name: Shape Attribute
head: Forma
body: Shape Attribute (Forma) is a feature-based classification operator prepared on segmented volumes to discriminate objects by examining three shape aspects: tubiness (cylindrical aspect), surfaceness (planar aspect), and blobbiness (bubble aspect). It generates a transfer function that maps these geometric properties to visual attributes, distinct from intensity- or size-based transfer functions. The method requires the input volume to be partitioned into distinct objects prior to evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A segmented volume dataset. Output: A transfer function that maps the computed shape aspects to visual attributes. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Prepare the volume dataset by segmenting it into distinct objects. 2. For each object, examine three geometric aspects to discriminate it: tubiness (cylindrical aspect), surfaceness (planar aspect), and blobbiness (bubble aspect). 3. Construct a shape-based transfer function using the evaluated aspects to visualize the object. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Segmentation Thresholds: Not given in the sources. Neighborhood Size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A set of three scalar values derived from the eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor to characterize shape within a triangular domain. Unlike the parent Shape Attribute operator which works on general segmented volumes, these metrics are specifically defined for diffusion tensors to distinguish between fiber-like, sheet-like, and isotropic structures. name: Geometric Anisotropy Metrics (Shape Domain)
head: DT-MRI Scalar Metrics, Diffusion Metrics, Westin metrics
body: Geometric Anisotropy Metrics (also known as Westin metrics) are a set of three scalar values derived from the eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor to characterize its shape within a triangular domain. They measure the certainty of the tensor being linear, planar, or spherical, providing orientation-independent shape discrimination. Unlike the parent Shape Attribute which operates on segmented volumes, these metrics are specifically defined for diffusion tensors to distinguish between fiber-like, sheet-like, and isotropic structures. Inputs and Outputs Input: A symmetric 3 \times 3 tensor D at a specific spatial location. Output: Three scalar values (cl, cp, cs) representing linear, planar, and spherical certainty, respectively. Data Structures The input tensor D is a symmetric matrix: D = \begin{bmatrix} D{xx} & D{xy} & D{xz} \\ D{yx} & D{yy} & D{yz} \\ D{zx} & D{zy} & D{zz} \end{bmatrix} where D{ij} = D{ji}. Steps 1. Eigen Decomposition: Compute the three eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of the tensor D. 2. Sorting: Sort the eigenvalues in descending order: \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0. 3. Trace Calculation: Compute the trace of the tensor, which equals the sum of the eigenvalues and the sum of the diagonal elements: \text{Trace}(D) = \lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3 = D{xx} + D{yy} + D{zz}. 4. Metric Calculation: Compute the three barycentric coordinates using the sorted eigenvalues and the trace: Linear Certainty (cl): cl = \frac{\lambda1 - \lambda2}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Planar Certainty (cp): cp = \frac{2(\lambda2 - \lambda3)}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Spherical Certainty (cs): cs = \frac{3\lambda3}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Parameters \lambdai: The sorted eigenvalues of the diffusion tensor. The metrics define a triangular domain where cl, cp, cs act as barycentric coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Trace: If the tensor is the zero matrix, the trace is zero, leading to division by zero. Guard against this by checking if \sum \lambdai < \epsilon and returning a default value. Precision: For nearly isotropic tensors (\lambda1 \approx \lambda2 \approx \lambda3), numerical precision in eigenvalue decomposition can affect the stability of the metrics, particularly cs which depends on the smallest eigenvalue. Boundary Conditions: The metrics sum to 1: cl + cp + cs = 1. The corners of the triangle correspond to pure shapes: Linear (cl=1, cp=0, cs=0), Planar (cp=1, cl=0, cs=0), and Spherical (cs=1, cl=0, cp=0). Pseudocode Unverified code. Args: tensor: A 3x3 list of lists representing the symmetric tensor D. Returns: A tuple (cl, cp, cs) representing linear, planar, and spherical certainty. """ # Step 1: Compute trace from diagonal elements trace = tensor[0][0] + tensor[1][1] + tensor[2][2] # Guard against zero trace if trace < 1e-9: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Step 2: Compute eigenvalues # Standard numerical eigenvalue solver for 3x3 symmetric matrices required. # Returns sorted eigenvalues [lambda1, lambda2, lambda3] descending. lambda1, lambda2, lambda3 = compute3x3symmetriceigenvalues(tensor) # Step 3: Calculate metrics cl = (lambda1 - lambda2) / trace cp = 2.0 (lambda2 - lambda3) / trace cs = 3.0 lambda3 / trace return (cl, cp, cs) def compute3x3symmetriceigenvalues(tensor: list[list[float]]) -> tuple[float, float, float]: """ Computes the eigenvalues of a 3x3 symmetric matrix and returns them sorted descending. Implementation uses a standard analytical cubic solver or Jacobi iteration. """ # Standard linear algebra routine. It solves the problem of visualizing specific geometric shapes (linear, planar, spherical) within tensor fields by allowing users to select regions in a 2D barycentric space, which is more intuitive than manipulating multi-dimensional transfer functions directly. Unlike standard eigenvalue thresholding, it leverages the geometric relationship between shape indices (cp, cl, cs) to highlight structural features in synthetic and Diffusion Weighted Imaging (DWI) data. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, dominated by the eigenvalue decomposition of a 3 \times 3 matrix. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per voxel. Strengths: Orientation-independent; provides a clear geometric interpretation of tensor shape; useful for classifying fiber, sheet, and isotropic regions in DT-MRI. Limitations: Only applicable to symmetric tensors; sensitive to noise in eigenvalue estimation, especially for the smallest eigenvalue \lambda3. When to use: When shape-based classification of diffusion tensors is required, independent of orientation. When not to use: For non-symmetric tensors or when orientation information is critical. They are widely used in Diffusion Tensor Magnetic Resonance Imaging (DT-MRI) visualization to reduce tensor data to scalar metrics that describe the shape of diffusion. name: Barycentric Mapping for Tensor Shape Exploration
head: Barycentric Shape Mapping, Tensor Anisotropy Barycentric Mapping
body: Barycentric Mapping is a feature-based classification technique that projects tensor anisotropy indices onto a 2D hyper-plane to control opacity and color transfer functions in volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from scalar transfer functions by mapping the geometric shape of diffusion tensors directly to a triangular domain, allowing distinct visual separation of isotropic, linear, and planar diffusion regimes. This method emphasizes important structural features (linear and planar anisotropy) while rendering unimportant regions (isotropic diffusion) transparent. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A symmetric tensor field where each tensor has eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 sorted such that \lambda1 > \lambda2 > \lambda3. Output: A 2D coordinate vector \mathbf{v} used to index a 2D opacity transfer function \alphab(\mathbf{v}) and/or a color lookup table. Data Structures: The method relies on three anisotropy indices (cl, cp, cs) which form a barycentric coordinate system. These indices satisfy the constraint cp + cl + cs = 1. Steps: 1. Compute Anisotropy Indices: Calculate the three shape indices from the sorted eigenvalues \lambda1 > \lambda2 > \lambda3 using the following formulas: cp = \frac{\lambda2 - \lambda3}{\lambda3} cl = \frac{\lambda1 - \lambda2}{\lambda3} cs = \frac{\lambda1}{\lambda3} Note: While the source states cp + cl + cs = 1, the provided formulas for cp, cl, cs do not mathematically sum to 1 for arbitrary eigenvalues. For example, if \lambda1=3, \lambda2=2, \lambda3=1, then cp=1, cl=1, cs=3, summing to 5. The source text explicitly claims the sum is 1. Implementers should verify if the indices are normalized differently in practice or if the formula definitions in the source contain a typo (e.g., division by \lambda1 or normalization by the sum). However, the mapping step below uses cs directly. 2. Normalize Indices (Optional but Recommended): To utilize the full range of the transfer function, normalize the indices across the dataset or a local neighborhood: ci' = \frac{ci - \min(ci)}{\max(ci) - \min(ci)} where ci \in \{cl, cp, cs\}. 3. Map to 2D Barycentric Space: Construct the 2D vector \mathbf{v} from the indices. The source defines this as: \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - cl - 0.5cs \\ cs \end{pmatrix} This vector \mathbf{v} serves as the coordinate for the 2D transfer function. 4. Lookup Transfer Function: Use \mathbf{v} to sample the opacity transfer function \alphab(\mathbf{v}) and/or color lookup table. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def barycentricmapping(eigenvalues): """ Computes the 2D barycentric coordinate vector v from tensor eigenvalues. Args: eigenvalues: Tuple or list of three floats (lambda1, lambda2, lambda3) sorted such that lambda1 > lambda2 > lambda3. Returns: v: Tuple (vx, vy) representing the 2D coordinate for transfer function lookup. """ lambda1, lambda2, lambda3 = eigenvalues # Guard against division by zero or invalid eigenvalue ordering if lambda3 == 0: # Handle degenerate case: Not given in the sources. # Typically, clamp lambda3 to a small epsilon or handle isotropic case separately. lambda3 = 1e-9 # 1. Compute anisotropy indices as defined in source # Note: Source claims cp + cl + cs = 1, but formulas provided do not satisfy this. # Implementation follows source formulas exactly. cp = (lambda2 - lambda3) / lambda3 cl = (lambda1 - lambda2) / lambda3 cs = lambda1 / lambda3 # 2. Map to 2D vector v # v = (1 - cl - 0.5cs, cs) vx = 1.0 - cl - 0.5 cs vy = cs return (vx, vy) Parameters: Normalization: The normalization step ci \rightarrow (ci - \min(ci)) / (\max(ci) - \min(ci)) is optional but used to stretch the map to utilize the entire range of anisotropy indices. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Eigenvalue Ordering: The formulas require \lambda1 > \lambda2 > \lambda3. If eigenvalues are equal (isotropic tensor), the indices may become undefined or zero depending on implementation. Zero Eigenvalues: Division by \lambda3 requires \lambda3 \neq 0. If \lambda3 = 0, the indices are undefined. A guard is required. Sum Constraint Contradiction: The source states cp + cl + cs = 1 but provides formulas that do not sum to 1. This is a significant inconsistency in the source material. Uses the barycentric coordinates to control opacity, emphasizing structural features and making isotropic regions transparent. Choose this when visual separation of diffusion regimes is the primary goal. Time Complexity: The computation per tensor is O(1), involving a few arithmetic operations (subtractions, divisions, multiplications). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per tensor for storing indices and the 2D vector. Performance: The method allows hardware-accelerated lookup at framebuffer rates, as demonstrated with 1.8M texture pixels on a 94 \times 128 \times 32 DWI dataset. Strengths: Interactive exploration of tensor anisotropies; distinct visual separation of isotropic, linear, and planar regimes; supports both opacity and color mapping. Limitations: The mathematical inconsistency in the source regarding the sum of indices may lead to implementation confusion; requires sorted eigenvalues. When to use: When exploring the shape characteristics of tensor fields (e.g., diffusion MRI) and needing to highlight specific anisotropy types (linear, planar, spherical). When not to use: When the tensor field is not symmetric or when eigenvalue sorting is not feasible. The method was introduced in the paper "Tensor Splats: Visualising Tensor Fields by Texture Mapped Volume Rendering". It was used to visualize synthetic data (cube, sphere, radiating spikes) and Diffusion Weighted Imaging (DWI) data, specifically highlighting white-matter fiber tracks. The technique is part of a broader family of feature-based classification methods for tensor visualization. name: Barycentric Opacity Mapping
head: Barycentric Color Map
body: Barycentric Opacity Mapping is a feature-based classification technique that uses three barycentric coordinates derived from the eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor to control opacity in volume rendering. It emphasizes important structural features (linear and planar anisotropy) while making unimportant regions (isotropic diffusion) transparent. Unlike general scalar transfer functions, it maps the shape of the diffusion tensor directly to a 2D barycentric space, allowing distinct visual separation of isotropic, linear, and planar diffusion regimes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A symmetric 3 \times 3 diffusion tensor T at a voxel. Output: An opacity value \alpha (and optionally color) for the voxel, determined by the barycentric coordinates of the tensor's eigenvalues. Data Structures: Tensor: A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. Eigenvalues: Three real numbers \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3. Barycentric Coordinates: Three values cl, cp, cs (or \lambdal, \lambdap, \lambdas) summing to 1. Steps: 1. Diagonalization: Compute the three real eigenvalues of the symmetric diffusion tensor T. 2. Sorting: Order the eigenvalues such that \lambda1 \geq \lambda2 \geq \lambda3. 3. Coordinate Calculation: Compute the three barycentric coordinates representing linear anisotropy (cl), planar anisotropy (cp), and isotropy (cs) using the formulas below. 4. Transfer Function Lookup: Use the coordinates (cl, cp, cs) to sample an opacity transfer function. Typically, high opacity is assigned to regions with high cl or cp (significant anisotropy), and low opacity to regions with high cs (isotropy). Formulas: Let \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 be the ordered eigenvalues. The sum of eigenvalues is S = \lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3. Linear anisotropy coordinate: cl = \frac{\lambda1 - \lambda2}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Planar anisotropy coordinate: cp = \frac{2(\lambda2 - \lambda3)}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Isotropy coordinate: cs = \frac{3\lambda3}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Note: cl + cp + cs = 1. The coordinates form a point in a 2D barycentric triangle where the vertices represent pure linear, pure planar, and pure isotropic diffusion, respectively. Parameters: Eigenvalues: Must be real (guaranteed for symmetric tensors). Thresholds: Not specified in the core definition, but practical implementations often filter noise by checking if \lambda{mean} > \epsilon or if anisotropy indices exceed a threshold. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Denominator: If \lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3 = 0 (e.g., all eigenvalues are zero), the coordinates are undefined. A small epsilon or a default isotropic value should be used. Numerical Stability: When eigenvalues are very close (near-isotropic), floating-point errors may cause cl or cp to be slightly negative or positive due to precision limits. Clamping to [0, 1] is recommended. Ordering: Incorrect ordering of eigenvalues will swap the meaning of cl and cp, leading to incorrect classification of linear vs. planar structures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def barycentricopacitymapping(tensor): """ Computes barycentric coordinates for a 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensor. Returns (cl, cp, cs). """ # 1. Compute eigenvalues of the symmetric 3x3 tensor # Note: In practice, use a robust symmetric eigensolver. eigenvalues = computeeigenvaluessymmetric3x3(tensor) # 2. Sort eigenvalues: lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3 eigenvalues.sort(reverse=True) lambda1 = eigenvalues[0] lambda2 = eigenvalues[1] lambda3 = eigenvalues[2] # 3. Compute sum of eigenvalues sumeigenvalues = lambda1 + lambda2 + lambda3 # 4. Handle zero sum to avoid division by zero if sumeigenvalues == 0: # Default to isotropic if tensor is zero return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # 5. Compute barycentric coordinates # Linear anisotropy cl = (lambda1 - lambda2) / sumeigenvalues # Planar anisotropy cp = 2.0 (lambda2 - lambda3) / sumeigenvalues # Isotropy cs = 3.0 lambda3 / sumeigenvalues # 6. Clamp to [0, 1] to handle numerical noise cl = max(0.0, min(1.0, cl)) cp = max(0.0, min(1.0, cp)) cs = max(0.0, min(1.0, cs)) return (cl, cp, cs) A variant that maps the barycentric coordinates to color rather than just opacity, visualizing the shape of diffusion directly. An illumination-based technique that interpolates between linear (streamline-like) and planar (surface-shading) lighting models based on the same anisotropy indices. A geometric visualization method that segments streamlines based on anisotropy and mean diffusivity thresholds, often using similar eigenvalue criteria. Time Complexity: Dominated by the eigenvalue decomposition of the 3 \times 3 symmetric tensor, which is O(1) per voxel. The coordinate calculation is also O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per voxel for storing eigenvalues and coordinates. Strengths: Intuitively separates isotropic noise from meaningful linear (fiber) and planar (sheet) structures. Provides a compact 2D representation of tensor shape. Limitations: Sensitive to noise in eigenvalue estimation. Does not encode direction, only shape. Requires accurate tensor estimation. When to use: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) visualization where distinguishing fiber tracts (linear) from sheet-like structures (planar) from isotropic regions (CSF, gray matter) is critical. Barycentric mapping for tensor shape exploration was developed as a method to visualize the geometric shape of diffusion tensors in medical imaging, particularly Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI). The technique leverages the fact that the eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor can be mapped to a barycentric coordinate system, where the vertices represent the three canonical tensor shapes: linear, planar, and isotropic. This approach was introduced to provide a more intuitive and feature-based classification than scalar transfer functions, allowing users to emphasize specific structural features while suppressing isotropic noise. It is commonly used in conjunction with volume rendering and tensor ellipsoid visualization. name: High-Dimensional Classification with Color Data
head: RGB Volume Classification
body: This method classifies color volume data by assigning opacity based on a high-dimensional classification function that utilizes RGB values, neighbor colors, and spatial position, thereby avoiding the difficulty of specifying three-dimensional transfer functions for RGB data. Unlike methods using Independent Component Analysis (ICA) that require users to work in a derived data space, this method allows users to work directly with original RGB data. It builds on Data Feature-Based Classification by extending the input domain from scalar values to multi-dimensional feature vectors derived from color and geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A color volume dataset where each voxel has an associated RGB color value. The classification function takes a feature vector \mathbf{x} constructed from the voxel's color, its six immediate neighbors' colors, and its position. Output: An opacity value \alpha \in [0, 1] for each voxel. Color is preserved from the original data; only opacity is modulated by the classification function. Data Structures: The classification function operates on a feature vector \mathbf{x} with up to 24 dimensions. The layout is: 1. Voxel Color: 3 dimensions (R, G, B). 2. Neighbor Colors: 6 neighbors \times 3 dimensions (R, G, B) = 18 dimensions. The neighbors are defined as the six immediate spatial neighbors (\pm x, \pm y, \pm z in the grid). 3. Position: Up to 3 dimensions (x, y, z) to provide spatial context, completing the 24-dimensional vector. Steps: 1. Training Data Acquisition: The user paints on 2D slices passing through the volume to provide training data. 2. Feature Extraction: For each voxel, construct the feature vector \mathbf{x} by concatenating the voxel's RGB values, the RGB values of its six neighbors, and its spatial coordinates. 3. Classification: Evaluate the high-dimensional classification function C(\mathbf{x}) to determine the opacity \alpha. The specific mathematical form of C is not detailed in the provided notes, but it maps the 24-dimensional input to a scalar opacity. 4. Rendering: Use the computed opacity \alpha and the original RGB color for volume rendering. Parameters: Input Dimensions: Up to 24 dimensions. Neighbor Count: 6 neighbors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Voxels on the volume boundary have fewer than 6 neighbors. The implementation must handle missing neighbors (e.g., by padding, clamping, or excluding spatial dimensions for boundary voxels), though the exact strategy is not specified in the sources. Dimensionality: The method relies on a high-dimensional space. Care must be taken to ensure the classification function generalizes well from the limited training data (painted slices) to the full 3D volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns: alpha: float in [0, 1]. """ # Construct feature vector x featurevector = list(voxelrgb) # 18 dims for 6 neighbors' colors for neighbor in neighborsrgb: featurevector.extend(neighbor) # Up to 3 dims for position featurevector.extend(position) # Evaluate classification function C(x) # The specific implementation of the intelligent system classifier is not detailed in the sources alpha = evaluateclassifier(featurevector) return alpha def evaluateclassifier(x): # Intelligent system classifier implementation not detailed in sources return 0.5 This method creates an interactive 1D opacity transfer function for photographic volumes by mapping 3D RGB colors to a 1D axis of 256 representative colors, allowing users to classify voxels based on color intuition rather than abstract scalar values. Unlike local decolorization methods which apply different mapping functions in different regions, this method uses a global non-linear mapping to ensure same colors map to the same value. It builds on High-Dimensional Classification with Color Data by providing the specific mechanism to reduce the 3D color space to a 1D index for classification. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves constructing a 24-dimensional feature vector per voxel and evaluating a classification function. Measured Performance: The method was tested on datasets including a 256³ cryosection color brain dataset, a 128³ MRI head dataset, and tumor datasets. Specific performance metrics (frame rates, accuracy) are not provided in the notes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows users to work directly with original RGB data without transforming to a derived space (unlike ICA-based methods). Handles color data sets in the same manner as scalar data sets, using 2D slice painting for training. Limitations: The high-dimensional feature space (up to 24 dimensions) may require careful tuning of the classification function. The method is limited to assigning opacity; color is not modified by the classification function. When to Use: Use when classifying color volume data (e.g., photographic volumes, cryosections) where users prefer to work with RGB colors directly and need to distinguish materials based on color and local context (neighbors). When Not to Use: Not suitable if the data is scalar-only or if the user prefers to work in a transformed feature space (e.g., ICA space). It contrasts with Takanashi et al.'s ICA-based method, which transforms RGB values into a derived space. Where it is Used: Used for visualizing color volume data such as cryosection color brain data, where it is necessary to remove surrounding materials (ice, table) and gaps in the brain that have similar colors. name: Color-Based 1D Transfer Function for Photographic Volumes
head: Color mapping approach, Non-linear color mapping method
body: This method creates an interactive 1D opacity transfer function for photographic volumes by mapping 3D RGB colors to a 1D axis of 256 representative colors, allowing users to classify voxels based on color intuition rather than abstract scalar values. Unlike local decolorization methods which apply different mapping functions in different regions, this method uses a global non-linear mapping to ensure same colors map to the same value. It builds on High-Dimensional Classification with Color Data by providing the specific mechanism to reduce the 3D color space to a 1D index for classification. Inputs: Volume data V containing voxels with RGB color values (r, g, b). Number of bins N = 256. Weights (wr, wg, wb) for linear projection. Outputs: A 1D axis consisting of N representative colors and their corresponding opacity values. A mapping function that assigns each voxel to a bin index. Data Structures: Bins: An array of size 256. Each bin stores a list of colors mapped to it and a representative color. Representative Colors: An array of 256 RGB values, one per bin. Weights: A triplet (wr, wg, wb) used for linear projection. Parameters: Number of bins: 256. This is chosen because the index of these representative colors can be represented by a byte (8 bits). Weights (wr, wg, wb): Subject to wr + wg + wb = 1, wr \ge 0, wg \ge 0, wb \ge 0. The specific selection method for weights is discussed in the source but not detailed in the provided notes. Steps: 1. Linear Projection: Map all voxel colors from the volume data to a 1D value C using a linear combination of RGB components. C = wr \cdot r + wg \cdot g + wb \cdot b where r, g, b are the color components and wr, wg, wb are the weights. 2. Binning: Divide the 1D axis into 256 uniform segments (bins). Assign each mapped color C to the corresponding bin based on its value. 3. Remove Empty Bins: Identify and remove empty bins from the sequence to compact the axis. The remaining bins form a contiguous sequence of non-empty bins. 4. Calculate Variance: For each non-empty bin, calculate the variance of the colors within it to measure color difference. To measure perceptual difference, convert colors to the CIELUV color space, as it is perceptually uniform. Let \Delta E(c1, c2) denote the Euclidean distance between color c1 and c2 in the CIELUV space. The variance is computed based on these distances. 5. Non-linear Adjustment: Apply a non-linear mapping adjustment strategy to move quite different colors from crowded bins (high variance) into empty bins. This ensures better use of the 1D space and preserves more color information. 6. Select Representative Colors: For each bin, select one color from the colors mapped to that bin to serve as the representative color. The selection minimizes color loss when the representative color substitutes for others in the bin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rgbtocieluv(rgb): # Standard sRGB to CIELUV conversion r, g, b = rgb # Linearize sRGB r = 1.055 (r (1/2.4)) - 0.055 if r > 0.04045 else r / 12.92 g = 1.055 (g (1/2.4)) - 0.055 if g > 0.04045 else g / 12.92 b = 1.055 (b (1/2.4)) - 0.055 if b > 0.04045 else b / 12.92 # RGB to XYZ (D65) x = 0.4124564 r + 0.3575761 g + 0.1804375 b y = 0.2126729 r + 0.7151522 g + 0.0721750 b z = 0.0193339 r + 0.1191920 g + 0.9503041 b # XYZ to CIELUV xn, yn, zn = 0.95047, 1.00000, 1.08883 u = 4 x / (x + 15 y + 3 z) if (x + 15 y + 3 z) != 0 else 0 v = 9 y / (x + 15 y + 3 z) if (x + 15 y + 3 z) != 0 else 0 un = 4 xn / (xn + 15 yn + 3 zn) vn = 9 yn / (xn + 15 yn + 3 zn) L = 116 (y / yn) (1/3) - 16 if y > 0.008856 else 903.3 (y / yn) L = max(0, L) U = 13 L (u - un) V = 13 L (v - vn) return (L, U, V) def euclideandistance(c1, c2): return math.sqrt((c1[0]-c2[0])2 + (c1[1]-c2[1])2 + (c1[2]-c2[2])2) def colorbased1dtf(volumedata, numbins=256, weights=(1/3, 1/3, 1/3)): wr, wg, wb = weights bins = [[] for in range(numbins)] # Step 1 & 2: Linear Projection and Binning cvalues = [wr r + wg g + wb b for r, g, b in volumedata] minc, maxc = min(cvalues), max(cvalues) rangec = maxc - minc if maxc != minc else 1.0 for i, c in enumerate(cvalues): binidx = int(((c - minc) / rangec) numbins) if binidx >= numbins: binidx = numbins - 1 bins[binidx].append(volumedata[i]) # Step 3: Remove Empty Bins nonemptybins = [bin for bin in bins if len(bin) > 0] # Step 4: Calculate Variance in CIELUV space binvariances = [] for bincolors in nonemptybins: luvcolors = [rgbtocieluv(c) for c in bincolors] meanluv = (sum(c[0] for c in luvcolors)/len(luvcolors), sum(c[1] for c in luvcolors)/len(luvcolors), sum(c[2] for c in luvcolors)/len(luvcolors)) variance = sum(euclideandistance(c, meanluv)2 for c in luvcolors) / len(luvcolors) binvariances.append((variance, bincolors)) # Step 5: Non-linear Adjustment # Move quite different colors from crowded bins to empty bins emptybinindices = [i for i, b in enumerate(bins) if len(b) == 0] for variance, bincolors in sorted(binvariances, reverse=True): if not emptybinindices: break if variance == 0: break # Find the color most distant from the bin's mean in CIELUV luvcolors = [rgbtocieluv(c) for c in bincolors] meanluv = (sum(c[0] for c in luvcolors)/len(luvcolors), sum(c[1] for c in luvcolors)/len(luvcolors), sum(c[2] for c in luvcolors)/len(luvcolors)) maxdist = -1 outlieridx = 0 for i, cluv in enumerate(luvcolors): d = euclideandistance(cluv, meanluv) if d > maxdist: maxdist = d outlieridx = i # Move outlier to first empty bin targetbinidx = emptybinindices.pop(0) bins[targetbinidx].append(bincolors[outlieridx]) # Step 6: Select Representative Colors representativecolors = [] for bincolors in nonemptybins: luvcolors = [rgbtocieluv(c) for c in bincolors] minloss = float('inf') bestcolor = bincolors[0] for i, cluv in enumerate(luvcolors): loss = sum(euclideandistance(cluv, otherluv) for j, otherluv in enumerate(luvcolors) if i != j) if loss < minloss: minloss = loss bestcolor = bincolors[i] representativecolors.append(bestcolor) return representativecolors, weights Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Bins: Linear mapping may result in empty bins and uneven histogram distribution if colors are clustered, leading to inefficient use of the 1D space. The method explicitly addresses this by removing empty bins and redistributing colors. Perceptual Uniformity: RGB space is not perceptually uniform. Variance calculations must use CIELUV space to ensure equal distances correspond to equal perceptual differences. Color Consistency: Local decolorization methods are unsuitable because they map the same color to different values depending on the region. This method uses global mapping to ensure consistency. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Intuitive for general users; 1D transfer function is easy to understand and convenient for interaction; global mapping ensures color consistency; effective use of 1D space through non-linear adjustment. Limitations: Requires selection of weights wr, wg, wb; non-linear adjustment strategy is complex to implement precisely. When to use: When designing interactive transfer functions for photographic volumes where user intuition on color is preferred over abstract scalar values. When not to use: When local contrast preservation is more important than global color consistency. The method was proposed to address the difficulty of creating intuitive interactive transfer functions for photographic volumes, as existing methods often require interaction in derived 3D spaces which are not convenient for general users. It builds on the concept of decolorization, adapting global linear parametric grayscale models and non-linear adjustments to the volume rendering context. name: Robust Material Graph Deduction
head: Graph-based TF Creation, Material Graph Generation
body: Robust Material Graph Deduction is an automated method for constructing transfer functions by discovering the topological structure of materials within a volume. It solves the problem of manual transfer function creation by automatically identifying material interiors and their spatial interconnectivity, producing a graph where nodes represent materials and edges represent interfaces. Unlike sibling methods that focus on local feature extraction or high-dimensional clustering, this approach explicitly models the adjacency relationships between materials to enable automatic background removal and fine control over opacity based on depth. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset V with scalar intensity values. Output: A material graph G(M, I), where M is the set of discovered materials and I is the set of interfaces between adjacent materials. Each material Mk is defined by a Gaussian intensity distribution Vk \sim \mathcal{N}(\muk, \sigmak) and a mean occlusion value \etak. Data Structures Initial Edge Set \hat{I}: A collection of interface samples, where each sample is a pair of intensity values (L, H) representing the low and high sides of an interface. Distance Matrix D: A symmetric matrix where D{ij} is the Bhattacharyya distance between material distributions Vi and Vj. Material Graph G: A graph structure with nodes M and edges I. Algorithm Steps 1. Compute Initial Edge Set \hat{I}: For each edge pixel in the volume, perform a bidirectional traversal along the local gradient to find a low value L and a high value H in a small neighborhood. These values are samples from adjacent intensity distributions V{i,1} and V{i,2}. 2. Cluster Interfaces: Cluster the (L, H) samples from \hat{I} using the HDBSCAN algorithm to define distinct material interfaces. Subsample the interface set from their distribution to maintain computational tractability for large volumes. 3. Define Base Threshold \theta{base}: Calculate the minimum Bhattacharyya distance between any two materials in the initial interfaces: \theta{base} = \min{i \in \{1, \dots, k\}} dB(V{i,1}, V{i,2}) where dB is the Bhattacharyya distance. 4. Search for Optimal Threshold \theta: Define a search range [\epsilon \theta{base}, \zeta \theta{base}] where \epsilon \ll 1 and \zeta \gg 1. For each candidate \theta, perform greedy merging to construct a graph and calculate the separation energy E{sep}: E{sep}(G(M, I)) = \frac{1}{|I|} \sum{j=1}^{|I|} dB(V{j,1}, V{j,2}) Select the \theta that maximizes E{sep}. Maximizing this energy results in a graph with fewer, well-separated interface edges. 5. Greedy Merging (for a fixed \theta): Find Materials to Merge: Walk through the distance matrix D to create sets of similar materials. A set may include a material from an interface, but not both materials of that interface (to avoid collapsing an interface into a single material). Reduce each set to a single material using a parent-child hierarchy, merging all children with their respective parents. Reconstruct Graph: Merge nodes of similar materials and merge repeating interface edges into a single interface edge. Update Distributions: Compute the resulting material intensity distributions as a weighted average of the constituent material distributions (means and standard deviations). 6. Assign Occlusion: Calculate the mean occlusion value \eta for each material, indicating its depth inside the volume, which is used to assign transparency values. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def robustmaterialgraphdeduction(volume): # Step 1: Compute initial edge set Ihat initialedges = [] for pixel in volume.edgepixels(): L, H = bidirectionalgradienttraversal(pixel, volume) initialedges.append((L, H)) # Step 2: Cluster interfaces and subsample samplededges = initialedges[:min(1000, len(initialedges))] clusters = clusteredges(samplededges) materials = [] for cid, edges in clusters.items(): vals = [v for e in edges for v in e] mu = sum(vals) / len(vals) sigma = math.sqrt(sum((v - mu)2 for v in vals) / len(vals)) materials.append({'id': cid, 'mu': mu, 'sigma': sigma, 'edges': edges}) # Step 3: Compute base threshold n = len(materials) distances = [[0.0]n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(i+1, n): d = bhattacharyya(materials[i], materials[j]) distances[i][j] = d distances[j][i] = d interfacepairs = getinterfacepairs(materials) thetabase = min(distances[i['id']][j['id']] for i, j in interfacepairs) # Step 4: Search for optimal theta epsilon = 0.1 zeta = 10.0 besttheta = thetabase maxenergy = -float('inf') bestgraph = None for logt in range(int(math.log10(epsilon thetabase) 10), int(math.log10(zeta thetabase) 10)): theta = 10 (logt / 10.0) if theta < epsilon thetabase or theta > zeta thetabase: continue mergedmaterials, mergedinterfaces = greedymerge(materials, distances, theta) if len(mergedinterfaces) == 0: continue energy = sum(bhattacharyya(m1, m2) for m1, m2 in mergedinterfaces) / len(mergedinterfaces) if energy > maxenergy: maxenergy = energy besttheta = theta bestgraph = (mergedmaterials, mergedinterfaces) finalmaterials, finalinterfaces = greedymerge(materials, distances, besttheta) for material in finalmaterials: material['occlusion'] = computemeanocclusion(material, volume) return finalmaterials, finalinterfaces def bidirectionalgradienttraversal(pixel, volume): grad = volume.gradient(pixel) lowval = volume[pixel] highval = volume[pixel] for in range(5): lowval = min(lowval, volume[pixel - grad]) highval = max(highval, volume[pixel + grad]) return lowval, highval def bhattacharyya(v1, v2): mu1, sigma1 = v1['mu'], v1['sigma'] mu2, sigma2 = v2['mu'], v2['sigma'] avgsigma = (sigma1 + sigma2) / 2 distsq = (mu1 - mu2)2 / (2 avgsigma2) coeff = 0.25 math.log(avgsigma2 / (sigma1 sigma2)) return distsq + coeff def clusteredges(edges): # Groups edges by proximity using a simple distance threshold clusters = {} threshold = 0.5 for edge in edges: placed = False for cid, clustedges in clusters.items(): if any(math.sqrt((e[0]-edge[0])2 + (e[1]-edge[1])2) < threshold for e in clustedges): clusters[cid].append(edge) placed = True break if not placed: clusters[len(clusters)] = [edge] return clusters def getinterfacepairs(materials): # Extracts pairs of materials sharing an interface in Ihat pairs = [] for mat in materials: for i, e1 in enumerate(mat['edges']): for j, e2 in enumerate(mat['edges']): if i < j: pairs.append((materials[e1[0]], materials[e2[0]])) return pairs def greedymerge(materials, distances, theta): n = len(materials) parent = {i: i for i in range(n)} # Step 5a: Find materials to merge for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): if distances[i][j] < theta and not interfacecollapses(materials[i], materials[j], materials): parent[j] = i # Reduce sets to single materials via parent-child hierarchy uniquematerials = [] for i in range(n): root = i while parent[root] != root: root = parent[root] if root not in [m['id'] for m in uniquematerials]: uniquematerials.append(materials[i]) # Step 5b: Reconstruct graph and merge repeating interfaces interfaces = [] for i, m1 in enumerate(uniquematerials): for j, m2 in enumerate(uniquematerials): if i < j and areadjacent(m1, m2, materials): mergeddist = weightedaveragedist(m1, m2) interfaces.append((mergeddist, mergeddist)) return uniquematerials, interfaces def interfacecollapses(m1, m2, materials): for mat in materials: ids = {e[0] for e in mat['edges']} if m1['id'] in ids and m2['id'] in ids: return True return False def areadjacent(m1, m2, materials): for mat in materials: ids = {e[0] for e in mat['edges']} if m1['id'] in ids and m2['id'] in ids: return True return False def weightedaveragedist(v1, v2): w1, w2 = v1['sigma'], v2['sigma'] totalw = w1 + w2 return {'mu': (w1v1['mu'] + w2v2['mu'])/totalw, 'sigma': (w1v1['sigma'] + w2v2['sigma'])/totalw} def computemeanocclusion(material, volume): # Not given in the sources. Computes depth-based transparency weight return 0.5 Parameters \epsilon: Lower bound multiplier for threshold search. Must be much less than 1 (\epsilon \ll 1). \zeta: Upper bound multiplier for threshold search. Must be much greater than 1 (\zeta \gg 1). \theta: Distance threshold for merging materials. Searched in [\epsilon \theta{base}, \zeta \theta{base}]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noise: Noise in volume data can result in repeating boundaries for the same interface. The clustering and merging steps help mitigate this, but subsampling is critical for performance. Disconnected Components: Materials may have multiple disconnected components. The graph deduction assumes valid material-material interfaces from clustering. Background: The background material is typically set to invisible (white node) to hide it from rendering. Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the initial edge detection and the HDBSCAN clustering. The greedy merging is efficient, but the search for optimal \theta requires evaluating multiple graph configurations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the initial edge set, distance matrix, and the final graph. Subsampling helps manage memory for large volumes. Performance: Implemented in a real-time GPU volume renderer with a Python backend. Graph deduction takes approximately 2 seconds on standard datasets, with voxel classification taking ~4 seconds and interface clustering taking negligible time. Strengths: Automatic discovery of materials and interfaces; fine control over color and opacity; automatic background removal; robust to noise via clustering. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial edge detection; assumes materials can be modeled by Gaussian distributions; may struggle with highly complex or overlapping intensity distributions. The method was proposed to address the limitation of existing techniques that focus on material boundaries without adequately representing material interiors. It builds on the LH histogram approach for edge detection. The algorithm was implemented and tested on datasets from The Volume Library. Robust Material Graphs for Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/pg20181282, fetched 2026-11-04 (unofficial)

name: Feature Graph
head: Feature Graph Construction, Feature Graph building
body: The Feature Graph is a hierarchical data structure for volume rendering that represents classified voxel models as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). It solves the problem of visualizing complex semantic hierarchies where a single voxel belongs to multiple non-exclusive classes simultaneously, enabling focus+context rendering through multiresolution support. It differs from standard single-criterion classification by explicitly modeling the subset relationships between disjoint classes of different criteria, creating a graph where nodes are features—defined as sets of values for a subset of the boolean expressions used in classification such that at least one voxel fulfills them—and edges represent inclusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A labeled voxel model where each voxel v has a set of nc boolean labels ri(v) for i \in [1, nc], indicating fulfillment of nc non-exclusive classification criteria. Output: A Feature Graph DAG where nodes represent features and arcs represent inclusion of voxel sets, along with a Feature Hash Table for direct node access. Data Structures: 1. Feature Hash Table: A hash table providing direct index access to feature nodes. The hash code for a voxel is derived from its set of labels. 2. Feature Node: Represents a feature f. Contains: Label signature (subset of boolean expressions). Reference to a Set of Voxels (SOV). Parent pointers (for traversal to ancestors). Child pointers (for traversal to descendants). 3. Set of Voxels (SOV): The spatial representation of a feature. Stored only in leaf nodes to avoid redundancy. Representation: Can be a list of voxels or a voxel submodel (octree). List-based: Stores voxel coordinates. No spatial ordering. Convenient for non-compact distributions. Submodel-based: Octree representation. Voxels not belonging to the feature are assigned zero value, ensuring a voxel has a non-zero value in only one unique leaf SOV. Preserves spatial ordering. Compaction: Homogeneous regions within an SOV are compacted using different voxel sizes. For submodels, an octree is used. For lists, only black nodes of the octree with their associated size are stored. Algorithm Steps: 1. Clustering (High Resolution): Traverse the labeled voxel model. For each voxel v, compute its label set \{r1(v),..., r{nc}(v)\}. Use this label set as a hash code to index into the Feature Hash Table. Add v to the SOV list indexed by this hash code. After traversal, for each non-empty SOV: Compute the bounding box. Create a voxel submodel (octree) for the SOV. Compress the submodel. Optionally, traverse the octree to create a list-based representation with variable-sized voxels. Create leaf nodes in the graph for each non-empty SOV and associate them with the computed SOVs. 2. Hierarchy Creation: Derive the graph hierarchy iteratively using boolean operations on feature labels. Recursively create common ancestor nodes for all nodes sharing a bit in their hash code (i.e., features that are supersets of other features). Update the Feature Hash Table to reference the newly created ancestor nodes. If the graph consists of multiple disconnected hierarchies, create a common root node called fall (feature all) that includes all features without an ancestor. Storage Policy: Store SOVs only in leaf nodes. Ancestor SOVs are obtained by recursively traversing descendant nodes down to the leaves. 3. Multiresolution Handling: Compute label sets at coarser resolution levels of the voxel model. Repeat the clustering process for larger voxels at each coarser level. Distribute the SOVs computed from these coarser clusters through the graph hierarchy, attaching them to corresponding nodes. Each node can contain SOVs from different resolution levels. Note that some clusters non-empty at high resolution may become empty at lower resolution, so not all features exist at all levels. A feature can be a leaf at one resolution and an intermediate node at another. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeboundingbox(voxels): minx, miny, minz = float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf') maxx, maxy, maxz = float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf') for v in voxels: minx = min(minx, v.x); maxx = max(maxx, v.x) miny = min(miny, v.y); maxy = max(maxy, v.y) minz = min(minz, v.z); maxz = max(maxz, v.z) return (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) def buildoctree(voxels, bbox): root = OctreeNode(bbox, voxels) root.build() return root class OctreeNode: def init(self, bbox, voxels): self.bbox = bbox self.voxels = voxels self.children = [None] 8 self.isleaf = len(voxels) <= 1 def build(self): if self.isleaf: return # Standard recursive octree subdivision omitted for brevity pass class FeatureNode: def init(self, labeltuple): self.labeltuple = labeltuple self.sov = None self.children = [] self.parent = None class FeatureGraph: def init(self, voxelmodel, nc): self.nc = nc self.hashtable = {} self.nodes = [] self.fallnode = None def build(self): clusters = {} for voxel in voxelmodel: labels = tuple(voxel.getlabel(i) for i in range(self.nc)) if labels not in clusters: clusters[labels] = [] clusters[labels].append(voxel) leafnodes = [] for labels, voxels in clusters.items(): if not voxels: continue bbox = computeboundingbox(voxels) octree = buildoctree(voxels, bbox) sov = octree node = FeatureNode(labels) node.sov = sov self.hashtable[labels] = node self.nodes.append(node) leafnodes.append(node) self.createhierarchy(leafnodes) self.createfallnode() def createhierarchy(self, leafnodes): existingsigs = set(n.labeltuple for n in leafnodes) allsigs = set(existingsigs) for bit in range(self.nc): nodeswithbit = [n for n in leafnodes if n.labeltuple[bit]] if len(nodeswithbit) > 1: sharedsig = tuple(1 if i == bit else 0 for i in range(self.nc)) if sharedsig not in self.hashtable: newnode = FeatureNode(sharedsig) self.hashtable[sharedsig] = newnode self.nodes.append(newnode) allsigs.add(sharedsig) for sig in allsigs: node = self.hashtable[sig] for othersig in allsigs: if othersig == sig: continue othernode = self.hashtable[othersig] if all(s <= o for s, o in zip(sig, othersig)): if node not in othernode.children: othernode.children.append(node) node.parent = othernode elif all(o <= s for s, o in zip(sig, othersig)): if othernode not in node.children: node.children.append(othernode) othernode.parent = node def createfallnode(self): roots = [n for n in self.nodes if n.parent is None] if len(roots) > 1: self.fallnode = FeatureNode(None) for root in roots: root.parent = self.fallnode self.fallnode.children.append(root) self.nodes.append(self.fallnode) elif len(roots) == 1: self.fallnode = roots[0] else: self.fallnode = None Parameters: nc: The number of non-exclusive classification criteria (boolean conditions). fall: The entry point node of the graph, representing a feature that includes all features that do not have an ancestor. Leaf nodes: Nodes in the graph that do not include any other feature. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Clusters: Many theoretical clusters (2^{nc}) may be empty. The algorithm only creates nodes for non-empty clusters. Multiresolution Disappearance: Clusters non-empty at high resolution may become empty at lower resolution. Not all features exist at all levels. Redundancy: SOVs are stored only in leaf nodes to avoid redundancy. Ancestor SOVs are derived by traversal. Spatial Ordering: List-based SOVs do not preserve spatial ordering, requiring view-aligned splatting for rendering. Submodel-based SOVs preserve ordering but may have overlapping bounding boxes. Builds a directed acyclic graph representing inclusion relationships between isoclasses in a voxel model classified by multiple independent criteria. It differs from standard single-criterion classification by explicitly modeling subset relationships between disjoint classes of different criteria, creating a graph where nodes are class identifiers and edges represent inclusion. Time Complexity: Construction involves clustering (O(V) where V is number of voxels) and hierarchy creation. Hierarchy creation depends on nc. The number of possible features is 2^{nc}, but only non-empty ones are created. Memory Complexity: Depends on the SOV representation. List-based SOVs store only voxel coordinates. Submodel-based SOVs store octrees. SOVs are stored only in leaves, reducing redundancy. Performance: View-aligned splatting is used for list-based SOVs to handle lack of spatial ordering. Multiresolution support reduces aliasing and provides focus+context visualizations. Strengths: Handles non-exclusive classification, supports multiresolution, allows focus+context rendering. Limitations: List-based SOVs require view-aligned splatting. Submodel-based SOVs may have overlapping bounding boxes. The Feature Graph was introduced in the paper "Splatting multiresolution volume data using the feature graph". It is used for visualizing complex semantic hierarchies in volume data. name: Multiclassified Structure Graph Construction
head: Isoclass Graph, Structure Graph
body: Multiclassified Structure Graph Construction builds a directed acyclic graph representing the inclusion relationships between isoclasses in a voxel model classified by multiple independent criteria. It solves the problem of visualizing complex semantic hierarchies where a single voxel can belong to multiple classes simultaneously, enabling users to explore structural semantics through focus+context rendering. It differs from standard single-criterion classification by explicitly modeling the subset relationships between disjoint classes of different criteria, creating a graph where nodes are class identifiers and edges represent inclusion. It builds on Feature Graph. Inputs and Outputs Input: A voxel model V and nc independent classification criteria. Each criterion i defines a set of disjoint class identifiers \tilde{c}i = \{c{i1}, \dots, c{i n{ci}}\} and a classification function Ci: V \to \tilde{c}i. Output: A directed graph G = (I, E) where I is the set of all isoclass identifiers and E represents inclusion relationships, a labelled voxel model LV, and a cluster list R with a binary relation F. Data Structures 1. Graph Nodes (I): Each node represents an isoclass identifier c{ij}. 2. Adjacency Table: A matrix storing the number of voxels for each pair of isoclasses. Rows correspond to potential included isoclasses and columns to potential includers. Non-zero entries indicate voxel overlap and zero entries indicate non-inclusion. 3. Labelled Voxel Model (LV): A voxel model aligned with V, where each voxel value is a cluster identifier r \in R. 4. Cluster List (R): A list of unique cluster identifiers, each associated with a tuple of isoclass identifiers CR. Steps 1. Construct Isoclasses: Separate the classified voxels into sets based on each criterion. For each isoclass, compute the number of voxels, the bounding box, the opacity as a factor of the bounding sphere radius and voxel count, and the initial color using Stone’s coloring model. Create one graph node per isoclass. 2. Compute Inclusion Hierarchy: Process input voxels slice by slice to avoid excessive memory load for huge models. Construct an adjacency table storing the number of voxels of included isoclasses as non-zero values and non-included isoclasses as zero. Sort the rows of the adjacency table by increasing number of voxels. Derive the inclusion hierarchy through a simple matrix traversal of the sorted table. 3. Construct Labelled Voxel Model and Clusters: For each voxel v, identify the set of isoclasses it belongs to as an nc-tuple. Compute a cluster identifier r as a hash code of the isoclass identifiers in the tuple. Label voxel v in LV with r and insert r into the cluster list R if it is new. Codify the relationship F between graph nodes and clusters in the hash code. Formulas Implication/Inclusion: c{kj} \Rightarrow c{li} \iff \text{isoclas}(c{kj}) \subset \text{isoclas}(c{li}) Where c{kj} implies c{li} if the isoclass of c{li} includes all voxels of c{kj}. Edges in G are directed from the inclusor isoclass to the included isoclass, which is opposite to the implication direction. Cluster-Node Relationship (F): \forall i \in I \land \forall r \in R, i F r \iff \exists ci \in CR \mid i = ci \land \neg(\exists cj \in CR, cj \neq ci \mid cj \Rightarrow ci) Node i is related to cluster r if i is in the cluster's isoclass tuple CR and no descendant of i in G has an identifier in CR. Stone’s Coloring Model Arithmetic: Let c1 = (r1, g1, b1) and c2 = (r2, g2, b2). Negation: \bar{c}1 = (MAX - r1, MAX - g1, MAX - b1). Union: c1 \cup c2 = (\max(r1, r2), \max(g1, g2), \max(b1, b2)). Intersection: c1 \cap c2 = (\min(r1, r2), \min(g1, g2), \min(b1, b2)). Parameters nc: Number of independent classification criteria. MAX: Maximum intensity value used in color arithmetic operations. \beta: User-specified blending factor, 0 \le \beta \le 1. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructmulticlassifiedstructuregraph(V, classificationfunctions): nc = len(classificationfunctions) I = [] E = [] adjacencytable = {} MAX = 255 # Step 1: Construct Isoclasses for i in range(nc): Ci = classificationfunctions[i] isoclasssets = {} for v in V.voxels: cid = Ci(v) if cid not in isoclasssets: isoclasssets[cid] = [] isoclasssets[cid].append(v) if cid not in I: I.append(cid) for cid, voxels in isoclasssets.items(): voxelcount = len(voxels) bbox = computeboundingbox(voxels) radius = computeradius(bbox) opacity = computeopacity(radius, voxelcount) color = stonecoloringmodel(cid, MAX) # Step 2: Compute Inclusion Hierarchy for slice in V.slices: for v in slice.voxels: voxelisoclasses = [Ci(v) for Ci in classificationfunctions] for incid in voxelisoclasses: for inclid in voxelisoclasses: if incid != inclid: key = (incid, inclid) adjacencytable[key] = adjacencytable.get(key, 0) + 1 sortededges = sorted(adjacencytable.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]) for (incid, inclid), count in sortededges: if count > 0: E.append((inclid, incid)) # Step 3: Construct Labelled Voxel Model and Clusters LV = createvoxelmodelalignedwith(V) R = [] clustermap = {} for v in V.voxels: voxelisoclasses = tuple(Ci(v) for Ci in classificationfunctions) hashcode = computehash(voxelisoclasses) if hashcode not in clustermap: newclusterid = len(R) R.append({'id': newclusterid, 'isoclasstuple': voxelisoclasses}) clustermap[hashcode] = newclusterid LV.setvalue(v, clustermap[hashcode]) F = {} for r in R: for nodeid in r['isoclasstuple']: hasdescendant = any(isdescendant(otherid, nodeid, E) for otherid in r['isoclasstuple'] if otherid != nodeid) if not hasdescendant: F[nodeid] = r['id'] return I, E, LV, R, F def computeboundingbox(voxels): return (min(v.coords for v in voxels), max(v.coords for v in voxels)) def computeradius(bbox): return sum((c - (bbox[0][i] + bbox[1][i])/2)2 for i in range(3)) 0.5 def computeopacity(radius, voxelcount): return radius voxelcount def stonecoloringmodel(cid, MAX): h = (cid 137) % 360 s, v = 0.8, 0.9 c = v s x = c (1 - abs((h / 60) % 2 - 1)) m = v - c if h < 60: rgb = (c, x, 0) elif h < 120: rgb = (x, c, 0) elif h < 180: rgb = (0, c, x) elif h < 240: rgb = (0, x, c) elif h < 300: rgb = (x, 0, c) else: rgb = (c, 0, x) return tuple(int((ch + m) MAX) for ch in rgb) def createvoxelmodelalignedwith(V): return type(V)(V.resolution, V.origin) def computehash(tupledata): return hash(tupledata) def isdescendant(descid, ancid, E): visited = set() queue = [ancid] while queue: current = queue.pop(0) if current == descid: return True if current in visited: continue visited.add(current) for parent, child in E: if parent == current and child not in visited: queue.append(child) return False Edge Cases and Pitfalls Memory Load: Processing all voxels at once for huge models with many criteria can exceed memory. The method specifies slice-by-slice processing for the adjacency table construction. Empty Classes: The source notes that "empty" classes across different criteria are equivalent and should be handled (remapped) to avoid spurious inclusion relationships. Precision: Opacity and color computations depend on bounding box accuracy and MAX value consistency. This subtopic defines the binary relation F that links graph nodes to clusters in the labelled voxel model LV. A node i is related to a cluster r if i is present in the cluster's isoclass tuple CR and no descendant of i in the graph G is also present in CR. This ensures that each cluster is associated with the most specific (highest) isoclass in the hierarchy that contains it, allowing efficient access to voxels during graph traversal queries. Time Complexity: The inclusion hierarchy construction involves processing voxels slice by slice and sorting an adjacency table. The complexity depends on the number of voxels, the number of classification criteria nc, and the number of classes per criterion. Sorting the adjacency table adds a logarithmic factor relative to the number of isoclass pairs. Memory Complexity: The method uses an adjacency table and a labelled voxel model LV. Slice-by-slice processing of the input voxels reduces peak memory usage during hierarchy construction. Strengths: Enables structural focus+context rendering by providing a clear hierarchy of semantic relationships. Allows users to explore complex multiclassified data through boolean queries on isoclasses. Limitations: The construction process can be memory-intensive for very large models if not processed carefully. The reliance on Stone’s coloring model may not suit all visual preferences, though it is interactive. When to use: When visualizing volume data classified by multiple independent criteria where the inclusion relationships between classes are semantically important and need to be explored interactively. The Multiclassified Structure Graph Construction method was introduced in the paper "Structural focus+context rendering of multiclassified volume data". It builds on the concept of Feature Graphs, extending them to handle multiple classification criteria simultaneously. The method uses Stone’s coloring model for initial color assignment. It employs multimodal 3D texture-mapping for rendering, composing proxy polygons parallel to the viewing plane. name: Attribute Ranking Heuristic
head: Attribute Selection Ranking, Ranking de Atributos
body: The Attribute Ranking Heuristic is a greedy method for selecting relevant volumetric attributes to construct voxel signatures for multidimensional transfer function (MTF) classification. It solves the problem of high-dimensional data complexity by ranking candidate attributes based on their information content and redundancy, presenting the top n candidates to the user for signature construction. It differs from its child Attribute Selection Heuristic for Multidimensional Transfer Functions by using entropy for the initial selection, whereas the child explicitly balances entropy against redundancy for sequential attribute selection. Inputs: D: The set of all available candidate attributes (dimensions) in the volume data. R: The set of ranked/selected attributes, initially empty. Outputs: R: An ordered list of attributes ranked by relevance. Data Structures: D: A set or list of attribute identifiers. R: A list of attribute identifiers. Parameters: n: The number of top-ranked candidates to present to the user. This is not computed by the algorithm but chosen empirically by the user. Steps: 1. Initialize R = \emptyset and D as the set of all available attributes. 2. Compute the entropy H(a) for each attribute a \in D. 3. Select the attribute d^ with the maximum entropy: d^ = \arg\max{a \in D} H(a). 4. Remove d^ from D and add it to R: D \leftarrow D \setminus \{d^\}, R \leftarrow R \cup \{d^\}. 5. While D is not empty: a. For each remaining attribute a \in D, compute a score based on its multiple correlation with the attributes already in R. b. The score uses linear regression to estimate the multiple correlation between a and the set R. c. Select the attribute d^ with the highest score. d. Remove d^ from D and add it to R: D \leftarrow D \setminus \{d^\}, R \leftarrow R \cup \{d^\}. 6. Return R. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def attributerankingheuristic(attributesdata): """ Greedy heuristic to rank attributes by relevance. attributesdata: dict mapping attribute name to list of numeric values. Returns: list of attribute names sorted by relevance. """ available = list(attributesdata.keys()) selected = [] if not available: return selected # Step 1: Select attribute with highest entropy # Standard Shannon entropy calculation (source does not specify binning method) def calculateentropy(values): counts = {} for v in values: counts[v] = counts.get(v, 0) + 1 total = len(values) entropy = 0.0 for count in counts.values(): p = count / total if p > 0: entropy -= p math.log2(p) return entropy firstattr = max(available, key=lambda a: calculateentropy(attributesdata[a])) available.remove(firstattr) selected.append(firstattr) # Step 2: Iteratively select attributes based on multiple correlation while available: bestattr = None bestscore = -1.0 for attr in available: # Score based on multiple correlation with selected attributes # Multiple correlation coefficient R^2 from linear regression of target # against all attributes in selected. Source cites Abdi (2007) for linear regression. score = computemultiplecorrelationscore(attributesdata[attr], {s: attributesdata[s] for s in selected}) if score > bestscore: bestscore = score bestattr = attr available.remove(bestattr) selected.append(bestattr) return selected def computemultiplecorrelationscore(target, predictors): """ Computes the coefficient of determination (R^2) for linear regression of target against all predictor vectors. Standard least-squares implementation for multiple correlation (source does not provide code). """ if not predictors: return 0.0 n = len(target) predmatrix = [[predictors[p][i] for p in predictors] for i in range(n)] # Add bias term for intercept predmatrix = [[1.0] + row for row in predmatrix] numpredictors = len(predmatrix[0]) # Solve normal equations (X^T X) beta = X^T y using Gaussian elimination XtX = [[sum(predmatrix[i][k] predmatrix[i][j] for k in range(numpredictors)) for j in range(numpredictors)] for i in range(numpredictors)] Xty = [sum(predmatrix[i][j] target[i] for i in range(n)) for j in range(numpredictors)] for i in range(numpredictors): maxrow = i for k in range(i+1, numpredictors): if abs(XtX[k][i]) > abs(XtX[maxrow][i]): maxrow = k XtX[i], XtX[maxrow] = XtX[maxrow], XtX[i] Xty[i], Xty[maxrow] = Xty[maxrow], Xty[i] for k in range(i+1, numpredictors): factor = XtX[k][i] / XtX[i][i] for j in range(i, numpredictors): XtX[k][j] -= factor XtX[i][j] Xty[k] -= factor Xty[i] beta = [0.0] numpredictors for i in range(numpredictors - 1, -1, -1): beta[i] = Xty[i] for j in range(i+1, numpredictors): beta[i] -= XtX[i][j] beta[j] beta[i] /= XtX[i][i] # Calculate R^2 ypred = [sum(predmatrix[i][j] beta[j] for j in range(numpredictors)) for i in range(n)] ymean = sum(target) / n ssres = sum((target[i] - ypred[i]) 2 for i in range(n)) sstot = sum((target[i] - ymean) 2 for i in range(n)) rsquared = 1.0 - (ssres / sstot) if sstot != 0 else 0.0 return rsquared Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Adding too many attributes to the voxel signature causes high false-positive sensitivity and fragments clusters, making graph exploration exhaustive. The user must empirically decide the number n of attributes to use; the algorithm does not determine this. The method relies on linear regression for multiple correlation; non-linear relationships may not be captured. Extends this method by generating a full ranking of candidate attributes using multiple correlation with all previously selected attributes, rather than just the initial one, and explicitly balances entropy against redundancy for sequential attribute selection. Choose this when higher accuracy in attribute selection is needed and computational cost is acceptable. Time Complexity: The heuristic step is O(c^2 \cdot n) where c is the number of dimensions and n is the number of instances. The total complexity is O(c^3 \cdot n) because the heuristic executes c linear regressions. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple, greedy approach that reduces the complexity of specifying MTFs by ranking attributes. Limitations: Greedy selection may not find the globally optimal set of attributes. Performance depends on the linear regression assumption. When to use: When exploring multidimensional volume data and needing a quick, automated way to identify relevant attributes for classification. When not to use: When non-linear attribute relationships are dominant or when the computational cost of O(c^3 \cdot n) is prohibitive for very high-dimensional data. The method is designed to support the definition of multidimensional transfer functions by providing a ranked list of candidate attributes for voxel signatures. name: Attribute Selection Heuristic for Multidimensional Transfer Functions
head: Heuristic for generation of ranking of candidate attributes, Zhou, Schott and Hansen heuristic (adapted)
body: This method provides a greedy heuristic to rank volumetric attributes for inclusion in voxel signatures, thereby reducing the complexity of specifying multidimensional transfer functions (MTFs). It extends the original Zhou, Schott, and Hansen (2012) pairwise selection by generating a full ranking of candidate attributes using multiple correlation with all previously selected attributes, rather than just the initial one. It builds on Attribute Ranking Heuristic by refining the scoring mechanism to explicitly balance information content (entropy) against redundancy (correlation) for sequential attribute selection. Inputs: A: A set of N candidate volumetric attributes. \eta: The decision factor (weighting parameter), where 0 \leq \eta \leq 1. Outputs: R: A ranked list of attributes, ordered by relevance for voxel signature composition. Data Structures: Yi: The i-th attribute in the candidate set A. Y{prev}: The set of attributes already selected for the signature (initially empty). E(Y): The entropy of attribute Y. Corr(Y{prev}, Y): The multiple correlation coefficient between the set of previously selected attributes Y{prev} and the candidate attribute Y. Formulas: 1. Shannon Entropy: For a discrete attribute x with n histogram classes, the entropy E(x) is calculated as: E(x) = -\sum{k=1}^{n} p(xk) \logb p(xk) where p(xk) is the probability of the k-th class occurring, n is the number of histogram classes, and b is the logarithm base (typically b=2 for Shannon Entropy). 2. Normalized Entropy: The entropy of each attribute is normalized by the maximum entropy observed in the dataset to allow comparison across attributes with different value ranges: \hat{E}(Yi) = \frac{E(Yi)}{\max{Y \in A} E(Y)} 3. Scoring Function: The score si for a candidate attribute Yi is computed as: si = -\eta |Corr(Y{prev}, Yi)| + (1 - \eta) \hat{E}(Yi) where: \eta is the decision factor. |Corr(Y{prev}, Yi)| is the absolute value of the multiple correlation coefficient. \hat{E}(Yi) is the normalized entropy. Interpretation: A score closer to 0 indicates high relevance (low correlation with existing attributes, high entropy). A value of \eta close to 0 favors low correlation (minimizing redundancy). A value of \eta close to 1 favors high entropy (maximizing information content). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the ranked list R as empty. 2. Calculate the entropy E(Y) for all attributes Y \in A. 3. Determine E{max} = \max{Y \in A} E(Y). 4. Normalize the entropy for all attributes: \hat{E}(Y) = E(Y) / E{max}. 5. First Selection: Select the attribute Y{first} with the highest normalized entropy \hat{E}(Y) from A. Add Y{first} to R. Remove Y{first} from A. Set Y{prev} = \{Y{first}\}. 6. Iterative Selection: While A is not empty: a. For each remaining attribute Yi \in A, calculate the multiple correlation coefficient Corr(Y{prev}, Yi). b. Compute the score si = -\eta |Corr(Y{prev}, Yi)| + (1 - \eta) \hat{E}(Yi). c. Select the attribute Y{best} with the maximum score si. d. Add Y{best} to R. e. Remove Y{best} from A. f. Update Y{prev} = Y{prev} \cup \{Y{best}\}. 7. Return R. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def attributeselectionheuristic(attributes, eta): """ attributes: List of attribute objects. Each object must provide: gethistogram(): returns list of bin counts (int/float) getvalues(): returns list of voxel-wise values (float) eta: Decision factor in [0, 1]. Returns: Ranked list of attributes. """ # Step 1: Calculate and normalize entropy entropies = {} for attr in attributes: hist = attr.gethistogram() total = sum(hist) if total == 0: entropies[attr] = 0.0 continue entropy = 0.0 for count in hist: if count > 0: p = count / total entropy -= p math.log2(p) entropies[attr] = entropy maxentropy = max(entropies.values()) if entropies else 0.0 if maxentropy == 0: normalizedentropies = {attr: 0.0 for attr in attributes} else: normalizedentropies = {attr: e / maxentropy for attr, e in entropies.items()} ranked = [] remaining = list(attributes) selected = [] # Step 2: Select first attribute (highest entropy) firstattr = max(remaining, key=lambda x: normalizedentropies[x]) ranked.append(firstattr) remaining.remove(firstattr) selected.append(firstattr) # Step 3: Iteratively select remaining attributes while remaining: bestattr = None maxscore = float('-inf') for attr in remaining: # Compute multiple correlation coefficient R between selected attributes and candidate corrvalue = computemultiplecorrelation(selected, attr) # Score: maximize to prefer high entropy and low correlation score = -eta abs(corrvalue) + (1 - eta) normalizedentropies[attr] if score > maxscore: maxscore = score bestattr = attr ranked.append(bestattr) remaining.remove(bestattr) selected.append(bestattr) return ranked def computemultiplecorrelation(selectedattributes, candidateattribute): """ Computes the multiple correlation coefficient R between the candidate and the set of selected attributes using linear regression. """ n = len(selectedattributes) if n == 0: return 0.0 # Extract voxel-wise data arrays X = [attr.getvalues() for attr in selectedattributes] y = candidateattribute.getvalues() m = len(y) # Compute correlation matrix Rxx and correlation vector ryx def std(v): return math.sqrt(sum(vi2 for vi in v) / m) def corr(a, b): sa, sb = std(a), std(b) if sa == 0 or sb == 0: return 0.0 return sum(a[i]b[i] for i in range(m)) / (m sa sb) Rxx = [[corr(X[i], X[j]) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] ryx = [corr(y, X[i]) for i in range(n)] # Invert Rxx (Gaussian elimination) Rxxinv = invertmatrix(Rxx) # R^2 = ryx^T Rxxinv ryx temp = [sum(Rxxinv[i][j] ryx[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)] rsquared = sum(ryx[i] temp[i] for i in range(n)) rsquared = max(0.0, min(1.0, rsquared)) # Clamp for numerical stability return math.sqrt(rsquared) def invertmatrix(M): """Gaussian elimination to invert matrix M.""" n = len(M) A = [row[:] + [1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i, row in enumerate(M)] for i in range(n): pivot = A[i][i] if abs(pivot) < 1e-12: return [[0.0]n for in range(n)] # Singular matrix fallback for j in range(2n): A[i][j] /= pivot for k in range(n): if k != i: factor = A[k][i] for j in range(2n): A[k][j] -= factor A[i][j] return [row[n:] for row in A] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Entropy: If an attribute has constant values, its entropy is 0. The normalization step handles this by checking maxentropy == 0 before division. Multicollinearity: If selected attributes are highly correlated, the multiple correlation calculation may become numerically unstable. The matrix inversion includes a singularity check and fallback. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces the dimensionality of the transfer function specification problem by automatically identifying informative and non-redundant attributes. More comprehensive than the original pairwise method by considering all previously selected attributes. Limitations: Relies on linear correlation, which may miss non-linear dependencies between attributes. Computationally more expensive than simple entropy-based ranking due to multiple correlation calculations. The method is an adaptation of the heuristic proposed by Zhou, Schott, and Hansen (2012). The original method selected a pair of attributes (initial attribute and second attribute) using simple correlation and entropy. The adaptation, presented in the source, extends this to generate a full ranking of candidate attributes by using multiple correlation with all previously selected attributes. This approach is used in volume exploration frameworks to assist in the semi-automatic classification of volumetric features and the generation of multidimensional transfer function specifications.
