name: Feature Visualization
head: 3D PCA Feature Visualization
body: Feature Visualization maps high-dimensional learned feature vectors to RGB colors to make abstract neural representations interpretable. It solves the problem of visualizing latent spaces by projecting features onto the first three principal components, allowing semantic structures to be perceived as color fields. It differs from standard scalar transfer functions by operating on multi-dimensional feature embeddings rather than raw intensity or gradient values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of feature vectors \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^D associated with spatial locations (voxels, primitives, or tokens). Output: A color image or volume where each location is colored (R, G, B) based on its projection onto the principal components. Data Structures: Feature Matrix: A matrix F \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} where N is the number of samples and D is the feature dimension. Principal Components: A matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times 3} containing the top 3 eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of F. Steps: 1. Feature Collection: Gather feature vectors \mathbf{f}i for all relevant spatial elements. In NeRF contexts, these are teacher network feature maps from the first frame of training view images. 2. PCA Computation: Compute the 3-dimensional Principal Component Analysis (PCA) components of the collected features. Let \mu be the mean of the feature vectors. Compute the covariance matrix C = \frac{1}{N-1} \sum{i=1}^{N} (\mathbf{f}i - \mu)(\mathbf{f}i - \mu)^T. Extract the top 3 eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 corresponding to the largest eigenvalues. 3. Projection: Project each feature vector \mathbf{f}i onto the principal components to obtain 3D coordinates: p{i,1} = \mathbf{f}i \cdot \mathbf{v}1 p{i,2} = \mathbf{f}i \cdot \mathbf{v}2 p{i,3} = \mathbf{f}i \cdot \mathbf{v}3 4. Normalization and Outlier Removal: Identify outliers in the projected values and remove them to prevent color saturation. Normalize the remaining projected values to the range [0, 1] using min-max scaling: Ri = \frac{p{i,1} - \min(p1)}{\max(p1) - \min(p1)} Gi = \frac{p{i,2} - \min(p2)}{\max(p2) - \min(p2)} Bi = \frac{p{i,3} - \min(p3)}{\max(p3) - \min(p3)} 5. Rendering: Assign the normalized values (Ri, Gi, Bi) to the color channels of the corresponding spatial elements. Parameters: Number of Components: Fixed at 3 for RGB visualization. Outlier Removal: Method not specified in detail, but explicitly mentioned as necessary. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Independence of PCA: PCA is fitted independently for each method-object pair or scene. Dimensionality Loss: 3D PCA cannot perfectly visualize the full feature space, potentially losing semantic information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def featurevisualization(features): """ Visualizes high-dimensional features using 3D PCA. Args: features: np.ndarray of shape (N, D), N samples, D dimensions. Returns: colors: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3), RGB values in [0, 1]. """ # Step 1: Compute mean and covariance mean = np.mean(features, axis=0) centered = features - mean covmatrix = np.cov(centered, rowvar=False) # Step 2: Compute PCA components (top 3 eigenvectors) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covmatrix) idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] top3eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx[:3]] # Step 3: Project features projections = np.dot(centered, top3eigenvectors) # Shape (N, 3) # Step 4: Outlier removal and normalization # Outlier removal algorithm not specified in sources # Assuming standard min-max normalization on remaining data minvals = np.min(projections, axis=0) maxvals = np.max(projections, axis=0) rangevals = maxvals - minvals rangevals[rangevals == 0] = 1 normalized = (projections - minvals) / rangevals # Clip to [0, 1] to handle numerical issues colors = np.clip(normalized, 0.0, 1.0) return colors Maps continuous frozen encoder features to RGB by projecting token features onto the first three principal components. It solves the problem of visualizing high-dimensional latent representations in 3D scenes by reducing dimensionality while preserving structural coherence. Unlike standard RGB rendering, it reveals semantic or geometric relationships within the feature space, distinguishing object parts from background noise. It is distinct from uncertainty visualization and from global embedding organization using t-SNE. PCA Feature Fields Visualization Concatenates all computed feature vectors into a high-dimensional feature space encoding shape-based distances to reference or composite volumes. Maps the high-dimensional vectors to a 2D scatterplot using either Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or Locally Linear Embedding (LLE). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides an intuitive, color-based overview of high-dimensional semantic structures. Effective for comparing semantic resolution between different models (e.g., LSeg vs. DINO). Limitations: Colors are relative to the specific dataset/scene and not globally comparable. Information loss due to dimensionality reduction from D to 3. When to use: Exploratory analysis of learned feature spaces, debugging feature consistency, or qualitative comparison of model semantics. When not to use: When quantitative, globally consistent color mapping is required. Originating from the need to interpret deep learning features, this method applies Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to visualize high-dimensional data. It has been used to analyze NeRF feature fields (e.g., LSeg, DINO). The technique relies on standard linear algebra tools like sklearn.decomposition.PCA. name: PCA Feature Fields Visualization
head: Feature Map Visualization, PCA Feature Visualization
body: PCA Feature Fields Visualization is a technique that maps continuous, frozen encoder features to RGB color space by projecting token features onto the first three principal components. It solves the problem of visualizing high-dimensional latent representations in 3D scenes by reducing dimensionality while preserving structural coherence. Unlike standard RGB rendering, this method reveals semantic or geometric relationships within the feature space, distinguishing object parts from background noise. It is distinct from uncertainty visualization, which maps scalar variance values, and from global embedding organization, which uses t-SNE for 2D scatter plots rather than spatial field rendering. Inputs: Frozen encoder token features propagated to input primitives (e.g., Gaussians). A set of frames or views containing pixel-aligned feature vectors. Outputs: RGB images where each pixel's color corresponds to the projected feature vector. Data Structures: Feature Vectors: For each primitive or pixel, a vector \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^D, where D is the latent dimension. PCA Components: A 3 \times D matrix \mathbf{W} containing the top 3 eigenvectors of the feature covariance matrix. Steps: 1. Feature Propagation: Propagate frozen encoder token features to the input primitives (e.g., 3D Gaussians). 2. Collection: Collect all pixel-aligned feature vectors across all frames or views for a specific method-object pair. 3. PCA Fitting: Fit Principal Component Analysis independently for each method-object pair on the collected features. Compute the covariance matrix of the feature vectors. Extract the top 3 eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues. 4. Projection: Project each feature vector \mathbf{f}i onto the first three principal components: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{f}i where \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. 5. RGB Mapping: Map the components of \mathbf{p}i to RGB channels. Typically, the three components are assigned directly to Red, Green, and Blue channels. 6. Background Handling: Fill background areas with low density with noise according to the feature sampling equation (Eq. 3 in). In latentSplat, this is consistent with setting background standard deviation to one. Parameters: Number of Components: 3 (fixed for RGB visualization). PCA Scope: Independent per method-object pair. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Incomparability: Absolute colors are not comparable across different panels or methods because PCA is fitted independently for each method-object pair. Colors must be interpreted within each panel. Background Noise: Background areas with low density are filled with noise, which may appear as uniform or random patterns depending on the sampling equation. Normalization: In global embedding analysis, features are \ell2-normalized before PCA, but for field visualization, direct projection is used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pcafeaturefieldsvisualization(frozenfeatures, primitives, frames): """ Visualize frozen encoder features using PCA. Args: frozenfeatures: List of feature vectors for each primitive/frame. primitives: List of primitives (e.g., Gaussians) with positions and densities. frames: List of frames/views to process. Returns: RGB images for each frame. """ # Step 1: Collect all pixel-aligned feature vectors across all frames allfeatures = [] for frame in frames: # Propagate frozen encoder token features to input primitives # This step assumes features are already propagated to primitives # Collect features for visible primitives/pixels framefeatures = getpixelalignedfeatures(frame, primitives) allfeatures.extend(framefeatures) # Step 2: Fit PCA independently for each method-object pair # Compute covariance matrix mean = np.mean(allfeatures, axis=0) centeredfeatures = allfeatures - mean covmatrix = np.cov(centeredfeatures, rowvar=False) # Extract top 3 eigenvectors eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covmatrix) # Sort by eigenvalue descending idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] top3eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx[:3]] # Step 3: Project features onto first three principal components projectedfeatures = np.dot(centeredfeatures, top3eigenvectors) # Step 4: Map to RGB channels # Normalize projected features to [0, 1] for display minval = np.min(projectedfeatures, axis=0) maxval = np.max(projectedfeatures, axis=0) normalizedfeatures = (projectedfeatures - minval) / (maxval - minval + 1e-8) # Assign to RGB rgbimages = [] for frameidx, frame in enumerate(frames): # Reconstruct frame-specific projected features frameprojected = projectedfeatures[framestart:frameend] framergb = np.clip(frameprojected, 0, 1) # Step 5: Handle background areas with low density # Fill with noise according to feature sampling equation # This is a placeholder for the specific noise generation method backgroundmask = getlowdensitymask(frame, primitives) framergb[backgroundmask] = generatenoise(framergb.shape) rgbimages.append(framergb) return rgbimages Time Complexity: Dominated by PCA fitting, which is O(N \cdot D^2) or O(N \cdot D) with iterative methods, where N is the number of feature vectors and D is the feature dimension. Projection is O(N \cdot D). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D) to store features and O(D^2) for covariance matrix. Strengths: Reveals coherent fields over extended structures and preserves variation between object parts. Clearly separates background from foreground. Limitations: Colors are not comparable across different methods or objects due to independent PCA fitting. Requires frozen encoder features, which may not be available in all pipelines. When to Use: When visualizing high-dimensional latent features in 3D scenes to understand semantic or geometric structure. When Not to Use: When absolute color consistency across different methods or objects is required. Origin: Introduced in Gaussian-JEPA and latentSplat for visualizing frozen encoder features in 3D Gaussian splats. Development: Used to analyze the quality of learned feature representations in novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction tasks. Usage: Applied in research on joint-embedding predictive learning and variational Gaussians for 3D scene representation. Gaussian-JEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for 3D Gaussian Splats, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15651v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) latentSplat, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16292, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: High-Dimensional Feature Projection
head: Feature Space Mapping, PCA/LLE Volume Projection
body: High-Dimensional Feature Projection maps high-dimensional feature vectors, which encode shape-based distances between volumetric datasets, into a two-dimensional scatterplot for visual overview and browsing. It distinguishes itself from pairwise distance visualization techniques (such as Self-Organizing Maps or Multidimensional Scaling) by focusing on comparing a small set of reference volumes against a large set of test volumes, where global linear or local non-linear projections are more efficient than all-pairs comparisons. Inputs: 1. A set of N volumetric datasets (e.g., virtual mastoidectomies). 2. A set of M reference or composite volumes. 3. Feature extraction method (e.g., distance field histogram) producing a feature vector fi for each volume i. Outputs: A 2D scatterplot where each point represents a volumetric dataset, positioned according to its high-dimensional feature similarity to the references. Data Structures: Feature Matrix F: An N \times D matrix, where N is the number of test volumes and D is the dimensionality of the feature space. Each row fi is the concatenated feature vector for volume i. Projection Matrix W: A D \times 2 matrix containing the projection vectors (eigenvectors for PCA, or embedding weights for LLE). Projected Points P: An N \times 2 matrix where each row pi is the 2D coordinate (xi, yi) for volume i. Steps: 1. Feature Vector Construction: For each volume i, compute the feature vector fi by concatenating shape-based distance metrics. These metrics typically encode the distance field histogram between volume i and the reference/composite volumes. Additional features (e.g., from Sec. 3.3.2 in the source) may be appended to fi. fi = [d1, d2, \dots, dD] Where dj are the individual feature components. 2. Projection Selection: Choose between Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) based on user preference or data characteristics. 3. Dimensionality Reduction: Map the high-dimensional vectors F to 2D space using the selected method. Option A: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) 1. Center the data: \bar{f} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} fi. 2. Compute the covariance matrix C = \frac{1}{N-1} (F - \mathbf{1}\bar{f}^T)^T (F - \mathbf{1}\bar{f}^T). 3. Compute the eigenvectors of C. 4. Select the two eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues. Let these be w1 and w2. 5. Project each vector: pi = [(fi - \bar{f}) \cdot w1, (fi - \bar{f}) \cdot w2]. Option B: Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) 1. For each point fi, find its k nearest neighbors in the high-dimensional space. 2. Compute reconstruction weights W{ij} such that fi \approx \sum{j \in neighbors(i)} W{ij} fj, minimizing \sumi ||fi - \sumj W{ij} fj||^2 subject to \sumj W{ij} = 1. 3. Find the 2D coordinates yi that minimize the embedding cost function E = \sumi ||yi - \sumj W{ij} yj||^2. 4. Visualization: Render the points pi in a 2D scatterplot. Users can browse the dataset by inspecting the spatial distribution of volumes relative to reference points. Parameters: Projection Method: PCA or LLE. Feature Components: The specific distance metrics and histograms used to construct fi. k (for LLE): Number of neighbors. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Choice of Algorithm: PCA is suitable for linear structures and global comparisons. LLE captures local nonlinear structures. The source notes that PCA and LLE are well-suited for comparing a small number of references to many tests, whereas Self-Organizing Maps or Multidimensional Scaling are better for all-pairwise distance comparisons. Feature Selection: The quality of the projection depends on the relevance of the appended features. The source mentions that features from Sec. 3.3.2 can be appended, but their specific effects are discussed elsewhere. This method is a visualization pipeline that uses subspace clustering to identify low-dimensional linear subspaces within high-dimensional multivariate volumetric data, enabling effective Transfer Function (TF) design through animated transitions (dynamic projections) between 2D views of these subspaces. It sets itself apart from static high-dimensional projection methods (like PCA) by mitigating structural illusions inherent in single-view projections; unlike random projection techniques (e.g., GGobi's grand tour), it uses data-driven subspace clustering to define meaningful transitional targets. Time and Memory Complexity: PCA: Computing the covariance matrix is O(N D^2) or O(N^2 D) depending on implementation. Eigendecomposition is O(D^3). Projection is O(N D). LLE: Finding neighbors is O(N D \log N) or O(N^2 D). Solving for weights is O(N k^3). Solving for embedding is O(N^3) or less with sparse solvers. Memory: O(N D) to store the feature matrix. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficient overview of large-scale datasets compared to flat lists. PCA and LLE are well-suited for comparing a small number of references to a large number of test volumes. Limitations: Single-view projections may suffer from structural illusions (addressed by subspace clustering variants). PCA assumes linear relationships. LLE is computationally more expensive and sensitive to parameter k. When to Use: When browsing a large dataset of volumes against a few reference/composite volumes. When shape-based distance features are available. When Not to Use: When comparing all pairwise distances in a set (use Self-Organizing Maps or Multidimensional Scaling instead). The method was introduced in the context of virtual mastoidectomy performance evaluation, providing a large-scale dataset overview tool. It builds on distance field histogram methods for feature extraction. The approach leverages established dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA and LLE) adapted for volumetric shape comparison. name: Subspace Clustering for Multivariate Volume Visualization
head: Subspace-based TF Design
body: This method is a visualization pipeline that uses subspace clustering to identify low-dimensional linear subspaces within high-dimensional multivariate volumetric data, enabling effective Transfer Function (TF) design through animated transitions (dynamic projections) between 2D views of these subspaces. It sets itself apart from static high-dimensional projection methods (like PCA) by mitigating structural illusions inherent in single-view projections; unlike random projection techniques (e.g., GGobi's grand tour), it uses data-driven subspace clustering to define meaningful transitional targets. The pipeline consists of three main stages: Data Reduction, Subspace Clustering, and Dynamic Projections for TF Design. Input: Multivariate volumetric dataset V with N voxels, each having D attributes. Output: A Transfer Function (colormap) and volume rendering parameters, visualized via dynamic projections. 1. Attribute Space Points: A set of points \{xi \in \mathbb{R}^D\}{i=1}^T representing the volumetric data. 2. Representatives: A reduced set of points R derived from clustering, serving as proxies for the full volume. 3. Coefficient Matrix W: A T \times T matrix where W{ik} describes the relationship between sample i and sample k. 4. Adjacency Matrix A: A T \times T symmetric matrix used for spectral clustering. 5. Subspace Basis Uj: A D \times dj matrix containing the basis vectors for subspace Sj. 6. Labels: An array mapping each representative (and by extension, volume voxels) to a subspace index. The goal is to reduce the computational load while preserving the structure of the attribute space. 1. Histogram Construction: Construct a histogram of the data points in the attribute space based on their \ell2-norm. 2. Sampling: Sample a fixed percentage of points within each discrete interval of the histogram to ensure coverage of the attribute space. Parameter: Sampling rate. Typical values are 10% to 30%. 3. Clustering: Perform k-means++ clustering on the sampled points. Parameter: Number of clusters k. Typical values are 1500 or 3000. 4. Approximation: Obtain cluster centers during convergence. Approximate these cluster centers with their nearest neighbors within the initial volumetric dataset. These approximated centers serve as the representatives of the entire volume. Represent the high-dimensional attribute space as a collection of low-dimensional linear subspaces. 1. Reconstruction Model: Solve for the coefficient matrix W such that: X \approx XW subject to W{ii} = 0 for i = 1 \dots T. X is the data matrix of representatives. Regularization penalties on W include sparsity, low-rank, or L2 norms. 2. Adjacency Matrix: Compute the adjacency matrix for spectral clustering: A = |W| + |W^T| Here, |W| denotes the element-wise absolute value. 3. Segmentation: Perform spectral clustering on A to segment the representatives into clusters \Lambdaj, where each cluster corresponds to a subspace Sj. 4. Basis Estimation: For each subspace Sj with index set \Lambdaj, estimate the basis Uj \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times dj} by solving: Uj = \arg \minU \sum{i \in \Lambdaj} \left\| U^T xi - \sum{k \neq i, k \in \Lambdaj} W{ik} U^T xk \right\|2^2 subject to U^T U = I. The solution is obtained via generalized eigenvalue decomposition of Xj (I - Wj)^T (I - Wj) Xj^T. Uj consists of the eigenvectors corresponding to the dj smallest eigenvalues. 1. View Definition: Use the estimated basis vectors of each subspace to define viewpoints. Create projections onto pairs of basis vectors to generate a set of 2D views from each subspace. Note: A subspace of dimension dj produces \binom{dj}{2} 2D views by projecting onto all pairs of basis vectors. 2. Dynamic Projections: Define dynamic projections as animated transitions between pairs of linear projections (views). Unlike methods that use random generation (e.g., grand tour) or projection pursuit, transitional targets are obtained via the subspace clustering framework. 3. Point Selection: Provide two approaches for selecting points in the dynamic projection canvas: Lasso Selection: Paints individual points for sculpting TF regions. Neighborhood Selection: Paints a point and its neighbors within a chosen radius in the high-dimensional attribute space. Three modes of TF design are supported, leveraging subspace labels assigned to representatives: 1. Automatic TF Design: Assign colors based on subspace labels. During dynamic transitions, points in the subspace of the target view increase opacity, while all other subspaces increase transparency. This yields smooth color transitions in the volume visualization. 2. Semi-automatic TF Design: Import subspace labels as an initial design. Modify and refine the TF by exploiting relations among data parts via animated transitions among multiple views. 3. Manual TF Design: Sculpt the colormap manually across multiple views. Subspace labels are treated as latent information to provide freedom and flexibility. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random import numpy as np def createhistogram(values, numbins=20): """Bins values into discrete intervals.""" minval, maxval = min(values), max(values) binwidth = (maxval - minval) / numbins bins = [{'low': minval + i binwidth, 'high': minval + (i + 1) binwidth} for i in range(numbins)] return bins def kmeanspp(points, k): """Standard k-means++ initialization and convergence.""" centers = [random.choice(points)] for in range(1, k): dists = np.array([min(np.linalg.norm(p - c)2 for c in centers) for p in points]) probs = dists / dists.sum() centers.append(random.choices(points, weights=probs, k=1)[0]) # Standard Lloyd's iterations omitted for brevity; returns final centers return centers def findnearestneighbor(target, dataset): """Returns the dataset point closest to target.""" return min(dataset, key=lambda p: np.linalg.norm(np.array(p) - np.array(target))) def solvereconstruction(X): """Solves X ≈ XW with Wii = 0 using standard constrained optimization.""" n, d = X.shape W = np.zeros((n, n)) # Standard sparse/low-rank/L2 regularization solver applied here return W def spectralclustering(A): """Standard spectral clustering returning list of index arrays.""" # Standard graph Laplacian eigenvector partitioning return [] def estimatedimension(eigenvalues): """Determines subspace dimension from eigenvalue gap.""" return max(1, int(np.sum(eigenvalues > np.mean(eigenvalues) 0.1))) def subspaceclusteringvizpipeline(volumedata, samplingrate=0.1, numclusters=1500, numhistbins=20): # 1. Data Reduction norms = [math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in x)) for x in volumedata] histogrambins = createhistogram(norms, numhistbins) sampledpoints = [] for bin in histogrambins: pointsinbin = [volumedata[i] for i, n in enumerate(norms) if bin['low'] <= n < bin['high']] numtosample = max(1, int(len(pointsinbin) samplingrate)) sampledpoints.extend(random.sample(pointsinbin, numtosample)) clustercenters = kmeanspp(sampledpoints, k=numclusters) representatives = [findnearestneighbor(center, volumedata) for center in clustercenters] volumelabels = [findnearestneighbor(pt, representatives) for pt in representatives] # Maps to cluster index # 2. Subspace Clustering X = np.array(representatives) nsamples, D = X.shape W = solvereconstruction(X) A = np.abs(W) + np.abs(W.T) clusters = spectralclustering(A) # 3. Basis Estimation subspacebases = {} for j, clusterindices in enumerate(clusters): Xj = X[clusterindices,:] Wj = W[clusterindices,:] Ij = np.eye(len(clusterindices)) diff = Ij - Wj M = Xj @ diff.T @ diff @ Xj.T eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(M) sortedindices = np.argsort(eigenvalues) dj = estimatedimension(eigenvalues) subspacebases[j] = eigenvectors[:, sortedindices[:dj]] # 4. View Generation views = [] for j, basis in subspacebases.items(): for i in range(basis.shape[1]): for k in range(i + 1, basis.shape[1]): views.append((j, basis[:, [i, k]])) return representatives, volumelabels, views, subspacebases Sampling Rate: Fixed percentage of points sampled from histogram intervals. Typical value: 10% to 30%. Number of Clusters (k): For k-means++. Typical values: 1500 or 3000. Regularization: Choice of penalty on W (sparsity, low-rank, L2). Structural Illusions: High dimensionality and complex attribute space structure mean no single projection faithfully represents structural relations. Dynamic projections across multiple views are required to mitigate errors caused by these illusions. Intersecting Subspaces: Standard PCA on each subspace independently fails when subspaces intersect. The proposed method uses a generalized eigenvalue decomposition that accounts for inter-sample relationships via W. Scalability: Hardware capacities limit the size of raw volumetric data and the number of points for smooth animation. Data reduction is essential. Time Complexity: k-means++: O(n k^2 \cdot \text{iterations}), where n is the number of data points and k is the number of clusters. Subspace Clustering: O(m^2 d) time to construct the affinity matrix, where m is the number of samples (representatives) and d is the dimension. Memory Complexity: O(m^2) to store the affinity matrix in subspace clustering. Strengths: Reveals unseen structures (e.g., separated subspaces) that appear connected in static PCA views. Provides a multi-view canvas for effective TF design, reducing structural illusions. Automatic TF design yields smooth color transitions during dynamic projections. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large datasets without reduction. Requires careful selection of sampling rate and number of clusters. When to use: When exploring high-dimensional multivariate volumetric data where structural relationships are complex and static projections are insufficient. When not to use: When real-time interaction on very large raw datasets is required without pre-processing, or when the attribute space does not exhibit low-dimensional subspace structure. The method was introduced in the paper "Multivariate volume visualization through dynamic projections". It builds upon infrastructure developed for high-dimensional data exploration. It adapts the infrastructure for multivariate TF design and volume rendering. The dynamic projection technique uses mathematical formulation similar to GGobi. It replaces random generation with subspace clustering-derived targets. The implementation uses C++ and Qt for the interface. It uses k-means++ from the Mobile Robot Programming Toolkit. It uses MATLAB for subspace clustering prototyping. Multivariate volume visualization through dynamic projections, https://doi.org/10.1109/ldav.2014.7013202, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Machine Learning and Feature Extraction
body: This family applies machine learning algorithms and feature extraction techniques to determine the optical properties of volume data, moving beyond manual transfer function design. It solves the problem of classifying complex, high-dimensional volumetric structures automatically or semi-automatically by learning decision boundaries from training data or extracting statistical features. It differs from Data Feature-Based Classification by explicitly using learned models (e.g., SVMs, Neural Networks, Boosting) or statistical clustering (e.g., K-means) rather than static, user-defined heuristic functions. Builds on Data Feature-Based Classification, which evaluates a classification function C(\mathbf{x}) for each sample point \mathbf{x} in the volume to produce optical properties. K-means-based hybrid segmentation is an image processing approach that enhances ray casting object distinction by assigning object membership information (ID tags) to cubical vertices in the volume. It differs from standard clustering by combining Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) for robust initialization, K-means for preliminary grouping, and Fisher discriminant analysis for statistical optimization, specifically designed to generate binary, non-overlapping transfer functions for color and opacity assignment. AdaBoost Look Up Table (LUT) Classification is a machine learning method for volume rendering that accelerates multi-class segmentation by storing trained AdaBoost weak classifiers in a compact lookup structure. It solves the problem of interactive volume classification by replacing iterative model evaluation with fast table lookups, enabling real-time testing after an interactive training phase. It differs from AdaBoost Volume Classification by explicitly encoding the decision stumps into a 3-row LUT structure optimized for GPU parallel testing, and from K-means-based hybrid segmentation by using boosting-based binary dichotomizers within an Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) framework rather than centroid-based clustering. AdaBoost Volume Classification is an interactive, data-driven method for multi-class segmentation of volumetric data using a framework of Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) and Discrete AdaBoost classifiers. It solves the problem of classifying multiple regions of interest on demand without requiring preprocessing or complex optimization procedures. Unlike graph cuts or random walker methods, it avoids segmentation dependencies among neighboring voxels, making it suitable for real-time applications and handling thinned or complex structures. Two-stage k-means streamline clustering is a method for abstracting 3D vector fields by decomposing a large set of streamlines into coherent bundles and extracting representative streamlines for visualization. It solves the problem of visual clutter and high computational complexity associated with rendering raw streamline data by reducing the dataset to a concise set of representative paths. Unlike standard k-means which operates on high-dimensional point vectors, this method uses low-dimensional feature vectors (spatial coordinates and entropy metrics) to ensure efficiency and coherence in flow structure representation. This method suggests the optimal viewpoint for features of interest in a given input volume and transfer function by considering the similarity between input features and features in a collected image set. It sets itself apart from image-based viewpoint selection models by separating viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation into distinct stages solved by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), rather than applying a single similarity measure to mix these stages. Definition: Saving a trained neural network or SVM configuration to apply it to new data sets with similar characteristics, reducing classification time. Step: Apply the saved classifier to the new data set. If misclassification occurs, the user can refine it by supplying additional training data. Parameter: Saved classifier size: under 30 kilobytes. Pitfall: Position information is specific to a given data set; using it reduces reusability because location changes between scans. It should be excluded if reusability is intended. Reused classifiers may misclassify materials if the new data set does not share similar characteristics (e.g., data value ranges or material locations). Number: SVM IoU on CT-ORG dataset with DINO features: 0.24 (liver), 0.36 (bones), 0.0 (other classes), mean 0.09. Fit time: 407s. Inference time: 2077s. Definition: A technique using Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to represent voxel signatures via linear transformation into a space where manual classification is simpler, often achievable using separator planes perpendicular to the new coordinate axes. ICA infers the linear transformation coefficients to simplify the signature representation. Step: 1. Apply ICA to voxel signatures. 2. Infer appropriate linear transformation coefficients. 3. Transform voxel signatures into the new space. 4. Perform manual classification using separator planes perpendicular to the new axes. The application of machine learning to volume rendering classification emerged in the early 2000s as a response to the complexity of high-dimensional data. Tzeng et al. introduced intelligent systems using Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and neural networks for higher-dimensional classification, demonstrating the reuse of classifiers across similar datasets. Concurrently, Takanashi et al. proposed using Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to simplify the classification space for multidimensional volumes. More recently, self-supervised vision transformers (e.g., DINO) have been leveraged for segmentation-based transfer function design, although computational costs remain a challenge. name: K-means-based hybrid segmentation
head: hybrid segmentation
body: K-means-based hybrid segmentation is an image processing approach that enhances ray casting object distinction by assigning object membership information (ID tags) to cubical vertices in the volume. It differs from standard clustering by combining Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) for robust initialization, K-means for preliminary grouping, and Fisher discriminant analysis for statistical optimization, specifically designed to generate binary, non-overlapping transfer functions for color and opacity assignment. Inputs: Volume data (typically RGB color bands, though gray levels are supported). Optional: Noise reduction filters and histogram equalization parameters. Outputs: Object membership ID tags assigned to cubical vertices. Optimum segments representing inherent color and formation characteristics. Data Structures: Neural Map: A 2D grid of nodes with dimensions mapwidth \times maplength. Each node stores a weight vector wv. Feature Vector: For K-means, features are limited to three color bands and a Diagonal Busyness Factor (DF). DF Calculation: Computed for each pixel using four diagonal neighbors xi and center C: DF = \sum{i=1}^4 |C - xi|. Parameters: SOM Learning Rate: Starts at 0.9, reduces to 0.1 in Stage 1; 0.01 in Stage 2. SOM Neighborhood Size: Starts at half map size, reduces to 1 in Stage 1; remains 1 in Stage 2. Feature Normalization: RGB values normalized from [0, 255] to [-1, 1]. Steps: 1. Pre-processing (Optional): Apply high pass/low pass filters and histogram equalization to remove noise and rectify intensity imbalance. 2. Neural Map Initialization: Calculate NumberofMapNodes = mapwidth \times maplength. Find SmallestAvailableColorValue = \min(R, G, B) and LargestAvailableColorValue = \max(R, G, B). Calculate Range = LargestAvailableColorValue - SmallestAvailableColorValue. Calculate Interval = Range / (NumberofMapNodes - 1). Initialize nodes by setting the first node to SmallestAvailableColorValue, then incrementing by Interval for each subsequent node. 3. SOM Training Stage 1: Randomly select pixels as input vectors D(t). Find Best Matching Unit (BMU) u for each input. Adjust BMU and neighborhood weights using: wv(s+1) = wv(s) + \theta(u,v,s)\alpha(s)(D(t) - wv(s)) where \alpha(s) is the monotonically decreasing learning coefficient and \theta(u,v,s) is the neighborhood function based on lattice distance. Reduce learning rate from 0.9 to 0.1 and neighborhood size from half map size to 1. 4. SOM Training Stage 2 (Refinement): Stabilize feature vectors with a learning rate of 0.01. Neighborhood size remains 1 (only BMU adjusted). 5. K-means Clustering: Use SOM output as initial cluster centers. Perform few rounds of K-means clustering using features: 3 color bands + DF. Identify preliminary groups/elementary clusters. 6. Statistical Optimization: Apply Fisher discriminant ratio to convert preliminary groups into optimum segments. Use edge detection to exempt important boundary/pattern information from irrelevant recombination. Apply recombination and epsilon tolerance factor for spatial tuning. Pseudocode: Unverified code. minval interval = rangeval / (numberofmapnodes - 1) nodes = [minval + i interval for i in range(numberofmapnodes)] # Helper: Normalize data to [-1, 1] def normalizetominusoneone(data): return (data / 255.0) 2 - 1 normalizeddata = normalizetominusoneone(processeddata) # Helper: Linear decay def decay(current, target, epoch, maxepoch): return current - (current - target) (epoch / maxepoch) # Helper: Lattice distance on 2D grid def latticedistance(idx1, idx2, width): r1, c1 = divmod(idx1, width) r2, c2 = divmod(idx2, width) return abs(r1 - r2) + abs(c1 - c2) # Helper: Neighborhood function (Gaussian) def neighborhoodfunction(dist, size): return math.exp(-(dist 2) / (2 (size / 2) 2)) # Helper: Find BMU def findbmu(pixel, nodes): dists = [np.linalg.norm(pixel - w) for w in nodes] return np.argmin(dists) # Phase 1.2: Training Stage 1 learningrate = 0.9 neighborhoodsize = mapwidth / 2 maxepochsstage1 = 100 # Not given in the sources for epoch in range(maxepochsstage1): for pixel in normalizeddata: bmuindex = findbmu(pixel, nodes) for i, node in enumerate(nodes): dist = latticedistance(i, bmuindex, mapwidth) theta = neighborhoodfunction(dist, neighborhoodsize) nodes[i] = node + theta learningrate (pixel - node) learningrate = decay(learningrate, 0.1, epoch, maxepochsstage1) neighborhoodsize = max(1, neighborhoodsize / 2) # Phase 1.2: Training Stage 2 learningrate = 0.01 neighborhoodsize = 1 maxepochsstage2 = 100 # Not given in the sources for epoch in range(maxepochsstage2): for pixel in normalizeddata: bmuindex = findbmu(pixel, nodes) nodes[bmuindex] = nodes[bmuindex] + learningrate (pixel - nodes[bmuindex]) # Phase 1.3: K-means Clustering # Features: 3 color bands + Diagonal Busyness Factor (DF) def extractfeatures(data): features = [] h, w, = data.shape for y in range(h): for x in range(w): c = data[y, x] df = 0.0 for dx, dy in [(-1, -1), (1, -1), (-1, 1), (1, 1)]: nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < w and 0 <= ny < h: df += np.linalg.norm(c - data[ny, nx]) else: df += 0.0 features.append(np.concatenate([c, [df]])) return np.array(features) features = extractfeatures(processeddata) initialcenters = nodes # Not given in the sources: kmeansclustering(features, initialcenters, rounds=3) # Statistical Optimization # Not given in the sources: applyfisherdiscriminant(clusters) # Not given in the sources: applyedgedetectionandrecombination(optimumsegments) # Not given in the sources: assignidtags(optimumsegments) Time Complexity: Dominated by SOM training iterations and K-means convergence. The use of SOM for initialization reduces the risk of local optima, potentially reducing the number of K-means iterations required compared to random initialization. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the neural map nodes and feature vectors (color + DF) for each voxel. Strengths: Improves clustering accuracy by avoiding random initialization pitfalls; handles noise via pre-processing; generates binary transfer functions suitable for clear object distinction. Limitations: Requires tuning of SOM parameters (map size, learning rates); DF calculation adds computational overhead per pixel; limited to 3 color bands + DF for K-means features. The method was proposed by Azimzadeh & Pourgholi in 2020 to enhance ray casting object distinction by integrating image processing techniques with volume rendering. It addresses the issue of K-means converging to local optima when initialized randomly by using a Self-Organizing Map (SOM) to provide rational initial cluster centers. name: AdaBoost Look Up Table (LUT) Classification
head: Discrete AdaBoost with ECOC, Voxel-based AdaBoost Classification
body: AdaBoost Look Up Table (LUT) Classification is a machine learning method for volume rendering that accelerates multi-class segmentation by storing trained AdaBoost weak classifiers in a compact lookup structure. It solves the problem of interactive volume classification by replacing iterative model evaluation with fast table lookups, enabling real-time testing after an interactive training phase. It differs from AdaBoost Volume Classification by explicitly encoding the decision stumps into a 3-row LUT structure optimized for GPU parallel testing, and from K-means-based hybrid segmentation by using boosting-based binary dichotomizers within an Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) framework rather than centroid-based clustering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N classes (volume structures) and a training dataset T consisting of voxel samples (\rho, l(\rho)). Output: A Look Up Table (LUT) L containing the parameters for n dichotomizers, and a classification map assigning each voxel in the volume to one of the N classes. Data Structures: The core data structure is the LUT L, which stores the parameters for all weak classifiers across all dichotomizers. It is organized as a table with 3 rows and n \times M columns (where n is the number of dichotomizers and M is the number of stumps per dichotomizer): Row 1: Codifies the 8 sample features \rhos (s \in [1..8]) used for splitting. Row 2: Codifies the polarity (p) for each weak classifier. Row 3: Codifies the threshold (t) for each weak classifier. Numbered Steps: 1. Define Classes: Define N classes representing the volume structures to be segmented. 2. Form Dichotomizers: Create n binary partitions (dichotomizers) of the N classes using an ECOC design. 3. Train Dichotomizers: For each dichotomizer hi: a. Select a subset of training voxels T. b. Train an AdaBoost classifier using Decision Stumps as weak learners. c. Extract the polarity and threshold for each stump's selected feature. d. Populate the corresponding columns in the LUT L with the feature index (Row 1), polarity (Row 2), and threshold (Row 3). 4. Test (Classify): For each voxel in the volume: a. Compute the 8 features \rho for the voxel. b. For each dichotomizer i: i. Retrieve the feature index s, polarity p, and threshold t from LUT L. ii. Evaluate the decision stump: if p=1, check if \rhos > t; if p=-1, check if \rhos < t. c. Aggregate the binary outputs from all n dichotomizers using the ECOC decoding scheme to determine the final class label. Formulas: Training Cost: The total cost of sequential training for one dichotomizer is O(|T| \times M), where |T| is the cardinality of the training data set T and M is the number of iterations/stumps. Feature Vector: \rho = [x, y, z, gx, gy, gz, |g|, v]. Parameters: Features: 8 features per voxel. Weak Classifier: Decision Stumps. Number of Stumps: 30 per dichotomizer. Training Data Size: Small subset of voxels, ranging from 1,880 (first iteration) to 14,200 (last iteration) in simulations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Data Selection: The method relies on user-selected voxels. Serial Bottleneck: While dichotomizers are trained in parallel, the training of a single dichotomizer is serial due to dependencies between AdaBoost iterations. ECOC Design: The choice of ECOC design affects the number of dichotomizers n. For N classes using one-versus-one, n = N(N-1)/2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainadaboostlut(classes, trainingsamples, numstumps=30): nclasses = len(classes) # One-versus-one ECOC design dichotomizers = [] for i in range(nclasses): for j in range(i + 1, nclasses): dichotomizers.append((classes[i], classes[j])) ndichotomizers = len(dichotomizers) totalstumps = ndichotomizers numstumps # LUT structure: 3 rows, totalstumps columns # Row 0: Feature indices (0-7) # Row 1: Polarity (-1 or 1) # Row 2: Thresholds (float) lut = [[0.0] totalstumps for in range(3)] for didx, (classa, classb) in enumerate(dichotomizers): binfeatures = [] binlabels = [] for features, label in trainingsamples: if label == classa: binfeatures.append(features) binlabels.append(1) elif label == classb: binfeatures.append(features) binlabels.append(-1) if not binfeatures: continue weights = [1.0 / len(binlabels)] len(binlabels) stumps = [] for m in range(numstumps): stump = traindecisionstump(binfeatures, binlabels, weights) stumps.append(stump) errors = [] for i in range(len(binlabels)): pred = stump.evaluate(binfeatures[i]) errors.append(1 if pred != binlabels[i] else 0) errorrate = sum(w e for w, e in zip(weights, errors)) if errorrate >= 0.5: break alpha = 0.5 math.log((1.0 - errorrate) / max(errorrate, 1e-10)) for i in range(len(weights)): weights[i] = math.exp(-alpha binlabels[i] (1 if errors[i] == 0 else -1)) wsum = sum(weights) weights = [w / wsum for w in weights] for m, stump in enumerate(stumps): col = didx numstumps + m lut[0][col] = stump.featureindex lut[1][col] = stump.polarity lut[2][col] = stump.threshold return lut, dichotomizers def traindecisionstump(features, labels, weights): beststump = None minweightederror = float('inf') for fidx in range(8): values = [f[fidx] for f in features] thresholds = sorted(set(values)) for t in thresholds: for p in [1, -1]: weightederror = 0.0 for i in range(len(labels)): pred = p if values[i] > t else -p if pred != labels[i]: weightederror += weights[i] if weightederror < minweightederror: minweightederror = weightederror beststump = {'featureindex': fidx, 'threshold': t, 'polarity': p} return beststump def classifyvoxel(lut, voxelfeatures, dichotomizers, numstumps): ndichotomizers = len(dichotomizers) classvotes = {c: 0 for c in set(c for pair in dichotomizers for c in pair)} for didx in range(ndichotomizers): vote = 0 for k in range(numstumps): col = didx numstumps + k fidx = int(lut[0][col]) p = lut[1][col] t = lut[2][col] val = voxelfeatures[fidx] pred = p if val > t else -p vote += pred classa, classb = dichotomizers[didx] if vote > 0: classvotes[classa] += 1 else: classvotes[classb] += 1 return max(classvotes, key=classvotes.get) Time Complexity: Training one dichotomizer is O(|T| \times M). Total training time is interactive, with a worst-case bound of 5 seconds for the tested datasets. Testing is real-time. Memory Complexity: The LUT size is proportional to 3 \times n \times M entries, where n is the number of dichotomizers and M is the number of stumps per dichotomizer. For N classes using one-versus-one, n = N(N-1)/2. Performance: Mean accuracy exceeds 90% by the 5th iteration across datasets. Brain: 0.960 accuracy (Ref: 0.968). Foot: 0.989 accuracy (Ref: 1.000). Thorax: 0.922 accuracy (Ref: 0.922). Data Efficiency: High accuracy is achieved with very few training samples (0.1% to 4% of voxels). Strengths: Real-time testing, interactive training, high accuracy with minimal user input, GPU parallelization of dichotomizer training. Limitations: Training of individual dichotomizers is serial; accuracy depends on user-provided training samples; ECOC design complexity grows with number of classes. The method was proposed by S. Grau, A. Puig, S. Escalera, and M. Salamó in the paper "Intelligent Interactive Volume Classification" presented at Eurographics 2013. It builds on Discrete AdaBoost and ECOC frameworks for multi-class classification, adapting them for volume rendering by using decision stumps and a LUT for efficient evaluation. The approach addresses the need for interactive segmentation in volume visualization, where traditional machine learning methods are too slow for real-time feedback. name: AdaBoost Volume Classification
head: ECOC-AdaBoost Volume Classification, GPU-Parallelized AdaBoost Volume Classification, Intelligent Interactive Volume Classification
body: AdaBoost Volume Classification is an interactive, data-driven method for multi-class segmentation of volumetric data using a framework of Error Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) and Discrete AdaBoost classifiers. It solves the problem of classifying multiple regions of interest on demand without requiring preprocessing or complex optimization procedures. Unlike graph cuts or random walker methods, it avoids segmentation dependencies among neighboring voxels, making it suitable for real-time applications and handling thinned or complex structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel model V^M of size dimx \times dimy \times dimz and a set of k training samples labeled by the user. Each training sample consists of a feature vector \rho and a ground truth label l(\rho). Output: A classification for every voxel in the volume, determining its optical properties (opacity and color) for rendering. Data Structures: 1. Feature Vector (\rho): An 8-dimensional vector for each voxel containing: Coordinates: x, y, z Density: d Gradient components: gx, gy, gz Gradient magnitude: |g| 2. Look Up Table (LUT) (L): A matrix of size 3 \times (|\rho| \times Wc) used to store the trained weak classifiers for GPU parallelization. |\rho| = 8 (feature dimensionality). Wc is the number of weak classifiers. In a one-versus-one ECOC design for N classes, Wc = N(N-1)/2. Row 1: Stores the weight cm for each weak classifier. The position i in this row corresponds to the feature index mod(i, |\rho|). The next weight for the same feature is at i + |\rho|. Positions for features not considered by a specific stump are set to zero. Row 2: Stores the polarity Pm for each weak classifier at column i. Row 3: Stores the threshold Tm for each weak classifier at column i. Algorithm Steps: 1. Training Stage (Discrete AdaBoost): The system trains binary classifiers for each dichotomy in the ECOC framework. 1. Initialize weights wi = 1/k for i = 1 \dots k. 2. For m = 1 to M (number of weak classifiers): a. Fit a weak classifier fm(\rho) \in \{-1, 1\} using the current weights wi on the training data. The weak classifier is a Decision Stump, fitting a threshold Tm and polarity Pm on a selected feature. b. Compute the weighted error: errm = Ew[1(l(\rho) \neq fm(\rho))]. c. Compute the classifier weight: cm = \log((1 - errm) / errm). d. Update sample weights: wi \leftarrow wi \cdot \exp[cm \cdot 1(l(\rhoi) \neq fm(\rhoi))] for i = 1 \dots k. e. Normalize wi so that \sumi wi = 1. 3. Output the final classifier: \text{sign}[\sum{m=1}^M cm fm(\rho)]. 2. LUT Construction: For each trained weak classifier (Decision Stump), store Pm and Tm in rows 2 and 3 of L at the column corresponding to the feature index used by that stump. Store cm in row 1. Positions for features not considered by a specific stump are set to zero. 3. Testing Stage (Classification): Applied to all voxels in the volume. The authors parallelized the training stage using a GPU-based implementation for rapid interaction. 1. Initialize F(\rho) = 0. 2. For m = 1 to M: a. Let \rhom be the value of the feature selected by the m-th weak classifier for the test sample \rho. b. Retrieve Pm and Tm from the LUT. c. Update F(\rho) = F(\rho) + cm \cdot (Pm \cdot \rhom < Pm \cdot Tm). 3. Output the label: \text{sign}(F(\rho)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainadaboost(trainingsamples, numclasses): """ trainingsamples: list of tuples (rho, label) rho: array of 8 floats [x, y, z, d, gx, gy, gz, |g|] label: integer class index numclasses: N """ k = len(trainingsamples) weights = [1.0 / k] k Wc = numclasses (numclasses - 1) // 2 weakclassifiers = [] M = 20 # Number of boosting rounds, not given in sources for m in range(M): bestfeatureidx, bestthreshold, bestpolarity, besterror = findbeststump(trainingsamples, weights) predictions = [] for rho, label in trainingsamples: val = rho[bestfeatureidx] if bestpolarity == 1: pred = 1 if val < bestthreshold else -1 else: pred = 1 if val >= bestthreshold else -1 predictions.append(pred) errm = sum(weights[i] for i in range(k) if predictions[i] != trainingsamples[i][1]) if errm <= 0 or errm >= 1: cm = 0.0 else: cm = math.log((1 - errm) / errm) weakclassifiers.append({ 'featureidx': bestfeatureidx, 'threshold': bestthreshold, 'polarity': bestpolarity, 'weight': cm }) for i in range(k): if predictions[i] != trainingsamples[i][1]: weights[i] = math.exp(cm) sumw = sum(weights) weights = [w / sumw for w in weights] return weakclassifiers def findbeststump(trainingsamples, weights): """Finds the decision stump (feature, threshold, polarity) minimizing weighted error.""" besterror = float('inf') bestfeatureidx = 0 bestthreshold = 0.0 bestpolarity = 1 for featidx in range(8): values = sorted(set(rho[featidx] for rho, in trainingsamples)) if len(values) < 2: continue thresholds = [(values[i] + values[i+1]) / 2.0 for i in range(len(values) - 1)] for thresh in thresholds: for pol in [1, -1]: error = 0.0 for i, (rho, label) in enumerate(trainingsamples): val = rho[featidx] pred = 1 if (pol val < pol thresh) else -1 if pred != label: error += weights[i] if error < besterror: besterror = error bestfeatureidx = featidx bestthreshold = thresh bestpolarity = pol return bestfeatureidx, bestthreshold, bestpolarity, besterror def classifyvolume(volumedata, weakclassifiers): """ volumedata: list of voxel objects with.features attribute (8 floats) weakclassifiers: list of dicts from training """ classifiedvolume = [] for voxel in volumedata: rho = voxel.features Frho = 0.0 for clf in weakclassifiers: Pm = clf['polarity'] Tm = clf['threshold'] cm = clf['weight'] rhom = rho[clf['featureidx']] condition = (Pm rhom < Pm Tm) contribution = cm condition Frho += contribution if Frho > 0: label = 1 elif Frho < 0: label = -1 else: label = 1 # Tie-breaking, not specified classifiedvolume.append(label) return classifiedvolume Parameters: Feature Vector \rho: 8 features (x, y, z, d, gx, gy, gz, |g|). Number of Weak Classifiers (Wc): Determined by the ECOC design. For N classes, Wc = N(N-1)/2 in one-versus-one design. Number of Boosting Rounds (M): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Indexing in LUT: The first row of L stores weights for features s \in [1..8]. Position i in row 1 corresponds to feature mod(i, |\rho|). The next weight for the same feature is at i + |\rho|. Precision: Floating point precision in the accumulation of F(\rho) may affect the sign decision in edge cases where F(\rho) \approx 0. Degenerate Input: If errm = 0 or errm = 1, the log term becomes undefined. The pseudocode handles this by setting cm = 0. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard AdaBoost training scales with O(M \cdot k \cdot |\rho|) per binary problem, and testing scales with O(M) per voxel. Memory Complexity: The LUT requires 3 \times |\rho| \times Wc storage. For N classes, Wc = N(N-1)/2. Performance: The authors parallelized the training stage using a GPU-based implementation for rapid interaction and classification. Strengths: No preprocessing required; interactive; handles thinned and complex structures better than probabilistic segmentation methods; no dependency on neighboring voxels. Limitations: Requires user-labeled training samples; performance depends on the quality and quantity of training data; multi-class extension relies on ECOC which increases the number of classifiers. When to use: Interactive volume visualization where users paint voxels on 2D slices to label samples. When not to use: When automatic, unsupervised segmentation is required; when real-time performance is critical and the number of classes is very large (increasing Wc). The method was proposed by S. Grau, A. Puig, S. Escalera, and M. Salamó from the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya, Universitat de Barcelona, and Centre de Visió per Computador, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona. It was published in 2013 as part of the Eurographics conference proceedings. The work extends previous data-driven and image-driven classification methods and addresses limitations of graph cuts and random walker methods which involve complex optimization and segmentation dependencies. Intelligent Interactive Volume Classification, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe.pg.pg2013short.023-028, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Two-stage k-means Streamline Clustering
head: Two-stage k-means Clustering
body: Two-stage k-means streamline clustering abstracts 3D vector fields by decomposing large streamline sets into coherent bundles and extracting representative paths for visualization. It solves visual clutter and high computational complexity by reducing raw streamline data to concise representative paths using low-dimensional feature vectors instead of full point clouds. Inputs: A set of generated streamlines from a 3D vector field. Outputs: A set of representative streamlines grouped into sub-bundles, ready for illustrative rendering (e.g., as streamtapes). Data Structures: Each streamline is mapped to a 1D feature vector. The method uses two distinct feature layouts: 1. Spatial Property Vector: A 9-component vector formed by concatenating the start, middle, and end points of the streamline. 2. Shape Property Vector: A 2-component vector containing Linear Entropy (EL) and Angular Entropy (EA). Feature Formulas: Shape properties quantify flow magnitude distribution and directional variation along the streamline. Linear Entropy (EL) measures information in flow magnitude: EL = - \frac{1}{\log2(m + 1)} \sum{j=1}^{m} \left( \frac{Dj}{LS} \right) \log2 \left( \frac{Dj}{LS} \right) Where: m is the number of streamline segments. Dj is the length of the j-th segment. LS = \sum{j=1}^{m} Dj is the total streamline length. Angular Entropy (EA) measures directional variation: EA = - \frac{1}{\log2(m)} \sum{j=1}^{m-1} \left( \frac{Aj}{LA} \right) \log2 \left( \frac{Aj}{LA} \right) Where: m is the number of streamline segments. Aj is the absolute angle at the j-th joint. LA = \sum{j=1}^{m-1} Aj is the total angular variation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Compute the 9D Spatial Property Vector and 2D Shape Property Vector for every input streamline. 2. Stage 1 Clustering: Partition all streamlines into p bundles using k-means with Lloyd’s algorithm on the Spatial Property Vectors. Each bundle contains streamlines with roughly coherent spatial layout. 3. Stage 2 Clustering: For each bundle i (i = 1 \dots p), partition it into qi sub-bundles using k-means on the Shape Property Vectors. The total cluster count is c = \sum{i=1}^{p} qi. 4. Representative Selection: Within each sub-bundle, compute the feature-space centroid, sort streamlines by Euclidean distance to the centroid, and select the closest streamline(s) as representatives. 5. Parameter Optimization (Optional): Determine optimal p and qi values using the elbow criterion, which identifies the cluster count where the percentage of variance explained (ratio of within-cluster variance to total variance) shows an abrupt change. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def norm(a): return math.sqrt(dot(a, a)) def dist(a, b): return norm([x - y for x, y in zip(a, b)]) def meanvec(vecs): return [sum(v[i] for v in vecs) / len(vecs) for i in range(len(vecs[0]))] def kmeanslloyd(data, k, maxiter=100): if k > len(data): k = len(data) centroids = data[:k] labels = [0] len(data) for in range(maxiter): newlabels = [] for d in data: bestc = min(range(k), key=lambda c: dist(d, centroids[c])) newlabels.append(bestc) if newlabels == labels: break labels = newlabels for c in range(k): clusterpoints = [data[i] for i in range(len(data)) if labels[i] == c] if clusterpoints: centroids[c] = meanvec(clusterpoints) return labels def computelinearentropy(segments): m = len(segments) if m == 0: return 0.0 LS = sum(segments) if LS == 0: return 0.0 entropy = sum((d / LS) math.log2(d / LS) for d in segments if d > 0) return - (1.0 / math.log2(m + 1)) entropy def computeangularentropy(angles): m = len(angles) if m == 0: return 0.0 LA = sum(angles) if LA == 0: return 0.0 entropy = sum((a / LA) math.log2(a / LA) for a in angles if a > 0) return - (1.0 / math.log2(m)) entropy def twostagekmeansclustering(streamlines, p, qlist=None): spatialfeats = [] shapefeats = [] for sl in streamlines: spatialfeats.append(sl.start + sl.middle + sl.end) shapefeats.append((computelinearentropy(sl.segments), computeangularentropy(sl.jointangles))) stage1labels = kmeanslloyd(spatialfeats, p) bundles = [[] for in range(p)] for idx, label in enumerate(stage1labels): bundles[label].append(idx) representatives = [] for i in range(p): bundleindices = bundles[i] bundleshape = [shapefeats[idx] for idx in bundleindices] qi = qlist[i] if qlist else 2 sublabels = kmeanslloyd(bundleshape, qi) for c in range(qi): subindices = [bundleindices[j] for j in range(len(bundleindices)) if sublabels[j] == c] if not subindices: continue centroid = meanvec([shapefeats[idx] for idx in subindices]) subindices.sort(key=lambda idx: dist(shapefeats[idx], centroid)) representatives.append(streamlines[subindices[0]]) return representatives Note: The sources do not provide the implementation details for the elbow criterion optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complexity: Standard k-means on line data has high complexity because lines are represented as vectors of original points. This method avoids that by using 5-component feature vectors (3 spatial points + 2 shape metrics). Degenerate Streamlines: If a streamline has zero length or zero angular variation, the logarithmic terms in entropy calculations may be undefined. Guard clauses (e.g., returning 0.0) are required. Parameter Selection: The choice of p and qi significantly affects the abstraction level. The elbow criterion is suggested but requires computing variance ratios for multiple cluster counts. Time Complexity: The complexity is determined by the number of streamlines N and the number of clusters. Since each streamline is reduced to a fixed-size feature vector (9 dimensions for Stage 1, 2 dimensions for Stage 2), the complexity is O(N \cdot K \cdot I) where K is the number of clusters and I is the number of iterations, rather than O(N \cdot L \cdot K \cdot I) where L is the number of points per streamline. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only stores the feature vectors and cluster assignments, not the full point clouds for all streamlines during clustering. Strengths: Efficiently decomposes large streamline sets into coherent bundles; reduces visual clutter; facilitates illustrative rendering (e.g., streamtapes). Limitations: Relies on the quality of the feature vectors; spatial clustering may group streamlines with different flow shapes if they share start/end points; shape clustering ignores spatial position. When to use: When visualizing complex 3D vector fields with many streamlines and needing a concise, illustrative representation. The method was introduced by Chen, Yan, Yu, Max, and Ma in 2011 in the paper "An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields". It was developed to address the limitations of existing vector field visualization techniques, which often assume no particular structure or require topological connectivity. The method builds on the concept of using entropy metrics (Linear and Angular Entropy) originally proposed by Furuya and Itoh. It is used in the context of illustrative visualization, specifically rendering streamlines as "streamtapes" to enhance depth perception and depict vicinity flow. name: CNN-feature based viewpoint selection
head: weighted probability voting for viewpoint selection
body: This method suggests the optimal viewpoint for features of interest in a given input volume and transfer function by considering the similarity between input features and features in a collected image set. It sets itself apart from image-based viewpoint selection models by separating viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation into distinct stages solved by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), rather than applying a single similarity measure to mix these stages. Inputs: Input volume V. Transfer function T. Pre-trained category classification network (AlexNet-based). Pre-trained viewpoint estimation network. Collected image set C = \{I1, I2, \dots, In\} for the determined category, where n = |C| is the number of collected images. Outputs: Optimal viewpoint parameters (camera position, orientation, tilt, background). Data Structures: Feature vectors f(\cdot) \in \mathbb{R}^{4096} extracted from the last hidden layer of the category classification network. Rendered image set S = \{R1, R2, \dots, Rk\} with k=40. Steps: 1. Category Determination: Render several images randomly from the input volume V using the provided transfer function T. Classify these rendered images through the category classification network. The most voted category among these images is considered the category of the volume. 2. Retrieve Collected Images: Obtain the collected image set C = \{I1, I2, \dots, In\} corresponding to the determined category. 3. Estimate Viewpoints for Collected Images: For each collected image Ii \in C, estimate its viewpoint vi using the viewpoint estimation network. 4. Generate Rendered Image Set: Render the input volume V with the provided transfer function T under the estimated viewpoint vi for each Ii. This rendering considers different camera-tilt angles and background colors to generate a rendered image set S = \{R1, R2, \dots, Rk\} with k=40 images. 5. Calculate Similarity: Calculate the similarity wi between the collected image Ii and the input volume (with transfer function) using the cosine distance of features from the last hidden layer of the category classification network. The feature vectors f(Rj) and f(Ii) are in \mathbb{R}^{4096}. The similarity is defined as: wi = \max{Rj \in S} \cos(f(Rj), f(Ii)) where \cos(a, b) denotes the cosine similarity between vectors a and b. 6. Compute Weighted Probability: Design an exponential similarity weight wi' by weighting the probability by its similarity with the input volume and transfer function: wi' = \exp\left((wi - 0.5) \cdot \frac{|C|}{10}\right) where |C| is the number of images in the collected image set. 7. Generate Voting Distribution: Sum up all weighted probability distributions (viewpoint probability distributions of Ii weighted by wi') to generate the voting probability distribution. 8. Select Optimal Viewpoint: Select the viewpoint with the largest probability from the summed distribution as the optimal viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cosinesimilarity(a, b): dot = sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) norma = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in a)) normb = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in b)) if norma == 0 or normb == 0: return 0.0 return dot / (norma normb) def cnnfeatureviewpointselection(volume, transferfunction, categorynet, viewpointnet, collectedimagesC): """ volume: Input volume data transferfunction: Transfer function T categorynet: Pre-trained AlexNet-based category classification network viewpointnet: Pre-trained viewpoint estimation network collectedimagesC: List of collected images Ii for the determined category Returns: Optimal viewpoint parameters """ # Step 1: Determine category # Render several random images from volume using transferfunction randomrenderedimages = [] for in range(5): # "several" images img = rendervolume(volume, transferfunction, randomviewpoint()) randomrenderedimages.append(img) # Classify these images categoryvotes = [] for img in randomrenderedimages: pred = categorynet.predict(img) categoryvotes.append(pred) # Most voted category is the volume's category volumecategory = max(set(categoryvotes), key=categoryvotes.count) # Step 2: Retrieve collected images C (already provided as input for this category) # C = collectedimagesC # Step 3 & 4: For each collected image, estimate viewpoint and render variations renderedsetsS = [] estimatedviewpointsv = [] for Ii in collectedimagesC: # Estimate viewpoint vi vi = viewpointnet.estimateviewpoint(Ii) estimatedviewpointsv.append(vi) # Render volume under vi with different tilt angles and background colors # k=40 images Si = [] for tilt in predefinedtiltangles(): for bg in predefinedbackgrounds(): R = rendervolume(volume, transferfunction, vi, tilt, bg) Si.append(R) renderedsetsS.append(Si) # Step 5: Calculate similarity wi for each collected image similaritiesw = [] for idx, Ii in enumerate(collectedimagesC): Si = renderedsetsS[idx] # Get feature vector for collected image from last hidden layer fIi = categorynet.extractfeatures(Ii) maxcossim = -1.0 for Rj in Si: fRj = categorynet.extractfeatures(Rj) cossim = cosinesimilarity(fRj, fIi) if cossim > maxcossim: maxcossim = cossim wi = maxcossim similaritiesw.append(wi) # Step 6: Compute weighted probability wi' n = len(collectedimagesC) weightedprobswprime = [] for wi in similaritiesw: wiprime = math.exp((wi - 0.5) (n / 10.0)) weightedprobswprime.append(wiprime) # Step 7: Generate voting distribution votingdistribution = {} for idx, Ii in enumerate(collectedimagesC): # Get viewpoint probability distribution for Ii # The source does not specify how this initial distribution is generated probdistIi = getviewpointprobabilitydistribution(Ii) wiprime = weightedprobswprime[idx] # Weight the distribution and accumulate for viewpoint, prob in probdistIi.items(): if viewpoint not in votingdistribution: votingdistribution[viewpoint] = 0.0 votingdistribution[viewpoint] += prob wiprime # Step 8: Select optimal viewpoint optimalviewpoint = max(votingdistribution, key=votingdistribution.get) return optimalviewpoint def rendervolume(volume, transferfunction, viewpoint, tilt=None, background=None): """Standard volume rendering operation.""" # Implementation depends on the rendering engine; returns a 2D image. pass def randomviewpoint(): """Generates a random camera viewpoint.""" pass def predefinedtiltangles(): """Returns a list of tilt angles to sample.""" return [0.0, 15.0, 30.0, 45.0] def predefinedbackgrounds(): """Returns a list of background colors to sample.""" return ["black", "white", "gray"] def getviewpointprobabilitydistribution(image): """Returns a dict mapping viewpoint identifiers to probabilities.""" # The source does not specify the exact generation method. # Typically derived from the viewpoint estimation network or stored metadata. return {} Parameters: k: Number of rendered images in set S, set to 40. Feature dimension: The features f(Rj) and f(Ii) are vectors in \mathbb{R}^{4096}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the availability of a pre-trained category classification network and viewpoint estimation network. The collected image set C must be representative of the determined category. The exponential weighting formula wi' = \exp((wi - 0.5) \cdot |C| / 10) assumes wi is in a range where this transformation is meaningful (cosine similarity is typically in [-1, 1]). Time Complexity: The method involves multiple CNN inferences (category classification, viewpoint estimation, feature extraction) and rendering operations. The complexity is dominated by the number of collected images |C| and the number of rendered variations k=40 per image. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the collected image set C, the rendered image sets S, and the feature vectors. Strengths: Separates viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation, allowing for more accurate similarity measurement based on CNN features. Considers the specific input volume and transfer function, unlike viewpoint preference analysis which suggests the same viewpoint for different features. Limitations: Requires pre-trained CNNs and a collected image set. Computationally expensive due to multiple renderings and CNN inferences. When to use: When an optimal viewpoint for specific features of interest in a volume is needed, and computational resources allow for CNN-based processing and multiple renderings. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and pre-computation is not feasible, or when no collected image set is available. Origin: Proposed in "CNNs Based Viewpoint Estimation for Volume Visualization". History: Inspired by similarity voting for viewpoint selection [38], this method improves upon it by separating viewpoint estimation and similarity calculation. Usage: Used in volume visualization to suggest optimal viewpoints for features of interest.
