name: Similarity-based Classification
body: Similarity-based classification determines optical properties by measuring the distance or agreement between a sample's feature vector and a reference set, rather than relying on absolute scalar thresholds. This family solves the problem of segmenting complex, high-dimensional, or semantically rich data where intensity alone is insufficient, by mapping spatial points to the nearest exemplar or by evaluating structural alignment. Unlike basic intensity-based methods, these techniques leverage geometric, spectral, or learned latent relationships to define classification boundaries. Builds on Data Feature-Based Classification. Projects high-dimensional function samples into scalar fields based on distance to exemplar functions, preserving spatial layout unlike MDS. Choose when segmenting hyperspectral or time-varying data by functional similarity. Measures angular agreement between feature vectors, factoring out magnitude. Choose when semantic content depends on direction (e.g., gradients) rather than intensity scale. Evaluates monotonic agreement between feature dimensions by computing Pearson correlation on ranks. Choose when data exhibits non-linear but order-preserving relationships. Evaluates the preservation of relational structure (manifold geometry) between latent spaces. Choose when verifying if a learned latent space captures the same representational organization as a reference. Retrieves transfer functions by matching high-level spatial semantics from co-planar images. Choose when differentiating segments with similar intensities but distinct shapes or textures. A discrete voxel classification technique for multidimensional signatures where users perform merge or bipartition operations on existing classes and define visual properties. Preprocessing establishes an initial classification based on voxel similarity criteria, which are also respected during rapid bipartition operations. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Automatically establish initial classification respecting voxel similarity criteria. 2. User performs merge or bipartition operations on classes. 3. User defines visual properties for each class. 4. Bipartition operations are executed rapidly, respecting similarity criteria. A self-supervised approach to spatiotemporal similarity learning using a Siamese neural network trained on a binary pretext task to predict spatial-temporal proximity, eliminating the need for labeled data. Steps: 1. Train a Siamese neural network on a binary pretext task: predict if two spatiotemporal patches originate from nearby locations in space and time. 2. Use the resulting latent space for similarity queries. 3. Users supply example patches as a query; S4 ranks the rest of the ensemble by learned similarity. A clustering algorithm to select a representative subset of particle trajectories to display as arrows, based on similarity of pathlines over three time steps. Steps: Select any pathline not already in a cluster to serve as the reference pathline. Examine all other pathlines not already in a cluster as candidates. If the similarity score between the reference pathline and the candidate pathline is less than a preset threshold, add the candidate to the cluster. After examining all candidates, output the reference pathline as the trajectory arrow for that cluster. Choose the next pathline not in a cluster and repeat the process. Filter out pathlines shorter than a preset threshold. Discard clusters that do not have a preset minimum number of pathlines. Similarity Metric: The sum of squared distances between particle positions at each time step in the three-time-step window. Parameters: Time Window: The number of time steps considered for trajectory similarity. Default: 3. Similarity Threshold: Determines cluster size. It is determined separately for each dataset based on distances between particles and can be changed interactively. A linear correlation coefficient across feature dimensions of latent vectors, probing per-dimension structure agreement. It measures stricter equivalence than cosine similarity by detecting poorly coordinated feature dimensions that high cosine similarity might miss. Formula: \rhoP = \frac{\sumk (z{render,k} - \bar{z}{render})(z{target,k} - \bar{z}{target})}{\sqrt{\sumk (z{render,k} - \bar{z}{render})^2} \sqrt{\sumk (z{target,k} - \bar{z}{target})^2}} where z{render,k} and z{target,k} are the k-th feature dimensions of the rendered and target latent vectors, and \bar{z} denotes their mean. Parameter: z{render}, z{target}: Latent vectors in \mathbb{R}^d. Comparison: Unlike cosine similarity which measures aggregate direction, Pearson correlation measures the coordination of individual feature dimensions. A gap between Pearson (\rhoP) and Spearman (\rhoS) indicates if mismatch is driven by outlier dimensions (large gap) or systematic non-linear warp (small gap). A method to identify target objects in a scene by computing cosine similarity between a user query embedding and pre-computed object embeddings. Steps: Generate a CLIP embedding E{query} for the user's natural language query. Identify objects corresponding to the highest similarity scores as the target of the user's query. Formula: S(E{query}, E{objecti}) = \frac{E{query} \cdot E{objecti}}{\|E{query}\| \cdot \|E{objecti}\|}, where S is the cosine similarity, E{query} is the query embedding, and E{objecti} is the embedding of the i-th object. A method to automatically position a new DVRI in a radial DVRI wheel based on its similarity to N primary DVRIs already positioned on the wheel boundary. Steps: Users manually choose and position primary DVRIs on the boundary of the DVRI wheel. Compute similarity values S1 \dots SN between the new DVRI and each of the N primary DVRIs. Compute the final position P using the weighted average formula based on similarities and primary positions. Formula: P = \frac{\sum{k=1}^N Sk \times Pk}{\sum{k=1}^N Sk}, where P is the final position of the DVRI in the wheel, N is the number of primary DVRIs, Pk is the position of primary DVRI k, and Sk is the similarity value between the DVRI and primary DVRI k. Similarity-based classification emerged from the need to handle multidimensional and semantically complex volume data where simple intensity thresholds fail. Early work focused on discrete classification of multidimensional signatures using voxel similarity criteria for rapid user interaction. The field expanded with self-supervised learning, such as S4, which uses Siamese networks to learn spatiotemporal proximity without labels. Recent extensions incorporate deep learning and natural language interfaces for semantic querying. In the context of neural rendering and latent space analysis, techniques like Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and correlation-based metrics (Pearson, Spearman) are used to decompose and probe latent spaces for editing and verification. name: Range-Space Segmentation
head: Function Field Visualization via Range-Space Segmentation, Function-space distance segmentation, Range-Space Segmentation Visualization
body: Range-Space Segmentation is a method for visualizing and analyzing function field data by projecting high-dimensional function samples into scalar fields based on their distance to a set of user-defined exemplar functions. It solves the problem of intelligently segmenting complex datasets (such as hyperspectral imagery or time-varying pollution data) by creating a classification field that assigns each spatial point to the nearest exemplar, thereby enabling feature-based visualization and surface extraction. Unlike multidimensional scaling (MDS) techniques which lose spatial layout, this method preserves the original spatial structure of the data while reducing the functional dimensionality to a scalar distance field and an integer label field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A function field F defined over a spatial domain \mathbb{R}^n, where each point \mathbf{p} has an associated function f\mathbf{p}. A set of m exemplar functions M = (f1, f2, \dots, fm) selected by the user (via probes, analytic definitions, or statistics). A similarity metric \|\cdot\|. Output: Two scalar fields defined on \mathbb{R}^n: 1. A multi-function scalar distance field S^, where S^(\mathbf{p}) is the minimum distance from f\mathbf{p} to any exemplar in M. 2. An integer-valued classification field L, where L(\mathbf{p}) is the index i of the exemplar fi \in M that minimizes the distance. Data Structures: Distance Field (S^): A scalar grid of size N (number of spatial points). Each element stores a floating-point value representing the minimal function-space distance. Classification Field (L): An integer grid of size N. Each element stores an integer index i \in \{1, \dots, m\}. Exemplar Set (M): A list of m function samples. Each sample fi is typically represented as a discrete vector of k values (e.g., spectral bands). Similarity Metric: The distance between two functions f and g is computed using a weighted norm. For a function f defined over a closed interval I with weight function w(x): \|f\| = \left( \intI w(x) f(x)^2 dx \right)^{1/2} For discrete functions represented by a sequence of k points (f1, \dots, fk) with weights (w1, \dots, wk): \|f\| = \left( \sum{j=1}^k wj fj^2 \right)^{1/2} The distance between two functions f and g is \|f - g\|. If weights are constant, this corresponds to a Voronoi tessellation in range-space. Algorithm Steps: 1. Define Metric: Select the similarity metric \|\cdot\| (e.g., weighted Euclidean, Earth Mover’s Distance). 2. Select Exemplars: Define the ordered set M = (f1, \dots, fm). Exemplars can be user-probed points f\mathbf{p}, analytic functions, or derived statistics. 3. Compute Single-Function Distance Fields: For each exemplar fi \in M and for each spatial point \mathbf{p}, compute the scalar distance field S{fi}: S{fi}(\mathbf{p}) = \| fi - f\mathbf{p} \| 4. Compute Multi-Function Distance Field (S^): For each point \mathbf{p}, find the minimum distance across all exemplars: S^(\mathbf{p}) = \min{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} S{fi}(\mathbf{p}) = \min{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} \| fi - f\mathbf{p} \| 5. Compute Classification Field (L): For each point \mathbf{p}, store the index of the exemplar that achieved the minimum distance: L(\mathbf{p}) = \arg \min{i \in \{1, \dots, m\}} \| fi - f\mathbf{p} \| 6. Visualization: Single Exemplar (m=1): Map S^ directly to color/opacity using a 1D transfer function. Multiple Exemplars (m>1): Associate a transfer function ti with each exemplar fi. The color at \mathbf{p} is determined by applying the transfer function corresponding to the classification label: \text{color}(\mathbf{p}) = t{L(\mathbf{p})}(S^(\mathbf{p})) 7. Feature Segmentation (Optional): Extract surfaces separating features by isosurfacing the classification field L. For m=2, use an isovalue of 0.5 with Marching Cubes. For m>2, use multi-label segmentation algorithms (e.g., multi-label Marching Cubes, Dual Contouring). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rangespacesegmentation(volumefunctions, exemplars, metricfunc): """ volumefunctions: List of functions fp for each spatial point p. Each fp is a vector/array of values. exemplars: List of m exemplar functions M = [f1,..., fm]. metricfunc: Function that computes ||f - g||. Returns: Sstar: List of minimal distances for each point. L: List of integer labels (1-based, matching mathematical definition). """ numpoints = len(volumefunctions) numexemplars = len(exemplars) # Initialize fields Sstar = [0.0] numpoints L = [0] numpoints # Precompute distances for all exemplars to optimize min/argmin # distances[i][p] = distance from exemplar i to point p distances = [[0.0] numpoints for in range(numexemplars)] for i in range(numexemplars): fi = exemplars[i] for p in range(numpoints): fp = volumefunctions[p] distances[i][p] = metricfunc(fi, fp) # Compute S and L for p in range(numpoints): mindist = float('inf') minidx = -1 for i in range(numexemplars): d = distances[i][p] if d < mindist: mindist = d minidx = i Sstar[p] = mindist # Convert 0-based index to 1-based to match mathematical definition L(p) = i L[p] = minidx + 1 return Sstar, L def visualizerangespace(Sstar, L, transferfunctions, numexemplars): """ Sstar: Minimal distance field. L: Classification field (integer labels, 1-based). transferfunctions: List of m transfer functions [t1,..., tm]. """ resultcolors = [] for p in range(len(Sstar)): label = L[p] # Ensure label is within bounds if label < 1 or label > numexemplars: label = 1 t = transferfunctions[label - 1] distanceval = Sstar[p] color = t(distanceval) resultcolors.append(color) return resultcolors Parameters: m: Number of exemplar functions. Typically large, leading to tens or hundreds of samples per data point. Transfer Functions: 1D transfer functions are standard for volume rendering, but 2D, multidimensional, or local transfer functions may be applied to emphasize local structures. Probes: User-specified points in the data domain \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n used to define exemplars f\mathbf{p}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voronoi Tessellation: If the weight function/vector is constant, the segmentation corresponds to a Voronoi tessellation of the range-space. Interactive Latency: When modifying a single function sample (e.g., repositioning a probe), only one of the m distance fields changes. The remaining m-1 fields remain unchanged. The latency experienced is S + S^, where S is the time to compute one single-function distance field and S^ is the time to combine all fields. Metric Choice: The choice of distance metric (e.g., weighted Euclidean, Earth Mover’s Distance, Chang’s spectral distance) significantly affects segmentation results. Feature Query is a method for identifying spatial regions in a function fields where 1-dimensional functions are similar to a user-defined exemplar. It solves the problem of intelligently paring down large scientific datasets by identifying regions of interest based on user-specified selection queries, allowing for the analysis of smaller, more meaningful subsets rather than processing the entire dataset. Unlike traditional visualization which processes the whole dataset, this approach constrains computational complexity to the number of items returned by a query. Time Complexity: Computing the distance field for one exemplar takes time S. Combining m fields to produce S^ and L takes time S^. Total generation time is proportional to m \times S + S^. Memory Complexity: Requires storing m distance fields temporarily or computing them on the fly, plus the final S^ and L fields. Measured Performance: On an Apple MacBook Pro (2.33 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo, 2 GB memory, ATI Radeon X1600): Hyperspectral Imagery segmentation: 336 ms total (80 ms for S, 16 ms for S^). H2O Aerosol (National): 51 ms total (20 ms for S, 11 ms for S^). SO4 Aerosol (CRPAQS): 104 ms total (27 ms for S, 23 ms for S^). Strengths: Preserves original spatial layout (unlike MDS); allows interactive exploration via probes; supports time-varying fields by treating probes as points in \mathbb{R}^n \times T. Limitations: Performance scales with the number of exemplars m; requires careful selection of distance metric and exemplars. When to Use: Ideal for hyperspectral imagery and particulate pollution data where functional similarity is more important than spatial proximity. Range-Space Segmentation was introduced in the context of scientific visualization for function field data, specifically for hyperspectral imagery and time-varying particulate pollution data (CRPAQS). The method was developed to address the limitations of dimension reduction and clustering techniques that either lose spatial information or require fragile high-dimensional queries. It builds on the concept of function-space distance metrics and Voronoi tessellations in range-space. name: Feature Query
head: Function Field Feature Query, Range Query
body: Feature Query identifies spatial regions in a function field where 1-dimensional functions are similar. It pares down large scientific datasets by identifying regions of interest via user-specified selection queries, constraining computational complexity to the number of returned items rather than processing the whole dataset. Inputs and Outputs Input: A dataset containing m samples per function, where each spatial point p has an associated 1-dimensional function f^p. Output: A binary mask or subset of spatial points p that satisfy the query constraints. Data Structures The query is defined by a set of constraints over a closed interval I. The specific layout includes three modifiable curves: 1. Minimum Constraint Curve: Defines the lower bound for each sample index. 2. Maximum Constraint Curve: Defines the upper bound for each sample index. 3. Sample Weights Curve: Defines the importance of each sample index. Control points for these curves can be added, removed, and manipulated by the user. Algorithm Steps 1. Exploration: The user explores the function field using distance field renderings to identify potential features. 2. Constraint Definition: The user sketches a pair of curves to define the feature query's minimum and maximum constraints. Let Qi be the minimum-maximum interval constraint for sample index i, where i = 1, \dots, m. 3. Evaluation: For each point p in the dataset with function f^p, evaluate the condition: f^pi \in Qi \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, m\} A point p is part of the feature if and only if its function value at every sample index i falls within the corresponding interval Qi. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def featurequery(dataset, m, mincurve, maxcurve): """ dataset: List of point objects, each with a.function attribute (list of m floats). m: Number of samples per function. mincurve: Callable or list returning the lower bound Qmin[i] for sample index i. maxcurve: Callable or list returning the upper bound Qmax[i] for sample index i. Returns: List of point objects that satisfy the query constraints. """ matchingpoints = [] # Pre-calculate constraint intervals for all sample indices # Qi corresponds to the closed interval [Qmin[i], Qmax[i]] constraints = [] for i in range(m): qmin = mincurve(i) if callable(mincurve) else mincurve[i] qmax = maxcurve(i) if callable(maxcurve) else maxcurve[i] constraints.append((qmin, qmax)) for point in dataset: ismatch = True for i in range(m): fi = point.function[i] qmin, qmax = constraints[i] # Check if f^pi is within the closed interval Qi if not (qmin <= fi <= qmax): ismatch = False break if ismatch: matchingpoints.append(point) return matchingpoints Parameters m: The number of samples per function in the dataset. Qi: The minimum-maximum interval constraint for sample i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The constraints are defined over closed intervals, so implementation must handle floating-point comparisons carefully to ensure boundary inclusion matches the mathematical definition f^pi \in Qi. Degenerate Input: If the minimum curve exceeds the maximum curve at any index i, the interval Qi is empty, and no points will match for that index. Time Complexity: The computational complexity is constrained to the number of items returned by the query, rather than the size of the entire dataset. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tested on a 2.6 GHz Mobile Pentium 4-M laptop with 1.0 GB RAM and nVidia GeForce 4200 Go graphics card: Hyperspectral image query execution times were 320ms (Water), 218ms (Golf Courses), 257ms (Evaporation Ponds), and 23ms (High SO4 Concentration). Distance fields were generated at ~6 per second for hyperspectral images and ~25 per second for CRPAQS. Strengths: Allows for the extraction of reusable query constraints across multiple datasets and enables rapid identification and visualization of regions of interest. Limitations: Performance depends on the number of samples m and the dataset size during the initial exploration phase (distance field generation). When to use/not: Use when intelligently paring down large scientific datasets to analyze smaller, meaningful subsets is required; avoid when processing the entire dataset simultaneously is necessary. The concept of coupling visualization with high-performance query technology was first presented by Stockinger et al., who introduced the DEX software system utilizing the FastBit indexing infrastructure to identify regions of interest. Feature Query applies these Query-Driven Visualization (QDV) techniques specifically to extract features from function fields. The method was evaluated on datasets including AVIRIS hyperspectral images of Moffett Field and the San Francisco Bay area, and air quality simulations from the California Regional Particulate Air Quality Study (CRPAQS). name: Cosine Similarity
head: Cosine Similarity on Unit Hypersphere
body: Cosine similarity measures the angular agreement between two vectors by computing the inner product of their L2-normalized forms, effectively factoring out magnitude variations to focus on directional information. In volume rendering classification, this allows transfer functions to distinguish semantic content based on the orientation of feature vectors (e.g., gradients or latent codes) rather than their scalar intensity or norm, which may be affected by scale or activation statistics. It is distinct from magnitude-dependent methods and correlation-based methods like Pearson or Spearman, which assess linear or monotonic agreement across individual feature dimensions rather than global direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two feature vectors \mathbf{z}{\text{render}}, \mathbf{z}{\text{target}} \in \mathbb{R}^d associated with a sample point \mathbf{x} in the volume. Output: A similarity score sim \in [-1, 1], representing the cosine of the angle between the vectors. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{z} are dense arrays of floating-point numbers of dimension d. No additional lookup tables or textures are required; the computation is algebraic. Steps: 1. Compute the squared L2 norm for each vector by summing the squares of its components. 2. Take the square root of the sum to obtain the L2 norm. 3. Divide each component of the original vectors by their respective L2 norm plus a stability constant \epsilon to obtain normalized vectors on the unit hypersphere. 4. Compute the dot product of the two normalized vectors. 5. Return the dot product as the similarity score. Formulas: L2 norm: \|\mathbf{z}\|2 = \sqrt{\sum{k=1}^d zk^2}. Normalization map: \hat{\mathbf{z}} = \phi(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{\mathbf{z}}{\|\mathbf{z}\|2 + \epsilon}, where \phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to S^{d-1} maps to the unit hypersphere. Similarity: sim = \hat{\mathbf{z}}{\text{render}}^\top \hat{\mathbf{z}}{\text{target}} = \cos \theta, where \theta is the angle between the original vectors. Parameters: \epsilon: A small positive constant added for numerical stability in the denominator. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Vectors: If a feature vector is zero, the L2 norm is zero. The addition of \epsilon ensures the denominator is non-zero, resulting in a normalized vector of zeros, which yields a similarity of 0 against any other vector. Dimensionality: The method assumes vectors are in the same space \mathbb{R}^d. Mismatched dimensions are undefined. A pairwise cosine similarity metric normalized per query to remove encoder-specific global structure, averaged by class pair to summarize within-class and between-class affinity. It computes a query-wise normalized affinity a{ij} for every non-self pair using the mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma of the non-self gallery for each query, then averages a{ij} by class pair. This normalization ensures that zero denotes the query-specific gallery average, not absolute similarity, revealing stronger class-relative organization in the feature space. Parameters include an embedding dimension of 768 and query-wise normalization using gallery statistics. Time Complexity: O(d) per pair, where d is the vector dimension. The normalization and dot product are linear in dimensionality. Memory Complexity: O(d) to store the vectors. No auxiliary structures like LUTs are needed for the core calculation. Strengths: Scale-invariant; robust to variations in vector magnitude caused by activation statistics or training dynamics. Focuses on directional semantic content. Limitations: Ignores magnitude information, which may be relevant in some physical contexts. Sensitive to the dimensionality d; high-dimensional spaces may suffer from the "curse of dimensionality" where distances become less discriminative. When to use: When feature vectors encode semantic content primarily through orientation (e.g., deep latent representations) rather than norm. When not to use: When magnitude carries critical information (e.g., density magnitude in some physical simulations) or when linear correlation across dimensions is more important than global direction (use Pearson/Spearman instead). The method is applied in probing vision models for 3D scene understanding using differentiable rendering. It is used to handle latent representations from deep networks where semantic content is encoded by vector orientation rather than norm, which can be affected by scale or training dynamics. The method maps vectors to S^{d-1} via L2-normalization and computes the inner product, which corresponds to \cos \theta. It is contrasted with Pearson and Spearman correlations, which assess agreement across individual feature dimensions rather than global direction. name: Spearman Correlation
head: Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficient, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
body: Spearman Correlation is a similarity-based classification method that evaluates the monotonic agreement between feature dimensions by computing the Pearson correlation on the ranks of the entries. Unlike Pearson correlation, which measures linear correlation, Spearman measures rank agreement, making it robust to non-linear but order-preserving distortions. It is used in volume rendering to classify data based on the relative ordering of features rather than their absolute linear relationships. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two feature vectors, \mathbf{z}{render} and \mathbf{z}{target}, each of dimension d. These vectors represent the feature values at a specific spatial location or across a set of samples. Output: The Spearman rank correlation coefficient, \rhoS, a scalar value in [-1, 1]. Data Structures: The method operates on arrays of floating-point numbers representing feature values. Ranks are typically stored as integers or floats in an array of size d. Steps: 1. Rank Transformation: Replace each value in \mathbf{z}{render} and \mathbf{z}{target} with its rank within its respective vector. Let R(\mathbf{z}) denote the vector of ranks. The rank of a value is its position when the vector is sorted in ascending order. Ties are typically handled by assigning the average rank of the tied values. 2. Compute Pearson Correlation on Ranks: Calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient between the rank-transformed vectors R(\mathbf{z}{render}) and R(\mathbf{z}{target}). Formula: Let r{i} be the rank of the i-th element in \mathbf{z}{render} and s{i} be the rank of the i-th element in \mathbf{z}{target}. Let \bar{r} and \bar{s} be the mean ranks. The Spearman correlation coefficient \rhoS is defined as: \rhoS = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{d} (ri - \bar{r})(si - \bar{s})}{\sqrt{\sum{i=1}^{d} (ri - \bar{r})^2} \sqrt{\sum{i=1}^{d} (si - \bar{s})^2}} Alternatively, if there are no ties, it can be computed using the sum of squared rank differences Di = ri - si: \rhoS = 1 - \frac{6 \sum{i=1}^{d} Di^2}{d(d^2 - 1)} The simple formula using Di^2 is an approximation that becomes less accurate with many ties. Parameters: d: The dimensionality of the feature vectors. Typical values depend on the feature space (e.g., number of spectral channels, gradient components). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ties: If feature values are identical, their ranks must be averaged. The general Pearson-on-ranks formula is preferred for robustness. Constant Vectors: If all values in a vector are identical, the variance is zero, and the correlation is undefined. Monotonicity: Spearman correlation detects monotonic relationships. It will be 1 if one variable is a strictly increasing function of the other, regardless of the specific non-linear mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getranks(values): """ Computes ranks for a list of values, handling ties by averaging. Returns 1-based ranks as floats. """ n = len(values) if n == 0: return [] # Create list of (value, originalindex) indexedvalues = [(v, i) for i, v in enumerate(values)] # Sort by value indexedvalues.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) ranks = [0.0] n i = 0 while i < n: # Find the range of ties j = i while j < n and indexedvalues[j][0] == indexedvalues[i][0]: j += 1 # Average rank for the tied group (1-based) avgrank = (i + 1 + j) / 2.0 for k in range(i, j): originalindex = indexedvalues[k][1] ranks[originalindex] = avgrank i = j return ranks def spearmancorrelation(zrender, ztarget): """ Computes the Spearman rank correlation coefficient between two feature vectors. Args: zrender (list[float]): Feature values from the rendered volume. ztarget (list[float]): Feature values from the target/reference volume. Returns: float: Spearman correlation coefficient. """ n = len(zrender) if n != len(ztarget): raise ValueError("Vectors must have the same length") if n < 2: return 0.0 # Undefined for single point, return 0 as default # Step 1: Rank transformation ranksrender = getranks(zrender) rankstarget = getranks(ztarget) # Step 2: Compute Pearson correlation on ranks meanr = sum(ranksrender) / n means = sum(rankstarget) / n numerator = 0.0 denomr = 0.0 denoms = 0.0 for i in range(n): ri = ranksrender[i] si = rankstarget[i] diffr = ri - meanr diffs = si - means numerator += diffr diffs denomr += diffr 2 denoms += diffs 2 denominator = (denomr denoms) 0.5 if denominator == 0: return 0.0 # Undefined if variance is zero return numerator / denominator A statistical method to determine if the association between cross-seed instability (\sigma{ens}) and ensemble mean error (\epsilon{mean}) persists after controlling for an oracle inverse-emissivity proxy (\bar{E}), treating low-emissivity regions as a signal-strength confound. It is chosen when one needs to isolate the rank-based relationship between two variables by removing the influence of a third confounding variable. The method involves rank-transforming all three variables and computing the standard partial Pearson correlation on the ranks. The formula is: \rho(\sigma{ens}, \epsilon{mean} | \bar{E}) = \frac{\rho(\sigma{ens}, \epsilon{mean}) - \rho(\sigma{ens}, \bar{E})\rho(\bar{E}, \epsilon{mean})}{\sqrt{(1 - \rho^2(\sigma{ens}, \bar{E}))(1 - \rho^2(\bar{E}, \epsilon{mean}))}} A strong positive partial correlation indicates a nontrivial linear association between the rank-transformed \sigma{ens} and \epsilon{mean}, after linear adjustment for the rank-transformed \bar{E} proxy. A pitfall is that mismatch conditions intentionally retain the nominal, unscaled Ground Truth (GT) emissivity for \bar{E} to ensure it remains an oracle probe of the underlying physical signal rather than an observation-consistent proxy. The method is evaluated on a 30×18×8 longitude-latitude-radius grid, with radial coordinates spanning 1.05-3 R⊙. Time Complexity: O(d \log d) due to the sorting step required for rank transformation, where d is the feature dimension. The subsequent Pearson correlation is O(d). Memory Complexity: O(d) to store the rank vectors. Strengths: Robust to non-linear monotonic relationships. Does not assume linearity or normality of the data distribution. Effective when the relationship between features is consistent in order but not in magnitude. Limitations: Less powerful than Pearson correlation if the relationship is truly linear and the data is normally distributed. Sensitive to ties. Does not capture non-monotonic relationships (e.g., U-shaped). When to use: When the feature dimensions have a monotonic but potentially non-linear relationship, or when the data contains outliers that would distort linear correlation. When not to use: When the relationship is known to be linear and Gaussian, or when non-monotonic relationships are of interest. Spearman correlation is a rank-based correlation coefficient introduced by Charles Spearman. In the context of volume rendering and 3D scene understanding, it is used as a metric to probe vision models by comparing rendered features against target features. It is distinct from cosine similarity (which measures direction) and Pearson correlation (which measures linear co-variation). It probes a stricter notion of equivalence than cosine, as a reconstruction can align in aggregate direction (high cosine) yet have poorly coordinated feature dimensions (low Pearson). The gap between Pearson and Spearman correlation can indicate whether a mismatch is driven by outlier dimensions or systematic non-linear warps. name: Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)
body: Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) evaluates the quality of a learned latent space by comparing the relational structure (manifold geometry) of two sets of representations against each other. Unlike pointwise similarity measures that assess individual latent codes in isolation, RSA assesses whether the pairwise similarity structure across an entire set of views is preserved. Inputs: Two sets of latent vectors representing the same N views. Let m \in \{1, 2\} denote the two representational spaces. For each view i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, let zi^{(m)} \in \mathbb{R}^{dm} be the latent vector produced by model gm for input xi. Outputs: A scalar RSA score \rho{RSA}, which is the Pearson correlation coefficient between the dissimilarity structures of the two spaces. Data Structures: Latent Vectors: zi^{(m)} of dimension dm. Normalized Vectors: \hat{z}i^{(m)} of dimension dm. Representational Similarity Matrix (RSM): S^{(m)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}. Dissimilarity Matrix: D^{(m)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}. Steps: 1. L2-Normalization: Map each latent vector onto the unit hypersphere to ensure scale invariance. For each i and m: \hat{z}i^{(m)} = \frac{zi^{(m)}}{\|zi^{(m)}\|2 + \epsilon} where \epsilon is a small constant to prevent division by zero. 2. Construct RSM: For each representational space m, compute the pairwise cosine similarities between all normalized latent vectors. The entry S{ij}^{(m)} is defined as: S{ij}^{(m)} = k(\hat{z}i^{(m)}, \hat{z}j^{(m)}) = (\hat{z}i^{(m)})^\top \hat{z}j^{(m)} where k(a, b) = a^\top b is the dot product, serving as the cosine similarity since vectors are normalized. 3. Compute Dissimilarity Matrix: Convert the similarity matrix to a dissimilarity matrix D^{(m)} using: D{ij}^{(m)} = 1 - S{ij}^{(m)} This transforms the similarity metric into a distance-like metric where higher values indicate greater dissimilarity. 4. Vectorize Upper Triangular Entries: Extract the off-diagonal entries from the upper triangular part of both dissimilarity matrices. Let \text{vec}{\triangle}(\cdot) denote this operation. This yields two vectors of length N(N-1)/2. 5. Calculate RSA Score: Compute the Pearson correlation coefficient between the vectorized dissimilarity matrices: \rho{RSA} = \text{corr}(\text{vec}{\triangle} D^{(1)}, \text{vec}{\triangle} D^{(2)}) A high \rho{RSA} indicates that pairs of views that are similar (or dissimilar) in one latent space tend to be similarly related in the other, implying the two spaces encode a similar representational structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def representationalsimilarityanalysis(z1, z2, epsilon=1e-8): """ Compute the RSA score between two sets of latent vectors. Args: z1: numpy array of shape (N, d1), latent vectors for space 1. z2: numpy array of shape (N, d2), latent vectors for space 2. epsilon: small constant for numerical stability. Returns: rhorsa: float, the Pearson correlation coefficient of dissimilarity matrices. """ N = z1.shape[0] # Step 1: L2-Normalization norms1 = np.linalg.norm(z1, axis=1, keepdims=True) z1hat = z1 / (norms1 + epsilon) norms2 = np.linalg.norm(z2, axis=1, keepdims=True) z2hat = z2 / (norms2 + epsilon) # Step 2: Construct RSM (Cosine Similarity) S1 = np.dot(z1hat, z1hat.T) S2 = np.dot(z2hat, z2hat.T) # Step 3: Compute Dissimilarity Matrix D1 = 1.0 - S1 D2 = 1.0 - S2 # Step 4: Vectorize upper triangular (off-diagonal) entries idxi, idxj = np.triuindices(N, k=1) vecD1 = D1[idxi, idxj] vecD2 = D2[idxi, idxj] # Step 5: Calculate Pearson correlation meanD1 = np.mean(vecD1) meanD2 = np.mean(vecD2) diffD1 = vecD1 - meanD1 diffD2 = vecD2 - meanD2 cov = np.mean(diffD1 diffD2) stdD1 = np.sqrt(np.mean(diffD12)) stdD2 = np.sqrt(np.mean(diffD22)) if stdD1 == 0 or stdD2 == 0: return 0.0 rhorsa = cov / (stdD1 stdD2) return rhorsa Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in normalization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Autocorrelation in Training Trajectories: RSA collapses across all views into a single scalar per epoch, resulting in strong autocorrelation in the training trajectory. Statistical Testing Error: Treating training steps as independent observations for statistical testing (e.g., calculating Bayes factors) would inflate the effective sample size and yield spuriously decisive evidence. RSA scores should not be used for per-step statistical inference in the same way as per-view metrics. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: It provides a global perspective on the latent space geometry, ensuring that the relational structure is preserved, which is crucial when reconstructing a latent space. Limitations: It is a global metric and does not provide pointwise error estimates. When to use: When evaluating reconstructed latent spaces where the goal is to preserve the manifold structure of the data. When not to use: When pointwise accuracy of individual latent codes is the primary concern, or when performing statistical hypothesis testing on training dynamics due to autocorrelation issues. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) is used in the context of differentiable rendering and latent space evaluation to assess whether a reconstructed latent space captures the same representational organization as a ground-truth space. It complements pointwise similarity measures by focusing on the geometry of the manifold induced over a set of views. name: CNN-based Image Retrieval
head: AlexNet retrieval, CNN-Based Image Matching, Image retrieval compartment
body: This method retrieves transfer functions from a knowledge database by matching high-level spatial semantics extracted from co-planar images along a ray, rather than relying solely on 1D intensity profiles. It solves the problem of differentiating Segments of Interest (SOIs) that share similar intensity values but differ in shape, texture, or spatial relationships. Unlike sibling methods that use local intensity statistics, this approach leverages deep learning to capture regional image semantics. Inputs: TIQ (Transfer Function Input Query): A set of images extracted from the volume along a specific ray, containing two co-planar images aligned with primary axes and the 1D intensity profile along the ray. Knowledge Database: A collection of pre-labeled medical volume datasets, each associated with a known transfer function and its corresponding TIQ representation. Outputs: Retrieved Transfer Function: The transfer function associated with the most similar image pair in the database. Optical Properties: Opacity (\alpha) and Color (C) values derived from the retrieved transfer function, applied to the volume samples. Data Structures: Image Pair: Two 2D images (I1, I2) extracted from the volume, aligned with primary axes, with resolution 224 \times 224 pixels. Feature Vector: A 4096-dimensional vector \mathbf{f} extracted from the FC7 layer of the AlexNet network. Database Index: A mapping from image pairs to their corresponding transfer functions and feature vectors. Algorithm Steps: 1. Image Extraction: Extract two co-planar images along the ray from the TIQ. 2. Feature Extraction: Pass each image through a pre-trained AlexNet network to produce a 4096-dimensional feature vector. 3. Similarity Measurement: Compare each query image with the corresponding database image aligned with the same primary axes, calculating the Euclidean distance between their CNN feature vectors. D(\mathbf{f}{query}, \mathbf{f}{db}) = \|\mathbf{f}{query} - \mathbf{f}{db}\|2 4. Retrieval: Identify the top N database entries with the smallest Euclidean distances. 5. Re-ranking: Re-rank the top N results based on the similarity of 1D intensity profiles using Dynamic Time Warping to refine the selection. 6. Transfer Function Application: Retrieve the transfer function associated with the best-matching database entry and apply it to the volume samples along the ray to determine opacity and color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cnnbasedimageretrieval(queryimages, database, alexnetmodel): """ queryimages: List of two 2D arrays (224x224), representing co-planar images along a ray. database: List of tuples (dbimages, dbtf, dbfeatures), where dbimages is a list of two arrays, dbtf is the transfer function, and dbfeatures is the 4096-dim feature vector. alexnetmodel: Pre-trained AlexNet model, outputting 4096-dim features from FC7. Returns: besttf: The transfer function from the best matching database entry. """ queryfeatures = [] for img in queryimages: processed = preprocessimage(img) feat = alexnetmodel.forwardfc7(processed) queryfeatures.append(feat) distances = [] for dbentry in database: dbimages, dbtf, dbfeatures = dbentry totaldist = 0.0 for qfeat, dbfeat in zip(queryfeatures, dbfeatures): totaldist += euclideandistance(qfeat, dbfeat) avgdist = totaldist / len(queryfeatures) distances.append((avgdist, dbtf)) distances.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Re-rank top N results using Dynamic Time Warping on 1D intensity profiles return distances[0][1] def preprocessimage(image): # Standard AlexNet preprocessing: resize to 224x224, normalize to ImageNet mean/std resized = resizeto224(image) mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] std = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225] h, w, c = len(resized), len(resized[0]), len(resized[0][0]) normalized = [[(resized[i][j][k] - mean[k]) / std[k] for k in range(c)] for j in range(w) for i in range(h)] return normalized def resizeto224(image): # Bilinear interpolation to 224x224 h, w = len(image), len(image[0]) scaleh, scalew = h / 224.0, w / 224.0 resized = [[image[int(i scaleh)][int(j scalew)] for j in range(224)] for i in range(224)] return resized def euclideandistance(v1, v2): return sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) 0.5 Parameters: Network: AlexNet, pre-trained on 1.2 million natural images from ImageNet. Feature Dimension: 4096 (from FC7 layer). Input Resolution: 224 \times 224 pixels. Similarity Metric: Euclidean Distance (ED). Top N: Number of retrieval results to consider (value not specified in sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Domain Gap: AlexNet is trained on natural images; deeper networks (GoogleNet, ResNet) yield lower recall on medical data due to overfitting to general image features. Intensity Differentiation: CNN features successfully differentiate SOIs with similar intensity values, which intensity profile retrieval alone cannot achieve. Alignment: Images must be aligned with the same primary axes for valid comparison. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieved an average recall of 0.719 on medical images, outperforming GoogleNet and ResNet. Strengths: Provides regional image semantics (shapes, textures, spatial relationships), enabling differentiation of SOIs with similar intensity values. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to CNN inference; requires a pre-labeled knowledge database. When to Use: When SOIs have similar intensity profiles but distinct spatial structures or textures (e.g., artery vs. kidney in CT scans). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Proposed by Younhyun Jung et al. in "A Transfer Function Design for Medical Volume Data Using a Knowledge Database Based on Deep Image and Primitive Intensity Profile Features Retrieval" (2024). Development: Builds upon earlier work using 1D intensity profile retrieval (DTW). Developed to address limitations of intensity-only retrieval, which fails to distinguish SOIs with similar intensity values but different spatial characteristics. Usage: Applied in medical volume visualization for automatic transfer function design, specifically for segmenting organs like liver, bone, kidney, and spleen. A Transfer Function Design for Medical Volume Data Using a Knowledge Database Based on Deep Image and Primitive Intensity Profile Features Retrieval, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11390-024-3419-7, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Local Histogram-based Classification Probability
head: Classification Probability (Local Histogram-based Tissue Separation), neighborhood histogram classification
body: Local Histogram-based Classification Probability is a method for separating overlapping tissues in volume rendering by using local histogram range weights as a second attribute alongside intensity. It allows a 2D Transfer Function to distinguish materials with identical intensity values but different neighborhood contexts, such as vessels and spongy bone in CT angiographies. Unlike standard intensity-based classification, this method computes a signed classification certainty P derived from the narrowness of local intensity distributions, enabling the separation of materials that are indistinguishable by scalar value alone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (typically 12-bit precision) and a set of n classification criteria \Phii, where each criterion defines a target intensity range (e.g., the mutual range of all vessels or range of muscle tissue). Output: A classification probability P \in [-1.0, 1.0] stored alongside the voxel intensity, used to modulate opacity or color in the transfer function. Data Structures: The method utilizes a 12-bit voxel data layout where the top 4 bits store the classification probability P and the lower 8 bits store the original intensity value. This exploits unused precision in 12-bit datasets. For histogram computation, the volume is processed using block neighborhoods. The block size is 8^3 voxels. Histograms are simplified into 12 piece-wise constant segments with a minimum width of 10 to preserve peak shapes efficiently. Parameters: \Phii: The intensity range defining criterion i (e.g., the mutual range of all vessels or range of muscle tissue). w{Ai}, w{Bi}: Confidence levels for criterion i. w{Ai} is the range weight where classification as material A is confident, and w{Bi} is the range weight where classification as material B is confident. These values are not restricted to [0, 1]. \lambdai: Weight for criterion i in the final sum. The paper uses equal weighting \lambdai = 1/n such that \sum \lambdai = 1. Block Size: 8^3 voxels. Steps: 1. Compute Local Histograms: For each voxel, compute the local histogram of intensities within its neighborhood. The neighborhood is defined by double block neighborhoods, where interpolation weights c1 and c2 are determined by the inverse distance to the center of each block (d1, d2) such that c1 + c2 = 1 and c1/c2 = d2/d1. The histogram is simplified into 12 piece-wise constant segments. 2. Calculate Range Weight wr(\Phii): For each criterion \Phii, calculate the range weight wr(\Phii), which represents the "narrowness" or density of the local histogram within the range \Phii. 3. Compute Individual Certainty pi: For each criterion i, calculate the mean \mui and delta \deltai of the confidence levels: \mui = \frac{w{Ai} + w{Bi}}{2} \deltai = \frac{w{Bi} - w{Ai}}{2} Then, calculate the signed classification certainty pi using the clamping function C2 (clamping to [-2.0, 2.0]): pi = C2\left( \frac{wr(\Phii) - \mui}{\deltai} \right) The sign of pi denotes the most likely tissue (e.g., negative for large vessels), and the magnitude denotes confidence. 4. Compute Total Probability P: Calculate the weighted sum of individual certainties and clamp the result to [-1.0, 1.0] using function C1: P = C1\left( \sum{i=1}^n \lambdai pi \right) where \sum \lambdai = 1. 5. Store Result: Pack P into the top 4 bits of the 12-bit voxel data, leaving the lower 8 bits for intensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeclassificationprobability(volume, criteria, blocksize=8): """ Computes local histogram-based classification probability for a volume. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel intensities (12-bit), shape (depth, height, width). criteria: List of tuples (Phistart, Phiend, wA, wB) for each tissue type. blocksize: Size of the block neighborhood (default 8). Returns: P: 3D array of classification probabilities in [-1.0, 1.0]. """ depth, height, width = volume.shape P = [[[0.0] width for in range(height)] for in range(depth)] ncriteria = len(criteria) if ncriteria == 0: return P for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): localhist = getsimplifiedhistogram(volume, x, y, z, blocksize) totalcertainty = 0.0 for Phistart, Phiend, wA, wB in criteria: wr = calculaterangeweight(localhist, Phistart, Phiend) mu = (wA + wB) / 2.0 delta = (wB - wA) / 2.0 if delta == 0: pi = 0.0 else: rawp = (wr - mu) / delta pi = clamp(rawp, -2.0, 2.0) totalcertainty += pi / ncriteria P[z][y][x] = clamp(totalcertainty, -1.0, 1.0) return P def clamp(value, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(value, maxval)) def getsimplifiedhistogram(volume, x, y, z, blocksize): # Standard histogram computation over the neighborhood. # The paper uses a piece-wise constant simplification with 12 segments # and a minimum width of 10, but does not detail the exact algorithm. hist = [0.0] 256 half = blocksize // 2 for dz in range(-half, half + 1): for dy in range(-half, half + 1): for dx in range(-half, half + 1): nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if 0 <= nx < volume.shape[2] and 0 <= ny < volume.shape[1] and 0 <= nz < volume.shape[0]: val = volume[nz][ny][nx] if 0 <= val < 256: hist[int(val)] += 1.0 return hist def calculaterangeweight(histogram, phistart, phiend): # Range weight is the sum of histogram bin counts within the target range. weight = 0.0 for i in range(phistart, phiend + 1): weight += histogram[i] return weight Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Histogram Simplification: The use of piece-wise constant segments with a minimum width of 10 is a simplification that may lose fine-grained histogram details but preserves peaks. Complexity: The method requires computing local histograms for every voxel, which is computationally expensive. The use of block neighborhoods (8^3) and histogram simplification (12 segments) reduces this cost. Memory: Requires storing the classification probability P alongside intensity. In 12-bit data, this uses no additional memory by packing P into unused bits. Strengths: Effectively separates overlapping tissues (e.g., vessels and bone) that have identical intensity values but different local contexts. Limitations: Requires manual definition of confidence levels (w{Ai}, w{Bi}) by the physician, which can be tedious. The simplification of histograms may lose some accuracy. The method was introduced by C. Lundström, P. Ljung, and A. Ynnerman in 2005. It is based on the idea that neighborhood histogram analysis can extend the capabilities of transfer function design in medical volume rendering, particularly for CT angiographies. The approach is related to morphological filtering. Extending and Simplifying Transfer Function Design in Medical Volume Rendering Using Local Histograms, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/eurovis05/263-270, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Critical Point Classification
head: Hessian Eigenvalue Classification, Stationary Point Classification
body:
Critical Point Classification identifies and categorizes stationary points (where the gradient vanishes) in a differentiable scalar field based on the signs of the Hessian matrix eigenvalues. It builds on Data Feature-Based Classification by evaluating second-order derivative features to produce optical properties. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A differentiable scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) defined on a 3D grid. Output: For each voxel \mathbf{x}, a classification label (Maximum, Minimum, Saddle, or Flat). Optical properties (opacity \alpha, color C) are mapped from these labels per parent principles. Data Structures: Data structure layouts are not given in the sources. Mathematical Definitions: A point \mathbf{x} is a critical point if 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}. The Hessian matrix H at \mathbf{x} contains second partial derivatives: H{ij} =  rac{\partial^2 f}{\partial xi \partial xj}. Let \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 be the eigenvalues of H. Classification depends on the signs of these eigenvalues: 1. Maximum: \lambda1 < 0, \lambda2 < 0, \lambda3 < 0 (all negative). 2. Minimum: \lambda1 > 0, \lambda2 > 0, \lambda3 > 0 (all positive). 3. Saddle: Mixed signs (e.g., two negative, one positive). 4. Flat/Degenerate: Singular Hessian (at least one eigenvalue is zero). These represent plateaus or line-like structures. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Gradient: Calculate 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) for all voxels using finite differences. 2. Identify Candidates: Find voxels where \|
abla f(\mathbf{x})\| < \epsilon for a small threshold \epsilon. 3. Compute Hessian: For each candidate, calculate the 3 	imes 3 Hessian matrix H(\mathbf{x}) using second-order finite differences. 4. Eigenvalue Decomposition: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of H(\mathbf{x}). 5. Classify: Apply the sign rules above. 6. Transfer Function Mapping: Map the classification label to opacity \alpha and color C using a lookup table or shader function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifycriticalpoints(field, epsilon=1e-6, delta=1e-6): labels = {} # Iterate over interior voxels to avoid boundary checks for x in field.interiorindices: # Compute gradient using central differences grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for d in range(3): offset = tuple(1 if k == d else 0 for k in range(3)) grad[d] = (field[x + offset] - field[x - offset]) / 2.0 # Identify candidates where gradient norm is near zero if sum(g2 for g in grad)0.5 >= epsilon: continue # Compute Hessian using second-order central differences H = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): if i == j: off = tuple(1 if k == i else 0 for k in range(3)) H[i][j] = field[x + off] - 2field[x] + field[x - off] else: offi = tuple(1 if k == i else 0 for k in range(3)) offj = tuple(1 if k == j else 0 for k in range(3)) H[i][j] = (field[x + tuple(a+b for a,b in zip(offi,offj))] field[x + tuple(a-b for a,b in zip(offi,offj))] field[x + tuple(-a+b for a,b in zip(offi,offj))] + field[x + tuple(-a-b for a,b in zip(offi,offj))]) / 4.0 # Solve characteristic polynomial for eigenvalues lambdas = solveeigenvalues(H) # Classify based on eigenvalue signs if any(abs(l) < delta for l in lambdas): labels[x] = "Flat" elif all(l < 0 for l in lambdas): labels[x] = "Maximum" elif all(l > 0 for l in lambdas): labels[x] = "Minimum" else: labels[x] = "Saddle" return labels Pitfalls: Singular Hessians: Critical points with a singular Hessian mark flat spots, representing line-like degenerate critical-points or (partial) plateaus. Discretization and Noise: True critical points rarely align exactly with voxel centers, and noise creates spurious points. Sub-voxel refinement and field smoothing are standard implementation guards. Extracts gradient flow structures connected to critical points: ascending manifolds (starting at a critical point) and descending manifolds (ending at a critical point). In 2D scalar fields, these manifolds may be zero-dimensional (the ascending manifold of a maximum is the position of the maximum itself), one-dimensional (the ascending manifolds of a saddle are separatrices), or two-dimensional (ascending manifold of a source). This allows for the visualization of ridges, valleys, and flow paths rather than just point locations. Not given in the sources. The classification of stationary points based on Hessian eigenvalues is a standard mathematical definition. The concept of ascending and descending manifolds and the Morse-Smale complex further extends this to topological graph representation of scalar fields. name: Vertex Classification for Piecewise Linear Fields
head: Edge graph classification, Gerstner and Pajarola's Vertex Classification for Piecewise Linear Fields, Local tetrahedral partitioning, Surrounding polyhedron method, Vertex Classification via Implicit Tetrahedrization
body: This method classifies mesh vertices in piecewise linear (C⁰-continuous) scalar fields as regular, maximum, minimum, or saddle points by analyzing the connectivity of an edge graph derived from the vertex's local neighborhood. It distinguishes itself from differentiable field methods (like Critical Point Classification) by operating on discrete, non-differentiable data where critical points are restricted to mesh vertices, using topological connectivity rather than Hessian eigenvalues. Inputs: A scalar field f defined on a mesh (tetrahedral or hexahedral/trilinear), and a target vertex v0 with value f(v0). Outputs: A classification label for v0: {Regular, Maximum, Minimum, Saddle}. Data Structures: 1. Surrounding Polyhedron: The set of all tetrahedra (or cells) sharing an edge connected to v0. The vertices of these cells form the local neighborhood. 2. Edge Graph: A graph where nodes are the neighborhood vertices (excluding v0) and edges are the connections between them within the surrounding polyhedron. 3. Polarity Map: A mapping from each neighborhood vertex vi to a sign si \in \{+, -\}. Steps: 1. Identify Neighborhood: Determine the "surrounding polyhedron" consisting of all cells sharing an edge connected to v0. Let V{nb} be the set of vertices in this polyhedron excluding v0. 2. Assign Polarity: For each vi \in V{nb}: If f(vi) > f(v0), set si = '+'. If f(vi) < f(v0), set si = '-'. If f(vi) = f(v0), ignore vi (do not include in graph or count). 3. Construct Edge Graph: Create a graph G=(V{nb}, E) where E contains all edges from the surrounding polyhedron connecting vertices in V{nb}. 4. Filter Edges: Remove all edges (u, v) \in E where su \neq sv (i.e., edges connecting vertices of different polarities). 5. Count Components: Calculate the number of connected components C in the remaining graph. 6. Classify: If C = 1: The vertex is a Maximum if the component consists of '+' vertices, or a Minimum if it consists of '-' vertices. If C = 2: The vertex is a Regular point. If C > 2: The vertex is a Saddle point. Alternative Implementation (Hexahedral/Trilinear): For hexahedral cells, the method leverages the fact that trilinear interpolation near a vertex mimics linear interpolation. 1. Identify the three edge-connected neighbors v1, v2, v4 of v0 within the same cell. 2. Treat v0, v1, v2, v4 as an implicit tetrahedron. 3. Apply the polarity and connectivity logic to these 4 vertices (plus any other edge-connected neighbors if the topology is more complex, but the core lemma relies on the 3 neighbors). 4. The sources note that for trilinear fields, a case table of 2^6=64 entries can be precomputed based on the signs of the 6 edge-connected vertices in a hexahedron, mapping the configuration to a classification. Formulas and Definitions: Let F: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R} be the scalar field. Let U\delta be a small neighborhood of v0. Let R = U\delta \cap C be the intersection with the cell C containing v0. Let N1 be the preimage of (-\infty, F(v0)) in R \setminus \{v0\} and P1 be the preimage of [F(v0), +\infty) in R \setminus \{v0\}. The classification is determined by the number of connected components nn (negative) and np (positive) in the neighborhood: Regular: np = nn = 1 and P1 \neq N1. Minimum: np = 1 and nn = 0. Maximum: nn = 1 and np = 0. Saddle: np + nn > 2. The edge graph method approximates these topological properties. The deletion of edges between different polarities effectively isolates the connected regions of higher/lower values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifyvertex(v0, mesh, scalarfield): """ Classifies vertex v0 in a piecewise linear scalar field. v0: The vertex index to classify. mesh: Object providing connectivity (edges, cells). scalarfield: Array of scalar values for all vertices. """ v0val = scalarfield[v0] # Step 1: Identify surrounding polyhedron vertices # Get all cells (tetrahedra or hexahedra) that share an edge with v0 # For simplicity, assume we can get all neighbors connected by an edge # and all vertices in the cells sharing those edges. neighbors = set() cellssharingedge = getcellssharingedgewithvertex(v0, mesh) for cell in cellssharingedge: neighbors.update(cell.vertices) # Remove v0 itself neighbors.discard(v0) # Step 2: Assign polarity and build graph graphnodes = [] nodetoidx = {} for i, v in enumerate(neighbors): val = scalarfield[v] if val == v0val: continue # Ignore equal values if val > v0val: polarity = '+' else: polarity = '-' graphnodes.append({'id': v, 'polarity': polarity}) nodetoidx[v] = i # Step 3: Construct edge graph and filter # Get edges between nodes in neighbors edges = getedgesbetweenvertices(neighbors, mesh) remainingedges = [] for u, v in edges: if u in nodetoidx and v in nodetoidx: upolarity = graphnodes[nodetoidx[u]]['polarity'] vpolarity = graphnodes[nodetoidx[v]]['polarity'] if upolarity == vpolarity: remainingedges.append((u, v)) # Step 4: Count connected components # Build adjacency list from remainingedges adj = {v: [] for v in neighbors if v in nodetoidx} for u, v in remainingedges: adj[u].append(v) adj[v].append(u) visited = set() components = 0 componentpolarity = None for v in adj: if v not in visited: components += 1 # Determine polarity of this component # All nodes in a component must have the same polarity # because edges between different polarities were removed. comppolarity = graphnodes[nodetoidx[v]]['polarity'] componentpolarity = comppolarity # BFS/DFS to mark visited stack = [v] while stack: curr = stack.pop() if curr not in visited: visited.add(curr) for neighbor in adj[curr]: if neighbor not in visited: stack.append(neighbor) # Step 5: Classify if components == 1: if componentpolarity == '+': return 'Maximum' else: return 'Minimum' elif components == 2: return 'Regular' else: return 'Saddle' def getcellssharingedgewithvertex(v0, mesh): """ Returns all cells that contain at least one edge connected to v0. Implementation detail: Iterate over all edges connected to v0, then find all cells containing those edges. """ cells = set() for neighbor in mesh.getedgeneighbors(v0): edge = (v0, neighbor) cells.update(mesh.getcellscontainingedge(edge)) return list(cells) def getedgesbetweenvertices(vertices, mesh): """ Returns list of edges (u, v) where both u and v are in vertices. """ edges = [] for u in vertices: for v in mesh.getneighbors(u): if v in vertices and u < v: # Avoid duplicates edges.append((u, v)) return edges Parameters: Neighborhood definition: "Surrounding polyhedron" defined by cells sharing an edge with the vertex. Equality handling: Vertices with equal scalar values are ignored. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Equal Values: Vertices with f(vi) = f(v0) are excluded from the graph. This can reduce the number of nodes and potentially affect component counting if not handled consistently. Degenerate Input: If the neighborhood is too small or disconnected, the component count may be ambiguous. Trilinear Approximation: The method relies on the lemma that trilinear interpolation near a vertex partitions space similarly to linear interpolation. This is an approximation and may not hold for all field configurations, though it is the basis for the method. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of edges in the surrounding polyhedron. The dominant step is graph traversal (BFS/DFS) to count components. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the size of the local neighborhood. Strengths: Robust for discrete, piecewise linear data where derivatives are undefined. Simple to implement using standard graph algorithms. Limitations: Only classifies vertices, not interior critical points. Accuracy depends on the mesh resolution and the validity of the trilinear-to-linear approximation assumption. When to use: When analyzing critical points in tetrahedral or hexahedral meshes with piecewise linear or trilinear interpolation, especially in adaptive refinement contexts where edge collapsing is performed. The method was introduced by Gerstner and Pajarola. It is based on the observation that for piecewise linear interpolation on tetrahedral grids, critical points can only occur at mesh vertices. The method extends to trilinear fields by leveraging the local linear behavior near vertices (Lemma 3 in the source). It is used in the context of feature-based visualization and adaptive refinement of scalar fields. name: Subspace Clustering via Spectral Clustering
head: Spectral Subspace Clustering, Subspace Clustering
body: Subspace Clustering via Spectral Clustering is a feature-based classification method that identifies low-dimensional linear subspaces within high-dimensional attribute spaces to group volume samples. It solves the problem of segmenting complex, multivariate data where samples belong to distinct structural regimes (e.g., different materials or physical phenomena) that are not separable by simple scalar thresholds. Unlike Similarity-based Classification which relies on pairwise distances, this method exploits the geometric property that samples from the same subspace can be linearly reconstructed from one another, revealing cluster structure through algebraic relationships rather than metric proximity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of T data samples \{\mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^D\}{i=1}^T, where each \mathbf{x}i is a feature vector (e.g., intensity, gradient, color) associated with a spatial position in the volume. Output: A clustering assignment for each sample, identifying which linear subspace it belongs to. This assignment drives the transfer function design, mapping subspace labels to opacity and color values. Data Structures: 1. Data Matrix X: A D \times T matrix where each column is a sample \mathbf{x}i. 2. Coefficient Matrix W: A T \times T matrix where W{ij} represents the weight of sample \mathbf{x}j in the reconstruction of sample \mathbf{x}i. 3. Affinity Matrix A: A symmetric T \times T matrix used for spectral clustering, derived from W. Algorithm Steps: 1. Assumption: Assume the data samples are drawn from a union of n \ge 1 linear subspaces \{Sj\}{j=1}^n with unknown dimensions 0 < dj < D. 2. Coefficient Matrix Construction: Construct the coefficient matrix W such that the data is approximately reconstructed by itself: X \approx XW Subject to the constraint: W{ii} = 0 \quad \text{for } i = 1, \dots, T This constraint ensures that a sample is not used for its own reconstruction. The problem is highly ill-posed; therefore, an appropriate regularization penalty must be applied to W. Common choices include: Sparsity (L1 norm) Low-rank constraint L2 norm regularization Note: The specific optimization solver is not detailed in the source, but the formulation requires solving for W under the chosen regularization. 3. Affinity Matrix Construction: Compute the adjacency (affinity) matrix A from W: A = |W| + |W^T| Here, |W| denotes the element-wise absolute value of W. This step creates a symmetric graph where edges represent the linear dependency between samples. 4. Spectral Clustering: Perform spectral clustering on the graph defined by A to segment the data into distinct subspaces. The source notes that "Any suitable clustering... can be used," but specifies spectral clustering as the effective method for revealing subspace structure. 5. Subspace Fitting (Post-Clustering): Once samples are segmented into clusters, fit a linear model (e.g., via PCA) to each subspace to estimate its dimension and basis. This step is crucial for understanding the transitions between subspace views in dynamic projections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def subspaceclusteringspectral(X, regularizationtype='sparsity'): """ X: numpy array of shape (D, T), D features, T samples. regularizationtype: string, one of 'sparsity', 'lowrank', 'L2'. Returns: clusterlabels array of shape (T,) """ T = X.shape[1] # Step 1 & 2: Construct Coefficient Matrix W # Solve X = X W subject to Wii = 0 and regularization # This is an optimization problem. # For sparsity: min ||W||1 s.t. X = XW, diag(W)=0 # For L2: min ||X - XW||F^2 + lambda ||W||F^2 s.t. diag(W)=0 # For low-rank: min rank(W) s.t. X = XW, diag(W)=0 W = solvecoefficientmatrix(X, regularizationtype) # Step 3: Construct Affinity Matrix # A = |W| + |W^T| A = abs(W) + abs(W.T) # Step 4: Spectral Clustering # Standard spectral clustering involves: # 1. Compute Laplacian L = D - A (where D is degree matrix) # 2. Compute eigenvectors of L corresponding to smallest eigenvalues # 3. Normalize rows of eigenvector matrix # 4. Cluster rows using k-means # The number of clusters 'n' is typically unknown. # The source mentions using 3000 clusters for a specific dataset, # but generally, this must be determined or provided. # For implementation completeness, we assume 'nclusters' is provided. # If not, eigen-gap analysis on L is required. nclusters = determinenumberofclusters(A) # Implementation detail clusterlabels = spectralcluster(A, nclusters) return clusterlabels def solvecoefficientmatrix(X, regtype): """ Placeholder for the specific optimization solver. The source states the problem is ill-posed and requires regularization. """ # Implementation depends on the chosen regularization. # Example for L2 with diagonal constraint: # W = (X^T X + lambda I)^-1 X^T X - lambda diag(...) # However, the exact solver is not specified in. raise NotImplementedError("Specific optimization solver for W is not defined in source.") def determinenumberofclusters(A): """ Heuristic to determine n. Source uses 3000 for a specific case, but this is not a general rule. """ # Not given in the sources. return 10 # Placeholder def spectralcluster(A, nclusters): """ Standard spectral clustering algorithm. """ import numpy as np from sklearn.cluster import KMeans # Compute Degree Matrix D = np.diag(np.sum(A, axis=1)) # Compute Laplacian L = D - A # Compute Eigenvectors # Get the nclusters eigenvectors corresponding to the smallest eigenvalues eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(L) U = eigenvectors[:,:nclusters] # Normalize rows rownorms = np.linalg.norm(U, axis=1, keepdims=True) Unormalized = U / rownorms # K-means clustering on the rows kmeans = KMeans(nclusters=nclusters, randomstate=42) labels = kmeans.fitpredict(Unormalized) return labels Parameters: Regularization Type: Determines how the ill-posed reconstruction problem is solved. Options cited: Sparsity, Low-rank, L2. Number of Clusters: The source example uses 3000 clusters for a hyperspectral dataset, but this is dataset-specific. In general, this is a hyperparameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posedness: The reconstruction X \approx XW has multiple solutions without regularization. Scalability: The method requires constructing an m \times m affinity matrix, leading to high memory and time costs for large datasets. Subspace Dimension: The dimensions of the subspaces are unknown and must be estimated post-clustering (e.g., via PCA), which may not fully exploit relationships between subspaces. Time Complexity: O(m^2 d) to construct the affinity matrix, where m is the number of samples and d is the data dimension. Memory Complexity: O(m^2) to store the affinity matrix. Strengths: Effectively handles high-dimensional attribute spaces by exploiting linear dependencies; suitable for dynamic projections and transfer function design in multivariate visualization. Limitations: High computational cost limits the number of samples that can be processed; requires data reduction (sampling) for large volumetric datasets to terminate in reasonable time. When to Use: When data exhibits distinct linear structures in feature space (e.g., different physical materials with distinct spectral signatures) and scalar-based classification fails. When Not to Use: For very large datasets where O(m^2) memory is prohibitive, or when the data does not conform to linear subspace assumptions. Origin: The method is described in the context of multivariate volume visualization through dynamic projections. History: It adapts techniques from machine learning literature on subspace clustering, specifically spectral clustering methods, to the domain of volume rendering and transfer function design. Usage: Used to find low-dimensional linear subspaces in the attribute space for dynamic projections and transfer function design. It allows for the identification of meaningful regions (e.g., water, urban, vegetation) in high-dimensional data like hyperspectral images.
