name: Magnetosheath Draped Field Line Generation
head: draped IMF field lines
body: Generates draped field line samples within the magnetosheath region, bounded by the bow shock and the magnetopause. Unlike the parent method which traces single lines from ionospheric footpoints, this method seeds lines randomly in the dayside magnetosheath to capture the draped topology of the solar wind magnetic field. It is distinct from general stream line tracing by its specific geometric constraints (dayside-only seeding) and reliance on external magnetosheath field models. Inputs: nlines: Number of field lines to generate. npts: Maximum number of sample points per field line. magnetopauseradius(theta): Callable returning the radial distance of the magnetopause surface for a given polar angle theta. bowshockradius(theta): Callable returning the radial distance of the bow shock surface for a given polar angle theta. magnetosheathfield(x, y, z): Callable returning the magnetic field vector (Bx, By, Bz) at position (x, y, z). Outputs: A flat list of dictionaries. Each record contains keys: x, y, z (float position coordinates), Bx, By, Bz (float magnetic field components), intensity (float magnitude |B|), and source (string 'magnetosheath'). Parameters: step: Fixed Euler integration step size, set to 0.20 Earth radii (RE). thetamax: Polar angle upper bound for seeding, set to 1.4 radians. cosclamp: Lower bound for \cos(\theta), set to -0.98. boundarymargin: Offset from surface boundaries for seeding, set to 0.3. Algorithm: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def generatemagnetosheathlines(nlines, npts, magnetopauseradius, bowshockradius, magnetosheathfield): records = [] for in range(nlines): # Seed selection phi = random.uniform(0.0, 2.0 math.pi) theta = random.uniform(0.0, 1.4) tcos = max(math.cos(theta), -0.98) mpr = magnetopauseradius(math.acos(tcos)) bsr = bowshockradius(math.acos(tcos)) rseed = random.uniform(mpr + 0.3, bsr - 0.3) if rseed <= mpr: continue # Initialization x = rseed math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) y = rseed math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) z = rseed math.cos(theta) step = 0.20 # Tracing loop for in range(npts): thetasun = math.atan2(math.sqrt(y2 + z2), max(x, -40.0)) mpr2 = magnetopauseradius(thetasun) bsr2 = bowshockradius(thetasun) r2 = math.sqrt(x2 + y2 + z2) if r2 < mpr2 or r2 > bsr2: break Bx, By, Bz = magnetosheathfield(x, y, z) mag = math.sqrt(Bx2 + By2 + Bz2) if mag < 1e-9: break records.append({ "x": x, "y": y, "z": z, "Bx": Bx, "By": By, "Bz": Bz, "intensity": mag, "source": "magnetosheath" }) x += step Bx / mag y += step By / mag z += step Bz / mag return records Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dayside Restriction: The method enforces a dayside-only generation by limiting \theta to [0, 1.4] radians and clamping \cos(\theta) to \ge -0.98. This prevents seeding in the nightside magnetosheath. Boundary Precision: The boundary check uses the current position's projected angle \theta{\text{sun}} to query surface radii. If the field line crosses the boundary between steps, it may be recorded outside the valid region before the next check breaks the loop. Zero Field: If the field magnitude drops below 10^{-9}, tracing stops to avoid division by zero. Seeding Gap: The seed radius is restricted to (r{mp} + 0.3, r{bs} - 0.3). If r{bs} - r{mp} \le 0.6, no valid seeds exist for that angle. The code checks if rseed <= mpr but relies on the uniform distribution to naturally fail if the interval is invalid or empty. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is nlines and P is npts. Each step requires a field evaluation and boundary checks. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot P) to store the output records. The source implementation truncates the output to 5,000 records if the total count exceeds this limit. Strengths: Simple to implement; captures the general draped structure of the magnetosheath field; efficient random seeding avoids bias towards specific regions. Limitations: Does not trace lines back to their source (solar wind) or footpoints; relies on external functions for magnetopause/bow shock shapes and field values; fixed step size may lead to inaccuracies in high-gradient regions. This method is part of a pipeline for volumetric visualization of astrophysical vector fields, specifically focusing on Earth's magnetosphere. It builds on Magnetosphere Field Line Tracing by providing complementary data for the magnetosheath region, which is not covered by ionospheric footpoint tracing. name: Particle Traces on 2D Surfaces
head: Particle traces on surfaces, Surface particle traces, Trace lines on surfaces
body: Particle traces on 2D surfaces is a visualization technique that represents the magnitude and direction of a 3D vector field on arbitrary 2D surfaces (not necessarily contour surfaces) by drawing long, evenly spaced particle trace lines. Unlike random seed placement which does not guarantee coverage near every point, this method uses a hierarchical integer lattice to ensure some seed point is near every point on the surface, avoiding density issues where the visualization becomes too dense or too sparse. It sets itself apart from its parent Integral Surface by explicitly breaking traces into segments of contrasting color to resolve directional ambiguity in still images and by projecting the vector field onto the surface geometry rather than integrating within the volume. Inputs: A set of arbitrary 2D surfaces (represented as piecewise linear meshes). A 3D vector field defined over the domain containing the surfaces. A length threshold parameter L{thresh} (initially large, reduced gradually). A constant time interval \Delta t for segment length calculation. Outputs: A set of particle trace lines rendered on the surfaces, composed of colored segments. Data Structures: Octree: The surfaces are scan-converted into an octree. Each cell in the octree holds a plane equation (four numbers: Ax + By + Cz + D = 0). Only cells intersecting the surfaces are present. Surfaces are subdivided down to a constant size cell. Seed Lattice: An integer lattice used for seed point selection, organized spatially hierarchically. Trace Storage: A list of segments for each trace. Each segment stores its start and end points, color, and length. Cell History: For each octree cell, store the length of the longest erased trace that passed through it, to prevent extensive recalculation during backtracking. Steps: 1. Surface Representation: Scan convert the input surfaces into an octree. Subdivide surfaces until they fit into constant-size cells. Each cell stores a plane equation. 2. Seed Selection: Choose seed points on an integer lattice in a spatially hierarchical manner. This ensures the first particle traces start well away from each other. 3. Advection Loop: For each seed point: a. Initialize particle position P at the seed point. b. Advect the particle along the surface in both forward and backward directions using variable step size Euler's method. c. At each step, project the 3D vector field \vec{V} onto the surface to get the tangent direction \vec{T}. d. Calculate segment length L{seg} = \Delta t \cdot |\vec{V}|, where |\vec{V}| is the magnitude of the vector field. e. Create a segment from the previous position to the new position. Color the segment using a sawtooth-shaped color map to resolve directional ambiguity in still images. f. Check termination conditions: i. Particle reaches a stagnation zone (velocity approaches zero). ii. Particle reaches an edge of the surface. iii. Particle becomes too close to its own trace or another particle's trace. g. If the total trace length L{trace} is greater than the current length threshold L{thresh}, keep the trace. h. If L{trace} < L{thresh}, erase the trace. Preserve the length of the erased trace in the octree cells it passed through to prevent extensive recalculation while backtracking. 4. Threshold Reduction: After all seed points at the current resolution are tried, reduce the length threshold L{thresh} and repeat the process. Gradually reducing the threshold from maximum to minimum produces an aesthetically pleasing distribution but takes longer than using a single threshold value. 5. Rendering: Render the trace segments. Color table animation can be used to add motion, making the lines "flow" in the direction of the vector field with velocity proportional to the magnitude. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def magnitude(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def normalize(v): m = magnitude(v) return (v[0]/m, v[1]/m, v[2]/m) if m > 0 else (0, 0, 0) def projectvectorontosurface(v, normal): return (v[0] - dot(v, normal)normal[0], v[1] - dot(v, normal)normal[1], v[2] - dot(v, normal)normal[2]) def calculatesawtoothcolor(mag, period=1.0): return (mag % period) / period class Segment: def init(self, start, end, color, length): self.start = start self.end = end self.color = color self.length = length def scanconverttooctree(surfaces): # Scans surfaces into an octree where each cell holds a plane equation (A,B,C,D). # Only cells intersecting surfaces are stored. Subdivided to constant size. # Not given in the sources. return {} def generatehierarchicalintegerlattice(boundingbox, maxres=8): # Generates seed points on an integer lattice, starting coarse and doubling resolution. # Not given in the sources. return [] def getsurfacenormal(planeeq, point): A, B, C, D = planeeq return normalize((A, B, C)) def updatecellhistory(cellhistory, segment, length): # Not given in the sources: exact cell ID computation for octree traversal cellid = hash(segment.start) if cellid not in cellhistory or cellhistory[cellid] < length: cellhistory[cellid] = length def isedge(point, octree): # Not given in the sources: exact implementation for surface boundary check return False def istooclosetoothertrace(point, segments, threshold=0.01): # Not given in the sources: exact implementation for proximity check against own/other traces for seg in segments: if magnitude((point[0]-seg.start[0], point[1]-seg.start[1], point[2]-seg.start[2])) < threshold: return True return False def advectalongsurface(startpos, vectorfield, octree, deltat, cellhistory, direction=1): segments = [] currentpos = startpos prevpos = startpos epsilon = 1e-6 while True: v = vectorfield(currentpos) if magnitude(v) < epsilon: break # Not given in the sources: exact octree cell lookup mechanism cellid = hash(currentpos) planeeq = octree.get(cellid, (0, 0, 0, 1)) normal = getsurfacenormal(planeeq, currentpos) t = projectvectorontosurface(v, normal) t = normalize(t) stepsize = deltat magnitude(v) nextpos = (currentpos[0] + direction stepsize t[0], currentpos[1] + direction stepsize t[1], currentpos[2] + direction stepsize t[2]) color = calculatesawtoothcolor(magnitude(v)) segment = Segment(prevpos, nextpos, color, stepsize) segments.append(segment) updatecellhistory(cellhistory, segment, segment.length) prevpos = nextpos currentpos = nextpos if isedge(currentpos, octree): break if istooclosetoothertrace(currentpos, segments): break return segments def particletraceson2dsurfaces(surfaces, vectorfield, deltat, initialthreshold, minthreshold): octree = scanconverttooctree(surfaces) seeds = generatehierarchicalintegerlattice(surfaces) traces = [] cellhistory = {} currentthreshold = initialthreshold while currentthreshold >= minthreshold: newtraces = [] for seed in seeds: tracesegments = [] forwardsegments = advectalongsurface(seed, vectorfield, octree, deltat, cellhistory, direction=1) backwardsegments = advectalongsurface(seed, vectorfield, octree, deltat, cellhistory, direction=-1) tracesegments.extend(forwardsegments) tracesegments.extend(backwardsegments) totallength = sum(seg.length for seg in tracesegments) if totallength >= currentthreshold: newtraces.append(tracesegments) else: for seg in tracesegments: updatecellhistory(cellhistory, seg, totallength) traces.extend(newtraces) currentthreshold = 0.5 return traces Parameters: \Delta t: Constant time interval for segment length calculation. L{thresh}: Length threshold. Initially set to a large value, then gradually reduced to minimum. L{min}: Minimum length threshold. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Directional ambiguity in still images is resolved using a sawtooth-shaped color map across each segment. Random seed placement does not guarantee coverage near every point on the surfaces. This family defines methods for projecting a 3D vector field onto a 2D surface to determine the direction of particle trace segments, as required by Particle Traces on 2D Surfaces. The primary distinction among siblings is viewpoint dependency: most techniques are viewpoint independent, while the vieweye projection requires recalculation when the viewpoint changes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, the method involves hierarchical seed selection and advection, which may be computationally expensive for large surfaces and complex vector fields. Gradually reducing the threshold increases computation time compared to using a single threshold. Memory Complexity: The octree representation is more memory efficient than a full 3D grid, storing only cells intersecting the surfaces. Performance: Real-time rotation and particle motion can be achieved on small data sets, and interactive performance on large data sets, using hardware texture mapping on an Onyx2 workstation. Strengths: Guarantees coverage near every point on the surface, avoids density issues, allows for long flowlines to be easily understood, and supports color table animation for motion. Limitations: Viewpoint dependent projection techniques require recalculation of particle traces when the viewpoint changes. Gradually reducing the threshold takes longer to calculate. The technique was introduced in the paper "Visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces" by Van Gelder and Wilhelms. The authors experimented with several different projections of the vector field to the surfaces, including normal, xy normal, cylinder, and eye projections. Color table animation, an old technique [Shoup79], was applied to flow visualization by Van Gelder and Wilhelms [VanGelder92] and was a primary goal of this technique. name: Vector Field Projection onto Surface
head: Normal projection, Projections for Particle Traces, Vieweye projection, XY normal projection
body: This family defines methods for projecting a 3D vector onto a 2D surface to determine the direction of particle trace segments, as required by Particle Traces on 2D Surfaces. The primary distinction among siblings is viewpoint dependency: normal, xy normal, and cylinder projections are viewpoint independent, while the vieweye projection requires recalculation when the viewpoint changes. All techniques in this family operate on a 3D vector \mathbf{v} at a point \mathbf{p} on a 2D surface. The goal is to compute a 2D direction vector \mathbf{d} tangent to the surface at \mathbf{p}, which represents the projected flow direction. The surface is assumed to be defined such that its normal \mathbf{n} at \mathbf{p} is available. The resulting direction \mathbf{d} is used to orient the particle trace segments. Normal projection projects the 3D vector at a point on the surface onto the surface in a direction parallel to the surface normal at that point. This technique is viewpoint independent. It is straightforward but can yield unintuitive particle traces. The XY normal projection is designed for producing film loops where the viewpoint is rotated about the z (vertical) axis. It projects the vector onto the surface using the XY plane normal. Like the normal projection, it is viewpoint independent. Cylinder projection is a viewpoint-independent technique. It projects the 3D vector onto the surface along a direction defined by a cylinder axis, typically aligned with the vertical axis. The vieweye projection is viewpoint dependent. It projects the 3D vector onto the surface relative to the current camera viewpoint. Consequently, the particle traces must be recalculated every time the viewpoint changes. This family of techniques originates from research into visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. The specific comparison of these four projection methods (normal, xy normal, cylinder, and vieweye) was conducted to evaluate their ability to indicate 3D flow on 2D surfaces. The study used a simple test case of a constant velocity field to assess the intuitiveness of the resulting particle traces. Visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. name: Multi-Seed Streamline Tracking
head: Adaptive Stream Line Tracking, ChomboVis Streamline Integration, ChomboVis backward Euler integration, parallel streamline tracking, volume seeding
body: Multi-Seed Streamline Tracking visualizes vector and tensor fields by integrating streamlines from multiple simultaneous seed points. It overcomes sparse flow representation by seeding a 26-neighbourhood of voxels around a target point or all volume points at a specified interval, rather than relying on isolated seeds. It differs from Adaptive Stream Line Seeding by using fixed spatial intervals or local neighborhoods instead of dynamic divergence-based subdivision, and from Entropy-based Seeding by not using information-theoretic metrics for seed density. Inputs: A vector or tensor field defined on a voxel grid. Seed points, either a local 26-neighbourhood or a global volume grid. Integration parameters: user-specified step length and step count. Outputs: A set of 3D streamlines representing the flow field. Arrow heads at the start and end of each streamline for display orientation. Data Structures: Streamline: An ordered list of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Seed Point: A 3D coordinate in voxel or physical space. Steps: 1. Seed Generation: Generate seeds via a 26-neighbourhood of voxels around a target point, or globally at a specified step interval. For interactive cut-views, seed with higher precision on the 2D window to resolve Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) depth ambiguities. 2. Integration: Integrate forward or backward using the specified step length and step count. Sources specify either backward Euler integration or 4th order Runge-Kutta. For tensor fields, take both forward and backward steps to resolve eigenvector sign ambiguity. 3. AMR Boundary Handling: After each step, check if the current position remains inside the current Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) box. If outside, search the AMR hierarchy from finest to coarsest to find a valid box for continuation. 4. Probabilistic Validation: Compute the probability P{total} that the current sample point represents a nerve fibre tract. P{total} = P{anisotropy} \times P{mean\diffusivity}. If P{total} < 0.60, terminate the streamline as the point is likely not in a tract. Parameters: Step Interval: Determines global seeding density; exact numerical value is not specified, but the interval is user-defined. Minimum Length Threshold: 8.2 mm for final fibre tracts. Maximum Curvature: Controlled to ensure realistic paths, but the specific value is not specified. Probability Threshold: 60% for nerve fibre tract validity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: Setting seed positions from a MIP alone causes depth ambiguity; precision seeding on a cut-view display window resolves this. Performance: Seeding all points in the data volume at a specified step interval is computationally slow. Tensor Sign Ambiguity: Eigenvectors have arbitrary signs; bidirectional stepping from the seed point overcomes this. AMR Boundary Crossing: Integration crossing box boundaries requires a hierarchy search, adding computational overhead. Pseudocode: A variant used in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) to determine seed points based on tissue classification probabilities. It computes the probability that a sample point is within a nerve fibre tract using the weighted product of anisotropy and mean diffusivity probabilities (P{total} = P{anisotropy} \times P{mean\diffusivity}). It generates potential seed points in the vicinity of a sample point, where the number of points is determined by the computed probability. It tests at each integration step if the probability exceeds 60% to ensure validity. This method creates around 9500 start points from 1 million voxels. It is chosen when visualizing nerve fibre tracts in brain anatomy where distinguishing white matter from grey matter and CSF is critical. A technique for exploring vector field datasets where a stylus effector acts as a dynamic particle source. It positions the stylus within the dataset to define the particle generation location. It generates a number of particles at the defined location with slight temporal or spatial offsets so their trajectories do not completely overlap. It animates particles following the vector field to visually identify structures. Time Complexity: Global volume seeding is "quite slow" compared to local neighbourhood seeding. Parallel tracking of multiple seeds enables efficient computation on modern hardware. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of generated streamlines; global seeding consumes significantly more memory than local seeding. Strengths: Provides superior flow connectivity visualization compared to static vector displays. Resolves MIP depth ambiguity via precision seeding. Effectively visualizes dense 3D nerve fibre structures in DTI. Limitations: Global seeding incurs high computational cost. DTI variants require careful tuning of probability thresholds and geometric constraints. When to Use: Comprehensive flow connectivity analysis or complex tensor field visualization (e.g., brain tracts). When Not to Use: Real-time applications where global seeding latency is prohibitive, or simple/laminar flows where sparse seeding suffices. The method originates from the ChomboVis/Amrvis toolkit for AMR data visualization and the Angiotool project for MRI vector and tensor fields. It was developed to address the complexity of multi-dimensional diffusion tensor datasets. It is used for interactive exploration of vector fields and nerve fibre tract extraction in brain anatomy. name: Entropy-based Seeding
head: Information-Theoretic Streamline Seeding, Shannon Entropy Seeding
body: Entropy-based Seeding is a method for selecting streamline seed locations in 3D vector fields by using Shannon’s entropy to measure local information content. It places seeds proportionally to entropy values to quantitatively capture critical flow features, such as turbulent cores, ensuring important regions are densely sampled. Inputs: A 3D vector field V. Outputs: A set of streamlines traced from the placed seeds. Data Structures: Entropy Volume: A 3D scalar grid of the same resolution as the input vector field, storing H(x) for each voxel. Seed List: A collection of 3D coordinates (x, y, z) where streamlines originate. Parameters: Number of bins (n): The number of partitions for vector quantization. The sources do not specify a default value but refer to suggestions by Xu et al. [XLS10]. Neighborhood size: The spatial extent around each voxel used to compute local entropy. The sources do not specify a default value but refer to suggestions by Xu et al. [XLS10]. Integration method: Fourth-order Runge-Kutta. Steps: 1. Calculate Local Entropy Field: For each voxel in the vector field, compute the local Shannon entropy H(x) based on the distribution of vectors in its neighborhood. The entropy of a discrete random variable X is defined as: H(x) = - \sum{xi \in X} p(xi) \log2 p(xi) Where p(xi) is the probability mass function for bin xi. This probability is approximated by creating a histogram of vectors in the local neighborhood using vector quantization [Leo06]: p(xi) = \frac{C(xi)}{\sum{j=1}^{n} C(xj)} Here, C(xi) is the number of vectors falling into bin xi, and n is the total number of bins. 2. Determine Seed Probabilities: Set the probability of seeding at each voxel to be proportional to its scalar value in the computed entropy volume. 3. Place Seeds: Place a sufficient number of seeds in the field based on the probability associated with each voxel to cover as many important areas as possible. 4. Trace Streamlines: Trace streamlines from the placed seeds using fourth-order Runge-Kutta integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def entropybasedseeding(vectorfield, numbins, neighborhoodsize): """ vectorfield: 3D list of vectors (Vx, Vy, Vz) numbins: integer, number of bins for vector quantization neighborhoodsize: tuple (dx, dy, dz), spatial size for local calculation """ # Step 1: Calculate Entropy Field nx, ny, nz = len(vectorfield), len(vectorfield[0]), len(vectorfield[0][0]) entropyvolume = [[[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] # Leopardi's vector quantization partitions vectors into bins. # The sources do not specify the exact binning routine. for x in range(nx): for y in range(ny): for z in range(nz): localvectors = [] for dx in range(-neighborhoodsize[0], neighborhoodsize[0] + 1): for dy in range(-neighborhoodsize[1], neighborhoodsize[1] + 1): for dz in range(-neighborhoodsize[2], neighborhoodsize[2] + 1): vx, vy, vz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if 0 <= vx < nx and 0 <= vy < ny and 0 <= vz < nz: localvectors.append(vectorfield[vx][vy][vz]) if len(localvectors) == 0: entropyvolume[x][y][z] = 0.0 continue bincounts = [0] numbins for v in localvectors: # Map vector v to a bin index using vector quantization [Leo06] # The sources do not specify the exact quantization algorithm. pass totalvectors = sum(bincounts) probabilities = [0.0] numbins for i in range(numbins): if totalvectors > 0: probabilities[i] = bincounts[i] / totalvectors entropy = 0.0 for p in probabilities: if p > 0: entropy -= p math.log2(p) entropyvolume[x][y][z] = entropy # Step 2 & 3: Place Seeds seeds = [] totalentropy = sum(entropyvolume[x][y][z] for x in range(nx) for y in range(ny) for z in range(nz)) # The exact number of seeds is not given in the sources. # A common implementation defines a target seed count Nseeds. Nseeds = 1000 for x in range(nx): for y in range(ny): for z in range(nz): pseed = entropyvolume[x][y][z] / totalentropy if totalentropy > 0 else 0.0 if random.random() < pseed Nseeds: seeds.append((x, y, z)) # Step 4: Trace Streamlines streamlines = [] for seed in seeds: # Fourth-order Runge-Kutta integration is used to trace streamlines # The sources do not specify the exact integration routine. line = [] streamlines.append(line) return streamlines Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Vectors: If a neighborhood contains no vectors, entropy is undefined or zero. The pseudocode handles this by setting entropy to 0.0. Bin Count Selection: The choice of n (number of bins) significantly impacts the entropy value. The sources defer to Xu et al. [XLS10] for specific suggestions. Neighborhood Size: The spatial extent of the neighborhood affects the smoothness and locality of the entropy field. The sources defer to Xu et al. [XLS10] for specific suggestions. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Quantitatively captures critical flow features; emphasizes important regions with high entropy (e.g., turbulent cores). Limitations: The number of streamlines generated in the first step can be large, necessitating a subsequent clustering step. Origin: Proposed by C.-K. Chen, S. Yan, H. Yu, N. Max & K.-L. Ma in "An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields". History: The method builds upon the concept of Shannon’s entropy in information theory and uses vector quantization techniques proposed by Leopardi [Leo06]. It relies on parameter suggestions from Xu et al. [XLS10]. Usage: Used as the first step in an illustrative visualization framework, followed by streamline clustering to simplify the large number of generated streamlines. An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields, http://vis.cs.ucdavis.edu/papers/pg2011paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Feature Streamlines
head: Automatic Streamline Placement, DOI-based Streamline Seeding
body: Feature Streamlines is a method for visualizing vector fields by automatically placing streamlines near significant flow features using a user-defined Degree of Interest (DOI) function. It extends Jobard et al.'s evenly-spaced placement by applying a smooth DOI function to control both seeding locations and the termination of streamline computation. Unlike sibling methods that rely on entropy or multi-seed strategies, this approach allows explicit, brush-based definition of focal interest regions, reducing occlusion by suppressing streamlines in low-interest areas. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D vector field \mathbf{V}(x,y,z); a scalar Degree of Interest (DOI) function D(x,y,z) mapping spatial locations to [0, 1]; a rendering style (color/opacity mapping or shading). Output: A set of 3D streamlines, each associated with a unique feature color and intensity derived from the DOI. Data Structures DOI Field: A 3D grid or texture storing scalar values D \in [0, 1]. D=1 indicates "focal interest"; D=0 indicates "context" or "ignore". Streamline: A sequence of points \mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \dots, \mathbf{p}n where \mathbf{p}0 is the seed. Each streamline has an associated featureid and colorintensity. Algorithm Steps The method supports two seeding modes. Non-random seeding is preferred for deterministic results and explicit control. 1. Feature Identification: Identify significant features (e.g., object surfaces, high velocity regions, vortices) to define the DOI function D(x,y,z). 2. Seeding: Mode 1 (Focal Interest): Allow seeding only at locations where D(x,y,z) = 1. Mode 2 (Probability): Randomly sample a spatial location \mathbf{p}. Generate a random float n \in (0, 1). If n < D(\mathbf{p}), use \mathbf{p} as a seed. 3. Integration: Compute the streamline starting from the seed \mathbf{p}0 by integrating the vector field \mathbf{V} (e.g., using RK4) to generate points \mathbf{p}i. 4. Termination Condition: Stop integration if: The endpoint leaves the scene boundary. The endpoint enters a region where D(\mathbf{p}) = 0 (for Mode 1, integration continues while D > 0; for Mode 2, similar logic applies to break computation in non-interest areas). 5. Rendering Mapping: Assign a unique color to the streamline based on its featureid. Map the color intensity or opacity of each point on the streamline proportional to the DOI value D(\mathbf{p}i) at that point. Alternatively, apply the Zöckler shading model. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefeaturestreamlines(vectorfield, doifield, seedingmode='focal', maxsteps=1000): """ vectorfield: function V(x,y,z) -> (vx, vy, vz) doifield: function D(x,y,z) -> float in [0,1] seedingmode: 'focal' or 'probability' """ streamlines = [] # Step 2: Seeding seeds = [] if seedingmode == 'focal': # Non-random seeding for deterministic results and highest density # Evaluate condition in every point to ensure equal positions after update for point in gridpoints: if doifield(point) == 1.0: seeds.append(point) elif seedingmode == 'probability': # Random sampling for in range(numsamples): point = randomsamplespatiallocation() n = randomfloat(0, 1) if n < doifield(point): seeds.append(point) # Step 3 & 4: Integration and Termination for seed in seeds: streamline = [seed] currentpos = seed featureid = assignuniquecolorid() for step in range(maxsteps): # Integrate one step velocity = vectorfield(currentpos) nextpos = integratestep(currentpos, velocity) streamline.append(nextpos) # Check termination if not isinsidescene(nextpos): break if doifield(nextpos) == 0.0: # Break computation in non-interest regions break currentpos = nextpos # Step 5: Rendering Mapping colorintensitymap = [] for point in streamline: doival = doifield(point) # Map intensity proportional to DOI intensity = doival # Or apply Zöckler shading model here colorintensitymap.append((intensity, featureid)) streamlines.append({ 'points': streamline, 'colors': colorintensitymap }) return streamlines Parameters and Edge Cases DOI Threshold: D=1 is the strict focal interest. D=0 terminates or hides. Values in (0,1) provide context. Precision: Non-random seeding ensures deterministic results, avoiding the influence of random entities during focus variation. Pitfall: Random seeding speeds up computation but lacks explicit control over placement. Complexity: Depends on the number of seeds and streamline length. Non-random seeding requires evaluating the DOI function at every grid point, which is O(N) where N is the number of grid cells. Random seeding is O(M) where M is the number of samples. Strengths: Reduces visual clutter by suppressing streamlines in low-interest areas; allows intuitive, brush-based definition of focus. Deterministic with non-random seeding. Limitations: Requires a user-defined DOI function, which can be difficult to construct for complex flows. Random seeding lacks explicit control. When to use: When the user wants to focus on specific features (e.g., vortices, surfaces) and reduce occlusion from background flow. Feature Streamlines was introduced by Mlejnek et al. in 2003 as an extension of Jobard et al.'s evenly-spaced streamline placement. It was developed to address occlusion problems in volume rendering of simulation data by using a focus-and-context approach. The method integrates concepts from Löffelman et al. for probability-based seeding and Zöckler for shading. It is used in interactive frameworks for visualizing computational simulation data, particularly in aerodynamic and fluid dynamics contexts. name: Directional Textured Tracelines
head: Animated Line Tracelines, Texture Map Animation for Vector Magnitude, Textured Streamlines
body: Directional Textured Tracelines is a flow visualization technique that enhances standard 1D line primitives (streamlines) by overlaying an animated 1D texture to explicitly convey flow direction. While standard lines indicate orientation and extent, they fail to show the direction of the underlying vector field; this method solves that ambiguity by moving a structured texture (e.g., a zebra-like pattern) along the line in the direction of the flow. It builds on Stream Lines by animating texture coordinates along the computed trajectories. Inputs: A set of streamlines, each defined as an ordered sequence of vertices. A 1D texture map T, containing a visual structure (e.g., alternating dark/light bands) that varies monotonically in intensity. A global time parameter \Delta t. Outputs: Rendered streamlines with apparent motion indicating flow direction. Data Structures: Vertices: Each vertex vi of a line is assigned a local texture coordinate ui. Texture Coordinate Range: The coordinates are normalized such that u0 = 0 at the first vertex and un = 1 at the last vertex. Texture Map: A static 1D image computed on the CPU and downloaded to GPU memory once; it does not change during animation. Steps: 1. Assign Texture Coordinates: For each vertex vi in a streamline, assign a local texture coordinate ui with a range between [0, 1] from the first to the last vertex respectively. 2. Select Texture: Choose a 1D texture map whose intensity varies monotonically from dark to light. 3. Shift Coordinates: For each frame, shift the local texture coordinate of each vertex by the global parameter \Delta t to move the texture along the line in the direction of the underlying flow field. The effective coordinate is computed as u'i = (ui + \Delta t) \mod 1. 4. Render: Render the lines using the shifted texture coordinates, which creates the illusion of the line crawling in the direction of the vector field. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdirectionaltracelines(streamlines, texturemap, deltat): """ streamlines: List of lists of vertices. Each vertex is a 3D point. texturemap: 1D array of color/intensity values. deltat: Global float parameter for animation time shift. """ for line in streamlines: n = len(line) if n < 2: continue # Step 1: Assign base texture coordinates [0, 1] baseu = [i / (n - 1) for i in range(n)] # Step 3: Shift texture coordinates shiftedu = [(u + deltat) % 1.0 for u in baseu] # Step 4: Render line with texture # Standard rasterization: interpolate shiftedu across segments, # sample texturemap for fragment colors, and draw to framebuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Direction Ambiguity: Lines alone fail to indicate flow direction; the animated texture is required to resolve this. Texture Selection: The texture must have visual structure (e.g., zebra-like pattern) for motion to be perceivable. Precision & Boundaries: The modulo operation handles coordinate wrapping seamlessly, but large \Delta t values may cause visual aliasing if the texture lacks sufficient high-frequency detail. Degenerate lines with fewer than two vertices must be skipped to avoid division by zero during coordinate assignment. Determines optimal seed points for streamlines. Choose when uniform seeding is insufficient. 2D surfaces generated by streamlines. Choose when surface topology is more important than individual trajectory paths. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Real-time visualization is possible, especially with GPU acceleration, as the texture map is static and downloaded once. Strengths: Clearly indicates flow direction; computationally inexpensive; works well with semi-transparent volume rendering via depth testing. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Originated in GPU-assisted multi-field video volume visualization. The technique leverages texture coordinate animation to add apparent motion to geometric objects, a concept also applied to hedgehogs for vector magnitude visualization. It is used in scientific visualization to enhance the readability of vector fields in dynamic environments. name: Stream Surfaces
head: Stream Surface as Isosurface, Streamsheet, Van Wijk Stream Surface Method, Van Wijk's method, van Wijk's Stream Surface Method
body: Stream surfaces visualize steady-state vector fields by stitching together adjacent streamlines to form a continuous geometric sheet, solving the problem of ascertaining overall flow direction in areas of substantial directional change where individual streamlines curl around each other. Unlike its parent Stream Lines, which represents flow as discrete trajectories, stream surfaces provide a coherent topological separation of the flow volume. The method is distinct from Stream-Balls in that it relies on explicit geometric stitching of trajectories rather than implicit scalar field extraction, and from Streak Surface as it assumes steady-state flow rather than tracking particle history. The method constructs a surface defined as the infinite set of streamlines emanating from a starting line segment or curve. Two primary algorithmic approaches exist: the advancing front method (Hultquist) and the isosurface reformulation (van Wijk). Input: A steady-state vector field \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) defined on a domain; a seeding curve \mathcal{C} (line segment or closed loop); optionally, a discretized grid for the isosurface method. Output: A mesh representing the stream surface. 1. Vector Field: Stored as a grid or unstructured mesh. 2. Surface Mesh: A list of vertices and connectivity. 3. Scalar Field (Isosurface Method): A regular grid where each cell stores a scalar value representing the boundary intersection identifier. This method explicitly integrates streamlines to build the surface geometry. 1. Initialization: Define the seeding curve \mathcal{C}. Discretize \mathcal{C} into a set of seed points \{\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1, \dots, \mathbf{p}n\}. 2. Integration: For each seed point \mathbf{p}i, integrate the streamline forward using a numerical integrator (e.g., Runge-Kutta) to generate a trajectory \mathbf{s}i(t). 3. Stitching: Connect adjacent streamlines \mathbf{s}i(t) and \mathbf{s}{i+1}(t) at corresponding parameter values t to form quadrilateral strips. 4. Adaptive Refinement: Monitor the divergence of adjacent streamlines. If the distance between \mathbf{s}i(t) and \mathbf{s}{i+1}(t) exceeds a threshold or if the surface mesh distorts significantly (e.g., around obstacles), insert new seed points between \mathbf{p}i and \mathbf{p}{i+1} on the curve \mathcal{C} and integrate new streamlines. 5. Handling Tears: If the flow divergence causes the surface to tear (adjacent streamlines separate beyond connectivity), allow the mesh to split or handle the boundary explicitly. This method reformulates the stream surface construction as an isosurface extraction problem. 1. Grid Precomputation: Precompute a discretized volume on a regular grid covering the flow domain. 2. Backward Integration: For every interior grid point \mathbf{x}k, compute a backward streamline by integrating -\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) until the trajectory intersects the boundary of the domain \partial \Omega. 3. Boundary Labeling: Store the position or unique identifier \mathbf{b}k of the boundary intersection point for each interior grid point \mathbf{x}k. 4. Scalar Field Definition: Assign scalar function values to the boundary points. The scalar value at an interior grid point \mathbf{x}k is defined by the scalar value of its boundary intersection \mathbf{b}k. This results in a scalar function f(\mathbf{x}) defined over the regular grid. 5. Iso-Contour Extraction: Extract the iso-contour surface of f(\mathbf{x}) using a standard algorithm to construct the stream surface. Steady-State Assumption: The method assumes the flow is steady. The utility is lost for unsteady flows. Boundary Conditions: The flow must enter or exit the volume boundaries for the isosurface method to work. Artificial boundaries can be placed to rectify this if the flow is confined. Directional Ambiguity: The flow direction tangential to the surface is lost because merging many streamlines prevents determining if the flow went straight or weaved. This is often mitigated by superimposing textures like LIC. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestreamsurfaceisosurface(vectorfield, gridpoints, boundarypoints, stepsize=0.1, maxsteps=1000): """ Constructs a stream surface by reformulating it as an isosurface of a scalar field derived from backward integration to the boundary. Args: vectorfield: Function v(x) returning velocity at x. gridpoints: List of 3D points on the regular grid. boundarypoints: Set of 3D points defining the domain boundary. stepsize: Integration step length. maxsteps: Maximum integration steps to prevent infinite loops. Returns: scalarfield: Dictionary mapping grid points to boundary identifiers. """ scalarfield = {} # Step 1 & 2: Backward integration for interior points for x in gridpoints: if x in boundarypoints: continue currentpos = x reachedboundary = False for in range(maxsteps): v = vectorfield(currentpos) vnorm = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if vnorm == 0: break # Euler integration backward along -v(x) currentpos = (currentpos[0] - stepsize v[0]/vnorm, currentpos[1] - stepsize v[1]/vnorm, currentpos[2] - stepsize v[2]/vnorm) if currentpos in boundarypoints: # Step 3: Store boundary identifier boundaryid = boundarypoints.index(currentpos) # Step 4: Assign scalar value based on boundary scalarfield[x] = boundaryid reachedboundary = True else: scalarfield[x] = None # Step 5: Extract iso-contour # The stream surface corresponds to the iso-surface separating # regions tracing back to different parts of the seeding curve. # Standard marching cubes or similar grid-based iso-surface extraction # is applied to scalarfield to generate the final mesh. return scalarfield Replaces explicit geometric stitching with an implicit scalar field using blobby functions, allowing the surface to gracefully split in high divergence areas. Superimposes Line Integral Convolution texture onto stream surfaces to resolve the lack of directional information inherent in standard surface rendering. Visualizes time-dependent flows by tracking particles from a seeding curve at different ages, capturing flow history unlike steady-state stream surfaces. Grows tiny, segmented hairs from contour surfaces that bend with the flow, offering a discrete alternative when surface continuity fails. Represents individual streamlines as twisted surfaces (streamtapes) using local torsion to manage visual complexity, rather than stitching adjacent lines into a continuous sheet. Texture maps arrows onto stream surface geometry to convey local flow direction, solving orientation ambiguity in curling flows. A continuous representation of a tensor field constructed by sweeping a geometric primitive along a streamline of one of the eigenfields. It selects one of the three eigenfields (major, medium, or minor) to define the longitudinal direction, constructs a streamline through it, and sweeps a geometric primitive (ellipse or cross) along the trajectory. For an ellipse primitive, the other two eigenvectors define the major and minor axes of the cross-section; for a cross primitive, they control the length and orientation of the arms. Color and trajectory represent the longitudinal eigenvector, while the cross-section encodes the two transverse eigenvectors. When using a cross primitive, the arms may rotate in some tensor fields, resulting in a helical shape. Critical points occur where the longitudinal eigenvector vanishes (locus) or where the cross-section becomes singular (surface). Time Complexity: The advancing front method is expensive due to the need for adaptive refinement and handling severe mesh distortion as flow diverges around obstacles. The isosurface method requires increased computational effort to advect a boundary-defined scalar field throughout the entire volume domain. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the vector field, the surface mesh (or scalar grid), and integration history. The isosurface method requires a full scalar grid representation. Strengths: A single surface can be rendered efficiently using standard graphics hardware. It provides a clear topological separation of the flow, especially for closed curves where it divides the volume into bounded and unbounded regions. Limitations: The method is limited to steady-state flows. The tangential flow direction is lost on the surface. Multiple surfaces may occlude each other, requiring careful examination from multiple viewpoints. The advancing front method suffers from severe distortion and requires complex tear handling. When to Use: When visualizing steady-state flows where the overall topology and separation of flow regions are critical, and individual streamline curling makes discrete lines hard to interpret. When Not to Use: For unsteady flows, or when precise tangential flow direction on the surface is required without additional texturing. Stream surfaces were introduced as an extension of streamlines to address the difficulty of ascertaining overall flow in 3D vector fields where streamlines curl around each other. Hultquist [1] proposed the original method of stitching adjacent streamlines to build a stream surface, including adaptive refinement to handle mesh distortion. Van Wijk [2] later proposed a simpler scheme for closed environments by reformulating stream surfaces as isosurfaces, which avoids explicit mesh stitching but requires global integration to the boundary. The method is widely used in computational fluid dynamics visualization for steady-state flows. name: Stream-Balls
body: Stream-Balls is a technique for visualizing steady-state vector fields that constructs a scalar potential field from advected particles or streamlines using blobby functions, then extracts iso-contours to mimic stream surfaces. It sets itself apart from its parent Stream Surfaces by replacing explicit geometric stitching with an implicit scalar field, which allows the resulting surface to gracefully split apart in areas of high divergence and break apart in areas of high velocity to indicate magnitude. Inputs: A set of seed points and a steady-state vector field to advect particles. Outputs: Iso-contour surfaces that mimic stream surfaces. Data Structures: Grid: A regular 3D grid for sampling the analytical function. Particle Trajectories: A list of positions \mathbf{p}{i,t} for each particle i at time step t. Steps: 1. Advect Particles: Generate trajectories from the seed points through the vector field to obtain a sequence of positions for each particle over time. 2. Define Kernel: Place a Gaussian blobby function at each advected particle position. 3. Sum Contributions: Compute the total potential field by summing the Gaussian functions over all time steps for each particle, and then summing over all particles, yielding an analytical scalar function. 4. Sample Grid: Evaluate the analytical function at the centers of a regular 3D grid covering the domain of interest. 5. Extract Surface: Compute an iso-contour of the sampled scalar grid to produce the final visualization surface. Formulas: The potential field is constructed as V(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i} \sum{t} \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}{i,t}\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), where \mathbf{p}{i,t} is the position of particle i at time t, and \sigma controls the blobby spread. Parameters: The exact mathematical form of the Gaussian kernel and the iso-contour threshold value are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: In areas of high divergence, the surface gracefully splits apart, losing the strict separation property inherent in explicit stream surfaces. In areas of high velocity, the surface breaks apart, which helps indicate velocity magnitude but fragments the visualization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def streamballs(seedpoints, vectorfield, gridbounds, gridspacing, sigma, threshold): # Initialize scalar grid grid = creategrid(gridbounds, gridspacing) # Advect particles and accumulate potential for seed in seedpoints: path = integratetrajectory(seed, vectorfield) for pos in path: for cell in grid.cells: distsq = dot(cell.center - pos, cell.center - pos) cell.value += exp(-distsq / (2 sigma2)) # Extract iso-contour surface = extractisocontour(grid, threshold) return surface Visualizes 3D vector fields by integrating trajectories from seed points and generating explicit tube geometry around the path, colored by vector magnitude. It sets itself apart from Stream-Balls by replacing the scalar potential field extraction with direct geometric tube primitives, offering explicit control over tube radius and cross-sectional shape. Choose it when analyzing specific trajectories without occlusion from neighboring flows is required, rather than when visualizing divergence and velocity magnitude through implicit surfaces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Indicates velocity magnitude through surface fragmentation; handles divergence gracefully. Limitations: Loses the nice property of separation inherent in stream surfaces; surface breaks apart in areas of high velocity. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Stream-Balls were proposed by Brill. The concept is similar to van Wijk’s implicit stream surfaces but uses blobby functions (meta-balls) to build the scalar potential field. It is an alternative to stream surfaces and flow volumes for visualizing steady-state flows. name: Streamtube Rendering
head: CUDA Streamtube Visualization, Stream tubes
body: Streamtube Rendering visualizes 3D vector fields by integrating trajectories from seed points and generating tube geometry around the path, colored by vector magnitude. It generates explicit pentagonal cross-sections along each streamline, offering direct visual control over the tube radius and cross-sectional shape. Unlike stream surfaces which connect multiple streamlines, streamtubes isolate individual flow paths, making them suitable for analyzing specific trajectories without occlusion from neighboring flows. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D vector field stored as a 3D texture (enabling hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation). An array of seed points (seeds). Output: A linear vertex buffer containing pentagonal cross-sections and a linear index buffer defining the triangular faces connecting them. Data Structures: Vector Field: 3D texture. Seeds: Array of 3D positions (float3). Output Buffer: Linear array of vertices. Each pentagonal cross-section consists of 5 vertices. The stride between cross-sections is maxSteps / geometrySampling + 1 sections. Index Buffer: Linear array of indices. Each segment between two cross-sections generates 10 indices connecting the previous 5 vertices to the current 5 vertices. Parameters: radius: The radius of the streamtube cross-section. maxSteps: Maximum number of integration steps per streamline. geometrySampling: Frequency of geometry generation (e.g., generate a cross-section every N integration steps). seedsCount: Number of seed points. Steps: 1. Initialization: For each thread id: If id >= seedsCount, terminate. Calculate outputPos = id (maxSteps / geometrySampling + 1) 5. Initialize position from seeds[id]. Lookup vector v and color c at position using trilinear interpolation. Call createTubeBaseVertices to generate 5 vertices for the first pentagonal cross-section at outputPos. Increment outputPos by 5. Initialize geometryStep = geometrySampling. 2. Integration Loop: Iterate step from 1 to maxSteps: Check boundary conditions. If position is out of bounds, terminate the streamline. Integrate position using Euler or RK4 method with the current vector v. Update position. Decrement geometryStep. If geometryStep == 0: Reset geometryStep = geometrySampling. Lookup vector v and color c at new position. Call createTubeBaseVertices to generate 5 vertices for the current cross-section. Call createTubeIndices to generate 10 triangle indices connecting the previous 5 vertices to the current 5 vertices. Increment outputPos by 5. Formulas: Tube Base Vertices: Given position P, vector V, and radius r. Calculate perpendicular vector U = \text{findPerpendicular}(V). Calculate binormal vector W = V \times U (normalized). Vertices Vi for i=0..4: Vi = P + r \cdot (\cos(\thetai) U + \sin(\thetai) W) where \thetai = \frac{2\pi i}{5}. Find Perpendicular: \text{findPerpendicular}(V) = (-V.y, V.x, 0.0f). Note: This assumes V is not parallel to the Z-axis in a degenerate way. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def streamtuberender(seeds, vectorfield, radius, maxsteps, geometrysampling, fieldbounds): seedscount = len(seeds) vertices = [] indices = [] def samplevector(pos): # Trilinear interpolation from 3D texture return vectorfield[pos] def magnitudetocolor(vec): # Map vector magnitude to color return math.sqrt(vec.x2 + vec.y2 + vec.z2) def isinside(pos): # Check bounds return (fieldbounds.min.x <= pos.x <= fieldbounds.max.x and fieldbounds.min.y <= pos.y <= fieldbounds.max.y and fieldbounds.min.z <= pos.z <= fieldbounds.max.z) def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2) return (v.x/l, v.y/l, v.z/l) def cross(a, b): return (a.yb.z - a.zb.y, a.zb.x - a.xb.z, a.xb.y - a.yb.x) def findperpendicular(v): # Returns (-v.y, v.x, 0.0f) return (-v.y, v.x, 0.0) def createtubebasevertices(position, vector, radius, outputpos): vnorm = normalize(vector) u = normalize(findperpendicular(vnorm)) w = normalize(cross(vnorm, u)) sectionverts = [] for i in range(5): theta = 2.0 math.pi i / 5.0 vx = position.x + radius (math.cos(theta) u.x + math.sin(theta) w.x) vy = position.y + radius (math.cos(theta) u.y + math.sin(theta) w.y) vz = position.z + radius (math.cos(theta) u.z + math.sin(theta) w.z) sectionverts.append((vx, vy, vz)) return sectionverts, outputpos + 5 def createtubeindices(prevstart, currstart): # Generates 10 triangle indices connecting previous 5 to current 5 vertices idx = [] for i in range(5): pcurr = prevstart + i pnext = prevstart + (i + 1) % 5 ccurr = currstart + i cnext = currstart + (i + 1) % 5 idx.append(pcurr) idx.append(ccurr) idx.append(pnext) idx.append(pnext) idx.append(ccurr) idx.append(cnext) return idx[:10] for id in range(seedscount): position = seeds[id] outputpos = id (maxsteps // geometrysampling + 1) 5 geometrystep = geometrysampling vector = samplevector(position) color = magnitudetocolor(vector) sectionverts, outputpos = createtubebasevertices(position, vector, radius, outputpos) vertices.extend(sectionverts) for step in range(1, maxsteps + 1): if not isinside(position): break vector = samplevector(position) position = (position.x + vector.x, position.y + vector.y, position.z + vector.z) geometrystep -= 1 if geometrystep == 0: geometrystep = geometrysampling vector = samplevector(position) color = magnitudetocolor(vector) prevstart = outputpos - 5 sectionverts, outputpos = createtubebasevertices(position, vector, radius, outputpos) vertices.extend(sectionverts) idx = createtubeindices(prevstart, prevstart + 5) indices.extend(idx) return vertices, indices A simpler technique that only draws lines along the trajectory, without tube geometry. Choose when performance is critical and occlusion is not a concern. Streamlines Connects multiple streamlines to form a surface. Choose when visualizing flow bands or vortices. Stream Surfaces Uses blobby functions to create a scalar field from particles, then extracts iso-contours. Choose for smooth, organic-looking flow visualization. Stream-Balls Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of seeds and M is the number of integration steps. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot \frac{M}{\text{geometrySampling}} \cdot 5) for vertices and O(N \cdot \frac{M}{\text{geometrySampling}} \cdot 10) for indices. Performance: Real-time visualization is achievable on CUDA-enabled GPUs due to hardware-accelerated texture lookups and parallel thread execution per seed. Strengths: Direct geometric representation, easy to color by magnitude, real-time capable. Limitations: Pentagonal cross-sections may appear faceted if radius is large or sampling is low. Perpendicular vector calculation is not robust for all vector orientations. When to use: When individual flow paths need to be highlighted with a consistent radius. When not to use: When flow bands or surfaces are more appropriate, or when robustness to vector orientation is critical. Streamtube Rendering was implemented as part of a CUDA-based 3D vector field visualization project by Marek Fiser. The project demonstrates real-time visualization using RK4 integration and 3D texture lookups. It is part of a suite of techniques including glyphs, stream lines, and stream surfaces. name: Optimized LIC
head: Fast LIC, LIC with Streamline Reuse, Stalling and Hege LIC
body: Optimized LIC (also known as Fast LIC) accelerates the Line Integral Convolution algorithm by eliminating redundant numerical integrations and reusing convolution results for adjacent pixels along the same streamline. It differs from standard Line Integral Convolution (LIC) by computing long field line segments once and incrementally updating the convolution integral for all pixels covered by that segment, rather than recomputing the integral independently for each pixel. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D vector field, a random noise texture T, and parameters for integration step size ht, convolution half-length n, and minimum hit count minNumHits. Output: An image where each pixel p contains the accumulated and normalized LIC intensity. Data Structures: Hit Counter Array: An integer array numHits of the same dimensions as the output image, initialized to zero. It tracks how many field lines have passed through each pixel to enable normalization. Accumulator Array: A floating-point array accumulatedIntensity of the same dimensions as the output image, initialized to zero. It stores the sum of convolution values for each pixel. Parameters: ht: Distance between sample points along the field line. Typically ht = 0.5 \times \text{width of a texture cell}. n: Half-length of the convolution kernel in terms of sample steps. k: Normalization constant for the kernel, set to k = 1/(2n + 1). M: Maximum number of steps to traverse along a field line from the starting point. The field line length is typically larger than the convolution length. minNumHits: Threshold to determine if a new field line needs to be computed for a pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize numHits and accumulatedIntensity to zero for all pixels. 2. Field Line Generation and Convolution: Iterate through each pixel p in the output image. If numHits(p) < minNumHits: Set the starting point x0 to the center of pixel p. Compute the field line segment \sigma(s) starting at x0 using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. Sample the texture T at evenly spaced locations xi = \sigma(s0 + i \cdot ht) for i = -n, \dots, n. Compute the initial convolution integral I(x0): I(x0) = k \sum{i=-n}^{n} T(xi) Add I(x0) to accumulatedIntensity(p). Increment numHits(p). Set m = 1. Incremental Update Loop: While m \le M: Update the convolution integral for the forward point xm: I(x{m+1}) = I(xm) + k [T(x{m+1+n}) - T(x{m-n})] Update the convolution integral for the backward point x{-m}: I(x{m-1}) = I(xm) + k [T(x{m-1-n}) - T(x{m+n})] Determine the pixels containing x{m+1} and x{m-1}. Add I(x{m+1}) to accumulatedIntensity of the pixel containing x{m+1}. Add I(x{m-1}) to accumulatedIntensity of the pixel containing x{m-1}. Increment numHits for the pixels containing x{m+1} and x{m-1}. Increment m. 3. Normalization: Iterate through each pixel p. Normalize intensity according to numHits(p). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedlic(vectorfield, texture, width, height, ht, n, M, minnumhits): k = 1.0 / (2 n + 1) numhits = [[0] width for in range(height)] accumulated = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] def samplefieldline(x0, y0, steps, stepsize): pts = [(x0, y0)] x, y = x0, y0 for in range(steps): k1 = vectorfield(x, y) k2 = vectorfield(x + 0.5 stepsize k1[0], y + 0.5 stepsize k1[1]) k3 = vectorfield(x + 0.5 stepsize k2[0], y + 0.5 stepsize k2[1]) k4 = vectorfield(x + stepsize k3[0], y + stepsize k3[1]) x += (stepsize / 6.0) (k1[0] + 2k2[0] + 2k3[0] + k4[0]) y += (stepsize / 6.0) (k1[1] + 2k2[1] + 2k3[1] + k4[1]) pts.append((x, y)) return pts for py in range(height): for px in range(width): if numhits[py][px] < minnumhits: totalpts = 2 (M + n) + 1 line = samplefieldline(px + 0.5, py + 0.5, totalpts - 1, ht) center = M + n Icurr = 0.0 for i in range(-n, n + 1): Icurr += texture(line[center + i][0], line[center + i][1]) Icurr = k accumulated[py][px] += Icurr numhits[py][px] += 1 idx = center for m in range(M): Icurr += k (texture(line[idx + 1 + n][0], line[idx + 1 + n][1]) - texture(line[idx - n][0], line[idx - n][1])) pxnext, pynext = line[idx + 1] if 0 <= pxnext < width and 0 <= pynext < height: accumulated[pynext][pxnext] += Icurr numhits[pynext][pxnext] += 1 idx += 1 idx = center Icurrback = 0.0 for i in range(-n, n + 1): Icurrback += texture(line[center + i][0], line[center + i][1]) Icurrback = k for j in range(1, M + 1): Icurrback += k (texture(line[idx - 1 - n][0], line[idx - 1 - n][1]) - texture(line[idx + n][0], line[idx + n][1])) pxprev, pyprev = line[idx - 1] if 0 <= pxprev < width and 0 <= pyprev < height: accumulated[pyprev][pxprev] += Icurrback numhits[pyprev][pxprev] += 1 idx -= 1 output = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for py in range(height): for px in range(width): if numhits[py][px] > 0: output[py][px] = accumulated[py][px] / numhits[py][px] return output Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: If the step size ht is too large, pixels along the field line may be missed, causing aliasing artifacts. Accuracy: Accuracy is critical near vortex centers; incorrect field lines disturb the LIC pattern. The method uses fourth-order Runge-Kutta to ensure this accuracy, unlike the variable step Euler's method used in CL-LIC. Boundary Conditions: Field lines may exit the domain. The algorithm must handle indices out of bounds when accessing the texture or updating pixel accumulators. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than standard LIC. By reusing field lines and updating integrals incrementally, it avoids redundant numerical integrations for pixels on the same streamline. The cost is proportional to the number of unique field lines generated (determined by minNumHits) rather than the total number of pixels. Strengths: Great saving in computing time compared to standard LIC; maintains accuracy by using fourth-order Runge-Kutta integration. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of ht to avoid aliasing; accuracy depends heavily on the integration method. Optimized LIC was proposed by Stalling and Hege in 1995. It was introduced as an improvement over the original Line Integral Convolution algorithm by Cabral and Leedom (CL-LIC). The method addresses the computational expense of LIC by exploiting the redundancy in field line coverage and convolution integrals. name: Fast-Oriented LIC (Fast-OLIC)
head: Asymmetric Fast-LIC, Exponential Fast-LIC
body: Fast-Oriented LIC (Fast-OLIC) is a volume rendering technique that generates line integral convolution textures with directional orientation by combining the computational efficiency of fast-LIC with an asymmetric exponential filter. It solves the problem of conveying flow direction (forward and backward) in 3D vector fields, which standard fast-LIC cannot do because it relies on a symmetric box filter. Unlike its sibling Optimized LIC, which optimizes for speed by reusing adjacent pixel calculations, Fast-OLIC specifically modifies the filtering kernel to encode orientation while maintaining incremental update efficiency. Fast-OLIC modifies the texture generation pass of fast-LIC. Instead of averaging a fixed number of samples (box filter), it applies a weighted sum where the weight decreases exponentially for samples further along the streamline. This asymmetry allows the resulting texture intensity to vary based on the direction of flow relative to the viewer or a reference frame, effectively conveying orientation. Input: A 3D texture containing the scalar field values to be convolved (e.g., density or velocity magnitude) and a 3D texture defining the streamline paths (or a vector field from which streamlines are traced). Output: A 3D texture containing the integrated intensity values for the LIC visualization. The method operates on a sliding window of sample values along a streamline. Window Array v: An array of fixed size flength + 1 storing the input texture values vi at the i-th sample point along the streamline. Current Intensity I': A scalar value representing the current integrated intensity at the current voxel. c: A constant controlling the rate of decrease in contribution for samples farther along the streamline. Must satisfy c < 1. flength: The length of the filter kernel, defined as the number of weighted samples in the forward direction along the streamline from each point that combine to determine the value at the corresponding point in the output texture. The core of Fast-OLIC is the exponential filter kernel and its incremental update rules. Initial Filter Kernel: The integrated intensity I0' at the current position is calculated as: I0' = \frac{1}{c^{flength+1}} \sum{i=0}^{flength} vi c^i where: vi is the input texture value at the i-th sample point. c is the exponential decay constant (c < 1). flength is the kernel length. Incremental Update (Forward): When moving to the next voxel along the streamline (forward direction), the new intensity I1' is computed from the previous intensity I0' without re-summing the entire window: I1' = \frac{I0' - v0}{c} + v{flength+1} c^{flength} where: v0 is the value leaving the window (the oldest sample). v{flength+1} is the new value entering the window (the newest sample). Incremental Update (Backward): When moving to the previous voxel (backward direction), the new intensity I{-1}' is computed as: I{-1}' = (I0' - v{flength} c^{flength}) c + v{-1} where: v{flength} is the value leaving the window. v{-1} is the new value entering the window. The following Python-like pseudocode demonstrates the forward incremental update logic. It assumes a function tracestreamline yields sample values v sequentially. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastolicforward(vstream, flength, c): """ Computes Fast-OLIC texture values using incremental updates. Args: vstream: Iterator yielding input texture values vi along the streamline. flength: Integer, length of the filter kernel. c: Float, exponential decay constant (0 < c < 1). Returns: List of integrated intensity values I'. """ # Initialize the window with the first flength + 1 samples window = [] for i in range(flength + 1): window.append(next(vstream)) # Calculate initial intensity I0' # Formula: I0' = (1 / c^(flength+1)) sum(vi c^i) for i=0 to flength sumval = 0.0 for i in range(flength + 1): sumval += window[i] (c i) currentintensity = sumval / (c (flength + 1)) results = [currentintensity] # Incremental updates for subsequent samples while True: try: newval = next(vstream) except StopIteration: break # The value leaving the window is the oldest one (index 0) vout = window[0] # Shift window: remove oldest, append new window.pop(0) window.append(newval) # Incremental update formula: # I1' = (I0' - v0) / c + v{flength+1} c^{flength} # Note: v{flength+1} in the formula corresponds to the newval just entered. # In the shifted window, newval is at index flength. currentintensity = (currentintensity - vout) / c + newval (c flength) results.append(currentintensity) return results Precision: Division by c in the forward update can amplify numerical errors if c is very small. Ensure c is not too close to 0 to maintain stability. Boundary Conditions: The initial calculation requires flength + 1 samples. At the start or end of a streamline segment, padding or clamping may be required if the source does not provide sufficient samples. Degenerate Input: If the streamline length is less than flength + 1, the filter cannot be applied as defined. [Not given in the sources.] Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels along the streamline, due to the incremental update which is O(1) per step. This matches the efficiency of standard fast-LIC. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per streamline (storing only the window of size flength + 1 and current intensity), plus storage for the output texture. Strengths: Conveys flow direction (orientation) similar to OLIC while retaining the high performance of fast-LIC. It avoids the "halo" artifacts mentioned in some OLIC implementations by using a decaying weight. Limitations: The orientation is implicit in the intensity gradient; it may be less intuitive than explicit arrow-based methods. The choice of c affects the visual balance between forward and backward contributions. When to use: When visualizing 3D flow fields where directionality is critical and performance is a constraint, and when a volumetric representation is preferred over line-based methods. Fast-Oriented LIC was introduced in 1998 by Interran et al. in the paper "Visualizing 3D Flow" published in IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications. The method was developed to address the limitation of the fast-LIC algorithm, which used a symmetric box filter and thus could not distinguish flow direction. By adapting the filter to an asymmetric exponential function, the authors achieved the orientation capabilities of OLIC (Oriented LIC) by Wegenkittl et al. while preserving the incremental calculation efficiency of fast-LIC.
