name: Filtering and Aliasing Reduction
body: Filtering and Aliasing Reduction is a family of techniques applied to Line Integral Convolution (LIC) to mitigate visual artifacts such as stair-stepping, high-frequency noise, and incoherent textures. It addresses the problem that standard LIC, which convolves noise along streamlines, can produce jagged or noisy results due to discrete sampling and the nature of the underlying vector field. What sets this family apart from its parent Line Integral Convolution (LIC) is the explicit modification of the input texture, the convolution kernel, or the rendering pipeline to smooth or structure the output, rather than just integrating raw noise. The shared mechanism across all methods in this family is the application of a smoothing or low-pass operation to either the input noise texture or the LIC output, or the modification of the LIC kernel itself to reduce high-frequency aliasing. The core problem addressed is that LIC is a spatially varying filtering operation that does not warp texture coordinates, making it susceptible to aliasing when the noise texture has high-frequency components or when the streamlines are sampled sparsely. The general approach involves: 1. Input Pre-filtering: Applying a low-pass filter to the noise texture before LIC convolution. This is preferred over creating a thick LIC filter with a low-pass cross-section because it incurs no additional cost to the LIC algorithm itself. 2. Kernel Modification: Replacing the standard box or Hanning window with filters that have specific frequency responses, such as periodic motion filters or box filters with phase shifting. 3. Post-processing/Rendering Interpolation: Using interpolation techniques (e.g., trilinear) during the rendering of the LIC texture to smooth the discrete voxel representation. A variation of LIC that replaces the standard Hanning windowed filter with a simple box filter to facilitate the visualization of dye advection in vector fields. While standard LIC produces static textures, this method introduces a phase-shift mechanism that allows the "dye" to move along streamlines over time, creating natural flow motion. It is distinguished from its parent method by its specific kernel choice and temporal animation capability, and from siblings like Variable Convolution Length by its focus on temporal phase shifting rather than spatial length variation. See Box Filter Dye Advection. Using trilinear interpolation during rendering to reduce the 'stair-stepped' aliasing appearance of voxel-based field lines in LIC textures. This technique is particularly effective for Seed LIC, which is more influenced by aliasing than Fast LIC because it assigns values only to voxels along field lines, whereas Fast LIC smears values to nearby voxels. Applying trilinear interpolation not only reduces aliasing but also, with proper color and opacity tables, creates a halo effect which makes it easier to separate the individual lines from one another. Uses a Hanning filter function, defined as 1/2(1 + \cos(\omega+\beta)), which has low band-pass filter characteristics and creates periodic low-pass filters to blur the underlying texture in the direction of the vector field. The general form of the windowed Hanning ripple function k(\omega) is: k(\omega) = \left[ \frac{1 + \cos(d\omega + \beta)}{2} \right] \times \left[ \frac{1 + \cos(e\omega)}{2} \right] Here, c and d are dilation constants for the Hanning window and ripple function respectively. \beta is the ripple function phase shift in radians. The integral of k(\omega) from a to b, used in the convolution, is: \inta^b k(\omega) d\omega = \frac{\sin(bd) - \sin(ad)}{d} + \frac{\sin(bd + \beta) - \sin(ad + \beta)}{d} + \frac{\sin(b(c-d) + \beta) - \sin(a(c-d) + \beta)}{2(c-d)} + \frac{\sin(b(c+d) + \beta) - \sin(a(c+d) + \beta)}{2(c+d)} Note: The source text mentions c in the integral formula but does not define c in the function definition; c likely represents the window width or a related dilation constant. Low-pass filters the input image before applying LIC. This is preferable to creating a thick LIC filter with a low-pass filter cross-section as it comes at no additional cost to the LIC algorithm. A fourth-order Butterworth filter can be used for low-pass filtering the input image. Cutoff frequencies such as 128, 84, 64, and 32 were used in experiments. A combined technique that alternates between Adaptive Filtering (F) and CLIC (C). An image is generated by applying one method to the input texture, and that result is used as the input texture for the other method. Operation C (CLIC) smooths the result, providing continuity and coherence. Operation F (Filtering) highlights the dynamic behavior, potentially causing discontinuities perpendicular to the vector field. Two-step sequences (FC, CF) and three-step sequences (FCF, CFC) are used. Two-step evaluations are faster, taking between 1 and 2 seconds using Double CLIC, because convolution filtering is very fast. Using a symmetric filter (like Sobel) in a CF sequence further smooths the C stage, giving a sense of three-dimensionality while suggesting isoclines and critical points. The problem of aliasing in LIC was identified early in the development of the technique. Van Wijk's original work noted that LIC is a spatially varying filtering operation. Subsequent research explored various methods to mitigate these artifacts, including the use of trilinear interpolation in visualization tools like Viz and Volumizer, the application of periodic motion filters with Hanning windows, and the combination of LIC with adaptive filtering techniques. The use of low-pass filtering on the input noise texture was proposed as a computationally efficient alternative to modifying the LIC kernel itself. name: Box Filter Dye Advection
head: Hanning filter replacement, Phase-shifted box filter
body: Box Filter Dye Advection is a variation of Line Integral Convolution (LIC) that replaces the standard Hanning windowed filter with a simple box filter to facilitate the visualization of dye advection in vector fields. While standard LIC produces static textures, this method introduces a phase-shift mechanism that allows the "dye" to move along streamlines over time, creating natural flow motion. It is distinguished from its parent method by its specific kernel choice and temporal animation capability, and from siblings like Variable Convolution Length by its focus on temporal phase shifting rather than spatial length variation. Inputs: A 2D vector field \mathbf{V}(x,y). A scalar noise field (dye texture). The current animation step l. The total number of animation steps \text{steps}. The filter box length \Delta L. Outputs: A rendered scalar field F{out}(l,x,y). Data Structures: The algorithm operates on pixel coordinates (x,y). Streamlines are computed by integrating the vector field. The filter box is defined by a start position L and length \Delta L along the streamline parameter s. Steps: 1. For each pixel (x,y), compute the streamline path through the vector field. 2. Determine the integration interval for the current frame using the start position L and length \Delta L. 3. Calculate the predicate T(I, si) for each sample point si along the streamline: T(I, si) = 1 if the sample point lies within the filter box range [L, L + \Delta L). T(I, si) = 0 otherwise. 4. Handle wrap-around: if L + \Delta L exceeds the streamline period or maximum length, apply modulo arithmetic to map the interval back into bounds. 5. Compute the output value using uniform weighting over the box interval. Formulas: Predicate: T(I, si) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } si \in [L, L + \Delta L) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Output: F{out}(l,x,y) = \frac{\sum{i} T(I, si) \cdot \text{Noise}(si)}{\sum{i} T(I, si)} The denominator acts as a normalization factor for the uniform box filter weights. The source text implies uniform weighting 1/\Delta L over the segment, which simplifies to the average of noise values within the box. Parameters: \Delta L: Length of the filter box. Not given in the sources. \text{steps}: Number of LIC animation steps. Not given in the sources. l: Current animation step, l \in [0, \text{steps}-1]. Pitfalls: Box filters can cause artifacts when the boxes re-enter the interval, particularly in periodic flows or when the box length is large relative to the streamline length. A solution to avoid this problem is referenced in external literature but not detailed in the source text. Precision issues may arise if the wrap-around logic is not handled correctly for closed streamlines. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boxfilterdyeadvection(streamlineparams, noisevalues, l, steps, deltaL, maxs): """ Compute the output value for a single pixel using Box Filter Dye Advection. Args: streamlineparams: List of arc-length parameters si along the streamline. noisevalues: List of noise field values sampled at each si. l: Current animation step. steps: Total number of animation steps. deltaL: Length of the filter box. maxs: Total length or period of the streamline. Returns: The output scalar value for the pixel. """ # Calculate start position L based on animation step l L = (l / steps) maxs # Define box end and handle wrap-around per source description Lend = (L + deltaL) % maxs sumval = 0.0 count = 0 for s, n in zip(streamlineparams, noisevalues): # Check if sample parameter s is within [L, Lend) if L < Lend: if L <= s < Lend: sumval += n count += 1 else: # Wrapped interval: [L, maxs) U [0, Lend) if s >= L or s < Lend: sumval += n count += 1 return sumval / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points along the streamline. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points along the streamline. Strengths: Simple to implement; easier to control dye concentration and motion compared to Hanning filters; allows for natural dye advection effects. Limitations: Can cause artifacts when boxes re-enter the interval; less smooth than Hanning filters due to the sharp edges of the box filter. When to use: When visualizing time-varying flow with dye advection is desired, and simplicity of parameter control is important. When not to use: When smooth, high-quality static textures are required, or when artifacts from box re-entry are unacceptable without additional processing. The method addresses the limitations of the Hanning windowed filter used in earlier LIC implementations, which were difficult to tune for smooth dye advection due to their periodic nature and attenuation at the ends. The box filter was chosen for its simplicity and ease of control. name: Fabric-like Visualization of Tensor Field Data
head: Fabric-like visualization, Image-space tensor fabric visualization
body: Fabric-like visualization is a multi-pass image-space rendering technique that visualizes symmetric second-order tensor fields on arbitrary, non-self-intersecting surfaces by mapping the two surface-projected eigendirections as thread-like structures. It solves the problem of visualizing complex directional data on complex geometries without requiring explicit surface parameterization or 3D noise textures, distinguishing itself from standard Line Integral Convolution (LIC) by using smooth reaction-diffusion noise instead of high-frequency white noise to allow the compositing of two distinct eigenvector textures. The method consists of four major rendering passes: Projection, Silhouette Detection, Advection, and Compositing. Data is transferred between passes using textures. Inputs: A surface representation (mesh or implicit) providing depth and normals; a 2D or 3D tensor field defined in world space; camera parameters (modelview MM and projection MP matrices). Outputs: A final image where the surface is textured with two thread-like structures representing the principal eigendirections. Surface Textures: Depth buffer and surface normal buffer generated in Pass 1. Eigenvector Textures: Two 8-bit integer textures storing the scaled projected eigenvectors. Noise Textures: Two 2D textures (channels a and b) generated via reaction-diffusion, mapped to the surface geometry. Da = 0.125: Diffusion constant for chemical a. Db = 0.031: Diffusion constant for chemical b. s: Scalar controlling spot size; smaller s yields larger spots. l: Edge length of the implicit voxel grid defining the parameterization resolution. b{min}: Minimum coordinate of the geometry's bounding box. 1. Render the surface using the standard OpenGL pipeline to obtain depth and surface normal n for each pixel. 2. Interpolate the tensor field T from the world-space tensor field at the surface point. 3. Project T onto the surface tangent plane using the projection matrix P derived from the surface normal n: T' = P \cdot T \cdot P^T where P is defined as: P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - nx^2 & -ny nx & -nz nx \\ -nx ny & 1 - ny^2 & -nz ny \\ -nx nz & -ny nz & 1 - nz^2 \end{pmatrix} 4. Decompose the projected tensor T' into eigenvectors v{\lambdai} and eigenvalues using the method from Hasan et al. [10]. 5. Project the 3D eigenvectors v{\lambdai} (where i \in \{1, 2\}) into 2D image space: \gamma'{\lambdai} = MP \times MM \times v{\lambdai} 6. Scale the projected 2D eigenvectors to fit 8-bit storage and avoid numerical instability. Calculate the infinity norm: \|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty = \max\{|vx|, |vy|\} Scale the vector: v'{\lambdai}' = \frac{v'{\lambdai}}{\|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty} If \|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty = 0 (surface normal perpendicular to view direction), ignore the division. Perform silhouette detection on the surface to identify boundaries. This step guarantees the integrity of the advection step in Pass 3. This pass produces the two eigenvector textures by advecting a noise field along the projected eigenvector fields. Generate a seamless 2D noise texture using a reaction-diffusion scheme (Turing [24]) to create smooth "spots" rather than high-frequency white noise. The discrete equations for channels a and b are: \Delta a{i,j} = F(i,j) + Da \cdot (a{i+1,j} + a{i-1,j} + a{i,j+1} + a{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot a{i,j}) \Delta b{i,j} = G(i,j) + Db \cdot (b{i+1,j} + b{i-1,j} + b{i,j+1} + b{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot b{i,j}) Source terms: F(i,j) = s(16 - a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j}) G(i,j) = s(a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j} - b{i,j} - \beta{i,j}) [Note: \beta{i,j} is not defined in the provided sources; assumed to be a constant or external input]. Use continuous boundary conditions to ensure the texture is seamless in both directions. Map the 2D reaction-diffusion texture to the 3D surface geometry using an implicit voxel-based parameterization. 1. Define a regular grid of voxels filling the geometry's bounding box. Each voxel has base coordinate bi and edge length l. 2. Transform an object-space vertex coordinate vg to voxel space v{voxel}: v{voxel} = vg \cdot M where M is a 4 \times 4 matrix: M = \begin{pmatrix} l & 0 & 0 & -b{\minx} \\ 0 & l & 0 & -b{\miny} \\ 0 & 0 & l & -b{\minz} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 3. Transform to local coordinate system v{hit} (components in [0,1]): v{hit} = v{voxel} - [v{voxel}] where [v{voxel}] denotes the integer part (floor). 4. Determine texture coordinates t = (v{hiti}, v{hitj}) by selecting the two components of v{hit} corresponding to the voxel side-plane whose normal is most similar to the surface normal n. Specifically, if nk = \max\{ni, nj, nk\}, then i \neq j \neq k: t = (v{hiti}, v{hitj}) 5. Sample the reaction-diffusion texture at t to initialize the noise field on the surface. 6. Advect the noise field along the projected eigenvector fields \gamma'{\lambda1} and \gamma'{\lambda2} to produce the two eigenvector textures. 1. Compose the intermediate textures (silhouette mask, eigenvector textures) in a final rendering pass. 2. Apply postprocessing steps to add shading and improve perceptual quality. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fabricvisualization(surface, tensorfield, camera, l, s, Da, Db): # Pass 1: Projection depthbuffer = surface.renderdepth(camera) normalbuffer = surface.rendernormals(camera) eigtex1 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] eigtex2 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] noisea, noiseb = generatereactiondiffusionnoise(l, s, Da, Db) bboxmin = surface.getboundingboxmin() Mvoxel = [[l, 0, 0, -bboxmin[0]], [0, l, 0, -bboxmin[1]], [0, 0, l, -bboxmin[2]], [0, 0, 0, 1]] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): n = normalbuffer.get(x, y) if n is None: continue pworld = camera.unproject(x, y, depthbuffer.get(x, y)) Tworld = tensorfield.interpolate(pworld) P = computeprojectionmatrix(n) Tprime = matmul(matmul(P, Tworld), transpose(P)) eigvals, eigvecs3d = decomposetensor(Tprime) v13d = eigvecs3d[:, 0] v23d = eigvecs3d[:, 1] v14d = v13d + [0.0] v24d = v23d + [0.0] v1img = matmul(matmul(camera.MP, camera.MM), v14d) v2img = matmul(matmul(camera.MP, camera.MM), v24d) v12d = [v1img[0]/v1img[3], v1img[1]/v1img[3]] v22d = [v2img[0]/v2img[3], v2img[1]/v2img[3]] v1scaled = scalefor8bit(v12d) v2scaled = scalefor8bit(v22d) eigtex1[y][x] = v1scaled eigtex2[y][x] = v2scaled vg = pworld vvoxel = matmul(Mvoxel, vg + [1.0]) vhit = [vvoxel[i] - int(vvoxel[i]) for i in range(3)] k = argmax(abs(n)) indices = [0, 1, 2] indices.remove(k) t = (vhit[indices[0]], vhit[indices[1]]) vala = noisea.sample(t) valb = noiseb.sample(t) # Pass 3: Advection (Standard LIC step) finaltex1 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] finaltex2 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] for in range(10): newtex1 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] newtex2 = [[0.0] 2 for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): dir1 = eigtex1[y][x] dir2 = eigtex2[y][x] srcx1, srcy1 = x - dir1[0], y - dir1[1] srcx2, srcy2 = x - dir2[0], y - dir2[1] newtex1[y][x] = noisea.sample(srcx1, srcy1) newtex2[y][x] = noiseb.sample(srcx2, srcy2) noisea, noiseb = newtex1, newtex2 finaltex1, finaltex2 = noisea, noiseb # Pass 4: Compositing and Postprocessing # Sources do not specify the exact compositing and postprocessing implementation. # image = composite(finaltex1, finaltex2, silhouettemask) # image = applypostprocessing(image) return image def computeprojectionmatrix(n): nx, ny, nz = n return [[1 - nx2, -nynx, -nznx], [-nxny, 1 - ny2, -nzny], [-nxnz, -nynz, 1 - nz2]] def scalefor8bit(v2d): norminf = max(abs(v2d[0]), abs(v2d[1])) if norminf == 0: return [0, 0] vscaled = [v / norminf for v in v2d] return [int((v + 1.0) 127.5) for v in vscaled] def generatereactiondiffusionnoise(l, s, Da, Db): # Not given in the sources. pass # Not given in the sources. Zero Infinity Norm: If \|v'{\lambdai}\|\infty = 0, the scaling division is undefined. This occurs when the surface normal is perpendicular to the view direction. The method states this case can be ignored. Non-Orthogonality: Projected 3D eigenvectors are not necessarily orthogonal in 2D image space. The method handles this by treating them independently as texture directions. Parameterization: The implicit voxel parameterization avoids the need for explicit texture atlases or 3D noise textures, but the choice of l affects the level of detail and coherence. Time Complexity: The algorithm performs at interactive frame rates for large datasets on current desktop PCs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for depth/normal buffers, two eigenvector textures (8-bit), and two noise textures. Strengths: Works on arbitrary non-self-intersecting surfaces; no explicit parameterization required; maintains local coherence during transformation; uses smooth noise suitable for compositing two directions. Limitations: Limited to non-self-intersecting surfaces; relies on image-space rendering which may suffer from aliasing if not supersampled; the reaction-diffusion noise generation is a pre-processing step. When to use: When visualizing tensor fields on complex surfaces (e.g., neural pathways in the brain) where standard LIC's white noise is visually cluttered or unsuitable for multi-direction compositing. When not to use: For self-intersecting surfaces or when explicit surface parameterization is already available and preferred. The method was introduced by Bernd Hamann and Gerik Scheuermann. It is motivated by image-space Line Integral Convolution (LIC) but adapts it for tensor visualization using a fabric metaphor. It overcomes drawbacks of previous image-space LIC implementations by defining a fixed parameterization on the surface via implicit voxel space, avoiding the need for 3D noise textures at sub-voxel resolution. Fabric-Like Visualization of Tensor Field Data on Arbitrary Surfaces in Image Space, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-27343-84, fetched 2026-10-27 (book)

name: Streak Surface
body: Streak surfaces visualize time-dependent flows by tracking particles emerging from a seeding curve at different ages, modeling the region of flow passing through a domain. Unlike stream surfaces which assume steady-state flow, streak surfaces capture the history of particle advection in unsteady fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A time-dependent velocity field f(\mathbf{x}, t), a univariate seeding curve c: [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^3, and a current time t. Output: An integral surface S parameterized by age r \in [0, t] and curve index s. Data Structures: The surface is defined parametrically. Numerical implementations discretize the integration interval into segments. Formulas: The streak surface S at time t is defined by the integral: S(r, s, t) = c(s) + \int{t-r}^{t} f(S(r - (t - \tau), s, \tau), \tau) d\tau Where: r \in [0, t] is the particle age parameter identifying individual particle instances. s indexes the seeding curve c(s). f is the velocity field. For constant s, S reduces to a streakline. Steps: 1. Define the seeding curve c(s) for s \in [0, 1]. 2. For each point on the curve s, compute the trajectory of particles emitted at different times. 3. The position of a particle with age r at current time t is found by integrating the velocity field backwards from t to t-r, starting from c(s). 4. Numerical integration (e.g., Riemann sums) is required as analytic integration is usually not possible. 5. Collect points S(r, s, t) for discrete values of r and s to form the surface representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestreaksurface(c, f, t, Nr, Ns, dt): # c: callable returning position for parameter s in [0, 1] # f: callable returning velocity vector for position x and time tau # t: current simulation time # Nr, Ns: discretization steps for age r and curve s # dt: time step for numerical integration surfacepoints = [] for j in range(Ns): s = j / (Ns - 1) pos = c(s) surfacepoints.append(pos) # Integrate backwards from t to t-r for i in range(1, Nr): r = i dt tau = t - r # Numerical integration scheme not specified in sources; using standard backward Euler discretization. vel = f(pos, tau) pos = pos + vel dt surfacepoints.append(pos) return surfacepoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Integration: Analytic integration is generally impossible; discretization errors depend on the step size in time and curve parameterization. Backwards Integration: Streak surfaces can also be modeled using backwards integration to trace flow regions. Approaches for computing time and streak surfaces vary by hardware and dataset size. CPU-based parallel algorithms are used for treating large CFD datasets, while GPU-based approaches are designed for real-time visualization of smaller datasets. These methods often employ point-based algorithms with dense particle sets advected at interactive speeds, combined with point-based rendering, rather than explicit mesh generation. Visualization options include striped textures and advanced transparency via depth peeling. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: CPU-based approaches handle large datasets but are not real-time. GPU-based approaches enable real-time visualization for smaller datasets. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Captures time-dependent flow history; suitable for both large offline analysis (CPU) and interactive exploration (GPU). Limitations: Requires numerical integration. The concept of streaklines and streak surfaces was defined in the context of multi-field visualization. Approaches for time and streak surface computation were presented by Krishnan et al. [21], Bürger et al. [5], and von Funck et al. [34]. name: Hairs
body: Hairs is a visualization technique for representing steady-state flow fields near or around contour surfaces, specifically addressing the failure of fiber bundles (or line bundles) when the flow vector points slightly into the surface. It solves this by growing tiny, segmented hairs from the surface that bend according to the local velocity field. Inputs: A 3D velocity vector field \mathbf{V}. A scalar field defining the contour surface \phi(\mathbf{x}) = 0. Surface normal field \mathbf{N} derived from the gradient of the scalar field. User parameters: number of segments N{seg}, velocity scale Velocity\Scale, segment weights wi, interpolation coefficients ti, root color \mathbf{C}{root}, head color \mathbf{C}{head}, jitter scales, and transparency values \alphai. Outputs: A set of rendered hairs, each defined by a sequence of vertices and associated colors and transparency values. Data Structures: Each hair is a list of N{seg} + 1 vertices P0, P1, \dots, P{N{seg}}. Each vertex Pi has an associated color \mathbf{C}i and transparency \alphai. Splat positions are derived from the contour surface. Steps: 1. Splat Positioning: Scatter splats near the contour surface using Levoy's method. Move each splat position towards the contour surface by a multiple of the gradient to ensure they originate from the surface. Let the final base position be \mathbf{P}0. 2. Hair Generation (Per Hair): Initialize the current position \mathbf{P}{curr} = \mathbf{P}0. For each segment index i from 0 to N{seg} - 1: a. Direction Calculation: Retrieve the normalized surface normal \mathbf{n} and the velocity vector \mathbf{v} at \mathbf{P}{curr}. Calculate the direction vector \mathbf{d}i using the formula: \mathbf{d}i = wi \left( ti \mathbf{n} + (1 - ti) \mathbf{v} \cdot Velocity\Scale \right) Where wi is the weighting factor for segment i, ti is the user-specified interpolation coefficient, and Velocity\Scale is the user-specified velocity scale parameter. The normal vector is normalized, and the velocity is scaled by Velocity\Scale. b. Vertex Update: Compute the next vertex: \mathbf{P}{i+1} = \mathbf{P}{curr} + \mathbf{d}i. Set \mathbf{P}{curr} = \mathbf{P}{i+1}. c. Color Calculation: Determine the color \mathbf{C}i for vertex i. A splat color \mathbf{C}{splat} is derived from the scalar field value at \mathbf{P}i mapped to a color table. The user specifies fractions f{root}, f{splat}, f{head} for the endpoint of segment i. The final color is computed in HSV space as a weighted function of the root color, splat color, and vector head color. A random jitter is added to this final color, controlled by scale factors for each component. All computations are performed in HSV space, with hue wrapping from one to zero, and saturation/value components clamped at zero and one. d. Transparency Assignment: Assign the user-specified transparency \alphai to vertex i. No jittering is applied to transparency. 3. Rendering: Render the line segments connecting \mathbf{P}i to \mathbf{P}{i+1} using the computed colors and transparency values. Parameters: N{seg}: Number of connected line segments per hair. Default is six. Velocity\Scale: Velocity scale parameter. wi: Weighting factor per segment to control apparent stiffness. Greater weights on initial segments favor the normal direction; lower weights on middle segments; large weights on the last one or two segments favor the velocity direction for longer hairs. ti: User-specified interpolation coefficients at each line segment point. \mathbf{C}{root}: User-specified root color. \mathbf{C}{head}: User-specified vector head color. Jitter scales: Scale factors for each HSV component. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flow into Surface: The method is designed for flow that is "slightly into" the surface, where fiber bundles break down. Precision: HSV hue wrapping must be handled correctly to avoid discontinuities in color. Degenerate Input: If the gradient is zero, the normal is undefined. In practice, a fallback normal (e.g., view vector or previous normal) should be used, though not specified in the source. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for visualizing flow near surfaces where fiber bundles fail due to inward flow. Provides clear indication of flow direction and magnitude via bending. Limitations: Discrete nature may not convey smooth flow topology as well as stream surfaces. When to use: Near-surface flow visualization, especially when flow vectors point into the surface. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Hairs were introduced by Brian Cabral and Lieth Leedom in their work on visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. The technique was developed to address limitations of fiber bundles in specific flow scenarios near surfaces. name: Streamtape Rendering
head: Illustrative Rendering of Streamtapes, Streamtape Generation, Streamtape Generation and Illustrative Rendering
body: Streamtape rendering is a technique for visualizing steady-state vector fields by representing selected representative streamlines as twisted surfaces (streamtapes) rather than simple lines or ribbons. It solves the problem of visual clutter and poor depth perception inherent in traditional streamline visualization, particularly in complex flows where streamlines curl and twist. Unlike Stream Surfaces, which stitch adjacent streamlines into a continuous sheet, streamtapes operate on individual representative streamlines, using local torsion to determine width and orientation to automatically manage visual complexity and convey local flow structure without the orientation-dependent flaws of streamribbons. Inputs: A set of representative streamlines r(s), parameterized by arc length s. Outputs: A set of streamtape meshes rendered with illustrative techniques. Data Structures: Streamline: A sequence of points r(si) sampled at equal arc length intervals. Frenet Frame: At each sample point, the tangent \mathbf{T}, normal \mathbf{N}, and binormal \mathbf{B} vectors are computed. Streamtape Mesh: A surface defined by two rows of vertices corresponding to the endpoints of orthogonal line segments at each sample point. Parameters: Sampling Density: Number of points per streamline. Not given in the sources. Torsion Normalization Range: Fixed to [0, 1]. Width Scaling Factor: Implicitly 1.0 in the formula \omega = 1.0 - \tau. Steps: 1. Sample the Streamline: Sample a series of points r(si) at equal arc length intervals along the representative streamline. 2. Compute Local Geometry: For each sample point r(si), compute the derivatives r'(si), r''(si), and r'''(si) with respect to arc length s. Compute the tangent vector \mathbf{T}: \mathbf{T} = \frac{dr}{ds} Compute the normal vector \mathbf{N}: \mathbf{N} = \frac{d\mathbf{T}/ds}{||d\mathbf{T}/ds||} Compute the binormal vector \mathbf{B}: \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N} 3. Compute Torsion: Calculate the local torsion \tau using the determinant of the derivatives: \tau = \frac{\det(r', r'', r''')}{||r' \times r''||^2} 4. Normalize Torsion and Compute Width: Normalize the torsion \tau to the range [0, 1] to prevent self-intersection. Let \tau{norm} be the normalized torsion. Calculate the streamtape width \omega: \omega = 1.0 - \tau{norm} 5. Generate Orthogonal Segments: At each sample point r(si), generate an orthogonal line segment centered at r(si). Direction: The segment lies along the binormal vector \mathbf{B}. Length: The total length of the segment is 2 \times \omega (extending \omega/2 on either side), as the sources state the length is determined by torsion and the width is \omega = 1.0 - \tau. 6. Construct Surface: Connect the successive line segments to form a twisted surface. The mesh consists of quadrilateral faces connecting the endpoints of segment i to the endpoints of segment i+1. 7. Add Direction Indicator: Place an arrow at the end of the streamtape to indicate flow direction. 8. Illustrative Rendering: Render the streamtape surfaces using an illustrative style to enhance depth cues and simplify depiction: Silhouettes: Use silhouettes (outlines) as visual cues to simplify the depiction of the streamtapes. Half-tone Shadow: Apply half-tone hatching/shadow to reveal twists of the streamtape surfaces, emphasizing intrinsic directional and structural information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computefrenetframe(rprime, rdoubleprime): """ Computes T, N, B from derivatives. rprime: tangent vector (dr/ds) rdoubleprime: second derivative (d^2r/ds^2) """ T = rprime / np.linalg.norm(rprime) Nvec = rdoubleprime normN = np.linalg.norm(Nvec) if normN < 1e-9: # Degenerate case: straight line. Normal is undefined by curvature. return T, np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) N = Nvec / normN B = np.cross(T, N) return T, N, B def computetorsion(rprime, rdoubleprime, rtripleprime): """ Computes torsion tau. """ numerator = np.linalg.det(np.vstack([rprime, rdoubleprime, rtripleprime])) denominator = np.linalg.norm(np.cross(rprime, rdoubleprime)) 2 if denominator < 1e-9: return 0.0 # Degenerate case return numerator / denominator def generatestreamtape(streamlinepoints): """ Generates a streamtape mesh from a list of points representing a streamline. Assumes points are sampled at equal arc length. Returns list of vertices and faces. """ n = len(streamlinepoints) vertices = [] faces = [] derivatives = [] # Precompute derivatives using finite differences for i in range(n): if i == 0: rp = streamlinepoints[1] - streamlinepoints[0] rpp = (streamlinepoints[2] - streamlinepoints[1]) - rp rppp = ((streamlinepoints[3] - streamlinepoints[2]) - (streamlinepoints[2] - streamlinepoints[1])) - rpp elif i == n - 1: rp = streamlinepoints[-1] - streamlinepoints[-2] rpp = (streamlinepoints[-1] - streamlinepoints[-2]) - (streamlinepoints[-2] - streamlinepoints[-3]) rppp = ((streamlinepoints[-1] - streamlinepoints[-2]) - (streamlinepoints[-2] - streamlinepoints[-3])) - rpp else: h = 1.0 # Normalized arc length step rp = (streamlinepoints[i+1] - streamlinepoints[i-1]) / (2h) rpp = (streamlinepoints[i+1] - 2streamlinepoints[i] + streamlinepoints[i-1]) / (h2) rppp = (streamlinepoints[i+2] - 2streamlinepoints[i+1] + 2streamlinepoints[i-1] - streamlinepoints[i-2]) / (2h3) derivatives.append((rp, rpp, rppp)) for i in range(n): rp, rpp, rppp = derivatives[i] T, N, B = computefrenetframe(rp, rpp) tau = computetorsion(rp, rpp, rppp) # Normalize torsion to [0, 1] taunorm = max(0.0, min(1.0, tau)) # Width omega = 1.0 - taunorm # Center point center = streamlinepoints[i] # Endpoints of the orthogonal segment halfwidth = omega / 2.0 p1 = center - halfwidth B p2 = center + halfwidth B vertices.append(p1) vertices.append(p2) if i > 0: # Connect to previous segment prevp1idx = 2 (i - 1) prevp2idx = 2 (i - 1) + 1 currp1idx = 2 i currp2idx = 2 i + 1 # Create two triangles for the quad faces.append([prevp1idx, prevp2idx, currp1idx]) faces.append([prevp2idx, currp2idx, currp1idx]) return vertices, faces Complexity: The generation of streamtapes is performed on the CPU. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of sample points per streamline and the number of representative streamlines. Strengths: Enhances depth perception by representing streamlines as surfaces. Automatically manages visual clutter and avoids orientation-dependent flaws associated with streamribbons by using the binormal vector and torsion-based width. Conveys local flow structural information (curvature and torsion). Limitations: Requires careful handling of torsion normalization to prevent self-intersection when flow twists sharply. Relies on the selection of representative streamlines, which depends on the preceding clustering and seeding steps. When to use: Use when visualizing complex 3D vector fields where depth perception and local flow structure (twist) are critical, and visual clutter from dense streamlines is a concern. Streamtape rendering was introduced by C.-K. Chen, S. Yan, H. Yu, N. Max, et al. in 2011 as part of an illustrative visualization framework for 3D vector fields. The work builds on the concept of streamribbons but addresses their limitations in handling complex, long streamlines by introducing a torsion-based width and binormal orientation. It is part of a broader effort to apply principles of abstraction and emphasis from technical illustration to scientific visualization. An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields, http://vis.cs.ucdavis.edu/papers/pg2011paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Stream Arrows
head: Texture Mapping of Arrows
body: Stream arrows are a technique for visualizing integral surfaces by texture mapping arrows onto the surface geometry to convey the local direction of the flow. It builds on Stream Surfaces by adding directional cues to the surface representation. Unlike Stream-Balls, which use discrete glyphs, stream arrows provide a continuous directional field across the surface. Inputs: A triangulated stream surface mesh and a vector field. Outputs: A rendered image of the surface with arrow textures. Data Structures: Stream Surface: A mesh defined by vertices and connectivity, generated by advancing particles from seed points. Texture Coordinates: UV coordinates mapped to the surface vertices. Arrow Texture: A 2D image containing an arrow graphic, typically with a transparent background. Steps: 1. Surface Generation: Generate the stream surface using particle propagation. The surface is formed on-the-fly using a greedy approach. Divergence and convergence of particles in the advancing front are treated using a simple distance criterion that inserts and removes particles to ensure a balanced resolution of the surface. 2. Texture Mapping: Map arrow textures onto the stream surface. The texture coordinates are assigned to the surface vertices such that the arrow orientation aligns with the local vector field direction at each point. 3. Rendering: Render the textured surface. The arrows are drawn according to the texture mapping, providing a visual indication of the flow direction across the integral surface. Parameters: Arrow Size: Not given in the sources. Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distortion: The original method does not address stretching and divergence of the surface, which distorts the parameterization and results in very large or small arrows. This can lead to visual clutter or unreadable arrows in regions of high shear or expansion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderstreamarrows(surfacemesh, vectorfield): """Render stream arrows on a given surface mesh.""" # Step 1: Surface generation handles particle insertion/removal # based on distance criteria to ensure balanced resolution. # (Handled externally during surface construction) # Step 2: Assign texture coordinates and orientations for vertex in surfacemesh.vertices: localvector = vectorfield(vertex.position) orientation = localvector / norm(localvector) # # Map orientation to UV coordinates and rotation for rendering # The exact mapping depends on the texture atlas and rendering engine vertex.uv = orientation.xy # vertex.rotation = atan2(orientation.y, orientation.x) # # Step 3: Render the textured surface # Draw the surface with the arrow textures applied # Standard rasterization of textured triangles is performed here # (Sources do not specify the exact rendering pipeline) A refinement of stream arrows using a regular, hierarchical tiling of texture space to adjust for surface stretching and divergence. It applies a regular, hierarchical tiling of texture space and adjusts the arrow textures based on the tiling to compensate for distortion. This addresses the pitfall of the original method where surface stretching results in distorted arrow sizes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides continuous directional cues on integral surfaces, enhancing the understanding of flow direction. Limitations: High visual complexity of the resulting surfaces makes stream arrows rarely used in integral surface visualization from CFD data. The original method suffers from distortion due to surface stretching and divergence. When to use: When continuous directional information on an integral surface is required and the surface geometry is relatively uniform. When not to use: When the surface exhibits significant stretching or divergence, leading to distorted arrows, or when visual clarity is prioritized over continuous directional cues. Stream arrows were introduced by Löffelmann as an advanced visualization of integral surfaces, with the goal of conveying the local direction of the flow. The same authors subsequently addressed the issue of distortion by proposing a regular, hierarchical tiling of texture space that results in adjusted arrows. Despite these improvements, stream arrows are rarely used in integral surface visualization from CFD data due to the high visual complexity of the resulting surfaces. name: Hyperstreamlines
head: Tensor Streamlines
body: Hyperstreamlines are a visualization technique for tensor fields that extends the concept of streamlines from vector fields by defining the longitudinal direction via an eigenvector and encoding the transverse tensor structure in the cross-section. Unlike standard streamlines which only show flow direction, hyperstreamlines provide a continuous representation of the local anisotropy and orientation of the tensor field, solving the problem of visualizing directional diffusion or stress in 3D space. They are distinct from Stream Surfaces by explicitly using the tensor's eigen-decomposition to define the geometry of the primitive being swept, rather than stitching adjacent vector streamlines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D tensor field T(\mathbf{x}) (typically symmetric positive definite, e.g., diffusion tensors in DT-MRI or stress tensors). Output: A set of geometric primitives (tubes or ribbons) representing the hyperstreamlines. Data Structures: Tensor Field: A grid where each cell contains a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. Eigen-decomposition: For each point \mathbf{x}, compute eigenvalues \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 and corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. Primitive: A geometric shape (ellipse or cross) defined in the local frame of the streamline. Steps: 1. Select Longitudinal Eigenvector: Choose one of the three eigenfields to define the direction of propagation. Commonly, the major eigenvector \mathbf{v}1 (associated with \lambda1) is used, but medium (\mathbf{v}2) or minor (\mathbf{v}3) eigenvectors can be selected to create "medium" or "minor" hyperstreamlines. 2. Integrate Streamline: Compute the streamline curve \mathbf{r}(t) by integrating the selected eigenvector field \mathbf{v}{long}: \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt} = \mathbf{v}{long}(\mathbf{r}(t)) using a numerical integrator (e.g., Runge-Kutta). 3. Define Cross-Section: At each point \mathbf{r}(t) along the streamline, the remaining two eigenvectors \mathbf{v}{trans1} and \mathbf{v}{trans2} define the orientation of the cross-section. 4. Sweep Primitive: Sweep a geometric primitive along the streamline. Two common primitives are defined in: Ellipse: The major and minor axes of the ellipse are aligned with \mathbf{v}{trans1} and \mathbf{v}{trans2}. The lengths of these axes are typically proportional to the square roots of the corresponding eigenvalues (\sqrt{\lambda{trans1}}, \sqrt{\lambda{trans2}}) or fixed constants. This results in a tubular shape. Cross: Two line segments intersecting at the streamline center, aligned with \mathbf{v}{trans1} and \mathbf{v}{trans2}. The length of the arms is controlled by the transverse eigenvalues. This results in a helical shape if the transverse eigenvectors rotate along the path. 5. Coloring: Color the hyperstreamline based on the longitudinal eigenvector or the scalar value of the longitudinal eigenvalue. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehyperstreamline(tensorfield, startpoint, primitivetype='ellipse'): """ Computes a single hyperstreamline. tensorfield: Function T(x) returning 3x3 matrix. startpoint: Initial 3D vector. primitivetype: 'ellipse' or 'cross'. """ # 1. Select major eigenvector as longitudinal direction # In practice, one might select v1, v2, or v3. Here we assume v1. currentpos = startpoint pathpoints = [currentpos] # Integration parameters dt = 0.01 maxsteps = 1000 for i in range(maxsteps): # Get tensor at current position T = tensorfield(currentpos) # Eigen-decomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigendecompose(T) # Sort eigenvalues: lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3 # Corresponding eigenvectors: v1, v2, v3 # Longitudinal direction (major eigenvector) vlong = eigenvectors[:, 0] # v1 # Transverse directions vtrans1 = eigenvectors[:, 1] # v2 vtrans2 = eigenvectors[:, 2] # v3 # Integrate step nextpos = currentpos + dt vlong # Store cross-section data for rendering crosssection = { 'position': currentpos, 'vlong': vlong, 'vtrans1': vtrans1, 'vtrans2': vtrans2, 'lambda1': eigenvalues[0], 'lambda2': eigenvalues[1], 'lambda3': eigenvalues[2] } pathpoints.append(crosssection) currentpos = nextpos # Check for termination (e.g., leaving domain or critical point) if not isindomain(currentpos): break return pathpoints def rendercrosssection(crosssection, primitivetype): """ Generates geometry for the cross-section at a specific point. """ v1 = crosssection['vtrans1'] v2 = crosssection['vtrans2'] l1 = crosssection['lambda2'] # Using lambda2 for transverse axis 1 l2 = crosssection['lambda3'] # Using lambda3 for transverse axis 2 if primitivetype == 'ellipse': # Create ellipse in local frame defined by v1, v2 # Major axis length proportional to sqrt(l1), minor to sqrt(l2) axisa = sqrt(l1) axisb = sqrt(l2) return createellipse(center=crosssection['position'], axis1=v1 axisa, axis2=v2 axisb) elif primitivetype == 'cross': # Create cross with arms along v1 and v2 armlen = sqrt(l1) # Example scaling arm1 = v1 armlen arm2 = v2 armlen return createcross(center=crosssection['position'], arm1=arm1, arm2=arm2) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Isotropic Regions: In regions where eigenvalues are nearly equal (isotropic), the eigenvectors are undefined or unstable due to noise and partial voluming effects, leading to ambiguous or erratic hyperstreamline orientations. Critical Points: Locus: Points where the longitudinal eigenvector vanishes (e.g., \lambda1 \to 0 or direction becomes undefined). Surface: Points where the cross-section becomes singular (e.g., \lambda2 \to 0 or \lambda3 \to 0, reducing the ellipse to a line or point). Helical Artifacts: When using the cross primitive, the transverse eigenvectors may rotate significantly along the streamline, causing the cross arms to twist and form a helical shape, which may be visually confusing. A variation that stabilizes the propagation direction by blending the major eigenvector with the input velocity vector, reducing ambiguity in isotropic regions. Used in linear anisotropic regions, often implying a simpler tubular representation without the explicit cross-sectional encoding of transverse eigenvectors. Used in planar anisotropic surfaces, representing a 2D manifold of flow rather than a 1D line with a cross-section. Time Complexity: Dominated by the eigen-decomposition at each integration step. For a streamline of length L with step size h, complexity is O(L/h \cdot C{eigen}), where C{eigen} is the cost of 3 \times 3 eigen-decomposition (constant time). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the path points and cross-section data, where N is the number of integration steps. Strengths: Provides a rich, continuous visualization of tensor orientation and anisotropy; intuitive mapping of eigenvectors to geometry. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to repeated eigen-decompositions; sensitive to noise in isotropic regions; visual clutter in dense fields. When to use: When the primary interest is the direction of maximum diffusion/stress and the local anisotropy structure (e.g., fiber tracking in DT-MRI). When not to use: In highly isotropic regions where eigenvectors are unstable; when computational resources are limited. Hyperstreamlines were introduced by Delmarcelle and Hesselink in 1992/1993 as an extension of streamlines to tensor fields. They are widely used in the visualization of diffusion tensor MRI (DT-MRI) data to visualize neural pathways, where the major eigenvector represents the direction of axonal fibers. The technique addresses the limitations of scalar or vector-only visualizations by incorporating the full tensor information into the geometry of the visualization primitive. name: Higher Order Tensor (HOT) Lines
head: Generalized Tensor Lines, HOT-Lines, Higher Order Tensor Line Tracking, Major tensor lines, Median higher order tensor lines, Minor tensor lines, Tracking Lines in Higher Order Tensor Fields [S1, book]
body: Higher Order Tensor (HOT) Lines is a method for visualizing higher-order tensor fields by tracking lines that follow the local maxima of the tensor's spherical function. It solves the problem of detecting fiber crossings locally without reducing spatial resolution, which is a limitation of second-order tensor lines that follow only the major eigenvector. Unlike second-order tensor lines, which are separated by a separatrix that cannot be crossed, HOT-lines allow for the representation of multiple directions within a single volume element, enabling the visualization of complex fiber structures such as the corpus callosum and pyramidal tract crossing. Inputs and Outputs Input: A symmetric higher-order tensor field T of order r and dimension d=3, defined on a domain U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3. The tensor field is typically derived from MRI diffusion data. Output: A set of curves (HOT-lines) representing the trajectories of mass-less particles advected by the direction fields defined by the maxima (major), minima (minor), or saddle points (median) of the tensor function on the unit sphere. Data Structures The tensor field is represented either as a set of tensor components T{j1 \dots jr} or via a spherical harmonic expansion. Spherical Harmonic Representation: For symmetric tensors, the field is represented as: f\sigma(g) = \suml \summ al^m Yl^m(g) where only even orders l are used for symmetric tensors. This requires (l+1)(l+2)/2 real coefficients per voxel. Tensor Components: For a tensor of order r, the components are stored in an array of size corresponding to the number of independent components of a symmetric tensor of order r in 3D. Mathematical Foundation A tensor T of order r is a multilinear form mapping r vectors to a scalar: T: (\mathbb{R}^d)^r \to \mathbb{R}, \quad (v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(r)}) \mapsto T{i1 \dots ir} v^{(1)}{i1} \dots v^{(r)}{ir} At each position p, the tensor is interpreted as a scalar function fT(p) on the unit sphere S^2 using a normalized direction vector g: fT(p)(g) = T{j1 \dots jr}(p) \cdot g{j1} \dots g{jr} Degeneracy Definition A position p is defined as degenerated if there exists a point (\theta, \phi) on S^2 where the spherical gradient is zero AND the determinant of the spherical Hessian is zero: \nabla{S^2} fT(p)(\theta, \phi) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \det |\nabla^2{S^2} fT(p)(\theta, \phi)| = 0 Pure order zero tensors (scalar fields, a{00}) are degenerate as they have no orientation. For second-order tensors, \lambda0 = \lambda1 is degenerate, but \lambda0 > \lambda1 = \lambda2 is not. Line Definitions Major HOT-Lines: Follow the maxima of fT. At a regular point q, there are M isolated maxima m1 \dots mM. Using the implicit function theorem, unique C^1 functions wm(p) = (\thetam(p), \phim(p)) parameterize these maxima in neighborhoods Um. The line xm(t) is defined by: \frac{\partial xm(t)}{\partial t} = wm(xm(t)), \quad xm(0) = q Minor HOT-Lines: Follow the minima of fT. This is equivalent to tracking streamlines on the negated tensor field for first-order tensors. Median HOT-Lines: Follow the saddle points of fT. Algorithm Steps 1. Tensor Reconstruction: Compute the higher-order tensor T from raw MRI signals s(n) and baseline s(0) using the signal equation: s(n) = s(0) e^{-b T{i1 \dots ir} \cdot g{i1} \dots g{ir}} where b is the diffusion weighting factor. Solve for T using least squares fitting. 2. Initialization: For each seed point p, identify all isolated maxima (for major lines) of fT(p) on S^2. 3. Tracking Loop: Maintain a set totrack containing tuples (position, direction, stepsize). While totrack is not empty, pop a triple (pos, dir, step). Call trackline(pos, dir, step). 4. Integration (trackline): Initialize stopped = false. While not stopped: While step not accepted or stopped: If stepsize is too small (below lower limit), stop (degenerated point reached). Calculate nextpos = pos + dir stepsize. Evaluate directions at nextpos. If there is a single direction close to dir: Accept step: pos = nextpos. If new direction is close enough, increase stepsize (adaptive control). Else if there are multiple directions close to dir: Append pos to a set of degenerated points. Stop tracking this line. Else (no direction close): Reduce stepsize and retry. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trackhotlines(tensorfield, seedpoints, bfactor, minstep, maxstep, directionthreshold, initialstepsize): """ tensorfield: 3D array of tensors (represented as spherical harmonic coefficients or components) seedpoints: list of (x, y, z) coordinates bfactor: float, diffusion weighting factor minstep: float, minimum step size before stopping maxstep: float, maximum step size directionthreshold: float, angular tolerance for direction matching initialstepsize: float, starting step size for tracking """ alllines = [] degeneratepoints = set() for seed in seedpoints: # The sources do not specify the numerical optimization algorithm for finding spherical maxima. # A standard implementation evaluates f(g) on a fine grid of S^2 and returns peak directions. initialdirections = findsphericalmaxima(tensorfield[seed]) totrack = [] for dirvec in initialdirections: totrack.append((seed, dirvec, initialstepsize)) while totrack: pos, direction, stepsize = totrack.pop(0) linepoints = [pos] stopped = False while not stopped: stepaccepted = False if stepsize < minstep: stopped = True break nextpos = pos + direction stepsize if not isinsidegrid(nextpos): stopped = True break # The sources do not specify how to evaluate directions at nextpos. # Standard practice evaluates the spherical function f(g) and finds local extrema. candidates = findsphericalmaxima(tensorfield[nextpos]) if not candidates: stopped = True break closedirs = [c for c in candidates if anglebetween(direction, c) < directionthreshold] if len(closedirs) == 1: stepaccepted = True pos = nextpos linepoints.append(pos) direction = closedirs[0] if anglebetween(direction, candidates[0]) < directionthreshold / 2: stepsize = min(stepsize 1.1, maxstep) else: stepsize = max(stepsize 0.9, minstep) elif len(closedirs) > 1: degeneratepoints.add(tuple(pos)) stopped = True else: stepsize = stepsize / 2.0 if linepoints: alllines.append(linepoints) return alllines, degeneratepoints def findsphericalmaxima(tensoratpoint): # The sources do not specify the numerical optimization algorithm. # A standard implementation evaluates f(g) on a fine grid of S^2 and returns peak directions. return [] def isinsidegrid(pos): # Standard boundary check implementation return True def anglebetween(v1, v2): # Standard dot product formula dot = sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) return math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot))) Parameters b-factor: Diffusion weighting factor, assumed constant. Step size limits: Lower and upper limits related to data smoothness. Direction accuracy: Depends on tracking accuracy and tensor order (higher orders produce closer maxima). Anisotropy Threshold (for switching variant): 0.2–0.3 depending on SNR. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Points: Positions where the Hessian determinant is zero. Lines are not uniquely defined. Tracking stops or branches. Scalar Fields: Pure order zero tensors (a{00}) make tracking impossible. Multiple Directions: If multiple directions are close to the current direction during tracking, the point is considered degenerate and tracking stops. Precision: Higher-order tensors can produce many maxima close together, requiring high direction accuracy. A variant that improves speed by using simple second-order tensor tracking in areas with one dominant fiber direction and switching to higher-order tensor analysis when anisotropy is low or direction deviation is large. It monitors local anisotropy measurements and orientation change. If anisotropy is below a threshold (typically 0.2–0.3) or direction deviation is too large, it processes the next step with higher-order lines; otherwise, it accepts the second-order step. This leverages the similarity of HOT-lines with second-order tensor lines in dominant direction areas. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Applied to datasets of size 128 \times 128 \times 44 with voxel size 1.7 \times 1.7 \times 3.0 mm^3. Uses 36 gradient directions. Strengths: Detects crossings locally without reducing resolution; preserves high angular resolution; generalizes streamlines and tensor lines. Limitations: Sensitive to noise and degenerate points; requires careful step-size control. When to use: When visualizing fiber crossings in diffusion MRI data where second-order tensors fail (e.g., corpus callosum/pyramidal tract crossing). When not to use: When data is purely scalar/isotropic. HOT-lines were introduced by Hlawitschka and Scheuermann. The method generalizes streamlines (first-order tensors) and tensor lines (second-order tensors) to arbitrary even-order symmetric tensors. It was applied to MRI data to solve the tractography problem, specifically to address the limitation of second-order tensors in representing fiber crossings. The approach uses spherical harmonic representation for efficiency and relies on the implicit function theorem to ensure C^1 continuity of the tracked lines. Tracking Lines in Higher Order Tensor Fields, https://doi.org/10.4230/dfu.sciviz.2010.124, fetched 2026-10-26 (book) HOT- Lines: Tracking Lines in Higher Order Tensor Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/vis.2005.48, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Speedlines
head: Motion Streaks, Speedlines Effect, Streak Lines
body: Speedlines are an illustrative visualization technique used to indicate the motion and history of specific features within time-varying datasets. Unlike standard stream lines that trace particle trajectories through a continuous vector field, speedlines superimpose geometric primitives (cones) along the receding bounding contour of a moving feature to provide intuitive visual cues of direction and velocity history. Inputs: Feature geometry f. Feature motion data: average velocity vector \mathbf{v}{avg} and angular velocity vector \boldsymbol{\omega}. User parameters: number of speedlines N, cone base radius r{base}, time-difference \Delta t, number of cone facets n{facets}, and color/intensity. Outputs: A mesh geometry containing cones representing the speedlines, colored according to user specifications. Data Structures: Bounding Contour (bc): A list of 3D points representing the smoothed boundary of the feature. Centroid (c): The 3D center of the feature. Indices (i{min}, i{max}): Integer indices into the contour list identifying the start and end of the trailing portion. Algorithm Steps: 1. Obtain Bounding Contour: Compute the bounding contour bc for feature f. 2. Smooth Contour: Apply Gaussian smoothing to bc. 3. Identify Trailing Edge: Initialize d{min} = \infty and d{max} = -\infty. Initialize i{min} = 0 and i{max} = 0. For each point pi in bc, calculate the distance metric di = (pi - c) \cdot \mathbf{v}{avg}. If di < d{min}, set d{min} = di and i{min} = i. If di > d{max}, set d{max} = di and i{max} = i. 4. Extract Trailing Segment: Reduce bc to the subset of points lying between indices i{min} and i{max} along the contour path. 5. Distribute Seeds: Distribute N seed points evenly along the extracted trailing segment of bc. 6. Calculate Local Velocity: For each seed point sj, calculate the local velocity vector \mathbf{v}{local} = \mathbf{v}{avg} + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times (sj - c). 7. Construct Cones: Determine cone length Lj = \|\mathbf{v}{local}\| \cdot \Delta t. Orient the central axis of the cone opposite to the estimated velocity vector (-\mathbf{v}{local}). Generate a cone geometry with base radius r{base}, length Lj, and n{facets} sides, centered at sj and aligned with -\mathbf{v}{local}. 8. Render: Add the generated cones to the output mesh geometry and apply the user-specified color/intensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vectoradd(a, b): return [a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]] def vectorsub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def dotproduct(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def crossproduct(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def vectorlength(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def vectorscale(v, s): return [v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s] def normalize(v): l = vectorlength(v) if l < 1e-9: return [0, 0, 1] return [v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l] def computecentroid(points): # Standard average of points n = len(points) if n == 0: return [0, 0, 0] return [sum(p[0] for p in points)/n, sum(p[1] for p in points)/n, sum(p[2] for p in points)/n] def generatespeedlines(featuremesh, vavg, omega, N, rbase, deltat, nfacets, color): # Step 1 & 2: Obtain and smooth contour (Algorithm 3 and Gaussian smoothing referenced) # Sources do not provide implementation details for contour extraction/smoothing. bc = [] # Placeholder for external contour extraction/smoothing # Step 3: Identify trailing edge centroid = computecentroid(bc) dmin = float('inf') dmax = float('-inf') imin = 0 imax = 0 for i, pi in enumerate(bc): diff = vectorsub(pi, centroid) di = dotproduct(diff, vavg) if di < dmin: dmin = di imin = i if di > dmax: dmax = di imax = i # Step 4: Extract trailing segment # Assumes linear ordering of contour points trailingbc = bc[imin: imax + 1] # Step 5: Distribute seeds evenly seedpoints = distributepointsevenly(trailingbc, N) speedlines = [] for sj in seedpoints: # Step 6: Calculate local velocity rj = vectorsub(sj, centroid) crossterm = crossproduct(omega, rj) vlocal = vectoradd(vavg, crossterm) # Step 7: Construct cone vmag = vectorlength(vlocal) length = vmag deltat axis = normalize(vectorsub([0,0,0], vlocal)) cone = generatecone(center=sj, axis=axis, length=length, radius=rbase, facets=nfacets) cone.color = color speedlines.append(cone) return speedlines def distributepointsevenly(polyline, N): # Linear interpolation along polyline segments if len(polyline) < 2: return polyline totallen = sum(vectorlength(vectorsub(polyline[i+1], polyline[i])) for i in range(len(polyline)-1)) if totallen < 1e-9: return polyline step = totallen / N points = [] currentdist = 0.0 segidx = 0 for i in range(N): targetdist = step (i + 1) while segidx < len(polyline) - 1: seglen = vectorlength(vectorsub(polyline[segidx+1], polyline[segidx])) if currentdist + seglen < targetdist: currentdist += seglen segidx += 1 else: break seglen = vectorlength(vectorsub(polyline[segidx+1], polyline[segidx])) if seglen > 1e-9: t = (targetdist - currentdist) / seglen points.append(vectoradd(polyline[segidx], vectorsub(polyline[segidx+1], polyline[segidx]) t)) else: points.append(polyline[segidx]) return points def generatecone(center, axis, length, radius, facets): axis = normalize(axis) vertices = [center] # Apex indices = [] basecenter = vectorsub(center, vectorscale(axis, length)) if abs(axis[0]) < 0.9: perp1 = normalize(crossproduct(axis, [1, 0, 0])) else: perp1 = normalize(crossproduct(axis, [0, 1, 0])) perp2 = crossproduct(axis, perp1) for i in range(facets): angle = 2 math.pi i / facets offset = vectoradd(vectorscale(perp1, radius math.cos(angle)), vectorscale(perp2, radius math.sin(angle))) vertices.append(vectoradd(basecenter, offset)) for i in range(1, facets + 1): indices.append((0, i, (i % facets) + 1)) return {"vertices": vertices, "indices": indices, "color": None} Parameters: \Delta t: User-defined time-difference controlling streak length. N: Number of speedlines. r{base}: Cone base radius. n{facets}: Number of cone facets. Color: User-specified color/intensity for the speedlines. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Velocity: If \mathbf{v}{avg} and \boldsymbol{\omega} are zero, \mathbf{v}{local} is zero, resulting in zero-length cones. Contour Ordering: The algorithm assumes the bounding contour points are ordered such that the segment between i{min} and i{max} represents the trailing edge. If the contour is a closed loop, the "between" logic must handle wrap-around or select the appropriate arc. Angular Velocity: If \boldsymbol{\omega} is not available, it is assumed to be zero. Adjusts seed point density based on flow complexity. Choose when uniform distribution is insufficient. Link Uses texture mapping on lines to show direction. Choose for high-density flow visualization. Link Generates surfaces from stream lines. Choose for volumetric flow visualization. Link Visualizes tensor fields. Choose for diffusion or stress data. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Intuitively conveys motion direction and history for discrete moving features. Limitations: Only applicable to discrete features with defined centroids and motion vectors. When to use: Visualizing the trajectory of specific, identifiable objects in time-varying data. When not to use: Continuous vector fields without distinct features. Speedlines were introduced by Joshi and Rheingans as part of a set of illustrative visualization techniques for time-varying datasets. The technique is motivated by the human perception of motion streaks, where moving objects leave a visual trace. Generalized Framework and Algorithms for Illustrative Visualization of Time-Varying Data on Unstructured Meshes, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc838861/?q=illustrative volume rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) Visualization
head: DTI Visualization
body: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) Visualization is a method for rendering 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensors acquired via MRI to visualize water diffusion patterns and structural neural connections in biological tissues. It solves the problem of interpreting complex, direction-dependent diffusion data by mapping tensor properties to visual attributes such as color, opacity, or geometric primitives. Unlike scalar volume rendering, it handles multi-component tensor fields, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like Domain Colouring by explicitly leveraging the geometric structure of the diffusion ellipsoid rather than just angular phase. Inputs: A 3D volume where each voxel contains a 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. Outputs: A rendered image or geometric representation (streamlines, glyphs) of the diffusion field. Data Structures: The diffusion tensor \mathbf{D} at position \mathbf{x} is stored as a symmetric 3x3 matrix: \mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix} D{xx} & D{xy} & D{xz} \\ D{xy} & D{yy} & D{yz} \\ D{xz} & D{yz} & D{zz} \end{bmatrix} Each tensor is typically stored as 6 floating-point values (D{xx}, D{yy}, D{zz}, D{xy}, D{xz}, D{yz}) due to symmetry. Steps: 1. Tensor Decomposition: For each voxel, compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 and corresponding eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 of \mathbf{D}, sorted such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0. 2. Geometric Interpretation: The tensor represents a diffusion ellipsoid where the eigenvectors define the principal axes and the eigenvalues define the squared lengths of the semi-axes. 3. Visualization Mapping: Apply one of the following strategies: Tractography: Extract and visualize fiber tract trajectories from DTI data. Tensor Lines: Visualize tensor lines for tractography. Direct Volume Rendering: Perform direct volume rendering of DTI data. Formulas: Orthogonality: Eigenvectors are orthogonal in Cartesian space: \langle \mathbf{v}{\lambda1}, \mathbf{v}{\lambda2} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}{\lambda2}, \mathbf{v}{\lambda3} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}{\lambda1}, \mathbf{v}{\lambda3} \rangle = 0. Cross Product Relation: \mathbf{v}{\lambda1} \times \mathbf{v}{\lambda2} = \mathbf{v}{\lambda3}. This relation can be used to reduce calculation effort if two eigenvectors are known. Parameters: Sorting order: \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3. Integration step size for tractography: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Critical Points: Occur when two eigenvalues are equal (\lambdai = \lambdaj). At these points, the corresponding eigenvectors are not uniquely defined, and anisotropy measures become zero. Orientation Ambiguity: Eigenvectors are orientationless (direction only, no sign). This causes interpolation problems if adjacent sample points have contrary orientations (e.g., \mathbf{v} vs -\mathbf{v}). Visualizes diffusion tensor fields by generating a scalar volume from an anisotropically correlated random noise field, preserving high-frequency components in transversal directions while smearing noise along the direction of greatest diffusivity. Unlike glyphs, streamlines, or line integral convolution, it is not sensitive to occlusion, does not depend on starting points, and provides a continuous scalar field representation that handles non-linear diffusion better. Choose when occlusion resistance and continuous scalar representation are required. Interprets the tensor as a distortion of a flat metric, transforming the tensor field into a metric tensor field visualized using a texture resembling fabric, where eigenvalues control texture density and eigenvectors control alignment. Unlike Domain Colouring or Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization, which often suffer from clutter or local view limitations, this method provides a continuous, global representation that explicitly distinguishes between positive (expansion) and negative (compression) eigenvalues. Choose for global, continuous metric visualization. A scalar quantity describing the diffusion along a specific direction vector \mathbf{v}, derived directly from the diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. Unlike rotationally invariant metrics such as Mean Diffusivity (MD) or Fractional Anisotropy (FA) that summarize the entire tensor, ADC is direction-dependent, quantifying diffusion intensity along a chosen axis. Choose when directional intensity mapping is required rather than global tensor shape analysis. The Diffusion Tensor is a 3x3 symmetric positive-definite matrix that serves as the native measurement quantity in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), modeling the local anisotropic diffusion of water molecules in biological tissue. It is defined by three orthogonal eigenvectors and their corresponding eigenvalues, which geometrically represent the principal axes and magnitudes of a diffusion ellipsoid. Choose when full second-order directional information is required for fiber tracking, distinct from scalar metrics like ADC or derived visualizations. Acquisition of 40 or more diffusion weighted volumes to calculate and visualize water diffusion and structural neural connections in the brain. Extends standard DTI by capturing more complex diffusion profiles, allowing for the visualization of crossing fibers which standard DTI cannot resolve. Choose when high angular resolution is needed to resolve crossing fibers. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance with hardware, resolution and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) was introduced by Basser in 1994 as an MRI-based acquisition modality yielding 3x3 symmetric diffusion tensors as its native measurement quantity. In 1998, Basser and colleagues published the first work extracting and visualizing fiber tract trajectories from DTI data of the brain. By 2000, the visualization community had developed methods for tensor line tractography and direct volume rendering of DTI data. The method is primarily used in medical imaging for therapy planning and understanding structural neural networks.
