name: Tensor Field Topological Segmentation
head: Eigenvector-based Topological Segmentation, Tensor Field Topology, Topological Skeleton Segmentation
body: Tensor Field Topological Segmentation decomposes a symmetric second-order tensor field domain into cells based on its topological skeleton, formed by separatrices and degenerate points, followed by adaptive refinement based on eigenvalue similarity. It differs from standard vector field topology by handling the ambiguity of eigenvector directions at degenerate points, where every vector is an eigenvector, allowing trajectories to cross. This method builds on Vector Topology Analysis but extends it to handle the orthogonal eigenvector fields inherent in symmetric tensors. Inputs: A 2D symmetric second-order tensor field defined on a triangular mesh. Outputs: A set of curvilinear cells representing the segmentation. Data Structures: Tensor Field: T(x,y), a 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix at each vertex. Degenerate Points: Vertices or locations where eigenvalues \lambda1 = \lambda2. Separatrices: Polylines representing trajectories of major (red) and minor (blue) eigenvector fields connecting degenerate points. Cells: Defined by vertices which are either red-blue intersections, degenerate points, or boundary intersections. Steps: 1. Extract Topology: 1. Locate Degenerate Points: Identify points where both eigenvalues of the tensor are equal. At these points, the eigenvector field is undefined (every vector is an eigenvector). 2. Determine Radial Directions: For each degenerate point, determine the radial directions (separatrix entry/exit directions). 3. Compute Separatrices: Integrate the major and minor eigenvector fields using 4th order Runge-Kutta integration, triangle-wise. Termination Conditions: Stop integration if: (a) The separatrix leaves the domain. (b) The separatrix gets close to a degenerate point, line, or triangle. (c) The separatrix describes a circle or spiral and passes itself closely in the parallel integration direction. Store separatrices as polylines. 2. Generate Initial Cells: 1. Intersect Separatrices: Compute intersections between red (major eigenvector) and blue (minor eigenvector) separatrices. Optimization: Track separatrices per triangle; only consider triangles containing at least one red and one blue line. 2. Define Vertices: Cell vertices are: Red-blue intersection points. Degenerate points. Intersections of tensorlines with the domain boundary. 3. Form Cells: Connect vertices to form curvilinear cells. Cells may lack degenerate points internally. 3. Adaptively Refine Cells: 1. Coarsening: Merge adjacent cells that do not exhibit enough structural information on their own. 2. Subdivision: Split cells that exceed defined criteria of similarity with respect to eigenvalue behavior by introducing new tensorlines. 3. Hanging Node Management: Use a growing strategy to merge or subdivide consecutive cells to minimize hanging nodes caused by divergence/convergence of tensor lines. Formulas: Degeneracy Condition: \lambda1 = \lambda2. Orthogonality: Eigenvectors v1, v2 are orthogonal (v1 \cdot v2 = 0) except at degenerate points. Parameters: Integration order: 4th order Runge-Kutta. Similarity criteria: Based on scalar invariants derived from eigenvalues. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Points: These are the only points where eigenvector trajectories can cross because eigenvectors are otherwise orthogonal. Hanging Nodes: Adaptive segmentation inevitably causes hanging nodes; a growing strategy is required to manage them. Interpolation: Eigenvector-based interpolation may lead to rare configurations of degenerate points compared to component-based interpolation. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures global features of the tensor field structure; handles the unique topology of symmetric tensors. Limitations: Requires careful handling of degenerate points and hanging nodes; adaptive refinement can be complex to implement. When to use: When analyzing the structural organization of symmetric tensor fields, such as in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI). The topological representation of symmetric second-order tensor fields was introduced by Lambertus Hesselink and Thierry Delmarcelle in 1994. The method is particularly relevant for visualizing neuroanatomy from DTI data, where it helps interpret water diffusion structures in the brain. name: Candy Cane Visualization
head: Candy cane, Polkagris, Polkagris visualization, Two Fields Visualization
body: Candy Cane Visualization is a multi-field direct volume rendering technique that simultaneously visualizes two distinct fields by assigning one field to control opacity and the other to control color. It specifically addresses the challenge of revealing the internal structure of vortical flow regions while preserving the directional information of the vorticity field. Unlike standard two-field visualization which may use independent transfer functions for both color and opacity for each field, Candy Cane Visualization couples the fields such that enstrophy defines the volumetric presence and a Line Integral Convolution texture of the vorticity field defines the surface appearance. This creates vortex tube structures that resemble "candy canes" or "polkagris". The method requires a velocity field \mathbf{u} as input. It computes two derived fields: the vorticity field \boldsymbol{\omega} and the enstrophy field \eta. It also requires a pre-computed or dynamically generated Seed LIC texture for the vorticity field. Inputs: 1. Velocity field \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) defined on a 3D grid. 2. Transfer function for opacity T{\eta}(\eta), mapping enstrophy values to opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. 3. Transfer function for color T{LIC}(\text{LIC}(\mathbf{x})), mapping LIC texture values to RGB color. Outputs: 1. A rendered image where vortex tubes are visible via opacity and colored by the directional flow structure via LIC. Data Structures: Velocity Field: 3D array of vectors \mathbf{u}. Vorticity Field: 3D array of vectors \boldsymbol{\omega}. Enstrophy Field: 3D array of scalars \eta. LIC Texture: 3D array of scalar values representing the convolved line integral intensity. Formulas: 1. Vorticity: The curl of the velocity field: \boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{u} 2. Enstrophy: The squared magnitude of the vorticity field: \eta = \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\|^2 = \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega} 3. LIC Texture: The Seed LIC texture is generated by convolving the velocity field with a kernel along streamlines. Steps: 1. Compute Vorticity: Calculate \boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla \times \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) for all grid points. 2. Compute Enstrophy: Calculate \eta(\mathbf{x}) = \|\boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x})\|^2 for all grid points. 3. Generate LIC Texture: Compute the Seed LIC texture for the vorticity field \boldsymbol{\omega}. 4. Map Enstrophy to Opacity: For each sample point \mathbf{x} during rendering, evaluate the opacity transfer function: \alpha(\mathbf{x}) = T{\eta}(\eta(\mathbf{x})). 5. Map LIC to Color: For each sample point \mathbf{x}, evaluate the color transfer function using the LIC texture value: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) = T{LIC}(\text{LIC}(\mathbf{x})). 6. Volume Rendering: Perform standard direct volume rendering using the computed opacity \alpha(\mathbf{x}) and color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) at each sample point along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def candycanevisualization(velocityfield, opacitytf, colortf, rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples): """ velocityfield: 3D array of vectors u(x,y,z) opacitytf: function mapping scalar enstrophy to opacity alpha colortf: function mapping scalar LIC value to RGB color rayorigin: 3D array of ray origins raydirection: 3D array of ray directions numsamples: integer number of samples per ray """ # Step 1: Compute Vorticity (curl of velocity) vorticityfield = computecurl(velocityfield) # Step 2: Compute Enstrophy (squared magnitude of vorticity) enstrophyfield = computesquaredmagnitude(vorticityfield) # Step 3: Generate Seed LIC Texture for Vorticity lictexture = computeseedlic(vorticityfield) # Step 4 & 5 & 6: Ray casting with direct volume rendering image = np.zeroslike(rayorigin[:,:, 0]) # Grayscale placeholder for alpha compositing colorimage = np.zeros((rayorigin.shape[:2], 3)) for i in range(rayorigin.shape[0]): for j in range(rayorigin.shape[1]): origin = rayorigin[i, j] direction = raydirection[i, j] accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for k in range(numsamples): t = k / numsamples point = origin + t direction # Sample fields at point (interpolation assumed) etaval = sample3d(enstrophyfield, point) licval = sample3d(lictexture, point) # Map to opacity and color alpha = opacitytf(etaval) color = colortf(licval) # Front-to-back compositing weight = alpha np.exp(-accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += weight color accumulatedalpha += weight colorimage[i, j] = accumulatedcolor return colorimage def computecurl(vectorfield): """Computes the curl of a 3D vector field using central differences.""" # Standard central difference approximation for curl on a uniform grid ux, uy, uz = vectorfield[..., 0], vectorfield[..., 1], vectorfield[..., 2] curlx = np.gradient(uz, axis=1) - np.gradient(uy, axis=2) curly = np.gradient(ux, axis=2) - np.gradient(uz, axis=0) curlz = np.gradient(uy, axis=0) - np.gradient(ux, axis=1) return np.stack([curlx, curly, curlz], axis=-1) def computesquaredmagnitude(vectorfield): """Computes the squared magnitude of a 3D vector field.""" # Dot product of vector with itself return np.sum(vectorfield 2, axis=-1) def computeseedlic(vectorfield): """Computes the Seed LIC texture for a 3D vector field.""" # Integration of a kernel along streamlines defined by the vector field # The exact integration algorithm is not given in the sources. # A 3x3 smoothing kernel is applied to smear field lines outwards, # making strokes thicker and smoother to improve 3D perception. raise NotImplementedError("Streamline integration algorithm not provided in sources.") def sample3d(field3d, point): """Samples a 3D field at a continuous point using trilinear interpolation.""" # Standard trilinear interpolation from grid coordinates coords = np.floor(point).astype(int) weights = point - coords # Boundary clamping assumed return np.interp(point, [0, 1], [0, 1]) # Placeholder for actual interpolation logic Parameters: LIC Kernel: A smoothing kernel (e.g., 3x3 filter) is used to smear field lines outwards, making strokes thicker and smoother to improve 3D perception. Transfer Functions: Specific transfer functions for enstrophy (opacity) and LIC (color) are required. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Computing the curl and squared magnitude requires careful handling of numerical precision, especially near boundaries or in regions of low velocity. Degenerate Input: If the velocity field is zero or has no vorticity, the enstrophy will be zero and the LIC texture will be undefined or uniform, resulting in no visible structure. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively visualizes vortex tubes by combining structural information (enstrophy) with directional information (LIC). Limitations: The technique requires pre-computation of the LIC texture and enstrophy field before rendering. When to Use: When visualizing vortical structures in flow fields where both the intensity of rotation (enstrophy) and the direction of rotation (vorticity/LIC) are important. When Not to Use: When the flow field has no significant vorticity. The Candy Cane Visualization technique was introduced in the context of visualizing vector fields using Seed LIC and Volume Rendering. It is also known as "polkagris" visualization, a term derived from Norwegian. The method was developed to address the limitations of visualizing multiple fields simultaneously, specifically by leveraging the strengths of LIC for directional information and volume rendering for structural information. The technique is particularly useful in fluid dynamics for analyzing vortex tubes. name: Continuous Indexed Points for Multivariate Volume Visualization
head: Indexed Points Computation, Indexed points calculation, Parallel coordinates indexed points
body: Continuous indexed points is a technique for multivariate volume visualization that encodes local correlations of multi-attribute data by representing linear structures in parallel coordinates. It improves spatial perception and interactive exploration by visualizing local linear fitting results as a density representation of indexed points in a continuous domain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multivariate volume dataset \tau: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m (typically n=3 for volumetric data). Output: A volume-rendered image with interactive multivariate transfer function widgets operating in the parallel coordinates image plane. Data Structures: Hierarchical Spatial Data Structure: An octree used to accelerate local neighborhood queries for principal component analysis (PCA). It stores reconstructed local linear information (\xi, e1, e2) for every sample in a new multivariate volume. 1-flat and 2-flat Indexed Points: Represent linear structures where a 1-flat corresponds to a line (correlation between two variables) and a 2-flat corresponds to a plane (correlation between three variables). Steps: 1. Saliency Map and Octree Construction: Compute a saliency map Sf(x) = \zeta(x) S(x) by convolving the gradient magnitude S(x) with a low-pass filter \zeta. Build an octree where a node subdivides if the value range of Sf in the region exceeds threshold ts. 2. Local Linear Fitting: For each volume sample \mathbf{x}, perform local PCA on its spatial neighborhood to extract the data value \xi = \tau(\mathbf{x}) and eigenvector matrix X \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times m}. If a leaf node's variance is below threshold te, reuse the node's linear fit for all samples within it. 3. 1-flat Indexed Points: Compute \eta{1,2}, \dots, \eta{m-1,m} by projecting \xi and \xi+e1 to all (m-1) 2D subspaces spanned by adjacent attribute pairs in parallel coordinates. 4. 2-flat Indexed Points: Compute \eta{1,2,3}, \dots, \eta{m-2,m-1,m} by calculating the normal vector n = e1 \times e2, then projecting \xi and \xi+n to all (m-2) 3D subspaces visualized as points on 2D image planes. 5. Angle-Uniform Transformation: Apply an angle-uniform transformation to bound and symmetrize the indexed points for visualization. 6. Density Representation: Generate a density representation using kernel density estimation (KDE) with dynamic bandwidth. The density \rho(\boldsymbol{\tau}) on the image domain is computed using geometric measure theory as \rho(\boldsymbol{\tau}) = \frac{s(x)}{|\text{Vol}(Dh)(x)|} integrated over h^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\tau}) with respect to d^{(n-2)}x. 7. Rendering and Interaction: Render the volume using an interactive occlusion shading model to facilitate spatial perception of volumetric correlation characteristics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def continuousindexedpoints(volumedata, m, n=3, ts=0.0, te=0.0): # Step 1: Saliency map and Octree construction gradientmagnitude = computegradientmagnitude(volumedata) saliencymap = convolvelowpass(gradientmagnitude) octree = buildoctree(saliencymap, ts) indexedpoints1flat = [] indexedpoints2flat = [] # Step 2: Local PCA and reconstruction for leaf in octree.leaves(): neighbors = leaf.getspatialneighbors() xi, e1, e2 = localpca(neighbors, volumedata) samples = leaf.getsamples() if leaf.variance < te else [leaf.center] for x in samples: # Step 3: 1-flat indexed points (2 variables) for i in range(m - 1): p1 = projectto2dsubspace(xi, i, i+1) p2 = projectto2dsubspace(xi + e1, i, i+1) indexedpoints1flat.append((p1, p2)) # Step 4: 2-flat indexed points (3 variables) nvec = crossproduct(e1, e2) for i in range(m - 2): q1 = projectto3dsubspace(xi, i, i+1, i+2) q2 = projectto3dsubspace(xi + nvec, i, i+1, i+2) indexedpoints2flat.append((q1, q2)) # Step 5: Angle-uniform transformation bounded1flat = angleuniformtransform(indexedpoints1flat) bounded2flat = angleuniformtransform(indexedpoints2flat) # Step 6: Density representation via KDE densitymap = computekdedensity(bounded1flat + bounded2flat, dynamicbandwidth=True) # Density formula: rho(tau) = s(x) / |Vol(Dh)(x)| integrated over h^{-1}(tau) w.r.t d^{(n-2)}x finaldensity = applygeometricmeasuretheory(densitymap) # Step 7: Rendering and interaction image = rendervolumewithocclusion(volumedata, finaldensity) widgets = createparallelcoordinateswidgets(bounded1flat, bounded2flat) return image, widgets def computegradientmagnitude(data): return standardgradient(data) def convolvelowpass(data): return standardconvolution(data, gaussiankernel) def buildoctree(saliency, threshold): return standardoctreeconstruction(saliency, threshold) def localpca(neighbors, data): return standardpca(neighbors.values) def projectto2dsubspace(point, axisi, axisj): return standardprojection(point, [axisi, axisj]) def projectto3dsubspace(point, axisi, axisj, axisk): return standardprojection(point, [axisi, axisj, axisk]) def crossproduct(v1, v2): return standardcrossproduct(v1, v2) def angleuniformtransform(points): return standardangleuniformmapping(points) def computekdedensity(points, bandwidth): return standardkde(points, bandwidth) def applygeometricmeasuretheory(density): return standardgeometricintegration(density) def rendervolumewithocclusion(vol, density): return standardvolumerendering(vol, density, occlusionshading=True) def createparallelcoordinateswidgets(p1, p2): return standardwidgetcreation(p1, p2) Parameters: Flat Dimensionality: Supports 1-flat (two variables) and 2-flat (three variables). Spatial Neighborhood: Size/radius for PCA neighborhood is not given in the sources. Octree Subdivision Threshold (ts): A node is subdivided if the difference between the minimum and maximum values of Sf in the region is greater than ts. Variance Threshold (te): If a leaf node's variance is smaller than te, the linear fit computed for the node is reused for every sample within it. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: False Positives: Indexed points computed without spatial embedding result in a large number of false positives compared to the method with spatial embedding. Computational Cost: Computing local PCA for every volume sample is costly; the octree construction must consider every volume attribute because local PCA involves all m dimensions of the multivariate volume. Rendering Continuous Indexed Points is a visualization technique that encodes local correlation of multivariate volume data by representing linear structures in parallel coordinates using continuous indexed points. It improves multivariate volume visualization by providing directional occlusion shading for spatial perception and allowing users to classify features based on density patterns. It differs from its sibling, Multivariate Indexed Points Transfer Function, by focusing on the rendering of the indexed point layer itself within the parallel coordinate space rather than defining transfer functions for volume raycasting. This method defines the transfer function lookup mechanism for continuous indexed points, mapping multivariate volume data samples to color and opacity values via precomputed indexed point locations in image space. It solves the problem of efficiently applying multivariate transfer functions by avoiding costly on-the-fly local fitting transformations during rendering, instead relying on precomputed volumes that map spatial positions directly to indexed point coordinates. It differs from general multivariate transfer functions by utilizing a subspace-aware ID map to handle overlapping indexed points from different subspaces, distinguishing it from its sibling Rendering Continuous Indexed Points which focuses on the rasterization of the points themselves rather than the transfer function logic. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows analysis of multivariate volume data using eigenvector information from local spatial embeddings; supports identification of correlations between two and three variables; facilitates good spatial perception via occlusion shading. Limitations: Parallel coordinates are difficult to interpret when there is a large number of attributes involved. When to use: When analyzing local correlations in multi-attribute volume data and needing interactive exploration via parallel coordinates. When not to use: When the dataset has a very large number of attributes, making parallel coordinates hard to interpret. The method was introduced by Liang Zhou, Xinyi Gou, and Daniel Weiskopf in December 2025. It builds on earlier work in parallel coordinates interfaces for volume visualization, such as Pradhan, Bartz, and Mueller (2005), and extends it with dimensionality reduction techniques like LLE (Zhao and Kaufman, 2010) and MDS (Guo, Xiao, and Yuan, 2011). The technique is demonstrated through case studies, expert user studies, and domain expert feedback. name: Parallel Coordinates with Dimensionality Reduction
head: Pradhan et al. interface, Zhao and Kaufman system
body: A user interface technique for multivariate volume visualization that maps volumetric attributes to axes in Parallel Coordinates (PCs), where user-specified values act as control points. It addresses the difficulty of interpreting PCs with a large number of attributes by incorporating dimensionality reduction methods, such as Locally Linear Embedding (LLE), to project arbitrary dimensions into a 2D space for global data investigation and manipulation. It builds on Continuous Indexed Points for Multivariate Volume Visualization by providing a global exploration mechanism for the local correlations encoded therein. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multivariate volume data attributes; user-defined control points for specific attribute values. Output: A 2D projection of the high-dimensional attribute space allowing for global data investigation. Data Structures: Parallel Coordinates Plot: A set of parallel axes, one for each volumetric attribute. Control Points: User-defined values on specific axes. Dimensionality Reduction Projection: A 2D coordinate space derived from the high-dimensional data using algorithms like LLE or Multidimensional Scaling (MDS). Steps: 1. Map Attributes: Map each volumetric attribute of the dataset to a distinct axis in the Parallel Coordinates plot. 2. Set Control Points: The user specifies values for the attributes by placing control points on the corresponding axes. 3. Global Investigation (Zhao and Kaufman): Incorporate global data investigation by applying a dimensionality reduction method, specifically Locally Linear Embedding (LLE), to project the arbitrary dimensions of the data into a 2D space. This allows the user to manipulate widgets in the 2D space to explore global correlations. 4. Alternative Global Investigation (Guo, Xiao, and Yuan): Use Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) to generate scatter plots for global data investigation. Formulas: LLE (Locally Linear Embedding): The sources cite Roweis and Saul (2000) for LLE but do not provide the mathematical formulation. MDS (Multidimensional Scaling): The sources cite Kruskal (1964) for MDS but do not provide the mathematical formulation. Parameters: Dimensionality Reduction Method: LLE or MDS. Number of Dimensions: Arbitrary, but PCs are noted as difficult to interpret when a large number of attributes are involved. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpretability: PCs are difficult to interpret when a large number of attributes are involved. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializeparallelcoordinates(attributes): """ Map each volumetric attribute to an axis in the Parallel Coordinates plot. """ axes = [] for attr in attributes: axes.append(Axis(attr)) return axes def setcontrolpoints(axes, uservalues): """ User specifies values for attributes by placing control points on axes. uservalues: dict mapping attribute name to value """ for attrname, value in uservalues.items(): for axis in axes: if axis.name == attrname: axis.addcontrolpoint(value) break def applydimensionalityreduction(data, method='LLE'): """ Project high-dimensional data into 2D space for global investigation. method: 'LLE' for Locally Linear Embedding, 'MDS' for Multidimensional Scaling """ if method == 'LLE': # LLE algorithm as described by Roweis and Saul (2000) # 1. Find k-nearest neighbors for each data point. # 2. Compute reconstruction weights that best reconstruct each point from its neighbors. # 3. Find low-dimensional embedding that preserves these reconstruction weights. projection = llealgorithm(data) elif method == 'MDS': # MDS algorithm as described by Kruskal (1964) # 1. Compute distance matrix between all data points. # 2. Find coordinates in lower-dimensional space that preserve these distances. projection = mdsalgorithm(data) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported dimensionality reduction method") return projection def visualize(axes, projection): """ Render the Parallel Coordinates plot and the 2D projection. """ renderparallelcoordinates(axes) render2dprojection(projection) A visualization technique used to present many metrics simultaneously, allowing quick comparison between nodes and outlier spotting, chosen over scatter plots or bar charts to minimize occlusion. Users can interact by rearranging and scaling the axes and brushing the poly-lines for selection. Each poly-line in the plot represents the metrics for one frame. The history of frames kept in the plot is 20 to reduce clutter and overdraw. Collecting metrics and rendering the plot on one node takes approximately 10 ms for the sort-first approach on five display nodes. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Collecting metrics and rendering the parallel coordinates plot on one node takes approximately 10 ms for the sort-first approach on five display nodes. Memory: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On five display nodes using a sort-first approach, metric collection and rendering take ~10 ms per node. With sort-last volume rendering, metric collection is negligible (4 bytes per metric per frame per node) relative to image data, but the resulting plot may become unreadable due to the increased number of nodes. Scaling: The approach scales to multiple display nodes, but advanced techniques (density-based approaches, clustering, bundling) are required when the number of nodes providing metrics is large to maintain readability. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Minimizes occlusion of the application; allows quick comparison of metrics between nodes and outlier spotting; distinct patterns between dimension axes help identify relations between metrics. Limitations: Can become unreadable with a large number of nodes providing metrics; requires advanced techniques for large-scale distributed systems. When to Use: Use for exploratory performance analysis and tuning of parallel interactive volume visualization on large displays. Use when minimizing occlusion of the application is critical. When Not to Use: Not suitable for post-mortem analysis if real-time collection overhead is a concern, although post-mortem approaches can offload metrics. Not suitable for large-scale distributed systems without advanced techniques like clustering or bundling. The concept was introduced by Pradhan, Bartz, and Mueller (2005) as a user interface of Parallel Coordinates where each volumetric attribute is an axis and the specified value is a control point. Zhao and Kaufman (2010) developed a complementary system that incorporates global data investigation using Locally Linear Embedding (LLE). Guo, Xiao, and Yuan (2011) utilized scatter plots generated by Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) for a similar purpose. The technique is used in the context of multivariate volume visualization to support the definition of multidimensional transfer functions. name: Rendering Continuous Indexed Points
head: Indexed points rendering, Parallel coordinates visualization
body: Rendering Continuous Indexed Points is a visualization technique that represents linear structures in parallel coordinates using continuous indexed points to visualize multivariate volumes. It improves multivariate volume visualization by providing directional occlusion shading for good spatial perception and allowing users to classify features based on density patterns. It differs from its sibling, Multivariate Indexed Points Transfer Function, by focusing on the rendering of the indexed point layer within the parallel coordinate space rather than defining transfer functions for volume raycasting. The method maps multivariate data to parallel coordinates, computes density in subspaces, and renders these densities as a continuous indexed point layer overlaid on the parallel axes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multivariate volume data; parallel coordinate axes definitions; user-defined parameters (gamma contrast, blending weight). Output: Composite image containing the parallel coordinate plot with the alpha-blended indexed point layer. Data Structures: High Dynamic Range (HDR) Image Buffer: A floating-point buffer storing the density \rho(\eta) for each pixel in the parallel coordinate subspace. Discrete Categorical Colormap: A lookup table mapping subspace indices to specific colors, visually positioned below the label of the parallel axes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercontinuousindexedpoints(subspaces, axes, gamma, alpha): # 1. Store continuous indexed points for each subspace in an HDR image buffer hdrbuffer = allocatehdrbuffer(axes.resolution) for subspace in subspaces: computedensity(subspace, hdrbuffer) # Stores ρ(η) # 2. Logarithmic transformation and normalization vmin = min(hdrbuffer) vmax = max(hdrbuffer) normalizedbuffer = emptylike(hdrbuffer) for pixel in hdrbuffer: vlog = log(pixel.value) # ρ(η) normalizedbuffer[pixel] = (vlog - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) # 3. Color mapping indexedpointlayer = emptylike(normalizedbuffer, dtype=color) for pixel in normalizedbuffer: subspaceidx = getsubspaceindex(pixel) indexedpointlayer[pixel] = discretecategoricalcolormap[subspaceidx][normalizedbuffer[pixel]] # 4. Gamma correction gammacorrectedlayer = indexedpointlayer (1.0 / gamma) # 5. Alpha blending originalplot = loadparallelcoordinatesplot() composite = alpha gammacorrectedlayer + (1.0 - alpha) originalplot return composite Formulas: Logarithmic transformation: v' = \log(\rho(\eta)). Normalization: v{\text{norm}} = \frac{v' - v{\min}}{v{\max} - v{\min}}. Gamma correction: v{\text{final}} = v{\text{norm}}^{1/\gamma}. Alpha blending: C{\text{out}} = \alpha C{\text{indexed}} + (1 - \alpha) C{\text{original}}. Parameters: Gamma (\gamma): User-controlled slider to change contrast. Blending Weight (\alpha): User-changeable weight for alpha blending. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density: If \rho(\eta) = 0, the logarithm is undefined. The implementation must clamp to a small epsilon or treat as zero density before applying the logarithm. Dynamic Range: The use of an HDR buffer is critical to preserve density information before normalization. Using a low dynamic range buffer would lose detail in high-density regions. This variant uses lasso widgets to classify features in the volume based on the patterns of continuous indexed points. The classification links to scatterplots via brushing-and-linking to verify feature separation. It allows users to interactively select regions in the parallel coordinate space and see the corresponding volume features. Data domain computation yields more spread-out signatures than spatial domain computation, but may select noisy samples that act as false positives. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires an HDR image buffer proportional to the resolution of the parallel coordinate plot. Strengths: Provides directional occlusion shading for spatial perception; enables interactive feature classification with lasso widgets; supports verification via brushing-and-linking with scatterplots. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Visualizing multivariate volume data to identify local linear correlations and directional patterns. When not to use: When spatial domain computation is preferred, as data domain computation may introduce noise and false positives. The method was introduced by L. Zhou, X. Gou, and D. Weiskopf in the paper "Continuous Indexed Points for Multivariate Volume Visualization". It is used in the context of multivariate volume visualization to enhance the understanding of local linear information and directional occlusion shading. name: Multivariate Indexed Points Transfer Function
head: Volume rendering with indexed points TF
body: This method defines the transfer function lookup mechanism for continuous indexed points, mapping multivariate volume data samples to color and opacity values via precomputed indexed point locations in image space. It solves the problem of efficiently applying multivariate transfer functions by avoiding costly on-the-fly local fitting transformations during rendering, instead relying on precomputed volumes that map spatial positions directly to indexed point coordinates. It differs from general multivariate transfer functions by utilizing a subspace-aware ID map to handle overlapping indexed points from different subspaces, distinguishing it from its sibling Rendering Continuous Indexed Points which focuses on the rasterization of the points themselves rather than the transfer function logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric sample value at spatial location \mathbf{x}; precomputed indexed point volume; ID map; color and opacity maps; subspace ID (sID); transfer function ID (tID). Output: Final color and opacity for the fragment. Data Structures: 1. Indexed Point Volume: A 3D volume where each voxel stores the 2D indexed point location \eta corresponding to the spatial location \mathbf{x}. This volume is precomputed for a fixed axis order of the parallel coordinates. 2. ID Map: A 3D volume storing two identifiers for each indexed point \eta. Subspace ID (sID): Distinguishes subspaces in overlapping regions. Transfer Function ID (tID): Identifies and links specific transfer functions. 3. Color and Opacity Maps: 2D lookup tables indexed by \eta, sID, and tID. Steps: 1. Sample: Sample the multivariate data at spatial location \mathbf{x}. 2. Retrieve Indexed Point: Look up the precomputed indexed point location \eta from the Indexed Point Volume at \mathbf{x}. This avoids computing the local fitting information (\xi, \mathbf{X}) transformation for every fragment, which is computationally expensive. 3. Retrieve IDs: Look up the Subspace ID (sID) and Transfer Function ID (tID) from the ID Map at \mathbf{x}. 4. Lookup Transfer Function: Use \eta, sID, and tID to index into the color and opacity maps. If sID = -1 (default), the widget applies across all subspaces. If multiple transfer functions are active, they are combined: Default: OR-operation of brushes. Linked: If tID is used, transfer functions with the same tID are joined using an AND operation. 5. Output: Return the resulting color and opacity. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: sID (Subspace ID): Default value is -1, indicating the widget lives in the image plane across all subspaces. tID (Transfer Function ID): Used to link transfer functions for AND operations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Computing the transformation from local fitting information (\xi, \mathbf{X}) to \eta for every fragment is costly. The method mitigates this by precomputing indexed points for a given axis order. Overlapping Subspaces: Indexed points of positive correlations may overlap with neighboring subspaces. The ID map is required to distinguish these using sID. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lookupmultivariatetf(x, indexedpointvol, idmap, colormap, opacitymap): """ x: 3D spatial coordinate indexedpointvol: 3D volume mapping x -> 2D indexed point eta idmap: 3D volume mapping x -> (sID, tID) colormap: 4D lookup table indexed by (etax, etay, sID, tID) opacitymap: 4D lookup table indexed by (etax, etay, sID, tID) """ # Step 1 & 2: Retrieve precomputed indexed point location eta = indexedpointvol[x] # Step 3: Retrieve IDs from ID map sID, tID = idmap[x] # Step 4: Lookup color and opacity using eta, sID, and tID color = colormap[eta.x, eta.y, sID, tID] opacity = opacitymap[eta.x, eta.y, sID, tID] # Step 5: Return results for accumulation return color, opacity This is the specific lookup process that realizes the multivariate transfer functions using a lookup table. It requires color/opacity maps and an ID map to handle overlapping indexed points from different subspaces. Transfer functions are constructed using the OR-operation of brushes by default, or linked via tID for AND operations. The ID map stores both sID and tID for each indexed point \eta. Time and Memory Complexity: Precomputation: The time to compute indexed points volumes depends on the subdivision threshold (ts), eigenvector interpolation threshold (te), and dataset noise. Octrees are effective in reducing computation time for certain datasets. Rendering: The lookup is O(1) per fragment, assuming precomputed volumes are available. Measured Performance: Measured on a machine with 3.5 GHz Intel i7 CPU, 32 GB main memory, and NVIDIA Quadro P6000 graphics card. Data processed with a neighborhood size of 7 \times 7 \times 7 voxels after normalization. Specific timing values vary with thresholds and noise. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables flexible parallel coordinates manipulations (e.g., changing axis order) without per-fragment fitting costs. Handles overlapping subspaces effectively. Limitations: Precomputation is required for a fixed axis order; changing axis order may require recomputation. When to Use: Use when visualizing multivariate volume data with linear structures and local correlations, especially when interactive manipulation of parallel coordinates is desired. This method is part of the "Continuous Indexed Points for Multivariate Volume Visualization" technique, which represents linear structures in parallel coordinates to encode local correlation of multivariate volume data. It addresses the limitation of traditional gradient-based shading in multivariate volumes by providing a shading model that does not rely on gradients, which are undefined for general multivariate attributes. name: Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization
head: Glyphs, Vector Glyphs, Tensor Glyphs
body: Glyph-based visualization maps vector or tensor field values at discrete sample points to geometric primitives placed in space, allowing the viewer to perceive local field properties such as direction, magnitude, and anisotropy through shape and orientation. It differs from line-integral methods like Stream Lines by providing discrete, point-wise sampling rather than continuous trajectories, and from domain coloring by using explicit 3D geometry rather than scalar color mapping on surfaces. Builds on Multi-field, vector and tensor volume visualization Shared principles. Represents vectors as simple line segments. Distinguished by extreme computational efficiency and low memory usage, allowing millions of glyphs, but suffers from direction ambiguity and poor 3D orientation perception due to lack of shading. Uses arrow-shaped primitives (cone + shaft) to explicitly encode flow direction. Distinguished by resolving the direction ambiguity of line glyphs and allowing for 3D shading, implemented on GPU for performance, but requires more memory and computation per glyph. An iterative packing algorithm for tensor glyphs using Delaunay triangulation to optimize placement and avoid overlap. Distinguished by its focus on interactive placement and clustering acceleration for complex tensor fields. Maps scalar error metrics to texture attributes (shape, size, blur, or transparency) applied directly to mesh facets generated by marching cubes. Distinguished from vector field glyphs because it represents scalar confidence intervals on a static surface rather than field direction and magnitude. Objects at every data point representing scalar, vectorial, or tensorial information (eigenvalues/eigenvectors) to overcome the limitation of colormaps displaying only three metrics. Definition: Display B-field direction vectors over the splat field with a local 'Directional Pulse' animation for direction reading. Steps: Render B-field direction vectors. Apply 'Directional Pulse' local animation as a visual cue for direction. Pitfall: Directional Pulse is a visual cue only, not a time-evolution simulation. Definition: Simplifying the diffusion tensor model to display only the principal eigenvector for each voxel to represent connectivity. Steps: Express the diffusion tensor T as a linear sum of outer products of its principal components using tensors of rank 1 \le i \le 3, Ti. For tracking/display, use the rank 1 (line) case where diffusion has taken place anisotropically in the direction e1. Formula: T = (\lambda1 - \lambda2)T1 + (\lambda2 - \lambda3)T2 + \lambda3 T3, where \lambdai are the eigenvalues, and Ti = ei ej^T are the sum of the outer product of eigenvectors respectively. v(r) = f(r)e1(r), where f can be any appropriate scalar measure e.g. \lambda1 = \sumi \lambdai. Glyph-based visualization is a foundational technique in scientific visualization, originating from the need to visualize vector fields in fluid dynamics and electromagnetism. Early work established the use of arrows and lines for vector fields. The technique has evolved to include complex tensor glyphs (e.g., ellipsoids for diffusion tensors) and GPU-accelerated implementations for real-time interaction. name: Line Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization
head: Line Glyphs, Vector Field Glyph Rendering, flow field display, vector arrow display
body: Line Glyphs is a visualization technique that represents a 3D vector field as a grid of line segments, where vector orientation and magnitude are encoded geometrically and chromatically. Unlike Arrow Glyphs, which use directional markers to resolve orientation ambiguity, Line Glyphs rely on color coding and interactive camera rotation to convey direction, offering significantly higher performance and memory efficiency for dense visualizations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D vector field texture storing vectors as float4 (x, y, z components and magnitude w); a 1D color transfer function texture mapping magnitude to color; grid dimensions (glyphsCount); world size (worldSize); and a fixed X-coordinate (x) defining the visualization plane. Output: Two arrays of vertices (outVertices) and colors (outColors). Each glyph produces two vertices (start and end) and two identical color values. Data Structures: vectorFieldTex: 3D texture, format float4. vectorMangitudeCtfTex: 1D texture, format float4 (RGBA). outVertices: Array of float3. Size is 2 \times N, where N is the number of glyphs. outColors: Array of float3. Size is 2 \times N. Parameters: glyphsCount: uint2 specifying the number of glyphs along the Y and Z axes, where glyphsCount.x maps to Y and glyphsCount.y maps to Z. worldSize: float2 specifying the physical span of the Y and Z axes, where worldSize.x maps to Y and worldSize.y maps to Z. x: float specifying the fixed X-coordinate for the visualization plane. Threshold: A user-defined magnitude threshold filters out stationary vectors or air to avoid visual clutter. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute the global thread ID id from block and thread indices. 2. Calculate the total number of glyphs totalCount as glyphsCount.x glyphsCount.y. 3. Check bounds: if id >= totalCount, terminate the thread. 4. Compute the Y and Z grid coordinates: y = (id \pmod{\text{glyphsCount.x}}) \times \frac{\text{worldSize.x}}{\text{glyphsCount.x}} z = \lfloor id / \text{glyphsCount.x} \rfloor \times \frac{\text{worldSize.y}}{\text{glyphsCount.y}} 5. Sample the vector field at (x, y, z) to obtain vector (x, y, z, w). 6. Compute the start vertex: \text{start} = (x, y, z). 7. Compute the end vertex: \text{end} = \text{start} + \text{normalize}(\text{vector}{xyz}) \times \text{vector}w. 8. Sample the color from the magnitude transfer function using the vector magnitude vector.w. 9. Assign the start and end vertices and colors to the output arrays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) if mag > 0 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def sample3dtexture(tex, x, y, z): # Performs trilinear interpolation or nearest-neighbor lookup on the 3D texture return tex[x, y, z] def sample1dtexture(tex, t): # Performs linear interpolation or nearest-neighbor lookup on the 1D texture return tex[t] def glyphlineskernel(blockidx, blockdim, threadidx, glyphscount, worldsize, xcoord, vectorfieldtex, magnitudectftex, outvertices, outcolors): id = blockidx.x blockdim.x + threadidx.x totalcount = glyphscount.x glyphscount.y if id >= totalcount: return y = (id % glyphscount.x) (worldsize.x / glyphscount.x) z = (id // glyphscount.x) (worldsize.y / glyphscount.y) vector = sample3dtexture(vectorfieldtex, xcoord, y, z) vertexidx = id 2 outvertices[vertexidx] = (xcoord, y, z) norm = normalize((vector.x, vector.y, vector.z)) outvertices[vertexidx + 1] = (xcoord + norm[0] vector.w, y + norm[1] vector.w, z + norm[2] vector.w) color = sample1dtexture(magnitudectftex, vector.w) outcolors[vertexidx] = (color.x, color.y, color.z) outcolors[vertexidx + 1] = (color.x, color.y, color.z) Color Encoding (Alternative/Supplementary): In some implementations, vector orientation is encoded directly into RGB channels rather than using a separate transfer function. For each component (vx, vy, vz), the color channel is calculated as: r = \frac{vx + \max(|vx|)}{2} with similar mappings for g and b, normalized to the appropriate range. This ensures vectors with the same orientation share the same color. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Direction Ambiguity: Line glyphs do not inherently indicate vector direction (head vs. tail). Shading Limitations: Lines lack surface normals for shading, making 3D orientation harder to perceive compared to arrows. Clutter: High density can lead to visual clutter. A threshold on vector magnitude is recommended to filter out stationary regions or noise. Performance: Extremely fast. Computation time for nearly any amount of glyphs is less than 20 ms, and nearly 13 million glyphs can be computed in 26 ms on an NVIDIA Quadro K5000. Memory Efficiency: Very high. Each glyph requires only one vector field query and stores two vertices and two colors. Scalability: Can render huge amounts of lines simultaneously, effectively creating a solid wall of glyphs to visualize magnitude fields. Strengths: High interactivity due to low computation time; suitable for real-time exploration; efficient for dense fields. Limitations: Ambiguous direction and length perception without color or interaction; hard to read in static views compared to arrows. When to use: When performance is critical, when the field is very dense, or when interactive camera rotation is available to resolve direction ambiguity. When not to use: When static, unambiguous direction representation is required without user interaction; use Arrow Glyphs instead. Line Glyphs were introduced as a simple, efficient method for visualizing 3D vector fields, particularly in the context of MRI vector and tensor fields (e.g., blood flow). The technique was further popularized in real-time CUDA-based visualizations of aerodynamic data (e.g., delta-wing airflow), where its speed allowed for interactive exploration of high-density fields. It serves as a foundational glyph-based method, often compared against Arrow Glyphs for its trade-off between performance and clarity. name: Uncertainty Visualization Using Glyphs
head: Error Glyph Mapping, Glyph-based Uncertainty Visualization
body: This method visualizes data uncertainty by mapping error values to visual properties of triangular facets generated during surface extraction. It solves the problem of conveying reliability information alongside geometry, allowing users to distinguish authentic data from noisy or interpolated regions. It differs from sibling methods like Line Glyphs or Arrow Glyphs, which encode vector direction and magnitude, by focusing exclusively on scalar error metrics. It differs from Uncertainty Visualization Using Blurring Texture and Uncertainty Visualization Using Transparency by using distinct geometric shapes or sizes rather than texture distortion or alpha blending, providing categorical or magnitude-based visual cues that are distinct from the underlying surface color. The core technique iterates over every triangular facet of the iso-surface. For each facet, an error value is computed, and this value determines the visual representation of the facet. Inputs: Triangular mesh (list of vertices and faces). Per-vertex error values (scalar fields). Base texture or glyph set. Outputs: Rendered image where each triangular facet displays a visual cue corresponding to its error level. Vertex: Contains position (x, y, z) and error value ev. Face: Contains indices to three vertices v1, v2, v3. Glyph Set: A collection of textures or geometric primitives. In the primary implementation, this includes: Set 1: Distinct shapes (triangle, diamond, rectangular, trapezoidal, crescent, round, heart, pentagram). Set 2: Shapes with varying sizes (e.g., gradient shapes of the moon). Base state: Solid color texture for error-free or low-error data. 1. Iterate over every triangular facet in the mesh. 2. Calculate Error: Compute the error value for the facet using a weighted average of the errors from the three vertices. Let e1, e2, e3 be the error values of the three vertices. The facet error Ef is calculated as: Ef = \frac{w1 e1 + w2 e2 + w3 e3}{w1 + w2 + w3} Where wi are weights. The exact weighting formula is not specified in the sources. 3. Map Error to Visual: Map the calculated error Ef to a specific visual property based on the chosen variant (Glyphs, Blurring, or Transparency). For Glyphs: Select a glyph texture or shape from the predefined set based on the magnitude of Ef. For Blurring: Determine the blurring level corresponding to Ef. For Transparency: Normalize Ef to the range [0, 1] and assign it to the alpha component. 4. Render: Map the selected visual property (glyph texture, blurred texture, or alpha value) to the triangular facet during rendering. Glyph Set 1: Uses distinct shapes to distinguish error levels apparently. Shapes include: triangle, diamond, rectangular, trapezoidal, crescent, round, heart, pentagram. Glyph Set 2: Uses shapes with different sizes (gradient shapes of the moon) to allow easier perception of error levels. Low Error Representation: Error-free or low-error data is represented by a solid color texture. Blurring Scales: 11 scales mapping error ranges. Clearest texture: Error range 0.0 to 18.18. Most blurring texture: Error range > 181.81. Intermediate scales are gradient from top to bottom (most blurring to clearest). Texture Pre-processing: Blurring effects can be pre-processed using tools like Photoshop or generated by a user-defined program. Graphical Overload: Using too many tiny triangular facets can cause graphical overload, making it difficult to get a fast overview of error patterns compared to blurring techniques. Interaction Requirement: Due to the potential for overload, interaction techniques (rotation, translation, zooming) are recommended to inspect individual facet errors. Vertex Error Source: The method relies on pre-existing vertex errors (e.g., from multi-resolution decomposition or measurement noise). The method itself does not compute the error but maps it. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamp(value, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(value, maxval)) def setfacetexture(faceidx, texture): """Assigns a texture to a face for rendering.""" pass def setfacergba(faceidx, r, g, b, a): """Assigns RGBA color values to a face for rendering.""" pass def renderuncertaintyglyphs(mesh, vertexerrors, glyphset, errorthresholds): """Renders a mesh with uncertainty visualization using glyphs.""" for face in mesh: v1, v2, v3 = face e1 = vertexerrors[v1] e2 = vertexerrors[v2] e3 = vertexerrors[v3] # Weighted average (uniform weights assumed when unspecified) faceterror = (e1 + e2 + e3) / 3.0 glyphindex = 0 for i, threshold in enumerate(errorthresholds): if faceterror < threshold: glyphindex = i break else: glyphindex = len(errorthresholds) setfacetexture(face, glyphset[glyphindex]) def renderuncertaintyblurring(mesh, vertexerrors, blurscales): """Renders a mesh with uncertainty visualization using blurring textures.""" for face in mesh: v1, v2, v3 = face e1 = vertexerrors[v1] e2 = vertexerrors[v2] e3 = vertexerrors[v3] faceterror = (e1 + e2 + e3) / 3.0 blurtexture = blurscales[-1][2] for mine, maxe, tex in blurscales: if mine <= faceterror <= maxe: blurtexture = tex break setfacetexture(face, blurtexture) def renderuncertaintytransparency(mesh, vertexerrors, minerror=0.0, maxerror=1.0): """Renders a mesh with uncertainty visualization using transparency.""" for face in mesh: v1, v2, v3 = face e1 = vertexerrors[v1] e2 = vertexerrors[v2] e3 = vertexerrors[v3] # Normalize error to [0, 1] n1 = clamp((e1 - minerror) / (maxerror - minerror), 0.0, 1.0) n2 = clamp((e2 - minerror) / (maxerror - minerror), 0.0, 1.0) n3 = clamp((e3 - minerror) / (maxerror - minerror), 0.0, 1.0) # Map normalized error to alpha component # The more opaque the facet is, the more reliable the data is a1 = 1.0 - n1 a2 = 1.0 - n2 a3 = 1.0 - n3 setfacergba(face, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, a1) Maps error information to blurring levels of a texture applied to triangular facets; higher error results in more blurring. It uses 11 scales mapping error ranges from 0.0-18.18 (clearest) to >181.81 (most blurring). Textures can be pre-processed using Photoshop or generated by a user-defined blurring program. It is advantageous over glyphs for avoiding graphical overload when dealing with many tiny facets. Maps error values to the transparency (alpha component) of triangular facets; higher error results in lower opacity. It normalizes vertex errors to [0, 1] and maps them to the alpha component of RGBA. The more opaque the triangular facet is, the more reliable the data is and vice versa. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangular facets N, O(N), as it iterates once over the mesh to compute errors and assign visual properties. Memory Complexity: Linear, O(N), to store the mesh and error values. Additional memory is required for the glyph/texture sets, which is constant relative to N. Performance: Implemented in C++ using OpenGL and GLUT on a dual processor 2.4GHz laptop with an ATI 3450 graphics card (256MB memory). Strengths: Provides immediate visual feedback on data reliability. Glyphs with distinct shapes allow categorical distinction of error levels. Limitations: Can cause graphical overload if the mesh has too many tiny triangular facets, obscuring the overall error pattern. Requires interaction (zoom/rotate) for detailed inspection. When to use: When categorical distinction of error levels is preferred over continuous gradients, or when texture distortion (blurring) is undesirable. When not to use: When the mesh is extremely dense and performance or visual clarity of the overall structure is prioritized over per-facet error inspection. Originated in research on visualizing uncertainty in multi-resolution volumetric data using the Marching Cubes algorithm. The work was presented in a paper discussing the application of blurring textures and glyph-based mappings to MRI human brain data sets. The implementation was based on low-level APIs (OpenGL/ GLUT) to allow control over the Marching Cubes algorithm and rendering. Visualizing uncertainty in multi-resolution volumetric data using marching cubes, https://doi.org/10.1145/2254556.2254649, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Diffusion Tensor Principal Eigenvector Display
head: principal eigenvector display, rank 1 tensor display
body: This method simplifies the diffusion tensor model to display only the principal eigenvector for each voxel, representing local connectivity and anisotropy. It reduces full tensor information to a dominant directional component suitable for direct rendering or tracking, differing from full tensor glyphs like Tensor Glyphs by focusing exclusively on the primary diffusion direction. Inputs: A diffusion tensor field T(\vec{r}) over a 3D volume, where each voxel stores a symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix. Outputs: A derived vector field \vec{v}(\vec{r}) per voxel for rendering or tracking. Data Structures: Input Tensor: Stored as 6 unique components per voxel or a 3 \times 3 matrix. Eigen Decomposition: Yields eigenvalues \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0 and orthogonal eigenvectors \vec{e}1, \vec{e}2, \vec{e}3. Output Vector: A 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3). Steps: 1. Eigen Decomposition: For each voxel, compute eigenvalues \lambdai and eigenvectors \vec{e}i of T. 2. Select Principal Component: Identify \vec{e}1 corresponding to the largest eigenvalue \lambda1, representing the direction of maximum diffusion. 3. Compute Scalar Modulator: Calculate a scalar measure f(\vec{r}) to weight the vector magnitude, such as \lambda1 or the trace \sum{i=1}^3 \lambdai. 4. Construct Vector Field: Compute the display vector \vec{v}(\vec{r}) = f(\vec{r})\vec{e}1(\vec{r}), treating the tensor as a rank-1 tensor aligned with \vec{e}1. Formulas: The diffusion tensor decomposes as T = (\lambda1 - \lambda2)T1 + (\lambda2 - \lambda3)T2 + \lambda3 T3, where Ti = \vec{e}i \vec{e}i^T. For display, \vec{v}(\vec{r}) = f(\vec{r})\vec{e}1(\vec{r}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeprincipaleigenvectordisplay(tensorfield): """ Computes the principal eigenvector display vector field from a diffusion tensor field. Args: tensorfield: A 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 6) representing symmetric diffusion tensors. Returns: vectorfield: A 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) containing the display vectors. """ Nx, Ny, Nz = tensorfield.shape[:3] vectorfield = [[[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(Nz)] for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] for x in range(Nx): for y in range(Ny): for z in range(Nz): # Extract tensor T at voxel (x,y,z) from 6 components [Txx, Tyy, Tzz, Txy, Txz, Tyz] c = tensorfield[x][y][z] T = [[c[0], c[3], c[4]], [c[3], c[1], c[5]], [c[4], c[5], c[2]]] # Eigen decomposition step eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eigendecompose3x3symmetric(T) # Sort eigenvalues and eigenvectors in descending order indices = sorted(range(3), key=lambda i: eigenvalues[i], reverse=True) eigenvalues = [eigenvalues[i] for i in indices] eigenvectors = [[eigenvectors[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in indices] # Principal eigenvector e1 e1 = eigenvectors[0] # Scalar measure f(r) (e.g., trace) f = sum(eigenvalues) # Construct display vector v = [f e1[0], f e1[1], f e1[2]] vectorfield[x][y][z] = v return vectorfield Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tensors: In regions where fibre tracts meet or cross, the tensor may be rank 2 or 3. The principal eigenvector display cannot optimally handle these points, as it assumes a single dominant direction. Precision: Numerical stability in eigen decomposition should be ensured, particularly for near-isotropic tensors where eigenvalues are close. Boundary Conditions: At volume boundaries, tensor estimation may be unreliable, leading to noisy eigenvectors. A visualization technique that maps the spatial direction of the principal eigenvector directly to RGB colors. The X, Y, and Z components of the principal eigenvector \vec{e}1 are mapped to the Red, Green, and Blue color channels, respectively. The saturation of the resulting RGB color is modulated by an anisotropic metric (e.g., Fractional Anisotropy, or CL/CP/CS metrics) to indicate the strength of anisotropy. This is useful for displaying spatial patterns of coherence, as the principal eigenvector aligns with coherent fibers. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Computationally efficient compared to full tensor rendering (e.g., ellipsoids). It simplifies the visual clutter of tensor data and is a direct prerequisite for streamline tractography. Limitations: Loses information about the shape of diffusion (e.g., planar vs. linear anisotropy) and cannot resolve crossing fibers. Structural boundaries may be harder to distinguish compared to anatomical or MIP images. When to use: When the primary goal is to visualize connectivity or dominant flow directions, or as an intermediate step for tracking algorithms. When not to use: When detailed microstructural information (shape of the diffusion ellipsoid) or crossing fiber resolution is required. This method is used in interactive visualization tools for MRI vector and tensor fields. It simplifies the ellipsoid model to displaying the principal eigenvector for each voxel to address connectivity questions. name: Tensor Glyphs
head: DT-MRI Glyphs, Eigenvalue-based Glyphs, Ellipsoid Glyphs, Superquadric Glyphs, Tensor Axes Glyphs
body: Tensor Glyphs are point-icon visualization techniques that represent scalar, vectorial, or tensorial information (specifically eigenvalues and eigenvectors) at every data point in space, overcoming the limitation of colormaps which can display only three distinct metrics or one direction per point. Unlike Ellipsoid Glyphs which suffer from ambiguity in projection, or Tensor Axes Glyphs which may be hard to distinguish, Tensor Glyphs map the tensor shape space (linear, planar, spherical) to geometric primitives that satisfy continuity, uniqueness, and unambiguity criteria. They are primarily used in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) to visualize the orientation and anisotropy of diffusion. Inputs: A 3×3 symmetric diffusion tensor D at each voxel. Outputs: Geometric glyphs (ellipsoids, superquadrics, cylinders, boxes, or spheres) positioned at voxel centers. Data Structures: Tensor Field: Array of 3×3 symmetric matrices. Stored as 6 floats per voxel (diagonal D{xx}, D{yy}, D{zz} and off-diagonals D{xy}, D{xz}, D{yz}). Eigen Decomposition: For each tensor, compute eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 and eigenvectors \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. Constraint: \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0. \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 are the major, medium, and minor eigenvectors, respectively. Numbered Steps: 1. Eigen Decomposition: For each tensor D, compute eigenvalues \lambdai and normalized eigenvectors \mathbf{v}i, ordered \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3 \ge 0. 2. Metric Calculation: Compute scalar anisotropy metrics CL, CP, CS using the formulas below. 3. Glyph Selection: Determine the glyph type based on the dominant metric: if CL is high (linear diffusion), render a cylinder oriented along \mathbf{v}1; if CS is high (isotropic diffusion), render a sphere; if CP is high (planar diffusion), render a box. Alternatively, use a single superquadric surface parameterized by CL, CP, CS to smoothly interpolate between these shapes. 4. Transformation: Transform a base glyph geometry G to the tensor glyph geometry GT using the rotation matrix R (formed by eigenvectors) and scaling by eigenvalues: GT = R^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} \lambda1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \lambda3 \end{pmatrix} R G. 5. Rendering: Render the transformed glyphs. For superquadrics, use GPU-based raytracing for efficiency. Formulas: Linear Anisotropy (CL): CL = \frac{\lambda1 - \lambda2}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Planar Anisotropy (CP): CP = \frac{2(\lambda2 - \lambda3)}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Spherical Anisotropy (CS): CS = \frac{3\lambda3}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} Note: CL + CP + CS = 1 Rotation Matrix: R = [\mathbf{v}1 | \mathbf{v}2 | \mathbf{v}3] Transformation: GT = R^{-1} S R G, where S = \text{diag}(\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3) Parameters: Thresholds for glyph selection are not explicitly defined in the sources; typical implementations use values around 0.6 for dominance. Display density must be kept low to avoid visual clutter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetensorglyph(tensorD): # 1. Eigen Decomposition (standard 3x3 symmetric solver) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = solveeigen3x3symmetric(tensorD) # Sort descending: lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3 idx = argsortdescending(eigenvalues) lambda1, lambda2, lambda3 = eigenvalues[idx] v1, v2, v3 = eigenvectors[:, idx] # 2. Calculate Scalar Metrics trace = lambda1 + lambda2 + lambda3 if trace == 0: return None, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) CL = (lambda1 - lambda2) / trace CP = 2.0 (lambda2 - lambda3) / trace CS = 3.0 lambda3 / trace # 3. Construct Rotation Matrix R R = columnstack((v1, v2, v3)) # 4. Construct Scaling Matrix S S = diag([lambda1, lambda2, lambda3]) # 5. Transformation Matrix T = R^-1 S R. Since R is orthogonal, R^-1 = R^T T = transpose(R) @ S @ R return T, (CL, CP, CS) def renderglyphs(tensorfield): for voxeltensor in tensorfield: T, metrics = computetensorglyph(voxeltensor) if T is None: continue CL, CP, CS = metrics # Glyph selection based on dominant metric if CL > 0.6: shape = 'cylinder' elif CS > 0.6: shape = 'sphere' elif CP > 0.6: shape = 'box' else: shape = 'superquadric' # Render primitive at voxel center with transformation T rasterizeorraytrace(shape, T) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unambiguity: Boxes/cuboids fail criterion (g3) because they are not distinguishable from every view direction. Ellipsoids also suffer from this ambiguity. Superquadrics are preferred as they meet all criteria (g1-g3). Visual Clutter: Display density must be kept low to avoid visual clutter when rendering many icons. Continuity: Minimal changes in neighboring tensors must not cause discontinuities in glyph geometry. Uniqueness: The mapping from tensor shape to glyph geometry must be unique. Provides a direct analytical expression for 2D rank-two tensors, ensuring invariance, uniqueness, and continuity, overcoming numerical interpolation constraints. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, for eigen decomposition and glyph placement. Rendering complexity depends on the glyph type; superquadrics require raytracing, which is more expensive than simple ellipsoids but manageable with GPU acceleration. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the tensor field and glyph parameters. Performance: Hlawitschka et al. introduced a fast, GPU-based raytracing method for superquadrics, allowing real-time rendering of thousands of glyphs. Strengths: Can display multiple metrics (direction, anisotropy type) simultaneously; unambiguous shape representation with superquadrics. Limitations: Visual clutter at high densities; computationally expensive for raytraced superquadrics compared to simple colormaps; ellipsoids are ambiguous. When to use: When understanding the local tensor shape (linear vs. planar vs. spherical) is critical, such as in DTI fiber tractography analysis. When not to use: When performance is critical and only dominant direction is needed (use Arrow Glyphs or Line Glyphs); when data density is very high. Tensor Glyphs were introduced to overcome the limitations of colormaps in displaying tensor information. Superquadrics, a specific type of tensor glyph, were introduced by A. H. Barr in 1981 and suggested for DTI visualization by Kindlmann in 2004. Hlawitschka et al. later optimized their rendering for GPUs. name: Analytical Tensor Glyph for Rank Two Tensors in a Plane
head: Analytic tensor glyph visualization, Analytical Symmetric Tensor Glyph Generation, Analytical Tensor Glyph Visualization in a Plane, Rank two tensor component derivation in a plane
body: This method provides a direct analytical expression for visualizing rank-two tensors in a 2D plane, generating omnidirectional graphical representations (glyphs) that are accurate and unambiguous. Unlike numerical interpolation methods which may fail to preserve tensor invariants, this approach satisfies strict requirements including invariance under isometric domain transformation, scaling invariance, direct encoding of real eigenvalues/eigenvectors, glyph uniqueness, and continual glyph changes. It overcomes the numerical constraints of existing imaging methods by analytically solving for tensor components at arbitrary rotation angles using eigenvalues and invariants. Inputs and Outputs Input: A rank-two tensor matrix B in 2D space, defined by four components b{ij}. Output: A set of symmetric tensor components (a{11}, a{12}, a{21}, a{22}) for any rotation angle \phi, allowing the construction of a glyph representing the tensor's shape in all directions. Data Structures The tensor is represented as a 2 \times 2 matrix. For a general tensor B: B = \begin{bmatrix} b{11} & b{12} \\ b{21} & b{22} \end{bmatrix} The method decomposes B into a symmetric part TS and an antisymmetric part TA: TS = \begin{bmatrix} a{11} & a{12} \\ a{21} & a{22} \end{bmatrix}, \quad TA = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & c{12} \\ c{21} & 0 \end{bmatrix} where a{ij} are symmetric components and c{ij} are antisymmetric components. Steps 1. Decomposition: Decompose the general tensor B into symmetric TS and antisymmetric TA parts: a{ij} = \frac{1}{2}(b{ij} + b{ji}) c{ij} = \frac{1}{2}(b{ij} - b{ji}) The method focuses the analytical calculation solely on the symmetric tensor TS, as the antisymmetric part TA does not depend on the symmetric part's size and simplifies the visualization. 2. Calculate Invariants: Compute the first invariant (trace m), second invariant (determinant n), and the third invariant (squared Frobenius norm l) from the symmetric components: m = a{11} + a{22} n = a{11}a{22} - a{12}a{21} l = a{11}^2 + a{22}^2 + 2a{12}a{21} = m^2 - 2n The third invariant l corresponds to the square of the initial vector's length and is necessary for the analytical calculation. 3. Solve for Eigenvalues: Solve the characteristic quadratic equation to find eigenvalues \lambda1 and \lambda2: \lambda^2 - m\lambda + n = 0 \lambda{1,2} = \frac{m \pm \sqrt{m^2 - 4n}}{2} To ensure real solutions, enforce \lambda1 \ge \lambda2. If the discriminant is negative, the roots are complex; the method requires swapping eigenvalues to satisfy \lambda1 > \lambda2 to ensure real solutions. 4. Determine Initial Angle: Calculate the initial angle \alpha for the vector r0(\lambda1, \lambda2): \alpha = \arctan\left(\frac{\lambda2}{\lambda1}\right) \quad \text{for } \alpha \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{4}\right] Typical values for the initial state are \alpha = 0^\circ or 45^\circ. At \alpha = 0^\circ, the maximum values of tensor component parts in the x-axis direction display the golden section ratio \phi \approx 0.618. 5. Calculate Rotation Angle: Determine the rotation angle \phi of the coordinate system using the eigenvector u(u1, u2) of the tensor: \tan \phi = \frac{u1}{u2} = \frac{-(a{11} - \lambda1)}{a{12}} 6. Compute Rotated Components: Solve the quadratic equation for the component a{22} at the rotation angle \phi: a{22}^{1,2} = \frac{(2\lambda2 \cot^2 \phi + m) \mp \sqrt{(2\lambda2 \cot^2 \phi + m)^2 - 4(1 + \cot^2 \phi)(n + \lambda2^2 \cot^2 \phi)}}{2(1 + \cot^2 \phi)} The quadratic yields two roots for a{22}; one corresponds to the initial tensor state and the other to the state rotated by angle \phi. The root corresponding to the rotated state is selected. 7. Derive Remaining Components: Calculate the remaining symmetric components using the solved a{22}: a{11} = \lambda1 + \lambda2 - a{22} a{21} = \cot \phi (\lambda1 - a{11}) a{12} = a{21} Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticaltensorglyph(tensormatrix, rotationanglephi): """ Computes symmetric rank-two tensor components at a given rotation angle phi. Args: tensormatrix: 2x2 list of lists [[b11, b12], [b21, b22]] rotationanglephi: float, rotation angle in radians Returns: list: [a11, a12, a21, a22] components of the symmetric tensor at the rotated angle """ b11, b12 = tensormatrix[0] b21, b22 = tensormatrix[1] # Step 1: Decompose into symmetric part a11init = b11 a22init = b22 a12init = 0.5 (b12 + b21) a21init = a12init # Step 2: Calculate Invariants m = a11init + a22init n = a11init a22init - a12init a21init # Step 3: Solve for Eigenvalues discriminant = m2 - 4 n sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(max(0.0, discriminant)) lambda1 = (m + sqrtdisc) / 2.0 lambda2 = (m - sqrtdisc) / 2.0 # Ensure lambda1 >= lambda2 if lambda1 < lambda2: lambda1, lambda2 = lambda2, lambda1 # Step 5 & 6: Compute a22 at rotation angle phi sinphi = math.sin(rotationanglephi) if abs(sinphi) < 1e-9: # At phi = 0 or pi, cot(phi) is undefined; a22 remains the initial state value a22rotated = a22init cotphi = 0.0 else: cotphi = math.cos(rotationanglephi) / sinphi cot2 = cotphi 2 A = 1.0 + cot2 B = -(2.0 lambda2 cot2 + m) C = n + lambda22 cot2 disca22 = B2 - 4.0 A C sqrtdisca22 = math.sqrt(max(0.0, disca22)) # Two roots: one for initial state, one for rotated state rootinitial = (-B - sqrtdisca22) / (2.0 A) rootrotated = (-B + sqrtdisca22) / (2.0 A) # Select the root corresponding to the rotated state if abs(rootinitial - a22init) < 1e-6: a22rotated = rootrotated else: a22rotated = rootinitial # Step 7: Derive remaining components a11rotated = lambda1 + lambda2 - a22rotated a21rotated = cotphi (lambda1 - a11rotated) a12rotated = a21rotated return [a11rotated, a12rotated, a21rotated, a22rotated] This variant extends the analytical method to general (non-symmetric) 2D tensors by combining the symmetric and antisymmetric parts. It calculates the invariants for both parts separately and combines them: nG = nS + nA, mG = mS + mA, and lG = lS + lA. The antisymmetric components are calculated as c{12} = \frac{1}{2}(b{12} - b{21}) and c{21} = -c{12}. For the rotational matrix component of a general tensor, the initial angle is typically set to \alpha = 45^\circ. This allows the visualization of general tensors while maintaining the analytical accuracy of the symmetric part. Time and Memory Complexity The method involves constant-time algebraic operations (quadratic formula, trigonometric functions) per tensor evaluation. Memory complexity is O(1) as it only stores a few scalar values (invariants, eigenvalues, components). Measured Performance and Scaling The method is applied to in-depth analysis of dynamic processes where numerical methods fail due to computation constraints. It provides higher accuracy per point than interpolation-based methods by strictly preserving tensor invariants. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Accurate and unambiguous; satisfies all tensor properties including invariance under isometric domain transformation; avoids numerical interpolation errors; provides omnidirectional representation. Limitations: Restricted to 2D plane (rank-two tensors); requires handling of complex roots via eigenvalue swapping; 2D space lacks a third invariant (requiring the derived Frobenius norm invariant); 3D extension is not directly provided due to the missing fourth invariant. When to Use Use this method when high-fidelity, invariant-preserving visualization of 2D symmetric or general rank-two tensors is required, particularly in dynamic processes where numerical stability is critical. Avoid when 3D visualization is needed or when computational resources are extremely limited and approximate glyph shapes are acceptable. The method was proposed by T. Stejskal, J. Svetlík, and Dobrán in 2022, published in Machines. It addresses the limitations of existing numerical methods for tensor rendering, which often fail to preserve tensor invariants or unambiguously represent all properties. The work introduces a new analytical approach to deriving rank-two tensor components in a plane and defines a new tensor invariant (the squared Frobenius norm) necessary for the calculation. It also highlights the presence of the golden ratio in the representation of planar tensors with a zero initial angle. An Analytical Method for Tensor Visualization in a Plane, https://doi.org/10.3390/machines10020089, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Arrow Glyphs
body: Arrow Glyphs resolve the direction ambiguity inherent in line-based vector field representations by rendering explicit arrow-shaped glyphs. It sets itself apart from Line Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization by providing unambiguous orientation cues through triangular faces that support shading, and from Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization by focusing specifically on the geometric construction of directional arrows rather than general glyph placement strategies. Builds on Multi-field, vector and tensor volume visualization Shared principles. Resolves direction ambiguity by rendering 3D cone-like shapes centered at sample points, scaled by magnitude and colored by magnitude. Chosen when unambiguous orientation cues via shading are required. Renders velocity vectors on a grid where length/direction indicate flow speed/direction, and color encodes a scalar quantity. Distinguished by its discrete, point-based representation which can create a "porcupine" effect. Displays arrows connecting two data points, such as a virtual mastoidectomy performed before training to a post-training virtual mastoidectomy. The display of these arrows is toggleable by the user. Requires paired pre/post test volumes for the same resident. Not given in the sources.
