name: Arrow Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization
head: Arrow Glyph Rendering, Arrow Plot, Glyph Arrows, Vector Glyphs as Arrows, Vector field arrow visualization
body: Arrow Glyphs is a visualization technique that resolves the direction ambiguity inherent in line-based vector field representations by rendering explicit arrow-shaped glyphs. It samples a vector field on a 2D grid (typically at a fixed coordinate) and renders each vector as a 3D cone-like shape centered at the sample point, scaled by magnitude and colored by magnitude. It sets itself apart from Line Glyphs for Vector Field Visualization by providing unambiguous orientation cues through triangular faces that support shading, and from Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization by focusing specifically on the geometric construction of directional arrows rather than general glyph placement strategies. Inputs: vectorfieldtex: A 3D texture containing the vector field data, where each texel stores a 4-component vector (vx, vy, vz, magnitude). xfixed: The fixed x-coordinate defining the 2D plane on which glyphs are sampled. glyphscount: A 2D integer vector (countx, county) specifying the number of arrows in the y and z directions. worldsize: A 2D float vector (width, height) defining the spatial extent of the glyph plane in world units. glyphlength: A scalar scaling factor for the length of the arrow shaft. magnormmult: A normalization factor for the color lookup table, typically vectormagnitudectflength / maxmagnitude. colormaptex: A 1D texture mapping magnitude values to colors. coordmult: A 3D vector mapping world coordinates to texture coordinates (optional, used when coordinate spaces differ). Outputs: outvertices: A buffer of float3 values, storing 9 vertices per arrow. outfaces: A buffer of uint3 values, storing 6 triangle indices per arrow. outvertexnormals: A buffer of float3 values, storing 9 normals per arrow. outvertexcolors: A buffer of float3 values, storing 9 colors per arrow. Each arrow glyph consists of exactly 9 vertices and 6 triangular faces. The vertices are indexed locally from 0 to 8 relative to the start of the arrow's block in the output buffers. Vertices Layout: v0: Tip of the arrow. v1, v2, v3, v4: Base vertices forming a square cross-section. v5, v6, v7, v8: Base vertices (duplicate positions to v1-v4 but with different normals for flat shading). Faces Layout: f0: (v0, v1, v2) f1: (v0, v2, v3) f2: (v0, v3, v4) f3: (v0, v4, v1) f4: (v5, v6, v7) f5: (v5, v7, v8) 1. Calculate Global Thread ID: Compute the global thread ID threadid from the execution configuration. 2. Boundary Check: Calculate totalcount = glyphscount.x glyphscount.y. If threadid >= totalcount, terminate the kernel. 3. Grid Coordinates: Compute column and row indices: col = thread\id \pmod{glyphs\count.x} row = \lfloor thread\id / glyphs\count.x \rfloor 4. Sample Position: Calculate the 3D position of the arrow base: position = (x\fixed, \ col \cdot \frac{world\size.x}{glyphs\count.x}, \ row \cdot \frac{world\size.y}{glyphs\count.y}) 5. Vector Sampling: Sample the vector field at the position, applying coordinate space multiplication if necessary: vector = \text{sample\vector\field}(vector\field\tex, position.x \cdot coord\mult.x, position.y \cdot coord\mult.y, position.z \cdot coord\mult.z) 6. Basis Vector Computation: Compute the forward axis (direction of flow): forward = \text{normalize}(vector.xyz) Compute a perpendicular axis xAxis using a robust helper that returns a unit vector orthogonal to forward. Compute the second perpendicular axis: yAxis = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(forward, xAxis)) 7. Face Index Assignment: For each arrow threadid, compute global indices: face\id = thread\id \cdot 6 vert\id = thread\id \cdot 9 Assign the 6 faces to outfaces as defined in the Data Structures section. 8. Normal Assignment: Assign normals to the 9 vertices: outvertexnormals[vertid + 0] = forward (Tip) outvertexnormals[vertid + 1] = xAxis outvertexnormals[vertid + 2] = yAxis outvertexnormals[vertid + 3] = -xAxis outvertexnormals[vertid + 4] = -yAxis outvertexnormals[vertid + 5] = -forward outvertexnormals[vertid + 6] = -forward outvertexnormals[vertid + 7] = -forward outvertexnormals[vertid + 8] = -forward 9. Scale Basis Vectors: Scale forward by the arrow length and magnitude: forward = forward \cdot glyph\length \cdot vector.w \cdot mag\norm\mult \cdot 0.5 Scale xAxis and yAxis by a fixed width factor and length: xAxis = xAxis \cdot glyph\length \cdot 0.1 yAxis = yAxis \cdot glyph\length \cdot 0.1 (Note: uses a simpler scaling of forward = vector.w and xAxis = 0.1.) 10. Vertex Position Computation: Compute the 9 vertex positions relative to position. Note that forward was negated in step 8 for normals, so position - forward places the tip in the direction of the vector: outvertices[vertid + 0] = position - forward (Tip) outvertices[vertid + 1] = position + xAxis outvertices[vertid + 2] = position + yAxis outvertices[vertid + 3] = position - xAxis outvertices[vertid + 4] = position - yAxis outvertices[vertid + 5] = position + xAxis outvertices[vertid + 6] = position + yAxis outvertices[vertid + 7] = position - xAxis outvertices[vertid + 8] = position - yAxis 11. Color Assignment: Sample the color from the magnitude lookup table: color = \text{sample\color\map}(color\map\tex, vector.w \cdot mag\norm\mult) Assign this color to all 9 vertices of the arrow: out\vertex\colors[vert\id + i] = color.xyz \quad \text{for } i \in [0, 8] In some implementations, the vector components at the arrow tail are computed using piecewise-bilinear interpolation of the four corner grid points. For a query point (x, y) in the x-y plane, with lower-left grid point (xi, yi) and grid widths (dx, dy), the weights are: b1 = \frac{(xi + dx - x)(yi + dy - y)}{dx \cdot dy} b2 = \frac{(xi - x)(yi + dy - y)}{dx \cdot dy} b3 = \frac{(xi + dx - x)(yi - y)}{dx \cdot dy} b4 = \frac{(xi - x)(yi - y)}{dx \cdot dy} The components are computed via piecewise-bilinear interpolation of the four corner grid points. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findperpendicular(v): # Robust perpendicular vector computation if abs(v.x) < abs(v.y): return normalize(cross(v, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0))) else: return normalize(cross(v, (0.0, 1.0, 0.0))) def samplevectorfield(tex, x, y, z): # Standard 3D texture lookup return tex[(x, y, z)] def samplecolormap(tex, t): # Standard 1D texture lookup return tex[t] def glypharrowskernel(xfixed, glyphscount, worldsize, vectorfieldtex, colormaptex, glyphlength, magnormmult, coordmult): # Simplified Python representation of the CUDA kernel totalcount = glyphscount.x glyphscount.y for threadid in range(totalcount): col = threadid % glyphscount.x row = threadid // glyphscount.x position = (xfixed, col (worldsize.x / glyphscount.x), row (worldsize.y / glyphscount.y)) samplepos = (position.x coordmult.x, position.y coordmult.y, position.z coordmult.z) vector = samplevectorfield(vectorfieldtex, samplepos.x, samplepos.y, samplepos.z) forward = normalize((vector.x, vector.y, vector.z)) xAxis = findperpendicular(forward) yAxis = normalize(cross(forward, xAxis)) faceid = threadid 6 vertid = threadid 9 outfaces[faceid] = (vertid, vertid + 1, vertid + 2) outfaces[faceid + 1] = (vertid, vertid + 2, vertid + 3) outfaces[faceid + 2] = (vertid, vertid + 3, vertid + 4) outfaces[faceid + 3] = (vertid, vertid + 4, vertid + 1) outfaces[faceid + 4] = (vertid + 5, vertid + 6, vertid + 7) outfaces[faceid + 5] = (vertid + 5, vertid + 7, vertid + 8) outvertexnormals[vertid] = forward outvertexnormals[vertid + 1] = xAxis outvertexnormals[vertid + 2] = yAxis outvertexnormals[vertid + 3] = -xAxis outvertexnormals[vertid + 4] = -yAxis baseforward = -forward outvertexnormals[vertid + 5] = baseforward outvertexnormals[vertid + 6] = baseforward outvertexnormals[vertid + 7] = baseforward outvertexnormals[vertid + 8] = baseforward forwardscaled = forward glyphlength vector.w magnormmult 0.5 xAxisscaled = xAxis glyphlength 0.1 yAxisscaled = yAxis glyphlength 0.1 outvertices[vertid] = position - forwardscaled outvertices[vertid + 1] = position + xAxisscaled outvertices[vertid + 2] = position + yAxisscaled outvertices[vertid + 3] = position - xAxisscaled outvertices[vertid + 4] = position - yAxisscaled outvertices[vertid + 5] = position + xAxisscaled outvertices[vertid + 6] = position + yAxisscaled outvertices[vertid + 7] = position - xAxisscaled outvertices[vertid + 8] = position - yAxisscaled colorval = samplecolormap(colormaptex, vector.w magnormmult) for i in range(9): outvertexcolors[vertid + i] = (colorval.x, colorval.y, colorval.z) Minimum Arrows: At least 2 arrows in each direction are required to form a valid surface representation. Arrow Width Factor: The base width of the arrow is scaled by a factor of 0.1 relative to the length. Fixed Coordinate: The visualization is typically performed on a 2D slice at a fixed x-coordinate x. Glyph Length: Controls the shaft length scaling. Magnitude CTF Normalization: Scales the magnitude value before color lookup. Zero Vector: If the sampled vector magnitude is zero, normalize will fail or produce undefined results. A guard clause should handle zero vectors, typically by rendering a small sphere or skipping the glyph. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when computing findperpendicular for vectors aligned with the primary axes. The helper uses a component comparison to avoid degeneracy. Boundary Conditions: If the sample position falls outside the vector field texture bounds, samplevectorfield should handle wrapping or clamping appropriately to avoid artifacts. Uses line segments instead of arrows. Simpler geometry but ambiguous direction. Choose when performance is critical and direction is less important than flow patterns. Focuses on optimal placement of glyphs in tensor fields to avoid clutter. Choose for complex tensor data where automatic placement is insufficient. Extends glyphs to represent uncertainty in vector/tensor data. Choose when data quality is variable or noisy. Uses ellipsoids or other shapes to represent tensor fields. Choose for stress/strain or diffusion data. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of glyphs. The computation is performed entirely on the GPU, avoiding CPU-GPU transfer overhead. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing vertices, faces, normals, and colors. Each glyph requires 9 vertices, 6 faces, 9 normals, and 9 colors. Performance: Arrow glyphs are roughly 2x faster than line glyphs (approx. 10 ms for typical scenes) because fewer glyphs are needed due to their larger visual size. Strengths: Unambiguous direction indication; supports shading for 3D depth perception; efficient GPU computation. Limitations: Can become cluttered in dense vector fields; requires careful tuning of glyph density and size. When to Use: When direction clarity is paramount and the vector field density is moderate. When Not to Use: In extremely dense fields where arrows overlap significantly, or when performance constraints are tighter than those for line glyphs. Arrow glyphs were introduced as a method to resolve the direction ambiguity of line-based vector field visualizations. The technique involves adding arrows to active surfaces in x, y, and z directions, with tails on surfaces and components computed via interpolation. The GPU-based implementation using CUDA allows for real-time visualization by computing all glyph geometry on the fly. It is commonly used in fluid dynamics and aerodynamics, such as visualizing wind flow near aircraft wings. name: Flow Vector Visualization
head: Flow direction arrows, Vector Glyph Visualization, Velocity vector plot
body: Flow Vector Visualization renders velocity vectors on a grid where the length and direction indicate flow speed and direction, while color encodes a scalar quantity. It solves the problem of visualizing vector fields by copying a generic object (glyph), positioning it at sample points, and scaling/coloring it based on vector data. It is distinguished from streamline methods by its discrete, point-based representation, which can create a "porcupine" effect. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vector field containing a positions component (to identify sample points) and a data component (containing vector quantities). Optionally, a connections component may exist. Output: A set of glyphs (arrows or rockets) representing the vector field. Data Structures: Field: Must include: positions: Coordinates of sample points. data: Vector values at those points. Glyph: A generic object (e.g., arrow) with a base and a tip. A directional dot is drawn at the vector tip to indicate flow direction. Parameters: vectordensityskip: Integer step for sampling grid cells. Default is 1 (all vectors). Setting to 2 skips every other vector to reduce density. vectorscale: Float multiplier for vector length. Adjusted interactively. Steps: 1. Position the Base: For position-dependent data: Fix the base of the vector glyph at the vertex position (sample point). For connection-dependent data: Fix the base at the center of the connection element. 2. Scale the Length: Scale the length of each vector glyph based on the vector magnitude relative to all other vectors in the field. 3. Orient the Glyph: Point the glyph in the direction of the vector given by the datum at that point. 4. Color the Glyph: Color the vector based on the value of the currently displayed scalar quantity. 5. Draw the Tip: Draw a small dot at the end of the line to indicate flow direction. 6. Reduce Density (Optional): Use a Reduce module to downsample the data field or a Sample module to extract a subset of points (e.g., from an isosurface) to feed to the Glyph module, thereby decreasing visual clutter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderflowvectors(field, vectorscale, vectordensityskip): """ Renders flow vectors for a given field. Args: field: Object with 'positions' and 'data' components. vectorscale: Float multiplier for vector length. vectordensityskip: Integer step for sampling grid cells. """ positions = field.positions vectors = field.data # Get magnitude of all vectors for relative scaling magnitudes = [norm(v) for v in vectors] maxmagnitude = max(magnitudes) if magnitudes else 1.0 renderedglyphs = [] for i, pos in enumerate(positions): # Apply density skip if i % vectordensityskip != 0: continue vector = vectors[i] magnitude = magnitudes[i] # Calculate scaled length # Note: Sources state scaling is relative to all other vectors. # A common implementation normalizes by max magnitude and applies scale factor. scaledlength = (magnitude / maxmagnitude) vectorscale # Determine base position # Assuming position-dependent data for simplicity as per S2 default basepos = pos # Determine tip position # Direction is given by vector datum if magnitude > 0: direction = vector / magnitude tippos = basepos + direction scaledlength else: tippos = basepos # Create glyph (arrow from base to tip) glyph = createarrowglyph(basepos, tippos) # Color based on scalar quantity (not explicitly defined in sources, assumed available) # scalarvalue = field.scalardata[i] # Assumed scalar data exists # glyph.color = mapscalartocolor(scalarvalue) # Add directional dot at tip glyph.addtipdot(tippos) renderedglyphs.append(glyph) return renderedglyphs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intersection and Occlusion: High density of vectors or large value disparities can cause vectors to intersect or occlude each other, making interpretation difficult. Visual Clutter: Fine meshes can result in very dense vector plots. Strengths: Provides immediate visual feedback on flow direction and relative magnitude at specific points. Limitations: Can become hard to interpret if there are many vector data points or if vectors intersect/occlude each other. Performance: Rendering time depends on the number of vectors. Downsampling via Reduce or Sample modules can improve performance and clarity. When to use: When discrete vector information at specific points is needed, and the field is not excessively dense. When not to use: When the field is very dense or when continuous flow paths are more important than discrete vectors (consider streamlines instead). Flow Vector Visualization is a technique used in scientific visualization, particularly in tools like Data Explorer and Smokeview. It is part of the broader category of glyph-based vector field visualization. name: Stress Analysis Visualization
head: Linear Elasticity Stress Visualization, Von Mises Stress Visualization
body: Stress Analysis Visualization renders the internal mechanical stress state of a deformed object, typically derived from linear elasticity simulations. It solves the problem of visualizing scalar stress metrics (such as Von Mises stress) computed from tensor fields that are often not stored directly but must be derived from displacement fields on the fly. It is distinguished from general tensor visualization by its specific reliance on on-the-fly derivation of strain and stress tensors from displacement data in isogeometric analysis contexts, rather than pre-computed cell-centered values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A displacement field u: P \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 defined over a parametric domain P, typically represented as cubic B-splines or similar basis functions in isogeometric analysis. Output: A volume-rendered image where color and opacity map to the Von Mises stress scalar \rho. Data Structures: Displacement Field: Defined by control points and basis functions (e.g., cubic B-splines). The specific topology (e.g., volume blocks with control points) is defined by the simulation mesh. Stress Tensor: Computed per sample point. In some pipelines (e.g., physiological mesh data), stress is stored as point-associated data rather than cell-associated data. Formulas: 1. Strain Tensor Calculation: The strain tensor \sigma is calculated using the Jacobian of the deformation. Let Ju be the Jacobian of the displacement field u and J\phi be the Jacobian of the geometry parametrization \phi. The term J{u \circ \phi^{-1}} is the solution to the linear system: [J\phi(p)]^T J{u \circ \phi^{-1}}(g) = [Ju(p)]^T Then, the strain tensor is: \sigma = \frac{1}{2} \left( J{u \circ \phi^{-1}} + (J{u \circ \phi^{-1}})^T \right) 2. Von Mises Stress: The scalar Von Mises stress \rho is derived from the components of the strain/stress tensor \sigma: \rho = \frac{(\sigma{11} - \sigma{22})^2 + (\sigma{22} - \sigma{33})^2 + (\sigma{33} - \sigma{11})^2 + 6(\sigma{12}^2 + \sigma{23}^2 + \sigma{31}^2)}{2} Steps: 1. Sample: For each sample point \mathbf{x} in the volume rendering integral, evaluate the displacement field u(\mathbf{x}) and its Jacobian Ju(\mathbf{x}), and the geometry parametrization Jacobian J\phi(\mathbf{x}). 2. Solve for Strain: Solve the linear system [J\phi(\mathbf{x})]^T \mathbf{y} = [Ju(\mathbf{x})]^T for \mathbf{y} (representing J{u \circ \phi^{-1}}). 3. Compute Strain Tensor: Calculate \sigma = \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{y}^T). 4. Compute Von Mises Stress: Calculate \rho using the formula above with components of \sigma. 5. Map: Apply a transfer function (e.g., logarithmic scaling and colormap) to \rho to determine color and opacity. 6. Composite: Integrate along the ray using standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., midpoint method). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computevonmisesstressatpoint(x, Jphifunc, Jufunc): """ Computes Von Mises stress at a single point x. Jphifunc: Returns Jphi(p) Jufunc: Returns Ju(p) """ Jphi = Jphifunc(x) Ju = Jufunc(x) # Solve [Jphi]^T Y = [Ju]^T for Y using standard numerical linear algebra Y = solvelinearsystem(Jphi.T, Ju.T) # Compute Strain Tensor Sigma = 0.5 (Y + Y^T) Sigma = 0.5 (Y + Y.T) # Extract components s11 = Sigma[0, 0] s22 = Sigma[1, 1] s33 = Sigma[2, 2] s12 = Sigma[0, 1] s23 = Sigma[1, 2] s31 = Sigma[2, 0] # Compute Von Mises Stress rho rho = ((s11 - s22)2 + (s22 - s33)2 + (s33 - s11)2 + 6 (s122 + s232 + s312)) / 2.0 return rho def solvelinearsystem(A, B): """Solves the linear system A X = B for X using standard Gaussian elimination.""" # Standard linear algebra solver implementation. # Returns the solution matrix X. pass def renderstressvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, Jphifunc, Jufunc, maxraylength, samplespacing, tf, stressepsilon): """ Renders the volume using on-the-fly stress calculation. tf: Transfer function mapping scalar stress to (r, g, b, a) """ t = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alpha = 0.0 while t < maxraylength: x = rayorigin + t raydirection # Calculate stress on the fly rho = computevonmisesstressatpoint(x, Jphifunc, Jufunc) # Apply transfer function (e.g., log scaling) mappedvalue = math.log10(rho + stressepsilon) rgba = tf(mappedvalue) # Front-to-back compositing color = ( color[0] + rgba[3] rgba[0] (1 - alpha), color[1] + rgba[3] rgba[1] (1 - alpha), color[2] + rgba[3] rgba[2] (1 - alpha)) alpha = alpha + rgba[3] (1 - alpha) t += samplespacing if alpha > 0.99: break return color Parameters: Sample Distance: Dictated by the volume render integral; methods like RK2 (midpoint) use a fixed sample distance. Colormap: Dark-red-to-yellow is used in specific physiological mesh pipelines. Scaling: Logarithmic scaling (\log{10}) is applied to stress values in mesh-based pipelines. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degeneracies: Boundary conditions may introduce degeneracies in the Jacobian or displacement field, requiring robust solvers. Point vs. Cell Data: In mesh-based pipelines, stress must be computed as point-associated data to ensure correct averaging during smoothing; using cell-associated data leads to errors. Mesh Inversion: Smoothing operations applied to the full tetrahedral volume can invert tetrahedra. Filtering must be restricted to the rendered surface geometry to prevent topological failure. A specialized pipeline for physiological stress data on tetrahedral meshes. It differs from standard volume rendering by explicitly handling mesh topology for smoothing. It computes Von Mises stress from point-associated tensors, applies \log{10} scaling, maps to a dark-red-to-yellow colormap, smooths nodal stress across mesh edges, and applies a median filter exclusively to rendered surface positions to prevent tetrahedron inversion. A key implementation detail is deduplicating bidirectional edge pairs in celledges to ensure each distinct directed neighbor is averaged exactly once during the nodal smoothing pass. Time Complexity: High per-sample cost due to the on-the-fly solution of linear systems for the strain tensor. The second-order midpoint method is noted as the fastest among tested ODE-based methods for the integration step. Memory: Low storage overhead for stress data as it is computed on the fly, but requires efficient access to displacement field control points and basis functions. Performance: In isogeometric analysis benchmarks (e.g., TERRIFIC project twisted bar), RK2 (midpoint) achieved ~78 ms total render time for a specific model, outperforming higher-order Runge-Kutta methods. Strengths: Pixel-accurate geometry representation; handles complex deformations defined by B-splines; avoids pre-computation storage costs. Limitations: Computationally expensive per sample; sensitive to degeneracies at boundaries. Originating from the field of isogeometric analysis, this method was detailed in work by the TERRIFIC project researchers. It addresses the need for visualizing structural analysis results where external forces lead to displacement fields u: P \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3. The approach was developed to allow interactive visualization of stress in complex geometries (e.g., twisted bars, backstep flows) without pre-computing stress fields on a dense grid. Later adaptations extended these concepts to physiological tetrahedral meshes, incorporating smoothing and surface filtering techniques. name: Anisotropic Deformation
head: Layer-based deformation, Normal Vector Deformation, Rubber sheet deformation, Tensor Field Deformation, Tensor Field Deformation via Spring Lattice
body: Anisotropic Deformation is a volume deformation technique that visualizes the directional information of a tensor field by deforming an entire volume using the tensor field as a force field acting on the object's normal vectors. It is capable of illustrating the compressing and shearing properties of the tensor field. Unlike Normal Vector Deformation, which emphasizes tensor information in one primary direction and requires a user-specified interrogation vector, Anisotropic Deformation allows the interrogation to vary over space and time, deforming the entire volume to represent tensor information in all directions. It provides an approximation of the tensor field's effect, specifically visualizing the symmetric portion of the tensor, as rigid rotation does not affect lengths. The method assumes the tensor field is sufficiently smooth so that there are no sudden changes in neighboring tensors, and tensors vary linearly between neighboring tensors. It also assumes that the tensor data resides in a structured grid such as a rectilinear or curvilinear grid. The tensor field is considered a special force field with different properties in all directions. Input: A tensor field T(x) defined on a structured 3D grid. Output: A deformed volume where the geometry reflects the local tensor properties (enlarging, compressing, shearing). The volume is represented as a lattice of nodes. In 3D, each node is connected to its immediate neighbors, requiring 26 springs per point. Node: Stores position P(x), initial position P{init}(x), and normal vector N(x) (for Normal Vector Deformation variant). Spring: Connects two nodes. Stores rest length L and spring constant K. Tensor Field: Structured grid of 3 \times 3 tensors T(x). TimeStep: Integration time step. Must be less than 0.1 for stability. Typical value: 0.01 (range 0.005 to 0.05 for better results). \lambda: User-specified parameter controlling the amount of deformation. Range: [0, 1]. Typical value: 0.1 to 0.9. If too small, deformation is undetectable. If 1, springs may degenerate to 0 due to singular tensors. K: Spring constant. Homogeneous in the Anisotropic Deformation variant. Interrogation Vector: In the Normal Vector Deformation variant, this is the normal vector of the current layer. It can be replaced by a user-specified vector. This variant traverses the tensor volume along one of the 3 axes in computational space, processing the volume one layer or sheet at a time. 1. Initialize: Set the normal vectors N(x) as the normals to the current layer in physical space. Set the rest length of each spring to the distance between the initial positions of the two nodes straddling it. 2. Iterate until equilibrium: a. Calculate External Force: For each node x, calculate the deforming force Fe(x) by multiplying the tensor T(x) and the normal vector N(x): Fe(x) = T(x) \cdot N(x) b. Calculate Internal Force: Calculate the internal force Fi(x) based on the deformation function D(x) and the displacement relative to rest length: Fi(x) = - \oint \frac{\partial D}{\partial x} \cdot \left( \frac{\left\| \frac{\partial D}{\partial x} \Delta x \right\|}{\left\| \Delta x \right\|} - 1 \right) \cdot \Delta x where the integral represents the summation over connected springs. c. Calculate Combined Force: Sum the external and internal forces: Fc(x) = Fe(x) + Fi(x) = T \cdot N + Fi(x) d. Update Position: Update the position of the deformed layer node P{k+1}(x) using the combined force and a time step: P{k+1}(x) = Pk(x) + Fc(x) \cdot \text{TimeStep} e. Update Normals: Update normals according to the new surface orientation as the layer deforms. 3. Termination: Stop when the values in the combined force fields are zero at all points (equilibrium). This variant does not require an interrogation vector or tensor decomposition. It adjusts lengths connecting a node to its neighboring nodes by minimizing resultant displacement force. 1. Initialize: Establish a spring model where each node is connected to its neighbors in 3D. Spring constants are homogeneous. Set the rest length of each spring to the original distance between neighboring nodes. 2. Iterate until equilibrium: a. Recalculate Rest Length: For each pair of neighboring points x0 and x1, recalculate the rest length L(x0, x1) using a weighted average of the tensor-transformed distance and the original distance: L(x0, x1) = \lambda \|T(x0) \cdot (x0 - x1)\| + (1 - \lambda) \|x0 - x1\| b. Calculate Internal Force: Compute internal forces F(x0) by summing contributions from all connected neighbors x1, using the spring constant K and the deviation of current length from rest length L: F(x0) = \sum{x1} K \cdot (x1 - x0) \cdot \left( \frac{\|x0 - x1\|}{L(x0, x1 + x0)} - 1 \right) c. Update Position: Use F(x) to compute new positions of all points in each iteration. 3. Termination: Stop when the magnitude of F(x) is below a threshold everywhere (equilibrium). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def anisotropicdeformation(tensorfield, gridnodes, lambdaparam, timestep, maxiterations): """ Implements the Anisotropic Deformation algorithm (Variant 2). Args: tensorfield: 3D array of 3x3 tensors T(x). gridnodes: List of Node objects with position P and neighbors. lambdaparam: Deformation control parameter [0, 1]. timestep: Integration time step (< 0.1). maxiterations: Maximum number of iterations. Returns: Deformed gridnodes. """ # Initialize rest lengths based on initial positions for node in gridnodes: for neighbor in node.neighbors: # Calculate initial distance dist = norm(neighbor.P - node.P) # Set rest length to initial distance (Variant 2 default) # Note: Variant 1 sets rest length to initial distance too, but # Variant 2 recalculates it every iteration based on tensor. neighbor.restlength = dist for iteration in range(maxiterations): equilibriumreached = True maxforce = 0.0 for node in gridnodes: internalforce = Vector3(0, 0, 0) for neighbor in node.neighbors: # Recalculate rest length L(x0, x1) # T(x0) is tensor at node # v = x0 - x1 v = node.P - neighbor.P tensortransformedv = tensorfield[node.index] @ v tensordist = norm(tensortransformedv) originaldist = norm(v) # L(x0, x1) = lambda ||T(x0) (x0 - x1)|| + (1 - lambda) ||x0 - x1|| newrestlength = lambdaparam tensordist + (1 - lambdaparam) originaldist # Update rest length for the spring connecting node and neighbor neighbor.restlength = newrestlength # Calculate internal force contribution # F(x0) = sum K (x1 - x0) (||x0 - x1|| / L(x0, x1) - 1) # Note: The formula in source uses L(x0, x1 + x0) which implies L depends on direction or is symmetric. # Assuming L is symmetric for simplicity in implementation unless specified otherwise. # Source formula: F(x0) = sum{x1} K (x1 - x0) (||x0 - x1|| / L(x0, x1 + x0) - 1) currentdist = norm(neighbor.P - node.P) direction = neighbor.P - node.P # Avoid division by zero if newrestlength < 1e-9: springterm = 0.0 else: springterm = (currentdist / newrestlength) - 1 # K is homogeneous spring constant K = 1.0 # Default spring constant forcecontribution = K direction springterm internalforce += forcecontribution # In Variant 2, there is no external force Fe. Fc = Fi. combinedforce = internalforce # Update position node.P += combinedforce timestep # Check equilibrium forcemag = norm(combinedforce) if forcemag > maxforce: maxforce = forcemag if forcemag > 1e-6: # Threshold for equilibrium equilibriumreached = False if equilibriumreached: break return gridnodes def normalvectordeformation(tensorfield, gridlayers, timestep, maxiterations): """ Implements the Normal Vector Deformation algorithm (Variant 1). Args: tensorfield: 3D array of 3x3 tensors T(x). gridlayers: List of layers, each containing nodes. timestep: Integration time step (< 0.1). maxiterations: Maximum number of iterations. Returns: Deformed gridlayers. """ for layer in gridlayers: # Initialize normals as normals to the current layer in physical space for node in layer.nodes: node.N = computelayernormal(node, layer) for layer in gridlayers: for iteration in range(maxiterations): equilibriumreached = True maxforce = 0.0 for node in layer.nodes: # Calculate External Force Fe(x) = T(x) N(x) externalforce = tensorfield[node.index] @ node.N # Calculate Internal Force Fi(x) # This requires summing over connected springs in the layer internalforce = Vector3(0, 0, 0) for neighbor in node.neighborsinlayer: # Approximate derivative term or use spring model # Source formula: Fi(x) = - integral... # Implementation note: The source describes a spring lattice model. # We approximate the integral as a sum over neighbors. # The term inside the integral involves the deformation gradient. # For a spring lattice, internal force is typically derived from spring extensions. # However, the source explicitly gives a formula for Fi involving D(x). # Since D(x) is the position P(x), we approximate the gradient. # Simplified spring force for internal force calculation # Note: The source formula for Fi is complex. # A common implementation for rubber sheet deformation uses spring forces. # Let's use the standard spring force for internal consistency with the lattice. # Fspring = -K (currentlength - restlength) direction # But the source formula is specific. # Re-reading source: "Fi(x) is then defined as follows: [formula]" # The formula involves partial derivatives of D. # In a discrete lattice, we can approximate this. # However, to keep it implementable from text, we use the spring model logic # described for the lattice. # Let's stick to the spring model for internal forces as described in the context # of "physics-based model to constrain the movement". # The formula provided might be a continuous approximation. # For implementation, we use the discrete spring force. # Actually, the source says: "To restore this balance, the system will have to displace... # until the internal and external forces reach a new equilibrium state." # And "Fc(x) = Fe(x) + Fi(x)". # And "Fi(x) = - integral...". # Given the complexity of implementing the exact integral formula from text, # and the fact that it's a spring lattice, we approximate Fi as the sum of spring forces. # This is a gap fill. dist = norm(neighbor.P - node.P) direction = neighbor.P - node.P restlen = neighbor.restlength # Set to initial distance if restlen < 1e-9: springforce = Vector3(0,0,0) else: # Standard spring force springforce = -1.0 (dist - restlen) / restlen direction # Note: Source formula has a more complex term. # The term (||dD/dx dx|| / ||dx|| - 1) is essentially (currentlength / restlength - 1). # So Fi is proportional to (currentlength / restlength - 1) direction. # The negative sign indicates restoring force. internalforce += springforce # Combined Force combinedforce = externalforce + internalforce # Update Position node.P += combinedforce timestep # Update Normals node.N = computelayernormal(node, layer) # Check equilibrium forcemag = norm(combinedforce) if forcemag > maxforce: maxforce = forcemag if forcemag > 1e-6: equilibriumreached = False if equilibriumreached: break return gridlayers def computelayernormal(node, layer): """ Computes the normal vector for a node in a layer. Approximation using cross product of two edge vectors from neighbors. """ if len(layer.nodes) < 3: return Vector3(0, 0, 1) # Default normal # Get two neighbors to define the plane n1 = layer.nodes[0].P - node.P n2 = layer.nodes[1].P - node.P normal = cross(n1, n2) if norm(normal) < 1e-9: return Vector3(0, 0, 1) return normalize(normal) Instability: Heterogeneous tensors in small areas can cause wild fluctuations in normal vectors. This is solved by using a physics-based spring model to constrain movement and reach equilibrium. Visual Clutter: Displaying multiple deformed slices can cause clutter. This is solved by adding weak spring links between layers to make deformation regular. Smooth Deformation Hiding Non-Smooth Fields: A smooth-looking deformation may hide a non-smooth tensor field, leading to high error rates. Users should specify smaller volumes to inspect details if error is high. Approximation: The method provides an approximation, not an exact solution. It only visualizes the symmetric portion of the tensor because rigid rotation (from polar decomposition) does not affect lengths. Singular Tensors: If \lambda is set to 1, springs may degenerate to 0 due to singular tensors. Time Complexity: The method is iterative and stops when equilibrium is reached. The number of iterations depends on the smoothness of the tensor field and the time step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the tensor field, node positions, and spring connections. In 3D, each node requires 26 springs. Measured Performance: On the single point load dataset, the maximal error detection factor was 0.0311 (3.11%). On the delta wing dataset, the maximal error rate was 7.61%. On the cylinder with hemispherical cap dataset, the maximal error rate was 6.35%. The error factor is below 10% for most simulations. Strengths: Good at exhibiting enlarging, compressing, and shearing properties in all directions. It provides an approximation that preserves anisotropy information in high-error regions. Limitations: It is an approximation, not an exact solution. It is less accurate than normal vector deformation in some metrics. The resulting deformation differs when different layer orientations are used to sweep the volume (for Normal Vector Deformation). Anisotropic Deformation was introduced in the paper "Volume Deformation For Tensor Visualization". It is an improvement over previous methods like Boring and Pang's Normal Vector Deformation, which used a homogeneous interrogation vector. The method is applied to visualize stress due to deformation in linear elasticity isogeometric analysis, where external forces lead to a displacement field [Parent]. It has been applied to the single point load tensor dataset, the delta wing velocity gradient tensor dataset, and the cylinder with hemispherical cap rate of strain tensor dataset. Volume Deformation For Tensor Visualization, https://avis.soe.ucsc.edu/images.tensordef/vis02.tensordef.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Combined DTI/MRI Volume Rendering
head: Combined MRI and DTI Volume Rendering, Interactive Volume Rendering of Diffusion Tensor Data, Magic Lens Selection for DTI/MRI, Multi-modal volume rendering
body: Combined DTI/MRI Volume Rendering is a technique that integrates the visualization of conventional scalar-valued MRI (providing high-resolution gyral structure and blood vessels) with Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data in a single volume rendering pass to aid surgical planning and navigation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by restricting the diffusion tensor color map to the standard RGB model to avoid misleading color mixing, while using MRI data solely to highlight object boundaries via a grayscale transfer function. Unlike methods that apply different transfer functions to a single dataset, this approach selects different transfer functions on different modalities to build a combined image without distorting geometry. The method extends a standard GPU-based raycasting volume renderer to handle two distinct data modalities simultaneously. It relies on a single-pass rendering pipeline for interactive performance, utilizing a "magic lens" concept to allow interactive selection of the weighting between MRI context and DTI fiber data. Inputs: Scalar MRI volume data representing anatomical structures. DTI volume data representing diffusion tensors. A "magic lens" region (defined by position and size) that determines where DTI data is emphasized versus where MRI context is dominant. Outputs: A composite RGB image where DTI fibers are color-coded and MRI structures provide geometric context. The implementation uses a 3D texture-based approach for storing volume data. MRI Data: Stored as a 3D texture of scalar values. DTI Data: Stored as a 3D texture of tensor values. Transfer Functions: MRI Transfer Function: A 2D lookup table (LUT) mapping scalar value and gradient magnitude to opacity and grayscale color. DTI Transfer Function: Evaluated analytically on the GPU based on tensor properties (e.g., Fractional Anisotropy) and potentially MRI scalar values. Lighting Parameters: OpenGL light sources are repurposed to encode parameters for the transfer functions. Specifically, unused light sources (typically five or more in medical imaging where only one or two are used) provide global parameters like cut-off angle and exponent for smooth step functions. 1. Compute Stencil: Determine the spatial region of interest, often defined by the "magic lens" or clipping planes. 2. Compute Tensor Volume Rendering: Cast rays through the DTI volume, sample tensor values along the ray, compute color based on the principal eigenvector for directional coloring, and apply opacity based on FA. The tensor transfer function is evaluated analytically on the GPU to allow real-time manipulation without texture updates. 3. Compute Conventional MRI Overlay: Cast rays through the MRI volume, sample scalar values, apply a 2D grayscale transfer function based on value and gradient magnitude to highlight boundaries, and apply special material attributes and gradient-based shading to improve 3D perception of surfaces. 4. Composite: Combine the DTI rendering and MRI overlay in a single rendering pass. The magic lens allows the user to interactively adjust the weighting between the DTI fiber visualization and the MRI structural context. Tensor Color Mapping: The color C is derived from the principal eigenvector \vec{v} of the diffusion tensor \mathbf{D}. The specific mapping is restricted to the RGB model. Transfer Function Evaluation: MRI TF: T{MRI}(v, g) \rightarrow (r, g, b, \alpha), where v is scalar value and g is gradient magnitude. DTI TF: T{DTI}(tensor, v{MRI}) \rightarrow (r, g, b, \alpha). The sources note that 2D functions can be based on two scalar values, e.g., MRI signal and FA. Light Parameterization: Smooth step functions for transfer functions are parameterized using OpenGL light parameters: cut-off angle (\thetac) and exponent (e). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generaterayfromcamera(pixel, cameraorigin, cameradirection, cameraup, cameraright, pixelspacing): """Generates a ray origin and direction for a given pixel.""" origin = cameraorigin direction = cameradirection + (pixel.x cameraright + pixel.y cameraup) pixelspacing return origin, direction / math.linalg.norm(direction) def sample3dtexture(volume, point): """Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D texture.""" # Standard trilinear interpolation implementation return volume.interpolate(point) def computegradient(volume, point): """Computes gradient magnitude using central differences.""" # Standard central difference implementation dx = (sample3dtexture(volume, point + (1,0,0)) - sample3dtexture(volume, point - (1,0,0))) / 2 dy = (sample3dtexture(volume, point + (0,1,0)) - sample3dtexture(volume, point - (0,1,0))) / 2 dz = (sample3dtexture(volume, point + (0,0,1)) - sample3dtexture(volume, point - (0,0,1))) / 2 return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) def computefractionalanisotropy(tensor): """Computes FA from a 3x3 symmetric tensor.""" # Standard FA formula using eigenvalues eigenvalues = math.linalg.eigvals(tensor) l1, l2, l3 = sorted(eigenvalues, reverse=True) numerator = math.sqrt(1.5) math.sqrt((l1-l2)2 + (l2-l3)2 + (l3-l1)2) denominator = math.sqrt(l12 + l22 + l32) return numerator / denominator if denominator > 1e-8 else 0.0 def getprincipaleigenvector(tensor): """Returns the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue.""" # Standard eigenvector extraction eigenvalues, eigenvectors = math.linalg.eigh(tensor) return eigenvectors[:, math.argmax(eigenvalues)] def evaluatemritf(value, gradient): """Returns grayscale color and opacity based on 2D LUT lookup.""" # Standard 2D LUT mapping to grayscale (r=g=b) return (value, value, value, gradient) def evaluatedtitf(tensor, fa, lightparams): """Returns RGB color and opacity based on analytical evaluation.""" eigenvector = getprincipaleigenvector(tensor) color = (abs(eigenvector.x), abs(eigenvector.y), abs(eigenvector.z)) cutoff = lightparams['cutoffangle'] exponent = lightparams['exponent'] t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (fa - (1.0 - cutoff)) / cutoff)) opacity = t t (3 - 2 t) exponent return (color[0], color[1], color[2], opacity) def isinsidelens(point, lenscenter, lensradius): """Checks if a point is within the magic lens sphere.""" return math.linalg.norm(point - lenscenter) <= lensradius def fronttobackcomposite(acccolor, accalpha, newcolor, newalpha): """Performs standard front-to-back alpha compositing.""" outalpha = accalpha + newalpha (1.0 - accalpha) outcolor = ( acccolor[0] accalpha + newcolor[0] newalpha (1.0 - accalpha), acccolor[1] accalpha + newcolor[1] newalpha (1.0 - accalpha), acccolor[2] accalpha + newcolor[2] newalpha (1.0 - accalpha)) return outcolor, outalpha def rendercombineddtimri(mrivolume, dtivolume, lenscenter, lensradius, lightparams, cameraparams): """Renders a combined view of MRI and DTI data in a single pass.""" imagewidth, imageheight = 1920, 1080 image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): rayorigin, raydirection = generaterayfromcamera((x, y), cameraparams) acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 for t in range(0, 1000, 2): point = rayorigin + raydirection t if not mrivolume.contains(point): break mrival = sample3dtexture(mrivolume, point) mrigrad = computegradient(mrivolume, point) mritf = evaluatemritf(mrival, mrigrad) dtitensor = sample3dtexture(dtivolume, point) fa = computefractionalanisotropy(dtitensor) dtitf = evaluatedtitf(dtitensor, fa, lightparams) inlens = isinsidelens(point, lenscenter, lensradius) weightdti = 1.0 if inlens else 0.2 weightmri = 0.2 if inlens else 1.0 combinedcolor = ( mritf[0] weightmri + dtitf[0] weightdti, mritf[1] weightmri + dtitf[1] weightdti, mritf[2] weightmri + dtitf[2] weightdti) combinedalpha = (mritf[3] weightmri + dtitf[3] weightdti) 0.5 acccolor, accalpha = fronttobackcomposite(acccolor, accalpha, combinedcolor, combinedalpha) if accalpha > 0.99: break image[y][x] = (acccolor[0] / max(accalpha, 1e-8), acccolor[1] / max(accalpha, 1e-8), acccolor[2] / max(accalpha, 1e-8), accalpha) return image Gray/White Matter Interface: There is an area of approximately two to three millimeters in the outer gyri where streamline tracking algorithms fail due to ambiguity of tensor information at the interface between gray and white matter. Volume rendering combined with cortex extraction shows the limits of these algorithms. Misleading Line Structures: Pre-computed line structures (streamlines) can be misleading because they are often started and stopped based on parameters like FA, implying single lines with defined start and end points. Color Model Restriction: The diffusion tensor color map is restricted to the RGB model. Introducing additional colors from MRI would be misleading. Performance: The method provides interactive frame rates on a full-screen application. Scalability: The speed of the algorithm is independent of the size of the magic lens. No change in frame rate was experienced for different sizes of DTI and MRI data sets. Strengths: Context-preserving visualization: MRI provides gyral structure and blood vessels, while DTI provides fiber connectivity. Interactive: The magic lens allows real-time adjustment of the weighting between modalities. Single-pass rendering: Efficient compositing of both datasets. Limitations: MRI data is volume rendered only to highlight boundaries of objects using a standard 2D grayscale transfer function. Gradient computation can be performed either on the GPU or on the CPU, depending on the available graphics board or user choice. This method was developed to address the limitations of pseudo-colored slices and fiber tracking algorithms in neuro-surgery and brain connectivity research. It specifically targets the need to understand neural fiber connectivity in brain gyri while maintaining the anatomical context provided by conventional MRI. It was applied to study conditions like Deletion 22q Syndrome, characterized by increased FA and ADC in certain brain areas. The approach contrasts with earlier methods like Wang et al. [WZMK05] by using separate transfer functions for separate modalities rather than modifying a single dataset's transfer function. Interactive Volume Rendering of Diffusion Tensor Data, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-88378-48, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Scalarization of Vector Fields
body: Scalarization of Vector Fields converts multi-component vector data into single-component scalar fields to enable standard volume rendering or surface extraction techniques. It sets itself apart from direct vector visualization methods (like Stream Lines) by projecting the vector information onto a scalar metric, allowing the use of established transfer functions for opacity and color mapping. All methods in this family evaluate a mapping function M(\mathbf{x}) at sample points \mathbf{x} within the volume to produce visual attributes. The core mechanism involves sampling the multi-component data field at \mathbf{x}, decomposing or normalizing the value (e.g., extracting magnitude, direction, eigenvalues, or phase), and applying a transfer function or geometric construction to map these features to rendering parameters such as color, opacity, or primitive geometry. Helicity Visualization maps the dot product of velocity and vorticity to opacity and color to identify vortices and their rotation direction in fluid flows. It sets itself apart from siblings like Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields by explicitly leveraging the alignment between flow direction and local rotation to highlight swirling features, whereas metric methods often rely on magnitude or strain. See Helicity Visualization. Metric Scalar Field Rendering converts vector field data into scalar values to enable standard surface or volume rendering techniques. It solves the problem of visualizing vector fields, which lack a single intensity value, by calculating metrics such as velocity magnitude, vorticity, or divergence. It differs from Helicity Visualization by focusing on general magnitude-based scalarization rather than the specific alignment of curl and velocity. See Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields. Visualizing specific components of the velocity field (e.g., x-component) to identify flow separation and reversal. Map the smallest x velocity values (including negative values) to cyan and high opacity. Map the largest x velocity components to yellow and near transparency. The technique originated in early computational fluid dynamics (CFD) visualization research. Volume Rendering for Computational Fluid Dynamics: Initial Results (1991) demonstrated the use of scalarization to visualize perturbation velocity fields, specifically mapping negative x-components to cyan to highlight flow separation from surfaces. [PDF] Volume Rendering for Computational Fluid Dynamics: Initial Results, https://www.nas.nasa.gov/assets/nas/pdf/techreports/1991/rnr-91-026.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Helicity Visualization
head: Helicity Calculation
body: Helicity Visualization maps the scalar helicity field to color and opacity to identify vortices and their rotation direction in fluid flows. It sets itself apart from siblings like Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields by explicitly utilizing the directional relationship between velocity and vorticity via a dot product, allowing distinction of vortex chirality through signed color mapping. Inputs: Velocity field \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = (u, v, w) defined on a grid. Vorticity field \boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla \times \mathbf{F}. Outputs: Color C(\mathbf{x}) and Opacity \alpha(\mathbf{x}) for each sample point. Data Structures: The helicity scalar field h(\mathbf{x}) is computed per voxel. Transfer function T(h) maps scalar value to (R, G, B, \alpha). Steps: 1. Compute Vorticity: Calculate the curl of the velocity field at each grid point \mathbf{x}: \boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla \times \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) 2. Compute Helicity: Calculate the dot product of the velocity and vorticity vectors: h(\mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\omega}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) This scalar represents the curl in the direction of the velocity. 3. Map Opacity: Map the magnitude of helicity |h(\mathbf{x})| to opacity \alpha: large magnitude maps to high opacity (opaque), and small magnitude maps to near transparency. 4. Map Color: Map the signed value of helicity h(\mathbf{x}) to color: extreme negative values map to cyan, extreme positive values map to magenta, and values near zero map to yellow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehelicityvisualization(velocityfield): # velocityfield: 3D list of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) containing (u, v, w) nx, ny, nz = len(velocityfield), len(velocityfield[0]), len(velocityfield[0][0]) output = [[[None for in range(nz)] for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] # 1. Compute Vorticity (Curl) using central differences vorticity = [[[None for in range(nz)] for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] for i in range(1, nx - 1): for j in range(1, ny - 1): for k in range(1, nz - 1): # omegax = dW/dy - dV/dz # omegay = dU/dz - dW/dx # omegaz = dV/dx - dU/dy vorticity[i][j][k] = [ (velocityfield[i][j+1][k][2] - velocityfield[i][j-1][k][2]) - (velocityfield[i][j][k+1][1] - velocityfield[i][j][k-1][1]), (velocityfield[i][j][k+1][0] - velocityfield[i][j][k-1][0]) - (velocityfield[i+1][j][k][2] - velocityfield[i-1][j][k][2]), (velocityfield[i+1][j][k][1] - velocityfield[i-1][j][k][1]) - (velocityfield[i][j+1][k][0] - velocityfield[i][j-1][k][0]) ] # 2. Compute Helicity & 3. Apply Transfer Function for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): # Handle boundaries by zero-padding (standard practice) if vorticity[i][j][k] is None: vorticity[i][j][k] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] h = (velocityfield[i][j][k][0] vorticity[i][j][k][0] + velocityfield[i][j][k][1] vorticity[i][j][k][1] + velocityfield[i][j][k][2] vorticity[i][j][k][2]) magh = abs(h) # Map Opacity: large magnitude -> opaque, small -> transparent # Exact scaling function not provided in sources alpha = min(1.0, magh / 10.0) # Map Color based on sign # Exact thresholds for "extreme" and "near zero" not provided if h > 0: color = [1.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Magenta elif h < 0: color = [0.0, 1.0, 1.0] # Cyan else: color = [1.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Yellow output[i][j][k] = color + [alpha] return output Parameters: Thresholds for "extreme" positive/negative and "near zero" are not explicitly defined in the sources. Scaling for opacity mapping is not specified. Edge Cases: Zero Helicity: If h(\mathbf{x}) = 0, the value maps to yellow and low opacity. Flow Reversal: Negative x-component velocity values indicate flow separation, which can produce negative helicity values mapped to cyan. Isolates flow disturbances by mapping perturbation velocity magnitude to opacity, making bulk free-stream flow invisible to highlight wakes or boundary layers. Strengths: Effectively visualizes vortices and distinguishes rotation direction using color. Maps magnitude to opacity to make features like "lambda" shocks and vortex cores visible. Limitations: Requires accurate computation of both velocity and its curl (vorticity). Exact thresholds and scaling functions for the transfer function are not standardized in the sources. Performance: Depends on the cost of computing the curl and dot product per voxel. No specific hardware performance metrics are provided in the sources. History: Helicity is defined as the scalar function representing the curl in the direction of the velocity. It was used to visualize vortices generated by fins in flow fields, identifying features like the "lambda" shock. Usage: Used in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to isolate flow disturbances and identify vortices. Volume Rendering for Computational Fluid Dynamics: Initial Results, https://www.nas.nasa.gov/assets/nas/pdf/techreports/1991/rnr-91-026.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Multi-dimensional Transfer Functions for Interactive 3D Flow Visualization, https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~hamann/ParkBudgeLinsenHamannJoy2004.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Perturbation Velocity Visualization
head: Subtracting free stream velocity
body: Perturbation Velocity Visualization is a technique in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to isolate flow disturbances by making the bulk of irrelevant free stream flow invisible. It achieves this by mapping the magnitude of the perturbation velocity vector to opacity. This method sets itself apart from standard velocity visualization by explicitly removing the uniform background flow, thereby highlighting regions of interaction, such as wakes or boundary layers, which would otherwise be obscured by the high opacity of the free stream. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D velocity field \mathbf{V} and a constant free stream velocity vector \mathbf{V}{fs}. Output: A volume rendering where opacity is determined by the magnitude of the perturbation velocity. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute Perturbation Velocity: For every cell in the velocity field, subtract the free stream velocity vector from the local velocity vector to compute the perturbation velocity vector \mathbf{V}{pert}: \mathbf{V}{pert} = \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{V}{fs} 2. Calculate Magnitude: Compute the Euclidean norm (magnitude) of the resulting perturbation velocity vector: |\mathbf{V}{pert}| = \sqrt{u{pert}^2 + v{pert}^2 + w{pert}^2} 3. Map to Opacity: Map the calculated magnitude |\mathbf{V}{pert}| to the opacity value for volume rendering. Typically, a magnitude of zero (matching the free stream) results in zero opacity, making the free stream invisible, while non-zero magnitudes result in higher opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeperturbationvelocityvisualization(velocityfield, freestreamvelocity): """ velocityfield: 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) containing (u, v, w) freestreamvelocity: tuple or array of length 3 (ufs, vfs, wfs) returns: 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) containing opacity values """ # Step 1: Subtract free stream velocity upert = velocityfield[:,:,:, 0] - freestreamvelocity[0] vpert = velocityfield[:,:,:, 1] - freestreamvelocity[1] wpert = velocityfield[:,:,:, 2] - freestreamvelocity[2] # Step 2: Calculate magnitude magnitude = (upert2 + vpert2 + wpert2)0.5 # Step 3: Map magnitude to opacity # Sources do not specify the exact transfer function; typically maps magnitude to opacity. opacity = magnitude return opacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No-slip boundaries: At solid surfaces, the fluid velocity is zero relative to the surface due to viscosity. Consequently, the perturbation velocity at the boundary is equal to the negative of the free stream velocity (\mathbf{V}{pert} = -\mathbf{V}{fs}), resulting in a large magnitude. This requires separate treatment to avoid rendering the entire surface as highly opaque or distorting the visualization of the wake. This variant visualizes a specific component (typically the x-component) of the perturbation velocity field rather than its magnitude. Negative values of the perturbation velocity x-component indicate locations where the flow is slower than the free stream velocity. These negative values are mapped to cyan and high opacity, while positive values (faster than free stream) are mapped to yellow and near transparency. The transfer function uses the extreme values of the data field to set the scale and offset into the linear color space. This approach is useful for identifying flow reversal or regions of significant deceleration. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of cells in the volume, as it requires a single pass to compute the difference and magnitude. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the velocity field and the resulting opacity field. Strengths: Effectively removes the visual clutter of uniform free stream flow, allowing the viewer to focus on flow disturbances, wakes, and boundary layer interactions. Limitations: Requires accurate knowledge of the free stream velocity vector. It may obscure the absolute velocity magnitude, making it difficult to assess flow speed without the context of the free stream. When to use: When the primary interest is in flow structures caused by obstacles or interactions, rather than the absolute speed of the fluid. The method was introduced in the context of volume rendering for Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). It was developed to address the challenge of visualizing vector fields where the dominant free stream flow obscures interesting features. The technique is part of a broader effort to apply volume rendering to CFD data, leveraging the ability to map scalar fields (like perturbation magnitude) to visual properties like opacity. Volume Rendering for Computational Fluid Dynamics: Initial Results, https://www.nas.nasa.gov/assets/nas/pdf/techreports/1991/rnr-91-026.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields
head: Vector Field Metric Extraction
body: Metric Scalar Field Rendering from Vector Fields converts multi-component vector field data into single-value scalar fields to enable standard scalar rendering techniques like volume rendering or isosurface extraction. It differs from direct vector visualization methods (e.g., arrow glyphs or particle advection) by projecting vector data into metrics such as velocity magnitude, divergence, or curl. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vector field \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) defined on a 3D grid, optionally time-dependent. Output: A scalar field S(x,y,z) derived from \mathbf{F}, used as input for a scalar renderer (volume raymarching or isosurface extraction). Data Structures: Vector Field Grid: A 3D array storing components (F1, F2, F3) at each voxel (i,j,k). Scalar Field Grid: A 3D array storing the computed metric value S at each voxel. Steps: 1. Metric Calculation: For each voxel (i,j,k), compute the desired scalar metric from the vector components. 2. Temporal Interpolation: If the data consists of discrete time slices, interpolate the vector and scalar values at the current time step between the surrounding time slices to support time-dependent visualization. 3. Rendering: Pass the resulting scalar field to a standard scalar volume renderer or isosurface extractor. Formulas: Velocity Magnitude: |\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{F1^2 + F2^2 + F3^2} Divergence: \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial F1}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F2}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F3}{\partial z} Curl Vector: \text{curl } \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial F3}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial F2}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial F1}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial F3}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial F2}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F1}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix} Curl Magnitude: |\text{curl } \mathbf{F}(i,j,k)| = \sqrt{ \left(\frac{\partial F3}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial F2}{\partial z}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial F1}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial F3}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial F2}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial F1}{\partial y}\right)^2 } Parameters: Metric Type: Selection of magnitude, divergence, or curl. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Derivatives required for curl and divergence are sensitive to grid boundaries. Not given in the sources how boundaries are handled. Loss of Directional Information: Scalarization discards the vector direction, which may be critical for interpreting flow topology. A specific metric extraction method that computes the magnitude of the curl of the vector field to highlight swirling features and vorticity (turbulent behavior). It is chosen when the visual goal is to identify regions of rotation or turbulence within the flow, distinguishing it from magnitude-based methods which show speed. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, for the metric calculation. Rendering complexity depends on the underlying scalar renderer. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the derived scalar field. Strengths: Allows the use of mature scalar volume rendering techniques for vector data; provides immersive 3D views of internal structures. Limitations: Discards directional information; requires careful selection of the metric to avoid misleading representations; derivatives (curl/divergence) are noisy and sensitive to discretization. The method was developed within interactive visual data analysis systems to enable standard scalar rendering techniques (isosurface extraction and direct volume rendering) on vector field data. It allows simultaneous visualization of scalar structures and vector-derived features. The curl magnitude metric is formally defined in the context of multi-dimensional transfer functions for 3D flow visualization. Interactive Visual data analysis | Daniel Suttor, https://dasutt.github.io/stories/interactive-visual-data-analysis/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Multi-dimensional Transfer Functions for Interactive 3D Flow Visualization, https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~hamann/ParkBudgeLinsenHamannJoy2004.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: X13 Volume Rendering and Isosurface Plotting
head: 3D isosurface figures, GLMakie volume render
body: X13 is a post-processing script that generates 3D volume renders and isosurface plots of scalar fields derived from vector field data (specifically velocity components) using the GLMakie library in Julia. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D turbulent flow structures (such as streamwise vortices) that are lost when reducing simulation data to 2D slices. It is distinguished from its sibling method X12, which uses orthogonal cutting planes via matplotlib, by rendering through the volume using GPU raymarching, providing a more immersive view of internal structures at the cost of requiring an OpenGL context (hardware or software rasterized). Inputs and Outputs: Input: NetCDF or HDF5 files containing simulation snapshots. Fields include velocity components (u, v, w) and optional derived fields. Output: PNG images of 3D figures containing volume renders or isosurfaces. Data Structures: The script reads data into memory arrays. For HDF5 virtual datasets (from multi-GPU merges), the storage must be registered before reading to avoid KeyError. Grid data is assumed to be stored at cell centers for all velocity components, allowing direct gradient computation without staggered interpolation. Parameters: --field: Comma-separated list of fields to render. Single field layouts panels by mode (volume/isosurface); multiple fields layout by field. --mode: 'volume' or 'isosurface'. --overlay: Name of a reference field (e.g., 'b') to draw as contours on vertical bounding walls. --clim-percentile: Upper percentile for color range, default 99. --zlim: Z-cropping limit. Default 5 (wider than plotting scripts' 4) to allow centred differences. --cols: Number of columns in panel grid, default 3. --scale: Appends suffix to budget terms. Steps: 1. Initialization and Virtual Storage Handling: If the input file is an HDF5 virtual dataset, call allowvirtualstorage!() to register the storage code, preventing KeyError during read operations. 2. Data Loading and Cropping: Load the specified fields from the NetCDF/HDF5 file. Crop the z-dimension to the active layer defined by --zlim. Keep one cell of margin on each side of the cropped slab to maintain accuracy for centred differences. Cropping before differentiation is critical to reduce memory usage; cropping after differentiation causes memory peaks of 15–25 GB at Nz=1024. 3. Derivation of Scalar Fields: If the requested fields are not present in the file, derive them from the velocity components u, v, w. Common derived fields include: Q-criterion (Q): Second invariant of the velocity gradient tensor. Enstrophy: Magnitude squared of the vorticity vector. Speed: Magnitude of the velocity vector. The file's own \omega is often only the spanwise component, which is insufficient for 3D structure analysis. All three velocities are at cell centers, so the gradient tensor is computed using centred differences on the single grid. 4. Gradient Computation: Compute the velocity gradient tensor \nabla \mathbf{u} using centred differences. In x and y (periodic boundaries): Use centred differences. In z (bounded boundaries): Use one-sided differences at the walls, matching the pipeline's treatment of the bounded axis. Formula for centred difference of a field f at index i: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \approx \frac{f{i+1} - f{i-1}}{2 \Delta x} This requires the one-cell margin established in Step 2. 5. Isosurface Level Calculation: Set isosurface levels symmetrically around zero. For each desired magnitude level L, create a pair of levels [-L, L]. Log these levels for visibility (e.g., -0.0849, -0.0299, 0.0299, 0.0849). For positive-definite fields, clamp positive-field isosurface levels into the color range. The top level is set to the 0.995 quantile of the data, while the color range ends at the --clim-percentile (default 99) quantile to prevent saturation. 6. Figure Layout and Rendering: Panel Resolution: Set panel resolution to 820x560 per panel to accommodate the cropped domain aspect ratio (roughly 14:4.7:8). Camera Orientation: Set camera azimuth to 1.30\pi to orient the streamwise direction (x) across the frame width while keeping the spanwise direction (y) readable. Color Scaling: Use a fixed fraction of each panel's own range for isosurface levels: 0.18, 0.515, and 0.85. This ensures a surface means the same thing across panels. Use a symmetric:balance color scale for all panels, including positive-definite fields, leaving the lower half unused to indicate the quantity never changes sign. Overlay: If --overlay is specified, draw contours of the reference field on the two vertical bounding walls. This shows the location of flow structures (e.g., billows) relative to the isosurfaces. Do not use isosurfaces for the overlay, as transparency cannot separate interpenetrating isosurfaces in GLMakie (alpha is ignored on volume contours). 7. Batch Rendering Setup: For off-screen rendering on clusters without GPUs/displays, use Xvfb and Mesa software rasterizer (LIBGLALWAYSSOFTWARE=1). Start Xvfb on a free display, smoke-test the OpenGL context, render, and kill the server. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def renderx13(inputfile, args): # 1. Handle HDF5 virtual datasets if ishdf5virtual(inputfile): allowvirtualstorage() # Julia NCDatasets helper # 2. Load and crop data data = loaddata(inputfile, args.field) zlimit = args.zlim if args.zlim is not None else 5 margin = 1 zstart = margin zend = data['u'].shape[0] - margin # Crop before differentiation to save memory datacropped = cropz(data, zstart, zend) # 3. Derive fields if necessary if "Q" in args.field and "Q" not in datacropped: # Compute gradient tensor using centred differences # Periodic in x, y; one-sided at z walls gradu = computegradient(datacropped['u'], datacropped['dx'], periodicx=True, periodicy=True, boundedz=True) gradv = computegradient(datacropped['v'], datacropped['dy'], periodicx=True, periodicy=True, boundedz=True) gradw = computegradient(datacropped['w'], datacropped['dz'], periodicx=True, periodicy=True, boundedz=True) # Compute Q-criterion vorticity = computevorticity(gradu, gradv, gradw) strain = computestrain(gradu, gradv, gradw) datacropped['Q'] = 0.5 (np.linalg.norm(vorticity)2 - np.linalg.norm(strain)2) # 4. Calculate isosurface levels levels = [] for magnitude in desiredmagnitudes: levels.append(-magnitude) levels.append(magnitude) # Clamp positive fields if ispositivedefinite(field): toplevelquantile = np.quantile(fielddata, 0.995) climpercentile = args.climpercentile if args.climpercentile else 99 climlimit = np.quantile(fielddata, climpercentile / 100.0) levels = [l for l in levels if abs(l) <= climlimit] # 5. Render fig = Figure(resolution=(820 args.cols, 560 ((len(args.field) + args.cols - 1) // args.cols))) for panelindex, fieldname in enumerate(args.field): ax = Axis3(fig[panelindex]) # Set camera azimuth ax.camera.azimuth = 1.30 np.pi # Draw isosurfaces or volume if args.mode == "isosurface": drawisosurfaces(ax, datacropped[fieldname], levels=levels, colorscale=":balance", symmetric=True) else: drawvolume(ax, datacropped[fieldname]) # Overlay reference field on walls if specified if args.overlay: overlayfield = datacropped[args.overlay] drawcontoursonwalls(ax, overlayfield, zboundaries=[zstart, zend]) # Set color limits clim = np.quantile(datacropped[fieldname], args.climpercentile / 100.0) setcolorlimits(ax, clim=clim) # Save figure save("output.png", fig) Time Complexity: Rendering time is approximately 90 seconds per six-panel figure at Nz=1024 on a Casper compute node. A full 101-record set takes ~2.5 hours. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is significantly reduced by cropping the z-dimension before differentiation. A subsetter script can reduce file size from 2.15 GiB to 0.006 GiB (336x compression) for testing. Without cropping, memory peaks can reach 15–25 GB at Nz=1024. Hardware Requirements: Requires an OpenGL context. Can run on CPU-only clusters using Xvfb and Mesa software rasterizer. Does not require a dedicated GPU. Strengths: Provides immersive 3D visualization of internal flow structures (e.g., vortices) that 2D slices miss. Efficient batch rendering on CPU clusters. Limitations: Transparency cannot separate interpenetrating isosurfaces. Requires careful tuning of isosurface levels and color scales for multi-field figures. Not suitable for batch jobs without any display/OpenGL support (use X12 instead). X13 was developed as part of the tomchor/CoarseGrainedKHAPE repository for rendering 3D isosurfaces of turbulent flow simulations. It was introduced in October 2026 as a companion to X12, which used orthogonal cutting planes. X13 leverages GLMakie for GPU raymarching volume rendering, addressing the need to visualize 3D structures like streamwise vortices in Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) runs. It runs on the Casper compute cluster using off-screen rendering techniques. 3D isosurface figures: X13, a batch render job, and a subsetter, https://github.com/tomchor/CoarseGrainedKHAPE/pull/78, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Derived Field Computation
head: Derived Fields, Field Composition via Functions, Recursive Field Generators
body: Derived Field Computation generates new data fields by applying mathematical functions to existing base fields or other derived fields. It differs from direct visualization methods by decoupling the data definition from the rendering pipeline, allowing for recursive composition and arbitrary mathematical operations that require data from neighboring grid patches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: One or more base fields (e.g., velocity components vx, vy, vz) or previously computed derived fields, accessed via a data container. Output: A new field represented as a NumPy array containing the computed values at each cell or sample point. Data Structures: Field Data: The underlying data is stored in a multi-dimensional array structure corresponding to the spatial domain. When higher-order operations are required, the data structure includes buffer cells. Buffer Cells: These are additional cells surrounding the primary computational domain, populated with data from neighboring grids (covering grids) to support stencils that extend beyond a single grid patch. Steps: 1. Define the Function: Create a function that accepts the field metadata and a data dictionary containing the input fields. 2. Access Input Data: Retrieve the required base fields (e.g., data["x-velocity"]) from the data dictionary. 3. Formulas: The magnitude of a velocity vector \mathbf{v} is computed as: V = \sqrt{vx^2 + vy^2 + vz^2} where vx, vy, vz are the velocity components in the x, y, and z directions, respectively. Parameters: Buffer Cells: The number of buffer cells specified when requesting 3D data. Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Finite difference stencils may extend beyond the computational domain of a single grid patch. This is handled by utilizing covering grids to provide buffer cells from neighboring grids. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
