name: Multi Field Visualization
body: Multi Field Visualization is a DOP node that visualizes multiple field data, combining and ramping fields to preview rendering behavior. It operates as a fast preview tool within the dynamics network, prioritizing speed and parameter tuning over photorealistic accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: The node accepts an optional object stream input (First Input) to specify which simulation objects are modified; objects connected here matching the Group parameter are modified. If unconnected, the node can be used with an Apply Data node or as input to another data node. Other data nodes attached to subsequent inputs act as modifiers for the data created by this node. The output is an object stream (if an object stream input is provided) containing the same objects with the visualization data attached, or a data output connectable to Apply Data DOP or other data nodes. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: Not given in the sources. Formulas: Volume values v are linearly remapped from a per-field mapping range [R{min}, R{max}] into v' \in [0, 1] using v' = \frac{v - R{min}}{R{max} - R{min}}. For the Emission Color Physical Blackbody mode, the temperature T corresponding to a normalized field value is interpolated between T0 (value 0.0) and T1 (value 1.0), then scaled by Ts before mapping to color via the blackbody radiation spectrum. Parameters: Field: Specifies the name of the field to visualize. If a color field (diffuse/emission) is specified, a scalar field is treated as monochromatic. If a vector field is specified, its components are tied to the red, green, and blue channels. Minimum, Maximum: Defines the density volume range remapped to 0..1. It acts as the default range for all other volumes unless overridden. Range: Per-field mapping range [R{min}, R{max}]. Mode: Controls ramp usage. 'No Ramp' uses values unclamped and unaffected. 'Clamped Ramp' clamps values to 0..1 before applying the ramp. 'Periodic Ramp' takes the modulus of values with 1 before sending to the ramp, useful for checkerboard or striped effects. Ramp: Volume values (after range conversion) are looked up in the ramp. If a color ramp has one volume bound, the value looks up the color. If two or three volumes are bound, each looks up R, G, B independently. Emission Color Physical Blackbody: Maps Emission Color Field values using the blackbody radiation spectrum, similar to the Physical (Black-Body) Color Mode on the Pyro Shader VOP. Temperature Scale (Ts): Scale applied to Emission Color Field values before mapping to color via blackbody spectrum. Temperature at 0 (K) (T0): Sets the Kelvin temperature corresponding to a value of 0.0 in the Emission Color Field. Temperature at 1 (K) (T1): Sets the Kelvin temperature corresponding to a value of 1.0 in the Emission Color Field. Adaptation: Manipulates the low end of the generated intensity. Burn: Manipulates the high end of the generated intensity. Density Scale: Fixed multiplier for the density field to control opacity. Shadow Scale: Multiplier applied to the Density Field after density scale, used for lighting. Equivalent to multiplying all light shadow intensities by this value. Max Vis Res: Default maximum volume resolution is 128 voxels per side to ensure fast shading and avoid texture memory issues. Visualization Mode: When set, 2D volumes are visualized as a height field instead of smoke. Bounding Box: Draws a bounding box encompassing the field. Bounding Box Hash: Adds hash marks along axes from the origin, marking voxel divisions. Marks are larger for every tenth and hundredth division. Local Variables: The node defines local variables for each channel/parameter on the Data Options page, evaluating to the previous value stored in attached data. Key variables include: channelname: Shortcut for dopfield(DOPNET, OBJID, dataName, "Options", 0, channelname). Returns 0 or empty string if data doesn't exist. DATACT/DATACF: Simulation time (ST) and frame (SF) at which current data was created. ST/SF: Simulation time and frame for node evaluation. SF equals ST divided by TIMESTEP. TIMESTEP: Size of a simulation timestep. SFPS is its inverse. SNOBJ/NOBJ: Total objects in simulation and objects evaluated by the current node, respectively. OBJ: Index of specific object being processed (0 to NOBJ-1). -1 if not processed sequentially. OBJID: Unique integer identifier for the object. Best way to look up info via dopfield. -1 if not processed sequentially. ALLOBJIDS/ALLOBJNAMES: Space-separated lists of unique object identifiers and names being processed. OBJCT/OBJCF: Simulation time and frame at which current object was created. OBJNAME: String name of object being processed. Empty string if not processed sequentially. DOPNET: Full path of the current DOP network. RELNAME, RELOBJIDS, RELOBJNAMES, RELAFFOBJIDS, RELAFFOBJNAMES: Set only when attaching data to a relationship, containing relationship name, affected object IDs/names, and affector object IDs/names. Pitfalls: Fog density is per unit and independent of resolution. Small boxes become transparent, especially without HDR rendering. Enable HDR rendering in the Effects tab of the Display Options dialog to fix this. Performance: Restricted to a default maximum of 128 voxels per side to ensure reasonably fast shading times and avoid texture memory problems. Scaling: Density is per unit, meaning opacity depends on scene scale rather than voxel count alone. Limitations: Provides a preview of rendering behavior rather than a final photorealistic render. Multi Field Visualization is a node within the Houdini Dynamics (DOP) network, introduced in version 12.0. It is part of the suite of dynamics nodes designed to manipulate and visualize simulation data. Multi Field Visualization - SideFX, https://www.sidefx.com/docs/houdini/nodes/dop/multifieldvisualization.html, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Dual Volume Rendering
head: Dual-field volume rendering, Multi-field correlation visualization
body: Dual Volume Rendering is a visualization technique for displaying two scalar fields simultaneously within a volume to investigate their correlations. It extends standard texture-based volume rendering by using the transparency (opacity) values of one scalar field to define the isocontours (isobars) onto which the second scalar field is color-mapped. Unlike overlaid rendering, which conceals features in regions of rapid value changes or high concentrations, Dual Volume Rendering allows the viewer to follow steep gradients of both quantities simultaneously. Inputs and Outputs Input: Two scalar fields, F1(\mathbf{x}) and F2(\mathbf{x}), defined on a 3D grid or point set. Output: A 2D image where color encodes one field and opacity/structure encodes the other. Data Structures Two scalar grids of identical dimensions (or resampled to match). Transfer functions for color mapping (Tc) and opacity mapping (To). Method The method constructs a composite visual attribute for each sample point \mathbf{x} along a ray. Let FA be the field defining the structural opacity (the "carrier") and FB be the field defining the color (the "content"). 1. Sample Fields: At sample point \mathbf{x}, retrieve values vA = FA(\mathbf{x}) and vB = FB(\mathbf{x}). 2. Compute Opacity: Determine the opacity \alpha using the transfer function for the carrier field: \alpha = To(vA) Typically, To is designed to highlight isocontours or gradients of FA, often resulting in high opacity at specific threshold values of FA and low opacity elsewhere. 3. Compute Color: Determine the color C using the transfer function for the content field: C = Tc(vB) Tc maps the range of FB to a color spectrum (e.g., red-blue for low-high). 4. Composite: Accumulate the color and opacity along the ray using standard volume integration (e.g., front-to-back compositing). Pseudocode The following pseudocode implements the per-sample computation for Dual Volume Rendering. It assumes standard front-to-back volume rendering integration. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualvolumerendersample(x, raydirection, gridA, gridB, To, Tc): """ Computes the color and opacity contribution for a single sample point in a Dual Volume Rendering setup. Args: x: Current 3D position in world space. raydirection: Normalized ray direction vector. gridA: Scalar field defining opacity (carrier). gridB: Scalar field defining color (content). To: Opacity transfer function mapping value -> [0, 1]. Tc: Color transfer function mapping value -> RGB color. Returns: color: RGB color contribution. alpha: Opacity contribution. """ # 1. Sample the two scalar fields at position x # Note: Interpolation (e.g., trilinear) is required if x is not on grid nodes. valA = gridA.sample(x) valB = gridB.sample(x) # 2. Map the carrier field (A) to opacity # This defines the "isocontours" or structural visibility alpha = To(valA) # 3. Map the content field (B) to color # This provides the visual information about the second quantity color = Tc(valB) return color, alpha def dualvolumerenderray(rayorigin, raydirection, gridA, gridB, To, Tc, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using Dual Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: Start of the ray. raydirection: Direction of the ray. gridA: Scalar field for opacity. gridB: Scalar field for color. To: Opacity transfer function. Tc: Color transfer function. numsamples: Number of steps along the ray. Returns: finalcolor: The resulting RGB color for this ray. """ # Standard front-to-back compositing initialization accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 # Step size stepsize = 1.0 / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): # Calculate current sample position t = i stepsize x = rayorigin + t raydirection # Check if x is within volume bounds if not isinsidevolume(x): break # Get contribution from this sample color, alpha = dualvolumerendersample(x, raydirection, gridA, gridB, To, Tc) # Front-to-back compositing # Weight of current sample relative to what has already been accumulated weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + color weight accumulatedalpha = accumulatedalpha + weight # Early ray termination if fully opaque if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor Parameters and Typical Values Transfer Functions: To is often a threshold or gradient-based function to highlight isocontours of FA. Tc is typically a linear or diverging colormap (e.g., red-blue) for FB. Symmetry: The method is symmetric in concept; one can map F1 color onto F2 isocontours or vice versa. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Occlusion: If To for the carrier field is too opaque, it may obscure the color information of the content field in regions where both fields are significant. Gradient Concealment: Unlike simple overlay, this method is specifically designed to avoid concealing features in regions of rapid value changes, but poor choice of To can still lead to loss of detail. General techniques for combining multiple data fields, including additive blending and layering. Choose when simple overlay is sufficient and correlation analysis is not the primary goal. Multi-field Visualization Combination Methods that map multiple scalar components to color directly (e.g., via color space mapping). Choose when the number of fields exceeds two or when complex multivariate relationships need direct color encoding. Multivariate Volume Rendering Techniques for defining how data values map to visual attributes. Essential for tuning the Tc and To functions in Dual Volume Rendering. Transfer Function and Color Mapping Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples, identical to standard volume rendering. The additional cost is the sampling of a second grid and the evaluation of an additional transfer function. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two scalar fields. If the fields are large, memory bandwidth may become a bottleneck during ray traversal. Strengths: Reveals correlations between two scalar fields that are otherwise hidden in overlaid rendering. Preserves visibility of steep gradients for both quantities simultaneously. Intuitive interpretation: structure is defined by one field, content by the other. Limitations: Limited to two scalar fields. Requires careful tuning of transfer functions to balance visibility of both fields. May suffer from visual clutter if both fields have high-frequency variations. When to Use: Investigating correlations between plasma properties (e.g., magnetic pressure and density) in astrophysical simulations or other domains where two scalar quantities interact. When Not to Use: When more than two fields need to be visualized simultaneously, or when the primary goal is to visualize vector/tensor directions rather than scalar correlations. Dual Volume Rendering was introduced in the context of visualizing numerical astrophysics data, specifically for investigating correlations between plasma properties in the intra-cluster medium (ICM) from magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. The technique extends the usual color-mapping algorithm of texture-based volume rendering to use transparency values from a second scalar field, allowing the display of two scalar fields at once. It addresses the limitation of overlaid rendering, which conceals features in regions of rapid value changes or high concentrations. Visualization Methods for Numerical Astrophysics, https://doi.org/10.5772/32203, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Tensor Shape and Invariant Analysis
head: Tensor Invariant Analysis, Shape Space Visualization
body: Tensor Shape and Invariant Analysis is a family of visualization mapping techniques that decompose second-order tensor fields into scalar invariants (such as eigenvalues, norms, or directional distributions) to reveal structural properties like anisotropy, stress type, or dominant orientation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization by abstracting the tensor into statistical or geometric descriptors rather than rendering local geometric primitives, and from Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) Visualization by offering robust Cartesian-based representations (Shape Space) that remain stable for indefinite tensors where spherical coordinates fail. All methods in this family evaluate a mapping function M(\mathbf{x}) at sample points \mathbf{x} within the volume to produce visual attributes. The core mechanism involves sampling the multi-component data field at \mathbf{x}, decomposing or normalizing the value (e.g., extracting magnitude, direction, eigenvalues, or phase), and applying a transfer function or geometric construction to map these features to rendering parameters such as color, opacity, or primitive geometry. Shape Space is a visualization mapping technique that represents the shape of a second-order tensor by mapping its three eigenvalues to a point in a 3D vector space. It provides a coordinate system where the tensor's structural properties are explicit. Unlike spherical coordinate systems (tensor norm, fractional anisotropy, tensor mode) used in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), which become unstable for tensors with small norms because angular coordinates are undefined at the origin, Shape Space uses Cartesian-like descriptors that remain stable for indefinite tensors where eigenvalues may be positive, negative, or zero. The Directional Histogram is a visualization method for analyzing the distribution of principal directions (such as eigenvectors or shear directions) within a tensor field by projecting them onto a unit sphere. It differs from sibling methods like Domain Colouring or Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization by aggregating directional data into statistical bins on a sphere rather than mapping values directly to color at spatial locations or rendering geometric primitives. This allows for the identification of dominant orientations and anisotropy in the field. A 2D plot depicting the relation between two scalar invariants, specifically principal stresses, to quantify normal and shear stresses. Sort the three principal stresses in descending order: \sigma1 \ge \sigma2 \ge \sigma3. Plot \sigma1 on the x-axis and \sigma3 on the y-axis, dividing the plot into four quadrants (A, B, C, D). Apply a sign-preserving logarithmic mapping to the eigenvalues: f(\sigmai) = \log(\sigmai + 1) for \sigmai \ge 0, and f(\sigmai) = -\log(1 - \sigmai) for \sigmai < 0. Linearly map the results of the logarithmic mapping to the range [-1, 1]. Unlike standard logarithmic mappings that require positive domains, this method preserves signs to distinguish between positive (tensile) and negative (compressive) invariants. A method to estimate local frequency content and orientation by analyzing image structure across multiple scales using Gaussian blur kernels and aggregating normalized structure tensors weighted by texture energy. Construct a Gaussian scale space using kernels G{\tilde{\tau}l} with increasing standard deviations \tilde{\tau}l = 1.5^l for l \in 0, \dots, L (where L=4 in practice), maintaining full spatial resolution at all levels to yield images Il. At each level l, compute per-pixel structure tensors Sl using an integration scale \rhol = 3\tilde{\tau}l. Normalize the tensor to remove influence of overall signal magnitude: \hat{S}l = \frac{Sl}{\text{tr}(Sl) + \epsilon}, where \epsilon > 0 ensures numerical stability. Aggregate structure tensors weighted by energy and squared frequency: \bar{S} = \frac{\sum{l=0}^L El^\gamma \omegal^2 \hat{S}l}{\sum{l=0}^L El^\gamma + \epsilon}, where \gamma=3.0 controls weighting sharpness. The concept of Shape Space and Mohr diagrams for stress tensor analysis was formalized in engineering visualization contexts, notably presented in "A Visual Approach to Analysis of Stress Tensor Fields" (2011). This work introduced Shape Space Scatterplots and Mohr diagrams as tools to quantify normal and shear stresses, addressing the limitations of spherical coordinates for indefinite tensors. The application of multi-scale structure tensor analysis for frequency-aware visualization was later adapted for 3D Gaussian Splatting convergence in "Faster 3D Gaussian Splatting Convergence via Structure-Aware Densification" (2025), extending tensor analysis to scale-space representations for structure-aware densification. name: Shape Space (Tensor Eigenvalue Space)
head: Eigenvalue Space for Tensors, Tensor Shape Space
body: Shape Space is a visualization mapping technique that represents the shape of a second-order tensor by mapping its three eigenvalues to a point in a 3D vector space. It provides a coordinate system where the tensor's structural properties are explicit. Unlike spherical coordinate systems (tensor norm, fractional anisotropy, tensor mode) used in Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), which become unstable for tensors with small norms because angular coordinates are undefined at the origin, Shape Space uses Cartesian-like descriptors that remain stable for indefinite tensors where eigenvalues may be positive, negative, or zero. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A second-order tensor field \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x}) evaluated at sample points \mathbf{x}. Output: A point in Shape Space with coordinates (\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3), where \lambdai are the eigenvalues, serving as shape descriptors for further mapping (e.g., glyph sizing, color, opacity). Data Structures: Tensor: 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix at each \mathbf{x}. Shape Space Point: 3D vector [\lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3]. Steps: 1. Sample Tensor: Evaluate the tensor field \mathbf{T} at the current sample point \mathbf{x}. 2. Compute Eigenvalues: Solve for the three real eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 of the symmetric tensor matrix. 3. Assign Coordinates: Map the eigenvalues to the Shape Space axes. The standard reference frame maps the major eigenvalue to the x-axis, the minor eigenvalue to the y-axis, and the medium eigenvalue to the z-axis. 4. Optional Transformation: Apply a change of basis if specific invariants are required. A rotation around the medium eigenvalue (\sigma2) axis by 45 degrees transforms the coordinates into Mohr’s Circle parameters: shear stress \tau, center c, and radius R. 5. Map to Visuals: Use the resulting coordinates (raw eigenvalues or transformed invariants) to determine rendering parameters. The radius R distinguishes planar from linear stresses. Formulas: Tensor Norm: \|\mathbf{T}\|^2 = \lambda1^2 + \lambda2^2 + \lambda3^2. Mohr’s Circle Radius: R = \frac{\lambda{\text{max}} - \lambda{\text{min}}}{2}. Mohr’s Circle Center: c = \frac{\lambda{\text{max}} + \lambda{\text{min}}}{2}. Maximum Shear Stress: \tau = R. Parameters: Orthogonality: Descriptors should ideally be orthogonal to exhibit maximum independence, isolating changes of one invariant from variations of the others. Axis Scaling: The scale of the shape space’s coordinate axes has a high impact on the visualization result and must be considered for diagram views and rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Norm: Derived spherical coordinates are unstable when \|\mathbf{T}\|^2 \approx 0 because angular coordinates are undefined at the origin. Indefinite Tensors: Shape Space is preferred over spherical coordinates for indefinite tensors because Cartesian-like descriptors handle positive, negative, or zero eigenvalues naturally. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshapespacepoint(tensormatrix): # Step 1: Compute eigenvalues of the 3x3 symmetric tensor matrix # Standard symmetric eigenvalue decomposition for 3x3 matrix eigenvalues = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # # Step 2: Sort eigenvalues into major (max), medium (median), minor (min) major = max(eigenvalues) minor = min(eigenvalues) medium = sum(eigenvalues) - major - minor # Step 3: Assign to Shape Space axes: x=major, y=minor, z=medium return (major, minor, medium) def transformtomohrparameters(shapepoint): # Optional transformation: rotation around medium axis by 45 degrees major, minor, medium = shapepoint # Radius distinguishes planar and linear stresses R = (major - minor) / 2.0 c = (major + minor) / 2.0 tau = R return (tau, c, R) Maps tensor invariants to a scale suitable for visualization, addressing the challenge that indefinite tensors have positive, negative, or zero eigenvalues while many visualization methods require positive values. It distinguishes itself from siblings like the Mohr Diagram by focusing on the direct transformation of eigenvalue magnitudes for glyph sizing and color/opacity mapping in the spatial domain, rather than projecting stress states onto invariant planes. A visualization technique representing the most important invariants for stress tensors, plotting normal stress vs. shear stress. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, dominated by eigenvalue decomposition of a 3 \times 3 matrix. Memory Complexity: O(1) per sample point to store the 3 eigenvalues. Strengths: Stable for indefinite tensors; provides intuitive geometric interpretation of tensor shape; orthogonal descriptors allow independent analysis of invariants. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: When visualizing stress or diffusion tensors where the sign of eigenvalues matters (indefinite tensors) or when a Cartesian-like representation of tensor shape is preferred over spherical coordinates. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Shape Space was introduced in the context of stress tensor field analysis. The concept is detailed in "A Visual Approach to Analysis of Stress Tensor Fields" by A. Kratz, B. Meyer, and I. Hotz. The method builds on the idea that tensor shape can be represented as a point in a vector space spanned by its eigenvalues, allowing for the application of standard geometric transformations (like Mohr’s Circle) to visualize complex tensor states. name: Shape Space Scaling
head: Antisymmetric Mapping, Antisymmetric Mapping for Tensor Glyphs, POS mapping, Sign-preserving mappings
body: Shape Space Scaling maps tensor invariants (eigenvalues) to a scale suitable for visualization, addressing the challenge that indefinite tensors have positive, negative, or zero eigenvalues while many visualization methods require positive values. It provides a positive-definite metric for glyph sizing that distinguishes between positive and negative eigenvalues. It directly transforms eigenvalue magnitudes for glyph sizing and spatial domain rendering, operating differently from sibling methods like the Mohr Diagram. Inputs and Outputs Input: Tensor eigenvalues \bar{\sigma}i (where i indexes the three principal values). Output: Scaled values f(\bar{\sigma}i) suitable for positive-definite metrics or sign-preserving visualization. Data Structures The method operates on scalar eigenvalues. Eigenvectors are already normalized and do not require scaling or mapping. Steps 1. Determine the visualization requirement: whether the downstream method requires strictly positive values (POS) or can handle signed values (SP). 2. If using Sign-preserving mappings (SP), apply a linear, logarithmic, or histogram equalization mapping that preserves the sign of the input eigenvalues. 3. If using Mapping to R+ (POS), apply the antisymmetric mapping function to convert eigenvalues to the positive domain while maintaining the distinction between positive and negative inputs. 4. Apply a global scale parameter to adapt the final glyph size or visual intensity. Formulas For the POS mapping (Antisymmetric Mapping), the function is defined as: f(\bar{\sigma}i, c, \alpha) = \exp(\alpha \arctan(c \cdot \bar{\sigma}i)) Where: \bar{\sigma}i is the i-th eigenvalue of the tensor. c is a parameter determining the slope of the function in the origin. \alpha is a scaling parameter for the antisymmetric mapping function. Parameters c: Determines the slope of the antisymmetric mapping function in the origin. Typical values are not specified in the sources. \alpha: A scaling parameter for the antisymmetric mapping function. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Global scale parameter: Used to adapt the glyph's size. Value depends on the desired visual output. Pitfalls Eigenvectors do not require scaling as they are already normalized. The choice of mapping (SP vs POS) depends heavily on the specific dataset and the desired visualization outcome; an optimal mapping is not universal. Indefinite tensors pose a challenge because their sign reveals important physical characteristics, which may be lost if mapped to R+ without care. Not given in the sources. Shape Space Scaling is discussed in the context of visual analysis of stress tensor fields, specifically within the framework of Shape Space (Tensor Eigenvalue Space) visualization. It was proposed to handle the scaling of coordinate axes in shape space diagrams and spatial rendering where tensor invariants define color, transparency, glyph shape, and glyph size. The method references prior work on antisymmetric mappings [23, 29] within the source text. name: Mohr Diagram
head: Mohr's Circle
body: The Mohr Diagram is a visualization technique for stress tensors that plots normal stress against shear stress to represent the most important invariants. It sets itself apart from scalar volume rendering by explicitly mapping the relationship between the three eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor to geometric circles, allowing for the inspection of maximum shear stress and the transition between tensile and compressive forces. It builds on Shape Space (Tensor Eigenvalue Space) by projecting tensor invariants onto a 2D plane. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A symmetric second-order tensor field. The three eigenvalues of each tensor are extracted. Output: A 2D plot where the horizontal axis represents normal stress and the vertical axis represents shear stress. Data Structures: Tensor: A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. Eigenvalues: A tuple (\sigma1, \sigma2, \sigma3) representing the principal stresses. Mohr Circle: Defined by a center C and radius R. Formulas: For a tensor with eigenvalues \sigma1, \sigma2, \sigma3, three Mohr circles are constructed between the eigenvalues: 1. Outer Circle: Connects the maximum and minimum eigenvalues. Center: C{outer} = \frac{\sigma1 + \sigma3}{2} Radius: R{outer} = \frac{\sigma1 - \sigma3}{2} 2. Middle Circle: Connects the maximum and middle eigenvalues. Center: C{mid1} = \frac{\sigma1 + \sigma2}{2} Radius: R{mid1} = \frac{\sigma1 - \sigma2}{2} 3. Inner Circle: Connects the middle and minimum eigenvalues. Center: C{mid2} = \frac{\sigma2 + \sigma3}{2} Radius: R{mid2} = \frac{\sigma2 - \sigma3}{2} The shaded region between the circles represents all possible combinations of normal and shear forces for a given cutting plane. A point within this region corresponds to the orientation of the plane’s normal. Parameters: Sign Convention: Negative eigenvalues are interpreted as compressive forces (volume reduction); positive eigenvalues as tensile forces (volume expansion). Some application areas use the reverse sign convention. Clutter Reduction: To equalize circle distribution and reduce clutter around the origin (high shear and tensile/compressive transitions), the diagram is divided into three separate sub-diagrams based on anisotropic behavior (isotropic, linear, planar). Semi-circles are drawn in context regions to achieve a compact visualization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemohrcircles(eigenvalues): sigma1, sigma2, sigma3 = eigenvalues return [ {"center": (sigma1 + sigma3) / 2.0, "radius": (sigma1 - sigma3) / 2.0, "type": "outer"}, {"center": (sigma1 + sigma2) / 2.0, "radius": (sigma1 - sigma2) / 2.0, "type": "mid1"}, {"center": (sigma2 + sigma3) / 2.0, "radius": (sigma2 - sigma3) / 2.0, "type": "mid2"} ] def classifytensor(eigenvalues): sigma1, sigma2, sigma3 = eigenvalues # Categorization thresholds not given in the sources. if abs(sigma1 - sigma3) < 1e-6: return "isotropic" elif abs(sigma2 - sigma3) < abs(sigma1 - sigma2): return "planar" else: return "linear" Edge Cases: Isotropic Tensors: If \sigma1 \approx \sigma2 \approx \sigma3, the circles collapse to a single point. Precision: Numerical stability in eigenvalue decomposition is critical for accurate circle placement. An extension of the standard Mohr diagram designed to reduce clutter and analyze the relationship between three eigenvalues and their relative strength. It categorizes tensors by anisotropic behavior (isotropic, linear, or planar) and divides the diagram into three separate sub-diagrams to equalize circle distribution. Tensors with similar eigenvalue behavior are clustered using Euclidean distance in shape space as the similarity measure, and the number of occurrences in each cluster is encoded by color. Semi-circles are drawn in context regions to achieve a compact visualization without losing information. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides immediate visual insight into maximum shear stress (radius of the outer circle) and the balance between tensile and compressive forces (position on the x-axis). Limitations: Best used after a selection has been specified in other diagram views, as it is not suitable for inspecting large, unselected datasets due to potential clutter. Scaling: The extended version scales better for dense datasets by using clustering and separation by anisotropy. The Mohr diagram originates from the analysis of stress tensors, where it represents the most important invariants. It is based on the classical Mohr's circle method from continuum mechanics [10] (cited in). The specific visualization techniques described, including the extended diagram with clustering and anisotropy-based separation, were proposed by A. Kratz, B. Meyer, and I. Hotz in 2011. name: Eigenvalue wheel
head: Cubic characteristic polynomial wheel, Nickalls wheel
body: The eigenvalue wheel is a geometric visualization method that maps the three real eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor to the projections of equally spaced spokes on a circle. It solves the problem of visualizing tensor shape by encoding the mean, variance, and skewness of the eigenvalues into the circle's center, radius, and spoke orientation, respectively. Unlike the Mohr circle diagram which uses nested circles to convey pairwise differences, or trilinear coordinate systems that map eigenvalues to a single point in a triangular space, the eigenvalue wheel uses continuous geometric parameters of a single circle to display the full shape information. Inputs: The three eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3. Outputs: A geometric representation defined by a center \mu1, a radius R, and an orientation angle \Theta. Data Structures: The method computes three scalar invariants from the eigenvalues: 1. Mean (\mu1): The first central moment. 2. Variance-related Radius (R): Derived from the second central moment \mu2. 3. Skewness-related Angle (\Theta): Derived from the third central moment \mu3 and the standard deviation. Formulas and Definitions: Let the eigenvalues be sorted such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3. 1. Mean (\mu1): \mu1 = \frac{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3}{3} = \frac{J1}{3} where J1 is the first principal invariant (trace). 2. Second Central Moment (\mu2) and Radius (R): \mu2 = \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=1}^3 (\lambdai - \mu1)^2 The radius of the wheel is: R = 2\sqrt{Q} = \sqrt{2\mu2} = \sigma\sqrt{2} where \sigma = \sqrt{\mu2} is the standard deviation of the eigenvalues, and Q is the second principal invariant of the deviatoric tensor. 3. Third Central Moment (\mu3) and Skewness (\alpha3): \mu3 = \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=1}^3 (\lambdai - \mu1)^3 \alpha3 = \frac{\mu3}{\sigma^3} 4. Spoke Orientation (\Theta): \Theta = \frac{1}{3} \cos^{-1}(\sqrt{2} \alpha3) Note: The argument to \cos^{-1} must be clamped to [-1, 1] to handle numerical precision errors. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the mean \mu1 from the input eigenvalues. 2. Compute the standard deviation \sigma and the skewness \alpha3. 3. Calculate the radius R = \sigma\sqrt{2}. 4. Calculate the orientation angle \Theta = \frac{1}{3} \cos^{-1}(\sqrt{2} \alpha3). 5. Define three spokes at angles \Theta, \Theta - 2\pi/3, and \Theta + 2\pi/3 relative to the horizontal axis. 6. The eigenvalues are the projections of the spoke ends onto the horizontal axis passing through \mu1. The projections are given by: \lambda1 = \mu1 + R \cos(\Theta) \lambda2 = \mu1 + R \cos(\Theta - 2\pi/3) \lambda3 = \mu1 + R \cos(\Theta + 2\pi/3) These formulas inherently produce sorted eigenvalues \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def eigenvaluewheel(lambda1, lambda2, lambda3): """ Computes the geometric parameters of the eigenvalue wheel. Args: lambda1, lambda2, lambda3: The three eigenvalues of a symmetric tensor. Returns: mu1: Center of the wheel (mean). R: Radius of the wheel. Theta: Orientation angle of the spokes. """ # Step 1: Compute Mean mu1 = (lambda1 + lambda2 + lambda3) / 3.0 # Step 2: Compute Standard Deviation (sigma) # mu2 is the variance mu2 = ((lambda1 - mu1)2 + (lambda2 - mu1)2 + (lambda3 - mu1)2) / 3.0 sigma = math.sqrt(mu2) # Edge case: If sigma is 0, all eigenvalues are equal. # The wheel collapses to a point. Theta is undefined but irrelevant. if sigma == 0: return mu1, 0.0, 0.0 # Step 3: Compute Skewness (alpha3) mu3 = ((lambda1 - mu1)3 + (lambda2 - mu1)3 + (lambda3 - mu1)3) / 3.0 alpha3 = mu3 / (sigma3) # Step 4: Compute Orientation Angle (Theta) # Clamp argument to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors arg = math.sqrt(2.0) alpha3 arg = max(-1.0, min(1.0, arg)) Theta = (1.0 / 3.0) math.acos(arg) # Radius R = sigma math.sqrt(2.0) return mu1, R, Theta def reconstructeigenvalues(mu1, R, Theta): """ Reconstructs the sorted eigenvalues from the wheel parameters. """ l1 = mu1 + R math.cos(Theta) l2 = mu1 + R math.cos(Theta - 2.0 math.pi / 3.0) l3 = mu1 + R math.cos(Theta + 2.0 math.pi / 3.0) return l1, l2, l3 Parameters: \mu1: Center location on the real axis. R: Radius, proportional to the standard deviation. \Theta: Angle in radians, typically in [0, \pi/3] due to symmetry and sorting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Plane: The circle does not lie on the complex plane. The symmetry of the tensor \mathbf{D} ensures three real eigenvalues, avoiding the case of one real and two complex-conjugate eigenvalues. Degenerate Input: If all eigenvalues are equal (\sigma = 0), the radius is 0 and the wheel collapses to a single point. The angle \Theta is undefined but does not affect the result. Numerical Precision: The argument to \cos^{-1} must be clamped to [-1, 1] to prevent domain errors due to floating-point inaccuracies when \alpha3 is close to \pm 1/\sqrt{2}. Normalizes the shape space coordinates. Uses nested circles to convey eigenvalues and pairwise differences. Time Complexity: O(1) for computing the invariants and geometric parameters from three eigenvalues. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only three scalar values (\mu1, R, \Theta). Strengths: Provides an intuitive geometric interpretation of tensor shape using continuous parameters. It clearly separates the mean (position), variance (size), and skewness (orientation) of the eigenvalues. Limitations: It is a visualization aid rather than a direct data structure. It requires the eigenvalues to be computed first. When to use: When visualizing the shape of symmetric tensors (e.g., in Diffusion Tensor Imaging) and needing to distinguish between linear, planar, and spherical shapes based on the spoke orientation. When not to use: When pairwise differences between eigenvalues are the primary focus (use Mohr diagram instead) or when a compact point-based representation is needed (use trilinear coordinates). The eigenvalue wheel was introduced by Kindlmann in his 2004 PhD thesis "Visualization and Analysis of Diffusion Tensor Fields". It is based on a geometric analogy for solving cubic characteristic polynomials, originally presented by Nickalls in the context of general cubic equations. Kindlmann adapted this construction specifically for visualizing the shape of diffusion tensors, noting its superficial similarity to the Mohr circle diagram from continuum mechanics but highlighting its distinct use of a single circle with oriented spokes. name: Directional Histogram
head: Spherical histogram
body: The Directional Histogram is a visualization method for analyzing the distribution of principal directions (such as eigenvectors or shear directions) within a tensor field by projecting them onto a unit sphere. It differs from sibling methods like Domain Colouring or Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization by aggregating directional data into statistical bins on a sphere rather than mapping values directly to color at spatial locations or rendering geometric primitives. This allows for the identification of dominant orientations and anisotropy in the field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of direction vectors \mathbf{v}i derived from the tensor field at sample points. Output: A histogram representing the frequency distribution of these directions on a hemisphere, visualized via color mapping or discrete binning. Data Structures: Sphere Representation: A triangulation of the unit sphere. Surface Division: The surface is divided into discrete patches (triangles) or continuous regions (Voronoi cells). Histogram Storage: An array or map storing counts for each patch, normalized by patch surface area. Steps: 1. Projection: Project each input direction vector \mathbf{v}i onto the surface of a unit sphere. 2. Orientation Handling: Because symmetric tensor directions are non-oriented, flip all vectors to the positive half-space defined by a user-selected viewing axis (x, y, or z). This restricts the analysis to a hemisphere. 3. Binning: Perform region-dependent binning by counting the number of vectors that intersect with each surface patch on the sphere. Discrete Approach: Bin by triangle. Each triangle is colored uniformly based on the count. Continuous Approach: Bin by the Voronoi cell of each vertex, allowing interpolation of frequencies. 4. Normalization: Normalize the counted frequencies by the respective surface area of each patch to account for variations in patch size, ensuring accurate density representation. 5. Visualization: Map the normalized frequencies to visual attributes (e.g., color in a Mohr diagram context). Formulas: Let Np be the number of vectors falling into patch p, and Ap be the surface area of patch p. The normalized frequency Fp is: Fp = \frac{Np}{Ap} Parameters: Viewing Axis: User-selected axis (x, y, or z) for flipping vectors. Triangulation Resolution: Determines the granularity of the binning. Uniform subdivision is crucial for accuracy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Isotropic Tensors: In simulations, isotropic tensors may exhibit numeric instabilities, leading to increased noise ratios. The Directional Histogram aggregates these, potentially obscuring noise if not handled, though the related Directional Scatterplot variant explicitly addresses this via transparency mapping. A variant of the directional histogram where each vector is represented as an individual point on the unit sphere rather than being aggregated into bins. Definition: A scatterplot on a unit sphere where each vector is represented by an individual point, allowing mapping of tensor properties to visual attributes. Steps: Map shear stress to transparency: low transparency for low shear stresses (isotropic tensors) and high opacity for high shear stresses. Pitfalls: Isotropic tensors exhibit increased noise ratio due to numeric instabilities in simulations. When to choose: Use when a direct representation of individual vectors and emphasizing pronounced directions via transparency mapping is preferred over aggregated statistical distribution. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of input vectors N, O(N), for projection and binning, assuming constant-time patch lookup. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of bins (triangles or vertices) in the sphere triangulation. Strengths: Provides a clear statistical overview of directional anisotropy; handles the non-oriented nature of symmetric tensors effectively. Limitations: Loses spatial context (it is a global or region-dependent statistic, not a spatial map); resolution is limited by the triangulation density. When to use: Analyzing the overall distribution of principal directions in a tensor field. When not: When spatial localization of directions is required (use Glyph-based Vector/Tensor Visualization instead). The Directional Histogram originates from the analysis of stress tensor fields, specifically for inspecting the distribution of principal shear directions or eigenvectors. It was developed as part of a visual approach to analyzing stress tensor fields, utilizing spherical diagrams to project directions onto a hemisphere. The method accounts for the non-oriented nature of symmetric tensors by flipping vectors to a positive half-space. name: Eigenvalue computation from principal invariants
head: Cubic eigenvalue solver, Invariant-based eigenvalue extraction
body: This method computes the three eigenvalues of a symmetric 3 \times 3 diffusion tensor directly from its principal invariants, avoiding explicit matrix diagonalization. It leverages the fact that tensor eigenvalues are invariant under coordinate rotation, allowing the characteristic cubic polynomial to be solved analytically using only arithmetic operations and trigonometric functions. Unlike direct diagonalization, which requires eigenvector computation, this approach is computationally cheaper and inherently sorts the eigenvalues in descending order due to the standard branch choice of the arccosine function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A symmetric 3 \times 3 tensor \mathbf{D} represented in the laboratory frame, with components D{xx}, D{yy}, D{zz} (diagonal) and D{xy}, D{xz}, D{yz} (off-diagonal). Output: Three scalar eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, sorted such that \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3. Data Structures: The tensor \mathbf{D} is typically stored as a flat array of 6 or 9 floating-point values. For a symmetric tensor, only the 6 unique components are required: D[0]: D{xx} D[1]: D{yy} D[2]: D{zz} D[3]: D{xy} D[4]: D{xz} D[5]: D{yz} Steps: 1. Compute Principal Invariants: Calculate J1, J2, J3 from the tensor components. 2. Compute Intermediate Invariants: Calculate Q and R using combinations of Ji. 3. Compute Angle: Calculate \Theta using the arccosine formula. 4. Compute Eigenvalues: Calculate \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 using cosine formulas. Formulas: The principal invariants are defined as: J1 = \text{tr}(\mathbf{D}) = D{xx} + D{yy} + D{zz} J2 = D{xx}D{yy} + D{xx}D{zz} + D{yy}D{zz} - D{xy}^2 - D{xz}^2 - D{yz}^2 J3 = 2D{xy}D{xz}D{yz} + D{xx}D{yy}D{zz} - D{xz}^2D{yy} - D{xx}D{yz}^2 - D{xy}^2D{zz} Alternatively, J2 can be computed using the trace of the square of the tensor: J2 = \frac{\text{tr}(\mathbf{D})^2 - \text{tr}(\mathbf{D}^2)}{2} where \text{tr}(\mathbf{D}^2) = D{xx}^2 + D{yy}^2 + D{zz}^2 + 2D{xy}^2 + 2D{xz}^2 + 2D{yz}^2. The squared norm invariant J4 is useful for computing Q and R with potentially better numerical stability or simpler expressions: J4 = \|\mathbf{D}\|^2 = D{xx}^2 + 2D{xy}^2 + 2D{xz}^2 + D{yy}^2 + 2D{yz}^2 + D{zz}^2 The intermediate invariants Q and R are: Q = \frac{J1^2 - 3J2}{9} = \frac{3J4 - J1^2}{18} R = \frac{-9J1J2 + 27J3 + 2J1^3}{54} = \frac{-5J1J2 + 27J3 + 2J1J4}{54} The angle \Theta is: \Theta = \frac{1}{3} \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{R}{\sqrt{Q^3}} \right) The eigenvalues are: \lambda1 = \frac{J1}{3} + 2\sqrt{Q} \cos(\Theta) \lambda2 = \frac{J1}{3} + 2\sqrt{Q} \cos\left(\Theta - \frac{2\pi}{3}\right) \lambda3 = \frac{J1}{3} + 2\sqrt{Q} \cos\left(\Theta + \frac{2\pi}{3}\right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeeigenvaluesfrominvariants(D): """ Computes eigenvalues of a symmetric 3x3 tensor D from its components. D is a list/tuple of 6 elements: [Dxx, Dyy, Dzz, Dxy, Dxz, Dyz] Returns sorted eigenvalues [lambda1, lambda2, lambda3] with lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3. """ Dxx, Dyy, Dzz, Dxy, Dxz, Dyz = D # Step 1: Compute Principal Invariants J1 = Dxx + Dyy + Dzz # J2 calculation using component-wise formula J2 = (Dxx Dyy + Dxx Dzz + Dyy Dzz Dxy2 - Dxz2 - Dyz2) # J3 calculation using component-wise formula J3 = (2 Dxy Dxz Dyz + Dxx Dyy Dzz Dxz2 Dyy Dxx Dyz2 Dxy2 Dzz) # Compute J4 (squared norm) for Q and R calculation J4 = (Dxx2 + Dyy2 + Dzz2 + 2 Dxy2 + 2 Dxz2 + 2 Dyz2) # Step 2: Compute Intermediate Invariants Q and R # Using the forms involving J4 for consistency with source Q = (3 J4 - J12) / 18.0 R = (-5 J1 J2 + 27 J3 + 2 J1 J4) / 54.0 # Step 3: Compute Theta # Guard against numerical errors causing argument > 1 or < -1 arg = R / (Q1.5) if arg > 1.0: arg = 1.0 elif arg < -1.0: arg = -1.0 Theta = (1.0 / 3.0) math.acos(arg) # Step 4: Compute Eigenvalues mean = J1 / 3.0 radius = 2 math.sqrt(Q) costheta = math.cos(Theta) costhetaminus2pi3 = math.cos(Theta - 2 math.pi / 3) costhetaplus2pi3 = math.cos(Theta + 2 math.pi / 3) lambda1 = mean + radius costheta lambda2 = mean + radius costhetaminus2pi3 lambda3 = mean + radius costhetaplus2pi3 # The standard branch choice of acos in [0, pi] ensures Theta in [0, pi/3] # which inherently sorts lambda1 >= lambda2 >= lambda3. # However, floating point inaccuracies might slightly violate this. # Sorting ensures correct order for downstream applications. eigenvalues = sorted([lambda1, lambda2, lambda3], reverse=True) return eigenvalues Parameters: No tunable parameters. The method is deterministic based on the input tensor components. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: When Q is very small or zero, the term \sqrt{Q^3} in the denominator of the arccosine argument may cause division by zero or instability. If Q=0, the tensor is spherical (\lambda1=\lambda2=\lambda3), and all eigenvalues are equal to J1/3. Argument Clipping: Due to floating-point precision, the value R/\sqrt{Q^3} may slightly exceed [-1, 1]. It must be clipped to this range before passing to \cos^{-1}. Sorting: The standard branch choice \cos^{-1}(x) \in [0, \pi] bounds \Theta to [0, \pi/3], which inherently sorts the eigenvalues in descending order (\lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3). A different branch choice yields a different fixed ordering. Degenerate Cases: When \Theta = \pi/3, \lambda1 = \lambda2 (minimal skewness). When \Theta = 0, \lambda2 = \lambda3 (maximal skewness). This variant focuses specifically on the calculation of the three principal invariants J1, J2, J3 of a symmetric diffusion tensor \mathbf{D} directly from its laboratory-frame matrix components, serving as precursors to solving for eigenvalues. It involves evaluating the characteristic polynomial \det(\lambda\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{D}) = \lambda^3 - J1\lambda^2 + J2\lambda - J3 = 0 in the laboratory frame. Computing invariants first avoids unnecessary computational expense compared to directly solving for individual eigenvalues, as the moments are precursors to the eigenvalue computation. It is chosen when only the shape characteristics (derived from invariants) are needed, or as a necessary first step for the full eigenvalue solver. Time Complexity: O(1) per tensor. The method involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and one trigonometric function evaluation. It is generally faster than iterative diagonalization methods and avoids the overhead of eigenvector computation. Memory Complexity: O(1). Requires storage for a few temporary scalar variables (J1, J2, J3, Q, R, \Theta). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids eigenvector computation; uses only arithmetic and trigonometric functions; inherently sorts eigenvalues; numerically stable for symmetric tensors if implemented with care (e.g., clipping arccos argument). Limitations: Requires the tensor to be symmetric; potential numerical instability if Q is near zero; does not provide eigenvectors (which may be needed for some visualization techniques like glyph orientation). When to use: When only eigenvalues are needed for transfer function mapping or shape analysis, and computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: When eigenvectors are required, or when the tensor is not symmetric (though diffusion tensors are theoretically symmetric, numerical errors in estimation might break symmetry, requiring symmetrization before application). This method originates from the analytical solution of cubic polynomials, adapted for tensor eigenvalue computation in the context of Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and visualization. The symmetry of diffusion tensors is a nontrivial result of statistical physics, explained by Onsager’s principle of “microscopic reversibility”. The specific formulation using principal invariants J1, J2, J3 and the intermediate variables Q, R follows standard formulas for solving cubic equations, as adapted in the literature on tensor visualization. The "eigenvalue wheel" geometric analogy was introduced to provide an intuitive understanding of the degrees of freedom in tensor shape. name: Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering
head: Volume illustration, NPR volume rendering
body: Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering (NPR) augments physics-based illumination pipelines with artistic techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth in volumetric data. It solves the problem of ambiguous internal structure in traditional physics-based or classification-based renderings by applying feature enhancement and depth cues derived from local volumetric properties rather than sample values alone. Unlike surface-based NPR where features are well-defined boundaries, volume illustration determines feature areas through continuous analysis of local gradients and properties, requiring less manual tuning of transfer functions than traditional direct volume rendering. The family shares the goal of enhancing volume visualization through stylized lighting and feature abstraction. All methods operate on fragment-level data, typically utilizing the volume sample gradient as a proxy for surface normal orientation. They decouple illumination from the physical light transport equation, instead using mathematical functions of the view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. Common inputs include the normalized gradient \nabla fn, light vectors L, and base colors derived from transfer functions. The output is a final color c that combines ambient/gaseous components with directed illumination effects. The framework utilizes four types of properties for enhancement: 1. Volume sample location and value. 2. Local volumetric properties, such as gradient and minimal change direction. 3. View direction. 4. Light information. Volumetric illustration differs from surface-based NPR in several important ways. In surface NPR, surfaces (features) are well-defined, whereas with volumes, feature areas within the volume must be determined through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) is a Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) technique that decouples geometric analysis from shading by storing per-pixel geometric properties (e.g., depth, normals) in intermediate 2D images. It solves the problem of efficiently generating illustrative effects (such as line drawings and edge enhancement) for complex 3D volumes by leveraging fast 2D image processing algorithms instead of expensive 3D analytic computations. Unlike sibling methods that may compute shading or illumination directly in 3D space, G-buffers provide hidden surface elimination for free and allow NPR parameters to be tweaked interactively without re-traversing the volume. The base renderer used for volume illustration examples, implementing physics-based illumination of gaseous phenomena. It can be replaced by a Phong illumination and linear accumulation renderer. Orientation-Based Color Modification simulates medical illustration techniques by altering the color, saturation, value, and transparency of volume samples based on the angle between the volumetric gradient and the viewer. It addresses the lack of depth cues in translucent volume rendering by using HSV color space to desaturate features facing the viewer and darken/saturate receding surfaces, thereby enhancing spatial understanding. A technique to create halo effects in planes orthogonal to the view vector by making regions just outside features darker and more opaque, obscuring background elements to reinforce depth perception. Context-Preserving Volume Rendering (CPVR) is an illustrative volume rendering technique that selectively reduces opacity in less important data regions to visualize interior structures while preserving exterior context. It solves the problem of context loss inherent in conventional clipping techniques by modulating sample opacity based on shading intensity, gradient magnitude, distance to the eye point, and previously accumulated opacity. Unlike clipping planes which remove context information, CPVR retains it by making homogeneous areas (high lighting intensity) transparent, allowing users to inspect the interior of an object without hiding occluded objects. Volume illustration is a non-photorealistic volume rendering method that augments a physics-based illumination pipeline with artistic techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth in volumetric data. It solves the problem of ambiguous internal structure in traditional physics-based or classification-based renderings by applying feature enhancement and depth cues derived from local volumetric properties rather than sample values alone. Unlike surface-based NPR where features are well-defined boundaries, volume illustration determines feature areas through continuous analysis of local gradients and properties, requiring less manual tuning of transfer functions than traditional direct volume rendering. A technique to create a sketch-like appearance by making non-volumetric silhouettes (areas not near silhouette edges) transparent and using a specific sketch color (e.g., white or black), with shadows calculated based on original volume opacity. Exact Projection Full Opacity is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that simplifies the visual output by identifying a single primary front object and optionally one significant background object, blending them based on density and distance thresholds rather than performing full front-to-back accumulation. It differs from standard front-to-back compositing by skipping the accumulation of intermediate samples, storing only the first significant object (primary) and potentially one background object, then blending them directly to create a stylized, illustrative result. Illumination and Tone Shading Models provide non-photorealistic lighting cues to enhance the visual clarity and artistic style of volume renderings. Unlike photometric models that simulate physical light transport, these methods map geometric or scalar properties to pre-defined color variations, prioritizing interpretability and aesthetic control over physical accuracy. They are distinct from Geometric Buffers by focusing on color modulation rather than depth/normal encoding, and from Base Gaseous Illumination Renderer by incorporating directed shading components. An interactive object-space technique for illustrating volumetric data by simulating free-hand line art (hatching) using hardware-assisted volume and line rendering, with data-driven seed point selection to minimize memory and generation time. Line and Edge Detection is a family of Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) techniques designed to detect and render lines within volume data to communicate structure, shape, and boundaries. It solves the problem of visualizing complex geometry and internal structures in volumetric datasets where traditional photorealistic rendering may obscure topological details. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its specific focus on line-based abstraction rather than surface shading or contour outlines; it distinguishes itself from Face-based volume rendering with edge highlights by generating lines that represent intrinsic surface properties (like curvature) rather than just silhouette edges, and from Outline and Contour Generation by often utilizing vector-oriented or texture-based approaches that are viewpoint-independent or analytically derived, rather than purely image-space depth-difference extraction. An interactive direct volume illustration system that simulates traditional stipple drawing by generating point lists based on volume characteristics (gradient magnitude/direction) and applying feature enhancements (silhouette curves, varying point sizes, resolution adjustments) to convey tone, texture, and shape. A method to visualize inter-penetrating volumetric objects by decomposing a scalar field into three distinct logical objects: selection, ghost, and background, allowing independent control of appearance and spatial transformation. Efficient non-photorealistic rendering of 3D polygonal meshes in OpenGL for non-living subjects, using specific conventions different from scientific illustration. Supported effects include line weighted depth cueing, fast silhouettes, shading using cool-to-warm lighting methods, light and highlight motion, and a non-parametric method of representing metal. A system that attempts to predict what kind of illustration a viewer would like to see by using an intent-based approach borrowing from AI knowledge bases. Rules that describe communicative intent are defined, and stylistic decisions that reflect particular goals are used to generate the actual illustrations. A visualization technique to emphasize differences in information content between two rendered fields by storing voxel-wise color differences. It calculates the l2-norm of opacity-weighted color values for each voxel to store in the residual map, which is then rendered interactively from arbitrary perspectives. Procedural coloring for butterfly wings using polar coordinates in wing space to generate veins, margins, bands, and apex patterns. It converts wing coordinates to polar, calculates base field color, vein patterns using sine waves, and mixes colors for veins, margins, and bands. A visualization mode to reveal structural differences between a reference volume (rendered with Tr) and an optimized volume (rendered with To) by rendering the residual field between them. It applies transfer functions to both fields, computes the residual by subtracting per-voxel colors and computing the l2-norm of the RGB\alpha difference vector, and uses RGB colors pre-multiplied with \alpha to ensure transparent regions have less contribution. Visualizes level sets of large CT scans (e.g., 1024^3) using slicemaps, which are small enough to fit in GPU memory and can be created by one slicing pass on the GPU. It estimates normals to compensate for the lack of binary information and reflect surface appearance, keeping several level sets at the same time and blending them together for interactive display. This avoids texture transfer stalls associated with slicing and the infeasibility of Marching Cubes at 1024^3 resolution. Cutaways remove occluding objects to reveal structures of interest, using a simplified three-object setup (Background, Ghost, Selection) with static importance functions to skip costly importance compositing. Ghosting selectively reduces opacity of occluding regions to preserve edges and spatial location impression, controllable from no ghosting to full cutaway. The degree of ghosting is smoothly controllable from no ghosting (opacity not reduced) to full cutaway view (occluding structures completely suppressed). The term "illustration" in the context of volume rendering was introduced by Ebert in 2000. The field is primarily motivated by the attempt to create renditions that consider the perceptual capabilities of humans. Visualization primarily motivated by this attempt includes boundary enhancement based on gradient approximation and curvature-based transfer functions. The approach augments a physics-based rendering process with non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques to enhance the expressiveness of the visualization. NPR draws inspiration from fields such as art and technical illustration to develop automatic methods to synthesize images with an illustrated look from geometric surface models. While NPR research had effectively addressed surface shape and 2D data, it had virtually ignored the rendering of volume models until this work. Early systems like SIV (Scientific Illustrator for Volumes) separated a 3D volume into segments using seeded region growing with thresholding, assigning interest labels to abstract groups of voxels, which were then rendered using NPR techniques. SIV used Saito and Takahashi's G-buffer idea extensively. In 2003, GPU raycasting was introduced by Krüger, making it feasible from a computational standpoint to apply illustrative visualization techniques in practice, overcoming previous performance constraints. name: Geometric Buffers (G-buffers)
head: 2D Image Processing for NPR, G-buffer approach, Intermediate geometric buffers, Pixel-Based Geometric Buffer Approach
body: Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) is a Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) technique that decouples geometric analysis from shading by storing per-pixel geometric properties (e.g., depth, normals) in intermediate 2D images. It solves the problem of efficiently generating illustrative effects for complex 3D volumes by leveraging fast 2D image processing algorithms instead of expensive 3D analytic computations. Unlike sibling methods that may compute shading or illumination directly in 3D space, G-buffers provide hidden surface elimination for free and allow NPR parameters to be tweaked interactively without re-traversing the volume. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset, camera position, and camera orientation. Outputs: A final 2D NPR image. Data Structures: G-buffers: A set of 2D images (arrays) corresponding to the screen resolution. Each buffer stores a single geometric property for every pixel. Common buffers include: Depth Buffer: Stores the distance from the camera to the visible surface along the view ray. Normal Buffer: Stores the surface normal vector (nx, ny, nz) of the visible surface at each pixel. Steps: 1. Single Volume Traversal: Traverse the 3D volume once from the camera's perspective to project the geometric scene onto a viewplane. For each pixel, determine the visible surface intersection, implicitly removing hidden surfaces. 2. Buffer Construction: For each pixel where a surface is visible, compute and store the relevant geometric properties into the corresponding G-buffers. Depth: Store the ray-surface intersection distance. Normal: Store the surface normal vector encapsulated during the projection phase. 3. 2D Image Processing: Apply various 2D image processing techniques to the G-buffers to achieve different NPR effects. Edge/Profile Extraction: Extract features such as profiles and internal edges from the depth map using a first-order differential operator. 4. Compositing: Apply image processing operators to the G-buffers to obtain the final rendering. 5. Reuse: If NPR parameters change but the scene geometry and camera position do not change, skip the traversal and reuse the existing G-buffers to avoid re-traversal. Formulas: Edge Detection: A first-order differential operator D applied to the depth buffer D{buf} yields the edge map E: E = |D(D{buf})| Pixels where E exceeds a threshold are marked as edges. Parameters: Thresholds: Used for edge detection in G-buffers. Determining the most suitable combination of enhancement techniques depends on the scene, purpose, and viewer's preferences, requiring trial and error. Reconstruction Resolution: High-resolution illustrations communicate more information, but source volume models are often smaller than final 2D images, necessitating consideration of reconstruction and interpolation issues. Variable Gaussian blurring reduces visible artifacts from the Nyquist limit. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Sharp surface borders may exhibit aliasing artifacts and digitization problems due to pixel discretization. Transparency/Reflection: The basic method assumes all objects are opaque and cannot natively enhance reflected or transparent images without extensions. Parameter Tuning: There is no automatic way to determine the optimal combination of enhancement techniques; it requires manual trial and error based on scene context and viewer preference. Resolution Mismatch: If the source volume is significantly smaller than the target image, reconstruction artifacts appear due to the discrete sampled nature of the original volume models. Addresses the mismatch between low-resolution volume data and high-resolution NPR output. It is chosen when source volumes are significantly smaller than the target image to mitigate Nyquist limit artifacts. See Reconstruction and Interpolation. Modifies the opaque assumption to handle semi-transparent or reflective surfaces. It is chosen when the scene requires rendering of non-opaque objects. Time Complexity: Dominated by the single 3D volume traversal. Subsequent NPR effect generation is fast since much of the processing is done in 2D rather than 3D. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of pixels and geometric properties stored per pixel. Performance: Fast enough for interactive user experimentation. Pixel-based techniques handle large or complex datasets better than analytic alternatives. Strengths: Reusability: G-buffers can be reused without recalculation if scene geometry and camera position do not change. Hidden Surface Elimination: Provided automatically by the traversal and buffering process. Scalability: Handles large or complex datasets better than analytic alternatives. Limitations: Assumes opacity without extensions. Susceptible to aliasing and digitization artifacts. Subjective tuning required for comprehensibility. The G-buffer approach was proposed by Saito and Takahashi [ST90] to enable line generation and NPR effects. The authors claim these techniques help make hand-drawn illustrations more comprehensible, and apply them to various digital domains like edge enhancement, line drawing illustrations, topographical maps, medical imaging, and surface analysis. The method is a foundational technique in pixel-based NPR for volume visualization, allowing for interactive user experimentation by decoupling geometry from style. name: Illumination and Tone Shading Models
head: Illustrative Lighting, NPR Illumination
body: Illumination and Tone Shading Models are non-photorealistic rendering techniques that enhance volume visualization by decoupling lighting from physical light transport, using mathematical functions of view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. They simulate artistic lighting styles, such as painterly effects, cel-shading, or warm-to-cool gradients, to solve the problem of missing depth cues and feature abstraction in translucent volume rendering. Unlike photometric models, these methods map normal vectors or scalar values directly to pre-computed artistic colors or discrete tone bands, providing view-dependent or orientation-dependent shading that rotates with the camera or adapts to local data structure. The family shares the goal of enhancing volume visualization through stylized lighting and feature abstraction. All methods operate on fragment-level data, typically utilizing the volume sample gradient as a proxy for surface normal orientation. They decouple illumination from the physical light transport equation, instead using mathematical functions of the view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. Common inputs include the normalized gradient \nabla fn, light vectors L, and base colors derived from transfer functions. The output is a final color c that combines ambient/gaseous components with directed illumination effects. The framework utilizes four types of properties for enhancement: 1. Volume sample location and value. 2. Local volumetric properties, such as gradient and minimal change direction. 3. View direction. 4. Light information. Volumetric illustration differs from surface-based NPR in several important ways. In surface NPR, surfaces (features) are well-defined, whereas with volumes, feature areas within the volume must be determined through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. Maps eye-space normal vectors to a pre-computed sphere texture to capture artistic lighting styles. It provides view-dependent lighting that rotates with the camera, ignoring front/back face ambiguity. Adjusts HSV color components based on the angle between the gradient and view direction. It simulates painterly effects where facing surfaces are desaturated/bright and receding surfaces are darkened/saturated. Maps gradient orientation relative to a light source to a warm-to-cool color gradient. It uses a positive dot product threshold to ensure zero contribution at orthogonal orientations, matching diffuse illumination models. A post-processing effect that darkens image corners based on the cubic alignment between ray direction and pixel frame normal, simulating projection falloff. Applies Blinn-Phong lighting followed by aggressive quantization (posterization) of diffuse bands and binary thresholding of specular highlights. Applies cel-shading to volumetric data using a pre-computed 3D normal map and hardware texture combiners, operating directly on the voxel gradient field without mesh extraction. Enhances material boundaries by using two scalar samples along the gradient direction as inputs to a 2D lighting transfer function, dynamically adjusting lighting coefficients based on local data structure. Uses the illumination model for curves of Banks to provide a better sense of curvature in line bundle rendering. Line bundles can be more opaque in this variant. A non-photorealistic rendering method used to visualize important information in an abstract but coherent way. The parameter \theta determines the effect of surrounding features, with higher values causing more distant features to increase shading variation. Tested values include 50^\circ and 85^\circ. The concept of Tone Rendering as a non-photorealistic method for abstract visualization was introduced in the context of volume visualization methods, contrasting with Phong Illumination which guarantees higher realistic images. The Banks illumination model for curves was applied in flow visualization techniques to enhance the perception of curvature in vector fields. name: Lit Sphere Shading
head: Lit sphere map shading, Sphere map shading
body: Lit sphere shading is a non-photorealistic rendering technique that captures artistic lighting styles by using an image of a sphere, shaded in a desired style, as a lookup table. It represents the shading of an object as a function of eye-space normal orientation, allowing the sphere to act as a proxy object for illumination. Unlike physical illumination models, it decouples lighting from light transport equations and relies on view-dependent mapping. It is distinct from Blinn-Phong Toon Shading and Volumetric Toon Shading because it does not compute lighting analytically per fragment but rather samples a pre-rendered or extracted artistic style map. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A lit sphere map texture T (square image), the normalized eye-space gradient \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) derived from the volume sample. Output: The final fragment color c. Data Structures: Lit Sphere Map (T): A square texture. The valid data is contained within an inscribed disk centered at (0.5, 0.5) in texture coordinates. Texels outside this disk are unused. Steps: 1. Sphere Map Acquisition: Obtain or render an image of a sphere under orthographic projection, shaded in the target artistic style. This image serves as the lit sphere map T. The sphere provides coverage of the complete set of unit normals on one hemisphere. 2. Normal Computation: For each volume fragment, compute the normalized eye-space gradient \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz). This vector serves as the proxy surface normal. 3. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the nx and ny components of \mathbf{n}, which are in the range [-1, 1], to texture coordinates (u, v) in the range [0, 1]. 4. Lookup: Sample the lit sphere map T at (u, v) to retrieve the stylized color. 5. Output: Assign the sampled color to the fragment. Formulas: The texture coordinates (u, v) are calculated from the eye-space normal \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) as follows: u = \frac{nx + 1}{2} v = \frac{ny + 1}{2} Where: nx, ny \in [-1, 1] are the x and y components of the normalized eye-space gradient. u, v \in [0, 1] are the resulting texture coordinates. Parameters: Light Source Position: The light source is treated as a "headlight," rotating with the camera (view-dependent lighting). This is considered the desired setup in volume visualization. Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-Component Ignorance: The nz component of the normal is ignored during indexing. Consequently, lighting does not distinguish between front and back faces. This is intentional because the gradient direction in volume data (used as the normal) might be flipped depending on data values at a material boundary. Boundary Access: Texture coordinates must be clamped to [0, 1] to prevent out-of-bounds sampling if \mathbf{n} is not perfectly normalized or due to precision errors, though the sources state texels outside the disk are "never accessed" by design. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def litsphereshading(normaleyespace, litspheremap, mapheight, mapwidth): """ Shading method using a lit sphere map. Args: normaleyespace: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) of the normalized eye-space gradient. litspheremap: 2D array of shape (mapheight, mapwidth, 3) representing the lit sphere map. mapheight: Integer height of the texture. mapwidth: Integer width of the texture. Returns: Color value sampled from the lit sphere map. """ nx, ny, nz = normaleyespace # Convert eye-space normal components from [-1, 1] to [0, 1] # The nz component is intentionally ignored as per the method definition u = (nx + 1.0) / 2.0 v = (ny + 1.0) / 2.0 # Clamp coordinates to valid texture range u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) # Map to array indices (assuming top-left origin for array indexing) # In practice, this step uses hardware texture sampling with interpolation colidx = int(u (mapwidth - 1)) rowidx = int(v (mapheight - 1)) # Sample the lit sphere map color = litspheremap[rowidx, colidx] return color Lit sphere shading is often used as a component of style transfer functions, where the sphere map defines the lighting style while other parameters modulate color based on scalar values. Lit sphere maps can be extracted from non-spherical regions in existing pieces of artwork using interactive tools, allowing for the rapid creation of style databases. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the lookup, assuming constant-time texture sampling. Memory Complexity: O(R^2) for the lit sphere map texture, where R is the resolution. Strengths: Well-suited to represent the general shading style of an object; images are relatively easy to obtain; allows for a large database of styles with little effort; view-dependent lighting effects appear regular. Limitations: Fails to capture complex aspects of realistic illumination. Cannot distinguish front/back faces, which may be undesirable in some surface-based contexts but is accepted for volume gradients. When to use: When a stylized, artistic lighting appearance is desired that moves with the camera, and computational efficiency is prioritized over physical accuracy. When not to use: When physically accurate light transport or complex shadowing/occlusion effects are required. Lit sphere shading was originally presented by Sloan et al. [SMGG01] for non-photorealistic rendering of polygonal models. It was adapted for illustrative volume rendering in the paper [Style Transfer Functions for Illustrative Volume Rendering]. The technique leverages the fact that a sphere under orthographic projection covers the complete set of unit normals on one hemisphere, making it an ideal proxy for capturing normal-dependent shading variations.
