name: Halftone Shading
head: Disk-based halftone
body: Halftone shading is a non-photorealistic illumination technique that represents gradual lighting variations through shading patterns of varying sizes, specifically disks whose radii are inversely proportional to illumination intensity. It distinguishes itself from standard photorealistic shading by replacing continuous tone gradients with discrete, scalable geometric primitives, creating an illustrative aesthetic suitable for anatomical or technical visualization. It builds on Lit Sphere Shading by providing a specific pattern-based shading option within that framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D model (point cloud or polygonal mesh), light position LP, surface normals ni, and view direction. Output: A rendered image containing scaled disks representing the shading intensity. Data Structures: Lighting Model: Phong illumination model is used to compute light intensity Li at a point xi with normal ni. Formula: Li = ka + kd \max(0, ni \cdot (LP - xi)) + ks \max(0, ni \cdot v)^{shininess}. Note: The exact coefficients (ka, kd, ks) and shininess exponent are not specified in the source, but Li is defined as the result of this standard Phong calculation. Scaling Factor: A scalar value S{shd} determines the size of the disk. Parameters: S{all}: Global normalization factor for the scaling factor. I{shd}: Parameter controlling the overall intensity (darkness) of shading. A{shd}: Parameter controlling the stretching of the shading. n: Parameter controlling the transition within the shade. Steps: 1. Compute Illumination: For each point or triangle, calculate the illumination intensity Li using the Phong model. 2. Calculate Scaling Factor: Compute the scaling factor S{shd} using the following formula: S{shd} = S{all} \cdot I{shd} \cdot A{shd} \cdot Li^{-n} Note: The source presents the formula as S{shd} = S{all} \cdot I{shd} \cdot A{shd} \cdot Li^{-n}. The order of multiplication for I{shd} and A{shd} is commutative. 3. Render Disks: For Point Models: Scale each shading disk by S{shd}. For Polygonal Models: Render scaled shading disks at the midpoints of triangles, oriented orthogonal to the viewing direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def halftoneshading(points, normals, lightposition, viewdirection, params): """ points: List of 3D coordinates (x, y, z) normals: List of 3D unit vectors (nx, ny, nz) lightposition: 3D coordinate (lx, ly, lz) viewdirection: 3D unit vector (vx, vy, vz) params: Dictionary containing Sall, Ishd, Ashd, n, ka, kd, ks, shininess """ Sall = params['Sall'] Ishd = params['Ishd'] Ashd = params['Ashd'] n = params['n'] ka = params['ka'] kd = params['kd'] ks = params['ks'] shininess = params['shininess'] rendereddisks = [] for i in range(len(points)): xi = points[i] ni = normals[i] # Compute Phong illumination # Vector from point to light lightvec = (lightposition[0] - xi[0], lightposition[1] - xi[1], lightposition[2] - xi[2]) # Diffuse term dotndl = max(0, ni[0]lightvec[0] + ni[1]lightvec[1] + ni[2]lightvec[2]) diffuse = kd dotndl # Specular term # Reflection vector r = 2 (n. l) n - l # However, standard Phong uses view vector v. # Assuming v is fixed view direction for simplicity as per source context # Specular: ks (n. v)^shininess dotnv = max(0, ni[0]viewdirection[0] + ni[1]viewdirection[1] + ni[2]viewdirection[2]) specular = ks (dotnv shininess) # Ambient term ambient = ka Li = ambient + diffuse + specular # Avoid division by zero or negative base for negative exponent if Li <= 0: Li = 1e-6 # Calculate scaling factor # Sshd = Sall Ishd Ashd Li^(-n) Sshd = Sall Ishd Ashd (Li (-n)) # Determine disk properties # Radius is inversely proportional to illumination intensity. # The source states radii are inversely proportional to illumination intensity. # Sshd is the scaling factor. The base radius is not explicitly defined, # but Sshd scales the disk. disk = { 'position': xi, 'scale': Sshd, 'normal': ni, # For point models, orientation might be based on surface normal or view 'type': 'point' } rendereddisks.append(disk) return rendereddisks def halftoneshadingpolygonal(triangles, lightposition, viewdirection, params): """ triangles: List of triangles, each defined by 3 vertices (v1, v2, v3) """ Sall = params['Sall'] Ishd = params['Ishd'] Ashd = params['Ashd'] n = params['n'] ka = params['ka'] kd = params['kd'] ks = params['ks'] shininess = params['shininess'] rendereddisks = [] for tri in triangles: v1, v2, v3 = tri # Compute triangle midpoint midpoint = ( (v1[0] + v2[0] + v3[0]) / 3.0, (v1[1] + v2[1] + v3[1]) / 3.0, (v1[2] + v2[2] + v3[2]) / 3.0) # Compute triangle normal edge1 = (v2[0]-v1[0], v2[1]-v1[1], v2[2]-v1[2]) edge2 = (v3[0]-v1[0], v3[1]-v1[1], v3[2]-v1[2]) normal = crossproduct(edge1, edge2) normal = normalize(normal) # Compute illumination at midpoint lightvec = (lightposition[0] - midpoint[0], lightposition[1] - midpoint[1], lightposition[2] - midpoint[2]) dotndl = max(0, normal[0]lightvec[0] + normal[1]lightvec[1] + normal[2]lightvec[2]) diffuse = kd dotndl dotnv = max(0, normal[0]viewdirection[0] + normal[1]viewdirection[1] + normal[2]viewdirection[2]) specular = ks (dotnv shininess) ambient = ka Li = ambient + diffuse + specular if Li <= 0: Li = 1e-6 Sshd = Sall Ishd Ashd (Li (-n)) disk = { 'position': midpoint, 'scale': Sshd, 'normal': viewdirection, # Orthogonal to viewing direction 'type': 'polygonal' } rendereddisks.append(disk) return rendereddisks def crossproduct(v1, v2): return ( v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0]) def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if mag == 0: return (0, 0, 0) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Illumination: If Li is zero or negative, the term Li^{-n} becomes undefined or infinite. A guard value (e.g., 1e-6) should be applied to Li before exponentiation. Negative Exponent: The parameter n controls the transition. If n is negative, the relationship between illumination and disk size inverts. The source implies n is positive to achieve "inversely proportional" behavior. Polygonal Orientation: For polygonal models, disks are rendered orthogonal to the viewing direction, not the surface normal. This ensures the disks appear as circles in screen space, maintaining the halftone aesthetic regardless of surface orientation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points or triangles, as each primitive requires one illumination calculation and one scaling factor computation. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of primitives to store the disk data structures. Strengths: Provides a clear, illustrative representation of lighting gradients. The use of discrete disks can help emphasize form and structure in anatomical or technical visualizations. Limitations: The discrete nature of disks may introduce aliasing or a "stippled" appearance if the resolution is insufficient. The reliance on a specific lighting model (Phong) may not capture complex global illumination effects. When to Use: Suitable for illustrative rendering where artistic style is prioritized over photorealism, particularly in medical or educational contexts. When Not to Use: Not suitable for photorealistic rendering or scenes requiring accurate light transport simulation. Halftone shading was introduced as one of the illustrative shading options in the GMS (Current Topics in Computer and Robot Assisted Surgery) journal article by. It is designed to create expressive anatomical illustrations based on scanned patient data. The technique is part of a broader set of non-photorealistic rendering methods aimed at enhancing the clarity and aesthetic appeal of medical visualizations. name: Orientation-Based Color Modification
head: HSV Color Orientation, HSV color modification, oriented fading
body:
Orientation-Based Color Modification is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that modulates the color, saturation, value, and transparency of volume samples based on the orientation of the local volumetric gradient relative to the viewer. It addresses the lack of depth cues in translucent volumes by simulating illustrative "oriented fading," where structures facing the viewer are desaturated and structures oriented away are darkened and saturated. It sets itself apart from general illumination models by operating directly in the HSV color space to decouple brightness from hue and saturation, enabling painterly effects that mimic traditional medical illustration techniques. Inputs: Volume sample color C{rgb} (from transfer function). Normalized volumetric gradient 
abla fn (proxy for surface normal). View direction V (normalized vector from sample to camera). Outputs: Modified color C'{rgb} and potentially modified opacity \alpha'. Data Structures: The method operates on per-fragment (or per-sample) data. No persistent global data structures are required beyond the volume grid and transfer function. Intermediate state uses HSV color space components: Hue (H), Saturation (S), Value (V). Steps: 1. Compute Orientation: Calculate the angle 	heta between the normalized gradient 
abla fn and the view direction V using the dot product: \cos 	heta = 
abla fn \cdot V. The angle 	heta ranges from 0 (gradient aligned with view, facing viewer) to \pi (gradient opposed to view, receding). 2. Convert to HSV: Convert the input RGB color C{rgb} to HSV space (H, S, V). 3. Modulate Value (Brightness): Decrease the Value component V as the angle 	heta increases, simulating "oriented fading". The modified value is computed as V' = V \cdot \max(0, \cos 	heta). 4. Modulate Saturation (Optional): Desaturate surfaces oriented toward the viewer (small 	heta) and saturate surfaces oriented away from the viewer (large 	heta). The modified saturation is computed as S' = S \cdot (1.0 - 0.5 \cdot \max(0, \cos 	heta)). 5. Modulate Transparency (Optional): Adjust opacity \alpha based on orientation to enhance depth cues. 6. Convert to RGB: Convert the modified HSV values (H, S', V') back to RGB space to obtain C'{rgb}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orientationbasedcolormodification(rgbcolor, gradientnormalized, viewdirection): # 1. Compute orientation factor (cos theta) costheta = max(-1.0, min(1.0, gradientnormalized[0]viewdirection[0] + gradientnormalized[1]viewdirection[1] + gradientnormalized[2]viewdirection[2])) # 2. Convert RGB to HSV h, s, v = rgbtohsv(rgbcolor) # 3. Modulate Value: decrease as angle increases (costheta decreases) vmodified = v max(0.0, costheta) # 4. Modulate Saturation: desaturate facing, saturate receding smodified = s (1.0 - 0.5 max(0.0, costheta)) # 5. Convert back to RGB return hsvtorgb(h, smodified, vmodified) def rgbtohsv(rgb): r, g, b = rgb cmax = max(r, g, b) cmin = min(r, g, b) delta = cmax - cmin if delta == 0: h = 0.0 elif cmax == r: h = 60.0 (((g - b) / delta) % 6) elif cmax == g: h = 60.0 (((b - r) / delta) + 2) else: h = 60.0 (((r - g) / delta) + 4) s = 0.0 if cmax == 0 else delta / cmax v = cmax return h, s, v def hsvtorgb(h, s, v): c = v s x = c (1.0 - abs((h / 60.0) % 2 - 1.0)) m = v - c if h < 60: r, g, b = c, x, 0 elif h < 120: r, g, b = x, c, 0 elif h < 180: r, g, b = 0, c, x elif h < 240: r, g, b = 0, x, c elif h < 300: r, g, b = x, 0, c else: r, g, b = c, 0, x return (r + m, g + m, b + m) Oriented Color Modification is a technique that adjusts the color value (brightness) of volume samples based on the orientation of the surface gradient relative to the viewer, simulating illustrative "oriented fading". It sets itself apart from general illumination models by operating directly in the HSV color space to decouple brightness from hue and saturation, allowing for painterly effects where facing surfaces remain bright and edge-on surfaces fade. Choose this when aiming for medical illustration styles where depth is conveyed through color intensity changes rather than shadows. A method to avoid false color effects in volume rendering where semi-transparency causes hue changes during color mixing, by adjusting saturation and blending weights. It reduces the global or local (in the overlap region only) saturation and blending weight of the background object in the mixture to control hue. Choose this when blending semi-transparent volumes to maintain harmonic color scales and avoid non-harmonic hue shifts caused by color mixing. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample/fragment, as it involves a dot product, HSV conversion, and simple arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Strengths: Provides strong depth cues in translucent volumes where traditional shadows are absent; operates directly in HSV space for intuitive control. Limitations: Relies on the quality of gradient estimation; the effect is stylized and not physically based. When to use: Medical visualization and scientific illustration requiring enhanced depth perception in translucent data without photorealism. The method originates from non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques for volume visualization, specifically drawing inspiration from medical illustration practices where anatomical structures oriented toward the viewer are desaturated and those oriented away are darkened and saturated. It was formalized in the context of "Non-Photorealistic Rendering of Volume Models" presented at IEEE Visualization '00. The approach leverages the HSV color space to provide an intuitive framework for applying these illustrative rules. name: Oriented Color Modification
body: Oriented Color Modification is a technique that adjusts the color value (brightness) of volume samples based on the orientation of the surface gradient relative to the viewer, simulating illustrative "oriented fading". It sets itself apart from general illumination models by operating directly in the HSV color space to decouple brightness from hue and saturation, allowing for painterly effects where facing surfaces remain bright and edge-on surfaces fade. Inputs: Volume sample color C in RGB. Volume sample opacity \alpha. Gradient vector \mathbf{g} at the sample point. View direction vector \mathbf{v} (typically from sample to camera). Outputs: Modified color C' and opacity \alpha'. Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{g} and \mathbf{v} are 3D floating-point vectors. Color is converted to HSV space for modification. Steps: 1. Compute the angle \theta between the gradient \mathbf{g} and the view direction \mathbf{v}. \cos \theta = \frac{\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{g}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|} 2. Convert the sample color from RGB to HSV. Let the value component be V. 3. Decrease V as \theta increases (i.e., as the surface becomes more edge-on to the viewer). The exact mapping function is not specified in the primary source, but the trend is monotonic decrease with increasing angle. 4. Convert the modified HSV color back to RGB to obtain C'. 5. (Optional/Variant) Modulate opacity \alpha based on the same or similar orientation metrics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orientedcolormodification(rgbcolor, gradient, viewdirection): # Normalize vectors glen = (gradient[0]2 + gradient[1]2 + gradient[2]2)0.5 vlen = (viewdirection[0]2 + viewdirection[1]2 + viewdirection[2]2)0.5 gnorm = (gradient[0]/glen, gradient[1]/glen, gradient[2]/glen) vnorm = (viewdirection[0]/vlen, viewdirection[1]/vlen, viewdirection[2]/vlen) # Calculate cosine of the angle between gradient and view costheta = gnorm[0]vnorm[0] + gnorm[1]vnorm[1] + gnorm[2]vnorm[2] # Convert RGB to HSV hsvcolor = rgbtohsv(rgbcolor) h, s, v = hsvcolor # Decrease value V as angle increases (costheta decreases) # Note: Exact formula for V' vs theta is not provided in # Assuming a linear fade for implementation completeness: vmodified = v (0.5 + 0.5 costheta) # Clamp value to [0, 1] vmodified = max(0.0, min(1.0, vmodified)) # Convert back to RGB newrgb = hsvtorgb((h, s, vmodified)) return newrgb def rgbtohsv(rgb): # Standard RGB to HSV conversion r, g, b = rgb[0]/255.0, rgb[1]/255.0, rgb[2]/255.0 cmax = max(r, g, b) cmin = min(r, g, b) delta = cmax - cmin if delta == 0: h = 0 elif cmax == r: h = 60 (((g - b) / delta) % 6) elif cmax == g: h = 60 (((b - r) / delta) + 2) else: h = 60 (((r - g) / delta) + 4) s = 0 if cmax == 0 else delta / cmax v = cmax return (h, s, v) def hsvtorgb(hsv): # Standard HSV to RGB conversion h, s, v = hsv c = v s x = c (1 - abs((h / 60) % 2 - 1)) m = v - c if h < 60: r1, g1, b1 = c, x, 0 elif h < 120: r1, g1, b1 = x, c, 0 elif h < 180: r1, g1, b1 = 0, c, x elif h < 240: r1, g1, b1 = 0, x, c elif h < 300: r1, g1, b1 = x, 0, c else: r1, g1, b1 = c, 0, x return ((r1 + m) 255, (g1 + m) 255, (b1 + m) 255) Edge Cases: Zero Gradient: If \|\mathbf{g}\| = 0, the direction is undefined. Handle by preserving original color or using a default view-aligned value. Precision: Floating-point errors in dot product near boundaries. A specific implementation of oriented color modification within the Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR) framework. It modulates color by calculating a new specular intensity based on modified gradients along cut-away borders and modulates the opacity of the current sample point prior to adapted compositing. It is integrated into the IDVRMImPCompositingModelSW class. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves basic vector operations and color space conversion. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample. Strengths: Provides intuitive, painterly control over visual emphasis; decouples brightness from color identity. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Illustrative volume rendering, medical visualization where edge-on structures need to be deemphasized. Introduced within volume illustration for non-photorealistic rendering. It adapts traditional illustration techniques of oriented fading to 3D volume data, leveraging the HSV color space for intuitive control. name: Hue-Balls
head: Direct Volume Rendering of Tensor Fields
body: Hue-Balls is a volume rendering technique that visualizes the anisotropy of a symmetric second-order tensor field by color-coding the deflection of a fixed input vector after tensor multiplication, mapped onto a sphere. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Lit-tensors by relying on direct hue mapping of vector deflection rather than illumination and shading to convey direction and curvature. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A symmetric second-order tensor field T(\mathbf{x}) defined over a 3D volume, and a fixed, arbitrary input vector \mathbf{v}{in} (e.g., user-specified). Output: A color volume where each voxel is assigned a color based on the transformation of \mathbf{v}{in} by T(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Tensor Field: Stored as a 3D texture or grid where each voxel contains a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. Color Map: A mapping from the angle of deflection (or related geometric properties) to a hue value on the color sphere. Steps: 1. Define Input Vector: Select a fixed, arbitrary input vector \mathbf{v}{in}. 2. Tensor Multiplication: For each voxel \mathbf{x}, compute the output vector \mathbf{v}{out} by multiplying the tensor T(\mathbf{x}) with \mathbf{v}{in}: \mathbf{v}{out} = T(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{v}{in} 3. Compute Deflection: Determine the relationship between \mathbf{v}{in} and \mathbf{v}{out}. The deflection angle \theta is typically the angle between \mathbf{v}{in} and \mathbf{v}{out}. 4. Map to Color: Map the deflection angle \theta to a hue value on a sphere. This color represents the anisotropy at that point. 5. Volume Rendering: Render the volume using standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., ray casting), applying the computed colors and an opacity function. Parameters: Input Vector \mathbf{v}{in}: A fixed vector, such as one specified by the user. Opacity Function: Can be defined using barycentric coordinates based on eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 (where \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge \lambda3) to emphasize important features. For example: cs = \frac{3\lambda3}{\lambda1 + \lambda2 + \lambda3} where cs is a component of the opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hueballrender(tensorfield, inputvector, opacityfunction): """ Renders a tensor field using the Hue-Balls technique. Args: tensorfield: 3D array of 3x3 symmetric matrices. inputvector: 3D vector (numpy array). opacityfunction: Function mapping eigenvalues to opacity. Returns: colorvolume: 3D array of RGB colors. """ # Initialize output color volume height, width, depth = tensorfield.shape[0], tensorfield.shape[1], tensorfield.shape[2] colorvolume = np.zeros((height, width, depth, 3)) for x in range(height): for y in range(width): for z in range(depth): # Get tensor at voxel T = tensorfield[x, y, z] # Multiply tensor with fixed input vector vout = T @ inputvector # Compute deflection angle between input and output vectors # Normalize vectors to handle magnitude changes vinnorm = inputvector / np.linalg.norm(inputvector) voutnorm = vout / np.linalg.norm(vout) # Dot product gives cosine of angle costheta = np.dot(vinnorm, voutnorm) # Clamp to avoid numerical errors costheta = np.clip(costheta, -1.0, 1.0) theta = np.arccos(costheta) # Map deflection angle to hue # Assuming a simple linear mapping from [0, pi] to [0, 1] hue hue = theta / np.pi # Convert hue to RGB (simplified) color = huetorgb(hue) # Compute opacity using eigenvalues eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(T) # Sort eigenvalues descending eigenvalues = np.sort(eigenvalues)[::-1] lambda1, lambda2, lambda3 = eigenvalues # Calculate opacity component cs sumeigs = lambda1 + lambda2 + lambda3 if sumeigs == 0: opacity = 0.0 else: cs = (3 lambda3) / sumeigs opacity = opacityfunction(cs) # Apply opacity to color colorvolume[x, y, z] = color opacity return colorvolume def huetorgb(h): """ Converts a hue value [0, 1] to an RGB color. This is a placeholder for a standard HSV to RGB conversion. """ # Simplified implementation for demonstration # In practice, use a proper HSV to RGB conversion r = 1.0 g = 1.0 - h b = 1.0 - h return np.array([r, g, b]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tensors: At points where eigenvalues are equal (degenerate points), every vector is an eigenvector, and the deflection may be undefined or zero. Precision: Numerical stability in computing the angle between vectors, especially when vectors are nearly parallel or anti-parallel. Boundary Conditions: Handling tensors at the boundaries of the volume, ensuring consistent input vector definition. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel requires a matrix-vector multiplication and angle computation. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the tensor field and the output color volume. Strengths: Directly visualizes anisotropy through color, making it intuitive for biological applications. Limitations: Relies on a fixed input vector, which may not capture all directional information; less effective for isotropic regions. When to Use: When the primary goal is to visualize anisotropy in tensor fields, such as in diffusion tensor imaging. When Not to Use: When detailed curvature or direction information is required, in which case Lit-tensors might be more appropriate. Hue-Balls was introduced by Gordon Kindlmann and Frank Weinstein in 1999. It is part of a broader effort to visualize tensor fields in scientific computing, particularly in biological applications where anisotropy is a key feature. The technique has been implemented in various visualization tools, often using 3D textures and color mapping to indicate tensor properties. name: Volume Illustration Tone Shading
head: Gooch tone shading for volumes, Modified Gooch tone shading for volume, Modified Gooch tone shading for volume models, Tone illumination model, Volumetric tone shading
body:
Volume Illustration Tone Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model that enhances the perception of 3D shape in volume rendering by modulating color temperature based on the orientation of volume samples relative to a light source. It assigns warm colors (yellows/reds) to regions facing the light and cool colors (blues) to receding regions, creating an illustrative effect suggestive of warm directional illumination like sunlight. Unlike standard Gooch shading which uses the full signed dot product for illumination, this method modifies the illuminated object contribution to be zero at orientations orthogonal to the light vector, matching familiar diffuse illumination models more closely. It builds on Illumination and Tone Shading Models by combining gaseous illumination with directed tone shading. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume scalar field f, transfer function T(v) mapping scalar value v to base color and opacity, normalized volume sample gradient 
abla fn at each sample location, light direction unit vectors Li for i = 1 \dots NL, gaseous illumination color IG, and illuminated object color contribution Ii derived from the transfer function and gaseous illumination. Outputs: Final fragment color c. Data Structures: Gradient Field: A 3D vector field storing 
abla fn for each voxel, typically computed via central differences during ray marching or rasterization. Light Vectors: Array of normalized 3D vectors Li. Parameters: Scalars k{ta}, k{td}, k{ty}, k{tb}. Formulas: The final color c is a weighted sum of gaseous illumination and the total tone and directed shading from all light sources: c = k{ta} IG + \sum{i=1}^{NL} (It + k{td} Io) Where: k{ta} controls the amount of gaseous illumination IG included. NL is the number of light sources. k{td} controls the amount of directed illumination included. It is the tone contribution to volume sample color. Io is the illuminated object color contribution. Tone Contribution (It): For a single light source with direction L, the tone contribution interpolates between a warm color cw and a cool color cc based on the signed dot product between the normalized gradient 
abla fn and L: It = \left(  rac{1.0 + 
abla fn \cdot L}{2} ight) cw + \left( 1 -  rac{1.0 + 
abla fn \cdot L}{2} ight) cc Where: cw = (k{ty}, k{ty}, 0) is the warm tone color vector. cc = (0, 0, k{tb}) is the cool tone color vector. k{ty} controls yellow intensity. k{tb} controls blue intensity. Directed Illumination Component (Io): Unlike standard Gooch shading, the illuminated object contribution is calculated using only the positive dot product, becoming zero at orientations orthogonal to the light vector: Io =  egin{cases} Ii (
abla fn \cdot L) & 	ext{if } 
abla fn \cdot L > 0 \ 0 & 	ext{if } 
abla fn \cdot L \le 0 \end{cases} Where Ii is the illuminated object color contribution. The original paper contains a typo defining Io with an extra k{td} factor, which would cause double-scaling when combined with the main summation; the corrected definition above matches the intended control and the pseudocode. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeillustrationtoneshading(samplevalue, gradient, transferfunction, lightvectors, kta, ktd, kty, ktb): # IG and Ii are base colors from transfer function, possibly modulated by ambient light basecolor = transferfunction(samplevalue) IG = basecolor Ii = basecolor c = kta IG for L in lightvectors: d = dot(gradient, L) w = (1.0 + d) / 2.0 cw = vec3(kty, kty, 0.0) cc = vec3(0.0, 0.0, ktb) It = w cw + (1.0 - w) cc if d > 0: Io = Ii d else: Io = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) c += It + ktd Io return c Parameters: k{ta}: Gaseous illumination weight. Typical value: 1.0. k{td}: Directed illumination weight. Typical value: 0.6. k{ty}: Warm tone yellow intensity. Typical value: 0.3 for medical volumes, 0.15 for iron protein. k{tb}: Cool tone blue intensity. Typical value: 0.3 for medical volumes, 0.15 for iron protein. NL: Number of lights. Recommended: A few (e.g., 1-3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Lights: Using more than a few light sources is likely to result in confusing images because humans are not used to interpreting complex illumination from many lights. Orthogonal Gradients: The directed contribution Io becomes zero when 
abla fn \cdot L = 0, ensuring no illumination from surfaces orthogonal to the light, matching diffuse models. Gradient Noise: Noisy gradients can cause flickering tone shading; smoothing or filtering the gradient field may be required. Gooch Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model for volume rendering that maps surface orientation relative to a light source to a warm-to-cool color gradient to convey shape. It is distinguished from standard Gooch shading by its specific integration with on-the-fly central difference normal estimation in rasterization pipelines, ensuring consistent visual output across different extraction methods (rasterization vs. ray-marching). Choose it when consistent normal estimation across rendering backends is required. Cool to warm shading is a tone-based illumination model that enhances 3D shape perception by mapping surface orientation to a color gradient, assigning warmer colors to regions facing the reference direction and cooler colors to receding regions. Unlike physically based models like Phong, which may obscure shape information in shadowed areas, this method preserves orientation cues across the visible surface. It is a standard technique in technical illustration and volume rendered illustrations. Choose it when preserving orientation cues in shadowed or back-facing regions is prioritized. name: Gooch Shading
head: Central Difference Normal Shading, Gooch Shading with Central Difference Normals, Gooch Tone Shading, Phong/Tone Shading
body: Gooch Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model for volume rendering that maps surface orientation relative to a light source to a warm-to-cool color gradient to convey shape. It is distinguished from standard Gooch shading by its specific integration with on-the-fly central difference normal estimation in rasterization pipelines, ensuring consistent visual output across different extraction methods (rasterization vs. ray-marching). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume data V(x,y,z), light direction vector \mathbf{L}, warm color Cw, cool color Cc, warm/cool ratios kw, kc, base ray sample color Ir, and opacity \alpha. Output: Final fragment color c. Data Structures: Vertex Normals: Computed on the fly using central differences on the scalar field. No pre-computed normal buffer is required for the rasterization approach. Steps: 1. Normal Estimation: For each vertex or sample point on the isosurface, compute the gradient \mathbf{G} using central differences: \mathbf{G} = [\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}], where \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} \approx \frac{V(x+1, y, z) - V(x-1, y, z)}{2}, and similarly for y and z. Normalize \mathbf{G} to unit length. 2. Pass to Fragment Shader: The computed normal \mathbf{G} and normalized light direction \mathbf{L} are passed to the fragment shader. 3. Dot Product Factor: Compute \kappa = \mathbf{G} \cdot \mathbf{L}. The illuminated contribution uses only the positive dot product, becoming zero at orthogonal orientations. 4. Tone Contribution: Calculate It by interpolating between Cw and Cc based on \kappa: It = \left(kw \frac{1.0 + \kappa}{2}\right) Cw + \left(kc \left(1 - \frac{1.0 + \kappa}{2}\right)\right) Cc. 5. Final Color: Combine the tone contribution with the base ray sample color Ir and opacity \alpha: c = It \alpha + Ir (1 - \alpha). For multiple light sources, sum over all NL lights: c = \sum{i=1}^{NL} (I{ti} \alpha + I{ri} (1 - \alpha)). Parameters: Warm Color (Cw): Typically yellow, defined as RGB (Rw, Gw, Bw). Cool Color (Cc): Typically blue, defined as RGB (Rc, Gc, Bc). Ratios (kw, kc): Weights for warm and cool color contribution to the final result. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Central difference requires neighboring voxels; boundary handling is not specified in the sources. Degenerate Normals: If the scalar field is flat (zero gradient), the normal is undefined. Orthogonal Orientations: The dot product \kappa naturally handles values between -1 and 1, but the illuminated contribution becomes zero at orthogonal orientations (\kappa = 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecentraldifferencenormal(volume, x, y, z): # Central difference gradient approximation dx = (volume[x + 1, y, z] - volume[x - 1, y, z]) / 2.0 dy = (volume[x, y + 1, z] - volume[x, y - 1, z]) / 2.0 dz = (volume[x, y, z + 1] - volume[x, y, z - 1]) / 2.0 length = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) 0.5 if length == 0.0: return vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Degenerate case: flat field return vec3(dx / length, dy / length, dz / length) def goocheshadingfragment(G, L, Cw, Cc, kw, kc, alpha, Ir): # Compute dot product factor kappa, clamped to positive values per source kappa = max(0.0, dot(G, L)) # Calculate tone contribution interpolation factor t = (1.0 + kappa) / 2.0 # Interpolate between warm and cool colors It = (kw t) Cw + (kc (1.0 - t)) Cc # Blend tone contribution with base ray sample color using opacity c = It alpha + Ir (1.0 - alpha) return c Time Complexity: Normal computation is O(1) per vertex/sample. Shading is O(1) per fragment. Memory Complexity: No additional memory for normals if computed on the fly. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Consistent visual appearance across different rendering techniques (rasterization and ray-marching) due to identical fragment shader implementation. Limitations: Relies on central difference normal estimation, which requires neighboring voxels and may produce undefined normals in flat regions. Boundary handling is not specified in the sources. Gooch Shading was originally proposed by Gooch et al. in 1998. It is used in volume rendering to provide illustrative shading that enhances shape perception by mapping orientation to warm and cool tones. The specific application with central difference normals in rasterization is described in. name: Cool to Warm Shading
head: Tone-based shading, Warm-to-cool Shading
body: Cool to warm shading is a tone-based illumination model that enhances 3D shape perception by mapping surface orientation to a color gradient, assigning warmer colors to regions facing the reference direction and cooler colors to receding regions. Unlike physically based models like Phong, which may obscure shape information in shadowed areas, this method preserves orientation cues across the visible surface. It is a standard technique in technical illustration and volume rendered illustrations. Inputs: Volume scalar field data. Camera position and a reference direction (light vector \mathbf{l} or view direction \mathbf{v}). Outputs: Per-sample color value C{final}. Data Structures: Two color endpoints C{cool} and C{warm}, typically RGB triplets. Normal vector \mathbf{n} at the sample point, derived from the volume gradient. Direction vector \mathbf{d}, defined as the reference direction and normalized. Steps: 1. Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the current volume sample from the scalar field gradient. 2. Determine the reference direction vector \mathbf{d} as either the light direction or the view direction. 3. Calculate the dot product k = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 4. Map k \in [-1, 1] to a blending factor \alpha \in [0, 1] using linear interpolation: \alpha = \frac{k + 1}{2}. Clamp \alpha to [0, 1] if numerical errors occur. 5. Interpolate between the cool and warm colors: C{final} = (1 - \alpha) C{cool} + \alpha C{warm}. 6. Use C{final} as the base color in the volume rendering integration equation, combining it with opacity and density. Parameters: C{cool} and C{warm} define the color temperature range (e.g., blue to red). Reference vector determines whether shading is light-relative or view-relative. Edge Cases: Degenerate Normals: If the gradient is zero (flat region), \mathbf{n} is undefined. Default to a neutral color or the average scene color. Precision: Dot product precision may cause banding in smooth volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cooltowarmshading(normal, direction, colorcool, colorwarm): # Normalize direction dlen = (direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2)0.5 direction = (direction[0]/dlen, direction[1]/dlen, direction[2]/dlen) # Normalize normal nlen = (normal[0]2 + normal[1]2 + normal[2]2)0.5 normal = (normal[0]/nlen, normal[1]/nlen, normal[2]/nlen) # Dot product dotproduct = normal[0]direction[0] + normal[1]direction[1] + normal[2]direction[2] # Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle numerical errors if dotproduct < -1.0: dotproduct = -1.0 elif dotproduct > 1.0: dotproduct = 1.0 # Map to [0, 1] alpha = (dotproduct + 1.0) / 2.0 # Interpolate colors finalcolor = ( (1.0 - alpha) colorcool[0] + alpha colorwarm[0], (1.0 - alpha) colorcool[1] + alpha colorwarm[1], (1.0 - alpha) colorcool[2] + alpha colorwarm[2]) return finalcolor Uses the view direction as the reference vector. Surfaces facing the observer are assigned warmer colors, and those oriented away are assigned cooler colors, assisting in shape perception of 3-D features projected into the view plane. Uses the light direction as the reference vector. Regions facing the light source are colored warmer, and regions facing away are colored cooler, preserving shape information that physically based models may lose in shadowed areas. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, requiring only a dot product and linear interpolation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for color parameters and direction vectors. Strengths: Enhances shape perception in regions that would otherwise be dark or featureless in physically based shading. Simple to implement and tune. Limitations: Does not simulate physical light interaction. Color choice is subjective and may not suit all data types. When to use: When shape perception is critical and physical accuracy is not required, often combined with silhouette edges. The cool to warm shading model was proposed by Gooch et al. in 1998. It is a tone-based shading model used in technical illustration and volume rendered illustrations to enhance visual communication rather than photorealism. It is closely related to Gooch shading [1670-gooch-shading.md], sharing the goal of using color temperature to convey orientation. name: Vignette Shading
head: Cubic Vignette, Vignette, Vignette Effect
body: Vignette Shading is a post-processing technique applied to display images to darken the corners and edges, simulating the optical falloff of light intensity due to projection onto a flat plane. It enhances the visual focus on the center of the image by modulating brightness based on the distance from the focal point or the alignment of the view ray with the camera's optical axis. Inputs and Outputs: The method operates on the final rendered image (or fragment color) before tonemapping. Inputs include pixel coordinates (or UVs), the ray direction \mathbf{r}, and camera frame information. The output is a modulated color c{\text{final}} = c{\text{base}} \cdot V, where V is the vignette factor. Data Structures: No complex volumetric data structures are required. The method relies on screen-space UV coordinates or ray vectors. Formulas and Parameters: Two primary formulations exist in the sources: 1. Cubic Alignment Vignette: This variant calculates the factor based on the alignment between the ray direction and the camera's z-axis (the third component of the pixel frame). V = (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{f}z)^3 Where: \mathbf{r} is the normalized ray direction. \mathbf{f}z is the third component (z-axis) of the pixel frame. The result is cubed to create a smooth falloff. Alternatively, expressed using geometric parameters: \text{Factor} = \frac{f^2}{f^2+rp^2}(\mathbf{v}p \cdot \mathbf{n}p) = (\cos \theta)^3 = (\mathbf{v}p \cdot \mathbf{n}p)^3 Where: f is the focal distance. rp is the radial distance between pixel p and the line of focus. \mathbf{n}p is the unit normal of pixel p. \mathbf{v}p is a unit vector from pixel p to the focal point. \theta is the angle between the view vector and the normal. 2. UV Coordinate Vignette Effect: This variant uses normalized UV coordinates to darken corners. V = 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot (16 \cdot u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v))^{0.25} Where: u, v are normalized UV coordinates ranging from 0 to 1. The term 16 \cdot u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v) peaks at the center (0.5, 0.5) and drops to 0 at the edges. Pseudocode: The following implementation combines the cubic alignment method and the UV method. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vignetteshadingcubic(raydirections, pixelframes): """ Applies cubic vignette shading based on ray alignment with camera z-axis. Args: raydirections: Tensor of shape (..., 3) containing normalized ray directions. pixelframes: Tensor of shape (..., 3, 3) containing camera frame vectors. The z-axis is at index 2. Returns: Tensor of vignette factors. """ # Extract the z-axis (third component) of the pixel frame cameraz = pixelframes[..., 2] # Calculate dot product between ray direction and camera z-axis dotproduct = (raydirections cameraz).sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Cube the result to create the vignette falloff vignettefactor = dotproduct.pow(3) return vignettefactor def vignetteshadinguv(uvcoords): """ Applies vignette shading based on UV coordinates. Args: uvcoords: Tensor of shape (..., 2) containing normalized UV coordinates (u, v). Returns: Tensor of vignette factors. """ u = uvcoords[..., 0] v = uvcoords[..., 1] # Calculate the term inside the root term = 16.0 u v (1.0 - u) (1.0 - v) # Apply the formula: 0.5 + 0.5 (term)^0.25 vignettefactor = 0.5 + 0.5 term.pow(0.25) return vignettefactor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Direction Normalization: The cubic method requires \mathbf{r} to be normalized; otherwise, the dot product will scale with ray length, causing incorrect shading. Negative Dot Products: If the ray direction points away from the camera's forward axis, the dot product may be negative. Cubing a negative number preserves the sign, potentially leading to inverted or dark artifacts. Clamping the dot product to [0, 1] or using absolute values may be necessary depending on the desired visual effect. UV Coordinate Range: The UV method assumes u, v \in [0, 1]. Coordinates outside this range will produce unexpected results. A specific variant of vignette shading that relies solely on screen-space UV coordinates rather than ray geometry. It produces a symmetric darkening centered on the image midpoint. Time and Memory Complexity: The method is O(1) per pixel and requires minimal memory, as it only needs local pixel data (UVs or ray vectors). It is computationally inexpensive compared to volumetric illumination models. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The effect is applied per-pixel, with computational cost independent of resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; effective at directing viewer attention; works well with both ray marching and rasterization. Limitations: It is a post-processing effect applied before tonemapping. When to Use: Use when a stylized, cinematic look is desired, or when the optical properties of the camera need to be simulated for illustrative purposes. When Not to Use: Avoid when physical accuracy is required, as the effect is not based on light transport physics. Vignette shading originates from photographic optics, where lenses naturally produce darker corners due to light falloff and sensor orientation. In computer graphics, it has been adopted as a stylized post-processing effect to enhance image composition. name: Vignette Effect
head: Post-processing Vignette, Vignetting Post-Processing
body: The Vignette Effect darkens the corners and edges of a rendered image relative to the center by multiplying the color by a factor derived from the pixel's normalized UV coordinates. It is applied as a post-processing step to the final color buffer, distinct from volumetric illumination models like Vignette Shading which modulate lighting based on ray alignment within the volume. Inputs and Outputs Input: Final rendered color buffer (RGB or RGBA), image dimensions (W \times H). Output: Vignette-modified color buffer. Data Structures UV Coordinates: Normalized coordinates (u, v) where u \in [0, 1] and v \in [0, 1], representing the pixel's position in the image plane. Steps 1. For each pixel, calculate normalized UV coordinates: u = \frac{x}{W}, \quad v = \frac{y}{H} where x and y are pixel coordinates. 2. Compute the vignette factor. Two formulations exist in the sources: Formulation A (Polynomial/Root-based): \text{vignette\factor} = 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot \left( 16 \cdot u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v) \right)^{0.25} The final color is multiplied by this factor. Formulation B (Power-based with Fringe): Let pos{2d} be the 2D position vector from the image center, and fr be a fringe radius parameter. \text{vignetting} = \min\left(\frac{\|pos{2d}\|}{fr}, 1.0\right) \text{vignetting} = \left( 1.0 - \text{vignetting}^{20.0} \right)^{2.0} The color is mixed with a background color weighted by this factor: \text{color}{out}.xyz = \text{mix}(\text{vignetting\background} \cdot \text{color}w, \text{color}{xyz}, \text{vignetting}) where \text{color}w is the alpha channel and \text{color}{xyz} is the RGB channels. Parameters fr: Fringe radius. Not given in the sources. Exponent (20.0 in Formulation B): Controls the steepness of the vignette. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The term u \cdot v \cdot (1-u) \cdot (1-v) in Formulation A is zero at the edges and center, potentially causing floating-point underflow or exact zero results if not handled, though the root operation is stable. Boundaries: Formulation A naturally goes to 0.5 at the corners (since u,v \to 0 or 1), while Formulation B can go to 0 depending on the exponent and fr. Degenerate Input: If W or H is 0, UV calculation fails. Ensure W, H > 0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def applyvignette(colorbuffer, width, height, fringeradius=1.0, vignettebackground=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)): """ Applies vignette effect. colorbuffer is a 2D list of [r, g, b, a] floats in [0, 1]. Returns a tuple of (resulta, resultb) implementing Formulation A and B. """ h = len(colorbuffer) w = len(colorbuffer[0]) centerx = width / 2.0 centery = height / 2.0 resulta = [[None] w for in range(h)] resultb = [[None] w for in range(h)] for y in range(h): for x in range(w): pixel = colorbuffer[y][x] r, g, b = pixel[0], pixel[1], pixel[2] a = pixel[3] if len(pixel) > 3 else 1.0 # Normalized UV coordinates u = x / width v = y / height # Formulation A terma = 16.0 u v (1.0 - u) (1.0 - v) terma = max(terma, 0.0) factora = 0.5 + 0.5 math.pow(terma, 0.25) resulta[y][x] = [r factora, g factora, b factora, a] # Formulation B if fringeradius > 0.0: posx = (x - centerx) / width posy = (y - centery) / height pos2dlen = math.sqrt(posx posx + posy posy) vignetting = min(pos2dlen / fringeradius, 1.0) vignetting = math.pow(1.0 - math.pow(vignetting, 20.0), 2.0) # Linear mix: mix(a, b, t) = a (1.0 - t) + b t bgr, bgg, bgb = vignettebackground outr = (bgr a) (1.0 - vignetting) + r vignetting outg = (bgg a) (1.0 - vignetting) + g vignetting outb = (bgb a) (1.0 - vignetting) + b vignetting resultb[y][x] = [outr, outg, outb, a] else: resultb[y][x] = [r, g, b, a] return resulta, resultb Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The vignette effect is a common post-processing technique in computer graphics and photography. name: Blinn-Phong Toon Shading
head: Toon Blinn-Phong
body: Blinn-Phong Toon Shading is a non-photorealistic illumination model that applies posterization to the diffuse component and binary thresholding to the specular component of the standard Blinn-Phong lighting equation. It differs from its siblings by explicitly discretizing continuous lighting values into distinct bands. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Normalized light direction vector L, normalized normal N (derived from volume gradient), normalized view direction V, normalized half-vector H = \frac{L+V}{\|L+V\|}, base color C{base}, shininess exponent k, and diffuse thresholds A=0.1, B=0.3, C=0.6, D=1.0. Outputs: Final fragment color C{final}. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values and vectors computed per fragment. Parameters: Shininess k: Not given in the sources. Diffuse Thresholds: A=0.1, B=0.3, C=0.6, D=1.0. Steps: 1. Compute the diffuse factor fd using the dot product of the light direction and normal: fd = \max(0, L \cdot N) 2. Compute the specular factor fs using the dot product of the half-vector and normal, raised to the shininess power: fs = \max(0, H \cdot N)^k 3. Posterize the diffuse factor fd into discrete levels: If fd < 0.1, set fd = 0.0. Else if fd < 0.3, set fd = 0.3. Else if fd < 0.6, set fd = 0.6. Else, set fd = 1.0. 4. Apply a harsh cut (binary threshold) to the specular factor fs: fs = \text{step}(0.2, fs) 5. Combine the components with an ambient term C{amb} and specular color C{spec}: C{final} = C{amb} + (C{base} \cdot fd) + (C{spec} \cdot fs) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blinnphongtoonshading(L, N, V, Cbase, Cspec, k, Camb=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)): L = normalize(L) N = normalize(N) V = normalize(V) H = normalize(L + V) diffusefactor = max(0.0, dot(L, N)) specularfactor = pow(max(0.0, dot(H, N)), k) if diffusefactor < 0.1: diffusefactor = 0.0 elif diffusefactor < 0.3: diffusefactor = 0.3 elif diffusefactor < 0.6: diffusefactor = 0.6 else: diffusefactor = 1.0 specularfactor = 1.0 if specularfactor >= 0.2 else 0.0 return Camb + (Cbase diffusefactor) + (Cspec specularfactor) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A shading mode that enhances edges by darkening pixels where the surface normal is nearly perpendicular to the view direction. It calculates dv = \text{dot}(V, N) and ev = \text{pow}(1.0 - |dv|, 0.3). If ev \ge 0.1, it mixes the color towards black using \text{mix}(color.rgb, \text{vec3}(0), \text{pow}((ev-0.1)/(1.0 - 0.1), 6)). The edge threshold et is 0.1. Not given in the sources. The method is a toon-shaded variant of the Blinn-Phong model. fargiolas/qvrc, https://github.com/fargiolas/qvrc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Toon Shading
head: Fragment Shader Toon-Shading for Volumes, Interactive volume cartoon shading, Toon-Shading for Volumes, Toon-shading via 3D normal map
body: Volumetric Toon Shading is a non-photorealistic rendering technique that simulates cel shading for volumetric datasets without requiring explicit surface vertices or mesh extraction. It differs from surface-based NPR methods by operating directly on fragment-level data using a 3D normal map, allowing for interactive rendering of stylized volumes where features are defined by local gradient properties rather than discrete geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data), a parallel light direction vector L, and two user-specified tone registers. Output: A 2D image with discrete tonal shading. Data Structures: 1. 3D Normal Map: A 3D texture storing gray-scale gradients of the volume data in its RGB components. 2. Toon-Shading Texture: A 1D texture used for nearest-neighbor interpolation to create discontinuities between illuminated and shadowed points. Steps: 1. Render a three-dimensional normal map storing gray-scale gradients in the RGB components. 2. Issue the parallel light vector L as a constant color in the texture combiner stage. 3. For each fragment, look up the normal vector N from the 3D normal map and compute the dot product D = L \cdot N using per-fragment arithmetic. 4. Add an optional offset to D to enable arbitrary mapping of shades to tones. 5. Use the resulting dot product value to trigger a multiplexer in the texture combiner stage. 6. If the value is greater than 0.5, the multiplexer outputs the first register; otherwise, it outputs the second register. 7. Write user-specified tones to the two registers to define the final rendered shades. Parameters: Threshold: The multiplexer threshold is 0.5, separating illuminated points from shadow points. Offset: An additive offset applied to the dot product before the threshold comparison, allowing arbitrary mapping of shades to tones. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def samplenearest(tex, coord): # Standard nearest-neighbor lookup: clamp and index idx = max(0, min(len(tex) - 1, int(coord len(tex)))) return tex[idx] def volumetrictoonshading(fragmentpos, normalmap3d, lightdir, toonlut1d, tone1, tone2, threshold=0.5, offset=0.0): # 1. Look up normal from 3D normal map (gray-scale gradients in RGB) N = normalmap3d.sample(fragmentpos).rgb # 2. Compute dot product with light direction (issued as constant color) D = dot(N, lightdir) # 3. Apply offset Dadjusted = D + offset # 4. Trigger multiplexer based on threshold if Dadjusted > threshold: selectedtone = tone1 else: selectedtone = tone2 # 5. Alternative software path: use dot product as 1D texture coordinate # with nearest-neighbor interpolation to create discontinuity # color = samplenearest(toonlut1d, Dadjusted) return selectedtone Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D normal map (same resolution as volume data) and the 1D toon-shading texture. Strengths: Interactive performance due to hardware-accelerated fragment shading and texture combiners; avoids the need for explicit surface vertices. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Interactive volume illustration". It adapts polygonal toon-shading techniques to volumetric data by replacing vertex-based normal interpolation with per-fragment gradient lookup via a 3D normal map. The approach integrates directly with direct volume rendering algorithms via 3D texture maps and can be combined with hatch-based rendering methods. name: Lighting Transfer Function with Gradient Aligned Sampling
head: Gradient Aligned Sampling, LTF, Lighting Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering, Lum and Ma In-Rendering TF
body:
Lighting Transfer Function (LTF) with Gradient Aligned Sampling is a direct volume rendering technique that enhances material boundaries by decoupling illumination from opacity. Unlike methods that attenuate lighting based solely on gradient magnitude, this method indexes a 2D transfer function with two scalar samples taken along the normalized gradient direction (one forward, one opposite) to modulate specular and diffuse lighting coefficients. This enables independent control of surface lighting and opacity, allowing translucent material boundaries to be illustrated without being obscured by uniform absorption. Inputs: Volume scalar field data V. Precomputed volume gradients 
abla V. 1D Color Transfer Function (ColorTF) mapping scalar values to base color and opacity. Three 2D Lighting Transfer Functions (LTFs) for ambient (LTF{ka}), diffuse (LTF{kd}), and specular (LTF{ks}) coefficients. Light direction vector L and view direction vector V{dir}. Light scaling factor S{light} (typically >1 for high dynamic range). Sample pair distance d (typically 1 voxel). Current sample position P in voxel coordinates. Outputs: Final fragment color C and opacity \alpha. 1. 2D Lighting Transfer Function (LTF). Implemented as 2D texture lookups indexed by the pair of scalar values (S1, S2) sampled along the gradient. Three separate textures store the coefficients: LTF{ka}(S1, S2): Ambient coefficient. LTF{kd}(S1, S2): Diffuse coefficient. LTF{ks}(S1, S2): Specular coefficient. Hybrid Gradient Sign Storage: The alpha channel of the LTF texture stores a precomputed sign value indicating the difference between post-classified sample densities at the two sample locations. This sign determines whether the pre-classified gradient should be flipped to point toward maximum variation in post-classified density. Sample Pair Distance (d): The distance between the two supplemental scalar samples read along the gradient direction. Typical value: 1 voxel in each direction. Light Scaling Factor (S{light}): A multiplier passed to the fragment program that modulates all light intensities. Values >1 are required to accommodate high dynamic range lighting where RGB color exceeds alpha, as surfaces rendered with this method do not have enhanced opacity. Specular Exponent (n): Phong shading exponent. 1. Preprocessing: Precompute gradients 
abla V of the original scalar field. Precompute the hybrid gradient sign for the LTF lookup tables based on the sign of the difference between post-classified sample densities. 2. Per-Sample Rendering (Fragment Program): 1. Read the current sample's scalar value S and gradient 
abla V from the volume data. 2. Normalize the gradient to obtain the unit vector N =  rac{
abla V}{\|
abla V\|}. 3. Gradient Aligned Sampling: Calculate the positions for two additional samples: P1 = P + d \cdot N and P2 = P - d \cdot N. Linearly interpolate and read the scalar values S1 and S2 from the volume data along the normalized gradient direction. 4. Hybrid Gradient Flipping: Query the precomputed sign from the alpha channel of the LTF texture at indices (S1, S2). If the sign indicates the pre-classified gradient points opposite to the direction of maximum variation in post-classified density, flip N to -N. 5. Color and Opacity Lookup: Use the center sample value S to lookup base color C{base} and opacity \alpha from the 1D ColorTF. 6. Lighting Coefficient Lookup: Use the pair (S1, S2) as texture indices to lookup coefficients from the 2D LTFs: ka = LTF{ka}(S1, S2) kd = LTF{kd}(S1, S2) ks = LTF{ks}(S1, S2) 7. Lighting Computation: Compute the reflection vector R based on N and V{dir}. Calculate the final color C using the Phong model modulated by the LTF coefficients: C = C{base} \cdot (ka + kd \max(N \cdot L, 0)) + ks \max((N \cdot R)^n, 0) Apply the light scaling factor: C = C \cdot S{light}. 8. Alpha Modulation: Perform alpha modulation of the source color in the fragment program rather than in the framebuffer blending stage to handle cases where RGB color exceeds alpha. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderfragment(S, gradV, L, Vdir, n, d, Slight, ColorTF, LTFka, LTFkd, LTFks, VolumeData, P): """ Renders a single volume sample using Lighting Transfer Function with Gradient Aligned Sampling. Args: S: Scalar value at current sample point. gradV: Gradient vector at current sample point. L: Normalized light direction vector. Vdir: Normalized view direction vector (pointing from eye to surface). n: Specular exponent. d: Distance between sample pairs (e.g., 1.0 voxel). Slight: Light scaling factor (>1 for HDR). ColorTF: 1D texture for base color and opacity. LTFka, LTFkd, LTFks: 2D textures for lighting coefficients. VolumeData: Volume scalar field for interpolation. P: Current sample position in voxel coordinates. Returns: C: Final color vector. alpha: Final opacity. """ # 1. Normalize gradient N = gradV / math.sqrt(dot(gradV, gradV)) # 2. Gradient Aligned Sampling # Sample points displaced along the normalized gradient direction P1 = P + d N P2 = P - d N # Read scalar values at displaced points via trilinear interpolation S1 = trilinear(VolumeData, P1) S2 = trilinear(VolumeData, P2) # 3. Hybrid Gradient Flipping # Query precomputed sign from the alpha channel of the LTF texture at (S1, S2) sign = LTFka.samplealpha(S1, S2) if sign < 0: N = -N # 4. Color and Opacity Lookup basecolor, alpha = ColorTF.lookup(S) # 5. Lighting Coefficient Lookup ka = LTFka.lookup(S1, S2) kd = LTFkd.lookup(S1, S2) ks = LTFks.lookup(S1, S2) # 6. Lighting Computation (Phong Model) # Compute reflection vector R = 2 dot(N, -Vdir) N + Vdir R = 2.0 dot(N, -Vdir) N + Vdir diffuseterm = kd max(dot(N, L), 0.0) specularterm = ks pow(max(dot(R, L), 0.0), n) # Combine ambient and diffuse with base color, add specular C = basecolor (ka + diffuseterm) + specularterm # 7. Apply Light Scaling Factor for HDR C = C Slight # 8. Alpha Modulation (performed in fragment program, not framebuffer) C = C alpha return C, alpha Gradient Direction Mismatch: Pre-classified gradients may point opposite to the classified opacity distribution (e.g., dentin in tooth scans), causing surfaces to be unlit with single-sided lighting. High Dynamic Range: Since opacity is not enhanced, the alpha-multiplied RGB color can exceed the alpha value. Boundary Thickness Sensitivity: The method is sensitive to the thickness of material boundaries. Two-Sided Lighting Artifacts: Using two-sided lighting without gradient flipping illuminates back-facing surfaces incorrectly. Time and Memory Complexity: Requires approximately twice as many texture reads as traditional opacity-based transfer function methods due to the two additional scalar samples along the gradient. Memory usage increases by the storage of three 2D LTF textures and the hybrid sign data. Measured Performance: Rendering a 256 	imes 256 	imes 256 volume to a 512 	imes 512 buffer on an Nvidia GeForce 6800 at rendered sample spacing equal to the original volume resolution: LTF with Gradient Aligned Sampling: ~7.3 fps. Uniform lighting baseline: ~13.5 fps. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Independent control of lighting and opacity; effectively illustrates material boundaries in translucent volumes; handles high dynamic range lighting. Limitations: Sensitive to boundary thickness; requires precomputation of gradients and hybrid signs; higher texture read count reduces frame rate compared to simple methods. When to Use: When illustrating material boundaries independent of opacity is required, such as in CT scans of engines, protein electron probability distributions, vortex flows, and fuel injection simulations. Origin: The method was introduced by Lum and Ma in their paper "Lighting Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering". It builds on Illumination and Tone Shading Models and differs from Drebin et al. [2] by using a hybrid of pre-classified gradients and post-classified density differences for direction flipping. History and Development: The technique was implemented in graphics hardware using view-aligned textured polygons and fragment programs. It was designed to address the limitations of uniform lighting and simple gradient-based attenuation, providing a user interface for specifying 2D lighting transfer functions that emphasize edges. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for enhancing the perception of structure in volumetric data where traditional opacity-based methods fail to distinguish material boundaries. Lighting Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g7h4kx, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Lighting Transfer Functions Using Gradient Aligned Sampling, https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~ma/papers/lightingtf.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 Especificação de funções de transferência unidimensionais e multidimensionais para visualização volumétrica direta, http://hdl.handle.net/10183/12077, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Shading
head: Hybrid CVR, Mixture of gradient-based shading with volumetric shading
body: Hybrid Shading blends gradient-based shading, which captures local surface details, with volumetric shading, which provides global ambient occlusion, to balance an image's local and global features while reducing noise. It distinguishes itself from pure gradient-based methods by introducing a dynamic interpolation controlled by opacity and gradient magnitude, offering a softer appearance that is particularly effective for noisy data such as ultrasound. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: v: User-defined blending factor, a scalar in the range [0, 1]. g: Gradient magnitude at the current sample point. \alpha x': Opacity value at the current sample point. L{phong}: Incident light computed via Phong lighting model. L{vs}: Incident light computed via volumetric shadow lighting. Output: L{in}: Final incident light value for the fragment. Data Structures No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard fragment shader inputs (gradient, opacity, light vectors). The method operates on per-sample values. Steps 1. Calculate the gradient-based shading value (L{phong}) using standard Phong illumination. 2. Calculate the volumetric shading value (L{vs}) using volumetric shadow lighting. 3. Compute the blending coefficient c{blend} using the formula below. 4. Interpolate between the two lighting models using c{blend} to produce the final incident light. Formulas The blending coefficient c{blend} is calculated as: c{blend} = v \left( 1 - e^{|g|^{\frac{1}{\alpha x'}}} \right) Where: v is the user-defined blending factor (0 \le v \le 1). g is the gradient magnitude. \alpha x' is the opacity value. The final incident light L{in} is calculated as: L{in} = (1 - c{blend}) L{phong} + c{blend} L{vs} Where: L{phong} is the Phong lighting contribution. L{vs} is the volumetric shadow lighting contribution. Parameters VolumetricScatteringBlending (v): A user-defined coefficient controlling the interpolation between gradient-based and volumetric shading. The blending factor ranges between 0 and 1. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Exponentiation Stability: The term |g|^{\frac{1}{\alpha x'}} involves exponentiation where the exponent depends on the inverse of opacity. If \alpha x' approaches zero, the exponent approaches infinity, potentially causing numerical instability or overflow if |g| > 1. If |g| < 1, the term approaches zero. Implementers should guard against division by zero or extreme values in the exponent. Noise Reduction vs. Detail Loss: Setting the method to favor volumetric shading (higher v or conditions where c{blend} is high) results in a softer appearance and reduces image noise, which is beneficial for ultrasound data. However, small features may be dampened, which can be undesirable if fine detail preservation is required. Stochasticity vs. Interpolation: The method uses deterministic interpolation rather than stochastic blending to reduce artifacts introduced by random sampling. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hybridshading(v, g, alphaxprime, Lphong, Lvs): """ Computes hybrid shading by interpolating between Phong and volumetric shading. Args: v (float): User-defined blending factor [0, 1]. g (float): Gradient magnitude. alphaxprime (float): Opacity value. Lphong (float): Phong lighting intensity. Lvs (float): Volumetric shadow lighting intensity. Returns: float: Final incident light Lin. """ # Guard against division by zero in exponent if alphaxprime <= 0.0: alphaxprime = 1e-6 # # Calculate exponent term: |g|^(1 / opacity) exponent = 1.0 / alphaxprime base = abs(g) # Compute e^(base^exponent) expterm = math.exp(math.pow(base, exponent)) # Calculate blending coefficient: cblend = v (1 - expterm) cblend = v (1.0 - expterm) # Clamp blending coefficient to [0, 1] for valid interpolation weights cblend = max(0.0, min(1.0, cblend)) # Final incident light Lin = (1.0 - cblend) Lphong + cblend Lvs return Lin Uses a sphere texture to simulate lighting on volumetric primitives. Choose when spherical symmetry is appropriate. Lit Sphere Shading Modifies color based on the angle between the view direction and the gradient. Choose for edge highlighting. Orientation-Based Color Modification Applies tone shading techniques to volume data for illustrative effects. Choose for artistic rendering. Volume Illustration Tone Shading Darkens the edges of the volume to focus attention on the center. Choose for compositional emphasis. Vignette Shading Applies toon shading using the Blinn-Phong model. Choose for stylized, non-photorealistic surfaces. Blinn-Phong Toon Shading Extends toon shading to volumetric data. Choose for cartoon-like volume rendering. Volumetric Toon Shading Aligns sampling with gradients to improve lighting accuracy. Choose for high-fidelity lighting. Lighting Transfer Function with Gradient Aligned Sampling Enhances details using multi-scale unsharp masking. Choose for detail enhancement. Volumetric Unsharp Masking with Multi-scale Hierarchy Provides multiple visualization modes for shading and context. Choose when flexible display options are needed. Shading and Context Visualization Modes Applies directional shading along flow or structural lines. Choose for anisotropic feature visualization. Anisotropic Line/Streamtube Shading Time Complexity: The method adds a constant number of mathematical operations (exponentiation, multiplication, addition) per sample. It avoids the computational cost of stochastic blending by using deterministic interpolation. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond standard volume data and fragment state. Performance: The method is designed for interactive, in-browser rendering, balancing quality and speed. Strengths: Reduces noise in volumetric data (e.g., ultrasound) by favoring volumetric shading in noisy regions; balances local and global features. Limitations: May dampen small features if volumetric shading is favored too strongly. Numerical stability of the exponent term requires careful handling of low opacity values. Hybrid Shading was developed by the CVR team at Kitware as part of their Cinematic Volume Rendering work. It was theorized to balance local and global features by combining gradient-based and volumetric shading. The method was implemented and evaluated for interactive, in-browser cinematic volume rendering of medical images. The original formula was adopted and modified to increase speed and reduce speckle artifacts.
