name: Volumetric Unsharp Masking with Multi-scale Hierarchy
head: Darkening Shadowed Regions, Enhanced perception method, Feature enhancement technique, Lightening Salient Features, Volumetric Unsharp Masking, feature enhancement by unsharp masking
body: Volumetric Unsharp Masking with Multi-scale Hierarchy is a feature enhancement technique for volume rendering that improves the perception of local details (edges, superficial features) by increasing local contrast through lightening salient features and darkening shadowed regions. Unlike classical unsharp masking which requires storing full-resolution smoothed radiance volumes, this method reduces memory consumption by using one or two levels of a multi-scale volume hierarchy of the original data to compute the smoothed signals required for the unsharp masking operation. It differs from Lit Sphere Shading and Volume Illustration Tone Shading by explicitly decoupling feature enhancement from the base shading model, applying a post-shading contrast modification in the CIELab color space. The method operates on the radiance signal computed along viewing rays during ray casting. It enhances local contrast by modifying the shading of each sample using unsharp masking in the CIELab color space, utilizing a multi-scale hierarchy to approximate the smoothed background signal without storing full-resolution auxiliary volumes. Inputs: Original volume dataset V with resolution Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Transfer function TF mapping density to color and opacity. Lighting parameters (light direction L, view direction V, material properties for Phong shading). Hierarchy levels H = \{h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, h{16}, h{32}\}, where hi represents the volume downsampled by factor i. Parameters: \gamma (lightening intensity), level for lightening L{lev}, level for darkening D{lev}. Outputs: Enhanced final color C{final} for each sample along the ray. 1. Original Volume (V): 3D texture containing the scalar field. 2. Multi-scale Hierarchy (H): A set of 3D textures. Each level hi has dimensions \lceil Dx/i \rceil \times \lceil Dy/i \rceil \times \lceil Dz/i \rceil. The hierarchy is computed on the CPU and uploaded to the GPU. Only one or two levels are stored in memory at a time, significantly reducing memory usage compared to storing full-resolution smoothed radiance volumes. 3. Ray Casting State: Accumulated color and opacity. 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Compute the multi-scale volume hierarchy from the original data set V. For each level i \in \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 16, 32\}, generate a volume where dimensions are divided by i. Upload V and the selected hierarchy levels to GPU 3D textures. 2. Ray Casting Loop (GPU): For each sample point P along the viewing ray: 2.1. Compute Base Radiance: Query the density d at P from V. Compute the Phong shading color C{phong} using the local gradient \nabla f, light vector, and view vector. Transform C{phong} from RGB to CIELab, yielding [L, a, b]. 2.2. Compute Lightening Signal (S{light}): Query the density d{smooth} at P from the hierarchy level L{lev} using trilinear interpolation. Compute the Phong shading color C{smooth} for density d{smooth} using the same lighting model. Transform C{smooth} to CIELab, yielding [L{level}, a{level}, b{level}]. Edge Case: If the opacity assigned by TF to d{smooth} is zero, replace [L{level}, a{level}, b{level}] with a color having lower luminance than [L, a, b] to ensure the unsharp masking results in lightening. Calculate the unsharped CIELab color UCIELab(C): L{new} = L + \gamma(L - L{level}) k = \frac{L{new}}{L} a{new} = k \cdot a b{new} = k \cdot b UCIELab(C) = [L{new}, a{new}, b{new}] where \gamma is the user-defined scaling factor for lightening intensity. Transform UCIELab(C) back to RGB to get C{light}. 2.3. Compute Darkening Signal (S{dark}): Query the density d{tf} at P from the hierarchy level D{lev} using trilinear interpolation. Compute the color C{tf} assigned by the transfer function for density d{tf}. Transform C{tf} to CIELab, yielding [L{tf}, a{tf}, b{tf}]. Calculate the darkened CIELab color DCIELab(C): L{dark} = L + \gamma(L - L{tf}) k{dark} = \frac{L{dark}}{L} a{dark} = k{dark} \cdot a b{dark} = k{dark} \cdot b DCIELab(C) = [L{dark}, a{dark}, b{dark}] The formula applies the same \gamma for darkening intensity, but uses the difference between the sample's luminance and the transfer function's luminance at the hierarchy level. Transform DCIELab(C) back to RGB to get C{dark}. 2.4. Combine Effects: Compute the final enhanced color for the sample: C{sample} = 0.5 \cdot (C{light} + C{dark}) Use the original opacity \alpha from the transfer function for compositing. 2.5. Compositing: Composite C{sample} and \alpha into the ray accumulator using standard front-to-back alpha compositing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeenhancedshading(samplepos, volume, hierarchylevels, transferfunc, lightingparams, gamma, levellight, leveldark): """ Computes the enhanced shading for a single sample point. Args: samplepos: (x, y, z) coordinates in volume space. volume: 3D texture of the original dataset. hierarchylevels: Dictionary mapping level index (int) to 3D texture. transferfunc: Function mapping density to (colorrgb, opacity). lightingparams: Object containing light direction, view direction, etc. gamma: Scaling factor for unsharp masking intensity. levellight: Integer, hierarchy level index for lightening. leveldark: Integer, hierarchy level index for darkening. Returns: finalcolorrgb: RGB color for the sample. opacity: Float, opacity for compositing. """ # 1. Get original density and compute base Phong color densityorig = volume.sampletrilinear(samplepos) colororigrgb = computephongshading(densityorig, samplepos, lightingparams) colororiglab = rgbtocielab(colororigrgb) L, a, b = colororiglab # 2. Lightening Component # Query smoothed density from hierarchy densitysmooth = hierarchylevels[levellight].sampletrilinear(samplepos) # Compute smoothed Phong color colorsmoothrgb = computephongshading(densitysmooth, samplepos, lightingparams) colorsmoothlab = rgbtocielab(colorsmoothrgb) Lsmooth, asmooth, bsmooth = colorsmoothlab # Edge case: if opacity of smoothed density is 0, use a darker color for Lsmooth # to ensure lightening effect. Assuming transferfunc provides opacity. opacitysmooth = transferfunc.getopacity(densitysmooth) if opacitysmooth == 0: # Replace with a color of lower luminance than original Lsmooth = L 0.5 asmooth = 0 bsmooth = 0 # Apply Unsharp Masking in CIELab Lnew = L + gamma (L - Lsmooth) # Preserve saturation by scaling a and b by the ratio of new luminance to old luminance if L != 0: k = Lnew / L else: k = 1.0 # Avoid division by zero, though L=0 is rare in shaded regions anew = k a bnew = k b colorlightlab = [Lnew, anew, bnew] colorlightrgb = cielabtorgb(colorlightlab) # 3. Darkening Component # Query density from hierarchy for darkening densitytf = hierarchylevels[leveldark].sampletrilinear(samplepos) # Get color assigned by transfer function for this density colortfrgb, = transferfunc.getcolorandopacity(densitytf) colortflab = rgbtocielab(colortfrgb) Ltf, atf, btf = colortflab # Apply Unsharp Masking formula for darkening Ldarknew = L + gamma (L - Ltf) if L != 0: kdark = Ldarknew / L else: kdark = 1.0 adarknew = kdark a bdarknew = kdark b colordarklab = [Ldarknew, adarknew, bdarknew] colordarkrgb = cielabtorgb(colordarklab) # 4. Combine finalcolorrgb = 0.5 (colorlightrgb + colordarkrgb) # 5. Get opacity for compositing (from original sample), opacity = transferfunc.getcolorandopacity(densityorig) return finalcolorrgb, opacity def computephongshading(density, pos, lightingparams): """Standard Phong shading model.""" grad = computegradient(pos) normal = normalize(grad) # Standard Phong calculation using lightingparams return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for standard Phong math def computegradient(pos): """Central difference gradient approximation.""" return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for gradient math def rgbtocielab(rgb): """Standard RGB to CIELab conversion.""" return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for color space math def cielabtorgb(lab): """Standard CIELab to RGB conversion.""" return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for color space math \gamma: User-defined scaling factor controlling the intensity of the lightening/darkening effect. L{lev} (Level for lightening): Determines the scale of features to enhance. Levels 2 to 5 are typically used. Low scaling factors (e.g., level 2) detect small features; higher factors (e.g., level 8) enhance larger features. D{lev} (Level for darkening): Determines the scale of shadowed regions to darken. Levels 2 or 3 are typically used. Using lower resolution levels (higher scaling factors) for darkening produces extra, unpleasant shadowed regions. Zero Opacity in Hierarchy: If the opacity assigned by the transfer function to the average density (from the hierarchy level) is zero, the Phong color of the average must be replaced by a color with lower luminance than the sample's to ensure the unsharp masking results in lightening. Darkening Level Selection: Using lower resolution levels (higher scaling factors) for darkening produces extra, unpleasant shadowed regions. Levels 2 or 3 are recommended. Isosurface Sampling: Applying unsharp masking only at the isosurface level produces poor results because the contribution of a single sample to the final color may be quite low, especially when semi-transparent materials are traversed before reaching the isosurface. Performance gain is only 2% to 10%. Performance with Different Levels: Using different levels for lightening and darkening reduces texture coherence, causing frame rates to decrease up to 50% compared to using the same level (which decreases up to 20%). Time Complexity: Hierarchy building is O(N) where N is the number of voxels, but the constant factor is low. Building times for various datasets range from 192ms (192x180x168) to 4559ms (512x512x512). Memory Complexity: The method stores the original volume and one or two levels of the hierarchy. In the worst case (using levels 2 and 3), memory consumption increases by less than a sixth of the original volume, compared to triple storage in Tao et al.'s method. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core2 DUO CPU at 3.0 GHz and nVidia GeForce GTX 280 GPU with 1GB RAM: Using the same level for lightening and darkening: Frame rates decrease up to 20% compared to standard Phong shading. Using different levels: Frame rates decrease up to 50% due to less texture coherence. This is an improvement over Tao et al.'s method, which saw up to 70% frame rate decay. Strengths: Significantly reduced memory requirements compared to full-resolution smoothed radiance volumes. Effective enhancement of local features in both opaque and semi-transparent volumes. User studies show 72% preference for this method over Phong and Tao's method. Limitations: Performance penalty when using different hierarchy levels for lightening and darkening. Requires careful selection of hierarchy levels based on feature size. Not suitable for real-time applications requiring very high frame rates on low-end hardware if different levels are used. The method was proposed to overcome the high memory consumption limitations of the volumetric unsharp masking technique by Tao et al. [105], which required storing two additional full-resolution volumes (radiance and smoothed radiance). The multi-scale volume hierarchy approach allows for non-power-of-two levels and sparse storage, making it more efficient. The technique was evaluated in a user study involving 252 participants, where it was preferred for feature perception. Enhanced perception in volume visualization, https://doi.org/10.5821/dissertation-2117-94929, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Shading and Context Visualization Modes
head: Focus and Context Shading
body: Shading and Context Visualization Modes is a volume rendering technique that separates data into "focus" (primary interest) and "context" (surrounding structure) clusters to enhance perceptual clarity. It solves the problem of visual clutter in complex multiclassified volumes by rendering the focus with high-fidelity shading while rendering the context as simplified, semi-transparent proxies. It is distinct from its siblings, such as Lit Sphere Shading or Volume Illustration Tone Shading, by explicitly decoupling the rendering pipeline into two distinct semantic layers with different shading models and opacity modulations, rather than applying a single stylized lighting model to the entire volume. The method operates on a pre-segmented volume where voxels are classified into focus clusters and context clusters. The context is often represented as a hierarchical structure (ghosting depth). Inputs: Volume data V with classification labels. Focus cluster bounding box and center. Context cluster hierarchy (depth levels). Shading type parameter \Sigma \in \{\text{Phong}, \text{E+A}, \text{E+A+S}\}. Context visualization mode \Omega \in \{\text{All Voxels}, \text{Boundary Voxels}, \text{Bounding Boxes}\}. Outputs: Final color c for each fragment. Data Structures: Context Cluster Hierarchy: A tree where nodes represent clusters. Each node has a depth (ghosting depth) and opacity factor. Gradient Modulation Transfer Function (GMTF): A function mapping local gradient magnitude to a width/opacity factor for boundary context. Steps: 1. Camera Setup: Compute view reference point P{cam} as the center of the focus clusters. Compute projection window as the bounding box of the union of focus and all context clusters. 2. Context Opacity Pre-computation (Parser Stage): If \Omega = \text{Bounding Boxes}: Set Context Transfer Function (CTF) opacity to 0 for all context voxels to prevent them from being rendered during standard texture slicing. If \Omega = \text{Boundary Voxels}: Compute GMTF factor g for each context voxel based on its gradient magnitude. Modulate context surface width/opacity using g. Deeper hierarchy levels (higher ghosting depth) result in thinner, more transparent surfaces. If \Omega = \text{All Voxels}: Render context voxels with standard opacity derived from their cluster hierarchy depth. 3. Fragment Shader Execution (Per Sample): Determine if the current sample belongs to Focus (F) or Context (C). If Focus: Compute shading using the global parameter \Sigma. If \Sigma = \text{Phong}: Use Phong illumination model with normal \nabla fn. If \Sigma = \text{E+A}: Compute emission and absorption. If \Sigma = \text{E+A+S}: Combine emission, absorption, and shading. Color cF is derived from the focus transfer function (typically RGB). If Context: Convert context cluster RGB values to grayscale to enhance contrast with the colored focus. Compute shading using the same global parameter \Sigma. Apply opacity modulation based on ghosting depth and/or GMTF. Color cC is the grayscale representation of the context cluster. 4. Compositing: Apply per-plane opacity modulation to proxy polygons (if used) in front of the focus bounding box to increase transparency of foreground context. Composite cF and cC using standard volume rendering integration (e.g., front-to-back alpha blending). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shadingandcontextvisualizationmode(sample, focusbbox, contexthierarchy, shadingtype, contextmode): """ sample: dict with 'value', 'gradient', 'clusterid', 'depth' focusbbox: bounding box of focus clusters contexthierarchy: dict mapping clusterid to {'depth': int, 'color': (r,g,b)} shadingtype: str ('Phong', 'E+A', 'E+A+S') contextmode: str ('All Voxels', 'Boundary Voxels', 'Bounding Boxes') """ clusterid = sample['clusterid'] isfocus = clusterid in focusclusters # Assumed global check if isfocus: # Focus Rendering normal = normalize(sample['gradient']) if shadingtype == 'Phong': color = phongshading(normal, sample['value']) elif shadingtype == 'E+A': color = emissionabsorption(sample['value']) elif shadingtype == 'E+A+S': color = emissionabsorptionshading(normal, sample['value']) # Focus color is typically RGB from transfer function finalcolor = applyfocustransferfunction(color) alpha = 1.0 # Focus is opaque/highly visible else: # Context Rendering clusterinfo = contexthierarchy[clusterid] depth = clusterinfo['depth'] basecolor = clusterinfo['color'] # Convert to grayscale for contrast graycolor = rgbtograyscale(basecolor) # Compute shading for context (same model as focus) normal = normalize(sample['gradient']) if shadingtype == 'Phong': shade = phongshading(normal, sample['value']) elif shadingtype == 'E+A': shade = emissionabsorption(sample['value']) elif shadingtype == 'E+A+S': shade = emissionabsorptionshading(normal, sample['value']) contextcolor = graycolor shade # Opacity Modulation if contextmode == 'Bounding Boxes': alpha = 0.0 # Prevent rendering during texture slicing elif contextmode == 'Boundary Voxels': # GMTF modulation based on gradient gmtffactor = computegmtf(sample['gradient']) # Depth-based transparency: deeper = thinner/more transparent depthfactor = 1.0 / (1.0 + depth) alpha = gmtffactor depthfactor else: # All Voxels # Standard depth-based transparency alpha = 1.0 / (1.0 + depth) finalcolor = contextcolor alpha = clamp(alpha, 0.0, 1.0) return finalcolor, alpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Definition: If the focus cluster boundary is ill-defined, the context bounding box may overlap incorrectly with focus data, causing visual artifacts. Gradient Noise: In low-resolution volumes, gradient estimation for GMTF may be noisy, leading to erratic context opacity. Performance: Computing shading for both focus and context layers doubles the shading computation cost compared to single-layer rendering. A method for binary voxel models that uses a divide-and-conquer strategy to estimate surface normals from a 3x3x3 neighborhood. It represents the neighborhood with three orthogonal 3x3 planes, computes 2D normal vectors for the 256 possible patterns in each plane into a lookup table, and combines them at runtime. To handle ambiguous cases, multiple normal vectors are encoded and selected based on the viewing direction quadrant. It also adds diagonal vectors from occupied corner voxels to account for vertex-adjacent influences neglected by the orthogonal planes. It achieves a mean error of 0.0337 and standard deviation of 0.0518 compared to polygon models, performing slightly better than gray-level methods near corners. An extension of the 3x3x3 method using a 5x5x5 neighborhood. Due to the impractical size of a full lookup table for 5x5 planes (25 entries each), it employs systematic elimination of interior and redundant entries that have little effect on the normal vector. This reduces the effective combinations to fewer than 1,000, keeping the lookup table size manageable while capturing smoother surface inclinations than the 3x3x3 method. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, with a constant factor roughly doubled due to dual-layer shading. The 3x3x3/5x5x5 normal estimation is O(1) per voxel using lookup tables. Memory Complexity: O(N) for volume data. The 3x3x3 method requires a small lookup table (256 entries per plane). The 5x5x5 method requires a reduced lookup table (<1,000 entries). Performance: Real-time performance is achievable for the 3x3x3 method on standard hardware. Strengths: Enhances perception of complex structures by separating focus and context; reduces visual clutter; real-time capable. Limitations: Requires pre-segmentation of focus and context; context shading may obscure fine details if opacity is not carefully tuned. The concept of focus and context rendering was introduced to address the limitations of traditional volume rendering in displaying complex, multiclassified data. The specific 3-D contextual shading methods (3x3x3 and 5x5x5) were developed by Chen et al. in the mid-1990s to overcome the limitations of existing methods like Hohne’s gray-scale shading, which was sensitive to distance value distributions. The 3x3x3 method was designed for binary voxel models, while the 5x5x5 method extended this to larger neighborhoods with optimized pattern reduction. name: 3-D Contextual Shading (5x5x5)
head: 5x5x5 Contextual Shading Method
body: 3-D Contextual Shading (5x5x5) is an illumination model for volume rendering that computes surface normals from a 5x5x5 voxel neighborhood to generate non-photorealistic shading. It improves upon the 3x3x3 contextual shading method by using a larger neighborhood to capture smoother surface inclinations, while employing systematic elimination of interior and redundant entries to keep the lookup table size manageable (reducing effective combinations to fewer than 1,000). It is distinct from gradient-based methods by relying on topological border detection rather than intensity derivatives, and from the 3x3x3 method by its larger context and optimized pattern reduction. Input: A 3D voxel grid V where each voxel is either occupied (surface) or unoccupied (background). The method operates on a central voxel C assumed to lie on the surface. Output: A surface normal vector \mathbf{n} for voxel C, used for shading calculations. Voxel Grid: Binary occupancy grid. Lookup Table (LUT): Maps a reduced set of pattern indices to precomputed normal vectors. The LUT size is less than 1,000 entries. 1. Define Neighborhood: Consider the 5x5x5 neighborhood centered at voxel C. Divide this cube into three orthogonal planes: XY, YZ, and XZ. 2. Identify Open Directions: Determine the "open direction(s)" of C by checking if C is a border point in the global grid. A voxel is an X-border point if it has an unoccupied neighbor in the \pm X direction. A direction (e.g., North/South, East/West, Front/Back) is an open direction if C is a border point in that direction but not in the opposite direction. If C is a border point in both opposite directions (e.g., both North and South), neither is an open direction. If no open directions are found (e.g., C is surrounded in all 6 cardinal directions), the normal cannot be determined by this method; use a fallback (e.g., gradient or default). 3. Plane Contribution Check: For each of the three orthogonal planes: Check the 4 direct neighbors of C in that plane. If all 4 direct neighbors are occupied, check the 4 indirect neighbors (diagonal neighbors in the plane, sharing only a corner with C). If all 4 indirect neighbors are also occupied, the plane contributes nothing to the normal. Skip this plane. 4. Column Traversal for Open Directions: For each identified open direction: Divide the 5x5 plane of that direction into five 5x1 columns parallel to the open direction. Traverse each column starting from the open direction towards the center. Identify the first surface voxel encountered in each column. If no surface voxel is found in a column, record a null value. There are 5 columns, each having 6 possible states (5 positions for the first surface voxel, or 1 state for "no surface"). This yields 6^5 = 7,776 raw patterns. 5. Pattern Reduction: Center Constraint: Since C is on the surface, the first surface voxel in the center column cannot be beyond C (i.e., it must be at or before C). This halves the possibilities for the center column, reducing the total patterns by half. Parallel Surface Elimination: If there are no surface voxels in the second column (adjacent to center) or the fourth column, the surface is effectively parallel to the column length. In such cases, any surface voxels in the first or fifth column (farthest from center) have negligible influence on the normal and are neglected. The effective number of combinations is reduced to fewer than 1,000. 6. Normal Computation: Map the reduced pattern to an entry in the LUT to retrieve a precomputed normal vector \mathbf{n}{plane} for that plane. The final normal \mathbf{n} is typically the normalized sum of the contributions from the three orthogonal planes: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{n}{XY} + \mathbf{n}{YZ} + \mathbf{n}{XZ}}{\|\mathbf{n}{XY} + \mathbf{n}{YZ} + \mathbf{n}{XZ}\|}. If a plane contributed nothing, its vector is zero. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenormal5x5x5(voxelgrid, centercoords): """ Computes the surface normal for a surface voxel using the 5x5x5 contextual shading method. Args: voxelgrid: 3D array of booleans (True for occupied, False for unoccupied). centercoords: Tuple (x, y, z) of the center voxel index. Returns: Normal vector (nx, ny, nz). """ x, y, z = centercoords # Define 5x5x5 neighborhood bounds # Note: Boundary checks should be added in practice neighborhood = get5x5x5neighbors(voxelgrid, x, y, z) # Step 1 & 2: Identify open directions # Check if center is a border point in each axis # A voxel is a border point if at least one neighbor in that axis is unoccupied isnorthborder = not all(neighborhood[x, y, z+1],...) # Simplified logic # More precisely: # North/South (Z), East/West (X), Front/Back (Y) - assuming standard axes # Let's define directions: # Z+: North, Z-: South # X+: East, X-: West # Y+: Front, Y-: Back opendirs = [] # Check Z (North/South) hasunocczpos = any(not voxelgrid[x, y, z+1+i] for i in range(1, 3)) # Simplified hasunocczneg = any(not voxelgrid[x, y, z-1-i] for i in range(1, 3)) # A direction is open if it is a border point but not the converse # Border point means unoccupied neighbor exists isnorthborder = hasunocczpos issouthborder = hasunocczneg if isnorthborder and not issouthborder: opendirs.append('Z+') elif issouthborder and not isnorthborder: opendirs.append('Z-') # Repeat for X and Y axes... #... normals = [] # Step 3 & 4: Process each open direction for direction in opendirs: # Determine the plane and columns if direction == 'Z+': plane = 'XY' # Columns are parallel to Z # Traverse from Z+ towards Z- #... elif direction == 'Z-': plane = 'XY' # Traverse from Z- towards Z+ #... #... # For the plane, check if it contributes # Check 4 direct neighbors in the plane directneighborsoccupied = checkdirectneighbors(voxelgrid, x, y, z, plane) if not directneighborsoccupied: # Plane contributes # Divide 5x5 plane into 5 columns # Traverse each column from the open direction # Find first surface voxel pattern = getpatternfromcolumns(voxelgrid, x, y, z, direction) # Reduce pattern reducedpattern = reducepattern(pattern, direction) # Lookup normal nplane = lookupnormal(reducedpattern) normals.append(nplane) # Step 6: Combine normals if not normals: return [0, 0, 0] # Fallback finalnormal = sum(normals) return normalize(finalnormal) Neighborhood Size: 5x5x5. Effective LUT Size: < 1,000 entries. No Open Directions: If the central voxel is surrounded by occupied voxels in all 6 cardinal directions, no open direction is found. The method fails to determine a normal from context alone. A fallback strategy is required. Boundary Conditions: Voxels near the edge of the volume grid do not have a full 5x5x5 neighborhood. Boundary handling (e.g., padding, clamping) must be defined. Precision: The method relies on binary occupancy. Noise in the voxelization process can lead to incorrect border detection. The source notes that fuzzy objects were generated using Gaussian filtering before voxelization to mitigate this. Degenerate Input: If the surface is extremely thin (1 voxel thick) or has complex topology, the "first surface voxel" logic may need careful definition to ensure consistency. Time Complexity: The method involves checking neighbors and traversing columns. The lookup table access is O(1). The preprocessing (LUT construction) is done once. Per-voxel cost is constant but higher than 3x3x3 due to the larger neighborhood. Memory Complexity: The LUT size is < 1,000 entries, which is small. The 5x5x5 neighborhood requires accessing 125 voxels per query. Measured Performance: Compared to a polygon model, the 5x5x5 contextual shading method has a mean error of 0.0376 and a standard deviation of 0.0573. This is slightly higher error than the 3x3x3 method (mean 0.0295, std 0.0460) but provides smoother shading due to the larger context. Strengths: Captures smoother surface inclinations than 3x3x3; lookup table size is manageable due to pattern reduction. Limitations: Higher computational cost than 3x3x3; sensitive to voxelization quality; requires handling of edge cases where no open direction exists. When to use: When smoother shading is desired and the voxel grid is clean (or pre-filtered). When the 3x3x3 method produces too much noise or jagged shading. When not to use: When computational resources are very limited (use 3x3x3 or gradient methods); when the voxel grid is noisy without pre-filtering. The 3-D Contextual Shading (5x5x5) method was developed as an improvement over the 3x3x3 contextual shading method. It was presented in a final report on visualization techniques for die casting part and die design. The report dates from July 1, 1995, to September 30, 1997. The method was compared against polygon models and grayscale gradient shading methods applied with Gaussian filters. Simple visualization techniques for die casting part and die design. name: Anisotropic Line/Streamtube Shading
head: Anisotropic shading for lines and streamtubes
body: Anisotropic Line/Streamtube Shading illuminates one-dimensional fiber representations, such as lines or streamtubes, to provide depth cues and shape perception that unshaded lines lack, while avoiding the polygonal overhead of explicit tube geometry. It distinguishes itself from surface-based NPR methods by applying an anisotropic parameter (specifically sheen) to model specular highlights along the fiber tangent, thereby revealing coherent structure. Inputs: The method requires fiber geometry defined as a sequence of points for the streamline or line segment. It also requires the view direction V and light direction L. An anisotropic parameter controls the sheen roughness or sharpness. Finally, a base color derived from transfer functions or fiber direction interpolation is needed. Data Structures: The streamline is represented as a polyline or parametric curve. For hardware implementation, this may be rasterized as a set of quads or triangles approximating a thin tube, or rendered as lines with a custom shader. An optional precomputed texture encodes illumination results for varying view angles, light directions, and streamline tangents. Steps: 1. Tangent Estimation: For each fragment on the line or streamtube, compute the local tangent vector T of the streamline. 2. Normal Approximation: Since lines lack a unique surface normal, define a plane of possible normals orthogonal to T. The effective normal N for shading is derived from the view vector V and tangent T. 3. Illumination Calculation: Compute the anisotropic highlight. This can be implemented efficiently in hardware by sampling the precomputed texture using normalized coordinates derived from V, L, and T. Alternatively, a shader-based anisotropic model applies the anisotropic parameter to modulate specular highlights along the tangent. 4. Color Composition: Combine the base color C{base} with the anisotropic highlight I{spec} and ambient term C{amb}: C{final} = C{base} \cdot C{amb} + I{spec} \cdot C{highlight}. Formulas: Exact mathematical formulas for the anisotropic BRDF or sheen model are not given in the sources. Standard implementations typically compute the specular term based on the alignment of the view direction with the tangent plane orthogonal to T. Parameters: The sheen roughness or sharpness parameter controls the spread of the anisotropic highlight, where higher values create sharper highlights along the fiber axis. The sheen tint parameter modulates the color of the specular reflection, allowing control over the perceived material properties. Edge Cases: At endpoints or singularities, the tangent may be undefined, requiring interpolation or fallback to a default normal. When fibers are densely packed, explicit streamtubes cause visual cluttering and aliasing, but illuminated streamlines avoid this by using the plane-of-normals approach to preserve overlay depth cues. This technique illuminates streamlines using a Phong illumination model to provide depth cues missing in simple streamlines. It replaces missing surface normals with planes of possible normals orthogonal to the streamline. The method is implemented efficiently in hardware by precomputing a texture that encodes illumination for different view points, light directions, and streamline tangents. It provides finer 3D details and better depth cues than simple non-illuminated streamlines, which perform poorly when examining complex fiber tract arrangements closely. Performance: Rendering is significantly faster than creating high-quality polygonal tubes, which require many polygons to avoid aliasing and visual clutter. Hardware acceleration is achieved via precomputed textures or efficient shader calculations. Visual Quality: The method provides better shape and depth cues than unshaded lines. It avoids the visual cluttering and aliasing issues associated with dense explicit streamtubes. Limitations: Simple non-illuminated streamlines perform poorly when examining complex fiber tract arrangements closely, but the illuminated variant resolves this by providing finer 3D details. Interpretation by laymen may still be ambiguous compared to explicit geometry, though less so than unshaded lines. The method originated in the context of medical imaging visualization, particularly for fiber tractography such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). It draws inspiration from human hair rendering techniques, which similarly handle many polyline-like objects with specific shapes and coherencies. The technique is implemented in tools like Horizon to compare plain gray coloring, anisotropic lighting, and interpolated colors. Earlier foundational work by Stalling et al. (1997) and Mallo et al. (2005) explored illuminated lines for visualizing fiber bundles. name: Sline
head: Seamless Line Illustration for Interactive Biomedical Visualization
body: Sline is a surface-based illustrative rendering method that provides a smooth, interactive transition between abstract silhouettes and detailed Phong shading by integrating silhouettes, contours, suggestive contours, and hatching. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by achieving these stylistic transitions without relying on pre-existing texture coordinates or assumptions about the underlying mesh topology, making it particularly suitable for medical surface data derived from volumes. Unlike pure volume rendering methods, Sline operates on explicit surface meshes, using local geometric properties to generate line-based features that enhance shape perception. Sline processes a scene containing one or more meshes M. For each mesh, a rendering style is selected from a hierarchy of abstraction levels: (1) Silhouettes and Contours, (2) Suggestive Contours, (3) Hatching, and (4) Phong Shading. The method relies on preprocessing geometric properties and then applying specific algorithms for each style level. Inputs: Mesh M with vertices and faces. View vector v (pointing from camera to mesh). Light gradient vector field k. Feature size F (bounding sphere radius of M). Style level parameter (1-4). Outputs: Final rendered image with illustrative line styles or Phong shading. Mesh M: Standard triangle mesh representation. Light Gradient Field k: A vector field defined on the mesh surface, computed as described in (based on Lawonn et al. [LKEP14]). Radial Surface Curvature \kappaw(p): Scalar field on M, where w is the projection of view vector v onto the tangent plane at p. Directional Derivative Dw \kappaw: Derivative of \kappaw in direction w. Preparation Texture TEXp: Screen-space texture storing fragment 3D locations and normals for hatching seed computation. Stencil Buffer: Used to isolate silhouette contours from inner contours. 1. Compute the light gradient vector field k on M. 2. Compute radial surface curvature \kappaw(p) for all points p \in M. 3. Compute the directional derivative Dw \kappaw using the method by Judd et al. [JDA07]. 4. Define feature size F as the radius of the bounding sphere of M. This step identifies object boundaries and internal feature lines. 1. Silhouette/Contour Detection: Iterate over all triangle edges. For each edge, interpolate the normal \hat{n} along the edge. Find zero crossings where \langle \hat{n}, v \rangle = 0. 2. Contour Patch Generation: If zero crossings are found on two edges of a triangle, create a contour patch with four vertices. The vertices are defined as: \hat{p}1 = \hat{p}0 + a \cdot \hat{n} \cdot F where \hat{p}0 is the zero crossing location, \hat{n} is the interpolated normal at that location, a is a parameter controlling contour width, and F is the feature size. 3. Silhouette-Only Mode (Optional): If only silhouettes are required: Render mesh M into the stencil buffer. Render the generated contour patches with the stencil test enabled. This ensures contours are drawn only where M has not been drawn, effectively discarding inner contour patches. Suggestive contours extend actual contours to support shape perception by identifying contours that would appear as silhouettes from nearby viewpoints. 1. Zero Crossing Search: For each triangle edge, search for a point \hat{p} where \kappaw(\hat{p}) = 0. 2. Condition Checks: For each zero crossing \hat{p}, verify two conditions: Condition 2: 0 < td < \frac{Dw \kappaw(\hat{p})}{\|w\|}. Here, td is a threshold parameter ensuring Dw \kappaw is positive and suppressing noise-induced sign changes. Condition 3: 0 < \thetac < \arccos\left( \frac{-\langle n(\hat{p}), v(\hat{p}) \rangle}{\|v(\hat{p})\|} \right). This discards contours where the angle between view vector v and normal n is too small. \thetac is a threshold parameter. 3. Patch Generation: If two or more edges of a triangle meet the conditions, generate suggestive contour patches. These patches are oriented orthogonally to the corresponding triangle surface. Hatching generates thick, non-merging lines using "smart seeds" mapped to the mesh without texture coordinates. 1. Seed Mapping (Polycube Projection): Define a 3D grid in local coordinates of M. For each surface point p with normal pn, project p onto the grid. The point is projected onto the grid face f with normal fn if \langle pn, fn \rangle is the maximum dot product among all face normals of the grid cell. This projection minimizes distortion and allows points to project outside their original cell. 2. Smart Seed Definition: Seeds consist of three concentric regions based on distance from the cell center c: Core: Radius rc = \frac{1}{2} sr. Always black (actual stroke). Halo: Radius rh = sr. Adjustable brightness for contrast. Contact: Radius r{cont} = \beta sr. Drawn lighter to prevent merging. sr = \frac{1}{4} cs, where cs is the cell size. \beta = 1.8 is the contact region size factor. Cell size cs is chosen dependent on feature size F and camera distance. 3. Seed Trimming: Render mesh M to preparation texture TEXp to get screen-space fragment location p and normal. Project p to grid point p' based on normal. Project light gradient k(p) to grid cell face to get normalized vector k'(p). Trim the seed in the direction of k'(p) to ensure accessibility from outside. Compute: q1 = c + sr \cdot \frac{k'(p)}{4} q2 = c - sr \cdot \frac{k'(p)}{4} d1 = \langle k'(p), (q1 - p') \rangle d2 = \langle k'(p), (q2 - p') \rangle If d1 and d2 have the same sign, the fragment is invalid (discarded). 4. Perspective Compensation: For faces turning away from the viewer, increase the seed radius: s{rm} = sr (2 - |\langle v, n \rangle|) This compensates for perspective distortion and prevents rasterizer discard of small, clinched seeds. 5. Line Search: Perform a line search from the seed regions to generate thick lines that do not merge. The core produces the black stroke, the halo adjusts contrast, and the contact region ensures strokes remain distinct. Standard Phong illumination model is applied if the highest level of abstraction is selected. a: Contour width factor. td: Threshold for suggestive contour condition 2. \thetac: Threshold for suggestive contour condition 3. \beta: Contact region size factor, typically 1.8. cs: Cell size for hatching grid, dependent on F and camera distance. F: Feature size (bounding sphere radius). Noise: Frequent sign changes in Dw \kappaw due to noise can generate spurious suggestive contours. Condition 2 with td suppresses these. Merging Strokes: Without the contact region and trimming, hatching strokes may merge into broad, indistinct bands. The smart seed design and line search address this. Perspective Distortion: Small seeds on faces turning away from the viewer may be discarded by the rasterizer. The radius modification s{rm} mitigates this. Lack of Texture Coordinates: Sline is designed to work without texture coordinates, which are often absent in medical surface data. Time Complexity: Depends on mesh resolution and grid density for hatching. Preprocessing requires curvature and derivative computations per vertex/face. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for mesh data, curvature fields, and preparation texture TEXp. Strengths: Seamless transition between abstraction levels; no reliance on texture coordinates; interactive performance. Limitations: Surface-based only (not direct volume rendering); requires preprocessing of curvature fields; parameter tuning for td, \thetac, and cs. When to Use: Interactive biomedical visualization where abstract to detailed transitions are needed, especially for meshes without texture coordinates. When Not to Use: Direct volume rendering without surface extraction; scenes requiring texture-based hatching. Sline was introduced in the paper "Sline: Seamless Line Illustration for Interactive Biomedical Visualization". It builds upon previous work in illustrative rendering, such as suggestive contours by De Carlo et al. [DFRS03] and hatching techniques by Lawonn et al. [LKEP14]. The method was developed to address the need for interactive, stylized visualization of medical data, where texture coordinates are often unavailable. name: Residual-based Difference Visualization
head: Residual DVR
body: Residual-based Difference Visualization is a comparative volume rendering technique designed to reveal structural discrepancies between a reference volume field and an optimized volume field. It solves the problem of identifying regions where an optimized transfer function fails to compensate for differences in the underlying data, thereby guiding further analysis or optimization. It is distinct from standard difference visualization by explicitly rendering the residual field derived from the difference of two transfer-function-applied volumes, rather than comparing raw scalar values. Inputs: 1. Reference volume field Vr. 2. Optimized volume field Vo. 3. Reference transfer function Tr. 4. Optimized transfer function To. Outputs: A residual volume field V{res} representing the magnitude of difference between the two rendered fields. Data Structures: The residual field V{res} is a 3D scalar field with dimensions matching the input volumes. Each voxel stores a single scalar value representing the residual magnitude. Steps: 1. Apply Transfer Functions: For each voxel i in the domain, compute the color output for both fields: cr(i) = Tr(Vr(i)) co(i) = To(Vo(i)) Where cr and co are RGBA vectors. 2. Pre-multiply Alpha: Ensure the RGB components are pre-multiplied with the alpha component for both colors to weight transparency correctly: c'r = (Rr\alphar, Gr\alphar, Br\alphar, \alphar) c'o = (Ro\alphao, Go\alphao, Bo\alphao, \alphao) 3. Compute Residual: Calculate the difference vector between the pre-multiplied colors and compute the l2-norm to obtain the scalar residual value for voxel i: V{res}(i) = \| c'r(i) - c'o(i) \|2 The sources specify using the l2-norm of the RGB\alpha difference vector, suggesting all 4 components are included in the norm calculation. 4. Render: Render the resulting residual field V{res} using standard Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) or a specific visualization mapping to highlight high-difference regions. Parameters: Norm type: l2 (Euclidean). Alpha handling: Pre-multiplication is required. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency Weighting: Failing to pre-multiply RGB by alpha will cause highly transparent regions to contribute equally to the residual as opaque regions, potentially obscuring structural differences in dense areas. Transfer Function Sensitivity: The method reveals differences in the rendered output, not just the scalar field. An imaging technique used to enhance the visualization of changes in tissue contrast by subtracting a reference image from a current image. It sets itself apart by operating on 2D image streams rather than 3D volumes. The reference image can be fixed in time or dynamic (to approximate a time derivative). It is chosen when temporal changes in tissue contrast need to be highlighted in interventional guidance. Strengths: Directly highlights where optimization or changes in data structure affect the visual output; handles transparency correctly via pre-multiplication. Limitations: Only reveals differences in the rendered appearance, not raw data differences; sensitive to transfer function choices. When to use: When comparing two volume datasets or two transfer functions to identify regions of significant visual discrepancy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the context of transfer function optimization for comparative volume rendering. It supports improved analysis by guiding users toward regions in the domain where structural differences are high and cannot be compensated by the optimized transfer function. A related technique, Complex Subtraction Imaging, was used in real-time volume rendered MRI for interventional guidance to enhance visualization of changes in tissue contrast. name: Pilot Network
body: The Pilot Network is an auxiliary training mechanism used in Volume Feature Rendering (VFR) to stabilize the convergence of neural radiance fields during the early stages of training. It solves the problem of convergence failure in scenes with complex geometry (e.g., the 'ship' scene from the NeRF synthetic dataset) when using large neural networks. Unlike the main VFR framework, which integrates features from all samples along a ray before passing them to a large network, the Pilot Network performs standard volume rendering by evaluating a small network for each sample individually. This approach helps the model find coarse geometry before switching to the main VFR framework. The Pilot Network is a small, temporary neural network used exclusively during the initial phase of training. It is discarded after a fixed number of training steps, after which the main VFR framework takes over. Inputs: The input to the Pilot Network is the feature vector F(xi) and the view direction d for a specific sample point xi along a ray. Outputs: The output is the predicted color contribution Ci for that specific sample. The Pilot Network is a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with the following architecture: Hidden Layers: 2 hidden layers. Neurons per Layer: 64 neurons per hidden layer. Activation: Not specified in the sources. Standard practice implies ReLU or similar. Output Layer: Produces color values (RGB). 1. Initialization: Initialize the Pilot Network with 2 hidden layers, each containing 64 neurons. 2. Early Training (Steps 1–300): For each ray, sample points xi along the ray. For each sample point xi, compute its feature vector F(xi). Pass F(xi) and the view direction d into the Pilot Network to predict the color contribution Ci for that sample. Compute the final ray color C(r) using standard volume rendering integration: C(r) = \sumi wi \text{PilotNet}(F(xi), d) where wi = Ti \alphai are the standard volume rendering weights derived from transmittance Ti and opacity \alphai. 3. Switch to Main Framework (Step 301+): Discard the Pilot Network. Switch to the main VFR framework, which uses a larger network (e.g., 4 hidden layers). The main framework integrates features from all samples along the ray before passing the aggregated feature to the large network. Pilot Network Architecture: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons each. Pilot Network Duration: 300 training steps. Total Training Steps: Approximately 20,000 steps (the pilot phase is negligible in duration). Convergence Failure: Without the Pilot Network, VFR fails to converge on certain scenes (e.g., 'ship') when using large neural networks (e.g., 4 hidden layers). This is attributed to the model's inability to find correct geometry due to feature integration of all samples (including empty space) in the early training stage. Network Size: The convergence failure is more likely to occur with comparably large neural networks. The standard VFR converges with a smaller network (2 hidden layers, 256 neurons) but fails with larger ones without the Pilot Network. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainvfrwithpilotnetwork(totalsteps=20000, pilotsteps=300): # Initialize networks mainnet = MLP(hiddenlayers=4, neuronsperlayer=256) pilotnet = MLP(hiddenlayers=2, neuronsperlayer=64) for step in range(1, totalsteps + 1): points, features, viewdirs, opacities = sampledata() transmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if step <= pilotsteps: # Pilot phase: standard volume rendering (evaluate network per sample) for i in range(len(points)): alpha = opacities[i] wi = transmittance alpha ci = pilotnet.forward(features[i], viewdirs[i]) finalcolor = [finalcolor[j] + wi ci[j] for j in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) loss = sum((finalcolor[j] - targetcolor[j])2 for j in range(3)) / 3 for param in pilotnet.parameters(): param -= learningrate gradient(loss, param) else: # Main VFR phase: integrate features, then evaluate network aggregatedfeature = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(len(points)): alpha = opacities[i] wi = transmittance alpha aggregatedfeature = [aggregatedfeature[j] + wi features[i][j] for j in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) finalcolor = mainnet.forward(aggregatedfeature, viewdirs[0]) loss = sum((finalcolor[j] - targetcolor[j])2 for j in range(3)) / 3 for param in mainnet.parameters(): param -= learningrate gradient(loss, param) def MLP(hiddenlayers, neuronsperlayer): # Standard multi-layer perceptron with ReLU activations return NeuralNetwork(layers=[neuronsperlayer] hiddenlayers) def sampledata(): # Returns sample points along rays, feature vectors F(xi), view directions d, and opacities alphai pass def gradient(loss, param): # Standard backpropagation gradient computation pass Time Complexity: The Pilot Network adds negligible overhead to the total training time because it is only used for a small number of steps (300 out of ~20,000). Memory Complexity: The Pilot Network is small (2 hidden layers, 64 neurons), so its memory footprint is minimal. Strengths: Stabilizes training for large neural networks in VFR, preventing convergence failure on complex scenes. Limitations: Only applicable during the early training phase; requires switching networks after a fixed number of steps. When to Use: When using large neural networks (e.g., 4 hidden layers) in VFR and experiencing convergence issues on complex scenes. When Not to Use: Not required when using smaller networks (e.g., 2 hidden layers, 256 neurons) that converge reliably without it. The Pilot Network was introduced in the paper "Volume Feature Rendering for Fast Neural Radiance Field Reconstruction". It was designed to address convergence issues observed when scaling up the neural network size in the VFR framework. The authors hypothesized that the failure was due to the integration of features from all samples (including empty space) in the early training stage, which prevented the model from finding correct geometry. The Pilot Network was tested on the NeRF synthetic dataset, specifically the 'ship' scene, which was prone to convergence failure. name: Importance-Driven Visualization Model
head: Importance-Driven Visualization
body: The Importance-Driven Visualization Model is a framework that dynamically adjusts visual representation based on computed feature importance to resolve occlusion and maximize perceptible information. It replaces viewpoint-independent classification with a pipeline of importance specification, compositing, and sparseness representation. It differs from siblings like Geometric Buffers (G-buffers) and Volume Illustration by focusing on a unified pipeline of importance specification, compositing, and sparseness representation rather than specific shading or edge-detection techniques. The framework operates on the principle that visual clarity is improved when less important features are made transparent or desaturated, while important features remain opaque and saturated. The core mechanism involves three stages: 1. Importance Specification: Computing a scalar importance value for each voxel or region. 2. Compositing: Integrating the importance values into the rendering pipeline to modulate the contribution of samples. 3. Sparseness Representation: Adjusting the visual density of the representation (e.g., opacity, color saturation) based on the importance level. The importance value is a scalar in the range [0, \text{max}]. Typical visualization levels use specific importance thresholds (e.g., 0, 0.1, 0.7, max) to define distinct layers of sparseness. The model supports automatic specification of importance based on feature classification or user-steered assignment to segmented objects. Saliency-based Opacity Modulation is an illustrative volume rendering technique that dynamically adjusts voxel opacity based on computed spatial importance (saliency) values to guide viewer attention toward salient features, such as boundaries, while suppressing less relevant internal structures. It differs from standard volume rendering by replacing fixed transfer functions with a data-driven modulation pipeline that enhances perceptible information through thresholding and scaling of opacity based on local intensity gradients. See Saliency-based Opacity Modulation. Semantic Shader Augmentation is a technique that automatically extends an input GPU shader program with rule-based rendering functionality, replacing static visualization mappings (such as fixed transfer functions) with dynamic mappings defined by semantic rules and fuzzy membership functions. It solves the problem of rigid, hard-coded semantic layers by allowing arbitrary existing shaders to be dynamically augmented with the capability to evaluate illustration rules, enabling domain experts to interactively explore semantic mappings without programming skills. Unlike the original semantic-layers approach where rule-based functionality is hard-coded a priori, or UberShader/SuperShader which combine pre-coded fragments, this method generates code fragments entirely on the fly, allowing minimal overhead and quick exploration of different semantic mappings for various visualization techniques. See Semantic Shader Augmentation. A system that attempts to predict what kind of illustration a viewer would like to see by using an intent-based approach borrowing from AI knowledge bases. It defines rules that describe communicative intent and uses stylistic decisions that reflect particular goals to generate the actual illustrations. A measure of regional importance for voxels, defined as the magnitude of the gradient of the obscurance field. It highlights edges, occlusion variations, and corners. The saliency S(p) for a voxel p is computed as: S(p) = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} where A, B, C are components of the obscurance gradient estimated by 4D linear regression: A = \sumk w(k)O(k)x(k), \quad B = \sumk w(k)O(k)y(k), \quad C = \sumk w(k)O(k)z(k) Here, k iterates over voxels in a 5^3 neighborhood centered at p, w(k) is the distance between p and k, O(k) is the obscurance of voxel k, and x(k), y(k), z(k) are the components of the vector from p to k. The resulting saliency is scaled to [0, 1]. It is used to select the best viewpoints by maximizing visible saliency and to enhance visualization by modifying the transfer function (opacity modulation) based on saliency. Regulation of dot density in stipple rendering based on the normalized absolute spatial importance map, where higher importance leads to denser dots or white regions. The density of the dots is modulated by the spatial importance map. Two user-defined parameters are used: a threshold t above which everything is rendered white, and a factor f that regulates the density scale. Additionally, a random value r(s) is generated for each sample s in the ray casting. The Importance-Driven Visualization Model was introduced by Ivan Viola and M. Eduard Gröller. It was implemented in the VolumeShop tool for interactive direct volume illustration, supporting multi-object rendering, 3D painting segmentation, stylized rendering, smart visibility, and labeling. The model addresses the problem of occlusion in 3D visualization, where important features are often hidden by less important ones. Traditional techniques classify features independently of the viewpoint, limiting the ability to reveal important structures. The model allows for automatic specification of importance based on feature classification or user-steered assignment. name: Saliency-based Opacity Modulation
head: Opacity Modulation via Spatial Importance, Saliency-guided Enhancement
body: Saliency-based Opacity Modulation is an automated technique that enhances volume visualization by modifying voxel opacity based on computed saliency values to guide viewer attention. It solves occlusion and visual clutter by making less important regions transparent while preserving or enhancing the visibility of salient parts. Unlike static transfer functions, this method is data-driven, relying on spatial importance maps to determine which features deserve visual prominence. It builds on the Importance-Driven Visualization Model by implementing the compositing stage where importance values directly modulate the optical density of samples. The method operates by computing a spatial importance map for the volume data and using these values to scale the original opacity of each voxel during rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original volume dataset V, original opacity transfer function A(z), spatial importance map \Delta D(z), and modulation parameters (thresholds tl, th and factors kl, kh). S1 also supports a single binary threshold parameter. Output: Rendered image with modulated opacity A'(z). Data Structures: Spatial Importance Map: A 3D grid of the same dimensions as the volume data, where each voxel z stores a scalar value \Delta D(z) representing local intensity variation. The absolute value |\Delta D(z)| is normalized to the range [0, 1]. Parameters: tl: Low threshold for absolute spatial importance. th: High threshold for absolute spatial importance. kl: Factor regulating modulation for importance < tl. kh: Factor regulating modulation for importance > th. S1 uses a single saliency threshold of 0.2 to separate transparent voxels from preserved/enhanced ones. Steps: 1. Compute Spatial Importance: Calculate the spatial importance map \Delta D(z) for the volume, typically using an unsharp mask filter. 2. Normalize: Normalize |\Delta D(z)| to the range [0, 1]. 3. Modulate Opacity: For each voxel z, compute the new opacity A'(z) based on the original opacity A(z) and the importance value |\Delta D(z)| using the piecewise function from S2: A'(z) = \begin{cases} A(z) \cdot kl \cdot |\Delta D(z)| & \text{if } |\Delta D(z)| < tl \\ A(z) \cdot kh \cdot |\Delta D(z)| & \text{if } |\Delta D(z)| > th \\ A(z) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Alternatively, a simpler binary thresholding approach can be used: If |\Delta D(z)| < 0.2, set A'(z) = 0 (transparent). If |\Delta D(z)| \ge 0.2, set A'(z) = A(z) (preserve) or A'(z) = 2 \cdot A(z) (enhance). 4. Render: Perform standard volume raycasting using the modulated opacity values A'(z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, val)) def boxblur3d(volume, radius=1): dimsx = len(volume) dimsy = len(volume[0]) dimsz = len(volume[0][0]) result = [[[0.0 for in range(dimsz)] for in range(dimsy)] for in range(dimsx)] for x in range(dimsx): for y in range(dimsy): for z in range(dimsz): sumval = 0.0 count = 0 for dx in range(-radius, radius + 1): for dy in range(-radius, radius + 1): for dz in range(-radius, radius + 1): nx = clamp(x + dx, 0, dimsx - 1) ny = clamp(y + dy, 0, dimsy - 1) nz = clamp(z + dz, 0, dimsz - 1) sumval += volume[nx][ny][nz] count += 1 result[x][y][z] = sumval / count return result def subtractarrays(a, b): dimsx = len(a) dimsy = len(a[0]) dimsz = len(a[0][0]) return [[[a[i][j][k] - b[i][j][k] for k in range(dimsz)] for j in range(dimsy)] for i in range(dimsx)] def absolutevalues(arr): dimsx = len(arr) dimsy = len(arr[0]) dimsz = len(arr[0][0]) return [[[abs(arr[i][j][k]) for k in range(dimsz)] for j in range(dimsy)] for i in range(dimsx)] def maxelement(arr): m = arr[0][0][0] for i in range(len(arr)): for j in range(len(arr[0])): for k in range(len(arr[0][0])): if arr[i][j][k] > m: m = arr[i][j][k] return m def dividearrays(arr, scalar): dimsx = len(arr) dimsy = len(arr[0]) dimsz = len(arr[0][0]) return [[[arr[i][j][k] / scalar for k in range(dimsz)] for j in range(dimsy)] for i in range(dimsx)] def createzeroslike(arr): dimsx = len(arr) dimsy = len(arr[0]) dimsz = len(arr[0][0]) return [[[0.0 for in range(dimsz)] for in range(dimsy)] for in range(dimsx)] def computemodulatedopacity(volumedata, originalopacity, tl, th, kl, kh): """ Computes modulated opacity based on spatial importance. Args: volumedata: 3D list of intensity values. originalopacity: 3D list of original opacity values. tl: Low threshold for importance. th: High threshold for importance. kl: Factor for low importance. kh: Factor for high importance. Returns: modulatedopacity: 3D list of new opacity values. """ # Step 1: Compute spatial importance (unsharp masking) blurredvolume = boxblur3d(volumedata, radius=1) diff = subtractarrays(volumedata, blurredvolume) absdiff = absolutevalues(diff) maxval = maxelement(absdiff) if maxval > 0: importancemap = dividearrays(absdiff, maxval) else: importancemap = absdiff # Step 2: Modulate opacity dimsx = len(volumedata) dimsy = len(volumedata[0]) dimsz = len(volumedata[0][0]) modulatedopacity = createzeroslike(volumedata) for x in range(dimsx): for y in range(dimsy): for z in range(dimsz): val = importancemap[x][y][z] if val < tl: modulatedopacity[x][y][z] = originalopacity[x][y][z] kl val elif val > th: modulatedopacity[x][y][z] = originalopacity[x][y][z] kh val else: modulatedopacity[x][y][z] = originalopacity[x][y][z] return modulatedopacity A dynamic focus+context technique that modulates voxel opacity based on the distance from a central reference point, inspired by the angular velocity of a viscous fluid rotating around its center. It solves the problem of occlusion in volume rendering by making voxels further from the center more transparent, thereby revealing inner structures during rotation or zooming interactions. Unlike static saliency methods, it adapts opacity in real-time to user interaction, specifically distinguishing between global rotation (center-based) and local zooming (focus-based). See Radial Opacity Change. This method computes a 3D spatial importance map by subtracting the original volume intensity values from a low-pass filtered (blurred) version of itself, effectively creating an unsharp mask. It captures salient boundary and separability information to modulate color and opacity in illustrative volume rendering, distinguishing itself from radiance-based saliency methods by relying solely on input intensity, which allows it to be computed as a preprocessing step independent of lighting and transfer functions. See Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking. A technique to modify visual prominence by controlling optical properties (color and opacity) based on the level of sparseness. It sets itself apart from siblings like Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking by directly altering the saturation and transparency of ray samples rather than just the opacity or spatial weighting, ensuring that sparse objects recede visually while dense objects remain prominent. See Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation. Smart Visibility is a category of illustrative visualization techniques that extends traditional light-propagation-based visibility by incorporating high-level abstractions of human cognition, such as object relevance and viewer pre-knowledge. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies solely on optical depth and occlusion, Smart Visibility explicitly handles semantic importance to ensure relevant data remains visible even when geometrically occluded by less important structures. See Smart Visibility. Modulation of voxel color based on the spatial importance map to emphasize boundaries, using either raw importance values or absolute importance values. The color I' is computed as I' = I + \Delta D \cdot \lambda for raw values or I' = I + |\Delta D| \cdot \lambda for absolute values, where I is the original color, \Delta D is the importance value, and \lambda is a modulation factor. Typical \lambda values are -10, 0, 10, 20 for raw values and -5, 0, 5, 10 for absolute values. A pitfall is that with raw values and positive \lambda, the image becomes darker because most importance values are negative; with absolute values, darkening and brightening effects are reversed because all values are positive. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In, the method was applied to CT head and body models. The modulation allows for interactive adjustment of parameters like kl and kh. Strengths: Effectively emphasizes boundaries and structural details. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the spatial importance map. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The concept of saliency-based modulation in volume rendering was introduced in the context of obscurance-based rendering frameworks. The specific implementation using spatial importance maps derived from intensity filtering was proposed by Ruiz, Boada, Feixas, and Sbert in 2010. The work builds on earlier ideas of importance-driven visualization and interactive volume illustration. name: Radial Opacity Change
head: Angular velocity metaphor opacity, Distance-based opacity modulation
body: Radial Opacity Change is an illustrative volume rendering technique that modulates voxel opacity based on radial distance from a reference point to create a focus+context effect during user interaction. It reveals inner structures by making peripheral voxels more transparent, inspired by the physics of viscous rotation. Inputs: Voxel position \vec{P}{voxel} in object space. Reference center position \vec{P}{center}. Style function S(t), a scalar representing interaction intensity (e.g., angular velocity). Optional focus point \vec{P}{focus} for zooming semantics. Outputs: Modulated opacity \alpha{voxel}. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Standard volume grid access is assumed. Steps: 1. Calculate the Euclidean distance \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) from the voxel to the reference center. 2. Retrieve the interaction intensity S(t). 3. Compute the modulated opacity using the exponential decay formula. Formulas: For standard rotation or center-based modulation: \alpha{voxel} = e^{-S(t) \cdot \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center})} For zooming interaction, where the transparency gradient shifts to a user-defined focus point: \alpha{voxel} = e^{-S(t) \cdot \max(0, \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) - \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{focus}))} Parameters: S(t): Style function controlling modulation strength. \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}): Distance from voxel to center. \vec{P}{focus}: Initial point of interaction on the object for zooming. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeradialopacity(voxelpos, centerpos, stylefunction, focuspos=None): dx = voxelpos[0] - centerpos[0] dy = voxelpos[1] - centerpos[1] dz = voxelpos[2] - centerpos[2] rhocenter = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if focuspos is None: exponent = -stylefunction rhocenter else: fx = voxelpos[0] - focuspos[0] fy = voxelpos[1] - focuspos[1] fz = voxelpos[2] - focuspos[2] rhofocus = math.sqrt(fxfx + fyfy + fzfz) distancediff = rhocenter - rhofocus if distancediff < 0: distancediff = 0 exponent = -stylefunction distancediff alpha = math.exp(exponent) return alpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If S(t) and \rho are large, the exponent underflows to -\infty, yielding \alpha{voxel}=0. This is expected behavior. Boundary Conditions: The formula assumes \vec{P}{center} is well-defined. For non-convex or disconnected volumes, the geometric center may lie outside the data, producing unintuitive transparency gradients. Zooming Logic: The \max(0, \rho{center} - \rho{focus}) term ensures voxels closer to the focus point than the center receive zero exponent (opacity 1), leaving context untouched while revealing inner parts near the focus. Radial Opacity Change (Zooming) is an illustrative volume rendering technique that reveals inner structures by modulating voxel opacity based on the distance from a user-defined focus point, rather than the distance from the volume center. Unlike its sibling Radial Opacity Change, which uses angular velocity and distance from the center to create a "tunnel" effect during rotation, this method shifts the transparency gradient to follow the user's interaction point, allowing for detailed inspection of specific regions while maintaining context elsewhere [14595-radial-opacity-change-zooming.md]. Depth Opacity-Modulation is a technique to ensure visibility of voxels at the back of an atomic structure by modulating opacity based on depth, preventing self-occlusion from hiding rear features. It is chosen when rendering complex atomic structures where rear features are frequently occluded by front features. Formula: \alphav = \begin{cases} Z(v), & \text{if } Z(v) \le 1 \\ 1, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where Z(v) = \alphas \cdot G(gv) \cdot r^{dv - d{min}(s)} Parameters: \alphav: Opacity of voxel v. \alphas: Seed opacity value for the atomic structure s, provided by a genetic algorithm. G(gv): Monotonically-increasing gradient magnitude opacity-modulation function mapping gradient magnitudes gv to opacity-modulation factors. dv: Depth value of voxel v. d{min}(s): Minimum depth of all voxels in the atomic structure s. r: Depth opacity-modulation rate, controlling the influence of voxel depth in modulation. Pitfalls: Voxels with high depth values (back side) are assigned high opacity to ensure visibility even if occluded by low depth voxels (front side). Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel/sample, involving basic arithmetic and exponential evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per voxel; no additional large data structures are required. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Standard GPU/CPU exponential evaluation applies. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Performance scales linearly with voxel/sample count. Strengths: Effective for dynamic focus+context visualization during interaction; naturally reveals inner structures without complex preprocessing. Limitations: The "angular velocity" metaphor may not intuitively map to all interaction types (e.g., panning); the choice of center point can be arbitrary for complex shapes. When to use: When the goal is to dynamically reveal internal structures during rotation or zooming in a volume visualization. When not to use: When precise quantitative analysis of outer structures is required, as they are intentionally made transparent. The Radial Opacity Change technique was proposed by Sikachev, Rautek, Bruckner, and Gröller in 2010 as part of a dynamic focus+context framework for volume rendering. It is inspired by the metaphor of a viscous fluid rotating around its center, where particles at the border have the highest speed and are candidates to disappear. The method was designed to aid users in exploring data efficiently and detecting unknown features during interaction. It is often used in conjunction with DVR-MIP interpolation to enhance the visual feedback during user interaction. name: Radial Opacity Change (Zooming)
body: Radial Opacity Change (Zooming) is an illustrative volume rendering technique that reveals inner structures by modulating voxel opacity based on the distance from a user-defined focus point during zooming interactions. Unlike its parent Radial Opacity Change, which uses angular velocity and distance from the center to create a tunnel effect during rotation, this method shifts the transparency gradient to follow the user's interaction point, allowing detailed inspection of specific regions while maintaining context elsewhere. Inputs and Outputs Input: Volume dataset V, camera parameters, user interaction point \vec{P}{focus} (initial point of interaction on the object), and a scaling factor S(t). Output: Rendered image with modulated opacity. Data Structures Volume Data: Standard 3D grid of scalar values. Focus Point: A 3D vector \vec{P}{focus} representing the location in world or object space where the user is focusing. Algorithm For each voxel \vec{P}{voxel} along the viewing ray: 1. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the voxel to the rendering area center \vec{P}{center}: \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) = \| \vec{P}{voxel} - \vec{P}{center} \| 2. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the voxel to the focus point: \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{focus}) = \| \vec{P}{voxel} - \vec{P}{focus} \| 3. Compute the radial difference: \Delta \rho = \max(0, \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{center}) - \rho(\vec{P}{voxel}, \vec{P}{focus})) 4. Apply exponential attenuation to determine the effective opacity: \alpha{voxel} = e^{-S(t) \cdot \Delta \rho} Parameters \vec{P}{focus}: The initial point of interaction on the object. This point defines the center of the "zoom" effect. S(t): A scaling factor that controls the strength of the opacity modulation. It may be constant or vary with time/interaction. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls If \vec{P}{focus} is outside the volume, the distance calculations still hold, but the effect may be unintuitive. Precision issues may arise if \vec{P}{voxel} and \vec{P}{focus} are very close, leading to \Delta \rho \approx 0 and thus \alpha{voxel} \approx 1. The term \max(0, \dots) ensures that opacity is only reduced when the voxel is closer to the focus point than to the center, preventing unintended brightening of outer layers. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computezoomopacity(voxelpos, centerpos, focuspos, scalefactor): distcenter = norm(voxelpos - centerpos) distfocus = norm(voxelpos - focuspos) deltarho = max(0.0, distcenter - distfocus) return exp(-scalefactor deltarho) This variant extends the Maximum Intensity Display (MIDA) technique by modulating only the opacity contribution based on importance measurements, rather than applying the maximum operator to both color and opacity. It accumulates colors and opacities along rays as in DVR but modulates opacity when a local maximum is found. The modulation is driven by importance measurements derived from gradient magnitudes, depth, intensity information, or a combination of these values. This approach aims to enhance depth perception and reveal the arrangement of rendered structures with minimum loss of information. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(N) per frame, where N is the number of voxels or samples, as it requires computing distances for each voxel. Memory: O(1) additional memory per voxel for storing the focus point and intermediate distance calculations. Measured Performance Not given in the sources. Scaling The method scales linearly with the number of voxels. Performance may be impacted by the computational cost of distance calculations on large volumes. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Allows for detailed inspection of specific regions without losing context. Effective for revealing inner structures near the focus point. Limitations: The loss of information is a key issue, as modifying opacity may conceal some information that is worth preserving. The effectiveness depends on the choice of \vec{P}{focus} and S(t). When to Use Use when the user needs to inspect specific inner structures of a volume while maintaining a sense of the overall context. Suitable for interactive exploration where the focus point changes frequently. When Not to Use Not suitable when preserving all information is critical, as opacity modulation may hide details. Less effective if the focus point is not well-defined or if the volume has no clear inner/outer structure. The Radial Opacity Change (Zooming) technique was introduced in the paper "Dynamic Focus + Context for Volume Rendering". It is part of a broader effort to enhance depth perception and reveal inner structures in volume visualization. The MIDA extension, described in "Enhanced perception in volume visualization", further refines this approach by integrating importance-based opacity modulation.
