name: Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking
head: Gaussian Blur Difference Map, Intensity Filtering, Intensity-based Saliency Map, Spatial Importance Map Computation, Unsharp Masking for Volume
body: This method computes a 3D spatial importance map by subtracting the original volume intensity values from a low-pass filtered (blurred) version of itself, effectively creating an unsharp mask. It captures salient boundary and separability information to modulate color and opacity in illustrative volume rendering, distinguishing itself from radiance-based saliency methods by relying solely on input intensity, which allows it to be computed as a preprocessing step independent of lighting and transfer functions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar volume model V: \mathbb{N}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}, where \mathbb{Z} represents the scalar intensity values of the voxels. Output: A spatial importance map \Delta D, a 3D volume of the same dimensions as V, containing signed values representing boundary saliency. Data Structures Volume Data: Stored as a 3D array of floating-point values for computation. Gaussian Kernel: A 1D array of normalized weights sampled from the Gaussian function, clamped to a specific radius. Parameters Radius (R): The spatial extent of the Gaussian kernel in voxels. Typical values used in implementations are 5 and 10. Standard Deviation (\sigma): Controls the spread of the Gaussian blur. It is defined as one-third of the radius: \sigma = R / 3. Formulas The spatial importance map is computed as: \Delta D = G V - V where G V is the Gaussian blur of the volume. The 1D Gaussian function is defined as: G(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}} where x is the distance from the origin and \sigma is the standard deviation. In 3D, the Gaussian kernel G is the product of three 1D Gaussians, one for each axis. Steps 1. Preprocessing: Convert the input volume data V to floating-point values. 2. Kernel Generation: Determine the kernel radius R and calculate \sigma = R / 3. Clamp the Gaussian kernel at a distance of 3\sigma from the center, as values further than this are negligible. Sample the 1D Gaussian function at the center of each voxel within the radius, then normalize the weights so that they sum to 1. 3. Separable Filtering: Compute the blurred volume G V by exploiting the separability of the Gaussian function. This requires three consecutive 1D convolutions: convolve V with the 1D kernel along the X-axis, then convolve the result along the Y-axis, and finally convolve that result along the Z-axis. 4. Subtraction: Compute the spatial importance map \Delta D by subtracting the original volume from the blurred volume for each voxel: \Delta D[i, j, k] = (G V)[i, j, k] - V[i, j, k]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computespatialimportancemap(volume: list[list[list[float]]], radius: int) -> list[list[list[float]]]: """ Computes the spatial importance map using unsharp masking via separable Gaussian filtering. Args: volume: 3D list of floats representing the input volume V. radius: Integer radius R for the Gaussian kernel. Returns: 3D list of floats representing the spatial importance map Delta D. """ # 1. Prepare volume data (assumed already float) # 2. Generate 1D Gaussian Kernel sigma = radius / 3.0 kernelsize = 2 radius + 1 kernel = [] sumweights = 0.0 for x in range(-radius, radius + 1): weight = (1.0 / math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi sigma sigma)) math.exp(-(x x) / (2.0 sigma sigma)) kernel.append(weight) sumweights += weight # Normalize kernel so it sums to 1 kernel = [w / sumweights for w in kernel] # 3. Separable Filtering dimx = len(volume) dimy = len(volume[0]) dimz = len(volume[0][0]) # Allocate intermediate volumes vxy = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] vxyz = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] vblur = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] # Convolve along X-axis for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): for x in range(dimx): sumval = 0.0 for k in range(-radius, radius + 1): xneighbor = x + k if xneighbor < 0: xneighbor = 0 elif xneighbor >= dimx: xneighbor = dimx - 1 sumval += volume[xneighbor][y][z] kernel[k + radius] vxy[x][y][z] = sumval # Convolve along Y-axis for x in range(dimx): for z in range(dimz): for y in range(dimy): sumval = 0.0 for k in range(-radius, radius + 1): yneighbor = y + k if yneighbor < 0: yneighbor = 0 elif yneighbor >= dimy: yneighbor = dimy - 1 sumval += vxy[x][yneighbor][z] kernel[k + radius] vxyz[x][y][z] = sumval # Convolve along Z-axis for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): sumval = 0.0 for k in range(-radius, radius + 1): zneighbor = z + k if zneighbor < 0: zneighbor = 0 elif zneighbor >= dimz: zneighbor = dimz - 1 sumval += vxyz[x][y][zneighbor] kernel[k + radius] vblur[x][y][z] = sumval # 4. Subtraction deltad = [[[0.0] dimz for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): deltad[x][y][z] = vblur[x][y][z] - volume[x][y][z] return deltad Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Voxels: Boundary voxels have non-zero importance values because the blurred volume smooths boundaries, creating intensity differences compared to the original. Implementation must handle boundary conditions (e.g., clamping) during convolution. Memory Usage: Using radiance instead of intensity would require significantly more memory. This method uses original intensity values to minimize memory requirements and remain independent of the transfer function and lighting. Sign Interpretation: Positive values in \Delta D indicate voxels near boundaries with higher density material (intensity increased in blur relative to original), while negative values indicate boundaries with lower density material (intensity decreased in blur relative to original). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: CT Body (256×256×415) with radius 5: Total time 335.05 ms (1D filter: 20.85 ms, Subtraction: 18.03 ms). CT Head (512×512×297) with radius 10: Total time 1570.10 ms. Salmon (336×173×511) with radius 10: Total time 617.24 ms. Strengths: Interactive rates achievable with GPU implementations (CUDA); independent of lighting and transfer functions; low memory footprint compared to radiance-based methods. Limitations: Relies on intensity values rather than radiance or gradient-based metrics. When to use: As a preprocessing step for illustrative volume rendering to modulate color and opacity based on boundary saliency. The method was proposed by Marc Ruiz, Imma Boada, Miquel Feixas, and Mateu Sbert from the Graphics and Imaging Laboratory, Universitat de Girona, Spain. It extends the spatial importance function \Delta D proposed by Luft [LCD06] to 3D volumes. The approach was presented in the context of interactive volume illustration, aiming to enhance perceptual quality and interpretation by modulating color and opacity based on boundary saliency. It contrasts with methods like Tao et al. [TLB09] that use radiance, arguing for the efficiency and preprocessing capability of using intensity. name: Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation
head: Color an Opacity Modulation, Color and Opacity Modulation, Sparseness-guided Modulation
body: A technique to modify visual prominence by controlling optical properties (color and opacity) based on the level of sparseness. It sets itself apart from siblings like Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking by directly altering the saturation and transparency of ray samples rather than just the opacity or spatial weighting, ensuring that sparse objects recede visually while dense objects remain prominent. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Pre-computed sparseness value s for each object/region (where low s indicates dense/important, high s indicates sparse/less important). Input: Initial color C{init} and opacity \alpha{init} for each ray sample, resulting from local rendering steps (shading and compositing). Output: Modulated color C{mod} and opacity \alpha{mod} used in global compositing. Data Structures: Sparseness value: Scalar float s \in [0, 1] (normalized). Color: RGB vector C = [R, G, B]. Opacity: Scalar float \alpha \in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Convert Color to HSV: Convert the initial color C{init} from RGB to HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) space to isolate saturation. 2. Modulate Saturation: Adjust the saturation component S based on sparseness s. Sparse objects (high s) receive low saturation (approaching gray), while dense objects (low s) maintain or amplify saturation. Formula: S{mod} = f(s, S{init}). Note: The exact function f is not specified in the sources. 3. Modulate Opacity: Adjust opacity \alpha based on sparseness s. Increasing sparseness makes the object more transparent to reveal underlying data. Formula: \alpha{mod} = g(s, \alpha{init}). Note: The exact function g is not specified in the sources. 4. Convert Back to RGB: Convert the modulated HSV color [H, S{mod}, V] back to RGB to get C{mod}. 5. Apply Smooth Transitions: Ensure smooth transitions between different levels of sparseness to prevent misinterpretations caused by abrupt visual changes within the same object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modulatecolorandopacity(Cinit, alphainit, sparseness): """ Modulates color and opacity based on sparseness. Args: Cinit: Initial color as RGB tuple (0.0-1.0) alphainit: Initial opacity (0.0-1.0) sparseness: Sparseness value (0.0=dense, 1.0=sparse) Returns: Cmod: Modulated color as RGB tuple alphamod: Modulated opacity """ # Step 1: Convert RGB to HSV H, Sinit, V = rgbtohsv(Cinit) # Step 2: Modulate Saturation # Sparse objects (high sparseness) get low saturation (gray) # Dense objects (low sparseness) maintain or amplify saturation # Note: Exact function f is not specified in sources # Implementation detail: Use a linear or sigmoidal decay Smod = Sinit (1.0 - sparseness) # Clamp to valid range Smod = max(0.0, min(1.0, Smod)) # Step 3: Modulate Opacity # Increasing sparseness makes object more transparent # Note: Exact function g is not specified in sources # Implementation detail: Linear decay alphamod = alphainit (1.0 - sparseness) # Clamp to valid range alphamod = max(0.0, min(1.0, alphamod)) # Step 4: Convert HSV back to RGB Cmod = hsvtorgb(H, Smod, V) # Step 5: Smooth transitions are handled by the continuous nature of sparseness # and the smooth functions f and g return Cmod, alphamod def rgbtohsv(rgb): """Standard RGB to HSV conversion.""" r, g, b = rgb maxc = max(r, g, b) minc = min(r, g, b) diff = maxc - minc if diff == 0: h = 0.0 elif maxc == r: h = 60.0 (((g - b) / diff) % 6) elif maxc == g: h = 60.0 (((b - r) / diff) + 2) else: h = 60.0 (((r - g) / diff) + 4) v = maxc s = diff / maxc if maxc != 0 else 0.0 return h, s, v def hsvtorgb(h, s, v): """Standard HSV to RGB conversion.""" c = v s x = c (1 - abs((h / 60.0) % 2 - 1)) m = v - c if h < 60: r, g, b = c, x, 0 elif h < 120: r, g, b = x, c, 0 elif h < 180: r, g, b = 0, c, x elif h < 240: r, g, b = 0, x, c elif h < 300: r, g, b = x, 0, c else: r, g, b = c, 0, x return (r + m, g + m, b + m) Parameters: Sparseness threshold: Not given in the sources. Saturation modulation function: Not given in the sources. Opacity modulation function: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Changing only saturation does not increase the visibility of occluded objects; color and opacity must be changed simultaneously. Different visual appearances within the same object can cause misinterpretations; smooth transitions between different levels of sparseness must be applied. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray sample, as it involves simple arithmetic operations and color space conversions. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Described as a "very simple and fast method". Strengths: Directly controls visual prominence; highly saturated colors attract focus more than gray colors. Limitations: Requires pre-computed sparseness values; smooth transitions are necessary to avoid misinterpretations. When to use: When the goal is to enhance visual prominence by making sparse objects less visible and dense objects more prominent. When not to use: When occlusion of important objects is a concern and only saturation is changed. Origin: Introduced in the context of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR). History: Part of the IDVR framework developed by Thurner et al.. Usage: Used in volume visualization to guide viewer attention by modifying transfer functions based on sparseness. name: Smart Visibility
body: Smart Visibility is a category of illustrative visualization techniques that extends traditional light-propagation-based visibility by incorporating high-level abstractions of human cognition, such as object relevance and viewer pre-knowledge. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies solely on optical depth and occlusion, Smart Visibility explicitly handles semantic importance to ensure relevant data remains visible even when geometrically occluded by less important structures. Smart Visibility is not a single algorithm but a set of principles and techniques for modifying visual representations to emphasize relevant data. It operates by altering the visibility determination process to account for semantic relevance rather than just physical occlusion. Inputs: Volumetric dataset or polygonal mesh representing the scene. Viewer pre-knowledge or semantic importance map defining the relevance of individual objects or regions. Camera view parameters. Outputs: Modified visual representation where important objects are emphasized, potentially through artificial cuts, deformations, or transparency adjustments. Data Structures: Not specified in the sources. Implementation requires a mechanism to store object relevance/importance values, typically associated with voxels or mesh primitives. Steps: 1. Determine Relevance: Assign a relevance score to individual objects or data regions based on user intent, domain knowledge, or automated saliency metrics. 2. Apply Cognitive Rules: Modify the visibility calculation to override standard occlusion based on relevance. If an important object is occluded by a less important one, the occluding object is rendered with increased transparency or removed to allow the important object to shine through. 3. Exploit Pre-knowledge (Cut-aways/Deformations): For objects with known shapes, apply local modifications such as artificial cuts or spatial deformations to reveal inner structures. This relies on the viewer's mental model to complete the object from partial information, such as cut-aways along symmetry axes. 4. Enforce Illustration Rules: Apply specific rules for section views and cut-away views to maintain clarity: Distinguish inside and outside objects. Represent section views as the intersection of two half-spaces. Ensure cut-outs consist of a single hole in the outside object. Ensure interior objects are visible from any viewing angle. Apply transparency fall-off close to edges of transparent objects. Ensure faces of transparent objects never shine through other transparent objects. Ensure objects occluded by two transparent objects do not shine through. Parameters: Relevance threshold: Determines which objects are considered "important" enough to override occlusion. Not given in the sources. Cut-away extent: The depth or area of artificial cuts. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simple Visibility Calculation: A common pitfall is relying solely on light propagation and occlusion, which hides important structures behind less important ones. Smart Visibility must explicitly handle relevance to avoid this. Ambiguity: Over-modification (e.g., excessive cut-aways) may lead to loss of spatial context or confusion about the object's overall shape. Volumetric Clipping: The source notes that algorithms for cut-away views were applied to polygonal data and are "generally applicable in computer graphics," but does not provide specific volumetric clipping algorithms. Implementation for volumes requires adapting these polygonal rules to voxel-based rendering, potentially via transfer function modulation or ray-marching modifications. A technique involving artificial cuts to reveal inner structures, relying on viewer pre-knowledge. Chosen when inner details of a symmetrical or complex object are critical. See Spatial Importance Map via Unsharp Masking for a related saliency-based approach. Represented by the intersection of half-spaces, used to inspect internal structures. Chosen for cross-sectional analysis. See Sparseness-based Color and Opacity Modulation for opacity modulation alternatives. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the complexity of the relevance calculation and the rendering technique used (e.g., ray marching with modified opacity). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for relevance/importance maps if not pre-computed. Strengths: Enhances interpretability by ensuring critical data is visible; leverages human cognitive strengths (pattern completion, attention guidance). Limitations: Requires semantic information or viewer pre-knowledge; may introduce artificial artifacts (cuts, deformations) that do not represent physical reality; primarily defined for polygonal data in the source, requiring adaptation for volumes. When to Use: When the goal is illustrative communication of specific features rather than photorealistic representation; when viewer attention needs to be guided to specific structures. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy of occlusion is required; when semantic relevance is unknown or ambiguous. Smart Visibility was introduced as part of illustrative visualization techniques in scientific visualization, particularly for medicine and science. It draws inspiration from technical illustrations (e.g., cut-aways, exploded views) and applies these high-level abstractions to computer graphics. The concept emphasizes that visibility should be determined not just by light propagation but by the relevance of objects and the viewer's cognitive abilities. The specific rules for cut-away and section views were developed for polygonal data but are considered generally applicable to computer graphics, including volumetric data. name: Voxel Saliency
head: Saliency map
body: Voxel Saliency is a feature importance metric for volume data defined as the magnitude of the gradient of the obscurance field. It identifies regions of high perceptual importance, such as edges, occlusion variations, and corners, by measuring how rapidly obscurance changes across a local neighborhood. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on direct intensity gradients or semantic labels, Voxel Saliency is derived from volumetric shadowing information (obscurance), making it particularly effective for highlighting structural boundaries in complex, self-occluding datasets. It serves as the core importance specification mechanism in the Importance-Driven Visualization Model, enabling viewpoint selection and transfer function modulation. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset V. The precomputed obscurance field O, where O(k) is the obscurance value for voxel k. Outputs: A scalar saliency map S, where S(p) \in [0, 1] for each voxel p. Data Structures: Obscurance Field: A 3D array of floating-point values, same dimensions as the input volume. Saliency Map: A 3D array of floating-point values, same dimensions as the input volume. Parameters: Neighborhood Size: A cubic neighborhood of 5^3 voxels centered at the query voxel p. (Note: A 3^3 neighborhood was used in [NCKG00], but 5^3 yields smoother results). Scaling: Linear scaling to [0, 1] per data volume. Algorithm: 1. Compute Obscurance: Calculate the obscurance O(k) for all voxels k in the volume. 2. Iterate Voxels: For each voxel p in the volume: a. Define the neighborhood \mathcal{N}p as the set of voxels k within a 5^3 cube centered at p. b. Initialize gradient components A = 0, B = 0, C = 0. c. For each voxel k \in \mathcal{N}p: i. Calculate the vector components \vec{d}{pk} = (x(k), y(k), z(k)) from p to k. ii. Calculate the distance weight w(k) between voxels p and k. iii. Accumulate components: A \leftarrow A + w(k) \cdot O(k) \cdot x(k) B \leftarrow B + w(k) \cdot O(k) \cdot y(k) C \leftarrow C + w(k) \cdot O(k) \cdot z(k) d. Compute the saliency magnitude: S(p) = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2} 3. Normalize: For the specific volume dataset, scale the map to [0, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computevoxelsaliency(obscurancefield, dims): """ Computes voxel saliency as the magnitude of the obscurance gradient. obscurancefield: 3D list of lists of lists of floats, O(k). dims: tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) of the volume dimensions. Returns: 3D list of lists of lists of floats, S(p) scaled to [0, 1]. """ # Initialize output saliency map saliencymap = [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] # Precompute neighborhood offsets for a 5x5x5 cube (radius 2) offsets = [] for dx in range(-2, 3): for dy in range(-2, 3): for dz in range(-2, 3): offsets.append((dx, dy, dz)) # Compute raw saliency for each voxel p for px in range(dims[0]): for py in range(dims[1]): for pz in range(dims[2]): A = 0.0 B = 0.0 C = 0.0 for dx, dy, dz in offsets: kx, ky, kz = px + dx, py + dy, pz + dz # Boundary check if not (0 <= kx < dims[0] and 0 <= ky < dims[1] and 0 <= kz < dims[2]): continue # Vector components from p to k xk, yk, zk = dx, dy, dz # Obscurance at k Ok = obscurancefield[kx][ky][kz] # Weight w(k) is the distance between p and k wk = math.sqrt(xk2 + yk2 + zk2) # Accumulate gradient components A += wk Ok xk B += wk Ok yk C += wk Ok zk # S(p) = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + C^2) saliencymap[px][py][pz] = math.sqrt(A2 + B2 + C2) # Normalize to [0, 1] per data volume maxsaliency = 0.0 for px in range(dims[0]): for py in range(dims[1]): for pz in range(dims[2]): if saliencymap[px][py][pz] > maxsaliency: maxsaliency = saliencymap[px][py][pz] if maxsaliency > 0: for px in range(dims[0]): for py in range(dims[1]): for pz in range(dims[2]): saliencymap[px][py][pz] /= maxsaliency return saliencymap The XS Map is a combined importance map used in perceptual rendering of participating media. It integrates the Saliency map (S) with an Extinction map (X) to guide selective rendering. The combination is defined as XS(wx, ws, op), where wx and ws are weighting coefficients and op is the combination operator. The default configuration uses equal weighting (wx=0.5, ws=0.5) and an additive operator (+) to preserve all weighted features. A key limitation is that the XS Map fails to identify areas of strong multiple scattering around light sources, leading to poor sampling and visible artifacts in those regions. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is scale-dependent; the saliency value depends on the size of the neighborhood considered. Strengths: Effectively highlights structural edges, occlusion variations, and corners in volumetric data. Limitations: Does not account for light scattering artifacts around sources, which can cause visible artifacts if used alone. Usage: Primarily used for automatic viewpoint selection (maximizing visible saliency) and for modulating transfer functions (opacity/color) to enhance salient features. Voxel Saliency was proposed in the Obscurance-based Volume Rendering Framework. It adapts the concept of mesh saliency [LVJ05] to volumetric data. The gradient estimation technique is based on the 4D linear regression method proposed in [NCKG00]. The method emphasizes that obscurance, representing occlusion information, varies perceptually at edges and corners, making its gradient a suitable saliency measure. name: Ghosting and Cutaway Techniques
head: Cutaway views, Ghosting
body: Ghosting and Cutaway Techniques are illustrative volume rendering methods that resolve occlusion by selectively suppressing or removing foreground objects to reveal interior structures of interest. Unlike standard clipping which discards context, these methods maintain spatial awareness through opacity modulation (ghosting) or explicit visual cues. They distinguish themselves from Context-Preserving Volume Rendering by using discrete object separation (Selection, Ghost, Background) rather than continuous opacity modulation based on shading intensity. The family operates on a three-object logical model: Selection (the object of interest), Ghost (the original position of the selection, often moved), and Background (the occluding environment). 1. Object Decomposition: The volume is conceptually split into these three sets. 2. Occlusion Handling: Cutaways remove the Background partially or fully in regions occluding the Selection or Ghost. Ghosting reduces the Background opacity in occluding regions to preserve edge cues and spatial context. 3. Visual Conventions: Auxiliary geometry clarifies the relationship between Ghost and Selection: Boxes provide orientation cues, Arrows depict translation between positions, and Fans indicate alternative depictions. 4. Rendering Strategy: Efficient implementation avoids costly per-voxel importance compositing by using static importance functions. Feature Halos reinforces depth perception by darkening and increasing opacity in regions just outside strong volumetric features, obscuring background elements. It distinguishes itself by generating these effects directly during the illumination pass using local spatial properties (gradient orientation relative to view and neighbors), rather than relying on post-processing or explicit surface extraction. The method is inherently view-dependent, ensuring features do not cast halos on themselves. Context-Preserving Volume Rendering (CPVR) selectively reduces opacity in less important data regions to visualize interior structures while preserving exterior context. It solves the problem of context loss inherent in conventional clipping techniques by modulating sample opacity based on shading intensity, gradient magnitude, distance to the eye point, and previously accumulated opacity. Unlike clipping planes which remove context information, CPVR retains it by making homogeneous areas (high lighting intensity) transparent, allowing users to inspect the interior of an object without hiding occluded objects. Exact Projection Full Opacity is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that simplifies visual output by identifying a single primary front object and optionally one significant background object, blending them based on density and distance thresholds rather than performing full front-to-back accumulation. It differs from standard front-to-back compositing by skipping the accumulation of intermediate samples, storing only the first significant object (primary) and potentially one background object, then blending them directly to create a stylized, illustrative result. Multi-object volume rendering with ghosting is a technique for visualizing inter-penetrating volumetric objects by decomposing a scalar field into three distinct logical objects: selection, ghost, and background, allowing independent control of appearance and spatial transformation. It solves the problem of occlusion in complex scenes by selectively reducing opacity in occluding regions to preserve features such as edges, aiding mental reconstruction of structures and spatial location. Unlike Cutaways and Ghosting which may remove occluding regions completely, this method allows smooth control from no ghosting (opacity not reduced) to full cutaway (occluding structures completely suppressed). It sets itself apart from single-pass multi-object compositing by using three separate rendering passes to avoid computational overhead and dynamic branching penalties. Cutaways remove occluding objects to reveal structures of interest, using a simplified three-object setup (Background, Ghost, Selection) with static importance functions to skip costly importance compositing. Definition: A technique where the occluding object is cut out to reveal the structure of interest, determined by an importance function. Step: In VolumeShop's simplified three-object setup, the importance function is statically defined to skip costly importance compositing, allowing efficient implementation. Cutaways are performed only on the background and can be independently defined for ghost and selection. Definition: Boxes: 3D bounding boxes providing cues on position and orientation. Useful during design but distracting during presentation. Arrows: Depict translation between ghost and selection (original to current position). Used to suggest movement or insertion. Fans: A connected pair of shapes (rectangles or circles) indicating a more detailed or alternative depiction. Constructed by connecting screen-space bounding rectangles of ghost and selection. Step: Control arrow curvature using screen-space depth difference to avoid very short arrows when ghost and selection project to nearby positions, creating bent arrows. The concepts of cutaways and ghosting originate from illustrative practices in information visualization and technical drawing. Viola et al. introduced importance-driven volume rendering as a general framework for determining which objects to cut. VolumeShop later provided an interactive system for direct volume illustration, implementing these concepts with a simplified three-object model to enable efficient real-time interaction. The techniques are applied in contexts such as surgical procedures and assembly instructions to clarify spatial relationships. Illustrative Focus+Context Approaches in Interactive Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.4230/dfu.sciviz.2010.136, fetched 2026-10-26 (book) VolumeShop: An Interactive System for Direct Volume Illustration, https://doi.org/10.1109/vis.2005.135, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Feature Halos
head: Auxiliary volume halos, Feature Halos Effect, Halo Effects, Null Halos
body:
Feature Halos is an illustrative volume rendering technique that enhances depth perception by generating dark, opaque regions around structures of interest, thereby obscuring background elements that would otherwise cause visual clutter. Unlike standard photorealistic rendering, this method uses view-dependent darkening and opacity increases in planes orthogonal to the viewing direction to create a visual separation around features, making foreground structures stand out more clearly. The method operates during the illumination/compositing pass of volume rendering. It computes a halo intensity value for each voxel based on the spatial relationship between that voxel and its neighbors, specifically targeting empty regions adjacent to strong features. Input: Volume data V (scalar field). View direction vector V (normalized). Parameters: k{hpe} (halo potential exponent, typically 1.0), k{hse} (halo separation exponent, typically 2.0). Output: Modified color C' and opacity \alpha' for each voxel, where halos are darker and more opaque than the base volume rendering. Volume Grid: Standard 3D array of scalar values. Gradient Field: 3D array of 3D vectors, computed via finite differences. Halo Field: 3D array of floats, storing the computed halo influence h(i) for each voxel. 1. Compute Gradient Field: Calculate the gradient 
ablaf(P) at every voxel P in the volume. 2. Initialize Halo Field: Create a halo field H of the same dimensions as the volume, initialized to zero. 3. Compute Halo Influence: For each voxel i at position Pi: a. Initialize h(i) = 0. b. Iterate over a specified neighborhood of voxels n at positions Pn. c. For each neighbor n: i. Calculate the displacement vector D = Pi - Pn and distance d = \|D\|. ii. Calculate the normalized direction u = D / d. iii. Compute the halo potential hn for the neighbor: hn = \left( 
ablaf(Pn) \cdot u ight)^{k{hpe}} (1 - 
ablaf(Pn) \cdot V)^{k{hse}} iv. Add the distance-weighted influence to the current voxel's halo field: h(i) \leftarrow h(i) +  rac{hn}{d^2} d. Weight the accumulated halo influence by the complement of the current voxel's gradient magnitude to restrict halos to less interesting (low-gradient) regions: h(i) \leftarrow h(i) \cdot (1 - \|
ablaf(Pi)\|) 4. Apply Visual Appearance: For each voxel i, adjust the base color C and opacity \alpha computed from the volume transfer function: a. Decrease brightness: C' = C \cdot (1 - k{dark} \cdot h(i)), where k{dark} is a scalar controlling the darkness of the halo. b. Increase opacity: \alpha' = \min(1.0, \alpha + k{opaque} \cdot h(i)), where k{opaque} is a scalar controlling the opacity increase. 5. Composite: Perform standard volume compositing (e.g., front-to-back or back-to-front) using the modified C' and \alpha' values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computefeaturehalos(volume, viewdirection, khpe=1.0, khse=2.0): """ Compute feature halos for volume rendering. Args: volume: 3D numpy array of scalar values. viewdirection: 3D numpy array, normalized view vector. khpe: Halo potential exponent. khse: Halo separation exponent. Returns: halofield: 3D numpy array of halo intensities. """ # Step 1: Compute gradient field grad = np.gradient(volume) # Returns tuple of 3 arrays (dz, dy, dx) gradientmagnitude = np.sqrt(sum(g2 for g in grad)) maxgrad = np.max(gradientmagnitude) normalizedgradmag = gradientmagnitude / maxgrad if maxgrad > 0 else gradientmagnitude # Step 2: Initialize halo field halofield = np.zeroslike(volume) # Neighborhood radius (specified neighborhood) radius = 1 neighborhoodindices = np.arange(-radius, radius + 1) vx, vy, vz = viewdirection # Step 3: Compute halo influence for z in range(volume.shape[0]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[2]): hi = 0.0 currentgradmag = normalizedgradmag[z, y, x] for dzoff in neighborhoodindices: for dyoff in neighborhoodindices: for dxoff in neighborhoodindices: if dzoff == 0 and dyoff == 0 and dxoff == 0: continue nz, ny, nx = z + dzoff, y + dyoff, x + dxoff if not (0 <= nz < volume.shape[0] and 0 <= ny < volume.shape[1] and 0 <= nx < volume.shape[2]): continue dxvec, dyvec, dzvec = dxoff, dyoff, dzoff distsq = dxvec2 + dyvec2 + dzvec2 dist = np.sqrt(distsq) ux, uy, uz = dxvec / dist, dyvec / dist, dzvec / dist gradnz, gradny, gradnx = grad[0][nz, ny, nx], grad[1][nz, ny, nx], grad[2][nz, ny, nx] dotproduct = gradnz ux + gradny uy + gradnx uz costheta = gradnz vx + gradny vy + gradnx vz # Halo potential formula from potential = max(0.0, dotproduct) khpe viewfactor = (1.0 - costheta) khse hn = potential viewfactor hi += hn / distsq halofield[z, y, x] = hi (1.0 - currentgradmag) return halofield def applyhalos(basecolor, baseopacity, halofield, kdark=0.5, kopaque=0.5): """ Apply halo effects to color and opacity. Args: basecolor: RGB array. baseopacity: Float. halofield: Float halo intensity. kdark: Scalar for brightness reduction. kopaque: Scalar for opacity increase. Returns: modifiedcolor, modifiedopacity """ modifiedcolor = basecolor (1.0 - kdark halofield) modifiedopacity = np.minimum(1.0, baseopacity + kopaque halofield) return modifiedcolor, modifiedopacity k{hpe}: Controls how directly the neighbor's gradient must be oriented toward the current location. Typical value: 1.0. k{hse}: Controls how tightly halos are kept in the plane orthogonal to the view direction. Typical value: 2.0. k{dark}: Scalar controlling the amount of brightness reduction in halo regions. Not given in the sources. k{opaque}: Scalar controlling the amount of opacity increase in halo regions. Not given in the sources. Self-Obscuration: Since halos are view-dependent and computed based on the relationship between neighbors and the current voxel, features do not cast halos on themselves. This avoids the self-obscuration issues present in other methods like Line Integral Convolution (LIC). Gradient Normalization: The gradient magnitude must be normalized to [0,1] before being used in the weighting term (1 - \|
ablaf(Pi)\|) to ensure consistent behavior across different datasets. Boundary Conditions: Neighbors outside the volume bounds must be handled, typically by ignoring them or padding with zeros. Performance: The naive implementation is O(N \cdot R^3) where N is the number of voxels and R is the neighborhood radius. Optimization via separable filters or GPU parallelization is recommended for large volumes. A variant that uses a dual-layer splat presentation: an inner core for the primary structure and an outer halo for softer support. The inner core is rendered as the primary measured structure, while the outer halo is rendered as a softer support shell. The intensity of the halo can be tuned using a "Halo Strength" slider, which can be reduced to zero. A technique that enhances depth perception by processing the volume model in view-aligned slices to generate halos around structures of interest, using hue changes rather than just brightening/darkening. The steps are: 1) Classify structures to highlight based on density, direction, and position, and place seeds around them; 2) Generate the halo region of influence by filtering the seeds; 3) Assign colors and opacities to the halo regions and composite them with the volume rendering. Unlike previous techniques that only brighten or darken color, this approach considers hue changes. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R^3) for a naive implementation, where N is the number of voxels and R is the neighborhood radius. Can be optimized to O(N) with separable filters or GPU acceleration. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the gradient field and halo field. Measured Performance: In medical volume rendering (e.g., liver and kidneys), halos make foreground structures stand out more clearly. Strengths: Enhances depth perception, reduces visual clutter from background elements, view-dependent (no self-obscuration), applicable to any type of data. Limitations: View-dependent (halos change with camera angle), requires gradient computation, may obscure fine details if parameters are not tuned correctly. When to Use: When depth perception is critical and background clutter is a problem, especially in medical or scientific visualization. When Not to Use: When photorealism is required, or when performance is extremely constrained and gradient computation is prohibitive. Feature Halos were introduced in non-photorealistic rendering literature. The technique builds on earlier work by Interrante and Grosch who applied halos to flow visualization. It is part of the broader family of Ghosting and Cutaway Techniques [8497-ghosting-and-cutaway-techniques.md]. name: Context-Preserving Volume Rendering
head: CPVR, Context-preserving clipping, Feature-aware clipping, Illustrative Context-Preserving Volume Rendering
body: Context-Preserving Volume Rendering (CPVR) is a technique that selectively reduces opacity in less important data regions to visualize interior structures while preserving exterior context, serving as an alternative to conventional clipping. Unlike clipping techniques which remove context information, this method retains context by making homogeneous areas (high lighting intensity) transparent while keeping feature-rich regions (contours) visible. It is controlled by two user-specified parameters, \kappat and \kappas, which provide an intuitive interface for interactively browsing through the volume without the need for tedious opacity tuning in the transfer function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A continuous volumetric scalar field f(Pi), a viewing ray, an eye point E, and two user parameters \kappat and \kappas. Output: Accumulated color ci and opacity \alphai for each pixel along the ray. Data Structures: Scalar Field: f(Pi), the value at sample position Pi. Gradient: \mathbf{g}(Pi) = \nabla f(Pi), the gradient vector at Pi. Normalized Gradient Magnitude: \|\mathbf{g}(Pi)\|, normalized to [0, 1], where 0 is the lowest gradient magnitude in the dataset and 1 is the highest. Shading Intensity: s(Pi), computed via a lighting model (e.g., Phong-Blinn). Accumulated Values: \alpha{i-1} (opacity) and c{i-1} (color) from previous samples along the ray. Parameters: \kappat: Controls the depth of the clipping effect. Higher values reveal more of the volume interior. Typical values: 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0. \kappas: Controls the sharpness of the cut between attenuated and visible regions. Higher values result in sharper cuts. Typical values: 0.4, 0.6, 0.8. Extension: \kappat and \kappas can be made data-dependent by replacing them with \kappat \cdot \lambdat(f{Pi}) and \kappas \cdot \lambdas(f{Pi}), where \lambdat, \lambdas \in [0, 1] are scalar-value-dependent functions. Steps: 1. Normalize Gradient Magnitude: Compute \|\mathbf{g}(Pi)\| normalized to [0, 1]. 2. Normalize Distance: Compute the distance from the eye point E to the sample Pi, normalized to [0, 1], where 0 is closest to the eye and 1 is farthest. 3. Compute Shading Intensity: Calculate s(Pi) using the chosen illumination model. 4. Compute Base Opacity: Determine the base opacity contribution \alpha{tf}(f{Pi}) from the transfer function based on the scalar value f{Pi}. 5. Compute Exponent Term: Calculate E{term} = \kappat \cdot s(Pi) \cdot (1 - d{norm}) \cdot (1 - \alpha{i-1}). 6. Compute Final Opacity: Calculate \alpha(Pi) using the context-preserving formula: \alpha(Pi) = \alpha{tf}(f{Pi}) \cdot \|\mathbf{g}(Pi)\|^{(E{term})^{\kappas}}. If \kappat = 0, the opacity remains unmodified (normal direct volume rendering). If \kappas = 0, the opacity is directly modulated by the gradient magnitude. 7. Approximate Exponentiation: To reduce computational cost, approximate x^{(a \cdot y)^b} using Schlick's approximation: x^{(a \cdot y)^b} \approx \frac{x \cdot (b + a \cdot y - a \cdot b \cdot y)}{a \cdot y + b \cdot (a \cdot x \cdot y)} This requires 4 multiplications, 2 additions, 1 subtraction, and 1 division. 8. Accumulate: Update accumulated opacity and color using front-to-back rendering: \alphai = \alpha{i-1} + \alpha(Pi) \cdot (1 - \alpha{i-1}) ci = c{i-1} + c(Pi) \cdot \alpha(Pi) \cdot (1 - \alpha{i-1}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def contextpreservingvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, eyepoint, kappat, kappas): """ Renders a single ray using Context-Preserving Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the viewing ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the viewing ray (normalized). volumedata: Object providing scalar values f(P), gradients g(P), shading s(P), and transfer functions. eyepoint: 3D vector, position of the camera eye. kappat: float, controls clipping depth. kappas: float, controls cut sharpness. Returns: color: 3D vector, accumulated color. opacity: float, accumulated opacity. """ alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Determine ray bounds for distance normalization [0, 1] mindist = 0.0 maxdist = volumedata.maxdistancealongray(rayorigin, raydirection) for samplepos in volumedata.samplesalongray(rayorigin, raydirection): # 1. Get scalar value and gradient fval = volumedata.scalar(samplepos) gradvec = volumedata.gradient(samplepos) # 2. Normalize gradient magnitude to [0, 1] gradmag = volumedata.normalizegradientmagnitude(gradvec) # 3. Compute shading intensity s(Pi) shading = volumedata.shadingintensity(samplepos, gradvec) # 4. Get base opacity from transfer function alphatf = volumedata.transferfunctionopacity(fval) # 5. Compute normalized distance to eye [0, 1] disttoeye = length(samplepos - eyepoint) distnorm = (disttoeye - mindist) / (maxdist - mindist) if maxdist > mindist else 0.0 # 6. Compute the exponent term Eterm eterm = kappat shading (1.0 - distnorm) (1.0 - alphaacc) # 7. Compute final opacity alpha(Pi) using Schlick's approximation for x^(ay)^b x = gradmag ay = eterm b = kappas if b == 0: alphasample = alphatf x elif ay == 0: alphasample = alphatf else: num = x (b + ay - ay b) den = ay + b (ay x) if den == 0: alphasample = alphatf x else: alphasample = alphatf (num / den) # 8. Get color contribution c(Pi) colortf = volumedata.transferfunctioncolor(fval) colorsample = colortf shading # 9. Accumulate alphaacc = alphaacc + alphasample (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc = coloracc + colorsample alphasample (1.0 - alphaacc) # Break if fully opaque if alphaacc >= 1.0: break return coloracc, alphaacc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exponentiation Cost: The most costly part is exponentiation. Schlick's approximation is used to reduce cost from a 15% increase to a 5% increase compared to normal direct volume rendering. Loss of Shape Cues: Reducing opacities generally causes a loss of shape cues due to reduced shading contributions per sample. This method mitigates this by preserving context and using lighting-driven feature classification. Semi-transparent Regions: Structures located behind semi-transparent regions appear more opaque due to the term (1 - \alpha{i-1}) in the exponent. Distance Effect: The effect of the model decreases as distance from the eye increases, due to the term (1 - \|Pi - E\|). Time Complexity: Adds approximately 5% computational overhead compared to normal direct volume rendering when using Schlick's approximation for exponentiation. Without approximation, the cost increase is 15%. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory requirements beyond standard volume rendering buffers and gradient/shading pre-computation if applicable. Strengths: Preserves context information unlike clipping. Simplifies transfer function specification; users mainly assign colors and use \kappat, \kappas for visibility. Intuitive user control with two parameters. Unifying extension of direct volume rendering and gradient-magnitude opacity-modulation. Limitations: May cause loss of shape cues if opacities are reduced too much. Requires shading computation, which adds complexity compared to unshaded DVF. When to Use: Medical imaging (e.g., contrast-enhanced CT scans like angiography, tooth, hand, leg, torso) to visualize internal structures without segmentation. When the user wants to browse through the volume interactively. When Not to Use: When strict quantitative opacity values are required, or when shading is not desired/appropriate for the data. Origin: Proposed by Bruckner et al. in 2004 in the paper "Illustrative Context-Preserving Volume Rendering". Also cited as Bruckner 2006 in some contexts. History: Inspired by techniques from technical illustration (ghosting). It serves as an alternative to conventional clipping techniques. Usage: Integrated into high-quality software volume ray casting systems. Can be used in GPU-based ray casting implementations. Used in medical imaging for contrast-enhanced CT scans. Related Work: Builds on direct volume rendering and gradient-magnitude opacity-modulation. Related to clipping techniques. Advanced illumination and view-selection techniques for volume rendering and its application to medical imaging, http://hdl.handle.net/10803/371154, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) (PDF) Illustrative Context-Preserving Volume Rendering., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220778350IllustrativeContext-PreservingVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Illustrative Context-Preserving Volume Rendering, https://www.cg.tuwien.ac.at/research/publications/2005/TR-186-2-05-01/TR-186-2-05-01-Technical%20Report.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Exact Projection Full Opacity
head: Background Object Blending, Full Opacity Rendering, Primary/Background Object Selection
body: Exact Projection Full Opacity is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that simplifies visual output by identifying a single primary front object and optionally one significant background object, blending them based on density and distance thresholds rather than performing full front-to-back accumulation. It differs from standard front-to-back compositing by skipping the accumulation of intermediate samples, storing only the first significant object (primary) and potentially one background object, then blending them directly to create a stylized, illustrative result. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume texture (volumeTexture), a 4D color map texture (colorMap), ray origin (startPos), ray direction (rayDir), near/far clipping planes (tNear, tFar), volume dimensions (volumeDimensions), and boolean flags for lighting (enableLighting) and shadows (enableShadow). Output: A fragment color FragColor (vec4). Data Structures: The method maintains state variables during ray traversal: foundPrimaryObject (bool): Indicates if the front-most significant object has been found. foundBackgroundObject (bool): Indicates if a significant background object has been found. primaryObjectPos, backgroundObjectPos (vec3): World-space positions of the primary and background objects. primaryObjectColor, backgroundObjectColor (vec4): RGBA colors sampled from the color map. primaryObjectDistance, backgroundObjectDistance (float): Ray parameter t values for the objects. primaryObjectDensity (float): Scalar value from the volume texture at the primary object's position. accumulatedColor (vec3): The final blended color. accumulatedAlpha (float): The final blended alpha. Constants: HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD = 0.7: Density value above which front objects obscure back objects. DISTANCETHRESHOLD = 0.5: Distance beyond which back objects are ignored or blended minimally. minDensityThreshold, maxDensityThreshold: Bounds for valid volume data. MAXITERATIONS = 2000: Safety counter to prevent infinite loops. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize foundPrimaryObject = false, foundBackgroundObject = false. Initialize accumulatedColor = vec3(0.0), accumulatedAlpha = 0.0. Initialize primaryObjectPos = vec3(0.0), backgroundObjectPos = vec3(0.0). Initialize primaryObjectColor = vec4(0.0), backgroundObjectColor = vec4(0.0). Initialize primaryObjectDistance = 0.0, backgroundObjectDistance = 0.0. Initialize primaryObjectDensity = 0.0. Initialize iterations = 0. 2. Ray Traversal Loop: While t < tFar and iterations < MAXITERATIONS: a. Sample Position: Calculate samplePos = startPos + rayDir t. b. Boundary Check: If any(lessThan(samplePos, vec3(0.0))) or any(greaterThan(samplePos, vec3(1.0))): Increment t by a small fixed step (e.g., 0.01) or dt. Increment iterations. Continue to next iteration. c. Voxel Traversal (Optional but implied for efficiency): Calculate voxelPos = samplePos volumeDimensions. Determine nextVoxel boundaries based on rayDir signs. Calculate dtVec components: dtVec.x = (rayDir.x > 0.0001) ? (nextVoxel.x - voxelPos.x) / (rayDir.x volumeDimensions.x): tFar dtVec.y = (rayDir.y > 0.0001) ? (nextVoxel.y - voxelPos.y) / (rayDir.y volumeDimensions.y): tFar dtVec.z = (rayDir.z > 0.0001) ? (nextVoxel.z - voxelPos.z) / (rayDir.z volumeDimensions.z): tFar dt = max(min(dtVec.x, min(dtVec.y, dtVec.z)), 0.0001). d. Volume Sampling: val = texture(volumeTexture, samplePos).r. If val < minDensityThreshold or val > maxDensityThreshold: Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. Continue. e. Color Mapping: color = texture(colorMap, val). If color.a < 0.05: Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. Continue. f. Primary Object Identification: If !foundPrimaryObject: Set foundPrimaryObject = true. Set primaryObjectPos = samplePos. Set primaryObjectColor = color. Set primaryObjectDistance = t. Set primaryObjectDensity = val. If val > HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD or color.a > 0.9: Break loop (high opacity/density obscures background). Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. Continue. g. Background Object Identification: If foundPrimaryObject and !foundBackgroundObject and color.a > 0.6: Set foundBackgroundObject = true. Set backgroundObjectPos = samplePos. Set backgroundObjectColor = color. Set backgroundObjectDistance = t. Calculate distanceBetweenObjects = backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance. If primaryObjectDensity > 0.5 or distanceBetweenObjects > DISTANCETHRESHOLD: Set foundBackgroundObject = false (effectively ignore background). Break loop (found primary and potentially background). h. Advance Ray: Increment t by dt. Increment iterations. 3. Fallback: If !foundPrimaryObject: Set FragColor = vec4(0.0). Return. 4. Lighting and Blending: a. Primary Color: If enableLighting: normal = calculateNormal(primaryObjectPos). primaryColor = calculateLighting(normal, -rayDir, primaryObjectPos, primaryObjectColor.rgb). Else: primaryColor = primaryObjectColor.rgb. b. Initialize Accumulation: accumulatedColor = primaryColor. accumulatedAlpha = primaryObjectColor.a. c. Background Blending (if found): If foundBackgroundObject: Calculate distanceFactor = clamp((backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance) / DISTANCETHRESHOLD, 0.0, 1.0). Calculate densityFactor = clamp(1.0 - primaryObjectDensity / HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD, 0.0, 1.0). Calculate backgroundContribution = min(distanceFactor, densityFactor) 0.7. Calculate backgroundLitColor: If enableLighting: bgNormal = calculateNormal(backgroundObjectPos). backgroundLitColor = calculateLighting(bgNormal, -rayDir, backgroundObjectPos, backgroundObjectColor.rgb). Else: backgroundLitColor = backgroundObjectColor.rgb. Blend: accumulatedColor = mix(accumulatedColor, backgroundLitColor, backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha)). accumulatedAlpha = accumulatedAlpha + backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha). 5. Final Output: FragColor = vec4(accumulatedColor, max(accumulatedAlpha, 0.5)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exactprojectionfullopacity(startPos, rayDir, tNear, tFar, volumeTexture, colorMap, volumeDimensions, enableLighting, enableShadow): # Constants HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD = 0.7 DISTANCETHRESHOLD = 0.5 MAXITERATIONS = 2000 # State foundPrimaryObject = False foundBackgroundObject = False primaryObjectPos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] backgroundObjectPos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] primaryObjectColor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] backgroundObjectColor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] primaryObjectDistance = 0.0 backgroundObjectDistance = 0.0 primaryObjectDensity = 0.0 t = tNear iterations = 0 while t < tFar and iterations < MAXITERATIONS: samplePos = [startPos[i] + rayDir[i] t for i in range(3)] # Boundary check if any(p < 0.0 for p in samplePos) or any(p > 1.0 for p in samplePos): t += 0.01 iterations += 1 continue # Voxel traversal logic for dt voxelPos = [samplePos[i] volumeDimensions[i] for i in range(3)] nextVoxel = [ (voxelPos[0] + 1.0 if rayDir[0] > 0.0 else voxelPos[0] - 1.0), (voxelPos[1] + 1.0 if rayDir[1] > 0.0 else voxelPos[1] - 1.0), (voxelPos[2] + 1.0 if rayDir[2] > 0.0 else voxelPos[2] - 1.0) ] dtVec = [tFar, tFar, tFar] if abs(rayDir[0]) > 0.0001: dtVec[0] = (nextVoxel[0] - voxelPos[0]) / (rayDir[0] volumeDimensions[0]) if abs(rayDir[1]) > 0.0001: dtVec[1] = (nextVoxel[1] - voxelPos[1]) / (rayDir[1] volumeDimensions[1]) if abs(rayDir[2]) > 0.0001: dtVec[2] = (nextVoxel[2] - voxelPos[2]) / (rayDir[2] volumeDimensions[2]) dt = max(min(dtVec[0], min(dtVec[1], dtVec[2])), 0.0001) # Sample volume val = volumeTexture(samplePos) # Simplified texture lookup if val < 0.0 or val > 1.0: t += dt iterations += 1 continue color = colorMap(val) # Simplified color map lookup if color[3] < 0.05: t += dt iterations += 1 continue # Primary Object if not foundPrimaryObject: foundPrimaryObject = True primaryObjectPos = samplePos primaryObjectColor = color primaryObjectDistance = t primaryObjectDensity = val if val > HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD or color[3] > 0.9: break t += dt iterations += 1 continue # Background Object if foundPrimaryObject and not foundBackgroundObject and color[3] > 0.6: foundBackgroundObject = True backgroundObjectPos = samplePos backgroundObjectColor = color backgroundObjectDistance = t distanceBetweenObjects = backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance if primaryObjectDensity > 0.5 or distanceBetweenObjects > DISTANCETHRESHOLD: foundBackgroundObject = False break t += dt iterations += 1 if not foundPrimaryObject: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Lighting Primary if enableLighting: normal = calculateNormal(primaryObjectPos) # Standard normal calculation primaryColor = calculateLighting(normal, [-r for r in rayDir], primaryObjectPos, primaryObjectColor[:3]) # Standard lighting else: primaryColor = primaryObjectColor[:3] accumulatedColor = primaryColor accumulatedAlpha = primaryObjectColor[3] if foundBackgroundObject: # Lighting Background if enableLighting: bgNormal = calculateNormal(backgroundObjectPos) # Standard normal calculation backgroundLitColor = calculateLighting(bgNormal, [-r for r in rayDir], backgroundObjectPos, backgroundObjectColor[:3]) # Standard lighting else: backgroundLitColor = backgroundObjectColor[:3] distanceFactor = max(0.0, min(1.0, (backgroundObjectDistance - primaryObjectDistance) / DISTANCETHRESHOLD)) densityFactor = max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - primaryObjectDensity / HIGHDENSITYTHRESHOLD)) backgroundContribution = min(distanceFactor, densityFactor) 0.7 accumulatedColor = [accumulatedColor[i] (1.0 - backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha)) + backgroundLitColor[i] backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha) for i in range(3)] accumulatedAlpha = accumulatedAlpha + backgroundContribution (1.0 - accumulatedAlpha) return [accumulatedColor[0], accumulatedColor[1], accumulatedColor[2], max(accumulatedAlpha, 0.5)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The dt calculation uses a small epsilon (0.0001) to avoid division by zero or zero-step traversal. Boundaries: Explicit checks ensure the ray does not sample outside the [0,1] volume space. Degenerate Input: If no primary object is found (empty volume or all values out of range), the output is black. High Density: If the primary object has density > 0.7 or alpha > 0.9, the loop breaks immediately, ignoring any potential background objects. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than standard front-to-back volume rendering because it terminates early. The loop breaks after finding the primary object (if high density/opacity) or after finding the primary and one background object. It does not process all samples along the ray. Memory Complexity: Low. It only stores state for two objects (primary and background) rather than accumulating color/alpha for every sample. Strengths: Efficient for illustrative rendering where full volumetric accuracy is not required. It provides a clean separation between foreground and background elements. Limitations: Loses detailed volumetric information from intermediate samples. The blending is heuristic-based (distance and density thresholds) rather than physically based. When to use: When performance is critical and a stylized, non-photorealistic look is desired. When the scene has distinct foreground and background objects that need to be highlighted. When not to use: When physically accurate volume visualization is required. When the scene contains many overlapping semi-transparent structures where intermediate accumulation is important. Exact Projection Full Opacity is described in the context of illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering. The method is designed to simplify the visual output by focusing on primary and significant background objects, blending them based on specific criteria rather than full accumulation. viljanvr/VisualNifty, https://github.com/viljanvr/VisualNifty, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-object volume rendering with ghosting
head: Direct multi-object volume visualization, Ghosting, Multi-Pass Rendering Implementation, VolumeShop multi-object rendering
body: Multi-object volume rendering with ghosting is a technique for visualizing inter-penetrating volumetric objects by decomposing a scalar field into three distinct logical objects: Selection (the primary focus), Ghost (the original position of the selection), and Background (the occluding environment). It solves the problem of spatial ambiguity in complex, overlapping structures by allowing independent control of appearance and spatial transformation for each object. Unlike standard volume rendering, it distinguishes itself by using a three-pass rendering strategy with depth-buffer-based occlusion culling to efficiently handle intersections and apply "ghosting" (selective opacity reduction) or "cutaways" (complete suppression) to the background, preserving edge cues and spatial context. Inputs: fV: Scalar-valued volumetric function defined for every point p in space (e.g., CT values). fS: Selection function defined for every point p in space, with values in [0, 1], where 0 means 'not selected' and 1 means 'fully selected'. T: Transformation applied to the selection object (move, rotate, scale). cS, \alphaS: Color and opacity transfer functions for the selection, based on fV(T(p)). cG, \alphaG: Color and opacity transfer functions for the ghost, based on fV(p). cB, \alphaB: Color and opacity transfer functions for the background, based on fV(p). Ghosting factor: User-defined value controlling the degree of ghosting, ranging from no ghosting (opacity not reduced) to full cutaway (occluding structures suppressed). Optional: Depth map of opaque geometry intersections. Outputs: Final color and opacity image with three logical objects composited, respecting intersections and ghosting/cutaway rules. Bricked Memory Layout: Data volumes and selection volumes are stored in a bricked memory layout using reference counting. Subdivision: Volumes are subdivided into small cubes accessed via an index data structure. Redundancy Handling: Redundant bricks are stored only once. Copy-on-Write: Used for handling modifications to shared bricks, particularly for the sparse selection volume, to avoid corrupting other references. Meta Information: Min-max octrees, bounding boxes, and transformations are stored for both volumes and updated on modification to allow quick extraction of tight bounding volumes. Depth Textures: Two depth maps are generated for the ghost and selection bounding volumes, and optionally one for opaque geometry. The method defines three fuzzy selection sets (SS, SG, SB) and three volume sets (VS, VG, VB) based on membership functions \mu: \begin{aligned} \mu{SS}(p) &= fS(T(p)) \\ \mu{SG}(p) &= fS(p) \\ \mu{SB}(p) &= 1 - fS(p) \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} \mu{VS}(p) &= \alphaS(fV(T(p))) \\ \mu{VG}(p) &= \alphaG(fV(p)) \\ \mu{VB}(p) &= \alphaB(fV(p)) \end{aligned} The final object sets (S, G, B) are the intersections of the corresponding selection and volume sets: \begin{aligned} S &= SS \cap VS \\ G &= SG \cap VG \\ B &= SB \cap VB \end{aligned} The final opacity \alpha(p) at point p is defined as the grade of membership in the union of all object sets: \alpha(p) = \mu{S \cup G \cup B}(p) The implementation uses three volume rendering passes with increasing complexity to avoid the computational overhead of single-pass multi-object compositing and dynamic branching. Preprocessing: 1. Extract bounding volumes for background, ghost, and selection by traversing hierarchical data structures. 2. Render the bounding volumes of the ghost and selection into separate depth textures with depth test set to LESS. 3. Filter these depth maps with a large kernel to enable smooth cutaways. 4. (Optional) If opaque geometry intersections are present, generate an additional depth map before the background pass and blend geometry color contributions into the frame buffer. Pass 1: Background 1. Set depth test to LESS and render the bounds of the background object into the depth buffer. 2. Disable depth buffer writes. 3. Set depth test to GREATER. This skips empty space up to the first intersection with the background bounding volume (early-z culling). 4. Render view-aligned slices in back-to-front order. 5. In the fragment program, shade the background object. Pass 2: Ghost 1. Clear the depth buffer. 2. Render the bounding volume of the ghost object with depth test set to GREATER. 3. Disable depth buffer writes. 4. Set depth test to LESS. 5. In the fragment program: Perform shading for both background and ghost objects. Discard fragments whose depth value is greater than or equal to the corresponding value in the selection depth map (effectively cutting out regions containing the selection from the background/ghost view). If cutaways are enabled, modulate the background opacity by the user-defined ghosting factor for fragments whose depth value is greater than or equal to the corresponding value in the ghost depth map. Pass 3: Selection 1. Render the selection bounds into the cleared depth buffer with depth test set to GREATER. 2. Disable depth buffer writes. 3. Set depth test to LESS. 4. Pass two sets of texture coordinates to the fragment program: Unmodified coordinates for background and ghost data access. Transformed coordinates (using T) for selection data access. 5. In the fragment program: Perform shading for background, selection, and ghost objects. Handle intersections (background/selection and ghost/selection) using intersection transfer functions. For cutaways, modulate the background's opacity if the fragment's depth value is greater than or equal to the corresponding values in the ghost or selection depth maps. Visual Conventions: Display auxiliary geometry (boxes, arrows, fans) as 3D objects with correct intersection handling or as overlays. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastmultiobjectghosting(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, volumefV, selectionfS, transformT, tfS, tfG, tfB, ghostingfactor, depthmapghost, depthmapselection): """ CPU raycasting implementation of the three-object ghosting method. Implements front-to-back compositing with depth-map occlusion culling. """ # Initialize compositing state alphaout = 0.0 colorout = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = 0.0 # Step through the ray while t < 1.0 and alphaout < 1.0: p = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] # Depth map occlusion check (simulating GPU depth test) # Assume depthmap stores depth values per pixel; use p[2] as depth proxy depthval = p[2] if depthval >= depthmapselection.get(tuple(p[:2]), float('inf')): t += stepsize continue if depthval >= depthmapghost.get(tuple(p[:2]), float('inf')): # Apply ghosting factor to background opacity when occluded by ghost depth pass # Compute membership functions fVval = volumefV(p) fSval = selectionfS(p) pT = transformT(p) fVTval = volumefV(pT) fSTval = selectionfS(pT) muSS = fSTval muSG = fSval muSB = 1.0 - fSval muVS = tfS.alpha(fVTval) muVG = tfG.alpha(fVval) muVB = tfB.alpha(fVval) # Object opacities alphaS = muSS muVS alphaG = muSG muVG alphaB = muSB muVB # Apply ghosting factor to background if occluded by ghost depth map if depthval >= depthmapghost.get(tuple(p[:2]), float('inf')): alphaB = ghostingfactor # Composite front-to-back alphastep = alphaS + alphaG + alphaB if alphastep > 0: cS = tfS.color(fVTval) cG = tfG.color(fVval) cB = tfB.color(fVval) # Weighted color contribution for this step cstep = [ (alphaS cS[i] + alphaG cG[i] + alphaB cB[i]) / alphastep for i in range(3) ] # Standard front-to-back compositing colorout = [ colorout[i] + cstep[i] alphastep (1.0 - alphaout) for i in range(3) ] alphaout = alphaout + alphastep (1.0 - alphaout) t += stepsize return colorout, alphaout Shared Bricks: Modifications to shared bricks in the bricked memory layout require copy-on-write to avoid corrupting other references to the same data. Performance Scaling: Performance depends heavily on the size of the selection. Non-Intersecting Selections: If the selection does not intersect the background or ghost (checked via bounding box test), a simplified fragment program can be executed in the selection pass. Ghosting vs. Cutaway: Ghosting preserves edge cues by reducing opacity, while cutaways remove occluding regions completely. Time Complexity: The method uses three rendering passes. Complexity Dominance: Complexity is dominated by the selection size. Time Complexity: The method uses three rendering passes. Complexity is dominated by the selection size. If the selection is small, performance is close to conventional slice-based rendering due to early-z culling. Memory Complexity: Uses a bricked memory layout with reference counting and copy-on-write, which is efficient for sparse selection volumes. Requires storage for two additional depth textures (ghost and selection) and their filtered versions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient handling of inter-penetrating objects; preserves spatial context through ghosting; allows smooth control between ghosting and cutaway; leverages hardware early-z culling for performance. Limitations: Performance degrades with large selection sizes; requires careful management of depth maps for smooth cutaways; complex fragment program logic in the selection pass. When to use: When visualizing inter-penetrating volumetric objects where spatial context and edge cues of occluding structures are important. When not to use: When simple, fast visualization of non-intersecting or fully opaque objects is sufficient, or when hardware does not support efficient depth buffering and early-z culling. Origin: The method was introduced in the VolumeShop system, an interactive system for direct volume illustration. History: Developed as part of the VolumeShop project, which aimed to provide illustrative enhancement methods and selective illustration techniques for volumetric data. Usage: Used in medical visualization and scientific data exploration where understanding the spatial relationship between overlapping structures is critical. name: Cutaways and Ghosting
head: Cut-away views, Ghosting, Selective Illustration
body: Cutaways and Ghosting are illustrative volume rendering techniques that selectively suppress or reduce the opacity of occluding background structures to reveal a primary object of interest (Selection). The method employs a three-object logical model (Selection, Ghost, Background) to create "magic views" that aid mental reconstruction of spatial relationships. It sets itself apart from siblings like Feature Halos by explicitly managing occlusion through opacity reduction or removal rather than edge enhancement, and from Context-Preserving Volume Rendering by allowing full suppression (cutaway) rather than just context preservation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset; a user-defined transformation (translation, rotation) for the Selection; a user-defined "Ghosting Degree" parameter \alpha \in [0, 1]; and a lighting transfer function that enhances opacity at contours. Output: A 2D image where the Selection is fully visible, the Ghost is visible in its displaced position, and the Background is occlusion-culled or ghosted. Data Structures: The volume is conceptually decomposed into three sets: 1. Selection (S): The primary object of interest. 2. Ghost (G): The original position or alternative state of the Selection. 3. Background (B): All other data not part of S or G. Rendering Strategy: To avoid costly per-voxel importance compositing, the method uses static importance functions defined by the three-object setup. Steps: 1. Define Selection and Ghost: Identify the voxels belonging to the Selection S. Define the Ghost G as the spatially transformed version of S (e.g., translated). 2. Define Background: Identify voxels belonging to the Background B (all voxels not in S or G). 3. Calculate Ghosting Factor: Determine the opacity reduction for Background voxels based on the user-defined Ghosting Degree \alpha. 4. Apply Occlusion Culling/Reduction: For Cutaways (\alpha = 1): Completely suppress Background voxels that occlude the Selection or Ghost. For Ghosting (0 < \alpha < 1): Reduce the opacity of Background voxels that occlude the Selection or Ghost. The reduction is combined with the opacity-enhancement component of the lighting transfer function to preserve edge cues. For No Ghosting (\alpha = 0): No reduction is applied. 5. Render: Composite the Selection, Ghost, and modified Background. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The effective opacity of a Background voxel is calculated by combining the user-defined ghosting factor with the opacity-enhancement component of the lighting transfer function. Regions with high contour enhancement (edges) are less suppressed during ghosting. Parameters: Ghosting Degree (\alpha): Smoothly controllable from 0 (no ghosting) to 1 (full cutaway). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A visual convention used to indicate a more detailed or alternative depiction of a structure. It consists of a connected pair of shapes (e.g., rectangles or circles) linking the screen-space bounding rectangles of the Ghost and Selection. It is constructed by connecting these bounding boxes in screen space. Time Complexity: Efficient implementation avoids per-voxel importance compositing by using static importance functions, allowing for faster rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the three-object decomposition masks. Strengths: Provides clear spatial context and aids mental reconstruction of structures by preserving edge cues (Ghosting) or removing occlusions (Cutaways). Allows for expressive "magic views". Limitations: Relies on user-defined transformations and may not automatically adapt to complex scene layouts without manual intervention. When to use: When illustrating specific anatomical or mechanical structures where occlusion by surrounding tissue/material hinders understanding. Originated in the context of interactive volume illustration systems, specifically VolumeShop. The method was developed to bridge the gap between scientific visualization and traditional illustration techniques, allowing users to create expressive views that aid in the interpretation of complex 3D data. It is part of the broader family of Illustrative Focus+Context approaches. name: Cutaways
head: Cut-away views
body: Cutaways are an illustrative volume rendering technique where occluding objects are removed to reveal the structure of interest. They solve the problem of visual obstruction in complex volumetric scenes by selectively suppressing background elements. Unlike ghosting, which reduces opacity to preserve spatial context, cutaways completely remove the occluding regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset containing three logical object sets: Selection (object of interest), Ghost (original position of selection), and Background (occluding environment). Output: A rendered image where background voxels are suppressed based on an importance function. Data Structures: The method relies on a static importance function I(\mathbf{x}) defined per voxel \mathbf{x}. In the simplified VolumeShop setup, this function is pre-computed and static to avoid costly per-voxel importance compositing. Steps: 1. Define Importance Function: Assign an importance value to each voxel. The function determines which object (Selection, Ghost, or Background) is subject to the cutaway. 2. Apply Cutaway to Background: For voxels belonging to the Background set, if the importance function indicates the voxel is occluding the Selection or Ghost, its opacity is set to zero (removed). 3. Independent Definition: The cutaway criteria can be defined independently for the Ghost and Selection objects. 4. Render: Composite the remaining voxels using standard volume rendering techniques. Parameters: Importance Function: Static definition used to skip costly compositing. Cutaway Degree: The user can control the degree of cutaway, ranging from no cutaway (full background) to full cutaway (complete suppression of occluding structures). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Static importance functions may lack the nuance of dynamic importance-driven rendering but offer efficiency. Boundaries: Care must be taken to ensure cutaways do not inadvertently remove parts of the Selection or Ghost. A technique to remove portions of Regions of Interest (ROIs) using axis-aligned, surface-aligned, or feature-based (segment-aligned) cuts. It identifies obscuring features and applies cuts to remove them without impinging on ROI geometry. Cut types include axis-aligned (global coordinates), surface-aligned (distances from isosurfaces), and feature-based (segment-aligned). Time Complexity: Efficient implementation due to static importance function, avoiding costly per-voxel importance compositing. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the static importance function. Strengths: Efficient removal of occluding objects; clear revelation of structures of interest. Limitations: Complete removal of background may reduce spatial context compared to ghosting. When to Use: When the primary goal is to reveal internal structures obscured by external objects, and spatial context preservation is secondary. When Not to Use: When maintaining a strong sense of the object's position within the larger scene is critical. Cutaways are frequently found in information visualization and are an important tool employed by illustrators. Viola et al. introduced importance-driven volume rendering, a general framework for determining which object is to be cut using an importance function. VolumeShop's simplified three-object setup allows a static definition of this importance function, enabling efficient implementation. Correa et al. demonstrated the value of using feature data for generating cut-away views of 3-D volumetric data, including axis-aligned, surface-aligned, and feature-based cuts.
