name: Virtual Magic Lantern
head: Magic Lantern metaphor
body: The Virtual Magic Lantern (VML) is an interaction metaphor for volumetric data inspection that uses a virtual right circular cone, guided by a 3D pointer device, to define a region of interest (ROI). Inside this cone, the volume is rendered using a secondary transfer function or shading style, while the exterior uses the primary style, allowing simultaneous visualization of the focal region and its context. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Virtual Magic Window by providing explicit contextual information at the boundary of the ROI, whereas VMW acts as a restricted implementation where the lantern aligns with the viewing direction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volumetric dataset (texture), primary transfer function (TF), secondary transfer function (TF), cone geometry (apex position, axis direction, aperture angle), and camera parameters. Outputs: Rendered image with dual-style visualization. Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture storing voxel values. In the source implementation, resolution is 512 \times 512 \times 512. Cone Parameters: Apex: \mathbf{a} (vec3), position of the pointer device. Axis: \mathbf{d} (vec3), normalized direction vector of the pointer. Aperture: \alpha (float), half-angle of the cone in radians, adjustable via joystick. Algorithm Steps: The method modifies the fragment shader of a classical GPU ray casting algorithm. 1. Initialization: Pass the transfer functions and cone geometry (\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{d}, \alpha) to the GPU. Initialize ray origin and direction based on screen coordinates (e.g., glFragCoord). 2. Ray Casting Loop: For each sample point \mathbf{p} along the ray: a. Sample Volume: Retrieve scalar value v from the volume texture at \mathbf{p}. b. Inclusion Test: Determine if \mathbf{p} lies inside the inspection cone. c. Color Calculation: If inside: Calculate material color \mathbf{c}{in} using the secondary transfer function and shading style. If outside: Calculate material color \mathbf{c}{out} using the primary transfer function and shading style. d. Shading: Apply Phong shading to the selected material color \mathbf{c}. e. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. f. Update: Advance \mathbf{p} along the ray. Point-in-Cone Test: A point \mathbf{p} is inside the cone defined by apex \mathbf{a}, axis \mathbf{d}, and aperture \alpha if the angle between the vector \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a} and the axis \mathbf{d} is less than or equal to \alpha, and \mathbf{v} points in the general direction of \mathbf{d} (dot product positive). Mathematically: \frac{(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}\|} \ge \cos(\alpha) \quad \text{and} \quad (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d} > 0 In practice, to avoid division by zero when \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{a} and improve performance, the test is implemented as: (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d} \ge \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}\| \cos(\alpha) with a guard that \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}\| > \epsilon and (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{d} > 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfragment(glfragcoord): # 1. Calculate Ray (standard raycasting setup) rayorigin, raydirection = calculaterayfromscreen(glfragcoord) # 2. Initialize Compositing acccolor = vec4(0.0) accopacity = 0.0 position = rayorigin # 3. Ray Casting Loop for in range(maxsteps): # Sample Volume v = samplevolume(volumetexture, position) # Inclusion Test vectopoint = position - a dotprod = dot(vectopoint, d) lensq = dot(vectopoint, vectopoint) if lensq > epsilon and dotprod > 0: cosangle = dotprod / sqrt(lensq) isinside = cosangle >= cos(alpha) else: isinside = False # 4. Determine Material Color if isinside: material = applytf(tfinside, v) else: material = applytf(tfoutside, v) # 5. Shading and Compositing shadedcolor = phongshading(material, position) alpha = material.opacity acccolor = acccolor + shadedcolor alpha (1.0 - accopacity) accopacity = accopacity + alpha (1.0 - accopacity) # 6. Update Position position = position + stepsize raydirection return acccolor Helper definitions (standard operations): calculaterayfromscreen generates ray origin/direction from pixel coordinates; samplevolume trilinearly interpolates the 3D texture; applytf maps scalar v to color/opacity via the transfer function; phongshading computes diffuse/specular lighting; vec4, dot, sqrt, cos are standard math/vector operations. Parameters: Aperture Angle: Adjustable via joystick on the Wanda device. Resolution: Tested on 512 \times 512 \times 512 voxel models. Window Size: 900 \times 900 pixels. Samples: Typically 1 sample per voxel for real-time performance, though 2 samples are supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Navigation Misalignment: When navigating through a model, the cone apex (device position) may not point exactly in front of the user, causing the entire volume to be rendered with the primary transfer function if the cone misses the view frustum or relevant data. Solution: Generate the inspection cone with the apex at the observer position while keeping the direction guided by the hand/device. Abrupt Region Changes: The pointed region may change more abruptly than expected if the geometry is closer than supposed. Solution: Place the apex of the cone at a fixed distance back from the device. Performance Penalty: The inclusion test adds a rendering penalty compared to classical ray casting, but real-time framerates are maintained on the tested hardware. A restricted implementation of VML where the virtual lantern aligns with the viewing direction, creating a window. It incurs no performance penalty compared to classical volume ray casting but provides less contextual information at the ROI boundary [11345-virtual-magic-window.md]. Time and Memory Complexity: The method adds a constant-time geometric inclusion test per sample point to the standard ray casting loop. Memory usage: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tests were conducted on a 3.00 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo PC, 8GB RAM, GeForce 8800 GTX (768MB RAM) in a stereo PowerWall system with a 900 \times 900 window. | Model | Samples | RC (fps) | VML (fps) | VMW (fps) | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Feet | 1 | 32 | 17 | 32 | | Feet | 2 | 18.5 | 9.8 | 18.5 | | Manix | 1 | 18 | 13 | 18 | | Manix | 2 | 10 | 6.5 | 10 | | Head | 1 | 28 | 15.3 | 28 | | Head | 2 | 15 | 10 | 15 | | Rips | 1 | 32 | 14.8 | 32 | | Rips | 2 | 18 | 8.4 | 18 | VML incurs a performance penalty compared to classical Ray Casting (RC) and Virtual Magic Window (VMW). VMW has no penalty compared to RC. Framerates drop roughly 40% if the volume covers the whole viewport (close inspection). Disabling stereo rendering doubles framerates. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Intuitive interaction, provides rich contextual information at the ROI boundary, maintains interactive framerates. Limitations: Performance penalty relative to RC, potential for abrupt region changes during navigation, requires 3D pointer device (Wanda) for optimal interaction. When to Use: Immersive stereo systems (PowerWall) for volumetric data inspection. Scenarios requiring simultaneous view of a focal region and its context (e.g., surgery planning, injury diagnosis). When Not to Use: When maximum performance is required and contextual boundary information is not needed, VMW or classical ray casting are preferred. When the hardware is significantly older than the tested GeForce 8800 GTX, as the penalty may become prohibitive. The Virtual Magic Lantern was presented by A. Andujar, M. Fairen, and F. Argelaguet in 2007. It is tailored to facilitate volumetric data inspection, particularly in Virtual Reality setups with large screens. The metaphor is inspired by the historical magic lantern, where a virtual illumination cone provides the focal region. The implementation builds on classical GPU ray casting. name: Virtual Magic Window
head: Magic Window
body: The Virtual Magic Window (VMW) is a volume rendering inspection metaphor that allows users to view a specific region of interest (ROI) within a volumetric dataset through a virtual "window" defined by a 3D pointer device, while the rest of the volume is rendered using a different style or transfer function. It serves as an efficient, restricted implementation of the Virtual Magic Lantern (VML), where the virtual lantern is constrained to align with the viewing direction, effectively creating a window through which the volume is seen. Unlike VML, VMW does not provide contextual information on the boundary of the ROI, but it incurs no performance penalty compared to classical volume ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric dataset, primary transfer function (TF), secondary TF, viewing parameters (camera position, direction), and 3D pointer device state (origin and direction). Output: Rendered image where the ROI is visualized with the secondary TF and the exterior with the primary TF. Data Structures: Ray Start Position Textures: Two textures store the starting positions for ray casting. Texture 1: Stores starting positions for rays inside the ROI. Texture 2: Stores starting positions for rays outside the ROI. Volume Bounding Box: Defines the spatial extent of the volume. Steps: 1. Define ROI: Construct a virtual cone using the origin and direction from the 3D pointer device (e.g., Wanda device). 2. Intersect: Intersect this cone with the volume's bounding box to determine the ROI. 3. Label Rays: Determine which rays cast from the observer pass through the ROI; rays passing through the intersection are labeled "inside", others "outside". 4. Split Ray Initialization: Initialize the input ray directions by splitting the texture storing ray starting positions into two: for rays inside the ROI, initialize starting positions for the outside rays as if they were outside the volume; vice versa for the other texture. 5. Render ROI (Secondary Pass): Perform a classical ray casting pass using the secondary TF for rays identified as lying inside the cone/ROI. 6. Render Exterior (Primary Pass): Perform a second classical ray casting pass using the primary TF for rays lying outside the cone/ROI. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def virtualmagicwindow(volume, primarytf, secondarytf, camera, pointer, bbox): # camera: {origin, direction, right, up, width, height} # pointer: {origin, direction} # bbox: {min: [x,y,z], max: [x,y,z]} # Step 1 & 2: Define ROI by intersecting virtual cone with volume bounding box # Precompute pixel coordinates that fall inside the ROI shape roipixels = set() for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): raydir = normalize(camera.direction + (x - camera.width/2) camera.right + (y - camera.height/2) camera.up) if rayintersectsroi(camera.origin, raydir, pointer.origin, pointer.direction, bbox): roipixels.add((x, y)) # Step 3 & 4: Split ray initialization textures # Texture A: for secondary TF pass (inside ROI) # Texture B: for primary TF pass (outside ROI) # Rays not belonging to the current pass are initialized as "outside volume" to be skipped texa = [[None for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] texb = [[None for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): raydir = normalize(camera.direction + (x - camera.width/2) camera.right + (y - camera.height/2) camera.up) startpos = computeraystart(camera.origin, raydir, bbox) if (x, y) in roipixels: texa[y][x] = startpos texb[y][x] = None # Mark as outside volume to skip else: texa[y][x] = None # Mark as outside volume to skip texb[y][x] = startpos # Step 5: Render ROI with secondary TF imgroi = renderpass(volume, texa, secondarytf) # Step 6: Render Exterior with primary TF imgext = renderpass(volume, texb, primarytf) # Composite: ROI pixels overwrite exterior pixels where valid imgfinal = [[imgext[y][x] for x in range(camera.width)] for y in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): if imgroi[y][x] is not None: imgfinal[y][x] = imgroi[y][x] return imgfinal def rayintersectsroi(rayorigin, raydir, coneorigin, conedir, bbox): # Check if ray passes through the intersection of the cone and bounding box if not rayhitsbbox(rayorigin, raydir, bbox): return False dot = dotproduct(raydir, conedir) return dot > 0.9 # Threshold approximating cone alignment def rayhitsbbox(rayorigin, raydir, bbox): # Standard ray-AABB intersection test tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < bbox.min[i] or rayorigin[i] > bbox.max[i]: return False else: t1 = (bbox.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (bbox.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmax >= 0 and tmin <= tmax def computeraystart(rayorigin, raydir, bbox): # Returns entry point of ray into bounding box; None if no intersection tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < bbox.min[i] or rayorigin[i] > bbox.max[i]: return None else: t1 = (bbox.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (bbox.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return None return [rayorigin[i] + tmin raydir[i] for i in range(3)] def renderpass(volume, texture, tf): # Classical GPU ray casting pass using given texture and transfer function img = [[None for in range(len(texture[0]))] for in range(len(texture))] for y in range(len(texture)): for x in range(len(texture[0])): start = texture[y][x] if start is None: continue color = samplevolumealongray(volume, start, tf) img[y][x] = color return img Parameters: Primary TF: Transfer function for the background/exterior region. Secondary TF: Transfer function for the ROI. Pointer Device: Provides the origin and direction for the virtual cone. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Context: VMW does not provide contextual information on the boundary of the ROI, which can make it harder to understand the spatial relationship of the ROI to the rest of the volume compared to VML. Performance: While VMW incurs no performance penalty with respect to classical volume ray casting, the implementation requires managing two ray casting passes and splitting the ray initialization. Time Complexity: Two passes of classical volume ray casting. The complexity is O(N) where N is the number of pixels, assuming constant time per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two ray start position textures and two intermediate images (or a mechanism to composite on the fly). Measured Performance: The implementation runs in real time and incurs no performance penalty with respect to classical volume ray casting. Strengths: Efficient, simple implementation, intuitive interaction, flexible shading style and region shape without volume deformation. Limitations: Lack of contextual information at the ROI boundary compared to VML. When to Use: When comparing rendering motifs or inspecting a specific region with a different style, and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When contextual information at the boundary of the ROI is important. The Virtual Magic Window (VMW) was introduced as a collateral implementation of the Virtual Magic Lantern (VML) in the paper "The virtual magic lantern". It is based on the Magic Lens metaphor but adapted for volume rendering with a 3D pointer device (Wanda device). The method was designed to be efficient and easy to adapt to GPU ray casting algorithms. The virtual magic lantern, https://doi.org/10.1145/1643928.1643955, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Flow and Trajectory Visualization
head: Flow Visualization, Trajectory Rendering, Flow Volumes
body: Flow and Trajectory Visualization is a family of illustrative volume rendering techniques designed to visualize vector fields and time-varying particle systems by mapping flow data into geometric or volumetric primitives. It solves the problem of visualizing complex fluid dynamics, such as separation, convergence, and recirculation, which are difficult to perceive in standard scalar volume renderings or sequential image sets. This family is distinguished from sibling methods like Geometric Buffers or Illumination and Tone Shading Models by its explicit construction of flow-dependent geometry (arrows or tetrahedra) rather than relying solely on scalar shading or post-processing effects. The family shares the goal of enhancing volume visualization through stylized lighting and feature abstraction. All methods operate on fragment-level data, typically utilizing the volume sample gradient as a proxy for surface normal orientation. They decouple illumination from the physical light transport equation, instead using mathematical functions of the view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. Common inputs include the normalized gradient \nabla fn, light vectors L, and base colors derived from transfer functions. The output is a final color c that combines ambient/gaseous components with directed illumination effects. The framework utilizes four types of properties for enhancement: 1. Volume sample location and value. 2. Local volumetric properties, such as gradient and minimal change direction. 3. View direction. 4. Light information. Volumetric illustration differs from surface-based NPR in several important ways. In surface NPR, surfaces (features) are well-defined, whereas with volumes, feature areas within the volume must be determined through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. Trajectory Arrow Rendering is an illustrative technique that overlays directional arrows on volume renderings of time-varying particle systems to visualize feature movement and provide temporal context within a single static image. Unlike sequential volume renderings, which make it difficult to track features visually, this method integrates pathline geometry into the volumetric depth buffer to highlight flow properties such as separation, convergence, and recirculation. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by explicitly decoupling the representation of particle trajectories from the scalar field density, using a multi-pass approach to ensure arrows are correctly occluded by and blended with the volume interior. It builds on Flow and Trajectory Visualization and differs from sibling methods like Flow Volumes by rendering explicit trajectory geometry rather than volumetric flow representations. Flow Volumes is a technique for visualizing flow fields by generating volumetric primitives (prisms and tetrahedra) from advected streamlines, rendered using volume rendering to simulate the appearance of smoke or dye. It solves the occlusion and sorting issues inherent in rendering semi-transparent stream surfaces by converting the flow into a volume of tetrahedra that can be composited in any order without affecting the final color. Unlike Trajectory Arrow Rendering, which uses discrete glyphs, Flow Volumes provides a continuous, organic representation of the flow's density and structure. step Enhance splatting of modeled clouds by employing line integral convolution to form various types of convoluted and asymmetric textures, mapped on billboards. definition Coloring the flow volume based on the time particles were released (age) to provide a depth cue and visualize flow history. step Particles in dynamic flows record the time they were released. Assign colors to vertices using the recorded release time as a scalar value, similar to other scalar fields like pressure or temperature. usage Demonstrated in Figure 9 with simulated wind data over Indonesia, colored by age after 72 time steps. definition A technique to animate blood flow characteristics by rendering multiple volumes simultaneously: one raw volume with standard shading, and a second volume containing distance information modulated by a time-varying sinusoid to color the first volume. step Sample the second volume (distance data) at the current position: vec4 volumeSample = SampleVolume (volumeIndex, pos); Compute a time-varying sine wave along vessels: float sineVal =.75 + sin (1000.0 volumeSample.x + time float(5.0)) / 4; Multiply the color of the first volume by the sine wave: sampleRGBA.rgb = sineVal; parameter time: Built-in variable representing time, used to offset the sinusoid. volumeSample.x: Contains the distance within vessels between the entry of blood and the current voxel. The concept of visualizing flow using volumetric primitives was introduced by Liao et al. in the paper "Unsteady flow volumes". This work demonstrated the interactive exploration of vector fields by constructing tetrahedral volumes from advected streamlines. The technique has been applied to various datasets, including simulated wind data over Indonesia and aerodynamic data for delta wings with oscillating flaps. The use of trajectory arrows for volume rendering was documented in a survey of cloud modeling and rendering, which cited the work of Yu and Wang. This approach focuses on enhancing the perception of flow direction and structure within volumetric data, such as clouds, by integrating explicit geometric cues. Further extensions include the "Blood Flow Animation" technique described in the context of the PRISM framework. This method utilizes multiple volume rendering passes to animate blood flow in angiographic data, modulating the appearance of the raw volume with a sinusoidal wave derived from distance-to-vessel data. name: Trajectory Arrow Rendering
head: speed lines
body: Trajectory Arrow Rendering is an illustrative technique that overlays directional arrows on volume renderings of time-varying particle systems to visualize feature movement and provide temporal context within a single static image. Unlike viewing sequential volume renderings, which makes it difficult to track features visually, this method integrates pathline geometry into the volumetric depth buffer to highlight flow properties such as separation, convergence, and recirculation. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by explicitly decoupling the representation of particle trajectories from the scalar field density, using a multi-pass approach to ensure arrows are correctly occluded by and blended with the volume interior. Inputs: Time-varying particle system data (positions at current time step and previous time step, or velocity vectors). Arrow width parameter. Minimum pathline length threshold and minimum cluster size. Volume rendering parameters, camera matrices, and final composite image layout: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Final composite image containing the volume rendering with trajectory arrows blended at correct depths. Data Structures: Pathlines representing particle trajectories. Arrow geometry rendered as triangle strips. Frame buffers for arrow color and depth. Steps: 1. Pathline Filtering: Compute pathlines from temporal particle data. Discard pathlines shorter than a preset threshold. Discard clusters with fewer than a preset minimum number of pathlines. 2. Pass 1 (Arrow Geometry): Render arrow geometry to a frame buffer as triangle strips. In the vertex shader, expand the arrow width to ensure it always faces the viewer by rotating the line corresponding to the particle trajectory by the viewing matrix and adding the arrow width to the rotated line. 3. Pass 2 (Background Composition): Render a full-screen quad containing the image of the arrows to a background buffer. 4. Pass 3 (Raycaster): Pass the depth texture of the arrow geometry into the raycaster. Change the ray termination condition to check if the current depth of the sample position along the ray is behind the arrow depth. If the sample is behind the arrow depth, stop the ray and blend the current color with the background image of the arrows. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertrajectoryarrows(particles, viewmatrix, arrowwidth, minlength, minclustersize): # Step 1: Filter Pathlines pathlines = integrateparticles(particles) # Standard temporal integration validpathlines = [p for p in pathlines if length(p) >= minlength] clusters = groupspatially(validpathlines) # Standard spatial clustering validpathlines = [p for c in clusters if len(c) >= minclustersize for p in c] # Step 2: Pass 1 - Render Arrow Geometry to Frame Buffer arrowcolorbuffer = allocatebuffer() arrowdepthbuffer = allocatedepthbuffer() for pathline in validpathlines: start = pathline[0] end = pathline[-1] direction = end - start # Rotate trajectory line by viewing matrix viewdir = transformview(direction, viewmatrix) # Compute perpendicular vector in view plane for billboarding up = vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) if abs(dot(viewdir, up)) > 0.999: up = vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) perp = normalize(cross(viewdir, up)) halfw = arrowwidth / 2.0 # Generate triangle strip vertices by expanding width along perpendicular vertices = [] for i in range(len(pathline) - 1): p1 = pathline[i] p2 = pathline[i+1] vertices.append(p1 + perp halfw) vertices.append(p1 - perp halfw) vertices.append(p2 + perp halfw) vertices.append(p2 - perp halfw) drawtrianglestrip(vertices, arrowcolorbuffer, arrowdepthbuffer) # Step 3: Pass 2 - Render Full Screen Quad backgroundimage = drawfullscreenquad(arrowcolorbuffer) # Step 4: Pass 3 - Volume Raycasting with Depth-Aware Blending finalimage = allocatebuffer() for pixel in finalimage: rayorigin = cameraposition raydirection = computeraydirection(pixel, viewmatrix) accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for t in range(0, maxdepth, stepsize): samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t depthsample = length(samplepos - rayorigin) deptharrow = readdepth(arrowdepthbuffer, pixel) if depthsample > deptharrow: arrowcolor = readcolor(backgroundimage, pixel) accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) + arrowcolor accumulatedalpha break density = readvolume(samplepos) color = applytf(density) alpha = density stepsize accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor (1.0 - alpha) + color alpha accumulatedalpha += alpha finalimage[pixel] = accumulatedcolor return finalimage Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides immediate temporal context in a single image; effectively visualizes flow features without requiring animation. Limitations: Requires pre-computed or real-time pathline generation; filtering parameters are critical and may require tuning to avoid visual clutter or loss of detail. When to use: When analyzing time-varying particle systems or flow fields where static visualization of motion is needed. When not to use: When precise quantitative tracking of individual particles over time is required, or when the volume density itself is the primary focus without need for motion cues. Trajectory Arrow Rendering was introduced by J. Chandler, H. Obermaier, and K. I. Joy in 2013 as part of their work on illustrative rendering of particle systems. It addresses the limitation of standard volume rendering, which only provides information about a single time step, making it difficult to track features in time-varying data. The method was applied to datasets such as the von Karman vortex street and jet flow fields to demonstrate its ability to reveal internal flow structures. name: Flow Volumes
head: Dye Flow Visualization, Prism/Tetrahedron Flow Visualization, Streamline-based Volume Rendering
body: Flow Volumes is a technique for visualizing flow fields by generating volumetric primitives (prisms and tetrahedra) from advected streamlines, rendered using volume rendering to simulate the appearance of smoke or dye. It solves the occlusion and sorting issues inherent in rendering semi-transparent stream surfaces by converting the flow into a volume of tetrahedra that can be composited in any order without affecting the final color. Unlike Trajectory Arrow Rendering, which uses discrete glyphs, Flow Volumes provides a continuous, organic representation of the flow's density and structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vector field \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}), an initial surface patch (typically a quadrilateral), a time step \Delta t, and rendering parameters (compressibility mode, dye color). Output: A rendered image simulating dye/smoke in the flow. Data Structures: The core data structure is a set of tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron is defined by four vertices in 3D space. For steady flows, the volume is built layer by layer. For unsteady flows, the volume evolves over time. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Starting Surface: Define a small surface patch comprised of quadrilaterals. Rotate the initial surface automatically such that it is perpendicular to the flow vector at the center point of the patch. Split each quadrilateral along its diagonal to form a triangular surface mesh. This mesh serves as the starting surface for advection. 2. Advection and Prism Generation: Advect streamlines from the grid points (vertices) of the starting surface using the vector field \mathbf{v} over a time step \Delta t. The advected streamlines bound prism solids. A prism is formed by the original triangular face and the corresponding advected triangular face. 3. Adaptive Subdivision: In areas where the flow diverges, the algorithm must adaptively start new grid points or streamlines to maintain resolution and prevent gaps. For steady flows, a new layer of tetrahedra is added to the flow volume for each time step. 4. Tetrahedron Decomposition: Split each individual prism into tetrahedra. Ensure a consistent subdivision of the mesh into tetrahedra to avoid rendering artifacts. 5. Rendering (Scan-Conversion): Apply a special scan-conversion routine to render each tetrahedron. The tetrahedra are projected and composited. If all tetrahedra have the same dye color C/\tau, the final color is independent of the compositing order, eliminating the need for sorting. To ensure dyed regions are correctly obscured by opaque geometry, render opaque objects into the z-buffer first. Formulas and Parameters: Compressibility Mode: Determines particle density behavior. Incompressible: Models a fixed density of particles per unit volume. As the tetrahedron's volume increases (due to diverging flow), the opacity increases, making the smoke appear thicker. Compressible: Models a fixed number of particles per tetrahedron. As the volume increases, the opacity decreases. For compressible flows, the concentration \rho must be adjusted to account for volume changes during flow. Dye Color: The color C is applied to the tetrahedra. The term C/\tau suggests a normalization by thickness or time, though the exact definition of \tau is not provided in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderflowvolume(vectorfield, initialquad, timesteps, compressiblemode): """ Renders a flow volume using the Flow Volumes technique. Args: vectorfield: Function v(x, t) returning velocity at position x and time t. initialquad: A quadrilateral defined by 4 vertices. timesteps: Number of advection steps. compressiblemode: Boolean, True for compressible, False for incompressible. Returns: Rendered image. """ # 1. Initialize Starting Surface # Split quadrilateral into two triangles trimesh = splitquadintotriangles(initialquad) # Rotate mesh to be perpendicular to flow at center center = computecenter(trimesh) flowatcenter = vectorfield(center, 0) trimesh = rotatetoperpendicular(trimesh, flowatcenter) # List of tetrahedra to render tetrahedralist = [] # 2. Advect and Build Volume currentmesh = trimesh for step in range(timesteps): # Advect vertices nextmesh = advectmesh(currentmesh, vectorfield, dt=1.0, time=step) # Form prisms from currentmesh and nextmesh prisms = formprisms(currentmesh, nextmesh) # Split prisms into tetrahedra newtetrahedra = splitprismsintotetrahedra(prisms) # Add to list tetrahedralist.extend(newtetrahedra) # Update current mesh for next iteration currentmesh = nextmesh # 3. Adaptive Subdivision (Simplified) # In areas of divergence, insert new grid points and advect them # This is a high-level placeholder for the adaptive logic described in if isdivergingflow(currentmesh): newpoints = adaptivelyaddpoints(currentmesh) advectedpoints = advectpoints(newpoints, vectorfield, dt=1.0, time=step) # Connect new points to form additional tetrahedra/prisms # Details of connectivity are not fully specified in sources pass # 4. Rendering # Clear z-buffer with opaque geometry (if any) clearzbuffer() # Render tetrahedra # Since compositing order is independent for same dye color, no sorting is needed for tet in tetrahedralist: # Calculate density/opacity based on compressibility mode volume = computevolume(tet) if compressiblemode: # Fixed number of particles: opacity decreases as volume increases opacity = computecompressibleopacity(tet) else: # Fixed density: opacity increases as volume increases opacity = computeincompressibleopacity(tet) # Scan-convert tetrahedron with calculated opacity and dye color scanconverttetrahedron(tet, opacity, dyecolor) return getframebuffer() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: For time-varying data, the flow volume changes over time and can self-intersect, leading to incorrect rendering. Divergence: The algorithm must handle areas where the flow diverges by adaptively starting new grid points or streamlines; failure to do so results in gaps in the visualization. Compressibility: For compressible flows, the concentration \rho must be correctly adjusted to account for volume changes; incorrect adjustment leads to inaccurate density representation. Time Complexity: Real-time performance is achievable because the sorting step is eliminated if all tetrahedra have the same dye color. The complexity is dominated by the advection and scan-conversion of tetrahedra. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of tetrahedra generated, which scales with the resolution of the starting surface, the time steps, and the adaptive subdivision density. Strengths: Eliminates the need for complex sorting of semi-transparent geometry; allows interactive movement of the smoke injector; provides a continuous, organic appearance. Limitations: Self-intersection in time-varying flows can cause artifacts; adaptive subdivision adds complexity; requires careful handling of compressibility. When to use: When visualizing steady or slowly varying flows where the organic appearance of smoke/dye is desired and real-time performance is important. When not to use: For highly turbulent, time-varying flows with significant self-intersection, or when precise quantitative density measurement is required without careful calibration of the compressibility model. Flow Volumes were introduced by Max et al. to render multiple stream surfaces efficiently without occlusion issues and slow ray-tracing. The technique was applied to visualize underground water transport and global climate simulations. Becker, Lane, and Max extended the technique to time-varying flows. The method is part of the broader family of illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques. name: Stylization and Non-Photorealistic Rendering Styles
body: This family encompasses methods that apply non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques to volumetric data to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth. Unlike traditional physics-based volume rendering, which often results in ambiguous structural interpretation due to the continuous nature of volumetric data, these methods decouple illumination from physical light transport to modulate color and opacity based on local volumetric properties. They are distinguished from surface-based NPR by deriving features from continuous 3D scalar or vector field properties rather than well-defined geometric surfaces. The family shares the goal of enhancing volume visualization through stylized lighting and feature abstraction. All methods operate on fragment-level data, typically utilizing the volume sample gradient as a proxy for surface normal orientation. They decouple illumination from the physical light transport equation, instead using mathematical functions of the view direction, light direction, and scalar field properties to modulate color. Common inputs include the normalized gradient \nabla fn, light vectors L, and base colors derived from transfer functions. The output is a final color c that combines ambient/gaseous components with directed illumination effects. The framework utilizes four types of properties for enhancement: 1. Volume sample location and value. 2. Local volumetric properties, such as gradient and minimal change direction. 3. View direction. 4. Light information. Volumetric illustration differs from surface-based NPR in several important ways. In surface NPR, surfaces (features) are well-defined, whereas with volumes, feature areas within the volume must be determined through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. Stylization and Pattern Generation applies non-photorealistic rendering techniques to volume data to enhance feature visibility and aesthetic appeal. It solves the ambiguity of internal structures in complex volumes by replacing photorealistic shading with abstract patterns, such as stippling or example-based textures. Unlike Geometric Buffers which focus on geometric abstraction, or Illumination and Tone Shading Models which refine lighting, this family explicitly decouples illumination from physical light transport to modulate color and density based on user-defined artistic styles. This family encompasses methods that apply non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques to volumetric data to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth. Unlike traditional physics-based volume rendering, which often results in ambiguous structural interpretation due to the continuous nature of volumetric data, these methods decouple illumination from physical light transport to modulate color and opacity based on local volumetric properties. They are distinguished from surface-based NPR by deriving features from continuous 3D scalar or vector field properties rather than well-defined geometric surfaces. CartoonVolumeStyle is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that produces a cel-shaded appearance by mapping surface normal orientations to a discrete set of flat colors. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric structure without the smooth gradients of photorealistic rendering, instead using distinct color bands to emphasize shape and boundaries. It differs from Boundary Enhancement Volume Style by relying on normal-view angle quantization rather than gradient magnitude, and from Stylization and Pattern Generation by using a fixed HSV-based interpolation scheme for its color palette. This variant applies tone selection based on the distance between the camera and the object. It applies saturation adaptation based on the distance from the ray intersection point to the external contour of the object. It includes silhouettes for neurons that are close to the camera. It highlights bifurcations in dendrites and connection points between dendrites and somas. An ad-hoc ray-casting method is used for computing intersections between rays and dendrites/somas and assigning proper colors according to these illustrative strategies rather than standard shading. This variant defines a seamless transition among shader stages using a user parameter \Gamma \in [0,5]. The transition parameters T{S,C,SC,H,P} \in [0,1] describe the transition from one rendering style to the next and depend on \Gamma. Silhouettes: TS = 1. Contours: TC = \text{clamp}{[0,1]}(\Gamma). Suggestive Contours: T{SC} = \text{clamp}{[0,1]}(\Gamma-1). Hatching: TH = \text{clamp}{[0,1]}(\Gamma-2). Phong: TP = \text{clamp}{[0,1]}(\Gamma-3). Contour width a is defined as a = \text{width} \cdot T{S,C}, where width is a predefined parameter (0.006) controlling the maximal contour width as a fraction of the bounding sphere. Suggestive contour parameters are set as td = (1 - T{SC})t{d,\min} + t{d,\min} and \theta{c} = \frac{\pi}{2} - (\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta{c,\min})T{SC}, where t{d,\min} and \theta{c,\min} are predefined minimal thresholds. Hatching threshold is set as \theta{c} = \frac{1}{2}\pi(1 - TH). Phong shading opacity Op is calculated using \theta{c}(TP) = \frac{1}{2}\pi(1 - TP), wa(TP) = \text{clamp}{[0,1]}(\frac{\arccos(-\langle \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v} \rangle) - \theta{c}(TP)}{\frac{1}{2}\pi - \theta{c}(TP)}), wk(TP) = -\langle \mathbf{k}, \mathbf{v} \rangle(1 - TP) - TP, and Op = \text{clamp}{[0,1]}(wa(TP) \cdot wk(TP)). For \Gamma > 4, T{S,C,SC,H,P} = 1 - \text{clamp}{[0,1]}(\Gamma-4) and the final Phong opacity is O{pm} = TP \cdot Op + (1 - TP). The concept of non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) for volumes emerged to address the ambiguity inherent in standard volume rendering, where continuous scalar fields make feature boundaries difficult to perceive. Early work focused on adapting surface-based NPR techniques, such as cel-shading and hatching, to volumetric data by estimating surface normals from gradients. The field has developed to include complex transition mechanisms that allow users to seamlessly blend between different illustrative styles, such as silhouettes, contours, and hatching, to highlight specific anatomical or structural features. These methods are primarily used in biomedical visualization to enhance the interpretability of complex structures like neural cells and internal organs. name: Stipple Volume Rendering
head: Illustrative Interactive Stipple Rendering, Interactive Volume Stippling, Stipple Volume Renderer, Stippling, The Stipple Volume Renderer, Volumetric Stippling, volume stipple renderer
body:
Stipple Volume Rendering is an object-space, point-based non-photorealistic rendering technique that replaces standard rasterization with stippled points to create an illustrative, sketch-like appearance. It solves the problem of conveying complex volumetric shape and features efficiently by abstracting unimportant details and utilizing attentive focus, making it suitable for initial volume investigation, data previewing, and medical education. Unlike Example-Based Volume Illustration, which relies on example textures, Stipple Volume Rendering generates point lists based on volume characteristics (gradient magnitude/direction) and applies feature enhancements (silhouette curves, varying point sizes, resolution adjustments) to convey tone, texture, and shape. It is distinct from image-space stippling because it determines stipples per geometric primitive (voxel) rather than computing grey levels in the image space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume dataset (scalar field), camera parameters (view direction, near plane), light direction, and user-defined enhancement parameters. Output: A set of point primitives (stipples) and optionally line segments (silhouette curves) rendered to the screen. Data Structures: Voxel Data: Normalized scalar values vi, positions, and precomputed gradient vectors 
abla Vi and magnitudes ||
abla Vi||. Edge Field: A binary or scalar field generated by applying a Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) filter to the voxel data to identify features for enhancement. Stipple List: A pre-generated list of stipple positions for each voxel. For a voxel i, this list contains up to N{max} points. The positions are distributed to approximate a Poisson disc distribution within a subvolume defined by planes parallel to the gradient plane. Preprocessing Stage (Viewpoint-Independent): 1. Normalization: Normalize voxel values and gradients. 2. Gradient Estimation: Estimate the gradient 
abla Vi for each voxel. The method uses a three-dimensional regression hyperplane approximation (Neumann et al. [16]) to minimize a four-dimensional error function, providing a smoothed dataset and accurate gradient simultaneously. 3. Resolution Adjustment: Apply a simple box-filter to adjust the volume resolution so that the average projection of a voxel on the screen is at least 5 	imes 5 pixels. 4. Calculate N{max}: Calculate the maximum number of stipples per voxel based on screen projection: N{max} = k{max}  rac{A{vol}}{(X{res} Y{res} Z{res})^{2/3}} Where A{vol} is the volume, X{res}, Y{res}, Z{res} are resolution dimensions, and k{max} is a constant. 5. Initial Point Generation: For voxels with gradient magnitude above a user-specified threshold, generate up to N{max} stipples. Place them randomly around the voxel center, between two planes p1 and p2 parallel to the tangent plane p0 (defined by the gradient), separated by a user-chosen distance. Adjust locations to be relatively equally spaced. Interactive Rendering Loop (Per Frame): 1. Calculate Enhancement Factors: For each voxel, compute the total enhancement factor T as the product of selected factors: T = Tb \cdot Ts \cdot Tr \cdot Td \cdot Tt \cdot Tl Each factor is normalized to [0, 1]. If a feature is not selected, its factor is excluded (effectively 1). 2. Determine Point Count: Calculate the number of stipples to draw for voxel i: Ni = N{max} \cdot T 3. Select Stipples: Select the first Ni stipples from the pre-generated list for voxel i. This maintains frame-to-frame coherence. 4. Render Points: Render the selected stipples as point primitives. The point size Si is scaled by the gradient magnitude: Si = ||
abla Vi|| \cdot S{max} 5. Render Silhouettes (Optional): Identify silhouette voxels using the LoG edge field and view direction. Render silhouette curves as line segments for these voxels. Formulas for Enhancement Factors: Boundary Factor (Tb): Tb = vi \cdot (k{gc} + k{gs} \cdot (||
abla Vi||^{k{ge}})) Where vi is the original voxel scalar value, k{gc} controls direct influence, k{gs} indicates maximum boundary enhancement, and k{ge} controls sharpness. Silhouette Factor (Ts): Constructed similarly to Tb using silhouette-specific parameters (k{sc}, k{ss}, k{se}), though defines it as Ts = 1 - (L \cdot 
abla Vi). Resolution Factor (Tr): Tr = \left[  rac{D{near} + di}{D{near} + d0} ight]^{k{re}} Where D{near} is the near plane location, di is the distance from the current volume location to the near plane, d0 is the distance from the initial volume location to the near plane (reference), and k{re} controls the rate of change. If k{re}=0, no enhancement. Distance Factor (Td): Td = 1 + \left(  rac{z}{a} ight)^{k{de}} Where z is the depth of the current voxel, a defines the original distance range (-a, a), and k{de} controls distance attenuation. k{de} can be negative or positive. Interior Transparency Factor (Tt): Tt = ||
abla Vi||^{k{te}} Where ||
abla Vi|| is the gradient magnitude to the center of the volume, and k{te} controls the falloff. Lower gradient voxels become more transparent. Lighting Factor (Tl): Tl = 1 - (L \cdot 
abla Vi) Where L is the light direction and 
abla Vi is the gradient vector. Parameters: Default rendering style: k{gc}=0.39, k{gs}=0.51, k{ge}=1.0. Boundary & Silhouette enhancement style: k{sc}=0.279, k{ss}=0.45, k{se}=1.11. Interactive thresholds: T{hLOG}, T{heye}, T{hgrad}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Aliasing: Occurs during rotation near silhouette edges and illuminated boundaries as new points are added. Alleviated by implementing simple partial opacity point rendering to fade points. Noisy Data: Noisy volume data creates incorrect gradient directions, affecting feature enhancements. The Neumann gradient estimation method helps mitigate this. Silhouette Approximation: Silhouette detection in volumes approximates surface normal using volume gradient direction and detects boundaries using volume gradient magnitude, which may not always align with true geometric boundaries. A proposed optimization to move feature enhancements onto the graphics card using programmable vertex programs, avoiding expensive vertex downloads. Preprocessed points are stored as display lists or vertex arrays in the graphics card’s memory. Vertex programs evaluate the thresholds of feature enhancements; if a vertex falls below the threshold, its coordinates are modified to a position off screen to effectively cull it. This culling is possible because the system uses vertices rather than polygons, allowing simple thresholding formulae to be implemented directly. However, this technique is not generally possible for polygons due to the lack of connectivity information in vertex programs. An application of volume stippling to flow data, where flow features (critical points, vortices, etc.) are conveyed with simple strokes, avoiding high-gradient boundary emphasis. Flow data often lacks high gradients, so boundaries are not the main concern. Instead, the method identifies flow features such as vortices, sources, and sinks from the vector field data. Stipples are generated to represent these structures, potentially using silhouette curves and contouring transfer functions to show major structures, avoiding visual clutter. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is viewpoint-independent and takes seconds to a minute depending on dataset size and resolution. Interactive rendering is frame-rate dependent on the number of points (5,000 to 2,000,000) and silhouette curves (1,000 to 300,000). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, precomputed gradients, edge fields, and the pre-generated stipple lists. Not limited by texture memory size for the stipple points themselves, as they are rendered as point primitives. Measured Performance: On a dual processor Intel Xeon 2.00 GHz computer with a Geforce 3 Ti 500 display card, frame rates ranged from 3.5 fps to 60.4 fps for datasets with resolutions from 64 	imes 64 	imes 64 to 341 	imes 341 	imes 93, depending on whether stipples, silhouettes, or both were rendered. Strengths: Interactive previewing, concise representation of complex data, frame-to-frame coherence, and suitability for medical education and initial investigation. Limitations: Temporal aliasing near edges, reliance on accurate gradient estimation for noisy data, and potential loss of fine detail due to abstraction. When to use: Initial volume investigation, data previewing, and medical education/teaching anatomy. When not to use: When photorealistic detail is required or when the volume data is extremely noisy and gradient estimation fails. Stipple Volume Rendering was introduced by Lu et al. in the paper "Non-Photorealistic Volume Rendering Using Stippling Techniques" (2003). It is part of the broader field of illustrative volume rendering, which applies principles from artistic and scientific illustration to volume data. The technique builds on the concept of object-space stippling, where stipples are determined per geometric primitive, as opposed to image-space stippling. It is used in medical illustration and flow visualization. name: Example-Based Volume Illustration
head: Color Transfer for Illustration, Example-Based Illustrative Visualization, Example-Based Rendering, Volume Illustration Using Wang Cubes
body: Example-Based Volume Illustration is a technique that generates multiple illustrative styles (e.g., pen and ink, watercolor) by combining 3D pattern textures with color transfer from example images. It solves the problem of simulating professional illustrator styles while simplifying user interaction, which previously required manual assignment of textured cubes per object. It sets itself apart from siblings like Stipple Volume Rendering by using Wang Cubes for pattern synthesis and explicit color transfer algorithms rather than procedural stippling or curve generation. Inputs: 1. Target volume data (scalar field). 2. Source illustration example (image). 3. Segmentation data (optional): Object IDs or Opacity values. Outputs: Stylized volume rendering with transferred colors and patterns. Data Structures: Wang Cubes: A set of 3D textured cubes where each cube has a "cube tiling" (face colors) and "cube contents" (internal pattern). Cube Sets: A collection of Wang Cubes assigned to objects or regions; for segmented datasets, one cube set per Object ID is used, while for un-segmented datasets, cube sets are defined by opacity ranges. Steps: 1. Sampling: The user samples the source illustration example and the target volume data. 2. Color Transfer: Apply a color transfer algorithm to map color statistics from the source example to the target volume data, utilizing standard methods such as Reinhard et al. (2001) or Welse et al. (2002). 3. Assignment: For each object or region, assign one set of textured Wang Cubes based on segmented datasets (Object ID) or un-segmented datasets (opacity). 4. Synthesis: Render the volume using the transferred colors and the assigned Wang Cubes, utilizing cube tiling for pattern similarity and cube contents for style. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def examplebasedvolumeillustration(volumedata, sourceimage, segmentation=None): # Step 1: Sampling # User provides sourceimage and volumedata # Step 2: Color Transfer # Map color statistics from sourceimage to volumedata # Standard operation: Reinhard et al. (2001) or Welse et al. (2002) transferredcolors = applycolortransfer(sourceimage, volumedata) # Step 3: Assignment if segmentation is not None: # Segmented datasets: assign one cube set per Object ID cubesets = {} for objid in unique(segmentation): cubesets[objid] = assigncubesetforobjectid(objid) else: # Un-segmented datasets: assign cube sets by opacity cubesets = assigncubesetsbyopacity(volumedata) # Step 4: Synthesis # Render using transferred colors and cube sets # Wang Cubes provide pattern via tiling and style via contents result = rendervolumewithcubes(volumedata, transferredcolors, cubesets) return result def applycolortransfer(source, target): # Standard color transfer algorithm return remapcolorstatistics(source, target) def assigncubesetforobjectid(objid): # Assign one set of textured Wang Cubes for the given object ID return getcubeset(objid) def assigncubesetsbyopacity(voldata): # Assign cube sets based on opacity ranges of un-segmented data return generatecubesetsfromopacity(voldata) def rendervolumewithcubes(voldata, colors, cubesets): # Render volume using transferred colors and assigned Wang Cubes return compositevolume(voldata, colors, cubesets) Parameters: User Interaction: Limited to sampling the source example and selecting illustration examples. Assumptions: Simpler representation and similar object distributions are assumed to allow automatic transferring. Edge Cases: Segmentation: If no segmentation is available, opacity-based assignment is used, which may be less precise for distinct objects. Object Distribution: The method assumes similar object distributions between the example and target for effective color transfer. A method for generating 3D patterns and textures using non-periodic indexing and shared cube tiling. Algorithms for mapping color statistics from a source image to a target volume. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables multiple styles (pen and ink, watercolor, etc.) with less storage by sharing one cube tiling. Simplifies user interaction by requiring only sampling and example selection. Limitations: Assumes similar object distributions between source and target for automatic color transfer. When to use: When simulating professional illustrator styles is desired with minimal user interaction. When not to use: When precise per-object style control is required without segmentation, as the method relies on simplified representations and automatic transfer. Originated in the context of medical illustration and flows, aiming to convey object properties through multiple illustrative styles. It builds on previous approaches that required one set of textured cubes per object or segmentation, proposing a simpler representation. The technique is used in medical illustration and surgical simulation. name: Fake Media Methods
head: Appearance-based methods, Non-physically based methods
body: Fake media methods are rendering techniques that do not account for the physical phenomena of light transport but instead generate visually pleasant, realistic appearances suitable for applications where physical accuracy is not required. They differ from physically based volume rendering by decoupling illumination from the radiative transfer equation, relying on empirical models, texture synthesis, or simplified analytical solutions to achieve specific aesthetic goals. Unlike surface-based non-photorealistic rendering, these methods must determine volumetric features through local property analysis, as features vary continuously in three-dimensional space. Inputs: View direction, light direction, scalar field values (e.g., density), and pre-defined empirical parameters (e.g., attenuation coefficients, noise seeds). Outputs: Final color c for each pixel or fragment. 1. Procedural Models (Gardner, Perlin): No explicit volumetric grid is required. Noise functions and mathematical primitives (ellipsoids) are evaluated on-the-fly. 2. Analytical Models (Premoze & Ashikmin, Biri): Require integration along the view ray. For Biri's fog, the extinction coefficient \kappat is defined as a function allowing analytical integration. 1. Determine the intersection of the view ray with the medium boundaries to obtain entry and exit points. 2. Evaluate procedural noise/turbulence functions or analytical extinction functions along the ray segment. 3. Compute transmittance \tau using the integrated extinction coefficient. 4. Calculate in-scattered or diffuse radiance using empirical or constant source terms. 5. Composite the background/target radiance with the in-scattered radiance using the analytical formula. L(0) = e^{-\kappat R} L(z) + \left(1 - e^{-(\kappat + \kappad \cos \theta)R}\right) L{df}(0) L(0): Apparent radiance just below the air-water interface. L(z): Radiance of the target at depth z. R: Total path length, calculated as R = -z / \cos \theta. \theta: Angle counted from the vertical direction (positive z-axis). \kappat: Extinction coefficient. \kappad: Apparent water diffuse attenuation coefficient. L{df}(0): Diffused radiance just below the sea surface, estimated using empirical equations relating it to downwelling irradiance from the sun and skylight. L(x) = \tau(x0, x) L(x0) + (1 - \tau(x0, x)) J{fog} L(x): Radiance at position x. L(x0): Radiance at the entry point x0. \tau(x0, x): Transmittance from x0 to x, computed efficiently due to the specific definition of \kappat. J{fog}: Constant source radiance within the fog. \kappat: Extinction coefficient. Defined as a well-chosen function allowing analytical integration for real-time performance. \kappad: Apparent water diffuse attenuation coefficient. Typical values depend on water type (e.g., deep ocean vs. tropical water). J{fog}: Constant source radiance. Typically derived from ambient light or sky color. Noise seeds and turbulence scales: Control procedural variation for clouds, fire, and marble. Shadowing: Fake media methods are generally not suited for proper self-shadowing or shadows cast by the medium. Texture-based methods (Gardner, Perlin, Yaeger) focus on modeling the medium but not its interaction with the scene. Analytical methods (Premoze & Ashikmin, Biri) use color blending without integrating the fog/medium into a global illumination scheme, thus ignoring shadows. Atmospheric Opacity: Yaeger et al.'s method assumes the atmosphere is opaque because the observer is restricted to being far away from the planet. Dimensionality: Premoze and Ashikmin's model assumes a one-dimensional dependency (depth only), which limits its applicability to scenes where lateral variations are negligible or handled separately. Division by Zero: Horizontal rays (\cos \theta \approx 0) in the water model cause division by zero in the path length calculation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderfakemediafog(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, kappat, Jfog, backgroundcolor): """ Renders fog using Biri et al.'s analytical integration model. Assumes a medium bounded by tmin and tmax along the ray. """ distance = tmax - tmin transmittance = math.exp(-kappat distance) return transmittance backgroundcolor + (1.0 - transmittance) Jfog def renderfakemediawater(depthz, theta, kappat, kappad, sunirradiance, targetradiance): """ Renders water using Premoze and Ashikmin's 1D depth-dependent model. """ costheta = math.cos(theta) if abs(costheta) < 1e-6: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) R = -depthz / costheta # Ldf(0) is estimated using empirical equations relating it to downwelling irradiance Ldf0 = sunirradiance 0.5 # Simplified empirical scaling factor return math.exp(-kappat R) targetradiance + (1.0 - math.exp(-(kappat + kappad costheta) R)) Ldf0 def rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax): """ Standard ray-box intersection returning entry and exit distances. """ tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): invd = 1.0 / raydirection[i] t1 = (boxmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd t2 = (boxmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < tmin: return None, None return tmin, tmax Performance: These methods are generally computationally inexpensive compared to physically based path tracing or even single-scattering approximations. Biri et al.'s method achieves real-time animation by using functions for \kappat that allow analytical integration. Realism: They produce "visually pleasant" results that can appear realistic in specific contexts (e.g., clouds, fog, water surfaces) but lack physical correctness. Limitations: Inability to handle complex light transport effects such as multiple scattering, self-shadowing, and dynamic shadow casting. Use Cases: Applications where physical accuracy is not required, such as stylized visualization, real-time games, or specific cinematic effects where aesthetic control is prioritized over physical fidelity. The term "fake media methods" was coined in the context of participating media rendering surveys to categorize techniques that prioritize appearance over physical accuracy. [107]: Applied fluid dynamics and particle systems to simulate Jupiter's atmosphere for the film 2010. name: Hatching and Stroke-based Rendering
body: Hatching and Stroke-based Rendering is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that simulate hand-drawn line art, such as hatching, stippling, or paint strokes, to convey shape, spatial relationships, and aesthetic qualities of 3D volumetric data. It solves the problem of abstracting continuous volumetric features into discrete, interpretable graphical elements that mimic traditional artistic media. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly combining line-strip primitives or textured quads with direct volume rendering (DVR) or particle systems, using data-driven seed point selection and curvature-guided tracing to minimize memory and generation time while maintaining interactivity. This family builds on the shared principles of Stylization and Pattern Generation. Volumetric illustration differs from surface-based NPR in several important ways. In surface NPR, surfaces (features) are well-defined, whereas with volumes, feature areas within the volume must be determined through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. Interactive Volume Illustration (Hatching) is an object-space technique for illustrating volumetric data by simulating free-hand line art (hatching) using hardware-assisted volume and line rendering. It solves the problem of conveying shape and spatial relationships in 3D volumes by tracing hatches as polylines over implicit surfaces along either a fixed direction or a smoothed principal curvature direction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly combining line-strip primitives with direct volume rendering (DVR) in a two-pass pipeline, using data-driven seed point selection to minimize memory and generation time. Choose it when interactivity and explicit curvature-guided hatching are required. Fast Paint Texture is a stylization technique that simulates 3D paint undulations and overlap shadows on 2D strokes by generating a height field from stroke height maps and overlap counts, rendered via Phong shading, thereby avoiding the computational cost of 3D mesh generation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Interactive Volume Illustration (Hatching) by explicitly modeling paint layer accumulation through a 2D height field rather than relying solely on surface normals or simple shading. Choose it when simulating physical paint properties like overlap and shadow without 3D mesh generation is needed. Visual Complexity (VC) Algorithm is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that simulates the local visual variations found in hand-painted artworks to enhance aesthetic judgment and detail perception. Unlike Interpretational Complexity (IC), which establishes global trends across the volume, VC focuses on local variations in stroke properties such as color, thickness, and contour to create a dense, textured appearance. It differs from Interactive Volume Illustration (Hatching) by employing a single-region, full-coverage painting strategy with varied stroke geometries rather than structured hatching lines, and from Fast Paint Texture by integrating embossing as a post-processing lighting effect on 2D stroke textures rather than a primary geometric modeling step. Choose it when simulating local hand-painted aesthetic variations is the goal. An interactive illustrative visualization framework for real-time pen-and-ink style rendering of volume data, based on a particle system. Input: Volume data stored in a 3D texture; Proxy geometry comprising a 3D grid of equally spaced vertices. Uses the VolumeFlies hidden surface removal filter: iso-surface is splatted with uniquely colored cones generated by the geometry shader; particle visibility is determined by an off-screen framebuffer. A methodology for sampling and rendering 3D volume data to simulate classical ink-and-paint non-photorealistic styles, addressing the lack of artist-friendly NPR volume rendering tools. Scatter point data within the 3D volume data based on density values, or create a custom point cloud. Ray cast from the camera to the hit position of the volume. From the ray's hit position, cast a secondary ray towards a direction, either towards a light source for shading or continuing in the same direction for a headlamp effect. Tally and normalize the number of scattered points found within a radius of the direction of the secondary ray. Interpolate between the lit color of the volume and the background color using the normalized value from the previous step. A method to render strokes as Bézier curves with control points positioned based on data attribute orientations. Query data attribute values at three sample points s0, s1, s2. Compute associated orientations θ0, θ1, θ2 to position control points A, B, C, D. Place control points so that segment BC has orientation θ0, AB has orientation θ1, and CD has orientation θ2. If max(d1, d2) is large, draw the stroke as a curve; otherwise, likely draw as linear segments (implied by contrast with 'draw stroke as a curve'). A technique to simulate paint variation by drawing strokes as three quadrilaterals with varying colors and widths. Sample center color C=(R,G,B) and length l, width w. Vary C to C1, C2 in small interval. Vary w to w1, w2 such that 0 <= w1, w2 < w/8. Draw q centered on sample with length l, width w-(w1+w2), color C. Draw q1 next to q with length l, width w1, color C1. Draw q2 opposite q1 with length l, width w2, color C2. A raymarching renderer that produces SVG files with hatching lines, where strokes follow surface tangent directions and density is controlled by lighting to produce an engraving or etching aesthetic. Pass 1: A Rust backend raymarches the SDF scene per-pixel using rayon parallelism, producing hit, brightness, and hatch angle buffers. Pass 2: A flow field line tracer connects polylines through the 2D angle field, enforcing minimum spacing that varies with brightness to create light and shadow. Pass 3: The polylines are written out as SVG. RenderConfig parameters: width (int), height (int), bufscale (int, default 18 in example), lightdir (tuple of 3 floats, e.g., (0.7, 1.0, 0.4)), shadows (bool, default True). TraceConfig parameters: stepsize (float, e.g., 0.04), minspace (float, e.g., 0.06), maxspace (float, e.g., 0.7). strokewidth (float, e.g., 0.04) is passed to renderscene to define the width of the output strokes. Scene definition uses a tree of SDF nodes (spheres, boxes, tori, boolean operations, transforms) evaluated natively in Rust via PyO3. Native Rust evaluation via PyO3 provides roughly 150x speedup over pure Python execution of the scene graph. A technique to help distinguish faces of wound stream surfaces using halftones and hatching, in addition to feature/boundary lines and cut-aways. 1. Render stream surfaces. 2. Apply halftones and hatching to distinguish faces of wound surfaces. Support for multiple stamp shapes including sphere, cylinder, box, cone, and procedural Perlin noise. For spherical stamping, support sweeping to create tapered capsules connecting consecutive stroke path samples. The VolFliesGPU framework, introduced by Busking et al. in 2008, pioneered the use of GPU-based particle systems for interactive illustrative volume rendering, leveraging GPGPU paradigms for real-time performance. The Visual Complexity algorithm, developed by Liao et al., introduced sophisticated stroke placement, variegation, and flank texturing to simulate hand-painted aesthetics. Fast Paint Texture provided a method for simulating physical paint properties like overlap and shadow without 3D mesh generation. More recent methodologies, such as those by, have explored point-sampling techniques to generalize ink-and-paint styles for volume data. Halftones and hatching were proposed to help distinguish faces of wound stream surfaces. Brush stamping methods support multiple shapes including sphere, cylinder, box, cone, and procedural Perlin noise, with sweeping to create tapered capsules. HatchForge provides a raymarching renderer that produces SVG files with hatching lines following surface tangent directions, controlled by lighting to produce an engraving aesthetic. name: Interactive Volume Illustration (Hatching)
head: Hatching, Object space hatching, Stroke-based volume rendering, Two-Pass Hatching Rendering
body: Interactive Volume Illustration (Hatching) is an object-space technique for illustrating volumetric data by simulating free-hand line art (hatching) using hardware-assisted volume and line rendering. It solves the problem of conveying shape and spatial relationships in 3D volumes by tracing hatches as polylines over implicit surfaces along either a fixed direction or a smoothed principal curvature direction. Unlike surface-based NPR methods where features are well-defined, this method determines feature areas through analysis of local volumetric properties because volumetric features vary continuously throughout three-dimensional space. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly combining line-strip primitives with direct volume rendering (DVR) in a two-pass pipeline, using data-driven seed point selection to minimize memory and generation time. The method operates in two main phases: stroke generation (preprocessing/seed placement) and rendering (two passes). Inputs: 3D scalar volume data V, transfer function (for volume rendering), light direction \vec{L}, view direction \vec{V}{dir}, user-defined fixed direction \vec{s}T, smoothing weight wT, flatness threshold \epsilon, cross-hatch angle threshold. Outputs: Final image combining hatching strokes and volumetric data. 1. Volume Data: 3D texture map or scalar grid. 2. Gradient/Normal Map: Precomputed or on-the-fly gradients \nabla f used to derive surface normals \vec{N} and principal curvatures. 3. Seed Points: A set of 3D positions \{pj\} representing iso-surfaces, selected at run time to ensure an optimal number of points. 4. Stroke Buffer: Stores line-strip primitives. Memory usage is at most one-eighth of the volume data set size. To guide hatches, principal curvature directions are computed. Direct tracing along raw principal curvature directions yields messy results when the main direction is not robustly defined. Therefore, the field is smoothed. 1. Reconstruct Derivatives: Use fast cubic B-spline filtering to reconstruct partial derivatives from volume data. 2. Compute Principal Curvatures: Calculate principal curvature magnitudes \kappa1, \kappa2 and shape index s for each particle pj. s = \frac{2}{\pi} \arctan \left( \frac{\kappa1 + \kappa2}{\kappa2 - \kappa1} \right) where \kappa1 \ge \kappa2 and |\kappa1| + |\kappa2| > 0. 3. Compute Surface Reliability: Determine if the local curvature is suitable for hatching: \rho(\kappa1, \kappa2) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |\kappa1| < \epsilon \text{ and } |\kappa2| < \epsilon \\ 1 - |2(|s| - 1/2)| & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Here \epsilon defines which nearly flat surfaces are considered flat. 4. Smooth Direction Field: Compute the smoothed direction \vec{s}i for a particle pi by averaging the main principal curvature directions \vec{\kappa}{1j} of neighboring particles pj: \vec{s}i = wT \frac{\sumj \rhoj \vec{\kappa}{1j}}{\sumj \rhoj} + (1 - wT) \vec{s}T The trace reliability weight wT is determined by averaging the surface reliability of all neighboring particles: wT = \frac{\sumj \rhoj}{\sumj 1} This smoothing is executed on the GPU, estimating curvature information of neighboring particles on the fly. 1. Seed Placement: Select seed points at run time to represent iso-surfaces, ensuring an optimal number of points. 2. Trace Hatches: In a geometry shader, use particle positions as seed points. Determine vertices connecting hatch segments by projecting the smoothed direction \vec{s}i to the tangent plane. 3. Store Strokes: Represent hatches as line-strip primitives. These can be pre-computed since the approach is not view-dependent. Pass 1: Render Hatching Strokes 1. Fetch line-strips from the texture buffer. 2. Anisotropic Shading: Illuminate using stored gradients. Apply anisotropic shading model for lines. 3. Front/Back Facing: Determine orientation using surface normal \vec{N} and view vector \vec{V}. Calculate two 2D lookup textures (varying diffuse/specular color). Interpolate color contributions based on \vec{N} \cdot \vec{V} in the per-fragment shader. 4. Cross-Hatches: For each seed, compute \vec{N} \cdot \vec{L}. If the angle is above a constant, generate an additional stroke along the minimal curvature direction. Cross-hatches are shorter than initial strokes. 5. Depth Test: Enable depth test and update depth buffer. Render transparent volume structures in back-to-front order without changing OpenGL state. Pass 2: Render Volumetric Data 1. Render the volumetric data set using 3D texture maps (Direct Volume Rendering). 2. Alpha/Depth Test: Use alpha-test and depth-test during re-sampling to render only texture samples closest to the viewpoint and above/below a threshold. 3. Hatch Visibility: To ensure only hatches in front of the iso-surface remain visible for opaque rendering, write white color to the frame buffer after rendering hatches, then render volume with alpha/depth test.
