dot normal[i] for i in range(3)] def findnearestparticle(position, particles): # Returns index of nearest particle to position return 0 def interpolatelookuptexture(dotnv): # Interpolates color from 2D lookup textures based on N.V return [0.8, 0.8, 0.8] def drawline(p1, p2, color): # Renders a line segment pass def enabledepthtest(): # Enables depth testing and updates depth buffer pass def depthtestpass(position): # Checks if sample is closest to viewpoint return True def drawsample(sample, alpha): # Draws volume sample pass def writewhitetoframebuffer(): # Writes white color to frame buffer pass def generatehatchingstrokes(seeds, normals, sT, epsilon, maxsegments=10): linestrips = [] for i, seed in enumerate(seeds): normal = normals[i] smootheddir = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Computed from neighbors dironplane = projecttotangentplane(smootheddir, normal) strip = [seed] currentpos = seed currentdir = dironplane for in range(maxsegments): nextpos = [currentpos[j] + currentdir[j] for j in range(3)] strip.append(nextpos) currentpos = nextpos newnormal = normals[findnearestparticle(currentpos, seeds)] newsmoothed = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Computed from neighbors currentdir = projecttotangentplane(newsmoothed, newnormal) linestrips.append(strip) return linestrips def renderstrokes(linestrips, normals, viewvector, lightdirection, crosshatchthreshold, seeds): for strip in linestrips: for i in range(len(strip) - 1): p1, p2 = strip[i], strip[i+1] normal = normals[findnearestparticle(p1, seeds)] dotnv = sum(n v for n, v in zip(normal, viewvector)) color = interpolatelookuptexture(dotnv) if dotnv > 0: color = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Front facing blue else: color = [1.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Back facing yellow drawline(p1, p2, color) dotnl = sum(n l for n, l in zip(normal, lightdirection)) angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dotnl))) if angle > crosshatchthreshold: crossdir = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] # Minimal curvature direction crossstrip = generatehatchingstrokes([p1], [normal], crossdir, 0.0, maxsegments=5) # Shorter renderstrokes(crossstrip, normals, viewvector, lightdirection, crosshatchthreshold, seeds) enabledepthtest() def rendervolume(volumedata, threshold): for sample in volumedata.backtofront(): if sample.value > threshold: alpha = sample.alpha if depthtestpass(sample.position): drawsample(sample, alpha) writewhitetoframebuffer() \epsilon: Parameter defining which nearly flat surfaces are considered flat. Not given in the sources. wT: Smoothing weight. Not given in the sources. Viewport Resolution: 600x600 pixels. Strokes per Example: 20K to 50K strokes generated. Average Line Segments: 10 line segments per stroke. Memory Usage: At most one eighth of the memory consumed by the volume data set is required to store the selected strokes. Messy Results: Directly tracing along principal curvature directions yields messy results when the main direction is not robustly defined. Smoothing is required. Hatch Visibility: To ensure only hatches in front of the iso-surface remain visible for opaque rendering, write white color into the frame buffer after rendering hatches, then render volume with alpha/depth test. Intersections: Long hatch strokes might lead to intersections. A non-photorealistic technique combining line drawings with direct volume rendering (DVR) by placing hatching lines along principal curvature directions of structures before compositing with the volume model. It involves identifying structures of interest, computing principal curvature directions, generating hatching lines aligned with these directions in object space, and combining them with the direct volume rendering of the volume model. Time Complexity: Preprocessing time is significant for large datasets (1.3 minutes for a 256^3 volume dataset, including curvature estimation and octree construction). Seed placement takes between 0.5 and 4 seconds. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is at most one-eighth of the volume data set size to store selected strokes. Performance: Rendering performance is 4 to 8 fps for various datasets (engine block, hydrogen molecule, iron protein, aneurysm, human foot, human skull) on a 600x600 viewport. Toon shader performance is about 7 fps. Strengths: Interactive, hardware-assisted, minimizes memory and generation time via data-driven seed point selection, effectively conveys shape and spatial correlations. Limitations: Direct curvature tracing can be messy without smoothing. The method was presented by R.F.P. van Pelt, A. Vilanova, and H.M.M. van de Wetering in 2008. It builds on the work of Sigg and Hadwiger [SH05] for fast cubic B-spline filtering and anisotropic shading models for lines. The shape index was introduced by Koenderink and Van Doorn [KvD92]. The technique is part of the broader field of interactive non-photorealistic volume rendering, aiming to bring NPR techniques and real-time 3D graphics to the visualization community. name: Fast Paint Texture
head: Fast Paint Texturing, Hertzmann’s fast paint texture
body: Fast Paint Texture is a stylization technique that simulates 3D paint undulations and overlap shadows on 2D strokes by generating a height field from stroke height maps and overlap counts, rendered via Phong shading, thereby avoiding the computational cost of 3D mesh generation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Interactive Volume Illustration by explicitly modeling paint layer accumulation through a 2D height field rather than relying solely on surface normals or simple shading. Inputs: A list of strokes, where each stroke has an associated color, opacity map, and height map. The background is initialized to (0,0,0,1). Outputs: A final RGB image with simulated paint depth and lighting. Data Structures: 1. Color Buffer: Stores the RGB components of the base stroke colors. Initialized to (0,0,0). 2. Overlap Weight Buffer: Stores the red component of the color buffer after the Overlap Pass, representing the count of overlapping strokes. Initialized to 0. 3. Height Buffer: Stores the red component of the color buffer after the Height Pass, representing the height map value of the last drawn stroke. Initialized to 0. Steps: 1. Color Pass: Draw each stroke colored and textured with an opacity map. Save the RGB components in the Color Buffer. Stroke color is set to (1,1,1,\alpha). Background is (0,0,0,1). This pass records the base color information. 2. Overlap Pass: Draw each stroke white and textured with the same opacity maps used in the Color Pass. Alpha blend with transparency 0 < \alpha \le 1 to count overlapping strokes. Save the red component of the color buffer in the Overlap Weight Buffer. The red component R{i,k} at pixel pi after drawing stroke k is calculated as: R{i,k} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } k = 0 \\ \alpha + R{i,k-1}(1 - \alpha) & \text{if } k > 0 \end{cases} This compactly defines the count of overlapping strokes. 3. Height Pass: Draw each stroke white and textured with the height map paired with the opacity map. Each pixel pi contains the grey value (height value) of the last stroke drawn at pi. Save the red component of the color buffer in the Height Buffer. This pass records the local texture height of the most recent stroke. 4. Height Field Calculation: For each pixel pi, compute the final height value h(pi) as the sum of the stroke’s height map value at pi plus a weight representing the number of strokes overlapping at pi. h(pi) = \text{height\map}(pi) + \text{overlap\weight}(pi) Calculate per-pixel normals using directional derivatives of the height field. 5. Final Rendering: For each pixel pi, combine the stroke’s diffuse color components (from Color Pass) and the surface normal (from Height Pass) using the Phong model to obtain the final RGB color value. The diffuse component for the red channel is: Ci^R = Ia Rk^a Oi^R dR + f{att} Ip^R Oi^R dR (Ni \cdot L) + \dots Similar calculations are performed for Green and Blue channels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastpainttexture(strokes, width, height): # Initialize buffers colorbuffer = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] overlapweightbuffer = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] heightbuffer = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Pass 1: Color Pass for stroke in strokes: for y in range(height): for x in range(width): if stroke.opacitymap[y, x] > 0: colorbuffer[y][x] = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Pass 2: Overlap Pass for stroke in strokes: for y in range(height): for x in range(width): if stroke.opacitymap[y, x] > 0: alpha = stroke.alpha overlapweightbuffer[y][x] = alpha + overlapweightbuffer[y][x] (1.0 - alpha) # Pass 3: Height Pass for stroke in strokes: for y in range(height): for x in range(width): if stroke.opacitymap[y, x] > 0: heightbuffer[y][x] = stroke.heightmap[y, x] # Height Field Calculation finalheight = [[heightbuffer[y][x] + overlapweightbuffer[y][x] for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] # Compute per-pixel normals using directional derivatives normals = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Clamp indices for boundary handling xprev = max(0, x - 1) xnext = min(width - 1, x + 1) yprev = max(0, y - 1) ynext = min(height - 1, y + 1) dx = finalheight[y][xnext] - finalheight[y][xprev] dy = finalheight[ynext][x] - finalheight[yprev][x] length = (dxdx + dydy + 1.0)0.5 normals[y][x] = (-dy/length, -dx/length, 1.0/length) # Final Rendering with Phong shading finalimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): basecolor = colorbuffer[y][x] normal = normals[y][x] Ia, ka, Ip, kd = 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 0.8 lightdir = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) dot = normal[0]lightdir[0] + normal[1]lightdir[1] + normal[2]lightdir[2] factor = ka + kd max(0.0, dot) finalimage[y][x] = (basecolor[0]factor, basecolor[1]factor, basecolor[2]factor) return finalimage Parameters: Alpha (\alpha): Transparency value used in blending passes. Range: 0 < \alpha \le 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stroke Orientation Approximation: Bézier curves approximate, not interpolate, control points. The curve may not pass through control points B and C but is pulled in their direction. Curved strokes are only drawn where the underlying data attribute mapped to orientation varies rapidly. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of strokes and image resolution, as it requires three passes over the stroke list and one pass over the image for shading. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for three buffers (Color, Overlap, Height) of size proportional to the image resolution. Strengths: Avoids rendering expensive 3D mesh models of strokes while producing similar visual results (shadows/undulations) by using a 2D height field and lighting. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that stroke overlap can be approximated by alpha blending, which may not perfectly represent physical paint accumulation in all cases. Fast Paint Texture was introduced by Hertzmann in 2002 as a method to simulate the visual properties of paint on a canvas, specifically undulations and overlap shadows, without the computational overhead of 3D geometry. It is widely used in non-photorealistic volume rendering, particularly within the Visual Complexity (VC) algorithm, to create embossed strokes that enhance the perception of depth and texture in volumetric data. name: Illustrative and Non-Photorealistic Rendering Styles
head: Illustrative Volume Rendering, NPR Volume Visualization
body: This family encompasses methods that apply non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques to volumetric data to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth. Unlike traditional physics-based volume rendering, which often results in ambiguous structural interpretation due to the continuous nature of volumetric data, these methods decouple illumination from physical light transport to modulate color and opacity based on local volumetric properties. They are distinguished from surface-based NPR by deriving features from continuous 3D scalar or vector field properties rather than well-defined geometric surfaces. All methods in this family modify the standard volume rendering pipeline to incorporate stylized enhancements. The core mechanism involves transforming voxel properties (color and opacity) before compositing, based on an analysis of local volumetric features such as gradients, view direction, and light direction. 1. Feature Analysis: For each sample along a ray, local properties are computed. This typically includes the scalar value s, the gradient \nabla f (normalized to \nabla fn), and the view \vec{v} and light \vec{l} directions. 2. NPR Transformation: Mathematical functions of these properties modulate the base color c{base} and opacity \alpha derived from the transfer function. Common transformations include boundary enhancement (triggered by high gradient magnitude) and tone shading (based on dot products with light/view vectors). 3. Compositing: The transformed values are composited using standard front-to-back volume compositing: C{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} c{final,i} \cdot \alpha{final,i} \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{final,j}) All voxels contribute to the final image, but their contribution is stylized. A unified framework that augments physics-based rendering with NPR techniques like boundary detection and tone shading. It is chosen when a general enhancement of structural perception in scalar fields is needed without specific artistic constraints. Combines Phong shading, half-tone hatching, and silhouette outlines specifically for 3D vector fields (streamtapes). It is chosen for visualizing flow structures where avoiding complex line patterns on narrow objects is critical. Simulates artistic brush-strokes using user-defined directional texture maps and Perlin noise. It is chosen when a painterly, artistic effect is desired, requiring the simulation of stroke direction and width in 3D space. A strategy for classifying anatomical objects into focus, context, and container categories to apply specific styles (silhouettes, shading, transparency). It is chosen to reduce visual clutter and guide viewer attention in complex medical scenes. The concept of decoupling illumination from physical light transport in volume rendering was introduced to address the limitations of photorealistic rendering in conveying structural information. Volume Illustration, a foundational method in this family, was developed to enhance the perception of shape and depth in volumetric data by applying stylized enhancements such as silhouettes and tone shading. Subsequent methods like Illustrative Rendering and Volume Painting extended these principles to specific data types (vector fields) and artistic styles (brush strokes). The classification-based approach (Focus/Context/Container) was developed to manage visual hierarchy in complex anatomical visualizations.

name: Volume Illustration
head: Ebert and Rheingans volume illustration, Non-photorealistic Volume Rendering
body:
Volume Illustration is a method that augments a physics-based volume rendering pipeline with non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth relationships in volumetric data. It solves the problem of ambiguous structural interpretation in traditional physics-based renderings by applying stylized enhancements such as boundary detection, silhouettes, and tone shading. Unlike surface-based NPR, which relies on well-defined geometric surfaces, Volume Illustration determines features through the analysis of local volumetric properties that vary continuously throughout 3D space. It is distinguished from its siblings by its unified framework that decouples illumination from physical light transport, using mathematical functions of view, light, and scalar field properties to modulate color and opacity. The method operates by modifying the standard volume rendering pipeline. It begins with a base renderer that implements physics-based illumination (e.g., atmospheric or Phong illumination with linear accumulation). The core innovation lies in the transformation of voxel properties before compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field V(x,y,z), a transfer function TF mapping scalar values to base color c{base} and opacity \alpha, view direction \vec{v}, and light direction \vec{l}. Output: A final 2D image where voxels contribute to the final color via standard volume compositing, but with modified color and opacity values derived from NPR transformations. Data Structures: For each voxel sample i along a ray, the renderer computes or accesses: 1. Scalar Value: si = V(xi, yi, zi). 2. Gradient: 
abla fi = ( rac{\partial f}{\partial x},  rac{\partial f}{\partial y},  rac{\partial f}{\partial z})i. This is normalized to 
abla f{n,i} to serve as a proxy for surface normal orientation. 3. Minimal Change Direction: The direction of least variation in the scalar field, often derived from the gradient's orthogonal complement or principal component analysis of local neighborhoods. 4. Base Color and Opacity: c{base,i} and \alphai obtained from the transfer function applied to si. Numbered Steps: 1. Classification: Apply the transfer function to the voxel's scalar value to obtain initial color c{base} and opacity \alpha. 2. Feature Analysis: Compute local volumetric properties for the voxel: Calculate the gradient 
abla f. Determine the minimal change direction. Retrieve view direction \vec{v} and light direction \vec{l}. 3. NPR Transformation: Apply transformation functions to c{base} and \alpha using the properties from Step 2. These transformations encapsulate specific illustration techniques (e.g., boundary enhancement, tone shading). Note: The specific mathematical forms of these transformations vary by technique (see Subtopics). Common parameters include sample location, value, gradient magnitude, view angle, and light angle. 4. Compositing: Perform standard front-to-back volume compositing using the transformed color and opacity. The compositing equation remains unchanged from physics-based rendering: C{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} c{final,i} \cdot \alpha{final,i} \cdot \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{final,j}) All voxels in the volume still contribute to the final image. Formulas and Parameters: Gradient Normalization: 
abla fn =  rac{
abla f}{\|
abla f\|}. Boundary Enhancement: Often triggered when \|
abla f\| exceeds a threshold, increasing opacity or altering color to highlight edges. Tone Shading: Modulates brightness based on the dot product 
abla fn \cdot \vec{l} and 
abla fn \cdot \vec{v}. Parameters: Tunable parameters include thresholds for gradient magnitude, intensity of halos, and color blending factors. These parameters are dataset-dependent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeillustrationrender(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, transferfunction, lightdirection, cameraposition): """ Renders a single ray using the Volume Illustration framework. """ coloraccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaaccum = 0.0 # Iterate along the ray through the volume for sample in raysamples(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata): # 1. Classification scalarval = sample.value basecolor, basealpha = transferfunction(scalarval) # 2. Feature Analysis # Compute gradient at sample position using standard finite differences gradient = computegradient(sample.position, volumedata) # Guard against zero gradient to avoid division by zero gradmag = magnitude(gradient) if gradmag > 1e-6: gradientnorm = [g / gradmag for g in gradient] else: gradientnorm = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # View direction from sample to camera viewvec = [cameraposition[i] - sample.position[i] for i in range(3)] viewmag = magnitude(viewvec) if viewmag > 1e-6: viewdirection = [v / viewmag for v in viewvec] else: viewdirection = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 3. NPR Transformation # Apply transformations based on local properties. # Sources do not specify exact mathematical forms for all techniques. # Example: Boundary enhancement increases opacity if gradient magnitude exceeds a threshold. boundarythreshold = 0.5 # Dataset-dependent parameter if gradmag > boundarythreshold: finalalpha = basealpha 1.5 # Example enhancement factor finalcolor = [c 0.8 for c in basecolor] # Example darkening for edges else: finalalpha = basealpha finalcolor = basecolor # Example: Tone shading modulates color based on light and view directions # Dot product for diffuse lighting lightdot = sum(gradientnorm[i] lightdirection[i] for i in range(3)) viewdot = sum(gradientnorm[i] viewdirection[i] for i in range(3)) ambientlight = 0.2 diffusecoeff = 0.8 lightingfactor = ambientlight + diffusecoeff max(0.0, lightdot) finalcolor = [c lightingfactor for c in finalcolor] # 4. Compositing # Standard front-to-back volume compositing alphaterm = finalalpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) coloraccum = [coloraccum[i] + finalcolor[i] alphaterm for i in range(3)] alphaaccum = alphaaccum + finalalpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) if alphaaccum > 0.99: break return coloraccum Note: The specific transformation logic in Step 3 is highly variable depending on the chosen NPR technique (e.g., stippling, hatching, halos). The pseudocode above illustrates the pipeline structure. For specific techniques, refer to the Subtopics. A flexible framework associating user-defined interest labels with rendering techniques to allow variable detail levels and artistic styles per segment. It solves programmatic bias by prioritizing communicative abstraction over physical accuracy. Choose when different volume regions require distinct illustrative styles. Simulates traditional pen-and-ink hatching styles interactively using local volumetric properties for stroke placement. Choose when a hand-drawn, sketch-like appearance is desired. Generates stipple drawing effects by varying dot density and size based on scalar values and gradients. Choose for textured, illustrative appearances mimicking pen-and-ink stippling. Extracts and enhances contours and edges from volume data using gradient analysis. Choose when emphasizing structural boundaries and sketch-like lines is the primary goal. Adds glowing or darkened outlines around features to enhance depth perception and separation. Choose when distinguishing overlapping structures or enhancing depth cues is needed. Uses intermediate buffers storing geometric information to guide NPR techniques, adapted for volumes by deriving normals from gradients. Choose when precise geometric guidance is required for stylization. Provides the underlying physics-based illumination model that Volume Illustration augments. Choose as the foundational lighting layer before applying NPR effects. Modifies colors based on gradient orientation relative to view and light directions. Choose when enhancing structural cues through directional shading is required. Maintains global context while applying local NPR enhancements, often using focus+context techniques. Choose when balancing detailed local illustration with overall scene context is necessary. Enhances silhouettes and sketch lines by modulating transparency and color along boundaries. Choose when a pen-and-ink silhouette effect is desired. Renders fully opaque features with precise boundaries, often used with NPR to define clear extents. Choose when crisp, unambiguous feature boundaries are critical. Defines mathematical models for lighting and shading, decoupling illumination from physical transport. Choose when custom lighting behaviors are needed for illustrative purposes. Renders multiple objects with ghosting effects to show internal structure while maintaining external context. Choose when visualizing overlapping or nested volumetric objects requires transparency and depth layering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard volume rendering scales linearly with the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the volume dataset and temporary per-sample buffers for gradients and transformed properties. Measured Performance: Tested on datasets such as 256 	imes 256 	imes 128 abdominal CT volumes. Scaling: Scales linearly with resolution and dataset size. Interactive frame rates are achievable with optimization techniques like adaptive sampling or GPU acceleration. Strengths: Enhances structural perception significantly more than physics-based rendering alone; requires less manual tuning of transfer functions than traditional methods; flexible framework allowing combination of multiple NPR techniques. Limitations: Local implementation requires significant parameter tuning dependent on exact voxel intensity values and dataset characteristics; features are not as well-defined as in surface rendering, leading to potential ambiguity in feature detection. When to Use: When the goal is to create illustrative, textbook-quality images that emphasize structure and depth; when traditional volume rendering fails to convey internal structure clearly. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy is required; when real-time performance is critical and computational resources are limited; when the dataset has low contrast or noisy gradients that make feature detection unreliable. Volume Illustration was introduced by Penny Rheingans and David Ebert in 2000 (Vis '00) and published in TVCG in July 2001. It combines the familiarity of physics-approximated illumination with the expressive power of NPR techniques. The method was developed to address the limitations of traditional volume rendering in conveying complex 3D structures, particularly in medical imaging and scientific visualization. Popular styles include stippling, hatching, and silhouettes, drawing inspiration from the pen-and-ink family of illustration. The framework allows for the augmentation of a physics-based renderer with various NPR techniques, providing a unified approach to enhancing volumetric data. Advanced illumination and view-selection techniques for volume rendering and its application to medical imaging, http://hdl.handle.net/10803/371154, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration, https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstream/10012/1104/1/jlmckinl2002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Volume illustration: nonphotorealistic rendering of volume models..., https://www.csee.umbc.edu/~rheingan/pubs/volillus.tvcg01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 PDF Transfer Functions for Direct Volume Rendering, https://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/xmt/classes/slides/CS530/TransferFunctions.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Interest-Based NPR Toolkit
head: Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) Toolkit, Variable-Detail NPR
body: The Interest-Based NPR Toolkit is a flexible framework within the Volume Illustration pipeline that generates 2D non-photorealistic illustrations by associating user-defined interest labels with subsets of rendering techniques. It solves the problem of programmatic bias in automated visualization by allowing variable detail levels per segment, where different labels trigger different artistic styles simultaneously. Unlike physics-based rendering, it prioritizes communicative abstraction and artistic vision over physical accuracy. The method operates on an enriched model consisting of a geometric model (identified segments) and a structural model (associated interest labels). Inputs: 1. Geometric Model: A set of segments derived from segmentation. 2. Structural Model: A mapping from segment IDs to interest labels. 3. NPR Technique Library: A set of implemented techniques (greyscale shading, simple outlines, copper plate lines, short hatching lines). Outputs: A single 2D illustration image where each segment is rendered according to the NPR techniques associated with its interest label. Data Structures: Segment Map: A shadow volume recording the segment associated with each voxel. Label Map: A mapping SegmentID -> InterestLabel (integer). Technique Map: A mapping InterestLabel -> Subset{NPRTechnique} representing a one-to-many association. Numbered Steps: 1. Segmentation: Identify segments in the volume data. The system assumes all voxels in a segment are equally interesting (Single Interest Volume assumption). 2. Enrichment: Assign an interest label to each segment to augment the geometric model with structural information, forming an enriched model. 3. Association: The user defines a one-to-many mapping where each interest label is associated with a subset of available NPR techniques to avoid programmatic biases. 4. Rendering: Render all NPR techniques associated with all interest labels simultaneously to generate the final 2D illustration. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of Interest Labels: Defaults to 5, an arbitrary decision generalizable to any number. Default Label: All segments default to label 3 if not explicitly assigned. Technique Properties: Techniques are customizable to portray silhouettes, surface geometry, value, light and shade, and a primitive form of texture. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Segmentation avoids the algorithmic deficiencies of isosurfacing, such as poor topological properties and the need for prior dataset knowledge. Automatic label allocation is impossible because the system cannot infer the user's artistic vision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createblankimage(width, height): """Initialize a 2D buffer with zero values.""" return [[0.0] width for in range(height)] def applynprtechnique(voxels, techniquename, imagebuffer): """ Applies a specific NPR technique to the geometry defined by voxels. The sources do not provide the mathematical implementation for the NPR techniques. Standard operations would compute gradients, lighting, or line projections per voxel. """ # Apply technique rendering logic to voxels in imagebuffer pass def renderinterestbasednpr(segmentmap, labelmap, techniquemap, width, height): """ segmentmap: Dict mapping SegmentID to list of Voxels labelmap: Dict mapping SegmentID to InterestLabel (int) techniquemap: Dict mapping InterestLabel to List of Technique Strings """ outputimage = createblankimage(width, height) for segmentid, voxels in segmentmap.items(): interestlabel = labelmap[segmentid] techniques = techniquemap.get(interestlabel, []) for technique in techniques: applynprtechnique(voxels, technique, outputimage) return outputimage A generalization of binary segmentation where the level of interest in each segment is quantified by assigning an interest label. The relationship between segments and labels is many-to-one. The user assigns one of five labels to each segment in a synchronized structural view. This supports variable detail levels without enforcing a specific hierarchy. Complexity: Rendering uses a fast, pixel-based, geometric buffer approach to maintain interactivity. Memory: Supports single-level undo; multiple-level undo is a future improvement requiring extra memory or computation. Strengths: High flexibility, avoidance of programmatic biases, and creative artistic control. Limitations: Requires manual label assignment and technique mapping, making it non-fully automatic. Originated in the 2002 thesis "Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration" by J.L. McKinley. It builds on the concept of enriched models combining geometric and structural information. It follows the lead of Ebert and Rheingans in providing a flexible NPR toolkit. Volume Visualisation Via Variable-Detail Non-Photorealistic Illustration, https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/bitstream/10012/1104/1/jlmckinl2002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Illustrative Rendering
head: Illustrative visualization, Streamtape illustrative rendering
body: Illustrative rendering is a non-photorealistic visualization technique that combines Phong shading, half-tone hatching shadows, and silhouette outlines to enhance the depth and structural perception of volumetric objects, specifically streamtapes in 3D vector fields. It differs from procedural texture-based methods (e.g., Hummel et al.) by avoiding complex line patterns on narrow objects, which would increase visual complexity, instead relying on stylized lighting and edge detection to clarify geometry. Inputs: 3D vector field data. Pre-computed streamtapes (narrow tubular surfaces representing flow). Camera position and light direction. Outputs: Final illustrative image combining Phong shading, hatched shadows, and silhouette outlines. Data Structures: Framebuffer Object (FBO) for storing luminance. Color buffer for storing normalized normal vectors (RGB) and clamped depth (Alpha). Discontinuity mask buffer for silhouette detection. Parameters: Torsion normalization: \tau is normalized to [0, 1]. Streamtape width formula: \omega = 1.0 - \tau. Discontinuity threshold: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Phong Shading Pass: Render the streamtapes using standard Phong shading. Record the resulting luminance into a framebuffer object. 2. Hatched Shadow Generation: Generate a hatched shadow image using half-tone rendering styles to incorporate lighting and display depth/rotation information. 3. Silhouette Extraction Pass: Render the scene again to obtain silhouettes. Write the normalized normal direction of each fragment to the RGB channels of the output color. Clamp the depth value to [0, 1] and write it to the alpha channel. 4. Silhouette Detection: Check for discontinuities in the up, down, left, and right directions in image space on the output from Step 3. Mark pixels with large discontinuities as silhouette pixels. 5. Composition: Compose the hatched shadow image and the silhouette image with the Phong shaded image. 6. Coloring: Color the streamtapes either by cluster ID using a predefined color table or by local features such as curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def illustrativerender(streamtapes, camera, lightdir): # Step 1: Phong Shading Pass phongluminance = renderphongpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir) # Step 2: Hatched Shadow Generation hatchedshadow = renderhatchedshadowpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir) # Step 3: Silhouette Extraction Pass normaldepthbuffer = rendernormalsanddepthpass(streamtapes, camera) # Step 4: Silhouette Detection silhouettemask = detectsilhouettes(normaldepthbuffer) # Step 5: Composition finalimage = composeimages(phongluminance, hatchedshadow, silhouettemask) # Step 6: Coloring finalimage = applycoloring(finalimage, streamtapes) return finalimage def renderphongpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir): buffer = createbuffer(streamtapes.width, streamtapes.height) for frag in streamtapes.fragments: diffuse = max(dot(frag.normal, lightdir), 0.0) specular = pow(max(dot(reflect(-lightdir, frag.normal), camera.viewdir), 0.0), 32.0) lum = frag.basecolor (0.5 + 0.5 diffuse + 0.2 specular) buffer.set(frag.u, frag.v, lum) return buffer def renderhatchedshadowpass(streamtapes, camera, lightdir): buffer = createbuffer(streamtapes.width, streamtapes.height) for frag in streamtapes.fragments: intensity = max(dot(frag.normal, lightdir), 0.0) # Half-tone hatching style based on lighting and depth buffer.set(frag.u, frag.v, intensity) return buffer def rendernormalsanddepthpass(streamtapes, camera): buffer = createbuffer(streamtapes.width, streamtapes.height) for frag in streamtapes.fragments: norm = normalize(frag.normal) depth = clamp(frag.depth, 0.0, 1.0) buffer.setrgb(frag.u, frag.v, norm) buffer.seta(frag.u, frag.v, depth) return buffer def detectsilhouettes(buffer): mask = createbuffer(buffer.width, buffer.height) for y in range(buffer.height): for x in range(buffer.width): pixel = buffer.get(x, y) up = buffer.get(x, min(y + 1, buffer.height - 1)) down = buffer.get(x, max(y - 1, 0)) right = buffer.get(min(x + 1, buffer.width - 1), y) left = buffer.get(max(x - 1, 0), y) # Mark pixels with large discontinuities as silhouette pixels if (absdiff(pixel, up) > 0.1 or absdiff(pixel, down) > 0.1 or absdiff(pixel, right) > 0.1 or absdiff(pixel, left) > 0.1): mask.set(x, y, 1.0) return mask def composeimages(phong, shadow, silhouette): result = createbuffer(phong.width, phong.height) for y in range(phong.height): for x in range(phong.width): # Compose hatched shadow and silhouette with Phong shaded image base = phong.get(x, y) shadowval = shadow.get(x, y) sil = silhouette.get(x, y) result.set(x, y, base shadowval + sil 0.8) return result def applycoloring(image, streamtapes): for frag in streamtapes.fragments: # Assign colors by cluster ID or local features like curvature if frag.colormode == 'cluster': color = clustercolortable[frag.clusterid] else: color = curvaturetocolor(frag.curvature) image.set(frag.u, frag.v, color) return image def createbuffer(w, h): return [[None]w for in range(h)] def absdiff(a, b): return sum(abs(a[i]-b[i]) for i in range(len(a))) clustercolortable = {0: [1,0,0], 1: [0,1,0], 2: [0,0,1]} def curvaturetocolor(curv): return [curv, curv, curv] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: When local flow twists sharply, streamtape surfaces can self-intersect. This is addressed by normalizing torsion \tau to [0, 1] and setting width \omega = 1.0 - \tau. Visual Complexity: Procedural line stripes (e.g., Hummel et al.) are incompatible because streamtapes are narrow objects where complex patterns increase visual complexity. Time Complexity: Entropy field calculation and streamline generation are implemented on the GPU (CUDA) and complete within a few seconds for given flow datasets. K-means clustering and streamtape generation are implemented on the CPU. Memory: Requires 1.5GB of video memory for the GPU (tested on Geforce GTX 480) and 16GB system memory (tested on Xeon 5450). Strengths: Enhances depth and structural perception; reveals structural information via curvature-based coloring. Limitations: Not suitable for integral surfaces requiring adaptive line stripes; limited to narrow objects like streamtapes. The method was introduced in 2011 as part of an illustrative visualization framework for 3D vector fields. It was implemented on the GPU and used to visualize streamtapes generated from vector field data. The half-tone rendering style references the work of Freudenberg et al. [FMS01] for an overview of half-tone rendering techniques. An Illustrative Visualization Framework for 3D Vector Fields, http://vis.cs.ucdavis.edu/papers/pg2011paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Volume Painting
head: Artistic brush-stroke volume rendering, Non-photorealistic volume rendering with brush strokes
body: Volume Painting is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that visualizes 3D volume datasets with artistic brush-strokes controlled by user-defined directional texture maps. It solves the problem of generating painterly, stylized 3D imagery by combining volumetric ray casting with vector fields derived from texture maps to simulate traditional painting strokes. Unlike general volume rendering which produces photorealistic results, Volume Painting produces artistic effects by using noise and vector fields to define stroke direction and width. It builds on Illustrative and Non-Photorealistic Rendering Styles by focusing specifically on brush-stroke simulation in 3D space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular mesh model (created in Alias Maya or Topmod), a user-defined directional texture map (vector field), and camera parameters. Output: A 2D image with artistic brush-stroke effects. Data Structures: The volume dataset is a 3D voxel array. The file structure contains four components per voxel: 1. Voxel Index: Identifier for the voxel. 2. Signed Distance Field (SDF): A float value. Positive values indicate outside the surface, negative values indicate inside, and zero indicates the boundary. The absolute value is the distance to the closest surface point. 3. Color: RGB value derived from UV texture coordinates. 4. Directional Information: Vector data derived from UV texture coordinates. Voxelization (Preprocessing): 1. Generate the SDF for the input mesh. The sign is determined by the dot product of the surface normal and the vector from the voxel center to the closest surface point. 2. Assign color and directional values to each voxel by accessing UV texture coordinates based on the quadratic equation for triangles. 3. Convert the SDF to density information using a transfer function. Volume Ray Casting and Surface Estimation: 1. Emit rays from the camera through the voxel block. 2. Instead of standard compositing, use the bisection method to find the surface boundary. Divide the distance between temporary exterior (positive SDF) and interior (negative SDF) intersection points in half. Place the surface point between them until the distance is less than a given threshold. 3. Estimate the real boundary by adding the voxel density to the value of Perlin noise applied with Line Integral Convolution (LIC) to create a new value. 4. Check if the new value is within defined threshold parameters to determine the surface point \tilde{p}. Gradient Estimation: Two methods are described for estimating the gradient vector \vec{N} = [Nx, Ny, Nz]: Central Difference Method: Calculate the gradient from the voxel density function f(x,y,z): Nx = f(x-1, y, z) - f(x+1, y, z) Ny = f(x, y-1, z) - f(x, y+1, z) Nz = f(x, y, z-1) - f(x, y, z+1) This method requires the derivative of voxel densities to exist. Geo-Dome Method: Position a Geo-Dome (spherical geometry with unit-length vertices) at the surface point. Calculate the gradient \nabla f as: \nabla f \approx \sum{i=0}^{K} ai \vec{v}i where \vec{v}i are the Geo-Dome vertices and ai = 1 if f(\vec{v}i + p) \ge 0 (outside) and ai = 0 otherwise (inside). Sum the outside vectors and subtract the inside vectors. Normalize the result. Rotate the Geo-Dome around a random axis with random magnitude to remove artifacts caused by limited vertex count. Brush-Stroke Noise Generation: 1. Normalize the surface point P to get h(p) = \text{normalize}(P(wp)), where w is the frequency. 2. Compute the noise value g(p): g(p) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N} h(pi) where P() is the Perlin noise function, p is the surface point, pi are sample positions along the brush-stroke direction \vec{v}, and N is the number of samples. Opacity Calculation: The opacity \alpha is computed based on the desired structure: 1. Solid Internal Structure: \alpha = g(p) + f(p) 2. Empty Inside: \alpha = g(p) + |f(p) - a| where a is an arbitrary real number that changes the thickness of the painted area, and f(p) normalizes the signed distance field between 0 and 1. The surface point \tilde{p} is estimated by determining if \alpha is larger than a given threshold. Illumination and Shading: 1. Convolve the color information of the surface point \tilde{p} along the brush-stroke direction \vec{v} to get the diffuse color C(\tilde{p}). 2. Apply the Phong illumination model: I = ka C(\tilde{p}) + \sum{i=1}^{n} [kd C(\tilde{p})(\vec{N} \cdot \vec{L}i) + ks Os (\vec{R}i \cdot \vec{V}n)] where I is the illumination color, ka, kd, ks are ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients, \vec{L}i are light vectors, \vec{R}i are reflection vectors, \vec{V}n is the view vector, and Os is the specular exponent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumepainting(camerarays, volumedataset, texturemap, threshold): """ Renders a volume dataset with artistic brush strokes. Args: camerarays: List of rays from camera. volumedataset: 3D voxel array with SDF, color, direction. texturemap: User-defined directional texture map. threshold: Threshold for surface boundary detection. Returns: Image buffer. """ image = createemptyimage() for ray in camerarays: # 1. Volume Ray Casting with Bisection # Find initial exterior (possdf) and interior (negsdf) points possdf, negsdf = findrayvoxelintersections(ray, volumedataset) # Bisection to find precise boundary while abs(possdf - negsdf) > threshold: mid = (possdf + negsdf) / 2.0 sdfval = samplesdf(ray, mid, volumedataset) if sdfval > 0: possdf = mid else: negsdf = mid surfacepoint = (possdf + negsdf) / 2.0 sdfval = samplesdf(ray, surfacepoint, volumedataset) # 2. Gradient Estimation (Geo-Dome Method preferred for robustness) gradient = estimategradientgeodome(surfacepoint, volumedataset) # 3. Brush-Stroke Noise Generation # Get brush direction from texture map at surface point brushdirection = getdirectionfromtexture(surfacepoint, texturemap) # Sample Perlin noise along brush direction noisesamples = [] for i in range(Nsamples): samplepos = surfacepoint + i brushdirection # Normalize position scaled by frequency w hp = normalize(samplepos frequency) noiseval = perlinnoise(hp) noisesamples.append(noiseval) gp = sum(noisesamples) / len(noisesamples) # 4. Opacity Calculation # Normalize SDF between 0 and 1 fp = normalizesdf(sdfval) # Choose structure type (Solid or Empty) # For this example, assuming Solid Internal Structure alpha = gp + fp # 5. Surface Point Estimation if alpha > threshold: # 6. Illumination and Shading # Convolve color along brush direction color = convolvecoloralongdirection(surfacepoint, brushdirection, volumedataset) # Phong shading lightcontrib = 0.0 for light in scenelights: L = normalize(light.position - surfacepoint) R = reflect(-L, gradient) V = normalize(camera.position - surfacepoint) lightcontrib += kd color dot(gradient, L) + ks specularexponent dot(R, V) illumination = ka color + lightcontrib # Composite into image image.setpixel(ray.pixelindex, illumination) else: image.setpixel(ray.pixelindex, backgroundcolor) return image Parameters: Voxel Array Size: 30x30x30, 50x50x50, or the maximum size allowed by physical memory. Threshold parameters: Used to determine if the calculated new value defines the surface boundary. Frequency of Perlin noise: Adjusts the width of the brush-stroke. Vector field: Obtained from a user-defined texture map, controls the direction and style of the brush-stroke. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Estimation: The Central Difference Method fails if the derivative of voxel densities does not exist. The Geo-Dome method is used as an alternative but may require rotation to remove artifacts from limited vertex count. Memory Usage: Larger voxel sizes generate higher quality images but require large amounts of physical memory and longer processing times. Standard Compositing: The method explicitly avoids standard compositing (C{out} = C{in} + (1 - \alpha{in})Ci) which uses early termination at \alpha{in} = 0.9999, in favor of the bisection method for boundary detection. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but processing time increases with voxel array size. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the voxel array size. Limited by physical memory of the processing computer. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows intuitive adjustment of brush-stroke direction via texture maps; simulates artistic painterly effects in 3D space; can be animated by simulating the vector field. Limitations: Requires significant memory for large voxel arrays; relies on user-defined texture maps for style control; not photorealistic. When to use: When artistic, non-photorealistic, brush-stroke style visualization of 3D volume data is desired. When not to use: When photorealistic rendering is required. Volume Painting was proposed by Ebert and Rheingans [13] (Note: The source text attributes the method to the author of the thesis, citing Ebert and Rheingans as related work for LIC, but the thesis itself presents the Volume Painting method). name: Illustrative Style Selection and Attribute Tuning
head: Object Classification for Illustrative Rendering, Style Selection Strategy
body: This method provides a strategy for classifying anatomical objects into focus, context, and container categories to select appropriate rendering styles, shading, transparency, color, and silhouettes for expressive combined illustrations. It solves the problem of visual clutter and ambiguity in complex volume-rendered scenes by establishing a visual hierarchy that guides the viewer's attention to high-interest structures while maintaining spatial context. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Volume Illustration by explicitly defining a tripartite classification system (focus/context/container) and mapping specific stylistic attributes (silhouette thickness, color saturation, shading type) to these roles rather than relying solely on geometric stylization or texture mapping. The method operates on a set of segmented objects extracted from medical scan data. It assumes the input includes object segmentation labels and optionally geometric properties (curvature, size). The output is a rendered image where each object is styled according to its assigned category. Object List: A collection of objects, each with properties: category: Enum {FOCUS, CONTEXT, CONTAINER}. doi: Degree of Interest (float, 0.0 to 1.0), where 1.0 is highest interest. geometrytype: Enum {POINTBASED, POLYGONAL}. curvaturevariance: Float (optional, for style selection). nestinglevel: Integer (distance from viewer or hierarchical depth). 1. Classify Objects: Assign each object to one of three categories: Focus: Objects of highest interest (e.g., internal organs like kidney, heart, colon). Context: Surrounding or neighboring objects that provide spatial reference. Container: Objects that enclose a subset of focus and context objects (e.g., skin). The current implementation typically defines only one container object. 2. Select Rendering Style: Choose between point-based and polygonal-based rendering based on object properties: Use Point-Based Algorithm if: Segmentation is provided. Object is of moderate or large size. Object does not exhibit extreme curvature variances (e.g., most internal organs). Object is a Focus object. Use Polygonal-Based Rendering if: Object is a Container. Object has sharp edges. Object is a relatively thin structure. Note: Point-based rendering avoids the triangulation step required by polygonal methods. 3. Select Shading Style: Assign shading to enhance distinction between categories: Container: Standard or discrete shading. Context: Cool-to-warm shaded. This style makes context objects clear and distinctive. Focus: Halftoning. This is particularly effective for large, innermost organs. Constraint: Do not apply the same shading style to both container and context objects, as they become indistinguishable. 4. Set Degree of Transparency: Apply transparency based on category and Degree of Interest (doi): Container: Must be very translucent. Focus: Rendered almost or totally opaque. Context and other non-container objects: Apply the degree of interest concept (doi). Objects at the same nesting level are assigned transparencies inversely proportional to their doi. Formula: Let T be transparency, doi be degree of interest. For objects at the same nesting level, T \propto \frac{1}{doi}. Focus objects have doi \approx 1.0, thus T \approx 0 (opaque). 5. Set Color: Assign colors to emphasize hierarchy: Container: Light skin-like colors. This produces acceptable visual effects even if the container is not skin. Focus: Fully saturated, preferably warm colors (e.g., red or orange). Context: Cooler colors than focus objects. 6. Set Silhouette: Render silhouettes to improve expressiveness and shape perception: Focus and Context: Always render with outlined silhouettes. Container: May be rendered without silhouettes. Silhouette Thickness: Proportional to the degree of object importance. Focus objects receive thicker silhouettes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyillustrativestyle(objectlist): """ Applies illustrative style selection and attribute tuning to a list of objects. Assumes objectlist contains objects with properties: category, doi, geometry, curvaturevariance. """ for obj in objectlist: # Step 1: Classification is assumed to be pre-computed based on semantic labels # obj.category is one of: 'FOCUS', 'CONTEXT', 'CONTAINER' # Step 2: Select Rendering Style if obj.category == 'CONTAINER': obj.renderingstyle = 'POLYGONAL' elif obj.category == 'FOCUS': # Point-based preferred for focus objects of moderate/large size without extreme curvature if obj.size >= THRESHOLDMODERATE and obj.curvaturevariance < THRESHOLDEXTREME: obj.renderingstyle = 'POINTBASED' else: obj.renderingstyle = 'POLYGONAL' else: # CONTEXT # Context objects often have sharp edges or are thin structures in this context if obj.hassharpedges or obj.isthin: obj.renderingstyle = 'POLYGONAL' else: obj.renderingstyle = 'POINTBASED' # Fallback, though context often benefits from polygonal for sharpness # Step 3: Select Shading Style if obj.category == 'CONTAINER': obj.shadingstyle = 'STANDARD' elif obj.category == 'CONTEXT': obj.shadingstyle = 'COOLTOWARM' elif obj.category == 'FOCUS': obj.shadingstyle = 'HALFTONING' # Step 4: Set Degree of Transparency if obj.category == 'CONTAINER': obj.transparency = 0.9 # Very translucent elif obj.category == 'FOCUS': obj.transparency = 0.0 # Almost or totally opaque else: # Inverse proportionality to doi for same nesting level # Note: In practice, this requires normalizing doi within the nesting level # For simplicity, assuming doi is normalized 0-1 obj.transparency = 1.0 - obj.doi # Step 5: Set Color if obj.category == 'CONTAINER': obj.color = LIGHTSKINCOLOR elif obj.category == 'FOCUS': obj.color = WARMSATURATEDCOLOR # e.g., Red or Orange else: # CONTEXT obj.color = COOLERCOLOR # Step 6: Set Silhouette if obj.category in ['FOCUS', 'CONTEXT']: obj.hassilhouette = True # Thickness proportional to importance (doi) obj.silhouettethickness = obj.doi MAXTHICKNESS else: # CONTAINER obj.hassilhouette = False obj.silhouettethickness = 0 Thresholds: THRESHOLDMODERATE, THRESHOLDEXTREME, MAXTHICKNESS are implementation-specific constants not defined in the source. Nesting Level: The transparency formula requires objects to be grouped by nesting level. If nesting levels are not explicitly defined, a fallback strategy (e.g., global doi normalization) must be used. Container Definition: The source notes that only one container object is typically defined (skin). If multiple containers exist, the "very translucent" rule applies to all. Curvature Variance: Extreme curvature variances disqualify an object from point-based rendering, even if it is a focus object. This prevents artifacts on highly irregular surfaces. Time Complexity: Depends on the rendering style. Point-based rendering avoids triangulation, potentially reducing preprocessing time for large datasets. Polygonal rendering requires mesh generation, which is more expensive. Memory Complexity: Point-based methods may require storing more points if high resolution is needed, while polygonal methods store mesh topology. Strengths: Provides a clear visual hierarchy. Enhances shape perception through silhouettes. Distinguishes between object types via color and shading. Limitations: Relies on accurate segmentation and classification. The "one container" assumption may not hold for all anatomical scenes. When to Use: Medical visualization where specific organs (focus) need to be highlighted against surrounding structures (context) and body surface (container). When Not to Use: Scenes without clear hierarchical relationships or where photorealism is preferred over illustrative clarity. The method originates from work on expressive anatomical illustrations based on scanned patient data, presented in the context of computer and robot-assisted surgery. It builds on the concept of Degree of Interest (doi) [32] for transparency control. The approach integrates point-based and polygonal rendering algorithms with various shading styles (standard, cool-to-warm, halftoning) to create a flexible illustration system. It was tested with diverse models extracted from segmentation data. name: CartoonVolumeStyle
head: X3D CartoonVolumeStyle, flat-shaded volume stylization
body: CartoonVolumeStyle is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that produces a cel-shaded appearance by mapping surface normal orientations to a discrete set of flat colors. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric structure without the smooth gradients of photorealistic rendering, instead using distinct color bands to emphasize shape and boundaries. It differs from BoundaryEnhancementVolumeStyle by relying on normal-view angle quantization rather than gradient magnitude, and from Stylization and Pattern Generation by using a fixed HSV-based interpolation scheme for its color palette. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (scalar field) and its associated surface normals. Output: A 2D image where each pixel is assigned one of N discrete colors based on the angle between the local surface normal and the view direction. Data Structures: Surface Normals: A 3D texture (X3DTexture3DNode) with at least 3 components (RGB representing X, Y, Z). Dimensions must match the source volume data. Colors: SFColorRGBA fields for parallelColor and orthogonalColor. Parameters: colorSteps (integer), parallelColor, orthogonalColor, surfaceNormals. Parameters: parallelColor: Default (0, 0, 0, 1). Color for normals orthogonal to the viewer (surface plane parallel to view direction). orthogonalColor: Default (1, 1, 1, 1). Color for normals parallel to the viewer (surface plane orthogonal to view direction). colorSteps: Default 4, range [1, 64]. Number of distinct color bands. surfaceNormals: Default NULL. If missing, the implementation must interpolate, average, or algorithmically generate normals from the source data. Algorithm: 1. Normal Retrieval: For each voxel, retrieve the surface normal vector \mathbf{n} from the surfaceNormals texture. If surfaceNormals is null, compute \mathbf{n} from the gradient of the scalar field. 2. Angle Calculation: Calculate the angle \theta between the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the view direction vector \mathbf{v} (pointing from the surface to the camera). \theta = \arccos(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) Note: \mathbf{v} must be normalized. The dot product assumes \mathbf{n} and \mathbf{v} are unit vectors. 3. Back-face Culling: If \theta > \pi/2 (i.e., the dot product is negative, meaning the surface is back-facing), the voxel is not rendered. No color is calculated. 4. Color Band Determination: If colorSteps == 1, the color is orthogonalColor for all visible surfaces. If colorSteps > 1: Divide the valid angle range [0, \pi/2] into colorSteps equal intervals. The width of each interval is \Delta \theta = \frac{\pi}{2 \cdot \text{colorSteps}}. The first interval [0, \Delta \theta) uses orthogonalColor. The last interval [\frac{\pi}{2} - \Delta \theta, \frac{\pi}{2}] uses parallelColor. For intermediate intervals i (where 1 \le i < \text{colorSteps} - 1), calculate the midpoint angle \thetai: \thetai = i \cdot \Delta \theta + \frac{\Delta \theta}{2} Determine the interpolation factor t for this midpoint relative to the full range [0, \pi/2]: t = \frac{\thetai}{\pi/2} = \frac{2 \thetai}{\pi} Note: The specification states colors are interpolated between parallelColor and orthogonalColor. Based on the example where \theta=0 yields orthogonalColor (1,1,1,1) and \theta=\pi/2 yields parallelColor (0,0,0,1), t=0 corresponds to orthogonalColor and t=1 corresponds to parallelColor. 5. Color Interpolation: Convert parallelColor and orthogonalColor to HSV. Interpolate the Hue, Saturation, and Value components linearly using t. Interpolate the Alpha component linearly using t. Convert the resulting HSV back to RGB. Assign this color to the voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cartoonvolumestyle(volumedata, surfacenormals, viewdirection, parallelcolor, orthogonalcolor, colorsteps): """ Renders a volume using the CartoonVolumeStyle method. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values (used only if surfacenormals is None). surfacenormals: 3D array of vectors (Nx, Ny, Nz) matching volume dimensions. viewdirection: 3D vector (normalized) pointing from surface to camera. parallelcolor: Tuple (R, G, B, A) for back-facing/parallel normals. orthogonalcolor: Tuple (R, G, B, A) for front-facing/orthogonal normals. colorsteps: Integer number of color bands. Returns: 2D image array. """ # 1. Handle missing normals if surfacenormals is None: # Implementation detail: Compute normals from volumedata gradient # This is a placeholder for the algorithmic generation mentioned in surfacenormals = computenormalsfromvolume(volumedata) # Precompute HSV for colors phsv = rgbtohsv(parallelcolor) ohsv = rgbtohsv(orthogonalcolor) # 2. Determine color bands if colorsteps == 1: finalcolor = orthogonalcolor # No interpolation needed bands = [] else: deltatheta = (math.pi / 2) / colorsteps bands = [] # First band: orthogonalColor bands.append({'range': (0, deltatheta), 'color': orthogonalcolor}) # Intermediate bands for i in range(1, colorsteps - 1): midtheta = i deltatheta + deltatheta / 2 t = (2 midtheta) / math.pi # Interpolate HSV h = lerp(phsv[0], ohsv[0], t) s = lerp(phsv[1], ohsv[1], t) v = lerp(phsv[2], ohsv[2], t) a = lerp(parallelcolor[3], orthogonalcolor[3], t) bands.append({'range': (i deltatheta, (i + 1) deltatheta), 'color': hsvtorgb((h, s, v, a))}) # Last band: parallelColor bands.append({'range': ((colorsteps - 1) deltatheta, math.pi / 2), 'color': parallelcolor}) # 3. Render image = emptyimage() for each voxel in volume: n = surfacenormals[voxel] # Normalize normal if not already n = normalize(n) # Calculate angle with view direction # Note: viewdirection is from surface to camera. # Dot product n. v gives cos(theta) costheta = dot(n, viewdirection) # Back-face culling if costheta <= 0: continue # No color calculated theta = acos(costheta) # Find band color = orthogonalcolor # Default fallback for band in bands: if band['range'][0] <= theta < band['range'][1]: color = band['color'] break # Handle edge case for last band inclusive upper bound if theta == math.pi / 2: color = parallelcolor break image[voxel] = color return image def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def rgbtohsv(color): # Standard RGB to HSV conversion r, g, b, a = color maxc = max(r, g, b) minc = min(r, g, b) diff = maxc - minc if diff == 0: h = 0 elif maxc == r: h = 60 (((g - b) / diff) % 6) elif maxc == g: h = 60 (((b - r) / diff) + 2) else: h = 60 (((r - g) / diff) + 4) s = 0 if maxc == 0 else diff / maxc v = maxc return (h, s, v, a) def hsvtorgb(hsv): h, s, v, a = hsv c = v s x = c (1 - abs((h / 60) % 2 - 1)) m = v - c if 0 <= h < 60: r, g, b = c, x, 0 elif 60 <= h < 120: r, g, b = x, c, 0 elif 120 <= h < 180: r, g, b = 0, c, x elif 180 <= h < 240: r, g, b = 0, x, c elif 240 <= h < 300: r, g, b = x, 0, c else: r, g, b = c, 0, x return (r + m, g + m, b + m, a) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back-facing surfaces: Surfaces with \theta > \pi/2 are completely invisible. This can lead to holes in the volume visualization if the view direction changes significantly. Normal Accuracy: If surfaceNormals is not provided, the quality of the stylization depends entirely on the gradient estimation algorithm. Noisy data will result in noisy normal vectors and erratic color banding. ColorSteps=1: Results in a single-color rendering using orthogonalColor. No shading effect is visible. HSV Interpolation: Interpolating in HSV space can produce unexpected hues if the start and end colors have very different hues (e.g., red to blue might pass through purple). This is a known artifact of HSV interpolation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, assuming normal lookup is O(1). If normals must be computed, it adds the cost of gradient calculation. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the volume and normal textures. Performance: Generally fast as it avoids complex lighting calculations and ray marching integration for color. The primary cost is the normal lookup and color band lookup. Strengths: Produces a clear, stylized look that emphasizes shape and boundaries. Simple to implement. Limitations: Lacks depth cues provided by smooth shading. Back-face culling can obscure internal structures if not handled carefully. The discrete color bands can appear jagged if the resolution is low. When to use: When a non-photorealistic, illustrative style is desired, such as in educational visualizations or artistic representations of medical data. When not to use: When photorealism or subtle intensity variations are required. CartoonVolumeStyle is defined in the X3D standard specification for volume rendering styles. It was developed as part of the X3D amendment for medical image volume rendering, segmentation, and registration. The style is part of the X3D Volume Rendering API, providing a standardized way to apply cel-shading effects to volumetric data. name: Steamlet Emission
head: Particle Systems for Volume, Steam Rendering
body: Steamlet Emission is a technique for visualizing 3D data by emitting and propagating particles, referred to as "steamlets," through the volume to directly visualize exterior structure without surface extraction. It differs from traditional ray casting by replacing continuous volume integration with a discrete particle system approach, simulating phenomena like advection and diffusion. This method is particularly noted for its ability to obscure internal details while highlighting boundaries, making it suitable for illustrative visualization but potentially unsuitable for volumes with fuzzy boundaries or intricate external details where precise structural fidelity is required. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data), a set of emission strategies (uniform, density-based, or gradient-based), and optical properties for the steamlets (color, opacity, velocity). Output: A 2D image produced by integrating steamlet contributions along viewing rays. Data Structures: Each steamlet is represented as a particle with the following fields: position: 3D vector (x, y, z) indicating location within the volume. velocity: 3D vector (vx, vy, vz) indicating direction and speed of propagation. opticalproperties: Scalar or vector values defining color and opacity contribution. Steps: 1. Emission: Emit a multitude of steamlets from various points within the volume. The distribution strategy is chosen from the following options: Uniform Distribution: Steamlets are emitted evenly across the volume. Density-Based Distribution: More steamlets are emitted from regions of low density to enhance visibility in sparse areas. Gradient-Based Distribution: Steamlets are emitted along gradients to highlight boundaries and feature edges. 2. Propagation (Simulation): Simulate the movement of steamlets using a particle system approach. Each steamlet updates its position based on its velocity, simulating simple phenomena such as advection and diffusion. In a standard implementation, this involves iterating through time steps t, updating position P{t+1} = Pt + Vt \cdot \Delta t, and potentially applying diffusion noise to the velocity or position to simulate the "steam" effect. 3. Integration: Integrate the contributions of all steamlets along viewing rays to produce the initial image. This involves accumulating the color and opacity values of each steamlet intersected by a ray. 4. Compositing: Apply compositing techniques, such as front-to-back or back-to-front compositing, to ensure correct blending of steamlet contributions. Front-to-back compositing is typically preferred for alpha-blended steamlets to handle transparency correctly: C{out} = C{in} + C{steam} \cdot \alpha{steam} \cdot (1 - \alpha{accumulated}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersteamletemission(volumedata, camera, emissionstrategy): """ Renders a volume using Steamlet Emission. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. camera: Camera object with ray generation function. emissionstrategy: Enum or string ('uniform', 'density', 'gradient'). Returns: 2D image array. """ # 1. Emit Steamlets steamlets = [] volumebounds = getvolumebounds(volumedata) if emissionstrategy == 'uniform': # Emit N particles uniformly distributed in volumebounds steamlets = emituniform(volumebounds, count=N) elif emissionstrategy == 'density': # Emit more particles in low-density regions # Implementation: Sample volume, invert density, use as probability distribution steamlets = emitdensitybased(volumedata, volumebounds, count=N) elif emissionstrategy == 'gradient': # Emit particles along gradients # Implementation: Compute gradient field, emit along gradient vectors steamlets = emitgradientbased(volumedata, volumebounds, count=N) # 2. Propagate Steamlets (Simplified single-step for illustration) # In practice, this may involve multiple time steps for particle in steamlets: particle.position += particle.velocity deltatime # Apply diffusion/advection noise if simulating physical steam behavior particle.velocity += getdiffusionnoise(particle.position) # 3. Integrate and Composite imagewidth, imageheight = camera.resolution image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): ray = camera.generateray(x, y) accumulatedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedalpha = 0.0 # Sort steamlets by distance along ray for front-to-back compositing intersectingparticles = getintersectingparticles(ray, steamlets) intersectingparticles.sort(key=lambda p: distance(ray.origin, p.position)) for particle in intersectingparticles: # Sample particle optical properties at intersection # Assuming particle has a spatial extent or is a point sample color = particle.color alpha = particle.opacity # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = Cin + Cparticle alphaparticle (1 - alphaaccumulated) contribution = color alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += contribution accumulatedalpha += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) # Break if fully opaque if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break image[y, x] = accumulatedcolor return image Parameters: N: Number of steamlets. Not given in the sources. deltatime: Time step for propagation. Not given in the sources. emissionstrategy: Determines particle distribution. Options: 'uniform', 'density', 'gradient'. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fuzzy Boundaries: The method is unsuitable for visualizing volumes with fuzzy boundaries or intricate external details, as it directly visualizes exterior structure without surface extraction. Performance: The particle system approach is typically faster than ray casting but may still be unsuitable for real-time applications depending on the number of steamlets and complexity of propagation. Distribution Bias: Choosing an inappropriate emission strategy (e.g., uniform for sparse data) can lead to obscure or uninformative visualizations. Time Complexity: Typically faster than ray casting, but performance depends on the number of steamlets and the complexity of the propagation simulation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of steamlets stored in memory. Each steamlet requires storage for position, velocity, and optical properties. Strengths: Directly visualizes exterior structure without surface extraction; can simulate phenomena like advection and diffusion; offers editability of individual components. Limitations: Unsuitable for volumes with fuzzy boundaries or intricate external details; may produce obscure visualizations if distribution is not carefully chosen. When to Use: When an illustrative, obscured view of the volume's exterior structure is desired, or when simulating steam-like phenomena is beneficial. When Not to Use: When precise structural fidelity of fuzzy boundaries or intricate external details is required. Steamlet Emission, also known as Steam Rendering or Particle Systems for Volume, is a technique for visualizing 3D data by emitting and propagating particles through the volume. It was developed as an alternative to traditional surface rendering methods that rely on extracting surfaces from the data. The technique is particularly relevant in fields such as industrial inspection, molecular modeling, and geological visualization, where understanding the exterior structure of volumetric data is crucial.
