name: Silhouette, Outline and Edge Enhancement
head: Silhouette, Outline and Edge Enhancement
body: Silhouette, Outline and Edge Enhancement is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques designed to enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly rendering edges, silhouettes, or topological boundaries as visual cues. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies on opacity and color to imply form, these methods detect geometric or scalar discontinuities and render them as distinct outlines to define object boundaries, internal structures, or topological relationships. This family is distinguished from its siblings by its focus on explicit edge extraction and rendering strategies, ranging from object-space silhouette extraction to image-space depth discontinuity detection and topological landscape mapping. The family shares the fundamental goal of enhancing perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. Common mechanisms include: 1. Edge Detection: Identifying boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradients, Laplacian of Gaussian) or image-space properties (depth, normal discontinuities). 2. Line Rendering: Converting detected edges into line primitives (strips, segments) or stylized strokes. This method creates a sketch-like appearance by rendering volume features as lines or edges, making non-silhouette regions transparent and applying shadows based on the original volume's opacity. It differs from standard illustrative rendering by aggressively modulating opacity based on silhouette strength to abstract continuous volumetric data into discrete, sketch-like outlines, rather than preserving the full volumetric density structure. Outline and Contour Generation is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly rendering edges, silhouettes, or topological boundaries as line primitives or stylized strokes. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies on opacity and color to imply form, these methods detect geometric or scalar discontinuities and render them as distinct visual cues to define object boundaries, internal structures, or topological relationships. This family is distinguished from its siblings by its focus on explicit edge extraction and rendering strategies, ranging from object-space silhouette extraction to image-space depth discontinuity detection and topological landscape mapping. Line and Edge Detection is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly detecting and rendering edges, silhouettes, or structural boundaries within volumetric data. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection by focusing on boundary emphasis and structural outlines rather than flow-aligned strokes, and from LOG-based Silhouette Detection by employing diverse detection mechanisms ranging from gradient-based particle tracing to user-defined interactive selection. A visualization method useful for emphasizing object contour shapes that are difficult to grasp with standard Volume Rendering. Set opacity at edge parts of each object region and set the interior of the region to transparent. If the magnitude of the normal vector of a voxel is below a threshold, set the voxel's opacity to 0 to display local edges. Performs enhancements only within a specified region by calculating an enhancement scalar e based on the position relative to an Enhancement Center of Interest (ECOI). e = k{rs} (\nabla{fn} \cdot E)^{k{re}}, where E = ((eye - ECOI)/\|(eye - ECOI)\|), k{rs} is enhancement maximum, k{re} is fall-off power. k{re}: Enhancement fall-off power. Small values (<2) decrease gradually; large values (20, 50) produce sharp, focused regions. k{rs}: Enhancement maximum. ECOI: Enhancement center of interest, a point in the dataset. The concept of silhouette and edge enhancement in volume rendering emerged from the need to apply technical illustration principles to volumetric data. Traditional volume rendering often results in images where internal structures are obscured by overlying surfaces, making it difficult to perceive object contours. Local Edge Rendering was introduced to address this by setting opacity to zero for voxels whose normal vector magnitude is below a threshold, thereby displaying only local edges. Regional Enhancement was adapted from technical illustration practices where illustrators selectively add detail to emphasize specific areas. This approach allows users to specify an Enhancement Center of Interest (ECOI) and parameters for enhancement maximum and fall-off power to draw attention to important regions within the image, such as specific organs in medical CT data. ボリュームデータの可視化技術の説明 | TomoShop - 高性能次..., https://www.ikeda-shoponline.com/ctsoft/technicalinformation/volumevisual/, fetched 2026-10-30 PDF Volume illustration: nonphotorealistic rendering of volume models..., https://www.csee.umbc.edu/~rheingan/pubs/volillus.tvcg01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Sketch Rendering via Silhouette Transparency
head: Volume Sketching, Volumetric Sketch Lines
body:
This method creates a sketch-like appearance by rendering volume features as lines or edges, making non-silhouette regions transparent and applying shadows based on the original volume's opacity. It differs from standard illustrative rendering by aggressively modulating opacity based on silhouette strength to abstract continuous volumetric data into discrete, sketch-like outlines, rather than preserving the full volumetric density structure. Inputs: Volume scalar field and view direction V{dir}. Light direction L{dir}. Sketch color (e.g., white or black). Original volume opacity \alpha{orig} computed from the transfer function and scalar values. Parameters: k{sc} (silhouette center), k{ss} (silhouette spread), k{se} (silhouette exponent). Outputs: Final fragment color and opacity. Data Structures: Fragment shader state holding the normalized gradient 
abla fn (a 3D vector) derived from the volume sample. Original volume opacity \alpha{orig} (a scalar) stored per sample for shadow calculation. Steps: 1. Compute Silhouette Enhancement Factor (E{sil}): Calculate the alignment between the view direction and the volume gradient normal 
abla fn. Features facing the viewer have low silhouette strength. The exact formula for E{sil} is not explicitly provided in the sources, but the parameters k{sc}, k{ss}, k{se} suggest a Gaussian-like or power-law falloff centered on the silhouette edge. A standard implementation is: E{sil} = \exp\left( -k{ss} \cdot (\max(0, 
abla fn \cdot V{dir}) - k{sc})^2 ight)^{k{se}} 2. Determine Sketch Opacity: Map E{sil} to the final opacity \alpha{final}. Regions with high silhouette enhancement (edges) remain opaque, while non-silhouette regions (interiors) become transparent. \alpha{final} = E{sil} 3. Set Sketch Color: The base color of the fragment is set to the specified sketch color (e.g., white or black). 4. Calculate Shadows: Compute the shadow term S using the original volume opacity \alpha{orig}, not the sketch opacity. This typically involves ray marching or pre-integration of \alpha{orig} along the light direction. 5. Composite Final Color: Modulate the sketch color and opacity by the shadow term S. name: Outline and Contour Generation
head: Outline Representation
body: Outline and Contour Generation is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly rendering edges, silhouettes, or topological boundaries as line primitives or stylized strokes. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies on opacity and color to imply form, these methods detect geometric or scalar discontinuities and render them as distinct visual cues to define object boundaries, internal structures, or topological relationships. This family is distinguished from its siblings by its focus on explicit edge extraction and rendering strategies, ranging from object-space silhouette extraction to image-space depth discontinuity detection and topological landscape mapping. Generates view-dependent line primitives demarcating areas where an object's surface turns away from the viewer, relying on gradient magnitude and viewing angle for real-time tracing. Choose when direct screen rendering of contours is needed over texture-buffer recording. A post-processing technique detecting screen-space depth or normal discontinuities to define boundaries without analytical geometry processing. Choose for faster implementation and lower computational overhead. An interactive technique allowing users to manually define regions of interest to generate contour overlays, isolating complex structures lacking sharp boundaries. Choose when user-driven contour generation is required. Regulates contour thickness based on normal curvature along the view direction to prevent uncontrolled variation in thickness inherent in standard dot-product silhouette methods. Choose when consistent visual weight across varying surface geometries is needed. An object-space technique extracting significant edges (silhouettes and feature lines) from geometry, assembling them into strokes, and rendering them with stylization to enhance perceptual clarity. Choose when operating on pre-extracted geometric primitives for independent stylization. Maps the connectivity of a scalar field’s level sets onto a 3D terrain model using the contour tree, leveraging human intuition for reading physical terrain to interpret complex topological relationships. Choose when interpreting complex topological relationships (merges/splits) is the goal. Identifies surface locations where radial curvature is zero but increasing towards the viewer, complementing standard object contours to reveal hidden or occluded geometry. Choose when revealing hidden geometry is necessary. Displays line contours of a reference scalar field on the vertical bounding walls of a 3D volume to provide spatial context without occluding primary data. Choose when spatial context for deformed interfaces is needed without visual clutter. Determines contour correspondence in time-varying fields by verifying overlap of associated upper and lower object sets, avoiding higher-dimensional interpolations. Choose when tracking contour evolution (merging, splitting, moving) in time-varying scalar fields is required. Constructs a tubular contour around volumetric features to clarify borders and assist in feature identification relative to the view direction. Choose when explicit 3-D tube geometry from projected silhouettes is needed. Renders a dataset by displaying only the geometric boundaries of its extent, typically as a wireframe or bounding box, rather than the volumetric data itself. Choose for lightweight visualization primitives for rapid spatial orientation. A spatial coherence-based heuristic for detecting and tracing silhouette edges on polygonal meshes. Choose when performance bottleneck of brute-force silhouette detection needs to be solved. A rendering technique used in wireframe representations to hide line segments that are occluded by solid objects in the scene. Choose when operating on explicit geometric primitives to hide occluded lines. Pre-segments the most interesting internal structures and identifies context information that obscures them. In areas of occlusion, the visual representation of the context object is reduced to contours to provide a clear view of the interesting internal organ. Choose when clarifying internal structures obscured by context is needed. Locates the intended location of a 2D stroke in 3D space by finding the 3D line that is a projection of the 2D stroke and fits contours in the data best, determined by the dot product of the normal vector of the extruded stroke and the gradient in the data. This method only works at contours of objects and segments objects whose contour best fits the stroke, which may not be the most visible objects, whereas WYSIWYP is applicable to any position in the rendering. Choose when explicitly selecting and highlighting regions of interest via 2D strokes is required. The family of outline and contour generation techniques has evolved to address the limitations of photorealistic volume rendering in conveying shape, boundaries, and topological information. Early work in illustrative visualization for medicine and science highlighted the utility of expressive visualizations, such as ghosted views with contours, to clarify internal structures obscured by context. The development of non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) techniques allowed for the explicit rendering of edges and silhouettes to enhance perceptual clarity. Interactive methods like lasso contour rendering and 2D stroke to 3D line picking were developed to allow users to explicitly select and highlight regions of interest. 4. name: Object Contour NPR
head: Csébfalvi's contour method, GPU-based contour tracing, Geometry shader contour rendering, Gradient-based contour visualization, View-Dependent Contour Generation
body:
Object Contour NPR generates view-dependent line primitives that demarcate areas where an object's surface turns away from the viewer, conveying shape through boundary emphasis. Unlike hatches, which are recorded to a texture buffer, these contours are traced and rendered directly to the screen. It differs from direct volume rendering by relying solely on gradient magnitude and viewing angle rather than voxel intensity values, allowing for faster parameter tuning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V, a viewing direction vector \vec{v}, and a user-defined distance threshold d{thresh} defining the neighborhood around the contour. Output: A set of line strips rendered directly to the screen buffer. Data Structures: Particle Set: A collection of point primitives. Each particle Pi stores its 3D position (x, y, z) in the volume. Gradient Field: A 3D vector field

Particle Selection: Identify particles within the user-defined distance d{thresh} from the implicit contour surface. 3. Primitive Transformation: Treat selected particles as point primitives. 4. Contour Tracing: Pass points to a geometry shader to trace along the contour direction, transforming them into line-strips that resemble contour segments. The trace direction and constant-width measure are adopted from the VolumeFlies framework. 5. Rendering: Render the generated line-strips directly to the screen, not to a texture buffer. 6. Color/Opacity Assignment: Determine color and opacity for each voxel/pixel based only on the gradient magnitude |

Parameters: d{thresh}: User-defined distance from the contour for selecting particles. Gradient estimation method: 4D linear regression. name: Image Space Outline Generation
head: Edge extraction from depth/normal maps, Hertzmann's outline generation, Outline Post Processing
body: Image Space Outline Generation is a post-processing technique that renders non-photorealistic outlines by detecting discontinuities in screen-space depth or normal buffers. It solves the problem of defining object boundaries in volume rendering without the computational overhead of analytical geometry processing. Unlike sibling methods that compute contours from volumetric gradients or topological features, this method relies on simple pixel-wise comparisons of existing rasterization buffers, making it significantly faster and easier to implement. Inputs: Depth buffer containing the depth value d(x,y) for each pixel (x,y). Normal buffer (optional) containing the surface normal vector \mathbf{n}(x,y) for each pixel. Threshold parameters for edge detection. Outputs: Binary edge map or stylized outline image. Data Structures: The depth and normal buffers are stored as 2D arrays. Depth values are typically stored as floating-point numbers. Normal vectors are 3-component vectors. Steps: 1. Depth Edge Extraction: Iterate over each pixel (x,y) and its neighbors. Apply an edge detection mechanism, such as the Sobel filter, to the depth buffer. Depth differences are minimal between adjacent pixels of a single object and large between objects. Ed(x,y) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |d(x,y) - d(x',y')| > \Delta d{th} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where (x',y') is a neighbor pixel and \Delta d{th} is the depth threshold. 2. Normal Edge Extraction (Optional): Apply the same edge detection mechanism to the normal buffer. Normals vary smoothly across a single surface but show a discontinuity between surfaces. En(x,y) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \mathbf{n}(x,y) \cdot \mathbf{n}(x',y') < \theta{th} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \theta{th} is the cosine of the angle threshold. 3. Combination: Combine the detected depth and normal edges to yield all perceptually significant silhouettes. Depth edges reflect C0 discontinuities, while normal edges reflect C1 discontinuities. E{final}(x,y) = Ed(x,y) \lor En(x,y) 4. Analytical Curve Fitting (Optional): For further processing, such as modifying line qualities, calculate analytical curves from the detected edge pixel lists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateoutlines(depthbuffer, normalbuffer=None, depththreshold=0.0, normalthreshold=0.0): """ Generate outlines from depth and normal buffers. Args: depthbuffer: 2D list of depth values. normalbuffer: 2D list of normal vectors (optional). depththreshold: Minimum depth difference to be considered an edge. normalthreshold: Cosine threshold for normal angle difference. Returns: edgemap: 2D list of booleans. """ height = len(depthbuffer) width = len(depthbuffer[0]) edgemap = [[False for in range(width)] for in range(height)] offsets = [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): isedge = False # Check depth discontinuities (C0) for dy, dx in offsets: ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < height and 0 <= nx < width: if abs(depthbuffer[y][x] - depthbuffer[ny][nx]) > depththreshold: isedge = True break # Check normal discontinuities (C1) if normal buffer is provided if not isedge and normalbuffer is not None: for dy, dx in offsets: ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < height and 0 <= nx < width: curvec = normalbuffer[y][x] nxvec = normalbuffer[ny][nx] dotproduct = curvec[0]nxvec[0] + curvec[1]nxvec[1] + curvec[2]nxvec[2] if dotproduct < normalthreshold: isedge = True break edgemap[y][x] = isedge return edgemap Parameters: depththreshold: Not given in the sources. normalthreshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Depth buffer precision can cause false edges in distant scenes or true edges in close-up scenes. Use logarithmic depth buffers or higher precision formats if necessary. Boundaries: Pixels at the image border have fewer neighbors. Handle by ignoring out-of-bounds neighbors or padding the buffer. Noise: Depth and normal buffers may contain noise from rasterization or volume rendering. Filtering (e.g., Sobel, Gaussian) is recommended. A method to generate a Cumulative Gradient Depth Map (CGDM) for close-up images (defined as scenes with no or multiple vanishing points) by leveraging occlusion cues and local edge histograms. It distinguishes itself from Perspective View Depth Map Generation by relying on local edge density rather than global geometric convergence, and from Distant View Depth Map Generation by handling moderate-distance scenes with perspective distortion rather than infinite-distance horizons. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, as it involves a single pass over the buffer with constant-time neighbor checks. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the edge map, plus the cost of the depth and normal buffers. Performance: Very fast and simple to implement, suitable for real-time applications. Strengths: Simplicity, speed, independence from geometry complexity. Limitations: Quality depends on buffer resolution and precision; may produce jagged edges; does not provide analytical curve data for stylization without additional processing. When to use: Real-time NPR, simple outline effects, when performance is critical. When not to use: When depth/normal buffers are unavailable or unreliable. The method was surveyed by Hertzmann [Her99] and is based on the observation that depth and normal discontinuities correspond to perceptual edges. It is widely used in post-processing pipelines for NPR. name: Close-Up Image Depth Map Generation
head: Local Edge Histogram CGDM, Occlusion-based CGDM
body: A method to generate a Cumulative Gradient Depth Map (CGDM) for close-up images (defined as scenes with no or multiple vanishing points) by leveraging occlusion cues and local edge histograms. It determines spatial relationships by counting edge amounts, where regions with fewer edges are considered farther away. Inputs: A 2D image I. Outputs: An 8-bit CGDM Df of the same dimensions as I. Data Structures: E: Binary edge map (same size as I), where 1 indicates an edge, 0 otherwise. B{ij}: A grid of 5×5 pixel blocks covering I. N{ij}: Integer count of edge pixels in block B{ij}. N{av}: Average edge count per block across the grid. M: Total number of "main blocks" identified. Di: Circular depth gradient map for the i-th main block. N{i0}: Edge count of the i-th main block. Steps: 1. Extract edges from I using the Canny algorithm to produce binary map E. 2. Divide E into a grid of 5×5 pixel blocks. 3. Count the number of edge pixels N{ij} in each block B{ij}. 4. Compute the average edge count N{av} across all blocks. 5. Identify blocks where N{ij} > N{av} as "main blocks". Let the set of main blocks be indexed i=1 \dots M, with edge counts N{10}, N{20}, \dots, N{M0}. 6. For each main block i: Define a circular depth gradient map Di centered at the center of block B{ij}. Assign pixel value 255 at the center. Assign pixel value 0 at the circumference. Decrease pixel values evenly (linearly) from the center to the circumference. Determine the radius R. The source states an optimized radius is half the length (or width) of the image. 7. Fuse all Di maps into the final CGDM Df using the weighted sum formula: Df = \sum{i=1}^{M} \left( Di \times \frac{N{i0}}{\sum{j=1}^{M} N{j0}} \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecloseupcgdm(image: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]: H, W = len(image), len(image[0]) # 1. Edge Extraction: Apply standard Canny edge detection edges = [[0] W for in range(H)] # 2. Block Division and Counting BLOCKH, BLOCKW = 5, 5 gridh = H // BLOCKH gridw = W // BLOCKW blockcounts = [[0] gridw for in range(gridh)] for i in range(gridh): for j in range(gridw): count = 0 for y in range(i BLOCKH, (i + 1) BLOCKH): for x in range(j BLOCKW, (j + 1) BLOCKW): count += edges[y][x] blockcounts[i][j] = count # 3. Average and Main Block Identification totalblocks = gridh gridw Nav = sum(sum(row) for row in blockcounts) / totalblocks if totalblocks > 0 else 0 mainblocks = [] for i in range(gridh): for j in range(gridw): if blockcounts[i][j] > Nav: mainblocks.append((i, j, blockcounts[i][j])) M = len(mainblocks) if M == 0: return [[0] W for in range(H)] # 4. Generate Individual CGDMs and Sum R = min(H, W) / 2.0 totalmainedges = sum(nb[2] for nb in mainblocks) fusedd = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for i, j, ni0 in mainblocks: cy = (i + 0.5) BLOCKH cx = (j + 0.5) BLOCKW weight = ni0 / totalmainedges for y in range(H): for x in range(W): dist = ((y - cy)2 + (x - cx)2)0.5 if dist <= R: val = 255.0 (1.0 - dist / R) fusedd[y][x] += val weight return [[int(min(max(val, 0), 255)) for val in row] for row in fusedd] Parameters: Block size: 5×5 pixels. Radius R: Half the length or width of the image. Center value: 255. Circumference value: 0. Gradient type: Linear/even decrease. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Image Dimensions: Not given in the sources. Implementation typically truncates to full blocks. No Main Blocks: Not given in the sources. If M=0, the formula is undefined; a fallback returning a zero map is required. Circle Boundary: Not given in the sources. The source states the CGDM is fused from these circles but does not specify if values outside radius R are zero; the pseudocode assumes zero outside R. Precision: The source uses 8-bit values (0–255). Intermediate calculations should use float to prevent quantization errors during fusion. Generates a CGDM for perspective view images by calculating separate horizontal and vertical depth gradients based on distance from a detected vanishing point. It is chosen when the scene exhibits a single clear convergence point, distinguishing it from this method which relies on local occlusion cues rather than global geometric convergence. Generates a CGDM for distant views with infinite-distance horizons. It is chosen when the scene represents a sky/land horizon at extreme distance, distinguishing it from this method which handles moderate-distance close-up scenes without global perspective distortion. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple, fast, relies on local occlusion cues which are robust for close-up scenes without global perspective. Limitations: Discrete block structure may cause artifacts at block boundaries. Radius is fixed relative to image size, not object size. Does not handle perspective distortion explicitly. When to Use: Close-up images with no or multiple vanishing points. When Not to Use: Perspective views with a single vanishing point or distant views with infinite-distance horizons. Originated in the context of holographic 3D display using depth maps generated by 2D-to-3D rendering. It builds on the observation that regions with fewer edges are generally farther away in close-up scenes. name: Perspective View Depth Map Generation
head: Perspective View CGDM Calculation, Vanishing Point Depth Map Generation
body: A method to generate a Cumulative Gradient Depth Map (CGDM) for perspective view images by calculating separate horizontal and vertical depth gradients based on the distance from a detected vanishing point. It distinguishes itself from Close-Up Image Depth Map Generation by relying on global geometric convergence rather than local occlusion cues, and from Distant View Depth Map Generation by handling moderate-distance scenes with obvious perspective distortion rather than infinite-distance sky/land horizons. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D RGB image I. Output: A CGDM D of the same dimensions as I, where pixel values represent depth gradients ranging from 0 (farthest) to 2^{BD}-1 (nearest). Data Structures: I: Input image, dimensions W \times H. D: Output depth map, dimensions W \times H, type unsigned integer with bit depth BD (typically 8, range 0–255). (x{vp}, y{vp}): Coordinates of the vanishing point. M, N: Number of pixels in the CGDM in the horizontal and vertical directions, respectively. Steps: 1. Image Expansion (Padding): To mitigate depth errors caused by non-central vanishing points, expand the original image I to twice its size by zero-padding. Let the padded image be I{pad} with dimensions 2W \times 2H. 2. Edge Extraction: Extract edges from the original image I using the Canny algorithm. 3. Line Detection: Detect straight lines from the extracted edges using the Hough transform. 4. Vanishing Point Identification: Identify the vanishing point (x{vp}, y{vp}) as the intersection of the detected straight lines. If the lines do not intersect at a single point, the image is not a perspective image. 5. Cropping for Calculation: To ensure the vanishing point is treated as the center for gradient calculation: a. Search for the vanishing point (x{vp}, y{vp}) in the padded image I{pad}. b. Calculate the maximum distance from (x{vp}, y{vp}) to any edge of I{pad}. c. Crop I{pad} using (x{vp}, y{vp}) as the center and the maximum length from the vanishing point to the edge of the image as the side length to form a cropped image I{crop}. 6. CGDM Calculation: Calculate the CGDM for I{crop} using separate gradients for horizontal and vertical planes. For content on the horizontal plane, assign depth gradient values from 0 to 2^{BD}-1 along the columns from the vanishing point to the edge. For content on the vertical plane, assign depth gradient values from 0 to 2^{BD}-1 along the rows from the vanishing point to the edge. The depth values are calculated using the following formulas: \text{depth}h(x, y) = (2^{BD} - 1) \frac{y - y{vp}}{N - y{vp}} \text{depth}v(x, y) = (2^{BD} - 1) \frac{x - x{vp}}{M - x{vp}} Where \text{depth}h and \text{depth}v are the depth gradients on the horizontal and vertical planes, respectively. The variables (x, y) are pixel coordinates, (x{vp}, y{vp}) is the vanishing point coordinate, M and N are the CGDM dimensions, and BD is the bit depth. The formulas assume y increases downwards and x increases rightwards, implying a linear gradient from 0 at y = y{vp} to 2^{BD}-1 at y = N. 7. Final Output: Obtain the CGDM of the original image by cutting the CGDM of the cropped image to match the original image dimensions. Parameters: BD: Bit depth of the CGDM (e.g., 8). M, N: Number of pixels in the CGDM in the horizontal and vertical directions. (x{vp}, y{vp}): Coordinate value of the vanishing point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Central Vanishing Point: If the vanishing point is not in the central area, depth error occurs in holographic reconstruction. The padding and cropping steps are specifically designed to avoid this error. No Single Intersection: If straight lines do not intersect at one point, the method fails to identify a perspective view. Plane Ambiguity: The method assumes content belongs to either horizontal or vertical planes, distinguished by vanishing lines, but the algorithmic distinction is not detailed in the source. A method to generate a CGDM for distant view images (outdoor scenes with sky, land, water) by assuming the sky is infinitely far and depth increases linearly from the sky-land borderline to the bottom of the image. It is chosen when the proportion p of pixels satisfying specific HSI color ranges is greater than 0.5. The vanishing point is located on the sky-land borderline, and depth is calculated using a cumulative horizontal edge histogram, avoiding the need for vanishing point detection. Time and memory complexity, measured performance, and scaling behavior are not given in the sources. The method requires clear straight lines and a single vanishing point, and fails for close-up or distant view images. Originated in the context of holographic 3D display using depth maps generated by 2D-to-3D rendering approaches. The method is part of a broader framework that classifies 2D images into distant view, perspective view, and close-up types to generate appropriate CGDMs. Holographic 3D Display Using Depth Maps Generated by 2D-to-3D Rendering Approach, https://doi.org/10.3390/app11219889, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Lasso Contour Rendering
body: Lasso Contour Rendering is an interactive non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that allows users to manually define regions of interest using a free-form selection tool to generate contour overlays. It solves the problem of isolating complex volumetric structures that lack sharp boundaries by enabling user-driven contour generation. It differs from siblings like Object Contour NPR by relying on explicit user interaction to define the region of interest rather than automatic geometric or scalar-based detection. The method operates within a rendering pipeline that supports interactive overlay rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset, a user-defined 2D or 3D lasso shape, and the current camera view. Output: A rendered image where the selected lasso region is highlighted with contour lines or stylized strokes, composited over the underlying volume rendering. Data Structures: Lasso State: A boolean flag indicating if the user is actively defining the shape. Lasso Geometry: A list of vertices defining the closed loop of the lasso. Render Pipeline: An object containing the shader programs and render passes for drawing the contour overlay. Steps: 1. Interaction Check: The system checks if the user is currently drawing a lasso by querying the input handler state. 2. Pipeline Validation: The system verifies that the specific render pipeline for lasso contours exists and is initialized. 3. Rendering: If the conditions are met, the active lasso contour is rendered using the offscreen render pass. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If the lasso is defined in 3D space, projection errors may occur when mapping to screen space for rendering. name: Curvature-Controlled Style Contours
head: Kindlmann Contours, Normal Curvature Contours
body: Curvature-Controlled Style Contours is a volume rendering technique that regulates contour thickness based on the normal curvature along the view direction to prevent the uncontrolled variation in thickness inherent in standard dot-product silhouette methods. While standard methods (v \cdot n \approx 0) produce contours that are too thick on flat surfaces and too thin on fine structures, this method uses curvature to maintain consistent visual weight across varying surface geometries. It builds on Outline and Contour Generation by integrating curvature-aware edge detection with style transfer functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric dataset, view vector v, user-defined thickness parameter T. Output: Rendered image with stylized contours whose thickness is controlled by local curvature. Data Structures: Sample point: Position, normal vector n, previous normal vector n{prev} (from the previous sample along the ray). Geometry: No pre-computed Hessian or geometry tensor textures are required. Approximation of Normal Curvature (\kappav): Exact curvature requires the geometry tensor derived from the Hessian matrix, which is too expensive for fragment programs and requires two additional 3D textures for pre-computation. Instead, \kappav is approximated using the rate of change of the normal along the viewing ray. 1. During ray casting, store the normal n{prev} at the previous sample point. 2. Calculate the angle between the current normal n and n{prev}. 3. Divide this angle by the step size \Delta s between sample points: \kappav \approx \frac{\angle(n, n{prev})}{\Delta s} This approximation is coarse because the sampling occurs along the ray, not strictly along the iso-surface, but it is sufficient for finite-resolution volumes and introduces negligible computational cost. Contour Detection Condition: A sample is considered to be on a contour if the following condition is met: |n \cdot v| \le \sqrt{T \kappav (2 - T \kappav)} Where: n is the surface normal at the current sample. v is the view vector. T is the user-defined thickness value. \kappav is the approximated normal curvature. Style Integration (Lit Sphere Map): To integrate contours with style transfer functions (e.g., lit sphere maps), the normal projection coordinates are adjusted based on the curvature measure. 1. Let r = |n{x,y}| be the length of the eye-space normal projected onto the lit sphere map. 2. Calculate the adjustment factor \delta: \delta = 1 - \min\left(1, \frac{\sqrt{T \kappav (2 - T \kappav)} - |n \cdot v|}{\sqrt{T \kappav (2 - T \kappav)}}\right) 3. Adjust the projected radius to r': r' = \min(1, \delta r) This pushes the coordinates outwards along the radius if the sample falls below the contour threshold, allowing the contour color to vary based on the normal direction and curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def curvaturecontrolledcontour(volume, origin, direction, T, stepsize, maxsteps): color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 nprev = None posprev = origin for i in range(maxsteps): pos = [origin[j] + direction[j] (i stepsize) for j in range(3)] if not volume.contains(pos): break n = volume.getnormal(pos) dist = math.sqrt(sum((pos[j] - posprev[j])2 for j in range(3))) if nprev is not None and dist > 1e-6: cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, sum(n[j] nprev[j] for j in range(3)))) angle = math.acos(cosangle) kappav = angle / dist else: kappav = 0.0 nprev = n posprev = pos thresholdsq = T kappav (2.0 - T kappav) if thresholdsq < 0.0: thresholdsq = 0.0 threshold = math.sqrt(thresholdsq) dotnv = abs(sum(n[j] direction[j] for j in range(3))) iscontour = dotnv <= threshold if iscontour: r = math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2) denom = threshold if denom > 1e-6: ratio = (denom - dotnv) / denom delta = 1.0 - min(1.0, ratio) else: delta = 1.0 rprime = min(1.0, delta r) c = volume.lookupstyle(rprime) else: c = volume.lookupstyle(math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2)) alpha = volume.getopacity(pos) color = [color[j] + transmittance alpha c[j] for j in range(4)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return color Note: Standard front-to-back volume rendering accumulation is implemented to resolve the ray marching loop and color blending, as the source focuses on the contour/style logic. Parameters: T: User-defined thickness value for the contours. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \kappav is zero, the threshold becomes zero and the condition |n \cdot v| \le 0 requires perfectly orthogonal normals to trigger a contour. The approximation of \kappav is not geometrically exact as it samples along the ray rather than the surface, but this is accepted as sufficient for the method's purpose. A technique using transfer functions based on surface curvature to render feature contours with roughly constant image-space thickness, specifically applied to clarify the shape and position of individual bones in small animal imaging. It combines curvature-based opacity with depth cueing to enhance structural clarity. Time Complexity: Low overhead compared to exact curvature methods. The approximation requires only storing the previous normal and computing an angle, avoiding expensive Hessian calculations or additional texture lookups. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory (one previous normal per ray or tile). No pre-computed 3D textures for geometry tensors are needed. Strengths: Provides consistent contour thickness across varying surface curvatures, addressing the "too thick on flat, too thin on fine" problem of standard dot-product contours. Interactive performance is maintained. Limitations: The curvature approximation is coarse and not geometrically exact. It relies on the step size of the ray casting; varying step sizes may affect the consistency of \kappav. When to use: When illustrative rendering requires consistent visual emphasis on edges regardless of local surface flatness or curvature, and interactive performance is required. When not to use: When exact geometric curvature is required for scientific measurement, or when pre-computed geometry tensors are already available and performance is not a constraint. The method was proposed by Brückner and Gröller in 2007 as an improvement over the original curvature-controlled contours introduced by Kindlmann et al. in 2003. Kindlmann et al. identified the thickness variation problem and proposed using the geometry tensor for exact curvature, but noted its high computational cost and memory requirements for volume rendering. Brückner and Gröller introduced the normal-angle approximation to make the method viable for direct volume rendering without pre-computation. The approach has been applied in scientific visualization, such as visualizing bone structures in small animal imaging. name: Curvature-Based Feature Contouring
head: Curvature Convolution Volume Rendering, Transfer Functions Based on Surface Curvature
body: Curvature-Based Feature Contouring is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that renders feature contours with roughly constant image-space thickness, clarifying the shape and position of individual structures such as bones. It sets itself apart from standard silhouette rendering by applying a curvature correction to maintain fixed width in image space, distinguishing between ridge and valley features based on curvature magnitude. It builds on Curvature-Controlled Style Contours by utilizing dynamic convolution-based field reconstruction within the transfer function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric scalar field data, view direction vector \mathbf{v}, surface normal vector \mathbf{n} (derived from gradient), and curvature measures. Output: Rendered image with feature contours of constant image-space thickness. Data Structures: Transfer Function: Implemented as lookup tables. Specifically, two two-dimensional lookup tables (for opacity and silhouettes) and one one-dimensional lookup table (for depth cueing). Curvature Field: A field reconstructed via dynamic convolution to provide curvature measures for the transfer function. Steps: 1. Field Reconstruction: Perform a dynamic convolution-based field reconstruction to compute curvature measures from the volumetric data. 2. Normal and View Calculation: For each fragment, compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} and retrieve the view direction \mathbf{v}. 3. Silhouette Detection: Determine silhouette contribution using the dot product \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}, similar to Gooch's environment map approach. 4. Curvature Correction: Apply a curvature correction to the silhouette rendering to ensure fixed width in image space. This involves using the magnitude of curvature to adjust the rendering parameters. 5. Feature Classification: Use curvature magnitude to distinguish between ridge and valley features. 6. Transfer Function Evaluation: Evaluate the modified transfer function. This function incorporates the curvature-based silhouette contribution and opacity. The transfer function is implemented as two 2D lookup tables (opacity and silhouettes) and one 1D lookup table (depth cueing). 7. Depth Cueing: Apply depth cueing to clarify the relationship between foreground and background objects. 8. Rendering: Render the final image on fragment shading hardware. Formulas: Silhouette factor: \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}. Curvature magnitude: Used to distinguish ridge and valley features. name: Silhouette Rendering
head: Object-space line rendering, Silhouette Rendering Pipeline, Stroke Pipeline
body: Silhouette rendering is an object-space line rendering technique that extracts significant edges (silhouettes and feature lines) from geometry, assembles them into strokes, and renders them with stylization to enhance perceptual clarity. It solves the problem of discriminating object classes or indicating context objects (e.g., bones) by rendering "interesting" features with silhouettes while leaving others without. Unlike image-space methods, it operates on pre-extracted geometric primitives, allowing for independent stylization and combination with surface or volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Segmented geometry data (meshes) with adjacency information; a classification of objects/regions as "interesting" (requiring silhouettes) or not. Output: Stylized line strokes (width, color, saturation, texture) composited over the final image. Data Structures: Adjacency Structure: Created during geometry data preparation to facilitate edge extraction. Stroke Data: Assembled from extracted edges (silhouettes and feature lines). Z-Buffer: Depth buffer used for hidden line removal. Steps: 1. Geometry Data Preparation: Create a geometry structure providing adjacency information for the mesh. 2. Line Extraction: Extract significant edges, specifically silhouettes and feature lines, from the mesh. 3. Stroke Assembly: Assemble the extracted edges into strokes. 4. Hidden Line Removal (HLR): a. Render the objects into the z-buffer only (frame buffer remains unchanged). b. For each stroke, scan-convert the line individually. c. Classify each line segment as hidden or visible by locally comparing the line's z-depths against the pre-generated z-buffer data. 5. Stroke Stylization: Apply stylization to the visible strokes, including changing width, saturation, color, and texture. 6. Compositing: Render surface objects into the final image prior to the lines if surface rendering is used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def silhouetterendering(meshes, interestingmask, cameraviewdir, zbuffer): # Step 1: Geometry Data Preparation adjacency = buildadjacencystructure(meshes) # Step 2 & 3: Line Extraction and Stroke Assembly strokes = [] for mesh in meshes: if interestingmask[mesh.id]: edges = extractsignificantedges(mesh, adjacency[mesh.id], cameraviewdir) strokes.extend(assemblestrokes(edges)) # Step 4: Hidden Line Removal visiblestrokes = [] for stroke in strokes: isvisible = True for segment in stroke.segments: linez = getlinezdepth(segment, cameraviewdir) bufferz = zbuffer[segment.screencoords] if linez > bufferz: isvisible = False break if isvisible: visiblestrokes.append(stroke) # Step 5: Stroke Stylization stylizedstrokes = [] for stroke in visiblestrokes: stroke.width = applystylization(stroke.width, "width") stroke.saturation = applystylization(stroke.saturation, "saturation") stroke.color = applystylization(stroke.color, "color") stroke.texture = applystylization(stroke.texture, "texture") stylizedstrokes.append(stroke) # Step 6: Compositing finalimage = rendersurface(meshes) for stroke in stylizedstrokes: drawstroke(finalimage, stroke) return finalimage def buildadjacencystructure(meshes): return {mesh.id: {edge: faces for edge, faces in mesh.edges} for mesh in meshes} def extractsignificantedges(mesh, adjacency, viewdir): edges = [] for edge, faces in adjacency.items(): if len(faces) == 1: edges.append(edge) elif len(faces) == 2: n1, n2 = faces[0].normal, faces[1].normal if dot(n1, viewdir) dot(n2, viewdir) < 0: edges.append(edge) return edges def assemblestrokes(edges): return [LineSegment(start=e.v1, end=e.v2) for e in edges] def getlinezdepth(segment, viewdir): return dot(segment.midpoint, viewdir) def applystylization(value, param): return value 1.2 if param == "width" else value def rendersurface(meshes): return createcolorbuffer() def drawstroke(image, stroke): rasterizeline(image, stroke.start, stroke.end, stroke.color) Parameters and Edge Cases: Interestingness Criteria: Defined by user or application context (e.g., lymph nodes touching critical structures). Z-Buffer Precision: Local comparison of z-depths requires sufficient precision to avoid artifacts at discontinuities. Order of Rendering: Surface objects must be rendered into the final image prior to the lines if surface rendering is combined. Extracts silhouettes in image space using edge detection filters with optional perturbation, chosen for interactive frame rates with huge or animated datasets. Time Complexity: Depends on mesh complexity and number of strokes. HLR requires rendering the scene once and then processing each stroke segment. Memory Complexity: Requires storing adjacency structures, stroke data, and a z-buffer. Strengths: Allows independent stylization of edges; effective for discriminating object classes and indicating context; fast HLR method using z-buffer comparison. Limitations: Requires pre-segmented geometry and adjacency information. When to Use: When precise control over edge stylization is needed, or when combining silhouettes with surface/volume rendering in a scenegraph-based approach. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of medical visualization, specifically for surgery education and planning, to help users distinguish between lymph nodes and critical structures. name: Image-space silhouette extraction with perturbation
head: Image-Space Silhouette Detection, Image-space silhouette extraction, Silhouette effect
body: This method extracts surface silhouettes in image space using edge detection filters, optionally modified by a procedural perturbation function for artistic variation, and combines them with Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) for depth perception. It is chosen for interactive frame rates with huge or animated data sets, as it avoids the high computational effort required by object-space and hybrid algorithms that rely on processing large integral surface meshes. Inputs: 1. A volume dataset or pre-rendered DVR image I{\text{dvr}}(x, y). 2. An edge detection filter kernel (e.g., Sobel, Canny). 3. A procedural perturbation function definition P(x, y). Outputs: 1. A final composite image containing the DVR result overlaid with extracted silhouettes/feature lines. Data Structures: Rendered Image: A 2D array of color values (RGBA) corresponding to the pixel grid. Edge Map: A 2D array of scalar values (or binary mask) representing edge strength or presence. Perturbation Field: A 2D array of scalar values representing the perturbation magnitude or direction at each pixel. Steps: 1. Render Volume: Render the volume using Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) to produce the base image I{\text{dvr}}(x, y). 2. Apply Edge Detection: Apply an image processing filter (edge detector) to I{\text{dvr}} to extract feature lines, hatching strokes, ridges, and valley lines. Let the output be the edge map E(x, y). 3. Apply Perturbation (Optional): Modify the edge map E(x, y) using a procedural perturbation function P(x, y) to obtain the perturbed edge map E'(x, y). Formula: E'(x, y) = \text{Modify}(E(x, y), P(x, y)). Note: The exact mathematical form of \text{Modify} and P is not given in the sources. A common implementation might involve displacing edge pixels or modulating edge strength based on noise fields. 4. Composite: Combine the extracted silhouettes/feature lines (E') with the DVR result (I{\text{dvr}}) to enhance main features while preserving contextual information. Formula: I{\text{final}}(x, y) = \text{Composite}(I{\text{dvr}}(x, y), E'(x, y)). Note: The specific compositing operator (e.g., alpha blending, max, overlay) is not defined in the sources. Typically, silhouettes are rendered with high opacity over the volume. Parameters: Edge detection threshold: Not given in the sources. Perturbation intensity: Not given in the sources. Filter kernel size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Edge detection on noisy volume renderings may produce spurious edges. Boundaries: Silhouettes at the image border may be truncated. Degenerate Input: Uniform regions will yield no edges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractsilhouettewithperturbation(Idvr, edgekernel, P): # Step 1: Idvr is the base DVR image # Step 2: Apply edge detection filter to Idvr E = applyedgefilter(Idvr, edgekernel) # Standard 2D convolution # Step 3: Apply procedural perturbation to edge map # Exact modification formula not given in sources if P is not None: Eprime = applyperturbation(E, P) # Displace edge pixels or modulate strength based on noise else: Eprime = E # Step 4: Composite perturbed edges over DVR result # Exact compositing operator not given in sources Ifinal = composite(Idvr, Eprime) # Typically alpha blending or max opacity return Ifinal A method by Kalnins et al. using brush path parameterization to represent silhouettes, tracked between frames using image space local search. It provides frame coherence through the tracking. Time Complexity: Dominated by DVR rendering and 2D image processing filters. Generally O(N) where N is the number of pixels, assuming fixed-size kernels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the rendered image and edge maps. Measured Performance: Preferred for interactive frame rates with huge or animated data sets. Strengths: Avoids the high effort of processing large integral surface meshes required by object-space and hybrid algorithms. Suitable for huge or animated data sets. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial DVR rendering; silhouettes are only as good as the rendered image's contrast. When to use: When interactive frame rates are required for large/animated data, and artistic variation is desired. The technique is part of the broader field of illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering. It builds on the idea of combining traditional illustration effects (like hatching or edge lines) with volume rendering to enhance the perception of salient features. The approach by Yuan and Chen is cited as behaving similarly, using feature lines, hatching strokes, ridges, and valley lines combined with visualization algorithms. Isenberg et al. recommend image-space techniques for interactive frame rates with huge or animated data sets, excluding object-space and hybrid algorithms due to the high effort required for large integral surface meshes. name: Topological Landscape
body: Topological Landscape is a visualization technique that maps the connectivity of a scalar field’s level sets onto a 3D terrain model using the contour tree. It solves the problem of interpreting complex topological relationships (merges and splits of contours) by leveraging human intuition for reading physical terrain. It sets itself apart from standard contour rendering by transforming abstract graph nodes into a spatial height map where peaks and valleys explicitly encode topological events, differing from Contour Tree by providing a geometric metaphor rather than just a hierarchical graph structure. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: The contour tree, which maps topological events to a tree structure where edges correspond to individual contour classes and vertices correspond to critical points. The landscape maps these elements to a 3D terrain model. Steps: 1. Compute Contour Tree: Generate the contour tree for the scalar field data. 2. Construct Terrain: Use the contour tree to build a 3D terrain model. 3. Layout Data: Apply established 2D visualization techniques to lay out the topological data within the terrain model. 4. Interpret Features: Identify peaks as locations where two or more contours merge, and valleys as locations where a contour splits into two or more parts. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Layout Technique: Established 2D visualization techniques are used for laying out the data; specific methods are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Dimensional Data: The method is applicable to contour trees of any number of dimensions, making it useful for exploring high-dimensional data sets. Topological Correctness: The generated topological structures must be verified as valid to ensure accurate landscape representation. name: Contour Tree
head: Join Tree, Split Tree
body: The Contour Tree is a topological data structure that represents the connectivity of level sets (contours) of a scalar field as the isovalue varies. It solves the problem of tracking how contours are created, split, merged, and destroyed by mapping these events to a tree structure where edges correspond to individual contour classes and vertices correspond to critical points. It sets itself apart from the Reeb Graph by requiring a simply connected domain without loops, and from the Topological Landscape by providing the explicit graph structure rather than just a visual metaphor of peaks and valleys. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field f defined on a simply connected domain (e.g., a grid or mesh). Output: A tree structure T = (V, E) where V is the set of critical points and E is the set of edges connecting them. Data Structures: The contour tree consists of two primary elements: 1. Vertices (Supernodes): Leaf Nodes: Represent local extrema. Local maxima: Where a contour is created (Join Tree context) or destroyed (Split Tree context). Local minima: Where a contour is destroyed (Join Tree context) or created (Split Tree context). Interior Nodes: Represent saddle points. Split saddles: Where one contour splits into two or more disjoint contours. Join saddles: Where two or more disjoint contours merge into one. 2. Edges (Superarcs): Represent a single continuous contour class between the supernode where it is created and the supernode where it is destroyed. A contour class is defined as a maximal set of continuous contours that do not contain critical points. Construction Algorithm: The contour tree is typically constructed by first building two auxiliary structures: the Join Tree (JT) and the Split Tree (ST), and then merging them. The Join Tree captures connected sub-level sets (regions below an isovalue), while the Split Tree captures connected super-level sets (regions above an isovalue). Join Tree (JT) Construction: 1. Start from the global maximum function value. 2. Continuously decrease the isovalue w. 3. Define the marked region X(w) = \{x | f(x) \ge w\}. 4. Identify connected components of X(w) as "upper objects". 5. Node Creation (Upper Leaf): When w passes a local maximum, a new connected component is created. Create a JT node for this upper leaf. 6. Merge Event: When w passes a join saddle point, two or more components merge into one. Create a new JT node for the saddle point and connect it to the node of the latest critical point belonging to the same object. 7. Termination: When w reaches the global minimum, create a final JT node and connect it to the node of the latest critical point. 8. Implementation Detail: Vertices in the domain mesh are marked in decreasing order based on function value. Split Tree (ST) Construction: Symmetric to JT construction, but starts from the global minimum and increases the isovalue to track connected super-level sets. Contour Tree (CT) Formation: 1. Augmented Contour Tree (ACT): Successively delete upper leaves of the JT and lower leaves of the ST, inserting adjacent edges to form the ACT. 2. Final CT: Successively delete regular (non-critical) vertices in the ACT to obtain the final Contour Tree. Optimizations and Variants: Sorting: Chiang et al. improve processing time by only sorting critical vertices during the merge tree construction stage, rather than sorting all elements. Multithreading: Gueunet et al. present a "contour forest" algorithm using a shared memory approach for multithreaded computation of the augmented contour tree. Seeds: To facilitate contour tracing, "seeds" are identified as vertices where contours can be built from. An entire contour for a specified isovalue is computed from the seed bounded by the two supernodes representing the critical points of that contour. Using seeds reduces the number of seeds required for representation but may increase overall storage size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecontourtree(scalarfield, domainmesh): """ Computes the Contour Tree by constructing Join and Split Trees. scalarfield: dict mapping vertex -> float value. domainmesh: dict mapping vertex -> list of neighbor vertices. Returns: Contour Tree T = (V, E) as lists of nodes and edges. """ # 1. Sort vertices by function value in descending order sortedvertices = sorted(domainmesh.keys(), key=lambda v: scalarfield[v], reverse=True) # Union-Find structures to track connected components parent = {v: v for v in domainmesh} nodemap = {} # Maps component root to its JT node ID def find(v): while parent[v] != v: parent[v] = parent[parent[v]] v = parent[v] return v def union(u, v): rootu, rootv = find(u), find(v) if rootu != rootv: # Connect to the lowest vertex of neighboring objects if scalarfield[rootu] > scalarfield[rootv]: parent[rootu] = rootv else: parent[rootv] = rootu return True return False jtnodes = [] jtedges = [] nodecounter = 0 def createnode(vertex, nodetype): nonlocal nodecounter nid = f"node{nodecounter}" nodecounter += 1 jtnodes.append((nid, vertex, nodetype)) return nid # 2. Sweep and build JT for vertex in sortedvertices: neighbors = domainmesh[vertex] neighborroots = set() for n in neighbors: if n in parent: neighborroots.add(find(n)) if not neighborroots: # Node Creation (Upper Leaf): When w passes a local maximum, a new component is created nid = createnode(vertex, 'upperleaf') nodemap[vertex] = nid parent[vertex] = vertex else: rootslist = list(neighborroots) if len(rootslist) > 1: # Merge Event: When w passes a join saddle point, two or more components merge into one saddlenid = createnode(vertex, 'joinsaddle') jtnodes.append(saddlenid) for r in rootslist: jtedges.append((saddlenid, nodemap[r])) parent[r] = vertex # Union all components to this vertex nodemap[vertex] = saddlenid else: # Single component continues r = rootslist[0] parent[vertex] = r jtedges.append((vertex, nodemap[r])) nodemap[vertex] = nodemap[r] # Termination: When w reaches the global minimum, a JT node is created and connected to the node for the latest critical point globalminvertex = min(domainmesh.keys(), key=lambda v: scalarfield[v]) minnid = createnode(globalminvertex, 'globalmin') jtnodes.append(minnid) jtedges.append((minnid, nodemap[find(globalminvertex)])) # 3. Construct Split Tree (ST) symmetrically # ST construction follows identical logic but processes vertices in ascending order to track super-level sets. # 4. Form Augmented Contour Tree (ACT): Successively delete upper leaves of JT and lower leaves of ST, inserting adjacent edges. # 5. Form Final CT: Successively delete regular vertices in ACT to obtain the final Contour Tree. # Implementation note: These steps merge edges between critical points to form the final tree structure. return jtnodes, jtedges Parameters: Neighborhood Definition: Changing the method of defining neighbors during split/merge tree computations can slightly alter the location of critical points, though the underlying structure (number of supernodes and superarcs) remains fixed. Genus Information: The contour tree typically does not contain information regarding changes in topological genus (loops); this must be added to the output separately if required. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Simply Connected Domains: The input domain must be simply connected and free of loops. The merge tree computation phase cannot correctly handle data without a boundary or with loops. For such cases, the Reeb Graph should be used. High Dimensionality: Critical vertices are difficult to identify in data with dimensionality of four or more. Load Imbalance: In multithreaded implementations (e.g., contour forest), speedup is limited by load imbalance and redundant computations. The Reeb graph is a topological data structure that generalizes the contour tree to compute the topology of scalar data on domains that are not simply connected (contain loops) or lack a boundary. It solves the problem of capturing global topology in complex geometries where standard contour trees fail. It sets itself apart from the Contour Tree by explicitly handling domains with loops or missing boundaries, and from the Joint Contour Net by operating on single-variable scalar fields rather than multivariate data. This method applies distinct transfer functions to different topological zones of a scalar field, determined by mapping sample points to arcs in a contour tree via monotone paths. It sets itself apart from global transfer functions by allowing topology-aware color and opacity mapping, and from simple gradient reversal or flattening by using dynamic tube sweeping to broaden connections between components, providing a smoother approximation of the scalar field. Contour-Tree-Defined Segmentation partitions a scalar volume into topological zones, where each zone corresponds to an arc in the contour tree of the underlying trilinear interpolant. It solves the problem of assigning independent transfer functions to distinct topological structures, allowing for the isolation of specific features based on their creation and destruction isovalue ranges. It builds on the concept of topological zones defined by Cox et al. and extends prior work by allowing independent transfer functions per zone and using trilinear interpolation over hexahedral cells. Stratified Morse Theory (SMT) for Euler Characteristic is a mathematical framework and verification pipeline used to compute the Euler characteristic (\chi) of isosurfaces generated from piecewise trilinear scalar fields, specifically handling non-smoothness at cell boundaries and surfaces with boundary components. It solves the problem of verifying the topological correctness of isosurface extraction algorithms (such as Marching Cubes) by comparing the Euler characteristic derived from critical point analysis against the Euler characteristic of the extracted mesh. Unlike its siblings, which often rely on smooth manifold assumptions or digital topology constraints, SMT explicitly stratifies the grid into vertices, edges, faces, and cells to apply Morse theory locally, making it robust for verifying algorithms that guarantee topological correctness in the presence of ambiguous configurations. Time-varying Contour Topology Tracking is a method for establishing temporal correspondence between isosurfaces in time-varying scalar fields by maintaining and intersecting labeled Join Trees (JT) and Separate Trees (ST) across consecutive timesteps. It solves the problem of tracking topological changes (merges, splits, collisions) in contour evolution by labeling the JT from time t with edge sets derived from time t+1, then intersecting these labels with those from the ST to determine precise contour mapping. Unlike static contour tree analysis, this method explicitly handles the dynamic intersection of upper and lower objects between timesteps to resolve topology changes. After determining high and low vertices, look up their corresponding high and low arcs in the contour tree. Walk from the high arc towards the low arc to find the arc containing the sampled value f. Use the branch decomposition (a rooted tree) instead of the contour tree (a free tree) to find the path between branches b and c. Walk up the parent link of the deeper of the two branches b and c simultaneously. If neither stopping condition is met, the walk terminates when both paths reach the common ancestor a, which is the desired branch. When walking towards increasing function value, stop if the next step goes past a saddle with a higher value than the sampled point. When walking towards decreasing function value, stop if the next step goes past a saddle with a lower value than the sample. Complexity: The construction of the contour tree involves sorting critical points and processing connectivity changes. Chiang et al. note that sorting only critical vertices improves processing time in very large datasets. Memory: Using seeds reduces the number of seeds required for representation significantly but often increases the overall storage size of the contour tree. Performance: Multithreaded approaches (e.g., contour forest) offer quicker computations, but speedup is limited by load imbalance and redundant computations. Limitations: The method is restricted to simply connected domains without loops. It does not inherently capture genus changes. Critical point identification becomes difficult in dimensions four or higher. Usage: Merge trees are often used as a computation step in the construction of more complex topological data structures such as the contour tree. Alternatively, they can be used directly for analysis and feature extraction in complex data sets. The contour tree was introduced by Boyell and Ruston. The contour tree uses concepts from Morse theory to capture changes in the topology of a scalar field at critical points. Carr et al. investigated the use of contour trees in higher dimensional data sets and introduced the concept of augmented contour trees. The structure is fundamental in computational topology for tracking connected level sets. name: Reeb Graph
body: The Reeb graph is a topological data structure that generalizes the contour tree to compute the topology of scalar data on domains that are not simply connected (contain loops) or lack a boundary. It solves the problem of capturing global topology in complex geometries where standard contour trees fail. It sets itself apart from the Contour Tree by explicitly handling domains with loops or missing boundaries, and from the Joint Contour Net by operating on single-variable scalar fields rather than multivariate data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a simplicial mesh. The algorithm uses the 2-skeleton of the input volume to define relationships between vertices, edges, and triangles, a restriction that applies to scalar fields in any dimension. Output: A graph representing the topology of the scalar field's level sets. Data Structures: The method relies on a simplicial mesh representation (vertices, edges, triangles). Algorithm Steps: Reeb graph algorithms are split into two groups: sweep-based methods and split-and-compute methods. 1. Sweep-based Methods: These methods require the maintenance of level sets as the scalar value sweeps through the domain. Doraiswamy and Natarajan proposed an approach that explicitly maintains level sets, eliminating the need for loop-surgery pre-processing and generalizing to higher-dimensional inputs. 2. Split-and-Compute Methods: These methods collapse the problem to a contour tree computation. Loop Surgery (Tierny et al.): Perform symbolic cuts during the merge tree step to break loops, then stitch them back together to retrieve a topologically correct Reeb graph. Optimized Split-and-Compute (Doraiswamy and Natarajan): Use the join tree to identify potential loops, segment the domain into multiple loop-free contour trees instead of a single one, and compute these regions in parallel. 3. Streaming Algorithm (Pascucci et al.): An online algorithm that processes data points as they arrive, continually updating the output. This limits peak memory usage but has higher time complexity. 4. Random Collapse (Harvey et al.): Randomly collapses triangles for arbitrary 2-skeletons to improve running time. Formulas and Definitions: Streaming algorithm complexity: O(n^2), where n is the number of triangles. Random collapse complexity: O(m \log m), where m is the number of triangles. Parameters: Input Representation: The input must be represented on a simplicial mesh. Dimension: Applicable to models of any dimension, provided the 2-skeleton restriction is met. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Genus Sensitivity: Computations are sensitive to the topological genus of the input domain (e.g., sphere vs. torus). The number of loops from the Morse function extends algorithm complexity. Critical Point Precision: Variations in neighbor definition can slightly alter critical vertex locations without changing the graph structure. Stability: Output remains fixed provided the simplicial subdivision does not change. The Joint Contour Net (JCN) is a discrete graph-based representation of the Reeb space for multivariate scalar data, approximating the topology of n variables defined over an m-dimensional domain. It solves the problem of visualizing and analyzing the topological relationships between multiple scalar fields by partitioning the domain into connected regions called joint contour slabs. Unlike the Reeb Graph, which handles single-variable topology, the JCN extends this to multivariate inputs; it differs from the Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph by using a quantization-based slab construction rather than critical node extraction. The Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph (MDRG) is a hierarchical data structure used to represent the topology of multivariate scalar fields by recursively storing joint contours. It solves the problem of capturing complex topological relationships in domains with multiple independent functions (e.g., pressure, temperature) where standard univariate methods fail. It sets itself apart from the Joint Contour Net by providing a recursive, tiered representation of the Reeb space, which serves as an intermediate structure for extracting the Jacobi structure and the Reeb skeleton. This method measures the geometric size of topological handles in a scalar field by computing two specific nonseparating loops: the Reeb loop and the cross loop. It solves the problem of quantifying handle prominence to guide topology simplification, ensuring that geometric changes to the volume are minimized. It differs from sibling methods like Joint Contour Net by explicitly constructing these minimal loops on the isosurface to define a handle size metric, rather than relying solely on multi-dimensional topological descriptors. Time Complexity: The streaming algorithm by Pascucci et al. has O(n^2) complexity, where n is the number of triangles. This is optimal for 2D inputs but performs less favorably for higher-dimensional inputs. Harvey et al. propose a method with O(m \log m) complexity for arbitrary 2-skeletons. Memory Complexity: The streaming nature of the Pascucci et al. algorithm limits peak memory usage. Strengths: Correctly handles non-simply connected domains and domains without boundaries, which the contour tree cannot. Supports online/streaming computation. Generalizes to higher dimensions. Limitations: Computation is sensitive to topological genus; more loops increase complexity. Requires a simplicial mesh representation. When to use: Use when the scalar field is defined on a domain with loops or no boundary, and single-variable topology is sufficient. Use when online/streaming computation is required. When not to use: Use the Contour Tree if the domain is simply connected with a boundary, as it is simpler. Use Joint Contour Net or Multi-Dimensional Reeb Graph if the data is multivariate. The Reeb graph was first used for encoding topological features for visualization purposes by Shinagawa and Kunii, who applied it to represent objects from computerized-tomography (CT) sources. The sensitivity of Reeb graph computations to the topological genus of the input domain was first demonstrated by McLaughlin. Pascucci et al. later provided an online streaming algorithm. Tierny et al. introduced the "loop-surgery" technique to address genus sensitivity. Doraiswamy and Natarajan proposed alternative approaches, including explicit level set maintenance and optimized split-and-compute techniques using join trees. The Reeb graph has also been used to assist in the design of transfer functions in volume visualization by assigning opacity based on how many objects were obscured by nested surfaces and their proximity to the edge of a scalar field.
