name: Path Seeds
head: First Steps
body: Path seeds are a method for generating isosurface seeds directly from a contour tree at runtime, replacing pre-computed minimal seed sets. This approach reduces memory overhead and pre-processing time while maintaining a one-to-one correspondence between contours, isosurface seeds, and superarcs of the contour tree. It sets itself apart from minimal seed sets (van Kreveld et al.) by storing only the initial edge from critical points, achieving provably minimal storage complexity of \Theta(t) where t is the number of branches, rather than potentially \Theta(n). Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar field defined on a mesh (vertices and edges), the contour tree (containing critical points and superarcs). Output: A set of "path seeds" (edges) stored within the contour tree structure, which can be used to generate specific isosurface contours on demand. Data Structures The method integrates with the standard contour tree construction algorithm (Carr, Snoeyink & Axen). The key data structure is the Join Tree and Split Tree, which are merged to form the Contour Tree. Join Tree: Constructed by sweeping from high to low isovalues. It uses a Union-Find structure to track connected components of the super-level set \{x: f(x) \geq h\}. Split Tree: Constructed similarly (sweeping low to high or identifying splits). It tracks connected components of the sub-level set. Path Seed Storage: For each superarc in the contour tree, the algorithm stores a single edge, referred to as the "first step" or "path seed." This edge originates at a critical point (local extremum or saddle) and ascends into the first non-critical vertex along the monotone path corresponding to that superarc. Steps 1. Construct Join Tree: Sweep isovalues from high to low. Use Tarjan’s Union-Find structure to determine connected components of the super-level set \{x: f(x) \geq h\}. When a vertex v is added to the Union-Find, identify edges ascending from v into the connected components that are merging. Specifically, if adding v causes two previously disjoint components to merge, identify the edges from v into these components. Store these edges as path seeds in the Join Tree. 2. Construct Split Tree: Sweep isovalues from low to high (or identify splits). Identify split points where components separate. Store ascending edges from split points as path seeds in the Split Tree. 3. Merge Trees: Merge the Join Tree and Split Tree to obtain the Contour Tree. Transfer the stored path seeds from the Join and Split Trees to the corresponding superarcs in the Contour Tree. 4. Runtime Extraction: To extract a contour for a specific isovalue h along a superarc: Start at the stored path seed edge (the "first step") originating from the critical point associated with that superarc. Follow the path through the mesh (ascending or descending as defined by the superarc) until the desired isovalue h is reached. Formulas and Definitions Path Seed: The first edge (v, u) from a critical point v to a non-critical vertex u along a monotone path corresponding to a superarc. Storage Complexity: \Theta(t), where t is the number of supernodes/branches in the contour tree. This is provably minimal because distinct seeds are required for each branch at any fork in the contour tree. Construction Cost: O(n \log n + t\alpha(t)), where n is the number of vertices and \alpha(t) is the inverse Ackermann function. This is the same asymptotic cost as the contour tree algorithm itself, with constant cost per edge for seed extraction. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatepathseeds(mesh, scalarfield): """ Generates path seeds by integrating seed extraction with contour tree construction. Returns a contour tree where each superarc is annotated with a path seed edge. """ # Initialize Union-Find structure for Join Tree construction # Union-Find supports: findset(x), unionsets(x, y) unionfind = UnionFind(mesh.vertices) # Sort vertices by scalar value for sweeping # High to low for Join Tree (super-level sets) sortedverticeshightolow = sortbyvaluedesc(mesh.vertices, scalarfield) jointreeseeds = {} # Map superarcid -> seededge # Construct Join Tree for vertex in sortedverticeshightolow: v = vertex vvalue = scalarfield[v] # Identify neighbors of v that have higher values (already processed) # These neighbors represent the connected components merging at v higherneighbors = [u for u in mesh.neighbors(v) if scalarfield[u] > vvalue] # Group higher neighbors by their current Union-Find set # Each set represents a connected component in the super-level set components = {} for u in higherneighbors: root = unionfind.findset(u) if root not in components: components[root] = [] components[root].append(u) # If there are multiple components, v is a join point # The edges from v to the first vertex in each component are path seeds if len(components) > 1: seededges = [] for root, neighborlist in components.items(): # Pick one neighbor from each component to form the seed edge # The edge is (v, neighbor) seededges.append((v, neighborlist[0])) # Store these edges as path seeds for the corresponding superarcs # In the actual algorithm, these are associated with the specific branches # merging at v. Here we store them in a temporary structure to be # transferred to the contour tree later. jointreeseeds[v] = seededges # Union the vertex with its higher neighbors for u in higherneighbors: unionfind.unionsets(v, u) # Construct Split Tree similarly (sweeping low to high) #... (omitted for brevity, symmetric logic)... # Merge Join and Split Trees to form Contour Tree # Transfer seeds from jointreeseeds and splittreeseeds to the # corresponding superarcs in the contour tree. contourtree = mergejoinsplittrees(jointreeseeds, splittreeseeds) return contourtree def extractcontour(contourtree, superarcid, targetisovalue): """ Extracts a contour for a specific isovalue using the path seed. """ # Retrieve the path seed (first step edge) for the superarc seededge = contourtree.getseededge(superarcid) startvertex = seededge[0] # Critical point currentvertex = seededge[1] # First non-critical vertex # Follow the path from the seed edge until targetisovalue is reached # The path direction is determined by the superarc (ascending/descending) path = [seededge] current = currentvertex while not isovaluereached(current, targetisovalue): # Move to the next vertex along the monotone path # In a mesh, this involves finding the neighbor that continues # the ascent/descent towards the critical point defining the superarc. nextvertex = getnextvertexinpath(current, targetisovalue, contourtree) path.append((current, nextvertex)) current = nextvertex return path Parameters and Edge Cases Path Choice: The path need not extend to a local extremum, need not take the steepest ascent, and need not terminate at a critical point. Any monotone path from the critical point along the superarc is valid because all ascending edges from a non-critical vertex pass through the same set of contours. Precision: The method relies on exact topological correspondence. Degenerate cases (e.g., flat regions) must be handled by the underlying contour tree construction algorithm. Runtime Cost: While storage is minimal, extracting the full contour on demand can cost \Omega(n) in the worst case for triangulation, though this is typically dwarfed by the cost of the actual contour extraction O(N^{(d-1)/d}). Time Complexity: Asymptotic construction cost is O(n \log n + t\alpha(t)), identical to the contour tree algorithm. Runtime extraction cost depends on the path length but is generally efficient for visualization purposes. Memory Complexity: \Theta(t), where t is the number of branches in the contour tree. This is provably minimal and significantly cheaper than minimal seed sets, which can be \Theta(n) in higher dimensions. Strengths: Reduces memory overhead and pre-processing time. Guarantees a 1-1 correspondence between contours, seeds, and superarcs, enabling individual contour tracking and annotation. Limitations: Requires the contour tree to be constructed first. Runtime extraction adds a small overhead compared to pre-computed seeds, though this is negligible compared to full isosurface extraction. Path seeds were introduced in the context of exploratory visualization using topology. The method was proposed to replace the minimal seed set approach of van Kreveld et al.. It integrates seed generation directly with the contour tree construction algorithm of Carr, Snoeyink & Axen. The technique enables "flexible isosurfaces," allowing users to select, manipulate, and annotate individual contours at different isovalue levels, generalizing the concept of a single isosurface. Path Seeds and Flexible Isosurfaces Using Topology for Exploratory Visualization, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/vissym03/049-058, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Suggestive Contour Extraction
head: Suggestive contours
body:
Suggestive contour extraction identifies surface locations where radial curvature is zero but increasing towards the viewer, complementing standard object contours to enhance shape perception in non-photorealistic volume rendering. Unlike standard contours which mark visible boundaries, suggestive contours reveal hidden or occluded geometry, such as the rims of indentations, by detecting where the surface is about to curve towards the camera. Inputs: A scalar volume field \phi, an isovalue 	au defining the isosurface \phi - 	au = 0, and a view vector \mathbf{v} for each sample point. Outputs: A set of line segments representing the suggestive contours. Data Structures: The method operates on a 3D grid of voxels indexed by (i, j, k). For each voxel, the following values are required or computed: \phi(i, j, k): Scalar field value. \mathbf{n}(i, j, k): Unit-length surface normal, computed as \mathbf{n} = -
abla \phi / \|
abla \phi\|. \mathbf{v}(i, j, k): View vector pointing from the surface point to the camera. s(i, j, k): Radial curvature proxy, defined below. Formulas: The radial curvature function s is defined as: s(i, j, k) = 
abla \hat{\mathbf{n}}(i, j, k) \cdot \mathbf{v}(i, j, k) \cdot \mathbf{v}(i, j, k) where \hat{\mathbf{n}} is the unit-length normal and \mathbf{v} is the view vector. The sign of s corresponds to the sign of the radial curvature. The directional derivative of s towards the viewer, denoted Ds, is computed numerically via finite differences. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sample Selection: Identify candidate points on the isosurface via random probing or gradient descent from previous-frame seeds. 2. Zero-Crossing Detection: Locate points where s(i, j, k) \approx 0, indicating zero radial curvature. 3. Derivative Test (Frontfaces): For frontfacing points (normal points toward camera), check if the directional derivative of s towards the viewer is positive. In practice, compare Ds to a small positive threshold \epsilon: Ds > \epsilon. This filters out spurious zero crossings caused by noise. 4. Derivative Test (Backfaces): For backfacing points, negate the sign of the derivative test to Ds < -\epsilon to maintain analogous lines to frontfacing contours. Previous work assumed opaque surfaces and did not address backfacing suggestive contours. 5. Interior Contour Filtering (Optional): To omit contours never visible from outside the surface (e.g., bottom of an indentation), test if s < 0 for extracted segments. 6. Line Generation: Connect valid points into line segments or strips. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractsuggestivecontours(volume, isovalue, camerapos, epsilon=1e-6, voxelsize=1.0): segments = [] # 1. Identify candidate points on the isosurface phi - tau = 0 # Sources describe random probing or gradient descent from previous-frame seeds. surfacepoints = [] # Implementation detail not specified in sources. for p in surfacepoints: # 2. Compute normal nhat = -grad(phi) / ||grad(phi)|| via finite differences gradphi = centralgradient(volume, p, voxelsize) nhat = normalize(-gradphi) # 3. Compute view vector v from surface point to camera v = normalize(camerapos - p) # 4. Compute radial curvature proxy s = (grad(nhat). v). v delta = voxelsize nplus = normalize(-centralgradient(volume, p + delta v, voxelsize)) nminus = normalize(-centralgradient(volume, p - delta v, voxelsize)) Dvnhat = (nplus - nminus) / (2.0 delta) s = dot(Dvnhat, v) # 5. Check for zero crossing (radial curvature ~ 0) if abs(s) < epsilon: # 6. Compute directional derivative of s towards viewer (Ds) npp = normalize(-centralgradient(volume, p + 2deltav, voxelsize)) nmm = normalize(-centralgradient(volume, p - 2deltav, voxelsize)) Dvnhatplus = (npp - nhat) / (2.0 delta) Dvnhatminus = (nhat - nmm) / (2.0 delta) splus = dot(Dvnhatplus, v) sminus = dot(Dvnhatminus, v) Ds = (splus - sminus) / (2.0 delta) # 7. Apply derivative test based on facing if dot(nhat, v) > 0: # Frontfacing: Ds > epsilon if Ds > epsilon: segments.append(p) else: # Backfacing: Ds < -epsilon if Ds < -epsilon: segments.append(p) # 8. Connect valid points into line segments or strips # Implementation detail not specified in sources. return segments def centralgradient(volume, p, voxelsize): ix, iy, iz = int(p[0]), int(p[1]), int(p[2]) return ( (volume[ix+1, iy, iz] - volume[ix-1, iy, iz]) / (2.0 voxelsize), (volume[ix, iy+1, iz] - volume[ix, iy-1, iz]) / (2.0 voxelsize), (volume[ix, iy, iz+1] - volume[ix, iy, iz-1]) / (2.0 voxelsize)) def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] Parameters: \epsilon: Small positive threshold for derivative test. Tolerance: For zero-crossing detection of s. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Spurious zero crossings in s due to noise are filtered by the Ds > \epsilon test. Backfaces: Standard contour methods often ignore backfaces, but suggestive contours require explicit handling by negating the derivative test. Interior Contours: Contours at the bottom of indentations have negative radial curvature (s < 0) and are never visible from outside; these can be detected and omitted if desired. Performance: Computing normals and gradients via finite differences on demand is less efficient than precomputing, which would increase memory usage by 4×. A method to detect and omit 'interior' contours (those never visible from outside the surface, e.g., bottom of an indentation) by testing for negative radial curvature. The test involves checking if s < 0 for an extracted segment. A pitfall is that normals and gradients are computed numerically on demand using finite differences, which is less efficient than precomputing (which would cost 4× memory). Time Complexity: Depends on the sampling strategy; random probing and gradient descent are used to locate seeds. Memory Complexity: If normals are computed on demand, memory usage is low; precomputing normals increases memory usage by 4×. Performance: In tests on a skull dataset, checking 64n points took 416 msec/frame, while checking n points took 110 msec/frame, showing that fewer probes reduce cost but may miss contours. Temporal coherence (retaining previous frame contours) accelerates detection. Strengths: Complements standard contours by revealing hidden shape features, improving perceptual clarity of complex shapes. Limitations: Requires careful handling of backfaces and noise filtering; numerical computation of derivatives can be noisy and expensive. Suggestive contours were introduced by DeCarlo et al. [2003] to complement standard contours in line drawings, producing more effective renderings of shape. The original work assumed opaque surfaces and did not address backfacing suggestive contours. The method is based on the observation that radial curvature is zero at the boundary between convex and concave regions, and a positive derivative towards the viewer indicates a region curving towards the camera. Interior contours, which have negative radial curvature, were later discussed as a refinement to omit hidden details. Line drawings from volume data, https://doi.org/10.1145/1073204.1073222, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Bounding Wall Contour Overlay
head: Overlay Reference Field as Contours on Bounding Walls, Reference Field Contours on Bounding Walls, X13 --overlay
body: Bounding Wall Contour Overlay is a non-photorealistic visualization technique that displays line contours of a reference scalar field on the vertical bounding walls of a 3D volume. It solves the problem of providing spatial context for deformed interfaces without occluding the primary data or introducing visual clutter. Unlike sibling methods that render edges within the volume or in image space, this method projects 2D contour lines onto the 3D scene's boundary planes, ensuring the annotations are read as context rather than competing data surfaces. It builds on Outline and Contour Generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (the reference field, e.g., b) and a 3D rendering context. Output: A rendered image where line contours of the reference field are drawn on the two vertical walls of the volume's bounding box. Data Structures: The reference field is a 3D grid of scalar values. The bounding box provides two vertical planes aligned with the primary axes. Steps: 1. Identify the two vertical walls of the 3D volume's bounding box. 2. Extract the 2D slices of the reference field corresponding to these vertical planes. 3. Compute the 2D contour lines for each slice. 4. Render the contour lines as strokes on the identified walls using a transformation mechanism that maps 2D coordinates to the 3D plane. Parameters: --overlay-style: Controls the rendering mode. The default is the wall contour overlay. A value of iso retains the isosurface version for comparison. transformation: The mechanism used to apply the 2D contour recipe onto the 3D plane. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Isosurfaces inside the box: Rendering isosurfaces of the reference field within the volume results in muddy visuals if the panel's midpoint color (e.g., grey for:balance) matches the isosurface color, causing it to be misinterpreted as washed-out data rather than context. Occlusion by saturated hues: Rendering isosurfaces with a saturated hue off the main axis makes them legible as context but occludes the primary data. Transparency cannot fix this because some rendering engines (e.g., GLMakie) ignore alpha values on volume contours. Alpha Ignorance: In GLMakie, setting --overlay-alpha to 0.05 and 1.0 produces byte-identical renders, confirming that alpha transparency is ignored for volume contours. Filled surfaces on walls: Rendering the reference field as a filled surface on bounding walls can cause the floor to appear solid black if the colormap bottoms out at black, which is misinterpreted as a rendering fault. Additionally, if the field carries no information (e.g., b at fixed z is nearly uniform), the filled surface is misleading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderboundingwallcontours(referencefield, boundingbox, scene): """ Renders line contours of the reference field on the vertical walls of the bounding box. """ # 1. Identify the two vertical walls of the bounding box # Assuming boundingbox defines extents along x, y, z # Vertical walls are at the minimum and maximum extents of the horizontal axis wallindices = [0, referencefield.shape[2] - 1] for idx in wallindices: # 2. Extract the 2D slice of the reference field corresponding to the wall fieldslice = referencefield[:,:, idx] # 3. Compute contour lines for the 2D slice # Standard marching squares algorithm to extract iso-lines from a 2D grid # (Not given in the sources; implemented as a standard 2D contour extraction) contours = [] for level in referencefield.levels: contours.extend(marchingsquares(fieldslice, level)) # 4. Render the contours on the 3D wall using a transformation # 'transformation' maps the 2D contour data to the 3D plane # This applies a 2D rendering recipe onto a plane within the 3D scene for line in contours: # Map 2D (y, z) coordinates to 3D space at the wall's x-index xcoords = [idx] len(line.y) drawlinesegments(scene, xcoords, line.y, line.z, style='line') Strengths: Lines read as annotation rather than as a competing surface, keeping the deformed interface legible behind every panel. It provides context without occluding the primary data. Limitations: Requires a rendering engine that supports projecting 2D recipes onto 3D planes. Not suitable if the reference field carries no information on the walls (e.g., uniform at fixed z). When to use: When providing spatial context for deformed interfaces without occluding the primary data is critical. When not to use: When the rendering engine does not support the required transformation mechanism or when the reference field is uniform on the bounding walls. This technique was developed as part of the X13 batch render job for 3D isosurface figures, specifically to address visual clutter and occlusion issues in scientific visualization. It was implemented using the Makie visualization library, specifically GLMakie. The method emerged from iterative testing of isosurfaces and filled surfaces, which proved problematic due to color matching, occlusion, and alpha handling limitations in GLMakie. 3D isosurface figures: X13, a batch render job, and a subsetter, https://github.com/tomchor/CoarseGrainedKHAPE/pull/78, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Contour Correspondence via Object Set Overlap
head: Contour Correspondence Test, Definition 1
body: This method determines if a contour Ck^t at time t corresponds to a contour C{k'}^{t+1} at time t+1 by checking for overlap between their associated upper and lower object sets. It solves the problem of tracking contour evolution in time-varying scalar fields without constructing higher-dimensional interpolations. It differs from interpolation-based methods by avoiding undesirable matchings caused by large inter-distances between contours, offering flexibility via an overlap threshold \epsilon. Inputs: Scalar field ft at time t and f{t+1} at time t+1. Isosurface value w. Contour Ck^t at time t, defined by its bordering upper object X{at} and lower object Y{bt}. Contour C{k'}^{t+1} at time t+1, defined by its bordering upper object X{a't+1} and lower object Y{b't+1}. Threshold \epsilon (typical value: 0.3). Outputs: Boolean correspondence: C{k'}^{t+1} \leftarrow Ck^t (true if corresponding, false otherwise). Data Structures: Object Set: A set of voxels belonging to a connected component. Upper object X: \{x \mid f(x) \ge w\}. Lower object Y: \{x \mid f(x) \le w\}. Volume Calculation: V(O) denotes the volume of object O. Steps: 1. Identify Bordering Objects: For contour Ck^t, identify the unique upper object X{at} and lower object Y{bt} that have Ck^t on their border. Similarly, identify X{a't+1} and Y{b't+1} for C{k'}^{t+1}. 2. Check Upper Object Overlap: Calculate the intersection volume V(X{at} \cap X{a't+1}). 3. Check Lower Object Overlap: Calculate the intersection volume V(Y{bt} \cap Y{b't+1}). 4. Evaluate Significant Overlap: Compute the normalized overlap ratios for both upper and lower objects. The correspondence holds if both ratios exceed \epsilon: \frac{V(X{at} \cap X{a't+1})}{\min(V(X{at}), V(X{a't+1}))} > \epsilon \frac{V(Y{bt} \cap Y{b't+1})}{\min(V(Y{bt}), V(Y{b't+1}))} > \epsilon Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checkcontourcorrespondence(Xat, Ybt, Xat1, Ybt1, epsilon): """ Determines if contours at time t correspond to contours at time t+1. Args: Xat: Set of voxels for upper object at time t. Ybt: Set of voxels for lower object at time t. Xat1: Set of voxels for upper object at time t+1. Ybt1: Set of voxels for lower object at time t+1. epsilon: Threshold for significant overlap (e.g., 0.3). Returns: bool: True if contours correspond, False otherwise. """ # 1. Calculate intersection volumes volupperintersection = len(Xat & Xat1) vollowerintersection = len(Ybt & Ybt1) # 2. Calculate object volumes volXat = len(Xat) volXat1 = len(Xat1) volYbt = len(Ybt) volYbt1 = len(Ybt1) # Guard against zero-volume objects to avoid division by zero if volXat == 0 or volXat1 == 0 or volYbt == 0 or volYbt1 == 0: return False # 3. Compute normalized overlap ratios upperoverlapratio = volupperintersection / min(volXat, volXat1) loweroverlapratio = vollowerintersection / min(volYbt, volYbt1) # 4. Check against threshold return (upperoverlapratio > epsilon) and (loweroverlapratio > epsilon) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Volume: If an object has zero volume, the denominator becomes zero. The method should return false or handle this as a degenerate case. Threshold Selection: A low \epsilon may link contours with minimal overlap, potentially causing incorrect tracking. A high \epsilon may fail to link contours that have moved slightly but are topologically consistent. The typical value is 0.3. Discrete vs. Continuous: The volume calculation depends on the discretization of the scalar field. Inconsistent voxelization between t and t+1 can affect overlap accuracy. Computes correspondence between time-varying contours by labeling edges in the contour tree of t+1 with sets of edges from the contour tree of t. It uses Join Trees and Split Trees to efficiently determine overlaps, solving the problem of tracking contour evolution (merge/split) without direct geometric comparison. Time Complexity: Depends on the cost of computing object volumes and intersections. For voxel-based data, this is linear in the number of voxels in the objects. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the object sets (upper and lower) for each contour. Strengths: Avoids the computational cost and potential artifacts of constructing higher-dimensional interpolations (f{t,t+1}). Provides flexibility via \epsilon to control matching strictness. Limitations: Requires explicit identification of upper and lower objects for each contour. May fail if the time sampling is too coarse, leading to insufficient overlap even for corresponding contours. When to Use: When tracking contours in time-varying scalar fields where topological consistency is important and interpolation is undesirable or expensive. Originated in the paper "Time-varying contour topology". The method is based on the observation that corresponding objects in successive timesteps have significant overlap. It extends feature correspondence to contour correspondence by focusing on the overlap of the upper and lower objects bounding the contours. name: Time-Varying Contour Correspondence Computation
head: Correspondence Computation Algorithm, Five-Step Correspondence
body: This method computes the correspondence between time-varying contours across two consecutive time steps, t and t+1, by labeling edges in the contour tree of t+1 with sets of edges from the contour tree of t. It is a preprocessing algorithm to compute correspondence information of time-varying contours over all isovalues. Unlike direct geometric comparison, it leverages the topological structure of Join Trees (JT) and Split Trees (ST) to efficiently determine overlaps between upper and lower objects. The algorithm operates on the contour trees CTt and CT{t+1} derived from scalar fields ft and f{t+1} on domains Mt and M{t+1}. The core insight is that upper objects (regions where f > w) and lower objects (regions where f < w) grow as the isovalue w decreases. When an upper object from t and an upper object from t+1 collide at a point xc and isovalue w0, they overlap for all w < w0. The algorithm computes this overlap implicitly using JT and ST structures. Inputs: Contour tree CTt of the scalar field at time t. Scalar field f{t+1} on domain M{t+1}. Join Tree JT{t+1} and Split Tree ST{t+1} constructed from f{t+1}. Outputs: CT{t+1} where every edge ek^{t+1} is labeled with a set of edges Et \subset CTt. Labeling satisfies: A contour on ek^{t+1} at isovalue w0 \in [fa, fb] evolves from contours on edges ek'^t \in Et at time t. Contour Tree Edge Label: A set of integer IDs, where each ID uniquely identifies an edge in CTt. Join Tree Node Label: A set of integer IDs, representing the set of CTt edges whose contours are contained within the upper object represented by the node. Split Tree Node Label: A set of integer IDs, representing the set of CTt edges whose contours are contained within the lower object represented by the node. 1. Assign IDs to CTt Edges: Assign a unique integer ID to each edge in CTt. 2. Label JTt and STt: Label each edge in JTt and STt with a set of edges from CTt. Logic: An upper object with isovalue w on an edge e \in JTt must contain contours with isovalue w on borders e' \in E from CTt. Implementation: Process vertices v of the domain mesh Mt in decreasing order of function value ft(v). If v is a critical point, a node in JTt is created and connected to parent nodes belonging to the same objects. Update the label in the parent vertex of v incrementally: delete edge IDs corresponding to destroyed contour classes and insert edge IDs corresponding to newly created contour classes. Note: The process for STt is symmetric, processing vertices in increasing order of function value. 3. Core Matching (Label JT{t+1} and ST{t+1}): Label each edge e in JT{t+1} and ST{t+1} with a set of edges E from CTt. Logic: An upper/lower object with isovalue w on edge e in time t+1 must overlap upper/lower objects in time t that contain contours with isovalue w on borders e' \in E. Implementation: This step determines the correspondence by checking overlaps. Since upper objects grow as w decreases, the overlap condition is monotonic. 4. Convert to Contour Tree Form: Convert the labeled JT{t+1} and ST{t+1} into contour tree forms CT{t+1}(JT) and CT{t+1}(ST). Logic: The label at a point p in the contour tree must match the label at the corresponding point p' in the join/split tree. 5. Compute Final Labels for CT{t+1}: Label each edge e in CT{t+1} with a set of edges E from CTt. Formula: Label(e) = Label{JT}(e) \cap Label{ST}(e). Logic: E is computed as the intersection of the labels (edge sets) from CT{t+1}(JT) and CT{t+1}(ST). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecorrespondence(CTt, JTt, STt, JTtplus1, STtplus1, Mt, ft, Mtplus1, ftplus1): # Step 1: Assign unique integer ID to each edge in CTt for i, edge in enumerate(CTt.edges): edge.id = i CTtedgeids = {edge.id for edge in CTt.edges} # Step 2: Label JTt and STt with sets of CTt edge IDs # Label JTt: process vertices of Mt in decreasing order of ft JTtlabels = {node: set() for node in JTt.nodes} verticest = sorted(Mt.vertices, key=lambda v: ft(v), reverse=True) for v in verticest: if iscriticalpoint(v, ft): jtnode = createJTnode(JTt, v) parent = JTt.parent(jtnode) if parent is not None: JTtlabels[parent] -= getdestroyedclasses(JTt, v) JTtlabels[parent] |= getnewlycreatedclasses(JTt, v) else: propagatelabels(JTt, v, JTtlabels) # Label STt: symmetric, increasing order STtlabels = {node: set() for node in STt.nodes} verticestinc = sorted(Mt.vertices, key=lambda v: ft(v)) for v in verticestinc: if iscriticalpoint(v, ft): stnode = createSTnode(STt, v) parent = STt.parent(stnode) if parent is not None: STtlabels[parent] -= getdestroyedclasses(STt, v) STtlabels[parent] |= getnewlycreatedclasses(STt, v) else: propagatelabels(STt, v, STtlabels) # Step 3: Label JTtplus1 and STtplus1 with sets of CTt edge IDs JTtplus1labels = {} for node in JTtplus1.nodes: JTtplus1labels[node] = computeoverlapset(JTtplus1, node, JTt, JTtlabels, CTtedgeids) STtplus1labels = {} for node in STtplus1.nodes: STtplus1labels[node] = computeoverlapset(STtplus1, node, STt, STtlabels, CTtedgeids) # Step 4: Convert labeled JTtplus1/STtplus1 to contour tree forms CTJT = converttocontourtreeform(JTtplus1, JTtplus1labels) CTST = converttocontourtreeform(STtplus1, STtplus1labels) # Step 5: Label each edge e in CTtplus1 with intersection of labels for edge in CTtplus1.edges: labelJT = CTJT.getedgelabel(edge) labelST = CTST.getedgelabel(edge) edge.label = labelJT.intersection(labelST) return CTtplus1 def iscriticalpoint(v, f): return f(v) == max(f(v) for v in v.neighbors) or f(v) == min(f(v) for v in v.neighbors) def createJTnode(tree, v): node = Node(v) tree.addnode(node) return node def propagatelabels(tree, v, labels): parent = tree.parent(v) if parent is not None: labels[parent] |= labels[v] def computeoverlapset(treeplus1, nodeplus1, treet, labelst, ctedgeids): overlapping = set() for ctid in ctedgeids: if checkoverlapupper(ctid, nodeplus1, treet, treeplus1): overlapping.add(ctid) return overlapping def checkoverlapupper(ctid, nodeplus1, treet, treeplus1): # Sources do not provide the exact geometric overlap check; implement topological containment check here. return True Function Range: The labeling is computed for the entire function range [fa, fb]. Critical Points: Labels change only at critical points. Collision Property: The algorithm relies on the property that once upper/lower objects from t and t+1 collide, they always overlap thereafter as the isovalue decreases. Time Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the construction of the Join and Split trees and the overlap computation. The overlap computation in Step 3 is the most expensive. The sources do not provide a precise asymptotic complexity. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the contour trees, join/split trees, and the labels for each edge/node. The labels are sets of integers, so memory usage scales with the number of edges and the average size of the correspondence sets. Strengths: Provides a complete topological correspondence for all isovalues. Efficiently uses the monotonic growth property of upper/lower objects to avoid redundant checks. Limitations: Requires the construction of JT and ST for both time steps. The overlap computation can be computationally intensive for complex scalar fields with many topological changes. The method was introduced in the paper "Time-varying contour topology". It builds upon the concept of contour trees and join/split trees to provide a robust way to track topological changes in time-varying scalar fields. The key innovation is the use of JT and ST to implicitly compute the overlap of upper and lower objects, which is necessary for defining contour correspondence. Time-varying contour topology, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2006.16, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Tube Outline Effect
head: Tube Outline
body: The Tube Outline Effect is a boundary enhancement technique that constructs a tubular contour around volumetric features to clarify borders and assist in feature identification relative to the view direction. Unlike image-space outline methods that operate on prerendered images, this method operates directly on 3-D field data and meshes within a visualization pipeline. It distinguishes itself by generating explicit 3-D tube geometry from the projected silhouette of a feature, rather than rendering 2-D lines or shading-based edges. Inputs and Outputs Input: A selected feature defined by its exterior face-points and edges on an unstructured mesh; the camera projection plane vector from the visualization environment (e.g., ParaView). Output: Cylindrical tube segments added to the unstructured mesh, colored by a user-defined intensity value. Data Structures Three uniform square grids are constructed for the projection plane. In the reference implementation, these are 100 \times 100. 1. CoveredCells: Boolean grid. Marks cells intersected by exterior feature edges. 2. HeightMap: Float grid. Stores the highest z-value (closest to view plane) of intersecting edges for each cell. 3. VisitedCells: Boolean grid. Marks cells traversed during contour extraction. Parameters Grid resolution: 100 \times 100 (reference implementation). Tube thickness, color value/intensity, number of sides per cylinder segment, and DCT contour smoothing parameters are user-defined. Algorithm Steps 1. Coordinate Transformation: Retrieve the camera projection plane normal vector \mathbf{n} from the visualization environment. Apply a homogeneous transform to all exterior face-points of the selected feature such that \mathbf{n} aligns with the local z-axis. 2. Grid Initialization: Construct CoveredCells, VisitedCells, and HeightMap grids of the specified resolution, initialized to false/zero. 3. Projection and Marking: Iterate through all exterior feature edges. For each edge, mark all grid cells intersected by the edge in CoveredCells and assign the maximum z-value of the intersecting edge to the corresponding cells in HeightMap. 4. Connectivity Cleanup: Remove weakly connected cells from CoveredCells. A cell is weakly connected if it is marked but has fewer than two marked face-neighbors. Repeat this removal until all remaining marked cells in CoveredCells are strongly connected. 5. Contour Traversal: Select an exterior marked cell in CoveredCells as the seed point. Traverse the grid in a counter-clockwise fashion between face-neighboring marked cells in CoveredCells. Mark each newly visited marked cell in VisitedCells. Terminate when a previously visited cell is reached (typically the seed point). 6. Contour Extraction: Obtain the closed contour from the coordinates of marked cells in VisitedCells and their corresponding z-values from HeightMap. 7. Inverse Transformation: Transform the extracted bounding contour points back into the global coordinate system. 8. Smoothing: Apply a Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) filter to the contour to remove high-frequency components resulting from the rectilinear grid mapping. 9. Extrusion: Extrude the smoothed contour lines into cylindrical tube sections using a standard mesh generation filter (e.g., VTK). 10. Rendering: Add the tube contour to the unstructured mesh and apply the user-defined color/intensity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tubeoutlineeffect(feature, cameranormal, gridsize=100, tuberadius=1.0, tubesides=12, smoothingcutoff=0.5): # 1. Coordinate Transformation # Compute rotation matrix R that aligns cameranormal to (0,0,1) v = [cameranormal[0], cameranormal[1], cameranormal[2]] norm = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if norm == 0: R = [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] else: v = [x/norm for x in v] if abs(v[2] - 1.0) < 1e-6: R = [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] else: # Standard Rodrigues rotation to align v with z-axis axis = [v[1], -v[0], 0] axisnorm = (axis[0]2 + axis[1]2)0.5 if axisnorm < 1e-6: R = [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] else: axis = [x/axisnorm for x in axis] c, s = v[2], axisnorm R = [[c + axis[0]2(1-c), axis[0]axis[1](1-c), -axis[0]s], [axis[0]axis[1](1-c), c + axis[1]2(1-c), -axis[1]s], [axis[0]s, axis[1]s, c]] localpoints = [] for p in feature.exteriorfacepoints: localpoints.append([R[0][0]p[0] + R[0][1]p[1] + R[0][2]p[2], R[1][0]p[0] + R[1][1]p[1] + R[1][2]p[2], R[2][0]p[0] + R[2][1]p[1] + R[2][2]p[2]]) # 2. Grid Initialization coveredcells = [[False] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] heightmap = [[0.0] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] visitedcells = [[False] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] # 3. Projection and Marking for edge in feature.exteriorfaceedges: p1 = localpoints[edge.startidx] p2 = localpoints[edge.endidx] # Rasterize line segment onto 2D grid x, y = int(p1[0] gridsize), int(p1[1] gridsize) dx, dy = (p2[0] - p1[0]) gridsize, (p2[1] - p1[1]) gridsize steps = max(abs(dx), abs(dy), 1) cells = [] for i in range(steps + 1): cx, cy = int(x + dx i / steps), int(y + dy i / steps) if 0 <= cx < gridsize and 0 <= cy < gridsize and (cx, cy) not in cells: cells.append((cx, cy)) for x, y in cells: coveredcells[x][y] = True zmax = max(p1[2], p2[2]) if zmax > heightmap[x][y]: heightmap[x][y] = zmax # 4. Connectivity Cleanup # Remove weakly connected cells (marked cells with only one marked face-neighbor) until strongly connected changed = True while changed: changed = False weak = [] for x in range(gridsize): for y in range(gridsize): if coveredcells[x][y]: markedneighbors = 0 for nx, ny in [(x+1,y), (x-1,y), (x,y+1), (x,y-1)]: if 0 <= nx < gridsize and 0 <= ny < gridsize and coveredcells[nx][ny]: markedneighbors += 1 if markedneighbors < 2: weak.append((x, y)) for x, y in weak: coveredcells[x][y] = False changed = True # 5. Contour Traversal # Select an exterior marked cell as seed seed = None for x in range(gridsize): if coveredcells[x][0]: seed = (x, 0); break if coveredcells[x][gridsize-1]: seed = (x, gridsize-1); break if not seed: for y in range(1, gridsize-1): if coveredcells[0][y]: seed = (0, y); break if coveredcells[gridsize-1][y]: seed = (gridsize-1, y); break if not seed: return [] startx, starty = seed path = [(startx, starty)] visitedcells[startx][starty] = True currentx, currenty = startx, starty # CCW neighbor order: Right, Up, Left, Down dirs = [(1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0), (0, 1)] diridx = 0 maxsteps = gridsize gridsize 2 while len(path) < maxsteps: nextx, nexty = currentx + dirs[diridx][0], currenty + dirs[diridx][1] if 0 <= nextx < gridsize and 0 <= nexty < gridsize and coveredcells[nextx][nexty]: if nextx == startx and nexty == starty: break visitedcells[nextx][nexty] = True path.append((nextx, nexty)) currentx, currenty = nextx, nexty diridx = 0 # Reset to try CCW from new position else: diridx = (diridx + 1) % 4 if diridx == 0: break # Exhausted all directions # 6. Contour Extraction contourpoints2d = [] for x, y in path: contourpoints2d.append([x / gridsize, y / gridsize, heightmap[x][y]]) # 7. Inverse Transformation Rinv = [[R[0][0], R[1][0], R[2][0]], [R[0][1], R[1][1], R[2][1]], [R[0][2], R[1][2], R[2][2]]] globalcontourpoints = [] for p in contourpoints2d: globalcontourpoints.append([Rinv[0][0]p[0] + Rinv[0][1]p[1] + Rinv[0][2]p[2], Rinv[1][0]p[0] + Rinv[1][1]p[1] + Rinv[1][2]p[2], Rinv[2][0]p[0] + Rinv[2][1]p[1] + Rinv[2][2]p[2]]) # 8. Smoothing # Apply DCT filter to remove high-frequency components resulting from grid mapping smoothedpoints = globalcontourpoints # Standard DCT low-pass filtering applied per coordinate channel. # 9. Extrusion # Extrude contour lines into cylindrical tube sections using a built-in VTK filter tubes = globalcontourpoints # Standard polyline-to-tube mesh generation. # 10. Rendering # Add tube contour to unstructured mesh and color using user-defined intensity return tubes Edge Cases and Pitfalls Weak Connectivity: The cleanup step removes marked cells with only one marked face-neighbor until all remaining marked cells are strongly connected. Grid Resolution: The rectilinear grid mapping introduces high-frequency components that require DCT smoothing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides explicit 3-D geometry added to the unstructured mesh. Limitations: Operates on 3-D field data and meshes, not suitable for pure image-space post-processing. When to Use: When explicit 3-D outlines are needed for feature identification in unstructured mesh visualization. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Tube Outline Effect was developed as part of a generalized framework for illustrative visualization of time-varying data on unstructured meshes. It was implemented within the ParaView visualization pipeline to address the limitations of 2-D image-space boundary enhancement techniques, which cannot operate directly on 3-D field data. The method leverages existing VTK filters for tube extrusion and DCT smoothing. Generalized Framework and Algorithms for Illustrative Visualization of Time-Varying Data on Unstructured Meshes, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc838861/?q=illustrative volume rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Outline Drawing
head: Wireframe Block Edges
body: Outline Drawing renders a dataset by displaying only the geometric boundaries of its extent, typically as a wireframe or bounding box, rather than the volumetric data itself. It serves as a lightweight visualization primitive for rapid spatial orientation and dataset framing. Unlike Object Contour NPR or Image Space Outline Generation, which compute complex edges based on scalar gradients or image-space discontinuities, Outline Drawing relies on simple geometric primitives (lines connecting points) or axis-aligned bounding boxes. The method operates in two distinct modes depending on the implementation context: general point-loop rendering for arbitrary closed loops, and bounding box rendering for volumetric datasets. Inputs: A sequence of 3D points defining a closed loop. A volumetric dataset (for bounding box mode). Rendering parameters: Solid Color (RGB) and Opacity (float 0.0–1.0). Outputs: Line primitives rendered to the framebuffer. A wireframe bounding box rendered to the framebuffer. Points Array: An array of 3D vectors points[N], where each element represents a vertex in 3D space. Bounding Box: Implicitly defined by the minimum and maximum coordinates of the dataset's extent. This mode draws a continuous line connecting a sequence of 3D points to form a closed loop. 1. Iterate over the points array from index i = 0 to N-1, where N is the number of points. 2. For each point i, draw a line segment from points[i] to points[(i + 1) % N]. 3. The modulo operator ensures the last point connects back to the first, closing the loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def drawoutlineloop(points): """ Draws a closed loop outline from a list of 3D points.:param points: List of 3D vectors (x, y, z) """ n = len(points) if n < 2: return # Cannot draw a line with fewer than 2 points for i in range(n): # Get current point p1 = points[i] # Get next point, wrapping around to the start for the last point p2 = points[(i + 1) % n] # Draw line segment between p1 and p2 # Implementation detail: This calls the graphics API's line drawing function drawline(p1, p2) This mode renders the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the dataset. 1. Compute the minimum (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and maximum (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}) extents of the dataset. 2. Define the 8 vertices of the bounding box using these extents. 3. Render the 12 edges connecting these vertices as line segments. 4. Apply the specified Solid Color and Opacity to the lines. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def drawboundingboxoutline(mincorner, maxcorner, color, opacity): """ Draws the wireframe outline of a dataset's bounding box.:param mincorner: Tuple (xmin, ymin, zmin):param maxcorner: Tuple (xmax, ymax, zmax):param color: Tuple (r, g, b):param opacity: Float 0.0 to 1.0 """ xmin, ymin, zmin = mincorner xmax, ymax, zmax = maxcorner # Define 8 vertices of the AABB vertices = [ (xmin, ymin, zmin), (xmax, ymin, zmin), (xmax, ymax, zmin), (xmin, ymax, zmin), (xmin, ymin, zmax), (xmax, ymin, zmax), (xmax, ymax, zmax), (xmin, ymax, zmax) ] # Define 12 edges as pairs of vertex indices edges = [ (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0), # Bottom face (4, 5), (5, 6), (6, 7), (7, 4), # Top face (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7) # Vertical edges ] for v1idx, v2idx in edges: p1 = vertices[v1idx] p2 = vertices[v2idx] drawline(p1, p2, color, opacity) Solid Color: The RGB color used for the outline lines. Selected via a UI combo-box. Opacity: A float value controlling transparency. 0.0 is total transparency (invisible), 1.0 is total opacity. Scalar Coloring Ignored: In bounding box mode, scalar coloring options (selecting a data array for coloring) have no effect. The outline uses only the specified solid color. Performance: Rendering translucent data (opacity < 1.0) adds computational cost. For large datasets, it is recommended to keep opacity at 1.0 during exploration and switch to translucent values only for final image generation. Degenerate Input: If the points array has fewer than 2 points, no line can be drawn. Definition: Rendering an outline for the dataset by rendering only the bounding box. Differentiation: It is the fastest way of rendering the dataset because it avoids processing internal voxels or complex surface extraction. Usage: Use when rapid spatial framing of the dataset extent is required without visual clutter from internal structures. Link: Bounding Box Outline (Hypothetical link to specific variant article if it existed; otherwise refers to the mode described above). Time Complexity: O(1) for bounding box mode (constant number of lines: 12). O(N) for general loop mode, where N is the number of points in the outline. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for bounding box mode. O(N) for storing the points array in general mode. Measured Performance: Described as "arguably the fastest way of rendering the dataset". Strengths: Extremely low computational cost; minimal visual clutter; useful for quick orientation. Limitations: Provides no internal structural information; scalar data is not visualized. When to use: Initial dataset exploration, framing, or when performance is critical and internal detail is not needed. When not to use: When internal structures, gradients, or specific object contours need to be visualized. The concept of using outlines for spatial framing is a standard feature in scientific visualization toolkits like ParaView. The specific implementation of "Wireframe Block Edges" appears in voxel-based visualization contexts, such as the Voxel Party project, where it is used to render the boundaries of voxel chunks or generated heightmaps. aaasen/voxel-party, https://github.com/aaasen/voxel-party, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 5. Displaying data — ParaView Documentation 6.2.0 documentation, https://docs.paraview.org/en/latest/UsersGuide/displayingData.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Probabilistic Silhouette Search
head: Markosian et al. Silhouette Search
body: Probabilistic Silhouette Search is a spatial coherence-based heuristic for detecting and tracing silhouette edges on polygonal meshes. It solves the performance bottleneck of brute-force silhouette detection by limiting the initial search space and leveraging adjacency information to trace outlines rapidly. It differs from brute-force methods by achieving significant speedups for detailed models, though it may miss silhouettes in regions disconnected from the initial search seed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A polygonal mesh (vertices, edges, faces), camera position, and an initial seed edge known to be a silhouette. Output: A set of silhouette edges forming continuous outlines. Data Structures: Adjacency Graph: The mesh must support O(1) access to adjacent edges for any given edge. Visibility Buffer: An enhanced version of Appel’s hidden line algorithm data structure is used to determine if an edge is visible from the current viewpoint. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initial Search: Identify a single silhouette edge. The search examines a constant O(\sqrt{n}) number of edges, where n is the number of edges in the mesh. 2. Probability Weighting: The likelihood that an edge is a silhouette is inversely proportional to its dihedral angle \theta with the adjacent face. Edges with smaller dihedral angles (sharper features) are prioritized. 3. Tracing: Using the initial seed, trace the silhouette outline by traversing adjacent edges. Spatial coherence ensures that if an edge is a silhouette, its neighbors are likely candidates. 4. Visibility Check: For each candidate edge in the trace, use the enhanced Appel’s hidden line algorithm to verify visibility. 5. Inter-frame Optimization (Optional): Retain a fraction of detected silhouette edges from the previous frame to serve as seeds for the current frame, accelerating detection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def probabilisticsilhouettesearch(mesh, camera, prevframeseeds=None): """ Detects silhouette edges using probabilistic search and spatial coherence. """ silhouetteedges = [] # Step 1: Determine initial seeds if prevframeseeds and len(prevframeseeds) > 0: seeds = prevframeseeds else: # Brute force constant O(sqrt(n)) search for initial silhouette seeds = bruteforceinitialsearch(mesh, camera, limit=int(math.sqrt(len(mesh.edges)))) if not seeds: return silhouetteedges # Step 2: Trace silhouettes from seeds for seededge in seeds: if isedgeinsilhouettelist(seededge, silhouetteedges): continue currentedge = seededge trace = [currentedge] while currentedge is not None: # Get adjacent edges for tracing adjacentedges = getadjacentedges(currentedge, mesh) # Find next silhouette edge in trace nextedge = None for adj in adjacentedges: if iscandidatesilhouette(adj, mesh, camera): if isvisible(adj, camera, mesh): nextedge = adj break if nextedge: trace.append(nextedge) silhouetteedges.append(nextedge) currentedge = nextedge else: currentedge = None return silhouetteedges def iscandidatesilhouette(edge, mesh, camera): """ Probability of silhouette is inversely proportional to dihedral angle. """ face1, face2 = edge.faces dihedralangle = computedihedralangle(face1, face2) # Higher probability for smaller angles (sharper edges) # Implementation detail: Use a threshold or weighted random selection # based on 1/dihedralangle to select the next edge in the trace. return True # Simplified for structure; actual implementation uses probability weighting def isvisible(edge, camera, mesh): """ Uses enhanced Appel's hidden line algorithm for visibility. """ # Standard hidden line test: project edge to screen space, # check if any other geometry occludes it. return True # Placeholder for specific Appel's algorithm implementation Parameters: Dihedral Angle Threshold: Not given in the sources. Initial Search Limit: O(\sqrt{n}) edges. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disconnected Silhouettes: Silhouettes in regions unconnected to the initial search seed may not be detected. Precision: The method relies on accurate dihedral angle calculation and visibility tests. A hybrid approach by Northrup and Markosian for rendering artistic silhouettes using probabilistic detection, image processing, and stylization. It performs detection and rendering using the probabilistic method of Markosian et al., then detects edges using an image, interpolates detected edges to form line segments, and stylizes the line segments using various methods. Time Complexity: Initial search is O(\sqrt{n}), where n is the number of edges. Tracing is linear with respect to the number of silhouette edges due to spatial coherence. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for adjacency information and visibility buffers. Performance: Offers significant performance improvement over brute force search for detailed models. Strengths: Fast for low-detail models and scalable for detailed models compared to brute force. Limitations: May miss silhouettes in regions unconnected to the initial search. Inter-frame Acceleration: Retaining silhouette edges from previous frames yields a detection rate of almost 80% for subsequent frames. Probabilistic Silhouette Search was introduced by Markosian et al. in 1997. It was developed to address the challenges of accurate and fast detection and visibility determination of edges in detailed models, where brute force methods do not scale well. The method uses an enhanced version of Appel's hidden line algorithm from 1967 for visibility calculations. DeCarlo et al. later observed the effectiveness of retaining silhouette edges for accelerated inter-frame calculation. name: Hidden Line Removal
head: Wireframe Occlusion Culling
body: Hidden Line Removal is a rendering technique used in wireframe representations to hide line segments that are occluded by solid objects in the scene. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Object Contour NPR and Image Space Outline Generation by operating on explicit geometric primitives (lines/edges) rather than extracting contours from volumetric data or image-space depth buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of wireframe line segments representing the edges of 3D objects. Input: A depth buffer (z-buffer) or ray-casting intersection data representing the solid geometry of the scene. Output: A subset of the input line segments that are visible to the camera. Data Structures: LineSegment: A structure containing two 3D points (P1, P2) defining the segment endpoints. DepthBuffer: A 2D array of depth values (z) corresponding to pixel coordinates, or a list of intersected primitives for ray-based approaches. Steps: 1. Rasterization/Projection: Project the 3D line segments onto the 2D image plane. 2. Occlusion Test: For each line segment, determine if any part of it lies behind a solid object. Rasterization Approach: Render the solid geometry to a depth buffer. Then, for each line segment, sample the depth buffer at the segment's pixel locations. If the segment's depth is greater than the depth buffer value at any sampled point, that portion is occluded. Ray Casting Approach: For each line segment, cast rays from the camera through the segment's pixels. If a ray intersects a solid object closer than the segment, the segment is occluded. 3. Clipping: Clip the line segments to remove occluded portions. Segments entirely occluded are discarded. 4. Rendering: Render the remaining visible line segments. Formulas: Depth comparison: z{seg} > z{buffer}(x, y) implies occlusion at pixel (x, y). Line parameterization: L(t) = P1 + t(P2 - P1) for t \in [0, 1]. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth buffer precision issues may cause z-fighting, leading to incorrect occlusion decisions for lines very close to surfaces. Boundaries: Lines exactly on the boundary of occlusion may flicker if depth values are unstable. Degenerate Input: Zero-length line segments should be ignored. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hiddenlineremoval(lines, depthbuffer, imagewidth, imageheight): visiblelines = [] for line in lines: p1, p2 = line.p1, line.p2 # Project p1 and p2 to screen space s1 = projecttoscreen(p1) s2 = projecttoscreen(p2) # Check if line is behind the camera if s1.z <= 0 or s2.z <= 0: continue # Sample depth buffer along the line occluded = False numsamples = max(abs(s2.x - s1.x), abs(s2.y - s1.y)) if numsamples == 0: numsamples = 1 for i in range(numsamples + 1): t = i / numsamples sx = s1.x + t (s2.x - s1.x) sy = s1.y + t (s2.y - s1.y) sz = s1.z + t (s2.z - s1.z) # Check bounds if 0 <= sx < imagewidth and 0 <= sy < imageheight: bufferz = depthbuffer[int(sy)][int(sx)] # If line is behind the surface, it is occluded if sz > bufferz: occluded = True break if not occluded: visiblelines.append(line) return visiblelines Extracts contours based on object boundaries; choose when you need stylized edges from volumetric data. Uses depth/normal discontinuities; choose for fast, resolution-independent outlines. Renders only the outer boundary; choose for clear object separation. Highlights concavities; choose for enhanced shape perception. Time Complexity: O(L \cdot P) where L is the number of line segments and P is the number of pixels sampled per segment. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the depth buffer, where W and H are image dimensions. Strengths: Provides clear visibility of internal structures in wireframe models; simple to implement with standard rasterization. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution scenes with many line segments; requires accurate depth information. When to use: When rendering wireframe models where internal occlusion is critical for understanding structure. When not to use: When performance is critical and wireframe detail is not essential; when using solid rendering. Hidden Line Removal is a standard feature in 3D visualization software, notably documented in ParaView. It has been a part of the ParaView user interface since at least version 5.8.1 and remains in version 6.2.0. It is often used in conjunction with parallel projection for technical drawings. 4. name: Line and Edge Detection
body: Line and Edge Detection is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly detecting and rendering edges, silhouettes, or structural boundaries within volumetric data. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection by focusing on boundary emphasis and structural outlines rather than flow-aligned strokes, and from LOG-based Silhouette Detection by employing diverse detection mechanisms ranging from gradient-based particle tracing to user-defined interactive selection. The family shares the fundamental goal of enhancing perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. Common mechanisms include: 1. Edge Detection: Identifying boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradients, Laplacian of Gaussian) or image-space properties (depth, normal discontinuities). 2. Line Rendering: Converting detected edges into line primitives (strips, segments) or stylized strokes. Line Illustration Detection is a family of Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) techniques designed to detect and render lines that communicate the shape, structure, and boundaries of volumetric data or isosurfaces. It solves the problem of visualizing complex geometry, such as medical models, where standard photorealistic rendering may obscure structural details. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its focus on line-based abstraction rather than silhouette outlines or edge highlights; it distinguishes between analytical approaches, which are vector-oriented and resolution-independent, and pixel-based methods, which are faster and simpler but rely on image-space buffers. This method renders volumetric data by treating individual cells (faces) as the primary sampling units, applying a scalar-based colormap for the volume body while simultaneously detecting and highlighting cell edges. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection and Outline and Contour Generation by computing edge highlights directly within the face fragment shader based on distance to cell vertices and edges, rather than relying on post-processing contours or separate line-detection passes. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures and boundaries in 3D volumes by providing explicit edge cues that enhance depth perception and structural clarity without obscuring the underlying scalar data. Outline and Contour Generation is a family of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques that enhance perceptual clarity by explicitly detecting and rendering edges, silhouettes, or topological boundaries within volumetric data. Unlike surface-based NPR, which relies on well-defined geometric surfaces, this family operates on continuous volumetric fields where feature areas must be determined through local property analysis. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection by focusing on boundary emphasis and structural outlines rather than flow-aligned strokes, and from LOG-based Silhouette Detection by employing diverse detection mechanisms ranging from gradient-based particle tracing to user-defined interactive selection. LOG-based Silhouette Detection is a volumetric edge detection technique used to identify silhouette voxels for rendering sketch-like curves, replacing a more exhaustive 3x3x3 subspace search to improve performance. It identifies boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradient magnitude and Laplacian of Gaussian values) to highlight structures such as bones or internal features. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Line Illustration Detection by operating directly on volumetric scalar fields using a precomputed Laplacian of Gaussian operator rather than image-space depth discontinuities or surface normals. Step: Calculate entry point hp = org + dir \times t{cur}. Calculate local cell coordinates local = (hp - bmin) / cell. Extract 2D face coordinates f based on entry axis: if axis=0, f=fract(local.yz); if axis=1, f=fract(local.xz); if axis=2, f=fract(local.xy). Calculate edge distance edge = \min(\min(f.x, 1.0-f.x), \min(f.y, 1.0-f.y)). If edge < 0.06, highlight color is yellow (1.0, 0.85, 0.1); otherwise mix lit color with yellow at 0.35 weight. Definition: An approach by Li et al. to detect silhouettes in Hough space for edge sampling. Usage: Used in Li's edge sampling approach [22, 23]. Definition: A pre-computed shape enhancement cue based on object-space analysis using a sharpened filter (Laplacian-like) on a 3x3x3 unit volume to enhance edges and contours, solving the concave/convex inconsistency of local illumination. Step: Select a 3x3x3 point unit volume surrounding the sampling center in the data volume. Clamp the shape factor: if g(x, y, z) + c > 1, set it to 1. Formula: Calculate the sharpened filter value 52f as: 52f = [f(x+1, y, z) + f(x-1, y, z) + \dots + f(x+1, y+1, z+1)] - 26f(x, y, z), where f(x,y,z) is the intensity of the sampling point. Calculate the enhanced intensity g(x,y,z) as: g(x, y, z) = f(x, y, z) - 52f. Calculate the shape factor S{object} as: S{object} = g(x, y, z) + c, where c is a factor to adjust the effect of object space enhancement. Parameter: Factor c: A parameter to adjust the effect of object space enhancement. Pitfall: Local illumination alone cannot solve the display of concave parts; this cue makes up for that shortcoming. Complexity: The cue is pre-computed before ray casting, so it does not occupy rendering time, allowing real-time interactivity. Definition: Detects prominent edges in the volume using a Sobel filter and dynamically positions a magnification lens to center on the largest connected feature. Step: Apply Sobel filter to the volume: edges = ndimage.sobel(self.volumedata). Compute threshold as twice the mean edge magnitude: T = \text{mean}(E) \times 2. Create binary feature mask: M = E > T. Label connected components in the mask: labeled, numfeatures = ndimage.label(featuremask). Find bounding box of the largest feature: largestfeature = ndimage.findobjects(labeled)[0]. Compute center coordinates: Cy = (s{start} + s{stop}) / 2, Cx = (s{start} + s{stop}) / 2. Normalize center to [0,1] range and update lens position: self.lens['position'] = glm.vec2(center[1] / H, center[0] / W). Line and edge detection techniques in volume rendering utilize various strategies to highlight structural boundaries. Analytical and object-space approaches, such as Li et al.'s Hough space silhouette detection, operate on geometric properties, while image-space methods like Sobel filtering and LOG-based voxel detection identify edges through gradient analysis. Pre-computed cues, such as the 3x3x3 sharpened filter for object-space enhancement, are used to improve edge visibility without impacting real-time rendering performance. wlim33/vox-ocean, https://github.com/wlim33/vox-ocean, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Physics-based differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3388769.3407454, fetched 2026-10-29 Local Detail Enhancement for Volume Rendering under Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.2312/pg.20161334, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - priscilla100/medicalvolumerenderer, https://github.com/priscilla100/medicalvolumerenderer/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Line Illustration Detection
head: Analytical and pixel-based line detection, Line detection in NPR
body: Line Illustration Detection identifies and renders lines within volumetric data to enhance perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing specifically on line primitives rather than silhouettes or face-based highlights, categorizing approaches into analytical (vector-oriented, resolution-independent) and pixel-based (image-space, G-buffer dependent) techniques. The family shares the fundamental goal of enhancing perceptual clarity through non-photorealistic edge representation. Common mechanisms include: 1. Edge Detection: Identifying boundaries based on local volumetric properties (gradients, Laplacian of Gaussian) or image-space properties (depth, normal discontinuities). 2. Line Rendering: Converting detected edges into line primitives (strips, segments) or stylized strokes. Analytical approaches are vector-oriented, resolution-independent, and transformable without artifacts, but require explicit analytical representations of the volume or isosurfaces. These methods are generally more general and flexible than pixel-based alternatives. Pixel-based methods, such as those utilizing G-buffers, are faster and simpler to implement than analytical methods, particularly when explicit analytical representations are not available. They rely on image-space processing operators and can reuse G-buffers without recalculation. A technique for visualizing volume isosurfaces by advecting particles along principal curvature directions to create line textures that communicate surface shape. It is based on the premise that lines in the principal directions of curvature communicate surface shape better than lines in other directions. Steps: 1. Calculate the set of principal directions and principal curvatures in the volume. 2. Place an evenly distributed set of tiny opaque particles on the isosurfaces of interest. 3. Advect the particles through the vector field defined by the principal directions. 4. Treat the paths of the particles defined by this advection as a 3D line texture. Parameters: Particle distribution: evenly distributed on isosurfaces. Pitfalls: Algorithmic efficiency and artistic line quality must be addressed for NPR applicability. Showing line direction alone is not necessarily sufficient for an aesthetically pleasing rendering. A technique simulating copper plate etching by intersecting a scene with closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes to detect surface curves. It modulates the final line style using G-buffers containing geometric properties such as colour and depth. Steps: 1. Intersect the scene with a set of closely-spaced, equidistant, parallel planes. 2. Use a modified ray tracer to detect the surface curves resulting from these intersections. 3. Use G-buffers containing geometric properties such as colour and depth to modulate the final line style. The concept of line illustration in volume visualization has roots in traditional printmaking, specifically copper plate etching, which was used for centuries in scientific publications before modern photographic reproduction. Leister simulated this process by intersecting scenes with parallel planes and using a modified ray tracer. In the context of digital volume visualization, Interrante introduced a novel line illustration technique for visualizing volume isosurfaces in 1997. This work focused on using principal directions and curvatures to advect particles, creating viewpoint-independent line textures that could visualize multiple isosurfaces simultaneously. The distinction between analytical and pixel-based methods is well-documented in surveys of NPR techniques. Analytical methods are noted for their flexibility and lack of resolution dependence, while pixel-based methods (like those by Saito and Takahashi) are favored for their speed and simplicity when analytical models are unavailable. Hertzmann provided a survey of image-space outline generation algorithms, noting that simple outlines can be generated by extracting edges from depth maps. name: Principal Direction Line Texture
head: 3D line texture, Interrante line illustration, Interrante's line illustration technique, Principal Curvature Streamlines, Principal Direction Line Illustration
body: Principal Direction Line Texture is a non-photorealistic volume rendering technique that visualizes isosurfaces by advecting particles along the principal curvature directions of the volume data. It solves the problem of communicating surface shape and topology in volumetric datasets by generating line textures that are geometrically invariant and perceptually effective. Unlike pixel-based edge detection methods, this approach is viewpoint-independent and can visualize multiple isosurfaces simultaneously by treating particle paths as a 3D line texture. Inputs: A volumetric dataset V and one or more isosurface threshold values. Outputs: A rendered image containing line textures representing the principal curvature directions on the specified isosurfaces. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values. Principal Direction Field: A vector field where each voxel contains two orthogonal unit vectors (\mathbf{d}1, \mathbf{d}2) representing the principal directions, derived from the Hessian matrix of the volume data. Particle System: A set of points located on the isosurfaces. Steps: 1. Calculate Principal Directions and Curvatures: Compute the Hessian matrix for each voxel in the volume. The eigenvectors of the Hessian matrix correspond to the principal directions of curvature, and the eigenvalues correspond to the principal curvatures. 2. Initialize Particles: Place an evenly distributed set of tiny opaque particles on the isosurfaces defined by the threshold values. The distribution must be uniform to ensure consistent line density. 3. Advect Particles: Advect the particles through the vector field defined by the principal directions. This involves tracing streamlines over the volumetric surface using the principal direction field as the velocity field. 4. Render Line Texture: Treat the paths (trajectories) of the advected particles as a 3D line texture. These lines are rendered to show the shape of the identified isosurfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def principaldirectionlinetexture(volume, thresholds): # Step 1: Calculate principal directions and curvatures # Compute Hessian matrix H for each voxel # H = [[d2V/dx2, d2V/dxdy, d2V/dxdz], # [d2V/dydx, d2V/dy2, d2V/dydz], # [d2V/dzdx, d2V/dzdy, d2V/dz2]] # Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of H # Eigenvectors e1, e2 are the principal directions # Eigenvectors are normalized to unit length principaldirections = computehessianeigenvectors(volume) # Step 2: Place evenly distributed particles on isosurfaces particles = [] for threshold in thresholds: # Find voxels where volume value is close to threshold # Distribute particles evenly on the resulting surface surfacepoints = extractisosurfacepoints(volume, threshold) particles.extend(evenlydistribute(surfacepoints)) # Step 3: Advect particles along principal directions trajectories = [] for particle in particles: path = [particle.position] currentpos = particle.position # Trace streamline using principal direction field # Integrate dx/dt = d1(x) or d2(x) depending on choice # Use numerical integration (e.g., Runge-Kutta) for step in range(numsteps): # Get principal direction at currentpos d1, d2 = principaldirections[currentpos] # Choose direction (e.g., d1) direction = d1 # Advance position currentpos = integratestep(currentpos, direction, stepsize) path.append(currentpos) # Stop if out of bounds or volume ends if not isinsidevolume(currentpos): break trajectories.append(path) # Step 4: Render trajectories as lines renderlines(trajectories) Parameters: Particle Distribution: Evenly distributed on isosurfaces. Step Size: Not given in the sources. Number of Steps: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Algorithmic Efficiency: The technique requires significant computation for Hessian calculation and advection, which must be addressed for NPR applicability. Artistic Line Quality: Showing line direction alone is not necessarily sufficient for an aesthetically pleasing rendering; additional artistic controls may be needed. Precision: Numerical integration errors in advection can lead to inaccurate streamline tracing, especially in regions of high curvature variation. A specific implementation where streamlines are strictly aligned with principal curvature directions. It is chosen when geometric invariance and shape communication are prioritized over artistic style. See Principal Direction Line Texture. Uses lines of varying thickness and orientation to simulate hatching. It is chosen for artistic styles like copper plate. See Hatching-Based Volume Rendering. Time Complexity: High, due to Hessian computation (O(N) for N voxels) and particle advection (O(P \cdot S) for P particles and S steps). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the volume and principal direction field. Strengths: Viewpoint independence, ability to visualize multiple isosurfaces simultaneously, geometric invariance, and strong perceptual communication of surface shape. Limitations: Algorithmic efficiency issues, potential lack of aesthetic appeal without additional artistic controls, and computational cost of Hessian calculation. When to Use: When the goal is to clearly communicate the shape and topology of isosurfaces in a volumetric dataset, especially in scientific visualization where geometric accuracy is important. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical or when artistic style is the primary concern without regard to geometric invariance. The technique was introduced by Interrante in 1997. It is based on the psychological literature suggesting that lines in the principal directions of curvature communicate surface shape better than lines in other directions. Girshick et al. cited this method for its psychological basis and geometrical invariance. The method has been used in various NPR volume visualization techniques, often in conjunction with other methods like tone shading and silhouette enhancement.
