name: YCoCg Color Space Rectification
head: Color Space Selection for History Rectification, YCrCb Rectification
body: YCoCg Color Space Rectification is a history rectification method used in temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) for volumetric rendering that transforms reprojected historical color data into a luminance-chrominance color space (specifically YCoCg or YCrCb) before applying bounding-box clipping. It solves the problem of temporal color bleeding artifacts caused by high correlation between RGB channels, which leads to poorly aligned bounding boxes and stale color information persisting across frames. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Variance Clipping, by operating on a fixed geometric bounding box oriented along the luminance axis rather than a statistical distribution, and from its sibling AABB Clamping by explicitly decoupling luminance and chrominance to reduce chroma-related ghosting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Reprojected historical color sample h{reprojected} (RGB vector), current frame neighborhood samples (RGB vectors). Output: Rectified historical color sample h{clipped} (RGB vector). Data Structures: Color vectors are 3-element arrays/tuples. YCoCg space: [Y, Co, Cg]^T. YCrCb space: [Y, Cr, Cb]^T. Steps: 1. Transform to Luminance-Chrominance Space: Convert the reprojected historical color h{reprojected} and the current frame neighborhood samples from RGB to the chosen color space (YCoCg or YCrCb). 2. Define Bounding Box: Determine the minimum and maximum values for each component (Y, Co, Cg or Y, Cr, Cb) across the current frame's neighborhood samples. This creates an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) in the transformed space. 3. Clamp History: Clamp each component of the transformed historical sample h{reprojected} to the corresponding min/max bounds of the AABB. 4. Transform Back to RGB: Convert the clamped historical sample back to RGB space to produce h{clipped}. Formulas: RGB to YCoCg Transform: \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Co \\ Cg \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{4} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} Inverse YCoCg to RGB Transform: \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Co \\ Cg \end{bmatrix} RGB to YCrCb Transform: \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Cr \\ Cb \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.299 & 0.587 & 0.114 \\ -0.5 & -0.4187 & 0.0813 \\ -0.1687 & -0.3313 & -0.5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} Inverse YCrCb to RGB Transform: \begin{bmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1.402 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.714 & -0.344 \\ 1 & 0 & 1.772 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Cr \\ Cb \end{bmatrix} Parameters: Color Space Selection: YCoCg or YCrCb. YCoCg is preferred for better decorrelation of luminance and chrominance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color-Related Artifacts in RGB: Performing history rectification directly in RGB space causes the AABB to be poorly aligned with the actual distribution of color samples because RGB channels are highly correlated, leading to ghosting artifacts. Temporal Color Bleeding: In RGB space, abrupt color changes (e.g., a light turning from red to yellow) cause stale color information to bleed into subsequent frames, taking many frames to converge. Luminance Artifacts: While YCoCg and YCrCb reduce chrominance bleeding, they can increase luminance artifacts. For example, when color shifts from green to blue, stale luminance information in the green channel may bleed into the next frame, causing excess luminance around the light source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rectifyhistoryycocg(hreprojectedrgb, neighborhoodsamplesrgb): """ Rectifies historical color using YCoCg color space rectification. Args: hreprojectedrgb: Tuple (R, G, B) of the reprojected historical sample. neighborhoodsamplesrgb: List of tuples [(R, G, B),...] of current frame neighborhood samples. Returns: Tuple (R, G, B) of the rectified historical sample. """ # Step 1: Transform historical sample to YCoCg hy, hco, hcg = rgbtoycocg(hreprojectedrgb) # Step 2: Transform neighborhood samples to YCoCg and find bounds # Initialize bounds with extreme values ymin, ymax = float('inf'), float('-inf') comin, comax = float('inf'), float('-inf') cgmin, cgmax = float('inf'), float('-inf') for samplergb in neighborhoodsamplesrgb: y, co, cg = rgbtoycocg(samplergb) # Update bounds if y < ymin: ymin = y if y > ymax: ymax = y if co < comin: comin = co if co > comax: comax = co if cg < cgmin: cgmin = cg if cg > cgmax: cgmax = cg # Step 3: Clamp historical sample components to bounds yclamped = max(ymin, min(ymax, hy)) coclamped = max(comin, min(comax, hco)) cgclamped = max(cgmin, min(cgmax, hcg)) # Step 4: Transform back to RGB hclippedrgb = ycocgtorgb(yclamped, coclamped, cgclamped) return hclippedrgb def rgbtoycocg(rgb): r, g, b = rgb y = 0.25 r + 0.5 g + 0.25 b co = 0.5 r + 0.0 g - 0.5 b cg = -0.25 r + 0.5 g - 0.25 b return (y, co, cg) def ycocgtorgb(ycocg): y, co, cg = ycocg r = 1.0 y + 1.0 co - 1.0 cg g = 1.0 y + 0.0 co + 1.0 cg b = 1.0 y - 1.0 co - 1.0 cg return (r, g, b) AABB Clamping is a history rectification method that individually limits each channel of the reprojected historical color to the minimum and maximum values of the current frame's neighborhood samples. It builds on YCoCg Color Space Rectification, which transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance space before applying rectification. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of a simple Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) approximation constructed from per-channel minimum and maximum values, whereas variants like Variance Clipping use statistical distributions to define bounds. Color Space Conversion for TAA is a variant that involves transforming volumetric samples into a specific color space (RGB, YCoCg, or YCrCb) before blending, then transforming back to RGB for storage. It is evaluated as a general approach to handling color space selection in TAA for volumetric rendering, with YCoCg and YCrCb shown to reduce chrominance artifacts compared to RGB. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of neighborhood samples, due to the linear transformation and min/max operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample for storing transformed values and bounds. Measured Performance: In tests involving abrupt color changes (e.g., spot light changing from red to yellow), YCoCg and YCrCb significantly reduced temporal color bleeding artifacts compared to RGB, as measured by SSIM scores over time. However, these color spaces introduced increased luminance artifacts during specific color transitions (e.g., green to blue). Strengths: Reduces color-related ghosting and chrominance bleeding by decoupling luminance and chrominance. YCoCg provides better decorrelation than YCrCb. Limitations: Can introduce luminance artifacts when chrominance changes rapidly. Requires additional transform operations. When to Use: When temporal color bleeding is a prominent issue, especially with high-contrast color changes. When Not to Use: When luminance stability is critical during rapid color shifts, or when computational overhead of color space transforms is prohibitive. YCoCg Color Space Rectification originated in the context of temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It was explored as an improvement over RGB-space history rectification to mitigate color-related artifacts. The method leverages the properties of luminance-chrominance color spaces, specifically YCoCg and YCrCb, to align the history rectification bounding box with the direction of luma, which typically has high local contrast. The approach was evaluated in a study on advances in volumetric temporal anti-aliasing, comparing RGB, YCoCg, and YCrCb color spaces in terms of artifact reduction and convergence speed. name: AABB Clamping
head: AABB Clamping History Rectification
body: AABB Clamping is a history rectification method that individually limits each channel of the reprojected historical color to the minimum and maximum values of the current frame's neighborhood samples. It builds on YCoCg Color Space Rectification, which transforms colors into a luminance-chrominance space before applying rectification. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of a simple Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) approximation constructed from per-channel minimum and maximum values, whereas variants like Variance Clipping use statistical distributions to define bounds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reprojected historical color ch, and a set of N current-frame neighborhood samples ci \in \mathbb{R}^k (where k is the number of channels, e.g., 3 or 4). Output: The rectified color cr. Data Structures: AABB Bounds: Two vectors, c{min} and c{max}, each of size k. c{min}[j] = \min{i=1..N}(ci[j]) for each channel j. c{max}[j] = \max{i=1..N}(ci[j]) for each channel j. Steps: 1. Construct AABB: Compute the component-wise minimum and maximum across all current-frame neighborhood samples to define the bounding box bounds c{min} and c{max}. 2. Clamp: For each channel j of the historical color ch, clamp the value between the corresponding bounds c{min}[j] and c{max}[j]. Formula: The rectified color cr is obtained by clamping ch component-wise: cr = \min(\max(ch, c{min}), c{max}) \quad (2.2) where \min, \max, and arithmetic operations are performed component-wise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbclamp(historicalcolor, neighborhoodsamples): """ Rectifies historical color by clamping it to the AABB defined by neighborhood samples. Args: historicalcolor: List/Array of floats, shape (k,) representing ch. neighborhoodsamples: List/Array of floats, shape (N, k) representing ci. Returns: List/Array of floats, shape (k,) representing cr. """ k = len(historicalcolor) N = len(neighborhoodsamples) # Step 1: Construct AABB bounds cmin = [0.0] k cmax = [0.0] k for j in range(k): cmin[j] = min(sample[j] for sample in neighborhoodsamples) cmax[j] = max(sample[j] for sample in neighborhoodsamples) # Step 2: Clamp historical color to bounds rectifiedcolor = [0.0] k for j in range(k): val = historicalcolor[j] if val < cmin[j]: val = cmin[j] elif val > cmax[j]: val = cmax[j] rectifiedcolor[j] = val return rectifiedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Accumulation: Because each channel is individually clamped, values tend to collect in the corners of the AABB. Color Artifacts: This corner accumulation can lead to strange color-related artifacts in scenes with significant color information, although it is generally not an issue for grayscale scenes. Accuracy: This method is a fast approximation of the tighter convex hull approach. It is less accurate but much cheaper to build and intersect against. History Rectification is a class of Temporal Anti-Aliasing techniques that correct historical color values before blending by restricting the reprojected history to a region defined by current-frame neighborhood samples. It solves the problem of temporal lag and ghosting during abrupt scene changes where a baseline Exponential Moving Average fails to react quickly enough. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is the use of a spatial neighborhood of current-frame samples to define a "color extent" or bound; if the historical value falls outside this extent, it is considered stale and is corrected prior to blending. This approach builds on AABB Clamping, which uses a simpler Axis-Aligned Bounding Box approximation, whereas History Rectification encompasses more sophisticated variants like Variance Clipping and AABB Clipping that better handle color information and statistical distributions. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot k) to compute min/max over N samples with k channels, followed by O(k) for clamping. It is computationally efficient compared to convex hull projection. Memory Complexity: O(k) to store the min and max bounds. Strengths: Fast approximation of history rectification; easy to implement and intersect against; ensures history remains within valid color extent. Limitations: Less accurate than convex hull methods; prone to color artifacts due to channel-wise clamping causing values to collect in AABB corners. When to use: When performance is critical and the scene is predominantly grayscale or has limited color variation. When not to use: In scenes with complex color information where color artifacts are noticeable, or when higher fidelity rectification (like AABB Clipping or Variance Clipping) is required. AABB Clamping is a history rectification method implemented and evaluated in the context of temporal anti-aliasing for real-time froxel-based volumetric rendering. It serves as a fast approximation to the computationally expensive convex hull projection, which is too costly for real-time rendering constraints. name: History Rectification
head: AABB Clipping
body: History rectification is a class of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) techniques that correct historical color values before blending by restricting the reprojected history to a region defined by current-frame neighborhood samples. It solves the problem of temporal lag and ghosting during abrupt scene changes (such as light introduction or sudden movement) where a baseline Exponential Moving Average (EMA) fails to react quickly enough. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is the use of a spatial neighborhood of current-frame samples to define a "color extent" or bound; if the historical value falls outside this extent, it is considered stale and is corrected (clamped or clipped) prior to blending. This approach builds on AABB Clamping, which uses a simpler Axis-Aligned Bounding Box approximation, whereas History Rectification encompasses more sophisticated variants like Variance Clipping and AABB Clipping that better handle color information and statistical distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The reprojected history buffer value H for the current pixel, and a neighborhood of current-frame color samples C{neighbor} (typically a 3x3 grid of pixels surrounding the current pixel). Output: A rectified history value H{rect} ready for blending with the current frame. Data Structures: Neighborhood Samples: A set of color vectors \{c1, c2,..., cn\} representing the RGB(A) values of the neighboring pixels in the current frame. Bounds: A minimum vector min and a maximum vector max defining the rectification region. For AABB-based methods, these are component-wise min/max. For Variance Clipping, these are derived from statistical moments. Steps: 1. Sample Neighborhood: Gather the color values of the neighboring pixels in the current frame. The standard evaluation uses a 3x3 neighborhood to avoid averaging across depth slices, which would act as a spatial stabilizer and hide flicker artifacts. Alternatives like 3x3x3 or 6-tap neighborhoods smooth across depth but are not used in the primary evaluation context. 2. Define Bounds: Calculate the bounding region based on the chosen variant (see Subtopics). For AABB variants: min = \min(ci), max = \max(ci) for each color channel independently. For Variance Clipping: Bounds are expanded beyond min/max using the standard deviation of the neighborhood values to account for statistical distribution. 3. Rectify History: Compare the reprojected history value H against the defined bounds. If H is within the bounds, H{rect} = H. If H is outside the bounds, H{rect} is adjusted to the nearest boundary value (clamping) or projected onto the boundary (clipping). 4. Blend: Blend H{rect} with the current frame color C{current} using the temporal blend factor \alpha (typically \alpha = 0.05 for evaluation comparability). Formulas: For AABB Clamping/Clipping, the rectified value for a single channel is: H{rect} = \text{clamp}(H, min, max) Where \text{clamp}(v, a, b) returns a if v < a, b if v > b, and v otherwise. For Variance Clipping, the bounds are extended by a factor of the standard deviation \sigma: min{var} = \mu - k \cdot \sigma max{var} = \mu + k \cdot \sigma Where \mu is the mean of the neighborhood, \sigma is the standard deviation, and k is a scaling factor. The first and second sample moments used for variance clipping are defined as m1 = \sum{i=1}^N ci and m2 = \sum{i=1}^N ci^2, from which \mu = m1/N and \sigma^2 = m2/N - \mu^2 are derived. Parameters: Neighborhood Size: 3x3 is the standard for evaluation to preserve depth separation. Blend Factor (\alpha): 0.05 is used in the cited evaluations to match baseline EMA conditions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Extent: When the light turns off, the neighborhood extent becomes 0 (a single point). The history is clamped to this point, eliminating temporal lag instantly. Gradual Color Change: AABB clamping struggles with gradual color transitions (e.g., red to blue fade). It exhibits an especially big RMSE spike at frame 500 and takes around 50 frames for the error to converge back down to the level of AABB clipping. Temporal Instability (TI): Tighter bounds allow faster adaptation but increase TI, perceived as visual flicker. The distance between highest error peaks is exactly 16 frames, corresponding to the jitter sequence length. Grayscale Scenes: AABB clipping and clamping produce identical results in grayscale scenes because color rectification is irrelevant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def historyrectification(historyvalue, currentframecolor, neighborhoodcolors, method='aabbclamp'): """ Rectifies the history value based on the current frame neighborhood. Args: historyvalue: list of 3 floats, the reprojected history color [R, G, B]. currentframecolor: list of 3 floats, the current frame's color. neighborhoodcolors: list of lists of 3 floats, colors of neighboring pixels. method: str, one of 'aabbclamp', 'aabbclip', 'varianceclip'. Returns: list of 3 floats, the rectified history value. """ # Step 1: Calculate bounds from neighborhood if method in ('aabbclamp', 'aabbclip'): # Component-wise min and max across the neighborhood minval = [min(c[i] for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] maxval = [max(c[i] for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] if method == 'aabbclamp': # Clamp history to AABB bounds per channel rectified = [max(minval[i], min(historyvalue[i], maxval[i])) for i in range(3)] else: # aabbclip # Project history onto AABB towards the current frame sample # The current frame sample is guaranteed to be inside the AABB dirvec = [currentframecolor[i] - historyvalue[i] for i in range(3)] tmin = 1.0 for i in range(3): if abs(dirvec[i]) > 1e-6: t1 = (minval[i] - historyvalue[i]) / dirvec[i] t2 = (maxval[i] - historyvalue[i]) / dirvec[i] tlo = min(t1, t2) thi = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tlo) # Clamp t to [0, 1] to stay within the segment between history and target t = max(0.0, min(1.0, tmin)) rectified = [historyvalue[i] + t dirvec[i] for i in range(3)] elif method == 'varianceclip': # Calculate first and second sample moments per channel n = len(neighborhoodcolors) m1 = [sum(c[i] for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] m2 = [sum(c[i]2 for c in neighborhoodcolors) for i in range(3)] meanval = [m1[i] / n for i in range(3)] variance = [m2[i] / n - meanval[i]2 for i in range(3)] stddev = [max(0.0, v)0.5 for v in variance] # Guard against negative variance due to precision k = 1.0 # Scaling factor not specified in sources minval = [meanval[i] - k stddev[i] for i in range(3)] maxval = [meanval[i] + k stddev[i] for i in range(3)] rectified = [max(minval[i], min(historyvalue[i], maxval[i])) for i in range(3)] else: rectified = list(historyvalue) # Fallback to no rectification return rectified A history rectification method that uses the statistical distribution of values in the current frame neighborhood to create the bounds of the AABB used for clipping. It calculates the mean and standard deviation of the neighborhood colors to define a range that is typically tighter than the raw min/max but accounts for variance. It consistently introduces less bias than AABB-based methods during movement, reducing ghosting artifacts more effectively, but exhibits higher Temporal Instability (flicker). In step response scenarios, it achieves the lowest RMSE (0.002977) but the highest TI P (0.004217, +190.23% increase over baseline). A history rectification method that projects the history onto the AABB defined by the minimum and maximum values in each color channel of the current frame neighborhood. In grayscale scenes, it produces identical results to AABB Clamping because color rectification is not relevant. It performs better than EMA in abrupt change scenarios and has lower TI than Variance Clipping (TI P of 0.002373, +63.32% over baseline). However, it struggles with gradual color changes, showing a large RMSE spike when a light fades from red to blue. Clipping the historical value against the convex hull formed by neighboring color samples, representing the smallest convex region containing all neighboring colors. Constructing and projecting history onto the convex hull is too computationally expensive for real-time rendering performance constraints. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of neighbors in the sampling kernel (e.g., 9 for 3x3). The operations are simple min/max or mean/std calculations per pixel. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel for storing neighborhood samples during the rectification pass. Measured Performance: Hardware/Resolution: Not given in the sources. Scene: Evaluated in step response (abrupt light on/off) and gradual change (moving/rotating light) scenarios. Metrics: Baseline EMA: RMSE 0.009724, TI P 0.001453. AABB Clamp/Clip: RMSE 0.003136, TI P 0.002373 (+63.32% TI). Variance Clip: RMSE 0.002977, TI P 0.004217 (+190.23% TI). Scaling: Performance scales with neighborhood size. Larger neighborhoods (3x3x3, 6-tap) smooth the signal across depth, reducing visible flicker but potentially blurring details. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Superior to EMA in abrupt change scenarios; immediately drops error to zero when intensity drops, eliminating temporal lag. Variance clipping produces the lowest error spike when reconstructing the signal during quick illumination introduction. Limitations: Higher Temporal Instability (flicker) compared to EMA, especially with Variance Clipping. AABB Clamping struggles with gradual color changes, taking ~50 frames to converge after a color fade. Jittering causes periodic error patterns (16-frame cycle) perceived as flicker. When to use/not use: Use: When rapid reaction to scene changes (light on/off, fast motion) is prioritized over absolute temporal stability, and ghosting must be minimized. Not Use: In scenes with gradual color transitions where AABB clamping is used, or when visual flicker is unacceptable and higher TI is a dealbreaker. History rectification techniques were developed as part of the broader effort to improve Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) for real-time rendering, specifically in the context of froxel-based volumetric rendering. The specific evaluation of these methods (Variance Clipping, AABB Clamping, AABB Clipping) is detailed in the work on "Advances in volumetric temporal anti-aliasing for real-time rendering of participating media". The mathematical definition for each method remains unchanged from their original pixel-space TAA counterparts. name: Clipped Cropping Region Planes
head: ClipCroppingRegionPlanes, Cropping Region Plane Clipping, Volume Bounding Box Clipping
body: Clipped Cropping Region Planes is a preprocessing step for volume rendering that constrains user-defined cropping planes to the physical bounds of the input volume dataset. It solves the problem of invalid or out-of-bounds clipping regions by computing the intersection of user-defined cropping planes with the volume's bounding box to ensure valid clipping regions before rendering. Unlike its sibling Cropping, which defines the logical clipping region, this method ensures the region is geometrically valid and contained within the data before rendering proceeds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The input volume dataset (typically vtkImageData), the user-defined cropping planes array CroppingRegionPlanes[6], and the volume's bounding box bounds volBounds[6]. Output: The clipped cropping planes array ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[6]. Data Structures: volBounds[6]: An array of 6 doubles representing the axis-aligned bounding box of the volume. Indices 0-1 correspond to the minimum and maximum X coordinates, 2-3 to Y, and 4-5 to Z. CroppingRegionPlanes[6]: An array of 6 doubles representing the user-defined clipping planes. Indices 0-1 define the min/max X planes, 2-3 for Y, and 4-5 for Z. ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[6]: An array of 6 doubles storing the clamped result. Steps: 1. Validate Input: Assert that the input volume exists (this->GetInput(0) != 0). 2. Retrieve Bounds: Obtain the volume's bounding box into volBounds[6] using the dataset's GetBounds method (this->GetInput(0)->GetBounds(volBounds)). 3. Validate Cropping Order: Assert that cropping is enabled and the planes are ordered correctly: CroppingRegionPlanes[0] < CroppingRegionPlanes[1], CroppingRegionPlanes[2] < CroppingRegionPlanes[3], and CroppingRegionPlanes[4] < CroppingRegionPlanes[5]. 4. Clip Min Planes: For each axis i \in \{0, 2, 4\} (representing X, Y, Z minimums): if CroppingRegionPlanes[i] < volBounds[i], set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = volBounds[i]; otherwise, set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = CroppingRegionPlanes[i]. 5. Clip Max Planes: For each axis i \in \{1, 3, 5\} (representing X, Y, Z maximums): if CroppingRegionPlanes[i] > volBounds[i], set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = volBounds[i]; otherwise, set ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[i] = CroppingRegionPlanes[i]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clipcroppingregionplanes(croppingregionplanes, volbounds): """ Clamps user-defined cropping planes to the volume's bounding box. Args: croppingregionplanes (list[float]): 6-element list [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz]. volbounds (list[float]): 6-element list [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz]. Returns: list[float]: Clipped cropping planes. """ # Precondition checks assert len(croppingregionplanes) == 6 assert len(volbounds) == 6 # Assert ordering: min < max for each axis assert croppingregionplanes[0] < croppingregionplanes[1], "X planes not ordered" assert croppingregionplanes[2] < croppingregionplanes[3], "Y planes not ordered" assert croppingregionplanes[4] < croppingregionplanes[5], "Z planes not ordered" clippedplanes = [0.0] 6 # Clip minimum planes (indices 0, 2, 4) for i in [0, 2, 4]: if croppingregionplanes[i] < volbounds[i]: clippedplanes[i] = volbounds[i] else: clippedplanes[i] = croppingregionplanes[i] # Clip maximum planes (indices 1, 3, 5) for i in [1, 3, 5]: if croppingregionplanes[i] > volbounds[i]: clippedplanes[i] = volbounds[i] else: clippedplanes[i] = croppingregionplanes[i] return clippedplanes Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Ordering: If the user-defined planes are not ordered (min > max), the method fails the precondition check. The parent Render() method silently stops if this check is not enforced by the caller. Out-of-Bounds Input: If a user plane is outside the volume bounds, it is clamped to the nearest bound. Polygon-based cropping is a voxel-wise volume rendering technique that masks voxels based on a user-defined 2D polygon drawn in the display (screen) coordinate space. It solves the problem of interactive, free-form region-of-interest selection by converting screen-space constraints into volume-space visibility masks. It differs from planar clipping methods by supporting arbitrary convex or non-convex polygonal shapes rather than just axis-aligned or arbitrary planar cuts, and it operates by explicitly iterating over voxels to test their projected positions against the polygon boundary. Interactive cropping enables real-time adjustment of the volume along X, Y, and Z axes using keyboard controls. Cropping is toggled on/off by pressing 'C' or 'c'. The X-axis is adjusted with Left/Right Arrow keys, the Y-axis with Up/Down Arrow keys, and the Z-axis with PageUp/PageDown keys. Holding Shift while pressing arrow keys expands the crop region. Pressing 'R' resets the crop to the full volume bounds. The crop planes are initialized at full bounds using vtk.vtkPlanes and vtk.vtkPoints with 8 corner points. Physical coordinates for crop planes are calculated from normalized ranges and volume bounds, then passed to the mapper via SetCroppingRegionPlanes. A minimum crop width of 0.1 must be enforced to prevent degenerate planes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. name: Polygon-based Cropping
head: CutLineInside, CutLineOutside, CutingImagedata, Voxel-wise 2D Polygon Clipping
body: Polygon-based cropping is a voxel-wise volume rendering technique that masks voxels based on a user-defined 2D polygon drawn in the display (screen) coordinate space. It solves the problem of interactive, free-form region-of-interest selection by converting screen-space constraints into volume-space visibility masks. It differs from planar clipping methods by supporting arbitrary convex or non-convex polygonal shapes rather than just axis-aligned or arbitrary planar cuts, and it operates by explicitly iterating over voxels to test their projected positions against the polygon boundary. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vtkImageData object containing the volume scalar data, a vtkRenderer for coordinate transformation, a QPolygonF defining the 2D clipping boundary in screen coordinates, and an integer type flag determining the clipping mode. Output: The modified vtkImageData where voxels outside the valid region are set to zero (transparent), effectively cropping the volume. Data Structures: vtkImageData: Stores voxel data. The implementation assumes the scalar type is unsigned char. If the type differs, pointer casting must be adjusted. QPolygonF: A 2D polygon defined by a sequence of QPointF vertices. vtkCoordinate: Used to transform world coordinates to display coordinates. Steps: 1. Retrieve volume metadata: dimensions, spacing, and origin. 2. Iterate over all voxel coordinates (i, j, k) within the volume bounds. 3. Compute the world position of the current voxel. 4. Transform the world position to display coordinates using a coordinate mapper. 5. Check if the display position lies inside the user-drawn polygon using the Qt::OddEvenFill rule. 6. Apply clipping based on type: if type == CutLineInside and the point is inside the polygon, set the voxel value to 0; if type == CutLineOutside and the point is outside the polygon, set the voxel value to 0. 7. After modification, update the volume and re-add it to the renderer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polygonbasedcropping(imagedata, volume, renderer, polygon, cliptype): # Retrieve metadata imgdims = imagedata.GetDimensions() imgspacing = imagedata.GetSpacing() imgorigian = imagedata.GetOrigin() # Standard coordinate transformation helper def transformworldtodisplay(worldpos, renderer): # VTK coordinate system conversion to screen space return renderer.GetActors()[0].GetMapper().GetInput().GetCoordinate().GetComputedDoubleDisplayValue(renderer) # Iterate over all voxels for k in range(imgdims[2]): for j in range(imgdims[1]): for i in range(imgdims[0]): # Compute world position worldpos = [ i imgspacing[0] + imgorigian[0], j imgspacing[1] + imgorigian[1], k imgspacing[2] + imgorigian[2] ] # Transform to display coordinates displaypos = transformworldtodisplay(worldpos, renderer) # Check if point is inside polygon using OddEvenFill rule containspoint = pointinpolygon(displaypos, polygon, fillrule="oddeven") # Get pointer to voxel data (assumes unsigned char) voxelptr = imagedata.GetScalarPointer(i, j, k) # Apply clipping logic if cliptype == CLIPINSIDE: if containspoint: voxelptr[0] = 0 elif cliptype == CLIPOUTSIDE: if not containspoint: voxelptr[0] = 0 # Update volume and renderer volume.Update() renderer.RemoveVolume(volume) renderer.AddVolume(volume) Parameters: cliptype: Enum or integer flag. CutLineInside (remove inside polygon), CutLineOutside (remove outside polygon). fillrule: Qt::OddEvenFill is used for point-in-polygon testing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The implementation assumes the bounding box origin starts at (0,0,0). Production code must validate actual bounds. Do not use vtkImageIterator as it cannot retrieve spatial positions; direct indexing is required. The scalar type is assumed to be unsigned char. If the scalar type differs, the pointer cast and assignment must be adjusted. A CPU-based clipping algorithm that intersects a sequence of parallel sampling planes against a user-defined convex Volume of Interest (VOI) to reduce the computational load on the GPU. It solves the problem of unnecessary volume rendering computation in empty or irrelevant regions by transmitting only the clipped, valid portions of sampling planes to the GPU. It sets itself apart from general convex clipping algorithms by exploiting the coherence between parallel planes and using a Weighted Sweep Graph (WSG) to efficiently manage topological changes (vertex events) during the sweep, avoiding the recomputation of edge lists from scratch for every plane. A variant that calculates crop offsets from screen coordinates, computes a new image resolution, updates the principal point to preserve the original principal axis, validates dimensions, and updates the camera's image size and principal point. It is chosen when precise camera parameter adjustment is required after defining a rectangular crop region. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels in the volume, as every voxel is visited and transformed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as it modifies the volume in place. Performance: The method is CPU-bound due to the per-voxel coordinate transformation and polygon containment test. It is suitable for interactive editing but may be slow for very large volumes compared to GPU-based clipping. Strengths: Supports arbitrary 2D polygonal shapes in screen space, allowing for intuitive free-form cropping. Limitations: Requires full volume iteration; not suitable for real-time rendering of large datasets without optimization. Assumes specific data types and coordinate systems. When to use: Interactive volume editing where the user draws a custom 2D shape to define the region of interest. When not to use: Real-time rendering of large volumes where performance is critical; use GPU-based clipping or the Convex VOI Clipping method instead. The method is described in the open-source project kpengk/VolumeClipping. It is part of a larger system for interactive volume visualization using VTK and Qt. name: Convex VOI Clipping via Weighted Sweep Graph
head: Clipper, WSG-based clipping
body: This method is a CPU-based clipping algorithm that intersects a sequence of parallel sampling planes against a user-defined convex Volume of Interest (VOI) to reduce the computational load on the GPU. It solves the problem of unnecessary volume rendering computation in empty or irrelevant regions by transmitting only the clipped, valid portions of sampling planes to the GPU. It sets itself apart from general convex clipping algorithms by exploiting the coherence between parallel planes and using a Weighted Sweep Graph (WSG) to efficiently manage topological changes (vertex events) during the sweep, avoiding the recomputation of edge lists from scratch for every plane. Inputs: 1. A convex VOI defined by a user via a carving approach starting from a basic convex shape (e.g., a cube). 2. A sequence of parallel sampling planes. Outputs: A sequence of convex polygons, one for each sampling plane that intersects the VOI. Each polygon is defined by an ordered list of vertices lying on the edges of the VOI. Data Structures: Weighted Sweep Graph (WSG): A graph structure that encodes the topological structure of the convex volume. It maintains the current list of edges intersected by the sweep plane, ordered to form the convex polygon. It detects vertex events and facilitates edge list updates by adding or removing edges incident to the vertex generating the event. Algorithm Steps: 1. VOI Definition: The user defines the convex VOI starting from a basic convex shape (e.g., a cube). Cutting planes are added to slice the volume. Each cutting plane is specified by a normal vector, controlled by dragging a line endpoint from the VOI center, and a reference point, controlled by a slider specifying the distance from the VOI center. 2. Intersection Algorithm: Compute the intersection of parallel sampling planes against the convex VOI. The algorithm exploits coherence between parallel planes. 3. Polygon Generation: The intersection of a single plane against the convex VOI results in a convex polygon defined by an ordered list of vertices lying on the edges of the VOI. 4. Edge List Reuse: For a parallel plane near the previous one, compute the new polygon vertices by intersecting the same list of edges from the previous calculation against the new plane. 5. Vertex Event Handling: If a VOI vertex lies between two planes, the edge list must be updated by adding or removing edges incident to that vertex. The WSG encodes the topological structure to maintain edge order and detect vertex events. Parameters: VOI Center: The reference point for user interaction (normal vector direction and plane distance). Plane Normal: The viewing direction, which is parallel for all sampling planes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertex Events: A vertex lying exactly between two sampling planes triggers an edge list update. Parallel Edges: An edge parallel to the sampling plane yields no unique intersection point and must be skipped or handled as a degenerate boundary case. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when determining if a vertex is between two planes or if an intersection point lies exactly on an edge. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convexvoiclipping(voiedges, voivertices, samplingplanes, sweepnormal): """ voiedges: List of edges, each edge is a tuple (vertexindexA, vertexindexB) voivertices: List of vertices, each vertex is a 3D point (x, y, z) samplingplanes: List of distances along the sweepnormal for each plane sweepnormal: Unit vector (nx, ny, nz) parallel to the viewing direction Returns: List of polygons, each polygon is a list of 3D points """ # Precompute vertex projections along the sweep direction vertexprojections = [dot(v, sweepnormal) for v in voivertices] # Sort sampling planes by distance along the sweep direction sortedplaneindices = sorted(range(len(samplingplanes)), key=lambda i: samplingplanes[i]) polygons = [] # Initialize edge list with edges intersecting the first plane currentedges = [] firstplanedist = samplingplanes[sortedplaneindices[0]] for eidx, (va, vb) in enumerate(voiedges): proja = vertexprojections[va] projb = vertexprojections[vb] # Edge crosses the plane if endpoints are on opposite sides or on the plane if (proja - firstplanedist) (projb - firstplanedist) <= 0: currentedges.append(eidx) # Order edges to form a convex polygon cycle currentedges = sortedgestopolygonorder(currentedges, voiedges) for i, pidx in enumerate(sortedplaneindices): planedist = samplingplanes[pidx] # Check for vertex events between previous plane and current plane if i > 0: prevplanedist = samplingplanes[sortedplaneindices[i-1]] for vidx in range(len(voivertices)): projv = vertexprojections[vidx] # Vertex lies strictly between the two planes if (prevplanedist < projv < planedist) or (planedist < projv < prevplanedist): currentedges = updateedgelistforvertexevent(currentedges, vidx, voiedges) currentedges = sortedgestopolygonorder(currentedges, voiedges) # Compute polygon vertices by intersecting current edges with the plane polygonvertices = [] for eidx in currentedges: va, vb = voiedges[eidx] proja = vertexprojections[va] projb = vertexprojections[vb] denom = projb - proja if abs(denom) < 1e-9: continue # Edge parallel to plane t = (planedist - proja) / denom if 0.0 <= t <= 1.0: p = add(voivertices[va], scale(sub(voivertices[vb], voivertices[va]), t)) polygonvertices.append(p) polygons.append(polygonvertices) return polygons def sortedgestopolygonorder(edgeindices, voiedges): """Order edges to form a convex polygon cycle via graph traversal.""" if not edgeindices: return [] adj = {} for eidx in edgeindices: v1, v2 = voiedges[eidx] adj.setdefault(v1, []).append(v2) adj.setdefault(v2, []).append(v1) startv = voiedges[edgeindices[0]][0] path = [startv] currentv = startv visited = {startv} while len(path) < len(edgeindices) + 1: neighbors = adj.get(currentv, []) nextv = None for n in neighbors: if n not in visited: nextv = n break if nextv is None: if path[0] in neighbors: nextv = path[0] else: break path.append(nextv) visited.add(nextv) currentv = nextv orderededges = [] for k in range(len(path) - 1): for eidx in range(len(voiedges)): if voiedges[eidx] == (path[k], path[k+1]) or voiedges[eidx] == (path[k+1], path[k]): orderededges.append(eidx) break return orderededges def updateedgelistforvertexevent(currentedges, vidx, voiedges): """Toggle inclusion of edges incident to a vertex when the sweep passes it. Removes the two edges in currentedges incident to vidx, and adds the two edges not in currentedges that are incident to vidx.""" incidentedges = [eidx for eidx, (va, vb) in enumerate(voiedges) if vidx in (va, vb)] newedges = [e for e in currentedges if e not in incidentedges] newedges.extend([e for e in incidentedges if e not in currentedges]) return newedges def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def sub(v1, v2): return (v1[0]-v2[0], v1[1]-v2[1], v1[2]-v2[2]) def add(v1, v2): return (v1[0]+v2[0], v1[1]+v2[1], v1[2]+v2[2]) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) GPU-based eraser and digger tools are interactive visualization methods that allow users to selectively remove voxels from a volume rendering using a "painting" paradigm. They solve the problem of intuitive, real-time data manipulation by mapping 2D screen interactions to 3D voxel selection via line-of-sight projection. Unlike the parent Convex VOI Clipping via Weighted Sweep Graph, which defines a static convex boundary for the entire Volume of Interest (VOI), these tools define dynamic, user-controlled removal zones that persist across multiple interaction strokes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces GPU computation by clipping empty regions. Exploits coherence between parallel planes. Supports interactive VOI definition. Limitations: Adds CPU overhead for clipping calculations. Limited to convex VOIs. When to use: When the VOI is convex and the user wants to interactively define the clipping region. When the GPU is the bottleneck and can benefit from reduced sampling. When not to use: When the VOI is non-convex. When the CPU is the bottleneck. The method was proposed in the paper "Real-time interactive visualization and manipulation of the volumetric data using GPU-based methods". It addresses the need for efficient clipping of volumetric data to improve rendering performance. The WSG is a novel data structure introduced in this work to manage the topological changes during the sweep. name: GPU-based Eraser and Digger Tools
head: Painting paradigm clipping, Sculpting tools
body: GPU-based eraser and digger tools are interactive visualization methods that allow users to selectively remove voxels from a volume rendering using a "painting" paradigm. They solve the problem of intuitive, real-time data manipulation by mapping 2D screen interactions to 3D voxel selection via line-of-sight projection. Unlike the parent Convex VOI Clipping via Weighted Sweep Graph, which defines a static convex boundary for the entire Volume of Interest (VOI), these tools define dynamic, user-controlled removal zones that persist across multiple interaction strokes. Inputs: ClippedImage: The resampled 3D volume data defined by the parent clipper. Sight-Reference-Point (SRP): A 2D point (u, v) on the screen selected by the user via mouse input. Circle-of-Interest Radius (R): A scalar parameter defining the extent of the selection area on the projection plane. Digging Depth (D{dig}): A scalar parameter (for Digger tool only) defining the maximum depth from the surface along the viewing direction. Outputs: SculptBuffer: A 3D texture buffer storing visibility/distance information. Final rendered image where selected voxels are invisible. SculptBuffer Type: 3D Texture Buffer. Layout: Scalar values. Content: Stores the minimum screen-coordinate distance between any previously set SRP and the voxel's projection on the screen. Initialization: All voxels initialized to the largest representable number (infinity), indicating all voxels are visible. Update Logic: For a new SRP, if the new projected distance d{new} for a voxel is less than the stored value d{old}, update d{old} \leftarrow d{new}. Otherwise, leave unchanged. This ensures the buffer tracks the closest SRP encountered for each voxel. ClippedImage Type: 3D Volume Texture. Content: The original 3D image resampled by the parent convex clipper. 2DSculptBuffer Type: 2D Texture Array / Side-by-side slices. Purpose: Intermediate representation used to bypass hardware limitations regarding 3D texture writes from fragment shaders. 1. SRP Acquisition: The user places a 2D point (SRP) on the screen. 2. Line-of-Sight Calculation: Apply the inverse viewing transformation to the SRP to obtain the line of projective equivalent points in 3D space. For perspective projection, this defines a cone. For parallel projection, this defines a cylinder. 3. Voxel Projection: For every voxel in the ClippedImage: Project the voxel center onto the 2D projection plane (screen). Compute the 2D Euclidean distance d between the projected voxel center and the SRP. 4. SculptBuffer Update: Calculate the new distance d{new} for the current SRP. If d{new} < \text{SculptBuffer}[voxel], update \text{SculptBuffer}[voxel] \leftarrow d{new}. 5. Visibility Determination (Eraser): A voxel is considered for removal if \text{SculptBuffer}[voxel] \le R. Voxels satisfying this condition are marked invisible in the final rendering. 6. Visibility Determination (Digger): First, identify voxels selected by the Eraser criteria (\text{SculptBuffer}[voxel] \le R). For these selected voxels, determine the depth along the viewing direction from the first point of intersection with the volume. If the depth is less than the Digging Depth (D{dig}), write a specific value to the SculptBuffer that forces the voxel to be invisible. Voxels with depth \ge D{dig} remain visible (or retain their previous visibility state based on the distance check). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatesculptbuffer(sculptbuffer, clippedimage, srp2d, radius, diggingdepth, isdiggermode): """ Updates the SculptBuffer based on the current SRP and tool parameters. Args: sculptbuffer: 3D array, initialized to infinity. clippedimage: 3D volume data. srp2d: Tuple (u, v), the 2D screen coordinates of the SRP. radius: Float, the Circle-of-Interest radius. diggingdepth: Float, the max depth for the Digger tool. isdiggermode: Boolean, True for Digger, False for Eraser. """ # 1. Get inverse view ray for SRP # This yields a ray origin and direction in world space rayorigin, raydirection = inverseviewtransform(srp2d) # 2. Iterate over all voxels in ClippedImage for voxel in clippedimage.voxels: # Project voxel center to screen space projectedcenter = projecttoscreen(voxel.center, rayorigin, raydirection) # Compute 2D Euclidean distance to SRP dist2d = euclideandistance(projectedcenter, srp2d) # Update SculptBuffer with minimum distance if dist2d < sculptbuffer[voxel]: sculptbuffer[voxel] = dist2d # Determine visibility isincircle = dist2d <= radius if isdiggermode: # Digger Logic: Check depth along viewing direction # Find first intersection of ray with volume boundary firstintersectiondepth = getdepthfromsurface(voxel, rayorigin, raydirection) if isincircle and firstintersectiondepth < diggingdepth: # Force invisibility sculptbuffer[voxel] = INVISIBLEMARKER # Else: Keep existing value (which might be <= radius, making it invisible, # or > radius, keeping it visible) else: # Eraser Logic: Simple radius check if isincircle: # Mark as invisible. # Note: The source says "ignored (invisible) in further image generation". # We store a value that signifies invisibility. # If the buffer stores distance, we might store a special flag or # rely on the renderer to check <= radius. # Based on source: "All voxels 'touched'... being ignored". # We assume the renderer checks sculptbuffer[voxel] <= radius. pass # Else: Keep existing value def render(clippedimage, sculptbuffer, radius): """ Renders the volume using the SculptBuffer for visibility. """ for voxel in clippedimage.voxels: # Check visibility based on SculptBuffer # If the buffer stores the min distance, check against radius if sculptbuffer[voxel] <= radius: continue # Skip rendering this voxel (invisible) else: rendervoxel(voxel, clippedimage[voxel]) def generate2dsculptbuffer(sculptbuffer3d): """ Generates a 2D representation of the 3D SculptBuffer to bypass hardware limitations on 3D texture writes from fragment processing. """ # Store slices side-by-side width = sculptbuffer3d.width sculptbuffer3d.depth height = sculptbuffer3d.height buffer2d = newtexture(width, height) for z in range(sculptbuffer3d.depth): for y in range(sculptbuffer3d.height): for x in range(sculptbuffer3d.width): buffer2d[x + z sculptbuffer3d.width, y] = sculptbuffer3d[x, y, z] return buffer2d def load3dsculptbuffer(buffer2d, sculptbuffer3d): """ Reads back the 2D buffer to CPU and reconstructs the 3D buffer on GPU. """ # Read back to CPU memory cpudata = readtexturetocpu(buffer2d) # Reconstruct 3D structure for z in range(sculptbuffer3d.depth): for y in range(sculptbuffer3d.height): for x in range(sculptbuffer3d.width): sculptbuffer3d[x, y, z] = cpudata[x + z sculptbuffer3d.width, y] SRP: 2D point (u, v) on the screen. Circle-of-Interest Radius (R): Controls the extents of the imaginary volume on the projection plane. Defined by a slider. Digging Depth (D{dig}): Specifies the depth from the first point of intersection with the volume along the viewing direction. Defined by a slider. Hardware Limitation: Current graphics hardware prevents 3D textures from being written as the output of fragment processing. Solution: Generate a 2D representation (2DSculptBuffer) using several slices stored side-by-side, read back to CPU, then pass pointer to GPU to create 3D SculptBuffer without further processing. Precision: The distance calculation is performed in screen coordinates (2D Euclidean distance). Degenerate Input: If the SRP is outside the volume bounds, no voxels may be selected depending on the projection geometry. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the ClippedImage, as every voxel must be projected and checked against the SRP. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the SculptBuffer. Performance: Real-time interactive performance is achieved by offloading the selection logic to the GPU. Strengths: Intuitive "painting" interaction; supports persistent selection (accumulation of SRPs) via the SculptBuffer. Limitations: Dependent on hardware capabilities for 3D texture writes, requiring a CPU-GPU round-trip workaround. The "Digger" tool requires additional depth calculations. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Real-time interactive visualization and manipulation of the volumetric data using GPU-based methods". Context: It is part of a suite of interactive tools for volumetric data, including a convex VOI clipper using Weighted Sweep Graphs (WSG). Usage: Used for real-time interactive visualization and manipulation of volumetric data. Real-time interactive visualization and manipulation of the volumetric data using GPU-based methods, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.536578, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Clipping Geometry Illumination
head: Clipping Surface Shading
body:
Clipping Geometry Illumination is a shading technique for volume rendering that replaces the volume's internal gradient with the geometric surface normal at the boundary of user-defined clipping geometry to provide correct lighting. It solves the problem of visual discontinuities and unlit surfaces that occur when parts of the volume are made transparent via clipping. It builds on Cropping and differs from sibling methods such as Variance Clipping, Clipped Cropping Region Planes, Clipping Cube and Cutting Plane Interaction, Depth-based Clipping for Focus and Context Volume Rendering, Pre-integrated Clipping Boundary Handling, Camera and Clipping Setup, and Plane-based Clipping by specifically substituting the gradient with the clipping geometry's surface normal for illumination. Inputs: Volume dataset V with scalar values. Transfer function T mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Clipping geometry defined by planes or surfaces. Light source position and direction. Camera position and view direction. Outputs: Final pixel color with correct illumination at clipping boundaries. Data Structures: Ray structure with origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and length L. Sample point structure with position \mathbf{p}, scalar value s, opacity \alpha, and color \mathbf{c}. Normal vector \mathbf{n} computed from either the volume gradient 
abla V(\mathbf{p}) or the clipping geometry. Steps: 1. Cast a ray through the volume for each pixel. 2. Advance along the ray, sampling the volume at discrete intervals. 3. At each sample point \mathbf{p}, determine if it lies on the clipping geometry boundary. If inside the volume and not on a boundary, compute \mathbf{n} using 
abla V(\mathbf{p}). If on the boundary, compute \mathbf{n} using the geometric surface normal of the clipping geometry at \mathbf{p}. 4. Compute the lighting model using \mathbf{n}, light direction \mathbf{l}, and view direction \mathbf{v}. 5. Accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing, applying the lighting result to the sampled color. Formulas: Gradient normal: \mathbf{n}{vol} =  rac{
abla V(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla V(\mathbf{p})\|}. Geometric normal: \mathbf{n}{clip} = 	ext{Normal of clipping geometry at } \mathbf{p}. Final normal: \mathbf{n} =  egin{cases} \mathbf{n}{vol} & 	ext{if not on clipping boundary} \ \mathbf{n}{clip} & 	ext{if on clipping boundary} \end{cases}. Parameters: Clipping geometry defined by plane equations ax + by + cz + d = 0 or mesh surfaces. Lighting coefficients kd, ks, \alpha{spec} follow the standard Phong model. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Detecting exact boundary intersection requires tolerance handling to avoid gaps or overlaps between normals. Degenerate input: Non-watertight or self-intersecting clipping geometry causes ambiguous normal computation. Overrides standard Phong illumination with purely emissive coloring at clipped volume boundaries. It sets itself apart by preserving classified material appearance directly at the cut plane while maintaining specular reflections elsewhere, solving noisy lighting in homogeneous materials and dark back-facing surfaces. Choose it when boundary material fidelity is prioritized over gradient-based shading. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides visually consistent lighting at clipping boundaries, avoiding unlit or noisy appearances at sharp cuts. Limitations: Requires explicit definition of clipping geometry normals; does not handle internal volume gradients at the boundary, which may appear discontinuous if the geometry normal does not align with the volume structure. Clipping Geometry Illumination was described by Weiskopf et al. in TVCG 2003. It is used in direct volume rendering to improve visual quality during interactive exploration by addressing lighting discontinuities when parts of the volume are made transparent via clipping geometry. name: Emissive Clip Planes
head: emissive illumination for clip planes
body: Emissive Clip Planes is a volume rendering technique that eliminates visual artifacts at the boundary of clipped volume data by overriding standard Phong illumination with purely emissive coloring. It solves two specific problems inherent in gradient-based lighting: random, noisy lighting in homogeneous materials caused by estimated gradient noise, and dark, unlit back-facing surfaces revealed when the volume is cut. Unlike methods that modify gradient normals or ignore clipped voxels, this approach preserves the classified material appearance directly at the cut plane while maintaining specular reflections on the rest of the volume. Inputs: Volume dataset: 3D grid of scalar values. Clip plane: Defined by a point and a normal vector. Classification map: Function mapping scalar values to RGBA. Lighting parameters: Light positions and material properties for the Phong model. Outputs: Final image with emissive illumination at clip boundaries and standard illumination elsewhere. Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D grid of scalar values. Classification Map: Function mapping scalar values to RGBA. Clip Plane: Defined by a point and a normal vector. Steps: 1. Identify the clip plane surface, which defines the boundary where the volume is cut. 2. Cast rays through the volume. 3. For each sample along a ray, determine if it lies on the clipped side. Samples on the clipped side are treated as transparent. 4. For samples immediately adjacent to the clip plane, override the standard Phong illumination calculation with purely emissive illumination. 5. For samples not adjacent to the clip plane, compute standard Phong illumination using gradients estimated from neighboring voxels. 6. Composite the color and opacity along the ray to produce the final pixel color. Formulas: Emissive Color: C{emissive} = C(v), where C(v) is the color output from the classification map for scalar value v. Gradient Estimation: \mathbf{g} is estimated using central differences on neighboring voxels. Phong Illumination: I = ka + kd (\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}) + ks (\mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{V})^n, where \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{g} / \|\mathbf{g}\| is the normalized gradient, \mathbf{L} is the light vector, \mathbf{V} is the view vector, \mathbf{R} is the reflection vector, and ka, kd, ks, n are Phong coefficients. Note: The exact mathematical formula for the clip plane test and the distance threshold for adjacency are not given in the sources. Parameters: Adjacency threshold: Not given in the sources. Phong coefficients (ka, kd, ks, n): Standard lighting parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Random Lighting: In homogeneous materials, estimated gradients \mathbf{g} have random orientations due to noise in neighboring voxels, causing random lighting artifacts when used as normals in the Phong model. Dark Back-Facing Surfaces: Clipping reveals inner structures that may be back-facing relative to light sources, appearing as dark, unlit regions. Incorrect Materials via Interpolation: If clipping is done by setting voxel values to zero before classification, interpolation of zero values leads to incorrect material appearance. Specular Reflections on Cut Plane: Customers disliked specular reflections on the cut plane itself, even though they wanted them on the volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderemissiveclipplanes(volume, clipplane, classificationmap, lightpos, viewpos): # clipplane: (point, normal) # volume: 3D array of scalars # classificationmap: function scalar -> RGBA image = emptyimage() for each pixel in image: ray = castraythroughpixel(pixel, camera) color = vec4(0.0) alpha = 0.0 for sample in raysamples: if dot(sample.position - clipplane.point, clipplane.normal) < 0: continue # Clipped side is transparent v = interpolatevolume(volume, sample.position) rgba = classificationmap(v) if isadjacenttoclipplane(sample.position, clipplane): # Override lighting with emissive samplecolor = rgba.color else: # Standard Phong illumination grad = centraldifferencegradient(volume, sample.position) N = normalize(grad) L = normalize(lightpos - sample.position) V = normalize(viewpos - sample.position) R = reflect(-L, N) diffuse = max(dot(N, L), 0.0) specular = pow(max(dot(R, V), 0.0), shininess) samplecolor = rgba.color (ambient + diffuse diffusefactor + specular specularfactor) color += samplecolor rgba.alpha (1.0 - alpha) alpha += rgba.alpha (1.0 - alpha) image[pixel] = color (Note: isadjacenttoclipplane and centraldifferencegradient are standard implementations. The adjacency threshold is not specified in the sources.) Time Complexity: Same as standard volume rendering with gradient-based lighting, plus a simple adjacency check per sample. Memory Complexity: No additional memory required beyond standard volume rendering buffers. Performance: Implemented in hardware (TeraRecon VolumePro 1000), suggesting efficient execution. Strengths: Eliminates noisy lighting artifacts at clip boundaries; preserves material appearance; avoids dark back-facing surfaces; maintains specular highlights on the volume body. Limitations: Does not provide gradient-based shading on the cut plane itself; may appear less "realistic" if specular highlights are desired on the cut surface (though this was a customer preference). When to Use: When clipping volumes and visual artifacts (noise, darkness) at the cut plane are unacceptable, and specular highlights on the cut plane are undesirable. When Not to Use: When gradient-based shading (e.g., specular highlights) is required on the cut plane surface itself. Emissive Clip Planes were developed to address illumination issues in volume rendering, specifically in the context of the TeraRecon VolumePro 1000 hardware renderer. The technique was documented in an unofficial supplement to a paper on volume rendering, highlighting common problems in gradient-based lighting when clipping is applied. The approach leverages the concept of emissive illumination from OpenGL, where the color is taken directly from the classification without lighting modification. The problem of random lighting in homogeneous materials was also discussed by Kniss et al. in 2002, who proposed using gradient magnitude to interpolate between lit and unlit results, but this was deemed too expensive and visually unsatisfactory for cut planes due to unwanted specular reflections. name: Clipping Cube and Cutting Plane Interaction
head: Focus-plus-context clipping
body: This method enables interactive, selective suppression of volume datasets using an axis-aligned Clipping Cube and an arbitrary Cutting Plane, implemented via client-side widgets controlling server-side RTVR clipping capabilities. It distinguishes itself from standard polygon clipping by supporting non-uniform cube resizing via corner spheres and rendering the context region outside the cube as non-photorealistic contours rather than transparent geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a 3D input device (pen and PIP pad), and a rendering engine supporting RTVR axis-aligned and oblique clipping planes. Output: A rendered view where the interior of the clipping cube (or correct side of the cutting plane) is rendered as a solid surface (focus) and the exterior is rendered as invisible, transparent, or NPR contours (context), or where a single cutting plane isolates a specific slice. Data Structures: 1. Clipping Cube Widget: Represented as a wireframe cube with spheres at its corners, remaining axis-aligned, with spheres serving as interaction handles. 2. Cutting Plane: Defined by an arbitrary alignment, acting like a single face of the clipping cube, rendered as a visual indicator during placement. Parameters: Clipping Mode: Determines the behavior of the volume outside the clipping cube, supporting "invisible" (hard clip), "transparent", or "NPR" (focus-plus-context). Interaction Mode: Switches the PIP pad between "moving object", "cutting plane", and "clipping cube" modes. Steps: 1. Initialize Clipping Cube: The system renders a wireframe cube with spheres at the corners, which light up when the pen enters their trigger volume. 2. Resize Clipping Cube: The user drags a lit sphere, causing the cube to resize non-uniformly while maintaining its axis-aligned orientation, updating the six face planes. 3. Place Cutting Plane: The user switches the PIP pad to "cutting" mode, where the pad itself acts as the cutting plane, moves the pad to position the plane through the volume, and presses the second pen button to freeze the plane in place. The primary pen button is reserved for moving the volume object, enabling two-handed interaction (one hand moves the plane via the pad, the other moves the object via the pen). 4. Render Focus and Context: The region inside the clipping cube (or on the correct side of the cutting plane) is rendered using standard surface shading, while the region outside is rendered using Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) contours or other specified modes. Selected segmented objects can be excluded from the clipping effect, remaining shaded even when intersected by the clipping boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateinteraction(pen, pad, cube, plane, mode): if mode == "CLIPPINGCUBE": for i, sphere in enumerate(cube.spheres): if distance(pen.position, sphere.center) <= sphere.radius: sphere.highlight = True if pen.isdragging(): cube.spheres[i].center = pen.position cube.updateaxisalignedbounds() else: sphere.highlight = False elif mode == "CUTTINGPLANE": plane.position = pad.position plane.normal = pad.normal if pen.secondbuttonpressed: mode = "CLIPPINGCUBE" return mode def computeclippingplanes(cube, plane): planes = [] for i in range(6): planes.append(cube.getfaceplane(i)) planes.append(plane) return planes def rendervolume(clippingplanes, outsidemode): # Apply clipping planes to volume data clippeddata = applyplanestovolume(clippingplanes) # Render inside region as surface rendersurface(clippeddata, region="inside") # Render outside region according to mode if outsidemode == "NPRCONTOURS": rendernprcontours(clippeddata, region="outside") elif outsidemode == "INVISIBLE": pass elif outsidemode == "TRANSPARENT": rendertransparent(clippeddata, region="outside") Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: The combination of image-based rendering with polygon-based interaction widgets yields occlusion problems. Convoluted Objects: For complex structures like vessels, distinguishing cut parts from the context can be difficult, making the NPR context rendering particularly valuable for clarity. This variant specifically utilizes Non-Photorealistic Rendering (NPR) for the context region. It isolates a focus region using a clipping cube widget (rendered as a surface) while rendering the context outside the cube as non-photorealistic contours. This approach is chosen when the user needs to see the structural outline of the clipped volume without the visual clutter of full volume rendering. The clipping cube widget is resizable via corner dragging and defines the bounded region for clipping. Selected segmented objects can be excluded from clipping, remaining shaded even when covered by the clipping planes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows intuitive, direct manipulation of the clipping region. Two-handed interaction (pad for plane, pen for object) improves workflow. NPR context reduces visual clutter. Limitations: The clipping cube is axis-aligned, limiting its orientation flexibility. The cutting plane is single-sided. Stereoscopic occlusion can be problematic with image-based rendering and polygon widgets. When to use: When exploring internal structures of a volume while needing to see the surrounding context's shape. This method was developed for distributed software-based volume visualization in a virtual environment. It builds on earlier focus-plus-context work [FG98] and integrates with RTVR capabilities for axis-aligned and oblique clipping. The approach was presented at the Eurographics conference in 2005. Distributed Software-Based Volume Visualization in a Virtual Environment, https://doi.org/10.2312/egve/iptegve2005/129-140, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth-based Clipping for Focus and Context Volume Rendering
head: Four-Pass Depth Clipping, Interactive Lens via Depth Clipping
body: This method decomposes a volume rendering into a high-quality 'focus' region and a lower-quality 'context' region using depth-based clipping and early-z rejection. It is implemented in four rendering passes to maximize fragment shader discard efficiency. It is chosen over tessellating proxy geometry or tagging volume regions because it supports arbitrary convex clip objects and large bricked volumes without performance-complicating side effects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (potentially bricked), a clip object (representing the focus region boundary) defined by front-facing and back-facing polygons, and a depth buffer. Output: A rendered image where the focus region is rendered with full sampling/quality and the context region is rendered with reduced sampling/quality. Data Structures: Clip Texture: A high-resolution depth component texture storing back-face depth values of the clip object. Depth Buffer: Standard framebuffer depth buffer. Opaque Depth Texture (Optional): If opaque geometry is present, a texture storing depths of opaque objects. Parameters: Depth Test Modes: LESS (used in Pass 1) and GREATER (used in Passes 3 and 4). Clip Texture Resolution: High-resolution, matching the screen resolution. Steps: 1. Pass 1: Initialize Depth Buffer for Front Region. Render the front-facing polygons of the clip object into the depth buffer. Set the depth test to LESS. Draw all volume slices in front-to-back order. 2. Pass 2: Capture Back-Face Depth. Render the back-facing polygons of the clip object. Copy the resulting depth values into the high-resolution depth component clip texture. 3. Pass 3: Render Front Half of Focus Region. Change the depth test to GREATER. Draw volume slices from the front of the volume until the center of the clip object. Fragment Shader Logic: At the beginning of the fragment shader, read the corresponding back-face depth value from the clip texture. If the fragment's depth is greater than the fetched clip texture value, terminate shader execution (discard fragment). 4. Pass 4: Render Back Half of Focus Region and Context. Repeat the process for slices from the center of the clip object to the back of the volume, with roles reversed: use the back faces to initialize the depth buffer and the front faces to set the clip texture. Use the back faces of the clip object to initialize the depth buffer, set the depth test to GREATER, and render slices from the front of the clip object to the back of the volume. Fragment Shader Logic: Same as Pass 3: read front-face depth from the clip texture and discard if fragment depth > fetched value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderclipobjectfrontfacesintodepthbuffer(): drawclipobjectfaces(facing='front') def drawvolumeslicesfronttoback(): drawslices(order='fronttoback') def renderclipobjectbackfaces(): drawclipobjectfaces(facing='back') def copydepthbuffertotexture(): return readdepthbufferastexture() def drawvolumeslicesfromfronttoclipcenter(): drawslices(start='front', end='clipcenter') def drawvolumeslicesfromfronttobackofvolume(): drawslices(start='clipfront', end='volumeback') depthfunction = LESS renderclipobjectfrontfacesintodepthbuffer() drawvolumeslicesfronttoback() renderclipobjectbackfaces() cliptexture = copydepthbuffertotexture() depthfunction = GREATER drawvolumeslicesfromfronttoclipcenter() depthfunction = LESS renderclipobjectbackfacesintodepthbuffer() renderclipobjectfrontfaces() cliptexture = copydepthbuffertotexture() depthfunction = GREATER drawvolumeslicesfromfronttobackofvolume() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Screen Space Lenses: If the lens is screen-space based, the focus does not need to be divided, and a clip texture is not required. However, opaque geometry and acceleration techniques (early ray termination/empty space skipping) require two additional depth textures: one for opaque object depths, one for the current pass's depth buffer. Opaque Geometry: To incorporate opaque geometry, the opaque depth texture is used to initialize the depth texture at the beginning of the passes, and the current pass's depth buffer is used to initialize the depth buffer for intermediate steps of the acceleration technique. Transition Region: Additional passes are needed for adding a transition region for blending the results. Time Complexity: Four rendering passes are required, increasing the overhead compared to single-pass methods. Memory Complexity: Requires a high-resolution depth component clip texture. For screen-space lenses with opaque geometry, two additional depth textures are needed. Strengths: Supports arbitrary convex clip objects and large bricked volumes without performance-complicating side effects. Maximizes early-z rejection efficiency. Limitations: Requires multiple passes, which can be costly on hardware with limited render target flexibility. Incorporating opaque geometry and acceleration techniques requires two additional depth textures and additional passes. When to Use: When interactive focus and context rendering is required with arbitrary convex clip regions and large volumes. When Not to Use: When screen-space lenses are sufficient and opaque geometry/acceleration techniques are not needed, as the clip texture and multiple passes are unnecessary. This method was developed by I. K. et al. and published in the paper "A Focus and Context Interface for Interactive Volume Rendering". It was chosen over alternative approaches like tessellating proxy geometry or tagging volume regions due to its ability to handle arbitrary convex clip objects and large bricked volumes efficiently.
