name: Pre-integrated Clipping Boundary Handling
body: A method to handle artifacts at clip boundaries when using pre-integrated volume rendering with low sampling rates, by mapping an opaque texture onto the clip geometry. It sets apart from Clipping and Clipped Cropping Region Planes by explicitly computing the optical contribution of the gap between the clipping surface and the first volume slice, rather than relying solely on depth buffering or simple suppression. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Clipping surface geometry (proxy polygons), volume texture, viewing ray, fragment shader program. Output: Correctly composited color and opacity at the clip boundary, avoiding artifacts caused by discrete sampling gaps. Data Structures: Clipping Surface: Defined by proxy polygons. Each polygon has vertices with 3D coordinates. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values v. Fragment Shader State: Current fragment position P on the clipping surface, and the intersection point Q on the first proxy polygon behind P. Numbered Steps: 1. Render the clipping surface before the clipped volume behind it. 2. For each fragment P on the clipping surface, find the intersection Q of the viewing ray with the first proxy polygon behind P. 3. Look up data values vP at P and vQ at Q from the volume texture. 4. Compute the corresponding sampling distance d{\Delta} based on vP and vQ. 5. Compute the contribution of the ray segment between the surface and the first slice in the clipped volume in a fragment program. 6. For consistency, do not compute the actual geometric length of the ray segment between P and Q if it deviates from the pre-integrated model assumptions. Formulas: Sampling distance: d{\Delta} is computed based on vP and vQ to determine the contribution of the ray segment. Contribution: The contribution of the ray segment between P and Q is computed in the fragment program using d{\Delta}. Parameters: Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on accurate intersection detection between the viewing ray and the proxy polygons. Boundaries: The method assumes that the clipping surface is rendered before the volume. Pitfall: An optical model for clipping using a boundary layer of finite thickness requires interleaved rendering of volume and clip surface, which is more complex. Goal: The primary goal is often to show relationships between features (e.g., distances between isosurfaces), which opaque textures might obscure if not handled carefully. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preintegratedclippingboundaryhandling(clippingsurface, volumetexture, viewingray, stepsize): # Step 1: Clipping surface is rendered before the volume (caller responsibility) for fragment in clippingsurface.fragments: P = fragment.position # Step 2: Find intersection Q with first proxy polygon behind P Q = findintersection(viewingray.origin, viewingray.direction, P, clippingsurface.proxypolygons) if Q is None: # No proxy polygon found behind P; skip boundary contribution fragment.color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) fragment.opacity = 0.0 continue # Step 3: Look up data values vP = volumetexture.sample(P) vQ = volumetexture.sample(Q) # Step 4: Compute sampling distance ddelta = computesamplingdistance(vP, vQ, stepsize) # Step 5: Compute contribution of ray segment color, opacity = computecontribution(vP, vQ, ddelta) # Set fragment color and opacity fragment.color = color fragment.opacity = opacity def findintersection(rayorigin, raydir, pointonsurface, proxypolygons): # Returns the first intersection point Q behind pointonsurface along the ray closestQ = None mint = float('inf') for poly in proxypolygons: t, Q = raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydir, pointonsurface, poly) if t is not None and t > 0 and t < mint: mint = t closestQ = Q return closestQ def raytriangleintersect(origin, direction, point, triangle): # Standard Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection # Returns (t, Q) if intersection is behind point, else (None, None) v1, v2, v3 = triangle.vertices E1 = [v2[i] - v1[i] for i in range(3)] E2 = [v3[i] - v1[i] for i in range(3)] D = [direction[i] for i in range(3)] N = [E1[1]E2[2] - E1[2]E2[1], E1[2]E2[0] - E1[0]E2[2], E1[0]E2[1] - E1[1]E2[0]] det = D[0]N[0] + D[1]N[1] + D[2]N[2] if abs(det) < 1e-8: return None, None invdet = 1.0 / det T = [v1[i] - point[i] for i in range(3)] u = (T[0]N[0] + T[1]N[1] + T[2]N[2]) invdet if u < 0 or u > 1: return None, None T = [D[1]E2[2] - D[2]E2[1], D[2]E2[0] - D[0]E2[2], D[0]E2[1] - D[1]E2[0]] v = (T[0]N[0] + T[1]N[1] + T[2]N[2]) invdet if v < 0 or u + v > 1: return None, None t = (T[0]E1[0] + T[1]E1[1] + T[2]E1[2]) invdet if t <= 0: return None, None Q = [point[i] + t D[i] for i in range(3)] return t, Q def computesamplingdistance(vP, vQ, stepsize): # Compute sampling distance based on values and step size # Guard against zero division and negative distances return max(stepsize, 1e-6) def computecontribution(vP, vQ, ddelta): # Compute optical contribution for the gap segment # Uses linear interpolation as a standard pre-integration fallback if ddelta <= 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 avgval = (vP + vQ) / 2.0 color = [avgval, avgval, avgval] opacity = min(1.0, avgval ddelta) return color, opacity Volume clipping is a technique to reveal internal structures of a volume model by setting unwanted parts to transparent, complementing transfer function specifications. It sets apart from sibling methods by allowing arbitrary clip geometry (polygons, voxelized geometry, or iso-surfaces) to define the visible region, often implemented via fragment shaders that modify alpha based on geometric distance. Unlike stencil-based approaches which decouple geometry from volume data, this method integrates clipping logic directly into the rendering pipeline of texture slicing. When to Use: When using pre-integrated volume rendering with low sampling rates. When Not to Use: When the goal is to show relationships between features, as opaque textures might obscure them if not handled carefully. Origin: Not given in the sources. History and Development: Not given in the sources. Where it is Used: Not given in the sources. name: Volume Clipping (Texture Slicing)
head: Clipping Node, Clipping in Texture Slicing, FSClipper, Volume Clipping Node, Volumetric Clipping
body: Volume clipping is a technique to reveal internal structures of a volume model by setting unwanted parts to transparent, complementing transfer function specifications. It sets apart from sibling methods by allowing arbitrary clip geometry (polygons, voxelized geometry, or iso-surfaces) to define the visible region, often implemented via fragment shaders that modify alpha based on geometric distance. Unlike stencil-based approaches which decouple geometry from volume data, this method integrates clipping logic directly into the rendering pipeline of texture slicing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume texture (3D), SculptMap texture (3D, stores clipping state), PolygonCoord texture (2D, stores projection coordinates), clipPlane (4D vector), ProjPlane (4x4 projection matrix), and tool point P (4D vector). Output: Rendered color/alpha buffer with clipped regions. Data Structures: SculptMap: A 3D texture where each voxel stores a mask value, with voxels inside the clip geometry initialized to 0 (transparent) and remaining voxels set to 1 (opaque). PolygonCoord: A 2D texture mapping fragment coordinates to 3D projection space. ProjPlane: A uniform 4x4 matrix representing the projection transformation required to map texture coordinates to clip space. clipPlane: A uniform float4 defining the clipping plane equation. P: A uniform float4 where P{xyz} represents a 3D point and Pa represents the tool radius. Steps: 1. Coordinate Projection: Sample the PolygonCoord texture at the input fragment coordinates to obtain 3D texture coordinates. 2. Mask Sampling: Sample the SculptMap texture at the obtained 3D coordinates to retrieve the current alpha mask value. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Subtract 0.5 from the 3D coordinate components, append 1.0, and multiply by the ProjPlane matrix. 4. Perspective Division: Divide the transformed vector's x, y, and z components by its w component. 5. Distance Calculation: Compute the 2D Euclidean distance D = \frac{\| \text{PlaneCoordinates}{xy} - P{xy} \|}{Pz}, where P{xy} and Pz are components of the tool point vector. 6. Alpha Update: If D is less than the current alpha value, update the alpha value to D. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mulrowvecmat(vec, mat): """Multiplies a row vector by a 4x4 matrix.""" return [sum(vec[i] mat[i][j] for i in range(4)) for j in range(4)] def FSClipper(v2fTex0, SculptMap, PolygonCoord, ProjPlane, P): # 1. Coordinate Projection texCoord = PolygonCoord.sample(v2fTex0) # 2. Mask Sampling Col = SculptMap.sample(texCoord[:3]) # 3. Coordinate Transformation centered = [texCoord[0] - 0.5, texCoord[1] - 0.5, texCoord[2] - 0.5, 1.0] PlaneCoordinates = mulrowvecmat(centered, ProjPlane) # 4. Perspective Division PlaneCoordinates[0] /= PlaneCoordinates[3] PlaneCoordinates[1] /= PlaneCoordinates[3] PlaneCoordinates[2] /= PlaneCoordinates[3] # 5. Distance Calculation D = math.sqrt((PlaneCoordinates[0] - P[0])2 + (PlaneCoordinates[1] - P[1])2) / P[2] # 6. Alpha Update if D < Col[3]: Col[3] = D return Col Parameters: Clipping Mode 1: The part inside the clipping geometry is the clipped object (removed). Clipping Mode 2: The part outside the clipping geometry is the clipped object (removed). Clipping Mode 3: Initializes the clipped volume model and attaches it to the clipping geometry. Tool Radius: Stored in Pa, defines the effective radius of the clipping tool. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-volume Clipping: Issuing the same clipping operation twice does not realize multi-volume clipping directly; a clipping-geometry-list must be created to arrange different clipping geometries. Performance: Multi-model clipping can seriously affect the interactive rate at runtime if not optimized. Occlusion: There is unavailability of volume-based depth buffering, meaning the final rendered frame with multiple volume models cannot always show correct occlusions like wireframe ones. Uses the OpenGL stencil buffer to restrict rendering to pixels inside or outside an arbitrary closed surface geometry. Sets apart by decoupling clipping boundary definition from volume data, allowing any triangle mesh to act as a clipper without voxelization overhead. Choose when hardware stencil support is available and arbitrary mesh clippers are needed. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of slices and the cost of texture sampling and distance calculation per fragment. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the SculptMap texture, which scales with the volume resolution. Performance: Multi-step slicing with oversampling (e.g., four-times) yields the best quality-performance tradeoff due to increased cache coherency. Strengths: Allows arbitrary clip geometry (polygons, voxelized, iso-surface) and provides high-quality shading for clip boundaries. Limitations: Multi-model clipping impacts interactive rate and lack of volume-based depth buffering leads to incorrect occlusions in multi-volume scenes. Volume clipping was introduced as part of hybrid rendering frameworks for real-time manipulation of volume and surface models. It complements transfer function specifications by providing geometric control over visibility. Techniques for volume clipping in 2D and 3D texture slicing methods were proposed by Weiskopf et al., who also presented high-quality shading techniques for clip boundaries. The method is used in medical visualization (e.g., anatomical atlases) and engineering visualization (e.g., engine box clipping). name: Stencil-based Clipping Geometries
head: Clipping geometries and Stenciling
body: Stencil-based clipping is a hardware-accelerated method for volume clipping that uses the stencil buffer to restrict rendering to pixels inside or outside an arbitrary closed surface geometry. It sets apart from sibling methods by decoupling the clipping boundary definition from the volume data itself, allowing any triangle mesh to act as a clipper without voxelization or ray-casting overhead. Inputs: A closed surface geometry defined by a list of triangles. A current slicing plane position and orientation. The volume texture data. Outputs: A rendered slice where pixels are either accepted or rejected based on their intersection with the clipping geometry's cross-section. Data Structures: Stencil Buffer: A per-pixel integer buffer that tracks which pixels are covered by the clipping cross-section. Clipping Geometry: A closed triangle mesh representing the arbitrary shape to clip against. Numbered Steps: 1. Enable Clipping Plane: Enable an additional clipping plane in the rasterization stage with the same orientation and position as the current slicing plane. 2. Render Back Faces: Render the back faces of the clipping object in polygon mode. This sets the stencil buffer for pixels covered by the cross-section without altering frame buffer color values. 3. Correct Stencil Errors: Render front faces into pixels where the stencil buffer was already set. Clear the stencil buffer entry for these pixels if the pixel passes the depth test, correcting erroneous stencil entries caused by back-face-only rendering. 4. Render Volume: Render the textured volume polygon. Configure the stencil test to accept or reject pixels based on the initialized stencil buffer, restricting drawing to pixels inside or outside the cross-section. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Stencil Bits: The number of bits provided by the visual hardware. Stencil Planes: Multiple stencil planes can be used to avoid clearing the buffer between slices. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Geometries: Rendering only back faces fails to determine the cross-section exactly for complex geometries. This is corrected by the subsequent front-face pass. Stencil Buffer Overflow: The number of slices that can be processed without clearing the buffer depends on the number of stencil bits provided by the visual hardware. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderclippedslice(clippingmesh, slicingplane, volumetexture, stencilbuffer, stencilbits): """ Renders a volume slice clipped by an arbitrary closed surface using the stencil buffer. """ # Step 1: Enable clipping plane matching the slicing plane enableclippingplane(slicingplane) # Step 2: Render back faces to set stencil buffer setstencilop(passdepth=REPLACE, faildepth=KEEP, failstencil=KEEP) setstencilfunc(compare=ALWAYS, ref=1, mask=0xFF) setcullmode(cullfront=True) setcolorwrite(enabled=False) setdepthwrite(enabled=False) drawmesh(clippingmesh) setcolorwrite(enabled=True) setdepthwrite(enabled=True) # Step 3: Correct stencil errors by rendering front faces setstencilop(passdepth=ZERO, faildepth=KEEP, failstencil=KEEP) setstencilfunc(compare=EQUAL, ref=1, mask=0xFF) setcullmode(cullfront=False) setcolorwrite(enabled=False) setdepthwrite(enabled=False) setdepthtest(enabled=True) drawmesh(clippingmesh) setcolorwrite(enabled=True) setdepthwrite(enabled=True) setdepthtest(enabled=False) # Step 4: Render volume with stencil test setstencilfunc(compare=EQUAL, ref=1, mask=0xFF) setstencilop(passdepth=KEEP, faildepth=KEEP, failstencil=KEEP) drawvolumeslice(volumetexture, slicingplane) disableclippingplane() Uses different stencil planes to process multiple slices without clearing the buffer, limited by stencil bit depth. Allows any closed triangle mesh to define the clip boundary, supporting transformations without additional overhead. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Independent of the used geometry, allowing arbitrary shapes to be specified. Transformations of the geometry can be handled without any additional overhead. Limitations: The number of slices that can be processed without clearing the buffer depends on the number of stencil bits provided by the visual hardware. When to Use: When arbitrary closed surface geometries are needed for clipping. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was described by Meissner in the context of volume visualization and rendering techniques. It leverages existing rasterization features to provide a flexible tool for carving portions out of the data in an intuitive way. name: Stencil Clip Mask Generation
head: ClipMaskOperation, RenderToClipMask
body: Stencil Clip Mask Generation creates a stencil buffer mask for user interface clipping by applying a sequence of stencil operations based on a requested ClipMaskOperation (Set, SetInverse, or Intersect). It differs from standard depth-based clipping by allowing arbitrary closed surface geometries to define clipping regions via the stencil buffer, enabling complex UI overlays and split-screen effects. Inputs: A compiled geometry object stored in this->geometries. A creation shader (must be non-null). A translation vector (translation.x, translation.y). A projection matrix and a transform matrix. A ClipMaskOperation enum value (Set, SetInverse, Intersect). A scissor region (optional). Outputs: Updated stencil buffer contents defining the clipping mask. Data Structures: BgfxFrameBuffer: Contains width (int), height (int), color (sharedptr<gfx::Texture>), depthstencil (sharedptr<gfx::Texture>), and fb (sharedptr<gfx::FrameBuffer> or equivalent handle). stencilValue: A monotonically increasing integer tracking the current stencil reference value. stencilRef: The current stencil reference value used in BGFXSTENCILFUNCREF, stored as a class member. Steps: 1. Locate the compiled geometry in this->geometries. If not found or if the creation shader is null, return immediately. 2. Compute the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix: Create a translation matrix: translatemat = Rml::Matrix4f::Translate(translation.x, translation.y, 0.0f). Compute mvp = projection transform translatemat. 3. Convert the mvp matrix to a 16-element float array and set it as the utransform uniform. 4. Apply stencil operations based on ClipMaskOperation: Set: Increment stencilValue, assign it to stencilRef. Configure stencil to always pass, write the reference value, and zero on stencil/depth fail. SetInverse: First, draw a fullscreen quad with an identity transform to fill the stencil with stencilRef using REPLACE operations. Then, draw the geometry with REPLACE operations and stencil reference 0. Intersect: Save oldref = stencilRef. Increment stencilValue. If stencilRef == oldref + 1 (sequential), use EQUAL test with INCR operation; otherwise, use LEQUAL test with REPLACE operation. 5. Re-apply the scissor region if enabled, set the final stencil state, and submit the draw call. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateclipmask(geometries, shader, translation, projection, transform, operation, scissorenabled, scissorregion, stencilvalue, stencilref): # Step 1: Locate geometry geometry = geometries.get(translation) # Assuming translation or ID maps to geometry if geometry is None or shader is None: return # Step 2: Compute MVP translatemat = Rml.Matrix4f.translate(translation.x, translation.y, 0.0f) mvp = projection transform translatemat # Step 3: Set uniform mvparray = mvp.tofloatarray16() shader.setuniform("utransform", mvparray) # Step 4: Apply stencil operations if operation == "Set": stencilvalue += 1 stencilref = stencilvalue # Configure stencil: always pass, write ref, zero on fail setstencilfunc(BGFXSTENCILFUNCALWAYS, stencilref, 0xFF) setstencilop(BGFXSTENCILOPKEEP, BGFXSTENCILOPKEEP, BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE) setdepthfunc(BGFXDEPTHFUNCALWAYS) # Assuming depth is handled via stencil zeroing on fail elif operation == "SetInverse": # Draw fullscreen quad with identity transform identitymat = Rml.Matrix4f.identity() shader.setuniform("utransform", identitymat.tofloatarray16()) setstencilfunc(BGFXSTENCILFUNCALWAYS, stencilref, 0xFF) setstencilop(BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE, BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE, BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE) drawfullscreenquad() # Draw geometry with stencil ref 0 shader.setuniform("utransform", mvparray) setstencilfunc(BGFXSTENCILFUNCALWAYS, 0, 0xFF) setstencilop(BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE, BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE, BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE) drawgeometry(geometry) elif operation == "Intersect": oldref = stencilref stencilvalue += 1 if stencilref == oldref + 1: setstencilfunc(BGFXSTENCILFUNCEQUAL, stencilref, 0xFF) setstencilop(BGFXSTENCILOPKEEP, BGFXSTENCILOPKEEP, BGFXSTENCILOPINCR) else: setstencilfunc(BGFXSTENCILFUNCLEQUAL, stencilref, 0xFF) setstencilop(BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE, BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE, BGFXSTENCILOPREPLACE) # Step 5: Finalize if scissorenabled: setscissorregion(scissorregion) setfinalstencilstate() submitdrawcall(geometry) Parameters: stencilValue: Monotonically increasing integer tracking the current stencil reference value. Incremented on each Set or Intersect operation. stencilRef: Current stencil reference value used in BGFXSTENCILFUNCREF. Stored as a class member. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the geometry is not found or the shader is null, the function returns immediately without modifying the stencil buffer. Precision issues may arise if stencilValue overflows, though this is unlikely given typical UI clipping scenarios. The Intersect operation relies on sequential increments; if the sequence is broken, it falls back to a less restrictive LEQUAL test. Time Complexity: O(1) per clipping operation, assuming constant-time matrix multiplication and stencil buffer updates. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it relies on the existing stencil buffer and frame buffer structures. Performance: Performance depends on the complexity of the geometry and the number of clipping operations. Fullscreen quad draws for SetInverse may be costly if done frequently. Strengths: Allows for complex, arbitrary clipping shapes using standard stencil buffer operations. Efficient for UI clipping where the clipping region is static or changes infrequently. Limitations: Limited by the stencil buffer width (typically 8 bits, allowing up to 256 levels of nesting). Not suitable for dynamic, high-frequency clipping updates. When to use: Ideal for UI clipping, split-screen effects, and other scenarios requiring precise, arbitrary clipping regions. When not to use: Not suitable for volumetric data clipping where depth-based methods are more appropriate, or for dynamic scenes with frequent clipping changes. Stencil Clip Mask Generation is part of the Damascene engine's UI rendering system, specifically designed to handle clipping for UI elements using the BGFX graphics library. It leverages the stencil buffer to create masks that can be used to clip subsequent rendering passes, enabling features like split-screen and custom clipping regions. name: Camera and Clipping Setup
head: View Reference and Clipping Planes
body: Camera and Clipping Setup defines the initial camera parameters and clipping boundaries for focus+context volume rendering. The view reference point is computed as the center of the focus clusters, while the projection window covers both focus and contextual clusters to keep the whole context visible while centering the image on the focus. It integrates distance-based voxel culling for surface proximity filtering. Inputs: A set of identified clusters, categorized as "focus" and "context". User-defined clipping plane parameters (initially derived from focus bounds). A distance map voxel model containing the distance of each voxel to the nearest surface boundary. User-defined threshold for surface proximity culling. Outputs: Camera view reference point. Camera projection window (bounding box). Clipping plane positions. Culling mask for voxels based on distance threshold. Data Structures: Clusters: List of 3D centroids (x, y, z) for focus and context groups. Distance Map: 3D voxel grid where each voxel stores a scalar distance value d to the nearest boundary. Clipping Planes: User-defined planes defined by normal vector \mathbf{n} and distance D from origin, or plane equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0. Steps: 1. Compute View Reference Point: Calculate the centroid of the focus clusters. Let F be the set of focus cluster centers. The view reference point \mathbf{V}{ref} is: \mathbf{V}{ref} = \frac{1}{|F|} \sum{c \in F} c 2. Compute Projection Window: Determine the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) that encloses both the focus clusters and the context clusters. Let C be the set of context cluster centers. The projection window is the AABB of F \cup C. 3. Initialize Clipping Planes: Set the initial position of user-defined clipping planes to coincide with the faces of the focus bounding box. 4. Load Distance Map: Load the third voxel model containing the precomputed distance map of all voxels to the nearest surface boundary. 5. Apply Distance-Based Culling: During rendering, for each voxel v with distance value dv and user-defined threshold T: if dv > T, cull the voxel (do not render). This applies to both focus and context voxels. 6. Apply Opacity Modulation: During 3D texture rendering, apply per-plane opacity modulation to all proxy polygons in front of the focus bounding box to make slices traversing only contextual information more transparent. Parameters: Distance Threshold (T): User-defined value for surface proximity culling. Clipping Plane Initial Position: Bounding box of focus clusters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Point Optimization: Not currently applied; camera orientation is specified interactively by users. Context Opacity: The parser sets the opacity of the Color Transfer Function (CTF) to zero for context voxels to prevent them from being rendered during texture slicing, while context bounding boxes are shown. Opacity modulation is then applied to proxy polygons in front of the focus bounding box. A variant where clipping is implemented via shader uniforms. The method passes a 4D homogeneous plane equation to a shader to enable custom clipping of rendered geometry. The plane equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 is uploaded as a 4-component float uniform clipeqn[0..3]. The shader program is bound, the uniform location is retrieved, and the plane components are uploaded as floats. This allows for dynamic, per-fragment clipping decisions based on the plane equation. Not given in the sources. This method originates from research on structural focus+context rendering of multiclassified volume data. It integrates cluster-based view framing with distance-based culling to enhance the visualization of complex, multi-class volumetric datasets. name: Shader Clip Plane Setup
head: Clip Plane Uniform Setup, Custom Clip Plane Uniform, Exclusion Plane Clipping
body: A clipping technique using user-defined planes to cut away parts of a volume, enabling the visualization of interior structures by excluding points on the positive side of the plane. It differs from fixed hardware clipping by passing a 4D homogeneous plane equation to a shader as a uniform, allowing dynamic, per-frame updates of the clipping boundary without rebuilding geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of active exclusion planes, each defined by a normal vector and a distance/offset. In the shader, these are accessed via a uniform array or single uniform depending on the variant. Output: A rendered volume where fragments/voxels satisfying the clipping condition are discarded (not colored), effectively "cutting" the volume. Data Structures: The plane is represented as a 4-component vector (often vec4 in GLSL/HLSL). Format A (Homogeneous/Standard): (A, B, C, D) representing the plane equation Ax + By + Cz + D = 0. The normal is (A, B, C) and D = -\text{dot}(\text{normal}, \text{point}). Format B (Normal/Distance): (nx, ny, nz, w) where (nx, ny, nz) is the unit normal and w is the signed distance from the origin to the plane along the normal. Numbered Steps: 1. Bind Shader: Retrieve the uniform location for the clip plane equation (e.g., clipeqn) from the target shader program. 2. Upload Data: Pass the 4 components of the plane equation as floats to the uniform. Unbind the shader program if necessary for other operations. 3. Shader Evaluation (Per Point/Voxel): For each intersection point p (or voxel center) in world space: Iterate through all active exclusion planes. Check Condition: If using Format A: Calculate d = \text{dot}(p, \text{vec3}(A,B,C)) + D. If d > 0, the point is on the "cut" side (positive side). Mark planetestpassed = false and break. If using Format B: Calculate d = \text{dot}(p, \text{vec3}(nx,ny,nz)). If d \ge w (or > w depending on strictness), the point is outside the valid region. Mark planetestpassed = false and break. If planetestpassed is false, discard the fragment/voxel (continue to next iteration or return). If all planes pass, color the point using the volume transfer function. Formulas: Format A (Homogeneous): \text{clip\test} = \text{dot}(p{xyz}, \text{plane}{xyz}) + \text{plane}w Discard if \text{clip\test} > 0. Note: Some implementations use w=-1 for homogeneous coordinates in specific contexts, but standard plane equation evaluation uses the 4th component as the offset D. Format B (Normal/Distance): \text{clip\test} = \text{dot}(p, \text{clippingPlane}{xyz}) Discard if \text{clip\test} \ge \text{clippingPlane}w. Parameters: clipeqn: 4-component float uniform. Format A: [A, B, C, D]. Format B: [nx, ny, nz, w]. MAXEXCLUSIONPLANES: Maximum number of planes supported in the shader loop. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors near the plane boundary may cause flickering or artifacts. It is common practice to add a small epsilon bias to the comparison or the plane distance to stabilize the boundary. Normal Direction: The "positive" side definition depends on the normal direction. Ensure the normal points away from the volume interior if the condition is dot > 0 (Format A) or dot >= w (Format B). Multiple Planes: The order of plane checks does not matter for correctness, but early-out optimization (breaking on first failure) is critical for performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isinsidevolume(p, clipplane): # Calculate signed distance from point to plane # Plane equation: Ax + By + Cz + D = 0 # dot(p, normal) + D normal = vec3(clipplane.x, clipplane.y, clipplane.z) d = clipplane.w # Evaluate plane equation # If result > 0, point is on the positive side (excluded) distance = dot(p, normal) + d if distance > 0.0: return False # Point is clipped return True # Point is inside A method to represent a clipping plane using a 4D vector where the first three components (xyz) define the plane's normal vector and the fourth component (w) defines the signed distance from the origin to the plane along that normal. It is simpler than managing three separate planes or using sine/cosine rotations for X and Y axes, allowing rotation in all directions (X, Y, and Z) through a single plane definition. The core check is dot(point, clippingPlane.xyz) < clippingPlane.w. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of fragments/voxels processed and P is the number of active exclusion planes. The check is a simple dot product per plane. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory on the GPU for the uniform storage. Performance: Very fast as it avoids geometry reconstruction. Performance depends on the number of active planes and the cost of the volume ray-marching loop. Early-out in the plane loop helps if many points are clipped. Strengths: Dynamic, per-frame updates; no geometry rebuild; works with any volume rendering technique (ray marching, splatting) that supports fragment/voxel discard. Limitations: Requires shader modification or specific uniform support; not all volume rendering engines expose a generic clip plane uniform. When to use: When interactive, dynamic cropping is needed without the overhead of modifying the underlying volume data structure or geometry. Originating from general graphics clipping techniques, this specific implementation for volume rendering leverages the flexibility of fragment shaders to apply custom clipping logic. It is commonly used in medical imaging and scientific visualization tools (e.g., Godot volume layers, Three.js extensions) to allow users to "slice" through volumes to see internal structures. blackears/godotvolumelayers, https://github.com/blackears/godotvolumelayers, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) qqdiguo/CloudRender-PointSplatting, https://github.com/qqdiguo/CloudRender-PointSplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Multiple Angle Clipping in Volume - Questions - three.js forum, https://discourse.threejs.org/t/multiple-angle-clipping-in-volume/9242, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Plane-based Clipping
body: Plane-based clipping is a cropping technique that restricts volume visualization using one or more arbitrary planes, allowing for cutaway views, interior reveals, and specific anatomical plane inspections that axis-aligned cropping cannot provide. It sets itself apart from Cropping by supporting arbitrary orientations and complex cutaways rather than just rectilinear slabs, and from Variance Clipping by operating on geometric position rather than statistical variance. Plane-based clipping defines a half-space or slab using a plane equation \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} - D = 0, where \mathbf{n} is the normal vector and D is the distance from the origin. Visibility is determined by the signed distance of a sample point \mathbf{x} to the plane. If the distance is negative (or outside a defined slab), the sample is suppressed. Implementation typically involves calculating this distance in the rendering pipeline (vertex, fragment, or ray-casting step) and modulating opacity or discarding samples. Removes specific regions to reveal interior structures or resolve occlusion using arbitrary planes, often with a smooth transition falloff. Choose this for complex cutaways or when smooth blending between visible and suppressed regions is required. Allows interactive resizing of an axis-aligned bounding box via controller or widget manipulation. Choose this for intuitive, real-time exploration of internal structures without manual dataset editing. Restricts visualization to a single, opaque, user-specified planar cross-section. Choose this for precise inspection of internal structures at a specific depth or orientation. A feature allowing users to view different anatomical planes (sagittal, transverse, coronal) by selecting them via a virtual laser from the Oculus Touch controller and moving along provided axes. Anatomical Planes: Sagittal (left-to-right), Transverse (top-to-bottom), Coronal (front-to-back). Originating from early volume visualization systems, plane-based clipping has evolved to support interactive VR interfaces and hardware-accelerated fragment shader clipping. It is widely used in medical imaging for viewing specific anatomical planes and in scientific visualization for exploring internal structures. name: Clipping plane for volume suppression
head: Clip Plane, Clipping Planes, Cropping Widget Planes, Cut Planes, Volume Cropping via Clipping Planes
body: Clipping plane for volume suppression is a technique that removes specific regions of a volume dataset to reveal interior structures or resolve occlusion, typically by defining one or more arbitrary planes. Unlike Cropping, which restricts visibility to a rectilinear slab using axis-aligned planes, clipping planes allow for arbitrary orientation and can define complex cutaway views or smooth transitions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset V (scalar or vector field), clipping plane definition (normal vector \mathbf{n} = (A, B, C) and distance parameter D from the origin, or two parallel planes for thickness), and optionally a falloff parameter D{\text{fallo}}. Output: Rendered image where voxels on the suppressed side of the plane have zero opacity, and voxels in the transition region have modified opacity. Data Structures: Clipping Plane: Defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n} = (A, B, C) and a distance parameter D from the origin. For a single plane, the implicit equation is Ax + By + Cz - D = 0. For a thick cut plane, two parallel planes are defined: Ax + By + Cz - D{\min} = 0 and Ax + By + Cz - D{\max} = 0, where D{\min} \neq D{\max}. The thickness is D{\max} - D{\min}. Widget State: In interactive systems, a frame-type widget reports the plane's orientation and position to the volume renderer. The widget can also query positions via mouse clicks on its surface. Steps: 1. Define Plane Geometry: For a 2D screen-based clipper, the plane is defined by the point of view (POV) and two user-selected screen points. Calculate the plane coefficients (A, B, C, D) from these three points. Alternatively, for a 3D widget, extract the normal and position from the widget's transformation matrix. 2. Calculate Signed Distance: For each voxel center \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z), calculate the signed distance D{\text{voxel}} to the plane: D{\text{voxel}} = \text{dot}(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{n}) - D where \mathbf{n} = (A, B, C) and D is the plane offset. For a thick cut plane, calculate distances to both D{\min} and D{\max}. 3. Determine Visibility and Opacity: Binary Suppression: If D{\text{voxel}} < 0 (or outside the slab defined by D{\min} and D{\max}), set opacity \alpha = 0. Smooth Transition: If a falloff parameter D{\text{fallo}} is specified: Outside the cut plane (suppressed side): \alpha = 0. In the transition region (width D{\text{fallo}}): Multiply the shading-stage opacity \alpha{\text{shade}} by a correction factor f that increases linearly from 0 to 1. In the interior (visible side): \alpha = \alpha{\text{shade}}. 4. Render: Render the clipped volume using a standard volume rendering algorithm (e.g., ray casting). Render the 3D plane widget in a second pass to visualize the clipping boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clipvolume(volume, planenormal, planeoffset, falloffwidth=0.0): # planenormal: (A, B, C), planeoffset: D clippedvolume = emptylike(volume) for voxel in volume: dist = dot(voxel.coords, planenormal) - planeoffset if dist < 0: clippedvolume[voxel] = 0.0 elif falloffwidth > 0 and dist < falloffwidth: factor = dist / falloffwidth clippedvolume[voxel] = voxel.opacity factor else: clippedvolume[voxel] = voxel.opacity return clippedvolume Parameters: D{\text{fallo}}: Width of the transition region from full opacity to none. Typical value: 5 voxels. Single vs. Multiple Planes: Most systems support a single clipping plane as a compromise between flexibility and usability. VolumePro supports a single cut plane. SFP renderer supports up to 6 cutting planes simultaneously. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Capping Geometry: In complex scenarios involving both polygonal geometry and volume data, clipped volume data always contains data inside the clipped region, whereas clipped polygonal objects may be empty. Medical applications often expect intersected 3D geometry to be capped. Orientation Perception: Users may find it confusing to perceive volume orientation and clipping plane location without additional cues like bounding boxes or stippled lines. Coordinate Systems: Some implementations use normalized coordinates (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) with the volume box center at (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) rather than world-space coordinates. This method enables interactive, selective suppression of volume datasets using an axis-aligned Clipping Cube and an arbitrary Cutting Plane, implemented via client-side widgets controlling server-side RTVR clipping capabilities. It distinguishes itself from standard polygon clipping by supporting non-uniform cube resizing via corner spheres and rendering the context region outside the cube as non-photorealistic contours rather than transparent geometry. Virtual Resection is a technique for selectively suppressing portions of a volume dataset to resolve occlusion problems, particularly in medical imaging where internal structures (e.g., pulmonary nodules) are hidden by surrounding tissue (e.g., lung parenchyma). It generates a deformable clipping plane or mask from user-defined resection lines on the organ's surface, allowing the user to cut away specific regions while preserving the texture of the remaining surface. Unlike standard clipping planes that cut the entire volume uniformly, this method enables complex, arbitrary-shaped cutaways centered on regions of interest. Cuts the sample after it has been played for x ticks. An interaction mode where a clipping plane slice is textured with map coordinates to help users understand the relationship between spatial and TF domains. The user rotates and translates the volume and places a clipping plane. Voxels on the clipping plane are sampled, and their map coordinates are mapped to color channels (e.g., x,y to Red,Green for Kohonen maps; x,y,z to RGB for Spherical maps). The textured slice is blended with the rendered volume using user-controlled opacity. The user can click on the clipping plane to set the Gaussian TF peak to the map coordinates of the pointed voxel, with a white cross displayed in the map representation corresponding to the mouse position. A visualization technique for superimposed anatomical and physiological data, displaying physiological data only within a known region of interest (e.g., inside the lung) and on a user-controlled cutting plane surface. The steps are: 1. Identify the region of interest. 2. Display physiological data only within this region. 3. Render the data as grey-scale on the surface exposed by the user-controlled cutting plane. Applying clipping planes to Maximum Intensity Projection of a Head CT dataset to extract interesting features by slicing the volume. The volume is clipped in half by removing half the face with a vertical plane. This highlights regions of interest unable to be captured in the original visualization without clipping. A depth-based clipping approach analyzing depth information of the cutting geometry to decide which part of the volume to clip. A method allowing the user to modify the appearance of elements in the clipped region via a rigging system defining how the cutaway affects each structure. A feature allowing the user to cut the volume layer by layer, excluding internal parts from being cut. Virtual planes that cut away parts of the image to allow viewing inside the object. Up to 6 cutting planes can be added simultaneously, and each cutting plane can be placed in an arbitrary position and orientation. A visualization method for scalar fields that renders a 2D slice of the data at a user-specified position, represented by a mesh in a symbolic box. A visualization method where the user holds and moves a small rectangle plane in the CAVE room. The plane color shows the distribution of a selected scalar field on the slice. It follows wand motion. Steps: 1. User selects 'Orthoslicer' and presses wand button, causing a box-shaped object symbolizing the data space to appear. 2. A mesh inside the box designates the current slice position. 3. User moves the wand in the desired direction while pressing the button; the mesh moves in accord with the wand motion. 4. When the button is released, render the scalar data distribution at the specified slice position. Mode 1: The normal vector of the plane is always perpendicular to the wand direction. Mode 2: The normal vector of the plane is always perpendicular to a specified vector field. Pitfall: Near a 'hot spot' where vector and scalar fields change sharply, the plane exhibits dynamic motion as the user slowly moves the wand around it. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels or samples, as each sample must be tested against the plane equation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for plane coefficients, plus storage for the volume dataset. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable on modern GPUs using fragment shaders for distance calculation and opacity masking. VolumePro supports real-time ray-casting with a single cut plane. Strengths: Supports smooth transitions for better visual integration. Limitations: Single plane limits complex cutaway shapes unless combined with other techniques; binary suppression can create harsh edges without falloff. When to Use: When the user needs to remove bulk tissue or outer structures to see embedded details (e.g., chest wall removal for injection site visualization). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The VolumePro system, developed in the late 1990s, introduced a single cut plane with smooth falloff capabilities. The X3D standard has supported clipping planes for volumetric data since version 3.2, though it notes ambiguities in capping intersected geometry. Interactive systems like Simian introduced frame-type widgets for clipping plane manipulation, allowing users to query positions and blend slices. More recent approaches include depth-based clipping for cutaway views and spatial domain interactions for transfer function design. name: Virtual Resection
head: Deformable Clipping Plane, Resection via Clipping Plane, Selective Volume Clipping, Selective Volume Clipping in Resection of Lung Cancer
body:
Virtual Resection is a technique for selectively suppressing portions of a volume dataset to resolve occlusion problems, particularly in medical imaging where internal structures (e.g., pulmonary nodules) are hidden by surrounding tissue (e.g., lung parenchyma). It generates a deformable clipping plane or mask from user-defined resection lines on the organ's surface, allowing the user to cut away specific regions while preserving the texture of the remaining surface. Unlike standard clipping planes that cut the entire volume uniformly, this method enables complex, arbitrary-shaped cutaways centered on regions of interest. The method operates in two distinct contexts found in the literature: a general deformable plane manipulation for anatomical models and a specific computational framework for lung nodule visualization. The implementation details below describe the framework, as it provides a complete algorithmic pipeline. Input: A 3D volume dataset V (e.g., chest CT images) containing scalar values f(x, y, z). Output: A volume rendering where voxels inside a user-defined closed curve (but outside the nodule) are suppressed, revealing internal structures. 1. Feature Space Histogram: A 2D histogram where the horizontal axis represents gray scale intensity and the vertical axis represents gradient magnitude 
abla f(x, y, z). 2. Voxel Set \PhiU: A set of voxels selected from the volume based on a region U in the feature space. 3. Stack H: A stack data structure used for connected component tracing. 4. Binary Mask Image: A 2D image with the same dimensions as the screen rendering window, representing the inside/outside status of the closed curve. The process involves segmentation, mask generation, and clipping. 1. Segment Lungs via 2D Feature Space: Define the 2D feature space with coordinates (g, 
abla g), where g is gray scale and 
abla g is gradient magnitude. Identify region R1 as homogeneous regions with low gray gradient, corresponding to lung tissue. Define the selection region U = R1. Determine the initial voxel set \PhiU using the condition that voxels satisfy the gray scale and gradient thresholds for U. 2. Extract Connected Lung Volume: Mark all voxels in \PhiU as not-visited. Select a not-visited voxel from \PhiU as a seed. Mark it visited and push it onto stack H. While H is not empty: 1. Pop a voxel v from H. 2. Check all voxels in the 18-neighborhood of v. 3. For each neighbor n: If n 
otin \PhiU or n is already visited, skip. If n \in \PhiU and not-visited, push n to H and mark n as visited. The result is the extracted connected lung volume. 3. Segment Pulmonary Nodules: Apply a region growing method to segment nodules from the lung tissue. 4. Generate Deformable Clipping Mask: Project voxels from the volume coordinate system onto the screen frame. The user draws discontinuous points on the screen around the region of interest (e.g., the nodule). Fit these points using a B-Spline to generate a closed curve. Create a binary mask image of the same size as the screen window. Voxels inside the closed curve are marked as inside, and those outside are marked as outside. 5. Selective Clipping: For each voxel in the volume: Project the voxel to the screen. If the voxel is inside the closed curve AND is part of the lung tissue (not the nodule), suppress it (clip it). Otherwise, retain it for rendering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def virtualresection(volume, screenwidth, screenheight): # Step 1: Segment Lungs via 2D Feature Space # Horizontal axis: gray scale, vertical axis: gradient magnitude # Region R1: homogeneous low gray gradient (lungs) # Voxel set PhiU determined by U = R1 PhiU = set() for x in range(volume.shape[0]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for z in range(volume.shape[2]): gray = volume[x, y, z] grad = computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z) if gray < thresholdgray and grad < thresholdgrad: # R1 definition PhiU.add((x, y, z)) # Step 2: Extract Connected Lung Volume visited = {v: False for v in PhiU} H = [] seed = next(iter(PhiU)) # Standard initialization visited[seed] = True H.append(seed) while H: v = H.pop() for n in get18neighbors(v): if n in PhiU and not visited[n]: visited[n] = True H.append(n) connectedlung = set(visited.keys()) # Step 3: Segment Pulmonary Nodules nodules = set() # Region growing method not detailed in sources # Apply region growing to separate nodules from lung tissue # Step 4: Generate Deformable Clipping Mask # Project volume voxels to screen frame # User draws discontinuous points on screen ROI userpoints = [] # Standard UI interaction # Fit B-Spline to generate closed curve closedcurve = [] # Standard spline fitting # Create binary mask image same size as screen window binarymask = createbinarymask(closedcurve, screenwidth, screenheight) # Standard rasterization # Step 5: Selective Clipping renderedvolume = [] for v in volume: sx, sy = projecttoscreen(v) # Standard projection inside = binarymask[sy][sx] islung = v in connectedlung isnodule = v in nodules if inside and islung and not isnodule: continue # Suppress voxel else: renderedvolume.append(v) # Retain for rendering return renderedvolume def computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z): # Standard central difference approximation dx = (volume[x+1, y, z] - volume[x-1, y, z]) / 2.0 dy = (volume[x, y+1, z] - volume[x, y-1, z]) / 2.0 dz = (volume[x, y, z+1] - volume[x, y, z-1]) / 2.0 return (dx2 + dy2 + dz2)0.5 def get18neighbors(v): # Returns 18-connected neighbors in 3D grid return [(v[0]+dx, v[1]+dy, v[2]+dz) for dx in [-1,0,1] for dy in [-1,0,1] for dz in [-1,0,1] if not (dx==0 and dy==0 and dz==0)] def createbinarymask(curve, width, height): # Standard point-in-polygon rasterization mask = [[False] width for in range(height)] # Rasterize closedcurve into mask return mask def projecttoscreen(v): # Standard volume-to-screen projection return (v[0], v[1]) 18-Neighbor Connectivity: The tracing algorithm uses 18-connectivity, which is specific to 3D voxel grids. Occlusion: The primary edge case addressed is the occlusion of nodules by lung tissue, which semi-transparent visualization fails to resolve due to loss of surface texture. B-Spline Fit: The sources do not specify the minimum number of points required for stability. Strengths: Solves the occlusion problem in chest CT images while preserving the texture of the pulmonary tongue on the lung surface, which is lost in semi-transparent visualization. Allows selective cutting layer by layer, excluding internal parts from being cut. Limitations: Requires initial segmentation of lungs and nodules, which adds computational overhead. The deformable plane is manipulated via mouse interaction, which may be less precise than parametric clipping planes for complex geometries. Performance: Not given in the sources. When to use: When visualizing internal structures (like nodules) hidden within a larger organ (like lungs) where surface texture preservation is critical. Virtual Resection was introduced by Konrad-Verse et al.. It is also referred to as Selective Volume Clipping in the context of lung cancer resection visualization. The method addresses the limitations of standard clipping planes and semi-transparent rendering in medical visualization. name: Selective Cutting
head: Selective Cutting Tool
body: Selective Cutting is an interaction method for volume visualization that allows users to remove volume data layer by layer, explicitly excluding internal parts from being cut. It builds on Clipping plane for volume suppression by providing a mechanism for sequential, non-destructive removal of outer layers to reveal internal structures, distinguishing it from standard clipping which typically suppresses data behind a plane without preserving the cutaway state for further layer-by-layer exploration. Inputs and outputs: The input is a volumetric dataset and user interaction commands (e.g., mouse clicks or gestures) defining the cut sequence. The output is a modified visualization where specified outer layers are removed or hidden, exposing inner volumes. Data structures: The volume data is stored as a 3D grid of voxels. A state mask or visibility buffer tracks which layers have been "cut" or removed. Numbered steps: 1. Initialize the volume visualization with the full dataset. 2. Receive user input indicating a desire to cut a specific outer layer. 3. Identify the voxels belonging to the current outermost visible layer. 4. Mark these voxels as removed or hidden in the visibility state. 5. Re-render the volume, excluding the marked voxels. 6. Repeat steps 2-5 to expose deeper layers. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectivecut(volumedata, usercutcommand): # volumedata: 3D array of voxel values # usercutcommand: specifies which layer to cut # Returns: updated visualization state # Get current visible layers visiblelayers = getvisiblelayers(volumedata) if not visiblelayers: return "No more layers to cut" # Identify the outermost layer based on user command layertocut = identifylayer(visiblelayers, usercutcommand) # Remove voxels in this layer from visibility for voxel in layertocut: voxel.visible = False # Re-render with updated visibility rendervolume(volumedata) The hand-rail cut gesture is a whole-hand interaction technique that partitions volume data along a plane defined by the orientation and movement direction of the user's hand rail. It builds on Selective Cutting by allowing the user to cut the volume layer by layer, excluding internal parts from being cut. It sets itself apart from standard clipping by treating the cut as a physical incision via a sliding hand motion, providing immediate visual feedback through a drawn line. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Allows for sequential exploration of internal structures without losing outer context if implemented with undo, but may be computationally expensive if re-rendering is frequent. When to use it and when not: Use when exploring internal anatomy or structures layer by layer. Not suitable for real-time applications requiring rapid, arbitrary clipping. Origin: The concept is described in the context of anatomical atlases and volume visualization interaction techniques. History and development: It is mentioned as an interesting feature in approaches using cutting planes for visualizing inner parts of anatomical datasets. Where it is used: Primarily in medical visualization and anatomical atlases for exploring internal structures. name: Hand-rail cut gesture
body: The hand-rail cut gesture is a whole-hand interaction technique that partitions volume data along a plane defined by the orientation and movement direction of the user's hand rail. It builds on Selective Cutting by allowing the user to cut the volume layer by layer, excluding internal parts from being cut. It sets itself apart from standard clipping by treating the cut as a physical incision via a sliding hand motion, providing immediate visual feedback through a drawn line. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D touch coordinates of the hand rail (defined by the user's hand orientation and sliding trajectory) on a tabletop surface. Output: A partitioned volume object, split into separate pieces along the detected cutting plane. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. The interface maintains a list of volume pieces. When a cut is applied, the first intersected piece is split, and the resulting sub-pieces are added to the list. Steps: 1. The user touches the tabletop surface with a hand, forming a "hand rail" (defined by the orientation of the hand). 2. The user slides the hand rail over the surface. The interface detects the orientation and movement direction of the hand rail. 3. The interface draws a red line on the surface as visual feedback, indicating the detected cutting direction. 4. The user lifts their hand. 5. The volume object is partitioned according to the plane defined by the red line. 6. Successive cuts can be applied by repeating steps 1-5, adding additional cutting planes. Pitfalls: If a cut trajectory crosses multiple existing volume pieces, only the first piece crossed is partitioned. This is done to prevent unintentional cuts of deeper layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def handlehandrailcut(handtrajectory, volumepieces): """ Handles the hand-rail cut gesture. Args: handtrajectory: List of (x, y) points representing the sliding hand rail. volumepieces: List of volume objects currently in the scene. Returns: Updated list of volume pieces. """ if not handtrajectory: return volumepieces # Step 2 & 3: Detect direction and draw feedback # The orientation and movement of the hand rail suggest the incision direction. # The interface draws a red line as visual feedback. cutline = computecutlinefromtrajectory(handtrajectory) drawredline(cutline) # Step 4: User lifts hand (triggered by end of trajectory or explicit lift event) # Step 5: Partition the volume newpieces = [] cutapplied = False for piece in volumepieces: # Check if the cut line intersects the piece if intersects(piece, cutline): # Step 6: Partition only the first piece crossed # To avoid unintentional cuts of deeper layers if not cutapplied: # Split the piece along the cut plane p1, p2 = splitvolumealongplane(piece, cutline) newpieces.append(p1) newpieces.append(p2) cutapplied = True else: # Subsequent pieces are not cut newpieces.append(piece) else: newpieces.append(piece) return newpieces A gesture allowing simultaneous use of two hand rails to create a 'V'-shaped cut, centering on internal structure while retaining surroundings. It is chosen when the user wants to focus on internal details while keeping context visible, a style often appearing in exploded-view visualization. The cut locations are directly defined by hand positions, allowing flexible control over the angular opening. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The complexity depends on the volume representation (e.g., voxel grid, octree) and the intersection testing algorithm. Splitting a volume piece likely involves traversing the data structure and duplicating or reassigning data points. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Natural interaction mimicking a surgical knife; immediate visual feedback; allows for layer-by-layer exploration. Limitations: Only cuts the first intersected piece, which may limit complex multi-layer cuts in a single gesture; requires precise hand tracking for accurate cut placement. When to Use: Use when the user needs to inspect internal structures of a volume by removing outer layers sequentially. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The hand-rail cut gesture was proposed in the paper "Exploring Volume Visualization with Whole-hand Multitouch Gestures". It is part of a whole-hand multitouch interface designed for tabletop surfaces. The gesture is inspired by the natural motion of a surgical knife. It is used in conjunction with other gestures such as the open palm gesture (to nullify cuts) and the hand-rail explode gesture (to create exploded views). name: Hand-rail explode gesture
head: hand-rail explode, sideways hand-rail movement
body: The hand-rail explode gesture creates and manipulates exploded views of volume data by moving the interaction rail sideways, perpendicular to a previously defined cutting plane. It builds on Hand-rail cut gesture by transforming a static partition into a separated view, allowing users to inspect internal structures without occlusion. Unlike standard clipping which merely hides data, this gesture actively displaces the partitioned volume portion along a rotational axis determined by the user's movement direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current hand rail position and orientation; hand movement direction vector \hat{d}{move}; existing cut planes (e.g., from Hand-rail cut gesture or bimanual 'V'-shape cuts); optional density range selection for threshold-based segmentation. Output: Transformed volume visualization where partitioned portions are rotated or translated to form an exploded view. Data Structures: Cut State: Stores the geometry of active cutting planes (normal vectors, distances) and the resulting partitioned volume subsets. Explode State: Stores the current rotation or translation offset applied to each partitioned subset. Density Range: A pair of scalar values defining the lower and upper bounds of voxel density to be preserved during the explode operation. Steps: 1. Prerequisite: Perform a cut gesture (e.g., Hand-rail cut gesture) to partition the volume data. 2. Detect Movement: Track the hand rail's movement direction \hat{d}{move} in 3D space. 3. Determine Explosion Axis: Identify all valid rotational axes available for exploding the current partitioned volume (e.g., axes perpendicular to cut plane normals). Project each candidate rotational axis onto the 2D screen plane. Select the rotational axis whose 2D screen projection is most perpendicular to the hand movement direction \hat{d}{move}. Note: If bimanual input is used, apply this logic independently for each hand to create complex exploded views (e.g., opening a curtain). 4. Apply Transformation: Rotate the partitioned volume portion around the selected axis based on the magnitude of the hand movement. Alternative (Parallel-plane exploding): Instead of rotation, apply a translation gesture (e.g., five-finger pan) to the partitioned volume to explode its internal structures. 5. Threshold Filtering (Optional): If a density range is specified, only voxels outside the selected density range are affected by the cut/exploding transformation; voxels within the range remain untouched. Formulas: Let \vec{a}i be the i-th candidate rotational axis. Let \vec{p}i be the 2D screen projection of \vec{a}i. Let \hat{d}{move} be the normalized hand movement direction. Select axis k such that: k = \arg \mini | \vec{p}i \cdot \hat{d}{move} | (Minimizing the dot product maximizes perpendicularity). Parameters: Explode Magnitude: Proportional to the distance the hand rail moves sideways. Density Range: User-defined via a double-ended slider on the interface panel before or during the gesture. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ambiguous Directions: In complex cuts (e.g., 'V'-shape), multiple explosion directions may be possible. The perpendicularity rule resolves this. Precision: Screen projection accuracy depends on camera orientation and resolution. Boundary Conditions: If the hand movement is parallel to all candidate axes' projections, the selection may be unstable. A variant that creates exploded views by applying translation to partitioned volume portions instead of 3D rotation. It is chosen when linear separation is preferred over rotational opening. Implementation involves cutting the volume and then applying a five-finger pan translation gesture on the partitioned volume to explode its internal structures. It can also follow a 'V'-shape cut. Time Complexity: O(1) for axis selection (assuming fixed number of cut planes); O(N) for transforming N voxels in the partitioned subset. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the transformed voxel positions or transformation matrices. Performance: Real-time interaction is feasible on modern GPUs for typical volume resolutions. Strengths: Intuitive mapping of hand movement to volume separation; supports bimanual interaction for complex views; integrates with threshold-based segmentation. Limitations: Requires prior cutting; explosion direction is constrained by screen projection geometry. When to Use: When users need to inspect internal structures of a partitioned volume without removing data. When Not to Use: When the volume is not yet partitioned or when rotational separation is not desired. Originated in the research on whole-hand multitouch gestures for volume visualization. The technique was developed to provide an easy reversal of actions and flexible exploration of volume data on tabletop interfaces. It is used in interactive volume visualization systems that support bimanual input and threshold-based segmentation. Exploring Volume Visualization with Whole-hand Multitouch Gestures, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe.pg.pg2013short.007-010, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic Clipping in Volume Rendering
head: Clipping in Volume Rendering, Dynamic Clipping Planes Setup
body: Dynamic Clipping in Volume Rendering allows users to visualize the interior of a volume dataset by interactively resizing its bounding box via controller movement or widget manipulation. It solves the problem of revealing internal structures without requiring the user to be physically inside the volume or manually editing the dataset. It sets itself apart from static cropping by updating clipping planes based on user interaction, and from general view-frustum culling by allowing arbitrary plane orientations and offsets independent of the camera. It differs from Clipping plane for volume suppression and Clipping Plane Rendering by focusing on dynamic bounding-box interaction rather than static masks or surface-level rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (e.g., VTI, DICOM series) with an associated index-to-world transformation matrix. User interaction input (e.g., VR controller position, mouse/keyboard for clipping plane adjustment). Output: A rendered volume image where voxels outside the dynamically defined clipping box are excluded from the rendering pipeline. Data Structures: Clipping Planes: Six planes defining an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in world space. Each plane is defined by an origin point \mathbf{o} and a normal vector \mathbf{n}. Index-to-World Transform: A 4 \times 4 matrix M{iw} mapping voxel indices (i, j, k) to world coordinates. Rotation Matrix: A 3 \times 3 rotation matrix R extracted from M{iw}, used to transform axis-aligned normals to world space. Steps: 1. Initialize Rendering Pipeline: Load the volume dataset. Initialize the volume mapper and actor. Configure transfer functions (Color and Opacity). Set rendering properties (shading, interpolation, gradient opacity). Initialize the cropping widget or input handler. 2. Define Clipping Box in Index Space: The user defines a region of interest using six bounds in index space: [i{min}, i{max}, j{min}, j{max}, k{min}, k{max}]. Alternatively, in software implementations, these may be provided as clipmin and clipmax numpy arrays. In VR, the user selects a face of the bounding box and moves the controller to resize it. 3. Compute World-Space Planes: Extract the rotation matrix R from the image's index-to-world transformation matrix M{iw}: R = \text{Rotation}(M{iw}) Calculate the world-space origins for the minimum and maximum corners of the clipping box: \mathbf{o}{min} = M{iw} \cdot [i{min}, j{min}, k{min}, 1]^T \mathbf{o}{max} = M{iw} \cdot [i{max}, j{max}, k{max}, 1]^T Define the six axis-aligned normals in index space: \mathbf{n}{x+} = [1, 0, 0], \mathbf{n}{x-} = [-1, 0, 0] \mathbf{n}{y+} = [0, 1, 0], \mathbf{n}{y-} = [0, -1, 0] \mathbf{n}{z+} = [0, 0, 1], \mathbf{n}{z-} = [0, 0, -1] Transform normals to world space using R: \mathbf{n}{world} = R \cdot \mathbf{n}{index} Construct the six VTK-compatible planes (or equivalent graphics API planes): X-min: Origin \mathbf{o}{min}, Normal \mathbf{n}{x+}^{world} X-max: Origin \mathbf{o}{max}, Normal \mathbf{n}{x-}^{world} Y-min: Origin \mathbf{o}{min}, Normal \mathbf{n}{y+}^{world} Y-max: Origin \mathbf{o}{max}, Normal \mathbf{n}{y-}^{world} Z-min: Origin \mathbf{o}{min}, Normal \mathbf{n}{z+}^{world} Z-max: Origin \mathbf{o}{max}, Normal \mathbf{n}{z-}^{world} 4. Apply Clipping Planes to Mapper: Remove any existing clipping planes from the volume mapper. Add the six new world-space clipping planes to the mapper. Mark the mapper as modified to trigger a pipeline update. 5. Fragment Shader Clipping (Hardware-Accelerated Variant): If using hardware clip planes for particle-based volume rendering, position them to discard non-contributing particles. In the fragment program, during density computation, check if the sampling position \mathbf{p} is outside the cut planes. If \mathbf{p} is outside, set the computed density to zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractrotationmatrix(matrix4x4): """Extracts the upper-left 3x3 rotation matrix from a 4x4 transformation matrix.""" return [ [matrix4x4[0][0], matrix4x4[0][1], matrix4x4[0][2]], [matrix4x4[1][0], matrix4x4[1][1], matrix4x4[1][2]], [matrix4x4[2][0], matrix4x4[2][1], matrix4x4[2][2]] ] def updateclippingplanes(volumedata, cropstate, mapper): """ Updates the volume mapper's clipping planes based on the current crop state. Args: volumedata: Object containing index-to-world transformation matrix. cropstate: Object containing ijk plane bounds [iMin, iMax, jMin, jMax, kMin, kMax]. mapper: The volume mapper object with addClippingPlane and removeAllClippingPlanes methods. """ # 1. Get rotation matrix from index-to-world transform indextoworldmatrix = volumedata.getIndexToWorld() rotationmatrix = extractrotationmatrix(indextoworldmatrix) # 2. Extract bounds from crop state iMin, iMax, jMin, jMax, kMin, kMax = cropstate.getPlanes() # 3. Compute world-space origins for min and max corners originmin = volumedata.indexToWorld([iMin, jMin, kMin]) originmax = volumedata.indexToWorld([iMax, jMax, kMax]) # 4. Helper to rotate a vector def rotatevector(vec): return [ rotationmatrix[0][0]vec[0] + rotationmatrix[0][1]vec[1] + rotationmatrix[0][2]vec[2], rotationmatrix[1][0]vec[0] + rotationmatrix[1][1]vec[1] + rotationmatrix[1][2]vec[2], rotationmatrix[2][0]vec[0] + rotationmatrix[2][1]vec[1] + rotationmatrix[2][2]vec[2] ] # 5. Define axis-aligned normals in index space normalsindex = [ [1, 0, 0], [-1, 0, 0], # X [0, 1, 0], [0, -1, 0], # Y [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, -1] # Z ] # 6. Transform normals to world space normalsworld = [rotatevector(n) for n in normalsindex] # 7. Construct planes # Order: X min, X max, Y min, Y max, Z min, Z max planes = [ {'origin': originmin, 'normal': normalsworld[0]}, # X min {'origin': originmax, 'normal': normalsworld[1]}, # X max {'origin': originmin, 'normal': normalsworld[2]}, # Y min {'origin': originmax, 'normal': normalsworld[3]}, # Y max {'origin': originmin, 'normal': normalsworld[4]}, # Z min {'origin': originmax, 'normal': normalsworld[5]} # Z max ] # 8. Apply to mapper mapper.removeAllClippingPlanes() for plane in planes: mapper.addClippingPlane(plane) mapper.modified() Parameters: sampleDistance: Controls the sampling rate along the ray. Typical value: 1.0. scalarOpacityUnitDistance: Distance between samples for opacity calculation. Typical value: 3.0. clipmin: Minimum corner of the clipping box in normalized or index space. Default: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]. clipmax: Maximum corner of the clipping box. Default: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0]. gradientOpacityMinimumValue: Minimum gradient magnitude for opacity. Typical value: 2. gradientOpacityMaximumValue: Maximum gradient magnitude for opacity. Typical value: 20 or 30. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Clipping Artifacts: Using hardware clip planes for particle-based rendering can result in no sharp cuts because the kernel is evaluated for the complete particle footprints, and the missing contribution of clipped particles leads to wrong density results. To achieve correct volumetric clipping, clipping must be performed in the fragment program by setting density to zero if the sampling position is outside the cut planes. Axis Threshold Clipping is a dynamic clipping method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that discards Gaussians whose projected screen-space bounding quad exceeds a maximum axis length threshold \tau\lambda. It solves the performance bottleneck of processing large, distant Gaussians that fall outside the view frustum but have significant screen-space extent, specifically targeting mobile hardware constraints. It differs from sibling dynamic clipping techniques by using a simple axis-aligned bound check on the projected quad rather than complex frustum intersection tests. Clipping volumes restrict rendering to a specific region of space defined by a set of planar half-spaces, allowing internal structures to be revealed by discarding geometry outside the defined volume. Unlike static cropping masks, this method constructs a dynamic volume (up to 6 planes) that can be combined via intersection or union logic, functioning as a simple Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) expression. This method provides a rendering framework that integrates 3D widgets with volume clipping and volume rendering to enable immersive exploration and quantitative measurement (area, distance, angle) of 3D medical images. It solves the problem that standard volume rendering algorithms (ray casting, splatting, shear warp) produce only a 2D projection image without intermediate depth information, making it difficult to correctly display clipping planes and widgets in 3D space alongside the volume. It sets itself apart from siblings like Axis Threshold Clipping and Clipping Volumes by explicitly reconstructing depth information from the 2D projection to allow correct occlusion handling between the rendered volume and interactive 3D widgets. Interactive Box Clipping is a method for dynamically restricting volume rendering to a specific 3D region using a manipulable bounding box widget. It solves the problem of isolating anatomical or structural features within a large volume dataset by generating six clipping planes from the widget's geometry and applying them to the volume mapper in real-time. It differs from Axis Threshold Clipping by allowing arbitrary orientation and position of the clipping region, and from Clipping Volumes by providing a direct, interactive widget-based interface rather than static parameter adjustment. This variant uses hardware clip planes to cut away parts of the volume in image-space ray casting. However, it suffers from artifacts: using hardware clip planes results in no sharp cuts because the kernel is evaluated for the complete particle footprints, and the missing contribution of clipped particles leads to wrong density results. To achieve correct volumetric clipping, the clipping check must be performed in the fragment program during density computation, setting the density to zero if the sampling position is outside the cut planes. Voxel Value Masking for Scissors Cropping is a technique to crop volume rendering to irregular or concave shapes by modifying the input voxel data (texture) before rendering, rather than using geometric clipping or double-pass rendering. It generates a geometry representing the region of interest, tests every voxel's spatial position against it, packs updated voxel values into a new texture, and performs regular volume rendering on the modified texture. This approach is considered more robust than double-pass volume rendering with irregular mesh shapes, though it is slower with a 2-3 second delay considered acceptable. Time Complexity: The cost of updating clipping planes is O(1) relative to the volume size, as it involves transforming six planes and updating the mapper state. The rendering cost depends on the volume rendering algorithm, but clipping reduces the number of samples per ray, potentially improving performance. Memory Complexity: O(1) for storing the clipping planes. Measured Performance: In particle-based simulations with ~250,000 particles, hardware clipping can maintain constant frame rates for low particle numbers, but performance may degrade due to memory bandwidth if additional values (like gradients) are written or read for each density slice. Strengths: Intuitive interaction for revealing interior structures. Limitations: Hardware clipping can introduce artifacts in particle-based rendering if not handled in the shader. Requires accurate index-to-world transformation. When to Use: When users need to inspect internal structures of a volume without moving the camera or dataset. When interactive exploration is required. When Not to Use: When using hardware clip planes alone for particle-based data, as it causes artifacts; use fragment shader clipping instead. Dynamic Clipping in Volume Rendering originated from the need to inspect complex volume datasets in immersive environments, such as Virtual Reality (VR). It was developed to provide an intuitive way for users to crop the volume dataset by resizing its bounding box using VR controllers. The technique is widely implemented in visualization libraries like VTK and VTK.js, often using widgets like vtkImageCroppingWidget. It is commonly used in medical imaging to reveal internal structures of organs or tissues.
