name: Focus+Context Visualization via Deformation
head: Feature Magnification, Interactive Deformation System
body: Focus+Context Visualization via Deformation is an interactive technique that magnifies regions of interest within a high-resolution volume dataset while shrinking less important regions to fit within the original volume boundary. It solves the problem of inspecting detailed features on low-resolution displays by leveraging color gradient magnitudes derived from the user-specified transfer function to determine importance. Unlike binary focus/context methods or explicit lens-based techniques, this method provides continuous, varying extents of magnification for entire features without requiring explicit feature specification. The method computes a deformation field that maps the original voxel grid to a deformed grid, optimizing for feature preservation and minimal distortion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: High-resolution volume dataset V, user-specified transfer function T, initial scaling factor s (typically > 1.0). Output: Deformed volume dataset V' rendered within the original bounding box. Data Structures: The volume is discretized into a 3D grid of space cubes. Each cube C{i,j,k} is associated with an importance value w{i,j,k}. The deformation is defined by a displacement vector \mathbf{d}{i,j,k} for each grid vertex or cube center. The system maintains a sparse linear system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}, where \mathbf{x} contains the unknown deformation parameters (e.g., vertex displacements). Steps: 1. Compute Importance Values: For each space cube C{i,j,k}, compute the importance value w{i,j,k} based on the magnitude of the color gradient in the transfer function output. High importance is assigned to cubes covering features, identified by sharp color boundaries. w{i,j,k} = \| \nabla T(V{i,j,k}) \| Where \nabla T is the gradient of the transfer function applied to the scalar data. 2. Construct Linear System: Formulate a linear system to solve for the deformation field. The system minimizes a distortion energy function \Psi subject to boundary constraints. High-weight regions are constrained to expand (magnify). Low-weight regions are constrained to compress (shrink). Continuity constraints are applied between neighboring cubes to prevent smoothing artifacts. 3. Solve Deformation Field: Solve the linear system A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} for the deformation parameters \mathbf{x}. Due to the frequent changes in the matrix A (as the transfer function or scaling factor changes), a direct solver like Cholesky is inefficient. Instead, use an iterative solver such as the Conjugate Gradient method, potentially accelerated by GPU computation, to achieve real-time performance. 4. Apply Deformation and Render: Map the original volume data to the deformed grid using the computed displacement field. Render the deformed volume. The user can interactively adjust the scaling factor s to control the degree of magnification. Parameters: Scaling Factor (s): An interactive operator value that adjusts the degree of magnification. Typically s > 1.0. Increasing s increases magnification until distortion \Psi increases rapidly, indicating that less important regions are fully squeezed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Edge Flipping: If s is increased too much, less important regions are squeezed dramatically, leading to edge flipping (inversion of geometry). Termination Condition: The system should stop increasing s when the distortion \Psi increases rapidly. This occurs when most less important regions are already well-squeezed, and no more space is available for features. Matrix Updates: The coefficient matrix A changes frequently with transfer function adjustments or edge flips. Using an expensive factorization step for every change is inefficient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def focuscontextdeformation(volumedata, transferfunction, initialscalingfactor): # Step 1: Compute Importance Values # Apply transfer function to scalar data to get color/opacity values tfoutput = [transferfunction(v) for v in volumedata] # Compute gradient magnitude of TF output using central differences importance = computegradientmagnitude3d(tfoutput, volumedata.shape) # Step 2: Construct Linear System dimx, dimy, dimz = volumedata.shape # Grid vertices are at cube corners: (dimx+1) x (dimy+1) x (dimz+1) numvertices = (dimx + 1) (dimy + 1) (dimz + 1) # Initialize displacement vectors for grid vertices displacements = [0.0] (numvertices 3) # High importance regions expand, low importance compress, with continuity constraints. # The exact matrix assembly algorithm is not provided in the sources. # A = assemblelinearsystem(importance, initialscalingfactor) # b = assemblerhsvector(importance, initialscalingfactor) # Step 3: Solve Deformation Field # Use Conjugate Gradient method for efficiency with changing matrices. # Standard iterative solver implementation # displacements = solveconjugategradient(A, b) # Step 4: Apply Deformation and Render # Map original volume data to deformed grid positions # deformedvolume = interpolatedeformedvolume(volumedata, displacements, transferfunction) return deformedvolume def computegradientmagnitude3d(values, shape): # Central difference approximation for gradient magnitude gradx = [values[i + 1] - values[i] for i in range(0, len(values) - 1, shape[1] shape[2])] grady = [values[i + shape[2]] - values[i] for i in range(0, len(values) - shape[2])] gradz = [values[i + shape[1] shape[2]] - values[i] for i in range(0, len(values) - shape[1] shape[2])] return [abs(gx) + abs(gy) + abs(gz) for gx, gy, gz in zip(gradx, grady, gradz)] Time Complexity: Solving the linear system dominates the computation. Using an iterative solver like Conjugate Gradient allows for real-time performance, especially with GPU acceleration. The matrix A must be rebuilt or updated frequently, making direct solvers like Cholesky inefficient. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, importance grid, and the sparse matrix A and vector \mathbf{b}. The sparse matrix size depends on the grid resolution and the number of constraints. Strengths: Allows varying extents of magnification. Magnifies whole features without explicit feature specification. Intuitive feature specification via transfer function color boundaries. Minimizes feature distortion. Limitations: Prone to edge flipping if scaling factor is too high. Requires careful tuning of the scaling factor. Distortion increases rapidly when less important regions are fully compressed. When to Use: When visualizing high-resolution volume data on low-resolution displays and the user needs to inspect specific features in context. Particularly useful for interior and non-regular features surrounded by homogeneous materials. When Not to Use: When explicit feature specification is preferred over automatic detection via transfer function gradients. When real-time performance is critical and GPU acceleration is not available due to iterative solver overhead. This method was introduced in the paper "Feature-Preserving Volume Data Reduction and Focus+Context Visualization" by C. Wang et al. (2011). It addresses limitations in previous focus+context techniques, such as the binary discrimination of focus/context regions in [33] and the need for explicit feature specification in lens-based techniques. The method leverages the fact that transfer functions typically provide sharp color boundaries around features, allowing for automatic importance assignment. name: Frustum Culling for Hierarchical Navigation
head: Context-aware Frustum Culling, Focus and Context with Interactive Filtering, Frustum Culling in Navigation, Interactive Filtering
body: Frustum Culling for Hierarchical Navigation is a focus-and-context technique designed to reduce visual clutter during the exploration of large, hierarchical datasets by culling nodes outside the current viewing frustum from the primary rendering window. It distinguishes itself from standard geometric culling by synchronizing the culling state with interactive selection mechanisms in coordinated 2D views (overview maps and treemaps), ensuring that culled data remains visible as contextual cues rather than disappearing entirely. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current Level of Detail (LOD) hierarchy, viewing frustum parameters, and 2D view states. Output: Rendered 3D window containing visible nodes; updated 2D views where culled nodes are greyed out and non-selectable. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify nodes in the current LOD that are outside the viewing frustum. 2. Cull these nodes from the rendering window (no squares drawn at their point locations). 3. Deactivate these nodes from selection. 4. Draw line segments through their point locations in the overview map to show the cut for context. 5. Fill their corresponding rectangle regions with grey colors in the treemap to provide context. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatehierarchicalnavigation(lodnodes, frustum, overviewmap, treemap): """ Updates rendering and 2D views based on frustum culling. Assumes frustum.intersects(boundingvolume) returns a boolean. Assumes overviewmap and treemap expose drawsquare, drawlinesegment, and drawrectangle. """ for node in lodnodes: isvisible = frustum.intersects(node.boundingvolume) if isvisible: render3dwindow.add(node.geometry) overviewmap.drawsquare(node.pointlocation) treemap.drawrectangle(node.rectangle, color=node.defaultcolor) else: overviewmap.drawlinesegment(node.pointlocation) treemap.drawrectangle(node.rectangle, color="grey") The view system methods (drawsquare, drawlinesegment, drawrectangle) and 3D window rendering are assumed to be provided by the parent interaction framework. Parameters: Context Color: Grey is used for rectangle regions of culled nodes in the treemap. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Precision: Nodes exactly on the frustum boundary should be treated as visible to prevent flickering during navigation. Selection Consistency: The selection state in the 2D views must strictly mirror the frustum culling state to prevent users from selecting data not visible in the 3D view. Interactive Filtering: The specific implementation of culling nodes based on the viewing frustum and updating 2D views accordingly. It sets itself apart by keeping contextual lines and greyed-out regions rather than hiding data completely. Choose this when maintaining orientation during hierarchical navigation is more important than maximizing the detail of the visible subset. Interactive Filtering Direct Transformation: A complementary technique allowing users to translate, scale, and rotate the 3D volume and 2D maps. It sets itself apart by providing the user input mechanism that drives the frustum changes. Choose this when fine-grained control over the view is required. Direct Transformation Siblings: Cropping, 3D Cursor, Focus+Context Visualization via Deformation, Dynamic Focus+Context Framework, Depth-based Clipping for Focus and Context Volume Rendering, Selection and Manipulation, Hybrid Rendering for Stress Tensor Fields. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces visual clutter significantly during navigation; maintains user orientation by showing context in 2D views; prevents selection errors by deactivating culled nodes. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When navigating large hierarchical datasets where visual clutter obscures the current focus. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This technique originates from the "Hierarchical Navigation Interface" (HNI) presented by Wang et al. in 2005. It was developed to address the challenges of visualizing large and high-dimensional datasets, where focus-and-context techniques are employed to assist users in data exploration and Level of Detail (LOD) selection. The method integrates interactive filtering with coordinated 2D views (overview map and treemap) to provide a seamless navigation experience. name: Dynamic Focus+Context Framework
head: Dynamic Focus+Context Visualization Framework
body: The Dynamic Focus+Context Framework is a visualization system that enhances user interaction in volume rendering by dynamically adjusting the visual presentation based on real-time engagement metrics rather than pre-defined regions of interest. It distinguishes itself from static focus+context techniques (such as Cropping or Depth-based Clipping for Focus and Context Volume Rendering) by using an intermediate Engagement Estimation module to drive animation and rendering style changes, allowing for continuous, context-aware navigation. The framework operates as a four-stage pipeline where user input is transformed into visual feedback through an intermediate estimation of user intent. The core mechanism relies on decoupling raw interaction from rendering output via an animation module that modulates style parameters. 1. Interaction Module: Captures raw user inputs (cursor position, button events) and translates them into geometric transformations. It supports rotation, panning, and zooming. Rotation and panning are based on a trackball metaphor. For zooming, it employs a shift of the object's center of interest based on the initial click position, modifying the model-view matrix MV to MV' using a magnification factor R, the interaction point \vec{P}{interaction}, and the object center \vec{P}{center}. 2. Engagement Estimation Module: Analyzes the interaction stream to determine the type of engagement, its duration, and speed. This module predicts user intent without requiring explicit selection of regions. 3. Animation Module: Takes the engagement parameters and outputs style parameters, flags for cut-aways, and factors for rendering styles. It drives the dynamic transition between different visual representations. 4. Rendering Module: Applies the style parameters to generate the final image. It can switch between or blend rendering techniques such as Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) and Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), or apply radial opacity effects. Mathematically, the framework can be viewed as a function V = R(S(E(I(u)))), where u is user input, I is the interaction transformation, E is the engagement estimation, S is the style generation, and R is the rendering function. Interprets the manner of interaction (speed, duration) to trigger visual changes. Allows seamless transitions between visualization styles (e.g., from DVR to MIP) based on the animation module's output. The framework was introduced by Sikachev, Rautek, Bruckner, and Gröller in their paper "Dynamic Focus+Context for Volume Rendering". It builds upon earlier work in information visualization, such as Carpendale et al.'s techniques for distorting 3D layouts, and extends concepts from StyleCam by Burtnyk et al., which allowed for constrained camera movements. Unlike StyleCam, which focused on authoring constrained interactions, this framework focuses on animations during user interaction to enhance navigation in large 3D scenes without pre-defined regions. It is used in volume rendering to enhance user interaction without pre-defined regions. name: Selection and Manipulation
body: Selection and Manipulation enables users to identify specific subsets of volumetric data or graphical primitives for modification, highlighting, or analysis, and to interactively alter their geometric or visual properties. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Cropping and Clipping by focusing on semantic or spatial selection of data elements rather than global view frustum or plane-based visibility culling, allowing for targeted editing and complex interaction states. This method connects 1D visualization views with 3D volume rendering by using Hilbert space-filling curve codes to define selection ranges. It differs from standard spatial selection by mapping the selection criterion to a 1D range of Hilbert codes rather than a 3D bounding box, allowing for compact representation of non-contiguous spatial regions. Choose this when working with structured-regular or AMR data where 1D data views are available and efficient transmission of selection ranges is required. The 3D Widget Interaction Model provides a framework for creating interactive, scene-represented objects that users can directly manipulate to control visualization parameters or data processing pipelines. It distinguishes itself from siblings by decoupling interaction handling from camera control and associating a visual representation with the widget, allowing the widget's state to drive downstream data transformations via an event-driven observer pattern. Choose this when a robust, event-driven framework for creating and manipulating 3D graphical handles is needed. The Lock Tool is an interaction mechanism that specifies data points immune to modification by subsequent brush or dig tools, allowing users to protect specific data subsets during volumetric exploration. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Brushing and Linking with Hilbert Codes by operating on a binary visibility state (locked/unlocked) rather than continuous selection weights, and from the 3D Widget Interaction Model by focusing on data subset protection rather than geometric transformation. Choose this when isolating regions of interest from accidental modification or visual clutter during interactive volume rendering is required. Definition: An approach where users instantly highlight all splats that intersect with the brush during selection, contrasting with indirect approaches that compute intersections after brushing. Steps: Selection/deletion brushes may be either circular (screen space) or spherical (world space). Users may choose selections based on splat centers or their border. In case of circular brushes and splat-border intersection tests, apply an approximation that checks whether the center of the brush circle is inside an ellipse that is enlarged by the radius of the brush. Sort all splats by their deletion flag, putting the deleted splats towards the end of the buffer. Unmap and release physical allocations at the buffer's end in steps of the GPU's granularity. Pitfalls: Using radix sort is not required; developers may implement this functionality with GPU-friendly stream compaction. Definition: Integrated: Selection acts as fully belonging to the 3D scene. Movement depends on distance to origin; can move out of viewport or be occluded. Decoupled: Selection fully decoupled from scene. Independently manipulated, not affected by viewing transformation. Useful for fixed orientation. Pinned: Hybrid mode. Object pinned to current image space position. On-screen location static, but affected by rotations (same relative rotation as viewpoint). Definition: A selection technique where 3D objects are projected onto a 2D image plane, and a cursor defines a perpendicular ray to select the first intersected object. A selection technique where users select objects that visually lie behind a hand-attached cursor, defined by the vector joining the user's eye and hand. Steps: For stereoscopic displays, define the image plane as the viewpoint from only a single eye to create a one-eyed cursor. Aperture-based variant: Cast cone from eye through finger. Distance between finger and eye controls cone divergence angle. Use device orientation for disambiguation when multiple objects intersect. Head Crusher: Select objects lying between index finger and thumb. Sticky Finger: Select objects occluded by the tip of the index finger. Lifting Palm: Flatten hand and position palm underneath object to select it. Framing Hands: Use both hands to define a bounding box around object using thumbs and index fingers. The concepts of selection and manipulation in volume rendering and 3D visualization have evolved from simple ray-casting techniques to complex, state-aware interaction models. Early work on image plane selection and ray cursors established the foundation for 3D interaction. Direct selection techniques, particularly for emerging media like Gaussian Splatting, emphasize immediate visual feedback to enhance user experience in interactive editing tasks. The 3D Widget Interaction Model relies on the VTK command/observer pattern to bridge user input gestures with specific application logic. name: Brushing and Linking with Hilbert Codes
head: Brushing and Linking for DVL and 3D Views, Hilbert code selection
body: This method connects 1D visualization views with 3D volume rendering by using Hilbert space-filling curve codes to define selection ranges. When a user selects a Region of Interest (ROI) in the 1D plot, the corresponding cells in the 3D view are highlighted. It differs from standard spatial selection by mapping the selection criterion to a 1D range of Hilbert codes rather than a 3D bounding box, allowing for a compact representation of non-contiguous spatial regions. Inputs: A set of ROIs defined in the 1D view, each specified by a start and end Hilbert code (H{start}, H{end}). A 3D volume dataset (structured-regular or AMR). A transfer function T mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Outputs: Highlighted cells in the 3D view corresponding to the selected ROIs. Data Structures: ROI Range: A pair of integers (H{start}, H{end}) defining the selection interval. Steps: 1. User Selection: The user selects one or more ROIs in the 1D view, and the system records the first and last Hilbert codes of each selected ROI. 2. Shader Initialization: The 3D rendering shader receives the list of ROI ranges (H{start}, H{end}) as uniform variables. 3. Ray Casting: For each pixel, a ray is cast through the volume. At each sample point p along the ray: a. Coordinate to Hilbert Conversion: The 3D coordinates of the sample point p are transformed into its corresponding Hilbert code H(p). b. Containment Test: The shader checks if p falls within any active ROI range. For structured-regular volumes, this is a direct integer comparison H{start} \le H(p) \le H{end}. For AMR data, the cell centroid's Hilbert code is insufficient; the shader must explicitly locate the cell to verify that p lies within the ROI's exact bounds. c. Value Lookup: If contained, the scalar value at p is retrieved and passed to the transfer function T to determine color and opacity. 4. Compositing: Standard front-to-back compositing accumulates the sampled color and opacity values along the ray. Formulas: ROI Containment (Structured): A sample at position p is part of ROI k if: H{start}^{(k)} \le H(p) \le H{end}^{(k)} where H(p) is the Hilbert code of the cell containing p. Alpha Approximation (1D View): For the 1D plot, the alpha value for a ROI is approximated by: V\alpha = \max{m \in M} \left( \max{a \in [i, j]} A(m, a) - \min{a \in [i, j]} A(m, a) \right) where A denotes a lookup to the transfer function to retrieve the alpha value, [i, j] is the Hilbert code range, and M is the set of fields. Parameters: Hilbert Order: Determined by the resolution of the volume grid. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Structured-Regular Volumes: Cell bounds can be derived implicitly from the Hilbert code because cells are uniform in size. AMR Data: The Hilbert code of the cell centroid is insufficient to determine if a sample falls inside an ROI because cell sizes vary. The shader must explicitly locate cells to know the ROI's exact size when checking containment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastpixel(rayorigin, raydirection, roiranges, volumebounds, isamr, transferfunction): color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 step = 0.5 # Typical step size maxt = computemaxt(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) # Standard ray-volume intersection while t <= maxt: p = rayorigin + t raydirection hcode = computehilbertcode(p) # Maps 3D coord to Hilbert integer insideroi = False for hstart, hend in roiranges: if hstart <= hcode <= hend: if isamr: # For AMR, explicitly locate cell bounds to verify containment if pointincellbounds(p, hcode): # Standard AMR cell lookup insideroi = True break else: insideroi = True break if insideroi: scalar = volumedata.sample(p) rgba = transferfunction(scalar) color = ( color[0] + rgba[0] rgba[3] (1.0 - alpha), color[1] + rgba[1] rgba[3] (1.0 - alpha), color[2] + rgba[2] rgba[3] (1.0 - alpha), alpha + rgba[3] (1.0 - alpha)) if alpha >= 1.0: break t += step return color The GPU-accelerated implementation of Dynamic Volume Lines that uses this brushing and linking technique for real-time interaction with large AMR data. The process of mapping 3D voxel coordinates to 1D Hilbert codes. This is a prerequisite for the selection method. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The containment test is O(1) per sample per ROI range, and the overall complexity is dominated by the ray casting steps. Memory Complexity: The ROI ranges are stored as small lists of integers, making the memory footprint for selection data minimal. Performance: The method is efficient for GPU implementation using CUDA, as the compact representation of ROIs as Hilbert codes reduces memory bandwidth usage compared to storing lists of cell indices. Strengths: Compact representation of complex, non-contiguous ROIs; efficient GPU implementation; seamless integration between 1D and 3D views. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of Hilbert codes; AMR data requires explicit cell location for accurate containment testing, which may be more expensive than structured grids. This method was introduced in the context of visual analysis of large multi-field AMR data on GPUs using Interactive Volume Lines. It was presented at IEEE VIS 2023. The technique builds on the concept of Dynamic Volume Lines (DVL) and extends it to support 3D view interaction through Hilbert space-filling curves. name: RemoveInstancesOp
head: Instance Deletion with Undo, Ordered Instance Removal
body: RemoveInstancesOp is an interaction primitive that removes selected Gaussian instances from the live rendering list while preserving their underlying data to enable strict Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) undo operations. It differs from standard undo mechanisms by enforcing a rigid edit history where older operations cannot be undone until the current operation is reversed, ensuring that selection ranges remain meaningful for subsequent actions. The method operates on a list of Gaussian splats, managing their active state and history. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of instances with associated state flags (specifically State.selected and State.locked), and a selection range definition. Output: The modified instance list (with selected instances removed from the active set) and a history stack entry containing the removed instances for undo. Data Structures: instances: A dynamic list or array of Gaussian splats. flags: An array or bitmask parallel to instances, where flags[i] indicates the state of instance i. removed: A temporary storage buffer holding the instances removed in the current operation. ranges: A data structure defining the contiguous or scattered indices of selected instances. Steps: 1. Compute Selection Ranges: Iterate through the instance list to identify indices where the selection predicate is true. Predicate: flags[i] === State.selected. Constraint: Exclude instances where flags[i] === State.locked. Locked instances are immune to removal. 2. Execute Removal: Call the removal routine on the instance container: this.splat.instances.remove(this.ranges). Store the removed instances in the undo buffer: this.removed. Update the rendering state: updateState(). 3. Undo Operation: Restore instances: Call this.splat.instances.insert(this.removed). Clear the undo buffer: this.removed is cleared. Update the rendering state: updateState(). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class RemoveInstancesOp: def init(self, splatsystem): self.splat = splatsystem self.removed = [] def execute(self): # 1. Compute selection ranges # Identify indices where selected is true AND locked is false selectedindices = [] for i in range(len(self.splat.instances)): isselected = (self.splat.flags[i] == State.selected) islocked = (self.splat.flags[i] == State.locked) # Pitfall: Locked instances survive deletion if isselected and not islocked: selectedindices.append(i) # Convert indices to ranges if the underlying structure requires it ranges = self.indicestoranges(selectedindices) # 2. Execute removal # Remove instances from the live list self.removed = self.splat.instances.remove(ranges) # Update rendering state (e.g., rebuild acceleration structures) self.splat.updatestate() def undo(self): # 3. Undo operation if not self.removed: return # Insert previously removed instances back into the list self.splat.instances.insert(self.removed) # Clear the undo buffer self.removed = [] # Update rendering state self.splat.updatestate() def indicestoranges(self, indices): # Helper to convert a list of indices into contiguous ranges #: Standard algorithm to group consecutive integers if not indices: return [] ranges = [] start = indices[0] end = indices[0] for i in range(1, len(indices)): if indices[i] == end + 1: end = indices[i] else: ranges.append((start, end)) start = indices[i] end = indices[i] ranges.append((start, end)) return ranges Parameters: State.selected: Boolean flag indicating user selection. State.locked: Boolean flag preventing modification. Typical values: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Locked Instances: Instances marked as locked must be excluded from the removal range even if selected. LIFO Enforcement: The method strictly enforces LIFO order. Older operations remain blocked from undoing until the current operation is undone. In scenarios where instances do not have explicit bounding boxes, object removal is accomplished by reducing the density of points associated with the target instance to zero. This approach avoids the need for geometric bounding volume calculations, relying instead on attribute manipulation to effectively hide or remove the instance from the rendered scene. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of selected instances for range computation. Removal and insertion complexity depends on the underlying data structure of splat.instances (e.g., O(N) for array-based lists, O(1) for linked lists with pointers). Memory Complexity: O(K) where K is the number of removed instances, stored in this.removed for undo. Strengths: Strict LIFO undo history ensures predictable interaction behavior; locked instance protection prevents accidental data loss. Limitations: Relies on a specific state flag system; undo history is strictly linear and cannot branch. When to use: Interactive editing of Gaussian splat scenes where undo/redo fidelity is critical. When not to use: When non-LIFO undo is required or when instances lack a selectable state flag. The method originates from the supersplat project, an interactive Gaussian Splatting editor. It addresses the need for robust scene editing in neural rendering workflows, where users frequently need to remove specific instances (e.g., artifacts, unwanted objects) while maintaining the ability to reverse mistakes. The strict LIFO undo mechanism was designed to prevent the ambiguity that can arise when multiple overlapping selection operations are undone out of order. playcanvas/supersplat, https://github.com/playcanvas/supersplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Semantically-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Visual Scene Understanding: A Comprehensive Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-025-02663-5, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Ray-based Picking
head: Ray casting selection, View-ray picking
body: Ray-based picking determines user selection intent by casting a geometric ray from the camera viewpoint through the input device's position into the 3D scene. It solves the problem of mapping 2D screen interactions or 3D hand poses to specific volumetric or geometric entities. It is distinguished from siblings like Brushing and Linking with Hilbert Codes by its reliance on precise geometric intersection rather than spatial indexing, and from Object Manipulation by its focus on identification rather than transformation. The core mechanism involves three steps: ray generation, intersection testing, and selection resolution. 1. Ray Generation: A ray R(t) = O + tD is defined, where O is the origin and D is the direction vector. Standard Projection: For screen-based input, O is the eye position E, and D is the vector from E to the cursor position C on the image plane (D = C - E). Hand Tracking: For gesture-based input, O is the eye position E, and D is derived from hand features (e.g., fingertip F) such that D = F - E. 2. Intersection Testing: The ray is tested against scene geometry. For volume rendering, this often involves marching along the ray to sample data values or opacity. 3. Selection Resolution: The system identifies the target based on intersection properties. Common strategies include: First-Hit: Selecting the closest object to the camera. Opacity Threshold: Selecting objects where accumulated opacity exceeds a specific value. Maximum Data Value: Selecting the point with the highest scalar value along the ray. Image plane selection projects 3D objects onto a 2D plane, using a cursor to define a perpendicular ray. It extends desktop mouse interaction to 3D by relying on visual alignment rather than explicit 3D coordinates. Variants include stereoscopic "one-eyed" cursors to avoid depth ambiguity, aperture-based cones controlled by finger distance, and gesture-based volumes like "head crushers" or "sticky fingers". For aperture-based selection, if multiple objects intersect, disambiguation is performed by matching the device orientation to the object's normal. See Image Plane Selection. This method extends VTK's trackball camera to allow 3D coordinate picking via mouse clicks. It maps 2D screen events to 3D world coordinates by querying a vtkCellPicker against the default renderer. Unlike image-plane selection, it operates in 3D space but relies on VTK's internal picking logic, often fixing the pick depth at z=0 in normalized device coordinates. See 3D Cell Picking with Trackball Camera. A method tailored to medical data in DICOM format. It uses meta information to deduce intended anatomical parts (e.g., angiography \rightarrow vessels) and matches initial user-specified ray profile samples against the data curve along the viewing ray. Unlike WYSIWYP, it requires metadata and searches for features in the data rather than in the visible rendering (profile of accumulated opacity). A two-click method where the user clicks on the desired location from two different viewing directions. The picked position is the (fuzzy) intersection of the two viewing rays. It requires the desired location to be visible from both viewing directions, whereas WYSIWYP provides picking with only one mouse click from one viewing direction. Ray-based picking is a fundamental interaction technique in volume visualization. Early implementations used first-hit approaches, as seen in Voreen and Avizo. VTK and ParaView employ opacity threshold methods. More sophisticated techniques include contextual picking by Kohlmann et al., which uses DICOM metadata to match ray profiles to anatomical structures. Peng et al. proposed a two-click multi-view method for arbitrary data, which WYSIWYP improves upon by enabling single-click picking from one view. Unlike techniques targeting real geometric objects (e.g., Argelaguet and Andujar), volume picking must handle semi-transparent, occluded data. WYSIWYP: What You See Is What You Pick, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2012.292, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Image Plane Selection
head: one-eyed cursor
body: Image plane selection projects 3D objects onto a 2D image plane, where a cursor defines a perpendicular ray to select the first intersected object. It extends desktop mouse interaction to 3D environments by using visual alignment or specific hand configurations as the selection mechanism. Unlike direct 3D cursors that specify X, Y, and Z coordinates explicitly, this method relies on the user's input device visually overlapping the target. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: User hand position or orientation (tracked via gloves, optical sensors, or head-tracking), camera viewpoint (eye position), and 3D scene geometry. Outputs: A selected object or set of objects identified by intersection with the selection ray or volume. Data Structures: Hand Pose: Vector H representing the position of the relevant hand feature (e.g., fingertip, palm center). Eye Position: Vector E representing the user's eye position. Scene Geometry: List of 3D primitives or volume data. Steps: 1. Define Selection Ray/Volume: Standard Image Plane: Define a ray R(t) = E + t(C - E), where E is the eye position and C is the cursor position on the image plane. One-Eyed Cursor (Stereoscopic): For stereoscopic displays, define the image plane as the viewpoint from only a single eye to create a "one-eyed cursor". Aperture-Based: Cast a cone from the eye E through the user's finger, where the distance between the finger and the eye controls the cone's divergence angle. Head Crusher: Define a selection volume between the index finger and thumb. Sticky Finger: Define a ray from the eye E through the tip of the index finger. Lifting Palm: Define a plane or volume underneath the flattened palm. Framing Hands: Use both hands to define a bounding box around the object using thumbs and index fingers. Icon Wall: Use a virtual laser pointer from the hand to a point on the projection screen plane. 2. Intersection Test: Cast the ray or test the volume against the 3D scene geometry. For Ray Cursor (Laser Gun): The first object intersected by the ray is selected. For Occlusion Selection: Objects visually lying behind the hand-attached cursor are selected. For Aperture-Based: If the ray intersects multiple objects, use device orientation for disambiguation by selecting the object whose orientation is most closely matched by the input device. 3. Selection Confirmation: Click or gesture confirmation selects the identified object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectobject(handpose, eyeposition, sceneobjects, technique="standard"): origin = eyeposition if technique in ("aperture", "stickyfinger"): direction = handpose['fingertip'] - origin else: cursor = handpose.get('cursor', handpose['fingertip']) direction = cursor - origin direction = direction / norm(direction) intersections = [] for obj in sceneobjects: t = intersectrayobject(origin, direction, obj) if t is not None and t > 0: intersections.append((t, obj)) intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) if not intersections: return None if len(intersections) > 1 and technique == "aperture": bestobject = None bestscore = -float('inf') for t, obj in intersections: score = dot(normalize(obj.normal), handpose['orientation']) if score > bestscore: bestscore = score bestobject = obj return bestobject return intersections[0][1] def intersectrayobject(origin, direction, obj): # Standard ray-AABB intersection test tmin = max((obj.bboxmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) tmax = min((obj.bboxmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('-inf') for i in range(3)) thit = max(tmin) if thit <= min(tmax) and thit > 0: return thit return None Parameters: Cone Divergence Angle: Controlled by the distance between the finger and the eye. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Intersections: In aperture-based selection, multiple objects may intersect the ray, requiring orientation matching for disambiguation. Stereoscopic Ambiguity: Without the one-eyed cursor technique, stereoscopic displays may lack a well-defined image plane, leading to selection errors. Occlusion: Users must visually align the cursor with the target, which can be difficult in cluttered scenes. Icons are drawn in the plane of the projection screen to allow both head-tracked and non-headtracked viewers to clearly view them at all times. Users interact with icons by pointing at them with a virtual laser pointer and clicking a button. Check boxes change state on click; dials are changed by clicking and twisting the hand. Strengths: Intuitive mapping from 2D desktop interaction; effective for 3D environments when combined with occlusion cues. Limitations: Requires precise hand tracking; ambiguous in cluttered scenes without disambiguation mechanisms. Originated from desktop mouse interaction, where objects are projected onto a 2D image plane. Extended to 3D displays by Ware and Lowther (1997) with the "one-eyed cursor" technique. Liang and Green (1994) implemented a "laser gun" selection mechanism. Forsberg et al. (1996) explored aperture-based selection. Pierce et al. (1997) explored several occlusion selection techniques including Head Crusher, Sticky Finger, Lifting Palm, and Framing Hands. name: 3D Cell Picking with Trackball Camera
head: VTK Trackball 3D Picking
body: An interaction method extending VTK's trackball camera to allow 3D coordinate picking via left mouse button click. It maps 2D screen events to 3D world coordinates by querying a vtkCellPicker against the default renderer, distinct from image-plane selection which operates strictly in 2D. Inputs and outputs: Input: 2D screen coordinates (x, y) from a left mouse button down event. Output: 3D world coordinates (X, Y, Z) and a formatted string representation. Data structures: mpnClickedPos: Array of two integers representing screen pixel coordinates. picker: Instance of vtkCellPicker. pos: Pointer to double array of size 3 containing world coordinates. Steps: 1. On OnLeftButtonDown, capture the 2D screen coordinates using the interactor's event position: \text{m\pnClickedPos} = \text{GetInteractor()->GetEventPosition()} 2. Instantiate vtkCellPicker and execute the pick at z=0 against the default renderer: \text{picker->Pick}(m\pnClickedPos[0], m\pnClickedPos[1], 0, \text{this->GetDefaultRenderer()}) 3. Retrieve the 3D world coordinates from the picker: \text{pos} = \text{picker->GetPickPosition()} 4. Format the coordinates to 2 decimal places and display in the window title: \text{str} = \text{Format}("%.2lf,%.2lf,%.2lf", \text{pos}[0], \text{pos}[1], \text{pos}[2]) \text{g\pMainDlg->SetWindowText(str)} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def onleftbuttondown(interactor, maindlg): # Step 1: Capture 2D screen coordinates clickedpos = interactor.geteventposition() x = clickedpos[0] y = clickedpos[1] # Step 2: Instantiate picker and execute pick # Note: z is fixed at 0, renderer is the default one picker = vtkcellpicker() picker.pick(x, y, 0, interactor.getdefaultrenderer()) # Step 3: Retrieve 3D world coordinates pos = picker.getpickposition() # pos is an array of 3 doubles: [X, Y, Z] # Step 4: Format and display # Format to 2 decimal places formattedstr = "%.2lf,%.2lf,%.2lf" % (pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) maindlg.setwindowtext(formattedstr) Parameters: z coordinate for pick: 0. Decimal precision: 2. Edge cases and pitfalls: The pick is performed at z=0 in normalized device coordinates or screen space depending on VTK's internal mapping, which may not correspond to the actual depth of the clicked object if the camera is not orthographic or if the object is far from the near plane. If no cell is picked, GetPickPosition() may return undefined or zero values; the source does not specify error handling for this case. A variant that uses vtkCellPicker specifically for 3D spatial picking within VTK. It sets itself apart by leveraging VTK's built-in cell picking mechanism rather than manual ray casting. Choose it when working within the VTK framework and needing to pick against existing VTK actors or volumes. Link: VTK CellPicker. Time complexity: O(1) for the pick operation assuming the renderer's picking data structures are pre-computed, but depends on the complexity of the scene graph traversal within VTK. Memory complexity: O(1) additional memory for the picker instance and coordinate storage. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple integration with VTK's event system; provides direct 3D world coordinates. Limitations: Relies on VTK's internal picking logic; may be inaccurate if the pick ray does not intersect any cell; fixed z=0 may lead to incorrect depth interpretation in non-orthographic views. When to use: When using VTK and needing quick 3D coordinate extraction from mouse clicks. When not: When high precision depth picking is required or when not using VTK. Originated in the VTK (Visualization Toolkit) framework, specifically in the IGS (Image Guided Surgery) application context. It is used in medical imaging applications where 3D spatial coordinates from mouse clicks are needed for further processing or display. name: Object Manipulation
head: Face manipulation
body: Object manipulation allows users to alter 3D data geometry or orientation, such as changing a model's curvature, to support inter-user understanding in collaborative settings. It differs from Ray-based Picking by directly modifying scene state via face dragging rather than merely selecting data, and from Tangible Dataset Manipulation by using depth rays and standard input devices instead of physical reference objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User input device movements and a depth ray generated from the viewpoint; for the tangible variant, rotation of a physical reference object. Output: Modified 3D model geometry (displaced faces) or a rotated volume dataset rendered on a tablet screen. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Selection: Cast a depth ray from the user's viewpoint through the input device position to intersect the 3D model and select its faces. 2. Activation: The user initiates a drag operation on the selected faces by moving the input device. 3. Transformation (Face): Move each selected face along its normal vector proportional to the input device movement. 4. Transformation (Tangible): Rotate the physical reference object with the hand, map its rotation to the virtual volume dataset, and render the rotated volume on the tablet screen. 5. Parallel Access: Multiple users can modify the scene simultaneously. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Depth Ray: Used for face selection. Reference Object Shape: Cuboctahedron, chosen to increase the odds that at least one marker remains visible during rotation while retaining quarter-turn resting positions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Fingers may obscure markers on the reference object during tangible manipulation, hiding the last visible marker. Parallel Access Limitations: Users can modify the scene in parallel, but if they work on areas that are too far apart or require different zoom levels, parallel access fails without implementing scene splitting. A technique where rotating a physical reference object (shaped as a cuboctahedron) rotates the corresponding virtual volume dataset, providing natural 6 DOF interaction. It is chosen when natural, bare-hand exploration of volume orientation is preferred over precise digital control. It differs from standard object manipulation by using a physical reference object observed through a handheld tablet window for tracking rather than a depth ray. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports inter-user understanding; allows natural 6 DOF interaction with bare hands; supports parallel access. Limitations: Requires specific hardware (depth ray system or physical reference object with tablet); scene splitting is needed for distant areas or different zoom levels; finger occlusion can hinder tangible manipulation. When to use: Collaborative design reviews where demonstrating geometric changes (e.g., curvature) is critical; natural exploration of volume orientation. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in collaborative volumetric display research. introduced face manipulation for car designers to demonstrate curvature changes. introduced tangible manipulation using a cuboctahedron reference object for portable volume exploration.
