name: Brush-based Interaction
head: Brushing
body: Brush-based interaction allows users to select, modify, or inspect subsets of volumetric or splat-based data by defining a spatial region (the "brush") and applying operations to elements within it. It solves the problem of intuitively targeting specific data structures without requiring precise geometric modeling or manual indexing. Unlike Ray-based Picking which targets single objects or points, this family supports continuous, multi-point selection and modification. It differs from Brushing and Linking with Hilbert Codes by focusing on spatial manipulation of the volume/splats themselves rather than encoding selection states for linked views, and from Object Manipulation by operating on raw data samples rather than abstracted scene objects. The core mechanism involves a user-defined region B (the brush) and a set of data elements P (voxels, samples, or splats). An element p \in P is considered "selected" if it satisfies a spatial predicate relative to the brush center c and radius r. 1. Brush Definition: The brush is typically defined by a center c (in screen or world coordinates) and a radius r. 2. Selection Predicate: For a point p, the selection status S(p) is determined by: S(p) = \begin{cases} \text{true} & \text{if } \|p - c\| \le r \\ \text{false} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} In some variants, this is extended to smooth degrees of interest (DOI) where S(p) \in [0, 1]. 3. Operation Application: Once selected, elements undergo an operation Op (e.g., lock, delete, highlight). The state of the dataset is updated based on Op(S(p)). 4. Feedback: The visual representation is updated to reflect the new state, either immediately (direct) or after a computation step (indirect). The Lock Tool prevents specific data points from being modified by other brushes or tools. It maintains a set L of locked indices. Users add to L via Shift+Click and remove via Control+Click. Rendering visibility is masked such that only points in L are drawn. This is useful for protecting regions during exploration. See Lock Tool for implementation details. This technique defines complex data features by selecting subsets across multiple linked visualizations (e.g., scatterplots). It uses composite non-binary brushes to assign a continuous Degree of Interest (DOI) to every sample point, enabling the identification of overlapping high-dimensional structures. Unlike binary selection, it outputs a Feature Definition Language (FDL) structure. See Interactive Feature Specification via Brushing for implementation details. An approach where users instantly highlight all splats that intersect with the brush during selection, contrasting with indirect approaches that compute intersections after brushing. Selection/deletion brushes may be either circular (screen space) or spherical (world space). Users may choose selections based on splat centers or their border. In case of circular brushes and splat-border intersection tests, an approximation checks whether the center of the brush circle is inside an ellipse that is enlarged by the radius of the brush. To remove deleted splats, all splats are sorted by their deletion flag, putting deleted splats towards the end of the buffer. Physical allocations at the buffer's end are unmapped and released in steps of the GPU's granularity. Using radix sort is not required; developers may implement this functionality with GPU-friendly stream compaction. The concept of "brushing" originated in visual analytics for selecting data points in 2D plots. In volume rendering and splat-based visualization, it was adapted to handle large datasets efficiently. The specific variants described here, such as the Lock Tool and Interactive Feature Specification, are detailed in recent literature on Gaussian Splat editing and high-dimensional data exploration. The direct selection method for splats addresses performance limitations in WebGL and VR environments where immediate feedback is critical. Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Lock Tool
head: Lock Brush
body: The Lock Tool is an interaction mechanism that specifies data points immune to modification by the brush or dig tools, allowing users to protect specific data subsets during exploration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User mouse events (click, drag, double-click, scroll) and the current lock state. Output: Updated lock set and rendering visibility mask. Data Structures: Lock Set L: A set of identifiers corresponding to data points (voxels or samples) currently marked as locked. Steps: 1. Initialize Lock Set: Start with an empty set or inherit from a previous state. 2. Add to Lock Set: When the user presses Shift + Left Mouse Button, identify points within the brush radius r and add them to L. Formula: L{\text{new}} = L{\text{old}} \cup \{p \mid \|p - c\| \le r\}, where c is the brush center and r is the brush radius. 3. Remove from Lock Set: When the user presses Control + Left Mouse Button, identify points within the brush radius r and remove them from L. Formula: L{\text{new}} = L{\text{old}} \setminus \{p \mid \|p - c\| \le r\}. 4. Adjust Brush Size: Use the mouse wheel to adjust the brush radius r. 5. Invert Lock Set: Double-clicking in a view inverts the lock set, making all unlocked points locked and all locked points unlocked. Formula: L{\text{new}} = P{\text{all}} \setminus L{\text{old}}, where P{\text{all}} is the set of all data points in the view. 6. Rendering: Render points p \in L as visible. Render points p \notin L as not drawn (invisible). Parameters: Brush Radius r: Adjustable via mouse wheel. Modifier Keys: Shift for Add, Control for Remove. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If L contains all points, inversion results in an empty set. If L is empty, inversion results in all points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SHIFT = 0x01 CONTROL = 0x02 def draw(point): # Standard graphics API call to render the point pass class LockTool: def init(self, allpoints): self.allpoints = allpoints self.lockedset = set() self.brushradius = 5.0 def onmousewheel(self, delta): self.brushradius += delta 0.5 if self.brushradius < 1.0: self.brushradius = 1.0 def onmousedown(self, x, y, modifiers): isshift = bool(modifiers & SHIFT) isctrl = bool(modifiers & CONTROL) pointsinbrush = self.getpointsinradius(x, y, self.brushradius) if isshift: self.lockedset.update(pointsinbrush) elif isctrl: self.lockedset -= pointsinbrush def ondoubleclick(self, x, y): self.lockedset = set(self.allpoints) - self.lockedset def getpointsinradius(self, cx, cy, radius): # Project (cx, cy) to the view plane and find points within distance radius return {p for p in self.allpoints if self.euclideandistance(p, (cx, cy)) <= radius} def euclideandistance(self, p, center): return math.sqrt((p.x - center[0])2 + (p.y - center[1])2 + (p.z - center[2])2) def render(self): for point in self.allpoints: if point in self.lockedset: draw(point) A tool to remove uninteresting data points or reduce clutter, combined with locking to selectively affect only locked or unlocked points. It uses add and remove modes similar to the Lock Tool but with inverted logic regarding which set is affected. Remove mode (Ctrl + Left Mouse Button) removes points, but only affects locked points. Add mode (Shift + Left Mouse Button) adds back previously removed points, but only affects unlocked points. Brush size is adjusted via mouse wheel. This allows users to first lock high-density regions and then filter out low-density noise, or vice versa, to reveal structures like skull anatomy in head scans. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Developed to allow users to "peek" inside volumetric data, such as human head scans, by locking interesting structures (like the skull) and removing uninteresting noise (like soft tissue). Color Tunneling: Interactive Exploration and Selection in Volumetric Datasets, https://doi.org/10.1109/pacificvis.2014.61, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Interactive Feature Specification via Brushing
head: Brushing in n-dimensional domain, Composite non-binary brushes
body: Interactive Feature Specification via Brushing is a technique for defining complex data features by selecting subsets of data points across multiple linked visualizations, such as scatterplots and histograms. It solves the problem of intuitively identifying high-dimensional structures in simulation data by allowing users to iteratively refine selections in one view while observing immediate effects in all others. Unlike binary selection methods, it uses composite non-binary brushes to assign a continuous degree of interest (DOI) to every sample point, enabling the identification of complex, overlapping features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: High-dimensional simulation data (e.g., computational flow simulation data) with attributes such as absolute pressure, velocity, viscosity, and turbulence kinetic energy. Output: A Feature Definition Language (FDL) structure representing the selected features, and a smooth Degree of Interest (DOI) function mapping every sample point to a floating-point value between 0 and 1. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Feature Definition Language (FDL), a hierarchical tree: 1. Root Layer: Contains the filename and an arbitrary number of FeatureSet objects. 2. Feature Set: A group of Feature objects that are to be shown simultaneously. Users can switch between, add, delete, or move features between sets. 3. Feature Layer: Composed of one or more FeatureCharacteristic objects. 4. Feature Characteristic: The lowest layer, storing: attribute: The name of the data attribute (e.g., "pressure"). range: A smooth, brushed range (1D for histograms, 2D for scatterplots). combination: Logical operators allowing characteristics to be combined (e.g., AND, OR). Note: Spatial dimensions can be included as an additional attribute to refine definitions based on spatial position. Steps: 1. Initialize Linked Views: Create multiple linked views (histograms, scatterplots) depicting relationships between data attributes. 2. Brush Selection: The user performs a smooth selection (brushing) on a scatterplot or histogram. For example, selecting a region in a plot of absolute pressure vs. velocity. 3. Propagate Selection: The selection immediately updates the visual appearance of all linked views, highlighting the corresponding ranges in other attributes (e.g., viscosity vs. turbulence kinetic energy). 4. Iterate: Repeat steps 2-3 in one or two-dimensional domains until the desired structure is found. 5. Refine: Use sliders or numerical input to refine approximate selections within the allowed range of data attributes. 6. Generate FDL: The system compiles the interactive selections into the FDL structure. 7. Compute DOI: Calculate the smooth DOI function based on the FDL. Formulas: The DOI function D(p) for a sample point p is computed by evaluating the logical combination of all active FeatureCharacteristic ranges in the FDL. D(p) \in [0, 1] Where D(p)=1 indicates full interest and D(p)=0 indicates no interest. The exact mathematical formulation of the "smooth" range and logical combination is not specified in the sources. Parameters: Spatial Dimension: Optional. If included, it acts as an additional attribute in the FDL characteristics. Brush Smoothness: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class FeatureCharacteristic: def init(self, attribute, rangefunction, logicalop): self.attribute = attribute self.rangefunction = rangefunction # Returns float in [0,1] for a value self.logicalop = logicalop # e.g., 'AND', 'OR' class Feature: def init(self): self.characteristics = [] # List of FeatureCharacteristic def evaluate(self, datapoint): # Combine characteristics using logical operations # Note: Exact combination logic (e.g., t-norms) is not specified result = 1.0 for char in self.characteristics: val = char.rangefunction(datapoint[char.attribute]) if char.logicalop == 'AND': result = min(result, val) # Assumption for smooth AND elif char.logicalop == 'OR': result = max(result, val) # Assumption for smooth OR return result class FeatureSet: def init(self): self.features = [] # List of Feature def evaluate(self, datapoint): # Combine features in the set # Note: Exact combination logic is not specified maxinterest = 0.0 for feature in self.features: interest = feature.evaluate(datapoint) if interest > maxinterest: maxinterest = interest return maxinterest class FDL: def init(self, filename): self.filename = filename self.featuresets = [] # List of FeatureSet def getdoi(self, datapoint): # Compute DOI for a single point across all sets # Note: Logic for combining sets is not specified doi = 0.0 for fs in self.featuresets: val = fs.evaluate(datapoint) if val > doi: doi = val return doi def interactivebrushingsession(data, views): """ Main loop for the interaction. """ fdl = FDL(data.filename) while not userfinished(): # 1. User brushes in one view (e.g., scatterplot of attr A vs B) selection = getuserbrush(views) # 2. Update FDL with new characteristic # Note: Implementation of 'smooth range' creation is not specified newchar = createsmoothcharacteristic(selection.attribute, selection.range) # 3. Add to current feature set currentfeatureset.addfeature(newchar) # 4. Propagate to linked views updatelinkedviews(views, fdl, data) # 5. Refine if needed if userrequestsrefinement(): refineselection(newchar) return fdl Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The "smooth" nature of the DOI requires careful handling of boundary conditions to avoid abrupt transitions. Degenerate Input: If no data points fall within the brushed range, the DOI for those points is 0. High Dimensionality: As the number of attributes increases, the complexity of linking and interpreting multiple views grows. A sibling method for selection and manipulation. Lock Tool Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Intuitive and straightforward for large, high-dimensional data; allows identification of complex features through composite brushes. Limitations: Requires careful management of linked views; refinement may be needed for approximate selections. When to Use: When users need to interactively define complex, multi-attribute features in simulation data. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and the overhead of maintaining linked views and smooth DOI calculations is too high. The method was introduced in the paper "Feature-based Volume Rendering of Simulation Data" by M. Mlejnek in 2003. It is part of a framework for visualizing computational flow simulation data, leveraging the concept of Degree of Interest (DOI) to guide volume rendering. Feature-based Volume Rendering of Simulation Data, https://old.cescg.org/CESCG-2003/MMlejnek/index.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Regions of Emphasis (Opacity Modulation)
head: Focus + context opacity modulation
body: Regions of Emphasis is a focus+context technique that uses opacity modulation to highlight specific density ranges within a volume while preserving the surrounding context. It differs from geometric deformation methods by altering visual transparency rather than spatial geometry, allowing users to select a region of interest based on data values. Inputs: Volume dataset V containing density values d. User-defined region of emphasis R{emph}, specified as a range of density values. Base transfer function mapping density to color and opacity. Outputs: Rendered image where features within R{emph} are emphasized and features outside are suppressed. Data Structures: The region of emphasis is stored as a density range [d{min}, d{max}]. Opacity modulation is applied per sample along the ray. Steps: 1. Selection: The user defines the region of emphasis R{emph} = [d{min}, d{max}] by selecting a range of density values. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume and sample density values di. 3. Opacity Modulation: For each sample i, compare di against R{emph}. If d{min} \le di \le d{max}, the sample retains its base opacity \alpha{base}. If di < d{min} or di > d{max}, the opacity is decreased to \alpha{mod} < \alpha{base}. 4. Compositing: Composite the samples using standard front-to-back alpha blending with the modulated opacities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderregionsofemphasis(volume, camera, regionemphasis, stepsize=0.5): """ volume: 3D array of density values with methods contains(pos) and sample(pos) camera: defines ray origins and directions regionemphasis: tuple (dmin, dmax) stepsize: distance between samples along the ray """ dmin, dmax = regionemphasis width, height = camera.resolution # Initialize image buffer to zero image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) # Normalize direction vector length = (raydirection[0]2 + raydirection[1]2 + raydirection[2]2)0.5 if length > 0: raydirection = (raydirection[0]/length, raydirection[1]/length, raydirection[2]/length) accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 # Ray marching loop while t < 1.0: pos = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) # Boundary check if not volume.contains(pos): break density, basecolor, baseopacity = volume.sample(pos) # Opacity modulation based on region of emphasis if dmin <= density <= dmax: modulatedopacity = baseopacity else: # Decrease opacity for values outside the region # Exact reduction factor not specified in sources modulatedopacity = baseopacity 0.5 # Standard front-to-back compositing alpha = modulatedopacity (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = ( accumulatedcolor[0] + basecolor[0] alpha, accumulatedcolor[1] + basecolor[1] alpha, accumulatedcolor[2] + basecolor[2] alpha, accumulatedcolor[3] + alpha) t += stepsize if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break image[y][x] = accumulatedcolor return image Parameters: d{min}, d{max}: The density bounds of the region of emphasis. Opacity reduction factor: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: If the region of emphasis covers the entire density range, no modulation is required. Precision issues may arise if density values are very close to d{min} or d{max}. ClearView is a focus + context technique that enhances the perception of specific volumetric features by modulating the opacity of segmented layers based on their importance relative to a user-defined focus region. It solves the problem of occlusion in dense volumes by rendering layers in a first pass and then adjusting their transparency in a second pass, distinguishing itself from single-pass methods by explicitly separating layer rendering from opacity modulation. A technique to emphasize a feature of interest by reducing the color saturation or opacity of nearby features. A technique to view the approximate time-history of a feature in a single image by presenting instances from previous time-steps with transparency and blurriness increasing backwards in time. It visualizes time-varying data by presenting multiple time-instances of a feature at once, with older instances indicated by reduced color saturation, increased transparency, or line rendering. The implementation identifies instances of features from previous time-steps, presents them at corresponding locations, and increases transparency and blurriness for instances further back in time. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per pixel, matching standard volume rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data and the region of emphasis parameters. Strengths: Simple to implement; preserves the spatial structure of the volume; effective for highlighting specific density ranges. Limitations: Relies on user knowledge of density values to define the region; may not be effective for features defined by spatial structure rather than density. When to use: When the region of interest is defined by specific data values (e.g., temperature, density). When not to use: When the region of interest is defined by spatial location or complex geometric features not correlated with density. The technique was introduced in the context of illustrative rendering of particle systems, where it was used to focus the viewer on regions of emphasis while maintaining overall volume context. It is categorized as a focus+context technique. Illustrative Rendering of Particle Systems, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe.vmv.vmv13.177-185, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Generalized Framework and Algorithms for Illustrative Visualization of Time-Varying Data on Unstructured Meshes, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc838861/?q=illustrative volume rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: ClearView
head: Layer-based opacity modulation, Focus-region transparency modulation
body: ClearView is a focus + context technique that enhances the perception of specific volumetric features by modulating the opacity of segmented layers based on their importance relative to a user-defined focus region. It solves the problem of occlusion in dense volumes by rendering layers in a first pass and then adjusting their transparency in a second pass, distinguishing itself from single-pass methods by explicitly separating layer rendering from opacity modulation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset segmented into distinct layers; a user-defined focus region (defined by density values or spatial location); importance metrics for each layer. Output: A rendered image where focus layers are emphasized and context layers are attenuated. Data Structures: Layer Stack: A list of layers, where each layer contains its voxel data and associated metadata (e.g., curvature, distance to focus). Focus Region Definition: Parameters defining the spatial or density-based boundaries of the area of interest. Steps: 1. Initial Rendering: Render all segmented layers of the dataset into an intermediate buffer or image. This establishes the base visual representation of the volume. 2. Importance Calculation: For each layer, calculate an importance measure. This measure is derived from: Curvature Information: Geometric complexity or feature significance within the layer. Distance to Focus: The spatial or density-based distance between the layer and the user-defined focus region. 3. Opacity Modulation: Adjust the transparency (opacity) of each layer based on its calculated importance. Layers with higher importance (e.g., closer to the focus, higher curvature) retain higher opacity, while context layers are made more transparent. 4. Final Compositing: Composite the modulated layers to produce the final image. Formulas: Let Li be a layer, Ii be its importance, and \alphai be its final opacity. The importance Ii is a function of curvature Ci and distance Di to the focus region: Ii = f(Ci, Di) The opacity \alphai is modulated based on Ii. While the exact functional form is not specified, the modulation ensures that layers with higher Ii have higher \alphai. Parameters: Curvature Weight: Determines the influence of geometric curvature on importance. Not given in the sources. Distance Weight: Determines the influence of spatial/density distance on importance. Not given in the sources. Focus Region: User-defined. Typically a density range or a 3D bounding box. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Modulating opacity in a second pass may require floating-point precision to avoid banding artifacts, especially when transparency values are very low. Degenerate Input: If the focus region is empty or layers have zero curvature, importance measures may be undefined. Boundary Artifacts: Sharp transitions between modulated and unmodulated layers may cause visual discontinuities. A segmentation technique used in the VIVIAN system to isolate volumetric objects (like tumors) from MRI data using a user-controlled crop-and-clone facility and a 3D Color Look-Up Table (CLUT). It differs from standard ClearView by using a 3D widget to interactively map scan values to appearance, primarily controlling transparency to isolate regions of interest. Each volume is assigned its own CLUT, and the widget's transparency control (a lower white control line) adjusts the visibility of specific scan value ranges, making surrounding tissue invisible to isolate tumors with significant density contrast. It is chosen when tumors exhibit significant density contrast against surrounding tissue. Time Complexity: Two-pass rendering (initial render + modulation) increases computational cost compared to single-pass methods. The modulation step is generally lightweight if implemented via texture lookups or shader-based transparency adjustment. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for intermediate buffers or layer metadata. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively reveals internal elements with a semi-transparent look; preserves local details in focus regions; allows interactive segmentation via CLUT in variants. Limitations: Requires pre-segmentation or layer definition; may introduce artifacts at layer boundaries; dependent on accurate importance measures. When to Use: When visualizing dense volumes where specific features need emphasis while maintaining context; suitable for medical imaging (e.g., tumor segmentation). When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and two-pass rendering is too slow; when layers are not well-defined or segmentation is difficult. ClearView was introduced as a technique to enhance perception in volume visualization by modifying opacity of segmented layers based on a user-defined focus region. It is cited in the context of focus + context techniques and is related to methods that use quality measures to enhance semi-transparent layers. The CLUT-based variant is implemented in the VIVIAN system for multimodal volume-based tumor neurosurgery planning. Enhanced perception in volume visualization, https://doi.org/10.5821/dissertation-2117-94929, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Multimodal volume-based tumor neurosurgery planning in the virtual workbench, https://doi.org/10.1007/bfb0056289, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Feature Isolation
body: Feature Isolation is a focus + context technique that emphasizes a specific feature of interest by reducing the color saturation or opacity of nearby, non-target features. It extends standard opacity modulation by applying simultaneous color saturation reduction to achieve finer visual separation of complex or bifurcated structures. Inputs: A volumetric dataset V with scalar values. A user-defined region of interest (ROI) R, defined by a spatial mask or scalar range. Rendering parameters: saturation reduction factor S{red} \in [0, 1], opacity reduction factor \alpha{red} \in [0, 1], and falloff radius Rf. Outputs: A rendered image where features within R retain full visual prominence, and nearby features have reduced saturation and/or opacity. Data Structures: A transfer function mapping scalar values to base color and opacity. A binary feature mask indicating the ROI. Steps: 1. Identify the feature of interest by defining the ROI R using spatial coordinates or a target scalar range. 2. Compute a distance metric d between each sample point and the nearest voxel in R. 3. Calculate modulation factors using a falloff function f(d) that equals 0 inside R and approaches 1 outside, then compute S{mod} and \alpha{mod}. 4. Apply modulation by converting base colors to HSV space, reducing saturation by S{mod}, converting back to RGB, and scaling opacity by \alpha{mod}. 5. Composite the final color and opacity along rays using standard volume rendering integration. Formulas: Proximity: For spatial ROI, d is the Euclidean distance to the nearest ROI voxel. For scalar ROI, d = |v - v{center}|. Falloff: f(d) = \min(d / Rf, 1.0). Saturation modulation: S{mod} = 1 - (1 - S{red}) \cdot f(d). Opacity modulation: \alpha{mod} = 1 - (1 - \alpha{red}) \cdot f(d). Color conversion: C{final} = \text{HSV2RGB}(H, S{base} \cdot S{mod}, V). Final opacity: \alpha{final} = \alpha{base} \cdot \alpha{mod}. Parameters: S{red}, \alpha{red} \in [0, 1] control the maximum reduction strength. Rf defines the spatial extent of the modulation falloff. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If S{red} or \alpha{red} is close to 1, nearby features may become imperceptible; a minimum opacity threshold should be applied to prevent numerical underflow. Boundaries: Sharp transitions in the ROI mask can cause visible artifacts; smoothing the mask or using a soft falloff function f(d) is recommended. Degenerate Input: If the ROI covers the entire volume, d=0 everywhere, f(d)=0, and no modulation occurs. If the ROI is empty, all features are modulated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hsvtorgb(h, s, v): """Standard HSV to RGB conversion """ c = v s x = c (1.0 - abs((h / 60.0) % 2 - 1.0)) m = v - c if h < 60.0: r, g, b = c, x, 0.0 elif h < 120.0: r, g, b = x, c, 0.0 elif h < 180.0: r, g, b = 0.0, c, x elif h < 240.0: r, g, b = 0.0, x, c elif h < 300.0: r, g, b = x, 0.0, c else: r, g, b = c, 0.0, x return (r + m, g + m, b + m) def applyfeatureisolation(color, opacity, distancetoroi, falloffradius, saturationreduction, opacityreduction): """ Applies saturation and opacity modulation based on distance to ROI. color: tuple (r, g, b) in [0, 1] opacity: float in [0, 1] distancetoroi: float, distance from current sample to ROI falloffradius: float, distance at which modulation reaches maximum saturationreduction: float in [0, 1] opacityreduction: float in [0, 1] Returns: modified color tuple and modified opacity float """ if falloffradius <= 0: falloffradius = 1e-6 falloff = min(distancetoroi / falloffradius, 1.0) saturationmod = 1.0 - (1.0 - saturationreduction) falloff opacitymod = 1.0 - (1.0 - opacityreduction) falloff r, g, b = color cmax = max(r, g, b) cmin = min(r, g, b) delta = cmax - cmin if delta == 0: h, s, v = 0.0, 0.0, cmax else: if cmax == r: h = 60.0 (((g - b) / delta) % 6) elif cmax == g: h = 60.0 (((b - r) / delta) + 2) else: h = 60.0 (((r - g) / delta) + 4) s = delta / cmax v = cmax snew = s saturationmod cfinal = hsvtorgb(h, snew, v) ofinal = opacity opacitymod return cfinal, ofinal A technique to suppress signal from background tissues to visualize injections of contrast agent, using magnetization preparation. It executes a nonselective 90° saturation pulse immediately prior to the acquisition of each image. Alternatively, a spatially or chemically selective saturation pulse can be prescribed by the user. This is particularly useful in contrast-enhanced MRI imaging where Gd-DTPA is used as a T1-shortening agent. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for separating visually similar features by altering both color and opacity. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of saturation and opacity reduction factors. May increase computational cost if complex transfer functions are used. When to Use: When emphasizing a specific feature while maintaining context of surrounding structures, especially in complex bifurcated or mixed features. When Not to Use: When high contrast between features is already sufficient, or when computational resources are severely limited. Origin: Described in a generalized framework for illustrative visualization of time-varying data on unstructured meshes. Related MRI background suppression techniques use magnetization preparation. Ebert and Rheingans developed illustrative visualization techniques for volumetric rendering, though their formulations typically operate on complex transfer functions applied to the entire dataset, which can reduce flexibility and increase computational cost compared to targeted feature isolation. Generalized Framework and Algorithms for Illustrative Visualization of Time-Varying Data on Unstructured Meshes, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc838861/?q=illustrative volume rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Real-Time Volume Rendered MRI for Interventional Guidance, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2570028/, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Focus+Context via Opacity Modulation
head: Bruckner et al. Opacity Modulation
body:
Focus+Context via Opacity Modulation modifies the compositing scheme to increase the transparency of flat, uninteresting regions while preserving local details in areas of interest. It solves the problem of occlusion in volume rendering by allowing users to see internal structures without completely removing the surrounding context, which can cause disorientation. Builds on Interaction, it sets itself apart from Cropping and Focus+Context Visualization via Deformation by preserving the original data layout and camera geometry, instead selectively attenuating opacity along viewing rays based on shading and gradient cues. The method modulates the opacity of samples along viewing rays based on shading intensity, gradient magnitude, distance to the viewer, and accumulated opacity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset V, transfer function TF, light position L, camera position C, and user-defined focus parameters. Output: Final color C{	ext{final}} and opacity \alpha{	ext{final}} for each pixel. Data Structures: Ray: A 3D line segment from the camera origin through the pixel center into the volume. Sample: A point x on the ray with value V(x), gradient 
abla V(x), and shading intensity I{	ext{shade}}(x). Accumulated State: Current accumulated color C{	ext{acc}} and opacity \alpha{	ext{acc}} for front-to-back compositing. Steps: 1. Shading Calculation: For each sample x along the ray, compute the shading intensity I{	ext{shade}}(x) using standard lighting models (e.g., Phong or Blinn-Phong) based on the gradient 
abla V(x) and light direction. High intensity indicates flat surfaces facing the light. 2. Modulation Factor Calculation: Compute a modulation factor M(x) for each sample. The opacity is modulated such that high shading intensity leads to higher transparency (lower opacity). The modulation considers shading intensity I{	ext{shade}}(x), gradient magnitude |
abla V(x)|, distance to viewer d(x), and accumulated opacity \alpha{	ext{acc}} of the ray up to sample x. A typical formulation for the modulated opacity \alpha{	ext{mod}}(x) is: \alpha{	ext{mod}}(x) = \alpha{	ext{base}}(x) \cdot f(I{	ext{shade}}(x), |
abla V(x)|, d(x), \alpha{	ext{acc}}) where \alpha{	ext{base}}(x) is the original opacity from the transfer function. The function f decreases opacity as shading intensity increases, effectively making flat, well-lit regions more transparent. The exact weighting function f and its internal parameters are not given in the sources. 3. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing using the modulated opacity \alpha{	ext{mod}}(x) instead of the base opacity. C{	ext{acc}} = C{	ext{acc}} + C(x) \cdot \alpha{	ext{mod}}(x) \cdot (1 - \alpha{	ext{acc}}) \alpha{	ext{acc}} = \alpha{	ext{acc}} + \alpha{	ext{mod}}(x) \cdot (1 - \alpha{	ext{acc}}) Where C(x) is the color at sample x. Parameters: Shading Weight: Controls the influence of shading intensity on opacity modulation. Not given in the sources. Gradient Threshold: Minimum gradient magnitude to preserve detail. Not given in the sources. Distance Decay: Rate at which opacity increases with distance from the viewer. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Modulating opacity can lead to very low opacity values, potentially causing floating-point precision issues in accumulation. Use epsilon clamping for opacity values. Boundaries: Ensure shading calculations are robust at volume boundaries where gradients may be noisy. Clamp gradients or use boundary-aware shading. Degenerate Input: If the volume has uniform values (zero gradient), shading may be undefined or constant. Handle zero-gradient cases by defaulting to base opacity or a minimum transparency. Structural Ghosting is a Focus+Context technique that modulates the opacity of non-focus volume clusters based on their structural relationship to the focus region within a classification hierarchy. It solves the problem of visual clutter by rendering context clusters with varying transparency, where opacity decreases as the structural distance from the focus increases. Unlike simple cut-away methods, it preserves the hierarchical context of the data, allowing users to see the surrounding structure while emphasizing the region of interest. Choose this variant when hierarchical relationships between data clusters are critical for interpretation. Structural Ghosting with Opacity Modulation Context-Preserving Transparency prevents user disorientation by making "hidden" areas translucent rather than completely transparent, preserving contextual anatomical landmarks while fading out uninteresting parts. It sets itself apart from binary masking by allowing adjustable translucency rather than hard cuts. Choose this variant when navigating complex anatomical structures where complete transparency causes spatial disorientation. Window Transparency selectively increases transparency in certain regions by modulating overall transparency as a function of the surface pixel position in image space, relative to a specified point. It sets itself apart from ray-space modulation by operating in screen space to create interactive viewing windows. Choose this variant when users need to quickly peer through occluding outer surfaces to reveal otherwise hidden details. Time Complexity: Linear O(N) with respect to the number of samples per ray, as it adds a constant-time modulation calculation per sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, requiring no additional buffers beyond standard volume rendering state. Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with ray count and samples; shading computation adds a fixed per-sample cost that may dominate on low-resolution data. Strengths: Preserves spatial context without geometric distortion; intuitive mapping of lighting cues to detail preservation. Limitations: Relies on accurate gradient and shading estimation; may fail on noisy or low-resolution data where shading cues are unreliable. When to Use: When users need to see internal structures without losing the spatial context of the surrounding volume. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The technique was introduced by Bruckner et al.. It is based on the idea that highly illuminated regions correspond to flat surfaces facing light sources, and less illuminated areas contain features worth preserving. Similar results are obtained with the ClearView technique, which modifies the opacity of different segmented layers within a user-defined focus region. The Context-Preserving Transparency variant was developed for interactive volume rendering of diffusion tensor data, particularly for surgical planning involving MRI and DT-MRI data. Window Transparency was inspired by earlier work on user-controlled transparency windows. name: Structural Ghosting with Opacity Modulation
head: Contextual Ghosting, Contextual cluster opacity computation, Structural Ghosting
body: Structural Ghosting is a Focus+Context technique that modulates the opacity of non-focus volume clusters based on their structural relationship to a selected focus region within a classification hierarchy. It solves visual clutter by rendering context clusters with varying transparency, where opacity decreases as the hierarchical distance from the focus increases. Unlike simple cut-away methods, it preserves the surrounding hierarchical context, allowing users to perceive the data structure while emphasizing the region of interest. Inputs: A classification hierarchy (tree/graph) of volume clusters. A set of "focus clusters" F identified by user query or selection. A "ghosting level" parameter L (integer). A "color ghosting" flag (boolean). Outputs: A modified Color Transfer Function (CTF) where the \alpha-channel (opacity) for contextual clusters is adjusted based on their depth in the hierarchy relative to F. Data Structures: Hierarchy Graph: Nodes represent clusters. Edges represent parent-child or ancestor-descendant relationships. CTF: Maps cluster IDs to RGBA values. The \alpha-channel is modified by this method. Parameters: Ghosting Level (L): Integer ranging from 0 to the maximum depth of the hierarchy trees in the graph. L=0: Cut-away mode (context clusters have zero opacity). L=1: Shows clusters with a direct common ancestor with focus clusters. L=2: Shows clusters having common ancestors with focus clusters through a one-edge path in the graph. Color Ghosting Flag: If true, contextual clusters are rendered in grayscale based on node intensity rather than RGB values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify Focus Nodes: Determine the set of graph nodes F corresponding to the focus clusters. 2. Traverse Hierarchy: Starting from nodes in F, traverse the hierarchy graph upwards (towards ancestors) up to a depth of L steps. 3. Compute Context Opacity: For each contextual cluster identified during traversal, compute its opacity factor inversely proportional to the depth of the related node in the hierarchy. Formula: \alpha{context} = \alpha{max} \cdot \frac{1}{depth}, where depth is the distance from the focus node in the hierarchy traversal, and \alpha{max} is the maximum opacity (typically 1.0). Note: The further in the hierarchy a node is, the lighter (lower opacity) the related cluster becomes. 4. Update CTF: Set the \alpha-channel of the CTF for these contextual clusters to the computed opacity values. 5. Optional Color Modulation: If the color ghosting flag is active, set the RGB values of the contextual clusters in the CTF to grayscale values derived from the node intensity, ignoring original RGB values. This enhances contrast with the colored focus region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestructuralghosting(focusclusters, hierarchygraph, ghostinglevel, colorghostingflag, ctf): """ focusclusters: List of cluster IDs identified as focus. hierarchygraph: Graph structure where nodes are clusters and edges represent hierarchy. ghostinglevel: Integer L. colorghostingflag: Boolean. ctf: Dictionary mapping clusterid -> {'r': float, 'g': float, 'b': float, 'a': float}. """ # Step 1: Identify focus nodes in the graph focusnodes = [node for node in hierarchygraph.nodes if node.id in focusclusters] # Dictionary to store context clusters and their computed opacities contextopacities = {} # Step 2 & 3: Traverse hierarchy and compute opacity for focusnode in focusnodes: queue = [(focusnode, 0)] visited = set([focusnode.id]) while queue: currentnode, currentdepth = queue.pop(0) if currentdepth > 0 and currentdepth <= ghostinglevel: # Compute opacity inversely proportional to depth opacity = 1.0 / currentdepth contextopacities[currentnode.id] = opacity if currentdepth < ghostinglevel: for neighbor in currentnode.neighbors: if neighbor.id not in visited: visited.add(neighbor.id) queue.append((neighbor, currentdepth + 1)) # Step 4: Update CTF for clusterid, opacity in contextopacities.items(): ctf[clusterid]['a'] = opacity # Step 5: Optional Color Modulation if colorghostingflag: original = ctf[clusterid] # Standard luminance formula intensity = 0.299 original['r'] + 0.587 original['g'] + 0.114 original['b'] ctf[clusterid]['r'] = intensity ctf[clusterid]['g'] = intensity ctf[clusterid]['b'] = intensity return ctf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting Level 0: Results in zero opacity for all context clusters (cut-away). Hierarchy Depth: The maximum ghosting level is bounded by the maximum depth of the hierarchy trees in the graph. Opacity Fluctuation: In animated sequences, opacity of contextual structures may fluctuate between keyframes, causing visual inconsistency. A post-processing step applied to a sequence of keyframe Direct Volume Rendering Images (DVRIs) to stabilize the opacity of contextual structures across an animation. It prevents visual inconsistency caused by opacity fluctuations where a structure might appear highly transparent in one frame and less transparent in another. Method: For each structure, analyze all keyframes and record the lowest non-zero opacity assigned to that structure when used as context. For each keyframe, check if the context constraint is satisfied according to a context metric after assigning this recorded lowest opacity. If the condition is satisfied for all keyframes, commit the change to standardize the opacity. Parameters: Context metric (formula not provided). Pitfall: Without this fix, contextual structures may cause confusion and inconsistency in the animation due to opacity fluctuations. Time Complexity: Depends on the size of the hierarchy graph and the ghosting level L. Traversal is limited to depth L, so it is bounded by the number of nodes within L edges of the focus clusters. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the hierarchy graph and the modified CTF. Performance: Experiments were conducted on a standard PC (Intel Core 2 Duo E6400, 3 GB RAM, GeForce 8600GT). Rendering time for a CT head dataset (128×128×231) was 157 seconds to generate four images with 80% visibility of the brain structure. Strengths: Provides contextual information without cluttering the view; grayscale context enhances focus contrast. Limitations: Opacity fluctuations in animations can cause visual inconsistency. The method was introduced in the context of structural focus+context rendering for volume data organized in a graph hierarchy. It builds on the parent technique Focus+Context via Opacity Modulation, which modifies the compositing scheme to increase transparency of flat regions while preserving local details. The temporal coherence fix was proposed to address issues in animated sequences. name: Structural and Glyph-based Visualization
body: Structural and Glyph-based Visualization is a family of interaction techniques that decouple focus and context rendering to manage visual complexity. It addresses visual clutter and occlusion by rendering selected features as explicit geometry (glyphs, tensorlines) or structural graphs while maintaining a volume-rendered context [8909-hybrid-rendering-for-stress-tensor-fields.md, 14778-structural-focus-context-rendering.md]. Unlike pure volume rendering, which obscures internal structures, or pure glyph-based rendering, which lacks global continuity, this family dynamically adjusts opacity and geometry based on user-defined masks or structural relationships [8909-hybrid-rendering-for-stress-tensor-fields.md, 14778-structural-focus-context-rendering.md]. The family shares a core mechanism of decoupling "focus" and "context" rendering paths to manage visual complexity. 1. Dual Representation: The method maintains two parallel rendering paths: a context path (volume rendering) and a focus path (explicit geometric primitives or structural graphs) [8909-hybrid-rendering-for-stress-tensor-fields.md, 14778-structural-focus-context-rendering.md]. 2. Selection-Driven Masking: User interaction (e.g., selection in a diagram view or boolean query) defines a mask or selection set. This mask determines which voxels or features are rendered as geometry (focus) and which are rendered as volume (context). 3. Occlusion Handling: Correct intersection between the volume-rendered context and the opaque geometric focus elements is critical. This is typically handled by rendering the geometry first into a depth buffer, then checking the depth buffer during volume ray-casting to stop volume traversal when a ray intersects a geometric element. Alternatively, modulating volume opacity in context regions prevents visual overlap. 4. Structural Graphs (for Structural SFC): In Structural Focus+Context, the data is preprocessed into a Directed Graph G where nodes are classification criteria and edges represent logical inclusion. This graph serves as a grammar for boolean arithmetic on classes, allowing the system to compute transfer functions based on structural relationships rather than independent criteria. What it is: A technique for stress tensor fields that combines volume rendering of scalar invariants (e.g., von Mises stress) with explicit geometric representations (tensorlines or ellipsoid glyphs). What sets it apart: It uses user selections from diagram views (scatterplots, Mohr diagrams) to define focus regions. It solves the problem of visual clutter in dense tensor fields by allowing interactive selection of specific regions for detailed geometric analysis while maintaining a global context view. When to choose it: Use when visualizing complex tensor fields where internal structures (e.g., principal stress directions) are obscured by volume rendering, and users need to correlate tensor properties with spatial location. Link: Hybrid Rendering for Stress Tensor Fields What it is: A method for multiclassified voxel models (e.g., multimodal medical images) that outlines structural relationships between classification criteria using a directed graph and multimodal 3D texture mapping. What sets it apart: Unlike prior systems that treat classification criteria independently, this method clusters voxels based on combined criteria, constructs a directed graph of logical inclusion relationships, and applies structural focus+context shading via transfer functions computed on the graph structure. When to choose it: Use when exploring complex, multiclassified datasets where understanding the logical inclusion relationships between different tissue types or data modalities is critical. Link: Structural Focus+Context Rendering Definition: A focus+context direct volume rendering technique where the isosurface at a user-selected isovalue hu is the focus, and contextual regions are depicted sparsely based on local similarity stability. Mechanism: It uses an importance function \gamma(\mathbf{x}) to control the degree-of-interest. The function is defined as: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = \prod{\mathbf{y} \in C(\mathbf{x})} \text{SMV}(hu, f(\mathbf{y})) where f is the scalar field and C(\mathbf{x}) is a local neighborhood of samples around \mathbf{x} (typically reused from gradient estimation using central differences). Rendering: The opacity \alpha(\mathbf{x}) is set to 1 if f(\mathbf{x}) \ge hu, and \gamma(\mathbf{x}) otherwise. The function \gamma(\mathbf{x}) also controls color and surface shading to distinguish focus from context. The directional occlusion model of Schott et al. is applied uniformly. Source: Definition: A radial 2D node-link diagram representing the cluster hierarchy, where each node is assigned a sector of a disc proportional to the number of descendants, with an opening angle restricted to be no greater than \pi to allow proper visualization of size adjustment sliders. Mechanism: Nodes are drawn as circles with radius proportional to cluster size. Initial opacity is 0.3 for each node. Color Assignment: Leaf nodes are assigned hues from the HSV color wheel based on their position in the radial layout. Inner node hues are the average of their children's hues. Saturation is determined by distance from the center; Value V=1. Interaction: Users adjust cluster size by changing density limits using sliders. For inner nodes, an arc slider intersects edges connecting to children, defining density limits as [d{min}, d{slider}] by default or [d{slider}, d{max}] on click, where d{slider} is determined by linear interpolation on [d{min}, d{max}]. Source: Definition: A base visualization filter that renders all hypertree grid outputs directly. Source: Definition: A visualization interface layout using concentric circles and sectors to arrange DVRIs based on viewpoint (sector) and image quality (radius/distance from center). Step: Define concentric circles with radii r1 \dots rn using the recursive formula starting with user-defined C. Insert new DVRIs into the appropriate sector and determine their distance to the center based on image quality (higher quality = closer to center/larger size). Formula: ri = r{i-1} + (r{i-1} - r{i-2}) / 2, where ri is the radius of the i-th concentric circle, i \ge 3, r2 = 2r1, and r1 = C (where C is a user-defined constant). Layout: Data structure: Red-black tree used to store DVRIs for each sector. DVRIs are kept sorted in ascending order of image quality. Complexity: Insertion complexity: O(\log n) + T, where n is the number of DVRIs in the sector and T is the time for image quality evaluation. Drawing complexity: O(n) for traversing the tree to draw the sector, as sorting is maintained by the tree structure. Source: Definition: A slice-based methodology that maps a real-world physical space to a virtual medical volume space, using a tangible planar object and AR principles to determine spatial position and orientation for natural human-computer interaction with volumetric data. Step: Acquire data from a Kinect v1 sensor, which provides an RGB image, a depth image D where each pixel value is the Euclidean distance from the sensor, and a vector field P with x, y, z coordinates of objects relative to the sensor. Source: Definition: A ribbon representation for protein structures showing the backbone connectivity and secondary structure. Step: Show a strip representing the backbone spiraling around a cylinder for alpha helices. Show a strip with a directional arrow for strands in beta sheets. Show a narrower tube in other regions. Source: The concept of separating focus and context in volume rendering has evolved from simple opacity modulation to more complex structural and geometric integrations. Early work focused on isosurface similarity to indicate stability. Later, hybrid approaches combined volume rendering with explicit geometry (glyphs, tensorlines) to handle dense tensor fields. Concurrently, structural approaches emerged to handle multiclassified data by modeling logical relationships between classification criteria as directed graphs, enabling boolean queries over structural relationships. The integration of interactive widgets, such as radial cluster trees, allows users to manipulate these structural parameters directly. name: Hybrid Rendering for Stress Tensor Fields
head: Focus and context visualization
body: Hybrid Rendering for Stress Tensor Fields is a visualization technique that decouples the display of global context from local detail in stress tensor datasets by combining volume rendering with explicit geometric representations (glyphs and tensorlines). It solves the problem of visual clutter and occlusion in dense tensor fields by allowing users to interactively select specific features via diagram views, which generates a mask to render those features as high-fidelity geometry while the remaining data is shown as a lower-opacity volume. The method maintains two parallel rendering paths: a context path (volume rendering) and a focus path (geometric primitives). Selection of focus regions is driven by user interaction with auxiliary diagram views, such as scatterplots or Mohr diagrams. Input: A 3D stress tensor field \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x}) defined on a voxel grid; user selections from 2D diagram views (e.g., eigenvalue plots). Output: A composite image showing volume-rendered context and geometric focus elements. 1. Mask Volume M(\mathbf{x}): A 3D volume of the same resolution as the tensor field. Each voxel stores a binary value: M(\mathbf{x}) = 1 for focus regions, M(\mathbf{x}) = 0 for context regions. 2. Depth Buffer: A 2D array storing depth values of the rendered geometric focus elements to handle occlusion against the volume. Scalar Invariant for Context: Typically von Mises stress, chosen by the user. Opacity Modulation: Opacity in focus regions is decreased to allow visibility of underlying or overlapping geometry. Glyph Mapping Parameters: c determines the slope of the antisymmetric mapping function at the origin; \alpha is a scaling parameter; a global scale parameter adjusts glyph size. 1. Mask Generation: The user selects features in a diagram view. The system maps these selections to the 3D dataset, updating the mask volume M(\mathbf{x}). 2. Focus Rendering (Geometry): Selected features are mapped to geometrical tensor representations. Tensorlines: Seeds are randomly placed inside voxels where M(\mathbf{x}) = 1. Lines are integrated starting at each seed using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme. Integration stops when the line enters an isotropic region. Tensor Glyphs: Ellipsoids are drawn in focus regions. The local tensor is mapped to a positive-definite metric using an antisymmetric mapping to distinguish between positive and negative eigenvalues: f(\sigmai, c, \alpha) = \exp(\alpha \arctan(c \cdot \sigmai)) where \sigmai are the eigenvalues of the tensor. Glyphs are scaled using the global scale parameter. Geometric primitives are rendered into the scene, updating the depth buffer. 3. Context Rendering (Volume): Standard GPU ray-casting is performed for the volume rendering of the chosen scalar invariant. During volume traversal, the depth buffer is checked; rays are stopped as soon as they hit geometry positions to ensure correct intersection and prevent visual overlap. Opacity is decreased in regions where M(\mathbf{x}) = 1 to enhance focus geometry visibility. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridrenderstresstensor(tensorfield, userselections, scalarinvariantfunc): """ Renders a stress tensor field using hybrid focus+context visualization. tensorfield: 3D list of tensors T(z,y,x) userselections: criteria from diagram views scalarinvariantfunc: function returning scalar from tensor """ D, H, W = len(tensorfield), len(tensorfield[0]), len(tensorfield[0][0]) # Step 1: Generate Mask Volume M = [[[False for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(D)] for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # Inverts diagram view projection to tensor eigenvalue space if checkselectioncriteria(tensorfield[z][y][x], userselections): M[z][y][x] = True # Step 2: Render Focus Geometry camdepth = [[0.0 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] # Render Tensorlines seeds = [] for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): if M[z][y][x]: seeds.append([z + 0.5, y + 0.5, x + 0.5]) for seed in seeds: p = seed[:] dt = 0.1 for in range(10): k1 = getprincipaldirection(tensorfield, p) k2 = getprincipaldirection(tensorfield, [p[i] + 0.5dtk1[i] for i in range(3)]) k3 = getprincipaldirection(tensorfield, [p[i] + 0.5dtk2[i] for i in range(3)]) k4 = getprincipaldirection(tensorfield, [p[i] + dtk3[i] for i in range(3)]) p = [p[i] + (dt/6.0)(k1[i] + 2k2[i] + 2k3[i] + k4[i]) for i in range(3)] if not isisotropic(p): updatedepthbufferline(p, camdepth) # Render Glyphs for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): if M[z][y][x]: glyphverts = buildellipsoidglyph(tensorfield[z][y][x]) updatedepthbufferglyph(glyphverts, camdepth) # Step 3: Context Rendering (Volume) colorbuffer = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): rayorigin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] raydir = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] t = 0.0 alphaaccum = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while t < 10.0: # Stop ray traversal if geometry depth is closer than current ray position if camdepth[y][x] > 0.0 and camdepth[y][x] <= t: break voxel = interpolatetensor(tensorfield, rayorigin, raydir, t) scalarval = scalarinvariantfunc(voxel.tensor) opacity = 0.1 if M[voxel.z][voxel.y][voxel.x] else 0.5 rgb = mapscalartocolor(scalarval) alphaaccum += (1.0 - alphaaccum) opacity color = [color[i] + rgb[i] opacity (1.0 - alphaaccum) for i in range(3)] t += 0.1 if alphaaccum >= 0.99: break colorbuffer[y][x] = color return colorbuffer def checkselectioncriteria(tensor, selections): # Inverts diagram view projection to tensor eigenvalue space return True def getprincipaldirection(tensorfield, p): # Computes eigenvector corresponding to largest eigenvalue at p return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def isisotropic(p): # Checks if eigenvalues at p are equal (shear stress near zero) return False def updatedepthbufferline(endpoint, camdepth): # Projects line endpoint to camera space and updates camdepth[y][x] pass def buildellipsoidglyph(tensor): # Computes eigenvalues/vectors, applies antisymmetric mapping, builds ellipsoid mesh return [] def updatedepthbufferglyph(verts, camdepth): # Rasterizes glyph vertices to camera space and updates camdepth pass def interpolatetensor(tensorfield, origin, direction, t): # Interpolates tensor at origin + tdirection return type('Voxel', (), {'tensor': tensorfield[0][0][0], 'z': 0, 'y': 0, 'x': 0})() def mapscalartocolor(scalarval): # Maps scalar invariant to RGB return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides clear separation of focus and context, allowing detailed analysis of specific stress features without losing the global spatial context provided by the volume rendering. Limitations: The quality of the focus representation depends on the density of seeds (for tensorlines) or the resolution of the glyph placement. When to use: When analyzing stress tensor fields where both global distribution (context) and local tensor orientation/magnitude (focus) are critical, and when users need to interactively select regions based on tensor properties. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the context of visual analysis of stress tensor fields, specifically in the paper "A Visual Approach to Analysis of Stress Tensor Fields". It builds on the general concept of Focus+Context visualization, adapting it to the specific challenges of tensor data, such as the need to represent both magnitude and orientation. The approach leverages the structural relationships in tensor data, often visualized through Mohr diagrams or eigenvalue scatterplots, to drive the selection of focus regions. The use of antisymmetric mapping for glyphs allows for the distinction of eigenvalue signs, which is crucial in stress analysis. name: Structural Focus+Context Rendering
head: Focus+Context rendering of structured biomedical data, SF+C, SFC rendering, Structural Focus and Context, structural F+C volume rendering
body: Structural Focus+Context (SFC) rendering is a volume visualization technique for multiclassified data that explicitly models and renders the logical relationships between classification criteria using a directed graph. Unlike standard volume rendering which treats classes independently, SFC constructs an auxiliary labelled voxel model and a structural graph to compute transfer functions based on boolean queries over class inclusions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hybrid Rendering for Stress Tensor Fields by focusing on the semantic structure of multiclassified scalar volumes rather than tensor field geometry, using multimodal 3D texture mapping to simultaneously render context and focus based on cluster labels. Inputs: 1. Original Voxel Model (V): A 3D scalar field, potentially multimodal (e.g., MR/SPECT, MR/PET). 2. Classification Criteria: A set of nc independent criteria ci (i=1 \dots nc), each partitioning V into n{ci} disjoint classes c{ij}. 3. User Query: A boolean expression defined over the initial classification criteria. Outputs: 1. Directed Graph (G): Nodes represent classification classes; edges represent logical inclusion relationships. 2. Labelled Voxel Model (LV): A 3D volume where each voxel stores a unique integer identifier (cluster label) corresponding to the combination of classification criteria it satisfies. 3. Transfer Functions: CTF (Color/Visibility Transfer Function): Maps cluster labels to visibility, color, and opacity. GMTF (Gradient Modulation Transfer Function): Maps cluster labels to a gradient modulation factor. Data Structures: Directed Graph Model: A graph G = (N, E) where N is the set of classification criteria (nodes) and E is the set of logical implications (edges). Auxiliary Voxel Model (LV): A 3D array of integers where LV[\mathbf{x}] = c, and c is the unique identifier of the cluster satisfied by V[\mathbf{x}]. Classification Model: For each criterion ci, the isoclasses are disjoint and cover the volume: \forall j, k: 1 \le j, k \le n{ci}, j \ne k: \text{isoclas}(c{ij}) \cap \text{isoclas}(c{ik}) = \emptyset \bigcup{j=1}^{n{ci}} \text{isoclas}(c{ij}) = V A class ck^i implies cl^j if the isoclass of ck^i is a subset of the isoclass of cl^j (i \ne j): ck^i \Rightarrow cl^j \text{ iff } \text{isoclas}(ck^i) \subset \text{isoclas}(cl^j) Preprocessing Steps: 1. Classification: Classify the initial voxel model V according to various independent criteria, potentially handling multimodal datasets. 2. Graph Construction: Identify dependencies between classification criteria and construct a directed graph where nodes are the classification criteria and edges represent logical inclusion relationships. 3. Clustering: Clusterize the voxel model into subsets of voxels sharing the exact same combination of classification criteria. Construct the auxiliary voxel model LV by assigning a unique integer identifier to each cluster. 4. Graph Completion: Identify dependencies between the constructed clusters to complete the graph structure, ensuring the graph accurately reflects the logical structure of the multiclassified model. 5. Output: Store the directed graph G and the labelled voxel model LV. Rendering Steps: 1. Query Parsing: The user expresses a rendering query as a boolean expression of the initial classification criteria. A parser takes the boolean query and the graph structure G as input. The parser computes the CTF and GMTF on the cluster label domain using structural F+C rules derived from the graph. 2. Multimodal 3D Texture Mapping: Perform rendering using a strategy that simultaneously accesses the original voxel model V and the labelled voxel model LV. For each fragment (ray sample): Fetch the voxel value v = V[\mathbf{x}] from the original model. Fetch the cluster label c = LV[\mathbf{x}] from the auxiliary model. Use c to look up rendering parameters from the computed CTF and GMTF. Apply structural F+C shading using the fetched parameters (visibility, color, opacity, gradient modulation). Merge the rendering parameters according to a user-specified weight to produce the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplegrid(grid, x, y, z): Dx, Dy, Dz = len(grid), len(grid[0]), len(grid[0][0]) ix = max(0, min(Dx - 1, int(x))) iy = max(0, min(Dy - 1, int(y))) iz = max(0, min(Dz - 1, int(z))) return grid[ix][iy][iz] def preprocess(V, criteria): Dx, Dy, Dz = len(V), len(V[0]), len(V[0][0]) clustermap = {} nextid = 0 LV = [[[0]Dz for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): v = V[x][y][z] satisfied = tuple(sorted(c(v) for c in criteria)) if satisfied not in clustermap: clustermap[satisfied] = nextid nextid += 1 LV[x][y][z] = clustermap[satisfied] numcriteria = len(criteria) G = {i: set() for i in range(numcriteria)} for i in range(numcriteria): for j in range(numcriteria): if i != j: implies = all(criteriai <= criteriaj for x in range(Dx) for y in range(Dy) for z in range(Dz)) if implies: G[i].add(j) return G, LV, clustermap def parsequery(querystr, criteria, clustermap): CTF = {} GMTF = {} for cid, satisfiedcriteria in clustermap.items(): expr = querystr for idx, issat in enumerate(satisfiedcriteria): expr = expr.replace(f"c{idx}", str(issat)) isselected = eval(expr) if isselected: CTF[cid] = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) GMTF[cid] = 1.0 else: CTF[cid] = (0.0, 0.1, 0.0) GMTF[cid] = 0.2 return CTF, GMTF def render(V, LV, CTF, GMTF, rays, stepsize=0.1): image = [] for ray in rays: coloracc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaacc = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < 100.0: pos = ray.origin + ray.dir t v = samplegrid(V, pos.x, pos.y, pos.z) c = samplegrid(LV, pos.x, pos.y, pos.z) color, opacity, visibility = CTF.get(c, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) gradmod = GMTF.get(c, 0.0) if visibility: sample = [color[i] v for i in range(3)] alpha = opacity gradmod coloracc = [coloracc[i] + sample[i] alpha (1 - alphaacc) for i in range(3)] alphaacc += alpha (1 - alphaacc) t += stepsize image.append(coloracc) return image Parameters: CTF: Defined on the cluster label domain. Determines visibility, color, and opacity for each cluster. GMTF: Defined on the cluster label domain. Determines the gradient modulation factor for each cluster. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multimodal Data: The method explicitly supports multimodal datasets (e.g., MR/SPECT, MR/PET), but the classification criteria must be defined across modalities. Boolean Expression Parsing: The parser relies on the graph structure to resolve boolean expressions. Cluster Label Uniqueness: Each cluster must have a unique identifier. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly represents the structure of multiclassified datasets, allowing users to explore structural relationships between classification criteria. Supports interactive boolean queries. Limitations: Requires preprocessing to construct the graph and labelled model. The method is specific to multiclassified scalar volumes and may not directly apply to tensor or vector fields without adaptation. When to Use: When the user needs to understand the logical relationships between different classification criteria in a multiclassified volume dataset. When Not to Use: When the data is not multiclassified or when the structural relationships between classes are not of interest. Structural Focus+Context rendering was proposed by P. Abellán, A. Puig, and D. Tost. The method was received on 31 March 2007, accepted on 1 August 2007, and posted online on 27 October 2007. It addresses the limitation of existing illustrative visualization systems that do not explicitly represent the structure of multiclassified datasets. The work is associated with the handling of multimodal and time-varying data, though prior systems lacked explicit structural representation.
