name: Glyph Vis Layer
head: 3D Glyphs, 3D Glyphs Representation, Glyph rendering with density sampling
body: The Glyph Vis Layer renders instances of 3D geometry (glyphs) or 2D image sprites at coordinates specified by a point set data object. It solves the problem of visualizing discrete features, vectors, or scalar fields by mapping data attributes to the position, orientation, size, and color of geometric primitives. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific reliance on geometry instancing for performance, whereas Hybrid Rendering for Stress Tensor Fields focuses on tensor-specific glyph alignment and Structural Focus+Context Rendering emphasizes the decoupling of focus/context paths via structural graphs. Inputs: 1. Point Set Data: A dataset containing coordinates (and optionally associated scalar/vector arrays). 2. Glyph Geometry: A source 3D mesh (e.g., arrow, cone, sphere) or 2D image sprite. 3. Configuration Parameters: Settings for alignment, color, size, and sampling strategy. Outputs: A rendered scene containing multiple instances of the glyph geometry, transformed according to the input data attributes. Data Structures: Point Set: Array of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Glyph Mesh: A single 3D geometry definition (vertices, normals, texture coordinates). Transformation Matrix: A 4 \times 4 matrix per glyph instance, computed from position, orientation, and scale. Steps: 1. Sampling: Determine the subset of points from the input dataset where glyphs will be placed. Strategies include: Regular: Uniform distribution. Random: Stochastic distribution. Density-based: Uses a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm (Markov Chain Monte Carlo method) to sample points based on data density. 2. Positioning: For each selected point, set the glyph's translation to the point's coordinates (x, y, z). 3. Orientation: Align the glyph's local axes. Options include: Axis-aligned: Fixed orientation. Direction-vector aligned: Oriented along a selected vector variable from the dataset. Random: Random rotation. 4. Sizing: Determine the glyph's scale. Options include: Constant: Defined as a percentage of the largest extent of the data object. Axial Radius: Constant value or driven by a selected width scalar variable. 5. Coloring: Assign color to the glyphs. Options include: Constant: Single solid color. Data-driven: Pseudocoloring based on a selected scalar data array. 6. Rendering Optimization: Use geometry instancing to draw the same geometry at many different locations. This avoids generating many copies of the source geometry into a single large mesh, which consumes more memory and is slower. 7. Special Handling: Apply normal maps if available. For image-based glyphs, apply alpha masks to mask away negative space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderglyphs(pointset, glyphmesh, config): """ Renders glyphs using geometry instancing. Args: pointset: List of (x, y, z) coordinates. glyphmesh: Source 3D geometry (vertices, indices). config: Dictionary with keys: sampling: 'regular', 'random', or 'density' alignment: 'axisaligned', 'directionvector', or 'random' colormode: 'constant' or 'datadriven' sizemode: 'constant' or 'axialradius' colorvalue: scalar for constant color colorarray: data array for data-driven color sizevalue: scalar for constant size sizearray: data array for axial radius directionarray: vector array for alignment """ # Step 1: Sampling if config['sampling'] == 'density': # Metropolis-Hastings algorithm implementation required selectedpoints = metropolishastingssample(pointset, config) elif config['sampling'] == 'random': selectedpoints = randomsample(pointset, config) else: # regular selectedpoints = pointset # Step 2-5: Compute transformations and attributes instances = [] for i, point in enumerate(selectedpoints): # Position translation = point # Orientation if config['alignment'] == 'directionvector': direction = getvectorfromarray(config['directionarray'], i) rotation = aligntovector(direction) elif config['alignment'] == 'random': rotation = randomrotation() else: # axisaligned rotation = identitymatrix() # Size if config['sizemode'] == 'axialradius': scale = getscalarfromarray(config['sizearray'], i) else: # constant scale = config['sizevalue'] # Color if config['colormode'] == 'datadriven': color = getscalarfromarray(config['colorarray'], i) else: # constant color = config['colorvalue'] # Combine into instance data instance = { 'translation': translation, 'rotation': rotation, 'scale': scale, 'color': color } instances.append(instance) # Step 6: Render using geometry instancing # Draw glyphmesh once per instance with the computed transformation drawinstanced(glyphmesh, instances) Parameters: Glyph Size: Defined as a percentage of the largest extent of the data object. Axial Radius: Specified as a constant or according to a selected width scalar variable. Glyph Color: Can be set to a single color or pseudocolored by a data array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Using the generic "Glyph filter" (which generates many copies of the source geometry) is significantly slower and more memory-intensive than the 3D Glyph representation (geometry instancing). Occlusion: Overlapping glyphs may obscure data. Transparency-based solutions or selection menus can help, but may require different techniques if dataset size doubles. Jitter: Avoid position jitter (offset) for continuous data as it is misleading. Points representation renders a dataset as a collection of points by first extracting its surface mesh. It serves as a lightweight alternative to solid surface rendering, allowing users to avoid translucent geometries during interactive exploration while reserving them for final presentations. It is distinguished from Surface by rendering only discrete vertices rather than filled polygons, and from Wireframe by omitting edge connectivity information. A filter that extracts cell center positions for glyphing. It extracts cell centers from the hypertree grid and hooks the output to a glyphing filter to render spheres at each center, colored by depth. A technique to resolve overlapping data points in continuous scatterplots by rendering points with partial transparency and providing a selection menu during drag operations. It avoids jitter (position offset), which is misleading for continuous data, and avoids filtering or distortion that removes or alters data representation. A pitfall is that the current transparency solution may be insufficient if the dataset size doubles. Rendering of labeled synapses stored in tabular format, including position, textual label, and IDs of connected objects (axon and dendrite). The system allows users to add new synapses to the data, which are stored in the visualization archive. Synapses are rendered as small geometric shapes at specified positions, and users can select individual synapses to center them in the view. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of glyph instances. Geometry instancing allows for efficient GPU rendering, making it typically much faster than generating and rendering a single large mesh of all glyph copies. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of glyph instances and the size of the source glyph geometry. It is significantly lower than the "Glyph filter" approach, which stores a copy of the geometry for every instance. Strengths: High performance via instancing; flexible mapping of data attributes to visual properties (position, orientation, size, color); supports various sampling strategies including density-based. Limitations: Overlapping glyphs can cause occlusion issues; density-based sampling requires complex MCMC implementation; not suitable for continuous field visualization without significant sampling. When to use: When visualizing discrete features, vectors, or sparse data points where geometric representation is more informative than volume or surface rendering. When not to use: When the dataset is extremely large and occlusion becomes unmanageable without advanced techniques; when continuous field visualization is required without sampling artifacts. The Glyph Vis Layer is part of an extensible rendering engine that supports multiple visualization layers. It was developed to provide expressive and engaging 3D visualizations by harnessing natural and traditional visual media. The concept of drawing 3D geometry at a subset of points has been implemented in various visualization tools, including ParaView, where it is recommended over the generic Glyph filter for performance reasons. The method has been applied in diverse fields, including stress tensor field visualization [8909-hybrid-rendering-for-stress-tensor-fields.md], structural focus+context rendering [14778-structural-focus-context-rendering.md], and petascale volume visualization of microscopy data streams. name: CakES MCS Layout
head: CakES, Cake View, MCS View
body: CakES MCS Layout is a 3D visualization metaphor for Minimal Cut Sets (MCSs) in fault tree analysis, representing MCSs as cylindrical "cakes" arranged in concentric rings and levels based on their Fault Probability (FP). It solves the problem of visualizing hierarchical probabilistic dependencies in complex systems by mapping abstract logical structures into a spatial layout where proximity and height encode risk and composition. It sets itself apart from general volume rendering methods by being a structural, glyph-based layout algorithm specifically designed for fault tree analysis, decoupling the geometric placement of MCSs from the internal structure of their constituent Basic Events (BEs). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Minimal Cut Sets (MCSs). Each MCS has a computed Fault Probability (FP) and a list of Basic Events (BEs). The number of BEs in an MCS is denoted as n. Output: A 3D layout where each MCS is represented as a cylinder (cake) positioned at specific coordinates (x, y, z) and height h. Data Structures: MCS Object: Contains a list of BEs, the computed FP, and the number of BEs n. Level: A grouping of MCSs with similar FP ranges. Ring: A concentric circle within a level, indexed by RingNo. Parameters: Rs: Base radius of an MCS plus empty distance. Fixed at 18.5 (derived from source text 0.5 + 1 8, interpreted as 0.5 + 18). RingNo: Integer index of the ring (1-based or 0-based, implied by multiplication). h: Height of the MCS cylinder in the y-direction. Steps: 1. Compute Fault Probability: For each MCS, compute its FP as the product of the FPs of its constituent BEs. 2. Determine Levels: Group MCSs into levels based on their FP values. The user can manipulate level boundaries using menu sliders. 3. Compute Radii: Calculate the base radius Rs = 18.5. For each ring in a level, calculate the ring radius Rc using: Rc = Rs \times \text{RingNo} Calculate the level radius Rh using: Rh = Rs + Rc 4. Calculate MCS Counts: Calculate the number of MCSs per ring mr. The source provides the formula: mr = \max(\text{NoMCS}) = \frac{\text{length}}{\text{width}} \times \frac{\text{height}}{\text{width}} \times \frac{\text{width}}{\text{length}} Note: The source text also mentions π arcsin Rs Rc in a garbled context, but the explicit formula given is the fraction product. The angular distribution logic is implied but not fully defined in the provided text. Calculate the number of MCSs per level mh by summing mr for all rings in that level: mh = \sum{r \in \text{ring}} mr Calculate the total number of MCSs m by summing mh for all levels: m = \sum{h \in \text{levels}} mh 5. Place MCSs: Each MCS is represented as a cylinder. The radius of the cylinder is determined by Rs. The height h in the y-direction is determined by the number of BEs n in the MCS. Placement of BEs within the MCS cylinder depends on n: If n = 1, the BE is placed in the center of the MCS (x, y, z). If n = 2, BEs are placed in a specific configuration (details cut off in source, but implied to be symmetric). MCSs are distributed within the rings defined by Rc and Rh. 6. Visual Enhancements: A black ring is placed around each group of MCSs to improve distinguishability and reduce color contrast errors. Coloring is applied based on risk level (Low, Medium, High) with specific colors for normal vision and color vision deficiency (Protanopia, Deuteranopia, Tritanopia). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecakeslayout(mcslist, rsbase=18.5): """ Computes the 3D layout for CakES MCS visualization. Args: mcslist: List of MCS objects, each with 'fps' (list of BE probabilities) and 'bes' (list of BEs). rsbase: Base radius Rs (default 18.5). Returns: List of MCS layout objects with 'x', 'y', 'z', 'h', 'ringno', 'levelidx'. """ # Step 1: Compute Fault Probability for each MCS for mcs in mcslist: # FP is product of BE FPs mcs.fp = 1.0 for befp in mcs.fps: mcs.fp = befp mcs.n = len(mcs.bes) # Step 2: Group into Levels based on FP # Note: Exact binning logic depends on user sliders, assumed pre-sorted or binned here levels = groupmcsbyfp(mcslist) layouts = [] for levelidx, levelmcs in enumerate(levels): # Step 3: Determine Rings for this level # Assume rings are determined by some capacity or user setting # For simplicity, assume all MCS in a level are in one ring or distributed # The source implies multiple rings per level. # We need to distribute MCSs into rings. # Calculate max MCSs per ring mr # Using the formula from source: mr = (length/width) (height/width) (width/length) # This formula seems to simplify to 1 or is context-dependent. # We will use a placeholder for ring capacity if not explicitly defined by geometry. # However, the source says mr = max(NoMCS) =... # Let's assume a fixed capacity or derived from geometry. # Since the formula is garbled, we use a generic capacity Cr for implementation. ringcapacity = 10 # Placeholder, source formula unclear rings = [] currentringmcs = [] for mcs in levelmcs: currentringmcs.append(mcs) if len(currentringmcs) >= ringcapacity: rings.append(currentringmcs) currentringmcs = [] if currentringmcs: rings.append(currentringmcs) # Step 4: Calculate Radii and Place MCSs for ringno, ringmcs in enumerate(rings): # RingNo is 1-based for calculation ringnocalc = ringno + 1 # Rc = Rs RingNo rc = rsbase ringnocalc # Rh = Rs + Rc rh = rsbase + rc # Distribute MCSs in the ring # Assuming uniform angular distribution nummcsinring = len(ringmcs) anglestep = 2 math.pi / nummcsinring for i, mcs in enumerate(ringmcs): angle = i anglestep # Position in x-z plane # Radius from center is Rc? Or between Rs and Rh? # Source says "radius of the ring holding the MCS Rc is Rc = Rs RingNo" # And "level radius Rh is Rh = Rs + Rc" # It implies the MCS is placed at radius Rc from the center of the level? # Or Rc is the radius of the ring itself. # Let's assume MCS center is at distance Rc from level center. x = rc math.cos(angle) z = rc math.sin(angle) y = 0 # Base y # Height h based on n # Source: "h be the height of the MCS's cylinder in y direction" # And "If n=1... If n=2..." # Let's assume h is proportional to n or fixed. # Source doesn't give explicit h(n) formula, only placement of BEs. # We'll set h = n unitheight unitheight = 1.0 h = mcs.n unitheight layouts.append({ 'mcs': mcs, 'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z, 'h': h, 'ringno': ringnocalc, 'levelidx': levelidx }) return layouts def groupmcsbyfp(mcslist): """Placeholder for FP-based binning.""" # Sort by FP sortedmcs = sorted(mcslist, key=lambda m: m.fp) # Simple equal binning for demonstration # In reality, this is controlled by user sliders if not sortedmcs: return [] # Assume 3 levels for example chunksize = len(sortedmcs) // 3 levels = [] for i in range(0, len(sortedmcs), chunksize): levels.append(sortedmcs[i:i+chunksize]) return levels Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Levels: If a level contains no MCSs, it should not be displayed. Color Vision Deficiency: Colors must be chosen to avoid confusion for Protanopia, Deuteranopia, and Tritanopia. Red and Green should not be neighbors. Garbled Formulas: The formula for mr is ambiguous in the source. Implementers should verify the intended geometric distribution logic. BE Placement: The exact placement of BEs within the MCS cylinder for n > 2 is not fully detailed in the source. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of MCSs for placement, assuming constant ring capacity. Sorting by FP is O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of MCSs. Strengths: Intuitive representation of hierarchical risk; supports color-blind users; interactive manipulation of levels. Limitations: Limited to fault tree analysis; scalability depends on the number of MCSs and rings; formulas for ring capacity are unclear. When to Use: Visualizing fault trees with a moderate number of MCSs where probabilistic hierarchy is key. When Not to Use: Large-scale fault trees with thousands of MCSs may suffer from occlusion and clutter. CakES MCS Layout was introduced in the context of fault tree analysis visualization. It is described in the DFU Volume 2, Scientific Visualization: Interactions, Features, Metaphors. The method aims to provide a 3D metaphor for Minimal Cut Sets, using "cakes" to represent MCSs. name: Interactive UI for Volume Rendering
head: Dear ImGui UI for Volume Rendering, Interactive IV Decomposition Interface, Interactive Panes and Gizmos, Interactive UI, Peeling IVs interface, Smooth viewpoint transition
body: This method provides a structured graphical user interface for interacting with volume rendering parameters, specifically focusing on the interactive decomposition of isovolume (IV) layers and the dynamic adjustment of the camera viewpoint. It solves the problem of navigating complex, multi-layered volumetric structures by allowing users to "peel" IVs from outside to inside while simultaneously optimizing the viewing angle to maximize information visibility. It sets itself apart from general clipping or cropping methods by integrating a specific IV decomposition workflow with an entropy-based viewpoint optimization system, where the camera position is automatically adjusted via smooth interpolation to reflect the new structural state. The method implements a feedback loop where user selection of an IV triggers a visual preview, a structural update, and a camera transition. The interface is typically composed of three coordinated windows. Inputs: User mouse clicks/selections on UI elements; current volume dataset; current transfer function; current camera state (position/orientation). Outputs: Updated rendering image; updated camera position; updated UI state (highlighted/grayed elements). The interface maintains three synchronized views: 1. Left Window (Level-set Graph): Displays the hierarchical inclusion relationships of IVs. Each IV is represented as a node/link. 2. Middle Window (Peeling View): Renders the decomposed feature IVs. Supports transparency for previewing inner structures. 3. Right Window (Entropy Distribution): Displays a color-coded distribution of viewpoint entropy on the viewing sphere, calculated from the remaining combinations of IVs. IV Status: Boolean flag indicating if an IV is active, transparent (preview), or removed. Viewpoint Entropy: A scalar value representing the information content of a specific viewpoint given the current set of visible IVs. Quaternion: Used to represent the camera orientation for smooth interpolation. 1. Initialization: Render the initial volume with all IVs active. Calculate the initial optimal viewpoint based on the full set of IVs and display the entropy distribution in the right window. 2. Selection: User selects an IV via the Left Window (Level-set graph) or Middle Window. The interface changes the status of the selected IV to "transparent" in the Middle Window, allowing the user to see the interior structure. The corresponding link in the Left Window is emphasized (highlighted). 3. Confirmation: User confirms the selection (e.g., via a button or double-click). The selected IV is removed from the active rendering set in the Middle Window. Silhouettes of the removed IV are left in its place to maintain spatial context. The corresponding link in the Left Window is grayed out. 4. Recalculation: The interface recalculates the viewpoint entropy distribution for the updated combination of remaining IVs. 5. Viewpoint Transition: Identify the new optimal viewpoint (often marked as a black spot on the projection of the upper viewing hemisphere). Move the viewpoint smoothly from the previous best viewpoint to the next optimal position. This movement is achieved using Spherical Linear Interpolation (SLERP) based on quaternion representations of the camera orientation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. currentivs = set(allivs) currentviewpointquaternion = initialoptimalquaternion(currentivs) entropymap = calculateentropydistribution(currentivs) def onivselected(ivid): """User selects an IV for peeling.""" # Step 2: Preview setivtransparency(ivid, alpha=0.5) # Render transparently highlightlinkinleftwindow(ivid) return "preview" def onivconfirmed(ivid): """User confirms removal of the IV.""" # Step 3: Remove removeivfromrendering(ivid) renderivsilhouette(ivid) # Leave silhouette grayoutlinkinleftwindow(ivid) # Update state currentivs.remove(ivid) # Step 4: Recalculate newentropymap = calculateentropydistribution(currentivs) newoptimalquaternion = findbestviewpointquaternion(currentivs) # Step 5: Smooth Transition oldquaternion = currentviewpointquaternion currentviewpointquaternion = slerp(oldquaternion, newoptimalquaternion, t=0.0) # Animation loop would interpolate t from 0 to 1 return newentropymap, newoptimalquaternion def renderloop(): while running: rendermiddlewindow(currentivs) renderleftwindow(currentivs) renderrightwindow(entropymap) updatecameraorientation(currentviewpointquaternion) Degenerate IVs: If an IV has no volume or is fully occluded, its removal may not change the entropy distribution significantly. The system should handle cases where the "next optimal viewpoint" is identical to the current one to avoid unnecessary camera jitter. Precision in SLERP: When the previous and next viewpoints are nearly identical or opposite (antipodal), quaternion interpolation can become unstable. A guard condition should check for the dot product of the quaternions; if close to -1, use an alternative interpolation path or normalize carefully. Synchronization: The three windows must update in lockstep. A delay in updating the entropy map (Right Window) while the volume (Middle Window) is already modified can confuse the user. This method enables interactive editing of volumetric data by mapping 2D user input to 3D space using a proxy plane. It solves the ambiguity of depth selection in volumetric displays or 3D Gaussian splatting where a fixed projection plane is not naturally available or intuitive. It sets itself apart from Focus Marker with Smooth Interpolation by using an explicit geometric proxy for input rather than implicit field interpolation, and from Omniview View Volume Control by focusing on editing operations rather than view volume navigation. This method provides a system to maintain a visible focus marker in 3D volume rendering and linked 2D slices, using fractional coordinates for interpolation and smooth animation between target positions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Interactive Editing with Proxy Plane Manipulation by decoupling the logical position (fractional) from the display coordinate (world mm), ensuring alignment during orbit, zoom, resize, and PNG export, whereas proxy planes typically manipulate the view volume directly. Omniview View Volume Control is a user interface technique for a true 3-D display device that allows users to control the position and size (radius) of the 3D view volume using a mouse tracking window and a joystick. It provides a direct manipulation alternative to the indirect WIMP (Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer) interface, enabling rapid large-scale movements to a desired display area. While the WIMP interface offers finer control, it requires the user to be 3-4 feet from the display, whereas the direct manipulation methods allow for more immersive interaction. A method for interactive 3D visualization using the VTK.js library, supporting camera rotation, zooming, and spatial exploration of the volume representation. It renders the 3D volume using VTK.js to allow interactive camera rotation, zooming, and spatial exploration. The surface and volume appearance depends on the configuration of the transfer function and image density. Time Complexity: The recalculation of viewpoint entropy is the most expensive operation. It depends on the number of IV combinations and the resolution of the viewing sphere discretization. SLERP is O(1). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the level-set graph, IV data, and the entropy map. The entropy map size depends on the discretization of the viewing sphere. Strengths: Provides an intuitive way to explore nested volumetric structures ("peeling"). The automatic viewpoint adjustment ensures the user always has an informative view of the remaining data. Limitations: The "peeling" workflow is specific to IV decomposition and may not be suitable for all volume visualization tasks. The reliance on entropy calculation assumes that information content correlates with visual clarity, which may not always hold for all datasets. When to use: When analyzing complex, multi-layered volumetric data (e.g., scientific simulations with multiple isovolumes) where understanding the internal structure is critical. When not to use: For simple volume visualization where only the outer surface is of interest, or when real-time performance is critical and entropy calculation is too slow. The method originates from research on interactive volume decomposition and optimal viewpoint selection. The specific implementation using Dear ImGui and OpenGL for auxiliary elements is described in the context of NeRFshop. The core algorithm for IV decomposition and entropy-based viewpoint selection was introduced in "Previewing Volume Decomposition Through Optimal Viewpoints". The VTK.js variant represents a web-based implementation of interactive volume rendering. name: Interactive Editing with Proxy Plane Manipulation
head: Intrinsic Field Selection and Albedo Editing via Proxy Planes, Proxy Plane Manipulation
body: This method enables interactive editing of volumetric data by mapping 2D user input to 3D space using a proxy plane. It solves the ambiguity of depth selection in volumetric displays or 3D Gaussian splatting where a fixed projection plane is not naturally available or intuitive. It sets itself apart from Focus Marker with Smooth Interpolation by using an explicit geometric proxy for input rather than implicit field interpolation, and from Omniview View Volume Control by focusing on editing operations rather than view volume navigation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User 2D screen coordinates (mouse/touch), current camera/viewpoint parameters, and the 3D scene data (volumetric voxels or 3D Gaussians). Output: Modified 3D scene data (e.g., updated albedo values, added/removed primitives). Data Structures: Proxy Plane: A 2D plane defined in 3D space. In 3D Gaussian splatting contexts, this is often a textured plane used to initialize new Gaussians. Scene Data: Volumetric: Voxel grid or point cloud. Gaussian Splatting: Set of 3D Gaussians, each with position, covariance, color/albedo, and opacity. Steps: 1. Define Proxy Plane: Establish the proxy plane relative to the user's line of sight or a fixed reference frame. Dynamic Approach: Update the plane orientation to remain orthogonal to the user's line of sight as the viewpoint changes. Fixed Approach: Keep the plane fixed but make it highly visible to aid user understanding. 2. Map Input: Project the user's 2D screen coordinates onto the proxy plane to determine the 3D interaction point. If using a dynamic plane, recalculate the projection matrix based on the current viewpoint. 3. Select/Modify Data: For Volumetric Displays: Identify the voxel or point at the intersection of the interaction ray and the proxy plane. Apply edits (e.g., color change, deletion). For 3D Gaussian Splats: a. Identify the target Gaussian or region on the proxy plane. b. Initialize new Gaussians on the textured proxy plane with user-defined properties (e.g., albedo). c. Place these new Gaussians in 3D space using the proxy depth information. d. Add the new Gaussians to the existing set. 4. Optimize/Update: Re-optimize the scene parameters to match the edited state. In Gaussian splatting, re-optimize albedo values of the augmented set. Remove primitives with high counter values (indicating redundancy or error) before densification steps. Parameters: Proxy Plane Visibility: High visibility is recommended for fixed planes to prevent confusion. Optimization Iterations: Densification steps may occur every 100 iterations from iteration 500 to 15000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewpoint Change During Drag: Fixing the input mapping at the start of a drag becomes confusing if the user's viewpoint changes significantly. Solutions include dynamic plane updates or high visibility of the fixed plane. Lack of Fixed Projection Plane: Volumetric displays lack an explicit projection plane, requiring careful definition of the input plane. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def editwithproxyplane(scene, userinput2d, viewpoint): # Define proxy plane based on strategy if strategy == "dynamic": # Plane orthogonal to user's line of sight proxyplane = Plane.orthogonalto(viewpoint.direction) else: # Fixed plane, ensure high visibility proxyplane = getfixedproxyplane() highlight(proxyplane) # Map 2D input to 3D point on proxy plane interactionpoint3d = project2dto3d(userinput2d, proxyplane, viewpoint) if scenetype == "gaussiansplatting": # Initialize new Gaussians on the proxy plane newgaussians = [] for edit in useredits: g = Gaussian() g.position = interactionpoint3d + edit.offset g.albedo = edit.color g.opacity = edit.opacity newgaussians.append(g) # Add to scene scene.gaussians.extend(newgaussians) # Re-optimize albedo reoptimizealbedo(scene.gaussians) # Remove redundant primitives if necessary removehighcounterprimitives(scene.gaussians) elif scenetype == "volumetric": # Identify voxel/point at interactionpoint3d target = findvoxelat(interactionpoint3d) if target: applyedit(target, useredits) return scene A technique to handle 3D manipulators on volumetric displays by defining the input plane relative to the user's line of sight. It sets itself apart by adapting to viewpoint changes, preventing confusion when the user moves. Choose this when the user frequently changes their viewing angle during interaction. Pitfall: Fixing the input mapping at the start of a drag becomes confusing if the viewpoint changes significantly. Time Complexity: Depends on the optimization step. For Gaussian splatting, re-optimization can be costly, occurring every 100 iterations from 500 to 15000. Memory Complexity: Increases with the number of added Gaussians or modified voxels. Strengths: Intuitive editing in 3D space without a fixed projection plane. Effective for intrinsic decomposition and editing of 3D Gaussian splats. Limitations: Confusion if viewpoint changes during drag without dynamic updates. Requires careful handling of volumetric display constraints. When to Use: Interactive editing on volumetric displays or 3D Gaussian splatting where 2D GUI techniques are insufficient. When Not to Use: When the user's viewpoint is static and a fixed projection plane is sufficient. Originated from research into user interfaces for volumetric displays and intrinsic decomposition of 3D Gaussian splats. The concept of using a proxy plane for editing in 3D Gaussian splatting was implemented in an interactive viewer by Shah et al.. The challenge of input mapping on volumetric displays, which lack a fixed projection plane, was addressed by defining input planes relative to the user's line of sight. name: Focus Marker with Smooth Interpolation
head: Focus Marker Animation, Smooth Focus Transition
body: This method provides a system to maintain a visible focus marker in 3D volume rendering and linked 2D slices, using fractional coordinates for interpolation and smooth animation between target positions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Interactive Editing with Proxy Plane Manipulation by decoupling the logical position (fractional) from the display coordinate (world mm), ensuring alignment during orbit, zoom, resize, and PNG export, whereas proxy planes typically manipulate the view volume directly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User interaction events (mouse wheel, clicks) providing target positions; current volume dimensions. Output: Updated current focus position; redrawn 3D volume and 2D slices with updated crosshairs/markers. Data Structures: The core state is held in a FocusLocation object: mm: number[] — World coordinates in millimeters. frac: number[] — Fractional coordinates, range [0, 1]. visible: boolean — Visibility flag for the marker. Parameters: duration: Animation duration in milliseconds. Typical value: 110 ms. notifyInterval: Minimum time between listener notifications in milliseconds. Typical value: 45 ms. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set current and target positions to [0.5, 0.5, 0.55]. 2. Rendering Hook: Override the core scene drawing function (e.g., drawSceneCore) to call drawMarkers() if the marker is enabled and volumes exist. 3. Trigger: On a location change event, call the moveTo function with the desired fractional coordinates. 4. Cancel Previous: Inside moveTo, cancel any existing animation frame to prevent queueing. 5. Capture Start: Calculate the from position as the current current value. 6. Set Target: Update the target position. Clamp the input fractional coordinates to [0, 1]. 7. Accessibility Check: If the reducedMotion flag is true, set current = target immediately and skip animation. 8. Start Animation: Otherwise, start a requestAnimationFrame loop with the specified duration. 9. Progress Calculation: In each tick, calculate progress: progress = \min\left(1, \frac{now - started}{duration}\right) where now is the current timestamp and started is the animation start time. 10. Easing: Apply cubic ease-out: eased = 1 - \text{Math.pow}(1 - progress, 3). 11. Interpolation: Update current using linear interpolation with the eased factor: current = from + (target - from) \times eased. 12. Apply: Call apply() to update the crosshair positions in the 3D and 2D views based on the new current. 13. Notify: Notify listeners every 45 ms or at completion of the animation. Wheel Scrolling Logic: 1. Check for modifier keys (ctrl, meta, alt, shift) or if deltaY is zero; return immediately if present. 2. Get the canvas rect and calculate pixel coordinates relative to the tile. 3. Get the tile index and tile object. 4. Return if the tile is null or axCorSag > 2. 5. Determine the axis from axCorSag using the mapping [2, 1, 0][axCorSag]. 6. Calculate voxel movement: voxels = \frac{pixels}{50} Clamp voxels to [-4, 4]. 7. World Mode (isSliceMM is true): Convert current target to world mm. Add direction voxels to the axis component. Convert back to fractional coordinates. Check bounds: if the new fractional position is outside [0, 1] (i.e., < 0 or > 1), abort the move to prevent invalid states. Call moveTo with the new fractional coordinates. 8. Fractional Mode (isSliceMM is false): Update the fractional coordinate directly. Clamp to [0.5/dim, 1 - 0.5/dim] where dim is the dimension size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time import math class FocusMarker: def init(self, volumedims): # volumedims: list of int, e.g., [512, 512, 100] self.volumedims = volumedims self.current = [0.5, 0.5, 0.55] self.target = [0.5, 0.5, 0.55] self.animationid = None self.lastnotifytime = 0 self.duration = 110 # ms self.notifyinterval = 45 # ms self.reducedmotion = False self.isslicemm = False def drawscenecore(self, drawmarkersenabled, volumesexist): if drawmarkersenabled and volumesexist: self.drawmarkers() def drawmarkers(self): # Implementation specific to renderer (e.g., NiiVue) # Updates crosshairs based on self.current pass def apply(self): # Updates the visual representation of the focus marker # and synchronizes with peer views if necessary pass def notifylisteners(self, now): if now - self.lastnotifytime >= self.notifyinterval: # Trigger UI update or event dispatch self.lastnotifytime = now def moveto(self, newfraccoords): # Cancel existing animation if self.animationid is not None: cancelAnimationFrame(self.animationid) self.animationid = None # Clamp target to [0, 1] clampedtarget = [max(0.0, min(1.0, c)) for c in newfraccoords] self.target = clampedtarget frompos = list(self.current) # Accessibility: reduced motion if self.reducedmotion: self.current = list(self.target) self.apply() self.notifylisteners(time.time() 1000) return # Start animation started = time.time() 1000 # ms self.animationid = requestAnimationFrame(lambda nowms: self.tick(frompos, started, nowms)) def tick(self, frompos, started, now): progress = min(1.0, (now - started) / self.duration) eased = 1.0 - math.pow(1.0 - progress, 3) # Linear interpolation with eased factor self.current = [frompos[i] + (self.target[i] - frompos[i]) eased for i in range(3)] self.apply() self.notifylisteners(now) if progress < 1.0: self.animationid = requestAnimationFrame(lambda nowms: self.tick(frompos, started, nowms)) else: self.current = list(self.target) self.apply() self.notifylisteners(now) self.animationid = None def handlewheel(self, event, canvasrect, tile, axcorsag): # Check modifiers and deltaY if event.ctrlKey or event.metaKey or event.altKey or event.shiftKey or event.deltaY == 0: return # Get pixel coordinates relative to tile # Assuming event provides clientX/Y and tile provides offset/size # pixels = (event.clientX - tile.offsetX) / tile.scale... (simplified) # For this implementation, we assume 'pixels' is calculated as delta in pixels pixels = event.deltaY # Check tile validity if tile is None or axcorsag > 2: return # Determine axis: [2, 1, 0][axcorsag] axismap = [2, 1, 0] axis = axismap[axcorsag] # Calculate voxel movement voxels = pixels / 50.0 voxels = max(-4.0, min(4.0, voxels)) direction = 1.0 if voxels > 0 else -1.0 absvoxels = abs(voxels) if self.isslicemm: # Convert current target to world mm # Assuming volume has spacing and origin, or we map frac to mm # fractomm is a helper not defined in source, assumed to exist worldpos = self.fractiontomm(self.target) # Add direction voxels to axis worldpos[axis] += direction absvoxels # Convert back to frac newfrac = self.mmtofraction(worldpos) # Check bounds if newfrac[axis] < 0 or newfrac[axis] > 1: return # Abort move self.moveto(newfrac) else: # Update fractional coordinate directly # Clamp to 0.5/dim and 1 - 0.5/dim dim = self.volumedims[axis] minfrac = 0.5 / dim maxfrac = 1.0 - 0.5 / dim currentfrac = self.target[axis] step = direction absvoxels # Note: voxels here is in voxel units, but we are in frac mode? # Source says "update fractional coordinate directly with clamping". # It implies the 'voxels' calculated from pixels is added to the frac coordinate? # Or is 'voxels' converted to frac? # Source: "Calculate voxel movement: pixels / 50... If not isSliceMM, update fractional coordinate directly" # It does not explicitly state conversion from voxels to frac for the non-MM case. # However, adding raw voxel count to fractional coordinate [0,1] is dimensionally inconsistent. # Given the clamp is 0.5/dim, it suggests the step size might be normalized or 'voxels' is actually a frac delta. # Re-reading: "Calculate voxel movement: pixels / 50... If not isSliceMM, update fractional coordinate directly with clamping..." # It is likely that 'voxels' in the non-MM case is treated as a fractional step or the source implies a direct addition # where the magnitude is small enough or normalized. # Let's assume the 'voxels' value is added directly to the fractional coordinate as per the literal instruction, # though this is physically ambiguous without a scale factor. # However, looking at the MM case, it adds 'direction voxels' to mm. # In the non-MM case, it updates frac. # Let's assume the 'voxels' variable holds the delta in the respective unit system. # But 'pixels/50' is pixels. # Pitfall note: "When scrolling in world millimeters...". This implies the other case is fractional. # Let's assume the step size in frac is derived from the pixel delta. # Since no conversion formula is given for non-MM, we assume the 'voxels' value is used as the delta in frac space? # Or perhaps 'voxels' is converted to frac by dividing by dim? # Source does not give the conversion. # We will implement the literal "update fractional coordinate directly" with the calculated 'voxels' value, # but this is a likely gap. # Actually, looking at the clamp: 0.5/dim. If dim=512, clamp is ~0.001. # If voxels=4, adding 4 to 0.5 is impossible. # Therefore, 'voxels' must be converted to fractional units. # Standard conversion: fracdelta = voxeldelta / dim. # We will add this assumption as it is necessary for implementation. fracstep = direction absvoxels / dim newfracval = self.target[axis] + fracstep newfracval = max(minfrac, min(maxfrac, newfracval)) newfrac = list(self.target) newfrac[axis] = newfracval self.moveto(newfrac) def fractiontomm(self, fraccoords): # Helper to convert frac to world mm # Assumes volume origin and spacing are available # Not defined in source, assumed to be a standard utility return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for implementation detail def mmtofraction(self, mmcoords): # Helper to convert world mm to frac return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for implementation detail Subtopics: Interactive Editing with Proxy Plane Manipulation: Manipulates the view volume directly using proxy planes. Choose when direct view volume control is preferred over marker-based navigation. Link Omniview View Volume Control: Controls the view volume across multiple views simultaneously. Choose when synchronized multi-view volume adjustment is required. Link Time Complexity: Animation is frame-rate dependent via requestAnimationFrame. Notification overhead is bounded by notifyInterval (45 ms). Memory Complexity: Constant space for FocusLocation and animation state. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The use of fractional coordinates ensures that the marker remains aligned with the volume data regardless of orbit, zoom, resize, or PNG export operations. Strengths: Smooth user experience via cubic ease-out; robust handling of accessibility (reduced motion); prevents invalid states by clamping and aborting out-of-bounds moves in world mode. Limitations: Animation duration is fixed at 110 ms in the source implementation; world mode requires conversion between fractional and millimeter coordinates which depends on volume metadata. When to use: When a smooth, animated focus marker is needed for both 3D and linked 2D slice views. When not: When immediate, non-animated position changes are required, or when proxy plane manipulation is the preferred interaction model. This method is implemented in the OpenMRI application, an open-source tool for viewing and comparing MRI studies. It was developed by lev1nson and is part of the interactive UI components for volume rendering. The system uses NiiVue for rendering and SimpleITK for registration. lev1nson/OpenMRI, https://github.com/lev1nson/OpenMRI, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Omniview View Volume Control
head: Direct Manipulation via Joystick, Tracking Window
body: Omniview View Volume Control is a user interface technique for a true 3-D display device that allows users to control the position and size (radius) of the 3D view volume using a mouse tracking window and a joystick. It provides a direct manipulation alternative to the indirect WIMP (Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer) interface, enabling rapid large-scale movements to a desired display area. While the WIMP interface offers finer control, it requires the user to be 3-4 feet from the display, whereas the direct manipulation methods allow for more immersive interaction. The method combines two input modalities: a 2D mouse-based tracking window for spatial orientation and a joystick for precise control of the view volume's location, scale, and data value. Inputs: Mouse (for tracking window), Joystick (stick movement, forward/backward tilt, top button, bottom button). Outputs: Updated 3D view volume parameters (center position, radius, displayed value range) rendered on the Omniview display. The tracking window is a 2D map representing the area of interest, similar to a topographic or road map. Tracking Map: A 2D coordinate system representing the global area of interest. View Volume Indicator: A circle rendered on the tracking map. Center: Represents the center of the Omniview display. Radius: Represents the area being viewed. View Volume Radius: The radius of the view volume. In the described battlefield environment, this is typically greater than 2,500 meters and up to 500,000 meters. Joystick State: stickx, sticky: Horizontal and vertical displacement of the joystick stick. tiltnorth: Boolean, true if joystick is tilted forward. tiltsouth: Boolean, true if joystick is tilted backward. btntop: Boolean, true if top button is pressed. btnbottom: Boolean, true if bottom button is pressed. 1. Initialize Tracking Window: Display a 2D map of the area of interest. Render a circle on this map representing the current center and radius of the Omniview view volume. 2. Mouse Control (Position): Detect user drag of the circle on the tracking map. Update the center position of the view volume based on the drag delta. Update the circle's position on the tracking map to reflect the new center. 3. Joystick Position Control: Map joystick stick movement (horizontal/vertical displacement) to changes in the location of the view volume center. 4. Joystick Scale Control: If neither button is pressed: If tiltnorth is true, increase the view volume radius. If tiltsouth is true, decrease the view volume radius. 5. Joystick Value Control: If btntop is pressed: If tiltnorth is true, raise the value being viewed. If tiltsouth is true, lower the value being viewed. If btnbottom is pressed: If tiltnorth is true, raise the value being viewed. If tiltsouth is true, lower the value being viewed. 6. Feedback Update: Update the tracking map to show the change in location and size of the volume being displayed. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OmniviewViewVolumeControl: def init(self, initialradius=2500): # View volume state self.viewcenter = (0, 0) self.viewradius = initialradius self.viewedvalue = 0.0 # Tracking window state self.trackingmapcenter = self.viewcenter self.trackingmapradius = self.viewradius # Joystick state self.joystickstick = (0, 0) self.joysticktiltnorth = False self.joysticktiltsouth = False self.joystickbtntop = False self.joystickbtnbottom = False # Mouse state self.mousedragging = False self.mousedragstart = (0, 0) self.mousedragcurrent = (0, 0) def updatemouse(self, event): """Handle mouse events for tracking window interaction.""" if event.type == "dragstart": self.mousedragging = True self.mousedragstart = event.position self.mousedragcurrent = event.position elif event.type == "dragmove": if self.mousedragging: self.mousedragcurrent = event.position # Update view center based on drag delta delta = ( self.mousedragcurrent[0] - self.mousedragstart[0], self.mousedragcurrent[1] - self.mousedragstart[1]) self.viewcenter = ( self.viewcenter[0] + delta[0], self.viewcenter[1] + delta[1]) self.trackingmapcenter = self.viewcenter self.mousedragstart = self.mousedragcurrent elif event.type == "dragend": self.mousedragging = False def updatejoystick(self, state): """Handle joystick input for position, scale, and value control.""" self.joystickstick = state.stick self.joysticktiltnorth = state.tiltnorth self.joysticktiltsouth = state.tiltsouth self.joystickbtntop = state.btntop self.joystickbtnbottom = state.btnbottom # Position Control: Map stick movement to location change # Note: Exact mapping factor not specified in sources positionscale = 1.0 self.viewcenter = ( self.viewcenter[0] + self.joystickstick[0] positionscale, self.viewcenter[1] + self.joystickstick[1] positionscale) self.trackingmapcenter = self.viewcenter # Scale Control: Map tilt to radius change if not self.joystickbtntop and not self.joystickbtnbottom: scalestep = 100.0 # Placeholder step size if self.joysticktiltnorth: self.viewradius += scalestep elif self.joysticktiltsouth: self.viewradius -= scalestep # Clamp radius if necessary self.viewradius = max(0, self.viewradius) self.trackingmapradius = self.viewradius # Value Control: Map tilt + button to value change valuestep = 1.0 # Placeholder step size if self.joystickbtntop or self.joystickbtnbottom: if self.joysticktiltnorth: self.viewedvalue += valuestep elif self.joysticktiltsouth: self.viewedvalue -= valuestep def rendertrackingwindow(self): """Render the 2D map and view volume indicator.""" # Draw 2D map of area of interest draw2dmap() # Draw circle representing view volume center and radius drawcircle(self.trackingmapcenter, self.trackingmapradius) def renderomniview(self): """Render the 3D view volume on the Omniview display.""" # Render 3D scene with current view center, radius, and value render3dscene(self.viewcenter, self.viewradius, self.viewedvalue) Precision vs. Scale: For increasingly large view volumes (up to 500,000 meters), accurate scaling of objects may cause them to become smaller than a single voxel, making them invisible. The system prioritizes relative positioning and spacing over precise detail. User Distance: The direct manipulation interface (joystick/voice) does not provide all controls that the indirect WIMP interface does. Users relying solely on direct manipulation may lack fine-grained control. Button Ambiguity: Both the top and bottom buttons perform the same function (raising/lowering value based on tilt direction). The distinction between top and bottom buttons is not explained in the sources. Uses proxy planes for editing volume data. Chosen when precise local editing is needed. Interactive Editing with Proxy Plane Manipulation Uses a focus marker for smooth transitions. Chosen when smooth visual transitions are prioritized over direct manipulation. Focus Marker with Smooth Interpolation Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows rapid large-scale movements to the desired display area. Provides direct manipulation which can be more intuitive for spatial tasks. Limitations: Does not provide all controls available in the indirect WIMP interface. Requires user to be close to the display for effective joystick use, whereas WIMP allows for distance. When to Use: When rapid navigation and direct spatial control are prioritized over fine-grained parameter adjustment. When Not to Use: When fine-grained control is required, or when the user needs to be at a distance from the display. The Omniview View Volume Control method was developed for the SIMNET battlefield simulation environment. It was part of a user interface designed for a true 3-D display device, aiming to provide effective visualization of battlefield data. The system was described in a report from the Defense Technical Information Center (DTIC). DTIC ADA258995: A User Interface to a True 3-D Display Device, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA258995, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Masking with Gaussian Transition
head: Focus+Context Masking, Mask lens
body: Masking with Gaussian Transition provides a focus+context interaction technique that smoothly fades the visibility of specific volume regions or parameters from a center point outward, rather than using hard clipping boundaries. It solves the problem of abrupt visual discontinuities in volume rendering by applying a Gaussian weighting function to parameter weights (such as opacity or color) within a defined masking region. Unlike Clipping which removes data entirely, this method preserves context by gradually reducing the influence of masked elements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User-defined mask center/region parameters, volume data, and current rendering parameters (opacity, color, etc.). Output: A rendered image where the masked region exhibits a smooth transition from full visibility to full transparency (or parameter suppression). Data Structures: G-Buffer (Geometric Buffer): A 2.5D data structure storing per-pixel view-dependent information required for blending. Fields typically include: Rendering Color (RGB) Depth Opacity/Transparency Virtual Thickness (optional, for depth-based blending) Normal Vectors (optional) Object ID (optional) Texture Coordinates (optional) Method Steps: 1. Define Mask Region: Identify the center and extent of the masking region in the view space. 2. Calculate Gaussian Weight: For each pixel or sample point within the masking region, calculate a weight w based on its distance d from the mask center c. The weight follows a Gaussian function: w(d) = e^{-\frac{d^2}{2\sigma^2}} Where \sigma controls the spread of the transition. The weight is 1.0 at the center (d=0) and approaches 0.0 at the edges. 3. Apply Weight to Parameters: Multiply the original rendering parameters (e.g., opacity \alpha, color C) by the calculated weight w. \alpha{masked} = \alpha{original} \times w C{masked} = C{original} \times w This effectively fades the parameters from the center to the edge of the masking region. 4. Render and Blend: Render the scene using the weighted parameters. The G-Buffer stores these intermediate results. Final image composition uses 3D blending techniques (e.g., depth-based blending) to composite the masked and unmasked regions into a single view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applygaussianmask(renderingparams, maskcenter, masksigma, pixelposition): """ Applies Gaussian masking to rendering parameters. Args: renderingparams: Tuple of (opacity, color) for the current pixel. maskcenter: 2D or 3D coordinates of the mask center. masksigma: Standard deviation for the Gaussian falloff. pixelposition: 2D or 3D coordinates of the current pixel/sample. Returns: Tuple of (maskedopacity, maskedcolor). """ # Calculate squared distance from mask center distsq = sum((p - c)2 for p, c in zip(pixelposition, maskcenter)) # Calculate Gaussian weight # w = exp(-dist^2 / (2 sigma^2)) weight = math.exp(-distsq / (2 masksigma2)) # Apply weight to parameters originalopacity, originalcolor = renderingparams maskedopacity = originalopacity weight maskedcolor = originalcolor weight return maskedopacity, maskedcolor Parameters: masksigma: Controls the smoothness of the transition. Larger values create a wider, softer fade. maskcenter: The focal point of the mask. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient for small distances to avoid numerical instability in the exponential function. Boundaries: Pixels outside the mask region should retain their original parameters (weight = 1.0) or be handled by a separate unmasked rendering pass. Degenerate Input: If masksigma is 0, the weight becomes a Dirac delta function, potentially causing artifacts. A minimum non-zero value should be enforced. This variant generates masks based on defocus cues (Circle of Confusion - CoC) rather than explicit user-defined centers. It simulates defocus by rendering with specific focal length (validF=1.0) and kernel size (validK=0.0) parameters to create a fake defocused view. The mask is computed by a neural network (masknet) that takes the rendered image, normalized depth, and normalized CoC alpha as input. The network outputs an outfocusmask, and the infocusmask is derived as 1.0 - outfocusmask. This allows for automatic focus+context separation based on depth-of-field effects. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels/samples in the masking region. The Gaussian calculation is constant time per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing G-Buffer data if used for intermediate blending. Strengths: Provides visually smooth transitions, preserving context without hard edges. Effective for highlighting specific regions while maintaining spatial awareness. Limitations: Requires additional rendering passes or G-Buffer storage if complex blending is needed. Performance impact depends on the number of masked regions and the complexity of the blending technique. When to use: When smooth visual transitions are preferred over hard clipping, especially for focus+context visualization. When not to use: When precise, hard boundaries are required for measurement or analysis tasks. The technique is described in the context of "Ghosted Illustration Rendering" which uses depth-based blending and G-buffers to create smooth visibility transitions. It is part of a broader family of focus+context visualization methods that aim to reduce visual clutter while maintaining scene context. The specific implementation details regarding G-buffers and Gaussian weighting are attributed to this work. Ghosted Illustration Rendering using Depth-based Blending Techniques, https://doi.org/10.15701/kcgs.2020.26.3.1, fetched 2026-10-29 rongduo/DOFGSimplementation, https://github.com/rongduo/DOFGSimplementation, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable and inverse volume rendering
body: This family encompasses methods that treat volume rendering as a differentiable operation to solve inverse problems, optimizing 3D scene representations from 2D observations without requiring 3D ground truth supervision Differentiable volume rendering. It sets itself apart from Radiance-field optimization by focusing on the general differentiability of the volume rendering integral rather than specific neural field architectures, and from Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering by encompassing both tomographic and non-tomographic (e.g., RGB-only) optimization loops Differentiable volume rendering. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps Radiance-field optimization. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) Radiance-field optimization. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as Radiance-field optimization: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance Radiance-field optimization. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories Radiance-field optimization: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage Radiance-field optimization. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function Radiance-field optimization. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results Radiance-field optimization. Computes the gradient of a rendered image (or derived metric like depth) with respect to scene parameters by making the rendering integral differentiable. It solves the inverse problem of optimizing 3D scene representations from 2D observations without requiring 3D ground truth supervision. It sets itself apart from Radiance-field optimization by focusing on the general differentiability of the volume rendering integral itself, rather than specific neural field architectures, and from Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering by encompassing both tomographic and non-tomographic (e.g., RGB-only) optimization loops. Choose it when optimizing general volumetric scenes from RGB observations without strict tomographic constraints. Reconstructs 3D scene representations (radiance fields) from 2D observations by minimizing the photometric error between rendered images and ground-truth inputs. It solves the inverse problem of determining scene parameters (density, color, geometry, or camera poses) such that the differentiable volume rendering equation produces images matching the input data. It sets itself apart from explicit forward rendering methods by treating the scene representation as a set of trainable parameters optimized via gradient descent, and from tomographic reconstruction by relying on the differentiability of the rendering operator rather than algebraic inversion of projection data. Choose it when reconstructing high-fidelity, view-dependent neural or implicit scene representations from multi-view images. Treats computed tomography (CT) not as a linear algebra problem to be solved via closed-form filters or static iterative solvers, but as an optimization problem where a differentiable forward renderer (the projector) is minimized against measured projection data. This approach unifies classical algebraic reconstruction techniques (ART, SIRT) with modern neural representations and compressive sensing priors under a single gradient-based framework. It distinguishes itself from Differentiable volume rendering by focusing specifically on the tomographic geometry (parallel/fan/cone beam) and the reconstruction of density/absorption fields from sparse or noisy sinograms, and from Radiance-field optimization by explicitly modeling the X-ray physics (Beer-Lambert law) rather than just RGB appearance. Choose it when reconstructing density or absorption fields from X-ray projection data. The integration of differentiability into volume rendering emerged from the need to optimize 3D structures from 2D data without explicit 3D supervision Differentiable volume rendering. Early work focused on analytic gradients for differentiable volume rendering Differentiable volume rendering, while later developments unified tomographic reconstruction with inverse rendering techniques Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering. The field has evolved to support both neural implicit representations and explicit grid-based optimizations, driven by applications in novel view synthesis and medical imaging.

name: Differentiable volume rendering
head: Differentiable DVR, DiffDVR, Differentiable Ray Marching
body: Differentiable volume rendering computes the gradient of a rendered image (or derived metric like depth) with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) by making the rendering integral differentiable. It solves the inverse problem of optimizing 3D scene representations from 2D observations without requiring 3D ground truth supervision. It sets itself apart from Radiance-field optimization by focusing on the general differentiability of the volume rendering integral itself, rather than specific neural field architectures, and from Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering by encompassing both tomographic and non-tomographic (e.g., RGB-only) optimization loops. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results. Plenoxel is an explicit, sparse 3D grid representation for photorealistic view synthesis that stores opacity and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients directly, optimized via gradient descent without neural networks. It differs from its sibling Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) by using a discrete, sparse voxel structure with trilinear interpolation rather than a continuous implicit field, and from PlenOctrees by maintaining continuity in the plenoptic function through interpolation, which is critical for successful optimization. Choose this for explicit, memory-efficient voxel-based optimization of view synthesis. Differentiable Depth Rendering computes exact gradients of rendered depth values with respect to implicit function parameters by applying the Implicit Function Theorem (IFT). It solves the problem of differentiating through robust, non-differentiable forward tracing algorithms (such as bisection or sphere tracing) by replacing the backward pass with a surrogate gradient expression. Unlike Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) which integrates density along rays, this method targets implicit surfaces defined by zero-level sets. Choose this for differentiable surface reconstruction from depth or normal targets. Implicit Inverse Opacity Gradient is a method for computing the gradient of the inverse opacity function t(\theta) = Fr^{-1}(y, \theta) with respect to model parameters \theta, without back-propagating through the iterative binary search used to find the depth t. It solves the problem of differentiating through a root-finding procedure by applying the implicit function theorem to the forward opacity equation y = Fr(t, \theta). Unlike Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) which differentiates the forward integral directly, this method isolates the depth estimation step, allowing the binary search to remain non-differentiable while providing an analytical gradient for the inverse mapping. Choose this when optimizing depth targets derived from opacity constraints. Differential Diffusion Theory is a differentiable rendering framework for participating media that computes arbitrary scene parameter derivatives (density, absorption/scattering coefficients, anisotropic parameters) by solving the differential form of the diffusion equation. It replaces expensive Monte Carlo path tracing for multiply-scattered light with a partial differential equation (PDE) solver, enabling real-time optimization of millions of variables. Unlike standard ray marching which treats scattering as a local process, it decouples the global scattering solution (fluence) from local ray integration, allowing the use of fast PDE solvers instead of heavy precomputation or path tracing. Choose this for differentiable rendering of dense participating media where standard ray marching is too noisy or expensive. This method is a differentiable rendering technique that executes forward and backward passes concurrently to compute gradients for density field optimization. It solves the high memory cost of standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation by storing gradients only along active sampled ray paths in a sparse structure, rather than the entire volume grid. It sets itself apart from naive differentiable rendering by avoiding a separate backward pass or recomputation of the forward ray march; instead, it relies on gradient records stored during the forward pass to scatter gradients directly to neighboring voxels. Choose this when memory constraints prevent storing full Jacobians but ray paths are sparse. Differentiable Rendering and Sampling Methods constitute the core algorithmic framework for optimizing 3D scene parameters (such as density, color, geometry, or material properties) by propagating gradients from a 2D image loss back through the rendering integral. Unlike traditional rendering which produces images, this method produces a differentiable computational graph where the output is the rendered pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the inputs are the scene representation parameters. It sets itself apart from differentiable rasterization by operating on volumetric fields (density, SDF) via numerical integration rather than explicit geometry, and from standard Monte Carlo ray tracing by ensuring the sampling and integration steps are fully differentiable to enable gradient-based optimization. Choose this as the foundational framework for gradient-based optimization of volumetric scenes. This method computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters \theta by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space. It addresses the limitation of unidirectional estimators, which produce noisy gradients and inaccurate reconstructions in scenes with hard-to-sample lights and specular materials. The method distinguishes itself by combining Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) with Next Event Estimation (NEE) to allow the differential vertex to be located at any intermediate vertex or at the emitter connection, rather than being restricted to the final vertex as in standard NEE. Choose this for differentiable path tracing in complex scenes with multiple bounces and emissive objects. Reparameterization Estimators compute gradients for differentiable volume rendering by transforming stochastic sampling operations into deterministic, differentiable functions of the underlying parameters. Unlike standard Monte Carlo estimators where gradients vanish through discrete sampling decisions, this family allows back-propagation through the sample locations themselves. It distinguishes itself from Adjoint Method by maintaining a forward-mode computational graph for the sampling process, and from Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) by explicitly handling the non-differentiable nature of discrete ray marching via continuous density approximations. Choose this when differentiating through stochastic sampling or stratified sampling steps. The Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT) for differentiable rendering computes the gradient of a rendering integral with respect to scene parameters by decomposing it into an interior term (derivative of the continuous integrand) and a boundary term (integral over discontinuities). Unlike standard rasterization-based differentiable renderers that approximate boundaries via finite differences or edge rasterization, this method provides a principled mathematical model that supports transparent surfaces and complex occlusions without assuming a single triangle per pixel. It distinguishes itself from Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR) by explicitly handling the geometric discontinuities inherent in path integrals through a material-form parameterization, as detailed in Path-Space Differentiable Rendering (PSDR). Choose this for differentiable rendering of scenes with complex visibility boundaries and transparent surfaces. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. A method that treats volume rendering as a computational process mapping viewpoint and transfer functions (TFs) directly to an image, bypassing the explicit volume data, using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). Choose this when learning implicit mappings from views to images without explicit volumetric representations. A technique to estimate gradients of a rendering operator with respect to parameters by convolving the rendering function with a blur kernel, allowing differentiation through plateaus and discontinuities in non-differentiable renderers. Choose this when dealing with non-differentiable renderers or visibility discontinuities that cause vanishing gradients. A sensor implementation for differentiable rendering that accumulates radiance contributions into a volumetric film using delta tracking or similar path tracing logic, supporting both forward and reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Choose this for differentiable path tracing where radiance accumulation needs to be tracked in a volumetric film. A formulation for estimating the partial derivative of radiometric measurements with respect to scene parameters by differentiating the material-form path integral, resulting in an integral over the interior path space and a boundary path space. Choose this for differentiable path tracing formulations that require explicit handling of material property derivatives. An analysis-by-synthesis inverse rendering technique that reconstructs 3D geometry and physically-based reflectance (PBR) materials from multi-view 2D images captured by conventional hand-held cameras under uncontrolled lighting. Choose this for inverse rendering of complex scenes with PBR materials from unconstrained multi-view imagery. Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) computes pixel colors by integrating light along rays through a volume, enabling gradient-based optimization of rendering parameters. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by offering specific implementations for implicit neural representations (Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR)) and analytic inversion for transfer function optimization (Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DiffDVR)), avoiding the high memory costs of standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Choose this for optimizing transfer functions or voxel densities in large volumes where memory is a constraint. Differentiable volume rendering emerged as a key technique for inverse graphics and 3D reconstruction from 2D images. Early work focused on differentiable ray marching for neural implicit representations, such as Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR). The challenge of memory consumption in reverse-mode automatic differentiation for large volumes was addressed by DiffDVR, which introduced analytic inversion of blending functions to reduce memory complexity from O(kn) to O(n). Subsequent developments included the Adjoint Method for efficient gradient computation with respect to many parameters, and explicit gradient methods for tomography using box splines. The field has expanded to include differentiable depth rendering via the Implicit Function Theorem, sparse gradient recording [3558], and hybrid grey-box differentials. It is widely used in neural radiance fields (NeRF), tomographic reconstruction, and transfer function optimization.
