name: Variance-aware Adaptive Pixel Sampling
head: Adaptive pixel sampling for inverse rendering, Image-Space Adaptive Sampling, Pixel-level mini-batching, Variance-minimizing pixel sampling
body: Variance-aware adaptive pixel sampling accelerates gradient-based inverse rendering by dynamically allocating a fixed per-iteration pixel sampling budget based on the estimated variance of loss gradient contributions. Unlike uniform mini-batching or sampling proportional only to loss gradient magnitude, this method accounts for the variance of the differentiable rendering derivative, minimizing the total variance of the gradient estimator. It acts as a form of pixel-level mini-batching, rendering only a subset of pixels per iteration while maintaining low gradient noise. The method operates within an inverse rendering pipeline where the goal is to minimize a loss \mathcal{L} with respect to scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}. It assumes the availability of an adjoint method or equivalent mechanism to compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the image, \partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L}, and the derivative of the image with respect to parameters, d\mathbf{I}/d\boldsymbol{\theta}. Scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\theta}. Target image \mathbf{I}^{\text{target}}. Per-iteration sampling budget N{\text{pix}} (number of pixels to render per iteration). Current estimate of pixel sampling probabilities pj (initialized uniformly or from previous iteration). Updated scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} (via gradient descent step). Updated sampling probabilities pj for the next iteration. Pixel Grid: A 2D array of size H \times W (image resolution). Sampling Weights: A 2D array of size H \times W storing the unnormalized weights wj for each pixel. Probability Map: A 2D array of size H \times W storing normalized probabilities pj. Gradient Estimators: Buffers to store \langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle and \langle dIj/d\theta \rangle (or their squared second moments) for variance estimation. 1. Primal Pass (Image Rendering): Render the current scene parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} to obtain the current image \mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta}). This pass may use a higher sample budget per pixel to ensure accurate image values for loss computation and weight estimation. 2. Compute Loss Gradient Derivatives: Compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the image, \partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L}, for all pixels. 3. Estimate Rendering Gradient Variance: Estimate the second moment of the rendering derivative, p{j2}, for each pixel by rendering the gradient dIj/d\theta (or its components) for a subset of pixels. For scalar \theta: p{j2} \approx \mathbb{E}[\langle dIj/d\theta \rangle^2]. For vector \boldsymbol{\theta}: p{j2} \approx \sum{k=1}^{m\theta} \mathbb{E}[\langle \partial Ij / \partial \thetak \rangle^2]. 4. Compute Sampling Weights: Calculate the unnormalized weight wj for each pixel j using the formula: wj = \sqrt{p{j1} p{j2}}. Here, p{j1} = \mathbb{E}[\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle^2] is the second moment of the loss derivative estimator. 5. Normalize Probabilities: Normalize the weights to obtain sampling probabilities: pj = \frac{wj}{\sum{k=1}^{mI} wk}, where mI is the total number of pixels. 6. Sample Pixels: Randomly select N{\text{pix}} pixels according to the probability distribution pj. This forms the "mini-batch" of pixels to render in this iteration. 7. Adjoint/Gradient Pass: For each sampled pixel j, render the gradient dIj/d\theta (or compute it via the adjoint method) to obtain the estimator \langle dIj/d\theta \rangle. 8. Estimate Gradient: Compute the unbiased gradient estimator for the selected pixels using the single-sample Monte Carlo formula: \left\langle \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle = \sum{j \in \text{sampled}} \frac{\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle}{pj} \left\langle \frac{dIj}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle. 9. Update Parameters: Use the estimated gradient to update \boldsymbol{\theta} via a gradient descent step. 10. Update Variance Estimates: Update the running estimates of p{j1} and p{j2} to adapt to changes in the scene parameters. Loss Minimization: \boldsymbol{\theta}^ = \arg \min{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L} \left( \mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta}); \mathbf{I}^{\text{target}} \right) \quad (4.1) Chain Rule: \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \sum{j=1}^{mI} (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \frac{dIj}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \quad (4.2) Monte Carlo Estimator: \left\langle \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle = \frac{\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle}{pj} \left\langle \frac{dIj}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} \right\rangle \quad (4.4) Optimal Probability (Scalar Case): pj \propto \sqrt{p{j1} p{j2}} \quad (4.8) where p{j1}:= \mathbb{E}[\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle^2] and p{j2}:= \mathbb{E}[\langle dIj/d\theta \rangle^2]. Optimal Probability (Vector Case): pj \propto \sqrt{p{j1} p{j2}} \quad (4.12) where p{j1}:= \mathbb{E}[\langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle^2] and p{j2}:= \sum{k=1}^{m\theta} \mathbb{E}[\langle \partial Ij / \partial \thetak \rangle^2]. Sampling Budget (N{\text{pix}}): The number of pixels sampled per iteration. This is fixed per iteration. Primal:Adjoint Sample Ratio: The optimal ratio found in practice is 3:1 (75% of samples for primal rendering, 25% for adjoint/gradient rendering). Independence Assumption: The derivation assumes that the loss derivative estimator \langle (\partial{\mathbf{I}} \mathcal{L})j \rangle and the rendering derivative estimator \langle dIj/d\theta \rangle are independent. If they are correlated, the variance minimization derivation does not hold directly. Negative Adjoint Radiance: The adjoint radiance \partialI \mathcal{L} can have negative values. Sampling proportional to its absolute value |\partialI \mathcal{L}| introduces sign variance. While positivization (sampling positive and negative components separately) removes this variance, it was found to have little effect on overall estimation variance in practice, so the simpler absolute value method is used. High Variance with Uniform Sampling: Naively reducing the sampling budget by uniformly sampling pixels results in high gradient variance, degrading performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def varianceawareadaptivesampling( theta, Itarget, renderfunc, rendergradfunc, lossfunc, lossgradfunc, Npix, maxiter=1000, lr=0.01): """ Variance-aware adaptive pixel sampling for inverse rendering. Args: theta: Initial scene parameters. Itarget: Target image. renderfunc: Function to render image I(theta). rendergradfunc: Function to render squared gradient magnitude for all pixels. lossfunc: Function to compute loss L(I, Itarget). lossgradfunc: Function to compute gradient dL/dI. Npix: Number of pixels to sample per iteration. maxiter: Maximum number of iterations. lr: Learning rate. Returns: theta: Optimized scene parameters. """ H, W = Itarget.shape[:2] mI = H W # Initialize variance estimates pj1 and pj2 pj1 = np.ones((H, W)) pj2 = np.ones((H, W)) # Initialize probabilities uniformly p = np.ones((H, W)) / mI for iteration in range(maxiter): # Step 1: Primal Pass Icurr = renderfunc(theta) dLdI = lossgradfunc(Icurr, Itarget) # Step 2 & 3: Estimate second moments # pj1:= E[<dL/dIj>^2] pj1 = dLdI 2 # pj2:= E[<dIj/dtheta>^2] (scalar or sum over params) pj2 = rendergradfunc(theta) # Step 4: Compute Sampling Weights weights = np.sqrt(pj1 pj2) weights = np.maximum(weights, 1e-8) # Step 5: Normalize Probabilities p = weights / np.sum(weights) # Step 6: Sample Pixels pflat = p.flatten() pixelindices = np.random.choice(mI, size=Npix, replace=False, p=pflat) # Step 7 & 8: Adjoint/Gradient Pass & Estimate Gradient gradestimates = np.zeroslike(theta) for idx in pixelindices: y, x = np.unravelindex(idx, (H, W)) dLdIj = dLdI[y, x] dIdthetaj = rendergradfuncpixel(theta, y, x) pj = p[y, x] gradest = (dLdIj / pj) dIdthetaj gradestimates += gradest # Step 9: Update Parameters theta -= lr gradestimates return theta def rendergradfuncpixel(theta, y, x): """Computes the rendering derivative dIj/dtheta for pixel (y, x).""" # Standard operation: evaluate differentiable renderer gradient at pixel (y, x) return np.zeroslike(theta) Time Complexity: O(N{\text{pix}} \cdot C{\text{render}}) per iteration, where C{\text{render}} is the cost of rendering a single pixel. This is significantly faster than full-image rendering O(mI \cdot C{\text{render}}) when N{\text{pix}} \ll mI. Memory Complexity: O(mI) to store the probability map and variance estimates. Measured Performance: Reduces loss gradient variance by 1–2 orders of magnitude compared to uniform sampling or BRDF-only sampling. Outperforms uniform mini-batching by allowing faster convergence at equal time. Strengths: Accelerates inverse rendering by reducing sampling budget without sacrificing performance. Lowers gradient variance by accounting for rendering derivative variance. Limitations: Requires estimation of rendering derivative variance, which can be costly if not approximated. Assumes independence between loss and rendering derivative estimators. When to Use: Inverse rendering pipelines for SVBRDF reconstruction, shape optimization, and inverse volume rendering where computational cost is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When the independence assumption is strongly violated, or when the cost of estimating p{j2} outweighs the benefits of adaptive sampling. The method was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering and inverse rendering to address the high computational cost of rendering all pixels during optimization. It builds on the concept of mini-batching in gradient-based optimization and applies it to the image space. The theoretical foundation for optimal sampling probabilities is derived from minimizing the variance of the Monte Carlo estimator for the loss gradient. The technique has been applied to various inverse rendering problems, including SVBRDF reconstruction and shape optimization. Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/337282320, fetched 2026-11-02 (unofficial) Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/sr.20241148, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Path Replay Backpropagation
head: Reverse-mode differentiation benchmark
body: Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) is an adjoint-based differentiable rendering method that computes gradients of a scalar loss function with respect to scene parameters without storing the full Monte Carlo computation graph. It solves the quadratic runtime complexity of its sibling, Radiative Backpropagation (RB), by using a two-pass approach: a primal pass to generate samples and store state, followed by an adjoint pass that replays the path using the same random seed to recover incident radiance. Unlike RB, which requires an intertwined simulation of adjoint and primal radiance leading to quadratic complexity, PRB achieves linear time complexity in path length. PRB transforms the derivative of a light transport simulation into an equivalent simulation of differential radiation, leveraging physical reciprocity and pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) replay to avoid explicit storage of the computational graph. Inputs: Scene parameters \pi (e.g., density, albedo, BRDF parameters), camera parameters, loss function L(I), and a random seed \bar{\boldsymbol{p}}. Outputs: Gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \pi}. The method is decomposed into three self-contained megakernels: 1. Megakernel #1 (Primal Path Tracer): Generates Monte Carlo samples. Implicitly depends on scene parameters. Outputs a primal rendering I and stores per-ray information (vertex positions, directions, BSDF evaluations) in a state array. 2. Megakernel #2 (Replay Sampler): Regenerates the same set of samples using the same random seed but a different pseudorandom sequence. Outputs a per-sample state array containing the specific random numbers used for each path segment. 3. Megakernel #3 (Adjoint Megakernel): Contains adjoint versions of all rendering steps. Takes the state array from Megakernel #2 and the primal rendering from Megakernel #1. Accumulates scene parameter gradients. 1. Primal Pass (Megakernel #1): Trace rays from the camera. For each ray, generate a path \bar{\boldsymbol{p}} using a PRNG. Store the path estimate \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) and per-ray information (vertices, directions, BSDF values). Compute the image I and the loss L(I). 2. Replay Pass (Megakernel #2): Regenerate the path \bar{\boldsymbol{p}} using the same initial random seed to ensure the same sequence of vertices and intersections is visited. Store the specific random numbers used for each segment n. 3. Adjoint Pass (Megakernel #3): Compute the adjoint radiance in image space: \frac{\partial L}{\partial I}. Emit this signed radiation from the camera into the scene. For each path segment n, replay the path using the stored random numbers to compute the segment weight gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}). Compute the derivative of the segment weight \frac{\partial gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} using automatic differentiation on the specific segment n. Combine using the product rule to compute the gradient contribution. At every intersection, absorb the accumulated differential light by backpropagating to the scene parameters \pi. 4. Optimization Step: Compute one further decorrelated primal rendering to provide to the image loss function, resulting in three integration steps total. The gradient of the loss L with respect to parameters \pi is derived using the chain rule and the material form parameterization: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \pi} = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \frac{\partial L}{\partial I} \frac{\partial \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial I} \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} d\mu(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) This avoids explicitly computing or storing \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi}. The path estimator \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) is decomposed into segment weights gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}): gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) = \begin{cases} fv(\bar{x}, n) J(pn), & 0 \le n \le N \\ G(x{n-N-1} \leftrightarrow x{n-N}), & N < n \le 2N \end{cases} where N is the path length, fv is the volume scattering term, J is the Jacobian, and G is the geometry term. The derivative of the path estimator is computed via the product rule: \frac{\partial \hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} = \sumn \frac{\partial gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} \prod{n' \ne n} g{n'}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}) = \sumn \frac{\partial gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{\partial \pi} \frac{\hat{f}(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})}{gn(\bar{\boldsymbol{p}})} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pathreplaybackpropagation(scene, camera, params, lossfn, seed): """ Implements Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB). scene: Scene representation with differentiable parameters. camera: Camera configuration. params: Scene parameters pi to optimize. lossfn: Scalar loss function L(I). seed: Random seed for path generation. """ # Pass 1: Primal Path Tracing (Megakernel #1) # Generate paths and store per-ray information paths, pathestimates, rayinfo = traceprimalpaths(scene, camera, params, seed) # Compute image and loss image = reconstructimage(paths, pathestimates) loss = lossfn(image) # Pass 2: Replay Sampling (Megakernel #2) # Regenerate paths with same seed to get specific random numbers used # This ensures we visit the same vertices but can access the RNG state replayrngstates = replayrngstates(seed, rayinfo) # Pass 3: Adjoint Path Tracing (Megakernel #3) # Initialize gradient accumulator gradparams = zeroslike(params) # Compute adjoint radiance at the sensor adjointradiance = computeadjointradiance(loss, image) for pathidx in range(numpaths): # Replay the path using stored RNG states to get segment weights # and the specific random numbers used for each segment segments = [] for n in range(pathlength): rngstate = replayrngstates[pathidx][n] # Re-evaluate segment n using the same random numbers # This allows computing gn and its derivative d(gn)/d(pi) segmentweight, segmentderiv = computesegmentandderiv( scene, camera, params, pathidx, n, rngstate) segments.append((segmentweight, segmentderiv)) # Compute total path estimate for normalization totalestimate = pathestimates[pathidx] # Accumulate gradients using the product rule formula # d(L)/d(pi) = sumn ( d(gn)/d(pi) (totalestimate / gn)) for n in range(pathlength): gn, dgndpi = segments[n] if gn != 0: # Contribution from segment n contribution = dgndpi (totalestimate / gn) # Backpropagate to parameters gradparams += contribution return gradparams Quadratic Complexity: The sibling method RB suffers from quadratic complexity because it computes incident primal radiance at every intersection by building another complete light path integral. PRB avoids this by replaying the path. Visibility Discontinuities: When differentiated parameters affect visibility, derivatives can be severely biased, breaking shape reconstruction. Special precautions are needed. Memory: PRB uses minimal GPU memory compared to storing full computation graphs, which is critical for large scene representations like 3D volumes. Polymorphic Calls: The reverse-mode derivative of polymorphic calls (e.g., BSDF evaluation with large intersection records) creates redundancies. Global dead code elimination, constant propagation, and value numbering are required for efficiency. Time Complexity: Linear in path length. RB is quadratic. Memory Complexity: Constant memory complexity, avoiding the storage of per-bounce data required by standard AD. Performance: In the Veach Door scene (480x270, 16 spp primal, 4 spp adjoint), PRB peak memory was 3.00 GiB and gradient computation time was 2.46s, compared to RB's 3.51 GiB and 2.52s. On CPU, megakernel-style evaluation provides speedups reaching ~166x compared to baseline. GPU speedups from redundancy elimination reach 3.3x. Strengths: Unbiased gradients, low memory usage, linear complexity. Limitations: Requires careful handling of visibility discontinuities. The method is write-heavy, accumulating gradients rather than querying scene representation. PRB was introduced by Vicini et al. [2021] as an improvement over Radiative Backpropagation (RB) [Nimier-David et al. 2020]. It is used as a baseline in inverse rendering optimization experiments, such as optimizing BRDF material properties in the Veach door scene. The method is implemented in the Dr.Jit differentiable rendering framework. name: Reservoir Light Replay Backpropagation
head: ResLRB, Reservoir Light Tracing with Backpropagation
body: Reservoir Light Replay Backpropagation (ResLRB) is a constant-memory, reverse-mode differentiable light tracing method that compresses per-path sensor connections into a single stochastically selected representative using weighted reservoir sampling. It preserves the two-pass structure of Path Replay Backpropagation but trades gradient fidelity for bounded memory by discarding N-1 of N candidate connections per path. Unlike LRB-3-pass, which retains all connections via a third traversal, ResLRB achieves constant memory at the cost of increased gradient variance. Inputs: Light path vertices \{x0, \dots, x{N-1}\}, emitter parameters \theta, sensor geometry. Outputs: Unbiased gradient estimate \nabla\theta \hat{S}. Data Structures: Reservoir Entry: Stores the selected vertex index R, the cumulative weight sum \Omegak, the weight of the selected connection \omegaR, and the accumulated ray-segment Jacobian J{0 \rightarrow R}^{\text{ray}} (for attached formulation). Ray-Segment Jacobian (J{0 \rightarrow i}^{\text{ray}}): A 4 \times 4 matrix representing the derivative of the ray-segment parameterization with respect to emitter parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Primal Pass (Streaming Reservoir): For each vertex xi along the light path: a. Compute the sensor connection radiance Li and its weight \omegai (typically proportional to the BSDF PDF and radiance). b. Update the running total weight \Omegak \leftarrow \Omegak + \omegai. c. Reservoir Update: With probability pi = \omegai / \Omegak, replace the current reservoir entry with the candidate at xi. If attached formulation: Cache the current accumulated Jacobian J{0 \rightarrow i}^{\text{ray}} with the new entry. Update J{0 \rightarrow i}^{\text{ray}} for the next iteration using forward-mode differentiation: J{0 \rightarrow i+1}^{\text{ray}} = J{\text{ray}}^{(i)} \cdot J{0 \rightarrow i}^{\text{ray}}. d. Advance the path. 2. Termination: When the path terminates, the reservoir holds a single index R \in \{1, \dots, N\} selected with probability: \Pr(R = i) = \frac{\omegai}{\Omegak} \quad (8) where \Omegak = \sum{j=1}^k \omegaj is the total weight sum. 3. Splat Contribution: Compute the reweighted splat contribution: \hat{S}(\bar{x}; \theta) = \frac{\Omegak}{\omegaR} \cdot LR(\theta) \quad (9) This estimator is unbiased because \mathbb{E}R[\hat{S}] = \sum{i=1}^k Li. 4. Adjoint Pass (Replay): a. Re-seed the PRNG with the stored seed to synchronize state. b. Replay the path from x0 up to the selected depth R. c. Reservoir Sync: Re-execute the reservoir update logic (specifically the random number consumption) at each vertex to keep the PRNG state synchronized with the primal pass, even though the selection outcome is known. d. Jacobian Reconstruction: At each replayed vertex xj (j \le R), rebuild J{0 \rightarrow j}^{\text{ray}} using the same forward-mode process as the primal pass. e. Backpropagation: i. Compute the sensor-connection Jacobian at the selected vertex R: JR^{\text{sensor}} = \frac{\partial(LR, uR)}{\partial \mathbf{p}R} \in \mathbb{R}^{5 \times 4} \quad (12) where \mathbf{p}R is the ray-segment parameterization, LR is the 3-channel radiance, and uR is the 2-component sensor coordinate. ii. Compute the total splat Jacobian: JR^{\text{splat}} = JR^{\text{sensor}} \cdot J{0 \rightarrow R}^{\text{ray}} \quad (13) iii. Project the image-space adjoint \tilde{L}R into the local frame via the inverse of J{0 \rightarrow j}^{\text{ray}}. iv. Perform two backward operations: Through the radiance channel weighted by \tilde{L}R. Through the position channel weighted by the position adjoint \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial uR. v. Apply the log-derivative identity at each vertex xj using the downstream adjoint \delta{\text{rem}} and BSDF PDF fs^{(j)}: \nabla{\theta} fs^{(j)} \cdot \frac{\delta{\text{rem}}}{fs^{(j)}} \quad (17) where \delta{\text{rem}} is the remaining downstream adjoint. Parameters: N: Number of candidate sensor connections. Trade-off between gradient fidelity and memory. res.depth: The depth R of the selected connection, determining the extent of the adjoint replay loop. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance: Variance increases proportional to the number of discarded connections. In worst-case scenes (high path-sensor connectivity, e.g., Living Room), effective sample count reduces by a factor proportional to path length. PRNG Synchronization: The PRNG state must remain synchronized between primal and adjoint passes. Failure to re-execute reservoir update logic causes desynchronization. Jacobian Inversion: In attached formulation, invert J{0 \rightarrow j}^{\text{ray}}. Use a determinant threshold to substitute zero matrix if |\det J| is small. Inject stochastic noise for regularization at non-specular vertices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reslrbprimal(pathvertices, emitterparams): """ Primal pass for ResLRB. Returns: reservoirentry, rngstate """ reservoir = None omegatotal = 0.0 jray = identitymatrix(4, 4) # J{0->0} for i, xi in enumerate(pathvertices): # Compute connection weight and radiance omegai, Li = computesensorconnection(xi, emitterparams) # Update total weight omegatotal += omegai # Reservoir sampling if omegatotal > 0: paccept = omegai / omegatotal if random() < paccept: # Cache current Jacobian with the new candidate jraycached = copy(jray) reservoir = { 'index': i, 'omega': omegai, 'omegatotal': omegatotal, 'jray': jraycached, 'L': Li } # Update Jacobian for next segment jray = jraysegmentjacobian(xi) @ jray return reservoir, getrngstate() def reslrbadjoint(reservoirentry, rngstate, pathvertices, emitterparams): """ Adjoint pass for ResLRB. Returns: gradientestimate """ setrngstate(rngstate) R = reservoirentry['index'] omegaR = reservoirentry['omega'] omegatotal = reservoirentry['omegatotal'] jrayR = reservoirentry['jray'] LR = reservoirentry['L'] # Reweighting factor wfactor = omegatotal / omegaR # Image space adjoint (from loss) LtildeR = getimageadjoint(R) # Replay path up to R jray = identitymatrix(4, 4) deltarem = LtildeR # Initial downstream adjoint for j in range(R + 1): xj = pathvertices[j] # Re-synchronize PRNG if j < R: # Re-execute reservoir logic to consume RNG # (Simplified: assume we know the path and can re-run the exact same random calls) # In practice, this involves re-computing the acceptance probability and consuming RNG pass # Rebuild Jacobian if j > 0: jray = jraysegmentjacobian(pathvertices[j-1]) @ jray # Backpropagation at vertex j if j == R: # Compute Sensor Jacobian jsensor = computesensorjacobian(xj, LR) jsplat = jsensor @ jrayR # Project adjoint #... (projection logic using inverse of jray) # Radiance channel backward gradL = wfactor LtildeR #... (backprop through radiance) # Position channel backward gradu = wfactor getpositionadjoint(R) #... (backprop through position) else: # Log-derivative identity for intermediate vertices fs = computebsdfpdf(xj) gradtheta = computebsdfgradient(xj) (deltarem / fs) #... (accumulate gradient) # Update deltarem for next step (if needed for attached formulation) # In detached, deltarem is constant LtildeR scaled? # Note: Eq 17 implies deltarem is used. In detached, it's simpler. pass return accumulatedgradient A constant-memory method that retains all connections via a third traversal, matching naive AD in expectation but requiring more computation time. Extends ResLRB to track geometric perturbations through the path to shift splatted sensor coordinates, adding constant storage per sample (4 \times 4 Jacobian matrix). Memory: Constant with respect to path length. Stores only one reservoir entry per sample (one 4 \times 4 matrix for J{0 \rightarrow R}^{\text{ray}} and one two-component vector for position adjoint in attached formulation). Time Complexity: Two passes. The adjoint pass replays only up to the selected depth R. Variance: Increased compared to naive AD. Proportional to the number of discarded connections. Worst-case reduction in effective sample count by a factor proportional to path length. Strengths: Enables differentiable light transport at path lengths where AD-based approaches are not feasible on consumer hardware due to memory limits. Limitations: Higher variance than LRB-3-pass. Becomes competitive with LRB-3-pass only in scenes with high path-sensor connectivity (e.g., Living Room), where the cost of the third traversal in LRB-3-pass outweighs the reservoir overhead. When to use: When memory is constrained and path lengths are long, and scene connectivity is low to moderate. When not to use: When gradient fidelity is critical and memory is sufficient for LRB-3-pass or naive AD. ResLRB was introduced by Linas Beresna and Eugene Fiume from Simon Fraser University in the paper "Constant-Memory Differentiable Light Tracing" (2026). It addresses the obstruction of applying Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) to light tracing in constant memory, where buffered two-pass variants retain linear memory scaling with path length. name: Checkpointing for Reverse-Mode Memory Optimization
head: Checkpointing, Griewank checkpointing, Logarithmic checkpointing, re-evaluation from checkpoints
body: Checkpointing is an optimization for reverse-mode automatic differentiation (AD) that reduces memory complexity by storing only a sparse subset of intermediate variables and recomputing loop segments during the backward pass. It addresses the scalability issue of exhaustive storage, where memory usage is proportional to the number of instructions, by trading increased time complexity for logarithmic memory usage. Unlike Inversion Trick or Path Replay Backpropagation, which exploit problem-specific structures to avoid differentiation entirely, checkpointing is a general-purpose mechanism applicable to any traced computation. Inputs: A primal computation consisting of N sequential operations (or a loop of length N). Outputs: Gradients of a scalar loss with respect to the input parameters. Data Structures: 1. Checkpoint Storage: A dictionary or array storing the full state at specific indices. The size is O(\log N). 2. Primal State: The current state of variables during recomputation. Algorithm: The method divides the sequence of N operations into segments. During the forward pass, the state is saved at predefined checkpoint indices. During the backward pass, the algorithm iterates backwards through the segments. For each segment, it restores the state from the nearest preceding checkpoint and re-executes the forward operations to reconstruct intermediate values required for gradient computation. 1. Forward Pass with Checkpointing: Initialize the primal state x0. Iterate i from 0 to N-1. Compute x{i+1} = fi(xi). If i is a checkpoint index, save xi to the Checkpoint Storage. Note: The optimal strategy for selecting checkpoint indices to minimize total recomputation time while maintaining O(\log N) memory is to use a recursive doubling or tree strategy. 2. Backward Pass with Recomputation: Initialize gradient accumulator \bar{x}N (typically \partial L / \partial xN). Iterate backwards through the segments defined by the checkpoints. Let the checkpoints be at indices c0, c1, \dots, ck where c0 = 0 and ck = N. For each segment from cj to c{j+1}: Restore the primal state x{cj} from the Checkpoint Storage. Recompute the forward operations for indices i from cj to c{j+1}-1: x{i+1} = fi(xi). Compute gradients for this segment in reverse order (i from c{j+1}-1 down to cj): \bar{x}i = \bar{x}{i+1} \cdot \frac{\partial fi}{\partial xi}. Accumulate \bar{x}i into the global gradient accumulator. Note: If the computation involves recursive function calls, a tree structure may be used instead of a stack to store intermediate results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checkpointedbackward(N, f, fprime, checkpoints, x0, gradout): savedstates = {} state = x0 # Forward pass: save state before update to enable correct segment restoration for i in range(N): if i in checkpoints: savedstates[i] = state state = f(state) grad = gradout # Sort checkpoint boundaries in descending order to process segments backwards segmentends = sorted(checkpoints + [N], reverse=True) for j in range(len(segmentends) - 1): endidx = segmentends[j] startidx = segmentends[j+1] # Restore primal state at segment start; default to x0 if startidx is 0 currentstate = savedstates.get(startidx, x0) forwardstates = [currentstate] tempstate = currentstate # Recompute forward operations for the segment for i in range(startidx, endidx): tempstate = f(tempstate) forwardstates.append(tempstate) # Compute gradients in reverse order for the segment for i in range(endidx - 1, startidx - 1, -1): xi = forwardstates[i - startidx] xnext = forwardstates[i - startidx + 1] # Standard reverse-mode adjoint update: xbari = xbarnext f'(xi) grad = fprime(xi, xnext, grad) return grad Parameters: Checkpoint Frequency: The number of checkpoints K. To achieve O(\log N) memory, K \approx \log2 N. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Recursive Calls: If the function f calls itself, the checkpointing strategy must handle the call stack correctly, potentially using a tree structure instead of a linear stack. Memory vs. Time Trade-off: While memory is reduced to O(\log N), time complexity increases to O(N \log N). Differentiation techniques that exploit problem-specific traits to reduce storage and reevaluation overheads, generally preferable to checkpointing when available. For Newton's method, the implicit function theorem provides the answer directly from the iteration's fixed point instead of differentiating through all steps. For ordinary differential equations, reverse time integration provides an efficient adjoint. A checkpointing mechanism that arises naturally from the combined AD/JIT system without intentional implementation effort. The JIT layer recomputes intermediate steps and temporaries from the last evaluation point. In systems like Dr.Jit, calling dr.backward(data) causes the AD layer to reference intermediate steps produced by f, which the JIT layer recomputes from the last dr.eval checkpoint. Checkpointing is not ideal for Path Replay Backpropagation (PBDR) workloads due to the large size of even a small number of checkpoints. Time Complexity: O(N \log N), where N is the number of operations or loop length. Memory Complexity: O(\log N), where N is the number of operations. Scaling: Reduces memory complexity to O(\log N), addressing scalability issues where exhaustive storage generates terabytes of intermediate state. Strengths: General applicability to any traced computation; significant memory savings for long sequences of operations. Limitations: Increased computational overhead due to recomputation; not ideal for workloads with large checkpoint sizes (e.g., PBDR). When to Use: When memory is the bottleneck and the computation is too large for exhaustive storage, and no custom adjoint is available. When Not to Use: When custom adjoints are available (e.g., Inversion Trick, Path Replay Backpropagation). Checkpointing for reverse-mode automatic differentiation was introduced by Andreas Griewank in 1992. The technique addresses the "age-old question" of how to manage intermediate state in reversed program references, where exhaustive storage does not scale due to the volume of data generated by modern processors. The concept of storing state at sparse checkpoints and recovering it via reevaluation was previously noted by Volin and Ostrovskii in 1985. Automatic recursive usage of this pattern was further analyzed by Siskind and Pearlmutter in 2018, formalizing the O(\log t) overhead for a program with t operations. In the context of differentiable rendering, checkpointing is a key component of general-purpose AD systems like Dr.Jit, enabling the differentiation of complex rendering programs without requiring custom adjoints for every operation. name: Halide Scheduling for Gradient Kernels
head: Halide AD Scheduling, Register-aware Checkpointing Scheduling
body: Halide Scheduling for Gradient Kernels is a heuristic-based strategy for optimizing reverse-mode automatic differentiation (AD) programs on GPUs, specifically within the Halide compiler framework. It addresses the trade-off between register spilling and memory I/O overhead by splitting gradient computation into multiple smaller kernels. Unlike standard checkpointing which focuses solely on recomputation vs. storage, this method explicitly manages register pressure by selecting which intermediate values to checkpoint based on a linear cost model, ensuring efficient utilization of GPU hardware resources. The method operates on a forward-pass program and its corresponding reverse-mode AD gradient program. The core challenge is that Halide’s common sub-expression elimination (CSE) pass prevents fine-grained control over recomputation within a single kernel. To work around this, the scheduling strategy splits the gradient program into multiple sub-kernels and decides for each intermediate value in the forward pass whether to checkpoint it (write to memory) or recompute it (risk register spilling). Input: The forward-pass computation graph (represented as a sequence of nodes), hardware register limits, and discrete scheduling options. Output: A compiled Halide schedule consisting of multiple kernels, a loggedtrace list of checkpoint nodes, and potentially a separate contloggedtrace for non-Dirac parameters. loggedtrace: A list of node indices or identifiers from the forward pass that are designated as checkpoints. These values are stored in memory during the forward pass and read during the reverse pass. contloggedtrace: A strict subset of loggedtrace used specifically for computing gradients with respect to non-Dirac parameters. Cost Model: An approximate linear model estimating register usage by counting the number of intermediate computations for each node in the forward pass. The backward pass can be split into sub-programs based on two discrete choices: 1. separatecont: If True, the gradient with respect to non-Dirac parameters is computed in a separate reverse-mode AD sub-program. This sub-program reads from contloggedtrace instead of loggedtrace. Since this sub-program is typically smaller, it may have more available register space for recomputation, potentially saving memory I/O. 2. separatesample: Determines how gradient approximations for Dirac parameters are split. Dirac parameter gradients involve pre-filtering four different kernels (left and right kernels on image coordinates x and y). 'axis': Computes the gradient approximation for each sampling axis (left/right on x, left/right on y) in a different sub-program. 'kernel': Separates the approximation to each pre-filtering kernel into different parts. The scheduling space is combinatorial and too large for exhaustive search. An autoscheduler uses a greedy heuristic search to find an optimal loggedtrace. 1. Initialize Cost Model: Build an approximate linear cost model by counting intermediate computations for each node in the forward pass. This model estimates register usage. 2. Greedy Search for Potential Checkpoints: Start with an empty potential checkpoint list. Iteratively add nodes to this list. Selection Criterion: A newly added node should approximately halve the current maximum cost among all nodes in the graph. Update the cost model after every iteration based on the current potential list. 3. Search for Optimal loggedtrace: Let the nodes added in the greedy search be ordered as n1, n2, \dots, nm. Search for an integer k (1 \le k \le m) such that checkpointing every node found before iteration k (i.e., \{n1, \dots, nk\}) yields the best profiled runtime. Set loggedtrace to this optimal subset. 4. Determine contloggedtrace: Choose between the optimal loggedtrace and a default checkpointing list. Select the one that provides the best runtime for the non-Dirac gradient sub-program. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def halidegradientschedule(forwardnodes, hardwareregisterlimit): """ forwardnodes: List of node objects, each having: id: unique identifier compcount: number of intermediate computations (for cost model) hardwareregisterlimit: int, max registers available per thread/block """ # Step 1: Initialize Cost Model # The cost model estimates register usage based on compcount. # For simplicity, assume cost(node) = node.compcount # Max cost is the maximum register pressure if no nodes are checkpointed. currentmaxcost = max(node.compcount for node in forwardnodes) potentialcheckpoints = [] # Step 2: Greedy Search # We iterate through nodes, potentially adding them to checkpoints # if they significantly reduce the max cost. # Note: The exact definition of "halve the current maximum cost" # implies a reduction in the peak register pressure of the remaining # uncheckpointed computation graph. # Since the source describes an iterative process where the model is # updated, we simulate the selection of nodes that offer the best # reduction-to-cost ratio or simply the largest reduction until # the marginal gain is insufficient. # Simplified greedy approach based on source description: # "newly added nodes should approximately halve the current maximum cost" uncheckpointednodes = list(forwardnodes) while uncheckpointednodes: # Find the node that, if checkpointed, reduces the max cost # of the remaining uncheckpointed nodes the most. bestnode = None bestreduction = 0 for node in uncheckpointednodes: # Estimate new max cost if this node is checkpointed remainingcosts = [n.compcount for n in uncheckpointednodes if n != node] if not remainingcosts: newmaxcost = 0 else: newmaxcost = max(remainingcosts) reduction = currentmaxcost - newmaxcost if reduction > bestreduction: bestreduction = reduction bestnode = node # Check if the reduction is significant (approx. halving) # Source says: "newly added nodes should approximately halve..." # We interpret this as: if the new max cost is <= half of the old max cost. if bestnode and (currentmaxcost - bestreduction) <= currentmaxcost / 2: potentialcheckpoints.append(bestnode) uncheckpointednodes.remove(bestnode) currentmaxcost = currentmaxcost - bestreduction else: break # Step 3: Search for optimal k # Checkpointing every node found before iteration k # We profile or estimate runtime for k from 0 to len(potentialcheckpoints) bestk = 0 bestruntime = infinity # In practice, this involves compiling and running the kernel with # different checkpoint sets. Here we assume a runtime estimation function. for k in range(len(potentialcheckpoints) + 1): currentcheckpointset = set(potentialcheckpoints[:k]) # Estimate runtime based on memory I/O (proportional to len(checkpoints)) # and register pressure (proportional to max cost of uncheckpointed) # This is a placeholder for the actual profiling step described in runtime = estimateruntime(currentcheckpointset, forwardnodes) if runtime < bestruntime: bestruntime = runtime bestk = k loggedtrace = potentialcheckpoints[:bestk] # Step 4: Determine contloggedtrace # Choose between optimal loggedtrace or default list for non-Dirac params defaultcheckpointlist = getdefaultcheckpoints(forwardnodes) runtimecontoptimal = estimateruntime(loggedtrace, forwardnodes, mode='cont') runtimecontdefault = estimateruntime(defaultcheckpointlist, forwardnodes, mode='cont') if runtimecontoptimal < runtimecontdefault: contloggedtrace = loggedtrace else: contloggedtrace = defaultcheckpointlist return loggedtrace, contloggedtrace def estimateruntime(checkpointset, nodes, mode='full'): """ Placeholder for profiling. In the actual implementation, this would compile the Halide schedule and measure execution time. """ # Heuristic: Runtime ~ Memory I/O + Compute # Memory I/O increases with checkpoint size # Compute increases with register pressure (uncheckpointed nodes) memio = len(checkpointset) uncheckpointedcosts = [n.compcount for n in nodes if n not in checkpointset] registerpressure = max(uncheckpointedcosts) if uncheckpointedcosts else 0 # Simple linear model for estimation return memio 10 + registerpressure 5 Register Spilling: If the cost model underestimates register usage, the generated kernels may spill to local memory, drastically reducing performance. The heuristic aims to prevent this by aggressively checkpointing nodes with high computational cost. Memory I/O Overhead: Over-checkpointing leads to excessive memory reads/writes. The autoscheduler balances this by stopping the greedy search when the reduction in register pressure no longer justifies the memory cost. CSE Interference: Halide’s CSE pass can merge computations, making it difficult to isolate specific nodes for recomputation. Splitting into multiple kernels mitigates this by isolating the gradient computations. Discrete Choice Impact: The choice of separatesample affects the granularity of the kernels. 'axis' may lead to more balanced register usage across axes, while 'kernel' might be better if certain kernels have significantly different computational profiles. Time Complexity: The autoscheduler uses a greedy search, which is polynomial in the number of nodes, but the profiling step (finding optimal k) requires multiple compilations and runs, making the scheduling phase itself expensive. The runtime of the generated kernel depends on the balance between memory I/O and register pressure. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to storing all intermediates, as only nodes in loggedtrace are stored. The size of loggedtrace is determined by the autoscheduler. Performance: Measured performance depends on the specific GPU hardware and the complexity of the gradient kernels. The method is designed to minimize register spilling, which is critical for high-performance GPU execution. Strengths: Explicitly handles register pressure, which is often overlooked in standard checkpointing. Works well within the Halide framework. Limitations: The autoscheduler requires profiling, which adds to the compilation time. The heuristic may not find the global optimum. This method was introduced in the context of differentiable volume rendering, specifically for optimizing the gradient computation of raymarching loops with Dirac delta parameters. It builds on the principles of reverse-mode automatic differentiation and checkpointing. The work is part of the "A \delta" paper, which focuses on differentiable rendering with discontinuities. name: Implicit Gradients for Forward LBS
head: Implicit Differentiation for LBS, Detached Jacobian Inverse
body: This method computes differentiable point samples for volume rendering by solving a root-finding problem via implicit differentiation, allowing gradients to flow through the inverse of a forward Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) network. It solves the problem of back-propagating gradients through non-invertible or complex deformation networks by treating the canonical-to-observation mapping as an implicit function defined by a residual equation. It differs from the Adjoint Method by avoiding the storage of all intermediate activations for a full backward pass; instead, it computes the gradient analytically using the inverse Jacobian of the deformation function, detached from the computational graph. Inputs: \bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}: Sampled points in observation space (e.g., camera rays or depth samples). \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}: Initial estimates of canonical correspondences, obtained via iterative root-finding (e.g., Newton-Raphson). LBS{\sigma\omega}: The forward LBS network parameterized by \sigma\omega, mapping canonical points to observation space. f{\sigmaf}: The SDF network parameterized by \sigmaf (used in joint root-finding variant). Outputs: \hat{\mathbf{x}}: Differentiable point samples in canonical space that satisfy the implicit constraint. Gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \sigma\omega} (and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \sigmaf} in joint variant) computed via standard back-propagation from the photometric loss. Data Structures: \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{}: Tensor of shape (N, 3), detached from the graph. \mathbf{J}^: Jacobian matrix of shape (3, 3) for single point, or (4, 4) for joint root-finding, computed at \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{} and detached. Steps: 1. Initial Root-Finding: For each observation point \bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}, find a canonical point \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} such that the residual is minimized: LBS{\sigma\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}) - \bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \approx 0 This is done using iterative numerical methods. 2. Jacobian Computation: Compute the Jacobian of the LBS function with respect to the canonical input at the detached solution \hat{\mathbf{x}}^{}: \mathbf{J}^ = \frac{\partial LBS{\sigma\omega}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{x}}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^) This matrix is detached from the computational graph. 3. Implicit Gradient Correction: Compute the differentiable sample \hat{\mathbf{x}} by applying the implicit differentiation formula: \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}^ - (\mathbf{J}^)^{-1} \cdot \left( LBS{\sigma\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}) - \bar{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \right) Here, \hat{\mathbf{x}}^ and \mathbf{J}^ are treated as constants (detached), while the residual term allows the gradient to flow through the LBS network to \sigma\omega. 4. Back-Propagation: Use \hat{\mathbf{x}} as input to subsequent networks (e.g., SDF f{\sigmaf} and color networks). Compute the photometric loss \mathcal{L} and perform standard back-propagation to obtain gradients with respect to \sigma\omega (and \sigmaf). Pitfalls: Detachment: \hat{\mathbf{x}}^ and \mathbf{J}^ must be explicitly detached from the computational graph. If gradients flow through them, the method fails to provide the correct implicit gradient and may introduce instability. Jacobian Inversion: The Jacobian \mathbf{J}^ must be non-singular. Degenerate poses or singularities in the LBS network can make inversion unstable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def implicitgradientsforwardlbs(obspoints, lbsnetwork, initialcanonicalguess): """ obspoints: Tensor of shape (N, 3), observation space points. lbsnetwork: Differentiable LBS function fsigmaw. initialcanonicalguess: Tensor of shape (N, 3), detached canonical points xhatstar. """ # Step 1: Compute residual at detached guess # Note: initialcanonicalguess is detached, so this forward pass # does not contribute to the gradient graph for the correction term. lbsoutput = lbsnetwork(initialcanonicalguess) residual = lbsoutput - obspoints # Step 2: Compute Jacobian at detached guess # Jstar = d(LBS) / d(xhat) evaluated at xhatstar # This requires computing the Jacobian-vector product or full Jacobian. # We detach the result to prevent gradient flow through the Jacobian computation. with torch.nograd(): # Compute Jacobian matrix J of shape (N, 3, 3) # Assuming lbsnetwork(x) returns (N, 3) Jstar = computejacobian(lbsnetwork, initialcanonicalguess) # Invert Jacobian. name: Adjoint Backpropagation to Tree Nodes
head: Adjoint query to tree nodes, Backpropagation to Nodes
body: This method computes the gradients of a rendering loss with respect to moment attributes stored in a spatial tree (such as a Barnes-Hut tree) by backpropagating derivatives from the differentiable rendering stage to all tree nodes that contributed to the primal query. It sets itself apart from naive automatic differentiation by allowing the spatial pruning performed during the primal query to apply to the adjoint computation, thereby avoiding the linear complexity of visiting all leaves when the primal query terminates early at a cluster node. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The derivative db\varepsilon(x) provided by the differentiable rendering stage, where x is the query point and \varepsilon is the smoothing parameter. Output: Updated vector-valued gradient attributes dbt for all tree nodes t that contributed to the dipole sum during the corresponding primal query. Data Structures: Tree Nodes (t): Each node stores a moment attribute b (geometry f or appearance \ell^k) and its accumulated gradient dbt. Node Properties: \widehat{A}t: The aggregated attribute value (mass/weight) of node t. \widehat{p}t: The centroid (center of mass) of node t. Parameters: \varepsilon: The smoothing parameter used in the primal query. b: A stand-in variable for any moment attribute stored in the tree \mathcal{P}, specifically the geometry attribute f and appearance attributes \ell^k for k = 1, \dots, K. Steps: 1. Identify the set of tree nodes \mathcal{T}{contrib} that contributed to the dipole sum during the primal query for point x. 2. For each node t \in \mathcal{T}{contrib}: a. Compute the displacement vector \Deltat = \widehat{p}t - x. b. Compute the squared distance Dt = \|\Deltat\|^2. c. Evaluate the smoothing function S\left(\frac{\|\Deltat\|}{\varepsilon}\right). d. Compute the gradient increment: \Delta (dbt) = \widehat{A}t S\left(\frac{\|\Deltat\|}{\varepsilon}\right) \frac{\Deltat}{Dt^{3/2}} \cdot db\varepsilon(x) Note: The dot product \cdot indicates the interaction between the directional derivative term and the scalar/vector derivative from rendering. e. Update the node's gradient attribute: dbt \leftarrow dbt + \Delta (dbt) Pseudocode: Unverified code. This method computes the derivatives of per-point attributes through a Barnes-Hut tree with logarithmic complexity, avoiding the linear complexity of naive automatic differentiation. It solves the problem where backpropagating gradients to leaf nodes would normally require visiting all leaves, even if the primal query terminated early at a cluster node. It sets itself apart from naive AD by decoupling the gradient accumulation from the gradient propagation, allowing the primal query's spatial pruning to apply to the adjoint computation as well. This is significantly faster than visiting all leaves M if N{contrib} \ll M. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradient attributes dbt for all nodes in the tree. Strengths: Reuses the spatial hierarchy and pruning logic of the primal query, ensuring efficiency. Limitations: Requires storing the list of contributing nodes from the primal query or re-traversing the tree to identify them. name: Accelerated Adjoint Queries for Barnes-Hut
head: Adjoint dipole sum queries, Two-stage backpropagation
body: This method computes the derivatives of per-point attributes through a Barnes-Hut tree with logarithmic complexity, avoiding the linear complexity of naive automatic differentiation. It solves the problem where backpropagating gradients to leaf nodes would normally require visiting all leaves, even if the primal query terminated early at a cluster node. It sets itself apart from naive AD by decoupling the gradient accumulation from the gradient propagation, allowing the primal query's spatial pruning to apply to the adjoint computation as well. The method uses a two-stage backpropagation scheme. It relies on the Barnes-Hut tree structure where each node t stores centroidal radius \widehat{r}t, centroid \widehat{p}t, area \widehat{A}t, and moment attributes \widehat{b}t. Inputs: \widetilde{b}\varepsilon: The gradient of the loss with respect to the dipole sum output for a specific query point x and regularization parameter \varepsilon. x: The query point location. \text{node}: The root of the Barnes-Hut tree. \varepsilon: The regularization parameter. \beta: The Barnes-Hut opening angle parameter (threshold for cluster acceptance). Outputs: Accumulated gradients in the mutable gradient attributes \widetilde{db}t of the tree nodes. Updated point cloud attributes after the full traversal. Each tree node t stores mutable gradient attributes \widetilde{db}t. One such attribute exists for each geometry and appearance attribute being differentiated (e.g., geometry f and appearance \ell\alpha). These attributes accumulate backpropagated gradients during Stage 1. Stage 1: Local Gradient Accumulation During inverse rendering, for each primal query, an adjoint query is performed. This query backpropagates gradients only to the nodes visited by the corresponding primal query. 1. Detach Attributes: At the start of the iteration, after tree updates, detach node attributes from leaf node attributes to ensure gradients flow correctly through the tree structure rather than just the leaves. 2. Adjoint Query: For each query (x, \varepsilon) with incoming gradient \widetilde{b}\varepsilon, call ADJOINTQUERY starting from the root node. 3. Pruning Check: In ADJOINTQUERY, check if the current node is sufficiently far from the query point x. The condition is: \| x - \text{node}.\widehat{p} \| > \beta \cdot \text{node}.\widehat{r} If this condition holds, the node's contribution to the gradient is computed and accumulated, and the node's children are not visited. 4. Leaf Handling: If the node is a leaf (has no children), its contribution is computed and accumulated. 5. Recursive Descent: If the node is not a leaf and does not satisfy the pruning condition, recursively call ADJOINTQUERY on all children. Stage 2: Global Gradient Propagation After inverse rendering concludes, a single full tree traversal is performed. 1. Traverse Tree: Perform a post-order traversal (children before parents) or a top-down propagation depending on implementation, but the source specifies propagating from nodes to leaves. Specifically, the accumulated gradients \widetilde{db}t in internal nodes are propagated to their successor leaf nodes. 2. Update Attributes: The resulting gradients at the leaf nodes are used to update the point cloud attributes. Unverified code. This method avoids that by accumulating gradients at the node level and propagating them later. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Barnes-Hut Primal Queries The mathematical foundation for the primal and adjoint computations, involving the kernel functions S and P\varepsilon. Regularized Dipole Sums Time Complexity: O(Q \log N + Q \log N) = O(Q \log N) total per iteration, where Q is the number of queries and N is the number of points. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Enables inverse rendering at speeds competitive with rasterization methods. Strengths: Logarithmic complexity for both primal and adjoint queries, making it scalable for large point clouds. Limitations: Requires a two-stage process, which may complicate implementation compared to naive AD. When to use: When differentiating through Barnes-Hut based dipole sums for large point clouds. When not to use: When N is small enough that O(N) is acceptable, or when the tree structure is not available. The method is based on the work of Barill et al. [2018] who showed how to perform primal queries for the winding number with logarithmic complexity using the classical Barnes-Hut fast summation method [Barnes and Hut 1986]. The authors of adapt this approach to regularized dipole sums and extend it to adjoint queries. name: Forward-Mode Automatic Differentiation
head: Forward Differentiation, Forward mode differentiation, Tangent Mode AD, Tape-based Automatic Differentiation, Tracing (Automatic Differentiation), Wengert tape, computation graph
body: Forward-mode automatic differentiation (AD) computes derivatives by recursively applying the chain rule to elementary operations, propagating derivative information from input variables to output variables simultaneously with the forward simulation pass. It solves the problem of computing exact gradients without symbolic manipulation or finite differences by replacing every variable with a tuple of the original value and its derivative with respect to a parameter. Unlike reverse-mode AD, which traverses the graph from output to input, forward-mode traverses from input to output, making it efficient when the input dimension is low and the output dimension is high, but typically less suitable for optimization in high-dimensional scenes because each parameter requires a separate rendering pass or significant memory overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A primal computational graph representing the rendering function f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m, where n is the number of input parameters (scene variables, camera parameters, etc.) and m is the number of output variables (pixel colors). Outputs: The primal values (rendered image) and the Jacobian-vector products (gradients) of the outputs with respect to the specified input parameters. Data Structures: The core data structure is the forward variable (often called fvar or dual number), which wraps a scalar value and its derivative information. 1. Dual Number / Forward Variable (fvar): Layout: A struct containing: value: The primal scalar value (T). derivatives: An array or vector of size p storing the partial derivatives with respect to p input parameters (T[p]). Bit Packing: Not given in the sources. Fields: value: Stores x. derivatives[i]: Stores \frac{\partial x}{\partial wi} for i \in \{0, \dots, p-1\}. 2. Computation Graph / Tape (Optional for Tracing-based AD): If using a tracing approach (Wengert tape), the graph records the sequence of operations. The trace ignores control flow constructs and stores unrolled versions of all loops and taken branches. Each edge carries a weight indicating sensitivity. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize constant variables with zero derivative: \tilde{x}{\text{const}} = \langle x{\text{const}}, 0 \rangle. Initialize parameters of interest with unit derivative: \tilde{w}i = \langle wi, ei \rangle, where ei is a vector with 1 at index i and 0 elsewhere. If computing derivatives for multiple parameters, extend the derivatives array to size p. 2. Forward Propagation (Primal and Tangent): Traverse the computational graph from inputs to outputs. For each operation c = f(a, b), compute the primal value and the derivative using the chain rule: \tilde{c} = \tilde{f}(\tilde{a}, \tilde{b}) = \left\langle f(a, b), \frac{\partial f}{\partial a} \frac{da}{dw} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial b} \frac{db}{dw} \right\rangle Apply operator overloading for elementary arithmetic operations: Addition: value += rhs.value; grad += rhs.grad; Multiplication: grad = value rhs.grad + rhs.value grad; value = rhs.value; Division: grad = (grad rhs.value - value rhs.grad) / (rhs.value rhs.value); value /= rhs.value; Elementary Functions (e.g., \sin, \cos, \sqrt{}): \sin(\tilde{a}): value = sin(d.value); grad = d.grad cos(d.value); \cos(\tilde{a}): value = cos(d.value); grad = -d.grad sin(d.value); \sqrt{\tilde{a}}: value = sqrt(d.value); grad = value 0.5 d.grad / d.value; |\tilde{a}|: returns -d if value < 0, else d 3. Accumulation: Derivatives are accumulated forward in time using the chain rule. If using a tracing-based approach with latent variables, ensure gradients are kept in all variables during traversal to handle dependencies between scene parameters (e.g., using a ClearEdges flag). 4. Output Retrieval: Extract the derivatives component from the output variables (e.g., the rendered image). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class fvar: def init(self, value, derivatives): self.value = value self.derivatives = derivatives # List or array of size p def add(self, other): # Addition: c = a + b newvalue = self.value + other.value newderivs = [self.derivatives[i] + other.derivatives[i] for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def mul(self, other): # Multiplication: c = a b newvalue = self.value other.value newderivs = [self.value other.derivatives[i] + other.value self.derivatives[i] for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def truediv(self, other): # Division: c = a / b denom = other.value other.value newvalue = self.value / other.value newderivs = [(other.value self.derivatives[i] - self.value other.derivatives[i]) / denom for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def sin(self): # sin(a) newvalue = math.sin(self.value) newderivs = [math.cos(self.value) self.derivatives[i] for i in range(len(self.derivatives))] return fvar(newvalue, newderivs) def computeforwardmode(): # 1. Initialize parameters # Parameter w with derivative 1 w.r.t itself w = fvar(value=2.0, derivatives=[1.0]) # Constant c with derivative 0 c = fvar(value=3.0, derivatives=[0.0]) # 2. Forward propagation # Example operation: y = w c + sin(w) temp1 = w c # temp1.value = 6.0, temp1.derivatives = [3.0] temp2 = w.sin() # temp2.value = sin(2.0), temp2.derivatives = [cos(2.0)] y = temp1 + temp2 # y.value = 6.0 + sin(2.0), y.derivatives = [3.0 + cos(2.0)] return y def computeforwardmodemulti(): # Parameters w0, w1 # w0 derivative vector: [1, 0] w0 = fvar(value=2.0, derivatives=[1.0, 0.0]) # w1 derivative vector: [0, 1] w1 = fvar(value=3.0, derivatives=[0.0, 1.0]) # Operation: y = w0 w1 y = w0 w1 # y.value = 6.0 # y.derivatives[0] = w0.val w1.deriv[0] + w1.val w0.deriv[0] = 20 + 31 = 3 # y.derivatives[1] = w0.val w1.deriv[1] + w1.val w0.deriv[1] = 21 + 30 = 2 return y Parameters: p: The number of parameters to differentiate with respect to. The derivatives array size is p. Typical values: p is small (e.g., 2 for camera viewpoint) for efficient use; large p (e.g., thousands for Transfer Functions) makes it inefficient. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Dimensionality: Forward differentiation becomes unfeasible for high-dimensional input data (like Transfer Functions or 3D volumetric fields) because the number of parameters p is large, requiring the process to be repeated for each parameter or extending the derivatives array significantly. Latent Variables: If gradients of latent variables are not propagated to scene parameters before rendering, the loop tracing may destroy the part of the computational graph outside the loop, resulting in incorrect gradients. Visualization: Gradient values are not necessarily within [0, 1]. Directly displaying them as RGB floats will clip or distort the visualization; use a colormap and clamp the display range. Control Flow: Differentiating long-running loops can be challenging in tracing-based implementations due to overheads from repeated tracing and unrolling. Computes exact gradients of scalar fields using dual numbers, primarily for computing vertex normals for implicit surfaces. Chosen when exact gradients are needed for geometric primitives, avoiding finite difference errors. Combines tracing (Wengert tape) with dynamic compilation to reduce overhead in dynamic dispatch scenarios. Chosen when runtime performance and compilation time are critical for complex, dynamic rendering code. Time Complexity: O(d) times the time complexity of the original algorithm, where d is the number of input variables (parameters). Scales linearly with the number of parameters p. Memory Complexity: O(np), where n is the size of intermediate results (e.g., image dimensions) and p is the number of parameters. Only the current state needs to be stored, unlike reverse mode which may require caching all states. Measured Performance: Efficient for functions with few input variables (e.g., viewpoint selection with 2 parameters). Inefficient for functions with thousands or millions of input variables (e.g., volume density fields). Strengths: Simpler implementation than source transformation; easier to incorporate into existing code; efficient for low-dimensional inputs; computes derivatives for arbitrary number of outputs in one pass. Limitations: Unfeasible for high-dimensional inputs; requires separate pass per parameter if p is large; runtime overheads dominate in scalar programs. When to Use: When the number of input parameters is small (e.g., camera pose optimization) and the number of outputs is large. When Not to Use: When the number of input parameters is large (e.g., optimizing a high-resolution Transfer Function or volume density field). Forward-mode automatic differentiation computes derivatives by replacing variables with tuples of values and derivatives, propagating them from inputs to outputs in the computation graph. It is historically used in optimal control (linear quadratic regulators, trajectory optimization) and robotics toolboxes. In the context of differentiable rendering, it is used to visualize the effect of individual scene parameters on the rendered image, such as how changes in a wall's color affect global illumination. Forward mode is typically less suitable for optimization than reverse-mode (backpropagation) because each parameter requires a separate rendering pass.
