name: Dual Number Automatic Differentiation for Scalar Fields
head: Exact Normals via Forward Automatic Differentiation, Forward-mode AD via dual numbers, dual_object gradient computation
body: This method computes the exact gradient of a scalar field f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} at a point by evaluating the field on dual numbers that automatically propagate derivative information alongside the primal value. It is primarily used to compute exact vertex normals for implicit surfaces, avoiding the numerical instability and approximation errors inherent in finite difference methods. Input: A point p = (x, y, z) in 3D space and a scalar field function f(x, y, z). Output: The normalized gradient vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) representing the surface normal at p. The implementation uses a templated dual number type, typically autodiff::Real<1, T> or a custom dualobject. A base class object<Scalar> declares pure virtual valuegrad() returning the dual type and value() returning the scalar type. Derived classes override these methods and use the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP) via a derived() method to enable static polymorphism. 1. Extract the floating-point coordinates x, y, z from the input point p. 2. Construct three dual numbers representing coordinate perturbations: dx = \text{dual}(x, (1, 0, 0)), dy = \text{dual}(y, (0, 1, 0)), dz = \text{dual}(z, (0, 0, 1)). 3. Pack the dual numbers into a dual vector and pass them to the scalar field evaluation function. 4. Compute derivatives along each axis using the automatic differentiation API: nx = \text{derivative}(f, \text{wrt}(x), \text{at}(x, y, z)), ny = \text{derivative}(f, \text{wrt}(y), \text{at}(x, y, z)), nz = \text{derivative}(f, \text{wrt}(z), \text{at}(x, y, z)). 5. Normalize the gradient: compute reciprocal norm nn = 1 / \sqrt{nx^2 + ny^2 + nz^2} and return (nx \cdot nn, ny \cdot nn, nz \cdot nn). The following Python-like pseudocode implements the core logic. It defines a self-contained Dual class with overloaded arithmetic operators and implements the derivative helper exactly as specified in the evidence. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Dual: def init(self, value, grad): self.value = value self.grad = grad def add(self, o): return Dual(self.value + o.value, tuple(a + b for a, b in zip(self.grad, o.grad))) def mul(self, o): return Dual(self.value o.value, tuple(a o.value + o.value b for a, b in zip(self.grad, o.grad))) def truediv(self, o): return Dual(self.value / o.value, tuple((a o.value - self.value b) / (o.value 2) for a, b in zip(self.grad, o.grad))) def pow(self, n): return Dual(self.value n, tuple(n (self.value (n - 1)) b for b in self.grad)) def wrt(axis): return axis def at(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def derivative(f, axis, coords): x, y, z = coords if axis == 0: dx = Dual(x, (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) dy = Dual(y, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) dz = Dual(z, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) elif axis == 1: dx = Dual(x, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) dy = Dual(y, (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) dz = Dual(z, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) elif axis == 2: dx = Dual(x, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) dy = Dual(y, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) dz = Dual(z, (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) result = f(dx, dy, dz) return result.grad[axis] def computenormal(p, f): x, y, z = p nx = derivative(f, wrt(0), at(x, y, z)) ny = derivative(f, wrt(1), at(x, y, z)) nz = derivative(f, wrt(2), at(x, y, z)) normsq = nx nx + ny ny + nz nz if normsq == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) invnorm = 1.0 / (normsq 0.5) return (nx invnorm, ny invnorm, nz invnorm) Vertex Property Registration: In some implementations, the normal computation is registered as a vertex property using metadata such as VertexProperty("normal", fname="computenormal", dtype="T", shape=("dim",)). Type Parameter: The scalar type T (e.g., float, double) determines the precision of the primal and dual values. Stationary Points: If the gradient magnitude is zero (e.g., at a local extremum or saddle point), normalization fails; a guard returns a zero vector or a default normal. Function Differentiability: The scalar field function f must be differentiable everywhere in the domain of interest. Focuses on the application of this method specifically for computing surface normals for implicit geometry, highlighting its advantage over finite differences in avoiding aliasing and approximation errors. The broader category of AD techniques that compute derivatives by propagating tangent vectors forward through the computation graph, suitable for functions with many inputs and few outputs Forward-mode Automatic Differentiation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Computes exact analytical gradients, avoiding the truncation and round-off errors of finite differences. Limitations: Requires the scalar field function to be implemented with dual number support (operator overloading). When to Use: When exact normals are required for implicit surfaces and the field is differentiable. When Not to Use: When the field involves non-differentiable operations that cannot be adapted to dual number arithmetic. The method originates from forward-mode automatic differentiation for computing exact normals in implicit surface rendering. It is implemented in libraries such as planaria/dmc and keckj/cupmb to compute vertex normals by evaluating the exact gradient of the scalar field, avoiding finite differences. planaria/dmc, https://github.com/planaria/dmc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) keckj/cupmb, https://github.com/keckj/cupmb, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Tracing-based Automatic Differentiation with Dynamic Compilation
head: Hybrid AD, JIT-traced AD
body: This method is an automatic differentiation (AD) approach that ingests computation via tracing (Wengert tape) but combines it with dynamic compilation and function-level differentiation to produce output resembling source transformation AD. It solves the problem of high compilation overhead and poor runtime performance in dynamic dispatch scenarios common in differentiable rendering by dynamically specializing differential algorithms to the scene and problem statement while removing redundant steps introduced by the AD transformation. The method operates by tracing at two levels simultaneously: the AD layer traces differentiable computation, and the underlying JIT compiler traces the resulting derivative-related computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A primal computation graph (Wengert tape) containing primal variables and their dependencies. Output: A compiled residue of ordinary computation (machine code or optimized IR) ready for execution as part of a (mega-) kernel. Data Structures: Wengert Tape: A computation graph that captures operations for subsequent derivative propagation. It associates every primal variable x with a differential version \bar{x} (or \delta x) and records inter-variable dependencies. JIT Intermediate Representation (IR): The representation used by the underlying JIT compiler to trace the derivative-related computation residue. Steps: 1. Trace Primal and Differential Variables: Associate every primal variable x with a differential version \bar{x} and record inter-variable dependencies on the Wengert tape. 2. Traverse Tape for Derivatives: Traverse the tape to compute differentiable variables, producing a flurry of operations referencing primal program state. 3. Trace Residue with JIT: The derivative-related computation generated in Step 2 is itself traced by the underlying JIT compiler. This step effectively destroys the AD data structures (the tape), leaving a residue of ordinary computation. 4. Compile and Execute: The residue is traced by the JIT compiler one level below so that it can run as part of a (mega-) kernel at a later point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tracingadwithdynamiccompilation(primalinput): # Step 1: Trace primal and differential variables # Associate every primal variable x with a differential version dx # and record inter-variable dependencies on the Wengert tape. tape = [] primaloutput = primalfunction(primalinput, tape) # Step 2: Traverse tape for derivatives # Traverse the tape to compute differentiable variables. # This produces a flurry of operations referencing primal program state. derivativeops = [] for node in reversed(tape): derivativeops.append(computederivative(node)) # Step 3: Trace residue with JIT # The derivative-related computation is traced by the underlying JIT compiler. # This destroys the AD data structures (tape), leaving a residue of ordinary computation. jitir = jittrace(derivativeops) # Step 4: Compile and execute # The residue is traced one level below to run as part of a (mega-) kernel. kernel = jitir.compile() result = kernel.execute() return result def primalfunction(x, tape): y = x 2.0 tape.append(('mul', x, 2.0, y)) return y def computederivative(node): op, a, b, out = node return ('dmul', a, b, out) def jittrace(ops): return {'ir': ops, 'compiled': False} Parameters and Typical Values: Tape Retention: The destruction of the AD tape is immaterial if multiple AD traversals are needed; the tape is often retained in such cases. Checkpointing: The system supports checkpointing without intentional effort, as shown in unrolled loops with intermediate evaluation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Traversals: If multiple AD traversals are required, the tape must be retained rather than destroyed. Developer Responsibility: The method does not free the developer from thinking about subtle details of the differentiation process. It facilitates but does not automate the introduction of physical and mathematical “reversibilities”. The JIT Compilation Pipeline is a computational substrate that captures Python or C++ code execution into an Intermediate Representation (IR) for later compilation into machine code, supporting asynchronous execution on CPU or GPU. It solves the problem of high compilation overhead and poor runtime performance in dynamic dispatch scenarios common in differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from alternatives like JAX/XLA by generating indirect calls to separate subroutines rather than merging all functions into a single large kernel body or committing loop state to memory at every iteration, thereby reducing backend compilation time and register allocation costs. Time Complexity: The method reduces backend compilation time and register allocation costs by generating indirect calls to separate subroutines rather than merging all functions into a single large kernel body. Memory Complexity: The AD data structures are destroyed during the tracing of the residue, leaving only the ordinary computation residue in memory, which reduces memory overhead compared to retaining full AD graphs during execution. Performance: The approach enables dynamic specialization of differential algorithms to the scene and problem statement, removing redundant steps introduced by the AD transformation. Strengths: Combines the flexibility of tracing AD with the performance of source transformation AD; supports checkpointing naturally; reduces compilation overhead. Limitations: The method does not free the developer from thinking about subtle details of the differentiation process. It facilitates—but does not automate—the introduction of physical and mathematical “reversibilities”. Tape destruction is immaterial if multiple AD traversals are needed; the tape is often retained. When to Use: Suitable for differentiable rendering scenarios where dynamic dispatch and scene-specific specialization are beneficial, and where compilation overhead is a concern. When Not to Use: Not suitable if the developer requires full automation of differentiation details or if multiple AD traversals are needed without retaining the tape. This method is based on the Dr.Jit system, a Just-In-Time Compiler for Differentiable Rendering. It lies between tracing and source transformation AD, ingesting computation using tracing but producing output resembling source transformation AD through the combination with dynamic compilation and function-level differentiation. The approach is not unique to Dr.Jit and also underlies other hybrid AD systems, such as CppADCodeGen. The system was introduced in the paper "Dr.Jit: A Just-In-Time Compiler for Differentiable Rendering". DR.JIT, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530099, fetched 2026-10-26

name: JIT Compilation Pipeline
head: Dr.Jit Compilation Pipeline, Dr.Jit IR generation, Dr.Jit JIT compilation, Dr.Jit Tracing and Compilation Pipeline
body: The JIT Compilation Pipeline is a computational substrate that captures Python or C++ code execution into an Intermediate Representation (IR) for later compilation into machine code, supporting asynchronous execution on CPU or GPU. It solves the problem of high compilation overhead and poor runtime performance in dynamic dispatch scenarios common in differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from alternatives like JAX/XLA by generating indirect calls to separate subroutines rather than merging all functions into a single large kernel body or committing loop state to memory at every iteration, thereby reducing backend compilation time and register allocation costs. The pipeline consists of five main phases: Tracing, Kernel Assembly, Backend Compilation, Kernel Execution, and Evaluation. Input: Python or C++ source code using custom arithmetic types (e.g., Float, UInt32) that represent dynamically sized 1D arrays rather than scalar variables. These arrays act as scalar variable declarations within a loop (e.g., for index in range(..)), where the index typically refers to a Monte Carlo sample. Output: Executable machine code (via LLVM for CPU or OptiX/CUDA for GPU) and asynchronous execution results. Computation Graph: A graph data structure recording operations during tracing. Kernel Cache: An in-memory and on-disk cache storing previously compiled kernels to avoid redundant backend compilation. Loop State: Variables modified in the loop body and accessed in subsequent iterations or after termination. 1. Tracing: The system executes the program using custom arithmetic types that record operations into the computation graph. Local Optimizations: During tracing, the system performs constant folding/propagation, basic algebraic simplifications (e.g., fma(a, b, 0) = a \cdot b; a \cdot 1 = a), and local value numbering (reusing equivalent variables based on operation type and input dependencies). Loop Handling: Standard Python for loops unroll the loop body, producing unnecessarily large traces. Instead, a Loop object is instantiated with a lambda function specifying state variables (e.g., random number generator, counter, result). The implementation invokes this lambda before and after the loop to catch redefinitions of Python variables. The loop runs for only one iteration to capture the effect of an individual iteration, wiring it into the generated kernel. Dynamic Dispatch (vcall): For polymorphic methods, Dr.Jit traces all reachable method implementations (scene objects register themselves). The operation acts as a demultiplexer-multiplexer. 2. Kernel Assembly: This phase removes redundancies at a global level and produces a program in the desired IR (LLVM IR or PTX). Global Optimizations: Includes dead code elimination, devirtualization (moving identical computations out of calls), and deduplication (identical sub-traces produce a single function definition). Control Flow Preservation: The generated IR preserves the control flow (loops, subroutines) of the original program, resembling source transformation output. Dynamic dispatch produces IR performing an indirect branch to one of multiple subroutines. 3. Backend Compilation: The generated IR is compiled into executable machine code using LLVM (CPU) or OptiX/CUDA (GPU). Caching: Backend compilation is relatively costly. The system consults the kernel cache (in-memory and on-disk) to see if the computation was previously encountered. In typical Path-Based Differentiable Rendering (PBDR) usage, this step is only necessary during the first gradient descent step. 4. Kernel Execution: The kernel is launched for asynchronous execution on the CPU (via a thread pool) or GPU (via CUDA/OptiX). This allows tracing and kernel execution to continue in parallel. 5. Evaluation (Triggered by Access): Accessing array contents (e.g., print) triggers evaluation via dr.eval(..). This compiles and launches a fused kernel to commit requested variables to device memory. Subsequent references use the stored version, allowing unused trace parts to expire. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr from drjit.cuda import Float, UInt32, Loop, PCG32 x = dr.linspace(Float, -1, 1, num=1024) y = dr.linspace(Float, -1, 1, num=1024) x, y = dr.meshgrid(x, y) rng = PCG32(size=1024 1024) i, result = UInt32(0), Float(0) loop = Loop(state=lambda: (rng, i, result)) intersectionvalid = True while loop(intersectionvalid & (i < 128)): # Loop body operations are traced # Dynamic dispatch (vcall) is traced here for polymorphic scene objects pass i += 1 print(x) Backend Compilation Frequency: Typically only necessary during the first gradient descent step in typical PBDR usage. Tracing/Assembly Time: Highly optimized, taking on the order of 1-15ms in typical cases. Loop Unrolling: Standard Python for loops unroll the loop body, producing unnecessarily large traces. Dr.Jit uses a Loop object to preserve loop structure instead. Backend Compilation Cost: Backend compilation time in OptiX and LLVM grows superlinearly with kernel size. Preserving control flow (loops/polymorphism) avoids creating an immensely large unrolled program that breaks the backend. Dynamic Dispatch Boundary: Dynamic dispatch presents an opaque boundary that breaks interprocedural optimizations in LLVM/OptiX. Dr.Jit handles this by generating indirect branches to subroutines. Dr.Jit Optimizations are a set of global transformations applied during the tracing phase to improve code generation, specifically addressing the opaque boundary of dynamic dispatch that breaks interprocedural optimizations in backends like LLVM and OptiX. Unlike ML-centric IR and tensorial optimizations which are costly for rendering, Dr.Jit's optimizations are tailored for the large amount of arithmetic in PBDR workloads. Choose it when rendering workloads require aggressive arithmetic simplification without the overhead of tensor-centric passes. Dr.Jit Tracing and Compilation is a just-in-time (JIT) system that converts traced Python-like computation graphs into optimized kernels for CPUs and GPUs. It solves the problem of high compilation overhead and poor runtime performance in dynamic dispatch scenarios common in differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from alternatives like JAX/XLA by generating indirect calls to separate subroutines rather than merging all functions into a single large kernel body or committing loop state to memory at every iteration, thereby reducing backend compilation time and register allocation costs. Choose it when control flow preservation is critical to avoid backend compilation bottlenecks. Time Complexity: Tracing and kernel assembly are highly optimized, taking on the order of 1-15ms in typical cases. Backend compilation is relatively costly but cached. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In typical PBDR usage, backend compilation is only necessary during the first gradient descent step. Scaling: Backend compilation time in OptiX and LLVM tends to grow superlinearly with kernel size. Strengths: Preserves control flow (loops, subroutines) of the original program, resembling source transformation output. Supports asynchronous execution on CPU or GPU. Effective for the large amount of arithmetic in PBDR workloads where rich ML-centric IR and tensorial optimizations are costly. Limitations: Backend compilation is costly if caching misses occur. Dynamic dispatch presents an opaque boundary for interprocedural optimizations in backends. When to use: Differentiable rendering workloads with large amounts of arithmetic, particularly when control flow preservation is needed to avoid excessive kernel size. When not to use: Workloads where rich tensorial optimizations are beneficial and the arithmetic intensity is lower (e.g., standard ML neural network training). Dr.Jit is a just-in-time compiler for differentiable rendering. It was introduced in the paper "Dr.Jit: A Just-In-Time Compiler for Differentiable Rendering". The system shares similarities with array programming frameworks like PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX, but is tailored for the specific needs of rendering. It is a hybrid system that ingests computation using tracing but generates kernels that preserve the control flow of the original program. name: Dr.Jit Optimizations
head: Global optimizations, Polymorphism-aware optimizations
body: Dr.Jit Optimizations are a set of global transformations applied during the tracing phase to improve code generation, specifically addressing the opaque boundary of dynamic dispatch that breaks interprocedural optimizations in backends like LLVM and OptiX. Unlike ML-centric IR and tensorial optimizations which are costly for rendering, Dr.Jit's optimizations are tailored for the large amount of arithmetic in PBDR workloads. Inputs: Traced computation graph containing polymorphic calls and variable references. Outputs: Optimized intermediate representation (IR) ready for backend compilation. Data Structures: Variable Reference Count: Tracks the number of active references to each variable to identify dead code. Value Numbering Map: Maps identical computational results to a single canonical ID to enable deduplication. Steps: 1. Constant Propagation: Automatically performed during tracing to replace variables with their constant values where possible. 2. Dead Code Elimination: Performed via variable reference counting; if a variable is unreferenced, it is removed. 3. Unreferenced Output Removal: The system removes unreferenced outputs from function calls, which triggers a cascade effect removing unreferenced inputs and further reducing the surrounding program's computational load. 4. Devirtualization: Computation that is identical in all sub-traces is devirtualized; if all sub-traces output a variable with the same ID, that variable is moved out of the call. 5. Trace and Merge: The system traces every reachable instance of polymorphic functions (e.g., ubershader materials) without making assumptions about parameter subsets, then merges the resulting identical functions into a single subroutine. 6. Deduplication: Built on value numbering; identical traces are collapsed into a single subroutine to handle scenes with thousands of objects of the same type. Pitfalls: Type Equivalence vs. Operation Sequence: Type equivalence does not imply identical operation sequences for complex materials. For example, Disney’s Principled BSDF may have different active subsets of parameters, procedural textures, or derivative tracking requirements depending on the instance. Dr.Jit avoids assumptions and traces every instance to ensure correctness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizetracedprogram(program): # Step 1: Constant Propagation (automatic during tracing) # Replace variables with constant values where possible for node in program.nodes: if isconstant(node): node.value = evaluate(node) # Step 2: Dead Code Elimination via Reference Counting # Track active references; remove variables with zero references refcounts = computereferencecounts(program) program.nodes = [n for n in program.nodes if refcounts[n.id] > 0] # Step 3: Remove Unreferenced Outputs and Inputs # Remove unreferenced outputs, cascading to remove dependent inputs for call in program.calls: if not isreferenced(call.outputs): remove(call.outputs) for inp in call.inputs: if not isreferenced(inp): remove(inp) # Step 4: Devirtualize Identical Sub-traces # Move variables out of calls if all sub-traces output the same ID for call in program.calls: outputids = {subtrace.outputid for subtrace in call.subtraces} if len(outputids) == 1: call.body = liftidenticalcomputationoutofcall(call.body) # Step 5: Trace Polymorphic Instances # Trace every reachable instance without assuming parameter subsets tracedinstances = [] for func in program.polymorphicfunctions: tracedinstances.append(traceinstance(func)) # Step 6: Deduplicate and Merge Identical Traces # Collapse identical traces into single subroutines using value numbering valuemap = {} for instance in tracedinstances: canonicalid = valuenumber(instance) if canonicalid not in valuemap: valuemap[canonicalid] = instance else: mergesubroutines(program, instance, valuemap[canonicalid]) return program def isconstant(node): return node.type == CONSTANT def evaluate(node): return node.op([n.value for n in node.inputs]) def computereferencecounts(prog): return {v.id: count(v) for v in prog.variables} def isreferenced(var): return var.usagecount > 0 def remove(var): var.active = False def liftidenticalcomputationoutofcall(body): return body def traceinstance(func): return func.trace() def valuenumber(instance): return hash(instance.ir) def mergesubroutines(prog, inst1, inst2): return prog.replace(inst1, inst2) Performance Impact: Removing unreferenced computation, arguments, and return values improves performance by an average factor of 2.5x in the OptiX backend. CPU Impact: On the CPU, removing unreferenced computation has essentially no impact on performance, likely because modern superscalar CPUs can absorb redundant computation by issuing multiple instructions per clock cycle. Compilation Time: Subroutine deduplication reverts growth in compilation time caused by other optimizations and provides a speed boost by reducing divergence under vectorized execution. Strengths: Tailored for the large amount of arithmetic in PBDR workloads, avoiding the cost of ML-centric tensorial optimizations. Effective at handling scenes with thousands of identical objects. Limitations: The optimization strategy relies on tracing every instance, which can increase compilation time if deduplication is not effective. Dr.Jit Optimizations were introduced in the Dr.Jit library, designed for differentiable programming and volume rendering. The approach addresses the limitations of standard backend compilers (LLVM/OptiX) when faced with dynamic dispatch boundaries. The optimizations are specifically tailored for the arithmetic intensity of PBDR workloads, distinguishing them from optimizations designed for neural network computations. name: Dr.Jit Tracing and Compilation
head: DrJit
body: Dr.Jit Tracing and Compilation is a just-in-time system that converts traced Python-like computation into optimized kernels for CPUs and GPUs. It solves high compilation overhead and poor runtime performance in dynamic dispatch scenarios common in differentiable rendering by generating indirect calls to separate subroutines rather than merging functions into a single large kernel body or committing loop state to memory at every iteration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Python program containing tensor operations, loops, and polymorphic function calls (e.g., closures, instance attributes). Output: Compiled kernels and execution metadata. Data Structures: Traced Graph: A representation of the computation where operations, loops, and function calls are recorded as nodes. Kernel Registry: Stores compiled subroutines. Dr.Jit exploits redundancy by identifying identical functions and generating indirect calls to them, allowing separate compilation. Side Effect Queue: Tracks variables affected by mutable operations (e.g., scatter, atomic scatter-reductions). Steps: 1. Tracing: The Python interpreter is wrapped to record operations into a graph. Loops are either recorded as single nodes or executed via wavefront-style kernels depending on configuration flags. 2. Redundancy Detection: The system analyzes the traced graph to identify identical subroutines from dynamic dispatch. Deduplication reduces backend compilation time to a constant when functions are identical. 3. Kernel Assembly: For megakernels, the entire traced program is assembled into a single kernel preserving control flow. For wavefront-style, loops are executed using a sequence of wavefront-style kernels, or wavefronts are grouped by instance to launch maximally coherent kernels. 4. Compilation: The assembled IR is passed to the backend compiler. Dr.Jit generates indirect calls to subroutines for separate compilation, unlike JAX which merges functions into one large body. 5. Execution: The compiled kernel is launched. Read access or arithmetic involving variables marked as affected by queued side effects triggers a kernel launch to materialize them. Parameters: Loop Handling: Flags control whether loops are traced (trace) or executed via wavefront-style kernels (wavefront). Dispatch Handling: Flags control whether polymorphic calls use indirect calls (indirectcall) or are inlined (inline). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Compilation Timeout: Nontrivial examples with custom computation, loops, and dynamic dispatch tracing can cause JAX/XLA to timeout. Side Effects: Mutable operations (scatter, atomic reductions) require explicit kernel launches to materialize state before read access or arithmetic. Register Pressure: Merging all functions into one large kernel (as JAX does with jax.lax.switch()) exacerbates register allocation costs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceandcompile(program, loopmode='trace', dispatchmode='indirectcall'): # 1. Tracing: wrap the Python interpreter to record tensor operations, loops, and polymorphic calls into a computation graph graph = [] for node in program.nodes: graph.append(recordoperation(node)) # 2. Redundancy Detection: identify identical subroutines to reduce compilation time uniquesubroutines = set() deduplicatedgraph = [] for node in graph: if node.isfunctioncall(): if node.functionid not in uniquesubroutines: uniquesubroutines.add(node.functionid) deduplicatedgraph.append(node) else: deduplicatedgraph.append(node) # 3. Kernel Assembly: generate IR based on tracing flags if loopmode == 'trace' and dispatchmode == 'indirectcall': kernelir = assemblesinglekernel(deduplicatedgraph) # standard IR generation elif loopmode == 'wavefront': kernelir = assemblewavefrontkernels(deduplicatedgraph) # wavefront kernel generation # 4. Side Effect Handling: materialize state for variables affected by scatter/atomic ops if any(node.ismutable() for node in kernelir.nodes): kernelir = insertkernellaunchesformaterialization(kernelir) # inserts kernel launches # 5. Compilation: pass IR to backend compiler (e.g., LLVM) compiledkernel = invokebackendcompiler(kernelir) return compiledkernel A tracing behavior mode where Dr.Jit executes loops using a sequence of wavefront-style kernels, or groups wavefronts by instance to launch maximally coherent kernels per group. It provides an intermediate configuration between full megakernel and full wavefront-style evaluation resembling Enoki. Wavefront-style execution reduces GPU performance by a factor of 2.0–7.7× compared to megakernels, while the same experiment on the CPU can increase cost by a factor of more than 100×. Memory usage is significant in this configuration, and tracing and kernel assembly only constitute a small portion of the total computation time. Time Complexity: Backend compilation time is reduced to a constant when functions are identical due to deduplication and indirect calls, whereas JAX/XLA compilation time grows with input program size. Memory Complexity: Megakernels have lower memory overhead than wavefront-style evaluation, which requires significant memory for intermediate data. Performance: Megakernels outperform wavefront-style evaluation significantly. On GPU, wavefront-style is 2.0–7.7× slower; on CPU, it is >100× slower. Micro-benchmark results for loop iteration count 10 show DrJit at 0.72s versus JAX at 12.51s, and for instance count 150 with de-duplicated functions, DrJit at 0.26s versus JAX at 26.09s. Strengths: Handles dynamic dispatch efficiently; avoids compilation timeouts; reduces register pressure via indirect calls. Limitations: Wavefront-style mode has high runtime cost and memory usage; megakernels may have high memory usage for very large programs. When to Use: Use megakernels for performance-critical rendering. Avoid JAX/XLA for nontrivial dynamic dispatch due to timeout risks. Dr.Jit was introduced by Wenzel Jakob et al. in 2022. It was developed to address the limitations of existing automatic differentiation systems in the context of differentiable rendering, particularly regarding compilation time and runtime performance for dynamic dispatch and loop handling. It is used in differentiable volume rendering and other graphics applications requiring efficient JIT compilation. DR.JIT, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530099, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Field Derivatives via Autograd
head: Differential Operators (Gradient, Divergence, Laplace), Gradient, Laplace via Autograd, autograd operators, neural field derivatives
body:
This method computes spatial differential operators (gradient, divergence, Laplacian) of neural field outputs with respect to their spatial inputs using automatic differentiation (autograd). It enables supervision on gradient targets, such as Eikonal loss or surface smoothness constraints, by leveraging the computational graph built during the forward pass. It builds on Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A differentiable neural field model f: \mathbb{R}^d 	o \mathbb{R}^k and a batch of input points X \in \mathbb{R}^{N 	imes d}. Outputs: The computed derivative field (gradient, divergence, or Laplacian) with the same spatial shape as X. Data Structures: The neural field is implemented as a differentiable module where weights are tracked parameters. Inputs X must be leaf tensors with requiresgrad=True to enable gradient computation with respect to spatial coordinates. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Compute the field output Y = f(X). 2. Gradient Computation: To compute the gradient 
ablaX Y \in \mathbb{R}^{N 	imes d 	imes k}: If k=1 (scalar field), compute 
ablaX Y =  rac{\partial Y}{\partial X} directly. If k>1 (vector field), compute the Jacobian matrix J \in \mathbb{R}^{N 	imes k 	imes d} where J{n,i,j} =  rac{\partial Y{n,i}}{\partial X{n,j}}. In PyTorch, this is done using torch.autograd.grad with creategraph=True to allow higher-order derivatives. 3. Divergence Computation: For a vector field Y \in \mathbb{R}^{N 	imes d}, the divergence 
abla \cdot Y \in \mathbb{R}^N is the trace of the Jacobian. This is computed by summing the diagonal elements of the Jacobian for each sample point. 4. Laplacian Computation: The Laplacian \Delta Y = 
abla \cdot (
abla Y) is computed as the divergence of the gradient. For a scalar field, this is the trace of the Hessian matrix. Formulas: Gradient: 
ablaX Y =  rac{\partial Y}{\partial X} Divergence: 
abla \cdot Y = 	ext{Tr}\left( rac{\partial Y}{\partial X}ight) = \sum{j=1}^d  rac{\partial Yj}{\partial Xj} Laplacian: \Delta Y = 
abla \cdot (
abla Y) = \sum{j=1}^d  rac{\partial^2 Y}{\partial Xj^2} Parameters: creategraph=True: A boolean flag in torch.autograd.grad that keeps the gradient computation in the computational graph, allowing for higher-order derivatives (e.g., Laplacian). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computegradient(model, x, creategraph=True): """ Compute the gradient of model output with respect to input x. Args: model: Differentiable neural field model. x: Input points [N, d], requiresgrad=True. creategraph: Whether to create a computation graph for higher-order derivatives. Returns: grad: Gradient [N, d] for scalar output, or [N, d, k] for vector output. """ y = model(x) # [N, k] if y.shape[-1] == 1: grad = torch.autograd.grad( y.sum(), x, creategraph=creategraph, retaingraph=True)[0] # [N, d] else: grad = [] for i in range(y.shape[1]): gradi = torch.autograd.grad( y[:, i].sum(), x, creategraph=creategraph, retaingraph=True)[0] # [N, d] grad.append(gradi) grad = torch.stack(grad, dim=-1) # [N, d, k] return grad def computedivergence(model, x, creategraph=True): """ Compute the divergence of a vector field output by the model. Args: model: Differentiable neural field model outputting a vector field [N, d]. x: Input points [N, d], requiresgrad=True. creategraph: Whether to create a computation graph for higher-order derivatives. Returns: div: Divergence [N]. """ y = model(x) # [N, d] grads = [] for i in range(y.shape[1]): gradi = torch.autograd.grad( y[:, i].sum(), x, creategraph=creategraph, retaingraph=True)[0] # [N, d] grads.append(gradi) grads = torch.stack(grads, dim=1) # [N, d, d] d = grads.shape[1] div = grads[:, torch.arange(d), torch.arange(d)].sum(dim=1) # [N] return div def computelaplacian(model, x, creategraph=True): """ Compute the Laplacian of a scalar field output by the model. Args: model: Differentiable neural field model outputting a scalar field [N]. x: Input points [N, d], requiresgrad=True. creategraph: Whether to create a computation graph for higher-order derivatives. Returns: laplacian: Laplacian [N]. """ y = model(x) # [N] grad = torch.autograd.grad( y.sum(), x, creategraph=creategraph, retaingraph=True)[0] # [N, d] laplacian = 0.0 for i in range(grad.shape[1]): laplacian += torch.autograd.grad( grad[:, i].sum(), x, creategraph=creategraph, retaingraph=True)[0][:, i] # [N] return laplacian Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Autograd provides exact derivatives, but numerical stability depends on the model's architecture and input scaling. Boundaries: For fields defined on bounded domains, derivatives at boundaries may be inaccurate if the model is not trained to respect boundary conditions. Degenerate Input: If input points are identical, gradients may be undefined or noisy. This method computes the gradients of the sphere tracing output with respect to input parameters (such as SDF parameters) using implicit differentiation, avoiding the need to backpropagate through the iterative sphere tracing loop. It differs from naive backpropagation by treating the converged ray positions as fixed points and computing gradients via the chain rule on the SDF evaluation, while explicitly handling the convergence mask. Choose this when sphere tracing is part of the differentiable pipeline and memory efficiency is critical. See Implicit Differentiation for Sphere Tracing. A numerical estimation of the Laplacian \Delta f of an SDF f at a point p, using the average value of f over a small sphere centered at p. The formula is: \overline{f}(p, h) \approx f(p) -  rac{(\Delta f)(p)}{2n}h^2 \overline{f}(p, \epsilon) \approx  rac{1}{4}\sum{i=0}^3f(p+\epsilon vi) (\Delta f)(p) \approx  rac{6}{\epsilon^2} \left( f(p) -  rac{1}{4}\sum{i=0}^3f(p+\epsilon vi) ight) Parameters: n is the dimension of the space (3 for 3D SDFs), \epsilon is the radius of the small sphere, and vi are vectors defining the points on the sphere for averaging (i=0 to 3). Pitfall: The sign convention for the Laplacian is positive-definite. In Jax, compute the Jacobian Jf(\mu) application without explicit matrix construction by using the linearize operator, applying it twice in sequence to \Sigma, with dimensions of the covariance matrix transposed after each application. This reduces memory overhead compared to explicit Jacobian computation. A technique to compute second-order derivatives of ReLU-based MLPs efficiently by exploiting the property that the second derivative of the MLP output with respect to its input is zero, simplifying the chain rule calculations for backpropagation of Eikonal loss. Define Pl^j as the product of matrices Gl, H{l-1},..., G2, H1^{(-j)} where H1^{(-j)} is the j-th column of H1. Define Sl^i as the product of matrices HL^{(i,-)}, GL,..., H{l+1}, G{l+1} where HL^{(i,-)} is the i-th row of HL. Define Gl as a diagonal matrix with 1s where H{l-1}... g(H1 x) > 0 and 0 otherwise. Use Theorem 1 to determine that \partial^2 e/\partial e^2 = 0 because e is computed by a ReLU-based MLP. Formulas: Pl^j = Gl H{l-1}... G2 H1^{(-j)} Sl^i = HL^{(i,-)} GL... H{l+1} G{l+1} Gl =  egin{cases} 1, & H{l-1}... g(H1 x) > 0 \ 0, & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases}  rac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x^2} = 0 Parameters: L is the number of hidden layers in the ReLU-based MLP, Hl is the weight matrix for layer l with dimensions \mathbb{R}^{nl 	imes \mathbb{R}^{n{l-1}}}, nl is the number of neurons in layer l, Pl^j is a matrix in \mathbb{R}^{n{l-1} 	imes 1} used in second-order derivative calculation, and Sl^i is a matrix in \mathbb{R}^{1 	imes nl} used in second-order derivative calculation. Not given in the sources. Originating from the rise of differentiable rendering and neural implicit representations, this method leverages automatic differentiation frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, Jax) to compute spatial derivatives of neural fields. The method is widely used in neural radiance fields (NeRF), signed distance fields (SDF), and other neural implicit representations for 3D reconstruction and rendering. name: Implicit Differentiation for Sphere Tracing
head: Implicit Differentiation for Sphere Tracing Gradients, Sphere Tracing Gradients via Implicit Differentiation
body:
This method computes the gradients of the sphere tracing output with respect to input parameters (such as SDF parameters) using implicit differentiation, avoiding the need to backpropagate through the iterative sphere tracing loop. It differs from naive backpropagation by treating the converged ray positions as fixed points and computing gradients via the chain rule on the SDF evaluation, while explicitly handling the convergence mask. Inputs: signeddistancefunction: A differentiable function f(\mathbf{p}, 	heta) mapping 3D positions \mathbf{p} and model parameters 	heta to signed distances. positions: The converged ray positions after sphere tracing, shape (N, 3). directions: The ray directions for each point, shape (N, 3). converged: A boolean mask indicating which rays successfully converged, shape (N,). gradoutputs: The upstream gradient flowing back from the loss with respect to the output positions, shape (N, 3). parameters: The learnable parameters 	heta of the SDF. Outputs: gradparameters: The gradients of the loss with respect to the model parameters 	heta. Data Structures: Tensors are assumed to be floating-point tensors for positions, directions, and parameters, with a boolean tensor for the convergence mask. Steps: 1. Detach Positions: The converged positions are detached from the computational graph to prevent backpropagation through the sphere tracing iterations. 2. Re-evaluate SDF: Compute the signed distance values and their gradients with respect to the detached positions. d = f(\mathbf{p}, 	heta) 
abla{\mathbf{p}} d =  rac{\partial d}{\partial \mathbf{p}} This is computed using automatic differentiation with retaingraph=True. 3. Project Output Gradient: Compute the dot product of the upstream gradient \mathbf{g}{	ext{out}} and the ray direction \mathbf{v}. g{	ext{dot}} = \mathbf{g}{	ext{out}} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum{i=1}^3 g{	ext{out}, i} vi Shape: (N, 1). 4. Project SDF Gradient: Compute the dot product of the SDF spatial gradient 
abla{\mathbf{p}} d and the ray direction \mathbf{v}. p{	ext{dot}} = 
abla{\mathbf{p}} d \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum{i=1}^3  rac{\partial d}{\partial pi} vi Shape: (N, 1). 5. Regularize Denominator: To avoid division by zero when the ray direction is tangent to the surface (p{	ext{dot}} \approx 0), clamp the denominator away from zero. If p{	ext{dot}} > 0, clamp to \max(p{	ext{dot}}, \epsilon); if p{	ext{dot}} \le 0, clamp to \min(p{	ext{dot}}, -\epsilon), where \epsilon = 10^{-6}. p{	ext{dot}}^{	ext{reg}} =  egin{cases} \max(p{	ext{dot}}, 10^{-6}) & 	ext{if } p{	ext{dot}} > 0 \ \min(p{	ext{dot}}, -10^{-6}) & 	ext{if } p{	ext{dot}} \le 0 \end{cases} 6. Compute Intermediate Gradient: Apply the implicit differentiation formula. \mathbf{g}{	ext{param\input}} = - rac{g{	ext{dot}}}{p{	ext{dot}}^{	ext{reg}}} Shape: (N, 1). 7. Mask Unconverged Points: Zero out gradients for rays that did not converge, as their positions are not well-defined by the SDF root. \mathbf{g}{	ext{masked}} = \mathbf{g}{	ext{param\input}} \odot \mathbb{I}(	ext{converged}) Shape: (N, 1). 8. Backpropagate to Parameters: Compute the final gradients with respect to the model parameters 	heta using the masked scalar gradient. 
abla{	heta} L =  rac{\partial d}{\partial 	heta} \cdot \mathbf{g}{	ext{masked}} This is computed via autograd.grad with outputs=d, inputs=parameters, and gradoutputs=gmasked. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def implicitdiffspheretracing( signeddistancefunction, positions, directions, converged, gradoutputs, parameters): """ Compute gradients for sphere tracing using implicit differentiation. Args: signeddistancefunction: Callable f(p, params) -> distances positions: Tensor (N, 3), converged ray positions directions: Tensor (N, 3), ray directions converged: Tensor (N,), boolean mask of converged rays gradoutputs: Tensor (N, 3), upstream gradients w.r.t positions parameters: Tensor or list of Tensors, model parameters Returns: gradparameters: Gradients w.r.t parameters """ # 1. Detach positions to break the iterative loop graph pdetached = positions.detach() pdetached.requiresgrad(True) # 2. Compute SDF and its spatial gradient signeddistances = signeddistancefunction(pdetached, parameters) # Compute gradient of SDF w.r.t positions gradpositions, = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=signeddistances, inputs=pdetached, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(signeddistances), retaingraph=True,) # 3. Dot product of output gradient and ray direction gradoutputsdotdirections = torch.sum(gradoutputs directions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # 4. Dot product of SDF gradient and ray direction gradpositionsdotdirections = torch.sum(gradpositions directions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # 5. Regularize denominator to avoid division by zero epsilon = 1e-6 gradpositionsdotdirections = torch.where( gradpositionsdotdirections > 0, torch.max(gradpositionsdotdirections, torch.fulllike(gradpositionsdotdirections, epsilon)), torch.min(gradpositionsdotdirections, torch.fulllike(gradpositionsdotdirections, -epsilon))) # 6. Compute intermediate gradient using implicit differentiation formula gradintermediate = -gradoutputsdotdirections / gradpositionsdotdirections # 7. Zero out gradients for unconverged points gradintermediate = torch.where(converged.unsqueeze(-1), gradintermediate, torch.zeroslike(gradintermediate)) # 8. Compute final parameter gradients gradparameters = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=signeddistances, inputs=parameters, gradoutputs=gradintermediate, retaingraph=True,) return gradparameters Parameters: epsilon: Regularization constant for the denominator. Default value: 10^{-6}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Occurs when the ray direction is tangent to the surface, making 
abla{\mathbf{p}} d \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0. Unconverged Rays: Rays that fail to converge within the iteration limit or tolerance should have their gradients zeroed out, as the position is not a valid root of the SDF. Graph Detachment: It is critical to detach the positions before re-evaluating the SDF. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids the computational overhead of backpropagating through the iterative sphere tracing loop. Limitations: Only valid for converged points and requires a differentiable SDF. When to use: When gradients with respect to SDF parameters are needed for differentiable rendering. When not to use: When gradients with respect to ray origins or directions are required. This method is documented in a repository named Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D. It leverages implicit differentiation to differentiate through the fixed-point iteration of sphere tracing, a common technique in differentiable rendering and inverse graphics. The approach avoids the need to manually derive the Jacobian of the sphere tracing iteration or backpropagate through the loop. skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Advection Gradients
head: Differentiable SL Advection Gradients
body:
Differentiable Advection Gradients provide the backward pass for semi-Lagrangian (SL) advection operators used in differentiable volume rendering and fluid reconstruction. They solve the problem of computing gradients of the advected field with respect to both the input scalar field (e.g., density) and the velocity field, enabling end-to-end optimization via automatic differentiation. Unlike implicit differentiation methods that solve linear systems for sphere tracing [2012-implicit-differentiation-for-sphere-tracing.md], this method relies on explicit gradient scattering and component-wise multiplication, leveraging the structure of the interpolation kernel. The method computes the gradients 
abla hot^A =  rac{\partial A(hot, ut)}{\partial hot} and 
abla ut^A =  rac{\partial A(hot, ut)}{\partial ut} required for back-propagation through the advection operator A. The implementation is typically provided as a custom CUDA operation (e.g., for TensorFlow) to handle the non-differentiable nature of standard grid lookups. Inputs: hot: Input scalar field (density) on a 3D grid. ut: Input velocity field on a 3D grid. 
abla ho{t+1}^A: Gradient of the loss with respect to the advected output A(hot, ut). Outputs: 
abla hot^A: Gradient with respect to the input density. 
abla ut^A: Gradient with respect to the input velocity. Data Structures: Grids are stored as dense 3D arrays. Interpolation uses bilinear or trilinear weights wi associated with the 8 neighboring grid cells for each particle trace. Algorithm Steps: 1. Forward Trace: For each grid cell (i,j,k) in the output domain, trace the particle backward using ut to find the source position p in the hot grid. 2. Interpolation Weights: Compute the interpolation weights w0, \dots, w7 based on the fractional part of p. 3. Compute 
abla ut^A: Compute the spatial gradient of the scalar field 
abla hot at the source positions. This is done by applying the same interpolation weights to the gradient of the loss with respect to the output, but specifically for the velocity term. The formula is: 
abla ut^A = A(
abla hot, ut) In practice, this means the gradient flowing back to the velocity is the advected spatial gradient of the density. Specifically, the gradient 
abla ho{t+1}^A is multiplied component-wise with the advected spatial gradients of hot. 4. Compute 
abla hot^A: Scatter the gradient 
abla ho{t+1}^A back to the source grid positions. For each output cell, distribute 
abla ho{t+1}^A to the 8 neighboring source cells, scaled by the corresponding interpolation weight wi. Formula: 
abla hot^A = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi \cdot 
abla ho{t+1}^A The gradients are scattered to the grid positions used for interpolation in the forward step, multiplied by interpolation weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiablesladvectionbackward( rhot: Tensor, ut: Tensor, gradoutput: Tensor, gridsize: Tuple[int, int, int]) -> Tuple[Tensor, Tensor]: """ Computes gradients for differentiable semi-Lagrangian advection. Args: rhot: Input density field [D, H, W, C] ut: Input velocity field [D, H, W, 3] gradoutput: Gradient of loss w.r.t. advected output [D, H, W, C] gridsize: Spatial dimensions (D, H, W) Returns: gradrho: Gradient w.r.t. input density gradu: Gradient w.r.t. input velocity """ # Initialize gradients gradrho = torch.zeroslike(rhot) gradu = torch.zeroslike(ut) # 1. Trace particles backward to find source positions # This step is identical to the forward pass but accumulates gradients sourcepositions, weights = tracebackward(ut, gridsize) # 2. Compute gradrho: Scatter gradoutput back to source positions # For each output voxel, scatter gradoutput weight to the 8 neighbors for voxel in outputvoxels: pos = sourcepositions[voxel] w = weights[voxel] # Scatter operation: add w gradoutput to the 8 neighboring grid cells scatteradd(gradrho, pos, w gradoutput[voxel]) # 3. Compute gradu: Multiply gradoutput with advected spatial gradients of rho # First, compute spatial gradient of rhot (e.g., using finite differences or autograd) gradrhospatial = computespatialgradient(rhot) # The gradient w.r.t. velocity is the advection of the spatial gradient of density # Formula: gradu = A(gradrhospatial, ut) # This involves tracing gradrhospatial with ut and interpolating advectedgradrho = advectfield(gradrhospatial, ut, gridsize) # Component-wise multiplication with the gradient of the output # Note: The source states "multiplied component wise with the advected spatial gradients" # This implies the gradient flow to u is driven by how changes in u affect the advection of gradrho gradu = advectedgradrho gradoutput # Element-wise return gradrho, gradu Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: Open boundaries are used. Velocities at boundaries are unconstrained. Look-ups falling outside the volume are clamped to the boundary values. Gradients are accumulated at the boundaries accordingly. Precision: The scattering operation must handle overlapping contributions from multiple output voxels tracing to the same source voxel correctly (additive accumulation). Uses these gradients to enforce physical fluid motion constraints between frames. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of grid cells and particles traced. The backward pass requires a second trace (for velocity gradient) and a scatter operation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the forward pass intermediate values (source positions, weights) or recomputing them, plus gradients for ho and u. Strengths: Efficient implementation via CUDA kernels; compatible with standard automatic differentiation frameworks when wrapped as a custom op. Limitations: Relies on the differentiability of the interpolation kernel; open boundaries may introduce artifacts if not handled carefully. The method was introduced in the context of global transport for fluid reconstruction with learned self-supervision. It enables the optimization of both density and velocity fields in differentiable fluid simulations by providing explicit gradients for the semi-Lagrangian advection step, which is otherwise non-differentiable due to grid lookups. Global Transport for Fluid Reconstruction with Learned Self-Supervision, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00168, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Physical Prior / Transport Losses
head: Density transport loss, Differentiable Transport Operator Loss, LA(s), Navier-Stokes based transport, Per-frame transport loss, Self-advection loss
body:
Physical Prior / Transport Losses enforce temporal coherence and physical plausibility in fluid reconstruction by minimizing the discrepancy between predicted and observed states using a differentiable transport operator. Unlike standard temporal smoothing, this method explicitly incorporates the Navier-Stokes equations as a physical prior, ensuring that the reconstructed velocity and density fields adhere to incompressible fluid dynamics. It builds on Differentiable Advection Gradients by providing the gradient signal necessary to update velocity fields from sparse or noisy observations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of state fields s (density ho or velocity u) at discrete time steps t-1, t, t+1; a velocity field u; and physical parameters (kinematic viscosity 
u). Outputs: Gradient updates for the velocity field u and density ho derived from the transport loss LA and divergence loss L{div}. Data Structures: State Field s: A 3D grid or implicit representation storing scalar (density) or vector (velocity) values at each voxel/point. Velocity Field u: A 3D vector field where each element is (ux, uy, uz). Transport Operator A(s, u): A differentiable function that advects field s by velocity u over one time step. Parameters: Transport Scheme: Second-order transport scheme is used in the discretized operator A to preserve small-scale content. Kinematic Viscosity (
u): A scalar parameter in the Navier-Stokes equations. Time Step: Implicitly handled by the operator A; the loss connects adjacent frames t-1 to t and t to t+1. Formulas: The core transport loss LA(s) for a state s at time t is defined as the sum of squared errors between the transported previous state and the current state, and the transported current state and the next state: LA(s) = \| A(s{t-1}, u{t-1}) - st \|^2 + \| A(st, ut) - s{t+1} \|^2 where: s is the field (either density ho or velocity u). A(s, u) is the differentiable transport operator advecting s by u. u is the velocity field. For velocity fields, this self-advection loss LA(u) induces temporal coherence. For density fields, LA(ho) is used to build the initial velocity sequence. The physical prior is grounded in the Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible fluid motion:  rac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \cdot 
abla u = -
abla p + 
u 
abla^2 u, \quad 	ext{s.t.} \quad 
abla \cdot u = 0 where u is velocity, p is pressure, and 
u is kinematic viscosity. To enforce the incompressibility constraint (
abla \cdot u = 0), an additional divergence-free constraint loss is minimized: L{div} = \| 
abla \cdot u \|^2 Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Velocity: Acquire an initial velocity sequence u0, \dots, uF via a forward-only pre-optimization pass. This is required to create the initial density transport At(ho0). 2. Compute Transported States: For each frame t, compute the transported previous state A(s{t-1}, u{t-1}) and the transported current state A(st, ut) using the second-order transport scheme. 3. Calculate Transport Loss: Compute LA(s) for both density ho and velocity u using the formula above. 4. Calculate Divergence Loss: Compute L{div} = \| 
abla \cdot u \|^2 to enforce incompressibility. 5. Back-propagate Gradients: Compute gradients for density ho and velocity u using the transport loss LA. Back-propagate gradients through the density advection operator A to update ho. Back-propagate gradients through the density advection operator A to update u. Crucial Constraint: Do not back-propagate gradients further through velocity self-advection (i.e., do not differentiate through A(ut, ut) with respect to ut for the purpose of updating u from the velocity loss term itself, though u is updated via density transport gradients). The velocity receives gradients 
abla ut^A =  rac{\partial Lho(hoi)}{\partial ut} =  rac{\partial A(hot, ut)}{\partial ut} 
abla ho{t+1}^A from the back-propagation through the density advection. 6. Update Fields: Update the velocity and density fields using the computed gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetransportlossandgradients(sprev, scurr, snext, uprev, ucurr, unext, transportop, divergenceop): """ Computes the physical prior transport loss and gradients for a state s (rho or u). Note: This function assumes the caller handles the specific back-propagation constraints described in the source, particularly regarding velocity self-advection. """ # Step 1: Advect previous state using previous velocity sprevtransported = transportop(sprev, uprev) # Step 2: Advect current state using current velocity scurrtransported = transportop(scurr, ucurr) # Step 3: Compute transport loss # LA(s) = ||A(s{t-1}, u{t-1}) - st||^2 + ||A(st, ut) - s{t+1}||^2 lossterm1 = normsquared(sprevtransported - scurr) lossterm2 = normsquared(scurrtransported - snext) transportloss = lossterm1 + lossterm2 # Step 4: Compute gradients for transport loss # Note: In a real autograd engine, this is done automatically. # Here we conceptually define the components. gradsprev = transportop.gradientwrtinput(sprev, uprev) (sprevtransported - scurr) graduprev = transportop.gradientwrtvelocity(sprev, uprev) (sprevtransported - scurr) gradscurr = transportop.gradientwrtinput(scurr, ucurr) (scurrtransported - snext) graducurr = transportop.gradientwrtvelocity(scurr, ucurr) (scurrtransported - snext) # Combine gradients for the current state scurr # The source specifies that for velocity u, gradients come from density transport back-propagation. # For density rho, gradients come from density transport. # This function returns the loss and the raw gradient components. return transportloss, gradscurr, graducurr def computedivergenceloss(ucurr, divergenceop): """ Computes the divergence-free constraint loss. """ divu = divergenceop(ucurr) lossdiv = normsquared(divu) gradu = divergenceop.gradientwrtinput(ucurr) divu return lossdiv, gradu def optimizevelocitysequence(initialu, rhosequence, transportop, divergenceop, numframes): """ Main optimization loop for velocity sequence. """ # Initialize velocity sequence from pre-optimization pass usequence = initialu for t in range(1, numframes - 1): # Get states at t-1, t, t+1 rhoprev = rhosequence[t-1] rhocurr = rhosequence[t] rhonext = rhosequence[t+1] uprev = usequence[t-1] ucurr = usequence[t] unext = usequence[t+1] # Compute transport loss for density rho # LA(rho) is used to build the initial velocity sequence and provides gradients for u rholoss, gradrhocurr, graducurrfromrho = computetransportlossandgradients( rhoprev, rhocurr, rhonext, uprev, ucurr, unext, transportop, divergenceop) # Compute divergence loss for velocity u # Ldiv = ||div(u)||^2 divloss, graducurrfromdiv = computedivergenceloss(ucurr, divergenceop) # Total gradient for ucurr # Source: "Those [gradients for u] are, however, not back-propagated further through velocity self-advection." # This implies we use the gradients derived from density transport and divergence, # but do not chain gradients through u's own advection loss term for u's update. totalgraducurr = graducurrfromrho + graducurrfromdiv # Update ucurr using totalgraducurr usequence[t] = updatestep(ucurr, totalgraducurr) # Update rhocurr using gradrhocurr rhosequence[t] = updatestep(rhocurr, gradrhocurr) return usequence Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Velocity Self-Advection: Gradients must not be back-propagated through velocity self-advection. This is a critical implementation detail to avoid incorrect gradient flow. Initial Velocity: A forward-only pre-optimization pass is required to acquire the initial velocity sequence before the global transport optimization can begin. Small-Scale Content: Using a first-order transport scheme may lose small-scale details; a second-order scheme is recommended. A specific instance of the transport loss where s = ho. It is used to build the initial velocity sequence and provides gradients for velocity updates via back-propagation through the density advection operator. A specific instance of the transport loss where s = u. It induces temporal coherence in the velocity fields. A loss term L{div} = \| 
abla \cdot u \|^2 used to enforce the incompressibility constraint of the Navier-Stokes equations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is applied to sparse-view input sequences for fluid reconstruction. It helps reconstruct inflow regions and motion within the visual hull. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enforces physical plausibility (Navier-Stokes) and temporal coherence; helps reconstruct motion in regions with sparse visual data (inflow regions). Limitations: Requires an initial velocity sequence from a pre-optimization pass; relies on a differentiable transport operator. When to use: When reconstructing fluid dynamics from sparse or noisy observations and physical consistency is required. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and pre-optimization is not feasible, or when the fluid is compressible (the method assumes incompressibility). The method originates from the paper "Global Transport for Fluid Reconstruction with Learned Self-Supervision" by Aleksandra Franz, Barbara Solenthaler, and Nils Thuerey, presented at CVPR 2021. It leverages recent progress in gradient-based differentiable rendering to connect physical priors to target observations. The approach uses a discriminator with RaLSGAN loss for training stability. It sets itself apart by using a symplectic integrator to propagate both the ray state and its sensitivity to the initial velocity, ensuring numerical stability and energy conservation during the optimization of initial conditions. The method computes the derivatives of the ray's position \mathbf{x}{s^} and velocity \mathbf{v}{s^} with respect to the initial velocity \mathbf{v}0 at a target geometric distance s^. These derivatives are necessary to calculate  rac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\mathbf{v}0} for BFGS optimization. Inputs: n(\mathbf{x}): Refractive index scalar field.

Outputs:  rac{\partial \mathbf{x}{s^}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0}: Updated position Jacobian.  rac{\partial \mathbf{v}{s^}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0}: Updated velocity Jacobian. Half-step velocity update: Update the velocity derivative using the current position derivative and the Hessian of the refractive index at the current ray position.  rac{\partial \mathbf{v}{s^}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0} \leftarrow  rac{\partial \mathbf{v}{s^}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0} + 0.5s Hn(	ext{ray}.\mathbf{x})  rac{\partial \mathbf{x}{s^}}{\partial \mathbf{v}0} Simultaneously, update the ray's velocity vector for the next position step: 	ext{ray}.\mathbf{v}0 = 0.5s

Memory Complexity: O(d^2) for storing the Jacobian matrices. Strengths: Symplectic integration preserves the geometric structure of the Hamiltonian system, leading to stable gradients over long integration paths, which is crucial for BFGS optimization. Limitations: Requires access to the Hessian of the refractive index Hn(\mathbf{x}), which may be expensive to compute or approximate. The method is described in "Path tracing estimators for refractive radiative transfer". It is used to compute gradients for optimizing initial ray velocities to hit specific surface points in refractive media, enabling differentiable rendering techniques that rely on Type-1 direct connections. name: Differentiable Rendering via Gradient-Based Optimization
head: Gradient-based optimization through a renderer, AD-based gradient computation, Density Reconstruction via Gradient Descent, Differentiable Ray Tracing with Automatic Differentiation, Image-Based Optimization, Inverse Rendering with Mitsuba 3, Source-to-source AD in Julia
body: Differentiable rendering via gradient-based optimization is an iterative inverse rendering technique that recovers scene parameters (such as volumetric density, albedo, geometry, or illumination) by minimizing the difference between rendered images and observed reference images. It solves the problem of non-differentiable rendering pipelines by integrating automatic differentiation (AD) into the forward rendering process, allowing gradients of a loss function to flow from the image space back to the scene parameters. Unlike finite-difference methods, which require multiple forward passes per parameter, AD computes exact gradients in a single backward pass, reducing wall-clock time by approximately 60% for scenes with more than 50 optimized parameters and lowering approximation error by two orders of magnitude. It sets itself apart from Adjoint Method by relying on source-to-source AD tools rather than hand-coded adjoint equations, and from Forward-Mode Automatic Differentiation by being more efficient for high-dimensional parameter spaces. The method formulates inverse rendering as a constrained optimization problem. The goal is to find parameters \theta (e.g., density field \rho, albedo a, pose \theta{pose}) that minimize a loss function L between the rendered image IR(\theta) and a reference image I. Inputs: Reference image I (high-quality, low-noise); initial scene parameters \theta0 (e.g., initial density field, albedo values); scene geometry and lighting definitions. Outputs: Optimized parameters \theta^; final rendered image IR(\theta^). Scene Parameters: Stored in a traversable structure or a flat array of tensors, with each parameter explicitly marked for gradient tracking. Optimizer State: Maintains moving averages of gradients (e.g., Adam) and learning rate schedules. Gradient Buffer: Accumulates gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} computed during the backward pass. 1. Setup: Initialize the rendering engine with an AD-supporting variant (e.g., cudaadrgb). Load the scene description (XML or programmatic). Render a high-quality reference image I{ref} using a high sample count (e.g., spp=512) to minimize noise-induced optimization instability. Initialize the optimizer (e.g., Adam with learning rate lr=0.05) and assign target parameters to it. 2. Forward Pass (Rendering): For each pixel (i, j) in the image dimensions (ImgW, ImgH): Cast a single ray (x, \boldsymbol{u}) per pixel. Note: Single-ray-per-pixel is required to avoid stochastic sampling non-differentiability. Compute radiance L{out}(x, \boldsymbol{u}) using the differentiable renderer. If the ray hits geometry, compute color based on barycentric coordinates and interpolated surface normals. If the ray misses, return background color (gradients are zero). Edge Case: At geometric boundaries (edges shared by triangles), apply a deterministic tie-breaking rule (prefer lower face index) to ensure a well-defined computational graph, accepting potentially biased gradients for the selected path. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the loss L using the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the current rendered image I{curr} and the reference image I{ref}: L = \text{MSE}(I{curr}, I{ref}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{k=1}^{N} (I{curr}[k] - I{ref}[k])^2 where N is the number of pixels. Alternatively, for formulations involving geometry \theta, illumination L, and albedo a: L(\theta, L, a{0,...,n}) = ||IR(\theta, L, a{0,...,n}) - I||^22 where IR(\theta, L, a{0,...,n}) = R(B(\theta x0),..., B(\theta xn), P). 4. Backward Pass (Gradient Computation): Call the automatic differentiation engine to compute gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} for all tracked parameters. The AD engine traverses the computational graph from the loss variable, applying the chain rule to sum gradient variables [Parent]. 5. Parameter Update: Perform an optimizer step (e.g., Adam step). Clip parameters to valid ranges (e.g., albedo [0.0, 1.0]). Update the scene state with the new parameters. Volumetric Specific: For density field reconstruction, accumulate density gradients and update voxel positions vp: \text{densityGrad}[vp] \leftarrow \text{densityGrad}[vp] + 2 \times diff \times grad \rho[vp] \leftarrow \rho[vp] - LR \times \text{densityGrad}[vp] where diff = I[i, j] - L{out}(x, \boldsymbol{u}). 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–5 for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 50). Unverified code.
