name: Depth from Ray Distance
body: Depth from Ray Distance converts the scalar ray distance d (the Euclidean distance from the camera center to the intersection or accumulation point along the ray) into camera-space depth zc (the distance along the camera's optical axis). It solves the problem of interpreting differentiable volume rendering outputs, which naturally produce distances along the viewing ray, into a coordinate system compatible with standard depth maps and RGB-D sensors. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Expected Term Rendering and Median Depth Rendering by providing a direct geometric projection of the ray distance rather than computing statistical moments or threshold crossings of the volume density. Inputs and outputs: Input: Ray distance d (scalar or tensor of shape Q), pixel coordinates (x, y), camera intrinsic matrix K (3 \times 3). Output: Camera-space depth zc (scalar or tensor of shape Q). Data structures: K: 3 \times 3 matrix containing focal lengths fx, fy and principal point cx, cy. (x, y): Pixel coordinates in image space. Steps: 1. Compute the normalized homogeneous coordinate vector \mathbf{v}{\text{norm}} by applying the inverse camera intrinsics to the pixel coordinates: \begin{bmatrix} x{\text{tilde}} \\ y{\text{tilde}} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = K^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} This yields the direction vector components x{\text{tilde}} and y{\text{tilde}} in the camera coordinate system, normalized such that the z-component is 1. 2. Calculate the norm of the normalized direction vector: \|\mathbf{v}{\text{norm}}\| = \sqrt{x{\text{tilde}}^2 + y{\text{tilde}}^2 + 1} 3. Compute the camera-space depth zc by dividing the ray distance d by this norm: zc = \frac{d}{\sqrt{x{\text{tilde}}^2 + y{\text{tilde}}^2 + 1}}. Formulas: zc = d / \sqrt{x{\text{tilde}}^2 + y{\text{tilde}}^2 + 1}. Where zc is the camera-space depth, d is the ray distance, and (x{\text{tilde}}, y{\text{tilde}}, 1)^T = K^{-1}(x, y, 1)^T is the normalized homogeneous coordinate derived from pixel coordinates (x,y) and camera matrix K. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: Division by the norm is stable as the norm is always \ge 1. However, if K is ill-conditioned, K^{-1} may introduce numerical noise. Boundaries: If pixel coordinates (x, y) are outside the valid image bounds, x{\text{tilde}} and y{\text{tilde}} will be large, resulting in a small zc. This is mathematically correct for rays pointing far off-axis, but may require clamping in practice. Degenerate input: If K is singular, K^{-1} is undefined. This is a precondition failure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthfromraydistance(d: torch.Tensor, pixelcoords: torch.Tensor, K: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Convert ray distance d to camera-space depth zc. Args: d: Ray distance tensor of shape (Q,) or (H, W). pixelcoords: Pixel coordinates tensor of shape (Q, 2) or (H, W, 2) with (x, y). K: Camera intrinsic matrix of shape (3, 3). Returns: zc: Camera-space depth tensor of the same shape as d. """ # Ensure pixelcoords is (..., 2) if pixelcoords.dim() == 2: x = pixelcoords[:, 0] y = pixelcoords[:, 1] else: x = pixelcoords[..., 0] y = pixelcoords[..., 1] # Compute inverse of camera intrinsics Kinv = torch.inverse(K) # Construct homogeneous vector [x, y, 1] homocoords = torch.stack([x, y, torch.oneslike(x)], dim=-1) # Apply inverse intrinsics: [xtilde, ytilde, 1] normvec = torch.matmul(homocoords, Kinv.T) xtilde = normvec[..., 0] ytilde = normvec[..., 1] # Compute norm of the direction vector norm = torch.sqrt(xtilde2 + ytilde2 + 1.0) # Compute camera-space depth zc = d / norm return zc Computes the expected termination distance (depth) for each ray traversing a volume, returning a tensor of size Q. It differs from standard depth rendering by calculating the weighted mean of sample depths along the ray, where weights are derived from transmittance and absorption. It builds on Depth from Ray Distance by implementing the expected value strategy. Choose it when volumetric averaging is required over a single surface hit. Computes a binary mask indicating the sample index where cumulative weight accumulation exceeds a specified density threshold, effectively identifying a 'surface' location along the ray. It serves as a differentiable depth estimation method that renders a binary or thresholded output based on whether volume density exceeds a given value, referencing the approach used in Dex-NeRF. Unlike Expected Term Rendering which computes the mean distance, or Median Depth Rendering which finds the median, this method identifies the depth at which the accumulated opacity crosses a hard boundary. It builds on Depth from Ray Distance by introducing a termination condition based on accumulated sigma rather than fixed sample counts or probabilistic expectations. Choose it when a sharp, threshold-based surface approximation is needed. Computes the geometric depth of a volume by identifying the sample along a ray where the accumulated transmittance drops to 0.5. It solves the bias introduced by residual density in free space that affects Expected Depth Rendering, providing a sharper and less biased geometric representation for ambiguous or sparse scenes. Unlike Expected Depth Rendering, which integrates the entire ray's contribution to find a weighted average, Median Depth Rendering selects a single threshold-crossing point, making it robust to noise in empty regions. Choose it when robustness to empty-region noise is prioritized over volumetric averaging. Estimates a robust clipped depth range [z{\text{min}}, z{\text{max}}] for binning by sampling visible Gaussians, applying a near-depth shift, and selecting percentiles via exact order statistics. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Median Depth Rendering by using percentile-based range estimation with exact order statistics rather than a single median value, ensuring the binning range covers the majority of contributing geometry while excluding outliers. Choose it when adaptive binning ranges are required for efficient ray marching. Is a differentiable volume rendering method that jointly optimizes a neural scene representation and lighting parameters from monocular video to recover physically plausible albedo, normals, semantics, and shadows. It solves the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering in urban environments by computing visibility via volume rendering transmittance rather than explicit geometry, ensuring consistency between the learned density field and shadow casting. Unlike sibling methods that focus on depth estimation or expected terms, this method explicitly models the interaction between sunlight and scene geometry to enable realistic relighting and shadow removal. Choose it for urban inverse rendering tasks requiring shadow and lighting consistency. Is a differentiable volume rendering technique implemented in Taichi using fixed-step ray marching and trilinear interpolation on a 3D density grid. It differs from sibling methods by relying on a fixed-step traversal with explicit alpha accumulation rather than expected terms or thresholding, and is implemented using Taichi's autodiff engine rather than PyTorch. A PyTorch equivalent uses adaptive-step ray marching with bounding box intersection and grid sampling. It computes ray direction from pixel coordinates, principal point, focal length, and camera rotation, then normalizes. It computes ray-box intersection parameters t{\text{min}} and t{\text{max}} for box [-1, 1]^3. It adds random jitter to starting t: t = t - self.dt torch.randlike(t). It initializes ray position, color, and alpha accumulators. In a while loop, it checks validity inside box, samples density with F.gridsample, computes step with jitter, and updates done flag. It computes alpha contribution: contrib = ((rayalpha + samplealpha step).clamp(max=1.) - rayalpha) validf. It accumulates color and alpha, updates ray position and t. It uses stepjitter (jitter scale) as a parameter. Tensor layouts: raydir shape [N, H, W, 3] (NHWC), rayrgb shape [N, 3, H, W] (NCHW), rayalpha shape [N, 1, H, W] (NCHW). Choose it when Taichi's parallel execution model or PyTorch's adaptive marching is preferred over other backends. Photometric loss Lp is the mean squared error between rendered color \hat{C} and input color C: Lp(\hat{C}(\sigma, c)) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^{M} \|\hat{C}(\sigmai, ci) - C\|^2. Geometric depth loss Lg is the mean squared error between rendered depth \hat{D} and input depth D: Lg(\hat{D}(\sigma)) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^{M} \|\hat{D}(\sigma) - D\|^2. Total loss is L = Lp + \lambdad Lg, where \lambdad is the scaling factor of the geometric loss. Partial derivative of rendered color \hat{C} w.r.t. color ci is \frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial ci} = wi(\sigma) = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). Partial derivative of rendered depth \hat{D} w.r.t. density \sigmai is \frac{\partial \hat{D}}{\partial \sigmai} = \deltai \left[ ti T{i+1}(\sigma) - \hat{D} + \sum{j=0}^{i} tj wj(\sigma) \right], derived by interpreting distance ti as color ci. The derivatives are implemented directly in a custom CUDA kernel, building on the code developed for Plenoxel to boost computational speed. Choose it when optimizing radiance fields with known RGB-D poses. Estimates camera pose by treating pose as the variable and radiance field parameters (\vec{\sigma}, \vec{c}) as static, performing image-to-model alignment using RGB-D input. Derivative of rendered depth \hat{D} w.r.t. ray \vec{r} is \frac{\partial \hat{D}}{\partial \vec{r}} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial \hat{D}}{\partial \sigmai} \frac{\partial \sigmai}{\partial \vec{p}i} \frac{\partial \vec{p}i}{\partial \vec{r}}. Derivative of sample point \vec{p}i w.r.t. ray \vec{r} is decomposed as \frac{\partial \vec{p}i}{\partial \vec{r}} = \left[\frac{\partial \vec{p}i}{\partial \vec{o}}, \frac{\partial \vec{p}i}{\partial \vec{d}}\right] = [1, ti]. Adam is used for tracking (mapping uses RMSProp). The partial derivatives \frac{\partial \sigmai}{\partial \vec{p}i}, \frac{\partial ci}{\partial \vec{p}i}, and \frac{\partial \vec{p}i}{\partial \vec{r}} are model-specific and produce messy functions for trilinear interpolation; complete analytical equations are reserved for Appendix A. Choose it when tracking camera poses against a fixed radiance field. Is a method for aggregating coloring based on depth, using Gumbel-Max/Min distributions, resulting in the softmin function. Unlike no depth perturbations or taking the closest triangle, Gumbel depth perturbations are truly continuous. Choose it when continuous depth-dependent aggregation is required for differentiable rendering. Is a depth rendering technique that identifies the most significant Gaussian contributing to the depth by selecting the depth of the Gaussian with the highest weight. name: Expected Term Rendering
head: depth rendering via expected termination
body: Expected Term Rendering computes the expected termination distance (depth) for each ray traversing a volume, returning a tensor of size Q (number of rays). It differs from standard depth rendering by calculating the weighted mean of sample depths along the ray, where weights are derived from the volume's transmittance and absorption properties. This method builds on Depth from Ray Distance by specifically implementing the expected value strategy for depth estimation. Inputs: rays: A tensor containing ray origins and directions, with shape (Q, 3) for origins and (Q, 3) for directions, where Q is the number of rays. grid: The volume representation containing density (\sigma) and other attributes. opt: Rendering configuration options, including sampling bounds and step counts. Outputs: results: A tensor of dtype and device matching rays.origins, with size {Q} (or rays.origins.size(0)), containing the expected depth for each ray. Data Structures: SingleRaySpec: A structure holding the origin, direction, and bounds for a single ray. CUDANBLOCKSNEEDED(Q, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS): A macro or function calculating the number of CUDA blocks required for Q rays, given a thread block size. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a result tensor results with shape (rays.origins.size(0),) and dtype float32 on the same device as rays.origins. Set requiresgrad to False. 2. Ray Specification: For each ray i, construct a SingleRaySpec object. This involves determining the near and far bounds of the volume intersection for the ray. 3. Kernel Launch: Calculate the number of blocks B using CUDANBLOCKSNEEDED(Q, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS), where Q is the total number of rays. Launch the CUDA kernel device::renderrayexpectedtermkernel with B blocks. Pass the grid, rays, options, and the data pointer of results as arguments. 4. Kernel Execution (Per Ray): Inside the kernel, for each ray: a. Trace the ray through the volume, sampling density \sigma at discrete points along the ray segment defined by the bounds. b. Compute the transmittance T(t) at each sample point t: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{t{near}}^{t} \sigma(s) ds\right) In discrete form, with sample distances \Delta tj: Tj = \exp\left(-\sum{k=0}^{j-1} \sigmak \Delta tk\right) c. Compute the weight wj for each sample j as the probability of termination at that sample: wj = Tj \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \Delta tj)) d. Compute the expected depth D as the weighted mean of the sample depths tj: D = \sum{j} wj \cdot tj e. Store D in the corresponding position in results. Parameters: TRACERAYCUDATHREADS: The number of threads per CUDA block for the expected term rendering kernel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential decay in transmittance can lead to underflow for large depths or high densities. Use log-space computations if necessary. Boundaries: Incorrect near/far bounds can lead to sampling outside the volume or missing relevant density. Ensure bounds are tightly fitted to the volume geometry. Degenerate Input: Rays with zero length or invalid directions should be handled or filtered out before kernel launch. name: Expected Term Ray Tracing

body: Expected Term Ray Tracing computes the expected distance to the first opaque surface (or significant density threshold) along a ray passing through a sparse voxel grid. It differs from standard volume rendering by outputting a scalar expected depth value rather than a color or opacity-weighted sum, making it suitable for uncertainty estimation or specific depth-based loss functions. It builds on Expected Term Rendering by providing the specific CUDA kernel implementation for this metric. Inputs and Outputs: grid: Sparse voxel grid containing densitydata (trilinearly interpolatable density field). ray: Ray specification including origin, direction, tmin, tmax, and worldstep (physical length of one voxel step). opt: Options struct containing sigmathresh (density threshold for opacity calculation), stopthresh (transmission threshold for early termination), and stepsize (number of samples per voxel). out: Output buffer for the computed expected term. Data Structures: grid.densitydata: Array of density values \sigma. ray: Struct with origin (float3), direction (float3), tmin (float), tmax (float), worldstep (float). opt: Struct with sigmathresh (float), stopthresh (float), stepsize (int). Algorithm: 1. Handle edge case: if ray.tmin > ray.tmax, set out = 0.f and return. 2. Initialize t = ray.tmin, outv = 0.f, and logtransmit = 0.f. 3. Loop while t <= ray.tmax: a. Compute ray position and lattice indices identically to traceraycuvol using fmaf, clamp, floor, and fractional position calculations. b. Trilinearly interpolate density \sigma from grid.densitydata at the current ray position. c. If \sigma > \text{opt.sigma\thresh}: i. Compute \text{pcnt} = \text{ray.world\step} \cdot \sigma. ii. Calculate weight w = e^{\text{log\transmit}} \cdot (1 - e^{-\text{pcnt}}). iii. Update \text{log\transmit} \leftarrow \text{log\transmit} - \text{pcnt}. iv. Accumulate expected term: \text{outv} \leftarrow \text{outv} + w \cdot \frac{t}{\text{opt.step\size}} \cdot \text{ray.world\step}. d. If e^{\text{log\transmit}} < \text{opt.stop\thresh}: set \text{log\transmit} = -1000.0f and break. e. Advance t \leftarrow t + \text{opt.step\size}. 4. After loop, write out = outv. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tracerayexpectedterm(grid, ray, opt, out): # Edge case: invalid ray bounds if ray.tmin > ray.tmax: out[0] = 0.0 return t = ray.tmin logtransmit = 0.0 outv = 0.0 worldstep = ray.worldstep sigmathresh = opt.sigmathresh stopthresh = opt.stopthresh stepsize = opt.stepsize while t <= ray.tmax: # Compute ray position and lattice indices identically to traceraycuvol # Standard sparse voxel traversal: pos = ray.origin + t ray.direction # lattice = floor(pos / voxelsize), frac = (pos - lattice voxelsize) / voxelsize # sigma = trilinearinterpolate(grid.densitydata, lattice, frac) sigma = trilinearinterpolate(grid.densitydata, ray.position(t)) if sigma > sigmathresh: pcnt = worldstep sigma weight = math.exp(logtransmit) (1.0 - math.exp(-pcnt)) logtransmit -= pcnt outv += weight (t / stepsize) worldstep if math.exp(logtransmit) < stopthresh: logtransmit = -1000.0 break t += stepsize out[0] = outv Parameters: sigmathresh: Density threshold above which opacity is calculated. Typical value: Not given in the sources. stopthresh: Transmission threshold for early termination. Typical value: Not given in the sources. stepsize: Number of samples per voxel. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the function returns 0.f immediately to avoid invalid traversal. If sigma never exceeds sigmathresh, outv remains 0. If exp(logtransmit) drops below stopthresh, logtransmit is clamped to -1000.0f to prevent floating-point underflow and the loop terminates early. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray, with early termination possible if transmission drops below stopthresh. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, plus access to the sparse voxel grid. Performance: Implemented as a CUDA kernel for parallel execution on GPUs. Strengths: Efficient computation of expected depth metrics for differentiable rendering. Limitations: Requires a sparse voxel grid structure; performance depends on density distribution and threshold settings. When to use: When expected depth or uncertainty estimation is required for volume rendering. When not to use: When color or opacity-weighted accumulation is needed instead of a scalar depth metric. name: Plenoxel Sigma Threshold Ray Tracing
head: Dex-NeRF sigma threshold ray tracing
body: Plenoxel Sigma Threshold Ray Tracing is a CUDA kernel function that computes the distance to the first sample along a ray where the volume density (\sigma) exceeds a specified threshold, returning the normalized distance to that sample. It differs from standard volume rendering by discretizing the volume into opaque/transparent regions based on a density cutoff rather than integrating transmittance, and it differs from its parent Expected Term Ray Tracing by using a hard threshold on density rather than integrating the expected distance contribution. Inputs: ray: A ray structure containing tmin, tmax, and world-space step size worldstep. opt: An options structure containing stepsize (the step size in lattice units) and sigmathresh (the density threshold). grid.densitydata: A sparse voxel grid storing density values. Outputs: out: A float pointer storing the result. If no sample exceeds the threshold, it remains 0.0. Data Structures: The density grid is accessed via lattice indices l and fractional positions derived from the ray position. Trilinear interpolation is used to sample \sigma from grid.densitydata. Algorithm: 1. If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, set out = 0.f and return. 2. Initialize t = ray.tmin and out = 0.f. 3. Loop while t <= ray.tmax: a. Compute the ray position at t. b. Clamp the position if necessary. c. Compute the lattice indices l and the fractional position within the voxel. d. Trilinearly interpolate the density \sigma from grid.densitydata using l and the fractional position. e. If \sigma > \text{sigma\thresh}: i. Set out = (t / opt.stepsize) ray.worldstep. ii. Break the loop. f. Advance t by opt.stepsize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceraysigmathresh(ray, opt, griddensitydata): # Guard: invalid ray range if ray.tmin > ray.tmax: return 0.0 t = ray.tmin out = 0.0 while t <= ray.tmax: # Compute ray position at t pos = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Clamp position (implementation detail for boundary handling) pos = clamp(pos, grid.bounds.min, grid.bounds.max) # Compute lattice indices and fractional part l, frac = computelatticeandfraction(pos, grid.voxelsize) # Trilinear interpolation of density sigma = trilinearinterpolate(griddensitydata, l, frac) # Check threshold if sigma > opt.sigmathresh: # Normalize distance: t is in world units, opt.stepsize is in lattice steps? # Formula from sources: (t / opt.stepsize) ray.worldstep # Note: This formula implies t and opt.stepsize are in compatible units, # and ray.worldstep scales the result. out = (t / opt.stepsize) ray.worldstep break # Advance t t += opt.stepsize return out Parameters: sigmathresh: The density threshold. Typical values are not given in the sources. opt.stepsize: The step size for ray marching. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the function returns 0.0 immediately. Precision issues may arise if opt.stepsize is very small or very large relative to ray.worldstep. If the ray never encounters a density above the threshold within tmax, out remains 0.0. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of steps along the ray, O((t{max} - t{min}) / \text{step\size}). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, plus access to the sparse voxel grid. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast convergence if the threshold is low. Limitations: Discontinuous output with respect to ray direction or density changes. When to use: When a binary opaque/transparent representation is sufficient. When not to use: When soft boundaries or alpha blending are required. body: Sigma-Threshold Depth Rendering computes a binary mask indicating the sample index where cumulative weight accumulation exceeds a specified density threshold, effectively identifying a 'surface' location along the ray. It serves as a differentiable depth estimation method that renders a binary or thresholded output based on whether volume density exceeds a given value, referencing the approach used in Dex-NeRF. Unlike Expected Term Rendering which computes the mean distance, or Median Depth Rendering which finds the median, this method identifies the depth at which the accumulated opacity crosses a hard boundary. It builds on Depth from Ray Distance by introducing a termination condition based on accumulated sigma rather than fixed sample counts or probabilistic expectations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: rays: Ray origins and directions (tensor of shape [Q, 3], where Q is the number of rays). weights: Array of density weights from the NeRF model for each sample along each ray. sigmathresh: The density threshold value used for comparison. depththreshold: Float accumulation threshold for depth termination (default 0.5). Outputs: results: A result tensor of size Q (one value per ray), with dtype and device matching rays.origins, requiresgrad=False. The value indicates the depth or sample index where the threshold was crossed. Data Structures: SingleRaySpec: A structure holding ray specification details (origin, direction, bounds) for a single ray. cum: Cumulative sum of weights. op: Boolean mask where cum >= depththreshold. opshifted: op shifted right by one position, padded with zeros at the beginning. mask: XOR of op and opshifted, cast to weights dtype. Steps: 1. Initialize Ray Specification: For each ray, create a SingleRaySpec and find the intersection bounds with the volume grid. 2. Compute Cumulative Weights: Calculate the cumulative sum of the per-sample weights along the ray: cum = \text{cumsum}(weights) 3. Create Threshold Mask: Generate a boolean mask indicating where the cumulative weight exceeds the threshold: op = cum \ge depth\threshold 4. Shift Mask: Shift the boolean mask op to the right by one position and pad with a zero at the start to identify the first crossing: op{shifted} = [0, op[:-1]] 5. Compute Crossing Mask: Compute the XOR of the original and shifted masks to find the exact sample index where the threshold was crossed: mask = op \oplus op{shifted} Cast mask to the weights' data type. 6. Trace Ray (CUDA Implementation): Launch the CUDA kernel device::renderraysigmathreshkernel. Calculate number of blocks: blocks = CUDANBLOCKSNEEDED(Q, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS). Pass grid, rays, opt, sigmathresh, and the output tensor pointer to the kernel. Inside the kernel, for each ray, march along the ray until the accumulated density exceeds sigmathresh. 7. Finalize Output: Return the results tensor containing the depth or index for each ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cumsum(arr, axis=1): """Standard cumulative sum along an axis.""" result = [] for i in range(len(arr)): row = [] acc = 0.0 for val in arr[i]: acc += val row.append(acc) result.append(row) return result def sigmathresholddepthrendering(raysorigins, raysdirections, weights, sigmathresh, depththreshold=0.5, sampledistances=None): """ Compute depth using sigma thresholding. Args: raysorigins: Tensor of ray origins [Q, 3]. raysdirections: Tensor of ray directions [Q, 3]. weights: Tensor of per-sample weights [Q, N]. sigmathresh: Density threshold for early termination. depththreshold: Accumulation threshold for mask computation (default 0.5). sampledistances: Tensor of sample distances along each ray [Q, N]. Returns: results: Tensor of depth values for each ray [Q]. """ Q = len(raysorigins) N = len(weights[0]) results = [0.0] Q # Step 1: Compute cumulative sum of weights cum = cumsum(weights, axis=1) # Step 2: Create boolean mask where cumulative weight exceeds threshold op = [[1 if c >= depththreshold else 0 for c in row] for row in cum] # Step 3: Shift op right by one and pad with zeros opshifted = [[0] + row[:-1] for row in op] # Step 4: Compute XOR mask to find the first crossing mask = [[op[i][j] ^ opshifted[i][j] for j in range(N)] for i in range(Q)] # Step 5: Compute depth based on the mask for i in range(Q): depth = 0.0 crossed = False for j in range(N): if mask[i][j] == 1: depth = sampledistances[i][j] crossed = True break results[i] = depth if crossed else 0.0 # Default to 0.0 if not crossed # Step 6: CUDA kernel launch (implementation detail) # blocks = (Q + TRACERAYCUDATHREADS - 1) // TRACERAYCUDATHREADS # renderraysigmathreshkernel<<<blocks, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS>>>(grid, rays, opt, sigmathresh, resultsptr) # The kernel performs the ray marching and threshold check directly on the density grid. return results Parameters: sigmathresh: Density threshold value for early ray termination during volume rendering. depththreshold: Accumulation threshold for depth termination (default 0.5). maxdepth: 10 (specific to ScanNet dataset). mindepth: 0.001 (specific to ScanNet dataset). thresholdmultiplier: 0.0001 (applied to the depth range). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Not Reached: If the cumulative weight never exceeds depththreshold, the mask will be all zeros and the depth remains at its default initialization. Precision: Floating-point precision in cumulative sum can affect the exact crossing point. Boundaries: Ray bounds must be correctly computed to avoid sampling outside the volume. A variant that uses a small threshold \tau to evaluate the uncertainty of a depth map. The threshold is calculated as \tau = (max\depth - min\depth) \cdot 0.0001, where max\depth = 10 and min\depth = 0.001 for the ScanNet dataset. This method is used to assess depth reliability rather than just computing a single depth value. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The CUDA implementation is optimized for GPU execution. The CUDA kernel allows for parallel processing of rays. Strengths: Provides a clear, binary surface indication, which can be useful for tasks requiring explicit depth boundaries. It is differentiable, allowing for gradient-based optimization. Limitations: Sensitive to the choice of threshold. If the threshold is too high or too low, it may fail to detect surfaces or detect noise. When to Use: When a binary surface mask is needed, or when the scene has clear density boundaries. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. name: Median Depth Rendering
head: 50% transmittance depth, Depth Renderer (Median), Median Depth Calculation, Median Depth Visualization, Median termination depth
body: Median Depth Rendering computes the geometric depth of a volume by identifying the sample along a ray where the accumulated transmittance drops to 0.5. It solves the bias introduced by residual density in free space that affects Expected Depth Rendering, providing a sharper and less biased geometric representation for ambiguous or sparse scenes. Unlike Expected Depth Rendering, which integrates the entire ray's contribution to find a weighted average, Median Depth Rendering selects a single threshold-crossing point, making it robust to noise in empty regions. Inputs: Ray samples: A set of N points along a ray, defined by their depths zi and densities \sigmai for i = 0, \dots, N-1. Step sizes: \Delta zi = z{i+1} - zi representing the distance between consecutive samples. Outputs: Depth value D for the pixel corresponding to the ray. Data Structures: zvals: Array of shape (N,) containing depths zi. sigma: Array of shape (N,) containing densities \sigmai. T: Array of shape (N,) storing accumulated transmittance values. Parameters: depththreshold: The transmittance threshold for median definition. Default is 0.5. Steps: 1. Compute Transmittance: Calculate the accumulated transmittance Ti for each sample. Ti represents the probability that a ray passes through all samples up to i without interacting. T0 = 1.0 T{i+1} = Ti \cdot \exp(-\sigmai \Delta zi) \quad \text{for } i = 0, \dots, N-2 2. Find Median Index: Identify the first sample index i^ such that the accumulated transmittance T{i^} is greater than or equal to the threshold. i^ = \min \{ i \mid Ti \ge 0.5 \} 3. Assign Depth: The rendered depth is the depth value of the identified sample. D = z{i^} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mediandepthrendering(zvals: list[float], sigma: list[float], threshold: float = 0.5) -> float: """ Compute median depth rendering for a single ray. Args: zvals: List of depths along the ray, sorted ascending. sigma: List of densities at each depth sample. threshold: Transmittance threshold (default 0.5). Returns: The depth value at the median termination point. """ n = len(zvals) if n == 0: return 0.0 # Fallback for empty ray # Step 1: Compute accumulated transmittance T T = [0.0] n T[0] = 1.0 for i in range(n - 1): deltaz = zvals[i+1] - zvals[i] T[i+1] = T[i] math.exp(-sigma[i] deltaz) # Step 2: Find the first index where T[i] >= threshold medianindex = 0 for i in range(n): if T[i] >= threshold: medianindex = i break # Step 3: Return depth at medianindex return zvals[medianindex] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fully Opaque Ray: If the accumulated transmittance drops below 0.5 immediately, the definition Ti \ge 0.5 still finds an index because T0=1.0 always satisfies the condition. The "first sample" logic ensures that if the object starts at the first sample, that depth is returned. Free Space Bias: In regions with no geometry (density \approx 0), transmittance remains near 1.0. Expected depth would pull the value towards the far plane, but median depth ignores this residual density, staying anchored to the actual surface where opacity accumulates. Discontinuity: The depth output is discontinuous with respect to small changes in density, as it jumps between sample indices. This can cause artifacts in differentiable rendering if not handled carefully (e.g., via soft approximations). Expected Depth Rendering estimates scene depth by computing the weighted average of depth samples along a ray, normalized by the accumulated weight. This method provides a stable geometric signal for pseudo-normal supervision and ray-tracing initialization, offering superior reconstruction quality and downstream stability compared to inverse-depth variants. It differs from Median Depth Rendering, which identifies the sample index where cumulative opacity crosses a threshold, by integrating the entire ray's contribution rather than selecting a single median point. Choose Expected Depth Rendering when smooth, differentiable depth fields are required for downstream tasks like normal estimation. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Finding the threshold index is a linear scan. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store transmittance values if computed explicitly, or O(1) if computed on the fly with early termination. Strengths: Robust to residual density in empty space; provides sharper depth boundaries than expected depth. Limitations: Discontinuous output can hinder gradient-based optimization in differentiable settings without smoothing. Sensitive to the choice of threshold (though 0.5 is standard). When to use: When geometric accuracy is prioritized over smoothness, or when residual density in free space biases expected depth significantly. Median Depth Rendering was introduced in the context of Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFies) to address the bias in depth visualization caused by residual density in free space. While standard NeRF uses expected termination distance for depth, NeRFies found that median depth provides a less biased geometric representation, particularly for deformable scenes. It is used in NeRFies for depth visualization and potentially for initialization or supervision in deformable reconstruction tasks. name: Expected Depth Rendering
head: Expected Depth Calculation, Weighted Mean Depth
body: Expected Depth Rendering computes the geometric center of mass of a ray's interaction with a volume or Gaussian mixture by calculating the weighted average of sample depths, normalized by the accumulated transmittance weight. It provides a continuous, differentiable depth signal that is numerically stable for downstream tasks such as pseudo-normal estimation and ray-tracing initialization. Unlike Median Depth Rendering, which selects a discrete sample index based on a cumulative opacity threshold, Expected Depth Rendering integrates contributions from all samples along the ray, resulting in smoother gradients and superior reconstruction quality for inverse rendering pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: z: Tensor or array of depth samples (or sample positions ti) along each ray. w: Tensor or array of per-sample weights. For Gaussian mixtures, wi = Ti gi \alphai. For volumetric density, wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). T: Transmittance tensor, where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) or the product of (1-\alphaj) for Gaussians. rayindices: Optional packed indices mapping samples to rays (used in sparse implementations). numrays: Total number of rays (used in sparse implementations). Outputs: depth: Tensor or array of expected depth values for each ray. Data Structures: Samples: Stored as 1D or 2D arrays. In packed formats (e.g., nerfacc), samples are flattened into a 1D array with a corresponding rayindices array indicating which ray each sample belongs to. Weights: Must be non-negative. In Gaussian splatting, this combines the Gaussian response gi, opacity \alphai, and transmittance Ti. Steps: 1. Compute Sample Positions: Determine the depth value zi for each sample. If only frustum bounds are available, compute midpoints: zi = (\text{starts}i + \text{ends}i) / 2. 2. Compute Weights: Calculate the weight wi for each sample. For Gaussian mixtures: wi = Ti gi \alphai. For volumetric density: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). 3. Accumulate Weights: Compute the total accumulated weight W for each ray: W = \sum{i \in N} wi. 4. Compute Expected Depth: Calculate the weighted sum of depths and normalize by the total weight: zE = \frac{\sum{i \in N} wi zi}{W}. 5. Numerical Stability: Add a small constant \epsilon to the denominator to prevent division by zero in empty regions. 6. Clipping: Clip the resulting depth to [\min(z), \max(z)] to handle boundary artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def expecteddepthrendering(z, weights, eps=1e-7): """ Compute expected depth from sample depths and weights. Args: z: 2D array of shape (Nrays, Nsamples) containing sample depths. weights: 2D array of shape (Nrays, Nsamples) containing per-sample weights. eps: Small constant for numerical stability. Returns: depth: 1D array of shape (Nrays) containing expected depth. """ depth = [] for rayz, rayw in zip(z, weights): weightedsum = sum(w zval for w, zval in zip(rayw, rayz)) totalw = sum(rayw) d = weightedsum / (totalw + eps) d = max(min(d, max(rayz)), min(rayz)) # Clip to [min(z), max(z)] depth.append(d) return depth def expecteddepthrenderingpacked(z, weights, rayindices, numrays, eps=1e-7): """ Compute expected depth for packed ray samples. Args: z: 1D array of sample depths. weights: 1D array of sample weights. rayindices: 1D array mapping each sample to a ray index. numrays: Total number of rays. eps: Small constant for numerical stability. Returns: depth: 1D array of shape (numrays) containing expected depth. """ depthsum = [0.0] numrays weightsum = [0.0] numrays for i in range(len(z)): r = rayindices[i] depthsum[r] += weights[i] z[i] weightsum[r] += weights[i] depth = [d / (w + eps) for d, w in zip(depthsum, weightsum)] return depth Parameters: eps: Small constant for numerical stability to prevent division by zero. method: Strategy for computing depth. The value 'expected' denotes the weighted mean approach. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Rays: If a ray hits no geometry, W=0. Division by zero is prevented by adding \epsilon. Boundary Conditions: Depth values at the start/end of the ray may be biased if the volume extends beyond the sampled interval. Clipping to [z{min}, z{max}] mitigates this. Computes the expected depth of a ray by calculating the weighted mean of sample depths, where weights are derived from the Gaussian's opacity, 2D contribution, and transmittance. It differs from Mode Depth Rendering, which selects the single Gaussian with the highest weight, by integrating contributions from all Gaussians along the ray to produce a continuous depth value. This method builds on Expected Depth Rendering. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples per ray, requiring a single pass to compute weights and a second pass for the weighted sum and normalization. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of samples to store depths and weights. Strengths: Provides a smooth, continuous depth signal that is robust to noise and suitable for normal estimation. It integrates information from the entire ray, reducing artifacts from sparse sampling. Limitations: Produces a continuous average rather than a discrete surface location, which may not suit methods requiring exact hit points. When to Use: When a continuous depth signal is needed for gradient-based optimization, pseudo-normal estimation, or ray-tracing initialization. Preferred over inverse-depth variants for overall reconstruction quality. When Not to Use: When a discrete surface location is required. Expected Depth Rendering originates from foundational volumetric rendering techniques, computing depth by weighting samples by their depth position analogous to color rendering. It is widely used in 3D Gaussian Splatting variants for geometry supervision, where it provides a stable geometric signal for pseudo-normal estimation and ray-tracing initialization. The method is often compared with Median Depth Rendering, which uses a threshold-based accumulation point. name: Mean Gaussian Depth Rendering
head: Expected Depth, Mean Depth Calculation
body: Mean Gaussian Depth Rendering computes the expected depth of a ray by calculating the weighted mean of sample depths, where weights are derived from the Gaussian's opacity, 2D contribution, and transmittance. It differs from Mode Depth Rendering, which selects the single Gaussian with the highest weight, by integrating contributions from all Gaussians along the ray to produce a continuous depth value. This method builds on Expected Depth Rendering. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \{Gk\}{k=1}^N. For each Gaussian k: center position \mathbf{c}k (from which depth dk is derived, typically the z-coordinate in camera space), opacity \alphak (or density \sigmak converted to opacity), 2D covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}k (projected to image plane), view direction and camera intrinsics. Outputs: A scalar depth value d(\mathbf{x}) for each pixel \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: Gaussians are sorted by depth dk along the ray to ensure correct front-to-back compositing for transmittance calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemeandepth(gaussians, pixelx): # Sort Gaussians by depth dk front-to-back gaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) T = 1.0 accumulateddepth = 0.0 for k in range(len(gaussians)): G = gaussians[k] # Calculate 2D Gaussian contribution at pixel x Gcontrib = evaluate2dgaussian(G.covariance, G.center, pixelx) # Calculate opacity contribution ok ok = G.opacity # Calculate weight wk wk = ok Gcontrib T # Update accumulated depth accumulateddepth += G.depth wk # Update transmittance T = T (1 - ok Gcontrib) # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if T < 1e-5: break return accumulateddepth Formula: The mean depth d(\mathbf{x}) for a pixel \mathbf{x} is computed as the weighted sum of Gaussian depths: d(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^N dk ok \mathcal{G}k^{\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) Tk \quad (5) where: dk is the depth of the k-th Gaussian. ok is the opacity contribution of the k-th Gaussian. \mathcal{G}k^{\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) is the 2D Gaussian contribution (density) at pixel \mathbf{x}. Tk = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - oj \mathcal{G}j^{\text{D}}(\mathbf{x})) is the transmittance up to the k-th Gaussian. An alternative normalization used in meshing processes divides by the accumulated alpha to ensure planar 2D disk rendering: z{\text{mean}} = \frac{\sumi \omegai zi}{\sumi \omegai + \epsilon} \quad (18) where \omegai is the weight contribution of the i-th Gaussian and \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in normalization. Typical value: 10^{-5}. Transmittance threshold for early termination: 10^{-5}. Pitfalls: Inconsistency with Volumetric Density: Fitting volumetric density (e.g., from ToF phase encoding) does not guarantee consistency with the rendered mean depth. If multiple density peaks exist along a ray but only one surface exists, the rendered mean depth diverges from the depth derived from raw quads. Jensen's Inequality: The discrepancy arises because sine/cosine functions in phase encoding oscillate, preventing equality in the finite form of Jensen's inequality. Clustering Requirement: The gap between fitted density and rendered depth reduces only when all Gaussians are clustered at the same z-position along each ray. Normalization: Without normalization, the output is an unnormalized moment rather than a true expected value. Mode Depth Rendering selects the depth of the single Gaussian with the largest contributing weight wi = Ti \alphai as the pixel depth. The formula is d{\text{mode}{x,y}} = d{\arg \maxi (wi)}. It differs from Mean Gaussian Depth Rendering by ignoring all other Gaussians, making it discrete and sensitive to the highest-opacity Gaussian rather than a weighted average. It is chosen when a sharp, single-surface depth is preferred over a continuous expected depth, though it may create ambiguity if low-weight Gaussians with greater depths influence the scene geometry. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Suitable for meshing processes and differentiable training. Integrates contributions from all Gaussians along the ray to produce a continuous depth value. Limitations: Fitting volumetric density does not guarantee consistency with rendered mean depth. Diverges from raw quad-derived depth when multiple density peaks exist along a ray. When to use: When a continuous depth estimate is required for meshing or differentiable rendering. When not to use: When a sharp, single-surface depth is required, or when the scene has multiple distinct surfaces along a ray and averaging is undesirable. Mean Gaussian Depth Rendering is used in optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for depth estimation, particularly from Time-of-Flight (ToF) cameras. It addresses the challenge that optimized volumetric properties (phasors or raw quads) are not the same as the property of interest (depth). The method also supports meshing processes where normal consistency and accurate depth are required. 2D Gaussian Splatting for Geometrically Accurate Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3641519.3657428, fetched 2026-10-27 Time of the Flight of the Gaussians: Optimizing Depth Indirectly in Dynamic Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01958, fetched 2026-10-26 Sparsegs: Sparse View Synthesis Using 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00100, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Median Depth Estimation via Binary Search
head: GGGS Depth Rendering, Geometry-Grounded Gaussian Splatting Depth Rendering
body: A method for computing the median depth of a ray and its analytical gradients for geometric regularization in Gaussian Splatting by performing a binary search for the depth where transmittance equals 0.5. It differs from Expected Depth Rendering by targeting the median (50% transmittance) rather than the mean, providing a robust geometric prior that is less sensitive to outliers in depth distribution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial median depth estimate t{init} (from RaDe-GS), Gaussian parameters \theta (centers \mathbf{x}c, opacities o, covariances \Sigma), camera extrinsics \mathbf{W}, projection Jacobian \mathbf{J}, and pixel location \mathbf{u}. Output: Median depth t{med} and gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \thetai} for each Gaussian i along the ray. Data Structures: Gaussian List: A list of Gaussians intersecting the pixel's screen-space support, sorted by depth. Each Gaussian i has parameters \thetai = \{\mathbf{x}c, o, \Sigma\}. Search Interval: A pair [t{min}, t{max}] defining the current depth range. Preliminaries: The scene is represented as 3D Gaussians: G(\mathbf{x}) = o \exp \left( -(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}c)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}c) \right) The covariance is transformed to the camera frame: \Sigma{cam} = \mathbf{W} \Sigma \mathbf{W}^\top And to screen space: \Sigma'{2D} = \mathbf{J} \Sigma{cam} \mathbf{J}^\top = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \Sigma \mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{J}^\top The per-pixel alpha for a Gaussian at pixel \mathbf{u} is: \alpha(\mathbf{u}) = o e^{-(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}c)^\top \Sigma{2D}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}c)} Transmittance T(t) is the product of (1-\alphai) for all Gaussians i up to depth t. Parameters: r: Half-width of the initial search interval. Typical value: 0.4 during training. num\iterations: Number of binary search iterations. Value: 5. num\segments: Number of segments the interval is divided into. Value: 8 (creating 7 internal segment points). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Interval: Set t{min} = t{init} - r and t{max} = t{init} + r. 2. Boundary Check: Compute transmittance T(t{min}) and T(t{max}). If both are > 0.5 or both are < 0.5, mask the pixel for geometric regularization (no gradient update). 3. Iterative Search: Repeat for k = 1 to num\iterations: a. Divide [t{min}, t{max}] into num\segments equal parts. Calculate 7 internal points tj = t{min} + j \cdot \frac{t{max}-t{min}}{num\segments} for j=1..7. b. Traverse Gaussians along the ray to compute T(tj) for each tj. c. Find the segment [tj, t{j+1}] where T(tj) and T(t{j+1}) bracket 0.5 (i.e., one is >0.5 and the other <0.5). d. Update t{min} = tj and t{max} = t{j+1}. 4. Final Depth: Set t{med} = \frac{t{min} + t{max}}{2}. The final depth error is bounded by 0.8 \times 8^{-5} \approx 2.441 \times 10^{-5}. Backward Pass: The gradient of the loss L with respect to Gaussian parameters \thetai is computed as: \frac{\partial L}{\partial t{med}} \cdot \frac{\partial t{med}}{\partial \thetai} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial t{med}} \cdot \frac{\partial T(t{med}; \theta)}{\partial \thetai} / \left( -\frac{\partial T(t; \theta)}{\partial t} \right)|{t=t{med}} This requires two traversals of the Gaussians at t{med}: 1. Compute \frac{\partial T}{\partial t}|{t{med}}: \frac{\partial T(t; \theta)}{\partial t}|{t=t{med}} = \sumi \frac{0.5}{Ti(t{med}; \thetai)} \frac{\partial Ti(t; \thetai)}{\partial t}|{t=t{med}} 2. Compute \frac{\partial T}{\partial \thetai}|{t{med}} for each Gaussian: \frac{\partial T(t; \theta)}{\partial \thetai} = \frac{0.5}{Ti(t{med}; \thetai)} \frac{\partial Ti(t{med}; \thetai)}{\partial \thetai} The terms \frac{\partial Ti}{\partial t} and \frac{\partial Ti}{\partial \thetai} are derived from the closed-form formulation of Ti. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mediandepthrendering(gaussians, tinit, r, numiterations=5, numsegments=8): """ Compute median depth and gradients for geometric regularization. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: xc: center (3,) o: opacity (scalar) Sigma: covariance (3x3) W: world-to-camera rotation (3x3) J: projection Jacobian (2x3) uc: projected center (2,) alpha(u): method to compute per-pixel alpha tinit: Initial median depth estimate r: Half-width of initial interval """ tmin = tinit - r tmax = tinit + r # Boundary check Tmin = computetransmittance(gaussians, tmin) Tmax = computetransmittance(gaussians, tmax) if (Tmin > 0.5 and Tmax > 0.5) or (Tmin < 0.5 and Tmax < 0.5): return None, None # Mask pixel # Binary search for in range(numiterations): stepsize = (tmax - tmin) / numsegments segmentpoints = [tmin + j stepsize for j in range(1, numsegments)] transmittances = [computetransmittance(gaussians, t) for t in segmentpoints] # Find bracketing segment found = False for j in range(numsegments - 1): tstart = segmentpoints[j] if j > 0 else tmin tend = segmentpoints[j+1] if j+1 < numsegments else tmax # Use precomputed or recompute boundary transmittances if needed # For simplicity, assume we have T at segmentpoints and boundaries Tstart = Tmin if j == 0 else transmittances[j-1] Tend = transmittances[j] if (Tstart > 0.5 and Tend < 0.5) or (Tstart < 0.5 and Tend > 0.5): tmin = tstart tmax = tend found = True break if not found: # Fallback or error handling if no segment found (should not happen if boundaries bracket) break tmed = (tmin + tmax) / 2 # Backward pass # Compute dT/dt at tmed dTdt = 0.0 dTdtheta = {} for i, g in enumerate(gaussians): Ti = computetransmittancesinglegaussian(g, tmed) # Ti is (1-alphai) if Ti == 0: continue # dT/dt = sumi [0.5 / Ti] dTi/dt dTidt = computedTidt(g, tmed) dTdt += (0.5 / Ti) dTidt # dT/dthetai = [0.5 / Ti] dTi/dthetai dTidtheta = computedTidtheta(g, tmed) dTdtheta[i] = (0.5 / Ti) dTidtheta # Gradient backprop # dL/dtmed is provided by the caller # dL/dthetai = dL/dtmed dT/dthetai / (-dT/dt) return tmed, dTdtheta, dTdt def computetransmittance(gaussians, t): """Compute total transmittance at depth t.""" T = 1.0 for g in gaussians: # Check if Gaussian is in front of t if isinfront(g, t): alpha = g.alpha(g.uc) # Simplified: alpha at center, usually evaluated at pixel # In practice, alpha is evaluated at the intersection point or projected center # For ray marching, we evaluate alpha along the ray # This is a simplification; actual implementation requires ray-Gaussian intersection T = (1.0 - alpha) return T def computetransmittancesinglegaussian(g, t): """Compute Ti = 1 - alphai at depth t.""" # Simplified: assume alpha is computed at the projected center # In reality, alpha varies along the ray alpha = g.alpha(g.uc) return 1.0 - alpha def computedTidt(g, t): """Compute derivative of Ti with respect to t.""" # Derived from closed-form Ti # dTi/dt = -d(alphai)/dt # This requires chain rule through Gaussian parameters and position pass # Implementation depends on specific Gaussian parameterization def computedTidtheta(g, t): """Compute derivative of Ti with respect to Gaussian parameters.""" # Derived from closed-form Ti pass # Implementation depends on specific Gaussian parameterization def isinfront(g, t): """Check if Gaussian is in front of depth t.""" # Check if Gaussian center is in front and ray intersects pass Time Complexity: O(N \cdot I \cdot S) per pixel, where N is the number of Gaussians, I is the number of iterations (5), and S is the number of segments (8). This is significantly faster than full ray marching for high-resolution depth estimation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian parameters. Accuracy: The final depth error is bounded by 2.441 \times 10^{-5} with 5 iterations. Strengths: Provides a robust geometric prior for Gaussian Splatting optimization. Efficient compared to iterative root-finding methods. Limitations: Requires an initial estimate t{init} (e.g., from RaDe-GS). If the initial interval does not bracket the median, the pixel is masked. Originated in "Geometry-Grounded Gaussian Splatting" (GGGS). It builds on Median Depth Rendering and uses an initial estimate from RaDe-GS. name: Robust Depth-Range Estimation
head: Robust Clipped Depth Range Estimation
body: Estimates a robust clipped depth range [z{min}, z{max}] for binning by sampling visible Gaussians, applying a near-depth shift, and selecting percentiles via exact order statistics. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Median Depth Rendering by using percentile-based range estimation with exact order statistics rather than a single median value, ensuring the binning range covers the majority of contributing geometry while excluding outliers. Inputs: Projected depths of visible Gaussians, Gaussian scales (specifically maximum projected scale s{max}), optional emitted flat IDs, near and far clipping planes (z{near}, z{far}), sample count S = 8192, near-depth shift parameters \alpha = 1.0, \gamma = 0.25, percentiles p{lo} = 1.0, p{hi} = 99.0, padding fraction f{pad} = 0.05, numerical floor \epsilon = 10^{-4}. Outputs: Robust clipped range [z{min}, z{max}]. Data Structures: List of sampled depth candidates. Steps: 1. Sample up to S depth candidates from the visible Gaussians or emitted flat IDs. 2. If near-depth mode is enabled (default), convert each sampled depth zc to a key z{key} using z{key} = zc - \min(\alpha \cdot s{max}, \gamma \cdot zc), where s{max} is the Gaussian's maximum projected scale. 3. Discard candidates where z{key} \le 0. Clamp remaining values to the range [\max(z{near}, \epsilon), z{far}]. 4. Select the exact p{lo} and p{hi} percentile values of the sampled candidates using order statistics (e.g., kthvalue) to obtain z{lo} and z{hi}. 5. Calculate the span: \text{span} = \max(z{hi} - z{lo}, 10^{-6}). 6. Calculate the final bounds: z{min} = \max(z{near}, z{lo} - f{pad} \cdot \text{span}) and z{max} = \min(z{far}, z{hi} + f{pad} \cdot \text{span}). 7. Return [z{min}, z{max}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def robustdepthrangeestimation( projecteddepths, gaussianscales, znear, zfar, S=8192, alpha=1.0, gamma=0.25, plo=1.0, phi=99.0, fpad=0.05, epsilon=1e-4): # Step 1: Sample up to S depth candidates def samplecandidates(depths, scales, maxcount): n = len(depths) count = min(maxcount, n) # Standard uniform sampling without replacement indices = list(range(n)) return [(depths[i], scales[i]) for i in indices[:count]] candidates = samplecandidates(projecteddepths, gaussianscales, S) if not candidates: return [znear, zfar] zkeys = [] # Step 2: Near-depth shift for zc, smax in candidates: shiftterm = min(alpha smax, gamma zc) zkey = zc - shiftterm zkeys.append(zkey) # Step 3: Filter and clamp validkeys = [] lowerbound = max(znear, epsilon) for zkey in zkeys: if zkey <= 0: continue clamped = max(lowerbound, min(zfar, zkey)) validkeys.append(clamped) if not validkeys: return [znear, zfar] # Step 4: Percentile selection via order statistics validkeys.sort() n = len(validkeys) def kthvalue(sortedarr, ppercentile): # Exact order statistics: select the k-th smallest element # Nearest-rank method: k = ceil(p/100 n) k = int((ppercentile / 100.0) n) k = max(0, min(n - 1, k)) return sortedarr[k] zlo = kthvalue(validkeys, plo) zhi = kthvalue(validkeys, phi) # Step 5: Span calculation span = max(zhi - zlo, 1e-6) # Step 6: Range expansion zmin = max(znear, zlo - fpad span) zmax = min(zfar, zhi + fpad span) return [zmin, zmax] Parameters: S = 8192: Maximum number of depth candidates sampled. \alpha = 1.0, \gamma = 0.25: Near-depth shift parameters. p{lo} = 1.0, p{hi} = 99.0: Percentiles for robust range estimation. f{pad} = 0.05: Padding fraction (5% of clipped span) added to the percentile range. \epsilon = 10^{-4}: Numerical floor for depth values. Pitfalls: The near-depth shift is used only to form the binning key; it does not change the projected Gaussian attributes or the alpha-compositing equations used by the raster kernel. Precision issues may arise if z{hi} - z{lo} is very small; the span is floored at 10^{-6} to prevent division by zero or degenerate ranges. Uses a single median depth value for binning. Choose when memory is extremely constrained and a single representative depth is sufficient. Parent method providing the general framework for estimating depth from ray intersections. Time complexity is dominated by sampling S candidates and sorting them for order statistics, O(S \log S). Memory complexity is O(S) to store candidates. Not given in the sources for measured performance with specific hardware, resolution, scene, or scaling behavior. Strengths include robustness to outliers due to percentile selection and the avoidance of histogram approximation errors via exact order statistics. Limitations include the requirement for a sorting or selection algorithm and sensitivity to the choice of percentiles p{lo}, p{hi}. Use it when accurate binning range is critical for performance and correctness in Gaussian Splatting rasterization. Do not use it when hardware lacks efficient sorting primitives or when memory bandwidth is strictly limited to O(1) auxiliary storage. Originated in the TileGS paper (2026) for tile-local depth binning in Gaussian Splatting rasterization. It improves upon previous methods by using exact order statistics instead of histogram approximations for percentile selection.
