name: UrbanIR Inverse Rendering
head: Inverse Rendering with Visibility Guidance
body: UrbanIR Inverse Rendering jointly optimizes a neural scene representation and lighting parameters from monocular video to recover physically plausible albedo, normals, semantics, and shadows. It solves the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering in urban environments by computing visibility via volume rendering transmittance rather than explicit geometry, ensuring consistency between the learned density field and shadow casting. Unlike explicit geometry shadow casting which may be inconsistent with neural fields, this method computes visibility via volume rendering transmittance, ensuring consistency with the learned density field. The method trains a neural field F(\cdot) representing density \sigma and color components (albedo \mathbf{a}, normal \mathbf{n}, semantic \mathbf{s}) and a lighting model \mathcal{L} jointly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera rays \mathcal{R}, ground-truth RGB images C{gt}, shadow masks M (from external detector [MTMT]), semantic priors, normal priors. Outputs: Rendered color C(r), albedo A, normal N, semantic S, visibility V, lighting parameters (ambient L{amb}, sky color C{sky}). Data Structures: The neural field F maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density and color attributes. Density: \sigma \in \mathbb{R} Albedo: \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Normal: \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Semantic: \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^k (where k is the number of classes) Numbered Steps: 1. Volume Rendering of Intrinsics: For each camera ray r, sample points xi along the ray. Compute density \sigmai and attributes \mathbf{a}i, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{s}i using F. Compute alpha-composition weights: wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. Render the final color, normal, and semantic maps: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{a}i, \quad N(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{n}i, \quad S(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{s}i 2. Depth Estimation for Shading Point: Compute the expected depth \hat{t} for the ray to determine the 3D point x(r) being shaded: \hat{t} = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ti Substitute \hat{t} into the ray equation to get the 3D position x(r). 3. Visibility Estimation via Volume Rendering: To estimate visibility V(x, \text{sun}) of point x to the sun, cast a ray from x in the direction of the sun \mathbf{l}{\text{sun}}. Compute transmittance along this segment using the same neural field: V(x, \text{sun}) = \exp\left(-\sumi \sigmai(xi) \deltai\right) \quad \text{where } xi = x + ti \mathbf{l}{\text{sun}} 4. Guidance Visibility Head: To avoid instability from direct 2D shadow mask supervision (which is inconsistent across frames), train an intermediate MLP head \hat{V}(r) to reproduce the 2D shadow masks M(r). This provides a consistent guidance signal. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{visibility}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{semantics}} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} Formulas: Rendering Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} = \sum{r} \| C{gt}(r) - C(r) \|2^2 Visibility Loss: The loss encourages V(x, \text{sun}) to be low where the guidance head \hat{V}(r) predicts shadow, and high otherwise. Specifically, it constrains geometry along the ray from the pixel to the sun based on shadow masks. Normal Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}} supervises the rendered normal against priors from Omnidata. Semantic Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{semantics}} supervises the rendered semantic against priors. Regularization Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{albedo}} + \| L{\text{amb}} \|2^2 where \mathcal{L}{\text{albedo}} regularizes ground albedo to be homogeneous: \mathcal{L}{\text{albedo}} = \sum{r \in \text{ground}} \| A(r) - \bar{A}g \|2^2 and \bar{A}g is the average ground albedo. \| L{\text{amb}} \|2^2 prevents unnatural color shifts from large ambient light intensity. Parameters: \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4: Weights for visibility, normal, semantics, and regularization losses. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Pitfalls: Instability from 2D Masks: Direct supervision of visibility with 2D shadow masks is unstable due to inconsistency across frames. Solved by using the intermediate MLP head \hat{V} for guidance. Ill-posed Optimization: Large ambient light intensity causes unnatural color shifts in recovered albedo. Solved by regularizing \| L{\text{amb}} \|2^2. Inconsistency with Explicit Geometry: Explicit geometry shadow casting may be inconsistent with neural fields. This method avoids this by computing visibility via volume rendering transmittance. The training pipeline retrieves scene intrinsics (albedo, normal, semantic) via volume rendering from camera rays, guided by semantic and normal priors. Transmittance along tracing rays is supervised with shadow masks. Inputs include the input image I, Instruct-Pix2Pix output I{p2p}, shadow mask M from MTMT, RGB ground truth C{gt}, albedo A, and sky color C{sky}. The pipeline uses losses \mathcal{L}{render} and \mathcal{L}{visibility} for volume rendering (Eq. 4 and 5), and \mathcal{L}{seman/c}, \mathcal{L}{normal}, \mathcal{L}{reg} for intrinsic decomposition. Priors come from Normal [Omnidata] and Semantic models. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on KITTI-360 and Waymo Open Dataset. The method successfully removes dark shadows with sharp boundaries and enables realistic nighttime rendering by introducing new light sources. Scaling: Evaluated on large-scale urban video sequences. Strengths: Consistency between learned density field and shadow casting; effective shadow removal in albedo; handles relighting. Limitations: Ill-posed nature requires strong regularization; dependency on external shadow masks and priors. When to use: When recovering physically plausible inverse rendering results (albedo, normals, shadows) from monocular urban video is required. When not: Not given in the sources. UrbanIR was introduced in the paper "UrbanIR: Large-Scale Urban Scene Inverse Rendering from a Single Video" published in 3DV 2025. It addresses the challenges of inverse rendering in urban driving sequences, where shadows and lighting variations complicate the recovery of intrinsic scene properties. The method builds on Depth from Ray Distance and differentiable volume rendering, and integrates semantic and normal priors to guide the optimization. UrbanIR: Large-Scale Urban Scene Inverse Rendering from a Single Video, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00052, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Differentiable Ray Marching (Taichi)
head: Taichi Differentiable Volume Rendering
body: A differentiable volume rendering technique implemented in Taichi using fixed-step ray marching and trilinear interpolation on a 3D density grid. It differs from sibling methods by relying on a fixed-step traversal with explicit alpha accumulation rather than expected terms or thresholding, and is implemented using Taichi's autodiff engine rather than PyTorch. Inputs: Camera position (campos), camera rotation matrix (camrot), pixel coordinates (pixelcoords), and a 4D density grid (density) containing RGBA values. Outputs: A rendered image (targetimage) with RGBA channels. Data Structures: density: Shape [8, 128, 128, 128, 4] (batch, x, y, z, rgba). targetimage: Shape [8, 4, 128, 128] (batch, rgba, height, width). campos: Shape [8, 3]. camrot: Shape [8, 3, 3]. pixelcoords: Shape [8, 128, 128, 2] (batch, height, width, xy). Parameters: dx = 0.015625 (fixed step size). densityres = 128 (grid resolution). focalx = 875., focaly = 875.. princptx = 400., princpty = 400.. Steps: 1. For each pixel (x, y) and batch index n:. 2. Compute ray direction components: a = (y - \text{princpt}y) / \text{focal}y, b = (x - \text{princpt}x) / \text{focal}x. 3. Compute direction vector: \mathbf{dir} = \text{cam\rot}[n] \cdot [a, b, 1]^T and normalize it. 4. Iterate k from 0 to 299:. a. Compute sample point: \mathbf{point} = \text{cam\pos}[n] + (k + 1) \cdot dx \cdot \mathbf{dir}. b. Check if \mathbf{point} is inside the box [-1, 1]^3. If so, set flag = 1, else flag = 0. c. Map point to grid coordinates: tx = (\mathbf{point}[0] + 1.) \cdot 127 / 2., similarly for ty, tz. d. Perform trilinear interpolation on density at (tx, ty, tz) to get r, g, b, a. e. Compute alpha contribution: \Delta \alpha = (\min(\text{current\alpha} + a \cdot dx, 1.) - \text{current\alpha}) \cdot \text{flag}. f. Accumulate color: \text{target\image}[n, c, x, y] += rc \cdot \Delta \alpha for c \in \{r, g, b\}. g. Update alpha: \text{target\image}[n, 3, x, y] = \min(\text{current\alpha} + a \cdot dx, 1.). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import taichi as ti ti.init(defaultfp=ti.f32, arch=ti.cuda) densityres = 128 dx = 0.015625 focalx = 875. focaly = 875. princptx = 400. princpty = 400. density = ti.field(dtype=ti.f32, shape=(8, 128, 128, 128, 4)) targetimage = ti.field(dtype=ti.f32, shape=(8, 4, 128, 128)) campos = ti.field(dtype=ti.f32, shape=(8, 3)) camrot = ti.field(dtype=ti.f32, shape=(8, 3, 3)) pixelcoords = ti.field(dtype=ti.i32, shape=(8, 128, 128, 2)) @ti.func def inbox(x, y, z): return x >= -1.0 and x <= 1.0 and y >= -1.0 and y <= 1.0 and z >= -1.0 and z <= 1.0 @ti.func def clip(x): return int(ti.max(0, ti.min(int(x), densityres - 1))) @ti.func def trilinearinterpolation(n, z, y, x, channel): ix = int(x) iy = int(y) iz = int(z) fx = x - ix fy = y - iy fz = z - iz ix = clip(ix) iy = clip(iy) iz = clip(iz) c000 = density[n, ix, iy, iz, channel] c100 = density[n, ix+1, iy, iz, channel] c010 = density[n, ix, iy+1, iz, channel] c110 = density[n, ix+1, iy+1, iz, channel] c001 = density[n, ix, iy, iz+1, channel] c101 = density[n, ix+1, iy, iz+1, channel] c011 = density[n, ix, iy+1, iz+1, channel] c111 = density[n, ix+1, iy+1, iz+1, channel] c00 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx c10 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx c01 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx c11 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1 - fy) + c11 fy c = c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz return c @ti.kernel def raymarch(res: ti.i32): targetimage.fill(0.0) for pixel in range(res res): for n in range(8): xind = pixel // res yind = pixel - xind res x = pixelcoords[n, xind, yind, 0] y = pixelcoords[n, xind, yind, 1] cameraorigin = ti.Vector([campos[n, 0], campos[n, 1], campos[n, 2]]) a = (y - princpty) / focaly b = (x - princptx) / focalx dir = ti.Vector([ camrot[n, 0, 0] a + camrot[n, 1, 0] b + camrot[n, 2, 0], camrot[n, 0, 1] a + camrot[n, 1, 1] b + camrot[n, 2, 1], camrot[n, 0, 2] a + camrot[n, 1, 2] b + camrot[n, 2, 2]]) length = ti.sqrt(dir[0] dir[0] + dir[1] dir[1] + dir[2] dir[2]) dir /= length for k in range(300): point = cameraorigin + (k + 1) dx dir flag = 0 if inbox(point[0], point[1], point[2]): flag = 1 templatex = (point[0] + 1.) 127 / 2. templatey = (point[1] + 1.) 127 / 2. templatez = (point[2] + 1.) 127 / 2. rinterp = trilinearinterpolation(n, templatez, templatey, templatex, 0) ginterp = trilinearinterpolation(n, templatez, templatey, templatex, 1) binterp = trilinearinterpolation(n, templatez, templatey, templatex, 2) ainterp = trilinearinterpolation(n, templatez, templatey, templatex, 3) contributionr = rinterp flag contributiong = ginterp flag contributionb = binterp flag contributiona = ainterp flag currentalpha = targetimage[n, 3, xind, yind] deltaalpha = (ti.min(currentalpha + contributiona dx, 1.0) - currentalpha) flag targetimage[n, 0, xind, yind] += contributionr deltaalpha targetimage[n, 1, xind, yind] += contributiong deltaalpha targetimage[n, 2, xind, yind] += contributionb deltaalpha targetimage[n, 3, xind, yind] = ti.min(currentalpha + contributiona dx, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradients computed by Taichi's autodiff may be rotated/translated compared to PyTorch due to implementation differences in differentiation rules for ray marching. Points outside the [-1, 1]^3 box are ignored via flag. Grid coordinates are clipped to [0, 127] to avoid out-of-bounds access. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot K) where N is batch size, H, W are image dimensions, and K is number of steps (300). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot R^3 \cdot C) for the density grid, where R is resolution (128) and C is channels (4). Strengths: Simple implementation, differentiable via Taichi's autodiff. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or inefficiency; gradient mismatches with PyTorch. When to use: When using Taichi for differentiable volume rendering and PyTorch compatibility is not critical for gradients. When not to use: When precise gradient alignment with PyTorch is required. Originated from a GitHub issue discussing gradient mismatches between Taichi and PyTorch implementations of differentiable ray marching. The code is based on examples from the Taichi repository. Gradients Computed by Taichi Don't Match Gradients Computed by PyTorch, https://github.com/taichi-dev/taichi/issues/2241, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Approximated Gradient Back-Propagation
body: Approximated Gradient Back-Propagation is a method for computing gradients in differentiable volume rendering by ignoring high-order gradient terms, specifically the dependence of sample point positions on the latent code, to reduce memory usage. It sets itself apart from exact gradient methods by using only the direct gradient of the Signed Distance Function (SDF) network, making it particularly useful for optimizing latent codes in implicit shape representations like DeepSDF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A latent code \mathbf{z}, camera ray origin \mathbf{p}^{(0)}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, and SDF network parameters \theta. Output: Gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}} for a loss function L. Data Structures: \mathbf{z}: Latent code vector. \mathbf{p}^{(i)}: Sample points along the ray, computed using a fixed initialization \mathbf{z}0. f\theta(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{z}): SDF network evaluating the distance at point \mathbf{p} given latent code \mathbf{z}. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the first point \mathbf{p}^{(0)} as the intersection between the camera ray and the unit sphere. If the ray does not intersect, mark as background. 2. Forward Marching: Perform sphere tracing to compute sample points \mathbf{p}^{(i)} along the ray. Crucially, these points are computed using a fixed latent code \mathbf{z}0 (e.g., from a previous iteration or initialization), not the current \mathbf{z} being optimized. 3. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF network f\theta(\mathbf{p}^{(i)}(\mathbf{z}0), \mathbf{z}) for the current \mathbf{z} at the fixed points. 4. Gradient Approximation: Compute the gradient of the rendered distance d' with respect to \mathbf{z} by ignoring the residual term involving \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}^{(i)}}{\partial \mathbf{z}}. Formula: The full chain rule for the gradient of the SDF output with respect to the latent code is: \frac{\partial f{\theta}(\mathbf{p}^{(i)}(\mathbf{z}), \mathbf{z})}{\partial \mathbf{z}} = \frac{\partial f{\theta}(\mathbf{p}^{(i)}(\mathbf{z}0), \mathbf{z})}{\partial \mathbf{z}} + \frac{\partial f{\theta}(\mathbf{p}^{(i)}(\mathbf{z}), \mathbf{z}0)}{\partial \mathbf{p}^{(i)}(\mathbf{z})} \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}^{(i)}(\mathbf{z}0)}{\partial \mathbf{z}} The method approximates this by keeping only the first term: \frac{\partial d'}{\partial \mathbf{z}} \approx \alpha \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{\partial f{\theta}(\mathbf{p}^{(i)}(\mathbf{z}0), \mathbf{z})}{\partial \mathbf{z}} where \alpha is the transmittance/weight factor and N is the number of samples. Parameters: \mathbf{z}0: Fixed latent code used for point position calculation. \alpha: Weighting factor for samples. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: The residual term e (the second term in the full chain rule) is ignored. High-order gradients empirically have less impact on the optimization process, but this approximation may fail if point positions are highly sensitive to \mathbf{z}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def norm(a): return math.sqrt(dot(a, a)) def add(a, b): return tuple(x + y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def scale(a, s): return tuple(x s for x in a) def raysphereintersection(origin, direction, radius=1.0): oc = origin a = dot(direction, direction) halfb = dot(oc, direction) c = dot(oc, oc) - radius radius discriminant = halfb halfb - a c if discriminant < 0: return None t = (-halfb - math.sqrt(discriminant)) / a if t < 0: t = (-halfb + math.sqrt(discriminant)) / a return t if t > 0 else None def computegradient(func, x, target): """Standard automatic differentiation operation.""" return func.backward(target) def approximatedgradientbackprop(z, z0, rayorigin, raydirection, sdfnetwork, maxsteps=256, threshold=1e-3): # 1. Initialize point on unit sphere tinit = raysphereintersection(rayorigin, raydirection) if tinit is None: return scale(z, 0.0) # Background ray p = add(rayorigin, scale(raydirection, tinit)) points = [p] transmittance = 1.0 gradz = scale(z, 0.0) # 2. Forward marching with fixed z0 for in range(maxsteps): dist = sdfnetwork(p, z0) if dist < threshold: break step = max(dist, 1e-4) # Prevent zero-step p = add(p, scale(raydirection, step)) points.append(p) # Compute sample weight alpha (transmittance opacity) alpha = transmittance (1.0 - math.exp(-max(0.0, dist))) transmittance = math.exp(-max(0.0, dist)) # 3. Gradient approximation for i, p in enumerate(points): # Evaluate SDF with current z sdfval = sdfnetwork(p, z) # Compute gradient w.r.t. z only (ignoring dp/dz) zgrad = computegradient(sdfnetwork, p, z) gradz = add(gradz, scale(zgrad, alpha)) return gradz This method computes gradients for material and light parameters in differentiable volume rendering by avoiding the storage of a computational graph during the forward pass, thereby significantly reducing memory footprint. It differs from standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation by deferring gradient computation to a separate backpropagation pass that casts rays with gradients from the camera, rather than storing intermediate values during the forward pass. The forward pass calls cubvh.floodfill(occ) to get floodfillmask, computes emptylabel from floodfillmask[0,0,0], computes emptymask and occmask, computes sdf = udf - 1e-6, computes innermask = occmask & (sdf > 0), updates nearestpoints for inner points, saves xflat and nearestpoints for backward, and returns udf.view(x.shape[:-1])[...,None]. The backward pass retrieves x and nearestpoints from ctx.savedtensors, computes diff = x - nearestpoints, computes norm = diff.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8, computes gradudf = gradoutput.view(-1, 1), computes gradinput = gradudf (diff / norm), reshapes gradinput to match x, and returns gradinput, None, None, None. The gradient formula is \text{grad\input} = \text{grad\output} \times \frac{\mathbf{x} - \text{nearest\points}}{\|\mathbf{x} - \text{nearest\points}\|}. Parameters include an epsilon of 10^{-8} added to the norm to prevent division by zero, and an offset of 10^{-6} subtracted from the UDF to create the SDF before determining the inner mask. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N and the cost of the SDF network evaluation. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to exact backpropagation because the computational graph for point positions is not stored. Strengths: Enables optimization of latent codes in memory-constrained environments; bridges the gap between shape priors and partial observations. When to use: When optimizing latent codes for implicit shapes (e.g., DeepSDF) and memory is a bottleneck. The method originates from the paper "DIST: Rendering Deep Implicit Signed Distance Function With Differentiable Sphere Tracing". It was developed to address the memory limitations of differentiable sphere tracing when optimizing latent codes for 3D shape representation. The approach leverages the observation that high-order gradients have less impact on the optimization process, allowing for a simplified gradient computation. DIST: Rendering Deep Implicit Signed Distance Function With Differentiable Sphere Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr42600.2020.00209, fetched 2026-10-26 jjjkkyz/DCx, https://github.com/jjjkkyz/DCx, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Efficient Gradient Computation without Computational Graph
head: Nimier-David et al. method
body: This method computes gradients for material and light parameters in differentiable volume rendering by avoiding the storage of a computational graph during the forward pass, thereby significantly reducing memory footprint. It differs from standard reverse-mode automatic differentiation by deferring gradient computation to a separate backpropagation pass that casts rays with gradients from the camera, rather than storing intermediate values during the forward pass. Inputs: Scene representation (e.g., SDF, volume density). Material and light parameters \theta. Camera configuration. Outputs: Gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} with respect to the loss L. Data Structures: Ray structures containing position, direction, and accumulated gradient values. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. No persistent computational graph or tape is stored in memory during rendering. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Render the image normally without storing the computational graph or intermediate derivative states. 2. Backpropagation Ray Casting: Cast new rays from the camera, initialized with gradients propagated from the pixel loss. 3. Gradient Propagation: As rays traverse the scene, gradients are propagated along the ray path. 4. Occlusion Handling: Gradients are propagated to surfaces at occlusion points. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: The method is implemented in Mitsuba 2, which explores approaches between forward- and reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Changes: The method does not account for the non-differentiability of object visibility changes (e.g., an object entering or leaving the frame). This makes optimizing shapes challenging. Memory vs. Compute: The approach trades arithmetic operations for memory traffic by avoiding graph storage, which is beneficial on modern hardware where memory access is costly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computegradients(scene, params, camera, lossfn): # Forward pass: render image without storing computational graph image = [] for pixel in camera.pixels: ray = camera.buildray(pixel) transmittance = 1.0 color = 0.0 for sample in ray.samples: density = scene.density(sample) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density stepsize) color += transmittance alpha scene.color(sample) transmittance = 1.0 - alpha image.append(color) # Initialize parameter gradients gradparams = {k: 0.0 for k in params} # Backpropagation: cast rays with gradients from camera for pixelidx, pixel in enumerate(camera.pixels): ray = camera.buildray(pixel) currentgrad = lossfn.derivative(image[pixelidx]) # Traverse scene to find interaction points hit = None for sample in ray.samples: if scene.isoccluded(sample): hit = sample break if hit is not None: # Compute local gradient contribution at hit point # Not given in the sources. localgrad = scene.evaluategradient(hit, params) # Accumulate gradient # Note: Visibility changes are ignored for k in params: gradparams[k] += localgrad currentgrad return gradparams An algorithm that finds common factors in the computational graph to optimize derivative computation, trading arithmetic operations for memory traffic. It is used in Mitsuba 2 to explore approaches between forward- and reverse-modes. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower than full reverse-mode AD because no computational graph is stored during rendering. Time Complexity: Requires two passes (forward and backward ray casting), potentially increasing compute time compared to a single forward pass, but avoids the overhead of graph traversal and storage. Strengths: Suitable for scenes with large memory footprints where storing a computational graph is infeasible. Limitations: Cannot handle non-differentiable visibility changes, limiting its applicability to shape optimization. The method was proposed by Nimier-David et al.. It addresses the high memory footprint of automatic differentiation in differentiable rendering, which limits applications to simple scenes. Mitsuba 2 adopted this approach to explore the spectrum between forward- and reverse-mode AD, utilizing a greedy vertex elimination algorithm to optimize derivative computation. Differentiable Rendering: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2006.12057, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Physics-based differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3388769.3407454, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Differentiable Volume Rendering via Box Splines
head: Differentiable X-ray Transform with Ray-Trace Gradients, Differentiable X-ray transform, Differentiable XRT Forward Projection, xrt_ad_t (Geometry Gradient w.r.t Ray Anchor) [S1, unofficial]
body: This method computes the forward projection of a volume defined by box splines and its analytical gradients with respect to ray parameters (origin \mathbf{t} and direction \mathbf{n}) and volume data coefficients. It solves the differentiable X-ray transform (XRT) for uniform 2D and 3D grids with interpolation orders 0, 1, and 2. Unlike standard differentiable renderers that rely on finite differences or implicit automatic differentiation through the entire ray-marching loop, this method explicitly computes ray-traced geometry gradients using specific adjoint functions for ray anchors and directions, while using the standard adjoint transform for volume coefficients. The method implements the differentiable X-ray transform operator \mathcal{X}f = \int{\mathbb{R}} f(\mathbf{t} + \tau \mathbf{n}) d\tau for a volume f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{\mathbf{q} \in \text{discreteRange}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}-1)} f{\mathbf{q}} \psi(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}{\mathbf{q}}), where \psi is a box spline basis function determined by the interpolation order. The volume is defined on a uniform grid with start \mathbf{x}0, step \mathbf{\Delta}, and dimensions \mathbf{Q}. Inputs: rayspec: Tuple (tspec, nspec) of shape (L,) containing ray anchors \mathbf{t} and directions \mathbf{n}. knotspec: UniformSpec object containing volume properties (\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{\Delta}, \mathbf{Q}). data: Flattened volume weights of shape (Q1, \dots, QD). order: Integer specifying interpolation order (0, 1, or 2). mode: String for AD mode, typically 'symbolic'. Outputs: proj: Array of shape (L,) containing projection values. Gradients w.r.t. data, tspec, and nspec are computed during the backward pass. Data Structures: ArrayNf: Ray type (e.g., drjit.Array3f). ArrayNi: Integer type (int32). ArrayNu: Unsigned integer type (uint32). Float: Scalar value type. Bool: Mask type. stride: Linear indexing stride. For 2D: (Qy, 1). For 3D: (Qy Qz, Qz, 1). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute bounding box: \mathbf{bbox}{ll} = \mathbf{x}0 - (\mathbf{\Delta} / 2), \mathbf{bbox}{ur} = \mathbf{x}0 - (\mathbf{\Delta} / 2) + (\mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta}). Compute stride based on dimension D and \mathbf{Q}. Initialize accumulator buffer of size L to zeros. Initialize state: For order 0, state = (buffer,). For order 1 (2D) and order > 0 (3D), state = (buffer, indexprev) with indexprev = ArrayNi(-1). 2. Ray Bounding Box Intersection: Compute intersection: active, t1, t2 = raybboxintersect(bboxll, bboxur, rayt, rayn). Compute tmin = minimum(t1, t2). Adjust ray origin: rayt = select(active & bboxcontains(bboxll, bboxur, rayt), rayt + (tmin - 1) rayn, rayt). 3. DDA Traversal: Execute DDA loop: dda(rayo=rayt, rayd=rayn, raymax=inf, gridres=Q, gridmin=bboxll, gridmax=bboxur, func=project, state=state, active=active, mode=mode, maxiterations=-1). The project callback is invoked for each cell (index, pa, pb, active) where pa, pb are entry/exit fractional positions. 4. Projection Callback (project): The implementation of project depends on the dimension D and order: Case 1: 3D, Order 0 (Voxel) Compute closed-form gradient for each dimension idx \in \{0, 1, 2\}: \sigma = \text{select}(pa[idx] < \epsilon, 1, 0) + \text{select}(pb[idx] < \epsilon, 1, 0) - \text{select}(pa[idx] > 1.0 - \epsilon, 1, 0) - \text{select}(pb[idx] > 1.0 - \epsilon, 1, 0). n{abs} = |n[idx]|. g = \text{select}(n{abs} > \epsilon, \sigma / n{abs}, 0). Accumulate: accum += fq g where fq is gathered from data at offset = dot(index, stride). Case 2: 2D (Any Order) or 3D Order > 0 (Using AD) Setup: Compute perpendicular vector: \mathbf{n}{perp} = \text{normalize}((-ny, nx)). Compute box spline parameters: E, E{mask} = \text{box\spline\1d\E}(order, \mathbf{\Delta}, \mathbf{n}{perp}). Determine movement direction: \text{direction} = \mathbf{n} / \mathbf{\Delta}, \text{look\lr} = |\text{direction}.x| \ge |\text{direction}.y|, \text{mv\dir} = \text{select}(\text{look\lr}, (1, 0), (0, 1)). Define shifts: \text{shift}l = \text{reverse}(-\text{mv\dir}), \text{shift}m = (0, 0), \text{shift}r = \text{reverse}(\text{mv\dir}). Processing Shifts: For each shift s \in \{\text{shift}l, \text{shift}m, \text{shift}r\}: Compute indexs = index + shift. Check bounds: actives = all((0 <= indexs) & (indexs < Q)). Gather fq = gather(data, dot(indexs, stride), actives). Compute cell center: \mathbf{c} = (0.5, 0.5) + \text{shift}. Enable gradients on local copies: \mathbf{p}{local} = \mathbf{p}a, \mathbf{n}{local} = \mathbf{n}, enablegrad(plocal, nlocal). Define contribution function: \text{contribution}(\mathbf{p}a, \mathbf{n}) = \text{box\spline\1d\dr}(E, E{mask}, \mathbf{n}{perp} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} \cdot (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}a)) where \mathbf{n}{perp} = \text{normalize}((-ny, nx)). Run backward pass: backward(contribution(plocal, nlocal)). Compute gradient: g = \mathbf{n}{local}.grad[idx] + \text{fac\t} \cdot \mathbf{p}{local}.grad[idx]. Note: \text{fac\t} is computed as \text{select}(n{norm\sq} > \epsilon^2, \mathbf{p}{phys} \cdot \mathbf{n} / n{norm\sq}, 0) where \mathbf{p}{phys} = \mathbf{bbox}{ll} + (\text{index} + \mathbf{p}a) \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} and n{norm\sq} = |\mathbf{n}|^2. Return fq and g (length L). Accumulation Logic: Compute displacement = index - indexprev. Select fqlmr based on dot(displacement, mvdir) != 0. Accumulate: accum += dot(fqlmr, (Ll, Lm, Lr)). Update indexprev = index. Case 3: 3D Order > 0 (Using Neural Network for Spline) Setup: Normalize \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{n}). Compute direction: \text{direction} = |\mathbf{n} / \mathbf{\Delta}|. Compute dominant axis: \text{dominant\axis} = \text{floor}(\text{direction} / \max(\text{direction}) + 10^{-6}). Compute shifts: \text{shift}x = (dy, dz, dx), \text{shift}y = \text{cross}(\text{dominant\axis}, \text{shift}x). Compute perpendiculars: \mathbf{n}{perp\x} = \text{normalize}(\text{shift}x - \text{dot}(\text{shift}x, \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n}), \mathbf{n}{perp\y} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{n}{perp\x}). Define shifts: \text{shift}m, \text{shift}x, -\text{shift}x, \text{shift}y, -\text{shift}y, \text{shift}x+\text{shift}y, -\text{shift}x-\text{shift}y, \text{shift}x-\text{shift}y, -\text{shift}x+\text{shift}y. Processing Shifts: For each shift, compute indexs, gather fq, compute \mathbf{c} = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) + \text{shift}, compute x = \mathbf{n}{perp\y} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} \cdot (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}a), y = \mathbf{n}{perp\x} \cdot \mathbf{\Delta} \cdot (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}a), and L = \text{spline\3d\dr}(net, x, y, \mathbf{n}). Accumulation Logic: Compute displacement = index - indexprev. Use ifstmt to select fqlmr and fqdmu based on dot(displacement, shiftx) and dot(displacement, shifty). Zero out corner weights if displacement conditions are not met. Accumulate: accum += dot(fqdmu, Ldmu) + dot(fqlmr, Llmr) + fqll Lll + fqrr Lrr + fqlr Llr + fqrl Lrl. 5. Backward Pass (Gradients): Retrieve output gradient g = self.gradout(). Gradient w.r.t. Volume (x): If wantx, compute adjoint transform using xrtadjoint(rs, knotspec, order, g). Gradient w.r.t. Ray Anchors (t): If wantt, compute partial derivatives. For 2D: gt[0] = g xrtadtx(...), gt[1] = g xrtadty(...). For 3D: additionally gt[2] = g xrtadtz(...). Gradient w.r.t. Ray Directions (n): If wantn, compute partial derivatives. For 2D: gn[0] = g xrtadnx(...), gn[1] = g xrtadny(...). For 3D: additionally gn[2] = g xrtadnz(...). Parameters: order: 0, 1, or 2. Order 0 uses \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{\Delta}. Order 1 (2D) uses \mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}2, \mathbf{\Delta}2]. Order 2 (2D) uses \mathbf{E} = [\mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}1, \mathbf{\Delta}1, 0, \mathbf{\Delta}2, \mathbf{\Delta}2, -\mathbf{\Delta}2]. eps: Small constant for numerical stability (e.g., 10^{-6}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When n[idx] = 0, the ray never crosses idx-faces; \sigma=0 too, so return 0 to avoid division by zero. Enabling grad on loop-external rayn breaks symbolic tracing; must use local copies nlocal and plocal. Forward-mode differentiation is not implemented; only reverse-mode (backward) differentiation is supported. 3D order 0 uses a closed-form gradient calculation (Algorithm vox2) instead of the general box-spline projection weight differentiation used for other orders/dimensions. A neural network used to evaluate the 3D box spline projection for orders > 0. It takes inputs related to position and direction and outputs the spline value. Weights are loaded from splineweights.npz file. The network architecture is dnn.Sequential with layers: dnn.Linear(4, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 16), dnn.ReLU(), dnn.Linear(16, 1). Weights are stored in TensorXf16 format. It is called as spline3ddr(net, x, y, n) where x and y are projected coordinates and n is the normalized ray direction. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by rays, determined by the DDA traversal. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output size, enabling single-pass or tightly coupled backward passes. The state maintains indexprev for tracking cell transitions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays and intersected voxels. Strengths: Explicit computation of ray-traced geometry gradients for anchors and directions using specific adjoint functions (xrtadt, xrtadn), while using the standard adjoint transform for volume coefficients. Supports 2D and 3D uniform grids with interpolation orders 0, 1, and 2. Limitations: Forward-mode differentiation is not implemented. 3D projections only support order 0 in the general case, with higher orders requiring a neural network approximation. When to use: Geometry calibration in tomography, specifically for differentiable ray-based models. When not to use: When forward-mode differentiation is required or when non-uniform grids are used. The method is based on the differentiable X-ray transform operator, implemented as a vector-Jacobian product within Dr.Jit's automatic differentiation framework. It implements Algorithms 1-2 of the reference paper. The approach explicitly expands the chain rule across the continuous stages of the rendering pipeline, bypassing the computational graph storage required by reverse-mode AD. For volumetric methods, the rendering integral is differentiated term-by-term, yielding a direct term for local emission and an indirect term for downstream transmittance or visibility attenuation. The implementation is part of the differentiablexrt library. HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, https://github.com/HaouchatY/differentiablexrt, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Volume Rendering with Analytical Gradients
head: Analytical Differentiable Rendering, DiffRenderer
body: A rendering technique that computes radiance and its analytical derivatives with respect to volume density directly, avoiding the overhead of propagating gradients through long computational graphs inherent in automatic differentiation. It solves the problem of inefficient optimization for dynamic volumetric densities, such as in fluid reconstruction, by providing a closed-form gradient calculation. Unlike Differentiable Volume Rendering via Box Splines, which relies on basis function smoothness, this method operates on the standard emission-absorption model with explicit step-wise differentiation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{x}a, ray direction \boldsymbol{u}, volume density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}), step size \triangle d, and ray exit boundary \mathbf{x}b. Outputs: Radiance L and its analytical gradient with respect to density parameters. Data Structures: Ray state: Current position xu, accumulated transmittance T, accumulated radiance L. Step history: Lists storing \sigmai, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i, and Ti for each sampled step. Steps: 1. Initialize L \leftarrow 0, T \leftarrow 1, xu \leftarrow \mathbf{x}a. 2. Iterate along the ray from xa to xb with step size \triangle d: a. Sample density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i at xu. b. Compute step transmittance attenuation: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \triangle d). c. Compute emitted radiance contribution: Ci = T \cdot \alphai \cdot \mathbf{c}i. d. Update accumulated radiance: L \leftarrow L + Ci. e. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai). f. Store step data (\sigmai, \alphai, \mathbf{c}i, Ti) for gradient computation. g. Advance ray position: xu \rightarrow xu + \boldsymbol{u} \triangle d. 3. Compute analytical gradient \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigmak} for each step k using a backward pass: a. Initialize backward accumulator B \leftarrow 0. b. Iterate steps k from N down to 1: i. Direct term: Dk = Tk \triangle d \exp(-\sigmak \triangle d) \mathbf{c}k. ii. Indirect term: Ik = \triangle d \cdot B. iii. Gradient: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigmak} = Dk - Ik. iv. Update accumulator: B \leftarrow B (1 - \alphak) + Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k. Formulas: The standard emission-absorption model computes color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is density, \deltai is step size, \mathbf{c}i is color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is transmittance. The analytical gradient with respect to density \sigmak is derived by differentiating the sum term-by-term. \frac{\partial \hat{C}}{\partial \sigmak} = Tk \triangle d \exp(-\sigmak \triangle d) \mathbf{c}k - \triangle d \sum{j=k+1}^N Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \triangle d)) \mathbf{c}j Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticalgradientrendering(rayorigin, raydir, densityfield, stepsize, rayexit): xu = rayorigin.copy() T = 1.0 L = 0.0 steps = [] # Forward pass: sample and accumulate radiance while True: # Guard: check if current position is within volume bounds tmin = max((rayorigin - xu) / (raydir + 1e-8)) tmax = min((rayexit - xu) / (raydir + 1e-8)) if tmin > tmax: break sigmai = densityfield.sample(xu) ci = densityfield.color(xu) alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai stepsize) Tk = T contribution = Tk alphai ci L += contribution T = (1.0 - alphai) # Store history for backward gradient pass steps.append({'sigma': sigmai, 'alpha': alphai, 'color': ci, 'T': Tk}) # Advance ray position xu = xu + raydir stepsize # Backward pass: compute analytical gradients grads = [] B = 0.0 for k in range(len(steps) - 1, -1, -1): s = steps[k] direct = s['T'] stepsize math.exp(-s['sigma'] stepsize) s['color'] indirect = stepsize B grad = direct - indirect grads.append(grad) B = B (1.0 - s['alpha']) + s['T'] s['alpha'] s['color'] return L, list(reversed(grads)) Computes continuously differentiable upper and lower bounds on cumulative mass consistent with power moments. It solves the truncated Hamburger moment problem. It is distinguished from standard visibility functions by generalizing to arbitrary moment sequences (2n+1 moments) for tighter bounds, and from its parent method by providing a robust, numerically stable implementation that handles singularities. Choose it when differentiable rendering requires guaranteed bounds on scene parameters rather than point estimates. Complexity: O(N) time and memory per ray, where N is the number of steps, as it avoids storing a full computational graph. Performance: Improves optimization speed for dynamic volumetric densities like fluid reconstruction by eliminating gradient tracking overhead. Strengths: Constant memory overhead relative to parameters; enables single-pass or tightly coupled backward passes. Limitations: Requires explicit analytical derivation of the rendering equation; less flexible than automatic differentiation for arbitrary, non-differentiable operations. Usage: Use for differentiable inverse rendering and optimization tasks where density gradients are needed; avoid when the scene contains hard, non-differentiable visibility changes or complex discrete selection logic. Originated in physics-based differentiable rendering for fluid modeling from monocular video. The work builds upon insights that automatic differentiation fundamentally relies on propagating gradients through long computational graphs, which carries inherent overhead compared to direct analytical derivatives. It is applied in dynamic volumetric reconstruction and fluid simulation pipelines. Physics-Based Differentiable Rendering for Efficient and Plausible Fluid Modeling from Monocular Video, https://doi.org/10.3390/e25091348, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Differentiable Moment Bounds
body: Differentiable Moment Bounds is a technique that computes continuously differentiable upper and lower bounds on the cumulative mass of a measure consistent with a given sequence of power moments. It solves the truncated Hamburger moment problem by constructing a unique "canonical" discrete measure that tightly bounds the set of all valid measures. Unlike standard visibility functions based on Chebyshev's inequality, which use only the first two moments (n=1), this method generalizes to arbitrary moment sequences (2n+1 moments) to provide tighter bounds. It is distinguished from its parent method, Differentiable Volume Rendering with Analytical Gradients, by providing a robust, numerically stable implementation of these bounds that handles singularities, enabling their use in differentiable rendering pipelines where gradients with respect to scene parameters are required. Inputs: Moments \mathbf{m} = (m0, \dots, m{2n}), a sequence of 2n+1 power moments. Evaluation point \eta \in \mathbb{R}. Overestimation weight \beta \in [0, 1]. Bias parameter \alpha \in [0, 1]. Reference moment vector \mathbf{m}^\star (used for biasing). Outputs: Bound b = (1 - \beta)L + \beta U, where L and U are the lower and upper bounds on the cumulative mass. Data Structures: Hankel Matrix H: A symmetric positive-definite matrix of size (n+1) \times (n+1) constructed from the biased moments. The entry H{i,j} corresponds to the moment m{i+j} for 0 \le i, j \le n. Coefficient Vector \mathbf{c}: A vector of size n+1 resulting from the Cholesky solve. Roots \mathbf{x}: A vector of size n containing the roots of the kernel polynomial. Weights \mathbf{w}: A vector of size n+1 containing the weights of the canonical discrete measure. Steps: 1. Biasing: Regularize the input moments to ensure numerical stability. Compute \mathbf{m}' = (1 - \alpha)\mathbf{m} + \alpha\mathbf{m}^\star. 2. Hankel Construction: Construct the Hankel matrix H from \mathbf{m}' such that H{i,j} = m'{i+j}. 3. Cholesky Solve: Solve the linear system H\mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\eta} for \mathbf{c}, where \boldsymbol{\eta} = (1, \eta, \eta^2, \dots, \eta^n)^\top. This is done using Cholesky decomposition. 4. Root Finding: Find the roots x1, \dots, xn of the kernel polynomial defined by coefficients \mathbf{c}. Roots can be found in closed-form for low n or as eigenvalues of the companion matrix for higher n. 5. Partial Moments: Define the partial moment vector \bar{\mathbf{m}} = (m0, \dots, mn). 6. Vandermonde Solve: Solve the Vandermonde system for weights \mathbf{w} = (w0, \dots, wn) using inputs \eta, x1, \dots, xn and \bar{\mathbf{m}}. The system enforces that the discrete measure matches the moments up to order n. 7. Bound Aggregation: Initialize b = \beta w0. Iterate i from 1 to n: if xi < \eta, add wi to b. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiablemomentbounds(m, eta, beta, alpha, mstar): n = (len(m) - 1) // 2 # Step 1: Biasing mbiased = [(1 - alpha) m[i] + alpha mstar[i] for i in range(len(m))] # Step 2: Construct Hankel Matrix H H = [[mbiased[i + j] for j in range(n + 1)] for i in range(n + 1)] # Step 3: Cholesky Solve H c = etavec etavec = [etai for i in range(n + 1)] c = choleskysolve(H, etavec) # Step 4: Find roots of kernel polynomial defined by c roots = findpolynomialroots(c) # Step 5: Partial moments mpartial = m[:n + 1] # Step 6: Solve Vandermonde system for weights w w = solvevandermondesystem(eta, roots, mpartial) # Step 7: Aggregate bound b = beta w[0] for i in range(1, n + 1): if roots[i - 1] < eta: b += w[i] return b def choleskysolve(A, b): """Solves Ax=b using Cholesky decomposition A=LL^T.""" n = len(A) L = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1): s = sum(L[i][k] L[j][k] for k in range(j)) L[i][j] = (A[i][j] - s) / (L[j][j] if j < i else 1.0) y = [0.0] n for i in range(n): y[i] = (b[i] - sum(L[i][k] y[k] for k in range(i))) / L[i][i] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): x[i] = (y[i] - sum(L[j][i] x[j] for j in range(i + 1, n))) / L[i][i] return x def findpolynomialroots(c): """Finds roots of polynomial with coefficients c using companion matrix eigenvalues.""" n = len(c) - 1 coeffs = [c[i] / c[n] for i in range(n)] comp = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for i in range(n - 1): comp[i][i + 1] = 1.0 for i in range(n): comp[n - 1][i] = -coeffs[i] return eigenvalues(comp) def solvevandermondesystem(eta, roots, mpartial): """Solves Vw = mpartial where V0j=1, Vij = roots[j-1]^i for i>0.""" n = len(roots) size = n + 1 V = [[0.0] size for in range(size)] for i in range(size): V[i][0] = 1.0 for j in range(1, size): V[i][j] = roots[j - 1] i aug = [V[i] + [mpartial[i]] for i in range(size)] for i in range(size): pivot = aug[i][i] for j in range(size + 1): aug[i][j] /= pivot for k in range(size): if k != i: factor = aug[k][i] for j in range(size + 1): aug[k][j] -= factor aug[i][j] return [aug[i][size] for i in range(size)] def eigenvalues(M): """Returns eigenvalues of matrix M using the QR algorithm.""" n = len(M) A = [row[:] for row in M] for in range(100): Q = [[0.0]n for in range(n)] R = [[0.0]n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(i, n): rij = sum(A[k][i] A[k][j] for k in range(i)) if i == j: rij = max(rij, 1e-12) R[i][j] = rij qij = A[i][j] / R[i][j] Q[i][j] = qij for k in range(i + 1, n): for j in range(i, n): A[k][j] -= qij R[i][j] newA = [[0.0]n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): for k in range(n): newA[i][j] += Q[i][k] R[k][j] A = newA return [A[i][i] for i in range(n)] Parameters: \beta \in [0, 1]: Overestimation weight blending between lower and upper bounds. \alpha \in [0, 1]: Bias parameter for moment regularization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularities: The representation has singularities where evaluating the bound is numerically challenging. The differentiability analysis reveals the behavior of the bound and its derivatives near these singularities to enable robust implementation. Numerical Stability: A straightforward implementation using automatic differentiation is numerically unstable and inefficient in terms of memory and runtime. Careful consideration of the derivative calculation (via the adjoint algorithm) is required for stability. This method computes differentiable upper and lower bounds on the cumulative mass of any measure consistent with a given sequence of moments \mathbf{m}. It solves the truncated Hamburger moment problem by constructing a unique "canonical" discrete measure that tightly bounds the set of all valid measures. Unlike standard visibility functions based on Chebyshev's inequality, which use only the first two moments (n=1), this method generalizes to arbitrary moment sequences (2n+1 moments) to provide tighter bounds. See Moment Bounds for Measures. This is the specific algorithmic implementation of the differentiable moment bounds described in the main method. It involves biasing the input moments, constructing the Hankel matrix, solving for coefficients via Cholesky decomposition, finding polynomial roots, solving a Vandermonde system for weights, and aggregating the bound based on the evaluation point. It is designed to be robust against numerical singularities and efficient for use in differentiable rendering pipelines. Time and Memory Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the Cholesky decomposition of the (n+1) \times (n+1) Hankel matrix and the root finding of the degree-n polynomial. The Cholesky decomposition is O(n^3), and root finding is typically O(n^2) or O(n^3) depending on the method (e.g., companion matrix eigenvalues). The Vandermonde solve is also O(n^2). Memory complexity is O(n^2) for the Hankel matrix and O(n) for vectors. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the order of the moment sequence n. Higher n provides tighter bounds but increases computational cost. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides continuously differentiable bounds, enabling their use in differentiable rendering pipelines. More accurate than existing differentiable shadow mapping techniques for the same computational cost. Generalizes Chebyshev's inequality to arbitrary moment sequences. Limitations: Numerically unstable if not implemented carefully, particularly near singularities. Straightforward automatic differentiation implementations are inefficient. When to use it and when not: Use when differentiable shadow mapping or visibility estimation is required with tighter bounds than Chebyshev's inequality can provide. Do not use when computational resources are extremely limited and n must be large, or when numerical stability cannot be guaranteed due to the presence of singularities. The method originates from the work of Peters and Klein (2015) and Peters et al. (2019), who introduced moment-based approximations for visibility. The differentiability of these bounds was formally proven and an efficient implementation was developed in the paper "Moment Bounds are Differentiable: Efficiently Approximating Measures in Inverse Rendering" (2026). It is used in differentiable shadow mapping, generalizing existing techniques by Donnelly and Lauritzen (2006) and Worchel and Alexa (2023). Moment Bounds are Differentiable: Efficiently Approximating Measures in Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3730899, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Moment Bounds for Measures
head: Canonical representation bounds, Chebyshev-Markov bounds, Moment Bounds for Inverse Rendering, Moment-based bounds, Truncated Hamburger moment problem bounds
body: This method computes differentiable upper and lower bounds on the cumulative mass of any measure consistent with a given sequence of moments \mathbf{m}. It solves the truncated Hamburger moment problem by constructing a unique "canonical" discrete measure that tightly bounds the set of all valid measures. Unlike standard visibility functions based on Chebyshev's inequality, which use only the first two moments (n=1), this method generalizes to arbitrary moment sequences (2n+1 moments) to provide tighter bounds. Inputs: Moment sequence \mathbf{m} = (m0, m1, \dots, m{2n}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2n+1}, where n > 0. Evaluation point \eta \in \mathbb{R}. Outputs: Lower bound L(\eta): The mass in the interval (-\infty, \eta). Upper bound U(\eta): The mass in the interval (-\infty, \eta]. Data Structures: Hankel Matrix H: A (n+1) \times (n+1) symmetric matrix where H{ij} = m{i+j} for 0 \le i, j \le n. Kernel Polynomial Vector \eta{\text{vec}}: A column vector of size n+1 representing the evaluation point \eta in the monomial basis: \eta{\text{vec}} = (1, \eta, \eta^2, \dots, \eta^n)^\top. Support Points \{xi\}{i=1}^n: The n distinct real roots of the kernel polynomial. Weights \{wi\}{i=0}^n: The weights of the canonical discrete measure, where x0 = \eta and w0 is the weight at \eta. Steps: 1. Construct the Hankel Matrix: Build H from the input moments: H{ij} = m{i+j} \quad \text{for } 0 \le i, j \le n 2. Compute the Kernel Polynomial Coefficients: Calculate the coefficient vector \mathbf{c} of the kernel polynomial K(x) by inverting H and multiplying by \eta{\text{vec}}: \mathbf{c} = H^{-1} \eta{\text{vec}} The kernel polynomial is defined as: K(x) = \sum{k=0}^{n} ck x^k = x^\top H^{-1} \eta{\text{vec}} where x = (1, x, \dots, x^n)^\top. 3. Find Support Points: Find the n distinct real roots \{xi\}{i=1}^n of the polynomial K(x) = 0. These roots are the support points of the canonical representation. If \mathbf{m} is strictly positive and \eta is not a root of K(x), the roots are guaranteed to be real and simple. 4. Compute Weights: The canonical measure \mu\eta is a discrete measure with support \{x0, x1, \dots, xn\} where x0 = \eta. The weights wi satisfy the moment equations: mk = \sum{i=0}^{n} wi xi^k, \quad k = 0, \dots, 2n The weights for the roots can be computed individually using the inverse Hankel matrix: wi = \frac{1}{xi^\top H^{-1} xi} \quad \text{for } i=1,\dots,n The weight w0 at \eta is determined by satisfying the total mass constraint m0 = w0 + \sum{i=1}^n wi. 5. Compute Bounds: Sort the support points \{xi\}{i=1}^n such that x1 < x2 < \dots < xn. The lower bound L(\eta) is the sum of weights of all support points strictly less than \eta: L(\eta) = \sum{i: xi < \eta} wi The upper bound U(\eta) is the sum of weights of all support points less than or equal to \eta: U(\eta) = \sum{i: xi \le \eta} wi If \eta coincides with a support point xj, then L(\eta) = \sum{i=1}^{j-1} wi and U(\eta) = \sum{i=1}^{j} wi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def momentbounds(m, eta, n): """ Compute differentiable upper and lower bounds for a measure consistent with moments m at evaluation point eta. Args: m: list of 2n+1 moments [m0,..., m2n] eta: float, evaluation point n: int, order parameter (moments are 0 to 2n) Returns: L: float, lower bound (mass in (-inf, eta)) U: float, upper bound (mass in (-inf, eta]) """ # Step 1: Construct Hankel Matrix H (n+1 x n+1) H = [[m[i+j] for j in range(n+1)] for i in range(n+1)] # Step 2: Compute Kernel Polynomial Coefficients c = H^-1 etavec etavec = [etak for k in range(n+1)] c = solvelinearsystem(H, etavec) # Step 3: Find roots of K(x) = sum(ck x^k) # Find roots of polynomial c using a standard companion matrix eigenvalue solver roots = findpolynomialroots(c) realroots = sorted([r.real for r in roots if abs(r.imag) < 1e-9]) # Step 4: Compute Weights Hinv = invertmatrix(H) weights = [] for x in realroots: xvec = [xk for k in range(n+1)] denom = dotproduct(xvec, multiplymatrixvector(Hinv, xvec)) weights.append(1.0 / denom) # Compute w0 at eta using mass constraint m0 = w0 + sum(wi) w0 = m[0] - sum(weights) # Step 5: Compute Bounds allpoints = [eta] + realroots allweights = [w0] + weights pointsweights = sorted(zip(allpoints, allweights)) L = 0.0 U = 0.0 for p, w in pointsweights: if p < eta: L += w U += w elif p == eta: U += w return L, U def solvelinearsystem(A, b): # Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting n = len(b) M = [A[i][:] + [b[i]] for i in range(n)] for i in range(n): pivot = max(range(i, n), key=lambda k: abs(M[k][i])) M[i], M[pivot] = M[pivot], M[i] for j in range(i+1, n): factor = M[j][i] / M[i][i] for k in range(i, n+1): M[j][k] -= factor M[i][k] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): x[i] = (M[i][n] - sum(M[i][j]x[j] for j in range(i+1, n))) / M[i][i] return x def findpolynomialroots(c): # Standard companion matrix eigenvalue method import numpy as np return np.roots(c[::-1]) def invertmatrix(M): n = len(M) I = [[1.0 if i==j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] aug = [M[i][:] + I[i][:] for i in range(n)] for i in range(n): pivot = max(range(i, n), key=lambda k: abs(aug[k][i])) aug[i], aug[pivot] = aug[pivot], aug[i] div = aug[i][i] for j in range(2n): aug[i][j] /= div for k in range(n): if k != i: factor = aug[k][i] for j in range(2n): aug[k][j] -= factor aug[i][j] return [row[n:] for row in aug] def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def multiplymatrixvector(M, v): return [sum(row[k]v[k] for k in range(len(v))) for row in M] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Strict Positivity: The method requires the moment sequence to be strictly positive. If not, the roots may not be real or simple, and the bounds may not be valid. Boundary Conditions: The bounds are continuously differentiable within regions where the set of support points less than \eta remains constant. Transitions occur when \eta crosses a support point xi. Precision: Inverting the Hankel matrix can be numerically unstable if the moments are ill-conditioned. High-precision arithmetic may be required for large n. Time Complexity: Computing the bounds requires inverting the Hankel matrix (O(n^3)) and finding roots of a degree-n polynomial (O(n) or O(n^2) depending on the root-finding method), then summing O(n) weights. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides tighter bounds than Chebyshev's inequality by using more moments. The bounds are differentiable with respect to the moment parameters, enabling use in differentiable rendering pipelines. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than 2-moment bounds. Requires the moment sequence to be strictly positive. Performance degrades with large n due to matrix inversion and root finding. When to Use: When tighter bounds are needed than Chebyshev's inequality allows, and differentiability is required. Suitable for shadow mapping and order-independent transparency where moment sequences are available. The method is based on the theory of moments, specifically the truncated Hamburger moment problem. The bounds are known as Chebyshev-Markov inequalities, originating from the work of Kreĭn and Nudel’man [1977] and Tari et al. [2005]. In computer graphics, these bounds have been used in efficient methods for shadow mapping [Peters and Klein 2015; Peters et al. 2016] and order-independent transparency [Münstermann et al. 2018]. The differentiability of these bounds was highlighted in recent work on differentiable volume rendering.
