name: Caching for SCL Training
head: Caching for Efficient Training, Codec Cache, Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL) caching
body: This method reduces the computational cost of invoking a standard codec round trip on every mini-batch during Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL) training, particularly for dynamic scenes where video codecs operate on sequences of frames. It maintains a per-frame cache of decoded feature planes and density volumes, refreshing them only when necessary based on time or parameter drift. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current global training step g, cached last refresh step g{cache}, current unquantized TriPlane features P^{ax}t for each axis ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}, current unquantized density grid Dt, and a frame index t with associated rays \{(o, d)\} and camera pose \pi. Outputs: Updated cached decoded planes \widehat{P}^{ax}t, cached decoded density \widehat{D}t, and the rendered image I. Data Structures: Cache: Stores the decoded TriPlane \widehat{P}^{ax}t and a snapshot of the raw plane P^{ax}t at the time of refresh for each axis ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}. Cache: Stores the decoded density grid \widehat{D}t and a snapshot of the raw density Dt at the time of refresh. Scalar: g{cache}, the global step at which the last cache refresh occurred. Parameters: M: The maximum interval between step-based refreshes. Typical value: M=128. \epsilon: Threshold for relative change (drift) to trigger change-based refresh. Measured by normalized \ell2 difference. Value not given in the sources. Algorithm: 1. Sample a frame index t, rays \{(o, d)\}, and camera pose \pi. 2. Determine if a refresh is required: Step-based refresh: If the cache is empty or g - g{cache} \ge M, mark refresh as true. Change-based refresh: Calculate the relative change between the current (P^{ax}t, Dt) and their cached snapshots. If this relative change exceeds \epsilon (measured by normalized \ell2 difference), mark refresh as true, even if g - g{cache} < M. 3. If refresh is true: Run the encode–decode codec round trip for the video segment to update the cache. Update g{cache} \leftarrow g. 4. Perform Straight-Through Estimator (STE) substitution using cached reconstructions: For each axis ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}: \widehat{P}^{ax}t \leftarrow \text{cached decoded plane} \widetilde{P}^{ax}t \leftarrow \widehat{P}^{ax}t + (P^{ax}t - \texttt{detach}(P^{ax}t)) For density: \widehat{D}t \leftarrow \text{cached decoded density} \widetilde{D}t \leftarrow \widehat{D}t + (Dt - \texttt{detach}(Dt)) Here, \widehat{P} and \widehat{D} are the quantized/cached values, \widetilde{P} and \widetilde{D} are the values used for rendering/loss, and P and D are the current unquantized values. 5. Render and compute losses: I \leftarrow \mathcal{R}(\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}t, \widetilde{D}t, \pi; \phi) where \mathcal{R} is the rendering function and \phi represents the network parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenormalizedl2drift(current, cached): diff = current - cached normdiff = sqrt(sum(diff2)) normcurrent = sqrt(sum(current2)) if normcurrent == 0: return 0.0 return normdiff / normcurrent def codecroundtrip(planes, density): # Source does not specify codec implementation details return planes, density def volumetricrender(planes, density, rays, pose): # Standard volumetric rendering step return renderoutput def scltrainingstepwithcaching( globalstep, frameindex, rays, camerapose, currentplanes, currentdensity, cacheddecodedplanes, cachedrawplanes, cacheddecodeddensity, cachedrawdensity, lastrefreshstep, refreshinterval, driftthreshold): refreshneeded = False # Step-based refresh if lastrefreshstep == -1 or (globalstep - lastrefreshstep) >= refreshinterval: refreshneeded = True # Change-based refresh if not refreshneeded: totaldrift = 0.0 for ax in ['xy', 'xz', 'yz']: totaldrift += computenormalizedl2drift(currentplanes[ax], cachedrawplanes[ax]) totaldrift += computenormalizedl2drift(currentdensity, cachedrawdensity) if totaldrift > driftthreshold: refreshneeded = True if refreshneeded: newdecodedplanes, newdecodeddensity = codecroundtrip(currentplanes, currentdensity) cacheddecodedplanes = newdecodedplanes cacheddecodeddensity = newdecodeddensity cachedrawplanes = {ax: currentplanes[ax] for ax in currentplanes} cachedrawdensity = currentdensity lastrefreshstep = globalstep renderedplanes = {} for ax in ['xy', 'xz', 'yz']: renderedplanes[ax] = cacheddecodedplanes[ax] + (currentplanes[ax] - detach(currentplanes[ax])) rendereddensity = cacheddecodeddensity + (currentdensity - detach(currentdensity)) renderedimage = volumetricrender(renderedplanes, rendereddensity, rays, camerapose) return renderedimage, lastrefreshstep, cacheddecodedplanes, cachedrawplanes, cacheddecodeddensity, cachedrawdensity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The STE substitution relies on the difference between the current unquantized value and its detached version. Boundaries: The change-based refresh depends on the normalized \ell2 difference. If the current planes or density are near zero, the normalization factor becomes small, potentially leading to numerical instability or false triggers. Degenerate Input: If the cache is empty, a refresh is always triggered. Time Complexity: The cost of the codec round trip is amortized over M training steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional cached decoded planes and density grids, as well as snapshots of the raw planes and density at the time of refresh. Measured Performance: Tab. 4 in shows that increasing M yields a favorable trade-off between accuracy and training efficiency. M=128 captures most of the benefit of SCL training. Strengths: Reduces training time significantly for dynamic scenes by avoiding frequent codec invocations. The change-based refresh ensures responsiveness to rapid parameter changes early in training. Limitations: The cache may lag behind rapid parameter changes if the drift threshold \epsilon is not set appropriately. When to use: When training SCL models on dynamic scenes where codec round trips are computationally expensive. This caching mechanism was introduced in the CATRF (Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields) paper. It addresses the computational bottleneck of invoking standard codecs in the training loop, which is particularly problematic for dynamic scenes. name: Hybrid STE+SPSA Gradient Estimation
head: STE+SPSA
body: Hybrid STE+SPSA is a gradient estimation strategy for differentiable volume rendering that combines vanilla Straight-Through Estimator (STE) with Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA) to handle non-differentiable codecs within a training loop. It uses vanilla STE during cached steps and applies SPSA only when the codec cache is refreshed. This hybrid approach avoids the prohibitive cost of applying SPSA at every step, though it yields the worst reconstruction quality and highest training time among tested methods due to high variance and poor signal-to-noise ratio from codec non-linearity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current parameter vector \mathbf{P} (e.g., feature planes), codec cache state, perturbation scale \epsilon, and objective function \mathcal{C}q (e.g., reconstruction loss). Output: Gradient estimate \hat{g}(\mathbf{P}) for the optimizer. Data Structures: Codec Cache: Stores the output of the non-differentiable codec for the current parameters to avoid redundant encoding/decoding. Perturbation Vector \Delta: A vector of the same dimension as \mathbf{P}, where each element \Deltai is sampled independently from a symmetric Bernoulli distribution (\Deltai = \pm 1 with probability 0.5). Steps: 1. Check Cache Status: Determine if the codec cache is active (valid for current \mathbf{P}) or needs refresh. 2. If Cache is Active: Use vanilla STE. The gradient is computed by backpropagating through the decoder as if the codec were the identity function, copying the gradient directly to the pre-codec feature plane. 3. If Cache is Refreshed: Sample a random perturbation vector \Delta where \Deltai = \pm 1 with probability 0.5. Compute the perturbed parameters \mathbf{P}^+ = \mathbf{P} + \epsilon \Delta and \mathbf{P}^- = \mathbf{P} - \epsilon \Delta. Evaluate the objective function \mathcal{C}q for both perturbed states, which requires running two additional full codec round trips per iteration. Compute the SPSA gradient estimate for each component i using the formula. Use this estimate for the optimizer step. Parameters: \epsilon (Perturbation Scale): A small scalar value. Not given in the sources. \Deltai: Random variable, \pm 1 with p=0.5. Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Applying SPSA at every step is prohibitively expensive because it requires multiple additional codec round trips per iteration. Gradient Quality: SPSA yields the worst reconstruction quality and highest training time among tested methods due to the high variance of zeroth-order estimates and poor signal-to-noise ratio from severe codec non-linearity. Alignment: Although SPSA is less biased in principle, its gradient estimates can be substantially noisier for complex black-box codec round-trips, making them less aligned with the descent direction needed for radiance-field optimization compared to vanilla STE. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def computegradienthybridstespsa(P, cache, epsilon, objectivefn): """ Compute gradient using Hybrid STE+SPSA. Args: P: Current parameter vector (e.g., feature planes). cache: Codec cache object with isvalid(P) method. epsilon: Perturbation scale. objectivefn: Function computing loss Cq, handling codec encoding/decoding. Returns: gradient: Estimated gradient vector. """ # Check if cache is valid for current P if cache.isvalid(P): # Step 1: Use vanilla STE for cached steps # Vanilla STE: Backpropagate through decoder assuming identity codec # Gradient is copied directly to pre-codec features loss = objectivefn(P, usecache=True) loss.backward() return P.grad else: # Step 2: Cache needs refresh, use SPSA # Sample random perturbation vector Delta # Deltai = +/- 1 with probability 0.5 Delta = [1.0 if random.random() < 0.5 else -1.0 for in P] # Compute perturbed parameters Pplus = [p + epsilon d for p, d in zip(P, Delta)] Pminus = [p - epsilon d for p, d in zip(P, Delta)] # Evaluate objective function for both perturbed states # This triggers codec encoding/decoding, updating the cache Cplus = objectivefn(Pplus, usecache=False) Cminus = objectivefn(Pminus, usecache=False) # Compute SPSA gradient estimate # gi = (C(P + eDelta) - C(P - eDelta)) / (2 e Deltai) gradient = [(Cplus - Cminus) / (2 epsilon d) for d in Delta] return gradient Time Complexity: Significantly higher than vanilla STE. When the cache is refreshed, SPSA requires two additional full codec round trips per iteration. Applying SPSA at every step is described as "prohibitively expensive". Memory Complexity: Requires storing the codec cache and the perturbation vector \Delta. No additional major memory overhead compared to standard SCL with caching. Measured Performance: High-Rate: PSNR 29.63, SSIM 0.930, LPIPS 0.459, Training Time 3h 18m. Low-Rate: PSNR 27.94, SSIM 0.909, LPIPS 0.650, Training Time 3h 18m. Training time is reported as identical for high and low rates in the source. Limitations: Worst reconstruction quality and highest training time among compared methods (vanilla STE, mSTE, STE+SPSA) due to high variance and poor signal-to-noise ratio from codec non-linearity. When to Use: Only when cache refreshes are infrequent enough that the computational cost of SPSA is manageable, and when reducing bias during updates is critical. However, the source notes that vanilla STE is more robust and provides better overall quality, especially in low-bitrate regimes. When Not to Use: When computational efficiency is a priority, or when codec non-linearity introduces too much noise for zeroth-order estimates to be effective. Vanilla STE is preferred as the default due to robustness. The Hybrid STE+SPSA method was introduced in the context of Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields (CATRF) for volumetric content delivery. It was proposed as a way to improve upon vanilla STE by incorporating insights from black-box gradient approximation methods, specifically SPSA. The method was evaluated in ablation studies alongside vanilla STE and modified STE (mSTE). The authors found that while SPSA is less biased in principle, its practical performance was inferior due to the specific challenges of differentiating through non-linear codecs. CATRF: Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields for Volumetric Content Delivery, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprf71909.2026.00048, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Modified Straight-Through Estimator (mSTE)
head: mSTE
body: Modified Straight-Through Estimator (mSTE) is a gradient extension technique for differentiable volume rendering that addresses the zero-gradient problem in the backward pass by rescaling the detached codec-induced perturbation using its standard deviation. Unlike the parent method, Straight-Through Estimator (STE) for Gradient Extension, which uses a simple identity surrogate to copy gradients directly to the pre-codec feature plane, mSTE modulates the backward signal based on the observed scale of quantization errors. This approach aims to provide a more informative gradient signal than vanilla STE in high-bitrate regimes, though it is less robust than vanilla STE under strong codec distortion. Inputs and Outputs Input: Pre-codec feature plane \mathbf{P} and decoded feature plane \hat{\mathbf{P}} (output of the differentiable codec). Output: Modified feature plane \widetilde{\mathbf{P}} used for gradient computation in the backward pass. Data Structures \mathbf{P}: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) representing the pre-quantization features. \hat{\mathbf{P}}: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) representing the post-quantization features. \epsilon: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) representing the codec-induced perturbation. \sigma(\epsilon): Scalar representing the standard deviation of the perturbation tensor. Steps 1. Compute the codec-induced perturbation \epsilon as the difference between the decoded feature plane and the pre-codec feature plane: \epsilon = \hat{\mathbf{P}} - \mathbf{P} 2. Compute the standard deviation \sigma(\epsilon) of the perturbation tensor \epsilon. 3. In the backward pass, compute the modified feature plane \widetilde{\mathbf{P}} using the following formula: \widetilde{\mathbf{P}} = \mathbf{P} + \operatorname{sg}(\epsilon) \cdot \frac{\sigma(\epsilon)}{\operatorname{sg}(\sigma(\epsilon))} where \operatorname{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator, which prevents gradients from flowing through its argument. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sg(x): """Stop-gradient operator: returns x but blocks gradient flow in autograd frameworks.""" return x def mSTEforward(P, codecfunction): """Forward pass: quantize P using codecfunction.""" Phat = codecfunction(P) return Phat def mSTEbackward(P, Phat): """Backward pass: compute modified gradient signal.""" # Step 1: Compute perturbation epsilon = Phat - P # Step 2: Compute standard deviation of perturbation over all elements sigmaepsilon = np.std(epsilon) # Step 3: Compute modified feature plane # Apply stop-gradient to epsilon and sigmaepsilon sgepsilon = sg(epsilon) sgsigma = sg(sigmaepsilon) # Guard against division by zero when quantization error is zero sgsigma = np.maximum(sgsigma, 1e-8) # Rescale the detached error rescalederror = sgepsilon (sigmaepsilon / sgsigma) # Add to original P Pmodified = P + rescalederror return Pmodified Parameters Standard deviation calculation: Computed over the perturbation tensor. Epsilon for numerical stability: 10^{-8}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: If \sigma(\epsilon) is zero (e.g., no quantization error), the ratio becomes undefined. A small epsilon value should be added to the denominator. Low Bitrate Degradation: At low bitrates, the perturbation \epsilon reflects non-linear artifacts rather than small local quantization residuals. In this regime, standard-deviation reweighting becomes a poor proxy for true local sensitivity, leading to less stable and less effective optimization compared to vanilla STE. A method that integrates codec constraints directly into the training loop. It sets itself apart by enforcing codec fidelity during optimization rather than treating the codec as a fixed black-box perturbation. Choose it when minimizing codec artifacts during training is a primary objective. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: High-rate: PSNR 33.62, SSIM 0.968, LPIPS 0.195, training time 1h 25m. Low-rate: PSNR 30.96, SSIM 0.948, LPIPS 0.368, training time 1h 28m. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Performs competitively at high bitrate. Limitations: Degrades noticeably at low bitrate. Less robust than vanilla STE under strong codec distortion. When to Use: High-bitrate regimes where codec-induced distortions are small and local quantization residuals are a good proxy for sensitivity. When Not to Use: Low-bitrate regimes or when strong codec distortion is present, as vanilla STE is more robust. Modified Straight-Through Estimator (mSTE) was introduced in the context of Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields for Volumetric Content Delivery. It is a variant of the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) designed to improve gradient estimation by incorporating information about the scale of quantization errors. The method was proposed to address the limitations of vanilla STE, which uses a simple identity surrogate in the backward pass. While vanilla STE is robust, mSTE aims to provide a more informative gradient signal in high-bitrate regimes by rescaling the detached codec error using the standard deviation of the quantization error. name: Scene Parameter Saliency via Differentiable Light Transport
head: Gradient-based Saliency, Metric Saliency Maps, gradient-based saliency for differentiable rendering, per-parameter gradients of a scalar objective
body: Metric saliency maps identify which scene parameters most influence a specific scalar image-space metric by computing per-parameter gradients through a differentiable renderer. Unlike neural saliency methods that propagate attribution through learned weights, this method propagates gradients through the physical light transport simulation, capturing multi-bounce dependencies and parameter interactions that are opaque to manual inspection. It serves as an interpretability tool for inverse rendering and scene understanding, providing a local sensitivity characterization at the cost of a single reverse-mode differentiation pass, avoiding the expensive re-renders required by finite-difference sensitivity analysis. The method consists of three stages: (1) render an image through a differentiable pipeline, (2) evaluate a scalar metric on that image, and (3) backpropagate through both the metric and the renderer to obtain per-parameter gradients, which are then mapped back to image space for visualization. Inputs: Scene parameters \theta: A vector including surface reflectances, roughness values, indices of refraction, emitter intensities, and geometric quantities. Scalar metric M: A function evaluating a property of the light transport simulation, defined as M: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}, where I = R(\theta) \in \mathbb{R}^D is the rendered image (generalized sensor response). Differentiable renderer R: A function computing the image I from \theta, such as a physically-based Monte Carlo path tracer with multi-bounce global illumination. Outputs: Parameter-space gradient g: A vector where each component gi = \partial M / \partial \thetai measures the sensitivity of the metric to the corresponding parameter. Saliency map: An image-space visualization where pixels are colored by the saliency of the material visible at that location. Scene Parameters (\theta): Stored as a structured object containing differentiable attributes for each material and light source. This work focuses on uniform material parameters; spatially-varying saliency fields are left to future work. Rendered Image (I): A tensor of shape H \times W \times C (height, width, channels) representing the generalized sensor response. Material Identity Map: A per-pixel map generated by tracing primary rays from the camera, identifying the hit scene object and its associated material parameters. 1. Render an image I through a differentiable pipeline using I = R(\theta). 2. Evaluate a scalar metric M on the rendered image. 3. Backpropagate through both the metric and the renderer to obtain per-parameter gradients g = \partial M / \partial \theta. 4. Map the obtained per-parameter gradients back to image space for visualization by tracing primary rays from the camera, identifying hit scene objects, and coloring each pixel with the saliency value of the visible material. The parameter-space gradient g is computed via the chain rule: g = \frac{\partial M(R(\theta))}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial M}{\partial I} \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} The product is obtained automatically by backpropagation through the metric and the light transport simulation jointly. The saliency of a parameter \thetai is defined as the magnitude of its gradient component: \text{Saliency}(\thetai) = |gi|, \quad \text{where } gi = \frac{\partial M}{\partial \thetai} For vector-valued parameters (e.g., RGB reflectance), the saliency is the \ell2 norm of the gradient components: \text{Saliency}(\mathbf{v}) = \left\| \frac{\partial M}{\partial \mathbf{v}} \right\|2 Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computemetricsaliency(sceneparams, metricfn, renderer, camera, materialtoparammap): # Stage 1: Render image through differentiable pipeline image = renderer(sceneparams) # Stage 2: Evaluate scalar metric on the image metricvalue = metricfn(image) # Stage 3: Backpropagate through metric and renderer # Compute dM/dI (metric sensitivity to image) dMdI = metricfn.gradient(image) # Compute dI/dtheta (image sensitivity to parameters) via reverse-mode AD # The chain rule g = (∂M/∂I) (∂I/∂θ) is applied automatically by the AD engine # Implementation detail: reverse-mode AD traverses the computational graph backward gradients = renderer.backwardpass(dMdI) # Compute saliency magnitudes saliencyvalues = [] for grad in gradients: if grad.isvector: # L2 norm of gradient components saliency = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in grad.flatten())) else: saliency = abs(grad) saliencyvalues.append(saliency) # Normalize saliency values to [0, 1] for visualization maxval = max(saliencyvalues) if saliencyvalues else 1.0 normalizedsaliency = [s / maxval for s in saliencyvalues] # Stage 4: Map gradients to image space # Trace primary rays from camera to identify hit scene objects materialidentitymap = [] for y in range(camera.height): row = [] for x in range(camera.width): ray = camera.generateray(x, y) hit = renderer.scene.intersect(ray) row.append(hit.objectid if hit else -1) materialidentitymap.append(row) # Color each pixel with the saliency of the visible material saliencymap = [[0.0] camera.width for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): objid = materialidentitymap[y][x] if objid != -1 and objid in materialtoparammap: paramidx = materialtoparammap[objid] saliencymap[y][x] = normalizedsaliency[paramidx] return saliencymap, gradients Renderer: Must be differentiable. The implementation uses Mitsuba 3 with Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) to handle multi-bounce global illumination gradients. Metric M: Can be qualitatively different objectives, including psychovisual glare indices (e.g., Unified Glare Rating), mean scene luminance, and neural perceptual scores (e.g., ResNet-50 logits). Maximum path depth: 6 bounces. Samples per pixel (SPP): 1024 for main results. Learning rate for validation: 0.01 (used for ablation validation to verify gradient accuracy). Metric Specificity: The saliency map is specific to the metric and not an intrinsic property of the scene. Parameters that dominate one objective may be negligible for another. Monte Carlo Variance: Gradient estimators inherit variance from the path tracer. At low sample counts, saliency values are noisy. Stable rankings require moderate sample counts (64–256 spp); fine-grained spatially-varying fields require higher budgets or variance reduction. Non-differentiable Metrics: Metrics with hard thresholds or discrete decisions (e.g., binary glare detection) are not differentiable. They must be relaxed into smooth approximations (e.g., sigmoid relaxations for visibility checks), which affects the resulting saliency map. First-Order Limitation: Gradient magnitude only measures local, first-order sensitivity. It does not capture parameter interactions (second-order effects) or physical constraints (e.g., roughness clamping at 1.0). Time Complexity: The method requires a single forward pass for rendering and a single reverse-mode differentiation pass (backpropagation) for gradient computation. This is significantly faster than finite-difference sensitivity analysis, which requires dozens of independent simulation evaluations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage depends on the differentiable renderer's implementation. Storing intermediate states for reverse-mode AD can be high, though PRB-based renderers like Mitsuba 3 manage memory efficiently for multi-bounce paths. Measured Performance: In experiments with 1024 SPP and 6 bounces, the method successfully isolated and ranked true physical drivers of discomfort glare and mean luminance, validating against finite-difference steps with a learning rate of 0.01. Strengths: Provides a local sensitivity characterization at the cost of a single backward pass; captures multi-bounce light transport dependencies; works with any differentiable renderer and metric. Limitations: Noisy at low sample counts; requires differentiable metrics; does not capture second-order effects or physical constraints; saliency is metric-specific. When to use: When interpreting which scene parameters drive a specific image-space metric, especially for multi-bounce global illumination scenarios where manual inspection is difficult. When not to use: When second-order interactions are critical, when metrics are inherently non-differentiable and cannot be relaxed, or when computational resources are too limited for stable Monte Carlo gradient estimation. The method was introduced by Linas Beresna and Eugene Fiume in "Scene Parameter Saliency via Differentiable Light Transport". It builds on Differentiable volume rendering, extending the concept of gradient-based attribution from neural networks to physical light transport simulations. The approach addresses the need for interpretability in inverse rendering and scene understanding, offering an alternative to traditional sensitivity analysis methods like parametric sweeps or finite-difference probing. It is implemented using Mitsuba 3 and DrJit, leveraging Path Replay Backpropagation for efficient gradient computation. Scene Parameter Saliency via Differentiable Light Transport, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2607.21562, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Differentiable Regularization Framework for Participating Media
head: Differentiable Regularization for Participating Media, Differentiable Regularization-based Approach, Radiance Prediction via Gradient, Radiance prediction via albedo gradient
body: This method reduces variance in high-order scattering dominant participating media by rendering a low-albedo version of the scene, computing the gradient of radiance with respect to albedo, and predicting the high-albedo result using a novel prediction function. It is designed for scenarios with low time budgets where standard path tracing is too noisy. Unlike path space regularization methods which cannot correct regularization error, this method extrapolates from the regularized result to predict the original configuration using gradient information. It builds on Differentiable volume rendering by utilizing differentiable path tracing to compute gradients with respect to material parameters. The method operates in three main steps: differentiable volumetric path tracing on a modified low-albedo configuration, temporal denoising of the computed gradient, and prediction of the final high-albedo radiance. Inputs: Target albedo \alphat and extinction coefficient \sigmat for the participating media. Phase function p(\omega, \omega') (typically Henyey–Greenstein). Camera parameters and scene geometry. Source albedo \alphas, chosen as 0.9 - 0.95 \times \alphat. A sequence of frames for temporal denoising. Outputs: Predicted radiance image \hat{L}{target} for the target albedo \alphat. The method relies on standard volumetric path tracing data structures but extends them to store gradients. Radiance Image: A 2D array of color values L(x, \omega). Gradient Image: A 2D array of values \frac{\partial L}{\partial \alpha} representing the derivative of radiance with respect to the albedo parameter. Path Contribution: For a path \tilde{p} with K scattering events, the contribution is defined as: f(\tilde{p}) = \prod{k=1}^K wk g(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) where wk is the weight of the path segment x{k-1} \leftrightarrow xk: wi = \begin{cases} \alpha \sigmat \text{Tr}(x{i-1} \leftrightarrow xi) & \text{if } xi \in \text{medium} \\ \text{Tr}(x{i-1} \leftrightarrow xi) & \text{if } xi \in \text{surface} \end{cases} and g(\omega{k-1}, \omegak) is the phase function evaluation. 1. Differentiable Volumetric Path Tracing: Render the scene using a modified media configuration with source albedo \alphas < \alphat. Compute the radiance Ls and the gradient \frac{\partial Ls}{\partial \alpha} with respect to the albedo. This is performed using automatic differentiation tools (e.g., Eigen library) integrated into the renderer (e.g., Mitsuba). The radiative transfer equation is modeled as: L(x, \omega) = \text{Tr}(x \leftrightarrow xs)L(xs, \omega) + \int0^s \text{Tr}(x \leftrightarrow xt)\sigmas(xt)Li(xt, \omega)dt where \text{Tr}(x \leftrightarrow xs) = \exp(-\sigmat \|x - xs\|). The in-scattering radiance is: Li(xt, \omega) = \int{\Omega{4\pi}} p(\omega, \omegat)L(xt, \omegat)d\omegat Monte Carlo estimation is used: L(x, \omega) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^M \frac{f(\tilde{p}i)}{\text{pdf}(\tilde{p}i)}. 2. Temporal Denoising: Apply temporal denoising to the gradient image \frac{\partial Ls}{\partial \alpha} using information from neighboring frames to produce a noise-free gradient estimate. The specific denoising algorithm is not detailed in the source, but it is noted that the cost is negligible compared to rendering. 3. Radiance Prediction: Predict the final radiance \hat{L}{target} for the target albedo \alphat using the rendered low-albedo radiance Ls and the denoised gradient \frac{\partial Ls}{\partial \alpha}. The prediction function is novel and designed to fit the behavior of media rendering, differing from linear or log-linear functions used in prior work. The exact formula for the prediction function is not provided in the source text, but it utilizes the gradient to extrapolate from \alphas to \alphat. Source Albedo (\alphas): The albedo used for the differentiable path tracing step. The optimal value is 0.9 - 0.95 \times \alphat. Using a source albedo far from the target albedo (e.g., with 0.5 or 0.7 as a factor) results in a large bias. Phase Function: Henyey–Greenstein is used in all test scenes. Extinction Coefficient (\sigmat): The method is robust across varying extinction coefficients, consistently producing less noise than path tracing in the tested range of \sigmat \in \{5, 10, 15, 20, 50\}. Bias-Variance Trade-off: The method introduces bias as a trade-off for variance reduction. The error increases compared to path tracing when the sample rate is high. Low-Albedo Failure: The method does not benefit low-albedo media. A failure case is shown for \alphat = 0.5. High Source Albedo: Increasing the source albedo decreases bias but increases variance. Time Complexity: The method is significantly faster than reference path tracing for equivalent quality. In tested scenes, it achieves lower MSE in less time than equal-time path tracing. The cost of prediction and denoising is negligible (e.g., 0.2s for a 512x512 image) compared to rendering time. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly stated, but relies on storing radiance and gradient images per frame for temporal denoising. Performance: Bunny (500x500): MSE 1.1 \times 10^{-4} in 0.49 min vs. PT MSE 2.3 \times 10^{-4} in 0.50 min. Reference MSE 1.1 \times 10^{-4} in 45.61 min. Candle (256x256): MSE 6.1 \times 10^{-5} in 1.21 min vs. PT MSE 1.3 \times 10^{-4} in 1.17 min. Reference MSE 6.1 \times 10^{-5} in 15.89 min. Lucy (512x512): MSE 1.5 \times 10^{-5} in 1.14 min vs. PT MSE 4.4 \times 10^{-5} in 1.16 min. Reference MSE 1.5 \times 10^{-5} in 60.00 min. Strengths: Reduces noise in high-order scattering dominant media; robust across varying extinction coefficients; suitable for low time budgets. Limitations: Introduces bias; ineffective for low-albedo media; less accurate than high-sample path tracing when time is not constrained. When to use: High-albedo participating media with strict time constraints. When not to use: Low-albedo media or when high sample counts are available. The method was proposed by authors publishing in 2023. It builds on the observation that lower-albedo media have less noise than higher-albedo media in Monte Carlo path tracing. It differs from previous differentiable regularization approaches by using a novel prediction function and temporal denoising of the gradient. It is implemented inside the Mitsuba renderer using automatic differentiation tools from the Eigen library. Efficient Participating Media Rendering with Differentiable Regularization, https://iccvm.org/2023/papers/s8-3-284-CVMJ.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Differentiable Transient Rendering with Implicit Geometry
head: Differentiable Transient Rendering, Path-space differentiable transient rendering
body: This method computes time-resolved illumination at sensor points by simulating third-bounce light transport between a laser source and a non-line-of-sight (NLOS) sensor using implicit surface geometry. It differs from standard differentiable volume rendering by operating in path space for transient measurements, discretizing continuous time-of-flight into bins via Gaussian smoothing, and bypassing explicit binary visibility checks by relying on volumetric intensities as a visibility estimator. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Implicit geometry representation G with parameters \ThetaG, laser parameters \Theta{ls}, sensor parameters, laser position xl, sensor position xs, and transient bin index \tau. Outputs: Sensed transient data matrix HR(xl, xs, \tau) representing time-resolved illumination at the sensor. Data Structures: Implicit Surface: Defined by parameters \ThetaG. Points xg and normals ng are estimated from volumetric intensities. Transient Bins: Discrete time indices \tau. Continuous time t is mapped to \tau via Gaussian weighting. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays originating from the sensor points xs. 2. Implicit Surface Estimation: Estimate implicit surface points xg and normals ng along the sampled rays. The geometry is derived from volumetric intensities, which depend on illumination reaching the surface without occluders. 3. Radiometric Contribution Calculation: Compute the radiometric contribution K(\bar{x}, t) for a path \bar{x} \equiv xl \to xg \to xs. This represents time-resolved transport in path space. The method avoids computing the binary visibility term V (typically required for path throughput \mathbb{T}) because the implicit surface estimation relies on volumetric intensities that inherently reflect unoccluded illumination. 4. Time Discretization: Discretize the continuous time t of the path contribution K(\bar{x}, t) into transient bins \tau using a differentiable Gaussian distribution: \hat{K}(\bar{x}, \tau) = |K(\bar{x}, t)| \exp \left( - \frac{(\tau - t)^2}{2\sigmat^2} \right) where \tau is the transient bin index, t is the continuous time, and \sigmat is the standard deviation for time bin discretization. 5. Path Summation: Approximate the time-resolved measurement Hr(xl, xs, \tau) by summing the discrete path contributions \hat{K}(\bar{x}, \tau) for all paths \bar{x} starting at xl and ending at xs, sampled via concentric disk mapping: Hr(xl, xs, \tau) \approx \sum{\bar{x} \in X} \hat{K}(\bar{x}, \tau) where X is the set of such paths. 6. Laser-Sensor Model Application: Apply the joint laser-sensor model to obtain the final sensed transient data HR by convolving with the system response \Psi(\tau) and adding an intensity offset \etas: HR(xl, xs, \tau) = \Psi(\tau) Hr(xl, xs, \tau) + \etas where \etas accounts for ambient light and sensor dark count rate. Parameters: \sigmat: Standard deviation for Gaussian discretization. Set to 0.62 to ensure the Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) covers a unit time bin. \etas: Intensity offset parameter for ambient light and dark count rate. Pitfalls: Differentiating the binary visibility function V is challenging. The method mitigates this by assuming volumetric intensities are a good estimator of geometry visible from both laser and sensor positions, thus avoiding explicit visibility computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def differentiabletransientrendering(implicitgeometry, laserpos, sensorpos, sigmat=0.62, etas=0.0, systemresponse=None, numbins=100, c=1.0): """ Computes time-resolved illumination HR using implicit geometry. Args: implicitgeometry: Object providing ray sampling, surface estimation, and radiometric contribution calculation. laserpos: 3D vector, position of the laser source xl. sensorpos: 3D vector, position of the sensor xs. sigmat: Float, standard deviation for time bin discretization (default 0.62). etas: Float, intensity offset for ambient light/dark count (default 0.0). systemresponse: List or array, Psi(tau) convolution kernel. numbins: Integer, number of transient bins. c: Float, speed of light constant (default 1.0 for normalized units). Returns: HR: List of sensed transient data indexed by tau. """ # 1. Sample rays from sensor positions (standard ray generation) rays = implicitgeometry.sampleraysfromsensor(sensorpos) # 2. Estimate implicit surface points and normals surfacepoints = [] surfacenormals = [] for ray in rays: xg, ng = implicitgeometry.estimatesurfaceandnormal(ray) surfacepoints.append(xg) surfacenormals.append(ng) # 3. Compute radiometric contribution K(xbar, t) for each path pathcontributions = [] pathtimes = [] for xg, ng in zip(surfacepoints, surfacenormals): # Path xbar = xl -> xg -> xs distlasertosurf = math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(laserpos, xg))) distsurftosensor = math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(xg, sensorpos))) totaldist = distlasertosurf + distsurftosensor # Continuous time t t = totaldist / c # Radiometric contribution K (Equations 5-9 in source) # Binary visibility V is avoided; volumetric intensity acts as visibility estimator kval = implicitgeometry.computeradiometriccontribution(laserpos, xg, sensorpos, ng) pathcontributions.append(kval) pathtimes.append(t) # 4. Discretize into transient bins using Gaussian distribution Hr = [0.0] numbins for kval, t in zip(pathcontributions, pathtimes): for tau in range(numbins): # Gaussian weighting: exp(-(tau - t)^2 / (2 sigmat^2)) weight = math.exp(-((tau - t) 2) / (2 sigmat 2)) Hr[tau] += abs(kval) weight # 5. Apply laser-sensor model # HR = Psi Hr + etas if systemresponse is not None: HR = discreteconvolution(Hr, systemresponse) for i in range(len(HR)): HR[i] += etas else: HR = list(Hr) return HR def discreteconvolution(signal, kernel): """Standard 1D discrete convolution.""" outlen = len(signal) + len(kernel) - 1 out = [0.0] outlen for i, s in enumerate(signal): for j, k in enumerate(kernel): out[i + j] += s k return out Time Complexity: Linear in the number of sampled paths and transient bins. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate path contributions and transient bins. Strengths: Enables gradient-based optimization of NLOS scene parameters (geometry, albedo, system parameters) by providing differentiable transient measurements. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that volumetric intensities approximate visibility, which may fail in highly occluded scenes. Discretization error depends on \sigmat. When to use: For inverse rendering problems involving NLOS transient measurements where implicit geometry representation is preferred or necessary. Originated in the context of Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) inverse rendering, specifically for self-calibrating and fully differentiable NLOS reconstruction. The method addresses the challenge of differentiating through transient rendering pipelines by using implicit surfaces and Gaussian time discretization. name: AutoInt
head: Automatic Integration, Learning the volume integral directly
body: AutoInt is a framework for learning efficient, closed-form solutions to integrals using coordinate-based neural networks, specifically applied to accelerate neural volume rendering. It solves the problem of extreme computational and memory requirements in neural volume rendering caused by Monte Carlo sampling, which requires hundreds of forward passes per ray to approximate integrals. Unlike standard differentiable volume rendering which relies on numerical quadrature or reverse-mode automatic differentiation through the rendering integral, AutoInt learns an antiderivative network that allows definite integrals to be computed via two network evaluations using the Newton-Leibniz formula. This reduces the number of network queries from hundreds to just two, improving render times by greater than 10× compared to NeRF, at the cost of slightly reduced image quality. AutoInt approximates the volume rendering equation (VRE) by separating it into piecewise sections, allowing the rendering step to use far fewer samples. The core mechanism involves training a "grad network" (representing the derivative of the output with respect to input coordinates) and automatically deriving an "integral network" (the antiderivative) from it. Inputs: Training images \mathbf{C} with known camera poses (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}); ground truth pixel values. Outputs: An optimized integral network \Phi{\theta^} capable of evaluating definite integrals of the signal f(\mathbf{x}) (e.g., radiance weighted by transmittance) along rays. The method relies on two coordinate-based neural networks with shared parameters \theta: 1. Integral Network (\Phi\theta): A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) representing the antiderivative. Architecture: \Phi\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}n(\phi{n-1} \circ \dots \circ \phi0)(\mathbf{x}). Layer definition: \phik(\mathbf{y}) = \text{NL}k(\mathbf{W}k \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{b}k). Parameters: \theta = \{\mathbf{W}k \in \mathbb{R}^{Nk \times Mk}, \mathbf{b}k \in \mathbb{R}^{Mk}, \forall k\}. Nonlinearity: Swish is recommended for best generalization. 2. Grad Network (\Psi\theta^i): Represents the partial derivative \partial\Phi\theta/\partial xi. Structure: Derived from the Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of \Phi\theta. Computation: \Psi\theta^i(\mathbf{x}) = \hat{\phi}{n-1} \circ (\phi{n-2} \circ \dots \circ \phi0)(\mathbf{x}) \odot \dots \odot \hat{\phi}1 \circ \phi0(\mathbf{x}) \odot \mathbf{W}0 \mathbf{e}i. Helper: \hat{\phi}k(\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{W}k^T \text{NL}'{k-1}(\mathbf{W}{k-1} \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{b}{k-1}). \mathbf{e}i is the unit vector with 1 at the i-th component. \odot is the Hadamard product. Inputs are mapped to a higher dimensional space using normalized positional encoding to improve performance in the grad network: \bar{w}(p) = (\dots, \omegai^{-1} \sin(\omegai p), \omegai^{-1} \cos(\omegai p), \dots) where \omegai = 2^i \pi. Standard positional encoding \gamma(p) is avoided in the grad network as it introduces exponentially increasing amplitude scaling. 1. Instantiate Integral Network: Choose MLP architecture (layers, features, nonlinearities) for \Phi\theta. 2. Instantiate Grad Network: Use a custom AutoDiff framework to trace the computational graph of \Phi\theta and explicitly instantiate \Psi\theta^i while maintaining shared parameters \theta. The graph is represented as a DAG using Python Networkx. 3. Optimize Grad Network: Optimize shared parameters \theta by minimizing the loss: \theta^ = \arg \min\theta \mathcal{L}(\Psi\theta^i(\mathbf{x}), f(\mathbf{x})) where f(\mathbf{x}) is the target signal (e.g., the integrand of the VRE). Use conventional AutoDiff and optimization tools (e.g., Adam). 4. Reassemble Integral Network: After training, the optimized parameters \theta^ are used to evaluate \Phi{\theta^}. The grad network is discarded or kept for reference, but inference uses \Phi{\theta^}. 5. Compute Definite Integrals: Calculate any definite integral using the Newton-Leibniz formula: \int{ai}^{bi} \Psi{\theta^}^i(\mathbf{x}) \, dxi = \Phi{\theta^}(\mathbf{x}) \Big|{xi=bi} - \Phi{\theta^}(\mathbf{x}) \Big|{xi=ai} This requires only two evaluations of the integral network. The VRE cannot be directly integrated due to nested integrals (transmittance). AutoInt approximates the ray with N piecewise sections. 1. Sampling Network: Train a small MLP S(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}) to predict interval lengths \delta \in \mathbb{R}^N. This allocates more sections in regions with large variations in density. 2. Stratified Sampling: Subdivide each interval \deltai into M bins. Samples t{i,j} are drawn uniformly: t{i,j} \sim U\left[t{i-1} + \frac{j-1}{M} \deltai, t{i-1} + \frac{j}{M} \deltai\right] for j = 1, \dots, M. 3. Rendering: Evaluate the integral network at the bounds of each piecewise section to compute the contribution, summing them to approximate the final color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class IntegralNetwork(nn.Module): """ The integral network Phitheta. Uses Swish nonlinearity. """ def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim, numlayers): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): indim = inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim outdim = hiddendim layers.append(nn.Linear(indim, outdim)) layers.append(nn.SiLU()) # Swish layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) # Output dimension depends on signal self.net = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class GradNetwork(nn.Module): """ The grad network Psitheta^i. In practice, this is instantiated by tracing the IntegralNetwork and computing the derivative w.r.t input coordinate i. For implementation, one can use torch.autograd.grad or a custom DAG tracer. Here we show the conceptual structure for training. """ def init(self, integralnet, inputdim, targetcoordindex): super().init() self.integralnet = integralnet self.targetcoordindex = targetcoordindex # Note: In the actual AutoInt paper, a custom AutoDiff framework # explicitly builds this graph to share weights and avoid re-computation. # We simulate the forward pass of the derivative here for clarity. def forward(self, x): # Compute the derivative of the integral network output w.r.t x[targetcoordindex] # This requires the integral network to output a scalar or we sum over outputs x.requiresgrad(True) y = self.integralnet(x) # Sum over output dimensions if y is multi-dimensional ysum = y.sum() grad = torch.autograd.grad( ysum, x, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] return grad[:, self.targetcoordindex] def normalizedpositionalencoding(p, L=10): """ Normalized positional encoding for AutoInt. """ freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(L, device=p.device) torch.pi # p shape: [..., 1] # freqbands shape: [L] # Output shape: [..., 2L] s = torch.sin(p freqbands) c = torch.cos(p freqbands) # Normalize by frequency to prevent amplitude explosion in derivatives s = s / freqbands c = c / freqbands return torch.cat([s, c], dim=-1) def trainautoint(scenedata, numlayers=8, hiddendim=256, lr=5e-4, numepochs=100000): """ Training loop for AutoInt. """ # 1. Instantiate Integral Network # Input: 3D position (x,y,z) + direction (dx, dy, dz) -> encoded # Standard NeRF uses 3+3=6 dims. AutoInt paper uses positional encoding. inputdimraw = 6 # With positional encoding L=10 for pos, L=4 for dir -> 20+8=28 dims # However, the integral network takes the encoded coordinates. # Let's assume the network takes raw coords and handles encoding internally or externally. # The paper says: "positions along the ray are calculated as x = o + t d and passed... together with d" # For simplicity, we assume the network input is the encoded coordinate vector. # Let's define the network to take raw 3D pos and 3D dir, and we encode before passing? # The paper states: "We use a normalized version of the positional encoding for the integral network" # So the input to the MLP is the encoded vector. # Let's assume we have a function to encode. # Input dim to MLP = 2Lpos + 2Ldir = 28. mlpinputdim = 28 integralnet = IntegralNetwork(mlpinputdim, hiddendim, numlayers) # 2. Instantiate Grad Network (Conceptually) # In the paper, this is done via a custom AutoDiff framework that parses the DAG. # Here we use PyTorch's autograd to compute the gradient for the loss. # The "Grad Network" is the computational graph of d(Phi)/dt. optimizer = optim.Adam(integralnet.parameters(), lr=lr) # 3. Training Loop for epoch in range(numepochs): # Sample rays from training images rays = samplerays(scenedata) # Returns origins o, directions d, ground truth colors Cgt losstotal = 0 for o, d, Cgt in rays: # Predict interval lengths using a separate sampling network S(o,d) # delta = samplingnet(o, d) # Returns N intervals # For this pseudocode, we assume a fixed number of intervals N for simplicity # or that the sampling network is trained jointly. # The core AutoInt step is the integration. # Calculate positions along the ray # t values are determined by stratified sampling within intervals delta # ti,j ~ U[...] # For the AutoInt integration step: # We need to evaluate the integral network at bounds. # The VRE is approximated piecewise. # Let's assume we have bounds ta and tb for a segment. # The integrand is T(t) sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), d). # AutoInt learns the antiderivative of this integrand w.r.t t. # However, the paper notes that AutoInt learns the antiderivative of the SIGNAL. # In volume rendering, the signal is complex. # The paper approximates the VRE piecewise. # Simplified Step: # 1. Forward pass through integral network to get Phi(tb) and Phi(ta) # 2. Integral = Phi(tb) - Phi(ta) # But we need to train Phi to be the antiderivative of the radiance/transmittance product. # The loss is computed on the grad network output vs the target signal. # Prepare inputs # x = o + t d # Input to network: encoded(x) concatenated with encoded(d) # Example for one segment bounds ta, tb # We need to compute the gradient of Phi w.r.t t at various points to train it. # Create tensors for ta and tb tatensor = torch.tensor(ta, device=device).view(1, 1) tbtensor = torch.tensor(tb, device=device).view(1, 1) # Compute positions posa = o + tatensor d posb = o + tbtensor d # Encode encposa = normalizedpositionalencoding(posa, L=10) encposb = normalizedpositionalencoding(posb, L=10) encd = normalizedpositionalencoding(d, L=4) inputa = torch.cat([encposa, encd], dim=-1) inputb = torch.cat([encposb, encd], dim=-1) # Forward pass Integral Network phia = integralnet(inputa) phib = integralnet(inputb) # Approximate integral for this segment integralsegment = phib - phia # Accumulate segments to get rendered color Cpred # (Simplified: assuming only one segment or summing up) Cpred = integralsegment # Placeholder for piecewise summation logic # Loss loss = torch.mean((Cpred - Cgt) 2) # Backprop to train the Grad Network (which is derived from Integral Network) # The paper optimizes the grad network to fit the signal f(x). # Here, we are optimizing the integral network such that its derivative fits the signal. # In the paper, they explicitly build the grad network and train it. # Here, we use autograd to compute the gradient of Phi w.r.t t. # To train the grad network, we need the target signal f(x) = d(Phi)/dt # We compute the gradient of Phi w.r.t t. # Note: Phi depends on t via pos = o + td. # We need to compute d(Phi)/dt = d(Phi)/d(pos) d(pos)/dt = d(Phi)/d(pos) d # This is the "Grad Network" output. # Let's compute the gradient of the integral network output w.r.t the input position # But we need w.r.t t specifically. # Re-evaluate with requiresgrad on t ttrain = torch.tensor(ta, device=device, requiresgrad=True) postrain = o + ttrain d encpostrain = normalizedpositionalencoding(postrain, L=10) inputtrain = torch.cat([encpostrain, encd], dim=-1) phitrain = integralnet(inputtrain) # Compute gradient w.r.t t gradphidt = torch.autograd.grad( phitrain.sum(), ttrain, creategraph=True)[0] # The target signal f(x) is the radiance transmittance product. # In the paper, they supervise the grad network to behave like a standard NeRF MLP output? # No, they supervise the grad network to fit the signal to integrate. # For volume rendering, the signal is the integrand of the VRE. # This requires knowing the density and color at t. # Usually, NeRF predicts sigma and c. # AutoInt learns the integral of the VRE integrand. # The paper states: "Optimize the grad network to fit the signal to integrate." # And "Supervise the gradient of the network to behave like a standard NeRF MLP." # This implies the grad network output is compared to the VRE integrand. # Let's assume we have a separate network or the same network predicting sigma/c? # The paper says: "The networks representing volume density and color each have 8 hidden layers..." # It seems AutoInt replaces the standard sampling-based rendering with the integral network. # Loss for Grad Network: # Lgrad = || gradphidt - f(x) ||^2 # where f(x) is the VRE integrand. # However, f(x) depends on sigma and c, which are also learned. # The paper mentions training the grad network using backpropagation on a loss calculated from the derivative. # For this pseudocode, we assume f(x) is available or computed from a parallel standard NeRF head? # The paper implies the integral network IS the representation. # Let's stick to the core AutoInt mechanism: # 1. Build Grad Network from Integral Network. # 2. Train Grad Network to match target signal. # 3. Use Integral Network for inference. # Since we can't easily separate the "Grad Network" module in standard PyTorch without custom ops, # we simulate the training objective. # Target signal f(t) = T(t) sigma(t) c(t) # We need sigma and c. # If we use the same network for sigma/c, it's complex. # The paper uses separate networks for density and color in the standard NeRF baseline, # but for AutoInt, it learns the integral of the combined signal. # Let's assume we have a target signal tensor targetsignal for this ray segment. # targetsignal = computevreintegrand(o, d, ttrain) # Placeholder # Loss lossgrad = torch.mean((gradphidt - targetsignal) 2) optimizer.zerograd() lossgrad.backward() optimizer.step() losstotal += lossgrad.item() if epoch % 1000 == 0: print(f"Epoch {epoch}, Loss: {losstotal}") return integralnet def renderwithautoint(integralnet, rayo, rayd, boundst): """ Render a single ray using the trained integral network. """ # boundst is a list of t values [t0, t1,..., tN] # The integral over [ti, t{i+1}] is Phi(t{i+1}) - Phi(ti) renderedcolor = 0.0 for i in range(len(boundst) - 1): ta = boundst[i] tb = boundst[i+1] posa = rayo + ta rayd posb = rayo + tb rayd encposa = normalizedpositionalencoding(posa, L=10) encposb = normalizedpositionalencoding(posb, L=10) encd = normalizedpositionalencoding(rayd, L=4) inputa = torch.cat([encposa, encd], dim=-1) inputb = torch.cat([encposb, encd], dim=-1) phia = integralnet(inputa) phib = integralnet(inputb) segmentintegral = phib - phia renderedcolor += segmentintegral return renderedcolor Network Architecture: 8 hidden layers, 256 hidden units. Nonlinearity: Swish. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 4, with 1024 rays sampled from each image. Learning Rate Decay: Factor of 0.2 every 10^5 iterations. Positional Encoding Depth: L=10 for position \mathbf{x}, L=4 for direction \mathbf{d}. Sampling Configuration: M = 128/N samples within each piecewise interval for N \in \{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\} intervals. ReLU Nonlinearities: Using ReLU in the integral network results in step functions in the grad network (derivative is zero almost everywhere), making training difficult. Quality vs. Speed Trade-off: Computational speedups come with a reduction in image quality compared to standard NeRF. Precision: The method relies on the accuracy of the learned antiderivative. Poor generalization of the nonlinearity (e.g., SIREN overfitting) can lead to errors. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) where N is the number of piecewise intervals, but each interval requires only 2 network evaluations. Total evaluations per ray: 2N. Standard NeRF requires hundreds of evaluations per ray. Memory Complexity: Training memory is reduced by 15% compared to standard two-step AutoDiff. Inference memory is dominated by the network weights. Measured Performance: On 8 Blender scenes, AutoInt (N=16) achieves 26.0 dB PSNR, 15.0 GB memory, and 4.8 s/frame runtime, compared to NeRF's 31.0 dB, 15.6 GB, and 30 s/frame. Strengths: >10× faster rendering than NeRF; reduced training iteration time by 1.8×; reduced memory by 15%. Limitations: Lower image quality (PSNR) than NeRF; trade-off between speed and quality controlled by N. When to use: When rendering speed is critical and slight quality degradation is acceptable. When not to use: When photorealistic quality (high PSNR/SSIM) is required. AutoInt was introduced in the paper "AutoInt: Automatic Integration for Fast Neural Volume Rendering". It is used for neural volume rendering on synthetic datasets with challenging geometries and reflectance properties, evaluated on Blender scenes, Local Light Field Fusion, and DeepVoxels datasets. It is analogous to conventional fast volume rendering methods like shear-warping and Fourier projection-slice methods, as all use approximations that trade image quality for computational efficiency. name: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering
body: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering is a method that utilizes surface rendering primitives to compute gradients analytically, performing inference via a CNN encoder. It distinguishes itself from linear or additive lighting models by accounting for complex non-linear lighting effects, specifically absorption and self-shadowing, which are critical for accurately capturing the visual appearance of real-world phenomena such as fluid markers. The method operates within a fully differentiable volumetric rendering pipeline that integrates physical constraints with image-space observations. Unlike prior works that rely on linear image formation models suitable for thin marker densities with little absorption under uniform lighting, this approach handles non-linear attenuation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A small number of input views (potentially unposed or posed depending on the specific instantiation like SinGRAF, though the core [NG20] reference implies a general differentiable pipeline) and physical priors (e.g., Navier-Stokes equations for fluid reconstruction). Outputs: Reconstructed volumetric fields (density \rho, velocity \mathbf{u}) or 3D radiance fields that match the input views while adhering to physical transport constraints. Data Structures: Volumetric Field: Represented as a density field \rho and potentially a velocity field \mathbf{u} for dynamic scenes. CNN Encoder: Used for inference to map input images to latent codes or scene parameters. Surface Representation: The method uses surface rendering primitives, implying a representation of the volume boundaries or isosurfaces rather than pure voxel marching for the gradient computation. Steps: 1. Scene Representation: The scene is represented using a structure that supports surface rendering (e.g., a neural radiance field or a latent code optimized via a hypernetwork). 2. Differentiable Rendering: The rendering process computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} using a model that accounts for absorption and self-shadowing. This involves non-linear attenuation of light as it passes through the medium. 3. Analytic Gradient Computation: Gradients are computed analytically with respect to the scene parameters (e.g., density, velocity, latent codes) rather than relying solely on reverse-mode automatic differentiation through the entire volumetric integral. This reduces memory overhead compared to storing O(kn) intermediate states. 4. Inference/Optimization: For generative tasks (e.g., SinGRAF), a CNN encoder infers latent codes from unposed 2D images, which are then decoded into 3D radiance fields. For reconstruction tasks (e.g., fluid), the method optimizes initial density \rho0 and velocity sequence \{\mathbf{u}0, \dots, \mathbf{u}{t-1}\} to minimize a composite loss \mathcal{L}\rho that enforces correct transport over the fluid flow trajectory. Formulas: The rendering model accounts for non-linear attenuation. While the standard emission-absorption model is: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i This method extends the model to include self-shadowing and absorption effects, moving beyond the linear additive model \hat{C} = \sum \mathbf{c}i \deltai. The exact closed-form gradient expressions are derived analytically. Parameters: Loss Function: A composite loss \mathcal{L}\rho constrains the density fields. Physics Priors: Navier-Stokes equations are used as physical priors for fluid reconstruction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thin Densities: Linear models fail for thick densities with significant absorption; this method is required in such cases. Small Input Views: Reconstruction from a very small number of input views is challenging and requires physical priors to reduce the solution space. A 3D-aware generative model that uses surface rendering, computes gradients analytically, and performs inference via a CNN encoder. It distinguishes itself by employing a progressive-scale patch discrimination strategy and operating on unposed inputs with a tri-plane representation. Memory: Analytic gradient computation reduces memory consumption compared to standard reverse-mode AD, which requires storing O(kn) intermediate states. Accuracy: Handles non-linear attenuation and self-shadowing, providing higher fidelity for real-world marker observations and fluids compared to linear models. Data Requirements: Can operate on a very small number of input views if physical priors (like Navier-Stokes) are introduced. SinGRAF variant operates on unposed 2D images of a single scene. Complexity: The use of surface rendering and analytic gradients simplifies the optimization landscape compared to full volumetric integration backpropagation. The method is attributed to [NG20] (Neural Graphics Primitives or similar, cited as Differentiable Volumetric Rendering [NG20] in). It was developed to address the limitations of linear lighting models in volumetric reconstruction. It is used in 3D-aware generative modeling (e.g., SinGRAF) and fluid reconstruction (e.g., Global Transport for Fluid Reconstruction). head: SinGRAF, Single Scene 3D GAN
body: SinGRAF is a 3D-aware generative model trained on a small set of unposed 2D images of a single scene to generate diverse 3D radiance fields that preserve appearance while varying scene layout. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a progressive-scale patch discrimination strategy during training, where the discriminator is conditioned on the spatial scale of the rendered patch, allowing the model to learn structural information at large scales and fine details at small scales. Unlike methods that require posed data or large datasets, SinGRAF operates on unposed inputs and uses a tri-plane representation for efficient 3D synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N unposed images \{I1, \dots, IN\}, each of resolution H' \times H' \times 3. Camera intrinsic parameters are assumed available. Output: A 3D generative model G that produces diverse 3D radiance fields. The generator takes a noise vector and outputs RGB predictions for query rays. Data Structures: 1. Latent Code: The mapping network outputs a latent code vector w \in \mathbb{R}^{128} from a noise vector z \sim \mathbb{R}^{128}. 2. Tri-planes: The synthesis network produces a 2D feature image F \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N \times 3C}. This is split into three axis-aligned feature planes: F{xy} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N \times C} F{xz} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N \times C} F{yz} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N \times C} 3. Decoder: A small multilayer perceptron (MLP) mapping \mathbb{R}^{3C} \to \mathbb{R}^4 (RGB + density). Algorithm Steps: 1. Sampling: For each training iteration, sample a patch scale s from a uniform distribution s \sim U(s{min}(t), s{max}(t)), where t is the current training epoch. The schedule decreases s from large values (structural info) to small values (quality/diversity) over epochs. 2. Ray Generation: Define a virtual camera image plane P with the same field of view (FOV) \theta as the input images. Sample a random patch location on P. Generate rays \Gamma\rho corresponding to a fixed resolution H \times H patch with spatial extent s on P. If s=1.0, the patch covers the entire image plane. 3. Feature Aggregation: For each ray origin o and direction d, define the ray parametrically as r(t) = o + td. Sample 96 points along the ray between near bound tn and far bound tf. For each point x = r(t), aggregate tri-plane features: \mathbf{F}{agg}(x) = \mathbf{F}{xy}(x) + \mathbf{F}{xz}(x) + \mathbf{F}{yz}(x) 4. Field Query: Pass the aggregated features through the MLP decoder to obtain color \mathbf{c}(x) and density \sigma(x): (\mathbf{c}(x), \sigma(x)) = \text{mlp}(\mathbf{F}{xy}(x) + \mathbf{F}{xz}(x) + \mathbf{F}{yz}(x)) 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the accumulated color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray using quadrature: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \, dt T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) \, ds\right) 6. Ground Truth Sampling: Crop the input images \{Ii\} using the same patch scale s and random location to obtain ground truth patches. 7. Discriminator Input: Condition the discriminator D with the scale value s. Implementation detail: repeat the scalar s to match the patch resolution before feeding it to D. 8. Discriminator Output: The discriminator D: G(\Gamma\rho, z) \times s \mapsto \mathbb{R} outputs a scalar indicating patch realism. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstep(images, cameraintrinsics, epoch, generator, discriminator, optimizerG, optimizerD): # 1. Sample scale s based on epoch t smin = schedulesmin(epoch) smax = schedulesmax(epoch) s = uniformsample(smin, smax) # 2. name: Path Integral and Path-Space Differentiation
head: Differentiable Path Tracing, Path-Space Gradients
body: Path Integral and Path-Space Differentiation computes gradients of the rendering equation by differentiating the path integral formulation directly, rather than differentiating a discretized volume rendering approximation. It solves the problem of obtaining accurate gradients for complex light transport involving subsurface scattering and visibility discontinuities, where standard volume rendering gradients fail to account for boundary movements. It sets itself apart from Differentiable Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by operating in continuous path space, allowing it to handle arbitrary participating media and surface interactions simultaneously, and from Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode) by providing explicit analytic forms for the gradient terms (interior and boundary) which can be more memory-efficient and physically interpretable. The core mechanism relies on the Reynolds Transport Theorem or the divergence theorem applied to the path integral. The rendering measurement I is expressed as an integral over a path space \hat{\Omega}: I = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \hat{f}(\vec{p}) d\mu(\vec{p}) where \hat{f} is the path contribution function and \mu is the path measure. When differentiating with respect to a scene parameter \pi (such as geometry or material properties), the derivative decomposes into two distinct terms: 1. Interior Term: The integral of the derivative of the path contribution function \frac{\partial \hat{f}}{\partial \pi} over the fixed path space. This accounts for changes in the integrand (e.g., scattering coefficients, geometry derivatives at fixed path vertices). 2. Boundary Term: The integral over the boundary of the path space \partial \hat{\Omega}, weighted by the velocity of the visibility boundaries V{\partial}. This accounts for the movement of the integration domain boundaries, such as silhouettes and shadow edges, as the scene parameters change. \frac{dI}{d\pi} = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \frac{\partial \hat{f}}{\partial \pi} d\mu + \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}} \hat{f} V{\partial} d\mu{\partial} The method requires mapping spatial paths to a fixed "material space" or "reference configuration" to handle domain deformation, ensuring the integration domain is independent of the parameter \pi. Estimates gradients for translucent object shape parameters by converting interior volume integrals into boundary area integrals. It avoids expensive tetrahedralizations by assuming no refractive/reflective boundaries. Choose when optimizing the shape of translucent objects without complex refraction. Transforms the integration domain from deforming spatial path space to a fixed material space. It reduces boundary terms to only visibility-related discontinuities (silhouettes), ignoring static mesh edges. Choose for subsurface scattering and implicit surfaces where domain deformation is significant. Explicitly handles visibility discontinuities (silhouettes and shadow edges) in the gradient estimation. It distinguishes itself by sampling primary and secondary boundaries separately. Choose for accurate gradients in translucent or complex surface materials where visibility changes are critical. The method originates from the application of calculus of variations and Reynolds Transport Theorem to rendering equations. It was developed to address the limitations of differentiating discrete volume rendering approximations, which do not capture the continuous nature of light transport in participating media. The approach is fundamental to differentiable rendering of complex scenes involving subsurface scattering and dynamic geometry.

name: Boundary Path Integral Formulation

body:
The Boundary Path Integral Formulation is a method for estimating the derivatives of the path integral formulation in differentiable volume rendering with respect to object shape parameters. It solves the problem of computing gradients for translucent objects by converting interior volume integrals into boundary area integrals using the divergence theorem. This approach sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Reparameterized Volume Sampling and Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering, by eliminating the need to evaluate the deformation mapping inside the volume, thereby avoiding expensive tetrahedralizations. Unlike Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE which handles visibility discontinuities, this formulation assumes no refractive/reflective boundaries or 	heta-dependent shadows, focusing instead on the shape derivative of translucent media. The method differentiates the reparameterized path integral by separating the result into an interior term and a boundary term. The interior term accounts for changes in the integrand due to parameter-dependent transmittance, while the boundary term arises from the movement of the volume boundary. Sample interior paths from material path space \hat{\Omega} interiorpaths = samplepathsfrommaterialspace(numsamples // 2) for path in interiorpaths: h = computemeasurementcontribution(path) gradh = computegradientofmeasurement(path) dJdtheta = computederivativeofjacobian(path) velocities = computevelocityfield(path.vertices) pdf = computepathprobability(path) term = 0.0 for n in range(len(path.vertices)): pn = path.vertices[n] if isinvolumeinterior(pn): term += dot(gradh[n], velocities[n]) term += h dJdtheta[n] interiorsum += term / pdf # 2. Sample boundary paths from volume boundary path space \partial \hat{\Omega} boundarypaths = samplepathsfromboundaryspace(numsamples // 2) for path in boundarypaths: K = findboundaryvertexindex(path.vertices) pK = path.vertices[K] fp = computemeasurementcontribution(path) vK = computevelocityfield([pK])[0] normalK = computeboundarynormal(pK) vperp = dot(vK, normalK) pdf = computepathprobability(path) boundarysum += (fp vperp) / pdf return interiorsum + boundarysum def computemeasurementcontribution(path): weight = 1.0 for n in range(len(path.vertices)): weight = path.vertexterms[n] for n in range(1, len(path.vertices)): weight = path.geometricterms[n] return weight def computegradientofmeasurement(path): return [computemeasurementgradient(path, n) for n in range(len(path.vertices))] def computederivativeofjacobian(path): return [computejacobianderivative(path, n) for n in range(len(path.vertices))] def computevelocityfield(vertices): return [computevelocity(p) for p in vertices] def computevelocity(p): # Velocity is the derivative of the deformation mapping X(p, theta) w.r.t theta at theta=0 return scene.computedeformationvelocity(p) def computeboundarynormal(p): return scene.computeboundarynormal(p) def isinvolumeinterior(p): return scene.ispointinvolume(p) def findboundaryvertexindex(vertices): for i, p in enumerate(vertices): if scene.ispointonboundary(p): return i return -1 def samplepathsfrommaterialspace(n): return scene.tracepaths(n, referencegeometry=True) def samplepathsfromboundaryspace(n): return scene.tracepathsconstrainedboundary(n, referencegeometry=True) def computepathprobability(path): return scene.computepathpdf(path) def computemeasurementgradient(path, n): return scene.computemeasurementgradient(path, n) def computejacobianderivative(path, n): return scene.computejacobianderivative(path, n) Visibility Discontinuities: The derivation assumes no refractive/reflective boundaries or 	heta-dependent shadows (Assumption S.1). If violated, the velocity of visibility boundaries is nontrivial to compute without tetrahedralization. Multiple Boundary Vertices: Paths with two or more vertices constrained on the boundary have zero measure and make no contribution to the first-order derivatives. Performance: Computation of gradients for a single rendered image takes between a few seconds to tens of seconds, making it impractical for training neural networks. Tetrahedralization Avoidance: Unlike previous methods (e.g., Zhang et al. [ZYZ21]), this method avoids tetrahedralizations and point-in-tetrahedron lookups by moving terms to the boundary. A Monte Carlo estimator for the boundary path integral using unidirectional path tracing. It is straightforward to implement but may exhibit high variance in complex lighting scenarios. Choose when scene complexity is low and implementation simplicity is prioritized. A Monte Carlo estimator for the boundary path integral using bidirectional path tracing. It handles complex lighting and indirect illumination more effectively than unidirectional variants. Choose when indirect lighting dominates or when unidirectional sampling yields insufficient coverage. Applies Multiple Importance Sampling to combine unidirectional and bidirectional estimators for the boundary path integral, reducing variance across different scene configurations. Choose when lighting conditions vary significantly or when robustness across diverse geometries is required. Time Complexity: The method is unbiased but computationally expensive, requiring seconds to tens of seconds per image. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Avoids interior mapping evaluations, improving performance for multi-bounce lighting compared to tetrahedralization-based methods, though dense meshes still pose sampling challenges. Strengths: Unbiased, eliminates explicit silhouette edge finding, and avoids expensive tetrahedralizations for translucent objects. Limitations: Assumes no refractive/reflective boundaries or 	heta-dependent shadows, and is too slow for neural network training. When to Use: Differentiable volume rendering of translucent objects with respect to shape parameters where high accuracy is prioritized over speed. When Not to Use: Scenes with complex visibility discontinuities dependent on 	heta, or applications requiring real-time gradient computation. The Boundary Path Integral Formulation was introduced by Zhang et al. in the context of Path-Space Differentiable Rendering (PSDR). It extends the PSDR framework to participating media by reparameterizing interior differential path integrals as boundary path integrals. The method was validated against finite-difference gradients and compared with other differentiable rendering techniques like Nimier-David et al.'s approach. It is part of the broader effort to differentiate the path integral formulation directly, rather than the rendering equation.
