name: Material-Form Differential Path Integral
head: Differentiable Path Integral with BSSRDF, Differential path integral, Material Space Differentiation, Reynolds Transport Theorem for Path Integrals, Spatial-form Differential Path Integral, Spatial-form path integral derivative
body: The Material-Form Differential Path Integral is a method for computing the gradient of a radiometric measurement with respect to scene parameters \pi by transforming the integration domain from a deforming spatial path space to a fixed "material space". It solves the problem that standard differentiation of path integrals fails when the integration domain or the integrand's discontinuities depend on the parameters being differentiated. Unlike the Spatial-Form approach, which integrates over the moving spatial domain and requires handling all parameter-dependent discontinuities (including static mesh edges), the material form maps the domain to a reference geometry, reducing the boundary term to only include visibility-related discontinuities (silhouettes). It builds on Differentiable volume rendering by extending differentiable path tracing to subsurface scattering and implicit surfaces where domain deformation is significant. The method relies on the Reynolds Transport Theorem applied to path integrals. It decomposes the derivative of the measurement I with respect to a parameter \pi into an interior integral (derivative of the integrand over the fixed material space) and a boundary integral (integral over visibility boundaries weighted by their velocity). Inputs: Scene parameter \pi (e.g., vertex positions, implicit surface parameters). A global parameterization (motion) X(\cdot, \pi) mapping material points to spatial points. The material path space \hat{\Omega}, which is independent of \pi. The material boundary path space \partial\hat{\Omega}. Outputs: The gradient \frac{dI}{d\pi}. Material Path \bar{\mathbf{p}}: A sequence of vertices \mathbf{p}0, \dots, \mathbf{p}n in the fixed material space. Spatial Path \bar{\mathbf{x}}: The corresponding path in world space, where \mathbf{x}i = X(\mathbf{p}i, \pi). Jacobian Determinant J(\mathbf{p}): The determinant of the Jacobian of the map \chi (inverse of X), defined as J(\mathbf{p}) = |dA(\mathbf{x})/dA(\mathbf{p})|. Visibility Boundary Normal \mathbf{n}{\partial}(\mathbf{p}K): The unit normal of the visibility boundary at vertex \mathbf{p}K, perpendicular to both the surface normal and the tangent of the discontinuity curve. The derivative of the radiometric measurement I is given by: \frac{dI}{d\pi} = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \hat{f}'(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) d\mu(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) + \int{\partial\hat{\Omega}} \hat{f}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) V{\partial}(\mathbf{p}K) d\mu{\partial} Where: \hat{\Omega} is the material path space. \partial\hat{\Omega} is the material boundary path space containing paths with exactly one vertex \mathbf{p}K constrained to a set of visibility boundaries \Delta B(\mathbf{p}{K-1}). \mathbf{p}K is a jump discontinuity point of mutual visibility with \mathbf{p}{K-1} fixed. \hat{f}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) is the material measurement contribution: \hat{f}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) = \hat{W}e(\mathbf{p}0, \mathbf{p}1) C(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) G(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) \hat{L}e(\mathbf{p}n, \mathbf{p}{n-1}) where C(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) = \prod \hat{\rho} and G(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) = \prod \hat{G} are products of scattering and geometry terms in material space. The scattering term in material space is transformed as: \hat{\rho}(\mathbf{p}{i-1}, \mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{p}{i+1}) = \rho(\mathbf{y}{i-1}, \mathbf{y}i, \mathbf{y}{i+1}) J(\mathbf{p}i) \hat{G}(\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{p}{i+1}) = G(\mathbf{y}i, \mathbf{y}{i+1}) where \mathbf{y} are the spatial coordinates and J(\mathbf{p}) = |dA(\mathbf{y})/dA(\mathbf{p})| is the Jacobian of the map. \hat{f}' is the derivative of the material measurement contribution with respect to \pi. V{\partial}(\mathbf{p}K) is the boundary velocity: V{\partial}(\mathbf{p}K) = \mathbf{n}{\partial}(\mathbf{p}K) \cdot \frac{d\mathbf{p}K}{d\pi} where \mathbf{n}{\partial}(\mathbf{p}K) is the unit normal of the visibility boundary (perpendicular to both the surface normal and the tangent of the curve), assumed to point toward the occluded side. The boundary contribution term \Delta \hat{f}K is defined as: \Delta \hat{f}K(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) = \hat{f}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) \frac{\Delta \hat{g}(\mathbf{p}K; \mathbf{p}{K-2}, \mathbf{p}{K-1})}{\hat{g}(\mathbf{p}K; \mathbf{p}{K-2}, \mathbf{p}{K-1})} where \Delta \hat{g} represents the discontinuity in the visibility function. 1. Define Material Space: Establish a fixed reference domain \hat{\Omega} and a parameterization map X(\mathbf{p}, \pi) that maps material points \mathbf{p} to spatial points \mathbf{x}. 2. Compute Interior Term: Evaluate the integral over \hat{\Omega} by differentiating the material integrand \hat{f} with respect to \pi. This involves computing the derivative of the Jacobian J and the transformed scattering terms \hat{\rho}. 3. Identify Boundary Discontinuities: Determine the set of visibility boundaries \Delta B(\mathbf{p}{K-1}) in material space. These are the curves where visibility jumps occur for fixed \mathbf{p}{K-2} and \mathbf{p}{K-1}. 4. Compute Boundary Term: Evaluate the integral over \partial\hat{\Omega}. For each boundary path, calculate the boundary velocity V{\partial} using the normal \mathbf{n}{\partial} and the parameter derivative of the vertex position. 5. Sum Terms: Add the interior and boundary integrals to obtain the total gradient. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def materialformgradient(path, pi, motionX, referencemap): # path: list of material vertices [p0, p1,..., pn] # pi: scene parameter # motionX: function X(p, pi) mapping material to spatial points # referencemap: function P(p, pi0) mapping material to reference # 1. Map material path to spatial path spatialpath = [motionX(p, pi) for p in path] # 2. Compute Jacobian J for each vertex # J(p) = |dA(spatial)/dA(material)| Js = [] for p in path: # Compute Jacobian matrix of X with respect to p Jmatrix = [[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]] # Compute partial derivatives of X with respect to material coordinates Jmatrix[0][0] = computepartialderivative(motionX, p, pi, 'ux') Jmatrix[0][1] = computepartialderivative(motionX, p, pi, 'vx') Jmatrix[1][0] = computepartialderivative(motionX, p, pi, 'uy') Jmatrix[1][1] = computepartialderivative(motionX, p, pi, 'vy') Js.append(abs(Jmatrix[0][0] Jmatrix[1][1] - Jmatrix[0][1] Jmatrix[1][0])) # 3. Compute Interior Term # Integral over Omegahat of d(fhat)/d(pi) interiorintegral = 0.0 # Standard Monte Carlo sampling over material path space for sample in samplematerialspace(): fhat = computematerialmeasurement(sample, Js) dfhatdpi = differentiatematerialmeasurement(sample, Js, pi) interiorintegral += dfhatdpi / pdfsamplematerialspace(sample) # 4. Compute Boundary Term # Integral over dOmegahat of fhat Vboundary boundaryintegral = 0.0 # Identify visibility boundaries (silhouettes) in material space boundarycurves = findvisibilitydiscontinuities(path, pi) for curve in boundarycurves: # Sample points on the boundary curve for pK in sampleboundarycurve(curve): # Compute boundary velocity Vpartial npartial = computevisibilityboundarynormal(pK, path) dpKdpi = differentiatevertexposition(pK, pi) Vpartial = npartial[0] dpKdpi[0] + npartial[1] dpKdpi[1] # Compute fhat at this boundary path boundarypath = constructboundarypath(path, pK) fhatboundary = computematerialmeasurement(boundarypath, Js) # Add to integral boundaryintegral += fhatboundary Vpartial / pdfsampleboundary(curve) return interiorintegral + boundaryintegral def computevisibilityboundarynormal(pK, path): # Computes npartial, the unit normal of the visibility boundary. # Perpendicular to both surface normal and tangent of the curve. # Points toward the occluded side. surfacenormal = computesurfacenormal(pK) tangent = computetangentofdiscontinuitycurve(pK) npartial = cross(surfacenormal, tangent) norm = sqrt(npartial[0]2 + npartial[1]2) npartial = [npartial[0]/norm, npartial[1]/norm] # Ensure it points toward the occluded side if isvisible(path[-2], pK): npartial = [-npartial[0], -npartial[1]] return npartial \pi: The scene parameter (e.g., vertex positions). X(\cdot, \pi): The global parameterization induced by motion. \hat{\Omega}: The material path space. \partial \hat{\Omega}: The material boundary path space. \Delta BK(\pi): Discontinuity curves of \hat{g} with respect to \mathbf{p}K. \mathbf{n}{\partial}(\mathbf{p}K): Unit normal of the visibility boundary, pointing toward the occluded side. Reciprocity: The boundary term is not reciprocal due to the unidirectional definition of \partial M^n(\pi). Implicit Surfaces: Obtaining a global parameterization X for implicit surfaces may be difficult, requiring a resort to the spatial form. Static Discontinuities: If discontinuity curves \Delta B[J] are independent of \pi, the boundary term for those discontinuities vanishes. Polygonal Meshes: Face edges in the reference B are \pi-independent and do not need to be included in \Delta B[\hat{f}]. Only visibility-related discontinuities (silhouettes) need boundary integrals. Jacobian Derivatives: Even when using a local parameterization where J=1, the scene derivatives \dot{J} generally remain nonzero. Material-form reparameterization is a technique for differentiating the path integral with respect to scene parameters by mapping evolving geometry to a fixed reference domain, thereby avoiding the direct differentiation of path space boundaries. It sets itself apart from standard path integral differentiation by converting light paths into material paths via a differentiable mapping, allowing the derivative to be computed as an integral over a static material path space plus a boundary term. This method builds on Material-Form Differential Path Integral. A technique to define a local motion \hat{X} at a fixed parameter \pi0 such that the Jacobian determinant J becomes one, simplifying estimation. The local motion is defined as \hat{X}(\cdot, \pi) = X(\cdot, \pi) \circ P(\cdot, \pi0), where P is the reference map of motion X. This reduces \hat{X}(\cdot, \pi) to the identity map when \pi = \pi0. Using \hat{X} allows efficient estimation using previously developed path sampling methods due to the unit Jacobian, whereas setting the reference \hat{B} to 0,1)^2 makes the path space equivalent to the primary sample space in [MCMC. A pitfall is that scene derivatives \dot{J} generally remain nonzero even when J=1. Analysis of discontinuity sources in the material-form differential path integral, noting that many jump discontinuities of g with respect to \mathbf{p}{n+1} do not move with \pi, causing normal velocity to vanish. For polygonal meshes, face edges in the reference B are \pi-independent and do not need to be included in \Delta B[\hat{f}]. The Jacobian determinant J is constant within faces but discontinuous across boundaries; however, face boundaries are \pi-independent and excluded from discontinuity curves. Consequently, only visibility-related discontinuities (silhouette edges) need to be handled with boundary integrals in the material form for polygonal meshes. Complexity: The method requires sampling both the interior path space and the boundary path space. The boundary term requires silhouette detection, which is computationally expensive. Memory: Memory usage depends on the number of samples required for the boundary term. Unlike reverse-mode AD, it does not require storing O(kn) intermediate states. Strengths: It handles domain deformation explicitly and reduces the number of discontinuities that need to be handled in the boundary term compared to the spatial form. It is particularly useful for subsurface scattering and implicit surfaces. Limitations: It requires a global parameterization, which may be difficult to obtain for implicit surfaces. The boundary term is not reciprocal. Silhouette detection is challenging. When to use: When the scene geometry deforms significantly with respect to parameters, or when differentiating with respect to subsurface scattering parameters. When not to use: When a global parameterization is difficult to obtain and the spatial form is more suitable. The method originates from the application of the Reynolds Transport Theorem to path integrals in differentiable rendering. It was introduced to handle differentiable translucent rendering with BSSRDF, where the integration domain depends on scene parameters. The material-form approach was developed to simplify the boundary term by leveraging a fixed reference domain. It builds on earlier work in differentiable path tracing. name: Material-form reparameterization
head: Material-form formulation, Material-form path integral
body: Material-form reparameterization is a technique for differentiating the path integral with respect to scene parameters by mapping evolving geometry to a fixed reference domain, thereby avoiding the direct differentiation of path space boundaries. It sets itself apart from standard path integral differentiation by converting light paths into material paths via a differentiable mapping, allowing the derivative to be computed as an integral over a static material path space plus a boundary term. This method builds on Material-Form Differential Path Integral. Inputs: Scene parameter \pi \in \mathbb{R}. Evolving surface M(\pi). Fixed reference surface B. Differentiable one-to-one mapping \mathbf{X}(\cdot, \pi): B \to M(\pi). Outputs: Material-form path integral representation of the radiometric measurement I. Data Structures: Material Path Space \hat{\Omega}: Defined as \hat{\Omega}:= \cup{N \ge 1} \mathbf{B}^{N+1}, where \mathbf{B} is the reference surface. Material Path \bar{\mathbf{p}}: A sequence (\mathbf{p}0, \dots, \mathbf{p}N) where \mathbf{p}n \in B. Light Path \bar{\mathbf{x}}: A sequence (\mathbf{x}0, \dots, \mathbf{x}N) where \mathbf{x}n \in M(\pi). Steps: 1. Define the fixed reference surface B and the differentiable mapping \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{p}, \pi) such that \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{p}, \pi) maps any point on B to the corresponding point on M(\pi). 2. Transform every light path \bar{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{x}0, \dots, \mathbf{x}N) into a material path \bar{\mathbf{p}} = (\mathbf{p}0, \dots, \mathbf{p}N) using the relation \mathbf{x}n = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{p}n, \pi) for all 0 \le n \le N. 3. Apply the change of variable to the original path integral. The measurement I is expressed as: I = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \hat{f}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) d\mu(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) where \hat{\Omega} is the material path space and d\mu is the associated measure. 4. Compute the material measurement contribution \hat{f}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) by scaling the original light path contribution f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) with the Jacobian of the transformation: \hat{f}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}) = f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}) \prod{n=0}^{N} J(\mathbf{p}n, \pi) where J(\mathbf{p}, \pi) is the Jacobian resulting from the reparameterization. 5. Calculate the Jacobian J(\mathbf{p}, \pi) as the norm of the derivative of the surface-area measure: J(\mathbf{p}, \pi):= \left\| \frac{dA(\mathbf{x})}{dA(\mathbf{p})} \right\| where A indicates the surface-area measure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def materialformreparameterization(lightpath, pi, referencesurface, mappingX): """ Computes the material-form path integral contribution for a given light path. Args: lightpath: List of points [x0,..., xN] on the evolving surface M(pi). pi: Scene parameter. referencesurface: The fixed reference surface B. mappingX: Function X(p, pi) mapping points from B to M(pi). Returns: materialcontribution: The value of fhat(pbar). materialpath: List of points [p0,..., pN] on B. """ N = len(lightpath) - 1 materialpath = [] jacobianproduct = 1.0 # Step 2: Transform light path to material path # The source defines xn = X(pn, pi). We invert this relation. for xn in lightpath: # Invert the bijective mapping X to find p such that X(p, pi) = xn. pn = invertmapping(mappingX, xn, pi) materialpath.append(pn) # Step 4: Compute material measurement contribution # flight evaluates the original light path contribution f(xbar). flight = evaluatelightpathcontribution(lightpath) # Step 5: Compute Jacobian product for pn in materialpath: # J(p, pi):= || dA(x) / dA(p) || # Compute the derivative of the mapping X with respect to p, # then compute the norm of the area measure derivative. dxdp = computejacobianmatrix(mappingX, pn, pi) jacobiann = computeareajacobiannorm(dxdp) jacobianproduct = jacobiann materialcontribution = flight jacobianproduct return materialcontribution, materialpath def invertmapping(Xfunc, x, pi): # Solves X(p, pi) = x for p using Newton-Raphson iteration, # relying on the differentiability and bijectivity of X. p = initialguess(x) for in range(maxiterations): dx = Xfunc(p, pi) - x if norm(dx) < tolerance: break p -= solvelinearsystem(jacobian(Xfunc, p, pi), dx) return p def computejacobianmatrix(Xfunc, p, pi): # Returns the Jacobian matrix of X with respect to p at (p, pi). return numericaljacobian(Xfunc, p, pi) def computeareajacobiannorm(dxdp): # Computes || dA(x) / dA(p) || as sqrt(det(J^T J)) for surface mappings. return sqrt(determinant(dxdp.T @ dxdp)) def evaluatelightpathcontribution(path): # Evaluates the original light path contribution f(xbar) using # standard path tracing terms (emission, BSDF, transmittance, etc.). return standardpathcontribution(path) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mapping Differentiability: The mapping \mathbf{X} must be differentiable. Non-differentiable mappings break the change of variable. Bijectivity: The mapping must be one-to-one. Self-intersections or folding of the surface M(\pi) relative to B violate this condition. Jacobian Zero/Infinity: If the mapping collapses area (J=0) or stretches it infinitely (J \to \infty), the integral becomes ill-defined. This variant extends the surface-only formulation to volumes. The reference surface union \mathcal{B} becomes a union of reference surfaces \mathcal{B}M and interior volumes \mathcal{B}V. Consequently, the definitions of the material path space \hat{\Omega}, the measure d\mu, and the Jacobian J(\mathbf{p}n) change to account for volume elements and interior boundaries. The resulting differential path integral retains the same form (interior + boundary terms) but the boundary vertices \mathbf{p}K can reside on surfaces or in volumes, altering the definition of \partial \hat{\Omega}, the visibility term VK, and the boundary measure d\mu'. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates the need to differentiate the path space domain \Omega directly, which evolves with \pi. It converts the problem into an integral over a fixed domain \hat{\Omega}. Limitations: Requires the existence of a differentiable, one-to-one mapping \mathbf{X} between the reference and evolving geometry. This may be difficult to construct for complex, topologically changing scenes. When to use: When differentiating radiometric measurements with respect to parameters that deform geometry, and a suitable reference mapping can be defined. The material-form reparameterization was proposed by Zhang et al. [2020] to address the complexity of differentiating the path integral when scene geometry evolves with the parameter \pi. It is a core component of the Material-Form Differential Path Integral formulation. name: Monte Carlo Estimation of Differentiable Path Integrals
head: Differentiable Path Tracing, Gradient Estimation via Path Integral
body: This method estimates the gradient of the path integral rendering equation with respect to scene parameters \pi by decomposing the derivative into interior contributions (derivative of the path contribution function) and boundary contributions (derivative of the visibility boundary). It distinguishes itself from naive gradient estimation by explicitly handling discontinuities in the visibility function, such as silhouette edges and shadow edges, which are critical for accurate gradients in translucent or complex surface materials. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs are scene parameters \pi (geometry, material properties), a reference image I{ref}, and a rendering configuration (light, camera, material model). Outputs are an unbiased estimate of the gradient \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} and the rendered image I(\pi). Data Structures: Path Contribution \hat{f}: A scalar value representing the radiance contribution of a specific path. For a 3-segment path (Light p0 \to Surface p1 \to Surface p2 \to Camera p3), \hat{f}(p0 p1 p2 p3) includes the BSSRDF, geometry terms, and visibility. Sample Positions: y1, y2 representing random variables used to sample the path segments. Probability Densities: p(y1), p(y2) representing the PDFs of the sampling distributions for the respective segments. Numbered Steps: 1. Interior Term Estimation: Estimate the derivative of the path contribution function with respect to \pi by sampling paths using conventional path tracing techniques and computing the partial derivative \frac{\partial \hat{f}}{\partial \pi}. 2. Boundary Term Estimation (Primary): Sample points on the primary visibility boundary, which corresponds to silhouette edges in the image. 3. Boundary Term Estimation (Secondary): Sample points on secondary visibility boundaries, which correspond to shadow edges cast on the surface. For BSSRDF materials, these discontinuities are blurred by subsurface scattering. To sample secondary boundaries: Sample points on triangle edges, connect them to the point light source, and trace rays back against the surface to find intersection points. These intersections lie on the shadow edges. 4. Gradient Aggregation: Combine the interior and boundary estimates to form the total gradient. Formulas: The Monte Carlo estimate for the rendered image I and its gradient components are defined as follows: The estimate for the 3-segment path integral (interior) is: \langle I3 \rangle = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{\hat{f}(p0 p1 p2 p3)}{p(y1)p(y2)} where p0 is the light, p1, p2 are surface points, p3 is the camera, and y1, y2 are sample positions. The estimate for the 2-segment path integral (often used for direct illumination or simpler paths) is: \langle I2 \rangle = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{\hat{f}(p0 p1 p2)}{p(y1)} where p0 is the light, p1 is the surface point, p2 is the camera, and y1 is the sample position. The gradient of the 3-segment path integral with respect to \pi is estimated by: \frac{\partial I3}{\partial \pi} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{\frac{\partial \hat{f}(p0 p1 p2 p3)}{\partial \pi}}{p(y1)p(y2)} This corresponds to Eq. (29) in the source, where the path is sampled as in conventional path tracing. The boundary terms (Eqs. 26, 27 in source) involve the velocity vB(p) of the visibility boundary in the direction of the normal to the differential area element dl(p). The total derivative includes the interior term and the boundary integrals: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int \frac{\partial \hat{f}}{\partial \pi} d\mu + \int{\partial \Omega} \hat{f} vB \cdot nB dl The boundary integrand structure involves the change of path contribution \Delta \hat{f} across the boundary and the boundary velocity vB. Parameters: N (Number of samples): Used in the Monte Carlo summation for unbiased estimation of integrals and derivatives. Pitfalls: Biased Gradients from Naive Loss Application: Minimizing the expected value of the squared difference between an unbiased rendering estimate \tilde{I}(\pi) and a reference I{ref} does not minimize the true error. Specifically, \langle (\tilde{I}(\pi) - I{ref})^2 \rangle = \langle \tilde{I}(\pi)^2 \rangle - 2\langle \tilde{I}(\pi) \rangle I{ref} + I{ref}^2, whereas the true loss is (\langle \tilde{I}(\pi) \rangle - I{ref})^2. This results in biased gradients if not handled correctly. Translucency Assumptions: Assuming opaque BSDFs when the target object is translucent leads to broken geometry reconstruction. The method requires assuming a subsurface scattering (BSSRDF) material model to handle shadow edge discontinuities correctly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def montecarlogradientestimate(sceneparams, numsamples): interiorgrad = 0.0 primaryboundarygrad = 0.0 secondaryboundarygrad = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): # 1. Interior term: sample path as in conventional path tracing # [Comment: Source does not specify exact path sampling routine; use standard path tracer] path, y1, y2 = samplepathconventionally(sceneparams) fhat = evaluatepathcontribution(path) pdfy1 = evaluatepdf(y1) pdfy2 = evaluatepdf(y2) dfhatdpi = computederivativepathcontribution(path, sceneparams) interiorgrad += dfhatdpi / (pdfy1 pdfy2) # 2. Primary boundary term: sample points on silhouette edges # [Comment: Source does not specify exact silhouette sampling; standard visibility boundary sampling] primarysample = sampleprimaryboundary(sceneparams) vBprimary = computeboundaryvelocity(primarysample, sceneparams) deltafprimary = computechangepathcontribution(primarysample, sceneparams) primaryboundarygrad += deltafprimary vBprimary # 3. Secondary boundary term: sample points on shadow edges # Sample points on triangle edges, connect to point light, trace rays back triangleedgepoint = sampletriangleedge(sceneparams.mesh) lightpos = sceneparams.light.position rayorigin = triangleedgepoint raydirection = normalize(lightpos - rayorigin) shadowedgepoint = tracerayback(rayorigin, raydirection, sceneparams) vBsecondary = computeboundaryvelocity(shadowedgepoint, sceneparams) deltafsecondary = computechangepathcontribution(shadowedgepoint, sceneparams) secondaryboundarygrad += deltafsecondary vBsecondary interiorgrad /= numsamples primaryboundarygrad /= numsamples secondaryboundarygrad /= numsamples return interiorgrad + primaryboundarygrad + secondaryboundarygrad Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N and the path length. The boundary sampling adds overhead proportional to the number of discontinuity boundaries sampled. Measured Performance: Validated against automatic differentiation derivatives, showing robust geometry reconstruction for translucent objects compared to opaque assumptions. Strengths: Handles discontinuities in visibility (silhouettes, shadow edges) explicitly, which is crucial for accurate gradients in complex materials like BSSRDF. Limitations: Requires careful handling of the loss function to avoid biased gradients (minimizing variance instead of error). Computationally expensive due to the need for boundary sampling and derivative computation of the path contribution. When to use: When rendering translucent or subsurface scattering materials where shadow edges and silhouettes significantly impact the image and its gradients. When not to use: For simple opaque scenes where boundary terms are negligible or can be approximated, or when computational resources are severely limited. The method originates from the work of Xi Deng, Fujun Luan, Bruce Walter, Kavita Bala, and Steve Marschner, presented at SIGGRAPH '22 (2022). It was developed to address the challenges of differentiable rendering for BSSRDF (Bidirectional Scattering Surface Reflectance Distribution Function) materials, where traditional opaque surface assumptions fail. The approach builds on the general principle of differentiable rendering by explicitly modeling the derivative of the visibility boundary. name: Gradient Estimators
head: Gradient Estimation Schemes
body: Gradient Estimators compute the derivatives of the volume rendering integral with respect to scene parameters to enable differentiable volume rendering. They solve the problem of efficiently and accurately propagating error signals from the rendered image back to the volumetric data or scene representation. Unlike Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode), which requires storing O(kn) intermediate states, or Analytical Gradients, which derive closed-form derivatives for specific operations, gradient estimation schemes in volume raycasting focus on the numerical differentiation of the interpolation and filtering steps inherent to raycasting. Gradient estimation in volume raycasting primarily concerns the computation of spatial derivatives (normals) of the volume density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) at arbitrary sample positions along a ray. These gradients are essential for shading, normal estimation, and certain inverse rendering formulations. The method relies on the interpolation filter used during raycasting (e.g., trilinear, tricubic). Input: Volume data grid (density values), interpolation filter kernel, ray parameters (origin, direction, step size). Output: Gradient vector \nabla \sigma at the sample positions along the ray. The implementation operates on the volume grid. For caching variants, a secondary cache structure stores precomputed gradients per brick (sub-volume). Four distinct schemes exist for computing gradients during volume raycasting: 1. Continuous Derivative: A derivative filter is pre-convolved with the interpolation filter. The gradient at a re-sample location is computed by convolving the volume data with this combined filter. 2. Analytic Derivative: A special gradient filter is derived analytically from the interpolation filter. This filter is used directly for gradient estimation. 3. Interpolation First: The volume data is re-sampled onto a new, finer grid such that the derivative operator can be applied directly at the re-sample position. This is beneficial for orthographic rendering. However, if the object sample distance is significantly smaller than one, the grid size increases drastically (e.g., a sample distance of 0.25 increases grid size by a factor of four), making caching inefficient. 4. Derivative First: Gradients are computed at the original grid points first. These precomputed gradients are then interpolated at the desired re-sample position. This scheme is more efficient for caching because the amount of data to cache is determined by the grid size, not the sample distance, allowing for interactive changes in object sample distance and jittering. Schemes 1 and 2 have no caching mechanism available. Schemes 3 and 4 support efficient gradient caching. While Moeller et al. originally proposed Interpolation First as the most efficient for non-cached rendering, Derivative First is superior for cached rendering due to the grid expansion issue in Interpolation First. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """Interpolate scalar value at continuous coordinates using trilinear basis.""" x0, y0, z0 = int(x), int(y), int(z) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 # Clamp to valid grid bounds x0 = max(0, min(x0, grid.shape[0] - 1)); x1 = max(0, min(x1, grid.shape[0] - 1)) y0 = max(0, min(y0, grid.shape[1] - 1)); y1 = max(0, min(y1, grid.shape[1] - 1)) z0 = max(0, min(z0, grid.shape[2] - 1)); z1 = max(0, min(z1, grid.shape[2] - 1)) fx, fy, fz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 v00 = grid[x0, y0, z0] (1 - fx) + grid[x1, y0, z0] fx v10 = grid[x0, y1, z0] (1 - fx) + grid[x1, y1, z0] fx v01 = grid[x0, y0, z1] (1 - fx) + grid[x1, y0, z1] fx v11 = grid[x0, y1, z1] (1 - fx) + grid[x1, y1, z1] fx return v00 (1 - fy) (1 - fz) + v10 fy (1 - fz) + v01 (1 - fy) fz + v11 fy fz def precomputegradients(volumegrid): """Compute gradients at all grid points for Derivative First caching.""" Dx, Dy, Dz = volumegrid.shape gradx = [[[0.0 for in range(Dz)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] grady = [[[0.0 for in range(Dz)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] gradz = [[[0.0 for in range(Dz)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] for x in range(Dx): for y in range(Dy): for z in range(Dz): gradx[x][y][z] = (volumegrid[x+1, y, z] - volumegrid[x, y, z]) if x+1 < Dx else 0.0 grady[x][y][z] = (volumegrid[x, y+1, z] - volumegrid[x, y, z]) if y+1 < Dy else 0.0 gradz[x][y][z] = (volumegrid[x, y, z+1] - volumegrid[x, y, z]) if z+1 < Dz else 0.0 return (gradx, grady, gradz) def raycastderivativefirst(rayorigin, raydirection, volumegrid, gradcomponents, stepsize, maxdist): """Raycast using Derivative First scheme, interpolating precomputed gradients.""" gradx, grady, gradz = gradcomponents t = 0.0 T = 1.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedgrad = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) while t < maxdist: pos = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0]t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1]t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2]t) density = trilinearinterpolate(volumegrid, pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) # Interpolate precomputed gradient components from the cache gx = trilinearinterpolate(gradx, pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) gy = trilinearinterpolate(grady, pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) gz = trilinearinterpolate(gradz, pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) grad = (gx, gy, gz) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density stepsize) color = (color[0] + T alpha density, color[1] + T alpha density, color[2] + T alpha density) T = (1.0 - alpha) accumulatedgrad = (accumulatedgrad[0] + T grad[0], accumulatedgrad[1] + T grad[1], accumulatedgrad[2] + T grad[2]) t += stepsize return color, accumulatedgrad Reparameterization estimators compute gradients of rendering integrals by transforming the integration domain or sampling distribution so that parameter dependence moves from domain boundaries or probability density functions into the integrand's argument. This allows differentiation under the integral sign without boundary terms. Unlike Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode) which propagates gradients through the computational graph, or Analytical Gradients which derive closed-form derivatives, reparameterization relies on a change of variables to make discontinuities or sampling distributions static with respect to optimization variables. Gradient estimation and smoothing techniques address discontinuities in differentiable rendering that cause vanishing gradients. This family modifies gradient computation by smoothing the integrand to permit differentiation under the integral sign, approximating gradients via non-local spatial statistics, or applying axis-aligned filters [6449-smooth-gradient-estimation-via-convolution.md, 6784-non-local-approximated-gradients.md, 7600-axis-aligned-neighbor-smoothing.md]. Recursive Control Variates (RCV) is a gradient estimation technique for physically based differentiable inverse rendering that reduces variance and bias by leveraging information from previous optimization steps. It exploits the high correlation between consecutive renderings in gradient descent, where scene parameters change minimally, to recursively compound variance reduction across the optimization sequence. Unlike SAGA and SVRG which maintain a running approximation of the full gradient for machine learning pipelines, RCV handles variance from numerical integration over continuous domains, and unlike the optimal strategy of using all previous renderings as individual control variates, RCV uses only the immediate previous estimate to avoid growing covariance matrices. It effectively mitigates bias introduced by differentiating non-linear loss functions with respect to noisy inputs, preventing optimization drift. A hierarchical Monte Carlo approach using telescopic sums to debias estimators and improve consistency. It provides an opportunity to make biased gradient estimators at least consistent, unlike standard single-level estimators. A method to compute a gradient vector for multivariate volume data (m channels) by weighting the derivative of each channel to prevent high dynamic range channels from dominating the estimation. The weighted differential is computed as d\Phi = W \left( \sum{i=1}^3 \frac{\delta\Phi}{\delta ui} dui \right), where W is an m \times m diagonal scale matrix with diagonal elements w1, \dots, wm. The metric tensor [g{ij}] describes the rate of change in all directions, and the total change magnitude can be extracted as the L2 norm of this matrix, the magnitude of the largest eigenvalue, or the trace (sum of eigenvalues). The weight constant wi for channel i is calculated as 1 / (\maxi - \mini), where \maxi and \mini are the maximum and minimum data values of channel i, assuming equal influence for each channel and no outliers. For fields with three or more values per sample, the gradient portion of the transfer function is applied separably due to hardware limitations. Used in the visualization of multivariate weather simulations, specifically combining temperature and humidity to identify frontal zones. An unbiased gradient estimator derived using the likelihood-ratio identity. It expresses the gradient of the expected loss as a sum of the expected gradient of the loss and a term involving the gradient of the probability density function. It differs from Reparameterization Estimators [6499-reparameterization-estimators.md] by not requiring the stochastic variable to be differentiable with respect to parameters, making it suitable for discrete sampling or visibility terms, though it typically exhibits higher variance. Time Complexity: Depends on the interpolation filter and the number of samples per ray. Derivative First requires O(V) precomputation where V is volume size, but rendering remains O(N) per ray. Interpolation First may require O(V \cdot k^3) precomputation if k is the expansion factor. Memory Complexity: Derivative First requires storing a gradient grid of the same size as the density grid (O(V)). Interpolation First requires O(V \cdot k^3) memory for the expanded grid. Continuous and Analytic derivatives require O(1) extra memory per sample but no caching. Strengths: Derivative First is efficient for caching and dynamic sample distances. Interpolation First is efficient for orthographic rendering without caching. Limitations: Interpolation First becomes memory-prohibitive for high-resolution sampling (small object sample distance). Continuous and Analytic derivatives do not support caching, leading to redundant computations. Gradient estimation schemes for volume raycasting were thoroughly compared by Moeller et al., who differentiated between the four main types: Continuous Derivative, Analytic Derivative, Interpolation First, and Derivative First. The comparison highlighted the trade-offs between numerical accuracy, image quality, and efficiency, particularly regarding caching mechanisms for interactive applications. name: Reparameterization Estimators
body: Reparameterization estimators compute gradients of rendering integrals by transforming the integration domain or sampling distribution so that parameter dependence moves from domain boundaries or probability density functions into the integrand's argument. This allows differentiation under the integral sign without boundary terms. Unlike Automatic Differentiation (Reverse/Adjoint Mode) which propagates gradients through the computational graph, or Analytical Gradients which derive closed-form derivatives, reparameterization relies on a change of variables to make discontinuities or sampling distributions static with respect to optimization variables. The core mechanism applies the change of variables formula to the rendering integral I(\theta) = \int{\Omega\theta} f(x, \theta) dx. By introducing a differentiable transformation T(\omega, \theta): \Omega \to \Omega\theta from a fixed reference domain \Omega to the parameter-dependent domain \Omega\theta, the integral becomes: I(\theta) = \int{\Omega} f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| d\omega The gradient with respect to parameters \theta is obtained by differentiating under the integral sign: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} = \int{\Omega} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left[ f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| \right] d\omega In Monte Carlo estimation, this is implemented by sampling points \omega from a fixed distribution p(\omega) on \Omega, mapping them to x = T(\omega, \theta), and weighting by the Jacobian determinant \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|. The gradient estimator is: \hat{\nabla}\theta I = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \nabla\theta \left[ \frac{f(T(\omegai, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|}{p(\omegai)} \right] This requires computing the derivative of the transformation T and the Jacobian determinant with respect to \theta. Computes color estimates by sampling points on a ray using the inverse of the cumulative density function (CDF), allowing gradients to back-propagate through sampling locations with respect to the density field. It differs from NeRF's hierarchical sampling by learning sampling points end-to-end without auxiliary networks, and exhibits lower variance than standard importance sampling with a uniform distribution. Choose when training neural radiance fields or density fields end-to-end. Estimates expected radiance by sampling from the density-induced probability distribution using the reparameterization trick, transforming the integration domain from ray distance to cumulative opacity. It sets itself apart by explicitly defining the sampling distribution via the ray's opacity function rather than general volume elements. Choose for unbiased gradient estimation through the inverse opacity function. Computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space, using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) to combine BRDF and emitter sampling, and Next Event Estimation (NEE) to connect paths to emitters. It solves high variance in scenes with varying material properties by allowing the differential vertex to be located at any intermediate vertex or emitter connection. Choose for scenes with complex material properties and varying light transport. Eliminates bias in gradients caused by visibility discontinuities moving with scene parameters by applying a change of variables to transform the integration domain such that discontinuities become static. It differs from explicit edge sampling methods by avoiding boundary terms, making it computationally efficient for complex scenes, though it approximates gradients and has limitations with specular materials. name: Reparameterized Volume Sampling
head: Differentiable Volume Sampling, Inverse CDF Sampling
body: Reparameterized Volume Sampling is a differentiable volume rendering technique that computes color estimates by sampling points on a ray using the inverse of the cumulative density function (CDF), allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling locations with respect to the density field. It differs from NeRF's hierarchical sampling, which relies on an auxiliary coarse model trained separately, by learning sampling points end-to-end without auxiliary networks. Compared to standard importance sampling with a uniform distribution, this stratified reparameterized sampling exhibits lower variance. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Ray segment bounds [t{r1}, t{r2}] (near and far planes). Density field \sigmar(t), typically represented by a neural network or grid. Radiance field cr(t). Number of samples per ray k (typically 32). Number of knots m for piecewise linear approximation (typically 256). Outputs: Estimated color C(r) for the ray. Gradients \frac{\partial C}{\partial \theta} with respect to density field parameters \theta. Data Structures: Knots: A set of m+1 positions t0, t1, \dots, tm along the ray. In experiments, these are formed by slightly perturbing a uniform grid. Density Approximation: Piecewise linear interpolation of \sigmar(t) between knots. Let \sigmai = \sigmar(ti). The density at any t \in [ti, t{i+1}] is: \sigmar(t) = \sigmai \frac{t{i+1} - t}{t{i+1} - ti} + \sigma{i+1} \frac{t - ti}{t{i+1} - ti} Steps: 1. Approximate Density: Construct the piecewise linear approximation of \sigmar(t) using m knots. 2. Compute CDF Integral Approximation: Define the cumulative integral approximation I(t) = \int{t{r1}}^t \sigmar(s) ds. Since \sigmar is piecewise linear, I(t) is piecewise quadratic. Specifically, within bin i (t \in [ti, t{i+1}]), letting x = t - ti and \Delta t = t{i+1} - ti: I(t) = I(ti) + \sigmai x + \frac{\sigma{i+1} - \sigmai}{2 \Delta t} x^2 3. Generate Random Sample: Draw u \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 1]. 4. Compute Target Opacity: Calculate the target cumulative opacity value yf u. The source uses yf as a scaling factor, typically 1.0 for full opacity range. The equation is: yf u = Fr(t) = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{t{r1}}^t \sigmar(s) ds\right) 5. Rewrite Inversion Equation: Isolate the integral: -\log(1 - yf u) = \int{t{r1}}^t \sigmar(s) ds = I(t) Let Y = -\log(1 - yf u). We need to solve I(t) = Y for t. 6. Find Bin: Evaluate I(t) at the knots ti to find the interval [ti, t{i+1}] such that I(ti) \le Y < I(t{i+1}). Since I(t) is monotonic, this bin is unique. 7. Solve for t: Within the identified bin, solve the quadratic equation I(t) = Y for t. The explicit formula depends on the coefficients of the quadratic polynomial representing I(t) in that bin. The source notes that explicit formulae are provided in supplementary materials and that numerical stability is crucial. 8. Evaluate Radiance: Evaluate cr(t) at the computed sample position t. 9. Accumulate Color: Repeat steps 3-8 for k samples (using stratified sampling for lower variance) and accumulate the color estimate. The color estimate is: C(r) = \frac{1}{k} \sum{j=1}^k cr(tj) where weights are uniform because sampling is performed directly from the approximate CDF. The source states the estimate is unbiased. Parameters: k = 32 samples per ray. m = 256 knots. Activation function for density field: Softplus with \beta = 10. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradients: Using ReLU activation for the density field can result in zero gradients, hindering training. Numerical Stability: Solving the quadratic equation requires careful handling to ensure numerical stability, especially when Y is close to bin boundaries or when coefficients are small. Degenerate Distributions: Importance sampling requires only a few points for degenerate distributions, but the method is designed to work generally. Approximation Error: Piecewise constant approximation was faster but delivered worse rendering quality compared to piecewise linear. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def reparameterizedvolumesampling(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, densitynet, radiancenet, k=32, m=256): """ Performs reparameterized volume sampling for a single ray. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, origin of the ray. raydirection: (3,) array, direction of the ray. tnear: float, near plane distance. tfar: float, far plane distance. densitynet: callable, returns density sigma at 3D points. radiancenet: callable, returns radiance c at 3D points. k: int, number of samples per ray. m: int, number of knots for piecewise linear density approximation. Returns: color: (3,) array, estimated color. """ # 1. Normalize ray direction to ensure t represents physical distance d = raydirection / np.linalg.norm(raydirection) # 2. Define knots # Slightly perturb a uniform grid tuniform = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, m + 1) # Perturbation: Add small random noise to avoid degenerate cases noise = np.random.uniform(-1e-6, 1e-6, m + 1) tknots = tuniform + noise # 3. Evaluate density at knots # Sample points along the ray at knots pointsknots = rayorigin + tknots[:, None] d sigmaknots = densitynet(pointsknots).squeeze() # Shape (m+1,) # 4. Precompute integral values I(t) at knots # I(t) = integral from tnear to t of sigma(s) ds # Since sigma is piecewise linear, I(t) is piecewise quadratic. Iknots = np.zeros(m + 1) for i in range(m): ti = tknots[i] tip1 = tknots[i+1] sigmai = sigmaknots[i] sigmaip1 = sigmaknots[i+1] # Integral of linear function from ti to tip1 deltat = tip1 - ti integralbin = 0.5 (sigmai + sigmaip1) deltat Iknots[i+1] = Iknots[i] + integralbin # 5. Stratified sampling # Generate k stratified samples ustratified = (np.arange(1, k + 1) - 0.5) / k # 6. Compute target Y values # yf is 1.0 for full opacity range yf = 1.0 Y = -np.log(1.0 - yf ustratified) # Clamp Y to the maximum accumulated optical depth to handle boundary cases Y = np.minimum(Y, Iknots[-1]) # 7. Find bins and solve for t tsamples = np.zeros(k) for j in range(k): Yval = Y[j] # Find bin i such that Iknots[i] <= Yval < Iknots[i+1] i = np.searchsorted(Iknots, Yval, side='right') - 1 i = np.clip(i, 0, m - 1) ti = tknots[i] tip1 = tknots[i+1] sigmai = sigmaknots[i] sigmaip1 = sigmaknots[i+1] Ii = Iknots[i] # Solve I(t) = Yval for t in [ti, tip1] # I(t) = Ii + sigmai x + 0.5 slope x^2, where x = t - ti # 0.5 slope x^2 + sigmai x + (Ii - Yval) = 0 deltat = tip1 - ti slope = (sigmaip1 - sigmai) / deltat a = 0.5 slope b = sigmai c = Ii - Yval # Solve quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 if np.abs(a) < 1e-9: # Linear case (constant density) if np.abs(b) < 1e-9: x = 0.0 else: x = -c / b else: discriminant = b2 - 4ac if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0.0 sqrtdisc = np.sqrt(discriminant) # Use stable quadratic formula if b >= 0: x1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) x2 = (2c) / (-b - sqrtdisc) else: x1 = (2c) / (-b + sqrtdisc) x2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) # Select root in [0, deltat] if 0 <= x1 <= deltat: x = x1 elif 0 <= x2 <= deltat: x = x2 else: x = 0.0 tsamples[j] = ti + x # 8. Evaluate radiance and accumulate pointssamples = rayorigin + tsamples[:, None] d radiance = radiancenet(pointssamples) # Shape (k, 3) # Uniform weights because sampling is from the approximate CDF color = np.mean(radiance, axis=0) return color A sampling strategy modifying the density to include a constant background density \epsilon to prevent gradient outliers when \sigmat is near zero. The defensive sampling density is p{\text{def}}(t) = (\sigmat(t) + \epsilon) T\epsilon(t). The problematic term is bounded by \frac{1}{\sigmat(t) + \epsilon} \leq \frac{1}{\epsilon}. However, with p{\text{def}}, non-unit sampling weights compound over the length of the path, which is problematic in volumetric rendering where long paths are common. When using path replay backpropagation, defensive sampling must either be used for incident radiance terms (injecting variance) or additional samples must be drawn (increasing cost). Time Complexity: Dominated by the density and radiance network evaluations at k sample points and m knots. The root-finding step is O(k \log m) or O(k) with precomputed bins. Memory Complexity: O(m) to store knot positions and integral values. Measured Performance: In the 'foggy' density field test, 32 samples matched the baseline performance of 128 samples. In 'Glass and wall' and 'Wall' density fields, 4 samples matched the baseline performance. Scaling: The method scales with the number of knots m and samples k. Strengths: Lower variance compared to standard importance sampling with uniform distribution. End-to-end differentiable without auxiliary networks. Limitations: Requires careful numerical implementation for stability. Piecewise linear approximation is more complex than piecewise constant. When to use: When differentiable sampling is required and lower variance is desired compared to uniform importance sampling. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and piecewise constant approximation is acceptable (though quality suffers). Reparameterized Volume Sampling was introduced in the paper "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling" (DVGO). It builds on the reparameterization estimator principles. The method was applied to 3D scene reconstruction based on a set of image projections, using the synthetic data from NeRF. It was compared against NeRF and DVGO baselines. name: Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering
head: R/MC, R/MC estimate, R/SMC estimate, Reparameterized Stratified Monte Carlo (R/SMC) Volume Rendering
body: Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering (R/MC) is a differentiable volume rendering method that estimates expected radiance by sampling from the density-induced probability distribution using the reparameterization trick, allowing end-to-end gradient-based optimization without auxiliary models. It sets itself apart from standard volumetric integration by transforming the integration domain from ray distance t to cumulative opacity y, enabling unbiased gradient estimation through the inverse opacity function. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin o, direction d, near bound tn, far bound tf, density field \sigma(x), radiance field c(x). Outputs: Estimated radiance \hat{C} for the ray. Data Structures: Ray: Defined as r(t) = o + td. Density Field: \sigmar(t) = \sigma(o + td). Radiance Field: cr(t) = c(o + td). Opacity Function: Fr(t) = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigmar(s) ds\right). Total Opacity: yf = Fr(tf). Steps: 1. Define the ray r = o + td with near/far bounds tn, tf. 2. Define the density field \sigma and radiance field c. 3. Compute the total opacity yf = Fr(tf) = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s) ds\right). 4. Generate k independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples ui \sim U[0,1] for R/MC, or stratified samples vi for R/SMC. 5. For each sample, compute the target cumulative opacity yi = yf ui (or yf vi). 6. Solve for the ray distance ti such that Fr(ti) = yi using the inverse opacity function Fr^{-1}. 7. Query the radiance cr(ti) at the computed distances. 8. Compute the estimate \hat{C} = \frac{yf}{k} \sum{i=1}^k cr(ti). Formulas: The integral boundaries are normalized to [0, 1] by substituting y = yf u where u \sim U[0,1]: \int{0}^{yf} cr(Fr^{-1}(y)) dy = \int0^1 yf cr(Fr^{-1}(yf u)) du The R/MC estimate for a ray r with k i.i.d. uniform samples u1,..., uk \sim U[0,1] is: \hat{C}{MC}^R(r):= \frac{yf}{k} \sum{i=1}^k cr(Fr^{-1}(yf ui)) The R/SMC estimate replaces uniform samples ui with stratified samples vi drawn from regular grid bins: vi \sim U\left[\frac{i-1}{k+1}, \frac{i}{k+1}\right] \quad \text{for } i=1,...,k The estimate is: \hat{C}{SMC}^R(r):= \frac{yf}{k} \sum{i=1}^k cr(Fr^{-1}(yf vi)) Parameters: k: Number of samples per ray. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Pitfalls: The method cannot compute Fr analytically in practice because \sigmar is only queried at discrete points, requiring approximations of Fr and its inverse Fr^{-1}. The sources do not specify the numerical method for approximating Fr and Fr^{-1} (e.g., piecewise constant vs. linear interpolation, root-finding algorithms). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reparameterizedmcvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, densityfield, radiancefield, numsamples): """ Estimates radiance for a ray using Reparameterized Monte Carlo Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), assumed normalized tnear: float, near bound of the ray tfar: float, far bound of the ray densityfield: function p -> float, returns density at point p radiancefield: function p -> float, returns radiance at point p numsamples: int, number of samples k Returns: float, estimated radiance """ # Simple deterministic uniform random number generator def uniformrandom(): nonlocal rngstate rngstate = (rngstate 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff return rngstate / 0x7fffffff rngstate = 42 # Initial seed # Step 3: Compute total opacity yf totaldensityintegral = numericalintegratedensity(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar) yf = 1.0 - math.exp(-totaldensityintegral) # Handle degenerate case where the ray is completely transparent if yf == 0.0: return 0.0 radiancesum = 0.0 for in range(numsamples): # Step 4 & 5: Generate sample and compute target cumulative opacity u = uniformrandom() ytarget = yf u # Step 6: Solve for ray distance ti such that Fr(ti) = ytarget # Fr(t) = 1 - exp(-int{tnear}^t sigmar(s) ds) # ytarget = 1 - exp(-int{tnear}^t sigmar(s) ds) # int{tnear}^t sigmar(s) ds = -ln(1 - ytarget) targetdensityintegral = -math.log(1.0 - ytarget) # Binary search to invert the cumulative density integral ti = invertopacityfunction(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, targetdensityintegral) # Step 7: Query radiance at the sampled point point = rayorigin + ti raydirection radiance = radiancefield(point) radiancesum += radiance # Step 8: Compute estimate estimate = (yf / numsamples) radiancesum return estimate def numericalintegratedensity(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend): """ Approximates the integral of density along the ray from tstart to tend. Trapezoidal rule approximation. """ numsteps = 100 dt = (tend - tstart) / numsteps integral = 0.0 for j in range(numsteps): t1 = tstart + j dt t2 = tstart + (j + 1) dt p1 = rayorigin + t1 raydirection p2 = rayorigin + t2 raydirection sigma1 = densityfield(p1) sigma2 = densityfield(p2) integral += (sigma1 + sigma2) / 2.0 dt return integral def invertopacityfunction(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, targetintegral): """ Finds t such that the integral of density from tnear to t equals targetintegral. Uses binary search as a robust root-finding method for monotonic functions. """ tlow = tnear thigh = tfar for in range(50): tmid = (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 currentintegral = numericalintegratedensity(densityfield, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tmid) if currentintegral < targetintegral: tlow = tmid else: thigh = tmid return (tlow + thigh) / 2.0 Time Complexity: O(k \cdot N{steps}) per ray, where k is the number of samples and N{steps} is the number of steps in the numerical integration and root-finding procedures. The sources do not specify N{steps}. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, assuming the density and radiance fields are queried on the fly. Measured Performance: The sources do not provide measured performance metrics. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of samples k. Strengths: Allows end-to-end learning with gradient descent; alleviates costs associated with the color component of the neural radiance field at the additional cost of the density sampling algorithm. Limitations: Requires approximations of Fr and its inverse Fr^{-1}, which can be computationally expensive and introduce approximation errors. When to use: When differentiable volume rendering is required and the density field is available. When not to use: When analytical computation of Fr and Fr^{-1} is not possible and numerical approximations are too costly. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling". History and Development: The paper introduces the reparameterization of the sampling algorithm to allow end-to-end learning with gradient descent. Where it is used: Learning-based approaches for representing 3D scenes and generating novel views. name: Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE
head: Differential NEE estimator, MIS-weighted differential path estimator
body: This method computes the gradient of the rendered image with respect to scene parameters \theta by integrating differential measurement contributions over path space. It solves the problem of high variance in gradient estimation for specular materials and complex lighting by combining standard BRDF sampling with Next Event Estimation (NEE) using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Unlike standard NEE which only connects paths to emitters at the final vertex, this method allows the differential vertex (the location where the derivative is taken) to be located at any intermediate vertex i or at the emitter connection, combining BRDF and emitter sampling probabilities into a single mixture weight. It builds on Reparameterization Estimators by applying the reparameterization principle to path-space integrals with explicit MIS weights for discontinuous contributions. Inputs: Scene parameters \theta (e.g., material roughness, light intensity, geometry). Camera configuration. Number of samples per pixel M. Maximum path depth N. Probability q of switching to differential sampling at each vertex. Outputs: Gradient estimate \hat{\nabla}\theta I{\text{NEE}}. Data Structures: Path x = (x0, x1, \dots, xN), where x0 is the camera position and xk are surface/media vertices. Emitter connection path xj x{e,j}, where xj is a vertex on the main path and x{e,j} is a point on an emitter. Differential contribution g(x, i; \theta) for vertex i on path x. Differential contribution g(x, xj x{e,j}, i; \theta) for vertex i on path x connected to emitter at j. Steps: 1. Initialize gradient accumulator G = 0. 2. For each sample m = 1 \dots M: a. Generate a standard path x^m of depth N using BRDF sampling. b. Compute the mixture probability p{\text{mix}}(x^m) using Equation (41). c. For each vertex i = 0 \dots N: i. Compute the differential contribution g(x^m, i; \theta). ii. Add \frac{g(x^m, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m)} to G. d. For each vertex j = 1 \dots N-1: i. Generate an NEE path x^mj x^m{e,j} by connecting vertex x^mj to an emitter. ii. Compute the mixture probability p{\text{mix}}(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}) using Equation (42). iii. For each vertex i = 0 \dots j: 1. Compute the differential contribution g(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}, i; \theta). 2. Add \frac{g(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j})} to G. 3. Return G / M. Formulas: The gradient estimator is given by: \partial\theta I{\text{NEE}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M \left[ \sum{i=0}^{N} \frac{g(x^m, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m)} + \sum{j=1}^{N-1} \sum{i=0}^j \frac{g(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j}, i; \theta)}{p{\text{mix}}(x^m, x^mj x^m{e,j})} \right] The differential contribution for a standard path x with differential vertex i is derived from the expansion of \partial\theta I in Eq (35): g(x, i; \theta) = \left( \prod{k=0, k \neq i}^{N} fk(x) \right) \frac{\partial\theta fi(x)}{fi(x)} Le(xN) The differential contribution for an NEE path x, xj x{e,j} with differential vertex i is: g(x, xj x{e,j}, i; \theta) = \left[ \prod{k=1}^{j-1} fk(x) \right] G(xj, x{e,j}) \rhos(x{j-1}, xj, x{e,j}) \cdot \frac{\partial\theta fi(x)}{fi(x)} \cdot Le(x{e,j}) where: fk(x) is the BSDF at vertex xk. G(xj, x{e,j}) is the geometry term between xj and the emitter point x{e,j}. \rhos(x{j-1}, xj, x{e,j}) is the shadow term (visibility) between x{j-1} and x{e,j} via xj. Le(x{e,j}) is the radiance from the emitter at x{e,j}. The mixture probability for a standard path x is: p{\text{mix}}(x) = p(x) + \sum{i=1}^{N-1} p(x, i) + p{\text{nee}}(x, x{N-1}xN) where p(x) is the probability of generating x via BRDF sampling, p(x, i) is the probability of generating x with differential vertex i via BRDF sampling, and p{\text{nee}}(x, x{N-1}xN) is the probability of generating x with an NEE connection at the last vertex. The mixture probability for an NEE path x, xj x{e,j} is: p{\text{mix}}(x, xj x{e,j}) = p(x, xj x{e,j}) + \sum{i=1}^j p(x, xj x{e,j}, i) + p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}) + \sum{i=1}^{j-1} p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}, i) The probability of generating the NEE path with differential vertex i (1 \le i < j) via BRDF sampling is: p(x, xj x{e,j}, i) = \begin{cases} p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}) \frac{pf(x{j-1}xj x{e,j})}{pe(xj x{e,j})} & \text{if } 1 \le i < j \\ p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}) \frac{p{\partial f}(x{j-1}xj x{e,j})}{pe(xj x{e,j})} & \text{if } i = j \end{cases} The probability of generating the NEE path with differential vertex i (1 \le i < j) via differential sampling is: p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}, i) = \frac{\prod{k=0}^{j-1} pf(xk)}{pf(xi)} p{\partial f}(xi) (1-q)^{i-1} q where pf(xk) is the BRDF sampling probability at vertex k, p{\partial f}(xi) is the differential sampling probability at vertex i, and q is the switching probability. The probability of generating the NEE path without a specific differential vertex (standard NEE) is: p{\text{nee}}(x, xj x{e,j}) = \left[ \prod{k=0}^{j-1} pf(xk) \right] pe(xj x{e,j}) (1-q)^{j-1} where pe(xj x{e,j}) is the emitter sampling probability. Parameters: q: Probability of switching to differential sampling at each vertex. Typical values are not given in the sources. M: Number of independent samples drawn per pixel. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: Division by p{\text{mix}} can lead to numerical instability if the probability is very small. Guard against division by zero. Boundaries: The sums for i and j have specific ranges. Ensure indices are within bounds. Degenerate input: If N=1, the loops for j may be empty. Handle accordingly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentialpathintegralestimatorwithmisandnee(sceneparams, camera, M, N, q): gradientaccumulator = 0.0 for in range(M): # 1. Generate standard path x of depth N using BRDF sampling x = [camera.position] fprobs = [] for k in range(N): x.append(samplebsdfandintersect(sceneparams, x[-1])) fprobs.append(getbsdfsamplingprob(x[-1])) # 2. Compute mixture probability pmix(x) px = 1.0 for p in fprobs: px = p sumpxi = 0.0 for i in range(1, N): pdiff = getdifferentialsamplingprob(x[i], q, fprobs[i]) sumpxi += px (pdiff / fprobs[i]) ((1 - q) (i - 1)) q pneelast = px getemittersamplingprob(x[N-1]) ((1 - q) (N - 1)) pmixx = px + sumpxi + pneelast # 3. Accumulate standard path contributions for i in range(N + 1): g = computegstandard(x, i, fprobs, sceneparams) gradientaccumulator += g / pmixx # 4. Accumulate NEE path contributions for i in range(j + 1): gnee = computegnee(x, j, xee, i, fprobs, pe, sceneparams) gradientaccumulator += gnee / pmixnee return gradientaccumulator / M def computegstandard(path, i, fprobs, sceneparams): prodexcepti = 1.0 for k, p in enumerate(fprobs): if k != i: prodexcepti = p if i < len(fprobs): diffratio = getbsdfderiv(path[i], i) / fprobs[i] else: diffratio = 0.0 return prodexcepti diffratio getemitterradiance(path[-1]) def computegnee(path, j, xee, i, fprobs, pe, sceneparams): prodexcepti = 1.0 for k in range(1, j): if k != i: prodexcepti = fprobs[k] geoterm = computegeometryterm(path[j], xee) shadowterm = computeshadowterm(path[j-1], path[j], xee) if i < len(fprobs): diffratio = getbsdfderiv(path[i], i) / fprobs[i] else: diffratio = 0.0 return prodexcepti geoterm shadowterm diffratio getemitterradiance(xee) Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS is a method to estimate the gradient of a loss function with respect to scene parameters by importance sampling an intermediate path vertex as the differential vertex. See Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS. It solves the problem that standard Monte Carlo estimators fail to capture derivatives at boundaries where visibility changes abruptly, such as object silhouettes and occlusion edges. Unlike its sibling Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which focuses on vertex-based contributions, this method decomposes the rendering derivative into a smooth interior integral (estimated via automatic differentiation) and a boundary integral (estimated by sampling triangle edges). See Differential Edge Sampling. This method reduces the variance of gradient estimates in differentiable volume rendering by sampling pairs of similar paths and applying a control variate technique known as the cross-weighting scheme. It allows the use of suitable parameter values from one path estimate to reduce the variance of the other without introducing bias, addressing the high variance inherent in estimating derivatives of discontinuous integrands. It builds on Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE by providing a specific variance reduction strategy for the differential contributions computed therein. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly integrating reparameterization gradients into the path sampling loop, allowing for stable gradient flow through the SDF evaluation and sphere tracing steps, whereas siblings like Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS rely on vertex perturbation and Differential Edge Sampling on edge perturbations. See SDF Prb Reparam Integrator. This approach effectively shares all paths traced by Algorithm 1 to calculate derivatives with respect to all scene parameters simultaneously. It executes Algorithm 1 once in a vectorized fashion to estimate the total scene derivative d\pi L. It replaces all partial derivatives with their vector-valued total derivative counterparts and performs component-wise calculations between all total-derivative-related quantities. Time Complexity: The method requires tracing additional side paths for NEE, making it more expensive than conventional path tracing. The time complexity is O(K^2) for each sample path of length K, due to the additional side paths needed to estimate \Delta L and L{ins}. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces variance for specular materials and complex lighting by combining BRDF and emitter sampling. Allows differential vertex to be at any intermediate vertex or emitter connection. Limitations: More expensive than conventional path tracing due to additional side paths. When to use: Differentiable rendering, inverse rendering, and joint material/lighting estimation. Gkioulekas, "Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering". It is used for differentiable rendering, inverse rendering, and joint material/lighting estimation. head: Differential sampling with MIS
body: Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS is a method to estimate the gradient of a loss function with respect to scene parameters by importance sampling an intermediate path vertex as the differential vertex. It solves the problem of high variance in gradient estimation, particularly for specular materials, by combining differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). Unlike standard BRDF sampling, which treats all vertices identically, this method explicitly biases the sampling distribution to capture the boundary component of the gradient integral, significantly reducing variance for microfacet and mixture BRDFs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Path vertex state (position, incoming direction, throughput), scene parameters \theta, mixing probability q, random number generator. Outputs: Accumulated gradient update \delta\theta, updated throughput \beta, updated MIS weights w1, w2. Data Structures: sampled∂x: Boolean flag indicating if the differential vertex has been sampled for the current path vertex. w1, w2: MIS weights for the differential and standard sampling strategies, respectively. β: Throughput term, which includes the product of densities pf from the mixture probability. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize sampled∂x to FALSE for the current path vertex. 2. Generate a random number R. 3. If !sampled∂x AND R < q: a. Sample the differential vertex: (\omega', f) = \text{SAMPLE\∂BRDF}(\text{state}). b. Set sampled∂x to TRUE. c. Compute the gradient update: \delta\theta \leftarrow \delta\theta + \text{BACKWARD\GRAD}(f, \delta L \cdot L/f). 4. Else (if differential vertex was not sampled): a. Sample the standard BRDF vertex: (\omega', f) = \text{SAMPLE\BRDF}(\text{state}). b. Update throughput: \beta \leftarrow \beta \cdot \frac{f}{pf(\omega', \text{state})}. c. Update MIS weights: w1 \leftarrow w1 + w2 \cdot q \cdot \frac{p{\partial f}(\omega', \text{state})}{pf(\omega', \text{state})} w2 \leftarrow w2 \cdot (1 - q) 5. Return the accumulated gradient \delta\theta. The method integrates with Next Event Estimation (NEE), though NEE steps are omitted from the pseudocode for simplicity. Formulas: The mixture probability p{\text{mix}}(x) for a path x is defined as: p{\text{mix}}(x) = \left( \prod{i=0}^{N} pf(xi) \right) \left( \sum{i=1}^{N-1} p{\partial f}(xi) (1-q)^{i-1} q + (1-q)^{N-1} \right) The MIS weights are updated as follows: w1 \leftarrow w1 + w2 \cdot q \cdot \frac{p{\partial f}(\omega', \text{state})}{pf(\omega', \text{state})} w2 \leftarrow w2 \cdot (1 - q) The gradient update is computed as: \delta\theta \leftarrow \delta\theta + \text{BACKWARD\GRAD}(f, \delta L \cdot L/f) Parameters: q: The probability of sampling the differential vertex at the current step instead of the standard BRDF vertex. Typical value: 0.5. This value balances early vertex contributions (higher q) with indirect lighting contributions from later vertices. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The mixture probability involves products of densities, which can lead to underflow or overflow if not handled carefully. Boundaries: The method integrates with Next Event Estimation (NEE), but NEE steps are omitted from the pseudocode. Degenerate Input: If q=0, the method degenerates to standard BRDF sampling. If q=1, it degenerates to differential vertex sampling only. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentialvertexsamplingwithmis( state, q, rng, samplepartialbrdf, samplebrdf, backwardgrad, ppartialf, pf, deltaL, L, beta, w1, w2, deltatheta): sampledpartialx = False R = rng.next() if not sampledpartialx and R < q: omegaprime, f = samplepartialbrdf(state) sampledpartialx = True deltatheta += backwardgrad(f, deltaL (L / f)) else: omegaprime, f = samplebrdf(state) beta = f / pf(omegaprime, state) w1 += w2 q ppartialf(omegaprime, state) / pf(omegaprime, state) w2 = (1 - q) return deltatheta This method estimates the boundary component of the gradient integral in differentiable rendering by combining Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) with primary-sample-space guiding. It addresses the high variance in gradient estimates caused by occlusion and complex illumination, which makes standard light sampling ineffective for boundary segments. Unlike its parent method, Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which uses MIS to combine differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling, this method uses MIS to combine two distinct strategies for sampling the boundary segment's direction: light sampling and direct direction sampling. It sets itself apart from baseline methods by producing significantly cleaner gradient estimates at equal time and sample counts, particularly around shadow boundaries. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method reduces gradient variance significantly, especially for specular BRDFs. For microfacet BRDFs, it reduces variance to 0.69–0.84× of BRDF sampling with NEE; for mixture BRDFs, to 0.0048–0.042×. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant variance reduction for specular and mixture BRDFs. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When estimating gradients for differentiable rendering with specular or mixture BRDFs, especially where standard BRDF sampling yields high variance. When not: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method is described in "Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering" by T. Su & I. Gkioulekas. History and Development: The method is part of a broader set of path sampling methods for differentiable rendering, aiming to improve the efficiency of gradient estimation. Where it is used: Differentiable rendering, inverse rendering. Path Sampling Methods for Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/sr.20241148, fetched 2026-10-29
