name: Primary-Sample-Space Guided MIS with Edge Sorting
head: Boundary Path Integral Estimation, Primary-Sample-Space Guiding with Multiple Importance Sampling and Edge Sorting, Guided boundary integral estimation, MIS with light and direction sampling, Primary-Sample-Space Guiding with Multiple Importance Sampling, Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering, Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering with MIS and Edge Sorting
body: This method estimates the boundary component of the gradient integral in differentiable rendering by combining multiple importance sampling (MIS) with primary-sample-space guiding. It addresses high variance in gradient estimates caused by occlusion and complex illumination, which makes standard light sampling ineffective for boundary segments. Unlike its parent method, Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which uses MIS to combine differential vertex sampling with standard BRDF sampling, this method uses MIS to combine light sampling and direction sampling for the boundary segment. It sets itself apart from baseline methods like Zhang et al. (2020) by producing significantly cleaner gradient estimates at equal time and sample counts, particularly around shadow boundaries. Inputs: A polygonal mesh M, a camera, a light environment, and target functions \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and \tilde{F}{\text{dir}} derived from the boundary integral formulation. Outputs: Unbiased estimators for the boundary integral component of the gradient. 1. Kd-trees: Two Kd-trees are built during preprocessing, one for \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and one for \tilde{F}{\text{dir}}. Each leaf node stores a probability mass. 2. Edge Chains: A list of chains, where each chain is a sequence of mesh edges constructed via edge sorting. 1. Edge Sorting: To reduce discontinuities in the mapping from primary samples to mesh edges, build chains of mesh edges. Start with an arbitrary edge (v0, v1). Initialize chain with this edge. Set v{\text{prev}} = v0, v{\text{cur}} = v1. While v{\text{cur}} has unused edges: Select an unused edge (v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{next}}) such that the direction of (v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{next}}) is closest to (v{\text{prev}}, v{\text{cur}}). Append (v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{next}}) to chain. Update v{\text{prev}} = v{\text{cur}}, v{\text{cur}} = v{\text{next}}. Repeat for all edges to form a set of chains. 2. Guiding: Apply primary-sample-space guiding to \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and \tilde{F}{\text{dir}} to build the Kd-trees. 3. Normalization: Compute normalization constants c{\text{light}} and c{\text{dir}} by summing the probability masses stored in all leaf nodes of the respective Kd-trees. 1. Target Functions: Calculate the target functions for light and direction sampling: \tilde{F}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}1, \mathbf{u}2) = \left| \hat{f}^B(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \right|{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}1, \mathbf{u}2) \hat{h}^S(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \hat{h}^D(\mathbf{p}0^S, \mathbf{p}0^D) \tilde{F}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2) = \left| \tilde{F}^B(\mathbf{p}0^D, \mathbf{p}0^D) \right| F{\text{dir}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2) \tilde{h}^S(\mathbf{p}0^D, \mathbf{p}0^D) \tilde{h}^D(\mathbf{p}0^D, \mathbf{p}0^D) where \mathbf{p}0^S and \mathbf{p}0^D are determined by the boundary segment direction \omegaB. Note that \mathbf{p}0^S and \mathbf{p}0^D take different values in these equations for the same primary sample (u1, \mathbf{u}2) because they are determined by different \omegaB mappings. 2. Sampling: Draw two sets of primary samples: (u1^{\text{light}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{light}}) from density p{\text{light}} (guided by \tilde{F}{\text{light}}). (u1^{\text{dir}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{dir}}) from density p{\text{dir}} (guided by \tilde{F}{\text{dir}}). 3. Estimators: Compute two unbiased estimators of the boundary integral: E{\text{light}} = \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{light}}(u1^{\text{light}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{light}})}{p{\text{light}}(u1^{\text{light}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{light}})} E{\text{dir}} = \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{dir}}(u1^{\text{dir}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{dir}})}{p{\text{dir}}(u1^{\text{dir}}, \mathbf{u}2^{\text{dir}})} 4. Rewritten Densities: Rewrite the probability densities with respect to xB and \omegaB using Jacobians J{\text{light}}^B and J{\text{dir}}^B: \hat{p}{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2):= \frac{p{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{J{\text{light}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2):= \frac{p{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{J{\text{dir}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} 5. Approximation: Approximate the rewritten densities using the target functions and normalization constants: \hat{p}{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2) \approx \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{light}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{c{\text{light}} J{\text{light}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2) \approx \frac{\tilde{F}{\text{dir}}(u1, \mathbf{u}2)}{c{\text{dir}} J{\text{dir}}^B(u1, \mathbf{u}2)} This approximation allows O(1) calculation of the densities. 6. MIS Weighting: Apply the balance heuristic to weight the contributions: w{\text{light}} = \frac{\hat{p}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{light}})}{\hat{p}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{light}}) + \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{light}})} w{\text{dir}} = \frac{\hat{p}{\text{dir}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{dir}})}{\hat{p}{\text{light}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{dir}}) + \hat{p}{\text{dir}}(\mathbf{u}^{\text{dir}})} The final estimator is w{\text{light}} E{\text{light}} + w{\text{dir}} E{\text{dir}}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocess(mesh, Flightfunc, Fdirfunc): chains = [] unusededges = set(getalledges(mesh)) while unusededges: startedge = unusededges.pop() chain = [startedge] vprev, vcur = startedge while vcur in unusededges: candidates = [e for e in unusededges if e[0] == vcur] if not candidates: break vnext = min(candidates, key=lambda e: anglebetween(e[1] - vcur, chain[-1][1] - chain[-1][0]))[1] edge = (vcur, vnext) chain.append(edge) unusededges.discard(edge) vprev, vcur = vcur, vnext chains.append(chain) kdlight = buildkdtree(Flightfunc, chains) kddir = buildkdtree(Fdirfunc, chains) clight = sum(kdlight.leafnodes) cdir = sum(kddir.leafnodes) return kdlight, kddir, clight, cdir def render(kdlight, kddir, clight, cdir, mesh, camera, lightenv): u1light, u2light = samplefromkd(kdlight) u1dir, u2dir = samplefromkd(kddir) omegaBlight = getdirectionfromlight(u1light, u2light, mesh, lightenv) omegaBdir = getdirectionfromdir(u1dir, u2dir, mesh) p0Slight, p0Dlight = getboundarypoints(omegaBlight, mesh) p0Sdir, p0Ddir = getboundarypoints(omegaBdir, mesh) Flight = abs(FhatB(p0Slight, p0Dlight)) hhatS(p0Slight, p0Dlight) hhatD(p0Slight, p0Dlight) Fdir = abs(FtildeB(p0Ddir, p0Ddir)) FdirB(u1dir, u2dir) htildeS(p0Ddir, p0Ddir) htildeD(p0Ddir, p0Ddir) plight = evaluatekd(kdlight, u1light, u2light) pdir = evaluatekd(kddir, u1dir, u2dir) Elight = Flight / plight Edir = Fdir / pdir Jlight = computejacobianlight(u1light, u2light, omegaBlight) Jdir = computejacobiandir(u1dir, u2dir, omegaBdir) phatlight = Flight / (clight Jlight) phatdir = Fdir / (cdir Jdir) phatdiratlight = Fdir(u1light, u2light) / (cdir computejacobiandir(u1light, u2light, getdirectionfromdir(u1light, u2light, mesh))) phatlightatdir = Flight(u1dir, u2dir) / (clight computejacobianlight(u1dir, u2dir, getdirectionfromlight(u1dir, u2dir, mesh, lightenv))) wlight = phatlight / (phatlight + phatdiratlight) wdir = phatdir / (phatlightatdir + phatdir) return wlight Elight + wdir Edir c{\text{light}}, c{\text{dir}}: Normalization constants from Kd-tree leaf sums. Hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper Pro 3975WX CPU, Nvidia RTX Titan. Occlusion: Light sampling can be ineffective for complex illumination (e.g., image-based lighting) because the sampled direction \omegaB may be invalid due to occlusion, causing the boundary segment to penetrate the object. Discontinuities: Highly discontinuous target functions cause Kd-trees to require large depths, degrading performance. This is mostly caused by discontinuities of xB as a function of u1. Edge sorting mitigates this. Rough Dielectrics: Warped-area sampling implementation does not support rough dielectric BSDF, requiring diffuse objects for certain evaluations. Shadow Boundaries: Direction sampling results in cleaner overall results but estimated gradients around shadow boundaries become slightly worse. MIS combines both to handle this. Participating Media: The technique focuses on surface-only light transport and does not currently support participating media, where the primary-sample space dimensionality increases from three to five. Time Complexity: \tilde{F}{\text{light}} and \tilde{F}{\text{dir}} can be calculated in O(1) time in the approximation equation. Memory Complexity: Guiding memory ranges from 80 KB to 4 MB depending on scene complexity. Performance: Dodoco: 70 target images, 450,000 parameters, batch size 2, 3000 iterations. Guiding memory 4 MB, guiding time 1.34 s, render time 2.59 s, postproc time 0.310 s. Jumpy Dumpty: 140 target images, 60,000 parameters, batch size 2, 520 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.61 s, render time 1.11 s, postproc time 0.016 s. Klee: 40 target images, 60,000 parameters, batch size 1, 200 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.33 s, render time 0.82 s, postproc time 0.016 s. Kirby: 35 target images, 15,000 parameters, batch size 1, 400 iterations. Guiding memory 80 KB, guiding time 0.91 s, render time 3.67 s, postproc time 0.017 s. Bunny in glass: 50 target images, 30,000 parameters, batch size 2, 2000 iterations. Guiding memory 128 KB, guiding time 1.79 s, render time 17.55 s, postproc time 0.022 s. Bunny shadow 2: 70 target images, 30,000 parameters, batch size 2, 600 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.47 s, render time 0.72 s, postproc time 0.012 s. Duck: 35 target images, 3,205,728 parameters, batch size 1, 400 iterations. Guiding memory 2 MB, guiding time 0.34 s, render time 0.94 s, postproc time 0.092 s. Mora: 70 target images, 150,001 parameters, batch size 1, 1600 iterations. Guiding memory 4 MB, guiding time 0.43 s, render time 1.01 s, postproc time 0.109 s. Glass Dodoco: 140 target images, 60,000 parameters, batch size 1, 700 iterations. Guiding memory 400 KB, guiding time 0.94 s, render time 5.76 s, postproc time 0.093 s. Strengths: Produces significantly cleaner gradient estimates than Zhang et al. (2020) at equal time and sample counts. Significantly faster and lower noise than Warped-Area Sampling (WAS) at equal sample counts, with greater quality advantage at equal time. Yields significantly lower noise around shadow boundaries, resulting in better geometry reconstruction in non-line-of-sight configurations. Faster convergence than Zhang et al. due to lower variance boundary integral estimates. Limitations: Does not support participating media. Direction sampling alone performs worse around shadow boundaries. Origin: The method was introduced in "Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering". It builds on the baseline method by Zhang et al. (2020) for estimating the interior term of the gradient integral. History: Zhang et al. (2020) introduced the baseline method for estimating the interior term of Eq. 3.3 and was compared against in inverse-rendering experiments. Nicolet et al. (2021) introduced the method used to update mesh vertex positions based on estimated gradients. Usage: Used in inverse-rendering problems, particularly where remeshing can be applied to make input meshes field-aligned. Used in inverse-rendering optimizations for scenes including Dodoco, Jumpy Dumpty, Klee, Kirby, Bunny in glass, Bunny shadow 2, Duck, Mora, and Glass Dodoco. Efficient estimation of boundary integrals for path-space differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530080, fetched 2026-10-28 Variance-aware Differentiable Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/337282320, fetched 2026-11-02 (unofficial)

name: Differential Edge Sampling
head: Boundary Path Integral Estimation via Edge Sampling, Differential Spherical Integral / Edge Sampling, LADL18, Li et al, Monte Carlo edge sampling, Stochastic Monte Carlo Gradient Estimation
body: Differential Edge Sampling computes the gradient of physically-based rendered images with respect to arbitrary scene parameters (camera, lights, materials, geometry) by explicitly sampling visibility discontinuities. It solves the problem that standard Monte Carlo estimators fail to capture derivatives at boundaries where visibility changes abruptly, such as object silhouettes and occlusion edges. Unlike its sibling Differential Vertex Sampling with MIS, which focuses on vertex-based contributions, this method decomposes the rendering derivative into a smooth interior integral (estimated via automatic differentiation) and a boundary integral (estimated by sampling triangle edges). The method computes the gradient of the pixel filter’s integral by splitting the integrand into smooth and discontinuous regions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry (triangle meshes), material properties, light sources, camera parameters, and scene parameters \theta to differentiate with respect to. Outputs: Rendered image value and its gradient \nabla\theta I. Data Structures: Mesh Representation: Triangle meshes where discontinuities are identified at triangle edges. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Edge Hierarchy: A spatial hierarchy used to efficiently reject interior edges and find silhouette edges for secondary boundaries. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Split the rendering integral into smooth parts and discontinuous parts. 2. Smooth Region Estimation: For smooth parts of the integrand, employ traditional area sampling combined with automatic differentiation to estimate the gradient. 3. Discontinuous Region Estimation (Edge Sampling): For discontinuous parts, explicitly sample edges to estimate the boundary integral contribution. Primary Boundaries: For boundaries directly observed by the detector (camera), project and clip all meshes into screen space and sample from the visible edges. Secondary Boundaries: For boundaries occurring at light bounces, the silhouette depends on the shading point. Use an importance sampling scheme with a hierarchy to quickly reject interior edges and find the relevant silhouette, avoiding per-bounce projection. 4. Combination: Combine the gradient estimates from smooth and discontinuous regions. Formulas: The rendering equation derivative is decomposed into an interior integral and a boundary integral. For mesh scenes, discontinuities occur at triangle edges. If shading is smooth, the focus narrows to silhouette edges. The complete equation for differentiating the radiative transfer equation (extended by Zhang et al. for volumes) is Lo = KT KC Li + Q, where Lo is outgoing radiance, KT is the transport operator, KC is the collision operator, Li is incoming radiance, and Q is the source term. Due to complexity, the specific derivative formula is referenced as Eq. 32 in the original paper. Parameters: Sampling Strategy: Importance sampling for secondary boundaries using a hierarchy. Assumptions: Meshes do not have interpenetration, no point light sources, no perfectly specular surfaces, and the scene is static. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpenetration: The method assumes meshes do not interpenetrate. Light Sources: Point light sources are not supported. Specular Surfaces: Perfectly specular surfaces are not supported. Dynamic Scenes: The scene must be static. Variance: Large variance in estimated gradients due to the difficulty of finding all object edges and sampling them. Performance: Rendering speed is slow. Secondary Boundaries: Inefficient to project for every light bounce due to shading-point-dependent silhouettes. Time Complexity: Slow rendering speed due to the computational cost of finding all object edges and sampling them. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Variance: Large variance in estimated gradients. Strengths: First method to achieve unbiased differentiation of the rendering equation for mesh scenes by explicitly handling discontinuities. Limitations: Limited to static scenes, no point lights, no perfect speculars, and high computational cost. When to Use: When unbiased gradients with respect to geometry and camera parameters are required for mesh-based scenes, and computational resources allow for high-variance, low-speed estimation. When Not to Use: For dynamic scenes, scenes with point lights or perfect speculars, or when real-time performance is required. Differential Edge Sampling was introduced by Li et al. in 2018 [LADL18] as the first work to compute derivatives of scalar functions over physically-based rendered images with respect to arbitrary input parameters using a stochastic Monte Carlo ray tracing approach. It achieved unbiased differentiation of the rendering equation [Kaj86] by directly sampling boundary discontinuities. Zhang et al. [ZWZ 19] later extended this method to support participating media by differentiating the radiative transfer equation. This work laid the foundation for path-space differentiable rendering (PSDR). name: Boundary Sampling Methods
body:
Boundary sampling methods are a category of physics-based differentiable rendering (PBDR) techniques that handle discontinuities in the rendering integrand by partitioning the domain and explicitly sampling geometric boundaries (edges) where discontinuities occur, rather than reparameterizing the integral domain. They solve the problem of computing gradients for scenes with triangle meshes where automatic differentiation fails due to discontinuous visibility and shading. Unlike reparameterization methods, which transform the integration domain to smooth out discontinuities, boundary sampling methods decompose the gradient into an interior integral (estimated via auto-diff) and a boundary integral (estimated by explicitly sampling visibility discontinuities). Inputs: Scene geometry (triangle meshes), scene parameters \pi (e.g., vertex positions, material properties), camera parameters, and the rendering equation for pixel intensity I. Outputs: The gradient of the pixel intensity with respect to the scene parameters,  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi}. Data Structures: Edge List: A collection of all triangle edges that contribute to geometric discontinuities. These are categorized into: 1. Boundary edges: Topological boundaries of the mesh (only if the mesh is not closed). 2. Silhouette edges: Edges causing occlusion between meshes or self-occlusion. 3. Sharp edges: Edges with discontinuous face normals (when smooth shading is disabled). Guiding Structures: Adaptive data structures (e.g., 6D Hough trees, edge-sorted lists) used to importance sample the boundary integrals. Mathematical Formulation: The pixel intensity I is expressed as a sum over subdivided domains using the Heaviside step function 	heta(\cdot) to ensure continuity within each sub-domain: I = \iint \sumi 	heta(\alphai(x, y)) fi(x, y) \, dx \, dy where: fi(x, y) is the scene function within the i-th sub-domain. 	heta(\cdot) is the Heaviside step function. \alphai(x, y) is the edge equation corresponding to the location of the discontinuity. The summation is over all subdivided small domains. The derivative of the pixel intensity I with respect to a scene parameter \pi is derived by applying the chain rule. Since the derivative of the Heaviside step function is the Dirac delta function \delta(\cdot), the gradient is:  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \iint \sumi 	hetai(x, y)  rac{\partial}{\partial \pi} fi(x, y) + \delta(\alphai(x, y)) 
abla{\alphai(x, y)} fi(x, y) \, dx \, dy where \delta(\cdot) is the Dirac delta function. This 2D integral containing the Dirac delta function reduces to a 1D integral over the domains where the delta function is non-zero (i.e., the edges). The physically correct gradient formula is:  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \iint  rac{\partial}{\partial \pi} f(x, y) \, dx \, dy + \sumi \int  rac{
abla \alphai(x, y)}{\|
abla{x,y} \alphai(x, y)\|} fi(x, y) \, dt where: The first term is the interior integral, estimated using automatic differentiation. The second term is the boundary integral, summed over all triangle edges i. The integral is over the triangle edges corresponding to the discontinuity's location. t is the parameter along the edge. Algorithm Steps: 1. Partition the Integrand: Identify all edges causing discontinuities in the scene function (boundary, silhouette, and sharp edges). 2. Decompose the Gradient: Separate the gradient computation into the interior term (smooth, handled by auto-diff) and the boundary term (discontinuous, handled by explicit sampling). 3. Precompute Edges (Primary Visibility): For primary visibility (the first segment of light paths), precompute all triangle edges that may contribute to geometric discontinuities. 4. Importance Sample Boundaries: Sample the boundary integrals. For primary visibility, importance sample the precomputed edges. For higher-order visibility (subsequent light path segments), importance sample geometric discontinuities viewed from arbitrary shading points. 5. Initialize Guiding Structures (Advanced): To reduce variance, project rays that intersect the shape being differentiated onto the corresponding geometry boundary. Calculate these projected rays' contributions to the boundary integral to initialize the guiding structure. 6. Adaptive Sampling (Advanced): Use adaptive data structures and edge-sorting algorithms to reorganize the boundary sample space and guide the sampling process for improved efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientboundarysampling(scene, camera, params): # 1. Compute interior term via automatic differentiation of the standard rendering equation interiorgradient = autodiffrender(scene, camera, params) # 2. Identify discontinuity edges: boundary, silhouette, and sharp edges edges = getalltriangleedges(scene.meshes) boundarygradient = 0.0 # 3. Primary visibility: precompute and importance sample edges primaryedges = filteredgesvisiblefromcamera(edges, camera) for edge in primaryedges: # Sample along the edge parameter t for t in sampleedgeparameter(edge, numsamples=K): # Evaluate scene function fi at the sample point by tracing a ray radiance = traceray(scene, camera, edge.pointat(t), params) # Compute boundary integrand: (gradalpha / ||gradalpha||) fi dt gradalpha = edge.gradientat(t) direction = gradalpha / vectornorm(gradalpha) boundarygradient += direction radiance edge.differentiallength(t) # 4. Higher-order visibility: sample discontinuities from arbitrary shading points # Project rays intersecting the differentiated shape onto the geometry boundary to initialize guiding structures gigradient = computeglobalilluminationboundaryterms(scene, camera, params, edges) boundarygradient += gigradient return interiorgradient + boundarygradient def autodiffrender(scene, camera, params): # Standard differentiable path tracing pass returning interior gradient return standarddifferentiablepathtrace(scene, camera, params) def getalltriangleedges(meshes): # Iterate over all triangles and collect unique vertex pairs return uniquevertexpairsfromtriangles(meshes) def filteredgesvisiblefromcamera(edges, camera): # Test each edge's bounding volume against camera frustum and visibility return [e for e in edges if isedgevisible(e, camera)] def sampleedgeparameter(edge, numsamples): # Uniform or importance sampling of parameter t in [0, 1] return uniformsampleinterval(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) def traceray(scene, camera, point, params): # Cast ray from camera through point, accumulate radiance return castcameraray(scene, camera, point, params) def computeglobalilluminationboundaryterms(scene, camera, params, edges): # Trace higher-order paths, project intersections onto geometry boundaries, # and accumulate boundary integral contributions return pathtracewithboundaryprojection(scene, camera, params, edges) def vectornorm(v): return math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in v)) def uniformsampleinterval(minval, maxval, count): return [minval + (maxval - minval) i / count for i in range(count)] Parameters: Number of samples per edge: Not given in the sources. Edge sorting threshold: Not given in the sources. Heaviside/Dirac approximations: Not given in the sources (exact functions are used). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Higher-order visibility: Importance sampling geometric discontinuities viewed from arbitrary shading points (higher-order visibility) is a much more complicated task than primary visibility. Inefficiency of early methods: The approach by Zhang et al. [12] remains confined to sampling edges from given shading points, which is considered inefficient from a modern viewpoint. Variance in complex scenes: The 6D Hough tree scheme by Li et al. [9] does not scale well to high-complexity scenes and does not match the contribution function shape closely, resulting in large variance. Handles discontinuities at pixel filter boundaries by explicitly integrating over the boundary, allowing box filters instead of Gaussian filters to reduce variance. Sets itself apart by avoiding the extra variance from the derivative of Gaussian weights in the divergence term. Choose when using box filters or when Gaussian filter derivatives introduce excessive noise. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Li et al. [9] results in relatively large variance because their scheme does not match the contribution function shape closely. Zhang et al. [11] significantly reduced the variance of the gradient estimator with less computation time by introducing multi-directional boundary integrals. Yan et al. [41] provided better exploration of the boundary sample space, resulting in lower variance for gradient estimates under equal-time configurations. Scaling: The 6D Hough tree scheme by Li et al. [9] does not scale well to scenes with high complexity. Strengths: Explicitly handles discontinuities, providing unbiased gradients. Modern variants (Zhang et al. [11], Yan et al. [41]) reduce variance significantly compared to early methods. Limitations: Complexity increases significantly for higher-order visibility (global illumination). Early importance sampling schemes (Li et al. [9]) suffer from high variance in complex scenes. When to use: When unbiased gradients are required for scenes with triangle meshes and discontinuities are a significant source of error. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and high-complexity scenes are used with early sampling schemes (Li et al. [9]). Origin: Li et al. [9] presented the first physics-based differentiable rendering technique for scenes composed of triangle meshes using an edge sampling method. They realized that automatic differentiation could not be used directly due to the discontinuity of the integrand in global illumination techniques like path tracing. Development: Zhang et al. [12] extended the edge sampling method to scenes containing participating media, supporting arbitrary surface and volumetric configurations. Zhang et al. [11] introduced a transport relation from fluid mechanics to establish a mathematical framework for modern boundary sampling techniques. They also introduced a multi-directional form of the boundary integral, allowing silhouette paths to be generated "from the middle" to reduce variance. Zhang et al. [13] extended the method of Zhang et al. [11] to scenes containing participating media. Yan et al. [41] employed adaptive data structures to guide the sampling process within the boundary sample space and proposed an edge-sorting algorithm to reorganize the boundary sample space to improve sampling efficiency. Zhang et al. [14] re-derived the local formulation of the perimeter and proposed the first local formulation of the interior. They also found that calculating the boundary term can benefit from information gathered during the interior term's simulation by projecting rays onto the geometry boundary to initialize the guiding structure. Usage: Used in differentiable rendering for inverse problems, shape optimization, and material estimation in scenes with triangle meshes. A Brief Review on Differentiable Rendering: Recent Advances and Challenges, https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics13173546, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Cross-reduction of variance using pairs of paths
head: Cross-weighting scheme, Variance cross-reduction
body: This method reduces the variance of gradient estimates in differentiable volume rendering by sampling pairs of similar paths and applying a control variate technique known as the cross-weighting scheme. It allows the use of suitable parameter values from one path estimate to reduce the variance of the other without introducing bias, addressing the high variance inherent in estimating derivatives of discontinuous integrands. It builds on Differential path integral estimator with MIS and NEE by providing a specific variance reduction strategy for the differential contributions computed therein. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Path Pair: Two paths, P0 and P1, generated for each sample index i. Path Contribution Components: For each path i \in \{0, 1\} and each emitter contribution index l: f{i,l}(\theta): Product of emitted radiance and path throughput at vertex l. W{i,l}(\theta): Product of all associated weights w{i,l}(\theta) for the path segment up to emitter l. Note: \mathbb{E}[\partial W{i,l} / \partial \theta] = 0 because weights are independent of the gradients of other weights. Steps: 1. Sample Path Pairs: For each sample i, generate a pair of paths (P0, P1). The paths must be "similar" (see Partially correlated path generation below). 2. Compute Contributions: For each path i \in \{0, 1\}, compute the total contribution ri as a sum over all emitter contributions l: ri = \sum{l=0}^{\infty} f{i,l}(\theta) W{i,l}(\theta) \quad (27) 3. Apply Cross-Reduction: Combine the contributions r0 and r1 to form the reduced variance estimate r' using the cross-weighting formula: \begin{aligned} r' = & \frac{1}{2} \sum f{0,l}(\theta) W{0,l}(\theta) - f{1,l}(\theta) (W{0,l}(\theta) - W{0,l}(\theta0)) \\ & + \frac{1}{2} \sum f{1,l}(\theta) W{1,l}(\theta) - f{0,l}(\theta) (W{1,l}(\theta) - W{1,l}(\theta0)). \end{aligned} \quad (28) Here, W{i,l}(\theta0) represents the weights evaluated at the reference parameters \theta0. The term (W{0,l}(\theta) - W{0,l}(\theta0)) acts as the control variate correction. 4. Accumulate Gradient: The gradient is estimated by averaging the derivatives of r' over all sampled pairs. Parameters: Samples per Integral: 4 samples (ray intersection queries) are used to estimate changes of variables in each emitter, BSDF, and pixel integral. Beckmann Roughness Threshold: 0.15 (root mean square of slopes in the microgeometry). Convolutions are applied when roughness exceeds this value to handle integrands that violate the small angular support assumption. von Mises-Fisher Concentration: \kappa = 1000. Used for spherical convolution kernels. Pitfalls: Degenerate Light Sources: Point or directional lights containing Dirac delta terms are incompatible because visibility-related discontinuities cause the integrals to collapse. Area Light Discontinuities: Area lights introduce two types of discontinuities (light source silhouette and occluder silhouettes), violating the single-discontinuity assumption. This is handled by replacing standard area lights with continuous analogues (e.g., smooth emission profiles falling to zero at boundaries). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crossreducevariance(path0, path1, theta, theta0): """ Computes the cross-reduced variance estimate for a pair of paths. Args: path0, path1: Path objects containing throughput, emittedradiance, and weights arrays. theta: Current scene parameters. theta0: Reference scene parameters for control variate. Returns: rprime: The variance-reduced contribution estimate. """ sum0 = 0.0 sum1 = 0.0 numconnections = len(path0.emitterconnections) for l in range(numconnections): f0l = computethroughputradiance(path0, l, theta) W0l = computeweightproduct(path0, l, theta) W0lref = computeweightproduct(path0, l, theta0) f1l = computethroughputradiance(path1, l, theta) W1l = computeweightproduct(path1, l, theta) W1lref = computeweightproduct(path1, l, theta0) term0 = 0.5 (f0l W0l - f1l (W0l - W0lref)) term1 = 0.5 (f1l W1l - f0l (W1l - W1lref)) sum0 += term0 sum1 += term1 return sum0 + sum1 def computethroughputradiance(path, l, theta): # Returns the product of emitted radiance and path throughput at vertex l return path.throughput[l] path.emittedradiance[l] def computeweightproduct(path, l, theta): # Returns the product of all associated weights w{i,l}(theta) up to l wprod = 1.0 for k in range(l + 1): wprod = path.weights[k] return wprod A method to generate path pairs that are highly correlated to maximize variance reduction while maintaining the statistical independence required to avoid bias. It reuses random numbers for all sampling steps except those affecting the weights W{i,l}, specifically the sampling of directions in re-parameterized integrals with small angular support. This ensures that f{0,l} is uncorrelated with \partial W{1,l}(\theta) / \partial \theta (and vice versa), which is a strict requirement for the unbiasedness of the cross-weighting scheme. Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of path pairs and the cost of evaluating weights at \theta0. The number of ray intersection queries increases by a factor related to the samples per integral (4 samples). Performance: Forward rendering and backpropagation for 512x512 images with 32 path pairs and 3 bounces take less than one minute on an NVIDIA TITAN RTX. Ray-triangle intersections account for approximately 9% of the computation time. Strengths: Substantially reduces variance of gradients without adding bias, enabling more stable optimization in differentiable rendering. Limitations: Incompatible with degenerate light sources (point/directional) and requires careful handling of area lights. Performance is sensitive to the number of samples used for variable change estimation. The method is based on the "cross-weighting scheme" introduced by Rousselle et al. [2016] for image-space gradients. It was adapted for differentiable path tracing to handle nested integrals corresponding to scattering events. The implementation described in the primary source uses Mitsuba 2 with automatic differentiation and a JIT compiler for GPU kernel generation. Reparameterizing discontinuous integrands for differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3355089.3356510, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SDF Prb Reparam Integrator
body: A differentiable path tracer that computes gradients of radiance with respect to scene parameters (e.g., Signed Distance Function shape parameters) by warping random samples via reparameterization, supporting both forward and backward mode automatic differentiation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene description containing an SDF field, camera parameters, random number generator state, and scene parameters \theta (e.g., SDF coefficients). Outputs: Primal radiance image L and gradient images \nabla\theta L (forward or backward). Data Structures and Parameters: self.primalimage: Tensor storing the computed radiance. self.warpfield: Optional field defining the reparameterization warp. reparammaxdepth: Maximum depth for reparameterization rays. shadegradientmaxdepth: Maximum depth for shading gradients, set equal to reparammaxdepth if warpfield is not None. reparamrays: Number of reparameterization rays (default 16). reparamkappa: Parameter for reparameterization (default 10^5). reparamexp: Exponent for reparameterization (default 3.0). rrdepth: Depth at which Russian Roulette is applied (default 5). useaovs: Boolean flag to enable Auxiliary Output Variables (default False). hideemitters: Boolean flag to hide emitters (default False). Core Algorithm: The integrator executes in two main phases depending on the differentiation mode, both following a consistent setup and sampling routine. 1. Primal Setup: Prepare the scene SDF via self.preparesdf(scene). Suspend gradients for primal setup using dr.suspendgrad(). Prepare the sampler and generate primary rays with reparameterization if self.warpfield is not None. Compute primal radiance L using self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Primal. Store primal image in self.primalimage. 2. Gradient Computation: Forward Mode: Resume gradients and compute sample position derivatives if enabled. Compute forward-mode gradients by calling self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Forward. Accumulate reparameterization result gradients into resultgrad. Backward Mode: Prepare the scene SDF via self.preparesdf(scene). Suspend gradients for primal setup using dr.suspendgrad(). Generate primary rays with reparameterization. Compute primal radiance L using self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Primal. Resume gradients and enable gradient tracking on L. Set gradient of image to gradin and enqueue backward pass. Compute backward-mode gradients by calling self.sample with mode=dr.ADMode.Backward. Sampling Loop (self.sample): The sampling loop handles path construction and reparameterization integration. 1. Initialize loop state: depth=0, L=0 (or statein), \beta=1, \eta=1, misem=1. 2. Perform preliminary ray intersection to get picur. 3. If warpfield is not None: Update reparammaxdepth to maxreparamdepth if >= 0, else 100,000. Set shadegradientmaxdepth equal to reparammaxdepth. 4. If reparameterization requires DRJITSTRUCT, start a loop named 'Path Replay Backpropagation'. 5. Sphere Tracing Step: Evaluate SDF value s = \text{SDF}(p) and gradient g = \nabla \text{SDF}(p). Compute silhouette weight w{sil}: w{sil} = \frac{1}{(10^{-7} + |s| + \text{SIL\WEIGHT\OFFSET} \cdot (n \cdot d)^2)^3} where n = g / \|g\|, d is the ray direction, and \text{SIL\WEIGHT\OFFSET} = 0.05. 6. Compute segment length and update integrals for warp position estimation using the trapezoid rule: W{int} \leftarrow W{int} + 0.5 \cdot \Delta t \cdot (w{prev} + w{sil}) T{warp} \leftarrow T{warp} + 0.5 \cdot \Delta t \cdot (t{prev} \cdot w{prev} + t \cdot w{sil}) where \Delta t is the segment length. 7. Update ray position: t \leftarrow t + s. Check for intersection (|s| < \epsilon) and boundary conditions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr def renderforward(scene, params): # Standard AD framework context manager to suspend gradients during primal setup with dr.suspendgrad(): sdf = scene.sdffield # Standard sampler initialization sampler = None # Standard primary ray generation with optional warp application rays = None primalimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Primal, sdf=sdf) scene.primalimage = primalimage # Resume gradients and compute sample position derivatives dr.resumegrad() gradimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Forward, sdf=sdf) # Standard accumulation of reparameterization gradients resultgrad = None return primalimage, resultgrad def renderbackward(scene, params, gradin): with dr.suspendgrad(): sdf = scene.sdffield sampler = None rays = None primalimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Primal, sdf=sdf) dr.resumegrad() dr.enablegrad(primalimage) primalimage.grad = gradin gradimage = sample(scene, rays, mode=dr.ADMode.Backward, sdf=sdf) return gradimage def sample(scene, rays, mode, sdf): depth = 0 L = 0.0 beta = 1.0 eta = 1.0 misem = 1.0 if scene.warpfield is not None: reparammaxdepth = scene.maxreparamdepth if scene.maxreparamdepth >= 0 else 100000 shadegradientmaxdepth = reparammaxdepth else: reparammaxdepth = 0 shadegradientmaxdepth = 0 weightintegral = 0.0 warptintegral = 0.0 prevsdfvalue = 0.0 prevsilw = 0.0 t = 0.0 active = True # Path Replay Backpropagation Loop while active and depth < shadegradientmaxdepth: # Standard ray-scene intersection returning hit point and mask picur = scene.intersect(rays) active = picur.hit if active: p = picur.position sdfval = sdf.eval(p) sdfgrad = sdf.evalgrad(p) n = sdfgrad / dr.norm(sdfgrad) ndotd = dr.dot(rays.d, n) silweightoffset = 0.05 wsil = 1.0 / (1e-7 + dr.abs(sdfval) + silweightoffset ndotd2)3 wsil = dr.maximum(wsil, 0.0) segmentlength = dr.maximum(prevsdfvalue, 0.0) prevt = t - prevsdfvalue weightintegral += 0.5 segmentlength (prevsilw + wsil) warptintegral += 0.5 segmentlength (prevt prevsilw + t wsil) t += sdfval prevsdfvalue = sdfval prevsilw = wsil depth += 1 if dr.abs(sdfval) < 1e-6: # Standard BSDF evaluation and MIS weighting L += beta 0.0 break else: break # Final warp position estimation from accumulated integrals if weightintegral > 0: warptintegral = warptintegral / weightintegral return L Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance depends heavily on the complexity of the SDF evaluation. The use of reparamrays=16 provides a balance between gradient accuracy and computational cost. Strengths: Provides stable gradients for SDF-based shape optimization. Supports both forward and backward mode AD, allowing flexibility in optimization setups. Limitations: Requires the SDF to be differentiable. The reparameterization warping may introduce bias if the warp field is poorly conditioned. High reparamkappa (10^5) and reparamexp (3.0) are used to stabilize the warping but may require tuning for specific scenes. When to use: When optimizing SDF parameters for shape reconstruction or editing. When not to use: When the scene does not involve SDFs or when memory is extremely constrained (due to path replay storage). The method originates from the work on Differentiable Signed Distance Function Rendering, specifically the implementation in the Mitsuba 3 renderer. It builds on the differential path integral estimator framework, incorporating reparameterization techniques to handle the non-differentiable nature of ray-SDF intersections by warping the random samples. The "Path Replay Backpropagation" loop is a key innovation to efficiently compute gradients through the iterative sphere tracing process. Differentiable Signed Distance Function Rendering, https://github.com/rgl-epfl/differentiable-sdf-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Reparametrized Integral Gradients
head: Reparameterized Integral Gradients, Loubet et al. method, Reparameterization for Discontinuous Integrands
body: Reparametrized Integral Gradients is a technique for differentiable rendering that eliminates bias in gradients caused by visibility discontinuities moving with scene parameters. Unlike explicit edge sampling methods that require detecting and sampling geometric boundaries, this method applies a change of variables to transform the integration domain such that discontinuities become static (parameter-independent). This allows differentiation under the integral sign without boundary terms, making it computationally efficient for complex scenes, though it approximates gradients and has limitations with specular materials. The method addresses the rendering integral I(\theta) where the integrand f(x, \theta) contains discontinuities at positions dependent on parameters \theta. Naïve differentiation yields incorrect gradients because the domain of integration or the location of discontinuities shifts. Inputs: Scene parameters \theta (e.g., camera position, light source position, triangle mesh vertices). Integrals over domains \Omega\theta containing discontinuities dependent on \theta. Outputs: Gradient \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} estimated via Monte Carlo sampling on a fixed domain. Data Structures: Transformation function T(\omega, \theta): \Omega \to \Omega\theta mapping a fixed reference domain \Omega to the parameter-dependent domain. Jacobian determinant J(\omega, \theta) = \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|. Steps: 1. Identify Discontinuities: Locate points in the integrand where visibility or material properties change abruptly, and determine how these points move as \theta changes. 2. Construct Transformation: Define a differentiable transformation T(\omega, \theta) that "warps" the domain such that the discontinuity in the transformed integrand is stationary. Specifically, choose T such that it yields the identity map when \theta = \theta0 (the parameter value for which gradients are evaluated). 3. Reparameterize Integral: Apply the change of variables to move the integral from \Omega\theta to the fixed domain \Omega: I(\theta) = \int{\Omega} f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| d\omega The discontinuities in the new integrand g(\omega, \theta) = f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| are now at fixed locations. 4. Differentiate: Since the domain \Omega and discontinuity locations are static, differentiate under the integral sign: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} = \int{\Omega} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left[ f(T(\omega, \theta), \theta) \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right| \right] d\omega No boundary term arises from the Reynolds Transport Theorem. 5. Estimate: Use Monte Carlo sampling on \Omega to estimate the gradient: Draw samples yi from a probability density function p(y) that does not depend on \theta. Evaluate the transformed integrand, density, and Jacobian determinant. Compute the estimator E = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{f(T(yi, \theta), \theta) |\det JT|}{p(yi)}. Apply automatic differentiation to E with respect to \theta to obtain the gradient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterizedgradient(theta, theta0, samples, p, integrandfn): """ Estimate gradient of rendering integral using reparameterization. theta: Current scene parameters. theta0: Parameter value for which gradients are evaluated (identity point). samples: Array of points omega drawn from fixed reference distribution p(omega). p: PDF function for the reference distribution. integrandfn: Function evaluating f(x, theta). """ gradsum = 0.0 N = len(samples) for omega in samples: # 1. Map reference sample to parameter-dependent domain x = transform(omega, theta, theta0) # 2. Compute Jacobian determinant |det(dT/domega)| jacobiandet = computejacobiandeterminant(omega, theta, theta0) # 3. Evaluate integrand at transformed point fval = integrandfn(x, theta) # 4. Form the transformed integrand transformedval = fval abs(jacobiandet) # 5. Compute gradient of the transformed integrand w.r.t theta # Using automatic differentiation on the composition gradval = computegradientwrttheta(transformedval, theta) # 6. Accumulate gradient estimate weighted by inverse PDF gradsum += gradval / p(omega) return gradsum / N def transform(omega, theta, theta0): # Standard translation example: T(omega, theta) = omega + theta - theta0 # For spherical domains, this would be a rotation R(omega, theta) return omega + theta - theta0 def computejacobiandeterminant(omega, theta, theta0): # For translation T(omega, theta) = omega + theta - theta0, dT/domega = 1 # For spherical rotations on S^2, the Jacobian determinant is 1. return 1.0 def evaluateintegrand(x, theta): # Evaluates the rendering integrand f(x, theta) at point x with parameters theta return 1.0 def computegradientwrttheta(val, theta): # Computes gradient using reverse-mode automatic differentiation # on the computational graph of val with respect to theta. return 0.0 Parameters: Sample count: The method produces high-quality gradients at low sample counts, specifically demonstrated at 64 samples per pixel (spp). \theta0: The specific value of the scene parameter \theta for which gradients are evaluated; T must be identity at this value. Sampling density p: Must not depend on \theta, otherwise discontinuities are reintroduced. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Specular Materials: The method does not support perfectly specular materials because the discontinuities in specular reflections cannot be easily reparameterized with a simple continuous warp. Dirac Delta Lights: Degenerate light sources containing Dirac delta functions are not supported. Multiple Discontinuities: The method struggles if multiple discontinuities exist within the support of the integrand, as a single global warp may not stabilize all of them. Approximation Error: Gradients are approximated and may not always be accurate. Small Angular Support: The method assumes integrands have small angular support (e.g., due to narrow BSDFs or small lights), where discontinuities consist of the silhouette of a single object. Warped-Area Sampling (WAS) is an unbiased method for differentiable rendering that eliminates the need for explicit boundary sampling by reparameterizing boundary integrals into interior integrals using a continuous warp field. It builds on Reparametrized Integral Gradients but improves upon the biased spherical rotation approach of Loubet et al. by satisfying the strict continuity requirements of the divergence theorem. Spherical Rotation Reparameterization is a technique for differentiable volume rendering that eliminates discontinuities in gradient estimates by applying a spherical rotation to the integration domain. It solves the problem of non-differentiable integrals caused by scene parameters \theta shifting discontinuity points across the sphere. Unlike Warped-Area Sampling, which explicitly samples and integrates over discontinuity boundaries, this method makes the discontinuity point parameter-independent through a change of variables, thereby removing the need for explicit boundary sampling. Time Complexity: Comparable to standard path tracing, as it avoids the overhead of explicit edge detection and sampling. However, it requires computing the Jacobian and its derivative, which may add computational cost per sample. Memory Complexity: Low, similar to standard path tracing, as it does not require storing edge lists or complex data structures for discontinuity tracking. Performance: Computationally efficient for scenes with many moving discontinuities where edge sampling would be expensive. Strengths: Eliminates bias from moving discontinuities without explicit edge sampling; works well with automatic differentiation. Limitations: Does not support perfectly specular materials, Dirac delta lights, or multiple discontinuities in one integrand; gradients are approximate. When to Use: When scene parameters cause visibility changes (e.g., object translation) and explicit edge sampling is too costly or complex. When Not to Use: For scenes with specular reflections, point lights, or complex multi-discontinuity integrands. Reparametrized Integral Gradients was introduced by Loubet et al. in "Reparameterizing Discontinuous Integrands for Differentiable Rendering" at SIGGRAPH Asia 2019. Unlike previous work (e.g., Li et al. 2018) which requires explicit sampling of silhouette edges, this method avoids edge sampling entirely by using changes of variables. The open source implementation of the method is part of version 2 of the Mitsuba renderer. name: Warped-Area Sampling
head: Warped-area reparameterization
body:
Warped-Area Sampling (WAS) is an unbiased method for differentiable rendering that eliminates the need for explicit boundary sampling by reparameterizing boundary integrals into interior integrals using a continuous warp field. It builds on Reparametrized Integral Gradients but improves upon the biased spherical rotation approach of Loubet et al. by satisfying the strict continuity requirements of the divergence theorem. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene parameters \pi, primal ray direction \omega, and the discontinuity boundary \Delta S^2 in the spherical domain S^2. Output: An unbiased estimator for the gradient  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} via a single interior integral over S^2. Data Structures: Warp Field \mathbf{V}: A vector field defined on S^2. It must be continuous everywhere and converge to the boundary velocity \mathbf{v}{\partial} as \omega approaches \Delta S^2. Discontinuous Warp Field \mathbf{V}{dis}: An intermediate field used to construct \mathbf{V}. It is discontinuous at \Delta S^2 because rays cast on different sides of the boundary typically intersect different objects, yielding different velocities. Smoothing Kernel w(\omega, \omega'): A convolution kernel used to smooth \mathbf{V}{dis} into \mathbf{V}. Steps: 1. Construct \mathbf{V}{dis}: Cast auxiliary rays around the primal sampled ray. For each auxiliary ray direction \omegap, if it intersects an object dependent on \pi, compute the velocity \mathbf{v}p:= \partial \omegap / \partial \pi by differentiating the ray intersection process. This ensures that as \omegap approaches the boundary \Delta S^2, \mathbf{v}p converges to \mathbf{v}{\partial}. 2. Smooth \mathbf{V}{dis}: Convolve \mathbf{V}{dis} with the kernel w to produce the continuous warp field \mathbf{V}. The kernel is defined as:  rac{1}{w(\omega, \omega')}:=  rac{1}{D(\omega, \omega') + B(\omega')} where D(\omega, \omega') is a distance function and B(\omega') is a boundary-test function that converges to 0 when \omega' 	o \Delta S^2. 3. Estimate Gradient: Apply the divergence theorem to reparameterize the boundary integral into an interior integral: \int{\partial S^2} (\Delta f \mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{n} d\ell(\omegai) = \int{S^2} (
abla \cdot \Delta f \mathbf{V}) d\sigma(\omegai) The total gradient estimator is the reparameterized spherical integral:  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int{S^2} \left[  rac{\partial f}{\partial \pi} + (
abla \cdot \Delta f \mathbf{V}) ight] d\sigma(\omegai) where f:= Li fs is the integrand. Parameters: Warp Field Requirements: (a) \mathbf{V} must be continuous; (b) \mathbf{V}(\omega) must converge to \mathbf{v}{\partial} as \omega 	o \Delta S^2. Kernel Parameters: D(\omega, \omega') is a distance function and B(\omega') is a boundary-test function that converges to 0 when \omega' 	o \Delta S^2. Pitfalls: Using only one auxiliary ray to approximate boundary motion (as in Loubet et al.) results in a biased estimator because the resulting warp field does not strictly satisfy the boundary requirement. Precision issues may arise if the smoothing kernel does not preserve the boundary velocity \mathbf{v}{\partial} correctly. An extension of WAS to differential path integrals by Xu et al. [XBLZ23], enabling multi-bounce light transport estimation without explicit boundary sampling in path space. It decomposes the boundary integral from PSDR into a sum of integrals over sub-spaces \partial \hat{\Omega}{N,K}: \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}} \Delta \hat{f}K( ar{p}) \mathbf{V}K(pK) d\mu'( ar{p}) = \sum{N=1}^{\infty} \sum{K=0}^{N-1} \int{\partial \hat{\Omega}{N,K}} \Delta \hat{f}K( ar{p}) \mathbf{V}K(pK) d\mu'( ar{p}) The reparameterized differential path integral is:  rac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int{\hat{\Omega}} \left[  rac{\partial \hat{f}( ar{p})}{\partial \pi} + \sum{K=0}^{N-1} 
abla \cdot \Delta \hat{f}K \mathbf{V}K(pK) ight] d\mu( ar{p}) Compared to the reparameterized spherical integral, this path integral has a more generalized form depicting multi-bounce light transport, enabling advanced Monte Carlo strategies like bidirectional path tracing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Unbiased estimation; avoids explicit boundary sampling; enables multi-bounce transport estimation (via the path integral variant). Limitations: Requires construction of a continuous warp field; the auxiliary ray approximation approach is biased if not handled correctly. When to use: When unbiased differentiable rendering is required and explicit boundary sampling is difficult or biased. When not to use: When biased estimators are acceptable and simpler methods (like spherical rotation) suffice. Warped-Area Sampling was proposed by Bangaru et al. [BLD20] as a refinement to the biased spherical rotation approach by Loubet et al. [LHJ19]. It draws inspiration from the divergence theorem to reparameterize boundary integrals into interior integrals. The method was later extended to differential path integrals by Xu et al. [XBLZ23] to support multi-bounce light transport. A Survey on Physics-based Differentiable Rendering - arXiv.org, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.01402, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Rotation Reparameterization
head: Discontinuity removal via rotation, Reparameterization with spherical rotations, Rotation-based change of variables
body: Spherical Rotation Reparameterization is a technique for differentiable volume rendering that eliminates discontinuities in gradient estimates by applying a spherical rotation to the integration domain. It solves the problem of non-differentiable integrals caused by scene parameters \theta shifting discontinuity points (e.g., object silhouettes) across the sphere. Unlike Warped-Area Sampling, which explicitly samples and integrates over discontinuity boundaries, this method makes the discontinuity point parameter-independent through a change of variables, thereby removing the need for explicit boundary sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An integrand f(\omega, \theta) defined on the unit sphere S^2, where \omega is a direction and \theta represents scene parameters (e.g., object position, camera pose). The integrand typically has discontinuities dependent on \theta. Output: A differentiable estimate of the integral I = \int{S^2} f(\omega, \theta) d\omega and its gradient with respect to \theta. Data Structures: Rotation R(\omega, \theta): A function mapping a direction \omega to a rotated direction \omega', parameterized by \theta. Sampling Distribution p(\omega, \theta0): The probability density function used to generate samples \omegai, using a fixed parameter \theta0 independent of the current \theta to ensure sample independence from the gradient path. Steps: 1. Identify Discontinuity Motion: Determine how the discontinuity point T(\theta) moves with respect to the parameter \theta. 2. Construct Rotation R: Choose a spherical rotation R(\omega, \theta) such that its derivative with respect to \theta matches the derivative of the discontinuity trajectory: \frac{\partial R}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial T}{\partial \theta} This ensures that the transformed discontinuity point \omega0, defined by R(\omega0, \theta) = T(\theta), is independent of \theta. 3. Reparameterize Integral: Apply the change of variables to the integral: I = \int{S^2} f(\omega, \theta) d\omega = \int{S^2} f(R(\omega, \theta), \theta) d\omega The Jacobian determinant of this spherical rotation is exactly 1. 4. Monte Carlo Estimation: Generate samples \omegai from a distribution p(\omega, \theta0) using a fixed parameter \theta0. Compute the estimate: E = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{f(R(\omegai, \theta), \theta)}{p(\omegai, \theta0)} Using \theta0 instead of \theta in the sampling distribution removes the dependency of the samples on \theta, preventing discontinuous jumps in the sample set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalrotationreparameterization(f, theta, theta0, N, samplefunc, pdffunc): """Estimate integral of f(w, theta) using spherical rotation reparameterization.""" # Rotation R is constructed to approximate discontinuity motion def R(omega, theta): # Returns rotated direction omega' = R(omega, theta) # Implementation depends on scene geometry to satisfy dR/dtheta = dT/dtheta return rotateomega(omega, theta) total = 0.0 for i in range(N): omegai = samplefunc(theta0) omegarotated = R(omegai, theta) pdfval = pdffunc(omegai, theta0) total += f(omegarotated, theta) / pdfval return total / N def rotateomega(omega, theta): # Standard spherical rotation (e.g., Rodrigues' formula or quaternion) # Returns a unit vector omega' return omega # Simplified structure; actual rotation applied per def constructrotation(theta): # Returns a rotation function R(omega, theta) # Construction matches discontinuity motion T(theta) via dR/dtheta = dT/dtheta return lambda omega: rotateomega(omega, theta) def evaluatepdf(omega, theta0): # Evaluates the probability density function p(omega, theta0) # Typically the default sampling scheme of the underlying renderer return pdffunc(omega, theta0) Parameters: \theta0: The fixed parameter used for sampling. It is chosen to remove the dependency of the samples on \theta. Rotation Approximation: The rotation R must accurately approximate the displacement of discontinuities. If the approximation is poor, bias remains. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Support: The method assumes the integrand has small angular support (vanishes outside a small neighborhood). If the support is large, the rotation approximation produces significant bias because the discontinuity structure is too complex to be modeled by a single rotation. Precision: The Jacobian is exactly 1, so no scaling factor is needed. A method to handle integrands with large support by convolving the integrand f with a spherical kernel k, allowing the small-support rotation technique to be applied to the inner integral. It is chosen when the integrand's discontinuities are localized, making direct rotation effective. The integral identity used is \int{S^2} f(\omega) d\omega = \int{S^2} \int{S^2} f(\mu) k(\mu, \omega) d\mu d\omega, where k satisfies \int{S^2} k(\mu, \omega) d\mu = 1. The kernel k can be any smooth distribution, such as a von Mises-Fisher distribution, with a concentration parameter controlling the trade-off between bias and variance. Small kernels reduce bias (better rotation approximation) but increase variance (lower probability of hitting discontinuities). The final estimator samples \omegai for the outer integral and \mui \sim k(\cdot, \omegai) for the inner integral, yielding: I \approx E = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{f(Ri(\mui, \theta), \theta) k(Ri(\mui, \theta), \omegai(\theta), \theta)}{p(\omegai(\theta), \theta) pk(\mui)}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Produces gradient images that closely match ground truth for scenes with small-support integrands. Performance degrades with large-support integrands due to bias. Strengths: Eliminates the need for explicit boundary sampling; simple to implement; Jacobian is 1. Limitations: High bias for large-support integrands; requires accurate estimation of discontinuity motion. When to Use: Suitable for differentiable rendering of scenes with sharp, localized discontinuities (e.g., specular highlights, small object silhouettes). When Not to Use: Unsuitable for diffuse shading or large-area lights where the integrand support is large. Spherical Rotation Reparameterization was introduced by Loubet et al. in 2019. It is part of the broader field of differentiable rendering, specifically addressing the challenge of differentiating through discontinuous integrals. The method builds on the idea of reparameterization estimators, which transform the integration domain to remove parameter dependency from discontinuities. It is used in differentiable volume rendering and path tracing to enable gradient-based optimization of scene parameters. name: Plateau-Reduced Differentiable Path Tracing
head: PR-DPT, Differentiable Path Tracing with Derivative-Kernel (Our∂κP), Convolutional Gradient Estimation, Our∂κP
body: Plateau-Reduced Differentiable Path Tracing (PR-DPT) is an inverse rendering technique that alleviates optimization plateaus (regions of zero gradient) by convolving the rendering equation with a smoothing kernel over the parameter space. Unlike standard differentiable path tracers that suffer from discontinuous gradients due to visibility changes, PR-DPT ensures that scene parameters continuously influence the objective function in expectation, allowing gradient-based optimizers to converge on problems with intricate light transport like caustics. It sets itself apart from siblings like Reparameterization Estimators by avoiding the need for a gradient tape, adjoint formulation, or special integrators for visibility discontinuities; instead, it relies on stochastic sampling of a blurred parameter space. Inputs: Scene function f(x, \theta): A forward renderer (path tracer) mapping light paths x \in \Omega and scene parameters \theta \in \Theta to pixel values. Current parameters \theta. Kernel standard deviation \sigma. Number of perturbation samples N (even integer). Outputs: Gradient estimate \hat{\nabla}\theta Q. Data Structures: \theta: Parameter vector, normalized to [0, 1] where possible (e.g., rotations). \tau: Parameter offset vector, sampled from the kernel distribution. Method: The method estimates the gradient of the plateau-reduced rendering equation Q(\theta), defined as the convolution of the original rendering equation P(\theta) with a symmetric, monotonous decreasing kernel \kappa(\tau): Q(\theta) = \int{\Theta} \int{\Omega} \kappa(\tau) f(x, \theta - \tau) \, dx \, d\tau The Monte Carlo estimator for Q(\theta) is: \hat{Q} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \kappa(\taui) f(xi, \theta - \taui) To compute the gradient \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \theta}, PR-DPT offers two paths depending on renderer differentiability. The paper primarily uses Eq. 10 for computational efficiency, as it skips the renderer's gradient computation. The gradient is estimated by sampling the derivative of the kernel: \frac{\partial Q}{\partial \theta} \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\taui) f(xi, \theta - \taui) For a Gaussian kernel \kappa(\tau) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{\tau^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), the derivative with respect to \theta (where \tau represents the offset \theta{\text{sample}} - \theta) is: \frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\tau) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\sigma^2 \pi}} \frac{-\tau}{\sigma^2} \exp\left(\frac{-\tau^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) Note that \frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta} is negative for \tau > 0. To perform importance sampling, the method uses "positivization" by sampling proportional to the absolute value |\frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\tau)|. Sampling Procedure: 1. Positivization: The PDF for sampling is proportional to |\frac{\partial \kappa}{\partial \theta}(\tau)|. 2. CDF Inversion: The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) for this PDF is: F(\tau) = 0.5 \, \text{sgn}(\tau) \exp\left(\frac{-\tau^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) + C where C=1 for \tau > 0 and C=0 otherwise. 3. Sample Generation: Inverting the CDF yields the sample generation formula: \tau = \sqrt{-2\sigma^2 \log(\xi)} where \xi \sim U(0,1). 4. Antithetic Sampling: To achieve a zero-variance estimator for the point-symmetric function, for every generated \tau, the algorithm also uses -\tau. Algorithm: The following pseudocode implements the gradient estimation for the non-differentiable case using antithetic sampling and importance sampling derived from the kernel gradient. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def estimategradient(P, theta, sigma, N): """ Estimates the gradient of the plateau-reduced rendering equation using the derivative-kernel method (Eq. 10 in). Args: P: Forward renderer function f(x, theta). theta: Current scene parameters. sigma: Standard deviation of the blur kernel. N: Total number of perturbation samples (must be even). Returns: Gradient estimate G. """ G = 0.0 # Loop runs for N/2 iterations to generate N samples via antithetic pairs for i in range(N // 2): # 1. Generate uniform random number xi = random.uniform(0, 1) # 2. Sample tau proportional to |dkappa/dtheta| using inverse CDF # Formula: tau = sqrt(-2 sigma^2 log(xi)) tau = math.sqrt(-2 (sigma 2) math.log(xi)) # 3. Evaluate renderer at perturbed parameters # Note: P returns the scalar pixel value (or integrated radiance) valplus = P(theta + tau) valminus = P(theta - tau) # 4. Accumulate difference # The term P(theta + tau) - P(theta - tau) effectively handles the # weighting by the signed kernel gradient and the positivization. # See Eq. 10 and Algorithm 1 in. G = G + (valplus - valminus) # 5. Normalize by N return G / N Parameters: \sigma: Standard deviation of the blur kernel. Controls the spread of perturbations. \sigma0: Initial value. Typical default: 0.5. The paper recommends setting \sigma0 to roughly 50% of the normalized parameter domain. \sigmam: Minimum value. Set to 0.01 to avoid numerical instabilities. N: Number of perturbations (samples) per optimization iteration. Typical values: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. N=2 (one sample + antithesis) is often sufficient for convergence. spp: Samples per pixel for the underlying path tracer. Not a hyperparameter of PR-DPT but must be set high enough so rendering noise is less than the optimization signal. LR: Optimizer learning rate (e.g., Adam). Values vary by task (0.125 to 0.800). Annealing Schedule: The bandwidth \sigma is decayed linearly to refine the solution: \sigma{t+1} = \sigma0 - t(\sigma0 - \sigmam) The schedule is warm-started after approximately 50% of the total optimization iterations have completed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small \sigma0 (< 0.2): Optimization fails to converge. As \sigma0 \to 0, the method approaches rigid optimization, and the loss landscape is not smoothed, causing stagnation. Large \sigma0 (\to 1): Perturbation samples may fall outside the view frustum. With small N, this produces noisy gradients causing divergence. Alleviated by enlarging the camera FOV (e.g., 40° to 60°). High Dimensions: Variance increases with parameter dimensionality. Mitigated by increasing N. Time Complexity: Runtime scales linearly with N. The bulk of time is spent evaluating the forward renderer f; sampling and gradient computation overhead is negligible. Memory Complexity: Low. Does not require storing a gradient tape or compute graph. Performance: On average 8× faster than differentiable rendering with Mitsuba. At N \approx 16, runtime equals Mitsuba's constant baseline (which uses re-parametrization/adjoint methods for 1 sample). Convergence: Convergence improves with N up to \sim 10, then stagnates. Final parameter MSE decreases slightly with higher N (9.5 \times 10^{-5} for N=2 vs 4.7 \times 10^{-6} for N=16), but N>2 yields no net benefit for the tested task due to offsetting runtime. Accuracy: Achieves parameter-space MSE errors as low as 10^{-7} on tested tasks. Strengths: Works with black-box/non-differentiable renderers; handles complex light transport (caustics, GI) where standard differentiable tracers fail; no gradient tape required. Limitations: Variance increases in high-dimensional spaces; requires careful tuning of \sigma0. PR-DPT was introduced by Fischer et al. in 2023. It addresses the issue of optimization plateaus in inverse rendering, where standard differentiable renderers fail to converge due to zero gradients in regions where scene parameter changes do not immediately affect the image (e.g., occlusion). The method connects variational optimization approaches with inverse rendering, interpreting the stochastic sampling as a Monte Carlo estimate of the gradient of a smoothed objective. name: Reparameterization
head: Ray Reparameterization, Silhouette Motion Compensation via Reparameterization
body: Reparameterization is a technique in differentiable rendering that counteracts parameter-dependent silhouette motion and the resulting bias in differentiated rendering. It solves the problem where changes in scene parameters cause discontinuities in the rendering integral to move across the sampling domain, violating standard differentiation assumptions. By applying a change of variables to freeze these discontinuities within spherical integrals, it enables unbiased gradient estimation. The method applies a change of variables to the rendering integral, mapping a parameter-dependent domain to a fixed reference domain. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray with direction d and scene parameters \theta. Output: A transformed ray direction d' and the Jacobian determinant \det = \left| \det \frac{\partial T}{\partial \omega} \right|. Data Structures: ray: Contains direction vector d. det: Scalar float representing the Jacobian determinant. Steps: 1. Primal Pass: The reparameterize() function is called. In primal computation, it returns the input ray direction unchanged and a Jacobian determinant of 1. 2. Differentiated Pass: When gradients are required, reparameterize() expands into intricate operations: a. Auxiliary Ray Tracing: Trace auxiliary rays to construct a warp field that counteracts silhouette motion. b. Jacobian Computation: Compute the determinant of the Jacobian of this warp field. c. Gradient Scattering: Use reverse-mode automatic differentiation on the warp field to scatter scene parameter gradients into the intersected geometry. This accounts for the dependence of the BSDF at adjacent vertices x{i-1} and x{i+1} on the reparameterized vertex position xi. Pseudocode: The implementation exposes reparameterizations through a CustomOp-based abstraction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterize(ray, differentiate=False): if not differentiate: # Primal pass: identity transformation return ray.d, 1.0 else: # Differentiated pass: trace auxiliary rays to construct warp field auxrays = traceauxiliaryrays(ray) # Compute Jacobian determinant of the change of variables det = computejacobian(auxrays) return ray.d, det def traceauxiliaryrays(ray): # Sample and trace rays to build the warp field return [] def computejacobian(auxrays): # Compute determinant from auxiliary intersection data return 1.0 def rayintersect(ray, scene): return scene.findintersection(ray) def scattergradients(si, det): # Use reverse-mode AD to scatter scene parameter gradients into geometry pass def render(scene, ray, det, differentiate=False): si = rayintersect(ray, scene) if differentiate: scattergradients(si, det) return scene.evaluate(si) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dielectric Interfaces: Derivatives are biased in scenes containing dielectric objects such as a glass of water. How to reparameterize through perfectly specular interfaces is an open research problem. Program Size: The introduction of reparameterizations and steps to evaluate derivatives of adjacent vertices leads to very large computational graphs compared to primal rendering. A variant of Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) that integrates reparameterizations. It introduces steps needed to evaluate the derivatives of adjacent vertices, leading to significantly larger programs than primal or non-reparameterized methods. Polymorphism-related optimizations (dead code elimination, value numbering, constant propagation) produce a 6.6x speedup on the OptiX backend. Loop state optimizations yield modest runtime improvements (a few percent) but may be more effective in methods using attached Monte Carlo sampling where large sets of derivatives are exchanged between loop iterations. Complexity: The method increases computational complexity due to the need for auxiliary ray tracing and the expansion of the AD tape. The generated kernel subroutines and data exchanged through function inputs/outputs are significantly larger than in non-reparameterized methods. Performance: On the OptiX backend, polymorphism-related optimizations provide a 6.6x speedup for reparameterized PRB. Loop state optimizations provide smaller gains. Limitations: Biased gradients in scenes with dielectric/specular interfaces. High memory and compilation overhead due to large program size. When to use: When optimizing scene geometry parameters (e.g., vertex positions) in differentiable rendering to avoid silhouette motion bias. Reparameterization was introduced in the context of differentiable path tracing to handle parameter-dependent geometry. It builds on the change of variables formula. The specific implementation using auxiliary rays to construct a warp field references prior work on warp fields. The technique is implemented within the DR.JIT framework.
