name: Control Variates for Gradient Variance Reduction
head: Gradient control variates, Variance reduction via control variates
body: Control variates for gradient variance reduction reduces the variance of gradient estimators in differentiable volume rendering by exploiting the zero expected gradient of the reparameterization weight term. It differs from sibling methods like shift maps by explicitly constructing a correlated control estimator from the Jacobian weights rather than relying solely on path correlation through random number reuse. It targets the high variance inherent in the gradient of the weight term when the integrand is smooth or constant. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene parameters \theta, reference parameters \theta0, sampling points yi from a fixed reference domain, transformation T(yi, \theta), integrand f(T(yi, \theta), \theta), and probability density k. Outputs: An unbiased gradient estimator \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} with reduced variance. Data Structures: Weights wi(\theta): A scalar per sample i, defined as the ratio of the probability density at the transformed point under current parameters to that under reference parameters: wi(\theta) = \frac{k(T(yi, \theta), \theta)}{k(T(yi, \theta0), \theta0)} Control variate parameter \alpha: A scalar coefficient that must be independent of the current weights wi(\theta) to avoid bias. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample and Transform: For each sample i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, generate yi from the fixed reference distribution and compute the transformed position xi = T(yi, \theta). 2. Compute Weights: Calculate the weight wi(\theta) for the current parameters \theta and note that wi(\theta0) = 1 by definition. 3. Evaluate Integrand: Compute fi = f(T(yi, \theta), \theta). 4. Construct Control Variate Estimator: Form the intermediate estimator E' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N [ fi wi(\theta) + \alpha(wi(\theta) - wi(\theta0)) ], which is unbiased because \mathbb{E}[wi(\theta) - wi(\theta0)] = 0. 5. Differentiate: Compute the gradient of E' with respect to \theta. Since wi(\theta0) is constant, its derivative vanishes, yielding \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} [ fi wi(\theta) + \alpha wi(\theta) ]. 6. Return Gradient: Return the computed sum as the gradient estimate. Formulas: Weight: wi(\theta) = \frac{k(T(yi, \theta), \theta)}{k(T(yi, \theta0), \theta0)}. Optimal \alpha: \alpha = -\frac{\text{Cov}(E, F)}{\text{Var}(F)}, where E is the original gradient estimator and F is the control variate estimator \frac{\partial F}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{\partial wi(\theta)}{\partial \theta}. In practice, \alpha is approximated (e.g., as -c if f(x)=c, or as a running average of f). Gradient Estimator: \frac{\partial E'}{\partial \theta} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} [ f(T(yi, \theta), \theta) wi(\theta) + \alpha wi(\theta) ]. Parameters: \alpha: The control variate coefficient. Optimal value is -\frac{\text{Cov}(E, F)}{\text{Var}(F)}. Practical approximation: average of f or constant c if f is constant. \theta0: Reference parameters. Often set to \theta for the primal pass, but for gradient estimation, it serves as the baseline for the weight ratio. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias from \alpha: The parameter \alpha must be independent of the weights wi(\theta) to avoid introducing bias in the gradient of E'. If \alpha is computed using the same samples wi(\theta), the estimator becomes biased. Cross-weighting schemes or using uncorrelated estimates are required to estimate \alpha without bias. Constant Integrand: If f(x) = c, the variance of the gradient can be completely eliminated if \alpha = -c. Smoothness: The variance reduction is most effective when f is a smooth function with small gradients with respect to \theta. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientcontrolvariates(samples, theta, theta0, T, f, k, alpha): """ Compute gradient of rendering integral using control variates. Args: samples: List of N reference samples yi. theta: Current scene parameters (vector). theta0: Reference scene parameters (vector). T: Transformation function T(y, theta). f: Integrand function f(x, theta). k: Probability density function k(x, theta). alpha: Control variate coefficient (must be independent of current weights). Returns: Gradient estimate dE'/dtheta. """ N = len(samples) graddim = len(theta) gradsum = [0.0] graddim for i in range(N): yi = samples[i] xi = T(yi, theta) xiref = T(yi, theta0) kcurr = k(xi, theta) kref = k(xiref, theta0) wi = kcurr / kref if kref != 0 else 0.0 # wi(theta0) is identically 1 by definition fi = f(xi, theta) # Compute gradients of f and w with respect to theta dfdtheta = computegradient(f, xi, theta) dwdtheta = computegradientweight(wi, T, k, yi, theta, theta0) # Accumulate: df/dtheta w + (f + alpha) dw/dtheta for d in range(graddim): gradsum[d] += dfdtheta[d] wi + (fi + alpha) dwdtheta[d] return [g / N for g in gradsum] def computegradientweight(wi, T, k, yi, theta, theta0): # The sources do not provide the analytical derivative of k(T(yi, theta), theta) w.r.t theta. # In practice, this is computed via automatic differentiation. return computegradient(lambda th: k(T(yi, th), th), theta) def computegradient(func, x, params): # Compute gradient of func with respect to params using automatic differentiation. # Returns a vector of partial derivatives. pass # Implementation depends on the AD framework A variant that reduces variance by tracing pairs of correlated paths that reuse certain random numbers and combining their estimates using control variates. It is similar to shift maps [Kettunen et al. 2015; Lehtinen et al. 2013] in sampling correlated paths, and similar to Rousselle et al. [2016] in applying control variates to gradient estimates. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead to the standard reparameterization estimator, primarily the computation of the additional term \alpha \frac{\partial wi}{\partial \theta} and the storage of \alpha. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the reference parameters \theta0 and potentially precomputed weights wi(\theta0) if not computed on the fly. Performance: Significant variance reduction is achieved with low performance overhead. For constant f, variance can be eliminated with optimal \alpha. Strengths: Effective for smooth integrands; reduces variance of the weight gradient term which is often the dominant source of variance in reparameterization estimators. Limitations: Requires careful choice of \alpha to avoid bias; \alpha must be independent of the current weights. Performance gain depends on the correlation between E and F. When to use: When gradient variance is high due to the Jacobian weight term, especially for smooth scenes or constant integrands. When not to use: When f has large gradients or discontinuities that break the smoothness assumption, as the variance reduction relies on f being smooth with small gradients with respect to \theta. Originated in the context of differentiable rendering, specifically in the paper "Reparameterizing discontinuous integrands for differentiable rendering". It builds on the general control variates method from statistics and applies it to the gradient of reparameterized rendering integrals. It is related to shift maps [Kettunen et al. 2015; Lehtinen et al. 2013] and Rousselle et al. [2016] who applied control variates to image-space gradients. Reparameterizing discontinuous integrands for differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3355089.3356510, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gradient Estimation and Smoothing
body: Gradient estimation and smoothing techniques address discontinuities in differentiable rendering that cause vanishing gradients. This family modifies gradient computation by smoothing the integrand to permit differentiation under the integral sign, approximating gradients via non-local spatial statistics, or applying axis-aligned filters [6449-smooth-gradient-estimation-via-convolution.md, 6784-non-local-approximated-gradients.md, 7600-axis-aligned-neighbor-smoothing.md]. Methods in this family either smooth the rendering integrand via convolution to allow Leibniz's rule to exchange differentiation and integration, or approximate gradients using differential filters on rendered images to propagate gradients beyond immediate primitive boundaries [6449-smooth-gradient-estimation-via-convolution.md, 6784-non-local-approximated-gradients.md]. Both aim to provide non-zero, directed gradients that guide optimization away from local minima [6449-smooth-gradient-estimation-via-convolution.md, 6784-non-local-approximated-gradients.md]. This method enables the computation of correct gradients for differentiable volume rendering by smoothing the rendering integrand via convolution, allowing the differential operator to move inside the integral via Leibniz's rule. It solves the problem where naive automatic differentiation yields incorrect gradients because the integrand is discontinuous with respect to scene parameters, causing classic gradients to be zero almost everywhere except at overlaps. It sets itself apart from Non-local Approximated Gradients by explicitly enforcing smoothness through convolution to permit differentiation under the integral sign, rather than approximating gradients via non-local statistics. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def samplegradientkernel(xi, sigma): """ Samples a parameter tau from the positivized, normalized CDF of the gradient-smoothing kernel using inverse transform sampling. """ if xi <= 0.5: return -math.sqrt(2 sigma2 math.log(2 xi)) else: return math.sqrt(2 sigma2 math.log(1 - xi)) def computesmoothgradient(R, theta, sigma, numsamples): """ Computes the smooth gradient of the rendering equation via convolution. """ gradientsum = np.zeroslike(theta) for in range(numsamples): # Standard light path sampling is performed here. omegai = np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=3) # Sample parameter tau from the gradient kernel xi = np.random.uniform(0, 1) taudiff = samplegradientkernel(xi, sigma) # Sample other dimensions independently from Gaussian tauother = np.random.normal(0, sigma, size=len(theta) - 1) # Construct full tau vector (assuming theta[0] is the differentiated dimension) tau = np.zeroslike(theta) tau[0] = taudiff tau[1:] = tauother # Evaluate integrand at shifted parameter shiftedtheta = theta - tau radiance = R(omegai, shiftedtheta) # Compute kernel derivative weight: -taui / sigma^2 N(tau, sigma) kernelval = np.exp(-0.5 (tau[0]2) / sigma2) / (math.sqrt(2 math.pi) sigma) weight = -tau[0] / sigma2 kernelval # Accumulate gradient contribution gradientsum += weight radiance return gradientsum / numsamples Non-local approximated gradients are a gradient estimation technique for differentiable volume and mesh rendering that computes pixel derivatives with respect to vertex positions using differential filters, allowing gradient flow from pixels outside the immediate primitive boundary. Unlike standard differentiable rendering which only propagates gradients through covered pixels, this method enables optimization objectives to influence vertices via boundary pixels, addressing the issue of poor local minima caused by the "localness" of standard rasterizer derivatives. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Smooth Gradient Estimation via Convolution by explicitly leveraging backpropagated loss gradients to make the gradient flow objective-aware, rather than relying solely on geometric or intensity-based smoothing. Introduced for homogeneous participating media by Gruson et al., taking advantage of the smoothness characteristics of rendered participating media to obtain smoother results than the original method. Four different gradient-based estimation methods were introduced: point to point, point to beam, beam to beam, and beam to light plane. With gradient domain rendering, smoother results are obtained than the original method. More recently, a deep learning based reconstruction approach for participating media has been proposed, yielding a better reconstruction solution than Poisson reconstruction. Implements a bilateral-like filter along a chosen axis, assuming the existence of a depth buffer and a normal buffer packed into a single texture alongside the color buffer. It solves the problem of vanishing gradients by smoothing the rendering integrand along a specific axis using a weighted average of neighboring pixels, preserving structural coherence via geometric priors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def axisalignedneighborsmoothing(u, v, R=7): # Current fragment data currentnd = samplenormaldepthtexture(u, v) currentcolor = samplecolortexture(u, v) n = np.array([currentnd[0], currentnd[1], currentnd[2]]) d = currentnd[3] c = currentcolor resultcolor = np.zeros(4) sumw = 0.0 # Precompute fwidth for depth scale invariance fw = fwidth(d) for i in range(-R, R + 1): uneighbor = u + i # Sample neighbor data neighbornd = samplenormaldepthtexture(uneighbor, v) neighborcolor = samplecolortexture(uneighbor, v) nprime = np.array([neighbornd[0], neighbornd[1], neighbornd[2]]) dprime = neighbornd[3] cprime = neighborcolor # Compute weights wz = math.exp(- (abs(d - dprime) 0.1) / (fw + 0.01)) wn = abs(np.dot(n, nprime)) wd = math.exp(- (i i) 0.005) colordistsq = np.dot(cprime - c, cprime - c) wc = math.exp(- colordistsq 2.0) # Total weight w = wn wz wd wc # Accumulate resultcolor += cprime w sumw += w # Normalize if sumw > 0.0: resultcolor = resultcolor (1.0 / sumw) else: pass return resultcolor Gradient estimation techniques in rendering have evolved to address the limitations of standard differentiable rendering. The concept of gradient-based rendering was introduced for homogeneous participating media by Gruson et al., leveraging the smoothness characteristics of multiple scattering. Frequency analysis of light transport was introduced for prefiltering and adaptive sampling in surface rendering, and later extended to participating media by Belcour et al., based on the observation that multiple scattering leads to a smooth appearance. More recently, deep learning-based reconstruction approaches have been proposed for participating media, yielding better reconstruction solutions than traditional Poisson reconstruction methods. A survey on rendering homogeneous participating media, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-021-0249-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Smooth Gradient Estimation via Convolution
head: Combined gradient-smoothing operator, Convolutional Smoothing for Gradients, Gradient Smoothing via Convolution, Leibniz Rule Gradient Estimation via Convolution, Smooth Differentiation via Convolution, Smooth Gradient
body: Smooth Gradient Estimation via Convolution enables the differentiation of the rendering equation by smoothing the integrand via convolution with a kernel, allowing the differential operator to move inside the integral via Leibniz's rule. It solves the problem of discontinuous integrands where naive automatic differentiation yields zero gradients almost everywhere (plateaus) except at exact overlaps, causing optimization to fail to converge. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly enforcing smoothness through convolution to permit the exchange of differentiation and integration, whereas Non-local Approximated Gradients approximates gradients using differential filters on rendered images and Axis-Aligned Neighbor Smoothing uses local neighbor averaging [6449-smooth-gradient-estimation-via-convolution.md, 6784-non-local-approximated-gradients.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The rendering integrand R(\omegai; \theta), where \omegai represents incoming light directions and \theta represents scene parameters. Output: The gradient of the smoothed rendering equation with respect to \theta, denoted D \bar{L}(x, \omegao; \theta). Data Structures: Smoothing Kernel \kappa: A Gaussian distribution is used in this work. Parameter Space \Theta: The domain of scene parameters \theta. Light Path Space \Omega: The domain of incoming light directions \omegai. Numbered Steps: 1. Define the smoothing operator S as a convolution with a kernel \kappa. For any function f in any dimension: S f (\theta) = \int{\Theta} \kappa(\tau)f (\theta - \tau)d\tau where \kappa is a smoothing kernel, specifically a Gaussian distribution. 2. Apply the smoothing operator S to the rendering integrand R to obtain the smoothed rendering equation \bar{L}: \bar{L}(x, \omegao; \theta) = \int{\Omega} S R(\omegai; \theta)d\omegai This smoothed integrand is now smooth, allowing the differential operator to move inside the integral via Leibniz's rule. 3. Compute the gradient of the smoothed loss by moving the differential operator D inside the integral: D \bar{L}(x, \omegao; \theta) = \int{\Omega} D S R(\omegai; \theta)d\omegai This step is valid because the convolution enforces the smoothness property that prevents the discontinuities which normally block this exchange. 4. Rearrange and expand the expression to yield an integral over the product space of light paths and scene parameters: D \bar{L}(x, \omegao; \theta) = \int{\Omega} \int{\Theta} D \kappa(\tau)R(\omegai; \theta - \tau)d\tau d\omegai Here, D \kappa(\tau) is the derivative of the smoothing kernel with respect to its argument. 5. Approximate the double integral via Monte Carlo (MC) sampling from the product space of light paths (\omegai \in \Omega) and scene parameters (\tau \in \Theta). Sample \omegai from \Omega using standard importance sampling strategies for incoming radiance and BRDF terms. Sample \tau from \Theta using importance sampling for the application of the differential operator to the smoothing kernel D \kappa(\tau). The integrand is a product of four terms: incoming radiance, BRDF, the kernel derivative D \kappa(\tau), and the shifted integrand R(\omegai; \theta - \tau). Formulas: Smoothed Rendering Equation: \bar{L}(x, \omegao; \theta) = \int{\Omega} S R(\omegai; \theta)d\omegai Smoothing Convolution: S f (\theta) = \int{\Theta} \kappa(\tau)f (\theta - \tau)d\tau Gradient of Smoothed Loss: D \bar{L}(x, \omegao; \theta) = \int{\Omega} \int{\Theta} D \kappa(\tau)R(\omegai; \theta - \tau)d\tau d\omegai Parameters: Smoothing Kernel \kappa: A Gaussian distribution is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Naive automatic differentiation computes \int{\Omega} D R(\omegai; \theta) d\omegai, which is incorrect because the integrand is discontinuous in \theta, preventing the exchange of integral and derivative operations. Classic gradients are zero almost everywhere (plateaus) except where overlaps occur, causing non-convergence. Smooth gradients point in the right direction but may make large steps far from the optimum. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def smoothgradientestimation(R, x, omegao, theta, numsamples): """ Computes the gradient of the smoothed rendering equation via Monte Carlo sampling. Args: R: Callable R(omegai, theta) returning radiance. x: Camera position. omegao: Outgoing direction. theta: Scene parameters (array-like). numsamples: Number of MC samples. Returns: Estimated gradient D Lbar(x, omegao; theta). """ gradientsum = np.zeroslike(theta, dtype=float) for in range(numsamples): # Sample light path omegai from Omega # Standard importance sampling for radiance/BRDF is assumed; # implementer must provide specific sampling strategy for R. omegai = np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, 3) # Sample tau from Theta based on importance sampling for D kappa(tau) # Sampling for D kappa(tau) is the essence of the problem at hand. tau = np.random.normal(0.0, 1.0, theta.shape[0]) # Evaluate the integrand: D kappa(tau) R(omegai; theta - tau) shiftedtheta = theta - tau radiance = R(omegai, shiftedtheta) # D kappa(tau) for standard Gaussian: -tau exp(-0.5 tau^2) / sqrt(2pi) kernelderiv = -tau np.exp(-0.5 tau2) / np.sqrt(2.0 np.pi) # Combine terms and divide by sampling PDFs # The integrand is a product of four terms. # p(omegai) and p(tau) are the probability densities of the samples. pdfomega = 1.0 / 2.0 # Uniform PDF over [-1, 1] for 1D example pdftau = np.exp(-0.5 tau2) / np.sqrt(2.0 np.pi) if pdfomega == 0 or pdftau == 0: continue weight = (kernelderiv radiance) / (pdfomega pdftau) gradientsum += weight return gradientsum / numsamples Computes the second-order spatial derivatives (the Hessian matrix) of a scalar volume function by convolving the function with a kernel that combines Gaussian smoothing and second-order differentiation. It sets itself apart from Smooth Gradient Estimation via Convolution by operating on the second derivative operator \nabla^2 rather than the first, and from Gradient Estimation (Our Grad.) by producing an n \times n matrix field instead of a vector field. Choose it when higher-order optimization requires stable, differentiable curvature information. Samples an n-dimensional Gaussian gradient by marginalizing the probability density function (PDF) over all dimensions except the one being differentiated, allowing individual dimension sampling. It sets itself apart from methods that only blur in the direction of differentiation by blurring all dimensions, which is more consistent with higher-order differentials. Choose it when consistent multi-dimensional gradient sampling is required for higher-order differentials. Computes the first-order gradient vector field of a scalar function with respect to its input dimensions, enabling differentiable volume rendering via stochastic sampling. It sets itself apart from siblings by specifically targeting the \nabla operator, mapping a scalar function f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} to an n-dimensional gradient vector field. Choose it when first-order gradient vector fields are sufficient for differentiable volume rendering. Time Complexity: The method requires Monte Carlo sampling from the product space of light paths and scene parameters. The complexity depends on the number of samples required to reduce variance, which is influenced by the smoothness of the kernel and the complexity of the integrand. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Classic gradients are zero almost everywhere (plateaus) except where overlaps occur, causing non-convergence. Smooth gradients point in the right direction but make large steps far from the optimum. An update taking into account the curvature of the loss landscape (via Hessians) lands at a point very close to the target. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables differentiation of discontinuous integrands by enforcing smoothness, allowing the use of gradient-based optimization. Limitations: Smooth gradients may make large steps far from the optimum, potentially requiring second-order information (Hessians) for efficient convergence. When to use: When naive automatic differentiation fails due to discontinuous integrands, and gradient-based optimization is desired. When not to use: When the integrand is already smooth, or when second-order information is not needed and first-order gradients are sufficient. The method originates from the work on Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-Order Differentiable Rendering. It addresses the issue that naive automatic differentiation computes the wrong gradients because the integrand is discontinuous in the scene parameters, preventing the exchange of integral and derivative operations. The solution involves enforcing smoothness via convolution to allow the application of Leibniz's rule. Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-Order Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51701.2025.02618, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Hessian Estimation via Convolution
head: Hessian Estimation (Our Hess.), Second-order derivative estimation using the Hessian operator
body:
Hessian Estimation via Convolution computes the second-order spatial derivatives (the Hessian matrix) of a scalar volume function by convolving the volume with a kernel that combines Gaussian smoothing and second-order differentiation. It solves the problem of obtaining stable, differentiable curvature information required for higher-order optimization in differentiable volume rendering. It sets itself apart from Smooth Gradient Estimation via Convolution by operating on the second derivative operator 
abla^2 rather than the first, and from Gradient Estimation (Our Grad.) by producing an n 	imes n matrix field instead of a vector field. Inputs: A scalar volume function V(\mathbf{x}) defined on \mathbb{R}^n; a smoothing parameter \sigma > 0. Outputs: An n 	imes n Hessian field H(\mathbf{x}), where H{ij} =  rac{\partial^2 V}{\partial xi \partial xj}. Data Structures: Volume Grid: V stored as a dense array or sparse structure. Hessian Field: H stored as an n 	imes n matrix per voxel. The method exploits symmetry (H{ij} = H{ji}) during sampling and estimation to reduce computational overhead. CDF Lookup Table: For diagonal elements, a 1D table mapping CDF values to spatial offsets 	aui. Method Steps: 1. Define the Kernel: The convolution kernel D^H \kappa{i,j}( oldsymbol{	au}) combines the Gaussian N( oldsymbol{	au}, \sigma) with the second-order differential operator. For dimensions i, j \in \{1, \dots, n\}: D^H \kappa{i,j}( oldsymbol{	au}) =  egin{cases} \left( - rac{	aui^2}{\sigma^2} +  rac{1}{\sigma^2} ight) N( oldsymbol{	au}, \sigma) & 	ext{if } i = j \  rac{	aui 	auj}{\sigma^4} N( oldsymbol{	au}, \sigma) & 	ext{if } i 
eq j \end{cases} where N( oldsymbol{	au}, \sigma) =  rac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}} \exp\left(- rac{\| oldsymbol{	au}\|^2}{2\sigma^2}ight). 2. Sampling Strategy (Stochastic Estimation): To estimate the Hessian efficiently, samples are drawn from a probability density function (PDF) derived from the kernel. The kernel is positivized and normalized to form a valid distribution. Off-Diagonal Elements (i 
eq j): The kernel factorizes into the product of two first-order gradient kernels. Sample 	aui from the PDF of the first derivative in dimension i, and 	auj from the PDF of the first derivative in dimension j. Diagonal Elements (i = j): The kernel is signed and must be positivized. The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) P^H{ii}(u) for the marginal distribution along dimension i is: P^H{ii}(u) =  egin{cases}  rac{1}{4\sigma} \exp\left(- rac{u^2}{2\sigma^2}ight) & 	ext{if } u < -\sigma \ 0.5 +  rac{u}{4\sigma} \exp\left(- rac{u^2}{2\sigma^2}ight) & 	ext{if } u \in [-\sigma, \sigma] \ 1 -  rac{1}{4\sigma} \exp\left(- rac{u^2}{2\sigma^2}ight) & 	ext{if } u > \sigma \end{cases} This is a transcendental equation with no closed-form inverse. 3. Inverse CDF Implementation: Tabulate P^H{ii}(u) on a discrete range [-10\sigma, 10\sigma] for each dimension i. Pre-compute and store the inverse indices (mapping CDF values to u) in a sorted array to allow O(1) lookup during sampling. 4. Estimation: For each sample, compute the contribution to the Hessian matrix by evaluating the volume at the sampled offset and multiplying by the kernel weight. Exploit symmetry: Estimate H{ij} and H{ji} simultaneously. Average contributions over M samples to reduce variance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def gaussianpdf1d(tau, sigma): """1D Gaussian PDF.""" return (1.0 / (math.sqrt(2 math.pi) sigma)) math.exp(-0.5 (tau tau) / (sigma sigma)) def computediagonalcdf(u, sigma): """CDF P^Hii(u) for diagonal Hessian elements.""" if u < -sigma: return (1.0 / (4 sigma)) math.exp(-0.5 (u u) / (sigma sigma)) elif u <= sigma: return 0.5 + (u / (4 sigma)) math.exp(-0.5 (u u) / (sigma sigma)) else: return 1.0 - (1.0 / (4 sigma)) math.exp(-0.5 (u u) / (sigma sigma)) def bisectleft(arr, target): """Returns the leftmost index where target could be inserted to keep arr sorted.""" low, high = 0, len(arr) while low < high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if arr[mid] < target: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid return low def samplediagonalelement(cdftable, inverseindices): """Samples taui from the diagonal Hessian distribution using inverse transform sampling.""" r = random.random() idx = bisectleft(cdftable, r) return inverseindices[idx] def samplegradientpdf1d(sigma): """Samples from the 1D first-order gradient PDF p(tau) ~ |tau| exp(-tau^2 / 2sigma^2) via rejection sampling.""" maxval = sigma math.exp(-0.5) while True: tau = random.uniform(-sigma, sigma) if abs(tau) < 1e-9: tau = 1e-9 u = random.random() if u <= (abs(tau) math.exp(-0.5 (tau tau) / (sigma sigma))) / maxval: return tau def estimatehessianvolume(volume, sigma, numsamples): """Estimates the Hessian field of a volume using stochastic convolution.""" n = len(volume.shape) numvoxels = volume.shape[0] hessianfield = [None] numvoxels # Pre-compute diagonal CDF tables for each dimension numbins = 1000 taurange = [(-10 sigma) + i (20 sigma / (numbins - 1)) for i in range(numbins)] cdftables = {} inverseindices = {} for i in range(n): cdfvals = [computediagonalcdf(t, sigma) for t in taurange] sortedindices = sorted(range(len(cdfvals)), key=lambda k: cdfvals[k]) cdftables[i] = [cdfvals[k] for k in sortedindices] inverseindices[i] = [taurange[k] for k in sortedindices] for voxelidx in range(numvoxels): hessian = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for in range(numsamples): # Diagonal elements for i in range(n): taui = samplediagonalelement(cdftables[i], inverseindices[i]) # Construct full tau vector: taui is fixed, others sampled from N(0, sigma) tau = [0.0] n tau[i] = taui for j in range(n): if j != i: u1 = random.random() u2 = random.random() tau[j] = sigma math.sqrt(-2.0 math.log(u1)) math.cos(2.0 math.pi u2) # Compute kernel weight: D^H kappa{ii} = (-taui^2/sigma^2 + 1/sigma^2) N(tau, sigma) nval = 1.0 for k in range(n): nval = gaussianpdf1d(tau[k], sigma) kernelval = (-tau[i]2 / sigma2 + 1.0 / sigma2) nval # Monte Carlo estimator: V(x + tau) Kernel(tau) vval = volume.evaluate(voxelidx, tau) hessian[i][i] += vval kernelval # Off-diagonal elements for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): taui = samplegradientpdf1d(sigma) tauj = samplegradientpdf1d(sigma) tau = [0.0] n tau[i] = taui tau[j] = tauj for k in range(n): if k != i and k != j: u1 = random.random() u2 = random.random() tau[k] = sigma math.sqrt(-2.0 math.log(u1)) math.cos(2.0 math.pi u2) # Kernel value: (taui tauj / sigma^4) N(tau, sigma) nval = 1.0 for k in range(n): nval = gaussianpdf1d(tau[k], sigma) kernelval = (tau[i] tau[j] / sigma4) nval vval = volume.evaluate(voxelidx, tau) hessian[i][j] += vval kernelval hessian[j][i] = hessian[i][j] # Symmetry # Average over samples for i in range(n): for j in range(n): hessian[i][j] /= numsamples hessianfield[voxelidx] = hessian return hessianfield Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The diagonal CDF is transcendental; numerical instability may occur near u = \pm \sigma if not handled with high-precision arithmetic or careful tabulation. Boundary Conditions: Sampling near volume boundaries requires handling out-of-bounds accesses (e.g., clamping, reflection, or zero-padding). Variance: Stochastic estimation has high variance; Aggregate Importance Sampling is recommended to reduce this. A variance reduction technique that samples from a mixture distribution of all convolution kernels, reducing computational complexity from O(n^2) to O(1) per iteration at the cost of slightly increased variance. Uses the Hessian to compute the second directional derivative along the gradient direction, providing sharper edge characterization than gradient magnitude alone. Locates step edges by finding the zero-crossing of the second-order derivative, relying on the continuity of the reconstruction filter. A deterministic method that exploits the separability of Gaussian derivative kernels to compute the Hessian matrix using sequential 1D convolutions. It reduces the complexity of a 3D convolution O(k^3) to three 1D convolutions O(3k). Computing the gradient requires 8 1D convolutions (reusing G\sigma(x)I twice and G'\sigma(x)I once), while computing the Hessian requires 15 1D convolutions (reusing G\sigma(x)I three times and G'\sigma(x)I twice). The formula for the derivative is \partial^o I = \partialx^a \partialy^b \partialz^c I = G\sigma^{(a)} G\sigma^{(b)} G\sigma^{(c)} I where a+b+c=o \in \{1, 2\}. Benchmarks on a Pentium III 800 MHz with kernel size k=7 show that computing Hessian eigenvalues is on average 2.7 times more expensive than computing gradient magnitude. Time Complexity: O(n^2) function evaluations per voxel without Importance Sampling (IS). With IS, it remains O(n^2) but with lower variance. With Aggregate IS, it reduces to O(1) per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) per voxel for the full Hessian matrix, though symmetry allows storing only n(n+1)/2 elements. Avoiding the full Hessian is possible by using Hessian-vector products (HVPs). Performance: Deterministic separable convolution reduces 3D convolution complexity O(k^3) to three 1D convolutions O(3k). Strengths: Provides full curvature information; stable via Gaussian smoothing; compatible with gradient-based optimization. Limitations: High computational cost for full Hessian; stochastic methods suffer from noise without sufficient samples or IS; deterministic methods are memory-intensive for large volumes. When to use: When second-order information is critical for convergence or edge detection. Avoid when memory is constrained or real-time performance is required without IS. The method originates from stochastic gradient estimation for differentiable rendering, specifically extending first-order gradient estimation to second-order derivatives. The core formulation for the Hessian kernel and its stochastic sampling via CDF inversion was introduced by Fischer and Ritschel in "Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-Order Differentiable Rendering" (2025). The separable convolution approach for Hessian computation in volume data was earlier established by Weinkauf et al. in "Salient Representation of Volume Data" (2001). Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-Order Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51701.2025.02618, fetched 2026-10-29 Salient Representation of Volume Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/vissym01/203-212, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Aggregate Importance Sampling
head: AIS
body: Aggregate Importance Sampling (AIS) is a sampling strategy to reduce function evaluations by importance-sampling the average of the convolution kernels across all dimensions or elements, rather than each individually. It addresses the high computational cost of non-aggregate importance sampling, which requires O(n) or O(n^2) evaluations for an n-dimensional output, by sampling from a mixture distribution representing the average of all convolution kernels. Unlike non-aggregate methods that optimize each dimension individually, AIS performs a single function evaluation per iteration, trading a slight increase in variance for a linear reduction in computational complexity. AIS estimates the derivative of a scalar function f with respect to n parameters by approximating the convolution of f with a differential kernel. The method reduces the number of rendering calls from proportional to the number of output elements to a constant O(1) per iteration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A differentiable rendering function f(\mathbf{x}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n is the parameter vector. A probability distribution p(\mathbf{z}) for sampling perturbation directions \mathbf{z}. Output: An unbiased estimator for the differential quantity (e.g., gradient vector or Hessian matrix). Data Structures: Differential Representation: For a Hessian, this is an n \times n matrix. For a gradient, it is a vector of size n. Kernel: The convolution kernel K(\mathbf{z}) associated with the differential operator (e.g., second-order derivative kernel for Hessian). Algorithm Steps: 1. Randomly decide which element of the differential representation to choose (e.g., which matrix element out of n^2 in the Hessian). 2. Compute the convolution sample for all n^2 elements using the same function value (single rendering call), weighting each by its respective kernel. Formulas: Let D be the differential operator (e.g., Hessian). The estimator for the (i,j)-th element \hat{D}{ij} after T iterations is: \hat{D}{ij} = \frac{1}{T{ij}} \sum{t=1}^{T{ij}} \frac{f(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{z}t) K{ij}(\mathbf{z}t)}{p(\mathbf{z}t)} Where: T{ij} is the number of times element (i,j) was selected. K{ij}(\mathbf{z}) is the kernel value for the (i,j)-th derivative at perturbation \mathbf{z}. p(\mathbf{z}) is the probability density of the sampling distribution. Parameters: Sampling Distribution p(\mathbf{z}): Typically a mixture distribution or a distribution matching the average kernel properties. The sources note that the average kernel shares properties like being zero at position 0 with individual kernels. Selection Probability: Uniform selection of the element index is implied by the "randomly decide" step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def aggregateimportancesampling(f, x, n, numiterations, sampledistribution, kernelfunc): """ Estimate the differential quantity of f at x using Aggregate Importance Sampling. """ # Initialize accumulator and counts H = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] counts = [[0] n for in range(n)] for in range(numiterations): # Step 1: Randomly decide which element of the differential representation to choose i = random.randint(0, n - 1) j = random.randint(0, n - 1) # Step 2: Sample perturbation from the mixture/average distribution z, pz = sampledistribution() # Step 3: Compute the convolution sample using the same function value (single rendering call) fval = f(x + z) # Step 4: Weight by the respective kernel for the selected element kval = kernelfunc(i, j, z) # Unbiased estimator contribution sample = (fval kval) / pz # Accumulate H[i][j] += sample counts[i][j] += 1 # Normalize by counts to get the average estimate for i in range(n): for j in range(n): if counts[i][j] > 0: H[i][j] /= counts[i][j] return H def kernelfunc(i, j, z): # Returns the kernel value for the (i,j)-th derivative at perturbation z # Exact implementation depends on the specific differential operator return 1.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance Increase: AIS increases variance compared to non-aggregate importance sampling because the average kernel is not identical to the individual kernels. Zero-Kernel Positions: Both average and individual kernels are zero at position 0, which must be handled correctly in the sampling distribution to avoid division by zero or undefined weights. Uneven Sampling: If certain elements are rarely selected, their estimates will have higher variance due to fewer samples. Sampling Convolutions is a technique to compute accurate gradients in integrands with large support using spherical convolutions, specifically addressing the mismatch between standard hemispherical sampling and the full-sphere support of a convolution. It differs from naive convolution sampling by introducing a precomputed correction factor that compensates for the energy loss incurred when the sampling distribution (typically a BRDF) is restricted to a hemisphere while the convolution kernel extends over the full sphere. Time Complexity: O(1) function evaluations per iteration for all differential methods (Gradient, Hessian, Hessian-Vector Product), compared to O(n) or O(n^2) for non-aggregate importance sampling. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) to store the Hessian matrix and counts, assuming a Hessian is being estimated. Variance: All estimators converge linearly in a log-log plot. The optimal estimator (sampling each dimension individually) has the lowest variance but requires quadratically many evaluations for Hessians. Aggregate sampling performs slightly worse than the optimal estimator but much better than uniform sampling. Strengths: Significant reduction in rendering calls, making higher-order derivatives feasible in differentiable rendering. Limitations: Higher variance than optimal sampling; requires careful design of the mixture sampling distribution to approximate the average kernel effectively. Aggregate Importance Sampling was proposed in the context of stochastic gradient estimation for higher-order differentiable rendering. It addresses the challenge of optimizing differentiable quantities where the number of parameters n is large, making non-aggregate methods computationally prohibitive. The method is analogous to Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) using the balance heuristic, where proposals are combined by sampling from a mixture. name: Sampling Convolutions
body: Sampling Convolutions is a technique to compute accurate gradients in integrands with large support using spherical convolutions, specifically addressing the mismatch between standard hemispherical sampling and the full-sphere support of a convolution. It differs from naive convolution sampling by introducing a precomputed correction factor that compensates for the energy loss incurred when the sampling distribution is restricted to a hemisphere while the convolution kernel extends over the full sphere. Inputs: The integrand function f(\mu), typically a product of a BSDF and incident illumination. The convolution kernel k(\mu, \omega), defined on the unit sphere S^2. The default sampling strategy PDF used by the renderer for f, denoted pf(\mu). Outputs: An unbiased estimate of the integral \int{S^2} f(\mu) d\mu. Data Structures: Correction Lookup Table: A precomputed array or function mapping direction \mu \in \mathcal{H} to the scalar correction factor C(\mu). Parameters: Kernel Width: The method assumes k is a narrowly peaked convolution kernel. Correction Factor Values: C(\mu) = 1/2 at grazing angles and C(\mu) \approx 1 for directions inside the hemisphere. Steps: 1. Precompute Correction Factor: Calculate C(\mu) = \int{\mathcal{H}} k(\mu, \omega) d\omega for the chosen kernel k. 2. Sample Direction: Sample a direction \mu from the hemisphere \mathcal{H} using the renderer's default sampling strategy for f. 3. Evaluate Integrand and Correction: Compute f(\mu) and retrieve C(\mu) from the lookup table. 4. Compute Weight: Calculate the sample weight as \frac{f(\mu)}{C(\mu) pf(\mu)} \int{S^2} k(\mu, \omega) d\omega. If the kernel is normalized over S^2, the inner integral equals 1. 5. Accumulate: Accumulate the weight to estimate \int{S^2} f(\mu) d\mu. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: f: Function evaluating the integrand f(mu). kernelk: Convolution kernel function k(mu, omega). pf: PDF function for the default sampling strategy of f. Clookup: Function or lookup table for C(mu). Returns: unbiasedestimate: Float, the unbiased estimate of the integral. """ # Step 2: Sample direction from hemisphere using default strategy mu, pdfvalue = pf.sample() # Guard: ensure sample is valid and correction factor is non-zero if mu.z <= 0 or Clookup(mu) == 0: return 0.0 # Step 3: Retrieve correction factor and evaluate integrand Cmu = Clookup(mu) fval = f(mu) # Step 4: Compute weight # The estimator derives from Eq. 35-37: f(mu) / (C(mu) pf(mu)) integral(k) over S^2 # Assuming kernelk is normalized over S^2, the integral equals 1.0 kernelintegral = 1.0 weight = (fval / (Cmu pdfvalue)) kernelintegral return weight Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hemispherical Mismatch: Standard BRDF sampling only covers the hemisphere \mathcal{H}, but the support of f \otimes k is the full sphere S^2, causing energy loss. Grazing Angles: At grazing angles, C(\mu) = 1/2, which halves the effective sampling weight if uncorrected. Kernel Width: The method relies on f \otimes k being similar to f, which holds when k is narrowly peaked. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the default sampling strategy for f is a good approximation for f \otimes k, which holds best for narrowly peaked kernels. name: Edge location estimation via second-order derivative
head: Second-order derivative edge estimation, Zero-crossing of second derivative
body: This method estimates the location of a step edge in continuous unsampled data by locating the zero-crossing of the second-order derivative of the signal. It relies on the principle that the first derivative of a step response equals the point-spread function of the acquisition apparatus, whose maximum corresponds to the edge location. Unlike value-based midpoint methods, it requires a reconstruction filter with a continuous second-order derivative, making it unreliable for standard low-order interpolation schemes applied to sampled data. Input: Discrete sample values, their positions, and a reconstruction filter capable of evaluating the continuous field and its derivatives. Output: The estimated edge position \mathbf{x}e. Not given in the sources. 1. Reconstruct the field: Evaluate the continuous scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) from discrete samples using a reconstruction filter that possesses a continuous second-order derivative. 2. Compute the second derivative: Calculate the second-order derivative of the reconstructed field at arbitrary points. 3. Find the zero-crossing: Search for the location where the second-order derivative equals zero, which corresponds to the maximum of the first derivative. The edge location xe satisfies: \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(xe) = 0 This zero-crossing identifies the peak of the first derivative \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, which acts as the point-spread function of the acquisition apparatus. Reconstruction Filter: Must have a continuous second-order derivative to ensure accurate edge localization. Linear Interpolation: The first derivative is piece-wise constant, so there is no unique location where the maximum is located. Quadratic Reconstruction: The first derivative is piece-wise linear, and its extreme always coincides with the boundaries of the piece-wise linear derivative. The second derivative is piece-wise constant and generally not significant for edge approximation. Cubic-Spline Interpolation: The second derivative is piece-wise linear but not continuous, making the zero-crossing an unreliable approximation of the edge location. General Limitation: Any reconstruction filter that lacks a continuous second-order derivative fails to provide an accurate edge location. Unverified code. Args: samples: Array of scalar sample values. positions: Array of sample positions. filtereval: Callable(x, samples, positions) -> (value, d1, d2) Evaluates the reconstructed field and its first two derivatives. Returns: Estimated edge position, or None if no zero-crossing is found. """ # Sources do not specify search bounds or step size xmin, xmax = min(positions), max(positions) step = (xmax - xmin) / 100.0 xprev = xmin d2prev = filtereval(xprev, samples, positions)[2] for in range(100): xcurr = xprev + step d2curr = filtereval(xcurr, samples, positions)[2] if d2prev d2curr <= 0: # Zero-crossing detected between xprev and xcurr # Refine root using bisection xlo, xhi = xprev, xcurr for in range(50): xmid = (xlo + xhi) / 2.0 d2mid = filtereval(xmid, samples, positions)[2] if d2prev d2mid <= 0: xhi = xmid else: xlo = xmid d2prev = d2mid return (xlo + xhi) / 2.0 xprev = xcurr d2prev = d2curr return None What it is: A method that combines importance sampling with aggregation techniques to improve the efficiency of gradient estimation. Difference: Focuses on sampling strategy rather than derivative computation. When to choose: When computational cost of sampling is a bottleneck. Link: Aggregate Importance Sampling What it is: Estimates the derivative along a specific direction rather than the full Hessian. Difference: Simpler than full Hessian estimation but less comprehensive. When to choose: When only directional information is needed. Link: Second Directional Derivative Time Complexity: Depends on the cost of evaluating the second derivative and the root-finding iterations. Memory Complexity: Low, as it operates on reconstructed field values. Strengths: Provides a theoretically sound method for edge location in continuous data. Limitations: Highly sensitive to the continuity of the reconstruction filter; fails for common low-order interpolation schemes. When to use: When a high-order reconstruction filter with continuous second derivatives is available and accurate edge localization is critical. When not to use: When using standard linear or quadratic interpolation, or when a simpler value-based midpoint method suffices. It addresses the partial volume effect, where edges are blurred in sampled data, by leveraging the properties of the point-spread function. name: Separable Convolution for Volume Reconstruction and Differentiation
head: Separable Reconstruction and Differentiation via 1D Kernel Product
body: This method computes 3D volume reconstruction and its spatial derivatives by decomposing the 3D convolution into a product of three 1D kernels, treating each dimension in isolation. It sets itself apart from direct 3D convolution by reducing computational complexity through separability, allowing efficient calculation of gradients and higher-order derivatives required for differentiable volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Discrete sampled volume data v[i, j, k] defined on a 3D grid. Input: A 1D reconstruction kernel h(x). Output: Reconstructed continuous field value (v h)(x, y, z). Output: Partial derivatives \frac{\partial(v h)}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial(v h)}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial(v h)}{\partial z}. Data Structures: The 3D kernel is defined as the tensor product of three identical 1D kernels: h(x, y, z) = h(x)h(y)h(z). The derivative kernel h'(x) is the analytic derivative of h(x). Parameters: Kernel choice: Cubic kernels, specifically the Mitchell and Netravali "BC" family, are recommended as a compromise between frequency response and cost. Parameters B and C define the specific cubic spline: Catmull-Rom: B=0, C=0.5. Uniform cubic B-spline: B=1, C=0. The B-spline is preferred for derivative computation because it is a non-interpolating smoothing kernel that attenuates high-frequency noise. Steps: 1. Define the 1D reconstruction kernel h(x) and its derivative h'(x). 2. For any point (x, y, z), compute the reconstructed value by convolving the data with the separable 3D kernel: (v h)(x, y, z) = \sum{i,j,k} v[i, j, k]h(x-i)h(y-j)h(z-k) 3. To compute the partial derivative with respect to x, convolve the data using h'(x) in the x-dimension and h(y), h(z) in the other dimensions: \frac{\partial(v h)(x, y, z)}{\partial x} = \sum{i,j,k} v[i, j, k]h'(x - i)h(y - j)h(z - k) 4. To compute the partial derivative with respect to y, use h(x), h'(y), and h(z): \frac{\partial(v h)(x, y, z)}{\partial y} = \sum{i,j,k} v[i, j, k]h(x - i)h'(y - j)h(z - k) 5. To compute the partial derivative with respect to z, use h(x), h(y), and h'(z): \frac{\partial(v h)(x, y, z)}{\partial z} = \sum{i,j,k} v[i, j, k]h(x - i)h(y - j)h'(z - k) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def separableconvolution3d(volume, kernel1d, derivativekernel1d, targetaxis='none'): """ Computes 3D reconstruction and optionally the partial derivative along targetaxis. volume: 3D array of samples v[i, j, k] kernel1d: function h(x) derivativekernel1d: function h'(x) targetaxis: 'x', 'y', 'z', or 'none' """ # Initialize output arrays reconstructed = zeroslike(volume) derivativex = zeroslike(volume) derivativey = zeroslike(volume) derivativez = zeroslike(volume) # Get dimensions dimx, dimy, dimz = volume.shape # Iterate over all sample points for i in range(dimx): for j in range(dimy): for k in range(dimz): val = volume[i, j, k] # The separable convolution sum is computed by iterating over the kernel support. # For implementation efficiency, this is typically done by iterating over the # kernel support relative to the target grid point, but here we show the # direct application of the formula for clarity. # Note: In practice, one would iterate over the target grid (x,y,z) and # sum over the kernel support (i,j,k). The formula below represents the # mathematical definition provided in the source. # To implement the sum efficiently, we assume a kernel support range. # Let support be defined by half-width W. # For each target point (tx, ty, tz): pass # Re-implementing the logic to match the source formula structure directly: # The source defines the sum over indices i,j,k of the sampled data. # This implies a convolution where the kernel is centered at (x,y,z). # Efficient implementation strategy: # 1. Convolve volume with h(x) along axis 0 -> temp1 # 2. Convolve temp1 with h(y) along axis 1 -> temp2 # 3. Convolve temp2 with h(z) along axis 2 -> reconstructed # For derivatives, replace h with h' for the specific axis. # Step 1: X-axis convolution # If targetaxis is 'x', use derivativekernel1d, else kernel1d kernelx = derivativekernel1d if targetaxis == 'x' else kernel1d temp1 = convolve1d(volume, kernelx, axis=0) # Step 2: Y-axis convolution # If targetaxis is 'y', use derivativekernel1d, else kernel1d kernely = derivativekernel1d if targetaxis == 'y' else kernel1d temp2 = convolve1d(temp1, kernely, axis=1) # Step 3: Z-axis convolution # If targetaxis is 'z', use derivativekernel1d, else kernel1d kernelz = derivativekernel1d if targetaxis == 'z' else kernel1d result = convolve1d(temp2, kernelz, axis=2) return result def convolve1d(data, kernel, axis): """ Performs 1D convolution along a specific axis. data: N-D array kernel: 1D array or function axis: integer index """ # Standard 1D convolution implementation # Pad data to handle boundaries # Apply kernel # Return result # Implementation detail: Use scipy.ndimage.convolve1d or manual loop # with appropriate boundary handling (e.g., zero-padding or replication). pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise sensitivity: Analytic differentiation has a linear frequency response, amplifying high-frequency noise. Using the derivative of a smoothing kernel (like the cubic B-spline) is preferable to mitigate this. Kernel Support: Cubic kernels have a larger support than simpler kernels, increasing computational cost. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of voxels and K is the kernel support size. Separability reduces the complexity from O(N \cdot K^3) for direct 3D convolution to O(N \cdot 3K). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input and output volumes, plus O(K) for the kernel storage. Strengths: Efficient computation of gradients and reconstruction; flexible kernel choice allows balancing between smoothing and detail preservation. Limitations: Noise amplification in derivatives if non-smoothing kernels are used; larger kernel support increases computation time compared to nearest-neighbor or linear interpolation. When to use: When differentiable volume rendering requires accurate gradient estimation and computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: When real-time performance is required with very large kernels or when noise is extremely high and cannot be pre-filtered. This method is based on the approach adopted in visualization for using separable convolution to treat each dimension of the image in isolation. It relies on the mathematical property that a 3D kernel can be generated as the product of three 1D kernels, simplifying the evaluation of partial derivatives. The technique is used throughout research in volume rendering, particularly in the context of rendering continuous field structures and their attributes. The specific kernel recommendations (Mitchell-Netravali BC family) are drawn from standard image processing literature. name: Smooth Gradient Marginalization
head: Marginalization of Gaussian Gradient
body:
Smooth Gradient Marginalization is a technique to sample an n-dimensional Gaussian gradient by marginalizing the probability density function (PDF) over all dimensions except the one being differentiated, allowing individual dimension sampling. It differs from methods that only blur in the direction of differentiation by blurring all dimensions, which is more consistent with higher-order differentials. Inputs: The n-dimensional Gaussian function N(	au), the dimension index i to differentiate, and the standard deviation \sigma. Outputs: A marginal PDF pG(	aui) for dimension i and the corresponding CDF for sampling. Data Structures: 	au: Vector of length n. N(	au): Scalar value of the Gaussian at 	au. pG(	aui): Scalar marginal PDF for dimension i. Formulas: The marginal PDF is obtained by integrating the joint gradient PDF over all dimensions j 
eq i: pG(	aui) = \int pG(	au) \, d	au{j 
eq i} Since the Gaussian is separable, N(	au) = \prod{j=1}^n N(	auj), the integration over all N(	auj) for j 
eq i evaluates to 1, leaving the magnitude of the 1D gradient. The 1D Gaussian gradient with respect to 	aui is: 
ablai N(	aui) = - rac{	aui}{\sigma^2} N(	aui) The marginal PDF is the positivized and scaled version of this gradient. Hessian Elements: The diagonal element of the Hessian is: 
abla^2 N(	au){ii} =  rac{\partial^2 N(	au)}{\partial 	aui^2} = \left( rac{	aui^2}{\sigma^4} -  rac{1}{\sigma^2}ight) N(	au) The off-diagonal element (i 
eq j) is: 
abla^2 N(	au){ij} =  rac{	aui 	auj}{\sigma^4} N(	au) A critical distinction is that the diagonal element is not a special case of the off-diagonal element because the variable appears twice in the differentiation (d(u^2)/du = 2u vs d(uv)/du = v). Sampling Steps: 1. Identify the roots of the second-order derivative at 	aui = \pm \sigma. 2. Calculate the scaling constant  eta using the gradient at -\sigma:  eta =  rac{1}{4 
abla N(-\sigma)}. 3. Construct the CDF P^H{ii}(	aui) by positivizing and scaling the second-order derivative such that the integral over [-\sigma, \sigma] is twice the integral outside, ensuring the CDF is 1/2 at -\sigma. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gaussian1d(t: float, sigma: float) -> float: """Standard 1D Gaussian PDF.""" return (1.0 / math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi sigma 2)) math.exp(-0.5 (t / sigma) 2) def gradient1d(t: float, sigma: float) -> float: """Derivative of the 1D Gaussian PDF.""" return -(t / (sigma 2)) gaussian1d(t, sigma) def computebeta(sigma: float) -> float: """Scaling constant for Hessian diagonal sampling.""" return 1.0 / (4.0 gradient1d(-sigma, sigma)) def marginalgradientpdf(taui: float, sigma: float) -> float: """Marginal PDF for the gradient along dimension i.""" return abs(gradient1d(taui, sigma)) def hessiandiagonalcdf(taui: float, sigma: float) -> float: """CDF for sampling the diagonal of the Hessian.""" beta = computebeta(sigma) g = gradient1d(taui, sigma) if taui < -sigma: return beta g elif taui <= sigma: return 0.5 + beta g else: return 1.0 - beta g This variant samples the diagonal elements of the Hessian matrix. It derives the valid distribution of the second-order derivative of the one-dimensional Gaussian by positivization and scaling, which then applies to higher dimensions. The 1D Gaussian second-order derivative is  eta \left(  rac{1}{\sigma^2} -  rac{	aui^2}{\sigma^4} ight) N(	aui). The roots are at 	aui = \pm \sigma. The PDF is p^H{ii} = | eta 
abla^2 N(	aui)|. The CDF is defined piecewise:  eta 
abla N(	aui) if 	aui < -\sigma; 1/2 +  eta 
abla N(	aui) if 	aui \in [-\sigma, \sigma]; 1 -  eta 
abla N(	aui) if 	aui > \sigma. Not given in the sources. This method is described in "Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-Order Differentiable Rendering". It builds on the work of Fischer and Ritschel [7] who derived 1D Gaussian gradient sampling, but extends it to n-dimensions via marginalization. name: Sampling Diagonal of Hessian
head: Diagonal Hessian PDF Derivation
body:
Sampling Diagonal of Hessian is a technique for constructing a probability density function (PDF) from the second-order derivative (Hessian) of a Gaussian function, enabling importance sampling of the diagonal elements of the Hessian matrix in differentiable volume rendering. It sets itself apart from standard gradient estimators by utilizing curvature information (second derivatives) rather than first-order gradients to determine sampling weights, which is particularly relevant for higher-order differentiable rendering and optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The standard deviation \sigma of the 1D Gaussian N(	aui). Output: A Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) P^H{ii}(	aui) and a scaling constant  eta, allowing for the generation of samples 	aui distributed according to the magnitude of the diagonal Hessian element. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the method relies on scalar arithmetic and standard mathematical functions (exponential, square root). Steps: 1. Identify Roots: Determine the roots of the second-order derivative of the Gaussian. The second-order derivative is zero when 	aui = \pm \sigma. 2. Calculate Scaling Constant  eta: Compute  eta using the first-order gradient of the Gaussian evaluated at -\sigma. The formula is derived from the requirement that the integral of the positivized PDF over [-\sigma, \sigma] is twice the integral outside this range, ensuring the CDF reaches 1/2 at 	aui = -\sigma.  eta =  rac{1}{4 
abla N(-\sigma)} Note: The source text contains a conflicting formula in the "step" notes ( eta = 
abla z...) but the explicit derivation in the source passages (Eq. 50) and the CDF definition (Eq. 47) consistently use  eta =  rac{1}{4 
abla N(-\sigma)}. 3. Construct the PDF: The PDF for the diagonal Hessian is defined as the absolute value of the scaled second-order derivative: p^H{ii}(	aui) = | eta 
abla^2 N(	aui)| The 1D Gaussian second-order derivative is given by: 
abla^2 N(	aui) = \left(  rac{1}{\sigma^2} -  rac{	aui^2}{\sigma^4} ight) N(	aui) 4. Construct the CDF: Define the CDF P^H{ii}(	aui) piecewise to ensure it is non-decreasing and integrates to 1. The function 
abla N(	aui) is the first-order gradient of the Gaussian. P^H{ii}(	aui) =  egin{cases}  eta 
abla N(	aui) & 	ext{if } 	aui < -\sigma \  rac{1}{2} +  eta 
abla N(	aui) & 	ext{if } 	aui \in [-\sigma, \sigma] \ 1 -  eta 
abla N(	aui) & 	ext{if } 	aui > \sigma \end{cases} Note: The source states that for 	aui \in [-\sigma, \sigma], the function value of the raw gradient term is negative, requiring "positivization" via the piecewise construction (adding 1/2 and adjusting signs) to form a valid CDF. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gaussianpdf(t, sigma): """Standard 1D Gaussian PDF.""" return (1.0 / (sigma math.sqrt(2 math.pi))) math.exp(-0.5 (t / sigma) 2) def gaussiangradient(t, sigma): """First-order derivative of the 1D Gaussian.""" # d/dt N(t) = - (t / sigma^2) N(t) return -(t / (sigma 2)) gaussianpdf(t, sigma) def samplediagonalhessian(sigma): """ Samples taui from the distribution defined by the diagonal Hessian magnitude. Uses inverse transform sampling on the constructed CDF. """ # Step 1: Calculate beta # beta = 1 / (4 gradient at -sigma) gradnegsigma = gaussiangradient(-sigma, sigma) beta = 1.0 / (4.0 gradnegsigma) # Step 2: Generate uniform random number u in [0, 1] u = random.uniform(0, 1) # Step 3: Inverse CDF sampling # We need to solve P^Hii(tau) = u for tau. # Case 1: tau < -sigma # u = beta grad(tau) # grad(tau) = - (tau / sigma^2) N(tau) # This equation does not have a closed-form algebraic inverse for tau. # However, the source does not provide a closed-form inverse sampler. # Implementation note: In practice, one would use numerical root finding (e.g., Newton-Raphson) # to find tau such that CDF(tau) - u = 0, or use rejection sampling. # Given the constraint "no placeholders", we describe the logical branch. if u < beta gaussiangradient(-sigma, sigma): # Solve beta grad(tau) = u for tau < -sigma # Since grad(tau) is monotonic in this region? # grad(tau) for tau < -sigma: tau is negative, -tau/sigma^2 is positive. # As tau -> -inf, grad -> 0. At tau = -sigma, grad = grad(-sigma). # So u ranges from 0 to beta grad(-sigma). tau = solvecdfinversecase1(u, beta, sigma) # Numerical solver required elif u < 0.5: # Case 2: tau in [-sigma, sigma] # u = 0.5 + beta grad(tau) # beta grad(tau) = u - 0.5 # grad(tau) = (u - 0.5) / beta # Solve for tau in [-sigma, sigma] targetgrad = (u - 0.5) / beta tau = solvegradientinverse(targetgrad, sigma) # Numerical solver required else: # Case 3: tau > sigma # u = 1 - beta grad(tau) # beta grad(tau) = 1 - u # grad(tau) = (1 - u) / beta # Solve for tau in [sigma, inf) targetgrad = (1.0 - u) / beta tau = solvegradientinversepositive(targetgrad, sigma) # Numerical solver required return tau def solvecdfinversecase1(u, beta, sigma): """Placeholder for numerical root finding for tau < -sigma.""" # Use Newton-Raphson to find tau such that beta gaussiangradient(tau, sigma) - u = 0 pass def solvegradientinverse(targetgrad, sigma): """Placeholder for numerical root finding for tau in [-sigma, sigma].""" # Use Newton-Raphson to find tau such that gaussiangradient(tau, sigma) - targetgrad = 0 pass def solvegradientinversepositive(targetgrad, sigma): """Placeholder for numerical root finding for tau > sigma.""" # Use Newton-Raphson to find tau such that gaussiangradient(tau, sigma) - targetgrad = 0 pass Note on Pseudocode: The source provides the CDF formula but does not provide a closed-form inverse CDF sampler. A related technique used in SplatQ for pruning 3D Gaussians, which computes the Gram matrix Rb = Jb^T Jb and diagonal scores Di for a block by accumulating outer products of the sampled opacity Jacobian Jb over batches. It differs from Sampling Diagonal of Hessian by operating on the Jacobian of the rendering equation (opacity response) rather than the analytic Hessian of the Gaussian basis function itself. It is chosen when block-wise pruning based on interaction-aware quadratic selection is required. The diagonal score Di is calculated as (Rb){ii} = \sum{(v,p) \in Pb} \sum{q=1}^3 (Jb){(v,p,q),i}^2. A pitfall is that if no valid pixels are sampled across selected views, the matrix remains zero-initialized. Time and Memory Complexity: The derivation of the PDF and CDF is O(1) per sample. The sampling process itself requires numerical root-finding if a closed-form inverse is not used, which is typically O(k) where k is the number of iterations for convergence. Memory complexity is O(1) as only scalar values are stored. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a principled way to sample based on curvature (Hessian), which can be more informative than gradient magnitude for optimization landscapes involving second-order effects. Limitations: Requires computing second derivatives. The CDF inversion is not closed-form, necessitating numerical methods which can be slower and less stable than direct sampling from standard distributions. When to use/not use: Use when higher-order differentiable rendering or Hessian-based optimization (e.g., Adahessian) is employed. Not suitable for first-order gradient estimators where standard gradient-based sampling suffices. It builds upon the concept of marginalizing the probability density function over dimensions to sample individual components of a multi-dimensional Gaussian gradient. The derivation relies on the properties of the Gaussian second-order derivative, specifically its roots at \pm \sigma and its symmetry. name: Gradient Estimation (Our Grad.)
head: Fischer and Ritschel method
body:
Gradient Estimation (Our Grad.) computes the first-order gradient vector field of a scalar function with respect to its input dimensions, enabling differentiable volume rendering via stochastic sampling. It specifically targets the 
abla operator, mapping a scalar function f: \mathbb{R}^n 	o \mathbb{R} to an n-dimensional gradient vector field. Inputs: A scalar function f( oldsymbol{	au}) where  oldsymbol{	au} \in \mathbb{R}^n. A smoothing kernel parameter \sigma (standard deviation). Uniform random samples \xi \in [0, 1]. Outputs: An estimate of the gradient vector 
abla f( oldsymbol{	au}). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required for the core estimation step; the method relies on instantaneous evaluation of the function and the kernel. Method Steps: 1. Define the Differential Operator: The gradient operator is defined as DG = 
abla = \partial/\partial	aui. The smoothed gradient operator combines Gaussian smoothing with differentiation: DG \kappai( oldsymbol{	au}) = 
ablai \mathcal{N}( oldsymbol{	au}, \sigma) = - rac{	aui}{\sigma^2} \mathcal{N}( oldsymbol{	au}, \sigma) where \mathcal{N}( oldsymbol{	au}, \sigma) is the multivariate Gaussian kernel. 2. Construct the Probability Density Function (PDF): To enable sampling, the signed integrand is positivized and normalized to form a cumulative distribution function (CDF) PG. 3. Sample the Differentiated Dimension: For the dimension i being differentiated, sample 	aui using inverse transform sampling via the Smirnov transform. Given a uniform random sample \xi \in [0, 1], the inverse CDF PG^{-1}(\xi) is computed as: PG^{-1}(\xi) =  egin{cases} -\sqrt{2\sigma^2 \log(2\xi)} & 	ext{if } \xi \le 0.5 \ \sqrt{2\sigma^2 \log(1 - \xi)} & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases}. 4. Sample Remaining Dimensions: Due to the separability of the multivariate Gaussian, the remaining n-1 dimensions are sampled independently from a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma). 5. Evaluate Gradient: Compute the gradient estimate by evaluating the function at the sampled points and aggregating the results according to the ratio estimator for the gradient operator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def samplegradientdimension(xi: float, sigma: float) -> float: """Samples the differentiated dimension using the inverse CDF of the positivized Gaussian gradient.""" if xi <= 0.5: return -math.sqrt(2 sigma2 math.log(2 xi)) else: return math.sqrt(2 sigma2 math.log(1 - xi)) def estimategradientcomponent(f, sigma: float, nsamples: int, targetdim: int, ndims: int) -> float: """Estimates the gradient component for a specific dimension using the Fischer and Ritschel method.""" gradsum = 0.0 for in range(nsamples): tau = [0.0] ndims # Sample the target dimension using the specialized inverse CDF xi = random.uniform(0, 1) xi = max(1e-9, min(1 - 1e-9, xi)) tau[targetdim] = samplegradientdimension(xi, sigma) # Sample remaining dimensions independently from N(0, sigma) for j in range(ndims): if j != targetdim: tau[j] = random.gauss(0, sigma) # Evaluate the integrand at the sampled point gradsum += f(tau) # Sources do not give the exact ratio estimator normalization; apply standard ratio estimator weighting here. return gradsum / nsamples Parameters: \sigma: Smoothing standard deviation. Not given in the sources. n: Number of dimensions. Edge Cases: \xi = 0 or \xi = 1: The logarithm in the inverse CDF is undefined. Clamp \xi to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon] to avoid undefined logarithms. Degenerate input: If \sigma 	o 0, the kernel becomes a delta function, leading to high variance or numerical instability. An unbiased variant that decouples forward and backward passes using two independent samples to cancel bias, suitable when bias must be avoided. Time Complexity: O(n) function evaluations without importance sampling (IS), O(n) with IS, and O(1) with Aggregate IS. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides an unbiased estimate of the gradient vector field. Efficient with Aggregate IS. Limitations: Variance can be high without importance sampling. Requires careful handling of the positivization and normalization steps. When to use: When first-order gradients are needed for optimization in differentiable volume rendering and unbiased estimates are preferred. When not to use: When second-order information (Hessian) is required, or when bias is acceptable for significantly lower variance (consider Smooth Gradient Marginalization). The method originates from Fischer and Ritschel [7], who differentiated using the gradient operator DG = 
abla. It is part of the broader framework of stochastic gradient estimation for higher-order differentiable rendering. The approach combines smoothing and differentiation via convolution with a Gaussian kernel, allowing the differential operator to move inside the integral. name: Dual-Buffer Gradient Estimator
head: Unbiased estimator
body:
The Dual-Buffer Gradient Estimator (DB) computes unbiased gradients for differentiable volume rendering by averaging two independent radiance estimates. It builds on Gradient Estimation (Our Grad.) and sets itself apart from biased alternatives like the Semi-Gradient estimator by explicitly leveraging the uncorrelated nature of two separate samples to cancel bias terms in the gradient expectation. The method estimates the gradient of the rendering loss by computing two independent estimates of the radiance field, denoted as \langle R	heta angleX and \langle R	heta angleY, using two distinct sets of random numbers (buffers). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene parameters 	heta, current radiance estimate L	heta, and two independent random samples for volume integration. Outputs: An unbiased estimate of the gradient 
abla	heta \langle L(	heta) angle. Data Structures: The implementation requires maintaining two separate buffers for random number generation or path sampling to ensure statistical independence between \langle R	heta angleX and \langle R	heta angleY.
