name: PG-NeuS
head: PG-NeuS: Point-Guided Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction by Volume Rendering, Point-NeuS
body: PG-NeuS is a point-guided neural implicit surface reconstruction method that enhances the base NeuS framework by modeling aleatoric uncertainty to capture point cloud noise distribution, using a Neural Projection module for geometric constraints, and employing a Bias Network to compensate for geometric bias between volume rendering and point modeling. It distinguishes itself from siblings like RegSDF and TUVR by estimating point reliability during geometry optimization via uncertainty modeling rather than using uniform smoothing or external MVS confidence maps, enabling robust handling of noisy and sparse point data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera center o, ray direction d, a noisy point cloud \{P\}, initial weights for the SDF network f, the Sigmoid parameter s, the Neural Projection module, the Bias Network, and observed pixel colors. Outputs: Reconstructed surface (zero-level set of f) and rendered colors. Data Structures: SDF Network (f): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates to signed distance values and aleatoric uncertainty. Neural Projection Module: A module that projects 3D points onto the implicit surface and then onto the 2D image plane to enforce photometric consistency. Bias Network: An MLP that takes high-fidelity points as input to output geometric corrections. Uncertainty Model: For each point pk \in P, the SDF value is modeled as a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(\muk, \sigmak^2), where \muk = f(pk) and \sigmak represents the aleatoric uncertainty. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling and Base Rendering: For each pixel, cast a ray p(t) = o + td for t > 0. Sample N points along the ray. Compute the discrete opacity \alphai for each sample point p(ti) using the NeuS formulation: \alphai = \max\left(\frac{\Phis(f(p(ti))) - \Phis(f(p(t{i+1})))}{\Phis(f(p(ti)))}, 0\right) where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} is the Sigmoid function with trainable parameter s, and f is the SDF network output. Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) and the rendered color \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai ci, where ci is the color predicted by the network at p(ti). 2. Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling: For each point pk in the input point cloud P, the SDF network predicts a mean value \muk = f(pk) and an uncertainty value \sigmak. The point's reliability is estimated based on \sigmak. 3. Neural Projection: The point data undergoes two projections within the Neural Projection module: a. Spatial Projection: Project the 3D point pk onto the implicit surface defined by f(x)=0. b. Image Projection: Project the spatially projected point onto the 2D image plane corresponding to the camera view. A photometric consistency constraint is imposed on these projected positions to serve as regularization for the SDF, ensuring the implicit surface aligns with the observed image colors. 4. High-Fidelity Point Filtering: Perform a filter operation utilizing the modeled uncertainty \sigmak to select high-fidelity points. 5. Bias Compensation: Feed the selected high-fidelity points into the Bias Network to compensate for the geometric bias between volume rendering and point modeling. 6. Optimization: Update the network weights (SDF, Projection, Bias) and parameter s by minimizing a combined loss function including photometric loss, geometric loss (from NeuS), uncertainty regularization, and photometric consistency constraints. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def pgneusrender(rayo, rayd, numsamples, sdfnet, sparam, colornet): # Ray parameterization: p(t) = o + td for t > 0 # Sample points along ray (simplified uniform sampling in t) tvals = [(i + 1) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] psamples = [[rayo[j] + t rayd[j] for j in range(3)] for t in tvals] # Query SDF network for mean and uncertainty # sdfnet(p) returns (sdfmean, sigma) sdfpreds = [sdfnet(p) for p in psamples] sdfmeans = [pred[0] for pred in sdfpreds] sdfuncert = [pred[1] for pred in sdfpreds] # Compute Phis(x) = (1 + exp(-sx))^-1 phis = [1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-sparam m)) for m in sdfmeans] # Opacity formula: alphai = max((Phis(ti) - Phis(t{i+1})) / Phis(ti), 0) alpha = [0.0] numsamples for i in range(numsamples - 1): phicurr = phis[i] phinext = phis[i + 1] if phicurr > 1e-6: alpha[i] = max((phicurr - phinext) / phicurr, 0.0) else: alpha[i] = 0.0 # Guard against division by zero # Transmittance: Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) T = [1.0] numsamples for i in range(1, numsamples): T[i] = T[i - 1] (1.0 - alpha[i - 1]) # Color accumulation: Chat = sum{i=1}^N Ti alphai ci colors = [colornet(p) for p in psamples] renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): for c in range(3): renderedcolor[c] += T[i] alpha[i] colors[i][c] return renderedcolor, sdfuncert, psamples Parameters: s: A trainable parameter in the Sigmoid function \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} used to define opacity. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the point cloud is extremely sparse, the Neural Projection module may fail to find valid surface projections. Precision: The uncertainty modeling requires the SDF network to output not just a value but a distribution parameter (\sigma). Boundary Conditions: The opacity formula involves division by \Phis(f(p(ti))). If \Phis is close to zero, numerical instability may occur. The base training objective combining photometric and geometric losses. PG-NeuS builds on this by adding uncertainty and projection losses. NeuS Training Loss Uses uniform smoothing for noise mitigation. PG-NeuS is preferred when noise characteristics vary significantly across regions, as RegSDF weakens precise point support. RegSDF Relies on MVS network confidence. PG-NeuS is preferred when depth camera data is used or when MVS confidence maps are unreliable, as PG-NeuS estimates reliability during optimization. TUVR Time Complexity: PG-NeuS achieves an 11x speedup compared to NeuS without masks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Achieves a 33.3% improvement in accuracy compared to NeuS without masks on DTU and BlendedMVS datasets. Scaling: Benefits from lightweight networks, allowing efficient convergence while maintaining high accuracy. Strengths: Robust to noisy and sparse point data; balances accuracy and efficiency; handles region-specific noise via uncertainty modeling. Limitations: Requires a point cloud prior; complexity of implementing uncertainty modeling and bias compensation. When to use: When high-quality point clouds are available but contain noise, and computational efficiency is a concern. When not to use: When no point cloud prior is available, or when the point cloud is extremely sparse to the point where projection is ambiguous. PG-NeuS was proposed to address challenges in neural implicit surface reconstruction, specifically limited accuracy, excessive time complexity, and the impact of point cloud noise. It was introduced in the paper "Point-NeuS: Point-Guided Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction by Volume Rendering". The method improves upon prior point-guided methods like RegSDF and TUVR by introducing aleatoric uncertainty estimation and a Bias Network to handle geometric bias. Point-NeuS: Point-Guided Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction by Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2310.07997, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Joint Optimization with NeuS
head: NeuS-based reconstruction
body: A framework for neural surface reconstruction that jointly optimizes camera poses and a neural implicit surface (SDF) by integrating photometric, geometric, and multi-view consistency losses into the NeuS architecture. It distinguishes itself from standard NeuS by explicitly handling outlier correspondences through a dual-network color loss strategy and by employing Intersection-of-Union (IoU) and re-projection losses to enforce geometric consistency across views, addressing the shape-radiance ambiguity that often causes standard methods to overfit to outliers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images \{Ii\}, initial camera poses \{(Ri, ti)\}, and matched keypoints \{k{pi}\} between image pairs. Outputs: Optimized camera poses, a signed distance field (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}), and a color field. Data Structures: Color Networks: Two networks are used: Co: Original color network, taking geometry features and viewing direction as input. Cn: Detached color network, taking only geometry features (no viewing direction). Gradients from L{color}(Cn) backpropagate only to Cn. Sampling: Points \mathbf{p}i are sampled along rays using a Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) distribution. Keypoint Representation: Keypoints are represented as 3D Gaussian distributions MoG(\mathbf{k}p) for volume intersection calculations. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, sample points \mathbf{p}i along the ray using the MoG distribution defined by the current SDF estimate. 2. SDF and Color Prediction: Compute the SDF value f(\mathbf{p}i) and its gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{p}i). Compute opacity \alphai and color \hat{C}i using volume rendering. Compute color \hat{C}n using the detached network Cn. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the components of the total loss L (see Formulas below). 4. Pose and Network Update: Inlier-Inlier Pairs: Jointly optimize camera poses and network parameters (SDF, Co, Cn). Outlier-Outlier Pairs: Bypass optimization (no gradients applied). Inlier-Outlier Pairs: Fix the inlier's pose and the NeuS backbone; optimize only the outlier's pose. 5. Confidence Update: Update confidence scores based on PSNR discrepancies between Co and Cn to filter outliers. Formulas: The total loss is defined as: L = L{NSR} + \alpha L{iou} + \beta L{rep} Where L{NSR} is the NeuS-based reconstruction loss: L{NSR} = L{color}(Co) + L{color}(Cn) + \lambda L{reg} Photometric Loss (L{color}): L{color} = \|\hat{C} - C\|2^2 where \hat{C} is the rendered color from volume rendering and C is the ground truth color. Eikonal Regularization (L{reg}): L{reg} = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^k (\|\nabla f(\mathbf{p}i)\|2^2 - 1)^2 where f(\mathbf{p}i) is the distance estimate for sampled point \mathbf{p}i. Intersection-of-Union Loss (L{iou}): Given matched keypoints \mathbf{k}{pi} and \mathbf{k}{pj} from images Ii and Ij: I = MoG(\mathbf{k}{pi}) \cdot MoG(\mathbf{k}{pj}) U = MoG(\mathbf{k}{pi}) + MoG(\mathbf{k}{pj}) - I L{iou} = 1 - \frac{I}{U} where MoG(\cdot) is the mixture of Gaussians for sampling points along the ray. Re-projection Loss (L{rep}): Approximate the depth di of \mathbf{k}{pi} by selecting the point with maximal weight. Let \mathbf{k}'{pi} be the re-projected point of \mathbf{k}{pi} into image Ij. L{rep} = L\delta(\mathbf{k}'{pi}, \mathbf{k}{pj}) where L\delta is the Huber loss. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for L{reg}, set to 0.1. \alpha: Weight for L{iou}, set to 0.2. \beta: Weight for L{rep}, set to 0.001. \tau: Threshold for scene graph sparsification (e.g., 70 for SG-NeRF, 45 for DTU). \tau1: Inlier-outlier threshold for PSNR discrepancy (e.g., 9). Np: Number of particles for Monte Carlo re-localization, set to 24. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jointoptimizationstep(images, poses, keypointpairs, sdfnet, colorneto, colornetn, lambdap, alphap, betap): """ Performs one step of joint optimization for NeuS-based reconstruction. """ totalloss = 0.0 lcoloro = 0.0 lcolorn = 0.0 lreg = 0.0 liou = 0.0 lrep = 0.0 for i, j, kpi, kpj in keypointpairs: # 1. Ray sampling and point generation rayo = generaterayfrompose(poses[i], kpi) rayj = generaterayfrompose(poses[j], kpj) ptso = samplealongray(rayo, numsamples=256) ptsj = samplealongray(rayj, numsamples=256) # 2. Photometric Losses # Co: takes geometry features and viewing direction feato, viewo = sdfnet(ptso), computeviewdirs(ptso, poses[i]) colo = colorneto(feato, viewo) rendero = volumerender(ptso, colo, sdfnet) gto = getpixelcolor(images[i], kpi) lcoloro += torch.sum((rendero - gto) 2) # Cn: detached, no viewing direction, gradients only to Cn featn = sdfnet(ptso) coln = colornetn(featn) rendern = volumerender(ptso, coln, sdfnet) lcolorn += torch.sum((rendern - gto) 2) # 3. Eikonal Regularization gradf = torch.autograd.grad(sdfnet(ptso).sum(), ptso, creategraph=True)[0] lreg += torch.mean((torch.norm(gradf, dim=1, p=2) 2 - 1) 2) # 4. IoU Loss iouvol = torch.sum(MoG(kpi) MoG(kpj)) unionvol = torch.sum(MoG(kpi) + MoG(kpj) - MoG(kpi) MoG(kpj)) liou += 1.0 - iouvol / unionvol # 5. Re-projection Loss weights = computerenderweights(ptso, colo, sdfnet) depthi = ptso[torch.argmax(weights)] kpireproj = reprojecttoimage(kpi, poses[i], depthi, poses[j]) lrep += huberloss(kpireproj, kpj) lnsr = lcoloro + lcolorn + lambdap lreg totalloss = lnsr + alphap liou + betap lrep # 6. Optimization routing if pairtype(i, j) == "inlier-inlier": totalloss.backward() elif pairtype(i, j) == "outlier-outlier": pass # Bypass elif pairtype(i, j) == "inlier-outlier": # Fix inlier pose and backbone, optimize outlier pose only # (Implementation masks gradients for inlier pose and network weights) pass return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shape-Radiance Ambiguity: Outliers may exhibit higher PSNR than inliers, leading to incorrect sampling. Mitigated by using the detached network Cn and comparing PSNR discrepancies. Epipolar Loss Invariance: Epipolar loss is invariant to the scale of the translation part, making it less reliable for scene geometry than re-projection loss. Precision: The Huber loss L\delta is used for re-projection to handle large errors robustly. A sibling method that extends the NeuS framework. No algorithm details provided in this article. Time Complexity: The method runs for 150k iterations on the SG-NeRF dataset (average 13 hours) and 300k iterations on the DTU dataset (average 22 hours) on NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles outliers effectively by bypassing outlier-outlier pairs and optimizing only outlier poses in inlier-outlier pairs. Re-projection loss is more reliable to scene geometry than epipolar loss. Limitations: Requires matched keypoints and initial pose estimation. When to use: When robustness to outlier correspondences is critical and high-quality mesh reconstruction is required. The method is built upon the NeuS framework. It addresses limitations in standard neural surface reconstruction where shape-radiance ambiguity leads to overfitting on outliers. The IoU loss was originally proposed by SG-NeRF, and the re-projection loss is cited from. The approach was validated on the SG-NeRF and DTU datasets. Robust SG-NeRF: Robust Scene Graph Aided Neural Surface Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.13620v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF-SH
head: NeRF with Spherical Harmonics, PlenOctrees, modified NeRF that predicts spherical harmonic coefficients
body: NeRF-SH is a variant of Neural Radiance Fields that replaces the direct RGB output with spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, allowing the neural network to predict only view-independent density and appearance weights while deferring view-dependent color calculation to a closed-form basis evaluation. This factorization eliminates the viewing direction as a network input, enabling the representation to be stored in a sparse voxel-based PlenOctree structure, which accelerates rendering by more than 3000 times compared to the original NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The viewing direction \mathbf{d} is not an input to the network during training or storage. Output: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and a vector of spherical harmonic coefficients \mathbf{k}. Data Structures: The method uses a PlenOctree, a sparse octree where each leaf node stores the density \sigma and the SH coefficients \mathbf{k} for the volume contained within that leaf. A sparsity prior is introduced during training to encourage empty or uniform regions to be pruned, improving memory efficiency. Spherical Harmonics Basis: Spherical Harmonics (SH) are used as a standard basis for functions defined on the surface of a sphere S^2. The SH basis functions Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) depend on the viewing direction defined by polar angle \theta and azimuthal angle \phi. Formulas: The network f maps position \mathbf{x} to coefficients \mathbf{k} and density \sigma: f(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{k}, \sigma) where \mathbf{k} = (k\ell^m){\ell: 0 \leq \ell \leq \ell{\max}}. Each coefficient k\ell^m \in \mathbb{R}^3 corresponds to the RGB color components. The view-dependent color \mathbf{c} at point \mathbf{x} for viewing direction \mathbf{d} (with angles \theta, \phi) is calculated by summing the weighted SH bases: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \sum{\ell=0}^{\ell{\max}} \sum{m=-\ell}^{\ell} k\ell^m \cdot Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) where k\ell^m are the RGB coefficients predicted by the network and Y\ell^m are the SH basis functions evaluated at the ray direction. Parameters: \ell{\max}: The maximum degree of the spherical harmonics. Not given in the sources. Sparsity Prior: A regularization term applied during training to promote sparsity in the octree. Steps: 1. Network Definition: Define a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) f that takes spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} as input and outputs density \sigma and SH coefficients \mathbf{k}. 2. Training: Train the network using standard NeRF volume rendering optimization against input images. The loss is computed by rendering rays using the SH-based color calculation. For each ray, sample points \mathbf{x}i. Query f(\mathbf{x}i) to get \sigmai and \mathbf{k}i. Compute color \mathbf{c}i using the SH formula based on the ray direction. Composite colors and opacities using standard volume rendering. 3. PlenOctree Construction: Densely sample the trained network throughout the volume around the target object to tabulate \sigma and \mathbf{k} values into the leaves of an octree structure. 4. Optional Optimization: The values stored in the PlenOctree can be further optimized directly using training images to improve quality, as the rendering procedure remains differentiable. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Projection Quality Loss: Directly projecting a standard trained NeRF (which outputs RGB) into SH coefficients via Monte Carlo estimation (sampling random directions and multiplying by SH component values) is inefficient and lossy. It takes several hours (e.g., ~2 hours for 10,000 samples per point) and results in a quality loss of approximately 2 dB (PSNR 29.21 vs. 31.02 for the direct NeRF-SH method). Training Time: Training NeRF-SH remains time-intensive, typically requiring one or two days for convergence. Basis Limitations: While Spherical Gaussians (SG) were experimented with, SHs were found to perform better for this specific volumetric use case. Rendering Speed: Accelerates rendering performance of the original NeRF by more than 3000 times. Achieves frame rates above 150 fps for 800x800 images. Training Speed: Training speed is similar to, but slightly faster than, standard NeRF (by about 10%). Image Quality: Produces images equal to or better in quality than the original NeRF after PlenOctree optimization. Memory: The use of a sparse octree (PlenOctree) with a sparsity prior improves memory efficiency compared to dense voxel grids, though caching radiance values in explicit structures is less compact than the implicit NeRF representation. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; view-independent network input simplifies the MLP; efficient storage of view-dependent effects. Limitations: Training is still slow (1-2 days); requires post-training conversion to explicit structure; limited by the basis functions' ability to represent high-frequency view-dependent effects (though SHs are generally sufficient for many scenes). NeRF-SH was introduced by Yu et al. in the paper "PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)". The method addresses the slow rendering speed of original NeRFs by factorizing appearance into view-independent coefficients (stored in a PlenOctree) and view-dependent basis functions (SHs). It builds on the original NeRF framework [1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md] but modifies the output layer and introduces a sparse voxel structure. PlenOctrees For Real-time Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), http://alexyu.net/plenoctrees/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Recursive-NeRF
head: Recursive Neural Radiance Fields
body: Recursive-NeRF is a volume rendering method that synthesizes novel views by routing query points through a hierarchy of branch networks based on predicted uncertainty, rather than outputting color and density from a single network layer. It adapts to scene complexity by dynamically growing the network structure during training, allowing simple regions to be resolved by shallow networks and complex regions to be refined by deeper branches. Unlike standard NeRF, which processes all points through the full network depth, Recursive-NeRF uses an early termination mechanism to finalize points with low uncertainty, reducing computational load while maintaining high fidelity. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses. A query point \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. An uncertainty threshold \epsilon (user-specified). A maximum number of training iterations. Outputs: A rendered image composed of color values C(\mathbf{r}) for each pixel ray \mathbf{r}. A dynamically grown neural network structure consisting of an initial network and multiple branch networks. The method uses a hierarchical network structure. The structure is defined by stages i = 1, 2, \dots, K. 1. Network Layers: Stage 1 (Initial Network \Phi1): 2 linear layers. Stage 2 (First Grown Network): 2 linear layers. Stage 3 (Second Grown Network): 4 linear layers. Stage 4 (Third Grown Network): 4 linear layers. Note: The network grows up to a maximum depth of 12 layers total across stages. 2. Outnet Module: Each branch network includes an "Outnet" module responsible for decoding features into density \sigma. The Outnet contains an "alpha linear" component. 3. Branch Regions (Ri): Ri is the set of query points contained in the i-th branch. Points are clustered and assigned to specific branch networks based on their spatial location or feature similarity during the growth phase. 4. Uncertainty Value (\deltai): A scalar value predicted by branch network i for a given query point, representing the confidence in the predicted color and density. Training Phase: 1. Initialization: Start with an initial network \Phi1 (2 linear layers). This network takes position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d} as input. 2. Forward Pass: For each query point, \Phi1 outputs color c1, density \sigma1, and uncertainty \delta1. 3. Uncertainty Evaluation: Check if \delta1 < \epsilon. If \delta1 < \epsilon, the point is considered "finalized" at this stage. If \delta1 \ge \epsilon, the point is marked as "uncertain" and forwarded to the next stage. 4. Clustering: Cluster the uncertain points from the current stage. 5. Dynamic Growth: Grow new branch networks for the next stage. The new networks have the same structure as the previous stage's grown networks (e.g., if moving to stage 3, use 4 linear layers). Initialization Pitfall Fix: To prevent density collapse (where density reduces to 0, causing missing geometry), initialize the "alpha linear" weights of the new sub-network's Outnet module to be identical to those of the parent network. 6. Training: Train the new branch networks on the clustered uncertain points. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-6 for subsequent stages until: All query points have uncertainty \delta < \epsilon, OR The maximal number of iterations is reached. 8. Termination: The training process terminates when uncertainties for all query coordinates are less than \epsilon or the iteration limit is hit. Rendering Phase: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 2. Query Point Routing: For each sample point t along the ray: Determine the branch index i such that the uncertainty \deltai is less than threshold \epsilon and the ray \mathbf{r} belongs to the region Ri of that branch. Select the minimum such i. Use the color ci and density \sigmai predicted by the selected branch network i to represent c(\mathbf{r}(t)) and \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)). 3. Volume Rendering: Calculate the final color C(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volume rendering equation: C(\mathbf{r}) = \int0^{+\infty} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) c(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) \, dt where cumulative transparency T(t) is: T(t) = \exp \left( - \int0^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) \, ds \right) 4. Composition: The final image is a composition of results from neural networks of all levels, where points exit at different times (stages) based on their uncertainty. The selection of the branch network for a query point \mathbf{r}(t) is defined by: \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) = \sigmai, \quad i = \min\{i \mid \deltai < \epsilon \wedge \mathbf{r} \in Ri\} c(\mathbf{r}(t)) = ci, \quad i = \min\{i \mid \deltai < \epsilon \wedge \mathbf{r} \in Ri\} Where: \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) is the volume density at point \mathbf{r}(t). c(\mathbf{r}(t)) is the emitted color at point \mathbf{r}(t). \sigmai and ci are the density and color predicted by branch network i. \deltai is the uncertainty predicted by branch network i. \epsilon is the uncertainty threshold. Ri is the set of points contained in the i-th branch. The base network function is: F\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) where \mathbf{x} is position and \mathbf{d} is viewing direction. Uncertainty Threshold (\epsilon): A user-specified threshold. If a query point's uncertainty \deltai < \epsilon, it exits the current stage. Training terminates when all points satisfy this condition. Maximal Iterations: A limit on the number of training iterations. Training stops if \epsilon is not reached within this count. Batch Size: 4096. Learning Rate: Initial value 5 \times 10^{-4}, with 10 times exponential decay after 250k iterations. Optimizer: Adam. Density Collapse: During staged training, directly growing a randomly initialized network can cause instability, leading the density of some grown networks to reduce to 0. This results in missing pieces in the rendered scene. Mitigation: Initialize the alpha linear weights of the grown sub-network's Outnet module to be the same as those of the parent network. This allows the density generation network to inherit density information from the parent, avoiding instability. Uncertainty Prediction Difficulty: Unlike classification tasks where probability naturally serves as confidence, Recursive-NeRF is a regression task. Predicting a confidence value (uncertainty) is harder to train than classification. Empty Space vs. Complex Geometry: Low uncertainty at early stages typically corresponds to empty spaces or surfaces with simple structure (e.g., floors). High uncertainty corresponds to complex geometry requiring deeper networks. import math def recursivenerfrender(rayo, rayd, epsilon, networks, regions, near=0.0, far=1.0): """ Renders a single ray using Recursive-NeRF. Args: rayo: Origin of the ray (3D vector). rayd: Direction of the ray (3D vector). epsilon: Uncertainty threshold. networks: List of branch networks. networks[i] is the network for stage i+1. regions: List of branch regions. regions[i] defines the cluster assignment for stage i+1. near, far: Ray clipping distances. Returns: color: Rendered color for the ray (RGB list). """ Nsamples = 192 tvals = [near + (far - near) i / Nsamples for i in range(Nsamples)] pts = [rayo + t rayd for t in tvals] Tcumulative = 1.0 coloraccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for k, t in enumerate(tvals): p = pts[k] selectedsigma = None selectedcolor = None for i, network in enumerate(networks): if not isinregion(p, regions[i]): continue c, sigma, delta = network.forward(p, rayd) if delta < epsilon: selectedsigma = sigma selectedcolor = c break if selectedsigma is None: lastnetwork = networks[-1] c, sigma, delta = lastnetwork.forward(p, rayd) selectedsigma = sigma selectedcolor = c dt = tvals[k+1] - tvals[k] if k < Nsamples - 1 else 0.01 alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-selectedsigma dt) coloraccum = [coloraccum[j] + Tcumulative alpha selectedcolor[j] for j in range(3)] Tcumulative = math.exp(-selectedsigma dt) if Tcumulative < 1e-4: break return coloraccum def isinregion(point, region): """ Checks if a point belongs to a specific branch region. Regions are defined by cluster IDs assigned during the training phase. """ return point.clusterid == region.clusterid The foundational method that Recursive-NeRF extends. NeRF uses a single MLP to predict color and density for all points. Recursive-NeRF differs by using a dynamic hierarchy and early termination based on uncertainty. Link Details the standard training setup (batch size, sampling, optimizer) which Recursive-NeRF adopts but modifies with dynamic growth. Link Uses spherical harmonics for view-dependent color. Recursive-NeRF does not specify SH usage but focuses on network depth/uncertainty. Link Addresses aliasing by rendering cones instead of rays. Recursive-NeRF addresses efficiency via network depth. Link Represents scenes as microflakes. Recursive-NeRF uses volumetric density. Link Optimized for ego-centric video. Recursive-NeRF is general-purpose. Link Decomposes scene into intrinsic properties. Recursive-NeRF focuses on rendering efficiency. Link Time Complexity: Recursive-NeRF reduces rendering time by 32.36% compared to standard NeRF. The average number of layers a sample point goes through is 4.95, compared to the full depth in NeRF. Memory Complexity: The total number of parameters is reduced because simple regions are handled by smaller networks. The method reduces computational effort (FLOPs) by 37% compared to NeRF. Measured Performance: Synthetic-NeRF Dataset: PSNR 31.34, SSIM 0.953, LPIPS 0.052, FLOPs 377,159, Time 17.68s. Cornell Box Dataset: PSNR 48.010, SSIM 0.996, LPIPS 0.010, FLOPs 198,361, Time 10.82s. Scaling: The method adapts to scene complexity. Simple scenes (like Cornell Box) see greater speed improvements. The maximum network depth can reach 12 layers, deeper than NeRF's 8 layers, but early termination keeps average load low. Strengths: Efficient rendering by skipping unnecessary calculations for simple points. High quality view synthesis with state-of-the-art results. Adaptive representation of scene complexity. Limitations: Training instability if not properly initialized (density collapse). Uncertainty prediction is harder to train than classification confidence. Requires dynamic graph execution support (e.g., Jittor) for dynamic network growth. When to use: When computational efficiency is critical and the scene has varying complexity (simple regions and complex details). When not to use: If the scene is uniformly complex and early termination provides little benefit, or if the framework does not support dynamic graph execution. Recursive-NeRF was proposed by G.-W. Yang, W.-Y. Zhou, H.-Y. Peng, D. Liang, T.-J. Mu, and S.-M. Hu from BNRist, Tsinghua University. It was published in the IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics in 2022. The method builds on the idea that complicated regions of a scene should be represented by large neural networks while simple regions can be encoded by small networks, balancing efficiency and quality. It addresses the limitations of standard NeRF, which processes all points through the full network depth regardless of complexity, and dynamic networks that adjust architecture based on hardware resources rather than training situation. The code was made available at https://github.com/Gword/Recursive-NeRF. Recursive-NeRF: An Efficient and Dynamically Growing NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2022.3204608, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mip-NeRF
head: Anti-aliased NeRF, Barron et al. 2021, Mip-360, MipNeRF, canonical sampling, multum in parvo NeRF
body: Mip-NeRF extends Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to represent the scene at a continuously-valued scale, rendering anti-aliased conical frustums instead of infinitesimal rays to reduce aliasing artifacts and improve the representation of fine details. Unlike traditional mipmapping which uses discrete downsampling scales, Mip-NeRF learns a single neural scene model that can be queried at arbitrary scales, effectively prefiltering the radiance field. This approach ameliorates the aliasing inherent in NeRF's point-sampling model while simultaneously allowing the merger of the separate "coarse" and "fine" MLPs used in standard NeRF into a single network. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and a pixel radius \dot{r} at the image plane. The method outputs a color value for the pixel by integrating radiance over a conical frustum. Output: A prefiltered pixel color C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \dot{r}). Data Structures: The core data structure is a 3D Gaussian distribution that approximates the conical frustum associated with a sampling interval. This Gaussian is characterized by: Mean distance along the ray: \mut Variance along the ray: \sigmat^2 Variance perpendicular to the ray: \sigmar^2 Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (shared for the frustum). Parameters: \dot{r}: The radius of the cone at the image plane. It is set to the width of the pixel in world coordinates scaled by 2/\sqrt{12}. This scaling ensures the cone's section on the image plane has a variance in x and y that matches the variance of the pixel's footprint. MLP Configuration: 8 layers with a skip connection concatenating the input to the fifth layer. Numbered Steps: 1. Cone Casting: For each pixel, instead of casting a single ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, cast a cone with apex at \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. The radius of the cone at distance t is determined by \dot{r}. 2. Frustum Division: Divide the cone into a series of conical frustums (cones cut perpendicular to their axis) corresponding to sampling intervals [t0, t1] along the ray. 3. Gaussian Approximation: Approximate each conical frustum with a multivariate Gaussian. Compute the mean \mut and variances \sigmat^2, \sigmar^2 for each frustum. 4. Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE): For each frustum, compute the IPE feature. This is the expected positional encoding over the volume of the frustum, approximated using the Gaussian parameters. 5. Neural Query: Query the single MLP with the IPE features and the view direction to obtain volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. 6. Volume Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering (alpha compositing) using the sampled densities and colors, integrating over the conical frustums. Formulas: The set of positions \mathbf{x} within a conical frustum between distances t0 and t1 is defined by the indicator function F: F(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \dot{r}, t0, t1) = \mathbb{1}\left\{ \left( t0 < \frac{\mathbf{d}^T(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{o})}{\|\mathbf{d}\|2^2} < t1 \right) \wedge \left( \frac{\mathbf{d}^T(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{o})}{\|\mathbf{d}\|2 \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{o}\|2} > \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\dot{r}/\|\mathbf{d}\|2)^2}} \right) \right\} where \mathbb{1}\{\cdot\} is 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise. The Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) \gamma^ is the expected positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) over the frustum: \gamma^(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \dot{r}, t0, t1) = \frac{\int \gamma(\mathbf{x}) F(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \dot{r}, t0, t1) d\mathbf{x}}{\int F(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, \dot{r}, t0, t1) d\mathbf{x}} Since the numerator has no closed-form solution, the frustum is approximated by a multivariate Gaussian. The Gaussian parameters for a frustum defined by interval [t\mu - ts, t\mu + ts] (where t\mu is the midpoint and ts is the half-width) are: \mut = t\mu + \frac{2t\mu ts^2}{3t\mu^2 + ts^2} \sigmat^2 = \frac{ts^2}{3} - \frac{4ts^4(12t\mu^2 - ts^2)}{15(3t\mu^2 + ts^2)^2} \sigmar^2 = r^2 \left( \frac{t\mu^2}{4} + \frac{5ts^2}{12} - \frac{4ts^4}{15(3t\mu^2 + ts^2)} \right) where r represents the radius of the cone at the mean distance t\mu, which is r = \dot{r} \frac{t\mu}{\|\mathbf{d}\|2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computegaussianparams(tmu, ts, rdot, dnorm): """ Compute Gaussian parameters for a conical frustum. Args: tmu: Midpoint distance of the frustum along the ray. ts: Half-width of the frustum along the ray. rdot: Radius of the cone at the image plane (world units). dnorm: Norm of the ray direction vector ||d||2. Returns: mut: Mean distance along the ray. sigmatsq: Variance along the ray. sigmarsq: Variance perpendicular to the ray. """ # Mean distance mut = tmu + (2 tmu ts2) / (3 tmu2 + ts2) # Variance along the ray sigmatsq = (ts2 / 3) - (4 ts4 (12 tmu2 - ts2)) / (15 (3 tmu2 + ts2)2) # Radius of the cone at the mean distance tmu r = rdot (tmu / dnorm) # Variance perpendicular to the ray sigmarsq = r2 (tmu2 / 4 + 5 ts2 / 12 - (4 ts4) / (15 (3 tmu2 + ts2))) return mut, sigmatsq, sigmarsq def integratedpositionalencoding(mut, sigmatsq, sigmarsq, d, o, numfreqs=15): """ Compute the Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) for a frustum. Args: mut: Mean distance along the ray. sigmatsq: Variance along the ray. sigmarsq: Variance perpendicular to the ray. d: Ray direction vector. o: Ray origin vector. numfreqs: Number of frequency bands for positional encoding. Returns: ipe: The integrated positional encoding vector. """ # The IPE is the expected positional encoding over the Gaussian volume. # For a Gaussian distribution, the expectation of sin/cos of linear functions # can be computed analytically. # The positional encoding typically involves sin(2^k pi x) for x in [x, y, z]. # The exact computation of IPE from Gaussian moments is complex and # relies on the property that E[cos(a^T x)] = cos(a^T mu) exp(-0.5 a^T Sigma a). # Construct the Gaussian covariance matrix Sigma in 3D space. # The Gaussian is aligned with the ray direction d. # Sigma = sigmarsq (I - dhat dhat^T) + sigmatsq (dhat dhat^T) # where dhat = d / ||d|| dhat = d / np.linalg.norm(d) I = np.eye(3) Sigma = sigmarsq (I - np.outer(dhat, dhat)) + sigmatsq np.outer(dhat, dhat) # The mean position of the frustum is mupos = o + mut dhat mupos = o + mut dhat ipe = [] for k in range(numfreqs): freq = 2k np.pi # Basis functions for positional encoding: sin and cos for x, y, z # We need E[cos(freq (mupos + delta)^T ei)] and E[sin(...)] # Using the Gaussian expectation formula: # E[cos(a^T x)] = cos(a^T mu) exp(-0.5 a^T Sigma a) # E[sin(a^T x)] = sin(a^T mu) exp(-0.5 a^T Sigma a) for i in range(3): a = np.zeros(3) a[i] = freq # a^T Sigma a aSigmaa = a @ Sigma @ a expterm = np.exp(-0.5 aSigmaa) # a^T mu amu = a @ mupos ipe.append(np.cos(amu) expterm) ipe.append(np.sin(amu) expterm) return np.array(ipe) def mipnerfrender(o, d, rdot, near, far, numsamples, mlp): """ Render a pixel using Mip-NeRF. Args: o: Ray origin. d: Ray direction. rdot: Radius of the cone at the image plane. near: Near clipping plane distance. far: Far clipping plane distance. numsamples: Number of sampling intervals. mlp: The Mip-NeRF MLP model. Returns: color: Rendered pixel color. """ dnorm = np.linalg.norm(d) tvals = np.linspace(near, far, numsamples + 1) tmus = (tvals[:-1] + tvals[1:]) / 2 tss = (tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1]) / 2 colors = [] alphas = [] for i in range(numsamples): mut, sigmatsq, sigmarsq = computegaussianparams(tmus[i], tss[i], rdot, dnorm) # Compute IPE ipe = integratedpositionalencoding(mut, sigmatsq, sigmarsq, d, o) # Query MLP # The MLP takes IPE and view direction as input # Output: density sigma and color c sigma, c = mlp(ipe, d) # Compute alpha for this interval # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma deltat) # However, for Mip-NeRF, the integration is over the frustum volume. # The standard NeRF alpha compositing is adapted. # The effective thickness is related to the frustum geometry. # For simplicity, we use the standard alpha formula with deltat = tss[i] 2 # Note: The exact integration weight for the frustum volume is non-trivial. # Standard NeRF uses alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma deltat). # Mip-NeRF uses the same compositing but with IPE features. deltat = tss[i] 2 # Approximation alpha = 1 - np.exp(-sigma deltat) colors.append(c) alphas.append(alpha) # Alpha compositing # C = sum(Ti alphai ci) # Ti = product(1 - alphaj) for j < i T = 1.0 finalcolor = np.zeros(3) for i in range(numsamples): alpha = alphas[i] color = colors[i] finalcolor += T alpha color T = (1 - alpha) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Medical Images: Mip-NeRF's regional (canonical) sampling smooths points, which adversely affects capturing fine details and complex spatial relationships in medical images, leading to lower performance compared to other NeRF variants in this domain. Precision: The approximation of the conical frustum with a Gaussian is an approximation; the exact integral has no closed form. Boundary Conditions: The radius \dot{r} must be scaled correctly to match the pixel footprint variance. The base method that Mip-NeRF extends. Mip-NeRF replaces point sampling with cone sampling and merges coarse/fine MLPs. NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) Mip-NeRF uses a single MLP, simplifying the training configuration compared to the coarse/fine setup of NeRF. NeRF Training Configuration Uses spherical harmonics for color. Mip-NeRF uses IPE for spatial encoding. NeRF-SH Uses recursive sampling. Mip-NeRF uses integrated encoding. Recursive-NeRF Uses microflakes. Mip-NeRF uses continuous scale representation. NeMF (Neural Microflake Field) For ego-motion. Mip-NeRF is general view synthesis. EgoNeRF Decomposes intrinsic properties. Mip-NeRF focuses on anti-aliasing. Intrinsic NeRF Uses sparse voxels. Mip-NeRF uses dense MLP. Sparse Neural Volume Representation Models distribution. Mip-NeRF models integrated features. Neural Radiance Distribution Field Uses confidence. Mip-NeRF uses scale. Incremental CONfidence (ICON) Uses Bayesian uncertainty. Mip-NeRF uses deterministic IPE. Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification for SeaThru-NeRF Uses control signals. Mip-NeRF uses geometric scale. Control-NeRF Time Complexity: Mip-NeRF is approximately 7% faster than NeRF. It matches the accuracy of brute-force supersampled NeRF while being 22x faster. Memory Complexity: Mip-NeRF has half the number of parameters of NeRF due to the merger of coarse and fine MLPs. Measured Performance: On the original NeRF dataset, Mip-NeRF reduces average error rates by 17% compared to NeRF. On a challenging multiscale variant dataset, it reduces error rates by 60%. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts, improves representation of fine details, allows for single MLP architecture, faster than supersampled NeRF. Limitations: In medical image reconstruction, Mip-NeRF consistently shows the lowest performance across experiments due to its regional sampling smoothing out fine details. In the Abdominal dataset, Mip-NeRF achieved a PSNR of 17.3 and SSIM of 0.709, which was lower than other models. When to Use: When anti-aliasing is critical and scene content is observed at different resolutions. When Not to Use: When fine detail preservation in complex spatial relationships is paramount, such as in medical image reconstruction, where other NeRF variants may perform better. Mip-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Mip-NeRF: A Multiscale Representation for Anti-Aliasing Neural Radiance Fields". The name "mip-NeRF" stands for "multum in parvo NeRF," analogous to "mipmap". It addresses the limitation that coordinate-based neural representations could previously only be anti-aliased using expensive supersampling. The method was developed to enable efficient rendering of anti-aliased images during both training and testing, and the use of multiscale images during training. name: NeMF (Neural Microflake Field)
head: Neural Microflake Field
body:
NeMF is a differentiable inverse volume rendering method that represents a scene as a distribution of microflakes at every point in space, enabling the recovery of physical attributes (shape, reflectance, illumination) from multi-view images under unknown natural illumination. Unlike standard NeRF which models view-dependent radiance, NeMF models light transportation via microflake normals and roughness, allowing it to handle complex geometry and translucent objects better than surface-based methods. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a scene, camera poses, and a bounding box defining the scene volume. Outputs: A continuous volumetric representation defined by the implicit microflake field \Phi, which outputs volume density \sigma, albedo a, microflake normal  oldsymbol{\omega}m, and roughness 	aum for any 3D position \mathbf{p}. The method also outputs optimized Spherical Gaussian (SG) parameters for environment illumination and visibility fields. Data Structures: The core data structure is the implicit microflake field, implemented via coordinate-based neural networks. 1. Geometry Network (\mathcal{F}g): An MLP that takes position \mathbf{p} and outputs volume density \sigma and microflake normal  oldsymbol{\omega}m, building on the vanilla NeRF structure. 2. Appearance Network (\mathcal{D}m): A U-shaped MLP that encodes the material to a feature vector, applies a sparsity constraint, and decodes it into albedo a and roughness 	aum. 3. Visibility Network (\mathcal{V}): An MLP that overfits visibility SG parameters for each spatial position. 4. Illumination Parameters: A set of 128-dimensional SGs representing infinitely faraway background lights. Mathematical Definitions: The microflake model assumes space is filled with infinite small flakes. The probability of normals in direction  oldsymbol{\omega} on the ellipsoid surface is modeled by the Normal Distribution Function (NDF): D( oldsymbol{\omega}) =  rac{1}{\pi\sqrt{|S|}( oldsymbol{\omega}^T S^{-1} oldsymbol{\omega})^2} where |S| is the determinant of the shape matrix S. The diffuse phase function is defined as: fp^d( oldsymbol{\omega}i,  oldsymbol{\omega}l) =  rac{1}{\pi 	au( oldsymbol{\omega}i)} \int{\Omega} \langle  oldsymbol{\omega}l,  oldsymbol{\omega} angle \langle  oldsymbol{\omega}i,  oldsymbol{\omega} angle D( oldsymbol{\omega}) d oldsymbol{\omega} where \langle \cdot angle is the dot product, \Omega is the hemisphere centered at  oldsymbol{\omega}m, and 	au( oldsymbol{\omega}) is the projected size of the ellipsoid along direction  oldsymbol{\omega}. The specular phase function is defined as: fp^s( oldsymbol{\omega}i,  oldsymbol{\omega}l) =  rac{D( oldsymbol{\omega}h)}{4	au( oldsymbol{\omega}i)} where  oldsymbol{\omega}h is the half-angle between the input light direction  oldsymbol{\omega}l and viewing direction  oldsymbol{\omega}i. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize \mathcal{F}g, \mathcal{D}m, \mathcal{V}, and 128-dimensional SG illumination parameters. 2. Sampling: For each ray \mathbf{r}, sample discrete positions \mathbf{p}k along the ray. 3. Feature Extraction: Query \mathcal{F}g(\mathbf{p}k) for \sigmak and  oldsymbol{\omega}{m,k}. Encode the material at \mathbf{p}k into a feature vector, apply a sparsity constraint, and query \mathcal{D}m to decode albedo ak and roughness 	au{m,k}. Query \mathcal{V}(\mathbf{p}k) for visibility SG parameters. 4. Visibility Calculation: To compute visibility of \mathbf{p}k w.r.t. light direction  oldsymbol{\omega}l, march a ray from \mathbf{p}k towards the light in the background and calculate opacity \eta using a pre-trained NeRF. Encode this visibility using SG parameterization. 5. Radiance Computation: Compute diffuse radiance 
ud(\mathbf{p}k) by summing the product of environment lighting and visibility: 
ud(x) = \sum{ oldsymbol{\omega}l \in \Omega} \{ [V(x,  oldsymbol{\omega}l) Y( oldsymbol{\omega}l)] \otimes [L^{	ext{sg}}( oldsymbol{\omega}l) Y( oldsymbol{\omega}l)] \cdot \langle  oldsymbol{\omega}l \cdot  oldsymbol{\omega}m angle \}. Compute specular radiance 
us(\mathbf{p}k) by checking visibility during ray sampling and setting radiance to 0 if the light is invisible. Total radiance is 
u^(\mathbf{p}k,  oldsymbol{\omega}i) = 
ud(\mathbf{p}k) + 
us(\mathbf{p}k). 6. Volume Rendering: Replace integrals with summations over discrete sampling positions. Perform importance ray sampling of light directions for calculating radiance, as elaborated in Algorithm 1 of Heitz et al. [22]. Render image color C(\mathbf{r}) via standard volume rendering integration. 7. Loss Calculation: Photometric loss \mathcal{L}c = \sum{\mathbf{r}, I} \|C(\mathbf{r}) - I(\mathbf{r})\|2^2. Density field loss \mathcal{L}\sigma = \sumk \etak (\| oldsymbol{\omega}m - \Delta \sigma\|2^2 + \max(0, \langle  oldsymbol{\omega}m,  oldsymbol{\omega}i angle)). Latent sparsity loss \mathcal{L}z = \sumj KL(ho \| \hat{ho}j) with ho=0.05. Smoothness loss \mathcal{L}s = \|\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{F}g(\mathbf{p})) - \mathcal{N}(\mathcal{F}g(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon))\|1 + \|\mathcal{D}m(\mathbf{z}) - \mathcal{D}m(\mathbf{z} + \epsilon)\|1 with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01). Total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \mathcal{L}\sigma + \mathcal{L}z + \mathcal{L}s. 8. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L} via gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerf(scenedata, numiterations): # Initialize networks Fg = MLP() # Outputs sigma, omegam Dm = UShapedMLP() # Outputs a, taum V = MLP() # Outputs visibility SG params SGLights = [SG(dim=128) for in range(128)] # Environment illumination # Pre-train NeRF for initial density and visibility NeRF = TrainNeRF(scenedata) for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0 for ray in scenedata.rays: # 1. Sample points along ray points = SamplePoints(ray, numsamples=64) # 2. Extract features sigmalist = [] omegamlist = [] albedolist = [] taumlist = [] visibilityparamslist = [] for p in points: sigma, omegam = Fg(p) sigmalist.append(sigma) omegamlist.append(omegam) z = EncodePosition(p) a, taum = Dm(z) albedolist.append(a) taumlist.append(taum) visparams = V(p) visibilityparamslist.append(visparams) # 3. Compute Visibility visibilities = [] for p, omegam in zip(points, omegamlist): opacity = 0.0 for lightdir in SGLights: opacity += NeRF.IntegrateRay(p, lightdir) visibilities.append(opacity) # 4. Compute Radiance radiancediffuse = 0.0 for p, omegam, visparams in zip(points, omegamlist, visibilityparamslist): for lightdir in SGLights: visterm = visparams lightdir.Y() lightterm = lightdir.L() lightdir.Y() radiancediffuse += (visterm lightterm) Dot(lightdir, omegam) radiancespecular = 0.0 for p, omegam, vis in zip(points, omegamlist, visibilities): if vis > 0: radiancespecular += ComputeSpecularPhase(omegam, ray.direction) else: radiancespecular += 0.0 totalradiance = radiancediffuse + radiancespecular # 5. Volume Rendering renderedcolor = 0.0 T = 1.0 for i, (p, sigma, radiance) in enumerate(zip(points, sigmalist, totalradiance)): alpha = 1.0 - Exp(-sigma ray.stepsize) renderedcolor += T alpha radiance T = (1.0 - alpha) # 6. Loss Calculation gtcolor = scenedata.GetGroundTruthColor(ray) lossc = L2Norm(renderedcolor - gtcolor) deltasigma = ComputeGradient(sigmalist) losssigma = Sum([vis (L2Norm(omegam - deltasigma) + Max(0, Dot(omegam, ray.direction))) for vis, omegam in zip(visibilities, omegamlist)]) lossz = KLDivergence(0.05, AverageChannels(z)) epsilon = RandomGaussian(variance=0.01) losss = L1Norm(Normalize(Fg(p)) - Normalize(Fg(p + epsilon))) + L1Norm(Dm(z) - Dm(z + epsilon)) totalloss += lossc + losssigma + lossz + losss GradientDescent(totalloss) def MLP(): return lambda x: (x.sum(), x) # Placeholder for actual network def UShapedMLP(): return lambda z: (z.mean(), z.std()) # Placeholder for actual network def SG(dim): return type('SG', (), {'Y': lambda self: 1.0, 'L': lambda self: 1.0})() def TrainNeRF(data): return type('NeRF', (), {'IntegrateRay': lambda self, p, d: 0.5})() def SamplePoints(ray, numsamples): return [ray.origin + ray.direction i for i in range(numsamples)] def EncodePosition(p): return p def ComputeSpecularPhase(omegam, direction): return 1.0 def L2Norm(x): return sum(x2)0.5 def ComputeGradient(lst): return [lst[i+1]-lst[i] for i in range(len(lst)-1)] def KLDivergence(rho, z): return 0.0 def AverageChannels(z): return z.mean() def RandomGaussian(variance): return (variance)0.5 def Normalize(x): return x / (x.norm() + 1e-8) def GradientDescent(loss): pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Estimation: Removing normal estimation ("w/o normal") bakes ambient lighting into surfaces, yielding significantly worse results (PSNR 15.4516 vs 23.6982). Visibility Modeling: Assuming environment illumination is visible to all points ("w/o vis.") leads to incorrect predictions around occlusion boundaries. Latent Space: Mapping points directly to parameters without a latent space ("w/o latent space") results in incorrect material extraction and vaguer edges. Precision: The integration in the diffuse phase function requires careful numerical handling. The sources note that integrals are replaced with summations over discrete sampling positions. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On synthetic Blender scenes (balloon, mic, spot, polyhedron), NeMF achieved PSNR 23.6982, SSIM 0.9387 (Albedo), and PSNR 25.7048 (Relighting), outperforming InvRender, NeRFactor, and PhySG. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fully relies on volume representation without needing to recover geometry explicitly, allowing it to handle scenes with complex geometry and translucent objects (e.g., clouds) which surface-based methods cannot handle well. Enables high-quality relighting, material editing, and volume scattering simulation. Limitations: Surface-based methods (e.g., NeRD, NeRFactor) may be more efficient for simple geometry. NeMF's reliance on inverse volume rendering and visibility modeling adds complexity. When to Use: Use NeMF when the scene contains complex geometry, translucent objects, or when high-quality relighting and material editing are required under unknown natural illumination. NeMF was proposed in the paper "NeMF: Inverse Volume Rendering with Neural Microflake Field". It extends the NeRF framework by incorporating a microflake model for light transportation, addressing the limitations of surface-based inverse rendering methods. The method builds on prior work in inverse rendering, such as InvRender and NeRD, but distinguishes itself by fully utilizing a volume representation. name: EgoNeRF
body: EgoNeRF is an efficient adaptation of NeRF [1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md] for large-scale scenes with casual input, utilizing a balanced spherical feature grid and maintaining uniform ray hit rates for individual cells for scenes captured with a short video of omnidirectional cameras. It addresses the inefficiency and artifact issues of Cartesian grids in wide-field-of-view settings by employing a spherical coordinate system that matches egocentric capture geometry. Unlike Mip-NeRF which relies on a proposal MLP for resampling, EgoNeRF shares a single density grid for coarse and fine sampling, enabling faster convergence and superior preservation of fine structures. EgoNeRF represents the scene using a continuous volumetric field parameterized by a balanced spherical feature grid and a lightweight MLP, optimized via differentiable volume rendering. Inputs: Multi-view equirectangular images from an omnidirectional camera; camera poses estimated via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: A neural volume representation allowing synthesis of novel views; rendered images with high fidelity to ground truth. The core data structure is the Balanced Spherical Feature Grid. Unlike Cartesian grids (e.g., DVGO or TensoRF), this grid is defined in spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi) to match the geometry of egocentric capture. 1. Radial Partition: Uniformly spaced concentric shells. 2. Angular Partition: Uses a Yin-Yang grid combined with a uniform radial partition to minimize valence variations at the poles. 3. Feature Storage: Each grid cell stores feature vectors, which are processed via vector-matrix factorization. 4. Density Grid (G\sigma): A shared grid used to query volume density for both coarse and fine sampling stages. Hardware: Experiments conducted on a single RTX-3090 GPU. Ray Batch Size: Same as baseline methods (DVGO, TensoRF) for fair comparison. Grid Resolution: Same number of feature grids as DVGO and TensoRF. Training Steps: High performance achieved at 5,000 steps. 1. Pose Estimation: Obtain camera poses from input video frames using the OpenMVG SfM library. 2. Grid Initialization: Initialize the balanced spherical feature grid with uniform radial partitions and Yin-Yang angular partitions. 3. Ray Sampling: Cast rays from the camera through each pixel. Sample points along the ray. Query the shared density grid G\sigma for volume density at these points. 4. Resampling: Employ resampling techniques to refine sample distribution based on the shared density grid G\sigma, rather than relying on a separate proposal MLP. 5. Feature Aggregation: Retrieve features from the spherical grid for each sample point. Apply vector-matrix factorization to combine features. 6. Rendering: Compute color and density for each sample. Perform volume rendering (compositing) to produce the final pixel color. 7. Optimization: Minimize the difference between rendered images and ground truth images. Update grid features and MLP parameters via gradient descent. 8. Environment Map: Include an environment map component to handle infinitely far regions, particularly in outdoor scenes.
