name: Inverse Rendering with Shadow Rays
head: Radiance field with explicit direct illumination
body: Inverse Rendering with Shadow Rays is a technique that augments a global illumination radiance field with explicit direct illumination terms from known point light sources, computed via shadow rays to improve mesh reconstruction and novel view synthesis accuracy. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like the base Radiance Field Prediction Network by decoupling direct lighting from the learned global illumination residual, allowing for physically accurate shadow casting that rasterization-based point-based methods cannot achieve. This method extends the radiance field representation by explicitly modeling direct illumination from known light sources while retaining a neural network to predict the residual appearance (indirect illumination and material properties). Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Scene geometry initialization: Dense point cloud, surface normals, and camera poses (typically extracted via COLMAP). Light source data: Positions of point light sources, which may vary per image in the experimental setup. Canonicalized 3D points x and view directions \omega. Outputs: Radiance L{\text{sh.rays}}(x, \omega) for a given point and view direction. Albedo \alpha(x) as an additional output of the MLP. Data Structures The method relies on the underlying Fast Dipole Sums representation. Key data structures include: Dipole Parameters: Stored per point, including the mean position and dipole strength. Kernel Outputs: \bar{\ell}\epsilon^k(x), the outputs of the Poisson kernel functions for K kernels. MLP: A neural network taking inputs (x, \omega, n{\text{imp}}(x), \bar{\ell}\epsilon^1(x), \dots, \bar{\ell}\epsilon^K(x)). Normals: n{\text{imp}}(x), the normal at point x. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the scene with a dense point cloud, normals, and camera poses using COLMAP. Use ground truth point light positions for each view. 2. Optimization Setup: Prepare two optimization runs: one using the standard radiance field representation (global illumination only) and one augmented with shadow rays. 3. Global Illumination Baseline: For the baseline, use the radiance field representation defined in Equation 21 of the source, which models global (direct and indirect) illumination implicitly through the MLP and kernel outputs. 4. Direct Illumination Augmentation: For the shadow ray method, augment the radiance field equation to include explicit direct illumination terms for each point light source. 5. Radiance Computation: For each ray passing through point x with direction \omega, compute the total radiance by summing the direct illumination from all light sources and the residual predicted by the MLP. 6. Albedo and Transmittance: Compute albedo \alpha(x) as an additional output of the MLP. Compute transmittance T(x, li) using quadrature and fast queries. 7. Regularization Guard: To prevent numerical errors and undefined values during training, apply a small cutoff (desingularization) in the denominator of the Poisson kernel. Do not set the kernel width parameter \epsilon to 0. Formulas The total radiance with shadow rays is defined as: L{\text{sh.rays}}(x, \omega) \equiv \sum{i=1,2} Ld^i(x, \omega) + \text{MLP}(x, \omega, n{\text{imp}}(x), \bar{\ell}\epsilon^1(x), \dots, \bar{\ell}\epsilon^K(x)) Where Ld^i(x, \omega) is the direct illumination from the i-th light source: Ld^i(x, \omega) \equiv \alpha(x) T(x, li) \frac{n{\text{imp}}(x) \cdot (li - x)}{\|li - x\|^3} Symbol Definitions: L{\text{sh.rays}}(x, \omega): Total radiance at point x in direction \omega with shadow rays. Ld^i(x, \omega): Direct illumination contribution from light source i. \alpha(x): Albedo at point x, predicted by the MLP. T(x, li): Exponential transmittance between point x and light source li, computed via quadrature. n{\text{imp}}(x): Normal vector at point x. li: Position of the i-th light source. x: 3D position of the point on the surface. \text{MLP}(\dots): Neural network predicting the residual appearance based on position, view direction, normal, and kernel outputs. \bar{\ell}\epsilon^k(x): Kernel outputs for k=1 \dots K. Parameters Light Sources: Two point light sources are used in the primary experiment. Kernel Regularization: A small cutoff is applied to the Poisson kernel denominator to avoid numerical instability; \epsilon \neq 0. Quadrature: Used for computing transmittance T(x, li). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Numerical Instability: Setting the kernel width parameter \epsilon to 0 (removing regularization) causes training failures due to numerical errors and undefined values. Mesh Artifacts: Using desingularization (a small cutoff in the denominator) without proper optimization can result in extracted meshes with strong artifacts. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes known light positions. If light positions are unknown or dynamic, the explicit shadow ray formulation requires adaptation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeradiancewithshadowrays(x, omega, normals, lightpositions, mlp, kerneloutputs): """ Computes radiance at point x for view direction omega using shadow rays. Args: x: 3D point position (vector) omega: View direction (vector) normals: Surface normal at x (vector) lightpositions: List of light source positions (list of vectors) mlp: Neural network function taking (x, omega, normal, kerneloutputs) kerneloutputs: List of kernel outputs [l1,..., lK] Returns: radiance: Scalar radiance value albedo: Scalar albedo value """ # 1. Get albedo and residual from MLP # The MLP takes position, view direction, normal, and kernel outputs residual = mlp(x, omega, normals, kerneloutputs) albedo = residual[-1] # Assuming albedo is the last output or extracted separately residualappearance = residual[:-1] # Remaining outputs for indirect illumination # 2. Compute direct illumination from each light source directillumination = 0.0 for lightpos in lightpositions: # Vector from point to light lightvec = lightpos - x # Distance squared for normalization and transmittance distsq = dot(lightvec, lightvec) dist = sqrt(distsq) # Normalized light direction lightdir = lightvec / dist # Compute transmittance T(x, li) using quadrature # Note: In implementation, this requires sampling along the ray from x to lightpos # and integrating the density. Here we assume a function computetransmittance exists. transmittance = computetransmittancequadrature(x, lightpos) # Lambertian shading term: n. l / dist^2 # Note: The formula uses dist^3 in denominator but dot product has one dist factor in numerator if l is not normalized? # Formula: (n. (l - x)) / ||l - x||^3 # Let's stick strictly to the source formula: # nimp(x). (li - x) / ||li - x||^3 # This is equivalent to (n. ldir) / dist^2 if ldir is normalized. # Source formula: n. (l-x) / ||l-x||^3 # (l-x) has length dist. So (n. (l-x)) / dist^3 = (n. (ldir dist)) / dist^3 = (n. ldir) / dist^2. dotproduct = dot(normals, lightvec) directterm = (albedo transmittance dotproduct) / (distsq dist) directillumination += directterm # 3. Sum direct and residual totalradiance = directillumination + sum(residualappearance) return totalradiance, albedo def computetransmittancequadrature(startpoint, lightpoint): """ Computes exponential transmittance between startpoint and lightpoint using quadrature. This requires access to the density field sigma(x) from the underlying radiance field. """ # Sample points along the segment from startpoint to lightpoint numsamples = 10 # Not given in sources, typical value for quadrature transmittanceintegral = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = i / numsamples samplepoint = lerp(startpoint, lightpoint, t) density = querydensity(samplepoint) # Query from underlying radiance field # Simple Riemann sum approximation stepsize = distance(startpoint, lightpoint) / numsamples transmittanceintegral += density stepsize # Exponential transmittance return exp(-transmittanceintegral) The underlying representation that models indirect and direct illumination implicitly through the MLP and kernel outputs. Choose this when light sources are unknown or when computational simplicity is prioritized over explicit shadow accuracy. See Radiance Field Prediction Network. Methods like Gaussian surfels that use rasterization instead of ray tracing. Choose these for real-time performance where explicit shadow casting is not required. See Gaussian Surfels. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of light sources and the cost of transmittance quadrature. Each ray requires querying the MLP and computing transmittance for each light source. Transmittance computation via quadrature adds a linear factor with respect to the number of quadrature samples. Memory Complexity: Similar to the base radiance field, plus storage for light source positions. The MLP and kernel outputs dominate memory usage. Measured Performance: In the Lego scene experiment, rendering 200 images from random viewpoints with two point lights showed that optimizing with shadow rays resulted in extracted meshes with fewer artifacts and finer details, and images with more accurate shadows compared to the method without shadow rays. Strengths: Enables rendering of direct illumination from known light sources, which rasterization methods cannot do. Leads to fewer mesh artifacts and more accurate shadows in novel views. Limitations: Requires known light source positions. Numerical instability can occur if regularization is removed. Desingularization can introduce mesh artifacts if not handled carefully. When to Use: When reconstructing scenes with known illumination and high-fidelity shadow casting is required. When Not to Use: When light sources are unknown, or when real-time performance is critical and rasterization is sufficient. The method originates from the paper "3D Reconstruction with Fast Dipole Sums". It builds upon the Fast Dipole Sums radiance field representation, which uses dipole sums to model global illumination. The specific augmentation with shadow rays was introduced to address the limitations of rasterization-based point-based methods in rendering explicit direct illumination and shadows. The technique was demonstrated on the NeRF Realistic Synthetic Lego scene, highlighting its ability to improve mesh reconstruction quality and novel view synthesis accuracy under varying lighting conditions. 3D Reconstruction with Fast Dipole Sums, https://doi.org/10.1145/3687914, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Flash Cache
head: Fast Cache, Fast Cache approximation
body: Flash Cache is a volumetric inverse rendering method that reduces bias and variance in radiance estimation by using a high-capacity Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) as a control variate for incoming illumination. Unlike prior radiance caches that use low-capacity models, which fail to capture high-frequency and near-field illumination, Flash Cache uses a high-capacity cache. Unlike methods that use a NeRF as a cache but render at only a single evaluation point, which causes bias, Flash Cache uses the cache as a control variate for unbiased estimation. It achieves this by replacing the recursive incoming radiance term with a NeRF-based cache output, evaluated via importance sampling, while maintaining computational tractability through a "Fast Cache" approximation. Flash Cache combines volumetric rendering with physically-based Monte Carlo light transport to optimize scene parameters \Phi (geometry, materials, lighting). The method avoids the recursive evaluation cost of standard path tracing by approximating the volume rendering integral with a single sample point per ray and using a NeRF as a radiance cache for incoming light. Inputs: A set of input images I(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o), where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \boldsymbol{\omega}o is the viewing direction. Scene representation parameters \Phi. Outputs: Optimized parameters \Phi that minimize the difference between measured images and rendered incident radiance. NeRF Radiance Cache: A neural network (MLP or grid-based) that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i to outgoing radiance L{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i). This cache acts as a proxy for incoming radiance Li. Mixture of von-Mises Fisher (vMF) Distributions: A spatially-varying probability distribution used to importance-sample incoming directions \boldsymbol{\omega}i based on the expected distribution of incoming radiance. 1. Ray Sampling: For each camera ray (\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o), sample a single point \mathbf{x}(tk) along the ray. This approximates the volume rendering integral with one sample. 2. Weight Calculation: Compute the quadrature weight wk for the sample point using the density \sigma along the ray: wk = \left(1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}(tk)) (t{k+1} - tk)}\right) \exp \left( - \sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigma(\mathbf{x}(tj))(t{j+1} - tj) \right) where tk is the distance along the ray, and t{k+1} - tk is the step size. 3. Importance Sampling: At the sample point \mathbf{x}(tk), use the spatially-varying mixture of vMF distributions to sample M incoming directions \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}. The distribution p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) is parameterized by the vMF mixture to capture spatially-varying illumination effects like occlusion and interreflections. 4. Radiance Cache Query: For each sampled direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}, query the NeRF radiance cache to obtain the estimated incoming radiance L{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}). This replaces the recursive evaluation of Li. 5. Outgoing Radiance Estimation: Compute the unbiased estimator for outgoing radiance \hat{L}o(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) using the BRDF f, the cache output, and the sampling distribution: \hat{L}o(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} f(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) L{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)}) \frac{(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)})}{p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i^{(j)})} where \mathbf{n} is the surface normal at \mathbf{x}(tk). 6. Incident Radiance Approximation: Approximate the incident radiance Li(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) for the camera ray using the single sample and its weight: \hat{L}i(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = wk \hat{L}o(\mathbf{x}(tk), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) The source describes approximating the volume rendering integral with a single sample point. The full integral is \int Lo T \sigma dt, approximated here as wk Lo. 7. Optimization: Minimize the loss function with respect to \Phi: \min{\Phi} \sum{\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o} \| I(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) - Li(\mathbf{o}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o; \Phi) \|^2 + \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}(\Phi) where Li is the estimated incident radiance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def flashcacherender(rayorigin, raydirection, tk, deltat, nerfcache, vmfmixture, brdf): """ Renders a single ray using Flash Cache approximation. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera origin o. raydirection: 3D vector, camera direction omegao. tk: float, distance to the single sample point along the ray. deltat: float, step size for quadrature weight calculation. nerfcache: Neural Radiance Field function providing density, normal, and radiance. vmfmixture: Spatially-varying mixture of vMFs for sampling omegai. brdf: Physically-based BRDF function f(x, omegai, omegao). Returns: incidentradiance: Scalar, estimated Li(o, omegao). """ # Sample point position xt = rayorigin + tk raydirection # Query NeRF cache for density and normal sigma = nerfcache.getdensity(xt) normal = nerfcache.getnormal(xt) # Compute transmittance T(o, x(tk)) = exp(-int0^{tk} sigma(x(s)) ds) # Approximated by numerical integration along the ray accumulatedsigma = 0.0 steps = 10 dt = tk / steps for s in range(steps): pos = rayorigin + (s dt) raydirection accumulatedsigma += nerfcache.getdensity(pos) dt transmittance = exp(-accumulatedsigma) # Compute quadrature weight wk # wk = (1 - exp(-sigma deltat)) exp(-sum{j=1}^{k-1} sigmaj deltatj) # The exponential term corresponds to the transmittance to the sample point weightk = (1 - exp(-sigma deltat)) transmittance # Importance sample M incoming directions from the vMF mixture M = 10 incomingdirections = vmfmixture.sample(M, xt) outgoingradiancesum = 0.0 for omegai in incomingdirections: # Query cache for incoming radiance Lcache(xt, omegai) lcache = nerfcache.query(xt, omegai) # Evaluate BRDF fval = brdf.evaluate(xt, omegai, raydirection) # Cosine term costheta = dot(normal, omegai) # Evaluate PDF pval = vmfmixture.pdf(omegai, xt) if pval < 1e-8: pval = 1e-8 # Accumulate estimator term outgoingradiancesum += fval lcache costheta / pval outgoingradiance = outgoingradiancesum / M incidentradiance = weightk outgoingradiance return incidentradiance M: Number of Monte Carlo samples for incoming directions. Not given in the sources. \Phi: Scene representation parameters (geometry, materials, lighting). Optimized via gradient descent. \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}: Regularization term. Not given in the sources. Recursive Evaluation: Naïve use of the rendering equation requires recursive evaluation of Li, leading to high computational cost. Flash Cache avoids this by using the cache as a control variate. Bias: Using low-capacity caches or single-point NeRF evaluation introduces bias. Flash Cache uses a high-capacity cache and control variate to avoid this. Precision: Division by p(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) requires care to avoid numerical instability when the PDF is near zero. A neural field that approximates incoming radiance Li to avoid recursive path tracing. It is cheaper to evaluate than full volume rendering. A variance reduction technique where the NeRF cache output is used to reduce the variance of the Monte Carlo estimator without introducing bias. A spatially-varying distribution used for importance sampling incoming directions, capturing effects like occlusion and interreflections. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples M and the cost of querying the NeRF cache. It is cheaper than recursive path tracing but more expensive than single-point NeRF evaluation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF cache parameters and the vMF distribution parameters. Strengths: Reduces bias and variance in inverse rendering. Captures high-frequency and near-field illumination. Preserves thin structures via volumetric representation. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than low-capacity cache methods. Requires careful tuning of the vMF distribution. When to Use: When unbiased estimation of complex lighting effects (interreflections, specularities) is required in volumetric inverse rendering. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and bias is acceptable. Flash Cache was introduced by Attal et al. in the paper "Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering". It addresses limitations in prior radiance cache methods, which either introduced bias through low-capacity models or single-point evaluations. The method builds on the principles of Neural Radiance Fields and physically-based Monte Carlo rendering. Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73390-12, fetched 2026-10-27

name: General Radiance Field (GRF)
body: General Radiance Field (GRF) is a neural rendering method that learns a 3D scene representation by extracting local features from 2D input images and projecting them into a canonical 3D space. It operates in canonical space rather than view-space, distinguishing it from methods like Generalizable Radiance Fields. The network models 3D geometry and appearance by constructing an internal representation for each point in 3D space and rendering appearance and geometry from an arbitrary position. Inputs: 1. A set of M input images with their corresponding camera poses and intrinsics: \{(I1, \xi1, K1), \dots, (IM, \xiM, KM)\}, where Im is the image, \xim is the pose, and Km is the intrinsic matrix. 2. A query 3D point p = \{xp, yp, zp\} in canonical space. 3. A query viewpoint Vp = \{x{vp}, y{pv}, z{pv}\} representing the camera position from which the point is observed. Outputs: 1. Predicted RGB color values \{rp, gp, bp\}. 2. Predicted volumetric density dp. The method utilizes a neural network architecture composed of four distinct components: 1. Feature Extractor: A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with an encoder-decoder structure that processes 2D images to extract pixel-level features. 2. Reprojector: A geometric module that transforms 2D features extracted from input images into the 3D canonical space corresponding to the query point p. 3. Aggregator: A module that combines features reprojected from multiple input views into a single general feature vector for point p. 4. Neural Renderer: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) based on the NeRF architecture that maps the aggregated general features and viewpoint information to density and color. 1. Preprocessing Input Images: For each input image Im, the camera's 3D location (xyz coordinates) is stacked (duplicated) to each pixel of the image. This allows the feature extractor to be explicitly aware of the pixel's relative position in 3D space. 2. Feature Extraction: The preprocessed images are passed through the shared CNN feature extractor. Skip connections between the encoder and decoder are used to preserve high-frequency local features, while fully connected layers in the middle learn global features. This produces a set of 2D feature maps, one for each input image. 3. Reprojection: For a given query point p, the 2D features from each input image Im are reprojected back to the 3D location of p. This aligns the features from different viewpoints to the same canonical coordinate. 4. Aggregation: The reprojected features from all M views are aggregated. An attention mechanism is integrated to handle visual occlusions implicitly, weighting features from visible views higher than those from occluded views. This results in a single general feature vector for point p. 5. Radiance Field Query: The aggregated general feature vector, along with the query viewpoint Vp, is fed into the NeRF MLP. The MLP predicts the density dp and color \{rp, gp, bp\} for point p. 6. Volume Rendering: To render a final pixel color for a camera ray, multiple points along the ray are sampled. The volume rendering equation is used to integrate the predicted densities and colors of these points to obtain the final pixel RGB value. The network fW with learnable parameters W is defined as: (rp, gp, bp, dp) = fW \left( (I1, \xi1, K1), \dots, (IM, \xiM, KM), (xp, yp, zp), (x{vp}, y{pv}, z{pv}) \right) Where: (rp, gp, bp, dp) are the predicted RGB value and volumetric density of point p observed from viewpoint Vp. fW is the network with learnable parameters W. (Im, \xim, Km) are the m-th image, pose, and intrinsics. (xp, yp, zp) are the coordinates of the query point p. (x{vp}, y{pv}, z{pv}) are the coordinates of the query viewpoint Vp. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np class GRF: def init(self, numimages, featureextractor, aggregator, renderer): self.numimages = numimages self.featureextractor = featureextractor self.aggregator = aggregator self.renderer = renderer def extract2dfeatures(self, images, camerapositions): # images: [M, H, W, 3], camerapositions: [M, 3] # Stack camera position to each pixel camposexpanded = np.expanddims(np.expanddims(camerapositions, axis=1), axis=1) camposstacked = np.broadcastto(camposexpanded, (images.shape[0], images.shape[1], images.shape[2], 3)) inputtensor = np.concatenate([images, camposstacked], axis=-1) return self.featureextractor(inputtensor) def reprojectfeatures(self, features2d, querypoints, cameraposes, Kmatrices): # features2d: [M, H, W, C] # querypoints: [N, 3] # cameraposes: [M, 4, 4] # Kmatrices: [M, 3, 3] N = querypoints.shape[0] M = features2d.shape[0] C = features2d.shape[-1] reprojected = np.zeros((M, N, C)) for m in range(M): camposeinv = np.linalg.inv(cameraposes[m]) phom = np.hstack([querypoints, np.ones((N, 1))]) pcamhom = (camposeinv @ phom.T).T pcam = pcamhom[:,:3] K = Kmatrices[m] pcamproj = (K @ pcam.T).T u = pcamproj[:, 0] / pcamproj[:, 2] v = pcamproj[:, 1] / pcamproj[:, 2] z = pcamproj[:, 2] unorm = (u / (features2d.shape[2] - 1)) 2 - 1 vnorm = (v / (features2d.shape[1] - 1)) 2 - 1 grid = np.stack([unorm, vnorm], axis=-1).reshape(1, 1, N, 2) featm = features2d[m].reshape(1, features2d.shape[1], features2d.shape[2], C) sampled = np.squeeze(gridsample(featm, grid)) reprojected[m] = sampled.T return reprojected def aggregatefeatures(self, reprojectedfeatures, querypoints): # reprojectedfeatures: [M, N, C] # querypoints: [N, 3] return self.aggregator(reprojectedfeatures, querypoints) def queryradiancefield(self, aggregatedfeatures, querypoints, queryviewpoints): # aggregatedfeatures: [N, Cagg] # querypoints: [N, 3] # queryviewpoints: [N, 3] inputdata = np.concatenate([aggregatedfeatures, querypoints, queryviewpoints], axis=-1) output = self.renderer(inputdata) color = output[:,:3] density = output[:, 3:4] return color, density def render(self, images, camerapositions, cameraposes, Kmatrices, raysorigins, raysdirections, numsamples): # raysorigins: [H, W, 3], raysdirections: [H, W, 3] tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) points = raysorigins[:,:, np.newaxis,:] + raysdirections[:,:, np.newaxis,:] tvals[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:, np.newaxis] H, W, N = points.shape[:3] pointsflat = points.reshape(-1, N, 3) features2d = self.extract2dfeatures(images, camerapositions) reprojected = self.reprojectfeatures(features2d, pointsflat, cameraposes, Kmatrices) aggregated = self.aggregatefeatures(reprojected, pointsflat) viewpointsflat = np.broadcastto(camerapositions[np.newaxis,:,:], (HW, N, 3)).reshape(-1, 3) color, density = self.queryradiancefield(aggregated, pointsflat, viewpointsflat) deltas = np.diff(tvals) delta = np.concatenate([deltas, [1e10]]) delta = np.broadcastto(delta[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:], (H, W, N)).reshape(-1, N) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density delta) T = np.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, axis=1) T = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], axis=1) weights = alpha T renderedcolor = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] color, axis=1) return renderedcolor.reshape(H, W, 3) def gridsample(inputtensor, grid): # Standard bilinear sampling implementation omitted for brevity; # assumes standard library or framework implementation. pass Number of Input Images (M): Not specified in the sources. CNN Architecture: Details are in the appendix of the source paper; not specified here. MLP Architecture: Based on NeRF; specific layer sizes not given in the provided notes. Lighting Sensitivity: Using raw RGB values as pixel features is sub-optimal because they are sensitive to lighting conditions and environmental noise. Camera Intrinsics/Rotations: Stacking additional camera rotation and intrinsics to each pixel does not noticeably improve performance. Occlusions: The attention mechanism in the aggregator implicitly handles visual occlusions by weighting features from visible views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach, but specific metrics are not provided in the notes. Strengths: Operates in canonical space, allowing for generalizable features across views. The use of CNNs for feature extraction provides robustness to lighting variations. Limitations: The method relies on accurate camera poses and intrinsics. The performance of the CNN feature extractor is critical and its optimal design is not detailed in the source. General Radiance Field (GRF) was introduced by Alex Trevithick and Bo Yang in October 2020. It is similar to pixelNeRF but operates in canonical space rather than view-space. The method models 3D geometries as a general radiance field, taking 2D images with camera poses and intrinsics as input, constructing an internal representation for each point of the 3D space, and rendering appearance and geometry from an arbitrary position. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 GRF: Learning a General Radiance Field for 3D Representation and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.01490, fetched 2026-10-26

name: C-ToF Gaussian Splatting Image Formation
head: C-ToF GS phasor formation model, C-ToF GS raw image formation model
body: This method defines the forward rendering equations for continuous-wave time-of-flight (C-ToF) cameras within a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework, enabling the reconstruction of dynamic scenes from monocular raw sensor samples. It extends standard Gaussian splatting by modeling the complex physics of modulated light propagation, specifically addressing the under-constrained nature of depth optimization in single-camera dynamic settings where the measured signal (phasor or raw quad) is not the property of interest (depth). Unlike neural volumetric approaches, this primitive-based method achieves 100× faster optimization and rendering while maintaining similar or better accuracy, and it avoids the need for additional constraints like camera motion or RGB integration required by prior works such as ToRF. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} = \{Gk\}{k=1}^N. Camera parameters: modulation frequency f, speed of light c, and intrinsic/extrinsic matrices. For the raw image model: a temporal offset t for each raw frame in the quartet. Outputs: Phasor Model: A complex-valued phasor image \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x}) at pixel coordinates \mathbf{x}. Raw Image Model: A vector of four raw intensity values \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}) corresponding to the phase offsets \phi \in \{0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\}. Mean Depth: A scalar depth map d(\mathbf{x}) derived from the Gaussian distribution (computed separately, see below). Each Gaussian Gk stores the following properties: 1. Center: \mathbf{x}k \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Covariance: \Sigmak \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, describing 3D scale and rotation. 3. Opacity: ok \in [0, 1]. 4. Reflectivity: rk \in [0, 1], view-dependent, parameterized by 16 spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. 5. Distance: dk, the distance from the camera center to the Gaussian center \mathbf{x}k. 6. Source Intensity: sk (or constant s), representing emitted signal intensity. Note: View-dependent color \mathbf{c}k is used in standard RGB splatting but is replaced by reflectivity rk and source intensity s in the C-ToF models. 1. Standard C-ToF Physics (Reference) The standard derivation of depth d{\text{ToF}} from raw frames Q\phi assumes simultaneous capture and opaque Lambertian surfaces: d{\text{ToF}} = \frac{c}{4\pi f} \psi, \quad \text{where} \quad \psi = \arctan\left(\frac{Q0 - Q\pi}{Q{\pi/2} - Q{3\pi/2}}\right) The complex phasor representation of the C-ToF signal is: a \cdot W(d{\text{path}}) = a \cdot \exp\left(i \frac{2\pi d{\text{path}} f}{c}\right) = (Q0 - Q\pi) + i(Q{\pi/2} - Q{3\pi/2}) where a = 2A, d{\text{path}} = 2d{\text{ToF}}, phase \psi = \angle W(d{\text{path}}), and amplitude A = |a \cdot W(d{\text{path}})| / 2. 2. C-ToF GS Phasor Formation Model This model renders the complex phasor \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x}) at pixel \mathbf{x}: \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{p}^{\text{bg}} TN + \sum{k=1}^N \frac{2s \cdot rk}{dk^2} W(dk) ok \mathcal{G}k^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) Tk^2 Definitions: \mathbf{p}^{\text{bg}}: Background phasor intensity. TN = \prod{l=1}^N (1 - ol \mathcal{G}l^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x})): Final transmittance. Tk = \prod{l=1}^{k-1} (1 - ol \mathcal{G}l^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x})): Transmittance before Gaussian k. \mathcal{G}k^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}): 2D Gaussian projection of Gk at pixel \mathbf{x}. W(dk) = \exp(i \psik): Phase weighting function, where \psik = \frac{4\pi dk f}{c}. The term Tk^2 accounts for the round-trip light travel (transmission squared). rk is the view-dependent surface reflectivity. 3. C-ToF GS Raw Image Formation Model This model renders the four raw intensity samples \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}) for dynamic scenes, allowing arbitrary time t: \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{q}^{\text{bg}} TN + \sum{k=1}^N \frac{sk \cdot TN}{dk^2} \phi(dk) ok \mathcal{G}k^{2\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) Tk^2 Definitions: \mathbf{q}^{\text{bg}}: Background raw intensity vector. \phi(dk): Modulated raw sample quad vector replacing the phasor: \phi(dk) = \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\psik) \\ \cos(\psik) \\ -\sin(\psik) \\ -\cos(\psik) \end{bmatrix} where \psik = \frac{4\pi dk f}{c}. sk \cdot TN: Source intensity modulated by final transmittance (strictly follows source notation sk^{TN}). 4. Mean Gaussian Depth The depth property of interest is computed as the weighted mean of Gaussian distances: d(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^N dk ok \mathcal{G}k^{\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) Tk Note: \mathcal{G}k^{\text{D}}(\mathbf{x}) refers to the 1D depth projection or the contribution of the Gaussian to the depth integral along the ray. Modulation Frequency (f): The frequency of the sinusoidal light modulation. Typical values result in an unambiguous depth range du of 5–10 m. Speed of Light (c): Physical constant. Unambiguous Depth Range (du): du = \frac{c}{2f}. Depths exceeding this range wrap around to [0, du]. Unverified code. H, W = pixelcoords.shape[:2] phasorimage = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.complex128) c = 299792458.0 f = camera.modulationfrequency T = np.ones((H, W)) # Running transmittance Tk for k in range(len(gaussians)): g = gaussians[k] # 1. Project Gaussian to 2D mu2d, Sigma2d = projectgaussian(g.center, g.cov3d, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projmatrix, (H, W)) # 2. Evaluate 2D Gaussian at pixel coordinates diff = pixelcoords - mu2d # (H, W, 2) invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) distsq = np.sum((diff @ invSigma) diff, axis=2) # (H, W) G2D = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) # 3. Compute Transmittance Tk and update T Tk = T.copy() T = T (1.0 - g.opacity G2D) # 4. Compute Phase Weighting W(dk) camcenter = camera.viewmatrix[:3, 3] dk = np.linalg.norm(camcenter - g.center) psik = 4 np.pi dk f / c Wdk = np.exp(1j psik) # 5. Compute Reflectivity rk viewdir = camcenter - g.center viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) rk = evaluatesh(g.reflectivitysh, viewdir) # 6. Accumulate contribution term = (2 g.sourceintensity rk / (dk2)) Wdk g.opacity G2D[:,:, np.newaxis] (Tk2)[:,:, np.newaxis] phasorimage += term # Add background phasorimage += camera.backgroundphasor T[:,:, np.newaxis] return phasorimage def renderctofraw(gaussians, camera, pixelcoords): """Renders the C-ToF raw image quartet using the raw image formation model.""" H, W = pixelcoords.shape[:2] rawimage = np.zeros((H, W, 4)) c = 299792458.0 f = camera.modulationfrequency T = np.ones((H, W)) for k in range(len(gaussians)): g = gaussians[k] mu2d, Sigma2d = projectgaussian(g.center, g.cov3d, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projmatrix, (H, W)) diff = pixelcoords - mu2d invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) distsq = np.sum((diff @ invSigma) diff, axis=2) G2D = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) Tk = T.copy() T = T (1.0 - g.opacity G2D) camcenter = camera.viewmatrix[:3, 3] dk = np.linalg.norm(camcenter - g.center) psik = 4 np.pi dk f / c viewdir = camcenter - g.center viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) rk = evaluatesh(g.reflectivitysh, viewdir) phivec = np.array([np.sin(psik), np.cos(psik), -np.sin(psik), -np.cos(psik)]) term = (g.sourceintensity T / (dk2)) phivec g.opacity G2D[:,:, np.newaxis] (Tk2)[:,:, np.newaxis] rawimage += term rawimage += camera.backgroundraw T[:,:, np.newaxis] return rawimage def computemeandepth(gaussians, camera, pixelcoords): """Computes the mean Gaussian depth.""" H, W = pixelcoords.shape[:2] depthmap = np.zeros((H, W)) T = np.ones((H, W)) for k in range(len(gaussians)): g = gaussians[k] mu2d, Sigma2d = projectgaussian(g.center, g.cov3d, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projmatrix, (H, W)) diff = pixelcoords - mu2d invSigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma2d) distsq = np.sum((diff @ invSigma) diff, axis=2) G2D = np.exp(-0.5 distsq) Tk = T.copy() T = T (1.0 - g.opacity G2D) camcenter = camera.viewmatrix[:3, 3] dk = np.linalg.norm(camcenter - g.center) depthmap += dk g.opacity G2D Tk return depthmap 1. Depth-Phasor Mismatch: Fitting C-ToF raw quads or phasors volumetrically does not guarantee consistency with the rendered mean depth. This discrepancy arises because sine/cosine functions oscillate between convex/concave regions, violating Jensen's inequality equality unless all Gaussians are clustered at the same z-position along each ray. 2. Motion Blur in Quartets: Capturing four frames for C-ToF requires 120 Hz raw capture for 30 Hz depth. If the scene moves within the quartet, depth errors occur because light arrives from different world points. The raw image model allows rendering at arbitrary time t, but correspondence across time must be resolved during optimization. 3. Unambiguous Depth Range: C-ToF cameras can only measure depth unambiguously up to du = c / 2f. Depths over this range map back to [0, du] due to sinusoidal periodicity. Typical du is 5–10 m. 4. Initialization Sensitivity: Optimization is sensitive to initialization and hyperparameters. Unlike ToRF, this method does not require moving the camera, making it suitable for static cameras but potentially brittle without good initialization. Time Complexity: The method achieves 100× faster optimization and rendering compared to neural volumetric approaches. This is due to the use of fast primitive-based scene representation (3D Gaussian Splatting) rather than neural networks. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N. Each Gaussian stores center, covariance, opacity, and SH coefficients for reflectivity (16 coefficients). Strengths: Fast optimization and rendering. Suitable for static cameras (unlike ToRF which requires camera motion). More stable optimization for dynamic scenes with a single camera compared to F-ToRF. Handles dynamic scenes by rendering raw quads at arbitrary time t. Limitations: Under-constrained depth optimization in single-camera dynamic settings. Depth-Phasor mismatch can lead to geometric inaccuracies if not addressed with heuristics. Sensitive to motion blur within the 4-frame quartet. Limited by the unambiguous depth range of the C-ToF sensor. When to Use: When high-fidelity dynamic 3D reconstruction from a single viewpoint is needed quickly, and the scene is within the unambiguous depth range of the C-ToF camera. When Not to Use: When the scene contains large motions within the 4-frame capture window, or when the scene depth exceeds the unambiguous range of the camera. The method was introduced by Runfeng Li, Mikhail Okunev, Zixuan Guo, Anh Ha Duong, Christian Richardt, Matthew O'Toole, and James Tompkin in the paper "Time of the Flight of the Gaussians: Optimizing Depth Indirectly in Dynamic Radiance Fields". It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting and C-ToF imaging principles. The work addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic scenes from monocular C-ToF cameras, where depth is not directly measured but derived from raw sensor samples. Previous works like ToRF required additional constraints (camera motion, RGB integration), while F-ToRF struggled with stability in dynamic single-camera settings. This method leverages the speed of Gaussian splatting to achieve faster optimization while incorporating C-ToF physics. name: Generative Neural Feature Fields (GIRAFFE)
head: GIRAFFE Object Representation, Neural Feature Fields
body: Generative Neural Feature Fields (GIRAFFE) is a scene representation framework that models individual objects within a scene using separate, compositional neural feature fields, enabling disentangled control over pose, shape, and appearance. Unlike its siblings NeRF and GRAF, which represent the entire scene with a single monolithic model, GIRAFFE assigns each object its own MLP that outputs a scalar density and a deep feature vector, composing the final scene via a density-weighted sum. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of object-specific latent codes \mathbf{z}s (shape) and \mathbf{z}a (appearance), sampled from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). Object transformation parameters \mathbf{T} = \{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{R}\}, where \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is scale, \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is translation, and \mathbf{R} \in SO(3) is rotation. A 3D query point \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: A rendered 2D image. Internally, each object field outputs a scalar density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+ and a feature vector \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{Mf}. Data Structures: Object Field MLP (h\theta): A shared architecture and weights across all objects. It maps encoded inputs to (\sigma, \mathbf{f}). Latent Codes: \mathbf{z}s \in \mathbb{R}^{Ms}, \mathbf{z}a \in \mathbb{R}^{Ma}. Transformation Parameters: \mathbf{T} containing \mathbf{s}, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{R}. Upsampling CNN: A 2D convolutional network that upsamples the rendered feature map to image resolution. Discriminator: A 2D CNN discriminator for adversarial training. Positional Encoding: Input components t (from \mathbf{x} or \mathbf{d}) are mapped to higher-dimensional features using positional encoding with L frequency octaves: \gamma(t, L) = (\sin(2^0 t\pi), \cos(2^0 t\pi), \dots, \sin(2^L t\pi), \cos(2^L t\pi)) This is applied element-wise to each component of \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Object Transformation: For each object k, transform the query point \mathbf{x} from object space to scene space using the affine transformation \mathbf{T}: k(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{R} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} s1 & & & \\ & s2 & & \\ & & s3 & \\ & & & s3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t} The source formula contains a typographical repetition of s3 in the diagonal matrix. Standard 3D implementation uses a 3 \times 3 scaling matrix \text{diag}(s1, s2, s3). 2. Feature Field Evaluation: For each object, evaluate its specific MLP h\theta using the transformed point k(\mathbf{x}), direction \mathbf{d}, and object-specific latent codes \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a: (\sigmak, \mathbf{f}k) = h\theta(\gamma(k(\mathbf{x})), \gamma(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a) where Mf is the dimensionality of the feature vector \mathbf{f}. 3. Scene Composition: Compose the scene's volume feature field by performing a density-weighted sum of the features from all objects. This is typically done during volume rendering by accumulating density-weighted features along the ray, similar to the standard emission-absorption model but accumulating \mathbf{f} instead of \mathbf{c}. \hat{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{f}i where \hat{\mathbf{F}} is the accumulated feature vector for ray \mathbf{r}, and Ti is the transmittance. 4. Image Synthesis: Render a small 2D feature map from the 3D volume feature field using volume rendering. Feed this 2D feature map into an upsampling CNN to produce the final image. 5. Adversarial Training: Train the model using adversarial loss. The synthesized image is compared against real images using a 2D CNN discriminator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def positionalencoding(t, L): """ Applies positional encoding element-wise to input t. t: tensor of shape (..., 1) L: number of frequency octaves Returns: tensor of shape (..., 2L) """ freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(L, device=t.device).float() return torch.cat([torch.sin(freqbands t torch.pi), torch.cos(freqbands t torch.pi)], dim=-1) class ObjectFieldMLP(nn.Module): """ The neural feature field MLP htheta. Shared architecture and weights across objects. """ def init(self, dimx, dimd, dims, dima, dimf): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dimx + dimd + dims + dima, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1 + dimf)) def forward(self, gammax, gammad, zs, za): x = torch.cat([gammax, gammad, zs, za], dim=-1) out = self.net(x) return torch.relu(out[:, 0:1]), out[:, 1:] class GIRAFFE: def init(self, numobjects, dimf, dims, dima, octavesx, octavesd): self.numobjects = numobjects self.dimf = dimf self.octavesx = octavesx self.octavesd = octavesd # Shared MLP across all objects self.objectfield = ObjectFieldMLP(2octavesx, 2octavesd, dims, dima, dimf) # Upsampling CNN self.upsampler = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(dimf, 64, 4, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(), nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 3, 4, 2, 1), nn.Tanh()) # Discriminator self.discriminator = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 4, 2, 1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 4, 2, 1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Conv2d(128, 1, 4, 1, 0), nn.Sigmoid()) def transformpoint(self, x, s, t, R): """ Transforms point x from object space to scene space. x: (N, 3), s: (3,), t: (3,), R: (3, 3) """ # Source formula uses a 4x4 matrix with repeated s3, which is a typo for 3D scaling. # We implement standard 3D scaling: R diag(s) x + t S = torch.diag(s) return torch.matmul(torch.matmul(R, S), x.t()).t() + t def render(self, rayorigins, raydirections, objectparams, zs, za, numsamples): """ rayorigins: (H, W, 3), raydirections: (H, W, 3) objectparams: list of dicts with 's', 't', 'R' zs: (numobjects, dims), za: (numobjects, dima) """ H, W = rayorigins.shape[:2] rayoriginsflat = rayorigins.reshape(-1, 3) raydirectionsflat = raydirections.reshape(-1, 3) numrays = rayoriginsflat.shape[0] # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples, device=rayorigins.device) xsamples = rayoriginsflat[:, None,:] + raydirectionsflat[:, None,:] tvals[None,:, None] # Initialize accumulation totalfeature = torch.zeros(numrays, self.dimf, device=rayorigins.device) transmittance = torch.ones(numrays, device=rayorigins.device) for i, obj in enumerate(objectparams): # Transform points to object space xobj = self.transformpoint(xsamples, obj['s'], obj['t'], obj['R']) # Positional encoding gammax = torch.cat([positionalencoding(xobj[..., j:j+1], self.octavesx) for j in range(3)], dim=-1) gammad = torch.cat([positionalencoding(raydirectionsflat[:, j:j+1], self.octavesd) for j in range(3)], dim=-1) # Get latent codes for this object zsobj = zs[i:i+1].expand(numrays, -1) zaobj = za[i:i+1].expand(numrays, -1) # Evaluate MLP sigma, f = self.objectfield(gammax, gammad, zsobj, zaobj) # Volume rendering step deltat = tvals[1] - tvals[0] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltat) weight = transmittance[:, None] alpha totalfeature += weight f transmittance = (1.0 - alpha).mean(dim=1) # Reshape to feature map (H, W, dimf) featuremap = totalfeature.reshape(H, W, self.dimf).permute(2, 0, 1) # Upsample to image image = self.upsampler(featuremap) image = image.permute(1, 2, 0) return image def computeloss(self, predimage, realimage): l1loss = nn.functional.l1loss(predimage, realimage) preddisc = self.discriminator(predimage.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)) realdisc = self.discriminator(realimage.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)) advloss = nn.functional.binarycrossentropy(preddisc, torch.oneslike(preddisc)) + \ nn.functional.binarycrossentropy(realdisc, torch.zeroslike(realdisc)) return l1loss + advloss Performance: GIRAFFE enables disentangled control over scene elements, allowing for fine-grained manipulation of pose, shape, and appearance. This comes at the cost of increased model complexity compared to single-NeRF approaches, as each object requires its own set of parameters and latent codes. Strengths: Disentangled representation, compositional scene modeling, and generative capabilities. Limitations: Requires explicit object segmentation or detection to assign latent codes and transformations to objects, which is not inherent to the method. The density-weighted sum composition assumes objects are opaque or semi-opaque and can be ordered or blended appropriately. GIRAFFE was introduced as an extension of GRAF (Generative RADiance Fields). While GRAF represents the entire scene with a single generative model, GIRAFFE assigns each object its own neural feature field, allowing for compositional scene modeling. The framework builds on the differentiable volume rendering principles established in prior radiance field optimization methods [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 GIRAFFE: Representing Scenes as Compositional Generative Neural Feature Fields, https://github.com/chaerinkong/paper-reviews/issues/63, fetched 2026-10-28

name: NeRDF Learning via Knowledge Distillation
head: Multi-View Distillation, NeRDF Distillation, Teacher-Student NeRF Distillation
body: NeRDF Learning via Knowledge Distillation is a training framework that accelerates the optimization of Neural Radiance Distribution Fields (NeRDF) by using a pre-trained teacher NeRF to generate dense, diverse pseudo-training views. Unlike standard NeRF optimization which relies solely on sparse input camera poses, this method synthesizes interpolated viewpoints to guide the student model, thereby avoiding the spatial high-frequency artifacts that occur when training a duplex field from scratch. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) by decoupling the geometry/radiance learning phase from the sparse input data constraint, enabling faster convergence and higher efficiency. The method trains a student NeRDF to mimic the radiance distribution of a teacher NeRF. The process involves generating synthetic views, encoding rays, and minimizing losses that match both pixel colors and volume density distributions. Inputs: Sparse set of training images with known camera poses. A pre-trained teacher NeRF model (e.g., TensoRF). Spherical coordinate ranges (r{min}, r{max}), (\theta{min}, \theta{max}), (\phi{min}, \phi{max}) derived from the training camera poses. Outputs: A trained student NeRDF model capable of real-time view synthesis. Distillation View: Defined by spherical coordinates (rs, \thetas, \phis) relative to the scene origin, converted to Cartesian coordinates for ray generation. Ray Encoding: A method capturing rich ray information, including position and direction, used as input to the student network. Volume Density Distribution: The scalar field \sigma predicted by the student and teacher networks, used for density matching. 1. Teacher Preparation: Train or load a pre-trained teacher NeRF model (e.g., TensoRF) on the sparse input images. 2. Pose Alignment and Coordinate Conversion: Align the view directions of all training cameras with the scene origin. Convert camera poses into spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi) relative to the origin. 3. Online View Sampling: Randomly sample radius rs \sim U(r{min}, r{max}), angle \thetas \sim U(\theta{min}, \theta{max}), and \phis \sim U(\phi{min}, \phi{max}). Convert sampled spherical coordinates to Cartesian coordinates to generate interpolated camera poses. Repeat to generate N{distill} distillation views (typically 1,000). 4. Synthesis of Pseudo-Training Data: Render images and volume density fields from the teacher NeRF using the sampled distillation viewpoints. 5. Student Training (Distillation Phase): Train the student NeRDF on the distilled views for the first half of the optimization iterations. Compute the color loss between student and teacher rendered colors. Compute the volume density constraint loss, matching the student's volume density distribution to the teacher's. 6. Fine-Tuning: Fine-tune the student NeRDF on the original sparse training images for the second half of the optimization iterations to sharpen appearance. The rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} remains the standard emission-absorption model: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. The total loss \mathcal{L} for the student network includes: 1. Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{color}): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between student and teacher rendered colors. 2. Density Loss (\mathcal{L}{density}): Matching loss between the volume density distribution of the student NeRDF and the teacher NeRF. \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{density} where \lambda is a weighting factor. Number of distillation views: 1,000. Teacher Model: TensoRF. Learning Rate: 10^{-3} initially, decaying exponentially to 10^{-5}. Training Split: 50% of iterations on distilled views, 50% on original training images. Spatial Artifacts: Training a neural duplex radiance field from scratch without distillation fails to match the high fidelity of original NeRFs and produces spatial high-frequency artifacts. Camera Pose Subspace: For real-world captures, camera poses may occupy a small subspace; the spherical sampling strategy ensures meaningful interpolated viewpoints even in this case. Training Time: The distillation process increases training time compared to standard NeRF due to the generation of pseudo-data and the sequential training schedule. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def trainnerdfwithdistillation(sparseimages, sparseposes, teachernerf, numdistillviews=1000, totaliterations=10000): """ Train a student NeRDF using knowledge distillation from a teacher NeRF. sparseimages: list of target color tensors sparseposes: list of camera pose objects with.position and.lookat attributes teachernerf: object with.render(pose) -> (color, density) """ # Initialize student network studentnerdf = createstudentnetwork() # Step 2: Align poses and convert to spherical coordinates origin = getsceneorigin(sparseposes) sphericalranges = converttosphericalranges(sparseposes, origin) rmin, rmax = sphericalranges['r'] thetamin, thetamax = sphericalranges['theta'] phimin, phimax = sphericalranges['phi'] # Step 3 & 4: Generate distillation views and teacher renderings distillationviews = [] teachertargets = [] for in range(numdistillviews): # Random sampling in spherical coordinates rs = uniformsample(rmin, rmax) thetas = uniformsample(thetamin, thetamax) phis = uniformsample(phimin, phimax) # Convert to Cartesian for camera pose campos = sphericaltocartesian(rs, thetas, phis, origin) campose = generatecamerapose(campos, origin) # Render from teacher teachercolor, teacherdensity = teachernerf.render(campose) distillationviews.append(campose) teachertargets.append((teachercolor, teacherdensity)) # Step 5: Distillation Phase (First half of iterations) halfiter = totaliterations // 2 for i in range(halfiter): # Sample a distillation view idx = randomindex(distillationviews) pose = distillationviews[idx] targetcolor, targetdensity = teachertargets[idx] # Student forward pass studentcolor, studentdensity = studentnerdf.render(pose) # Compute losses losscolor = mse(studentcolor, targetcolor) lossdensity = mse(studentdensity, targetdensity) # Total loss with weighting factor lambda loss = losscolor + 1.0 lossdensity # Backpropagate and update student studentnerdf.update(loss) # Step 6: Fine-Tuning Phase (Second half of iterations) for i in range(halfiter, totaliterations): # Sample from original sparse training images idx = randomindex(sparseimages) pose = sparseposes[idx] targetcolor = sparseimages[idx] # Student forward pass studentcolor, studentdensity = studentnerdf.render(pose) # Compute color loss only (standard supervision) loss = mse(studentcolor, targetcolor) # Backpropagate and update student studentnerdf.update(loss) return studentnerdf def createstudentnetwork(): # Standard MLP initialization for NeRDF return type('StudentNeRDF', (), {'render': lambda self, p: (None, None), 'update': lambda self, l: None}) def getsceneorigin(poses): # Average of camera positions return sum(p.position for p in poses) / len(poses) def converttosphericalranges(poses, origin): # Compute min/max of spherical coordinates for all poses coords = [tospherical(p.position, origin) for p in poses] return { 'r': (min(c[0] for c in coords), max(c[0] for c in coords)), 'theta': (min(c[1] for c in coords), max(c[1] for c in coords)), 'phi': (min(c[2] for c in coords), max(c[2] for c in coords)) } def tospherical(pos, origin): # Standard spherical conversion dx, dy, dz = pos[0]-origin[0], pos[1]-origin[1], pos[2]-origin[2] r = math.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) theta = math.acos(dz / r) if r > 0 else 0 phi = math.atan2(dy, dx) return (r, theta, phi) def sphericaltocartesian(r, theta, phi, origin): # Standard Cartesian conversion x = origin[0] + r math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) y = origin[1] + r math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) z = origin[2] + r math.cos(theta) return (x, y, z) def generatecamerapose(position, origin): # Construct look-at pose return type('Pose', (), {'position': position, 'lookat': origin})() def uniformsample(a, b): return random.uniform(a, b) def randomindex(lst): return random.randint(0, len(lst) - 1) def mse(a, b): return sum((x - y)2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) / len(a) A variant where the input data is augmented with synthetic renderings generated by a fully trained teacher model (e.g., NeRF) to improve quantitative metrics. It uses a 10x10 grid of renderings from the teacher. On the Real Forward-Facing dataset, this variant outperforms NeRF quantitatively in PSNR (e.g., Fern: 26.06 vs 26.92, Flower: 28.90 vs 28.57, Fortress: 32.60 vs 32.94) but requires increased training time. Time Complexity: Training time increases due to pseudo-data generation and the sequential training schedule. Inference speed reaches ~21 FPS, which is ~100× faster than the original NeRF. Memory Complexity: The student model uses an 8-layer MLP, comparable to NeRF. GPU memory consumption is quantified for WebGL applications. Strengths: Avoids spatial artifacts from scratch training; leverages dense teacher knowledge; fast inference. Limitations: Increased training time; requires a pre-trained teacher model. When to use: When high-fidelity view synthesis is required with limited input views and fast inference is desired. When not to use: When training time is a critical constraint and standard NeRF performance is acceptable. The method is based on knowledge distillation principles. It was proposed to address the limitations of training neural duplex radiance fields from scratch, which suffer from spatial artifacts. The approach extends the R2L method by incorporating volume density matching. The teacher model TensoRF was chosen for its high efficiency in reconstruction and synthesis. name: Fourier Feature Encoding
head: Fourier Feature Mapping, Fourier Feature Positional Encoding, Fourier Features, NeRF Positional Encoding, Positional Encoding (NeRF), Sinusoidal Positional Encoding
body: Fourier Feature Encoding is a preprocessing technique applied to scene coordinates and viewing directions to address the spectral bias of neural networks, which naturally favor low-frequency functions. By mapping input vectors into a high-dimensional space via sinusoidal functions, it provides high-frequency features directly to the network, greatly improving fine detail reconstruction in rendered views. It sets itself apart from standard positional encodings (like those in Transformers) by using fixed, non-trainable sinusoidal bases rather than learned embeddings, and from learnable frequency mappings by relying on a deterministic geometric progression of frequencies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vector \mathbf{v} representing either a 3D scene coordinate \mathbf{x} or a viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Output: A higher-dimensional vector \gamma(\mathbf{v}) containing sinusoidal features. Data Structures: The encoding is a static transformation applied element-wise or vector-wise. No persistent data structures are required beyond the input vector and the output vector. Parameters: L (or N): The number of frequency bands (or encoding dimensionality parameter). The output dimension is 2L. Typical values: In the original NeRF implementation, N=10 for coordinates \mathbf{x} and N=4 for directions \mathbf{d}. Formulas: The positional encoding function \gamma maps a vector \mathbf{v} to a vector of sines and cosines with exponentially increasing frequencies: \gamma(\mathbf{v}) = \left( \sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{v}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{v}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{v}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{v}) \right) The neural radiance field F{\Theta} is reformulated as a composition F{\Theta} = F^{\prime}{\Theta} \circ \gamma, where F^{\prime}{\Theta} is the MLP that takes the encoded features: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = F^{\prime}{\Theta}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \gamma(\mathbf{d})) Numbered Steps: 1. Normalize the input coordinate \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d} to the range [-1, 1]. 2. For each component v of the input vector: a. Initialize an empty list of features. b. For b from 0 to L-1: i. Calculate frequency \omega = 2^b \pi. ii. Append \sin(\omega v) to the list. iii. Append \cos(\omega v) to the list. 3. Concatenate the features for all components of the input vector to form the final encoded vector. 4. Pass the encoded vector into the MLP F^{\prime}{\Theta}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fourierfeatureencoding(v, numbands): """ Encodes a vector v using Fourier features. Args: v: A list or array of floats (coordinates or direction components), expected to be in range [-1, 1]. numbands: Integer L, the number of frequency bands. Returns: A list of floats representing the encoded features. """ features = [] for val in v: for b in range(numbands): # Frequency is 2^b pi freq = (2 b) math.pi features.append(math.sin(freq val)) features.append(math.cos(freq val)) return features def nerfforward(x, d, xbands, dbands, mlp): """ Simulates the forward pass of a NeRF with Fourier Feature Encoding. Args: x: 3D coordinate vector [x, y, z]. d: Viewing direction vector [dx, dy, dz]. xbands: Number of bands for coordinates (e.g., 10). dbands: Number of bands for directions (e.g., 4). mlp: A function representing the MLP F'Theta. Returns: Color c and density sigma. """ # Encode inputs xencoded = fourierfeatureencoding(x, xbands) dencoded = fourierfeatureencoding(d, dbands) # Concatenate encoded inputs inputfeatures = xencoded + dencoded # Pass through MLP c, sigma = mlp(inputfeatures) return c, sigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: High-frequency bands (2^{L-1}) can lead to numerical instability if inputs are not strictly normalized to [-1, 1]. Values outside this range may cause oscillations that the network cannot resolve or gradients that vanish/explode. Boundary Conditions: The encoding is periodic. If the scene geometry extends beyond the normalized bounding box, the encoding wraps around, potentially causing artifacts. Degenerate Input: If the input vector is zero, the encoding results in zeros for sines and ones for cosines, which is valid but provides no directional information for that component. Time Complexity: The encoding itself is O(L \cdot D), where D is the input dimension (3 for coordinates/directions). This is negligible compared to the MLP evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(L \cdot D) to store the encoded vector. No additional memory is required for the encoding process itself. Strengths: Significantly improves the reconstruction of high-frequency details (textures, sharp edges) compared to unencoded MLPs. It is simple to implement and requires no additional training parameters for the encoder. Limitations: The fixed frequency spectrum may not be optimal for all scenes. Very high frequencies can lead to aliasing or optimization difficulties if the sampling rate along rays is insufficient. When to use: Standard for NeRF-like implicit radiance fields where high-frequency detail is desired. When not to use: If the scene is inherently low-frequency or if computational resources are extremely constrained and the overhead of encoding is non-trivial (though it usually is not). Fixed sinusoidal positional encoding was introduced in the seminal paper "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It was motivated by the observation that standard MLPs struggle to learn high-frequency functions due to spectral bias. The technique was later analyzed theoretically using Neural Tangent Kernels. Modern variants include trainable parametric encodings, integral encodings, and hierarchical variants. name: Voxel-based Representation
head: Voxel Grids, 3D Grids, Discrete Radiance Fields
body: Voxel-based representations use discrete 3D grids to store volumetric features, density, or color. This approach trades spatial continuity for memory efficiency and inference speed, with resolution limits imposed by grid size. The family builds on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. FastNeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates inference by factorizing the view-dependent radiance field into position-dependent and direction-dependent components, enabling efficient caching of intermediate network outputs. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard NeRF by avoiding MLP evaluations at inference time, instead relying on hardware-accelerated ray tracing and grid lookups to achieve interactive frame rates (200Hz) on consumer hardware. It differs from its siblings, such as C-NeRF and V4D, by using a low-rank inner-product factorization to decouple spatial and directional information, whereas other methods may use spherical harmonics or explicit voxel grids for density only. C-NeRF is a voxel-based radiance field representation that uses a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) to generate feature volumes, which are then decoded by a NeRF-like multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to predict density and color. C-NeRF serves as a baseline for dynamic scene representation. When decomposing 4D volumes into a weighted summation of shared 3D volumes, this factorization is referred to as Volume Basis. V4D is a voxel-based architecture for 4D novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes that models the 4D neural radiance field directly without requiring a canonical space. It distinguishes itself from continuous neural radiance fields and other voxel-based methods by using separate 3D voxel grids for density and texture, combined with a conditional positional encoding (CPE) module and a look-up table (LUT) refinement module to mitigate the over-smoothing effects of total variation regularization. Unlike its sibling TiNeuVox which uses a canonical space and position offsets, V4D relies on temporal concatenation and total variation loss to enforce temporal consistency, resulting in longer training times but faster inference. RenderNet is a differentiable rendering convolutional neural network that generates 2D images from 3D voxel grids by jointly learning visibility computation and pixel color calculation (shading). Unlike traditional rasterization or ray tracing which rely on discrete, non-differentiable operations like z-buffering, RenderNet uses a CNN to encode spatial occlusion and shading automatically. It is distinguished from sibling methods like FastNeRF and VoxGRAF by its explicit use of a "Projection Unit" that collapses the 3D depth dimension into 2D feature maps while learning visibility, rather than relying on continuous volume rendering equations or sparse voxel structures. It handles low-resolution or noisy voxel inputs more robustly than mesh-based differentiable renderers. ExBluRF is a novel view synthesis method designed to reconstruct sharp 3D scenes from extreme motion-blurred images by jointly optimizing voxel-based radiance fields and 6-DOF camera trajectories. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like FastNeRF and C-NeRF, which focus on static scene acceleration, by addressing the ill-posed problem of deblurring through a trajectory-based blur model and memory-efficient voxel representations, unlike DeblurNeRF which relies on spatially varying 2D kernels and MLPs. Part-based MHE-augmented NeRF is a method for learning neural volumetric videos of dynamic humans from sparse view videos in minutes with competitive visual quality. It addresses the slow convergence of per-scene optimization methods by decomposing the canonical human body into multiple anatomical parts, assigning each part its own Multiresolution Hash Encoding (MHE)-augmented NeRF network with varying resolutions to efficiently distribute representational power. Unlike single-resolution voxelized representations or continuous implicit functions that treat the entire body uniformly, this method leverages a 2D motion parameterization scheme on a parametric mesh (SMPL) to accelerate deformation field learning. Object-NeRF is a composition model that separates and edits objects within a scene using a hybrid voxel-based approach with jointly optimized voxel grid features and MLP parameters. It differs from its siblings by explicitly partitioning the scene into a background "scene branch" and foreground "object branch," allowing for the shifting, addition, or removal of specific objects without retraining the entire radiance field. VoxGRAF is a 3D-aware Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that replaces the coordinate-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) scene representation with a sparse voxel grid generator. It solves the problem of slow rendering and viewpoint/content entanglement inherent in previous 3D-aware GANs by enabling fast, 3D-consistent image synthesis with a single forward pass. Unlike its siblings FastNeRF, C-NeRF, V4D, RenderNet, and Object-NeRF which often rely on dense coordinate-based queries or hybrid rendering, VoxGRAF generates the entire 3D radiance field on a sparse voxel grid using 3D convolutions, allowing for efficient rendering via alpha composition without reducing sample counts. Voxel-based Gaussian Splatting (VoxGS) is a volume representation that places isometric 3D Gaussians at the fixed centroids of a regular 3D voxel grid to enable efficient Computed Tomography (CT) volume extraction and differentiable X-ray rendering. Unlike standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) which optimizes primitive positions and uses spherical harmonics for view-dependent color, VoxGS fixes positions and removes color coefficients, retaining only opacity, scale, and rotation to support isotropic density modeling. This design solves the instability and inaccurate volume extraction issues associated with applying original 3DGS directly to CT data. Gaussian Voxel Kernel Functions (GVKF) is a method for efficient 3D surface reconstruction in open scenes that establishes a continuous scene representation based on discrete 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) through kernel regression. It differs from explicit 3DGS by using implicit continuous representation via kernel regression instead of explicit discrete summation, reducing memory consumption and improving surface continuity. Unlike standard volume rendering which relies on continuous sampling, GVKF integrates fast 3DGS rasterization with implicit scene representations to achieve high-fidelity open scene surface reconstruction without computationally intensive volume rendering. This method converts OpenVDB volumetric datasets into a set of non-overlapping 3D Gaussian particles to enable memory-efficient, lossy representation with Level of Detail (LOD) support, rendered via forward ray marching using NVIDIA OptiX. It differs from standard voxel-based representations by replacing the discrete grid sampling with continuous Gaussian primitives, allowing for hardware-accelerated bounding box intersections and real-time performance with millions of particles, while maintaining compatibility with traditional volume rendering transfer functions. Global Scene Generator (GSN) is a generative model that synthesizes unconstrained 3D scenes by decomposing them into local regions using a global generator and a locally conditioned radiance field. Unlike dictionary-based memory models that limit unseen viewpoints, GSN uses a learned scene prior to allow extrapolation beyond given observations. It sets itself apart from sibling voxel-based methods by explicitly generating a 2D latent "floorplan" grid to condition multiple local radiance fields, rather than storing static features in a 3D voxel grid. Definition: A framework that synthesizes realistic images given object voxels as input, providing editing functionalities for illumination, object geometry, and appearance. Parameters: Initial voxel resolution is 100^3. Scene volume is V \in 128^3 \times 4. Environment map resolution (realism variant) is 32 \times 32, processed by convolutional layers to extract a latent code supplied to NVR+. Performance: At 25^3 voxel resolution, performance decreases gracefully but still produces plausible outputs. Comparison: NVR captures color and structure but smooths fine texture details. NVR+ accurately renders geometry and texture, realistically synthesizing shadows, specular reflections, and highlights. Usage: Trained on ShapeNet chair category. Tested on Pix3D and Ikea datasets for sofas, tables, and miscellaneous objects. Not given in the sources.
