name: FastNeRF
head: Factorized NeRF, Factorized Neural Radiance Fields
body: FastNeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates the inference of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by factorizing the view-dependent color function into position-dependent and direction-dependent components, enabling efficient caching of intermediate radiance values. It solves the problem of high computational cost in standard NeRF, which requires hundreds of MLP evaluations per pixel, by reducing inference to memory-bound cache lookups and dot products, achieving speeds over 3000 times faster than the original NeRF. It differs from its siblings, such as C-NeRF and VoxGRAF, by explicitly separating the 5D radiance field into two independent low-dimensional manifolds (position and direction) to allow for compact, sparse caching of a "deep radiance map" rather than caching the full 5D function or using smaller local MLPs. FastNeRF builds on Voxel-based Representation by replacing the single monolithic MLP with two factorized networks and caching their outputs. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses; a bounding box V enclosing the scene. Outputs: A trained position-dependent network \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}}, a direction-dependent network \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}}, and optionally, cached grids for inference. 1. Position Cache: A sparse 3D grid storing outputs of \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}}. Fields: Density \sigma (scalar) and a deep radiance map components (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}) (each D-dimensional vectors). Layout: Stored as dense 16-bit floating point values in a grid of size k^3 (or sparse subset thereof). 2. Direction Cache: A sparse 2D grid storing outputs of \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}}. Fields: Weight vector \boldsymbol{\beta} (D-dimensional). Layout: Stored as dense 16-bit floating point values in a grid of size l^2 (parameterized by spherical coordinates \theta, \phi). 3. Collision Mesh: A triangle mesh derived from the density volume \sigma using Marching Cubes, used for hardware-accelerated ray tracing to skip empty space. \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}}: An 8-layer MLP with 384 hidden units (256 for LLFF scenes). Input: 3D position \mathbf{p}. Output: \{\sigma, (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})\}. \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}}: A 4-layer MLP with 128 hidden units. Input: 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d} (parameterized as a unit vector or spherical coordinates). Output: \boldsymbol{\beta}. Positional Encoding: Applied to inputs of both MLPs, as in standard NeRF. 1. Train \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}} and \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}} jointly using the standard NeRF loss (MSE between rendered and ground truth colors). 2. Define a bounding box V covering the scene. 3. Uniformly sample k values for x, y, z within V and l values for \theta \in [0, \pi], \phi \in [0, 2\pi]. 4. Compute \mathcal{F}{\text{pos}} for all position combinations and \mathcal{F}{\text{dir}} for all direction combinations to populate the caches. 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray \mathbf{r} defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Empty Space Skipping: Intersect \mathbf{r} with the collision mesh derived from the density volume via Marching Cubes. Start integration only after the first hit. 3. Sampling: Uniformly sample N points \mathbf{p}i along the ray within the mesh bounds. 4. Cache Lookup: For each \mathbf{p}i, lookup \sigmai and (\mathbf{u}i, \mathbf{v}i, \mathbf{w}i) from the Position Cache using nearest-neighbor interpolation. For the ray direction \mathbf{d}, lookup \boldsymbol{\beta} from the Direction Cache using trilinear sampling on the \theta, \phi grid. 5. Color Computation: Compute color \mathbf{c}i for each sample point: \mathbf{c}i = \boldsymbol{\beta}^T \cdot (\mathbf{u}i, \mathbf{v}i, \mathbf{w}i) = \sum{j=1}^D \betaj (u{i,j}, v{i,j}, w{i,j}) where D is the number of components (typically 8 for Synthetic 360, 6 for LLFF). 6. Volume Rendering: Integrate color and density along the ray using the standard NeRF volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) and \deltai is the distance between samples. 7. Termination: Terminate ray integration once transmittance Ti drops below a threshold (saturation). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, bounds): """Returns (tmin, tmax) for ray-AABB intersection. bounds = [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz].""" tmin = -math.inf tmax = math.inf for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds[2i] or origin[i] > bounds[2i+1]: return None, None else: t1 = (bounds[2i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[2i+1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def nearestneighborlookup(grid, point): """Simplified nearest-neighbor lookup returning (sigma, u, v, w).""" idx = [int(round(p)) for p in point] return grid[idx] def trilinearlookup(grid, theta, phi): """Simplified trilinear lookup returning beta vector.""" idxt = int(theta / math.pi (grid.shape[0] - 1)) idxp = int(phi / (2 math.pi) (grid.shape[1] - 1)) return grid[idxt, idxp] def fastnerfinfer(rayorigin, raydirection, poscache, dircache, D, bounds, stepsize): """ Renders a single pixel using FastNeRF caches. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, camera origin. raydirection: (3,) array, normalized ray direction. poscache: Sparse 3D grid storing {sigma, u, v, w}. dircache: Sparse 2D grid storing beta. D: Number of components (e.g., 8). bounds: [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz] of the scene bounding box. stepsize: Distance between samples (delta). Returns: color: (3,) array, RGB color. """ # 1. Empty Space Skipping: Intersect ray with collision mesh (approximated here by AABB) tnear, tfar = rayaabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, bounds) if tnear is None: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) tstart = max(0.0, tnear) tend = tfar numsamples = int(round((tend - tstart) / stepsize)) if numsamples <= 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Pre-fetch direction weights theta = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, raydirection[2]))) phi = math.atan2(raydirection[1], raydirection[0]) beta = trilinearlookup(dircache, theta, phi) totalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tstart + (i + 0.5) stepsize p = rayorigin + raydirection t # 2. Cache Lookup sigma, u, v, w = nearestneighborlookup(poscache, p) # 3. Color Computation r = sum(beta[j] u[j] for j in range(D)) g = sum(beta[j] v[j] for j in range(D)) b = sum(beta[j] w[j] for j in range(D)) c = (r, g, b) # 4. Volume Rendering Integration alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma stepsize) weight = transmittance alpha totalcolor = (totalcolor[0] + weight c[0], totalcolor[1] + weight c[1], totalcolor[2] + weight c[2]) transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return totalcolor D (Components): Dimensionality of the deep radiance map and direction weights. Typical values: 8 for NeRF Synthetic 360 scenes, 6 for LLFF scenes. k (Position Grid Size): Number of uniform samples for each worldspace coordinate (x, y, z) in the position cache bounding box. Typical values: 512, 768, 1024. l (Direction Grid Size): Number of uniform samples for each ray direction coordinate (\theta, \phi). Typical values: 256. Grid Resolution: Number of divisions of the longest side of the bounding volume. Typical values: 256^3, 384^3, 512^3, 768^3, 1024^3. Memory Limits: Discretizing the full 5D space with 512 bins per dimension would require ~176 TB, which is infeasible. FastNeRF reduces this to ~54 GB (dense) or ~3 GB (sparse). Memory Complexity: Caching standard NeRF is O(k^3 l^2). FastNeRF reduces this to O(k^3 (1 + 3D) + l^2 D). Aliasing: Caching the model to a grid after training can introduce aliasing artifacts, leading to a decrease in metrics as a function of grid resolution. Mesh Complexity: For density volumes larger than 512^3, the collision mesh must be downsampled by a factor of two to reduce complexity. Uncached Performance: Without caching, FastNeRF is slower than standard NeRF due to larger MLPs (384 hidden units vs 256), though it performs identically to NeRF when using 256 hidden units. Provides analytical formulas to calculate the memory footprint of the position-dependent and direction-dependent caches, solving the problem of determining if a configuration fits in hardware memory. Time Complexity: Inference is O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray, dominated by cache lookups and dot products, avoiding MLP evaluations. Memory Complexity: Caching standard NeRF is O(k^3 l^2). FastNeRF reduces this to O(k^3 (1 + 3D) + l^2 D). For k=l=1024, D=8, dense cache size is ~54 GB, compared to ~5600 TB for standard NeRF. Sparse cache size is ~3 GB. Performance: Renders high-fidelity photorealistic images at 200Hz on high-end consumer GPUs. It is on average more than 3000x faster than NeRF. On Nvidia Tesla V100, it renders 300x300 pixel images of a face at 30 fps in telepresence scenarios, ~50x faster than NeRF. Strengths: Extremely fast inference; compatible with hardware-accelerated ray tracing; maintains visual quality comparable to NeRF. Limitations: High memory usage for caches (several GBs); aliasing artifacts at lower resolutions; slower than NeRF when not cached. When to use: Scenarios requiring interactive rates on consumer hardware, such as mobile devices, mixed reality, and telepresence. When not to use: Memory-constrained embedded systems without large caches; scenarios where training speed is the primary bottleneck (FastNeRF does not address training speed). FastNeRF was proposed by Garbin et al. in March 2021. It was motivated by the need for real-time neural rendering on mobile and mixed reality devices. The method draws inspiration from real-time computer graphics techniques for approximating the rendering equation, such as spherical harmonics, by factorizing the 5D radiance field into position and direction components. It is a key development in the evolution of NeRF acceleration, preceding methods like KiloNeRF and PlenOctrees. name: FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation
body: FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation provides analytical formulas to calculate the memory footprint of the position-dependent and direction-dependent caches in the FastNeRF architecture. It addresses the impracticality of standard NeRF caches, which can exceed 60TB even for highly sparse volumes (\alpha = 0.01), by accounting for the factorized representation of the direction-dependent cache. The method calculates the total memory size M in bits for the position-dependent and direction-dependent caches. Inputs: \alpha \in 0, 1): Inverse volume sparsity, where \alpha = 1 indicates a dense volume. k: Number of bins per dimension in the position-dependent cache. l: Number of bins per dimension in the direction-dependent cache. D: Number of components or factors in the direction cache [decomposition. s\sigma: Size in bits of the stored transparency value. s{rgb}: Size in bits of the stored RGB color value. s{uvw}: Size in bits of the stored (ui, vi, wi) coordinate values. s{\beta}: Size in bits of the stored weights \betai. Outputs: M{NeRF}: Estimated memory size in bits for a standard NeRF cache. M{FastNeRF}: Estimated memory size in bits for the FastNeRF cache. Formulas: 1. Standard NeRF Cache Size: M{NeRF} = \alpha(s\sigma + s{rgb})k^3l^2 This formula assumes a dense lookup table for direction-dependent colors, requiring storage of full RGB vectors for every direction bin. 2. FastNeRF Cache Size: M{FastNeRF} = \alpha \left( (D \cdot s{uvw} + s{\sigma})k^3 \right) + D \cdot s{\beta}l^2 This formula accounts for the factorized representation, where the position cache stores D coordinate factors and transparency, and the direction cache stores D weight factors. Parameters and Typical Values: Standard implementation uses k = l = 1024. Number of factors D = 8. Color channels (r, g, b) are stored as individual bytes (s{rgb} = 24 bits). Coordinate, weight, and transparency values are stored as half-precision floats (s{uvw} = 16 bits, s{\beta} = 16 bits, s{\sigma} = 16 bits). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Memory Usage: Even for highly sparse volumes with \alpha = 0.01, the standard NeRF cache size is nearly 60TB, which exceeds the memory capacity of consumer-grade hardware. Dense Volume: If \alpha = 1, the memory requirements are maximized. Data Type Sensitivity: The choice of storage size (s{uvw}, s{\beta}, s{rgb}) significantly impacts the total memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateneRFcachesize(alpha, ssigma, srgb, k, l): """Calculate memory size in bits for standard NeRF cache.""" return alpha (ssigma + srgb) (k 3) (l 2) def calculatefastNeRFcachesize(alpha, D, suvw, ssigma, sbeta, k, l): """Calculate memory size in bits for FastNeRF cache.""" positioncachesize = alpha ((D suvw) + ssigma) (k 3) directioncachesize = D sbeta (l 2) return positioncachesize + directioncachesize Lightweight Profiling is a white-box model that predicts the representation data size and rendering quality of mesh-assisted Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) for specific configurations without training the network. It solves the problem of high computational cost in configuration search by providing an analytical approximation of performance metrics, avoiding the significant time and resource costs associated with full network training. It differs from black-box profiling models by using explicit polynomial functions derived from rendering knowledge, and it differs from its parent FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation by focusing on mesh-assisted NeRFs where geometry and texture knobs are decoupled from the MLP. name: Lightweight Profiling
head: Mesh-assisted NeRF Profiling Model, Polynomial-based Size and Quality Prediction
body: Lightweight Profiling is a white-box model that predicts the representation data size and rendering quality of mesh-assisted Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) for specific configurations without training the network. It solves the problem of high computational cost in configuration search by providing an analytical approximation of performance metrics, avoiding the significant time and resource costs associated with full network training. It differs from black-box profiling models (e.g., neural networks) by using explicit polynomial functions derived from rendering knowledge, and it differs from its parent FastNeRF Cache Size Estimation by focusing on mesh-assisted NeRFs (like mobile-NeRF) where geometry and texture knobs are decoupled from the MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two configuration knobs: g: Number of voxel grids allocated for each axis in the 3D voxel grid representation (geometry knob). p: One-dimensional size of the texture image allocated for each quad face (texture knob, p \times p pixels). Outputs: S: Total data size (memory load). Q: Rendering quality metric, specifically SSIM (Structural Similarity Index Measure). Data Structures: The model consists of two polynomial functions, fs and fq, parameterized by a set of coefficients \theta = \{m, a, b, k, a', b'\}. These coefficients are determined via curve fitting. Formulas: The size S and quality Q are calculated as follows: S = fs(g, p) = \frac{m}{3}(g + a)^3 \cdot (p + b)^2 Q = fq(g, p) = k \cdot (g + a')^3 \cdot (p + b')^2 Where: m, a, b are constants for the size model. k, a', b' are constants for the quality model. The exponent 3 on the geometry term (g+a) reflects the 3D nature of the voxel grid. The exponent 2 on the texture term (p+b) reflects the 2D nature of the texture image. The MLP size is excluded from S as it is negligible (a few KB) and has poor compatibility with commercial rendering engines when quantized. Parameters and Typical Values: Quality Metric Q: SSIM, evaluating luminance, contrast, and structure. Size Metric S: Total data size in bytes or KB. Knob g: Integer, number of voxels per axis. Knob p: Integer, texture resolution per face. Coefficients: Not given in the sources. They are determined by curve fitting on sampled data. Sampling Strategy for Curve Fitting: To minimize the number of sampling points required to fit the coefficients \theta, a variable step-size searching strategy is used: 1. Select g values using a step size of 2 \cdot g', where g' is the value of the previous sample point. 2. For each selected g, select three distinct p values: the maximum, minimum, and midpoint of the valid patch size range. 3. Pair each g with these three p values to generate sample points. """ # Extract data gvals = [pt[0] for pt in samplepoints] pvals = [pt[1] for pt in samplepoints] Svals = [pt[2] for pt in samplepoints] Qvals = [pt[3] for pt in samplepoints] # Fit Size Model: S = (m/3) (g + a)^3 (p + b)^2 # This is a non-linear least squares problem. # We define the residual function and solve for thetas = [m, a, b] def sizeresidual(theta, g, p, S): m, a, b = theta predicted = (m / 3.0) (g + a)3 (p + b)2 return predicted - S # Initial guess for size coefficients [G: Placeholder values, # actual values depend on the specific dataset and range of g, p] initialguesss = [1000.0, 0.0, 0.0] thetas = optimizenonlinearleastsquares(sizeresidual, initialguesss, gvals, pvals, Svals) # Fit Quality Model: Q = k (g + a')^3 (p + b')^2 def qualityresidual(theta, g, p, Q): k, aprime, bprime = theta predicted = k (g + aprime)3 (p + bprime)2 return predicted - Q # Initial guess for quality coefficients [G: Placeholder values] initialguessq = [0.5, 0.0, 0.0] thetaq = optimizenonlinearleastsquares(qualityresidual, initialguessq, gvals, pvals, Qvals) return thetas, thetaq def predictsizeandquality(g, p, thetas, thetaq): """ Predicts size and quality for a given configuration. Args: g: Geometry knob (voxels per axis). p: Texture knob (texture size per face). thetas: Coefficients (m, a, b) for size. thetaq: Coefficients (k, aprime, bprime) for quality. Returns: S: Predicted size. Q: Predicted quality (SSIM). This is valid because the MLP size is small (KBs) and quantization is incompatible with commercial engines. If the MLP size becomes significant for a specific variant, this model will underestimate total size. Mesh-Assisted Only: The model is designed for mesh-assisted NeRFs (e.g., mobile-NeRF, NeRF2Mesh) where geometry is converted to a voxel grid and textured meshes. It may not apply to pure voxel-based or pure grid-based NeRFs without texture mapping. SSIM Limitations: The quality metric is SSIM, which aligns with human perception but may differ from PSNR. If PSNR is required, the model must be re-fitted with PSNR targets. Extrapolation: The polynomial model is fitted within the sampled range. Extrapolating outside the range of g and p used for fitting may lead to inaccurate predictions. Time Complexity: The prediction itself is O(1) given the coefficients, as it involves simple arithmetic operations. The cost lies in the initial curve fitting, which requires sampling a small number of configurations (e.g., 45 pairs in validation). Memory Complexity: The model stores a small number of coefficients (6 for size, 3 for quality, total 9). Memory usage is negligible compared to the NeRF model itself. Measured Performance: Validated on four objects with 45 configuration pairs. Average error in quality prediction (SSIM): 0.0065, standard deviation 0.0088. Average error in size prediction: 3.3410, standard deviation 2.7345. Strengths: Avoids the hours-long training time required for full NeRF optimization (e.g., on RTX 3090 GPUs). Provides a white-box, interpretable model. Limitations: Limited to mesh-assisted NeRFs. Accuracy depends on the quality of the curve fitting and the representativeness of the sample points. Does not account for MLP configuration changes. Origin: Proposed in the NeRFlex paper. Context: Mobile-NeRF [6] and NeRF2Mesh [7] are examples of mesh-assisted real-time NeRF solutions that convert objects to voxel grid representations. The baking of data for these representations can take several hours on high-end GPUs. Development: The profiling module was designed to predict representation data size and rendering quality without training the network, addressing the high cost of configuration search. It uses SSIM for quality and total data size for memory load. Usage: Used in the NeRFlex framework for resource-aware real-time high-quality rendering on mobile devices. name: C-NeRF
head: Volume Basis
body: C-NeRF is a voxel-based radiance field optimization method that adopts a 3D convolutional neural network to produce feature volumes, which are then decoded by a NeRF-like MLP to predict radiance fields. It improves upon its predecessor Neural Volumes by leveraging 3D convolutions for volumetric data, though it still tends to lose high-frequency details due to its single shared MLP structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-view images and camera poses. Output: A differentiable radiance field representation consisting of a 3D feature volume and a decoding MLP, allowing for novel view synthesis and volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. 3D Feature Volume: A 3D grid of tensors produced by a 3D CNN. 2. Decoding MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes spatial coordinates and the sampled feature vector from the 3D volume as input, and outputs density (\sigma) and color (\mathbf{c}). Method Steps: 1. 3D CNN Encoding: A 3D Convolutional Neural Network processes the input data to produce a 3D feature volume. This step replaces the implicit coordinate mapping of standard NeRF with an explicit volumetric representation. 2. Ray Sampling: For each ray \mathbf{r}, sample N points along the ray within the scene bounding box. 3. Feature Interpolation: For each sample point, trilinearly interpolate the feature vector from the 3D feature volume based on the point's spatial coordinates. 4. Radiance Field Prediction: Pass the spatial coordinates and the interpolated feature vector into the NeRF-like MLP. The MLP outputs the density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for each sample point i. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the final pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard differentiable volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance, and \deltai is the distance between sample points. 6. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between rendered images and ground truth images using gradient descent. Gradients are backpropagated through the rendering equation and the MLP. The 3D CNN parameters are updated if the network is trained end-to-end from raw inputs. Parameters: Voxel Resolution: Not given in the sources. CNN Architecture: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Detail Loss: C-NeRF tends to lose details in high-frequency regions of the image compared to more advanced methods, attributed to the limitations of its single shared MLP model structure. Memory Usage: Storing a 3D feature volume requires significant memory, scaling with the cube of the resolution. Fast, generalizable radiance field reconstruction from multi-view stereo that learns a data prior to bypass per-scene optimization. Uses a pretrained CNN to extract 2D features, maps them to a 3D voxelized cost volume via plane sweeping, and uses a pretrained 3D CNN for a 3D neural encoding volume. Choose when per-scene optimization is too slow and multi-view inputs are available. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Dominated by the storage of the 3D feature volume and the CNN/MLP parameters. Time: Training time is significantly faster than coordinate-based NeRF due to the efficiency of 3D convolutions and parallelizable voxel access. However, specific complexity formulas are not provided. Measured Performance: Qualitative results show it produces sharper images than Neural Volumes but still suffers from blurring in high-frequency regions compared to methods using dynamic representations. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster training than MLP-only NeRF; better detail preservation than Neural Volumes; explicit volumetric representation allows for efficient 3D operations. Limitations: Loses high-frequency details due to its single shared MLP model structure. When to Use: When faster training than standard NeRF is required and the scene has moderate complexity. When an explicit volumetric representation is preferred for downstream 3D processing. When Not to Use: When high-frequency detail preservation is critical. When memory is constrained and high resolution is needed. C-NeRF was introduced as a follow-up work to Neural Volumes. It is part of the evolution of voxel-based radiance field representations, aiming to balance the efficiency of voxel grids with the expressive power of neural networks for volumetric video representation and novel view synthesis. name: MVSNeRF
head: MVS-NeRF
body: MVSNeRF is a method for fast, generalizable radiance field reconstruction from multi-view stereo that learns a data prior to bypass per-scene optimization. It extracts 2D image features using a pretrained CNN, maps them to a 3D voxelized cost volume through plane sweeping with a variance-based cost, and uses a pretrained 3D CNN to produce a 3D neural encoding volume. Inputs: A set of multi-view images \{It\} with known camera parameters. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{I}. Data Structures: 1. 2D Feature Volume: Extracted from input images using a pretrained CNN. 2. 3D Cost Volume: A voxelized grid constructed via plane sweeping. 3. 3D Neural Encoding Volume (V): A 3D tensor produced by a pretrained 3D CNN, storing latent codes for spatial points. 4. NeRF MLP: A multi-layer perceptron taking latent codes, coordinates, and viewing directions as input. Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Extract 2D features from each input image It using a pretrained CNN. 2. Cost Volume Construction: Map the 2D features to a 3D voxelized cost volume through plane sweeping using a variance-based cost metric. 3. 3D Neural Encoding: Pass the cost volume through a pretrained 3D CNN to produce the 3D neural encoding volume V. 4. Latent Code Interpolation: For any 3D point p, retrieve its latent code zp by interpolating values from V. 5. Radiance Field Prediction: Input zp, the 3D point coordinates p, and the viewing direction d into the NeRF MLP to predict density \sigma and color c. 6. Volume Rendering: Render the image by integrating predicted density and color along camera rays. 7. Joint Optimization: During training, jointly optimize the 3D feature volume (via the 3D CNN) and the NeRF MLP parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def interpolate(volume, point): # Standard trilinear interpolation from 3D tensor return volume[point] def mvsnerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, V, nerfmlp, near, far, numsamples): renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = near + (far - near) (i + 0.5) / numsamples p = [rayorigin[j] + raydirection[j] t for j in range(3)] zp = interpolate(V, p) sigma, color = nerfmlp(zp, p, raydirection) delta = (far - near) / numsamples alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha renderedcolor = [renderedcolor[j] + weight color[j] for j in range(3)] accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return renderedcolor def trainmvsnerf(images, gtimages, nerfmlp, optimizer): # Joint optimization of 3D feature volume and NeRF MLP rendered = mvsnerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, V, nerfmlp, near, far, numsamples) loss = sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, gtimages)) / len(gtimages) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: Plane sweeping depth range: Not given in the sources. Variance-based cost threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Interpolation from the 3D neural encoding volume requires careful handling of grid boundaries. Regresses a local neural volume for each input frame using neighboring images. It solves per-frame radiance field estimation by aggregating multi-view features in a canonical world coordinate frame. Unlike MVSNeRF, which builds perspective frustum volumes for small-baseline rendering, this method constructs volumes directly in canonical space to facilitate global fusion. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than baseline NeRF; on the DTU dataset, MVSNeRF reached results comparable to hours of baseline NeRF training within 15 minutes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D neural encoding volume and the cost volume. Strengths: Fast generalizable reconstruction. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Fast reconstruction from multi-view images where per-scene optimization is too slow. When not to use: Not given in the sources. MVSNeRF was introduced in March 2021. It differs from General Radiance Field (GRF) by taking a slightly different approach, whereas GRF operated in canonical space as opposed to view-space for pixelNeRF. It builds on the idea of using multi-view stereo to initialize or guide the radiance field representation. name: Local Sparse Volume Reconstruction
head: Local Radiance Field Reconstruction, Per-frame Local Radiance Field, Reconstructing Local Volumes
body: Local Sparse Volume Reconstruction regresses a local neural volume Vt for each input frame t using its image It and K-1 neighboring images. It solves per-frame radiance field estimation by aggregating multi-view features in a canonical world coordinate frame, ensuring alignment with a global volume for large-scale reconstruction. Unlike MVS-NeRF, which builds perspective frustum volumes for small-baseline rendering, this method constructs volumes directly in canonical space to facilitate global fusion. Inputs: A sequence of RGB images I1, \dots, IN with known camera parameters \Phi1, \dots, \PhiN. For each frame t, a set of K neighboring viewpoints \mathcal{N}t (typically temporal neighbors in monocular video). Outputs: A local sparse neural volume \mathcal{V}t representing the local radiance field for frame t in canonical world space. Data Structures: 1. 2D Feature Map Ft: A standard 2D tensor (height, width, channels) extracted for each image It using a deep 2D CNN. 2. Sparse Voxel Set: A set of 3D voxel centers \{v\} within an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) covering the frustums of all K neighboring viewpoints in the world coordinate frame, with voxels invisible to all views masked out. 3. 3D Feature Volume \mathcal{U}i: For each neighboring view i \in \mathcal{N}t, a 3D feature volume where each visible voxel v stores a concatenated feature vector. 4. Local Volume \mathcal{V}t: The output volume with the same spatial layout as \mathcal{U}i, containing the regressed local radiance field features. Parameters: K: Number of neighboring viewpoints used for reconstruction. Not given in the sources. G: MLP for computing direction features. Architecture details not given in the sources. J: Deep neural network for regressing the local volume from aggregated statistics. Architecture details not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Extract 2D Image Features: For each input image It in the sequence, pass it through a deep 2D convolutional neural network to extract a 2D feature map Ft. 2. Define Bounding Box and Sparse Voxels: Define an axis-aligned bounding box in the canonical world coordinate frame that encompasses the viewing frustums of all K neighboring viewpoints in \mathcal{N}t. Identify the set of voxels within this box and mask out any voxel that is not visible to at least one of the K neighboring views, resulting in a sparse set of active voxels. 3. Build 3D Feature Volumes (\mathcal{U}i): For each neighboring viewpoint i \in \mathcal{N}t and its corresponding feature map Fi, iterate over each visible voxel v in the sparse set. Compute the 2D projection ui of the voxel center v onto the image plane of view i. Fetch the 2D image feature Fi(ui) from the feature map at location ui. Compute the viewing direction di from viewpoint i to voxel v in world coordinates. Pass di through an MLP G to get direction features G(di). Concatenate the image and direction features to form the per-view feature at voxel v: \mathcal{U}i(v) = [Fi(ui), G(di)], where [\cdot, \cdot] denotes concatenation. 4. Aggregate and Regress Local Volume (\mathcal{V}t): For each visible voxel v, compute the element-wise mean and variance of the features \mathcal{U}i(v) across all K neighboring viewpoints i \in \mathcal{N}t: \text{Mean}v = \text{Mean}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v) and \text{Var}v = \text{Var}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v). These operations are invariant to the number and order of inputs, naturally handling voxels with varying numbers of visible viewpoints. Concatenate the mean and variance features: [\text{Mean}v, \text{Var}v]. Pass this concatenated vector through a deep neural network J to regress the local volume feature at voxel v: \mathcal{V}t(v) = J([\text{Mean}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v), \text{Var}{i \in \mathcal{N}t} \mathcal{U}i(v)]). The result \mathcal{V}t is the local neural volume for frame t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def reconstructlocalvolume(images, neighbors, K, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, featureextractor, directionmlp, regressor, voxelgrid): # Step 1: Extract 2D features for all K views featuremaps = [featureextractor(img) for img in images] # Step 2: voxelgrid contains 3D points v visible to at least one neighbor voxelstats = {} # v -> [sumfeatures, sumsqfeatures, count] for i in range(K): Fi = featuremaps[i] camintr = cameraintrinsics[i] camextr = cameraextrinsics[i] for v in voxelgrid: # Project voxel v to 2D image plane of view i ui = project2d(v, camintr, camextr) # Fetch 2D feature via bilinear interpolation feat2d = samplefeature(Fi, ui) # Compute viewing direction di from camera center to v camcenter = getcameracenter(camextr) di = normalize(v - camcenter) # Encode direction featdir = directionmlp(di) # Concatenate image and direction features Uiv = concatenate(feat2d, featdir) # Accumulate for mean/var if v not in voxelstats: voxelstats[v] = [zeroslike(Uiv), zeroslike(Uiv), 0] stats = voxelstats[v] stats[0] = [a + b for a, b in zip(stats[0], Uiv)] stats[1] = [a + b b for a, b in zip(stats[1], Uiv)] stats[2] += 1 localvolume = {} for v, stats in voxelstats.items(): sumfeat, sumsqfeat, count = stats meanfeat = [s / count for s in sumfeat] varfeat = [s / count - m m for s, m in zip(sumsqfeat, meanfeat)] inputtoJ = concatenate(meanfeat, varfeat) localvolume[v] = regressor(inputtoJ) return localvolume def project2d(v, intr, extr): vh = v + (1.0,) camcoord = [sum(extr[i][j] vh[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] u = [sum(intr[i][j] camcoord[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] return (u[0] / u[2], u[1] / u[2]) def samplefeature(F, u): # Bilinear interpolation assumed return F[u[1], u[0]] def getcameracenter(extr): R = extr[:3,:3] t = extr[:3, 3] return tuple(-sum(r ti for r, ti in zip(R[:, j], t)) for j in range(3)) def normalize(v): norm = math.sqrt(sum(c c for c in v)) return tuple(c / (norm + 1e-8) for c in v) def concatenate(a, b): return a + b def zeroslike(t): return [0.0] len(t) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Varying Visibility: Voxels have different numbers of visible viewpoints across the K neighbors. The mean and variance operations are invariant to the number and order of inputs, naturally handling this variation without requiring explicit masking or padding. Coordinate Frame: Volumes are built in the canonical world coordinate frame, not the view's perspective coordinate. This is crucial for aligning with the global volume Vg. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the number of voxels, K, and the depth of networks G and J. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the size of the bounding box and the sparsity of visible voxels. Strengths: Builds volumes in canonical space, facilitating global large-scale reconstruction and fusion. Uses mean and variance aggregation, which is robust to varying visibility and order of inputs. Incorporates viewing direction information to account for view-dependent effects. Limitations: Requires a sparse voxel grid and visibility checks, which may be computationally intensive to set up. Limited to local reconstruction per frame; requires a subsequent fusion step (e.g., GRU) for global consistency. When to use: For large-scale scene reconstruction from monocular video where global consistency is required, and when leveraging multi-view cues per frame is beneficial. When not to use: For small-baseline rendering where perspective frustum volumes (like MVS-NeRF) are sufficient and simpler. Local Sparse Volume Reconstruction was introduced in the paper "NeRFusion: Fusing Radiance Fields for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction". It is part of the NeRFusion framework, which aims to fuse radiance fields for large-scale scene reconstruction. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous approaches like MVS-NeRF, which built perspective frustum volumes for small-baseline rendering, by constructing volumes in canonical space for global reconstruction. The technique leverages mean and variance aggregation, a strategy widely used in MVS-based cost volumes, to fuse per-view appearance and geometry cues. name: V4D (Voxel for 4D Novel View Synthesis)
body: V4D is a voxel-based architecture for 4D novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes that models the 4D neural radiance field directly without requiring a canonical space. It addresses the limited representation capacity of MLPs under single-view constraints by using separate 3D voxel grids for density and texture, combined with a conditional positional encoding module and a look-up table (LUT) refinement module to preserve high-frequency details and prevent over-smoothing. Unlike continuous neural radiance fields that require per-pixel optimization, V4D pre-computes a shared volumetric representation, offering competitive reconstruction quality with shorter inference time than TiNeuVox. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single-view video sequence (providing spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}=(x,y,z), time index t, and view direction (\theta, \phi)) and ground-truth RGB images for supervision. Output: Rendered RGB images \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for novel viewpoints and time steps. Data Structures: 1. Density Volume: A 3D voxel grid initialized with dimensions 160 \times 160 \times 160 \times 12 storing features F{den}. 2. Texture Volume: A 3D voxel grid initialized with dimensions 160 \times 160 \times 160 \times 12 storing features F{tex}. 3. Basic LUTs: M=5 learnable 3D look-up tables, each with resolution 33 \times 33 \times 33. 4. MLPs: Density MLP (5 layers), Texture MLP (5 layers), and Weight Prediction MLP (10 layers). Numbered Steps: 1. Voxel Sampling: For a ray \mathbf{r} sampled at N points along its path, retrieve the feature vectors F{den} and F{tex} from the density and texture volumes at the 3D spatial location (x, y, z) using trilinear interpolation. 2. Conditional Positional Encoding (CPE): Apply CPE to the sampled texture features F{tex} to recover high-frequency details lost by regularization. The encoding is defined as: \gamma(pv) = \left( \sin\left(2^\pi pv + \frac{2\pi}{L-1}t\right), \cos\left(2^\pi pv + \frac{2\pi}{L-1}t\right) \right) where pv is the sampled feature vector, L=5 is the frequency order, and t is the time index. Pitfall: CPE is not applied to the density features F{den}. The density volume must be initialized to zero for correct initial volume rendering; applying CPE to density features breaks this initialization and causes learning collapse. Let the encoded texture feature be \hat{F}{tex}. The density feature remains F{den}. 3. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the time index t, the 3D location (x, y, z), the view direction (\theta, \phi), and the features (F{den} for density, \hat{F}{tex} for texture) into a single vector. 4. Field Estimation: Feed the concatenated vector into the 5-layer Density MLP to predict volume density \sigma. Feed the concatenated vector into the 5-layer Texture MLP to predict RGB color \mathbf{c}. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the coarse RGB color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray using the standard emission-absorption model: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the step size, and N is the number of sampled points. 6. Pseudo-Surface Depth Estimation: Compute the expected depth \hat{d} for the ray to guide the refinement module: \hat{d} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ti where ti represents the depth coordinate of the i-th sample point. 7. LUT Refinement (Pixel-Level): Treat the coarse RGB value \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) as a spatial coordinate in the RGB space. Perform trilinear interpolation on each of the M=5 basic LUTs using this coordinate to obtain interpolated RGB values \mathbf{r}m for m=1 \dots M. Use the pseudo-surface depth \hat{d} (and potentially spatial coordinates) as input to the 10-layer Weight Prediction MLP to predict spatial-aware weights wm for each basic LUT. Combine the interpolated values using the predicted weights to produce the refined RGB color. This process is repeated for Z=3 recurrent iterations. Loss Function: The total loss is a weighted sum of four components: Loss = w1 L{rgb} + w2 L{pt\rgb} + w3 L{bg} + w4 L{TV} RGB Loss (L{rgb}): Mean squared error between rendered and ground truth colors. L{rgb} = \frac{1}{R} \sum{r \in R} |\hat{C}(r) - C(r)|^2 where R is the set of training rays. Point-wise RGB Loss (L{pt\rgb}): Encourages consistency at sampled points. L{pt\rgb} = \frac{1}{R} \sum{r \in R} \sum{i=1}^{K} (Ti ai \hat{C}(r) - C(r))^2 where K is the number of queried points in the texture volume, Ti is accumulated transmittance, and ai is the probability of termination at point i. Background Loss (L{bg}): Encourages foreground/background separation by penalizing intermediate transmittance values. L{bg} = -T{K+1} \log(T{K+1}) - (1 - T{K+1}) \log(1 - T{K+1}) where T{K+1} is the transmittance after the last sample. Total Variation Loss (L{TV}): Applied directly to the voxel grids of the density and texture volumes to prevent over-fitting and maintain geometry. It is not applied to the LUTs. Parameters: Voxel Resolution: 160 \times 160 \times 160. Feature Dimension: 12. MLP Layers: 5 for density/texture fields, 10 for weight prediction. CPE Frequency Order (L): 5. Basic LUTs (M): 5. LUT Resolution: 33 \times 33 \times 33. Recurrent Iterations (Z): 3. Learning Rates: Voxel grids (density/texture): 0.1. Density/Texture MLPs: 1 \times 10^{-3}. LUTs refinement MLPs and voxels: 1 \times 10^{-4}. Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 8,196 rays (first stage), 4,196 rays (second stage). Loss Weights: w1=1.0, w2=0.01, w3=0.001, w4=0.1. TV Loss Decay: Exponential decay factor of 0.005 applied to w4 during training to alleviate over-smoothing. Training Iterations: 250k for datasets [23] and 100k for datasets [21]. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Over-smoothing: Total variation loss causes blurring and loss of high-frequency details. This is mitigated by the CPE module and the LUT refinement module. Initialization Collapse: Applying CPE to density features breaks the zero-initialization rule required for stable volume rendering at the start of training. CPE must only be applied to texture features. Spatial Awareness: Using low-resolution images to predict LUT weights loses 3D spatial awareness. Using pseudo-surface depth via an MLP preserves this awareness. MAV3D synthesizes time-varying 3D scenes directly from text prompts by optimizing a 4D neural radiance field (4D-NeRF) under the guidance of a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model. It is distinguished from its parent V4D by its data-free supervision strategy, which relies solely on text and video priors rather than multi-view video inputs, and from its sibling Explicit Neural View Synthesis (Voxel-based Neural Rendering) by its use of a hexplane-based hybrid representation for efficient spacetime encoding. Explicit Neural View Synthesis (ENR) is a novel view synthesis method that explicitly encodes sparse source observations into a volumetric representation (RGB\alpha volume) to enable amortized rendering, avoiding per-pixel ray sampling and scene-specific optimization. Unlike continuous neural radiance fields such as NeRF [26], which require independent ray integrals for each pixel and prevent amortization across views, ENR pre-computes a shared RGB\alpha volume that can be rendered for any target view via geometric transformations. This approach offers rendering speeds over 400x faster than continuous baselines while maintaining comparable or superior reconstruction quality. Time and Memory Complexity: Training requires 250k iterations for datasets [23] and 100k for datasets [21]. Memory usage consists of two 160^3 \times 12 voxel grids and five 33^3 LUTs. Measured Performance: V4D achieves state-of-the-art performance on synthetic dynamic scenes (e.g., PSNR 33.72, SSIM 0.98 on datasets [23]) and competitive performance on real dynamic scenes. It outperforms D-NeRF, NDVG, and TiNeuVox in PSNR/SSIM. Scaling: The method scales to 4K resolution in related real-time variants but standard V4D focuses on single-view dynamic scene synthesis. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths include no canonical space requirement, plug-and-play LUT refinement, and high-quality dynamic novel view synthesis from single-view video. Limitations include longer training time compared to canonical-space methods and potential for over-smoothing if TV loss is not balanced with CPE/LUT refinement. When to Use: Use V4D when synthesizing novel views of dynamic scenes from single-view video without requiring a canonical space or multi-view constraints. Avoid it when faster training convergence is prioritized over inference speed or when multi-view inputs are available. V4D was proposed to address the limited representation capacity of MLPs under single-view constraints, specifically the lack of multi-view constraints. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and extends 3D voxel-based representations to 4D by modeling density and texture fields separately. The method was evaluated on 8 synthetic dynamic scene datasets and 4 real scene datasets, demonstrating superiority over existing single-view dynamic novel view synthesis methods. V4D: Voxel for 4D Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2023.3312127, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MAV3D
body: MAV3D synthesizes time-varying 3D scenes directly from text by optimizing a 4D neural radiance field under guidance from a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model. It differs from its parent V4D by employing a data-free supervision strategy that uses only text and video priors to create dynamic 3D content without any 4D datasets. It differs from its sibling Explicit Neural View Synthesis by introducing a hexplane-based 4D representation for efficient spacetime encoding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt describing the desired dynamic scene. Output: A 4D neural radiance field parameterized by a hexplane representation. Data Structures: MAV3D uses a hexplane-based 4D representation that decomposes the spacetime volume into a set of 2D planes for efficient encoding. The exact tensor dimensions, layout, and aggregation operations are not given in the sources. Standard implementations typically use bilinear sampling across the planes and concatenate or sum the resulting feature vectors. This decomposition avoids the memory explosion of a full 4D voxel grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the six hexplane plane tensors and the MLP that maps aggregated plane features to density and color. 2. Multi-stage static-to-dynamic training: Optimize the representation in stages, applying temporal regularization to enforce coherence across adjacent time steps. 3. Data-free supervision: Render views from the current 4D-NeRF estimate and compute a loss against outputs from a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model guided by the input text prompt. 4. Parameter update: Backpropagate the combined loss and update all learnable parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmav3d(textprompt, numsteps, learningrate, staticsteps, lambdatemp, H, W, T, C): # Initialize hexplane planes and MLP Pxy = torch.zeros(H, W, C) Pyz = torch.zeros(H, W, C) Pxz = torch.zeros(H, W, C) Pxt = torch.zeros(H, T, C) Pyt = torch.zeros(H, T, C) Pzt = torch.zeros(H, T, C) mlp = MLP() diffusionmodel = loadpretrainedtexttovideodiffusion() optimizerstatic = torch.optim.Adam([Pxy, Pyz, Pxz, mlp], lr=learningrate) optimizerdynamic = torch.optim.Adam([Pxy, Pyz, Pxz, Pxt, Pyt, Pzt, mlp], lr=learningrate) for step in range(numsteps): # Sample time and camera t = torch.rand(1) camera = samplerandomcamera() rayo, rayd = samplerayoriginanddirection(camera) # Query hexplane: bilinearly sample 6 planes and aggregate features = torch.zeros(C) features += bilinearsample(Pxy, rayo[:2], rayd[:2]) features += bilinearsample(Pyz, rayo[1:3], rayd[1:3]) features += bilinearsample(Pxz, rayo[[0,2]], rayd[[0,2]]) features += bilinearsample(Pxt, rayo[0], t) features += bilinearsample(Pyt, rayo[1], t) features += bilinearsample(Pzt, rayo[2], t) density, color = mlpforward(mlp, features) # Volume render the ray renderedcolor = volumerenderray(rayo, rayd, density, color) # Diffusion guidance: compute gradient from text-to-video model diffusiongrad = computediffusionguidance(renderedcolor, textprompt, diffusionmodel) # Temporal regularization: penalize feature changes across adjacent times temporalloss = computetemporalsmoothness(Pxt, Pyt, Pzt) # Combine losses and update loss = computeloss(renderedcolor, diffusiongrad) + lambdatemp temporalloss if step < staticsteps: optimizerstatic.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizerstatic.step() else: optimizerdynamic.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizerdynamic.step() return Pxy, Pyz, Pxz, Pxt, Pyt, Pzt, mlp def bilinearsample(plane, u, v): # Standard bilinear interpolation u0, v0 = torch.floor(u).long(), torch.floor(v).long() u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 wu, wv = u - u0, v - v0 return (1-wu)(1-wv)plane[u0, v0] + wu(1-wv)plane[u1, v0] + (1-wu)wvplane[u0, v1] + wuwvplane[u1, v1] def volumerenderray(rayo, rayd, density, color): # Standard volumetric rendering tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, 64) zvals = rayo + tvals rayd rawdensity = density(zvals) rawcolor = color(zvals) alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-rawdensity 0.01) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1 - alpha, dim=0) weights = alpha transmittance return torch.sum(weights rawcolor, dim=0) Parameters: Temporal Regularization Weight (\lambda{temp}): Not given in the sources. HexPlane Resolution (H, W, T): Not given in the sources. Static Training Steps (static\steps): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Temporal Incoherence: Without sufficient regularization, the dynamic planes may produce flickering or jittering artifacts. Prompt Alignment: The output quality depends on the alignment between the text prompt and the diffusion model's generation priors. A video-to-4D generation method that introduces HexPlane as the dynamic representation. It constructs point clouds using generated multi-view images as 3D deformation pseudo ground truth. Proposes a temporally consistent multi-view diffusion model to generate multi-view videos for 4D reconstruction from monocular video or 4D generation. Time and Memory Complexity: The hexplane representation provides compression relative to a full 4D voxel-based representation and a significant speedup relative to fully implicit NeRF baselines. Training is iterative and scales with optimization steps and diffusion model query costs. Strengths: Data-free supervision requires no 4D datasets; efficient spacetime encoding; generates dynamic 3D content from text. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pretrained text-to-video diffusion model; temporal artifacts possible without sufficient regularization. When to use: Text-to-4D generation is required and no 4D video data is available. When not to use: High-fidelity 4D data is already available. MAV3D was introduced in January 2023. It addresses the challenge of synthesizing time-varying 3D scenes from text without requiring large-scale 4D datasets by optimizing a 4D neural radiance field with a hexplane representation. name: Explicit Neural View Synthesis (Voxel-based Neural Rendering)
head: Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis, explicit voxel-like scene representation, our model
body: Explicit Neural View Synthesis (ENR) is a novel view synthesis method that explicitly encodes sparse source observations into a volumetric representation (RGBα volume) to enable amortized rendering, avoiding per-pixel ray sampling and scene-specific optimization. Unlike continuous neural radiance fields such as NeRF [26], which require independent ray integrals for each pixel and prevent amortization across views, ENR pre-computes a shared RGBα volume that can be rendered for any target view via geometric transformations. This approach offers rendering speeds over 400x faster than continuous baselines while maintaining comparable or superior reconstruction quality. The method consists of four main stages: 2D feature encoding, inverse projection (back-projection), 3D feature decoding, and amortized rendering. Input: Source image(s) Is \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times h \times w} and camera intrinsic parameters K (assumed constant). For multi-view, multiple source images are aggregated into a single latent volume. Output: Target image \hat{I}t \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times h \times w} rendered from a target camera pose Pt. 1. 2D Feature Map (Fs): Layout: \mathbb{R}^{32 \times h \times w}. Spatial resolution matches the input image. Channels: 32. 2. Latent Volumetric Tensor (Zs): Layout: \mathbb{R}^{c \times ds \times hs \times ws}. ds, hs, ws are depth, height, and width of the volumetric representation. Spatial height and width are halved with respect to the input feature map (hs = h/2, ws = w/2). Depth ds corresponds to the depth of the voxel grid. 3. RGBα Volume (Vs): Layout: \mathbb{R}^{4 \times ds \times h \times w}. Channels: 4 (R, G, B, α). Spatial resolution matches the input image (h, w). Produced by a final 3D convolution and sigmoid activation. 1. 2D Feature Encoding: Process the source image Is through a 2D U-Net encoder with a ResNet-18 backbone. Downsampling: Intermediate feature channels are 64, 128, 256, 512 at each spatial resolution level. Upsampling: Perform deconvolution and fuse resulting features with skip encoder features at the same level through concatenation followed by two consecutive convolution blocks. Output: A 32-channel feature map Fs \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times h \times w} preserving the spatial resolution of Is. 2. Inverse Projection (Back-projection): Back-project Fs into a latent volumetric tensor Zs \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times ds \times hs \times ws}. Tiling: Tile the 2D features into a 3D cube to prepare for sampling. Homography: Leverage camera intrinsic parameters K to compute the homography matrix mapping the cube to the viewing frustum. Grid Mapping: Obtain the grid mapping function by multiplying the homography matrix with individual points from a fixed voxel mesh grid set. Sampling: Apply the gridsample function to perform the inverse projection. This step is critical to preserve 3D geometry and texture information, which is lost if 2D feature maps are reshaped directly into 3D volumes. 3. 3D Feature Decoding: Process the latent volume Zs with a 3D U-Net model to predict the final RGBα volume Vs. Architecture: 3D U-Net with ResNet-3D blocks. Channel Scaling: When spatial resolution is downscaled by 2 times, double the channel numbers. Output Feature Map: 16 channels with the same spatial resolution as the input image. Final Layer: Apply one 3D convolution to transform the tensor map into 4 channels. Activation: Apply sigmoid activation to produce the RGBα volume Vs \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times ds \times h \times w}. 4. Amortized Rendering: Render the transformed RGBα volume Vt into the target image \hat{I}t. Pose Transformation: Compute the relative rigid transformation P{st} = Pt Ps^{-1} between source pose Ps and target pose Pt. Apply this transformation to Vs to obtain Vt = T(P{st}, Vs), aligning the volume with the target view. This combines rotation (transferring volume from source to target view) and perspective deformation (mapping viewing frustum to output cube) via left matrix multiplication. Perspective Deformation: Apply inverse warping and trilinear sampling to the transformed volume. Similar to inverse projection, use mesh grid multiplication and gridsample to obtain the voxel volume aligned with the target camera. Alpha Blending: Calculate the expected color \hat{C}{i,j} for each pixel (i,j) using accumulated transmittance: \hat{C}{i,j} = \sum{k=1}^{ds} T{i,j}^k \alpha{i,j}^k \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k where: \mathbf{c}{i,j}^k is the color value (first 3 channels) of the voxel at depth k. \alpha{i,j}^k is the alpha value (4th channel) of the voxel at depth k. T{i,j}^k is the accumulated transmittance, calculated using the cumprod method: T{i,j}^k = \prod{m=1}^{k-1} (1-\alpha{i,j}^m) The product is over the depth dimension k=1 \dots ds. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ExplicitNeuralViewSynthesis(nn.Module): def init(self, intrinsicparams, voxeldepth=16, voxelheight=64, voxelwidth=64): super().init() self.K = intrinsicparams self.ds = voxeldepth self.hs = voxelheight self.ws = voxelwidth self.encoder2d = UNet2D(channelsin=3, channelsout=32) self.decoder3d = UNet3D(channelsin=32, channelsout=4) # Fixed voxel mesh grid for inverse projection and rendering # Shape: (1, ds, hs, ws, 3) normalized to [-1, 1] self.voxelgrid = self.createvoxelgrid() def createvoxelgrid(self): z = torch.linspace(-1, 1, self.ds) y = torch.linspace(-1, 1, self.hs) x = torch.linspace(-1, 1, self.ws) z, y, x = torch.meshgrid(z, y, x, indexing='ij') return torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0) def inverseprojection(self, Fs): B, C, h, w = Fs.shape hs, ws = self.hs, self.ws # Tile 2D features into a 3D cube (B, C, ds, h, w) Ftiled = Fs.unsqueeze(2).repeat(1, 1, self.ds, 1, 1) # Implementation detail: Compute homography matrix from K and map voxel centers to image pixels. # Returns grid of shape (B, ds, hs, ws, 3) in normalized [-1, 1] coordinates. samplinggrid = self.getinverseprojectiongrid(Fs) # Perform inverse projection using gridsample on 4D tensor Zs = F.gridsample(Ftiled, samplinggrid, aligncorners=True) return Zs def getinverseprojectiongrid(self, Fs): # Not given in the sources. Computes homography and maps voxel centers to image pixels. pass def forward(self, Is, Pt, Ps): Fs = self.encoder2d(Is) Zs = self.inverseprojection(Fs) Vs = self.decoder3d(Zs) return self.render(Vs, Pt, Ps) def render(self, Vs, Pt, Ps): B, C, ds, h, w = Vs.shape Pst = Pt @ torch.linalg.inv(Ps) # Apply rigid transformation to volume # Not given in the sources. Uses gridsample with a grid generated from Pst to rotate/translate the voxel grid. Vt = self.transformvolume(Vs, Pst) Ct = Vt[:,:3,:,:,:] Alphat = Vt[:, 3:4,:,:,:] oneminusalpha = 1.0 - Alphat cumprod = torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha, dim=2) ones = torch.oneslike(cumprod[:,:, 0:1,:,:]) T = torch.cat([ones, cumprod[:,:,:-1,:,:]], dim=2) weightedcolor = T Alphat Ct return torch.sum(weightedcolor, dim=2) def transformvolume(self, Vs, Pst): # Not given in the sources. Uses gridsample with a grid generated from Pst to rotate/translate the voxel grid. pass class UNet2D(nn.Module): def init(self, channelsin, channelsout): super().init() # Not given in the sources. 2D U-Net with ResNet-18 backbone. pass class UNet3D(nn.Module): def init(self, channelsin, channelsout): super().init() # Not given in the sources. 3D U-Net with ResNet-3D blocks. pass Learning Rate: 0.0016 (fixed throughout training). SSIM Loss Weight: 0.05. Training Epochs: 150. Nonlinearity: ReLU used throughout the model for each nonlinear transformation. Normalization: GroupNorm [54] used throughout the model for each nonlinear transformation. Data Normalization: ImageNet statistics applied only at the preprocessing stage. Intrinsic Camera Parameters: Used for inverse projection and perspective deformation; assumed constant. Geometry Preservation: Reshaping 2D feature maps directly into 3D volumes loses 3D geometry and texture information. The inverse projection step is essential to preserve this. Resolution Limits: The resolution of rendered images is capped by the explicit voxel-like scene representation. Continuous representations are resolution-free but slower. Future work plans to use octrees, mixture of volumetric primitives, or scene graphs to increase capacity for complex regions while minimizing resources for empty regions, and to enhance with super-resolution methods. View-Dependent Lighting: The current model cannot produce view-dependent lighting effects. It assumes a Lambertian RGBA model. Future work plans to incorporate physically based rendering with view direction, light sources, material properties (roughness, metalness), and surface information (normals, displacement maps), potentially using spherical harmonics or learned MLPs for specular effects. Rendering Speed: Over 400x faster than continuous baselines like NeRF. Complexity: Rendering is amortized across views because the RGBα volume is shared. The cost is dominated by the initial encoding and decoding, which are fixed per scene. Memory: Memory usage is determined by the size of the 3D voxel grid (ds \times h \times w). The source does not specify exact memory consumption in MB, but notes that resolution is capped by the explicit representation. Performance: On unseen-category view synthesis (Table 8 in), the two-view model achieves mean PSNR 24.80, SSIM 0.893, LPIPS 0.107, outperforming the ENR baseline (PSNR 23.16, SSIM 0.807, LPIPS 0.190). The single-view model achieves the same mean metrics (PSNR 24.80, SSIM 0.893, LPIPS 0.107). Strengths: Fast rendering, no per-pixel ray sampling, no scene-specific optimization, category-agnostic training. Limitations: Resolution capped by voxel grid, no view-dependent lighting effects. Explicit Neural View Synthesis was proposed by Pengsheng Guo et al. from Apple. It challenges the trend of continuous and implicit radiance field representations by proposing a simple, explicit volumetric approach that achieves comparable or better quality with significantly faster rendering speeds. Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv51458.2022.00009, fetched 2026-10-30

name: RenderNet
body: RenderNet is a differentiable rendering convolutional neural network that generates 2D images from 3D voxel grids by jointly learning visibility computation and pixel color calculation (shading). Unlike traditional rasterization or ray tracing which rely on discrete, non-differentiable operations like z-buffering, RenderNet uses a CNN to implicitly handle occlusion and complex shading, enabling inverse rendering tasks such as shape, pose, and texture estimation from single images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by learning the projection and shading via a dedicated "Projection Unit" rather than using surrogate gradients for discrete operations or approximate rasterization, allowing it to robustly handle low-resolution or noisy voxel inputs that would fail in mesh-based differentiable renderers. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D voxel grid V with dimensions HV \times WV \times DV \times CV (height, width, depth, channel). Typical input resolution is 64 \times 64 \times 64 \times 1. Parameters: Camera pose (azimuth \theta, elevation \eta, distance R), light position \tilde{l}, and optionally texture coefficients \phi. Output: A 2D RGB image I with dimensions HI \times WI \times CI (height, width, channel). Typical output resolution is 512 \times 512 \times 3. Data Structures The core data structure is the voxel grid tensor. The network processes this through a "Projection Unit" which reshapes the 4D tensor into a 3D squeezed tensor V' with dimensions W \times H \times (D \cdot C). Steps 1. Coordinate Transformation: Apply a rigid-body transformation to the input voxel grid V to convert from world coordinates to camera coordinates. The camera is assumed axis-aligned, looking along the negative z-axis. The transformation is parameterized by rotation around the y-axis (azimuth), rotation around the z-axis (elevation), and a distance R (scaling factor). 2. Resampling: Trilinearly sample the transformed input voxel grid to handle the coordinate change and ensure the object is not cut off (the input is embedded in a larger grid to accommodate rotation). 3. Geometry Encoding: Pass the sampled input through a sequence of 3D convolutions and PReLU activations to encode geometry. The specific sequence is: Conv3d, PReLU, Conv3d, PReLU, PReLU, Down-conv3d. 4. Projection and Visibility (Projection Unit): Reshaping: Collapse the depth dimension with the feature maps to map the incoming 4D tensor to a 3D squeezed tensor V' with dimension W \times H \times (D \cdot C). MLP/1x1 Convolution: Apply a Multilayer Perceptron (implemented as a 1x1 convolution) on each (D \cdot C) vector of the squeezed tensor to produce a 3D tensor with K channels. This allows the network to learn visibility along the depth axis, unlike max pooling which only creates a silhouette. The operation is defined as: I'{i,j,k} = \sum{dc} w{k,dc} \cdot V'{i,j,dc} + bk where i, j are pixel coordinates, k is the image channel, dc is the squeezed depth channel (combining original depth d and channel c), and w, b are the weights and biases of the 1x1 convolution. The Projection Unit outputs intermediate representations including a Normal Map and a Final Output (depth/visibility). 5. Shading and Rendering: Apply 2D convolutions and PReLU activations to the projected features to generate the final RGB image. The sequence is: Conv2d, PReLU, Conv2d, PReLU, Up-conv2d, PReLU, PReLU, Up-conv2d. Phong Illumination Extension: If rendering Phong shading, the network outputs a Normal Map and an Albedo Map. The shaded color S is calculated as S = \max(0, \tilde{l} \cdot \tilde{n} + a), where \tilde{l} is the light direction, \tilde{n} is the normal vector (from the Normal Map RGB channels), and a is an ambient constant. The final image is I = A \cdot S, where A is the Albedo Map. Texture Mapping: For texture, a separate network maps 1D texture vectors (e.g., PCA coefficients) to a 3D texture representation, which is concatenated with the input shape before rendering. An additional output branch renders the Normal Map. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rendernet(voxelgrid, cameraparams, lightparams=None): """ Renders a 2D image from a 3D voxel grid using RenderNet. Args: voxelgrid: Tensor of shape (Hv, Wv, Dv, Cv) cameraparams: Dict containing 'azimuth', 'elevation', 'distance' lightparams: Dict containing 'lightdirection' (optional) Returns: image: Tensor of shape (Hi, Wi, 3) """ # 1. Coordinate Transformation # Rigid-body transform: rotation around Y (azimuth), Z (elevation), scale by distance R # Camera is axis-aligned, looking along negative z-axis. transformedgrid = applyrigidtransform(voxelgrid, cameraparams) # 2. Resampling # Trilinearly sample the transformed grid. sampledgrid = trilinearinterpolation(transformedgrid) # 3. Geometry Encoding # Sequence: Conv3d, PReLU, Conv3d, PReLU, PReLU, Down-conv3d encodedfeatures = conv3dblock(sampledgrid) # 4. Projection Unit # Reshape: Collapse depth and channels -> (H, W, DC) squeezedtensor = reshapedepthchannels(encodedfeatures) # MLP / 1x1 Convolution: I'{i,j,k} = sum{dc} w{k,dc} V'{i,j,dc} + bk projectedfeatures = apply1x1conv(squeezedtensor) # Output intermediate maps: Normal Map, Final Output normalmap, finaloutput = extractintermediates(projectedfeatures) # 5. Shading and Rendering # Sequence: Conv2d, PReLU, Conv2d, PReLU, Up-conv2d, PReLU, PReLU, Up-conv2d if lightparams is not None: lightdir = lightparams['lightdirection'] shading = phongshading(normalmap, lightdir) albedomap = renderalbedo(finaloutput) image = albedomap shading else: image = renderrgb(finaloutput) return image def applyrigidtransform(grid, params): # Standard affine transformation: rotation matrices for azimuth/elevation, scaling by distance R # Generates voxel coordinates, applies transform, returns transformed grid. pass def trilinearinterpolation(grid): # Standard trilinear interpolation on transformed coordinates. pass def conv3dblock(tensor): # Standard 3D convolution sequence: Conv3d, PReLU, Conv3d, PReLU, PReLU, Down-conv3d pass def reshapedepthchannels(tensor): # Collapse depth and channel dimensions. H, W, D, C = tensor.shape return tensor.reshape(H, W, D C) def apply1x1conv(tensor): # Standard 1x1 convolution (MLP per spatial location) pass def extractintermediates(tensor): # Standard split into Normal Map and Final Output branches pass def phongshading(normalmap, lightdir): # S = max(0, l~. n~ + a) normals = normalmap / (np.linalg.norm(normalmap, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) light = lightdir / np.linalg.norm(lightdir) dotproduct = np.sum(normals light, axis=-1) return np.maximum(dotproduct + 0.1, 0) def renderalbedo(tensor): # Standard 2D convolution branch for albedo map pass def renderrgb(tensor): # Standard 2D convolution branch for RGB output pass Parameters Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 0.00001. Loss Function: Mean Squared Error (MSE) for colored images; Binary Cross Entropy for grayscale images. Training Strategy: Patch training. Random spatially cropped samples (width/height) are used, keeping depth/channel intact. Patch size starts at 1/8 of the full grid and increases to 1/2 at the end of training. Full-sized grid is used only during inference. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noisy/Low-Resolution Input: RenderNet handles erroneous or low-resolution voxel inputs robustly, unlike mesh renderers which require clean, high-quality meshes. Inverse Rendering Instability: Directly minimizing reconstruction loss for shape/pose/texture estimation leads to noisy, unstable results. This is mitigated by using a shape prior (a pre-trained 3D auto-encoder) to regularize the optimization. Instead of optimizing the shape z directly, the latent representation z' of the auto-encoder is optimized: \min{z', \theta, \phi', \eta} \| I - f(g(z'), \theta, h(\phi'), \eta) \|^2, where g is the decoder. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the Phong-shaded chair dataset, RenderNet achieved a PSNR of 25.39, compared to 22.37 for EC and 27.43 for EC-Deep. For Contour shading, RenderNet scored 24.21. Other shader PSNR scores for RenderNet include: 20.88 (Cartoon), 19.70 (AO), and 17.77 (Face). Strengths: Handles occlusion and complex shaders (ambient occlusion, cartoon shading) without explicit geometric visibility tests. Generalizes well to unseen categories and corrupted/low-resolution inputs. Differentiable end-to-end, enabling inverse rendering (shape, pose, texture, lighting estimation). Limitations: Requires voxel grid input, which can be memory inefficient for high-resolution scenes compared to sparse representations (though the paper notes recent work addresses this with octrees). When to use: When differentiable rendering from voxel data is required, especially for inverse rendering tasks involving complex shading or noisy inputs. When not to use: When high-resolution mesh-based rendering is preferred, or when explicit geometric visibility control is required rather than learned visibility. RenderNet was introduced by Thu Nguyen-Phuoc, Chuan Li, Stephen Balaban, and Yong-Liang Yang from the University of Bath and Lambda Labs. The paper "RenderNet: A deep convolutional network for differentiable rendering from 3D shapes" was published on arXiv in April 2019. It addresses the challenge of non-differentiable operations in traditional rendering pipelines (rasterization and ray tracing) which hinder inverse graphics tasks. By framing rendering as a feed-forward CNN, it allows the network to learn visibility and shading jointly. It is used for novel-view synthesis, pose prediction, and image-based 3D shape reconstruction.
