name: Neural Volume Super-Resolution
head: NVSR
body: Neural Volume Super-Resolution (NVSR) is a method that super-resolves volumetric neural scene representations to generate geometrically consistent, high-resolution novel views from low-resolution captures, operating directly on the 3D representation rather than post-rendered 2D images. It sets itself apart from post-rendering 2D SR methods by guaranteeing consistency across viewing directions and preventing inconsistent distortions, and from spatial Video SR methods by enabling novel views from arbitrary directions rather than being limited to the original camera trajectory. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of low-resolution (LR) captures I{lr} of a scene s along with their relative camera poses. Output: High-resolution (HR) novel views of the scene. Data Structures: The 3D scene representation uses four 2D feature planes: 1. Three planes encode spatial scene features. 2. A fourth plane is added to enable view-direction dependency for the RGB values. The representation model G comprises a decoder model D and learned feature planes Ps corresponding to each scene s. Parameters: \theta^Gs: Learned parameters for scene s (decoder weights and feature planes). \theta^F: Parameters of the learned super-resolution module F, learned independently of any specific scene. F: Learned super-resolution module that operates in feature space on the 2D planes. Steps: 1. Learn Coarse Representation: Train the scene representation model G using the low-resolution images I{lr} and their poses. 2. Render Low-Resolution Views: Render novel low-resolution views for new camera poses using the learned model: \hat{i}{lr}(\mathbf{r}) = G(\theta^Gs, \mathbf{r}) where \hat{i}{lr}(\mathbf{r}) is the rendered low-resolution pixel value, G is the scene representation model, \theta^Gs are its learned parameters for scene s, and \mathbf{r} denotes a pixel and its corresponding ray. 3. Super-Resolve Volumetric Representation: Apply the learned 2D super-resolution module F directly on the 2D feature planes in feature space before projecting 3D points onto them. The super-resolved parameters are F(\theta^F, \theta^Gs). 4. Render High-Resolution Views: Reconstruct each image pixel by marching along the camera ray, accumulating the density and view-direction dependent RGB values predicted by the model for each point along the ray, using the super-resolved features: \hat{i}{sr}(\mathbf{r}) = G(F(\theta^F, \theta^Gs), \mathbf{r}) where \hat{i}{sr} is the rendered super-resolved image. 5. Training: Train the NVSR framework end-to-end using low-resolution and matching high-resolution image pairs from synthetic scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def samplepointsalongray(origin, direction, near, far, numsamples): """Returns N 3D points along the ray from near to far.""" t = [near + i (far - near) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] return [[origin[d] + t[i]direction[d] for d in range(3)] for i in range(numsamples)] def projectontofeatureplanes(points, featureplanes, viewdirection): """Projects 3D points onto 3 spatial planes and concatenates view direction.""" features = [] for point in points: pfeat = [featureplanes[0][point[0]][point[1]], featureplanes[1][point[0]][point[2]], featureplanes[2][point[1]][point[2]]] pfeat.extend(viewdirection) features.append(pfeat) return features def decodefeatures(features, decoderweights): """Maps features to density (sigma) and RGB color via a small MLP.""" sigma = [] color = [] for f in features: h = [max(0.0, sum(f[j]decoderweights['W1'][j][k] for j in range(len(f))) + decoderweights['b1'][k]) for k in range(decoderweights['W1'][0].len())] s = math.log(1.0 + math.exp(sum(h[j]decoderweights['W2'][j] for j in range(len(h))) + decoderweights['b2'])) c = [1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-(sum(h[j]decoderweights['W3'][j][k] for j in range(len(h))) + decoderweights['b3'][k]))) for k in range(3)] sigma.append(s) color.append(c) return sigma, color def renderray(origin, direction, near, far, numsamples, featureplanes, decoderweights): """Standard volume rendering equation: C(r) = sum Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai delta)) ci""" points = samplepointsalongray(origin, direction, near, far, numsamples) features = projectontofeatureplanes(points, featureplanes, direction) sigma, color = decodefeatures(features, decoderweights) delta = (far - near) / (numsamples - 1) transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[i] delta) transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[k] + transmittance alpha color[i][k] for k in range(3)] return accumulatedcolor def trainnvsr(lrimages, hrimages, poses, srmodule, lrfeatureplanes, lrdecoder): """End-to-end training loop.""" thetaF = initsrmodule() for epoch in range(100): for lrimg, hrimg, pose in zip(lrimages, hrimages, poses): srfeatureplanes = srmodule(lrfeatureplanes, thetaF) srrendered = renderray(pose.origin, pose.direction, pose.near, pose.far, 128, srfeatureplanes, lrdecoder) loss = sum((srrendered[k] - hrimg[k])2 for k in range(3)) / 3.0 thetaF = [p - 0.001 grad for p, grad in zip(thetaF, computegradient(loss, thetaF))] lrfeatureplanes = [p - 0.001 grad for p, grad in zip(lrfeatureplanes, computegradient(loss, lrfeatureplanes))] return srfeatureplanes, lrdecoder Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the availability of matching high-resolution image pairs for training on synthetic scenes. Unlike post-rendering SR, NVSR requires the super-resolution module to be integrated into the volumetric representation pipeline, which may increase training complexity. A zero-shot super-resolution method that does not rely on external SR priors or HR reference images, learning a scene-specific degradation model on a coarse NeRF first. It trains a fine super-resolution NeRF via inverse rendering that backpropagates gradients through this degradation, together with a temporal ensemble at inference, which makes the whole pipeline fully zero-shot and single-scene internal. It accelerates training through an explicit coarse-to-fine schedule. Performance: Exceeds state-of-the-art image SR methods by over 1 dB in PSNR when trained on the same dataset. Consistency: Guarantees geometric consistency across all viewing directions, preventing inconsistent distortions such as slanted structures that appear in post-rendering 2D SR methods. Novel View Synthesis: Can render novel views from arbitrary directions, unlike spatial Video SR methods limited to positions along the original camera trajectory. Validation: Validated on diverse unseen 3D scenes from synthetic datasets. Limitations: Requires low-resolution and matching high-resolution image pairs for training, which may not be available for all real-world scenes. NVSR was proposed to address the task of rendering high-resolution views corresponding to a scene captured at low resolution. It builds on the principles of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). The method was validated on synthetic datasets, demonstrating the ability to exploit the volumetric domain for consistent super-resolution. name: Volumetric Supervision for NeRF
head: Hybrid NeRF reconstruction, NeRF with volumetric loss
body: Volumetric Supervision for NeRF is a hybrid reconstruction method designed to improve the fidelity of the canonical volume in dynamic tomography by combining projection-based training with volumetric supervision from high-fidelity static X-CT data at key time steps (t=0 and t=1). It addresses the observation that standard neural rendering methods often fail to achieve high normalized correlation coefficients for complex objects, whereas conventional data-rich X-CT can reconstruct such volumes with high fidelity. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF optimization by explicitly incorporating a ground-truth volumetric loss term derived from external high-resolution scans, rather than relying solely on 2D projection consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse 2D projections for intermediate time steps (e.g., 2 projections for t=0.1, \dots, 0.9). High-fidelity 3D X-CT volumes for key time steps (t=0 and t=1). A set of 2D projections for the canonical step (e.g., 256 projections for t=0). A deformation field parametrization (e.g., B-spline grid). Outputs: A high-fidelity canonical volume at t=0 (and optionally t=1). A trained deformation field mapping the canonical volume to dynamic states. Data Structures: Canonical Volume: Represented as a 3D density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) evaluated by a neural network or grid structure. Ground Truth X-CT: A 3D volume of density values \sigma{gt}(\mathbf{x}) obtained from high-fidelity static scans. Deformation Field: Parametrized by a B-spline grid with a cited resolution of 6 \times 6 \times 6. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the neural radiance field for the canonical volume and the deformation field (e.g., B-spline grid with resolution 6 \times 6 \times 6). 2. Initialize the volumetric supervision weight \lambda = 0. 3. For the first 200 iterations, render the canonical volume from the 256 projections at t=0, compute L{proj}, and optimize network parameters using L = L{proj}. 4. Set \lambda = 0.005. 5. For subsequent iterations, render the canonical volume from the 256 projections, compute L{proj}, compute L{vol} using the normalized correlation between the predicted canonical volume density and the high-fidelity X-CT ground truth at t=0, compute total loss L = L{proj} + 0.005 L{vol}, and optimize network parameters. 6. Using the reconstructed canonical volume, train the deformation field to map to intermediate time steps (t=0.1, \dots, 0.9) using the sparse 2 projections per step. Formulas: The total training loss L for the canonical volume reconstruction is defined as: L = L{proj} + \lambda L{vol} Where: L{proj} is the projection loss, computed by rendering the canonical volume from the available 2D projections and comparing against measured projection data. L{vol} is the volumetric loss, calculated as the negative normalized correlation C{cor} between the predicted density of the canonical volume and the ground truth X-CT volume. \lambda is a weighting coefficient for the volumetric supervision. C{cor} denotes the normalized correlation coefficient between the predicted density field and the ground truth X-CT volume. Parameters: \lambda: Volumetric supervision weight. Set to 0 for the first 200 iterations, then set to 0.005. B-spline Grid Resolution: 6 \times 6 \times 6. Projections at t=0: 256. Projections at intermediate steps: 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: The coefficient \lambda must be 0 initially to allow the projection-based loss to establish a basic geometry before introducing the volumetric constraint. Data Availability: This method requires high-fidelity static X-CT data at key time steps, which may not be available in all dynamic tomography scenarios. Accuracy: Volumetric supervision significantly improves reconstruction quality, improving both normalized correlation and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) on simulated lattice datasets compared to training purely with projections. Displacement Error: In simulated deformation experiments (Kelvin lattice), the displacement error E{disp} was 0.5 \times 10^{-5} when using both volumetric supervision and rich data at t=1, compared to 6.4 \times 10^{-5} with neither. Complexity: The method adds the computational cost of computing the normalized correlation between the predicted volume and the ground truth X-CT volume to the training loop. Strengths: Synergistically improves accuracy when combined with rich data at multiple time steps. Limitations: Requires high-fidelity X-CT data at key time steps, which increases data acquisition requirements. This method was proposed in the context of dynamic tomography, where neural rendering is used to reconstruct 4D volumes from sparse 2D projections. It leverages the observation that while neural rendering struggles with high normalized correlation for complex objects, conventional X-CT can achieve high fidelity when many projections are available. The method was tested on simulated lattice datasets and deformation experiments inspired by uniaxial tensile tests. name: NeRF-MAE
head: Masked AutoEncoders for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning for Neural Radiance Fields, Masked voxel-grid pretraining, NeRF Masked Auto Encoders, NeRF-MAE Masked Radiance and Density Grid Pretraining
body: NeRF-MAE is a self-supervised pretraining framework for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that learns 3D scene representations by masking and reconstructing patches from an explicit radiance and density grid. Unlike implicit NeRFs or point-cloud-based methods, it operates directly on the regular, high-density volumetric grid extracted from a trained NeRF, allowing the use of standard 3D Vision Transformers without adaptation. It disentangles representation learning from NeRF training, enabling the use of large-scale unlabeled data from diverse sources to improve downstream tasks such as 3D object detection and semantic labeling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Posed RGB images used to train an initial implicit NeRF, and the resulting explicit 4D radiance/density grid G. Output: A reconstructed 4D volume R \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times 4} containing predicted radiance (RGB) and opacity (\alpha). Data Structures: The core data structure is the explicit grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times 4}, where H, W, D are spatial dimensions and the 4 channels represent (r, g, b, \alpha). Patches: The grid is partitioned into cubic patches of size P = p \times p \times p with p=4. Tokens: Patches are converted into 3D tokens of size \frac{H}{p} \times \frac{W}{p} \times \frac{D}{p} \times E via a 3D convolutional embedding layer. Masking: A binary mask M indicates which patches are hidden. A masking ratio of m=0.75 is used. Parameters: Grid dimensions: H=W=D=160. Patch size: p=4. Masking ratio: m=0.75. Encoder Embedding dimension: E=96. Swin Transformer block depths: d=[2, 2, 18, 2]. Number of attention heads: [3, 6, 12, 24] for the four stages. Window size: W{win}=4. Preset distance for opacity calculation: \Delta x = 0.01. Steps: 1. Grid Extraction: Train an implicit NeRF f(x, \theta) (e.g., Instant-NGP) on posed images. Extract the explicit grid G by querying the NeRF for all training camera viewing directions \theta at each grid point (i, j, k) and averaging the output: (r{i, j, k}, g{i, j, k}, b{i, j, k}, \alpha{i, j, k}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{\theta=1}^{N} f(x{i, j, k}, \theta) where N is the number of training images. The opacity \alpha is derived from volume density \sigma and a preset distance \Delta x = 0.01: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \Delta x). 2. Masking: Randomly mask out patches of size p \times p \times p from G with ratio m=0.75 to create the masked grid M. 3. Patch Partitioning and Embedding: Divide M into patches using a 3D convolutional operation that merges partitioning and linear embedding into one step, creating tokens of size \frac{H}{p} \times \frac{W}{p} \times \frac{D}{p} \times E. 4. Positional Encoding: Add 3D positional embeddings to each token. No classification token is added. 5. Encoder (3D Swin Transformer): Process tokens through 4 stages. Each stage consists of Swin Transformer 3D blocks and patch merging layers (except the last stage). Block Structure: Each block contains local multi-head self-attention (W-MSA-3D) or shifted multi-head self-attention (SW-MSA-3D), a 2-layer MLP with GeLU activation, Linear Norm (LN) layers, and residual connections. Window Shifting: Windows are displaced by [\frac{W{win}}{2}, \frac{W{win}}{2}, \frac{W{win}}{2}] every layer. Patch Merging: Merges four volumetric patches, reducing spatial dimensions by 2 and increasing channel dimension by 2, followed by LN and MLP. Feature Pyramid: Concatenate outputs of all 4 stages to form feature pyramid F = [f0, f1, f2, f3]. The final encoder output has spatial size 5 \times 5 \times 5 and channel dimension 768. 6. Decoder: Reconstruct the grid using lightweight transposed 3D convolution decoders Di attached to the feature pyramid. Update Rule: di = \text{Conv}(d{i-1} + D(fi)) with d0 = f3, where D is a transposed 3D convolution with kernel size 3. Output Prediction: The final decoder output passes through a residual block with 3 \times 3 \times 3 convolutions and a sigmoid activation to predict R \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times 4}. 7. Loss Computation: Compute reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{recon} = \mathcal{L}{rad} + \mathcal{L}{\alpha}. Radiance Loss: \mathcal{L}{rad} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{i=1}^{N} (\hat{y}{radi} - y{radi})^2 where K is the number of voxels in the mask corresponding to patches where \alpha > \Delta x (\Delta x = 0.01). Opacity Loss: \mathcal{L}{\alpha} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} (\hat{y}{\alphaj} - y{\alphaj})^2 where M is the number of voxels in the mask corresponding to removed 3D patches. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class NeRFMAE: def init(self, H=160, W=160, D=160, p=4, m=0.75, E=96, windowsize=4): self.H, self.W, self.D = H, W, D self.p = p self.m = m self.E = E self.windowsize = windowsize self.numpatches = (H // p) (W // p) (D // p) # Patch embedding: 3D conv merging partitioning and linear embedding self.patchembed = nn.Conv3d(4, E, kernelsize=p, stride=p) # Encoder: 4 stages of Swin Transformer 3D blocks # Depths: [2, 2, 18, 2], Heads: [3, 6, 12, 24] self.encoderstages = nn.ModuleList() embeddims = [E, E2, E4, E8] # Patch merging doubles channels for i in range(4): stage = [] for in range([2, 2, 18, 2][i]): stage.append(SwinTransformer3DBlock(embeddims[i], windowsize, [3, 6, 12, 24][i])) self.encoderstages.append(nn.Sequential(stage)) if i < 3: # Patch merging after each block except last self.encoderstages.append(nn.Sequential( PatchMerging3D(embeddims[i], embeddims[i+1]), nn.LayerNorm(embeddims[i+1]), nn.Linear(embeddims[i+1], embeddims[i+1]))) # Decoder: 4 stages with transposed convs # d0 = f3. di = Conv(d{i-1} + D(fi)) self.decoderstages = nn.ModuleList() for i in range(3, -1, -1): self.decoderstages.append(nn.ConvTranspose3d(embeddims[i], embeddims[i], kernelsize=3, padding=1)) self.finalblock = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(embeddims[0], embeddims[0], kernelsize=3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv3d(embeddims[0], 4, kernelsize=3, padding=1), nn.Sigmoid()) def forward(self, G): # G: (B, 4, H, W, D) B = G.shape[0] # 1. Masking nummasked = int(self.numpatches self.m) maskindices = torch.randperm(self.numpatches)[:nummasked] patchmask = torch.zeros(self.numpatches) patchmask[maskindices] = 1.0 # Reshape to patches: (B, numpatches, ppp4) patches = G.unfold(2, self.p, self.p).unfold(3, self.p, self.p).unfold(4, self.p, self.p) patches = patches.permute(0, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3).reshape(B, -1, self.p2 4) # Zero out masked patches maskedpatches = patches (1 - patchmask.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1)) maskedgrid = maskedpatches.reshape(B, 4, self.H, self.W, self.D) # 2. Patch Embedding x = self.patchembed(maskedgrid) # (B, E, H/p, W/p, D/p) # 3. Positional Encoding posembed = self.get3dposembed(x.shape[2], x.shape[3], x.shape[4]) x = x + posembed # 4. Encoder -> Feature Pyramid F = [f0, f1, f2, f3] F = [] for stage in self.encoderstages: x = stage(x) F.append(x) # 5. Decoder # d0 = f3 d = F[3] # di = Conv(d{i-1} + D(fi)) for i=2,1,0 for i in range(2, -1, -1): fi = F[i] # D(fi) is transposed conv fiup = self.decoderstages3-i d = self.decoderstages3-i # Conv(d{i-1} + D(fi)) # 6. Output Prediction R = self.finalblock(d) return R, maskindices def computeloss(self, R, G, maskindices): # Reshape to patches Rpatches = R.unfold(2, self.p, self.p).unfold(3, self.p, self.p).unfold(4, self.p, self.p) Rpatches = Rpatches.permute(0, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3).reshape(R.shape[0], -1, self.p2 4) Gpatches = G.unfold(2, self.p, self.p).unfold(3, self.p, self.p).unfold(4, self.p, self.p) Gpatches = Gpatches.permute(0, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3).reshape(G.shape[0], -1, self.p2 4) Rmasked = Rpatches[:, maskindices,:] Gmasked = Gpatches[:, maskindices,:] # Split radiance (RGB) and opacity (Alpha) Rrad = Rmasked[:,:,:3] Grad = Gmasked[:,:,:3] Ralpha = Rmasked[:,:, 3:] Galpha = Gmasked[:,:, 3:] # Flatten to voxels Rradflat = Rrad.reshape(Rrad.shape[0], -1, 3) Gradflat = Grad.reshape(Grad.shape[0], -1, 3) Galphaflat = Galpha.reshape(Galpha.shape[0], -1, 1) # Lrad: K voxels where target alpha > 0.01 alphathresh = 0.01 validvoxels = (Galphaflat > alphathresh).squeeze(-1) # (B, nummaskedvoxels) Rradvalid = Rradflat[validvoxels] Gradvalid = Gradflat[validvoxels] K = Rradvalid.shape[0] Lrad = torch.mean((Rradvalid - Gradvalid)2) if K > 0 else torch.tensor(0.0) # Lalpha: M all masked voxels Lalpha = torch.mean((Ralpha.reshape(Ralpha.shape[0], -1) - Galpha.reshape(Galpha.shape[0], -1))2) return Lrad + Lalpha def get3dposembed(self, H, W, D): # Standard 3D sinusoidal positional embedding freqs = torch.arange(0, self.E // 4, dtype=torch.float32) freqs = (1.0 / (10000 (freqs / (self.E / 2)))) pos = torch.arange(H W D, dtype=torch.float32) out = torch.sin(torch.outer(pos, freqs)) out = torch.cat([out, torch.cos(torch.outer(pos, freqs))], dim=-1) return out.reshape(1, 1, H, W, D) class SwinTransformer3DBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, windowsize, numheads): super().init() self.attn = WindowAttention3D(dim, windowsize, numheads) self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.LayerNorm(dim), nn.Linear(dim, dim 4), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(dim 4, dim)) self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(dim) self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(dim) def forward(self, x): # x shape: (B, C, H, W, D) # Standard Swin requires shifting windows. Simplified for pseudocode. x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x)) return x class WindowAttention3D(nn.Module): def init(self, dim, windowsize, numheads): super().init() self.numheads = numheads self.scale = (dim // numheads) -0.5 self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, dim 3) self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim) self.windowsize = windowsize def forward(self, x): B, C, H, W, D = x.shape # Implementation details omitted for brevity, follows standard 3D window attention # Returns tensor of shape (B, C, H, W, D) return self.proj(self.qkv(x).view(B, -1, 3, C // 3, self.numheads, -1).permute(2, 0, 3, 4, 1, 5).mean(dim=0)) class PatchMerging3D(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels, outchannels): super().init() self.conv = nn.Conv3d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=2, stride=2) self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(outchannels) self.mlp = nn.Linear(outchannels, outchannels) def forward(self, x): # x shape: (B, C, H, W, D) x = self.conv(x) B, C, H, W, D = x.shape x = x.permute(0, 2, 3, 4, 1).reshape(B, -1, C) x = self.norm(x) x = self.mlp(x) return x.permute(0, 2, 1).reshape(B, -1, H, W, D) Time Complexity: The encoder uses shifted window attention, which reduces the quadratic complexity of global self-attention to linear with respect to the number of voxels, making it efficient for large volumes. Memory Complexity: The explicit grid storage requires O(H \times W \times D) memory. For 160^3, this is manageable. The attention mechanism's memory usage is proportional to the number of tokens and window size. Performance: NeRF-MAE significantly outperforms self-supervised 3D pretraining and NeRF scene understanding baselines on Front3D and ScanNet datasets, with an absolute performance improvement of over 20% AP50 and 8% AP25 for 3D object detection. Strengths: Utilizes standard 3D Transformers without adaptation; disentangles representation learning from NeRF training, allowing use of diverse data sources; handles dense volumetric information better than sparse point clouds. Limitations: Requires an initial trained NeRF to extract the grid; relies on posed images; the explicit grid extraction can be computationally expensive for very large scenes. NeRF-MAE was introduced by M.Z. Irshad et al. in 2024. It builds on the success of Masked Autoencoders (MAE) in 2D vision and extends it to 3D neural radiance fields. The method addresses the lack of large-scale self-supervised pretraining for NeRFs by leveraging the regular structure of the explicit radiance and density grid. It is used for downstream tasks such as 3D object detection, voxel-grid super-resolution, and semantic voxel labeling. NeRF-MAE: Masked AutoEncoders for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01300v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Distilled Feature Fields
head: Neural Perceptual Fields
body: Distilled Feature Fields (DFF) extend Neural Radiance Fields by adding a 3D neural feature field that maps every 3D coordinate to a semantic feature descriptor, enabling query-based local editing of NeRF scenes by semantically decomposing 3D space without re-training. Unlike methods that optimize NeRF parameters to match text prompts (which may affect unintended regions) or rely on costly instance segmentation annotations, DFF enables efficient, open-set decomposition and accurate selective editing of specific scene regions via decomposition. It builds on Neural Radiance Fields by distilling knowledge from off-the-shelf 2D image feature extractors (teachers) into the 3D field via volume rendering. Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses. A pre-trained 2D teacher network (e.g., LSeg for text/image queries or DINO for self-supervised features). User query: text string, image patch, or point-and-click selection. Outputs: A trained NeRF model (density \sigma and color c). A trained 3D Feature Field f(\mathbf{x}). Rendered images and decomposed/edited views based on user queries. Data Structures: NeRF MLP: Takes 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d}, outputs density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and color c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}). Feature Field MLP: Takes 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}, outputs a semantic feature vector f(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^D. Teacher Network: A frozen 2D encoder (LSeg or DINO) that takes an image I and returns feature maps f{img}(I, \mathbf{r}). Query Encoder: A frozen encoder (part of LSeg or DINO) that maps a text label l or image patch to a feature vector fq(l). Training Procedure: The method trains the NeRF and the Feature Field in parallel using a teacher-student distillation approach. 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, sample K points \mathbf{x}k along the camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} within bounds [t{near}, t{far}]. 2. NeRF Evaluation: Query the NeRF MLP for density \sigma(\mathbf{x}k) and color c(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{d}). 3. Feature Field Evaluation: Query the Feature Field MLP for the 3D feature vector f(\mathbf{x}k). 4. Volume Rendering (NeRF): Compute the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard emission-absorption model: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak) c(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{d}) where \hat{T}(tk) = \exp \left( -\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(\mathbf{x}{k'})\delta{k'} \right), \alpha(x) = 1 - \exp(-x), and \deltak = t{k+1} - tk. 5. Volume Rendering (Features): Compute the rendered feature vector \hat{F}(\mathbf{r}) by volume rendering the 3D features f(\mathbf{x}k) using the same transmittance weights as the color: \hat{F}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak) f(\mathbf{x}k) 6. Teacher Projection: Render the input image I from the current camera pose and pass it through the frozen teacher network to obtain the teacher's feature output f{img}(I, \mathbf{r}). 7. Loss Computation: Photometric Loss (Lp): Mean squared error between rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and ground-truth pixel color. Feature Loss (Lf): Mean squared error between rendered features \hat{F}(\mathbf{r}) and teacher features f{img}(I, \mathbf{r}). Total Loss: L = Lp + \lambda Lf, where \lambda is a weighting factor. 8. Optimization: Minimize L with respect to the parameters of the NeRF MLP and the Feature Field MLP using gradient descent. Query-based Decomposition and Editing: At test time, the trained DFF enables zero-shot segmentation and editing. 1. Query Encoding: Encode the user query (text l or image patch) into a feature vector fq(l) using the frozen query encoder. 2. Segmentation Probability: For any 3D point \mathbf{x}, calculate the probability p(l|\mathbf{x}) of belonging to label l using the dot product of the 3D feature f(\mathbf{x}) and the query feature fq(l), followed by a softmax over a set of labels \mathcal{L}: p(l|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(f(\mathbf{x})fq(l)^T)}{\sum{l' \in \mathcal{L}} \exp(f(\mathbf{x})fq(l')^T)} 3. Editing via Blending: To apply a geometric transformation g to a region defined by query l, blend the original scene (\sigma, c) with a transformed scene (\sigma2, c2). Define the original scene as Scene 1: \sigma1 = \sigma, c1(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}). Define the transformed scene as Scene 2: \sigma2(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(g^{-1}(\mathbf{x})), c2(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = c(g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), g^{-1}(\mathbf{d})). Compute the blend ratio \rhok for sample k using the segmentation probability p(l|\mathbf{x}k): \rhok = \frac{\alpha(\sigma1(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak)}{\alpha(\sigma1(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak) + \alpha(\sigma2(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak)} Set the effective opacity and color for the edited render: \alpha(\sigma1(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak){new} = (1 - p(l|\mathbf{x}k)) \alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak) \alpha(\sigma2(\mathbf{x}k)\deltak){new} = p(l|g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}k)) \alpha(\sigma(g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}k))\deltak) c1(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{d}){new} = (1 - p(l|\mathbf{x}k)) c(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{d}) c2(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{d}){new} = p(l|g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}k)) c(g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}k), g^{-1}(\mathbf{d})) Render the final image using the standard volume rendering equation with these modified opacities and colors. Parameters: Teacher Networks: LSeg (CLIP-inspired language-driven semantic segmentation) and DINO (self-supervised network aware of object boundaries). Loss Weight \lambda: Not given in the sources. Number of Samples K: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The goal is not state-of-the-art 3D semantic segmentation on discrete point clouds/voxelgrids, but smooth segmentation results on continuous 3D space for editing. Introducing view-dependency to the segmentation (e.g., for referring expressions like "the chair left to the table") is noted as an interesting extension but is not implemented in the base method. A technique to perform 3D zero-shot segmentation and editing by calculating the probability of a label l for a point \mathbf{x} using the dot product of the 3D feature f(\mathbf{x}) and a query feature fq(l). It uses teacher networks LSeg and DINO for obtaining image and text features. It enables geometric transformations of specific regions by blending the original and transformed scenes weighted by segmentation probabilities. Time Complexity: Training requires simultaneous optimization of two MLPs (NeRF and Feature Field) and forward passes through a large teacher network for every batch, increasing training time compared to standard NeRF. Rendering time is similar to NeRF, with the addition of querying the Feature Field MLP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for both the NeRF and Feature Field MLPs, plus the frozen teacher network weights. Strengths: Enables efficient, open-set decomposition without re-training; allows accurate selective editing of specific scene regions; leverages pre-trained foundation models for zero-shot segmentation. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D teacher network; segmentation is limited to the semantic space of the teacher (e.g., LSeg classes); does not support view-dependent segmentation in the base implementation. When to use: When interactive, query-based editing of NeRF scenes is required without re-training the scene representation. When not to use: When state-of-the-art discrete 3D semantic segmentation is the primary goal, or when view-dependent segmentation is required. Distilled Feature Fields were introduced by Sosuke Kobayashi, Eiichi Matsumoto, and Vincent Sitzmann in 'Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation' (arXiv:2205.15585v2, Oct 2022, NeurIPS 2022). The work addresses the challenge of editing NeRF scenes, which are not object-centric, by distilling 2D vision and language foundation models (LSeg, DINO) into a 3D feature field. Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation, https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1694, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeuralRadianceFieldPackedRenderer
head: NeRF Packed Renderer
body: The NeuralRadianceFieldPackedRenderer is a differentiable rendering component for pipelines combining a Neural Radiance Field with the PackedRFTracer. It serves as the default fallback renderer for BaseNeuralField subclasses using PackedRFTracer and supports interactive mode by dynamically reducing sampling steps to maintain real-time performance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of rays (origin and direction), the nef (ray-based neural field mapping 3D coordinates and view directions to RGB and density), the tracer, and configuration parameters. Outputs: A RenderBuffer containing the computed color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for each ray. Data Structures: The renderer maintains the following internal state variables: nef: Reference to the BaseNeuralField instance. tracer: Reference to the PackedRFTracer instance. batchsize: Integer specifying rays processed per batch. Default: 2^{14} (16384). numsteps: Integer for raymarching steps. Defaults to tracer.numsteps if None. numstepsinteractive: Integer for interactive mode steps, computed as \max(\lfloor \text{num\steps} / 4 \rfloor, 1). raymarchtype: String for the sampling strategy. Defaults to tracer.raymarchtype if None. bgcolor: Tuple for background color, initialized to (0.0, 0.0, 0.0). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the renderer with nef and tracer. 2. Set self.numsteps to the provided value or tracer.numsteps if None. 3. Compute self.numstepsinteractive = max(self.numsteps // 4, 1). 4. Set self.raymarchtype to the provided value or tracer.raymarchtype if None. 5. Initialize self.bgcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0). 6. In prerender, update self.bgcolor based on payload.clearcolor: set to (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if payload.clearcolor == (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), otherwise (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). 7. Split rays into batches of size self.batchsize. 8. For each batch, determine active steps: use self.numstepsinteractive in interactive mode, else self.numsteps. 9. Call tracer.trace(rays, nef, numsteps, raymarchtype) to compute accumulated color and final transmittance. 10. Apply background blending: \hat{C}{final}(\mathbf{r}) = \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) + TN(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \text{self.bg\color}. 11. Concatenate batch results into the final RenderBuffer. Formulas: The background blending follows the standard volume rendering composition rule: \hat{C}{final}(\mathbf{r}) = \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) + TN(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{C}{bg} where \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is the accumulated color from the tracer, TN(\mathbf{r}) is the transmittance after the last sample, and \mathbf{C}{bg} is the background color tuple. Parameters: batchsize (int): Amount of rays processed per batch during inference. Default: 2^{14} (16384). numsteps (int): Number of steps for raymarching. Defaults to tracer.numsteps if None. Overrides tracer default if specified. raymarchtype (str): Raymarch sampling strategy. Defaults to tracer.raymarchtype if None. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interactive Mode: Switching to interactive mode requires reducing numsteps to numsteps // 4 (minimum 1) to achieve real-time performance, which significantly reduces rendering quality. Background Color Logic: The background color update logic in prerender is binary (black or white) based on the clear color, which limits support for semi-transparent backgrounds or complex environment maps. Tracer Dependency: The renderer assumes the tracer is correctly configured and differentiable; invalid bounds or failed ray tracing will produce empty or erroneous results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class NeuralRadianceFieldPackedRenderer: def init(self, nef, tracer, batchsize=214, numsteps=None, raymarchtype=None): self.nef = nef self.tracer = tracer self.batchsize = batchsize self.numsteps = numsteps if numsteps is not None else tracer.numsteps self.numstepsinteractive = max(self.numsteps // 4, 1) self.raymarchtype = raymarchtype if raymarchtype is not None else tracer.raymarchtype self.bgcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def prerender(self, payload): if payload.clearcolor == (0.0, 0.0, 0.0): self.bgcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: self.bgcolor = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) def render(self, rays, interactive=False): results = [] numsteps = self.numstepsinteractive if interactive else self.numsteps for i in range(0, len(rays), self.batchsize): batch = rays[i:i + self.batchsize] accumulatedcolor, finaltransmittance = self.tracer.trace(batch, self.nef, numsteps, self.raymarchtype) bgcolor = torch.tensor(self.bgcolor, device=accumulatedcolor.device) finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + finaltransmittance.unsqueeze(-1) bgcolor results.append(finalcolor) return torch.cat(results, dim=0) An efficient hybrid scene representation for autonomous driving that uses explicit voxel grids for density and implicit hash grids for color, initialized with LiDAR point clouds to improve training speed and rendering quality. It separates foreground and background encodings, utilizing inverse cubic modeling for the background to warp 3D points into 4D coordinates, and employs separate view-independent and view-dependent MLPs for color decomposition. It achieves a five-fold increase in training speed and ten-fold improvement in rendering speed compared to state-of-the-art methods on real-world datasets. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and sampling steps (O(N{rays} \cdot N{steps})). Interactive mode improves frame rate by reducing steps by a factor of four. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the batch size (O(N{batch} \cdot N{steps})). The default batchsize of 16384 limits peak VRAM usage for high-resolution rendering. Performance: Rendering speed depends on PackedRFTracer efficiency in querying the neural field's acceleration structure (e.g., Octree or HashGrid). Strengths: Seamless integration with PackedRFTracer and BaseNeuralField, configurable batching for memory management, and built-in interactive mode for real-time preview. Limitations: Binary background color handling restricts complex environment map support, and interactive mode quality drops significantly due to reduced sampling. When to use: Standard NeRF training and inference pipelines requiring differentiable rendering with PackedRFTracer. When not: Applications requiring high-fidelity real-time rendering without step reduction, or complex background compositing beyond binary colors. The NeuralRadianceFieldPackedRenderer is part of the kaolin-wisp library developed by NVIDIA. It is registered as the default fallback renderer for BaseNeuralField subclasses that use PackedRFTracer, indicating its role as a standard rendering solution within the framework. It is utilized in applications such as the DemoApp for visualizing internal NeRF decoder layers and in multiview training pipelines for NeRF synthesis. NVIDIAGameWorks/kaolin-wisp, https://github.com/NVIDIAGameWorks/kaolin-wisp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LightningNeRF
head: Lightning NeRF
body: Lightning NeRF is an efficient hybrid scene representation for autonomous driving that uses explicit voxel grids for density and implicit hash grids for color, initialized with LiDAR point clouds to improve training speed and rendering quality. It separates foreground and background encodings, utilizing inverse cubic modeling for the background to warp 3D points into 4D coordinates, and employs separate view-independent and view-dependent MLPs for color decomposition. It achieves a five-fold increase in training speed and ten-fold improvement in rendering speed compared to state-of-the-art methods on real-world datasets. The method builds on NeuralRadianceFieldPackedRenderer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses, images, LiDAR point clouds (for initialization), scene bounding box (AABB). Outputs: Rendered RGB images, accumulation (opacity), depth. Data Structures: Foreground Density Grid: HashGrid encoding, 3D input, 1D output. Foreground Color Grid: Multi-resolution HashGrid encoding, 3D input, concatenated features. Background Density Grid: HashGrid encoding, 4D input (warped 3D + inverse norm), 1D output. Background Color Grid: Multi-resolution HashGrid encoding, 4D input, concatenated features. Occupancy Grid: Sparse grid for efficient sampling, updated based on density. MLPs: View-independent (Vi) and View-dependent (Vd) networks for color. Parameters: densityres: 256 (Foreground density base resolution). densitylog2hashmapsize: 24 (Foreground density hashmap size). colorbaseres: 16 (Foreground color base resolution). colormaxres: 256 (Foreground color max resolution). numlevels: 8 (Foreground color levels). featuresperlevel: 2 (Foreground color features per level). colorlog2hashmapsize: 19 (Foreground color hashmap size). bgdensityres: 32 (Background density base resolution). bgdensitylog2hashmapsize: 18 (Background density hashmap size). bgcolorbaseres: 32 (Background color base resolution). bgcolormaxres: 128 (Background color max resolution). bgcolorlog2hashmapsize: 16 (Background color hashmap size). vimlpnumlayers: 3. vimlphiddensize: 64. vdmlpnumlayers: 2. vdmlphiddensize: 32. initdensityvalue: 10.0. alphathre: 0.01. occgridbaseres: 256. occgridnumlevels: 2. occnumsamplesperray: 1000. pdfnumsamplesperray: 8. pdfsampleswarmupstep: 500. pdfsamplesfixedstep: 2000. pdfsamplesfixedratio: 0.5. coneangle: 0.004 (for real scenes). appearanceembeddingdim: 0 (default). Steps: 1. Scene Definition: Inspect camera frustums in a trajectory sequence. Define a foreground bounding box tightly wrapping all frustums. Define a background box by enlarging the foreground box proportionally along each dimension. 2. LiDAR Initialization: Load LiDAR point clouds P{pc} = \{pi | pi \in \mathbb{R}^3\}{i=1}^{N{pc}}. Transform points into normalized space using metadata transform matrix transpose and scale factor. 3. Background Augmentation: Generate augmented background points on the front, left, right, and top surfaces of the background box. Get AABB from occupancy grid. Generate grid points using torch.linspace and meshgrid. For frontal axis 'y': create augneg1 (x=x{min}+0.05, y=y{min}+0.05), augpos1 (x=x{max}-0.05, y=y{max}-0.05), augxz (y=y{max}-0.05), augxy (z=z{max}-0.05). For frontal axis 'x': create augneg1 (y=y{min}+0.20), augpos1 (y=y{max}-0.20), augyz (x=x{max}-0.05), augxy (z=z{max}-0.05). Concatenate all augmented points P{bg}. 4. Pretrain Density Grid (Foreground): Set model to train mode. Split foreground vertices into 50 batches. For each batch, query density, compute MSE loss against initdensityvalue (10.0), backpropagate, and step optimizer (lr=0.2). Update occupancy grid every iteration using \lambda x: \text{field.density\fn}(x) \text{render\step\size}. Run for 20 iterations. 5. Pretrain Density Grid (Background): Concatenate background (P{bg}) and augmented vertices. Split into 10 batches. For each batch, query density, compute MSE loss against initdensityvalue 0.8, backpropagate, and step optimizer (lr=0.2). Update occupancy grid every iteration. Run for 40 iterations. 6. Initialize Encodings: Foreground Density: tcnn.Encoding with ninputdims=3, otype='HashGrid', nlevels=1, nfeaturesperlevel=1, log2hashmapsize=24, baseresolution=256, interpolation='Linear'. Background Density: tcnn.Encoding with ninputdims=4, otype='HashGrid', nlevels=1, nfeaturesperlevel=1, log2hashmapsize=18, baseresolution=32, interpolation='Linear'. Initialize parameters for both density encodings uniformly in [-3, -2.8]. Foreground Color: Calculate growth factor g = \exp\left(\frac{\log(256) - \log(16)}{8 - 1}\right). tcnn.Encoding with ninputdims=3, otype='HashGrid', nlevels=8, nfeaturesperlevel=2, log2hashmapsize=19, baseresolution=16, perlevelscale=g. Background Color: Calculate growth factor g{\text{bg}} = \exp\left(\frac{\log(128) - \log(32)}{8 - 1}\right). tcnn.Encoding with ninputdims=4, otype='HashGrid', nlevels=8, nfeaturesperlevel=2, log2hashmapsize=16, baseresolution=32, perlevelscale=g{\text{bg}}. Appearance Embedding: If appearanceembeddingdim > 0, create Embedding(numimages, appearanceembeddingdim). View-Independent MLP: Input dim d{\text{color}} = 8 \times 2 + \text{appearance\embedding\dim}. tcnn.Network with ninputdims=d{\text{color}}, noutputdims=3, otype='FullyFusedMLP', activation='ReLU', outputactivation='Sigmoid', nneurons=64, nhiddenlayers=2. Direction Encoding: tcnn.Encoding with ninputdims=3, otype='Frequency', nfrequencies=4. View-Dependent MLP: Input dim d{\text{view}} = d{\text{color}} + 4 \times 2. tcnn.Network with ninputdims=d{\text{view}}, noutputdims=3, otype='FullyFusedMLP', activation='ReLU', outputactivation='Sigmoid', nneurons=32, nhiddenlayers=1. 7. Initialize Sampler: Calculate renderstepsize as \sqrt{\sum (\text{scene\aabb}[3:] - \text{scene\aabb}[:3])^2} / \text{occ\num\samples\per\ray}. Create nerfacc.OccGridEstimator with roiaabb, resolution=256, levels=2. Create LightningNeRFSampler with occupancy grid and density function. 8. Density Query (Foreground): Flatten positions to (-1, 3). Normalize positions to [0, 1] using SceneBox.getnormalizedpositions. Create selector for positions inside [0, 1]^3. If all positions inside: densitybeforeact = densityencoding(positionsnorm). 9. Density Query (Background): If some positions outside: Split into foreground and background selectors. For background positions: Shift bgpositionsnorm from [0, 1] to [-1, 1] by bgpositionsnorm = bgpositionsnorm 2.0 - 1.0. Compute inf norm bginfnorm = bgpositionsnorm.abs().max(-1, keepdim=True).values. Warp to [0, 1] for tcnn: bgpositionswarp = (bgpositionsnorm / bginfnorm + 1.0) / 2.0. Concatenate warped positions with inverse inf norm: bgpositionswarp = torch.cat([bgpositionswarp, torch.div(1., bginfnorm)], dim=-1). Compute bgdensitybeforeact = bgdensityencoding(bgpositionswarp). Combine foreground and background densities: Initialize densitybeforeact with zeros. Assign fgdensitybeforeact to fgselector indices and bgdensitybeforeact to bgselector indices. 10. Final Density: Apply truncexp to densitybeforeact to get final density \sigma = \text{trunc\exp}(\text{density\before\act}). Reshape to match input positions shape. 11. Color Query: Get density and color embeddings for ray samples. For foreground: fgcolorembedding = colorencoding(positionsnorm). For background: bgcolorembedding = bgcolorencoding(bgpositionswarp) (using same warping as density). Concatenate color embeddings and appearance embedding (if used). 12. Color Decomposition: View-Independent Color: c{\text{vi}} = \text{ViMLP}(\text{color\embedding}). View-Dependent Color: Encode viewing direction d using frequency encoding. c{\text{vd}} = \text{VdMLP}(\text{color\embedding}, \text{direction\encoding}(d)). Final color c = c{\text{vi}} + c{\text{vd}}. 13. Rendering: Query volume density \sigma and color embedding feature f from voxel grids for sample points along a ray. Combine with viewing direction d in separate MLPs for view-dependent and view-independent colors. Combine components to achieve the final rendered image using standard volume rendering integration. Use occupancy grid for sparse sampling, clustering around object surfaces. Update occupancy grid based on initialized density mapping to ensure sample locations are sparse in the scene and cluster around object surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def truncexp(x): """Stable exponential truncation.""" return torch.exp(torch.clamp(x, max=15.0)) class LightningNeRF: def init(self, aabb, numimages, config): self.aabb = aabb self.numimages = numimages self.config = config # Initialize foreground density encoding (3D -> 1D HashGrid) self.densityencoding = self.createencoding(3, 1, 1, config.densitylog2hashmapsize, config.densityres) self.densityencoding.params.data.uniform(-3., -2.8) # Initialize background density encoding (4D -> 1D HashGrid) self.bgdensityencoding = self.createencoding(4, 1, 1, config.bgdensitylog2hashmapsize, config.bgdensityres) self.bgdensityencoding.params.data.uniform(-3., -2.8) # Initialize foreground color encoding (multi-resolution HashGrid) growthfactor = np.exp((np.log(config.colormaxres) - np.log(config.colorbaseres)) / (config.numlevels - 1)) self.colorencoding = self.createencoding(3, config.numlevels, config.featuresperlevel, config.colorlog2hashmapsize, config.colorbaseres, growthfactor) # Initialize background color encoding (multi-resolution HashGrid) bggrowthfactor = np.exp((np.log(config.bgcolormaxres) - np.log(config.bgcolorbaseres)) / (config.numlevels - 1)) self.bgcolorencoding = self.createencoding(4, config.numlevels, config.featuresperlevel, config.bgcolorlog2hashmapsize, config.bgcolorbaseres, bggrowthfactor) if config.appearanceembeddingdim > 0: self.appearanceembedding = torch.nn.Embedding(numimages, config.appearanceembeddingdim) else: self.appearanceembedding = None indimcolor = config.numlevels config.featuresperlevel if config.appearanceembeddingdim > 0: indimcolor += config.appearanceembeddingdim self.vimlp = self.createmlp(indimcolor, 3, config.vimlphiddensize, config.vimlpnumlayers - 1) self.directionencoding = self.createfreqencoding(3, 4) indimview = indimcolor + self.directionencoding.noutputdims self.vdmlp = self.createmlp(indimview, 3, config.vdmlphiddensize, config.vdmlpnumlayers - 1) def createencoding(self, ninputdims, nlevels, nfeaturesperlevel, log2hashmapsize, baseresolution, perlevelscale=None): # Instantiates a tcnn.Encoding with otype='HashGrid' and the given parameters. # Returns an object supporting.forward(x) and.params. raise NotImplementedError("tcnn library required for HashGrid encoding.") def createfreqencoding(self, ninputdims, nfrequencies): # Instantiates a tcnn.Encoding with otype='Frequency' and the given parameters. # Returns an object supporting.forward(x) and.noutputdims. raise NotImplementedError("tcnn library required for Frequency encoding.") def createmlp(self, ninputdims, noutputdims, nneurons, nhiddenlayers): # Instantiates a tcnn.Network with otype='FullyFusedMLP', ReLU activations, and Sigmoid output. # Returns an object supporting.forward(x). raise NotImplementedError("tcnn library required for MLP network.") def getdensity(self, positions): positionsflat = positions.view(-1, 3) positionsnorm = self.normalizepositions(positionsflat) selector = ((positionsnorm > 0.0) & (positionsnorm < 1.0)).all(dim=-1) densitybeforeact = torch.zeros((positionsflat.shape[0], 1), device=positionsflat.device, dtype=positionsflat.dtype) if selector.all(): densitybeforeact = self.densityencoding(positionsnorm) else: fgselector = selector bgselector = ~selector fgdensitybeforeact = self.densityencoding(positionsnorm[fgselector]) bgpositionsnorm = positionsnorm[bgselector] bgpositionsnormshifted = bgpositionsnorm 2.0 - 1.0 bginfnorm = bgpositionsnormshifted.abs().max(-1, keepdim=True).values bgpositionswarp = (bgpositionsnormshifted / bginfnorm + 1.0) / 2.0 bgpositionswarp = torch.cat([bgpositionswarp, torch.div(1., bginfnorm)], dim=-1) bgdensitybeforeact = self.bgdensityencoding(bgpositionswarp) densitybeforeact[fgselector] = fgdensitybeforeact densitybeforeact[bgselector] = bgdensitybeforeact density = truncexp(densitybeforeact) return density.view(positions.shape[:-1], 1) def getcolor(self, positions, direction, imageidx): positionsflat = positions.view(-1, 3) positionsnorm = self.normalizepositions(positionsflat) selector = ((positionsnorm > 0.0) & (positionsnorm < 1.0)).all(dim=-1) colorembedding = torch.zeros((positionsflat.shape[0], self.config.numlevels self.config.featuresperlevel), device=positionsflat.device, dtype=positionsflat.dtype) if selector.all(): colorembedding = self.colorencoding(positionsnorm) else: fgselector = selector bgselector = ~selector colorembedding[fgselector] = self.colorencoding(positionsnorm[fgselector]) bgpositionsnorm = positionsnorm[bgselector] bgpositionsnormshifted = bgpositionsnorm 2.0 - 1.0 bginfnorm = bgpositionsnormshifted.abs().max(-1, keepdim=True).values bgpositionswarp = (bgpositionsnormshifted / bginfnorm + 1.0) / 2.0 bgpositionswarp = torch.cat([bgpositionswarp, torch.div(1., bginfnorm)], dim=-1) colorembedding[bgselector] = self.bgcolorencoding(bgpositionswarp) if self.appearanceembedding is not None: appemb = self.appearanceembedding(imageidx.view(-1)) colorembedding = torch.cat([colorembedding, appemb], dim=-1) cvi = self.vimlp(colorembedding) directionflat = direction.view(-1, 3) directionenc = self.directionencoding(directionflat) vdinput = torch.cat([colorembedding, directionenc], dim=-1) cvd = self.vdmlp(vdinput) c = cvi + cvd return c.view(positions.shape[:-1], 3) def normalizepositions(self, positions): minval = self.aabb[:3] maxval = self.aabb[3:] return (positions - minval) / (maxval - minval) Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than standard NeRF due to explicit density initialization and sparse sampling via occupancy grid. Rendering is also faster. Memory Complexity: Uses hash grids for color, which are memory efficient compared to dense voxel grids for color. Background uses 4D hash grids, which may consume more memory than 3D but avoids expanding the scene bounding box as in NGP. Measured Performance: Five-fold increase in training speed and ten-fold improvement in rendering speed on real-world datasets (KITTI-360, Argoverse2). Strengths: Efficient for large-scale outdoor scenes (autonomous driving). LiDAR initialization improves convergence and quality. Separate foreground/background handling handles unbounded scenes well. Limitations: Relies on LiDAR for initialization, which may not be available in all scenarios. Background modeling assumes a specific structure (inverse cubic). When to use: Autonomous driving scenarios with LiDAR data. Large-scale outdoor scenes. When not to use: Indoor scenes without LiDAR. Small-scale scenes where standard NeRF or NGP might be simpler. Lightning NeRF was proposed to address the challenges of applying NeRF to outdoor environments, specifically for autonomous driving. It builds on the idea of using LiDAR point clouds to provide geometric priors, which are often overlooked in terms of efficiency in previous methods. The method was evaluated on KITTI-360, Argoverse2, and a private autonomous driving dataset. It was presented in 2024.
