name: Semi-Gradient Method
head: Ours, Ours w/o VR, Partial derivative-based optimization, SG method, Semi-Gradient Estimator
body: The Semi-Gradient Method is a training optimization technique for neural radiance field caching that modifies the baseline loss function by applying a stop-gradient operation to the right-hand side (RHS) of the rendering equation. It solves the problem of gradient bias and high variance inherent in standard differentiable rendering optimization, where the correlation between the network gradient and the radiance estimate impedes convergence. It sets itself apart from the baseline by intentionally ignoring updates to the RHS, thereby removing the partial derivatives with respect to the RHS to achieve unbiased and low-variance gradient estimates. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Network parameters \theta, learning rate \eta, location vectors \{xj\}, outgoing directions \{\omegaj\}, incident directions \{\omega{in,j,k}\}, and reference radiance values. Outputs: Updated network parameters \theta. Data Structures Radiance Prediction Network: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) consisting of seven linear layers, each with 512 units. Six ReLU activations are used; the final output layer does not pass through an activation function. Encoding: Multi-resolution hash encoding (from InstantNGP) with base resolution 2, 14 hierarchy levels, 2 features per level, and a hashmap size of 2^{18}. Precision: Mixed precision is used. Inputs (x, \omega) are processed in 32-bit full precision, converted to 16-bit half-precision for the network, and outputs are converted back to full precision before the rendering engine. Parameters Learning Rate (\eta): 5 \times 10^{-4}, reduced by a factor of three every 12,000 steps. Incident Sample Count (M): 32 incident directions sampled per (x, \omega). Batch Size (N): 214 samples of (x, \omega). Training Steps: 36,000 steps per scene. Optimizer: Adam. Initialization: Xavier uniform distribution. Algorithm The method replaces the standard L2 loss gradient with a semi-gradient estimator. The baseline minimizes the L2 distance between the left-hand side (LHS, outgoing radiance L\theta) and the right-hand side (RHS, sum of emitted and reflected radiance \langle R\theta \rangle). The semi-gradient loss \langle L(\theta) \rangle{SG} is defined as: \langle L(\theta) \rangle{SG} = \frac{\| L\theta - \text{sg}(\langle R\theta \rangle) \|^2}{\| \text{sg}(L\theta) \|^2 + \epsilon} where \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator, which blocks the flow of gradients through its argument. The term \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. The gradient estimator for this loss eliminates the partial derivative with respect to the RHS, making \frac{\partial \langle L(\theta) \rangle{SG}}{\partial \langle R\theta \rangle} = 0. This prevents the network from pulling the RHS estimates towards the LHS, a behavior identified as the source of bias and high variance in the baseline. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class RadianceNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=512): super().init() # Seven linear layers, 512 units each self.layers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Linear(inputdim, 512) for in range(6) ] + [nn.Linear(512, 512)]) # Last layer output self.relu = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, x): h = x for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers[:-1]): h = self.relu(layer(h)) # Last layer: no activation h = self.layers-1 return h def semigradientstep(network, optimizer, positions, outgoingdirs, incidentdirs): """ Performs one optimization step using the semi-gradient method. Args: network: RadianceNetwork instance. optimizer: Adam optimizer instance. positions: Tensor of shape (N, 3) location vectors. outgoingdirs: Tensor of shape (N, 3) outgoing directions. incidentdirs: Tensor of shape (N, M, 3) incident directions. Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. """ optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Encode inputs # Sources do not provide the hash encoding implementation; typically uses tiny-cuda-nn. encodedpos = hashencode(positions) encodeddir = hashencode(outgoingdirs) inputvec = torch.cat([encodedpos, encodeddir], dim=-1) # 2. Evaluate LHS (Outgoing Radiance) Ltheta = network(inputvec) # 3. Evaluate RHS (Emitted + Reflected Radiance) # RHS is computed using Monte Carlo integration over incident directions. # We compute this without tracking gradients to stop gradient flow. with torch.nograd(): # Encode incident directions encodedincident = hashencode(incidentdirs) # Query network for radiance at incident directions incidentradiance = network(encodedincident) # Integrate over the hemisphere (simplified sum over M samples) Rtheta = torch.mean(incidentradiance, dim=1) # 4. Compute Semi-Gradient Loss epsilon = 1e-8 # Stop gradient on RHS (numerator) and LHS (denominator) Rthetasg = Rtheta.detach() Lthetasg = Ltheta.detach() numerator = (Ltheta - Rthetasg) 2 denominator = Lthetasg 2 + epsilon loss = torch.mean(numerator / denominator) # 5. Backpropagate loss.backward() # 6. Update parameters optimizer.step() return loss.item() def hashencode(x): # Sources do not provide the hash encoding implementation; typically uses tiny-cuda-nn. return torch.randnlike(x[...,:1]).expandas(x) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Bias in Baseline: The baseline method is a biased estimator because of the correlation between \nabla\theta \langle R\theta \rangle and \langle R\theta \rangle in the partial derivative with respect to the RHS. This bias impedes convergence to the minimum, causing the reconstruction to appear darker than the reference. Convergence Guarantee: Due to mathematical shortcomings in the definition of the stop-gradient operation, convergence of the L2-form loss cannot be prematurely guaranteed. Convergence is theoretically guaranteed only for scenes satisfying the energy absorption condition. Implementation Detail: To realize the speedup, unnecessary intermediate activations should not be stored for the backward pass, e.g., using PyTorch's nograd context manager. A technique to expedite initial convergence by integrating neural path guiding. It uses additional neural caches to sample incident directions, reducing the variance of the Right Hand Side (RHS) estimates and subsequently the variance of the semi-gradient estimator. The path guiding model consists of four linear layers of 256 units with three activations. It is trained alongside radiance caches for 1,000 to 5,000 iterations, then held fixed for the remaining iterations. It operates with next event estimation for multiple importance sampling to reduce variance. This reduction mitigates visual artifacts during early training and accelerates error reduction, but does not impact the error at final convergence. Time Complexity: Training time per iteration is reduced by 25-30% compared to the baseline. This efficiency is primarily due to the elimination of partial derivatives for the RHS, which obviates the need to store intermediate activations in memory. Memory Complexity: Lower memory usage than reverse-mode AD because intermediate activations for the RHS are not stored. Performance: On average, the semi-gradient method decreases the error to the reference by 8.8 times across various scenes compared to the baseline. In free-viewpoint video rendering, MAPE errors decrease by a factor of 2 to 35 times. On the arXiv cover figure, the Baseline MAPE is 0.318 (1.0x) and the Semi-Gradient MAPE is 0.069 (4.6x). Strengths: Removes gradient bias and high variance associated with the RHS derivative. Faster convergence and lower final error. Limitations: Convergence is not guaranteed for all scenes (only those satisfying energy absorption condition). Non-L2 losses (RMSE, Huber, MAE) still benefit (2-15 times lower error) but the theoretical justification is less robust than for L2. When to use: When training neural radiance caches for global illumination rendering and fast convergence is desired. When not to use: When strict theoretical convergence guarantees are required for all scene types, or when the scene is simple enough that stochasticity is low (where the baseline may perform comparably). The Semi-Gradient Method was proposed by In-Young Cho and JaeWoong Cho from Krafton, Republic of Korea, in the paper "Fast and Accurate Neural Rendering Using Semi-Gradients" (arXiv:2410.10149, October 14, 2024). It addresses issues in neural radiosity methods, specifically the baseline method by Hadadan et al. [2021], which minimizes the residual between the LHS and RHS of the rendering equation. The method builds on the observation that the stochasticity of Monte Carlo integration causes gradient bias and high variance in the RHS derivative. It is implemented using PyTorch, Mitsuba 3, and the tiny-cuda-nn library. Training is performed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, using 7GB or less of VRAM. Fast and Accurate Neural Rendering Using Semi-Gradients, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2410.10149, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Surface-Volume and Mesh Representation
head: Hybrid Neural Representations, Implicit-Explicit NeRF Hybrids
body: This family integrates explicit geometric primitives or implicit surface fields with neural radiance fields to decouple geometry reconstruction from appearance modeling. It addresses the slow convergence and ambiguous geometry of pure volumetric NeRFs by using surface boundaries to guide sampling and define radiance evaluation points. Represents scenes as a dynamic set of neural surfels (position, normal, radius, neural features) and uses differentiable rasterization for online integration. It distinguishes itself by using explicit surfel primitives with learned features rather than implicit occupancy fields, enabling fast rendering without per-scene optimization. Choose this for large-scale, dynamic indoor scenes requiring incremental updates. Replaces volume density with a continuous occupancy field o\theta where the zero-level set defines the surface. It unifies surface rendering with volume rendering by finding surface intersections via root-finding and sampling densely only near the surface with a decaying interval schedule. Choose this for high-precision static reconstruction where mesh extraction is required without per-pixel masks. Encodes scene geometry and appearance into disentangled latent codes anchored to the vertices of a mesh scaffold. It solves high-frequency detail preservation and efficient fine-grained editing in unbounded scenes by using a local space parameterization and hybrid blending with an implicit hash grid for backgrounds. Choose this for unbounded scenes requiring editable mesh geometry and per-vertex latent codes. Stores geometry and appearance latent codes at anchor nodes (typically mesh vertices) on a deformable mesh, enabling local editing and deformation tracking. It differs from implicit surface methods by using explicit mesh topology to define spatial relationships and resolves surface-normal ambiguity via a signed height indicator. Choose this for scenarios requiring local editing and deformation tracking of explicit mesh structures. A framework combining surface field and radiance field for high-fidelity human reconstruction and rendering, bridging them via a shared feature embedding and surface-guided sampling strategy. The core representation is a joint implicit function f{db} that bridges the surface field and the radiance field, allowing shared learning space for geometry and radiance reconstruction. Build associations between surface and radiance fields using a feature embedding shared by these fields in the network architecture. Apply a surface-guided sampling strategy to disentangle the geometry component from the appearance modeling. Input resolution: Ultra-high resolution images, e.g., 4K, are used as input to the method. Unlike PIFu which isolates geometry and texture making texture learning space discontinuous, DoubleField enables joint implicit function learning. Unlike NeRF which entangles density and color leading to inconsistent geometry with sparse views, DoubleField imposes geometry constraints on the radiance field. DoubleField was introduced to bridge surface and radiance fields for high-fidelity human reconstruction. The family builds on Neural Radiance Fields by introducing geometric priors to guide radiance field optimization. DoubleField: Bridging the Neural Surface and Radiance Fields for High-fidelity Human Reconstruction and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01541, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Neural Surfel Radiance Fields
head: SurfelNeRF
body: Neural Surfel Radiance Fields (SurfelNeRF) is an online photorealistic reconstruction method that represents large-scale indoor scenes using a dynamic set of neural surfels, enabling efficient incremental updates and fast rendering without per-scene optimization. It distinguishes itself from point-based representations by using explicit surfel primitives with learned neural features, allowing for easier location of overlapping surfels and simpler feature fusion. Unlike DeepSurfel, which performs appearance fusion only on fixed geometry, SurfelNeRF performs online appearance and geometry integration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of input images \{It\}, corresponding camera parameters ct, and estimated or sensor depth maps Dt. Outputs: A global neural surfel radiance field Sg and rendered photorealistic images for novel views. Data Structures: Each neural surfel si in the global set Sg stores the following attributes: Position \mathbf{p}^i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Normal \mathbf{n}^i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Radius r^i \in \mathbb{R}. Weight w^i \in \mathbb{R} (confidence based on depth measurement distance). Neural features \mathbf{f}^i \in \mathbb{R}^{32} (extracted from input images). Step 1: Local Neural Surfel Radiance Field Construction For each input frame It with camera ct and depth Dt: 1. Depth Refinement: If Dt is from a sensor or MVS, refine it using a U-Net structure to handle noise and incompleteness. 2. Unprojection: Unproject pixels in It to 3D space using ct to obtain initial 3D positions. 3. Attribute Estimation: Estimate normal, weight, and radius for each point. The weight wt^i measures confidence based on the distance of the depth measurement from the camera center. The radius rt^i represents the local support area. 4. Neural Feature Extraction: Extract multi-scale view-dependent features from It using a modified MnasNet (MasNet) pretrained on ImageNet. Project these 2D pixel features to 3D surfel features \mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{merge}} using an MLP. Step 2: Neural Surfel Association Integrate local surfels \{st^i\} into the global set Sg: 1. Projection: Project each global surfel sj \in Sg as an ellipse onto the image plane of the current view. 2. Rasterization: For each pixel, obtain the top-K global surfels that overlap with it. Discard surfels failing a normal filter. 3. Matching: Compare the depth distance between the local surfel and the top-M global candidates (sorted near to far). 4. Decision: If the minimum depth distance between a local surfel and its global candidates is < \delta{depth}, mark it for Merge. Otherwise, mark it for Add. Step 3: Neural Surfel Fusion 1. Addition: For surfels marked "Add", insert them directly into Sg with their estimated attributes and features. 2. Update (Merge): For surfels marked "Merge", update the corresponding global surfel sj using a GRU network for features and weighted sums for geometry. Feature Update: \mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{corrs}} = \mathtt{GRU}(\mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{merge}}, \mathbf{f}{t-1}^{\mathtt{corrs}}) Where \mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{merge}} is the input feature and \mathbf{f}{t-1}^{\mathtt{corrs}} is the hidden state (previous global feature). The GRU gates are computed as: \mathbf{z}t = \sigma(Mz([\mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{merge}}, \mathbf{f}{t-1}^{\mathtt{corrs}}])) \mathbf{r}t = \sigma(Mr([\mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{merge}}, \mathbf{f}{t-1}^{\mathtt{corrs}}])) \tilde{\mathbf{f}}t^{\mathtt{corrs}} = \tanh(Mt([\mathbf{r}t \mathbf{f}{t-1}^{\mathtt{corrs}}, \mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{merge}}])) \mathbf{f}t^{\mathtt{corrs}} = (1 - \mathbf{z}t) \mathbf{f}{t-1}^{\mathtt{corrs}} + \mathbf{z}t \tilde{\mathbf{f}}t^{\mathtt{corrs}} Where Mz, Mr, Mt are one-layer MLPs followed by sigmoid, sigmoid, and tanh activations, respectively, and [\cdot, \cdot] denotes concatenation. Geometry Update: \mathbf{p}t^j = \frac{wt^i \mathbf{p}t^i + w{t-1}^j \mathbf{p}{t-1}^j}{wt^i + w{t-1}^j} \mathbf{n}t^j = \frac{wt^i \mathbf{n}t^i + w{t-1}^j \mathbf{n}{t-1}^j}{wt^i + w{t-1}^j} rt^j = \frac{wt^i rt^i + w{t-1}^j r{t-1}^j}{wt^i + w{t-1}^j} wt^j = wt^i + w{t-1}^j Where i is the local surfel index and j is the global surfel index. Step 4: Rendering To render a target view with camera c{tar}: 1. Rasterization: Project all global surfels onto the target image plane. For each pixel px, gather the set of intersecting surfels \{si\}{i=1}^M (up to M=80). 2. Shading Point Intersection: For each surfel si, compute the intersection point \mathbf{x}i between the ray from c{tar} through px and the surfel surface. 3. Feature Interpolation: Compute the interpolated feature \mathbf{f}^i(\mathbf{x}i) at \mathbf{x}i: \mathbf{f}^i(\mathbf{x}i) = \frac{r^i - \|\mathbf{x}^i - \mathbf{p}^i\|}{r^i} \mathtt{F}(\mathbf{f}^i, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{n}^i, w^i) Where \mathbf{d} is the view direction. The network \mathtt{F} is: \mathtt{F}(\mathbf{f}^i, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{n}^i, w^i) = Ff([\mathbf{f}^i, \gamma(\mathbf{d}), \gamma(w^i), \gamma(\mathbf{n}^i), \gamma(\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{n})]) Ff is a two-layer MLP with ReLU activation and hidden size 256. \gamma(\cdot) is positional embedding with max frequency 5. 4. Density and Radiance Prediction: Predict volume density \sigmai and radiance ci using an MLP \mathtt{Render}: \sigmai, ci = \mathtt{Render}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{f}^i(\mathbf{x}i), \mathbf{d}) 5. Volume Rendering: Compute pixel color C(px): C(px) = \sum{i=1}^M \taui (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Deltai)) ci \taui = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Deltaj\right) Where \Deltaj is the distance between adjacent shading points. Parameters: K=8: Number of top global surfels considered per pixel during association. \delta{depth}=0.1m: Threshold for merging surfels based on depth distance. M=80: Maximum number of shading points (intersecting surfels) per pixel during rendering. \lambda=0.1: Balancing weight for depth loss. Image Resolution: 640 \times 480. Keyframe Sampling: 5% of the sequence. Learning Rate: 0.001 (training), 0.0002 (fine-tuning). Pitfalls: Inaccurate or noisy depth estimates cause geometry discontinuities or missing parts in the surfel representation, leading to rendering artifacts. The method relies on depth refinement; without it, incomplete sensor depths result in missing geometry. Speed: SurfelNeRF achieves a 10× speedup in training and inference compared to conventional NeRF methods. Rendering time is approximately 0.2s per image on a V100 GPU, compared to 30s for volume rendering. Complexity: The major computational cost is rasterization. Surfel construction and integration costs are negligible. The number of surfels grows sub-linearly with input frames due to fusion. Memory: Memory footprint grows linearly with the number of neural surfels. On ScanNet, the average number of rasterized surfels per pixel is 2.92, with a maximum of 10. Performance: On ScanNet, SurfelNeRF achieves 23.82 PSNR in feedforward inference and 29.58 PSNR with per-scene fine-tuning. Strengths: Efficient online reconstruction, scalable fusion, and fast rendering via rasterization-guided volume rendering. Limitations: Sensitive to depth quality; requires depth refinement for noisy/incomplete inputs. Performance drops slightly (0.5% PSNR) if depth resolution is halved. SurfelNeRF was introduced in 2023 by Gao et al.. It builds upon classical surfel-based geometric reconstruction methods [43] and neural radiance fields [22], aiming to combine the efficiency of explicit geometry with the appearance modeling of NeRFs. It is designed for online photorealistic reconstruction of large-scale indoor scenes, such as those in the ScanNet dataset. SurfelNeRF: Neural Surfel Radiance Fields for Online Photorealistic Reconstruction of Indoor Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00019, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Unified Neural Implicit Surface and Radiance Field Rendering
head: UNISURF rendering, Unified volume/surface rendering
body: UNISURF is a framework for reconstructing accurate 3D surfaces from multi-view RGB images without requiring per-pixel object masks. It solves the ambiguity of volume-only rendering and the mask-dependency of surface-only rendering by unifying them: it parameterizes occupancy directly via a continuous field o\theta instead of volume density \sigma, allowing the model to render both through the volume (for coarse structure) and directly on the surface (for geometric precision). Unlike Neural Radiance Fields which requires hierarchical two-stage sampling, UNISURF eliminates this need by using the occupancy field for root-finding and a decaying sampling interval. Unlike IDR (a sibling in Hybrid Surface-Volume and Mesh Representation), it does not rely on input masks. Inputs: Multi-view RGB images with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. No object masks are required. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a given ray \mathbf{r}, and implicitly, a 3D surface defined by the zero-level set of the occupancy field. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy Network (o\theta): An 8-layer MLP with Softplus activation and hidden dimension 256. Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} (encoded with Fourier features, k=6 octaves). Output: scalar occupancy o \in [0, 1]. 2. Color Network (c\theta): A 4-layer MLP with ReLU activation. Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} (encoded with Fourier features, k=6 octaves), surface normal \mathbf{n}, geometry feature vector \mathbf{h} (from the geometry network's intermediate layers), and viewing direction \mathbf{d} (encoded with Fourier features, k=4 octaves). Output: RGB color \mathbf{c} \in [0, 1]^3. 3. Ray Parameters: Camera origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and current sampling interval width \Delta. Numbered Steps: 1. Network Initialization: Initialize the occupancy network such that the decision boundary is a sphere. 2. Surface Intersection (Root-Finding): For a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, find the surface intersection point \mathbf{x}s. Sample 256 uniformly spaced points along the ray. Evaluate o\theta at these points. Identify the interval where the occupancy changes sign. Apply the secant method with 8 steps to refine the root ts within this interval. Compute \mathbf{x}s = \mathbf{o} + ts \mathbf{d}. 3. Surface Normal and Feature Extraction: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n}s using double backpropagation to get the gradient of the occupancy field: \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}s) = \frac{\nabla{\mathbf{x}s} o\theta(\mathbf{x}s)}{\|\nabla{\mathbf{x}s} o\theta(\mathbf{x}s)\|2}. Retrieve the geometry feature vector \mathbf{h}s from the intermediate layers of the occupancy network evaluated at \mathbf{x}s. 4. Volume Rendering Sampling: Determine the sampling interval [ts - \Delta, ts + \Delta] centered at the surface depth ts. Interval Samples: Draw N=64 query points \{ti\}{i=1}^N inside the interval using stratified sampling: ti \sim \mathcal{U} \left[ ts + \left( \frac{2i - 2}{N} - 1 \right) \Delta, ts + \left( \frac{2i}{N} - 1 \right) \Delta \right]. Compute \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d} for each i. Free Space Samples: Draw 32 points randomly in the free space between the camera and the lower bound of the interval (t < ts - \Delta) to reduce free space artifacts. No Intersection Fallback: If no surface intersection is found, use stratified sampling on the entire ray depth range. 5. Color Evaluation: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i in the interval, compute normal \mathbf{n}i and feature \mathbf{h}i at \mathbf{x}i using gradients and network features. Compute color \mathbf{c}i = c\theta(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{h}i, \mathbf{d}). For free space samples, color is typically background or black. 6. Unified Rendering Equation: Compute the rendered color \hat{C}v(\mathbf{r}) using the occupancy values oi = o\theta(\mathbf{x}i): \hat{C}v(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N oi \prod{j < i} (1 - oj) ci. This equation effectively selects the color of the first occupied sample along the ray, unifying volume integration with surface-like occlusion. 7. Surface Rendering (Optional for Inference): For faster inference, the color can be computed directly at the surface point: \hat{C}s(\mathbf{r}) = c\theta(\mathbf{x}s, \mathbf{n}s, \mathbf{h}s, \mathbf{d}). This is twice as fast as volume rendering. 8. Loss Computation: Reconstruction Loss: \mathcal{L}{rec} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\hat{C}v(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|1, where C(\mathbf{r}) is the observed color. Surface Regularization Loss: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \sum{\mathbf{x}s \in \mathcal{S}} \|\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}s) - \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}s + \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|2, where \boldsymbol{\epsilon} is a small random uniform 3D perturbation. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{reg}. 9. Optimization Schedule: Start with a large interval \Delta{\max} = 1.0 to capture coarse geometry. Decay \Delta monotonically using the schedule: \Deltak = \max(\Delta{\max} \exp(-k\beta), \Delta{\min}) where k is the iteration number, \beta = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}, and \Delta{\min} = 0.05. Perform two decay steps after 200k and 400k iterations. Optimize using Adam with learning rate 0.0001 for 450k total iterations, processing M=1024 pixels per iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Unlike UNISURF which unifies volume and surface rendering, Neural Surface Fields often isolate geometry and texture (e.g., PIFu predicts color on points where fs(\mathbf{x})=0.5), which can hinder geometry optimization under texture supervision. Time Complexity: Surface rendering is twice as fast as volume rendering. Volume rendering requires sampling N=64 points plus free space samples and computing gradients for normals/features at each point. Surface rendering only requires evaluation at the root \mathbf{x}s. Memory Complexity: Depends on the MLP sizes (8-layer for occupancy, 4-layer for color) and the number of samples per ray. No large voxel grids are stored, unlike traditional volume rendering. Performance: On the DTU MVS dataset, UNISURF attains results competitive with state-of-the-art implicit neural reconstruction methods like IDR, which use strong mask supervision, despite not using masks. Strengths: Eliminates the need for hierarchical two-stage sampling (unlike NeRF) and per-pixel masks (unlike IDR). Combines coarse structure learning (volume) with precise surface refinement (surface). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the sampling interval decay schedule. Root-finding can be unstable if the occupancy field is not smooth. UNISURF was introduced in the paper "UNISURF: Unifying Neural Implicit Surfaces and Radiance Fields for Multi-View Reconstruction". It builds on Neural Radiance Fields and IDR. The method addresses the limitation of surface rendering methods that require masks and the limitation of volume rendering methods that produce noisy surfaces. It is used for multi-view 3D reconstruction on datasets like DTU and BlendedMVS. name: NeuMesh++
head: Hybrid rendering for unbounded scenes, Learning Disentangled Neural Mesh-Based Implicit Field, Learning Disentangled Neural Mesh-Based Implicit Field for Geometry and Texture Editing, NeuMesh++ Neural Mesh-based Radiance Field, NeuMesh++ background blending, Unbounded Scene Rendering with NeuMesh++
body: NeuMesh++ is a mesh-based neural radiance field representation that encodes a scene using disentangled geometry, texture, and semantic codes attached to a mesh scaffold. It solves the problem of high-fidelity novel view synthesis while enabling efficient, fine-grained 3D editing (geometry deformation, texture swapping, painting, and semantic-guided editing) without UV mapping or pre-trained teacher models. Unlike its predecessor NeuMesh, which relied on distillation from an implicit SDF field and suffered from spatial ambiguity on single-layer vertex codes, NeuMesh++ introduces a novel local space parameterization and a decoder-free modification color to stabilize training and improve editing fidelity. For unbounded scenes, it learns an additional implicit hash grid for the background and blends it with the mesh-based foreground weighted by accumulated transmittance. Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses. Optional foreground masks for scenes with empty backgrounds. A foreground mesh scaffold (typically extracted from Neuralangelo and Marching Cubes). For editing: User interactions (vertex selection, painting masks, semantic clicks). Outputs: Volume-rendered color images for novel views. Editable latent codes (geometry, texture, modification color, semantic) stored on mesh vertices. Per-Vertex Storage (on mesh scaffold): Each vertex v stores a set of learnable parameters: 1. Geometry Code (lg): Latent vector for geometry. 2. Texture Code (lt): Latent vector for appearance. 3. Modification Color (cm): View-independent, decoder-free color attribute for editing. 4. Semantic Code (ls): Latent vector storing semantic attributes (aggregated from open-vocabulary segmentation). Query Point Interpolated Attributes: For a query point x, the system retrieves interpolated values from K nearest vertices: Interpolated Geometry Code (lg(x)): 32 dimensions. Interpolated Texture Code (lt(x)): 32 dimensions. Local Indicator Vector (h(x)): Computed from spatial relationships (see Formulas). Decoders: Two separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Geometry Decoder (FG): Decodes density \sigma. 2. Radiance Decoder (FR): Decodes base color c. 1. Mesh Acquisition: Extract a foreground mesh from an external reconstruction method (e.g., Neuralangelo) using Marching Cubes. The mesh serves as the scaffold for latent codes. 2. Occupancy Grid Initialization: Initialize an occupancy grid using the mesh scaffold to guide ray sampling, bypassing unoccupied space. Update this grid if the mesh is deformed. 3. Ray Casting and Sampling: Cast rays from camera viewpoints. Sample N points along each ray. NeuMesh++ uses 64 coarse points and 64 fine points (progressive up-sampling), totaling 128 samples per ray. Pre-compute near-far bounds based on ray-mesh intersections to accelerate this step. 4. Nearest Neighbor Search: For each query point x along a ray, find the K nearest vertices \{vk\}{k=1}^K from the mesh scaffold within a fixed radius. Default K=8. 5. Local Indicator Calculation: For each neighbor vk, calculate the local indicator vector hk to resolve spatial ambiguity (inner/outer distinction): Calculate normalized distance: wk = \frac{\|vk - x\|}{\sum{i=1}^K \|vi - x\|}. Calculate projection distance: pk = (vk - x) \cdot nk, where nk is the normal of vertex vk. Form local indicator: hk = (pk, wk). 6. Interpolation: Interpolate the vertex codes (lg, lt) based on spatial proximity to form inputs for the decoders. Local indicators (hk) are computed per neighbor and not interpolated. 7. Decoding: Feed lg and h into the Geometry Decoder FG to obtain density \sigma. Feed lt, h, viewing direction d, and vertex normal n into the Radiance Decoder FR to obtain base color c, then add the vertex-specific modification color cm: c{final} = c + cm. 8. Volume Rendering: Aggregate densities and colors using standard volume rendering equations: Opacity: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), where \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples. Transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Color: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai ci. 9. Background Blending (Unbounded Scenes): For unbounded scenes, render a background color \hat{C}(r){bg} using an implicit hash grid (following the NeuS approach). Blend foreground and background: \hat{C}(r){comp} = \hat{C}(r) T + \hat{C}(r){bg} (1 - T), where T is the accumulated transmittance of the NeuMesh++ foreground. 10. Training (Distillation-Free): NeuMesh++ does not require a pre-trained teacher model. It optimizes latent codes and decoders directly using photometric loss and regularization. Rendering Equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), \quad \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where \mathbf{r} is the ray, N is the number of samples, \sigmai is density, \mathbf{c}i is color, and \deltai is sample spacing. Local Indicator: wk = \frac{\|vk - x\|}{\sum{i=1}^K \|vi - x\|}, \quad pk = (vk - x) \cdot nk, \quad hk = (pk, wk) where vk is the k-th nearest vertex, nk is its normal, and x is the query point. Decoder Outputs: \sigmak = FG(\mathbf{l}k^g, \mathbf{h}k) \mathbf{c}k = FR(\mathbf{l}k^t, \mathbf{h}k, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{n}k) + \mathbf{c}k^m where \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction and \mathbf{c}k^m is the modification color. Loss Functions: 1. Photometric Loss: \mathcal{L}f = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \|\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + 0.01 \cdot \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \|\hat{C}^m(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 where C(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth color, and \hat{C}^m(\mathbf{r}) is the accumulated modification color. 2. Mask Loss (for empty backgrounds): Mm = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \text{BCE}(\hat{M}(\mathbf{r}), M(\mathbf{r})) where \hat{M}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai and M(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth mask. 3. Total Variation Loss: \mathcal{L}t = \sum{i=1}^N \sum{j \in \text{NR}(i)} |li - lj| where \text{NR}(i) contains the indices of the K{tv} closest vertices to vi. K (Nearest Neighbors): Number of vertices used for interpolation. Default: 8. Ktv: Number of closest vertices for Total Variation loss. Not given in the sources. Mesh Resolution: Marching Cubes voxel resolution 256, spatial range [-1, 1]. Positional Encoding Frequencies: Local indicators: 8 frequencies. Interpolated codes: 2 frequencies. Viewing directions: 4 frequencies. Geometry Decoder: 3 hidden layers, 256 hidden size, SoftPlus activation. Radiance Decoder: 4 hidden layers, 256 hidden size, ReLU activation. Samples per Ray: 128 total (64 coarse + 64 fine). Loss Weight: 0.01 for modification color photometric loss term. Rendering Resolution: 800 × 800 for performance benchmarks; 1600 × 1200 for DTU dataset training. Spatial Distinguishability: Naive trilinear interpolation of single-layer vertex codes fails to distinguish inner/outer queries perpendicular to the surface. NeuMesh++ resolves this with the local indicator vector hk (projection distance and normalized distance). Training Stability: Vertex-bounded representations lack the spatial continuity of MLP-based methods, risking unstable training. NeuMesh++ avoids the need for a teacher model (used in NeuMesh) by using the local space parameterization and Total Variation loss. View-Dependent Editing: Standard neural decoders limit the range of modifiable colors due to fixed weights and view conditioning. NeuMesh++ introduces a decoder-free, view-independent modification color (cm) per vertex to allow high-fidelity texture painting and swapping. Overfitting in Editing: Fine-tuning texture codes with a single image can cause artifacts in other views. NeuMesh++ uses a spatial-aware optimization strategy: it selects only the modification colors of vertices intersected by probing rays from painted pixels, fine-tuning only those to preserve other regions. Non-Watertight Meshes: The representation is agnostic to mesh topology (non-watertight, non-manifold) because it relies on local vertex neighborhoods rather than global surface continuity. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(x, freqs=8): """Standard positional encoding for input x.""" scales = np.array([2i for i in range(freqs)]) x = np.expanddims(x, axis=-1) scales return np.sin(x).flatten() def findknearestvertices(querypoint, vertices, K): """Finds K nearest vertices to querypoint.""" dists = np.linalg.norm(vertices - querypoint, axis=1) indices = np.argsort(dists)[:K] return indices def computeoccupancygridfrommesh(mesh): """Initializes occupancy grid using mesh bounding box and resolution.""" # Simplified: returns a boolean grid covering mesh bounds bounds = np.array([mesh.vertices.min(axis=0), mesh.vertices.max(axis=0)]) return np.zeros((32, 32, 32), dtype=bool) # Placeholder for actual grid logic def computeraymeshintersections(mesh, cameraposes): """Pre-computes near-far bounds for rays based on mesh intersections.""" # Simplified: returns min/max distances along ray directions return np.zeros((len(cameraposes), 2)) def generaterays(pose, imageshape): """Generates ray origins and directions from camera pose and image shape.""" # Simplified: origins = np.zeros((imageshape[0] imageshape[1], 3)) directions = np.zeros((imageshape[0] imageshape[1], 3)) return origins, directions def samplealongray(origins, directions, nearfarbounds, Ntotal): """Samples points along rays between near and far bounds.""" # Simplified: evenly spaced samples t = np.linspace(nearfarbounds[:, 0], nearfarbounds[:, 1], Ntotal) return origins[:, None,:] + directions[:, None,:] t[:,:, None] def neumeshplusplusrender(mesh, cameraposes, images, masks, geometrydecoder, radiancedecoder, K=8, numcoarse=64, numfine=64): """ NeuMesh++ Rendering and Training Loop. Args: mesh: Object containing vertices V, normals N, and latent codes (lg, lt, cm, ls). cameraposes: List of camera extrinsics/intrinsics. images: Ground truth images. masks: Ground truth foreground masks (optional). geometrydecoder: MLP FG. radiancedecoder: MLP FR. K: Number of nearest neighbors. numcoarse: Number of coarse samples. numfine: Number of fine samples. Returns: Rendered images, losses. """ # 1. Initialize Occupancy Grid from Mesh occupancygrid = computeoccupancygridfrommesh(mesh) # 2. Pre-compute Near-Far Bounds for Rays nearfarbounds = computeraymeshintersections(mesh, cameraposes) renderedimages = [] totalloss = 0 for pose, gtimage, gtmask in zip(cameraposes, images, masks): rayorigins, raydirections = generaterays(pose, gtimage.shape) N = len(rayorigins) renderedraycolors = np.zeros((N, 3)) # Combine coarse and fine samples Ntotal = numcoarse + numfine sampledistances = samplealongray(rayorigins, raydirections, nearfarbounds, Ntotal) # 3. Volume Rendering Loop for i in range(N): origin = rayorigins[i] direction = raydirections[i] # Get sample points along ray points = sampledistances[i] # Initialize accumulation variables Tacc = 1.0 coloracc = np.zeros(3) modcoloracc = np.zeros(3) for j, x in enumerate(points): # 4. Find K nearest vertices neighbors = findknearestvertices(x, mesh.vertices, K) # 5. Calculate Local Indicators and Interpolate densities = [] colors = [] modcolors = [] weights = [] for vidx in neighbors: v = mesh.vertices[vidx] n = mesh.normals[vidx] # Local Indicator Calculation distvec = v - x distnorm = np.linalg.norm(distvec) # Normalized distance sumdists = sum(np.linalg.norm(mesh.vertices[k] - x) for k in neighbors) wk = distnorm / sumdists if sumdists > 0 else 0 # Projection distance pk = np.dot(distvec, n) hk = np.array([pk, wk]) # Interpolate Codes (Weighted by inverse distance) weight = 1.0 / (distnorm + 1e-8) weights.append(weight) lginterp = mesh.lg[vidx] ltinterp = mesh.lt[vidx] cminterp = mesh.cm[vidx] # Positional Encoding hpe = positionalencoding(hk, freqs=8) lgpe = positionalencoding(lginterp, freqs=2) ltpe = positionalencoding(ltinterp, freqs=2) dpe = positionalencoding(direction, freqs=4) # 6. Decode sigma = geometrydecoder.forward(np.concatenate([lgpe, hpe])) basecolor = radiancedecoder.forward(np.concatenate([ltpe, hpe, dpe, n])) # Add modification color finalcolor = basecolor + cminterp densities.append(sigma) colors.append(finalcolor) modcolors.append(cminterp) # Fuse densities and colors from neighbors using weights totalweight = sum(weights) normweights = [w / totalweight for w in weights] sigmafinal = sum(d w for d, w in zip(densities, normweights)) colorfinal = sum(c w for c, w in zip(colors, normweights)) modcolorfinal = sum(m w for m, w in zip(modcolors, normweights)) # 7. Volume Rendering Step delta = sampledistances[i][j+1] - sampledistances[i][j] if j < Ntotal-1 else 0 alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmafinal delta) Tacc = (1.0 - alpha) coloracc += Tacc alpha colorfinal modcoloracc += Tacc alpha modcolorfinal if Tacc < 1e-4: break renderedraycolors[i] = coloracc renderedimages.append(renderedraycolors) # 8. Loss Calculation # Photometric Loss lossf = np.mean((renderedraycolors - gtimage) 2) # Accumulated modification color loss lossmod = 0.01 np.mean((modcoloracc - gtimage) 2) # Mask Loss # Mhat = sum(Ti alphai) # Mm = BCE(Mhat, M) lossmask = 0 # Placeholder for BCE calculation # Total Variation Loss (on latent codes) losstv = computetotalvariationloss(mesh, Ktv=10) totalloss += lossf + lossmod + lossmask + losstv return renderedimages, totalloss def computetotalvariationloss(mesh, Ktv=10): """ Computes Total Variation loss on latent codes. """ loss = 0 for i, vi in enumerate(mesh.vertices): neighbors = findknearestvertices(vi, mesh.vertices, Ktv) for j in neighbors: li = mesh.lg[i] lj = mesh.lg[j] loss += np.sum(np.abs(li - lj)) return loss Time Complexity: Rendering speed is approximately 15 fps on an Nvidia GTX 4070 GPU for 800×800 images. This is achieved by using compact latent codes, lightweight decoders, and an occupancy grid to skip unoccupied space. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of latent codes per vertex. For a mesh with 50K–150K vertices, this is significantly less than storing a dense voxel grid or a large hash grid for the entire scene. Performance: Outperforms BakedSDF quantitatively on the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, particularly in high-frequency details. Editing Efficiency: Geometry editing: ~1 second to update the occupancy grid after mesh deformation. Texture painting: ~1 second for fine-tuning modification colors. Semantic-guided editing: ~2 seconds for 3D semantic propagation. Texture swapping/filling: Immediate rendering without fine-tuning. Strengths: Enables fine-grained, mesh-guided editing (geometry, texture, semantics). No need for UV mapping. Agnostic to mesh topology (non-watertight). High-fidelity rendering of complex geometry and textures. Training stability without a pre-trained teacher model. Limitations: Requires an initial mesh scaffold (e.g., from Neuralangelo). Performance depends on mesh quality and vertex density. May suffer from artifacts if editing is not spatially aware (mitigated by the proposed strategy). Origin: NeuMesh++ is an extension of NeuMesh, published in TPAMI in 2025. Development: NeuMesh used a distillation approach from a pre-trained implicit SDF field (NeuS) to stabilize training but suffered from spatial ambiguity and limited editing fidelity. NeuMesh++ rebuilds the representation on the neural radiance field directly, introducing local space parameterization and modification colors to remove the need for distillation and improve editing. Usage: Evaluated on the DTU dataset (15 scenes) and NeRF 360 Synthetic dataset. Used for applications requiring interactive 3D editing, such as texture swapping, filling, painting, and semantic-guided manipulation. name: Structured Latent Codes Anchored to Mesh
head: anchor mesh latent codes, l_geo / l_rgb
body: This method stores structured geometry (l{geo}) and appearance (l{rgb}) latent codes at anchor nodes (typically mesh vertices) on a deformable mesh, enabling local editing and deformation tracking. It solves the ambiguity of point-to-latent mapping in 3D space by anchoring codes to a mesh surface, allowing the density field to track vertex movements for geometry editing. Unlike sibling methods that may use global parametric controls or unstructured point clouds, this approach leverages the mesh structure to support fine-grained, local manipulations such as bulges or texture transfers while maintaining 3D consistency. Inputs: A canonical mesh (e.g., SMPL in rest pose) defining anchor nodes (vertices); a 3D query point xt in target pose; Top-K nearest anchor vertices \{vi\}{i=1}^K; and pre-trained latent codes l{geo}^i, l{rgb}^i stored at each anchor node. Outputs: Interpolated latent codes l{geo}, l{rgb} for the query point; deformed position LBS(xt). Data Structures: Anchor Mesh: A set of vertices V. Each vertex vi has an associated latent code vector. Latent Codes: Vectors l{geo}^i, l{rgb}^i \in \mathbb{R}^{32} stored at each vertex vi. Steps: 1. Identify Nearest Anchors: For a query point xt in the target pose, determine the K nearest vertices \{vi\}{i=1}^K on the canonical mesh. 2. Compute Weights: Calculate inverse distance weights wi for each neighbor: wi = \frac{1}{\|xt - vi\|^2} Normalize weights to sum to 1: \tilde{w}i = \frac{wi}{\sum{j=1}^K wj}. 3. Interpolate Latent Codes: Compute the interpolated geometry and appearance codes using the normalized weights: l{geo} = \sum{i=1}^K \tilde{w}i l{geo}^i l{rgb} = \sum{i=1}^K \tilde{w}i l{rgb}^i. 4. Deform Position (Optional for Rendering): To obtain the deformed position for rendering, interpolate the Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) weights b^i from the anchor nodes using the same weights \tilde{w}i, then apply the skinning transformation: LBS(xt) = \left( \sum{i=1}^K \tilde{w}i B^i \right)^{-1} xt where B^i is the skinning matrix for vertex i. 5. Resolve Ambiguity (Signed Height): To handle points perpendicular to the surface, introduce a local signed height indicator \tilde{h} based on the signed distance and UV coordinates of xt, mapping the 3D point to a 2.5D volume. Parameters: Latent Dimension: 32 for both l{geo} and l{rgb}. K: Number of nearest neighbors (Not given in the sources). Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying to 5 \times 10^{-6} for networks; 10\times higher for latent codes. Edge Cases: Perpendicular Ambiguity: Points along the normal direction may have identical latent codes but different positions. Boundary Effects: For texture painting, masks are dilated to ensure smooth boundaries during fine-tuning. Texture swapping transfers appearance latent codes from a source mesh area to a target mesh area within a trained Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA) or similar neural mesh representation. It solves the problem of reusing textures between objects with slightly different geometries by performing non-rigid 3D alignment of anchor nodes (mesh vertices). Unlike Texture Painting, which modifies appearance directly on a single model, swapping operates between two distinct trained models or areas, leveraging pre-blended latent codes for better 3D consistency. Texture painting is a method for locally editing the appearance of a 3D avatar or mesh by fine-tuning specific latent codes to match a 2D input painting. It solves the problem of transferring 2D artistic intent to a 3D neural representation while preserving the geometry and appearance of unedited regions. Unlike global texture replacement, it operates on a sparse set of anchor nodes, allowing for independent, spatial-aware local edits. Definition: An editing technique allowing local manipulation of avatar geometry by moving anchor nodes on the mesh, with the density field tracking these movements. Steps: 1. Users move anchor nodes in 3D modeling software (e.g., Blender) or using mesh deforming methods (e.g., ARAP). 2. Copy movements of corresponding vertices from the canonical mesh to the target mesh to deform the skinning field in sync for animation. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of mesh vertices (anchor nodes) and the latent dimension (32). Interpolation is O(K) per query point, where K is the number of neighbors. Training requires joint optimization of motion and canonical fields (e.g., 300K iterations). Measured Performance: Training takes about 10 hours using two NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs for 9 performers from the ZJU-MoCap dataset with a batch size of 1024. Strengths: Enables local geometry editing (e.g., bulges) and texture painting while maintaining 3D consistency and novel view synthesis. The mesh-based skinning field allows synchronized deformation for animation. Limitations: Interpolation alone can lead to ambiguity for points perpendicular to the surface, requiring additional indicators like signed height. Fine-tuning the texture decoder locally is non-trivial. Originated in the Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA) method. The method builds on the idea that a skinning field is naturally a mesh-based representation, making it possible to track vertex movements and desired geometry editing. It uses parametric models like SMPL as the anchored mesh baseline. UVA: Towards Unified Volumetric Avatar for View Synthesis, Pose rendering, Geometry and Texture Editing, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2304.06969, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Texture Swapping
head: Texture transfer
body: Texture swapping transfers appearance latent codes from a source mesh area to a target mesh area within trained neural mesh representations. It solves the problem of reusing textures between objects with slightly different geometries by performing non-rigid 3D alignment of anchor nodes. Unlike Texture Painting, which modifies appearance directly on a single model, swapping operates between two distinct trained models or areas, leveraging pre-blended latent codes for better 3D consistency. Inputs: Source mesh area: A set of vertices VS and their associated latent codes CS from a trained source model. Target mesh area: A set of vertices VT and their associated latent codes CT from a trained target model. Correspondences: A set of K point pairs (pi^S, pi^T) where pi^S \in VS and pi^T \in VT, with K \in [4, 9]. Outputs: Updated latent codes CT' for the target vertices, allowing the target area to display the source texture. Data Structures: Mesh vertices: 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Latent codes: Vectors c stored at anchor nodes (mesh vertices). Steps: 1. Selection: Select source and target areas by choosing mesh vertices in a 3D editor (e.g., Blender). 2. Annotation: Annotate K point correspondences between the source and target areas. 3. Initial Alignment (Umeyama): Compute a scaled rigid transformation T{scale} that aligns the source correspondences to the target correspondences using the Umeyama algorithm. This minimizes the least-squares error between the point sets. 4. Non-Rigid Deformation (ARAP): Calculate the residual transformation for each corresponding point pair after applying T{scale}. Use As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation to deform the entire source mesh area VS to match the target shape, producing deformed source vertices VS'. 5. Code Interpolation: For each target vertex vj \in VT, identify the 4 nearest neighbors in the deformed source vertices VS'. 6. Code Assignment: Compute the new latent code cj' for vj using inverse distance weighting (IDW) of the latent codes from the 4 nearest deformed source vertices. cj' = \frac{\sum{k=1}^{4} wk ck'}{\sum{k=1}^{4} wk} where ck' is the latent code of the k-th nearest deformed source vertex, and wk = \frac{1}{dk} is the weight based on the Euclidean distance dk between vj and the k-th source vertex. 7. Decoding: Decode the updated latent codes CT' using the source decoder to render the swapped texture, as the pre-blended method is chosen for better 3D consistency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def textureswap(sourceverts, targetverts, sourcecodes, targetcodes, correspondences): # correspondences: list of (srcidx, tgtidx) # Step 3: Scaled rigid alignment (Umeyama) srcpts = [sourceverts[i] for i, in correspondences] tgtpts = [targetverts[i] for, i in correspondences] scale, rot, trans = umeyama(srcpts, tgtpts) # Apply rigid transform to all source vertices deformedverts = [] for v in sourceverts: rv = [sum(rot[j][k]v[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] deformedverts.append([rv[j] + trans[j] for j in range(3)]) # Step 4: Non-rigid deformation (ARAP) residuals = [] for srci, tgti in correspondences: tsrc = deformedverts[srci] tgtv = targetverts[tgti] residuals.append([tgtv[j] - tsrc[j] for j in range(3)]) deformedverts = arap(deformedverts, sourceverts, residuals, correspondences) # Step 5 & 6: Code interpolation updatedcodes = [] for i, tgtv in enumerate(targetverts): neighbors = knearest(tgtv, deformedverts, k=4) if not neighbors: updatedcodes.append(targetcodes[i]) continue weights = [] codes = [] for nidx in neighbors: d = dist(tgtv, deformedverts[nidx]) weights.append(1.0 / (d + 1e-6)) codes.append(sourcecodes[nidx]) wsum = sum(weights) newc = [0.0] len(sourcecodes[0]) for w, c in zip(weights, codes): for d in range(len(c)): newc[d] += w c[d] for d in range(len(newc)): newc[d] /= wsum updatedcodes.append(newc) return updatedcodes def dist(a, b): return sum((x - y) 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) 0.5 def knearest(p, pts, k): return [i for, i in sorted([(dist(p, pt), i) for i, pt in enumerate(pts)])[:k]] def umeyama(src, tgt): n = len(src) srcc = [sum(p[j] for p in src)/n for j in range(3)] tgtc = [sum(p[j] for p in tgt)/n for j in range(3)] srcc = [[p[j] - srcc[j] for j in range(3)] for p in src] tgtc = [[p[j] - tgtc[j] for j in range(3)] for p in tgt] H = [[sum(srcc[i][j]tgtc[i][k] for i in range(n)) for k in range(3)] for j in range(3)] U, S, Vt = svd3x3(H) d = 1 if det3x3(U)det3x3(Vt) > 0 else -1 D = [[S[i] if i==j else 0 for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] D[2][2] = d R = matmul(U, matmul(D, Vt)) scale = sum(S) / sum(sum((p[j]-srcc[j])2 for j in range(3)) for p in src) trans = [tgtc[j] - sum(R[j][k]srcc[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] return scale, R, trans def arap(current, original, residuals, correspondences): # Standard ARAP: solves for local rigid transforms minimizing deviation from original # then updates positions to satisfy residuals newverts = [list(v) for v in current] for i in range(len(original)): neighbors = getneighbors(i, original) if not neighbors: continue Hi = [[sum((current[n][j]-current[i][j])(original[n][k]-original[i][k]) for n in neighbors) for k in range(3)] for j in range(3)] U, S, Vt = svd3x3(Hi) d = 1 if det3x3(U)det3x3(Vt) > 0 else -1 D = [[S[j] if j==k else 0 for k in range(3)] for j in range(3)] D[2][2] = d Ri = matmul(U, matmul(D, Vt)) for n in neighbors: diff = [newverts[n][j] - newverts[i][j] for j in range(3)] rotdiff = [sum(Ri[j][k]diff[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] newverts[n] = [newverts[i][j] + rotdiff[j] for j in range(3)] return newverts def getneighbors(idx, verts): # Returns indices of adjacent vertices (e.g., from mesh connectivity) return [i for i, v in enumerate(verts) if i != idx and dist(verts[idx], v) < 1e-3] def svd3x3(M): # Standard 3x3 SVD implementation # Returns U, S, Vt pass def det3x3(M): return M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0]) def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k]B[k][j] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] Parameters: Number of correspondences: 4 to 9 points. Nearest neighbors for interpolation: 4. Weighting scheme: Inverse distance weighting. Edge Cases: Precision: Ensure distance calculations use sufficient precision to avoid division by zero in IDW. Boundaries: The method assumes the source and target areas can be reasonably aligned. Time Complexity: Dominated by the ARAP deformation and nearest neighbor search. ARAP is typically solved iteratively. Nearest neighbor search is O(N \log N) or O(N) with spatial indexing. Memory Complexity: Requires storing latent codes for all vertices in the source and target areas. Strengths: Provides better 3D consistency than pose-dependent inference methods by using pre-blended codes. Allows local editing without global shape parameter changes. Limitations: Requires manual annotation of correspondences (though automation is possible). Texture swapping was introduced in the context of Unified Volumetric Avatars (UVA) and NeuMesh for geometry and texture editing. The method leverages Umeyama alignment for initial rigid transformation and ARAP for non-rigid deformation. name: Texture Painting
head: local texture editing
body: Texture painting is a method for locally editing the appearance of a 3D avatar or mesh by fine-tuning specific latent codes to match a 2D input painting. It solves the problem of transferring 2D artistic intent to a 3D neural representation while preserving the geometry and appearance of unedited regions. It operates on a subset of anchor nodes, allowing for independent, spatial-aware local edits. Inputs: A 2D painting image, a binary mask indicating the region to edit, the current mesh scaffold (vertices and faces), and the neural implicit field parameters (shading network, signed height indicator, and latent codes). Outputs: Updated latent codes for the affected anchor nodes. Data Structures: Mesh Scaffold: Defined by vertices V and faces F, where each vertex vi stores an anchor latent code ci. Binary Mask: A 2D image M where M(u,v)=1 if the pixel (u,v) is painted, 0 otherwise. Neural Field Parameters: Shading network f{\text{shade}}, non-trainable signed height indicator h, and latent codes C = \{ci\}. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Shoot probing rays from the camera through the painted pixels in the 2D painting image towards the mesh scaffold. 2. Hit Detection: Identify the faces hit by these rays. Collect all vertices of the hit faces to determine the set of affected anchor nodes V{\text{affected}}. 3. Mask Dilation: Dilate the binary mask M slightly to create a boundary region. 4. Training Ray Sampling: Sample training rays using the dilated mask. This ensures smooth texture boundaries by including pixels adjacent to the painted region in the optimization. 5. Optimization Setup: Fix the shading network parameters. Fix the latent codes for all nodes vj \notin V{\text{affected}}. Enable gradient updates only for latent codes ci where vi \in V{\text{affected}}. 6. Loss Function: Minimize the difference between the rendered pixel values and the target painting pixel values. The pixel value is determined by the interpolated latent code, the local signed height indicator, and the shading factor. 7. Learning Rate Adjustment: Use a higher learning rate for the latent codes compared to other parameters to prevent the non-trainable signed height indicator from dominating the optimization. Specifically, increase the learning rate gap further during texture painting compared to standard training. 8. Iteration: Repeat steps 5-7 for a fixed number of iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texturepainting(paintingimg, mask, meshV, meshF, latentcodes, shadingnet, signedheight, lrcode, numiters=8000): # 1. Identify affected nodes via ray casting hitfaces = [] for u, v in zip(np.where(mask > 0)): rayorigin = cameraprojection(u, v) raydir = normalize(rayorigin - cameracenter) hit = raytriangleintersection(rayorigin, raydir, meshV, meshF) if hit is not None: hitfaces.append(hit.faceid) affectedV = set() for fid in hitfaces: affectedV.update(meshF[fid].vertices) # 2. Prepare optimizer state trainablemask = {v: (v in affectedV) for v in meshV} for v in meshV: if not trainablemask[v]: latentcodes[v].requiresgrad = False # 3. Dilate mask for smooth boundaries dilatedmask = morphologicaldilate(mask, kernelsize=3) # 4. Optimization loop optimizer = Adam([latentcodes[v] for v in affectedV], lr=lrcode) for i in range(numiters): rays = sampleraysthroughmask(dilatedmask) renderedcolors = [] targetcolors = [] for ray in rays: cinterp = interpolatelatents(ray.hitpoint, meshV, meshF, latentcodes) color = shadingnet(cinterp, signedheight[ray.faceid]) renderedcolors.append(color) targetcolors.append(paintingimg[ray.u, ray.v]) loss = mseloss(renderedcolors, targetcolors) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return latentcodes (Note: Helper functions cameraprojection, raytriangleintersection, morphologicaldilate, sampleraysthroughmask, interpolatelatents, mseloss, and Adam are standard operations.) Parameters: Learning Rate (Latent Codes): Significantly higher than other parameters (e.g., 10 times higher than standard training). Iterations: 8000 iterations. Optimization Duration: ~1 hour on the reported hardware. Optimizer: Adam. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting to Signed Height: The texture decoder may overfit to the non-trainable signed height indicator during single-image fine-tuning, generating artifacts at other positions. This is mitigated by increasing the learning rate gap. Boundary Artifacts: Without mask dilation, texture boundaries may appear sharp or aliased. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. Empirically, optimization takes ~1 hour for 8000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. Only a subset of latent codes are updated during optimization. Strengths: Allows precise, local 2D-to-3D texture transfer; preserves geometry and unedited appearance; supports novel view synthesis of edited textures. Limitations: Requires a neural implicit field setup; optimization can be slow (~1 hour); risk of artifacts if learning rates are not tuned correctly. When to use: When local appearance editing is required without retraining the entire model or altering geometry. Texture painting was introduced in the context of Unified Volumetric Avatars (UVA) and NeuMesh for editing human avatars and 3D objects. It addresses the challenge of disentangling geometry and appearance in neural implicit fields to allow for fine-grained editing. Previous methods relied on neural texture map replacement or separate implicit fields, which lacked the flexibility of this approach. name: Volume Relaxation
head: Heuristic-based generalization, relaxed variant, relaxed volumetric version
body: Volume Relaxation is a heuristic optimization strategy that allows a surface-based radiance field to revert to volumetric alpha blending in challenging regions (e.g., sub-pixel structures, directional materials) where the opaque surface assumption is insufficient, while retaining surface-like properties elsewhere. It differs from its siblings, such as Neural Surfel Radiance Fields and Unified Neural Implicit Surface and Radiance Field Rendering, by dynamically switching the loss supervision mode per sample based on a local heuristic, rather than using a fixed hybrid representation or separate surface/volume branches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained surface representation (e.g., from Hybrid Surface-Volume and Mesh Representation), a set of rays, and target pixel colors L{\text{target}}. Output: Gradients for the surface representation parameters, updated to minimize the relaxed loss. Data Structures: The method operates on standard ray-marching data structures. For each ray, a sequence of samples i=1 \dots m is evaluated. Each sample i yields: \alphai: Opacity (Heaviside-like for surface regions, continuous for relaxed regions). Li: Radiance (color) at the sample point. T{\text{prev}}: Transmittance from the camera to sample i, defined as T{\text{prev}} = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Surface Training: Train the surface representation for 20,000 iterations using the standard radiance field loss (Equation 8 in), which enforces the surface assumption. 2. Identify Challenging Regions: During subsequent training steps, evaluate the local loss for each sample to identify regions where the surface assumption fails. 3. Compute Modified Target Color: For each sample i, calculate the modified target color L{\text{goal}} which accounts for the color contribution of prior samples and the transmittance: L{\text{goal}} = \frac{L{\text{target}} - L{\text{prev}}}{T{\text{prev}}} = \frac{L{\text{target}} - \sum{j=1}^{i-1} \left( \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) \right) \alphaj Lj}{\prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj)} where L{\text{prev}} is the accumulated color from prior samples. 4. Heuristic Comparison: Compare the local loss without blending against the local loss with blending: Unblended Loss: \ell(Li, L{\text{goal}}) Blended Loss: \ell \left( \alphai Li + (1 - \alphai) \mathbb{E}{t > ti}[Lt], L{\text{goal}} \right) If \ell(Li, L{\text{goal}}) \leq \ell \left( \alphai Li + (1 - \alphai) \mathbb{E}{t > ti}[Lt], L{\text{goal}} \right), use the unblended loss term for sample i. Otherwise, use the blended loss term. Note: \mathbb{E}{t > ti}[Lt] represents the expected radiance of subsequent samples. In practice, this is often approximated or treated as a background color if not explicitly modeled, but the heuristic compares the potential blended result against the direct sample result. 5. Accumulate Ray Loss: Sum the weighted local losses for all samples i=1 \dots m along the ray: \mathcal{L}{\text{ray}}^{\text{vol}} = \sum{i=1}^m \left[ T{\text{prev}} \cdot \ell{\text{local}}(i) \right] where \ell{\text{local}}(i) is the chosen loss term (blended or unblended) for sample i. 6. Backpropagation: Compute gradients and update the model parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumerelaxationloss(rays, model, Ltarget, errormetric): """ Computes the volume relaxation loss for a batch of rays. Args: rays: List of ray origins and directions. model: The surface radiance field model. Ltarget: Target pixel colors for the rays. errormetric: Function l(a, b) computing the error between prediction a and target b. Returns: Total loss scalar. """ totalloss = 0.0 for ray, targetcolor in zip(rays, Ltarget): rayloss = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # Standard ray marching loop # Note: The number of samples m and their positions ti are determined by the sampling strategy # For surface methods, this often involves adaptive sampling or fixed steps near the surface. # We assume a list of samples (ti, alphai, Li) is generated by evalmodel. samples = [] tcurrent = ray.origin + ray.direction mint while tcurrent < ray.maxt: alpha, L = model.evaluate(ray, tcurrent) samples.append((tcurrent, alpha, L)) tcurrent += stepsize # Or adaptive step # Process samples in order (front to back) for i, (ti, alphai, Li) in enumerate(samples): # Calculate transmittance to current sample Tprev = transmittance # Calculate accumulated color from prior samples Lprev = accumulatedcolor # Calculate modified target color Lgoal # Avoid division by zero if Tprev is very small if Tprev < 1e-6: # If transmittance is effectively zero, the sample is occluded. # The loss contribution should be negligible or handled via gradient stopping. # Standard practice: if Tprev is near zero, skip gradient contribution # or treat Lgoal as undefined. We set localloss to 0. localloss = 0.0 else: Lgoal = (targetcolor - Lprev) / Tprev # Calculate expected radiance of subsequent samples # In many implementations, if no further samples are taken or # background is not modeled, E[Lt] might be assumed to be 0 or a # constant background color. The source implies it's part of the # blended term. For a pure surface method, subsequent samples are # often transparent. We assume a background color Lbg if needed, # or 0 if the volume is empty. # Here we assume Lbg is 0 for simplicity unless specified. Lbg = 0.0 ELsubsequent = Lbg # Unblended loss: sample matches Lgoal directly lossunblended = errormetric(Li, Lgoal) # Blended loss: sample contributes to a blended color # Blended color = alphai Li + (1 - alphai) ELsubsequent blendedcolor = alphai Li + (1 - alphai) ELsubsequent lossblended = errormetric(blendedcolor, Lgoal) # Heuristic: choose the smaller loss if lossunblended <= lossblended: localloss = lossunblended else: localloss = lossblended # Weight by transmittance rayloss += Tprev localloss # Update accumulated color and transmittance for next sample accumulatedcolor += Tprev alphai Li transmittance = (1 - alphai) totalloss += rayloss return totalloss / len(rays) Parameters: Initial Training Iterations: 20,000 iterations for the initial surface-only phase. Error Metric \ell: Typically L1 or L2 loss. Overhead: The heuristic comparison introduces no additional computational overhead, as all necessary values (\alphai, Li, T{\text{prev}}, L{\text{prev}}) are computed during the standard ray marching pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-Relaxation: When applied to refine a converged surface scene, the relaxed loss often converts the entire scene into a volumetric representation, even in visually adequate regions. This occurs because fitting colors in a volume (with more degrees of freedom) reduces the loss more easily than fitting colors on a surface. The heuristic is designed to mitigate this but may not prevent it entirely in highly underconstrained scenes. Division by Zero: If transmittance T{\text{prev}} becomes very small (near zero), L{\text{goal}} becomes numerically unstable. A guard condition is required. Expected Radiance: The term \mathbb{E}{t > ti}[Lt] requires a model for subsequent samples. If the scene is treated as opaque surfaces, subsequent samples are transparent, making the blended term effectively just \alphai Li. However, in relaxed regions, this term allows for volumetric blending. The exact implementation of this expectation depends on the background model or further sampling. Time Complexity: Comparable to standard NeRF or surface-based training, as the heuristic adds no extra passes. However, the initial 20,000 iterations are surface-only, after which the relaxation is applied. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond standard ray marching buffers. Performance: Empirically performs well as a volume reconstruction algorithm in challenging regions while preserving surface properties elsewhere. Convergence rate is comparable to NeRF in the Instant NGP codebase, though it may have a longer tail in the loss curve due to spawning more rays per iteration. Strengths: Handles sub-pixel structures and directional materials better than pure surface methods; retains sharp surface details in well-constrained regions. Limitations: Risk of over-relaxation; heuristic is not a fundamental part of the method and results may vary. When to Use: When refining a surface representation in regions with complex geometry or material properties that violate the opaque surface assumption. When Not to Use: When the scene is well-constrained and purely surface-based; or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of the heuristic (though minimal) is unacceptable. Origin: Proposed in "Radiance Surfaces: Optimizing Surface Representations with a 5D Radiance Field Loss". History: Developed as an optional, heuristic-based generalization to the core Radiance Surfaces method to handle limitations of the opaque surface assumption. Usage: Implemented in the Instant NGP and ZipNeRF codebases for novel view synthesis and geometry reconstruction experiments. Radiance Surfaces: Optimizing Surface Representations with a 5D Radiance Field Loss, https://doi.org/10.1145/3721238.3730713, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dynamic and Deformation Modeling
body: Dynamic and Deformation Modeling extends static Neural Radiance Fields to reconstruct time-varying scenes from multi-view video or sparse image collections, solving the problem of novel view synthesis for non-static content. It sets itself apart from static NeRF variants by explicitly incorporating temporal information, either through direct time-conditioned radiance fields or by warping spatial coordinates to a canonical space, allowing for the coherent reconstruction of moving objects that would otherwise appear inconsistent in a static model. Builds on Neural Radiance Fields. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). Deformation Field Parametrization methods map 3D spatial coordinates from a dynamic, time-varying state to a static canonical space (or vice versa) to enable the rendering of dynamic scenes using static neural radiance fields. This approach solves the problem of modeling non-rigid, time-varying geometry without requiring a separate radiance field for every time step. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by the specific mathematical representation of the deformation field: while some use cubic B-splines for sparse data efficiency, others use MLPs guided by parametric models like 3DMMs or inverse Linear Blend Skinning with neural residuals. Choose this when explicit geometric warping is preferred over direct temporal conditioning. Dynamic Scene Representation methods extend static radiance fields to model temporal variations, enabling novel view synthesis of non-static scenes. Unlike static methods, these approaches incorporate time or scene variables as inputs to the neural field or deformation operators to predict density and color for specific moments. They differ from sibling methods like Deformation Field Parametrization by explicitly handling the evolution of geometry and appearance over time, often through shared networks, explicit temporal interpolation, or deformation fields. Choose this when direct temporal conditioning or shared network architectures are sufficient for the scene's dynamics. Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies) reconstructs non-rigidly deforming scenes by decomposing the scene into a static canonical template volume (a standard NeRF) and a per-observation continuous deformation field that maps observation-space coordinates to canonical-space coordinates. Unlike methods that condition deformation on time or define it on discrete meshes/voxels, Nerfies conditions the deformation on a learned per-frame latent code and models the deformation as a continuous function using an MLP. It distinguishes itself from siblings by introducing elastic regularization to resolve ambiguities between motion and scaling, and a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy to avoid local minima. Choose this for high-quality reconstruction of non-rigid human deformation or elastic objects. JointRF is a compact residual feature grid representation for dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that handles large motions and long sequences by decomposing the radiance field into a long-reference basis feature grid and a coefficient feature grid. Unlike canonical space methods that warp features back to a static canonical space—making them fragile to large motions and topological changes—JointRF uses residual grids to capture temporal variations, thereby diminishing temporal redundancy and improving compression efficiency. Choose this when dealing with long sequences or large motions where canonical warping fails. D-TensoRF is a dynamic radiance field model that maps 3D location, viewing direction, and time instant to emitted color and volume density using factorized 4D/5D tensor grids. It extends TensoRF by incorporating a time dimension and applying Matrix-Matrix decomposition to reduce memory complexity. Unlike Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies), which rely on explicit deformation fields to warp static coordinates, D-TensoRF models temporal dynamics directly within the tensor structure, augmented by smoothing regularization to enforce temporal dependency. Choose this when memory efficiency and direct temporal modeling in tensor grids are prioritized over explicit deformation fields. The SE(3) Deformation Field encodes scene deformation as a rigid transformation (rotation and translation) per point using a screw axis representation. It replaces per-point translation fields to simplify optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space, rather than distinct translation vectors for each point. This method is primarily used in dynamic scene reconstruction to handle rotational motion more efficiently than pure translation-based deformation fields. Choose this when scenes exhibit significant rigid rotational motion and a simpler optimization landscape is desired. The extension of NeRF to dynamic scenes originated with the recognition that static radiance fields cannot represent temporal changes. Early approaches focused on direct time-conditioning, where the temporal variable is concatenated with spatial coordinates to predict density and color. Subsequent work introduced deformation fields to handle non-rigid motion, mapping points from observation space to a canonical space to leverage static NeRF priors. These methods are primarily used in novel view synthesis for video, 4D reconstruction, and dynamic scene analysis. Radiance Field Optimization, URL, date fetched

name: Deformation Field Parametrization
body: Deformation Field Parametrization methods map 3D spatial coordinates from a dynamic, time-varying state to a static canonical space (or vice versa) to enable the rendering of dynamic scenes using static neural radiance fields. This approach solves the problem of modeling non-rigid, time-varying geometry without requiring a separate radiance field for every time step. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by the specific mathematical representation of the deformation field: while some use cubic B-splines for sparse data efficiency Spline-based Deformation Field, others use MLPs guided by parametric models like 3DMMs Deformation-Guided Neural Fields or inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) with neural residuals Neural Deformation Field. Builds on Dynamic and Deformation Modeling. This method parametrizes the deformation field in dynamic volume rendering using cubic B-splines with time-modulated weights to map spatial coordinates (x, y, z) at time t to canonical coordinates (x0, y0, z0) Spline-based Deformation Field. It enables the reconstruction of dynamic scenes from sparse projection data by combining a pre-trained canonical volume with the learned deformation field Spline-based Deformation Field. Unlike Neural Deformation Fields which rely on MLPs and complex regularization, this approach allows reconstruction from as few as two projections due to the efficient encoding provided by B-splines Spline-based Deformation Field. Deformation-Guided Neural Fields address the problem of modeling dynamic, articulated subjects (specifically human faces) in neural radiance fields by decoupling identity from pose and expression Deformation-Guided Neural Fields. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly guiding the deformation field MLP with a parametric 3D morphable model (3DMM), ensuring that the learned deformations adhere to anatomical priors rather than relying solely on unconstrained neural predictions Deformation-Guided Neural Fields.
