It solves the problem of animating static neural representations without relying on rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL Neural Deformation Field. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Deformation-Guided Neural Fields by explicitly decoupling the rigid skeletal transformation (LBS) from the residual non-rigid displacement predicted by a neural network Neural Deformation Field. Local Rotation Estimation via SVD is a technique used in dynamic neural radiance fields to correct view-dependent rendering artifacts caused by large rigid-body rotations during deformation Local Rotation Estimation via SVD. It estimates the local rotation for each point in a deformed point cloud using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), inspired by As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) mesh deformation Local Rotation Estimation via SVD. This estimated rotation is then interpolated to query view directions to "bend" rays, ensuring consistency between the deformed space and the canonical space representation Local Rotation Estimation via SVD. It differs from sibling methods like Neural Deformation Field by explicitly modeling rotational components of the deformation field rather than relying solely on translation or dense deformation vectors, thereby handling complex fine-level deformations without introducing extra complexity into the radiance field model itself Local Rotation Estimation via SVD. The Polynomial Motion Field is a parametric deformation model used in dynamic volume rendering to represent temporal motion as a continuous function of time. It solves the problem of reconstructing 4D (3D space + time) scenes from sparse or limited view measurements by warping a static template volume to arbitrary time points using polynomial coefficients. Unlike neural deformation fields that map (x, y, z, t) to displacement via a network, this method explicitly parameterizes the motion trajectory at each voxel as a polynomial, allowing for efficient optimization and arbitrary temporal upsampling. It differs from spline-based methods by using global polynomial bases rather than piecewise continuous splines, and from neural fields by avoiding the computational overhead of network inference during rendering Polynomial Motion Field. name: Spline-based Deformation Field
head: Cubic B-spline deformation, Time-modulated spline deformation
body: This method parametrizes the deformation field in dynamic volume rendering using cubic B-splines with time-modulated weights to map spatial coordinates (x, y, z) at time t to canonical coordinates (x0, y0, z0). It enables the reconstruction of dynamic scenes from sparse projection data by combining a pre-trained canonical volume with the learned deformation field. Unlike Neural Deformation Field which relies on MLPs and complex regularization, this approach allows reconstruction from as few as two projections due to the efficient encoding provided by B-splines. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse few-projection data recorded at intermediate times t during a dynamic experiment; a pre-trained canonical volume obtained from rich many-projection data via traditional computed tomography. Outputs: A deformation field \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{x}, t) that maps dynamic coordinates to canonical space, and full spatio-temporal volumetric information. Data Structures: The deformation field is represented by a cubic B-spline grid of control points. The temporal evolution is handled by time-modulated weights associated with these control points. Grid resolution and bit-packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Pre-training (Canonical Volume): Reconstruct a static canonical volume using traditional computed tomography from rich, many-projection data acquired at a reference state. 2. Deformation Field Calculation: For each time step t where sparse data is available, calculate the deformation field parameters from the sparse few-projection data. 3. Spatio-Temporal Reconstruction: Combine the canonical volume and the calculated deformation field to obtain full field spatio-temporal information. For any point \mathbf{x} at time t, the canonical coordinate is computed as \mathbf{x}0 = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{x}, t), and the density/color is queried from the canonical volume at \mathbf{x}0. Formulas: The sources describe the parametrization conceptually but do not provide the explicit mathematical formula for the cubic B-spline basis functions or the time-modulation weights. The general mapping is described as: \mathbf{x}0 = f(\mathbf{x}, t; \text{B-spline parameters}) where \mathbf{x}0 is the canonical coordinate. Parameters: Number of Projections: As few as two. B-spline Order: Cubic (degree 3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Changes: Deformation fields based on canonical models fail when the scene topology changes over time, as they assume topology-preserving motion. Sparse Data: The reconstruction quality depends on the pre-training of the canonical volume. Fully-differentiable variable-knot splines are used as measurement representations. They allow optimization of spline control points and control point weights via automatic differentiation. This variant is faster to fit and simpler to interpret than implicit neural networks, while performing equally well in reconstruction quality. It is used in contexts such as uncalibrated imaging where measurement coordinates are uncertain. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Splines are noted to be faster to fit than implicit neural networks. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables reconstruction from very sparse data (as few as two projections). Simpler to interpret than neural fields. Limitations: Fails for scenes with topological changes over time. Requires a pre-trained canonical volume from dense data. When to use: Dynamic tomography with sparse projections where topology is preserved. When not to use: Scenes with significant topological changes. Originated in the context of dynamic X-ray computed tomography (X-CT). The method combines traditional CT in data-rich regimes with neural rendering in data-sparse regimes. It addresses the trade-off between detail and acquisition time in tomography by allowing efficient encoding of tomographic data. name: Deformation-Guided Neural Fields
head: Deformation Field NeRF, Morphable Model Guided NeRF, RigNeRF
body: Deformation-Guided Neural Fields construct a fully 3D face portrait with controllable pose and expression using deformation field MLPs guided by a morphable 3D face model. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly guiding the deformation field with a parametric 3D morphable model (3DMM) rather than relying on unconstrained neural predictions. Inputs: Training images with known camera poses and 3DMM parameters. A pre-trained 3D Morphable Model (3DMM). Outputs: A trained neural field capable of rendering novel views of the face with arbitrary pose and expression. Data Structures: Deformation field MLP guided by a morphable 3D face model. Appearance field MLP for density and color prediction. Exact layouts, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Canonical Space Definition: Define the canonical space as the neutral expression state of the subject, using the 3DMM mean shape. 2. Deformation Field Evaluation: For a query point \mathbf{x}{\text{canon}} in canonical space, compute the deformation \Delta \mathbf{x} using the deformation field MLP, taking canonical coordinates and expression/pose parameters \theta derived from the 3DMM fit as input. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Map the canonical coordinate to the deformed space \mathbf{x}{\text{def}} by adding the computed deformation. 4. Appearance Query: Query the appearance field with the deformed coordinate \mathbf{x}{\text{def}} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to obtain density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. 5. Volume Rendering: Render the image using the standard emission-absorption model (see 44-radiance-field-optimization.md) with the sampled (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) values along rays. 6. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between rendered and ground-truth images. Formulas: Deformation: \Delta \mathbf{x} = \mathcal{M}{\text{def}}(\mathbf{x}{\text{canon}}, \theta), where \mathcal{M}{\text{def}} is the deformation MLP, \mathbf{x}{\text{canon}} are canonical coordinates, and \theta are 3DMM coefficients. Transformed coordinate: \mathbf{x}{\text{def}} = \mathbf{x}{\text{canon}} + \Delta \mathbf{x}. Appearance query: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \mathcal{M}{\text{app}}(\mathbf{x}{\text{def}}, \mathbf{d}), where \mathcal{M}{\text{app}} is the appearance MLP, \sigma is density, \mathbf{c} is color, and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. Parameters: 3DMM coefficients (pose, expression): Not given in the sources. MLP hidden layers: Not given in the sources. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fitting Errors: If the 3DMM fit to the input images is inaccurate, the canonical space definition may be misaligned, leading to artifacts. A common mitigation is to include a mask supervision loss to ensure the rendered alpha channel aligns with the subject's silhouette. Degenerate Input: Extreme expressions outside the 3DMM basis may cause extrapolation errors in the deformation field. Canonical Face Space Transformation normalizes world coordinates to a canonical face space using a rigid transform to address face shape variations between training data and real-world inputs, making the NeRF robust to geometry and pose variations. It sets itself apart from methods that rely on detailed mesh priors or non-rigid deformation fields by using only a rigid alignment derived from a mean geometry, avoiding the need for mesh details during view synthesis. Choose it when rigid alignment is sufficient to handle pose variations without complex non-rigid warping. Mesh-anchored Hash Table Blendshapes is a 3D neural avatar system achieving real-time rendering with high fidelity and fine-grained control through mesh-anchored hash table blendshapes. It sets itself apart from standard global deformation fields by linking each vertex of a 3DMM mesh to a local hash table for expression-dependent embeddings and localized facial deformations. Choose it when real-time rendering and localized control are prioritized over global deformation fields. HiDe-NeRF is a neural radiation field technique for detailed, unobstructed dynamic head synthesis. It sets itself apart from other deformation methods by using a multi-scale generalized appearance module (MGA) and a streamlined expression-aware deformation module (LED) to enhance expression precision while preserving identity data. Choose it when high-fidelity dynamic head synthesis with strong identity preservation is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides explicit control over pose and expression; leverages strong anatomical priors from the 3DMM. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the 3DMM fit; limited to the expression range of the 3DMM basis; may struggle with non-facial regions or occlusions not covered by the face model. When to use: When controllable, high-fidelity 3D face avatars are required from video or image collections. When not to use: For non-rigid, non-anatomical dynamic scenes or when 3DMM fitting is unreliable (e.g., heavy occlusion, extreme angles). Deformation-Guided Neural Fields emerged as a solution to the limitations of standard NeRFs in handling moving subjects. While standard NeRFs struggle with moving bodies, mesh deformation approaches like Neural Body demonstrated the ability to interpolate between frames and poses. RigNeRF, introduced in June 2022, innovated on this topic by using deformation field MLPs guided by a morphable 3D face model, creating a fully 3D face portrait with controllable pose and expression. This approach built upon the popular paradigm of animating articulated bodies using a baseline skeleton equipped with an MLP-based deformation field, a paradigm established by works such as A-NeRF (Feb 2021) and Animatable NeRF (May 2021). name: Canonical Face Space Transformation
head: Canonical face coordinate, Rigid transform
body: Canonical Face Space Transformation normalizes world coordinates to a canonical face space using a rigid transform to address face shape variations between training data and real-world inputs, making the NeRF robust to geometry and pose variations. It addresses the challenge of rendering novel views of faces from a single frontal image by normalizing geometric variations across different subjects into a shared canonical space, allowing a single pre-trained NeRF model to be fine-tuned for individual subjects. It sets itself apart from methods that rely on detailed mesh priors or non-rigid deformation fields by using only a rigid alignment derived from a mean geometry, avoiding the need for mesh details during view synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point x in the subject’s world coordinate system; viewing direction \tilde{d} in world coordinates. Output: A point x0 in the face canonical space; color and occlusion values retrieved from the MLP f\theta. Parameters: Optimized scale sm, rotation Rm, and translation tm for subject m. Data Structures: Facial Geometry (Fm): Approximate 3D facial mesh for subject m, obtained from frontal image using a 3D morphable model and image-based landmark fitting. Mean Geometry (F): Average of all facial geometries in the training dataset. Rigid Transform: Tuple (sm, Rm, tm) where sm is a scalar, Rm is a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix, and tm is a 3 \times 1 translation vector. Steps: 1. Compute Subject Geometry: For each subject m in the training data, compute approximate facial geometry Fm from the frontal image using a 3D morphable model and image-based landmark fitting. 2. Compute Mean Geometry: Calculate the mean geometry F by averaging all facial geometries Fm in the dataset. 3. Optimize Rigid Transform: Optimize the rigid transform (sm, Rm, tm) by minimizing the L2 loss between corresponding vertices of Fm and F using SVD decomposition on vertex correspondences. 4. Warp Coordinates: During prediction, warp the input coordinate x from world space to canonical space using the optimized transform: x0 = sm Rm x + tm where x is the point in the subject's world coordinate and x0 is the point in the face canonical space. 5. Query MLP: Feed the warped coordinate x0 and the original viewing direction \tilde{d} (kept in world coordinates) to the MLP network f\theta to retrieve color and occlusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def canonicalfacespacetransform(xworld, viewingdirection, subjectid, subjecttransforms): """ Transforms world coordinates to canonical face space for a specific subject. Args: xworld: numpy array, shape (3,), point in subject's world coordinate. viewingdirection: numpy array, shape (3,), viewing direction in world coordinate. subjectid: int, identifier for the subject. subjecttransforms: dict mapping subjectid to (sm, Rm, tm). Returns: xcanonical: numpy array, shape (3,), point in face canonical space. viewingdirection: numpy array, shape (3,), unchanged viewing direction. """ # Retrieve pre-optimized rigid transform for the subject # sm: scalar scale factor # Rm: 3x3 rotation matrix # tm: 3x1 translation vector sm, Rm, tm = subjecttransforms[subjectid] # Apply rigid transform: x0 = sm Rm x + tm xcanonical = sm (Rm @ xworld) + tm # Viewing direction remains in world coordinates return xcanonical, viewingdirection Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The 3D mesh models are used only to obtain the rigid transform; mesh details and priors are not required or used in the view synthesis process itself. The viewing direction \tilde{d} is kept in the world coordinate and is not warped to canonical space. The parent method that uses deformation fields MLP guided by a morphable 3D face model. Canonical Face Space Transformation is a specific rigid alignment technique within this family. Deformation-Guided Neural Fields Performance: Using canonical coordinates yields better quality (higher PSNR/SSIM, lower LPIPS) than using world coordinates, particularly on chin and eyes. World Coordinate: PSNR 24.80, SSIM 0.8167, LPIPS 0.172 Canonical Coordinate: PSNR 24.98, SSIM 0.8178, LPIPS 0.156 Strengths: Robust to variation in face geometry and poses in training and testing inputs. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the initial 3D morphable model and landmark fitting to derive the mean geometry and subject geometries. It addresses the challenge of rendering novel views of faces from a single frontal image by normalizing geometric variations across different subjects into a shared canonical space, allowing a single pre-trained NeRF model to be fine-tuned for individual subjects. name: Neural Deformation Field
head: non-rigid deformation network
body: The Neural Deformation Field (NDF) is a method for modeling non-rigid, time-varying deformations in neural radiance fields by predicting per-point displacements in a canonical space. It solves the problem of animating static neural representations without relying on rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Deformation-Guided Neural Fields by explicitly decoupling the rigid skeletal transformation (LBS) from the residual non-rigid displacement predicted by a neural network. Builds on Deformation Field Parametrization. The method operates by mapping points from a target deformed space to a canonical space using a combination of inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) and a neural displacement field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point in the target deformed space \mathbf{x}t, the target pose \thetat, and the 2D UV coordinates [u, v] of the point on the underlying mesh surface. Output: The corresponding point \mathbf{x}c in the canonical space. Data Structures: Signed Height Indicator (\tilde{h}): A vector encoding the geometric relationship of the point to the mesh surface. It is defined as \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}], where [u, v] are the 2D UV coordinates and \bar{d} is the signed distance. Neural Network (F\Delta): An MLP that takes the position-encoded signed height indicator and the target pose as input to predict the displacement \Delta. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Project to Mesh Surface: Given a target point \mathbf{x}t, project it onto the mesh surface to find the nearest surface point \mathbf{x}0. 2. Calculate Signed Distance (\bar{d}): Compute the direction vector from the surface point to the target point: \tilde{\mathbf{r}} = \mathbf{x}t - \mathbf{x}0. Obtain the surface normal \tilde{\mathbf{n}} at \mathbf{x}0. Calculate the signed distance: \bar{d} = \text{sign}(\tilde{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{n}}) \|\tilde{\mathbf{r}}\|2 3. Construct Signed Height Indicator: Combine the UV coordinates and signed distance: \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}] 4. Predict Displacement (\Delta): Pass the position-encoded signed height indicator \phi(\tilde{h}) and the target pose \thetat through the neural deformation network F\Delta: \Delta = F\Delta(\phi(\tilde{h}), \thetat) 5. Compute Canonical Point (\mathbf{x}c): Apply the inverse LBS transformation to the target point and add the predicted displacement: \mathbf{x}c = LBS^{-1}(\mathbf{x}t) + \Delta Parameters: \phi(\cdot): Position encoding function. LBS^{-1}: Inverse Linear Blend Skinning transformation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Background: If a point's nearest SMPL vertex exceeds a certain threshold, it is classified as a static background point. In this case, the bone weight is set to zero, the background weight to one, and no non-rigid deformation is applied. Precision: The calculation of \bar{d} relies on the accuracy of the surface normal \tilde{\mathbf{n}} and the projection \mathbf{x}0. Dynamic Point Field Deformation (DPF) models non-rigid, time-varying deformations in point-based radiance fields by predicting translations between canonical and deformed space point clouds using a neural network. It animates static neural point clouds without rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL. Unlike cage-based or linear blend skinning methods, DPF generalizes to arbitrary objects and enables fine-level complex deformation through user-defined or algorithmically extracted key points. This variant addresses the consistency of learnable signed distances when deforming a neural implicit field by deforming the mesh scaffold. To maintain local consistency, the rotation of the surface normal is compensated in the learnable signed indicator \tilde{h}(x). The compensated signed indicator is calculated as: \tilde{h}'(x) = \tilde{h}(x) + \delta hx where \delta hx is the relative difference of the vertex normal (averaged from nearby surface normals) from the original mesh to the deformed mesh. This ensures that the interpolated signed distance of locally deformed or rotated regions remains consistent. Not given in the sources. The Neural Deformation Field was introduced in the context of unified volumetric avatars for view synthesis, pose rendering, and geometry editing. It was proposed to address the limitations of previous methods that relied on baking polygon meshes from pre-trained neural fields, which required manual parameter tuning. The method jointly optimizes the geometry field with other components from scratch. name: Dynamic Point Field Deformation
body: Dynamic Point Field Deformation (DPF) is a method for modeling non-rigid, time-varying deformations in point-based radiance fields by predicting the translation between a canonical space point cloud and a deformed space point cloud using a neural network. It solves the problem of animating static neural point clouds without relying on rigid body assumptions or human-specific priors like SMPL. Unlike cage-based or linear blend skinning methods, DPF generalizes to arbitrary objects and enables fine-level complex deformation through user-defined or algorithmically extracted key points. Inputs and Outputs: Canonical Space Point Cloud: A static neural point cloud X = \{(xi, fi, \gammai) \mid i = 1, \dots, N\}, where xi \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the position, fi is the neural feature, and \gammai \in [0, 1] is the scale confidence. Key Points: A sparse subset \{\hat{x}i\}{i=1}^{n} of size n extracted from the canonical space. Target Pose Key Points: A set of T frames of target key points \{xi^{(t)}\}{i=1}^{n} \subseteq X^{(t)} for t=1, \dots, T, which have fine correspondence with the source key points \{\hat{x}i\}. Output: A series of deformation networks \{g{\theta}^{(t)}\}{t=1}^{T} and the deformed point cloud positions. Data Structures: Key Points: Stored as a list or tensor of shape (n, 3) containing 3D coordinates. The number of key points N{kp} is a hyperparameter; experiments tested N{kp} \in \{20, 200, 2000\}. Deformation MLP (g{\theta}^{(t)}): A Multi-Layer Perceptron mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3. It takes a canonical point as input and outputs a displacement vector. Steps: 1. Extract Key Points: Identify a sparse set of key points \{\hat{x}i\} from the canonical neural point cloud X. These can be user-defined or derived from a mesh. 2. Define Target Poses: For each time step t, provide the corresponding target key point positions \{xi^{(t)}\}. 3. Train Deformation Network: Train the MLP g{\theta}^{(t)} to predict the translation using key points as supervision. 4. Compute Deformation: For any point p in the canonical space, compute its deformed position p^{(t)} using the trained network: p^{(t)} = p + g{\theta}^{(t)}(p) Specifically for key points: xi^{(t)} = \hat{x}i + g{\theta}^{(t)}(\hat{x}i) 5. Ray Bending (Rendering): To render the deformed scene, rays cast from the camera are bent along the volumetric marching path. The deformation induces an absolute transformation (translation and rotation) that maps the query point in deformed space back to the canonical space for feature query. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random class DeformationMLP: """MLP predicting displacement vector for canonical points.""" def init(self, hiddendim=256, numlayers=4): self.layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): insize = 3 if i == 0 else hiddendim outsize = 3 if i == numlayers - 1 else hiddendim self.layers.append({ 'W': [[random.uniform(-1, 1) for in range(outsize)] for in range(insize)], 'b': [0.0] outsize }) def forward(self, points): """points: list of [x, y, z] coordinates.""" h = points for layer in self.layers: h = [[sum(h[i][j] layer['W'][j][k] for j in range(len(h))) + layer['b'][k] for k in range(len(layer['b']))] for i in range(len(h))] if layer is not self.layers[-1]: h = [[max(0.0, v) for v in row] for row in h] return h def traindeformationnetwork(canonicalkeypoints, targetkeypoints, epochs=1000, lr=1e-3): """Trains the deformation MLP to map canonical keypoints to target keypoints.""" model = DeformationMLP() for in range(epochs): displacement = model.forward(canonicalkeypoints) predicted = [[canonicalkeypoints[i][j] + displacement[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(len(canonicalkeypoints))] loss = sum((predicted[i][j] - targetkeypoints[i][j])2 for i in range(len(canonicalkeypoints)) for j in range(3)) # Backpropagation and optimizer step would update model.layers here return model def deformpointcloud(canonicalpointcloud, trainedmodel): """Deforms the entire canonical point cloud using the trained model.""" displacement = trainedmodel.forward(canonicalpointcloud) return [[canonicalpointcloud[i][j] + displacement[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(len(canonicalpointcloud))] Parameters: Number of Key Points (N{kp}): The density of key points affects deformation quality. Experiments showed results for N{kp}=20, 200, 2000. MLP Architecture: Not explicitly defined in the notes, but standard MLPs are used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistent Rendering: Direct rendering of deformed points without ray bending can lead to inconsistent results if the deformation causes gaps or overlaps. Generalization: Unlike SMPL-based methods, DPF does not require a human prior, allowing it to handle non-human objects. A neural network approach that uses key points (user-defined or SMPL-derived) as input to predict point cloud deformations, avoiding restrictions to linear blend skinning. It generalizes to all kinds of objects, enabling fine-level complex deformation, unlike cage/tetrahedron-based barycentric methods or SMPL-prior methods which are limited to humans or coarse deformation. Complexity: The method relies on an MLP for deformation prediction, which is computationally attractive compared to complex skeletal rigs. Performance: The method demonstrates superior deformation and rendering quality for fine-level user editing compared to simple local deformation methods. Limitations: The quality depends on the selection and number of key points. Insufficient key points may lead to poor deformation fidelity. Hardware: Not specified in the sources. Dynamic Point Field Deformation was introduced in the context of point-based radiance fields, specifically building upon PointNeRF. It was proposed to allow efficient editing of point clouds and the synthesis of human motion without relying on linear blend skinning or human-specific priors like SMPL. The method was demonstrated on datasets generated using Blender NeRF and multi-view stereo algorithms. name: Local Rotation Estimation via SVD
head: SVD-based Rotation Estimation
body: Local Rotation Estimation via SVD is a technique used in dynamic neural radiance fields to correct view-dependent rendering artifacts caused by large rigid-body rotations during deformation. It estimates the local rotation for each point in a deformed point cloud using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), inspired by As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) mesh deformation. This estimated rotation is then interpolated to query view directions to "bend" rays, ensuring consistency between the deformed space and the canonical space representation. It differs from sibling methods like Neural Deformation Field by explicitly modeling rotational components of the deformation field rather than relying solely on translation or dense deformation vectors, thereby handling complex fine-level deformations without introducing extra complexity into the radiance field model itself. Inputs: 1. A set of canonical space points P{can} = \{(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{f}i, \gammai)\}{i=1}^N, where \mathbf{x}i is position, \mathbf{f}i is neural feature, and \gammai is scale confidence. 2. A deformed space point cloud P{def}, obtained by applying a deformation MLP to predict translations from canonical to deformed space. 3. A pre-trained static radiance field model (e.g., PointNeRF) that predicts density \sigma and radiance \mathbf{r} given a query location and view direction. 4. A query ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{v} in camera space. Outputs: 1. Corrected ray direction \mathbf{v}' in canonical space for accurate sampling. 2. Rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) consistent with the deformed pose. Data Structures: Point Cloud: List of tuples (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{f}, \gamma). Rotation Matrix: 3 \times 3 orthogonal matrix R with determinant +1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Deformation Translation: For each canonical point \mathbf{x}i, compute its deformed position \mathbf{x}'i using a deformation MLP D: \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x}i + D(\mathbf{x}i) 2. Local Rotation Estimation via SVD: For each point \mathbf{x}i, estimate the local rotation Ri that best aligns the local neighborhood in the canonical space to the deformed space. Let \mathcal{N}i be the set of k nearest neighbors of \mathbf{x}i in the canonical space. Construct two matrices A and B of size 3 \times k: Columns of A are vectors from \mathbf{x}i to its neighbors: \mathbf{a}j = \mathbf{x}{nj} - \mathbf{x}i for nj \in \mathcal{N}i. Columns of B are vectors from \mathbf{x}'i to the corresponding deformed neighbors: \mathbf{b}j = \mathbf{x}'{nj} - \mathbf{x}'i. Compute the cross-covariance matrix H: H = A B^T = \sum{j=1}^k (\mathbf{x}{nj} - \mathbf{x}i)(\mathbf{x}'{nj} - \mathbf{x}'i)^T Perform Singular Value Decomposition on H: H = U \Sigma V^T Compute the rotation matrix Ri: Ri = V U^T Correction for Reflection: If \det(Ri) = -1, the decomposition yields a reflection. Correct it by setting the last column of V to -V{last} before computing Ri (i.e., Ri = V \text{diag}(1, 1, -1) U^T). This ensures Ri is a proper rotation matrix (\det(Ri)=1). 3. Interpolation to Query Direction: Given a query ray with direction \mathbf{v} in camera space, determine the corresponding direction \mathbf{v}{can} in canonical space. First, find the intersection point \mathbf{x}{hit} of the ray with the deformed point cloud or use the nearest deformed point \mathbf{x}'k to the ray. Interpolate the rotation R{query} from the estimated local rotations Ri of nearby points. A common approach is inverse-distance weighting based on the distance from the query ray to the canonical points \mathbf{x}i: R{query} = \frac{\sum{i \in \mathcal{K}} wi Ri}{\|\sum{i \in \mathcal{K}} wi Ri\|{F}} where \mathcal{K} is a set of m nearest canonical points to the query ray, and wi = 1 / (\|\mathbf{x}{hit} - \mathbf{x}i\|^2 + \epsilon). The Frobenius norm normalization ensures the result is a valid rotation matrix. 4. Ray Bending: Rotate the query view direction \mathbf{v} using the interpolated rotation R{query} to obtain the canonical view direction \mathbf{v}{can}: \mathbf{v}{can} = R{query} \mathbf{v} 5. Rendering: Use the canonical radiance field to sample density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} at points along the ray using \mathbf{v}{can} and the canonical positions. Compute the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volume rendering equation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Parameters: k: Number of neighbors for SVD estimation. Typical value: 6-10. m: Number of neighbors for rotation interpolation. Typical value: 6-10. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability. Typical value: 10^{-6}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Neighbors: If neighbors are collinear or coplanar, H may be rank-deficient, leading to unstable SVD. Add a small regularization term to H or increase k. Reflection: As noted, SVD can produce reflections. The determinant check is mandatory. Boundary Points: Points on the boundary of the deformed object may have sparse neighbors. Use a larger search radius or fallback to identity rotation. ARAP Mesh Deformation is a technique for deforming a triangular mesh while preserving local rigidity, minimizing distortion energy by approximating local rotations. It solves the problem of transferring user-specified boundary edits to the interior of a mesh without excessive stretching or shearing. It differs from global rigid transformations by allowing local rotation estimation per vertex, and from linear blend skinning by avoiding skeletal dependencies, relying instead on the mesh connectivity and cotangent weights. Time Complexity: The SVD step is O(k) per point for covariance matrix construction and O(1) for 3 \times 3 SVD. Interpolation is O(m). Overall, it adds a small constant overhead per ray query compared to pure translation-based deformation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the deformation MLP and the point cloud. No additional large structures are needed beyond the point features. Strengths: Handles large rotations effectively without modifying the core radiance field architecture. Improves visual consistency for complex deformations (e.g., human motion). Limitations: Requires a well-defined point cloud structure. Performance degrades if the point cloud is sparse or noisy. The interpolation step can introduce artifacts if the rotation field is not smooth. When to Use: When deforming scenes with significant rigid-body motion (e.g., articulated characters) where translation-only deformation causes view-dependent artifacts. When Not to Use: For small deformations where translation is sufficient, or for scenes without a clear point cloud representation. This method was introduced in "Point-Based Radiance Fields for Controllable Human Motion Synthesis" by Zhang et al. (2023). It builds on the observation that direct rendering of deformed point clouds leads to inconsistencies due to changed viewing directions. By borrowing the SVD-based rotation estimation from ARAP mesh deformation, the method provides a simple yet effective "ray-bending" module. It is particularly relevant for dynamic NeRF applications involving digital humans and other 3D characters. name: ARAP Mesh Deformation
head: ARAP energy minimization, As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation
body: ARAP Mesh Deformation is a technique for deforming a triangular mesh while preserving local rigidity, minimizing distortion energy by approximating local rotations. It solves the problem of transferring user-specified boundary edits to the interior of a mesh without excessive stretching or shearing. It differs from global rigid transformations by allowing local rotation estimation per vertex, and from linear blend skinning by avoiding skeletal dependencies, relying instead on mesh connectivity and cotangent weights. Inputs and Outputs: Original mesh S with vertex positions vi \in \mathbb{R}^3 for i=1 \dots n. Connectivity information (adjacency list N(i) for each vertex). Boundary conditions: deformed positions v'i for a subset of vertices (user edits). Deformed mesh S' with vertex positions v'i for all i. Data Structures: Adjacency list: N(i) contains indices of vertices adjacent to i. Cotangent weights: w{ij} stored for each edge (i,j). Rotation matrices: Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} for each vertex i. Formulas: The ARAP energy is defined as: E(S') = \sum{i=1}^{n} \sum{j \in N(i)} w{ij} \| (v'i - v'j) - Ri(vi - vj) \|^2 where: w{ij} = \frac{1}{2}(\cot \alpha{ij} + \cot \beta{ij}) is the cotangent weight for edge (i,j). \alpha{ij}, \beta{ij} are the angles opposite to edge (i,j) in the two triangles sharing it. Ri is the local rotation matrix at vertex i. Steps: 1. Precompute Weights: Calculate w{ij} for all edges using the original mesh geometry. 2. Initialize: Set initial rotations Ri = I (identity) for all i. Fix boundary vertices v'i to user-specified positions. 3. Optimize Rotations: For each vertex i, compute the optimal rotation Ri that minimizes the energy term involving i and its neighbors, given current v'j. This typically involves a Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of a covariance matrix constructed from vectors (vi - vj) and (v'i - v'j). 4. Optimize Positions: Solve for v'i for all free vertices by setting the gradient of E(S') with respect to v'i to zero. This results in a linear system A v' = b, where A is a sparse matrix derived from the cotangent weights and Ri, and b incorporates boundary conditions and rotation terms. 5. Iterate: Repeat steps 3 and 4 until convergence (change in energy or positions below a threshold). Parameters: w{ij}: The cotangent weight for edge (i,j), calculated as 0.5 \times (\cot(\alpha{ij}) + \cot(\beta{ij})). Ri: The local rotation matrix at vertex i. Fixed points for optimization: All Gaussian kernels whose distance from the active handle is greater than 0.5s, where s is the scale of the scene's bounding box. Handle displacement magnitude: Scaled to 0.2s, where s is the scale of the scene's bounding box. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import math def computecotangentweights(vertices, faces): """Compute cotangent weights for all edges in a triangular mesh.""" weights = {} for face in faces: i, j, k = face pi, pj, pk = vertices[i], vertices[j], vertices[k] def angleat(p1, p2, p3): v1 = p1 - p2 v2 = p3 - p2 cosa = np.dot(v1, v2) / (np.linalg.norm(v1) np.linalg.norm(v2)) cosa = np.clip(cosa, -1.0, 1.0) return math.acos(cosa) alpha = angleat(pj, pi, pk) beta = angleat(pk, pj, pi) gamma = angleat(pi, pk, pj) cotalpha = 1.0 / math.tan(alpha) if alpha != 0 else 0.0 cotbeta = 1.0 / math.tan(beta) if beta != 0 else 0.0 cotgamma = 1.0 / math.tan(gamma) if gamma != 0 else 0.0 edgeij = (min(i, j), max(i, j)) edgejk = (min(j, k), max(j, k)) edgeki = (min(k, i), max(k, i)) weights[edgeij] = weights.get(edgeij, 0.0) + 0.5 cotalpha weights[edgejk] = weights.get(edgejk, 0.0) + 0.5 cotbeta weights[edgeki] = weights.get(edgeki, 0.0) + 0.5 cotgamma return weights def arapdeformation(vertices, faces, adjacency, boundaryindices, boundarypositions, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): n = len(vertices) v = np.array(vertices) vprime = v.copy() R = [np.eye(3) for in range(n)] weights = computecotangentweights(v, faces) fixedmask = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool) fixedmask[boundaryindices] = True for iteration in range(maxiter): # Step 1: Optimize Rotations for i in range(n): Mi = np.zeros((3, 3)) for j in adjacency[i]: difforig = v[i] - v[j] diffdeformed = vprime[i] - vprime[j] w = weights.get((min(i, j), max(i, j)), 0.0) Mi += w np.outer(difforig, diffdeformed) U,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Mi) R[i] = Vt.T @ U.T if np.linalg.det(R[i]) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1 R[i] = Vt.T @ U.T # Step 2: Optimize Positions Arows = [] brows = [] freeindices = [i for i in range(n) if not fixedmask[i]] freetoidx = {i: idx for idx, i in enumerate(freeindices)} for i in freeindices: row = np.zeros(n) rhs = np.zeros(3) for j in adjacency[i]: w = weights.get((min(i, j), max(i, j)), 0.0) row[i] += w rhs += w R[i] @ (v[i] - v[j]) if j in freetoidx: row[j] -= w elif fixedmask[j]: rhs += w vprime[j] Arows.append(row) brows.append(rhs) Asparse = np.array(Arows) bsparse = np.array(brows).reshape(-1) vprimefree = np.linalg.solve(Asparse, bsparse) for idx, i in enumerate(freeindices): vprime[i] = vprimefree[idx 3: (idx + 1) 3] if np.linalg.norm(vprime - v) < tol: break return vprime Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Incorrectly fixing boundary vertices can lead to unrealistic deformations. Degenerate Triangles: Cotangent weights become undefined for degenerate triangles (zero area). Handle by skipping or smoothing weights. Reflections: SVD may produce a reflection (\det(R) = -1). Ensure proper handling to maintain orientation. Applies As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) geometric deformation to tetrahedral meshes under constraints from surface mesh deformation. It differs from triangular ARAP by extending the energy formulation to volumetric cells and using barycentric coordinates to transfer surface vertex displacements to tetrahedron vertices. Choose it when deforming volumetric representations or implicit fields that require internal consistency beyond the surface. See Embedded Deformation (Stage I). Time Complexity: Each iteration requires O(N) work for the rotation step and a sparse linear solve for the position step. Memory Complexity: Proportional to O(N + E) for storing weights, rotations, and the sparse cotangent Laplacian stiffness matrix. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with vertex count per iteration; sparse solvers handle large meshes efficiently. Strengths: Preserves local rigidity well, handles complex deformations, avoids skeletal dependencies. Limitations: Iterative optimization can be slow for very large meshes; sensitive to boundary condition placement. When to Use: When rigid deformation is desired without skeletal animation, or for transferring deformations from a surface mesh to a volume representation. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and iterative convergence is too slow, or when non-rigid stretching/shearing is intentionally desired. ARAP mesh deformation was introduced in the context of NeRF editing, specifically in the paper "NeRF-Editing: Geometry Editing of Neural Radiance Fields". It is used to transfer user edits from a triangular mesh to an implicit volume representation, enabling geometry editing of neural radiance fields. The method is implemented based on libigl. name: Embedded Deformation (Stage I)
head: ARAP Deformation, Deformation Graph
body: Embedded Deformation (Stage I) applies As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) geometric deformation to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations using a deformation graph of control nodes. It displaces embedded geometries (Gaussian centers and endpoints) via affine transformations to approximate per-Gaussian rotation and scaling, but visual artifacts under large deformations remain due to the mismatch between deformed geometry and the deformed radiance field, necessitating a second alignment stage. Inputs: Set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by center pi, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonics coefficients Hi. User-defined constraints ql specifying desired deformed positions for selected control points. Outputs: Deformed Gaussian centers \tilde{p}i. Deformed covariance matrices \tilde{\Sigma}i derived from rotation r and scaling s. Rotated spherical harmonics coefficients. Data Structures: Deformation Graph: A graph where vertices are control points gj and edges connect neighbors via KNN. Control Point Affine Transform: Each node j stores a 3 \times 3 matrix Aj and a 3 \times 1 translation vector tj. Gaussian Endpoints: For each Gaussian, 6 endpoints located at \pm 2\sigma along the three principal axes. Steps: 1. Construct Deformation Graph: Select control points from Gaussian centers using Furthest Point Sampling (FPS). Construct edge connections between control points using the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm. 2. Define Energies: Minimize the total energy E{geo} to find optimal Aj and tj: E{geo} = \sumj \left( w{rot} E{rot}(Aj) + w{reg} E{reg}(Aj) \right) + w{con} E{con} where: E{rot}(A) measures deviation from rigid rotation. Let c1, c2, c3 \in \mathbb{R}^3 be the column vectors of A: E{rot}(A) = (c1 \cdot c2)^2 + (c1 \cdot c3)^2 + (c2 \cdot c3)^2 + (c1 \cdot c1 - 1)^2 + (c2 \cdot c2 - 1)^2 + (c3 \cdot c3 - 1)^2 E{reg}(A) penalizes sharp translational changes between adjacent control nodes k: E{reg}(A) = \sumk \| A(gk - g) + g + t - (gk + tk) \|^2 Here, g and t are the position and translation of the current node, and gk, tk are those of neighbor k. E{con} enforces user constraints ql for deformed control point positions \tilde{g}l: E{con} = \suml \| \tilde{g}l - ql \|^2 3. Optimize Transformations: Solve for Aj and tj that minimize E{geo}. 4. Displace Embedded Geometries: Compute the deformed position \tilde{v}i for any embedded geometry point vi (e.g., Gaussian center or endpoint) using weights wj(vi) inherited from control node j: \tilde{v}i = \sumj wj(vi) \left( Aj (vi - gj) + gj + tj \right) where gj is the original position of control node j. 5. Reconstruct Gaussians: For each Gaussian, select 6 endpoints along the three axes at twice the standard deviation from the center. Displace these endpoints using the Embedded Deformation formula above. Let Q \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6} be the matrix of original endpoint positions and P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6} be the matrix of deformed endpoint positions. Estimate the local deformation matrix M: M = P Q^\top (Q Q^\top)^{-1} Perform polar decomposition on M to obtain rotation r and scaling s. Update the Gaussian's covariance matrix using r and s. Rotate the spherical harmonics coefficients corresponding to the new rotation r. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def embeddeddeformationstagei(gaussians, constraints): # 1. Construct deformation graph controlpoints = furthestpointsampling(gaussians.centers) graph = buildknngraph(controlpoints) # 2. Optimize affine transforms A, t = minimizeenergy(graph, constraints) # 3. Displace geometries & reconstruct Gaussians deformedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Displace center centerdeformed = sum(wj(g.center) (Aj @ (g.center - gj) + gj + tj) for j in graph.neighbors(g.center)) # Displace endpoints endpointsorig = get6endpoints(g.center, g.sigma) endpointsdeformed = applydeformation(endpointsorig, A, t, graph) # Estimate local deformation M = endpointsdeformed @ endpointsorig.T @ inv(endpointsorig @ endpointsorig.T) r, s = polardecomposition(M) # Update Gaussian covdeformed = r @ g.covariance @ r.T s shdeformed = rotatesphericalharmonics(g.sh, r) deformedgaussians.append(Gaussian(centerdeformed, covdeformed, g.opacity, shdeformed)) return deformedgaussians Parameters: w{rot} = 1 w{reg} = 10 w{con} = 100 Pitfalls: Direct geometric deformation causes visual artifacts under large deformations due to the mismatch between deformed Gaussians and the deformed radiance field. This method addresses the geometry but requires Stage II to align with the radiance field. Anchor-Guided ARAP Deformation is a variational mesh deformation method that computes a globally rigid-consistent deformation of a template mesh by minimizing a combination of As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) energy and a sparse anchor fidelity term. It solves the problem of applying noisy or sparse motion flows (e.g., from voxelized geometry tracking) to a mesh without propagating noise across the entire surface. Unlike standard ARAP [SA07] which relies on fixed boundary conditions, this method uses a dynamically selected subset of high-curvature or high-motion vertices as anchors, making it resilient to input noise while preserving local geometric features. Neural Deformation Graph is a self-supervised modeling method that uses a graph structure to model objects, assigning an SDF to each node to describe shapes. It designs multiple loss functions to constrain the graph: covering the whole body, uniform node distribution within the contour, and sparse edge connections. It takes an SDF sequence as input and evaluates deformation using the relative displacement of graph nodes between frames, which is then used to generate dynamic skinning weights. Complexity: Depends on the number of control points, their KNN neighbors, and the number of Gaussians. Optimization of E{geo} is typically solved via least squares or iterative solvers. Strengths: Provides physically plausible, rigid-like deformation for point clouds and meshes; avoids the need for explicit mesh topology in Gaussian Splatting. Limitations: Does not fully correct radiance field misalignment artifacts on its own; requires a second stage for full consistency. Embedded deformation was originally introduced for meshes and point clouds. In the context of 3DGS, it is adapted to handle the particle-like nature of Gaussians. This method is part of a two-stage pipeline for ARAP deformation of Gaussian Radiance Fields. name: Anchor-Guided ARAP Deformation
head: Anchor-based ARAP, Global deformation
body: Anchor-Guided ARAP Deformation is a variational mesh deformation method that computes a globally rigid-consistent deformation of a template mesh by minimizing a combination of As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) energy and a sparse anchor fidelity term. It solves the problem of applying noisy or sparse motion flows (e.g., from voxelized geometry tracking) to a mesh without propagating noise across the entire surface. Unlike standard ARAP [SA07] which relies on fixed boundary conditions, this method uses a dynamically selected subset of high-curvature or high-motion vertices as anchors, making it resilient to input noise while preserving local geometric features. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Template mesh M0 with vertices pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 and one-ring neighborhoods N(i), target positions pi^{\text{target}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 derived from a noisy motion flow, edge weights w{ij}, and anchor weights w{ai}. Outputs: Deformed mesh positions p'i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and local rotation matrices Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} for each vertex. Data Structures: Mesh connectivity: Adjacency list storing N(i) for each vertex i=1 \dots n. Position arrays: ptemplate (n \times 3) for original vertices, ptarget (n \times 3) for target positions, pcurr (n \times 3) for deformed vertices. Weight arrays: wij (sparse map or dictionary mapping (i,j) to float), wai (n-vector). Rotation array: R (list of 3 \times 3 matrices, size n). Linear system data: Dense matrix L (n \times n), dense vector b (n \times 3). Numbered Steps: 1. Anchor Selection: For each vertex at time ti, compute a curvature score using [PGK02] and a motion vector score based on correspondence matching [BLNL14]. Normalize and sum these scores. Select the subset with the highest scores as anchors. Set w{ai} to the normalized score for anchors, and 0 otherwise. 2. Initialization: Set initial rotations Ri to identity matrices. Initialize deformed positions p'i to template positions pi. 3. Iterate until convergence: a. Solve Linear System: Construct L and b based on current Ri. Solve L p' = b for new positions p'. b. Update Rotations: For each vertex i, compute the optimal rotation Ri using SVD on the positions of pi and p'i (and their one-ring neighbors) as derived in [SA07]. 4. Convergence Check: Stop when \|p'{\text{new}} - p'{\text{old}}\| < \epsilon. Formulas: Total energy: E(M0) = E{\text{ARAP}}(M0) + E{\text{ANC}}(M0). ARAP energy: E{\text{ARAP}}(M0) = \frac{1}{2} \sum{i=1}^{n} \sum{j \in N(i)} w{ij} \|(p'i - p'j) - Ri(pi - pj)\|^2. Anchor energy: E{\text{ANC}}(M0) = \frac{1}{2} \sum{i=1}^{n} w{ai} \|p'i - pi^{\text{target}}\|^2, where w{ai} = 0 if vertex i is not an anchor. Optimality condition (fixed Ri): \sum{j \in N(i)} w{ij}(p'i - p'j) + w{ai}p'i = \sum{j \in N(i)} w{ij} \frac{1}{2} (Ri - Rj)(pi - pj) + w{ai}pi^{\text{target}}. This yields the linear system L p' = b, where L is the Laplacian of M0 with w{ai} added to the diagonal for anchor nodes, and b contains the right-hand side terms. Parameters: Anchor weights w{ai}: Confidence scores from selection, typically [0, 1] after normalization. Edge weights w{ij}: Standard cotangent or uniform weights. Convergence tolerance \epsilon: Typically 10^{-4} to 10^{-6}. Maximum iterations: Typically 10–20. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Solving the linear system requires a sparse solver (e.g., conjugate gradient or direct sparse LU) to handle ill-conditioning from low anchor weights. Boundaries: The method assumes a closed or well-connected mesh; disconnected components require separate anchor sets or global constraints. Degenerate input: If anchors are too sparse or weights are near zero, the system becomes under-constrained; a minimum anchor count or fallback to standard ARAP is needed. SVD reflection: The optimal rotation from SVD may yield a reflection (\det(Ri) = -1); it must be corrected by flipping the sign of the smallest singular vector [SA07]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def anchorguidedarap(ptemplate, neighbors, wij, ptarget, wai, maxiter=10, tol=1e-4): """ ptemplate: (n, 3) array of original vertex positions neighbors: list of lists, neighbors[i] contains indices of N(i) wij: dict mapping (i, j) to float edge weight ptarget: (n, 3) array of target positions from motion flow wai: (n,) array of anchor weights (0 if not anchor) """ n = len(ptemplate) pcurr = ptemplate.copy() R = [np.eye(3) for in range(n)] # Initial rotations for in range(maxiter): L = np.zeros((n, n)) b = np.zeros((n, 3)) for i in range(n): rhs = np.zeros(3) for j in neighbors[i]: w = wij.get((i, j), 0.0) L[i, i] += w L[i, j] -= w diffp = ptemplate[i] - ptemplate[j] diffR = R[i] - R[j] rhs += w 0.5 (diffR @ diffp) L[i, i] += wai[i] rhs += wai[i] ptarget[i] b[i] = rhs pnew = np.linalg.solve(L, b) # Standard dense solver if np.linalg.norm(pnew - pcurr) < tol: break pcurr = pnew # Update rotations via SVD [SA07] for i in range(n): H = np.zeros((3, 3)) for j in neighbors[i]: v1 = ptemplate[i] - ptemplate[j] v2 = pcurr[i] - pcurr[j] H += np.outer(v2, v1) U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H) R[i] = Vt.T @ U.T if np.linalg.det(R[i]) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1 R[i] = Vt.T @ U.T return pcurr, R Time Complexity: Dominated by solving the sparse linear system L p' = b and computing SVDs per vertex. Each iteration is O(n) for SVDs (constant size 3 \times 3) and O(nnz) for the linear solve, where nnz is the number of non-zeros in L. Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing vertices, rotations, and weights. O(nnz) for the sparse Laplacian matrix. Strengths: Resilient to noisy motion flows; preserves local geometric details better than direct application of flow; handles non-rigid deformation via ARAP while anchoring global pose. Limitations: Requires iterative convergence; sensitive to anchor selection quality; may smooth out fine details if anchors are too sparse or weights too low. When to use: When deforming a mesh based on sparse or noisy global motion data (e.g., from voxel tracking) and preserving local rigidity is important. When not to use: When high-frequency non-rigid details (like cloth folds) are the primary focus, as this method is a global deformation step; local optimization is needed subsequently. The method was introduced in the context of 4D mesh reconstruction from time-varying voxelized geometry. It builds on the As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation method [SA07] by introducing a sparse set of anchors guided by curvature and motion correspondence scores [PGK02, BLNL14]. The method was developed to handle the noise inherent in voxel-based motion tracking, providing a robust global deformation step before local regularization. 4D Mesh Reconstruction from Time-Varying Voxelized Geometry through ARAP Tracking, https://doi.org/10.2312/egsh.20151002, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Local Volume Orientation Estimation
head: Local Rotation Estimation via Heuristic
body: Local Volume Orientation Estimation is a heuristic method for computing the local rotation matrix of a point in a dynamic volume by analyzing its two nearest neighbors. It solves the problem of view-dependent rendering artifacts caused by large rotations in non-rigid deformation fields by ensuring that the estimated orientation transforms equivariantly with the input points. It differs from Local Rotation Estimation via SVD by using a direct geometric construction (cross products) rather than singular value decomposition, offering a computationally lighter alternative for establishing local coordinate frames. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The positions of a central point i and its two closest neighbors j and k at a specific time step t. Let these positions be denoted as \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2, \mathbf{p}3 respectively, where \mathbf{p}1 corresponds to point i. Output: A 3 \times 3 rotation matrix \mathbf{T}, where each row \mathbf{T}{m,\cdot} represents a basis vector of the local orientation frame. Data Structures: Point positions: 3D vectors (\mathbb{R}^3). Orientation Matrix: 3 \times 3 matrix where rows are orthonormal basis vectors. Steps: 1. Neighbor Selection: Identify the central point i and its two closest neighbors j and k in the spatial neighborhood at the current time step. Assign \mathbf{p}1 = \text{pos}(i), \mathbf{p}2 = \text{pos}(j), \mathbf{p}3 = \text{pos}(k). 2. First Basis Vector (\mathbf{T}{1,\cdot}): Compute the normalized cross product of the vectors formed by the edges of the triangle defined by the three points. This vector represents the normal to the triangle plane. \mathbf{T}{1,\cdot} = \frac{\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}1}{\|\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{p}1\|2} \times \frac{\mathbf{p}3 - \mathbf{p}1}{\|\mathbf{p}3 - \mathbf{p}1\|2} 3. Second Basis Vector (\mathbf{T}{2,\cdot}): Compute the vector from the central point \mathbf{p}1 to the centroid of the triangle formed by \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2, \mathbf{p}3, then normalize it. \mathbf{T}{2,\cdot} = \frac{\frac{\mathbf{p}1 + \mathbf{p}2 + \mathbf{p}3}{3} - \mathbf{p}1}{\left\| \frac{\mathbf{p}1 + \mathbf{p}2 + \mathbf{p}3}{3} - \mathbf{p}1 \right\|2} 4. Third Basis Vector (\mathbf{T}{3,\cdot}): Compute the cross product of the first two basis vectors to complete the orthonormal frame. \mathbf{T}{3,\cdot} = \mathbf{T}{1,\cdot} \times \mathbf{T}{2,\cdot} 5. Matrix Assembly: Construct the rotation matrix \mathbf{T} by stacking the basis vectors as rows: \mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{T}{1,\cdot} \\ \mathbf{T}{2,\cdot} \\ \mathbf{T}{3,\cdot} \end{bmatrix} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computelocalorientation(p1: np.ndarray, p2: np.ndarray, p3: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Compute the local orientation rotation matrix for a point p1 given neighbors p2 and p3. Args: p1: Position of the central point (3,) p2: Position of the first neighbor (3,) p3: Position of the second neighbor (3,) Returns: T: 3x3 rotation matrix where rows are the basis vectors T1, T2, T3. """ # Step 1: Compute edge vectors vec12 = p2 - p1 vec13 = p3 - p1 # Step 2: Compute T1 (Normal to the triangle) # Note: The source normalizes the edge vectors before cross product. # This is equivalent to normalizing the result of the cross product of unnormalized vectors # scaled by the product of their lengths, but the source explicitly normalizes inputs. norm12 = np.linalg.norm(vec12) norm13 = np.linalg.norm(vec13) # Guard against division by zero if points coincide if norm12 < 1e-8 or norm13 < 1e-8: # Fallback to identity or handle degenerate case return np.eye(3) unit12 = vec12 / norm12 unit13 = vec13 / norm13 T1 = np.cross(unit12, unit13) # Step 3: Compute T2 (Vector from p1 to centroid) centroid = (p1 + p2 + p3) / 3.0 vectocentroid = centroid - p1 normcentroid = np.linalg.norm(vectocentroid) if normcentroid < 1e-8: # Degenerate case: points are coincident return np.eye(3) T2 = vectocentroid / normcentroid # Step 4: Compute T3 (Cross product of T1 and T2) T3 = np.cross(T1, T2) # Step 5: Assemble matrix T = np.stack([T1, T2, T3], axis=0) return T Parameters: Neighbor count: Fixed at 2 neighbors. Distance metric: Euclidean distance (L2 norm) is implied by the normalization steps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degeneracy: If points p1, p2, p3 are collinear or coincident, the cross products in Step 2 or Step 3 may yield zero vectors, leading to undefined orientations. The source notes that degenerate cases are not explicitly handled in the formulas, relying on the heuristic of finding "closest neighbors" which implies distinct points in typical usage. Implementers must add guards for zero-length vectors. Equivariance: The method guarantees equivariance: if the input points are rotated by a matrix R, the resulting orientation matrix \mathbf{T} rotates by R as well (\mathbf{T}' = R\mathbf{T}). Time Complexity: O(1) per point, assuming neighbor lookup is pre-computed or provided. The calculation involves a constant number of vector operations (subtractions, norms, cross products). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per point. Strengths: Computationally efficient compared to SVD-based methods. It provides a robust local frame that respects the geometric structure of the point cloud neighborhood. Limitations: Sensitive to the quality of neighbor selection. If neighbors are not well-distributed or if the local geometry is flat (collinear points), the orientation estimate may be unstable. It does not enforce a specific global consistency, relying on local geometry. When to use: Suitable for real-time or resource-constrained dynamic volume rendering where full SVD decomposition is too expensive, and the local geometry is sufficiently non-degenerate. The method was introduced in the context of Neural Parametric Gaussians for Monocular Non-Rigid Object Reconstruction. It serves as a deformation basis component to handle non-rigid motion, specifically addressing artifacts arising from large rotations in dynamic scenes. The heuristic approach was chosen to provide an equivariant local coordinate frame without the computational overhead of more complex decomposition techniques. name: Polynomial Motion Field
head: Hierarchical motion model, Parametric Motion Field, Polynomial warp field
body: The Polynomial Motion Field is a parametric deformation model for dynamic volume rendering that represents temporal motion as a continuous function of time. It reconstructs 4D scenes from sparse or limited-view measurements by warping a static template volume to arbitrary time points using voxel-wise polynomial coefficients. Unlike neural deformation fields that map coordinates to displacement via a network, this method explicitly parameterizes the motion trajectory at each voxel, enabling efficient optimization and arbitrary temporal upsampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N sparse or limited-view 2D projections (sinograms) sampled at discrete time points t{i=0 \dots N-1}, and a static template volume \hat{\sigma}. Output: A Motion Coefficient Tensor C and the reconstructed dynamic volume \sigma(x, y, z, t) for any t \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: Motion Coefficient Tensor C: A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{\beta^3 \times k \times 3}. \beta^3: The spatial resolution of the scene (number of voxels). k: The polynomial order (degree). 3: The three spatial dimensions (x, y, z). Each voxel stores k coefficients for each of the 3 spatial displacement components. Time Samples: N time points ti linearly spaced in [0, 1]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Motion Coefficient Tensor C at a base spatial resolution \alpha (where \alpha < \beta), resulting in C\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{\alpha^3 \times k \times 3}. 2. Hierarchical Upsampling (Coarse-to-Fine): Iteratively increase the spatial resolution \alpha (e.g., 2^3 \to 4^3 \to 8^3 \to 16^3). At each step, upsample the current coefficient tensor C{\alphai} to the next resolution C{\alpha{i+1}} using linear upsampling U: C{\alpha{i+1}} = U(C{\alphai}) where U: \mathbb{R}^{\alphai^3} \to \mathbb{R}^{\alpha{i+1}^3}. 3. Warp Field Computation: For a specific time ti, compute the 3D displacement vector W(C, ti) for all voxels using the polynomial expansion: W(C, ti) = \sum{j=0}^{k} C{:, j,:} ti^j where W(C, ti) \in \mathbb{R}^{\beta^3 \times 3} is the warp field at time ti, and C{:, j,:} denotes the slice of coefficients for the j-th polynomial order across all voxels and spatial dimensions. 4. Differentiable Grid Sampling: Warp the template volume \hat{\sigma} using the computed displacement field. The volume at time ti is obtained via a differentiable grid sampling function fn: \sigma(x, y, z, ti) = fn(W(C, ti), \hat{\sigma}) This function interpolates the template values at the displaced coordinates. 5. Optimization: Minimize the reconstruction error between the rendered projections of \sigma(x, y, z, ti) and the measured sinograms. The optimization encourages the polynomial coefficients to fit a continuous representation of motion, allowing the model to be evaluated at arbitrary time points t not present in the training set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computewarpfield(C, timet): """ Compute the displacement field W for a given time t. C: Tensor of shape (numvoxels, k+1, 3) timet: Scalar in [0, 1] Returns: W of shape (numvoxels, 3) """ numvoxels, kplus1, = C.shape W = zeros((numvoxels, 3)) tpower = 1.0 for j in range(kplus1): if j > 0: tpower = timet W += C[:, j,:] tpower return W def hierarchicalupsample(Calpha, targetalpha): """ Upsample the coefficient tensor from resolution alpha to targetalpha. Calpha: Tensor of shape (alpha^3, k+1, 3) targetalpha: Integer target resolution Returns: Tensor of shape (targetalpha^3, k+1, 3) """ alpha = int(Calpha.shape[0] (1/3)) kplus1 = Calpha.shape[1] # Reshape to 3D grid for interpolation grid = Calpha.reshape(alpha, alpha, alpha, kplus1, 3) # Standard trilinear interpolation on spatial dimensions interpgrid = trilinearinterpolate(grid, targetalpha) return interpgrid.reshape(targetalpha3, kplus1, 3) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, targetsize): """ Perform trilinear interpolation on the spatial dimensions of grid. grid: Tensor of shape (oldsize, oldsize, oldsize, k+1, 3) targetsize: Integer target spatial dimension Returns: Tensor of shape (targetsize, targetsize, targetsize, k+1, 3) """ # Standard trilinear interpolation computes weighted averages of 8 neighboring voxels # Implementation details omitted for brevity; follows standard graphics literature pass def renderdynamicvolume(C, templatesigma, timet, resolutionbeta): """ Render the volume at time t. C: (beta^3, k+1, 3) templatesigma: (beta^3,) or (beta, beta, beta) timet: float in [0, 1] resolutionbeta: int """ # 1. Compute Warp W = computewarpfield(C, timet) # (beta^3, 3) # 2. Differentiable Grid Sampling # fn(W, sigma) samples templatesigma at displaced coordinates (x+Wx, y+Wy, z+Wz) # Standard differentiable grid sampler implementation warpedvolume = differentiablegridsample(templatesigma, W, resolutionbeta) return warpedvolume Parameters: Polynomial Order k: The degree of the polynomial. Typically k=5 is sufficient for deformable and periodic motion. Base Resolution \alpha: The initial resolution for coarse-to-fine optimization. Examples include 2^3, 4^3, 8^3, 16^3. Target Resolution \beta: The final spatial resolution of the scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Upsampling Accuracy: The parametric representation constrains the upsampling of the motion field itself to simple trilinear interpolation, which may limit accuracy compared to other interpolation methods. Resolution Scaling: Attempting to estimate the warp field directly at the full resolution \beta^3 without hierarchical initialization results in poor motion reconstruction. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is dominated by the Motion Coefficient Tensor C, which scales as O(\beta^3 \cdot k \cdot 3). The method allows optimizing on low-resolution measurements (e.g., 80^3) and upsampling to high resolutions (e.g., 256^3) post-optimization, bypassing substantial GPU memory requirements. Time Complexity: The warp field computation is O(\beta^3 \cdot k) per time point. Rendering involves grid sampling, which is typically O(\beta^3). The hierarchical optimization adds overhead but improves convergence. Strengths: Arbitrary Temporal Resolution: The polynomial representation allows evaluation at any time t \in [0, 1], enabling arbitrary frame rate upsampling (e.g., from 10 to 90 frames). Memory Efficiency: Parametric representation reduces memory footprint compared to storing discrete time steps. Differentiability: The method is fully differentiable, allowing gradient-based optimization of the coefficients. Limitations: Interpolation Constraint: Trilinear interpolation for upsampling the field itself may not capture complex motion details as well as learned upsamplers. When to Use: Suitable for dynamic CT reconstruction from sparse/limited views where temporal continuity is expected and memory is a constraint. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Polynomial Motion Field was introduced in the context of dynamic CT reconstruction from limited views. It leverages implicit neural representations and parametric motion fields to warp a template volume to different time values. The method was proposed to address the challenges of reconstructing objects from limited views, which is traditionally more challenging than from sparse views. It assumes only that the scene is sparse view sampled, without requiring specialized sampling schemes or phase information. The hierarchical coarse-to-fine estimation strategy was introduced to overcome poor motion reconstruction at full resolution. The approach builds on differentiable grid sampling functions. name: Dynamic Scene Representation
head: Dynamic Radiance Fields
body: Dynamic Scene Representation methods extend static radiance fields to model temporal variations, enabling novel view synthesis of non-static scenes. Unlike static methods, these approaches incorporate time or scene variables as inputs to the neural field or deformation operators to predict density and color for specific moments. They differ from sibling methods like Deformation Field Parametrization by explicitly handling the evolution of geometry and appearance over time, often through shared networks, explicit temporal interpolation, or deformation fields. This family builds on Neural Radiance Fields. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). DyNeRF represents volumetric videos using a single shared Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) that takes spatial coordinates and a temporal embedding as input to predict the radiance field for a specific video frame. It sets itself apart from Neural Rendering of Variable Scenes by using a monolithic shared network structure rather than decomposing the scene into static and dynamic components or using explicit voxel structures. While simple to implement, this single shared MLP structure tends to lose details in high-frequency regions of the image. This method explicitly incorporates scene variation into the training phase by encoding predefined ranges of dynamic scene elements into a structured vector representation. Unlike methods that constrain learning to a single static manifold, these approaches learn a surface radiance field capable of handling all possible permutations of the specified scene variables. This distinguishes them from sibling methods like DyNeRF, which typically model deformation or motion through explicit geometric transformations or temporal bases, whereas variable scene methods treat dynamic parameters as direct inputs to the neural field to capture higher-order interactions between moving objects and the static environment. Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting (Ex4DGS) achieves memory efficiency and rendering speed by separating scene primitives into static and dynamic categories and explicitly interpolating their attributes over time. Unlike implicit deformation fields or continuous trajectory models, Ex4DGS stores sparse keyframe data for dynamic Gaussians and uses specific interpolators to reconstruct continuous motion, handling complex phenomena like self-occlusion and object disappearance without requiring auxiliary masks or supervision. It builds on Dynamic Scene Representation by introducing a fully explicit temporal domain where attributes are sampled at discrete timestamps and interpolated. GauFRe augments 3D Gaussian Splatting with a time-conditioned forward-warping deformation field to enable real-time novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes. Unlike NeRF-based methods that use backward warps to query canonical space, GauFRe stores Gaussians in a canonical space and uses a neural network to output deformed attributes (position, rotation, scale) for each time step t. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly separating the scene into static and deformable Gaussian sets, preventing capacity waste and noise in static regions, and by modeling non-rigid deformations (scaling) in addition to rigid motion. Light-weight 4D Gaussian Splatting (LGS) is a memory-efficient method for reconstructing and rendering dynamic scenes, specifically designed for surgical endoscopy. It addresses the high memory consumption and computational cost of standard 4D Gaussian Splatting by combining three compression techniques: Deformation-Aware Pruning (DAP), Gaussian-Attribute Pruning (GAP), and Feature Field Condensation (FFC). Unlike Explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting which stores full attributes, or Gaussian Deformation Field (GauFRe) which uses a deformation network, LGS achieves compression by pruning redundant Gaussians and condensing the feature field resolution, maintaining real-time rendering speeds with significantly smaller model sizes. A neural radiance field that takes transformed 3D location, view direction, and aggregated features as input to predict volume density and color. The concept of representing dynamic scenes using neural radiance fields emerged with the need to extend static NeRF capabilities to video and dynamic content. The integration of the temporal dimension in a radiance field-based volumetric representation offers two benefits: it increases temporal homogeneity, reinforcing spatial information with temporal redundancy, and addresses temporary occluded areas. Deformation-based approaches achieve this by dividing the dynamic radiance field into a spatial radiance field and a dynamic deformation field.
