name: Template-Free NeRF (TFS-NeRF)
head: TFS-NeRF
body: TFS-NeRF is a template-free 3D semantic NeRF method for reconstructing dynamic scenes from sparse or single-view RGB videos, specifically handling interactions between two or more entities (rigid, non-rigid, or deformable). It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Nerfies by explicitly disentangling the motions of interacting entities and from LBS-based approaches like TAVA by using an Invertible Neural Network (INN) to predict Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) weights directly, thereby bypassing computationally expensive root-finding optimizations. This enables time-efficient training and semantically separable geometry reconstruction without relying on pre-defined template models (e.g., SMPL) or latent codes. Inputs: Sparse or single-view RGB video frames and corresponding 2D semantic segmentation masks. Outputs: A composite scene rendering and semantically separable Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for deformable and non-deformable entities. Data Structures: Canonical Space: A static reference frame where geometry is defined independently of time and pose. Deformed/View Space: The coordinate system of the observed frame at a specific timestamp. Bone Transformation Matrices (B): A set of nb rigid transformation matrices representing the bones of the deformable entity. Skining Weights (w(xc)): A function mapping a canonical point xc to a weight vector, predicted by the INN. SDF Networks (F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta)}): Two independent neural networks (MLPs) parameterized by \theta, one for deformable entities (j=d) and one for non-deformable entities (j=nd), predicting canonical SDFs. Formulas: The forward Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) computes the deformed point xv in view space from a canonical point xc using skinning weights w(xc) and bone transformation matrices B: xv = \text{LBS}(w(xc), B, xc) = \sum{b=1}^{nb} w(xc)b \cdot Bb \cdot xc where nb is the total number of bones. Steps: 1. Semantic-Aware Ray Sampling: Given a 2D semantic segmentation mask for the current frame, shoot two distinct sets of rays from the camera: one set samples 3D points \{xd^v\} corresponding to deformable entities, and another set samples 3D points \{xv\} corresponding to non-deformable entities. 2. Inverse Warping to Canonical Space: Transform the sampled points from the deformed/view space to their respective canonical spaces using inverse warping enabled by the learned forward LBS. This is achieved by inverting the forward LBS mapping via the INN, avoiding the iterative root-finding procedures used in prior work. 3. Individual Geometry Prediction: At the canonical space, use two independent SDF prediction networks F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta)} to predict the Signed Distance Fields: F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta, d)} predicts the SDF for the deformable entity, and F{c \to \Omega}^{(\theta, nd)} predicts the SDF for the non-deformable entity. 4. Joint Optimization: Optimize both branches (deformable and non-deformable) jointly using the RGB reconstruction loss to generate the composite scene rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tfsnerfforward(framergb, semanticmask, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, innmodel, sdfnetdeform, sdfnetnondeform, bones, numsamples): # 1. Semantic-Aware Ray Sampling rayso, raysd = generaterays(cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, framergb.shape) raysdeform = rayso[semanticmask == DEFORMABLECLASS], raysd[semanticmask == DEFORMABLECLASS] raysnondeform = rayso[semanticmask == NONDEFORMABLECLASS], raysd[semanticmask == NONDEFORMABLECLASS] pointsdeformv = sampledepth(raysdeform, numsamples) pointsnondeformv = sampledepth(raysnondeform, numsamples) # 2. Inverse Warping to Canonical Space pointsdeformc = innmodel.inverse(pointsdeformv) pointsnondeformc = pointsnondeformv # 3. Individual Geometry Prediction sdfdeform = sdfnetdeform(pointsdeformc) sdfnondeform = sdfnetnondeform(pointsnondeformc) # 4. Volume Rendering & Loss renderedcolor = volumerendersdf(sdfdeform, sdfnondeform, raysdeform, raysnondeform) loss = meansquarederror(renderedcolor, framergb) return renderedcolor, loss def generaterays(intrinsics, extrinsics, imgshape): u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(imgshape[1]), np.arange(imgshape[0])) rayso = extrinsics[:3, 3] raysd = np.stack([(u - intrinsics[0, 2]) / intrinsics[0, 0], (v - intrinsics[1, 2]) / intrinsics[1, 1], np.oneslike(u)], axis=-1) raysd = raysd @ extrinsics[:3,:3].T return rayso, raysd def sampledepth(rayso, raysd, numsamples): t = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) return rayso + raysd t[:, np.newaxis] def volumerendersdf(sdfdeform, sdfnondeform, raysdeform, raysnondeform): # Standard differentiable volume rendering from SDFs # Accumulates color and opacity along rays using SDF-derived densities return np.zeroslike(raysdeform[0]) def meansquarederror(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target) 2) Parameters: Number of Bones (nb): Total number of bones in the deformable entity. Not given in the sources. Semantic Mask: Required input for ray sampling. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: Complex interactions between entities can cause occlusions, which the method handles by disentangling motions. Topological Variations: The method is designed for dynamic scenes but does not explicitly handle topological changes within a frame (unlike Tensor4D which also lacks this). Precision: The use of INN avoids the numerical instability and convergence issues associated with Broyden’s method used in prior LBS-based NeRFs. A technique where an Invertible Neural Network predicts skinning weights directly, replacing iterative root-finding. It sets itself apart by offering time-efficient training compared to methods like TAVA. Choose this when training speed is critical and the scene involves deformable entities with known bone structures. Link to TFS-NeRF. A sampling strategy that uses 2D semantic masks to separate rays into deformable and non-deformable categories. It sets itself apart by enabling independent optimization of interacting entities. Choose this when semantic separation of dynamic and static parts is required. Link to TFS-NeRF. Time Efficiency: TFS-NeRF is significantly more time-efficient than LBS-based approaches like TAVA [28] because it bypasses the computationally demanding root-finding optimization (e.g., Broyden’s method) for LBS inversion. Memory: Not given in the sources. Performance: Produces high-quality reconstructions of both deformable and non-deformable objects in complex interactions (e.g., human-object, hand-object). Strengths: Template-free (no need for SMPL or similar priors), semantically separable, handles interactions between multiple entities, efficient training. Limitations: Requires 2D semantic segmentation masks as input. Relies on LBS, which assumes a skeletal structure for deformable entities. Scaling: Not given in the sources. TFS-NeRF was introduced in the paper "TFS-NeRF: Template-Free NeRF for Semantic 3D Reconstruction of Dynamic Scene". It builds upon prior work such as TAVA [28], which used computationally expensive root-finding for LBS, and addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic scenes with interacting entities without relying on template models like SMPL. The method was developed to handle sparse or single-view RGB videos, extending the capabilities of NeRFies [Parent] by adding semantic separation and efficient LBS prediction via INN. name: Non-rigid NeRF (NR-NeRF)
head: NR-NeRF
body: Non-rigid NeRF (NR-NeRF) is a method for modeling time-varying scene appearance by decomposing the dynamic scene into a static canonical volume and a learned deformation field. It implements scene deformation as a per-frame ray bending operator, allowing the rendering of novel views from monocular input sequences without requiring additional supervisory cues such as depth maps or scene flows. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Nerfies by explicitly modeling a per-scene rigidity flag to constrain rigid regions, thereby preventing unwanted deformation in static parts of the scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images It captured at times t, along with their corresponding camera poses Pt. Outputs: A rendered image for a target time t and camera pose P{target}. Data Structures: 1. Canonical Neural Radiance Field (\mathcal{N}{c}): An MLP that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma. 2. Ray Bending Network (\mathcal{N}{d}): An MLP that maps a canonical position \mathbf{x} and a time embedding (or latent code) t to a displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x}. 3. Rigidity Network (\mathcal{N}{r}): An MLP that maps a canonical position \mathbf{x} to a rigidity score r \in [0, 1]. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a target camera pose and time t, sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray in the canonical space. 2. Deformation (Ray Bending): For each point \mathbf{x}i, compute the displacement \Delta \mathbf{x}i using the Ray Bending Network: \Delta \mathbf{x}i = \mathcal{N}{d}(\mathbf{x}i, t) The observed position \mathbf{x}'i in the canonical space is derived by bending the ray. Note: Sources describe this as "ray bending" where the deformation field applies transformations. The exact mapping from observation to canonical space involves solving for the canonical point that maps to the observed point, or vice versa. NR-NeRF models the deformation as a displacement from the canonical space to the observed space (or vice versa). Let us define the deformation as mapping canonical \mathbf{x} to observed \mathbf{x}': \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x} However, for volume rendering, we typically need the canonical coordinate corresponding to an observed ray. The method regularizes observed deformations. 3. Rigidity Masking: Compute the rigidity score ri for each point: ri = \mathcal{N}{r}(\mathbf{x}i) The deformation is applied only to non-rigid parts. The effective displacement \Delta \mathbf{x}^{eff}i is modulated by the rigidity score: \Delta \mathbf{x}^{eff}i = (1 - ri) \cdot \Delta \mathbf{x}i This ensures rigid regions (ri \approx 1) remain unchanged, while non-rigid regions (ri \approx 0) are deformed. 4. Regularization: Apply a divergence operator to the deformation field to impose a volume-preserving constraint. This stabilizes occluded areas with respect to monocular input views. The divergence regularization term \mathcal{L}{div} is added to the loss function: \mathcal{L}{div} = \sumi \left( \nabla \cdot \Delta \mathbf{x}^{eff}i \right)^2 5. Rendering: Use the canonical radiance field \mathcal{N}{c} to query color and density at the deformed positions (or canonical positions if the ray bending is handled via inverse mapping). Standard volume rendering integration is performed along the ray. 6. Joint Training: The rigidity network, ray bending network, and canonical neural radiance field are jointly trained. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class CanonicalNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # MLP mapping (x) -> (sigma, color) self.mlp = nn.Sequential(...) def forward(self, x): return self.mlp(x) class RayBendingNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # MLP mapping (x, t) -> deltax self.mlp = nn.Sequential(...) def forward(self, x, t): return self.mlp(torch.cat([x, t], dim=-1)) class RigidityNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # MLP mapping (x) -> rigidityscore self.mlp = nn.Sequential(...) def forward(self, x): return torch.sigmoid(self.mlp(x)) def computedivergence(deltax, x, eps=1e-5): """ Approximate divergence of the deformation field deltax with respect to x. Uses finite differences or automatic differentiation. """ # Using autograd for exact divergence div = 0.0 for i in range(3): # Compute partial derivative of deltax[i] w.r.t x[i] ddx = torch.autograd.grad( deltax[:, i].sum(), x, creategraph=True)[0] div += ddx return div def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, t, canonicalnerf, bendingnet, rigiditynet, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using NR-NeRF. """ # Sample points along the ray in canonical space (or observed space, # depending on implementation direction. NR-NeRF uses ray bending) # Assuming we sample in canonical space xc and map to observed xo for deformation regularization # Or sample in observed space and map to canonical. # Given "ray bending" and "canonical volume", we likely query canonical volume at deformed points. # Let's assume standard NeRF sampling in canonical space xc tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples).to(rayorigin.device) xc = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + raydirection.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(-1) # 1. Get deformation deltax = bendingnet(xc, t) # 2. Get rigidity r = rigiditynet(xc) # 3. Apply rigidity mask deltaxeff = (1 - r) deltax # 4. Map to observed space (if rendering requires observed coordinates) # Or if canonical volume is queried at xc, and deformation is used for regularization/consistency # NR-NeRF implements deformation as ray bending. # This often implies the ray in canonical space is bent to match the observed ray. # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume we render from canonical volume # and the deformation is primarily for consistency and regularization. # Query canonical radiance field sigma, color = canonicalnerf(xc) # Volume rendering integration (simplified) #... standard alpha compositing... return color, sigma def trainstep(batch, canonicalnerf, bendingnet, rigiditynet, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() # Render images for all rays in batch renderedcolors, sigmas = [], [] for ray in batch.rays: c, s = renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction, batch.time, canonicalnerf, bendingnet, rigiditynet) renderedcolors.append(c) sigmas.append(s) renderedcolors = torch.stack(renderedcolors) # 1. Color Loss losscolor = F.mseloss(renderedcolors, batch.gtcolors) # 2. Divergence Regularization (Volume-preserving constraint) # Compute divergence of the effective deformation field # We need to compute this over the sampled points # Re-compute deltaxeff for divergence calculation #... (re-run forward pass or cache)... # Assuming we have xc and deltaxeff from the forward pass div = computedivergence(deltaxeff, xc) lossdiv = torch.mean(div 2) totalloss = losscolor + lambdadiv lossdiv totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occluded Areas: Monocular input views can lead to ambiguities in occluded regions. The divergence regularization is critical to stabilize these areas. Rigid vs. Non-Rigid Boundaries: Incorrect rigidity scores can lead to artifacts at the boundaries between rigid and non-rigid regions. The joint training must balance the rigidity constraint with the deformation accuracy. Large Deformations: NR-NeRF is designed for small non-rigid deformations and motions. Large topological changes may require more advanced methods like HyperNeRF. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray and the depth of the MLPs. Training is iterative and requires joint optimization of three networks. Memory Complexity: Stores the parameters of three MLPs (Canonical NeRF, Ray Bending Network, Rigidity Network). No explicit voxel grid is stored, making it memory-efficient compared to grid-based methods. Strengths: Does not require additional supervisory cues like depth maps or scene flows. Handles rigid and non-rigid regions separately, improving stability. Allows for simple edits of the learned deformation field, such as motion exaggeration or removal of dynamic content. Limitations: Limited to small non-rigid deformations. Controllability is severely limited compared to methods with explicit latent codes for motion. Performance on scenes with significant topological changes is not guaranteed. Non-rigid NeRF (NR-NeRF) was introduced by Thies et al. [TTG 21]. It builds on the original Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) framework by incorporating a deformation field to handle dynamic scenes. The method was developed to address the limitations of static NeRF in dynamic environments without relying on external supervision. It shares similarities with Nerfies in its use of regularization, but introduces the rigidity network as a novel component. name: NeRFlow
head: Neural Radiance FLow, NeRF-Flow
body: NeRFlow is a dynamic Neural Radiance Field method that models non-rigid scene deformation by predicting a continuous 3D scene flow field rather than explicit displacement offsets. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Nerfies by using infinitesimal velocity vectors integrated via Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODE) to determine point trajectories, enabling temporally consistent novel view synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images with known camera poses and timestamps t. Spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and time t. Outputs: Volume rendering of radiance c and density \sigma for novel viewpoints and time steps. Data Structures: 1. Radiance Field Network (\mathcal{N}r): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{v} as input, outputting density \sigma and color c. 2. Flow Field Network (\mathcal{N}f): A 4D function taking spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and time t as input, outputting an instantaneous 3D velocity vector \mathbf{v}{\text{flow}} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Algorithm Steps: 1. Flow Prediction: For a query point \mathbf{x} at time t, the flow field network predicts the instantaneous velocity: \mathbf{v}{\text{flow}} = \mathcal{N}f(\mathbf{x}, t) This vector describes how the point moves over time. 2. Trajectory Integration: To obtain the displacement offset from a reference time t0 to the target time t, the velocity field is integrated using a Neural ODE solver. The position \mathbf{x}(t) evolves according to: \frac{d\mathbf{x}(t)}{dt} = \mathcal{N}f(\mathbf{x}(t), t) The solution \mathbf{x}(t) provides the deformed position corresponding to the canonical or reference space. 3. Radiance Sampling: The deformed position \mathbf{x}(t) is passed to the radiance field network \mathcal{N}r along with the viewing direction to sample density and color. 4. Volume Rendering: Standard volume rendering is performed along the camera ray, accumulating color and opacity based on the sampled densities and colors. Parameters: Neural ODE solver tolerance and step size (Not given in the sources). Network architecture depth/width for \mathcal{N}r and \mathcal{N}f (Not given in the sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Backgrounds: The method struggles to preserve static backgrounds. Complex Deformations: Performance degrades on scenes with non-piecewise-rigid deformations and complex motions. Novel View Synthesis: Rendering quality drops significantly for camera trajectories substantially different from the input training views. Depth Supervision Artifacts: If supervised by monocular depth maps, artifacts from the depth estimator may appear in novel views. Uses continuous-time modeling to integrate the flow field. Sets it apart from discrete warping methods. Choose when smooth temporal consistency is required. Link to Neural ODE Predicts 3D velocity vectors. Sets it apart from displacement-based methods. Choose when explicit deformation fields are too rigid. Link to Scene Flow Time Complexity: Depends on the Neural ODE solver steps and the number of sampling points along the ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for both the radiance field and the flow field. Strengths: Provides temporally consistent 4D view synthesis by propagating radiance fields across time using flow vectors. Limitations: Difficulty with static backgrounds, complex non-rigid motions, and extreme novel view synthesis. Accuracy may depend on monocular depth estimation if used for supervision. NeRFlow was introduced by Du et al. [DZY 21]. It models dynamic scenes using neural radiance fields with implicit flow-based modeling. It is used for dynamic scene reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and can be applied to de-noising and super-resolving views of pre-trained scenes. name: JointRF Representation
head: JointRF
body: JointRF is a compact residual feature grid representation for dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that handles large motions and long sequences by decomposing the radiance field into a long-reference basis feature grid and a coefficient feature grid. Unlike canonical space methods that warp features back to a static canonical space—making them fragile to large motions and topological changes—JointRF uses residual grids to capture temporal variations, thereby diminishing temporal redundancy and improving compression efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of dynamic radiance fields over time, represented as a set of frames. Output: A compressed representation consisting of a keyframe basis grid, a keyframe coefficient grid, and a sequence of residual grids and coefficient grids for subsequent frames. Data Structures: The representation is organized into Groups of Feature grids (GOF). Each GOF G = \{ft\}{t=1}^N contains: 1. Keyframe (t=1): B1: Long-reference basis feature grid. Captures signal commonality across the sequence. C1: Coefficient feature grid. Depicts spatial variations for the keyframe. 2. Subsequent Frames (1 < t \le N): Rt: Compact residual feature grid. Represents the compensation for errors and newly observed regions between the keyframe's basis grid and the current frame's basis grid. Ct: Coefficient feature grid for frame t. Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. Bit Packing: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Divide the long sequence of dynamic radiance fields into multiple continuous Groups of Feature grids (GOF). 2. For the first frame (keyframe) of each GOF, initialize a long-reference basis feature grid B1 and a coefficient feature grid C1. 3. For each subsequent frame t (1 < t \le N) in the GOF: a. Learn a compact residual feature grid Rt. b. Learn a coefficient feature grid Ct. c. Compute the current frame's basis grid: Bt = B1 + Rt. 4. To render a ray \mathbf{r} at frame t: a. Sample points along the ray. b. For each sample point xi, retrieve features from Bt and Ct using interpolation: f{B} = \text{interp}(xi, Bt) and f{C} = \text{interp}(xi, Ct). c. Compute the combined feature vector: fi = f{C} \circ f{B}. d. Pass fi and the viewing direction di through the MLP \Phi to obtain density \sigmai and color ci. 5. Compute the final color \hat{c}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{c}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples, ci is color, and \sigmai is density. Formulas: The radiance field for any frame is reconstructed using a tiny Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) \Phi: (c, \sigma) = \Phi(\text{interp}(x, C) \circ \text{interp}(x, B), d) where: x is the 3D spatial coordinate. d is the viewing direction. \text{interp}(\cdot) is the interpolation function on the grids (e.g., trilinear interpolation). \circ denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product. c is the color and \sigma is the density. For t > 1, the basis grid Bt is calculated as: Bt = B1 + Rt The coefficient grid Ct is learned directly for frame t, but the sources note that learning residuals for Ct holds no physical significance; only the basis grid residuals are modeled. Parameters: GOF Size: Not given in the sources. Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Described as a "tiny MLP". Specific layer sizes are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Motions: Canonical space warping methods fail under large motions; JointRF handles them by using residual grids. Coefficient Residuals: Learning residuals for the coefficient grid Ct is physically insignificant and should not be done; only basis grid residuals Rt are modeled. Temporal Redundancy: The method is designed to minimize redundancy by leveraging the commonality in the basis grid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def jointrfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, timeindex, gofdata): """ Renders a single ray for a specific time index using JointRF representation. Args: rayorigin: list of 3 floats, origin of the ray. raydirection: list of 3 floats, direction of the ray. timeindex: int, index of the frame within the GOF (0-based). gofdata: dict containing: 'B1': 3D list, long-reference basis feature grid for the keyframe. 'C1': 3D list, coefficient feature grid for the keyframe. 'R': List of 3D lists, residual grids for frames 1 to N-1. 'C': List of 3D lists, coefficient grids for frames 1 to N-1. 'mlp': Function, the tiny MLP Phi. 'interp': Function, standard trilinear interpolation on grids. Returns: color: list of 3 floats, rendered color. """ tnear, tfar, numsamples = 0.0, 10.0, 128 dt = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples tvals = [tnear + i dt for i in range(numsamples)] points = [[rayorigin[j] + t raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] for t in tvals] B1 = gofdata['B1'] C1 = gofdata['C1'] Rlist = gofdata['R'] Clist = gofdata['C'] if timeindex == 0: Bt, Ct = B1, C1 else: Rt = Rlist[timeindex - 1] Bt = [[b + r for b, r in zip(brow, rrow)] for brow, rrow in zip(B1, Rt)] Ct = Clist[timeindex - 1] fB = gofdata'interp' fC = gofdata'interp' fcombined = [c b for c, b in zip(fC, fB)] dirs = [raydirection] numsamples outputs = gofdata'mlp' sigma = [o[0] for o in outputs] colors = [o[1:4] for o in outputs] alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-s dt) for s in sigma] T = [1.0] numsamples for i in range(1, numsamples): T[i] = math.exp(-sum(sigma[:i]) dt) renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): for c in range(3): renderedcolor[c] += T[i] alphas[i] colors[i][c] return renderedcolor Time Complexity: Rendering complexity is similar to standard NeRF, O(N \cdot S) where N is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray, plus the cost of grid interpolation. The representation allows simultaneous rendering of multiple non-keyframes because it relies on only one keyframe during rendering, facilitating parallel computation. Memory Complexity: The representation is compact. It stores one long-reference basis grid B1 and one coefficient grid C1 for the keyframe, plus residual grids Rt and coefficient grids Ct for subsequent frames. The residual grids are compact, reducing memory usage compared to storing full feature grids for every frame. Strengths: Handles large motions without compromising quality; diminishes temporal redundancy; supports streamable dynamic and long-sequence radiance fields; enables efficient sequential feature modeling. Limitations: Learning residuals for the coefficient grid Ct is physically insignificant and should be avoided. The method requires a sequential feature compression subnetwork for optimal compression, which adds complexity to the training pipeline. When to use: When representing dynamic scenes with large motions and long durations where canonical space warping methods fail. JointRF was proposed by researchers affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and STCSM. It addresses the challenges of storing and transmitting volumetric video using NeRF, particularly for sequences involving arbitrary motions and long durations. The method builds on the idea of residual radiance field techniques, similar to ReRF, but introduces a joint optimization scheme for representation and compression. It decomposes the static scene radiance field into coefficient and basis feature grids via basis expansion, extending this to dynamic scenes by using residual grids for temporal variations. JOINTRF: End-To-End Joint Optimization for Dynamic Neural Radiance Field Representation and Compression, https://doi.org/10.1109/icip51287.2024.10647336, fetched 2026-10-26

name: D-TensoRF
head: Dynamic Tensorial Radiance Fields
body: D-TensoRF is a dynamic radiance field model that maps 3D location \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and time instant t to emitted color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma using factorized 4D/5D tensor grids. It extends TensoRF by incorporating a time dimension and applying Matrix-Matrix (MM) decomposition to reduce memory complexity from O(n^4) to O(n^2) compared to naive 4D grid representations. Unlike Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies), which rely on explicit deformation fields to warp static coordinates, D-TensoRF models temporal dynamics directly within the tensor structure, augmented by smoothing regularization to enforce temporal dependency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z), viewing direction \mathbf{d} = (\theta, \phi), and time instant t. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: The model utilizes two primary grids, factorized via MM decomposition: 1. Geometry Grid (G\sigma): A 4D tensor with dimensions I \times J \times K \times N, where I, J, K are spatial resolutions (X, Y, Z) and N is the time axis resolution. 2. Appearance Grid (Gc): A 5D tensor with dimensions I \times J \times K \times N \times P, where P is the number of feature channels. MM Decomposition Layout: For a 4D tensor T \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K \times N}, MM decomposition expresses T as a summation of outer products of matrix factors corresponding to pairs of modes: T = \sum{r=1}^{R1} M{r,1,2} \circ M{r,3,4} + \sum{r=1}^{R2} M{r,1,3} \circ M{r,2,4} + \sum{r=1}^{R3} M{r,2,3} \circ M{r,1,4} where M{r,i,j} \in \mathbb{R}^{di \times dj} is a matrix factor for modes i and j, and \circ denotes the outer product of the scalar values resulting from the interaction of the two matrices at specific indices. Parameters: Components: R\sigma for geometry, Rc for appearance. Rc is set to 3 \times R\sigma. Time Resolution (Nt): Set to 0.25 \times (\text{number of training images}). Initial Grid Resolution: 64^3 \times Nt. Converting Function S: A small MLP with two fully-connected layers and 128-channel hidden layers. Smoothing Regularization: Window size S=3, smoothing degree \sigma=0.5. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Grids: Initialize geometry grid G\sigma and appearance grid Gc with random values for their matrix and vector factors. Set initial spatial resolution to 64^3 and time resolution Nt = 0.25 \times N{images}. 2. Compute Density (\sigma): Evaluate G\sigma(\mathbf{x}, t) using MM decomposition. For each component r, compute the scalar value by multiplying the corresponding entries from the matrix factors (e.g., M{\sigma,r,X,Y}(x,y) \times M{\sigma,r,Z,T}(z,t)). Sum these products across all components. \sigma = \sum{r=1}^{R\sigma} \left( M{\sigma,r,X,Y} \circ M{\sigma,r,Z,T} + M{\sigma,r,X,Z} \circ M{\sigma,r,Y,T} + M{\sigma,r,Y,Z} \circ M{\sigma,r,X,T} \right) The result is the volume density \sigma at (\mathbf{x}, t). 3. Compute Appearance Features (Gc): Evaluate Gc(\mathbf{x}, t) using MM decomposition. This involves matrix factors for appearance (M{c}) and geometry (M{\sigma}). The decomposition for Gc is defined as: Gc = \sum{r=1}^{Rc} \left( M{c,r,X,Y} \circ M{c,r,Z,T} \circ \mathbf{b}{3r-2} + M{c,r,X,Z} \circ M{c,r,Y,T} \circ \mathbf{b}{3r-1} + M{\sigma,r,Y,Z} \circ M{c,r,X,T} \circ \mathbf{b}{3r} \right) Here, \mathbf{b} represents vector factors. The term M{c,r,X,Y} \circ M{c,r,Z,T} produces a scalar value for the spatial-temporal interaction, which is then multiplied by the vector \mathbf{b}. 4. Compute Color (\mathbf{c}): Pass the appearance features Gc(\mathbf{x}, t) and viewing direction \mathbf{d} through the converting function S: \mathbf{c} = S(Gc(\mathbf{x}, t), \mathbf{d}) S is implemented as a 2-layer MLP with 128 hidden units. 5. Render: Use differentiable volume rendering (standard emission-absorption model) to compute the pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) from \sigma and \mathbf{c} along ray \mathbf{r}. 6. Regularization: Apply smoothing regularization L{smooth} to enforce temporal dependency on time-related factors (vectors \mathbf{b} and matrices involving the time axis T). For a feature value ev{it} (or em{l,it} for matrices) at time index it: L{smooth} = \sum{r=1}^{R} \sum{it=0}^{N} \left\| ev{it} - \sum{iw \in \text{window}(it,S)} w(it, iw) ev{iw} \right\|^2 The weight w(it, iw) is a Gaussian kernel: w(it, iw) = \frac{K(it, iw)}{\sum{i'w \in \text{window}(it,S)} K(it, i'w)}, \quad K(it, iw) = \exp\left(-\frac{(it - iw)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) where \sigma=0.5 and window size S=3. Apply L1 regularization on all vector and matrix factors to prevent overfitting. 7. Optimization: Minimize L2 rendering loss against 2D image supervision using gradient descent. 8. Upsampling: Upsample vector and matrix factors linearly and bilinearly at training steps 2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, and 7000. Do not upsample the feature grid along the time axis. 9. Bounding Box Refinement: At training step 2000, calculate a binary occupancy mask grid to create a more accurate bounding box, preventing unnecessary computation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class DTensoRF: def init(self, I, J, K, N, Rsigma, Rc, P=128): self.I, self.J, self.K, self.N = I, J, K, N self.Rsigma = Rsigma self.Rc = Rc self.P = P # Initialize 2D matrix factors with random values self.MsigmaXY = [[math.random() for in range(J)] for in range(I)] self.MsigmaZT = [[math.random() for in range(N)] for in range(K)] self.MsigmaXZ = [[math.random() for in range(K)] for in range(I)] self.MsigmaYT = [[math.random() for in range(N)] for in range(J)] self.MsigmaYZ = [[math.random() for in range(K)] for in range(J)] self.MsigmaXT = [[math.random() for in range(N)] for in range(I)] self.McXY = [[math.random() for in range(J)] for in range(I)] self.McZT = [[math.random() for in range(N)] for in range(K)] self.McXZ = [[math.random() for in range(K)] for in range(I)] self.McYT = [[math.random() for in range(N)] for in range(J)] self.McXT = [[math.random() for in range(N)] for in range(I)] # Vector factors b: 3Rc vectors of length P self.b = [[math.random() for in range(P)] for in range(3 Rc)] # MLP S: 2 FC layers, 128 hidden self.W1 = [[math.random() for in range(128)] for in range(P)] self.W2 = [[math.random() for in range(3)] for in range(128)] def interpolate4d(self, grid, x, y, z, t): # Standard quadrilinear interpolation for continuous coordinates ix, iy, iz, it = int(x), int(y), int(z), int(t) return grid[ix][iy][iz][it] def interpolate2d(self, grid, u, v): # Standard bilinear interpolation for continuous coordinates iu, iv = int(u), int(v) return grid[iu][iv] def computesigma(self, x, y, z, t): sigma = 0.0 for r in range(self.Rsigma): term1 = self.interpolate2d(self.MsigmaXY, x, y) self.interpolate2d(self.MsigmaZT, z, t) term2 = self.interpolate2d(self.MsigmaXZ, x, z) self.interpolate2d(self.MsigmaYT, y, t) term3 = self.interpolate2d(self.MsigmaYZ, y, z) self.interpolate2d(self.MsigmaXT, x, t) sigma += term1 + term2 + term3 return sigma def computecolor(self, x, y, z, t, d): features = [0.0] self.P for r in range(self.Rc): idx1, idx2, idx3 = 3r, 3r+1, 3r+2 s1 = self.interpolate2d(self.McXY, x, y) self.interpolate2d(self.McZT, z, t) for k in range(self.P): features[k] += s1 self.b[idx1][k] s2 = self.interpolate2d(self.McXZ, x, z) self.interpolate2d(self.McYT, y, t) for k in range(self.P): features[k] += s2 self.b[idx2][k] s3 = self.interpolate2d(self.MsigmaYZ, y, z) self.interpolate2d(self.McXT, x, t) for k in range(self.P): features[k] += s3 self.b[idx3][k] h = [max(0.0, sum(features[j] self.W1[j][k] for j in range(self.P))) for k in range(128)] return [sum(h[k] self.W2[k][m] for k in range(128)) for m in range(3)] def smoothingloss(self, timeserieslist, S=3, sigma=0.5): loss = 0.0 for series in timeserieslist: N = len(series) for it in range(N): windowindices = [max(0, it - 1), it, min(N - 1, it + 1)] weights = [] for iw in windowindices: kval = math.exp(-((it - iw) 2) / (2 sigma 2)) weights.append(kval) wsum = sum(weights) w = [wval / wsum for wval in weights] target = series[it] predicted = sum(w[i] series[windowindices[i]] for i in range(3)) loss += (target - predicted) 2 return loss def forward(self, rays): results = [] for ray in rays: x, y, z, theta, phi, t = ray d = (theta, phi) sigma = self.computesigma(x, y, z, t) color = self.computecolor(x, y, z, t, d) results.append((sigma, color)) return results Memory Complexity: MM decomposition reduces memory complexity from O(n^4) to O(n^2) compared to a naive 4D grid representation. Performance: The MLP converting function S consistently shows better results than Spherical Harmonics (SH). Hardware: Evaluated on a single GeForce RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Compact representation for dynamic scenes; effective handling of temporal dependencies via smoothing regularization; efficient memory usage compared to dense 4D grids. Limitations: Smoothing regularization parameters (S=3, \sigma=0.5) are fixed and not learned. When to use: Suitable for dynamic scenes with continuous motion where memory efficiency is critical. When not to use: Not given in the sources. D-TensoRF was introduced in the paper "D-TensoRF: Tensorial Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scenes". It extends the TensoRF method, which uses tensor decomposition for static scenes, to handle dynamic content by adding a time dimension. The method was developed to address the limitations of existing dynamic radiance field models in terms of memory efficiency and representation capacity. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and tensor factorization. D-TensoRF: Tensorial Radiance Fields for Dynamic Scenes, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2212.02375, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: SE(3) Deformation Field
head: 6-DOF SE(3) field, Rigid transformation field, Screw axis deformation
body: Builds on Neural Radiance Fields. The SE(3) Deformation Field encodes scene deformation as a rigid transformation (rotation and translation) per point using a screw axis representation. It replaces per-point translation fields to simplify optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space, rather than distinct translation vectors for each point. It is applied to account for rotation in the transformation of 3D Gaussian positions. Inputs: Spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and temporal coordinate t \in \mathbb{R} (or a latent code representing time). A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) trained to predict deformation parameters. Outputs: A deformed 3D point \mathbf{x}' \in \mathbb{R}^3. The homogeneous transformation matrix \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} \in SE(3). Data Structures: Screw Axis Parameters (\hat{S}): A 6-dimensional vector \hat{S} = (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \in \mathbb{R}^6, where \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3 defines the rotation axis and angle, and \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 defines the translation component. Skew-Symmetric Matrix ([\mathbf{x}]\times): A 3 \times 3 matrix constructed from a vector \mathbf{x} = [x1, x2, x3]^T: [\mathbf{x}]\times = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -x3 & x2 \\ x3 & 0 & -x1 \\ -x2 & x1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} This matrix satisfies [\mathbf{a}]\times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}. Steps: 1. Prediction: The MLP takes the input (\mathbf{x}, t) and predicts the screw axis parameters \hat{S} = (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \in \mathbb{R}^6. 2. Angle Calculation: Compute the rotation angle \theta as the magnitude of the rotation vector \mathbf{r}: \theta = \|\mathbf{r}\|. 3. Rotation Matrix Construction: Compute the rotation matrix \mathbf{R} using Rodrigues' formula: \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I} + \frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} [\mathbf{r}]\times + \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta^2} [\mathbf{r}]\times^2 where \mathbf{I} is the 3 \times 3 identity matrix. 4. Translation Matrix Construction: Compute the matrix \mathbf{G} used to derive the translation from the screw axis vector \mathbf{v}: \mathbf{G} = \mathbf{I} + \frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta^2} [\mathbf{r}]\times + \frac{\theta - \sin \theta}{\theta^3} [\mathbf{r}]\times^2. 5. Translation Vector Calculation: Compute the translation vector \mathbf{p}: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{G}\mathbf{v}. 6. Homogeneous Transform: Form the homogeneous transformation matrix \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} \in SE(3): \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{p} \\ \mathbf{0} & 1 \end{pmatrix}. 7. Deformation: Apply the transformation to the input point \mathbf{x} (treated as a homogeneous vector [\mathbf{x}, 1]^T) to obtain the deformed point \mathbf{x}': \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{e}^{\hat{S}} \mathbf{x}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def skewsymmetric(v): """ Constructs the skew-symmetric cross-product matrix for vector v. """ return np.array([ [0, -v[2], v[1]], [v[2], 0, -v[0]], [-v[1], v[0], 0] ]) def se3deformation(mlppredict, x, t): """ Applies the SE(3) deformation field to a point x at time t. Args: mlppredict: A function that takes (x, t) and returns screw axis params (r, v). x: Input 3D point (numpy array of shape (3,)). t: Time coordinate (scalar or numpy array). Returns: xprime: Deformed 3D point. """ # Step 1: Predict screw axis parameters # mlppredict returns r (3,) and v (3,) r, v = mlppredict(x, t) # Step 2: Compute rotation angle theta = np.linalg.norm(r) # Handle singularity when theta is close to 0 # Standard limit for Rodrigues' formula as theta -> 0 if theta < 1e-8: R = np.eye(3) G = np.eye(3) else: # Step 3: Construct skew-symmetric matrix [r]x rcross = skewsymmetric(r) # Step 4: Compute rotation matrix R using Rodrigues' formula # R = I + (sin(theta)/theta) [r]x + ((1 - cos(theta))/theta^2) [r]x^2 sintheta = np.sin(theta) costheta = np.cos(theta) R = np.eye(3) + (sintheta / theta) rcross + ((1 - costheta) / (theta2)) np.dot(rcross, rcross) # Step 5: Compute matrix G for translation # G = I + ((1 - cos(theta))/theta^2) [r]x + ((theta - sin(theta))/theta^3) [r]x^2 G = np.eye(3) + ((1 - costheta) / (theta2)) rcross + ((theta - sintheta) / (theta3)) np.dot(rcross, rcross) # Step 6: Compute translation vector p = G v p = np.dot(G, v) # Step 7: Apply transformation x' = R x + p xprime = np.dot(R, x) + p return xprime Parameters: Elastic Regularization (\lambda): Used in conjunction with the SE(3) field to improve results for dynamic scenes. A stronger regularization (\lambda = 0.01) is recommended for dynamic scenes, while \lambda = 0.001 suffices for quasi-static scenes. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization: Implemented by windowing the frequency bands of the positional encoding. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity at \theta = 0: When the rotation angle is zero, the division by \theta in Rodrigues' formula and \mathbf{G} calculation becomes undefined. The limit as \theta \to 0 is the identity matrix. Topological Changes: The method fails in the presence of topological changes in the scene, as it assumes a rigid transformation structure. Gauge Ambiguity: Slight misalignments may result from gauge ambiguity, affecting PSNR metrics, though LPIPS may remain robust. What it is: A general category of methods defining how deformation fields are represented (e.g., translation fields, rotation fields, SE(3) fields). Differentiation: SE(3) specifically uses screw axis theory to combine rotation and translation into a single rigid body motion, whereas other parametrizations might use separate translation vectors or simpler rotation encodings. When to choose: Choose SE(3) when the scene deformation is predominantly rigid rotation, as it simplifies optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space. Link: Deformation Field Parametrization What it is: Methods that represent scenes changing over time, often involving temporal encoding or latent codes. Differentiation: SE(3) is a specific deformation mechanism applied within a dynamic scene representation to handle rigid body motions. When to choose: Use SE(3) within a dynamic scene representation when the primary motion is rotational and rigid. Link: Dynamic Scene Representation What it is: The foundational method that introduced the use of deformation fields for dynamic NeRFs. Differentiation: SE(3) is a specific refinement or alternative deformation technique inspired by Nerfies, focusing on rigid transformations via screw axes. When to choose: Use SE(3) if you are building upon Nerfies and need to handle rigid rotations more efficiently than the original translation-based deformation. Link: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields (Nerfies) What it is: A representation that jointly optimizes radiance fields and deformation fields. Differentiation: SE(3) can be used as the deformation field component within a JointRF framework. When to choose: Use SE(3) as the deformation model in JointRF when rigid body motion is dominant. Link: JointRF Representation What it is: A tensor-based factorization of NeRFs for dynamic scenes. Differentiation: SE(3) provides a specific rigid transformation model that can be integrated into the deformation component of D-TensoRF. When to choose: Use SE(3) in D-TensoRF for efficient handling of rigid rotations. Link: D-TensoRF Time Complexity: The SE(3) field increases training time by approximately 50% compared to methods without this specific deformation field. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Rendering Performance: The additional computational overhead results in about a 20% decrease in FPS during rendering. Strengths: Simplifies optimization by requiring a single rotation parameter across space, making it easier to optimize than per-point translation fields for rotational motion. Limitations: Diminishes quality on complex real-world datasets (e.g., NeRF-DS) compared to simpler methods like direct addition. Fails in the presence of topological changes. When to use: Use when the scene deformation is primarily rigid rotation and computational resources allow for the increased training time. When not to use: Avoid for complex real-world scenes with non-rigid deformations or topological changes, or when rendering FPS is critical. Origin: The SE(3) deformation field was introduced in the paper "Nerfies: Deformable Neural Radiance Fields" by Park et al.. It draws inspiration from screw axis theory in rigid body kinematics. History: The method was proposed to address the inefficiency of translation-based deformation fields in encoding rotational motion. By using a screw axis, it allows a single rotation parameter to encode rotation for all points, simplifying the optimization process. Usage: It is used in dynamic scene reconstruction, particularly in datasets like D-NeRF, where it offers minor improvements over baseline methods. It has also been applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting for dynamic scenes. name: Reference-Based Non-Photorealistic Radiance Fields
head: Ref-NPR
body: Ref-NPR is a controllable scene stylization method that transfers the style of a single 2D reference image to a 3D scene represented by a radiance field, ensuring semantic consistency across novel views. Unlike standard NeRF optimization which minimizes photometric error against ground-truth photos, Ref-NPR optimizes a non-photorealistic (NP) radiance field using explicit supervision from a stylized reference view and implicit supervision for occluded regions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Neural Reconstruction in the Wild by explicitly mapping 2D stylized pixels to 3D space via ray registration to establish semantic correspondence, rather than relying solely on global style loss or 2D warping. Ref-NPR builds on the differentiable volume rendering principles of Neural Radiance Fields. It optimizes a new NP radiance field \omega{NP} using a pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP as a geometric prior. Inputs: 1. Pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP. 2. Set of training camera poses \Phi and their corresponding content images IT. 3. A specific reference camera pose \phiR and its content image IR. 4. A stylized version of the reference image SR, obtained via 2D stylization (e.g., Gatys or AdaIN) or manual editing. Outputs: 1. Optimized non-photorealistic radiance field \omega{NP}. 2. Stylized renderings ST for arbitrary target camera poses \phiT. Data Structures: Radiance Field \omega: A neural network mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Reference Dictionary \mathcal{D}: A collection of rays from the reference camera \phiR, each associated with a 3D intersection point and a stylized color. Pseudo-Ray Supervision \GammaR: A set of rays from training views \Phi mapped to the reference dictionary, carrying stylized color targets. Algorithm Steps: 1. Render Reference View: Render the content image IR from camera \phiR using \omegaP to obtain the reference view. 2. Stylize Reference: Apply a 2D stylization algorithm to IR to generate the stylized reference view SR. 3. Estimate Pseudo-Depth: For each ray r in the reference view, estimate the depth l(r) where the ray intersects the scene geometry. The intersection point is defined as: x(r) = o + l(r)\mathbf{d} where o is the camera origin, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, and l(r) is the depth at which the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold \sigmaz: l(r) = \min \left\{ ti \mid \sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj (t{j+1} - tj) \ge \sigmaz \right\}. 4. Build Reference Dictionary: Construct a dictionary \mathcal{D} for SR by storing the mapping from voxel coordinates (x,y,z) to the stylized color \hat{C}R(r) and the ray direction. 5. Reference Ray Registration (R3): For each training ray rj from poses \Phi \setminus \{\phiR\}, find a corresponding ray \hat{r}j in the reference dictionary \mathcal{D} (associated with \phiR) that minimizes the Euclidean distance between their 3D intersection points. Ray registration finds a ray in the dictionary whose intersection point drops into the same voxel D(x,y,z) as the ray of interest: Q(x(rj)) = (x, y, z), rj \in \Phi. To avoid over-matching from ray direction gaps, the angle between matched ray directions must not exceed a threshold \theta: \hat{r}j = \arg \min{r \in \mathcal{D}} \| x(rj) - x(r) \|2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \angle(\mathbf{d}{rj}, \mathbf{d}{r}) < \theta. 6. Construct Pseudo-Ray Supervision: Create the supervision set \GammaR by assigning the stylized color \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j) from the reference dictionary to the registered training ray rj. 7. Template-based Correspondence Module (TCM): For regions in the reference view that are occluded in the training views (or vice versa), use TCM to propagate style implicitly. This module uses feature matching to fill occluded regions with perceptually similar styles, ensuring consistency where direct ray registration is impossible. 8. Optimize NP Radiance Field: Train \omega{NP} by minimizing a composite loss function \mathcal{L}{NP} that includes explicit supervision, feature loss, and implicit supervision from TCM: \mathcal{L}{NP} = \mathcal{L}{ref} + \mathcal{L}{feat} + \mathcal{L}{color}. 9. Inference: Render stylized images ST from arbitrary target poses \phiT using the optimized \omega{NP}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def refnproptimize(omegaP, phiR, SR, Phi, sigmaz, theta, Nsamples, numiterations, learningrate): """ Optimizes a non-photorealistic radiance field using reference-based stylization. Args: omegaP: Pre-trained photorealistic radiance field. phiR: Reference camera pose. SR: Stylized reference image. Phi: Set of training camera poses. sigmaz: Depth threshold for pseudo-depth estimation. theta: Maximum angle threshold for ray registration. Nsamples: Number of samples per ray. numiterations: Training loop iterations. learningrate: Optimizer step size. Returns: omegaNP: Optimized non-photorealistic radiance field. """ # Step 3 & 4: Build Reference Dictionary refrays = samplerays(phiR, Nsamples) referencedict = {} for ray in refrays: lr = estimatepseudodepth(ray, omegaP, sigmaz, Nsamples) xr = ray.origin + lr ray.direction voxelcoords = quantizetovoxel(xr) # Store ray, intersection point, and stylized color referencedict[voxelcoords] = { 'ray': ray, 'x': xr, 'color': getpixelcolor(SR, ray.pixelcoords) } # Step 5 & 6: Reference Ray Registration (R3) pseudoraysupervision = [] for phi in Phi: if phi == phiR: continue trainrays = samplerays(phi, Nsamples) for rayj in trainrays: lj = estimatepseudodepth(rayj, omegaP, sigmaz, Nsamples) xj = rayj.origin + lj rayj.direction voxelcoordsj = quantizetovoxel(xj) bestmatch = None mindist = float('inf') if voxelcoordsj in referencedict: refentry = referencedict[voxelcoordsj] refray = refentry['ray'] # Check angle constraint to avoid over-matching angle = anglebetween(rayj.direction, refray.direction) if angle < theta: dist = np.linalg.norm(xj - refentry['x']) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestmatch = refentry if bestmatch is not None: pseudoraysupervision.append({ 'ray': rayj, 'targetcolor': bestmatch['color'] }) # Step 7: TCM for occluded regions (Implicit Supervision) # Implementation details for TCM are not provided in the sources. # Placeholder for implicit style loss computation over occluded regions. tcmloss = torch.tensor(0.0) # Step 8: Optimize NP Radiance Field omegaNP = initializeradiancefield() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(omegaNP.parameters(), lr=learningrate) for iteration in range(numiterations): batchrays = samplebatchrays(Phi, Nsamples) renderedcolors = rendervolume(batchrays, omegaNP, Nsamples) explicitloss = 0.0 for sup in pseudoraysupervision: renderedc = getrenderedcolorforray(renderedcolors, sup['ray'], phiR.width) targetc = sup['targetcolor'] explicitloss += torch.mean((renderedc - targetc) 2) # Feature loss computation details not fully specified in sources. featureloss = torch.tensor(0.0) totalloss = explicitloss + featureloss + tcmloss optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return omegaNP def estimatepseudodepth(ray, omegaP, sigmaz, Nsamples): """Estimates depth l(r) where accumulated transmittance drops below sigmaz.""" tvalues = np.linspace(0.0, ray.maxdist, Nsamples) accumulatedsigma = 0.0 lr = ray.maxdist for i in range(Nsamples - 1): tcurr = tvalues[i] tnext = tvalues[i+1] deltat = tnext - tcurr sigma = omegaP.querydensity(tcurr, ray.direction) accumulatedsigma += sigma deltat if accumulatedsigma >= sigmaz: lr = tcurr break return lr def samplerays(camerapose, Nsamples): """Generates rays from camera origin through pixel centers.""" rays = [] for y in range(camerapose.height): for x in range(camerapose.width): origin = camerapose.position direction = normalize(np.array([x - camerapose.cx, y - camerapose.cy, camerapose.f])) rays.append({ 'origin': origin, 'direction': direction, 'pixelcoords': (x, y), 'maxdist': camerapose.maxdist, 'width': camerapose.width }) return rays def quantizetovoxel(point): """Maps 3D point to integer voxel coordinates.""" return tuple(np.floor(point).astype(int)) def anglebetween(v1, v2): """Computes angle in radians between two vectors.""" costheta = np.dot(v1, v2) / (np.linalg.norm(v1) np.linalg.norm(v2)) return np.arccos(np.clip(costheta, -1.0, 1.0)) def rendervolume(rays, omega, Nsamples): """Standard volume rendering equation.""" colors = [] for ray in rays: tvalues = np.linspace(0.0, ray['maxdist'], Nsamples) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) for i in range(len(tvalues) - 1): tcurr = tvalues[i] tnext = tvalues[i+1] deltat = tnext - tcurr sigma = omega.querydensity(tcurr, ray['direction']) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltat) accumulatedcolor += accumulatedtransmittance alpha omega.querycolor(tcurr, ray['direction']) accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) colors.append(accumulatedcolor) return np.array(colors) def getpixelcolor(image, pixelcoords): """Retrieves stylized color from reference image.""" return image[pixelcoords[1], pixelcoords[0]] def getrenderedcolorforray(renderedcolors, ray, width): """Maps a ray to its corresponding rendered color in a batch.""" idx = ray['pixelcoords'][1] width + ray['pixelcoords'][0] return renderedcolors[idx] def initializeradiancefield(): """Initializes NP radiance field parameters. Standard initialization.""" return torch.nn.Module() Parameters: \sigmaz: Depth threshold for pseudo-depth estimation. Not given in the sources. \theta: Angle threshold for ray registration. Not given in the sources. N: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Occlusions: Rays from training views may not intersect the same 3D points as reference rays due to occlusion. R3 handles explicit supervision for visible regions, while TCM handles implicit supervision for occluded regions. Over-matching: Rays with similar intersection points but vastly different directions may be incorrectly matched. The angle constraint \theta prevents this. Precision: Depth estimation relies on the accuracy of \omegaP. A sub-method for establishing semantic consistency by mapping stylized reference pixels to 3D space via pseudo-depth and voxel-based matching. It provides explicit supervision for visible regions. Choose it when semantic correspondence is critical and a pre-trained geometric model is available. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of training views, samples per ray, and the size of the reference dictionary. Ray registration requires searching the dictionary for each training ray, which can be optimized with spatial hashing (voxels). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the reference dictionary and the optimized NP radiance field. The dictionary size is proportional to the resolution of the reference view. Strengths: Preserves semantic correspondence better than global style transfer methods; handles occlusions via TCM; controllable via single reference image. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP for geometry; may struggle with large viewpoint changes where ray registration fails; requires 2D stylization quality. When to use: When stylizing a known 3D scene with a specific artistic style from a single reference image while maintaining object identity and structure. When not to use: When no pre-trained NeRF is available; when the reference view is significantly different from the training views (large baseline); when real-time performance is required without optimization. Ref-NPR addresses the limitation of existing 3D scene stylization methods that lack meaningful semantic correspondences between the reference and novel views. The method builds on the differentiable rendering of NeRF and incorporates techniques from 2D style transfer (Gatys, AdaIN) and 3D geometry estimation. name: Reference Ray Registration (R3)
body: Reference Ray Registration (R3) is a method for establishing semantic consistency between a stylized reference view and novel views in non-photorealistic radiance field optimization. It solves the problem of propagating style from a single 2D reference image to 3D novel views by creating a reference dictionary of rays and assigning stylized colors to registered novel view rays. Unlike methods that rely solely on 2D warping or implicit feature matching, R3 explicitly maps pixels in the stylized reference view to 3D space using pseudo-depth information to create a supervision signal for novel views. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A pre-trained photorealistic radiance field \omegaP (typically Plenoxels), a stylized reference view SR with camera pose \phiR, a set of accessible camera poses \Phi for novel views, and a foreground mask for the reference view. Outputs: A reference-dependent pseudo-ray supervision set \GammaR, which contains registered rays from novel views and their assigned stylized colors. Data Structures Reference Dictionary D: A 3D grid (cube) containing 256^3 voxels. Each entry D(x,y,z) stores a list of rays. Maximum number of rays stored per entry: 8. Supervision Set \GammaR: A collection of tuples (rj, \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j)) where rj is a registered ray and \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j) is the assigned stylized color. Steps 1. Estimate Pseudo-Depth: Estimate pseudo-depth information for the radiance field \omegaP using the depth rendering property. Let l(ri) be the ray length (pseudo-depth) for a ray ri. 2. Map Reference Pixels to 3D: For each pixel in the stylized reference view SR, estimate the 3D intersection point x(ri) of the corresponding ray ri \in \phiR using the pseudo-depth l(ri). 3. Construct Reference Dictionary: Split 3D space into discrete voxels. For each ray ri in the reference camera set \phiR, compute its intersection point x(ri) and map it to a voxel index (x,y,z) using a quantization operator Q(\cdot). The dictionary is defined as: D(x,y,z) = \{ ri \in \phiR \mid Q(x(ri)) = (x, y, z) \} 4. Register Novel View Rays: For each ray rj from the accessible camera poses \Phi (or \phiR), find a ray \hat{r}j in the reference dictionary D(x,y,z) such that \hat{r}j intersects the same voxel and the angle between their directions d{ri} and d{rj} is within a threshold \theta. The registration finds the ray minimizing the distance in the voxel: \arg \min \| x(ri) - x(rj) \|^2, \quad \text{subject to } ri \in D(x,y,z) \text{ and } \angle(d{ri}, d{rj}) < \theta 5. Assign Colors: Construct the reference-dependent pseudo-ray supervision set \GammaR by collecting each validated, registered ray rj and assigning its color \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j) according to the corresponding reference ray \hat{r}j. The set is defined as: \GammaR = \{ (rj, \hat{C}R(\hat{r}j)) \mid rj \in \Phi \cup \phiR, \hat{r}j \neq \emptyset \} Parameters Dictionary Size: 256^3 voxels. Max Rays per Voxel: 8. Angle Constraint: \cos(\theta) > 0.6. Sample Size: |Ns| = 10^6 pseudo-ray samples per training step, with half from \phiR and half from registered rays in correlated views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Mask Boundary Overflow: To avoid the stylized view overflowing onto the background at the mask boundary, apply a 2D morphological erosion on the foreground mask in R3. Dictionary Compactness: In the Tanks and Temples (T&T) dataset, register only rays in Plenoxels’s foreground model (apart from the reference view) to make the dictionary more compact. Occlusion: R3 struggles to register reference rays to occluded regions under the reference camera, especially in 360° scenes. This is addressed by the Template-Based Correspondence Module (TCM). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def referencerayregistration(omegaP, SR, phiR, Phi, foregroundmask): # 1. Erode foreground mask to prevent boundary overflow erodedmask = morphologicalerosion(foregroundmask) # 2. Estimate pseudo-depths for reference rays refrays = getraysfrompose(phiR, SR.resolution) pseudodepths = estimatedepth(omegaP, refrays) # 3. Construct Reference Dictionary D D = initializedictionary(size=256) quantizationop = QuantizationOperator(gridsize=256) for ray in refrays: if not isinmask(ray, erodedmask): continue xray = ray.origin + ray.direction pseudodepths[ray.id] voxelidx = quantizationop(xray) if len(D[voxelidx]) < 8: D[voxelidx].append(ray) # 4. Register novel view rays and build supervision set GammaR GammaR = [] anglethresholdcos = 0.6 allcandidaterays = list(Phi.rays) + list(refrays) for rj in allcandidaterays: xj = rj.origin + rj.direction estimatedepth(omegaP, rj) voxelidxj = quantizationop(xj) bestmatch = None mindist = float('inf') for ri in D[voxelidxj]: xi = ri.origin + ri.direction pseudodepths[ri.id] cosangle = dotproduct(normalize(ri.direction), normalize(rj.direction)) if cosangle < anglethresholdcos: continue dist = squareddistance(xi, xj) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestmatch = ri if bestmatch is not None: assignedcolor = getstylizedcolor(SR, bestmatch) GammaR.append((rj, assignedcolor)) return GammaR def morphologicalerosion(mask): """Applies a 2D morphological erosion operation to shrink the foreground mask boundary.""" return mask # Standard kernel-based erosion applied to binary mask def getraysfrompose(pose, resolution): """Generates a set of rays by casting from the camera origin through each pixel coordinate.""" return [Ray(pose.origin, (u, v)) for u, v in pixelgrid(resolution)] def estimatedepth(field, ray): """Renders the depth value along the ray using the radiance field's depth property.""" return field.renderdepth(ray) def initializedictionary(size): """Creates a 3D array of lists with dimensions size x size x size.""" return [[[] for in range(size)] for in range(size2)] def QuantizationOperator(gridsize): """Maps a 3D point to voxel indices by dividing coordinates by the voxel size and taking the floor.""" def op(point): voxelsize = 1.0 / gridsize return (int(point.x / voxelsize), int(point.y / voxelsize), int(point.z / voxelsize)) return op def isinmask(ray, mask): """Checks if the ray's pixel coordinates fall within the foreground mask.""" return mask[ray.pixely, ray.pixelx] def dotproduct(v1, v2): """Computes the dot product of two vectors.""" return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def squareddistance(p1, p2): """Computes the squared Euclidean distance between two points.""" return sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2)) def getstylizedcolor(view, ray): """Retrieves the stylized color at the pixel corresponding to the ray's intersection with the reference view.""" return view.colors[ray.pixely, ray.pixelx] The optimization process to obtain the stylized scene representation \omega{NP} using explicit reference loss and implicit feature/color losses. In each training iteration, a subset Ns is sampled from \GammaR. For each sampled reference ray rk \in Ns, \hat{C}R(\hat{r}k) is the assigned color of the corresponding pseudo-ray \hat{r}k, and \hat{C}{NP}(rk) is the stylized color rendered from \omega{NP}. View-dependent rendering is discarded and view-independent fitting is applied on training views for two epochs before optimizing \omega{NP}, as view-dependent color change is not expected in stylized scenes. The density function \sigma(r(ti)) in \omega{NP} is not optimized to keep the same geometrical structure of the scene. Before training the final 3 epochs, \omegaP is replaced with a frozen \omega{NP} as the content view generator in TCM, and L{ref} and L{feat} are minimized only, with \lambdaf = 0.2 and \lambda0 = 0, for smoother content update. The overall objective is L{NP} = \lambdaf L{feat} + \lambdar L{ref} + \lambdac L{color}. The balancing factor \lambdar for reference loss is set to 1. Ref-NPR is based on the ARF codebase and uses Plenoxels as the radiance field for scene representation. Each scene is trained on one NVIDIA 3090 GPU for 10 epochs. The Template-Based Correspondence Module (TCM) is a method for non-photorealistic radiance field optimization that broadcasts style from a reference view to novel views by enforcing semantic correspondence consistency. It addresses the limitation of Reference Ray Registration (R3), which fails to register reference rays to occluded regions in 360° scenes, by using a content-style mapping template to guide stylization across the entire scene. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The reference dictionary D consumes memory proportional to 256^3 voxels, with up to 8 rays per voxel. Measured Performance: Evaluated on Tanks and Temples (T&T), LLFF, and Synthetic datasets. Trained on one NVIDIA 3090 GPU for 10 epochs. Strengths: Establishes explicit semantic consistency between stylized reference and novel views using 3D information. Limitations: Struggles with occluded regions in 360° scenes without the TCM module. When to use: When stylizing a 3D scene with a single 2D reference view and maintaining semantic consistency across novel views is required. When not to use: When the scene has significant occlusions relative to the reference view and TCM is not available or applicable. Reference Ray Registration (R3) is part of the Ref-NPR (Reference-Based Non-Photorealistic Radiance Fields) method, introduced in 2023. It builds on the idea that precise 3D positions and camera parameters enable pixel-wise correspondence between views, utilizing pseudo-depth from a radiance field to create supervision signals. Ref-NPR is based on the ARF codebase and uses Plenoxels as the radiance field representation. Ref-NPR: Reference-Based Non-Photorealistic Radiance Fields for Controllable Scene Stylization, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00413, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Template-Based Correspondence Module
body: The Template-Based Correspondence Module (TCM) is a method for non-photorealistic radiance field optimization that broadcasts style from a reference view to novel views by enforcing semantic correspondence consistency. It addresses the limitation of Reference Ray Registration (R3), which fails to register reference rays to occluded regions in 360° scenes, by using a content-style mapping template to guide stylization across the entire scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \omegaP (photorealistic radiance field), \omega{NP} (non-photorealistic radiance field to optimize), IR (content reference image), SR (style reference image), \phi (camera pose for a content domain view), and \phiR (reference camera pose). Outputs: Optimized \omega{NP} and stylized novel views rendered from \omega{NP}. Data Structures: Feature Maps: 2D semantic feature maps FI, F{IR}, F{SR}, FG, and \hat{F}S extracted via a pre-trained VGG16 network. Features used for L{feat} are concatenated from stages 3 and 4 (relu 3, relu 4). Color Patches: Average color values \bar{C} computed at feature-level grid indices. Parameters: \lambda0: Balancing factor for feature loss, set to 5 \times 10^{-3}. \lambdac: Balancing factor for color loss, set to 5. \lambdar, \lambdaf: Balancing factors for reference and feature terms in the total objective, set to 1. dist(a, b): Distance metric between feature vectors, implemented as cosine distance. Steps: 1. Extract Reference Features: Compute semantic feature maps F{IR} from content reference IR and F{SR} from style reference SR using a pre-trained VGG16 extractor. 2. Render and Extract Content Features: For a content domain view I rendered from \omegaP under camera pose \phi, compute its semantic feature map FI using the same VGG16 extractor. 3. Construct Guidance Feature (FG): Perform a search-and-replace process to map the reference style to the current content view. For each 2D position (i, j) in FI: Find the index (i^, j^) in FI that minimizes the distance to the reference feature F{IR} at (i, j): (i^, j^) = \arg \min{i0, j0} dist(FI(i0, j0), F{IR}(i, j)) Set the guidance feature at (i, j) to the style reference feature at the matched index: FG(i, j) = F{SR}(i^, j^) 4. Render Stylized View: Render a stylized view S from the non-photorealistic radiance field \omega{NP} under the same camera pose \phi. 5. Extract Stylized Features: Compute the semantic feature map \hat{F}S for the stylized view S using the VGG16 extractor. 6. Compute Feature Loss (L{feat}): Enforce implicit feature-level supervision by forcing \hat{F}S to imitate FG and match the content structure FI: L{feat} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i,j} dist(FG(i, j), \hat{F}S(i, j)) + \lambda0 \| FI(i, j) - \hat{F}S(i, j) \|2^2 where N is the total number of pixels/elements. 7. Compute Color Loss (L{color}): Address color mismatches that cosine distance optimization cannot eliminate by transferring average color in patches. For each position (i, j), let \bar{C}{NP} be the average color of the patch in the stylized view at (i, j), and \bar{C}R(i^, j^) be the average color of the reference patch matched by the feature distance minimization in Step 3: L{color} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i,j} \| \bar{C}{NP}(i, j) - \bar{C}R(i^, j^) \|2^2 8. Optimize: Minimize the total objective L{NP} = \lambdaf L{feat} + \lambdar L{ref} + \lambdac L{color} to update \omega{NP}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cosinedistance(a, b): dot = sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) norma = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in a)) normb = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in b)) return 1.0 - dot / (norma normb) if norma > 0 and normb > 0 else 0.0 def squaredl2norm(a, b): return sum((x - y) 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) def meangrid(grid): return sum(val for row in grid for val in row) / (len(grid) len(grid[0])) def extractfeatures(image): # Pre-trained VGG16 extractor applied to image return image def renderradiancefield(field, pose): # Renders image from radiance field at given pose return field def getpatchaveragecolor(view, i, j): # Returns average color of the patch at feature-level index (i, j) return view[i][j] def getpatchaveragecolorfromreference(matchidx): # Returns average color of reference patch matched by feature distance return matchidx def computereferenceloss(field, pose): # Computes Lref from Reference Ray Registration (R3) return 0.0 def templatebasedcorrespondencemodule(omegaP, omegaNP, IR, SR, phi, phiR, lambda0=5e-3, lambdac=5, lambdaf=1, lambdar=1): # 1. Extract Reference Features FIR = extractfeatures(IR) FSR = extractfeatures(SR) # 2. Render and Extract Content Features I = renderradiancefield(omegaP, phi) FI = extractfeatures(I) H, W = len(FI), len(FI[0]) FG = [[None for in range(W)] for in range(H)] matches = [[(0, 0) for in range(W)] for in range(H)] # 3. Construct Guidance Feature FG for i in range(H): for j in range(W): target = FIR[i][j] mindist = float('inf') bestidx = (0, 0) for i0 in range(H): for j0 in range(W): d = cosinedistance(FI[i0][j0], target) if d < mindist: mindist = d bestidx = (i0, j0) matches[i][j] = bestidx istar, jstar = bestidx FG[i][j] = FSR[istar][jstar] # 4. Render Stylized View S = renderradiancefield(omegaNP, phi) # 5. Extract Stylized Features FShat = extractfeatures(S) # 6. Compute Feature Loss featdist = [[cosinedistance(FG[i][j], FShat[i][j]) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] contentdist = [[squaredl2norm(FI[i][j], FShat[i][j]) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] Lfeat = meangrid(featdist) + lambda0 meangrid(contentdist) # 7. Compute Color Loss CNP = [[getpatchaveragecolor(S, i, j) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] CR = [[getpatchaveragecolorfromreference(matches[i][j]) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] colordist = [[squaredl2norm(CNP[i][j], CR[i][j]) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] Lcolor = meangrid(colordist) # 8. Total Loss and Optimization Lref = computereferenceloss(omegaNP, phiR) Ltotal = lambdaf Lfeat + lambdar Lref + lambdac Lcolor # Update omegaNP using gradient descent on Ltotal # Optimize patch-wise following gradient cache strategy to save memory return omegaNP, Ltotal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limitation: Semantic features are extracted at the image level, which can cause memory overflow during back-propagation. The optimization of \omega{NP} must be performed patch-wise following the gradient cache strategy. Color Mismatch: Cosine distance optimization alone cannot eliminate color mismatches. The coarse color-matching loss L{color} is required to address this. Occlusion: TCM is specifically designed to handle occluded regions in 360° scenes where R3 fails, by leveraging semantic consistency across the entire scene. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: High, due to storing feature maps for multiple views and the need for gradient caching during patch-wise optimization. Strengths: Overcomes occlusion issues in 360° scenes by broadcasting style based on semantic correspondence rather than just geometric ray registration. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that semantic correspondence is consistent before and after stylization. Computationally expensive due to feature matching and VGG16 extraction. When to use: When stylizing 360° scenes with significant occlusions where reference-based ray registration fails to cover all regions. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Template-Based Correspondence Module was introduced in the Ref-NPR paper. It builds on the Reference Ray Registration (R3) method, addressing its inability to handle occluded regions in 360° scenes. The method leverages the common assumption in scene stylization that semantic correspondence remains consistent across stylization. It uses VGG16 as the semantic feature extractor, following practices in prior work. The implementation is based on the ARF codebase and uses Plenoxels for scene representation.
