name: Space-Time Tomographic Projection (STP) Regularizer
head: Patch-based Jacobian Computation, Patch-based Jacobian Norm, STP Regularizer, STP Regularizer Computation, Space-Time Tomographic Prior, Structure Tensor Prior (STP)
body:
The Space-Time Tomographic Projection (STP) regularizer is a non-local regularization term for tomographic reconstruction that encourages the volume to exhibit low-rank structure tensors, effectively recovering thin 1D and 2D manifolds (surfaces, tubes, filaments) at resolutions below the Nyquist limit. It differs from standard Total Variation (TV) by aggregating gradient information from a local neighborhood (patch) of voxels using a structure tensor, rather than just the gradient at a single voxel, thereby allowing anisotropic regularization based on local geometry. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume field f defined on a grid of n voxels. Output: The scalar regularizer value STPp(f) and its gradient for optimization. Data Structures Volume f: Array of size n. Patch-based Jacobian JK(fi): For each voxel i, a matrix of size l 	imes 3 containing weighted local gradients of the voxel and its l-1 neighbors. Structure Tensor SK(fi): A 3 	imes 3 symmetric positive semi-definite matrix for each voxel i. Parameters Kernel K: A 3D rotationally-symmetric smoothing kernel. The sources specify a truncated 3D Gaussian kernel with support 3 	imes 3 	imes 3 voxels (l=27) and standard deviation \sigma = 0.5 voxels. Norm p: The Schatten p-norm parameter. Common choices are p=1 (nuclear norm), p=2 (Frobenius norm), or p=\infty (spectral norm). Neighborhood N(qi): The set of l neighbors of voxel i (including i itself) within the kernel support. Formulas 1. Local Gradient: The gradient 
abla fj at voxel j is computed using forward differences: 
abla fj =  egin{bmatrix} f{j1+1,j2,j3} - f{j1,j2,j3} \ f{j1,j2+1,j3} - f{j1,j2,j3} \ f{j1,j2,j3+1} - f{j1,j2,j3} \end{bmatrix}. 2. Patch-based Jacobian: The patch-based Jacobian JK(fi) \in \mathbb{R}^{l 	imes 3} is constructed by stacking weighted local gradients: JK(fi) =  egin{bmatrix} \kappa{j1} 
abla f{j1} \ \vdots \ \kappa{jl} 
abla f{jl} \end{bmatrix} where \{j1, \dots, jl\} = N(qi) and the weights are \kappa{jk} = K(qi - q{jk}). 3. Structure Tensor: The structure tensor is the weighted sum of outer products of local gradients: SK(fi) = \sum{j \in N(qi)} K(qj - qi) (
abla fj 
abla fj^T) = JK(fi)^T JK(fi). 4. STP Value: The regularizer value at voxel i is the Schatten p-norm of JK(fi), which equals the p-norm of the square roots of the eigenvalues \lambdaj of SK(fi): STPp(fi) = \| JK(fi) \|{Sp} = \left( \sum{j=1}^3 (\sqrt{\lambdaj})^p ight)^{1/p}. The total regularizer is the sum over all voxels: STPp(f) = \sum{i=1}^n STPp(fi) = \| JK f \|{1,p} where JK is the global linear operator mapping the volume to the stacked patch-based Jacobians. Special Case: Isotropic TV If the kernel K is a Dirac delta (K(q) = \delta(q)), the structure tensor simplifies to S\delta(fi) = 
abla fi 
abla fi^T. This matrix has rank 1 with one non-zero eigenvalue \lambda1 = \|
abla fi\|2^2. In this case, STPp(fi) = \sqrt{\lambda1} = \|
abla fi\|2, reducing to the standard isotropic TV regularizer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computestpregularizer(volume, kernelsigma=0.5, kernelsupport=3, p=2): """ Computes the STP regularizer value for a 3D volume. Args: volume: np.ndarray of shape (D, H, W), the input volume field. kernelsigma: float, standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel. kernelsupport: int, half-width of the kernel support (e.g., 3 for 3x3x3). p: float, Schatten p-norm parameter (default 2 for Frobenius norm). Returns: float: The total STP regularizer value. """ D, H, W = volume.shape # Define neighborhood offsets for a (2kernelsupport+1)^3 grid centered at 0 offsets = [] for dz in range(-kernelsupport, kernelsupport + 1): for dy in range(-kernelsupport, kernelsupport + 1): for dx in range(-kernelsupport, kernelsupport + 1): offsets.append((dz, dy, dx)) l = len(offsets) # Precompute kernel weights K(q) = exp(-||q||^2 / (2 sigma^2)) kernelweights = np.array([np.exp(-(dz2 + dy2 + dx2) / (2 kernelsigma2)) for dz, dy, dx in offsets]) # Compute forward differences for all voxels gradd = np.zeroslike(volume) gradh = np.zeroslike(volume) gradw = np.zeroslike(volume) gradd[:-1,:,:] = volume[1:,:,:] - volume[:-1,:,:] gradh[:,:-1,:] = volume[:, 1:,:] - volume[:,:-1,:] gradw[:,:,:-1] = volume[:,:, 1:,:] - volume[:,:,:-1] # Boundary handling: zero-gradient outside bounds gradd[-1,:,:] = 0 gradh[:, -1,:] = 0 gradw[:,:, -1] = 0 totalstp = 0.0 for i in range(D): for j in range(H): for k in range(W): localgrads = np.zeros((l, 3)) for idx, (dz, dy, dx) in enumerate(offsets): ni, nj, nk = i + dz, j + dy, k + dx if 0 <= ni < D and 0 <= nj < H and 0 <= nk < W: localgrads[idx, 0] = gradd[ni, nj, nk] localgrads[idx, 1] = gradh[ni, nj, nk] localgrads[idx, 2] = gradw[ni, nj, nk] else: localgrads[idx,:] = 0 weightedgrads = localgrads kernelweights[:, np.newaxis] S = weightedgrads.T @ weightedgrads eigenvalues = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(S))[::-1] sqrteigs = np.sqrt(eigenvalues) totalstp += np.sum(sqrteigsp)(1/p) return totalstp The proximal operator for the convex conjugate g^(H) of the STP regularizer corresponds to the projection of a matrix H onto the convex set \lambda B{\infty, q}, which is the unit ball of the dual (\infty, q) norm scaled by \lambda. The dual norm parameter q satisfies 1/p + 1/q = 1. The set is defined as \lambda B{\infty, q} = \{ H \in \mathbb{R}^{n 	imes 3}: \|Hi\|{Sq} \leq \lambda \quad  orall i = 1, \dots, N \}. Memory Complexity: The patch-based Jacobian JK(f) must be stored explicitly for the optimization algorithm (e.g., Chambolle-Pock). For every voxel, a matrix of size l 	imes 3 is stored. With l=27, this requires 81 times the size of the volume data plus the volume itself, totaling 82 times the volume size. For a volume of 690 	imes 668 	imes 776 voxels, this requires approximately 109 GB of memory. Time Complexity: The linear mapping JK is not stored explicitly but computed on the fly using discrete forward differences and kernel scaling. The adjoint JK^ is also computed on the fly. Strengths: Better recovers thin structures (surfaces, tubes) compared to isotropic TV by distinguishing between sheet-like, line-like, and isotropic structures based on eigenvalue ratios. Limitations: High memory consumption due to explicit storage of patch-based Jacobians. Non-local nature requires careful handling of boundaries and kernel support. The STP regularizer was introduced by [66, 65] in the context of tomographic reconstruction. It extends the Structure Tensor Prior from 2D images to 3D volumes, employing efficient proximal algorithms for computation. It is used in X-ray CT reconstruction, particularly for dynamic scenes where thin structures need to be preserved. name: Anisotropic Total Variation
head: Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) Prior, L1 Total Variation
body: Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) is a regularization prior used in tomographic reconstruction and radiance field optimization to enforce piecewise constant solutions with axis-aligned edges. It is defined as the sum of absolute differences along the three principal axes (forward differences in x, y, z). Unlike Isotropic Total Variation, which computes the Euclidean norm of the gradient vector at each voxel, ATV treats each axis independently, making it computationally cheaper and favoring structures aligned with the grid axes. It builds on Total Variation Regularization by using the L1 norm specifically along principal directions rather than a general Huber loss or isotropic magnitude. Inputs: A 3D volume grid \mathbf{x} of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, where n = Nx Ny Nz is the total number of voxels. Outputs: The regularized volume \mathbf{x} (after optimization steps) or the gradient vector \mathbf{z} = D\mathbf{x} and divergence D^T\mathbf{z}. Data Structures: The forward difference matrix D \in \mathbb{R}^{3n \times n} is defined implicitly and not stored in memory to save space. Each row of D corresponds to an edge (difference between two voxels). For an edge e connecting voxel i to voxel j, the entries are: D{ev} = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } v = i \\ 1 & \text{if } v = j \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The matrix has 3n rows (edges) and n columns (voxels). Note: While the mathematical definition sums forward differences (3 per voxel), the implementation of D^T considers all 6 neighbors (forward and backward) to compute the divergence. Parameters: \mu: Proximal operator step size or regularization weight. Typical values depend on the specific solver (e.g., SART) and noise level. Steps: 1. Compute Gradient (D\mathbf{x}): For each voxel v = (i, j, k), compute the 3 forward differences connecting it to its neighbors in the positive axes. The vector \mathbf{z}v for voxel v contains: \mathbf{z}v = \begin{bmatrix} x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j,k+1} - x{i,j,k} \end{bmatrix} Boundary handling: Voxels at the boundary are assumed to be replicated. Thus, if a neighbor is out of bounds, the difference is zero (i.e., x{boundary} = x{neighbor}). 2. Compute Divergence (D^T\mathbf{z}): For a specific vertex v = (i, j, k), sum the difference values \mathbf{z}e from all incident edges e, weighted by D{ev}. (D^T\mathbf{z})v = \sum{e \ni v} D{ev} ze Expanding this for voxel (i, j, k) considering all 6 neighbors: (D^T\mathbf{z}){i,j,k} = 6x{i,j,k} - x{i-1,j,k} - x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j-1,k} - x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k-1} - x{i,j,k+1} This operation is equivalent to the discrete Laplace operator D^T D applied to \mathbf{x}. 3. Proximal Operator (for optimization): In proximal algorithms (e.g., SART), the ATV prior h(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\|1 requires the proximal operator of its convex conjugate g^. The proximal operator for the L1 norm's conjugate is the projection onto the unit L\infty ball, computed component-wise as clipping: \text{prox}{\mu g^}(\mathbf{q}) = \Pi{B\infty}(\mathbf{q}) Component-wise definition for a value u: \text{clip}(u) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } u > 1 \\ u & \text{if } |u| \leq 1 \\ -1 & \text{if } u < -1 \end{cases} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeatvgradient(volume): """ Computes the 3 forward differences for each voxel. volume: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) returns: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) """ diffs = np.zeros((volume.shape, 3)) diffs[:-1,:,:, 0] = volume[1:,:,:] - volume[:-1,:,:] diffs[:,:-1,:, 1] = volume[:, 1:,:] - volume[:,:-1,:] diffs[:,:,:-1, 2] = volume[:,:, 1:] - volume[:,:,:-1] return diffs def computeatvdivergence(z): """ Computes D^T z for each voxel from the gradient tensor z. z: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3) storing forward differences along x, y, z returns: np.ndarray of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) """ # D^T z sums forward differences at (i,j,k) and subtracts forward differences # at neighbors (which represent backward differences at (i,j,k)) div = np.zeroslike(z[..., 0]) div += z[..., 0] + z[..., 1] + z[..., 2] div[:-1,:,:] -= z[1:,:,:, 0] div[1:,:,:] -= z[:-1,:,:, 0] div[:,:-1,:] -= z[:, 1:,:, 1] div[:, 1:,:] -= z[:,:-1,:, 1] div[:,:,:-1] -= z[:,:, 1:, 2] div[:,:, 1:] -= z[:,:,:-1, 2] return div def proxatvconjugate(q, mu=1.0): """ Proximal operator of the convex conjugate of the L1 norm (Projection onto Linf ball). q: np.ndarray (gradient or dual variable) mu: step size (not used in the projection step, kept for API consistency) returns: clipped q """ return np.clip(q, -1.0, 1.0) Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) extends ATV by considering a larger local neighborhood. While ATV sums absolute differences along only the three principal axes, SAD sums the absolute differences between a voxel and all voxels in its immediate 3x3 spatial neighborhood (excluding the voxel itself), thereby enforcing smoothness across more edges per voxel. It has been shown to produce excellent results in stochastic tomography reconstruction. Multi-dimensional Total Variation (TV) Loss computes the total variation regularization on multi-dimensional tensors by summing absolute differences along all spatial and channel dimensions. It serves as a smoothness prior for feature fields, encouraging piecewise constant solutions while preserving sharp boundaries. It extends the standard 3D TV prior by generalizing the difference operation to arbitrary tensor shapes, including batch and channel dimensions. The Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) Proximal Operator is a mathematical tool used to enforce sparsity in the gradient domain of a volume during optimization. It serves as the proximal mapping for the ATV regularizer, which penalizes the \ell1 norm of the discrete volume gradient. Unlike isotropic TV, which treats all gradient directions equally, ATV sums the absolute differences along the three principal axes (x, y, z) independently. This operator is distinct from Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) and Multi-dimensional Total Variation Loss by specifically applying soft-thresholding to the individual gradient components rather than the magnitude of the gradient vector. It is primarily used in differentiable and inverse volume rendering to denoise reconstructed volumes while preserving sharp edges. Time Complexity: Computing the gradient D\mathbf{x} and divergence D^T\mathbf{z} is O(n), where n is the number of voxels, as each voxel interacts with a constant number of neighbors (6). The proximal operator is also O(n). Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing the volume. The matrix D is not stored, saving significant memory compared to explicit sparse matrix storage. Performance: ATV is computationally efficient due to the simple L1 norm and axis-aligned differences. It is faster than Isotropic TV (ITV), which requires square root computations per voxel. Strengths: Promotes piecewise constant solutions with sharp, axis-aligned edges. Computationally cheap. Limitations: Can produce "staircasing" artifacts (piecewise constant regions) and may not preserve diagonal features as well as isotropic variants. Sensitive to the choice of regularization parameter \mu. When to use: When the target volume has strong axis-aligned structures and computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: When isotropic smoothness is required or diagonal features are important. Anisotropic Total Variation was introduced as a regularization prior for tomographic reconstruction, specifically within the context of proximal algorithms like SART (Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique). The formulation h(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\|1 leverages the convex conjugate's proximal operator, which is the projection onto the unit L\infty ball. It is used in industrial computed tomography reconstruction. name: Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD)
head: SAD Prior, Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) Prior
body: Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) is a regularization prior used in tomographic reconstruction that extends Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) by considering a larger local neighborhood. While ATV sums absolute differences along only the three principal axes, SAD sums the absolute differences between a voxel and all voxels in its immediate 3x3 spatial neighborhood (excluding the voxel itself), thereby enforcing smoothness across more edges per voxel. It has been shown to produce excellent results in stochastic tomography reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D voxel grid \mathbf{x} of size I \times J \times K, where each element x{i,j,k} represents the scalar value (e.g., density or radiance) at voxel coordinates (i,j,k). Output: The scalar energy value h(\mathbf{x}) representing the regularization cost, or the proximal operator applied to \mathbf{x} to produce a regularized version \mathbf{x}'. Data Structures The voxel grid is stored as a dense 3D array. The neighborhood N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k}) is defined implicitly by coordinate offsets relative to (i,j,k). No explicit adjacency matrix D is stored; operations are computed on-the-fly. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize the energy accumulator to zero. 2. Iterate over every voxel (i,j,k) in the grid bounds [0, I-1] \times [0, J-1] \times [0, K-1]. 3. For each voxel, identify the 8 neighbors in its 3x3 neighborhood N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k}) by applying offsets \deltai, \deltaj \in \{-1, 0, 1\} where (\deltai, \deltaj) \neq (0,0), while keeping the k-index fixed. 4. For each valid neighbor (i+\deltai, j+\deltaj, k) within grid boundaries, compute the absolute difference |\mathbf{x}{i+\deltai, j+\deltaj, k} - \mathbf{x}{i,j,k}|. 5. Accumulate the absolute differences into the energy value. 6. Return the final energy value h(\mathbf{x}). Formula The SAD energy function is defined as: h(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i,j,k} \sum{\mathbf{x}n \in N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k})} |\mathbf{x}n - \mathbf{x}{i,j,k}| Where: \mathbf{x}{i,j,k} is the value of the central voxel at coordinates (i,j,k). N(\mathbf{x}{i,j,k}) denotes the 3x3 neighborhood around the voxel excluding itself. The summation iterates over the 8 neighbors in the xy-plane at a fixed z-slice. Parameters None. The neighborhood size and structure are fixed by the definition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundaries: Voxels on the volume boundaries have fewer than 8 neighbors. The algorithm must clamp neighbor coordinates to the valid grid range [0, I-1] \times [0, J-1] \times [0, K-1] before accessing memory. Precision: Summing absolute differences across a large volume can accumulate floating-point error. Using double-precision accumulators prevents overflow and maintains numerical stability for large grids. Degenerate Input: If the grid dimensions are smaller than 3 \times 3 \times 1, the neighborhood definition still applies but yields fewer terms per voxel; the algorithm remains valid without modification. Pseudocode The following computes the SAD energy h(\mathbf{x}) for a 3D grid \mathbf{x} of dimensions I \times J \times K. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesadenergy(x, I, J, K): """ Computes the Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) regularization energy. Args: x: 3D numpy array of shape (I, J, K) containing voxel values. I: Width of the volume. J: Height of the volume. K: Depth of the volume. Returns: float: The SAD energy value. """ energy = 0.0 for i in range(I): for j in range(J): for k in range(K): currentval = x[i, j, k] for di in (-1, 0, 1): for dj in (-1, 0, 1): if di == 0 and dj == 0: continue ni, nj = i + di, j + dj if 0 <= ni < I and 0 <= nj < J: energy += abs(x[ni, nj, k] - currentval) return energy Note: The proximal operator for SAD is not explicitly derived in the sources, but is stated to be similar to the ATV proximal operator. Implementers should apply the standard l1 proximal projection onto the extended neighborhood graph, which couples the 8 neighbors per voxel. Time Complexity: Computing the energy is O(I \cdot J \cdot K), as each voxel processes a constant number (8) of neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if computed on-the-fly, or O(I \cdot J \cdot K) if storing intermediate neighbor differences. Strengths: Produces excellent results in stochastic tomography reconstruction compared to other priors. It enforces smoothness across more edges per voxel than ATV. Limitations: Requires more arithmetic operations per voxel than ATV due to the larger neighborhood. When to use: When tomographic reconstruction tasks benefit from the extended neighborhood smoothing provided by SAD. When not to use: When strict anisotropic smoothing along principal axes is required, or when minimal per-voxel computational overhead is critical. Origin: The SAD prior is discussed in the context of proximal algorithms for industrial computed tomography and space-time tomographic reconstruction. History: It is presented as an extension of the Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) prior. Usage: It is applied in stochastic tomography reconstruction. name: Multi-dimensional Total Variation Loss
body: Multi-dimensional Total Variation Loss computes the total variation regularization on multi-dimensional tensors by summing absolute differences along all spatial and channel dimensions. It generalizes the difference operation to arbitrary tensor shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor \mathbf{x} of shape (B, C, \dots), where B is batch size, C is channel size, and subsequent dimensions are spatial or feature dimensions. Output: A scalar loss value representing the sum of absolute differences across the specified dimensions. Data Structures: The input \mathbf{x} is a dense tensor. No auxiliary structures are required beyond standard tensor indexing. Algorithm: 1. Initialize tv = 0. 2. Loop over dimensions i from 2 to \text{len}(\mathbf{x}.shape) - 1. 3. Let n{res} = \mathbf{x}.shape[i]. 4. Create index sets idx1 = [1, 2, \dots, n{res}-1] and idx2 = [0, 1, \dots, n{res}-2]. 5. Select slices \mathbf{x}1 = \mathbf{x}.index\select(i, idx1) and \mathbf{x}2 = \mathbf{x}.index\select(i, idx2). 6. Compute the absolute difference and add its sum to tv. 7. Return tv. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multidimtvloss(x): tv = 0.0 for i in range(2, len(x.shape)): nres = x.shape[i] if nres < 2: continue idx1 = list(range(1, nres)) idx2 = list(range(0, nres - 1)) x1 = indexselect(x, i, idx1) x2 = indexselect(x, i, idx2) tv += sum(abs(v1 - v2) for v1, v2 in zip(flatten(x1), flatten(x2))) return tv def indexselect(tensor, dim, indices): if dim == 0: return [tensor[i] for i in indices] return [indexselect(sub, dim - 1, indices) for sub in tensor] def flatten(tensor): if not isinstance(tensor, list): return [tensor] return [item for sub in tensor for item in flatten(sub)] Parameters: None explicitly defined in the core algorithm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If any dimension has size 1, the difference along that dimension is zero or undefined. The loop bounds naturally handle this by producing empty index ranges, resulting in a zero contribution. Precision issues with large tensors are not specified in the sources. A variant used in inverse rendering to regularize material and lighting fields separately. It computes TV on a mask field \hat{M} and a light field \hat{E} using exponential weighting based on image intensity differences to preserve edges. Formula for Mask: TV{mat} = \frac{1}{|\hat{M}|} \sum{i,j} \Delta \hat{M}{ij}, where \Delta \hat{M}{ij} = \exp(-|I{i,j} - I{i-1,j}|) (\hat{M}{i,j} - \hat{M}{i-1,j})^2 + \exp(-|I{i,j} - I{i,j-1}|) (\hat{M}{i,j} - \hat{M}{i,j-1})^2. Formula for Light: TV{light} = \frac{1}{|\hat{E}|} \sum{i,j} \Delta \hat{E}{ij}, where \Delta \hat{E}{ij} = (\hat{E}{i,j} - \hat{E}{i-1,j})^2 + (\hat{E}{i,j} - \hat{E}{i,j-1})^2. PlaneTV Regularization computes the total variation of spatial planes within a feature tensor to encourage smoothness in the learned feature fields. It differs from standard isotropic TV by explicitly separating horizontal and vertical gradient computations across 2D spatial slices, making it suitable for multi-dimensional tensors where specific dimensions represent spatial planes. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use and when not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is adapted for multi-dimensional tensors in recent implementations. It builds on the anisotropic total variation prior by extending the difference operation to arbitrary tensor shapes. name: PlaneTV Regularization
head: PlaneTV, Total Variation on Planes
body: PlaneTV Regularization computes the total variation of spatial planes to encourage smoothness in feature fields. It operates on multi-dimensional tensors by summing differences along specified spatial dimensions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor t with batch size B, channels C, height H, and width W. Output: A scalar loss value representing the regularized TV. Data Structures: The tensor is treated as a collection of spatial planes. For a tensor with 3 dimensions, spatial dimensions are indices [0, 1, 2]. For a 4D tensor, spatial dimensions are indices [0, 1, 3]. Formula: The loss is computed as: L = 2 \times \left( \frac{\sum (t{i+1} - ti)^2}{counth} + \frac{\sum (t{j+1} - tj)^2}{countw} \right) Where: t{i+1} - ti represents the difference along the height dimension (rows). t{j+1} - tj represents the difference along the width dimension (columns). counth = B \times C \times (H-1) \times W. countw = B \times C \times H \times (W-1). Steps: 1. Compute the squared differences along the height dimension: \sum (t{i+1} - ti)^2. 2. Compute the squared differences along the width dimension: \sum (t{j+1} - tj)^2. 3. Normalize the height sum by counth. 4. Normalize the width sum by countw. 5. Sum the normalized values and multiply by 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeplanetv(t: list, B: int, C: int, H: int, W: int) -> float: sumh = 0.0 for b in range(B): for c in range(C): for h in range(H - 1): for w in range(W): diff = t[b][c][h+1][w] - t[b][c][h][w] sumh += diff diff counth = B C (H - 1) W sumw = 0.0 for b in range(B): for c in range(C): for h in range(H): for w in range(W - 1): diff = t[b][c][h][w+1] - t[b][c][h][w] sumw += diff diff countw = B C H (W - 1) termh = sumh / counth if counth > 0 else 0.0 termw = sumw / countw if countw > 0 else 0.0 return 2.0 (termh + termw) Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: If H=1 or W=1, the corresponding count becomes 0, leading to division by zero. The implementation must guard against this by setting the term to 0. Applies TV regularization to triplane features to smooth them and make gradients resemble natural images, which are modeled by a hyper-Laplacian with \alpha \in [0.5, 0.8]. The regularization target \alpha is typically set to 0.5. This variant is chosen when training generative models on triplanes to prevent high-frequency artifacts. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. Origin and history: Not given in the sources. Usage: Associated with Triplane Diffusion models for 3D neural field generation. name: Anisotropic Total Variation Proximal Operator
head: ATV Proximal Operator, ROF model proximal operator
body: The Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV) Proximal Operator computes the proximal mapping for the ATV regularizer, which is defined as the \ell1 norm of the discrete volume gradient. It applies the soft-thresholding function element-wise to the volume gradient components, distinguishing it from Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) and Multi-dimensional Total Variation Loss by operating on individual gradient directions rather than the gradient vector magnitude. The operator computes the proximal mapping of the ATV regularizer. It assumes that images with excessive noise have high total variation and are sparse in the gradient domain. Inputs and Outputs: 1. Input: A volume gradient tensor \mathbf{u} of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of voxels and the last dimension corresponds to the x, y, z components. 2. Input: A scalar regularization parameter \rho1 \ge 0. 3. Output: A denoised gradient tensor \mathbf{u}' of shape (N, 3), where each component has been soft-thresholded. Data Structures: The forward difference matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times N} is used to compute the initial gradient from a volume \mathbf{v} such that \mathbf{u} = K\mathbf{v}. The proximal operator itself operates directly on the pre-computed gradient components u{ni}. Formula: The proximal operator is defined as the soft-thresholding function applied element-wise to the volume gradient components: \text{prox}{\rho1 G{ATV}}(u{ni}) = \text{sign}(u{ni}) \times \max(0, |u{ni}| - \rho1) Where: u{ni} is the i-th component (i \in \{0, 1, 2\}) of the volume gradient at voxel n. \rho1 is the regularization parameter that controls how fast the volume gradient shrinks. \text{sign}(x) returns 1 if x > 0, -1 if x < 0, and 0 if x = 0. Parameters: \rho1: Regularization parameter. Higher values result in stronger shrinkage of small gradient components, promoting sparser gradients. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the element-wise soft-thresholding. It assumes gradient is a list of lists of shape (N, 3) and rho1 is a scalar. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def anisotropictvproximaloperator(gradient, rho1): # gradient: list of lists of shape (N, 3) # rho1: scalar regularization parameter result = [] for n in range(len(gradient)): row = [] for i in range(3): u = gradient[n][i] absu = abs(u) thresholded = absu - rho1 if absu > rho1 else 0.0 signu = 1.0 if u > 0.0 else (-1.0 if u < 0.0 else 0.0) row.append(signu thresholded) result.append(row) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: If u{ni} = 0, the output is 0. The soft-thresholding function is continuous but not differentiable at u{ni} = \pm \rho1. Precision: When |u{ni}| is very close to \rho1, floating-point precision errors may cause oscillations if the operator is called repeatedly in an iterative solver without momentum or step-size adjustments. Anisotropy: ATV sums absolute differences along the three principal axes independently, which means it does not enforce rotational symmetry. This variant implements the ATV proximal operator within a proximal gradient descent framework for TV minimization. It maintains a residual voltv from previous iterations to update the current estimate. The algorithm initializes ii = 0 and stopcount = 0, then loops while ii < 6 and stopcount < 3. Inside the loop, it computes a new volume estimate vol[:] = volt - la data.divergence(finalvoltv), clips vol to bounds if they exist, and updates the TV residual voltv[:] = finalvoltv - 1/(8la) data.gradient(vol). It computes the norm of the TV residual components, clamps values below 1 to 1, takes the square root, and normalizes voltv by this norm to avoid division by zero. It updates momentum using tau = tau; tau = (1 + numpy.sqrt(1 + 4tau2)) / 2, then updates finalvoltv = voltv + (tau - 1) / (tau) (voltv - voltvold). Convergence is checked via re = numpy.linalg.norm(vol - volold) / numpy.linalg.norm(vol); if re < 1e-3, stopcount increments, otherwise it resets to 0. The step size parameter la is calculated as lamb / L, where L is the Lipschitz constant of the data fidelity term. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels, as it performs element-wise operations on the gradient tensor. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the gradient tensor and the output. Strengths: Computationally efficient; promotes piecewise constant solutions; effective at removing noise while preserving sharp edges in the principal directions. Limitations: Can produce "staircasing" artifacts (piecewise constant regions) in smooth gradients; the anisotropic nature sums absolute differences along principal axes independently, which may lead to directional bias in reconstructed structures. When to use: When computational efficiency is critical and the volume exhibits strong edges aligned with the grid axes. When not to use: When rotational invariance is required (use Isotropic TV instead) or when smooth gradients are expected without staircasing artifacts. The Anisotropic Total Variation regularizer was conceived based on the idea that images with excessive noise have high total variation and are sparse in the gradient domain. The proximal operator for the \ell1 norm, which forms the basis of ATV, is the soft-thresholding function. This approach is widely used in tomographic reconstruction and inverse problems to denoise data. The proximal gradient implementation with momentum is found in open-source tomography libraries like flexTOMO. name: Isotropic Total Variation
head: ITV, TV Regularization, Total Variation (TV) Regularization
body: Isotropic Total Variation (ITV) is a regularization prior used in volume rendering and tomographic reconstruction to enforce piecewise constant solutions while preserving isotropic edge structures. Unlike Anisotropic Total Variation (ATV), which sums the absolute values of individual gradient components, ITV sums the Euclidean magnitude of the full 3D gradient vector at each voxel, treating the gradient components as a coupled group. This distinction makes ITV particularly effective for preventing overfitting and artifacts like floaters in explicit radiance field representations, especially when using rendering methods that do not inherently smooth across voxel boundaries. Input: A 3D voxel grid \mathbf{x} of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, where each element x{i,j,k} represents a scalar value (e.g., density \sigma or opacity) at voxel coordinates (i,j,k). Output: A scalar regularization loss value h(\mathbf{x}) or the proximal operator update for optimization algorithms. The method operates on the voxel grid \mathbf{x}. In matrix formulations, \mathbf{x} is often vectorized into a column vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n where n = Nx Ny Nz. Gradient Vector \mathbf{w}^v: At each voxel v=(i,j,k), the gradient is a 3-element vector defined by forward differences: \mathbf{w}^v = \begin{bmatrix} x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k} \\ x{i,j,k+1} - x{i,j,k} \end{bmatrix} Mask Matrix \mathbf{E}: A sparse matrix \mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{3n \times n} indicating the positions of forward differences. It is defined such that E{ev} = 1 if D{ev} = -1 (where \mathbf{D} is the forward difference matrix) and 0 otherwise. In implementation, \mathbf{E} is not stored explicitly; operations involving \mathbf{E} are computed on-the-fly. The ITV prior h(\mathbf{x}) is defined as the sum of the L2 norms of the gradient vectors at all voxels: h(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i,j,k} \sqrt{|x{i+1,j,k} - x{i,j,k}|^2 + |x{i,j+1,k} - x{i,j,k}|^2 + |x{i,j,k+1} - x{i,j,k}|^2} In compact matrix notation, let \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}. The prior is expressed as a weighted norm \|\mathbf{w}\|E: h(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{D}\mathbf{x}\|E = \sumv \|\mathbf{w}^v\|2 where the norm \|\mathbf{w}\|E is computed as \|\sqrt{\mathbf{E}^T \mathbf{w}^2}\|1. Here, squaring and square roots are component-wise operations. For continuous neural radiance fields (e.g., in Aug-NeRF), the regularization is approximated via quadrature over the domain [-1, 1]^3: R{\text{TV}}(\Theta) \approx \sum{i=1}^{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} \sum{k=1}^{N} |\nablax \sigma\Theta(\delta i, \delta j, \delta k)| \delta^3 where \sigma\Theta is the density branch of the network, \nablax is the spatial gradient computed via auto-differentiation, and \delta is the grid spacing. For optimization algorithms like Primal-Dual or ADMM, the proximal operator of the convex conjugate \tilde{g}^ of the ITV prior is required. This corresponds to the projection onto the unit ball of the dual norm: \text{prox}{\mu \tilde{g}^}(\mathbf{q}) = \Pi{B^}(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{\mathbf{q}}{\max\left(\sqrt{\mathbf{E}^T \mathbf{q}^2}, 1\right)} where division and max are component-wise. Intuitively, this scales the gradient vector \mathbf{q} at each voxel by 1/\|\mathbf{q}^v\|2 if the magnitude exceeds 1, and leaves it unchanged otherwise. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the computation of the ITV loss and its proximal step for a voxel grid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def isotropictotalvariationloss(x): """ Computes the Isotropic Total Variation loss for a 3D voxel grid. Args: x: numpy array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz). Represents the scalar field. Returns: scalar: The ITV regularization value. """ # Forward differences in x, y, z directions dx = np.diff(x, axis=0) dy = np.diff(x, axis=1) dz = np.diff(x, axis=2) # Compute magnitude of the gradient vector at each voxel # The resulting arrays are of shape (Nx-1, Ny-1, Nz-1) gradmagnitude = np.sqrt(dx2 + dy2 + dz2) # Sum all magnitudes loss = np.sum(gradmagnitude) return loss def proximalisotropictv(q): """ Computes the proximal operator of the convex conjugate of ITV. Equivalent to projecting q onto the unit dual norm ball. Args: q: numpy array of shape (3, H, W, D) representing the gradient vector field (stacked dx, dy, dz). Returns: numpy array: The proximal update PB(q). """ # q[0] is dx, q[1] is dy, q[2] is dz gradmag = np.sqrt(q[0]2 + q[1]2 + q[2]2) # Projection onto unit ball: scale by max(1, mag) scale = np.maximum(gradmag, 1.0) # Component-wise division qproj = q / scale return qproj Regularization Weight (\lambda or \mu): Controls the strength of the ITV penalty. In DiffVox, a GroupL1Norm weight of 0.26 was used for isotropic TV. In Primal-Dual algorithms, step sizes \tau and \sigma must satisfy \tau \sigma \|K\|^2 < 1. Grid Resolution (N): The number of voxels along each dimension. Higher resolution increases the number of gradient terms in the sum. Boundary Conditions: The forward difference definition requires voxels at i+1, j+1, k+1. For voxels on the boundary of the grid, these neighbors do not exist. The pseudocode handles this by using np.diff, which reduces the dimension by 1, effectively ignoring the last slice in each direction. Zero Gradient: If the gradient magnitude is zero, the proximal operator division is well-defined (division by 1). Matrix Storage: The matrix \mathbf{E} is not stored explicitly to save memory; operations are computed on-the-fly. Sums absolute values of individual gradient components (L1 norm of components). Chosen when directional smoothing is preferred or for simpler implementation. Ablation study comparing regularization effects in Plenoxels. Regularizer for dynamic scenes, uses ITV as a component. Time Complexity: Computing the loss is O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations per voxel. Proximal operators are also O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the voxel grid and intermediate gradient arrays. The matrix \mathbf{E} is not stored, saving memory. Strengths: Promotes piecewise constant solutions with isotropic edge preservation. Limitations: Can introduce "staircasing" artifacts (piecewise constant approximation). Removing TV norm has a far greater impact on Siddon's method than on trilinear interpolation, as trilinear interpolation provides inherent smoothing. When to use: When isotropic edge preservation is critical and the solution is expected to be piecewise constant. Useful in sparse-view CT and differentiable volume rendering to prevent overfitting. Total Variation regularization was introduced by Rudin, Osher, and Fatemi in 1992 in "Nonlinear total variation based noise removal algorithms". It has since been widely adopted in image processing and tomography. In the context of volume rendering and radiance fields, ITV is used to regularize the density field during optimization, particularly in methods like DiffVox and Aug-NeRF. The specific formulation using the proximal operator of the convex conjugate for Primal-Dual algorithms is detailed in works on industrial CT and space-time tomography. name: Perceptual Loss Training
head: Feature Matching Objective, PIPS Loss, Perceptual Distance Loss, Perceptual Loss for 3DGS, Perceptual loss for dynamic NeRF
body: Perceptual Loss Training is an optimization strategy that incorporates a perceptual loss term to improve the visual fidelity of rendered images, addressing the smoothness and texture distortion issues inherent in pixel-wise losses like L1 or L2. It sets itself apart from its siblings by leveraging features from pre-trained convolutional neural networks (typically VGG) to enforce high-level structural consistency, whereas methods like Total Variation Regularization operate directly on spatial gradients of the output or scene parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image \hat{I} (prediction), ground truth image Ig, pre-trained feature extractor network \Phi (e.g., VGG-19), and loss weights \lambdal or w{\cdot}. Output: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{perc}} used for backpropagation. Data Structures: Feature Maps: Intermediate activations from the pre-trained network. Weights: Scalars \lambdal balancing the contribution of each layer's feature distance. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Pass both the rendered image \hat{I} and the ground truth image Ig through the pre-trained network \Phi. Extract feature maps from a set of layers L. \mathbf{F}{\hat{I}}^l = \Phil(\hat{I}), \quad \mathbf{F}{Ig}^l = \Phil(Ig) \quad \forall l \in L 2. Distance Calculation: Compute the distance between the feature maps of the prediction and the ground truth. The L1 norm is commonly used. D^l = \| \mathbf{F}{\hat{I}}^l - \mathbf{F}{Ig}^l \|1 3. Aggregation: Sum the distances weighted by layer-specific coefficients \lambdal. \mathcal{L}{\text{perc}} = \sum{l \in L} \lambdal D^l Formulas: The general perceptual loss is defined as: L(Pf, \theta) = \suml \lambdal \| \Phil(Ig) - \Phil(f(Pf; \theta)) \|1 where Pf represents the scene parameters (e.g., point features), \theta are the network parameters, f is the rendering function, and \Phil are the VGG-19 layers. Some formulations normalize the distance by the total number of features Nl in layer l: L{\text{perc}}(G) = \mathbb{E}{x,y} \sum{t=1}^{T} \lambdat \frac{1}{Nt} \| F^{(t)}(G(x)) - F^{(t)}(y) \|1 where F^{(t)} is the feature extractor in the t-th layer of the pretrained network F with T layers total. In the context of Gaussian Splatting (PIPS), the total loss combines L1, SSIM, and Perceptual (PIPS) terms: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda1 - \lambda2)\mathcal{L}1 + \lambda1\mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} + \lambda2\mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{PIPS}} is the perceptual loss term. For large reconstruction models (GS-LRM), the loss combines MSE and Perceptual terms over M supervision views: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i'=1}^M \left( \mathrm{MSE}(\hat{I}^{i'}, I^{i'}) + \lambda \cdot \mathrm{Perceptual}(\hat{I}^{i'}, I^{i'}) \right) where \lambda is the perceptual loss weight. Parameters: VGG-19 Layers: Commonly used layers include 'input', 'conv1-2', 'conv2-2', 'conv3-2', 'conv4-2', and 'conv5-2'. Weights (\lambdal): Balancing weights for each layer. Specific values follow the scheme in Chen et al.. Weights (\lambda1, \lambda2): In the PIPS formulation, \lambda1 weights the SSIM term and \lambda2 weights the perceptual term. Exact values are not given. Optimization: Adam optimizer is typically used. Learning rate initialized at 0.01, decreased every 7 epochs: 0.01 \to 0.005 \to 0.001. DINER uses a learning rate of 10^{-4}. Pitfalls: Computational Overhead: CNN-based perceptual loss computation is expensive. It is recommended to compute it every 20 training iterations to alleviate overhead without significantly impacting quality. Color Shifts: Perceptual loss can introduce color shifts in the rendered output. This may require auxiliary terms like Anti-Bias Loss to correct. Visual Quality Degradation: Omitting perceptual loss increases LPIPS distance, indicating degraded visual quality even if pixel-wise metrics (PSNR/SSIM) remain acceptable. The learned generator using Lp norm tends to synthesize blurry images or average results over multiple plausible outputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit dependence on external proxy geometry (typically piecewise planar meshes) and access to all training images, whereas High-Frequency Aware Loss and WD-Regularized Loss operate within different optimization frameworks without this specific blending-and-proxy requirement. High-Frequency Aware Loss (LHF) is a perceptual regularization term designed to recover high-frequency details in rendered images while avoiding the texture distortion common in deeper perceptual losses. It sets itself apart from standard VGG-based perceptual losses by restricting feature extraction to the first block of the network, thereby preserving fine structural details without enforcing semantic texture consistency that may conflict with the ground truth. It builds on Perceptual Loss Training by providing a differentiable proxy for high-frequency similarity. WD-Regularized Loss (WD-R) is a training objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting that combines the Wasserstein Distance (WD) perceptual loss with a lightly weighted version of the original pixel-level loss. It solves the problem of visual artifacts that occur in regions with constrained Gaussian splat counts or limited training views, where the pure WD loss may fail to enforce sufficient pixel fidelity. Unlike its sibling Stable View Synthesis (SVS) Baseline which focuses on gradient stability, or High-Frequency Aware Loss which targets high-frequency details, WD-R specifically balances perceptual fidelity against raw pixel error to maintain compact representations without sacrificing sharpness. An l1 loss applied to downsampled versions of prediction and ground truth to eliminate color shifts introduced by perceptual loss while remaining robust against minor misalignments. Formula: Calculate L{ab} as the l1 distance between k-fold downsampled ground truth patch P and predicted patch \hat{P}: L{ab} = \| DSk(P) - DSk(\hat{P}) \|1 where DSk(\cdot) denotes k-fold downsampling. The full objective function is: L = w{l1} \cdot L{l1} + w{vgg} \cdot L{vgg} + w{ab} \cdot L{ab} where L{l1} is pixel-wise l1 distance, L{vgg} is perceptual loss, and w{\cdot} are weights. Strengths: Better visual fidelity, recovers high-frequency details, reduces structural artifacts. Limitations: Computationally expensive, prone to color shifts, requires careful tuning of weights. When to use: When visual quality is prioritized over training speed, and when pixel-wise losses result in overly smooth or blurry outputs. When not to use: When real-time training is required, or when color accuracy is critical and auxiliary bias correction is not feasible. Perceptual loss was originally introduced for image generation tasks. In the context of volume rendering and radiance fields, it has been adopted to address the "smoothness" problem of L1/L2 losses, which often produce blurry results. body: Stable View Synthesis (SVS) is a view synthesis method that renders novel views by blending a set of training images together, relying on proxy geometry produced by an external system. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit dependence on external piecewise planar mesh proxy geometry and direct access to all training images during rendering. SVS is trained using a perceptual loss. The method operates by blending training images together to render novel views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images; proxy geometry produced by an external system. Outputs: Rendered novel views. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Obtain proxy geometry from an external system. 2. Train the model using a perceptual loss. 3. Render novel views by blending training images together. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SVS may fail when the external proxy geometry is incorrect. It struggles particularly with distant or unobserved content, such as trees, where the proxy geometry reconstruction (e.g., via COLMAP) is poor. Pseudocode: Not given in the sources. Targets high-frequency details to improve perceptual quality, setting it apart from SVS's image-blending approach. Choose when SVS fails on natural content due to proxy geometry errors. See High-Frequency Aware Loss. Uses weight decay regularization for training stability, setting it apart from SVS's reliance on external geometry. Choose when SVS's requirement for external proxy geometry is unavailable. See WD-Regularized Loss. SVS requires multiple large CNNs and access to all training images to render novel views. It is better suited to large piecewise planar objects (e.g., vehicles) due to its reliance on piecewise planar mesh proxy geometry, whereas it performs poorly on scenes with natural content (trees, grass, flowers). name: High-Frequency Aware Loss
head: LHF, Shallow VGG Loss
body: High-Frequency Aware Loss (LHF) is a perceptual regularization term designed to recover high-frequency details in rendered images while avoiding the texture distortion common in deeper perceptual losses. It sets itself apart from standard VGG-based perceptual losses by restricting feature extraction to the first block of the network, thereby preserving fine structural details without enforcing semantic texture consistency that may conflict with the ground truth. It builds on Perceptual Loss Training by providing a differentiable proxy for high-frequency similarity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Gi (ground truth image patch after alignment), R (rendered image patch). Output: Scalar loss value L{HF}. Data Structures: Feature Extractor (F): The first block of a pre-trained VGG-19 model, consisting of convolutional layers and ReLU activations, explicitly excluding the max-pooling layer that follows this block in the standard architecture. Feature Maps: The output of F is a tensor of dimensions C \times W \times H, where C is the number of channels, and W, H are the width and height of the feature map. Parameters: w: Weight for the LHF term in the total loss function (value not specified in sources). F: Pre-trained VGG-19 weights, kept frozen during optimization. Steps: 1. Extract features from the ground truth patch Gi using the shallow VGG block: F(Gi). 2. Extract features from the rendered patch R using the same block: F(R). 3. Compute the squared Euclidean distance between the feature maps. 4. Normalize by the total number of elements in the feature map (C \times W \times H) and divide by 2. Formula: L{HF}(Gi, R) = \frac{1}{2CWH} \|F(Gi) - F(R)\|2^2 Where: \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences). C, W, H are the dimensions of the extracted feature maps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def highfrequencyawareloss(groundtruthpatch, renderedpatch, vggblock): """ Computes the High-Frequency Aware Loss using the first block of VGG-19. Args: groundtruthpatch (list of lists of lists): Ground truth image patch Gi. renderedpatch (list of lists of lists): Rendered image patch R. vggblock (callable): The first block of a pre-trained VGG-19 model (convolutions + ReLUs, no max-pooling). Returns: float: Scalar loss value LHF. """ # Extract features using the shallow VGG block # F(Gi) and F(R) are 3D structures of shape (C, W, H) featuresgt = vggblock(groundtruthpatch) featuresrendered = vggblock(renderedpatch) # Compute squared L2 distance between feature maps sumsquareddiff = 0.0 for c in range(len(featuresgt)): for w in range(len(featuresgt[0])): for h in range(len(featuresgt[0][0])): diff = featuresgt[c][w][h] - featuresrendered[c][w][h] sumsquareddiff += diff diff # Normalize by 2 C W H c = len(featuresgt) w = len(featuresgt[0]) h = len(featuresgt[0][0]) normalizationfactor = 2.0 c w h loss = sumsquareddiff / normalizationfactor return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Misalignment: The loss assumes Gi and R are aligned; misalignment prevents the recovery of high-frequency details, as the feature comparison penalizes structural shifts rather than texture errors. Texture Distortion: Using deeper VGG blocks can distort actual textures; restricting to the first block mitigates this. A differentiable loss function that measures perceptual similarity by comparing high-level features of rendered and reference image patches. It truncates a pre-trained VGG network to compute the Euclidean distance between extracted features, preserving high-level global details but suffering from loss-induced bias when rendered images contain noise. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves high-frequency details while preserving real textures, addressing the smoothness issues of pixel-wise MSE losses. Limitations: Sensitive to misalignment between ground truth and rendered patches. When to use: When optimizing radiance fields or images where high-frequency detail recovery is critical and standard MSE loss results in overly smooth outputs. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The High-Frequency Aware Loss was introduced in the AligNeRF paper. It modifies the original perceptual loss proposed by Johnson et al. by using only the output of the first block of a pre-trained VGG-19 model, before the max-pooling layer. This modification was motivated by observations in image restoration tasks where deeper perceptual losses distorted actual textures. The loss is typically combined with a patch-based MSE loss to handle misalignment, replacing the standard per-pixel MSE loss. name: VGG Loss for Image Patches
head: Content Loss, Feature Distance Loss, Feature Loss, Perceptual Loss (L_feat), VGG Loss, VGG feature distance
body: A differentiable loss function that measures perceptual similarity by comparing high-level features of rendered and reference image patches. It truncates a pre-trained VGG network to compute the Euclidean distance between extracted features, preserving high-level global details but suffering from loss-induced bias when rendered images contain noise. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Real image patches Ii, rendered (fake) image patches \hat{I}i, a pre-trained VGG network (typically VGG-19), and a loss multiplier parameter. Outputs: A scalar loss value representing the perceptual distance between the patches. Data Structures: Patches: 2D image arrays of shape (H, W, C) or (B, C, H, W) for batches. VGG Features: Activation maps from a specific truncated layer of the VGG network. The parent method High-Frequency Aware Loss specifies using only the first block of VGG-19 (before max-pooling) to preserve high-frequency details. Steps: 1. Extract real and fake patches from the training batch. 2. Slice the batch to include only the first numpatches if processing a subset. 3. Pass both real and fake patches through the truncated VGG network to obtain high-level feature representations \Phi(Ii) and \Phi(\hat{I}i). 4. Compute the squared Euclidean distance between the feature maps. 5. Average the distances over the number of patches N and multiply by the loss multiplier. Formula: Let N be the number of patches, \Phi(\cdot) be the feature extractor from the truncated VGG network, \hat{I}i be the rendered patch, and Ii be the reference patch. The VGG loss L{feat} is: L{feat} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \| \Phi(\hat{I}i) - \Phi(Ii) \|2^2 The final loss term added to the optimization objective is: L{final} = \text{vgg\loss\mult} \times L{feat} Parameters: vgglossmult: The multiplier for the VGG loss in the total loss computation. Value not given in the sources. \lambdap: Hyperparameter scaling the perceptual loss, typically set to 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise Sensitivity: High-level feature propagation amplifies rendering noise, making the loss highly sensitive to it and causing loss-induced bias that impedes optimization. This bias can push the optimizer toward suboptimal solutions when rendered images contain Monte Carlo noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevggloss(realpatches, fakepatches, vggmodel, vgglossmult): """ Computes the VGG perceptual loss for a batch of image patches. Args: realpatches: List or array of real image patches. fakepatches: List or array of generated image patches. vggmodel: A pre-trained VGG-19 model, truncated to the first block (before max-pooling). vgglossmult: Scalar multiplier for the loss. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Extract features from real and fake patches using the truncated VGG network featuresreal = vggmodel(realpatches) featuresfake = vggmodel(fakepatches) # 2. Compute the squared Euclidean distance between feature maps diff = featuresreal - featuresfake squareddiff = diff diff lossperpatch = sum(val 2 for val in squareddiff.flatten()) # 3. Average over the batch and apply multiplier numpatches = len(realpatches) avgloss = lossperpatch / numpatches finalloss = vgglossmult avgloss return finalloss A variant that uses the LPIPS metric for patch supervision. In each training step, it randomly renders a 300 × 300 image patch and compares it with the ground-truth patch to compute the LPIPS loss. The total training loss is L = L{reg} + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS}, where L{reg} = \lambda{color} L{color} + \lambda{density} L{density} is the regularization loss. The weight \lambda{LPIPS} is set to 0.025. Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple network evaluations per ray or small 32×32 patches, this method renders a large 300×300 patch in a single step, enabling efficient large-patch LPIPS supervision. On the light change dataset, ProLiF with large-patch LPIPS achieves higher SSIM and lower LPIPS than NeRF with 32×32 patch supervision or 256×256 up-sampled patch supervision. A variant that uses VGG perceptual loss with random geometric image-space augmentations to reduce gradient variance during inversion refinement. In each step, both the predicted and target images are randomly augmented with geometric transformations, and the losses from 16 augmentations are averaged. The number of augmentations is set to 16. A variant that optimizes the HrSRG representation by treating voxel values \{(c, \sigma, v)\} as learnable parameters alongside a tiny MLP weights \Phi, using perceptual loss to improve texture crispness and tolerate camera pose misalignment. It renders a 384×384 image patch per iteration, considers the first three convolution blocks of VGG-19, and sets the hyperparameter \lambdap to 0.01. The perceptual loss is computed as Lp = \frac{\lambdap}{Hj Wj} \sum{h,w} \|\phij(\hat{I}) - \phij(I)\|, where Hj and Wj are spatial dimensions of the feature maps, and \phij is the output of the j-th convolution block. It takes about 80 seconds to optimize HrSRG for 100 iterations (or 2.0×10^7 rays) on a single V100 GPU. Unlike SNeRG, which only fine-tunes its tiny MLP after obtaining the sparse radiance grid, HrSRG optimizes the voxel values directly as parameters. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of patches and the inference time of the truncated VGG network. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the patch size and batch size, as feature maps must be stored for the distance computation. Strengths: Preserves high-level global features and high-frequency details when using shallow VGG blocks, effectively preventing smoothing of textures. Limitations: Highly sensitive to rendering noise due to deep feature propagation, which can cause loss-induced bias and impede optimization. Not compatible with PSNR in varying light conditions. When to use: When perceptual quality and high-frequency detail preservation are prioritized over strict pixel-wise accuracy. When not to use: When rendered images contain significant noise that would bias the optimization toward suboptimal solutions. VGG loss was introduced by Johnson et al. [2016] as a differentiable proxy for perceptual similarity by truncating the VGG-19 network [Simonyan and Zisserman 2015] and computing the Euclidean distance between high-level features. It has been widely adopted in image synthesis and optimization tasks to align semantic content and style across views. In volume rendering, it is applied as a regularization loss to improve perceptual quality and prevent overly smooth textures. Specific applications to large-scale rendering and patch-based supervision are explored in methods like ProLiF and HrSRG. name: WD-Regularized Loss
head: WD with original loss regularizer, WD-R, WD-R Objective, WD-Regularized, Wasserstein Distortion (WD) Loss Optimization
body: WD-Regularized Loss (WD-R) is a training objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting that combines the Wasserstein Distance (WD) perceptual loss with a lightly weighted version of the original pixel-level loss. It solves the problem of visual artifacts that occur in regions with constrained Gaussian splat counts or limited training views, where the pure WD loss may fail to enforce sufficient pixel fidelity. It balances perceptual fidelity against raw pixel error to maintain compact representations without sacrificing sharpness. It is compared against sibling methods such as Stable View Synthesis (SVS) Baseline and High-Frequency Aware Loss. The method augments the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization by introducing a composite loss function. The core mechanism relies on computing the Wasserstein Distance between VGG feature pyramids of the rendered and ground-truth images, while adding a scaled original loss term to regularize the optimization. Inputs: Current 3D Gaussian parameters (means, covariances, opacities, colors, spherical harmonics). Camera poses and intrinsics for the current training view. Ground-truth image for the current view. Pre-computed ground-truth VGG features and pyramid statistics (if caching is enabled). Outputs: Rendered image. Scalar loss value L{WD-R}. Gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters. VGG Feature Pyramid: A stack of feature maps extracted from a pre-trained VGG network. The implementation uses 96 pyramid levels. Pyramid Weights: A scalar weight for each pyramid level i, computed as \text{ReLU}(1 - |\log2 \sigma - i|). Cached Statistics: Ground-truth VGG features and their corresponding pyramid statistics (mean and variance) are cached to avoid recomputation. The total loss is defined as: L{WD-R} = \gamma (d{WD} + \beta L{orig}) Where: L{WD-R} is the WD-Regularized loss. \gamma is a dataset-specific global scale factor. It modulates the magnitude of positional gradients to control the number of generated Gaussian splats, ensuring fair comparison with baselines under similar representation budgets. d{WD} is the Wasserstein Distance distortion metric computed in VGG feature space. \beta is the weighting factor for the original loss. It is chosen such that L{orig} acts as a mild pixel fidelity regularizer without overwhelming the WD term. L{orig} is the original 3DGS pixel-level loss (typically a combination of L1 and SSIM). The pure WD loss is defined as: L{WD} = \gamma d{WD} The per-level pyramid weight is calculated as: wi = \text{ReLU}(1 - |\log2 \sigma - i|) Where: \sigma = 4 is a constant. i is the pyramid level index. \beta: Set to 0.09 for all scenes. This value ensures that the gradient from the original loss is moderate; empirical analysis shows the gradient ratio \frac{\|\nabla d{WD}\|}{\|\nabla (\beta L{orig})\|} has a mean of \sim 1.6\times across training iterations, confirming WD remains the dominant signal. \gamma: A dataset-specific global scale. It is tuned per scene to align Gaussian counts across methods. Exact values are scene-dependent and not provided as a single constant. \sigma: Constant set to 4. 1. Warm-up Phase: Optimize the model using the standard 3DGS loss (L{orig}) for 3,000–5,000 iterations. 2. Perceptual Phase: For the remaining iterations (up to 30,000 total), switch to the WD-R objective. 3. Feature Extraction: Render the current view to obtain the predicted image. Extract VGG features from the predicted image. If caching is enabled, retrieve pre-computed VGG features and pyramid statistics for the ground-truth image. If caching is not enabled, extract VGG features from the ground-truth image and compute pyramid statistics. 4. Pyramid Weighting: Compute the weight wi for each pyramid level i using \sigma = 4. 5. Pruning: Identify pyramid levels where wi = 0. These levels do not contribute to the loss and can be skipped during computation. In the standard setup, only 20 of 96 pyramid levels contribute. 6. Loss Computation: Compute d{WD} using the weighted VGG feature differences. Compute L{orig} (L1 + SSIM). Calculate L{WD-R} = \gamma (d{WD} + \beta L{orig}). 7. Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to Gaussian parameters and update them. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computewdregularizedloss(gaussians, camera, gtimage, cachedgtfeatures, cachedgtstats, gamma, beta, sigma=4): # 1. Render current view predimage = forwardrender(gaussians, camera) # 2. Extract VGG features predfeatures = extractvggfeatures(predimage) if cachedgtfeatures is not None: gtfeatures = cachedgtfeatures gtstats = cachedgtstats else: gtfeatures = extractvggfeatures(gtimage) gtstats = computepyramidstatistics(gtfeatures) # 3. Compute pyramid weights and identify active levels numlevels = 96 activelevels = [] weights = {} log2sigma = math.log2(sigma) for i in range(numlevels): w = max(0.0, 1.0 - abs(log2sigma - i)) weights[i] = w if w > 0: activelevels.append(i) # 4. Compute WD distortion (dWD) dWD = 0.0 for i in activelevels: predfeat = predfeatures[i] gtfeat = gtfeatures[i] predmean = sum(predfeat) / len(predfeat) predvar = sum((x - predmean)2 for x in predfeat) / len(predfeat) gtmean = gtstats['mean'][i] gtvar = gtstats['var'][i] leveldist = wasserstein2distance(predmean, predvar, gtmean, gtvar) dWD += weights[i] leveldist # 5. Compute original loss (Lorig) Lorig = computel1loss(predimage, gtimage) + computessimloss(predimage, gtimage) # 6. Combine losses loss = gamma (dWD + beta Lorig) # 7. Backpropagation grads = computegradients(loss, gaussians) return loss, grads def forwardrender(gaussians, camera): # Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting forward rasterization return rasterizegaussians(gaussians, camera) def extractvggfeatures(image): # Standard VGG-16 feature extraction returning a list of feature maps return vggforwardpass(image) def computepyramidstatistics(features): stats = {'mean': [], 'var': []} for feat in features: n = len(feat) m = sum(feat) / n v = sum((x - m)2 for x in feat) / n stats['mean'].append(m) stats['var'].append(v) return stats def wasserstein2distance(m1, v1, m2, v2): # Wasserstein-2 distance between two 1D Gaussian distributions return (m1 - m2)2 + (math.sqrt(v1) - math.sqrt(v2))2 def computel1loss(pred, gt): return sum(abs(p - g) for p, g in zip(pred, gt)) / len(pred) def computessimloss(pred, gt): # Standard SSIM computation return 1.0 - structuralsimilarityindex(pred, gt) def computegradients(loss, params): # Standard automatic differentiation return autogradbackward(loss, params) Gradient Dominance: Although \beta=0.09 appears large, the WD gradient consistently exceeds the scaled original loss gradient (mean ratio \sim 1.6\times), preventing the original loss from overwhelming the perceptual signal. Pyramid Pruning: With \sigma=4, most of the 96 pyramid levels have zero weight. Ignoring these levels is critical for performance but must be handled correctly to ensure bit-exact gradients. Global Scale Tuning: \gamma must be tuned per dataset to align Gaussian counts for fair comparison with baselines. Warm-up Requirement: Skipping the warm-up phase with the original loss may lead to instability or artifacts, as the perceptual objective requires a stable initial representation. This variant refers to the specific optimizations applied to the WD loss computation to reduce overhead. It involves caching ground-truth VGG features and their pyramid statistics since the ground-truth view is constant across iterations, and pruning zero-weight VGG pyramid levels (only 20 of 96 levels contribute with \sigma=4). These optimizations reduce the per-iteration time by approximately 48%, lowering the relative training overhead from \approx 4.5\times to \approx 2.8\times over the original 3DGS. Time Complexity: The WD loss introduces significant computational overhead due to VGG feature extraction and statistical computation. At 1063 × 1600 resolution with 4.79M Gaussians, the forward/backward pass takes 273.9 ms/iteration compared to 61.1 ms for L1+SSIM, a 4.5× overhead. With caching and pruning optimizations, this is reduced to \approx 2.8\times overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing VGG features for the ground-truth image and potentially cached statistics. The VGG feature stack consists of 96 levels. Performance: WD-R consistently outperforms Original Loss and Perceptual-GS in perceptual metrics while maintaining compact representations (e.g., reducing Gaussian count on BungeNeRF from 6.92M to 4.89M). It trades higher training time for improved visual quality and fewer splats, which can partially offset rendering costs. Strengths: High perceptual fidelity, compact Gaussian representations, robust against artifacts in sparse-view regions. Limitations: High training time overhead (2.8×–4.5× slower than baseline), requires careful tuning of \gamma per dataset. When to Use: When perceptual quality and compactness are prioritized over training speed, and when artifacts from pure WD loss are observed in constrained regions. When Not to Use: When real-time training speed is critical, or when the scene has abundant training views and no constraint on Gaussian count. WD-Regularized Loss was introduced by Özyılkan and Chen et al. in the paper "Drop-In Perceptual Optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It builds upon the Wasserstein Distance (WD) perceptual loss for 3D Gaussian Splatting. The method addresses the limitations of pure WD loss by adding a regularizer to handle regions with constrained splat counts or small numbers of training views. It is part of the broader effort to improve perceptual quality in differentiable volume rendering and 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization. name: Color-Corrected Error Metrics
head: Per-image polynomial color correction, Photometric variation mitigation metrics
body: Color-Corrected Error Metrics are evaluation procedures designed to mitigate the impact of photometric variations—such as autoexposure shifts, white balance changes, and RGB clipping—in "in the wild" datasets. They solve the problem of ill-posed view synthesis evaluation where the ground truth image's photometric conditions may not match the model's neutral rendering. Unlike standard metrics that penalize brightness or color shifts as errors, these metrics first align the rendered image to the ground truth via a per-image least-squares fit, making models like Stable View Synthesis and GLO quantitatively comparable. Inputs: Rendered image \hat{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} Ground truth image I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} Saturated pixel mask M \in \{0, 1\}^{H \times W \times 3} indicating pixels to ignore Outputs: Corrected error metric value (e.g., PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) computed on the aligned images Data Structures: Standard image buffers and a small coefficient vector for the polynomial fit Steps: 1. Identify Saturated Pixels: Determine the set of pixels in the ground truth image I that are clipped or saturated. These pixels are excluded from the fitting process. 2. Fit Polynomial Expansion: Solve a per-image least-squares problem to find coefficients for a quadratic polynomial expansion that maps the rendered RGB values \hat{I} to the ground truth I. 3. Apply Correction: Transform the rendered image using the fitted polynomial: I{\text{corr}} = f(\hat{I}). 4. Compute Metric: Calculate the desired error metric between I{\text{corr}} and I. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def colorcorrectederror(renderedimg, gtimg, saturatedmask): """ renderedimg: np.array, shape (H, W, 3), float32 gtimg: np.array, shape (H, W, 3), float32 saturatedmask: np.array, shape (H, W, 3), bool (True if pixel is saturated/clipped) """ # 1. Filter out saturated pixels validpixels = ~saturatedmask if not np.any(validpixels): return np.inf # No valid pixels to fit # 2. Solve least squares for quadratic polynomial expansion # Quadratic expansion in 3 channels: 1, r, g, b, r^2, g^2, b^2, rg, rb, gb (10 terms) r, g, b = renderedimg[validpixels][:, 0], renderedimg[validpixels][:, 1], renderedimg[validpixels][:, 2] X = np.columnstack([ np.ones(len(r)), r, g, b, r2, g2, b2, rg, rb, gb ]) y = gtimg[validpixels] # Shape (N, 3) # Solve for coefficients beta (shape: 10, 3) beta,,, = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None) # 3. Apply the fitted transformation to the entire rendered image rall, gall, ball = renderedimg[:,:, 0], renderedimg[:,:, 1], renderedimg[:,:, 2] Xall = np.columnstack([ np.oneslike(rall), rall, gall, ball, rall2, gall2, ball2, rallgall, rallball, gallball ]) Icorr = Xall @ beta # 4. Compute standard metric (e.g., PSNR) between Icorr and gtimg mse = np.mean((Icorr - gtimg) 2) psnr = 10 np.log10(1.0 / mse) if mse > 0 else np.inf return psnr Parameters: Polynomial degree: Quadratic (2nd order) Saturated pixel threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Saturated Pixels: Ignoring saturated pixels is critical; including them would bias the polynomial fit towards the clipped values, which do not contain valid scene information. Ill-posedness: Without this correction, metrics become ill-posed because the model cannot be expected to replicate arbitrary autoexposure or white balance settings. The Textural Complexity Objective (T) is a metric used in active view planning for radiance-field optimization to identify camera poses that capture regions with high photometric variation. Unlike geometric metrics that analyze 3D mesh structure, T operates on 2D image projections, leveraging the fact that textural characteristics are readily discernible in 2D even if 3D geometry is ambiguous. It serves as a component of Color-Corrected Error Metrics, helping to mitigate photometric variations such as autoexposure shifts or white balance changes in "in the wild" datasets by prioritizing views with rich texture. A post-processing white balance technique using Bradford chromatic adaptation to map from a Planck/CIE-daylight illuminant to D65. It applies the Bradford chromatic adaptation transform, differing from simple gray-world or white-patch algorithms. For synthetic data, explicitly computes a 3-channel rescale factor for base color by taking the median value of all pixel-wise ratios between the model's prediction and ground truth. For real captures, omits the rescale procedure and presents only qualitative results as no ground truth on base color is provided. The PBR rendering pipeline operates in linear (HDR) space, and the final result is clipped to [0, 1] and mapped to SRGB just before calculating photometric loss or evaluation. A data augmentation technique simulating variable lighting and exposure by applying a random scale and shift transformation to RGB pixel values across training images. For each training image Ii \in [0, 1]^{800 \times 800 \times 3}, scale s{ij} and offset b{ij} are sampled uniformly. The transformation is applied to each channel j: \tilde{I}{ij} = \min(1, \max(0, s{ij} I{ij} + b{ij})) where s{ij} \sim \mathcal{U}(0.8, 1.2) and b{ij} \sim \mathcal{U}(-0.2, 0.2). Perturbations are applied to all training images except the first, which serves as the reference view. On the Lego dataset, this perturbation alone decreases NeRF's PSNR by approximately 10 dB on average compared to the original unperturbed dataset. Verification of camera localization performance on NeRF synthetic dataset scenes using reprojection error versus photometric error. Using reprojection error improves performance more than using photometric error alone, consistent with iNeRF results. In scenes with insufficient color uniqueness (e.g., Materials), reprojection error may degrade performance due to mismatches between corresponding points. In scenes with many local solutions for photometric errors (e.g., Mic, Ship), reprojection error does not avoid local solutions and does not improve performance. A potential improvement is to propagate unique features other than color to empty regions in the same way as color fields. Time and Memory Complexity: The fitting step involves solving a least-squares problem per image. The complexity depends on the number of polynomial terms (quadratic implies ~10 terms for RGB) and the number of valid pixels. It is generally fast relative to the rendering process itself. Memory usage is minimal, requiring only storage for the image buffers and the small set of polynomial coefficients. Measured Performance: On the Tanks and Temples dataset, using these color-corrected metrics allows for quantitative comparison between models like Stable View Synthesis (SVS) and models with Global Lighting Optimization (GLO), which would otherwise be incomparable due to photometric shifts. The correction makes SVS and the GLO model variant quantitatively comparable. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Mitigates the impact of autoexposure and white balance variations in "in the wild" datasets. Limitations: Does not solve the underlying issue of photometric variation during training; it is an evaluation procedure. Requires identification of saturated pixels, which may be ambiguous in some datasets. When to Use: Use when evaluating view synthesis on datasets with uncontrolled lighting or camera settings (e.g., Tanks and Temples, Phototourism). Use when comparing models that handle photometric variation differently (e.g., explicit appearance embeddings vs. neutral rendering). When Not to Use: Do not use for synthetic datasets with controlled, known lighting conditions where photometric consistency is expected and required. Do not use if the goal is to evaluate the model's ability to replicate specific lighting conditions (e.g., relighting tasks). Originating from the challenges of evaluating neural radiance fields on "in the wild" datasets, this method addresses the issue where camera autoexposure and white balance vary between images, making standard error metrics misleading. The approach was highlighted in the context of the Mip-NeRF 360 paper, which constructed a dataset with fixed photometric conditions to avoid these issues, but acknowledged the need for such metrics for existing uncontrolled datasets like Tanks and Temples. The concept of mitigating photometric variation is also related to NeRF in the Wild (NeRF-W), which uses appearance embeddings to isolate tinting, but Color-Corrected Error Metrics specifically refer to the post-hoc evaluation correction.
