name: Overall Training Objective
head: Overall Loss, Overall Optimization Strategy, SparseNeuS Total Training Loss
body: The Overall Training Objective defines the composite loss function used to optimize radiance fields by balancing pixel-wise fidelity, perceptual quality, and adversarial constraints. It addresses the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by combining multiple metrics to supervise optimization, addressing the problem of generating high-fidelity, visually consistent rendered images. The method minimizes a weighted sum of loss components during the training of a neural radiance field. The optimization is performed using the Adam optimizer. Inputs: Rendered images and ground truth images. Positive and negative text descriptions for adversarial and perceptual guidance. Camera parameters and sampling points. Outputs: Updated radiance field parameters. Data Structures: Loss weights: \lambdag (adversarial), \lambdal (local contrastive), \lambdap (perceptual), \lambdar (reconstruction). Text embeddings: Positive and negative text descriptions collected from a dataset. Parameters: \lambdag = 0.2, \lambdal = 0.1, \lambdap = 2.0, \lambdar = 0.1. Patch size: 1/10 of the original input image dimensions. Negative samples: ~200 text descriptions manually collected (e.g., "Zombie", "Tolkien elf"). \lambda{n\text{-}dmean} = 0.001, \lambda{n\text{-}dmed} = 0.001. \alpha (Eikonal weight), \beta (sparseness weight). Steps: 1. Reconstruction Stage: Sample 192 points per ray. Compute \mathcal{L}r (reconstruction), \mathcal{L}p (perceptual), \mathcal{L}l (local contrastive), and \mathcal{L}g (adversarial). Compute total loss \mathcal{L} = \lambdag \mathcal{L}g + \lambdal \mathcal{L}l + \lambdap \mathcal{L}p + \lambdar \mathcal{L}r. Train for 6 epochs with learning rate 0.0005 using Adam. 2. Stylization Stage: Use the same loss formulation. Train for 4 epochs with learning rate 0.001 using Adam. 3. Regularization Schedule: Apply \mathcal{L}{n\text{-}dmed} starting at iteration \tau = 1,000 and \mathcal{L}{n\text{-}dmean} starting at \tau = 2,000. 4. Iteration Limits: Train DTU scenes for 8,000 iterations and Tanks-and-Temples scenes for 10,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. lambdag, lambdal, lambdap, lambdar = 0.2, 0.1, 2.0, 0.1 lrrecon, lrstyl = 0.0005, 0.001 epochsrecon, epochsstyl = 6, 4 pointsperray = 192 patchratio = 0.1 taundmed, taundmean = 1000, 2000 lambdandmed, lambdandmean = 0.001, 0.001 negativetexts = ["Zombie", "Tolkien elf", "Self-Portrait by Van Gogh"] # ~200 texts from Pinterest def mse(a, b): return sum((a[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) def contrastiveloss(rendered, gt, patchh, patchw): # Extract and compare patches of size 1/10 of input return sum((rendered[i:i+patchh, j:j+patchw] - gt[i:i+patchh, j:j+patchw])2 for i in range(0, gt.shape[0], patchh) for j in range(0, gt.shape[1], patchw)) def adversarialloss(rendered, posemb, negemb, model): # Conditional adversarial score using text embeddings return model.adversarialscore(rendered, posemb) - model.adversarialscore(rendered, negemb) def perceptualloss(a, b): return sum((a[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) # Standard perceptual metric def normalmeandiff(a, b): return sum((a[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) # SVRaster normal mean difference regularizer def normalmeddiff(a, b): return sum((a[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) # SVRaster normal median difference regularizer def computetotalloss(rendered, gt, posemb, negemb, model, stage, iteration): lossr = mse(rendered, gt) lossp = perceptualloss(rendered, gt) patchh, patchw = gt.shape[0] // 10, gt.shape[1] // 10 lossl = contrastiveloss(rendered, gt, patchh, patchw) lossg = adversarialloss(rendered, posemb, negemb, model) total = lambdag lossg + lambdal lossl + lambdap lossp + lambdar lossr if stage == 'svrecon': if iteration >= taundmed: total += lambdandmed normalmeddiff(rendered, gt) if iteration >= taundmean: total += lambdandmean normalmeandiff(rendered, gt) return total def train(model, data, stage): lr = lrrecon if stage == 'reconstruction' else lrstyl epochs = epochsrecon if stage == 'reconstruction' else epochsstyl optimizer = GradientOptimizer(model.parameters(), lr=lr) # Standard gradient-based updater iteration = 0 for epoch in range(epochs): for batch in data: rendered = model.render(batch.cameras, batch.points) loss = computetotalloss(rendered, batch.gt, batch.posemb, batch.negemb, model, stage, iteration) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() iteration += 1 Composite training loss functions aggregate multiple error metrics to optimize the parameters of a radiance field or inverse rendering model. They address the ill-posed nature of inverse problems by combining pixel-wise accuracy, structural similarity, and perceptual fidelity. This method differs from single-metric approaches by balancing reconstruction error with high-frequency detail preservation, often incorporating specific priors (such as normals or semantics) depending on the variant. Deactivates the conditional adversarial loss (\mathcal{L}g) and retrains the model. This results in incomplete renderings with clear artifacts, demonstrating the importance of the adversarial component for style transfer. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of epochs and points per ray. Reconstruction stage uses 6 epochs with 192 points/ray; stylization uses 4 epochs. Memory Complexity: Reduced by processing at the patch level (1/10 of original input) for local contrastive loss. Strengths: Balances local pixel fidelity with global structural integrity and perceptual quality. Limitations: Requires manual collection of negative text samples. Adversarial loss is critical for style transfer; removing it degrades quality significantly. When to use: When high-fidelity stylization of radiance fields is required using text guidance. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited or when style transfer is not needed (use standard reconstruction loss). The method is based on NeRF-Art, which introduces text-driven neural radiance fields stylization. It builds on VolSDF as the base NeRF model. The approach addresses the limitations of single-metric losses in generating visually consistent stylized images. The "No conditional adversarial objective" variant is discussed in Pix2NeRF to highlight the role of adversarial training in conditional GANs for NeRF translation. SVRecon: Sparse Voxel Rasterization for Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2511.17364, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) SparseNeuS: Fast Generalizable Neural Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-313, fetched 2026-10-26 NeRF-Art: Text-Driven Neural Radiance Fields Stylization, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2023.3283400, fetched 2026-10-26 Pix2NeRF: Unsupervised Conditional \pi-GAN for Single Image to Neural Radiance Fields Translation, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00395, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Composite Training Loss
head: Composite Training Loss & Schedule, L1+SSIM+LPIPS Loss, LiteVoxel Training Objective
body: Composite training loss aggregates multiple error metrics to optimize radiance field or inverse rendering parameters by combining photometric, structural, and perceptual terms. It addresses the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by balancing reconstruction accuracy with high-frequency detail preservation and geometric/material priors. Inputs: Rendered image Ir, ground truth image I{gt}, and optionally auxiliary data such as estimated normals, semantic maps, shadow masks, or depth maps. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L} used for gradient-based optimization. Standard image tensors and scalar weights. Some variants require pre-computed auxiliary maps (e.g., normals from Omnidata, semantic maps from MMSegmentation). 1. Render: Generate the image Ir from the current model parameters. 2. Compute Auxiliary Priors (Variant-dependent): If required, estimate normals, semantics, or shadow masks using pretrained networks. 3. Compute Individual Loss Terms: Calculate each component loss (L1, SSIM, LPIPS, robust loss, etc.) between Ir and I{gt} (or priors). 4. Aggregate: Sum the weighted loss terms to produce the total loss \mathcal{L}. The specific formula depends on the variant: General Composite (MuRF): \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{L1} + \mathcal{L}{SSIM} + \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} Where \mathcal{L}{L1} is the mean absolute error, \mathcal{L}{SSIM} is the structural similarity index loss, and \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} is the learned perceptual image patch similarity loss. latentSplat: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{rec}} = \lambda1\|\hat{\mathbf{T}}-\mathbf{T}\|1 + \lambda2 \mathrm{LPIPS}(\hat{\mathbf{T}},\mathbf{T}) \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{aux}} = \lambda3\|\hat{\mathbf{T}}{\mathrm{aux}}-\mathbf{T}\|2^2 + \lambda4 \mathrm{LPIPS}(\hat{\mathbf{T}}{\mathrm{aux}},\mathbf{T}) \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{gen}}=E{\hat{\mathbf{T}}} [\log (1- D(\hat{\mathbf{T}}))], \quad \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{disc}} = E{\mathbf{X}}[\log (D(\mathbf{X}))] + E{\hat{\mathbf{T}}}[\log (1-D(\hat{\mathbf{T}}))] Where \hat{\mathbf{T}} is the decoded feature image, \mathbf{T} is the target image, \hat{\mathbf{T}}{\mathrm{aux}} is the color rendering, D is a pre-trained discriminator from LDM, and \mathbf{X} are real images. UrbanIR: \min {\theta, \mathbf{L}} \mathcal {L}{\text {render}} + \lambda 1\mathcal {L}{\text {visibility}} + \lambda 2\mathcal {L}{\text {normal}} + \lambda 3\mathcal {L}{\text {semantics}} + \lambda 4\mathcal {L}{\text {reg}} Where \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} is the base rendering loss, \mathcal{L}{\text{visibility}} enforces visibility consistency, \mathcal{L}{\text{normal}} aligns with estimated normals, \mathcal{L}{\text{semantics}} aligns with semantic maps, and \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} is a regularization term. SVG-IR / LiteVoxel: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{SSIM}\mathcal{L}{SSIM} + \lambda{Tc}\mathcal{L}{Tc} + \lambda{Ti}\mathcal{L}{Ti} + \lambda{NDM}\mathcal{L}{NDM} + \mathcal{L}{mask} + \mathcal{L}{tv} Where \mathcal{L}{SSIM} is a structure-aware penalty, \mathcal{L}{Tc} encourages final ray transmittance near 0 or 1, \mathcal{L}{Ti} discourages floating density, \lambda{NDM}\mathcal{L}{NDM} is median-based depth-normal consistency, \mathcal{L}{mask} is foreground/background supervision, and \mathcal{L}{tv} is total variation on the sparse density field. INPC: L = LR + L{D-SSIM} + \lambda{vgg} \cdot L{VGG} + \lambda{decay} \cdot L{Reg} Where LR is a robust per-pixel loss, L{D-SSIM} is differentiable SSIM, L{VGG} is VGG perceptual loss, and L{Reg} is normalized weight decay on hash grid parameters. LINGO: L{total} = L1(Ir, Im) + \lambda{ssim} L{ssim}(Ir, Im) + \lambda{tv} L{tv}(V{tv}) Tg = \max(0.01, \mathrm{Otsu}(Ir)) L{final} = L{total} \times \left(Tg + \frac{1}{4Tg}\right) Where Ir and Im are rendered and ground-truth images, V{tv} represents the density volume, and Tg is a dynamic loss-scaling coefficient. Water Gaussians: \mathcal{L}{RGB} = 0.8 \cdot \frac{\|Ir - I{gt}\|2^2}{\mathrm{stopgrad}(bI) + 10^{-3}}, \quad \mathcal{L}{Struct} = 0.2 \cdot (1 - \mathrm{SSIM}(Ir, I{gt})) \mathcal{L}{TV} = 10^{-4} \cdot \left(\text{mean absolute first differences along axes} + \text{within-cell deviation of FCC sites}\right) The RGB and structural terms supervise captured underwater RGB, while the TV penalty regularizes water densities. Pre-training: L = L{color} + \lambda \cdot L{lpips} L{color} = \frac{1}{H \times W} \sum{i=1}^{H \times W} (Ir(i) - I{gt}(i))^2 L{lpips} = \sum{l} \frac{1}{Ml} \sum{i=1}^{Ml} \| wl \odot (\hat{f}l(Ir(i)) - \hat{f}l(I{gt}(i))) \|2^2 Where H \times W is the pixel count, \hat{f}l is the normalized VGG feature map at layer l, and wl are channel-wise weights. latentSplat: \lambda1 = 1, \lambda2 = 1, \lambda3 = 10, \lambda4 = 0.5. UrbanIR: \lambda1 = 0.001, \lambda2 = 0.01, \lambda3 = 0.04, \lambda4 = 0.1. INPC: \lambda{vgg} = 0.075, \lambda{decay} = 0.1, robust loss parameters \alpha = 0, c = 0.2. LINGO: \lambda{ssim} = 0.25, \lambda{tv} = 0.05. Water Gaussians: RGB/Structural weights 0.8/0.2, TV penalty 10^{-4}, Adam learning rates 2.5 \times 10^{-3} (transport-density) and 10^{-3} (directional head), \epsilon = 10^{-15}, directional head decays to 1.5 \times 10^{-4} over 15k steps. Pre-training: \lambda = 0.05. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def l1loss(pred, target): return np.mean(np.abs(pred - target)) def mseloss(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target) 2) def ssimloss(pred, target): mup = np.mean(pred) mut = np.mean(target) sigmap = np.var(pred) sigmat = np.var(target) sigmapt = np.mean((pred - mup) (target - mut)) C1, C2 = 1e-4, 1e-4 ssim = ((2 mup mut + C1) (2 sigmapt + C2)) / \ ((mup2 + mut2 + C1) (sigmap + sigmat + C2)) return 1.0 - ssim def lpipsloss(pred, target): # Computes LPIPS using VGG-19 feature maps # Simplified as L2 distance on flattened tensors for demonstration return np.mean((pred.flatten() - target.flatten()) 2) def robustloss(pred, target, alpha=0.0, c=0.2): diff = pred - target return np.mean(np.sqrt(diff2 + c2)) def vggloss(pred, target): # Computes VGG perceptual loss return np.mean((pred.flatten() - target.flatten()) 2) def normalizedweightdecay(params): return np.mean(params 2) def otsuthreshold(image): hist, bins = np.histogram(image.flatten(), bins=256, range=(0, 1)) total = image.size sumf = np.dot(bins[:-1], hist) weightf1 = np.cumsum(hist) weightf2 = total - weightf1 meanf1 = np.cumsum(hist bins[:-1]) / (weightf1 + 1e-8) meanf2 = (sumf - np.cumsum(hist bins[:-1])) / (weightf2 + 1e-8) variance = weightf1 weightf2 (meanf1 - meanf2) 2 return np.argmax(variance) / 255.0 def totalvariation(volume): tvx = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(volume, axis=0))) tvy = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(volume, axis=1))) tvz = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(volume, axis=2))) return (tvx + tvy + tvz) / 3.0 def computecompositeloss(renderedimage, groundtruth, variant="standard", auxdata=None, params=None): if params is None: params = {} if variant == "standard": return l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruth) + ssimloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) + lpipsloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) elif variant == "latentSplat": lambda1 = params.get("lambda1", 1.0) lambda2 = params.get("lambda2", 1.0) lambda3 = params.get("lambda3", 10.0) lambda4 = params.get("lambda4", 0.5) rec = lambda1 l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruth) + lambda2 lpipsloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) aux = lambda3 mseloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) + lambda4 lpipsloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) return rec + aux elif variant == "urbanir": lambda1 = params.get("lambda1", 0.001) lambda2 = params.get("lambda2", 0.01) lambda3 = params.get("lambda3", 0.04) lambda4 = params.get("lambda4", 0.1) lossrender = l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruth) lossvis = l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruth) if auxdata and "visibilitymask" in auxdata else 0.0 lossnorm = 1.0 - np.mean(renderedimage auxdata.get("normals", renderedimage)) if auxdata and "normals" in auxdata else 0.0 losssem = l1loss(renderedimage, auxdata.get("semantics", renderedimage)) if auxdata and "semantics" in auxdata else 0.0 lossreg = normalizedweightdecay(renderedimage) return lossrender + lambda1 lossvis + lambda2 lossnorm + lambda3 losssem + lambda4 lossreg elif variant == "svgir": lossssim = ssimloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) losstv = totalvariation(renderedimage) return lossssim + losstv elif variant == "inpc": lambdavgg = params.get("lambdavgg", 0.075) lambdadecay = params.get("lambdadecay", 0.1) alpha = params.get("alpha", 0.0) c = params.get("c", 0.2) lossr = robustloss(renderedimage, groundtruth, alpha=alpha, c=c) lossdssim = ssimloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) lossvgg = vggloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) lossreg = normalizedweightdecay(renderedimage) return lossr + lossdssim + lambdavgg lossvgg + lambdadecay lossreg elif variant == "lingo": lambdassim = params.get("lambdassim", 0.25) lambdatv = params.get("lambdatv", 0.05) ltotal = l1loss(renderedimage, groundtruth) + lambdassim ssimloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) + lambdatv totalvariation(renderedimage) Tg = max(0.01, otsuthreshold(renderedimage)) return ltotal (Tg + 1.0 / (4.0 Tg)) elif variant == "water": bI = 1.0 rgbterm = 0.8 mseloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) / (bI + 1e-3) structterm = 0.2 ssimloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) tvterm = 1e-4 totalvariation(renderedimage) return rgbterm + structterm + tvterm elif variant == "pretrain": lambdalpips = params.get("lambdalpips", 0.05) lcolor = mseloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) llpips = lpipsloss(renderedimage, groundtruth) return lcolor + lambdalpips llpips else: raise ValueError("Unknown variant") Staged Training: latentSplat trains with auxiliary losses only for the first 100k iterations to prevent features from fitting to incorrectly positioned Gaussians, and delays generative loss until 125k iterations to prevent an overly strong discriminator. Dynamic Scaling: LINGO uses Otsu's threshold on the rendered image to compute a dynamic loss-scaling coefficient, strengthening gradients in low-density areas without causing gradient explosion. Auxiliary Dependency: UrbanIR requires pretrained 2D priors (MTMT for shadows, Omnidata for normals, MMSegmentation for semantics) which must be available or estimated before optimization. Initialization & Precision: Water Gaussians initializes direct/backscatter densities and directional heads with specific values and uses \epsilon = 10^{-15} for Adam stability. An optimization objective combining rendering loss, visibility, normal, semantic, and regularization losses, using pretrained 2D priors to address the ill-posed inverse problem. It estimates shadow masks using MTMT, refines geometry using Omnidata, and uses semantic maps from Kitti360 or MMSegmentation. It is chosen for large-scale urban scene inverse rendering from single videos. A composite objective function used to optimize the Spatially-Varying Gaussian Splatting (SVG-IR) representation for inverse rendering. It solves the problem of jointly optimizing geometric, photometric, and material properties from multi-view images by combining data fidelity terms with regularization constraints for normals, albedo, and roughness. It is distinguished from standard Gaussian Splatting optimization by the inclusion of physically-based inverse rendering losses, specifically radiance consistency and surface normal regularization, and differs from implicit neural representation methods like IGR by using a discrete Gaussian primitive set rather than a continuous signed distance function. A composite training loss combining a robust per-pixel loss, D-SSIM, VGG perceptual loss, and normalized weight decay on multi-resolution hash grid parameters. It is used for Implicit Neural Point Clouds, balancing perceptual quality with regularization of the hash grid. It is chosen for high-quality radiance field rendering with fixed model size. A staged training objective combining auxiliary, reconstruction, and generative losses with specific weights and adaptive scaling. It uses L1 and LPIPS for reconstruction, MSE and LPIPS for auxiliary color rendering, and VAE-GAN losses adapted from LDM for generative sampling. It is chosen when correct sampling and generation in uncertain regions is required. A dynamic loss-scaling strategy that computes total loss with L1, SSIM, and TV regularization, then scales it using Otsu's threshold on the rendered image to address vanishing gradients in low-density structural regions. It is chosen for sparse-view X-ray novel view synthesis and CT reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting. A convex combination of RGB and structural terms (weights 0.8 and 0.2) with a spatial total-variation penalty on water densities. The RGB term is mean squared residual after division by \mathrm{stopgrad}(bI) + 10^{-3}, and the structural term is 1 - \mathrm{SSIM} after the same normalization. It is chosen for per-scene underwater rendering with homogeneous-grid optical-mass identity. A weighted sum of image color loss (MSE) and LPIPS loss used to pre-train a point cloud encoder via 3D Gaussian Splatting. It encourages the encoder to capture precise geometric and spatial information for downstream tasks. It is chosen for unsupervised pre-training of 3D scene understanding models. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of loss terms and the complexity of auxiliary networks (e.g., VGG, Omnidata). latentSplat requires staged training over 125k+ iterations. UrbanIR requires 100 epochs with Adam optimizer. Memory Complexity: INPC uses a fixed-size hash grid (1.1 GB). UrbanIR uses Instant-NGP style hash tables. Water Gaussians uses a compact configuration with N=8 (2,048 fixed water Gaussians, 12,288 learned RGB transport parameters). Performance: INPC achieves high PSNR and LPIPS scores on MipNeRF360 and Tanks and Temples datasets. latentSplat improves on prior methods with view-synthesis benchmarks. LINGO reaches performance comparable to baselines trained with 30k iterations within only 5k iterations under sparse-view conditions. Hardware: INPC tested on RTX 4090 and A100. Strengths: Combines multiple metrics for robust optimization. Handles ill-posed problems via priors (UrbanIR). Dynamic scaling accelerates convergence in challenging regions (LINGO). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of weights. Auxiliary networks add complexity and dependency. Staged training increases total optimization time (latentSplat). Composite training losses are standard in differentiable rendering and inverse rendering to balance photometric accuracy with perceptual quality. The L1+SSIM+LPIPS combination is a common baseline. latentSplat adapts LDM VAE-GAN decoder losses for radiance field optimization. UrbanIR extends this with semantic and normal priors for urban scenes. SVG-IR adds radiance consistency and material-specific losses for Gaussian splatting. INPC uses robust losses and hash grid regularization for neural point clouds. LINGO addresses sparse-view X-ray synthesis with dynamic gradient optimization. Water Gaussians handles underwater optical-mass identity with specialized TV penalties. Pre-training objectives use 3DGS for point cloud encoder initialization. body: The SVG-IR Training Loss is the composite objective function used to optimize the Spatially-Varying Gaussian Splatting (SVG-IR) representation for inverse rendering. It solves the problem of jointly optimizing geometric, photometric, and material properties from multi-view images by combining data fidelity terms with regularization constraints for normals, albedo, and roughness. It is distinguished from standard Gaussian Splatting optimization by the inclusion of physically-based inverse rendering losses, specifically radiance consistency and surface normal regularization, and differs from implicit neural representation methods like IGR by using a discrete Gaussian primitive set rather than a continuous signed distance function. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image, ground truth image, predicted surface normals, pseudo-normals (from geometry), albedo map, roughness map, and normal offsets \Delta NM. Outputs: Scalar loss value L for backpropagation. Data Structures: Loss Weights: \lambda1, \lambda{ssim}, \lambda{rc}, \lambdan, \lambda{s,a}, \lambda{s,r}, \lambda{reg,n}. Typical values are not given in the sources. Radiance Consistency: Involves secondary Gaussian outgoing radiance L'{ind}(xj, \omega{ik}) and primary radiance L{ind}(xj, \omegai). Formulas: The total loss is defined as: L = \lambda1 L1 + \lambda{ssim} L{ssim} + \lambda{rc} L{rc} + \lambdan Ln + \lambda{s,a} L{s,a} + \lambda{s,r} L{s,r} + \lambda{reg,n} L{reg,n} Where: L1: L1 loss between rendered image and ground truth. L{ssim}: SSIM loss between rendered image and ground truth. L{rc}: Radiance consistency loss. Defined as the sum of absolute differences between primary and secondary Gaussian radiance: L{rc} = \sum |L'{ind}(xj, \omega{ik}) - L{ind}(xj, \omegai)| (Note: The source formula L{rc} = |L'{ind}(xj, \omega{ik})| appears incomplete; the standard consistency formulation implies a difference term, but the source explicitly writes the magnitude of the secondary radiance in the snippet. It is distinguished from SVG-IR by using a continuous implicit function f rather than discrete Gaussians. name: Sky Loss
head: Sky Transmittance Mask Loss
body: Sky Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering to prevent the invalid allocation of sparse voxels in unbounded free space. It isolates the sky region and enforces maximum global ray transmittance, ensuring that background color generation is routed exclusively through a 2D environment map rather than learned 3D primitives. It differs from standard photometric losses by targeting the transmittance field specifically in sky-masked pixels to suppress background noise. The method operates by identifying pixels corresponding to the sky and penalizing any residual density or occupancy that prevents rays from passing through to the background environment map. Inputs: skylabel: A binary mask indicating sky pixels (1.0 for sky, 0.0 otherwise). densityfieldweights or occupancyfieldweights: The accumulated weights along rays from the volume renderer. Tfinal: The residual transmittance accumulated at the terminal boundary of the composition pass. Msky: A binary mask derived from zero-depth LiDAR boundaries. Outputs: skyloss: A scalar loss value. Sky Label: A tensor of shape matching the image batch, containing float values 0.0 or 1.0. Mask: A binary tensor of the same spatial dimensions as the rendered image. 1. Compute Sky Label: Convert the input batch['sky'] to float and move to the computation device. Compute skylabel = 1.0 - skylabel. 2. Clip Weights: Clip the sum of field weights along the ray dimension (dim=1) to the range [10^{-3}, 1 - 10^{-3}] to prevent gradient vanishing or explosion at boundaries. 3. Compute Loss: For Density/Occupancy Fields (SDFStudio variant): Compute the Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) between the clipped sum of weights and skylabel. Multiply the result by a coefficient of 0.01. For Transmittance Fields (DrivingVoxels variant): Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the final transmittance T{\text{final}} and 1.0 for all pixels in the sky mask. SDFStudio Variant (BCE-based): \mathcal{L}{\text{sky}} = 0.01 \cdot \text{BCE}(\text{clip}(\sum w, 10^{-3}, 1-10^{-3}), \text{sky\label}) Where w are the field weights. DrivingVoxels Variant (MSE-based): \mathcal{L}{\text{sky}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}{\text{sky}}|} \sum{i \in \mathcal{M}{\text{sky}}} (T{\text{final}, i} - 1)^2 Where \mathcal{M}{\text{sky}} is the set of pixels in the sky mask and T{\text{final}} is the residual transmittance. Weight Coefficient: 0.01 (for SDFStudio variant). Clip Range: [10^{-3}, 1 - 10^{-3}]. Background Primitives: Without this loss, background primitives in the sky dome may be incorrectly optimized. This loss completely penalizes such primitives to ensure background color is generated exclusively through the 2D environment map. Mask Derivation: The sky mask \mathcal{M}{\text{sky}} must be derived from zero-depth LiDAR boundaries to accurately isolate unbounded free space. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeskylosssdfstudio(batch, fieldweights, usenerfacto=True): """ Computes Sky Loss for SDFStudio-style density/occupancy fields. """ # Step 1: Compute sky label # batch['sky'] is assumed to be 1 for sky, 0 for non-sky # skylabel is 1.0 for sky, 0.0 for non-sky skylabel = 1.0 - batch['sky'].float().to(device) # Step 2: Sum weights along ray dimension (dim=1) # Assuming fieldweights has shape [B, Nrays, Nsamples] or similar # Sum over the sample dimension sumweights = torch.sum(fieldweights, dim=1) # Step 3: Clip weights clippedweights = torch.clamp(sumweights, min=1e-3, max=1-1e-3) # Step 4: Compute BCE loss # BCE expects probabilities, so we treat clippedweights as predicted probability # skylabel is the target bceloss = torch.nn.functional.binarycrossentropy(clippedweights, skylabel) # Step 5: Scale by coefficient skyloss = bceloss 0.01 return skyloss def computeskylossdrivingvoxels(Tfinal, Msky): """ Computes Sky Loss for DrivingVoxels-style transmittance fields. """ # Msky is a binary mask (1.0 for sky pixels, 0.0 otherwise) # Tfinal is the residual transmittance tensor # Select pixels in the sky mask skypixelsTfinal = Tfinal[Msky.bool()] # Compute MSE against 1.0 # If no sky pixels, return 0 if skypixelsTfinal.numel() == 0: return torch.tensor(0.0, device=Tfinal.device) mseloss = torch.mean((skypixelsTfinal - 1.0) 2) return mseloss A specific implementation of Sky Loss used in DrivingVoxels. It uses a Mean Squared Error objective on the final transmittance T{\text{final}} rather than Binary Cross Entropy on weights. It relies on a binary mask \mathcal{M}{\text{sky}} derived from zero-depth LiDAR boundaries. It is chosen when using sparse voxel rasterization in unbounded driving scenes to prevent invalid voxel allocation in free space. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the sky mask. The operation is element-wise and parallelizable on GPU. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sky mask and intermediate transmittance/weight tensors. Strengths: Effectively suppresses background noise and prevents the network from learning incorrect 3D structures in the sky region. Limitations: Requires accurate sky masks (from LiDAR or other sensors). If the mask is inaccurate, it may penalize valid foreground geometry or fail to suppress background noise. When to use: In unbounded scenes where a 2D environment map is used for background rendering and 3D primitives should not contribute to the sky region. The concept of isolating sky regions for regularization appears in recent differentiable volume rendering literature for autonomous driving and large-scale scene reconstruction. The SDFStudio variant uses a BCE loss on density/occupancy weights. The DrivingVoxels variant introduces the MSE-based transmittance loss to handle sparse voxel allocation in unbounded free space. autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DrivingVoxels: Compositional Sparse Voxel Rasterization for Dynamic Driving Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.23031, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Skinning Weights Weak Supervision
head: Weak Supervision for Gaussian Skinning Weights
body: This method regularizes the skinning weights of 3D Gaussians by supervising them with ground-truth skinning weights from the SMPL parametric human model. It addresses the problem that training on a limited amount of gestures typically yields skinning weights that do not generalize well to novel poses. Unlike sibling methods that optimize photometric or perceptual image fidelity, this approach focuses specifically on the geometric consistency of deformation weights. Inputs: G: Set of N Gaussians. P: Canonical positions of Gaussians, pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. WG: Learned skinning weights for Gaussians, w(gi) \in \mathbb{R}^{24}. V: Vertices of the canonical SMPL mesh. WS: Ground-truth SMPL skinning weights for vertices, w(vi) \in \mathbb{R}^{24}. \tau{skn}: Threshold parameter. Outputs: Scalar loss value L{skn}. Data Structures: Skinning weights are vectors of size 24, corresponding to the 24 bones of the SMPL model. The distance metric is the Euclidean distance in 3D space. Steps: 1. For each Gaussian i with canonical position pi: a. Find the nearest vertex vi on the canonical SMPL mesh to pi. b. Retrieve the ground-truth skinning weight vector w(vi) for vertex vi. c. Retrieve the current learned skinning weight vector w(gi) for Gaussian i. d. Compute the Euclidean distance between the Gaussian and the nearest vertex: di = \|vi - pi\|2. e. Compute the squared L2 distance between the skinning weight vectors: \Delta wi = \|w(gi) - w(vi)\|2^2. f. Compute the loss term for this Gaussian: li = \text{ReLU}(\Delta wi - \tau{skn} \cdot di). 2. Sum the loss terms over all Gaussians: L{skn} = \sumi li. Formula: L{skn} = \sumi \text{ReLU}(\|w(gi) - w(vi)\|2^2 - \tau{skn} \|vi - pi\|2) Where: w(gi) is the skinning weight vector of Gaussian i. w(vi) is the skinning weight vector of the nearest SMPL vertex vi. vi is the position of the nearest SMPL vertex to Gaussian i. pi is the canonical position of Gaussian i. \tau{skn} is a threshold parameter controlling the trade-off between weight similarity and spatial proximity. Parameters: \tau{skn}: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Do not backpropagate the gradient of the distance term \|vi - pi\|2 through this loss. The distance term acts as a static threshold modifier; its gradient must be stopped to prevent instability in the nearest-vertex search or spatial optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeskinningweaksupervisionloss(gaussians, smplmesh, tauskn): """ Computes the skinning weights weak supervision loss. Args: gaussians: List of tuples (canonicalposition, skinningweights) smplmesh: Object with method nearestvertex(position) returning (vertexposition, vertexskinningweights) tauskn: Float threshold parameter. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 for pi, wg in gaussians: vi, wv = smplmesh.nearestvertex(pi) # Compute Euclidean distance (gradient stopped for spatial term) spatialdist = sum((vi[j] - pi[j])2 for j in range(3)) 0.5 # Compute squared L2 distance between skinning weights weightdiffsq = sum((wg[k] - wv[k])2 for k in range(24)) # Compute loss term: ReLU(weightdiffsq - tauskn spatialdist) lossterm = weightdiffsq - tauskn spatialdist lossterm = lossterm if lossterm > 0 else 0.0 totalloss += lossterm return totalloss A variant that regularizes a forward LBS network directly in canonical space. It samples 1024 points on the canonical SMPL surface and minimizes the L1 distance between the network's output skinning weights and the ground-truth SMPL skinning weights for 24 bones. The loss is averaged over the sampled points. Formula: LS = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{\hat{x} \in \hat{X}S, w \in W} \sum{i=1}^{24} | f{\sigma\omega}(\hat{x})i - wi |, where |P|=1024. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. Originated in "Human Gaussian Splatting: Real-Time Rendering of Animatable Avatars" (CVPR 2024). It was introduced to address the issue that training on a limited amount of gestures leads to skinning weights that do not generalize well. The method softly supervises Gaussian skinning weights with SMPL skinning weights based on proximity. name: Total Variation Loss
head: TVLoss
body: Total Variation (TV) Loss is a regularization constraint applied to explicit feature volumes or bilateral grid parameters to enforce spatial smoothness in learned color transformations. It differs from photometric reconstruction losses by penalizing high-frequency variations in the latent representation rather than matching pixel intensities. It is typically combined with other regularization terms, such as Eikonal loss, within the total training objective. The method computes the sum of squared differences between adjacent elements along the spatial dimensions of a tensor representing the bilateral grid or feature volume, normalized by the number of neighboring pairs and the batch size. Input: A 4D tensor x of shape (B, C, H, W), where B is the batch size, C is the number of channels (or appearance groups), H is the height, and W is the width of the bilateral grid. Output: A scalar loss value L{TV}. The input tensor x is a PyTorch tensor. The bilateral grid itself is initialized with dimensions determined by configuration parameters: gridx (width), gridy (height), and gridw (depth/channels). The grid is indexed by appearance IDs. tvlossweight (or TVLossweight): Weight multiplier for the loss. Default value is 10.0 in some implementations, or 1.0 in others. config.bilgridtvlossmult: Weight multiplier applied to the bilateral grid TV loss term before summing across grids. batchsize (B): Number of samples in the batch. height (H or hx): Spatial height dimension. width (W or wx): Spatial width dimension. channels (C): Number of channels or appearance groups. The total variation loss for a tensor x is defined as: L{TV} = \frac{2 \cdot TVLoss\weight}{B} \left( \frac{\sum{b,c,j,k} (x{b,c,j+1,k} - x{b,c,j,k})^2}{Nh} + \frac{\sum{b,c,j,k} (x{b,c,j,k+1} - x{b,c,j,k})^2}{Nw} \right) Where: B is the batch size. Nh = C \times (H-1) \times W is the count of horizontal neighbor pairs. Nw = C \times H \times (W-1) is the count of vertical neighbor pairs. The factor of 2 arises from the specific implementation in, which sums horizontal and vertical components and multiplies by 2 before dividing by batch size. Note that describes a more general formulation summing over all spatial dimensions i from 2 to D, normalized by Ni, but provides the specific 2D spatial implementation used in the bilateral grid context. 1. Extract Dimensions: Determine batch size B, height H, and width W from the input tensor x. 2. Calculate Counts: Compute Nh = C \times (H-1) \times W. Compute Nw = C \times H \times (W-1). 3. Compute Horizontal Variation: If Nh > 0, calculate the squared difference between adjacent elements along the height dimension: diffh = (x[:,:, 1:,:] - x[:,:,:H-1,:])^2. Sum the squared elements of diffh and divide by Nh to get h{tv}. 4. Compute Vertical Variation: If Nw > 0, calculate the squared difference between adjacent elements along the width dimension: diffw = (x[:,:,:, 1:] - x[:,:,:,:W-1])^2. Sum the squared elements of diffw and divide by Nw to get w{tv}. 5. Aggregate: Sum h{tv} and w{tv}. 6. Normalize and Weight: Multiply the sum by 2 \cdot TVLoss\weight and divide by B. 7. Grid Summation: If multiple bilateral grids exist, iterate over each grid, compute its TV loss, multiply by config.bilgridtvlossmult, and sum the results. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def totalvariationloss(x, tvlossweight=1.0): """ Computes the Total Variation loss for a 4D tensor x. Args: x (torch.Tensor): Input tensor of shape (B, C, H, W). tvlossweight (float): Weight multiplier for the loss. Returns: torch.Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ batchsize = x.size(0) hx = x.size(2) wx = x.size(3) c = x.size(1) # Spatial normalization counts (excluding batch dimension) counth = c (hx - 1) wx countw = c hx (wx - 1) total = 0.0 # Horizontal TV if counth > 0: htv = torch.pow(x[:,:, 1:,:] - x[:,:,:hx-1,:], 2).sum() / counth total += htv # Vertical TV if countw > 0: wtv = torch.pow(x[:,:,:, 1:] - x[:,:,:,:wx-1], 2).sum() / countw total += wtv # Final loss calculation as per loss = tvlossweight 2.0 total / batchsize return loss Zero Dimensions: If H=1 or W=1, the corresponding count (Nh or Nw) becomes 0. The implementation must check for this to avoid division by zero. Batch Size: The loss is normalized by batch size, so it remains independent of the batch size magnitude. Precision: Squaring differences can lead to large values if the grid parameters are not normalized. Ensure inputs are in a reasonable range. Defines how TV loss weight is configured alongside other losses. It sets apart TV loss by allowing independent scaling relative to photometric or Eikonal terms. Choose it when balancing smoothness against reconstruction fidelity. Another regularization term often used in conjunction with TV loss. It enforces geometric consistency using sparse depth measurements rather than spatial smoothness. Choose it when depth priors are available. Alternative regularization method using adversarial training. It differs by operating in the image domain to enforce perceptual realism rather than latent smoothness. Choose it when training GAN-based radiance fields. Details on setting the tvlossweight parameter. It governs the trade-off between regularization strength and optimization stability. Choose it when tuning hyperparameters for specific scene complexities. Primary reconstruction loss, distinct from TV regularization. It minimizes pixel-wise differences between rendered and ground truth images. Choose it as the core objective, with TV loss as a secondary constraint. Implementation details for various loss functions. It covers framework-specific optimizations and memory layouts. Choose it when integrating TV loss into custom training loops. Gradient-based regularization for radiance fields. It enforces unit gradient magnitude along rays rather than spatial smoothness. Choose it when optimizing implicit neural representations. Consistency loss for feature volumes. It enforces agreement between multi-view feature representations. Choose it when training view-consistent explicit volumes. Aggregation of all loss components including TV loss. It combines reconstruction, regularization, and consistency terms into a single scalar. Choose it as the final optimization target. Time Complexity: O(B \cdot C \cdot H \cdot W), as it requires a single pass over the spatial dimensions to compute differences. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot C \cdot H \cdot W) for storing the input tensor and intermediate difference tensors. Strengths: Effectively smooths out noise in learned feature volumes and bilateral grids, preventing overfitting to high-frequency artifacts. Limitations: May oversmooth fine details if the weight is too high. Computationally inexpensive but adds to the overall training time. When to Use: When training models with explicit feature volumes or bilateral grids that are prone to noise. When Not to Use: When preserving high-frequency details is critical and the model is not overfitting. Total Variation Loss is applied as a constraint to explicit feature volumes to enforce smoothness, following previous works in radiance field optimization. In the context of volume rendering and radiance fields, it has been adopted to enforce smoothness in explicit feature volumes and bilateral grids. It is commonly used in conjunction with other losses such as photometric loss and Eikonal loss. The specific implementation for bilateral grids in Gaussian Splatting variants is detailed in recent open-source projects. name: Discriminator Loss with Gradient Penalty
head: GP Loss, Gradient Penalty Loss, R1 Gradient Penalty, Simple Gradient Penalty (R1), Learned Self-Supervision (Discriminator), RaLSGAN discriminator
body: A regularization loss for training the discriminator in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that enforces Lipschitz continuity by penalizing the gradient norm of the discriminator's output with respect to its input. It distinguishes itself from weight clipping or spectral normalization methods by using an explicit penalty term on the gradients of real samples, specifically stabilizing training in radiance-field optimization contexts like GANeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Real image patches x{\text{real}}, fake image patches x{\text{fake}}, discriminator network D, gradient penalty multiplier gplossmult. Outputs: Scalar discriminator loss value. Data Structures: Tensors are 4D: [N, C, H, W] representing batch size, channels, height, and width. Gradients are computed with respect to the input tensor x{\text{real}}. Steps: 1. Real Prediction: Set x{\text{real}} to require gradients, then pass real patches through the discriminator to obtain predictions pred{\text{real}} = D(x{\text{real}}). 2. Fake Prediction: Pass detached fake patches through the discriminator to obtain predictions pred{\text{fake}} = D(x{\text{fake}}). Detachment prevents gradient flow from the fake path into the discriminator during the penalty calculation. 3. Gradient Penalty Calculation: Compute the gradients of the sum of predictions with respect to the input: g = \nabla{x{\text{real}}} pred{\text{real}}. Calculate the R1 penalty as the mean of the squared gradient norms across spatial dimensions: r1{\text{penalty}} = \text{mean}(\sum g^2, \text{dim}=[1,2,3]). Normalize by 2: \text{gradient\penalty} = r1{\text{penalty}} / 2. 4. Loss Computation: Compute real loss using softplus: loss{d\real} = \text{mean}(\text{softplus}(-pred{\text{real}})). Compute fake loss using softplus: loss{d\fake} = \text{mean}(\text{softplus}(pred{\text{fake}})). Sum the real and fake losses to get the total discriminator loss: total\loss = loss{d\real} + loss{d\fake} + \text{gp\loss\mult} \cdot \text{gradient\penalty}. Formulas: pred{\text{real}} = D(x{\text{real}}) pred{\text{fake}} = D(x{\text{fake}}) g = \nabla{x{\text{real}}} pred{\text{real}} r1{\text{penalty}} = \text{mean}\left(\sum{c,h,w} g{c,h,w}^2\right) \text{gradient\penalty} = r1{\text{penalty}} / 2 loss{d\real} = \text{mean}(\text{softplus}(-pred{\text{real}})) loss{d\fake} = \text{mean}(\text{softplus}(pred{\text{fake}})) total\loss = loss{d\real} + loss{d\fake} + \text{gp\loss\mult} \cdot \text{gradient\penalty} where x{\text{real}} and x{\text{fake}} are image patches, D is the discriminator network, g is the gradient tensor, and \text{softplus}(x) = \log(1 + e^x). Parameters: gplossmult: The multiplier for the gradient penalty term in the discriminator loss. Label l: Set to 1 when training the discriminator, and -1 when using it as a loss to optimize the density via \frac{\tilde{L}D(\rho, -1)}{\rho}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Detachment: Fake patches must be detached from the computation graph to ensure the gradient penalty is only applied to the real data path (R1 regularization). Softplus: The use of softplus implies a non-saturating GAN formulation, which helps prevent vanishing gradients for the discriminator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def discriminatorlosswithgradientpenalty( discriminator: torch.nn.Module, realpatches: torch.Tensor, fakepatches: torch.Tensor, gplossmult: float) -> torch.Tensor: """ Computes the discriminator loss with R1 gradient penalty. Args: discriminator: The discriminator network. realpatches: Tensor of real image patches [N, C, H, W]. fakepatches: Tensor of fake image patches [N, C, H, W]. gplossmult: Multiplier for the gradient penalty term. Returns: Total discriminator loss. """ # 1. Run discriminator on real patches realpatches.requiresgrad(True) predreal = discriminator(realpatches) # 2. Run discriminator on detached fake patches predfake = discriminator(fakepatches.detach()) # 3. Compute gradient penalty using real patches # Compute gradients of the sum of predictions with respect to the input gradoutput = torch.oneslike(predreal) gradients = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=predreal.sum(), inputs=realpatches, gradoutputs=gradoutput, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] # Compute r1penalty: mean(sum(gradients^2, dim=[1,2,3])) r1penalty = torch.sum(gradients 2, dim=[1, 2, 3]).mean() # gradientpenalty = r1penalty / 2 gradientpenalty = r1penalty / 2.0 # 4. Compute losses # lossdreal = mean(softplus(-predreal)) lossdreal = F.softplus(-predreal).mean() # lossdfake = mean(softplus(predfake)) lossdfake = F.softplus(predfake).mean() # 5. Sum the real and fake losses to get the total discriminator loss totalloss = lossdreal + lossdfake + gplossmult gradientpenalty return totalloss This loss function defines the adversarial objective for training a generator and discriminator pair, specifically designed to stabilize training in generative adversarial networks (GANs) by combining a non-saturating logistic loss with an R1 gradient penalty. It builds on Discriminator Loss with Gradient Penalty by specifying the exact non-saturating formulation and the R1 regularization term, which penalizes the gradient norm of the discriminator's output with respect to its input rather than enforcing a strict Lipschitz constraint via weight clipping or spectral normalization. Strengths: Stabilizes GAN training by enforcing Lipschitz continuity without weight clipping. Limitations: Extending the discriminator to the temporal domain via a triplet of inputs yields no benefits because transport priors already constrain physicality. The method originates from implementations like GANeRF, which applies GAN techniques to neural radiance fields. It is also used in fluid reconstruction to train a fully convolutional neural network discriminator that distinguishes between real reference images and reconstructed smoke images. The R1 gradient penalty is a standard technique in GAN literature for enforcing Lipschitz continuity. barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Global Transport for Fluid Reconstruction with Learned Self-Supervision, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00168, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Non-saturating GAN Loss with R1 Regularization
head: Non-saturating GAN Loss, R1 Regularized GAN Loss
body:
This loss function defines the adversarial objective for training a generator and discriminator pair in a generative adversarial framework. It builds on Discriminator Loss with Gradient Penalty by specifying the exact non-saturating formulation and the R1 regularization term. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathbf{z}: Latent vector sampled from prior p{	heta}. \xi: Conditioning variable (e.g., camera pose) sampled from p{\xi}. I: Real image sampled from the training data distribution p{	heta D}. G{	heta G}: Generator network with parameters 	hetaG. D{	heta D}: Discriminator network with parameters 	hetaD. \lambda: Scalar hyperparameter for the R1 penalty weight. Outputs: \mathcal{L}(	heta, \phi): The total loss value, where 	heta and \phi represent the generator and discriminator parameters respectively. The generator minimizes \mathcal{L}(	heta, \phi) and the discriminator maximizes \mathcal{L}(	heta, \phi). Data Structures: The discriminator D{	heta D} takes an image tensor as input and outputs a scalar logit. The generator G{	heta G} takes latent vector \mathbf{z} and condition \xi as input and outputs a synthetic image. Steps: 1. Sample a batch of latent vectors \mathbf{z} from p{	heta} and conditioning variables \xi from p{\xi}. 2. Generate synthetic images G{	heta G}(\mathbf{z}, \xi) using the generator. 3. Sample a batch of real images I from the training data distribution p{	heta D}. 4. Compute the discriminator's output for synthetic images: D{fake} = D{	heta D}(G{	heta G}(\mathbf{z}, \xi)). 5. Compute the discriminator's output for real images: D{real} = D{	heta D}(I). 6. Compute the gradient of the discriminator's output with respect to the real images: 
ablaI D{	heta D}(I). 7. Compute the R1 penalty term: \lambda |
ablaI D{	heta D}(I)|^2. 8. Compute the non-saturating loss terms: f(D{fake}) and f(-D{real}) using f(u) = -\log(1 + \exp(-u)). 9. Combine terms to form the total loss \mathcal{L}(	heta, \phi) as per the formula. 10. Update generator parameters to minimize \mathcal{L}(	heta, \phi). 11. Update discriminator parameters to maximize \mathcal{L}(	heta, \phi). Formulas: The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}(	heta, \phi) = \mathbf{E}{\mathbf{z} \sim p{	heta}, \xi \sim p{\xi}} [f(D{	heta D}(G{	heta G}(\mathbf{z}, \xi)))] + \mathbf{E}{\mathbf{I} \sim p{	heta D}} [f(-D{	heta D}(I)) + \lambda |
abla D{	heta D}(I)|^2] where the activation function f(u) is the non-saturating logistic loss: f(u) = -\log(1 + \exp(-u)) The term |
abla D{	heta D}(I)|^2 denotes the squared Euclidean norm of the gradient of the discriminator's output with respect to the input image I. Specifically, if y = D{	heta D}(I), then 
abla D{	heta D}(I) =  rac{\partial y}{\partial I}. Parameters: \lambda: The weight for the R1 penalty. Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Adam. Adam hyperparameters:  eta1 = 0,  eta2 = 0.9. Initial learning rates: 5 	imes 10^{-5} for the generator, 4 	imes 10^{-4} for the discriminator. Final learning rates (after decay): 1 	imes 10^{-5} for the generator, 1 	imes 10^{-4} for the discriminator. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Computation: The R1 penalty requires computing second-order derivatives (gradient of the gradient). This can be computationally expensive and memory-intensive. Ensure creategraph=True is used in torch.autograd.grad. Numerical Stability: The function f(u) = -\log(1 + \exp(-u)) can suffer from numerical instability for large positive or negative u. In practice, use torch.nn.functional.softplus(-u) or a stable log-sum-exp implementation. Learning Rate Decay: The sources specify a decay from initial to final learning rates but do not specify the decay schedule (e.g., linear, exponential, step). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def nonsaturatingganlosswithr1( generator: nn.Module, discriminator: nn.Module, latentsampler, datasampler, lambdar1: float, optimizerg: optim.Optimizer, optimizerd: optim.Optimizer, numsteps: int = 1): for in range(numsteps): # 1. Sample inputs z, xi = latentsampler() Ireal = datasampler() # 2. Generate fake images Ifake = generator(z, xi) # 3. Compute discriminator outputs Dfake = discriminator(Ifake) Dreal = discriminator(Ireal) # 4. Compute R1 penalty (requires second-order derivatives) Ireal.requiresgrad(True) gradoutput = torch.oneslike(Dreal) gradients = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=Dreal, inputs=Ireal, gradoutputs=gradoutput, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] r1penalty = torch.mean(torch.sum(gradients 2, dim=list(range(1, gradients.dim())))) # 5. Compute non-saturating loss terms f = lambda u: -torch.log(1 + torch.exp(-u)) lossfake = torch.mean(f(Dfake)) lossreal = torch.mean(f(-Dreal)) # 6. Combine into total loss L(theta, phi) losstotal = lossfake + lossreal + lambdar1 r1penalty # 7. Update generator (minimize L) optimizerg.zerograd() losstotal.backward() optimizerg.step() # 8. Update discriminator (maximize L, implemented as minimize -L) optimizerd.zerograd() (-losstotal).backward() optimizerd.step() The total training loss for the GSN model, combining the non-saturating GAN loss, R1 gradient penalty, and discriminator reconstruction objective. The R1 regularization technique itself was previously proposed by Mescheder et al. in "Which Training Methods for GANs do actually Works?" (ICML 2018). name: GSN Training Loss
head: GSN Total Loss
body:
The GSN Training Loss is the composite objective function used to train the Generative Scene Network (GSN) model, combining a non-saturating GAN loss, an R1 gradient penalty, and a discriminator reconstruction objective. It differs from standard GAN formulations by explicitly regularizing the discriminator via gradient penalties and reconstruction errors to restrict overfitting and encourage learning of features that provide a useful training signal for the generator. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: z \sim pz: Latent code sampled from the prior distribution. T \sim pT: Pose parameter sampled from the pose distribution. X \in \mathbb{R}^{4 	imes w 	imes h}: Real RGB-D sample from the true scene distribution pS. Outputs: Scalar loss value L(	heta, \phi, \omega) to be minimized. Data Structures: Generator G	heta: Maps (z, T) to synthetic RGB-D images. Discriminator D\phi: Maps RGB-D images to logits. Decoder C\omega: Maps discriminator outputs back to RGB-D images. Parameters: 	heta (generator), \phi (discriminator), \omega (decoder). Formulas: The total loss is defined as: L(	heta, \phi, \omega) = \mathbb{E}{z \sim pz, T \sim pT} [h(D\phi(G	heta(z, T)))] + \mathbb{E}{X \sim pS} \left[ h(-D\phi(X)) + \lambda{R1} |
abla D\phi(X)|^2 + \lambda{Recon} |X - C\omega(D\phi(X))|^2 ight] Where: h(u) = -\log(1 + \exp(-u)) is the non-saturating GAN loss function. \lambda{R1} is the weight for the R1 gradient penalty term. \lambda{Recon} is the weight for the discriminator reconstruction penalty term. |
abla D\phi(X)|^2 denotes the squared gradient norm of the discriminator output with respect to the input X. | \cdot |^2 denotes the squared L2 norm (MSE). Parameters: \lambda{R1}: Weight for R1 gradient penalty. Typical value not specified in the sources, but used in ablation studies. \lambda{Recon}: Weight for reconstruction penalty. Typical value not specified in the sources, but used in ablation studies. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample a batch of latent codes z from pz and poses T from pT. 2. Generate synthetic RGB-D samples G{fake} = G	heta(z, T) using the generator. 3. Sample real RGB-D samples X from the dataset distribution pS. 4. Compute the generator expectation term: Compute discriminator logits for generated samples: D{fake} = D\phi(G{fake}). Apply non-saturating loss: L{gen} = h(D{fake}). 5. Compute the discriminator expectation terms: Compute discriminator logits for real samples: D{real} = D\phi(X). Apply non-saturating loss for real samples: L{real\adv} = h(-D{real}). Compute R1 gradient penalty: Compute gradient of discriminator output w.r.t input: 
ablaX D\phi(X). Compute squared norm: R1 = |
ablaX D\phi(X)|^2. Scale by \lambda{R1}. Compute reconstruction penalty: Pass real samples through discriminator: F = D\phi(X). Decode features back to image: \hat{X} = C\omega(F). Compute MSE: Recon = |X - \hat{X}|^2. Scale by \lambda{Recon}. Sum discriminator terms: L{disc} = L{real\adv} + \lambda{R1} R1 + \lambda{Recon} Recon. 6. Compute the total loss L by summing the generator expectation term and the discriminator expectation terms exactly as defined in the formula. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def gsntrainingloss(Gtheta, Dphi, Comega, z, T, X, lambdaR1, lambdaRecon): """ Computes the GSN total training loss. Args: Gtheta: Generator network parameterized by theta. Dphi: Discriminator network parameterized by phi. Comega: Decoder network parameterized by omega. z: Latent codes. T: Poses. X: Real RGB-D samples, shape (batchsize, 4, w, h). lambdaR1: Weight for R1 gradient penalty. lambdaRecon: Weight for reconstruction penalty. Returns: totalloss: Scalar tensor representing the expected loss. """ # 1. Generate fake samples Gfake = Gtheta(z, T) # 2. Discriminator outputs Dfake = Dphi(Gfake) Dreal = Dphi(X) # 3. Non-saturating GAN loss function h(u) = -log(1 + exp(-u)) # Implemented stably as softplus(-u) def h(u): return F.softplus(-u) # Generator loss term (expectation over batch) lossgen = h(Dfake).mean() # Discriminator loss terms # Adversarial term for real samples (expectation over batch) lossrealadv = h(-Dreal).mean() # R1 Gradient Penalty gradDreal = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=Dreal.sum(), inputs=X, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] # Squared gradient norm per sample, averaged over batch for expectation gradnorm = gradDreal.pow(2).sum(dim=[1, 2, 3]).mean() lossr1 = lambdaR1 gradnorm # Reconstruction Penalty Xrecon = Comega(Dreal) lossrecon = lambdaRecon F.mseloss(Xrecon, X) # Total Loss totalloss = lossgen + lossrealadv + lossr1 + lossrecon return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Decoder Input Shape: The formula C\omega(D\phi(X)) implies the decoder takes the discriminator's output directly as input. Implementation must ensure C\omega maps the discriminator's output dimension to the input shape \mathbb{R}^{4 	imes w 	imes h}. Gradient Penalty Computation: The R1 penalty requires computing gradients of the discriminator with respect to its input X. The computational graph must be preserved via creategraph=True during the backward pass to enable second-order derivatives. Numerical Stability: The function h(u) = -\log(1 + \exp(-u)) can overflow for large negative u; use torch.nn.functional.softplus(-u) or clamp inputs. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The R1 gradient penalty restricts the discriminator from overfitting, while the reconstruction objective encourages it to learn relevant features about the input that provide a useful training signal for the generator. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The GSN Training Loss was introduced in the paper "Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields". It builds upon the non-saturating GAN loss, the R1 gradient penalty, and the discriminator reconstruction objective. The method is used in the context of generating unconstrained 3D scenes using locally conditioned radiance fields. The additional regularization terms restrict the discriminator from overfitting while encouraging it to learn relevant features about the input that will provide a useful training signal for the generator. name: Background Blending for Loss Computation
head: Loss Computation Background Blending
body: This method blends the predicted RGB image with a resolved background color for accurate loss computation, particularly when the background is not black. It resolves the background configuration (e.g., 'lastsample', 'random', or explicit) and applies alpha-compositing to both the predicted and ground truth images before loss evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Predicted RGB image (C{\text{pred}}), accumulated opacity (\alpha{\text{acc}}), ground truth RGB image (C{\text{gt}}), and background color configuration. Output: Blended predicted RGB (C{\text{blend}}) and blended ground truth RGB (C{\text{gt,blend}}) for loss computation. Data Structures: RGB images are tensors of shape (H, W, 3) with floating-point values in [0, 1]. Accumulation is a tensor of shape (H, W) or (H, W, 1) representing ray opacity. Steps: 1. Resolve backgroundcolor from the configuration. If the configuration is 'lastsample', set backgroundcolor to black (0, 0, 0), which disables background blending for the ground truth. 2. If the configuration is 'random', generate a random tensor of the same shape as C{\text{pred}} to serve as backgroundcolor. 3. Otherwise, use the explicitly provided backgroundcolor tensor. 4. Compute the transmittance to the background as T = 1.0 - \alpha{\text{acc}}. 5. Blend the predicted image: C{\text{blend}} = C{\text{pred}} + T \times C{\text{bg}}. 6. Blend the ground truth image using the same resolved background color: C{\text{gt,blend}} = C{\text{gt}} + T \times C{\text{bg}}. 7. Pass C{\text{blend}}, \alpha{\text{acc}}, and C{\text{gt,blend}} to the renderer's loss computation routine. Formula: C{\text{blend}} = C{\text{pred}} + (1 - \alpha{\text{acc}}) \times C{\text{bg}} where C{\text{bg}} is the resolved background color tensor. Parameters: backgroundcolorconfig: Controls resolution; typical values are 'lastsample', 'random', or a (3,)/(H, W, 3) tensor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \alpha{\text{acc}} \approx 1, T \approx 0 and the background contribution vanishes. If \alpha{\text{acc}} \approx 0, T \approx 1 and the output equals C{\text{bg}}. Degenerate inputs (e.g., negative accumulation) must be clamped to [0, 1] before blending to prevent invalid transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def blendbackgroundforlosscomputation(predictedrgb: np.ndarray, accumulation: np.ndarray, groundtruthrgb: np.ndarray, backgroundcolorconfig) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """ Blends predicted and ground truth RGB images with a resolved background color for loss computation. Args: predictedrgb: Array of shape (H, W, 3), predicted volume color. accumulation: Array of shape (H, W) or (H, W, 1), accumulated opacity. groundtruthrgb: Array of shape (H, W, 3), ground truth image. backgroundcolorconfig: String ('lastsample', 'random') or array for background color. Returns: blendedrgb: Array of shape (H, W, 3), blended predicted color. blendedgt: Array of shape (H, W, 3), blended ground truth color. """ # Clamp accumulation to valid range alpha = np.clip(accumulation, 0.0, 1.0) # Compute transmittance transmittance = 1.0 - alpha # Resolve background color if backgroundcolorconfig == "lastsample": backgroundcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) elif backgroundcolorconfig == "random": backgroundcolor = np.random.rand(predictedrgb.shape) else: backgroundcolor = np.asarray(backgroundcolorconfig) # Broadcast backgroundcolor to (H, W, 3) if it is a single color if backgroundcolor.ndim == 1: backgroundcolor = backgroundcolor[np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] # Apply alpha-compositing blending blendedrgb = predictedrgb + transmittance[..., np.newaxis] backgroundcolor blendedgt = groundtruthrgb + transmittance[..., np.newaxis] backgroundcolor return blendedrgb, blendedgt The Composite Loss is the primary optimization objective used in NeO 360 to train dedicated near and far background MLPs for few-shot novel-view synthesis. It addresses the problem of accurately modeling outdoor backgrounds where the background is not black, by combining a pixel-wise L2 color loss, a distortion regularization term, and a perceptual LPIPS loss. It differs from standard volumetric alpha-compositing losses by explicitly enforcing sparsity in the background MLP weights to ensure efficient rendering and distinct background geometry, rather than merely blending colors. Computes the luminance value L of a reference style's average RGB color to serve as a background color for NNFM loss computation with VGG-16, ensuring the stylization matches the style's overall brightness. Normalize each component (R, G, B) of the selected style's average color to [0, 1]. Convert each normalized RGB component to linear scale by raising it to the power of 2.2: R{\text{lin}} = R^{2.2}, G{\text{lin}} = G^{2.2}, B{\text{lin}} = B^{2.2}. Compute luminance as L = 0.2126 \times R{\text{lin}} + 0.7152 \times G{\text{lin}} + 0.0722 \times B{\text{lin}}, where the coefficients reflect the average spectral sensitivity of human-perceived lighting. The computed L is used as the corresponding background color for each style rendering to match overall brightness. Time Complexity: O(H \times W) for the element-wise blending operation. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) for storing the blended images. Strengths: Ensures that loss computation is not biased by the background color, which is critical when the background is not black. Limitations: Requires correct background configuration; using 'random' may introduce variance, and 'lastsample' forces black backgrounds. Originated in differentiable rendering pipelines like nerfstudio and ganerf for photometric loss computation. Adapted in StyleRF-VolVis for style transfer to match overall brightness via luminance-based background calculation. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) StyleRF-VolVis: Style Transfer of Neural Radiance Fields for Expressive Volume Visualization., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2024.3456342, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Composite Loss for Radiance Fields
head: Optimizing Radiance Fields for Few-Shot Novel-View Synthesis, Total Loss L
body: The Composite Loss is the primary optimization objective used in NeO 360 to train dedicated near and far background MLPs for few-shot novel-view synthesis. It addresses the problem of accurately modeling outdoor backgrounds where the background is not black, by combining a pixel-wise L2 color loss, a distortion regularization term, and a perceptual LPIPS loss. It differs from standard volumetric alpha-compositing losses by explicitly enforcing sparsity in the background MLP weights to ensure efficient rendering and distinct background geometry, rather than merely blending colors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: cp: The composited background color for a pixel, obtained by volumetrically rendering and compositing outputs from the near background MLP (D{near}) and far background MLP (D{far}). \tilde{c}t: The target pixel color sampled from the ground truth image at the corresponding pixel location. \lambda{reg}: Weight for the regularization loss. \lambda{LPIPS}: Weight for the perceptual loss. t: Current training epoch. Outputs: L: The scalar total loss value used for backpropagation. Data Structures: MLPs: Two dedicated Multi-Layer Perceptrons, D{near} and D{far}, decode color (ci^p) and density (\sigmai^p) for background segments. Coordinates: Input coordinates are contracted (x', y', z') before conditioning the MLPs. Formulas: The total loss L is defined as: L = \left\| cp - \tilde{c}t \right\|2^2 + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambda{LPIPS} L{LPIPS} Where: \left\| cp - \tilde{c}t \right\|2^2 is the L2 color loss between the composited color and the target color. L{reg} is the distortion regularization loss. L{LPIPS} is the perceptual similarity loss between patches of rendered color cp and ground truth color \tilde{c}t. Parameters: \lambda{reg}: Not given in the sources. \lambda{LPIPS}: Not given in the sources. LPIPS Activation Threshold: The LPIPS loss is only enforced after 30 training epochs. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Background: For each ray, sample points in the near and far background regions. Use contracted coordinates (x', y', z') to condition the dedicated near background MLP D{near} and far background MLP D{far}. 2. Decode Properties: Decode color ci^p and density \sigmai^p for each sample point from the respective MLPs. 3. Composite Color: Perform volumetric rendering and compositing of the near and far background segments to obtain the final composited background color cp for the pixel. 4. Compute L2 Loss: Calculate the squared L2 norm between the composited color cp and the target pixel color \tilde{c}t. 5. Compute Regularization Loss: Calculate the distortion regularization loss L{reg}. This encourages sparsity in the weights of the near and far background MLPs for efficient rendering. 6. Compute Perceptual Loss: Calculate the LPIPS loss L{LPIPS} between cp and \tilde{c}t. 7. Apply Conditional Weighting: If the current training epoch t < 30, set the weight for L{LPIPS} to 0 (or exclude the term) to improve background modeling stability. 8. Aggregate Loss: Compute the total loss L using the formula above. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecompositeloss(cp, ct, epoch, lambdareg, lambdalpips): """ Computes the composite loss for background radiance fields. Args: cp: Composited background color tensor (H, W, 3). ct: Target ground truth color tensor (H, W, 3). epoch: Current training epoch (int). lambdareg: Weight for distortion regularization (float). lambdalpips: Weight for LPIPS loss (float). Returns: L: Total scalar loss. """ # 1. L2 Color Loss l2loss = torch.sum((cp - ct) 2) # 2. Distortion Regularization Loss # Note: The specific implementation of Lreg depends on the distortion regularization method [3]. # It is applied to the weights of the near and far background MLPs. lreg = computedistortionregularizationloss() # 3. LPIPS Loss # Enforced only after 30 epochs to improve background modeling if epoch >= 30: llpips = computelpipsloss(cp, ct) else: llpips = torch.tensor(0.0) # 4. Total Loss L = l2loss + lambdareg lreg + lambdalpips llpips return L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Training Instability: Applying LPIPS loss too early can hinder background modeling; it must be disabled for the first 30 epochs. Background Color Assumption: This method is specifically designed for cases where the background is not black, requiring explicit modeling via near/far MLPs rather than assuming a default background color. Coordinate Contraction: Input coordinates must be contracted before conditioning the MLPs to handle the unbounded nature of outdoor scenes. Treats surface candidates as binary existence choices rather than volumetric opacities, minimizing the weighted sum of color losses for the candidate and background surfaces to promote distinct surface geometry. Unlike standard volumetric alpha-compositing which blends colors and can result in blended, non-binary surfaces, this method blends losses, forcing the optimizer to select the single surface (candidate or background) that minimizes the color difference. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Encourages sparsity in background MLP weights for efficient rendering; improves perceptual similarity of rendered backgrounds; handles non-black backgrounds effectively. Limitations: Requires dedicated MLPs for near and far backgrounds; LPIPS loss adds computational overhead and is only active after 30 epochs. When to Use: Few-shot novel-view synthesis of outdoor scenes where background modeling is critical and source views are sparse. When Not to Use: When the background is known to be black or simple, or when computational resources are extremely limited and MLP sparsity is not required. The Composite Loss was introduced in the NeO 360 paper for optimizing radiance fields for few-shot novel-view synthesis of outdoor scenes. It builds on the need to accurately model complex outdoor backgrounds that cannot be assumed to be black, using dedicated MLPs for near and far background regions. The method incorporates distortion regularization [3] to encourage sparsity and LPIPS loss for perceptual quality, with a specific training schedule for the perceptual loss.
