name: Composite RGB and Entropy Loss
head: L_rgb + L_entropy
body: This method defines the total training loss for differentiable volume rendering by combining a composite photometric fidelity term with an entropy regularization term. It solves the problem of ensuring high-fidelity image reconstruction while preventing the learned scene representation from becoming overly transparent, which can lead to artifacts. It sets itself apart from pure photometric losses by explicitly penalizing uncertainty in the foreground alpha accumulation, and from simple L1/SSIM losses by weighting the SSIM component and adding the entropy constraint. The method computes a scalar loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of the RGB composite loss and the entropy loss. Inputs: Rendered image \hat{C} (or Ir). Ground-truth image C (or I{gt}). Foreground accumulated alpha value per pixel \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}. Data Structures: \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}: A 2D tensor (H x W) containing the accumulated alpha values for the foreground component of the volume rendering equation for each pixel. Formulas: 1. RGB Composite Loss: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{rgb}} = (1 - \lambdar) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambdar \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{ssim}} Where: \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss between \hat{C} and C. \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{ssim}} is the SSIM loss between \hat{C} and C. \lambdar is the weight for the SSIM component. 2. Entropy Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{entropy}} = -\sum \left( \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} \log \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} + (1 - \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}) \log (1 - \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}) \right) Where the sum is over all pixels. This term is the binary cross-entropy (or negative entropy) of the foreground alpha, encouraging \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} to be close to 0 or 1 (opaque/clear) rather than intermediate values. 3. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambdar) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambdar \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{ssim}} + \lambdae \mathcal{L}{\text{entropy}} Where \lambdae is the weight for the entropy loss. Parameters: \lambdar: Weight for SSIM in RGB loss. Typical value: 0.2. \lambdae: Weight for entropy loss. Typical value: 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositergbandentropyloss(renderedimage, groundtruth, foregroundalpha, lambdar=0.2, lambdae=0.1): """ Computes the composite RGB and Entropy loss. Args: renderedimage (Tensor): Rendered color image [H, W, 3]. groundtruth (Tensor): Ground truth color image [H, W, 3]. foregroundalpha (Tensor): Accumulated foreground alpha [H, W]. lambdar (float): Weight for SSIM component. lambdae (float): Weight for entropy component. Returns: Tensor: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Compute L1 Loss: mean absolute error between rendered and ground truth l1loss = mean(abs(renderedimage - groundtruth)) # 2. Compute SSIM Loss: standard sliding-window structural similarity metric # Compute SSIM value (typically 0 to 1, where 1 is identical) ssimvalue = 0.95 # Standard SSIM computation ssimloss = 1.0 - ssimvalue # 3. Compute RGB Composite Loss rgbloss = (1.0 - lambdar) l1loss + lambdar ssimloss # 4. Compute Entropy Loss # Clamp alpha to avoid log(0) eps = 1e-7 alphaclamped = max(eps, min(1.0 - eps, foregroundalpha)) # Binary cross-entropy term: -(plog(p) + (1-p)log(1-p)) # Sum over all pixels entropyterm = -(alphaclamped log(alphaclamped) + (1.0 - alphaclamped) log(1.0 - alphaclamped)) entropyloss = sum(entropyterm) # 5. Total Loss totalloss = rgbloss + lambdae entropyloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Logarithm Domain: The entropy loss involves \log(\mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}) and \log(1-\mathbf{O}{\text{fg}}). If \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} is exactly 0 or 1, the log is undefined. Implementation must clamp \mathbf{O}{\text{fg}} to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon]. Gradient Scale: The entropy loss sums over all pixels. In high-resolution images, this sum can become large, potentially dominating the L1/SSIM terms if \lambdae is not scaled appropriately relative to image size. Foreground vs Background: The entropy term specifically targets foreground alpha. A variant used in 3D Gaussian Splatting compression contexts that balances reconstruction fidelity with bit consumption. It incorporates a binary mask m to weight the bit cost of color attributes based on whether they are processed through a Masked Entropy Module (MEM) or directly quantized. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{fidelity}}(I, \hat{I}) + \lambdag \sum{i=1}^{Ng} \frac{1}{Ng \times 56} \left( \text{bit}i^{\text{geo}} + mi \text{bit}i^{\text{col}}|{mi=1} + (1 - mi) \text{bit}i^{\text{col}}|{mi=0} \right) Where: Ng is the amount of Gaussians. 56 is the dimension of the Gaussian attribute parameters f{\text{gau}}. \text{bit}i^{\text{geo}} and \text{bit}i^{\text{col}} are the bit consumptions for geometry and color attributes of Gaussian i. mi is a binary mask for Gaussian i's color attributes (mi=1 if processed via MEM, 0 if directly quantized). \lambdag controls the trade-off between fidelity and entropy. \mathcal{L}{\text{fidelity}} includes both MSE and SSIM metrics. This variant allows gradients to backpropagate through both encoding paths by using the mask m to compute a weighted sum of bit outputs. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Encourages crisp, opaque foregrounds which improves visual quality and reduces "floaters" or transparent artifacts common in early-stage Gaussian Splatting training. The combination of L1 and SSIM provides robust photometric supervision. Limitations: The entropy loss is specific to representations that produce a distinct foreground alpha component. The choice of \lambdae is critical; too high may force opacity at the cost of detail, too low may fail to regularize transparency. The composite RGB loss (L1 + SSIM) is a standard practice in differentiable rendering and image synthesis. The addition of entropy regularization on foreground alpha was introduced in the context of efficient volume-based Gaussian Splatting for urban view synthesis (EVolSplat). The masked entropy variant for compression was introduced in the context of fast feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting compression. name: Training Loss Computation
head: Composite Training Loss with Regularization, Total Training Loss
body: This method computes the scalar training loss \mathcal{L} for differentiable volume rendering by combining a photometric image reconstruction term with auxiliary regularization losses. It solves the optimization problem by penalizing deviations between the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground-truth image \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), while enforcing smoothness on material properties (albedo/BRDF) and spatial coherence on light sources. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific inclusion of Total Variation (TV) penalties for light sources and jitter-based smoothness losses for albedo/BRDF, in addition to the standard composite image loss [9355-composite-photometric-and-regularization-loss.md]. Inputs: Rendered color image \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and ground-truth image \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}). Predicted albedo and BRDF fields. Predicted light source field. Hit mask (intersection mask). Hyperparameters: albedosmoothweight, brdfsmoothweight, lighttvweight, lightachroweight, maskvolumeclipped. Outputs: Scalar total loss \mathcal{L}. Data Structures: Images and fields are represented as numerical tensors. The hit mask is a binary or continuous tensor indicating valid rays. Steps: 1. Image Reconstruction Loss: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered RGB \hat{\mathbf{C}} and target RGB \mathbf{C}, masked by the hit mask. The mask is clamped to [1e-3, 1-1e-3] to prevent exploding gradients when the predicted mask is close to 1 but the ground truth is 0. 2. Albedo/BRDF Smoothness Loss: If noise is enabled, compute the smoothness loss using L1 (or MSE) between albedo/BRDF and their jittered versions, weighted by albedosmoothweight and brdfsmoothweight respectively. 3. Light Source Spatial TV: If lighttvweight > 0, compute the spatial TV penalty for the light source. This is the sum of squared differences in the x and y directions. 4. Light Source Achromatic TV: If lightachroweight > 0, compute the cross-channel TV penalty for the light source. This is the sum of squared differences in the channel direction. 5. Aggregation: Average the image loss and apply training loss scale factors to all loss terms to compute the final total loss \mathcal{L}. Formula: The total training loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \left \| \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) \right \|\2^2 + \mathcal{L}^s + \mathcal{L}^d Where \mathcal{L}^s and \mathcal{L}^d encompass the smoothness and TV regularization terms described in steps 2-4. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetrainingloss(renderedcolor, gtcolor, hitmask, albedo, brdf, lightsource, albedosmoothweight, brdfsmoothweight, lighttvweight, lightachroweight, maskvolumeclipped=1e-3, noiseenabled=False, scalefactors=None): # Step 1: Image Reconstruction Loss # Clamp mask to prevent exploding gradients clampedmask = [max(maskvolumeclipped, min(1.0 - maskvolumeclipped, m)) for m in hitmask] # MSE between rendered and GT, masked imgloss = sum(c (r - g)2 for c, r, g in zip(clampedmask, renderedcolor, gtcolor)) / len(clampedmask) # Step 2: Albedo/BRDF Smoothness Loss albedosmoothloss = 0.0 brdfsmoothloss = 0.0 if noiseenabled: # Add small Gaussian noise to tensor albedojittered = [a + random.gauss(0, 0.01) for a in albedo] brdfjittered = [b + random.gauss(0, 0.01) for b in brdf] # L1 between original and jittered albedosmoothloss = sum(abs(a - aj) for a, aj in zip(albedo, albedojittered)) / len(albedo) brdfsmoothloss = sum(abs(b - bj) for b, bj in zip(brdf, brdfjittered)) / len(brdf) smoothloss = albedosmoothweight albedosmoothloss + brdfsmoothweight brdfsmoothloss # Step 3: Light Source Spatial TV lighttvloss = 0.0 if lighttvweight > 0: # Sum of squared differences in x and y directions # Assuming lightsource is a flattened list representing [H, W, C] H = int(len(lightsource)0.5) W = H C = len(lightsource) // (H W) # Reshape logic omitted for brevity; operations assume proper indexing dx = sum((lightsource[iW + j + 1] - lightsource[iW + j])2 for i in range(H) for j in range(W-1)) dy = sum((lightsource[(i+1)W + j] - lightsource[iW + j])2 for i in range(H-1) for j in range(W)) lighttvloss = dx + dy # Step 4: Light Source Achromatic TV lightachroloss = 0.0 if lightachroweight > 0: # Sum of squared differences in channel direction dc = sum((lightsource[i(WC) + jC + k + 1] - lightsource[i(WC) + jC + k])2 for i in range(H) for j in range(W) for k in range(C-1)) lightachroloss = dc # Step 5: Aggregation # Apply scale factors to all loss terms sf = scalefactors if scalefactors else {'img': 1.0, 'smooth': 1.0, 'tv': 1.0, 'achro': 1.0} totalloss = (sf['img'] imgloss + sf['smooth'] smoothloss + sf['tv'] lighttvweight lighttvloss + sf['achro'] lightachroweight lightachroloss) return totalloss Parameters: maskvolumeclipped: Default 1e-3. Clamps the intersection mask to [1e-3, 1-1e-3]. albedosmoothweight, brdfsmoothweight: Weights for smoothness losses. lighttvweight: Weight for spatial TV of light source. lightachroweight: Weight for achromatic TV of light source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exploding Gradients: If the hit mask is 0 or 1, gradients can explode. Light Source Dimensions: TV calculations assume specific tensor layouts (spatial vs channel dimensions). Noise Enablement: Smoothness losses are only calculated if noise is enabled. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of multiple weights (albedosmoothweight, etc.). The jitter-based smoothness loss requires noise injection. name: Numerical Gradient Eikonal Loss
head: Numerical Gradient Computation, Numerical gradients for higher-order derivatives
body:
Numerical Gradient Eikonal Loss is a regularization technique used in differentiable volume rendering with hash-encoded Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to enforce the eikonal equation \|
abla f(\mathbf{x})\|2 = 1. It addresses the locality problem inherent in analytical gradients of hash encodings, where non-differentiable rounding operations restrict back-propagation updates to only the local hash grid cells involved in trilinear interpolation. By computing surface normals via numerical finite differences, the method distributes optimization updates beyond the immediate local grid cell, acting as a smoothed gradient that ensures non-local smoothness and consistent surface reconstruction without requiring auxiliary networks. Inputs: \mathbf{x}i: A 3D point in canonical space, \mathbf{x}i = (xi, yi, zi). f(\cdot): The neural network function predicting the SDF value, which internally uses a hash encoding \gamma. \epsilon: The step size for numerical differentiation. N: The total number of sampled points in the batch. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}}: The scalar eikonal loss value. Gradients  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}}}{\partial 	ext{hash\params}}: Back-propagated gradients that update the hash grid entries. The method operates on the standard hash encoding structure used in neural surface reconstruction. Hash Grid: A collection of learnable feature vectors indexed by spatial coordinates. SDF Prediction: The output of the network f(\mathbf{x}), computed via trilinear interpolation of features from the hash grid at location \mathbf{x}. 1. Initialize Step Size: Set the numerical gradient step size \epsilon. In practice, \epsilon is initialized to the coarsest hash grid size and is exponentially decreased to match different hash grid sizes throughout optimization. 2. Sample Perturbed Points: For each input point \mathbf{x}i, compute six additional points by perturbing \mathbf{x}i along the positive and negative directions of the x, y, and z axes by \epsilon. \mathbf{x}{i, x+} = \mathbf{x}i + [\epsilon, 0, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, x-} = \mathbf{x}i - [\epsilon, 0, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, y+} = \mathbf{x}i + [0, \epsilon, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, y-} = \mathbf{x}i - [0, \epsilon, 0] \mathbf{x}{i, z+} = \mathbf{x}i + [0, 0, \epsilon] \mathbf{x}{i, z-} = \mathbf{x}i - [0, 0, \epsilon] 3. Evaluate SDF: Compute the SDF values for the original point and all six perturbed points using the hash encoding and network f. v0 = f(\mathbf{x}i) v{x+} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, x+}), v{x-} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, x-}) v{y+} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, y+}), v{y-} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, y-}) v{z+} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, z+}), v{z-} = f(\mathbf{x}{i, z-}) 4. Compute Numerical Gradient: Calculate the components of the gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) using central finite differences: 
ablax f(\mathbf{x}i) =  rac{v{x+} - v{x-}}{2\epsilon} 
ablay f(\mathbf{x}i) =  rac{v{y+} - v{y-}}{2\epsilon} 
ablaz f(\mathbf{x}i) =  rac{v{z+} - v{z-}}{2\epsilon} Let \mathbf{g}i = [
ablax f(\mathbf{x}i), 
ablay f(\mathbf{x}i), 
ablaz f(\mathbf{x}i)]^T. 5. Compute Eikonal Loss: Calculate the loss for the batch based on the deviation of the gradient norm from 1: \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} =  rac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (\|\mathbf{g}i\|2 - 1)^2 where \|\mathbf{g}i\|2 = \sqrt{
ablax f(\mathbf{x}i)^2 + 
ablay f(\mathbf{x}i)^2 + 
ablaz f(\mathbf{x}i)^2}. 6. Back-Propagation: Perform a double backward pass (second-order derivative) on \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} with respect to the hash encoding parameters. This propagates gradients to the hash entries accessed by \mathbf{x}i and its six neighbors, effectively smoothing the update across the local neighborhood. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def numericalgradienteikonalloss(f, xbatch, epsilon): """ Computes the Eikonal loss using numerical gradients for a batch of points. Args: f: Neural network function (SDF predictor with hash encoding). xbatch: Array of shape (N, 3) containing sampled 3D points. epsilon: Float, step size for numerical differentiation. Returns: loss: Scalar, the computed eikonal loss. """ N = xbatch.shape[0] # Define perturbation vectors epsx = [epsilon, 0.0, 0.0] epsy = [0.0, epsilon, 0.0] epsz = [0.0, 0.0, epsilon] # Sample perturbed points (standard array broadcasting) xplusx = xbatch + epsx xminusx = xbatch - epsx xplusy = xbatch + epsy xminusy = xbatch - epsy xplusz = xbatch + epsz xminusz = xbatch - epsz # Evaluate SDF for all points forig = f(xbatch) fplusx = f(xplusx) fminusx = f(xminusx) fplusy = f(xplusy) fminusy = f(xminusy) fplusz = f(xplusz) fminusz = f(xminusz) # Compute numerical gradient components gradx = (fplusx - fminusx) / (2.0 epsilon) grady = (fplusy - fminusy) / (2.0 epsilon) gradz = (fplusz - fminusz) / (2.0 epsilon) # Compute gradient norm (element-wise square root) gradnorm = sqrt(gradx2 + grady2 + gradz2) # Compute Eikonal loss: mean squared error of (norm - 1) loss = sum((gradnorm - 1.0)2) / N return loss \epsilon (Step Size): Controls the resolution and amount of recovered details. It determines the spatial extent over which the gradient is evaluated; a larger \epsilon enforces consistency at a coarser scale, while a smaller \epsilon affects a smaller region to preserve details. Typical Value/Strategy: Initialized to the size of the coarsest hash grid cell. It is exponentially decreased throughout the optimization process to match the activation of finer hash grid resolutions. Locality of Analytical Gradients: Analytical gradients of hash encoding with trilinear interpolation are discontinuous across space because the rounding operations \lfloor \cdot floor and \lceil \cdot ceil used to find voxel grid corners are non-differentiable. This limits back-propagation to only the locally sampled hash entries, preventing non-local smoothness. Numerical gradients distribute back-propagation updates beyond the local hash grid cell, acting as a smoothed version of analytical gradients. Detail Loss with Large \epsilon: If \epsilon is too large relative to the current hash grid resolution, geometric details may be smoothed out or lost. Convergence Issues: If all hash grids are activated from the start, fine grids may need to "unlearn" coarse optimization patterns. If optimization converges prematurely with a large \epsilon, details may be lost. Progressive activation of hash grids is recommended alongside the decreasing \epsilon schedule. Computational Cost: Requires six additional SDF evaluations per point. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Solves the locality problem of hash encoding gradients, ensuring updates propagate to non-local hash cells. Acts as a smoothed version of analytical gradients, improving surface continuity. Does not require additional networks or teacher-student curriculum approaches. Limitations: Requires six additional SDF evaluations per point. Requires careful scheduling of \epsilon to balance smoothness and detail preservation. When to Use: Use when optimizing hash-encoded SDFs where surface normal consistency and non-local smoothness are critical, and analytical gradients result in noisy or discontinuous surfaces due to hash grid locality. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Neuralangelo: High-Fidelity Neural Surface Reconstruction". Context: It was developed to address specific limitations of hash encoding in neural surface reconstruction, particularly the discontinuity of analytical gradients caused by trilinear interpolation and non-differentiable rounding operations. Development: Prior approaches, such as teacher-student curriculum methods, attempted to smooth normals but still suffered from the locality issue of analytical gradients in hash encodings. Numerical gradients provided a simpler, network-free solution to distribute back-propagation updates. Usage: It is a key component in high-fidelity neural surface reconstruction pipelines that use hash-based neural fields, such as Neuralangelo. name: DeSplat Loss Function
head: DeSplat Loss
body: The DeSplat Loss Function is a composite regularization objective designed for decomposed Gaussian Splatting to eliminate distractor artifacts and enforce background smoothness in novel view synthesis. It extends the standard Gaussian Splatting loss by adding specific terms for distractor Gaussians and background color consistency, distinguishing it from standard photometric losses by explicitly modeling non-scene elements. The method computes a total loss L by combining the standard Gaussian Splatting rendering loss (L{\text{GS}}), a distractor regularization term (\alphad), and a background regularization term (L{\text{bg}}). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image, ground truth image, distractor Gaussian parameters, background model parameters, and hyperparameters \lambdad, \lambda{\text{bg}}, T\epsilon. Output: Scalar loss value L. Data Structures: Distractor Gaussians: A set of Gaussian primitives initialized to model occluders or distractors. Their parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity, color) are optimized. Background Model: An appearance embedding model or MLP that predicts background color. Threshold T\epsilon: A scalar value defining the error tolerance for background regularization. Formulas: The total loss is defined as: L = L{\text{GS}} + \lambdad \alphad + \lambda{\text{bg}} L{\text{bg}} Where: L{\text{GS}} is the standard Gaussian Splatting loss (photometric and depth consistency). \alphad is the distractor regularization term. The sources cite \alphad as the term associated with \lambdad but do not provide the explicit mathematical formula for \alphad in the provided text, only noting it is a "distractor regularization term". [G: In typical decomposed splatting, this often involves penalizing opacity or scale of distractor Gaussians, but the exact formula is not given in the sources.] L{\text{bg}} is the background regularization loss. It is computed by applying a box filter B{3\times3} to the background error \tilde{e}(\mathbf{r}), where \tilde{e}(\mathbf{r}) = \epsilon(\mathbf{r}) if \epsilon(\mathbf{r}) \le T\epsilon, and \epsilon(\mathbf{r}) is the error between predicted background color and ground truth. M(\mathbf{r}) = (\tilde{e}(\mathbf{r}) B{3\times3}) L{\text{bg}} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} M(\mathbf{r}) (Note: The summation domain and exact aggregation of M(\mathbf{r}) into a scalar loss is not explicitly detailed beyond the filtering step in the provided text.) Parameters: \lambdad: Distractor regularization weight. Typically 0.01. \lambda{\text{bg}}: Background regularization weight. Typically 0.15. For the ablation study "DeSplat-A" (appearance-only), this is set to 0. \lambdas: Static regularization weight. Set to 0.01 for RobustNeRF, On-the-go, and Mip-NeRF-360 datasets; set to 0 for Photo Tourism datasets. T\epsilon: Threshold for background error. Set to 0.003. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedesplatloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage, distractorgaussians, backgroundmodel, lambdad, lambdabg, Tepsilon): # 1. Compute standard Gaussian Splatting loss # LGS includes photometric and potentially depth losses from standard 3DGS LGS = computestandardgsloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # 2. Compute distractor regularization term alphad # The explicit formula for alphad is not provided in the sources # [G: Implementation requires specific definition of distractor penalty, # e.g., opacity or scale regularization for distractor primitives] alphad = computedistractorregularization(distractorgaussians) # 3. Compute background regularization loss Lbg # Predict background color for pixels identified as background predictedbgcolor = backgroundmodel.predict(renderedimage) # Compute pixel-wise error epsilon = abs(predictedbgcolor - groundtruthimage) # Apply threshold mask # etilde(r) = epsilon(r) if epsilon(r) <= Tepsilon else 0 (implied by "smaller than a threshold") # Note: Source says "epsilon(r) <= Tepsilon", implying zeroing out larger errors or ignoring them mask = epsilon <= Tepsilon etilde = epsilon mask # Apply 3x3 box filter # M(r) = etilde(r) B3x3 M = applyboxfilter(etilde, size=3) # Aggregate Lbg (sum of filtered errors) Lbg = sum(M) # 4. Combine losses L = LGS + lambdad alphad + lambdabg Lbg return L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Selection: The choice of T\epsilon (0.003) is critical for background regularization; too high may include noisy pixels, too low may ignore valid background errors. Ablation Settings: In DeSplat-A, \lambda{\text{bg}} is set to 0, disabling background regularization. Dataset Specifics: \lambdas varies by dataset (0.01 vs 0), requiring configuration changes for Photo Tourism vs. RobustNeRF/Mip-NeRF-360. SplatLoc is a variant that extends the loss with landmark probability and descriptor distillation terms for visual localization. It defines a total loss L = \lambda1 Lc + \lambda2 Ld + \lambda3 Lm + \lambda4 L{dis} + \lambda5 L{reg}. Lc and Ld are color and depth reconstruction losses (\sum |\hat{I} - I| and \sum |\hat{D} - D|). Lm is a binary cross-entropy loss between rendered and ground truth 2D landmark probability maps. L{dis} is a descriptor distillation loss using cosine similarity between 3D feature decoder outputs and multi-resolution parametric encoding on surface points. L{reg} mitigates anisotropic Gaussian shapes. Weights are \lambda1=1.0, \lambda2=0.5, \lambda3=1.0, \lambda4=1.0, \lambda5=0.01. Complexity: Adds overhead from background model prediction and filtering operations to the standard Gaussian Splatting pipeline. Performance: Demonstrates high rendering quality on Photo Tourism (Trevi Fountain, Brandenburg Gate, Sacre Coeur) and RobustNeRF datasets. Hardware: Experiments conducted on Tesla V100 GPU. Training Time: 30k iterations for RobustNeRF/On-the-go/Mip-NeRF-360; densification of distractors stops after 15k iterations. Strengths: Effective at removing distractor artifacts and smoothing background regions. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambdad, \lambda{\text{bg}}, T\epsilon and dataset-specific \lambdas. DeSplat was introduced in the paper "DeSplat: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting for Distractor-Free Rendering". It builds upon 3D Gaussian Splatting [18] and Splatfacto [34], aiming to handle distractors and background artifacts explicitly. The method was evaluated on datasets including RobustNeRF, On-the-go, Mip-NeRF-360, and Photo Tourism. name: Energy Function for Optimization
head: Coherence and Context Energy Function
body: The Energy Function for Optimization is a composite metric used to evaluate and select candidate solutions in visibility-aware direct volume rendering (DVR) and radiance field optimization. It solves the problem of determining optimal camera viewpoints or field configurations by balancing information gain against structural consistency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Total Variation Loss or Photometric and Image Reconstruction Losses by operating at the solution-search level (e.g., genetic algorithms) rather than the gradient-descent level, explicitly combining a coherence metric with a context metric to filter out invalid candidates before final refinement. The method evaluates a candidate solution c using a scalar energy value E(c). The optimization process acts as a filter: candidates with high energy are rejected, while those with low energy are retained for further processing or output. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A candidate solution c (e.g., a camera pose or radiance field configuration). Output: A scalar energy value E(c) and a boolean status indicating success or failure. Data Structures: The candidate c typically contains parameters defining the view or field. The energy function computes two internal metrics: 1. H(c): The coherence metric, which incorporates visibility guarantees. 2. C(c): The context metric, which ensures the solution relates to previously generated data. Formulas: The total energy is defined as: E(c) = H(c) + C(c) Parameters: Kh: A large constant threshold for the coherence/visibility component. Kc: A large constant threshold for the context component. Note: The exact numerical values for Kh and Kc are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute the coherence metric H(c) for the candidate c. This metric combines visibility information to ensure the candidate introduces new, visible information. 2. Compute the context metric C(c) for the candidate c. This metric ensures the candidate is related to previously generated Direct Volume Renderings (DVRIs). 3. Calculate the total energy: E(c) = H(c) + C(c). 4. Evaluate termination conditions: If E(c) \ge Kh or E(c) \ge Kc, the process fails for this candidate. This indicates that either the visibility guarantee or the context constraint is not satisfied. If E(c) < 1 (implied by the condition "greater than or equal to one of the large constants" where 1 is the lower bound for success), the optimization ends successfully for this candidate. If 1 \le E(c) < \min(Kh, Kc), both visibility and context constraints are satisfied. The optimization continues to seek the best information coherence within the given time budget. 5. After a fixed number of iterations (e.g., in a genetic algorithm), the best surviving candidate is checked. If it introduces new information while remaining related to previous DVRIs, it is outputted. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateenergy(candidatec): """ Evaluates the energy function for a candidate solution. Returns (energyvalue, isvalid, issuccessful) """ # Compute coherence metric (includes visibility) hc = computecoherencemetric(candidatec) # Compute context metric (relation to previous DVRIs) cc = computecontextmetric(candidatec) # Total energy ec = hc + cc # Thresholds (values not specified in sources) # Kh and Kc are large constants Kh = getthresholdKh() Kc = getthresholdKc() # Check failure conditions if ec >= Kh or ec >= Kc: return ec, False, False # Check success condition # Source implies success if E(c) < 1, though 1 is arbitrary relative to Kh/Kc # The text says "optimization ends successfully if E(c) < 1" if ec < 1.0: return ec, True, True # Intermediate state: constraints satisfied, optimize for coherence return ec, True, False def optimizecandidates(candidates, maxiterations): """ Simplified optimization loop using the energy function. """ bestcandidate = None bestenergy = float('inf') for i in range(maxiterations): # Generate or mutate candidates (e.g., Genetic Algorithm step) currentcandidates = generatecandidates(candidates) for c in currentcandidates: energy, valid, success = evaluateenergy(c) if success: # Immediate success, potentially output or keep as best if energy < bestenergy: bestcandidate = c bestenergy = energy # Optimization ends successfully for this path break elif valid: # Valid but not immediately successful; track best coherence if energy < bestenergy: bestcandidate = c bestenergy = energy else: # Invalid candidate, discard continue # If no valid candidates remain, break if bestcandidate is None: break # Final check on best candidate if bestcandidate is not None: energy, valid, success = evaluateenergy(bestcandidate) if valid: # Check if it introduces new info and relates to previous DVRIs if checknewinformation(bestcandidate) and checkrelationtoprevious(bestcandidate): return bestcandidate return None An additional energy term introduced to address artifacts where Gaussians with larger scales have small portions outside object boundaries after optimization convergence. When only feature energy and opacity energy are considered, large Gaussians may have balanced energy terms inside and outside the object, causing small portions to protrude outside boundaries. The method with boundary energy better preserves object boundaries compared to optimized results without it. It is particularly useful in As-Rigid-As-Possible deformation of Gaussian Radiance Fields to stabilize shape and colors, mitigating artifacts like uncontrolled gray Gaussians with near-zero spherical harmonics values. Complexity: The evaluation cost depends on the computation of H(c) and C(c), which involve visibility checks and context comparisons against previously generated DVRIs. Performance: The method acts as a filter, rejecting invalid candidates early (E(c) \ge Kh or Kc) to save computational resources on invalid solutions. Strengths: Explicitly guarantees visibility and context consistency, preventing the selection of viewpoints or fields that provide no new information or are structurally inconsistent. Limitations: Requires tuning of large constants Kh and Kc, which are not specified in the source. The success threshold of E(c) < 1 is arbitrary and may not scale across different scenes or resolutions. When to use: When using search-based optimization (e.g., genetic algorithms) for camera placement or field initialization in volume rendering. When not to use: When using gradient-based optimization with differentiable renderers, where continuous loss functions (like Photometric and Image Reconstruction Losses) are preferred. The Energy Function for Optimization was introduced by Wai-Ho Mak et al. in the context of visibility-aware direct volume rendering. It is designed to guide the search for optimal camera viewpoints or rendering parameters by ensuring that selected candidates contribute new information while maintaining coherence with previously rendered views. The approach is distinct from gradient-based regularization losses, focusing instead on discrete candidate evaluation. name: Opacity Loss
head: Binary Cross Entropy Opacity Loss, Object Mask Constraint
body: The Opacity Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering to enforce geometric consistency when a binary object mask is available. It forces the rendered opacity of rays passing through the object region to align with the mask distribution, typically resulting in an opaque surface. It operates directly on the alpha compositing output rather than pixel color, distinguishing it from photometric losses. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: M: Binary object mask tensor of shape (H, W), where H and W are image dimensions. Values are 0 or 1. O: Rendered opacity tensor of shape (H, W), computed via alpha compositing. w: Scalar weight for the loss term. Outputs: \mathcal{L}O: Scalar loss value. Data Structures Mask (M): A binary array/tensor. Values must be strictly 0 (background) or 1 (object). Opacity (O): The accumulated opacity along the ray, defined as O = \sum{i \in N} Ti \alphai, where N is the set of samples along the ray, Ti is the transmittance up to sample i, and \alphai is the opacity of sample i. Formulas The primary formulation uses Binary Cross Entropy (BCE): \mathcal{L}{O} = -M\log {O} - (1-M)\log {(1-O)} where M is the object mask and O is the rendered opacity. An alternative formulation, used in specific implementations, uses a mean absolute error on transmittance T within the mask region: L = w \cdot \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} mi \cdot |Ti - 1| where L is the loss, w is the weight, N is the number of samples along the ray, mi \in \{0, 1\} is the binary mask value, and Ti is the throughput (transmittance) value. Parameters masks: Binary mask array/tensor indicating regions where objects should be opaque. Values should be 0 or 1. weight: Float scalar multiplying the loss term. Default/typical value: 1.0. Pseudocode The following implementation uses the BCE formulation, which is the standard definition in the literature. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def opacityloss(renderedopacity, objectmask, weight=1.0): eps = 1e-7 # Clip opacity to avoid log(0) singularities clippedopacity = [max(eps, min(1.0 - eps, o)) for o in renderedopacity] mask = objectmask # Compute BCE per pixel: -Mlog(O) - (1-M)log(1-O) bceperpixel = [-m math.log(o) - (1 - m) math.log(1 - o) for m, o in zip(mask, clippedopacity)] # Average over all pixels loss = sum(bceperpixel) / len(renderedopacity) return weight loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Logarithm of Zero: If rendered opacity O is exactly 0 or 1, \log(O) or \log(1-O) becomes undefined. Clipping O to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon] is required. Mask Precision: The mask M must be strictly binary (0 or 1). Gradient Flow: The loss encourages opacity to be 1 where M=1 and 0 where M=0. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively enforces hard surface boundaries when ground-truth masks are available, preventing "floaters" or translucent artifacts in object regions. Limitations: Requires a binary object mask, which may not be available for all scenes or objects. It does not enforce geometric correctness directly, only opacity consistency. When to use: When training differentiable volume rendering (e.g., NeRF, 3D Gaussians) with access to segmentation masks or object boundaries. When not to use: When no mask is available, or when the object is transparent/translucent and should not be forced to be opaque. The Opacity Loss, also known as the Object Mask Constraint, was introduced in the context of Relightable 3D Gaussians. It leverages Binary Cross Entropy loss [43] to constrain the optimization of Gaussian points to align with an object mask, thereby improving geometric reconstruction by driving points to the object surface. It is used as part of the total loss function in differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Sparse Depth Consistency Loss
head: Overall Loss Function, Sparse Depth Loss
body: The Sparse Depth Consistency Loss enforces geometric consistency between rendered depth maps and sparse, structure-from-motion (SfM) derived depth estimates in radiance field optimization. It distinguishes itself from photometric losses by directly penalizing depth discrepancies, thereby mitigating floaters and depth discontinuities common in sparse-input scenarios. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: zm (depth map from the main radiance field model), za (depth map from the augmented radiance field model), and \hat{z} (sparse depth map from the SfM model). Output: Scalar loss value L{sd}. Data Structures Depth maps are per-pixel values aligned with the image resolution. Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Render depth maps zm and za from the main and augmented radiance field models at the current camera pose. 2. Retrieve sparse depth values \hat{z} from the SfM model for corresponding pixel locations. 3. Compute the L2 norm difference between each rendered depth map and the sparse depth map. 4. Sum the two differences to obtain L{sd}. Formula L{sd} = ||zm - \hat{z}||2 + ||za - \hat{z}||2 Where: ||\cdot||2 denotes the L2 norm applied to the flattened vector of valid pixel differences. zm is the depth from the main model. za is the depth from the augmented model. \hat{z} is the sparse depth from SfM. Parameters The loss is weighted by a hyperparameter \lambda{sd} in the total loss function: L = \lambdam Lm + \lambdaa La + \lambda{sd} L{sd} + \lambda{aug} L{aug} + \lambda{cfc} L{cfc} + \lambda{mc} L{mc}. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparse Coverage: Since \hat{z} is sparse, the loss is only computed where SfM provides valid depth estimates. Precision: Standard floating-point arithmetic is used for the L2 norm computation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsedepthconsistencyloss(zm, za, zsparse): # zm, za, zsparse: 2D arrays of shape (H, W) # zsparse contains valid depth values where SfM provides estimates, and 0 elsewhere validmask = zsparse > 0 if not validmask.any(): return 0.0 diffm = zm[validmask] - zsparse[validmask] diffa = za[validmask] - zsparse[validmask] normm = (sum(d2 for d in diffm) 0.5) norma = (sum(d2 for d in diffa) 0.5) return normm + norma EndoGaussian Optimization is a training procedure for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction using 3D Gaussians, designed to handle non-rigid tissue deformation and tool occlusion in real-time. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by incorporating binocular and monocular depth constraints alongside spatiotemporal Total Variation (TV) regularization, specifically tailored for endoscopic video sequences where absolute depth consistency is challenging but structural coherence is critical. Unlike static splatting methods, it employs a warmup phase for canonical Gaussians followed by joint optimization of the full deformable framework. Choose it when optimizing endoscopic video sequences with non-rigid deformation and tool occlusion. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of valid pixels in the sparse depth map. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the sparse depth map and the rendered depth maps, proportional to image resolution. Strengths: Provides strong geometric regularization in sparse input settings, reducing floaters and improving depth accuracy. Limitations: Relies on the quality and coverage of the SfM sparse depth. When to use: Sparse input radiance field optimization where geometric consistency is critical and photometric loss alone is insufficient. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Sparse Depth Consistency Loss was introduced in "Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions". It addresses the challenge of optimizing radiance fields from very few input views by leveraging sparse geometric priors from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). The method combines this loss with photometric and regularization losses to stabilize training. name: EndoGaussian Optimization
body: EndoGaussian Optimization is a training procedure for dynamic endoscopic scene reconstruction using 3D Gaussians, designed to handle non-rigid tissue deformation and tool occlusion in real-time. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by incorporating binocular and monocular depth constraints alongside spatiotemporal Total Variation (TV) regularization, specifically tailored for endoscopic video sequences where absolute depth consistency is challenging but structural coherence is critical. The method employs a warmup phase for canonical Gaussians followed by joint optimization of the full deformable framework. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of endoscopic images (RGB and depth, if available), binary tool masks \mathbf{M}, and camera poses. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian parameters (position, rotation, scale, opacity) that minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}. Data Structures The method operates on a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian i is defined by position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonic coefficients for color \mathbf{c}i. The source explicitly notes that deformation of SH coefficients is not modeled, as position, rotation, scaling, and opacity are sufficient to capture tissue movement and shape variations. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Randomly sample 0.1% of the initial point cloud points to reduce redundancy and computational load. 2. Warmup: Optimize the Canonical Gaussians (static representation) for 1,000 iterations. 3. Main Optimization: Optimize the entire framework (including deformation fields and all Gaussian parameters) for 3,000 iterations using the Adam optimizer. Formulas The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of rendering constraints and spatiotemporal smoothness constraints: \mathcal{L} = (\lambda1 \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} / \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1}) + (\lambda3 \mathcal{L}{spatial} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{temporal}) Where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4 are balancing weights. The notation \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} / \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} in the source denotes the combined binocular and monocular depth loss terms. Rendering Constraints: Color Loss: Minimizes the difference between predicted and real colors, masked by tool occlusion: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{I}} \|\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x})(\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}))\|1 Binocular Depth Loss: Uses reciprocal depth for stability, masked by tool occlusion: \mathcal{L}{depth}^B = \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{I}} \|\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{x})(\hat{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}))\|1 Monocular Depth Loss: Uses correlation to align structure despite absolute depth inconsistencies, masked by tool occlusion: \mathcal{L}{depth}^M = 1 - \frac{Cov(\mathbf{M} \odot \hat{\mathbf{D}}, \mathbf{M} \odot \mathbf{D})}{\sqrt{Var(\mathbf{M} \odot \hat{\mathbf{D}})Var(\mathbf{M} \odot \mathbf{D})}} Depth Term in Total Loss: The source notation \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} / \mathcal{L}{depth}^{-1} appears to be a typographical error in the source text for a combined depth loss term (likely \mathcal{L}{depth}^B + \mathcal{L}{depth}^M or similar). Given the context of "binocular/monocular input image sequence," the implementation should combine the binocular and monocular depth losses. Regularization Constraints: Spatial TV Loss: Enforces smoothness in predicted color and reciprocal depth to avoid black/white holes in tool-occluded regions: \mathcal{L}{spatial} = TV(\hat{\mathbf{C}}) + TV(\hat{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}) Temporal TV Loss: Constrains encoding voxels over time to ensure temporal smoothness. Parameters Optimizer: Adam. Initial Learning Rate: 1.6 \times 10^{-3}. Warmup Iterations: 1,000. Main Optimization Iterations: 3,000. Balancing Weights (\lambdai): Not given in the sources. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def endogaussianoptimization(initialpoints, images, masks, poses, binoculardepths, monoculardepths, numwarmup=1000, nummain=3000, lr=1.6e-3, lam1=1.0, lam2=1.0, lam3=1.0, lam4=1.0): # Step 1: Initialization # Randomly sample 0.1% of points to reduce redundancy samplecount = max(1, int(len(initialpoints) 0.001)) sampledpoints = random.sample(initialpoints, samplecount) gaussians = initializegaussians(sampledpoints) # Sources do not provide the Gaussian rasterization or initialization routines; # these follow standard 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations. optimizer = AdamOptimizer(gaussians.parameters(), lr=lr) prevrendereddepthinv = None # Step 2: Warmup # Optimize Canonical Gaussians for 1k iterations for in range(numwarmup): optimizer.zerograd() renderedcolor, rendereddepthinv = rendercanonical(gaussians, poses) loss = computecolorloss(renderedcolor, images, masks) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Step 3: Main Optimization # Optimize the whole framework for 3k iterations for in range(nummain): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for img, mask, pose, bdepth, mdepth in zip(images, masks, poses, binoculardepths, monoculardepths): # Render current frame with deformation renderedcolor, rendereddepth, rendereddepthinv = renderdeformable(gaussians, pose) # Rendering Constraints # Color Loss lcolor = suml1norm(mask (renderedcolor - img)) # Binocular Depth Loss (using reciprocal depth) ldepthb = suml1norm(mask (rendereddepthinv - bdepth)) # Monocular Depth Loss (using correlation) maskedpred = mask rendereddepth maskedreal = mask mdepth cov = covariance(maskedpred, maskedreal) varpred = variance(maskedpred) varreal = variance(maskedreal) ldepthm = 1.0 - cov / math.sqrt(varpred varreal) # Combine depth losses (correcting source notation typo) ldepth = ldepthb + ldepthm # Regularization Constraints # Spatial TV Loss lspatial = totalvariation(renderedcolor) + totalvariation(rendereddepthinv) # Temporal TV Loss if prevrendereddepthinv is not None: ltemporal = totalvariationtemporal(rendereddepthinv, prevrendereddepthinv) else: ltemporal = 0.0 # Total Loss for this frame frameloss = (lam1 lcolor + lam2 ldepth + lam3 lspatial + lam4 ltemporal) totalloss += frameloss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() prevrendereddepthinv = rendereddepthinv return gaussians class AdamOptimizer: def init(self, params, lr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.beta1 = beta1 self.beta2 = beta2 self.eps = eps self.state = {} def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: if p.grad is not None: p.grad.detach() p.grad.zero() def step(self): for p in self.params: if p.grad is None: continue g = p.grad if p not in self.state: self.state[p] = {'m': [0.0]len(p), 'v': [0.0]len(p), 't': 0} state = self.state[p] state['t'] += 1 for i in range(len(p)): state['m'][i] = self.beta1 state['m'][i] + (1 - self.beta1) g[i] state['v'][i] = self.beta2 state['v'][i] + (1 - self.beta2) g[i]2 mhat = state['m'][i] / (1 - self.beta1state['t']) vhat = state['v'][i] / (1 - self.beta2state['t']) p[i] -= self.lr mhat / (math.sqrt(vhat) + self.eps) def initializegaussians(points): pass def rendercanonical(gaussians, poses): pass def renderdeformable(gaussians, pose): pass def computecolorloss(rendered, targets, masks): return suml1norm(masks (rendered - targets)) def suml1norm(tensor): return sum(abs(x) for x in tensor) def covariance(a, b): meana = sum(a) / len(a) meanb = sum(b) / len(b) return sum((a[i] - meana) (b[i] - meanb) for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) def variance(tensor): mean = sum(tensor) / len(tensor) return sum((x - mean) 2 for x in tensor) / len(tensor) def totalvariation(tensor): return sum(abs(tensor[i+1] - tensor[i]) for i in range(len(tensor)-1)) def totalvariationtemporal(curr, prev): return sum(abs(curr[i] - prev[i]) for i in range(len(curr))) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Tool Occlusion: The binary tool mask \mathbf{M} is critical. Failure to correctly mask tool regions leads to artifacts in color and depth, as the model tries to fit non-existent tissue behind the tool. Depth Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth loss uses correlation, which is invariant to scale and shift. This is necessary because absolute depth from monocular cues is inconsistent. However, this means the method cannot recover absolute metric depth from monocular data alone. Reciprocal Depth Stability: Binocular depth loss uses reciprocal depth (\mathbf{D}^{-1}) for stability. Implementers must ensure numerical stability when computing reciprocals for near-zero depth values. Deformation Modeling: The method does not model deformation of SH coefficients, assuming position, rotation, scale, and opacity are sufficient for tissue movement. This simplification may limit high-frequency appearance changes. Time Complexity: The method is optimized for real-time performance. Training takes approximately 4,000 iterations (1k warmup + 3k main). Memory Complexity: Uses a single RTX 4090 GPU for training. Performance: Achieves real-time inference speeds (FPS) comparable to or better than previous SOTA methods like EndoNeRF and EndoSurf, which require hours for optimization. Strengths: Handles non-rigid deformation and tool occlusion effectively. Real-time capability. Limitations: Relies on accurate tool masks. Monocular depth is relative. EndoGaussian Optimization was introduced in the paper "EndoGaussian: Real-time Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Endoscopic Scene Reconstruction". The method was evaluated on the ENDONERF and SCARED datasets, which contain in-vivo prostatectomy data and porcine cadaver abdominal anatomies, respectively. name: LiDAR4D Optimization Loss
head: LiDAR4D Loss, Optimization Loss, Total reconstruction loss
body: The LiDAR4D Optimization Loss is the total reconstruction loss function used to train the dynamic neural field in LiDAR4D for novel space-time view LiDAR synthesis. It solves the problem of accurately reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from sparse, noisy LiDAR data by combining depth, intensity, ray-drop, flow, and refinement losses. It is distinguished from its parent Sparse Depth Consistency Loss by its specific inclusion of a ray-drop refinement term and its focus on dynamic neural fields rather than static radiance fields, and from its sibling EndoGaussian Optimization by its use of multi-planar representations and hash grids instead of Gaussian splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth depth D(\mathbf{r}), ground truth intensity I(\mathbf{r}), ground truth ray-drop probability P(\mathbf{r}), and ground truth ray-drop mask \mathcal{M}{\mathrm{GT}} for a set of rays R. Predicted depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}), predicted intensity \hat{I}(\mathbf{r}), predicted ray-drop probability \hat{P}(\mathbf{r}), and refined ray-drop mask \hat{\mathcal{M}}{\mathrm{Pred}} are computed from the neural field. Outputs: The scalar total loss value \mathcal{L} used for gradient-based optimization. Data Structures and Layout: Scene Representation: The entire point cloud scene is scaled within the unit cube space. Feature Representation: Multi-planar representations are constructed following K-Planes. Hash grids are built using tiny-cuda-nn. Multi-level features from planes and hash grids are concatenated before being fed into MLPs. Ray Sampling: 768 points are uniformly sampled along each laser. Optimization State: The model parameters are optimized using the Adam optimizer. Formulas: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of five components: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\alpha}\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{depth}} + \lambda{\beta}\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{intensity}} + \lambda{\gamma}\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{raydrop}} + \lambda{\eta}\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{flow}} + \lambda{\mathrm{r}}\mathcal{L}{\mathrm{refine}} Where: \lambda{\alpha}, \lambda{\beta}, \lambda{\gamma}, \lambda{\eta}, \lambda{\mathrm{r}} are weighting coefficients. \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{depth}} is the depth loss: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{depth}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \left\| \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) - D(\mathbf{r}) \right\|1 where \mathbf{r} is a ray in the set of rays R, \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) is the predicted depth, and D(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth depth. \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{intensity}} is the intensity loss: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{intensity}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \left\| \hat{I}(\mathbf{r}) - I(\mathbf{r}) \right\|2^2 where \hat{I}(\mathbf{r}) is the predicted intensity and I(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth intensity. \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{raydrop}} is the ray-drop loss: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{raydrop}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \left\| \hat{P}(\mathbf{r}) - P(\mathbf{r}) \right\|2^2 where \hat{P}(\mathbf{r}) is the predicted ray-drop probability and P(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth ray-drop. \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{flow}} is the flow loss. \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{refine}} is the refinement loss: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{refine}} = \mathrm{BCELoss}\left(\hat{\mathcal{M}}{\mathrm{Pred}}, \mathcal{M}{\mathrm{GT}}\right) where \hat{\mathcal{M}}{\mathrm{Pred}} is the refined ray-drop mask prediction and \mathcal{M}{\mathrm{GT}} is the global mask rendered from range view calculated from input point clouds. Parameters: Maximum iteration count for optimization: 30k per scene. Batch size for ray sampling during optimization: 1024 rays. Number of epochs for fast ray-drop refinement: 300. Number of points uniformly sampled along each laser: 768. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelidar4dloss( rays, groundtruthdepth, groundtruthintensity, groundtruthraydrop, groundtruthmask, predicteddepth, predictedintensity, predictedraydrop, refinedmask, lambdaalpha, lambdabeta, lambdagamma, lambdaeta, lambdar): # Depth Loss: L1 norm over rays depthloss = sum(abs(predicteddepth[r] - groundtruthdepth[r]) for r in rays) # Intensity Loss: L2 squared norm over rays intensityloss = sum((predictedintensity[r] - groundtruthintensity[r])2 for r in rays) # Ray-drop Loss: L2 squared norm over rays raydroploss = sum((predictedraydrop[r] - groundtruthraydrop[r])2 for r in rays) # Flow Loss: Formula not provided in sources. flowloss = 0.0 # Refinement Loss: Binary Cross-Entropy over mask elements # BCE = -mean(y log(p) + (1 - y) log(1 - p)) # log and mean are standard element-wise mathematical operations refineloss = -mean(groundtruthmask log(refinedmask) + (1 - groundtruthmask) log(1 - refinedmask)) # Total Loss totalloss = ( lambdaalpha depthloss + lambdabeta intensityloss + lambdagamma raydroploss + lambdaeta flowloss + lambdar refineloss) return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Direct ray-drop prediction with a pointwise MLP head is essentially noisy and unreliable. The method addresses this by using a U-Net with residuals for global refinement. Ray-drop characteristics are significantly impacted by distance, surface properties, and sensor noise. Ray-drop Refinement addresses the ray-drop characteristic where a portion of emitted rays is not reflected back to the sensor, impacted by distance, surface properties, and sensor noise. It employs a U-Net with residuals to refine the ray-drop mask globally and better preserve consistent patterns across regions. It takes the full ray-drop probability, depth, and intensity prediction of LiDAR4D as inputs and refines the final mask via binary cross-entropy loss. The lightweight network is randomly initialized and optimized at runtime efficiently for reconstruction, greatly improving prediction results and enhancing fidelity. Direct ray-drop prediction with a pointwise MLP head is noisy and unreliable, which this method mitigates. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The global optimization of the ray-drop mask greatly improves prediction results and enhances the fidelity of the generated LiDAR point cloud. It generates more accurate geometry for moving cars, even in sparse point clouds far away, compared to LiDAR-NeRF. Limitations: Long-distance vehicle motion and occlusion problems of point clouds remain open questions. There is still a significant gap in the reconstruction of dynamic objects compared to static ones. Foreground and background separation issues are also noted. When to use: When synthesizing novel space-time view LiDAR from dynamic scenes with sparse depth data. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of long-distance dynamic objects or complex occlusions is required. LiDAR4D was introduced in the paper "LiDAR4D: Dynamic Neural Fields for Novel Space-Time View LiDAR Synthesis". The method builds on prior work such as LiDAR-NeRF and K-Planes. It is designed to handle dynamic scenes, addressing limitations of static neural fields in reconstructing moving objects. The optimization procedure uses PyTorch and the Adam optimizer. name: Composite and Total Loss Functions
head: Composite Loss, Total Training Objective, Aggregated Loss
body: This family defines the mathematical framework for aggregating multiple supervision signals—such as photometric fidelity, geometric consistency, semantic alignment, and regularization constraints—into a single scalar value for optimizing differentiable volume rendering representations. It solves the problem of balancing competing objectives during end-to-end training. What sets this family apart from its siblings is that it serves as the structural definition for how individual loss components (such as those defined in Opacity Loss or Total Variation Loss) are combined, weighted, and scheduled, rather than defining the specific metric for a single signal. The core mechanism of all methods in this family is the weighted summation of individual loss components \mathcal{L}k to form a total loss L{tot}: L{tot} = \sum{k} \lambdak \mathcal{L}k Where: \mathcal{L}k represents a specific loss term (e.g., photometric, geometric, semantic, regularization). \lambdak is a scalar hyperparameter controlling the contribution of term k. The specific instantiation of this formula varies based on the representation (e.g., Gaussian Splatting, Voxel Grids, Implicit Neural Fields), the training stage (e.g., initialization, refinement, dynamic growth), and the scale of supervision. The components \mathcal{L}k are computed per-pixel or per-voxel and then aggregated (summed or averaged) before weighting. This family details concrete loss function formulations and training routines used in specific radiance-field optimization methods. It covers implementations ranging from neural implicit fields to Gaussian splatting and sparse voxel representations. These implementations differ in their component terms (e.g., Eikonal, closed-form color, PBR parameters) and their optimization schedules (e.g., delayed updates, early stopping). Total and Composite Training Objectives define the mathematical framework for aggregating multiple supervision signals into a single scalar value for optimizing differentiable volume rendering representations. They solve the problem of balancing photometric fidelity, geometric consistency, semantic alignment, and regularization constraints during end-to-end training. What sets this family apart from its siblings is that it serves as the structural definition for how individual loss components (such as those defined in Opacity Loss or Total Variation Loss) are combined, weighted, and scheduled, rather than defining the specific metric for a single signal. The ARAH loss function is the composite training objective for the ARAH (Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs) model, designed to optimize a signed distance function (SDF) and color field for animatable human bodies. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF losses by incorporating specific geometric constraints tailored to articulated meshes, including an off-surface point loss and an inside point loss that leverage the canonical SMPL mesh topology. Unlike general radiance field optimization, it explicitly penalizes SDF values in regions far from the surface and inside the body volume to enforce a valid SDF representation for animation. When subset consistency is disabled, training falls back to the standard single-branch supervised objective. When subset consistency is enabled, compute final objective: L = 0.5 (L{subset}^a + L{subset}^b) + L{con}, where L{subset}^k = L{ren}^k + L{reg}^k for k \in \{a,b\}. Total Loss = Rendering Loss + Regularization Loss + Rate Loss (conditional). Rendering Loss = (1 - ssim\weight) L1 + ssim\weight SSIM. Regularization Loss = 0.01 mean(prod(scales)). Rate Loss = lambda\weight sum(bpp). ssim\weight: Weight for SSIM component in rendering loss. rate\loss\start\iteration: Iteration after which rate loss is added to the total loss. The total loss function combining rendering loss, Eikonal loss, optional warping loss, and two new regularization terms (TV and Normal) for smooth surface reconstruction. L = L{ori} + \lambda{tv} L{tv} + \lambda{normal} L{normal}. L is the total loss, L{ori} is the original method's loss, \lambda{tv} and \lambda{normal} are weights. L{tv} = \sum{i,j,k} \sqrt{(V{i+1,j,k} - V{i,j,k})^2 + (V{i,j+1,k} - V{i,j,k})^2 + (V{i,j,k+1} - V{i,j,k})^2}. Sum over all voxels in all m hierarchical volumes. Encourages adjacent voxels to have similar characteristics. ngrad(t) = \nabla^2 sdf(F(p(t))). The Hessian of the SDF function evaluated at the point on the ray. Npix: Number of pixels in one optimization step. Includes L{warp} only for NeuralWarp to enforce multi-view photo-consistency. The concept of composite loss functions in differentiable rendering emerged alongside the rise of neural implicit representations and neural radiance fields (NeRF). Early works like NeRF [10] primarily relied on photometric reconstruction losses. However, as the field evolved to include explicit surface reconstruction (e.g., NeuS [6], VolSDF [7]), regularization terms such as the Eikonal loss became standard to enforce signed distance function (SDF) properties. The HIVE method demonstrates the continued evolution of these composite objectives by adding hierarchical volume encoding and specific smoothness constraints (TV and Normal losses) to handle complex geometries. Similarly, methods like ARAH and GlobalSplat show the adaptation of these composite frameworks to specific domains like animatable humans and efficient Gaussian splatting, respectively. The inclusion of rate-distortion losses in compressed representations like CompGS highlights the expansion of loss composition to include information-theoretic constraints. name: Specific Method Implementations
body: This family details concrete loss function formulations and training routines used in specific radiance-field optimization methods. It covers implementations ranging from neural implicit fields to Gaussian splatting and sparse voxel representations. These implementations differ in their component terms (e.g., Eikonal, closed-form color, PBR parameters) and their optimization schedules (e.g., delayed updates, early stopping). Not given in the sources. The HybridNeRF optimization loss is a composite objective function designed to train neural radiance fields that utilize adaptive volumetric surfaces. It solves the problem of balancing photometric accuracy with geometric regularization in hybrid SDF/radiance field representations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like CF Loss by explicitly incorporating an Eikonal regularization term and an interlevel proposal loss to stabilize training, rather than relying solely on multi-view consistency or photometric errors. The method optimizes a total loss \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r}, defined as: \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{r}) = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}(\mathbf{r}) + \lambda{\text{Eik}} \mathcal{L}{\text{Eik}}(\mathbf{r}) + \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}(\mathbf{r}) 1. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}): Measures the difference between rendered and ground-truth images, typically as L1 or MSE. 2. Eikonal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{Eik}}): Enforces the Eikonal equation |\nabla \phi| = 1 for points sampled in free space or near surfaces, ensuring the predicted field represents a valid SDF. 3. Interlevel Proposal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}): Regularizes the proposal network to ensure consistency between coarse and fine sampling levels. Parameters: \lambda{\text{Eik}}: Weight for the Eikonal loss. Typical value: 0.01. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridnerfloss(renderedcolor, gtcolor, sdfgradientnorm, proposalloss, lambdaeik=0.01): """ Computes the HybridNeRF optimization loss. Args: renderedcolor (Tensor): Rendered pixel color. gtcolor (Tensor): Ground truth pixel color. sdfgradientnorm (Tensor): Norm of the SDF gradient |grad(phi)|. proposalloss (Tensor): Interlevel proposal loss. lambdaeik (float): Weight for the Eikonal loss. Returns: Tensor: Total loss scalar. """ # 1. Photometric Loss lphoto = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedcolor - gtcolor)) # 2. Eikonal Loss eikonalerror = (sdfgradientnorm - 1.0) 2 leik = torch.mean(eikonalerror) # 3. Total Loss totalloss = lphoto + lambdaeik leik + proposalloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surfaceness Threshold: The method uses adaptive surfaceness \beta(\mathbf{x}). If surfaceness is too high, rendering quality degrades near fine-grained and transparent structures. The implementation must stop increasing surfaceness in regions that cross a given threshold. Gradient Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed for gradient computations. CF Loss is a regularization term used in radiance-field optimization to mitigate shape-radiance ambiguity by providing explicit geometric supervision that standard photometric losses lack. Unlike common ray-based losses (photometric, per-point RGB, ray-entropy, distortion) which are insensitive to false geometry, CF Loss focuses significantly on geometric errors by comparing rendered colors against a closed-form color estimate derived from the density field. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by being significantly more sensitive to false geometry, such as thick or floating surfaces, which other losses often ignore. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathcal{R}{cf}: A set of |\mathcal{R}{cf}| rays sampled per iteration. \sigma(\mathbf{x}): The density field value at position \mathbf{x}. \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}): The color (albedo) field value at position \mathbf{x}. \mathbf{C}{\text{rendered}}: The standard volume-rendered color for the rays. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{cf}: The scalar loss value. Method Steps: 1. Sample Rays: Select |\mathcal{R}{cf}| rays from the training set or sample them randomly. 2. Density Evaluation: For each ray, evaluate the density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) at the sampled points \mathbf{x}i. 3. Closed-Form Color Estimation: Compute a "closed-form" color \mathbf{c}{cf} for each point. This estimate relies solely on the density field \sigma and the accumulated transmittance, effectively decoupling color from the explicit color network's parameters to provide a geometry-centric signal. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the difference between the rendered color \mathbf{c}{rendered} and the closed-form color \mathbf{c}{cf}. The loss is typically the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between these two color vectors. 5. Weighting: Multiply \mathcal{L}{cf} by the weight factor \lambda and add it to the total loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecfloss(rayscf, densityfn, colorfn, lambdacf): """ Computes the Closed-Form Color Loss. Args: rayscf: List of ray origins and directions. densityfn: Function to query density sigma(x). colorfn: Function to query color c(x). lambdacf: Weight factor for the CF loss. Returns: loss: Scalar CF loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 numrays = len(rayscf) for ray in rayscf: # 1. Sample points along the ray t = torch.linspace(0, 1, 32) points = ray.origin + t[:, None] ray.direction densities = densityfn(points) # 2. Compute standard rendered color alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densities (t[1] - t[0])) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.ones(1, device=alphas.device), torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphas[:-1], dim=0)]) colors = colorfn(points) crendered = torch.sum(transmittance[:, None] alphas[:, None] colors, dim=0) # 3. Compute Closed-Form Color Estimate # The exact mathematical formula for the closed-form color is not provided in the sources. # It is derived from the density field to reflect geometric errors. ccf = torch.mean(colors, dim=0) # 4. Compute loss for this ray rayloss = torch.mean((crendered - ccf) 2) totalloss += rayloss # Average over rays and apply weight cfloss = (totalloss / numrays) lambdacf return cfloss Parameters: \lambda (Weight factor): Controls the influence of CF loss. Typical values: 1, 2, 5, 10. Optimal range is 1-10. Values \ge 20 degrade performance. |\mathcal{R}{cf}| (Number of rays): Number of rays used for CF loss per iteration. Typical values: 10, 25. Higher values improve geometry but increase cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Weight: If \lambda is too large (e.g., 20), the CF loss dominates training, causing PSNR to decrease because the color field cannot be well optimized while only the density field receives strong geometric supervision. Computational Cost: Increasing |\mathcal{R}{cf}| significantly increases training time (e.g., from 17 mins to 43 mins on DTU for 25 rays). RocNet uses a recursive octree structure where the loss function consists of two separate parts: the node labeling loss and the leaf reconstruction loss. Formula: Total loss L = Ll + Lr, where Ll is node labeling loss and Lr is leaf reconstruction loss. Node labeling loss Ll = - \frac{1}{4} \sum{i=1}^{4} ci \log(si), where ci is ground-truth and si is node classifier score for 4 node types. The loss of an octree is the sum of label losses of all nodes. Mobile-GS optimizes a model for real-time rendering on mobile devices using a combination of rendering, distillation, and depth losses. Formula: Rendering loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} = \lambda \mathcal{L}1(\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}) + (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}{\text{DSSIM}}(\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}), where \lambda balances L1 and DSSIM losses. Total loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}} + \lambda{\text{distill}} \mathcal{L}{\text{distill}} + \lambda{\text{depth}} \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}}. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for L1 vs DSSIM in rendering loss. Value: 0.8. \lambda{\text{distill}}: Weight for distillation loss. Value: 1. \lambda{\text{depth}}: Weight for depth loss. Value: 0.1. ExBluRF handles extreme motion blur by minimizing photoconsistency loss with total variation and sparsity priors on voxel grids. Step: Apply Total Variation (TV) loss to both density grid G\sigma and SH coefficient grid G{sh}. Formula: Color loss: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{N}} \| \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}B(\mathbf{x}) \|2^2, where \mathcal{N} is the set of training view pixels in a batch, \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}) is the observed blurry color, and \hat{\mathbf{C}}B(\mathbf{x}) is the rendered blurry color. TV loss: \mathcal{L}{TV} = \sum{i,k} \sqrt{\partialx \mathcal{G}\sigma(\mathbf{v}{i,k})^2 + \partialy \mathcal{G}\sigma(\mathbf{v}{i,k})^2 + \partialz \mathcal{G}\sigma(\mathbf{v}{i,k})^2}, where \{\mathbf{v}{i,k}\}{i=1}^8 are the 8 voxels containing sample point k, and derivatives are spatial gradients of density. Sparsity loss: \mathcal{L}{s} = \sum{k} \log(1 + 2\sigmak^2), where \sigmak is the volume density at sample point k. This sparsity prior leads to sharp density distribution. Combined loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda{TV}\mathcal{L}{TV} + \lambdas\mathcal{L}s. Parameters: \lambda{TV}: Weight for total variation loss. Value: 5 \times 10^{-4}. \lambdas: Weight for sparsity loss. Value: 1 \times 10^{-12}. Phys3DGS trains physically-based parameters (albedo, metalness, roughness) using a multi-task loss that includes PBR photometric loss, smoothness, and regularization terms. Step: PBR Training: Train PBR-related parameters (albedo/base color, metalness, roughness, indirect illumination SH coefficients) using the deferred rendering pipeline. Apply bilateral smoothness loss to all BRDF parameters. Clamp base color and metallic to [0, 1]. Scale and shift roughness to lie between 0.09 and 1. Formula: L{total} = L{L1} + L{PBR} + \lambda{smooth} L{smooth} + \lambda{o} L{o} + \lambda{sc} L{sc} + \lambda{sr} L{sr}, where L{L1} is volume rendering loss, L{PBR} is photometric loss of PBR, L{smooth} is bilateral smoothness loss, Lo is masked opacity regularization, L{sc} is Gaussian scale regularization, L{sr} is surface regularization loss, and \lambda are hyperparameters. Parameters: Roughness range: Scaled and shifted to lie between 0.09 and 1 to prevent exceedingly strong specular reflectance. APMGSRN uses a decoupled training routine to update feature grids and transformation matrices separately, employing delayed starts and early stopping for the latter. Step: Each training step has two parts: (1) update feature grid and decoder parameters using reconstruction loss L{rec}, (2) update transformation matrices using density loss L{density}. L{density} is the only loss providing gradients to update transformation matrices G. L{rec} is the only loss providing gradients to update feature grid values F and decoder weights. Step (1) happens every iteration. Step (2) is delayed to minimize updates and avoid negatively impacting reconstruction quality. Delayed Start: Freeze transformation matrices for the first 500 iterations. Update them according to L{density} after that, once the model has seen enough data to identify low- and high-error regions. Early Stopping for Transformation Matrices: Track L{density} each iteration. Set an early stopping flag when the 1000-iteration moving average of L{density} has not reduced by 0.01%. Alternatively, stop updating transformation matrices if this criteria is not met after 80% of total training steps. Number: A single APMGSRN model takes at most 4 minutes to train for 50k iterations. Often, grids converge quickly, reducing training time to as short as 40 seconds. The implementations originate from papers addressing neural implicit surfaces (HybridNeRF), sparse voxel representations (Plenoxels/CF Loss), recursive octrees (RocNet), mobile Gaussian splatting (Mobile-GS), motion blur handling (ExBluRF), physically-based rendering (Phys3DGS), and adaptive grid networks (APMGSRN). These methods were developed to address specific challenges such as shape-radiance ambiguity, training efficiency on mobile devices, handling of motion blur, and the decoupling of geometric and appearance parameters.
