Eikonal Regularization # Sample 1024 points in [-1, 1]^3 numeik = 1024 xeik = torch.rand(numeik, 3) 2 - 1 # Uniform in [-1, 1] # Compute SDF gradient xeik.requiresgrad(True) sdfeik = sdfnetwork(xeik) gradeik = torch.autograd.grad( sdfeik, xeik, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(sdfeik), creategraph=True)[0] # LE = mean(| ||grad|| - 1 |) # Note: Source divides by |P| (N), not numeik le = torch.mean(torch.abs(torch.norm(gradeik, dim=1) - 1.0)) / N N # Simplified: just mean over eik points, then scaled? # Correction based on source formula: sum / |P|. # Since sum is over eik points, and divisor is |P|, we compute mean over eik points and divide by |P|? # No, source: (1/|P|) sum(...). # Implementation: sum over eik points, then divide by N. le = torch.sum(torch.abs(torch.norm(gradeik, dim=1) - 1.0)) / N # 3. Off-surface Point Loss # Sample 1024 points > 20cm from SMPL mesh # Note: Exact sampling method for Xoff is not detailed, assumed to be provided or sampled via rejection numoff = 1024 xoff = samplepointsfarfrommesh(smplmesh, numoff, mindist=0.20) # 20cm = 0.20m? Source says 20cm. Units in SDF network unknown. Assuming consistent units. sdfoff = sdfnetwork(xoff) # LO = (1/|P|) sum(exp(-100 sdf)) lo = torch.sum(torch.exp(-100.0 sdfoff)) / N # 4. Inside Point Loss # Sample 1024 points inside mesh, > 1cm from surface numin = 1024 xin = samplepointsinsidemesh(smplmesh, numin, mindist=0.01) # 1cm sdfin = sdfnetwork(xin) # LI = (1/|P|) sum(sigmoid(5000 sdf)) li = torch.sum(torch.sigmoid(5000.0 sdfin)) / N # 5. Skinning Loss # Formula not provided in source excerpt ls = 0.0 # Placeholder # Total Loss totalloss = ( lambdac lc + lambdae le + lambdao lo + lambdai li + lambdas ls) return totalloss Sampling Constraints: The sets \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{off}} and \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{in}} require distance queries to the canonical SMPL mesh. If the mesh topology changes or is invalid, these samples cannot be generated. Normalization: The source formulas divide the sums for \mathcal{L}E, \mathcal{L}O, \mathcal{L}I by |P| (number of pixels) rather than the number of sampled points (1024). This implies the magnitude of these geometric losses scales with the image resolution, which is non-standard for regularization terms. Units: The distance thresholds (20cm, 1cm) and constants (1e2, 5e3) assume a specific unit system for the SDF network. If the canonical space is normalized to [-1, 1]^3, these physical distances must be converted to canonical units. A regularization term that penalizes SDF values for points inside the canonical SMPL mesh to ensure they are negative and large in magnitude. It uses a sigmoid function scaled by 5000. It is chosen when a tight, watertight volume is required for the human body. A regularization term that penalizes SDF values for points far from the surface (outside the mesh) to ensure they are positive and large in magnitude. It uses an exponential decay function scaled by 100. It is chosen to prevent the SDF from being zero or negative far from the surface. A standard SDF regularization term enforcing that the gradient of the SDF has unit norm everywhere. It is sampled in the canonical bounding box [-1, 1]^3. It is chosen to ensure the SDF represents a valid distance function. Time Complexity: Dominated by the forward passes of the SDF and color networks for all pixels and sampled points. The gradient computation for the Eikonal loss adds a backward pass through the SDF network for the 1024 eikonal points. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SDF and color network parameters, plus intermediate activations for the 1024 eikonal, off-surface, and inside points. Strengths: Explicitly handles the geometry of articulated humans using the SMPL mesh, leading to better surface reconstruction and animatability compared to generic NeRF losses. Limitations: Relies on the availability of a canonical SMPL mesh and its topology. The specific weighting coefficients (\lambda) are not provided, requiring empirical tuning. The normalization by |P| for geometric losses may make them sensitive to image resolution. When to use: When training an animatable human model using volume rendering of SDFs where surface accuracy and valid SDF properties are critical. When not to use: For static objects without articulated structure, or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of sampling and computing geometric losses is prohibitive. The ARAH loss function was introduced in the ARAH (Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs) paper by Wang et al. (2022). It builds upon differentiable volume rendering and signed distance function representations for human avatars. The method integrates concepts from Eikonal regularization and specific geometric constraints derived from the SMPL human body model. It is used in the context of self-supervised 3D human mesh recovery and animatable avatar creation from images. name: Joint Optimization with Loss Functions
head: Joint Optimization of Surfel Parameters and HDR Environment Map
body: Joint optimization with loss functions simultaneously updates scene geometry, material properties, and illumination parameters by minimizing a composite objective function. It solves the ill-posed inverse rendering problem by regularizing the solution space through geometric and photometric constraints, distinguishing itself from single-parameter optimization by enforcing consistency across depth layers, surface normals, and image appearance. Builds on Regularization losses. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground-truth images \mathbf{I}^, optional ground-truth masks \mathbf{M}^, camera poses, and initial surfel parameters (positions \mathbf{c}, normals \mathbf{n}, scales, albedo, metallic, roughness) and an HDR environment map. Outputs: Optimized surfel parameters and HDR environment map. Data Structures: Surfel Parameters: Positions \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, tangent vectors parameterized as unit quaternions \mathbf{q}, log-space scales (\log sx, \log sy), albedo \rho, metallic m, roughness r. HDR Environment Map: Equirectangular map of resolution 16 \times 32 storing radiance values L. Spatial Data Structure: A KNN (K-Nearest Neighbors) index built on surfel positions, rebuilt periodically and cached between optimization updates. Composite Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of four terms: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{sil}} \mathcal{L}{\text{sil}} + \lambda{\text{cons}} \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} + \lambda{\text{nc}} \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}} where \lambda{\text{sil}}, \lambda{\text{cons}}, \lambda{\text{nc}} are scalar weights. 1. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}): Combines \ell1 reconstruction and Structural Similarity (SSIM). For HDR targets, both rendered image \hat{\mathbf{I}} and ground-truth \mathbf{I}^ are transformed via log-space and sRGB transfer before loss computation to prevent gradient domination by bright pixels. \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = (1 - \lambda{\text{ssim}}) \|\hat{\mathbf{I}} - \mathbf{I}^\|1 + \lambda{\text{ssim}} (1 - \text{SSIM}(\hat{\mathbf{I}}, \mathbf{I}^)) where \lambda{\text{ssim}} is the weighting factor. 2. Silhouette Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{sil}}): Supervises total accumulated coverage using soft Intersection-over-Union (IoU). Provides a strong signal during early training and is disabled once adaptive density control begins. \mathcal{L}{\text{sil}} = \text{IoU}(1 - \bar{T}{K+1}, \mathbf{M}^) where \bar{T}{K+1} is the residual transmittance and \mathbf{M}^ is the ground-truth mask. 3. Depth Consolidation Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{cons}}): Penalizes spurious depth layers by enforcing geometric thinness. It is the average over all pixels \mathcal{P} of inter-layer and intra-layer terms: \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|} \sum{p \in \mathcal{P}} (\mathcal{L}{\text{inter-c}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{intra-c}}) Inter-layer term (\mathcal{L}{\text{inter-c}}): Penalizes weight allocation across distant layers. \mathcal{L}{\text{inter-c}} = \sum{i < j} wi wj |zi - zj| where wi, wj are compositing weights and zi, zj are mean depths of layers i, j. Intra-layer term (\mathcal{L}{\text{intra-c}}): Penalizes depth spread within layers. \mathcal{L}{\text{intra-c}} = \sumi wi^2 \sigmai^2 where \sigmai^2 is the depth variance of layer i. 4. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{nc}}): Penalizes angular deviation between a surfel's normal and its orientation-aware nearest neighbors in 3D space: \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}} = \frac{\sumi \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}i} w{ij} (1 - \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}j)}{\sumi \sum{j \in \mathcal{N}i} w{ij}} where \mathcal{N}i are nearest neighbors with compatible normal orientation, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{n}j are normals, and w{ij} = \exp(-\|\mathbf{c}i - \mathbf{c}j\|^2 / 2\sigma^2) are distance-dependent weights derived from local intersample spacing. Optimization Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize surfel parameters (positions, quaternions, log-scales, albedo, metallic, roughness) and HDR environment map (16 \times 32 equirectangular). 2. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients of \mathcal{L} with respect to all parameters using the Adam optimizer. 3. Parameter Update: Update parameters using the computed gradients. 4. Spatial Structure Update: Periodically rebuild and cache the KNN spatial data structure for normal consistency calculation. 5. Schedule Management: Disable \mathcal{L}{\text{sil}} once adaptive density control begins. Activate \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}} according to the training schedule. Parameters: \lambda{\text{ssim}}: SSIM weighting factor. Not given in the sources. \lambda{\text{sil}}, \lambda{\text{cons}}, \lambda{\text{nc}}: Scalar weights for respective losses. Not given in the sources. \sigma: Parameter for distance-dependent weights in \mathcal{L}{\text{nc}}, derived from local intersample spacing. Environment Map Resolution: 16 \times 32 equirectangular. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Domination: In HDR training, bright pixels can dominate gradients. Mitigated by applying log-space and sRGB transfer to both rendered and ground-truth images before loss computation. Spurious Depth Layers: Without regularization, multi-layer compositing may distribute surfels across incorrect depths. Mitigated by \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}}. Oversmoothing: Screen-space normal regularizers may oversmooth geometry. Mitigated by using 3D normal consistency on surfel primitives instead. Illumination Absorption: Long second-stage optimization may cause albedo to absorb illumination information, degrading relighting quality. Mitigated by limiting optimization duration. Models distant lighting as a high-dynamic-range spherical environment map in equirectangular coordinates. It sets itself apart by optimizing radiance values directly with solid-angle compensation for non-uniform texel area, preserving high-frequency angular detail for sharp cast shadows. It is chosen when accurate relighting is required. Uses normal-based hemisphere sampling to halve the number of rays per pixel compared to full-sphere sampling. After hemisphere culling and empty-space removal, there are 512 candidate directions. Map Resolution is 16 \times 32 equirectangular, limiting recoverable illumination bandwidth to the object's BRDF lobes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: A full second-stage optimization iteration takes approximately 1.25 s/it. Final PBR relighting renders at about 0.83 s/image. Forward relighting spends about 55% of its time on visibility queries and 44% on BRDF/environment-map integration. OptiX visibility pass takes approximately 436 ms at evaluation resolution, corresponding to about 127 MRays/s. Strengths: Enforces geometric thinness and normal consistency; handles HDR lighting; stable gradient-based optimization of illumination. Limitations: Compact environment map limits recoverable illumination bandwidth; long optimization may degrade relighting quality. When to use: Object-level inverse rendering requiring geometry reconstruction, novel view synthesis, and novel scene relighting. When not to use: When high-bandwidth illumination recovery is critical and the object's BRDF lobes are insufficient to constrain the environment map. Originated in the context of 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering (3DSS) and VisibilitySplat. 3DSS jointly optimizes surfel parameters and HDR environment maps using composite losses. VisibilitySplat uses ray-traced occlusion for relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting, optimizing an HDR environment map. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.24132/csrn.2026-e17, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light-SMAE
head: Smooth Manifold Auto-Encoder
body: Light-SMAE is a smooth manifold auto-encoder that learns a low-dimensional, differentiable latent representation of high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps, serving as a strong regularizer or prior for reflectance decomposition and inverse rendering. It sets itself apart from direct optimization of lighting parameters by constraining the solution space to a smooth manifold learned from data, which enables stable gradient-based optimization of illumination in ill-posed inverse problems. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An HDR environment map p, downscaled to 128 \times 256 resolution. Output: A 128-dimensional latent embedding zl \in \mathbb{R}^{128} (via Encoder) or a reconstructed HDR environment map \hat{p}0 (via Decoder). Data Structures: The architecture consists of an Encoder E, a Decoder G, and a Discriminator D, all based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) utilizing CoordConv layers. CoordConv Layer: A 2D convolution where the input tensor is augmented with coordinate channels (x, y) before convolution. Conv Layer: Standard 2D convolution. ConvT Layer: Transposed 2D convolution (upsampling). Network Architecture (Light-SMAE): The specific layer configurations are defined in the source. Encoder E: 1. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ELU. 2. ConvT: Kernel 1 \times 1, Stride 1, 64 features, Activation ELU. 3. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ReLU. Padding: No padding. Decoder G: 1. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ELU. 2. CoordConv: Kernel 4 \times 4, Stride 2, 21 features, Activation ELU. 3. ConvT: Kernel 4 \times 4, Stride 2, 58 features, Activation ELU. 4. Final Output Layer: Conv 1 \times 1, Stride 1, 3 features (RGB), Activation \exp(x - 1). Padding: Uses 'same' padding. Discriminator D: 1. CoordConv: Kernel 3 \times 3, Stride 1, 8 features, Activation ELU. 2. Conv: Kernel 4 \times 4, Stride 2, 21 features, Activation ELU. Padding: No padding. Training Procedure: The network is trained jointly to minimize a composite loss function. 1. Data Preprocessing: Rotate each of the 320 environment maps 10 times. Randomly blend two environment maps during training. Downscale inputs to 128 \times 256. Transform HDR input x to LDR for encoder: x{ldr} = \log(1 + x). 2. Forward Pass (Encoding): Pass x{ldr} through Encoder E to get latent vector z. 3. Forward Pass (Decoding & Reconstruction): Pass z through Decoder G to get reconstruction \hat{p}{ldr}. Transform LDR output to HDR: \hat{p}{hdr} = \exp(\hat{p}{ldr} - 1). 4. Latent Interpolation: Randomly sample two latent vectors from the mini-batch: za and zb. Sample m linearly interpolated embeddings uniformly spaced between za and zb: zn^0 = (1 - \alphan) za + \alphan zb for n = 1, \dots, m. Parameter: m = 5 interpolation steps between each of the batch halves. 5. Forward Pass (Interpolated Reconstruction and Re-encoding): Pass each zn^0 through Decoder G to obtain \hat{p}n^0. Pass each \hat{p}n^0 (transformed to LDR) through Encoder E to obtain re-estimated latents \hat{z}n^0. 6. Loss Calculation: The total loss L is a weighted sum of four components: L = Lr + \lambda1 La + \lambda2 Lc + \lambda3 Ls Reconstruction Loss (Lr): Calculated using the Mean Absolute Log Error (MALE) between the ground truth HDR x^ and the predicted HDR \hat{x}: Lr = |\log(1 + x^) - \log(1 + \hat{x})| Adversarial Loss (La): Standard adversarial loss from LSGAN applied to the discriminator D evaluating the interpolated reconstructions \hat{p}n^0. Cyclic Loss (Lc): L2-loss between the interpolated latents \{zn^0\} and their re-estimated counterparts \{\hat{z}n^0\}: Lc = \sum{n=1}^m \| zn^0 - \hat{z}n^0 \|^2 Smoothness Loss (Ls): Imposed on the gradient of the decoder G with respect to the interpolating scalar value \alpha: Ls = \frac{1}{m} \sum{n=1}^m \left( \nabla\alpha G(zn^0) \right)^2 7. Optimization: Update parameters of E, G, and D using the Adam optimizer. Parameters: Latent Dimension: zl \in \mathbb{R}^{128}. Loss Weights: \lambda1 = 0.01 (Adversarial), \lambda2 = 0.0001 (Cyclic), \lambda3 = 0.05 (Smoothness). Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 24. Training Steps: 4 million steps. Hardware: Single NVIDIA 1080 TI GPU. Training Time: Approximately 5 days. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hdrtoldr(x): return log(1 + x) def ldrtohdr(x): return exp(x - 1) def computesmoothnessloss(decoder, za, zb, m): loss = 0.0 for i in range(1, m + 1): alpha = i / (m + 1) zinterp = za + alpha (zb - za) zinterp.requiresgrad = True recon = decoder(zinterp) grad = gradient(recon.sum(), zinterp) dzdalpha = zb - za gradalpha = sum(grad dzdalpha) loss += gradalpha 2 return loss / m def computecyclicloss(encoder, decoder, za, zb, m): loss = 0.0 for i in range(1, m + 1): alpha = i / (m + 1) zinterp = za + alpha (zb - za) ldrrecon = decoder(zinterp) hdrrecon = ldrtohdr(ldrrecon) ldrreconenc = hdrtoldr(hdrrecon) zreest = encoder(ldrreconenc) loss += norm(zinterp - zreest) 2 return loss / m def computeadversarialloss(discriminator, hdrreconinterp): # Standard LSGAN loss for interpolated reconstructions pred = discriminator(hdrreconinterp) return mean((pred - 1.0) 2) def trainstep(encoder, decoder, discriminator, batch, lambdaa, lambdac, lambdas, m): ldrinput = hdrtoldr(batch) z = encoder(ldrinput) ldrrecon = decoder(z) hdrrecon = ldrtohdr(ldrrecon) lossr = mean(abs(hdrtoldr(batch) - hdrtoldr(hdrrecon))) za, zb = z[0], z[1] lossc = computecyclicloss(encoder, decoder, za, zb, m) losss = computesmoothnessloss(decoder, za, zb, m) # Compute interpolated reconstructions for adversarial loss alpha = 0.5 zinterp = za + alpha (zb - za) ldrreconinterp = decoder(zinterp) hdrreconinterp = ldrtohdr(ldrreconinterp) lossa = computeadversarialloss(discriminator, hdrreconinterp) loss = lossr + lambdaa lossa + lambdac lossc + lambdas losss return loss Time Complexity: Training requires 4 million steps. On a single NVIDIA 1080 TI GPU, this takes approximately 5 days. Memory Complexity: The latent space is 128-dimensional, which is significantly smaller than the 128 \times 256 \times 3 input resolution, reducing memory requirements for storing lighting parameters during optimization. Strengths: Provides a strong prior for ill-posed inverse problems (reflectance decomposition). The smoothness of the manifold enables stable gradient-based optimization. Handles HDR data effectively via specific HDR/LDR transformations and MALE loss. Limitations: Requires pre-training on a dataset of high-quality environment maps (320 maps augmented). The problem of jointly estimating 3D shape, materials, and lighting is highly underconstrained; the SMAE acts as a necessary regularizer but does not solve the ill-posedness alone. When to use: When optimizing illumination parameters in inverse rendering or reflectance decomposition tasks where direct optimization is unstable or prone to implausible solutions. When not to use: When no prior distribution of lighting is available or when real-time inference of lighting from a single image without pre-trained priors is required. Light-SMAE was introduced in the paper "Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition". It is based on the concept of Interpolating Auto-Encoders [5] and is designed to learn low-dimensional smooth manifolds for BRDFs and illuminations. The method was developed to address the ill-posedness of jointly estimating 3D shape, materials, and lighting. The Light-SMAE specifically targets environment maps, mapping them to a 128-dimensional latent space, while a companion BRDF-SMAE maps Cook-Torrance BRDF parameters to a 4D latent space. The networks are pre-trained on datasets of real-world BRDFs [10] and environment maps [61], with the Light-SMAE trained on 320 environment maps augmented by rotations and blending. Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.14373, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Forplane Optimization Losses
head: Forplane Losses
body: Forplane Optimization Losses are a set of regularization terms designed to stabilize the training of neural radiance fields that utilize orthogonal neural planes (Forplanes) for spatiotemporal volume representation. They solve the problem of entanglement between static and dynamic scene components in dynamic volume rendering, where the model may incorrectly assign dynamic motion to static geometry or vice versa. Unlike standard Total Variation regularization which smooths spatial features, Forplane losses specifically target the structural integrity of the orthogonal plane representations by enforcing spatial smoothness, temporal consistency, and static-field isolation. The method operates on a representation where the 4D volume (3D space + time) is decomposed into a set of 2D orthogonal planes. The optimization minimizes a composite loss function comprising a photometric term, a depth term, and three specific regularization terms derived from the plane structures. Inputs: \boldsymbol{\theta}: Parameters of the density MLP. \boldsymbol{\phi}: Parameters of the color MLP. \mathbf{V}{sd}^s: Set of static space planes (G{XY}, G{YZ}, G{XZ}). \mathbf{V}{3d}^d: Set of dynamic space-time planes (G{XT}, G{YT}, G{ZT}). \mathbf{V}{sd}^v: Set of space-time planes associated with the dynamic field initialization. \hat{\boldsymbol{C}}(\mathbf{r}): Rendered color for ray \mathbf{r}. \boldsymbol{C}i^{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r}): Ground truth color for ray \mathbf{r} in image Ii. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{total}: The scalar loss value to be minimized. The Forplane representation consists of 2D grids (planes). Static Space Planes (\mathbf{V}{sd}^s): 2D arrays representing spatial slices (XY, YZ, XZ). Dynamic Space-Time Planes (\mathbf{V}{3d}^d): 2D arrays representing slices combining one spatial dimension and time (XT, YT, ZT). Values: Each element g in a plane G is a scalar feature value. The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{total}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}D + \lambda{tv} \mathcal{L}{TV} + \lambda{ts} \mathcal{L}{TS} + \lambda{de} \mathcal{L}{DE} Where: 1. Photometric Loss (\mathcal{L}{rgb}): \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = \sumi \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{r} \sim Ii} \left[ \left\| \hat{\boldsymbol{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \boldsymbol{C}i^{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r}) \right\|2^2 \right] where \boldsymbol{C}i^{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth color. 2. Spatial Total Variation Loss (\mathcal{L}{TV}): \mathcal{L}{TV} = \sum{G \in \mathbf{V}{sd}^s} \sum{g \in G} \|\Deltah^2(G, g) + \Deltaw^2(G, g)\| where \mathbf{V}{sd}^s = \{G{XY}, G{YZ}, G{XZ}\} are the static space planes. \Deltah^2(G, g) is the squared difference between the g-th value in plane G:=(i,j) and G:=(i+1,j) normalized by resolution. 3. Temporal Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}{TS}): \mathcal{L}{TS} = \sum{G \in \mathbf{V}{3d}^d} \sum{g \in G} \|\Deltat^2(G, g)\| where \mathbf{V}{3d}^d = \{G{XT}, G{YT}, G{ZT}\} are the space-time planes. \Deltat^2(G, g) represents the squared difference along the time axis. 4. Disentangle Loss (\mathcal{L}{DE}): \mathcal{L}{DE} = \sum{G \in \mathbf{V}{sd}^v} \sum{g \in G} \|1 - g\| where \mathbf{V}{sd}^v refers to the space-time planes associated with the dynamic field initialization. This loss encourages features to remain at the initial value of 1. \lambdad: Weight for depth loss \mathcal{L}D. Default: 1. \lambda{tv}: Weight for spatial TV loss. Default: 0.001. \lambda{ts}: Weight for temporal smoothness loss. Default: 0.05. \lambda{de}: Weight for disentangle loss. Default: 0.001. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeforplanelosses(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors, staticspaceplanes, dynamicspacetimeplanes, dynamicfieldspacetimeplanes, lambdad=1.0, lambdatv=0.001, lambdats=0.05, lambdade=0.001): # 1. Photometric Loss (Lrgb) lrgb = sum((c - gt) 2 for c, gt in zip(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors)) / len(renderedcolors) # LD (depth loss) is not defined in the provided source notes. ld = 0.0 # 2. Spatial Total Variation Loss (LTV) ltv = 0.0 for plane in staticspaceplanes: # Deltah^2: squared difference between (i, j) and (i+1, j) hdiff = [(plane[i][j] - plane[i+1][j]) 2 for i in range(len(plane)-1) for j in range(len(plane[0]))] # Deltaw^2: squared difference between (i, j) and (i, j+1) wdiff = [(plane[i][j] - plane[i][j+1]) 2 for i in range(len(plane)) for j in range(len(plane[0])-1)] ltv += sum(hdiff) + sum(wdiff) # 3. Temporal Smoothness Loss (LTS) lts = 0.0 for plane in dynamicspacetimeplanes: # Deltat^2: squared difference along the time axis (assumed axis 1) tdiff = [(plane[i][j] - plane[i][j+1]) 2 for i in range(len(plane)) for j in range(len(plane[0])-1)] lts += sum(tdiff) # 4. Disentangle Loss (LDE) lde = 0.0 for plane in dynamicfieldspacetimeplanes: lde += sum(abs(1.0 - val) for row in plane for val in row) # Total Loss totalloss = lrgb + (lambdad ld) + (lambdatv ltv) + (lambdats lts) + (lambdade lde) return totalloss Initialization: The dynamic field planes \mathbf{V}{3d}^d are initialized to 1 to ensure they do not influence the static field features during element-wise multiplication in the rendering procedure. Failure to initialize correctly may cause immediate entanglement. Boundary Conditions: The definition of \Deltah^2 and \Deltaw^2 involves differences between adjacent grid cells. Boundary handling (e.g., zero-padding vs. wrapping) is not explicitly detailed in the source notes. Standard practice suggests zero-padding or ignoring boundary terms to avoid artifacts. Monocular Input: In endoscopic procedures with monocular cameras, the reliance on stereo depth can be limiting. The Forplane method is designed to work with monocular inputs, but the depth loss \mathcal{L}D may need adaptation or removal if depth supervision is unavailable. Apply SVD plane regularization exclusively to semantic classes expected to exhibit flat surfaces, such as roads and sidewalks. Group semantic classes that share the same physical plane into a single semantic group. Apply the regularization loss only when a single semantic group is detected within the current patch. Pitfalls: Multiple semantic classes within one patch likely indicate multiple distinct planes; skip regularization to avoid violating the single-plane assumption. Multiple semantic classes may belong to the same physical plane (e.g., road and lane markings); group them together and apply regularization. Time Complexity: The regularization losses are computed directly on the plane tensors. \mathcal{L}{TV} and \mathcal{L}{TS} involve simple finite difference operations on the planes, which is O(N{planes} \times N{cells}). Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the plane tensors themselves. Strengths: Enforces spatial smoothness, temporal consistency, and static-field isolation. The disentangle loss specifically prevents the dynamic field from learning static structures. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (\lambda{tv}, \lambda{ts}, \lambda{de}). The method assumes a specific orthogonal plane structure; it is not directly applicable to other volume representations like voxels or Gaussian splats without modification. Forplane Optimization Losses were introduced in the context of "Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction via Orthogonal Neural Plane". The method builds upon the concept of Neural Fields and specifically the use of orthogonal planes (Forplanes) to represent 3D and 4D volumes efficiently. The specific losses (\mathcal{L}{TV}, \mathcal{L}{TS}, \mathcal{L}{DE}) were proposed to address the challenges of reconstructing dynamic, deformable tissues (such as in endoscopic surgery) where static and dynamic elements coexist and must be separated for accurate modeling. name: Geometric and Normal Alignment Losses
body: Geometric and Normal Alignment Losses are a family of regularization techniques in differentiable volume rendering that enforce structural coherence by penalizing geometric inconsistencies, noisy normals, and high-frequency oscillations. This family sets itself apart from sibling methods like Total Variation Regularization or Distortion Loss by explicitly targeting the orientation, curvature, and spatial consistency of geometry and material fields rather than just photometric output. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results. Curvature Loss is a geometric regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering and neural implicit surface optimization to penalize high-frequency oscillations in the predicted scalar field [2911-curvature-loss.md]. It solves the problem of noisy, jagged, or topologically incorrect geometry by enforcing smoothness in the second-order derivatives of the model output [2911-curvature-loss.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Normal Consistency and Alignment by operating on the curvature (second derivative) of the field rather than the alignment of first-order normals, and from Surface Curvature Regularization by serving as the foundational mechanism that those methods build upon [2911-curvature-loss.md]. 2D Planar Image Alignment is a simplified joint optimization problem that aligns overlapping 2D image patches with learned content [6845-2d-planar-image-alignment.md]. It reconstructs a ground truth image from transformed patches by simultaneously optimizing the image content representation and the geometric transformation parameters [6845-2d-planar-image-alignment.md]. It differs from other geometric losses by operating in 2D patch space using homography parameters and low-rank tensor decompositions, rather than directly constraining 3D geometry or normals [6845-2d-planar-image-alignment.md]. Material Smoothness Loss is a regularization term applied to material fields to enforce spatial smoothness by penalizing differences in material parameters between neighboring surface points [7299-material-smoothness-loss.md]. A specific variant, the BRDF Smoothness Loss, enforces smoothness of BRDF parameters using a normalized difference weighted by pseudo-albedo gradients [7299-material-smoothness-loss.md]. It differs from standard smoothness losses by incorporating a bilateral weight derived from rendered color and irradiance to modulate the penalty, ensuring smoothness is preserved across material boundaries [7299-material-smoothness-loss.md]. This family enforces geometric plausibility in differentiable volume rendering by constraining predicted surface normals against ray directions, ground truth data, or density gradients [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md]. It solves the ambiguity of implicit surfaces in radiance fields, particularly in sparse-view or ill-posed reconstruction scenarios, by stabilizing optimization and improving surface quality [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md]. Unlike sibling methods that focus on curvature or material smoothness, these losses specifically target the orientation and consistency of the normal field [13295-normal-consistency-and-alignment.md]. Geometry Consistency Loss is a regularization technique used in differentiable volume rendering, specifically within style transfer frameworks like INS, to enforce view-consistent scene geometry. It addresses the problem of geometric distortions and inconsistencies that arise when applying style transformations to radiance fields by ensuring that the underlying 3D structure remains stable across different viewpoints. Unlike sibling methods such as Curvature Loss or Normal Consistency which focus on local surface properties or alignment with external normals, this method relies on self-distillation to maintain global geometric coherence without requiring explicit depth supervision [14883-geometry-consistency-loss.md]. Definition: A loss function that accounts for spatial misalignment between rendered and ground truth images by searching for the best-matching subpatch in the ground truth set, regularized by coordinate distance. Formula: L{PM}(G, R) = \min{i=1,...,N} (D(Gi, R) + \lambda \cdot D{coord}(Gi, R)). Here, D(Gi, R) = \|Gi - R\|2^2 and D{coord}(Gi, R) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}, where \Delta x and \Delta y are the horizontal and vertical offsets between the ground truth subpatch Gi and the rendered patch R. Parameters: \lambda is the regularization weight for the coordinate distance penalty, typically set to 0.01. The ground truth patch size (G) is sampled at 48 \times 48 pixels, and the rendered patch size (R) is 32 \times 32 pixels. Comparison: Unlike standard losses defined on single pixels, this loss is defined on patches, allowing alignment vectors (\Delta x, \Delta y) to be estimated more robustly. Definition: A depth loss function that enforces constraints on planar boundaries by directly addressing sample weights, effectively reducing ambiguity during the volume rendering procedure. Formula: L{bound} = \sum{r \in R} \sum{i} \left( wi - e^{-\frac{(ti - D(r))^2}{2\sigma^2}} \right)^2, where L{bound} is the boundary loss, wi is the weight, ti is the distance of the sample from the ray origin, D(r) is ground truth depth, and \sigma is a sigma parameter. Parameters: \delta is set to 1 mm as a tolerance/threshold parameter for boundary enforcement. D(r) is the ground truth depth of ray r, wi is the weight corresponding to a point sampled on ray r at distance ti from the ray origin. Pitfall: In open space, transmittance Ti remains high and opacity \alphai remains low, producing low weights and minimal interaction to indicate boundaries. At boundary surfaces, opacity \alphai rises due to increasing material density, causing weights to peak. Comparison: Produces fewer artifacts and cleaner renderings than MSE loss by directly addressing the weights of samples, effectively reducing ambiguity during volume rendering. Definition: A comparison of various ray-based regularization losses used during NeRF/DVGO training to evaluate their sensitivity to false geometry. The CF loss is noted as being more sensitive to false geometry than others. Data: On DTU scan 40 with false geometry, the percentage of loss value in the false geometry region (normalized [0,1]) for various losses: Background entropy loss (11.0%), Photometric loss (11.1%), Per-point RGB loss (12.4%), CF loss (6.5%), Ray-entropy loss (4.7%), Distortion loss (28.0%). Definition: A two-stage pipeline addressing the vector field counterpart to STNet, combining U-Net-based motion estimation with deformable alignment. These objectives reflect the additional fidelity constraints that vector data imposes. Steps: Introduces domain-motivated objectives including cosine direction loss and a Jacobian loss for capturing divergence and curl. Definition: Three regularization/alignment losses used in DP-GES: Ls enforces geometric alignment with ground-truth colors, Lt prevents background leakage from overlapping semi-transparent regions, and L{scale} regularizes surfel scaling for spatial uniformity. Steps: Apply Ls during optimization to align surfel geometry with ground-truth colors, preventing missing geometry. Apply Lt during optimization to prevent background leakage caused by stacks of overlapping semi-transparent regions. Apply L{scale} during optimization to regularize surfel scaling distribution, reducing color leakage from chaotic scaling. Pitfall: Stopping transmittance-mediated gradients (w/o trans. grad) leads to blurrier details and prominent small surfels, similar to GES artifacts. Data: Ablation PSNR (MipNeRF360 1080p): Ours (full) 28.11, Ours (base) 27.72, w/ 2 layers 27.02, w/ 4 layers 28.10, w/o trans. grad 27.82, w/o Ls 28.05, w/o L{scale} 28.07, w/o Lt 27.86. Definition: A variant of direct alignment that replaces the RGB alignment loss with feature and gradient alignment losses to mitigate artifacts from photo-consistency violations. Steps: Replace the RGB alignment loss with an alignment loss computed on DINO features and image gradients. Pitfall: Mitigates ghosting artifacts and structural inaccuracies, allowing recovery of semi-transparent objects such as glass supports. The use of geometric constraints in neural radiance fields emerged to address floaters and noisy geometry in sparse-view reconstruction. Early methods relied on photometric loss, leading to ambiguous geometry, prompting the introduction of curvature regularization and normal consistency losses. Subsequent works extended these principles to material fields and style transfer contexts. Specific variants target architectural surfaces, vector fields, and surfel rendering, while alignment-aware training addresses spatial misalignment between rendered and ground truth images and feature-space alignment mitigates photo-consistency violations. AligNeRF: High-Fidelity Neural Radiance Fields via Alignment-Aware Training, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00013, fetched 2026-10-26 Improving Geometric Consistency for 360-Degree Neural Radiance Fields in Indoor Scenarios, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13710v1, fetched 2026-10-27 Reducing Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in Radiance Fields with a Closed-Form Color Estimation Method, https://doi.org/10.52202/075280-2570, fetched 2026-10-26 PDF Deep Learning Methods and Neural Representations for Scientific Volume..., https://www.cs.uoregon.edu/Reports/AREA-202603-Mathai.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Depth Peeling for High-Fidelity Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.25345, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) ACCV 2024 Open Access Repository, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ACCV2024/html/GargDirectAlignmentforRobustNeRFLearningACCV2024paper.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Second-Order Chamfer Distance
head: Second-Order CD
body: Second-Order Chamfer Distance is a supervised geometric loss that measures the discrepancy between a predicted mesh vertex and a ground truth surface by incorporating local surface curvature. It applies a quadratic approximation of the point-to-point distance to penalize deviations along the principal curvature directions and surface normal. It serves as a supervised baseline for meshing implicit functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A predicted mesh vertex \mathbf{x} (output of network h\phi) and a ground truth mesh. Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L} representing the second-order distance error. Data Structures: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D coordinates of the query point (predicted vertex). \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The closest point on the reference (ground truth) surface to \mathbf{x}. \vec{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The unit surface normal at \mathbf{y}. \vec{e}1, \vec{e}2 \in \mathbb{R}^3: The orthonormal principal curvature directions at \mathbf{y}. \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2 \in \mathbb{R}: The magnitudes of the principal curvatures at \mathbf{y}. Steps: 1. Find Closest Point: For each predicted vertex \mathbf{x}, find the closest point \mathbf{y} on the ground truth mesh. 2. Compute Geometric Properties: At the reference point \mathbf{y}, compute the surface normal \vec{n}, the principal curvature directions \vec{e}1, \vec{e}2, and their magnitudes \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2. 3. Compute Displacement Vector: Calculate the vector \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}. 4. Project Displacement: Project \mathbf{d} onto the normal and the two principal curvature directions: dn = \vec{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}, d{e1} = \vec{e}1 \cdot \mathbf{d}, d{e2} = \vec{e}2 \cdot \mathbf{d}. 5. Calculate Loss: Compute the loss using the quadratic approximation formula: \mathcal{L} = \hat{\delta}1 (d{e1})^2 + \hat{\delta}2 (d{e2})^2 + (dn)^2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def secondorderchamferdistance(predictedvertices, groundtruthmesh): totalloss = 0.0 npoints = len(predictedvertices) for i in range(npoints): x = predictedvertices[i] y = groundtruthmesh.findclosestpoint(x) n = groundtruthmesh.getnormal(y) e1, e2 = groundtruthmesh.getprincipaldirections(y) delta1, delta2 = groundtruthmesh.getprincipalcurvatures(y) d = [x[j] - y[j] for j in range(3)] dotn = n[0]d[0] + n[1]d[1] + n[2]d[2] dote1 = e1[0]d[0] + e1[1]d[1] + e1[2]d[2] dote2 = e2[0]d[0] + e2[1]d[1] + e2[2]d[2] lossi = (delta1 dote12) + (delta2 dote22) + (dotn2) totalloss += lossi return totalloss / npoints Parameters: \mathbf{x}: The mesh vertex predicted by the network h\phi. \mathbf{y}: The closest point on the ground truth mesh from the training dataset (ABC dataset). \hat{\delta}1, \hat{\delta}2: Magnitude of principal curvatures at \mathbf{y}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) is a metric used to quantify the geometric discrepancy between a generated mesh and a ground truth mesh, specifically designed for scenarios where the ground truth is non-watertight or an analytic Signed Distance Field (SDF) is ill-defined. Unlike the Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P), which evaluates distance errors on a fixed grid near the surface, LSD-A measures the point-to-face distance from points sampled directly on the ground truth mesh to the generated mesh. It serves as a robust alternative to standard Chamfer Distance when strict watertightness cannot be guaranteed. Not given in the sources. The method is a supervised baseline for meshing implicit functions that uses a quadratic approximation of point-point distance proposed in [51] (cited in). It was applied in "Self-Supervised Dual Contouring" to measure distance between a query point and a reference surface using local surface curvature. The ground truth meshes used in the cited work were from the ABC dataset. Self-Supervised Dual Contouring, https://inria.hal.science/hal-04590906v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Approximate Level Set Discrepancy
head: LSD-A
body: Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) is a metric used to quantify the geometric discrepancy between a generated mesh and a ground truth mesh, specifically designed for scenarios where the ground truth is non-watertight or an analytic Signed Distance Field (SDF) is ill-defined. Unlike the Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P), which evaluates distance errors on a fixed grid near the surface, LSD-A measures the point-to-face distance from points sampled directly on the ground truth mesh to the generated mesh. It serves as a robust alternative to standard Chamfer Distance when strict watertightness cannot be guaranteed. Inputs: \mathcal{M}^: The ground truth mesh. \mathcal{M}: The generated (reconstructed) mesh. N: The number of points to sample on \mathcal{M}^. Outputs: A scalar value representing the average point-to-face distance. Data Structures: Points q: A set of N points sampled on the surface of \mathcal{M}^. Mesh \mathcal{M}: Represented as a collection of vertices and faces supporting point-to-face distance queries. Steps: 1. Sample N points q distributed over the surface of the ground truth mesh \mathcal{M}^. 2. For each point q \in \mathcal{M}^, compute the Euclidean distance to the closest point on the generated mesh \mathcal{M}. This distance is denoted as d^p(q, \mathcal{M}). 3. Sum these distances and divide by N to obtain the mean. Formula: \text{LSD-A} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{q \in \mathcal{M}^} d^p(q, \mathcal{M}) Where: \mathcal{M}^ is the ground truth mesh. \mathcal{M} is the generated mesh. q are points sampled on \mathcal{M}^. d^p(q, \mathcal{M}) is the point-to-face distance from point q to the generated mesh \mathcal{M}. N is the number of sampled points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximatelevelsetdiscrepancy(groundtruthmesh, generatedmesh, numsamples): """ Computes the Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A). Args: groundtruthmesh: Mesh object representing M. generatedmesh: Mesh object representing M. numsamples: Integer N, number of points to sample on M. Returns: float: The LSD-A score. """ # Step 1: Sample points on the ground truth mesh sampledpoints = samplepointsuniformly(groundtruthmesh, numsamples) totaldistance = 0.0 # Step 2 & 3: Compute point-to-face distance and average for q in sampledpoints: dist = pointtofacedistance(q, generatedmesh) totaldistance += dist return totaldistance / numsamples def samplepointsuniformly(mesh, numsamples): # Standard area-weighted uniform sampling on a triangle mesh faces = mesh.faces areas = [trianglearea(f.v0, f.v1, f.v2) for f in faces] totalarea = sum(areas) cumareas = [] acc = 0.0 for a in areas: acc += a cumareas.append(acc) points = [] for in range(numsamples): r = random.uniform(0, totalarea) idx = 0 for i, ca in enumerate(cumareas): if r <= ca: idx = i break v0, v1, v2 = faces[idx].v0, faces[idx].v1, faces[idx].v2 s, t = random.random(), random.random() if s + t > 1: s, t = 1 - s, 1 - t points.append(vectoradd(v0, vectoradd(vectormul(s, vectorsub(v1, v0)), vectormul(t, vectorsub(v2, v0))))) return points def trianglearea(v0, v1, v2): return 0.5 vectornorm(vectorcross(vectorsub(v1, v0), vectorsub(v2, v0))) def pointtofacedistance(point, mesh): mindist = float('inf') for face in mesh.faces: dist = distancepointtotriangle(point, face.v0, face.v1, face.v2) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist return mindist def distancepointtotriangle(point, v0, v1, v2): # Standard point-to-triangle distance closest = computeclosestpointontriangle(point, v0, v1, v2) return vectornorm(vectorsub(point, closest)) def computeclosestpointontriangle(point, v0, v1, v2): # Standard barycentric projection v0v1 = vectorsub(v1, v0) v0v2 = vectorsub(v2, v0) v0p = vectorsub(point, v0) d1 = vectordot(v0v1, v0v1) d2 = vectordot(v0v2, v0v2) d3 = vectordot(v0v1, v0v2) d = d1 d2 - d3 d3 u = (d2 vectordot(v0v1, v0p) - d3 vectordot(v0v2, v0p)) / d v = (d1 vectordot(v0v2, v0p) - d3 vectordot(v0v1, v0p)) / d if u <= 0 and v <= 0: return v0 if u > 1 and v <= 0: return v1 if v > 1 and u <= 0: return v2 if u + v > 1: e = vectorsub(v2, v1) w = vectorsub(point, v1) denom = vectordot(e, e) t = max(0, min(1, vectordot(w, e) / denom)) return vectoradd(v1, vectormul(t, e)) return vectoradd(v0, vectoradd(vectormul(u, v0v1), vectormul(v, v0v2))) Parameters: N: The number of points sampled on the ground truth mesh \mathcal{M}^. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight Ground Truth: LSD-A is specifically intended for cases where the ground truth mesh is non-watertight, making analytic SDF computation ill-defined. Distance Definition: The metric uses point-to-face distance, not point-to-vertex distance, ensuring that the entire surface area contributes to the error measurement. Precision: Floating-point comparisons in barycentric projection require epsilon guards to avoid degenerate edge cases. Precise Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-P) gauges the discrepancy in signed distance values between a reconstructed mesh and the ground truth mesh at fixed points sampled on a regular grid close to the ground truth surface. It is defined as \text{LSD-P} = \sum{g \in \tilde{\mathcal{G}}} \|\text{abs}(\mathbf{d}^p(\mathcal{M}^, g)) - \text{abs}(\mathbf{d}^p(\mathcal{M}, g))\|2, where \tilde{\mathcal{G}} is the grid of points and \mathbf{d}^p is the distance from a query point to its closest point on the surface. LSD-P is chosen when a fixed spatial grid is preferred over surface sampling, whereas LSD-A is preferred for non-watertight meshes where surface sampling is more robust. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Robust to non-watertight ground truth meshes; does not require an analytic SDF; directly measures surface proximity. Limitations: Requires sampling on the ground truth mesh; sensitive to the number of samples N; does not account for signed distance errors in the same way LSD-P does. When to Use: Use LSD-A when evaluating generated meshes against non-watertight ground truth meshes (e.g., ShapeNet dataset) where analytic SDF is ill-defined. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Approximate Level Set Discrepancy (LSD-A) was introduced in the context of self-supervised dual contouring for 3D mesh reconstruction. It was specifically designed to handle the challenges posed by datasets like ShapeNet, which contain non-watertight meshes, making traditional SDF-based metrics unreliable. The metric was used in experiments to evaluate the quality of reconstructed meshes against ground truth in these challenging scenarios. name: Distortion Loss
head: distloss
body: Distortion Loss is a regularization term for differentiable volume rendering that prevents "floaters" (disconnected volumetric artifacts) and "background collapse" (distant surfaces modeled as semi-transparent clouds near the camera) by encouraging rendering weights to be compact along the ray. It minimizes the expected distance between two independent samples drawn from the weight distribution, effectively penalizing spread-out density. Unlike sibling methods such as Total Variation Regularization which smooths spatial gradients, Distortion Loss operates on the 1D depth distribution along rays. It sets itself apart from Variance Loss by explicitly modeling the pairwise distances between all samples rather than just the variance around the mean depth, providing a more robust constraint against multi-modal depth distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \mathbf{s}: Array of normalized ray distances (sample positions) with shape (B, N+1), where B is batch size and N is number of intervals. Values are in [0, 1], derived from non-linear normalization of near-far clipping distances to prevent upweighting distant intervals. \mathbf{w}: Array of ray weights (opacity contributions) with shape (B, N). Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}: Scalar distortion loss value, averaged over the batch. Data Structures: s: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1). si is the start of interval i, s{i+1} is the end. w: Float tensor, shape (B, N). m: Float tensor, shape (B, N), storing interval midpoints mi = (si + s{i+1})/2. prefixw: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), prefix sums of w. prefixwm: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), prefix sums of w \odot m. suffixw: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), suffix sums of w. suffixwm: Float tensor, shape (B, N+1), suffix sums of w \odot m. Steps: 1. Compute Midpoints: Calculate the center of each interval i: mi = \frac{si + s{i+1}}{2} 2. Compute Intra-Interval Loss: Calculate the second term of the distortion loss, which penalizes the width of individual intervals: \mathcal{L}{\text{intra}} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi^2 (s{i+1} - si) 3. Compute Inter-Interval Loss (Efficient O(N)): The first term involves a double sum over all pairs. To achieve O(N) complexity, eliminate the diagonal (i=j) and split the sum into j < i and j > i cases. Since mi < m{i+1}, |mi - mj| = mi - mj for j < i. \mathcal{L}{\text{inter}} = 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi mi \left( \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj \right) - 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi \left( \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj mj \right) This is computed using prefix sums: Let Pw[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj and P{wm}[i] = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} wj mj. \mathcal{L}{\text{inter}} = 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi mi Pw[i] - 2 \sum{i=1}^{N-1} wi P{wm}[i]. 4. Combine: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{inter}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{intra}} 5. Average: Average \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} over the batch dimension B. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedistortionloss(s, w): """ s: list of lists or array of shape (B, N+1) normalized ray distances w: list of lists or array of shape (B, N) ray weights Returns: list of floats, shape (B,) distortion loss per ray """ B = len(w) N = len(w[0]) losses = [] for b in range(B): # 1. Compute midpoints m = [(s[b][i] + s[b][i+1]) / 2.0 for i in range(N)] # 2. Intra-interval loss: 1/3 sum(w^2 intervallength) intervallengths = [s[b][i+1] - s[b][i] for i in range(N)] lossintra = sum(w[b][i]2 intervallengths[i] for i in range(N)) / 3.0 # 3. Inter-interval loss: O(N) implementation via prefix sums # prefixw[i] stores sum{j=0}^{i-1} w[j], prefixwm[i] stores sum{j=0}^{i-1} w[j]m[j] prefixw = [0.0] (N + 1) prefixwm = [0.0] (N + 1) for i in range(N): prefixw[i+1] = prefixw[i] + w[b][i] prefixwm[i+1] = prefixwm[i] + w[b][i] m[i] # Compute sums for i from 1 to N-1 term1 = sum(2.0 w[b][i] m[i] prefixw[i] for i in range(1, N)) term2 = sum(2.0 w[b][i] prefixwm[i] for i in range(1, N)) lossinter = term1 - term2 losses.append(lossinter + lossintra) return losses Parameters: \lambda{\text{dist}}: Weight for the distortion loss in the total loss function. Typical value: 0.01. N: Number of sampled points per ray. The efficient implementation supports uneven N across rays. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: Using unnormalized ray distances t instead of normalized s significantly upweights distant intervals, causing nearby intervals to be ignored. Memory: A naive O(N^2) implementation consumes excessive GPU memory (e.g., >3GB for a batch of 4,096 rays with >256 samples). The prefix-sum method reduces this to O(N) memory and compute. Diagonal Term: The derivation explicitly eliminates the diagonal term (i=j) because |mi - mi| = 0, which is consistent with the integral definition. The 2D-GS Loss Configuration is a variant applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting that decomposes the penalty into a uniform term (penalizing weight magnitude) and a bi-directional term (penalizing variance of depth distribution). It balances uniformity and bi-directional consistency to stabilize training, differing from the standard Distortion Loss which focuses purely on compactness around true depth. A variant used in Gaussian Splatting that encourages the accumulated weights of primitives to concentrate around a single depth plane, effectively modeling an opaque surface. It sets itself apart from general depth supervision by operating directly on the internal weight distribution of the volume rendering equation rather than comparing rendered pixels to ground truth images. It is a specific instance of the broader Distortion Loss family. A heuristic adjustment rather than a direct loss term, used in conjunction with distortion-like constraints. It decreases the learning rate for scene reflectivity by 10× compared to position/opacity, encouraging the optimizer to fit data by varying occupancy (structure) rather than reflectivity. This avoids forcing Gaussians to be artificially close to each other as in the standard Depth Distortion Loss. A loss term that minimizes depth uncertainty by penalizing the variance of the depth distribution along rays, driving Gaussians toward the true surface. It explicitly formulates the penalty as the difference between the second moment of depth and the square of the first moment. It is distinct from the sibling Depth Distortion Loss by this explicit variance formulation. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray using the prefix/suffix sum optimization, where N is the number of samples. The naive implementation is O(N^2). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing prefix/suffix sums, compared to O(N^2) for the pairwise distance matrix in the naive approach. Performance: Significantly reduces artifacts like floaters and background collapse without degrading reconstruction quality, outperforming noise-injection regularizers. Strengths: Effective at enforcing compact depth distributions; differentiable; works well with both MLP-based NeRFs and point-based queries. Limitations: Implicitly assumes opaque surfaces when used with Gaussian variants; may oversmooth depth in complex light transport scenarios. When to use: When training unbounded or forward-facing scenes where background collapse is prevalent; when floaters appear in novel views. When not to use: When modeling transparent or complex light transport scenes where opaque assumptions are invalid. Distortion Loss was introduced in Mip-NeRF 360 (2022) as a regularizer to improve the quality of neural radiance fields in unbounded scenes. It was motivated by the observation that standard NeRF training often produces "floaters" and "background collapse". The efficient O(N) implementation was later popularized by DirectVoxGO (2022) to handle point-based queries with high sample counts. name: Depth Distortion Loss
head: DD Loss, L2 Depth Distortion, Nested Depth Distortion
body: Depth Distortion Loss (DD Loss) is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering and Gaussian Splatting optimization to penalize the spread of accumulated weights along a view ray. It encourages primitives to concentrate around a single depth plane, effectively modeling an opaque surface. It sets itself apart from standard depth supervision by operating directly on the internal weight distribution of the volume rendering equation rather than comparing rendered pixels to ground truth images. It is a specific instance of the broader Distortion Loss family [2755-distortion-loss.md]. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: \mathbf{x}: A 2D pixel coordinate. View ray direction and origin. For each of the N Gaussians intersecting the ray: dk: Raw depth of the Gaussian center along the view ray. ok: Intrinsic opacity of Gaussian k. \mathcal{G}k^{2D}(\mathbf{x}): 2D Gaussian density value at pixel \mathbf{x}. Tk: Transmittance accumulated up to (but not including) Gaussian k. Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L} for the pixel. Data Structures Standard per-Gaussian attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color) are used. For the current ray, the algorithm maintains arrays or registers for weights \omegak, NDC depths mk, and three running accumulators A, D, and D^2. Formula The Depth Distortion loss is defined as the sum over all pairs of Gaussians of the squared distance between their NDC-transformed depths, weighted by their rendering weights: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \sum{j=0}^{i-1} \omegai \omegaj (mi - mj)^2 where the rendering weight is \omegak = ok \mathcal{G}k^{2D}(\mathbf{x}) Tk, and mk = \text{NDC}(dk) is the depth transformed to normalized device coordinates. This expands to an efficient O(N) nested form: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \omegai \left( mi^2 A{i-1} + D{i-1}^2 - 2mi D{i-1} \right) where A{i-1} = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} \omegaj, D{i-1} = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} \omegaj mj, and D{i-1}^2 = \sum{j=0}^{i-1} \omegaj mj^2. Steps 1. For pixel \mathbf{x}, gather all N Gaussians intersecting the view ray and sort them front-to-back by raw depth dk. 2. Compute the 2D Gaussian density \mathcal{G}k^{2D}(\mathbf{x}) and transmittance Tk for each Gaussian. 3. Compute the rendering weight \omegak = ok \mathcal{G}k^{2D}(\mathbf{x}) Tk for each Gaussian. 4. Transform each raw depth dk to NDC space mk = \text{NDC}(dk) using near plane 0.2 and far plane 1000. 5. Initialize accumulators A = 0, D = 0, D2 = 0, and loss \mathcal{L} = 0. 6. Iterate i from 0 to N-1: add \omegai (mi^2 A + D2 - 2mi D) to \mathcal{L}, then update A \leftarrow A + \omegai, D \leftarrow D + \omegai mi, D2 \leftarrow D2 + \omegai mi^2. 7. Back-propagate the gradient of \mathcal{L} back-to-front through the intersection depths mi to update the Gaussians. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthdistortionloss(gaussians, nearplane=0.2, farplane=1000.0): """ Compute Depth Distortion Loss using the nested O(N) formulation. Args: gaussians: List of dicts/objects with keys: 'depth': float, raw depth dk 'opacity': float, ok 'density2d': float, Gk^2D(x) 'transmittance': float, Tk nearplane: float, NDC near plane (default 0.2) farplane: float, NDC far plane (default 1000.0) Returns: float: The DD loss value """ # Sort front-to-back by raw depth sortedgs = sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g['depth']) n = len(sortedgs) if n == 0: return 0.0 # Precompute weights and NDC depths weights = [] ndcdepths = [] for g in sortedgs: w = g['opacity'] g['density2d'] g['transmittance'] weights.append(w) # Standard linear NDC mapping: [near, far] -> [-1, 1] m = (2.0 g['depth'] - (nearplane + farplane)) / (farplane - nearplane) ndcdepths.append(m) loss = 0.0 accA = 0.0 accD = 0.0 accD2 = 0.0 for i in range(n): w = weights[i] m = ndcdepths[i] # Add nested term using accumulators from previous steps loss += w (m m accA + accD2 - 2.0 m accD) # Update accumulators for next step accA += w accD += w m accD2 += w m m return loss Parameters \lambda{dist}: Weight for the distortion loss term in the total loss function. Typical value: 0.1. NDC near plane: 0.2. NDC far plane: 1000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Opaque Surface Assumption: The loss implicitly assumes an opaque surface, which reduces the ability to model complex light transport and transparent structures. Oversmoothing: The loss tends to produce oversmoothed depth reconstructions. Scene Divergence: It may cause the scene reconstruction to diverge from accurate mean depth maps in scenes that do not conform to the opaque surface assumption. Gradient Flow: Gradients must be back-propagated back-to-front through the intersection depths to encourage Gaussians to move tightly together. Incorporates Depth Distortion Loss (R{dist}) into a broader training objective: L = L\psi + \lambdaT RT + \lambda{dist} R{dist} + \lambda{nf} R{nf}, where L\psi is a weighted L2 loss, RT is a transmittance regularization, and R{nf} is a near-far regularization. The distortion weight \lambda{dist} is set to 0.1. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel using the nested formulation, where N is the number of Gaussians along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store weights, NDC depths, and accumulators for the current ray. Strengths: Effectively pushes Gaussians towards a surface, improving depth accuracy for opaque scenes. Limitations: Fails to model transparency and complex light transport; causes oversmoothing. When to Use: When reconstructing opaque surfaces and depth accuracy is prioritized over transparency modeling. When Not to Use: For scenes with significant transparency, subsurface scattering, or complex light transport. The Depth Distortion Loss was introduced in the context of Gaussian Splatting for RGB scene reconstruction to regularize depth estimation by pushing Gaussians towards a surface. It is based on the observation that standard approaches in multi-view settings use this loss to encourage weight concentration. The method was further analyzed in "Time of the Flight of the Gaussians," which highlighted its implicit opaque surface assumption and tendency to oversmooth. It is also used in the LE3D framework for view synthesis. The implementation is based on Sun et al. 2022b and is powered by tile-based rendering. 2D Gaussian Splatting for Geometrically Accurate Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3641519.3657428, fetched 2026-10-27 Time of the Flight of the Gaussians: Optimizing Depth Indirectly in Dynamic Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01958, fetched 2026-10-26 SpaceCollectors/dust3r-3dgs, https://github.com/SpaceCollectors/dust3r-3dgs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Lighting Every Darkness with 3DGS: Fast Training and Real-Time Rendering for HDR View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-2549, fetched 2026-10-26

name: 2D-GS Loss Configuration
head: 2D-GS Training Loss, Distortion Regularization, Uni-Bi Distortion Loss
body: The 2D-GS Loss Configuration is a differentiable regularization method applied to volume rendering weights to reduce distortion artifacts. It sets itself apart from its sibling Distortion Loss by decomposing the penalty into two distinct components: a uniform term that penalizes weight magnitude, and a bi-directional term that penalizes the variance of depth distribution along rays. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: w (alpha weights, shape N{samples}), s (normalized depth parameters, shape N{samples}), rayid (ray identifiers, shape N{samples}), and nmax (maximum samples per ray). Outputs: Scalar loss and gradients for w; gradients for s, nmax, and rayid are None. Data Structures The method maintains prefix and suffix sums for weights and weighted distances, grouped by rayid: wprefix, wtotal, wsprefix, wstotal, wsuffix, and wssuffix. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forward(w, s, rayid, nmax): nrays = rayid.max() + 1 interval = 1.0 / nmax # Compute prefix sums grouped by rayid wprefix = torch.zeroslike(w) wtotal = torch.zeros(nrays) wsprefix = torch.zeroslike(w) wstotal = torch.zeros(nrays) for i in range(len(w)): rid = rayid[i] wprefix[i] = wtotal[rid] + w[i] wsprefix[i] = wstotal[rid] + w[i] s[i] wtotal[rid] = wprefix[i] wstotal[rid] = wsprefix[i] lossuni = (1.0 / 3.0) interval w w lossbi = 2.0 w (s wprefix - wsprefix) loss = (lossuni + lossbi) / nrays save(w, s, wprefix, wtotal, wsprefix, wstotal, rayid, interval) return loss def backward(gradback, savedtensors): w, s, wprefix, wtotal, wsprefix, wstotal, rayid, interval = savedtensors wsuffix = wtotal[rayid] - (wprefix + w) wssuffix = wstotal[rayid] - (wsprefix + w s) graduni = (1.0 / 3.0) interval 2.0 w gradbi = 2.0 (s (wprefix - wsuffix) + (wssuffix - wsprefix)) gradw = gradback (gradbi + graduni) return gradw, None, None, None Formulas Uniform loss: loss{uni} = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \text{interval} \cdot w^2. Bi-directional loss: loss{bi} = 2 \cdot w \cdot (s \cdot w{prefix} - ws{prefix}). Total loss: loss = \frac{loss{uni} + loss{bi}}{n{rays}}. Uniform gradient: grad{uni} = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \text{interval} \cdot 2 \cdot w. Bi-directional gradient: grad{bi} = 2 \cdot (s \cdot (w{prefix} - w{suffix}) + (ws{suffix} - ws{prefix})). Final gradient: \frac{\partial loss}{\partial w} = grad{back} \cdot (grad{bi} + grad{uni}). Suffix sums: w{suffix} = w{total}[\text{ray\id}] - (w{prefix} + w) and ws{suffix} = ws{total}[\text{ray\id}] - (ws{prefix} + w \cdot s). Parameters w: Alpha weights for each sample. s: Normalized depth parameter for each sample. nmax: Maximum number of samples per ray. rayid: Ray identifier for each sample. Distortion loss weight: 0.01. Normal loss weight: 0.05. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by zero: If nmax is 0, the interval calculation fails; ensure nmax >= 1. Gradient flow: Gradients for s, nmax, and rayid are explicitly returned as None. A distortion metric that combines L1, L2, MS-SSIM, and LPIPS error signals to align rendered images with human perception. It sets itself apart from its sibling Distortion Loss by explicitly aggregating four distinct error signals rather than relying on a single structural or pixel-wise distance. Choose it when perceptual alignment is prioritized over structural distortion penalties. A mechanism that activates new Gaussian primitives only in spatial regions where reconstruction quality falls below a prescribed fidelity target. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Composite Loss by using explicit quality metrics (PSNR and SSIM) to gate primitive activation rather than relying on non-differentiable pseudo-labels or density-based heuristics. Choose it when reducing primitive redundancy and maintaining controlled distortion levels is required. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance with hardware, resolution and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use it and when not: Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the repository "SegmentAnythingin3D". The broader use of distortion loss (Ld) and normal loss (Ln) in Gaussian Splatting variants is documented in "Octree-GS: Towards Consistent Real-time Rendering with LOD-Structured 3D Gaussians". name: Composite Loss
head: L1+L2+MS-SSIM+LPIPS, L1+L2+MS-SSIM+LPIPS loss
body: The Composite Loss is a distortion metric used in differentiable volume rendering, specifically within 3D Gaussian Splatting, that combines multiple perceptual and pixel-level metrics to align rendered images more closely with human visual perception than standard L1 or SSIM losses alone. It sets itself apart from its sibling Distortion Loss by explicitly aggregating four distinct error signals—L1, L2, Multi-Scale Structural Similarity (MS-SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS)—rather than relying on a single structural or pixel-wise distance. The method computes a weighted sum of four loss components, each measuring a different aspect of the difference between the rendered image and the ground truth image. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: I{\text{render}}: The rendered image tensor. I{\text{gt}}: The ground truth image tensor. \omega1, \omega2, \omega3, \omega4: Scalar weights for each loss term. Output: L{\text{composite}}: A scalar loss value. Data Structures: Images are treated as tensors of floating-point values. Formulas: The composite loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\textrm{composite}} = \omega1 \mathcal{L}{\textrm{L1}} + \omega2 \mathcal{L}{\textrm{L2}} + \omega3 \mathcal{L}{\textrm{MS-SSIM}} + \omega4 \mathcal{L}{\textrm{LPIPS}} Where: \mathcal{L}{\textrm{L1}} is the per-pixel L1 norm between I{\text{render}} and I{\text{gt}}. \mathcal{L}{\textrm{L2}} is the per-pixel L2 norm between I{\text{render}} and I{\text{gt}}. \mathcal{L}{\textrm{MS-SSIM}} is the multi-scale structural similarity loss. \mathcal{L}{\textrm{LPIPS}} measures perceptual distance using features extracted from a pretrained deep neural network. Parameters: The weights control the relative importance of each term. The specific configuration used in the source experiments is: \omega1 = 0.05 (L1) \omega2 = 0.30 (L2) \omega3 = 0.60 (MS-SSIM) \omega4 = 0.10 (LPIPS) Tuning these weights is described as non-trivial and engineering-intensive. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Overfitting to Training Metric: Using the same network backbone for training and evaluation causes overfitting to the specific features of the training metric. The recommended practice is to train with LPIPS-AlexNet and evaluate with LPIPS-VGG. This remains consistent with common evaluation practices in the 3D Gaussian Splatting literature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositeloss(Irender, Igt, weights=None): """ Computes the composite loss for volume rendering optimization. Args: Irender: List or array of pixel values for the rendered image. Igt: List or array of pixel values for the ground truth image. weights: Dict with keys 'w1', 'w2', 'w3', 'w4'. Defaults to [0.05, 0.30, 0.60, 0.10]. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ if weights is None: weights = {'w1': 0.05, 'w2': 0.30, 'w3': 0.60, 'w4': 0.10} # 1. L1 Loss: Mean absolute error l1 = sum(abs(r - g) for r, g in zip(Irender, Igt)) / len(Irender) # 2. L2 Loss: Mean squared error l2 = sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(Irender, Igt)) / len(Irender) # 3. MS-SSIM Loss: Multi-scale structural similarity # The sources do not provide the algorithm for MS-SSIM lmsssim = 1.0 - msssim(Irender, Igt) # 4. LPIPS Loss: Learned perceptual image patch similarity # The sources do not provide the algorithm for LPIPS llpips = lpips(Irender, Igt) # Combine with weights loss = (weights['w1'] l1 + weights['w2'] l2 + weights['w3'] lmsssim + weights['w4'] llpips) return loss Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The configuration \omega1=0.05, \omega2=0.30, \omega3=0.60, \omega4=0.10 provides a favorable trade-off between reconstruction quality and representation efficiency. Strengths: Better alignment with human visual perception compared to standard L1/SSIM losses by incorporating deep perceptual features (LPIPS) and multi-scale structural information (MS-SSIM). Limitations: Tuning the weights is non-trivial. When to use: Not given in the sources. The Composite Loss formulation was introduced in the context of "Drop-In Perceptual Optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting" by Özyılkan et al.. The authors studied three families of distortion losses: (i) L1 + SSIM, (ii) the Composite Loss (L1 + L2 + MS-SSIM + LPIPS), and (iii) Wasserstein Distortion. The composite loss generalizes the original L1 + SSIM loss by employing a weighted sum of more recent and commonly used distortion metrics. It was evaluated in a large-scale human subjective study comprising 39,320 pairwise ratings across 4 datasets and 3 distinct 3DGS frameworks. While Wasserstein Distortion emerged as a top performer in their specific analysis, the Composite Loss remains a significant baseline and alternative for perceptual optimization.
