name: Stage Control Strategy
head: Activation criteria, Explicit Stage-Control Mechanism, Quality-Constrained Stage Control, Stage Control
body: The Stage Control Strategy is a mechanism that activates new Gaussian primitives only in spatial regions where the current reconstruction quality falls below a prescribed fidelity target, avoiding redundancy and promoting compactness. It solves the problem of unnecessary primitive allocation by restricting new Gaussian introduction to under-reconstructed areas, thereby reducing the total number of Gaussians while maintaining controlled distortion levels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Composite Loss by using explicit quality metrics (PSNR and SSIM) to gate primitive activation rather than relying on non-differentiable pseudo-labels or density-based heuristics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground-truth image I{gt}, reconstructed image from the previous stage I{i-1}, candidate Gaussian set predicted by the current stage \Delta \hat{G}i, and fidelity thresholds \tau{psnr} and \tau{ssim}. Outputs: Effective Gaussian subset \Delta Gi to be added to the scene. Data Structures: Quality Maps: Two 2D maps, Q{i-1}^{psnr} and Q{i-1}^{ssim}, with dimensions matching the spatial resolution of the image patches. Activation Mask: A binary 2D map Mi with the same spatial dimensions as the patches, where each element is 0 or 1. Candidate Gaussians: A dense set of predicted Gaussian parameters \Delta \hat{G}i, one per spatial token/patch. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Quality Maps: Calculate the PSNR and SSIM between the ground-truth image I{gt} and the previous stage's reconstruction I{i-1} for each spatial location u. Q{i-1}^{psnr} = Q{psnr}(I{gt}, I{i-1}) Q{i-1}^{ssim} = Q{ssim}(I{gt}, I{i-1}) 2. Generate Activation Mask: Create a binary mask Mi(u) for each spatial location u. A location is marked for activation (1) if either the PSNR is below \tau{psnr} OR the SSIM is below \tau{ssim}. Otherwise, it is masked out (0). Mi(u) = \mathbb{I}(Q{i-1}^{psnr}(u) < \tau{psnr} \lor Q{i-1}^{ssim}(u) < \tau{ssim}) 3. Apply Mask to Candidates: Perform patch-wise masking on the dense candidate Gaussian set \Delta \hat{G}i using Mi to obtain the effective subset \Delta Gi. \Delta Gi = Mi \odot \Delta \hat{G}i where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication or masking, effectively zeroing out or discarding candidates where Mi(u) = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def stagecontrolstrategy(Igt, Iprev, candidategaussians, taupsnr, taussim, patchsize): """ Activates new Gaussians only where reconstruction quality is insufficient. Args: Igt: Ground truth image tensor (H, W, C). Iprev: Reconstructed image from previous stage (H, W, C). candidategaussians: Dense set of predicted Gaussian parameters, one per spatial token/patch. taupsnr: PSNR threshold (float, e.g., 35.0). taussim: SSIM threshold (float, e.g., 0.95). patchsize: Spatial dimension of each patch/token. Returns: effectivegaussians: Subset of candidategaussians activated by the mask. """ H, W, C = Igt.shape rows = H // patchsize cols = W // patchsize mask = [] for r in range(rows): for c in range(cols): y1, y2 = r patchsize, (r + 1) patchsize x1, x2 = c patchsize, (c + 1) patchsize pgt = Igt[y1:y2, x1:x2,:] pprev = Iprev[y1:y2, x1:x2,:] # Compute patch-wise PSNR mse = sum((pgt - pprev) 2) / (patchsize patchsize C) psnr = 10 math.log10(1.0 / (mse + 1e-8)) # Compute patch-wise SSIM using standard windowed statistics mux = sum(pgt) / (patchsize patchsize C) muy = sum(pprev) / (patchsize patchsize C) sigmaxsq = sum((pgt - mux) 2) / (patchsize patchsize C) sigmaysq = sum((pprev - muy) 2) / (patchsize patchsize C) sigmaxy = sum((pgt - mux) (pprev - muy)) / (patchsize patchsize C) C1, C2 = 1e-4, 1e-4 ssim = ((2 mux muy + C1) (2 sigmaxy + C2)) / \ ((mux2 + muy2 + C1) (sigmaxsq + sigmaysq + C2)) mask.append(psnr < taupsnr or ssim < taussim) effectivegaussians = [g for g, m in zip(candidategaussians, mask) if m] return effectivegaussians Parameters: \tau{psnr}: PSNR threshold. Default value: 35 dB. \tau{ssim}: SSIM threshold. Default value: 0.95. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Sensitivity: Increasing thresholds imposes a stricter fidelity target, activating more primitives. Decreasing them yields a more compact representation but may degrade quality. No Masking: If no mask is applied (all Gaussians activated), the method uses the maximum number of primitives (e.g., 58,114 in the cited experiment). Metric Complementarity: Using only PSNR or only SSIM provides an incomplete quality criterion. PSNR detects large local reconstruction errors, while SSIM captures structural distortions not fully reflected by pixel-wise error. Combining them covers both pixel-level errors and structural degradation. Time Complexity: The method requires computing PSNR and SSIM maps for the previous stage's reconstruction, which is O(H \times W) per stage, where H and W are image dimensions. The masking operation is also O(N), where N is the number of candidate Gaussians (proportional to H \times W / ps^2). Memory Complexity: Requires storing two quality maps (Q{psnr} and Q{ssim}) and the activation mask Mi, each of size proportional to the number of spatial tokens. Measured Performance: No mask: PSNR 30.89 dB, Utilization 1.00, #Gaussians 58,114. PSNR target 35 dB only: PSNR 30.60 dB, Utilization 0.69, #Gaussians 40,163. SSIM target 0.95 only: PSNR 30.29 dB, Utilization 0.75, #Gaussians 43,750. Joint PSNR 35 dB and SSIM 0.95: PSNR 30.76 dB, Utilization 0.79, #Gaussians 46,001. Joint PSNR 35 dB and SSIM 0.98: PSNR 30.87 dB, Utilization 0.90, #Gaussians 52,318. Utilization Ratio: The proportion of activated Gaussians among all candidate Gaussians, calculated as 4 \times (H/ps) \times (W/ps) where H, W are image dimensions and ps is patch size. Strengths: Reduces unnecessary primitives under a controlled distortion level. Improves over MSE-only and SSIM-only variants by combining complementary quality cues. Limitations: Requires access to ground-truth images for quality map computation during training (self-supervised context). Performance is sensitive to threshold selection. The Stage Control Strategy was proposed in the context of the AIR (Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework) for self-supervised feed-forward 2D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the drawbacks of scaling pipelines that inject inductive bias and are expensive to train. The method follows a constrained reconstruction objective: using as few Gaussians as possible while satisfying a prescribed fidelity target. It replaces non-differentiable pseudo-labels (like those used in Instant-GI) with an explicit quality-constrained mechanism. The default thresholds of 35 dB PSNR and 0.95 SSIM were chosen to keep utilization at a moderate level while maintaining competitive perceptual quality. AIR: Amortized Image Reconstruction Framework for Self-Supervised Feed-Forward 2D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.20820, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Depth Distribution Constraint
head: Depth Distortion Regularization, Depth Uncertainty Loss, Depth Variance Loss
body: The Depth Distribution Constraint is a regularization term applied during 3D Gaussian splatting optimization to constrain Gaussians to aggregate at object surfaces, improving 3D structural reconstruction quality. It minimizes depth uncertainty by penalizing the variance of the depth distribution along rays, driving Gaussians toward the true surface. It is distinct from the sibling Depth Distortion Loss by explicitly formulating the penalty as the difference between the second moment of depth and the square of the first moment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N Gaussians intersected by a ray. For each Gaussian i, the method requires the weight wi (contribution to the ray) and the depth di (distance from camera center to the Gaussian center along the ray). Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}u representing the depth uncertainty. Data Structures: N: The number of Gaussians contributing to the ray. wi: The transmittance-weighted contribution of the i-th Gaussian, typically computed as wi = \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the opacity. di: The depth of the i-th Gaussian along the ray. Steps: 1. Collect weights wi and depths di for all N Gaussians intersected by the ray. 2. Compute the expected depth \mathcal{D} = \sum{i \in N} wi di. 3. Compute the second moment \mathcal{D}{sq} = \sum{i \in N} wi di^2. 4. Calculate the uncertainty loss \mathcal{L}u = \mathcal{D}{sq} - \mathcal{D}^2. Formulas: The loss is defined as the variance of the depth distribution: \mathcal{L}u = \mathcal{D}{sq} - \mathcal{D}^2 where: \mathcal{D} is the expected depth (first moment), defined as \mathcal{D} = \sum{i \in N} wi di. \mathcal{D}{sq} is the second moment of the depth distribution, defined as \mathcal{D}{sq} = \sum{i \in N} wi di^2. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthdistributionconstraint(weights, depths): """ Computes the depth distribution constraint loss. Args: weights (list[float]): List of weights wi for each Gaussian along the ray. depths (list[float]): List of depths di for each Gaussian along the ray. Returns: float: The uncertainty loss Lu. """ # Calculate the expected depth D (first moment) expecteddepth = 0.0 for w, d in zip(weights, depths): expecteddepth += w d # Calculate the second moment Dsq secondmoment = 0.0 for w, d in zip(weights, depths): secondmoment += w (d 2) # Compute uncertainty loss loss = secondmoment - (expecteddepth 2) return loss Edge cases and pitfalls: If all weights are zero (no Gaussians intersect the ray), the sums evaluate to zero, resulting in a loss of 0. This is generally acceptable as there is no depth to constrain. Numerical precision: If the depth distribution is very narrow, \mathcal{D}{sq} \approx \mathcal{D}^2, leading to potential cancellation errors. In standard 3DGS optimization, this is rarely an issue due to the nature of the opacity accumulation. A sibling loss that also penalizes depth estimation errors but may use different formulations for distortion. Choose this when the primary goal is minimizing pixel-wise depth error rather than structural surface aggregation. Link A configuration for 2D Gaussian Splatting that may include similar regularization terms adapted for 2D primitives. Choose this when working with 2D Gaussian primitives instead of 3D. Link Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of Gaussians along the ray. This is negligible compared to the rendering and densification steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it only requires summing two values. Strengths: Improves 3D structural reconstruction, which is crucial for downstream tasks like refocusing. It effectively reduces foreground/background ambiguity by forcing Gaussians to the surface. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the object possesses an accurate surface. It may not be suitable for transparent or volumetric scenes where depth is inherently distributed. When to use: When structural fidelity is important for downstream applications (e.g., refocusing, normal estimation) and the scene consists of opaque surfaces. When not to use: For scenes with significant transparency or volumetric effects where depth is not concentrated at a single surface. The Depth Distribution Constraint was introduced in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to address structural reconstruction issues. It was notably used in the LE3D method to enhance structural details for downstream tasks like refocusing. The formulation as a variance minimization (\mathcal{D}{sq} - \mathcal{D}^2) is derived from the statistical definition of variance, treating the depth distribution as a probability distribution weighted by Gaussian contributions. name: Curvature Loss
body: Curvature Loss is a geometric regularization term that applies a curvature operator to the model output and scales the result by a configurable weight. It operates on second-order derivatives of the implicit function, distinguishing it from sibling methods that use first-order derivatives or pixel-space alignment. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Model output (scalar field values) at query points. Output: A scalar curvature loss value. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Method: 1. Evaluate the model output at the query points. 2. Apply the curvature operator C to the model output. 3. Multiply the result by the curvature loss weight \lambda{\text{curvature}}. Formula: L{\text{curv}} = \lambda{\text{curvature}} \cdot C(\text{model output}) where: \lambda{\text{curvature}} is the curvature loss weight. C(\cdot) is the curvature operator applied to the model output. Parameters: \lambda{\text{curvature}}: The weight for the curvature loss term, retrieved from self.config.system.loss.lambdacurvature. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecurvatureloss(modeloutput, lambdacurvature): """ Computes the curvature regularization loss. Args: modeloutput: Tensor of model predictions (e.g., SDF values). lambdacurvature: Float weight for the curvature loss. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # Compute curvature operator C on modeloutput. # Standard implementations use automatic differentiation of the network # to compute second-order derivatives (e.g., Laplacian). curvaturevalues = modeloutput # Represents C(modeloutput) # Multiply by the curvature loss weight weightedcurvature = lambdacurvature curvaturevalues # Reduce to a scalar by computing the arithmetic mean return weightedcurvature.mean() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Computing second-order derivatives can be numerically unstable if the network output is not smooth. Ensure the network architecture supports stable gradient computation (e.g., using smooth activation functions). Boundaries: Curvature is undefined or ill-behaved at domain boundaries. Exclude points near the boundary of the query volume or use appropriate padding. Degenerate Input: If the scalar field is constant, curvature is zero and provides no gradient. Focuses on sign changes at mesh edges to enforce zero-crossing consistency for discrete representations like FlexiCubes. Sets itself apart by targeting edge connectivity rather than continuous curvature. Choose when sharp features or correct topology at boundaries are required. Penalizes discontinuities in surface normals along viewing rays. Sets itself apart by operating on first-order derivatives (dot product of consecutive normals) rather than higher-order operators. Choose when enforcing spatial coherence of surface orientation is prioritized over curvature. Computes and penalizes Gaussian and Mean curvatures directly on the implicit function. Sets itself apart by operating on the final implicit function's differential geometry within the loss. Choose when direct surface regularization is needed. Dynamically scales down curvature regularization strength as optimization progresses. Sets itself apart by adapting intensity to spatial resolution rather than using a static weight. Choose when preserving high-frequency details during fine-grained optimization is critical. The method is implemented in the Instant-NSR-PL framework. Specific origin details and historical development are not given in the sources. bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, https://github.com/bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Edge Regularization Loss
body: A loss function that penalizes Signed Distance Function (SDF) values at mesh edges where the sign changes, encouraging sharp features or correct topology at boundaries. It differs from general curvature penalties by focusing specifically on discrete edge connectivity to enforce zero-crossing consistency. Inputs: sdf: Tensor of SDF values at vertices. Shape not given in the sources. alledges: Tensor of edge indices mapping vertices to edges. Shape not given in the sources. Outputs: loss: Scalar tensor representing the regularization loss. Data Structures: sdfedges: Intermediate tensor storing SDF values at edge endpoints, with shape [E, 2] where E is the number of edges. mask: Boolean tensor identifying edges with sign changes. Steps: 1. Gather SDF values at edge endpoints: sdfedges = sdf[alledges.reshape(-1)].reshape(-1, 2). 2. Create a mask for edges where signs differ: mask = torch.sign(sdfedges[:, 0]) != torch.sign(sdfedges[:, 1]). 3. Filter SDF values to only those edges with sign changes: sdffiltered = sdfedges[mask]. 4. Compute binary cross-entropy loss between the first endpoint and the boolean second endpoint, and vice versa. 5. Return the computed loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def sdfedgeregularizationloss(sdf, alledges): # 1. Gather SDF values at edge endpoints sdfedges = sdf[alledges.reshape(-1)].reshape(-1, 2) # 2. Create mask for edges where signs differ mask = torch.sign(sdfedges[:, 0]) != torch.sign(sdfedges[:, 1]) # 3. Filter SDF values to only those edges with sign changes sdffiltered = sdfedges[mask] if sdffiltered.numel() == 0: return torch.tensor(0.0, device=sdf.device) # 4. Compute binary cross-entropy loss between first endpoint and boolean second endpoint, and vice versa # Targets are boolean flags for the opposite endpoint's sign target0 = (sdffiltered[:, 1] > 0).float() target1 = (sdffiltered[:, 0] > 0).float() # SDF values are passed directly to BCE; a sigmoid or scaling step is typically applied in practice loss01 = F.binarycrossentropy(sdffiltered[:, 0], target0) loss10 = F.binarycrossentropy(sdffiltered[:, 1], target1) return (loss01 + loss10) / 2.0 Parameters: None explicitly defined in sources. Edge Cases: No edges with sign changes: Return 0 loss. Precision: SDF values near 0 may cause unstable gradients if not handled. A regularization term to prevent density from growing from background into foreground by enforcing the SDF decision boundary using low-resolution SDF values. It minimizes the SDF likelihood under a Laplacian distribution using low-resolution probe values. Formula: L{dec} = \sum{zhw} \exp(-2|S{zhw}|) where S{zhw} are SDF values from the low-resolution probe (192 \times 128 \times 128), z refers to the sample index, and h,w to pixel. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enforces sharp features and correct topology at boundaries. Limitations: Only applies to edges with sign changes, potentially ignoring smooth regions. When to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of differentiable volume rendering and mesh extraction, specifically associated with the FlexiCubes implementation. It is used to improve the geometric quality of extracted meshes by ensuring consistent SDF signs across edges. name: Normal Smoothness Loss
head: Normal Continuity Loss, Normal Smoothness
body: Normal Smoothness Loss is a regularization term for differentiable volume rendering that encourages geometric consistency by penalizing discontinuities in surface normals along a viewing ray. It differs from sibling methods like Surface Curvature Regularization by operating directly on the dot product of consecutive normals rather than higher-order differential operators, and from Normal Regularization Loss by relying solely on internal spatial coherence rather than external monocular depth/normal estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of surface normals \mathbf{n}i computed at sample points along a ray, and a scalar weight w. Outputs: A scalar loss value L representing the smoothness penalty. Data Structures: Normals Array: A list or tensor of 3D vectors \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, where each vector is normalized (\|\mathbf{n}i\| = 1). The order corresponds to the sampling order along the ray (e.g., from near to far). Steps: 1. Iterate through the sequence of normals along the ray. 2. For each sample point i (where i > 0), compute the dot product between the current normal \mathbf{n}i and the previous normal \mathbf{n}{i-1}. 3. Calculate the per-pair loss as 1.0 - (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}{i-1}). 4. Aggregate the loss by summing over all pairs along the ray. 5. Scale the aggregated loss by the weight w. Formula: L = w \cdot (1 - \mathbf{n}p \cdot \mathbf{n}{prev}) Where: L is the loss contribution for a pair of adjacent samples. w is the weight scalar. \mathbf{n}p is the normal at the current sample point. \mathbf{n}{prev} is the normal at the previous sample point along the ray. Parameters: Weight (w): Float scalar multiplying the loss term. Typical value: 1.0. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Ray Tracking: The method requires tracking adjacent sample normals along a ray. This is not natively supported by all standard volume renderers, which may process samples independently or in parallel batches without maintaining ray-wise history. Implementation Status: In some codebases, this is currently a placeholder for future implementation due to the difficulty of integrating ray-wise state into the integrator. Normalization: Normals must be normalized before computing the dot product to ensure the metric accurately reflects angular difference. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalsmoothnessloss(normals: list, weight: float = 1.0) -> float: """ Computes the Normal Smoothness Loss for a single ray. Args: normals: List of normalized 3D vectors representing surface normals at consecutive sample points along the ray, ordered from near to far. weight: Scalar weight for the loss term. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ if len(normals) < 2: return 0.0 totalloss = 0.0 for i in range(1, len(normals)): np = normals[i] nprev = normals[i-1] # Compute dot product dotproduct = sum(a b for a, b in zip(np, nprev)) # Clamp to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors dotproduct = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dotproduct)) # Calculate loss for this pair: 1.0 - dotproduct pairloss = 1.0 - dotproduct totalloss += pairloss # Scale the aggregated loss by the weight return weight totalloss A regularization term that uses the Jacobian of the map of normals to regularize scene geometry, derived from differential geometry principles. It differs from the basic smoothness loss by considering the spatial variation of the normal field across the image plane (or ray bundle) rather than just along a single ray. It is significantly slower to compute, processing approximately 1100 rays/s compared to ~5000 rays/s for depth regularization on an NVIDIA V100. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The Jacobian-based variant is much slower than depth regularization, with measured performance of ~1100 rays/s vs ~5000 rays/s on NVIDIA V100. Memory: Requires storing normals for adjacent samples along the ray, or recomputing them. The basic implementation requires minimal extra memory beyond the normal field itself. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA V100, normals regularization (Jacobian-based) processes ~1100 rays/s, while depth regularization processes ~5000 rays/s. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Encourages geometric smoothness by penalizing normal discontinuities. Limitations: Requires ray-wise state tracking which may not be supported by all integrators; slower than depth-based regularization if using Jacobian variants; may oversmooth fine geometric details if weight is too high. When to Use: Use when normal consistency is critical and computational budget allows for ray-wise processing. Avoid when high throughput is required and depth regularization suffices. The concept of normal smoothness as a regularization term in differentiable rendering is discussed in the context of Total Light Inverse Rendering (TLIR). The specific formula L = w \cdot (1 - \mathbf{n}p \cdot \mathbf{n}{prev}) is documented in the TLIR codebase. Differential geometry-based normal regularization, including Jacobian approaches, is detailed in "Regularization of NeRFs using differential geometry". name: Normal Regularization Loss
head: Monocular Normals Regularization
body:
Normal Regularization Loss enforces geometric consistency in differentiable volume rendering and Gaussian splatting by combining monocular normal supervision with a total variation smoothness prior on predicted normals. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Normal Smoothness Loss by explicitly incorporating external monocular normal estimates to anchor the geometry, rather than relying solely on internal spatial coherence. The method minimizes a composite loss \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}} defined as the sum of a monocular normal loss \mathcal{L}{\hat{N}} and a smoothness prior \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}}. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Predicted normal map \hat{ oldsymbol{N}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W 	imes 3}, monocular normal estimates  oldsymbol{N}{	ext{mono}}, and scaling parameters  oldsymbol{s}i for each Gaussian primitive i. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}}. Data Structures: \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j}: The predicted normal vector at pixel coordinates (i, j).  oldsymbol{s}i: A 3D vector representing the scaling axes of the i-th Gaussian. Formulas: 1. Monocular Normal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\hat{N}}): An L1 loss between the predicted normals and monocular estimates. \mathcal{L}{\hat{N}} = \sum{i,j} \| \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j} -  oldsymbol{N}{	ext{mono}, i,j} \|1 2. Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}}): Encourages spatial smoothness using finite differences. \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}} = \sum{i,j} \left( |
ablai \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j}| + |
ablaj \hat{ oldsymbol{N}}{i,j}| ight) Where 
abla is the finite difference operator convolving with [-1, 1] for the i-axis and [-1, 1]^	op for the j-axis. 3. Scale Loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{scale}}): Applied to force Gaussians to become disc-like surfels, aiding normal estimation convergence. \mathcal{L}{	ext{scale}} = \sumi \|\arg\min( oldsymbol{s}i)\|1 The normal \hat{ oldsymbol{n}}i is derived from the scaling axes via a rotation matrix R and a one-hot encoding of the minimum axis index: \hat{ oldsymbol{n}}i = R \cdot 	ext{OneHot}(\arg\min( oldsymbol{s}i)) The rotation matrix R is constructed from quaternion q = (w, x, y, z)^	op: R =  egin{bmatrix} 1 - 2(y^2 + z^2) & 2(xy - wz) & 2(xz + wy) \ 2(xy + wz) & 1 - 2(x^2 + z^2) & 2(yz - wx) \ 2(xz - wy) & 2(yz + wx) & 1 - 2(x^2 + y^2) \end{bmatrix} 4. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}} = \mathcal{L}{\hat{N}} + \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}}. Parameters: Weight for smoothness prior: Not given in the sources. Weight for scale loss: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Monocular Normal Loss (L1) lmono = 0.0 for i in range(H): for j in range(W): for k in range(3): lmono += abs(predictednormals[i, j, k] - monocularnormals[i, j, k]) # 2. Smoothness Loss (Total Variation) lsmooth = 0.0 for i in range(H): for j in range(W): # i-axis difference (row direction) if i < H - 1: diffi = [predictednormals[i+1, j, k] - predictednormals[i, j, k] for k in range(3)] lsmooth += sum(abs(d) for d in diffi) # j-axis difference (column direction) if j < W - 1: diffj = [predictednormals[i, j+1, k] - predictednormals[i, j, k] for k in range(3)] lsmooth += sum(abs(d) for d in diffj) # 3. Scale Loss (auxiliary, not included in Lnormal per source formula) lscale = 0.0 for i in range(N): minidx = 0 for k in range(1, 3): if scales[i, k] < scales[i, minidx]: minidx = k lscale += minidx # ||argmin(si)||1 for a scalar index is the index itself return lmono + lsmooth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Not given in the sources. It differs from the standard smoothness loss by using image intensity gradients as edge-aware weights. Parameters: \lambda{n-TV} = 5.0. When to choose: Use when working with inverse rendering tasks where preserving sharp edges in the normal map corresponding to object boundaries is critical, as the exponential weighting suppresses smoothing across intensity discontinuities. name: Normal Consistency Loss
head: Face normal smoothness, Structural Regularization
body: Normal Consistency Loss is a regularization term that penalizes geometric inconsistency between different normal estimates derived from a radiance field or mesh, thereby enforcing local surface smoothness and reducing artifacts such as floaters or mesh face flipping. It builds on Normal Smoothness Loss by explicitly comparing normals derived from distinct geometric proxies (e.g., density gradients versus depth maps, or adjacent mesh faces) rather than enforcing continuity along a single ray path. The method is applied in two representation contexts based on the source literature: radiance fields with depth supervision and joint optimization of explicit meshes with Gaussian splats. Inputs: 1. Radiance Field Context: \mathbf{N}\sigma: Rendered density-gradient normal. \mathbf{N}{\text{mean}}: Normal estimated from the expected (mean) depth map. \mathbf{N}{\text{med}}: Normal estimated from the median depth map. 2. Mesh Context: Nf: Set of all pairs of neighboring faces in the mesh. ni, nj: Surface normals of adjacent mesh faces i and j. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}n or L{nc}. Normals: 3D unit vectors \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Mesh Topology: Adjacency list or face-pair index set Nf defining neighboring triangles. 1. Radiance Field Variant (Structural Regularization) This variant addresses the issue where LiDAR depth supervision only constrains the field along measured rays, leaving the density to ripple or drift between anchors. It penalizes the inconsistency between the rendered density-gradient normal and normals estimated from rendered depth maps. \mathcal{L}n = \|\mathbf{N}\sigma - \mathbf{N}{\text{mean}}\|2^2 + \|\mathbf{N}\sigma - \mathbf{N}{\text{med}}\|2^2 \quad (15) Where: \mathbf{N}\sigma: The normal derived from the gradient of the volume density \nabla \sigma. \mathbf{N}{\text{mean}}: The normal computed from the expected depth. \mathbf{N}{\text{med}}: The normal computed from the median depth. 2. Mesh Variant (Face Normal Smoothness) This variant encourages a smoother surface and reduces mesh face flipping during optimization. L{nc} = \frac{1}{|Nf|} \sum{(i,j) \in Nf} (1 - ni \cdot nj) \quad (7) Where: Nf: The set of all pairs of neighboring faces in the mesh. ni, nj: The surface normals of adjacent mesh faces i and j. |Nf|: The number of such neighboring face pairs. \lambda{nc}: The weight of the normal consistency loss in the total training objective. \lambdan: The weight of the monocular normal loss in the total training objective, used in the combined loss L = L{img} + \lambda{lap} L{lap} + \lambda{nc} L{nc} + \lambdan Ln. (The radiance field variant does not specify a weighting coefficient in the provided sources.) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computenormalconsistencyloss(meshpairs, normals, mode="mesh"): """ Computes Normal Consistency Loss. Args: meshpairs: List of tuples (i, j) representing neighboring face indices. Ignored when mode is 'radiance'. normals: Dictionary containing normal vectors. For 'mesh' mode: Array-like of shape (numfaces, 3) for face normals. For 'radiance' mode: Dict with keys 'Nsigma', 'Nmean', 'Nmed'. mode: String, either "mesh" or "radiance". Returns: Scalar loss value. """ if mode == "mesh": totalloss = 0.0 numpairs = 0 for i, j in meshpairs: ni = normals[i] nj = normals[j] dotproduct = sum(a b for a, b in zip(ni, nj)) totalloss += (1.0 - dotproduct) numpairs += 1 if numpairs == 0: return 0.0 return totalloss / numpairs elif mode == "radiance": Nsigma = normals['Nsigma'] Nmean = normals['Nmean'] Nmed = normals['Nmed'] diffmean = [a - b for a, b in zip(Nsigma, Nmean)] lossmean = sum(d d for d in diffmean) diffmed = [a - b for a, b in zip(Nsigma, Nmed)] lossmed = sum(d d for d in diffmed) return lossmean + lossmed else: raise ValueError("Mode must be 'mesh' or 'radiance'") Precision: In the mesh variant, normals must be normalized before computing the dot product to ensure the range is [-1, 1]. Degenerate Input: If no neighboring face pairs exist (|Nf| = 0), the denominator in the mesh formula is zero. The pseudocode handles this by returning 0.0. Floaters: In the radiance field variant, without this loss, density can ripple or drift between LiDAR anchors, creating floaters. Time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory complexity is not given in the sources. It effectively suppresses floaters in front of occupied voxels in sparse voxel maps. It reduces mesh distortion (e.g., intersecting triangles) and face flipping during joint optimization. It acts as a geometric prior that constrains optimization, improving surface quality. It does not constrain the field along unmeasured rays in the radiance field variant; it only smooths between proxies. It requires accurate depth estimation or mesh topology. The radiance field variant was introduced in the context of Sparse Radiance Voxels (SpaRV) for LiDAR-Visual Mapping. It addresses the ambiguity in density fields between sparse LiDAR anchors. The mesh variant was inspired by conventional mesh optimization works [8, 22] and Laplacian smoothing [10, 25], and it was adopted in OMeGa for joint optimization of explicit meshes and Gaussian splats. name: Surface Curvature Regularization
head: Curvature Regularization, Curvature Regularization using Curvatures, Gaussian and Mean Curvature Loss, Mean Curvature Regularization, Surface Regularization using Curvatures
body:
Surface Curvature Regularization is a technique for regularizing neural implicit surfaces (specifically Signed Distance Functions, SDFs) by computing and penalizing Gaussian and Mean curvatures directly during training, rather than regularizing projections or depth maps. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating on the final implicit function's differential geometry within the loss function, enabling direct surface regularization. It builds on Curvature Loss. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained or training neural implicit surface model f(\mathbf{x}) (typically an SDF), a set of surface points S (points where f(\mathbf{x}) \approx 0), and hyperparameters w{	ext{curv}} (or \lambda{	ext{curv}}) and \kappa{	ext{curv}}. Output: A scalar curvature loss value \mathcal{L}{	ext{curv}} added to the total training loss. Data Structures: Surface Points S: A set of 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}i sampled near the zero-level set of the SDF. SDF Model f: A neural network mapping \mathbb{R}^3 	o \mathbb{R}. Gradients/Hessians: First and second-order derivatives of f with respect to spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}. Method Steps: 1. Sample Surface Points: Collect a batch of points \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^N located on or near the implicit surface. 2. Compute Derivatives: Calculate the gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}i) and the Hessian matrix H(f)(\mathbf{x}i) (or its discrete approximation) at each point. Pitfall: For hash-based encodings with trilinear interpolation, second-order analytical gradients are zero everywhere. Therefore, a discrete Laplacian approach (similar to numerical gradient computation) must be used to compute curvature, reusing the six additional SDF samples required for numerical surface normal computation to avoid extra forward passes. 3. Compute Curvature: Calculate the curvature metric \gamma(\mathbf{x}i) for each point. Two common metrics are used: Mean Curvature: Computed via the discrete Laplacian 
abla^2 f(\mathbf{x}i). Gaussian Curvature: Computed using the formula involving the gradient and the adjoint of the Hessian: \gamma{	ext{gauss}} =  rac{
abla F 	imes H^(F) 	imes 
abla F^t}{\|
abla F\|^4} where H^ is the adjoint of the Hessian of F. 4. Clip Curvature: Apply a clipping function to the absolute curvature to prevent large outliers from dominating the gradient: 	ext{clip}(|\gamma(\mathbf{x}i)|) = \min(|\gamma(\mathbf{x}i)|, \kappa{	ext{curv}}) where \kappa{	ext{curv}} is the clipping threshold. 5. Aggregate Loss: Compute the mean curvature loss over the batch. Using Mean Curvature (Neuralangelo style): \mathcal{L}{	ext{curv}} =  rac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N |
abla^2 f(\mathbf{x}i)| Using Gaussian or Mean Curvature with Clipping (VolSDF style): \mathcal{L}{	ext{curv}}(\kappa{	ext{curv}}) = \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{x} \in S}[\min(|\gamma(\mathbf{x})|, \kappa{	ext{curv}})] 6. Combine with Total Loss: Add the weighted curvature loss to the total loss function. Neuralangelo: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{	ext{RGB}} + w{	ext{eik}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} + w{	ext{curv}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{curv}} VolSDF: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{	ext{RGB}} + \lambda{	ext{SDF}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{SDF}} + \lambda{	ext{curv}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{curv}}(\kappa{	ext{curv}}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecurvatureloss(sdfmodel, surfacepoints, curvaturetype='mean', clippingthreshold=1.0, stepsize=1e-3): """Computes the surface curvature regularization loss.""" N = len(surfacepoints) curvatures = [] for i in range(N): x = surfacepoints[i] if curvaturetype == 'mean': # Discrete Laplacian using 6 neighbors (reuses normal computation samples) # 
abla^2 f \approx (f(x+h) + f(x-h) + f(y+h) + f(y-h) + f(z+h) + f(z-h) - 6f(x)) / h^2 fx = sdfmodel(x) fxh = sdfmodel(x + stepsize [1, 0, 0]) fxm = sdfmodel(x - stepsize [1, 0, 0]) fyh = sdfmodel(x + stepsize [0, 1, 0]) fym = sdfmodel(x - stepsize [0, 1, 0]) fzh = sdfmodel(x + stepsize [0, 0, 1]) fzm = sdfmodel(x - stepsize [0, 0, 1]) laplacian = (fxh + fxm + fyh + fym + fzh + fzm - 6 fx) / (stepsize 2) curvatures.append(abs(laplacian)) elif curvaturetype == 'gaussian': # Analytical gradient and Hessian adjoint (for non-hash encodings) gradf = computegradient(sdfmodel, x) hessianf = computehessian(sdfmodel, x) numerator = dot(gradf, matvec(hessianf, gradf)) denominator = norm(gradf) 4 curv = numerator / denominator curvatures.append(abs(curv)) abscurvatures = curvatures clipped = [min(c, clippingthreshold) for c in abscurvatures] loss = sum(clipped) / N return loss def computegradient(model, x): # Standard automatic differentiation for first-order derivatives return model.gradient(x) def computehessian(model, x): # Standard automatic differentiation for second-order derivatives return model.hessian(x) def dot(a, b): return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def norm(v): return dot(v, v) 0.5 def matvec(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))] Parameters: w{	ext{curv}} (or \lambda{	ext{curv}}): Curvature regularization strength. In Neuralangelo, this linearly warms up to 5 	imes 10^{-4} following the learning rate schedule and decays by the same spacing factor between hash resolutions every time \epsilon decreases. \kappa{	ext{curv}}: A clipping value for the curvature regularization loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Encoding Gradients: Second-order analytical gradients of hash encoding are zero everywhere when using trilinear interpolation. Using analytical Hessians will result in zero curvature loss. One must use a discrete Laplacian approach. Sharp Transitions: Without curvature regularization, surfaces tend to have undesirable sharp transitions and noise. Concave Shapes: Curvature regularization alone may not fully resolve concave shapes; topology warmup or other priors may be needed in conjunction. DiffNeRF Curvature Regularization is a technique for regularizing neural implicit surfaces (specifically VolSDF) by computing and penalizing Gaussian and Mean curvatures directly during training, rather than regularizing projections or depth maps. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating on the final implicit function's differential geometry within the loss function, enabling direct surface regularization. Time Complexity: Adds computational overhead proportional to the number of surface points N and the cost of computing second-order derivatives. However, by reusing samples from normal computation (discrete Laplacian), the number of forward passes is minimized. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradients and Hessians for the batch of surface points. No additional large data structures are needed. Strengths: Removes surface noise and prevents undesirable sharp transitions, leading to smoother reconstructed surfaces. Allows direct regularization of the surface geometry rather than indirect regularization via projections. Limitations: Requires careful handling of derivative computation, especially for hash-based encodings where analytical second derivatives vanish. May oversmooth fine details if the weight w{	ext{curv}} is too high. When to use: When high-fidelity surface reconstruction is required and the implicit model exhibits noisy or jagged surfaces. Particularly useful in Neuralangelo and VolSDF pipelines. When not to use: When preserving sharp features is critical and the regularization weight cannot be tuned low enough, or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of second-order derivative computation is prohibitive. Surface Curvature Regularization originates from the need to improve the smoothness and quality of neural implicit surface reconstructions. It was notably employed in Neuralangelo to regularize the mean curvature of SDFs computed via discrete Laplacian, addressing issues with hash encoding gradients. It was also explored in VolSDF where Gaussian and Mean curvatures were computed analytically to regularize the surface directly. The method addresses the tendency of unregularized neural implicit surfaces to exhibit noise and sharp, unnatural transitions. name: DiffNeRF Curvature Regularization
head: Gaussian/Mean Curvature Regularization for VolSDF, Regularization of NeRFs using differential geometry
body:
DiffNeRF Curvature Regularization is a technique for regularizing neural implicit surfaces (specifically VolSDF) by computing and penalizing Gaussian and Mean curvatures directly during training, rather than regularizing projections or depth maps. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating on the final implicit function's differential geometry within the loss function, enabling direct surface regularization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A neural network F representing an implicit signed distance function (SDF), where the surface S is defined as \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid F(x) = 0\}. Sample points x are drawn from the surface S and the volume \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A curvature regularization loss term L{curv} added to the total training loss. Data Structures: Implicit Function F: A neural network taking 3D coordinates x and outputting a scalar value F(x). Gradient 
abla F: A 3D vector field computed via automatic differentiation of F with respect to x. Hessian H(F): A 3 	imes 3 matrix of second-order partial derivatives of F with respect to x. Adjoint Hessian H^(F): The transpose of the Hessian matrix H(F)^T. For real-valued functions with continuous second derivatives, H(F) is symmetric, so H^(F) = H(F). Parameters: \lambda{curv}: Regularization weight. Typical values: 0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001. \kappa{curv}: Clipping value for curvature magnitude. Typical values: 1, 5, 10. Steps: 1. Compute Differential Quantities: For each sample point x, compute the gradient 
abla F(x) and the Hessian H(F)(x) using automatic differentiation. 2. Calculate Gaussian Curvature (\gamma{gauss}): \gamma{gauss} =  rac{
abla F^T H^(F) 
abla F}{\|
abla F\|^4} where the numerator is a quadratic form equivalent to 
abla F 	imes H^(F) 	imes 
abla F^t in the source notation. This equals the product of principal curvatures \gamma{min} \gamma{max}. 3. Calculate Mean Curvature (\gamma{mean}): \gamma{mean} =  rac{\gamma{min} + \gamma{max}}{2} The source defines it via principal curvatures but does not provide a direct analytical formula from 
abla F and H(F) without eigen-decomposition. 4. Compute Curvature Loss (L{curv}): L{curv}(\kappa{curv}) = \mathbb{E}{x \in S} [\min(|\gamma(x)|, \kappa{curv})] where \gamma is either \gamma{gauss} or \gamma{mean}. 5. Combine Losses: L = L{RGB} + \lambda{SDF} L{SDF} + \lambda{curv} L{curv}(\kappa{curv}) where L{SDF} = \mathbb{E}{x \in \mathbb{R}^3} (\|
abla F(x)\| - 1)^2 enforces the Eikonal constraint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecurvatureregularizationloss(F, samples, lambdacurv, kappacurv, curvaturetype='gauss'): # 1. Compute Gradient and Hessian via automatic differentiation x = samples.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) fval = F(x) gradf = computegradient(fval, x) # Standard AD operation hessf = computehessian(gradf, x) # Standard AD operation if curvaturetype == 'gauss': # gammagauss = (gradf^T H gradf) / ||gradf||^4 numerator = sum(gradf (hessf @ gradf.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2), dim=1) gradnormsq = sum(gradf2, dim=1) denominator = gradnormsq2 denominator = clamp(denominator, min=1e-8) gamma = numerator / denominator elif curvaturetype == 'mean': # Direct formula from grad/hess is not provided in the sources gamma = computemeancurvature(gradf, hessf) # Standard AD operation else: raise ValueError("curvaturetype must be 'gauss' or 'mean'") # 3. Compute Loss absgamma = abs(gamma) clippedgamma = min(absgamma, kappacurv) curvatureloss = mean(clippedgamma) return lambdacurv curvatureloss Note: computegradient, computehessian, computemeancurvature, sum, clamp, abs, min, mean are standard array/math operations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by \|
abla F\|^4 can lead to numerical instability if the gradient norm is near zero (off-surface points or flat regions). Clamping the denominator is required. Boundaries: The method assumes F is differentiable. Discontinuities in the neural network output can break automatic differentiation. Degenerate Input: If the surface is flat, Gaussian curvature is zero. If the surface is a sphere, both curvatures are constant. Over-regularization: High \lambda{curv} with low \kappa{curv} leads to "Cubist-style" surfaces with exaggerated edges and loss of detail. Hole Filling: Regularization tends to fill small gaps (e.g., mouth of a bunny model), so clipping is important to preserve small details. Penalizes the product of principal curvatures. Forces surfaces to be developable (flat with sharp edges). Tends to fill holes. Choose when a piece-wise developable surface is desired. Link: Gaussian Curvature Regularization. Penalizes the average of principal curvatures. Leads to surface smoothing. Choose when smoothing is the primary goal. Link: Gaussian Curvature Regularization. Time Complexity: Computing the Hessian via automatic differentiation is O(N \cdot D^2) where N is the number of samples and D=3 is the dimensionality. This is more expensive than gradient-only methods but feasible with modern frameworks. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Hessian matrix for each sample point during the backward pass, increasing memory usage compared to gradient-only regularization. Measured Performance: Tested on DTU dataset scenes using VolSDF. Parameters \lambda{curv}=0.0005, \kappa{curv}=5 produced strong regularization while keeping details. Strengths: Direct surface regularization; state-of-the-art novel view synthesis and depth estimation in few-shot neural rendering. Limitations: Can fill small details; "Cubist" artifacts with poor parameter tuning; requires differentiable SDF (VolSDF). When to use: When direct geometric regularization of the implicit surface is preferred over depth/normal regularization, and the scene benefits from smooth or developable surfaces. When not to use: When preserving fine small-scale details is critical and clipping cannot mitigate hole-filling; when computational resources are limited due to Hessian computation. Origin: Proposed in "Regularization of NeRFs using differential geometry" (DiffNeRF). History: The curvature formulas for implicit curves and surfaces are derived from Ron Goldman's work "Curvature formulas for implicit curves and surfaces" (2005). Usage: Used with VolSDF for surface estimation on DTU dataset scenes. Regularization of NeRFs using differential geometry, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2206.14938, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Curvature Regularization Decay
body: Curvature Regularization Decay is a dynamic weighting strategy for curvature-based geometric losses in differentiable volume rendering, designed to preserve high-frequency details during optimization. It addresses the trade-off between surface smoothness and detail retention by scaling down the curvature regularization strength (w{curv}) as the optimization step size (\epsilon) decreases and finer hash grid resolutions are activated. Unlike static curvature losses, which may overly smooth fine structures, this method adapts the regularization intensity to the current spatial resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current optimization step size \epsilon, current hash grid spacing s{curr}, previous hash grid spacing s{prev}, current curvature loss weight w{curv}. Output: Updated curvature loss weight w{curv}^{new}. Data Structures: The method operates on hierarchical hash grids where resolution and spacing change discretely as optimization progresses. Steps: 1. Monitor Step Size: Track the optimization step size \epsilon. 2. Detect Resolution Change: Identify when \epsilon decreases, indicating activation of a finer hash grid level. 3. Calculate Scaling Factor: Compute the spacing factor between the current and previous hash grid resolutions, defined as s{curr} / s{prev}. 4. Update Weight: Scale down the curvature regularization strength by the spacing factor. Formulas: w{curv}^{new} = w{curv}^{old} \times \frac{s{curr}}{s{prev}} This ensures that as the grid becomes finer (s{curr} < s{prev}), the regularization strength decreases proportionally. Parameters: Initial w{curv}: Not given in the sources. Step Size Schedule: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premature Decay: If the weight decays too quickly before the surface is sufficiently smooth, noise may persist. Insufficient Decay: If the weight does not decay sufficiently, fine details may be smoothed out as the optimizer attempts to fit high-frequency noise in the fine grids. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatecurvatureweight(wcurv, sprev, scurr, epsilonprev, epsiloncurr): """ Update curvature regularization weight based on step size decrease and hash grid spacing change. Args: wcurv (float): Current curvature loss weight. sprev (float): Spacing of the previous (coarser) hash grid level. scurr (float): Spacing of the current (finer) hash grid level. epsilonprev (float): Optimization step size from the previous update. epsiloncurr (float): Current optimization step size. Returns: float: Updated curvature loss weight. """ if epsiloncurr < epsilonprev: # Scale down the weight by the ratio of spacings # As scurr < sprev, the weight decreases proportionally wcurvnew = wcurv (scurr / sprev) return wcurvnew else: return wcurv A complementary strategy to prevent topology preservation issues during the initial stages of optimization. It initializes the SDF approximately as a sphere. During a short warmup period, the curvature loss strength is linearly increased from zero to its target value instead of being applied from the beginning. Applying L{curv} from the start preserves topology by preventing singularities in curvature, which makes forming concave shapes difficult. This strategy should be used in conjunction with Curvature Regularization Decay when the target geometry contains significant concave regions or complex topology. Time Complexity: Negligible overhead, involving a simple multiplication per resolution change. Performance: Improves image synthesis quality by preserving fine details that would otherwise be smoothed out by static curvature regularization. Strengths: Prevents over-smoothing of high-frequency details; adapts to the multi-resolution nature of hash grids. Limitations: Requires coordination with the step size schedule. When to use: High-fidelity neural surface reconstruction where fine details are critical. Curvature Regularization Decay was introduced in the context of Neuralangelo, a method for high-fidelity neural surface reconstruction. It builds on the observation that static curvature regularization, while effective at removing surface noise, can inadvertently smooth out fine details as the optimization progresses to finer hash grid resolutions. name: 2D Planar Image Alignment
head: Joint optimization of 2D image content and per-patch homography warps
body: 2D Planar Image Alignment is a simplified joint optimization problem that aligns overlapping 2D image patches with learned content. It reconstructs a ground truth image from transformed patches by simultaneously optimizing the image content representation and the geometric transformation parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of L{2d} overlapping image patches \{I1, \dots, I{L{2d}}\} cropped from a ground truth image. Outputs: Optimized 2D image content function F{2d}: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 and a set of homography parameters P{2d} = \{P1, \dots, P{L{2d}}\}. Data Structures: 1. Homography Parameters (Pi): Each Pi \in \mathfrak{sl}(3) is parameterized using the Lie algebra of SL(3) and initialized to \vec{0}. 2. Image Content (F{2d}): Parameterized by a 2D decomposed low-rank tensor T{2d} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w}, where h, w are image dimensions. 3. Low-Rank Tensor (T{2d}): Represented via Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition with rank R: T{2d} = \sum{r=1}^R v{rX} \otimes v{rY} where v{rX} \in \mathbb{R}^w and v{rY} \in \mathbb{R}^h are 1D vectors, and \otimes denotes the outer product. 4. Gaussian Kernel (N{2d}): A 2D Gaussian kernel used to filter T{2d} to prevent overfitting. It is constructed as the outer product of two 1D kernels: N{2d}(\sigma) = N{1d}(\sigma) \otimes N{1d}(\sigma) where N{1d}(\sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^{LN} is a discrete kernel of size LN. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set homography parameters Pi to zero (identity transform) and initialize vectors v{rX}, v{rY} for the low-rank tensor. 2. Construct Kernel: For a given bandwidth \sigma, generate the 1D kernel N{1d}(\sigma): If \sigma > 0.0001: N{1d}(\sigma)x = \min\left(1, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}}\right) for x \in [-LN/2, LN/2]. If \sigma < 0.001: Assign N{1d}(\sigma) to the discrete impulse function \delta to avoid numerical instability. Construct N{2d}(\sigma) = N{1d}(\sigma) \otimes N{1d}(\sigma). 3. Filter Content: Compute the filtered content function F{2d}(x) by convolving the tensor T{2d} with N{2d}: F{2d}(x) = (N{2d} {2d} T{2d})(x) = \left(N{2d} {2d} \left(\sum{r=1}^R v{rX} \otimes v{rY}\right)\right)(x) where {2d} denotes 2D convolution. 4. Warp Coordinates: For each patch i and pixel coordinate u \in U{2d} (the set of coordinates in the patch), compute the warped coordinate u' using the homography Pi: u' = W{2d}(Pi, u) where W{2d} maps the coordinate u from the ground truth space to the patch space via the homography parameterized by Pi \in \mathfrak{sl}(3). 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the reconstruction loss L{2d}: L{2d}(F{2d}, P{2d}) = \sum{i=1}^{L{2d}} \sum{u \in U{2d}} \| F{2d}(W{2d}(Pi, u)) - I{iu} \|^2 where I{iu} is the color of the pixel at location u in input patch Ii. 6. Optimize: Perform gradient-based optimization to minimize L{2d} with respect to F{2d} (via v{rX}, v{rY}) and P{2d}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generate1dkernel(sigma, LN): """Generates a 1D Gaussian kernel of size LN. Handles numerical instability for small sigma.""" if sigma < 0.001: kernel = np.zeros(LN) kernel[LN // 2] = 1.0 return kernel x = np.arange(-LN // 2, LN // 2 + 1) pdf = (1.0 / np.sqrt(2 np.pi sigma2)) np.exp(-x2 / (2 sigma2)) return np.minimum(1.0, pdf) def generate2dkernel(sigma, LN): """Generates a 2D Gaussian kernel as outer product of two 1D kernels.""" n1d = generate1dkernel(sigma, LN) return np.outer(n1d, n1d) def reconstructandfilter(vectorsx, vectorsy, kernel2d, h, w): """Computes F2d(x) by reconstructing T2d and convolving with the 2D Gaussian kernel.""" R = len(vectorsx) T2d = np.zeros((h, w)) for r in range(R): T2d += np.outer(vectorsy[r], vectorsx[r]) # Differentiable 2D convolution is applied. Using separable property: n1d = kernel2d[:, 0] filtered = np.convolve(T2d, n1d, axis=0, mode='same') return np.convolve(filtered, n1d, axis=1, mode='same') def warpcoordinatehomography(u, H): """Warps a 2D coordinate u using homography matrix H.""" uh = np.array([u[0], u[1], 1.0]) uprimeh = H @ uh return uprimeh[:2] / uprimeh[2] def bilinearsample(grid, x, y): """Performs bilinear interpolation on a 2D grid at coordinates (x, y).""" x0, y0 = int(np.floor(x)), int(np.floor(y)) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 dx, dy = x - x0, y - y0 x0 = np.clip(x0, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) x1 = np.clip(x1, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) y0 = np.clip(y0, 0, grid.shape[0] - 1) y1 = np.clip(y1, 0, grid.shape[0] - 1) top = grid[y0, x0] (1 - dx) + grid[y0, x1] dx bottom = grid[y1, x0] (1 - dx) + grid[y1, x1] dx return top (1 - dy) + bottom dy def computeloss(F2d, patches, homographies, kernelsigma, LN, h, w, vectorsx, vectorsy): """Computes the 2D Planar Image Alignment loss.""" kernel2d = generate2dkernel(kernelsigma, LN) F2d = reconstructandfilter(vectorsx, vectorsy, kernel2d, h, w) totalloss = 0.0 for i, patch in enumerate(patches): H = homographies[i] patchh, patchw, = patch.shape for y in range(patchh): for x in range(patchw): u = np.array([x, y]) uglobal = warpcoordinatehomography(u, H) val = bilinearsample(F2d, uglobal[0], uglobal[1]) target = patch[y, x] totalloss += np.sum((val - target)2) return totalloss Parameters: \sigma: Gaussian kernel bandwidth. Typical values not given in the sources. LN: Size of the discrete kernel. Not given in the sources. R: Rank of the low-rank decomposition. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: When \sigma < 0.001, the Gaussian kernel calculation becomes numerically unstable. The source specifies assigning the 1D kernel to a discrete impulse function \delta in this case. Overfitting: Naively applying low-rank decomposed tensors without filtering can limit the spectrum of the learned signal. Filtering with a Gaussian kernel is necessary to avoid overfitting. A 2D variant of radiance field estimation for homography-based panorama stitching. A 2D coordinate network renders a stitched image, and pixel pi in training patch i is warped with estimated homography Hi to the rendered image. At every iteration, a reference crop r is randomly selected to align other crops. Pixel pi from any crop i is warped by estimating composed homography H'{ri} = Hr^{-1} \cdot Hi to its location p'i = H'{ri} \cdot pi in the reference crop. Color constancy of the backward warps to the reference crop for all surrogate views is penalized with a huber function and minimized alongside the rendering MSE. Homography noise parameters used for evaluation include scale noise H \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.15\} and fixed translation noise of 0.2. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a simplified testbed for joint optimization of geometry and content, sharing computational properties with 3D alignment. Limitations: Limited to 2D planar images; does not account for 3D depth or occlusion explicitly. When to use: When validating differentiable rendering pipelines or joint optimization strategies in a simplified 2D setting. When not to use: For full 3D scene reconstruction where depth and volume rendering are required. The method is presented as a simpler example of joint optimization involving overlapping image patches transformed by 2D homography, serving as an analog to 1D and 3D alignment problems. The approach builds on the decomposed low-rank tensor representation (VM-decomposition) proposed by TensoRF. name: Material Smoothness Loss
head: Lmat
body: Material Smoothness Loss is a regularization term applied during material field optimization to enforce spatial coherence by penalizing color differences between neighboring surface points. It addresses high-frequency noise in decomposed material properties by assuming homogeneous areas exhibit smooth variations. It differs from standard smoothness priors by relying on spatial neighbor comparisons rather than global constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of surface points \mathbf{x}{surf} reconstructed from the scene; the material field values (specifically diffuse color \mathbf{b}d) at these points; a displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x} defining the neighborhood. Outputs: A scalar loss value L{mat} used to update material field parameters via gradient descent. Data Structures: Surface Points: A list or tensor of 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}{surf}. Material Field: A function or lookup table mapping 3D coordinates to color vectors \mathbf{b}d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Iterate over each surface point \mathbf{x}{surf} in the set. 2. Compute the neighboring coordinate \mathbf{x}{neighbor} = \mathbf{x}{surf} + \Delta \mathbf{x}. 3. Retrieve the diffuse color values \mathbf{b}d(\mathbf{x}{surf}) and \mathbf{b}d(\mathbf{x}{neighbor}) from the material field. 4. Compute the squared Euclidean distance between the retrieved colors. 5. Sum these distances over all surface points to produce the loss. Formula: The loss is defined as: L{mat} = \sum{\mathbf{x}{surf}} \| \mathbf{b}d(\mathbf{x}{surf}) - \mathbf{b}d(\mathbf{x}{surf} + \Delta \mathbf{x}) \|^2 Where: \mathbf{x}{surf} represents the surface points. \mathbf{b}d(\cdot) is the diffuse color component of the material at the given location. \Delta \mathbf{x} is the spatial offset to the neighbor. \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. Parameters: \Delta \mathbf{x}: The neighborhood distance. Weighting: The sources do not provide an explicit weighting formula or edge-aware mechanism for this base loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Material Boundaries: Standard uniform smoothing can blur material boundaries. Unconstrained Optimization: Without regularization, optimization leads to implausible results, such as materials being highly glossy only where highlights were observed. This is handled by combining smoothness with constancy assumptions (see Subtopics). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def materialsmoothnessloss(surfacepoints, materialfield, deltax): """ Computes the Material Smoothness Loss (Lmat). Args: surfacepoints: List of 3D coordinates [N, 3]. materialfield: Callable returning diffuse color [3] for a 3D coordinate. deltax: 3D vector defining the neighbor offset. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 for x in surfacepoints: xneighbor = [x[i] + deltax[i] for i in range(3)] colorcurrent = materialfield(x) colorneighbor = materialfield(xneighbor) diff = [colorcurrent[i] - colorneighbor[i] for i in range(3)] totalloss += sum(d d for d in diff) return totalloss BRDF Smoothness Loss is a regularization term applied during material field optimization to enforce spatial coherence in BRDF parameters such as roughness, albedo, and normals. It penalizes drastic changes between neighboring surface points based on the assumption that BRDF properties do not change drastically in homogeneous areas. It differs from standard smoothness priors by incorporating edge-aware weighting based on pseudo-albedo differences, which suppresses the loss across material boundaries. See BRDF Smoothness Loss. Bilateral Smoothness Regularization is a geometric and normal alignment loss applied to material fields to enforce spatial smoothness of BRDF parameters weighted by image gradients. It alleviates the ambiguity between material and illumination by constraining material gradients to correspond with image edges, preventing noisy and inconsistent material reconstructions. It differs from standard smoothness losses by using the image gradient as a bilateral weight to preserve material boundaries where the image shows sharp transitions. See Bilateral Smoothness Regularization. Definition: An assumption that roughness and specularity remain constant within a class of the surface segmentation, optimizing a single roughness & specularity value per object. This addresses the ambiguity that roughness can only be judged where an actual highlight is observed. Pitfall: Unconstrained optimization leads to implausible results, such as materials being highly glossy only where highlights were observed. This is handled by enforcing constancy per object. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces high-frequency noise in material fields. Prevents isolated glossy spots by enforcing spatial consistency. Limitations: Requires careful handling of material boundaries to avoid blurring. Relies on the availability of surface points and material field evaluations. When to Use: Use when optimizing spatially-varying material fields (BRDFs) to prevent noise and artifacts, particularly in homogeneous regions. When Not to Use: Avoid if the scene contains high-frequency material details that should not be smoothed, or if computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of evaluating neighbors is prohibitive (though specific costs are not given). Origin: The term L{mat} and the specific formulation using squared color differences between neighbors are defined in. The constancy assumption for roughness and specularity is introduced in. History and Development: The method is part of the broader effort in inverse rendering to decouple material properties from illumination and geometry. The constancy assumption reduces the number of parameters to optimize, speeding up convergence. Where it is used: Used in inverse rendering pipelines that optimize cascaded tensorial radiance fields, lighting, and materials from multi-view images, and in texture-space differentiable rendering for complex indoor scenes. name: BRDF Smoothness Loss
head: BRDF Smoothness Regularization, Smoothness Loss (BRDF), Smoothness Priors for BRDF
body: BRDF Smoothness Loss is a regularization term applied during material field optimization to enforce spatial coherence in BRDF parameters such as roughness, albedo, and normals. It penalizes drastic changes between neighboring surface points based on the assumption that BRDF properties do not change drastically in homogeneous areas. The method differs from standard smoothness priors by incorporating edge-aware weighting based on pseudo-albedo differences, which suppresses the loss across material boundaries. The method computes a loss value based on the relative difference of BRDF parameters between a reference point and a perturbed neighbor, weighted by the difference in pseudo-albedo. Inputs: \mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k: Position of the k-th sampled point on the surface. \boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}): Vector of BRDF parameters at position \mathbf{x}. \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}{\text{out}}): Rendered color at position \mathbf{x} for outgoing direction \mathbf{d}{\text{out}}. \mathbf{c}{\text{irradiance}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}{\text{out}}): Irradiance color at position \mathbf{x}, computed by setting the BRDF to perfectly Lambertian with albedo 1. \boldsymbol{\xi}: Perturbation vector. C{\text{BRDF}}: Loss weight coefficient. \epsilon: Perturbation scale. wk: Sampling weight for point k. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\text{BRDF}}: Scalar loss value. Data Structures: \boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}): Generic parameter vector containing BRDF properties. defines separate losses for roughness (R), normal (N), and albedo (B), while treats \boldsymbol{\beta} as a unified vector. Steps: 1. Sample a perturbation vector \boldsymbol{\xi} from a normal distribution \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \epsilon \mathrm{I}). 2. Compute the pseudo-albedo at the reference point \mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k and the perturbed point \mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi}: \mathbf{a}{\text{pseudo}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}{\text{out}})}{\mathbf{c}{\text{irradiance}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}{\text{out}})} 3. Compute the edge-aware weight \lambda based on the absolute difference of pseudo-albedos: \lambda(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k, \mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi}) = | \mathbf{a}{\text{pseudo}}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k) - \mathbf{a}{\text{pseudo}}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi}) | 4. Compute the relative difference of the BRDF parameters \boldsymbol{\beta}: \Delta \boldsymbol{\beta} = \left| \frac{\boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k) - \boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi})}{\operatorname{max}(\boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k), \boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi}))} \right| Division and maximum operations are performed element-wise. 5. Accumulate the loss over all sampled points k: \mathcal{L}{\text{BRDF}} = C{\text{BRDF}} \sum{k} wk \cdot \Delta \boldsymbol{\beta} \cdot \lambda(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k, \mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi}) Alternative Formulation (S1): proposes a gradient-based edge-aware smoothness prior. For roughness R: \mathcal{L}{s, r} = \Vert \nabla R \Vert \exp (-\Vert \nabla C{gt} \Vert) where R = \sum{i \in N} wi ri is the rendered roughness map. Similar constraints \mathcal{L}{s,n} and \mathcal{L}{s,b} are defined for normal and albedo. Parameters: \epsilon: Standard deviation of the perturbation noise. Set to 0.01 for the TensoIR dataset, 0.005 for other datasets. C{\text{BRDF}}: Loss coefficient. Set to 0.05 for the TensoIR dataset, 0.001 for other datasets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The denominator \operatorname{max}(\boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k), \boldsymbol{\beta}(\mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi})) can be zero if BRDF parameters are uninitialized or clamped to zero. A small constant is added to the denominator to prevent numerical instability. Boundary Conditions: The perturbed point \mathbf{x}{\text{pos}}k + \boldsymbol{\xi} may fall outside the valid surface or volume. Out-of-bounds queries must be handled by returning zero or clamping coordinates. Not given in the sources. The concept of BRDF smoothness priors originates from the observation that BRDF properties do not change drastically in homogeneous areas. The specific formulation using pseudo-albedo weighting and relative differences is a variant of TensoIR’s smoothness loss. The gradient-based exponential weighting variant is used in Relightable 3D Gaussians. name: Bilateral Smoothness Regularization
head: Image gradient-aware smoothness loss, Phys3DGS Smoothness Regularizer
body:
Bilateral Smoothness Regularization is a geometric and normal alignment loss applied to material fields to enforce spatial smoothness of BRDF parameters weighted by image gradients. It alleviates the ambiguity between material and illumination by constraining material gradients to correspond with image edges, preventing noisy and inconsistent material reconstructions. It differs from standard smoothness losses by using the image gradient as a bilateral weight to preserve material boundaries where the image shows sharp transitions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: x: The BRDF parameter field (e.g., base color, roughness ho, or specular tint \alpha). I: The ground truth RGB image. M: A binary mask indicating pixels belonging to the object. SI: The set of pixels on the object, used for normalization. Outputs: L{smooth}: The scalar regularization loss value. Data Structures: Image Gradient: Pre-computed gradient magnitude \|
ablap I(p)\| for each pixel p. The specific derivative operator is not explicitly defined in the sources, but standard finite differences are implied by the notation 
ablad. Material Field: A tensor or array storing the scalar BRDF parameter x for each surface point or pixel. Steps: 1. Pre-compute Image Gradient: Calculate the gradient magnitude \|
ablap I(p)\| for all pixels p in the ground truth image I before training. 2. Compute Material Gradient: For each BRDF parameter x and each pixel i in the mask M, compute the spatial derivative in the x and y dimensions. Source uses second-order derivatives 
abla^2d, while Source uses first-order gradients \|
abla{xs}\| for surface points xs. 3. Calculate Bilateral Weight: Compute the exponential weight using the pre-computed image gradient. Source uses e^{
ablad I(i)}, while Source uses e^{-\|
ablap I(p)\|}. 4. Aggregate Loss: Sum the product of the material gradient magnitude and the bilateral weight over all pixels in the mask. 5. Normalize: Divide by the number of pixels in SI when using the formulation from Source. Formula: Source defines the loss as: L{smooth}(x) = \sum {i\in M} \sum {d\in x,y} |
abla ^2d x(i)| e^{
abla d I(i)} where d iterates over x and y dimensions. Source defines the loss as: ls =  rac{1}{|SI|} \sum {p\in SI} (\|
abla{xs} \alpha(xs)\| + \|
abla{xs} ho(xs)\|) e^{-\|
ablap I(p)\|} where xs is the surface point corresponding to pixel p, and \alpha, ho are specular tint and roughness. Parameters: Mask M / Set SI: Defines the region of interest (the object). Image Gradient: Pre-computed, not learned. Pitfalls: Noise: Without this regularization, the model generates noisy materials that are inconsistent across the same material, making it unsuitable for material editing applications. Formula Discrepancy: Sources and use different gradient orders (second vs. first) and different signs in the exponential weight. Boundary Conditions: The handling of image gradient computation at image boundaries is not specified. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegradientmagnitude(field): """Computes gradient magnitude using central finite differences.""" h, w = len(field), len(field[0]) gradmag = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] for r in range(1, h - 1): for c in range(1, w - 1): dx = (field[r][c+1] - field[r][c-1]) / 2.0 dy = (field[r+1][c] - field[r-1][c]) / 2.0 gradmag[r][c] = (dx2 + dy2)0.5 return gradmag def bilateralsmoothnessloss(materialfield, groundtruthimage, mask): """ Computes the Bilateral Smoothness Regularization loss. Implements the variant from Source for surface points, as it explicitly handles normalization and distinct material parameters. """ # 1. Pre-compute image gradient magnitude imagegradmagnitude = computegradientmagnitude(groundtruthimage) # 2. Get material gradients for roughness and specular tint roughness = materialfield[..., 0] speculartint = materialfield[..., 1] roughgradmag = computegradientmagnitude(roughness) specgradmag = computegradientmagnitude(speculartint) # 3. Calculate bilateral weight: e^(-||grad I||) weight = [[0.0] len(groundtruthimage[0]) for in range(len(groundtruthimage))] for r in range(len(weight)): for c in range(len(weight[0])): weight[r][c] = import('math').exp(-imagegradmagnitude[r][c]) # 4. Aggregate loss over pixels in SI (mask) sumgrad = 0.0 numpixels = 0 for r in range(len(mask)): for c in range(len(mask[0])): if mask[r][c] > 0.5: sumgrad += (roughgradmag[r][c] + specgradmag[r][c]) weight[r][c] numpixels += 1 # 5. Normalize by |SI| if numpixels == 0: return 0.0 loss = sumgrad / numpixels return loss The parent category. Enforces spatial smoothness of material fields. Material Smoothness Loss The sibling category. Focuses on aligning geometry and normals. Geometric and Normal Alignment Losses Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the mask |SI| or M, as it involves a single pass over the pixels to compute gradients and sum the loss. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-computed image gradient and the material field gradients. Strengths: Effectively reduces noise in reconstructed materials and resolves ambiguity between material and illumination. Improves suitability for material editing applications. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of image gradients. Performance may vary depending on the choice of gradient operator and exponential weight sign. When to use: When reconstructing physically-based materials (BRDF) from images, especially when noise or material-illumination ambiguity is observed. When not to use: When computational resources for pre-computing gradients are unavailable, or when the material is expected to be highly noisy by nature. Origin: The term "Bilateral Smoothness Regularization" is attributed to Yao et al. 2022 in Source. Source refers to it as "image gradient-aware smoothness loss" and applies it in the context of Phys3DGS. History: It was introduced to address the ambiguity between material and illumination in inverse rendering tasks. Usage: Used in Phys3DGS for BRDF parameter smoothing and in NeIF (Neural Illumination Fields) for roughness and specular tint smoothing.
