name: Uncertainty Guided Policy with Region Clustering
head: Active View Selection via Entropy, Coarse-to-Fine Reconstruction Policy
body: This method is an active view selection policy for robotic 3D reconstruction using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It selects the next best views by maximizing information gain, approximated via the mean entropy of a candidate view's uncertainty map. It distinguishes itself from global greedy selection by enforcing spatial diversity through region clustering, preventing the selection of redundant, similar viewpoints that cause overfitting, while avoiding the slow coverage of single-view-per-iteration strategies. Inputs: A set of candidate camera poses \mathcal{C} distributed on a hemisphere surrounding the object. A current NeRF model \mathcal{N} trained on an initial dataset \mathcal{D}{init}. A target image resolution for uncertainty evaluation. Outputs: A set of selected camera poses \mathcal{S} to be captured in the current iteration. An updated NeRF model \mathcal{N}'. Data Structures: View Space: A hemisphere divided into 13 regions: 12 sections (clusters) and 1 middle circle (excluded from selection). Sections: The hemisphere is split into an upper half and a lower half relative to the middle circle. Each half is divided into 6 groups based on azimuthal angle \phi, resulting in 12 sections R1, \dots, R{12}. Candidate Poses: 30 poses per horizontal circle, 5 circles total, yielding 150 candidates. Parameters: Candidate Poses: 150 total (30 per circle \times 5 circles). Initialization Images: 6 for synthetic data, 15 for real-world data, sampled from the middle circle. Sampling: 64 samples for coarse network, 128 for fine network. Downsampling: Images are downsampled by a factor of 4 for entropy evaluation. Steps: 1. Initialization: Train an initial NeRF model \mathcal{N}0 using images from the middle circle (6 images for synthetic, 15 for real-world). 2. Region Definition: Divide the hemisphere into 12 sections for clustering. The middle circle is excluded from selection regions. 3. Iteration Loop: a. For each of the 12 sections Ri: i. Identify all candidate poses c \in \mathcal{C} that fall within section Ri. ii. For each candidate pose c, render the scene using \mathcal{N} to obtain the weight distribution w for each pixel. iii. Compute the entropy H(c, p) for each pixel p in the rendered image. The entropy is derived from the ray-based volumetric uncertainty estimation. iv. Calculate the mean entropy \bar{H}(c) for the entire image by averaging H(c, p) across all pixels. v. Select the candidate pose c^i with the highest mean entropy \bar{H}(c) within section Ri. b. Collect the 12 selected views \mathcal{S} = \{c^1, \dots, c^{12}\}. c. Update the training dataset \mathcal{D} \leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \mathcal{S}. d. Refine the NeRF model \mathcal{N} using the updated dataset \mathcal{D}, initializing from the previous model state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uncertaintyguidedpolicywithregionclustering(candidateposes, initialimages, numsections=12, maxiterations=10): # Step 1: Initialization # Standard NeRF optimization: initialize MLP parameters, run gradient descent on initialimages nerfmodel = trainnerf(initialimages) # Step 2: Define regions # Partition candidateposes into upper/lower hemispheres relative to middle circle, # then split each half into numsections/2 azimuthal sectors sections = definehemispheresections(candidateposes, numsections) selectedviews = [] dataset = list(initialimages) # Step 3: Iterative selection for iteration in range(maxiterations): currentselection = [] for section in sections: candidatesinsection = [c for c in candidateposes if c in section] bestcandidate = None maxmeanentropy = -1.0 for candidate in candidatesinsection: # Ray march NeRF to get color/weight distribution, downsampled by 4 renderedimage = render(nerfmodel, candidate) # Compute Shannon entropy from weight distribution per pixel entropies = computepixelentropy(renderedimage) meanentropy = sum(entropies) / len(entropies) if meanentropy > maxmeanentropy: maxmeanentropy = meanentropy bestcandidate = candidate currentselection.append(bestcandidate) # Acquire images at selected poses newimages = captureimages(currentselection) dataset.extend(newimages) # Continue NeRF optimization on updated dataset from previous checkpoint nerfmodel = refinenerf(nerfmodel, dataset) selectedviews.extend(currentselection) if iteration >= maxiterations - 1: break return selectedviews, nerfmodel def trainnerf(images): # Standard NeRF optimization: initialize MLP parameters, run gradient descent on images pass def definehemispheresections(poses, n): # Partition poses into upper/lower hemispheres relative to middle circle, # then split each half into n/2 azimuthal sectors based on azimuthal angle pass def render(model, pose): # Ray march NeRF to compute color and weight distribution per pixel pass def computepixelentropy(image): # Compute Shannon entropy from the normalized weight distribution along rays pass def captureimages(poses): # Acquire or simulate RGB images at the given camera poses pass def refinenerf(model, data): # Resume NeRF training on the expanded dataset from the previous model state pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Selecting top-k most uncertain viewpoints without region constraints or model updates may result in choosing similar viewpoints, leading to overfitting. Inefficiency: Selecting only one view globally per iteration without spatial constraints results in much longer acquisition processes to cover object geometry. Precision: Entropy calculation requires accurate weight distributions from the NeRF. Downsampling by a factor of 4 is used to speed up the process, which may affect precision. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of candidate poses (150) and the number of sections (12). For each iteration, 12 candidates are evaluated. Each evaluation requires rendering the scene and computing entropy for all pixels. Downsampling by a factor of 4 reduces computational cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model and the training dataset. The dataset grows with each iteration. Performance: The method is evaluated on synthetic and real-world data. It achieves high-quality 3D meshes with fewer images than dense sampling. The F-score metric is used for evaluation. Strengths: Ensures diverse view selection, prevents overfitting, and accelerates coverage compared to single-view strategies. Limitations: Requires a hemisphere view space definition. Performance depends on the quality of the initial coarse reconstruction. The method was proposed in "Uncertainty Guided Policy for Active Robotic 3D Reconstruction Using Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the concept of active robotic 3D reconstruction using NeRF, leveraging ray-based volumetric uncertainty estimation to guide view selection. The approach addresses the challenge of efficiently selecting novel views to improve 3D reconstruction quality. name: Pixel-wise Regression Model for Uncertainty
head: Meta-regression, Uncertainty prediction
body: This method estimates pixel-wise rendering or depth error for novel views in Gaussian Splatting by training a regression model on rendered uncertainty feature maps. It differs from direct uncertainty prediction losses by decoupling scene representation optimization from uncertainty estimation, using a separate meta-regression step trained on hold-out views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Rendered feature maps representing specific Gaussian primitive properties (e.g., Field of View count, coverage, or error metrics) instead of color. Output: A dense, pixel-wise map predicting the magnitude of rendering error or depth error for a target novel view. Data Structures: Feature Maps: 2D images where each pixel contains values derived from Gaussian primitives splatted to that pixel. Target Map: A 2D image of the same resolution as the feature maps, containing the ground truth error computed against a held-out ground truth view. Steps: 1. Render Feature Maps: For a set of hold-out views (not used for primary Gaussian splatting optimization), render the scene using the standard volume rendering equation, replacing the Gaussian color term with the chosen uncertainty primitive representation (e.g., coverage or FOV count). 2. Compute Target Error: For the same hold-out views, render the actual color/depth and compute the pixel-wise error against the ground truth image. The error metric is defined as \bar{e} = \| R(\bar{x}) - \hat{R}(\bar{x}) \|1, where R(\bar{x}) is the ground truth and \hat{R}(\bar{x}) is the rendered value at pixel \bar{x}. 3. Train Regression Model: Train a regression model to map the rendered feature maps to the target error maps using the hold-out views. 4. Inference: Apply the trained model to feature maps rendered from novel viewpoints or scenes to produce dense uncertainty maps. Parameters: Regression Algorithm: Gradient boosting regression is the default, with linear regression also tested. Training Data: One hold-out view per scene is typically used for training the meta-regression models. Separation: Separate regressors are trained for rendering error and depth error. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainpixelwiseregression(gaussians, holdoutviews, groundtruthviews): featuremaps = [] errormaps = [] for view, gtimage in zip(holdoutviews, groundtruthviews): # Step 1: Render uncertainty feature maps # Replace Gaussian color term with primitive representation (e.g., coverage) featuremap = splat(gaussians, view, outputtype='feature') # Step 2: Compute ground truth error renderedimage = splat(gaussians, view, outputtype='color') errormap = abs(renderedimage - gtimage) featuremaps.append(featuremap) errormaps.append(errormap) # Step 3: Train the regressor Xtrain = [fm.flatten() for fm in featuremaps] ytrain = [em.flatten() for em in errormaps] # Train gradient boosting regressor on Xtrain, ytrain regressor = traingradientboosting(Xtrain, ytrain) return regressor def predictuncertainty(gaussians, novelview, trainedregressor): featuremap = splat(gaussians, novelview, outputtype='feature') Xnovel = featuremap.flatten() predictederrorflat = trainedregressor.predict(Xnovel) uncertaintymap = predictederrorflat.reshape(featuremap.shape) return uncertaintymap def splat(gaussians, view, outputtype): # Perform standard Gaussian splatting to 2D image # If outputtype is 'feature', replace color term with chosen primitive representation # If outputtype is 'color', use standard color term return zeros(view.resolution) def traingradientboosting(X, y): # Train gradient boosting regressor on input features X and targets y return None Replaces pixel-wise gradient boosting with lightweight fully convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to incorporate uncertainty features from neighboring pixels. It uses 13 direction-independent primitive representations from the first three hold-out views of a scene as input to predict rendering and depth errors on foreground objects for the fourth hold-out view. The CNN architecture has 4 layers with uniform channel depths h \in \{32, 64, 128, 256\} and kernel sizes ki \in \{1, 3, 5\} satisfying kj + 2 \ge ki \ge kj for i < j. Training uses a batch size of 1, 2000 iterations, and a learning rate schedule decreasing from 10^{-3} to 10^{-5} with weight decay 10^{-5}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides dense, pixel-wise uncertainty estimates that correlate well with actual rendering errors. It is decoupled from the main optimization, allowing it to be applied post-hoc. Limitations: Requires hold-out views for training, which may not be available in all scenarios. Performance depends on the quality of the primitive-based feature maps. When to use: When dense uncertainty maps are needed for novel views in Gaussian Splatting, especially for applications like view selection or adaptive rendering. The method originates from the PRIMU paper, which introduces uncertainty estimation for novel views in Gaussian Splatting using primitive-based representations of error and coverage. PRIMU: Uncertainty Estimation for Novel Views in Gaussian Splatting from Primitive-Based Representations of Error and Coverage, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02443v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Photometric and Color Consistency Losses
head: Baseline Photo-consistency, Consistency Supervision, Frontal and Back Consistency Losses, Lambertian Prior, Photometric Consistency (Baseline)
body: This family of losses enforces pixel-level color fidelity and structural consistency between rendered images and ground-truth observations, serving as the primary supervisory signal for differentiable volume rendering. Unlike structural or geometric regularizers, these methods directly minimize the discrepancy in radiance values, often incorporating mechanisms to handle occlusion, temporal dynamics, or the density-color ambiguity inherent in the emission-absorption model. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs are rendered images, ground-truth images, scene parameters (density \sigma, color \mathbf{c}, geometry), and camera poses. Outputs are scalar loss values for backpropagation through the differentiable rendering pipeline. Data Structures: Scene parameters are typically stored in learnable tensors or explicit structures (e.g., voxel grids, point clouds, Gaussian attributes). Camera poses are 4×4 transformation matrices. Intermediate rendering states (transmittance, accumulated weights) are stored per ray for gradient computation. Numbered Steps: 1. Render images \hat{I} from current scene parameters using the emission-absorption model. 2. Compute per-pixel or per-surface photometric residuals against ground-truth observations I. 3. Apply occlusion or geometric consistency masks to exclude unreliable pixels (e.g., depth thresholding, top-NCC selection). 4. Aggregate residuals into a scalar loss, optionally weighting terms by opacity, blending weights, or consensus statistics. 5. Backpropagate gradients through the loss and rendering operator to update scene parameters. Formulas: The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is density, \deltai is step size, \mathbf{c}i is color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is transmittance. Baseline Lambertian Prior: Assumes non-occluded viewpoints yield similar photometric observations for points on the observed surface. The consistency measure accounts for the distance to the median observed value \Phi(X, I). A constant \Gamma\Phi prevents the product over all cameras from canceling out during occlusion, and \sigmac is a hyperparameter. Consistency Supervision (Frontal & Back): Aligns a frontal anchor image I with the xy-axes to supervise a rendered frontal image I{vf} via L{2D,vf} = \|I{vf} - I\|2^2. Ray intersection points X{inter} from sphere tracing are supervised against pixel-aligned RGB colors c{uv}(X{inter}) using L{3D\RGB} = \|c(X{inter}) - c{uv}(X{inter})\|2^2. A blending weight regularization L{reg,b} = \|1 - b(X{inter})\|2^2 enhances frontal blending. The total frontal loss is L{CS\front} = \lambda{2D\front} L{2D,vf} + \lambda{3D\RGB} L{3D\RGB} + \lambdab L{reg,b}. Back-view consistency uses a pretrained color prior: L{CS\back} = \lambda{2D\back} \|I{vb0} - I{vb\pred}\|2^2. View Direction Dependence: Addresses color inconsistency when training on a single view per instance by penalizing squared differences between sampled radiance c(x, d) and the average radiance over directions. The loss is E{x\sim px; d\sim pd} [\|c(x, d) - E{d'\sim pd}[c(x, d')]\|^2]. The inner expectation is approximated by sampling K directions di \sim pd and averaging: \frac{1}{K} \sum{i=1}^K c(x, di). LNCC Photometric Consistency: Constrains surface patches s across views using Normalized Cross Correlation. NCC(U{k1}'(s), U{k2}'(s)) = \frac{Cov(U{k1}'(s), U{k2}'(s))}{\sqrt{Var(U{k1}'(s)) Var(U{k2}'(s))}}. The loss sums the top three largest NCC scores among neighboring views to handle occlusion: LNCC = \sum{k2=1}^3 (1 - NCC(U{k1}'(s), U{k2}'(s))). Gray-level images U' are derived from ground-truth colors via a gray() function. VTC Appearance-Consistency Loss: Uses a Huber penalty \rho(\cdot) on the difference between current color estimates \hat{c}k and a precomputed consensus target \hat{c}^. A stop-gradient operator \text{sg}(\cdot) is applied to \hat{c}^ to prevent circular dependency where geometric errors absorb rendering errors. Parameters: \lambda weights control term contributions. K=64 for direction sampling. \sigmac, \Gamma\Phi for baseline prior. \lambda5 for LNCC anneals from 0 to 0.1 over 100 epochs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The baseline prior yields state-of-the-art results on synthetic data where Lambertian assumptions hold but performs poorly on real data. Adding view-direction regularization decreases average PSNR over color edits to 34.49. If the consensus target is updated with the training state, the geometric error term absorbs the current rendering error, creating a circular dependency that re-injects interference into the supervision signal. LNCC requires careful occlusion handling; using all neighboring views without top-NCC selection degrades performance on partially occluded surfaces. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeconsistencyloss(renderedimg, gtimg, radiancefield, consensustarget, K=64): # 1. Baseline 2D photometric loss (MSE) residual2d = renderedimg - gtimg loss2d = torch.mean(residual2d 2) # 2. View-direction dependence regularization # Approximate inner expectation E{d'}[c(x, d')] by sampling K directions directionloss = 0.0 for in range(K): dsample = sampledirection() # Uniform spherical sampling csample = radiancefield(dsample) directionloss += torch.mean((csample - torch.mean(csample, dim=0, keepdim=True)) 2) directionloss /= K # 3. VTC appearance-consistency loss with stop-gradient # Huber penalty on difference between current estimate and fixed consensus target consensusresidual = renderedimg - torch.stopgradient(consensustarget) lossconsensus = torch.mean(huberpenalty(consensusresidual)) # 4. Aggregate losses totalloss = loss2d + directionloss + lossconsensus return totalloss def huberpenalty(residual, delta=1.0): absresidual = torch.abs(residual) return torch.where(absresidual <= delta, 0.5 residual 2, delta (absresidual - 0.5 delta)) def sampledirection(): # Standard uniform direction generation on unit sphere u = torch.rand(1) v = torch.rand(1) theta = 2 torch.pi u phi = torch.acos(2 v - 1) return torch.tensor([torch.sin(phi) torch.cos(theta), torch.sin(phi) torch.sin(theta), torch.cos(phi)]) Computes the Mean Squared Error between predicted and target RGB values to serve as the primary photometric fidelity metric. It sets itself apart by focusing strictly on pixel-wise intensity error, penalizing large deviations more heavily than perceptual metrics. Choose it for stable convergence on synthetic data or when PSNR benchmarking is required. Combines a pixel-wise L1 term for color fidelity with a Structural Similarity (SSIM) term to preserve local structure and edges. Unlike pure L1 or MSE, which can produce blurry results, this hybrid approach aligns more closely with human perception. It is the standard training objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Computes photometric error only on pixels where the squared depth difference between reprojected source view depth and directly rendered target view depth is below a fixed threshold (\Delta d^2 < 0.001). It sets itself apart by explicitly masking out geometrically inconsistent pixels before applying the L1 loss. Choose it for SLAM or multi-view consistency pipelines where depth alignment is available. Improves convergence by combining a standard photometric term with a secondary term that normalizes the color error by the remaining opacity. It addresses volume rendering ambiguity by concentrating opacity on the object surface. It differs from standard losses by introducing a dynamic weighting scheme and thresholding mechanism that activates the opacity-normalized term only after a significant portion of training. Enforces smoothness in dynamic radiance fields by penalizing differences in the scene representation between adjacent time steps. It solves the problem of flickering and visual discontinuities in novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes. It sets itself apart by explicitly incorporating the temporal dimension. Choose it for video or dynamic scene reconstruction. A regularization technique for explicit radiance fields (e.g., Plenoxels, DVGO) that breaks the entanglement between density and color fields. It estimates a closed-form color field given the current density field and posed training images, then computes a photometric loss between this estimated color and the ground truth to supervise the density field. It is distinct from distortion loss in that it is sensitive to specific geometric errors. Leverages the correlation between surface texture and geometry (normals) to refine 3D reconstruction, effectively applying shape-from-shading principles to neural fields. It alleviates texture-induced artifacts by enforcing multi-view consistency during the joint training of geometry and color fields. Choose it when surface detail recovery is prioritized over photometric exactness, but avoid on textureless or decorrelated surfaces. Evaluates whether a focus structure's shading distribution is preserved in a rendered Direct Volume Rendering Image (DVRI), ensuring a clear and comprehensible presentation without distortion from partial occlusion. It sets itself apart by focusing on the structural integrity of a specific focus object rather than global pixel-wise error. Choose it for medical or scientific visualization where shading fidelity of specific structures is critical. A regularization prior used in inverse rendering and radiance field optimization to mitigate the inherent ambiguity between material properties and incident illumination. It operates on the assumption that natural environmental lighting is typically neutral or "white," penalizing illumination estimates that exhibit strong chromatic biases. Choose it when jointly optimizing lighting and geometry, rather than for standard photometric supervision. A photometric regularization term designed for neural surface reconstruction from sparse views. It solves the problem of noisy or distorted geometry caused by inconsistent radiance in unstructured scenes by automatically excluding regions where rendered colors do not match ground truth observations. It sets itself apart by weighting the error by the accumulated weight O(r) and applying logistic regularization to suppress inconsistent rays. Choose it for sparse-view reconstruction pipelines. A filtering function applied during training to maintain consistency, removed in ablation experiments. It sets itself apart by acting as a dynamic quality gate that discards inconsistent samples before loss computation. Choose it when training point-based or coarse-to-fine radiance fields to stabilize early optimization stages. Regularization to address color inconsistency across rendered views when training on only one view per instance. It sets itself apart by explicitly penalizing directional variance in the radiance field. Choose it for single-view or limited-view training scenarios where view-dependent appearance artifacts are prominent. A loss term constraining photometric consistency of surface patches across different views using Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC), considering occlusion by selecting top NCC scores. It sets itself apart from pixel-wise L1/MSE losses by operating on surface patches and using rank-based occlusion handling. Choose it for SDF-based reconstruction where surface patch constraints are available. Enforces appearance consistency using a precomputed consensus target and a stop-gradient operator to prevent gradient feedback loops. It sets itself apart by separating stable color statistics from instantaneous photometric residuals. Choose it for Gaussian reconstruction in texture-degraded scenes where consensus priors can be reliably estimated. Time and Memory Complexity: Computation scales linearly with the number of pixels and samples per ray. View-direction regularization adds O(K) radiance evaluations per point, increasing compute by a factor of K. Consensus-based losses require storing precomputed targets, adding O(N) memory overhead. Differentiation strategies (reverse-mode AD, adjoint, analytic inversion) trade memory for compute, with analytic inversion reducing memory to O(n) per pixel. Measured Performance: On the Blender dataset, applying a consistency filter improves PSNR from 29.1 dB to 30.3 dB and SSIM from 0.941 to 0.945, while removing it increases LPIPS from 0.078 to 0.103. Adding view-direction regularization decreases the average PSNR over three color edits to 34.49. Scaling: Photometric losses scale well with resolution when using differentiable rasterization or ray marching, but memory consumption grows with ray samples and batch size. Consensus and NCC-based methods scale poorly with extreme view counts due to pairwise or patch-wise computation. Strengths and Limitations: Directly minimizes radiance discrepancy, providing strong supervision for color and texture. Handles occlusion via depth thresholds or NCC ranking. Resolves density-color ambiguity via opacity normalization or closed-form estimation. Fails on textureless surfaces, strong specularities, or non-Lambertian materials where photometric assumptions break down. When to Use: Use for standard novel view synthesis, explicit radiance field training, and surface reconstruction where ground-truth images are available. Use visibility-based or adaptive variants for SLAM or ambiguous density fields. Avoid when training on highly dynamic lighting or non-diffuse scenes without appropriate priors. Originating from traditional multi-view stereo Lambertian priors, photometric consistency measures were adapted for differentiable rendering to supervise neural radiance fields. Early implementations relied heavily on MSE loss for its differentiability and simplicity. The adoption of L1+SSIM became standard in explicit representations like 3D Gaussian Splatting to mitigate blurriness. Subsequent research introduced visibility-based constraints for SLAM contexts, adaptive thresholding for density-color ambiguity, temporal consistency for dynamic scenes, and closed-form color estimation for voxel-based methods. Modern variants incorporate consistency filtering, view-direction regularization, surface patch NCC constraints, and consensus-based Gaussian supervision to address specific reconstruction challenges. name: MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion
head: Loss Function for Constant Model, MSE Loss, Mean Squared Error, Mean Squared Error Loss, Pixel-wise RGB Mean Squared Error (MSE)
body: MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion computes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and target RGB values (or volumes) and converts this error into Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for logging and evaluation. It serves as the primary photometric consistency loss for training differentiable volume rendering models, minimizing the pixel-wise intensity difference between rendered images and ground truth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Predicted image/volume \hat{I} (or \hat{C}), Target image/volume I (or C), and optionally a binary mask M indicating valid voxels/pixels. Outputs: Scalar MSE loss value, PSNR value (for logging), and optionally masked statistics. Data Structures: Predicted/Target Arrays: 3D arrays (H, W, 3) for images or 3D grids (D, H, W) for volumes, containing floating-point color/intensity values. Mask (Optional): Boolean array of same spatial dimensions as input, where True indicates valid regions. Steps: 1. Input Validation: Check that inputs are not empty and have compatible shapes. If using a mask, ensure it is not entirely false. 2. Compute Difference: Calculate the element-wise difference between predicted and target values: D = \hat{I} - I. 3. Square Difference: Square the difference element-wise: S = D^2. 4. Masking (Optional): If a mask M is provided, apply it to the squared errors. Let N be the number of elements where M is true. 5. Compute MSE: Average the squared errors over the valid elements: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i \in \text{valid}} (\hat{I}i - Ii)^2 For a constant intensity model parameterized by density \sigma and step size q, the predicted intensity is computed via a lookup function, and the loss is half the sum of squared residuals. 6. Compute PSNR: Convert MSE to PSNR in decibels (dB): \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \log{10}(\text{MSE}) Alternatively, using the signal-to-noise ratio form where the maximum signal value is 1 (for normalized RGB): \text{PSNR} = 20 \cdot \log{10}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}}}\right) If MSE is 0, PSNR is defined as infinity. Parameters: Mask Threshold (Optional): A relative threshold maskthresholdrel (default 0.01) applied to the normalized mask volume to create the boolean mask. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Mask: If the boolean mask has no true values, raise a RuntimeError. Zero MSE: If MSE is exactly 0.0, PSNR remains infinity to avoid division by zero in the log10 calculation. Precision: Ensure inputs are in linear color space (no gamma compression) for accurate photometric loss, especially when handling under/over-exposed values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computemseandpsnr(predicted: np.ndarray, target: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray = None) -> dict: """ Computes MSE and PSNR between predicted and target arrays. Args: predicted: Array of predicted values (H, W, C) or (D, H, W). target: Array of target values with same shape as predicted. mask: Optional boolean array of same spatial dimensions. Returns: Dictionary with 'mse', 'psnr', 'maskedvoxelcount', 'volumeshape'. """ # Validate inputs if predicted.shape != target.shape: raise ValueError("Predicted and target must have the same shape.") if mask is not None: # Apply mask threshold if mask is not boolean if not mask.dtype == bool: threshold = 0.01 np.max(mask) mask = mask > threshold if not np.any(mask): raise RuntimeError("Mask has no true values.") # Flatten spatial dimensions for masking predictedflat = predicted.flatten() targetflat = target.flatten() maskflat = mask.flatten() # Apply mask validpred = predictedflat[maskflat] validtarget = targetflat[maskflat] nvalid = len(validpred) else: validpred = predicted.flatten() validtarget = target.flatten() nvalid = len(validpred) # Compute squared differences squareddiff = (validpred - validtarget) 2 # Compute MSE mse = np.mean(squareddiff) # Compute PSNR if mse == 0.0: psnr = float('inf') else: psnr = 20.0 math.log10(1.0 / math.sqrt(mse)) return { 'mse': float(mse), 'psnr': psnr, 'maskedvoxelcount': int(nvalid) if mask is not None else int(nvalid), 'volumeshape': list(predicted.shape) } Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is a standard benchmark metric used to evaluate the photometric fidelity of reconstructed images or volumes in novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. It quantifies the error between a predicted image and a ground-truth reference by converting the Mean Squared Error (MSE) into a logarithmic decibel (dB) scale, where higher values indicate better quality. Unlike structural metrics such as SSIM, PSNR focuses strictly on pixel-wise intensity accuracy, making it sensitive to large smooth regions while largely ignoring small, high-frequency features like specular highlights. SSIM is a full-reference quality assessment metric that evaluates image fidelity by measuring perceptual similarity through local comparisons of luminance, contrast, and structure. Unlike pixel-wise error metrics such as MSE or PSNR, which often correlate poorly with human perception, SSIM captures structural information changes to approximate perceived distortion. It is widely used as a standard benchmark for image quality in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. The Normal-L2 Score computes the mean squared error between predicted surface normals and ground-truth normals to evaluate geometric fidelity in radiance-field optimization. It differs from sibling metrics like PSNR Metric Calculation by focusing on shading-critical surface orientation rather than color intensity, and from IoU Loss by measuring local geometric accuracy rather than global silhouette alignment. Minkowski's Metric (also known as the Lp norm or Lgamma loss) is a family of photometric consistency losses used in radiance-field optimization to quantify the dissimilarity between a rendered image and a ground-truth reference. It generalizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) by allowing the exponent \gamma to vary, enabling a trade-off between sensitivity to large errors and robustness to outliers. Unlike MSE, which penalizes large deviations quadratically, Minkowski's Metric with \gamma < 2 (e.g., L1) is less sensitive to outliers, while \gamma > 2 increases sensitivity to large errors. IoU Loss is a binary segmentation metric that computes the ratio of overlapping voxels above a threshold to the total union of predicted and target voxels. The perceptually-motivated variance metric quantifies the error between an 8-bit ambient occlusion (AO) approximation T and a high-fidelity ray-traced reference R. It differs from raw pixel Mean Squared Error (MSE) by operating on log-transformed values and spatial gradients, thereby aligning with human visual sensitivity to radiance and its changes. This metric is specifically designed for evaluating AO approximations where reflected ambient radiance is linear in accessibility. Depth Accuracy Metrics evaluate the geometric fidelity of predicted depth maps against ground truth data in radiance field optimization pipelines. They quantify scale- and translation-invariant errors on valid depth pixels. They are used to evaluate depth prior quality and monocular depth estimation outputs in NeRF pipelines. The Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) Loss is a regularization term for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that minimizes the difference between the frequency representations of rendered and ground-truth images by decomposing them into sub-bands. It addresses high-frequency overfitting in few-shot NeRF training by explicitly prioritizing low-frequency learning during early stages. Unlike its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion, which compares pixel-wise values globally, the DW loss operates on local structures using patch-based sampling to supervise low and mid-frequency components. Calculates the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) between observed intensity values and a predicted constant intensity model parameterized by density (\sigma) and step size (q). It serves as a photometric consistency loss in differentiable volume rendering, specifically fitting a constant radiance assumption along a ray. Unlike the parent MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion which operates on raw RGB predictions, this method explicitly models the physical integration of a constant source over a ray segment. Computes a normalized L1 loss between a reconstructed image and an original image, scaling the loss to the [0, 1] range. It is used in sparse pixel sampling optimization pipelines to provide an error metric for adaptive Gaussian densification and pruning. Masked and Weighted Losses is a family of techniques that modify the standard photometric error computation in differentiable volume rendering by applying spatial masks or per-pixel weights to the loss function. It solves the problem of training instability and evaluation bias caused by invalid background regions, sensor artifacts, multiscale resolution disparities, or structural inconsistencies. It sets itself apart from its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion by introducing selective suppression or amplification of error terms rather than computing a global average, and from Masked Volume Metrics by focusing on training-time gradient correction rather than evaluation-time metric definition. The Restricted Mean Error Metric is a loss function designed to optimize scalar weight factors for pre-computed scattering lobe shapes in volume rendering, specifically addressing parameter heterogeneity across voxel clusters. Unlike standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) which treats all pixels equally or global mean metrics that obscure local errors, this method computes the average intensity only for pixels "directly" visible to specific voxel clusters, allowing the optimizer to identify which clusters cause rendering artifacts (such as seams) and correcting them individually. It is primarily used in the context of optimizing SGGX lobe weights via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Silhouette Loss provides boundary supervision for differentiable volume rendering by penalizing discrepancies between predicted surface probabilities and ground-truth image masks. It ensures that the rendered alpha channel aligns with the object's silhouette, preventing geometric artifacts and providing warm-start supervision for fine-grained geometry. It is distinct from photometric losses (e.g., MSE) by operating on the alpha channel rather than RGB values, and from depth losses by focusing on binary boundary presence rather than metric distance. Treating the TAA algorithm as a biased estimator to analyze correctness using Mean Squared Error (MSE), decomposed into variance and bias squared. The formula is \text{MSE}[F] = \mathbb{E}[(F - G)^2] = V[F] + \beta[F]^2, where F is the output of the estimator, G is the true value (ground truth), V[F] is the variance of the estimator, and \beta[F] is its bias. A fast assignment strategy used during Phase 1 to compute the L2 matching loss between heuristic samples and learnt proposals. For each heuristic sample, find the closest proposal from the learnt proposer set. Optimal matching (Hungarian algorithm) or strict 1-1 greedy matching significantly slows training. Calculates Mean Squared Logarithmic Error between two RGB colors, optionally weighted by luminance. The formula is \text{MSLE} = \sumc (\log2(\frac{bc + 1.0}{ac + 1.0}))^2 \cdot wc where wc is 1.0 or luminance weight. L2 loss between the simulated blurry image and the input blurry image. The parameter B(x) is the input blurry image at pixel x. A pixel-wise mean squared loss operating in linear color space (no gamma compression) that handles under-exposed and over-exposed values using a one-sided difference based on clipping thresholds. The parameters are v{min} (lower clipping threshold) and v{max} (upper clipping threshold). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels or voxels, as it involves a single pass to compute differences and averages. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the squared differences, though this can be computed on-the-fly to reduce memory to O(1) if streaming. Measured Performance: Standard metric for NeRF training, often used in conjunction with Adam optimizer. Scaling: Scales linearly with resolution and batch size. Strengths: Simple to implement, differentiable, and widely understood. Provides a direct measure of pixel-wise error. Limitations: Does not correlate well with human perception for high-frequency details. Sensitive to outliers. When to use: Standard training loss for photometric consistency. When not to use: When perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy (use SSIM or LPIPS). MSE Loss is a fundamental metric in image processing and computer vision, originating from statistical error analysis. It is widely used in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis to evaluate the quality of reconstructed volumes and rendered views. name: PSNR Metric Calculation
head: PSNR Calculation, PSNR Metric, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio
body: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is a standard benchmark metric used to evaluate the photometric fidelity of reconstructed images or volumes in novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. It quantifies the error between a predicted image and a ground-truth reference by converting the Mean Squared Error (MSE) into a logarithmic decibel (dB) scale, where higher values indicate better quality. Unlike structural metrics such as SSIM, PSNR focuses strictly on pixel-wise intensity accuracy, making it sensitive to large smooth regions while largely ignoring small, high-frequency features like specular highlights. Inputs and Outputs Input x: Ground-truth image or volume. Input y: Predicted/reconstructed image or volume. Parameter MAX: The maximum possible representable pixel value (e.g., 1.0 for normalized float, 255 for 8-bit integer). Parameter eps: A small constant (typically 10^{-10}) added to MSE to prevent \log(0). Output: A scalar float representing the PSNR in decibels (dB). Data Structures The inputs are dense arrays or tensors containing pixel/voxel values. The computation aggregates errors over all elements in the array. Steps 1. Validation: Ensure x and y have identical dimensions; if not, return an error or maximum float value. 2. Compute Squared Error: Calculate the element-wise squared difference between x and y. 3. Compute MSE: Calculate the mean of the squared differences over all pixels/voxels. 4. Compute PSNR: Apply the logarithmic conversion using MAX and eps. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatepsnr(x: list, y: list, maxval: float = 1.0, eps: float = 1e-10) -> float: """Calculate Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio between two images/volumes x and y.""" if len(x) != len(y): raise ValueError("Input arrays must have identical dimensions") n = len(x) if n == 0: return 0.0 errorsum = 0.0 for i in range(n): diff = x[i] - y[i] errorsum += diff diff mse = errorsum / n psnr = 10.0 math.log10((maxval 2) / (mse + eps)) return psnr Parameters and Typical Values maxval: Default is 1.0 for normalized floating-point images. eps: Default is 10^{-10}. Interpretation: A difference of 3 dB corresponds to a halving of the squared error; a 6 dB difference corresponds to a quartering. Target PSNR for NeRF Blender scenes is typically 31–33 dB. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero MSE: If the prediction is perfect (MSE = 0), PSNR is infinite. The eps term prevents this from causing a runtime error but results in a very large finite number. Smooth Region Bias: PSNR averages over every pixel, weighting large smooth regions heavily and ignoring small bright features like specular highlights or grass blades. Noise Floor: In scientific volumes, if the noise level is zero (signal-limited), MAD estimators may return exactly zero, bounding nothing. 3D Evaluation Metrics quantify the fidelity of reconstructed volumetric or radiance-field representations against ground-truth references, addressing the problem of assessing both geometric accuracy and photometric consistency in 3D reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific aspects like mesh topology Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation or surface orientation Normal Consistency, this category encompasses a suite of metrics including PSNR, SSIM, and mIoU to provide a comprehensive assessment of reconstruction quality. It distinguishes itself from PSNR Metric Calculation by extending the evaluation to 3D volumes and multi-view consistency, and from Benchmark Performance Numbers by providing the specific algorithmic definitions of the scores rather than just reporting aggregated results. Benchmark Performance Numbers provide standardized quantitative baselines for evaluating radiance field optimization methods, primarily using the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset metrics (average PSNR and LPIPS). They serve as a reference point to compare the reconstruction quality of different variants (e.g., 3DGS, Mip-Splatting) against established baselines. Unlike raw metric calculation, these numbers aggregate results across a specific scene set to highlight trade-offs between visual fidelity, geometric accuracy, and resource efficiency. The PSNR Difference Metric for Ablation quantifies the performance degradation caused by removing a specific component from a rendering pipeline by comparing the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) of the ablated configuration against the full method. It isolates the error ratio independent of the bit depth (MAX), as MAX cancels out in the logarithmic difference, providing a scale-invariant measure of quality loss. Noise Floor Estimation via MAD estimates the noise standard deviation \sigma in volumetric data to determine the theoretical maximum achievable PSNR (noise floor). It uses Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) estimators: (1) Laplacian MAD applies the D-dimensional discrete Laplacian and scales the MAD of the response by 1/(0.6745 \sqrt{2D(2D+1)}); (2) Haar finite-difference MAD uses per-slice diagonal second differences d = I(y,x) - I(y,x+1) - I(y+1,x) + I(y+1,x+1), scaling MAD by 1/(0.6745 \sqrt{2}). The noise floor PSNR is then 10 \log{10}(1/\sigma^2). A pitfall is that MAD estimators may return exactly zero for signal-limited volumes (e.g., Mouse heart nuclei), bounding nothing. PSNR Loss computes the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio between predicted and target images, used as a regression metric during training. It is defined as \text{PSNR} = 20 \log{10}\left(\frac{\text{max\val}}{\sqrt{\text{MSE}}}\right). Unlike the standard PSNR metric which is used for evaluation, this variant is often used as a differentiable loss function (or its negative) during optimization, with maxval defaulting to 1.0. Color PSNR (YUV) computes color degradation by converting RGB to YUV and combining per-component PSNR values. Points in the distorted content are associated to reference points using a nearest neighbor algorithm, and RGB values are converted to YUV per ITU-R BT.709-3. PSNR is computed for Y, U, and V components separately, then combined using a weighted average: PSNRYUV = \frac{6 \cdot PSNRY + PSNRU + PSNRV}{8}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and widely understood as a standard benchmark for image quality. Limitations: Does not correlate well with human perception for structural details or textures; heavily biased towards smooth regions; sensitive to global brightness shifts. When to Use: Standard reporting for novel view synthesis benchmarks (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360, Blender scenes) where photometric accuracy is the primary concern. When Not to Use: When structural similarity or perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy; in such cases, SSIM or LPIPS should be used alongside or instead. In the context of volume rendering and neural radiance fields (NeRF), PSNR became a standard metric for evaluating novel view synthesis quality, with early benchmarks targeting 31–33 dB on Blender scenes. It is frequently reported alongside SSIM and LPIPS to provide a more complete picture of reconstruction fidelity, as PSNR alone fails to capture perceptual similarities in complex scenes. name: 3D Evaluation Metrics
body: 3D Evaluation Metrics quantify the fidelity of reconstructed volumetric or radiance-field representations against ground-truth references, addressing the problem of assessing both geometric accuracy and photometric consistency in 3D reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that focus on specific aspects like mesh topology Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation or surface orientation Normal Consistency, this category encompasses a suite of metrics including PSNR, SSIM, and mIoU to provide a comprehensive assessment of reconstruction quality. It extends evaluation to 3D volumes and multi-view consistency compared to PSNR Metric Calculation, and provides specific algorithmic definitions rather than just aggregated results like Benchmark Performance Numbers. Inputs: Reconstructed volume V{pred} (normalized to [0, 1] or binarized occupancy); Ground-truth volume V{gt} (normalized to [0, 1] or binary occupancy); Camera poses for novel view synthesis; Rendering engine for splats or direct volume access for voxels. Outputs: PSNR (dB), SSIM (0–1), and/or mIoU (0–100%). Volume: A 3D tensor of shape (D, H, W) or (N, D, H, W) for multiple views/channels. Occupancy Grid: A binary 3D tensor where 1 indicates occupied space and 0 indicates empty space. Splats: A list of Gaussian parameters (\mu, \Sigma, c, \alpha) used for rendering. 1. Photometric Evaluation (PSNR and SSIM): a. Normalization: Ensure V{pred} and V{gt} are normalized to the range [0, 1]. b. View Selection: Iterate over axial, coronal, and sagittal slices, or render novel views from held-out camera poses. c. MSE Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) averaged over all voxels, including background: MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (V{pred}[i] - V{gt}[i])^2 where N is the total number of voxels. d. PSNR Calculation: Compute PSNR using the normalized maximum value MAX=1: PSNR = 10 \log{10} \left( \frac{1}{MSE} \right). e. SSIM Calculation: Compute Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) using a window size of 11 and Gaussian weighting with \sigma = 1.5. f. Aggregation: Print or return the mean PSNR and SSIM across all views or slices. 2. Geometric Evaluation (mIoU for Occupancy): a. Alpha Extraction: Extract the predicted \alpha volume, which corresponds to the last channel of the predicted volume Vs. b. Binarization: Binarize the predicted \alpha volume using a fixed threshold \tau = 0.05: V{pred\bin}[i] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V{pred}[i] \ge \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} c. Ground Truth Preparation: Ensure V{gt} is a binary occupancy volume (upsampled to the target resolution, e.g., 64^3). d. IoU Calculation: For each semantic category c, compute the Intersection-over-Union: IoUc = \frac{|V{pred\bin}^c \cap V{gt}^c|}{|V{pred\bin}^c \cup V{gt}^c|} e. mIoU Aggregation: Average the per-category IoU scores to obtain the final mIoU metric. SSIM Window Size: 11. SSIM Sigma (\sigma): 1.5. Binarization Threshold (\tau): 0.05. MSE Scope: Includes all voxels (background included). Overfitting: Low error on training views but high error on held-out views indicates overfitting, usually caused by insufficient scene coverage. Background Inclusion: MSE must be averaged over all voxels including background to be comparable with standard definitions. Resolution Mismatch: Ground truth volumes may need upsampling (e.g., nearest-neighbor interpolation from 32^3 to 64^3) to match the prediction resolution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.ndimage import gaussianfilter def computepsnrssimvolume(predvol: np.ndarray, gtvol: np.ndarray) -> dict: """ Computes PSNR and SSIM for 3D volumes normalized to [0, 1]. MSE is averaged over all voxels including background. SSIM uses window size 11 and sigma 1.5. """ pred = predvol.astype(np.float32) gt = gtvol.astype(np.float32) # 1. Compute MSE mse = np.mean((pred - gt) 2) # 2. Compute PSNR if mse == 0: psnr = float('inf') else: psnr = 10 np.log10(1.0 / mse) # 3. Compute SSIM ssim = computessim3d(pred, gt, windowsize=11, sigma=1.5) return {"psnr": psnr, "ssim": ssim} def computessim3d(img1: np.ndarray, img2: np.ndarray, windowsize: int = 11, sigma: float = 1.5) -> float: """ Computes 3D SSIM using Gaussian kernel. Sources do not provide SSIM formula; standard implementation uses Gaussian kernel. """ C1 = (0.01 255) 2 C2 = (0.03 255) 2 mu1 = gaussianfilter(img1, sigma) mu2 = gaussianfilter(img2, sigma) mu1sq = mu1 2 mu2sq = mu2 2 mu1mu2 = mu1 mu2 sigma1sq = gaussianfilter(img1 2, sigma) - mu1sq sigma2sq = gaussianfilter(img2 2, sigma) - mu2sq sigma12 = gaussianfilter(img1 img2, sigma) - mu1mu2 ssimval = (2 mu1mu2 + C1) (2 sigma12 + C2) / \ ((mu1sq + mu2sq + C1) (sigma1sq + sigma2sq + C2)) return float(np.mean(ssimval)) def computemiou(predalphavol: np.ndarray, gtoccvol: np.ndarray, threshold: float = 0.05) -> float: """ Computes mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) for 3D occupancy. predalphavol: Predicted alpha volume (last channel of Vs). gtoccvol: Ground truth binary occupancy volume. """ # 1. Binarize predicted alpha volume predbin = (predalphavol >= threshold).astype(np.float32) # 2. Ensure GT is binary gtbin = (gtoccvol > 0.5).astype(np.float32) # 3. Compute IoU for the whole volume (single category) intersection = np.sum(predbin gtbin) union = np.sum(predbin) + np.sum(gtbin) - intersection if union == 0: return 0.0 iou = intersection / union # For multi-category, average per-category IoU # Here assuming single category for simplicity based on S3 description return iou 100.0 # Return as percentage Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation quantifies the geometric fidelity of a reconstructed triangular mesh against a ground-truth reference mesh. It solves the problem of assessing how well a surface reconstruction method captures the true shape, topology, and detail of the underlying scene. Unlike radiance-field metrics that evaluate visual appearance, this method focuses strictly on spatial accuracy, distinguishing it from PSNR Metric Calculation which measures pixel-level photometric error. Normal Consistency (NC) is a metric for 3D surface reconstruction that measures the angular deviation between estimated surface normals and ground truth normals. It quantifies how well the orientation of the reconstructed surface aligns with the underlying geometry, serving as a complementary measure to distance-based metrics like Chamfer Distance. Unlike distance metrics that assess positional accuracy, NC specifically evaluates surface smoothness and orientation fidelity. Standard Rendering Metrics provide an objective, numerical assessment of image fidelity for 3D reconstructions and novel view synthesis. The primary metric is the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), which quantifies pixel-wise reconstruction error in decibels by comparing rendered images against ground-truth references. While PSNR is the standard baseline due to its computational cheapness, it is widely recognized as insensitive to perceptual quality, often necessitating companion metrics like SSIM or LPIPS for a complete evaluation. Evaluates 3D geometry learned in a self-supervised manner by minimizing a novel view synthesis objective, using mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) between predicted and ground truth volumes. The predicted \alpha volume (last channel of Vs) is binarized using a threshold \tau = 0.05 and compared against the ground truth occupancy volume. The mIoU is averaged across categories. In benchmarks, this method achieved 63.25% mIoU, outperforming supervised baselines like 3D-R2N2 (55.1%). Evaluation requires holding out photos never trained on, rendering the trained splat from those poses, and comparing against real photos. Standard scores are PSNR (higher is better), SSIM (closer to 1 is better), and LPIPS (lower is better, correlates with human perception). A key pitfall is that low training-view error but high held-out error indicates overfitting, usually caused by insufficient scene coverage. Time Complexity: PSNR/SSIM computation is O(N) where N is the number of voxels or pixels. SSIM requires convolution, adding a factor related to window size. mIoU is O(N) for voxel-wise comparison. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the volumes and intermediate buffers for SSIM. Strengths: PSNR and SSIM are computationally cheap and provide a standard baseline. mIoU provides a direct geometric measure for occupancy grids. Limitations: PSNR is insensitive to perceptual quality. SSIM parameters (window size, sigma) must be chosen carefully. mIoU requires a threshold, which can be sensitive to the choice of \tau. When to Use: Use PSNR/SSIM for photometric evaluation of novel views or volume slices. Use mIoU for evaluating self-supervised 3D geometry reconstruction. Use LPIPS for perceptual quality assessment. 3D evaluation metrics have evolved alongside 3D reconstruction techniques. PSNR and SSIM were originally developed for 2D image compression and quality assessment but have been adapted for 3D volumes and radiance fields. The use of mIoU for 3D reconstruction evaluation in self-supervised settings was introduced in works like Fast and Explicit Neural View Synthesis. The evaluation of 3D Gaussian Splatting relies on held-out view metrics including LPIPS to assess generalization. name: Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation
body: Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation quantifies the geometric fidelity of a reconstructed triangular mesh against a ground-truth reference mesh. It solves the problem of assessing how well a surface reconstruction method captures the true shape, topology, and detail of the underlying scene. Unlike radiance-field metrics that evaluate visual appearance, this method focuses strictly on spatial accuracy, distinguishing it from PSNR Metric Calculation which measures pixel-level photometric error. The evaluation computes statistical distances between the vertices of the reconstructed mesh and the ground-truth surface. The primary metrics are Chamfer Distance and F-Score. Inputs: Reconstructed mesh \mathcal{M}{rec} and ground-truth mesh \mathcal{M}{gt}, typically represented as sets of vertices and faces. Outputs: Scalar scores for Chamfer Distance and F-Score. Data Structures: Point clouds or vertex sets for distance queries; KD-trees or spatial hashing for efficient nearest-neighbor search. Steps: 1. Sample points uniformly from the surface of \mathcal{M}{rec} and \mathcal{M}{gt} to obtain point sets P{rec} and P{gt}. 2. Compute the Chamfer Distance (CD) as the sum of squared nearest-neighbor distances in both directions: CD(P{rec}, P{gt}) = \frac{1}{|P{rec}|} \sum{p \in P{rec}} \min{q \in P{gt}} \|p - q\|^2 + \frac{1}{|P{gt}|} \sum{q \in P{gt}} \min{p \in P{rec}} \|p - q\|^2. 3. Compute the F-Score at a threshold distance \tau by calculating precision (fraction of P{rec} within \tau of P{gt}) and recall (fraction of P{gt} within \tau of P{rec}), then taking the harmonic mean: F(\tau) = \frac{2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}. Parameters: Threshold \tau for F-Score, typically 0.01 to 0.02 of the bounding box diagonal. Number of sampled points per mesh, typically 10^4 to 10^5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-explanation: The method focuses heavily on geometric details, which can cause over-explanation of texture on flat surfaces with complex geometry, leading to visible artifacts. Metric Discrepancy: Quantitative mesh metrics (F-score, Chamfer distance) are good, but visualizations show apparent artifacts compared to ground truth. Evaluators should always inspect visual results alongside metrics. A mesh regularization term that encourages geometric flatness by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of the vertex normal covariance matrix, weighted by vertex area. It distinguishes itself from smoothness-based regularizers like Laplacian smoothing by explicitly penalizing curvature to promote planar patches. Choose it when differentiable surface reconstruction requires explicit flatness constraints. It builds on Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation. name: Developability Regularizer
head: Stein et al. regularizer
body:
The Developability Regularizer is a mesh regularization term that encourages geometric flatness (developability) by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of the vertex normal covariance matrix, weighted by vertex area. It builds on Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation. The method computes a per-vertex contribution to the loss based on the local geometry of incident triangles. It aggregates normal covariances and areas, then computes the minimum eigenvalue as a measure of non-developability. Inputs: tripos: Tensor of shape (T, 3, 3), containing the 3D positions of the three vertices for each of the T triangles. tris: Tensor of shape (T, 3), containing the vertex indices for each triangle. V: Number of unique vertices in the mesh. Outputs: loss: Scalar tensor representing the total developability loss. Data Structures: vertnormalcovariancesum: Tensor of shape (V, 9), initialized to zeros. Stores the flattened 3 	imes 3 normal covariance matrix for each vertex. vertarea: Tensor of shape (V), initialized to zeros. Stores the weighted area contribution for each vertex. vertdegree: Tensor of shape (V), initialized to zeros (int32). Stores the number of triangles incident to each vertex. Parameters: RELEPS: 1 	imes 10^{-6}. Added to the covariance matrix to ensure numerical stability during eigenvalue decomposition. POSEPS: 1 	imes 10^{-6}. Used in normalization denominators to prevent division by zero. Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulators: Set vertnormalcovariancesum, vertarea, and vertdegree to zero tensors of the specified shapes. 2. Iterate Over Triangle Corners: For each triangle t in the mesh, and for each corner index iC \in \{0, 1, 2\}: a. Gather Vertices: Let p{Root} = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, iC], pA = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, (iC + 1) \pmod 3], and pB = 	ext{tri\pos}[t, (iC + 2) \pmod 3]. b. Compute Edge Vectors: vA = pA - p{Root}, vB = pB - p{Root}, and normalize them to v{An} and v{Bn}. c. Compute Face Geometry: area
ormal = vA 	imes vB, face\area = 0.5 	imes \|area
ormal\|, and normal =  rac{area
ormal}{\|area
ormal\| + 	ext{POS\EPS}}. d. Compute Corner Angle: corner\angle = \arccos(	ext{clamp}(	ext{dot}(v{An}, v{Bn}), -1, 1)). e. Compute Normal Outer Product: outer = normal \otimes normal (Resulting in a 3 	imes 3 matrix), then flatten to a vector of length 9. f. Scatter Updates: Let idx = 	ext{tris}[t, iC]. Accumulate outer to 	ext{vert
ormal\covariance\sum}[idx], add  rac{face\area}{3} to 	ext{vert\area}[idx], and add 1 to 	ext{vert\degree}[idx]. 3. Process Covariance Matrices: Reshape vertnormalcovariancesum to (V, 3, 3) and add 	ext{REL\EPS} 	imes I to each matrix, where I is the identity matrix. 4. Compute Minimum Eigenvalues: Compute the eigenvalues for each vertex's covariance matrix and take the minimum absolute value: 	ext{min\eigvals}[v] = \min(|\lambda1|, |\lambda2|, |\lambda3|). 5. Mask Degree-3 Vertices: Set 	ext{vert\area}[v] = 0 where 	ext{vert\degree}[v] == 3. 6. Normalize Area: Normalize 	ext{vert\area} by scaling it: 	ext{vert\area} \leftarrow 	ext{vert\area} 	imes  rac{V}{\sum 	ext{vert\area}}. 7. Compute Loss: Return the element-wise product 	ext{vert\area} 	imes 	ext{min\eigvals}, summed to a scalar. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computedevelopabilityregularizer(tripos, tris, V, releps=1e-6, poseps=1e-6): """ Compute the Developability Regularizer loss. Args: tripos: Tensor (T, 3, 3) - Vertex positions for each triangle. tris: Tensor (T, 3) - Vertex indices for each triangle. V: int - Number of vertices. releps: float - Regularization epsilon for eigenvalues. poseps: float - Epsilon for normalization. Returns: loss: Tensor (1,) - Scalar loss value. """ T = tripos.shape[0] # Initialize accumulators vertnormalcovariancesum = torch.zeros((V, 9), device=tripos.device) vertarea = torch.zeros((V), device=tripos.device) vertdegree = torch.zeros((V), dtype=torch.int32, device=tripos.device) # Loop over triangles and corners for iC in range(3): # Gather vertices proot = tripos[:, iC] pa = tripos[:, (iC + 1) % 3] pb = tripos[:, (iC + 2) % 3] # Edge vectors va = pa - proot vb = pb - proot # Normalize edges normva = torch.norm(va, dim=1, keepdim=True) normvb = torch.norm(vb, dim=1, keepdim=True) van = va / (normva + poseps) vbn = vb / (normvb + poseps) # Face area and normal areanormal = torch.cross(va, vb, dim=1) facearea = 0.5 torch.norm(areanormal, dim=1) normareanormal = torch.norm(areanormal, dim=1, keepdim=True) normal = areanormal / (normareanormal + poseps) # Compute corner angle (computed per source, but unused in final loss) cornerangle = torch.acos(torch.clamp(torch.sum(van vbn, dim=1), -1.0, 1.0)) # Outer product of normal (3x3 matrix) outer = torch.einsum('ti,tj->tij', normal, normal) outerflat = outer.reshape(T, 9) # Scatter updates indices = tris[:, iC] vertnormalcovariancesum.scatteradd(0, indices.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, 9), outerflat) vertarea.scatteradd(0, indices, facearea / 3.0) vertdegree.scatteradd(0, indices, torch.ones(T, dtype=torch.int32, device=tripos.device)) # Reshape covariance to (V, 3, 3) covmatrix = vertnormalcovariancesum.reshape(V, 3, 3) # Add regularization identity = torch.eye(3, device=tripos.device) covmatrix = covmatrix + releps identity # Compute eigenvalues eigvals = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(covmatrix) # Minimum absolute eigenvalue mineigvals = torch.min(torch.abs(eigvals), dim=1).values # Mask out degree-3 vertices maskdegree3 = (vertdegree == 3) vertarea = vertarea.clone() vertarea[maskdegree3] = 0.0 # Normalize area totalarea = vertarea.sum() vertarea = vertarea (V / (totalarea + poseps)) # Final loss loss = torch.sum(vertarea mineigvals) return loss Not given in the sources. The Developability Regularizer originates from the FlexiCubes framework. It is used as a regularization term in differentiable surface reconstruction to encourage mesh flatness. name: Normal Consistency
head: Mean Cosine Error
body: Normal Consistency (NC) is a metric for 3D surface reconstruction that measures the angular deviation between estimated surface normals and ground truth normals. It quantifies how well the orientation of the reconstructed surface aligns with the underlying geometry. Unlike Mesh Reconstruction Evaluation which may focus on vertex/face topology or Standard Rendering Metrics which focus on pixel-wise photometric error, NC specifically isolates geometric orientation accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N points on the surface. For each point i, an estimated normal vector \mathbf{n}i (or Ni) and a ground truth normal vector \mathbf{n}i^ (or Ni^). Both vectors must be normalized (unit length). Output: A scalar value representing the average angular error, typically expressed as a percentage or in radians/degrees depending on the variant. Data Structures: Two arrays of shape (N, 3) containing the estimated and ground truth normals, respectively. N: The total number of points sampled on the surface. Formula: The standard Normal Consistency (NC) metric is defined as: \text{NC} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (1 - \cos(Ni, Ni^)) \times 100\% Where: Ni is the estimated normal for the i-th point. Ni^ is the ground truth normal for the i-th point. \cos(Ni, Ni^) is the cosine similarity, calculated as the dot product Ni \cdot Ni^ for unit vectors. N is the number of points. An alternative formulation, often called Mean Cosine Error (MCE), computes the mean angle directly: \text{MCE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \cos^{-1} (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}i) Where \mathbf{n}i is the exact normal and \hat{\mathbf{n}}i is the estimated normal. Note that MCE yields results in radians, while NC yields a percentage where 0% indicates perfect consistency and 100% indicates orthogonal normals. Steps: 1. Sample N points on the surface of the reconstructed mesh. 2. Compute or retrieve the ground truth normal \mathbf{n}i^ for each point. 3. Compute the estimated normal \mathbf{n}i for each point. This is often done by computing the gradient of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) at the point and normalizing it, or by averaging face normals of the mesh. 4. Normalize both \mathbf{n}i and \mathbf{n}i^ to unit length. 5. Compute the dot product di = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}i^. 6. Apply the chosen formula (NC or MCE) to aggregate the errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computenormalconsistency(estimatednormals: np.ndarray, groundtruthnormals: np.ndarray) -> float: """ Computes the Normal Consistency (NC) metric. Args: estimatednormals: Array of shape (N, 3) with estimated unit normals. groundtruthnormals: Array of shape (N, 3) with ground truth unit normals. Returns: NC value as a percentage (0-100). """ # Ensure inputs are float32/64 for precision estimatednormals = np.asarray(estimatednormals, dtype=np.float64) groundtruthnormals = np.asarray(groundtruthnormals, dtype=np.float64) # Normalize to handle potential non-unit vectors from gradient computation estnorms = estimatednormals / (np.linalg.norm(estimatednormals, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) gtnorms = groundtruthnormals / (np.linalg.norm(groundtruthnormals, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) # Compute dot products # Clamp to [-1, 1] to avoid numerical errors in acos if using MCE, # though NC formula (1 - dot) is robust to slight overshoots if dot > 1. dots = np.sum(estnorms gtnorms, axis=1) # Standard NC formula: 1 - cos(angle) # cos(angle) is the dot product for unit vectors errors = 1.0 - dots # Average error meanerror = np.mean(errors) # Convert to percentage ncpercentage = meanerror 100.0 return ncpercentage def computemeancosineerror(estimatednormals: np.ndarray, groundtruthnormals: np.ndarray) -> float: """ Computes the Mean Cosine Error (MCE) in radians. Args: estimatednormals: Array of shape (N, 3). groundtruthnormals: Array of shape (N, 3). Returns: MCE value in radians. """ estnorms = estimatednormals / (np.linalg.norm(estimatednormals, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) gtnorms = groundtruthnormals / (np.linalg.norm(groundtruthnormals, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) dots = np.sum(estnorms gtnorms, axis=1) # Clamp to [-1, 1] to prevent NaN from acos due to floating point precision dots = np.clip(dots, -1.0, 1.0) # Compute angle in radians angles = np.arccos(dots) return np.mean(angles) Parameters: N: Number of points. Typical values range from thousands to millions depending on mesh resolution. Batch size: When processing large meshes, points are often processed in batches (e.g., 16,384) to manage memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Dot products may slightly exceed [-1, 1] due to floating-point arithmetic. If using the MCE variant (\arccos), this must be clamped to [-1, 1] to avoid NaNs. The NC variant (1 - \text{dot}) is less sensitive but should still be monitored. Normal Orientation: Surface normals can be flipped (inward vs outward). If the ground truth and estimated normals are opposite, the dot product is -1, resulting in an error of 2 (NC) or \pi radians (MCE). Some implementations use the absolute value of the dot product |\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}i^| to ignore orientation ambiguity, effectively treating opposite normals as consistent. This is common when the orientation is not guaranteed to be consistent. Degenerate Input: If the mesh has no surface (empty), N=0, the metric is undefined. A variant that explicitly reports the angle in degrees and provides statistical summaries (MAE, Std, Max, Median) rather than a single mean value. It samples points on the surface (default N=2,097,152), computes network gradients, and compares them against mesh face normals. It uses the formula \theta = \arccos( | \mathbf{n}{mesh} \cdot \mathbf{n}{net} |) \times \frac{180}{\pi}. This variant is useful for detailed debugging of normal estimation quality. Extends normal consistency to 2D image space for depth and normal map evaluation. It includes: 1. RMSE Normal Error: \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum (\cos^{-1}(\frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{n}^|}{||\mathbf{n}|| ||\mathbf{n}^||}))^2}. 2. Prop 30 deg: The proportion of pixels where the angle error is less than 30 degrees: \frac{1}{n} \sum \mathbb{I}(\cos^{-1}(\frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{n}^|}{||\mathbf{n}|| ||\mathbf{n}^||}) < 30^\circ). These metrics are used when evaluating rendered outputs rather than explicit 3D meshes. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of points. The computation involves a dot product and a mean aggregation per point. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the normal vectors. Performance: Computationally inexpensive. Can be batched for large meshes (e.g., batch size 16,384) to fit within GPU memory. Strengths: Directly measures geometric orientation accuracy, which is critical for applications like lighting and shading. It is robust to small positional errors if the normals are correct. Limitations: It does not measure positional accuracy (Chamfer Distance does that). It is sensitive to normal flipping if not handled (e.g., via absolute dot product). It cannot represent the variance of samples as effectively as correlation metrics derived from lighting. When to use: When surface orientation is more important than exact vertex positions, or as a complementary metric to Chamfer Distance in 3D reconstruction. Normal Consistency was introduced as a standard metric for 3D surface reconstruction tasks to evaluate the geometric consistency of estimated surfaces. It is frequently paired with Chamfer Distance to provide a comprehensive evaluation of both position and orientation. The Mean Cosine Error (MCE) variant was used in early volume rendering gradient estimation comparisons to measure the accuracy of gradient reconstruction. More recently, it has been adopted in neural implicit surface learning (e.g., TetraSDF, HelixSurf) to evaluate the quality of SDF gradients and mesh normals.
