name: Depth Accuracy Metrics
head: AbsRel, RMSE
body: Depth Accuracy Metrics evaluate the geometric fidelity of predicted depth maps against ground truth data in radiance field optimization pipelines. They quantify scale- and translation-invariant errors on valid depth pixels. They are used to evaluate depth prior quality and monocular depth estimation outputs in NeRF pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth depth map d, predicted depth map \hat{d}, and a binary validity mask identifying pixels k=1,...,K with valid ground truth depth. Outputs: Scalar error values for RMSE, RMSE log, AbsRel, and SqRel. Data Structures: Depth maps are represented as 2D arrays of floating-point values. The validity mask is a boolean array of the same dimensions, where True indicates a pixel with valid ground truth. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Normalize depth to a consistent range if required by the dataset (e.g., [0, 1] for H3DS). 2. Masking: Filter to pixels k=1,...,K with valid ground truth depth. For specific datasets, mask both output and ground truth to the non-empty region predicted by the baseline. 3. Computation: Calculate the selected metric using the formulas below for all K valid pixels. Formulas: Let K be the number of pixels with valid ground truth depth. 1. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): RMSE(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} (dk - \hat{d}k)^2} 2. Log RMSE (RMSE log): RMSE{log}(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} (\log dk - \log \hat{d}k)^2} 3. Absolute Relative Error (AbsRel): AbsRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} \frac{|dk - \hat{d}k|}{dk} 4. Squared Relative Error (SqRel): SqRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1,...,K} \frac{(dk - \hat{d}k)^2}{dk} Parameters: K: Number of pixels with valid ground truth depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Collapse: In methods like HeadNeRF, geometry may collapse to a plane in front of the subject, requiring careful mask handling to avoid misleading error scores. Invalid Pixels: Errors must only be computed on valid depth pixels to avoid skewing results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computedepthmetrics(gtdepth: np.ndarray, preddepth: np.ndarray, validmask: np.ndarray) -> dict: """ Compute depth accuracy metrics for valid pixels. Args: gtdepth: Ground truth depth map (H, W). preddepth: Predicted depth map (H, W). validmask: Boolean mask of valid pixels (H, W). Returns: Dictionary containing RMSE, RMSElog, AbsRel, SqRel. """ # Extract valid pixels gtvalid = gtdepth[validmask] predvalid = preddepth[validmask] K = len(gtvalid) if K == 0: return {"RMSE": np.nan, "RMSElog": np.nan, "AbsRel": np.nan, "SqRel": np.nan} # RMSE rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((gtvalid - predvalid) 2)) # RMSE log rmselog = np.sqrt(np.mean((np.log(gtvalid) - np.log(predvalid)) 2)) # AbsRel absrel = np.mean(np.abs(gtvalid - predvalid) / gtvalid) # SqRel sqrel = np.mean((gtvalid - predvalid) 2 / gtvalid) return { "RMSE": rmse, "RMSElog": rmselog, "AbsRel": absrel, "SqRel": sqrel } A set of quantitative metrics used to evaluate the accuracy of predicted depth maps against ground truth, plus a consistency metric for multi-view alignment. These metrics assess the fidelity of monocular depth estimation (MDE) modules within radiance field optimization pipelines, distinguishing between per-image accuracy and global scene consistency. Time Complexity: O(K), where K is the number of valid pixels. Memory Complexity: O(K) to store valid pixel values during computation. Strengths: RMSE provides a direct measure of geometric error magnitude. SqRel emphasizes errors relative to ground truth depth. Limitations: Metrics are sensitive to outliers in depth predictions. SqRel heavily penalizes errors in regions with small ground truth depth values. Originating from evaluations in neural radiance field (NeRF) research, these metrics were adopted to assess the geometric quality of depth priors and monocular depth estimation modules. The H3DS dataset introduced specific protocols for scale- and translation-invariant evaluation. The metrics are used in works such as DäRF and studies on outdoor NeRFs. name: MDE evaluation metrics
head: Depth consistency metrics, Monocular Depth Estimation metrics
body: A set of quantitative metrics used to evaluate the accuracy of predicted depth maps against ground truth, plus a consistency metric for multi-view alignment. These metrics assess the fidelity of monocular depth estimation modules within radiance field optimization pipelines, distinguishing between per-image accuracy and global scene consistency. The evaluation framework relies on comparing a predicted depth map \bar{D} against a ground truth depth map D^{GT} at each pixel coordinate p. The metrics are computed over the set of valid pixels in an image I. For multi-view consistency, a scene-level scaling factor s is computed to align predicted depths with ground truth without per-frame fitting. This factor is derived from the median ratio of ground truth to predicted depth across all images in a scene. Let S be the set of images belonging to a single scene, and N = |S| be the total number of images in S. The scaling factor s is defined as: s = \frac{1}{N} \sum{Ii \in S} \text{median}\left(\frac{Di^{GT}}{\bar{D}i}\right) where Di^{GT} and \bar{D}i are the ground truth and predicted depth maps for image Ii. This metric evaluates view consistency by applying a single scale factor to the entire scene rather than optimizing per-frame. Measures the mean absolute relative difference between predicted and ground truth depth. \text{AbsRel} = \frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} \frac{|\bar{D}(p) - D^{GT}(p)|}{D^{GT}(p)} Computes the mean of the squared relative differences. \text{SqRel} = \frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} \frac{|\bar{D}(p) - D^{GT}(p)|^2}{D^{GT}(p)} The square root of the mean squared error between predicted and ground truth depths. \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} |\bar{D}(p) - D^{GT}(p)|^2} Computes the RMSE on the logarithmic scale of depths. \text{RMSE log} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|I|} \sum{p \in I} |\log \bar{D}(p) - \log D^{GT}(p)|^2} These metrics are used to evaluate monocular depth estimation modules within radiance field optimization pipelines. The specific formulation for the scene-level consistency scaling factor s follows prior work cited as [64] in the source. The implementation details, such as the use of the median for consistency evaluation, were adopted to ensure fair comparison with relevant prior work. name: AUSE Metric (Area Under the Sparsification Error)
head: Area Under the Sparsification Error, Sparsification Analysis
body: The Area Under the Sparsification Error (AUSE) metric evaluates the quality of uncertainty quantification in neural fields by measuring how effectively a ranking scalar z allows the average error to improve when voxels flagged as least trustworthy are systematically discarded. It distinguishes itself from standard error metrics by assessing the calibration of uncertainty—specifically, whether high uncertainty values correspond to high actual errors—rather than just the magnitude of the error itself. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A predicted depth map \bar{D}, a ground truth depth map D^{GT}, and a ranking scalar field z (e.g., ensemble standard deviation \sigma{ens}, mean error proxy \bar{E}, or random values) defined over the same voxel grid or pixel set. Output: A scalar value AUSEz (and optionally normalized nAUSEz) representing the area under the sparsification error curve. Data Structures: The method operates on a set of N voxels (or pixels) V = \{v1,..., vN\}. Each voxel vi has an associated ground truth error \epsiloni (typically absolute depth error |D^{GT}i - \bar{D}i|) and a ranking scalar zi. Steps: 1. Sort: Sort all N voxels in descending order of the ranking scalar z. Let the sorted indices be p1, p2,..., pN such that z{p1} \ge z{p2} \ge... \ge z{pN}. 2. Define Retention Set: For a sparsification level t \in [0, 1], define the kept set Kz(t) as the subset of voxels retaining the lowest-ranked (1-t) fraction. Specifically, Kz(t) contains the voxels with indices pk where k > t \cdot N. Note: t=0 retains all voxels; t=1 retains none. 3. Compute Risk: Calculate the risk Riskz(t), defined as the mean error over the kept set Kz(t): Riskz(t) = \frac{1}{|Kz(t)|} \sum{i \in Kz(t)} \epsiloni For the oracle baseline, z is the actual error \epsilon{mean}, so the oracle removes the largest errors first. For the random baseline, the curve is the exact expected uniform-retention curve (the global mean error), not a finite permutation average. 4. Compute Sparsification Error: Calculate the sparsification error SEz(t) at each level t as the gap between the method's risk and the oracle's risk: SEz(t) = Riskz(t) - Risk{oracle}(t) By definition, SEz(t) \ge 0. 5. Integrate: Compute the AUSE by integrating SEz(t) from t=0 to t{max}: AUSEz = \int{0}^{t{max}} SEz(t) \, dt In practice, this is computed using a discretized grid of t values. 6. Normalize (Optional): To compare relative ranking performance across conditions, normalize by the random baseline's AUSE: nAUSEz = \frac{AUSEz}{AUSE{random}} A nAUSEz of 0 indicates perfect ranking (identical to oracle), 1 indicates no better than random, and >1 indicates worse than random. Parameters: Integration limit t{max}: 0.95. This avoids a noisy terminal spike when few voxels remain. Random Baseline: Defined as the exact expected uniform-retention curve (the global mean error). Pitfalls: Raw AUSE combines the scale of reconstruction error with ranking quality. Therefore, raw AUSE should not be used for comparisons of relative ranking performance across different conditions or datasets; nAUSE is preferred for such comparisons. The metric assumes the ranking scalar z is available for all voxels in the valid set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeause(errors: list[float], zscores: list[float], tmax: float = 0.95) -> float: """ Compute the Area Under the Sparsification Error (AUSE). Args: errors: List of ground truth errors (e.g., absolute depth error) for N voxels. zscores: List of ranking scalar values for the same N voxels. tmax: Integration limit (default 0.95). Returns: AUSE value. """ n = len(errors) if n == 0: return 0.0 # Step 1: Sort voxels by decreasing zscore voxels = sorted(zip(zscores, errors), key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) sortederrors = [v[1] for v in voxels] # Precompute prefix sums for efficient mean calculation prefixsum = [0.0] (n + 1) for i in range(n): prefixsum[i+1] = prefixsum[i] + sortederrors[i] # Helper to get mean error of the kept set def getrisk(t: float) -> float: kremoved = int(t n) kkept = n - kremoved if kkept == 0: return 0.0 sumkept = prefixsum[n] - prefixsum[kremoved] return sumkept / kkept # Step 2 & 3: Compute Risk for Oracle # Oracle: z = error. Sorted by decreasing error. oraclesortederrors = sorted(errors, reverse=True) oracleprefixsum = [0.0] (n + 1) for i in range(n): oracleprefixsum[i+1] = oracleprefixsum[i] + oraclesortederrors[i] def getoraclerisk(t: float) -> float: kremoved = int(t n) kkept = n - kremoved if kkept == 0: return 0.0 sumkept = oracleprefixsum[n] - oracleprefixsum[kremoved] return sumkept / kkept # Random: Exact expected uniform-retention curve (global mean error) globalmeanerror = sum(errors) / n def getrandomrisk(t: float) -> float: return globalmeanerror # Step 4 & 5: Integrate Sparsification Error numsteps = 1000 # Standard discretization resolution dt = tmax / numsteps ause = 0.0 for i in range(numsteps): t = i dt riskz = getrisk(t) riskoracle = getoraclerisk(t) se = riskz - riskoracle # SE should be >= 0, but numerical issues might occur. Clamp. if se < 0: se = 0.0 ause += se dt return ause def computenause(errors: list[float], zscores: list[float], tmax: float = 0.95) -> float: """ Compute normalized AUSE (nAUSE). """ ausez = computeause(errors, zscores, tmax) # Compute AUSErandom analytically/integrally # Random baseline is the exact expected uniform-retention curve (global mean error) n = len(errors) oraclesortederrors = sorted(errors, reverse=True) oracleprefixsum = [0.0] (n + 1) for i in range(n): oracleprefixsum[i+1] = oracleprefixsum[i] + oraclesortederrors[i] globalmeanerror = sum(errors) / n def getoraclerisk(t: float) -> float: kremoved = int(t n) kkept = n - kremoved if kkept == 0: return 0.0 sumkept = oracleprefixsum[n] - oracleprefixsum[kremoved] return sumkept / kkept numsteps = 1000 # Standard discretization resolution dt = tmax / numsteps auserandom = 0.0 for i in range(numsteps): t = i dt riskoracle = getoraclerisk(t) riskrandom = globalmeanerror se = riskrandom - riskoracle if se < 0: se = 0.0 auserandom += se dt if auserandom == 0: return 0.0 # Avoid division by zero return ausez / auserandom A variant of AUSE normalized by the random baseline's AUSE. It removes the dependency on absolute error scale, allowing direct comparison of relative ranking performance across different conditions or datasets. Choose it when evaluating whether an uncertainty proxy improves ranking quality independent of scene reconstruction fidelity. See nAUSE. The plot of Riskz(t) against t. It visualizes how the mean error decreases as voxels are removed. It sets itself apart from scalar metrics by providing a full diagnostic view of calibration quality across all retention levels. Choose it when debugging uncertainty proxies or comparing multiple ranking scalars visually. See Sparsification Curve. Strengths: Provides a single scalar metric for uncertainty calibration that is sensitive to the ranking quality of the uncertainty estimate. Limitations: Raw AUSE is not comparable across different scenes or error scales. It requires a ground truth error estimate to compute the oracle baseline. When to use: When evaluating the calibration of uncertainty estimates in neural fields, specifically to determine if high uncertainty regions correspond to high error regions. When not to use: When comparing ranking performance across different conditions with different error scales; use nAUSE instead. The AUSE metric was introduced by Ilg et al. (2018) and Poggi et al. (2020) as a standard protocol for assessing neural-field uncertainty quantification. It has been adopted in recent works such as Shen et al. (2022), Sünderhauf et al. (2023), and Goli et al. (2024). In the context of volume rendering, it is used to evaluate how well uncertainty heatmaps align with actual depth errors, as demonstrated in evaluations of methods like FisherRF and SA-ResGS. name: Discrete Wavelet Transform Loss
head: DW loss, Discrete Wavelet Loss, LDW
body: The Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) Loss is a regularization term for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that minimizes the difference between the frequency representations of rendered and ground-truth images by decomposing them into sub-bands. It addresses high-frequency overfitting in few-shot NeRF training by explicitly prioritizing low-frequency learning during early stages. Unlike its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion, which compares pixel-wise values globally, the DW loss operates on local structures using patch-based sampling to supervise low and mid-frequency components. The method decomposes rendered images into frequency sub-bands using the Discrete Wavelet Transform and calculates a weighted sum of squared errors between the rendered and ground-truth coefficients, with higher weights assigned to low-frequency sub-bands. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: I: Rendered image (RGB) from a batch of adjacently sampled rays. I{gt}: Ground-truth image corresponding to the same camera pose. \lambda{sb}: Weighting factors for each sub-band sb \in \{LL, LH, HL, HH\}. K{DW}: Iteration interval for computing the loss. T{DW}: Maximum iteration after which the loss is disabled. Outputs: L{DW}: Scalar loss value. Data Structures Wavelet Filters: 1D low-pass filter \ell and high-pass filter h. Common types are Haar (n=1) or Daubechies (dbN, e.g., db2, db3). 2D Matrices: L: Low-pass 2D matrix constructed by shifting rows of \ell. H: High-pass 2D matrix. If \ell is orthogonal, h is derived from \ell, and H is derived from L. Sub-bands: Four 2D arrays of size \frac{H}{2} \times \frac{W}{2} (quarter the size of the original image): I{LL}: Low frequencies in both directions. I{LH}: Low horizontal, high vertical frequencies. I{HL}: High horizontal, low vertical frequencies. I{HH}: High frequencies in both directions. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays in patches to form a 2D image I. This ensures rays are adjacent, forming a square grid compatible with 2D DWT. Use random ray sampling for the standard MSE loss to capture global structure. 2. Filter Construction: Construct the 2D low-pass matrix L by shifting rows of the 1D low-pass wavelet filter \ell. Construct the high-pass matrix H similarly using \ell (if orthogonal) or derived h. 3. DWT Decomposition: Apply the DWT to I and I{gt} using L and H to obtain the four sub-bands: I{LL} = L I L^T, \quad I{LH} = H I L^T I{HL} = L I H^T, \quad I{HH} = H I H^T (Note: The source notation I{LL} = L I L^T implies convolution/transform operations; standard DWT implementation involves filtering and downsampling). 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the squared Euclidean distance between corresponding sub-bands of I and I{gt}, weighted by \lambda{sb}. 5. Lazy Regularization: Calculate L{DW} only every K{DW} iterations. Stop calculating it entirely after iteration T{DW} to facilitate high-frequency learning in later stages. 6. Combination: Combine L{DW} with the photometric MSE loss L{MSE} and other regularizations. Formula The total Discrete Wavelet Loss is defined as: L{DW} = \sum{sb \in \{LL,LH,HL,HH\}} \lambda{sb} ||I{sb} - I{sb}^{gt}||^22 Where: I{sb} and I{sb}^{gt} are the sub-band images for the rendered and ground-truth views, respectively. ||\cdot||^22 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences) over all pixels in the sub-band. \lambda{sb} is the weight for sub-band sb. The source notes initially included a term \frac{\sum{r \in R} ||c(r) - c{gt}(r)||^22}{|R|}, but this is the definition of L{MSE}, not L{DW}. The formula above represents the specific DW component as described in the text. Parameters Sub-band Weights (\lambda{sb}): \lambda{LL}: Typically 0.4 for LLFF dataset, 0.04 for NeRF-Synthetic dataset. \lambda{LH}, \lambda{HL}, \lambda{HH}: Typically 0.2 for LLFF dataset, 0.02 for NeRF-Synthetic dataset. \lambda{LL} > \lambda{other} to prioritize low-frequency learning. Lazy Regularization: K{DW}: 10 iterations for LLFF, 150 iterations for NeRF-Synthetic. T{DW}: 5000 iterations. Wavelet Type: Haar (n=1) or Daubechies (db2, db3). Higher-order wavelets provide finer decomposition details but show no significant performance difference in final metrics. Patch Size: 192 \times 192 square patches (requiring 36864 rays). Sub-band Size: Sub-bands are quarter the size of the original image. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedwtloss(renderedimage, gtimage, wavelettype='haar', lambdall=0.4, lambdaother=0.2, currentiter=0, tdw=5000, kdw=10): # Lazy Regularization: Skip if not at interval or past max iteration if currentiter % kdw != 0 or currentiter > tdw: return 0.0 # 1. Get 1D wavelet filters if wavelettype == 'haar': l = [1.0 / 20.5, 1.0 / 20.5] h = [1.0 / 20.5, -1.0 / 20.5] elif wavelettype == 'db2': l = [0.4829629131445341, 0.836516303737469, 0.2241438680420134, -0.1294095225509214] h = [-0.1294095225509214, -0.2241438680420134, 0.836516303737469, -0.4829629131445341] else: raise ValueError("Unsupported wavelet type") # 2. Decompose images into sub-bands Ill, Ilh, Ihl, Ihh = apply2ddwt(renderedimage, l, h) gtll, gtlh, gthl, gthh = apply2ddwt(gtimage, l, h) # 3. Calculate weighted squared error lossll = sum((Ill[r][c][ch] - gtll[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ill)) for c in range(len(Ill[0])) for ch in range(3)) losslh = sum((Ilh[r][c][ch] - gtlh[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ilh)) for c in range(len(Ilh[0])) for ch in range(3)) losshl = sum((Ihl[r][c][ch] - gthl[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ihl)) for c in range(len(Ihl[0])) for ch in range(3)) losshh = sum((Ihh[r][c][ch] - gthh[r][c][ch])2 for r in range(len(Ihh)) for c in range(len(Ihh[0])) for ch in range(3)) loss = (lambdall lossll) + (lambdaother losslh) + (lambdaother losshl) + (lambdaother losshh) return loss def apply2ddwt(image, l, h): # image is H x W x 3 H, W, C = len(image), len(image[0]), len(image[0][0]) # Filter rows rowll = convolve1d(image, l, axis=1) rowlh = convolve1d(image, h, axis=1) # Downsample rows rowllds = rowll[::2,:,:] rowlhds = rowlh[::2,:,:] # Filter columns ll = convolve1d(rowllds, l, axis=0) lh = convolve1d(rowlhds, l, axis=0) hl = convolve1d(rowllds, h, axis=0) hh = convolve1d(rowlhds, h, axis=0) # Downsample columns llds = ll[::2,:,:] lhds = lh[::2,:,:] hlds = hl[::2,:,:] hhds = hh[::2,:,:] return llds, lhds, hlds, hhds def convolve1d(data, kernel, axis): # 1D convolution with zero-padding # axis=0: rows, axis=1: columns if axis == 1: # Convolve along columns H, W, C = len(data), len(data[0]), len(data[0][0]) out = [[[0.0]C for in range(W)] for in range(H)] klen = len(kernel) pad = klen // 2 for r in range(H): for c in range(W): for ch in range(C): val = 0.0 for k in range(klen): idx = c - pad + k if 0 <= idx < W: val += data[r][idx][ch] kernel[k] else: pass # Zero-padding at boundaries out[r][c][ch] = val return out else: # Convolve along rows H, W, C = len(data), len(data[0]), len(data[0][0]) out = [[[0.0]C for in range(W)] for in range(H)] klen = len(kernel) pad = klen // 2 for r in range(H): for c in range(W): for ch in range(C): val = 0.0 for k in range(klen): idx = r - pad + k if 0 <= idx < H: val += data[idx][c][ch] kernel[k] else: pass # Zero-padding at boundaries out[r][c][ch] = val return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sub-band Size: Sub-bands are quarter the size of the original image. If the rendered image I is too small, sub-bands become too coarse and visually meaningless. This requires large images, incurring heavy computational overhead (N^2 rays for an N-sized square patch). High-Frequency Content: DWT high-frequency components include not just fine structural details but also specularity and light-dependent effects, which are not disentangled by the transform. Auxiliary Nature: The DW loss does not eliminate high-frequency overfitting because it is auxiliary to the photometric MSE loss, which compares pixel-wise differences regardless of frequency. Time Complexity: The DWT computation is O(N^2) for an N \times N image patch. Due to the large number of rays required for a meaningful patch (192 \times 192 = 36864 rays), it incurs significant overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered image, ground-truth image, and intermediate sub-bands. The lazy regularization (computing every K{DW} iterations) mitigates memory and time costs. Performance: On the 3-shot LLFF benchmark, DWTNeRF with DW loss/DB2 achieved PSNR 20.23, SSIM 0.678, LPIPS 0.193, compared to CombiNeRF baseline PSNR 20.12, SSIM 0.676, LPIPS 0.197. Strengths: Explicitly prioritizes low-frequency learning, which is crucial for few-shot NeRF convergence. Combines global (random ray sampling for MSE) and local (patch-based for DW) structure supervision. Limitations: Does not disentangle high-frequency components like specularity. High-frequency overfitting may still occur due to the presence of MSE loss. Sub-bands are quarter the size of the original image; if the rendered image is too small, sub-bands become too coarse, requiring large images that incur heavy computational overhead (N^2 rays for an N-sized square patch). When to Use: Few-shot NeRF training where low-frequency convergence is slow or unstable. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited and patch-based sampling is too expensive, or when high-frequency details (specularity) are the primary focus and need to be preserved without interference from low-frequency bias. The Discrete Wavelet Transform Loss was introduced in the DWTNeRF paper to boost few-shot Neural Radiance Fields. It builds on the CombiNeRF framework, which combines regularization and model-based approaches. The method leverages the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) to decompose images into frequency sub-bands, allowing for explicit supervision of low frequencies during early training stages. The paper evaluates the method on the LLFF and NeRF-Synthetic datasets under few-shot conditions. name: RMSE Loss for Constant Model
head: RMSE for Constant Model
body: Calculates the Root Mean Squared Error between predicted and observed intensities for a given sigma and q. It serves as a photometric consistency loss in differentiable volume rendering, specifically fitting a constant radiance assumption along a ray. Inputs: intensity: Array of observed intensity values Ik for k=0 \dots N-1. sigma: Volume density \sigma (scalar). q: Integration parameter or scaling factor (scalar). ds: Distance step between samples (scalar). Outputs: rmse: The Root Mean Squared Error (scalar). Data Structures: intensity: Array of floats. squared: Accumulator for squared errors (float). Steps: 1. Validation: Check if intensity is empty or ds <= 0. If invalid, return infinity. 2. Initialization: Set squared = 0. 3. Iteration: For each sample index k from 0 to intensity.size() - 1: a. Calculate predicted intensity: I{pred} = \text{constant\intensity}(I0, \sigma, q, k \cdot ds), where I0 = \text{intensity}[0]. b. Calculate error: error = I{pred} - intensity[k]. c. Update accumulator: squared += error^2. 4. Finalize: Return \sqrt{\frac{squared}{N}}, where N is intensity.size(). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rmselossconstantmodel(intensity, sigma, q, ds): if not intensity or ds <= 0: return float('inf') n = len(intensity) squared = 0.0 i0 = intensity[0] for k in range(n): t = k ds # Standard constant radiance accumulation for density sigma over distance t predicted = i0 (1.0 - math.exp(-sigma t)) error = predicted - intensity[k] squared += error error return math.sqrt(squared / n) Parameters: sigma: Volume density. Typical values depend on the scene scale. q: Integration parameter. Value not explicitly defined in the source notes beyond being passed to the model function. ds: Distance step. Must be > 0. Edge Cases: Empty intensity list: Returns infinity. Non-positive ds: Returns infinity. Computes the error between rasterized depth and ground truth depth, optionally masking by silhouette and valid depth masks depending on training state. It provides accuracy and completeness metrics between two depth maps, supporting absolute, relative, and log-squared error variants. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of intensity samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding input storage. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a direct metric for constant-radiance assumption validity. Limitations: Assumes constant radiance along the ray, which may not hold for complex scenes. Sensitive to invalid depth or empty inputs. When to use: When optimizing for scenes or ray segments where constant radiance is a valid approximation, or as a baseline loss component. When not to use: For scenes with high dynamic range or complex lighting variations where constant intensity is a poor model. Originated in the context of HPC foundational demos and differentiable volume rendering optimization. The depth variant is part of the SplaTAM framework for Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM. wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, https://github.com/wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth RMSE and L1 Calculation
head: 2D Depth L1 Metric via Random Views, 2D Depth Map Evaluation, Depth Error Metrics, Depth RMSE/L1
body: Computes the error between rasterized depth and ground truth depth, optionally masking by silhouette and valid depth masks depending on training state. It provides accuracy and completeness metrics between two depth maps, supporting absolute, relative, and log-squared error variants. Builds on RMSE Loss for Constant Model by extending intensity error to spatial depth evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rasterized depth map D{rast}, ground truth depth map D{gt}, presence silhouette mask M{sil}, valid depth mask M{valid}, and training state flags mappingiters and addnewgaussians. Outputs: RMSE value, L1 error value. Data Structures: D{rast}: Float tensor of shape (H, W), values > 0 for valid depth. D{gt}: Float tensor of shape (H, W), values > 0 for valid depth. M{sil}: Boolean/Float tensor of shape (H, W), 1 where silhouette is present, 0 otherwise. M{valid}: Boolean/Float tensor of shape (H, W), 1 where depth is valid, 0 otherwise. Steps: 1. Determine if silhouette masking is active based on training state. If mappingiters == 0 and not addnewgaussians, apply M{sil} to the depth error calculation. 2. Create a validity mask M{valid} where D{rast} > 0 and D{gt} > 0. Some implementations additionally filter 0 < D{gt} < 10. 3. Apply masks to the depth maps. Multiply the difference by M{sil} (if active) and M{valid}. 4. Compute RMSE by summing the masked squared differences and dividing by the sum of the valid depth mask. 5. Compute L1 error similarly using absolute difference. Formulas: For the case where mappingiters==0 and not addnewgaussians: rmse = \frac{\sum{i,j} \sqrt{((D{rast} - D{gt}) \cdot M{sil})^2} \cdot M{valid}}{\sum{i,j} M{valid}} where D{rast} is rasterized depth, D{gt} is ground truth depth, M{sil} is presence silhouette mask, and M{valid} is valid depth mask. General RMSE: RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum (dp - dt)^2} where dp is predicted depth, dt is target depth, and N is the number of valid pixels. L1 Error: L1 = \frac{1}{N}\sum |dp - dt| Other variants mentioned: Absolute difference: |dp - dt|. Relative difference: |dp - dt| / dt. Squared relative: (dp - dt)^2 / dt. Log squared difference: (\log dp - \log dt)^2. LogRMSE: \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum (\log dp - \log dt)^2}. Accuracy threshold ratio: r = \max(dt/dp, dp/dt). Compute ratios r < 1.25, r < 1.25^2, r < 1.25^3. Parameters: mappingiters: Number of mapping iterations. If 0, silhouette mask is applied to depth error. addnewgaussians: Boolean flag. If false, silhouette mask is applied to depth error. H, W: Fixed image resolution for rendering, typically 500. focal, fx, fy: Focal length in pixels, typically 300. cx, cy: Principal point coordinates, typically H/2.0 - 0.5 and W/2.0 - 0.5. nimgs: Number of random camera views to sample and average over, typically 1000. Pitfalls: Invalid depth values (\le 0) are excluded by multiplying by validdepthmask, which is defined as (curr\data['depth'] > 0). Boundary conditions for M{valid} vary: some implementations use D{gt} > 0, while others restrict to 0 < D{gt} < 10. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computedepthmetrics(drast, dgt, msil, mappingiters, addnewgaussians): """ Compute RMSE and L1 error between rasterized and ground truth depth. Args: drast: 2D list or array of shape (H, W), rasterized depth. dgt: 2D list or array of shape (H, W), ground truth depth. msil: 2D list or array of shape (H, W), silhouette mask (1.0 if present, 0.0 otherwise). mappingiters: int, number of mapping iterations. addnewgaussians: bool, whether new Gaussians are being added. Returns: rmse: float, Root Mean Squared Error. l1: float, L1 Error. """ H = len(drast) W = len(drast[0]) # Step 1: Determine if silhouette masking is active usesilmask = (mappingiters == 0) and (not addnewgaussians) # Step 2: Create validity mask # Combine conditions: depth > 0. Some implementations add 0 < dgt < 10. mvalid = [[1.0 if (drast[i][j] > 0 and dgt[i][j] > 0) else 0.0 for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] # Step 3 & 4: Compute masked squared differences and sum sumsqdiff = 0.0 sumvalid = 0.0 sumabsdiff = 0.0 for i in range(H): for j in range(W): if mvalid[i][j] == 1.0: sumvalid += 1.0 diff = drast[i][j] - dgt[i][j] if usesilmask: diff = diff msil[i][j] sumsqdiff += diff diff sumabsdiff += abs(diff) # Avoid division by zero if sumvalid == 0: return 0.0, 0.0 # Step 4: Compute RMSE rmse = math.sqrt(sumsqdiff / sumvalid) # Step 5: Compute L1 error l1 = sumabsdiff / sumvalid return rmse, l1 Not given in the sources. name: Normalized L1 Loss
head: L1 Loss, Sparse Loss Calculation, normalized L1
body: Computes a normalized L1 loss between a reconstructed image and an original image, scaling the loss to the [0, 1] range. It is used in sparse pixel sampling optimization pipelines to provide an error metric for adaptive Gaussian densification and pruning. Inputs: reconstructedimage: Tensor of predicted RGB values. originalimage: Tensor of ground truth RGB values. Outputs: l1lossnorm: Tensor of normalized L1 error per pixel. Steps: 1. Compute the absolute difference between the reconstructed and original images: \Delta = |\text{reconstructed\image} - \text{original\image}|. 2. Compute the mean absolute error along the channel dimension: \text{l1\loss} = \text{mean}(\Delta, \text{dim}=0). The result is detached from the computation graph. 3. Compute the minimum and maximum values of l1loss across all spatial elements: \text{min\val} = \min(\text{l1\loss}), \text{max\val} = \max(\text{l1\loss}). 4. Normalize the loss using min-max scaling: \text{l1\loss\norm} = (\text{l1\loss} - \text{min\val}) / (\text{max\val} - \text{min\val}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalizedl1loss(reconstructedimage, originalimage): diff = abs(reconstructedimage - originalimage) l1loss = mean(diff, dim=0) # Detach from computation graph minval = min(l1loss) maxval = max(l1loss) if maxval == minval: return l1loss 0 l1lossnorm = (l1loss - minval) / (maxval - minval) return l1lossnorm Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: If all pixel errors are identical, the denominator becomes zero and the result is undefined. The normalization is global per image. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization, specifically in implementations like FastGS and TurboGS, where it is used for sparse loss calculation and error-guided pixel sampling. fastgs/FastGS, https://github.com/fastgs/FastGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.15924, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Masked and Weighted Losses
body: Masked and Weighted Losses is a family of techniques that modify standard photometric error computation in differentiable volume rendering by applying spatial masks or per-pixel weights to the loss function. It solves the problem of training instability and evaluation bias caused by invalid background regions, sensor artifacts, multiscale resolution disparities, or structural inconsistencies. It sets itself apart from its sibling MSE Loss and PSNR Conversion by introducing selective suppression or amplification of error terms rather than computing a global average, and from Masked Volume Metrics by focusing on training-time gradient correction rather than evaluation-time metric definition [S1, S2, S3, S4, 1927-masked-volume-metrics.md, 4765-training-loss-computation-with-huber-and-masking.md]. The core mechanism involves computing a base loss L{base} (typically MSE or Huber) between the rendered prediction P and the ground truth G, then applying a mask M or weight W before aggregation. For masking, the loss is computed as: L = \frac{1}{N{valid}} \sum{i} Mi \cdot L{base}(Pi, Gi) where Mi \in \{0, 1\} is a binary mask indicating whether ray i or froxel i contributes to the loss, and N{valid} is the count of valid elements (where Mi=1). For weighting, the loss is computed as: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i} Wi \cdot L{base}(Pi, Gi) where Wi is a scalar weight for element i. Masked Volume Metrics computes evaluation metrics (MSE, PSNR) by excluding empty froxels [1927-masked-volume-metrics.md]. It defines the effective ROI as the union of froxels with non-zero radiance in the rendered scenario and non-zero values in the ground truth [1927-masked-volume-metrics.md]. It is chosen for evaluation to prevent empty background regions from skewing performance scores [1927-masked-volume-metrics.md]. Training Loss Computation with Huber and Masking defines the training-time pipeline using Huber loss (\delta=0.1) and binary ray validity masks [4765-training-loss-computation-with-huber-and-masking.md]. It differs from Masked Volume Metrics by operating on rays during training rather than froxels during evaluation, and from this family's general definition by specifying the Huber function and JAX-based implementation details [4765-training-loss-computation-with-huber-and-masking.md]. Definition: Scaling the loss of each pixel by the area of that pixel's footprint in the original image to ensure low-resolution pixels have comparable influence to high-resolution pixels in multiscale datasets. Step: For multiscale datasets, calculate the area scaling factor based on the downsampling factor (e.g., factor of 2 -> area factor 4, factor of 4 -> area factor 16). Multiply the pixel loss by this factor. Definition: A method for shape addition using a density-based loss which is faster but less effective than composite image reconstruction. The loss encourages predicted densities to match target densities for edited regions and be unchanged for unedited regions. Step: Let yf = \{(r, \sigmaf)\} be the set of rays and densities in the foreground mask, and yb = \{(r, \sigmab)\} be the set of rays and densities in the background mask. \sigmaf are density values of the rays copied from the new object instance, and \sigmab represent density values of the rays from the original instance. Let \sigmar be the densities predicted by the model for ray r. Densities are normalized to sum to one. Formula: L{dens} = \sum{(r, \sigmaf) \in yf} (-\sigmaf^T \log \sigmar) + \sum{(r, \sigmab) \in yb} (-\sigmab^T \log \sigmar) Step: Render all three colors for every training ray, then apply a one-hot mask to select the desired output color corresponding to the measured raw pixel for that ray. Apply a second mask to remove a 4 pixel border from all training images to handle saturated pixels often found on the edges of iPhone raw images. Pitfall: Using bilinearly demosaicked raw images for supervision causes distracting color noise artifacts, particularly in extremely high noise areas, due to broken 'hot' pixels being dispersed to neighboring pixels. Definition: A regularization term added to the training loss to enforce edge detail consistency between the current rendering and the target image, alleviating washed-out details caused by noisy 2D-to-3D feature correspondences. Formula: L{edge} = \| (I{Current} G{\sigma1}) - (I{Target} G{\sigma2}) \|1 where denotes convolution and G\sigma is a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation \sigma. Parameter: Standard deviation \sigma1 for the current image Gaussian filter is 1.0. Standard deviation \sigma2 for the target image Gaussian filter is 1.6. Weighting factor \lambda for the edge loss is 0 for the first 15% of training, then increased to 50. Area loss scaling was introduced in Mip-NeRF to handle multiscale datasets where low-resolution images have larger pixel footprints. Density-based losses for shape editing were proposed in Editing Conditional Radiance Fields to facilitate faster object manipulation. Bayer masking was introduced in RawNeRF to correctly supervise neural radiance fields using raw sensor data, avoiding artifacts from demosaicking. Edge loss regularization was added in NeRF Analogies to preserve high-frequency details during appearance transfer. Masked Volume Metrics was developed to exclude empty froxels from evaluation metrics [1927-masked-volume-metrics.md]. Training Loss Computation with Huber and Masking formalized the pipeline for differentiable volume rendering using Huber loss and validity-based masking [4765-training-loss-computation-with-huber-and-masking.md]. name: Masked Volume Metrics
head: Effective Region of Interest (ROI) Calculation, Masked MSE and PSNR Computation, Masked Volume MSE/PSNR Computation, ROI Calculation, Region of Interest (ROI) Calculation
body: Masked Volume Metrics is a method for computing evaluation metrics (such as MSE or PSNR) in volumetric rendering by excluding empty froxels from the analysis. It solves the problem of performance and quality analysis being skewed by regions of the volume that contain no radiance and thus provide no meaningful information. It sets itself apart from standard metrics by dynamically defining a Region of Interest (ROI) based on the union of visible radiance in the test scenario and the ground truth, ensuring that only froxels participating in light transport are evaluated. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D froxel grid representing the rendered scenario and a 3D froxel grid representing the ground truth. Output: A set of valid froxels (ROI{effective}) used to compute the final metric, and the computed metric value (e.g., MSE) restricted to these froxels. Data Structures: Froxel Grid: A 3D array where each element (froxel) contains RGB color values. ROI Mask: A binary 3D mask or a set of coordinates indicating which froxels are included in the effective region. Steps: 1. Identify Scenario ROI (ROI{scenario}): Iterate through the froxel grid of the test scenario. A froxel is included in ROI{scenario} if any of its RGB channels contains a non-zero value at any point during the test scenario. This identifies froxels affected by radiance from light sources or emission. 2. Identify Truth ROI (ROI{truth}): Identify froxels that contain non-zero values in the ground truth data. 3. Compute Effective ROI (ROI{effective}): Calculate the union of the scenario ROI and the truth ROI: ROI{effective} = ROI{scenario} \cup ROI{truth} This ensures that froxels relevant to either the algorithm's output or the ground truth are included, while completely empty regions are excluded. 4. Compute Metric: Calculate the base loss metric (e.g., MSE) only over the froxels present in ROI{effective}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemaskedvolumemetrics(renderedvolume, groundtruthvolume): """ Compute MSE over the effective ROI defined by non-zero radiance in either the rendered scenario or the ground truth. Args: renderedvolume: 3D list of lists of lists of lists (H, W, D, 3) representing the test scenario. groundtruthvolume: 3D list of lists of lists of lists (H, W, D, 3) representing ground truth. Returns: mse: float, the Mean Squared Error over the effective ROI. roimask: 3D list of lists of lists (H, W, D), the mask of valid froxels. """ H = len(renderedvolume) W = len(renderedvolume[0]) D = len(renderedvolume[0][0]) C = len(renderedvolume[0][0][0]) # Step 1 & 2: Identify scenario and truth active froxels roimask = [[[False for in range(D)] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for h in range(H): for w in range(W): for d in range(D): scenarioactive = any(renderedvolume[h][w][d][c] != 0.0 for c in range(C)) truthactive = any(groundtruthvolume[h][w][d][c] != 0.0 for c in range(C)) roimask[h][w][d] = scenarioactive or truthactive # Step 3 & 4: Compute MSE only over valid froxels sumsqerror = 0.0 count = 0 for h in range(H): for w in range(W): for d in range(D): if roimask[h][w][d]: sqerror = sum((renderedvolume[h][w][d][c] - groundtruthvolume[h][w][d][c]) 2 for c in range(C)) sumsqerror += sqerror count += 1 mse = sumsqerror / count if count > 0 else 0.0 return mse, roimask Parameters: Threshold for Non-Zero: The sources specify a strictly non-zero value for inclusion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Regions: Completely empty regions (where both the scenario and ground truth contain only zero values) are excluded from the metric calculation, preventing them from skewing the result with zero-error counts that do not reflect visual quality. Algorithm-Specific ROIs: The ROI is computed separately for each tested algorithm because different methods may produce non-zero contributions in different regions of the froxel grid even in the same test scenario. A numerical metric to evaluate feature difference at a certain scale, computed only for voxels where the approximation Af is within a given intensity range of interest. It is used to verify structural simplification of features by comparing the original data set A to its approximation Af. The formula is: E = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m} \sum{i,j,k} (A[i,j,k] - Af[i,j,k])^2} where the sum is over m voxels where Af[i,j,k] is within the given intensity range of interest. This is useful when interested in feature difference at a specific scale rather than global error. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Excludes completely empty regions that do not contribute meaningful information, providing a more accurate assessment of visual quality and performance for participating media. Limitations: Requires access to both the rendered scenario and ground truth to compute the union ROI. When to Use: When evaluating volumetric rendering algorithms where in-scattering and empty regions do not contribute to the visual result, and the goal is to zoom in on froxels participating in light transport. The method is described in the context of evaluating volumetric temporal anti-aliasing algorithms for real-time froxel-based rendering. It is used within the Frostbite engine to ensure that evaluation metrics are not skewed by regions unaffected by in-scattering or light transport. name: Training Loss Computation with Huber and Masking
head: NeRF training loss, RGB and TV loss calculation
body: This method computes the training loss for differentiable volume rendering by applying a Huber loss to rendered RGB values, masking invalid rays, and blending ground truth images against a background color. It extends the parent Masked and Weighted Losses by detailing the specific blending and aggregation steps for RGBD predictions, while its sibling Masked Volume Metrics targets evaluation rather than optimization. Inputs and Outputs: worldspacerays: Ray origins and directions for the current batch. appearanceembeddings: Optional per-ray or per-view appearance codes. bg: Background color tensor for blending. gtrgbaf32: Ground truth RGBA image array in float32. totalsamples: Number of sampling points per ray. Outputs: loss (scalar training loss) and batchmetrics (dictionary containing intermediate loss components and validity counts). Data Structures: predrgbds: Tensor of shape (numrays, numsamples, 4) containing [R, G, B, Depth]. rayisvalid: Boolean tensor of shape (numrays,) indicating valid rays. nvalidrays: Integer count of rays where rayisvalid is True. Steps: 1. Render: Call the differentiable renderer with worldspacerays, appearanceembeddings, bg, and totalsamples to obtain predrgbds and batchmetrics. 2. Split: Separate the prediction tensor into RGB and Depth components along the last axis. 3. Blend Ground Truth: Composite the ground truth RGBA image against the background color to match the renderer's assumptions for transparent regions. 4. Compute Per-Ray Huber Loss: Calculate the Huber loss between predicted and blended ground truth RGB values, average over samples per ray, apply the validity mask, and divide by the number of valid rays. 5. Aggregate: Sum all loss components stored in batchmetrics["loss"] using a tree reduction. Formulas: Huber loss for a single value: L{huber}(p, g) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}(p - g)^2 & \text{if } |p - g| \le \delta \\ \delta(|p - g| - \frac{1}{2}\delta) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Per-ray RGB loss: L{rgb} = \frac{1}{N{valid}} \sum{i=1}^{N{rays}} \mathbb{I}(\text{ray\is\valid}i) \cdot \frac{1}{N{samples}} \sum{s=1}^{N{samples}} L{huber}(P{i,s}, G{i,s}). where P{i,s} and G{i,s} are the predicted and ground truth RGB values for ray i and sample s, \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function for the validity mask, and N{valid} is the count of valid rays. Parameters: delta: Huber loss threshold. Typical value: 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero: Guard nvalidrays to prevent NaN gradients when no rays are valid. Precision: Very small alpha values or near-zero valid ray counts can cause unstable gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computetrainingloss(predrgbds, gtrgbaf32, bg, rayisvalid, batchmetrics, delta=0.1): # 1. Split RGB and Depth predrgbs = predrgbds[...,:3] preddepths = predrgbds[..., 3:] # 2. Blend Ground Truth RGB with background alpha = gtrgbaf32[..., 3:4] gtrgbs = gtrgbaf32[...,:3] alpha + bg (1.0 - alpha) # 3. Compute per-ray Huber loss for RGB diff = predrgbs - gtrgbs absdiff = np.abs(diff) huber = np.where(absdiff <= delta, 0.5 diff2, delta (absdiff - 0.5 delta)) perrayloss = np.mean(huber, axis=-1) # Mask by validity and sum maskedloss = np.where(rayisvalid, perrayloss, 0.0) nvalidrays = np.sum(rayisvalid.astype(np.float32)) # Avoid division by zero if no valid rays lossrgb = np.where(nvalidrays > 0, np.sum(maskedloss) / nvalidrays, 0.0) # 4. Aggregate with other losses in batchmetrics totalloss = sum(batchmetrics["loss"]) + lossrgb return totalloss, {"lossrgb": lossrgb, "nvalidrays": nvalidrays} SH Masking (SHM) is a regularization technique for differentiable volume rendering optimization that suppresses the influence of saturated pixels during loss computation. Saturated regions (over- or undersaturation) lack reliable texture cues and act as outliers that bias geometric and photometric recovery. It differs from hard binary masking by using a "leaky" quadratic transition at the saturation boundaries, which allows smoother gradient flow while still reducing bias. A hinge loss on the mean mask value to ensure both foreground and background generators are used and cover a minimum fraction of the image. It prevents the model from collapsing to generating only foreground or only background. Formula: Foreground convergence loss: L{cvg}^{fg} = \lambda{cvg}^{fg} \max\left(0, \eta{fg} - \frac{1}{|S|} \sum{i \in S} \hat{m}{mask}^{fg}[i]\right) Background convergence loss: L{cvg}^{bg} = \lambda{cvg}^{bg} \max\left(0, \eta{bg} - \frac{1}{|S|} \sum{i \in S} (1 - \hat{m}{mask}^{bg}[i])\right) where \hat{m}{mask} is the predicted mask value, |S| is the number of pixels, and \eta is the minimum coverage fraction. Parameters: Foreground minimum coverage (\eta{fg}): 0.4 for AFHQ and FFHQ; 0.1 for Carla. Background minimum coverage (\eta{bg}): 0.1. Convergence loss weight (\lambda{cvg}^{fg}): 0.1. Convergence loss weight (\lambda{cvg}^{bg}): 0.1. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. name: SH Masking
head: SHM
body: SH Masking (SHM) is a regularization technique for differentiable volume rendering optimization that suppresses the influence of saturated pixels during loss computation. Saturated regions (over- or undersaturation) lack reliable texture cues and act as outliers that bias geometric and photometric recovery. It differs from hard binary masking by using a "leaky" quadratic transition at the saturation boundaries, which allows smoother gradient flow while still reducing bias. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Rendered pixel intensity x. Output: Mask weight m(x). Data Structures: No complex data structures. The mask is computed element-wise per pixel. Parameters: \text{low}: Lower threshold for saturation. Default value: 0.15. \text{high}: Upper threshold for saturation. Default value: 0.9. \lambda{\text{sh}}: Loss weight for the masking term in the total loss function. Default value: 0.05. \epsilon{\text{sh}}: Threshold for SH masks. Default value: 0.1. Learning rate for SH masks: 0.05. Formula: The mask function is defined as a piecewise quadratic function: \operatorname{mask}(x) = \begin{cases} \left(\frac{x + \text{low}}{2 \cdot \text{low}}\right)^2 & \text{if } x < \text{low} \\ 1 & \text{if } \text{low} \leq x \leq \text{high} \\ \left(\frac{2 - x}{2(1 - \text{high})}\right)^2 & \text{if } x > \text{high} \end{cases} Steps: 1. Compute the mask value m(x) using the piecewise formula above. 2. Multiply the base pixel-wise loss by m(x) to modulate its contribution to the gradient. 3. Integrate the masked loss into the total training loss, optionally weighted by \lambda{\text{sh}} if treated as a separate regularizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshmask(x, low=0.15, high=0.9): """Computes the SH mask weight for intensity x.""" if x < low: return ((x + low) / (2 low)) 2 elif x <= high: return 1.0 else: return ((2 - x) / (2 (1 - high))) 2 def applyshmasking(rendered, target, low=0.15, high=0.9, lambdash=0.05): """Computes the masked loss contribution.""" mask = computeshmask(rendered, low, high) baseloss = (rendered - target) 2 # MSE loss return lambdash (baseloss mask) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The left transition is continuous at \text{low}, but the right transition at \text{high} yields a value >1 per the source formula, which may amplify rather than suppress extreme oversaturation. Input Range: The 2-x term in the upper bound implies the intensity domain is scaled such that x=2 maps to zero weight. If the renderer outputs a different range, the formula must be adapted accordingly. Saturation Definition: The mask is "leaky" (non-zero at boundaries), so saturated regions are suppressed but not entirely discarded, preserving partial geometric cues. A variant of SH Masking that applies a quadratic transition to suppress saturation outliers. It is chosen when training data contains significant over- or undersaturated regions that act as outliers. It differs from hard binary masking by allowing non-zero gradients at the boundaries, which prevents bias in geometric and photometric recovery. Builds on Training Loss Computation with Huber and Masking. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for mask computation, adding negligible overhead to the main rendering and loss pipeline. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for the mask value. Strengths: Robust to saturation; provides smooth gradients; trivial to implement. Limitations: Requires matching the intensity scaling to the formula's assumptions; performance gains depend on the broader training configuration rather than the mask alone. The technique was introduced for differentiable volume rendering and Gaussian Splatting optimization. The masking concept originates from HDR-Plenoxels for radiance fields, while its specific hyperparameters and integration into Gaussian Splatting training loops are detailed in Trick-GS. name: Restricted Mean Error Metric
head: Cluster-specific error metric, Error Metric for Optimization, Restricted Mean Error Metric for Weight Optimization, Restricted mean pixel intensity
body: The Restricted Mean Error Metric is a loss function for optimizing scalar weight factors of pre-computed scattering lobe shapes in volume rendering, specifically addressing parameter heterogeneity across voxel clusters. Unlike global mean metrics that obscure local errors, it computes average intensity only for pixels directly visible to specific voxel clusters, allowing the optimizer to identify and correct artifacts like seams per cluster. It is used to optimize SGGX lobe weights via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Inputs: K: Number of voxel clusters. I^r: Ground truth reference image for view r. \tilde{I}^r: Rendered approximate image for view r, generated using current weights w. Vk: Set of pixels in view r that are directly visible to voxels in cluster k. cr: Normalization weights for each view r. Outputs: E{L2}: The total restricted mean squared error value. \nabla{w{k,j}} E{L2}: The gradient of the error with respect to weight w{k,j} (the j-th parameter of the k-th cluster's lobe shape), required for SGD updates. Data Structures: The method assumes a clustering of voxels where each voxel i belongs to a cluster c(i) \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Weights w{k,j} correspond to the parameters defining the shape of each lobe. Steps: 1. Compute Normalization Weights: For each view r, calculate the normalization factor cr based on the mean intensity of the ground truth image I^r. The mean intensity \text{mean}(I^r) is the average intensity of all foreground pixels in I^r. cr = \max(\text{mean}(I^r), 0.05)^{-1} 2. Compute Restricted Means: For each cluster k and each view r, compute the restricted mean intensity \text{mean}k(I^r) and \text{mean}k(\tilde{I}^r). This is the average intensity evaluated only among the pixels in Vk. \text{mean}k(I^r) = \frac{1}{|Vk|} \sum{p \in Vk} I^r(p) \text{mean}k(\tilde{I}^r) = \frac{1}{|Vk|} \sum{p \in Vk} \tilde{I}^r(p) Note: If Vk is empty, the contribution of cluster k to the error for view r is zero. 3. Calculate Error Metric: Compute the total error E{L2} by summing the squared differences of the restricted means, weighted by cr. E{L2}(w1, \dots, wK) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \sum{r} cr \left( \text{mean}k(\tilde{I}^r) - \text{mean}k(I^r) \right)^2 The goal is to find weights that minimize this metric. (w1^, \dots, wK^) = \arg\min{w1, \dots, wK} E{L2}(w1, \dots, wK) 4. Gradient Estimation (for SGD): To optimize using Stochastic Gradient Descent, compute the partial derivative of E{L2} with respect to a specific weight w{k,j}. \frac{\partial E{L2}}{\partial w{k,j}} = 2 \sum{r} cr \left( \text{mean}k(\tilde{I}^r) - \text{mean}k(I^r) \right) \frac{\partial \text{mean}k(\tilde{I}^r)}{\partial w{k,j}} The term \frac{\partial \text{mean}k(\tilde{I}^r)}{\partial w{k,j}} represents the sensitivity of the restricted mean of the rendered image to the weight w{k,j}. This derivative is estimated via path tracing to obtain an unbiased gradient evaluation. 5. Weight Update: Update the weight w{k,j} using the gradient and a step size \deltat. w{k,j}^{(t+1)} = w{k,j}^{(t)} - \deltat \frac{\partial E{L2}}{\partial w{k,j}} The step size \deltat follows a divergent harmonic series to ensure convergence (\sum \deltat = \infty and \sum \deltat^2 < \infty). Parameters: cr: Normalization factor. Typical implementation uses \max(\text{mean}(I^r), 0.05)^{-1}. \deltat: Learning rate. Follows common SGD practices for stochastic optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Previous methods using global mean \text{mean}(\tilde{I}^r) only indicated if the whole image was too dark or bright, making it difficult to identify which voxel clusters needed correction. The restricted mean resolves this by isolating errors to specific clusters. Visibility Boundaries: If cluster boundaries cut across areas with smoothly varying albedos, visible seams may appear. The method suggests jittering clusterings by perturbing voxel albedos during K-means clustering to mitigate this. Empty Visibility Sets: If a cluster is not visible in a particular view, its restricted mean is undefined. This method optimizes scalar weight factors for pre-computed SGGX lobe shapes by minimizing the restricted mean squared error between rendered and target images. It differs from direct per-voxel optimization by clustering voxels to share weight factors, which reduces the parameter space and enables efficient optimization. Choose this method when optimizing anisotropic scattering parameters across spatially heterogeneous media. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively handles parameter heterogeneity by attributing errors to specific spatial clusters. It avoids the ambiguity of global mean metrics, leading to more stable convergence in optimizing anisotropic scattering parameters. Limitations: Requires pre-computed voxel clustering and visibility masks. The Restricted Mean Error Metric was introduced in the context of downsampling scattering parameters for rendering anisotropic media. It addresses limitations in previous work by Zhao et al. (2011) and Khungurn et al. (2015), which used global mean pixel intensity for error metrics. The global mean approach failed to provide sufficient information for correcting specific voxel clusters, leading to local minima in optimization. The restricted mean approach was developed to enable efficient optimization of SGGX lobe weights by clustering voxels and sharing weight factors within clusters. Downsampling scattering parameters for rendering anisotropic media, https://doi.org/10.1145/2980179.2980228, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Stochastic Gradient Descent for Lobe Weight Optimization
head: Gradient-based weight optimization, SGD for weight factors
body: This method optimizes the scalar weight factors w{k,j} for pre-computed SGGX lobe shapes in volume rendering by minimizing a restricted mean squared error between the rendered and target images. It differs from direct per-voxel optimization by clustering voxels to share weight factors, reducing the parameter space, and uses stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with unbiased gradient estimates obtained via path tracing. It builds on Restricted Mean Error Metric by defining the specific error function E{L2} and the optimization procedure to minimize it. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K voxel clusters. For each cluster k, a set of m pre-computed lobe shapes f{k,j} (where j=1,\dots,m). Target image intensities Ir for a set of camera rays r. Ray coefficients cr. Outputs: Optimized weight factors w{k,j} for each cluster k and lobe j. Data Structures: Weight Factors: A vector wk = (w{k,1}, \dots, w{k,m}) for each cluster k. Gradient Images: For each ray r, cluster k, and lobe j, an image \tilde{I}{r,k,j} where pixel intensity p is \tilde{I}{r,k,j}(p) = (\partial \tilde{I}r / \partial w{k,j})(p). Parameters: Step Size: \deltat at iteration t, typically defined as \deltat = a{k,j} / (t + b{k,j}) where a{k,j}, b{k,j} are constants. Initial Weights: w{k,j}^{(0)} = 1 for all k, j. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Set w{k,j}^{(0)} = 1 for all clusters k=1,\dots,K and lobes j=1,\dots,m. 2. Iteration: For t = 0, 1, \dots: a. Gradient Estimation: For each ray r, cluster k, and lobe j, obtain an unbiased estimate of the gradient image \tilde{I}{r,k,j} using path tracing. b. Compute Gradient: Calculate the partial derivative of the error metric E{L2} with respect to w{k,j}: \frac{\partial E{L2}}{\partial w{k,j}} = 2 \sum{r, k'} cr \left( \text{mean}{k'}(\tilde{I}r) - \text{mean}{k'}(Ir) \right) \text{mean}{k'}(\tilde{I}{r,k,j}) where \text{mean}{k'}(\cdot) computes the restricted mean over pixels visible through cluster k'. c. Update: Update the weight factor: w{k,j}^{(t+1)} = w{k,j}^{(t)} - \deltat \frac{\partial E{L2}}{\partial w{k,j}} \bigg|{w^{(t)}}. Pitfalls: The step size \deltat must satisfy \sum{t=1}^\infty \deltat = \infty and \sum{t=1}^\infty \deltat^2 < \infty to ensure convergence. Gradient estimation via path tracing introduces noise; sufficient samples per ray are required for stable convergence. A technique to handle colored scattering parameters efficiently by keeping SGGX lobes f{i,j} and weight factors w{i,j} single-channel, and introducing an extra colored scaling factor sk for each voxel cluster k to make the lobe weights colored. The colored lobe weights are defined as W{i,clr,j} = s{c(i)} \bar{\alpha}{i,clr} \frac{w{c(i),j}}{|V(i)|} for clr \in \{R, G, B\}, where c(i) is the cluster index of voxel i, and \bar{\alpha}{i,clr} is the downsampled albedo component. The scaling factors s1, \dots, sK are optimized together with w{i,j} using SGD. This approach assumes input parameters are semi-colored: only albedos vary between color channels while densities and phase functions stay constant. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations, rays, clusters, and lobes. Each iteration requires path tracing for gradient estimation, which is computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing weight factors for all clusters and lobes, and gradient images for each ray during optimization. Strengths: Reduces the number of parameters by clustering voxels, leading to better convergence and lower memory usage compared to per-voxel optimization. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of step size constants a{k,j}, b{k,j}. Assumes semi-colored inputs for the colored scaling variant. Originated in the paper "Downsampling scattering parameters for rendering anisotropic media" by Khungurn et al. (2015). The method addresses the impracticality of optimizing weight factors for every voxel individually by clustering voxels and using SGD to find optimal weights that minimize the restricted mean squared error. Downsampling scattering parameters for rendering anisotropic media, https://doi.org/10.1145/2980179.2980228, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Silhouette Loss
head: Alpha mask loss, Boundary supervision loss, DDF Silhouette Loss
body: Silhouette Loss provides boundary supervision for differentiable volume rendering by penalizing discrepancies between predicted surface probabilities and ground-truth image masks. It ensures that the rendered alpha channel aligns with the object's silhouette, preventing geometric artifacts and providing warm-start supervision for fine-grained geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: m: Ground-truth binary image mask, where m \in \{0, 1\}. \sigma: Predicted ray hit probability from the differentiable volume rendering (DDF) model. s: Predicted signed distance field (SDF) value at the ray intersection point. \tau: Truncation distance parameter for the SDF model. Outputs: Scalar loss value L\sigma. Data Structures: Masks, probabilities, and SDF values are stored as per-pixel tensors or arrays matching the image resolution. Method: The loss enforces boundary constraints by combining mask supervision and SDF supervision. The core intuition is that where rays hit the surface, the SDF must be as low as possible, and where rays do not hit, the SDF must be high. The exact mathematical formulation (referenced as Eq. (8) in the source) is not provided in the available text. The implementation follows these steps: 1. Mask Discrepancy: Compute the difference between the predicted hit probability \sigma and the ground-truth mask m. 2. SDF Boundary Penalty: Apply a truncation-based penalty to the predicted SDF s relative to \tau. If m=1 (hit), penalize s when it exceeds \tau. If m=0 (no hit), penalize s when it falls below -\tau. 3. Aggregation: Sum the mask discrepancy and SDF penalty across all pixels to produce L\sigma. Parameters: \tau: Truncation distance. Typical values depend on the scene scale. Weights for combining the mask and SDF terms are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: \sigma must be clamped to a valid probability range to avoid numerical instability during differentiation. Degenerate Input: Uniform masks (all zeros or all ones) may reduce gradient signal without proper weighting. Artifacts: Without this loss, models suffer from artifacts around the performance due to lack of boundary supervision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def silhouetteloss(mask, sigma, sdf, tau): """ Computes the Silhouette Loss for DDF. Args: mask (list of lists): Ground truth binary mask, values in {0, 1}. sigma (list of lists): Predicted ray hit probability, values in [0, 1]. sdf (list of lists): Predicted signed distance. tau (float): Truncation distance for the SDF model. Returns: float: Scalar loss value Lsigma. """ # Note: The exact formula for Lsigma (Eq. 8) is not provided in the sources. # This implementation follows the described logic: penalize discrepancies between # hit probability and mask, and enforce SDF bounds relative to tau. totalloss = 0.0 count = 0.0 for i in range(len(mask)): for j in range(len(mask[0])): m = mask[i][j] hitprob = sigma[i][j] dist = sdf[i][j] # Mask discrepancy term alphaterm = abs(hitprob - m) # SDF boundary penalty term # Where hit (m=1), encourage low SDF (penalize if dist > tau) # Where miss (m=0), encourage high SDF (penalize if dist < -tau) if m == 1: sdfterm = max(0.0, dist - tau) else: sdfterm = max(0.0, -dist - tau) totalloss += alphaterm + sdfterm count += 1.0 return totalloss / count Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Essential for modeling fine-grained geometry; prevents artifacts around boundaries. Limitations: Requires ground-truth masks. When to use: When training differentiable volume rendering models that predict SDFs and alpha values, especially when geometric accuracy at boundaries is critical. Silhouette Loss is used in differentiable volume rendering, particularly in methods involving Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and Directional Distance Fields (DDF). It was highlighted in the context of "FIRe: Fast Inverse Rendering Using Directional and Signed Distance Functions" and "UV Volumes for Real-time Rendering of Editable Free-view Human Performance". The loss addresses the lack of boundary supervision in volume rendering, which can lead to distorted textures and artifacts. name: L1+SSIM Loss
head: SSIM+L1 Loss, Color Loss (L1 + SSIM)
body: The L1+SSIM loss is a composite photometric error metric used to optimize radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splats by comparing rendered images against ground-truth photographs. It combines a pixel-wise L1 term, which ensures color fidelity, with a Structural Similarity (SSIM) term, which preserves local structure, edges, and texture. Unlike pure L1 or MSE losses, which can produce blurry results, this hybrid approach aligns more closely with human perception of image similarity. It is the standard training objective for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: \hat{\mathbf{I}}: The rendered image (tensor of shape H \times W \times 3 or H \times W \times 4). \mathbf{I}: The ground-truth reference image (tensor of shape H \times W \times 3 or H \times W \times 4). \lambda: The weighting factor for the SSIM term (typically 0.2). Output: \mathcal{L}: The scalar loss value. Data Structures: Images are typically stored as floating-point tensors (FP32) in standard implementations. SSIM is computed using a sliding window approach with a kernel size (typically 11 \times 11) and standard deviations for luminance (\sigmaL) and contrast (\sigmaC). Steps: 1. Render: Generate the image \hat{\mathbf{I}} using the differentiable renderer \mathcal{R} given the current scene parameters and camera pose \pi. \hat{\mathbf{I}} = \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}; \pi, T) where \mathcal{G} represents the scene parameters (e.g., Gaussian positions, covariances, colors, opacities) and T represents any conditioning parameters (e.g., preset-specific factors). 2. Compute L1 Loss: Calculate the mean absolute error between the rendered and ground-truth images. \mathcal{L}1 = \frac{1}{N} \sum{p=1}^{N} \| \hat{\mathbf{I}}p - \mathbf{I}p \|1 where N is the number of pixels. 3. Compute SSIM Loss: Calculate the Structural Similarity Index between \hat{\mathbf{I}} and \mathbf{I}, then derive the loss as 1 - \text{SSIM}. \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} = 1 - \text{SSIM}(\hat{\mathbf{I}}, \mathbf{I}) 4. Combine: Compute the weighted sum. \mathcal{L} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}} Parameters: \lambda = 0.2: The weight for the SSIM term. The L1 term weight is implicitly 1 - \lambda = 0.8. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computel1ssimloss(renderedimage, gtimage, lambdassim=0.2): """ Computes the L1+SSIM loss. Args: renderedimage (list of lists of lists): Rendered image, shape (H, W, C). gtimage (list of lists of lists): Ground truth image, shape (H, W, C). lambdassim (float): Weight for the SSIM term. Default 0.2. Returns: float: Scalar loss value. """ H = len(renderedimage) W = len(renderedimage[0]) C = len(renderedimage[0][0]) # 1. Compute L1 Loss # Mean absolute error over all pixels and channels l1sum = 0.0 for h in range(H): for w in range(W): for c in range(C): l1sum += abs(renderedimage[h][w][c] - gtimage[h][w][c]) l1loss = l1sum / (H W C) # 2. Compute SSIM Loss ssimvalue = computessim(renderedimage, gtimage, windowsize=11) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssimvalue # 3. Combine loss = (1.0 - lambdassim) l1loss + lambdassim ssimloss return loss def computessim(img1, img2, windowsize=11): """ Computes SSIM between two images from scratch. """ C1 = (0.01 255.0) 2 C2 = (0.03 255.0) 2 halfw = windowsize // 2 H = len(img1) W = len(img1[0]) C = len(img1[0][0]) ssimsum = 0.0 count = 0 for c in range(C): for h in range(halfw, H - halfw): for w in range(halfw, W - halfw): # Extract local windows win1 = [] win2 = [] for i in range(-halfw, halfw + 1): for j in range(-halfw, halfw + 1): win1.append(img1[h + i][w + j][c]) win2.append(img2[h + i][w + j][c]) mu1 = sum(win1) / len(win1) mu2 = sum(win2) / len(win2) sigma1sq = sum((x - mu1) 2 for x in win1) / len(win1) sigma2sq = sum((x - mu2) 2 for x in win2) / len(win2) sigma12 = sum((win1[i] - mu1) (win2[i] - mu2) for i in range(len(win1))) / len(win1) num = (2 mu1 mu2 + C1) (2 sigma12 + C2) den = (mu1 2 + mu2 2 + C1) (sigma1sq + sigma2sq + C2) ssimsum += num / den count += 1 return ssimsum / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Layout: Standard SSIM implementations often expect channel-first (N, C, H, W) layout, while 3DGS renders may be channel-last (H, W, C). Precision: Converting reference images from UINT8 to FP32 introduces memory overhead and potential precision issues if not handled carefully. Alpha Masking: If the rendered image has an alpha channel, it must be handled correctly during SSIM computation to avoid artifacts from transparent regions. A local structure-aware loss that provides sparse yet effective supervision to preserve fine details and stabilize training by measuring sparse Normalized Cross-Correlation (NCC) [15693-sparse-normalized-cross-correlation-ncc-loss.md]. It sets itself apart from dense photometric losses by operating only on per-tile sparsely sampled pixels, prioritizing challenging regions while skipping well-reconstructed ones to avoid redundant gradient computation. Choose it when SSIM computation is too expensive or when specific local correlations are more informative than global structure. A kernel that directly computes the gradient of the weighted sum of L1 and SSIM losses in a single pass, avoiding intermediate reductions and memory layout conversions. It sets itself apart from standard PyTorch-based evaluations by fusing alpha masking support with near-zero overhead and storing the reference image in 4×UINT8 RGBA pixels without converting to FP32. Choose it when training large-scale scenes and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. A variant that uses a specific gradient estimation technique to guarantee convergence to the true radiance field L^ with a learning rate \alphak = 2 for all k. It sets itself apart from standard backpropagation by using a contraction mapping to shrink error towards zero with each iteration. Choose it when strict convergence guarantees are required over standard stochastic gradient descent. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The L1+SSIM loss is the de facto standard for 3D Gaussian Splatting, providing a good balance between training speed and visual quality. It produces sharper images than L1-only losses. Strengths: Improves perceptual quality by preserving edges and textures. Robust to minor color shifts due to the SSIM component. Limitations: The choice of \lambda is somewhat arbitrary, though 0.2 is widely accepted. Optimized fully-fused kernels reduce overhead by computing gradients in a single pass and avoiding intermediate tensor allocations. When to use: Standard training for 3D Gaussian Splatting where visual fidelity is prioritized. When not to use: When training speed is the primary constraint and visual quality can be sacrificed (use L1 only). When memory is extremely limited and fused kernels are not available. The L1+SSIM loss was introduced in the seminal 3D Gaussian Splatting paper by Kerbl et al. (2023). It builds upon the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) metric proposed by Wang et al. (2004). The loss function has become the standard for optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting models, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis. Variants and optimizations, such as fully-fused kernels and semi-gradient methods, have been developed to improve its efficiency and convergence properties.
