name: Light Regularization
head: Chromaticity Prior, Chromaticity Regularization
body: Light Regularization is a regularization prior used in inverse rendering and radiance field optimization to mitigate the inherent ambiguity between material properties and incident illumination. It operates on the assumption that natural environmental lighting is typically neutral or "white," penalizing illumination estimates that exhibit strong chromatic biases. Unlike sibling methods that enforce photometric consistency with observed image pixels, this method enforces a statistical prior on the estimated light field itself. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The estimated incident light field, represented as a set of color channels. In the context of environment maps or spherical harmonics, this is the RGB vector \mathbf{x}0 or L for each direction or basis coefficient. Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{light} or L{\text{chroma}} used during gradient-based optimization. Data Structures: The method operates on the color channels of the illumination estimate. Let the illumination estimate be denoted by x0 (in) or L (in). For each sample or direction, the estimate consists of three values corresponding to the Red, Green, and Blue channels. Formula: The loss is computed as the sum of the deviations of each color channel from the mean intensity of the three channels. For a single illumination estimate with channels x{c0} for c \in \{R, G, B\}, the loss is: L{\text{chroma}} = \sum{c=1}^{3} \left( x{c0} - \frac{1}{3} \sum{c=1}^{3} x{c0} \right) Alternatively, using notation Lc for the c-th channel: \mathcal{L}{\text{light}} = \sum{c \in \{R,G,B\}} \left( L{c} - \frac{1}{3}\sum{c \in \{R,G,B\}} L{c} \right) Note: The source formulas omit absolute value or squaring operators, which would mathematically sum to zero. Implementations apply an L1 or L2 norm to the deviations to ensure a non-negative penalty. Parameters: None. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightregularizationloss(channels): """ Computes the chromaticity regularization loss for a single illumination estimate. Args: channels: A list or array of 3 values [R, G, B]. Returns: A scalar loss value. """ # Calculate the mean intensity across the RGB channels meanintensity = sum(channels) / 3.0 # Calculate the absolute deviation of each channel from the mean # Absolute value is applied to ensure a non-negative penalty, as the raw sum of deviations is zero deviations = [abs(c - meanintensity) for c in channels] # Sum the deviations across the RGB channels loss = sum(deviations) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Intensity: If the illumination estimate is zero, the mean is zero and the loss is zero, providing no gradient signal. Negative Values: Illumination estimates should be non-negative for physical plausibility; the prior applies regardless but may conflict with physical constraints. What it is: A specific instance of Light Regularization focusing on the colorfulness of the environment map. Differentiation: Explicitly references the observation that natural illumination is not highly colorful. When to choose: When optimizing environment maps for novel view synthesis where lighting consistency is key. Link: Light Regularization What it is: The underlying physical assumption that incident light is near-white. Differentiation: Used to decouple material albedo from lighting color. When to choose: In inverse rendering tasks involving BRDF decomposition where lighting and material colors are entangled. Link: Light Regularization Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples or directions in the illumination estimate. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively breaks the symmetry between dark materials and bright lighting or colored materials and neutral lighting. Limitations: Assumes natural lighting. It may penalize artistic or stylized scenes with strong colored lighting if not weighted appropriately. Scaling: Scales linearly with the resolution of the environment map or the number of spherical harmonic coefficients. Origin: The concept is based on the observation that natural illumination is typically neutral. It follows the work of Munkberg et al. [2022] (NeRF-W) who introduced chromaticity priors for consistent novel view synthesis. History: It has been adopted in various inverse rendering frameworks to resolve material-lighting ambiguity. Usage: Used in differentiable rendering pipelines, particularly those involving environment map optimization or BRDF decomposition. name: SparseNeuS Consistency-Aware Color Loss
head: O(r) Weighted Loss
body: The SparseNeuS Consistency-Aware Color Loss is a photometric regularization term designed for neural surface reconstruction from sparse views. It solves the problem of noisy or distorted geometry caused by inconsistent radiance in unstructured scenes by automatically excluding regions where rendered colors do not match ground truth observations. It sets itself apart from standard photometric losses by weighting the error by the accumulated weight O(r) and applying logistic regularization to suppress inconsistent rays, rather than treating all pixels equally. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of query rays \mathbb{R}. For each ray r, the rendered pixel color C(r), ground truth pixel color \tilde{C}(r), rendered patch color P(r), ground truth patch color \tilde{P}(r), and the accumulated weight O(r). Output: The scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{color}. Data Structures: \mathbb{R}: Set of all query rays. O(r): Scalar, the sum of accumulated weights along ray r. C(r), \tilde{C}(r): Vectors of pixel colors (e.g., RGB). P(r), \tilde{P}(r): Vectors of patch colors (e.g., flattened local neighborhoods). \lambda0, \lambda1: Scalar regularization coefficients. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the accumulated weight O(r) for each query ray by summing the transmittance-weighted density contributions along the ray. 2. Compute the pixel-wise L1 distance \mathcal{D}{pix}(C(r), \tilde{C}(r)) between rendered and ground truth pixel colors. 3. Compute the patch-wise Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC) distance \mathcal{D}{pat}(P(r), \tilde{P}(r)) between rendered and ground truth patch colors. 4. Weight the pixel and patch losses by O(r) and sum over all rays in \mathbb{R}. 5. Compute the logistic regularization terms \log(O(r)) and \log(1-O(r)), scale them by \lambda0 and \lambda1, and sum over all rays. 6. Add the weighted photometric losses and the logistic regularization terms to obtain \mathcal{L}{color}. Formulas: The accumulated weight O(r) represents the opacity or the sum of contributions along the ray. It is calculated as: O(r) = \sum{i=1}^{PM} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai)) where: PM: Total number of samples along the ray. Ti: Transmittance at sample i. \sigmai: Density at sample i. The total loss combines the weighted photometric errors and the logistic regularization terms: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{r \in \mathbb{R}} O(r) \mathcal{D}{pix}(C(r), \tilde{C}(r)) + \sum{r \in \mathbb{R}} O(r) \mathcal{D}{pat}(P(r), \tilde{P}(r)) + \lambda0 \sum{r \in \mathbb{R}} \log(O(r)) + \lambda1 \sum{r \in \mathbb{R}} \log(1 - O(r)) Parameters: \mathcal{D}{pix}: Empirically chosen as L1 loss. \mathcal{D}{pat}: Empirically chosen as Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC) loss. \lambda0, \lambda1: Logistic regularization coefficients controlling the level of consistency. Decreasing the ratio \lambda0/\lambda1 leads to more regions being kept; increasing it excludes more regions, resulting in cleaner surfaces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Training Instability: In the early stages of generic training, the estimated geometry is inaccurate, and 3D surface points may have large errors. These errors do not provide clear clues on whether regions are radiance consistent. Therefore, the consistency-aware logistic terms are removed from the loss function during the generic model training phase and only applied during per-scene fine-tuning. Logarithm Domain: O(r) must be strictly between 0 and 1 for the log terms to be defined. Clamping or adding epsilon is required in implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparseNeusconsistencyawarecolorloss(renderedpixels, gtpixels, renderedpatches, gtpatches, accumulatedweights, lambda0, lambda1): """ Computes the SparseNeuS Consistency-Aware Color Loss. Args: renderedpixels: Array of shape (N, C) or (N,), rendered pixel colors C(r). gtpixels: Array of shape (N, C) or (N,), ground truth pixel colors C̃(r). renderedpatches: Array of shape (N, K), rendered patch colors P(r). gtpatches: Array of shape (N, K), ground truth patch colors P̃(r). accumulatedweights: Array of shape (N,), O(r) = sum of weights along ray. lambda0: Scalar, regularization coefficient for log(O(r)). lambda1: Scalar, regularization coefficient for log(1-O(r)). Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Pixel-wise L1 Loss weighted by O(r) pixeldiff = abs(renderedpixels - gtpixels) pixellossperray = sum(pixeldiff, axis=-1) weightedpixelloss = sum(accumulatedweights pixellossperray) # 2. Patch-wise NCC Loss weighted by O(r) eps = 1e-8 dotproducts = sum(renderedpatches gtpatches, axis=-1) normrendered = sqrt(sum(renderedpatches2, axis=-1) + eps) normgt = sqrt(sum(gtpatches2, axis=-1) + eps) correlation = dotproducts / (normrendered normgt) ncclossperray = 1.0 - correlation weightedpatchloss = sum(accumulatedweights ncclossperray) # 3. Logistic Regularization Terms wclipped = clamp(accumulatedweights, min=eps, max=1.0-eps) logo = log(wclipped) log1minuso = log(1.0 - wclipped) logisticloss0 = lambda0 sum(logo) logisticloss1 = lambda1 sum(log1minuso) # Total Loss totalloss = weightedpixelloss + weightedpatchloss + logisticloss0 + logisticloss1 return totalloss A strategy that enforces local and contextual radiance consistency between rendered colors and ground truth colors by combining pixel-based and patch-based blending. It uses pixel-based L1 loss for global consistency and patch-based NCC loss for local texture consistency. Combining both yields better Chamfer distance (1.28 on DTU) compared to pixel-only blending (1.39). Complexity: The loss computation is O(N) with respect to the number of rays, as it involves element-wise operations and sums over the ray set \mathbb{R}. Performance: On the DTU dataset, the consistency-aware scheme combined with multi-scale blending achieves a Chamfer distance of 1.21 (Fine-tuning, Cascaded volumes, Pixel+Patch), compared to 1.39 for pixel-only and 1.28 for pixel+patch without consistency awareness. Strengths: Automatically excludes inconsistent regions, leading to cleaner surfaces and avoiding distorted geometries caused by radiance inconsistencies. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \lambda0 and \lambda1. The ratio \lambda0/\lambda1 controls the trade-off between keeping regions and excluding them. Incorrect ratios may lead to over-exclusion or under-exclusion of valid geometry. Usage: Recommended for per-scene fine-tuning in sparse view reconstruction where generic initialization may be noisy. Not recommended for the initial generic training phase due to inaccurate geometry. The SparseNeuS Consistency-Aware Color Loss was introduced in the SparseNeuS paper ("SparseNeuS: Fast Generalizable Neural Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views") by X. Long et al.. It is part of a framework that uses cascaded volumes and a multi-scale color blending strategy to achieve high-quality reconstruction from sparse views without relying on 3D ground-truth shapes. The method builds on the differentiable volume rendering equation and extends it with consistency-aware regularization. name: Gaussian and Density Specific Regularization
body: This family of regularization techniques addresses the instability, overfitting, and geometric inaccuracies inherent in differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization by penalizing specific properties of the density field, model parameters, or output noise. Unlike sibling methods that focus on perceptual features, color consistency, or total variation smoothness, these methods operate directly on the scalar density/opacity values, the raw latent parameters of the scene representation, or the statistical distribution of the output noise to enforce physical plausibility and optimization stability. The core mechanism across this family is the injection of a penalty term into the total loss function L{total} that targets specific failure modes of neural scene representations: 1. Output Perturbation: Adding noise to raw density predictions before activation to encourage robustness against small input perturbations. 2. Parameter Constraint: Penalizing raw decoder outputs (e.g., residual rotations, spherical harmonics coefficients, scales) to keep them within numerically stable or physically plausible bounds. 3. Structural Fitting: Explicitly regularizing the amplitude and extent (covariance) of Gaussian splats to prevent extreme values and overfitting. 4. Spatial Density Control: Forcing density to zero in empty space (before scene boundaries) to correct geometry representation when multi-view cues are weak. All methods produce a scalar loss value L{reg} that is weighted by a hyperparameter \lambda and added to the reconstruction loss. A training-time technique that improves novel view synthesis by injecting Gaussian noise into predicted density (\sigma) or opacity values. It encourages the network to learn a robust density field less sensitive to small perturbations. Unlike sibling methods targeting geometric consistency, this operates directly on the radiance field's scalar output before activation. Applies penalties to the raw parameters of a neural scene representation (such as residual rotations or spherical harmonics coefficients) to prevent instability and overfitting. It distinguishes itself from output-based regularizations by constraining internal latent variables or decoder outputs directly, ensuring predicted attributes remain within stable bounds. Defines the objective for optimizing a set of K Gaussian splats to reconstruct a target volume, combining data fidelity with structural regularization. It differs from standard reconstruction losses by explicitly penalizing extreme splat amplitudes and extents to prevent overfitting. It is typically used in single-pass benchmarks for differentiable volume rendering. Defines a composite differentiable loss function used to optimize 3D Gaussians from video input. It solves the problem of shape reconstruction by combining segmentation mask supervision, photometric color fidelity, and optical flow consistency. A technique used in differentiable volume rendering to prevent large Gaussians from interfering with visibility tests and causing gradient explosion. It differs from conventional mask regularization by only penalizing opacity outside a specified binary mask, leaving opacity inside the mask unconstrained, thereby avoiding the degradation of BRDF parameter training and visibility accuracy. Definition: A regularization term to address inaccurate volume density predictions caused by small camera motion and lack of multi-view information, which leads to incorrect scene geometry representation. Step: Set the volume density of 3D points to 0 for all points before the ray reaches the scene boundary. Formula: \mathcal{L}{\text{density}} = \sum{\tau \in [1,N]} \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}f(\tau)} \|\sigma\tau(\mathbf{x})\|1 where \tau is the video frame index, N is the total number of frames, \mathcal{X}f(\tau) is the set of 3D points located before the object boundary at time \tau, and \sigma\tau(\mathbf{x}) is the predicted volume density. Comparison: The density loss focuses on the surface of the scene, while the rendering weight loss allows for more precise geometry representation; they complement each other. The need for specific regularization in volume rendering arises from the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering, particularly when multi-view information is sparse (e.g., small camera motion videos) or when using explicit representations like 3D Gaussians that can overfit to noise. The "Density Loss for Volume Density Regularization" originates from work on dynamic view synthesis from small camera motion videos, where traditional COLMAP-based camera initialization fails and NeRF struggles with spatial relationships due to lack of multi-view cues. Output noise regularization and model regularization are broader techniques adopted from neural network training stability practices, applied here to the specific domain of radiance fields and Gaussian splatting to prevent exploding gradients and unstable appearance coefficients. name: Output Noise Regularization
head: Density Noise Regularization, Gaussian Noise Regularization on Density, Training Regularization for Real Scenes
body: Output Noise Regularization is a training-time technique that improves novel view synthesis in real-world scenes by injecting Gaussian noise into predicted density (\sigma) or opacity values. It encourages the network to learn a robust density field that is less sensitive to small perturbations in the input space. Unlike sibling methods targeting geometric consistency or perceptual features, this method operates directly on the radiance field's scalar output before activation. The method modifies the forward pass of the neural radiance field during training by adding random noise to the raw density predictions. This forces the model to produce consistent rendering outputs even when underlying density estimates are slightly corrupted, effectively regularizing the optimization landscape. Input: The raw output tensor from the neural network, typically containing RGB color and density/opacity channels. Let this be \mathbf{raw} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times N \times C}, where B is batch size, N is the number of samples per ray, and C is the number of channels (typically 4: RGB + \sigma). Output: The modified raw tensor \mathbf{raw}' with noise added to the density channel. The implementation assumes a standard volume rendering output format: Tensor Shape: [batchsize, numsamples, 4]. Channels: Indices 0-2 correspond to Red, Green, Blue. Index 3 corresponds to density \sigma (or pre-activation opacity). Data Type: float32. noisestd: Standard deviation of the Gaussian noise. Default is None (disabled) or 0.0. usestratifiedsampling: Boolean flag. Noise is typically applied only when stratified sampling is active. noisemean: Mean of the Gaussian noise, typically 0. 1. Check Conditions: Verify if noise regularization is enabled (noisestd > 0) and if stratified sampling is active. 2. Generate Noise: If conditions are met, generate a noise tensor \mathbf{n} with the same shape as the density channel of the raw output. The noise is drawn from a standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and scaled by noisestd. 3. Add Noise: Add the generated noise to the density channel of the raw output. Crucially, this is done before any non-linear activation function (such as ReLU or Sigmoid) is applied to the density. 4. Concatenate: Combine the original RGB channels with the noisy density channel to form the final output tensor for the current step. 5. Forward Pass: Pass \mathbf{raw}' through the activation function and the volume rendering equation to compute the final pixel color. Noise generation: \mathbf{n} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \text{noise\std}^2). Noisy density: \sigma' = \sigma + \mathbf{n}. Output tensor: \mathbf{raw}' = [\mathbf{rgb}, \sigma + \mathbf{n}]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import random def concatenate(tensors, axis=-1): """Standard tensor concatenation along the specified axis.""" return np.concatenate(tensors, axis=axis) def normal(key, shape, dtype=np.float32): """Generate Gaussian noise with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.""" return np.random.defaultrng(key).normal(0.0, 1.0, shape).astype(dtype) def outputnoiseregularization(raw, noisestd, usestratifiedsampling, rngkey): """ Adds Gaussian noise to the density channel of the raw network output. Args: raw: numpy.ndarray, shape [batchsize, numsamples, 4], dtype float32. Channels 0-2 are RGB, channel 3 is density sigma. noisestd: float, standard deviation of the noise. If None or <= 0, no noise is added. usestratifiedsampling: bool, flag indicating if stratified sampling is used. rngkey: int, random number generator seed/key. Returns: rawnoisy: numpy.ndarray, same shape as raw, with noise added to channel 3. newkey: int, updated random key. """ if noisestd is None or noisestd <= 0.0 or not usestratifiedsampling: return raw, rngkey # Split key for noise generation rngkey, noisekey = rngkey + 1, rngkey + 2 # Generate noise with shape matching the density channel (channel index 3) noiseshape = raw[..., 3:4].shape noise = normal(noisekey, noiseshape, dtype=raw.dtype) noisestd # Add noise to the density channel (channel 3) # RGB channels (0-2) remain unchanged rawnoisy = concatenate([ raw[...,:3], # RGB channels raw[..., 3:4] + noise # Noisy sigma channel ], axis=-1) return rawnoisy, rngkey Activation Order: Noise must be added before the ReLU activation on \sigma. Adding it after ReLU would clip negative noise values, altering the distribution and potentially reducing the regularization effect. Stratified Sampling Dependency: Some implementations only apply this noise during stratified sampling. Applying it during uniform sampling may not yield the same benefits or could interfere with the uniform distribution assumptions. Precision: Ensure the noise is generated in the same precision (float32) as the network output to avoid casting issues during concatenation. Over-Regularization: Excessive noise standard deviation can destabilize training. The sources suggest unit variance (std=1) or specific scales depending on the context (e.g., opacity perturbation scales of 0.25-0.5). Smoothness priors are regularization terms applied during training and inference to reduce surface noise and improve geometric smoothness in neural surface reconstruction. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods by targeting the geometric consistency of the signed distance field (SDF) and its gradients, rather than just radiance or color consistency. Unlike Output Noise Regularization which perturbs the output, smoothness priors typically penalize the gradient of the SDF or the Laplacian of the field. This variant evaluates model robustness by injecting Gaussian noise into predicted opacity values before sigmoid activation to prevent negative values, then measuring segmentation metric degradation. It is used for sensitivity analysis rather than training regularization. At noise scale 0.25, mIoU drops from 50.75 to 50.13 and mAcc from 62.00 to 60.94. At scale 0.5, mIoU is 50.18 and mAcc is 60.88. Performance remains stable up to scale 0.5. At scale 1.0, mIoU drops to 47.13 and mAcc to 57.10. At scale 2.0, mIoU is 38.13 and mAcc is 44.11. At scale 4.0, mIoU collapses to 16.12 and mAcc to 32.19. A regularization technique that imposes sparsity constraints on the entire scene space to reduce noise using a relaxed geometry proxy. It improves PSNR from 20.01 (Model-C) to 20.07 (AR-NeRF) on DTU 3-view. It outperforms Emptiness loss and ray density entropy loss. Emptiness loss fails because wi is a biased geometry proxy. Ray density entropy loss encourages unimodal distribution, which is not necessarily true. A ray regularization technique that encourages a unimodal distribution for ray densities. It achieves 19.94 PSNR on DTU 3-view, performing worse than Model-C (20.01) and AR-NeRF (20.07). A pitfall is that it encourages a unimodal distribution for ray densities, which is not necessarily true in practice. A regularization technique that adds Gaussian noise to sigma values to encourage discreteness in the rendered output. If discretereg is True or training is active, it generates Gaussian noise with mean 0 and variance 1 for each sigma value. The free energy is calculated as \text{free\energy} = \text{ReLU}(\text{noise} + \sigma) \times \text{sampled\dists}, then scaled by 7.0. Directly applying a learned denoiser (e.g., OptiX denoiser) to primal renders in an inverse rendering pipeline reduces reconstruction quality because the added bias impedes gradient-based optimization. In a challenging indirect illumination scene, L1 error drops from 1.47e-02 (Baseline + Denoising) to 1.44e-02 (Ours + Denoising), and L2 error drops from 5.17e-04 to 4.60e-04. Denoising the control variate estimator progressively reduces bias and yields better results than denoising the primal render directly. A regularization technique for background points to avoid memory issues and handle outliers. It samples 16384 background points per iteration, jitters each input point using Gaussian noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.001), and computes loss using the Geman-McClure robust loss function with \alpha = -2 and c = 0.001. A technique to mitigate overfitting to training lightings by adding normal noise to environment coefficients. The modified shadow network computes S'(\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}, \mathbf {L}) = S(\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}, \mathbf {L} + \mathbf {\varepsilon }), where \mathbf {\varepsilon} \sim \mathcal {N}(0, 0.025\mathbf {I}). This is interpreted as a locality condition allowing smoother transitions between different lightings. Time Complexity: Adds negligible computational overhead. The noise generation is O(N) where N is the number of samples, and addition is element-wise. Memory Complexity: No additional memory storage is required beyond the noise tensor, which is generated on-the-fly and discarded after the forward pass. Performance: Slightly improves visual performance for rendering novel views in real scenes. It helps stabilize training and reduces artifacts. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for real-world data, does not require additional hyperparameters beyond noisestd. Limitations: May not be as effective for synthetic data or scenes with very different characteristics. When to Use: Recommended for training on real-world scene data where noise and artifacts are common. When Not to Use: May not be necessary for synthetic data or when other regularization methods are already sufficient. The method originated in the context of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for view synthesis. Tancik et al. introduced the technique of adding random Gaussian noise with zero mean and unit variance to the output \sigma values before ReLU activation during optimization for real scene data, finding that it slightly improves visual performance for rendering novel views. The implementation was done in TensorFlow. Later, this technique was adopted and adapted in various frameworks, including JAX-based implementations like Nerfies, where it is applied during stratified sampling. It has also been explored in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting for opacity perturbation analysis and in discrete regularization schemes. name: Denoising in Inverse Rendering
head: Learned Denoising, OptiX denoiser, Primal Denoising
body: This method applies a learned denoiser to Monte Carlo renders in inverse rendering pipelines to reduce variance. Unlike sibling methods that impose spatial constraints on radiance field parameters, it operates directly on pixel-space images. However, directly denoising the primal rendered image introduces bias that impedes gradient-based optimization, whereas applying the denoiser to a control variate estimator progressively reduces bias and improves reconstruction quality. Inputs: The noisy primal rendered image I{\text{primal}} (RGB). A pre-trained learned denoiser network D(\cdot), such as the OptiX denoiser based on Chaitanya et al. [2017]. Outputs: The denoised image I{\text{denoised}}. Data Structures: The denoiser D is a convolutional neural network trained on large datasets of rendered images. Architecture details are not provided in the sources. Steps: 1. Apply the learned denoiser to the primal image: I{\text{denoised}} = D(I{\text{primal}}). 2. Compute gradients for the inverse rendering optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias Introduction: Directly denoising the primal image adds bias that impedes optimization, potentially turning an unbiased optimization into a non-converging one. Artifacts: The bias can cause unrealistic artifacts, such as the brightening of the tea in a teapot. Denoiser Choice: The negative effects are observed with the OptiX denoiser, but similar behavior is expected with other learned denoisers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyprimaldenoiser(primalimage, denoiser): """Applies a learned denoiser to a primal rendered image.""" # Apply learned denoiser to primal rendered image denoisedimage = denoiser(primalimage) # Compute gradients for inverse rendering optimization return denoisedimage Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Directly applying the denoiser to the primal image reduces reconstruction quality. In a challenging indirect illumination scene, L1 error was 1.47e-02 and L2 error was 5.17e-04 for the baseline with denoising. The method reduces visual noise but introduces bias that impedes optimization. It is not recommended for direct primal denoising; instead, denoising the control variate estimator is preferred, which progressively reduces bias and yields better results (L1: 1.44e-02, L2: 4.60e-04 in the same scene). The method originates from "Recursive Control Variates for Inverse Rendering" by Nicolet et al. (2023). Learned denoisers are common in forward Monte Carlo rendering pipelines to reduce noise in final images, but their application in inverse rendering is counter-intuitive due to the requirement for differentiable gradients. The study demonstrates that while denoising reduces variance, the introduced bias is detrimental to the optimization process. The authors propose denoising the control variate estimator instead to mitigate these issues. name: Smoothness Priors
head: Geometric Smoothness Regularization, Gradient Smoothness Loss, SDF Total Variation Loss, Scene flow smoothness loss, Spatial and temporal smoothness priors
body:
Smoothness priors are regularization terms applied during training and post-processing to reduce surface noise and improve geometric smoothness in neural radiance fields and signed distance fields. This family builds on Output Noise Regularization and applies distinct loss formulations to enforce smoothness across different geometric representations. The family applies regularization losses to output fields to reduce artifacts. The core mechanism involves penalizing differences between neighboring values or enforcing alignment with ground-truth geometric cues. A spatial and temporal smoothness prior used to regularize scene flow in dynamic scene representations. It is chosen when optimizing for dynamic scenes where consistent motion fields are required. For a ray r, let x and x0 be neighboring points along the ray, t index the time step, and st^0(x, t) denote the scene flow value at point x and time t. The total loss sums over all time steps t and spatial points x along the ray. Two loss terms applied during training to enforce physical plausibility of the learned occupancy and normal fields. They are chosen to prevent specific artifacts in surface reconstruction, particularly for human faces or complex geometry. The method applies an opacity loss L{opacity} to constrain the opacity distribution and a normal loss L{normal} to constrain surface normals. name: Background Regularization
head: Background Point Regularization, Regularization for Background Artifacts
body: Background Regularization is a regularization technique that reduces background artifacts in object-centric scenes by sampling rays from pixels outside the input image space and constraining their rendered color to a constant background color. It addresses the issue where training rays are confined to the input image bounds (px \in [0, H], py \in [0, W]), causing extrapolated areas to exhibit apparent artifacts. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A batch of target pixels located outside the input image space, a fixed number of background samples per iteration, a background color constant \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}, and a radiance field model capable of rendering color \mathbf{C}(r) for a given ray r. Outputs: A scalar regularization loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{BR}} added to the total training loss. Data Structures Ray Batch \mathcal{R}o: A collection of rays generated from target pixels outside the input image space. Its size equals the fixed sample count parameter. Background Color \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}: A constant 3D vector (RGB) representing the assumed uniform background color for pixels outside the input image space. Steps 1. Sample Generation: Generate a fixed number of background points (rays) per iteration to avoid memory issues caused by scene-dependent background point counts. These points correspond to pixels outside the input image space [0, H] \times [0, W]. 2. Jittering: Apply Gaussian jittering to the input points to prevent overfitting to specific grid locations. Each point is perturbed by noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.001). 3. Rendering: For each ray r \in \mathcal{R}o, render the color \mathbf{C}(r) using the current state of the radiance field model. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between the rendered color and the constant background color. Formula \mathcal{L}{\text{BR}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}o|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}o} \|\mathbf{C}(r) - \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}\|2^2 where \mathcal{R}o is the batch of sampling rays, \mathbf{C}(r) is the rendered color, and \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}} is the background color. Some implementations replace the squared L2 norm with a Geman-McClure robust loss function with parameters \alpha = -2 and c = 0.001 to handle outliers. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computebackgroundregularizationloss(model, rays, backgroundcolor, userobustloss=False): """ Computes the Background Regularization loss for rays outside the input image space. Args: model: Radiance field model with a renderray(ray) method. rays: List of rays generated from pixels outside the input image space. backgroundcolor: 3D vector (RGB) constant for outside-space pixels. userobustloss: If True, uses Geman-McClure loss; otherwise uses L2 loss. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ renderedcolors = [] for r in rays: renderedcolors.append(model.renderray(r)) diffs = [] for cr, cbk in zip(renderedcolors, backgroundcolor): diffs.append(cr - cbk) n = len(rays) if userobustloss: cparam = 0.001 totalloss = 0.0 for d in diffs: xsq = sum(di2 for di in d) term = (cparam2) / (cparam2 + xsq) totalloss += cparam2 (1.0 - term2) return totalloss / n else: totalloss = 0.0 for d in diffs: totalloss += sum(di2 for di in d) return totalloss / n Parameters Sample Count: 16,384 points per iteration. Jitter Standard Deviation: 0.001. Geman-McClure Parameters: \alpha = -2, c = 0.001. Background Color \mathbf{C}{\text{bk}}: Assumed constant for pixels outside the image space in object-centric scenes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Extrapolation Artifacts: In object-centric scenes with few input views, training rays are only distributed inside the input image space (px \in [0, H], py \in [0, W]), leading to apparent artifacts in extrapolated input images outside this space. Memory Issues: The total number of background points varies per scene. Failing to fix the sample count per iteration (e.g., to 16,384) can cause memory overflow. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of background samples (16,384 per iteration). The jittering and loss computation are negligible compared to the ray marching and rendering cost. Memory Complexity: Constant per iteration, as the number of samples is fixed regardless of scene size. Strengths: Effectively removes background artifacts in object-centric scenes where the background is assumed to be uniform. Prevents memory overflow by fixing sample counts. Limitations: Assumes a constant background color, which may not hold for all scenes. When to use: When rendering object-centric scenes with limited input views and observing artifacts outside the input image bounds. When not to use: For scenes with complex, non-uniform backgrounds or when the background color is not constant. Background Regularization was introduced to reduce background artifacts in few-shot view synthesis scenarios. It is also employed to handle memory constraints and outliers in deformable radiance field optimization. The technique leverages the observation that pixels outside the input image space in object-centric scenes should ideally render as the background color. name: Complexity Dropout
body: Complexity Dropout is a training regularization technique that probabilistically excludes the complexity term from the importance score calculation during densification. It solves the problem of densification repeatedly targeting the same high-complexity regions, which prevents opacity sampling from covering remaining areas and leads to suboptimal reconstruction. It interpolates between always-applying the complexity term (\delta=0) and pure opacity sampling (\delta=1) via a single dropout rate parameter. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current set of Gaussian primitives, their attributes (position, covariance, opacity, color), the training loss gradients, and the dropout rate parameter \delta. Output: Modified importance scores used to select primitives for densification (splitting or cloning) and pruning. Data Structures: Primitive List: A list of N Gaussian primitives. Each primitive i stores a base importance score Ii (derived from loss gradients) and a complexity score Ci (derived from spatial extent or anisotropy). Dropout Mask: A binary vector M \in \{0, 1\}^N where mi=1 indicates the complexity term is kept, and mi=0 indicates it is dropped. Parameters: \delta: The dropout rate, \delta \in [0, 1]. \delta = 0: Always applies the complexity term. \delta = 1: Reduces to pure opacity sampling (complexity term always dropped). Default: \delta = 0.2. Steps: 1. Calculate Base Importance: For each primitive i, compute the base importance score Ii from the training loss gradients. 2. Calculate Complexity: Compute the complexity score Ci for each primitive. 3. Generate Dropout Mask: For each primitive i, sample mi \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1 - \delta). The mask is M = [m1, \dots, mN]. 4. Modify Importance Score: Compute the modified score I'i by excluding the complexity term when the mask is active. The exact combination is implementation-dependent. 5. Select Primitives: Rank primitives by I'i and select the highest values for densification. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: \delta = 0 is not beneficial and falls below opacity sampling on Deep Blending (29.00 vs 29.28 AUC PSNR). Large intermediate rates (\delta \in \{0.6, 0.8\}) perform worst on both evaluated datasets. Precision: Ensure Ci is normalized relative to Ii to prevent one term from dominating the selection signal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def complexitydropout(primitives, gradients, dropoutrate): """ Applies complexity dropout to primitive importance scores. Args: primitives: List of primitive objects with attributes 'complexity' (C) and 'opacity' (O). gradients: List of gradient magnitudes (G) for each primitive. dropoutrate: Float, delta (0 to 1). Returns: Modified importance scores. """ n = len(primitives) if n == 0: return [] complexities = np.array([p.complexity for p in primitives]) gradients = np.array(gradients) # Generate dropout mask: mi = 1 with probability (1 - delta), 0 with probability delta mask = np.random.binomial(1, 1 - dropoutrate, n) # Base importance score from gradients basescores = gradients # Modify score by excluding complexity term when mask is 0 # Note: The exact weighting of gradients vs complexity is not specified in the sources # Assuming additive combination for implementation: modifiedscores = basescores + mask complexities return modifiedscores Linearly Annealed Dropout (LAD) is a training regularization technique that applies a time-decaying Bernoulli mask to Gaussian primitives to suppress fragile co-adaptation and needle-like anisotropic structures in sparse-view tomography. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration for mask generation and score modification, where N is the number of primitives. This overhead is negligible compared to densification and rendering steps. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the dropout mask. Measured Performance: On the TandT dataset with \delta=0.2, the method yields PSNR 24.65, SSIM 0.868, LPIPS 0.150. On the DB dataset with \delta=0.2, it yields PSNR 29.92, SSIM 0.911, LPIPS 0.240. These are the best or near-best results compared to other \delta values (0, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1). Strengths: Prevents over-concentration on high-complexity regions, improves coverage, and leads to more stable training, especially on indoor scenes. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \delta; poor choices (0, 0.6, 0.8) degrade performance. When to use: When densification repeatedly targets the same high-complexity regions or overfits to local optima. When not to use: When opacity sampling alone is sufficient or when computational budget is extremely tight. The method was introduced in the KoalaGS paper. It is designed as a regularization technique for densification in Gaussian Splatting to balance structural refinement with spatial coverage. The technique is part of the broader family of output noise regularization methods used in differentiable volume rendering. KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28615, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Linearly Annealed Dropout
head: Linear Dropout Schedule
body: Linearly Annealed Dropout (LAD) is a training regularization technique that applies a time-decaying Bernoulli mask to Gaussian primitives to suppress fragile co-adaptation and needle-like anisotropic structures in sparse-view tomography. It enforces cross-view consistency by applying a single shared mask to all projection views in an iteration, preventing per-view masking from weakening the consistency signal. Unlike fixed dropout, which can over-smooth density structures, LAD gradually reduces regularization to allow late-stage refinement. Inputs and Outputs Input: Current set of Nt Gaussian primitives Gt, current training iteration t, initial dropout probability p0, annealing horizon T{\text{anneal}}, and SAES trigger iteration ts. Output: A masked Gaussian set Gt \odot m(t) used for rendering and loss computation, and the updated dropout probability pt for the next iteration. Data Structures Mask m(t): A binary vector of size Nt, where mi(t) \in \{0, 1\}. mi(t)=1 indicates the primitive is active; 0 indicates it is dropped. Gaussian Parameters: The standard 3DGS parameter tensor (position, scale, rotation, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients). Numbered Steps 1. Compute Dropout Probability: Calculate pt using the linear schedule. 2. Sample Mask: At iteration t, sample a single Bernoulli mask m(t) \in \{0, 1\}^{Nt} where each element mi(t) is drawn independently with probability 1 - pt of being 1. This mask is shared across all K projection views in the current iteration. 3. Apply Mask: Compute the masked Gaussian set G't = Gt \odot m(t), where \odot denotes element-wise masking (setting parameters of dropped primitives to zero or excluding them from rendering). 4. Render and Loss: Compute the projection loss \mathcal{L}{\text{proj}} using the masked set G't instead of the full set Gt. 5. Gradient Accumulation: Dropped primitives do not contribute to rendered projections and therefore do not accumulate position gradients in that iteration. To prevent biasing densification statistics, use the standard 3DGS gradient-accumulation buffer that averages gradients over the densification interval (100 iterations). This ensures each primitive contributes to densification proportionally to its expected retention probability 1 - pt. 6. SAES Check: If SAES triggers at iteration ts, set pt = 0 immediately for all subsequent iterations, even if ts < T{\text{anneal}}, to allow unconstrained late-stage refinement. Formulas The dropout probability pt at iteration t is defined as: pt = \begin{cases} p0 \cdot \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{t}{T{\text{anneal}}}\right) & \text{if } t < ts \\ 0 & \text{if } t \ge ts \end{cases} The base projection loss combines an L1 term and an SSIM term: \mathcal{L}{\text{proj}}(G) = \sum{v \in V} \left( \| \hat{P}v(G) - Pv \|1 + \lambda{\text{SSIM}} \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}(\hat{P}v(G), Pv) \right) with \lambda{\text{SSIM}} = 0.2. Parameters p0 = 0.9: Initial dropout probability. T{\text{anneal}} = 30,000: Annealing duration in iterations. ts: Iteration at which Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES) is triggered. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Per-view masking: Avoid sampling a separate mask per view, as it weakens the cross-view consistency signal. Densification bias: Dropped primitives do not accumulate position gradients. The gradient accumulation buffer must average over the densification interval to account for the variable retention probability. Parameter sensitivity: A too-small p0 weakens early co-adaptation suppression, while a too-large p0 over-regularizes the Gaussian field. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def linearlyannealeddropout(Gt, t, p0, Tanneal, ts): """ Gt: List of Nt Gaussian primitives t: Current training iteration p0: Initial dropout probability (0.9) Tanneal: Annealing horizon (30000) ts: SAES trigger iteration Returns: Masked Gaussian set Gmasked, dropout probability pt """ # 1. Compute dropout probability if t >= ts: pt = 0.0 else: # Linear annealing schedule pt = p0 max(0.0, 1.0 - t / Tanneal) # 2. Sample Bernoulli mask shared across all views # mi = 1 with probability (1 - pt), 0 with probability pt retentionprob = 1.0 - pt Nt = len(Gt) mt = [1 if random.random() < retentionprob else 0 for in range(Nt)] # 3. Apply mask to Gaussian parameters (equivalent to Hadamard product Gt ⊙ m(t)) Gmasked = [Gt[i] for i in range(Nt) if mt[i] == 1] return Gmasked, pt LADES is a ground-truth-free optimization controller for sparse-view Gaussian tomography that mitigates PVFD by combining Linearly Annealed Dropout (LAD) and Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES). Time Complexity: Computational overhead is below 1% of total per-iteration time, dominated by GPU rasterization. Memory Complexity: Adds one Bernoulli sampling per iteration (O(Nt)) and one element-wise mask multiplication on the Gaussian parameter tensor before rasterization. Strengths: Effectively controls early view-specific co-adaptation and mitigates Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence (PVFD) in sparse-view settings. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of p0 and T{\text{anneal}}; too extreme values lead to underfitting or over-regularization. LAD was introduced in the context of sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography to address the ill-posedness of recovering 3D density fields from a finite number of projections. It builds on the observation that needle-like anisotropic structures can fit projection data well but violate volumetric consistency. The method is part of the LADES framework, which also includes Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES). Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence: Diagnosing and Controlling Optimization Drift in Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.22525, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: LADES
head: Linearly Annealed Dropout and Structure-Aware Early Stopping, Linearly Annealed Dropout with Structure-Aware Early Stopping
body: LADES is a ground-truth-free optimization controller for sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography that mitigates Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence (PVFD) by combining Linearly Annealed Dropout (LAD) and Structure-Aware Early Stopping (SAES). It addresses the problem where improved projection fitting coincides with deteriorating volumetric fidelity due to structural degeneration, such as needle-like anisotropic primitives and fragile co-adaptation. Unlike fixed dropout or validation-based stopping, LADES disrupts premature co-adaptation via time-decaying stochastic masking and terminates densification based on intrinsic Gaussian population dynamics rather than external metrics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse-view X-ray projections Pv, a set of Gaussian primitives Gt (initialized via R2-GS or similar), and hyperparameters p0, T{anneal}, t{min}, \tau, W, \gamma{cool}. Outputs: A final set of Gaussian primitives G{final} and their parameters (position, scale, opacity, color) optimized for volumetric fidelity. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive i: Contains position \mathbf{x}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and color coefficients. Mask m^{(t)}: A binary vector where mi^{(t)} \in \{0, 1\} indicates if primitive i is active at iteration t. Population Counter Nj: The number of active Gaussians at monitoring step j. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian primitives G0. Set iteration counter t=0. Set monitoring step counter j=0. Initialize Adam optimizer moments for position and scaling parameters. 2. Dropout Probability Calculation: Compute the current dropout probability pt: pt = \begin{cases} p0 \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{t}{T{anneal}}\right), & t < ts \\ 0, & t \ge ts \end{cases} where p0 is the initial dropout probability, T{anneal} is the annealing horizon, and ts is the SAES trigger iteration (initially undefined or \infty). 3. Mask Sampling: For each Gaussian primitive i, sample a Bernoulli mask mi^{(t)} with retention probability 1 - pt: mi^{(t)} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1 - pt) mi^{(t)} = 1 means the primitive is retained for the forward and backward pass. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the projection loss using the masked Gaussian set Gt \odot m^{(t)}: L{LAD}^{(t)} = \sum{v \in V} \left\| \hat{P}v(Gt \odot m^{(t)}) - Pv \right\|^2 + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM}(\hat{P}v(Gt \odot m^{(t)}), Pv) where \hat{P}v is the rendered projection, Pv is the ground truth projection, and L{SSIM} is the SSIM loss. 5. Optimization Step: Perform gradient descent using the Adam optimizer to update Gaussian parameters based on L{LAD}^{(t)}. 6. Densification (Conditional): If t < ts, perform standard densification operations (clone, split, prune) according to the R2-GS densification rule. If t \ge ts, disable all topology-changing operations. 7. Monitoring (SAES): Every \Delta iterations, increment j and monitor the Gaussian population: Let Nj be the number of active Gaussians at step j. Compute the normalized population growth rate gj: gj = \frac{Nj - N{j-1}}{\max(N{j-1}, 1)} Compute the averaged growth rate \bar{g}j over a sliding window of size W: \bar{g}j = \frac{1}{W} \sum{q=j-W+1}^{j} gq Check for SAES trigger: If tj \ge t{min} and \bar{g}j < \tau, set ts = tj. 8. Transition to Fixed-Topology Refinement: Once ts is triggered (or if ts was never triggered, after T{anneal} or a max iteration limit): Set final training iteration T{final} = 2ts. Disable dropout (pt = 0). Cool down learning rates for geometry (\eta{xyz}) and scaling (\eta{scale}) parameters by factor \gamma{cool}: \eta{xyz} \leftarrow \gamma{cool} \eta{xyz}, \quad \eta{scale} \leftarrow \gamma{cool} \eta{scale} Reset the first- and second-order Adam moments for position and scaling parameters to remove optimization inertia. Continue optimization until T{final}. Parameters: p0: Initial dropout probability. Default: 0.9. T{anneal}: Annealing horizon. Default: 30,000 iterations. t{min}: Minimum iteration count before SAES can trigger. Default: 2,000. \tau: Growth threshold for SAES. Default: 10^{-3}. W: Sliding window size for SAES. Default: 5. \gamma{cool}: Learning rate cooling factor. Default: 0.2. \Delta: Monitoring interval. Default: 100 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-regularization: If p0 is too large, the model may underfit volumetrically, dropping 3D PSNR significantly (e.g., from 35.45 dB to 30.62 dB). Under-suppression: If p0 is too small, early co-adaptation is not sufficiently disrupted. Premature Stopping: If t{min} is too low, SAES may trigger before structural saturation, leading to incomplete reconstruction. Ground-Truth Dependency: SAES must not access ground-truth volumes or 3D PSNR during training; doing so violates the ground-truth-free design and may lead to overfitting to validation metrics. A regularization technique that applies strong stochastic masking in early training to disrupt premature primitive co-adaptation, then linearly decays the dropout probability to zero to restore full capacity for structural consolidation. Choose when early view-specific co-adaptation is a primary concern. See Linearly Annealed Dropout. A stopping criterion that monitors Gaussian population growth momentum to detect structural saturation and terminates densification without ground-truth metrics. Choose when volumetric fidelity degradation due to redundant late-stage densification is observed. See Structure-Aware Early Stopping. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to fixed-budget training because SAES terminates densification early, though the final refinement phase extends training to 2ts. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is determined by the number of active Gaussians, which is controlled by SAES to prevent excessive growth. Performance: On sparse-view CT reconstruction (e.g., 25-view FIPS dataset), LADES improves volumetric fidelity, suppresses structural degeneration, and maintains competitive projection accuracy (PSNR ~36.33 dB, SSIM ~0.853). Strengths: Ground-truth-free; mitigates PVFD; reduces training time; robust to hyperparameter variations. Limitations: Evaluated primarily on sparse-view CT with Gaussian-based backbones; generalization to other scanner geometries, noise levels, and clinical protocols requires further validation. When to Use: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian tomography where volumetric fidelity is critical and ground-truth volumes are unavailable during training. When Not to Use: Dense-view reconstruction where PVFD is less severe; non-Gaussian representations; scenarios where ground-truth validation metrics are available and preferred. LADES was introduced in the paper "Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence: Diagnosing and Controlling Optimization Drift in Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Tomography". The authors identified PVFD as a failure mode in sparse-view 3DGS-CT where projection fitting improves while volumetric fidelity deteriorates due to structural degeneration (needle-like primitives, fragile co-adaptation). LADES combines LAD and SAES to address this, using diagnostics like Geometric Anisotropy Index (GAI) and Volumetric Co-adaptation Score (VCS) to characterize the problem. The method was evaluated on real X-ray CT data from the Finnish Inverse Problems Society (FIPS) dataset. Projection-Volume Fidelity Divergence: Diagnosing and Controlling Optimization Drift in Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.22525, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Model Regularization
head: Residual Rotation Regularization, Rotation Regularization
body: Model Regularization applies penalties to the raw parameters of a neural scene representation (such as residual rotations or spherical harmonics coefficients) to prevent instability and overfitting during optimization. It distinguishes itself from output-based regularizations (like Distortion Loss) by constraining internal latent variables or decoder outputs directly, ensuring predicted geometric or appearance attributes remain within physically plausible or numerically stable bounds. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: The raw outputs from the neural network's decoder layers, including residual rotation vectors \mathbf{r}n, spherical harmonics coefficients c, and scale parameters sn. Outputs: A scalar regularization loss value L{reg} that is weighted by a hyperparameter \lambda and added to the total training objective. Data Structures: Residual Rotations (\mathbf{r}n): A vector of size 6 representing the 6D rotation residual predicted by the decoder. SH Coefficients (c): A vector of spherical harmonics coefficients for each Gaussian or voxel. Scales (sn): Log-space scale parameters predicted by the decoder. Steps: 1. Retrieve Decoder Outputs: Extract the raw parameters from the model's forward pass, typically via a dedicated regularization hook that returns a dictionary of raw parameters. 2. Compute Individual Loss Terms: Calculate specific regularization losses based on the parameter type using the formulas below. 3. Aggregate and Weight: Multiply each loss term by its corresponding weight (lambda) from the configuration dictionary and sum them into the total loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softplus(x): return np.logaddexp(0, x) def computemodelregularizationloss(rawparams, config): # rawparams: dict with keys 'rotations' (N, 6), 'shcoeffs' (N, C), 'scales' (N,) # config: dict with config.system.loss = {name: lambdaval} N = rawparams['rotations'].shape[0] losses = {} # 1. Rotation regularization: quadratic penalty on raw residual 6D rotations losses['rotation'] = np.mean(np.linalg.norm(rawparams['rotations'], axis=1)2) # 2. SH soft-cap regularization: soft penalty for coefficients exceeding cap c = rawparams['shcoeffs'] cmax = config.get('cmax') # Value not given in sources tauSH = config.get('tauSH') # Value not given in sources p = config.get('p', 2) shterm = softplus((np.abs(c) - cmax) / tauSH) tauSH losses['shsoftcap'] = np.mean(shtermp) # 3. Scale regularization: quadratic penalty for log-scales exceeding max s = rawparams['scales'] smax = config.get('smax') # Value not given in sources losses['scale'] = np.mean(np.maximum(np.log(s) - np.log(smax), 0)2) # 4. Aggregate and weight per loss name from config totalloss = 0.0 for name, lossval in losses.items(): lambdaval = config.system.loss.get(f"lambda{name}", 0.0) weighted = lossval lambdaval totalloss += weighted # Log the loss print(f"Logged {name}: {weighted}") return totalloss Formulas: Rotation Loss (L{rot}): Applies a quadratic penalty to raw residual 6D rotations \mathbf{r}n predicted by the decoder. L{rot} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^{N} \|\mathbf{r}n\|2^2 where N is the number of samples or Gaussians. SH Soft-Cap Loss (L{SH}): Softly penalizes spherical harmonics coefficients c whose magnitude exceeds a prescribed cap c{max}. L{SH} = \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \operatorname{softplus}\left( \frac{|c| - c{max}}{\tau{SH}} \right) \tau{SH} \right)^p \right] where \tau{SH} is the temperature parameter for the softplus function, and p is the power (typically 2). Scale Regularization (L{scale}): Penalizes scales sn that exceed a predefined maximum s{max} in log-space. L{scale} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^{N} \max(\log sn - \log s{max}, 0)^2 Parameters: c{max}: Prescribed cap for SH coefficient magnitude. Not given in the sources. \tau{SH}: Temperature parameter for the softplus function. Not given in the sources. s{max}: Maximum allowed scale. Not given in the sources. \lambda{name}: Weight for each regularization term. Configurable per loss name via a dictionary lookup. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Scales are predicted in log-space. Applies an L1 penalty to the opacity and color parameters of a transfer function to avoid unnecessary complexity when a simpler transfer function yields a similar result. It addresses convergence to complex transfer functions with multiple opacity peaks and redundant color mappings that are difficult for users to interpret. Choose this when transfer function interpretability is critical. Uses a small auxiliary neural network to reconstruct grid features from canonical coordinates and timestamps, preventing overfitting of the radiance field without affecting inference speed. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by regularizing the grid feature representation itself rather than the transfer function or output colors. Choose this for dynamic radiance fields where grid consistency is key. Applies L1 regularization to residual grids (Rt) during the optimization of dynamic radiance fields to enforce temporal continuity and minimize the magnitude of temporal changes. It is a core component of the JointRF training objective, distinguishing itself from static regularization by explicitly targeting the temporal residual structure to facilitate compression and stability. It builds on Model Regularization. Choose this for dynamic scene reconstruction. Evaluates the contribution of individual components within a neural scene reconstruction pipeline by systematically removing architectural branches, loss terms, or input signals and comparing performance against a baseline. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its diagnostic nature: rather than actively regularizing the model during training, it isolates marginal utility through parallel or sequential variant training. Choose this for architectural analysis. Applies specific loss terms to the outputs of a neural network (typically a scene manipulator or deformation field) to enforce physical plausibility or stability. It solves the problem of unrealistic deformations or artifacts by constraining translation residuals, rotation residuals, and ambient occlusion factors. It differs from general model regularization by targeting the semantic meaning of the output vectors rather than the network weights directly. Choose this for deformation fields or scene manipulators. Encourages predicted uncertainty \deltai to be as close to zero as possible to prevent blowing up. The formula is \mathcal{L}0 = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{i=1}^N \max(\delta{ci}, 0). It is used in uncertainty-aware NeRFs. Volume regularization loss is defined as L{vol} = \sum{i=1}^N \text{Prod}(si), weighted at 0.01. It is used in Scaffold-GS to control Gaussian volume. A training detail adopted from 3D-GS-MCMC that adds a compactness regularizer based on volume and opacity to the loss function. Adding the regularizer to the full model raises PSNR by 0.05 dB (to 27.80) and reduces the final Gaussian count by 2.5% (3.23M to 3.15M). It improves SSIM by 0.001 but worsens LPIPS by only 0.001 (0.203 to 0.204). A regularization term to avoid unstable appearance coefficients by softly penalizing spherical harmonics coefficients whose magnitude exceeds a prescribed cap. It uses a softplus function with temperature \tau{SH} and cap c{max}. Regularization applied to triplane features during optimization to simplify the data manifold for the diffusion model, ensuring feature planes do not contain spurious high-frequency information and discouraging outlier values. It includes total variation (TV) regularization terms to make the distribution of triplane features more similar to the manifold of natural images. The total loss is L = L{photo} + \lambda1 L{sparse} + \lambda2 L{TV}. L{photo} is MSE(\hat{I}, I), \lambda1 (sparse weight) is 1 \times 10^{-4}, and \lambda2 (TV weight) is 1 \times 10^{-5}. Without a density parameterisation correction (\Delta=0), neither regularization term receives a meaningful gradient signal because density is zero. Additional constraints applied during training to improve reconstruction quality and stability. These include shading the underlying geometry during training, randomly dropping out texture during training, smoothing the normals of the surface, and fitting the model in a coarse-to-fine fashion to capture overall structure first and fine-grained details later. Applies a constant penalty whenever the robot’s yaw angular speed is larger than \pi rad s^{-1} to encourage slow turning. It applies L2 regularization on joint angles towards a default standing pose. It applies a walking reward encouraging the average of feet velocities in the robot’s forward direction to be 0.3 m s^{-1}. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Prevents numerical instability (exploding scales/coefficients). Improves PSNR by 0.05 dB and reduces Gaussian count by 2.5%. Limitations: Requires tuning of caps (c{max}) and weights (\lambda). When to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated from techniques in 3D Gaussian Splatting and NeRF optimization. Rotation regularization and SH soft-cap regularization are detailed in GlobalSplat. Uncertainty regularization (L0) was introduced in Recursive-NeRF. Compactness regularization was adopted from 3D-GS-MCMC. Scaffold-GS uses volume regularization. The general framework of calling model.regularizations() is seen in instant-nsr-pl implementations. bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, https://github.com/bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GlobalSplat: Efficient Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Global Scene Tokens, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37595-710, fetched 2026-10-29 Recursive-NeRF: An Efficient and Dynamically Growing NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2022.3204608, fetched 2026-10-26 Octree-GS: Towards Consistent Real-time Rendering with LOD-Structured 3D Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3568201, fetched 2026-10-27 DART-3DGS: Distance-Aware Replication and Age-Gated Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13705904, fetched 2026-10-27 3D Neural Field Generation Using Triplane Diffusion, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.02000, fetched 2026-10-26 Sparse-View Lung Nodule Volumetry from Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs via AReT: Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.02639, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00816, fetched 2026-10-30 NeRF2Real: Sim2real Transfer of Vision-guided Bipedal Motion Skills using Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/icra48891.2023.10161544, fetched 2026-10-29

name: L1 Norm Regularization for Transfer Functions
head: L1 Regularization on Opacity and Color TFs, TF Regularization (L1 Norm)
body: L1 Norm Regularization for Transfer Functions applies an L1 penalty to the opacity and color parameters of a transfer function to avoid unnecessary complexity when a simpler transfer function yields a similar result. It addresses the problem where optimization algorithms converge to complex transfer functions with multiple opacity peaks and redundant color mappings that are difficult for users to interpret. Inputs and Outputs Input: The current opacity values \alpha and color values \mathbf{c} of the transfer function. Output: A scalar regularization loss value L{reg} added to the total optimization loss. Data Structures Opacity Vector (\alpha): A 1D array of size N, where N is the number of transfer function control points or grid entries. Color Vector (\mathbf{c}): A 1D array of size 3N (for RGB), corresponding to the color output for each opacity entry. Steps 1. Retrieve the opacity vector \alpha and color vector \mathbf{c} from the transfer function. 2. Compute the L1 norm for each vector by summing the absolute values of all entries. 3. Multiply each norm by its respective regularization weight and sum them to produce the scalar loss L{reg}. Formulas The regularization loss is the sum of the L1 norms of the opacity and color vectors: L{reg} = \lambda{\alpha} \sum{i=1}^{N} |\alphai| + \lambda{\mathbf{c}} \sum{j=1}^{3N} |cj| Where: \alphai is the opacity value at index i. cj is the color component value at index j. \lambda{\alpha} and \lambda{\mathbf{c}} are weighting hyperparameters. Parameters Regularization Weights (\lambda): Not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computel1tfregularizationloss(opacity: List[float], color: List[float], lambdaalpha: float, lambdacolor: float) -> float: """ Computes the L1 regularization loss for transfer function opacity and color. Args: opacity: List of opacity values for the TF. color: List of color values (RGB) for the TF. lambdaalpha: Weight for the opacity L1 term. lambdacolor: Weight for the color L1 term. Returns: Scalar regularization loss. """ # Sum of absolute values of opacity opacityl1 = sum(abs(val) for val in opacity) # Sum of absolute values of color colorl1 = sum(abs(val) for val in color) # Weighted sum loss = lambdaalpha opacityl1 + lambdacolor colorl1 return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-differentiability at zero: The absolute value function is not differentiable at 0. In practice, subgradients are used during backpropagation, or a small epsilon is added to avoid numerical instability. Boundary conditions: The regularization applies to all entries; care must be taken if certain TF regions are fixed or constrained by user interaction. L1 Sparsity Regularization applies an L1 norm penalty to the density field (or saliency grid) of a neural radiance field to enforce sparsity, reducing model complexity and eliminating unnecessary features. It differs from L1 Norm Regularization for Transfer Functions, which targets opacity and color transfer functions to avoid unnecessary complexity in the rendering pipeline, by directly constraining the volumetric density or feature saliency values. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of transfer function entries. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it only requires summing existing values. Strengths: Promotes simpler, more intuitive transfer functions by eliminating unnecessary opacity peaks and color mappings. Improves interpretability for users. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When the optimization process yields complex, oscillatory TFs that are hard to interpret, but the visual output is acceptable. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is used in text-based transfer function design for semantic volume rendering. The authors observed that optimization processes often converge to complex transfer functions even when simpler ones would yield similar results. To address this, they applied L1 norm regularization to both opacity and color transfer functions, demonstrating that this leads to simpler, more user-friendly transfer functions. name: L1 Sparsity Regularization
head: L1 Density Sparsity, L1 Norm Regularization for Density
body: L1 Sparsity Regularization applies an L1 norm penalty to the density field or saliency grid of a neural radiance field to enforce sparsity, reducing model complexity and eliminating unnecessary features. It builds on L1 Norm Regularization for Transfer Functions, which applies the penalty to opacity and color transfer functions, by instead constraining the volumetric density or feature saliency values directly. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a neural radiance field parameterized by \Theta (or \mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G}) as input. It outputs a regularized loss term R{l1} or an augmented loss function for optimization. Data Structures: The density field \sigma\Theta(x) is a continuous function mapping 3D coordinates to density. In discrete implementations, it is sampled on a grid. The saliency grid \mathcal{G} is a 3D tensor of size K \times K \times K (or mapped to a hashgrid) storing saliency values g for each voxel. The sigmoid operator S{sig}(\cdot) is applied element-wise to \mathcal{G} to bound saliency values, as the forward pipeline uses sigmoided saliency to weight feature vectors. Formulas: 1. Basic L1 Regularization (Density): R{l1}(\Theta) = \int{[-1,1]^3} |\sigma\Theta(x)| dx \approx \sum{i=1}^N \sum{j=1}^N \sum{k=1}^N |\sigma\Theta(\delta i, \delta j, \delta k)| \delta^3 where \delta is the grid spacing and N is the number of samples per dimension. 2. Basic L1 Regularization (Saliency Grid): \min{\mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G}} \left( L + \lambda \|S{sig}(\mathcal{G})\|1 \right) where L is the primary training loss (e.g., MSE), \lambda is a constant weight controlling sparsity, and \| \cdot \|1 denotes the L1 norm. 3. ADMM Pruner (Constrained Optimization): To overcome the sensitivity of \lambda, the problem is formulated as a constrained optimization: \min{\mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G}} L(\mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G}) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \|S{sig}(\mathcal{G})\|1 < C where C is the sparsity constraint. 4. Augmented Lagrangian (Unconstrained Minimax): The constrained problem is transformed into: \min{\mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G}} \max{\gamma \ge 0} L(\mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G}) + \frac{\rho\gamma}{2} \left[ \|S{sig}(\mathcal{G})\|1 - C \right]+^2 + \gamma \left( \|S{sig}(\mathcal{G})\|1 - C \right) where \gamma is the trainable dual variable (Lagrange multiplier), \rho\gamma is its learning rate, and [x]+ = \max(0, x). Parameters: \lambda: Constant weight for basic L1 regularization. Not given in the sources. C: Sparsity constraint threshold for ADMM. Not given in the sources. \gamma: Trainable dual variable. Updated via gradient ascent: \gamma^{(t+1)} = \gamma^{(t)} + \rho\gamma (\|S{sig}(\mathcal{G})\|1 - C). \rho\gamma: Learning rate for \gamma. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Basic Method: 1. Compute the L1 norm of the density field \sigma\Theta or sigmoided saliency grid S{sig}(\mathcal{G}). 2. Multiply by \lambda. 3. Add to the primary loss L. 4. Backpropagate to update \Theta (or \mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G}). 2. ADMM Pruner Method: 1. Initialize \gamma \ge 0. 2. Minimization Step: Update \mathcal{W}, \mathcal{H}, \mathcal{G} to minimize the augmented Lagrangian loss using gradient descent, treating \gamma as constant. 3. Dual Update Step: Update \gamma using gradient ascent: \gamma^{(t+1)} = \gamma^{(t)} + \rho\gamma (\|S{sig}(\mathcal{G})\|1 - C). 4. Repeat until convergence. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-pruning: If \lambda is too high or training runs too long, visible features may be pruned, degrading performance. Gradient Persistence: Even when the grid is sparse, the L1 term may provide gradients that further prune, requiring careful tuning of \lambda. Hash Collisions: In hashgrid-based methods (e.g., Instant-NGP), sparsity enforcement helps mitigate the impact of hash collisions by reducing the number of active features, but improper pruning can still affect accuracy. A pruning method using Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to enforce sparsity in the saliency grid \mathcal{G} by treating sparsity as a constrained optimization problem. It differs from basic L1 regularization by using a trainable dual variable \gamma instead of a fixed \lambda, adapting the sparsity constraint dynamically during training. Choose this when precise control over the sparsity level C is required and fixed \lambda tuning is difficult. Link: HollowNeRF. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead to the forward pass for L1 norm computation. The ADMM variant adds a dual variable update step via gradient ascent. Memory Complexity: Requires no additional memory for the basic method. The ADMM method requires storing the dual variable \gamma. Measured Performance: HollowNeRF uses 0.76M parameters for a 2^{14} hashgrid size compared to 0.50M for Instant-NGP, while maintaining or improving PSNR. Strengths: Reduces model size and complexity, mitigates hash collision effects in hashgrid-based NeRFs, and provides adaptive sparsity control via ADMM. Limitations: Basic L1 requires careful tuning of \lambda, and over-pruning can degrade quality. When to Use: When model size is a constraint or when using hashgrid-based NeRFs where sparsity mitigates collisions. When Not to Use: When high fidelity is required and sparsity might remove fine details. L1 regularization is a standard technique in optimization for promoting sparsity. In the context of neural radiance fields, it has been applied to density fields to encourage sparse representations. The ADMM pruner was introduced in HollowNeRF to address the limitations of simple L1 regularization in hashgrid-based NeRFs, specifically to handle hash collisions and enable adaptive sparsity control.
