name: Dual-Domain Deformation Model
body: The Dual-Domain Deformation Model (DDDM) represents temporal dynamics of 3D Gaussian particles by explicitly fitting attribute residuals to time-dependent curves, eliminating per-frame models or implicit neural fields. It sets itself apart from siblings like KNN Rigid Loss by focusing on parametric fitting of individual Gaussian attributes rather than spatial consistency constraints, and from Adaptive Spatio-Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting by introducing a specific dual-domain fitting strategy for attribute deformation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian particles. Each particle i has base attributes at a reference time t0: position \mu0, rotation q0, radiance c0, scaling s0, and opacity \alpha0. The input also includes the normalized frame index t \in [0, 1] for each observation. Output: Deformed attributes \mu(ts), q(ts), c(ts) for any time ts, while s(ts)=s0 and \alpha(ts)=\alpha0 remain constant. Data Structures: Each Gaussian particle stores: 1. Base Attributes: \mu0 \in \mathbb{R}^3, q0 \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion), c0 \in \mathbb{R}^3 (SH coefficients or RGB), s0 \in \mathbb{R}^3, \alpha0 \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Deformation Coefficients: Polynomial coefficients a = \{an\}{n=0}^N for each dimension of \mu, q, c. Fourier coefficients f = \{fl^{\sin}, fl^{\cos}\}{l=1}^L for each dimension of \mu, q, c. Scaling parameters \lambdas, \lambdab for adaptive timestamp scaling. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set reference time t0 (typically the first frame). Initialize base attributes \mu0, q0, c0, s0, \alpha0 from static 3DGS reconstruction. Initialize deformation coefficients a, f to zero or small random values. Initialize \lambdas = 1, \lambdab = 0. 2. Attribute Selection: Identify attributes to model over time: position \mu, rotation q, and radiance c. Scaling s and opacity \alpha are held constant. 3. Dimension-wise Assignment: Assign a separate deformation function D(t) for each dimension of the selected attributes. For position \mu, use \{D{\mui}(t)\}{i=0}^2. For rotation q, use \{D{qj}(t)\}{j=0}^3. For radiance c, use \{D{ck}(t)\}{k=0}^2 (or per SH coefficient). 4. Temporal Scaling: For each Gaussian, compute the scaled time input ts using the adaptive timestamp scaling technique: ts = \lambdas \cdot t + \lambdab where t is the normalized frame index. 5. Residual Calculation: Compute the time-dependent residual D(ts) for each dimension using the dual-domain model: D(ts) = PN(ts) + FL(ts) where PN(ts) is the polynomial component and FL(ts) is the Fourier series component. 6. Attribute Reconstruction: Compute the deformed attribute S(ts) for a dimension with base value S0: S(ts) = S0 + D(ts) For rotation, ensure the result is normalized to a unit quaternion after addition. Formulas: The residual D(ts) is defined as: D(ts) = \sum{n=0}^{N} an ts^n + \sum{l=1}^{L} \left( fl^{\sin} \cos(l ts) + fl^{\cos} \sin(l ts) \right) where: N is the polynomial order. L is the Fourier series order. an are polynomial coefficients. fl^{\sin}, fl^{\cos} are Fourier coefficients. ts is the scaled time input. Parameters: Polynomial Order N: Hyperparameter determining the complexity of the polynomial fit. Fourier Series Order L: Hyperparameter determining the complexity of the Fourier fit. In experiments, order 16 leads to best results on HyperNeRF; performance drops after order 32 due to over-parameterization. Reference Time t0: Usually set to the first frame. Scaling Factors: \lambdas initialized to 1, \lambdab initialized to 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Polynomial Overfitting: Polynomials alone can overfit violent motion if order is large, causing unreasonable oscillations in the fitted trajectory. Fourier Underfitting: Fourier series alone requires manual order reduction for smooth motion to avoid unnecessary complexity. Optimization Instability: Using standard normalized time t \in [0,1] for substantial motions in short time frames requires exceedingly large coefficients, inducing instability or breakdown in optimization. Adaptive timestamp scaling mitigates this. Rotation Normalization: Since q is a quaternion, adding a residual Dq(ts) may result in a non-unit quaternion. The result must be normalized. base value ts: scaled time polycoeffs: coefficients for this specific dimension fouriercoeffs: coefficients for this specific dimension isrotation: if True, normalize result to unit magnitude (for / norm if norm > 1e-8 else deformed return deformed def getgaussianattributes(gaussian, t, lambdas, lambdab, N, L): """ Returns deformed attributes for a Gaussian at time t. gaussian: object with attributes mu0, q0, c0, s0, alpha0 and deformation coefficients polymu, fouriermu, etc. t: normalized frame index [0, 1] """ ts = lambdas t + lambdab mu = np.zeros(3) for i in range(3): mu[i] = residuals between a Gaussian point and its K nearest neighbors. It addresses the instability caused by dynamic density control (adding/removing points) by restricting the application of spatial constraints to optimization stages where the point set is static. Adaptive Timestamp Scaling is a technique to scale the temporal input for each Gaussian point to prevent optimization instability caused by large coefficients when modeling substantial motions in short time frames. It uses a dilation factor \lambdas and a base factor \lambdab to transform the normalized time t into ts = \lambdas \cdot t + \lambdab. \lambdas is initialized to 1 and \lambdab to 0. Without this, standard normalized time t \in [0,1] for substantial motions requires exceedingly large coefficients, inducing instability or breakdown in optimization. Time Complexity: The deformation model adds a linear cost in the number of attributes and dimensions per Gaussian per frame. The joint polynomial and Fourier series fitting is computationally cheap compared to implicit neural fields, preserving the ultra-fast training and rendering speed of the original 3DGS. Memory Complexity: Each Gaussian stores additional coefficients for position, rotation, and radiance deformation. The memory overhead is proportional to (N + 2L) \times \text{dimensions} per attribute. Measured Performance: Achieves a 5× faster training speed compared to per-frame 3DGS modeling. Strengths: Capable of modeling complex scene deformations across long video footage; eliminates the need for training separate 3DGS for each frame or introducing an additional implicit neural field; preserves discretized nature of 3D Gaussian points. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of polynomial order N and Fourier order L to balance smooth and violent motions; over-parameterization (e.g., L > 32) can degrade performance. When to use: When ultra-fast training and rendering of 4D scenes are required, and the scene dynamics can be approximated by polynomial and Fourier series residuals. When not to use: When the scene dynamics are too complex to be captured by low-order polynomials and Fourier series, or when high-frequency, non-periodic motions dominate without sufficient data coverage. The Dual-Domain Deformation Model was proposed in the paper "Gaussian-Flow: 4D Reconstruction with Dynamic 3D Gaussian Particle". It builds on the advancements in point-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to address the slow training and rendering speeds of prevalent NeRF-based approaches for dynamic scenes. The method leverages the explicit deformation modeling of discretized Gaussian points to achieve efficiency comparable to static 3DGS. name: KNN Rigid Loss
head: Spatial Regularization
body: The KNN Rigid Loss is a regularization term used in dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting to enforce spatial local consistency by penalizing differences in attribute residuals between a Gaussian point and its K nearest neighbors. It addresses the instability caused by dynamic density control (adding/removing points) by restricting the application of spatial constraints to optimization stages where the point set is static. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussian particles. Each particle i has a position \mui, and a deformation function D^{(t)} that outputs attributes (e.g., position, rotation) at normalized time t \in [0, 1]. Output: A scalar loss value Ls representing the spatial rigidity error. Data Structures: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN): For each Gaussian i, a list of K indices j corresponding to the spatially nearest neighbors in the current frame. Scaled Time Input: ts = \lambdas \cdot t + \lambdab, where \lambdas is the dilation factor and \lambdab is the base factor. Parameters: \lambdas: Dilation factor for time scaling. Initialized to 1. \lambdab: Base factor for time scaling. Initialized to 0. K: Number of nearest neighbors. Not given in the sources. Algorithm: The optimization is divided into two alternating stages to handle dynamic point density: 1. Stage 1 (Density Control): Optimize all variables (including adding/removing points) without the KNN Rigid Loss. 2. Stage 2 (Attribute Optimization): Optimize attributes (position, rotation, etc.) without adding or removing points. The KNN Rigid Loss is applied in this stage. Formula: The loss is defined as the sum of squared differences between the deformation outputs of a Gaussian and its neighbors at time ts: Ls = \sum{i} \sum{j \in \text{KNN}(i)} \| D^{(ts)}i - D^{(ts)}j \|2^2 Where: i iterates over all Gaussian particles. \text{KNN}(i) is the set of K nearest neighbors to particle i. D^{(ts)}i is the attribute vector (e.g., position) of particle i predicted by its deformation function at scaled time ts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def knnrigidloss(gaussians, kneighbors, timet, lambdas, lambdab): """ Computes the KNN Rigid Loss for dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each having a deformation function D(t). kneighbors: Dictionary mapping Gaussian index i to a list of neighbor indices j. timet: Normalized frame index t in [0, 1]. lambdas: Dilation factor (default 1). lambdab: Base factor (default 0). Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # Calculate scaled time input ts = lambdas timet + lambdab loss = 0.0 # Iterate over each Gaussian and its neighbors for i, neighborindices in kneighbors.items(): # Get the deformation output for the current Gaussian at ts attri = gaussians[i].deformation(ts) for j in neighborindices: # Get the deformation output for the neighbor at ts attrj = gaussians[j].deformation(ts) # Compute squared L2 distance diff = attri - attrj loss += sum(d d for d in diff) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Density Control: Directly enforcing spatial consistency during density control (adding/removing points) is difficult because neighbors change constantly. The two-stage optimization sidesteps this by only applying the loss when the point set is static. Neighbor Stability: The KNN graph must be recomputed or maintained carefully between Stage 1 and Stage 2 to ensure consistent neighbor relationships. Locality Regularizers are a pair of constraints used in resource-linear Gaussian decoding to ensure that the spatial neighborhood of a Gaussian token remains consistent with its parent anchor's local context. They solve the problem of "neighbor drift," where optimized Gaussians move far enough from their initial positions that their true spatial neighbors no longer reside within the parent anchor's computed neighborhood N{anc}(nb), thereby breaking the validity of the hierarchical neighbor search. Unlike the parent KNN Rigid Loss, which enforces smoothness between a point and its K nearest neighbors, Locality Regularizers enforce topological consistency between a Gaussian and its anchor's local cluster structure. A regularizer penalizing squared differences between a splat's SH coefficient vector and its K nearest neighbors in canonical CAD space, acting as a graph Laplacian on appearance. At initialization, indices of K=20 nearest neighbors N(i) are precomputed for every splat i in the canonical CAD frame. During Stage II, the loss is computed as the average squared L2 norm of the difference between SH coefficients of splat i and its neighbors j: L{SH} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i} \sum{j \in N(i)} \|ci - cj\|2^2 where ci is the SH coefficient vector, N(i) is the neighbor set, and N is the total number of splats. The neighbor set is fixed in canonical space, making the loss invariant to small deformations \Delta \mu. A regularization term applied when K > 1 decoder heads output multiple Gaussians per superpixel to prevent them from collapsing into identical copies and to encourage spatial coverage of the original superpixel region. The weight scales each pair contribution: w{ij} = \sqrt{vi vj} where vi = \exp(\sumk s{k,i}) is the volume proxy of Gaussian i. The normalized gap is \gamma{ij} = \max(0, d{ij} - d{contact}) / d{contact} where d{ij} is the Euclidean distance between means and d{contact} is the sum of the two AABB half-extent norms. The profile function is: f(u{ij}, \gamma{ij}) = \begin{cases} \left(\frac{u{ij} - 0.5}{0.5}\right)^3 & u{ij} \ge 0.5 \\ \frac{0.5 - u{ij}}{0.5} - 3\gamma{ij} + 0.5(1 - e^{-3\gamma{ij}}) & u{ij} < 0.5 \end{cases} where u{ij} is the AABB IoU. The repulsion branch penalizes excessive overlap, and the attraction branch prevents Gaussians from drifting apart when non-overlapping. The geometric term averages these weighted profile values over all pairs P: L{geom} = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{(i,j) \in P} w{ij} f(u{ij}, \gamma{ij}). To prevent single-Gaussian dominance, pairwise opacity differences are penalized: L{opa} = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{(i,j) \in P} w{ij} |\alphai - \alphaj|^2. The combined loss blends both terms: L{div} = 0.75 L{geom} + 0.25 L{opa}. Without this regularizer, multiple Gaussians from the same superpixel may collapse into identical copies. Time Complexity: The loss computation is O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of Gaussians and K is the number of neighbors. Strengths: Enforces local rigidity, preventing unrealistic deformations in dynamic scenes. Limitations: Computationally expensive if K is large or if KNN queries are not optimized. Sensitive to the choice of K and the stability of the neighbor graph during dynamic density control. When to use: In dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting scenarios where spatial consistency is crucial and the optimization can be split into static attribute optimization stages. The KNN Rigid Loss was introduced in "Gaussian-Flow: 4D Reconstruction with Dynamic 3D Gaussian Particle". It addresses the challenge of maintaining spatial coherence in dynamic scenes where Gaussian particles are added or removed during optimization. The method builds on the Dual-Domain Deformation Model [12804-dual-domain-deformation-model.md], which models Gaussian dynamics using time-domain polynomials and frequency-domain Fourier series [12804-dual-domain-deformation-model.md]. name: Locality Regularizers
head: Anchor-based Locality Regularization, Voronoi and Offset Loss
body: Locality Regularizers are a pair of constraints used in resource-linear Gaussian decoding to ensure that the spatial neighborhood of a Gaussian token remains consistent with its parent anchor's local context. They solve the problem of "neighbor drift," where optimized Gaussians move far enough from their initial positions that their true spatial neighbors no longer reside within the parent anchor's computed neighborhood N{anc}(nb), thereby breaking the validity of the hierarchical neighbor search. Unlike the parent KNN Rigid Loss, which enforces smoothness between a point and its K nearest neighbors, Locality Regularizers enforce topological consistency between a Gaussian and its anchor's local cluster structure. The method operates on a set of B Gaussian tokens spawned from anchors. For each anchor n, the centroid of its initial Gaussians is computed as \bar{\mu}n = \frac{1}{kn} \sum{b: nb=n} \mub^0, where kn is the number of Gaussians spawned by anchor n and nb is the parent anchor of token b. The regularizers are applied during the refinement stage to constrain the initial centers \mub^0 and the residual corrections \Delta \mub. Inputs: B: Total number of Gaussian tokens. \mub^0: Initial center of token b. \Delta \mub: Residual correction predicted by the residual head for token b. N{anc}(nb): Set of neighboring anchor indices to the parent anchor nb. \bar{\mu}m: Centroid of anchor m. d{nb}: Local anchor spacing for anchor nb. \delta: Margin parameter. Outputs: Scalar loss values L{vor} and L{offset}. Data Structures: The neighbor set N{anc}(nb) is determined by a hierarchical neighbor search (e.g., using a spatial index like a KD-tree or grid) over the anchor centroids \bar{\mu}n. d{nb} is defined as the median distance from \bar{\mu}{nb} to its K{anc} nearest anchors. Steps: 1. Compute the centroid \bar{\mu}n for each anchor n that spawned at least one Gaussian. 2. For each anchor nb, identify its K{anc} nearest neighbors to compute the local spacing d{nb} as the median distance to these neighbors. 3. Identify the set of neighboring anchors N{anc}(nb) for each parent anchor nb. 4. Compute the Voronoi loss L{vor} to ensure each Gaussian stays closer to its parent anchor's centroid than to any neighboring anchor's centroid. 5. Compute the Offset loss L{offset} to limit the magnitude of the residual correction relative to the local anchor scale. Formulas: The Voronoi loss is defined as: L{vor} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{b=1}^B \sum{m \in N{anc}(nb)} \max\left(0, \|\mub^0 - \bar{\mu}{nb}\| - \|\mub^0 - \bar{\mu}m\|\right) where \mub^0 is the initial center of Gaussian b, \bar{\mu}{nb} is the centroid of its parent anchor, and \bar{\mu}m is the centroid of a neighboring anchor m. The Offset loss is defined as: L{offset} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{b=1}^B \max\left(0, \frac{\|\Delta \mub\|}{d{nb}} - \delta\right)^2 where \Delta \mub is the residual correction for Gaussian b, d{nb} is the local anchor spacing of the parent anchor, and \delta is a margin parameter. Parameters: \delta: Margin limiting Gaussian movement relative to local anchor scale. Typical value is 0.5. K{anc}: Number of nearest anchors used to compute local spacing. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def norm(v): """Euclidean norm of a vector.""" return math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in v)) def computelocalityregularizers( initialcenters: list, # mub^0 for b in 0..B-1 residualcorrections: list, # Delta mub for b in 0..B-1 parentanchors: list, # nb for b in 0..B-1 anchorcentroids: dict, # mubarn for each anchor n neighborsets: dict, # Nanc(nb) for each anchor nb localspacings: dict, # dnb for each anchor nb delta: float = 0.5) -> tuple: """ Computes Voronoi and Offset losses for locality regularization. Args: initialcenters: List of initial Gaussian centers mub^0. residualcorrections: List of residual corrections Delta mub. parentanchors: List mapping each Gaussian b to its parent anchor nb. anchorcentroids: Dictionary mapping anchor index n to its centroid mubarn. neighborsets: Dictionary mapping each anchor nb to a list of neighboring anchor indices m. localspacings: Dictionary mapping each anchor nb to its local spacing dnb. delta: Margin parameter for offset loss. Returns: Tuple of (Lvor, Loffset). """ B = len(initialcenters) sumvor = 0.0 sumoffset = 0.0 for b in range(B): mub0 = initialcenters[b] deltamub = residualcorrections[b] nb = parentanchors[b] # Get parent anchor centroid mubarnb = anchorcentroids[nb] # Voronoi Loss # Sum over all neighboring anchors m in Nanc(nb) neighbors = neighborsets[nb] for m in neighbors: mubarm = anchorcentroids[m] disttoparent = norm(mub0 - mubarnb) disttoneighbor = norm(mub0 - mubarm) # max(0, disttoparent - disttoneighbor) term = disttoparent - disttoneighbor if term > 0: sumvor += term # Offset Loss # Limit drift relative to local anchor spacing dnb = localspacings[nb] # Avoid division by zero if spacing is zero (edge case) if dnb > 1e-8: normdeltamu = norm(deltamub) ratio = normdeltamu / dnb marginterm = ratio - delta if marginterm > 0: sumoffset += marginterm 2 Lvor = sumvor / B Loffset = sumoffset / B return Lvor, Loffset Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If d{nb} is zero or very small, the Offset loss division may become unstable. A small epsilon should be added to the denominator. The neighbor set N{anc}(nb) must be computed consistently with the search used during inference to ensure the regularizer matches the operational context. If an anchor has no neighbors (isolated), the Voronoi loss sum is empty, contributing 0 to the loss. A regularizer that penalizes excessive center displacement in local orthogonal directions while preserving necessary positional adjustments within an allowed subspace, interpreted as MAP estimation with a generalized Gaussian prior. It uses an adaptive strength based on structural confidence: when the neighborhood direction is well-defined, orthogonal displacement is constrained more strongly; when local structure is uncertain, the constraint is weakened to prevent erroneous PCA directions from imposing incorrect restrictions. The loss is defined as \mathcal{L}{anchor} = \sum{i=1}^{K} \hat{C}i \| (I - Pi)(xi - x{0,i}) \|^2, where Pi is the allowed-direction projection matrix and \hat{C}i is the structural confidence. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures that the hierarchical neighbor search remains valid during optimization, preventing topological inconsistencies that could degrade rendering quality. Limitations: Depends on the accuracy of the initial anchor placement and neighbor search; if the initial topology is incorrect, the regularizer may enforce incorrect constraints. When to use: When using resource-linear Gaussian decoding with hierarchical neighbor search to maintain spatial locality. Locality Regularizers were introduced in RLSplat (Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting) to support resource-linear Gaussian decoding with hierarchical neighbor search. The method was developed to address the scalability issues of global attention in 3D Gaussian Splatting by restricting interactions to local neighborhoods, which requires strict control over Gaussian positions relative to their anchors. name: Multi-View Constraint
head: Patch Matching Regularization
body: Multi-View Constraint is a regularization technique that enforces color consistency between reference and neighborhood views using patch matching and homography warping to improve geometry reconstruction in textureless regions where standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) struggles. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Reference and neighborhood view images, camera poses (relative rotation R and translation t), intrinsic matrix K, and the current state of 3D Gaussians (positions, orientations, opacities, colors). Outputs: A scalar loss value L{mv} added to the total training objective. Data Structures Rendered Maps: Depth map D and normal map N for each view, generated by alpha-blending 3D Gaussians. Homography Matrix H: A 3 \times 3 matrix mapping pixels from reference to neighborhood view. Patch Pi: A set of neighboring pixels around a target pixel p. Formulas 1. Homography Warping: p' = H p Where H is defined as: H = K \left( R - \frac{t n^\top}{d} \right) K^{-1} Here, R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and t \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 3} are the relative rotation and translation between the reference and source views, K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is the camera intrinsic matrix, n \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 3} is the rendered normal at pixel p, and d is the distance from the camera origin to the spatial plane defined by n. 2. Multi-View Loss: L{mv} = \sum{p \in Pi} (1 - \text{NCC}(p, p')) Where \text{NCC}(p, p') is the Normalized Cross Correlation between the patch at p in the reference view and the patch at p' in the neighborhood view. 3. Total Loss Integration: L = (1 - \lambda)L1 + \lambda L{\text{SSIM}} + L{mv} Where L1 and L{\text{SSIM}} are standard image reconstruction losses from 3DGS. Numbered Steps 1. Identify Neighborhood Frames: For each reference image, identify its neighborhood frames from the subgraphs. 2. Render Depth and Normal Maps: For each image, render depth and normal maps by overlapping the positions and orientations of 3D Gaussians using alpha blending. 3. Establish Spatial Plane: For a pixel p in the reference view, establish a spatial plane defined by the rendered normal n and distance d from the camera origin. 4. Compute Homography: Calculate the homography matrix H using the relative pose (R, t), intrinsics K, and the local plane parameters (d, n). 5. Warp Pixel: Project pixel p to its corresponding pixel p' in the neighborhood view using p' = H p. 6. Construct Patch: Select neighboring pixels around p to form patch Pi. 7. Evaluate Consistency: Compute the Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC) between the patch at p and the warped patch at p'. 8. Accumulate Loss: Sum (1 - \text{NCC}) over all pixels in the patch to form L{mv}. Pseudocode Unverified code. """ # Render depth and normal maps via alpha blending depthmapref, normalmapref = rendergaussiansalphablend(gaussians, referenceimage) lossmv = 0.0 patchradius = 1 # Not given in the sources height, width = referenceimage.height, referenceimage.width # Iterate over pixels in the reference view for y in range(height): for x in range(width): p = (x, y) # Get normal and depth at pixel p n = normalmapref[y][x] # list of 3 floats d = depthmapref[y][x] # float # Compute Homography Matrix H: H = K (R - ncc) return lossmv def outerproduct(a, b): return [[a[i] b[j] for j in range(len(b))] for i in range(len(a))] def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k] B[k][j] for k in range(len(B))) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def matsub(A, B): return [[A[i][j] - name: Multi-view Regularization
head: Cycle Reprojection Regularizer, Geometric Multi-View Term, PGSR Multi-view Regularization
body: Multi-view Regularization is a technique that penalizes cycle reprojection error to enforce multi-view geometric consistency during the optimization of radiance fields. It sets itself apart from its sibling Multi-View Constraint by explicitly computing a forward-backward reprojection cycle error to handle occlusions and unreliable correspondences, rather than relying solely on patch matching and homography warping for color consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference image Ir, neighboring image In, camera intrinsics \mathbf{K}r, \mathbf{K}n, relative pose (\mathbf{R}{rn}, \mathbf{T}{rn}) from reference to neighbor, rendered depth map Dr, and rendered normal map \mathbf{N}r for the reference view. Outputs: Regularization loss L{mv} and its gradients with respect to the scene parameters (depth, normals, or Gaussian attributes). Data Structures: Images: Ir, In \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} (RGB). Depth: Dr \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} (depth along the ray). Normals: \mathbf{N}r \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} (surface normal in camera space). Homography: \mathbf{H}{rn} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} matrix. Parameters: w{pc}: Weight for photometric consistency. Typical value: 0.6. w{gc}: Weight for geometric consistency. Typical value: 0.02. Threshold for confidence weight: 1.0 pixel. Steps: 1. Back-project to 3D: For each pixel \mathbf{u}r = (u, v) in the reference image, retrieve the rendered depth dr = Dr(\mathbf{u}r) and normal \mathbf{n}r = \mathbf{N}r(\mathbf{u}r). Compute the 3D point \mathbf{p}r in the reference camera frame: \mathbf{p}r = dr \cdot \mathbf{K}r^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} 2. Compute Plane Homography: Approximate the local surface as a plane defined by \mathbf{p}r and \mathbf{n}r. Compute the homography \mathbf{H}{rn} that maps points from the reference view to the neighboring view: \mathbf{H}{rn} = \mathbf{K}n \left( \mathbf{R}{rn} + \frac{\mathbf{T}{rn} \mathbf{n}r^\top}{\mathbf{p}r^\top \mathbf{n}r} \right) \mathbf{K}r^{-1} where \mathbf{R}{rn}, \mathbf{T}{rn} are the rotation and translation from reference to neighbor. 3. Compute Forward-Backward Cycle Error: To handle occlusions, compute the homography \mathbf{H}{rr} mapping from the neighboring view back to the reference view (using inverse relative pose and potentially neighbor depth/normal if available, or assuming the same local plane approximation). Calculate the cycle reprojection error \phi(\mathbf{u}r): \phi(\mathbf{u}r) = \|\mathbf{u}r - \mathbf{H}{rr} \mathbf{H}{rn} \mathbf{u}r\|2 4. Compute Confidence Weight: Discard pixels with large cycle errors (likely occluded or mismatched): w(\mathbf{u}r) = \begin{cases} \exp(-\phi(\mathbf{u}r)) & \text{if } \phi(\mathbf{u}r) < 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 5. Compute Photometric Consistency Loss (L{pc}): Warp the neighboring image In to the reference frame using \mathbf{H}{rn} and enforce patch-level photometric consistency via Normalized Cross-Correlation (NCC): L{pc} = \sum{\mathbf{u}r} w(\mathbf{u}r) \left( 1 - \text{NCC}(Ir(\mathbf{u}r), In(\mathbf{H}{rn}\mathbf{u}r)) \right) 6. Compute Geometric Consistency Loss (L{gc}): Penalize the cycle reprojection error directly: L{gc} = \sum{\mathbf{u}r} w(\mathbf{u}r) \phi(\mathbf{u}r) 7. Combine Losses: The total multi-view regularization loss is: L{mv} = w{pc} L{pc} + w{gc} L{gc} 8. Gradient Accumulation: Accumulate gradients using a custom CUDA kernel for efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiviewregularization(Ir, In, Kr, Kn, Rrn, Trn, Dr, Nr, wpc=0.6, wgc=0.02): """ Computes the multi-view regularization loss. Args: Ir: Reference image (H, W, 3) In: Neighboring image (H, W, 3) Kr: Reference camera intrinsics (3, 3) Kn: Neighbor camera intrinsics (3, 3) Rrn: Rotation matrix from ref to neighbor (3, 3) Trn: Translation vector from ref to neighbor (3,) Dr: Rendered depth map (H, W) Nr: Rendered normal map (H, W, 3) wpc: Weight for photometric consistency wgc: Weight for geometric consistency Returns: Lmv: Scalar loss value """ H, W = Ir.shape[:2] # 1. Back-project to 3D # Create grid of pixel coordinates u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='xy') ones = torch.ones(H, W) pixelcoords = torch.stack([u, v, ones], dim=-1).float() # (H, W, 3) # Unproject to 3D in reference camera frame # pr = dr Kr^-1 [u, v, 1]^T Krinv = torch.linalg.inv(Kr) pixelcoordshom = pixelcoords.unsqueeze(-1) # (H, W, 3, 1) prhom = torch.matmul(Krinv, pixelcoordshom).squeeze(-1) # (H, W, 3) pr = Dr.unsqueeze(-1) prhom # (H, W, 3) nr = Nr # (H, W, 3) # 2. Compute Plane Homography Hrn # Hrn = Kn (Rrn + Trn nr^T / (pr^T nr)) Kr^-1 # Denominator: pr dot nr denom = torch.sum(pr nr, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # (H, W, 1) # Avoid division by zero denom = torch.clamp(denom, min=1e-8) # Outer product Trn nr^T Trncol = Trn.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, 3) nrrow = nr.unsqueeze(-1) # (H, W, 3, 1) Tnouter = Trncol nrrow # (H, W, 3, 3) # Term inside parenthesis innerterm = Rrn + Tnouter / denom.unsqueeze(-1) # (H, W, 3, 3) # Hrn = Kn @ innerterm @ Krinv Hrn = torch.matmul(Kn, torch.matmul(innerterm, Krinv)) # (H, W, 3, 3) # 3. Compute Forward-Backward Cycle Error # We need Hrr (neighbor to ref). Assuming symmetric plane approximation or using inverse. # For simplicity, if Hrr is not explicitly computed from neighbor depth, # we might approximate it or assume the same local plane holds. # However, the formula uses Hrr Hrn. # Let's assume we compute Hnr (neighbor to ref) similarly using neighbor depth/normal if available. # If not, we might use the inverse of Hrn as an approximation, but this is less accurate. # The source mentions Hrr maps from neighbor back to ref. # Let's assume we have Dn, Nn for the neighbor to compute Hnr accurately. # If not, this step is incomplete. Assuming Dn, Nn are available for robustness. # Re-compute pn and nn for neighbor # pn = dn Kn^-1 [u, v, 1]^T Kninv = torch.linalg.inv(Kn) pnhom = torch.matmul(Kninv, pixelcoordshom).squeeze(-1) pn = Dn.unsqueeze(-1) pnhom # (H, W, 3) nn = Nn # (H, W, 3) # Hnr = Kr (Rnr + Tnr nn^T / (pn^T nn)) Kn^-1 # Rnr = Rrn^T, Tnr = -Rrn^T Trn Rnr = Rrn.transpose(-2, -1) Tnr = -torch.matmul(Rnr, Trn) denomn = torch.sum(pn nn, dim=-1, keepdim=True) denomn = torch.clamp(denomn, min=1e-8) Tnrcol = Tnr.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) nnrow = nn.unsqueeze(-1) Tnnouter = Tnrcol nnrow innertermnr = Rnr + Tnnouter / denomn.unsqueeze(-1) Hnr = torch.matmul(Kr, torch.matmul(innertermnr, Kninv)) # Cycle error: ur - Hnr Hrn ur # Warp ur using Hrn to get un # Then warp un using Hnr to get ur' # ur' = Hnr Hrn ur # Vectorized homography warp def warpgrid(H, grid): # grid: (H, W, 2) # H: (H, W, 3, 3) # Returns warped grid (H, W, 2) # Convert grid to homogeneous (H, W, 3) gridh = torch.cat([grid, torch.ones(H, W, 1)], dim=-1) # (H, W, 3) # Apply H # gridh is (H, W, 3), H is (H, W, 3, 3) # result = H @ gridh^T -> (H, W, 3, 3) @ (H, W, 3, 1) -> (H, W, 3, 1) warpedh = torch.matmul(H, gridh.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) # (H, W, 3) # Normalize warped = warpedh[...,:2] / torch.clamp(warpedh[..., 2:], min=1e-8) # (H, W, 2) return warped gridref = torch.stack([u.float(), v.float()], dim=-1) # (H, W, 2) gridneighbor = warpgrid(Hrn, gridref) # (H, W, 2) gridcycle = warpgrid(Hnr, gridneighbor) # (H, W, 2) phi = torch.norm(gridref - gridcycle, dim=-1) # (H, W) # 4. Confidence Weight mask = phi < 1.0 w = torch.where(mask, torch.exp(-phi), torch.zeroslike(phi)) # 5. Photometric Loss # Warp In to reference frame using Hrn # Inwarped = sample(In, gridneighbor) # NCC calculation # For simplicity, assume NCC is computed over small patches or per-pixel if normalized. # The source says "patch-level photometric consistency via NCC". # Implementing full patch NCC is complex. We'll approximate with per-pixel if patch size not specified. # Or assume a small kernel. Let's assume per-pixel for the formula structure, # noting that in practice a patch is used. # Normalize images to [0, 1] Irnorm = Ir / 255.0 Inwarped = gridsample(In, gridneighbor, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') Inwarped = Inwarped / 255.0 # Per-pixel NCC (simplified) # NCC(a, b) = (a - mean(a))(b - mean(b)) / (std(a) std(b)) # If patch size is 1, NCC is sign(ab) if non-zero, which is unstable. # The source likely uses a small patch (e.g., 3x3 or 5x5). # Since patch size is not given, we note this as a gap. # We will assume a function computenccpatch exists. ncc = computenccpatch(Irnorm, Inwarped, patchsize=3) # (H, W) Lpc = torch.sum(w (1 - ncc)) # 6. Geometric Loss Lgc = torch.sum(w phi) # 7. Combine Lmv = wpc Lpc + wgc Lgc return Lmv def computenccpatch(Ir, In, patchsize=3): """ Computes NCC between Ir and In over local patches. """ # Pad images pad = patchsize // 2 Irpad = F.pad(Ir, (pad, pad, pad, pad, 0, 0), mode='reflect') Inpad = F.pad(In, (pad, pad, pad, pad, 0, 0), mode='reflect') # Extract patches # Irpatches: (H, W, C, patchsize, patchsize) Irpatches = F.unfold(Irpad, kernelsize=patchsize, stride=1) # (HW, CPP) Inpatches = F.unfold(Inpad, kernelsize=patchsize, stride=1) # Reshape to (H, W, CPP) H, W = Ir.shape[:2] Irpatches = Irpatches.view(H, W, -1) Inpatches = Inpatches.view(H, W, -1) # Flatten patches to vectors Irflat = Irpatches.view(H, W, -1) Inflat = Inpatches.view(H, W, -1) # Compute mean and std meanr = torch.mean(Irflat, dim=-1, keepdim=True) meann = torch.mean(Inflat, dim=-1, keepdim=True) stdr = torch.std(Irflat, dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False) stdn = torch.std(Inflat, dim=-1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False) # Avoid division by zero stdr = torch.clamp(stdr, min=1e-8) stdn = torch.clamp(stdn, min=1e-8) # NCC ncc = torch.mean(((Irflat - meanr) (Inflat - meann)) / (stdr stdn), dim=-1) return ncc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: The cycle reprojection error \phi(\mathbf{u}r) becomes large for occluded pixels. The confidence weight w(\mathbf{u}r) discards these pixels (\phi \ge 1), preventing incorrect gradients. Depth/Normal Accuracy: The homography \mathbf{H}{rn} relies on accurate rendered depth and normals. Errors in these estimates lead to incorrect warping and false cycle errors. Precision: Floating-point precision in homography multiplication and warping can introduce small errors. The threshold of 1 pixel is used to mitigate this. Textureless Regions: While the method helps in textureless regions by enforcing geometric consistency, it may struggle if depth/normal estimates are ambiguous. Enforces color similarity between warped views. Sets itself apart by using NCC for robustness to lighting changes. Choose when lighting is consistent. Enforces geometric consistency via cycle reprojection error. Sets itself apart by directly penalizing geometric inconsistency. Choose when geometry is the primary concern. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of pixels and the cost of homography warping and NCC computation. The custom CUDA kernel improves efficiency. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate warping grids and patches. Measured Performance: On DTU dataset, multi-view regularizers substantially boost accuracy. The method is faster than GeoSVR (15 vs. 53 min) and PGSR (25 vs. 30 min) due to efficient implementation. Strengths: Improves reconstruction accuracy, particularly on datasets like DTU. Handles occlusions via cycle error. Limitations: Marginal gains when combined with depth-rendering formulations that already enforce strong multi-view consistency (e.g., RaDe-GS). Relies on accurate depth and normal estimates. When to Use: When multi-view consistency is critical and depth/normal estimates are reliable. Particularly useful for datasets like DTU. When Not to Use: When the underlying depth-rendering formulation already provides strong multi-view consistency, as the additional term may offer only marginal gains. Multi-view Regularization, specifically the cycle reprojection variant, was introduced in the context of Gaussian Splatting optimization. It was notably used in PGSR (Photometric and Geometric Regularization for Gaussian Splatting). The method builds on the idea of enforcing consistency across multiple views to improve geometry, particularly in textureless regions. It has been applied to datasets like DTU and Tanks & Temples. name: Rendering-Guided Regularization for SLAM
head: Gaussian parameter regularization, L_reg regularization
body: This method introduces a regularization term to the mapping loss in 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM to prevent the model from "forgetting" previously observed geometry when optimizing for the current frame. Unlike original 3D Gaussian Splatting which requires queuing all frames for random selection, this approach allows the use of a small keyframe buffer, making it suitable for online continual mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame image, camera pose, existing 3D Gaussian parameters, and a small keyframe buffer. Outputs: Updated 3D Gaussian parameters and camera pose. Data Structures: Each Gaussian i maintains additional state variables \Deltai to track sensitivity and history: N^{seen}i: An integer counter recording the number of times this Gaussian has been involved in optimization. \Sigma{si}: Accumulated sum of gradients of the mapping loss with respect to the scale parameter si. \Sigma{ci}: Accumulated sum of gradients of the mapping loss with respect to the color parameter ci. \Sigma{di}: Accumulated sum of gradients of the mapping loss with respect to the depth parameter di. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussian parameters and \Deltai. 2. Optimization Loop: For each new frame to be optimized: a. Calculate Regularization Loss (L{reg}): Compute the regularization term based on the difference between current parameters and parameters from the previous step (t-1), weighted by importance weights \Omega. b. Update Importance Weights: After training on the current frame, update the importance weights \Omega by averaging the gradients of the mapping loss with respect to the parameters over the number of times the Gaussian has been seen. c. Minimize Total Loss: Minimize the combined loss L'{mapping} = L{mapping} + L{reg} using gradient descent to update Gaussian parameters and camera pose. 3. Iteration: Repeat for subsequent frames. Formulas: The regularization loss L{reg} is defined as: L{reg} = \sum{i \in G} \Omega{si} |s{i,t} - s^{i}| + \Omega{ci} |r{i,t} - r^{i}| + \Omega{di} |z{i,t} - z^{i}| Where: G is the set of Gaussians involved in the optimization for the current frame. s{i,t}, r{i,t}, z{i,t} are the scale, color, and depth parameters to be optimized at step t. s^{i}, r^{i}, z^{i} are the current parameter values (values achieved after step t-1). \Omega{si}, \Omega{ci}, \Omega{di} are the importance weights for scale, color, and depth, respectively. The final loss function used in the mapping is: L'{mapping} = L{mapping} + L{reg} The importance weight \Omega{si} for the scale parameter is calculated as: \Omega{si} = \frac{1}{N^{seen}i} \sum{j=1}^{N^{seen}i} \left| \frac{\partial L{mapping}}{\partial si} \right|j Similar formulas apply for \Omega{ci} and \Omega{di} using their respective gradient sums. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializegaussians(gaussians): for g in gaussians: g.Nseen = 0 g.Sigmas = 0.0 g.Sigmac = 0.0 g.Sigmad = 0.0 g.prevs = g.s g.prevc = g.c g.prevd = g.d def computeimportanceweights(gaussians): for g in gaussians: if g.Nseen > 0: g.Omegas = g.Sigmas / g.Nseen g.Omegac = g.Sigmac / g.Nseen g.Omegad = g.Sigmad / g.Nseen else: g.Omegas = 0.0 g.Omegac = 0.0 g.Omegad = 0.0 def computeregularizationloss(gaussians): Lreg = 0.0 for g in gaussians: Lreg += g.Omegas abs(g.s - g.prevs) Lreg += g.Omegac abs(g.c - g.prevc) Lreg += g.Omegad abs(g.d - g.prevd) return Lreg def optimizeframe(gaussians, currentframe, keyframebuffer, learningrate): # 1. Render current frame and compute mapping loss Lmapping renderedimage = renderscene(gaussians, currentframe.pose, keyframebuffer) Lmapping = computerenderingerror(renderedimage, currentframe.image) # 2. Compute regularization loss Lreg Lreg = computeregularizationloss(gaussians) # 3. Total loss Ltotal = Lmapping + Lreg # 4. Backward pass to get gradients for Ltotal gradstotal = computegradients(Ltotal, gaussians) # 5. Update Gaussians using gradient descent for g in gaussians: g.s -= learningrate gradstotal.s g.c -= learningrate gradstotal.c g.d -= learningrate gradstotal.d # 6. Accumulate absolute gradients of Lmapping for importance weights # Gradients of Lmapping are extracted from the backward pass of Lmapping gradsmapping = computegradients(Lmapping, gaussians) if g in gaussians: # G is the set of Gaussians involved in current frame g.Sigmas += abs(gradsmapping.s) g.Sigmac += abs(gradsmapping.c) g.Sigmad += abs(gradsmapping.d) g.Nseen += 1 # 7. Store current parameters as previous for next step g.prevs = g.s g.prevc = g.c g.prevd = g.d # 8. Update importance weights for next iteration computeimportanceweights(gaussians) return gaussians Parameters: Keyframe Buffer Size: Small, significantly smaller than the total number of frames. Exact size is not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources, but gradient descent is implied. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floaters: Without regularization, artifacts such as floaters appear at the edges of the generated image when processing many frames, as the map forgets previous observations. Time Complexity: Reduces processing time compared to optimizing with multiple previous frames, as only a small keyframe buffer is maintained. However, it adds overhead for computing and updating importance weights. Memory Complexity: Increases memory usage per Gaussian by storing \Deltai (4 additional fields). Measured Performance: On the Room0 Replica dataset with a V100 GPU, the method achieves better reconstruction and tracking accuracy compared to no regularization. Runtime results are reported in Table V of the source, but specific numbers are not provided in the notes. Strengths: Prevents forgetting, allows small keyframe buffer, suitable for online continual mapping, reduces floaters. Limitations: Requires additional state per Gaussian, adds computational overhead for weight updates. When to use: Online SLAM with 3D Gaussian Splatting where memory and processing time are constrained, and forgetting is a concern. This method was introduced in the paper "High-Fidelity SLAM Using Gaussian Splatting with Rendering-Guided Densification and Regularized Optimization". It addresses the limitation of original 3D Gaussian Splatting, which queues all frames for random selection, leading to long processing times unsuitable for online applications. The method builds on Adaptive Spatio-Temporal 3D Gaussian Splatting by adding a regularization term to the mapping loss. name: Ambiguous Gaussians Removal
head: SA3D-GS ambiguous Gaussians removal
body: Ambiguous Gaussians Removal is a post-processing strategy within SA3D-GS designed to eliminate 3D Gaussians located at the borders of two objects that share similar colors, such as reflective metal surfaces. It addresses the artifact generation inherent in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS), where the RGB-fitting optimization goal causes the model to merge adjacent objects with similar colors into a single or few Gaussians. Unlike sibling methods that rely on complex segmentation decoders, this method acts as a lightweight supplementary phase that bypasses SAM decoders, cross-view self-prompting, and IoU computations to achieve negligible additional time cost. Inputs and Outputs Input: The set of optimized 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} from the SA3D-GS pipeline, including their positions, covariances, opacities, and spherical harmonic coefficients. Output: A pruned set of 3D Gaussians with ambiguous boundary Gaussians removed. Data Structures The method operates on the standard 3D Gaussian representation without introducing new complex data structures, modifying the existing Gaussian list by filtering entries based on spatial and color properties relative to neighbors. Steps 1. Identify Ambiguous Regions: Scan the Gaussian cloud to locate boundaries between objects sharing similar RGB colors, as 3D-GS tends to model these borders with one or few Gaussians to fit multi-view RGB color consistency. 2. Evaluate Contribution: For Gaussians at these ambiguous borders, assess their contribution to rendering the segmentation target, noting that some contribute significantly even when occluded parts are small. 3. Gradient Analysis: During removal, the method evaluates gradient signals, specifically noting that the gradient from the negative refinement term may be smaller than the positive term. 4. Removal: Ambiguous Gaussians are selectively removed; those with insufficient negative refinement gradients relative to positive terms cannot be eliminated naively. Parameters Time Cost: The removal process completes within one second. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Imbalance: Some ambiguous Gaussians contribute significantly to rendering the segmentation target with relatively small occluded parts, causing the negative refinement gradient to be smaller than the positive term, preventing naive elimination. Reflective Surfaces: The method targets artifacts from reflective effects (e.g., metal basin vs. table) where color similarity confuses RGB-fitting optimization. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def removeambiguousgaussians(gaussians): """ Removes ambiguous Gaussians at object borders with similar colors. Args: gaussians: List of 3D Gaussian objects with position, covariance, opacity, SH coefficients. Returns: prunedgaussians: List of Gaussians with ambiguous boundary entries removed. """ prunedgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: # Step 1: Identify Gaussians at borders of objects with similar colors. # The sources do not specify the exact algorithm for detecting similar color borders. isambiguousboundary = False # Logic not given in the sources. if isambiguousboundary: # Step 2 & 3: Evaluate contribution and gradient signals. # The sources state that some ambiguous Gaussians contribute significantly # to rendering the target, and their negative refinement gradient is # smaller than the positive term, preventing naive elimination. # The sources do not specify the exact thresholding or gradient comparison logic. canremove = False # Logic not given in the sources. if canremove: continue else: prunedgaussians.append(g) else: prunedgaussians.append(g) return prunedgaussians Uses normal information to improve mesh extraction quality. Choose when mesh fidelity is prioritized over segmentation speed. [12069-3d-gaussian-splatting-with-normal-information-for-mesh-extra.md] Adds a frosting layer to handle surface details. Choose when surface texture refinement is needed. [12579-gaussian-frosting-layer-creation.md] Handles dynamic scenes via dual-domain deformation. Choose for temporal consistency in moving objects. [12804-dual-domain-deformation-model.md] Denoising approach for Gaussian Splatting. Choose when input data is noisy. [13430-dn-splatter.md] Integrates photometric stereo for better shading. Choose when lighting consistency is critical. [14017-gaussian-splatting-photometric-stereo.md] Uses rendering guidance for SLAM tasks. Choose for simultaneous localization and mapping. [15093-rendering-guided-regularization-for-slam.md] Time Complexity: The removal process completes within one second. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the 360-counter dataset, SA3D-GS with this strategy achieved mAcc 98.1% and mIoU 88.0% with 403 Grids, and mAcc 97.8% and mIoU 80.9% with MLP. Strengths: Negligible additional time cost; bypasses complex components like SAM decoders and IoU computations. Limitations: Cannot naively eliminate all ambiguous Gaussians due to gradient imbalance when they contribute significantly to rendering the target. Performance may be slightly below expectations on datasets lacking detailed textures (e.g., Replica) due to 3D-GS artifacts. Ambiguous Gaussians Removal was introduced in the SA3D-GS method, which is part of the broader effort to segment 3D scenes using radiance fields. The method addresses a specific limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting where the RGB-fitting optimization goal leads to artifacts at object borders with similar colors, such as reflective metal surfaces. The work is presented in "Segment Anything in 3D with Radiance Fields". Segment Anything in 3D with Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11263-025-02421-7, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Normal Supervision and Reconstruction
body:
Normal Supervision and Reconstruction refers to a family of techniques that enhance 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by incorporating surface normal constraints into the optimization process. These methods solve the problem of ambiguous or noisy geometry inherent in standard volumetric rendering, where photometric losses alone often fail to recover precise surface details or coherent normals. What sets this family apart from its siblings, such as Gaussian Frosting Layer Creation or Ambiguous Gaussians Removal, is the explicit use of normal alignment—either against monocular estimates, depth gradients, or photometric stereo cues—to enforce surface-aligned geometry rather than just density fitting. The core mechanism involves augmenting the standard 3DGS rendering pipeline with a normal regularization loss term. This requires: 1. Normal Representation: Extending the Gaussian primitive to include or infer a normal vector \mathbf{n}i. 2. Normal Rendering: Computing a rendered normal map \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} for a pixel (u,v) by alpha-blending the normals of contributing Gaussians in depth order: \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} = \sum{i}^{N} \mathbf{n}{i} \alpha{i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1-\alpha{j}) where \mathbf{n}i is the normal of the i-th Gaussian, \alphai is its opacity, and the product term represents the transparency of preceding Gaussians. 3. Supervision Signal: Comparing the rendered normal \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} against a target normal \mathbf{n}{uv}. Targets are derived from monocular normal estimation networks (e.g., Omnidata, MiDaS), gradients of estimated depth maps, or D-Normal regularization from back-projected depth. 4. Loss Function: A cosine distance or similarity loss is added to the total optimization loss: \mathcal{L}{	ext{total}} = \mathcal{L}{	ext{photometric}} + \lambda{	ext{normal}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}} where \mathcal{L}{	ext{normal}} measures alignment between \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} and \mathbf{n}{uv}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernormalsandcomputeloss(gaussians, camera, gtnormal): """ Renders normals for a view and computes the normal alignment loss. gaussians: list of dicts with keys 'mu', 'cov', 'alpha', 'n' (normal vector) camera: dict with 'viewmatrix', 'intrinsicmatrix' gtnormal: (H, W, 3) ground truth or predicted normal map """ H, W = gtnormal.shape[:2] renderednormal = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) transmittance = np.ones((H, W)) # Sort Gaussians by depth in view space viewmu = transformtoview(gaussians.mu, camera['viewmatrix']) sortedidx = np.argsort(viewmu[:, 2])[::-1] for i in sortedidx: g = gaussians[i] # Project center and compute 2D covariance screenpos = project(g.mu, camera['viewmatrix']) cov2d = compute2dcov(g.cov, camera['viewmatrix'], screenpos) # Bounding box and pixel loop bbox = getboundingbox(screenpos, cov2d) for u, v in pixelsinbbox(bbox, H, W): dist = np.array([u - screenpos[0], v - screenpos[1]]) sigma = np.exp(-0.5 dist.T @ np.linalg.inv(cov2d) @ dist) alphacontrib = g.alpha sigma Tprev = transmittance[u, v] alphafinal = alphacontrib Tprev # Alpha-blend normal renderednormal[u, v] += g.n alphafinal transmittance[u, v] = (1 - alphacontrib) # Normalize accumulated normal valid = transmittance < 0.99 renderednormal[valid] /= (1 - transmittance[valid, np.newaxis]) renderednormal = normalize(renderednormal) # Compute cosine distance loss dotproduct = np.sum(renderednormal gtnormal, axis=-1) dotproduct = np.clip(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0) loss = np.sum(1 - dotproduct) return loss, renderednormal This method enhances 3DGS by incorporating normal supervision derived from the gradients of an estimated depth map to improve geometric accuracy and enable high-quality mesh extraction. While standard 3DGS relies solely on photometric losses, which often result in imprecise geometry and noisy normals, this approach uses monocular normal estimates to regularize depth gradients, facilitating the reconstruction of surface-aligned Gaussians suitable for Poisson meshing. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly linking the depth gradient direction to monocular normal priors rather than relying on depth consistency or photometric stereo alone. Gaussian Splatting Photometric Stereo (GS-PS) is a calibrated photometric stereo method that represents the scene exclusively using 3D Gaussian primitives to estimate surface normals and albedo. It solves the problem of recovering high-frequency surface geometry from multi-view images under varying lighting by optimizing Gaussian parameters to minimize a combined photometric and normal alignment loss. Unlike deep neural network methods that predict normals directly from image features, GS-PS optimizes an explicit physical image formation model, making it more explainable and providing geometrically interpretable parameters. It builds on this family by integrating normal supervision directly into the Gaussian splatting optimization loop. Definition: A strategy to estimate scene normals in 3DGS by improving depth estimation and using the depth gradient to derive pseudo normals, which guide the optimization of normals stored in 3D Gaussians. Formula: Pseudo normals \hat{\mathbf{n}}{\hat{D}} are derived from the depth map gradient: \hat{\mathbf{n}}{\hat{D}} = 
abla{uv} \hat{D}. Definition: Learning 3D normal vectors by rendering normals from the 3D Gaussian field and comparing them with predictions from an off-the-shelf 2D normal estimation network (Omnidata). Step: Render the normal vector \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} for each pixel (u,v) by alpha-blending the normal vectors \mathbf{n}i of the Gaussians, weighted by their opacity \alphai and the transparency of preceding Gaussians in depth order. Formula: The normal loss is defined as \mathcal{L}{	ext{n}} = \sum{(u,v)} (1 - \langle \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} \cdot \mathbf{n}{uv} angle), where \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} is the rendered normal at pixel (u,v), and \mathbf{n}{uv} is the predicted normal from the 2D network. The rendered normal is computed as \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} = \sum{i} \mathbf{n}{i} \alpha{i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1-\alpha{j}). Definition: A regularizer that uses a normal prior \mathbf{N} from a pretrained monocular deep neural network to supervise the rendered normal map \hat{\mathbf{N}} with L1 and cosine losses. Step: Render the depth map \hat{D} by weighted summing the intersection depths di. Convert the rendered depth \hat{D} to a D-Normal  ar{\mathbf{N}}d by back-projecting the depth map into point clouds with the camera intrinsic matrix. Compute the confidence term w as the cosine distance between the rendered normal \hat{\mathbf{N}}d and predicted normal \mathbf{N} to emphasize high certainty areas. Formula: \mathcal{L}n = \|\hat{\mathbf{N}} - \mathbf{N}\|1 + (1 - \hat{\mathbf{N}} \cdot \mathbf{N}), where \hat{\mathbf{N}} = (\sum{i \in M} \mathbf{n}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj)) / (\sum{i \in M} \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj)).  ar{\mathbf{N}}d(n, p) = (
ablav d(n, p) 	imes 
ablah d(n, p)) / |
ablav d(n, p) 	imes 
ablah d(n, p)|, where 
ablav and 
ablah are horizontal and vertical finite differences from neighboring points. \mathcal{L}{dn} = w (\| ar{\mathbf{N}}d - \mathbf{N}\|1 + (1 -  ar{\mathbf{N}}d \cdot \mathbf{N})). \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}s + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}n + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{dn}, with \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 balancing the components. The integration of normal supervision into 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as a solution to the "floating geometry" and lack of explicit surface representation in standard 3DGS. Early works like 3D Gaussian Splatting with Normal Information for Mesh Extraction introduced depth-gradient-based normal regularization to enforce surface coherence. Concurrently, methods like Gaussian Splatting Photometric Stereo explored explicit normal parameterization and photometric constraints to improve geometric accuracy and enable inverse rendering tasks. These approaches leverage pretrained monocular normal estimators (e.g., Omnidata) or depth gradients as weak supervision signals to guide the 3D structure. name: 3D Gaussian Splatting with Normal Information for Mesh Extraction
head: GS with Normal Regularization, SDF Gradient Normal Supervision
body:
This method augments standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with a regularization term based on the gradients of an estimated Signed Distance Function (SDF) to enforce surface-aligned geometry. While standard 3DGS relies on photometric losses that often result in imprecise geometry and noisy normals, this approach uses monocular normal estimates to supervise the SDF gradients, enabling high-quality surface mesh extraction via Poisson reconstruction. It differs from DN-Splatter by explicitly deriving SDF gradients from the Gaussian density field rather than using differentiable normal splatting, and from Gaussian Splatting Photometric Stereo by relying on monocular priors rather than multi-view photometric stereo constraints. Inputs: A set of calibrated camera poses and images from Structure-from-Motion (SfM). A sparse point cloud from SfM for initialization. Pretrained monocular normal estimation network (e.g., Omnidata or MiDaS) to generate target normals \mathbf{n}p for training images. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians (means  oldsymbol{\mu}, covariances  oldsymbol{\Sigma}, opacities \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients). A surface mesh extracted via Poisson reconstruction from the optimized Gaussians. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Defined by mean  oldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix  oldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3}, opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and spherical harmonics coefficients for color. Covariance Parameterization:  oldsymbol{\Sigma} is parameterized by a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and a scaling matrix \mathbf{S} such that  oldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{S}^T \mathbf{R}^T to ensure positive semi-definiteness during optimization. Density Function: The scene density at point \mathbf{p} is defined as: d(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{g} \alphag \exp \left( - rac{1}{2} (\mathbf{p} -  oldsymbol{\mu}g)^T  oldsymbol{\Sigma}g^{-1} (\mathbf{p} -  oldsymbol{\mu}g) ight) where the sum is over all Gaussians g. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians using the sparse point cloud obtained from SfM. 2. Standard Optimization Loop: Project 3D Gaussians to 2D image plane as splats using fast tile-based rasterization. Render color and depth maps via \alpha-blending. Compute photometric loss (\mathcal{L}1) and D-SSIM loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{DSSIM}}) against input images. Update Gaussian parameters using gradient descent. 3. Adaptive Density Control: Interleave optimization with density control: Add Gaussians to empty areas or areas where a single Gaussian covers large parts of the scene. Prune transparent Gaussians with opacities close to 0. 4. SDF Estimation: For a point \mathbf{p} visible from a training viewpoint: Render the depth map d{	ext{rendered}} at the projection of \mathbf{p}. Estimate the SDF value \hat{f}(\mathbf{p}) as the difference between the depth of \mathbf{p} and d{	ext{rendered}}. 5. Normal Supervision (Regularization Phase): Obtain target monocular normals \mathbf{n}p from the pretrained network for the training image at pixel p. Compute the gradient of the estimated SDF, 
abla \hat{f}p, at point \mathbf{p}. Project 
abla \hat{f}p into camera space using the world-to-view transform. Rasterize the projected gradient to obtain 
abla \hat{f}p at the corresponding pixel position. Compute the normal regularization term R(\hat{f}): R(\hat{f}) = \sum{p \in P}  rac{|
abla \hat{f}p \cdot \mathbf{n}p|}{\|
abla \hat{f}p\| \|\mathbf{n}p\|} where P is the set of pixel points in the training images. Compute total loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}1 + \lambda{	ext{DSSIM}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{DSSIM}} + \lambdar R(\hat{f}) where \lambda{	ext{DSSIM}} = 0.2 and \lambdar \in [0.1, 0.4]. Apply entropy regularization for a short number of iterations to encourage binary opacities (avoiding semi-transparent Gaussians). 6. Mesh Extraction: Run Poisson reconstruction on points sampled on the optimized Gaussians to extract the mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizegaussianswithnormalregularization(cameras, images, sparsepoints, normalnet): # 1. Initialize Gaussians from sparse points gaussians = initializegaussians(sparsepoints) # 2. Standard optimization loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Adaptive density control gaussians = adaptivedensitycontrol(gaussians, cameras) # Render current view renderedcolor, rendereddepth = rendergaussians(gaussians, cameras) # Photometric losses lossl1 = computel1loss(renderedcolor, images) lossdssim = computedssimloss(renderedcolor, images) # Normal regularization (applied during specific iterations or always with weight) # Estimate SDF gradient sdfgradients = estimatesdfgradients(gaussians, cameras) # Get monocular normals from pretrained network monocularnormals = normalnet(images) # Project SDF gradients to camera space and rasterize rasterizedgradients = rasterizegradients(sdfgradients, cameras) # Compute normal regularization term # R(fhat) = sum(|grad. n| / (||grad|| ||n||)) normalloss = computecosinesimilarityloss(rasterizedgradients, monocularnormals) # Total loss lambdadssim = 0.2 lambdar = 0.2 # Tuned per scene, typically 0.1-0.4 totalloss = lossl1 + lambdadssim lossdssim + lambdar normalloss # Entropy regularization for binary opacities (short duration) if iteration in entropyregularizationiterations: totalloss += entropyregularization(gaussians.opacities) # Backpropagate and update updategaussians(gaussians, totalloss) # 3. Mesh extraction mesh = poissonreconstruction(samplepointsfromgaussians(gaussians)) return mesh Parameters: \lambda{	ext{DSSIM}}: Weight for D-SSIM loss, typically 0.2. \lambdar: Weight for normal regularization, typically between 0.1 and 0.4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Semi-transparent Gaussians: Without entropy regularization, Gaussians may remain semi-transparent, degrading mesh quality. Entropy regularization is applied for a short number of iterations to force binary opacities. Monocular Normal Accuracy: The method relies on pretrained networks (Omnidata, MiDaS) which may produce inaccurate normals in textureless or ambiguous regions. SDF Estimation: The SDF is estimated from depth maps, which may be noisy or incomplete in occluded regions. Time Complexity: Similar to standard 3DGS, dominated by rasterization and gradient descent updates. The additional SDF gradient estimation and normal supervision add computational overhead but remain efficient due to tile-based rasterization. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of Gaussians, similar to standard 3DGS. Performance: Scores higher on photorealism metrics (PSNR, SSIM) compared to other mesh-extracting methods like SuGaR and Baked-SDF on datasets such as Mip-NeRF360, Tanks and Temples, and Deep-Blending. Strengths: Enables high-quality surface mesh extraction; improves rendering quality in regions with high curvature or fine detail; leverages efficient 3DGS rasterization. Limitations: Relies on monocular normal estimation which may be inaccurate; requires careful tuning of \lambdar per scene. This method was proposed by Meenakshi Krishnan, Liam Fowl, and Ramani Duraiswami in 2025. It addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which relies on photometric losses and often results in imprecise geometry and noisy normals, particularly in regions with high curvature or fine detail. The method builds on the density function formulation from [8] (SuGaR) but diverges by supervising SDF gradients rather than target density. It is relevant for downstream applications in video generation, animation, AR-VR, and gaming where surface meshes are required. 3D Gaussian Splatting with Normal Information for Mesh Extraction and Improved Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/icasspw65056.2025.11011170, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DN-Splatter
head: DN-Splatter Regularization and Initialization, Depth and Normal Priors for Gaussian Splatting
body: DN-Splatter is a method that enhances 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction quality by incorporating depth and normal priors captured from common devices or predicted from general-purpose networks. It addresses the challenge of achieving both photorealism and geometric accuracy in challenging, ill-posed, and textureless indoor scenes where standard photometric optimization often fails. Unlike standard 3DGS which lacks explicit geometric constraints, DN-Splatter regularizes the optimization with depth information, enforces local smoothness of nearby Gaussians, and utilizes off-the-shelf monocular networks to align Gaussians with true scene geometry. It enables direct mesh extraction from the optimized Gaussian representation, yielding more physically accurate reconstructions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images (RGB), corresponding camera poses, and optionally sensor depth maps (e.g., from LiDAR or structured light) or monocular depth/normal predictions. Outputs: Optimized 3D Gaussian primitives (means \mu, covariances \Sigma, opacities \alpha, colors c) and a rendered normal map. Data Structures: The method extends the standard 3DGS primitive. While standard 3DGS does not explicitly store normals, DN-Splatter derives them. Gaussian Primitive: Parameterized by mean \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (decomposed into scaling s \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation q \in \mathbb{R}^4), opacity \alpha \in \mathbb{R}, and color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Implicit Normal: The normal \mathbf{n}i for the i-th Gaussian is derived from the gradient of the Gaussian density or by assuming the Gaussian aligns with the surface normal estimated from the depth/normal priors. The rendering pipeline computes a rendered normal map \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} by alpha-blending these normals. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Gaussian scene using either sparse COLMAP SfM points or dense sensor depth readings back-projected into 3D. Sensor depth initialization is preferred over COLMAP SfM as it enhances both mesh and novel-view synthesis metrics. Typical initialization uses 1 million Gaussians when using sensor depth. 2. Depth Rendering: Render per-pixel z-depth estimates \hat{D} using a discrete volume rendering approximation similar to color values: \hat{D}{uv} = \sum{i \in N} di \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1-\alphaj) where di is the i-th Gaussian's z-depth coordinate in view space, \alphai is its opacity, and the product term represents the transmittance of preceding Gaussians. Since 3DGS uses a single global sort for efficiency rather than per-pixel sorting, this depth rendering is an approximation. To handle pixels where accumulated transmittance Ti \neq 1, normalize depth estimates with the final accumulated transmittance per pixel to ensure correct depth values. Rasterize color and depths simultaneously per pixel in a single CUDA kernel forward pass to improve inference and training speed. 3. Normal Rendering: Extract normal directions from Gaussians. Compute the rendered normal map \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} for each pixel by alpha-blending the normals of contributing Gaussians in depth order: \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} = \sum{i}^{N} \mathbf{n}{i} \alpha{i} \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1-\alpha{j}) where \mathbf{n}i is the normal of the i-th Gaussian. 4. Loss Computation: Gradient-Aware Depth Loss (L{\hat{D}}): Apply an adaptive depth regularization based on the current RGB image. The loss is lowered in regions with large image gradients (edges) to enforce regularization more on smoother texture-less regions. Use a logarithmic penalty for the depth loss instead of linear or quadratic penalties to result in smoother reconstructions. Formula (implied from context of "gradient-aware" and "logarithmic penalty"): L{\hat{D}} = \sum{uv} w{uv} \log(1 + |\hat{D}{uv} - D{target, uv}|) where w{uv} is a weight inversely proportional to the image gradient magnitude at (u,v). Normal Loss (L{\hat{N}}): Align Gaussians along the scene geometry using normal cues from monocular networks (e.g., Omnidata) or depth gradients. Formula: L{\hat{N}} = \sum{uv} (1 - \hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} \cdot \mathbf{n}{target, uv}) where \mathbf{n}{target, uv} is the target normal. Normal Smoothing Prior (L{smooth}): Add a smoothing prior on rendered normal maps to better align nearby Gaussians during optimization. Formula: L{smooth} = \sum{uv} \|\hat{\mathbf{n}}{uv} - \text{mean}(\{\hat{\mathbf{n}}{neighbor}\})\|^2 where the mean is taken over neighboring pixels. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photometric}} + \lambda{\text{depth}} L{\hat{D}} + \lambda{\text{normal}} L{\hat{N}} + \lambda{\text{smooth}} L{smooth} where \lambda are hyperparameters. 5. Optimization: Optimize the Gaussian scene parameters using the total loss. Training iterations: 30k iterations for all reported experiments. 6. Mesh Extraction: Extract meshes directly from the optimized Gaussian scene using Poisson surface reconstruction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dnsplatteroptimize(inputimages, cameraposes, sensordepths=None, monocularnormals=None): """ Optimizes 3D Gaussians using DN-Splatter regularization. Args: inputimages: List of RGB images. cameraposes: List of camera pose matrices. sensordepths: Optional list of sensor depth maps. monocularnormals: Optional list of monocular normal maps. Returns: Optimized Gaussian primitives. """ # 1. Initialization if sensordepths is not None: # Back-project sensor depth to 3D points initpoints = backprojectdepth(sensordepths, cameraposes) # Initialize 1M Gaussians at these points gaussians = initializegaussians(initpoints, numgaussians=1000000) else: # Fallback to COLMAP SfM points initpoints = getcolmapsfmpoints() gaussians = initializegaussians(initpoints) # 2. Training Loop for iteration in range(30000): # Sample a random view viewidx = randomsample(inputimages) image = inputimages[viewidx] pose = cameraposes[viewidx] # Render Color, Depth, and Normal # Rasterize color and depths simultaneously in a single CUDA kernel renderedcolor, rendereddepth, renderednormal = rendergaussians(gaussians, pose) # Get target depth and normal if sensordepths is not None: targetdepth = sensordepths[viewidx] # Compute target normal from sensor depth or use monocular if available targetnormal = computenormalfromdepth(targetdepth) if monocularnormals is None else monocularnormals[viewidx] else: # Use monocular predictions if no sensor depth targetdepth = monoculardepthpredictions[viewidx] targetnormal = monocularnormals[viewidx] # Compute Photometric Loss lossrgb = mseloss(renderedcolor, image) # Compute Gradient-Aware Depth Loss # Calculate image gradient magnitude imggrad = computegradientmagnitude(image) # Weight inversely proportional to gradient (lower weight at edges) depthweight = 1.0 / (1.0 + imggrad) # Logarithmic penalty depthdiff = log(1.0 + abs(rendereddepth - targetdepth)) lossdepth = sum(depthweight depthdiff) # Compute Normal Loss # Ensure normals are normalized renderednormal = normalize(renderednormal) targetnormal = normalize(targetnormal) lossnormal = sum(1.0 - dot(renderednormal, targetnormal)) # Compute Normal Smoothing Prior # Average normals of neighboring pixels smoothednormal = averageneighbors(renderednormal) losssmooth = sum(squarednorm(renderednormal - smoothednormal)) # Total Loss totalloss = lossrgb + lambdadepth lossdepth + lambdanormal lossnormal + lambdasmooth losssmooth # Backpropagate and update Gaussians updategaussians(gaussians, totalloss) return gaussians Parameters: Logarithmic penalty: Used for depth loss to ensure smoother reconstructions. Number of initialized Gaussians: 1M points when using sensor depth initialization. Training iterations: 30k iterations. Hardware: Nvidia 4090 GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Approximation: 3DGS uses a single global sort for efficiency, making depth rendering an approximation. This is handled by normalizing depth estimates with the final accumulated transmittance Ti per pixel. Sensor Depth Inaccuracies: Sensor depths suffer from low resolution and inaccuracies, particularly at object edges. The gradient-aware loss mitigates this by lowering regularization at edges. Textureless Regions: Standard photometric regularization fails in textureless regions. Depth and normal priors are crucial here. Time Complexity: Training requires 30k iterations. Rasterization is optimized by rendering color and depth simultaneously in a single CUDA kernel. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians. 1M Gaussians are used for sensor depth initialization. Measured Performance: Depth Estimation (MuSHRoom left test set): Abs Rel 0.0228, Sq Rel 0.0089, RMSE 0.1280, \delta<1.25 0.9854, PSNR 24.58, SSIM 0.8558. Mesh Quality (ScanNet++): C-L1 0.0940, NC 0.8316, F1 0.7658. Scaling: Sensor depth initialization outperforms COLMAP SfM initialization. Strengths: Improves photorealism and geometric accuracy in challenging indoor scenes; enables direct mesh extraction; robust to textureless regions. Limitations: Relies on the quality of sensor depth or monocular predictions; sensor depths can be inaccurate at edges. When to use: When high-fidelity 3D reconstruction of indoor scenes is required, especially with textureless regions, and mesh extraction is desired. When not to use: If sensor depth is unavailable and monocular predictions are unreliable; if real-time rendering speed is critical and 30k iterations are too slow. Origin: DN-Splatter was introduced by Matias Turkulainen, Xuqian Ren, Iaroslav Melekhov, Otto Seiskari, Esa Rahtu, and Juho Kannala in the paper "DN-Splatter: Depth and Normal Priors for Gaussian Splatting and Meshing". History: It builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting [19] and addresses its limitations in geometric reconstruction. Usage: Evaluated on MuSHRoom (6 scenes) and ScanNet++ datasets. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y, fetched 2026-10-26 DN-Splatter: Depth and Normal Priors for Gaussian Splatting and Meshing, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv61041.2025.00241, fetched 2026-10-26
