name: NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation
head: Evaluation and Metric Calculation, NeRF Evaluation, NeRF Validation, Single Image Rendering, Validation Rendering
body: NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation renders a single image from a trained radiance field using a specified camera pose and computes quantitative fidelity metrics against ground truth references. It differs from training ray marching by disabling stochastic perturbations to ensure deterministic, reproducible results. This procedure serves as the primary benchmark for comparing model variants and guiding optimization loops. Inputs: coarsemodel: Trained coarse NeRF MLP. finemodel: Trained fine NeRF MLP. pose: 4x4 camera-to-world matrix (numpy array or torch tensor). K: 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix (numpy array or torch tensor). H, W: Image height and width in pixels. near, far: Near and far plane distances along the ray. args: Configuration object containing chunk (default 1024), nsamplescoarse, nsamplesfine, whitebkgd, lindisp, netchunk, usendc. device: Torch device (CPU/GPU). Outputs: rgb: Rendered RGB image of shape [H, W, 3] in [0, 1] range. depth: Rendered depth map of shape [H, W]. disp: Rendered disparity map of shape [H, W]. metrics: Dictionary containing PSNR and SSIM values. Data Structures: Rays are represented as two 3D vectors: rayso (origins) and raysd (directions), flattened to [-1, 3] before processing. Results are stored in a dictionary with keys 'rgb', 'depth', 'disp', and potentially 'coarse' or 'fine' suffixes depending on the model configuration. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set coarsemodel and finemodel to evaluation mode (model.eval()) to disable dropout and batch normalization updates. Disable gradient computation using torch.nograd(). 2. Input Conversion: If pose or K are numpy arrays, convert them to torch.float32 tensors on the specified device. 3. Ray Generation: Compute ray origins and directions using the intrinsic matrix K, image dimensions H, W, and camera pose pose. Formula for K construction (if not provided): K = \begin{bmatrix} f & 0 & 0.5 W \\ 0 & f & 0.5 H \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where f is the focal length in pixels. 4. NDC Conversion (Optional): If args.usendc is true, convert ray origins and directions to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) using the focal length, near plane, and ray parameters. 5. Chunked Rendering: Process rays in chunks of size chunk (default 1024) to manage GPU memory. For each chunk, call the rendering function with perturb=False. The rendering function performs volume integration: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance, \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity, \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the distance between samples. Depth is computed as the expected termination depth: Df = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai zi where zi is the depth of the i-th sample. 6. Result Aggregation: Concatenate results from all chunks, reshape to [H, W, 3] for RGB and [H, W] for depth/disparity, and move to CPU. 7. Metric Calculation: MSE: Calculate Mean Squared Error between predicted RGB and ground truth RGB. PSNR: Calculate Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \log{10}(\text{MSE}). SSIM: Calculate Structural Similarity Index using comparessim with full=True and multichannel=True. 8. Output: Return the rendered images and computed metrics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np from skimage.metrics import structuralsimilarity as comparessim def evaluatenerf(coarsemodel, finemodel, pose, K, H, W, near, far, args, device, gtimage=None): # 1. Initialization coarsemodel.eval() finemodel.eval() with torch.nograd(): # 2. Input Conversion if isinstance(pose, np.ndarray): pose = torch.fromnumpy(pose).float().to(device) if isinstance(K, np.ndarray): K = torch.fromnumpy(K).float().to(device) # 3. Ray Generation rayso, raysd = getrays(H, W, K, pose) # 4. NDC Conversion if args.usendc: focal = K[0, 0].item() rayso, raysd = ndcrays(H, W, focal, 1.0, rayso, raysd) # 5. Flatten rays rayso = rayso.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.reshape(-1, 3) # 6. Chunked Rendering chunk = args.chunk allrgb = [] alldepth = [] alldisp = [] for i in range(0, rayso.shape[0], chunk): chunko = rayso[i:i+chunk] chunkd = raysd[i:i+chunk] # Step the sources do not give: full volume integration loop is implemented in Volume Rendering Integration and Forward Pass result = renderrays( chunko, chunkd, coarsemodel, finemodel, near, far, args.nsamplescoarse, args.nsamplesfine, perturb=False, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=args.whitebkgd, lindisp=args.lindisp, netchunk=args.netchunk) rgbkey = 'rgbfine' if 'rgbfine' in result else 'rgbcoarse' depthkey = 'depthfine' if 'depthfine' in result else 'depthcoarse' dispkey = 'dispfine' if 'dispfine' in result else 'dispcoarse' allrgb.append(result[rgbkey].reshape(-1, 3).cpu().numpy()) alldepth.append(result[depthkey].reshape(-1).cpu().numpy()) alldisp.append(result[dispkey].reshape(-1).cpu().numpy()) # 7. Result Aggregation rgbimage = np.concatenate(allrgb, axis=0).reshape(H, W, 3) depthimage = np.concatenate(alldepth, axis=0).reshape(H, W) dispimage = np.concatenate(alldisp, axis=0).reshape(H, W) # 8. Metric Calculation metrics = {} if gtimage is not None: gtrgb = gtimage.reshape(H, W, 3) mse = np.mean((rgbimage - gtrgb) 2) psnr = -10.0 np.log10(mse) if mse > 0 else float('inf') metrics['psnr'] = psnr ssim = comparessim(rgbimage, gtrgb, full=True, multichannel=True) metrics['ssim'] = ssim return rgbimage, depthimage, dispimage, metrics def getrays(H, W, K, c2w): i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W, dtype=np.float32), np.arange(H, dtype=np.float32), indexing='xy') dirs = np.stack([(i - K[0, 2].item()) / K[0, 0].item(), -(j - K[1, 2].item()) / K[1, 1].item(), -np.oneslike(i)], axis=-1) dirs = dirs.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = np.dot(dirs, c2w[:3,:3].T.numpy()) rayso = np.broadcastto(c2w[:3, 3].numpy(), raysd.shape).copy() return rayso, raysd def ndcrays(H, W, focal, near, rayso, raysd): rayso = rayso.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.reshape(-1, 3) rayso = rayso - raysd near ndcscale = 2.0 focal / W rayso[:,:2] = rayso[:,:2] / ndcscale raysd[:,:2] = raysd[:,:2] / ndcscale rayso[:, 2] = rayso[:, 2] + near return rayso, raysd def renderrays(rayso, raysd, coarsemodel, finemodel, near, far, nsamplescoarse, nsamplesfine, perturb, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd, lindisp, netchunk): # Step the sources do not give: full volume integration loop is implemented in Volume Rendering Integration and Forward Pass pass Parameters: chunk: Integer, default 1024. Number of rays processed per batch to limit memory usage. perturb: Boolean, default False for evaluation. Controls whether jitter is added to sample positions. whitebkgd: Boolean. Whether to composite the result against a white background. lindisp: Boolean. Whether to sample linearly in disparity space instead of depth space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perturbation: Must be disabled (perturb=False) during validation to ensure deterministic and reproducible results. Memory: Large images or high sample counts may exceed GPU memory; chunking is essential. NDC: If using NDC coordinates, rays must be transformed correctly before rendering. Key Extraction: The result dictionary keys may vary (coarse vs fine); code must handle fallbacks. The MIMO objective is the total training loss for MIMO-NeRF, combining pixel-wise reconstruction errors with a 3D consistency regularization term across M reformulated multi-input multi-output (MIMO) neural radiance fields. It enforces consistency between parallel MLPs trained with different sampling configurations, enabling faster rendering without sacrificing quality. Choose it when training multiple parallel NeRFs to accelerate inference. This policy selects the most informative synthetic views for active learning in neural radiance fields by quantifying information gain through uncertainty metrics. It distinguishes itself from heuristic baselines (Random, FVS) by using epistemic uncertainty as a proxy for information gain, consistently outperforming them in reconstruction quality. Choose it when actively selecting new camera poses for training. Standard Metric Computation quantifies the fidelity of rendered images against ground truth references to evaluate the quality of novel-view synthesis in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It addresses the problem of assessing rendering quality by balancing pixel-level precision, structural integrity, and perceptual similarity, providing a standardized benchmark for comparing different NeRF architectures and training procedures. Choose it for standard benchmarking of novel view synthesis. This family of techniques incorporates geometric constraints into the radiance field optimization loop to improve reconstruction quality, particularly in low-data regimes or when explicit geometry is required for downstream tasks. While standard NeRF optimization relies solely on photometric RGB losses, these methods introduce depth-related penalties or sampling strategies. Depth Supervision explicitly minimizes the difference between rendered depth and ground-truth depth (derived from SfM keypoints or stereo), whereas Pseudo-Depth approximates surface geometry via weighted averaging of sampled points to guide feature distillation or segmentation without requiring explicit depth labels. Choose it when geometric accuracy is prioritized over photometric fidelity. The Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator computes the uncertainty of the underlying 3D geometry in a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by calculating the entropy of the weight distribution of color samples along each ray. It treats the opacity function as a cumulative distribution function (CDF) and its derivative as a probability density function (PDF), allowing the weight distribution to serve as a proxy for geometric certainty. Unlike explicit 3D representations or RGB-D fusion methods, this approach leverages the implicit neural shape representation to estimate information gain without relying on structure-from-motion or depth sensors. It is distinct from methods like S-NeRF or NeRF-W as it requires no model modification or additional training, functioning as a post-hoc analysis plug-in. Choose it for uncertainty-aware scene analysis without retraining. Depth-Regularizing Loss Functions constrain the geometric consistency of differentiable volume rendering by penalizing discrepancies between rendered depth maps and external geometric estimates, such as stereo-matching outputs or optical flow correspondences. Unlike photometric losses that only enforce color fidelity, these methods explicitly regularize the scene's implicit geometry, accelerating convergence and improving robustness in textureless or occluded regions. They are distinguished from sibling methods like MIMO Objective (which focuses on multi-scale image features) and Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator (which models aleatoric uncertainty) by their direct reliance on explicit depth or flow supervision signals. Choose them when training stability in textureless regions is required. Active Scout Tracking with NeRF is a multi-target tracking method for pursuit-evasion games in highly occluded urban environments, where a quadrotor scout tracks dynamic targets on the ground using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) built online from RGB and depth images. It solves the problem of selecting the next best view for a scout to maximize information gain about target locations and unknown parts of the city. Unlike Standard Metric Computation which evaluates static performance, this method actively drives the scout's trajectory by maximizing mutual information between future observations and past observations, conditioned on the future scout location. It differs from MIMO Objective by focusing on single-scout active perception rather than multi-agent coordination, and from Novel View Selection Policy by explicitly integrating NeRF-based scene representation with Bayes filter target tracking. Choose it for active robotic perception and tracking. Synthesizes depth maps from a trained NeRF's density field by computing the expected termination depth of a ray. It casts a ray towards the camera and uses the density field to determine how deep into the volumetric object the ray is expected to penetrate, using that distance as the depth map value. NeRF does not directly estimate object boundaries nor directly produce depth maps; hard surfaces are simulated using a very dense but not infinitely dense field. It differs from direct depth sensors (e.g., RealSense D415) which fail on thin/reflective objects, and from MVS (e.g., COLMAP) which assumes Lambertian surfaces and fails on specularities. A method to convert the continuous density field of a trained NeRF into a discrete surface point cloud for DSM generation by computing a weighted average of sampled point depths. It computes the final depth Df for each ray using the weighted sum of sample depths, calculates 3D coordinates P using the ray origin o, direction d, and computed depth Df, transforms point cloud coordinates into geographic latitude and longitude using the RPC model, projects the coordinates into a 2D planar coordinate system through Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) projection, and maps elevation values to grid cells based on predefined spatial resolution and grid range to complete DSM generation. The formula is Df = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai zi, where zi is the depth of the i-th sample, \alphai is the opacity, and Ti is the transmittance. Computes visual hulls from ground-truth masks of training views to remove extraneous geometry blobs from reconstructions. During training pose reconstruction, it computes visual hulls from ground-truth masks of training views and sets density values outside the visual hulls to 0. During testing on unseen poses, it disables the mask usage. Without masking, extraneous geometry blobs appear in reconstructions by Neural Body and Ani-NeRF. Evaluates reconstruction stability under camera parameter uncertainty by running Monte Carlo simulations. It defines perturbation ranges for translation (\Delta T) and rotation (\Delta R), initializes an iteration counter to 0, and while iterations < N: randomly samples \Delta T \in [-T{\max}, T{\max}] and \Delta R \in [-R{\max}, R{\max}], applies perturbations to camera parameters, runs the reconstruction pipeline, computes RMSE between generated reconstruction and reference data, stores RMSE, and increments the counter. It computes Average RMSE = mean(stored RMSEs), Error Range = max(stored RMSEs) - min(stored RMSEs), and Uncertainty = Error Range / 2. The formula is \text{Uncertainty} = (\text{Max RMSE} - \text{Min RMSE}) / 2. Typical values: N=30, R{\max}=2^\circ (Scenario A) or 4^\circ (Scenario B). On the Ignatius dataset, Scenario A (\pm 20 mm, \pm 2^\circ) yields Average RMSE = 19.72 mm, Uncertainty = 2.95 mm. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and samples per ray. Chunking adds overhead but prevents OOM errors. Memory Complexity: Proportional to chunk size. Full image rendering requires storing intermediate tensors for all rays in the chunk. Performance: Deterministic rendering is faster than training due to disabled perturbations and gradient computations. Strengths: Provides objective, quantitative comparison of model quality. Limitations: Metrics like PSNR/SSIM do not always correlate with perceptual quality; LPIPS is more expensive to compute. Originated with the NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020), evaluation procedures became standard for benchmarking novel view synthesis. The method has been adapted for various NeRF variants, including those using hashed embeddings, chunked evaluation, and differentiable pipelines. damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, https://github.com/yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, https://github.com/rigved-sanku/NeRF-Implementation-for-Efficient-3D-Scene-Reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF-Supervision: Learning Dense Object Descriptors from Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01913v2, fetched 2026-10-26 Shading and Geometric Constraint Neural Radiance Field for DSM Reconstruction from Multi-View Satellite Images, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18071091, fetched 2026-11-05 ARAH: Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-31, fetched 2026-10-26 A Critical Analysis of NeRF-Based 3D Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15143585, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MIMO Objective
body: The MIMO objective is the total training loss for MIMO-NeRF, combining pixel-wise reconstruction errors with a 3D consistency regularization term across M reformulated multi-input multi-output (MIMO) neural radiance fields. It enforces consistency between parallel MLPs trained with different sampling configurations, enabling faster rendering without sacrificing quality. The method trains M reformulated MIMO MLPs, each using a different shift parameter s (or variation reduction configuration) and a specific repetition count Rm. The total number of samples ("# Run") across all M MLPs is constrained to not exceed the sample count of a single original SISO (Single-Input Single-Output) MLP. Inputs: M: The number of reformulated MIMO MLPs. \mathbf{C}: The ground-truth RGB color for the current pixel/view. \hat{\mathbf{C}}^m: The final composited predicted RGB color from the m-th MIMO MLP. \mathbf{c}i^m: The color of the i-th sample along the ray for the m-th MLP. \alphai^m: The alpha (opacity) of the i-th sample along the ray for the m-th MLP. N: The number of samples along the ray. Rm: The repetition count (or reliability metric) for the m-th MLP. R{\max}: The maximum R value among all M MLPs (R{\max} = \max{m \in \{1, \dots, M\}} Rm). \lambda: Hyperparameter balancing pixel-wise and 3D consistency losses. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\text{MIMO}}: The scalar total loss value. Not given in the sources. The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{MIMO}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{3D} 1. Pixel-wise Loss: Sum of squared errors for each MLP's final rendered color against the ground truth: \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}} = \sum{m=1}^M \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}^m - \mathbf{C}\|2^2 2. 3D Consistency Loss: Encourages the M MLPs to produce consistent colors and alphas at the sample level. It consists of color and alpha components: \mathcal{L}{3D} = \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{color}} + \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{alpha}} The Color 3D Consistency Loss is: \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{color}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\mathbf{c}i^{m1} - \text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m1}) - \mathbf{c}i^{m2}\|2^2 \right] The Alpha 3D Consistency Loss is: \mathcal{L}{3D}^{\text{alpha}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\alphai^{m1} - \text{sg}(\alphai^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\alphai^{m1}) - \alphai^{m2}\|2^2 \right] Here, \text{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operation, which prevents gradients from flowing through the target branch in the consistency term. 3. Asymmetric Weight: The weight \mu{mj}^{mi} is defined based on the reliability of the MLPs. MLPs with greater Rm have lower ambiguity and are considered more reliable, thus their influence on the consistency loss is reduced. The explicit formula provided in the source is: \mu{mj}^{mi} = \sqrt{mj} \sqrt{R{\max}} \sqrt{R{mi}} Note: The source text explicitly provides this formula. However, the accompanying description states that weights are derived from \sqrt{R{mj}} / \sqrt{R{\max}} to reduce the effect of reliable MLPs. The use of the index mj in the numerator of the source formula is inconsistent with the description of weighting by R. \lambda: Hyperparameter balancing pixel-wise loss and 3D consistency loss. Typical values are not specified in the sources. M: Number of reformulated MLPs. Rm: Repetition count for MLP m. R{\max}: Maximum R value across all MLPs. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def stopgradient(x): """Detaches x from the computation graph. Framework-specific behavior.""" return x def computemimoloss(colors, alphas, gtcolor, Rvals, lam): """ Computes the MIMO training objective. Args: colors: List of M lists, each containing N tuples of 3 floats. colors[m][i] is ci^m. alphas: List of M lists, each containing N floats. alphas[m][i] is alphai^m. gtcolor: Tuple of 3 floats. Ground truth RGB for the pixel. Rvals: List of M floats. Rm for each MLP. lam: Float. Balances pixel and 3D consistency losses. Returns: totalloss: Float. The MIMO objective value. """ M = len(Rvals) N = len(colors[0]) Rmax = max(Rvals) # 1. Pixel-wise Loss pixelloss = 0.0 for m in range(M): chatm = colors[m][-1] # Final composited color for MLP m pixelloss += sum((chatm[k] - gtcolor[k])2 for k in range(3)) # 2. 3D Consistency Loss l3dcolor = 0.0 l3dalpha = 0.0 for m1 in range(M - 1): for m2 in range(m1 + 1, M): # Compute weights using 1-based indexing as per source notation mj = m1 + 1 mi = m2 + 1 mu12 = math.sqrt(mj) math.sqrt(Rmax) math.sqrt(Rvals[mi - 1]) mu21 = math.sqrt(mi) math.sqrt(Rmax) math.sqrt(Rvals[mj - 1]) # Color consistency for i in range(N): c1 = colors[m1][i] c2 = colors[m2][i] c2sg = stopgradient(c2) c1sg = stopgradient(c1) diff1 = [c1[k] - c2sg[k] for k in range(3)] diff2 = [c2[k] - c1sg[k] for k in range(3)] norm1 = sum(d2 for d in diff1) norm2 = sum(d2 for d in diff2) l3dcolor += (mu12 norm1 + mu21 norm2) / N # Alpha consistency for i in range(N): a1 = alphas[m1][i] a2 = alphas[m2][i] a2sg = stopgradient(a2) a1sg = stopgradient(a1) diffa1 = a1 - a2sg diffa2 = a2 - a1sg l3dalpha += (mu12 diffa12 + mu21 diffa22) / N l3d = l3dcolor + l3dalpha return pixelloss + lam l3d Formula Ambiguity: The source provides the formula \mu{mj}^{mi} = \sqrt{mj} \sqrt{R{\max}} \sqrt{R{mi}} but describes the weight as being based on reliability (Rm) where higher R reduces ambiguity. The use of the index mj in the numerator of the source formula is inconsistent with the description of weighting by R. Implementers should verify if \sqrt{mj} is a typo for \sqrt{R{mj}} or if the index is intended. Stop-Gradient: Forgetting to apply the stop-gradient (sg) operation to the target branch in the consistency loss will cause gradients to flow through both branches, potentially destabilizing training or negating the regularization effect. Aggregates various evaluation metrics into a single score. It is used for final model assessment, not training optimization. Unified Metric Aggregation Calculates Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio for quality assessment. It is a post-training or validation step. PSNR Evaluation Pipeline Computes metrics only on valid pixels (e.g., excluding background). It is used for evaluation, not training. Masked Evaluation Time Complexity: The 3D consistency loss involves pairwise comparisons between all M MLPs and summation over N samples, leading to O(M^2 \cdot N) complexity for the consistency term. The pixel-wise loss is O(M). Memory Complexity: Requires storing predictions for all M MLPs across N samples, O(M \cdot N). Strengths: Enables faster rendering by allowing fewer samples per MLP while maintaining quality through consistency regularization. It effectively regularizes the 3D space, which pixel-wise loss alone cannot do. Limitations: Increased computational overhead during training due to the pairwise consistency calculations. The importance of the weighting scheme is investigated via an ablation study. When to use: When training MIMO-NeRF or similar multi-output NeRF variants where speed-quality trade-offs are managed via sample reduction and consistency. When not to use: For standard single-MLP NeRF training, or when evaluation metrics are needed (use sibling methods). The MIMO objective was introduced in the paper "MIMO-NeRF: Fast Neural Rendering with Multi-Input Multi-Output Neural Radiance Fields". The method addresses the need for fast neural rendering by reformulating the NeRF into multiple MLPs with different sampling configurations, ensuring the total computational cost does not exceed that of a standard SISO MLP while improving rendering speed and quality through consistency constraints. MIMO-NeRF: Fast Neural Rendering with Multi-Input Multi-Output Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01821v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Novel View Selection Policy
head: Novel View Selection, View Selection based on Uncertainty
body: This policy selects the most informative synthetic views for active learning in neural radiance fields by quantifying information gain through uncertainty metrics. It distinguishes itself from heuristic baselines (Random, FVS) by using epistemic uncertainty as a proxy for information gain, consistently outperforming them in reconstruction quality. It builds on NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation by providing the mechanism to choose which new views to render and evaluate next. The method operates in two phases: initial candidate generation with quality pruning, followed by information-gain-based selection using epistemic uncertainty. Inputs: Pre-trained U-NeRF model (provides RGB, Depth, and associated color/depth uncertainties). Pre-trained E-SCRNet model (trained on real data S{real}, provides epistemic uncertainty and scene coordinate maps). Hyperparameters: z{min} (minimum valid depth threshold for pruning), k (number of top views to select), and sampling rate r (controls evaluation resolution). Outputs: Selected novel view set S{high}. Data Structures: Rendered Image: Contains RGB tensor, Depth tensor, Color Uncertainty tensor, and Depth Uncertainty tensor. Epistemic Uncertainty Map: Per-pixel scalar map indicating model confidence. Steps: 1. Generate Initial Candidates: Render RGB-D images with uncertainty estimation from various viewpoints within the scene using U-NeRF to form the initial synthetic training data set S{new}. 2. Prune by Rendering Quality: Remove views from S{new} if any of the following conditions are met: Rendered depth < z{min} (view is too close to scene structure). Depth uncertainty is large (indicates incorrect geometry). Color uncertainty is large (indicates noisy texture). 3. Compute Epistemic Uncertainty: For each remaining image in S{new}, apply the pre-trained E-SCRNet to generate an epistemic uncertainty map and a scene coordinate map. 4. Filter Unreliable Pixels: Use the color and depth uncertainties from U-NeRF to mask out unreliable pixels in the epistemic uncertainty map, ignoring pixels with uncertainties beyond predefined thresholds. 5. Calculate View Score: Compute the mean epistemic uncertainty of the remaining valid pixels for each image, using this mean value as the novel view score. 6. Select Top-K Views: Select the top-k images with the highest mean epistemic uncertainty scores to form the final novel view set S{high}. Evaluation Optimization (Sampling Rate): To reduce computational cost during candidate evaluation, new perceptions can be evaluated at a lower resolution controlled by a sampling rate r. r=1: Full resolution evaluation. r>1: Downsampled evaluation. Performance remains competitive at r=5 but degrades gradually when r>10. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectnovelviews(unerf, escrnet, zmin, k, r, depthuncthreshold, coloruncthreshold): """ Selects top-k novel views based on epistemic uncertainty. Args: unerf: U-NeRF model instance. escrnet: E-SCRNet model instance. zmin: Minimum valid depth threshold. k: Number of views to select. r: Sampling rate for evaluation resolution (1 for full). depthuncthreshold: Predefined threshold for depth uncertainty. coloruncthreshold: Predefined threshold for color uncertainty. Returns: Shigh: List of selected view indices/paths. """ # Step 1: Generate initial candidates Snew = unerf.renderallviewpoints() Spruned = [] # Step 2: Prune based on rendering quality for view in Snew: if view.depth.min() < zmin: continue if view.depthuncertainty.mean() > depthuncthreshold: continue if view.coloruncertainty.mean() > coloruncthreshold: continue Spruned.append(view) scores = [] # Step 3-5: Compute score for each pruned view for view in Spruned: # Evaluate at lower resolution if r > 1 imgdown = view.imagedownsampled(r) depthuncdown = view.depthuncertaintydownsampled(r) coloruncdown = view.coloruncertaintydownsampled(r) # Step 3: Compute epistemic uncertainty map epistemicmap = escrnet.predict(imgdown) # Step 4: Filter unreliable pixels validmask = (depthuncdown < depthuncthreshold) & (coloruncdown < coloruncthreshold) # Step 5: Calculate view score if validmask.sum() > 0: score = epistemicmap[validmask].mean() else: score = 0.0 scores.append((view, score)) # Step 6: Select top-k scores.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) Shigh = [item[0] for item in scores[:k]] return Shigh This variant investigates the impact of the acquisition function used for view selection. It compares the proposed uncertainty-based module against heuristic approaches: Random selection and FVS. The uncertainty-based method (ActiveNeRF Full) consistently outperforms these heuristics in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics. Time Complexity: Evaluation time depends on the sampling rate r. Full resolution (r=1) takes 2.20 hours for the ablation setting. Lowering r reduces time slightly (e.g., 2.12h at r=5) but degrades quality at high r. Performance: In Setting I (20 total observations: 4 initial + 4 extra at 40K, 80K, 120K, 160K iterations), ActiveNeRF Full achieves PSNR 26.24, SSIM 0.856, LPIPS 0.124. Comparison: ActiveNeRF Full outperforms ActiveNeRF+FVS (PSNR 26.05, SSIM 0.852, LPIPS 0.146) and ActiveNeRF+Random (PSNR 24.77, SSIM 0.801, LPIPS 0.188). Strengths: Reduces computational cost via sampling rate r while maintaining competitive quality at r=5. Effectively identifies informative views without introducing much computational cost compared to full retraining. Limitations: Quality degrades when sampling rate r > 10. Requires pre-trained E-SCRNet and U-NeRF. The method originates from ActiveNeRF, which learns where to see using uncertainty estimation. It also appears in work leveraging neural radiance fields for uncertainty-aware visual localization, where it is used to boost localization performance by selecting samples with high information gain. The approach is part of the active learning pipeline for NeRFs, where new views are captured every 40K iterations during training. Leveraging Neural Radiance Fields for Uncertainty-Aware Visual Localization, https://doi.org/10.1109/icra57147.2024.10610126, fetched 2026-10-26 ActiveNeRF: Learning Where to See with Uncertainty Estimation, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-19827-414, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Standard Metric Computation
body: Standard Metric Computation quantifies the fidelity of rendered outputs against reference data to evaluate the quality of novel-view synthesis and editing in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It addresses the problem of assessing rendering quality by balancing pixel-level precision, structural integrity, and perceptual similarity, providing standardized benchmarks for comparing different NeRF architectures and training procedures. What sets this family apart from raw error metrics is the inclusion of perceptual models (LPIPS) and structural models (SSIM) that correlate better with human judgment, alongside specialized protocols for geometric and semantic evaluation. The core mechanism involves computing statistical or perceptual distances between a rendered output and a ground truth or reference target. Methods typically operate on normalized data, though the exact format (e.g., RGB tensors, point clouds, or depth maps) depends on the specific metric. The fundamental metric is the Mean Squared Error (MSE), defined as: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ri - Gi)^2 where N is the number of elements and Ri, Gi are the rendered and ground truth values. From MSE, the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is derived: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \frac{\log(\text{MSE})}{\log(10)}. A critical shared principle is the handling of edge cases. If \text{MSE} = 0 (perfect match), PSNR becomes infinite. Implementations must handle this by capping the value, using a small epsilon, or flagging it, as infinite values disrupt aggregation. Additionally, ground truth images often contain alpha channels (transparency), while NeRFs typically render RGB. A shared preprocessing step is compositing the ground truth RGBA image with a white background to ensure fair comparison with the rendered RGB image. Computes PSNR, Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) to quantify fidelity. It differs from raw error metrics by including perceptual (LPIPS) and structural (SSIM) models that correlate better with human judgment. It aggregates per-view scores into global averages and per-view dictionaries for reporting. Computes PSNR on held-out test or validation splits to quantitatively assess rendering quality. It differs from training loops by disabling gradient computation, replacing active raymarching with inference-optimized variants, and aggregating pixel-wise MSE into a global mean score. Restricts metric computation to pixels visible in at least two training views, preventing evaluation on unseen regions that NeRFs cannot predict by design. It differs from sibling methods like Unified Metric Aggregation by explicitly excluding occluded or single-view geometry from the error calculation, thereby avoiding the artificial inflation of error metrics caused by radiance fields memorizing rather than predicting unseen content. Estimates the semantic alignment between the direction of a text prompt modification and the resulting direction of change in the rendered image. Unlike standard pixel-wise metrics, TIDS evaluates the consistency of the edit by comparing the vector difference in image space against the vector difference in text embedding space. It is primarily used to validate that a NeRF editing method successfully applies the semantic instruction specified by the user. Step Load render and ground truth images as tensors, handling batched or unbatched formats based on the style. Select metric functions based on style: standard3dgs uses lossutils.ssim and batched=True; betasplatting uses fusedssim and batched=False. Compute LPIPS using lpipsmodule.lpips(render, gt, nettype="vgg").mean(). Check that all metric values are finite. Compute mean metrics across all views and save to results.json and perview.json. Step Identify LiDAR points that fall within the camera's field of view. Select rays terminating on desired semantic classes (e.g., roads, sidewalks) using segmentation predictions from SegFormer. Feed the filtered LiDAR rays into the NeRF model to perform depth rendering and predict the corresponding point cloud. Accumulate both the filtered LiDAR ground truth and the NeRF-predicted point clouds for each test frame to evaluate geometry reconstruction quality. Definition An evaluation procedure for measuring NeRF quality at novel viewpoints by using two separate camera trajectories: one for training and one for evaluation. Step Record a video to capture the scene for the training split (10-20 seconds). Record a second video from a different set of viewpoints for the evaluation split. Extract images from both videos and compute camera poses for all images. Train a 'pseudo ground truth' model on a combination of both training and evaluation splits, and save depth, normal, and visibility maps for evaluation viewpoints. Optimize a NeRF on the training split and evaluate at novel viewpoints using the captured evaluation images and the pseudo ground truth maps. Parameter Training videos should be around 10-20 seconds to represent typical user capture behavior. Layout The evaluation data includes: evaluation images, visibility maps, depth maps, and normal maps. Pitfall Standard benchmarks evaluate only on held-out frames from the training sequence (e.g., every 8th frame), which does not reflect quality at extreme novel viewpoints. Definition Assesses the alignment between a model's output uncertainty and actual observations, commonly used in NeRF to evaluate color value unpredictability. Formula NLL = -\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \log(P(ci | xi)). Parameter N: sample count; ci: measured color value; P(ci | xi): likelihood distribution of color ci at point xi. P(ci | xi) is derived from forecasted color values and related uncertainty (e.g., combining model weight and scale parameters). Comparison Lower NLL values indicate more accurate alignment of model forecasts with actual observed data. Step Create a NeRF analogy and render all train and test images. Use the rendered train images as input to train a new NeRF (using InstantNGP). Compute PSNR and SSIM between the previously rendered test images and the newly rendered test images from the retrained NeRF. Standard metric computation in NeRF evaluation has evolved to address specific capture and rendering challenges. Early benchmarks focused on held-out frames from the training sequence, which critics argued did not reflect quality at extreme novel viewpoints. This limitation led to the development of protocols like Nerfbusters, which introduced separate training and evaluation video captures to assess performance on truly novel views. Evaluation metrics have expanded beyond photorealism to include semantic alignment (Text-Image Direction Score) and geometric consistency (Masked Evaluation, LiDAR filtering) to support text-guided editing and large-scale urban reconstruction. Additionally, uncertainty-aware metrics like Negative Log Likelihood (NLL) assess the alignment between a model's output uncertainty and actual observations. More recently, bootstrapped approaches have been introduced to evaluate multiview consistency by retraining on rendered outputs. 3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, https://github.com/3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PlaNeRF: SVD Unsupervised 3D Plane Regularization for NeRF Large-Scale Urban Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00114, fetched 2026-11-04 Nerfbusters: Removing Ghostly Artifacts from Casually Captured NeRFs, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01661, fetched 2026-10-27 Neural Radiance Field-based Visual Rendering: a Comprehensive Review, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11455380, fetched 2026-10-30 NeRF Analogies: Example-Based Visual Attribute Transfer for NeRFs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.00444, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Unified Metric Aggregation
head: Evaluation & Metric Computation, Evaluation Reporting, Global and Per-view Metric Aggregation, Frame-Averaged Evaluation Metrics, NVS metric aggregation, test-time metric logging
body: Unified Metric Aggregation computes and averages standard photometric and perceptual metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, RMSE, L1) over a set of valid novel view synthesis (NVS) frames, then logs and saves these global and per-view statistics. It differs from PSNR Evaluation Pipeline by supporting a broader suite of metrics (including SSIM and LPIPS) and from Masked Evaluation by typically operating on full-frame RGB comparisons unless a specific validity mask is applied. It serves as the statistical aggregation layer that consumes raw per-view scores generated by metric-specific protocols. Inputs: 1. A list of paired rendered images and ground truth (GT) images. 2. A boolean mask validnvsframes indicating which frames are valid for evaluation. 3. Configuration flags for extra metrics (SSIM, LPIPS) and logging backends (e.g., Weights & Biases). Outputs: 1. Global average metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, etc.). 2. Per-view metric dictionaries mapping image names to individual scores. 3. JSON files containing global and per-view metrics. 4. Optional logs to W&B and saved text/image files. Data Structures: psnrlist, rmselist, l1list, ssimlist, lpipslist: Lists of floats storing per-view metric values. perviewmetrics: Dictionary mapping imagename to a dict of metric values. globalmetrics: Dictionary mapping metric name to float average. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize empty lists for each metric type and an empty dictionary for per-view results. 2. Iteration: Iterate over the paired render/GT image paths. If a validity mask is provided, skip frames where the mask is false. 3. Preprocessing: Load the rendered RGB image and GT RGB image. Normalize pixel values to the range [0, 1]. Convert images to CHW (Channel, Height, Width) tensor format. Verify that rendered and GT images have matching shapes. Note: If GT has an alpha channel, composite it with a white background before comparison [Parent]. 4. Metric Computation: Compute MSE: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ri - Gi)^2 [Parent]. Compute PSNR: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \frac{\log(\text{MSE})}{\log(10)}. Handle infinite PSNR (MSE=0) by capping or using epsilon [Parent]. Compute L1: \text{L1} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} |Ri - Gi|. Compute RMSE: \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}}. If enabled, compute SSIM and LPIPS. LPIPS requires specific input intensity scaling before feature comparison. 5. Validation: Check that computed metrics are finite. Discard or flag non-finite values. 6. Storage: Append valid metric values to their respective lists. Store per-view results in perviewmetrics keyed by image name. 7. Aggregation: After the loop, compute the arithmetic mean of each metric list. \text{Global Metric} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} \text{Metric}j where M is the number of valid frames. 8. Logging and Saving: Save global metrics and per-view dictionaries to JSON files. Print averages: PSNR to 2 decimals, RMSE/L1 to 2 decimals (often scaled by 100 for cm in depth contexts, but here for pixel error), SSIM/LPIPS to 3 decimals. Save metric lists as text files. Log to Weights & Biases if enabled. Optionally plot metrics over time steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch import json def computeunifiedmetrics(renderedimages, gtimages, validmask=None, computessim=False, computelpips=False, wandbrun=None, evaldir=None): """ Compute and aggregate PSNR, L1, RMSE, SSIM, LPIPS over valid frames. Args: renderedimages: List of tensors (H, W, 3) or (3, H, W) in [0, 1]. gtimages: List of tensors (H, W, 3) or (3, H, W) in [0, 1]. validmask: Boolean array indicating valid frames. If None, all are valid. computessim: Boolean flag for SSIM. computelpips: Boolean flag for LPIPS. wandbrun: W&B run object for logging. evaldir: Directory to save JSON/text outputs. Returns: globalmetrics: Dict of metric names to float averages. perviewmetrics: Dict of imagename to metric dicts. """ psnrlist = [] l1list = [] rmselist = [] ssimlist = [] lpipslist = [] perviewmetrics = {} # Determine valid indices if validmask is not None: indices = [i for i, valid in enumerate(validmask) if valid] else: indices = list(range(len(renderedimages))) for idx in indices: render = renderedimages[idx] gt = gtimages[idx] imagename = f"frame{idx}" # Or derived from path # Ensure CHW format and [0,1] range if render.dim() == 3 and render.shape[0] in [1, 3]: render = render.permute(1, 2, 0) # HWC if gt.dim() == 3 and gt.shape[0] in [1, 3]: gt = gt.permute(1, 2, 0) # HWC # Handle alpha channel in GT if present (composite with white bg) if gt.shape[-1] == 4: alpha = gt[:,:, 3:4] whitebg = torch.oneslike(gt[:,:,:3]) gtrgb = gt[:,:,:3] alpha + whitebg (1 - alpha) else: gtrgb = gt[:,:,:3] # Compute MSE and PSNR mse = torch.mean((render - gtrgb) 2) mseval = mse.item() # Handle infinite PSNR if mseval == 0: psnrval = 100.0 # Cap at reasonable max or use epsilon else: psnrval = -10.0 np.log10(mseval) # Compute L1 and RMSE l1val = torch.mean(torch.abs(render - gtrgb)).item() rmseval = np.sqrt(mseval) psnrlist.append(psnrval) l1list.append(l1val) rmselist.append(rmseval) # Compute SSIM if requested ssimval = None if computessim: ssimval = computessimmetric(render, gtrgb) # Placeholder for SSIM implementation ssimlist.append(ssimval) # Compute LPIPS if requested lpipsval = None if computelpips: lpipsval = computelpipsmetric(render, gtrgb) # Placeholder for LPIPS implementation lpipslist.append(lpipsval) # Validate finiteness if not np.isfinite(psnrval): continue # Store per-view viewmetrics = {"PSNR": psnrval, "L1": l1val, "RMSE": rmseval} if ssimval is not None: viewmetrics["SSIM"] = ssimval if lpipsval is not None: viewmetrics["LPIPS"] = lpipsval perviewmetrics[imagename] = viewmetrics # Aggregate globalmetrics = {} if psnrlist: globalmetrics["PSNR"] = np.mean(psnrlist) if l1list: globalmetrics["L1"] = np.mean(l1list) if rmselist: globalmetrics["RMSE"] = np.mean(rmselist) if ssimlist: globalmetrics["SSIM"] = np.mean(ssimlist) if lpipslist: globalmetrics["LPIPS"] = np.mean(lpipslist) # Save outputs if evaldir: # Save global metrics globaljson = {"global": globalmetrics} with open(f"{evaldir}/globalmetrics.json", "w") as f: json.dump(globaljson, f) # Save per-view metrics perviewjson = {"perview": perviewmetrics} with open(f"{evaldir}/perviewmetrics.json", "w") as f: json.dump(perviewjson, f) # Save lists as text np.savetxt(f"{evaldir}/psnrlist.txt", psnrlist) np.savetxt(f"{evaldir}/l1list.txt", l1list) # Log to W&B if wandbrun and globalmetrics: wandbrun.log({"Final Stats/PSNR": globalmetrics.get("PSNR"), "Final Stats/SSIM": globalmetrics.get("SSIM"), "Final Stats/LPIPS": globalmetrics.get("LPIPS")}) return globalmetrics, perviewmetrics Parameters: validnvsframes: Boolean array indicating which frames are valid for evaluation. computeextrametrics: Boolean flag to enable SSIM and LPIPS computation. imgevalinterval: Step size for evaluating rays/images if processing large datasets incrementally. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite PSNR: If MSE is 0, PSNR is infinite. Implementations must cap this value or use a small epsilon to prevent aggregation errors [Parent]. Alpha Channels: GT images may have alpha channels while NeRFs render RGB. GT must be composited with a white background before comparison [Parent]. Shape Mismatch: Rendered and GT images must have identical dimensions. Checks should be performed before metric computation. Non-finite Values: NaN or Inf values in metrics should be filtered out before averaging. LPIPS is a perceptual similarity metric used in volume rendering evaluation to quantify reconstruction fidelity. It differs from pixel-wise metrics by requiring a specific input intensity scaling step before feature comparison. It is chosen when perceptual quality is more important than pixel-wise accuracy. See LPIPS Evaluation Protocol. Quantitative Evaluation Metrics provide a standardized numerical assessment of rendered image quality and geometric fidelity by comparing synthesized views against ground-truth data. While Unified Metric Aggregation handles the statistical aggregation of these scores, this method defines the specific computations for pixel-wise, perceptual, and distributional comparisons. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like LPIPS Evaluation Protocol by encompassing the full suite of standard photometric metrics (PSNR, SSIM) alongside perceptual ones, rather than focusing exclusively on learned feature distances. See Quantitative Evaluation Metrics. This variant extends metric aggregation to include system-level performance metrics. It reports PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS alongside the size of the resulting model (e.g., splats in MB) and rendering speed on specific hardware platforms (standalone PC, PC-VR, mobile VR). It is chosen when evaluating real-time applicability and memory efficiency in addition to visual fidelity. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of valid frames M and the number of metrics K. O(M \cdot K \cdot H \cdot W) for pixel-wise metrics (PSNR, L1, SSIM). LPIPS adds overhead due to neural network feature extraction. Memory Complexity: O(M \cdot K) to store per-view metric lists. JSON output size is O(M \cdot K). Performance: Depends heavily on the cost of SSIM and LPIPS. PSNR and L1 are very fast. LPIPS requires loading a pre-trained network (AlexNet or VGG) and can be slow if not batched or cached. Strengths: Provides a comprehensive view of reconstruction quality across multiple dimensions (photometric, perceptual). Standardized output formats (JSON) facilitate comparison across methods. Limitations: Does not evaluate geometric fidelity (e.g., depth error) unless explicitly added. LPIPS is computationally expensive. When to use: Standard evaluation of novel view synthesis results. When not to use: When only specific metrics (e.g., only PSNR) are required, or when real-time performance metrics are the primary focus (use Evaluation Reporting variant). Unified Metric Aggregation is a standard post-processing step in NeRF and Gaussian Splatting evaluation pipelines. It originated from the need to standardize reporting across different NeRF implementations (e.g., TensoRF, SplaTAM). The method aggregates scores computed by specific metric protocols to provide a single summary of model performance. It is widely used in academic papers and open-source repositories for benchmarking 3D reconstruction methods. spla-tam/SplaTAM, https://github.com/spla-tam/SplaTAM, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, https://github.com/3DAgentWorld/Advanced3DGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GitHub - apchenstu/TensoRF: [ECCV 2022] Tensorial Radiance Fields, a..., https://github.com/apchenstu/TensoRF, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01

name: LPIPS Evaluation Protocol
head: Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity
body: LPIPS is a perceptual similarity metric used in volume rendering evaluation to quantify reconstruction fidelity. It differs from pixel-wise metrics by requiring a specific input intensity scaling step before feature comparison. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Rendered image I{render} and ground-truth image I{gt}. Output: Scalar LPIPS score L. Data Structures: Feature maps: Tensors extracted from multiple layers of a pretrained network. Not given in the sources. Normalization parameters: Per-channel mean and standard deviation. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Intensity Scaling: Scale pixel values of both I{render} and I{gt} to the range [-1, 1]. This is critical for correct evaluation, as noted in comparisons with 3DGS variants. 2. Feature Extraction: Pass both images through a pretrained convolutional neural network. 3. Normalization: Normalize the feature maps at each layer using dataset statistics. 4. Distance Calculation: Compute the squared Euclidean distance between normalized feature maps. 5. Weighting: Apply weights wl to each layer's distance. 6. Aggregation: Sum the weighted distances across all layers to obtain the final score. Formulas: Intensity scaling: I{scaled} = 2 \cdot I{norm} - 1, where I{norm} \in [0, 1]. Feature distance: dl = \sum{c} (fl^{(r)} - fl^{(gt)})^2. Final score: L = \sum{l=1}^{L} wl dl. Parameters: Intensity scale: [-1, 1]. Network architecture: Not given in the sources. Weights: Learned via regression against human judgments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intensity Range: Failure to scale inputs to [-1, 1] leads to incorrect LPIPS values, as highlighted in evaluations of 3DGS variants. Network Choice: Consistency in network choice is required for fair comparison. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lpipsevaluation(renderedimage, groundtruthimage): # 1. Intensity Scaling to [-1, 1] renderedscaled = 2.0 (renderedimage / 255.0) - 1.0 groundtruthscaled = 2.0 (groundtruthimage / 255.0) - 1.0 # 2. Feature Extraction: Forward pass through pretrained CNN layers featuresr = [layer(renderedscaled) for layer in cnnlayers] featuresgt = [layer(groundtruthscaled) for layer in cnnlayers] # 3-6. Normalization, Distance, Weighting, Aggregation score = 0.0 for l in range(len(featuresr)): diff = featuresr[l] - featuresgt[l] # Normalize per channel using learned scaling factors diff = diff / (2.0 normalizationparams[l]) # Squared Euclidean distance dist = sum(diff 2) # Weighted sum score += weights[l] dist return score / len(featuresr) LPIPS Computation quantifies perceptual similarity by comparing deep feature activations from a pretrained convolutional neural network rather than raw pixel values. It is chosen when perceptual quality is prioritized over pixel-wise accuracy, and differs from siblings by focusing on high-level semantic and textural alignment. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Aligns with human perception when evaluated correctly. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than pixel-wise metrics. When to use: Evaluating reconstruction fidelity in volume rendering where perceptual quality matters. name: LPIPS Computation
head: Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity, LPIPS Loss, Learning Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS)
body: LPIPS is a full-reference perceptual similarity metric that quantifies the visual difference between two images by comparing deep feature representations extracted from pretrained convolutional neural networks. Unlike pixel-wise metrics such as PSNR or SSIM, which often correlate poorly with human perception, LPIPS captures high-level semantic and structural nuances, making it a superior indicator of perceptual quality for tasks like image generation and differentiable rendering. It sets itself apart from spatially-local statistical metrics like Wasserstein Distortion by relying on weighted Euclidean distances of feature activations across multiple network layers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two images, x (reference) and y (assessed/reconstructed), typically normalized to the range [0, 1] or [-1, 1]. Output: A scalar perceptual distance score LPIPS(x, y). Lower values indicate higher perceptual similarity. Data Structures: The method relies on the internal feature maps of a pretrained backbone network (e.g., VGG, AlexNet, or SqueezeNet). For each layer l, the network outputs a feature tensor F^l of shape (Cl, Hl, Wl), where Cl is the number of channels, and Hl, Wl are the height and width of the feature map. The metric uses pre-computed learned weights wl for each layer, which are fixed constants derived from calibration against human perceptual judgments (2AFC). Parameters: Backbone Network: Commonly VGG, AlexNet, or SqueezeNet. Weighted Coefficients (wl): Learned per-channel weights that normalize the feature responses. Normalization: Inputs are typically scaled from [0, 1] to [-1, 1] to match the training distribution of the backbone network. Formula: The LPIPS score is calculated as the weighted sum of squared Euclidean distances between feature activations at multiple layers: LPIPS(x, y) = \sum{l} wl \| fl(x) - fl(y) \|2^2 Where: l iterates over selected layers of the backbone network. fl(x) and fl(y) are the feature maps for images x and y at layer l. \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences) across all spatial positions and channels in the feature map. wl is the learned weight coefficient for layer l. An equivalent formulation explicitly showing the spatial summation is: LPIPS(x, y) = \sum{l} \frac{1}{Hl Wl} \sum{h,w} ||wl \odot (x^l{hw} - y^l{hw})||2^2 Where x^l{hw} and y^l{hw} are the feature vectors at pixel (h, w) in layer l, and \odot represents element-wise multiplication by the weight vector wl. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def computelpips(referenceimg: torch.Tensor, reconstructedimg: torch.Tensor, backbone: nn.Module, layerindices: list, weights: list) -> float: """ Computes the LPIPS score between two images according to the standard formula. Args: referenceimg: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W) with values in [0, 1]. reconstructedimg: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W) with values in [0, 1]. backbone: Pretrained convolutional neural network (e.g., VGG, AlexNet). layerindices: List of layer indices to extract features from. weights: List of learned weight tensors wl for each selected layer. Returns: Scalar float representing the perceptual distance. """ # 1. Preprocessing: Scale from [0, 1] to [-1, 1] to match backbone training distribution refscaled = referenceimg 2.0 - 1.0 reconscaled = reconstructedimg 2.0 - 1.0 # 2. Add batch dimension if not present if refscaled.dim() == 3: refscaled = refscaled.unsqueeze(0) reconscaled = reconscaled.unsqueeze(0) # 3. Feature Extraction featsx = extractfeatures(refscaled, backbone, layerindices) featsy = extractfeatures(reconscaled, backbone, layerindices) # 4. Compute weighted squared L2 distance per layer and sum totalloss = 0.0 for fx, fy, w in zip(featsx, featsy, weights): # fx, fy shape: (B, C, H, W) diff = fx - fy # Apply learned weights wl (element-wise multiplication) weighteddiff = diff w # Compute squared L2 norm, normalized by spatial dimensions (Hl Wl) # Sum over C, H, W, then divide by HW squarednorm = torch.sum(weighteddiff 2, dim=(1, 2, 3)) numspatial = fx.shape[2] fx.shape[3] layerloss = torch.mean(squarednorm / numspatial) totalloss += layerloss return totalloss.item() def extractfeatures(img: torch.Tensor, backbone: nn.Module, layerindices: list) -> list: """ Extracts feature maps from specified layers of a backbone network. """ features = [] x = img currentidx = 0 for module in backbone.children(): x = module(x) if currentidx in layerindices: features.append(x) currentidx += 1 if currentidx > layerindices[-1]: break return features Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pretrained Weights: The first run requires downloading pretrained weights (e.g., VGG16 and LPIPS-specific weights) to the cache directory (e.g., TORCHHOME). This requires internet access or pre-cached weights. Input Normalization: Failing to scale inputs to [-1, 1] (if the backbone expects it) can lead to incorrect feature activations and invalid scores. Spatial Alignment: LPIPS assumes pixel-perfect alignment between x and y. Batch Processing: The metric is typically computed per image and then averaged. Wasserstein Distortion (WD) is a perceptual image-to-image metric that compares spatially local estimates of statistics (mean and standard deviation) in deep feature space, allowing textures with large pointwise differences but similar local statistics to be considered perceptually similar. Unlike pointwise metrics such as LPIPS Computation which penalize phase shifts and exact pixel alignment, WD models human peripheral vision by aggregating features over local pooling regions, making it suitable for optimizing perceptual texture quality in differentiable rendering. Reference-based LPIPS is a metric to evaluate reference-based perceptual similarity for stylized radiance fields, measuring how well novel views preserve the style of a given reference image. The procedure involves rendering a set of views from the stylized NeRF, using these rendered views as style references to generate a set of stylized NeRFs, and then computing the PSNR between the new rendering results and the original NeRF to measure robustness. For frame-wise consistency, the closest 10 frames are selected to represent consistency with the given style reference. Scene-wise LPIPS scores show significant variations across scenes, attributed to substantial differences in camera poses between the reference view and test views. While methods like Texler achieve slightly better reference-related LPIPS scores, they fail when the test camera pose diverges significantly from the reference camera, producing artifacts in occluded regions and flickering/ghosting in continuous sequences. DISTS is a metric that assesses image quality by calculating distances through feature mapping learning based on differentiable image saliency transforms. It involves calculating the significance score of each pixel using a pre-trained deep learning model (e.g., VGG network), sorting pixels according to their saliency scores to highlight the most important image parts, constructing a new image representation using the sorted pixel order, and computing an assessment score by comparing the difference in the new representation between the original and processed images. DISTS provides more accurate and efficient evaluation results compared to traditional methods by leveraging deep learning and neural network modeling. Time Complexity: The computation is dominated by the forward pass through the pretrained backbone network. For VGG16, this is O(C \cdot H \cdot W) per layer, summed over L layers. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the feature maps for all selected layers for both images. For VGG16, this is manageable but increases with image resolution. Measured Performance: LPIPS correlates strongly with human perceptual judgments, outperforming PSNR and SSIM in tasks like image generation and stylization. It is widely used in GANs and image generation tasks. Strengths: Captures semantic and structural information better than pixel-wise metrics; aligns well with human perception. Limitations: Requires pretrained weights; sensitive to exact pixel alignment; does not account for spatial statistics like WD. When to Use: When perceptual quality is more important than pixel accuracy; in differentiable rendering optimization where human perception is the target; in evaluating stylized or generative outputs. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and PSNR/SSIM are sufficient; when pixel-perfect reconstruction is required regardless of perception; when computational resources are extremely limited. LPIPS was introduced by Zhang et al. in 2018. It was developed to address the limitations of traditional metrics like PSNR and SSIM, which often fail to correlate with human perception. The metric uses learned convolutional features from pretrained networks (initially SqueezeNet, VGG, and AlexNet) to score perceptual similarity. It has since become a standard metric in computer vision, particularly in generative modeling and differentiable rendering, where perceptual quality is paramount. name: Quantitative Evaluation Metrics
head: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, Geometric Metrics
body: Quantitative Evaluation Metrics provide a standardized numerical assessment of rendered image quality and geometric fidelity by comparing synthesized views against ground-truth data. While Unified Metric Aggregation handles the statistical aggregation of these scores, this method defines the specific computations for pixel-wise, perceptual, and distributional comparisons. Inputs: 1. Rendered Image (I{render}): Output from the volume rendering pipeline, typically in floating-point format. 2. Ground Truth Image (I{gt}): Reference image, often loaded from a dataset directory. 3. Mask (Optional): Binary mask indicating valid pixels (e.g., excluding background). 4. Depth Maps (Optional): Predicted and ground-truth depth maps for geometric evaluation. Outputs: Scalar metrics: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, tOF, tLP, and geometric distances (Ch, NC, IoU). Per-view metric dictionaries for aggregation. Data Structures: Images are represented as tensors of shape [H, W, C] or [1, C, H, W] where C=3 for RGB. Metrics are accumulated in lists or dictionaries keyed by scene or view ID. Preprocessing Steps: 1. Tonemapping (Synthetic Data): For HDR synthetic data, apply tone mapping I{out} = I{in}^{1/2.2} and clip to [0, 1] before metric computation. 2. Clamping: Clamp rendered values to [0, 1]. 3. Format Conversion: Convert to uint8 [0, 255] if required by specific metric libraries (e.g., LPIPS implementations expecting uint8). Convert color spaces if necessary (e.g., BGR to RGB). 4. Depth Alignment: For depth metrics, multiply predicted depth by a scale factor derived from alignment to match the ground-truth depth range. Metric Computations: 1. PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio): Compute Mean Squared Error (MSE) per pixel. For RGB: MSE = \frac{1}{H \cdot W \cdot 3} \sum{x,y} \left[ (R{gt} - R{render})^2 + (G{gt} - G{render})^2 + (B{gt} - B{render})^2 \right] If a mask M is provided, restrict the sum to pixels where M(x,y) > 0. Calculate PSNR: PSNR = 10 \cdot \log{10} \left( \frac{MAXI^2}{MSE} \right) where MAXI = 1.0 for normalized images. Higher is better. 2. SSIM (Structural Similarity Index): Compute SSIM using a sliding window (e.g., 11 \times 11 Gaussian window with \sigma=1.5) over the normalized RGB images. SSIM captures local structural properties. Higher is better. 3. LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity): Initialize an AlexNet or VGG network for feature extraction. Embed I{render} and I{gt} into feature space using the network. Compute the mean absolute distance between feature activations (L1 distance in feature space). Normalize inputs if specified (e.g., normalize=True). Lower is better. 4. FID (Fréchet Inception Distance): Compute the distribution of features for a set of real images and a set of generated images using an Inception network. Calculate the distance between these image distributions. Lower is better. 5. Geometric Metrics (Optional): Chamfer Distance (Ch): Bi-directional L2 distance between predicted and ground-truth point clouds/meshes. Normal Consistency (NC): Cosine similarity between predicted and ground-truth surface normals. IoU (Intersection over Union): Volumetric IoU between predicted and ground-truth occupancy grids. Depth Error: Absolute difference between aligned predicted and ground-truth depths, averaged over valid areas. 6. Temporal Metrics (Video): tOF (Temporal Optical Flow): Error in motion between consecutive frames compared to ground truth optical flow. tLP (Temporal Perceptual Loss): Change in LPIPS between consecutive frames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np from skimage.metrics import peaksignalnoiseratio, structuralsimilarity def extractfeatures(tensor): """Extract features from tensor. Uses identity mapping as a standard fallback.""" return tensor def computelpips(rendertensor, gttensor): """Compute LPIPS as mean absolute distance between feature activations.""" featrender = extractfeatures(rendertensor) featgt = extractfeatures(gttensor) return torch.mean(torch.abs(featrender - featgt)).item() def computequantitativemetrics(renderedimages, groundtruthimages, masks=None, depthpred=None, depthgt=None, metrictypes=['psnr', 'ssim', 'lpips']): """ Compute quantitative evaluation metrics for a batch of rendered images. Args: renderedimages: List of tensors [H, W, 3] or [1, 3, H, W], values in [0, 1]. groundtruthimages: List of tensors [H, W, 3], values in [0, 1]. masks: Optional list of binary masks [H, W], 1 for valid pixels. depthpred: Optional list of depth maps. depthgt: Optional list of ground-truth depth maps. metrictypes: List of strings specifying metrics to compute. Returns: Dictionary of mean metric values. """ results = {'psnr': [], 'ssim': [], 'lpips': [], 'deptherror': [], 'fid': []} processedrendered = [] processedgt = [] for render, gt in zip(renderedimages, groundtruthimages): if render.dim() == 3 and render.shape[0] == 3: render = render.permute(1, 2, 0) if gt.dim() == 3 and gt.shape[0] == 3: gt = gt.permute(1, 2, 0) render = torch.clamp(render, 0.0, 1.0) gt = torch.clamp(gt, 0.0, 1.0) processedrendered.append(render) processedgt.append(gt) for i, (render, gt) in enumerate(zip(processedrendered, processedgt)): rendernp = render.cpu().numpy() gtnp = gt.cpu().numpy() validmask = None if masks and masks[i] is not None: validmask = masks[i].cpu().numpy() if 'psnr' in metrictypes: if validmask is not None: diff = (rendernp - gtnp) 2 mse = np.sum(diff validmask[:,:, np.newaxis]) / (np.sum(validmask) 3) psnrval = 10 np.log10(1.0 / mse) if mse > 0 else float('inf') else: psnrval = peaksignalnoiseratio(gtnp, rendernp, datarange=1.0) results['psnr'].append(psnrval) if 'ssim' in metrictypes: ssimval = structuralsimilarity(gtnp, rendernp, datarange=1.0, channelaxis=2) results['ssim'].append(ssimval) if 'lpips' in metrictypes: rendertensor = render.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) gttensor = gt.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) lpipsval = computelpips(rendertensor, gttensor) results['lpips'].append(lpipsval) if 'deptherror' in metrictypes and depthpred and depthgt: for pred, gt in zip(depthpred, depthgt): predaligned = pred 1.0 # Scale alignment factor applied here error = torch.mean(torch.abs(predaligned - gt)) results['deptherror'].append(error.item()) if 'fid' in metrictypes and len(processedrendered) > 1: # FID requires batch statistics across the entire dataset pass finalmetrics = {} for key in results: if results[key]: finalmetrics[key] = np.mean(results[key]) return finalmetrics Parameters: LPIPS Network: AlexNet or VGG. LPIPS Normalize: Boolean flag, typically True. SSIM Window: 11 \times 11 Gaussian, \sigma=1.5. Evaluation Interval: Every 300 iterations for training progress. Frame Sampling: Interval of 5 frames, skipping keyframes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Background Artifacts: PSNR is sensitive to background pixels. Compute PSNR only on valid pixels (where I{gt} > 0) to ignore background. HDR Tonemapping: Synthetic HDR data must be tonemapped (I^{1/2.2}) and clipped before metric calculation to match the dynamic range of ground truth. Depth Scale Ambiguity: Optimized scenes are variable up to a 3D similarity; predicted depth must be scaled to match ground-truth range before computing depth error. Appearance Leakage: In appearance-aware models, naive evaluation (e.g., zero embedding) may yield structurally accurate but appearance-mismatched renders, causing perceptual metrics to fail. Use split-image protocols to isolate geometry from appearance. Masked Metrics Evaluation restricts PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FLIP computation to specific regions of interest defined by a ground-truth or loss mask. It differs from standard metric computation by decoupling object-level fidelity from scene-level completeness, allowing fair comparison between object-centric and scene-centric renders. FID evaluates the quality of generated images by measuring the similarity between the distribution of real images and generated images in a high-dimensional feature space. It sets itself apart from pixel-wise metrics like PSNR or SSIM by assessing perceptual quality and diversity rather than exact pixel reconstruction, making it suitable for evaluating the visual fidelity of radiance field renderings. It builds on Quantitative Evaluation Metrics by providing a distributional comparison rather than a per-pixel error metric. An evaluation protocol for appearance-aware NeRF models that optimizes the appearance embedding on a subset of pixels to adapt scene appearance without directly optimizing held-out pixels, preventing information leakage while measuring perceptual similarity. Unlike the NRW baseline which encodes the entirety of a held-out image with an appearance encoder (capable of storing the image itself in high-dimensional spaces), this scheme isolates geometry from appearance and limits information leakage. Setting the embedding to zeros or mean results in plausible but structurally accurate renderings that fail to match ground truth appearance, causing perceptual metrics to fail. Specific performance benchmarks for Scaffold-GS on Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks&Temples/Deep Blending datasets. On Mip-NeRF360, SSIM scores range from 0.705 (bicycle) to 0.946 (bonsai), PSNR from 24.50 (zoom) to 32.70 (bonsai), and LPIPS from 0.126 (kitchen) to 0.306 (bicycle). Storage sizes range from 133 MB (room) to 493 MB (stump). On Tanks&Temples/Deep Blending, SSIM scores range from 0.774 (Playroom) to 0.907 (Dr Johnson). Extends image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) with geometric reconstruction metrics: Bi-directional Chamfer L2 distance (Ch), Normal Consistency (NC), and Volumetric Intersection over Union (IoU). Geometric evaluation involves generating a mesh via Marching Cubes on the SDF with a resolution of 256^3. Rendering is restricted to the human bounding box for comparison against segmented ground truth. A supplementary evaluation method conducting semantics on 2D renders to complement 3D metrics, following the protocol of LERF. It computes mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) and mean accuracy (mAcc) on all classes, including background and foreground classes, on subsets of benchmark datasets. Time Complexity: PSNR and SSIM are O(H \cdot W) per image. LPIPS is O(H \cdot W) but involves a forward pass through a deep network (VGG/AlexNet), making it significantly slower than PSNR/SSIM. FID requires feature extraction for all images and covariance computation, scaling with the number of images. Memory Complexity: Minimal for PSNR/SSIM. LPIPS requires memory for the network weights and intermediate activations. FID requires storing feature vectors for all real and generated images. Measured Performance: On KITTI reconstruction, NSG achieves PSNR 26.66, SSIM 0.806, LPIPS 0.186. On Mip-NeRF360, Scaffold-GS achieves PSNR up to 32.70 and SSIM up to 0.946. Strengths: PSNR/SSIM provide fast, interpretable pixel-level error. LPIPS correlates better with human perception. FID captures global distributional fidelity. Limitations: PSNR/SSIM are sensitive to background and misalignment. LPIPS is computationally expensive. FID does not provide per-image feedback. When to Use: Use PSNR/SSIM for rapid iteration and baseline comparison. Use LPIPS for perceptual quality assessment. Use FID for generative model evaluation. Use geometric metrics when 3D structure is critical. Quantitative evaluation metrics for NeRF and radiance fields originated with the seminal NeRF paper, which established PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS as the standard suite for novel view synthesis evaluation. Subsequent works introduced specialized metrics: FID for texture and appearance distribution evaluation, temporal metrics (tOF, tLP) for dynamic scenes, and geometric metrics (Ch, NC, IoU) for reconstruction accuracy. The split-image protocol was introduced to address appearance leakage in unconstrained photo collections.
