name: Masked Metrics Evaluation
head: Loss-masked Metric Reporting, Masked PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, Object-crop image quality metrics
body: Masked Metrics Evaluation is a protocol for computing quantitative image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FLIP) restricted to specific regions of interest, typically defined by a ground-truth or loss mask, to isolate visible reconstruction quality from background artifacts. It differs from standard metric computation by decoupling object-level fidelity from scene-level completeness, allowing fair comparison between object-centric and scene-centric renders. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered image I{pred}, ground truth image I{gt}, binary mask M (where M{ij}=1 for pixels inside the region of interest, 0 otherwise). Outputs: Scalar metric values (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) computed over the masked region, often reported alongside full-image metrics. Data Structures: Mask M: Binary tensor of same spatial dimensions as I{pred} and I{gt}. Metric Functions: Standard implementations of PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, or FLIP. Steps: 1. Full-Image Baseline (Optional): Compute standard metrics over all pixels P{all} in I{pred} and I{gt}. 2. Mask Application: Identify valid pixels P{mask} = \{(i,j) | M{ij} = 1\}. 3. Restricted Computation: Compute the chosen metric Metric(I{pred}, I{gt}) using only pixels in P{mask}. 4. Reporting: Report the masked metric value, often in parentheses next to the full-image value. Formulas: For PSNR, the masked mean squared error (MSE) is: MSE{mask} = \frac{1}{|P{mask}|} \sum{(i,j) \in P{mask}} (I{pred}(i,j) - I{gt}(i,j))^2 PSNR{mask} = 10 \cdot \log{10} \left( \frac{MAXI^2}{MSE{mask}} \right) where MAXI is the maximum possible pixel value (e.g., 1.0 or 255). Parameters: Mask Source: Can be a loss mask (from training supervision) or a ground-truth object mask. Evaluation Views: For radiance field completion, metrics are averaged across evaluation views (typically 10 randomly chosen views). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Mask: If |P{mask}| = 0, the metric is undefined. Guard against division by zero. Boundary Precision: Mask boundaries may introduce aliasing if not aligned with pixel centers. Ensure mask and image resolutions match exactly. Depth Projection: In masked radiance field completion, the mask is projected into the image plane using depth estimated from the input radiance field f{in}. Errors in depth estimation affect the mask validity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemaskedpsnr(renderedimage, gtimage, mask): """ Compute PSNR restricted to pixels where mask is 1. renderedimage: numpy array (H, W, C) gtimage: numpy array (H, W, C) mask: numpy array (H, W) of 0s and 1s """ # Identify valid pixels validpixels = mask == 1 if not np.any(validpixels): return float('nan') # Guard against empty mask # Extract valid pixels predvalid = renderedimage[validpixels] gtvalid = gtimage[validpixels] # Compute MSE mse = np.mean((predvalid - gtvalid) 2) # Compute PSNR if mse == 0: return float('inf') maxval = 1.0 # Assuming normalized [0,1] images psnr = 10 np.log10((maxval 2) / mse) return psnr def evaluatemaskedmetrics(renderedimages, gtimages, masks, numviews=10): """ Average masked PSNR across evaluation views. renderedimages: list of images gtimages: list of images masks: list of masks """ psnrvalues = [] for i in range(numviews): psnr = computemaskedpsnr(renderedimages[i], gtimages[i], masks[i]) if not np.isnan(psnr): psnrvalues.append(psnr) if not psnrvalues: return float('nan') return np.mean(psnrvalues) A metric for evaluating masked radiance field completion that computes PSNR only on non-masked pixels projected from depth. Given a binary mask m of the input radiance field f{in}, the non-masked area is computed by depth-based projection into the image plane using depth estimated from f{in}. The mPSNR is then computed by averaging the PSNR on the non-masked pixels for all evaluation views (typically 10 randomly chosen views). This variant is specifically designed for scenarios where the mask is derived from the input field's geometry rather than a ground-truth object label. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the mask. Negligible overhead compared to rendering. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the mask and intermediate valid pixel arrays. Strengths: Isolates object reconstruction quality from background errors; enables fair comparison between object-centric and scene-centric methods. Limitations: Requires a reliable mask; metrics can be misleading if the mask is inaccurate or misaligned. When to Use: When evaluating object-level fidelity in the presence of background noise or when comparing methods with different scene coverage. When Not to Use: When scene-level completeness is the primary concern; use full-image metrics instead. The protocol originates from NeRS [38] as "Object-crop image quality" metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FLIP). It has been adopted in works like Splatt3R and CADSplat to report metrics on loss-masked regions. The mPSNR variant was introduced in DiffRF for masked radiance field completion. name: FID Evaluation
head: Fréchet Inception Distance
body: FID evaluates the quality of generated images by measuring the similarity between the distribution of real images and the distribution of generated images in a high-dimensional feature space. It sets itself apart from pixel-wise metrics like PSNR or SSIM by assessing perceptual quality and diversity rather than exact pixel reconstruction, making it suitable for evaluating the visual fidelity of radiance field renderings. It builds on Quantitative Evaluation Metrics by providing a distributional comparison rather than a per-pixel error metric. Inputs: 1. A set of N real images \mathcal{R} = \{r1, \dots, rN\}. 2. A set of M generated images \mathcal{G} = \{g1, \dots, gM\}. 3. A pretrained Inception-v3 model. Outputs: A single scalar score: the Fréchet Inception Distance. Lower scores indicate higher similarity in visual appearance and diversity. Data Structures: Feature Vectors: For each image, a feature vector z \in \mathbb{R}^k is extracted from the pool3 layer of the Inception-v3 network. The dimension k is typically 2048. Statistics: Two multivariate Gaussian distributions are characterized by their mean vectors \mur, \mug \in \mathbb{R}^k and covariance matrices \Sigmar, \Sigmag \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Resize all images to a fixed resolution (typically 128 \times 128) using antialiased resampling (area interpolation) if necessary, as FID is sensitive to resizing artifacts. Ensure backgrounds are handled consistently (e.g., empty background value 0/gray). 2. Feature Extraction: Pass each image through the pretrained Inception-v3 model. Extract the feature vector z from the pool3 layer for each image. 3. Statistics Calculation: Compute the sample mean and covariance for the real and generated feature sets: \mur = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N z{r,i}, \quad \Sigmar = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (z{r,i} - \mur)(z{r,i} - \mur)^T \mug = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^M z{g,j}, \quad \Sigmag = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^M (z{g,j} - \mug)(z{g,j} - \mug)^T 4. Distance Calculation: Compute the Fréchet distance between the two Gaussian distributions: \text{FID} = \|\mur - \mug\|^2 + \text{Tr}(\Sigmar + \Sigmag - 2(\Sigmar \Sigmag)^{1/2}) where \text{Tr}(\cdot) is the trace operator and (\Sigmar \Sigmag)^{1/2} is the matrix square root. Parameters: Resolution: 128 \times 128 is standard. Resampling: Antialiased (area interpolation) is required if resizing is needed. Background: For fair comparison in radiance field contexts, evaluate on empty backgrounds (value 0/gray). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sample Size: FID can be biased by small sample sizes. Ensure N and M are sufficiently large and consistent across comparisons. Resizing Sensitivity: FID is sensitive to resizing methods. Always use antialiased resampling. Implementation Consistency: When comparing against other methods, compute FID under identical settings by modifying their public implementations if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.linalg import sqrtm def extractfeatures(images, inceptionmodel): """ Extracts pool3 features from images using a pretrained Inception-v3 model. images: array of shape (N, H, W, C) Returns: array of shape (N, 2048) """ # Preprocess images: resize to 128x128 with antialiasing if needed # Pass through Inception-v3 and extract pool3 layer output features = [] for img in images: # Placeholder for actual model inference feat = inceptionmodel.predict(img) features.append(feat) return np.array(features) def calculatefid(realfeatures, generatedfeatures): """ Calculates the Fréchet Inception Distance between two sets of features. realfeatures: array of shape (N, 2048) generatedfeatures: array of shape (M, 2048) Returns: float FID score """ mur = np.mean(realfeatures, axis=0) sigmar = np.cov(realfeatures, rowvar=False) mug = np.mean(generatedfeatures, axis=0) sigmag = np.cov(generatedfeatures, rowvar=False) diff = mur - mug # Compute the trace of the sum of covariances minus 2 times the square root of the product # Note: sqrtm computes the matrix square root covmean = sqrtm(sigmar.dot(sigmag)) # Handle numerical errors if np.iscomplexobj(covmean): covmean = covmean.real fid = diff.dot(diff) + np.trace(sigmar + sigmag - 2.0 covmean) return fid KID is an extension of FID that measures the Maximum Mean Discrepancy between feature distributions using kernel functions. It provides an unbiased estimation of the true distance between distributions, ensuring a more accurate representation of similarity in feature space. KID is robust to the choice of sample size, minimizing variability from different sample sizes, and requires fewer samples for calculation compared to alternative metrics. Time Complexity: Dominated by the feature extraction step using the Inception-v3 model, which is computationally expensive. The statistical calculation is O(k^2) or O(k^3) depending on the matrix square root implementation, where k=2048. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature vectors for all real and generated images. For N images, this is O(N \cdot k). Strengths: Correlates well with human perception of image quality and diversity. Robust to minor pixel-level variations that PSNR/SSIM penalize heavily. Limitations: Sensitive to sample size and resizing methods. Does not provide per-image scores, only a global distributional metric. Computationally heavy due to the deep neural network. When to Use: When evaluating the perceptual quality and diversity of generated radiance field renderings, especially when pixel-perfect accuracy is less important than visual fidelity. When Not to Use: When per-pixel accuracy is required (use PSNR/SSIM) or when computational resources are extremely limited. FID was introduced as a metric for evaluating generative models and image synthesis tasks. It uses the Inception-v3 model pretrained on ImageNet to extract features. It has been adopted in radiance field evaluation to assess the visual quality of generated scenes, often in conjunction with other metrics like PSNR and SSIM. It is particularly useful for comparing the diversity and realism of generated images against real datasets. name: PSNR Evaluation Pipeline
head: NeRF validation loop, PSNR calculation, Quantitative Evaluation, Test Set PSNR, Validation and PSNR Evaluation Pipeline
body: The PSNR Evaluation Pipeline computes the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) on held-out test or validation splits to quantitatively assess the rendering quality of a trained NeRF model. It builds on Standard Metric Computation and differs from training metrics by using inference-optimized rendering paths and strictly handling ground truth transparency via white-background compositing to ensure fair comparison with the rendered RGB output. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Trained model state (coarse and/or fine MLPs), dataset split identifier ("test" or "val"), and optional resolution flag (halfres). Outputs: Per-frame PSNR values, mean PSNR, standard deviation, and optionally side-by-side visual comparisons of ground truth, rendered RGB, and depth. Data Structures Evaluation State: A model configuration object where the standard training raymarch and render functions are replaced with inference variants (e.g., stateeval = state.replace(raymarch=args.raymarcheval, render=args.rendereval)). Image Arrays: Ground truth images are stored as RGBA (uint8 or float32) and rendered images as RGB (float32). Steps 1. Load Data: Load the camera poses and images for the specified split. If halfres is true, images are loaded at half resolution (e.g., 200 \times 200 for Blender datasets). 2. Prepare State: Instantiate the evaluation state using inference-specific rendering functions. 3. Composite Ground Truth: For each ground truth image in the split, composite the RGBA image against a white background. 4. Render: Iterate over each validation view. For each view, extract the camera transform and render the image using the inference state. Chunked rendering is used to manage memory. 5. Compute MSE: Calculate the Mean Squared Error between the composite ground truth RGB and the rendered RGB. Formula: \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ri - Gi)^2, where Ri is the rendered pixel and Gi is the composite ground truth pixel. 6. Compute PSNR: Convert MSE to PSNR. Formula: \text{PSNR} = -10 \cdot \log{10}(\text{MSE}). Edge Case: If \text{MSE} = 0, PSNR is infinite. 7. Aggregate: Accumulate PSNR values across all frames in the split. Compute the mean and standard deviation. 8. Visualize (Optional): Concatenate ground truth, rendered RGB, and depth maps side-by-side for qualitative inspection. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def evaluatepsnr(modelstate, dataset, split="test", halfres=False): # Load test images and poses via loadblenderdata(..., split, halfres=True) images, poses = loaddata(dataset, split, halfres) # Standard data loading routine # Create evaluation state by replacing raymarch and render functions with inference variants evalstate = modelstate.replace(raymarch=modelstate.raymarcheval, render=modelstate.rendereval) psnrvalues = [] # Iterate over validation views, extracting camera transforms and rendering images for i, (imagergba, transform) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # Composite ground truth images with white background alpha = imagergba[..., 3:4] / 255.0 rgbgt = imagergba[...,:3] / 255.0 whitebg = np.oneslike(rgbgt) gtrgbcomposite = rgbgt alpha + whitebg (1 - alpha) # Render rays using chunked rendering rendered = renderimage(i, transform, evalstate) # Standard rendering routine renderedrgb = rendered['rgb'] # Compute MSE mse = np.mean((renderedrgb - gtrgbcomposite) 2) # Compute PSNR if mse == 0: psnr = float('inf') else: psnr = -10.0 math.log10(mse) psnrvalues.append(psnr) # Accumulate PSNRs, print per-frame and mean ± std meanpsnr = np.mean(psnrvalues) stdpsnr = np.std(psnrvalues) return meanpsnr, stdpsnr, psnrvalues Parameters split: Dataset split to evaluate ("test" or "val"). halfres: Boolean flag to load images at half resolution for faster evaluation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Infinite PSNR: Occurs when MSE is exactly zero. Alpha Handling: Failing to composite ground truth RGBA with a white background leads to incorrect MSE calculations against opaque RGB renders. Resolution Mismatch: Ensure rendered resolution matches ground truth resolution before computing MSE. A variant of the evaluation pipeline that focuses on comparing PSNR values across different methods (e.g., NeRF vs. SDF-based methods) on standard datasets like NeRFsynthetic. It highlights that NeRF often achieves higher PSNR than geometric regularization-based methods because it prioritizes color reproduction over strict geometric fidelity. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Standard, interpretable metric for image fidelity; easy to implement and compare across papers. Limitations: Does not measure geometric accuracy. When to Use: Standard validation for novel view synthesis tasks where photometric accuracy is the primary goal. The PSNR evaluation pipeline is used to benchmark rendering quality on datasets like NeRFsynthetic (Blender) and DTU. The specific handling of alpha compositing and inference state replacement is detailed in community implementations and forks. yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, https://github.com/yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) blurgyy/jaxngp, https://github.com/blurgyy/jaxngp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PET-NeuS: Positional Encoding Tri-Planes for Neural Surfaces, http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05594v1, fetched 2026-10-27

name: PSNR and Time Metrics Calculation
body: This method computes quantitative evaluation metrics for volume rendering, specifically Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for image quality and rendering time for computational performance. It parses training and rendering logs to identify the specific frames and views to evaluate, calculates per-pixel error against ground truth images, and aggregates these into mean scores. It is distinct from general metric computation by explicitly linking evaluation to specific training epochs and rendering configurations logged during the NeRF training loop. Inputs: trainlogfile: Path to the training log file containing timestamps and frame indices. renderlogfile: Path to the rendering log file containing experiment IDs and view indices. imagesbasedir: Root directory containing the rendered and ground truth images. viewstartidx: Starting index of the views to evaluate. numofviews: Number of views to evaluate. framestart: Starting frame index for evaluation. frameend: Ending frame index for evaluation. testsetviews: List of view indices included in the test set. Outputs: A CSV file containing per-view average PSNR and total rendering time statistics. Data Structures: datas: A dictionary or list of records storing metrics. Each record contains: viewid: Integer identifier of the camera view. avgpsnr: Float, average PSNR across all evaluated frames for this view. rendertime: Float, total time to render the sequence of frames for this view (if measured). Steps: 1. Parse Configuration: Read trainlogfile to extract trainexpid, imagesbasedir, viewstartidx, and numofviews. Read renderlogfile to extract renderexpid, framestart, frameend, and testsetviews. Ensure imagesbasedir exists and contains the expected image format (e.g.,.jpg). 2. Initialize Metrics Storage: Create an empty dictionary viewpsnrs mapping viewid to a list of PSNR values. Initialize totalrendertime to 0.0. 3. Iterate Over Frames and Views: For each frameidx in range framestart to frameend (inclusive): For each viewid in testsetviews: Construct origpath: Path to the rendered image. Format: {imagesbasedir}/{renderexpid}/{viewid}/{frameidx:04d}.jpg (format may vary by implementation). Construct targetpath: Path to the ground truth image. Format: {imagesbasedir}/{trainexpid}/{viewid}/{frameidx:04d}.jpg. Read origimg and targetimg using cv2.imread. Handle cases where images are not found or cannot be read (e.g., skip or log error). Calculate psnr using cv2.PSNR(origimg, targetimg). Append psnr to viewpsnrs[viewid]. 4. Calculate Rendering Time (Optional/Contextual): If rendering time is to be measured, parse trainlogfile for timestamps associated with the rendering of specific frames or views. Use regex patterns to extract start and end times: patternstarttraining = re.compile(r'\[(.?)\] - Start training frame(\d+)') patternendtraining = re.compile(r'\[(.?)\] - End training frame(\d+)') Note: The provided source uses these patterns for training frames, but the method description implies evaluating rendered frames. If measuring rendering time specifically, ensure the log contains corresponding "Render" events or use wall-clock time during the evaluation loop. If not available, report "Not given in the sources." for precise per-frame rendering time extraction from logs in this specific script context. 5. Aggregate Results: For each viewid in viewpsnrs: Calculate avgpsnr = sum(viewpsnrs[viewid]) / len(viewpsnrs[viewid]). Store viewid and avgpsnr in datas. 6. Save Results: Write datas to a CSV file with columns: viewid, avgpsnr. Formulas: PSNR: \text{PSNR} = 10 \cdot \log{10} \left( \frac{\text{MAX}I^2}{\text{MSE}} \right) Where \text{MAX}I is the maximum possible pixel value (e.g., 255 for 8-bit images) and \text{MSE} is the Mean Squared Error between the rendered and ground truth images. Average PSNR per View: \text{AvgPSNR}v = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \text{PSNR}{v,i} Where N is the number of frames evaluated for view v. Parameters: cv2.PSNR: Uses default parameters for 8-bit images. Image format: Typically.jpg or.png. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Images: If a rendered or ground truth image is missing, cv2.imread returns None. The implementation must handle this to avoid crashes. Dimension Mismatch: Ensure rendered and ground truth images have identical dimensions. Log Parsing Errors: Regex patterns for log parsing may fail if log format changes. provides specific patterns for "Start training frame" and "End training frame". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import cv2 import re import csv import os def calculatepsnrtimemetrics(trainlogfile, renderlogfile, imagesbasedir, viewstartidx, numofviews, framestart, frameend, testsetviews): # Parse renderlogfile for framestart, frameend, testsetviews # Note: Actual parsing logic depends on log format. Assuming these are extracted as inputs. viewpsnrs = {viewid: [] for viewid in testsetviews} for frameidx in range(framestart, frameend + 1): for viewid in testsetviews: # Construct paths - format may vary origpath = os.path.join(imagesbasedir, f"{frameidx:04d}{viewid}.jpg") targetpath = os.path.join(imagesbasedir, f"gt{frameidx:04d}{viewid}.jpg") if not os.path.exists(origpath) or not os.path.exists(targetpath): continue origimg = cv2.imread(origpath) targetimg = cv2.imread(targetpath) if origimg is None or targetimg is None: continue # Calculate PSNR psnr = cv2.PSNR(origimg, targetimg) viewpsnrs[viewid].append(psnr) # Aggregate results datas = [] for viewid, psnrlist in viewpsnrs.items(): if len(psnrlist) > 0: avgpsnr = sum(psnrlist) / len(psnrlist) datas.append({'viewid': viewid, 'avgpsnr': avgpsnr}) # Save to CSV with open('metrics.csv', 'w', newline='') as csvfile: fieldnames = ['viewid', 'avgpsnr'] writer = csv.DictWriter(csvfile, fieldnames=fieldnames) writer.writeheader() for row in datas: writer.writerow(row) return datas Measures the computational cost of rendering, typically in seconds per image. reports that rendering a single 800x800 image takes 25.59 seconds for Vanilla NeRF and 32.35 seconds for PL-NeRF on the Lego scene. Total rendering time varies with sample counts: (64+64) samples take 19.20 seconds, (64+128) take 25.85 seconds, and (128+64) take 32.35 seconds for PL-NeRF. Compares the efficiency and quality trade-offs between different NeRF variants. PL-NeRF converges to a higher training PSNR than Vanilla NeRF under different numbers of samples, despite requiring more FLOPS and being slightly slower due to importance sampling computations. Time Complexity: The PSNR calculation is O(P) per image pair, where P is the number of pixels. The total time is proportional to the number of frames and views evaluated. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot F) to store PSNR values, where V is the number of views and F is the number of frames. Images are loaded and discarded, so peak memory is O(P). Measured Performance: On an Nvidia V100 GPU, training times were 17.78 hours for Vanilla NeRF and 21.43 hours for PL-NeRF. Rendering times for 800x800 images range from 19.20 to 32.35 seconds depending on the method and sample count. Strengths: Provides a standard, quantitative measure of rendering quality (PSNR) and computational cost. Limitations: PSNR is not always correlated with perceptual quality. Rendering time measurements are hardware-dependent. When to Use: Standard evaluation of NeRF training progress and final model quality. When Not to Use: When perceptual metrics (e.g., LPIPS) are more relevant, or when real-time performance is the primary concern. The method is derived from evaluation scripts used in NeRF research, specifically those associated with Dynamic-NGPs and PL-NeRF. The use of PSNR as a primary metric is standard in the field. The specific log parsing and aggregation logic is detailed in the Dynamic-NGPs repository. name: Masked Evaluation
head: Depth reprojection masking, Evaluation Visibility Mask Generation
body: Masked Evaluation restricts radiance field metric computation to pixels visible in at least two training views, preventing metric degradation from evaluating regions that neural radiance fields cannot predict by design. Unlike sibling methods like Unified Metric Aggregation which may aggregate errors across all pixels, or PSNR Evaluation Pipeline which computes standard metrics on full images, this method explicitly excludes occluded or single-view-only geometry to ensure fair comparison of geometric consistency. It differs from View-Consistency Metric (Ewarp) by serving as a preprocessing step for standard metrics rather than a self-supervised regularizer, using depth reprojection to define the valid evaluation domain. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Set of training views with associated camera poses, intrinsics, and predicted depth maps generated by a Dense-NeRF model. Test view with associated camera pose, intrinsics, and predicted depth map from the same Dense-NeRF model. Threshold parameter \tau. Outputs: Binary visibility mask M{test} of the same spatial dimensions as the test view, where M{test}(x,y) = 1 if the pixel is visible in at least two training views, and 0 otherwise. Data Structures: Depth maps are 2D arrays of floating-point values representing distance from the camera center. The mask is a 2D binary array. Steps: 1. Initialize Visibility Counter: Create a zero-initialized integer array C{test} with the same height and width as D{test}. This array will count how many training views consider each pixel visible. 2. Iterate Training Views: For each training view vi: a. Reprojection: Warp the depth map Di from the coordinate system of vi to the coordinate system of v{test} using depth-based reprojection. Let the warped depth map be D{i \to test}. b. Depth Comparison: For each pixel (x,y) in v{test}: i. Retrieve the predicted depth from the test view: d{test} = D{test}(x,y). ii. Retrieve the warped depth from the training view: d{warped} = D{i \to test}(x,y). iii. Compute the absolute depth difference: \Delta d = |d{test} - d{warped}|. iv. Thresholding: If \Delta d < \tau, mark the pixel as visible in view vi by incrementing the counter: C{test}(x,y) \leftarrow C{test}(x,y) + 1. 3. Final Mask Generation: For each pixel (x,y) in v{test}: a. If C{test}(x,y) \ge 2, set M{test}(x,y) = 1. b. Otherwise, set M{test}(x,y) = 0. Parameters: Depth Difference Threshold (\tau): Set to 0.05 \times \max(D{train}), where \max(D{train}) is the maximum depth value in the training view's depth map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatemaskedevaluationmask( trainviews: list, testview: dict, thresholdfactor: float = 0.05) -> list: """ Generates a binary visibility mask for a test view based on depth consistency with at least two training views. Args: trainviews: List of dicts with keys 'id', 'K', 'P', 'depth'. testview: Dict with keys 'id', 'K', 'P', 'depth'. thresholdfactor: Factor to multiply max depth by for thresholding. Returns: 2D list representing the binary visibility mask. """ h, w = len(testview['depth']), len(testview['depth'][0]) visibilitycount = [[0 for in range(w)] for in range(h)] for trainview in trainviews: dtrain = trainview['depth'] dtest = testview['depth'] # Threshold calculation per training view maxdepthtrain = max(max(row) for row in dtrain) threshold = thresholdfactor maxdepthtrain # Warp depth from trainview to testview dwarped = warpdepth(dtrain, trainview['K'], trainview['P'], testview['K'], testview['P'], h, w) # Compute absolute difference and visibility for y in range(h): for x in range(w): dt = dtest[y][x] dw = dwarped[y][x] # Handle invalid depths (e.g., from occlusions in source view) if dt <= 0 or dw <= 0 or not (dt == dt and dw == dw): continue diff = abs(dt - dw) if diff < threshold: visibilitycount[y][x] += 1 # Generate final mask: visible in at least 2 views mask = [[1 if visibilitycount[y][x] >= 2 else 0 for x in range(w)] for y in range(h)] return mask def warpdepth(depthmap, Ksrc, Psrc, Kdst, Pdst, h, w): """ Warps a depth map from source view to destination view using standard pinhole camera geometry. """ # 1. Create 2D grid of pixel coordinates in source view # 2. Unproject to 3D points in source camera frame # 3. Transform 3D points to world frame using inverse of Psrc # 4. Transform 3D points to destination camera frame using Pdst # 5. Project to destination image plane using Kdst # 6. Interpolate depth values onto destination grid # Note: Exact matrix operations omitted for brevity; follows standard depth reprojection. # Returns 2D array of depth values in dstview coordinate system. pass # Implementation follows standard pinhole reprojection; see Cho et al. [2017], Kanchana et al. [2022] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Accuracy Dependency: Mask accuracy is entirely dependent on the accuracy of the Dense-NeRF depth estimation; incorrect Dense-NeRF depths produce incorrect masks. Specular Surfaces: Using depth-based reprojection is robust to specular objects, whereas color-based reprojection fails on such surfaces. Unseen Regions: Unmasked evaluation includes regions not visible in training views, which radiance fields memorize rather than predict, artificially inflating error metrics. Invalid Depths: Warping may produce invalid depths (e.g., from occlusions in the source view); these should be handled by ignoring pixels where d{warped} is invalid or zero. Generates a binary visibility mask to identify pixels in a reference view that are occluded (invisible) when observed from a new camera pose. It solves the problem of evaluating or inpainting regions that have no geometric correspondence in other views, which often leads to artifacts or incorrect depth predictions in radiance field optimization. It differs from sibling methods like View-Consistency Metric by explicitly using depth warping errors to detect occlusion rather than relying solely on photometric color differences or optical flow consistency. The View-Consistency Metric (E{\text{warp}}) evaluates the geometric and photometric consistency of a radiance field by measuring the reconstruction error between a rendered view and a neighboring view warped into the target viewpoint. It serves as a self-supervised regularizer or evaluation metric that penalizes inconsistencies arising from incorrect depth or color predictions, leveraging optical flow and occlusion masks to isolate valid correspondences. It differs from standard PSNR or LPIPS by explicitly accounting for viewpoint changes and occlusions, ensuring that errors are only measured where scene content is visible in both views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of training views. Strengths: Robust to specular objects; prevents metric degradation from evaluating unseen geometry; ensures fair comparison of geometric consistency. Limitations: Highly dependent on the accuracy of the Dense-NeRF depth estimation; incorrect depths lead to incorrect masks. When to Use: When evaluating radiance fields trained on sparse input views, particularly when comparing models that may memorize unseen regions. When Not to Use: When depth estimation is unreliable or when evaluating full-image fidelity including unseen regions is desired. Masked Evaluation was introduced in the context of regularizing sparse input Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to prevent them from being evaluated on regions they cannot predict by design. Radiance fields are designed to memorize a scene and are ill-equipped to predict unseen regions or the depth of objects seen in only one input view. The method was proposed to address the issue that unmasked evaluation artificially inflates error metrics by including these unpredictable regions. It relies on depth-based reprojection techniques similar to those described by Cho et al. [2017] and Kanchana et al. [2022]. The approach was implemented and released alongside the SimpleNeRF and Simple-RF models. name: Masked Evaluation (Depth-based Visibility Mask Generation)
head: Depth reprojection masking, Invisible Mask Computation, Invisible Region Detection via Depth Warping
body: This method generates a binary visibility mask to identify pixels in a reference view that are occluded (invisible) when viewed from a new camera pose. It solves the problem of evaluating or inpainting regions that lack geometric correspondence in other views, which prevents metric degradation from predicting unseen geometry or depth of single-view objects. It differs from sibling methods like View-Consistency Metric by explicitly using depth warping errors to detect occlusion rather than relying solely on photometric color differences or optical flow consistency. Inputs: A reference view with RGB image I{rgb} and depth map Id. A new (source) view with RGB image I'{rgb} and depth map I'd. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics for both views. A trained NeRF or depth estimation model to provide initial depth values if not given directly. Outputs: A final binary mask m of the same spatial dimensions as the reference view, where m{ij}=1 indicates an invisible (occluded) pixel and m{ij}=0 indicates a visible pixel. Masked RGB image \bar{I}{rgb} and masked depth map \bar{I}d for subsequent processing (e.g., inpainting). Data Structures: Id, I'd: 2D arrays of floating-point depth values. m, m': 2D binary arrays (uint8 or bool). v{ij}: Depth value at pixel (i,j) in the reference view. v'{ij}: Warped depth value at pixel (i,j) from the new view. Steps: 1. Depth Warping: For each pixel (i,j) in the reference view, project the corresponding 3D point from the new view's depth map I'd into the reference view's coordinate system using the relative camera pose. Let the resulting depth value be v'{ij}. 2. Per-View Invisible Mask Generation: Compute the intermediate mask m' for the current new view using the indicator function: m'{ij} = \mathbb{I}(v'{ij} - v{ij} > \varepsilon) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function (1 if true, 0 otherwise). If the warped depth v'{ij} is larger than the reference depth v{ij}, the point is considered occluded in the reference view because the surface seen in the new view is behind the surface seen in the reference view. 3. Final Mask Aggregation: If multiple new views are used, compute m' for each. The final mask m is the logical AND of all intermediate masks: m = \bigwedge{k} m'k A pixel is marked invisible only if it is occluded in all compared new views. 4. Masking Inputs: Apply the final mask to the reference RGB and depth images: \bar{I}{rgb} = I{rgb} \otimes (1 - m) \bar{I}d = Id \otimes (1 - m) where \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication. Parameters: \varepsilon: A small positive threshold value to allow for minor warping errors or depth estimation noise. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth values must be consistent in units and coordinate systems. Misalignment in camera poses will cause false occlusions. Degenerate Input: If Id or I'd contains invalid values (e.g., infinity or zero), they must be handled or filtered out before warping. Boundary Conditions: Pixels at the image border may not have valid correspondences in the new view. These should be treated as invisible or masked out. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatevisibilitymask(refdepth, newdepth, refK, newK, refpose, newpose, epsilon): """ Generates an invisible mask for a reference view based on depth warping from a new view. Assumes standard pinhole camera model and 4x4 pose matrices. """ height, width = len(refdepth), len(refdepth[0]) mask = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] # Precompute inverse intrinsics and relative pose Krefinv = invertmatrix(refK) relpose = multiplymatrix(newpose, invertmatrix(refpose)) R = relpose[:3,:3] t = relpose[:3, 3] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Unproject reference pixel to 3D: Pref = Kref^-1 [x, y, 1]^T dref uref = float(x) vref = float(y) zref = refdepth[y][x] camx = Krefinv[0][0] uref + Krefinv[0][1] vref + Krefinv[0][2] camy = Krefinv[1][0] uref + Krefinv[1][1] vref + Krefinv[1][2] camz = Krefinv[2][0] uref + Krefinv[2][1] vref + Krefinv[2][2] X = camx zref Y = camy zref Z = camz zref # Transform to new view coordinate system: Pnew = R Pref + t Xnew = R[0][0]X + R[0][1]Y + R[0][2]Z + t[0] Ynew = R[1][0]X + R[1][1]Y + R[1][2]Z + t[1] Znew = R[2][0]X + R[2][1]Y + R[2][2]Z + t[2] # Project to new view image plane: pnew = Knew Pnew unewhom = newK[0][0]Xnew + newK[0][1]Ynew + newK[0][2]Znew vnewhom = newK[1][0]Xnew + newK[1][1]Ynew + newK[1][2]Znew wnew = newK[2][0]Xnew + newK[2][1]Ynew + newK[2][2]Znew if wnew <= 0: mask[y][x] = 1.0 continue unew = unewhom / wnew vnew = vnewhom / wnew # Check bounds if unew < 0 or unew >= width - 1 or vnew < 0 or vnew >= height - 1: mask[y][x] = 1.0 continue # Bilinear interpolation of newdepth at (unew, vnew) u0, v0 = int(unew), int(vnew) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 du = unew - u0 dv = vnew - v0 d00 = newdepth[v0][u0] d01 = newdepth[v0][u1] d10 = newdepth[v1][u0] d11 = newdepth[v1][u1] d0 = d00 (1 - du) + d01 du d1 = d10 (1 - du) + d11 du vprime = d0 (1 - dv) + d1 dv # Handle invalid depth values if vprime <= 0 or vprime == float('inf'): mask[y][x] = 1.0 continue # Compute mask: 1 if warped depth is significantly larger (occluded) if vprime - zref > epsilon: mask[y][x] = 1.0 else: mask[y][x] = 0.0 return mask def invertmatrix(M): """Computes inverse of a 3x3 upper-triangular intrinsic matrix.""" inv = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] inv[0][0] = 1.0 / M[0][0] inv[0][1] = -M[0][1] / (M[0][0] M[1][1]) inv[0][2] = (M[0][1]M[1][2] - M[0][2]M[1][1]) / (M[0][0]M[1][1]M[2][2]) inv[1][1] = 1.0 / M[1][1] inv[1][2] = -M[1][2] / (M[1][1]M[2][2]) inv[2][2] = 1.0 / M[2][2] return inv def multiplymatrix(A, B): """Multiplies two 3x3 matrices.""" C = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): C[i][j] += A[i][k] B[k][j] return C Generates a consistency mask Ml to identify pixels with geometric inconsistencies during feature-level regularization. It distinguishes itself by explicitly comparing rendered depth maps between views to detect warping errors, rather than relying solely on photometric color differences or optical flow consistency. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the reference view and the number of new views used for comparison. Depth warping and interpolation are the dominant operations. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels, storing depth maps and masks. Strengths: Explicitly handles occlusions by leveraging geometric consistency. Effective for identifying regions that lack multi-view support. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation or rendering. Sensitive to camera pose errors and depth noise. Does not account for textureless regions where depth estimation might be unreliable. When to Use: When inpainting or regularizing radiance fields in regions that are occluded in some views but visible in others. When Not to Use: When depth information is unavailable or highly unreliable. When computational resources are extremely limited and a simpler photometric consistency check suffices. The method originates from the PERF (Panoramic Neural Radiance Field) paper, which addresses the challenge of completing large-size occlusions in complex 3D panoramic scenes using collaborative RGBD inpainting. It was developed to overcome the limitations of adversarial learning and high-level semantic constraints, which fail to fill large invisible regions effectively. PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2024.3387307, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Occlusion-Aware Masking
head: Depth-based Visibility Mask Generation, Invisible Mask Computation, Invisible Region Detection via Depth Warping
body: Occlusion-Aware Masking generates a consistency mask Ml to ignore regions with geometric inconsistencies (such as artifacts or self-occlusion) during feature-level regularization in NeRF optimization. It sets apart from its siblings by explicitly comparing rendered depth maps between a target view and a warped source view to identify invalid warps, rather than relying solely on pixel-space optical flow consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depth map of the target (unseen) view Dj, rendered depth map of the source (seen) view Di, camera intrinsic matrix K, relative rotation R{j \to i} between views, and a distance threshold \tau. Outputs: A binary consistency mask Ml aligned with the feature map of layer l. Data Structures: Dj, Di: 2D arrays of depth values, same resolution as the image. M: Binary mask (0 or 1) of the same resolution as Dj. Ml: Downsampled mask matching the spatial dimensions of the l-th layer feature map. Steps: 1. Reprojection: For each pixel pj in the target view j, compute its corresponding coordinate p{j \to i} in the source view i using the camera parameters and the depth of the target view: p{j \to i} \sim K R{j \to i} Dj(pj) K^{-1} pj where \sim indicates approximate equality and the result is a continuous coordinate. 2. Depth Sampling: Sample the depth value Di(p{j \to i}) from the source view's depth map at the reprojected coordinate. 3. Mask Generation: Compute the binary mask M for each pixel pj using the Iverson bracket: M(pj) = [ || Dj(pj) - Di(p{j \to i}) || < \tau ] If the Euclidean distance between the target depth and the reprojected source depth exceeds \tau, the pixel is considered occluded or inconsistent and is masked out (0); otherwise, it is valid (1). 4. Downsampling: Apply nearest-neighbor downsampling to M to produce Ml, matching the dimensions of the l-th layer feature map outputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateocclusionmask(Dj, Di, K, Rjtoi, tau): """ Generate occlusion-aware mask by comparing target depth Dj with reprojected source depth Di. Args: Dj: 2D array, depth of target view j. Di: 2D array, depth of source view i. K: 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix. Rjtoi: 3x3 rotation matrix from j to i. tau: float, depth distance threshold. Returns: M: 2D binary array, same shape as Dj. """ H, W = Dj.shape M = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=float) # Precompute inverse intrinsic matrix Kinv = np.linalg.inv(K) # Create grid of pixel coordinates for target view # pj is represented as homogeneous coordinates [x, y, 1] y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') pjhomogeneous = np.stack([x, y, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1).astype(np.float32) # Shape (H, W, 3) # Reshape for matrix multiplication: (HW, 3) pjflat = pjhomogeneous.reshape(-1, 3) # Step 1: Reprojection # Formula: p{j->i} ~ K R{j->i} Dj(pj) K^{-1} pj # Note: Dj(pj) is a scalar depth value for each pixel. # We perform element-wise multiplication of depth with the transformed coordinates. # Transform pixel coordinates to camera frame of j, then to i # pcamj = K^{-1} pjhomogeneous (unproject to normalized camera coords) pcamj = np.einsum('ij, nj -> ni', Kinv, pjflat) # (HW, 3) # Scale by depth Dj # Djflat is (HW,) Djflat = Dj.reshape(-1) pcamjscaled = pcamj Djflat[:, np.newaxis] # (HW, 3) # Rotate to source camera frame i pcami = np.einsum('ij, nj -> ni', Rjtoi, pcamjscaled) # (HW, 3) # Project back to image plane of i pihomogeneous = np.einsum('ij, nj -> ni', K, pcami) # (HW, 3) # Normalize to get 2D coordinates # pi2d = pihomogeneous[:,:2] / pihomogeneous[:, 2] # Handle division by zero or near-zero depth validdepth = pihomogeneous[:, 2] > 1e-5 pi2d = np.zeros((pihomogeneous.shape[0], 2)) pi2d[validdepth] = pihomogeneous[validdepth,:2] / pihomogeneous[validdepth, 2:3] # Step 2: Sample depth from Di at pi2d # Using bilinear or nearest neighbor sampling. The source mentions "differentiable sampler" for color, # but for depth consistency in masking, nearest neighbor is often used for robustness, # or bilinear if differentiable masking is required. The text implies standard sampling. # We assume a standard bilinear sampler for Di. Disampled = sampledepth(Di, pi2d) # Helper function to sample 2D array at float coordinates # Step 3: Mask Generation # Calculate Euclidean distance between Dj and sampled Di # Note: Djflat is the depth at pj. Disampled is the depth at reprojected pj. depthdiff = np.abs(Djflat - Disampled) # Apply threshold Mflat = (depthdiff < tau).astype(float) # Reshape back to image M = Mflat.reshape(H, W) return M def downsamplemask(M, targetshape): """ Nearest-neighbor downsampling of mask M to targetshape. """ # Implementation of nearest-neighbor downsampling # Using standard interpolation with mode='nearest' return scipy.ndimage.zoom(M, (targetshape[0]/M.shape[0], targetshape[1]/M.shape[1]), order=0) Parameters: \tau: Threshold for depth difference. If the distance between two rays' rendered depths is greater than \tau, the pixel is masked out. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Pixels reprojected outside the source view bounds must be handled (masked out). Precision: The reprojection formula uses approximate equality (\sim), implying floating-point precision issues may arise. Degenerate Input: If Dj(pj) is zero or invalid, reprojection fails. Distinguishes valid/invalid optical flow areas to handle occlusion and lighting errors. It sets itself apart by using pixel-space flow consistency rather than just depth-based visibility. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels N in the image, as it involves per-pixel reprojection and depth comparison. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the depth maps and masks. Strengths: Effectively filters out regions with geometric inconsistencies, artifacts, and self-occlusion, preventing them from corrupting feature-level regularization. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation; erroneous geometry in the source or target view can lead to incorrect masking. When to use: When performing feature-level consistency regularization in NeRF training, especially in few-shot settings where geometric errors are prominent. Originated in GeCoNeRF (Geometric Consistency NeRF), a method for few-shot Neural Radiance Fields. The technique addresses the issue of imperfect and distorted warping caused by erroneous geometry degrading reconstruction quality. name: Optical Flow Masking
head: Flow-based Occlusion Masking, Optical Flow Validity Masking
body: Optical Flow Masking distinguishes between valid and invalid optical flow areas to handle occlusion and lighting errors during NeRF optimization. It sets aside regions where geometric inconsistencies or artifacts would corrupt feature-level regularization, building on Occlusion-Aware Masking by using pixel-space flow consistency rather than just depth-based visibility. Inputs: Two adjacent RGB images (source Ia, target Ib), forward optical flow field f{a \to b}, backward optical flow field f{b \to a}, image dimensions H \times W, and a threshold \theta. Outputs: A binary validity mask M{a \to b} of size H \times W. Data Structures: f{a \to b}(r, c): 2D vector (u, v) representing flow at pixel (r, c). M{a \to b}: Binary matrix, M{a \to b}(r, c) \in \{0, 1\}. Steps: 1. Compute forward corresponding point coordinates F{a \to b}(r, c) for all r \in [0, H], c \in [0, W]: F{a \to b}(r, c) = (r, c) + f{a \to b}(r, c) Similarly for backward flow F{b \to a}(r, c) = (r, c) + f{b \to a}(r, c). 2. Calculate the absolute difference d between the target ground-truth image True{rgb} and the source image warped by the flow: d = |Flow{rgb} - True{rgb}| Where Flow{rgb} is the pixel value at F{a \to b}(r, c) sampled from Ia, and True{rgb} is the pixel value at (r, c) in Ib. 3. Set the mask value M{a \to b}(r, c): M{a \to b}(r, c) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } d \le \theta \text{ and } F{a \to b}(r, c) \in [W, H] \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The condition F{a \to b}(r, c) \in [W, H] checks if the corresponding point lies within the image bounds. Parameters: \theta: Threshold between optical flow prediction and ground truth. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: If F{a \to b}(r, c) falls outside image bounds, the mask is 0. Lighting changes or occlusions cause large d, resulting in mask 0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeopticalflowmask(Ia, Ib, fatob, H, W, theta): """ Ia: Source image (H, W, 3) Ib: Target image (H, W, 3) fatob: Forward flow field (H, W, 2) H, W: Image height and width theta: Consistency threshold """ mask = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32) # Get coordinates rows, cols = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') # Compute corresponding points # fatob contains (dx, dy) fx = cols + fatob[:,:, 0] fy = rows + fatob[:,:, 1] # Check bounds validbounds = (fx >= 0) & (fx < W) & (fy >= 0) & (fy < H) # Sample warped source image # Clamp coordinates for sampling to avoid index errors, though validbounds handles logic fxclamped = np.clip(fx, 0, W - 1).astype(np.int32) fyclamped = np.clip(fy, 0, H - 1).astype(np.int32) # Get RGB values from source image at corresponding points # Note: Ia shape is (H, W, 3) flowrgb = Ia[fyclamped, fxclamped] # Calculate absolute difference d = np.abs(flowrgb.astype(np.float32) - Ib.astype(np.float32)) # Sum differences across channels (or use mean, source says "absolute difference") # Source implies scalar d, likely sum or max of channel diffs dscalar = np.sum(d, axis=2) # Apply threshold and bounds validflow = dscalar <= theta mask = (validbounds & validflow).astype(np.float32) return mask Creates a soft [0,1] dynamism mask by comparing measured flow against rigid flow predicted by depth. Used in synthetic tests; real data uses the depth-free epipolar residual. Generates per-frame soft dynamism masks for a moving-camera clip by measuring dense flow to a neighbor, subtracting rigid flow predicted by recovered pose, and thresholding the residual. 1. Check for OpenCV availability and sufficient frames/poses; return empty masks if unavailable or insufficient. 2. Initialize DISOpticalFlow with PRESETMEDIUM and finest scale 0. 3. Convert RGB frames to grayscale. 4. For each frame i, determine neighbor j (i+1, or i-1 for last frame). 5. Calculate measured flow between frames i and j. 6. Compute rigid flow prediction and validity mask from depth and camera poses. 7. Calculate the residual as the L2 norm of the difference between measured flow and predicted flow, masked by validity. 8. Compute epipolar residual using measured flow and camera poses. 9. Apply the robust thresholding function to the residual. 10. Clean and threshold the residual to get the mask, then append to list. 11. Update statistics with the mean dynamic fraction (m > 0.5). Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Handles occlusion and lighting errors effectively. Limitations include sensitivity to lighting changes and occlusions which generate invalid flow areas. When to use it: When using optical flow to guide view synthesis or feature regularization in NeRF, specifically to ignore invalid flow regions. When not: When high-quality depth and pose information is available for rigid flow subtraction (use Per-Frame Soft Dynamism Masks instead). Origin: Introduced in "Bidirectional Optical Flow NeRF: High Accuracy and High Quality under Fewer Views". History and development: Used to preprocess optical flow graphs before NeRF optimization to ensure correct and photorealistic novel views under fewer input views. Where it is used: In NeRF training loops that incorporate bidirectional optical flow constraints. name: View-Consistency Metric (E_warp)
head: Warped View Consistency Metric
body: The View-Consistency Metric (E{\text{warp}}) evaluates geometric and photometric consistency in radiance fields by measuring the mean squared error between a rendered view and a neighboring view warped into the target coordinate system. It differs from standard metrics by explicitly masking occluded regions using optical flow, ensuring errors are only computed where scene content is visible in both views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered images Vi and V{i+\delta} from a pre-trained NeRF at camera poses separated by offset \delta, an optical flow estimator (RAFT), and an occlusion detection method (Ruder et al.). Outputs: A scalar consistency error E{\text{warp}}. Data Structures: V{i+\delta}: Rendered image at pose i+\delta (target view). \bar{V}{i+\delta}: Warped image at pose i+\delta (source view Vi warped to i+\delta). O: Binary occlusion mask of the same spatial dimensions as the images, where O(x,y)=1 if the pixel is visible in both views and 0 otherwise. |O|: The number of pixels where O(x,y)=1. Steps: 1. Render images Vi and V{i+\delta} from the NeRF at camera poses separated by offset \delta. 2. Estimate the optical flow field from Vi to V{i+\delta} using a pre-trained optical flow network (RAFT). 3. Derive the occlusion mask O using the occlusion detection method from Ruder et al.. 4. Warp Vi into the coordinate system of V{i+\delta} using the estimated flow to produce \bar{V}{i+\delta}. 5. Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between \bar{V}{i+\delta} and V{i+\delta} restricted to pixels where O=1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeewarp(Vi, Vip, flownet, occlusionnet, delta): # 1. Render Vi and Vip at poses separated by delta (handled externally) # 2. Estimate optical flow from Vi to Vip flow = flownet(Vi, Vip) # 3. Derive occlusion mask O O = occlusionnet(Vi, Vip, flow) # 4. Warp Vi to Vip coordinate system using bilinear sampling Vbarip = samplewithflow(Vi, flow) # 5. Compute MSE over valid pixels mask = O > 0 if not mask.any(): return 0.0 error = mean((Vbarip[mask] - Vip[mask]) 2) return error def samplewithflow(image, flow): # Standard bilinear warping: maps each pixel (x,y) in target to source coordinates # using the flow vector, then samples RGB values return bilinearsample(image, flow) Formula: E{\text{warp}}(V{i+\delta}, \bar{V}{i+\delta}) = \frac{1}{|O|} \left\| \bar{V}{i+\delta} - V{i+\delta} \right\|2^2 Where: V{i+\delta} is the rendered view at pose i+\delta. \bar{V}{i+\delta} is the warped view from pose i to i+\delta. O is the occlusion mask. \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm (sum of squared differences). Parameters: \delta: The offset between viewpoints. Short-range consistency: \delta = 1. Long-range consistency: \delta = 7. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion Handling: Pixels occluded in one view but visible in the other must be masked out (O=0) to prevent the metric from penalizing valid geometric changes as errors. Pre-trained Requirement: The optical flow must be estimated on a video sequence rendered from a pre-trained NeRF to ensure the flow corresponds to the scene geometry rather than training artifacts. Flow Estimation Limits: Incorrect flow in textureless regions or large displacements can warp pixels incorrectly, producing false consistency errors. The Warped LPIPS Metric is a no-reference evaluation method used to assess geometric and photometric consistency across viewpoints in novel view synthesis, particularly for stylized or super-resolved NeRFs. It quantifies consistency by computing the Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) between a target rendered view and a source view warped into the target's coordinate system using estimated depth. Unlike standard metrics that require ground truth, it measures how well the underlying 3D structure supports consistent appearance from nearby angles. It distinguishes itself from the base View-Consistency Metric (E{\text{warp}}) by using LPIPS instead of MSE, making it more sensitive to perceptual artifacts and texture consistency. Time Complexity: Dominated by NeRF rendering and the inference of the optical flow network and occlusion detector. The warping and error computation scale linearly with the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered images, the optical flow field, and the occlusion mask. Strengths: Provides a geometrically aware consistency check that does not require ground truth multi-view data, making it suitable for self-supervised training or evaluation of unstructured captures. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of external models (RAFT, occlusion detector) and degrades when flow estimation is ambiguous. When to use: Evaluating geometric coherence in NeRFs, particularly in video stylization or recoloring tasks where temporal or spatial consistency is critical. When not to use: When ground truth multi-view data is available and direct photometric error is preferred, or when the scene contains significant non-rigid motion that violates the optical flow assumption. The metric is based on the view-consistency evaluation introduced in SNeRF [31], which generalized the approach from Lai et al. [22] to the NeRF setting. It was adopted in LAENeRF for evaluating 3D-aware stylization and recoloring consistency, using short-range (\delta=1) and long-range (\delta=7) offsets. name: Warped LPIPS Metric
head: E_warp (LPIPS variant), Warped LPIPS Consistency Metric, Warped View Consistency with LPIPS
body: The Warped LPIPS Metric is a no-reference evaluation method used to assess geometric and photometric consistency across viewpoints in novel view synthesis, particularly for stylized or super-resolved NeRFs. It quantifies consistency by computing the Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) between a target rendered view and a source view warped into the target's coordinate system using estimated depth. Unlike standard metrics that require ground truth, it measures how well the underlying 3D structure supports consistent appearance from nearby angles. It distinguishes itself from the base View-Consistency Metric (Ewarp) by using LPIPS instead of MSE, making it more sensitive to perceptual artifacts. Inputs: Iv: Rendered image from target viewpoint v. I{v'}: Rendered image from source viewpoint v' (a nearby viewpoint). D{v'}: Predicted depth map corresponding to I{v'}. Kv, K{v'}: Intrinsic camera matrices for viewpoints v and v'. T{v \to v'}: Extrinsic transformation matrix from v to v'. M{v,v'}: Warping mask indicating valid pixels (occlusion-free regions). Outputs: E{warp}: Scalar LPIPS score representing inconsistency; lower values indicate higher consistency. Data Structures: Depth map D{v'}: 2D array of floats, shape (H, W), where each element represents the distance from the camera center to the surface along the ray. Warping mask M{v,v'}: 2D binary array, shape (H, W), where 1 indicates a valid pixel and 0 indicates an occluded or invalid region. Steps: 1. Select Source Viewpoint: Select v' as the 3rd nearest test pose from v. For short-range consistency, pairs with a gap of 5 indices (Oi, O{i+5}) are used; for long-range, a gap of 15 (Oi, O{i+15}) is used. 2. Backproject to World Space: Use predicted depths to backproject pixels in I{v'} to a point cloud in world space. 3. Reproject and Rasterize: Apply a point cloud rasterizer to render the warped image W(I{v'}) in viewpoint v. 4. Compute Warping Mask M{v,v'}: Identify pixels in the target view v that correspond to valid, non-occluded regions in v'. The mask ensures LPIPS is only computed on geometrically consistent regions. 5. Compute LPIPS Score: Calculate the LPIPS score between the masked target image M{v,v'} \cdot Iv and the warped image W(I{v'}). Formula: E{warp}(Iv, I{v'}) = \text{LPIPS}(M{v,v'} \cdot Iv, W(I{v'})) Only pixels where M{v,v'} = 1 contribute to the LPIPS calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computewarpedlpips(Iv, Ivprime, Dvprime, Kv, Kvprime, Tvtovprime, Tv): """ Compute the Warped LPIPS metric between view v and v'. Args: Iv: Target rendered image (H, W, 3) Ivprime: Source rendered image (H, W, 3) Dvprime: Depth map for source view (H, W) Kv, Kvprime: Camera intrinsics Tvtovprime: Extrinsics from v to v' Tv: Extrinsics for view v Returns: Ewarp: Scalar LPIPS score """ H, W = Iv.shape[:2] # 1. Backproject source pixels to world space u, v = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H)) fx, fy = Kvprime[0, 0], Kvprime[1, 1] cx, cy = Kvprime[0, 2], Kvprime[1, 2] xcam = (u - cx) / fx ycam = (v - cy) / fy Z = Dvprime X = xcam Z Y = ycam Z Pvprimehomo = np.stack([X, Y, Z, np.oneslike(Z)], axis=0) Tinv = np.linalg.inv(Tvtovprime) Pvhomo = Tinv @ Pvprimehomo Xv = Pvhomo[0] / Pvhomo[2] Yv = Pvhomo[1] / Pvhomo[2] Zv = Pvhomo[2] # 2. Project to target image coordinates fxv, fyv = Kv[0, 0], Kv[1, 1] cxv, cyv = Kv[0, 2], Kv[1, 2] uwarped = Xv fxv + cxv vwarped = Yv fyv + cyv # 3. Create Warped Image W(Ivprime) via bilinear sampling def bilinearsample(img, coords): y, x = coords[:,:,0], coords[:,:,1] y0, x0 = np.floor(y).astype(int), np.floor(x).astype(int) y1, x1 = np.clip(y0 + 1, 0, H-1), np.clip(x0 + 1, 0, W-1) wa = (x1 - x) (y1 - y) wb = (x1 - x) (y - y0) wc = (x - x0) (y1 - y) wd = (x - x0) (y - y0) return waimg[y0, x0] + wbimg[y0, x1] + wcimg[y1, x0] + wdimg[y1, x1] coords = np.stack([vwarped, uwarped], axis=-1) WIvprime = bilinearsample(Ivprime, coords) # 4. Compute Warping Mask Mv,v' validbounds = (uwarped >= 0) & (uwarped < W) & (vwarped >= 0) & (vwarped < H) validdepth = Zv > 0 Mvvprime = (validbounds & validdepth).astype(float) # 5. Compute LPIPS Score Ivmasked = Iv Mvvprime[..., np.newaxis] # Compute LPIPS using a standard pretrained perceptual network (e.g., VGG or AlexNet) Ewarp = computelpipsperceptualscore(Ivmasked, WIvprime) return Ewarp def computelpipsperceptualscore(img1, img2): # Standard LPIPS implementation using pretrained feature networks # Returns scalar perceptual distance pass Parameters: View Selection: v' is the 3rd nearest test pose. Consistency Range: Short-range uses view pairs with a gap of 5; long-range uses a gap of 15. LPIPS Model: Standard LPIPS network (typically VGG or AlexNet based). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: The warping mask must correctly identify occluded regions; incorrect masking leads to high LPIPS scores due to comparing background with foreground. Boundary Conditions: Pixels near image borders may not have valid correspondences, requiring careful handling of the mask. Measures consistency between view pairs with a gap of 5. Use when evaluating short-term geometric and photometric stability across closely spaced viewpoints. Measures consistency between view pairs with a gap of 15. Use when evaluating long-term structural coherence across widely spaced viewpoints. Time Complexity: Dominated by backprojection and rasterization steps, which are O(H \times W) per view pair. LPIPS computation is also O(H \times W) but involves neural network inference. Memory Complexity: O(H \times W) for storing depth maps, warped images, and masks. Measured Performance: On the LLFF dataset, scores range from 0.0018 (Trex) to 0.0037 (Orchids) for short-range consistency. For long-range, scores range from 0.0049 (Fern) to 0.0140 (Trex). Strengths: No-reference; perceptually relevant; measures short- and long-term consistency. Limitations: Requires predicted depth maps; sensitive to depth estimation errors. When to Use: Evaluating novel view synthesis methods where ground truth is unavailable, especially for stylized or super-resolved NeRFs. The Warped LPIPS Metric was introduced as a no-reference evaluator for assessing view consistency in NeRF-based super-resolution and stylization tasks. It builds on the concept of warping views using depth to detect inconsistencies, adapting the LPIPS metric for perceptual quality assessment. It is used in evaluating methods like DiSR-NeRF and stylization pipelines. name: Text-Image Direction Score
head: TIDS
body: The Text-Image Direction Score (TIDS) is a quantitative metric used in text-guided NeRF editing to estimate the semantic alignment between the direction of a text prompt change and the resulting change in the rendered image. Unlike pixel-level metrics such as MSE or PSNR, which measure visual fidelity, TIDS evaluates whether the edit performed by the model corresponds to the semantic intent of the instruction. It sets itself apart from sibling metrics like R-Precision by focusing on the directionality of the edit in embedding space rather than the retrieval accuracy of a single view against a caption. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: oIi: The original rendered image for view i. eIi: The edited rendered image for view i. oTi: The text caption/prompt describing the original scene. eTi: The text caption/prompt describing the edited scene. \mathbf{C}I: The CLIP image encoder. \mathbf{C}T: The CLIP text encoder. Output: A scalar value representing the cosine similarity between the image edit vector and the text edit vector. Data Structures: Embeddings are vectors of fixed dimensionality. Steps: 1. Encode the original rendered image oIi using the image encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}I(oIi). 2. Encode the edited rendered image eIi using the image encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}I(eIi). 3. Encode the original text prompt oTi using the text encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}T(oTi). 4. Encode the edited text prompt eTi using the text encoder to obtain \mathbf{C}T(eTi). 5. Compute the image direction vector: \Delta \mathbf{V}I = \mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi). 6. Compute the text direction vector: \Delta \mathbf{V}T = \mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi). 7. Calculate the cosine similarity between \Delta \mathbf{V}I and \Delta \mathbf{V}T. Formula: \text{TIDS} = \cos(\mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi), \mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi)) \text{TIDS} = \frac{(\mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi)) \cdot (\mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi))}{\|\mathbf{C}I(eIi) - \mathbf{C}I(oIi)\| \|\mathbf{C}T(eTi) - \mathbf{C}T(oTi)\|} where \cos denotes cosine similarity. Parameters: CLIP Model: The standard CLIP model is used for both \mathbf{C}I and \mathbf{C}T. Views: The score is computed per view i and averaged across the evaluation set. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Vectors: If the image or text embeddings do not change (i.e., \Delta \mathbf{V}I = \mathbf{0} or \Delta \mathbf{V}T = \mathbf{0}), the denominator becomes zero. Implementations must handle this by returning 0 or skipping the view, as the direction is undefined. Prompt Specificity: The metric assumes that oTi and eTi accurately reflect the semantic difference intended by the user. Ambiguous prompts may yield low scores even if the visual edit is correct. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def textimagedirectionscore(clipimageencoder, cliptextencoder, originalimage, editedimage, originaltext, editedtext): # 1. Encode images and text emboimg = clipimageencoder(originalimage) embeimg = clipimageencoder(editedimage) embotxt = cliptextencoder(originaltext) embetxt = cliptextencoder(editedtext) # 2. Compute direction vectors imgdirection = embeimg - emboimg txtdirection = embetxt - embotxt # 3. Compute cosine similarity dotproduct = torch.dot(imgdirection.flatten(), txtdirection.flatten()) imgnorm = torch.norm(imgdirection) txtnorm = torch.norm(txtdirection) # Handle zero vectors to avoid division by zero if imgnorm == 0 or txtnorm == 0: return 0.0 return dotproduct / (imgnorm txtnorm) R-Precision measures how well a rendered view of a synthesis object aligns with the text caption used to generate it. It computes the precision of rendered views over a group of text captions using a retrieval model. It is distinct from pixel-based metrics by evaluating semantic alignment rather than geometric fidelity. Choose it when evaluating text-to-3D generation quality rather than edit directionality. See R-Precision. Time Complexity: Dominated by the inference time of the CLIP image and text encoders. For a single view, it is O(1) relative to the number of pixels but depends on the encoder's depth. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the CLIP model weights and the embeddings for the original and edited images/text. Performance: In simple settings (e.g., 5 edits on NeRF-Art face scene), TIDS scores for methods like Instruct-NeRF2NeRF are around 0.1477, while ViCA-NeRF achieves 0.1545. Strengths: Directly measures semantic alignment with the text instruction, which is the primary goal of text-guided editing. Limitations: Does not measure visual fidelity or photorealism. The Text-Image Direction Score was introduced in the context of evaluating text-guided NeRF editing methods. It was adopted from prior work on image editing evaluation to quantify how well the visual changes in a NeRF correspond to the textual instructions provided. It is used alongside consistency scores to evaluate methods like ViCA-NeRF and Instruct-NeRF2NeRF. name: R-Precision
head: R-Precision Evaluation
body: R-Precision measures how well a rendered view of a synthesis object aligns with the text caption used to generate it. It computes the precision of rendered views over a group of text captions using a retrieval model. It is distinct from pixel-based metrics (e.g., LPIPS) by evaluating semantic alignment rather than geometric fidelity. Inputs: A set of N text captions \{c1, \dots, cN\} associated with a synthesis object. A rendered view I of the synthesis object. A vision-language model backbone M (CLIP or BLIP2). Data Structures: Caption list: Array of strings. Image tensor: RGB image corresponding to the rendered view. Steps: 1. Dataset Construction: Collect object-centric captions from the COCO dataset. Sample 20 captions for training. Use a total of 153 captions for evaluation. 2. View Selection: Render the object at a 30° elevation. This angle is chosen because it is not prone to overfitting issues seen in other methods. 3. Retrieval: For each caption ci, compute the similarity score between the rendered image I and the text ci using the backbone M. 4. Precision Calculation: Compute the precision of the rendered views over the group of text captions. Specifically, determine if the ground-truth caption is ranked within the top k results (where k is the number of relevant items, typically 1 for single-object retrieval). 5. Averaging: Average the metric over multiple azimuths to reduce variance. 6. Seeding: Evaluate all captions with 2 generation seeds unless otherwise noted. Parameters: Elevation angle: 30°. Backbone models: CLIP [51] and BLIP2 [32]. Caption count: 153 captions for evaluation. Training captions: 20 captions sampled from COCO. Edge Cases: Overfitting: Evaluating at training viewpoints can lead to overfitting; 30° elevation mitigates this. Variance: Single-view evaluation may have high variance; averaging over azimuths reduces this. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Evaluates semantic alignment with text prompts. The 30° elevation reduces overfitting issues. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the vision-language model backbone. When to Use: Use when evaluating text-to-3D generation quality based on semantic alignment. R-Precision was introduced in the context of text-to-3D generation evaluation. It is inspired by retrieval metrics in information retrieval. The method uses CLIP and BLIP2 as backbones. name: Depth Supervision and Pseudo-Depth
body: This family of techniques incorporates geometric constraints into the radiance field optimization loop to improve reconstruction quality, particularly in low-data regimes or when explicit geometry is required for downstream tasks. While standard NeRF optimization relies solely on photometric RGB losses, these methods introduce depth-related penalties or sampling strategies. Depth Supervision explicitly minimizes the difference between rendered depth and ground-truth depth (derived from SfM keypoints or stereo), whereas Pseudo-Depth approximates surface geometry via weighted averaging of sampled points to guide feature distillation or segmentation without requiring explicit depth labels. This family builds on NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation by extending metric calculation with geometric losses. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable volume rendering framework. The core mechanism involves computing a depth estimate \hat{D}(r) for a ray r during the forward pass of the renderer and incorporating this value into the loss function or sampling strategy. The predicted depth \hat{D}(r) is computed as the expected depth along the ray, weighted by the transmittance and density at each sample point ti: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \sigmai is the volume density, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the interval between adjacent samples, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. This formulation ensures that depth contributions are proportional to the opacity of the surface encountered at that depth. This variant applies explicit depth supervision to the TensoRF architecture to enhance performance in low-data scenarios. It differs from standard NeRF depth supervision by leveraging TensoRF's tensor decomposition for efficiency, while using COLMAP keypoints to generate sparse ground-truth depth labels. Definition TensoRF is augmented with a depth supervision term derived from COLMAP keypoints to improve low-data performance. Procedure 1. Extract 3D point locations and their corresponding 2D pixel coordinates from the COLMAP keypoints stored in the dataset. 2. Using the coordinate information and the camera matrix for the ground truth image, calculate the ray r(t) = o + td and the ground-truth depth D from the projection origin. 3. Sample the TensoRF model along these rays to calculate the model-estimated depths \hat{D}. Loss Function The depth loss is calculated using Mean Squared Error (MSE): L{\hat{D}} = \mathbb{E}{r \in R(P)} ||\hat{D}(r) - D(r)||2^2 where \hat{D}(r) is the predicted depth and D(r) is the ground-truth depth. The total loss combines this with the color loss LC and a weighting hyperparameter \lambdai: L{tot} = LC + \lambdai L{\hat{D}} Parameters and Context Dataset: LLFF dataset, consisting of 20-30 images of household/office environments captured with a smartphone in a grid pattern. Rationale: The LLFF dataset was chosen due to the small variance of angles, making it more suitable for this approach than 360-degree view datasets. Loss Choice: MSE loss was implemented as a baseline. Although the DS-NeRF paper reported slightly better results with KL loss, the improvements were of similar magnitude. Architecture: TensoRF was selected over standard NeRF due to faster training times and lower space complexity, fitting limited GPU and RAM resources. This technique approximates surface geometry without explicit depth labels. It is primarily used in feature field distillation (e.g., for CLIPNeRF) to enable efficient sampling around the "surface" for feature extraction. Procedure 1. Compute the pseudo depth of the surface as a weighted average of the depth of each sampled point during volume rendering. 2. Use this pseudo-surface point to compute features by sampling a small neighborhood (e.g., five points) around it with small perturbations during training and inference. Context This method is employed for computational efficiency in feature rendering, avoiding the complete process of volume rendering for features. It allows gradients to be backpropagated only to rays selected by specific semantic masks (e.g., "apple") during optimization. This method generates ground-truth depth for novel panoramic views by projecting 2D pixel coordinates onto a uniform sphere centered at the camera position. It enables the extraction of depth priors for 360-degree scenes. Definition A method to extract depth ground truths for novel panoramic views by projecting 2D pixel coordinates to a uniform sphere centered at the camera position. Procedure 1. For a pixel (x, y) on a panorama of height H and width W, calculate the vertical viewing angle \theta = \pi y / H and horizontal viewing angle \phi = 2\pi x / W. 2. Define the ray origin as the camera position (coordinate center) and the ray direction as the unit vector from the center to the sphere point defined by \theta and \phi. 3. Determine visibility for a novel view by moving the camera to a new position and checking which parts of the ground truth sphere are visible to the emitted rays from the new origin. Optimization The network parameters \theta are optimized using RGB-D frames. The geometric loss is the absolute difference between predicted and true depths, normalized by the depth variance. Depth supervision in NeRF-like models originated from the observation that photometric loss alone often leads to ambiguous geometry, especially in textureless regions or with sparse inputs. The DS-NeRF paper introduced depth supervision using KL divergence to align predicted depth distributions with ground truth. TensoRF-DS adapted this to tensor-decomposed fields for efficiency. Pseudo-depth techniques emerged in the context of feature distillation, where explicit depth is unavailable but surface proximity is needed for feature sampling. Panoramic depth extraction extends these concepts to 360-degree scenes using spherical projections.
