name: Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator
head: NeRF Uncertainty via Weight PDF, NeRF uncertainty estimator, Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimation, Weight Distribution Entropy, entropy of weight distribution
body: The Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator computes the uncertainty of the underlying 3D geometry in a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by calculating the entropy of the weight distribution of color samples along each ray. It treats the opacity function as a cumulative distribution function (CDF) and its derivative as a probability density function (PDF), allowing the weight distribution to serve as a proxy for geometric certainty. Unlike explicit 3D representations or RGB-D fusion methods, this approach leverages the implicit neural shape representation to estimate information gain without relying on structure-from-motion or depth sensors. It is distinct from methods like S-NeRF or NeRF-W as it requires no model modification or additional training, functioning as a post-hoc analysis plug-in. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained NeRF model (MLP parameters \Theta), a camera pose (origin o, direction d), and the number of samples N per ray. Outputs: A scalar uncertainty value (entropy H) for each ray, and optionally a mean entropy value for the entire image. Data Structures Ray Samples: An array of N positions ti along the ray r(t) = o + td. NeRF Query: For each sample point r(ti), the MLP returns volume density \sigmai and color ci. Weights: An array of N weights wi representing the contribution of each sample to the final color. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Sampling: For each ray r emanating from camera position o in direction d, sample N points along the ray at positions r(ti) for i = 1 \dots N. 2. NeRF Query: Query the NeRF MLP for volume density \sigmai and color ci at each sample point r(ti). 3. Transmittance Calculation: Calculate the transmittance factor pi for each sample using the volume density and the distance to the next sample: pi = \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between adjacent samples. 4. Weight Calculation: Calculate the weight wi for each sample using the accumulated transmittance from previous samples: wi = (1 - pi) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} pj This weight represents the contribution of the i-th sample to the final rendered color, derived from the opacity derivative. 5. Normalization: Normalize the weights wi to form a valid probability distribution P(xi) such that \sum{i=1}^N P(xi) = 1. The normalized probability for the i-th sample is: P(xi) = \frac{wi}{\sum{k=1}^N wk}. Note: In standard volume rendering, \sum wi \approx 1 for rays hitting an object, but normalization ensures a valid PDF for entropy calculation. 6. Entropy Calculation: Calculate the Shannon entropy H for each pixel (ray) using the normalized weights: H = -\sum{i=1}^N P(xi) \log P(xi). High entropy indicates a spread-out weight distribution (low certainty/incomplete geometry), while low entropy indicates a concentrated weight distribution (high certainty/concentrated surface). 7. Aggregation (Optional): Compute the mean entropy across all pixels in the image to serve as the uncertainty metric for that view. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computerayuncertainty(nerfmodel, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, numsamples): """ Computes the volumetric uncertainty (entropy of weight distribution) for a single ray. Args: nerfmodel: A callable that takes (points, directions) and returns (sigma, color). rayorigin: 3D vector (ox, oy, oz). raydirection: 3D vector (dx, dy, dz), assumed normalized. tmin: Float, near clipping distance along the ray. tmax: Float, far clipping distance along the ray. numsamples: Integer N, number of samples along the ray. Returns: float: Shannon entropy H of the weight distribution. """ # Step 1: Sample points along the ray tvals = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, numsamples + 1) tsamples = tvals[:-1] deltas = np.diff(tvals) # Step 2: Query NeRF points = rayorigin + np.outer(tsamples, raydirection) sigma, color = nerfmodel(points, raydirection) # Step 3 & 4: Calculate weights p = np.exp(-sigma deltas) # Calculate accumulated transmittance Ti = prod{j=1}^{i-1} pj accumulatedtransmittance = np.ones(numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples): accumulatedtransmittance[i] = accumulatedtransmittance[i-1] p[i-1] weights = (1 - p) accumulatedtransmittance # Step 5: Normalize weights to form probability distribution weightsum = np.sum(weights) if weightsum == 0: return 0.0 # Guard against division by zero for rays missing the object probabilities = weights / weightsum # Step 6: Calculate Shannon Entropy entropy = 0.0 for prob in probabilities: if prob > 0: entropy -= prob math.log(prob) return entropy def computeimageuncertainty(nerfmodel, rayorigin, raydirections, tmin, tmax, numsamples, downsamplefactor=4): """ Computes the mean entropy for an entire image given precomputed ray directions. """ totalentropy = 0.0 count = 0 # Iterate over downsampled grid for i in range(0, raydirections.shape[0], downsamplefactor): for j in range(0, raydirections.shape[1], downsamplefactor): raydir = raydirections[i, j] hval = computerayuncertainty(nerfmodel, rayorigin, raydir, tmin, tmax, numsamples) totalentropy += hval count += 1 return totalentropy / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Parameters Number of samples (N): 64 for the 'coarse' network and 128 for the 'fine' network. Downsampling factor: Images are downsampled by a factor of 4 during entropy evaluation to speed up computation. \sigmai: The volume density predicted by the NeRF MLP at the i-th sample point. ci: The color (r,g,b) predicted by the NeRF MLP at the i-th sample point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Transparency: The method is restricted to non-transparent objects with solid surfaces. It fails for transparent objects (e.g., glass) because Marching Cubes removes low density regions (noise) and transparent surfaces do not produce a clear single peak in weight distribution. Empty Space: If a ray does not hit any object, the weights will be near zero, leading to potential division by zero or undefined entropy. The implementation returns 0.0 in this case. Precision: The calculation of accumulated transmittance involves products of values less than 1, which can lead to underflow for very long rays or high densities. Log-space computation is recommended for stability in implementation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P) per image, where N is the number of samples per ray and P is the number of pixels. The method requires a forward pass through the NeRF MLP for every sample point. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray to store weights and transmittance values. Performance: The method is computationally expensive due to the need to query the MLP for every sample point on every ray. Downsampling by a factor of 4 is used to mitigate this. Strengths: It provides a direct measure of geometric uncertainty from the implicit representation without requiring explicit mesh extraction or additional training. It is applicable to any NeRF-based approach. Limitations: It is not suitable for transparent objects or scenes with significant transparency. It assumes that the weight distribution concentration correlates with geometric certainty, which may not hold for all scene types. When to use: Active robotic 3D reconstruction to determine the next best view for effective 3D reconstruction of an object. When not to use: Scenes with transparent objects or when explicit geometric meshes are required directly from the NeRF without further processing. The Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator was introduced in the paper "Uncertainty Guided Policy for Active Robotic 3D Reconstruction Using Neural Radiance Fields". The authors leveraged the popular neural radiance fields-based object representation to solve the next-best-view selection problem for dense 3D reconstruction. The key insight is that the weight distribution in NeRF, which is the derivative of the opacity function, can be treated as a probability density function. By computing the entropy of this distribution, the method provides a proxy for the uncertainty of the underlying 3D geometry. This approach distinguishes itself from explicit 3D representations and RGB-D fusion methods by using the implicit neural shape representation to estimate information gain without relying on structure-from-motion or depth sensors. It is also distinct from Bayesian NeRF variants like S-NeRF as it requires no model modification. name: Depth-Regularizing Loss Functions
head: Depth Supervision, Geometric Regularization
body: Depth-Regularizing Loss Functions constrain the geometric consistency of differentiable volume rendering by penalizing discrepancies between rendered depth maps and external geometric estimates, such as stereo-matching outputs or optical flow correspondences. Unlike photometric losses that only enforce color fidelity, these methods explicitly regularize the scene's implicit geometry, accelerating convergence and improving robustness in textureless or occluded regions. They are distinguished from sibling methods like MIMO Objective (which focuses on multi-scale image features) and Ray-Based Volumetric Uncertainty Estimator (which models aleatoric uncertainty) by their direct reliance on explicit depth or flow supervision signals. All depth-regularizing losses operate on the principle that the rendered depth \hat{\textbf{D}} must align with a geometric prior \textbf{D}{prior}. The rendered depth is computed via standard volumetric integration along rays \textbf{r}: \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) zi where zi is the sample position, \sigmai is the volume density, \deltai is the distance between samples, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. The loss function \mathcal{L}{depth} typically takes the form: \mathcal{L}{depth} = \sum{\textbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}{reg}(\hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}), \textbf{D}{prior}(\textbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}{reg} is a robust loss metric (e.g., Huber or L1) and \textbf{D}{prior} is derived from either stereo matching or optical flow projection. A training objective that combines photometric color loss with a depth-supervised loss using estimated stereo depth to accelerate convergence and remove the need for a depth refinement module. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF losses by explicitly constraining the rendered depth to match external stereo-matching estimates, thereby reducing training time compared to methods like STTR that require iterative depth refinement. Optical Flow Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering and NeRF optimization to supervise the implicit scene representation and camera poses using temporal or spatial optical flow correspondences. It differs from photometric losses by enforcing geometric consistency between adjacent views (or frames) through depth-derived flow, making it particularly effective for weakly supervised scenarios or scenes with textureless regions where color-based matching fails. A regularization loss applied to depth patches rendered from sampled unseen camera poses to improve scene geometry based on the piecewise-smooth hypothesis. It is defined as: \mathcal{L}{DS} = \frac{\lambda{DS}}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\textbf{r}c \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{(x,y)} \|\nabla D(x, y)\|2 where \mathcal{R} is the set of rays cast from sampled poses, D is the depth patch centered at \textbf{r}c, and \nabla D is computed using finite differences. The weight \lambda{DS} is set to 5 \cdot 10^{-4} for coarse-stage training and 10^{-5} for fine-stage training in bounded inward-facing scenes, and 5 \cdot 10^{-4} for forward-facing scenes. Camera poses are sampled from a uniform distribution over a hemisphere (inward-facing) or 2D plane (forward-facing), or via interpolation if the distribution is unknown. The concept of using depth regularization in NeRF stems from the observation that photometric loss alone often leads to ambiguous geometry, particularly in textureless regions. RegNeRF [Niemeyer et al., 2022] introduced depth smoothness loss on sampled viewpoints to enforce piecewise-smooth geometry. Subsequent works like VGOS and others extended this by incorporating external stereo-matching estimates (e.g., Unimatch) and optical flow constraints to provide stronger geometric priors, especially in dynamic or sparse-view settings. These methods are widely used in medical imaging (e.g., endoscopic surgery videos) and novel view synthesis from sparse inputs. name: Depth-Supervised EndoNeRF Loss
head: Depth-Supervised Loss, EndoNeRF Loss
body: A training objective that combines photometric color loss with a depth-supervised loss using estimated stereo depth to accelerate convergence and remove the need for a depth refinement module. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF losses by explicitly constraining the rendered depth to match external stereo-matching estimates, thereby reducing training time compared to methods like STTR that require iterative depth refinement. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: \mathcal{R}: The set of camera rays \textbf{r}(z). t \in [0,1]: The time parameter for dynamic scenes. \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The rendered color for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t. \textbf{C}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The ground truth pixel color for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t. \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The rendered depth for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t. \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z), t): The estimated stereo depth for ray \textbf{r}(z) at time t, obtained via stereo-matching feature correspondence of robotic surgery videos using Unimatch. \lambdad: The weight coefficient for the depth loss term. Output: \mathcal{L}: The total loss value. Data Structures Rays: Represented as \textbf{r}(z), where zj is the distance of the j-th sample along the ray. Depth Maps: \textbf{D} is treated as a dense per-ray value or 2D map derived from Unimatch. Steps 1. Estimate Stereo Depth: Compute the estimated stereo depth \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z),t) by performing stereo-matching on feature correspondence of the robotic surgery videos using the Unimatch algorithm. 2. Render Color and Depth: For each ray \textbf{r}(z) \in \mathcal{R} and time t \in [0,1], compute the rendered color \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) and rendered depth \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) from the current radiance field representation. 3. Compute Photometric Loss: Calculate the squared L2 norm between the rendered color and the ground truth color: \left\| \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) - \textbf{C}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right\| 2^2. 4. Compute Depth Loss: Calculate the Huber loss between the rendered depth and the estimated stereo depth: {\text {Huber}}\left( \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t), \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right). 5. Aggregate Loss: Sum the photometric and weighted depth losses over all rays and time steps to obtain \mathcal{L}. Formulas The total loss function is defined as: \mathcal {L}= \sum {\textbf{r}(z) \in \mathcal {R}, t\in [0,1]} \left\| \hat{\textbf{C}}(\textbf{r}(z), t) - \textbf{C}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right\| 2^2 + \lambda d {\text {Huber}}\left( \hat{\textbf{D}}(\textbf{r}(z), t), \textbf{D}(\textbf{r}(z), t) \right) Where: \textbf{r}(z) is the camera ray. zj is the distance of the j-th sample along the ray. t \in [0,1] is the time. \hat{\textbf{C}} is the rendered color. \textbf{C} is the ground truth pixel color. \hat{\textbf{D}} is the rendered depth. \textbf{D} is the estimated stereo depth from Unimatch. \lambdad is the weight for the depth loss. Parameters \lambdad: The weight coefficient for the Huber depth loss term. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls Outliers: Huber loss is adopted for the depth term because it is more stable to outliers than L2 loss. Stereo Quality: Convergence to the estimated stereo depth requires well-matched stereo correspondence. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def huberloss(diff, delta=1.0): """Standard Huber loss implementation.""" absdiff = abs(diff) quadratic = min(absdiff, delta) linear = absdiff - quadratic return 0.5 quadratic 2 + delta linear def depthsupervisedendonerfloss(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors, rendereddepths, stereodepths, lambdad, delta=1.0): """ Computes the Depth-Supervised EndoNeRF Loss. Inputs are flattened lists of values over all rays and time steps. """ # 1. Photometric Color Loss (L2 norm squared) colorloss = sum((cr - cg) 2 for cr, cg in zip(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors)) # 2. Depth Loss (Huber) depthloss = sum(huberloss(dr - ds, delta) for dr, ds in zip(rendereddepths, stereodepths)) # 3. Total Loss totalloss = colorloss + lambdad depthloss return totalloss Depth Supervision and Pseudo-Depth Uses external depth estimates to guide training. Sets itself apart by using stereo-matching (Unimatch) rather than pseudo-depth from other NeRF variants. Choose when stereo data is available and training speed is critical. Link MIMO Objective Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Supervising with Unimatch depth maps decreases training time compared to STTR. This is because the depth refinement module proposed in EndoNeRF (which requires depth rendering of all training images) is no longer needed. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Accelerates convergence; removes the need for a computationally expensive depth refinement module; robust to outliers via Huber loss. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Training dynamic radiance fields for robotic surgery videos where stereo depth estimates are available. When not: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the Efficient EndoNeRF reconstruction and its application for data-driven surgical simulation paper. It was developed to address the computational overhead of depth refinement in previous EndoNeRF variants. The approach leverages Unimatch for stereo depth estimation. name: Optical Flow Loss
head: Flow-guided shape reconstruction, Forward Optical Flow Loss, Optical Flow Weak Supervision
body: Optical Flow Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering and NeRF optimization to supervise the implicit scene representation and camera poses using temporal or spatial optical flow correspondences. It enforces geometric consistency between adjacent views through depth-derived flow, addressing textureless regions where photometric matching fails. The method computes a loss by comparing predicted optical flow (derived from rendered depth and camera poses) against ground-truth optical flow between adjacent views. Two primary formulations exist in the literature, differing in whether they operate on pixel coordinate shifts or explicit flow vectors. Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{D} for the current view (or novel view). Camera poses: Current pose \{R, t\} and adjacent pose \{R', t'\} (or relative transformation \{R, t\}{k \rightarrow k+1}). Ground-truth optical flow \mathcal{F} (or \mathcal{F}{k \rightarrow k+1}) between adjacent views. Inverse camera projection matrix (intrinsic parameters) \Pi^{-1}. Optical flow mask M (optional, for weighting). Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{flow} or \mathcal{L}{fa}. Depth Map: 2D array of floats representing distance along the ray. Camera Pose: 4 \times 4 transformation matrix or separate rotation R (3 \times 3) and translation t (3 \times 1). Optical Flow: 2D vector field (u, v). Mask: Binary weights Ml and Mr determined by photometric similarity thresholds. This approach maps 3D points from the novel view to adjacent views and minimizes the Euclidean distance between the projected pixel coordinates and the ground-truth flow coordinates. 1. Render Depth: Compute depth \hat{D}(r) for each ray r in the novel view using the standard NeRF integration formula. 2. Back-Project to 3D: For each pixel (x, y) with depth d = \hat{D}(x, y), compute the 3D point P{novel} in the world coordinate system: P{novel} = ro + rd \cdot d, where ro is the ray origin and rd is the ray direction. 3. Project to Adjacent Views: Transform P{novel} into the coordinate systems of the left (I{left}) and right (I{right}) adjacent input views. For a generic adjacent view with rotation R1 and translation T1: \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \end{bmatrix} = R1 \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} + T1. Project to 2D pixel coordinates (w0, h0) using the camera intrinsics. 4. Compute Loss: Calculate the mean squared error between the projected coordinates (w0, h0) and the ground-truth optical flow coordinates (w{g.t.}, h{g.t.}): \mathcal{L}{flow} = \sum{i,j} \left( \| w0 - w{g.t.} \|^2 + \| h0 - h{g.t.} \|^2 \right), where the sum is over valid pixels. 5. Masking (Optional): Apply a mask M to weight the loss, typically based on photometric consistency or flow magnitude thresholds. This approach explicitly computes the predicted optical flow vector from depth and pose, then compares it to the ground-truth flow vector using an L1 norm. 1. Back-Project: For each pixel (u, v) in the source frame k, back-project to 3D using the rendered depth \hat{D} and inverse intrinsics \Pi^{-1}: Pk = \Pi^{-1}(u, v, \hat{D}). 2. Transform Pose: Apply the relative camera pose transformation \{R, t\}{k \rightarrow k+1} to Pk to get the point in the target frame k+1: P{k+1} = \{R, t\}{k \rightarrow k+1} Pk. 3. Re-Project: Project P{k+1} back to 2D pixel coordinates in frame k+1 using \Pi: (u', v') = \Pi(P{k+1}). 4. Compute Predicted Flow: The predicted optical flow \hat{\mathcal{F}}{k \rightarrow k+1} is the displacement: \hat{\mathcal{F}}{k \rightarrow k+1} = (u', v') - (u, v). Note: The source formula (16) defines \mathcal{F}{k \rightarrow k+1} as the expected flow given the depth and pose, which serves as the "predicted" flow for the loss calculation against the "ground truth" flow \hat{\mathcal{F}} (notation varies in source, but the intent is comparing geometry-derived flow to observed flow). Correct interpretation from S2: \mathcal{F}{pred} = (u, v) - \Pi \left( \{R, t\}{k \rightarrow k+1} \Pi^{-1}(u, v, \hat{D}) \right). 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the L1 norm between the predicted flow and the ground-truth flow: \mathcal{L}{fa} = \| \mathcal{F}{pred} - \mathcal{F}{gt} \|1. Mask M: Binary mask used to weight the optical flow loss in the final composite loss. Values are 1 if the pixel is valid (e.g., within similarity threshold w), 0 otherwise. Similarity Threshold w: Used in S1 to determine if a pixel is consistent between views for mask generation. Loss Weights (\lambda): In S2, the total loss is \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}p + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}D + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{fa}. Depth Normalization: S2 uses scale- and shift-invariant normalization for depth estimation: t(D) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N Di, s(D) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N |Di - t(D)|, D^ = \frac{D - t(D)}{s(D)}. This is applied before computing flow to handle scale ambiguities. Coordinate System Consistency: Ray origins ro and directions rd must be in the same coordinate system as the camera poses R, t. Occlusions: Occluded regions in the adjacent view will produce incorrect depth projections. Masks M are required to handle these. Depth Ambiguity: In textureless regions, depth estimation is unstable, leading to noisy flow predictions. S2 addresses this by combining flow loss with photometric loss \mathcal{L}p and a depth term \mathcal{L}D. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of pixels in the image. Requires rendering depth and performing matrix multiplications for each pixel. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store depth maps, flow fields, and intermediate 3D points. Strengths: Improves geometric accuracy and robustness in challenging scenarios (e.g., low texture, dynamic scenes) where photometric loss alone is insufficient. Effective for few-view synthesis. Limitations: Requires ground-truth optical flow or accurate camera poses, which may not always be available. Computationally more expensive than photometric loss due to 3D projections. When to Use: When optimizing NeRFs with sparse views, dynamic scenes, or when camera poses are uncertain. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and only photometric consistency is needed, or when no adjacent frames/views are available. Optical Flow Loss was introduced in the context of NeRF optimization to enhance view synthesis quality, particularly under few-view conditions. It leverages the geometric consistency enforced by optical flow to guide the learning of the implicit scene representation. The method has been applied to synthetic and real-world scenes, demonstrating improvements in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics compared to standard NeRF and other variants. It is part of a broader trend of using weak supervision (flow, depth) to improve differentiable rendering. name: Active Scout Tracking with NeRF
head: Active Scout, GTmap+MAP, GTmap+MI, NeRF+MI, NeRF:2k+MI, NeRF:4k+MI, offlineNeRF+MI
body: Active Scout Tracking with NeRF is a multi-target tracking method for pursuit-evasion games in highly occluded urban environments, where a quadrotor scout tracks dynamic targets on the ground using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) built online from RGB and depth images. It solves the problem of selecting the next best view for a scout to maximize information gain about target locations and unknown parts of the city. Unlike Standard Metric Computation which evaluates static performance, this method actively drives the scout's trajectory by maximizing mutual information between future observations and past observations, conditioned on the future scout location. It differs from MIMO Objective by focusing on single-scout active perception rather than multi-agent coordination, and from Novel View Selection Policy by explicitly integrating NeRF-based scene representation with Bayes filter target tracking. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: RGB and depth images (320 \times 320 pixels) from the scout's camera (Field of View: 90 degrees); current NeRF representation of the scene; Bayes filters representing target location hypotheses; graph of the urban environment (e.g., from OpenStreetMap data). Outputs: Next best waypoint (pose) for the quadrotor; updated NeRF representation; updated Bayes filters. Data Structures: 1. NeRF Representation (\xi): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Since NeRFs are not probabilistic, an ensemble of NeRFs is built from bootstrapped data to calculate variance over color and depth. 2. Bayes Filter: Maintains a history of detected target locations. One extra unassigned filter is always maintained to promote exploration. When a new target is found, the extra filter is assigned to it, and a new filter with a uniform prior is created. 3. Target History (y{detect}): A list of graph nodes (particles) seen by the scout. Used by active targets to select unseen nodes. Parameters: Camera FOV: 90 degrees. Image Resolution: 320 \times 320. NeRF Training Iterations: 4,000 per planning step (default), 2,000 for NeRF:2k variant. Planning Steps: 40. Control Steps per Planning Step: 30. Target History Reset Interval: Every 10 planning steps. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Scout starts at origin. Increases altitude to maximum (150m for Philadelphia, 100m for NYC). Performs a 2\pi yaw rotation scan with random pitch perturbations, collecting 30 images (1 per step). Train the initial NeRF for 4,000 iterations. 2. Planning Loop (for k = 1 to 40): A. NeRF Update: After reaching the previous waypoint, retrain the NeRF for the specified number of iterations (e.g., 4,000) using new observations. B. Next Best View Selection: Sample future scout poses x{future} from the distribution \phi \equiv p(x{future} | y{past}). For each candidate pose, synthesize future observations y{future} using the NeRF ensemble. Calculate Mutual Information (MI) between future detections y{future,detect} and past detections y{past}: I = \sum{i=1}^{P} I(y{future,detect}^{(i)}; y{past}) where P is the number of targets. Select the pose u{future} that maximizes this MI: u{future} \in \text{argmax}{\theta} \mathbb{E}{\theta} [y{future,detect}; y{past} | x{future}] where \theta \equiv p(x{future} | y{past}). C. Trajectory Execution: Compute a dynamically feasible quadrotor trajectory to the selected waypoint. Execute 30 control steps to reach the waypoint. D. Observation and Update: Capture new RGB and depth images yt at the new location. Update the Bayes filter for each target using the new observations. Update the NeRF with the new observations. E. Target History Reset: If k is a multiple of 10, reset the buffer of observed particles y{detect}. This forces active targets to return to old nodes, ensuring the scout revisits previously seen locations. 3. Active Target Policy (Simulation Only): Targets maintain a history of graph nodes seen by the scout (y{detect}). Each iteration, an active target randomly selects a graph node from the list of unseen particles and moves there via Dijkstra's path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def activescouttracking(): # Initialization scoutpos = (0, 0, 0) maxaltitude = 150.0 # Example for Philadelphia scoutpos.z = maxaltitude # Collect initialization images initimages = [] for i in range(30): yaw = 2 pi (i / 30) pitch = randomperturbation() image = capturergbdepth(scoutpos, yaw, pitch) initimages.append(image) # Train initial NeRF nerf = trainnerf(initimages, iterations=4000) # Initialize Bayes Filters # One extra unassigned filter is always maintained bayesfilters = [createuniformpriorfilter()] targethistory = [] # List of seen graph nodes # Planning Loop for planningstep in range(40): # 1. Retrain NeRF with new data nerf = trainnerf(nerf, newobservations, iterations=4000) # 2. Select Next Best View bestpose = None maxmi = -infinity # Sample future poses from prior distribution phi candidateposes = sampleposes(phi, numsamples=100) for pose in candidateposes: # Synthesize future observations using NeRF ensemble futureobs = synthesizeobservations(nerf, pose) # Calculate Mutual Information over all targets totalmi = 0 for targetidx in range(numtargets): # I(yfuture; ypast) = H(ypast) - H(ypast | yfuture) # Approximated via variance in NeRF ensemble and Bayes filter mi = calculatemutualinformation( futureobs.detections[targetidx], bayesfilters[targetidx].history) totalmi += mi if totalmi > maxmi: maxmi = totalmi bestpose = pose # 3. Execute Trajectory trajectory = computequadrotortrajectory(scoutpos, bestpose) for controlstep in range(30): executecontrolstep(trajectory, controlstep) # Capture new observation newobs = capturergbdepth(scoutpos) newobservations.append(newobs) # 4. Update Bayes Filters for targetidx in range(numtargets): updatebayesfilter(bayesfilters[targetidx], newobs) # 5. Check for new targets if newtargetdetected(newobs): # Assign extra filter to new target assignedfilter = bayesfilters.pop() # Remove unassigned bayesfilters.append(assignedfilter) # Create new unassigned filter with uniform prior bayesfilters.append(createuniformpriorfilter()) # 6. Reset Target History periodically if planningstep % 10 == 0: targethistory = [] scoutpos = bestpose Formulas: Mutual Information: I(y; x) = \iint dy dx p(x, y) \log \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)p(y)} = H(y) - H(y|x), where H is Shannon entropy. Total MI over Targets: I = \sum{i=1}^{P} I(y{future,detect}^{(i)}; y{past}). MAP Policy (Baseline): u{future} \in \text{argmax}{\theta} \mathbb{E}{\theta} [y{future,detect}; y{past} | x{future}], where \theta \equiv p(x{future} | y{past}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Probabilistic NeRFs: NeRFs do not inherently provide uncertainty. An ensemble from bootstrapped data is required to calculate variance for MI computation. Motion Model Uncertainty: RMSE may increase for some targets if the simplistic dynamics model used in the Bayes filter introduces uncertainty, even if the target is stationary. Unbounded Altitude: If the scout can fly to unbounded heights, it can observe the entire map from a single point, trivializing the tracking problem. Altitude is bounded (150m/100m) to ensure meaningful active perception. Target Hiding: Active targets use Dijkstra's path to move to unseen graph nodes, actively hiding behind occlusions. The history reset mechanism is crucial to force the scout to revisit these areas. Time Complexity: Each planning step involves retraining the NeRF (4,000 iterations) and sampling future poses to calculate MI. The number of control steps per planning step is fixed at 30. Memory Complexity: Depends on the NeRF size (MLP weights) and the number of Bayes filters. The ensemble of NeRFs increases memory usage. Measured Performance: Stationary Targets: Can explore and locate 20 stationary targets within 300 steps in a simulator. GTmap+MAP is quickest, but MI policies are more thorough. Dynamic Targets (Philadelphia, 4 targets, Seed 88): GTmap+MI: Mean RMSE 124.671 ± 20.088 m. NeRF:4k+MI: Mean RMSE 133.818 ± 24.080 m. NeRF:2k+MI: Mean RMSE 153.711 ± 29.144 m. OfflineNeRF+MI: Mean RMSE 117.800 ± 21.931 m. Dynamic Targets (NYC StuyTown, 4 targets): GTmap+MAP: Mean RMSE 163.216 ± 18.319 m. GTmap+MI: Mean RMSE 137.121 ± 12.754 m. NeRF:4k+MI: Mean RMSE 145.057 ± 34.356 m. OfflineNeRF+MI: Mean RMSE 167.537 ± 24.989 m. Scaling: More training steps generally lead to better performance, but NeRF:2k is slower to converge than NeRF:4k. Strengths: Maintains a worst-case tracking error of 200m for dynamic targets, whereas a greedy baseline can have an error as large as 600m. Does not need to know the number of targets a priori. Limitations: Slower than a greedy baseline for stationary targets. Performance depends on the quality of the NeRF representation, which improves over time. Origin: The method was introduced by Christopher D. Hsu, Pratik Chaudhari, and others from the Department of Electrical & Systems Engineering and General Robotics, Automation, Sensing and Perception (GRASP) Laboratory at the University of Pennsylvania, and DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory. Paper: "Active Scout: Multi-Target Tracking Using Neural Radiance Fields in Dense Urban Environments" (2024). History: The work builds on the concept of using NeRFs for online scene representation and applying active perception strategies (mutual information) for robot navigation and tracking. Usage: Evaluated in a custom-built simulator using OpenStreetMap data of Philadelphia and New York City. name: NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings
head: HashNeRF query, Instant-NGP NeRF, NeRF with Hash Encoding, NeRF with Multiresolution Hash Encoding, Neural Radiance and Density Fields (NeRF) with Multiresolution Hash Encoding
body: This method queries a neural radiance field by mapping 3D spatial coordinates and 2D view directions into high-dimensional feature vectors using a multiresolution hash encoding, which are then processed by concatenated Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to predict volume density and view-dependent color. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF [Mildenhall et al. 2020] by replacing expensive positional encoding with a learnable, sparse hash grid that enables significantly faster training convergence and real-time rendering performance on consumer hardware. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A batch of 3D positions \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} and view directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Outputs: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N} and RGB color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. Data Structures Hash Grid: A collection of L resolution levels. Each level l consists of a hash table mapping integer coordinates to feature vectors. Hash Table: A flat array of size 2^{22} (or similar capacity) storing F-dimensional feature vectors. The hash function maps 3D grid coordinates to table indices. Feature Vector: A vector of size F (typically F=2) stored in the hash table. MLP Weights: Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 64 neurons. Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons. Numbered Steps 1. Reshape Inputs: Flatten the input positions to shape [-1, 3]. 2. Position Embedding: Apply the multiresolution hash encoding function embedfn to the positions. This involves: For each resolution level l, discretizing the position into grid coordinates. Hashing these coordinates to find indices in the level-l hash table. Trilinearly interpolating the F-dimensional features from the eight nearest neighbors in the hash table. Concatenating the interpolated features from all L levels along the last dimension to form the position embedding \mathbf{y}. Generate a validity mask keepmask to identify valid points (e.g., within bounds). 3. Direction Embedding: If view directions are provided: Expand directions to match the input batch shape and reshape to flat [-1, 3]. Project the view direction onto the first 16 coefficients of the spherical harmonics basis (up to degree 4). Apply direction embedding embeddirsfn. 4. Concatenate Embeddings: Concatenate the position embedding \mathbf{y} and the direction embedding along the last dimension to form the full input vector for the network. 5. Batched Network Evaluation: Apply the network function fn in batches of size netchunk (default 102464) to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. Density MLP: Input is \mathbf{y}. Output is 16 values. The first value is treated as log-space density \log(\sigma). Color MLP: Input is the concatenation of the 16 density MLP outputs and the spherical harmonics projected view direction. Color Output: Apply Sigmoid activation for low dynamic-range (sRGB) data or Exponential activation for high dynamic range (linear HDR) data. 6. Mask Invalid Points: Set density \sigma to 0 for points where ~keepmask is true. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def getgridcoords(x, level): """Discretize continuous positions to integer grid coordinates for a given resolution level.""" # Scale by 2^level and floor to get integer grid indices res = 2 level return torch.floor(x res + 0.5).long() def hashfunction(coords, tablesize): """Map 3D integer coordinates to hash table indices using a polynomial hash.""" idx = (coords[..., 0] 73856093 ^ coords[..., 1] 19349663 ^ coords[..., 2] 83492791) % tablesize return idx def computesphericalharmonics(d, degree=4): """Compute the first 16 coefficients of the spherical harmonics basis for unit vectors.""" # Standard SH basis computation for degree 0 to 4 (16 coefficients) # d shape: [N, 3], normalized to unit length d = d / (torch.norm(d, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) x, y, z = d[..., 0], d[..., 1], d[..., 2] # Simplified SH basis evaluation (degree 0-4) sh = torch.zeros(d.shape[0], 16, device=d.device) sh[:, 0] = 0.282095 sh[:, 1] = -0.488603 y sh[:, 2] = 0.488603 z sh[:, 3] = -0.488603 x sh[:, 4] = 1.092548 x y sh[:, 5] = -1.092548 y z sh[:, 6] = 0.315392 (3 z2 - 1) sh[:, 7] = -1.092548 x z sh[:, 8] = 0.546274 (x2 - y2) sh[:, 9] = 0.590592 y (3 x2 - y2) sh[:, 10] = -2.890611 x y z sh[:, 11] = 0.457045 y (5 z2 - 1) sh[:, 12] = 3.731763 z (5 z2 - 3) sh[:, 13] = -0.457045 x (5 z2 - 1) sh[:, 14] = 1.445306 x z (x2 - 3 y2) sh[:, 15] = -0.590592 y (x2 - 3 y2) return sh class HashNeRFQuery: def init(self, hashtablesize, numlevels, leveldim, hiddendim=64): self.numlevels = numlevels self.leveldim = leveldim self.hashtablesize = hashtablesize # Initialize hash tables for each level self.embeddings = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Embedding(hashtablesize, leveldim) for in range(numlevels) ]) # Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 64 neurons inputdim = numlevels leveldim self.densitymlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 16)) # Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons self.colormlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(16 + 16, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) # Activation for HDR or LDR self.coloractivation = nn.Sigmoid() def hashencode(self, x): features = [] for l in range(self.numlevels): gridcoords = getgridcoords(x, level=l) indices = hashfunction(gridcoords, self.hashtablesize) # Gather features from hash table feat = self.embeddingsl features.append(feat) return torch.cat(features, dim=-1) def directionalencoding(self, d): shcoeffs = computesphericalharmonics(d, degree=4) return shcoeffs[:,:16] def forward(self, x, d): # 1. Position Embedding posfeat = self.hashencode(x) # 2. Direction Embedding dirfeat = self.directionalencoding(d) # 3. Concatenate inputfeat = torch.cat([posfeat, dirfeat], dim=-1) # 4. Density MLP densityout = self.densitymlp(inputfeat) logdensity = densityout[:, 0] density = torch.exp(logdensity) # 5. Color MLP colorinput = torch.cat([densityout, dirfeat], dim=-1) colorout = self.colormlp(colorinput) color = self.coloractivation(colorout) return density, color Parameters Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 64 neurons. Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons. View Direction Encoding: First 16 coefficients of spherical harmonics (degree 4). Color Activation: Sigmoid for sRGB, Exponential for linear HDR. Batch Size (netchunk): Default 102464. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Hash Collisions: Cause "grainy" microstructure artifacts, especially visible in learned signed distance functions. The MLP cannot fully compensate for this. Concatenation vs. Reduction: Concatenating F-dimensional features from each resolution is preferred over reduction (e.g., summing) because reduction may result in dimensionality L \times F being too small to encode useful information. Linear Replacement: Replacing the MLP with a single linear matrix multiplication compromises quality significantly, failing to capture specular effects and resolve hash collisions, despite being cheaper. HybridNeRF is a neural radiance field architecture that combines dense multi-resolution 3D feature grids with multi-resolution triplanes to efficiently featurize 3D sample locations. It solves the trade-off between the high memory cost of pure 3D grids and the limited geometric expressiveness of pure 2D triplanes by using a hybrid representation. It sets itself apart from its sibling MVS Network Query by explicitly summing features across resolution levels rather than concatenating them, and from SqueezeNeRF by utilizing a spatially adaptive surfaceness field for density estimation. MVS Network Query prepares inputs for a neural network by embedding points and view directions, then applies the network in batches. It differs from standard NeRF network queries by explicitly handling multi-view geometric consistency through the generation of angle and point features derived from camera poses and depth candidates. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings and relates to HybridNeRF Model Architecture, Simple-ZipNeRF, VoxNeRF, Deformation Field Integration for Telepresence, and Multi-resolution Hash Encoding. SqueezeNeRF is a memory-efficient neural rendering method that further factorizes the position-dependent Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) of FastNeRF into three separate 2D networks operating on coordinate pairs (x,y), (y,z), and (z,x) to reduce cache size complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2). It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by replacing the dense 3D position cache with a set of 2D position caches and a 2D direction cache, enabling real-time inference with significantly lower memory overhead than FastNeRF or NeRF-SH while maintaining high rendering speeds. VoxNeRF is a neural rendering method that integrates explicit scene geometry priors (mesh, point cloud, or depth map) with implicit radiance field representation to improve sampling efficiency and reconstruction accuracy. It addresses the ill-posed nature of recovering 3D geometry from 2D images by using a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to model geometric uncertainty, which guides a hybrid sampling strategy. This method extends the FastNeRF architecture to support dynamic, expression-driven head avatars for telepresence by integrating a learnable deformation field network (F{deform}) and a non-trainable skeletal deformation field (F{bone}) into the ray marching process. It solves the problem of rendering animatable 3D heads from static multi-view images by warping sample positions based on an expression vector before querying the radiance field. It is distinguished from static NeRF variants by its explicit handling of temporal expression parameters and from other dynamic NeRF methods by its specific integration with the FastNeRF caching infrastructure and grid-based pruning. HDR-HexPlane is an end-to-end neural radiance field framework for dynamic scenes that learns 3D scene representations from dynamic 2D images captured with various exposures, allowing for novel view synthesis with adjustable exposure levels. It explicitly separates the modeling of dynamic scene geometry/radiance from the learning of scene illumination (exposure), addressing color inconsistency caused by objects moving between dark and bright regions. Unlike static HDR-NeRF methods, HDR-HexPlane handles dynamic scenes by incorporating temporal information (timestamp t) into the HexPlane representation. Multi-scale PointNeRF++ is a method for obtaining radiance (\rhoq) and density (\sigmaq) for a query point q by operating on a sparse, hierarchical point cloud representation at multiple granularity levels. It solves the problem of rendering in empty regions without relying on failure-prone region-growing heuristics. Unlike its sibling PointNeRF, this method naturally fills empty regions by averaging feature embeddings over valid scale levels where neighbors exist. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by replacing hash grids with a multi-scale point cloud hierarchy. FourieRF is a few-shot Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) estimation method that prevents high-frequency artifacts and catastrophic overfitting by parameterizing grid-based features with a Fourier Transform prior. Unlike sibling methods that rely on external data priors or complex occlusion regularization, FourieRF uses an explicit curriculum training procedure to progressively increase the maximum learnable Fourier frequency, ensuring stable convergence on sparse data. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by applying frequency control to the feature grids of grid-based NeRFs (specifically TensoRF) rather than MLP positional encodings. This family encompasses techniques that modify the hash-grid encoding mechanism in neural radiance fields to mitigate artifacts such as high-frequency aliasing and sparse-view floaters. It differs from standard hash-grid encoding by introducing either capacity constraints (smaller hash tables) to enforce feature sharing and geometric consistency, or statistical down-weighting factors to suppress high-frequency noise during rendering. NeRF-W extends Neural Radiance Fields to handle unconstrained internet photo collections by modeling temporal modifications, specifically variable illuminations and transient objects (people, cars, occlusions). It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by introducing per-image appearance embeddings to handle photometric variations and a secondary transient MLP head to model dynamic content, allowing the rendering of static geometry while accounting for scene changes. A geometry estimator and appearance model using UniSDF, a state-of-the-art volume rendering approach based on a signed distance function (SDF), which decouples geometry from appearance and allows mesh extraction for radiance cue computation. A method that modifies Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to reconstruct scenes in linear HDR color space by supervising directly on noisy raw input images, rather than postprocessed low dynamic range (LDR) images. A radiance field representation that uses two geometric proxy meshes (inner and outer) to define a ray segment. Instead of dense volumetric sampling, it learns to map the two endpoints of the ray segment (intersections with the inner and outer meshes) and the view direction to the final pixel color, reducing the number of sampled points per ray to two. A method to resample points along a ray based on the importance (weight) of previous samples, improving detail in high-density regions. It normalizes bin weights by adding epsilon (1e-5) and dividing by sum to create a PDF, computes the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) by cumsumming the PDF and padding with zeros at the start, generates uniform random values u in [0, 1] (or deterministic midpoints if det=True), finds indices in the CDF where u falls using searchsorted, identifies lower and upper bin indices for interpolation, and interpolates the final sample position within the bin using linear interpolation based on u's position in the CDF interval. A sparse neural rendering method that explicitly conditions the color prediction network on local features extracted from a pretrained network to improve color and feature consistency. It extracts local features F{gt}(r) from a pretrained VGG network's Relu1-1 layer for each ray r, concatenates bottleneck feature bi, prior feature fi, and view direction d, and predicts color ci = Mc(bi, fi, d). The loss function is L = Lc + \lambda Lf, where Lf = || F(r) - F^{gt}(r) ||2. It is trained at low resolution for 44K iterations with a batch size of 1024 due to memory limitations, and frequency regulation ends at 40K iterations. Using deeper VGG layers introduces interpolation artifacts because their output size differs from the input image; Relu1-1 is used because it is the same size as the input image. A post-training optimization step to ensure consistent appearance across adjacent Block-NeRFs by matching an appearance latent code from a target Block-NeRF to its neighbors. It selects a 3D matching location between pairs of adjacent Block-NeRFs where visibility prediction is high for both blocks, freezes the Block-NeRF network weights, and optimizes only the appearance code of the adjacent Block-NeRF to match the target appearance. Without appearance matching, randomly initialized appearance codes lead to different appearances in different blocks, causing inconsistencies during compositing. A rendering model that computes NeRF-based color by combining albedo, a shading scalar, and ambient color, replacing the standard transmittance/opacity accumulation with a shadow-aware irradiance formulation to handle illumination inconsistency. The rendered color is I{p1} = \rho(P) \times (s(P, w) + (1 - s(P, w)) \times a(w)), where \rho(P) is the albedo of surface point P, s(P, w) is the shading scalar (values 0 to 1), and a(w) is the ambient color indicating shadowed areas. The NeRF-based rendering color is C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti oi s{vi}, where C(r) is the rendered color, oi is opacity, Ti is transmittance, and s{vi} is the shadow value at the i-th sampled point. Opacity is oi = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), where \sigmai is the density value at the sampled point and \deltai is the distance between adjacent sampled points along the ray. Transmittance is Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - oj). Time Complexity: Training time is significantly reduced compared to standard NeRF. For example, accumulating 128 samples at 1080p on a single RTX 3090 GPU takes approximately 5 seconds for a modular synthesizer scene. Memory Complexity: The hash grid memory usage is determined by the hash table size and the number of levels. It is generally more memory-efficient than dense 3D grids for large scenes but can still be substantial depending on the number of levels and feature dimensions. Measured Performance: Rendering performance can reach 10 frames per second on an RTX 3090 GPU for a large natural 360 scene. Scaling: Performance scales well with hardware acceleration due to the efficient implementation of the hash encoding and MLPs. Strengths: Fast training convergence, real-time rendering capabilities, ability to handle large scenes with occupancy grid pruning. Limitations: Hash collisions can cause grainy artifacts. The quality is significantly compromised if the MLP is replaced with a simple linear lookup. When to Use: When real-time rendering or fast training is required, and the scene can benefit from sparse representations. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity specular details are critical and hardware constraints prevent the use of the MLP component, or when the scene is very small and the overhead of hash encoding is not justified. The method originates from the "Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding" paper by Müller et al.. It builds on the original NeRF architecture by Mildenhall et al., which uses positional encoding and concatenated MLPs. The key innovation is the introduction of a learnable multiresolution hash encoding that maps 3D coordinates to feature vectors, enabling efficient training and rendering. The method has been widely adopted in various NeRF variants and extensions, such as HybridNeRF, SqueezeNeRF, and VoxNeRF. name: HybridNeRF Model Architecture
body: HybridNeRF is a neural radiance field architecture that combines multi-resolution 3D feature grids with 2D triplanes to efficiently represent complex scenes. It solves the trade-off between the high memory cost of pure 3D voxel representations and the limited geometric expressiveness of pure 2D plane-based methods by using a hybrid query mechanism. Unlike its sibling MVS Network Query which relies on multi-view stereo consistency, or VoxNeRF which uses pure voxel grids, HybridNeRF explicitly separates geometric and appearance features into distinct multi-resolution structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: 1. 3D Feature Grids: 3 resolution levels at 128^3, 256^3, and 512^3. 2. Triplanes: 7 resolution levels ranging from 128^2 to 8,192^2. 3. Hash Tables: Length T = 2^{19}, feature dimension F = 2 per level. 4. MLPs: Density network \mathcal{F}{\mathbf{w}\theta} (1 hidden layer, 64 channels) and color network \mathcal{F}{\mathbf{w}\phi} (2 hidden layers, 64 channels each). Algorithm Steps: 1. Coarse-level encoding: Compute \gamma{\text{coarse}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \gammap(\mathbf{x}) \otimes \boldsymbol{\alpha}, where \gammap(\mathbf{x}) is fixed positional encoding with Lc=8 frequency bands, and \boldsymbol{\alpha} are learnable weights. 2. Fine-level encoding: Query multi-resolution hash grids \gamma{\text{fine}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\vartheta}) at Lf \in \{8, 16\} levels, with resolution Nl = \lfloor N{\min} b^l \rfloor and b = \exp((\ln N{\max} - \ln N{\min}) / (Lf - 1)), where N{\min}=180. 3. Cone tracing features: Compute covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} = \sigmat^2(\mathbf{d}\mathbf{d}^T) + \sigmar^2(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{d}\mathbf{d}^T/\|\mathbf{d}\|2^2), extract upper triangular elements f(\mathbf{x}) = \text{triu}(\mathbf{\Sigma}), and encode via \gammap. 4. Learnable weights: Predict \boldsymbol{\alpha} = \mathcal{F}{\mathbf{w}p}([\gamma{\text{fine}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\vartheta}), \gammap(f(\mathbf{x}))]). 5. Hybrid position encoding: Concatenate coarse and fine encodings: \gamma{\text{hyb}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\vartheta}) = [\gamma{\text{coarse}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\alpha}), \gamma{\text{fine}}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\vartheta})]. 6. Direction encoding: Transform \mathbf{d} into spherical harmonic features \xi(\mathbf{d}) up to the 4th degree. 7. Feature aggregation: Fetch K=4 features per level from 3D grids and triplanes via interpolation, sum across levels separately, and concatenate to obtain a 4K=16-dimensional input vector. 8. MLP prediction: Pass aggregated features through \mathcal{F}{\mathbf{w}\theta} to get density \sigma and intermediate features \mathbf{e}, then through \mathcal{F}{\mathbf{w}\phi} with \xi(\mathbf{d}) to get color \mathbf{c}. 9. Volume rendering: Compute pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i with transmittance Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). 10. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L} = \|\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 using Adam (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99, lr=5\times10^{-3}, batch size 256K). Parameters: Lc = 8 frequency bands. N{\min} = 180 coarsest resolution. Lf \in \{8, 16\} fine-level hash levels. T = 2^{19} hash table length, F = 2 feature dimension. Pitfalls: Aliasing: Multi-resolution grids can introduce aliasing artifacts; this is mitigated by the hybrid encoding design and cone tracing features. Boundary handling: Standard NeRF volume rendering bounds apply; out-of-bounds queries must be clamped or masked. Precision: Fixed positional encoding at coarse levels guarantees convergence, while trainable fine-level grids capture high-frequency details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridnerfforward(x, d, grids3d, triplanes2d, params): # 1. Fixed positional encoding (Lc=8) gammap = fixedpositionalencoding(x, Lc=8) # 2. Fine-level hash features (Lf=8 or 16) gammafine = fetchhashfeatures(x, grids3d, levels=params.Lf) # 3. Cone tracing features Sigma = params.sigmat2 outer(d, d) + params.sigmar2 (eye(3) - outer(d, d) / norm(d)2) fx = uppertriangular(Sigma) gammapcone = fixedpositionalencoding(fx, Lc=8) # 4. Learnable weights alpha alpha = mlpweightpredictor(concat(gammafine, gammapcone)) # 5. Coarse encoding with alpha gammacoarse = elementwisemultiply(gammap, alpha) # 6. Hybrid position encoding gammahyb = concat(gammacoarse, gammafine) # 7. Direction encoding (SH degree 4) dsh = sphericalharmonics(d, degree=4) # 8. Feature aggregation (3D + 2D) f3d = sumfeatures(fetch3dfeatures(x, grids3d, K=4)) f2d = sumfeatures(fetch2dfeatures(x, triplanes2d, K=4)) ftotal = concat(f3d, f2d) # 16-dimensional per evidence # 9. MLPs sigma, e = mlpdensity(ftotal) c = mlpcolor(concat(e, dsh)) return sigma, c A neural radiance field method for visualizing scenes in dispersed scattering media like fog or subaquatic environments. It extends standard NeRF by treating the scattering medium as a semi-transparent entity with distinct color and density parameters, enabling restoration of scene hue and 3D configuration in obscured areas. It builds on HybridNeRF by incorporating specific scattering physics into the volume rendering integral. Improves rendering efficiency on consumer hardware by combining a lightweight NeRF with a CNN-based super-resolution module. It trains the NeRF to produce low-resolution 3D-consistent features and upscales them to high-resolution outputs, requiring no architectural changes to the NeRF backbone. An end-to-end compression framework for plane-based hybrid NeRFs that integrates non-linear transform, quantization, and entropy coding. It compresses feature planes using a pre-trained 2D neural image codec backbone, achieving high-quality novel view synthesis within a strict memory budget of approximately 0.5 MB per scene. A few-shot local unposed NeRF method that jointly estimates camera poses and scene representation from a small subset of images without accurate pose initialization. It employs a local-to-global learning framework to optimize overlapping mini-scenes and synchronize them into a global reference frame, handling mirror symmetry ambiguities. A few-shot novel view synthesis method for dynamic articulated objects that reconstructs a current state using sparse inputs by leveraging a pretrained NeRF model of a previous state as a knowledge base. It uses a lightweight projection module to map points from the current state to the knowledge base, avoiding the limited clarity of monocular video deformation methods. Techniques that address lighting inconsistency when compositing objects into NeRF scenes or synthesizing novel views under varying illumination. Unlike standard methods that treat radiance as static, they explicitly model lighting interactions, inter-reflections, or shading correlations to enable physically plausible relighting and HDR synthesis. Not given in the sources. An optimization method for sparse-view satellite imagery that integrates dense depth supervision from Semi-Global Matching to resolve few-view reconstruction ambiguities. It uses a single coarse network with a hybrid ray sampling strategy (random for global structure, guided Gaussian around depth priors for local geometry) and explicitly models input depth uncertainty. A method for steganographic information embedding in NeRFs that allows accurate hidden information extraction from rendered images while preserving visual quality. Unlike 2D steganography, it hides information in a continuous neural representation, enabling viewpoint-independent recovery for copyright identification. Synthesizes out-of-trajectory driving views with semantic road consistency by incorporating map priors into neural radiance fields. It uses coarse ground surface and lane information as uncertain supervisory signals to guide the density field and depth warping, distinguishing itself from siblings that rely solely on image-based augmentation. Defines the radiance field decoder that predicts volume density and color for a 3D location and viewing direction, conditioned on global triplane features and residual local features. It replaces raw positional encoding with structured global features and local residuals, enabling effective 360° view synthesis from minimal input views. Optimization techniques that incorporate explicit depth information into NeRF training to resolve scale ambiguity and geometric inaccuracies. They differ from sibling methods by directly supervising geometric output rather than just photometric output, enforcing metric consistency and improving reconstruction speed in sparse-view scenarios. A NeRF-based burst denoising method that leverages inter-view and spatial information to handle high noise and large camera motion in 3D space. It treats the burst as an un-ordered set with potentially large parallax, explicitly reasoning about the scene's underlying 3D structure to cope with significant motion and occlusions under very high noise levels. A test-time method for transferring semantic or instance segmentation labels from a source view to novel target views in a trained NeRF. It perturbs network parameters along gradients of mutual information associated with labeled pixels, synthesizing perturbed images to assign labels, leveraging the second-order geometry of the radiance field. A hybrid neural representation that unifies volume rendering and surface rendering to achieve high-quality geometry and sharp textures without mask supervision. It replaces the density function with an occupancy network, leveraging volume rendering in early optimization stages and surface rendering in later stages to avoid blurry texture mapping. Extends static radiance field representations to handle temporal changes by introducing time as an explicit input and using deformation fields, scene flow, or canonical space mappings. Unlike static variants, these methods explicitly model motion, distinguishing themselves from siblings that handle lighting changes or interpolation without physical motion modeling. Addresses memory constraints and convergence issues of global NeRFs on large-scale scenes by partitioning the scene into multiple local radiance fields. Unlike global implicit representations, these methods use structured collections of local fields to enable efficient, structure-aware scene decomposition and interactive editing. Accelerates inference in pre-trained NeRFs by deriving density estimates from intermediate layer activations of the coarse MLP. Unlike coarse-to-fine sampling or sampling networks, it uses existing capacity from a single coarse NeRF's intermediate features to reduce computational requirements by up to 50% with minimal quality loss. Not given in the sources. A variant for inserting objects into scenes. It transforms sampling points from scene coordinates to object coordinates using the object's insertion position (translation and rotation). It composites density as the normalized sum of densities from the scene and object at the same position, and composites reflectance as a weighted sum of reflectance values weighted by voxel particle densities. A rendering pipeline that mixes a neural proxy sampler Sp for animated objects and a neural scene sampler Sc for static elements. It separates particles into a proxy set Xp and scene set Xc, finds the convex set bounded by intersections with the proxy mesh using triangle intersection methods to determine Barycentric coordinates, and samples the neural texture locally. Enhances new view creation from limited inputs in indoor settings by integrating structural indicators into self-guided depth estimation and applying planar coherence loss. It limits textured area shapes via patch-based multi-view coherent photometric loss and implements progressive training to reduce noise from limited depth point clouds in structure-from-motion. A generalizable human NeRF model for recovering animatable 3D humans from a single input image, forecasting varied depth assessments from each perspective. It uses conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation (cIMLE) to address intrinsic uncertainty in single-eye depth estimation and presents a spatial sculpting loss technique to merge theoretical depth maps across perspectives. A NeRF training method without camera poses that improves robustness by introducing implicit pose regularization via a scene codebook. It implicitly captures scene-specific camera pose distribution as a priori, consistently outperforming GNeRF in image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). Incorporates bidirectional optical flow to supervise and guide the network to learn scene structure and synthesize novel views under fewer input views. It estimates camera parameters using COLMAP, calculates forward/backward optical flow using RAFT, determines effective optical flow areas, and applies view-enhanced fusion to refine novel view details. Approximates high-resolution feature maps by upsampling low-resolution feature maps, allowing volume rendering to only generate low-resolution feature maps. It introduces multi-view inconsistency because pixel-space operations like upsampling compromise 3D consistency and capture spurious correlations in 2D observations. Combines image-based and neural 3D representations to render high-quality, view-consistent images for large-scale scenes. It extracts multiscale image features from nearby views, projects query points to retrieve features, constructs image-based features, obtains neural 3D features via k-nearest neighbor interpolation, and aggregates them using a 3D-guided fusion module. Exploits additional LIDAR data to supervise depth prediction in large-scale scenarios. Computes surface normal \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}) at the intersection point as \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{r})\mathbf{v}). Extracts features from several context views and leverages learned correspondence matching between pairwise features across context images to aggregate features. Decomposes the scene into 'soft Voronoi diagrams' to take advantage of accelerator memory architectures. Extends NeRF in the Wild to hallucinate novel appearances. A fusion-based approach that combines NeRF with photometric stereo methods to improve mesh resolution. Establishes a canonical space using NeRF representation, constructs a neural deformation field constrained by SMPL, feeds the output into a position encoder, and converts the encoder output into shape features and volume density via a density model. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The model uses 8.4M parameters (early-stop) or 16.8M parameters (fully-trained). Measured Performance: On the Blender dataset, Hyb-NeRF (early-stop, 8.4M params) achieves PSNR 33.28 dB and SSIM 0.960, trained in 4 minutes with 40k iterations; fully-trained (16.8M params) achieves PSNR 33.94 dB and SSIM 0.964, trained in 9 minutes with 40k iterations. Scaling: Uses Adam optimizer with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99, learning rate 5\times10^{-3}, and batch size 256K samples. Strengths: Fewer trainable parameters than Instant NGP (8.4M/16.8M vs 12.6M/24.4M) due to larger N{\min} and smaller Lf; fixed positional encoding at coarse levels guarantees convergence while trainable fine-level grids capture high-frequency details. Limitations: Shallow MLPs have limited representation power without cone tracing features; multi-resolution grids require careful handling to avoid aliasing artifacts. When to use: Suitable for high-quality, fast novel view synthesis on consumer hardware where memory efficiency and rapid convergence are prioritized. When not: Unsuitable for scenes requiring explicit surface extraction without auxiliary methods, or where strict metric scale is required without depth priors. HybridNeRF was introduced in 2024 by the authors of "Hyb-NeRF: A Multiresolution Hybrid Encoding for Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on multi-resolution hash encoding and learnable positional encoding concepts to balance rendering quality and computational efficiency. The method was evaluated on Blender, Synthetic-NSVF, and Tanks&Temples datasets, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced training times compared to prior methods. name: SeaThru-NeRF
head: SeaThru
body: SeaThru-NeRF is a neural radiance field method designed for visualizing and reconstructing scenes within dispersed scattering media, such as fog, haze, and subaquatic environments. It extends the standard NeRF formulation by treating the scattering medium as a semi-transparent entity with distinct color and density parameters, separate from opaque objects. This allows the model to distinguish between unblemished and backscattered segments of the scene, enabling the restoration of scene hue and 3D configuration in far-off areas that are typically obscured. It builds on HybridNeRF Model Architecture by incorporating a scattering model into the NeRF rendering formulas. SeaThru-NeRF modifies the standard volume rendering equation to account for the additive density and color contributions of a scattering medium. It assumes that the total density at any point along a ray is the sum of the object density and the medium density. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray r, scene geometry and appearance data (learned via MLPs). Output: Rendered color C(r), potentially decomposed into object-only and medium-only components. Data Structures: The method utilizes the standard NeRF MLP architecture but outputs two sets of parameters for each sampled point t along the ray: object density \sigma{obj}(t) and object color c{obj}(t), and medium density \sigma{med}(t) and medium color c{med}(t). Rendering Formulas: The rendered color C(r) is computed by integrating the accumulated color along the ray segment from tn to tf: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \left[ \sigma{obj}(t)c{obj}(t) + \sigma{med}(t)c{med}(t) \right] dt \quad (8) where T(t) is the transmittance, representing the probability that light travels from the camera to point t without being absorbed or scattered: T(t) = \exp \left( - \int{tn}^{t} \left[ \sigma{obj}(s) + \sigma{med}(s) \right] ds \right) \quad (9) Here, c{obj}(t) and c{med}(t) are the colors of the object and medium at t, respectively. Training: The model parameters are optimized by minimizing the squared distance between the expected color \hat{C}(r) and the ground truth color C{gt}(r). Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the rendering step for a single ray. The discrete volume rendering accumulation is a standard implementation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderseathruray(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, numsamples, queryobject, querymedium): """ Renders a single ray using the SeaThru-NeRF scattering model. Args: rayorigin: list of 3 floats, camera origin. raydirection: list of 3 floats, normalized ray direction. tnear: float, near plane distance. tfar: float, far plane distance. numsamples: int, number of sample points along the ray. queryobject: function, returns (sigmaobj, cobj) for a 3D point. querymedium: function, returns (sigmamed, cmed) for a 3D point. Returns: color: float, rendered color value. """ # Discretize the ray into uniformly spaced sample points tvals = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] deltat = (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tvals[i] point = [rayorigin[j] + t raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] # Query object and medium properties sigmaobj, cobj = queryobject(point) sigmamed, cmed = querymedium(point) # Total density at this point sigmatotal = sigmaobj + sigmamed # Skip if density is negligible to avoid division by zero if sigmatotal < 1e-6: accumulatedtransmittance = math.exp(-sigmatotal deltat) continue # Calculate opacity for this segment: alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma deltat) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmatotal deltat) # Weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha # Compute weighted color contribution: ctotal = (sigmaobjcobj + sigmamedcmed) / sigmatotal ctotal = (sigmaobj cobj + sigmamed cmed) / (sigmatotal + 1e-6) accumulatedcolor += weight ctotal # Update transmittance for next step: T{i+1} = Ti (1 - alpha) accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If the medium density is zero everywhere, the model reduces to standard NeRF. If object density is zero, it renders only the medium. Precision: The exponential function in transmittance calculation can lead to underflow for very dense media. Clamping or using log-space arithmetic may be necessary. Boundary Conditions: The integration limits tn and tf must be carefully chosen to include all relevant scattering and object contributions. Fast super-resolution NeRF. Link Compression for NeRF. Link Modifies shading for relighting. Link Uses hybrid representations for multi-space scenes. Link Hybrid representation for large-scale scenes. Link Panoramic NeRF. Link Depth estimation with ambiguity. Link Dynamic scenes. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray and the depth of the MLPs. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two sets of density and color parameters per point, effectively doubling the output size of the MLPs compared to standard NeRF. Strengths: Capable of restoring scene hue and 3D configuration in far-off areas obscured by scattering media. Can produce lifelike new-view composites while maintaining or eliminating the medium effect. Limitations: Performance in highly complex reflective and refractive scenes may require more subspaces, similar to MS-NeRF. Not given in the sources for specific hardware performance metrics. When to use: Underwater, fog, or haze visualization and reconstruction. When not to use: Clear air scenes where standard NeRF is sufficient and more efficient. SeaThru-NeRF was introduced in 2023. It is inspired by the SeaThru method. It extends the capability of NeRFs to handle scattering media such as underwater environments. The method showcases proficiency in depicting scenes in both simulated and actual settings, resulting in cutting-edge, realistic new-view composites.
