name: NeRF-based View Morphing
head: VM-NeRF
body: NeRF-based View Morphing (VM-NeRF) synthesizes intermediate training views from sparse input camera pairs using geometric constraints and disparity-based warping. It addresses the challenge of sparse training data in Neural Radiance Fields by generating photometrically consistent intermediate views, improving reconstruction quality over semantic-based augmentation methods like DietNeRF. VM-NeRF generates a set of morphed views M = \{M{(k,k'),\alpha}\} from a pair of input views k and k' with a mixing parameter \alpha. The process consists of rectification, disparity computation, image morphing, and coalescence, followed by integration into the training loop. Inputs: Two input views k and k', each consisting of an image I, a predicted depth map D, and a camera pose P (containing rotation R and translation t). Camera intrinsics include focal lengths fk, f{k'} and principal points ok, o{k'}. Outputs: A set of morphed images \hat{I}{k,\alpha} and \hat{I}{k',\alpha} which are fused into a single new training view. Camera Pose: P = [R, t], where R is a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix and t is a 3 \times 1 translation vector. Rectification Matrix: \tilde{R} = [ax, ay, az], a 3 \times 3 rotation matrix representing the common coplanar image plane. Disparity Map: E, a 2D array of the same spatial dimensions as the input image, storing disparity values. Baseline Direction: \tilde{\beta}k, a 3D vector. \gamma: Threshold for discarding camera pairs. Pairs with distance > \gamma are discarded to prevent morphing across invisible regions. Typical value: 6. \sigma: Standard deviation for the Gaussian distribution sampling \alpha. Chosen such that 3\sigma reaches the optic center positions. Typical value: 0.2. M: Number of new views regenerated every \eta iterations for each valid camera pair. Typical value: 1. \eta: Interval in training iterations after warm-up to regenerate VM-NeRF views. Typical value: 5. \lambda: Number of iterations NeRF warms up on known views before synthesizing VM-NeRF views. Typical value: 500. 1. Rectification: Rotate known camera poses Pk and P{k'} around their optical centers until their image planes become coplanar. Compute the common image plane rotation matrix \tilde{R} = [ax, ay, az] using a stereo rectification algorithm. Apply \tilde{R} to the original images \{Ik, I{k'}\} and depth maps \{Dk, D{k'}\} to generate rectified images \{\tilde{I}k, \tilde{I}{k'}\} and rectified depth maps \{\tilde{D}k, \tilde{D}{k'}\}. Pitfall: Conventional rectification assumes horizontal alignment. If the angle between az and the z-component of the original view poses Pk, P{k'} is greater than 45^\circ, rotate the warping matrices and poses by 90^\circ or 180^\circ to mitigate rectification error. 2. Disparity Computation: Compute disparity maps Ek and E{k'} as functions of the rectified estimated depths. Compute the baseline direction \tilde{\beta}k: \tilde{\beta}k = az \times ((ok - o{k'}) \times az) where \times denotes the cross product. Compute disparity maps: Ek = \frac{fk}{\tilde{D}k} \frac{1}{\|\tilde{\beta}k\|} E{k'} = \frac{f{k'}}{\tilde{D}{k'}} \frac{1}{\|\tilde{\beta}k\|} where fk, f{k'} are focal lengths and \tilde{D}k, \tilde{D}{k'} are rectified depths. 3. Pixel Correspondences: Determine the pixel correspondences qk(\tilde{I}k) using the disparity maps and baseline direction. Compute correspondences: qk(\tilde{I}k) = \tilde{I}k + \frac{\tilde{\beta}k}{\|\tilde{\beta}k\|^2} (1 \odot Ek) where 1 is a matrix of ones matching Ek's dimensions, \odot indicates the Hadamard product, and the operation yields a displacement field. Perform the same operation for k' to get q{k'}(\tilde{I}{k'}). 4. Image Morphing: Compute the position of each pixel on the morphed camera using warp functions parameterized by \alpha to obtain \hat{I}{k,\alpha} and \hat{I}{k',\alpha}. 5. Coalescence: Fuse pixels from the two views k and k' that fall in the same position. Concatenate the coordinates and pixel values from both warped views. For pixels occupying the same position, preserve only the pixel value of the point nearest to the camera. Use the rectified depth maps \{\tilde{D}k, \tilde{D}{k'}\} to determine the distance of the points. 6. View Sampling: Randomly sample new views for training. Sample \alpha from a Gaussian distribution centered halfway through the camera pair: \alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0.5, \sigma) with 0 \le \alpha \le 1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.ndimage import mapcoordinates def computebaselinedirection(az, ok, okprime): """Computes the baseline direction betatildek.""" ok3d = np.array([ok[0], ok[1], 0.0]) okprime3d = np.array([okprime[0], okprime[1], 0.0]) diff = ok3d - okprime3d return np.cross(az, np.cross(diff, az)) def computedisparity(f, Dtilde, betatildek): """Computes disparity map E.""" normbeta = np.linalg.norm(betatildek) if normbeta < 1e-8: return np.zeroslike(Dtilde) return (f / Dtilde) (1.0 / normbeta) def computedisplacementfield(betatildek, E): """Computes the pixel displacement field qk - Itilde.""" normbetasq = np.dot(betatildek, betatildek) if normbetasq < 1e-8: return np.zeroslike(E) onesmatrix = np.oneslike(E) displacement = (betatildek / normbetasq) (onesmatrix E) return displacement def warpimage(Itilde, displacement): """Warps an image using the computed displacement field.""" H, W = Itilde.shape[:2] y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') dispx = displacement[..., 0] dispy = displacement[..., 1] newx = x + dispx newy = y + dispy coords = np.stack([newy, newx], axis=0) coords[0] = np.clip(coords[0], 0, H - 1) coords[1] = np.clip(coords[1], 0, W - 1) return mapcoordinates(Itilde, coords, order=1, mode='nearest') def coalesce(I1, I2, D1, D2): """Fuses two warped views, keeping the nearest pixel to the camera.""" flatI1 = I1.reshape(-1, I1.shape[-1]) flatI2 = I2.reshape(-1, I2.shape[-1]) flatD1 = D1.flatten() flatD2 = D2.flatten() mask = flatD1 <= flatD2 result = np.where(mask[:, None], flatI1, flatI2) return result.reshape(I1.shape) def vmnerfmorph(Ik, Dk, Pk, Ikprime, Dkprime, Pkprime, fk, fkprime, ok, okprime): """Executes one VM-NeRF morphing step.""" # 1. Rectification Rtilde = stereorectification(Pk, Pkprime) az = Rtilde[:, 2] Itildek = applyrotation(Ik, Rtilde) Dtildek = applyrotation(Dk, Rtilde) Itildekprime = applyrotation(Ikprime, Rtilde) Dtildekprime = applyrotation(Dkprime, Rtilde) # 2. Disparity betatildek = computebaselinedirection(az, ok, okprime) Ek = computedisparity(fk, Dtildek, betatildek) Ekprime = computedisparity(fkprime, Dtildekprime, betatildek) # 3. Correspondences & 4. Image Morphing dispk = computedisplacementfield(betatildek, Ek) dispkprime = computedisplacementfield(betatildek, Ekprime) Ihatk = warpimage(Itildek, dispk) Ihatkprime = warpimage(Itildekprime, dispkprime) # 5. Coalescence return coalesce(Ihatk, Ihatkprime, Dtildek, Dtildekprime) def stereorectification(Pk, Pkprime): """Computes coplanar rotation matrix Rtilde = [ax, ay, az].""" # Standard stereo rectification aligns optical axes horizontally. # Returns a 3x3 rotation matrix. pass def applyrotation(image, R): """Applies rotation R to image coordinates.""" # Standard coordinate transformation for rectification. pass Rectification Error: If the angle between az and the z-component of the original view poses is > 45^\circ, rotate warping matrices and poses by 90^\circ or 180^\circ. Singular Configurations: Discard camera pairs where the optical center of one camera is within the field of view of another, as these violate geometric constraints. Distance Threshold: Discard camera pairs with distance > \gamma (Typical: 6) to avoid morphing across invisible regions. Noisy Depth: The depth NeRF renders at early iterations is noisy. A warm-up period of \lambda iterations (Typical: 500) is required before synthesizing VM-NeRF views. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead to the training loop for rectification, warping, and coalescence. New views are regenerated every \eta iterations (Typical: 5). Memory Complexity: Requires storing rectified images, depth maps, and disparity maps for the camera pairs. Performance: On the 8-view DietNeRF setup, VM-NeRF achieved a PSNR of 24.14 compared to DietNeRF's 23.59. On the 4-view setup, VM-NeRF improved PSNR by +1.02 on average compared to the baseline. Strengths: Interpolates original photometric information without losing detail through low-dimensional encoding, unlike CLIP-based methods. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation; noisy depth in early training requires warm-up. VM-NeRF was introduced by Matteo Bortolon, Alessio Del Bue, and Fabio Poiesi in the paper "VM-NeRF: Tackling Sparsity in NeRF with View Morphing". It adapts the classical view morphing technique to a learning-based NeRF pipeline to address sparse training data. name: Sparsesat-NeRF
head: SpS-NeRF
body: Sparsesat-NeRF is a neural radiance field optimization method for sparse-view satellite imagery that integrates dense depth supervision derived from Semi-Global Matching (SGM) to resolve reconstruction ambiguities. Unlike standard NeRF or Sat-NeRF, which rely on hierarchical coarse/fine models with importance sampling, Sparsesat-NeRF employs a single coarse network with a hybrid ray sampling strategy that uses random samples for global structure and guided Gaussian samples around depth priors for local geometry. It explicitly models input depth uncertainty to weight the depth loss and control the sampling distribution, enabling robust training with as few as two or three input images. Inputs: N input satellite images with refined RPC camera poses. N low-resolution depth maps (downsampled by factor 2^{-2}) and corresponding cross-correlation similarity maps generated via SGM. Scene envelope defined by near (tn) and far (tf) planes. Outputs: Optimized neural radiance field parameters (density \sigma and color c). Novel view images and depth maps. The method does not define unique persistent data structures beyond standard neural network weights and the pre-computed depth/similarity maps. The depth map D{input} and similarity map corr are indexed by pixel coordinates (u, v). 1. Pre-processing: Refine RPC camera poses using bundle adjustment. For each of the N input images, run an independent SGM algorithm to generate a low-resolution depth map D{input}(u,v) and a cross-correlation similarity map corr(u,v). If SGM depths are unavailable, substitute with a coarse global DEM (e.g., SRTM) and set corr(u,v) to a constant value. 2. Ray Casting and Sampling: For each training ray r, divide the total samples into two groups of equal cardinality N{sample} = 64. Group 1 (Random) samples N{sample} points uniformly at random within the scene envelope [tn, tf]. Group 2 (Guided) samples N{sample} points based on a Gaussian distribution centered on a depth prior. If the pixel has valid input depth during training, draw from \mathcal{N}(D{input}(r), \Sigma(r)). If the pixel lacks input depth (occlusion) or during testing, draw from \mathcal{N}(D(r), S(r)), where D(r) is the predicted depth and S(r) is the predicted standard deviation. 3. Network Query: Query the coarse neural network at each sample point xi along ray r to obtain density \sigmai and color ci. 4. Volume Rendering: Compute opacity \alphai and transmittance Ti for each sample: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between samples. Render the final color C(r): C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci 5. Depth Prediction and Uncertainty Estimation: Compute the predicted depth D(r) along the ray: D(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ti Compute the predicted standard deviation S(r) of the sample distribution: S(r)^2 = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai (ti - D(r))^2 Compute the input uncertainty \Sigma(r) from the similarity map: \Sigma(r) = \gamma \cdot (1 - corr(r)) + m where \gamma = 1.0 and m = 10^{-4}. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the mean squared error between rendered color C(r) and ground truth color \hat{C}(r) over all rays R: L{color}(r) = \| C(r) - \hat{C}(r) \|^2 L{color} = \sum{r \in R} L{color}(r) Define a subregion R{sub} for each ray where the depth loss is active. The condition for inclusion in R{sub} is: S(r) > \Sigma(r) \quad \text{OR} \quad |D(r) - D{input}(r)| > \Sigma(r) Compute the weighted depth loss over R{sub}: L{depth}(r) = \sum{r \in R{sub}} corr(r) (D(r) - D{input}(r))^2 Compute the total loss: L = L{color} + \lambda L{depth} where \lambda = 31 for urban areas and \lambda = 50 for rural areas. 7. Optimization: Update network parameters using gradient descent. Repeat for 30,000 iterations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def computeuncertainty(corrmap, gamma=1.0, m=1e-4): """Compute input uncertainty Sigma from cross-correlation similarity.""" return gamma (1.0 - corrmap) + m def generaterays(imageshape, camerapose, intrinsics): """Standard pinhole camera ray generation. Returns origins (H, W, 3) and directions (H, W, 3).""" h, w = imageshape y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(h), torch.arange(w), indexing='ij') # Back-project pixel coordinates to camera space fx, fy = intrinsics[0, 0], intrinsics[1, 1] cx, cy = intrinsics[0, 2], intrinsics[1, 2] zcam = torch.ones(h, w) xcam = (x - cx) / fx ycam = (y - cy) / fy rayscam = torch.stack([xcam, ycam, zcam], dim=-1) # Transform to world space using camera pose raysdir = (camerapose[:3,:3] @ rayscam.view(-1, 3).T).T.view(h, w, 3) raysdir = raysdir / torch.norm(raysdir, dim=-1, keepdim=True) raysorig = camerapose[:3, 3].expand(h, w, 3) return raysorig, raysdir def volumerender(points, network, tsamples, nearplane, farplane): """Query network and perform volume rendering.""" sigma, color = network(points) # Compute deltas: deltai = t{i+1} - ti deltas = torch.cat([tsamples[1:] - tsamples[:-1], torch.tensor([farplane - tsamples[-1]])]) # Compute opacity alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) # Compute transmittance: Ti = prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=0) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:1]), transmittance[:-1]]) # Render color weights = transmittance alpha renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=0) # Render depth rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights tsamples, dim=0) # Render depth variance S^2 depthvar = torch.sum(weights (tsamples - rendereddepth)2, dim=0) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvar def trainstep(images, depthmaps, corrmaps, cameraposes, intrinsics, network, optimizer, nearplane, farplane, lambdadepth=31): """Single training step.""" optimizer.zerograd() totalcolorloss = 0.0 totaldepthloss = 0.0 Nrandom = 64 Nguided = 64 for image, depthmap, corrmap, campose in zip(images, depthmaps, corrmaps, cameraposes): rayso, raysd = generaterays(image.shape[:2], campose, intrinsics) sigmainput = computeuncertainty(corrmap) # Group 1: Random samples trandom = torch.rand(Nrandom) (farplane - nearplane) + nearplane pointsrandom = rayso + trandom.unsqueeze(1) raysd # Group 2: Guided samples validdepthmask = ~torch.isnan(depthmap) guidedpointslist = [] tguidedlist = [] # Pixels with valid input depth if validdepthmask.any(): dinput = depthmap[validdepthmask] sinput = sigmainput[validdepthmask] z = torch.randn(validdepthmask.sum(), Nguided) tguidedvalid = dinput.unsqueeze(1) + z sinput.unsqueeze(1) tguidedvalid = torch.clamp(tguidedvalid, min=nearplane, max=farplane) pointsvalid = rayso[validdepthmask] + tguidedvalid.unsqueeze(2) raysd[validdepthmask] guidedpointslist.append(pointsvalid) tguidedlist.append(tguidedvalid) # Pixels without input depth (occlusions) -> fallback to scene bounds midpoint if (~validdepthmask).any(): dfallback = (nearplane + farplane) / 2.0 sfallback = (farplane - nearplane) / 4.0 z = torch.randn((~validdepthmask).sum(), Nguided) tguidedinvalid = dfallback + z sfallback tguidedinvalid = torch.clamp(tguidedinvalid, min=nearplane, max=farplane) pointsinvalid = rayso[~validdepthmask] + tguidedinvalid.unsqueeze(2) raysd[~validdepthmask] guidedpointslist.append(pointsinvalid) tguidedlist.append(tguidedinvalid) guidedpoints = torch.cat(guidedpointslist, dim=0) tguided = torch.cat(tguidedlist, dim=0) # Combine and render allpoints = torch.cat([pointsrandom, guidedpoints], dim=0) allt = torch.cat([trandom, tguided], dim=0) renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvar = volumerender(allpoints, network, allt, nearplane, farplane) # Color Loss colorloss = torch.mean((renderedcolor - image)2) # Depth Loss over Rsub diff = rendereddepth - depthmap sr = torch.sqrt(depthvar + 1e-8) sigmar = sigmainput # Rsub condition: S(r) > Sigma(r) OR |D(r) - Dinput(r)| > Sigma(r) masksub = (sr > sigmar) | (torch.abs(diff) > sigmar) # Only compute depth loss where input depth is valid and masksub is true validandactive = validdepthmask & masksub if validandactive.any(): activediff = diff[validandactive] activecorr = corrmap[validandactive] depthlossval = torch.sum(activecorr (activediff2)) else: depthlossval = torch.tensor(0.0) totalcolorloss += colorloss totaldepthloss += depthlossval loss = totalcolorloss + lambdadepth totaldepthloss loss.backward() optimizer.step() SGM Resolution Scale: 2^{-2} (depth maps downsampled by factor of 4). Uncertainty Scaling \gamma: 1.0. Uncertainty Shift m: 10^{-4}. Depth Loss Weight \lambda: 31 for urban areas, 50 for rural areas. Initial Random Samples: 64. Guided Samples: 64. Batch Size: 1024. Training Iterations: 30,000. Learning Rate: 10^{-5} (inherited from Sat-NeRF backbone). Learning Rate Decay: 0.9. Depth Loss Inactivity: The depth loss is inactive or clipped outside the subregion R{sub} defined by S(r) > \Sigma(r) or |D(r) - D{input}(r)| > \Sigma(r). This prevents the optimizer from being biased by inaccurate depth priors in occluded or low-texture regions. Missing Depth: If SGM depths are unavailable, the method falls back to a coarse global DEM (e.g., SRTM) with a constant similarity metric. High-Resolution Depth Bias: Using high-resolution SGM depths is avoided to prevent biasing the NeRF towards the SGM solution and to mitigate incomplete depth information at challenging surfaces (e.g., low texture). Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 2 hours on an NVIDIA GPU with 40GB RAM for 30,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Uses a single coarse network, reducing memory overhead compared to hierarchical NeRF models that require coarse and fine networks. Strengths: Efficiently handles sparse satellite views by leveraging external depth priors. The guided sampling reduces the number of samples needed to resolve geometry compared to pure random sampling. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the input SGM depth maps. Performance degrades if depth maps are missing or inaccurate. The method uses only a coarse model, potentially lacking the fine-detail resolution of hierarchical NeRFs. When to Use: Suitable for sparse-view satellite imagery reconstruction where dense depth maps can be generated via SGM. When Not to Use: Unsuitable for scenarios requiring high-frequency detail resolution that might require a fine model, or where SGM depth generation is not feasible. Sparsesat-NeRF was introduced in 2023 by researchers presenting at the ISPRS Geospatial Week. It builds upon the Sat-NeRF architecture but adapts it for sparse satellite imagery by integrating dense depth supervision. The method draws inspiration from Roessle et al. (2022) for guided sampling and depth loss formulation. It is specifically designed to address the challenges of photo-realistic novel view synthesis from very few satellite images (2-3 views). name: StegaNeRF
head: StegaNeRF: Embedding Invisible Information within Neural Radiance Fields
body: StegaNeRF is a method for steganographic information embedding in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that allows accurate hidden information extraction from rendered images while preserving original visual quality, solving the problem of copyright/ownership identification in shared 3D content. Unlike traditional 2D steganography which embeds signals only into specific source images, StegaNeRF allows recovery of the same hidden signal from NeRF renderings at arbitrary viewpoints. It differs from prior 3D mesh steganography by hiding information in a continuous neural representation (NeRF) rather than discrete mesh geometry, enabling viewpoint-independent recovery. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images \{Yi\} with corresponding camera poses \{Pi\}; hidden information I (e.g., an image or message); learning rates \eta = [\eta0, \eta1]. Outputs: Steganographic NeRF weights \theta and detector network weights \psi. Data Structures: NeRF (\theta, \theta0): The neural radiance field parameters. \theta0 are the initial weights trained without steganography; \theta are the final weights containing the steganographic information. Detector (F\psi): A U-Net network with learnable weights \psi used to decode the hidden information I from 2D renderings. Classifier (F{\psic}): A network used to classify whether a NeRF rendering contains hidden information. Mask (m): A gradient-based mask computed from \theta0 to steer steganographic updates toward less important weights. (Note: The exact formula for m is referenced as Eq. 3 in the source but not provided in the text snippets.) Algorithm Steps: 1. Stage 1: Initial Training. Train the initial NeRF weights \theta0 using standard photometric loss between rendered and ground truth pixels to guarantee visual quality. 2. Compute Mask. Compute the importance mask m for \theta0. 3. Stage 2: Steganographic Optimization. Initialize final NeRF weights \theta with \theta0. For each training iteration t: a. Randomly sample a training pose Pi and render the image \theta(Pi). b. Render the original NeRF image \theta0(Pi) for negative sampling. c. Compute steganographic losses (defined below). d. Compute standard rendering loss L{rgb}. e. Combine total loss L (defined below). f. Update detector weights \psi using learning rate \eta1: \psi \leftarrow \psi - \eta1 \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \psi}. g. Update NeRF weights \theta using learning rate \eta0 and mask m: \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta0 \cdot (m \odot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}). Formulas: Contrastive Detection Loss: L^+{dec} = |F\psi(\theta(P)) - I| L^-{dec} = |F\psi(\theta0(P)) - \emptyset| Where F\psi is the detector network, \theta is the steganographic NeRF weights, \theta0 is the original NeRF weights, P is the camera pose, I is the hidden information, and \emptyset is an empty image with all zeros. Classifier-Guided Recovery Loss: L^c{dec} = -\log F{\psic}(\theta(P)) - \log(1 - F{\psic}(\theta0(P))) Where F{\psic} is the classifier network outputting the probability of hidden information presence. Total Loss: L = \lambda0 L^c{dec} + \lambda1 L^+{dec} + \lambda2 L^-{dec} + \lambda3 L{rgb} Where \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are weighting coefficients. Parameters: \eta0: Learning rate for NeRF weight update. \eta1: Learning rate for detector weight update. \theta0: Initial NeRF weights trained in Stage 1 without steganography. \theta: Final NeRF weights containing steganographic information, initialized from \theta0. F\psi: Detector network with learnable weights \psi. F{\psic}: Classifier network. I: The customizable hidden information (e.g., image, message) to be embedded. \emptyset: An empty image with all zeros. Pitfalls: Naively applying 2D steganography methods (like LSB or DeepStega) to NeRF training images fails because the embedded information gets smoothed out and lost in the actual NeRF renderings, inhibiting detection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainsteganerf(trainingimages, trainingposes, hiddeninfo, eta0, eta1, lambda0, lambda1, lambda2, lambda3): # Stage 1: Train initial NeRF theta0 = initializenerf() for iteration in range(stage1iterations): pose = randomsample(trainingposes) gtimage = getgtimage(trainingimages, pose) renderedimage = rendernerf(theta0, pose) lossrgb = meansquarederror(renderedimage, gtimage) theta0 = updateweights(theta0, eta0, lossrgb) # Compute mask for gradient masking (implementation details not provided in source) mask = computeimportancemask(theta0) # Stage 2: Steganographic Optimization theta = copyweights(theta0) detector = initializeunet() classifier = initializeclassifier() for iteration in range(stage2iterations): # Sample pose and render pose = randomsample(trainingposes) stegorender = rendernerf(theta, pose) originalrender = rendernerf(theta0, pose) # Compute steganographic losses # L+dec: Recover hidden info from stego render lplusdec = meansquarederror(detector(stegorender), hiddeninfo) # L-dec: Detect empty image from original render emptyimage = zeroslike(hiddeninfo) lminusdec = meansquarederror(detector(originalrender), emptyimage) # Lcdec: Classifier-guided recovery # Classifier predicts probability of hidden info presence probstego = classifier(stegorender) proboriginal = classifier(originalrender) lcdec = -log(probstego) - log(1 - proboriginal) # Compute standard rendering loss gtimage = getgtimage(trainingimages, pose) lrgb = meansquarederror(stegorender, gtimage) # Combine total loss totalloss = (lambda0 lcdec + lambda1 lplusdec + lambda2 lminusdec + lambda3 lrgb) # Update detector detectorgrads = computegradients(totalloss, detector) detector = updateweights(detector, eta1, detectorgrads) # Update NeRF with gradient masking nerfgrads = computegradients(totalloss, theta) maskedgrads = elementwisemultiply(mask, nerfgrads) theta = updateweights(theta, eta0, maskedgrads) return theta, detector Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Extensive experimental results validate StegaNeRF balances between the rendering quality of novel views and the high-fidelity transmission of the concealed information. Strengths: Enables reliable extraction of the hidden signal from NeRF renderings at arbitrary viewpoints, unlike 2D steganography. Uses adaptive gradient masking to steer hidden information towards less important NeRF weights, balancing steganography ability and rendering visual quality. Limitations: Requires joint optimization of the NeRF and detector networks. When to use: Designed for ownership identification, copyright protection, and preserving multiple source identities in collaborative 3D scene reconstruction. StegaNeRF was introduced by Chenxin Li, Brandon Y. Feng, Zhiwen Fan, Panwang Pan, and Zhangyang Wang in arXiv:2212.01602v1 on Dec 3, 2022. It represents the first exploration of hiding information in NeRF models for ownership identification. name: MapNeRF
head: Map-NeRF, MapNeRF: Incorporating Map Priors into Neural Radiance Fields for Driving View Simulation
body: MapNeRF is a method for synthesizing out-of-trajectory driving views with semantic road consistency by incorporating map priors into neural radiance fields. Unlike standard NeRF methods that fail on view extrapolation and lack semantic consistency for deviated views, MapNeRF uses coarse ground surface and lane information as uncertain supervisory signals to guide the density field and depth warping. It sets itself apart from siblings like SeaThru-NeRF or FastSR-NeRF by explicitly leveraging structured map data (ground height, lane vectors) rather than relying solely on image-based augmentation or unsupervised consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images \{Ii\} with corresponding camera poses \{Pi\} and intrinsics; a map M containing ground height and lane vectors. Outputs: A 5D radiance field function F parameterized by an MLP, capable of rendering color and depth for arbitrary camera poses, including those outside the training trajectory. Data Structures: Radiance Field F: A function mapping 3D location x = (x, y, z) and 2D viewing direction d = (\theta, \phi) to density \sigma and color c. \sigma, c = F(d, x) Map M: Contains ground height and lane vectors. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling for Unseen Views: Propose sampling rays to simulate unseen views (view extrapolation), utilizing ground and lane information from map M in the sampling computations to guide the radiance field. 2. Ground Density Supervision: Employ ground information from M to supervise the density field \sigma of the NeRF, providing a more reliable road base for semantic entities. 3. Depth Warping with Uncertainty: Warp depth with uncertainty derived from unknown camera poses to ensure multi-view consistency. 4. Uncertainty Tempering: Model the supervision methods as weak supervision using an uncertainty parameter and propose an uncertainty tempering scheme to increase the uncertainty, ensuring map priors only guide rather than enforce training. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss combining photometric reconstruction and the map-guided supervisory losses. Formulas: Rendered Depth: For a ray r, the rendered depth \hat{D}(r) is calculated as: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \sum{j=1}^{i} \deltaj where N is the number of samples, \sigmai is the density at sample i, \deltai is the distance between sample i and i+1, and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance. Photometric Loss: The L2 photometric reconstruction loss supervises training: L{rgb} = \sum{r \in Ii} || \hat{C}(r) - C^{gt}(r) ||2^2 where \hat{C}(r) is the rendered color and C^{gt}(r) is the ground truth color. Parameters: Map M: Contains ground height and lane vectors. Uncertainty Parameter: Used to model weak supervision. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: View Extrapolation Failure: Existing NeRF methods fail on view extrapolation (synthesizing views outside the training trajectory). MapNeRF addresses this but requires careful handling of the uncertainty tempering to avoid over-constraining the model with potentially inaccurate map data. Map Accuracy: Errors from semantic-level map data can introduce training errors if not properly modeled as weak supervision with uncertainty. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Experimental results demonstrate that the approach produces semantic consistency in deviated views for vehicle camera simulation and improves rendering quality of interpolated novel view synthesis quantitatively. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves semantic consistency of deviated views; leverages commonly used map priors in AD scenes; ensures multi-view consistency through uncertainty modeling. Limitations: Relies on the availability and accuracy of map priors (ground height, lane vectors); weak supervision requires tuning of the uncertainty tempering scheme. When to use: When simulating camera sensors for autonomous driving, specifically for out-of-trajectory views where semantic road consistency is critical. Origin: Proposed by Chenming Wu, Jiadai Sun, Zhelun Shen, and Liangjun Zhang in "MapNeRF: Incorporating Map Priors into Neural Radiance Fields for Driving View Simulation" (arXiv:2307.14981v2, 6 Aug 2023). History and Development: Standard NeRF in autonomous driving simulations struggles with view extrapolation. Collecting extensive data for view interpolation is time- and cost-intensive, while relying on log data from road tests is labor-intensive, costly, and dangerous. MapNeRF addresses this by incorporating map priors with uncertainty to guide training. Usage: Used in autonomous driving simulation for training and evaluating AD software and algorithms, specifically for generating photorealistic views outside the recorded driving trajectory. name: Radiance Field Decoding with Hybrid Features
head: D(x, fr)
body: This method defines the radiance field decoder D that predicts volume density \sigma and color c for a 3D location x and viewing direction d, conditioned on global triplane features f{tp} and residual local features fr. It differs from standard NeRF decoders by replacing raw positional encoding with structured global features (triplanes) and local residuals, enabling effective 360° view synthesis from minimal input views. Inputs: 3D query point x = (x, y, z). Viewing direction d. Triplane set S = \{S{xy}, S{xz}, S{yz}\}, where each S is a 2D feature map. Residual local features fr associated with the query point or neighborhood. Outputs: Volume density \sigma. View-dependent color c. Data Structures: Triplanes (S): Three 2D tensors representing orthogonal projections of the scene. Dimensions are not explicitly given in the sources. Residual Features (fr): Local feature vectors. In the variant, these are enhanced by aggregating image features gi via an MLP: ri = r'i + \text{MLP}(r'i, gi). Steps: 1. Coordinate System Establishment: Establish the coordinate system using the view space of the input image to standardize scene scales. 2. Triplane Sampling: Orthogonally project point x into each plane in S. Perform bilinear sampling to obtain vectors from the xy, xz, and yz planes: f{tp} = [S{xy}(i, j), S{xz}(j, k), S{yz}(i, k)] where (i, j, k) are the projected coordinates. 3. Feature Conditioning: Concatenate the sampled triplane features f{tp} with the residual local features fr and the viewing direction d. 4. Decoding: Pass the conditioned features through a modular rendering MLP D to predict \sigma and c: \sigma, c = D(x, d, f{tp}, fr). 5. Near/Far Split (Optional): If implementing the NeRF++-style split: Calculate squared distance r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2. If r^2 < 1, use foreground MLP D{fg}. If r^2 > 1, use background MLP D{bg}. A coordinate remapping function M contracts points outside the unit sphere. 6. Multi-view Integration (Optional): To integrate multi-view observations, pool features along the view dimension in the rendering MLPs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decoderadiancefield(x, d, triplanes, residualfeatures, usenearfarsplit=True): """ Decodes radiance field using hybrid features. Args: x: 3D point (x, y, z) d: Viewing direction vector triplanes: Dict with keys 'xy', 'xz', 'yz' containing 2D feature maps residualfeatures: Local feature vector fr usenearfarsplit: Boolean flag for NeRF++ style split Returns: sigma: Volume density c: Color """ # Step 2: Triplane Sampling # Project x into each plane and bilinearly sample # Note: Exact projection indices (i,j,k) depend on coordinate system scaling # Assuming normalized coordinates for simplicity fxy = bilinearsample(triplanes['xy'], x[0], x[1]) fxz = bilinearsample(triplanes['xz'], x[0], x[2]) fyz = bilinearsample(triplanes['yz'], x[1], x[2]) # Concatenate triplane features ftp = concatenate([fxy, fxz, fyz]) # Step 3: Condition MLP with features # Combine triplane, residual, and direction inputfeatures = concatenate([ftp, residualfeatures, d]) # Step 4: Decode if usenearfarsplit: # Step 5: Near/Far Split rsquared = dot(x, x) if rsquared < 1.0: # Foreground MLP sigma, c = Dfg(inputfeatures) else: # Background MLP with coordinate remapping xmapped = remapcoordinate(x) # Contract outside unit sphere inputfeaturesmapped = concatenate([ftp, residualfeatures, d]) # Features might also need remapping or remain same sigma, c = Dbg(inputfeaturesmapped) else: # Single MLP sigma, c = Dsingle(inputfeatures) return sigma, c def bilinearsample(featuremap, u, v): """ Performs bilinear sampling on a 2D feature map. """ # Implementation depends on specific tensor library # Returns interpolated feature vector pass def remapcoordinate(x): """ Remaps coordinates outside the unit sphere. Similar to NeRF++ formulation. """ # Not given in the sources. Standard inverse sphere contraction: # if ||x|| > 1: x' = x (2 - 1/||x||) # else: x' = x norm = norm(x) if norm > 1.0: return x (2.0 - 1.0 / norm) return x Parameters: Triplane Resolution: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Modular implementation as proposed in [74] (NeRF++). Details refer to supplementary material. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Scaling: Using the view space of the input image is critical for standardizing scales across different data sources. Single View Generalization: While the method works for single views, performance may degrade without multi-view pooling. Predicts volume density \deltai for a query point using k nearby geometric-consistent point descriptors, leveraging the view-independent nature of 3D geometry. Estimates radiance values ci through hybrid neural features ri which contain rich details. The hybrid feature ri is enhanced by aggregating image features gi: ri = r'i + \text{MLP}(r'i, gi). Rendering uses standard volume rendering: c = \sum{i=1}^M \taui(1 - \exp(-\deltai\Deltai))ci, where \taui = \exp(-\sum{t=1}^{i-1} \deltat\Deltat). M is the number of query points, \Deltai is the distance between adjacent points. Random drop strategies (ray-based and query-point-based) are used to ensure both modalities of features are well-optimized. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the triplanes and residual features. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Combines local and global feature representations effectively, resulting in accurate 360° view synthesis from as minimal as a single view of an unbounded scene. Standardizes scales of scenes from various data sources. Limitations: Requires careful coordinate system establishment. Performance on single views may be limited compared to multi-view inputs. When to use: Sparse view synthesis, especially outdoor scenes or unbounded scenes. Large-scale scenes with motion blur. When not to use: Dense view settings where standard NeRF might suffice, or when computational resources for triplane storage are limited. Originated in NeO 360 for neural fields in sparse view synthesis of outdoor scenes. Also used in Hybrid Neural Rendering for large-scale scenes with motion blur. Builds on NeRF++ [74] for the modular MLP structure. name: Depth and Geometry Priors
head: Depth-supervised NeRF, RGB-D NeRF, Geometry-constrained NeRF
body: Depth and Geometry Priors are optimization techniques that incorporate explicit depth information (from sensors, stereo, or monocular estimation) into the training of neural radiance fields to resolve the inherent scale ambiguity and geometric inaccuracies of standard volume rendering. They differ from sibling methods like Relighting and Shading or Regularization and Constraints by directly supervising the geometric output (depth) rather than just the photometric output (color), thereby enforcing metric consistency and improving reconstruction speed and accuracy in sparse-view or ambiguous scenarios. The core mechanism involves augmenting the standard NeRF loss function with a geometric term that penalizes the discrepancy between the depth rendered by the neural field and a provided depth prior. 1. Depth Rendering: The expected depth \hat{D}(r) along a ray r is computed as the weighted average of sample depths ti, analogous to color rendering: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the weight of the i-th sample, \alphai is the opacity, and ti is the distance along the ray. 2. Geometric Loss: A loss term lg is added to the photometric loss lp. The most common formulation is the L1 norm between the rendered depth \hat{D}(r) and the ground truth or estimated depth D(r): lg = \sum{r \in R} |\hat{D}(r) - D(r)| In methods accounting for uncertainty, this is normalized by the depth variance \sigmaD(r) to discourage weights on uncertain measurements: lg = \sum{r \in R} \frac{|\hat{D}(r) - D(r)|}{\sigmaD(r)} 3. Sample Guidance: Depth priors are often used to guide the sampling strategy. Instead of uniform or stratified sampling along the entire ray, samples are concentrated around the expected depth value provided by the prior, reducing the number of required samples and accelerating convergence. Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates is a technique for learning a multimodal distribution of depth estimates conditioned on a single input image, using an implicit generative model to capture inherent ambiguities in monocular depth estimation such as non-opaque surfaces and albedo-shading confusion. Unlike GANs which optimize for similarity to a single ground truth, this method uses conditional Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (cIMLE) to prevent mode collapse by enforcing that all ground truth points are explained by at least one generated sample. It is chosen when monocular depth estimation is ambiguous and a single deterministic estimate is insufficient. See Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates. Mip-NeRF RGB-D is a neural scene representation method that reconstructs 3D scenes from multi-view RGB-D data by combining the conical frustum sampling of Mip-NeRF with explicit depth supervision. It solves the limitations of standard NeRF regarding geometric accuracy and training speed by using depth information for local sampling and geometric loss, reducing training time by 3–5 times compared to standard NeRF. Unlike DS-NeRF which relies on sparse point clouds and reprojection errors, Mip-NeRF RGB-D uses dense RGB-D frames and explicitly models depth uncertainty to improve photometry and geometry. It is chosen when high-quality dense RGB-D data is available and fast, accurate geometry is required. See Mip-NeRF RGB-D. SparseNeRF addresses the problem of synthesizing new views from finite perspectives by extracting depth priors from pre-trained depth models or rough depth maps captured by consumer-grade depth sensors. It introduces local depth ordering and spatial continuity constraints to extract robust depth priors from rough depth maps, thereby improving the performance of new view synthesis while maintaining geometric spatial continuity. It is chosen when only sparse or low-quality depth data is available from consumer sensors. Pitfall: Relies on pre-trained depth models or depth maps captured by consumer-grade sensors, the accuracy and quality of which can be limited by real-world conditions. Depth-Guided NeRF Training uses a multistage pipeline for depth supervision to guide NeRF sample placement. It applies a pretrained sparse-to-dense depth completion network to sparse structure-from-motion depth estimates to guide sample placement and supervise NeRF depth. The steps involve finetuning a single-view depth estimation network on sparse multiview stereo depth estimates, using the resulting dense depth maps to guide NeRF sample placement, and supervising the depth produced by NeRF. It is chosen when starting with sparse SfM depth estimates that need to be densified for effective NeRF training. NeRF with Depth Completion Guidance applies a pretrained sparse-to-dense depth completion network to sparse structure-from-motion depth estimates to guide sample placement and supervise NeRF depth. It uses the resulting depth and predicted uncertainty to guide sample placement and supervise the depth produced by NeRF. It is chosen when uncertainty-aware depth completion is needed to robustly handle sparse input data. The integration of depth priors into NeRF originated from the observation that standard NeRF suffers from scale ambiguity and poor geometric accuracy, especially with sparse views. Early works like NerfingMVS [WLR 21] and Roessle et al. [RBM 21] introduced multistage pipelines using sparse-to-dense depth completion to guide sampling and supervise depth. SparseNeRF [38] (2023) further advanced this by using local depth ordering and spatial continuity constraints from rough depth maps. Mip-NeRF RGB-D combined conical frustum sampling with explicit depth supervision to improve both geometry and training speed. These methods are widely used in applications requiring metric 3D reconstruction from limited or noisy depth data, such as autonomous driving, robotics, and cultural heritage digitization. name: Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates
head: Multimodal Depth Prior, cIMLE-based Depth Estimation
body: Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates is a technique for learning a multimodal distribution of depth estimates conditioned on a single input image, using an implicit generative model to capture inherent ambiguities in monocular depth estimation such as non-opaque surfaces and albedo-shading confusion. Unlike GANs which optimize for similarity to a single ground truth, this method uses conditional Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (cIMLE) to prevent mode collapse by enforcing that all ground truth points are explained by at least one generated sample. Inputs: A set of input images \{I1, I2,..., In\}, each with a corresponding ground truth depth map Di. Outputs: Network parameters \phi for the conditional distribution G\phi(I, z) and per-image scale/shift variables. Data Structures: G\phi: Implicit generative network parameterized by \phi. Takes image I and latent code z as input. z: Latent code sampled from standard normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). M: Number of samples drawn per image. \deltai: Threshold radius for the neighborhood around ground truth depth Di. wi: Weighting factor for training example i. Parameters: \phi: Network parameters for G\phi. z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I): Latent codes. M = 20: Typical number of samples. \deltai: Dependent on training example i. wi = 0: In the specific implementation cited, weights are zero. Learning Rate: 1e-6 for \phi and scale/shift variables. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize \phi and a 2-dimensional scale/shift variable for each input image. The depth estimates are in relative scale, so these variables directly optimize the scale and shift for each input image. 2. Sampling: For each training image Ii, sample M latent codes zj \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). Compute M depth estimates y{i,j} = G\phi(Ii, zj). 3. Distance Calculation: Compute the distance d(y{i,j}, Di) between each sampled depth estimate y{i,j} and the ground truth depth map Di. 4. Loss Computation: The objective is derived from maximizing the likelihood induced by the model. The kernel derivative \Phi'{\delta}(t) is defined as: \Phi'{\delta}(t) = \begin{cases} 1/\delta & \text{for } 0 \le t \le \delta \\ 0 & \text{for } t > \delta \end{cases} Maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the minimum distance across the M samples for each image. In the cited implementation, wi = 0 for all i, so the effective loss per image reduces to \min{j \in [M]} d(y{i,j}, Di). 5. Optimization: The scale and shift variables are jointly optimized with the NeRF for the first 400,000 iterations with a learning rate of 1e-6. Then, they are kept frozen for the last 100,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class SGD: def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = 0.0 def step(self): for p in self.params: if p.grad is not None: p.data = p.data - self.lr p.grad def samplenormal(): u1, u2 = random.random(), random.random() return math.sqrt(-2.0 math.log(u1)) math.cos(2.0 math.pi u2) def computel1(pred, gt): total = 0.0 count = 0 for prow, grow in zip(pred, gt): for p, g in zip(prow, grow): total += abs(p - g) count += 1 return total / max(count, 1) def trainambiguityawaredepth(images, gtdepths, phiweights, scaleshiftvars, M=20, numiters=500000, lr=1e-6): # phiweights: list of tensors representing network parameters # scaleshiftvars: list of 2D vectors for per-image scale/shift params = phiweights + scaleshiftvars optimizer = SGD(params=params, lr=lr) for iteration in range(numiters): totalloss = 0.0 for i, (Ii, Di) in enumerate(zip(images, gtdepths)): s, sh = scaleshiftvars[i] zsamples = [samplenormal() for in range(M)] ysamples = [phiweights(Ii, z) for z in zsamples] # Apply scale/shift to depth hypotheses as specified yshifted = [[s y + sh for y in row] for y in ysamples] distances = [computel1(y, Di) for y in yshifted] mindist = min(distances) totalloss += mindist totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \deltai is too small such that all sampled distances d(y{i,j}, Di) > \deltai, the loss becomes constant (\deltai - \deltai = 0), resulting in no gradients for \phi. The minimum viable \deltai is \min{j} d(y{i,j}, Di). Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples M and the cost of the generator G\phi. For each image, M forward passes are required. Memory Complexity: Stores the generator parameters \phi and the latent codes during the forward pass. Strengths: Captures multimodal depth distributions, handling ambiguities like non-opaque surfaces (e.g., glass) and albedo-shading confusion. Prevents mode collapse compared to GANs. Limitations: Requires ground truth depth maps for training. When to use: When monocular depth estimation is inherently ambiguous and a single deterministic estimate is insufficient. Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates was introduced in the SCADE paper (CVPR 2023). It builds on the concept of Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (IMLE). The method is used in the HybridNeRF model architecture to provide a multimodal depth prior. name: Mip-NeRF RGB-D
body: Mip-NeRF RGB-D is a neural scene representation method that reconstructs 3D scenes from multi-view RGB-D data by combining the conical frustum sampling of Mip-NeRF with explicit depth supervision. It solves the geometric inaccuracy and slow convergence of standard NeRF by using depth information for local sampling and geometric loss, reducing training time by 3–5 times compared to standard NeRF. Unlike DS-NeRF which relies on sparse point clouds and reprojection errors, Mip-NeRF RGB-D uses dense RGB-D frames and explicitly models depth uncertainty to improve photometry and geometry. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Multi-view RGB-D data consisting of color images, depth maps, and camera poses (origin o and direction d). Outputs: A neural radiance field represented by an MLP F\Theta that outputs volume density \tau and color C for any 5D coordinate, enabling novel view synthesis and depth estimation. Data Structures Conical Frustum: Defined by a mean position \mu and a covariance matrix \Sigma, approximating the Gaussian distribution of the pixel area at a given distance. Integrated Positional Encoding: A vector constructed from the mean and covariance of the frustum, used as input to the MLP. Network F\Theta: A multilayer perceptron mapping 5D coordinates to radiance and density. Steps 1. Ray to Cone Conversion: For each pixel, generate a ray r(t) = o + td. Replace the ray with a cone generated using the camera center and pixel size to account for the varying area of a pixel with distance. 2. Interval Splitting: Split the cone into N intervals Ti = ti, t{i+1}). 3. Compute Frustum Statistics: For each interval, compute the mean \mu and covariance \Sigma of the corresponding conical frustum. 4. Integrated Positional Encoding: Compute the integrated positional encoding \gamma(\mu, \Sigma) for each interval using the mean and covariance. 5. Network Query: Query the MLP F\Theta with the integrated positional encoding to output volume density \tau and color C. 6. Volume Rendering: Calculate the pixel color \hat{C}(r) and depth \hat{D}(r) using volume rendering over the conical frustum segments. 7. Local Sampling: Use depth information for local sampling to reduce the number of samples along the ray and replace the coarse [NeRF network. 8. Uncertainty Modeling: Incorporate depth uncertainty into a multivariate Gaussian method to query the MLP. 9. Optimization: Optimize network parameters by minimizing a joint loss function combining photometric and geometric losses. Formulas Implicit Function: The network maps 5D coordinates (3D location + viewing direction) to color and volume density: F\Theta: (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) \rightarrow (C, \tau) Integrated Positional Encoding: Encodes the Gaussian approximation of the conical frustum: \gamma(\mu, \Sigma) = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \sin(2^l \mu) \exp(-2^{l-1} \text{diag}(\Sigma)) \\ \cos(2^l \mu) \exp(-2^{l-1} \text{diag}(\Sigma)) \end{bmatrix} \right\}{l=0}^{L-1} where L is the number of frequency bands. Depth Representation: Depth is represented with volume density: \hat{D}(r) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N \deltai ti \alphai}{\sum{i=1}^N \alphai} where \deltaj = t{j+1} - tj is the distance between adjacent samples, ti is the distance along the ray, and \alphai is the opacity of the i-th sample. Photometric Loss: The L1-norm between predicted and ground truth color over a set of rays R: lp = \sum{r \in R} |\hat{C}(r) - C(r)| Geometric Loss: The absolute difference between predicted and true depths, normalized by depth variance to discourage weights with high uncertainty: lg = \sum{r \in R} \frac{|\hat{D}(r) - D(r)|}{\sigmaD(r)} where D(r) is the ground truth depth and \sigmaD(r) is the depth variance. Parameters Number of Intervals (N): Not given in the sources. Frequency Bands (L): Not given in the sources. Near/Far Bounds: Predefined bounds for sampling along the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth Uncertainty: High uncertainty in depth measurements should be handled by normalizing the geometric loss, as the method explicitly models depth uncertainty. Limited Views: The method is designed to improve geometry when a limited number of input views are given. Forward-Facing Scenes: The experiments are limited to forward-facing scenes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mipnerfrgbdforward(cameracenter, raydirection, pixelsize, nearbound, farbound, numintervals, L, mlp, depthdata): """ Forward pass for Mip-NeRF RGB-D. Args: cameracenter: 3D vector, origin o raydirection: 3D vector, direction d pixelsize: float, size of the pixel nearbound: float, near clipping plane farbound: float, far clipping plane numintervals: int, N L: int, number of frequency bands mlp: function, FTheta taking integrated positional encoding depthdata: dict with keys 'color', 'depth', 'variance' for the current ray's pixel Returns: predictedcolor: list of 3 floats, Chat(r) predicteddepth: float, Dhat(r) photometricloss: float, lp (per-ray) geometricloss: float, lg (per-ray) """ # 1. Stratified sampling along the ray tvalues = [nearbound + (farbound - nearbound) (i + 0.5) / numintervals for i in range(numintervals)] intervals = [] for i in range(numintervals): ti = tvalues[i] tiplus1 = tvalues[i+1] if i < numintervals - 1 else farbound delta = tiplus1 - ti mu = (ti + tiplus1) / 2.0 # Covariance computation for conical frustum sigmasq = (delta 2) / 12.0 + (pixelsize 2) / 4.0 # Integrated positional encoding encoding = [] for l in range(L): expterm = math.exp(-2(l-1) sigmasq) encoding.extend([math.sin(2l mu) expterm, math.cos(2l mu) expterm]) intervals.append({ 'mu': mu, 'sigmasq': sigmasq, 'encoding': encoding, 'ti': ti, 'delta': delta }) # 2. Volume rendering predictedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] predicteddepthnum = 0.0 predicteddepthden = 0.0 accumulatedopacity = 1.0 for interval in intervals: tau, color = mlp(interval['encoding']) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tau interval['delta']) weight = alpha accumulatedopacity accumulatedopacity = (1.0 - alpha) # Standard color accumulation for c in range(3): predictedcolor[c] += weight color[c] # Evidence formula for depth: Dhat = sum(deltai ti alphai) / sum(alphai) predicteddepthnum += interval['delta'] interval['ti'] alpha predicteddepthden += alpha predicteddepth = predicteddepthnum / predicteddepthden if predicteddepthden > 0 else 0.0 # 3. Loss computation (per-ray) gtcolor = depthdata['color'] gtdepth = depthdata['depth'] gtvariance = depthdata['variance'] photometricloss = sum(abs(predictedcolor[c] - gtcolor[c]) for c in range(3)) geometricloss = abs(predicteddepth - gtdepth) / gtvariance if gtvariance > 0 else abs(predicteddepth - gtdepth) return predictedcolor, predicteddepth, photometricloss, geometricloss def optimizemipnerfrgbd(dataloader, mlp, numepochs, learningrate): """ Training loop for Mip-NeRF RGB-D. """ params = list(mlp.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for batch in dataloader: totalloss = 0.0 for ray in batch.rays: predcolor, preddepth, lp, lg = mipnerfrgbdforward( ray.cameracenter, ray.direction, ray.pixelsize, ray.near, ray.far, ray.numintervals, ray.L, mlp, ray.depthdata) totalloss += lp + lg # Standard gradient descent update for p in params: if p.grad is not None: p.data -= learningrate p.grad Uses depth information to guide sampling along the ray, reducing the number of samples and replacing the coarse NeRF network. It is chosen when dense depth priors are available to accelerate convergence and improve geometry. Incorporates depth uncertainty into a multivariate Gaussian method to query the MLP, allowing the network to learn multiple scales of uncertainty. It is chosen when depth measurements have varying reliability, as it normalizes the geometric loss by variance. Minimizes a joint loss function combining photometric (L1 color difference) and geometric (L1 depth difference normalized by variance) losses. It is chosen when simultaneous photometric and geometric accuracy is required, particularly with limited input views. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced by 3–5 times compared to standard NeRF. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Improved accuracy in scene geometry and photometry compared to standard NeRF and DS-NeRF. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves geometric accuracy, reduces artifacts, faster training time, and shortened prediction time. Limitations: Experiments are limited to forward-facing scenes. When to use: When RGB-D data is available and faster training with better geometry is desired compared to standard NeRF. When not to use: For scenes with significant non-forward-facing geometry or when depth data is not available. Mip-NeRF RGB-D was proposed by Arnab Dey, Yassine Ahmine, and Andrew I. Comport from I3S-CNRS/Université Côte d’Azur. It builds on the Mip-NeRF approach, which uses conical frustums to account for the varying area of a pixel with distance from the camera center, and extends it to include depth uncertainty. The method addresses major limitations of NeRF-based approaches, including improving the accuracy of geometry, reducing artifacts, and reducing training time. It is compared to DS-NeRF, which uses sparse 3D point clouds and reprojection errors, and NerfingMVS, which uses monocular depth priors. name: NAN (Noise-Aware NeRFs for Burst-Denoising)
head: Noise-Aware NeRFs
body: NAN is a NeRF-based burst denoising method that leverages inter-view and spatial information to handle high levels of noise and large camera motion by operating in 3D space rather than the image plane. It solves the problem of generating a clean version of a target image from a burst of N noisy images, treating the burst as an un-ordered set with potentially large parallax between frames. Unlike sibling methods that operate in the 2D image plane (e.g., SeaThru-NeRF or FastSR-NeRF which may rely on optical flow or local kernels), NAN explicitly reasons about the scene's underlying 3D structure, allowing it to cope with significant motion and occlusions under very high noise levels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N noisy images \{In\}{n=1}^N of a scene. The method requires as few as 8 images for inference. Output: A single clean target image corresponding to one of the viewpoints in the burst. Data Structures: The method builds upon the IBRNet architecture. For each pixel in the target image, a ray r is projected into 3D space. The ray is sampled at M positions indexed by m = 1, \dots, M. Sample Point Representation: For each 3D point along the ray, the system accumulates features from all other views that image this point. This involves projecting the 3D point onto the other N-1 input images and extracting local image features. Feature Aggregation: The features from all viewing directions are aggregated by concatenating mean and variance vectors, which serve as signals for downstream density and color prediction. Noise Model: The noisy version of a clean linear image In(x) at coordinate x follows a Gaussian distribution: In(x) \sim \mathcal{N}(Ic(x), \sigmar^2 + \sigmas^2 Ic(x)) where Ic(x) is the clean intensity, \sigmar is the signal-independent read-noise parameter, and \sigmas is the signal-dependent shot-noise parameter. Rendering Equation: The density \rhom predicted for the m-th sample point determines the probability wm that an object exists at that location: wm = \frac{1 - e^{-\rhom}}{e^{\sum{j=1}^{m-1} \rhoj}} The final color \hat{C}(r) of the predicted target image pixel is the weighted sum of the point colors cm: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{m=1}^{M} wm cm Training Procedure: 1. Pre-training: The network builds upon IBRNet, which is pre-trained on different image sets to produce novel views in unseen scenes. 2. Novel View Selection: In training, the novel pose is taken to be one of the available (non-input) viewpoints. 3. Loss: A loss function measures rendering quality by comparing the rendered image to the ground truth clean image. 4. Noise Range: Training extends up to a gain level of 20, with a maximum noise level equivalent to a standard deviation of \sim 0.4 for images in [0,1]. Inference Steps: 1. Select a target view from the burst. 2. For each pixel in the target image: a. Project a ray r into 3D space. b. Sample the ray at M positions m=1 \dots M on an inverse-depth scale. c. For each sample point, project it onto all other input views to gather local features. d. Aggregate features by concatenating mean and variance vectors. e. Predict density \rhom and color cm for the point. f. Compute weights wm and accumulate color \hat{C}(r). 3. The process is repeated in two stages: 'coarse' and 'fine'. In the fine stage, sampling is refined around depth values that most influence the rendering (i.e., at visible surfaces). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nanburstdenoise(noisyimages, targetviewindex, numsamplescoarse, numsamplesfine): """ Performs burst denoising using the NAN method. Args: noisyimages: List of N noisy images. targetviewindex: Index of the target view to reconstruct. numsamplescoarse: Mcoarse, number of coarse samples. numsamplesfine: Mfine, number of fine samples. Returns: cleantargetimage: Reconstructed clean image. """ # 1. Feature Extraction (Pre-Net) # Pre-process all input images to extract initial features inputfeatures = prenet(noisyimages) # 2. Initialize Output Image H, W, C = noisyimages[0].shape cleantargetimage = np.zeros((H, W, C)) # 3. Ray Marching for each pixel for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # Project ray for target pixel (x, y) into 3D space ray = projectray(targetviewindex, x, y) # Stage 1: Coarse Sampling # Sample Mcoarse points on inverse-depth scale coarsepoints = sampleinversedepth(ray, numsamplescoarse) # Aggregate features for coarse points coarsedensities = [] coarsecolors = [] for point in coarsepoints: # Project 3D point to other views projectedpixels = [] for i, imgfeat in enumerate(inputfeatures): if i != targetviewindex: # Get local features at projected location feat = getlocalfeatures(imgfeat, point) projectedpixels.append(feat) # Concatenate mean and variance of features from other views aggregatedfeat = aggregatefeatures(projectedpixels) # Predict density and color using the main network density, color = predictdensitycolor(aggregatedfeat, point) coarsedensities.append(density) coarsecolors.append(color) # Stage 2: Fine Sampling # Refine sampling around depths that influence rendering (visible surfaces) # This typically involves using the coarse depth distribution to guide fine sampling finepoints = refinesampling(coarsedensities, coarsepoints, numsamplesfine) finedensities = [] finecolors = [] for point in finepoints: projectedpixels = [] for i, imgfeat in enumerate(inputfeatures): if i != targetviewindex: feat = getlocalfeatures(imgfeat, point) projectedpixels.append(feat) aggregatedfeat = aggregatefeatures(projectedpixels) density, color = predictdensitycolor(aggregatedfeat, point) finedensities.append(density) finecolors.append(color) # Combine coarse and fine samples (implementation detail: usually fine replaces or augments coarse) # For simplicity, we assume fine samples are used for final integration or combined alldensities = coarsedensities + finedensities allcolors = coarsecolors + finecolors # Compute weights and final color # wm = (1 - exp(-rhom)) / exp(sum{j=1}^{m-1} rhoj) cumulativedensity = 0.0 finalcolor = np.zeros(C) totalweight = 0.0 for density, color in zip(alldensities, allcolors): weight = (1.0 - np.exp(-density)) / np.exp(cumulativedensity) finalcolor += weight color totalweight += weight cumulativedensity += density cleantargetimage[y, x] = finalcolor return cleantargetimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Noise: The method is designed for noise levels up to \sigma \approx 0.4, which is higher than typical burst denoising benchmarks (\sigma \approx 0.1-0.2). Large Motion: Unlike methods relying on optical flow (e.g., DeepRep), NAN handles large camera motion and occlusions by working in 3D. Few Images: The method works with as few as 8 images, leveraging pre-trained IBRNet priors. Time Complexity: The method processes each pixel independently, projecting rays and aggregating features from N-1 other views for M sample points. This is computationally intensive compared to 2D methods but scales linearly with the number of samples and views. Memory Complexity: Requires storing features for all input images and intermediate aggregation states for each ray sample. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results in burst denoising, especially under high noise and large motion. Strengths: Explicit 3D reasoning handles large parallax and occlusions better than 2D alignment methods. Robust to very high noise levels (\sigma \approx 0.4). Limitations: Computationally more expensive than 2D CNN-based denoising. Requires a pre-trained model (IBRNet) which may have domain gaps if the scene differs significantly from training data. When to use: Low-light imaging with handheld devices where burst capture is possible, and significant camera motion or high noise is expected. When not to use: Real-time applications requiring low latency, or scenes with no inter-view overlap. NAN was introduced in the paper "NAN: Noise-Aware NeRFs for Burst-Denoising". It builds on the IBRNet architecture, which pre-trains on different image sets to produce novel views in unseen scenes. The method addresses the limitations of previous burst denoising methods that operate in the image plane and are prone to errors in high noise or large motion due to reliance on optical flow or local kernels. It extends the training noise range up to gain level 20, covering noise levels up to \sigma \approx 0.4. name: JacobiNeRF Label Propagation
head: Adaptive Gradient Sampling, J-NeRF 2D, J-NeRF 3D
body: JacobiNeRF Label Propagation is a test-time method for transferring semantic or instance segmentation labels from a source view to novel target views in a trained NeRF. It operates by perturbing the NeRF's network parameters along gradients of mutual information associated with labeled pixels, synthesizing perturbed images, and analyzing the response to assign labels. Unlike methods that append a semantic branch to the network (e.g., Semantic-NeRF) or rely on feature similarity in a separate latent space (e.g., DINO-NeRF), JacobiNeRF leverages the second-order geometry of the radiance field itself to propagate information through mutual-information-induced synergies. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by utilizing a "shaping" technique that aligns gradients of correlated entities, allowing value information to propagate via the network's parameter space rather than just the feature space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained JacobiNeRF model \PhiJ with parameters \theta; a source view with known labels (sparse: one pixel per class, or dense: all pixels labeled); a target view defined by camera pose (ot, v{ptt}); number of classes K. Output: Predicted semantic/instance labels for pixels in the target view. Data Structures: JacobiNeRF Model \PhiJ: The radiance field network. The specific internal architecture (hashing, MLPs) is defined in HybridNeRF Model Architecture. Gradients \partial \Phi{J,sk}: The gradient of the mutual information (or relevant loss) with respect to network parameters \theta, computed for a specific labeled pixel sk in the source view. The norm of these gradients is normalized to be close to 1.0. Perturbation Magnitude \sigma: A scalar hyper-parameter controlling the step size of the parameter perturbation. Parameters: \sigma = 0.1: Empirically set perturbation magnitude. K: Number of semantic/instance classes. N{sample} = 20: Number of gradient combinations sampled per iteration in the dense setting. N{select} = 5: Number of qualified gradient selections required to terminate the adaptive sampling loop. Algorithm Steps: The method supports two settings: Sparse and Dense. 1. Gradient Computation: For each labeled pixel sk in the source view (where k=1 \dots K), compute the gradient \partial \Phi{J,sk} of the mutual information shaping objective with respect to the network parameters \theta. Normalize \|\partial \Phi{J,sk}\| \approx 1.0. 2. Perturbation and Synthesis (Core Propagation): For each selected gradient index k \in \{1, \dots, K\}: a. Generate a perturbed model instance: \PhiJ^{(k)} = \PhiJ(\cdot; \theta + \sigma \partial \Phi{J,sk}) b. Synthesize the perturbed image at the target pixel p{ti} with origin ot and direction v{ptt}: Ik(p{ti}) = \PhiJ^{(k)}(ot, v{ptt}) This yields a K-dimensional response vector (logits or probabilities) for the target pixel, where the k-th component corresponds to the response induced by perturbing along the gradient of the k-th class label. 3. Label Assignment (Sparse Setting): For each target pixel, assign the label k corresponding to the maximum response in the K-dimensional vector: \hat{y} = \arg\maxk Ik(p{ti}) 4. Adaptive Gradient Sampling (Dense Setting): In the dense setting, perturbing along all labeled pixels is redundant. An adaptive sampling strategy selects representative gradients. a. Initialization: Randomly select 20 combinations of labeled pixels. Each combination contains K pixels (one for each class). b. Response Evaluation: For each combination, perturb the model along the corresponding K gradients and synthesize the response for the source view (where the ground truth dense label is known). c. Selection Metric: Calculate the gain in mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) between the predicted label (derived from the \arg\max of the response) and the ground truth dense label. d. Selection: Choose the combination of gradients that yields the largest positive gain. Discard the combination if the gain is \le 0. e. Iteration: Repeat steps (a-d) for subsequent iterations, sampling new combinations. f. Termination: Stop when 5 qualified selections (combinations) are obtained. This results in a total of 5 \times K selected gradients used for the final propagation. 5. Aggregation MLP (Dense Setting): To enhance the \arg\max operator, a lightweight decoding MLP is applied. a. Input: The K-dimensional perturbation response vector for each pixel. b. Process: Map the response to K-dimensional segmentation logits. c. Output: Refined logits used for final label assignment via \arg\max. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jacobilabelpropagation(modelphij, theta, sourcelabels, targetview, sigma=0.1, K=10): """ modelphij: The JacobiNeRF function PhiJ(theta, ray) theta: Current network parameters sourcelabels: List of (pixelcoord, classid) tuples for the source view targetview: Camera pose (origin, direction) for the target view sigma: Perturbation magnitude (default 0.1) K: Number of classes """ # Step 1: Compute gradients for source labels # Note: In practice, gradients are computed via backpropagation of the MI-shaping loss gradients = {} for pixel, classid in sourcelabels: grad = computegradient(modelphij, theta, pixel, classid) # Normalize gradient norm to ~1.0 grad = grad / norm(grad) gradients[classid] = grad # Step 2 & 3: Sparse Propagation # For each class k, perturb and synthesize responses = [] # List of K vectors, one per class for k in range(K): if k not in gradients: continue gradk = gradients[k] # Perturbed parameters thetaperturbed = theta + sigma gradk # Synthesize image at target view using perturbed model # This returns a tensor of shape (H, W, C) or similar, depending on implementation # Here we assume we query specific target pixels perturbedimage = modelphij(thetaperturbed, targetview) responses.append(perturbedimage) # Stack responses along the class dimension # responsemap[p, k] is the response for pixel p, class k responsemap = stack(responses, axis=-1) # Assign labels via Argmax predictedlabels = argmax(responsemap, axis=-1) return predictedlabels def jacobilabelpropagationdense(modelphij, theta, sourcedenselabels, targetview, sigma=0.1, K=10): """ Dense setting with adaptive sampling and aggregation MLP. sourcedenselabels: Dense label map (H, W) of the source view. """ # Step 4: Adaptive Gradient Sampling selectedgradients = [] qualifiedcount = 0 iteration = 0 while qualifiedcount < 5: # Sample 20 combinations of labeled pixels # Each combination has K pixels, one for each class candidates = [] for in range(20): combo = [] for k in range(K): # Find all pixels of class k in sourcedenselabels classpixels = getpixelswithlabel(sourcedenselabels, k) # Randomly select one pixel from this class pixel = random.choice(classpixels) combo.append(pixel) candidates.append(combo) bestgain = -1 bestcombo = None for combo in candidates: # Compute gradients for this combination combograds = [] for pixel in combo: classid = sourcedenselabels[pixel] grad = computegradient(modelphij, theta, pixel, classid) grad = grad / norm(grad) combograds.append(grad) # Evaluate response on SOURCE view (known ground truth) # Synthesize perturbed images for each gradient sourceresponses = [] for grad in combograds: thetapert = theta + sigma grad # Synthesize on source view camera srcimg = modelphij(thetapert, sourceviewcamera) sourceresponses.append(srcimg) # Aggregate responses to get prediction # Note: In the paper, this might involve the Aggregation MLP even during selection # or a simple aggregation. We assume a standard aggregation for selection metric. responsemap = stack(sourceresponses, axis=-1) # Apply Aggregation MLP if available, else identity if aggregationmlpexists: logits = aggregationmlp(responsemap) else: logits = responsemap predlabels = argmax(logits, axis=-1) # Calculate mIoU gain against ground truth gain = calculatemiougain(predlabels, sourcedenselabels) if gain > bestgain: bestgain = gain bestcombo = combo bestgrads = combograds # Discard if gain <= 0 if bestgain > 0: selectedgradients.extend(bestgrads) qualifiedcount += 1 else: # If no positive gain found, break or handle edge case break iteration += 1 if iteration > 100: # Safety break break # Step 5: Final Propagation with Selected Gradients # Use the selected 5K gradients to synthesize target view finalresponses = [] for grad in selectedgradients: thetapert = theta + sigma grad tgtimg = modelphij(thetapert, targetview) finalresponses.append(tgtimg) responsemap = stack(finalresponses, axis=-1) # Apply Aggregation MLP for final denoising if aggregationmlpexists: finallogits = aggregationmlp(responsemap) else: finallogits = responsemap finallabels = argmax(finallogits, axis=-1) return finallabels Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perturbation Magnitude (\sigma): If \sigma is too small, the propagation response is weak and noisy, leading to failure. If \sigma is too large, the first-order Taylor expansion approximation underlying the method becomes invalid, degrading results. The value \sigma=0.1 is recommended. Gradient Norm: Gradients must be normalized to have a norm close to 1.0 to ensure the cosine similarity approximation holds. Dense Sampling Failure: If the adaptive sampling yields no combinations with positive gain, the process may stall. The implementation should discard such gradients. An implementation scheme that utilizes the 2D structure of the NeRF (likely treating rays or pixels in a 2D grid manner) for label propagation. It differs from J-NeRF 3D in how it handles the spatial structure during perturbation and aggregation. Link An implementation scheme that leverages the 3D structure of the NeRF for label propagation. It differs from J-NeRF 2D by explicitly considering the volumetric nature of the radiance field during the gradient computation and perturbation steps. Link Time Complexity: The method requires O(N{grad} \cdot N{pixels}) forward passes, where N{grad} is the number of selected gradients (e.g., 5K in dense setting) and N{pixels} is the number of target pixels. In the dense adaptive sampling phase, this is multiplied by the number of iterations and candidate combinations (20 per iteration). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the perturbed model parameters for each gradient evaluation. Since perturbations are applied to the same base model, memory overhead is proportional to the number of simultaneous perturbations if parallelized, or linear with the number of sequential forward passes. Performance: On ScanNet, JacobiNeRF achieves higher mIoU and Total Accuracy compared to S-NeRF and D-NeRF, particularly in far-view scenarios (e.g., 0.47 mIoU vs 0.28 for S-NeRF in far views with 1 source view). Strengths: Does not require retraining the network; leverages mutual information gradients for robust propagation; effective for both sparse and dense label transfer. Limitations: Requires computing gradients of the NeRF parameters, which can be computationally expensive; sensitive to the choice of \sigma; the adaptive sampling in dense settings adds overhead. JacobiNeRF was introduced in the paper "JacobiNeRF: NeRF Shaping with Mutual Information Gradients". The method is based on the concept of "NeRF Shaping," where the network parameters are adjusted to align gradients of correlated entities (via mutual information) in the tangent space. This alignment allows the NeRF to propagate value information (such as semantic labels) from selected quantities to other correlated quantities through the network's parameter space. The label propagation technique was developed as a test-time application of this shaping framework, demonstrating its ability to transfer semantic and instance information without modifying the network architecture or retraining.
