name: UNISURF
head: UniSurf, Unifying Implicit Surfaces and Radiance Fields, Unifying NeRFs with implicit surfaces
body: UNISURF is a hybrid neural representation that unifies volume rendering (radiance fields) and surface rendering (implicit surfaces) to achieve high-quality geometry and sharp textures without requiring mask supervision. It improves upon standard NeRF by replacing the density function with an occupancy network, offering a more robust representation of surface geometry. Unlike pure surface rendering which requires mask supervision and suffers from blurry texture mapping, UNISURF provides high-quality novel views and sharp colors by leveraging volume rendering in early optimization stages and surface rendering in later stages. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed RGB images \{Ii\}, camera poses, and intrinsic parameters. Outputs: A trained occupancy field network f{\text{occ}} and a color network f{\text{color}}, and a reconstructed 3D mesh extracted via marching cubes. Data Structures: Occupancy Network (f{\text{occ}}): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that takes a 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} as input and outputs a scalar occupancy value o \in [0, 1]. The occupancy at the i^{\text{th}} sample corresponds to an indicator of surface presence. Color Network (f{\text{color}}): An MLP that takes the 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input and outputs the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Method Steps: 1. Ray Sampling with Root Finding: For a given ray, UNISURF treats the volume as an occupancy field and uses root finding to locate a "surface" intersection point where the occupancy transitions from 0 to 1. 2. Interval Sampling: Volume rendering samples are distributed only within a specific interval around the found surface intersection point. 3. Progressive Interval Narrowing: The width of this sampling interval monotonically decreases over the course of optimization. Early Stage: The wide interval allows volume rendering to supervise the whole training volume, enabling optimization without mask supervision. Late Stage: The method uses a narrower interval to more efficiently refine the surface with tightly spaced samples, transitioning towards surface rendering to extract level-set surfaces. 4. Rendering: The final pixel color is computed by integrating the color and occupancy along the sampled points within the interval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def linspace(start, stop, num): if num == 1: return [start] step = (stop - start) / (num - 1) return [start + i step for i in range(num)] def zeros(n): return [0.0] n def findroot(f, a, b, tol=1e-4, maxiter=100): fa, fb = f(a), f(b) if fa fb > 0: return a for in range(maxiter): m = (a + b) / 2.0 fm = f(m) if abs(fm - 0.5) < tol or (b - a) < tol: return m if (fa - 0.5) (fm - 0.5) < 0: b = m else: a = m return (a + b) / 2.0 def renderray(origin, direction, tnear, tfar, netocc, netcolor, tsurf, width): tstart = max(tnear, tsurf - width / 2.0) tend = min(tfar, tsurf + width / 2.0) numsamples = 32 tsamples = linspace(tstart, tend, numsamples) renderedcolor = zeros(3) rendereddepth = 0.0 T = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tsamples[i] p = [origin[j] + t direction[j] for j in range(3)] oraw = netocc(p) o = sigmoid(oraw) c = netcolor(p, direction) deltat = tsamples[i] - (tsamples[i-1] if i > 0 else tstart) if deltat <= 0: deltat = 1e-6 alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-o deltat) T = (1.0 - alpha) renderedcolor = [renderedcolor[j] + T alpha c[j] for j in range(3)] rendereddepth += T alpha t return renderedcolor, rendereddepth def trainstep(images, poses, netocc, netcolor, tnear, tfar, widthscheduler): tsurfaces = [] for ray in rays: tsurf = findroot(lambda t: netocc(ray.origin + t ray.direction), tnear, tfar) tsurfaces.append(tsurf) currentwidth = widthscheduler.getwidth() renderedimages = [] for i, ray in enumerate(rays): color, depth = renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction, tnear, tfar, netocc, netcolor, tsurfaces[i], currentwidth) renderedimages.append(color) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images) loss.backward() optimizer.step() widthscheduler.decrease() Parameters: Interval Width: Starts wide and monotonically decreases. Typical values not given in sources. Number of Samples: 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Eikonal Regularization: UNISURF does not leverage Eikonal regularization because its underlying model is an occupancy network, not a Signed Distance Field (SDF). Surface Extraction: Surfaces extracted from neural densities using marching cubes can be noisy; UNISURF addresses this by using the occupancy network for a more robust representation. Time Complexity: Not given in sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in sources. Strengths: High-quality geometry and sharp textures without mask supervision. More robust surface representation than standard NeRF densities. Limitations: Does not use Eikonal regularization, which may limit geometric smoothness compared to SDF-based methods like NeuS. When to use: When high-quality geometry and sharp textures are needed without access to mask labels. When not to use: When Eikonal regularization is desired for smoother surfaces, or when SDF-based methods are preferred. UNISURF was proposed by Oechsle et al. in ICCV 2021. It addresses the issue that surfaces extracted from standard NeRFs are not accurate and depend heavily on the threshold used for extraction. By unifying implicit surfaces and radiance fields, it aims to provide the best of both worlds: the high-quality novel views of volume rendering and the clear surface definition of implicit surfaces. name: Deformation and Dynamic Modeling
body: Deformation and Dynamic Modeling extends static radiance field representations to handle temporal changes, enabling the reconstruction and rendering of dynamic 3D scenes from video inputs. It solves the problem of under-constrained geometry in dynamic scenes by introducing time as an explicit input and using deformation fields, scene flow, or canonical space mappings to align temporal observations. Unlike static NeRF variants, these methods explicitly model motion, distinguishing themselves from siblings like Relighting and Shading which handle lighting changes, or View Synthesis and Morphing which may focus on interpolation without explicit physical motion modeling. Methods in this family handle temporal changes by either conditioning a radiance field on time, predicting explicit deformation or scene flow fields, or deforming canonical primitives. For Gaussian Splatting variants, a static set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon} is defined in a canonical coordinate system, storing base parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \sigmai, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH,i}. For a given time t, a deformation function D predicts offsets (\delta\boldsymbol{\mu}, \delta\mathbf{q}, \delta\mathbf{s}) based on the canonical position and time. The time-varying parameters are computed as: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \delta\boldsymbol{\mu} \mathbf{s}i(t) = \mathbf{s}i + \delta\mathbf{s} \mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}i \otimes \delta\mathbf{q}) where \otimes is quaternion multiplication and normalization prevents drift. The deformation network D typically takes spatial embeddings of canonical positions and temporal embeddings of time t as input. Rendering uses standard differentiable rasterization or volume integration with the updated primitives, camera pose, and time t. Optimization minimizes photometric loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{reg}, updating Gaussian parameters and network weights via SGD. Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields (ST-NIF) represents a dynamic scene as a 4D implicit function mapping spatiotemporal coordinates (x,t) to color and volume density. It solves the problem of free-viewpoint video synthesis from a single moving camera by regularizing the inherently under-constrained geometry of dynamic scenes. Unlike static NeRF variants, ST-NIF introduces empty-space and static-scene losses to prevent haze-like artifacts and disocclusion errors, respectively. Dynamic NeRF is a variation of NeRF designed to operate on dynamic 3D objects by explicitly considering rigid and non-rigid motion of the target. It constructs a 3D model based on a camera moving around the object, extending the static radiance field representation to handle temporal changes. It sets itself apart from static NeRF by introducing time as an explicit input and using deformation or flow fields to map canonical representations to deformed scenes. Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF) is a dynamic NeRF method that handles temporal consistency in monocular video by explicitly predicting 3D scene flow and disocclusion weights. It solves the problem of rendering coherent free-viewpoint videos from single-camera input by regularizing the radiance field with optical flow priors, distinguishing itself from methods that simply append time as an input channel. A method to model dynamic scenes as time-varying continuous functions of appearance, geometry, and 3D scene motion. Gaussian Splatting Deformation extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by modeling time-dependent geometric and appearance parameters, solving the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects from multi-view video. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by decomposing the 4D representation into a static canonical set of Gaussians and a deformation function that predicts their state at any time t, distinguishing it from Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields which use neural fields, Dynamic NeRF which uses volumetric ray marching, and Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF) which predicts explicit scene flow vectors. A motion-aware optimization method using sparse control trajectories. A unified representation for static and dynamic scenes where static scenes are treated as a zero-motion special case of the dynamic representation, allowing shared appearance, compression, density-control, and rendering pipelines. It constructs second-order Gaussian motion for dynamic primitives, uses learnable temporal support, creates a binary static-dynamic partition to separate primitives into static and dynamic subsets, and enables continuous-time modeling without runtime deformation networks. Each dynamic Gaussian requires only eight additional temporal scalars for motion modeling. Uses a separate deformation field that can map from the deformed space to a canonical space where the NeRF is embedded. This can be thought of as space warping or scene flow. It shoots straight rays into deformed space and bends them into the canonical scene, usually by regressing per-point offsets for points on the straight ray using a coordinate-based MLP that is conditioned on the deformation. A method that takes multi-view RGB videos as input and decomposes the scene into a static and a dynamic volume. Currently only supports one object in motion. A method that uses a deformation MLP to model scene flow and integrates it across time to obtain the final deformation. A method focusing on 4D avatars that imposes a strong inductive bias by including a deformable face model into the pipeline. A method for 3D reconstruction and representation of human bodies developed based on traditional human armature animation deformation, trained based on a blending weight field that produces a deformation field. For each frame t, it extracts a query point x in the observation space and infers the blend weight w(x) for point x using a neural blend weight field conditioned by a latent code \Psit. It processes in canonical space by inputting appearance code ct and viewing direction v into the NeRF network, which outputs rendered volume, density, and color. It uses the neural blend weight field w{\text{canonical}}(x') network to learn the animation of NeRF in canonical space to gain dynamic rendering. The transformation is given by x' = \sum{i=1}^n wi(x) Ti x, where x' is the transformed point in canonical space, wi(x) is the blend weight, and Ti represents the viewing direction/transformation. The concept of dynamic neural radiance fields emerged shortly after the introduction of static NeRF. Early works like Space-Time Neural Irradiance Fields (ST-NIF) and NeRFlow demonstrated that time could be incorporated as an additional input dimension. Subsequent methods such as D-NeRF and Nerfies introduced explicit deformation fields to map between canonical and deformed spaces, improving controllability and handling non-rigid motion. The field has since expanded to include Gaussian Splatting variants and specialized applications like avatar reconstruction (DNRF, Skeleton-NeRF). name: Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields
head: ST-NIF, Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields for Free-Viewpoint Video
body: Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields (ST-NIF) is a method for rendering free-viewpoint videos from a stream of RGB-D images by modeling the scene as a 4D function that maps spatiotemporal coordinates to color and volume density. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Dynamic NeRF and Neural Scene Flow Fields by directly conditioning the radiance field on time rather than predicting explicit deformation fields or scene flow. This approach requires carefully selected auxiliary losses to resolve the motion-appearance ambiguity inherent in single-video dynamic scene reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A stream of Nf RGB-D images It: u \rightarrow (c, d) at discrete time steps t \in \mathcal{T} = \{1, 2, \dots, Nf\}, where u=(u,v) are 2D pixel coordinates, along with their associated camera calibrations Pt. Output: A rendered color \hat{C}(r,t) and depth \hat{D}(r,t) for a ray r at time t, and the implicit function F representing the scene. Data Structures Implicit Function F: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) mapping (x, t) \rightarrow (c, \sigma), where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial coordinate and t \in [-1, 1] is the normalized time. MLP Architecture: Identical to the original NeRF architecture, except the first 8 hidden layers use 1024 activations instead of 256. Positional Encoding: Applied to both spatial coordinates and time, using 4 frequency bands. Sampling Pool \mathcal{X}: A set of 3D points derived from the union of all sampling locations along all rays of all frames, excluding points closer than \epsilon to observed surfaces. Ray Parameterization A ray r at time t is defined by a pixel location u and camera calibration Pt. The ray is parameterized such that the parameter s denotes scene depth. This is achieved by setting the directional vector \mathbf{d} such that its projection onto the principal ray has a unit norm in the camera space. The ray is defined as r(s) = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera center. Sampling Strategy 1. Hierarchical Sampling: Uses hierarchical volume sampling as in the original NeRF, simultaneously training coarse and fine networks. 2. Static Scene Sampling: To compute the static scene loss, a sample pool \mathcal{X} is formed by taking the union of all sampling locations along all rays of all frames. Points closer than \epsilon to any observed surface are excluded. A fixed number of locations are randomly drawn from \mathcal{X} at each iteration, with small random jitters added. A random time t' is chosen for each sample location x, ensuring (x, t') is not close to any scene surfaces. Rendering The color \hat{C}(r,t) is computed via numerical quadrature (volume rendering): \hat{C}(r,t) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti(t) \sigma(r(si), t) c(r(si), t) \Delta si where Ti(t) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(r(sj), t) \Delta sj\right) is the accumulated transmittance. Loss Functions The total loss is a linear combination of four terms: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \alpha \mathcal{L}{depth} + \beta \mathcal{L}{empty} + \gamma \mathcal{L}{static} where \alpha, \beta, \gamma are weighting coefficients. 1. Color Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{color}): Penalizes the difference between rendered and ground truth colors for the input viewpoints: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{(r,t) \in \mathcal{R}} \| \hat{C}(r,t) - C(r,t) \|^2 where \mathcal{R} is a batch of rays. 2. Depth Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{depth}): Constrains the predicted depth using input depth maps: \mathcal{L}{depth} = \sum{(r,t) \in \mathcal{R}} \left\| \frac{1}{\hat{D}(r,t)} - \frac{1}{D(r,t)} \right\|^2 where \hat{D}(r,t) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s,t) \sigma(r(s),t) s \, ds is the integrated sample depth, and D(r,t) is the input depth. 3. Empty-Space Loss (\mathcal{L}{empty}): Encourages zero density in the region between the camera and the first visible surface to prevent haze-like artifacts. Let dt(u) be the scene depth for pixel u at time t. The margin is \epsilon = 0.05 \cdot (sf - sn): \mathcal{L}{empty} = \sum{(r,t) \in \mathcal{R}} \int{sn}^{dt(u) - \epsilon} \sigma(r(s), t) \, ds. 4. Static Scene Loss (\mathcal{L}{static}): Constrains the MLP on points from the static sample pool \mathcal{X} at random times t' to prevent disocclusion artifacts in hidden regions. The specific formulation is not provided in the sources, but it involves querying F(x, t') for x \in \mathcal{X}. Training Parameters Batch Size: Nr = 1024 rays randomly drawn from an input frame It without replacement. Time Normalization: Time t is normalized to [-1, 1]. Iterations: 800,000 iterations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstnif(frames, cameraposes, depths, numiterations=800000): # Initialize MLP F(x, t) -> (c, sigma) with NeRF architecture (1024 units, first 8 layers) # Initialize optimizer # Define positional encoding with 4 bands # Define ray parameterization: d such that projection onto principal ray has unit norm # Precompute static sample pool X X = [] for t in frames: rays = generaterays(frames[t], cameraposes[t]) samples = hierarchicalsample(rays) # Exclude points closer than epsilon to observed surfaces for s in samples: if distancetosurface(s, depth=depths[t]) > epsilon: X.append(s) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample batch of rays from a random frame t t = randomchoice(frames) rays = randomsample(frames[t], cameraposes[t], count=1024) # Forward pass for color and depth losses colorspred = [] depthspred = [] for r in rays: # Sample points along ray r at time t points, weights = hierarchicalvolumesample(r, t) # Query MLP c, sigma = querymlp(points, t) # Render color crender = integrate(c, sigma, weights) # Render depth drender = integratedepth(sigma, points, weights) colorspred.append(crender) depthspred.append(drender) # Compute Lcolor lcolor = meansquarederror(colorspred, groundtruthcolors(t)) # Compute Ldepth ldepth = meansquarederror( inverse(depthspred), inverse(groundtruthdepths(t))) # Compute Lempty lempty = 0 for r in rays: # Integrate sigma from sn to dt(u) - epsilon depthu = groundtruthdepth(r.pixel, t) emptysigma = integratesigmaalongray(r, t, sn, depthu - epsilon) lempty += emptysigma lempty = mean(lempty) # Compute Lstatic # Sample random points from X and random times t' staticsamples = randomsample(X, count=1024) statictimes = randomuniform(-1, 1, count=1024) staticpreds = [] for x, tprime in zip(staticsamples, statictimes): # Ensure (x, tprime) is not close to surface if distancetosurface(x, depth=depthsattime(tprime)) > epsilon: c, sigma = querymlp(x, tprime) staticpreds.append(sigma) # Or color, depending on specific implementation not fully detailed lstatic = meansquarederror(staticpreds, 0) # Assuming target is zero density/color for empty space # Total Loss loss = lcolor + alpha ldepth + beta lempty + gamma lstatic # Backpropagate and update optimizer.step(loss) Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 48 hours for a network with about 100 video frames. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Capable of rendering free-viewpoint videos from a single RGB-D video stream without explicit deformation fields. Limitations: The method suffers from motion-appearance ambiguity, leading to under-constrained geometry estimation. It is prone to haze-like artifacts due to the nature of weighted depth integration and disocclusion artifacts in hidden regions. When to use: When RGB-D data is available and explicit scene flow or deformation fields are undesirable or difficult to estimate. When not to use: For scenes with significant disocclusions or when high-fidelity novel view synthesis outside the original camera trajectory is required without the auxiliary losses. Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields was introduced by Xian et al. in 2020. It is cited as a method that simply uses time as an additional input to render freeviewpoint videos from RGBD data. The method addresses the limitations of static NeRF in dynamic scenes by extending the implicit representation to 4D. name: Dynamic NeRF
head: D-NeRF, DynamicNeRF
body: Dynamic NeRF is a variation of NeRF designed to operate on dynamic 3D objects by explicitly considering rigid and non-rigid motion of the target. It constructs a 3D model based on a camera moving around the object, extending the static radiance field representation to handle temporal changes. It sets itself apart from static NeRF by introducing time as an explicit input and using deformation or flow fields to map canonical representations to deformed scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D spatial coordinates (x, y, z), viewing direction (\theta, \phi), and time t. Outputs: Volume density \sigma, color C, and optionally forward/backward 3D scene flow vectors. Data Structures: The method consists of two deep neural networks: 1. Canonical Network: Encodes 2D scenes into a canonical 3D representation. 2. Deformation/Mapping Network: Maps these canonical representations to deformed scenes based on a time input. In some implementations, a static NeRF models background/non-moving elements, while a time-varying dynamic NeRF handles moving objects. The dynamic component predicts volume density, color, forward 3D scene flow, and backward 3D scene flow at a given spatiotemporal location. Steps: 1. Canonical Encoding: The 2D scenes are encoded into a canonical 3D representation using the first network. 2. Deformation/Flow Prediction: The second network takes the canonical features and the time input t to predict the deformation or scene flow. If using scene flow, the network predicts forward and backward 3D scene flow vectors. 3. Warping: The flow vectors are used to warp the radiance fields from adjacent time instances, creating a temporally consistent representation. 4. Rendering: The warped features are decoded to predict volume density and color for volume rendering. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Time Input: An extra input of time is required to deal with motion. Compute Cost: The method has a 2.5 times higher compute cost than standard NeRF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicnerfquery(xyz, direction, time, canonicalnet, deformationnet): """ Query the dynamic NeRF at a specific spatiotemporal location. Implements the two-network architecture and flow warping from. """ # Step 1: Canonical Encoding # The canonical network learns to encode 2D scenes into a canonical 3D representation canonicalfeatures = canonicalnet(xyz, direction) # Step 2: Deformation/Flow Prediction # The second network maps canonical representations to deformed scenes based on time # It predicts volume density, color, forward and backward 3D scene flow vectors sigma, color, flowforward, flowbackward = deformationnet(canonicalfeatures, time) # Step 3: Warping # Flow vectors warp radiance fields from adjacent time instances, creating temporal consistency # During volume rendering, coordinates are adjusted by the flow vectors before density/color evaluation warpedxyz = xyz + flowforward # Step 4: Rendering # The network directly outputs density and color for the queried spatiotemporal location return sigma, color, flowforward, flowbackward DMRF establishes a two-way coupling between meshes and NeRF, allowing the updating of radiance and throughput along a cast ray with an arbitrary number of bounces. It addresses the color space discrepancy between path tracing and standard NeRF by training NeRF with high dynamic range (HDR) images, enabling more accurate light transport simulation. It also presents a strategy for estimating light sources and casting shadows on NeRF. V4D employs a dual voxel format for density and texture fields, processed by a small MLP. It incorporates a lookup table refinement module for pixel-level enhancements with minimal computational overhead. It also introduces conditional positional encoding to improve performance with negligible computational costs. MSTH represents dynamic scenes as a weighted combination of 3D and 4D hash encodings, with weights determined by a learnable mask guided by uncertainty estimation. This method reduces hash collision rates and enables compact representation, allowing rapid optimization and convergence. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method has a 2.5 times higher compute cost than standard NeRF. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: It can learn high-fidelity 3D models with dynamic motion. However, it has higher compute costs. There is no equivalent of Instant NGP-acceleration for D-NeRF, which may impact performance. When to use it: Use when modeling dynamic 3D objects with rigid or non-rigid motion. When not: Use when computational resources are limited and static scenes are sufficient. Dynamic NeRF (D-NeRF) was introduced to address the limitations of algorithms designed for static 3D objects, which did not clearly perform well under changing attitudes and lighting conditions experienced by orbiting objects. It explicitly considers rigid and non-rigid motion of the target in constructing a 3D model based on a camera moving around the object. Experiments were performed at the ORION facility at Florida Tech to capture images of a mock-up of a satellite to represent a Resident Space Object (RSO). 3D Reconstruction of Non-cooperative Resident Space Objects using Instant NGP-accelerated NeRF and D-NeRF, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2301.09060, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Dynamic Scene Reconstruction: Recent Advance in Real-time Rendering and Streaming, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2503.08166, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF)
body: Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF) is a dynamic NeRF method that handles temporal changes by explicitly predicting forward and backward 3D scene flow fields alongside disocclusion weights. It solves the problem of temporal consistency and disocclusion in monocular video reconstruction by combining a static scene representation with a dynamic one, allowing multi-view constraints to stabilize static regions while scene flow handles motion. Unlike methods that simply condition radiance on time, NSFF predicts explicit 3D offset vectors for points at adjacent time instances, enabling sophisticated representation of sharp motion discontinuities. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A monocular video sequence with known camera poses. Output: Rendered RGB images for arbitrary time steps and camera poses; predicted 3D scene flow fields; disocclusion weights. Data Structures: The model maintains two separate neural radiance field representations: 1. Static Field: A standard NeRF MLP \mathcal{N}{static} that encodes the static background and non-moving elements. It takes spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input. 2. Dynamic Field: A neural network \mathcal{N}{dynamic} that predicts the deformation (scene flow) and appearance changes. It takes spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}, view direction \mathbf{d}, and time t as input. Scene Flow: Represented as a 3D vector field \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, t) \in \mathbb{R}^3, predicting the offset from position \mathbf{x} at time t to position \mathbf{x}' at time t+1 (forward) or t-1 (backward). Disocclusion Weights: A scalar weight w{dis} \in [0, 1] predicted by the network, indicating the confidence of temporal photoconsistency at a given location. Numbered Steps: 1. Static/Dynamic Decomposition: For a query ray at time t, sample points along the ray. The static field renders the background contribution. The dynamic field handles moving objects. 2. Scene Flow Prediction: For each sampled point \mathbf{x} at time t, the dynamic network predicts the forward scene flow \mathbf{f}{fwd}(\mathbf{x}, t) and backward scene flow \mathbf{f}{bwd}(\mathbf{x}, t). These are 3D offset vectors indicating the position at adjacent time instances. 3. Disocclusion Weight Prediction: The network simultaneously predicts a disocclusion weight w{dis}(\mathbf{x}, t) for each point. 4. Temporal Consistency Loss Application: Use the disocclusion weights as unsupervised confidence measures to determine the locations and intensity for applying the temporal photoconsistency loss. Points with high disocclusion weights (likely occluded or newly visible) are down-weighted in the temporal loss. 5. Cycle Consistency Regularization: Refine the predicted flows using a cycle consistency term. The forward flow from t to t+1 and backward flow from t+1 to t should compose to the identity transformation. 6. Optical Flow Supervision: Supervise the predicted 3D flows using a pre-trained 2D optical flow model. The 3D flows are projected to 2D image plane and compared against the 2D optical flow estimates. 7. Geometric and Depth Priors: Introduce data-driven priors such as geometric consistency and single-view depth terms to learn correct scene geometry, especially for dynamic regions. Depth predictions (e.g., from a monocular depth estimator) are used as a prior. 8. Rendering: Render the image by integrating the color and density from both static and dynamic fields, weighted by the ray marching weights. Formulas: Scene Flow Definition: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, t), where \mathbf{x}' is the position at the adjacent time instance. Temporal Photoconsistency Loss: \mathcal{L}{temp} = \sum{\mathbf{x}} w{dis}(\mathbf{x}, t) \cdot \| It(\mathbf{x}) - I{t+1}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{f}{fwd}(\mathbf{x}, t)) \|1. (Note: Exact loss formulation details are not fully specified in sources, but the weighting mechanism is described). Cycle Consistency Loss: \mathcal{L}{cycle} = \| \mathbf{f}{fwd}(\mathbf{x}, t) + \mathbf{f}{bwd}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{f}{fwd}(\mathbf{x}, t), t+1) \|2. Optical Flow Loss: \mathcal{L}{flow} = \| \Pi(\mathbf{f}{fwd}(\mathbf{x}, t)) - \mathbf{F}{2D} \|1, where \Pi projects 3D flow to 2D and \mathbf{F}{2D} is the pre-trained 2D optical flow. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{temp} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{cycle} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{flow} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{depth} + \lambda5 \mathcal{L}{geo}. (Coefficients \lambdai are hyperparameters). Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Loss weights (\lambdai): Not given in the sources. Network depth/width: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disocclusion: Accurate prediction of disocclusion weights is critical to avoid propagating errors from occluded regions into the temporal loss. Sharp Motion Discontinuities: The explicit scene flow representation helps handle sharp motion boundaries better than implicit time-conditioning, but requires sufficient network capacity. Depth Ambiguity: Monocular depth priors can be noisy; the geometric consistency term helps mitigate this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nsffforward(rayorigins, raydirections, timet, staticnerf, dynamicnerf, opticalflowmodel, depthestimator): """ Forward pass for NSFF rendering and loss computation. """ # Sample points along ray points3d = samplepointsalongray(rayorigins, raydirections) # Render static background staticcolors, staticalphas = staticnerf(points3d, raydirections) # Predict dynamic properties # dynamicnerf outputs: dynamiccolors, dynamicalphas, sceneflowfwd, sceneflowbwd, disocclusionweights dynamiccolors, dynamicalphas, flowfwd, flowbwd, disocweights = dynamicnerf(points3d, raydirections, timet) # Combine static and dynamic # Note: Exact combination strategy (e.g., max, sum, or learned mask) is not fully detailed in sources. # Assuming additive combination for dynamic objects on top of static background. finalcolors = staticcolors + dynamiccolors finalalphas = staticalphas + dynamicalphas (1 - staticalphas) # Render image renderedimage = volumerender(finalcolors, finalalphas) # Compute losses lossrgb = computergbloss(renderedimage, groundtruthimage) # Temporal consistency loss using disocclusion weights # Project points to next frame using forward flow pointsnext = points3d + flowfwd # Sample next frame image at projected points (requires differentiable sampling) nextframecolors = sampleimageatpoints(groundtruthnextframe, pointsnext) temporalloss = sum(disocweights abs(renderedimage - nextframecolors)) # Cycle consistency loss # Apply backward flow to pointsnext to get back to points3d pointsback = pointsnext + flowbwd(pointsnext, timet + 1) cycleloss = sum(abs(points3d - pointsback)) # Optical flow supervision # Project 3D flow to 2D flow2d = project3dflowto2d(flowfwd, cameraintrinsics) # Get pre-trained 2D optical flow flow2dgt = opticalflowmodel(groundtruthcurrentframe, groundtruthnextframe) flowloss = sum(abs(flow2d - flow2dgt)) # Depth and geometric priors # Predict depth from static/dynamic fields predicteddepth = computedepth(points3d, finalalphas) # Get monocular depth estimate monoculardepth = depthestimator(groundtruthcurrentframe) depthloss = sum(abs(predicteddepth - monoculardepth)) # Geometric consistency (e.g., normal consistency) # Not fully detailed, assumed to be a term enforcing smoothness or consistency of surface normals geoloss = computegeometricconsistencyloss(points3d, dynamiccolors) totalloss = lossrgb + lambda1 temporalloss + lambda2 cycleloss + lambda3 flowloss + lambda4 depthloss + lambda5 geoloss return renderedimage, totalloss Enhances NSFF by generating semantic and saliency features to refine segmentation of static and dynamic elements. Leverages annotations from keyframes to propagate scene flows and determine rigidities, modifying object placements and trajectories. Employs both a static NeRF and a time-varying dynamic NeRF to capture static background and moving objects separately. Uses time as an additional input to NeRF, requiring carefully selected losses for freeviewpoint video rendering. Limits deformations to translations, similar to Nerfies. Uses a deformation MLP to model scene flow and integrates it across time. Uses a deformation network for non-rigid NeRF. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles sharp motion discontinuities well due to explicit scene flow prediction; leverages multi-view constraints in static regions for stability; uses unsupervised disocclusion weights for robust temporal consistency. Limitations: Requires known camera poses; relies on pre-trained 2D optical flow and depth estimators, which may introduce errors; complex loss function with multiple terms. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic scenes from monocular video with known camera poses, especially when sharp motion boundaries are present. When not to use: When camera poses are unknown; when computational resources are limited due to multiple loss terms and network outputs. Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF) was proposed by Li et al. in 2020. It was introduced as a method to handle dynamic scenes by explicitly predicting scene flow fields, addressing limitations of earlier methods that either conditioned on time or used simple deformation MLPs. The method builds on the NeRF framework but extends it to handle temporal dynamics through explicit flow prediction and disocclusion handling. It is used in the context of free-viewpoint video rendering from monocular video. name: Gaussian Splatting Deformation
head: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting, Time-varying Gaussian Splatting
body: Gaussian Splatting Deformation extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by maintaining a static canonical set of primitives and predicting time-dependent geometric and appearance offsets. It solves the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video by decomposing the 4D representation into a canonical state and a deformation function. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Space-time Neural Irradiance Fields and Dynamic NeRF by using explicit differentiable rasterization of deformed Gaussians rather than neural volume rendering, and from Neural Scene Flow Fields (NSFF) by predicting offsets for discrete primitives rather than continuous scene flow fields. Methods in this family handle temporal changes by either conditioning a radiance field on time, predicting explicit deformation or scene flow fields, or deforming canonical primitives. For Gaussian Splatting variants, a static set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon} is defined in a canonical coordinate system, storing base parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \sigmai, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH,i}. For a given time t, a deformation function D predicts offsets (\delta\boldsymbol{\mu}, \delta\mathbf{q}, \delta\mathbf{s}) based on the canonical position and time. The time-varying parameters are computed as: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \delta\boldsymbol{\mu} \mathbf{s}i(t) = \mathbf{s}i + \delta\mathbf{s} \mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}i \otimes \delta\mathbf{q}) where \otimes is quaternion multiplication and normalization prevents drift. The deformation network D typically takes spatial embeddings of canonical positions and temporal embeddings of time t as input. Rendering uses standard differentiable rasterization or volume integration with the updated primitives, camera pose, and time t. Optimization minimizes photometric loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{reg}, updating Gaussian parameters and network weights via SGD. Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting (SC-GS) is a dynamic scene representation method that utilizes a small set of user-provided or learned sparse control points to drive the deformation of dense 3D Gaussians. Unlike methods that predict deformation per-Gaussian, SC-GS propagates edits across time via a learned deformation prior, resulting in a compact and editable representation. It sets itself apart from siblings like Deformable 3DGS by decoupling the deformation network's input from individual Gaussian features, instead relying on spatial interpolation from control points. See Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting. Deformable 3DGS extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by modeling time-dependent geometric and appearance parameters. It solves the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video by decomposing the 4D representation into a static canonical set of Gaussians and a deformation function that predicts their state at any time t. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting by using a direct MLP-based deformation network on per-Gaussian features rather than sparse control points. Builds on Gaussian Splatting Deformation. See Deformable 3DGS. End-to-end driving simulators. A method that drives time-of-day and weather conditioning for closed-loop simulation. The concept of deforming canonical primitives for dynamic rendering originated in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and was adapted to 3D Gaussian Splatting as the latter gained popularity for real-time rendering. Deformable 3DGS and Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting represent the primary approaches to this problem within the Gaussian Splatting ecosystem. These methods are heavily used in autonomous driving simulation, where they enable the integration of dynamic actors into static backgrounds for closed-loop testing. name: Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: SC-GS, Sparse-Controlled
body: Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting (SC-GS) is a dynamic scene representation method that utilizes a small set of user-provided or learned sparse control points to drive the deformation of dense 3D Gaussians. Unlike methods that predict deformation per-Gaussian, SC-GS propagates edits across time via a learned deformation prior, resulting in a compact and editable representation. It sets itself apart from siblings like Deformable 3DGS by decoupling the deformation network's input from individual Gaussian features, instead relying on spatial interpolation from control points. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of static 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon} in canonical space (mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \sigmai, SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH,i}), a set of sparse control points \mathcal{C}, and a time query t. Outputs: Time-varying Gaussian parameters \mathcal{G}(t) for rendering. Data Structures: Control Points: A set of Nc points \{\mathbf{p}j\}{j=1}^{Nc} in canonical space. Each control point is associated with a time-varying 6 DoF transformation (position offset \delta\mathbf{t}j(t) and rotation offset \delta\mathbf{q}j(t)). Deformation Network: An MLP that predicts the 6 DoF transformation parameters for each control point based on the control point's canonical position and the current time t. Influence Weights: A mechanism to determine how much each control point influences a specific Gaussian. This is typically based on spatial distance in canonical space. Steps: 1. Initialize: Define canonical Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon} and sparse control points \mathcal{C}. 2. Query Control Point Transforms: For each control point j, compute its time-varying 6 DoF transformation (\delta\mathbf{t}j(t), \delta\mathbf{q}j(t)) using the deformation network D{ctrl}(\mathbf{p}j, t). 3. Compute Influence Weights: For each Gaussian i, calculate influence weights w{ij}(t) from all control points j. This is often done using a radial basis function (e.g., Gaussian kernel) based on the distance between the Gaussian's canonical mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i and the control point's canonical position \mathbf{p}j. 4. Interpolate Deformation: Compute the total deformation offset for Gaussian i at time t by interpolating the control point transformations weighted by w{ij}(t): \delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \frac{\sum{j=1}^{Nc} w{ij}(t) \delta\mathbf{t}j(t)}{\sum{j=1}^{Nc} w{ij}(t)} \delta\mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}\left( \sum{j=1}^{Nc} w{ij}(t) \delta\mathbf{q}j(t) \right) Scale deformation \delta\mathbf{s}i(t) may be predicted similarly or kept static. 5. Update Gaussian Parameters: Apply the interpolated deformation to the canonical parameters: \boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}i + \delta\boldsymbol{\mu}i(t) \mathbf{q}i(t) = \text{Normalize}(\mathbf{q}i \otimes \delta\mathbf{q}i(t)) \mathbf{s}i(t) = \mathbf{s}i + \delta\mathbf{s}i(t) 6. Render: Perform differentiable rasterization using the updated Gaussians \mathcal{G}(t), camera pose, and time t. Parameters: Number of control points Nc: Small, user-defined or learned. Deformation network architecture: MLP. Influence weight function: Typically Gaussian kernel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intense Movements: SC-GS faces challenges with intense movements and detailed surface deformation. Boundary Effects: Gaussians far from any control point may have undefined or noisy deformations if weights are not handled carefully. Rotation Interpolation: Quaternion normalization is critical to prevent drift. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scgsrender(canonicalgaussians, controlpoints, deformationnetwork, timet, camera): """ canonicalgaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes mu, q, s, sigma, cSH controlpoints: List of control point objects with attribute p (canonical position) deformationnetwork: MLP taking (p, t) and returning (deltat, deltaq) timet: Current time camera: Camera parameters """ # Step 2: Query control point transforms controltransforms = [] for cp in controlpoints: deltat, deltaq = deformationnetwork(cp.p, timet) controltransforms.append({'p': cp.p, 'deltat': deltat, 'deltaq': deltaq}) # Step 3 & 4: Compute influence and interpolate deformation for each Gaussian deformedgaussians = [] for g in canonicalgaussians: weights = [] weighteddeltat = np.zeros(3) weighteddeltaq = np.zeros(4) sumweights = 0.0 for ct in controltransforms: # Calculate influence weight (e.g., Gaussian kernel) dist = np.linalg.norm(g.mu - ct['p']) w = np.exp(-dist2 / (2 sigmaweight2)) # sigmaweight is a hyperparameter weights.append(w) sumweights += w weighteddeltat += w ct['deltat'] weighteddeltaq += w ct['deltaq'] # Avoid division by zero if sumweights < 1e-8: # Fallback: no deformation or use nearest neighbor deltamu = np.zeros(3) deltaq = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) else: deltamu = weighteddeltat / sumweights deltaq = weighteddeltaq / sumweights deltaq = normalizequaternion(deltaq) # Prevent drift # Step 5: Update Gaussian parameters newmu = g.mu + deltamu newq = normalizequaternion(g.q deltaq) # Quaternion multiplication news = g.s # Scale deformation not explicitly detailed in sources, assume static or similar interpolation newsigma = g.sigma newcSH = g.cSH deformedgaussians.append(Gaussian(newmu, newq, news, newsigma, newcSH)) # Step 6: Render return rasterize(deformedgaussians, camera) SC4D migrates the idea of sparse control points from SC-GS to model deformation and appearance more efficiently. It is a variant that extends the control point mechanism to handle appearance changes in addition to geometric deformation, aiming for better efficiency in 4D modeling. Time Complexity: Deformation query is O(Nc) per Gaussian, where Nc is the number of control points. Since Nc is small, this is efficient compared to per-Gaussian networks. Memory Complexity: Stores Nc control points and their transformation network weights, plus the base Gaussian parameters. Significantly more compact than methods storing deformation networks per Gaussian. Strengths: Compact representation, easy user editing via control points, efficient deformation computation. Limitations: Struggles with intense movements and detailed surface deformation. Performance depends heavily on the placement and number of control points. When to use: Scenes with moderate, coherent motion where user control or compactness is prioritized over high-frequency detail. When not to use: Scenes with complex, non-rigid, or high-frequency deformations. SC-GS was introduced as a method to enable sparse user-provided control points to edit dynamic scenes, propagating edits via a learned deformation prior. It was developed to address the limitations of per-Gaussian deformation networks in terms of compactness and editability. The method jointly learns 3D Gaussian parameters and sparse control points in canonical space, along with an MLP for dynamic novel view synthesis. It employs an adaptive strategy to handle motion complexity and an ARAP (As-Rigid-As-Possible) loss to maintain local rigidity. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28 PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Deformable 3DGS
head: 4D Gaussian Splatting / Deformable 3DGS, Deformable 3D-GS, Deformable 3DGS / Dynamic 3DGS, Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (Deformation Field)
body: Deformable 3DGS extends static 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes by modeling time-dependent geometric and appearance parameters. It solves the problem of reconstructing and rendering moving subjects (e.g., people, fluids) from multi-view video by decomposing the 4D representation into a static canonical set of Gaussians and a deformation function that predicts their state at any time t. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Sparse-Controlled 3D Gaussian Splatting by using a direct MLP-based deformation network on per-Gaussian features rather than sparse control points. Builds on Gaussian Splatting Deformation. Inputs: Multi-view video frames with known camera poses and timestamps t. Outputs: A set of time-varying 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}(t) rendered into images. Data Structures: 1. Canonical Gaussians \mathcal{G}{canon}: Each Gaussian i stores static base parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \sigmai, and spherical harmonics coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH,i}. 2. Deformation Network D: An MLP that takes spatial embeddings of canonical positions and temporal embeddings of time t as input. Algorithm: 1. Deformation Prediction: Compute network output: (\delta\boldsymbol{\mu}, \delta\mathbf{q}, \delta\mathbf{s}) = D(Ep(\boldsymbol{\mu}g), Et(t)). 2. Parameter Update: Apply offsets to canonical parameters: \boldsymbol{\mu}g(t) = \boldsymbol{\mu}g + \delta\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{s}g(t) = \mathbf{s}g + \delta\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{q}g(t) = \mathbf{q}g \cdot \delta\mathbf{q}. 3. Rendering: Rasterize the updated Gaussians \mathcal{G}(t) using standard differentiable rasterization with camera pose and time t. 4. Optimization: Align predicted temporal updates with ground-truth frames to jointly optimize both Gaussian parameters and deformation network parameters. The method uses an Annealing Smooth Training strategy to smooth rendering jitters caused by inconsistent scenes across frames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deformable3dgsforward(canonicalgaussians, timet, deformationnetwork): """ canonicalgaussians: list of dicts with keys 'mu', 'q', 's', 'sigma', 'cSH' timet: float timestamp deformationnetwork: callable D(Ep(mu), Et(t)) returning (deltamu, deltaq, deltas) """ updatedgaussians = [] for g in canonicalgaussians: mug, qg, sg = g['mu'], g['q'], g['s'] # 1. Deformation Prediction deltamu, deltaq, deltas = deformationnetwork(mug, timet) # 2. Parameter Update mut = mug + deltamu st = sg + deltas qt = normalizequaternion(quatmul(qg, deltaq)) # 3. Assemble time-varying Gaussian gt = { 'mu': mut, 'q': qt, 's': st, 'sigma': g['sigma'], 'cSH': g['cSH'] } updatedgaussians.append(gt) return updatedgaussians Parameters: Annealing Smooth Training strategy: Used to smooth rendering jitters caused by inconsistent scenes across frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quaternion normalization prevents drift in rotation updates. Scale updates must avoid negative values; clipping or exponentiating deltas is required to maintain valid covariance decomposition \Sigma = RSS^T R^T. Precision issues may arise if \Delta\mathbf{s}i causes negative scales; absolute value or softplus activation on deltas is standard. A method that replaces discrete per-frame deformation with a smooth spline modeling the trajectory of each primitive's center and rotation as a function of time, ensuring physically plausible, smooth motion with fewer parameters. It uses B-spline basis functions \mathbf{B}k(t) and control points \mathbf{p}{i,k}: \mui(t) = \sum{k=0}^K \mathbf{B}k(t) \mathbf{p}{i,k}. A neural network that takes local body pose and latent codes to predict residual transformations (translation, rotation) and shading for Gaussians. Input is the concatenation of local body pose vector \thetat and per-Gaussian learnable latent features l. Hidden layers: 2 layers, 64 neurons each, ReLU activations. Output heads: 3 separate heads, each with 2 layers, outputting: 1) Translation vector t{mlp}, 2) Rotation quaternion q{mlp}, 3) Scaling factor s. Using latent codes l instead of position leads to better performance. The final observed position and orientation are computed as: \mathbf {p}{\text {obs}} = \mathbf {p}{\text {lbs}} + (\mathbf {R}{t}\mathbf {t}{\text {mlp}}) \mathbf {q}{\text {obs}} = \mathbf {q}{\text {mlp}} \circ \mathbf {q}{\text {lbs}}. Applying the scale-adaptive Gaussian fitting method as a plug-in to dynamic 3DGS models to solve zoom-out dilation without disturbing the deformation network. Scaffold-GS and Pixel-GS lack multi-scale deformation, compromising robustness for unseen settings. Embeds between Gaussian band and MLP for deformation prediction. Assigns each Gaussian a latent learnable embedding for unique characteristics and uses typical temporal embeddings for different frames. MLP takes latent and temporal embeddings to predict changes in position, scale, and rotation. Separately conducts deformation for coarse and fine motions: leverages a 1D feature grid for N frames and interpolates temporally to decode embedding for fine deformation; downsamples feature grid for coarse deformation. Uses Local Smoothness Regularization to encourage nearby Gaussians to conduct similar deformation to capture textures and fine details. Groups 3D Gaussians into superpoints using a Property Reconstruction Loss. The deformation network takes canonical position of superpoints and time as input to predict deformation, applied to Gaussians within superpoints. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes (people moving, fluids). When to use: Dynamic scene reconstruction and rendering. Introduced by Yang et al. in CVPR'24. It extends 3D-GS to canonical space and leverages a deformation MLP network to learn the offsets of the canonical 3D-GS to the final 3D shape. It is part of the broader effort to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to 4D (spatiotemporal) representations. name: VolSegGS
body: VolSegGS is a method for segmenting and tracking structures across timesteps in dynamic volumetric scenes by representing the scene as deformable 3D Gaussians, thereby sidestepping the memory constraints associated with grid-based representations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by employing a two-level segmentation strategy guided by an affinity field network, which allows it to split segments beneath thin, semi-transparent layers and resolve inner color variations that confuse 2D-prompt-based approaches. Unlike 4DGS, which relies on expensive k-NN regularization for explicit 4D Gaussians, VolSegGS uses a hybrid deformation network that provides spatial smoothness naturally, offering a balance between real-time rendering performance and segmentation accuracy. Inputs: A set of training views (images) of a dynamic volumetric scene at specific timesteps. 2D segmentation prompts (masks) generated by SAM 2 for the training views. Time parameter t for dynamic scenes. Outputs: A set of deformable 3D Gaussians representing the scene geometry and appearance. An affinity field network that assigns segmentation labels to Gaussians. Segmentation masks for test views and tracked labels across timesteps. Data Structures: 1. Deformable 3D Gaussians: Each Gaussian i is defined by mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3, opacity \alphai \in [0, 1], and view-independent color ci \in \mathbb{R}^3 used for coarse clustering. Deformation state is managed by the hybrid network. 2. Hybrid Deformation Network: Consists of an explicit feature grid storing latent features and a lightweight MLP that takes Gaussian means and time as inputs to output deformation parameters, providing spatial smoothness without additional regularization. 3. Affinity Field Network: A neural network that predicts affinity scores between Gaussians to refine segmentation, trained to ensure smoothness and consistency among neighboring Gaussians. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Representation: Represent the dynamic volumetric scene as a set of deformable 3D Gaussians. The hybrid deformation network takes the Gaussian mean \mui and time t as inputs to predict the deformation, providing spatial smoothness without additional regularization terms. 2. Coarse-Level Segmentation: Cluster the Gaussians based on their view-independent colors ci to provide a rough segmentation of the scene structures. 3. Fine-Level Segmentation (Affinity Field Training): Initialize the affinity field network. Train the network for 5,000 iterations using a batch size of 8,192 pixels, the Adam optimizer, and a learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-3}. The network is guided by SAM 2D prompts to refine the coarse clusters into fine-level segments. The affinity field ensures smoothness and consistency, reducing noise in affinity features that might otherwise affect occluded parts. 4. Segment Tracking: Maintain segment labels across timesteps by propagating them through the deformation field. As Gaussians deform over time, their associated segmentation labels are updated based on the learned affinity and deformation continuity. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using standard differentiable volume rendering techniques with the deformable Gaussians and their assigned segmentation labels. Loss Functions and Training Strategy: Early Training: Use L2 loss during early training iterations. This more effectively penalizes large errors in small regions, preventing missing content in synthesized images caused by deformation network inaccuracies. Late Training: Postpone the application of DSSIM loss until the final 5,000 iterations of training. This ensures better structural preservation. Two-Level Segmentation: The strategy splits segments beneath thin, semi-transparent layers and removes inner parts of different colors within semi-transparent segments, addressing ambiguities that 2D prompts alone cannot resolve. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class HybridDeformationNetwork(nn.Module): """Hybrid deformation network combining an explicit feature grid and a lightweight MLP.""" def init(self, gridres, featdim, mlphid): super().init() self.gridres = gridres self.grid = nn.Embedding(gridres3, featdim) self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(featdim + 1, mlphid), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(mlphid, mlphid), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(mlphid, 6)) def forward(self, mu, t): # Quantize normalized mean positions to grid indices indices = torch.clamp((mu + 1.0) (self.gridres / 2).long(), 0, self.gridres - 1) gridfeat = self.grid(indices[:, 0] self.gridres2 + indices[:, 1] self.gridres + indices[:, 2]) texp = t.unsqueeze(1) return self.mlp(torch.cat([gridfeat, texp], dim=-1)) class AffinityFieldNetwork(nn.Module): """Network to predict affinity scores for segmentation refinement.""" def init(self, dim, hid): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dim, hid), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hid, hid), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hid, 1)) def forward(self, f1, f2): return self.net(torch.abs(f1 - f2)) def computedssim(rendered, gt, windowsize=11): """Standard differentiable SSIM/DSSIM computation.""" mur = torch.nn.functional.avgpool2d(rendered, windowsize) mug = torch.nn.functional.avgpool2d(gt, windowsize) sigmar = torch.nn.functional.avgpool2d(rendered2, windowsize) - mur2 sigmag = torch.nn.functional.avgpool2d(gt2, windowsize) - mug2 sigmarg = torch.nn.functional.avgpool2d(rendered gt, windowsize) - mur mug C1, C2 = 1e-4, 1e-4 ssim = (2 mur mug + C1) (2 sigmarg + C2) / ((mur2 + mug2 + C1) (sigmar + sigmag + C2)) return torch.mean(1 - ssim) def rendergaussians(mu, colors, alphas, width, height): """Standard 2D Gaussian rasterization with alpha blending.""" projected = mu[:,:2] scores = alphas colors[:, 0] sortedidx = torch.argsort(scores, descending=True) out = torch.zeros(1, 3, height, width) for idx in sortedidx: c = colors[idx] a = alphas[idx] out = out + (1 - out) a.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) c.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1) return out def clusterbycolor(colors, k=10): """K-means clustering on view-independent colors.""" return torch.zeros(len(colors), dtype=torch.long) def refineaffinity(labels, affinitynet, mu, samprompts): """Refine coarse labels using affinity scores and SAM prompts.""" return labels def propagatelabels(labels, deformedmu, affinitynet): """Propagate segmentation labels across timesteps via deformation continuity.""" return labels def trainvolseggs(gaussiansmu, gaussianscolors, gaussiansalphas, trainingviews, sammasks, timesteps, totaliters=10000, width=800, height=800): """Main training loop for VolSegGS.""" deformnet = HybridDeformationNetwork(gridres=64, featdim=32, mlphid=64) affinitynet = AffinityFieldNetwork(dim=32, hid=64) optaff = optim.Adam(affinitynet.parameters(), lr=1e-3) optdef = optim.Adam(list(deformnet.parameters()), lr=1e-3) for it in range(totaliters): view, timet = trainingviews[it % len(trainingviews)], timesteps[it % len(timesteps)] # Deform Gaussians defparams = deformnet(gaussiansmu, timet) deformedmu = gaussiansmu + defparams[:,:3] # Render scene rendered = rendergaussians(deformedmu, gaussianscolors, gaussiansalphas, width, height) gt = view.gtimage # Loss scheduling: L2 early, DSSIM late if it < totaliters - 5000: loss = torch.mean((rendered - gt)2) else: lossl2 = torch.mean((rendered - gt)2) lossdssim = computedssim(rendered, gt) loss = lossl2 + lossdssim loss.backward(retaingraph=True) optdef.step() optdef.zerograd() # Affinity field training (first 5000 iterations) if it < 5000: batchpixels = torch.randint(0, width, (8192, 2)) feata, featb = extractneighborfeatures(deformedmu, batchpixels) affpred = affinitynet(feata, featb) affgt = computegtaffinity(sammasks, batchpixels) affloss = torch.mean((affpred - affgt)2) affloss.backward() optaff.step() optaff.zerograd() return deformnet, affinitynet def segmentandtrack(deformnet, affinitynet, gaussiansmu, gaussianscolors, samprompts, timesteps): """Segment and track structures in dynamic scenes.""" # Coarse clustering by view-independent colors coarselabels = clusterbycolor(gaussianscolors) # Refine using Affinity Field Network refinedlabels = refineaffinity(coarselabels, affinitynet, gaussiansmu, samprompts) tracked = [] for t in timesteps: defparams = deformnet(gaussiansmu, t) deformedmu = gaussiansmu + defparams[:,:3] # Propagate labels via deformation continuity and affinity currentlabels = propagatelabels(refinedlabels, deformedmu, affinitynet) tracked.append(currentlabels) return tracked Parameters: Affinity field network training iterations: 5,000. Batch size for affinity field network training: 8,192 pixels. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Training view resolution: 800×800. Number of training views: 30. Number of test views: 181. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with 24 GB VRAM. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing content in small regions: Caused by deformation network inaccuracies. Mitigated by using L2 loss in early training and postponing DSSIM loss. Segmentation beneath thin, semi-transparent layers: 2D prompts fail here. Mitigated by the two-level segmentation strategy. Noise in affinity features: Can lead to suboptimal segmentation for occluded parts. Mitigated by the spatial smoothness provided by the MLP-based deformation field network. Inner color variations: Semi-transparent segments may contain different colors. Mitigated by the two-level segmentation strategy which removes inner parts of different colors. Rendering Performance: Achieves a minimum rendering framerate of 87 FPS. Across five time-varying datasets at resolutions up to 960×1440×240, it achieves PSNR values of 25.76–29.02 dB at 88–89 FPS. Training Time: Training time for the affinity field network ranges from 1.53 to 1.85 minutes across datasets. Total preparation and training time varies by dataset (e.g., 1.38+16.07 minutes for 'five jets' to 15.96+16.92 minutes for 'combustion'). Segmentation Time: Segmentation time ranges from 0.14 to 0.16 seconds across datasets. Memory: Uses a hybrid deformation network with an explicit feature grid, which slightly increases model size compared to D3DGS but reduces memory overhead compared to grid-based methods like DVR. Strengths: Real-time rendering (≥87 FPS), fast segmentation (~0.15s), effective handling of semi-transparent layers and dynamic tracking, no data loading overhead during inference compared to DVR. Limitations: Requires upfront preparation and training time. Slightly larger model size than D3DGS. When to use: Real-time exploratory visualization of dynamic scenes and interactive segmentation and tracking tasks. When not to use: When training time is strictly prohibited and real-time segmentation is not required (SAGD might be preferred for its training-free nature, though it is slower per prompt). VolSegGS was proposed by Yao et al.. It addresses the challenge of segmenting and tracking structures in dynamic volumes, which is more difficult than static segmentation due to the need to maintain consistent labels as features deform, split, and merge. The method sidesteps grid memory constraints by using deformable 3D Gaussians. It is positioned as a solution for real-time exploratory visualization, offering a balance between generation quality, rendering efficiency, and training cost. name: Deformation Network for 4D Gaussian Splatting
head: Deformation Field Estimation Network (CDF), Dynamic Gaussian Prediction, Trunk-Branch Deformation Network
body: The Deformation Network is a neural module within Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting that predicts the time-dependent evolution of Gaussian primitives (means, scales, rotations, opacity, and spherical harmonic coefficients) from static input features and a time coordinate. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic scenes by mapping a canonical Gaussian representation to a time-varying state, enabling 4D content reconstruction from multi-view video. It differs from sibling methods like VolSegGS by explicitly modeling temporal deformation via a dedicated time-conditioned MLP with a trunk-branch design rather than static or voxel-based approaches. The method constructs a neural network that takes static Gaussian attributes and a time coordinate as input, applies positional encoding, and passes them through a deformation network to output dynamic parameters for a specific timestamp. Inputs: point: Static 3D mean position of the Gaussian, shape (N, 3). scales: Static scale parameters, shape (N, 3). rotations: Static rotation parameters (quaternions), shape (N, 4). opacity: Static opacity, shape (N, 1). shs: Static spherical harmonic coefficients, shape (N, K, 3) where K is the number of bands. timessel: Time coordinates for the target frames, shape (M, 1) or broadcastable to N. Outputs: dynamicmeans: Predicted 3D means at time t, shape (N, 3). dynamicscales: Predicted scales at time t, shape (N, 3). dynamicrotations: Predicted rotations at time t, shape (N, 4). dynamicopacity: Predicted opacity at time t, shape (N, 1). dynamicshs: Predicted SH coefficients at time t, shape (N, K, 3). The Deformation class (referenced as self.deformationnet) contains: 1. self.timenet: A Sequential module consisting of Linear -> ReLU -> Linear that processes time inputs. 2. self.deformationnet: An instance of the Deformation MLP class. 3. Buffers (FloatTensors): timepoc: Powers of 2 for time positional encoding. pospoc: Powers of 2 for position positional encoding. rotationscalingpoc: Powers of 2 for scale/rotation positional encoding. opacitypoc: Powers of 2 for opacity positional encoding. Positional encoding is applied to inputs using a function pocfre. For an input tensor x and a buffer B (containing powers of 2 from 2^0 to 2^{n-1}): 1. Multiply x by B (broadcasted). 2. Flatten the result. 3. Apply \sin and \cos. 4. Concatenate [x, \sin(x \cdot B), \cos(x \cdot B)] along the last dimension. netwidth: Width of the deformation network layers. timebasepe: Number of frequency bands for time positional encoding. defordepth: Depth of the deformation network. posbasepe: Number of frequency bands for position positional encoding. scalerotationpe: Number of frequency bands for scale/rotation positional encoding. opacitype: Number of frequency bands for opacity positional encoding. timenetwidth: Width of the time network. timenetoutput: Output dimension of the time network. gridpe: Parameter passed to the Deformation class for grid positional encoding.
