name: Cage-based Deformation for 3DGS
head: Deformation Algorithm, GSDeformer Deformation Algorithm
body: Cage-based deformation for 3DGS (GSDeformer) is a real-time method that transfers geometric deformation from a proxy point cloud to a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene without retraining. It solves the problem of accurately modeling large bending deformations, which standard mean-only optimization fails to capture, by splitting Gaussians and transforming their covariances. Unlike sibling methods such as Deformation Network for 4D Gaussian Splatting or VolSegGS which only optimize existing Gaussians, GSDeformer explicitly subdivides ellipsoids to handle complex curvature. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Source 3DGS scene Ss (set of Gaussians), Source Cage Cs, Target Cage Cd, Split threshold angle t. Output: Deformed 3DGS scene Sd. Data Structures: Gaussian: Standard 3DGS representation defined by mean position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma (encoding rotation and scale), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics coefficients c{lm}. Cage: A polygonal mesh defining the deformation space. Points-represented ellipsoid (AP): A discrete point set approximating the Gaussian's ellipsoidal shape, used as a proxy for deformation. Steps: 1. Proxy Construction: For each Gaussian i in the source scene, generate a points-represented ellipsoid set APs using Equation (4). This typically samples points on the ellipsoid surface defined by \Sigmai and \mui. 2. Cage-based Deformation: Deform the points APs to APd using the source cage Cs and target cage Cd. Convert Euclidean points APs to cage-based coordinates using EulerToMVC(APs, Cs). Interpolate deformation based on the cage topology using standard cage-based deformation logic. Convert back to Euclidean coordinates using MVCToEuler(AP{mvc}, Cd) to obtain APd. 3. Splitting: Initialize split sets AP{ss} = [APs] and AP{ds} = [APd]. Call the Split function with threshold t to handle large deformations. The Split function iterates over axes a \in \{x, y, z\} and deformed ellipsoids di \in AP{ds}. For each axis, calculate the angle \alpha formed by the endpoints l, r of the axis and the center c of the ellipsoid (\alpha = \angle l-c-r). If \alpha < t, the ellipsoid is too bent to be represented by a single Gaussian and is split into two ellipsoids, dl and dr. dl center is set to \text{mean}(c, l), points are shifted from c to the new center, and the c-l vector becomes its new axis a. dr center is set to \text{mean}(c, r), points are shifted from c to the new center, and the c-r vector becomes its new axis a. The corresponding source ellipsoids in AP{ss} are split identically to maintain correspondence. 4. Gaussian Transformation: For each pair of source ellipsoid si \in AP{ss} and deformed ellipsoid di \in AP{ds}: Compute the affine transform T from si to di using Equation (6). This is the least-squares affine transform mapping the point set si to di. Compute translation t{vec} = \text{center}(di) - \text{center}(si). Transform the original Gaussian i using Equations (7) and (8). Equation (7) updates the mean position, and Equation (8) updates the covariance to account for rotation and scaling. Append the transformed Gaussian to the result set Sd. Spherical harmonics parameters are copied directly without rotation adjustment. Parameters: t: Split threshold angle used to determine when an ellipsoid must be subdivided during deformation. k: Split scaling factor. Theoretical analysis suggests k should be 3/1, but empirical testing shows a large k (e.g., 1.0) creates spikes on intricate surfaces, while a small k (e.g., 0.1) produces fragmented surfaces. Pitfalls: Mean-only deformation: Optimizing only the position causes significant striping artifacts. No splitting: Disabling splitting causes spiking artifacts in bent regions because a single Gaussian cannot model the deformation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def gsdeformerdeform(gsscene, sourcecage, targetcage, splitthreshold): """ Deforms a 3DGS scene using cage-based deformation. Args: gsscene: List of Gaussian objects. Each has.mu (3,),.cov (3,3),.opacity (float),.sh (array). sourcecage: Cage mesh for source space. targetcage: Cage mesh for target space. splitthreshold: Angle threshold for splitting ellipsoids. Returns: deformedgsscene: List of deformed Gaussian objects. """ deformedgsscene = [] for gaussian in gsscene: # 1. Convert Gaussian to points-represented ellipsoid aps = sampleellipsoidpoints(gaussian.mu, gaussian.cov) # 2. Deform points using cage-based deformation apmvc = eulertomvc(aps, sourcecage) apd = mvctoeuler(apmvc, targetcage) # 3. Perform splitting apss = [aps] apds = [apd] apss, apds = splitfunction(gaussian, apss, apds, splitthreshold) # 4. Transform Gaussians for si, di in zip(apss, apds): # Compute affine transform T from si to di T = computeaffinetransform(si, di) # Compute translation centersi = meanpoint(si) centerdi = meanpoint(di) tvec = centerdi - centersi # Transform Gaussian newmu = T @ gaussian.mu + tvec newcov = T @ gaussian.cov @ T.T # Create new Gaussian newgaussian = Gaussian() newgaussian.mu = newmu newgaussian.cov = newcov newgaussian.opacity = gaussian.opacity newgaussian.sh = gaussian.sh deformedgsscene.append(newgaussian) return deformedgsscene def splitfunction(gaussian, apss, apds, threshold): """ Splits ellipsoids if the bending angle is too large. """ newapss = [] newapds = [] for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: for si, di in zip(apss, apds): centerdi = meanpoint(di) l, r = getaxisendpoints(di, gaussian.cov, axis) # Calculate angle alpha v1 = l - centerdi v2 = r - centerdi alpha = math.acos(np.clip(np.dot(v1, v2) / (np.linalg.norm(v1) np.linalg.norm(v2) + 1e-8), -1.0, 1.0)) if alpha < threshold: # Split into two # Left ellipsoid dl = copyellipsoid(di) dl.center = (centerdi + l) / 2.0 shiftpoints(dl.points, centerdi, dl.center) dl.axis = dl.center - l # Right ellipsoid dr = copyellipsoid(di) dr.center = (centerdi + r) / 2.0 shiftpoints(dr.points, centerdi, dr.center) dr.axis = dr.center - r # Corresponding source splits centersi = meanpoint(si) sl = copyellipsoid(si) sl.center = (centersi + l) / 2.0 shiftpoints(sl.points, centersi, sl.center) sr = copyellipsoid(si) sr.center = (centersi + r) / 2.0 shiftpoints(sr.points, centersi, sr.center) newapss.extend([sl, sr]) newapds.extend([dl, dr]) else: newapss.append(si) newapds.append(di) return newapss, newapds def sampleellipsoidpoints(mu, cov): """ Sample points on the ellipsoid defined by mu and cov.""" eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) radii = np.sqrt(eigenvalues) npoints = 100 phi = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, npoints) theta = np.linspace(0, np.pi, npoints) points = [] for p in phi: for t in theta: x = np.sin(t) np.cos(p) y = np.sin(t) np.sin(p) z = np.cos(t) local = np.array([x, y, z]) world = mu + eigenvectors @ (local radii) points.append(world) return np.array(points) def eulertomvc(points, cage): """ Convert Euclidean points to Cage-based coordinates using barycentric interpolation.""" # Standard cage deformation: find enclosing tetrahedron, compute barycentric coords pass def mvctoeuler(pointsmvc, cage): """ Convert Cage-based coordinates back to Euclidean using target cage interpolation.""" # Standard cage deformation: interpolate using target cage weights pass def computeaffinetransform(sourcepoints, targetpoints): """ Compute affine transform T such that T sourcepoints ≈ targetpoints.""" # Least squares solution: T = targetpoints @ sourcepoints^+ sourcemean = np.mean(sourcepoints, axis=0) targetmean = np.mean(targetpoints, axis=0) centereds = sourcepoints - sourcemean centeredt = targetpoints - targetmean H = centeredt.T @ centereds U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H) Trot = Vt.T @ U.T if np.linalg.det(Trot) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1 Trot = Vt.T @ U.T Ttrans = targetmean - Trot @ sourcemean T = np.eye(4) T[:3,:3] = Trot T[:3, 3] = Ttrans return T[:3,:3] def meanpoint(points): return np.mean(points, axis=0) def getaxisendpoints(ellipsoidpoints, cov, axis): """ Get endpoints of the principal axis.""" eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) maxidx = np.argmax(eigenvalues) axisvec = eigenvectors[:, maxidx] scale = np.sqrt(eigenvalues[maxidx]) center = meanpoint(ellipsoidpoints) l = center - scale axisvec r = center + scale axisvec return l, r def copyellipsoid(ellipsoid): return Ellipsoid(ellipsoid.points.copy(), ellipsoid.center.copy()) def shiftpoints(points, oldcenter, newcenter): points += (newcenter - oldcenter) class Gaussian: def init(self): self.mu = np.zeros(3) self.cov = np.eye(3) self.opacity = 1.0 self.sh = np.array([]) class Ellipsoid: def init(self, points, center): self.points = points self.center = center self.axis = np.zeros(3) Time Complexity: Real-time performance is achieved through extensive caching, where AP{mvc} and parts of the transform T can be precomputed. The splitting and transformation steps scale linearly with the number of Gaussians and split ellipsoids. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the proxy point sets and split ellipsoids temporarily, but needs no additional training data or architectural changes. Strengths: Handles large bending deformations accurately via splitting; works on existing trained vanilla 3DGS without retraining; real-time capable. Limitations: Copies spherical harmonics without rotation adjustment, potentially causing color inaccuracies under rotation; point-based deformation is better suited for small deformations like facial expressions. When to use: When deforming large, complex shapes with significant bending where mean-only optimization fails. When not to use: For small, local deformations (e.g., facial expressions) where point-based methods might be more efficient, or when high-fidelity viewpoint-dependent color rotation is critical. GSDeformer was introduced by the authors of the paper "GSDeformer: Direct Cage-based Deformation for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It adapts traditional cage-based deformation techniques to the specific data structure of 3DGS. The method addresses limitations in prior works like ARAP-GS and VRGS, which only optimize existing Gaussians and fail to model bending accurately. The cage-building process is inspired by the 3DGS marching cube method proposed in SuGaR. GSDeformer: Direct Cage-based Deformation for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.15491, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical and Local Scene Decomposition
head: Local Neural Fields, Incremental Implicit Scene Representation, Adaptive Voronoi NeRFs
body: Hierarchical and Local Scene Decomposition addresses the memory constraints and convergence issues of global NeRF representations when applied to large-scale or long-sequence scenes by partitioning the scene into multiple local radiance fields. Unlike global implicit representations that evaluate a single large MLP for every sample, these methods use a structured collection of local fields (e.g., Nerflets or sliding-window local radiance fields) to enable efficient, structure-aware scene decomposition and interactive editing [S1, 20286-nerf-with-local-neural-fields-nerflets.md]. The family shares the mechanism of decomposing a 3D scene into a set of N local representations rather than a single global function. Each local representation i maintains its own spatial parameters (position, orientation, extent) and a local neural network or feature grid. 1. Local Coordinate Transformation: For a query point x, it is transformed into the local coordinate frame of each contributing local field i using the field's center \mui, rotation \thetai, and scale/radii ri. 2. Influence Weighting: Each local field contributes to the final density and color based on an influence weight w{k,i}, which typically falls off with distance from the field's center, often modeled by a Radial Basis Function (RBF) [S1, 20286-nerf-with-local-neural-fields-nerflets.md]. 3. Aggregation: The effective density \sigmak and color ck at a sample point are computed as weighted sums of the outputs from all nearby local fields: \sigmak = \sum{i} w{k,i} \sigma{k,i} ck = \frac{\sum{i} w{k,i} \sigma{k,i} c{k,i}}{\sum{i} w{k,i} \sigma{k,i}} [20286-nerf-with-local-neural-fields-nerflets.md] 4. Volume Rendering: Standard volume rendering integration is performed using the aggregated density and color values [S1, 20286-nerf-with-local-neural-fields-nerflets.md]. Nerflets represent a scene as an irregular collection of local neural radiance fields, where each "nerflet" maintains its own pose and influence region. It differs from global NeRF by evaluating only small MLPs of nearby nerflets, enabling efficient structure-aware reconstruction and 2D-supervised semantic/instance editing [20286-nerf-with-local-neural-fields-nerflets.md]. This method reconstructs large-scale scenes by dynamically allocating local radiance fields as the camera moves, using a sliding window of frames. It differs from global NeRF by using Vector-Matrix decomposition for feature grids, reducing space complexity from cubic O(n^3) to square O(n) and solving memory constraints for long sequences [21737-incremental-implicit-scene-representation.md]. A technique presented by Elsner et al. that enhances efficiency by employing Voronoi diagrams to partition the scene into cells. These cells are subsequently subdivided to effectively capture and represent intricate details, leading to improved performance and accuracy. The concept of decomposing scenes into local fields emerged to address the scalability limits of global NeRFs. Elsner et al. introduced Adaptive Voronoi NeRFs to improve efficiency through spatial partitioning. Concurrently, methods like Nerflets and Incremental Implicit Scene Representation were developed to handle large-scale environments and long sequences by avoiding the optimization of a single monolithic network, thereby reducing memory usage and improving convergence [20286-nerf-with-local-neural-fields-nerflets.md, 21737-incremental-implicit-scene-representation.md]. A Critical Analysis of NeRF-Based 3D Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15143585, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF with Local Neural Fields (Nerflets)
head: Local Radiance Fields, Nerflets
body: Nerflets represent a 3D scene as a structured, irregular set of local neural radiance fields, where each "nerflet" maintains its own spatial position, orientation, and extent to contribute to density, radiance, and semantic reconstructions within its region of influence. Unlike global implicit representations or methods requiring expensive 3D ground-truth supervision for decomposition, Nerflets optimize a joint set of local parameters using only 2D image and panoptic segmentation supervision, enabling efficient, scalable, and editable scene representation. Inputs: A set of M posed RGB images \{Im\}{m=1}^M with known camera poses. (Optional) 2D panoptic segmentation masks \{Sm\}{m=1}^M aligned with the images. The number of nerflets N (or a mechanism to dynamically add/remove them, though the core definition assumes a fixed set during the single training stage described). Outputs: A set of N nerflets, each defined by its pose parameters, MLP weights, semantic logit, and instance ID. Synthesized novel view images and associated semantic/instance maps. Each nerflet i stores the following fields: 1. Pose Parameters (9 DOF): \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D center position. ri \in \mathbb{R}^3: Per-axis radii (scale). \thetai \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D XYZ rotation angles. These define the local coordinate frame and the spatial extent of the nerflet's influence. 2. Miniature MLP (fi): A small neural network (typically a multi-layer perceptron) that takes local coordinates as input and outputs density \sigma and color c. Note: The exact architecture (layer sizes, activation functions) of the "miniature" MLP is not specified in the provided sources, other than it being "tiny" compared to global NeRF MLPs. 3. Semantic Logit Vector (si): si \in \mathbb{R}^C: A single vector storing semantic logits for C categories (e.g., "car", "person"). This replaces an MLP-based semantic decoder, reducing capacity burden and providing an inductive bias for 3D spatial consistency. 4. Instance ID (I{nsi}): An integer label indicating which real-world object instance the nerflet belongs to (e.g., "the third car"). Multiple nerflets can share the same instance ID to represent complex objects. The influence of nerflet i at a query point x is determined by a Radial Basis Function (RBF) gi(x), which falls off with distance from the center \mui. First, transform the query point x into the local coordinate frame of nerflet i: x'i = Ri^T (x - \mui) where Ri is the rotation matrix derived from \thetai. The normalized distance is computed using the per-axis radii ri = [r{i,x}, r{i,y}, r{i,z}]^T: di(x) = \sqrt{ \left(\frac{x'i[0]}{r{i,x}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{x'i[1]}{r{i,y}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{x'i[2]}{r{i,z}}\right)^2 } The influence weight w{k,i} for a sample point xk is typically modeled as a Gaussian RBF: w{k,i} = \exp(-di(xk)^2) Note: The exact functional form of the RBF (e.g., specific variance scaling) is not explicitly detailed in the provided text, but the fall-off behavior is described as dependent on orientation and radii. 1. Ray Sampling: For a given ray (defined by origin o and direction d), sample K points xk along the ray, as in standard NeRF. 2. Local Coordinate Transformation: For each sample point xk and each nerflet i, compute the local coordinates x'i using the nerflet's center \mui and rotation \thetai. 3. Influence Weight Calculation: Compute the influence weight w{k,i} for each nerflet i at sample xk using the RBF based on the distance in the local frame and the radii ri. 4. Nerflet Query: For each nerflet i with non-negligible influence (or all N nerflets), query the miniature MLP fi with the local coordinates x'i to obtain local density \sigma{k,i} and color c{k,i}. \sigma{k,i}, c{k,i} = fi(x'i) 5. Aggregation: Compute the aggregated density \sigmak and color ck at sample xk by weighting the outputs of all nerflets: \sigmak = \sum{i=1}^{N} w{k,i} \sigma{k,i} ck = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} w{k,i} \sigma{k,i} c{k,i}}{\sum{i=1}^{N} w{k,i} \sigma{k,i}} Note: If the denominator is zero, ck is undefined or set to a background color. 6. Volume Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering integration over the samples k=1 \dots K to compute the pixel color C: C = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak ck where \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak), Tk = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), and \deltak is the distance between samples. 7. Semantic Aggregation: The semantic logits for the pixel are aggregated similarly, weighted by the density contribution: s{pixel} = \frac{\sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak si}{\sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak} Note: The exact aggregation formula for semantics across samples and nerflets is not explicitly provided in the sources, but it follows the principle of blending values produced by individual nerflets. A reasonable implementation would aggregate semantic logits weighted by the final transmittance and density contribution of each nerflet's samples. 8. Training: Optimize all continuous parameters (pose, MLP weights, semantic logits) jointly using a single training stage with 2D supervision (photometric loss and optional panoptic segmentation loss). 9. Instance Assignment: After training, instance labels are assigned based on the scene structure (e.g., clustering nerflets with similar instance IDs or spatial proximity if not explicitly optimized). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def nerfletrender(rayorigin, raydirection, nerflets, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using the Nerflets representation. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, camera origin. raydirection: (3,) array, normalized ray direction. nerflets: List of Nerflet objects. numsamples: Integer, number of sample points along the ray. Returns: color: (3,) array, rendered RGB color. semanticlogits: (C,) array, aggregated semantic logits. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # Assuming a fixed range [tmin, tmax] for the scene bounds tmin, tmax = 0.1, 100.0 tvals = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, numsamples) points = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, np.newaxis] # (K, 3) aggregateddensity = 0.0 aggregatedcolor = np.zeros(3) aggregatedsemantic = np.zeros(nerflets[0].semanticlogit.shape[0]) transmittance = 1.0 for k in range(numsamples): xk = points[k] # 2. Aggregate contributions from all nerflets localdensitysum = 0.0 localcolorsum = np.zeros(3) localsemanticsum = np.zeros(nerflets[0].semanticlogit.shape[0]) for nerflet in nerflets: # 3. Compute influence weight # Transform point to local frame # Ri is rotation matrix from thetai # x'i = Ri^T (xk - mui) xlocal = nerflet.transformtolocal(xk) # Compute normalized distance # di = sqrt( (x'i[0]/rx)^2 + (x'i[1]/ry)^2 + (x'i[2]/rz)^2) normalizeddist = np.linalg.norm(xlocal / nerflet.radii) # Influence weight (Gaussian RBF) # w = exp(-d^2) weight = np.exp(-normalizeddist2) # 4. Query MLP # sigmai, ci = fi(xlocal) sigmai, colori = nerflet.mlp(xlocal) # 5. Weighted aggregation localdensitysum += weight sigmai localcolorsum += weight sigmai colori localsemanticsum += weight sigmai nerflet.semanticlogit # Avoid division by zero if localdensitysum < 1e-6: continue # Aggregated density and color at this sample sigmak = localdensitysum colork = localcolorsum / localdensitysum semantick = localsemanticsum / localdensitysum # 6. Volume Rendering Step # alphak = 1 - exp(-sigmak deltak) # deltak is the distance between samples (approximated as constant) deltat = tvals[1] - tvals[0] alphak = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmak deltat) # Contribution to final color contribution = transmittance alphak aggregatedcolor += contribution colork aggregatedsemantic += contribution semantick aggregateddensity += contribution sigmak # For debugging/analysis # Update transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - alphak) # Early termination if transmittance is very low if transmittance < 1e-4: break return aggregatedcolor, aggregatedsemantic class Nerflet: def init(self, center, radii, rotationangles, mlp, semanticlogit, instanceid): self.center = center # (3,) self.radii = radii # (3,) self.rotationangles = rotationangles # (3,) self.mlp = mlp # Miniature MLP function self.semanticlogit = semanticlogit # (C,) self.instanceid = instanceid def transformtolocal(self, xworld): """Transform world point to local coordinate frame.""" # Construct rotation matrix from XYZ angles R = self.rotationmatrixfromangles(self.rotationangles) Rinv = R.T # Inverse of rotation matrix is transpose # xlocal = Rinv (xworld - center) xlocal = Rinv @ (xworld - self.center) return xlocal def rotationmatrixfromangles(self, angles): """Construct rotation matrix from XYZ Euler angles.""" # Standard rotation matrices Rx = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, np.cos(angles[0]), -np.sin(angles[0])], [0, np.sin(angles[0]), np.cos(angles[0])]]) Ry = np.array([[np.cos(angles[1]), 0, np.sin(angles[1])], [0, 1, 0], [-np.sin(angles[1]), 0, np.cos(angles[1])]]) Rz = np.array([[np.cos(angles[2]), -np.sin(angles[2]), 0], [np.sin(angles[2]), np.cos(angles[2]), 0], [0, 0, 1]]) return Rz @ Ry @ Rx Number of Nerflets (N): Not given in the sources. Depends on scene complexity. MLP Size: "Miniature" or "tiny". Specific layer sizes not given. Pose Parameters: 9 per nerflet (3 center, 3 radii, 3 rotation). Training: Single stage, joint optimization. Zero Density: If \sum w{k,i} \sigma{k,i} = 0, the color aggregation is undefined. A guard condition should return a background color or transparent value. Degenerate Pose: If radii are zero or rotation is singular, the local transformation may fail. Initialization should ensure non-zero radii. Overlap: Nerflets may overlap. The RBF weighting handles this, but care must be taken to ensure smooth transitions and avoid artifacts from conflicting semantic labels. An alternative approach that builds the scene representation incrementally, adding new nerflets as needed, rather than optimizing a fixed set. It focuses on dynamic scene updates. Link Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to N \times K, where N is the number of nerflets and K is the number of samples per ray. However, only nearby nerflets contribute significantly due to the RBF fall-off, allowing for spatial indexing to optimize queries. Training time is comparable to global NeRF but with smaller MLPs per nerflet. Memory Complexity: Memory scales with N \times (\text{MLP size} + \text{pose size}). This can be more efficient than a single large MLP for complex scenes if N is small, but may be less efficient if N is very large. Strengths: Efficiency: Smaller MLPs per nerflet reduce computational load per query. Scalability: Local decomposition allows handling large scenes. Editability: Explicit structure allows direct editing of objects as geometric primitives. 2D Supervision: Requires only 2D images and panoptic masks, avoiding expensive 3D ground truth. Limitations: Complexity of Decomposition: Determining the optimal number and placement of nerflets is non-trivial. Overlap Artifacts: Improperly tuned RBFs or overlapping nerflets with conflicting semantics can cause artifacts. Instance Assignment: Post-training instance assignment may require additional heuristics. When to Use: Scenes requiring efficient, editable, and semantically aware 3D representation from 2D supervision. Ideal for robotics and AR/VR applications where object-level interaction is needed. When Not to Use: Scenes with very high frequency details that require a large number of nerflets, or where global coherence is more important than local editability. Nerflets were introduced by Xiaoshuai Zhang, Abhijit Kundu, Thomas Funkhouser, Leonidas Guibas, Hao Su, and Kyle Genova from Google Research, Stanford University, and UC San Diego in 2023. The work addresses the limitations of existing semantics-aware NeRF methods, such as Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF) and DM-NeRF, which either require expensive 3D supervision or lack explicit structure for editing. The method builds on the principles of hierarchical and local scene decomposition Link. Nerflets: Local Radiance Fields for Efficient Structure-Aware 3D Scene Representation from 2D Supervision, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00800, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Incremental Implicit Scene Representation
head: Incremental NeRF, Local Radiance Fields
body: Incremental Implicit Scene Representation is a method for reconstructing large-scale scenes by dynamically allocating multiple local neural radiance fields (LR) as the camera moves, rather than relying on a single global representation. It solves the problems of local minima convergence and cubic memory constraints inherent in global NeRF approaches for long sequences. It differs from NeRF with Local Neural Fields (Nerflets) by using a strictly sequential, incremental registration process where previous fields are frozen once the camera exits their spatial bounds, whereas Nerflets typically optimizes a fixed set of local fields jointly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of monocular images Ii and their corresponding estimated depth maps Di for i=1 \dots M. Camera intrinsics are required for ray generation. Outputs: A set of n local radiance fields \{\text{LR}{\theta1}^1, \dots, \text{LR}{\thetan}^n\} and optimized camera poses \{R, T\}, which render color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Data Structures: 1. Local Radiance Field (LR): Defined by parameters \thetaj. It contains a 3D feature grid \mathcal{G} factorized via Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition. 2. Vector-Matrix Grid (\mathcal{G}): Instead of storing a dense tensor, \mathcal{G} is stored as a sum of outer products of vectors and matrices: \mathcal{G} = \sum{r=1}^R \mathbf{v}r^X \circ \mathbf{M}r^{YZ} + \mathbf{v}r^Y \circ \mathbf{M}r^{XZ} + \mathbf{v}r^Z \circ \mathbf{M}r^{XY} where \mathbf{v}r^X, \mathbf{v}r^Y, \mathbf{v}r^Z are vectors corresponding to the XYZ axes, and \mathbf{M}r^{YZ}, \mathbf{M}r^{XZ}, \mathbf{M}r^{XY} are matrices. 3. Pose History: A list of camera poses \{R, T\} indexed by frame number. 4. Boundaries: Each local field j has an associated spatial boundary \text{Bound}j. Algorithm Steps: The optimization follows Algorithm 1: 1. Initialization: Set local field index j=1, pose start index p=1, and current frame index q=1. Initialize poses \{R, T\}{p..q} as identity. Initialize the first local radiance field \theta1. Set the center of the first field t1 based on the initial pose. 2. Iterative Registration (Loop over frames q < P): Local Optimization: For the current frame q, optimize the parameters \thetaj of the current local field for 100 iterations. Sliding Window Refinement: While the current camera pose \{R, T\}q is within the boundary \text{Bound}j of the current local field: 1. Increment q to include the next frame. 2. Append the new pose: \{R, T\}q \leftarrow \{R, T\}{q-1} (initially, then refined). 3. Jointly optimize the poses \{R, T\}{p..q} and the local field parameters \thetaj. Incremental Expansion: If q < P (more frames remain): 1. Increment j to create a new local field. 2. Initialize new field \thetaj. 3. Set the center of the new field tj to the last known pose tq. 4. Update the start index p \leftarrow p + n (where n is a step size, effectively stopping consideration of frames handled by the previous local field). 3. Freezing: Once the camera pose exceeds the boundary of a local field, optimization of that field's poses and network parameters ceases (freezes) to reduce memory usage. Ray Marching and Integration: Ray Generation: For each input image, generate rays \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{x}i + t \mathbf{d}i using the camera intrinsic matrix and pose. Sampling: Sample points \mathbf{x}i along the rays. The method uses estimated depth information to guide this sampling process. Query: Query the active local radiance field \text{LR}{\thetaj} to get color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Feature Interpolation: To compute features for a voxel, tri-linear interpolation is performed directly on the vector/matrix factors of the VM decomposition, rather than recovering eight individual tensor elements. Volume Rendering: The final color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) is computed via standard differentiable volume rendering: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i Ti = \exp \left( - \sum{j=1}^i \sigmaj \deltaj \right) where \sigmai is density, \deltai is the distance between samples, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalimplicitscenerepresentation(images, depths, intrinsics, totalframes): """ Implements the incremental registration of local radiance fields. """ # Initialization j = 1 # Current local field index p = 1 # Start index for pose optimization window q = 1 # Current frame index being processed poses = [IdentityPose()] # List of poses, index 1-based logic mapped to 0-based list localfields = [] # List of LR objects bounds = [] # List of boundaries for each LR # Initialize first local field theta1 = InitializeLR() localfields.append(theta1) bounds.append(CalculateBound(poses[0])) # Bound centered at initial pose # Set initial pose poses[0] = IdentityPose() # Main loop while q < totalframes: # 1. Optimize current field with current frame # Optimize thetaj for 100 iterations using image q and depth q for m in range(100): thetaj = localfields[j-1] OptimizeParameters(thetaj, images[q-1], depths[q-1], poses[q-1], intrinsics) # 2. Sliding window refinement # While current pose is within the boundary of the current local field while IsPoseInBound(poses[q-1], bounds[j-1]): q += 1 if q > totalframes: break # Append new pose (initially copy previous, then refine) # Note: Source says {R,T}q <- {R,T}{q-1} initially poses.append(poses[q-2].Copy()) # Jointly optimize poses p..q and local field thetaj # p is the start of the window, j is the current field index windowposes = poses[p-1: q] # Slice from p to q thetaj = localfields[j-1] JointOptimize(windowposes, thetaj, images[p-1: q], depths[p-1: q], intrinsics) # Update bound based on refined poses bounds[j-1] = CalculateBound(poses[q-1]) if q >= totalframes: break # 3. Incremental expansion if q < totalframes: j += 1 # Initialize new local field thetanew = InitializeLR() localfields.append(thetanew) # Center new field around last pose tj = poses[q-1] thetanew.center = tj # Update p: stop considering frames in last local radiance field # n is a step size parameter defined in source p = p + n # Initialize boundary for new field bounds.append(CalculateBound(tj)) return localfields, poses def IsPoseInBound(pose, bound): # Check if pose position is within the spatial extent of the bound # Implementation detail: Typically involves checking distance against radius or AABB return Distance(pose.position, bound.center) < bound.radius def JointOptimize(poslist, lrparams, imglist, depthlist, intrinsics): # Perform gradient descent on poses and LR parameters # Loss includes rendering loss and depth consistency pass Parameters: Optimization Iterations per Frame: 100. VM Decomposition Rank: R (Not given in the sources). Step Size n: Not given in the sources. Complexity: Reduces space complexity from cubic O(n^3) (typical voxel grid) to square O(n) via Vector-Matrix decomposition. Memory: Decreases memory usage by freezing and discarding supervisory frames for local fields once the camera moves beyond their boundaries. Strengths: Avoids local minima common in global NeRF for large-scale scenes; handles long sequences by decomposing the problem into manageable local optimizations. Limitations: Requires accurate initial depth estimation to guide sampling; performance depends on the definition of boundaries \text{Bound}j. Performance: On Tanks and Temples datasets, the method achieves higher PSNR than NoPe-NeRF and LocalRF. Origin: Proposed in 2025 by authors of "Incremental Joint Learning of Depth, Pose, and Implicit Scene Representation on Monocular Camera in Large-Scale Scenes". Context: Addresses limitations of existing implicit scene representations (like global NeRF) which struggle with large-scale scenes and converge to local minima. It builds on the concept of local neural radiance fields. Incremental Joint Learning of Depth, Pose, and Implicit Scene Representation on Monocular Camera in Large-Scale Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/tase.2025.3617654, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Activation-based Density Estimation for NeRF Acceleration
head: Activation-derived density estimate, Weight estimate from activations
body: This method accelerates inference in pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by deriving density estimates from intermediate layer activations of the coarse MLP, allowing for reduced sampling or early termination without modifying the network architecture or training protocol. Unlike coarse-to-fine sampling which uses two separate NeRFs, this method uses intermediate activations from a single coarse NeRF to derive weights, reducing computational requirements by up to 50% with only a slight hit in rendering quality. Unlike sampling networks that predict density with reduced capacity, this method leverages the existing capacity of the trained coarse NeRF's intermediate features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained coarse NeRF network \Theta{\text{coarse}}, a camera ray \vec{r} defined by origin \vec{o} and direction \vec{d}, near/far bounds tn, tf, and a layer index \ell. Output: An estimated color \hat{\mathcal{C}}(\vec{r}) and optionally a boolean flag indicating whether the fine pass was executed. Data Structures: Ray Samples: A set of positions ti for i=1 \dots Nc uniformly distributed in [tn, tf]. Positional Encoding: \gamma(\cdot) maps 3D coordinates to a higher-dimensional vector. Activation Feature Vector: f\ell \in \mathbb{R}^{Ns}, where Ns is the number of samples. This is derived from the raw activation matrix A^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{Ns \times Nh} by computing the mean over the hidden units dimension Nh: f{\ell, i} = \frac{1}{Nh} \sum{k=1}^{Nh} A^{(\ell)}{i,k} Density Estimate: \hat{d}i derived from f{\ell, i}. Weight Estimate: \hat{w}i derived from \hat{d}i. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting and Encoding: For each pixel, generate a ray \vec{r}(t) = \vec{o} + t\vec{d}. Place Nc samples uniformly at positions ti \in [tn, tf]. Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to each sample position ti. 2. Coarse Network Forward Pass: Pass the encoded samples through the coarse NeRF MLP \Theta{\text{coarse}}. Retrieve the raw activation matrix A^{(\ell)} for a specific intermediate layer \ell. 3. Feature Extraction: Compute the activation feature vector f\ell \in \mathbb{R}^{Nc} by averaging the activations across the hidden dimension Nh for each sample: f{\ell, i} = \frac{1}{Nh} \sum{k=1}^{Nh} A^{(\ell)}{i,k} 4. Density Estimation: Derive a density estimate \hat{d}i from the activation feature f{\ell, i}. The method relies on the observation that trained NeRFs map samples with high volumetric density \sigma to local minima in the activation feature space along a ray. Note: The specific mathematical function mapping f{\ell, i} to \hat{d}i is not explicitly defined in the provided sources, other than the qualitative relationship that minima in f\ell correspond to high \sigma. [G: In implementation, this typically involves normalizing the activations or applying a monotonic transformation that inverts the "minima = high density" relationship, such as \hat{d}i = \max(f\ell) - f{\ell, i} or similar scaling, but the exact formula is not given in the sources.] 5. Weight Estimation: Convert the density estimates \hat{d}i into weights \hat{w}i that approximate the standard NeRF weights wi = Ti(1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). These weights are normalized such that \sum \hat{w}i = 1 to form a piecewise-constant probability density function (PDF) along the ray. 6. Fine Pass Sampling (Optional): Use inverse transform sampling with the derived weight estimate \hat{w} to generate a new set of Nf samples for the fine pass. 7. Early Termination (Optional): To further reduce inference time, perform the fine pass only if a condition based on the activation value v\ell and a threshold \mu(V\ell) is met. Specifically, if v\ell < \mu(V\ell), the fine pass is skipped. Here, v\ell likely refers to a scalar summary of the activations (e.g., mean or min) and \mu(V\ell) is a learned or statistical threshold [G: The exact definition of v\ell and \mu(V\ell) is not provided in the sources, but it serves as a gate for computational cost]. 8. Rendering: If the fine pass is executed, render using all Nc + Nf samples with the fine network \Theta{\text{fine}}. If the fine pass is skipped, render using only the Nc coarse samples with \Theta{\text{coarse}}. The color \hat{\mathcal{C}}(\vec{r}) is estimated using the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{\mathcal{C}}(\vec{r}) = \sum{i} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \vec{c}i where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Parameters: Ns: The number of samples used to estimate the ray color in the standard NeRF formulation. Nc: The number of samples placed uniformly by the coarse NeRF. Nf: The number of samples generated for the fine pass via inverse transform sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded Scenes: For unbounded 3D scenes, coordinates must be mapped using the spatial contraction function \text{contract}(\cdot) from Mip-NeRF 360 to map \mathbb{R}^3 to a ball of radius 2: \text{contract}(\vec{x}) = \begin{cases} \vec{x} & \|\vec{x}\| \leq 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\vec{x}\|}\right)\left(\frac{\vec{x}}{\|\vec{x}\|}\right) & \|\vec{x}\| > 1 \end{cases} Precision: The method relies on the stability of intermediate activations. Degenerate inputs (e.g., rays with no intersection) may produce undefined activation patterns. [G: Standard NeRF handling of empty space should be applied.] Time Complexity: Reduces computational requirements of trained NeRFs by up to 50%. This is achieved by avoiding the full fine-pass network evaluation for a significant portion of pixels/rays. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead compared to standard coarse-to-fine NeRFs, as it reuses the existing coarse network activations. Strengths: Does not require retraining or architectural changes; leverages existing network capacity; simple to implement as a post-processing step on activations. Limitations: Slight hit in rendering quality compared to standard coarse-to-fine sampling. Performance depends on the correlation between activation minima and density, which may vary across different NeRF architectures or datasets. When to use: When inference speed is critical and a small quality trade-off is acceptable. When not to use: When maximum rendering quality is required or when the activation-density correlation is weak for the specific scene/network. Origin: Proposed in "Analyzing the Internals of Neural Radiance Fields". History: The method builds on the observation that NeRF-MLPs naturally partition themselves into structural and color layers. It contrasts with sampling networks that predict density with reduced capacity, arguing that the coarse NeRF's deep features already contain valuable density information. Usage: Applied to accelerate inference in synthetic and real-world NeRF datasets. Analyzing the Internals of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprw63382.2024.00288, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SpikingNeRF
head: SpikingNeRF: Making Bio-inspired Neural Networks See through the Real World
body: SpikingNeRF is a method that aligns the temporal dimension of spiking neural networks (SNNs) with radiance rays to enable spike-based, multiplication-free NeRF rendering, reducing energy consumption for neuromorphic hardware. It differs from standard differentiable rendering by replacing the continuous activation of Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with spiking dynamics, where the geometric sequence of points along a ray is mapped to the temporal sequence of input spikes. Unlike Liao et al. (2023), which uses an ANN with a post-processing function B-FIF, SpikingNeRF uses actual SNNs targeting neuromorphic hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera poses, intrinsics, and training images. Output: Rendered RGB images \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for given rays \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grids (\mathbf{V}\sigma, \mathbf{V}f): Explicitly stored volumetric parameters. \mathbf{V}\sigma: Stores density \sigma. \mathbf{V}f: Stores embedded features \mathbf{e}. Layout: 3D grid indexed by spatial coordinates. Values are accessed via trilinear interpolation. 2. Spiking MLP (sMLP): Implicitly yields volumetric color \mathbf{c}. Structure: Standard MLP layers replaced with spiking neuron models. Input shape: [\text{batch}, \text{time}, c], where time corresponds to the sampled point index along the ray. 3. Masked Point Set (A): A subset of sampled points retained for rendering based on thresholds. Parameters: \lambda1: Predefined threshold for point weight wi. \lambda2: Predefined threshold for point opacity \alphai. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling and Masking: For each ray \mathbf{r}, sample K points \mathbf{p}i along the ray. Calculate intermediate weight wi and opacity \alphai using standard volume rendering equations (derived from density \sigma). Define the active set A for each ray: A \triangleq \{i: wi > \lambda1, \alphai > \lambda2\} Points not in A are masked out to reduce computation. 2. Hybrid Feature Query: For each point \mathbf{p}i \in A: Query voxel grids to obtain density \sigmai and embedded feature \mathbf{e}i: \sigmai = \text{act}(\text{interp}(\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{V}\sigma)) \mathbf{e}i = \text{interp}(\mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{V}f) Here, \text{interp} denotes trilinear interpolation and \text{act} is an activation function (e.g., ReLU or shifted softplus). 3. Time-Ray Alignment (TRA): Pack the embedded features \mathbf{e}i for all active points in a batch. Original shape: [\text{ray}, \text{pts}, c], where ray is the ray index and pts is the index of the sampled point along that ray. Reshape to match SNN temporal input: [\text{batch}, \text{time}, c]. The mapping aligns the geometric consecutiveness of the ray with the temporal continuity of the SNN: \text{Input}{MLP}:= [\text{batch}, c] \Rightarrow [\text{ray}, \text{pts}, c] \Rightarrow [\text{batch}, \text{time}, c]:= \text{Input}{s{MLP}} Each sampled point \mathbf{p}i is matched to a specific time step t in the sMLP input. 4. Temporal Condensing-and-Padding (TCP): Due to masking, the number of active points varies per ray, creating irregular tensor lengths. Temporal Padding (TP): Pad shorter ray sequences with zeros to ensure regular tensor shapes for GPU parallel training. Temporal Condensing: Condense the data distribution to form a denser structure, optimizing for hardware-friendly computation on neuromorphic accelerators and GPUs. 5. Spiking Inference: Pass the aligned input \text{Input}{s{MLP}} through the sMLP. The sMLP processes the spike trains addition-only (multiplication-free) to output the color \mathbf{c}i for each time step. 6. Volume Rendering Integration: Compute the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the accumulated contributions from the active set A: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) \approx \sum{i \in A} wi \alphai \mathbf{c}i where wi and \alphai are the pre-computed weights and opacities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spikingnerfrender(ray, voxelgridsigma, voxelgridfeat, smlp, lambda1, lambda2): """ Renders a single ray using SpikingNeRF. Args: ray: Ray origin and direction. voxelgridsigma: 3D voxel grid for density. voxelgridfeat: 3D voxel grid for features. smlp: Spiking MLP model. lambda1: Weight threshold. lambda2: Opacity threshold. Returns: color: Rendered RGB color. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray # Assume K samples are generated at positions p0,..., p{K-1} # and depths t0,..., t{K-1} positions = samplepointsalongray(ray, numsamples=K) # 2. Query Voxel Grids for Density and Features # Interpolate from voxel grids densities = interpolatevoxel(positions, voxelgridsigma) features = interpolatevoxel(positions, voxelgridfeat) # Apply activation to density densities = activation(densities) # e.g., softplus # 3. Compute Opacity and Weight for Masking # Standard volume rendering accumulation to get alpha and weight # This part typically requires forward accumulation alphas = computeopacity(densities) weights = computeweights(alphas) # 4. Masking # Identify active points based on thresholds activeindices = [] for i in range(K): if weights[i] > lambda1 and alphas[i] > lambda2: activeindices.append(i) if not activeindices: return 0.0 # Or background color # 5. Extract Active Features activefeatures = features[activeindices] # 6. Time-Ray Alignment (TRA) # Reshape features to [1, len(activeindices), featuredim] # This aligns the spatial sequence to the temporal dimension of SNN smlpinput = activefeatures.reshape(1, len(activeindices), -1) # 7. Spiking MLP Inference # The sMLP processes the input spike train over time steps # Output is color for each active point colors = smlp(smlpinput) # Shape: [1, len(activeindices), 3] colors = colors.squeeze(0) # Shape: [len(activeindices), 3] # 8. Volume Rendering Integration # Retrieve active weights and alphas activeweights = weights[activeindices] activealphas = alphas[activeindices] # Accumulate color color = sum(activeweights[i] activealphas[i] colors[i] for i in range(len(activeindices))) return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Irregular Tensor Lengths: Masking causes different rays to have different numbers of active points. This breaks standard GPU batch processing. TCP (Temporal Condensing-and-Padding) is required to handle this. Precision: SNNs operate on spike trains. The transition from real-valued inputs to spikes requires careful encoding (TRA) to preserve geometric information without duplication. A method to accommodate SNNs to NeRF rendering by retaining real-valued input data (like direct-encoding) but matching each sample along a ray to a corresponding time step without duplication-based filling. It packs volumetric parameters (e.g., e, v) as input data with shape [\text{ray}, \text{pts}, c], where ray is the ray index, pts is the sampled point index, and c is the channel index. The input is reshaped to [\text{batch}, \text{time}, c] for the sMLP. TRA does not require input data pre-processing such as duplication (used in prior arts like Zhou et al. 2022) or Poisson generation (used in Garg et al. 2021). Energy Efficiency: SpikingNeRF reduces energy consumption by an average of 70.79% compared to ANN baselines. Performance: SpikingNeRF-D achieves 72.95% energy reduction with a 0.33 PSNR drop on the Tanks&Temples dataset. Hardware: Designed for neuromorphic hardware accelerators, benefiting from addition-only, spike-driven computation. Complexity: The hybrid representation (voxel grids + sMLP) reduces the querying burden on the MLP compared to pure NeRF. Limitations: Requires handling irregular tensor lengths due to masking, necessitating TCP. SpikingNeRF was proposed by researchers from the Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. It is the first work to accommodate SNNs to reconstruct 3D scenes (real RGB world) using neural radiance fields, making high-quality 3D rendering accessible to neuromorphic hardware. It builds on the concept of hybrid volumetric representations (voxel grids for density/features, MLP for color) and the temporal accumulation process of SNNs inspired by primate fovea imaging. SpikingNeRF: Making Bio-inspired Neural Networks See through the Real World, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2309.10987, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: MVS Network Query
body: MVS Network Query prepares inputs for a neural network by embedding points and view directions, then applies the network in batches. It differs from standard NeRF network queries by explicitly handling multi-view geometric consistency through the generation of angle and point features derived from camera poses and depth candidates. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings and relates to HybridNeRF Model Architecture, Simple-ZipNeRF, VoxNeRF, Deformation Field Integration for Telepresence, and Multi-resolution Hash Encoding. The method consists of two main phases: input preparation for the neural network and the MVS rendering pipeline that utilizes these outputs. Inputs: Points: 3D spatial coordinates. View directions: Unit vectors (dx, dy, dz). Optional embedding functions: embedfn for points, embeddirsfn for view directions. Optional alpha features: alphafeat concatenated with points. Reference pose: poseref for angle feature generation. Depth candidates: Discrete depth values for sampling. Input features: inputfeat for channel concatenation. Outputs: Raw network outputs: Tensors containing color, density, and auxiliary features. Final rendered images: Computed via warping and aggregation of features from multiple views. Points: Array of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of sample points. View Directions: Array of shape (N, 3), normalized. Angle Features: Array of shape (N, Fa), derived from the cosine of the angle between ray directions and reference camera axes. Point Features: Array of shape (N, Fp), derived from depth candidates and geometric constraints. Network Input: Concatenated tensor of shape (N, 3 + Fa + Fp + \dots). Network Output: Flat tensor of shape (N, C), where C is the number of output channels (typically \ge 4 for RGB + alpha, plus auxiliary features). 1. Process View Directions: Expand dimensions of viewdirs if necessary to match batch dimensions. If embeddirsfn is provided, apply it to viewdirs. 4. Determine Output Requirements: Check if only alpha (density) is needed based on the presence of viewdirs. If viewdirs is absent, the network may output only density. 6. Choose this variant when multi-view consistency is critical for accurate reconstruction, such as in structured scenes with known camera poses. head: SqueezeNeRF (1K cache)
body: SqueezeNeRF is a memory-efficient neural rendering method that further factorizes the position-dependent Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) of FastNeRF into three separate 2D networks operating on coordinate pairs (x,y), (y,z), and (z,x) to reduce cache size complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2). It builds on FastNeRF by replacing the dense 3D position cache with a set of 2D position caches and a 2D direction cache, enabling real-time inference with significantly lower memory overhead than FastNeRF or NeRF-SH while maintaining high rendering speeds. Inputs: Camera viewing direction (\theta, \phi). 3D spatial coordinates (x, y, z) of sample points along a ray. Pre-trained cache files containing outputs of the position-conditioned and view-conditioned networks. Outputs: Volume density \sigma. Radiance map components (u, v, w). Final pixel color (r, g, b) via volume rendering. The method relies on dense caches for the outputs of the neural networks. The cache layout differs between the default architecture and the alternate architecture. Default Architecture Cache: Position Caches: Three caches corresponding to networks F{pos}^{xy}, F{pos}^{yz}, and F{pos}^{zx}. Each cache stores outputs for np^2 coordinate pairs. For each pair, the network outputs a scalar \sigma0^j and three D-dimensional vectors (u0^j, v0^j, w0^j), along with scaling weights W\sigma^j (scalar) and Wk^j (D-dimensional vectors for k \in \{u,v,w\}). Storage: \sigma0^j is stored as a 32-bit float. u0^j, v0^j, w0^j and weights are stored as 16-bit floats. Total storage per 3D point combination (conceptually np^3) is 3np^2(3D + 1) values. Direction Cache: One cache for F{dir} storing \beta for nd^2 direction pairs (\theta, \phi). Storage: \beta is stored as 16-bit floats. Total storage is nd^2(D) values. Alternate Architecture Cache (SqueezeNeRF alt): Position Caches: Same structure as default, but outputs are vectors. F{pos}^j outputs \sigma^j \in \mathbb{R}^{D\sigma} and k^j \in \mathbb{R}^{Dk} for k \in \{u,v,w\}. Storage: All values stored as 16-bit floats. Total storage per 3D point combination is 3np^2(3D + D\sigma) values. Direction Cache: Same as default. Parameters: np: Number of bins per position dimension. Typical values: 512 ('512 cache') or 1024 ('1K cache'). nd: Number of bins per direction dimension. Typical values: 64 (synthetic 360° scenes) or 32 (LLFF dataset). D: Dimensionality of radiance map vectors. Typical value: 8. D\sigma, Dk: Dimensionality of outputs in alternate architecture. Typical values: D\sigma=12, Dk=8. MLP Hidden Dimensions: Position MLPs have 6 layers with 256 hidden units. View MLP has 4 layers with 128 hidden units. 1. Network Factorization: Split the position-dependent network F{pos} from FastNeRF into three separate MLPs: F{pos}^{xy}, F{pos}^{yz}, and F{pos}^{zx}. 2. Network Definition: For the default configuration, each F{pos}^j (where j \in \{(x,y), (y,z), (z,x)\}) maps 2D coordinates to: F{pos}^j: j \rightarrow \{(\sigma0^j, W\sigma^j), (wj^u, u0^j, wj^v, v0^j, wj^w, w0^j)\} where \sigma0^j is a scalar and u0^j, v0^j, w0^j are D-dimensional vectors. For the alternate configuration, F{pos}^j maps to \{\sigma^j, u^j, v^j, w^j\} where \sigma^j \in \mathbb{R}^{D\sigma} and k^j \in \mathbb{R}^{Dk}. The view-dependent network F{dir} remains unchanged from FastNeRF, mapping (\theta, \phi) \rightarrow \beta \in \mathbb{R}^D. 3. Cache Generation (Training Phase): Train the networks using standard NeRF training procedures, including hierarchical sampling and positional encoding. Discretize the input space into a grid of np \times np for each position pair and nd \times nd for directions. Compute the network outputs for all grid points and store them in the cache files using the precision specified (32-bit for \sigma0, 16-bit for others). 4. Inference Query (Ray Marching): Sample N=256 points along the ray. For each sample point with coordinates (x,y,z) and direction (\theta, \phi): a. Fetch Position Outputs: Retrieve \sigma0^j, u0^j, v0^j, w0^j (or \sigma^j, k^j for alt) from the three position caches using nearest neighbor interpolation. b. Fetch Direction Output: Retrieve \beta from the direction cache using bilinear interpolation. c. Compute Intermediate Density and Radiance (Default): \sigma^j = \sigma0^j \cdot W\sigma^j k^j = Wk^j \cdot k0^j \quad \forall k \in \{u, v, w\} where \cdot denotes pointwise multiplication. d. Combine Outputs (Default): \sigma = \prod{j \in \{xy, yz, zx\}} \sigma^j k = \sum{j \in \{xy, yz, zx\}} k^j \quad \forall k \in \{u, v, w\} Thus, u = \sum u^j, v = \sum v^j, w = \sum w^j. e. Combine Outputs (Alternate): \sigma = W\sigma [\text{concat}(\{\sigma^j\})] + b\sigma k = Wk [\text{concat}(\{k^j\})] + bk \quad \forall k \in \{u, v, w\} where W\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 3D\sigma}, b\sigma \in \mathbb{R}, Wk \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times 3Dk}, bk \in \mathbb{R}^D are learnable parameters stored in the cache. f. Compute Color: c = (r, g, b) = \sum{i=1}^D \betai (ui, vi, wi) = \beta^T \cdot (u, v, w). g. Volume Rendering: Compute final pixel color using standard volume rendering integration based on \sigma and c. Unverified code. Returns dicts for position (xy, yz, zx) and direction. File I/O is standard. """ # Returns structure matching Data Structures section pass def nearestneighborinterpolate(cachegrid, coord): """ Nearest neighbor interpolation on a 2D cache grid. coord: (u, v) float coordinates in [0, 1]. """ idxu = int(coord[0] (cachegrid.shape[0] - 1)) idxv = int(coord[1] (cachegrid.shape[1] - 1)) idxu = np.clip(idxu, 0, cachegrid.shape[0] - 1) idxv = np.clip(idxv, 0, cachegrid.shape[1] - 1) return cachegrid[idxu, idxv] def bilinearinterpolate(cachegrid, coord): """ Bilinear interpolation on a 2D cache grid. coord: (u, v) float coordinates in [0, 1]. """ u, v = coord u0, v0 = int(u (cachegrid.shape[0] - 1)), int(v (cachegrid.shape[1] - 1)) u1, v1 = np.clip(u0 + 1, 0, cachegrid.shape[0] - 1), np.clip(v0 + 1, 0, cachegrid.shape[1] - 1) du, dv = u (cachegrid.shape[0] - 1) - u0, v (cachegrid.shape[1] - 1) - v0 top = cachegrid[u0, v0] (1 - du) + cachegrid[u0, v1] du bot = cachegrid[u1, v0] (1 - du) + cachegrid[u1, v1] du return top (1 - dv) + bot dv def volumerender(tvals, sigma, color): """ Standard volume rendering integration. tvals: (N,) distances along ray. sigma: (N,) volume density. color: (N, 3) color at samples. """ dt = np.diff(tvals, prepend=0.0) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma dt) T = np.exp(-np.cumsum(sigma dt)) weights = alpha T return np.sum(weights[:, None] color, axis=0) def squeezenerfinferdefault(rayorigins, raydirections, nsamples=256, poscaches=None, dircache=None, D=8): """ Default SqueezeNeRF inference. """ tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nsamples) points = rayorigins[:, None,:] + raydirections[:, None,:] tvals[None,:, None] numrays = points.shape[0] sigmatotal = np.ones(numrays) utotal = np.zeros((numrays, D)) vtotal = np.zeros((numrays, D)) wtotal = np.zeros((numrays, D)) for i in range(nsamples): p = points[:, i,:] theta = np.arccos(np.clip(p[:, 2] / (np.linalg.norm(p, axis=1) + 1e-8), -1.0, 1.0)) phi = np.arctan2(p[:, 1], p[:, 0]) thetanorm = (theta / np.pi) 0.5 phinorm = (phi / (2 np.pi)) + 0.5 sigmaxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['sigma0'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) uxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['u0'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) vxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['v0'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) wxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['w0'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) wsigmaxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['wsigma'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) wuxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['wu'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) wvxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['wv'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) wwxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['ww'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) sigmayz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['sigma0'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) uyz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['u0'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) vyz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['v0'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) wyz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['w0'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) wsigmayz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['wsigma'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) wuyz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['wu'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) wvyz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['wv'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) wwyz = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['yz']['ww'], (p[:, 1], p[:, 2])) sigmazx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['sigma0'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) uzx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['u0'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) vzx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['v0'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) wzx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['w0'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) wsigmazx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['wsigma'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) wuzx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['wu'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) wvzx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['wv'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) wwzx = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['zx']['ww'], (p[:, 2], p[:, 0])) sigmaxy = sigmaxy wsigmaxy uxy = uxy wuxy vxy = vxy wvxy wxy = wxy wwxy sigmayz = sigmayz wsigmayz uyz = uyz wuyz vyz = vyz wvyz wzx beta = bilinearinterpolate(dircache['beta'], (thetanorm, phinorm)) color = beta np.stack([utotal, vtotal, wtotal], axis=-1) color = np.sum(color, axis=-1) return volumerender(tvals, sigmatotal, color) def squeezenerfinferalt(rayorigins, raydirections, nsamples=256, poscaches=None, dircache=None, D=8, Dsigma=12, Dk=8): """ Alternate SqueezeNeRF inference. """ tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, nsamples) points = rayorigins[:, None,:] + raydirections[:, None,:] tvals[None,:, None] numrays = points.shape[0] sigmatotal = np.ones(numrays) utotal = np.zeros((numrays, Dk)) vtotal = np.zeros((numrays, Dk)) wtotal = np.zeros((numrays, Dk)) for i in range(nsamples): p = points[:, i,:] theta = np.arccos(np.clip(p[:, 2] / (np.linalg.norm(p, axis=1) + 1e-8), -1.0, 1.0)) phi = np.arctan2(p[:, 1], p[:, 0]) thetanorm = (theta / np.pi) 0.5 phinorm = (phi / (2 np.pi)) + 0.5 sigmaxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['sigma'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) uxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['u'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) vxy = nearestneighborinterpolate(poscaches['xy']['v'], (p[:, 0], p[:, 1])) wxy = leads to considerably inferior results. Precision: Using 16-bit floats for radiance components and 32-bit for density scalars is critical for memory efficiency but may affect precision in extreme cases. Cache Size vs Quality: Smaller caches (512 vs 1K) reduce memory but may degrade image quality (PSNR/SSIM). Memory Complexity: O(np^2) for position caches and O(nd^2) for direction cache, compared to O(n^3) for FastNeRF. Memory Usage: SqueezeNeRF (1K cache, np=1024): ~155 MB. SqueezeNeRF addresses the substantial memory overhead of FastNeRF by reducing cache size complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2). It is designed for deployment on embedded systems and real-time applications where memory is constrained. name: VoxNeRF
body: VoxNeRF is a neural rendering method that integrates explicit scene geometry priors (mesh, point cloud, or depth map) with implicit radiance field representation to improve sampling efficiency and reconstruction accuracy. It addresses the ill-posed nature of recovering 3D geometry from 2D images by using a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to model geometric uncertainty, which guides a hybrid sampling strategy. Unlike standard NeRF methods that sample uniformly or via stratified noise, VoxNeRF concentrates samples near the estimated surface while maintaining coverage of free space, reducing computational waste in empty regions. Inputs: Input images with known camera poses. A scene geometry prior, which can be a mesh, point cloud, or depth map. Pseudo-depth labels D derived from the geometry prior for regularization. Outputs: Rendered RGB images for novel viewpoints. Volume accumulated depth \hat{D}. Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Represents the scene geometry prior. Each voxel is an axis-aligned bounding box with side length v. Voxel vertex coordinates are encoded using 8-bit Morton codes to map 3D coordinates to 1D representations, preserving spatial locality and reducing memory consumption. Used to determine ray-surface intersections. Multi-resolution Hash Grids (MHG) Represents the radiance field. Consists of several compact spatial hash tables indexed at different resolutions. Stores trainable feature vectors. Used to encode spatial features for the neural network. Neural Network Feature MLP: Takes concatenated tri-linear interpolated outputs from MHG tables and view direction encoding di as input, outputting density \sigmai and a hidden code. Color MLP: A 3-layer MLP that takes the hidden code concatenated with view direction encoding di as input, outputting radiance ci. The sampling strategy divides points into an "important region" near the surface and a "remaining region" for the rest of the ray. 1. Ray-Surface Intersection: Find the first non-empty leaf voxel hit by the ray in the SVO. Let z(pi) be the hitting point distance of the ray and the voxel. 2. Important Region: Model the sampling region as a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(z(pi), (\sqrt{3}vi)^2), where vi is the voxel size. The region length is 6\sqrt{3}vi, centered at z(pi). This captures 99.7% of the distribution, assuming the true surface lies within the cube defined by the voxel uncertainty. Sample points uniformly within this region. 3. Remaining Region: Generate additional sampling points using uniform distributions for the rest of the ray: U(0, z(pi) - 3\sqrt{3}vi) U(z(pi) + 3\sqrt{3}vi, \infty). Volume Rendering For each sample point i with density \sigmai, emitted radiance ci, and distance to the next adjacent sample \deltai: Termination probability \alphai and accumulated transmittance Ti are computed as: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\deltai \sigmai) Ti = \prod{j<i} (1 - \alphaj) (Note: Source Eq. 2 contains a typo 1 - exp(1 - δi σi); standard volume rendering uses the negative exponent). Rendered color C and accumulated depth \hat{D} are: C = \sumi \alphai Ti ci, \quad \hat{D} = \sumi \alphai Ti zi Loss Function The total loss L is defined as: L = Lc + \lambdad (Ld + L{reg}) where Lc is the color reconstruction loss. Robust Depth Loss (Ld) Let \hat{D} be the volume accumulated depth and D be the pseudo depth. Let \beta = 0.1. Ld = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} |\hat{D} - D|^2 & \text{if } |\hat{D} - D| < \beta \\ \frac{1}{2} |\hat{D} - D| + \ln\left(\frac{|\hat{D} - D|}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } |\hat{D} - D| \ge \beta \end{cases} This loss uses a squared error for small differences and a logarithmic function for large differences to reduce sensitivity to outliers. Regularization Loss (L{reg}) Penalizes gradients across different scales to enforce smoothness: L{reg} = \sum{s=1}^{S} \sum{i,j} M{i,j} (|Gx^{(s)}| + |Gy^{(s)}|) where Gx^{(s)} and Gy^{(s)} are gradient components at scale s, and M{i,j} is a mask. Voxel Size (v): Set to the maximal standard deviation \sigma across all scene points in the geometry prior: v = \max(\sigma1, \sigma2, \dots, \sigman). Batch Size: 4,096 rays per batch. Points per Ray: 128 points in the important sampling region and 128 points in the remaining region. Optimizer: ADAM with learning rate 0.01 and exponential schedule. Beta (\beta): 0.1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voxnerfrender(rayorigins, raydirections, svos, mhgs, featuremlp, colormlp, params): """ Renders a batch of rays using VoxNeRF sampling and volume integration. Args: rayorigins: (B, 3) Array of ray origins. raydirections: (B, 3) Array of ray directions. svos: Sparse Voxel Octree structures. mhgs: Multi-resolution Hash Grids structure. featuremlp: Function returning (hiddencodes, sigmas) from MHG features and view dirs. colormlp: Function returning radiance from hidden codes and view dirs. params: Dictionary containing hyperparameters. Returns: colors: (B, 3) Rendered colors. depths: (B,) Accumulated depths. """ B = rayorigins.shape[0] colors = np.zeros((B, 3)) depths = np.zeros(B) maxdist = params.get('maxdist', 100.0) Nimp = 128 Nrem = 128 for i in range(B): # 1. Ray-Surface Intersection # Traverses SVO to find first non-empty leaf voxel intersection # Returns distance to intersection and voxel side length zpi, vi = querysvo(rayorigins[i], raydirections[i], svos) # 2. Sampling halfwidth = 3.0 np.sqrt(3.0) vi impmin = zpi - halfwidth impmax = zpi + halfwidth ptsimp = np.linspace(impmin, impmax, Nimp) remmin = 0.0 remmax = maxdist # Split remaining points evenly between near and far intervals ptsnear = np.linspace(remmin, impmin, Nrem // 2) if impmin > remmin else np.array([]) ptsfar = np.linspace(impmax, remmax, Nrem // 2) if remmax > impmax else np.array([]) ptsrem = np.concatenate([ptsnear, ptsfar]) allpts = np.concatenate([ptsimp, ptsrem]) pts3d = rayorigins[i] + allpts[:, None] raydirections[i] # 3. Network Query # Tri-linear interpolation across multi-resolution hash tables mhgfeats = querymhgs(mhgs, pts3d) viewdirs = raydirections[i][None,:] hiddencodes, sigmas = featuremlp(mhgfeats, viewdirs) radiance = colormlp(hiddencodes, viewdirs) # 4. Volume Rendering deltas = np.diff(allpts, append=allpts[-1] + 1e-6) alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmas deltas) transmittances = np.cumprod(1.0 - alphas) transmittances = np.concatenate([[1.0], transmittances[:-1]]) weights = alphas transmittances colors[i] = np.sum(weights[:, None] radiance, axis=0) depths[i] = np.sum(weights allpts) return colors, depths def querysvo(origin, direction, svos): # SVO traversal implementation depends on specific octree layout raise NotImplementedError("SVO traversal not specified in sources") def querymhgs(mhgs, points3d): # MHG query implementation depends on hash table layout raise NotImplementedError("MHG query not specified in sources") Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sampling points (256 per ray in the reported setup) and the cost of querying the Multi-resolution Hash Grids and MLPs. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the MHG tables and the SVO structure. Performance: Evaluated on ScanNet and ScanNet++ datasets. Trained for 30,000 iterations on a single 24GB NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Strengths: Reduces unnecessary sampling in free space by focusing on the geometry prior. Handles noise in geometry priors via the Gaussian sampling model. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the geometry prior. If the prior is inaccurate, the sampling region may miss the true surface or include too much empty space. When to use: When a coarse geometry prior (point cloud, depth map) is available and efficient rendering is desired. Particularly useful in sparse-view settings. VoxNeRF was introduced to bridge the gap between voxel-based representations and neural radiance fields. It addresses the limitations of standard NeRF methods which often suffer from slow convergence and poor performance in textureless or ambiguous regions. By incorporating explicit geometry priors, it aims to provide a more robust and efficient rendering pipeline. The method was evaluated on real-world indoor datasets like ScanNet and ScanNet++. name: Deformation Field Integration for Telepresence
head: Dynamic Human Volume Rendering
body: This method extends the FastNeRF architecture to support dynamic, expression-driven head avatars for telepresence by integrating a learnable deformation field network (F{deform}) and a non-trainable skeletal deformation field (F{bone}) into the ray marching process. It solves the problem of rendering animatable 3D heads from static multi-view images by warping sample positions based on an expression vector before querying the radiance field. It is distinguished from static NeRF variants by its explicit handling of temporal expression parameters and from other dynamic NeRF methods by its specific integration with the FastNeRF caching infrastructure and grid-based pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D sample position \mathbf{p}, an expression vector \mathbf{e}, and a viewing direction (implicit in the view-dependent network). Outputs: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color coefficients (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}). Data Structures: 1. Deformation Network (F{deform}): A 6-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 64 units per layer. It takes the encoded position and expression vector as input and outputs a 3D offset vector. 2. Skeletal Deformation Field (F{bone}): A non-trainable function that maps \mathbf{p} and \mathbf{e} to a deformed position based on 3D model bones (shoulders and neck). 3. Position-Dependent Network (F{pos}): The FastNeRF position network. It takes the deformed position and outputs \sigma and (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}). It has 384 units per layer during training. 4. View-Dependent Network: A 2-layer MLP with 32 units per layer, used for view-dependent color. 5. Sparse Volume (Pruning Cache): A sparse 3D grid storing the minimum and maximum density values encountered for each grid cell around the face region. Numbered Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Encode the input sample position \mathbf{p} using the same positional encoding scheme as FastNeRF. 2. Skeletal Deformation: Compute the bone-deformed position \mathbf{p}{bone} = \mathcal{F}{bone}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{e}). This step accounts for large rigid movements of the head and shoulders. 3. Deformation Field Query: Compute the offset \mathbf{o} = \mathcal{F}{deform}(\mathbf{p}{bone}, \mathbf{e}). The network F{deform} is a 6-layer MLP with 64 units per layer. 4. Final Position: Compute the warped position \mathbf{p}{warped} = \mathbf{p}{bone} + \mathbf{o}. 5. Radiance Field Query: Query the position-dependent network to get density and color features: \{\sigma, (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})\} = \mathcal{F}{pos}(\mathbf{p}{warped}). 6. View-Dependent Color: Use (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}) and the viewing direction to compute the final RGB color. Formulas: The composition of deformation fields and the position network is defined as: \{\sigma, (\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})\} = \mathcal{F}{pos}(\mathcal{F}{deform}(\mathcal{F}{bone}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{e}), \mathbf{e})) where \mathbf{e} is the expression vector. The deformation network output is an offset applied to the position: \mathbf{p}{deform} = \mathcal{F}{deform}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{e}) Note: In the context of the full pipeline, this offset is added to the bone-deformed position. The synthesized pixel color C\mathbf{r} is computed by marching a ray and accumulating radiance at sampled points between near and far bounds: C\mathbf{r} = \sum{i=1}^{N} T(pi) \left[ (1 - e^{-\sigma{pi}\delta{pi}}) c{pi} \right] where T(pi) = e^{-\sum{k=1}^{i-1} \sigma{pk}\delta{pk}} is the transmittance, \delta(pi) = p{i+1} - pi is the distance between adjacent samples, c{pi} is the color at sample i, and N is the number of sampled points on the ray. Parameters: Training Samples: 64 samples in the coarse stage, 64 additional samples in the fine stage. Test Samples: 43 samples in the coarse stage. The fine stage is removed. Interpolation: Additional samples are added by linearly interpolating between samples generated by the deformation network. These interpolated samples are looked up in the FastNeRF cache. Pruning Samples: 50 randomly chosen samples of \mathbf{e} are used to populate the sparse volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def querydeformationfield(p, e, Fdeform, Fbone, Fpos): """Query radiance field with deformation for telepresence.""" pbone = Fbone(p, e) offset = Fdeform(pbone, e) pwarped = pbone + offset sigma, uvw = Fpos(pwarped) return sigma, uvw def computepruningvolume(gridpositions, Fdeform, Fpos, numesamples=50, edim=32): """Pre-compute min/max density for grid-based pruning at test time.""" sparsevolume = {} for idx, pgrid in enumerate(gridpositions): minsigma = float('inf') maxsigma = float('-inf') for in range(numesamples): erandom = np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, size=edim) # Pruning volume computation per evidence does not use Fbone offset = Fdeform(pgrid, erandom) pwarped = pgrid + offset sigma, = Fpos(pwarped) if sigma < minsigma: minsigma = sigma if sigma > maxsigma: maxsigma = sigma sparsevolume[idx] = (minsigma, maxsigma) return sparsevolume def pruneandquery(p, e, sparsevolume, Fdeform, Fbone, Fpos, cellsize=0.01, saturationthreshold=1e-3): """Query with pruning based on sparse volume.""" idx = tuple(np.floor(p / cellsize).astype(int)) if idx in sparsevolume: minsigma, maxsigma = sparsevolume[idx] if maxsigma == 0: return None if minsigma > saturationthreshold: return None pbone = Fbone(p, e) offset = Fdeform(pbone, e) pwarped = pbone + offset sigma, uvw = Fpos(pwarped) return sigma, uvw Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Linear Rays: The deformation network changes sample positions along rays, meaning rays are no longer straight. This prevents the use of hardware-accelerated ray tracing described in the main FastNeRF paper. Identity Constraint: Without an L2 regularizer constraining F{deform} to be an identity transform for a neutral expression, training is unstable. Performance Limit: The approach is limited to rendering 300x300 pixel images with a reduced sample count to maintain 30FPS. Test-Time Optimization: F{bone} is removed at test-time to improve performance, relying solely on F{deform} and caching for dynamic regions. Time Complexity: The primary bottleneck is the evaluation of F{deform} for all input samples. The grid-based pruning reduces the runtime of F{deform} by more than a factor of 2. Memory Complexity: Inherits the memory structure of FastNeRF, which is significantly more compact than standard NeRF due to the cache-based approach. Performance: Renders 300x300 pixel images at 30FPS with 43 coarse samples and no fine stage at test time. Strengths: Stabilizes training with L2 regularization; handles large movements via F{bone}; efficient test-time rendering via pruning and caching. Limitations: Cannot use hardware-accelerated ray tracing due to non-linear rays; limited resolution and frame rate compared to static NeRF; requires careful tuning of expression samples for pruning. When to Use: Telepresence applications requiring real-time, expression-driven head avatars from static multi-view data. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring hardware-accelerated ray tracing, as the deformation network bends rays and breaks straight-ray assumptions. Scenes with complex non-rigid deformations not captured by the expression vector. This method was introduced by Garbin et al. in the FastNeRF paper as a proof-of-concept for telepresence scenarios. It builds upon the FastNeRF architecture, which uses a cache-based approach to reduce memory usage. The deformation field approach allows for the animation of 3D heads from static images by learning a mapping from expression parameters to spatial deformations.
