name: UniSDF-based Latent NeRF
head: Latent NeRF Model with UniSDF
body:
UniSDF-based Latent NeRF is a geometry estimator and appearance model that utilizes UniSDF, a signed distance function (SDF) based volume rendering approach, to decouple geometry from appearance. It solves the problem of generating relightable 3D assets by extracting a mesh from the SDF for radiance cue computation via a standard rendering engine, while optimizing a latent NeRF for appearance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly leveraging SDF-based mesh extraction to compute physically-based shading normals and radiance cues, rather than relying solely on differentiable volume rendering for all geometric cues. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input images, camera poses, and a mask. Outputs: A mesh representing the geometry, a latent NeRF model for appearance, and radiance cues (shading normals, depth, etc.) rendered from the mesh. Data Structures: UniSDF Model: Parameterized similarly to the original UniSDF for the DTU dataset, with specific modifications to proposal sampling and encoding. Hash Grid Encoding: An additional hash grid encoding with 15 scales between a resolution of 32 and 4096, used exclusively for outputting predicted normals. GLO Embeddings: Applied via an MLP that predicts element-wise scale and shift values for the 'bottleneck' feature of UniSDF. Numbered Steps: 1. Geometry Estimation: Optimize the UniSDF model on the input images. The number of proposal sampling rounds is reduced from two to one, using 64 proposal samples. 2. Normal Prediction: Use the additional hash grid encoding (15 scales, resolution 32 to 4096) to output predicted normals. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the asymmetric predicted normal loss Lp and the smoothness loss Ls during optimization. 4. Mesh Extraction: Convert the optimized SDF representation to a mesh using marching cubes with a threshold set to zero. 5. Radiance Cue Rendering: Import the extracted mesh into a standard rendering engine (Blender Cycles) with predefined materials based on the GGX material model to render radiance cues. 6. Latent NeRF Optimization: Optimize the latent NeRF model. Incorporate GLO embeddings by using an MLP to predict element-wise scale and shift values applied to the UniSDF 'bottleneck' feature. Formulas: The asymmetric predicted normal loss Lp is defined as: Lp = \sumi \left( \lambda1 \omegai \|
abla ni - 
abla n'i \|2 + \lambda2 
abla \omegai \| ni - n'i \|2 + \lambda3 
abla \omegai \|
abla ni - n'i \|2 ight) where: \omegai is the volume rendering weight of the i-th sample. 
abla denotes the stop-gradient operator. ni is the i-th sample's density normal. n'i is the i-th sample's predicted normal. \lambda1 = 10^{-3}, \lambda2 = 10^{-3}, \lambda3 = 10^{-2}. The smoothness loss Ls is defined as: Ls = \lambda4 \sumi \omegai \| n'(xi + \epsilon) - n'(xi) \|2^2 where: xi is the 3D position of the i-th sample. \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) is an isotropic Gaussian random variable used to perturb the sample locations. \lambda4 = 0.1. \sigma = 0.01. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with  eta1 = 0.9,  eta2 = 0.99, and \epsilon = 1 	imes 10^{-15}. Learning Rate: Decayed logarithmically from 5 	imes 10^{-3} to 5 	imes 10^{-4} over 25k training iterations. Warmup: Cosine-scheduled warmup in the first 500 steps. Proposal Samples: 64 samples, with one round of proposal sampling. Hash Grid: 15 scales, resolution range 32 to 4096. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def samplerays(numproposalsamples, numrounds): positions = np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, (numproposalsamples, 3)) weights = np.ones(numproposalsamples) / numproposalsamples return positions, weights def computedensitynormals(densityfield): return np.zeroslike(densityfield) # Standard gradient computation of density field def computeasymmetricnormalloss(weights, densitynormals, predictednormals, lambda1, lambda2, lambda3): def stopgradient(x): return x term1 = lambda1 weights np.linalg.norm(stopgradient(densitynormals) - stopgradient(predictednormals), axis=1)2 term2 = lambda2 stopgradient(weights) np.linalg.norm(densitynormals - stopgradient(predictednormals), axis=1)2 term3 = lambda3 stopgradient(weights) np.linalg.norm(stopgradient(densitynormals) - predictednormals, axis=1)2 return np.sum(term1 + term2 + term3) def samplegaussiannoise(positions, sigma): return np.random.normal(0, sigma, positions.shape) def cosinewarmup(step, warmupsteps, initiallr, finallr): return initiallr + (finallr - initiallr) (1 + math.cos(math.pi step / warmupsteps)) / 2 def logarithmicdecay(step, totalsteps, startlr, endlr): return endlr + (startlr - endlr) (math.log(1 + step) / math.log(1 + totalsteps)) class Adam: def init(self, params, lr, beta1, beta2, eps): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.beta1 = beta1 self.beta2 = beta2 self.eps = eps self.m = {k: np.zeroslike(v) for k, v in params.items()} self.v = {k: np.zeroslike(v) for k, v in params.items()} self.t = 0 def step(self, grads): self.t += 1 for k in self.params: self.m[k] = self.beta1 self.m[k] + (1 - self.beta1) grads[k] self.v[k] = self.beta2 self.v[k] + (1 - self.beta2) grads[k]2 mhat = self.m[k] / (1 - self.beta1self.t) vhat = self.v[k] / (1 - self.beta2self.t) self.params[k] -= self.lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + self.eps) class UniSDFModel: def init(self): self.params = {'weights': np.random.randn(10)} def forward(self, positions): return np.zeroslike(positions), np.abs(np.sin(positions.sum(axis=1))) class HashGrid: def init(self, numlevels, resolutionmin, resolutionmax): pass def forward(self, positions): return np.random.randn(len(positions), 3) class GLOMLP: def init(self): pass def predict(self, feature): return {'scale': np.oneslike(feature), 'shift': np.zeroslike(feature)} class LatentNeRF: def optimize(self, cues, feature): pass def marchingcubes(sdffield, threshold): return "mesh" def renderwithblendercycles(mesh, materialmodel): return "radiancecues" model = UniSDFModel() hashgrid = HashGrid(numlevels=15, resolutionmin=32, resolutionmax=4096) optimizer = Adam(params=model.params, lr=5e-3, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.99, eps=1e-15) warmupsteps = 500 totalsteps = 25000 for step in range(totalsteps): lr = cosinewarmup(step, warmupsteps, 5e-3, 5e-4) if step < warmupsteps else logarithmicdecay(step - warmupsteps, totalsteps - warmupsteps, 5e-3, 5e-4) optimizer.lr = lr positions, weights = samplerays(64, 1) sdfvalues, densities = model.forward(positions) predictednormals = hashgrid.forward(positions) densitynormals = computedensitynormals(densities) lossp = computeasymmetricnormalloss(weights, densitynormals, predictednormals, 1e-3, 1e-3, 1e-2) epsilon = samplegaussiannoise(positions, 0.01) perturbednormals = hashgrid.forward(positions + epsilon) losss = 0.1 np.mean(weights np.linalg.norm(perturbednormals - predictednormals, axis=1)2) totalloss = lossp + losss grads = {k: np.oneslike(v) for k, v in model.params.items()} optimizer.step(grads) mesh = marchingcubes(sdffield=sdfvalues, threshold=0.0) radiancecues = renderwithblendercycles(mesh, 'GGX') bottleneckfeature = np.random.randn(10) scaleshift = GLOMLP().predict(bottleneckfeature) bottleneckfeature = bottleneckfeature scaleshift['scale'] + scaleshift['shift'] LatentNeRF().optimize(radiancecues, bottleneckfeature) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Decouples geometry from appearance, allowing fixed geometry weights and optimized appearance weights. Enables mesh extraction for radiance cue computation. Modifications result in better and smoother geometry necessary for relighting objects with specular highlights. Limitations: Relies on external rendering engine (Blender Cycles) for radiance cues. When to use: When relightable 3D assets with specular highlights are required. When not to use: When end-to-end differentiable volume rendering without external tools is required. UniSDF-based Latent NeRF is based on the IllumiNeRF paper. It uses UniSDF as the geometry estimator and Latent NeRF model. The method was implemented using JAX. IllumiNeRF: 3D Relighting without Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2406.06527, fetched 2026-10-29

name: RawNeRF
head: NeRF in the Dark
body: RawNeRF is a method for High Dynamic Range (HDR) view synthesis and denoising that adapts Mip-NeRF to train directly on raw linear images, preserving the scene's full dynamic range and enabling post-processing tasks like exposure adjustment and tonemapping after rendering. Unlike standard NeRF variants that use tonemapped low dynamic range (LDR) images, RawNeRF optimizes the neural radiance field in the linear raw domain, allowing it to recover correct colors in dark regions and unclipped highlights that are lost in standard camera pipelines. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A collection of N posed input raw images (typically 25–200 per scene), where N is the number of training images. Each image Ii has an associated shutter speed ti and camera pose. The raw images are 12-bit DNG files, converted to floating point by normalizing with white and black levels. Outputs: A trained NeRF model representing the scene in linear HDR color space. Novel views are rendered as raw linear HDR images, which can subsequently be tonemapped, exposed, or defocused. Data Structures NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that takes a 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input and outputs volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Exposure Parameters: For each unique shutter speed t present in the training set, a learned per-color-channel scaling factor \alpha{tc} is maintained, where c indexes the color channels (R, G, B). Numbered Steps 1. Preprocessing: Camera poses are calculated using full-resolution postprocessed JPEG images via COLMAP, as COLMAP does not support raw images directly. Inputs are not undistorted or downsampled to avoid affecting the raw noise distribution. Camera intrinsics are used to account for radial distortion when generating rays. Raw images are mosaicked (one color value per pixel). The loss is applied only to the active color channel for each pixel, effectively demosaicing the input during optimization. 2. Ray Marching and Integration: For each training image, rays are generated through the camera center. The NeRF is queried along the ray to sample points. Volume rendering is performed to accumulate color and opacity along the ray, producing a raw linear output color \hat{y}i for the pixel. 3. Exposure Scaling: To match the brightness of the input image Ii with shutter speed ti, the network's linear output \hat{y}i is scaled by ti and a learned per-channel scaling factor \alpha{ti c}. The final scaled value is clipped at 1 to account for pixel saturation in overexposed regions: \tilde{y}{ic} = \min(\hat{y}{ic} \cdot ti \cdot \alpha{ti c}, 1) The scaling factor for the longest exposure shutter speed t{max} is constrained to 1 (\alpha{t{max} c} = 1). 4. Loss Computation: A gradient supervision loss is applied using a linearization of the tone curve \psi(z) = \log(z + \epsilon) with \epsilon = 10^{-3}. The loss for a pixel i is: Li = \left( \frac{\tilde{y}i - yi}{\text{sg}(\tilde{y}i) + \epsilon} \right)^2 where yi is the target raw pixel value, \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator, and the denominator stabilizes training. Regularization: A regularization loss is applied to the variance of the weight distribution used to accumulate color values along the ray. This prevents partially transparent "floater" artifacts in extremely noisy scenes. 5. Optimization: The NeRF parameters and exposure scaling factors \alpha{tc} are jointly optimized using gradient descent. The Adam optimizer is used with a learning rate decaying from 10^{-3} to 10^{-5} over 500k steps. Batches consist of 16k random rays sampled across all training images. 6. Post-Processing (Inference): Rendered raw outputs are processed after training. This includes tonemapping, exposure adjustment, or synthetic defocusing. Synthetic Defocus: RGBA depth layers are precomputed from the trained model. A varying blur kernel is applied to different depth layers and composited together. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class RawNeRF: def init(self, numshutterspeeds, channels=3): self.neuralfield = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 4)) self.alpha = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(numshutterspeeds, channels)) self.alpha.data[0] = 1.0 self.epsilon = 1e-3 self.optimizer = optim.Adam(list(self.neuralfield.parameters()) + [self.alpha], lr=1e-3) self.scheduler = optim.lrscheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(self.optimizer, Tmax=500000, etamin=1e-5) def forward(self, rays): # rays: [numrays, 6] (xyz, xyz) # Returns raw accumulated color [numrays, 3] and rendering weights [numrays, numsamples] # Note: Volume rendering integration is handled by the parent NeRF article. rawcolor = self.neuralfield(rays)[:, 1:] return rawcolor def applyexposure(self, rawcolor, shutterspeed, shutterspeedidx): alphafactors = self.alpha[shutterspeedidx] scaled = rawcolor shutterspeed alphafactors return torch.clamp(scaled, max=1.0) def computeloss(self, scaledcolor, targetcolor, activechannelmask, weights): denominator = scaledcolor.detach() + self.epsilon lossperpixel = ((scaledcolor - targetcolor) / denominator) 2 maskedloss = lossperpixel activechannelmask pixelloss = torch.sum(maskedloss, dim=-1) meanloss = torch.mean(pixelloss) regloss = torch.var(weights, dim=1).mean() return meanloss + 0.1 regloss def trainstep(self, batch): self.optimizer.zerograd() rays = batch['rays'] shutterspeeds = batch['shutterspeeds'] shutterspeedindices = batch['shutterspeedindices'] targets = batch['targets'] masks = batch['activechannelmasks'] weights = batch['renderingweights'] rawcolors = self.forward(rays) scaledcolors = [] for i in range(len(rays)): scaledcolors.append(self.applyexposure(rawcolors[i:i+1], shutterspeeds[i], shutterspeedindices[i])) scaledcolors = torch.cat(scaledcolors, dim=0) loss = self.computeloss(scaledcolors, targets, masks, weights) loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.scheduler.step() Parameters Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Decays from 10^{-3} to 10^{-5} over 500k steps. Batch Size: 16k random rays sampled across all training images. Log Tonemap Epsilon: \epsilon = 10^{-3}. Exposure Constraint: \alpha{t{max}} = 1. Input Count: 25–200 images per scene. Shutter Speeds: Simulated speeds include 1/7, 1/15, 1/30, 1/60, 1/120, 1/240 seconds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sensor Miscalibration: Varying exposures cannot be precisely aligned using shutter speed alone due to sensor miscalibration. This is corrected by the learned per-color-channel scaling factor \alpha{tc}. LDR Bias: Training on LDR images corrupts the noise distribution, causing NeRF to recover incorrect colors in dark regions and clip highlights. RawNeRF avoids this by training on raw data. Preprocessing: Applying single-image denoisers to inputs before training RawNeRF results in oversmoothed renderings. Wide Baseline: RawNeRF handles wide-baseline captures where camera movement is larger than in typical burst video, unlike multi-image denoisers that assume small motion. Time Complexity: Optimization requires 500k steps of gradient descent on batches of 16k random rays sampled across all training images. Memory Complexity: Depends on the NeRF architecture and the number of training images stored for pose calculation. Raw images are large (12MP), requiring significant storage. Measured Performance: On a real dataset with 101 noisy images, RawNeRF achieved a PSNR of 28.76 at 1/240s simulated shutter speed, compared to LDR NeRF's 14.51. In synthetic ablation on the Lego scene with 120 training images, RawNeRF achieved 32.11 PSNR at 1/240s shutter speed, while LDR NeRF achieved 18.27. On affine-aligned sRGB, RawNeRF achieved PSNR 23.53, SSIM 0.536, and LPIPS 0.501, outperforming LDR NeRF (PSNR 19.43) and Un+RawNeRF (PSNR 23.35). Strengths: Robust to noise; recovers HDR information; enables post-processing (exposure, focus, tonemapping); handles wide-baseline captures. Limitations: Requires raw images (large storage); dependent on COLMAP for pose estimation (fails in very low light); cannot handle dynamic scenes. When to Use: High dynamic range view synthesis, denoising scenes captured in near-darkness, HDR view synthesis tasks like changing focus and exposure. When Not to Use: When storage is limited; when camera poses cannot be reliably estimated by COLMAP; for dynamic scenes. RawNeRF was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in November 2021. It adapts Mip-NeRF to train directly on linear raw HDR input data, exploiting NeRF's robustness to zero-mean noise distribution when aggregated across frames. The method was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF, which uses tonemapped LDR images that clip highlights and bias dark regions. It is used for high dynamic range view synthesis and denoising. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 NeRF in the Dark: High Dynamic Range View Synthesis from Noisy Raw Images, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01571, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Duplex Radiance Field
head: Duplex Radiance Field
body: The Neural Duplex Radiance Field is a real-time view synthesis method that replaces dense volumetric ray marching with a two-surface proxy representation. It solves the computational bottleneck of evaluating deep MLPs for every sample point by learning to map the two endpoints of a ray segment (defined by intersections with inner and outer meshes) and the view direction to the final pixel color. It sets itself apart from its parent NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by abandoning per-point MLP queries in favor of vertex-attached features interpolated via hardware rasterization, and from siblings like HybridNeRF Model Architecture by relying on explicit mesh proxies rather than hybrid voxel/grid structures for the primary geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pretrained NeRF density field (used to generate proxies), camera parameters (view direction \mathbf{d}), and two proxy meshes (inner \mathcal{T}i and outer \mathcal{T}o). Output: Pixel color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: 1. Inner Mesh (\mathcal{T}i): Extracted from the density field using a threshold of 10^{-4}. Contains vertices Vi and triangles Ti. 2. Outer Mesh (\mathcal{T}o): Extracted from the density field using a threshold of 10^{-2}. Contains vertices Vo and triangles To. 3. Vertex Features: Each vertex vk in both meshes has an associated learnable feature vector \mathbf{f}k \in \mathbb{R}^N. N=20 for CUDA implementation. N=8 for WebGL implementation. Numbered Steps: 1. Mesh Extraction: Extract \mathcal{T}i and \mathcal{T}o from a pretrained NeRF density field using marching cubes at the specified density thresholds. 2. Feature Initialization: Initialize learnable feature vectors \mathbf{f}k for every vertex vk in \mathcal{T}i and \mathcal{T}o. 3. Ray Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray with direction \mathbf{d}. Compute the depth-sorted intersection points \mathbf{x}1 with the outer mesh \mathcal{T}o and \mathbf{x}2 with the inner mesh \mathcal{T}i. 4. Feature Interpolation: For each intersection point \mathbf{x} \in \{\mathbf{x}1, \mathbf{x}2\}, determine the containing triangle and compute barycentric coordinates. Interpolate the vertex features to obtain \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}). This is performed via hardware rasterization. 5. Color Aggregation: Pass the interpolated features and view direction through a shallow aggregation network F\Theta to predict the color. Formula: The rendering equation is defined as: \mathbf{c} = F{\Theta}(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}1), \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}2), \mathbf{d}) where: \mathbf{x}1 \in \mathcal{T}o is the intersection with the outer mesh. \mathbf{x}2 \in \mathcal{T}i is the intersection with the inner mesh. \mathbf{d} is the view direction vector. F{\Theta} is a shallow network (3-layer convolutional network in CUDA, simplified in WebGL). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh, outermesh, aggregationnet, N): """Renders a single ray using the Neural Duplex Radiance Field.""" # Step 3: Find depth-sorted intersections with outer and inner meshes x1, bary1 = raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, outermesh) x2, bary2 = raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh) # Step 4: Initialize feature vectors f1 = [0.0] N f2 = [0.0] N # Interpolate features if intersections exist if x1 is not None: f1 = interpolatebarycentric(outermesh.vertices, outermesh.features, x1, bary1) if x2 is not None: f2 = interpolatebarycentric(innermesh.vertices, innermesh.features, x2, bary2) # Step 5: Aggregate color using shallow network color = aggregationnet(f1, f2, raydirection) return color def raytriangleintersect(origin, direction, mesh): """Finds the closest intersection of a ray with any triangle in the mesh.""" closestdist = float('inf') closestpoint = None closestbary = None for tri in mesh.triangles: v0, v1, v2 = tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2 e1 = [v1[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] e2 = [v2[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] normal = [e1[1]e2[2] - e1[2]e2[1], e1[2]e2[0] - e1[0]e2[2], e1[0]e2[1] - e1[1]e2[0]] denom = sum(direction[i] normal[i] for i in range(3)) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: continue t = sum((v0[i] - origin[i]) normal[i] for i in range(3)) / denom if t < 1e-6 or t > closestdist: continue point = [origin[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3)] v0v1 = [v1[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] v0v2 = [v2[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] v0p = [point[i] - v0[i] for i in range(3)] d11 = sum(v0v1[i]v0v1[i] for i in range(3)) d12 = sum(v0v1[i]v0v2[i] for i in range(3)) d22 = sum(v0v2[i]v0v2[i] for i in range(3)) d01 = sum(v0p[i]v0v1[i] for i in range(3)) d02 = sum(v0p[i]v0v2[i] for i in range(3)) inv = 1.0 / (d11 d22 - d12 d12) u = (d22 d01 - d12 d02) inv v = (d11 d02 - d12 d01) inv if u >= 0 and v >= 0 and u + v <= 1: w = 1.0 - u - v closestdist = t closestpoint = point closestbary = [w, u, v] return closestpoint, closestbary def interpolatebarycentric(vertices, features, point, barycentric): """Interpolates feature vector using barycentric coordinates.""" v0, v1, v2 = vertices[0], vertices[1], vertices[2] f0, f1, f2 = features[0], features[1], features[2] w, u, v = barycentric return [f0[i]w + f1[i]u + f2[i]v for i in range(len(f0))] Parameters: Feature Dimension (N): 20 (CUDA), 8 (WebGL). Inner Mesh Density Threshold: 10^{-4}. Outer Mesh Density Threshold: 10^{-2}. Aggregation Network: 3-layer convolutional network (CUDA); simplified network without final convolution layer (WebGL). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Intersections: Not all rays hit both proxy surfaces. The view direction \mathbf{d} is appended to the input of F\Theta to allow the network to handle cases where one intersection is missing. Occlusion Artifacts: Local sampling around a single surface suffers from missing geometry or visible occlusions, leading to hole artifacts. The duplex field mitigates this by learning to combine locations on two estimated surfaces. High-Frequency Artifacts: Training from scratch fails to match the fidelity of original NeRFs. Multi-view distillation from a pretrained teacher model (e.g., TensoRF) is required to guide optimization. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray for feature lookup and aggregation, dominated by rasterization and ray-triangle intersection. Significantly faster than dense volumetric sampling O(N) where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of vertices in the proxy meshes. Much lower than storing dense voxel grids or large hash tables for every sample point. Performance: Evaluated on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti GPU, achieving real-time rendering speeds comparable to efficiency-class methods like KiloNeRF and SNeRG. WebGL implementation offers cross-platform compatibility with some performance degradation. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability, reduced memory footprint compared to dense volumetric methods, handles view-dependent appearance via the aggregation network. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the proxy meshes; poor mesh extraction leads to artifacts. Requires a pretrained teacher model for stable training. May struggle with complex internal structures not captured by the two surface proxies. When to use: Real-time view synthesis where high fidelity is needed but dense volumetric rendering is too slow. When not to use: Scenes with highly complex internal geometry that cannot be approximated by two surfaces, or when training from scratch without distillation is required. The Neural Duplex Radiance Field was introduced in "Learning Neural Duplex Radiance Fields for Real-Time View Synthesis" (CVPR 2023). It addresses the computational cost of densely evaluating deep MLPs in NeRF-based methods. By leveraging two geometric proxy meshes and hardware rasterization, it enables real-time rendering. The method builds on the concept of using explicit geometry to guide neural rendering, contrasting with implicit volumetric approaches. It uses multi-view distillation from a pretrained teacher model (like TensoRF) to overcome the lack of high-frequency details when training from scratch. name: NeuRay Occlusion-Aware Parameterization
head: Neural Rays
body: NeuRay is a rendering method that parameterizes visibility and hitting probability directly using an occlusion probability function t(z), rather than deriving them from volume density as in NeRF. This allows for efficient computation of visibility and hitting probability without requiring multiple network forward passes for each sample point. Unlike NeRF, which computes visibility vi = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) from density di via alpha values \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\text{ReLU}(di)li), NeuRay computes visibility directly from the occlusion probability t(z) as vi = 1 - t(zi). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sample points pi \equiv p(zi) on a ray with zi < z{i+1} and zi \in \mathbb{R}^+; occlusion probability parameters decoded from the network; features from neighboring input views. Outputs: Hitting probability \tilde{h}i, visibility vi, and alpha value \hat{\alpha}i for the test ray. Data Structures: The method relies on the occlusion probability function t(z). The network outputs parameters that define t(z), from which \tilde{h}i and vi are derived. The visibility feature g is used to memorize visibility information during finetuning. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample Points: Given an input ray, sample points \{pi \equiv p(zi) | i = 1,..., N; zi < z{i+1}; zi \in \mathbb{R}^+\}. 2. Compute Hitting Probability and Visibility: Compute the hitting probability \tilde{h}i and visibility vi from the occlusion probability t(z): \tilde{h}i = t(z{i+1}) - t(zi) vi \equiv v(zi) = 1 - t(zi) Here, \tilde{h}i indicates the probability that the ray is not occluded by any depth up to zi and hits a surface in the range (zi, z{i+1}). 3. Compute Alpha Value on Input Ray: Derive the alpha value \tilde{\alpha}i on pi from \tilde{h}i and vi using the relationship \tilde{h}i = vi \tilde{\alpha}i: \tilde{\alpha}i = \frac{\tilde{h}i}{vi} = \frac{t(z{i+1}) - t(zi)}{1 - t(zi)} This is the inverse of the density definition in NeRF. 4. Aggregate Alpha Values for Test Ray: For a test ray, compute the alpha value \hat{\alpha}i as a weighted sum of alpha values \tilde{\alpha}{i,j} from all input rays j, weighted by their visibility v{i,j}: \hat{\alpha}i = \frac{\sumj \tilde{\alpha}{i,j} v{i,j}}{\sumj v{i,j}} By considering the visibility, only visible input rays can affect the alpha values \hat{\alpha} of the point. 5. Compute Final Hitting Probability: Use \hat{\alpha}i in the computation of the final hitting probability \hat{h}i for the test ray: \hat{h}i = \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \hat{\alpha}j) \right) \hat{\alpha}i 6. Finetuning with Consistency Loss: During finetuning, NeuRay uses a consistency loss \ell{consist} to memorize predicted surfaces. In one step, choose a pseudo test view A and aggregate features from neighboring input views B, C, D to predict hitting probability hi for the test ray on view A. Apply \ell{consist} to force the visibility feature g of the test ray of view A to produce \tilde{h}i consistent with hi. This memorizes the visibility (and thus geometry) in the feature g, since both are computed from t(z). In subsequent steps, when rendering a different pseudo test view D using views A, B, C, NeuRay checks the memorized visibility on view A to determine if points are invisible. It then predicts an accurate hi for view D, which is also memorized on D for future steps. Formulas: Hitting Probability (Input Ray): \tilde{h}i = t(z{i+1}) - t(zi) Visibility (Input Ray): vi = 1 - t(zi) Alpha Value (Input Ray): \tilde{\alpha}i = \frac{t(z{i+1}) - t(zi)}{1 - t(zi)} Alpha Value (Test Ray): \hat{\alpha}i = \frac{\sumj \tilde{\alpha}{i,j} v{i,j}}{\sumj v{i,j}} Hitting Probability (Test Ray): \hat{h}i = \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \hat{\alpha}j) \right) \hat{\alpha}i Parameters: Number of sample points N: Not given in the sources. Number of neighboring input views: Not given in the sources, but an example uses 8 views. Sample points per input ray: Not given in the sources, but an example uses 32 points. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost of Visibility from Density: Computing visibility from density in NeRF is computationally impractical for training because it requires Kr forward passes of the network F to compute visibility from one input view to one 3D point. For example, with 1 test ray, 8 input views, 128 sample points on the test ray, and 32 sample points per input ray, it requires 8 \times 128 \times 32 network evaluations. Such computation complexity is not affordable for training on a single 2080 Ti GPU to achieve reasonable results. NeuRay avoids this by parameterizing visibility directly. Time Complexity: NeuRay avoids the O(Kr) forward passes required by NeRF for visibility computation, where Kr is the number of sample points on input rays. The exact time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient computation of visibility and hitting probability without requiring multiple network forward passes for each sample point. Enables memorization of scene geometry in the visibility feature g during finetuning. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When efficient visibility computation is critical for training, especially in scenarios with many input views and sample points. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Origin: NeuRay was introduced in the paper "Neural Rays for Occlusion-aware Image-based Rendering". History and Development: The method was developed to address the computational impracticality of computing visibility from density in NeRF during training. It uses a consistency loss to memorize predicted surfaces and refine scene representation. Where it is used: Image-based rendering. name: SHINE-Mapping
head: Sparse Hierarchical Implicit Neural Representations
body: SHINE-Mapping is a large-scale incremental 3D mapping system that represents the environment as a continuous Signed Distance Field (SDF) using sparse hierarchical implicit neural representations. It solves the problem of memory-efficient, real-time mapping for autonomous robots by storing learnable feature vectors in an octree-based sparse structure and regressing SDF values via a shared shallow MLP. Unlike dense voxel methods (e.g., NICE-SLAM) or replay-based continual learning approaches (e.g., iMap/iSDF), SHINE-Mapping uses a sparse hash-table-based octree with feature update regularization to prevent catastrophic forgetting while maintaining limited memory usage. It differs from single-object hierarchical models like NGLOD by supporting incremental extension of the mapped area without pre-allocated memory. Inputs: 3D LiDAR point clouds with known sensor poses. Outputs: A continuous SDF representation of the environment, queryable at any resolution. Data Structures: The representation consists of H hash tables, one for each hierarchical level h \in \{0, \dots, H-1\}. Hash Table Layout: Each hash table maps Morton codes (Z-order/Lebesgue curve spatial hash codes) to feature vectors. Feature Vector: Stored in the corners of octree nodes. Each feature is a one-dimensional vector of length L. Morton Codes: Used to address hash tables, preserving spatial locality and allowing average-case O(1) access. MLP Decoder: A shared shallow multilayer perceptron with M hidden layers. The MLP takes the summed feature vector as input and outputs the SDF value. The query point coordinates are not stacked under the feature vector. Parameters: H: Number of hierarchical levels. Typical values are 3 or 4. Each level doubles the spatial extend in the x, y, and z directions relative to the previous level. L: Length of the feature vector. This is also the input dimension for the MLP. M: Number of hidden layers in the shared shallow MLP. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: When a new octree node corner is created (triggered by LiDAR measurements), its feature vector is randomly initialized. 2. Querying (Hierarchical Interpolation): For a query point \mathbf{x}: Start at the lowest level (level 0). Compute the Morton code for \mathbf{x} at the current level. Retrieve the feature vectors from the corners of the octree node containing \mathbf{x} at this level. Perform trilinear interpolation of these corner features at position \mathbf{x} to obtain the interpolated feature vector \mathbf{f}h for level h. Repeat steps 2a-2d for each level h from 0 to H-1. 3. Aggregation: Sum the interpolated feature vectors from all H levels to form the final input vector \mathbf{F}{sum}: \mathbf{F}{sum} = \sum{h=0}^{H-1} \mathbf{f}h 4. Decoding: Feed \mathbf{F}{sum} into the shared shallow MLP \phi to output the SDF value s: s = \phi(\mathbf{F}{sum}) 5. Optimization: Sample points along rays from LiDAR measurements. Calculate the projected signed distance from the sampled point to the beam endpoint as the supervision signal (label l). Compute the Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) loss between the network output s and the label l. Optimize feature vectors and MLP parameters jointly via backpropagation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getmortoncode(point, level): """ Computes the Morton code (Z-order) for the point at the specific hierarchical level. The spatial extent doubles at each level. Implementation detail: Not given in sources. Assumes a standard Morton encoding function that maps 3D coordinates to a 1D integer based on the grid resolution of the current level. """ # Placeholder for Morton code calculation logic pass def trilinearinterpolate(corners, point): """ Performs trilinear interpolation of 8 corner features at the query point. corners: List of 8 FeatureVectors (size L) corresponding to the octree node corners. point: 3D query coordinates relative to the node. Returns: Interpolated FeatureVector (size L). Implementation detail: Not given in sources. Standard trilinear interpolation using the relative coordinates of the point within the unit cube defined by the corners. """ # Placeholder for trilinear interpolation logic pass def querysdf(querypoint, hashtables, mlp, H): """ Queries the SDF value for a given 3D point. """ summedfeatures = None for level in range(H): # 1. Get Morton code for the current level mortoncode = getmortoncode(querypoint, level) # 2. Retrieve features from the hash table # Note: If the key does not exist, it implies no data has been stored there. # In a sparse structure, missing features might be treated as zero or require # handling. The sources do not specify the behavior for missing keys during # interpolation. Assuming missing features are treated as zero vectors # for the purpose of interpolation, or that the query point always falls # within a populated node. features = hashtables[level].get(mortoncode) if features is None: # Guard for sparse lookup: if no features exist at this level for this location, # the contribution is zero. interpolatedfeature = [0.0] L else: # 3. Trilinear interpolation # Note: 'features' here refers to the 8 corners of the octree node. # The hash table typically stores the feature for a specific corner. # The pseudocode in the source simplifies this by implying 'features' # are retrieved directly. In practice, one must retrieve the 8 corners # surrounding the query point. # The source pseudocode: "features = hashtables[level].get(mortoncode)" # followed by "trilinearinterpolate(features, querypoint)". # This implies the hash table might store the node's features or the # Morton code resolves to the node containing the point. # However, Morton codes usually identify specific cells. # To be implementable from text alone, we assume the hash table lookup # returns the necessary corner features or the node structure allows # interpolation. Given the source says "determine the grids... and determine # the interpolated feature... by trilinear interpolation of the vertex features", # we assume the retrieval step provides the 8 vertices. # Re-interpreting source pseudocode strictly: # "features = hashtables[level].get(mortoncode)" # If the hash table maps Morton Code -> Feature Vector (single vector), # trilinear interpolation is impossible with a single vector. # The text says: "store features in the corners... trilinear interpolation of the vertex features". # Therefore, the hash table likely maps Morton Code -> List of 8 Feature Vectors # OR the Morton Code identifies the node, and the 8 corners are retrieved # via neighbor lookups. # To make the pseudocode valid and self-contained based on the text: # We assume getmortoncode returns the code for the node containing the point. # We assume a helper to get the 8 corners. cornerfeatures = getoctreenodecorners(querypoint, level, hashtables) interpolatedfeature = trilinearinterpolate(cornerfeatures, querypoint) # 4. Aggregate if summedfeatures is None: summedfeatures = interpolatedfeature else: summedfeatures = addvectors(summedfeatures, interpolatedfeature) # 5. Decode sdfvalue = mlp.forward(summedfeatures) return sdfvalue def getoctreenodecorners(point, level, hashtables): """ Retrieves the 8 feature vectors from the corners of the octree node containing the query point at the given level. Implementation detail: Not given in sources. Requires mapping the point to the node index, then computing the 8 neighbor Morton codes and retrieving their features from the hash table. """ pass def addvectors(v1, v2): return [a + b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)] def trainstep(querypoints, labels, hashtables, mlp, learningrate): """ Optimizes features and MLP parameters. """ # 1. Forward pass predictions = [] for point in querypoints: pred = querysdf(point, hashtables, mlp, H) predictions.append(pred) # 2. Loss Calculation (Binary Cross Entropy) # Loss is sensitive to sign misprediction and changes near the surface. loss = binarycrossentropy(predictions, labels) # 3. Backpropagation # Update MLP parameters and feature vectors in hashtables # Implementation detail: Standard backpropagation through the MLP and # the interpolation graph. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Catastrophic Forgetting: In incremental mapping, updating features can cause the network to forget previously learned geometry. Mitigation: Use feature update regularization. In incremental mode, keep the pre-trained MLP fixed (do not update its parameters) to minimize forgetting effects. Sparse Lookup: If a query point falls in a region where no octree nodes have been created (no LiDAR data), the hash table lookup may return empty. The implementation must handle missing features (e.g., treating them as zero) to allow interpolation. Memory Management: While sparse, the hash tables grow with the scene. The system relies on the sparsity of the environment to keep memory low. Time Complexity: Average-case O(1) access to features via hash tables. Querying involves H interpolations and one MLP forward pass. Memory Complexity: Sparse. Memory usage depends on the number of occupied octree nodes, which is proportional to the surface area/volume of the scanned environment, significantly less than dense voxel grids. Performance: More accurate, complete, and memory-efficient than current state-of-the-art 3D mapping methods in large-scale outdoor scenes. Strengths: Supports incremental mapping without pre-allocating memory. Memory-efficient compared to dense voxel structures (e.g., NICE-SLAM). Robust to catastrophic forgetting via feature update regularization and fixed MLP in incremental mode. High-resolution querying via trilinear interpolation of hierarchical features. Limitations: Requires 3D LiDAR sensors with known poses. Memory usage can still become significant in extremely dense environments, though less than dense grids. Not designed for single-object modeling (unlike NGLOD) but for large-scale scenes. When to use: Large-scale outdoor autonomous systems, mobile robots, and self-driving cars using 3D LiDAR. When not to use: Single-object modeling, scenes without LiDAR, or scenarios where replay-based memory is acceptable and memory is not a constraint. SHINE-Mapping was proposed in 2023 by the authors of the paper "SHINE-Mapping: Large-Scale 3D Mapping Using Sparse Hierarchical Implicit Neural Representations". It builds upon the NGLOD method [34] but adapts it for incremental large-scale mapping by using hash tables instead of a fixed octree structure. It addresses the limitations of NICE-SLAM [40] (dense voxel memory cost) and iMap/iSDF [31, 23] (replay-based continual learning memory growth). name: NeRF-LiDAR
head: LiDAR simulation with NeRF
body: NeRF-LiDAR is a method for generating realistic LiDAR point clouds and semantic labels by leveraging real-world images and sparse LiDAR data to learn an implicit neural radiance field representation of driving scenes. It differs from physics-based simulators that rely on manually constructed 3D virtual worlds and from reconstruction-based methods that require dense LiDAR scans and expensive hardware to create meshes, instead using multi-view images and sparse LiDAR signals to implicitly reconstruct the scene and avoid domain gaps. Inputs: Multi-view RGB images from a driving dataset (e.g., nuScenes). Sparse LiDAR point clouds corresponding to the image timestamps. Weak semantic labels (sparse 3D point labels and weak 2D image labels). Virtual LiDAR sensor parameters (e.g., Velodyne HDL32E settings). Outputs: Realistic simulated LiDAR point clouds. Point-wise semantic labels for the generated point clouds. Data Structures: NeRF Representation: An implicit neural network using hash encoding (specifically Instant-NGP style hash grids as adopted from Barron et al. 2023) to represent scene density \sigma and color c. The hash encoding replaces the original unbounded NeRF to address training speed issues. Ray Parameters: Defined by origin o and direction d. The direction is determined by azimuth \theta and vertical angle \phi. The origin o is updated based on ego-vehicle velocity v and time interval \Delta t. Numbered Steps: 1. NeRF Reconstruction: Train an unbounded NeRF with hash encoding using multi-view images and sparse LiDAR depth supervision. The network learns to predict density \sigmai and color ci at sampled points ti along rays. The volume rendering equation for color is: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci where Ti = \exp \left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) is the accumulated transmittance, r = o + td is the ray, o is the origin, d is the direction, ci and \sigmai are color and density at sampled point ti, and \deltaj = t{j+1} - tj is the distance between adjacent sampled points. The rendered depth \hat{D}(r) is calculated as: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) zi where zi is the depth value at the sampled point ti on the ray r. The total loss combines RGB and depth losses: L{rgb} = \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|2^2 L{depth} = \|\hat{D}(r) - D(r)\|1 where \hat{C}(r) is the rendered color, C(r) is the ground truth color, \hat{D}(r) is the rendered depth, and D(r) is the ground truth depth derived from sparse LiDAR signals. 2. Virtual LiDAR Ray Generation: Define a virtual LiDAR sensor with parameters matching the real sensor (e.g., Velodyne HDL32E: 20Hz spinning speed, field of view from -30.67° to 10.67° across 32 channels). Generate ray directions d using azimuth \theta and vertical angle \phi: d = (\cos \theta \cos \phi, \sin \theta \sin \phi, \cos \phi)^T where \theta and \phi are determined by the laser time interval and sensor settings. Update the ray origin o based on ego-vehicle motion: o = o0 + \Delta t \cdot v where o0 is the initial position, \Delta t is the time interval, and v is the velocity of the ego car. 3. Coarse Point Cloud Generation: Cast the generated rays through the learned NeRF representation to sample points. Points are generated where the density \sigma exceeds a threshold or via volume rendering integration to determine hit locations. This produces initial coarse point clouds. 4. Projection to Equirectangular Image: Project the initial coarse 3D point clouds into 2D equirectangular images. 5. Refinement via U-Net: Utilize a U-Net architecture to process the equirectangular images. The network learns to correct "raydrop" (simulating the physical phenomenon where LiDAR rays pass through transparent or semi-transparent objects without reflecting) and alignment errors to make the generated point clouds more realistic. 6. Semantic Label Generation: Integrate sparse 3D point labels and weak 2D image labels into the training process to learn semantic radiance fields, allowing the generation of point-wise semantic labels for the simulated LiDAR data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class HashEncodedNeRF(nn.Module): """Implicit neural radiance field using hash encoding for spatial hashing.""" def init(self): super().init() # Hash grid and MLPs for density and color self.densitymlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1)) self.colormlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3)) def forward(self, x): # Query hash grid and interpolate features sigma = torch.relu(self.densitymlp(x)) c = torch.sigmoid(self.colormlp(x)) return sigma, c class UNet(nn.Module): """Convolutional neural network for processing equirectangular images.""" def init(self): super().init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 3, padding=1) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 3, 3, padding=1) self.relu = nn.ReLU() self.sigmoid = nn.Sigmoid() def forward(self, x): # Process equirectangular projection to correct raydrop and alignment return self.sigmoid(self.conv2(self.relu(self.conv1(x)))) def rendervolume(rayso, raysd, tvals, nerfmodel): """Render color and depth using volume rendering equations.""" # Sample points along rays: r = o + td points = rayso[:, None,:] + tvals[None,:, None] raysd[:, None,:] pointsflat = points.reshape(-1, 3) # Query NeRF for density and color sigmaflat, cflat = nerfmodel(pointsflat) sigma = sigmaflat.reshape(rayso.shape[0], -1) c = cflat.reshape(rayso.shape[0], -1, 3) # Compute deltas: deltaj = t{j+1} - tj delta = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] delta = torch.cat([delta, torch.tensor([1e10], device=tvals.device)], dim=0) # Compute transmittance: Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma delta), dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) # Render color: Chat(r) = sumi Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci weights = alpha T Chat = torch.sum(weights[:,:, None] c, dim=1) # Render depth: Dhat(r) = sumi Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) zi z = tvals Dhat = torch.sum(weights z, dim=1) return Chat, Dhat, T, alpha, delta def generatelidarsimulation(nerfmodel, egopose, egovelocity, t, lidarparams, numsamples): """Simulate LiDAR point cloud generation end-to-end.""" # 1. Generate ray directions from azimuth theta and vertical phi theta = torch.linspace(lidarparams['fovmin'], lidarparams['fovmax'], lidarparams['numchannels']) phi = torch.linspace(0, 2 torch.pi, lidarparams['numrotations']) azimuth, vertical = torch.meshgrid(theta, phi, indexing='ij') raysd = getraydirection(azimuth, vertical) # 2. Update ray origin based on ego-vehicle motion deltat = t rayso = getrayorigin(egopose, deltat, egovelocity) # 3. Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(lidarparams['near'], lidarparams['far'], numsamples) # 4. Render color and depth Chat, Dhat, T, alpha, delta = rendervolume(rayso, raysd, tvals, nerfmodel) # 5. Generate coarse point clouds from density threshold or integration coarsepoints = rayso[:, None,:] + tvals[None,:, None] raysd[:, None,:] coarsepoints = coarsepoints.reshape(-1, 3) # 6. Project to 2D equirectangular image # Standard spherical projection mapping from 3D points to 2D grid img2d = projecttoequirectangular(coarsepoints, lidarparams) # 7. Refine with U-Net to correct raydrop and alignment refinedimg = UNet()(img2d) # 8. Unproject to 3D to get final point clouds # Standard inverse mapping from 2D grid back to 3D coordinates finalpoints = unprojectfromequirectangular(refinedimg, lidarparams) return finalpoints, Chat, Dhat def getraydirection(azimuththeta, verticalphi): """Calculate ray direction d from azimuth and vertical angles.""" costheta = torch.cos(azimuththeta) sintheta = torch.sin(azimuththeta) cosphi = torch.cos(verticalphi) sinphi = torch.sin(verticalphi) dx = costheta cosphi dy = sintheta sinphi dz = cosphi return torch.stack([dx, dy, dz], dim=-1) def getrayorigin(o0, deltat, v): """Calculate ray origin o based on ego-vehicle motion.""" return o0 + deltat v def projecttoequirectangular(points3d, lidarparams): """Project 3D points to 2D equirectangular image.""" # Convert 3D coordinates to spherical angles and map to 2D grid # Not given in the sources. def unprojectfromequirectangular(img2d, lidarparams): """Unproject 2D equirectangular image back to 3D points.""" # Map 2D coordinates back to 3D ray directions and depths # Not given in the sources. A variant of NeRF using hash grids for spatial hashing to accelerate training and inference, adopted here to mitigate the slowness of original unbounded NeRF. A convolutional neural network architecture that processes the 2D equirectangular projections of the initial coarse point clouds to learn raydrop and alignment corrections. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than original unbounded NeRF due to the adoption of hash encoding. The original unbounded NeRF was reported to take about one day to train each NeRF block. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Generates realistic LiDAR data with semantic labels using only multi-view images and sparse LiDAR signals, avoiding the need for dense LiDAR scans or expensive hardware. Avoids domain gaps associated with physics-based virtual world creation by learning from real-world data. Can boost 3D segmentation model accuracy when used for pre-training, reducing the requirement for real labeled data. Limitations: Driving data often comes from unbounded outdoor scenes with small overlaps between adjacent views due to fast ego-car movement, making multi-view geometry challenging. Relies on the quality of sparse LiDAR signals for depth supervision. When to use: When realistic LiDAR simulation for autonomous driving training is needed, but dense LiDAR data or physics-based simulation environments are unavailable or too costly. When not to use: When high-fidelity physics-based interactions (e.g., complex material properties not captured by density/color) are required, or when real-world data collection is impossible. NeRF-LiDAR was introduced by Junge Zhang, Feihu Zhang, Shaochen Kuang, and Li Zhang from Fudan University, University of Oxford, and South China University of Technology at the Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-24). The method addresses the high cost and difficulty of labeling LiDAR point clouds for autonomous driving by leveraging Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for novel view synthesis and implicit 3D scene reconstruction. It builds upon unbounded NeRF (Barron et al. 2022) and hash-encoding NeRF (Barron et al. 2023) to handle large-scale driving scenes. name: DINER (Disorder-Invariant Implicit Neural Representation)
head: DINER with hash-table, Hash+SIREN
body: DINER is an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) technique that augments a traditional INR backbone (such as an MLP or SIREN) with a learnable full-resolution hash-table to map input coordinates. This mapping rearranges the coordinate order to modulate the signal's frequency spectrum, increasing low-frequency components to alleviate spectral bias and improve expressive power. Unlike traditional INRs where the arrangement order of input points affects the network's ability to learn, DINER is disorder-invariant: signals with the same histogram of attributes but different spatial arrangements share the same optimized network parameters. It breaks the paired relationship between input coordinates and output attributes, allowing the MLP to focus on fitting a curved manifold in the attribute space while the hash-table optimizes the coordinate projection. DINER represents a discrete signal Y = \{(\tilde{x}i, \tilde{y}i)\}{i=1}^N, where \tilde{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^{d{in}} is the i-th input coordinate and \tilde{y}i \in \mathbb{R}^{d{out}} is the corresponding attribute (e.g., RGB color). The method consists of a hash-table mapping module and a neural network backbone. 1. Hash-table (HM): A 2D array of learnable floating-point parameters with dimensions N \times L. N: The length of the hash-table, equal to the number of elements in the input signal Y. L: The width (dimensionality) of the hash-table. It determines the dimensionality of the projected space (1D curve for L=1, 2D curved-plane for L=2, 3D curved-volume for L=3). 2. Network Parameters (\theta): The weights and biases of the INR backbone function f'\theta. Input: A coordinate \tilde{x}i from the signal. Output: The predicted attribute \hat{y}i \in \mathbb{R}^{d{out}}. 1. Initialization: Initialize the hash-table HM of size N \times L with learnable parameters (e.g., all zeros). Initialize the network parameters \theta. 2. Hash-Mapping: For each input coordinate \tilde{x}i, query the hash-table to obtain the mapped coordinate M(\tilde{x}i). The index i is used directly to access the i-th row of HM: M(\tilde{x}i) = HM[i] \in \mathbb{R}^L Note: The mapping is independent of the value of \tilde{x}i; it depends only on the index i. 3. Network Query: Feed the mapped coordinate M(\tilde{x}i) into the INR backbone f'\theta to predict the attribute: \hat{y}i = f'\theta(M(\tilde{x}i)) 4. Joint Optimization: Optimize the hash-table parameters HM and the network parameters \theta jointly to minimize the loss between \hat{y}i and the ground truth \tilde{y}i. The INR backbone function f'\theta(x) for an input x \in \mathbb{R}^L is defined as: z0 = \gamma(x) zj = \rhoj(Wj z{j-1} + bj), \quad j = 1, \dots, J-1 f'\theta(x) = WJ z{J-1} + bJ where \gamma(\cdot) is a preprocess function (e.g., identity or frequency encoding), \rhoj is the activation function, Wj and bj are the weight and bias of layer j, and J is the number of layers. In DINER, x = M(\tilde{x}i). The expressive power of the underlying INR is modeled as: f(x) = \sum{\omega0 \in H\Omega} c{\omega0} \sin(\langle \omega0, x \rangle + \phi{\omega0}) where H\Omega is the frequency set determined by the preprocess function \gamma(\cdot). The set of possible functions S^\omegaL representable by DINER with hash-table width L and encoded frequencies \omega is nested: S^\omega1 \subset S^\omega2 \subset S^\omega3 \subset \dots For linearly-independent signals with attribute dimension d{out}, the expressive power saturates when L \ge d{out}: \forall i \ge d{out}, S^\omegai = S^\omega{d{out}} For linearly-dependent signals with attribute rank \rho(Y), the expressive power saturates when L \ge \rho(Y): \forall i \ge \rho(Y), S^\omegai = S^\omega{\rho(Y)} Hash-table Width (L): Determines expressive power. For RGB images (d{out}=3), L=3 is sufficient to cover the entire RGB space. In experiments, L=2 or L=3 is used for 2D images. Hash-table Size (N): Equal to the number of pixels/points in the signal. For a 1200 \times 1200 image, N = 1,440,000. Network Size: DINER uses a small MLP. Examples include 1 \times 128 (1 layer, 128 neurons), 2 \times 64 (2 layers, 64 neurons), or 4 \times 64 for 3D video. Backbone: Standard MLP with ReLU or SIREN with periodic activation (default frequency 30). Loss Function: L2 loss between predicted and ground truth values. Frequency Encoding (\omega): If used, increases the size of the supported frequency set H\Omega linearly, but has less impact on expressive power than increasing L. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DINER(nn.Module): def init(self, N, L, din, dout, backboneconfig): """ N: Number of signal points (hash-table length) L: Hash-table width (projected dimensionality) din: Dimensionality of input coordinates (usually 2 for images) dout: Dimensionality of attributes (e.g., 3 for RGB) backboneconfig: Configuration for the MLP/SIREN backbone """ super().init() # Hash-table: Learnable parameters of size N x L # Initialized to zeros self.HM = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(N, L)) # Backbone network: Maps L-dimensional mapped coordinates to dout-dimensional attributes # Example: Simple MLP layers = [] indim = L for hiddendim in backboneconfig['hiddendims']: layers.append(nn.Linear(indim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Or SIREN activation indim = hiddendim layers.append(nn.Linear(indim, dout)) self.backbone = nn.Sequential(layers) self.dout = dout def forward(self, indices): """ indices: Tensor of shape (batchsize,) containing indices i for each point Returns: Predicted attributes of shape (batchsize, dout) """ # Step 1: Query hash-table # HM[indices] retrieves the i-th row for each index in indices mappedcoords = self.HM[indices] # Shape: (batchsize, L) # Step 2: Feed mapped coordinates to backbone predictedattrs = self.backbone(mappedcoords) # Shape: (batchsize, dout) return predictedattrs def traindiner(model, indices, groundtruth, optimizer, epochs): """ indices: Tensor of shape (N,) containing 0..N-1 groundtruth: Tensor of shape (N, dout) """ for epoch in range(epochs): optimizer.zerograd() # Forward pass predictions = model(indices) # Loss calculation (L2 loss) loss = torch.mean((predictions - groundtruth) 2) # Backward pass and update loss.backward() optimizer.step() Interpolated Hash-Keys: For continuous signals, feeding interpolated mapped coordinates to the trained MLP yields poor results because the distance between mapped coordinates is larger than in the original space. Instead, apply post-interpolation to the network output. Large Hash-Table Size: Using a large hash-table increases training time due to memory/cache communication costs on the GPU. For example, in a 3D video task, DINER took 1309s vs 706s for SIREN. Floating Point Errors: Slight differences in values between different hash-table arrangements with the same histogram are caused by floating-point errors of GPU when summing matrices. Hash-Table Width Selection: Setting L higher than d{out} (for independent signals) or \rho(Y) (for dependent signals) does not improve expressive power and wastes parameters. Time Complexity: The computational cost of the hash-table derivation (back-propagation) is O(1) per iteration for batch size 1, assuming small hash-table size. However, large hash-tables increase training time due to memory transfer costs. Memory Complexity: The hash-table size is N \times L. For a 1200 \times 1200 image with L=3, this is 1.44 \times 10^6 \times 3 \times 4 bytes \approx 17 MB. This is comparable to the input signal size. Performance: On 2D image fitting (1200x1200), DINER with MLP backbone achieves ~54dB PSNR (30dB improvement over MLP alone), outperforming Instant-NGP by 6dB. On 3D video (30 frames, 1920x1080), DINER achieved 50.74 dB PSNR in 1309s, outperforming NeRV (36.08 dB, 7445s) by 14 dB and 5x speed. DINER(SIREN) is slightly stronger than DINER(MLP) in early epochs (first 3000) due to high-frequency encoding in SIREN, but they converge to similar performance (59.64dB vs 59.53dB) after 10000 epochs. Strengths: Disorder-invariant; small networks achieve high accuracy; alleviates spectral bias; fast computation for hash-table updates. Limitations: Large hash-tables cause memory/cache bottlenecks; not suitable for continuous signals without post-interpolation of outputs. When to use: When representing discrete signals (images, videos) with high-frequency details where traditional INRs suffer from spectral bias, and when disorder invariance is beneficial. When not to use: For continuous signals where interpolation is required during inference (use post-interpolation of output instead); when memory bandwidth is a severe bottleneck and N is very large. DINER was introduced by S. Xie, H. Zhu, Z. Liu, Q. Zhang, Y. Zhou, X. Cao, and Z. Ma in the Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2023. It extends the concept of Implicit Neural Representations by addressing the spectral bias problem through coordinate rearrangement via a hash-table. The method is used in image/video representation, phase retrieval, refractive index recovery, and neural radiance field optimization. It builds on NeRF Network Query with Hashed Embeddings by using a hash-table for coordinate mapping, but differs in that the hash-table is fully learnable and disorder-invariant, rather than a fixed spatial hashing scheme for acceleration. name: Generative Radiance Fields (GRAF)
body: Generative Radiance Fields (GRAF) is a method for 3D-aware image synthesis and shape estimation from unposed images, enabling volume reconstruction without explicit camera pose information. Unlike standard NeRF which requires known camera poses, GRAF uses an adversarial training scheme where a generator conditioned on pose, shape, and appearance codes learns to synthesize images that fool a patch-based discriminator. It builds on the original NeRF representation and rendering equation, replacing the supervised reconstruction loss with an adversarial objective to handle datasets where relative camera positions are unknown. Inputs: A dataset of unposed 2D RGB images. During training, the generator receives a requested viewing pose (elevation and azimuth angles), and optionally shape and appearance codes. The discriminator receives patches from real images and generated images. Outputs: Synthesized RGB images of the scene from specified viewpoints, depth maps, and the learned 3D implicit representation (NeRF weights). The core representation is a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) acting as the radiance field, identical to the original NeRF architecture. MLP Network: 8 fully-connected layers. Channels: 256 channels per layer. Activation: ReLU for hidden layers. Input to MLP: 5D coordinate consisting of 3D position (x, y, z) and 2D viewing direction (\theta, \phi). Output of MLP: Volume density (\sigma) and emitted RGB color (c). Generator Conditioners: Pose (elevation and azimuth angles), Shape Code (latent vector controlling volume density distribution), and Appearance Code (latent vector controlling color/albedo). Discriminator: Patch-based network operating on square arrays of pixels. 1. Patch Selection: Instead of predicting full images, the generator selects a patch position and a distance between pixels within that patch. A patch represents a square array of pixels. 2. Conditioning: The generator takes the requested pose, and optionally shape and appearance codes, as input. 3. Ray Marching: For each pixel in the patch, a ray is cast based on the requested pose. 4. NeRF Query: At each sample point along the ray, the MLP is queried with the 3D position and viewing direction to obtain density and color. 5. Volume Rendering: The color and density values are integrated along the ray using the standard NeRF rendering equation to produce the color for each pixel in the patch. 6. Adversarial Training (Generator): The generated patch is compared against a real patch from the dataset by the discriminator. 7. Discriminator Update: The discriminator learns to differentiate real patches from generated ones. 8. Generator Update: The generator's weights are updated to minimize the discriminator's ability to distinguish generated patches from real ones, effectively matching the probabilistic distribution of real image pixels. 9. Receptive Field Decay: The size of the receptive field of the patch (or the distance between pixels) is decreased during training. This allows the model to first capture global contours and progressively improve local details. 10. Inference: To synthesize an image, the generator is fed a specific viewing angle (pose). Optionally, shape and appearance codes can be varied to change the volume density or color, respectively. The internal NeRF representation and rendering equation are identical to the original NeRF. Let C(r) be the rendered color for a ray r passing through sample points ti: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \left( 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) \right) ci Where: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the accumulated transmittance. \sigmai is the volume density predicted by the MLP at ti. ci is the color predicted by the MLP at ti. \deltai is the distance between sample points ti and t{i+1}. MLP Layers: 8 fully-connected layers. MLP Channels: 256. Activation: ReLU. Image Resolution: 256 × 256 pixels (used in experiments for computational reasons). Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Overfitting: Training for a high number of iterations leads to overfitting, resulting in a heavily under-regularized depth map with many floating artifacts in the background, which decreases the Intersection over Union (IoU) score. Underfitting/Early Stopping: Stopping training after a smaller number of iterations results in a more accurate depth map but a blurry, non-detailed RGB image. Pose Ambiguity: While GRAF does not require pose input, the predicted pose may not be precise, shifting the depth map from ground truth, although the shape may be more plausible. Memory Constraints: Predicting color for every pixel in the target image in the same batch is too memory-intensive, necessitating the patch-based approach. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def tanh(x): return math.tanh(x) def relu(x): return max(0.0, x) def fullyconnected(x, weights, bias): return [sum(x[j] weights[j][k] for j in range(len(x))) + bias[k] for k in range(len(bias))] def concatenatevectors(a, b): return a + b def samplebatch(dataset, batchsize): return [dataset[i] for i in range(batchsize)] def sampleposes(batchsize): return [(math.random.uniform(0, math.pi), math.random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi)) for in range(batchsize)] def sampleshapecodes(batchsize, codedim): return [math.random.normal(0, 1, codedim) for in range(batchsize)] def sampleappearancecodes(batchsize, codedim): return [math.random.normal(0, 1, codedim) for in range(batchsize)] def definepatchgrid(patchsize, numpixelsperside): grid = [] for i in range(numpixelsperside): for j in range(numpixelsperside): grid.append((i patchsize, j patchsize)) return grid def castray(pose, pixeloffset): theta, phi = pose origin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] direction = [math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) + pixeloffset[0], math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) + pixeloffset[1], math.cos(theta)] return {"origin": origin, "direction": direction} def sampleray(ray, numsamples, near, far): tvals = [near + i (far - near) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] samples = [] for t in tvals: pos = [ray["origin"][k] + t ray["direction"][k] for k in range(3)] samples.append({"position": pos, "t": t}) return samples def mlpforward(input5d, shapecode, appearancecode, weightslist, biaseslist): x = concatenatevectors(input5d, shapecode) x = concatenatevectors(x, appearancecode) for i in range(8): x = fullyconnected(x, weightslist[i], biaseslist[i]) if i < 7: x = [relu(v) for v in x] density = sigmoid(x[0]) color = [tanh(v) for v in x[1:4]] return density, color def volumerender(densities, colors, distances): transmittance = 1.0 renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(len(densities)): sigma = densities[i] delta = distances[i] c = colors[i] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) weight = transmittance alpha renderedcolor = [renderedcolor[k] + weight c[k] for k in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return renderedcolor def computediscriminatorloss(realscores, fakescores): return sum(realscores) - sum(fakescores) def computegeneratorloss(fakescores): return -sum(fakescores) def updateweights(model, loss, learningrate): pass def traingraf(dataset, generator, discriminator, numiterations, learningrate): receptivefieldsize = 10.0 numpixelsperside = 16 batchsize = 4 codedim = 128 near, far = 0.1, 10.0 numsamples = 128 for iteration in range(numiterations): realimages = samplebatch(dataset, batchsize) poses = sampleposes(batchsize) shapecodes = sampleshapecodes(batchsize, codedim) appearancecodes = sampleappearancecodes(batchsize, codedim) generatedpatches = [] for i in range(batchsize): patchpixels = definepatchgrid(receptivefieldsize, numpixelsperside) renderedpatch = [] for pixeloffset in patchpixels: ray = castray(poses[i], pixeloffset) samples = sampleray(ray, numsamples, near, far) densities = [] colors = [] distances = [] for k in range(len(samples) - 1): densities.append(mlpforward(samples[k]["position"], shapecodes[i], appearancecodes[i], generator.weights, generator.biases)) colors.append(mlpforward(samples[k]["position"], shapecodes[i], appearancecodes[i], generator.weights, generator.biases)) distances.append(samples[k+1]["t"] - samples[k]["t"]) renderedpatch.append(volumerender(densities, colors, distances)) generatedpatches.append(renderedpatch) realscores = discriminator.forward(realimages) fakescores = discriminator.forward(generatedpatches) dloss = computediscriminatorloss(realscores, fakescores) updateweights(discriminator, dloss, learningrate) fakescoresgen = discriminator.forward(generatedpatches) gloss = computegeneratorloss(fakescoresgen) updateweights(generator, gloss, learningrate) receptivefieldsize = 0.99 def inferencegraf(generator, pose, shapecode, appearancecode, patchsize, numpixels): patchpixels = definepatchgrid(patchsize, numpixels) renderedpatch = [] for pixeloffset in patchpixels: ray = castray(pose, pixeloffset) samples = sampleray(ray, 128, 0.1, 10.0) densities = [] colors = [] distances = [] for k in range(len(samples) - 1): densities.append(mlpforward(samples[k]["position"], shapecode, appearancecode, generator.weights, generator.biases)) colors.append(mlpforward(samples[k]["position"], shapecode, appearancecode, generator.weights, generator.biases)) distances.append(samples[k+1]["t"] - samples[k]["t"]) renderedpatch.append(volumerender(densities, colors, distances)) return renderedpatch Combines voxel grids with neural radiance fields for efficiency. Choose when memory is constrained but high fidelity is needed. HybridNeRF Model Architecture Uses multi-view stereo features to initialize or condition the NeRF. Choose when sparse multi-view images are available. MVS Network Query Compresses NeRF models for mobile deployment. Choose for real-time applications on edge devices. SqueezeNeRF Uses voxel grids for spatial hashing to accelerate NeRF queries. Choose for faster training/inference with large scenes. VoxNeRF Adds time-varying deformation fields to NeRF. Choose for dynamic scenes. Deformation Field Integration for Telepresence Uses hexagonal planes for high-dynamic-range rendering. Choose for scenes with extreme lighting variations. HDR-HexPlane Aggregates features from multiple scales of point clouds. Choose for scenes with sparse geometry. Multi-scale PointNeRF++ Feature Aggregation Uses Fourier features for frequency bias. Choose for high-frequency detail reconstruction. FourieRF Matches appearance across views using consistency losses. Choose for unposed datasets with consistent lighting. Appearance Matching Applies anti-aliasing to hash grids. Choose to reduce artifacts in high-resolution renders. Hash-grid anti-aliasing and regularization Handles unposed images with weather conditions. Choose for outdoor scenes with varying lighting. NeRF-W Uses signed distance fields for better geometry. Choose when accurate surface reconstruction is critical. UniSDF-based Latent NeRF Processes raw sensor data. Choose for high-fidelity rendering from unprocessed camera data. RawNeRF Uses bidirectional rendering. Choose for view-dependent effects like specularities. Neural Duplex Radiance Field Handles occlusions explicitly. Choose for scenes with complex occlusions. NeuRay Occlusion-Aware Parameterization Maps lighting conditions. Choose for consistent lighting across views. SHINE-Mapping Integrates LiDAR data. Choose when depth sensors are available. NeRF-LiDAR Invariant to point cloud disorder. Choose for unordered point cloud inputs. DINER (Disorder-Invariant Implicit Neural Representation) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources, but the patch-based approach reduces memory usage compared to full-image prediction. Measured Performance: On CubeSat and SMOS satellite datasets, GRAF renders precise novel views with accurate details even when parts of the satellites are shadowed, whereas NeRF may struggle with dark scenes. NeRF generally renders more accurate images regarding material specularity and pose. GRAF's depth prediction captures shape accurately but the pose may be imprecise, shifting the depth map from ground truth. Scaling: The patch-based approach allows application to high-resolution images by avoiding memory-intensive full-image prediction. Strengths: Does not require camera pose information; disentangles shape and appearance; handles dark scenes better than NeRF; allows explicit camera control. Limitations: Prone to overfitting with high iteration counts (leading to floating artifacts in depth maps); early stopping leads to blurry RGB images; pose estimation is imprecise, shifting depth maps from ground truth, though shape capture remains plausible. When to use: When camera poses are unknown (unposed images); when dealing with dark or shadowed scenes; when disentangling shape and appearance is desired. When not to use: When high-fidelity material specularity is critical (NeRF may be better); when full-image rendering is necessary and memory is not constrained. Generative Radiance Fields (GRAF) was introduced by Schwarz et al.. It is based on the original NeRF paper and extends it with an adversarial training scheme. The method was applied to space situational awareness, specifically for identifying non-cooperative spacecraft from unposed images. The authors note that while other 3D-aware GANs use voxel grids, GRAF uses a NeRF as a 3D implicit representation, allowing it to learn without pose information. The method was evaluated on synthetic datasets of satellites generated using Unity.
