name: Instant NGP-based Surface Rendering
head: Radiance Surface Rendering, Radiance Surface Rendering via Instant NGP
body: Instant NGP-based Surface Rendering is a method that repurposes the Instant NGP ray-marching infrastructure for explicit surface reconstruction by treating the radiance field as an occupancy field and terminating rays at the first surface intersection. Unlike standard NeRF which integrates volumetric color along the entire ray, this approach returns the color of the first sample where the occupancy value exceeds a threshold, resulting in a 2.4× average speedup in frames per second (FPS) compared to the baseline on MipNeRF360 scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera rays, a radiance field represented by an interpolated hash grid lookup combined with a lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Output: Pixel color and depth (implicitly defined by the surface hit). Data Structures: Hash Grid: Stores feature vectors for spatial locations. The specific bit-packing or grid resolution is not detailed in the sources, but it is the core lookup structure used by Instant NGP. MLP: A lightweight network that processes the interpolated features to predict occupancy and color. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Marching: For each pixel, generate a ray and sample points along it. The field (\sigmap, cp) is evaluated at each sample point p using the hash grid lookup and MLP. 2. Occupancy Check: For each sample along the ray, retrieve the occupancy value \sigmap. 3. Surface Hit Detection: Check if the occupancy value exceeds the threshold \tau = 0.5. 4. Termination and Color Return: If \sigmap > 0.5, return the color cp of that sample and terminate the ray. If the threshold is not met within the ray bounds, the ray is considered to have missed the surface (background). Parameters: Occupancy Threshold (\tau): 0.5. Samples with occupancy > 0.5 are considered surface intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersurfaceray(rayorigin, raydirection, hashgrid, mlp, threshold=0.5): """ Renders a single ray using Instant NGP-based surface rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. hashgrid: Data structure for spatial hashing lookups. mlp: Lightweight MLP for feature processing. threshold: Float, occupancy threshold for surface detection (default 0.5). Returns: color: 3D vector, color of the surface hit. depth: Float, distance to the surface hit. """ # Standard ray marching setup for Instant NGP # The sources do not specify the exact number of samples or step size, # so we assume a standard fixed-step or adaptive step loop typical of NGP. t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 # Typical step size for NGP; not explicitly given in sources. maxsteps = 1000 # Safety limit; not explicitly given in sources. for i in range(maxsteps): # Current sample position pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Evaluate occupancy and color using Instant NGP's hash grid and MLP # This involves querying the hash grid at pos and passing features through MLP occupancy, color = evaluatengpfield(pos, hashgrid, mlp) # Check for surface intersection if occupancy > threshold: return color, t # Advance along the ray t += stepsize # If no surface is hit, return background color (e.g., black or white) # Background handling is not detailed in sources, assuming standard black. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], t def evaluatengpfield(pos, hashgrid, mlp): """ Evaluates the Instant NGP field at a position. """ # Query hash grid for multi-resolution features features = queryhashgrid(pos, hashgrid) # Process features through MLP # Specific MLP architecture (layers, activations) is not detailed in sources. # Assuming a standard lightweight MLP as described in Instant NGP. occupancy, color = mlp(features) return occupancy, color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the occupancy value crossing 0.5. If the network output is noisy near the surface, jittering may occur. Boundaries: If the ray does not intersect any surface within the sampled range, the method must handle the "miss" case, typically by returning a background color. Degenerate Input: Simple scenes with enough observations reconstruct surfaces accurately without additional constraints, but complex scenes may require regularization (e.g., Laplacian refinement) to smooth small kinks. An optimization that replaces ray-marching with the rasterization of a meshed isosurface extracted from the radiance field, boosting rendering performance while maintaining visual quality. The color network is used only for mesh shading. Performance can be further boosted by storing precomputed hash grid lookups alongside mesh vertices or by projecting the directional MLP dependence into spherical harmonics. This variant provides an additional 2× speedup over the ray-marching version. A variant that switches to volumetric rendering in hard regions where the surface representation is insufficient, improving visual quality. This approach encourages surface-like, sparse distributions, resulting in more empty space that the renderer can efficiently skip. Consequently, Instant NGP automatically spawns more rays at equal batch size, covering more reference pixels per batch. When restricted to match NeRF's ray count, the relaxed variant delivers results approximately equal to NeRF. Time and Memory Complexity: Speed: The method achieves a 2.4× average speedup in FPS compared to the baseline NeRF on MipNeRF360 scenes. The relaxed variant achieves a 2.0× speedup. Meshed Isosurface Rasterization provides an additional 2× speedup over the ray-marching version. Training Time: On the DTU dataset, the method achieves an average Chamfer distance of 0.80 with 1 minute of training time, compared to NeuS2's 0.68 with 5 minutes of training time. Measured Performance: MipNeRF360 Indoor: Mean PSNR of 29.02 dB (standard) and 29.41 dB (relaxed), compared to NeRF's 29.19 dB. MipNeRF360 Outdoor: Mean PSNR of 22.41 dB (standard) and 22.62 dB (relaxed), compared to NeRF's 22.47 dB. DTU Geometry: Average Chamfer distance of 0.80 (1 min training) vs. NeuS2's 0.68 (5 min training). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fast rendering due to early termination; efficient surface extraction at any point without intermediate volume representation. The relaxed variant can exceed NeRF's visual quality in hard regions. Limitations: The standard surface rendering may struggle in hard regions without the relaxed variant. Geometry quality (Chamfer distance) is lower than NeuS2, though training is significantly faster. When to Use: Use when fast surface extraction and rendering are prioritized over high-fidelity geometry reconstruction. Use when training time is a constraint (e.g., 1 minute vs. 5 minutes for NeuS2). When Not to Use: Use when high-fidelity geometry is required and training time is not a constraint (NeuS2 is better). Use when volumetric effects (transparency, subsurface scattering) are essential, as this method is designed for surface rendering. The method is based on the paper "Radiance Surfaces: Optimizing Surface Representations with a 5D Radiance Field Loss". It builds on the Instant NGP codebase, which uses interpolated hash grid lookups combined with a lightweight MLP to represent radiance fields. The approach was developed to leverage the efficiency of Instant NGP for surface rendering tasks, offering a trade-off between speed and geometric accuracy compared to traditional volumetric NeRF methods. name: Chunked Network Evaluation
head: Batched NeRF Evaluation, Neural Network Chunking
body: Chunked Network Evaluation is a memory-management technique that evaluates a NeRF network on batched points in chunks to avoid out-of-memory errors during training or rendering. It partitions the total set of query points into smaller subsets processed sequentially, rather than attempting to process all points in a single forward pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: pts (tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 3)), viewdirs (tensor of shape (N{rays}, 1, 3)), model (the NeRF network function), and netchunk (integer specifying the maximum number of points per chunk). Outputs: rgb (tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 3)) and sigma (tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}, 1)). Data Structures: allrgb and allsigma: Lists of tensors storing intermediate results from each chunk. Steps: 1. Flatten Inputs: Reshape pts and viewdirs into 2D tensors where the first dimension is the total number of points (N{total} = N{rays} \times N{samples}). pts{flat} = pts.reshape(-1, 3) viewdirs{flat} = viewdirs[:, None,:].expandas(pts).reshape(-1, 3) 2. Inputs and Outputs: Input: rayspts (tensor of sample points along rays), densityfeature (pre-computed density features corresponding to the points), chunk (integer, default 5120), networkqueryfn (callable that queries the network), networkfn (network function). Output: Tensor of density values for all input points. Data Structures: rayspts: Tensor of sample points along rays. densityfeature: Tensor of pre-computed density features corresponding to the points. densities: List of tensors storing chunk results. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list densities. 2. Determine the device (CPU/GPU) from the densityfeature tensor. 3. Iterate over rayspts in chunks of size chunk. For each chunk index i: a. Extract inputfeat = rayspts[i:i + chunk]. b. Move inputfeat to the device. c. Extract densityfeatchunk = densityfeature[i:i + chunk]. d. Call networkqueryfn(inputfeat, None, densityfeatchunk, networkfn) to get the density for the current chunk. e. Append the result to densities. 4. Concatenate all tensors in densities along the default dimension and return the result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Differentiable Volume Rendering Pipeline
body: The Differentiable Volume Rendering Pipeline orchestrates the training loop for Neural Radiance Fields by generating rays, sampling points through an implicit volume, evaluating the neural network, and aggregating results via differentiable alpha compositing. It solves the problem of optimizing 3D scene representations from 2D images by computing gradients of the rendered image loss with respect to network parameters. It differs from standard volume rendering by explicitly maintaining the computational graph through the sampling and integration steps to enable end-to-end backpropagation. Inputs: Camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics) for a batch of views. Ground truth images Ci for the corresponding pixel coordinates. Neural network model (implicit volume representation) with parameters \theta. Sampler configuration (number of samples per ray, hierarchical sampling settings). Training configuration cfg.training.batchsize (N), defining the number of random pixels sampled per iteration. Outputs: Rendered feature/color images \hat{C}i. Rendered depth maps. Data Structures: Ray Bundle: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the origin and direction for each ray in the batch. Sample Points: A tensor of shape (N, K, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of K samples along each ray. Network Outputs: Tensors of shape (N, K, 4) containing the predicted color (RGB) and density (\sigma) for each sample. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Loop over cameras, generate NDC grids, and create ray bundles. 2. Sampling: Pass the ray bundle through model.sampler to generate sample points. 3. Network Evaluation: Call model(raybundle) to evaluate the implicit volume and aggregate results. 4. Alpha Compositing: Compute transmittance Tk and weight wk for each sample: \deltak = t{k+1} - tk \hat{\sigma}k = \sigmak \deltak \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\hat{\sigma}k) Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \hat{\sigma}j\right) wk = \alphak Tk The rendered color \hat{C} is the weighted sum: \hat{C} = \sum{k=1}^{K} wk \mathbf{c}k 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between the rendered color \hat{C}i and the ground truth color Ci for the batch of N pixels: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (\hat{C}i - Ci)^2 6. Reshape & Return: Extract rendered features and depth, reshape to image dimensions, and save/return them. Parameters: cfg.training.batchsize (N): Number of random pixels sampled per training iteration. Controls memory usage and gradient noise. Number of samples per ray (K): Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: If the network is too expressive or view-dependence is not handled carefully, it may overfit to training images. Precision: Floating-point precision in transmittance calculation can lead to artifacts if not handled correctly (Standard practice: clamp \hat{\sigma}k or use log-space accumulation). Boundaries: Rays intersecting the bounding box of the scene must be clipped (Standard practice: use near/far planes or AABB intersection). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderimages(model, cameras, gtimages, cfg): """ Orchestrates the differentiable volume rendering pipeline. Args: model: Neural network model with 'sampler' and forward pass. cameras: List of camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics). gtimages: Ground truth images tensor. cfg: Configuration object containing training parameters. Returns: renderedimages: Rendered images tensor. depthmaps: Rendered depth maps tensor. loss: Scalar loss value. """ batchsize = cfg.training.batchsize renderedimages = [] depthmaps = [] totalloss = 0.0 for cam in cameras: # 1. Ray Generation: generate NDC grids and ray bundles raybundle = generateraybundle(cam, batchsize) # # 2. Sampling: pass through sampler samplepoints = model.sampler(raybundle) # # 3. Network Evaluation: evaluate implicit volume colors, densities = model(samplepoints) # # 4. Alpha Compositing (differentiable) deltas = [] for i in range(len(samplepoints) - 1): d = samplepoints[i+1] - samplepoints[i] deltas.append(d) deltas.append(deltas[-1]) deltas = [d if all(d) == 0 else d for d in deltas] # fix vector comparison bug deltas = [abs(d) for d in deltas] sigmadeltas = [densities[i] deltas[i] for i in range(len(deltas))] alphas = [1.0 - import('math').exp(-s) for s in sigmadeltas] transmittances = [] t = 1.0 for a in alphas: transmittances.append(t) t = (1.0 - a) weights = [a t for a, t in zip(alphas, transmittances)] renderedcolors = sum([w c for w, c in zip(weights, colors)]) rendereddepth = sum([w p[2] for w, p in zip(weights, samplepoints)]) # 5. Loss Calculation gtcolors = samplegtcolors(gtimages, raybundle) # loss = sum([(rc - gc) 2 for rc, gc in zip(renderedcolors, gtcolors)]) / len(gtcolors) totalloss += loss renderedimages.append(renderedcolors) depthmaps.append(rendereddepth) # 6. Reshape & Return renderedimages = reshapetoimage(renderedimages, cameras) # depthmaps = reshapetoimage(depthmaps, cameras) # return renderedimages, depthmaps, totalloss / len(cameras) A method to optimize camera poses and NeRF parameters jointly by using event data as a constraint to model non-uniform camera motion during exposure. It differs from standard NeRF training by incorporating event cameras and motion blur constraints. Choose this method when dealing with scenes captured with event cameras or significant motion blur. It renders virtual sharp images, converts them to grayscale, transforms to log domain, and computes event loss and blur loss. The event loss compares simulated events with real events, and the blur loss compares simulated blurry images with input blurry images. The final loss is a weighted sum of event and blur losses. Scaling: Scales with cfg.training.batchsize (number of random pixels sampled per iteration). Strengths: End-to-end differentiable rendering pipeline. name: Active Learning Strategy for NeRF Distillation
head: Important camera poses selection, Important sample points selection, Important sample rays selection, PVD-AL active learning
body: This method bridges the performance gap between teacher and student Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models during knowledge distillation by actively selecting challenging camera poses, sample rays, and sample points rather than processing all data uniformly. It distinguishes itself from standard uniform distillation by dynamically prioritizing difficult samples based on loss metrics, enabling student models to outperform those trained from scratch. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Teacher NeRF model, Student NeRF model, batch of training rays, camera poses, and hyperparameters for selection percentages and loss weights. Outputs: Updated Student NeRF parameters; sets of selected important poses, rays, and points for the next iteration. Data Structures lossrgb: Tensor of shape (Nrays,) storing the L2 loss per ray between teacher and student RGB outputs. lossimg: Tensor of shape (Nposes,) storing the accumulated image-level loss. Wt, Ws: Vectors of point weights for teacher and student, respectively, derived from density and distance. TSP: Set of indices for important sample points. TSR: Set of indices for important sample rays. TCP: Set of indices for important camera poses. Formulas The weight W^ for a sampling point i along a ray with N points is calculated as: W^ = \sum{i=1}^{N} (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \sigmai is the density and \deltai is the distance interval at point i. The density loss L{\sigma^2} constrains the numerical range of density \sigma to [a, b] for both teacher (\sigmat) and student (\sigmas): L{\sigma^2} = \| \min(\max(\sigmat, a), b) - \min(\max(\sigmas, a), b) \|2 This restriction avoids optimizing \sigma directly on \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), which is inefficient due to gradient saturation and high exponential computation cost during block-wise implementation. Parameters Distillation Loss Rates: Volume-aligned: 2 \times 10^{-3}, Density: 2 \times 10^{-3}, Color: 2 \times 10^{-3}, RGB: 1. Important Rays Percentage: 10\% of rays selected per iteration. Important Points Percentage: 30\% of sample points selected per iteration. Important Poses Percentage: 10\% of camera poses selected per epoch. Training Schedule: Stage 1 (3k steps), Stage 2 (5k steps), Stage 3 (remaining steps). Active learning is incorporated after Stages 1 and 2. Algorithm The active learning strategy operates within the training loop as follows: 1. Forward Pass & Loss Calculation: Compute the RGB loss between teacher and student outputs: \text{loss\rgb} = \text{L2}(\text{tea\out}['\text{rgb}'], \text{stu\out}['\text{rgb}']). Compute other losses (e.g., density, sigma) using the constrained density loss formula. 2. Record Image-Level Loss: Accumulate ray losses to their corresponding image indices: \text{loss\img}[\text{RaysMapToImgIdx}(\text{batch\rays})] += \text{loss\rgb}. 3. Backward Pass: Perform the optimization step. 4. Select Important Sample Rays (TSR): Sort rays by lossrgb in descending order. Select the top N{sr} rays (where N{sr} is 10\% of total rays) as important rays. 5. Select Important Camera Poses (TCP): Sort camera poses by lossimg in descending order. Select the top N{cp} poses (where N{cp} is 10\% of total poses) as important poses for the next epoch. 6. Select Important Sample Points (TSP): Calculate point weights W^ for both teacher and student using the density and distance. Concatenate teacher weights Wt and student weights Ws. Select the top N{sp} points (where N{sp} is 30\% of total sample points) with the largest combined weight values as important points. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def activelearningstep(teachermodel, studentmodel, batchrays, poses, hyperparams): # 1. Forward pass and loss calculation teaout = teachermodel(batchrays) stuout = studentmodel(batchrays) # Per-ray L2 loss between teacher and student RGB outputs lossrgb = [] for tr, sr in zip(teaout['rgb'], stuout['rgb']): lossrgb.append(sum((t - s) 2 for t, s in zip(tr, sr)) / len(tr)) # Density loss using constrained range [a, b] to avoid exp saturation a, b = hyperparams['sigmamin'], hyperparams['sigmamax'] teasigmac = [min(max(s, a), b) for s in teaout['sigma']] stusigmac = [min(max(s, a), b) for s in stuout['sigma']] lossdensity = sum((t - s) 2 for t, s in zip(teasigmac, stusigmac)) / len(teasigmac) # Other losses (volume-aligned, color) combined with specified rates lossother = lossdensity hyperparams['ratedensity'] # 2. Record image-level loss lossimg = [0.0] len(poses) for rayidx, poseidx in enumerate(batchrays['poseindices']): lossimg[poseidx] += lossrgb[rayidx] # 3. Backward pass totalloss = sum(lossrgb) hyperparams['ratergb'] + lossother optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 4. Select Important Sample Rays (TSR) sortedrayindices = sorted(range(len(lossrgb)), key=lambda i: lossrgb[i], reverse=True) nrays = len(batchrays) nimportantrays = int(nrays hyperparams['pctrays']) # 10% importantrayindices = sortedrayindices[:nimportantrays] # 5. Select Important Camera Poses (TCP) sortedposeindices = sorted(range(len(lossimg)), key=lambda i: lossimg[i], reverse=True) nposes = len(poses) nimportantposes = int(nposes hyperparams['pctposes']) # 10% importantposeindices = sortedposeindices[:nimportantposes] # 6. Select Important Sample Points (TSP) # Calculate point weights W = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) per point teaweights = [1.0 - math.exp(-teaout['sigma'][i] batchrays['delta'][i]) for i in range(len(teaout['sigma']))] stuweights = [1.0 - math.exp(-stuout['sigma'][i] batchrays['delta'][i]) for i in range(len(stuout['sigma']))] # Concatenate weights combinedweights = teaweights + stuweights # Select top N points npoints = len(teaweights) nimportantpoints = int(npoints hyperparams['pctpoints']) # 30% sortedpointindices = sorted(range(len(combinedweights)), key=lambda i: combinedweights[i], reverse=True) importantpointindices = sortedpointindices[:nimportantpoints] return { 'importantrays': importantrayindices, 'importantposes': importantposeindices, 'importantpoints': importantpointindices } Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Saturation: Optimizing \sigma directly on \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is inefficient because the gradient of the exponential function saturates easily, and computing exponentials increases calculation cost during block-wise implementation. The constrained density loss L{\sigma^2} is used to avoid this. Time Complexity: The active learning strategy adds overhead for sorting rays, poses, and points, and calculating point weights. By focusing computation on a subset of important samples (10% rays, 30% points), it improves the signal-to-noise ratio of gradient updates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing loss tensors for all rays and poses, and weight tensors for all sample points. This is O(N{rays}) and O(N{points}) respectively. Performance: PVD-AL yields student models that outperform those trained from scratch, breaking the upper limit of student capabilities. Strengths: Bridges the performance gap between teacher and student models; effectively transfers knowledge by focusing on challenging cases; flexible as a plugin for various methods. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained teacher model; adds complexity to the training loop with selection logic; performance depends on the quality of the teacher model. When to use: When distilling knowledge from a high-capacity teacher to a lower-capacity student, especially when the student struggles with specific views or details. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of selection is prohibitive, or when the teacher model is not significantly better than the student. The method originates from the "Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning for Efficient NeRF Architecture Conversion" paper. It was developed to address the inefficiencies and performance gaps in NeRF architecture conversion via distillation. The authors found that uniformly sampling data for distillation leads to suboptimal student performance, particularly under certain camera poses. By actively selecting challenging poses, rays, and points, the method improves the student's understanding of crucial knowledge. The approach has been validated on benchmark datasets using NVIDIA V100 GPUs, demonstrating significant advantages in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS metrics. name: Direct Matching Alignment Loss
head: Direct Alignment
body: Direct Matching Alignment Loss (L{align}) is a regularization term used during NeRF training to align a reference image with a set of surrogate views, thereby reducing overfitting and improving pose estimation accuracy. Unlike standard rendering losses that only compare rendered pixels against ground truth, this method enforces geometric consistency between different camera viewpoints by projecting 3D points from a reference view into surrogate views and comparing their appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference image Ir with pixel domain \Omega(Ir), camera intrinsics K (3 \times 3), rotation Rr (3 \times 3), translation \mathbf{t}r (3 \times 1); set of surrogate views \mathcal{N}r with poses (K, Rs, \mathbf{t}s); NeRF model parameters \Theta for depth estimation; depth threshold \deltad; Huber parameter \epsilon. Outputs: Scalar loss value L{align}. Data Structures: Pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} = [u, v]^T. Estimated depth \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) (scalar). Image intensities \mathcal{I}r(\mathbf{u}), \mathcal{I}s(\mathbf{u}s) (RGB vectors). Numbered Steps: 1. Sample Reference Frame and Points: Randomly select a reference frame r from the training set and pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} \in \Omega(Ir). Unless specified, the entire training set serves as \mathcal{N}r. 2. Estimate Reference Depth: Compute \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) as the weighted sum of sampled depths d{sample} along the ray, weighted by the ray termination distribution h: \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) = \sum {d{sample}} h(\mathbf{u},d{sample}) d{sample} 3. Project to Surrogate View: For each surrogate view s \in \mathcal{N}r, compute the corresponding pixel coordinate \mathbf{u}s by back-projecting \mathbf{u} to 3D using \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}), transforming to the surrogate camera frame, and projecting back to 2D: \mathbf{u}s = \Pi \left( K Rs \left( R{r}^{-1} K^{-1} [\mathbf{u}, 1]^T \bar {d}(\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{t}r \right) + \mathbf{t}s \right) where \Pi ([X,Y,Z]^T) = [X/Z, Y/Z]^T. 4. Check Occlusion (Visibility Indicator): Determine visibility using \mathcal{V}(\mathbf{u}s,\mathbf{u}): \mathcal{V}(\mathbf{u}s,\mathbf{u}) = \mathbbm {1}[ \bar {d}(\mathbf{u}s) < \mathcal {T}s (\mathbf{u}, \bar {d}(\mathbf{u})) - \delta d ] where \mathcal {T}s (\mathbf{u}, \bar {d}(\mathbf{u})) is the depth of the projected 3D point in the surrogate camera frame, calculated as the Z-component of the transformed point: \mathcal {T}s (\mathbf{u}, \bar {d}(\mathbf{u})) = \omega \left( K \left( Rs \left( R{r}^{-1} K^{-1} [\mathbf{u}, 1]^T \bar {d}(\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{t}r \right) + \mathbf{t}s \right) \right) and \omega ([X,Y,Z]^T) = Z. 5. Compute Alignment Loss: Sum the Huber penalty between \mathcal{I}{r}(\mathbf{u}) and \mathcal{I}s (\mathbf{u}s), weighted by visibility: L{align} = \sum {r=1}^{F} \sum {s \in \mathcal {N}r} \sum {\mathbf {u} \in \Omega (Ir)} \mathcal {V}(\mathbf {u}s,\mathbf {u}) \| \mathcal {I}s (\mathbf {u}s) - \mathcal {I}{r}(\mathbf {u}) \|\epsilon where \| \cdot \|\epsilon is the Huber penalty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedirectalignmentloss(Ir, K, Rr, tr, surrogateviews, nerfmodel, deltad, epsilon): """Computes Direct Matching Alignment Loss per.""" totalloss = 0.0 H, W = Ir.shape[:2] # Step 1: Sample pixels u on reference image for v in range(H): for u in range(W): # Step 2: Estimate depth d(u) dsamples = nerfmodel.getsampledepths((u, v), (K, Rr, tr)) hvalues = nerfmodel.getterminationdistribution((u, v), (K, Rr, tr)) dest = sum(h d for h, d in zip(hvalues, dsamples)) # Step 3: Project to surrogate view uhom = [u, v, 1.0] # Pcam = inv(K) @ uhom dest Pcam = vecscale(matvecmul(inv3x3(K), uhom), dest) # Pworld = Rr.T @ (Pcam - tr) Pworld = vecadd(vecscale(Rr.T, Pcam), vecscale(-Rr.T, tr)) for Is, Ks, Rs, ts in surrogateviews: # Transform to surrogate camera frame Pscam = vecadd(vecscale(Rs, Pworld), ts) if Pscam[2] <= 0: continue # Behind camera # Project to us us = [Pscam[0] / Pscam[2], Pscam[1] / Pscam[2]] if not isinbounds(us, Is.shape): continue # Step 4: Occlusion Reasoning # Ts is depth of projected point in surrogate frame Ts = Pscam[2] # Query NeRF at us in view s dsampless = nerfmodel.getsampledepths(us, (Ks, Rs, ts)) hvaluess = nerfmodel.getterminationdistribution(us, (Ks, Rs, ts)) dests = sum(h d for h, d in zip(hvaluess, dsampless)) vis = 1.0 if dests < (Ts - deltad) else 0.0 if vis > 0: # Step 5: Compute Loss Isus = bilinearsample(Is, us) Iru = Ir[v, u] diff = Isus - Iru totalloss += vis huberpenalty(diff, epsilon) return totalloss def huberpenalty(diff, epsilon): absdiff = abs(diff) return epsilon (absdiff - 0.5 epsilon) if absdiff > epsilon else 0.5 diff2 def bilinearsample(img, uv): u, v = uv u0, v0 = int(u), int(v) u1, v1 = min(u0 + 1, img.shape[1]-1), min(v0 + 1, img.shape[0]-1) wu, wv = u - u0, v - v0 top = img[v0, u0](1-wu) + img[v0, u1]wu bot = img[v1, u0](1-wu) + img[v1, u1]wu return top(1-wv) + botwv def isinbounds(uv, shape): return 0 <= uv[0] < shape[1] and 0 <= uv[1] < shape[0] def vecscale(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] def vecadd(v1, v2): return [a+b for a,b in zip(v1, v2)] def inv3x3(M): # Standard 3x3 matrix inversion invdet = 1.0 / (M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])) return [ [(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])invdet], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])invdet], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])invdet] ] def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] Parameters: \deltad: Depth threshold for occlusion reasoning. Value not given in the sources. \epsilon: Huber penalty parameter. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The projected pixel \mathbf{u}s is defined as the projection of the intersection point of the two rays by definition, ensuring geometric consistency for the occlusion check. Floating-point inaccuracies in depth estimation or projection can lead to incorrect occlusion decisions. Boundaries: Projected pixels \mathbf{u}s may fall outside the image boundaries of the surrogate view; these should be handled by skipping the pixel or assigning zero visibility. Degenerate Input: If the estimated depth \bar{d}(\mathbf{u}) is zero or negative, the back-projection is invalid; such rays should be skipped. This variant explicitly models visibility between views using a depth-based indicator. It calculates the depth of the 3D point projected from the reference view into the surrogate view and compares it with the NeRF's estimated depth at the corresponding pixel in the surrogate view. If the surrogate view's surface is closer than the projected point (minus a threshold \deltad), the point is considered occluded and excluded from the loss. This prevents the loss from penalizing the model for correct occlusions where the reference point is hidden in the surrogate view. This variant aligns the real-time camera viewpoint with the reconstructed model's observation vector to enhance spatial coherence and immersion. The alignment objective is defined as the squared L2 norm of the difference between perspective projections of the camera viewpoint V{cam} and the NeRF observation vector V{NeRF}: L{align} = \| \text{Proj}(V{cam}) - \text{Proj}(V{NeRF}) \|^2 where \text{Proj}(\cdot) is the perspective projection function. V{cam} is the real-time camera viewpoint from the user device, and V{NeRF} is the observation vector of the reconstructed model. This optimization improves spatial coherence between the user viewpoint and the virtual model, particularly for mobile and AR-enabled devices. Time Complexity: The loss calculation is O(F \cdot |\mathcal{N}r| \cdot |\Omega(Ir)|), where F is the number of reference frames, |\mathcal{N}r| is the number of surrogate views, and |\Omega(Ir)| is the number of pixels sampled. Since the entire training set is often used as surrogate views, this can be computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model and the training images, with no additional large data structures beyond the ray samples. Measured Performance: On the Fern sequence, using alignment increased PSNR from 23.06 to 24.50 and SSIM from 0.72 to 0.75. On the Trex sequence, it increased PSNR from 21.82 to 21.90 and SSIM from 0.76 to 0.78. Strengths: Reduces overfitting to training data, improves pose estimation, and enforces geometric consistency across views. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to cross-view projections and depth queries; relies on accurate depth estimation from the NeRF. When to use: When training NeRFs on datasets with significant overfitting or when pose estimation accuracy is critical. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or when the dataset is very large, making the O(N^2) cross-view comparison prohibitive. The Direct Matching Alignment Loss was proposed by R. Garg et al. in the paper "Direct Alignment for Robust NeRF Learning" presented at ACCV 2024. The work addresses the issue of NeRFs overfitting to training data, even with multiple views, by introducing a direct alignment term that encourages consistency between different camera viewpoints. The method builds on the standard NeRF rendering pipeline and integrates with the training loop using SGD. name: Volume Rendering Integration and Forward Pass
head: Alpha Compositing, Volume Rendering Integral Discretization, Ray Marching Integration
body: This family defines the forward pass that synthesizes a 2D image pixel color from a 3D implicit scene representation by integrating radiance along camera rays. It solves the problem of mapping a continuous 5D implicit function to a 2D image by discretizing the ray integral. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF Evaluation and Metric Calculation by focusing strictly on the geometric integration and compositing logic rather than loss computation or metric evaluation. All methods in this family compute the expected color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r by discretizing the medium interaction interval into steps and accumulating emission weighted by transmittance. The core mathematical formulation relies on the Beer-Lambert law to convert volume density \sigma into opacity \alpha and transmittance T. The discrete volume rendering equation is: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci Where: N is the number of samples along the ray. \sigmai is the volume density at sample i. ci is the emitted color at sample i. \deltai is the distance between sample i and i+1. Ti is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity of sample i. Numerical Stability: To prevent NaNs during gradient computation, a small epsilon \epsilon (typically 10^{-10}) is added to (1 - \alphaj) before the cumulative product or exponential calculation. Background Handling: If a background color c{bg} (typically white (1,1,1)) is assumed, the final color includes the contribution of rays that pass through the scene without terminating: \hat{C}{final}(r) = \hat{C}(r) + \left(1 - \sum{i=1}^{N} wi\right) c{bg} where wi = \alphai Ti is the weight of sample i. Depth Estimation: Expected depth \hat{D}(r) is computed analogously to color: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ti where ti is the distance of sample i from the camera origin. NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) is the forward pass method that synthesizes a 2D image pixel color from a 3D implicit scene representation by integrating radiance along camera rays. It solves the problem of differentiable volume rendering by approximating the continuous volume rendering integral as a discrete weighted sum, where weights are determined by the probability of the ray terminating at each sample point. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator by explicitly defining the standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) query pipeline, stratified sampling strategy, and the specific alpha-compositing formulation (\alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) that underpins the original NeRF architecture. This method computes the expected color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r by discretizing the medium interaction interval into fixed steps and accumulating emission weighted by transmittance. It differs from its sibling NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) by using a fixed-step marching loop with explicit throughput tracking and jittering, rather than bin-based stratified sampling. It is designed for dense grid-based media where direction-dependent emission is not required. This variant extends the standard forward pass by incorporating alpha masking and NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates) ray sampling. It handles rays that hit empty space in an alpha mask by marking them invalid. It adjusts distances by ray norm and normalizes view directions if NDC simulation is enabled. Density features are converted to sigma using feature2density if not component-wise, and alpha weights are computed using raw2alpha with distance scaling. The depth map is computed as a weighted sum of z-values, adjusted by background weight and ray direction Z component, and clamped if NDC Euclidean depth simulation is enabled. Not given in the sources. Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, https://github.com/Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing)
head: Alpha Compositing in NeRF, NeRF Integration, NeRF Rendering Equation, NeRF Rendering Process, Neural Radiance Field Volume Rendering
body: NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) is the differentiable forward pass that synthesizes a pixel's color and depth by integrating the volume density and emitted radiance predicted by a neural network along a camera ray. It solves the problem of mapping a continuous 5D implicit function (mapping spatial coordinates and view directions to density and color) to a 2D image by discretizing the ray integral. Unlike deterministic ray tracing which follows specific light paths, NeRF leverages a probabilistic density function to compute the expected color, handling view-dependent effects (non-Lambertian materials) that standard photogrammetry often assumes as diffuse. It sets itself apart from its sibling NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator by explicitly defining the standard alpha-compositing formulation with stratified sampling and background handling as the baseline for training and inference. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray r(t) = o + td, where o is the camera origin and d is the unit viewing direction. Near bound tn (camera center) and far bound tf (scene boundary). Number of samples N (typical value: 64 for both coarse and fine networks). Neural network model F\Theta (MLP) taking positional encoding of (x, d) and outputting density \sigma and color c. Optional background color c{bg}. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \hat{C}(r). Expected depth \hat{D}(r). Data Structures: Sample Points: Array of N distances ti along the ray. Predictions: Tensor of shape (N, 4) containing N samples, each with 3 RGB channels and 1 density channel. Deltas: Array of interval lengths \deltai = t{i+1} - ti for i=1 \dots N-1, plus a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) for the final segment to infinity. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the target image, generate a ray r(t) = o + td using the camera's intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. 2. Sampling: Divide the interval [tn, tf] into N equally spaced bins. Draw one sample ti uniformly at random from each bin (non-deterministic stratified sampling): ti \sim U\left[tn + \frac{i-1}{N}(tf - tn), tn + \frac{i}{N}(tf - tn)\right]. 3. Querying: For each sample point ti, compute the 3D position xi = o + ti d. Input xi and the ray direction d (often with positional encoding \gamma) into the MLP F\Theta to predict volume density \sigmai and color ci: [\sigmai, ci] = F\Theta(\gamma(xi), \gamma(d)). Apply ReLU to \sigmai and Sigmoid to ci to constrain ranges. 4. Delta Calculation: Compute the distance between adjacent samples: \deltai = t{i+1} - ti \quad \text{for } i=1 \dots N-1. Append a large value \delta\infty = 10^{10} (or tf - tN if bounded) for the last segment to handle rays that do not terminate within the scene. 5. Opacity Calculation: Compute the opacity \alphai for each sample using the Beer-Lambert law: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). 6. Transmittance Calculation: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti, representing the probability that the ray travels from tn to ti without being intercepted. Use a cumulative product with a small epsilon \epsilon (typically 10^{-10}) added to (1 - \alphaj) for numerical stability to prevent NaNs during gradient computation: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj + \epsilon). Note: T1 = 1. 7. Weight Calculation: Compute the weight wi for each sample, representing the probability that the ray terminates at sample i: wi = \alphai Ti. 8. Color Integration: Compute the final rendered color \hat{C}(r) as the weighted sum of colors: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci. 9. Background Handling (Optional): If a background color c{bg} is assumed, add the contribution of rays that pass through the scene without terminating. Let W = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi be the total accumulated opacity. The final color is: \hat{C}{final}(r) = \hat{C}(r) + (1 - W) c{bg}. 10. Depth Estimation: Compute the expected depth \hat{D}(r) analogously to color, using the sample distances ti as the value: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ti. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def nerfrendering(rayso, raysd, tvals, model, whitebackground=True, cbg=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), eps=1e-10): """ Render RGB and Depth for a batch of rays using NeRF alpha compositing. Args: rayso: (B, 3) Camera origins. raysd: (B, 3) Ray directions (unit vectors). tvals: (B, N) Sample distances along rays. model: Function that takes (points, directions) and returns (sigma, rgb). whitebackground: Boolean, whether to add background color. cbg: (3,) Background color. eps: Float, epsilon for numerical stability. Returns: rgb: (B, 3) Rendered colors. depth: (B,) Expected depths. """ B, N = tvals.shape # 1. Compute 3D points # points shape: (B, N, 3) points = rayso[:, np.newaxis,:] + raysd[:, np.newaxis,:] tvals[:,:, np.newaxis] # 2. Query model # model returns sigma (B, N) and rgb (B, N, 3) # Note: In practice, positional encoding is applied inside or before model call. # Here we assume model handles input or we pass raw coords. # For strict adherence to NeRF, positional encoding is applied to x and d. # We assume 'model' expects encoded inputs or handles them. # To be self-contained, we denote the query as: sigma, rgb = model(points, raysd) # 3. Apply activation functions if not done in model # sigma = np.maximum(sigma, 0) # ReLU # rgb = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-rgb)) # Sigmoid (if raw logits) # Assuming model outputs valid sigma >= 0 and rgb in [0,1] or logits. # Standard implementation applies sigmoid to rgb and relu to sigma. sigma = np.maximum(sigma, 0) rgb = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-rgb)) # 4. Compute deltas # deltas shape: (B, N-1) deltas = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] # Append infinity for the last segment # deltainf shape: (B, 1) deltainf = np.ones((B, 1)) 1e10 # Concatenate to get (B, N) deltas = np.concatenate([deltas, deltainf], axis=1) # 5. Compute opacity alpha # alpha shape: (B, N) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltas) # 6. Compute transmittance T # Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) # Use cumulative product with exclusive=True # (1 - alpha + eps) shape: (B, N) term = 1.0 - alpha + eps # cumprod along axis=1 (samples) # T shape: (B, N), T[:,0] = 1.0 T = np.cumprod(term, axis=1, exclusive=True) # 7. Compute weights # wi = alphai Ti # weights shape: (B, N) weights = alpha T # 8. Compute RGB # rgbfinal = sum(weights rgb) # weights needs to be broadcasted to (B, N, 1) rgbfinal = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] rgb, axis=1) # 9. Background handling if whitebackground: # Total opacity W = sum(weights) W = np.sum(weights, axis=1) # (B,) # Add (1 - W) cbg rgbfinal = rgbfinal + (1.0 - W[:, np.newaxis]) cbg[np.newaxis,:] # 10. Compute Depth # depth = sum(weights tvals) depth = np.sum(weights tvals, axis=1) return rgbfinal, depth Parameters: N: Number of samples per ray. Typical value: 64. \epsilon: Epsilon for stability. Typical value: 10^{-10}. c{bg}: Background color. tn, tf: Integration bounds. tn is camera center, tf is scene boundary. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: Without \epsilon, the cumulative product of (1-\alpha) can underflow to 0, causing NaNs in gradients. \epsilon = 10^{-10} is standard. Infinity Handling: The last segment \deltaN must be large enough to capture rays that exit the scene. Using 10^{10} ensures \alphaN \approx 1 if \sigmaN > 0, effectively terminating the ray. View-Dependent Effects: NeRF handles non-Lambertian materials by conditioning color on view direction d. Computational Cost: Original NeRF requires high computing power and long training times due to dense sampling and MLP queries. The complete workflow including data loading, ray generation, coarse/fine network sampling, and loss computation. Uses predicted depth maps to bias sample placement toward surfaces, reducing redundant sampling in free space. Uses rendered depth to warp images for consistency regularization, distinct from sampling strategies. Replaces uniform sampling with depth-prior guided stratified sampling to focus on likely surfaces. Uses SDFs instead of density, concentrating weight at the zero-level set for precise surface extraction. Models blur as a distribution of rays using a two-stage module. Approximates integrated positional encoding by treating rays as cones to solve aliasing. Simulates event camera data for motion blur supervision. A method for scaling NeRF rendering across multiple GPUs. It performs global composition by aggregating transmittance and color contributions from segments processed on different GPUs. Step: Initialize global transmittance T{1 \to i} = 1 and global color C{1 \to N+1} = 0. For each segment s in the GPU order list I, if the segment's GPU i \neq k (current GPU), gather T{i \to i+1} and C{i \to i+1}. Update global color: C{1 \to N+1} += T{1 \to i} \times C{i \to i+1}. Update global transmittance: T{1 \to i^} = T{i \to i+1}. Pitfall: During inference, data gathering is only required on a single GPU (e.g., GPU 0) to render the final image, reducing data transfer compared to training. Approximates the volume rendering integral by summing contributions from sampled spheres inside the cone using numerical quadrature. Formula: \text{Color} = \sumi Ti (1 - \exp(-\text{density}i (t{i+1} - ti))) \text{color}i, with Ti = \exp(-\sum{k<i} \text{density}k (t{k+1} - tk)). A rendering procedure using RM-LSTM to predict a single intersection point and output RGB directly, skipping volume rendering. Step: Extract latent features from PixelNeRF CNN encoder, feed into RM-LSTM. RM-LSTM predicts step length and updates depth for 10 steps with 512 feature channels. Pass final depth point through PixelNeRF network to obtain RGB. Comparison: ~80 times faster than baseline but slightly lower quality (PSNR 23.02 vs 23.34). Maps low-resolution feature maps to final images using upsampling and 2D convolution to alleviate multi-view inconsistent artifacts. Formula: \text{Upsample}(X) = \text{Conv2D}(Y, K), where Y = \text{Pixelshuffle}(\text{repeat}(X, 4) + \beta\zeta(X), 2). Parameter: Convolution kernel size is 1x1 to avoid multi-view inconsistencies. Real-time NeRF-based parametric head model inference. Step: Sample 64 points per ray, compute volume rendering to get feature map IF, pass IF through 2D neural rendering module (upsampling + 1x1 Conv) to get final image I. Performance: >40 fps on NVIDIA 3090 GPU. Extracts 3D point-cloud data by estimating depth where transmittance changes significantly. Formula: t{surface} \approx \arg \mint \left| \frac{dT(t)}{dt} \right|. Produces approximate rendering (RGB and features) at a target pose using input images. Step: Pass N input images through 2D U-Net to create feature images. Cast rays, sample 128 points (uniform up to distance 1, then linear in disparity). Reproject 3D points into input cameras, gather features. Append positionally-encoded 3D locations and statistics. Layout: Output tensor 64x64x131 (3 RGB + 128 features). Standard NeRF rendering using coarse and fine sampling. Step: Discretize integral using stratified sampling. Coarse sampling uses uniform distribution. Fine sampling uses volume density weights. Loss: Sum of squared errors for coarse and fine samples against ground truth. Models image motion blur by discretizing exposure time into p poses, rendering sharp images, and averaging them. Parameter: p (number of poses), typical value 5. Pitfall: Assumes uniform motion or linear interpolation for intermediate poses. Measured Performance: Original NeRF is slow; Instant NGP reduces processing time significantly using multi-resolution hash encoding. HeadNeRF achieves >40 fps on NVIDIA 3090 with 2D neural rendering module. Strengths: Handles view-dependent effects, high-quality novel view synthesis, fine details. Limitations: High computational cost, neither a point cloud nor a mesh (continuous voxels). When to Use: When high-quality novel view synthesis is required, especially for complex scenes with view-dependent effects. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical without acceleration techniques, or when explicit geometry (mesh/point cloud) is required. NeRF was first presented by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It represents a static scene as a continuous 5D function outputting volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance. The method was initially presented at CVPR 2020. Subsequent developments include Instant NGP by Müller et al. (2022) which introduced multi-resolution hash encoding. It is used in Cultural Heritage for reconstruction of metallic, translucent, and transparent surfaces. Implemented in platforms like Instant NGP, Nerfstudio, and Luma AI. name: NeRF Rendering Pipeline
head: NeRF Rendering Path
body: The NeRF Rendering Pipeline generates novel views from a trained neural radiance field by iterating over a sequence of camera poses, invoking the volume rendering primitive for each, and assembling the outputs. It handles resolution scaling, metric computation, and image I/O, differing from the core NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) method by managing the external pose traversal loop rather than the per-ray integration itself. Inputs: renderposes: Array of camera-to-world matrices. H, W: Integer height and width of the target image. focal: Scalar focal length in pixels. renderkwargs: Dictionary containing the model and rendering configuration passed to the volume renderer. renderfactor: Integer downsampling factor (default 0, meaning no downsampling). chunk: Integer number of rays to process in parallel (default 32768). gtimgs: Optional array of ground truth images for PSNR calculation. savedir: Optional directory path to save rendered images. Outputs: rgbs: List or array of rendered RGB images. disps: List or array of rendered depth/disparity maps. Data Structures: rgbs: List of numpy arrays, each shape (H', W', 3), where H' = H/render\factor and W' = W/render\factor. disps: List of numpy arrays, each shape (H', W'). Steps: 1. Initialize Output Containers: Create empty lists rgbs and disps. 2. Iterate Poses: For each camera pose c2w in renderposes: a. Downsample Resolution: If renderfactor != 0, downsample H, W, and focal by dividing by renderfactor before rendering. b. Render: Call the volume rendering function with arguments (H, W, focal, chunk, c2w, \text{render\kwargs}) to get rgb and disp. c. Store Results: Append rgb.numpy() to rgbs and disp.numpy() to disps. d. Compute PSNR (Optional): If gtimgs is not None and renderfactor == 0, compute PSNR = -10 \log{10}(\text{MSE}) where \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum (rgb - gt\img)^2. e. Save Image (Optional): If savedir is not None, convert rgb to 8-bit with to8b(), save as '{:03d}.png' using imageio.imwrite. 3. Return: Stack rgbs and disps along axis 0 and return them. Formulas: Rendered Color: \hat{C}(p) = \sumi Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci, where Ti = e^{-\sumj \deltaj}, \deltai is the interval between neighboring sampling points (often constant). PSNR: PSNR = -10 \log{10}(\text{MSE}). Parameters: renderfactor: Controls rendering speed vs. resolution. Typical values: 4 or 8 for previews. Default: 0. chunk: Controls memory usage during rendering. Default: 32768. Decrease if out-of-memory errors occur. MLP Structure: The underlying INR typically uses a large MLP (8 × 256 network structure) with 10 Fourier bases in the Positional Encoding (PE). Edge Cases: Memory Limits: If chunk is too large for the GPU, the rendering call may fail; reduce chunk size. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpipeline(renderposes, H, W, focal, renderkwargs, renderfactor=0, chunk=32768, gtimgs=None, savedir=None): rgbs = [] disps = [] for i, c2w in enumerate(renderposes): h, w, f = H, W, focal if renderfactor != 0: h = h // renderfactor w = w // renderfactor f = f / renderfactor rgb, disp = render(h, w, f, chunk=chunk, c2w=c2w[:3,:4], renderkwargs) rgbs.append(rgb.numpy()) disps.append(disp.numpy()) if gtimgs is not None and renderfactor == 0: mse = np.mean(np.square(rgb - gtimgs[i])) psnr = -10.0 np.log10(mse) if savedir is not None: imageio.imwrite(f'{savedir}/{i:03d}.png', to8b(rgb)) return np.stack(rgbs, axis=0), np.stack(disps, axis=0) ViiNeuS Hybrid Volume Rendering is a progressive training strategy for implicit neural surface reconstruction that transitions from pure volumetric density representation to signed distance field (SDF) representation during the optimization loop. It solves the initialization instability and slow convergence of pure SDF methods in complex scenes by initially leveraging a robust volumetric estimator, then gradually introducing SDF-based alpha compositing. Unlike standard NeRF rendering which uses only density-based alpha, or pure NeuS which uses only SDF-based alpha, this method dynamically assigns each sample's alpha value to either \alpha^{iv} or \alpha^{if} based on training stage and sample density, ensuring stable surface extraction. Sample and Blend Rendering generates a ray's final color by querying N nearby local MLPs (nerflets) and blending their outputs using spatial influence weights. For a ray sample k at (pos, dir), it queries N nerflet MLPs fi to get density \sigma{k,i} and color c{k,i}, then computes nerflet influence activation w(x) = \text{SoftMax}([\sigma1 g1(x), \dots, \sigmaN gN(x)]) to determine dominant nerflet contribution. The final ray color is \hat{C}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak ck, where Tk = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1-\alphaj). Semantic images are generated by averaging per-nerflet semantic logit vectors in the same weighted manner, while instance labels are assigned via \text{argmax}i w(r) or \text{argmax}i W(r) (accumulated influence map). The underlying INR uses an 8×256 MLP with 10 Fourier bases, resulting in long training and rendering times. Memory Complexity: Scales with chunk size and resolution; the default chunk=32768 balances VRAM usage and throughput. Performance: Rendering speed is directly proportional to the number of rays processed. Downsampling by renderfactor reduces the ray count by render\factor^2, significantly accelerating preview generation. Strengths: Modular pipeline that cleanly separates pose traversal, I/O, and metric computation from the per-ray volume integration primitive. Limitations: Not optimized for real-time inference; relies on batched ray processing and large MLPs that constrain throughput. The pipeline structure follows the evaluation and novel view synthesis workflow of the original NeRF implementation. The underlying volume rendering primitive models the attributes of a light ray in 3D space as an implicit neural representation (INR), taking ray position and direction as input to output color and density, which are then integrated via ray marching. name: ViiNeuS Hybrid Volume Rendering
head: Hybrid alpha composition, ViiNeuS Volume Rendering
body: ViiNeuS Hybrid Volume Rendering is a progressive training strategy for implicit neural surface reconstruction that transitions from pure volumetric density representation to signed distance field (SDF) representation during the optimization loop. It solves the initialization instability and slow convergence of pure SDF methods in complex scenes by initially leveraging a robust volumetric estimator, then gradually introducing SDF-based alpha compositing. Unlike standard NeRF rendering which uses only density-based alpha, or pure NeuS which uses only SDF-based alpha, this method dynamically assigns each sample's alpha value to either \alpha^{iv} or \alpha^{if} based on training stage and sample density, ensuring stable surface extraction. Inputs: Ray r defined by origin and direction. Sample points xi along the ray. Network outputs for each sample xi: Density \sigmai (from MLP F^h\Theta). Signed Distance Field value f(xi) (from MLP F^h\Theta). Color ci (from MLP F^c\Theta, using direction, latent vector, and normal). Current training step t and total training steps T{total}. Outputs: Rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r). The method relies on two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Geometry MLP (F^h\Theta): Input: Positional embedding embx(x). Output: Tuple (\sigma, f(x), h), where \sigma is density, f(x) is SDF value, and h is a latent vector. Architecture: 2 layers, 64 hidden units. 2. Color MLP (F^c\Theta): Input: Directional embedding embd(d), latent vector h, and normal vector -\vec{n}. Output: Color c. Architecture: 2 layers, 64 hidden units. Normal \vec{n} is computed as the gradient of the SDF: \vec{n} = \nabla f(x). Volumetric Stage Duration: First 100 training steps. Hybrid Stage End: 35% of total training time (0.35 \times T{total}). Sharpness Parameter (s): Controls the standard deviation of the SDF density distribution \phis (std = 1/s). It is regularized during training with weight decay from 10^{-3} to 10^{-5}. Sample Spacing (\deltai): Distance between adjacent samples along the ray. 1. Volumetric Alpha (\alpha^{iv}): Computed from predicted density \sigmai and sample spacing \deltai: \alpha^{iv} = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) 2. SDF-based Alpha (\alpha^{if}): Computed using the sigmoid function \Phis and its derivative \phis. Let \Phis(z) = (1 + e^{-sz})^{-1} and \phis(z) = \frac{se^{-sz}}{(1 + e^{-sz})^2}. For sample i at position pi and next sample i+1 at p{i+1}, the alpha is: \alpha^{if} = \max\left( \frac{\Phis(f(pi)) - \Phis(f(p{i+1}))}{\Phis(f(pi))}, 0 \right) 3. Final Rendered Color: Alpha compositing along the ray: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci where: wi = Ti \alphai is the weight of sample i. Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance. \alphai is the blending factor, determined by the training stage (see Steps). 1. Determine Training Stage: If current step t < 100: Volumetric Stage. If 100 \le t < 0.35 \times T{total}: Hybrid Stage. If t \ge 0.35 \times T{total}: Surface Stage. 2. Compute Network Outputs: For each sample xi on the ray: Compute embx(xi) using hash encoding. Query F^h\Theta(embx(xi)) to get \sigmai, f(xi), hi. Compute normal \vec{n}i = \nabla f(xi). SDF-Gradient Normalization: During the Hybrid Stage, normalize \vec{n}i to prevent large gradient values from compensating for alpha distribution differences. Let \vec{n}'i = \frac{\vec{n}i}{\|\vec{n}i\|}. Compute embd(d) using spherical harmonics. Query F^c\Theta(embd(d), hi, -\vec{n}'i) to get color ci. 3. Assign Alpha Value (\alphai): Volumetric Stage: Set \alphai = \alpha^{iv}i for all samples. Hybrid Stage: Identify samples with the highest predicted density values \sigmai. Assign \alphai = \alpha^{if}i to these high-density samples to facilitate SDF initialization near the surface. Assign \alphai = \alpha^{iv}i to the remaining samples. Note: The exact probability or threshold for "highest density" is not explicitly defined in the provided text, but the strategy is to prioritize high-density samples for SDF training. Surface Stage: Set \alphai = \alpha^{if}i for all samples. 4. Compute Transmittance and Weights: Initialize T1 = 1. For i = 1 to N: wi = Ti \alphai. T{i+1} = Ti (1 - \alphai). 5. Accumulate Color: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viineusvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, spacing, trainingstep, totalsteps, geometrymlp, colormlp, sparam): """ Renders a single ray using ViiNeuS hybrid volume rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector ray origin. raydirection: 3D vector ray direction. numsamples: Number of samples N along the ray. spacing: Distance deltai between adjacent samples. trainingstep: Current integer training step. totalsteps: Total number of training steps. geometrymlp: Function F^hTheta taking positional embedding. colormlp: Function F^cTheta taking direction embedding, latent, normal. sparam: Sharpness parameter s for sigmoid. Returns: renderedcolor: 3D vector color for the ray. """ N = numsamples renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 # Determine stages isvolumetricstage = trainingstep < 100 ishybridstage = 100 <= trainingstep < 0.35 totalsteps issurfacestage = trainingstep >= 0.35 totalsteps # Pre-compute geometry outputs for all samples sampledata = [] for i in range(N): # Compute sample position xi = rayorigin + (i spacing) raydirection # Get positional embedding (hash encoding) embx = hashencoding(xi) # Query Geometry MLP sigma, fx, h = geometrymlp(embx) # Compute normal from SDF gradient gradf = numericalgradient(lambda p: geometrymlp(hashencoding(p))[1], xi) normal = normalizevector(gradf) sampledata.append({ 'sigma': sigma, 'fx': fx, 'h': h, 'normal': normal, 'x': xi }) # Determine which samples get SDF alpha in hybrid stage alphaassignments = [] if ishybridstage: # Assign alphaif to samples with highest predicted density sortedindices = sorted(range(N), key=lambda k: sampledata[k]['sigma'], reverse=True) # Exact threshold for "highest density" not specified in sources thresholdindex = N // 2 highdensityindices = set(sortedindices[:thresholdindex]) for i in range(N): data = sampledata[i] sigmai = data['sigma'] fxi = data['fx'] normali = data['normal'] # Compute deltai deltai = spacing if i < N - 1 else 0.0 # Compute Volumetric Alpha alphaiv = 1.0 - exp(-sigmai deltai) # Compute SDF Alpha if i < N - 1: fxnext = sampledata[i+1]['fx'] else: fxnext = fxi deltai = 0.0 # Effectively alphaif will be 0 for last sample # Sigmoid function Phis phisfxi = sigmoid(fxi, sparam) phisfxnext = sigmoid(fxnext, sparam) # Alphaif formula if phisfxi > 1e-6: alphaif = max((phisfxi - phisfxnext) / phisfxi, 0.0) else: alphaif = 0.0 # Assign Alpha based on Stage if isvolumetricstage: alphai = alphaiv elif issurfacestage: alphai = alphaif else: # Hybrid Stage if i in highdensityindices: alphai = alphaif else: alphai = alphaiv # Compute Weight weighti = accumulatedtransmittance alphai renderedcolor += weighti getcolorfromdata(data, raydirection) # Update Transmittance accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alphai) # Early exit if transmittance is negligible if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break return renderedcolor def sigmoid(z, s): return 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-s z)) def normalizevector(v): norm = sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) if norm == 0: return v return [x/norm for x in v] def getcolorfromdata(data, direction): # Query Color MLP embd = sphericalharmonics(direction) h = data['h'] normal = data['normal'] # Note: Source says input is -n negnormal = [-n for n in normal] return colormlp(embd, h, negnormal) def hashencoding(x): # Standard positional encoding implementation return x def sphericalharmonics(d): # Standard spherical harmonics encoding implementation return d def numericalgradient(func, x, eps=1e-4): # Numerical gradient computation grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): xplus = x.copy() xplus[i] += eps xminus = x.copy() xminus[i] -= eps grad[i] = (func(xplus) - func(xminus)) / (2 eps) return grad Large SDF Gradients: During the hybrid stage, the SDF gradient can become large, causing \alpha^{if} to align incorrectly with \alpha^{iv}. This is addressed by normalizing the SDF gradient before computing \alpha^{if}. SDF Initialization: Pure SDF initialization assumes full scene observability and a centered region of interest, which may not hold for outdoor/autonomous driving scenes. The hybrid strategy mitigates this by starting with volumetric density. Parameter s: The sharpness parameter s controls the standard deviation of the density distribution. It is regularized during training to stabilize convergence. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N per ray, O(N), as each sample requires a forward pass through two MLPs and alpha computation. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to N to store intermediate values (sigma, f(x), h, normal) for all samples along the ray. Performance: The method is evaluated on autonomous driving datasets (KITTI-360, nuScenes, Waymo, Pandaset). It uses a single high-tier GPU with Adam optimizer. Strengths: Faster convergence of the density estimator by starting with pure volumetric representation. Robust SDF initialization in complex scenes with wide distance ranges and complex geometries by sampling near the surface. Stable transition from volumetric to surface representation. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the hybrid stage transition (35% of training time) and the probability-based sample association strategy. Relies on the accuracy of the SDF gradient for normal computation and alpha calculation. When to Use: Suitable for implicit neural surface reconstruction in urban/outdoor scenes with limited image overlap where pure SDF initialization is unstable. When Not to Use: Not necessary for scenes with full observability and simple geometry where pure SDF (NeuS) or pure Volumetric (NeRF) methods converge reliably. Origin: ViiNeuS was introduced in the paper "ViiNeuS: Volumetric Initialization for Implicit Neural Surface reconstruction of urban scenes with limited image overlap". History: The method builds upon NeuS, which introduced SDF-based volume rendering for neural rendering. ViiNeuS extends this by introducing a hybrid training strategy to address initialization issues in challenging environments like autonomous driving scenarios. Usage: It is used for 3D scene reconstruction from images, specifically targeting outdoor/urban datasets such as KITTI-360, nuScenes, Waymo Open Dataset, and Pandaset. The final mesh is generated using Marching Cubes.
