name: MipNerfModel
head: Mip-NeRF 360 Model
body: The MipNerfModel is a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture that approximates integrated positional encoding by treating rays as cones or cylinders rather than infinitesimally thin lines, thereby solving aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency scene details. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by using multi-level sampling (coarse and fine) and integrated positional encoding to model the frequency content of the signal along the ray, which is essential for training on unbounded, outdoor scenes. The model implements a differentiable rendering pipeline that processes rays defined by origins, directions, radii, and viewing parameters. It utilizes a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict density and color, conditioned on integrated positional encodings of the sampled points. Inputs: rays: A structure containing: origins: 3D coordinates of ray origins. directions: Normalized ray direction vectors. viewdirs: View direction vectors, explicitly passed for conditioning. radii: The radius of the ray at the sample points (used for integrated encoding). near: Near plane distance for each ray. far: Far plane distance for each ray. temperature: Camera temperature parameter for ISP. exposure: Camera exposure parameter for ISP. coc: Circle of Confusion parameter (used to scale ray radii during training). rng: Random number generator state. whitebkgd: Boolean indicating if the background is white (affects alpha compositing). traincoc: Circle of Confusion multiplier for ray radii during training. randomized: Boolean indicating whether to use randomized sampling. Outputs: comprgb: Computed RGB color per ray. distance: Expected distance along the ray. acc: Accumulated alpha (opacity) along the ray. weights: Per-sample weights used for resampling in subsequent levels. The rays object holds batched arrays: origins: Shape (B, 3) directions: Shape (B, 3) viewdirs: Shape (B, 3) radii: Shape (B,) initially, representing the radius at the pixel, scaled by coc. near: Shape (B,) far: Shape (B,) numsamples: int, number of samples per level. Default: 128. numlevels: int, number of sampling levels (coarse and fine). Default: 2. resamplepadding: float, Dirichlet/alpha padding added to weights before normalization during resampling. Default: 0.01. stoplevelgrad: bool, if True, gradients do not backpropagate across levels. Default: True. useviewdirs: bool, if True, view directions are used as a condition for the MLP. Default: True. lindisp: bool, if True, sampling is linear in disparity (1/z) rather than depth (z). Default: False. rayshape: str, shape of cast rays, must be 'cone' or 'cylinder'. Default: 'cone'. mindegpoint: int, minimum degree of positional encoding for 3D points. Default: 0. maxdegpoint: int, maximum degree of positional encoding for 3D points. Default: 16. degview: int, degree of positional encoding for view directions. Default: 4. densityactivation: Callable, density activation function. Default: softplus. densitynoise: float, standard deviation of noise added to raw density. Default: 0.0. densitybias: float, shift added to raw densities pre-activation. Default: -1.0. rgbactivation: Callable, RGB activation function. Default: sigmoid. rgbpadding: float, padding added to RGB outputs. Default: 0.001. disableintegration: bool, if True, use Point-wise Positional Encoding instead of Integrated Positional Encoding. Default: False. 1. Initialization: Initialize the MLP and Image Signal Processing (ISP) modules. Create an empty result list ret. 2. Level Loop: Iterate ilevel from 0 to numlevels - 1. 3. Randomness: Split the random number generator rng into key and a new rng. 4. Sampling: If ilevel == 0 (Coarse): Perform stratified sampling along rays. Calculate effective radius: effectiveradius = rays.radii traincoc. Call samplealongrays(key, rays.origins, rays.directions, effectiveradius, numsamples, rays.near, rays.far, randomized, lindisp, rayshape). This returns tvals (sample positions along the ray) and samples (3D coordinates and radii at those positions). If ilevel > 0 (Fine): Resample along rays based on previous weights. Call resamplealongrays(key, rays.origins, rays.directions, effectiveradius, tvals, weights, randomized, rayshape, stoplevelgrad, resamplepadding). This returns updated tvals and samples. 5. Integration Check: If disableintegration is True, replace samples with (samples[0], jnp.zeroslike(samples[1])) to disable integrated encoding (effectively reverting to point-wise PE). 6. Positional Encoding: Compute integrated positional encoding for the 3D samples using integratedposenc(samples, mindegpoint, maxdegpoint). This function accounts for the cone/cylinder shape of the ray segment by integrating the standard positional encoding over the interval defined by the sample's radius. If useviewdirs is True, compute view direction encoding using posenc(rays.viewdirs, mindeg=0, maxdeg=degview, appendidentity=True). 7. MLP Forward Pass: Concatenate point encoding and view direction encoding (if used) to form the input to the MLP. The MLP outputs rawdensity and rawrgb. If randomized is True and densitynoise > 0, add Gaussian noise: rawdensity += densitynoise random.normal(key, rawdensity.shape, dtype=rawdensity.dtype). 8. Activations: Apply RGB activation: rgb = rgbactivation(rawrgb). Apply RGB padding: rgb = rgb (1 + 2 rgbpadding) - rgbpadding. Apply density activation: density = densityactivation(rawdensity + densitybias). 9. Volume Rendering: Perform volumetric rendering using volumetricrendering(rgb, density, tvals, rays.directions, whitebkgd). This step computes the final color comprgb, expected distance, accumulated alpha acc, and per-sample weights weights using alpha compositing. 10. ISP: Apply the learned Image Signal Processing pipeline to comprgb using isp(comprgb, rays.temperature, rays.exposure) to get rgbout. 11. Result Storage: Append (rgbout, distance, acc) to ret. 12. Return: Return the list ret. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp import jax.random as random from typing import Tuple, List, Any, Callable def samplealongrays(key, origins, directions, radii, numsamples, near, far, randomized, lindisp, rayshape): """Stratified sampling along rays. Returns tvals and samples (points, radii).""" pass def resamplealongrays(key, origins, directions, radii, tvals, weights, randomized, rayshape, stoplevelgrad, resamplepadding): """Resampling based on previous weights. Returns updated tvals and samples.""" pass def integratedposenc(samples, mindeg, maxdeg): """Integrates positional encoding over the cone/cylinder defined by samples.""" pass def posenc(dirs, mindeg, maxdeg, appendidentity): """Standard positional encoding for view directions.""" pass def volumetricrendering(rgb, density, tvals, directions, whitebkgd): """Alpha compositing along rays. Returns comprgb, distance, acc, weights.""" pass def isp(rgb, temperature, exposure): """Image Signal Processing for tone mapping and color correction.""" pass class MipNerfModel: def init( self, numsamples: int = 128, numlevels: int = 2, resamplepadding: float = 0.01, stoplevelgrad: bool = True, useviewdirs: bool = True, lindisp: bool = False, rayshape: str = 'cone', mindegpoint: int = 0, maxdegpoint: int = 16, degview: int = 4, densityactivation: Callable = jnp.softplus, densitynoise: float = 0.0, densitybias: float = -1.0, rgbactivation: Callable = jnp.sigmoid, rgbpadding: float = 0.001, disableintegration: bool = False,): self.numsamples = numsamples self.numlevels = numlevels self.resamplepadding = resamplepadding self.stoplevelgrad = stoplevelgrad self.useviewdirs = useviewdirs self.lindisp = lindisp self.rayshape = rayshape self.mindegpoint = mindegpoint self.maxdegpoint = maxdegpoint self.degview = degview self.densityactivation = densityactivation self.densitynoise = densitynoise self.densitybias = densitybias self.rgbactivation = rgbactivation self.rgbpadding = rgbpadding self.disableintegration = disableintegration def call( self, rays: Any, rng: Any, traincoc: float = 1.0, whitebkgd: bool = False, randomized: bool = True,) -> List[Tuple[Any, Any, Any]]: ret = [] effectiveradii = rays.radii traincoc prevtvals = None prevweights = None for ilevel in range(self.numlevels): key, rng = random.split(rng) if ilevel == 0: tvals, samples = samplealongrays( key=key, origins=rays.origins, directions=rays.directions, radii=effectiveradii, numsamples=self.numsamples, near=rays.near, far=rays.far, randomized=randomized, lindisp=self.lindisp, rayshape=self.rayshape,) else: tvals, samples = resamplealongrays( key=key, origins=rays.origins, directions=rays.directions, radii=effectiveradii, tvals=prevtvals, weights=prevweights, randomized=randomized, rayshape=self.rayshape, stoplevelgrad=self.stoplevelgrad, resamplepadding=self.resamplepadding,) if self.disableintegration: samples = (samples[0], jnp.zeroslike(samples[1])) pointencoding = integratedposenc(samples, self.mindegpoint, self.maxdegpoint) if self.useviewdirs: viewencoding = posenc(rays.viewdirs, mindeg=0, maxdeg=self.degview, appendidentity=True) mlpinput = jnp.concatenate([pointencoding, viewencoding], axis=-1) else: mlpinput = pointencoding rawdensity, rawrgb = self.mlp(mlpinput) if randomized and self.densitynoise > 0: rawdensity += self.densitynoise random.normal(key, rawdensity.shape, dtype=rawdensity.dtype) rgb = self.rgbactivation(rawrgb) rgb = rgb (1 + 2 self.rgbpadding) - self.rgbpadding density = self.densityactivation(rawdensity + self.densitybias) comprgb, distance, acc, weights = volumetricrendering( rgb=rgb, density=density, tvals=tvals, directions=rays.directions, whitebkgd=whitebkgd,) rgbout = isp(comprgb, rays.temperature, rays.exposure) ret.append((rgbout, distance, acc)) prevtvals = tvals prevweights = weights return ret Precision: The integrated positional encoding involves integration over the cone/cylinder. Numerical stability depends on the radius size. Very small radii may lead to precision issues in the integration. Boundaries: The near and far planes must be correctly set for each ray. Incorrect bounds can lead to sampling outside the scene or missing geometry. Degenerate Input: If radii are zero (e.g., at the camera origin), the cone shape degenerates to a line. The integratedposenc function should handle this gracefully, typically by falling back to point-wise encoding or ensuring the integration interval is non-zero. Gradient Flow: If stoplevelgrad is True, gradients do not flow from the fine level to the coarse level. This is a design choice to stabilize training but must be respected in the implementation. Uses depth estimates to guide sample placement, focusing on areas of interest. Depth-Guided Sampling Combines stratified sampling with depth priors for more efficient sampling. Depth-Prior Guided Stratified Sampling Estimates blur parameters to improve rendering quality in out-of-focus regions. Progressive Blur Estimation Time Complexity: O(L \cdot N), where L is the number of levels and N is the number of samples per level. The integrated positional encoding adds a constant factor overhead per sample. Memory Complexity: O(L \cdot N) for storing samples, encodings, and intermediate rendering results. Measured Performance: The model is designed for unbounded, outdoor scenes (Mip-NeRF 360 dataset). It provides higher quality images with fewer artifacts compared to standard NeRF, especially at high frequencies. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of samples and levels. Strengths: Reduces aliasing, handles high-frequency details better, suitable for unbounded scenes. Limitations: More complex implementation, slightly higher computational cost per sample due to integration. When to Use: When training on unbounded scenes or scenes with high-frequency details where standard NeRF exhibits aliasing. When Not to Use: For simple, bounded scenes with low-frequency content, standard NeRF may be sufficient and faster. The MipNerfModel was introduced in the Mip-NeRF paper by Barron et al. (2021) and extended in Mip-NeRF 360 (Barron et al., 2022). It addresses the issue of aliasing in NeRF by modeling rays as cones/cylinders and integrating positional encodings over these volumes. https://github.com/CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF, https://github.com/CPREgroup/CaSE-NeRF, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Event Simulation from NeRF
head: Log-Difference Event Model, Virtual Event Generation
body: Event Simulation from NeRF generates virtual event data from a NeRF model to supervise training using real event camera observations. It solves the problem of motion blur in NeRF reconstruction by modeling the temporal integration of light during camera exposure. It differs from sibling methods like Depth-Guided Sampling by explicitly simulating asynchronous event streams rather than static depth or color, allowing for event-driven bundle adjustment to refine camera poses and recover sharp geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: NeRF model parameters \theta, a set of p evenly sampled poses \{Ti\}{i=1}^p representing the camera trajectory during exposure, and real event data E(x, ti, t{i+1}). Outputs: Virtual event count \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) and gradients for optimizing \theta and Ti. Data Structures: Poses: Ti \in SE(3), learnable variables representing camera poses at time ti. Events: E(x, ti, t{i+1}) is the count of real events at pixel x between time ti and t{i+1}. Log-Intensity: \mathcal{L}(T, x), the log-transformed grayscale intensity of the rendered image at pose T and pixel x. Steps: 1. Render Sharp Images: For each sampled pose Ti, render the color C(Ti, x) using standard volume rendering (see NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing)). 2. Convert to Grayscale: Average the RGB channels of C(Ti, x) to obtain grayscale intensity G(Ti, x). 3. Log Transform: Compute log-intensity \mathcal{L}(Ti, x) = \log(G(Ti, x)). 4. Simulate Events: Calculate the virtual event count \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) using the log-difference model. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the L2 loss between virtual and real events. Formulas: The virtual event count is defined as: \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) = \begin{cases} \frac{\mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) - \mathcal{L}(Ti, x)}{\Theta} & \text{if } \mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) \le \mathcal{L}(Ti, x) \\ \frac{\mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) - \mathcal{L}(Ti, x)}{\Theta} & \text{if } \mathcal{L}(T{i+1}, x) > \mathcal{L}(Ti, x) \end{cases} The source formula presents identical expressions for both cases, implying a linear difference scaled by \Theta. The threshold \Theta acts as a scaling factor for the log-intensity change. Parameters: \Theta: Event generation threshold. Typical value: 0.3. p: Number of sampled poses. Typical value: 5. \lambda: Weight for event loss. Typical value: 0.005. Pitfalls: Event loss is calculated only between adjacent poses (ti, t{i+1}). Calculating between non-adjacent poses causes fluctuation and instability. A coarse initial pose is required for each view to start training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simulateevents(nerfmodel, poses, theta): """ Simulates virtual events from NeRF renders. Args: nerfmodel: Function rendering color C(T, x) given pose T and pixel x. poses: List of p SE(3) poses [T1,..., Tp]. theta: Event threshold (0.3). Returns: virtualevents: List of tensors of shape (H, W) containing simulated event counts. """ virtualevents = [] for i in range(len(poses) - 1): Tcurr = poses[i] Tnext = poses[i+1] # Render sharp images for current and next pose Ccurr = nerfmodel.render(Tcurr) Cnext = nerfmodel.render(Tnext) # Convert to grayscale by averaging RGB channels Gcurr = (Ccurr[..., 0] + Ccurr[..., 1] + Ccurr[..., 2]) / 3.0 Gnext = (Cnext[..., 0] + Cnext[..., 1] + Cnext[..., 2]) / 3.0 # Log transform with epsilon guard to avoid log(0) Lcurr = log(Gcurr + 1e-8) Lnext = log(Gnext + 1e-8) # Calculate log difference deltaL = Lnext - Lcurr # Simulate events (linear scaling by theta as per source formula) Ehat = deltaL / theta virtualevents.append(Ehat) return virtualevents def computeeventloss(virtualevents, realevents): """ Computes L2 loss between virtual and real events. Args: virtualevents: List of tensors [H, W] for each interval. realevents: List of tensors [H, W] for each interval. Returns: loss: Scalar L2 loss averaged over intervals and pixels. """ totalloss = 0.0 count = 0 for Ehat, Ereal in zip(virtualevents, realevents): totalloss += sum((Ehat - Ereal) 2) count += 1 return totalloss / count The Event Loss is the L2 loss between simulated events \hat{E} and real events E, summed over all pixels x \in X and pose intervals i=1 \dots p-1. It serves as an intensity-change metric to supervise NeRF parameters and optimize adjunctive poses Ti and T{i+1} via event-driven bundle adjustment. The formula is: L{event} = \frac{1}{p-1} \sum{i=1}^{p} \frac{1}{m} \sum{x \in X} \| \hat{E}(x, ti, t{i+1}) - E(x, ti, t{i+1}) \|2^2 where p is the number of sampled poses and m is the number of pixels. This variant uses a trained NeRF to render the scene from novel viewpoints and camera intrinsics, specifically to model a robot's camera (Logitech C920) different from the one used for training data collection. It sets itself apart by bridging simulation and reality through explicit camera calibration, and is chosen when deploying NeRF-based perception to physical hardware. The step requires matching camera intrinsics between simulation and reality by calibrating the robot’s camera, then using the obtained focal length and distortion parameters to render the NeRF. Time Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of sampled poses p per view, as p renders are required per exposure interval. Training time is reported to be close to standard BAD-NeRF. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate renders for p poses per view. Performance: Improves PSNR, SSIM, and reduces ATE compared to baselines like BAD-NeRF. Strengths: Enables joint optimization of NeRF parameters and camera poses using asynchronous event data, handling motion blur effectively. Limitations: Requires synchronized event data and blurry images, and stability depends on adjacent pose intervals. Originated in the paper "Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields with Event-driven Bundle Adjustment" (EBAD-NeRF) by Yunshan Qi et al.. It builds on NeRF volume rendering and event-based vision models to address motion blur in dynamic scenes. Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields with Event-driven Bundle Adjustment, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3680569, fetched 2026-10-27 NeRF2Real: Sim2real Transfer of Vision-guided Bipedal Motion Skills using Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/icra48891.2023.10161544, fetched 2026-10-29

name: NeRF-style Volume Rendering Integrator
head: NeRF forward raymarching, NeRFIntegrator
body: This method computes the expected color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r by discretizing the medium interaction interval into fixed steps and accumulating emission weighted by transmittance. It differs from its sibling NeRF Rendering (Alpha Compositing) by using a dense grid-based density representation with no direction-dependent emission, and by employing a fixed-step marching loop with optional jittering rather than adaptive sampling or neural network queries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray r (origin, direction), scene geometry (for exit intersection), density grid (scalar field \sigma), emission field (vector field c), parameters: queriesperray, densitynoisestd, jitteringenabled, activation, hideemitters. Output: Rendered color \hat{C}(r) and accumulated weights. Data Structures: Density Grid: Dense 3D grid of scalar values \sigma. Emission Field: Dense 3D grid of RGB values c. State Variables: result (color accumulator), throughput (transmittance T), weightssum (accumulated opacity weight), stepj (current step index), ta (previous sample position), tb (current sample position). Parameters: queriesperray: Number of steps for ray marching. Default: 128. densitynoisestd: Standard deviation for noise added to density. Default: 0. jitteringenabled: Boolean flag enabling jittering for step positions. Default: True. activation: Activation function type for density ('identity', 'relu'). Default: 'identity'. hideemitters: Boolean flag to hide background emitters if weightssum is zero. Default: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize result = 0, throughput = 1, weightssum = 0, stepj = 0, ta = 0. 2. Exit Intersection: Intersect ray with scene geometry to find medium exit distance t{exit}. 3. Step Size Calculation: Calculate stepsize = t{exit} / \text{queries\per\ray}. Sample jittersample from a uniform sampler if jitteringenabled. 4. Marching Loop: While stepj < queriesperray: a. Calculate tb = ta + stepsize \times (1.0 + \text{jitter\sample}). Calculate actualstep = tb - ta. b. Query density \sigma and emission c at tb along the ray. c. Apply activation to \sigma if specified. d. Add Gaussian noise with standard deviation densitynoisestd to \sigma if enabled. e. Calculate alpharecip: if stepj + 1 < queriesperray, alpharecip = \exp(-\sigma \cdot \text{actual\step}); else alpharecip = 1.0. f. Numerical Stability: Add \epsilon = 10^{-10} to alpharecip to prevent NaNs during gradient computation. g. Calculate weight = (1.0 - \text{alpha\recip}) \cdot \text{throughput}. h. Accumulate Color: result += weight \times emission. i. Increment stepj. Update ta = tb. j. Update Throughput: throughput = alpharecip. k. Update Weights Sum: weightssum += weight. 5. Background Contribution: Calculate contribution = (1 - \text{weights\sum}) \cdot c{bg}. Add to result for active pixels. If hideemitters is true and weightssum is zero, do not add background emission. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def querydensity(rayorigin, raydirection, t): """Standard 3D grid trilinear lookup.""" return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual grid query def queryemission(rayorigin, raydirection, t): """Standard 3D grid trilinear lookup.""" return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Placeholder for actual grid query def nerfintegrator(rayorigin, raydirection, texit, queriesperray, densitynoisestd, jitteringenabled, activation, hideemitters): # Initialization result = 0.0 throughput = 1.0 weightssum = 0.0 stepj = 0 ta = 0.0 # Step size calculation stepsize = texit / queriesperray jittersample = random.uniform(0, 1) if jitteringenabled else 0.0 while stepj < queriesperray: # Calculate current sample position tb = ta + stepsize (1.0 + jittersample) actualstep = tb - ta # Query density and emission at tb along ray sigma = querydensity(rayorigin, raydirection, tb) c = queryemission(rayorigin, raydirection, tb) # Apply activation if activation == 'relu': sigma = max(0.0, sigma) # Add density noise if densitynoisestd > 0: sigma += random.gauss(0, densitynoisestd) # Calculate alpharecip (transmittance factor for this step) if stepj + 1 < queriesperray: alpharecip = math.exp(-sigma actualstep) else: alpharecip = 1.0 # Numerical stability alpharecip += 1e-10 # Calculate weight weight = (1.0 - alpharecip) throughput # Accumulate color (primal mode) result += weight c # Update throughput and weightssum throughput = alpharecip weightssum += weight # Update step variables stepj += 1 ta = tb # Background contribution cbg = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) if not hideemitters or weightssum > 0: result += (1.0 - weightssum) cbg return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Adding \epsilon = 10^{-10} to alpharecip is critical to prevent NaNs during gradient computation. Boundaries: Rays missing the scene return 0. Rays hitting the exit are processed up to queriesperray steps. Degenerate Input: If queriesperray is 0, the loop does not execute and only background is returned. If densitynoisestd is large, noise may dominate the signal. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is queriesperray. Total time is O(N \cdot R), where R is the number of rays. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the density and emission grids, where V is the volume of the grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with respect to queriesperray and number of rays. Strengths: Simple implementation, deterministic (with fixed jitter), easy to differentiate. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or inefficiency in sparse regions. No direction-dependent emission. When to Use: When a dense grid representation is sufficient and direction-dependent effects are not required. When Not to Use: When adaptive sampling is needed for efficiency or accuracy, or when direction-dependent emission is required. Origin: The method is a simplified NeRF-style integrator that accumulates emission along a ray through a medium, backed by a dense grid instead of a neural network, with no direction-dependent emission. History: The implementation originates from the unbiased-inverse-volume-rendering repository. Usage: The surrounding codebase provides finite-difference gradient computation and loss functions for differentiable optimization tasks. Unbiased Inverse Volume Rendering, https://github.com/rgl-epfl/unbiased-inverse-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Lightning-NeRF Rendering and Training Loop
head: Lightning NeRF
body: Lightning-NeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates training and inference by combining a hybrid density representation (voxel grid with hash encoding) with a decomposed view-independent/view-dependent MLP architecture. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by employing adaptive sampling warmup schedules and dynamic occupancy grid updates to prune empty space, enabling efficient training on large-scale real-world scenes. Inputs: Camera poses and intrinsics. Ground truth RGB images. Optional point cloud file (.ply) for initialization. Outputs: Rendered RGB image. Accumulated opacity (accumulation). Depth map. Number of samples per ray. Optional residual RGB loss. Data Structures: Occupancy Grid: A multi-resolution hash grid storing occupancy probabilities, updated dynamically based on density thresholds. Density Grid: A hybrid structure using a base voxel grid and hash encoding for density values. Color Grid: A multi-resolution hash grid for color features. MLPs: Two separate networks: View-Independent (VI) MLP encodes spatial position to intermediate features, and View-Dependent (VD) MLP encodes viewing direction and VI features to final RGB color. Parameters: nearplane: Near clipping plane. Default: 0.01. farplane: Far clipping plane. Default: 6.0 (KITTI-360) or 10.0 (Argoverse2). alphathre: Alpha threshold for occupancy culling. Default: 0.01 (KITTI-360) or 0.02 (Argoverse2). occnumsamplesperray: Coarse samples per ray. Default: 750. pdfnumsamplesperray: Fine samples per ray. Default: 8. pdfsampleswarmupstep: Steps to keep max fine samples. Default: 100000 (notes) / 500 (code). pdfsamplesfixedstep: Steps after which fine sampling ratio stabilizes. name: Training Configuration
head: Hyperparameter Configuration, Implementation Parameters, Optimization Configuration, Optimization Setup, Optimizer Settings, Training Details, Training Hyperparameters, Training Settings
body: Training Configuration specifies the hyperparameters, optimization strategies, and architectural settings required to train neural radiance fields or implicit surface representations. It solves the problem of reproducibly managing the training state by standardizing how models, optimizers, and datasets are initialized and how gradients are applied. It differs from Learning Rate Scheduling and Mixed Precision Training by focusing on the structural orchestration of the training state rather than numerical precision or adaptive step sizing. The training configuration establishes the execution environment for the optimization loop. It specifies the optimizer type, learning rates, batch sizes, sampling strategies, and loss function weights. Inputs: Scene data (images, poses), network architecture definition, hyperparameter dictionary (learning rates, batch sizes, iteration counts), and device specification (GPU/CPU). Outputs: Trained model weights (MLP parameters, voxel grid values, latent codes) and optionally checkpoints for resume training. The configuration is typically stored in a dictionary or object containing: optimizer: String identifier (e.g., "Adam", "AdamW", "RMSProp") and parameters (betas, eps, weight decay). lr: Initial learning rate, potentially split by parameter group (e.g., embeddings vs. networks). batchsize: Number of rays or pixels per iteration. iterations: Total number of training steps. lossweights: Dictionary mapping loss terms (e.g., L2, SSIM, regularization) to scalar multipliers. sampling: Parameters for ray marching (e.g., number of coarse/fine samples, step sizes). 1. Initialization: Initialize the model parameters (MLP weights, voxel grids, latent codes) using specific schemes (e.g., Gaussian noise for density, specific initialization for alpha values). 2. Optimizer Setup: Instantiate the optimizer with specified hyperparameters (e.g., Adam with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99, \epsilon=10^{-15}). 3. Data Loading: Load training images and camera poses. Create a data loader that samples pixels or rays. 4. Iteration Loop: a. Sample a batch of rays/pixels from the training set. b. Perform forward pass to render predicted colors. c. Compute loss (e.g., L = L2 + 0.2 \cdot L{SSIM}). d. Backpropagate gradients. e. Update model parameters using the optimizer. f. Apply learning rate schedule if configured. g. Apply regularization or pruning if scheduled (e.g., every 300 iterations). 5. Checkpointing: Save model state periodically for resume training or evaluation. Loss Function: L = L2 + 0.2 \cdot L{SSIM}, where L2 is the L2-loss and L{SSIM} is the perceptual loss. Dynamic Frequency Masking (FreeNeRF): \alphai(t, T, L) denotes the i-th bit value of the mask \alpha(t, T, L): \alphai(t, T, L) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \le \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor \\ \frac{t \cdot L}{T} - \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor & \text{if } \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor < i \le \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor + 3 \\ 0 & \text{if } i > \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor + 6 \end{cases} where t is current iteration, T is total iterations, and L is the tensor component length. Sampling Step Size: Points sampling step sizes are set to half of the voxel sizes: \delta^{(c)} = 0.5 \cdot s^{(c)} and \delta^{(f)} = 0.5 \cdot s^{(f)}. Optimizer: Adam is most common. Betas: (0.9, 0.99) or (0.9, 0.999). Epsilon: 10^{-15}. Learning Rate: Varies by method. Common values: 10^{-3}, 5 \times 10^{-4}, 0.1 for voxel grids. Batch Size: Ranges from 1 ray to 256 rays to 25,000 rays or 256 pixels. Iterations: 20,000, 25,000, 30,000 default, 200,000. Weight Decay: 0.1 for hash grid values, 2 \times 10^{-5}, 10^{-9}. Inaccurate Optical Flow: Can cause errors in later training phases; handled by disabling multi-sampling and using vanilla sampling with fewer but accurate data points. Overfitting: Mitigated by dynamic frequency masking or regularization. Narrow-Baseline Poses: COLMAP may struggle; treat camera pose parameters (focal length, parallax offset) as trainable variables. Non-determinism: GPU hashgrid optimization is nondeterministic; fixing seed does not guarantee bitwise-identical trajectories. Unverified code. Dynamically adjusts the optimizer's step size to balance convergence speed and quality. Replaces fixed background with random samples to prevent semi-transparent artifacts. Uses FP16 for forward/backward passes and FP32 for weights to accelerate training. Applies component-specific learning rate multipliers to address disparate convergence speeds. Restores optimization state from disk to continue training. Selects context and target camera views during training. Defines loss for high-resolution refinement after coarse stage convergence. Hyperparameters for specific NeRF variants (e.g., Mip-NeRF, DONeRF). Constraints beyond photometric reconstruction for physical plausibility. Initializes network weights from previous frame to reduce flickering in animated scenes. Reference training protocols for differentiable volume rendering. Configures Region Proposal Network for object detection in NeRFs. Handles outlier poses during training. Quantization strategy for tensor cores and biases using uniform 16-bit and non-uniform k-means quantization. Defines neural network architectures and data structures used to represent 3D scenes. A technique to mask tensor components (density or appearance feature) based on training iteration to enhance high-frequency details in later stages and mitigate overfitting. It calculates mask values using integer and fractional parts for smooth transition during training (t < T) and returns ones after training (t \ge T). Introduced in FreeNeRF and used in Few TensoRF. Pitfall: May struggle with intricate details and hidden angles in complex scenes like 'Drums'. Configures training for object detection in NeRFs. Involves random flipping (x, y axes, prob 0.5), random rotation (z-axis, \pi/2, prob 0.5), and slight rotation (\alpha \in [-\pi/18, \pi/18], prob 0.5). Uses AdamW optimizer with LR 0.0003 and weight decay 0.001. Loss weights: \lambda = 5.0 for Eq. (3) and \lambda = 1.0 for Eq. (6). Balances performance and efficiency by adjusting the ratio of past task rays (mp) to current task rays (mc). mp = mc/2 is chosen as optimal trade-off (e.g., PSNR 22.14 / MS-SSIM 0.836 on Tanks and Temples/Barn with mc=4096). Alternately removes and re-samples particles to manage count and convergence. Re-sampled count gradually decreases to zero as model converges (e.g., after 10K steps on D-NeRF). Initializes NeRF for structured light fields where camera pose parameters (focal length f, parallax offset \Delta) are trainable to handle narrow-baseline cases where COLMAP struggles. A self-supervised regularization technique that shifts the grouping of samples along the ray to assess each point in multiple ways using different groups, imposing consistency on the results. Shifts the head index k of the first group by s towards the camera, where s is randomly sampled from \{1, \dots, Np-1\} during training. A method that jointly optimizes the NeRF MLP and input camera poses, bypassing the need for structure-from-motion preprocessing for forward facing scenes. A variant of NeRF trained with 32-bit HDR images to produce 3-channel radiance in linear color space, reconciling the color space difference between NeRF (sRGB) and path tracing (linear). Achieves higher lighting realism compared to 8-bit LDR NeRF. Time Complexity: Training time varies significantly by method and hardware. Typical ranges: 15 minutes, 20 hours, 1-2 days, few hours to one day. Memory Complexity: Depends on batch size and model size. GPU memory usage can be ~10.5 GB. Mixed precision training reduces memory bandwidth requirements. Scaling: Performance generally increases with more training iterations and larger batch sizes, but with diminishing returns and higher computational cost. Strengths: Flexible configuration allows optimization for various scenes and constraints (e.g., sparse views, dynamic scenes). Limitations: Hyperparameter tuning is often empirical and method-specific. Some methods are sensitive to initialization and learning rate schedules. When to Use: Standard NeRF optimization requires generic hierarchical sampling with Adam [Parent]. Specific variants (e.g., Mip-NeRF, DONeRF) require tailored configurations. Originating from early neural radiance field formulations, training configuration has evolved to address challenges in convergence speed, memory efficiency, and generalization. Early methods used simple Adam optimization with fixed learning rates. Subsequent works introduced adaptive scaling, mixed precision, and dynamic sampling strategies. The field continues to develop specialized configurations for specific applications like object detection, dynamic scenes, and X-ray tomography. body: The method executes a single training iteration, including forward pass, loss computation, and optimizer update. It also sets up the training environment, including random seed fixing, data loading, log directory creation, and checkpoint reloading logic. It solves the problem of reproducibly managing the state required to train neural radiance fields or implicit surface representations by standardizing how models, optimizers, and datasets are loaded and how gradients are applied. It differs from Learning Rate Scheduling and Mixed Precision Training by focusing on the structural orchestration of the training state rather than numerical precision or adaptive step sizing. The method executes a single training iteration or configures the global training environment. It involves initializing random seeds, loading scene data and camera poses, managing checkpoint resumption, and performing the forward-backward pass sequence. Inputs: Configuration arguments (args): dataset type, paths, random seed, learning rate, batch size, GPU IDs, and checkpoint paths. Scene data: Images, camera poses, bounding boxes, and focal lengths. Model parameters: Neural network weights (coarse and optional fine networks). Optimizer state: Adam moments (expavg, expavgsq) if resuming. Outputs: Updated model weights. Loss metrics (RGB, SSIM, PSNR) for logging. Checkpoint files saved at specified intervals. Ray Data: Generated per view using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Shape: (NV, H, W, 8) where NV is number of views, H height, W width. Each ray vector contains 8 dimensions (typically origin xyz, direction xyz, and view metadata). Image Data: Input images shape: (SB, NV, 3, H, W) where SB is batch size. Source images selected shape: (SB, NS, 3, H, W) where NS is number of source views. Pixel values normalized to [0, 1] range via images 0.5 + 0.5. Checkpoint State: Weights stored as.npy files. Filename pattern includes step number: model.npy. Step number extracted from filename: int(ftweights[-10:-4]). 1. Environment Initialization: Set random seeds for reproducibility: np.random.seed(args.randomseed) and tf.compat.v1.setrandomseed (if using TensorFlow). Create log directory: os.makedirs(os.path.join(basedir, expname), existok=True). 2. Data Loading: Load images and transformation matrices from disk based on args.datasettype (e.g., llff, blender, deepvoxels). Transform poses and images to the target device (GPU). Normalize image values to [0, 1]. Generate camera rays for all views using util.genrays(poses, W, H, focal, znear, zfar). 3. Checkpoint Management: Check for existing checkpoints in the log directory. If args.ftpath is provided or latest checkpoint exists: Load weights: model.setweights(np.load(ftweights, allowpickle=True)). Set start step: start = int(ftweights[-10:-4]) + 1. If fine network exists, load corresponding fine weights. 4. View Selection (for multi-view methods): Randomly select currnviews source views from available views: np.random.choice(NV, currnviews, replace=False). Index into images and poses using util.batchedindexselectnd. Note: This selection is noted as "somewhat inefficient" in some implementations. 5. Network Encoding (if applicable): Encode source views into the network: net.encode(srcimages, srcposes, allfocals, c=allc). 6. Forward Pass: Render the scene by calling the parallel renderer on selected rays: renderdict = renderpar(allrays, wantweights=True). Outputs include coarse RGB, fine RGB (if enabled), and weights. 7. Loss Computation: Calculate RGB loss for coarse output: losscoarse = self.rgbcoarsecrit(coarse.rgb, allrgbgt). If fine rendering is used (len(fine) > 0), add fine RGB loss weighted by lambdafine: lossfine = lambdafine self.rgbfinecrit(fine.rgb, allrgbgt). Total loss: loss = losscoarse + lossfine. Normalize loss by lossInvN = 1.0 / (height width 3). 8. Backward Pass and Update: Compute gradients: loss.backward(). Step optimizer: optimizer.step(). Zero gradients: optimizer.zerograd(). 9. Logging and Checkpointing: Print metrics every iprint steps (default 100). Save weights every iweights steps (default 10000). Image Normalization: \text{images}{[0,1]} = \text{images} \times 0.5 + 0.5 Loss Normalization Factor: \text{lossInvN} = \frac{1.0}{\text{height} \times \text{width} \times 3} Scaling Factor for Bounding Box: \text{sc} = \begin{cases} 1. & \text{if } \text{bd\factor is None} \\ \frac{1}{\min(\text{bds}) \times \text{bd\factor}} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{coarse}} + \lambda{\text{fine}} \mathcal{L}{\text{fine}} where \lambda{\text{fine}} is loaded from config, default 1.0. iprint: Frequency of console printout and metric logging, default 100. iweights: Frequency of weight checkpoint saving, default 10000. lambdacoarse: Weight for coarse RGB loss, loaded from config. lambdafine: Weight for fine RGB loss, default 1.0. nobboxstep: Integer parameter; if globalstep >= nobboxstep, bbox sampling is disabled. randomseed: If not None, sets np.random.seed and tf.compat.v1.setrandomseed. Inefficient View Selection: Randomly selecting source views for each object in the batch loop is noted as inefficient. Checkpoint Resumption: Ensure step number extraction logic matches filename format exactly to avoid incorrect start steps. Device Placement: Ensure all data (images, poses, rays) are moved to the specified GPU device before computation. Precision: Use float32 for poses and images as specified. Unverified code. name: Training Ray Batching
head: Random Ray Batching, Random Ray Batching for NeRF Training, Random Ray Sampling, batch ray selection, partial ray sampling
body: Training Ray Batching is a data loading strategy for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that selects a random subset of pixel coordinates (and their corresponding rays) from the full training image grid per optimization iteration, rather than rendering complete images. It reduces the GPU memory footprint during the backward pass of gradient descent by processing only N{rand} rays per step, which controls gradient noise and enables efficient training. It differs from Training Loop for Refractive Index Field and Training Loop by explicitly managing the pre-computation, shuffling, and batch-slicing of ray tensors across multiple training images, whereas those siblings focus on the network forward/backward passes or specific physical models. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images tensor images of shape (N{img}, H, W, 3); camera poses tensor poses of shape (N{img}, 3, 4); camera intrinsic matrix K of shape (3, 3); image dimensions H, W; batch size N{rand}; boolean flag usebatching (default True). Outputs: A batch tensor batch of shape (3, N{rand}, 3) containing ray origins, ray directions, and target RGB values, ready for the NeRF forward pass. Data Structures: The core data structure is a flat tensor raysrgb of shape (N{total\rays}, 3, 3), where N{total\rays} = N{train} \times H \times W. The first dimension indexes the specific ray (image index, row, column). The second dimension indexes the component: index 0 is ray origin (x, y, z), index 1 is ray direction (dx, dy, dz), and index 2 is target RGB color (r, g, b). The third dimension is the coordinate value (3 floats). Data type is float32. Steps: 1. Generate Rays: For each training image, call getraysnp(H, W, K, p) for each pose p in poses[:,:3,:4] and stack them into a tensor rays of shape (N{img}, ro+rd, H, W, 3), where ro+rd=2 represents ray origins and directions. 2. Concatenate Targets: Concatenate rays with images[:,None] along axis 1 to create raysrgb of shape (N{img}, ro+rd+rgb, H, W, 3). 3. Transpose: Transpose raysrgb using [0,2,3,1,4] to shape (N{img}, H, W, ro+rd+rgb, 3). 4. Filter Training Set: Stack only the images in the training index list i{train} into raysrgb, resulting in shape (len(i{train}), H, W, ro+rd+rgb, 3). 5. Flatten: Reshape raysrgb to (-1, 3, 3), resulting in shape (N{train} \times H \times W, 3, 3). 6. Cast and Shuffle: Cast raysrgb to np.float32. Randomly shuffle the order of rays in raysrgb using np.random.shuffle(raysrgb) to ensure random sampling during training. 7. Batch Sampling (Per Iteration): Maintain a global index ibatch initialized to 0. Slice raysrgb[ibatch:ibatch+Nrand] to get the batch. Transpose the batch to shape (2+1, N{rand}, 3) where the first dimension represents ray origins, ray directions, and target values. Increment ibatch by N{rand}. If ibatch >= raysrgb.shape[0], shuffle raysrgb again using torch.randperm and reset ibatch to 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch def getraysnp(H, W, K, pose): # pose is (3, 4) [R|t] i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W, dtype=np.float32), np.arange(H, dtype=np.float32), indexing='xy') dirs = np.stack([(i - K[0, 2]) / K[0, 0], (j - K[1, 2]) / K[1, 1], np.oneslike(i)], axis=-1) dirs = dirs / np.linalg.norm(dirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) R = pose[:,:3] t = pose[:, 3] dirsworld = np.sum(np.expanddims(dirs, -2) R, axis=-1) origins = np.dot(-R.T, t) originsworld = np.broadcastto(origins, (H, W, 3)) rays = np.stack([originsworld, dirsworld], axis=0) return rays def prepareraybatch(images, poses, K, itrain, H, W, Nrand): Nimg = len(images) rays = np.stack([getraysnp(H, W, K, p) for p in poses[:Nimg]], axis=0) raysrgb = np.concatenate([rays, images[:, None]], axis=1) raysrgb = np.transpose(raysrgb, [0, 2, 3, 1, 4]) raysrgb = np.stack([raysrgb[i] for i in itrain], axis=0) raysrgb = raysrgb.reshape(-1, 3, 3) raysrgb = raysrgb.astype(np.float32) np.random.shuffle(raysrgb) raysrgb = torch.Tensor(raysrgb) return raysrgb def samplebatch(raysrgb, ibatch, Nrand): Ntotal = raysrgb.shape[0] batchflat = raysrgb[ibatch: ibatch + Nrand] batchtransposed = torch.transpose(batchflat, 0, 1) batchrays = batchtransposed[:2] targets = batchtransposed[2] newibatch = ibatch + Nrand if newibatch >= Ntotal: randidx = torch.randperm(Ntotal) raysrgb = raysrgb[randidx] newibatch = 0 return batchrays, targets, newibatch, raysrgb Parameters: Nrand: Number of rays per batch. Default value is 32 \times 32 \times 4 = 4096. Controls memory footprint and gradient noise. usebatching: Boolean flag. If True, rays are sampled from all training images globally. If False, rays are sampled from a single random image per iteration. K: Camera intrinsic calibration matrix, shape (3, 3). Simplified form: \begin{bmatrix} f{camera} & 0 & W/2 \\ 0 & f{camera} & H/2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. imagesize: Resolution of the target image, determines the search space for random sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: When ibatch reaches the end of the tensor, a full shuffle is required to maintain randomness for the next epoch. Precision: The tensor is explicitly cast to float32 during preparation to match standard training requirements. Memory: Pre-computing all rays consumes memory proportional to the number of training pixels, which can be significant for high-resolution datasets. This method prepares training and validation data for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by loading synthetic Blender dataset scenes, parsing JSON metadata for camera poses and images, and precomputing rays and RGB values. It differs from LLFF Dataset Loading by assuming known, precise camera poses provided in JSON rather than estimating them, and by using fixed depth bounds (near: 2.0, far: 6.0) instead of NDC normalization. It differs from NeRF Dataset Loading by explicitly handling the specific preprocessing steps for the Blender synthetic dataset, including focal length computation from cameraanglex and RGBA compositing. Batch Ray Sampling is a data loading strategy for training neural radiance fields (NeRF) that generates batches of random rays from training images per optimization iteration, rather than rendering complete images. It solves the memory bottleneck of full-image rendering by processing only a subset of pixels (e.g., 1024–8192 rays) per step, enabling efficient gradient updates and better memory utilization. It differs from image-based training by sampling randomly across the entire image pool, which allows for different training dynamics compared to frameworks like I-NGP that sample every pixel of n images. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces GPU memory usage during the backward pass of gradient descent. Enables training on large datasets by processing only a subset of pixels per step. Limitations: Requires pre-computation and shuffling of all rays, which consumes memory proportional to the training set size. When to use: Standard NeRF training with limited GPU memory. When not to use: When adaptive ray sampling is required for faster convergence, or when memory is extremely constrained (consider on-the-fly ray generation instead of pre-computation). name: NeRF System Data Preparation
head: Blender Dataset Loading, NeRF training data sampling, NeRF validation data sampling, Synthetic NeRF Dataset
body: NeRF System Data Preparation loads synthetic Blender dataset scenes, parsing JSON metadata for camera poses and images, and precomputes rays and RGB values for training and validation. It differs from generic loaders by enforcing specific coordinate system conversions (OpenCV to NeRF's right-handed convention), half-resolution resizing for the synthetic dataset, and alpha compositing onto a white background to handle transparent foregrounds. Unlike LLFF Dataset Loading, which handles sparse real-world poses and NDC normalization, this method assumes known, precise camera poses from synthetic renders. Inputs: transforms{split}.json: Metadata file containing cameraanglex, frames array (with filepath, transformmatrix), and optional bgcolor. split: String, either 'train', 'val', or 'test'. Outputs: rays: Tensor of shape (N, 6) or (H, W, 6) containing concatenated ray origins and normalized directions. rgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3) or (H, W, 3) containing the target RGB colors. masks: Tensor of shape (N, 1) or (H, W, 1) containing foreground alpha masks (optional, used for validation). Data Structures: rays: Float32 tensor. Columns 0-2 are ray origins (ox, oy, oz), columns 3-5 are normalized ray directions (dx, dy, dz). c2w: 4x4 camera-to-world transformation matrix. focal: Float scalar, computed from cameraanglex. Parameters: WHITEBG: Boolean, always True for Blender dataset. near: Float, typically 2.0. far: Float, typically 6.0. resizefactor: Integer, typically 2 (images are resized to half resolution). trainnumrays: Integer, number of random rays to sample per training step. batchimagesampling: Boolean, if True, samples random indices from all training images; otherwise, samples 1 random index per step. Steps: 1. Parse Metadata: Load transforms{split}.json. Extract cameraanglex. Compute focal length: f = \frac{0.5 \times W}{\tan(0.5 \times \text{camera\angle\x})} where W is the original image width. 2. Load and Preprocess Images: For each frame in the JSON: Load the image specified by filepath. Convert to RGBA. Resize to (W/2, H/2). Composite onto a white background: \text{rgb} = \text{rgba}{:,:3} \times \text{rgba}{:,:,3} + (1 - \text{rgba}{:,:,3}) Store the resulting RGB image and the alpha mask. 3. Compute Ray Directions (Precomputation): Generate a grid of pixel coordinates (i, j) for the resized image dimensions. Compute camera-space directions using the focal length and principal point (W/2, H/2): dx = \frac{i - W/2}{f}, \quad dy = -\frac{j - H/2}{f}, \quad dz = -1 (The negative sign on dy and dz accounts for the coordinate system flip from image space to NeRF's camera space). Store these directions in a tensor self.dataset.directions. 4. Sample Rays (Per Iteration/Step): If split is 'train': If batchimagesampling is True, sample trainnumrays random indices from self.dataset.allimages. Else, sample 1 random index. For each sampled index, retrieve the camera-to-world matrix c2w. Sample random pixel coordinates (x, y) within the image dimensions w, h. Extract ray origins from c2w and directions from self.dataset.directions based on the sampled coordinates. Extract RGB values and masks for the sampled pixels. If split is 'val' or 'test': Use the first camera for the index (or all cameras if generating full validation set). Extract all directions and full image RGB/masks. 5. Normalize and Concatenate: Normalize ray directions to unit length: \hat{d} = \frac{d}{\|d\|2} Concatenate origins and normalized directions: \text{rays} = [\text{ray\o}, \hat{d}] Shape is (N, 6) for sampled rays or (H, W, 6) for full images. 6. Set Background Color: If training, set self.model.backgroundcolor based on config. For Blender, this is torch.ones((3,), dtype=torch.float32) (white). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np import json from PIL import Image def loadblenderdata(datadir, split, resizefactor=2): """ Loads NeRF Blender dataset. Returns: rays, rgbs, masks (for validation), or rayindices, rgbs, masks (for training) """ with open(f"{datadir}/transforms{split}.json", 'r') as f: meta = json.load(f) Worig = meta['w'] Horig = meta['h'] focal = 0.5 Worig / np.tan(0.5 meta['cameraanglex']) W, H = Worig // resizefactor, Horig // resizefactor # Precompute directions for the resized image i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W), np.arange(H), indexing='xy') dirs = np.stack([ (i - W/2.0) / focal, -(j - H/2.0) / focal, -np.oneslike(i) ], axis=-1) # (H, W, 3) frames = meta['frames'] allimages = [] allmasks = [] allc2w = [] for frame in frames: imgpath = f"{datadir}/{frame['filepath']}" img = Image.open(imgpath).convert('RGBA') img = img.resize((W, H), Image.Resampling.BILINEAR) img = np.array(img).astype(np.float32) / 255.0 # Composite on white background rgba = img rgb = rgba[...,:3] rgba[..., 3:] + (1 - rgba[..., 3:]) mask = rgba[..., 3:] allimages.append(rgb) allmasks.append(mask) # Convert 4x4 transform matrix to 3x4 (c2w) c2w = np.array(frame['transformmatrix'])[:3,:] allc2w.append(c2w) allimages = np.stack(allimages, axis=0) allmasks = np.stack(allmasks, axis=0) allc2w = np.stack(allc2w, axis=0) return allimages, allmasks, allc2w, dirs, focal def sampletrainingrays(allimages, allmasks, allc2w, dirs, focal, trainnumrays=1024): """ Samples random rays for a single training step. """ numimages = allimages.shape[0] # Sample image indices if np.random.rand() < 0.5: # Example logic for batchimagesampling imgindices = np.random.choice(numimages, size=trainnumrays, replace=False) else: imgindices = np.random.choice(numimages, size=1) raysolist = [] raysdlist = [] rgbslist = [] maskslist = [] for idx in imgindices: c2w = allc2w[idx] rgb = allimages[idx] mask = allmasks[idx] # Sample random pixel coordinates h, w = rgb.shape[:2] x = np.random.randint(0, w) y = np.random.randint(0, h) # Get direction d = dirs[y, x] d = d / np.linalg.norm(d) # Get origin o = c2w[:, 3] raysolist.append(o) raysdlist.append(d) rgbslist.append(rgb[y, x]) maskslist.append(mask[y, x]) rayso = np.stack(raysolist, axis=0) raysd = np.stack(raysdlist, axis=0) rgbs = np.stack(rgbslist, axis=0) masks = np.stack(maskslist, axis=0) rays = np.concatenate([rayso, raysd], axis=-1) return rays, rgbs, masks def samplevalidationrays(allimages, allmasks, allc2w, dirs, focal): """ Samples all rays for validation. """ rayslist = [] rgbslist = [] maskslist = [] for idx in range(allimages.shape[0]): c2w = allc2w[idx] rgb = allimages[idx] mask = allmasks[idx] h, w = rgb.shape[:2] # Generate all rays i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h), indexing='xy') dirsfull = np.stack([ (i - w/2.0) / focal, -(j - h/2.0) / focal, -np.oneslike(i) ], axis=-1) # Normalize directions dirsnorm = dirsfull / np.linalg.norm(dirsfull, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Origins o = c2w[:, 3] rayso = np.broadcastto(o, (h, w, 3)) rays = np.concatenate([rayso, dirsnorm], axis=-1) rayslist.append(rays) rgbslist.append(rgb) maskslist.append(mask) rays = np.concatenate([r.reshape(-1, 6) for r in rayslist], axis=0) rgbs = np.concatenate([r.reshape(-1, 3) for r in rgbslist], axis=0) masks = np.concatenate([m.reshape(-1, 1) for m in maskslist], axis=0) return rays, rgbs, masks Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Systems: The Blender dataset uses a right-handed coordinate system with Y-up and Z-forward (or similar, depending on the exporter), while NeRF assumes a specific camera space (Z-back, Y-down). The getrays function must correctly flip the Y and Z axes of the direction vectors. Alpha Compositing: The synthetic dataset contains transparent backgrounds. Failing to composite onto a white background before training will result in the network learning to predict black or transparent values incorrectly, as the loss function expects RGB values. Resolution: The dataset is typically provided at high resolution (e.g., 800x800). Resizing to half resolution (400x400) is standard to reduce memory usage and training time. Selects 90 scenes from ScanNet, SceneNN, and INRIA datasets. For each scene, video frames are uniformly divided into 100 bins, and the sharpest frame in each bin is selected based on the variance of the Laplacian. Provided depth maps and a depth-guided NeRF are used for training. Minimum bounding boxes are computed based on annotated meshes, and objects of certain categories (e.g., text cut off) are discarded. Loads the NeRF-Synthetic (Blender) dataset by parsing JSON metadata for camera poses and images. It handles coordinate system conversions, half-resolution resizing, and alpha compositing to return normalized RGBA images and camera parameters. It differs from LLFF Dataset Loading by assuming known, precise camera poses from synthetic renders rather than estimating them from sparse, unstructured real-world photos. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(N \cdot H \cdot W) where N is the number of images, and H, W are the image dimensions. Ray sampling is O(R) where R is the number of rays per batch. Memory Complexity: Storing all precomputed rays for validation is O(N \cdot H \cdot W). For training, only the sampled rays are stored, O(R). The images themselves are stored in memory, O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C). Performance: The method is efficient for synthetic datasets due to the small number of images and the ability to precompute rays. However, loading and resizing images can be a bottleneck if not cached. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for synthetic data, handles transparency correctly. Limitations: Not suitable for real-world datasets without modification (e.g., LLFF, Tanks and Temples). Assumes perfect camera poses. The NeRF System Data Preparation method originates from the original NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020) and its accompanying codebase, which introduced the standard pipeline for training on the Blender synthetic dataset. It has become the de facto standard for evaluating NeRF variants on synthetic data. emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, https://github.com/bennyguo/instant-nsr-pl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF-RPN: A general framework for object detection in NeRFs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.02253, fetched 2026-10-26

name: LLFF Dataset Loading
head: LLFF Data Loading, Local Light Field Fusion Dataset Loading
body: LLFF Dataset Loading prepares forward-facing scenes from the Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) dataset for differentiable volume rendering by parsing COLMAP-derived camera poses, correcting axis conventions, rescaling the scene geometry, and generating rays in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). It differs from generic NeRF dataset loaders by enforcing specific coordinate system corrections (COLMAP's 'down-right-back' to 'right-up-back'), bounding-box-based scene rescaling to normalize depth, and the generation of a parametric spiral trajectory for novel view synthesis, which are required due to the LLFF dataset's unique metadata structure and forward-facing constraints. Inputs: posesbounds.npy: NumPy array of shape (N, 17), where N is the number of images. The first 15 columns contain the flattened 3 \times 5 pose matrix (rotation and translation), and the last 2 columns contain the near and far depth bounds for the scene. Image directory: Typically images/, optionally with a downsampling suffix (e.g., images/8 for 8x downsample). Configuration parameters: factor (downscale factor), holdout (validation split interval), whitebkgd (background compositing flag, always False for LLFF). Outputs: c2ws: Camera-to-world transformation matrices of shape (N, 4, 4). images: Loaded and potentially downsampled images of shape (N, H', W', 3). focal: Rescaled focal length in pixels. near, far: Depth bounds for ray sampling. rayo, rayd: Ray origins and directions, optionally in NDC space. Data Structures: posesbounds: Array of shape (N, 17). poses: Reshaped to (N, 3, 5), representing rotation (3x3) and translation (3x1) with an extra column for projection matrix details (often unused or zeroed in standard NeRF pipelines). bounds: Array of shape (N, 2), storing near and far depths per image. Steps: 1. Load Poses and Bounds: Load posesbounds.npy of shape (N, 17). Reshape the pose portion to (N, 3, 5) and extract the last two columns as bounds of shape (N, 2). 2. Extract Intrinsics: Extract height H, width W, and focal length f from the first pose's metadata, typically from poses[0,:, 4]. 3. Downscale Images: Determine the image directory suffix based on the factor parameter. If factor > 0, the suffix is {factor}; otherwise, it is empty. Load images from this directory, sorted by filename. Downscale images if downscale > 1 and pre-downscaled directory does not exist. 4. Rescale Focal Length: Adjust the focal length to match the training resolution. If the original image width is W{orig} and the training width is W{train}, update f \leftarrow f \times \frac{W{train}}{W{orig}}. 5. Correct Pose Axes: COLMAP uses a 'down-right-back' coordinate system. Convert to 'right-up-back' by concatenating columns: poses = np.concatenate([poses[..., 1:2], -poses[...,:1], poses[..., 2:4]], axis=-1). 6. Append Homogeneous Row: Append a row [0, 0, 0, 1] to each 3 \times 4 pose matrix to create full 4 \times 4 camera-to-world (c2w) matrices. 7. Compute Scale Factor: Calculate the minimum near bound across all images: d{min} = \min(\text{bounds}[:, 0]). Compute the scale factor: s = d{min} \times 0.75. 8. Rescale Scene: Divide all pose translations and depth bounds by s. This normalizes the scene so that the nearest depth is approximately 1/0.75 \approx 1.33 in normalized space. 9. Set Depth Bounds: Set the global near and far bounds for ray sampling: near = \min(\text{bounds}) \times 0.9 and far = \max(\text{bounds}) \times 1.0. 10. Split Data: Split images and poses into training and validation sets using a holdout interval. For example, valids = list(range(0, len(c2ws), holdout)). 11. Generate Rays: For each pixel (i, j) in each image, compute the ray direction in camera space: \text{dirs} = \left[ \frac{i - cx}{f}, -\frac{j - cy}{f}, -1 \right] where cx = W/2 and cy = H/2. Transform directions to world space: \mathbf{d}{world} = \mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{dirs}, and origins: \mathbf{o}{world} = \mathbf{t}. 12. NDC Normalization: Convert rays to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) to handle forward-facing scenes uniformly. This involves shifting ray origins to the near plane and projecting to NDC space. NDC Ray Conversion Formula: Given ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in world space, and near plane near: 1. Compute intersection with near plane: t = -\frac{near + oz}{dz} 2. Shift origin to near plane: \mathbf{o}0 = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d} 3. Project to NDC: o{0x}^{\text{ndc}} = -\frac{2f}{W} \frac{o{0x}}{o{0z}}, \quad o{0y}^{\text{ndc}} = -\frac{2f}{H} \frac{o{0y}}{o{0z}}, \quad o{0z}^{\text{ndc}} = 1 + \frac{2 \cdot near}{o{0z}} dx^{\text{ndc}} = -\frac{2f}{W} \left( \frac{dx}{dz} - \frac{o{0x}}{o{0z}} \right), \quad dy^{\text{ndc}} = -\frac{2f}{H} \left( \frac{dy}{dz} - \frac{o{0y}}{o{0z}} \right), \quad dz^{\text{ndc}} = -\frac{2 \cdot near}{o{0z}} The resulting NDC rays are (\mathbf{o}{ndc}, \mathbf{d}{ndc}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import os import imageio def loadllffdata( posesboundspath: str, imagespath: str, factor: int = 8, holdout: int = 8,) -> dict: """ Load and preprocess LLFF dataset. Args: posesboundspath: Path to posesbounds.npy (N, 17). imagespath: Path to images directory. factor: Downscale factor. holdout: Interval for validation split. Returns: Dictionary containing c2ws, images, focal, near, far, rayo, rayd. """ # 1. Load poses and bounds posesbounds = np.load(posesboundspath) posesarr = posesbounds[:,:-2].reshape(-1, 3, 5) bounds = posesbounds[:, -2:] # 2. Extract intrinsics from first pose H, W, focal = posesarr[0,:, 4] # 3. Determine image directory suffix suffix = f"{factor}" if factor > 0 else "" imgdir = os.path.join(imagespath, f"images{suffix}") # 4. Load images imgfiles = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(imgdir) if f.endswith(('.jpg', '.png'))]) N = len(imgfiles) images = np.stack([imageio.imread(os.path.join(imgdir, f)) for f in imgfiles], axis=0) # 5. Correct pose axes (COLMAP down-right-back to right-up-back) poses = np.concatenate([ posesarr[..., 1:2], -posesarr[...,:1], posesarr[..., 2:4] ], axis=-1) # 6. Append homogeneous row to create c2w matrices c2ws = np.zeros((N, 4, 4)) c2ws[:,:3,:4] = poses[:,:,:4] c2ws[:, 3, 3] = 1.0 # 7. Compute scale factor and rescale scene nearoriginal = np.min(bounds[:, 0]) scalefactor = nearoriginal 0.75 c2ws[:,:3, 3] /= scalefactor bounds /= scalefactor # 8. Set near/far bounds near = np.min(bounds) 0.9 far = np.max(bounds) 1.0 # 9. Split data valids = list(range(0, N, holdout)) trainids = [i for i in range(N) if i not in valids] # 10. Generate rays and convert to NDC i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(W, dtype=np.float32), np.arange(H, dtype=np.float32), indexing="xy") cx, cy = W / 2.0, H / 2.0 dirs = np.stack([(i - cx) / focal, -(j - cy) / focal, -np.oneslike(i)], -1) rayolist = [] raydlist = [] for idx in trainids: c2w = c2ws[idx] rayd = np.einsum("hwc,kc->hwk", dirs, c2w[:3,:3]) rayo = np.broadcastto(c2w[:3, 3], rayd.shape) rayondc, raydndc = ndcrays(H, W, focal, near, rayo, rayd) rayolist.append(rayondc.reshape(-1, 3)) raydlist.append(raydndc.reshape(-1, 3)) rayo = np.concatenate(rayolist, axis=0) rayd = np.concatenate(raydlist, axis=0) return { "c2ws": c2ws, "images": images, "focal": focal, "near": near, "far": far, "rayo": rayo, "rayd": rayd, "trainids": trainids, "valids": valids } def ndcrays(H, W, focal, near, rayo, rayd): """ Convert rays to NDC space. """ # Shift to near plane t = -(near + rayo[..., 2]) / (rayd[..., 2] + 1e-8) o0 = rayo + t[..., None] rayd # NDC projection o0x = -(2 focal / W) o0[..., 0] / (o0[..., 2] + 1e-8) o0y = -(2 focal / H) o0[..., 1] / (o0[..., 2] + 1e-8) o0z = 1.0 + 2.0 near / (o0[..., 2] + 1e-8) dx = -(2 focal / W) (rayd[..., 0] / (rayd[..., 2] + 1e-8) - o0[..., 0] / (o0[..., 2] + 1e-8)) dy = -(2 focal / H) (rayd[..., 1] / (rayd[..., 2] + 1e-8) - o0[..., 1] / (o0[..., 2] + 1e-8)) dz = -2.0 near / (o0[..., 2] + 1e-8) rayondc = np.stack([o0x, o0y, o0z], axis=-1) raydndc = np.stack([dx, dy, dz], axis=-1) return rayondc, raydndc Parameters: factor: Downscale factor for images. Default is often 8. holdout: Interval for validation split. Default is often 8. whitebkgd: Always False for LLFF dataset. scalefactor: Default multiplier is 0.75, ensuring nearest depth maps to ~1.33. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: NDC conversion involves division by dz. If dz is close to zero (ray parallel to image plane), this can cause numerical instability. Ensure rays are not perfectly parallel or add a small epsilon. Boundaries: The near and far bounds are set based on the minimum and maximum depths in the scene. If the scene has outliers, this can lead to poor sampling. Clamping or robust statistics may be needed. Degenerate Input: If posesbounds.npy is missing or malformed, the loader will fail. Ensure the file exists and has the correct shape. name: LLFF Data Loading and Spiral Path Generation
head: Real Scene NeRF Dataset Loading
body: This method loads LLFF-style datasets, corrects coordinate system conventions, rescales the scene, and generates a spiral render path for novel view synthesis. It sets itself apart from generic loaders by enforcing specific axis corrections, bounding-box-based rescaling, and parametric spiral trajectory generation. Inputs: Raw poses, bounds (bds), and images. Parameters: recenter (bool), bdfactor (float, default 0.75), spherify (bool), Nviews (int), pathzflat (bool), zdelta (float), zrate (float, default 0.5). File paths for train.txt and test.txt to split data. Outputs: Rescaled poses. Rescaled bounds (bds). Spiral render poses (renderposes). Split images and masks for training and testing. Data Structures: Poses: N \times 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrices. Bounds: N \times 2 array where each row is [min\depth, max\depth]. Images: Tensor of shape (N, H, W, 3). Steps: 1. Load and Downsample: Load raw poses, bounds, and images, and downsample images by a factor. 2. Correct Rotation Ordering: Concatenate columns poses[:, 1:2,:], -poses[:, 0:1,:], and poses[:, 2:,:], then move axis -1 to 0. 3. Rescale Scene: Compute scale factor sc = 1 / (\min(bds) \times bd\factor) if bd\factor is not None, and rescale all poses and bounds by sc. 4. Recenter (Optional): If recenter is True, center the poses around the origin. 5. Spherify (Optional): If spherify is True, adjust poses to lie on a sphere and update sc. 6. Compute Average Pose and Up Vector: If not spherify, compute the average pose c2w = \text{poses\avg}(poses) and the up vector up = \text{normalize}(\sum poses[:,:3, 1]). 7. Determine Focus Depth: Calculate close\depth = \min(bds) \times 0.9, inf\depth = \max(bds) \times 5.0, mean\dz = 1 / ((1-0.75)/close\depth + 0.75/inf\depth), and set focal = mean\dz. 8. Adjust Path Parameters: If pathzflat is True, set zloc = -close\depth \times 0.1, adjust c2w\path[:3, 3] += zloc \times c2w\path[:3, 2], set rads[2] = 0, N\rots = 1, and N\views = N\views / 2; else set N\rots = 2. 9. Generate Spiral Path: Generate render poses using \text{render\path\spiral}(c2w\path, up, rads, focal, zdelta, zrate=0.5, rots=N\rots, N=N\views). 10. Split Data: Split images into training and test sets based on indices listed in train.txt and test.txt. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def loadllffdata(basedir, factor=8, recenter=True, bdfactor=0.75, spherify=False, pathzflat=True, Nviews=120, zdelta=0.0, zrate=0.5): # 1. Load raw data poses, bds, imgs = loadrawllffdata(basedir, factor) # 2. Correct rotation matrix ordering poses = np.concatenate([poses[:, 1:2,:], -poses[:, 0:1,:], poses[:, 2:,:]], axis=1) poses = np.moveaxis(poses, -1, 0) # 3. Rescale sc = 1.0 / (np.min(bds) bdfactor) if bdfactor is not None else 1.0 poses = sc bds = sc # 4. Recenter if recenter: poses = recenterposes(poses) # 5. Spherify if spherify: poses, sc = spherifyposes(poses, bds, Nviews) # 6. Average pose and up vector c2w = posesavg(poses) up = normalize(np.sum(poses[:,:3, 1], axis=0)) # 7. Focus depth closedepth = np.min(bds) 0.9 infdepth = np.max(bds) 5.0 meandz = 1.0 / (((1 - 0.75) / closedepth) + (0.75 / infdepth)) focal = meandz # 8. Path parameters if pathzflat: zloc = -closedepth 0.1 c2wpath = c2w.copy() c2wpath[:3, 3] += zloc c2wpath[:3, 2] rads = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) rads[2] = 0.0 Nrots = 1 Nviewsfinal = Nviews / 2 else: c2wpath = c2w rads = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) Nrots = 2 Nviewsfinal = Nviews # 9. Generate spiral renderposes = renderpathspiral(c2wpath, up, rads, focal, zdelta, zrate, Nrots, Nviewsfinal) # 10. Split data itrain, itest = loadsplitindices(basedir) return poses, bds, imgs, renderposes, itrain, itest def loadrawllffdata(basedir, factor): # Standard LLFF loader: reads posesbounds.npy and images, applies downsampling pass def recenterposes(poses): # Centers poses around the origin center = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 3], axis=0) poses[:,:3, 3] -= center return poses def spherifyposes(poses, bds, Nviews): # Adjusts poses to lie on a sphere sc = 1.0 return poses, sc def posesavg(poses): # Computes average pose center = np.mean(poses[:,:3, 3], axis=0) rot = poses[:,:3,:3] avgrot = np.mean(rot, axis=0) # Re-orthogonalize rotation matrix U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(avgrot) avgrot = U @ Vt poseavg = np.eye(4) poseavg[:3,:3] = avgrot poseavg[:3, 3] = center return poseavg def normalize(v): return v / np.linalg.norm(v) def renderpathspiral(c2wpath, up, rads, focal, zdelta, zrate, rots, N): # Generates poses along a spiral trajectory poses = [] for i in range(int(N)): t = i / N theta = 2 np.pi rots t phi = np.pi / 2 + (np.pi / 2) np.sin(theta) x = rads[0] np.cos(theta) np.cos(phi) y = rads[1] np.sin(theta) np.cos(phi) z = rads[2] np.sin(phi) + zdelta t pos = c2wpath[:3, 3] + x c2wpath[:3, 0] + y c2wpath[:3, 1] + z c2wpath[:3, 2] pose = np.eye(4) pose[:3, 3] = pos poses.append(pose) return np.array(poses) def loadsplitindices(basedir): # Loads train.txt and test.txt indices return [0], [1] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Rescaling by bdfactor can lead to numerical instability if bds.min() is very small. Ensure bdfactor is not zero. Boundaries: If bds contains zeros or negative values, closedepth calculation may fail. Clamp bds to positive values before processing. Degenerate Input: If Nviews is odd and pathzflat is True, integer division Nviews / 2 may lose a view. Handle odd Nviews explicitly if needed.
