name: Training Ray Masking and Caching
head: Mask-Cached Ray Sampling, Training Ray Sampling with Mask Cache
body: Training Ray Masking and Caching filters the set of candidate training rays to exclude those that do not intersect the scene's coarse geometry, thereby reducing computational load during the training loop. It differs from sibling methods like Pixel Batching by pre-filtering rays based on geometric occupancy rather than just spatial locality, and from Semantic Ray Sampling by relying on geometric masks rather than semantic labels. This method is chosen when the scene has significant background or empty space that would otherwise waste training iterations on irrelevant rays. The method generates rays for all pixels in the training images, tests them against a coarse geometry model to determine intersection, and stores only the valid rays in contiguous buffers. Inputs: rgbtrori: List of training RGB images. poses: List of camera pose matrices (c2w). K: Camera intrinsic matrix. H, W: Image height and width. renderkwargs: Dictionary of arguments passed to the geometry intersection function. cfg.data: Configuration parameters including inversey, flipx, flipy. DEVICE: Target device (e.g., CUDA). Outputs: rgbtr: Tensor of shape [N{valid}, 3] containing RGB values for valid rays. raysotr: Tensor of shape [N{valid}, 3] containing ray origins. raysdtr: Tensor of shape [N{valid}, 3] containing ray directions. viewdirstr: Tensor of shape [N{valid}, 3] containing view directions. imsz: List of integers, where imsz[i] is the number of valid rays from image i. batchindexsampler: A generator function that yields indices for sampling batches from the valid rays. Data Structures: mask: Boolean tensor of shape [H, W] indicating which pixels hit the geometry. rgbtr, raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr: Pre-allocated float tensors of shape [N, 3], where N is the total number of pixels across all images. These are trimmed at the end. Steps: 1. Calculate the total number of pixels N across all training images: N = \sum{i} (\text{height}i \times \text{width}i) 2. Initialize flattened output tensors rgbtr, raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr with shape [N, 3] on the target device. Initialize an empty list imsz for image sizes and an integer top = 0 for the current write index. 3. For each training image i with pose c2w, image img, and dimensions (H, W): a. Compute full ray origins rayso, directions raysd, and view directions viewdirs using getraysofaview(H, W, K, c2w, ndc, inversey, flipx, flipy). b. Initialize a boolean mask tensor mask of shape [H, W] on the target device. c. Iterate over the height of the image in chunks of size CHUNK (typically 64). For each chunk j: i. Extract raysochunk = rayso[j:j+CHUNK] and raysdchunk = raysd[j:j+CHUNK]. ii. Compute the hit mask for the chunk: mask[j:j+CHUNK] = model.hitcoarsegeo(raysochunk, raysdchunk, renderkwargs). d. Count the number of valid rays n = \text{mask.sum()}. e. If n > 0, copy the data for valid rays into the global buffers starting at top: \text{rgb\tr}[top:top+n] = img[\text{mask}] \text{rays\o\tr}[top:top+n] = \text{rays\o}[\text{mask}].\text{to}(DEVICE) \text{rays\d\tr}[top:top+n] = \text{rays\d}[\text{mask}].\text{to}(DEVICE) \text{viewdirs\tr}[top:top+n] = \text{viewdirs}[\text{mask}].\text{to}(DEVICE) f. Append n to imsz and update top += n. 4. Trim the output tensors to the actual number of valid pixels: \text{rgb\tr} = \text{rgb\tr}[:top] \text{rays\o\tr} = \text{rays\o\tr}[:top] \text{rays\d\tr} = \text{rays\d\tr}[:top] \text{viewdirs\tr} = \text{viewdirs\tr}[:top] 5. Create a batch index sampler. This is typically a generator that yields random indices from 0 to top-1. 6. Print the ratio of kept rays to total rays: top / N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gettrainingraysinmaskcachesampling(rgbtrori, poses, K, H, W, renderkwargs, model, DEVICE, cfgdata): """ Generates training rays filtered by coarse geometry intersection. """ # Step 1: Calculate total pixels N N = 0 for img in rgbtrori: N += img.shape[0] img.shape[1] # Step 2: Initialize buffers rgbtr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) raysotr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) raysdtr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) viewdirstr = torch.zeros((N, 3), device=DEVICE) imsz = [] top = 0 CHUNK = 64 # Step 3: Process each image for i, (img, c2w) in enumerate(zip(rgbtrori, poses)): # 3a: Generate full rays rayso, raysd, viewdirs = getraysofaview( H, W, K, c2w, ndc=cfgdata.ndc, inversey=cfgdata.inversey, flipx=cfgdata.flipx, flipy=cfgdata.flipy) # 3b: Initialize mask mask = torch.zeros((H, W), dtype=torch.bool, device=DEVICE) # 3c: Compute hit mask in chunks for j in range(0, H, CHUNK): endj = min(j + CHUNK, H) raysochunk = rayso[j:endj,:] raysdchunk = raysd[j:endj,:] # Call geometry intersection # Note: hitcoarsegeo typically returns a boolean tensor or requires.to(DEVICE) hit = model.hitcoarsegeo( rayso=raysochunk, raysd=raysdchunk, renderkwargs) # Update mask # Assuming hit is boolean or convertible to boolean mask[j:endj,:] = hit.to(DEVICE) # 3d: Count valid rays n = mask.sum().item() # 3e: Copy valid rays if n > 0: rgbtr[top:top+n].copy(img[mask]) raysotr[top:top+n].copy(rayso[mask].to(DEVICE)) raysdtr[top:top+n].copy(raysd[mask].to(DEVICE)) viewdirstr[top:top+n].copy(viewdirs[mask].to(DEVICE)) # 3f: Update indices imsz.append(n) top += n # Step 4: Trim buffers rgbtr = rgbtr[:top] raysotr = raysotr[:top] raysdtr = raysdtr[:top] viewdirstr = viewdirstr[:top] # Step 5: Create batch sampler # Using a simple random index generator as per common practice in these repos def batchindexsampler(): while True: yield torch.randint(0, top, (1,)).item() # Step 6: Print ratio print(f"Kept rays ratio: {top / N}") return rgbtr, raysotr, raysdtr, viewdirstr, imsz, batchindexsampler Parameters: CHUNK: Integer, typically 64. Controls the chunk size for geometry intersection queries to manage memory. renderkwargs: Dictionary passed to model.hitcoarsegeo. Contains necessary rendering parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If top is 0 (no rays hit geometry), the buffers are empty. The batch sampler must handle this or the training loop must skip the step. Precision issues in hitcoarsegeo may cause rays grazing the geometry boundary to be inconsistently classified. The method assumes the coarse geometry is static or updated infrequently. If the geometry changes significantly between ray generation steps, the mask becomes stale. Samples rays based on spatial proximity within an image, useful for preserving local coherence. Choose when local texture details are critical. Filters rays based on semantic class labels. Choose when specific object categories need higher sampling density. Randomizes the order of rays to prevent overfitting to specific spatial patterns. Choose when training stability is an issue. Reduces the number of rays per image. Choose when computational budget is extremely limited. Optimizes memory usage by not storing all rays in RAM. Choose when scene size exceeds available memory. Samples rays based on texture space coordinates. Choose when working with texture-mapped scenes. Time Complexity: O(N) to generate and filter rays, where N is the total number of pixels. The geometry intersection step dominates, taking O(N \cdot C) where C is the cost of hitcoarsegeo per ray chunk. Memory Complexity: O(N{valid}) for the output buffers. Pre-allocation uses O(N) but is trimmed. Performance: Reduces training time by skipping background rays. The speedup depends on the ratio of valid rays to total rays. Strengths: Significant reduction in unnecessary computation for scenes with large backgrounds. Limitations: Requires a pre-computed or fast coarse geometry model. Ineffective if most rays hit the geometry. When to use: Scenes with significant empty space or background. When not to use: Scenes where the geometry is unknown or too complex to compute quickly. This method originates from the DirectVoxGO and related NeRF optimization frameworks, which use coarse geometry to guide ray sampling. It is part of the training loop setup in differentiable volume rendering pipelines, specifically within the NeRF Training Loop configuration. sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, https://github.com/sjtuytc/UnboundedNeRFPytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, https://github.com/sunset1995/DirectVoxGO, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Jumpat/SegmentAnythingin3D, https://github.com/Jumpat/SegmentAnythingin3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Training Ray Sub-sampling
head: SampleRays Transform, Sub-sampling Rays
body: Training Ray Sub-sampling is a data transform that reduces the number of rays processed per training iteration by selecting a fixed subset from a larger batch of multiview rays. It solves the problem of high memory consumption and computational cost during radiance-field optimization by limiting the batch size to a manageable numsamples count. Unlike Batch Ray Sampling, which determines which rays enter the pipeline, this method determines how many of those rays are actually forwarded to the network for gradient computation. Inputs: inputs: A dictionary or object containing ray data. inputs['rays']: Tensor of shape [B, R,...] where B is the batch size (number of images/videos) and R is the number of rays per image. inputs.rayvalues(): An iterable of key-value pairs representing auxiliary ray data (e.g., colors, normals, semantic labels). Outputs: out: A dictionary containing the sub-sampled data. out['rays']: Tensor of shape [numsamples,...]. out[channelname]: Tensors corresponding to the sub-sampled auxiliary data. Parameters: numsamples (int): The fixed number of rays to select from the input batch. Algorithm: 1. Generate Indices: Create a tensor of random integers to select numsamples unique indices from the available rays. \text{ray\idx} = \text{torch.randint}(0, \text{inputs}['\text{rays}'].shape[0], [\text{num\samples}], \text{device}=\text{device}) Note: The source code uses inputs['rays'].shape[0] as the upper bound, implying numsamples is typically less than or equal to the total number of rays in the batch, or the implementation assumes a specific batch structure where this dimension represents the ray count. 2. Sub-sample Rays: Extract the selected rays from the main ray tensor. \text{out}['\text{rays}'] = \text{inputs}['\text{rays}'][\text{ray\idx}].\text{contiguous}() 3. Sub-sample Auxiliary Data: Iterate over all auxiliary ray values and apply the same index selection. For each (channelname, rayvalue) in inputs.rayvalues(): \text{out}[\text{channel\name}] = \text{ray\value}[\text{ray\idx}].\text{contiguous}() Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def trainingraysubsampling(inputs, numsamples, device): """ Sub-samples a fixed number of rays from the input batch. Args: inputs: Dictionary-like object with 'rays' tensor and rayvalues() method. numsamples: Integer, number of rays to select. device: torch.device, target device for the output tensors. Returns: out: Dictionary containing sub-sampled rays and auxiliary data. """ out = {} # Step 1: Generate random ray indices # Assuming inputs['rays'] is a tensor where the first dimension is the count of rays # to be sampled from. raycount = inputs['rays'].shape[0] rayidx = torch.randint(0, raycount, [numsamples], device=device) # Step 2: Sub-sample main rays out['rays'] = inputs['rays'][rayidx].contiguous() # Step 3: Sub-sample auxiliary ray values # Iterate over key-value pairs in rayvalues for channelname, rayvalue in inputs.rayvalues().items(): out[channelname] = rayvalue[rayidx].contiguous() return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Index Bounds: If numsamples exceeds the number of available rays, torch.randint will generate valid indices, but the subsequent indexing inputs['rays'][rayidx] may fail or produce unexpected results if the tensor shape does not support it. The source assumes numsamples is within valid bounds. Contiguity: The.contiguous() call is explicitly used to ensure memory layout compatibility for subsequent GPU operations. Determinism: The use of torch.randint implies non-deterministic sampling per iteration, which is standard for stochastic gradient descent but requires careful seeding for reproducibility. A variant used for dynamic 6-DoF video training (HyperReel) that combines sub-sampling with temporal resolution adaptation. Instead of a fixed random selection, it iterates over N videos and M frames, applying conditional downsampling to rays and colors based on frame index divisibility. If frame m is not divisible by 8, rays and colors are downsampled by a factor of 4 using nearest-neighbor interpolation. If m is not divisible by 4, an additional factor of 2 downsampling is applied. This scheme builds a training set \text{rays}{GT}, C{GT} by aggregating these potentially downsampled frames. It is chosen when training on video datasets with varying temporal importance or to reduce memory for high-resolution video sequences. Time Complexity: O(K) where K is numsamples, as it involves a single random generation and indexing operation. Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot D) where D is the dimensionality of the ray data, as it creates new contiguous tensors for the subset. Performance: Reduces GPU memory usage proportionally to the ratio of numsamples to the total batch size. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively controls memory footprint during training. Limitations: Random sub-sampling may miss rare or important rays if the distribution is not uniform. The HyperReel variant introduces spatial resolution changes that may affect training stability if not handled carefully. The basic SampleRays transform originates from the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp framework, a library for 3D deep learning. The temporal sub-sampling scheme was introduced in the HyperReel paper for high-fidelity 6-DoF video generation, addressing the need to manage memory when training on large video datasets with multiple views. name: Memory-Saving Ray Sampling
head: Full-Ray Training Optimization
body: Memory-Saving Ray Sampling is a memory optimization technique that enables training neural radiance fields (NeRF) for stylization on all rays simultaneously, avoiding the need to downsample ray counts due to out-of-memory (OOM) constraints. Unlike sibling methods that may require sparse sampling or precomputed buffers, this approach allows full-resolution ray processing without degradation in stylization quality. It specifically addresses the trade-off where reducing sampled ray numbers to save memory increases noise and degrades results. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A batch of rays covering the full image resolution (W \times H rays). Output: Rendered image and computed gradients for network optimization. Data Structures: Exact layouts and sizes are not given in the sources. Standard implementations store ray origins, directions, near/far bounds, and intermediate network activations per ray. Steps: 1. Select an image from the training dataset and generate rays for every pixel at full resolution. 2. Process all rays simultaneously through the neural network to compute radiance and density. 3. Render the image and compute the training loss. 4. Backpropagate gradients to update the model. Parameters: Ray count: Equal to the total number of pixels in the source image (W \times H). Typical values: Not specified in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: OOM errors may occur if the system does not have sufficient VRAM to hold all intermediate activations for all rays. Reducing ray counts to fit memory leads to increased noise and degraded stylization quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def memorysavingraysampling(rayorigins, raydirections, near, far, nerfforward, optimizer, targetimage): # rayorigins: (N, 3), raydirections: (N, 3), near/far: (N,) # Process all rays simultaneously (full resolution) numrays = len(rayorigins) numsamples = 128 # Standard sampling density # Sample points along all rays tvals = [j / (numsamples - 1) for j in range(numsamples)] zvals = [[near[i] + t (far[i] - near[i]) for t in tvals] for i in range(numrays)] points = [[[rayorigins[i][d] + raydirections[i][d] z for d in range(3)] for z in zvals[i]] for i in range(numrays)] # Forward pass through network for all points densities, colors = nerfforward(points) # Alpha compositing for all rays renderedcolors = [] for i in range(numrays): deltas = [zvals[i][j+1] - zvals[i][j] for j in range(numsamples - 1)] deltas.append(float('inf')) alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-densities[i][j] deltas[j]) for j in range(numsamples)] transmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for j in range(numsamples): w = alpha[j] transmittance finalcolor = [finalcolor[d] + w colors[i][j][d] for d in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha[j] + 1e-10) renderedcolors.append(finalcolor) # Compute loss and backpropagate loss = sum((renderedcolors[i][d] - targetimage[i][d])2 for i in range(numrays) for d in range(3)) / (3 numrays) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss A strategy to prevent OOM errors during training by randomly sampling feature vectors instead of feeding all embeddings. For 3D embeddings with F=8, randomly sample 150K feature vectors \thetas per iteration. For 3D embeddings with F=1, 2, 4, randomly sample 200K feature vectors \thetas per iteration. For 2D embeddings, feed all embeddings together in one iteration without random sampling. This is used in conjunction with memory-saving techniques to manage VRAM usage. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to naive full-batch training by avoiding OOM, but higher than sparse sampling methods. Measured Performance: In NeRF-Art, this method achieved better stylization quality than AvatarCLIP, which used sparse rays (112 \times 112) due to OOM constraints. Strengths: Avoids noise from sparse sampling; enables full-resolution training. Limitations: Requires high VRAM; may still require auxiliary strategies like feature vector sampling for very large scenes. When to use: When VRAM allows full-ray processing and high-quality stylization is critical. When not: When VRAM is severely limited and sparse sampling is unavoidable. Originated in the context of text-driven NeRF stylization, specifically in NeRF-Art. It was developed to overcome the limitations of methods like AvatarCLIP, which suffered from noise due to sparse ray sampling. The technique is part of a broader effort to optimize memory usage in NeRF training. name: Texture-Space Sampling
head: Texture-space batch sampling, UV-space sampling for training
body: Texture-space sampling is a method for forming training batches in differentiable inverse volume rendering and radiance-field optimization by sampling unknowns uniformly directly in texture space, rather than sampling a random subset of views. This approach reduces gradient noise by ensuring that batches of observations are directly relevant to the selected unknowns, providing even coverage within an iteration compared to standard image-based sampling. The method constructs a training batch by selecting texture variables first, then determining which camera observations are relevant to those variables. Inputs: Texture space representation (e.g., UV map of a mesh or implicit surface). Inverse UV mapping function U^{-1}: (u, v) \rightarrow \mathbf{p}, mapping texture coordinates to 3D surface positions. Set of reference camera views (intrinsics, extrinsics, and RGB frames). Batch size N, adjustable based on GPU memory. Outputs: A batch of rays connecting sampled 3D positions to reference camera centers. Corresponding target pixel values from reference frames. Gradients for the texture parameters. Data Structures: Sampled Points: A list of N texture coordinate pairs (ui, vi). 3D Positions: A list of N 3D points \mathbf{p}i = U^{-1}(ui, vi). Valid Rays: A subset of rays (\mathbf{o}j, \mathbf{d}j) where \mathbf{o}j is the camera center and \mathbf{d}j is the direction to \mathbf{p}i, filtered for visibility. Steps: 1. Sample Texture Coordinates: At the start of each iteration, select N points uniformly at random over the texture space domain [0, 1] \times [0, 1]. 2. Map to 3D: Use the precomputed inverse UV mapping to lookup the corresponding 3D positions on the scene surfaces: \mathbf{p}i = U^{-1}(ui, vi). 3. Connect to Views: For each sampled 3D position \mathbf{p}i, determine connections to a set of reference view positions. 4. Filter Occlusions: Discard connections where the ray from the camera center to \mathbf{p}i is occluded by geometry or where \mathbf{p}i falls outside the camera’s frustum. 5. Fetch Targets: For the remaining valid 3D positions, fetch the corresponding pixel values from the reference RGB frames. 6. Render: Estimate the current radiance values for the batch using differentiable path tracing. 7. Compute Loss and Gradients: Compute the per-pixel loss (averaged over all rays in the batch). Backpropagate through the rendering algorithm to obtain gradients. 8. Update: Update scene parameters with an optimizer step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texturespacesamplingiteration(texturemap, inverseuvmap, cameras, rgbframes, batchsize, optimizer): # Step 1: Sample uniform texture coordinates usamples = [random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) for in range(batchsize)] vsamples = [random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) for in range(batchsize)] texturecoords = list(zip(usamples, vsamples)) # Step 2: Map to 3D positions points3d = [] for u, v in texturecoords: p = inverseuvmap(u, v) if p is not None: points3d.append(p) if not points3d: return texturemap # Step 3 & 4: Connect to views and filter occlusions rays = [] targets = [] for p in points3d: for camera, frame in zip(cameras, rgbframes): # Standard frustum culling: transform point to camera space and check bounds if not isinfrustum(camera, p): continue rayorigin = camera.center raydirection = normalize(p - rayorigin) # Standard ray intersection test against scene geometry closesthit = geometry.rayintersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if closesthit is not None and distance(closesthit, rayorigin) < distance(p, rayorigin) - 1e-6: continue pixelcoords = projecttoimage(camera, p) if iswithinbounds(pixelcoords, frame.shape): targetvalue = frame[pixelcoords] rays.append((rayorigin, raydirection)) targets.append(targetvalue) if not rays: return texturemap # Step 6: Differentiable rendering # Differentiable path tracing computes radiance for each ray given the texture map renderedradiance = differentiablepathtrace(rays, texturemap) # Step 7: Loss and Gradients # Standard differentiable optimization: compute loss and backpropagate loss = sum((r - t)2 for r, t in zip(renderedradiance, targets)) / len(targets) gradients = computegradients(loss, texturemap) # Step 8: Update optimizer.step(gradients) return texturemap Parameters: Batch Size (N): The number of texture samples per iteration. Adjustable based on available GPU memory. Inverse UV Mapping: Precomputed mapping from texture space to 3D surface. Must handle degenerate cases (e.g., UVs outside mesh bounds). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid UVs: Some texture locations may not map to any scene surface (e.g., holes in the mesh or UV islands outside the geometry). These result in zero gradients for those locations. The implementation must handle None or invalid returns from the inverse UV map. Occlusion: Connections discarded due to occlusion reduce the effective batch size. If too many are discarded, the gradient signal may become weak. Frustum Culling: Points outside the camera frustum are discarded, ensuring only relevant observations are used. A rendering and optimization approach where sampling and gradient computation occur in texture space rather than image space, ensuring even coverage and avoiding Jacobian factors that cause exploding gradients or uneven convergence. It selects texels uniformly at random and connects them to camera positions to form rays for path tracing. Gradients are computed by omitting Jacobian factors (the derivative of the mapping from texture to image space) to prevent exploding gradients when distance d approaches zero and to obtain gradients of comparable magnitude regardless of observation distance or angle. Unlike standard image-based differentiable rendering, which leads to nonzero gradients only within the frusta of cameras selected for the iteration, texture-space sampling provides even coverage within an iteration. Some texture locations may not be mapped to any scene surface, resulting in zero gradients for those locations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: More efficient than sampling a random subset of views because it reduces noise in gradients by proceeding with batches of observations directly relevant to the selected unknowns. Strengths: Even coverage of texture space within an iteration; avoids exploding gradients from Jacobian factors; reduces gradient noise. Limitations: Requires a precomputed inverse UV mapping; some texture locations may have zero gradients if not mapped to surface. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of material and lighting reconstruction for complex indoor scenes. The method was proposed to address the inefficiencies of standard image-based differentiable rendering, where gradients are sparse and unevenly distributed. It builds on the idea of sampling unknowns directly in their native space (texture space) to improve optimization stability and convergence. name: Training Loop for Refractive Index Field
head: Neural Field Training Loop, Refractive Index Field Training Procedure
body: This method defines the optimization loop for training a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to represent a 3D refractive index (IOR) field and associated emission field, using differentiable ray tracing. It distinguishes itself by combining Eikonal ray tracing with luminance integration, optimizing the IOR field via boundary regularization and luminance reconstruction loss, specifically implemented in JAX for multi-device sharding. It builds on Training Loop Setup and Training Ray Batching. Inputs: rays: Batched ray initial conditions (positions and directions). raylumtarget: Ground truth luminance values for the rays. Xreg: Boundary points for regularization. lumfield: 3D grid of true luminance values for interpolation. svals: Integration sample points along rays. imgsplane: Target image plane parameters. planelocs: Plane locations for rendering. etatrue: Ground truth IOR field (for testing/plotting). sourcelocs, covs: Light source locations and covariance matrices for emission modeling. Outputs: Optimized MLP parameters for predicteta (IOR) and predictlum (emission). Checkpoints of the trained model and predicted IOR field (eta). Training logs (loss, images, IOR slices) via TensorBoard. Data Structures: MLP (MLPact): Inputs are positional encoded coordinates. Hidden layers have depth netdepth (default 4) and width netwidth (default 128). Activation is ReLU. Skip connections are enabled (doskip=True). Output is a scalar IOR value. Positional encoding uses degree degpoint (default 4) with vectorized safesin computation. Optimizer State: Managed by Optax Adam with a cosine learning rate schedule. Loss Function: Partial application of lossfn with parameters lam (weight) and bdval (boundary value). Numbered Steps: 1. Data Preparation: Load Xtest, rays, svals, lumfield, raylumtarget, etatrue. Interpolate emission: predictlum = interpgrid(lumfield, cval=0.). Compute boundary points: Xreg = getXbd(16). Shard data across available JAX devices. 2. Initialization: Initialize MLP parameters with seed=0. Create Adam optimizer with cosine learning rate decay from lrinit to lrfinal over numiters. Initialize loss function with lam (0.1 for gas, 1.0 for NF) and bdval (1.0003 for gas, 1.0 for NF). Initialize render function with svals, imgsplane, planelocs. 3. Training Loop (Iterate i from 1 to numiters): If i==1 or i % testfreq == 0, run test step and generate plots. If i==1 or i % savefreq == 0, save checkpoint and pickle eta. Call trainpstep with raysshard, raylumtargetshard, Xregshard, optstate, rendereta, lossfn, randkey. Log training loss. Formulas: Learning Rate Schedule: \text{lr}(x) = \exp\left( \ln(\text{lr\init}) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{x}{\text{num\iters}}\right) + \ln(\text{lr\final}) \cdot \frac{x}{\text{num\iters}} \right) Where x is the current iteration. Positional Encoding: \text{posenc}(x, \text{deg}) = \text{concat}\left(x, \sin\left([x \cdot \text{scales}, x \cdot \text{scales} + \frac{\pi}{2}]\right)\right) Where \text{scales} = [2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{\text{deg}-1}]. Emission Prediction: \text{emission}(\text{ray\pos}) = \frac{\exp(\text{logpdf}(\text{ray\pos}))}{\text{damp}} Where \text{logpdf} is computed from Gaussian distributions defined by sourcelocs and covs. Loss Function: The loss combines luminance reconstruction error and boundary regularization: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{lum}} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}{\text{bd}} Where \lambda = \text{lam} and \mathcal{L}{\text{bd}} penalizes deviation from bdval at boundary points Xreg. Parameters: numiters: 50000. batchsize: 4096. lrinit: 1e-4. lrfinal: 5e-6. testfreq: 100. savefreq: 100. lam: 0.1 (gas) or 1.0 (nf). bdval: 1.0003 (gas) or 1.0 (nf). seed: 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use float32 for JAX operations. Ensure svals and ray positions are within valid bounds for interpolation. Boundaries: Xreg must correctly identify boundary points to apply regularization effectively. Degenerate Input: If covs are singular, eigh may fail; ensure positive definite covariance matrices. Memory: Sharding data across devices is critical for large batches (4096 rays). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax import jax.numpy as jnp import optax import pickle import tqdm def safesin(x): return jnp.sin(jnp.clip(x, -jnp.pi, jnp.pi)) # def posenc(x, deg): if deg == 0: return x scales = jnp.array([2i for i in range(deg)]) xb = jnp.reshape((x[..., None,:] scales[:, None]), list(x.shape[:-1]) + [-1]) fourfeat = safesin(jnp.concatenate([xb, xb + 0.5 jnp.pi], axis=-1)) return jnp.concatenate([x] + [fourfeat], axis=-1) # def interpgrid(grid, cval=0.0): def predictlum(pos): return jnp.zeroslike(pos[..., 0]) + cval # return predictlum # def getXbd(res): coords = jnp.mgrid[0:res, 0:res, 0:res] mask = (coords[0] == 0) | (coords[0] == res-1) | \ (coords[1] == 0) | (coords[1] == res-1) | \ (coords[2] == 0) | (coords[2] == res-1) return coords[:, mask].T # def mlpforward(params, x): xenc = posenc(x, degpoint) h = jnp.tanh(jnp.dot(xenc, params['w1']) + params['b1']) h = h + jnp.dot(xenc, params['wskip']) # h = jnp.tanh(jnp.dot(h, params['w2']) + params['b2']) return h # def renderfn(rays, predicteta, predictlum, svals): etavals = predicteta(rays) lumvals = predictlum(rays) return jnp.sum(lumvals svals, axis=-1) # def lossfn(pred, target, etaboundary, lam, bdval): lumloss = jnp.mean((pred - target) 2) bdloss = jnp.mean((etaboundary - bdval) 2) return lumloss + lam bdloss # def trainpstep(raysshard, raylumtargetshard, Xregshard, optstate, rendereta, lossfnpartial, randkey, optimizer): def lossfn(params): pred = rendereta(raysshard, params) etaboundary = rendereta(Xregshard, params) return lossfnpartial(pred, raylumtargetshard, etaboundary) grad = jax.grad(lossfn)(optstate.params) updates, newstate = optimizer.update(grad, optstate) newstate = optax.applyupdates(newstate, updates) # return 0.0, 0.0, newstate, None, None, randkey, grad # def testpstepandplot(rays, raylumtarget, etatrue, mlp, optstate, rendereta, lossfnpartial, randkey, imgsplane, planelocs, savedir, i): pred = rendereta(rays, optstate.params) eta = mlp.apply({'params': optstate.params}, jnp.zeros((1, 3))) # # TensorBoard logging omitted for brevity return 0.0, 0.0, eta # def trainnf(rays, raylumtarget, lumfield, svals, imgsplane, planelocs, etatrue, sourcelocs, covs, numiters=50000, batchsize=4096, lrinit=1e-4, lrfinal=5e-6, testfreq=100, savefreq=100, lam=0.1, bdval=1.0003, seed=0, savedir='./'): # 1. Data Preparation predictlum = interpgrid(lumfield, cval=0.0) # Xreg = getXbd(16) # raysshard = jax.treeutil.treemap(lambda x: jnp.reshape(x, (jax.devicecount(), -1) + x.shape[1:]), rays) # raylumtargetshard = jax.treeutil.treemap(lambda x: jnp.reshape(x, (jax.devicecount(), -1) + x.shape[1:]), raylumtarget) # Xregshard = jax.treeutil.treemap(lambda x: jnp.reshape(x, (jax.devicecount(), -1) + x.shape[1:]), Xreg) # # 2. Initialization key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed) # mlp = jax.nn.Module(lambda x: x) # params = {'w1': jnp.zeros((3, 128)), 'b1': jnp.zeros(128), 'wskip': jnp.zeros((3, 128)), 'w2': jnp.zeros((128, 1)), 'b2': jnp.zeros(1)} # def lrschedule(x): return jnp.exp(jnp.log(lrinit) (1 - x/numiters) + jnp.log(lrfinal) (x/numiters)) # optimizer = optax.adam(lrschedule) # optstate = optimizer.init(params) # lossfnpartial = jax.treeutil.Partial(lossfn, lam=lam, bdval=bdval) # rendereta = lambda rays, p: renderfn(rays, lambda x: mlpforward(p, x), predictlum, svals) # randkey = key # # 3. Training Loop for i in tqdm.tqdm(range(1, numiters + 1)): if i == 1 or i % testfreq == 0: start, diffvmax, eta = testpstepandplot( rays, raylumtarget, etatrue, mlp, optstate, rendereta, lossfnpartial, randkey, imgsplane, planelocs, savedir, i) # if (i % savefreq == 0) or (i == 1): with open(f"{savedir}etaout/etaout{i:04d}.p", 'wb') as f: pickle.dump(eta, f) # losstrain, loss2, optstate, raytrace, rendering, randkey, grad = trainpstep( raysshard, raylumtargetshard, Xregshard, optstate, rendereta, lossfnpartial, randkey, optimizer) # return params, optstate Handles the sampling and sharding of rays for efficient parallel processing. Training Ray Batching General framework for differentiable rendering optimization. Training Loop Time Complexity: Linear with respect to numiters and batch size. Each iteration involves forward pass (ray tracing), loss computation, and backward pass (gradient computation). Memory Complexity: Proportional to batch size and model size. Sharding helps distribute memory across devices. Measured Performance: Trained over 50,000 iterations with batch size 4096. Learning rate decays from 1e-4 to 5e-6. Strengths: Efficient multi-device training via JAX. Effective regularization for IOR fields. Detailed logging and visualization. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to ray tracing and gradient computation. Sensitive to hyperparameters (lr, lam, bdval). When to Use: When training neural fields for refractive index and emission from ray-based measurements. When Not to Use: For simple volume rendering without IOR optimization or when computational resources are limited. This method is based on the rtnf repository by Brandon Zhao, which implements differentiable ray tracing for refractive index field estimation. It uses JAX for automatic differentiation and Optax for optimization. The approach combines Eikonal ray tracing with luminance integration to reconstruct 3D fields from 2D measurements. brandonyzhao/rtnf, https://github.com/brandonyzhao/rtnf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Training Loop
head: NeRF Training Pipeline, RtStereoHumanModel Training Loop, Training Loop & Data Fetching
body: The Training Loop is the main optimization procedure for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), orchestrating data loading, ray sampling, model forward passes, loss calculation, and parameter updates. It solves the problem of iteratively refining a differentiable radiance field representation to match observed input images. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Training Ray Batching by managing the high-level control flow (epochs, validation, checkpointing) rather than just the geometry of ray selection, and from Camera Pose Optimization by typically assuming fixed camera poses unless explicitly extended. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training dataset (images, poses, intrinsics), model architecture (NeRF MLP/Gaussian Splatting), optimizer configuration (learning rate, weight decay), and hyperparameters (batch size, epochs, near/far bounds). Outputs: Trained model weights, optimizer state, and optionally rendered validation/test images. Data Structures: Batch: A dictionary or object containing tensors for image data (lmain, rmain for stereo; or single view), camera parameters (intrinsics K, extrinsics P), and metadata (view indices, bounds). Ray Bundle: A flat array of rays, where each ray is defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, concatenated with the ground truth RGB color \mathbf{c} at the sampled pixel. Metrics: Accumulators for L1 loss, SSIM, and Chamfer distance. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load training and validation datasets using getnerfdatasets. Create the NeRF model and optimizer via createmodel(cfg) or createnerf(args). Initialize the learning rate scheduler (e.g., LambdaLR or OneCycleLR). Initialize gradient scaler if using mixed precision. 2. Data Fetching: Fetch the next batch from trainloader. If StopIteration occurs, reset the iterator to iter(trainloader) and fetch again. Move all relevant tensors (images, camera matrices, masks) to the CUDA device. Dataset-Specific Bounds: LLFF: Near = \min(\text{bounds}) \times 0.9, Far = \max(\text{bounds}) \times 1.0 (or 0/1 if nondc). Blender: Near = 2.0, Far = 6.0. DeepVoxels: Near = \text{hemi\R} - 1.0, Far = \text{hemi\R} + 1.0. 3. Ray Sampling: Sample random pixels from the ground truth image. Generate a ray bundle from these pixels using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. If batching is enabled, stack rays and concatenate with RGB values, then reshape into a flat array. Parameter: Nrand (number of random rays per batch). 4. Forward Pass: Pass the ray bundle through the model with istrain=True. The model renders the scene, producing predicted RGB colors and optionally depth/alpha. Gaussian Splatting Variant: Render using pts2render with background color from config (e.g., (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)). 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the primary rendering loss (e.g., L1 or MSE) between predicted and ground truth RGB. Compute structural similarity (SSIM) loss. Optional Regularization: Chamfer Loss: If enabled, extract valid points from left/right XYZ, sample 10,000 points, and compute chamfer distance. Total Loss Formula: \text{Loss} = 0.8 \times L1 + 0.2 \times (1 - \text{SSIM}) + 0.5 \times \text{Chamfer Loss}. Adaptive/Two-Phase: Use adaptive rendering loss weights or two-phase supervision to balance low-frequency structure and high-frequency details. 6. Backpropagation and Optimization: Scale the loss using GradScaler if mixed precision is active. Perform backward pass: loss.backward(). Unscale gradients and clip them to a global norm of 1.0. Step the optimizer: optimizer.step(). Step the learning rate scheduler. Update the gradient scaler. Zero gradients: optimizer.zerograd(). 7. Logging and Validation: Accumulate loss metrics (L1, SSIM, Chamfer). Print averages every 100 steps. If totalsteps % evalfreq == 0: Set model to eval mode. Run evaluation (runeval()) on validation set. Set model back to train mode. Freeze BatchNorm layers if applicable (e.g., in Raft-Stereo). 8. Checkpointing and Rendering: If epoch % checkpointinterval == 0, save model and optimizer state. If epoch % renderinterval == 0 and epoch > 0, render test images using surround cameras. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainingloop(model, trainloader, valloader, optimizer, scheduler, cfg): """ Main training loop for NeRF. """ totalsteps = 0 scaler = GradScaler(enabled=cfg.mixedprecision) for epoch in range(cfg.startepoch, cfg.numepochs): for batch in trainloader: image = batch['image'].to(device='cuda') camera = batch['camera'].to(device='cuda') rays, gtrgb = samplerays(image, camera, cfg.Nrand) with autocast(enabled=cfg.mixedprecision): predrgb = model(rays, istrain=True) l1loss = l1lossfn(predrgb, gtrgb) ssimloss = 1.0 - ssimfn(predrgb, gtrgb) chamferloss = 0.0 if cfg.ifchamfer and totalsteps > cfg.iterfrom: chamferloss = computechamferloss(batch) totalloss = 0.8 l1loss + 0.2 ssimloss + 0.5 chamferloss scaler.scale(totalloss).backward() scaler.unscale(optimizer) clipgradnorm(model.parameters(), maxnorm=1.0) scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() optimizer.zerograd() totalsteps += 1 if totalsteps % 100 == 0: logmetrics(l1loss, ssimloss, chamferloss) scheduler.step() if totalsteps % cfg.evalfreq == 0: model.eval() runeval(valloader) model.train() if epoch % cfg.checkpointinterval == 0: savecheckpoint(model, optimizer, epoch) if epoch % cfg.renderinterval == 0 and epoch > 0: rendertestimages(model) class GradScaler: def init(self, enabled): self.enabled = enabled def scale(self, loss): return loss def backward(self): pass def unscale(self, optimizer): pass def step(self, optimizer): optimizer.step() def update(self): pass def samplerays(image, camera, nrand): # Samples nrand random pixels and constructs ray origins/directions return rays, gtrgb def l1lossfn(pred, target): return torch.mean(torch.abs(pred - target)) def ssimfn(pred, target): return 1.0 # Placeholder for SSIM calculation def computechamferloss(batch): return 0.0 def logmetrics(l1, ssim, chamfer): pass def runeval(valloader): pass def savecheckpoint(model, optimizer, epoch): pass def rendertestimages(model): pass MVDream is a guidance method that fine-tunes Stable Diffusion with 3D-aware components trained on Objaverse to improve multi-view consistency and alleviate the Janus problem in text-to-3D generation. It provides gradient guidance for 3D optimization by encoding RGB images and camera poses into a multi-view diffusion model, predicting noise, and stepping the DDIM scheduler. Unlike standard Stable Diffusion guidance which treats views independently, MVDream explicitly conditions on camera poses to enforce geometric coherence across multiple viewpoints. Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization uses the score function of a pretrained 2D diffusion model to provide gradient signals that guide the optimization of a differentiable radiance field parametrization z = g(\theta) towards the mode of a conditional probability distribution p(zt | y). It solves the problem of generating or refining 3D scenes from sparse views or text prompts by leveraging the rich prior knowledge of 2D diffusion models, effectively removing non-photorealistic artifacts and enforcing geometric consistency. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like VCCNF Training Loop by relying on a frozen, pre-trained diffusion prior rather than a learned multi-view consistency network, and from MVDream Multi-View Diffusion Guidance by typically using a single-view or text-conditioned 2D model without explicit multi-view joint training. Specific Architecture Training Procedures define the optimization loops and configuration strategies required to train distinct radiance field architectures, addressing their unique convergence challenges and data requirements. Unlike generic training loops, these methods often decouple network stages or employ specialized loss functions (e.g., latent code regression) to resolve instabilities inherent in joint optimization or conditional generation. This article details the supervision strategy for optimizing a hybrid lighting representation that combines a volumetric lighting field with a parametric sky model for street scenes. It solves the problem of estimating physically plausible illumination from single or multi-view LDR images to enable realistic virtual object insertion. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit separation of sky and volumetric lighting components, supervised via a pre-trained sky modeling network and adversarial feedback from object insertion realism rather than pure photometric consistency alone. Parameters: valCamerasCount (int, default 100), testCamerasCount (int, default 200), grayLized (bool, default true). Layout: Render class fields include renderRes (Image); groundTruth, traincameras, valcameras, testcameras (Image/Camera); valCamerasCount (int, default 100); testCamerasCount (int, default 200); grayLized (bool, default true); datasetSize (int); scene (ObjectScene); ray (rays); sceneOptimizer (Optimizer); currentHierarchy (int); trainingProcessIdx (int, default 0); sampleRaysIndexGPU, sampleRaysIndexHost (int); idx (int); config (Configuration). Definition: A design choice where the input features to the importance predictor are detached from the gradient computation to prevent trivial solutions and simplify loss scaling. Parameter: Importance predictor loss weight is not required as a separate hyperparameter because stop gradient decouples it from the main loss, allowing Adam to scale them independently. Pitfall: Without stop gradient, gradients could push the proposer and importance predictor toward a trivial solution where bad samples are predicted as unimportant to minimize loss. Definition: A mechanism that adaptively learns rendering loss weights to align frequency relationships between PE and pixel supervision. Pitfall: May be unstable in the early training phase, causing global structures to resemble the baseline. Number: Improves all metrics compared to Baseline (PSNR 19.73 on DTU 3-view). Comparison: Improves local details (e.g., hands become cleaner) compared to Baseline and Model-A, but requires two-phase supervision for stable global structure learning. Definition: A rendering supervision strategy that makes NeRF optimization focus more on learning low-frequency information. Number: Improves PSNR from 19.54 (Baseline) to 19.81 (Model-A) on DTU 3-view. Comparison: Better at rendering global structures (e.g., face) compared to Baseline, but lacks local detail refinement. Step: Train the model with a train/test split by passing the --eval flag to train.py. This withholds a test set for evaluation. Step: Generate renderings for the trained model using render.py, specifying the model path. Step: Compute error metrics on the generated renderings using metrics.py, specifying the model path. Definition: An optimization acceleration technique where back-propagated prior gradients (\nablax \lambda{diff} L{diff}) are cached and reused for multiple Adam steps on scene codes, while rendering gradients (\nablax \lambda{rend} L{rend}) are recomputed in each step. Step: In the outer loop, compute prior gradients g{xdiff} once per scene batch. Step: In the inner loop, compute new rendering gradients g{xrend} for the current ray batch. Step: Add the cached prior gradient g{xdiff} to the new rendering gradient g{xrend} to form the update gradient gx. Step: Update scene codes using gx, allowing fewer diffusion passes than rendering passes. Step: LOD generation phase: Freeze training of submodels for 5,000 iterations, then refine them and shared global deferred MLP jointly for an additional 10,000 iterations. Parameter: Training loss weights: \lambda1 = 1.0, \lambda2 = 1.0, \lambda3 = 0.01, \lambda4 = 0.05, \lambda5 = 0.001. Sample count for sparsity loss: 2^{14} samples. Step: Train MLPs alongside the last layer of the color MLP using the RGB loss (Eq. 4), without ground truth segmentation masks. Formula: cx = \alphax c'x + (1 - \alphax) cx where c'x is the new color from the retrained last layer, cx is the original color, and \alphax is the probability of the feature being part of the edited area. Layout: Soft segmentation MLP (MLPs): Two-layer MLP. Input: 32-dimensional multiresolution hash grid feature vector f. Hidden layer: 64 neurons. Output: 1-dimensional probability \alpha. Number: Convergence time for soft segmentation: typically less than 5 seconds. Definition: A self-supervised method to train a CNN-based encoder to predict camera parameters from rendered images, used for style inversion tasks. Step: Randomly sample a camera pose and latent codes to render the output image. Step: Use a CNN-based encoder (backbone initialized with pretrained ResNet18) to read the image and predict input camera parameters based on a smoothed L1 loss function. Definition: A regularization technique applied to the camera trajectory to prevent high-frequency predictions and improve trajectory estimation by leveraging the sequential nature of camera movement. Definition: A regularization term added to the loss function to enforce smooth and continuous camera trajectory estimation across adjacent Rolling Shutter (RS) frames, addressing the issue of high-frequency predictions in vanilla RS-NeRF. Step: For each pair of adjacent trajectory vectors \vec{d}k and \vec{d}{k+1}, compute the mid-point trajectory vector \vec{d}{mid}. Formula: \mathcal {L}{s}=||\overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{mid} - \operatorname {mean}(\overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}k + \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{k+1})||2. where \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}k and \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{k+1} are unit direction vectors of estimated camera trajectories for adjacent RS frames I^Rk and I^R{k+1}, and \overrightarrow {\mathbf {n}}{mid} is the unit direction vector for the camera trajectory during the exposure interval between these two frames. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of training steps and batch size. Each step involves a forward pass through the MLP/Gaussian splatter and a backward pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of model parameters and the batch size (storing gradients and optimizer states). Measured Performance: Varies by implementation. For example, IBRNet baseline training takes 0.33 sec/iteration with 33.3 sec/frame rendering. Scaling: Scales with batch size and number of rays sampled per step (Nrand). Larger batches improve gradient stability but increase memory usage. Strengths: Flexible, supports various loss functions (L1, SSIM, Chamfer), and integrates with standard PyTorch/TensorFlow optimization utilities. Limitations: Can be slow for high-resolution scenes due to ray sampling and rendering overhead. Prone to local minima without careful initialization or regularization (e.g., importance sampling, adaptive loss weights). When to use: Standard NeRF training for novel view synthesis. When not to use: When real-time training is required (consider MVDream or Diffusion-Based Guidance for faster convergence via priors). The NeRF training loop was introduced in the seminal paper "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" by Mildenhall et al. (2020). It established the standard pipeline of volumetric rendering integrated with gradient-based optimization. Subsequent works have extended this loop with various optimizations, such as importance sampling, adaptive loss weighting, and diffusion-based guidance. name: MVDream Multi-View Diffusion Guidance
head: MVDream Guidance, Multi-View Dream
body: MVDream is a guidance method that fine-tunes Stable Diffusion with 3D-aware components trained on Objaverse to improve multi-view consistency and alleviate the Janus problem in text-to-3D generation. It provides gradient guidance for 3D optimization by encoding RGB images and camera poses into a multi-view diffusion model, predicting noise, and stepping the DDIM scheduler. Unlike standard Stable Diffusion guidance which treats views independently, MVDream explicitly conditions on camera poses to enforce geometric coherence across multiple viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs Input: Text prompts, a batch of rendered RGB images (predrgb256) from the current 3D representation, and corresponding camera pose matrices. Output: Gradient signal for optimizing the 3D representation via the latent space update. Data Structures Camera Tensor: Shape [batchsize, 16], created by normalizing the 4×4 camera pose matrix and flattening it. Context Dictionary: Contains 'context' (text embeddings of shape [B, 77, 768]), 'camera' (camera tensor of shape [B, 16]), and 'numframes' (integer, typically 4). Parameters trange: List of floats, default [0.02, 0.98], defines the range of noise levels for training. minstep = int(1000 trange[0]), maxstep = int(1000 trange[1]). guidancescale: Float, default 100, multiplier for classifier-free guidance in noise prediction. Steps 1. Encode Text: Generate text embeddings and repeat them to match the number of views (typically 4). \text{pos\embeds} = \text{encode\text(prompts)}.repeat(4, 1, 1) 2. Convert Camera Convention: Convert camera poses to Blender convention by permuting axes and flipping the Y-axis. \text{camera} = \text{camera}[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] \text{camera}[:, 1] = -1 3. Normalize Camera: Normalize the camera poses and flatten to 16 dimensions. \text{camera} = \text{normalize\camera(camera)}.view(\text{batch\size}, 16) 4. Encode Images: Encode the rendered RGB images into latent space. \text{latents} = \text{encode\imgs(pred\rgb\256)} 5. Sample Timestep: Sample a timestep t uniformly between minstep and maxstep. 6. Forward Model with CFG: Pass the latents, timestep, and context through the model. Split the output into conditional and unconditional predictions and combine them using classifier-free guidance. \text{noise\pred} = \text{model.apply\model}(\text{latent\model\input}, t, \text{context}) \text{noise\pred\uncond}, \text{noise\pred\cond} = \text{noise\pred.chunk}(2) \text{noise\pred} = \text{noise\pred\uncond} + \text{guidance\scale} \times (\text{noise\pred\cond} - \text{noise\pred\uncond}) 7. Step Scheduler: Update the latents using the DDIM scheduler. \text{latents} = \text{scheduler.step}(\text{noise\pred}, t, \text{latents}).\text{prev\sample} Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mvdreamguidancestep(model, scheduler, encodetext, encodeimgs, prompts, predrgb256, cameraposes, batchsize, guidancescale=100, trange=(0.02, 0.98)): # 1. Encode text prompts posembeds = encodetext(prompts) posembeds = posembeds.repeat(4, 1, 1) # 2. Convert camera to Blender convention # cameraposes shape is assumed to be [batchsize, 4, 4] or [batchsize, 4, 16] # The source applies permutation and flip before normalization camera = cameraposes[:, [0, 2, 1, 3]] camera[:, 1] = -1 # 3. Normalize camera and flatten to [batchsize, 16] # normalizecamera is not defined in the sources camera = normalizecamera(camera).view(batchsize, 16) # 4. Encode RGB images to latents latents = encodeimgs(predrgb256) # 5. Sample timestep uniformly between minstep and maxstep minstep = int(1000 trange[0]) maxstep = int(1000 trange[1]) t = torch.randint(minstep, maxstep, (batchsize,)).to(latents.device) # 6. Forward model with Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) # Prepare null context for CFG nulltext = encodetext([""]) nulltext = nulltext.repeat(4, 1, 1) nullcamera = torch.zeroslike(camera) # Concatenate conditional and unconditional inputs along batch dimension latentscfg = torch.cat([latents, latents], dim=0) contextcfg = { 'context': torch.cat([posembeds, nulltext], dim=0), 'camera': torch.cat([camera, nullcamera], dim=0), 'numframes': 4 } noisepred = model.applymodel(latentscfg, t.repeat(2), contextcfg) noisepreduncond, noisepredcond = noisepred.chunk(2) noisepred = noisepreduncond + guidancescale (noisepredcond - noisepreduncond) # 7. Step scheduler latents = scheduler.step(noisepred, t, latents).prevsample return latents Edge Cases and Pitfalls Complex Prompts: MVDream tends to ignore specific prompt details (e.g., moss on a suit, vines on a car) compared to standard Stable Diffusion guidance. Janus Problem: While MVDream alleviates the Janus problem, it does not completely eliminate it due to the ill-posed nature of text-to-3D generation. GALA3D is a method for 3D scene generation that leverages both object-level and scene-level models to achieve realistic composition. It addresses the challenge of generating coherent 3D scenes by first synthesizing individual objects and then composing them into a global environment. Unlike single-stage text-to-3D methods, GALA3D separates the generation of local geometry (objects) from global layout (scenes), using MVDream for object synthesis and a scene-level diffusion model for composition. RealmDreamer utilizes diffusion priors from inpainting and depth estimation models to generate different viewpoints of a scene iteratively. This method generates high-quality viewpoint images of unobserved viewpoints by utilizing multidimensional features from MTL-FeatureNet and viewpoint data from an improved NeRF model, ensuring geometric and physical realism. It uses features from MTL-FeatureNet as inputs to the conditional diffusion model to guide the generation process, ensuring visual coherence and geometric/physical consistency with original viewpoints. It improves the traditional backward diffusion process by fusing and using conditional information c to determine the mean \mu\theta and covariance \Sigma\theta for the Gaussian transition from Ot to O{t-1}: \rho\theta(O{t-1}|Ot, c) = \mathcal{N}(O{t-1}; \mu\theta(Ot, c, t), \Sigma\theta(Ot, c, t)) The conditional information c is derived from features extracted via MTL-FeatureNet. Multi-View Consistency: MVDream significantly improves multi-view consistency and geometry completeness (e.g., Janus-free ostrich) compared to standard guidance. Prompt Adherence: It sacrifices fine-grained prompt adherence on complex scenes, tending to ignore specific prompt details (e.g., moss on a suit, vines on a car) compared to standard Stable Diffusion guidance. Performance: The method relies on the computational cost of the Stable Diffusion model and the DDIM scheduler steps. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Better 3D geometry and consistency. Limitations: Loss of detail for complex prompts; incomplete elimination of Janus problem due to the ill-posed nature of text-to-3D generation. MVDream was proposed as a concurrent work to improve text-to-3D generation by fine-tuning Stable Diffusion with 3D-aware components trained on Objaverse. It aims to enhance multi-view consistency and alleviate the Janus problem. The method is cited in the context of Gaussian Splatting for text-to-3D generation and is part of the broader family of diffusion-based guidance methods for radiance field optimization. name: GALA3D
body: GALA3D is a method for 3D scene generation that leverages both object-level and scene-level models to achieve realistic composition. It addresses the challenge of generating coherent 3D scenes by first synthesizing individual objects and then composing them into a global environment. Unlike single-stage text-to-3D methods, GALA3D separates the generation of local geometry (objects) from global layout (scenes), using MVDream for object synthesis and a scene-level diffusion model for composition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt describing the desired scene. Output: A composed 3D scene representation. Data Structures: Object-level representation: Generated by MVDream, typically a point cloud or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representation. Scene-level composition: A diffusion model that arranges and composes the generated objects into a coherent scene. Steps: 1. Object Generation: Use the object-level text-to-3D model MVDream to generate realistic 3D objects from the text prompt. 2. Scene Composition: Use a scene-level diffusion model to compose the generated objects into a coherent 3D scene. Parameters: Text prompt: Defines the semantic content of the scene. MVDream model: Pre-trained text-to-3D model. Scene-level diffusion model: Pre-trained model for scene composition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. This process simultaneously generates multiple views of the object as well as its 3D model. During inference, the viewset is initialized with Gaussian noise. The model iteratively denoises the viewset by applying a reconstruction model. Each image Ii in the viewset is replaced with Ii^t = \alphat Ii + \sigmat \epsiloni where t is the noising schedule, \alphat and \sigmat = \sqrt{1 - \alphat^2} are the noise level, and \epsiloni is a random Normal noise vector. This approach boosts scalability by increasing the amount of 2D information lifted to 3D and allows for larger model and batch sizes during training due to memory savings. Inference time for Lightplane is under 2 minutes, compared to 30 minutes for HoloFusion. It significantly outperforms HoloDiffusion and Viewset Diffusion on CO3Dv2, and beats HoloFusion in speed. Time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory complexity is reduced in the Lightplane-augmented variant, allowing for increased model and batch sizes during training. Performance benchmarks show improvements in scalability and speed for 3D tasks. Strengths include enabling the generation of complex scenes with multiple objects and scalability to large-scale 3D models. Limitations include the requirement for two separate models (object-level and scene-level) and dependency on pre-trained model quality. GALA3D was introduced to explore 3D scene generation by combining object-level and scene-level generation processes. It builds on the idea of using text-to-3D models like MVDream for object synthesis and extends it to scene-level composition. The method is part of the broader effort to improve the realism and coherence of generated 3D scenes.
