name: Masked Completion via GAN Inversion
head: GAN Inversion for 3D Completion
body: Masked Completion via GAN Inversion is a conditional sampling technique that completes a 3D radiance field by inverting a 2D discriminator-trained generator, using photometric error on non-masked regions to guide the optimization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Nerfiller and Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields by operating in the latent space of a pre-trained GAN generator (specifically EG3D) rather than optimizing a neural network's weights or using diffusion-based volumetric gradients directly. Inputs: A pre-trained 3D-aware GAN generator (e.g., EG3D) trained with 2D discriminator guidance. A target image with an associated 3D input mask indicating the region to be completed. A random initial latent code w{init}. Outputs: An optimized latent code w^ that, when passed through the generator, produces a 3D radiance field consistent with the non-masked regions of the input image. Data Structures: Latent Code (w): The optimization variable, initialized randomly. 3D Input Mask: A binary mask defining the region of interest in the 3D scene, projected onto 2D views. Parameters: Iterations: 200 iterations per masked sample. Views per Iteration: 8 views. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 10^{-2}. L2 Regularization Weight: 5 \times 10^{-2} applied to the latent code. Resolution: Rendering is performed at 128 \times 128 resolution. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start from a random initial latent code w. 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat for 200 iterations: a. Rendering: Render the current synthesized sample from 8 different views using the current latent code w. b. Mask Projection: Project the 3D input mask onto the synthesized views using the predicted depths from the rendering. c. Error Computation: Compute the photometric error between the rendered non-masked regions and the corresponding regions in the input images. d. Optimization: Update the latent code w using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10^{-2} and an L2 regularization term on the code weighted by 5 \times 10^{-2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskedcompletionviaganinversion(generator, targetimages, inputmask3d, numiterations=200, numviews=8): # Initialize with a random latent code w = [random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) for in range(generator.latentdim)] lr = 1e-2 l2weight = 5e-2 for i in range(numiterations): # Render the current synthesized sample from 8 views renderedimages = [] predicteddepths = [] for viewidx in range(numviews): img, depth = generator.forward(w, view=viewidx) renderedimages.append(img) predicteddepths.append(depth) # Project the 3D input mask onto the synthesized views using predicted depths viewmasks = [] for viewidx in range(numviews): # Standard 3D-to-2D projection using camera pose and depth mask2d = project3dmaskto2d(inputmask3d, predicteddepths[viewidx], generator.getcamerapose(viewidx)) viewmasks.append(mask2d) # Compute photometric error on non-masked regions totalerror = 0.0 gradw = [0.0] len(w) for j in range(numviews): renderedimg = renderedimages[j] targetimg = targetimages[j] nonmasked = [[1.0 - viewmasks[j][y][x] for x in range(len(viewmasks[j][0]))] for y in range(len(viewmasks[j]))] # Photometric error (MSE) on non-masked regions errorsum = 0.0 count = 0 for y in range(len(renderedimg)): for x in range(len(renderedimg[0])): diff = (renderedimg[y][x] - targetimg[y][x]) nonmasked[y][x] errorsum += diff 2 count += 1 error = errorsum / count totalerror += error # Compute gradient w.r.t latent code via automatic differentiation gradw = addvectors(gradw, generator.backward(w, renderedimg, nonmasked)) # Add L2 regularization on the latent code l2loss = l2weight sum(wi2 for wi in w) loss = totalerror + l2loss # Update latent code using Adam optimizer step # (Standard Adam update: m, v, t, biascorrection, w = w - lr (mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + eps) + l2weight w)) w = adamstep(w, gradw, lr, l2weight) return w def project3dmaskto2d(mask3d, depthmap, camerapose): # Standard perspective projection of 3D mask using depth and camera pose # Returns 2D mask where 1 indicates masked region return [[0.0] width for in range(height)] # Standard projection logic def addvectors(a, b): return [x + y for x, y in zip(a, b)] def adamstep(w, grad, lr, l2weight): # Simplified gradient descent step with L2 regularization # Full Adam state maintenance omitted for brevity; standard implementation applies bias correction and moment updates return [wi - lr (gw + l2weight wi) for wi, gw in zip(w, grad)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The method requires 200 iterations per sample, with each iteration involving rendering from 8 views. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the storage of the latent code and the intermediate rendered images and depths for the 8 views per iteration. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 2080 TI, the method requires 48.6 seconds per sample for 1000 iterations. Rendering Speed: Once synthesized, the explicit representation enables rendering at 128 \times 128 resolution with over 380 FPS. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Masked Completion via GAN Inversion is described in the context of DiffRF, which uses a rendering-guided 3D radiance field diffusion model. The specific technique of using GAN inversion for 3D masked completion is attributed to the use of the EG3D generator, which is trained via 2D discriminator guidance. This approach allows for conditional sampling in 3D by optimizing the latent code to match 2D image observations. name: Diffusion Model Preprocessing & Training Setup
head: SDG Preprocessing, Stable Diffusion Training Setup
body: This method defines the data preprocessing pipeline and hyperparameter configuration required to fine-tune a 2D diffusion model (specifically Stable Diffusion 1.5) to serve as a semantic prior for radiance field optimization. It solves the problem of overfitting to specific camera viewpoints and occlusion artifacts by decoupling semantic identity learning from spatial pose control, ensuring the model generalizes to novel views. It sets itself apart from methods like ReconFusion by explicitly managing the perspective gap between reference and training images through distinct cropping strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Raw images from the KITTI-360 dataset (original resolution 1408 \times 376), LiDAR point clouds, and text prompts. Output: Preprocessed image tensors (512 \times 512), masked depth maps, and a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 1.5 model ready for classifier-free guidance. Data Structures: Image Tensor: H \times W \times C float32, normalized to [0, 1]. Depth Mask: Boolean mask of size H \times W, where the top 80 rows are True (masked) and the rest are False. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Training Data): Crop: Apply a center crop to the original 1408 \times 376 image to obtain 600 \times 376. This step avoids over-distortion during the subsequent resize. Resize: Resize the 600 \times 376 image to 512 \times 512. Masking: Apply the depth mask to the corresponding depth map, setting the top 80 rows to invalid/empty values to account for LiDAR height limitations. 2. Reference Image Selection (Training): During training, reference images are selected from the temporal sequence. Randomly choose one frame from the five frames preceding the current training image. Randomly choose one frame from the five frames succeeding the current training image. Crop: Apply a random crop to these reference images (before resizing to 512 \times 512) to ensure a perspective gap between the reference and the training image. 3. Reference Image Selection (Inference): Standard Inference: Apply a center crop to the reference images before resizing to 512 \times 512. Novel View Inference: Identify the closest training viewpoint to the desired novel viewpoint. Use the adjacent frames of this closest training viewpoint as the reference images. Apply center crop and resize as above. 4. Training Configuration (Classifier-Free Guidance): To enable classifier-free guidance, randomly set both the text prompt and the reference images to empty/null with a probability of 10\% during training. 5. Model Initialization: Initialize the model with pre-trained Stable Diffusion 1.5 weights. Fine-tune on approximately 12,000 images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocesstrainingimage(imageraw, depthraw): """ Preprocesses a single training image and its depth map. imageraw: numpy array of shape (376, 1408, 3) depthraw: numpy array of shape (376, 1408) Returns: processedimage (512, 512, 3), processeddepth (512, 512) """ # Step 1: Center crop to 600x376 to avoid distortion h, w = imageraw.shape[0], imageraw.shape[1] neww = 600 startx = (w - neww) // 2 imagecropped = imageraw[:, startx:startx+neww,:] depthcropped = depthraw[:, startx:startx+neww] # Step 2: Resize to 512x512 imageresized = resize(imagecropped, (512, 512)) depthresized = resize(depthcropped, (512, 512)) # Step 3: Apply depth mask (top 80 rows) depthmask = np.zeros((512, 512), dtype=bool) depthmask[:80,:] = True processeddepth = np.where(depthmask, np.nan, depthresized) return imageresized, processeddepth def selectandpreprocessreference(referenceimagesraw): """ Selects and preprocesses reference images for training. referenceimagesraw: list of raw images (376, 1408, 3) Returns: list of processed reference images (512, 512, 3) """ processedrefs = [] for refimg in referenceimagesraw: # Random crop is applied to reference images during training # to ensure perspective gap. # Note: Exact random crop logic depends on implementation, # but must result in a crop that is then resized to 512x512. # We assume a random crop of size 600x376 is taken first, # similar to training image, but with random offset. h, w = refimg.shape[0], refimg.shape[1] neww = 600 startx = random.randint(0, w - neww) refcropped = refimg[:, startx:startx+neww,:] refresized = resize(refcropped, (512, 512)) processedrefs.append(refresized) return processedrefs def selectreferenceforinference(referenceimagesraw, isnovelview, closesttrainingviewrefs): """ Selects reference images for inference. Returns: list of processed reference images (512, 512, 3) """ if isnovelview: # Use adjacent frames of the closest training viewpoint rawrefs = closesttrainingviewrefs else: # Use pre-selected adjacent frames from the sequence rawrefs = referenceimagesraw processedrefs = [] for refimg in rawrefs: # Center crop for inference h, w = refimg.shape[0], refimg.shape[1] neww = 600 startx = (w - neww) // 2 refcropped = refimg[:, startx:startx+neww,:] refresized = resize(refcropped, (512, 512)) processedrefs.append(refresized) return processedrefs def applyclassifierfreeguidanceconditioning(textprompt, referenceimages, training=True): """ Applies CFG conditioning. Returns: modifiedtextprompt, modifiedreferenceimages """ if training and random.random() < 0.1: # 10% probability to empty both for CFG return "", [] return textprompt, referenceimages Image-Conditioned Diffusion Fine-Tuning is the first stage of a two-step procedure that adapts a pre-trained 2D diffusion model (specifically Stable Diffusion 1.5) to learn high-level semantic content of a specific scene from adjacent reference images, without using pose information. It sets itself apart from methods like ReconFusion by decoupling semantic identity learning from spatial pose control, thereby preventing the model from overfitting to specific camera viewpoints or occlusion artifacts common in complex driving scenes. StableMaterial Training Configuration defines the hyperparameters and data pipeline for finetuning a 2D diffusion model prior to estimate physically plausible material properties (albedo and ORM) from input images. It adapts a pretrained Stable Diffusion UNet by freezing the backbone and training only a custom adapter and the UNet weights, reducing computational requirements compared to full model training. This configuration serves as the foundation for the StableMaterial model, which provides strong material priors for inverse rendering pipelines like MaterialFusion. DeepFloyd IF 2D Guidance is a text-to-image guidance approach using DeepFloyd IF, which features an Imagen-like architecture and a T-5 text encoder for stronger text understanding. It requires downsampling the input image to 64 \times 64 pixels before passing it to the model due to its modular cascaded design. It produces better text-3D alignment than StableDiffusion due to the T-5 encoder, but yields blurrier assets because of the mandatory 64 \times 64 downsampling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is trained on 12,000 images from the KITTI-360 dataset. The 3D Gaussian Splatting model is trained for 50,000 iterations. Strengths: Prevents overfitting to training views by ensuring a perspective gap between reference and training images. Effectively handles missing depth data in the top 80 rows via inpainting capabilities. Limitations: The preprocessing steps (cropping and resizing) may introduce geometric distortions if not handled carefully, though the preliminary crop to 600 \times 376 mitigates this. When to use: When using Stable Diffusion 1.5 as a prior for street view synthesis or radiance field optimization where viewpoint generalization is critical. When not to use: When high-fidelity text alignment is required without blur, in which case DeepFloyd IF might be considered despite its blur. The method originates from the SGD (Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior) paper, which adapts Stable Diffusion 1.5 for 3D scene synthesis. It builds on the need to overcome overfitting in diffusion-guided radiance field optimization by introducing specific data augmentation and conditioning strategies. name: Image-Conditioned Diffusion Fine-Tuning
head: Training Stage 1
body: Image-Conditioned Diffusion Fine-Tuning is the first stage of a two-step procedure that adapts a pre-trained 2D diffusion model (specifically Stable Diffusion 1.5) to learn high-level semantic content of a specific scene from adjacent reference images, without using pose information. It sets itself apart from methods like ReconFusion by decoupling semantic identity learning from spatial pose control, thereby preventing the model from overfitting to specific camera viewpoints or occlusion artifacts common in complex driving scenes. This method fine-tunes the U-Net parameters of a diffusion model to condition generation on text prompts and latent features from adjacent reference frames. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An input image I (current frame), a previous reference image I{pre}, a next reference image I{next}, and a text prompt T. Output: A fine-tuned U-Net \theta capable of denoising latents conditioned on eT and e{I{ref}}. Data Structures: Latent Feature Map z0: Output of the frozen VAE encoder applied to I. Dimensions depend on the VAE's downsampling factor (typically H/8 \times W/8 for SD 1.5). Text Embedding eT: Sequence of token embeddings from the frozen CLIP Text Encoder. Shape: [LT, D], where LT is token length and D=768 (for clip-vit-B-32). Image Embedding e{Ii}: Sequence of patch embeddings from the frozen CLIP Image Encoder. Shape: [LI, D], where LI=50 (1 CLS token + 49 patch tokens) for 224 \times 224 input. Combined Condition c{img}: Concatenation of eT and [e{I{pre}}, e{I{next}}] along the sequence length dimension. Shape: [LT + 2LI, D]. Parameters: CLIP Image Encoder Input Size: 224 \times 224 \times 3. Batch Size: 4. Hardware: 4 NVIDIA V100 GPUs (32GB VRAM). Iterations: 625,000. Steps: 1. Reference Selection: For a given input image I, select the immediately preceding frame I{pre} and the immediately following frame I{next} as the reference set I{ref} = \{I{pre}, I{next}\}. 2. Latent Encoding: Encode I into latent space z0 using the frozen VAE encoder \mathcal{E}{VAE}: z0 = \mathcal{E}{VAE}(I) 3. Text Encoding: Tokenize T and encode it using the frozen CLIP Text Encoder \mathcal{E}{text}: eT = \mathcal{E}{text}(T) = [eT^0, \ldots, eT^{LT}], \quad eT^i \in \mathbb{R}^D \quad (1) where LT is the token sequence length and D is the embedding dimension. 4. Reference Image Encoding: Encode I{pre} and I{next} separately using the frozen CLIP Image Encoder \mathcal{E}{Image}: e{Ii} = \mathcal{E}{Image}(Ii) = [e{Ii}^0, \ldots, e{Ii}^{LI}], \quad i \in \{\text{pre}, \text{next}\} \quad (2) where LI is the number of image patches (50). 5. Condition Fusion: Concatenate the reference image features to the text embedding along the token length dimension to form the combined condition c{img}: c{img} = \text{Concat}(eT, e{I{pre}}, e{I{next}}) 6. Denoising Prediction: Pass the noisy latent zt (at timestep t), the timestep t, and the combined condition c{img} into the trainable U-Net \epsilon\theta to predict the noise \epsilon: \hat{\epsilon} = \epsilon\theta(zt, t, c{img}) 7. Loss Calculation: Optimize \theta by minimizing the mean squared error between the predicted noise and the actual random noise \epsilon: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}{z0, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}), t, T, I{ref}} ||\epsilon - \epsilon\theta(zt, t, eT, e{I{ref}})||2^2 \quad (3) where \epsilon is random noise, t is the denoising timestep, and zt is the noisy latent at timestep t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline def trainstage1(model, vae, textencoder, imageencoder, dataloader, optimizer, numiterations=625000, batchsize=4): """ Fine-tunes the U-Net of a Stable Diffusion model using image-conditioned diffusion loss. Args: model: The U-Net component of Stable Diffusion 1.5 (trainable). vae: Frozen VAE encoder. textencoder: Frozen CLIP Text Encoder. imageencoder: Frozen CLIP Image Encoder (clip-vit-B-32). dataloader: Iterator yielding batches of (I, Ipre, Inext, T). optimizer: Optimizer for model parameters. numiterations: Total training steps. batchsize: Batch size per GPU (total batch size = batchsize numgpus). """ model.train() vae.eval() textencoder.eval() imageencoder.eval() # Noise scheduler for sampling timesteps # Assuming standard DDPM noise schedule used in SD 1.5 noisescheduler = model.config.getnoisescheduler() for step in range(numiterations): # 1. Load batch # I: [B, 3, H, W], Ipre: [B, 3, H, W], Inext: [B, 3, H, W], T: list of strings I, Ipre, Inext, T = next(dataloader) # 2. Encode Input Image to Latent z0 with torch.nograd(): z0 = vae.encode(I) # 3. Encode Text Prompt with torch.nograd(): textinputs = textencoder.tokenizer(T, padding=True, returntensors="pt") eT = textencoder(textinputs.inputids, textinputs.attentionmask).lasthiddenstate # eT shape: [B, LT, D] # 4. Encode Reference Images with torch.nograd(): # Resize references to 224x224 if necessary, as per CLIP input requirements Ipreresized = F.interpolate(Ipre, size=(224, 224), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) Inextresized = F.interpolate(Inext, size=(224, 224), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) eIpre = imageencoder(Ipreresized).lasthiddenstate eInext = imageencoder(Inextresized).lasthiddenstate # eIpre, eInext shape: [B, LI, D] where LI=50 # 5. Concatenate Conditions # Concatenate along sequence dimension (dim=1) # eT: [B, LT, D], eIpre: [B, LI, D], eInext: [B, LI, D] combinedcondition = torch.cat([eT, eIpre, eInext], dim=1) # combinedcondition shape: [B, LT + 2LI, D] # 6. Sample Timestep and Noise t = torch.randint(0, noisescheduler.config.numtraintimesteps, (batchsize,), device=I.device) noise = torch.randnlike(z0) # 7. Add Noise to Latent zt = noisescheduler.addnoise(z0, noise, t) # 8. Predict Noise # model expects: sample, timestep, encoderhiddenstates predictednoise = model(zt, t, encoderhiddenstates=combinedcondition).sample # 9. Compute Loss loss = F.mseloss(predictednoise, noise) # 10. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() if step % 1000 == 0: print(f"Step {step}, Loss: {loss.item()}") A second fine-tuning stage that adds a ControlNet module to the frozen Stage 1 model to incorporate spatial relationships via depth maps derived from LiDAR point clouds. It addresses the limitation of Stage 1, which lacks awareness of spatial relationships between objects, by enabling depth-controlled generation. It sets itself apart from Stage 1 by introducing a separate trainable network (ControlNet) initialized as a copy of the U-Net encoder, rather than modifying the main U-Net weights directly. Steps: 1. Depth Map Generation: Derive depth maps D{I{ref}} for reference images and DI for the input image by projecting 3D LiDAR point clouds onto the image plane and completing them using an off-the-shelf depth completion model. 2. ControlNet Initialization: Initialize the ControlNet as a trainable copy of the U-Net’s encoder block from Stage 1. 3. Depth Encoding: Encode reference depth maps D{I{ref}} using a pre-trained depth encoder \mathcal{E}{depth} (structure identical to CLIP Image Encoder, pre-trained via contrastive learning): e{Di} = \mathcal{E}{Depth}(Ii) 4. Feature Fusion: Fuse encoded depth features e{Di} with CLIP image features e{Ii} via average pooling: \tilde{e}{Ii} = \text{AvgPool}(e{Ii}, e{Di}), \quad i \in \{\text{pre}, \text{next}\} \quad (5) 5. Injection: Concatenate the fused features \tilde{e}{I{ref}} with text embedding eT and inject into the ControlNet via cross-attention. 6. Training: Train the ControlNet parameters \tilde{\theta} using the loss function: \mathcal{L}(\tilde{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}{z0, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}), t, T, \{I{ref}, D{ref}\}} ||\epsilon - \epsilon\theta(zt, t, cD, eT, \tilde{e}{I{ref}})||2^2 \quad (6) where cD represents the depth condition. Parameters: Training Iterations: 125,000 steps. Time Complexity: The method requires significant computational resources due to the large number of iterations (625,000 for Stage 1, 125,000 for Stage 2) and the use of multiple encoders (VAE, CLIP Text, CLIP Image) per step. Memory Complexity: Requires 4 NVIDIA V100 GPUs (32GB VRAM each) with a batch size of 4 per GPU, indicating high memory usage for storing latent representations and model weights. Strengths: Effectively learns high-level semantic content and "what exists" in a scene without being biased by camera pose, which is crucial for complex driving scenes with occlusions. Limitations: Stage 1 alone does not capture spatial relationships or depth, requiring the subsequent ControlNet stage for geometric accuracy. The reliance on LiDAR for Stage 2 limits applicability to scenes with available depth data. When to use: When synthesizing novel views for a specific scene where semantic consistency across adjacent frames is more critical than initial geometric precision, and LiDAR data is available for the second stage. When not to use: When pose information is the primary constraint or when computational resources are limited to a single GPU. The method originates from the paper "SGD: Street View Synthesis with Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion Prior". It was developed to address the challenges of autonomous driving scene synthesis, where complex objects (buildings, vehicles, pedestrians) and mutual occlusions make it difficult for diffusion models to understand 3D structure from pose alone. The approach builds on Stable Diffusion 1.5 and utilizes CLIP encoders for conditioning. It is part of a pipeline that eventually regularizes 3D Gaussian Splatting training. name: Two-Stage Specified Diffusion
head: DreamBooth Fine-Tuning
body: Two-Stage Specified Diffusion is a fine-tuning procedure that specializes a 2D diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion) for a specific target object by gradually learning its visual style and identity details. It addresses the problem of adapting a pre-trained diffusion model to a novel object without requiring multi-view consistent training data, using Zero-1-to-3 generated images as intermediate style references. It sets itself apart from single-stage fine-tuning by decoupling style learning from identity preservation, thereby preventing the model from overfitting to the specific pose or artifacts of the initial generated views. Inputs: 1. A pre-trained 2D diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion). 2. A single input image of the target object. 3. A set of multi-view images generated from the input image using Zero-1-to-3. 4. A text prompt describing the object class. Outputs: A fine-tuned diffusion model specialized for the target object. Data Structures: Identifier [V]: A unique string token used in Stage 1 to represent the visual style of the target. Identifier [S]: An additional unique string token used in Stage 2 to represent the specific identity of the target. Steps: 1. Generate Intermediate Views: Use Zero-1-to-3 to generate a set of multi-view images from the input image. Note that these images may not be multi-view consistent but share the visual style of the input. 2. Stage 1: Visual Style Learning: Positive Samples: The multi-view images generated by Zero-1-to-3. Negative Samples: Images generated by the diffusion model using the text prompt alone (without the object identifier). Prompt Construction: Use the text prompt combined with the unique identifier [V] (e.g., "a photo of a [V]"). Objective: Fine-tune the diffusion model to associate the identifier [V] with the visual style present in the Zero-1-to-3 outputs. 3. Stage 2: Identity Refinement: Positive Samples: The original input image. Negative Samples: All multi-view images generated by Zero-1-to-3 in Step 1. Prompt Construction: Use the text prompt combined with the additional identifier [S] (e.g., "a photo of a [S]"). Objective: Fine-tune the model to associate the identifier [S] with the specific identity and finer details of the target, using the style-learned model from Stage 1 as the base. 4. Application (Denoising): Render images from the NeRF. Add a small level of noise to the NeRF renderings using the Stable Diffusion scheduler at timestep t=200. Use the fine-tuned diffusion model to denoise the renderings, ensuring they are consistent with the specialized object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagespecifieddiffusion(inputimage, textprompt, diffusionmodel): # Step 1: Generate intermediate views # Zero-1-to-3 generates multi-view images from a single input zero1to3views = zero1to3.generate(inputimage) # Stage 1: Learn visual style # Use a unique identifier [V] for style identifierV = "[V]" promptstyle = f"a photo of {identifierV}" # Positive samples: Zero-1-to-3 views # Negative samples: Text-prompt generated images (generic object) # Note: The specific loss function (e.g., DreamBooth loss) is implied by the source # but not explicitly defined with formulas in the provided text. # We assume standard fine-tuning loop. for view in zero1to3views: # Construct positive sample pair positivesample = view # Construct negative sample pair (generic class) negativesample = diffusionmodel.generate(prompt=textprompt) # Update model parameters to associate [V] with style diffusionmodel.finetune( positive=positivesample, negative=negativesample, prompt=promptstyle, identifier=identifierV) # Stage 2: Learn specific identity # Use an additional identifier [S] for identity identifierS = "[S]" promptidentity = f"a photo of {identifierS}" # Positive sample: Original input image # Negative samples: All Zero-1-to-3 views for view in zero1to3views: positivesample = inputimage negativesample = view # Update model parameters to associate [S] with identity diffusionmodel.finetune( positive=positivesample, negative=negativesample, prompt=promptidentity, identifier=identifierS) return diffusionmodel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-1-to-3 Bias: The method acknowledges that Zero-1-to-3 unconditional noise may have significant bias due to insufficient unconditional training. The two-stage approach mitigates this by first learning the style from potentially biased views, then refining identity against the ground truth input. Identifier Collision: Using distinct identifiers [V] and [S] is critical to separate style and identity learning. An image editing approach that leverages the large language model GPT3 and Stable Diffusion for generating image and instruction pairs, fine-tuning the diffusion model to perform editing. It serves as a baseline for instruction-based editing, contrasting with the object-specific specialization of Two-Stage Specified Diffusion. For example, it uses instructions like "change to night" or "It’s now midnight" to transform scene lighting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Gradually learns object details, separating style from identity, which helps in handling the inconsistency of Zero-1-to-3 generated views. Limitations: Relies on the quality of Zero-1-to-3 for intermediate views; if Zero-1-to-3 fails to generate coherent views, style learning may be affected. When to use: When specializing a diffusion model for a specific object from a single image, especially when multi-view consistent data is unavailable. Originated in the context of optimizing view and geometry distillation from multi-view diffusers. It leverages the DreamBooth technique for diffusion model specialization. The method is part of a pipeline that includes unbiased score distillation and NeuS for mesh reconstruction. name: StableMaterial Training Configuration
head: StableMaterial finetuning, StableMaterial setup
body: StableMaterial Training Configuration defines the hyperparameters and data pipeline for finetuning a 2D diffusion model prior to estimate physically plausible material properties (albedo and ORM) from input images. It adapts a pretrained Stable Diffusion UNet by freezing the backbone and training only a custom adapter and the UNet weights, reducing computational requirements compared to full model training. This configuration serves as the foundation for the StableMaterial model, which provides strong material priors for inverse rendering pipelines like MaterialFusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: RGB images resized to 256 \times 256 resolution. Input Conditioning: A concatenation of a CLIP embedding and a pose representation. Output: Factorized 2D maps for albedo (\hat{I}d) and ORM (Occlusion, Roughness, Metallicness) (\hat{I}{orm}). Data Structures: Pose Representation: Follows the format defined in Zero123. Fully Connected (FC) Layer: Converts the concatenated CLIP and pose embedding into a compatible embedding for the Stable Diffusion UNet, mapping from dimension 1028 to 1024. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Filtering: Filter the dataset using inclusion keys [pbr, pbrtexture, substance, substancepainter] and exclusion keys [style, stylized, cartoon, lowpoly, poly]. 2. Skip Procedural Objects: Skip objects with procedural generation features (approximately 300 objects). 3. Preprocessing: Resize input images to 256 \times 256 resolution. 4. Embedding Concatenation: Concatenate the CLIP embedding and the pose representation. 5. Adapter Projection: Pass the concatenated embedding through the fully connected layer to produce the conditioning embedding for the UNet. 6. Training: Train the fully connected layer and the Stable Diffusion UNet while freezing all other components. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Batch Size: 1536. Base Learning Rate: 10^{-4}. FC Layer Learning Rate: 10^{-3}. Optimizer: AdamW. Training Steps: 25,000. Hardware: 8× NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Training Duration: 2 days. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ensure input images are converted to RGB and sRGB tonemapped for the downstream L{recon} loss. Do not train the UNet backbone from scratch; only finetune the adapter and UNet weights to reduce compute. An inference-time modification to StableMaterial that enforces material consistency across multiple input views by modifying self-attention layers. It processes a batch of 4 images as a single large image within self-attention layers, allowing each latent pixel to attend to pixels in all other images, while non-self-attention layers process images independently. This mechanism is strictly for 2D inference and not used during 3D optimization or training. It improves albedo PSNR (24.70 vs 24.25) and handles difficult views better than the standard StableMaterial variant. Compute: Requires 8× NVIDIA H100 GPUs for 2 days to complete 25,000 steps with a batch size of 1536. Performance: The multi-view variant (StableMaterialMV) achieves an albedo PSNR of 24.70 and ORM L1 of 0.018, outperforming the single-view StableMaterial (PSNR 24.25) and baselines like IIR, IID, and Derender3D. Limitations: Multi-view attention is limited to 2D image inference and does not directly enhance 3D inverse rendering optimization, as the albedo/ORM representations are already optimized for multi-view consistency in the 3D pipeline. Usage: Best suited for generating material priors for inverse rendering (MaterialFusion) or for sparse-view 2D scenarios where 3D reconstruction is infeasible. StableMaterial was introduced in the MaterialFusion paper (2025) as a 2D diffusion model prior designed to refine multi-view data to estimate albedo and material properties (ORM) from input appearances. It addresses the challenge of recovering physically plausible material factors under unknown illumination by leveraging a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion architecture. The training configuration follows a similar approach to Zero123, adapting the Stable Diffusion UNet with a custom pose/CLIP adapter. MaterialFusion: Enhancing Inverse Rendering with Material Diffusion Priors, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00079, fetched 2026-10-29

name: StableMaterial
head: 2D Material Denoising Diffusion Prior
body: StableMaterial is a 2D diffusion model prior that refines multi-view data to estimate the most likely albedo and material properties from given input appearances. It addresses the challenge of recovering physically plausible material factors from images under unknown illumination by leveraging a fine-tuned Stable Diffusion architecture. Unlike generic denoising models, it is specifically conditioned on input RGB images to output factorized albedo (\hat{I}d) and ORM (\hat{I}{orm}) 2D maps, serving as a strong prior for inverse rendering pipelines such as MaterialFusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An RGB image x of an object under unknown illumination. Output: Two 2D maps: the albedo map \hat{I}d and the ORM (Occlusion, Roughness, Metallic) map \hat{I}{orm}. Data Structures and Layout: The model operates in the latent space of the pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE. Latent Channels: The noisy latent codes zt consist of 8 channels: 4 channels for albedo (z{td}) and 4 channels for ORM (z{torm}). UNet Input: The UNet input tensor has 12 channels in total: 4 channels for the clean latent encoding of the input image z{0x} = E(x), and 8 channels for the concatenated noisy latents zt = [z{td}, z{torm}]. Conditioning: The text conditioning of the original Stable Diffusion is replaced with a CLIP image embedding of the input image x. Training Data: The model is trained on triplets (x, Id, I{orm}) derived from a curated dataset of approximately 29K high-quality objects. This includes ~12K artist-designed synthetic Blender objects (BlenderVault), ~8.5K filtered Objaverse objects, and ~8K ABO objects. The total training dataset size is approximately 28K–29K synthetic objects with high-quality PBR assets. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Load pretrained Stable Diffusion 2.1 weights. Modify the UNet to accept 12 input channels and 8 output channels. Randomly initialize the first and last layers of the UNet to account for the different channel dimensions; keep all other UNet parameters unchanged. 2. Encoding: For a training triplet (x, Id, I{orm}), encode the input image x using the frozen VAE encoder E to obtain z{0x}. Encode the ground truth albedo Id and ORM I{orm} using E to obtain their clean latents, then concatenate them in the channel dimension to form the target latent z. 3. Noise Addition: Sample a diffusion timestep t and an 8-channel random noise vector \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). Compute the noisy latent zt by adding noise to z according to the diffusion scheduler parameters \alphat and \sigmat. 4. Conditioning: Compute the CLIP image embedding of x. Construct the UNet input by concatenating z{0x} and zt in the channel dimension, along with the timestep embedding t. 5. Prediction: Pass the concatenated input through the UNet \epsilon\theta to predict the noise component vt. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the diffusion loss L{diff} using the v-prediction objective. 7. Optimization: Update the UNet parameters \theta to minimize L{diff}. Formulas: The diffusion loss is defined as: L{diff} = \mathbb{E}{x, Id, I{orm}, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I), t} \|\epsilon\theta(E(x), zt, t) - vt\|2^2 where vt is the v-prediction target: vt = \alphat \epsilon - \sigmat z Here, \alphat and \sigmat are parameters from the diffusion scheduler. Parameters: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG): Input images, input image prompts (CLIP embeddings), or both are set to all zeros with a 5% probability each. Guidance Scale: Set to 3.0. Base Model: Stable Diffusion 2.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def trainstablematerial(unet, vae, clipencoder, optimizer, dataloader, numepochs, alphas, sigmas): """ Trains the StableMaterial model. unet: Modified UNet with 12 input channels, 8 output channels. vae: Pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE (encoder E and decoder D). clipencoder: Pretrained CLIP image encoder. optimizer: Optimizer for unet parameters. dataloader: Yields batches of (x, Id, Iorm). alphas, sigmas: Precomputed 1D tensors of scheduler parameters for each timestep. """ unet.train() vae.eval() clipencoder.eval() for epoch in range(numepochs): for x, Id, Iorm in dataloader: # 1. Encode inputs with torch.nograd(): z0x = vae.encode(x).latentdist.sample() zd = vae.encode(Id).latentdist.sample() zorm = vae.encode(Iorm).latentdist.sample() # Concatenate target latents: 4 channels albedo + 4 channels ORM z = torch.cat([zd, zorm], dim=1) # 2. Sample noise and timestep t = torch.randint(0, len(alphas), (x.shape[0],), device=x.device).long() noise = torch.randnlike(z) # 3. Add noise to get zt (standard forward diffusion process) sqrtalpha = torch.sqrt(alphas[t]) sqrtsigma = torch.sqrt(sigmas[t]) zt = sqrtalpha.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) z + \ sqrtsigma.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) noise # 4. Prepare UNet input unetinput = torch.cat([z0x, zt], dim=1) # 5. Classifier-Free Guidance Logic docondimg = torch.rand(1).item() > 0.05 docondclip = torch.rand(1).item() > 0.05 if not docondimg: z0x = torch.zeroslike(z0x) clipemb = clipencoder(x).imageembeds if not docondclip: clipemb = torch.zeroslike(clipemb) # 6. Forward pass predv = unet(unetinput, t, encoderhiddenstates=clipemb).sample # 7. Compute Loss targetv = alphas[t].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) noise - \ sigmas[t].unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) z loss = nn.functional.mseloss(predv, targetv) # 8. Backward pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() Complexity: The model inherits the computational complexity of Stable Diffusion 2.1 UNet inference and training, scaled by the batch size and resolution of the latent space. Performance: The model demonstrates superior performance in recovering albedo and materials from input images compared to prior state-of-the-art methods, particularly in novel view synthesis under relighting. Strengths: Provides a strong 2D prior for material properties, improving relighting performance in inverse rendering pipelines. It generalizes better to novel lighting conditions across diverse scenarios. Limitations: It is a 2D prior; it does not directly output 3D geometry or handle multi-view consistency without integration into a 3D optimization loop (e.g., via SDS). When to use: Use when a strong prior on albedo and material properties is needed for inverse rendering or relighting tasks, especially when input images are under unknown illumination. StableMaterial was introduced in the paper "MaterialFusion: Enhancing Inverse Rendering with Material Diffusion Priors". It builds upon Stable Diffusion 2.1 and is trained on a dataset comprising BlenderVault, filtered Objaverse, and ABO objects. The method is part of the MaterialFusion pipeline, which combines this 2D diffusion prior with score distillation sampling (SDS) for 3D inverse rendering. name: Two-Plane Diffusion Model (TPDM)
head: TDPM
body: Two-Plane Diffusion Model (TPDM) is a method for solving 3D inverse problems and generating 3D voxel volumes by training two separate 2D diffusion models on perpendicular planes and alternating their usage during the denoising process to maintain 3D consistency. It avoids the curse of dimensionality by assuming a 3D distribution is the product of 2D distributions, allowing it to handle 3D volumes without using a 3D diffusion model. Unlike Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization which guides optimization via gradients, TPDM performs conditional sampling directly on the volume using a primary model for measurement consistency and an auxiliary model for cross-plane consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Observed 3D measurement data Y \in \mathbb{R}^{d1 \times d2 \times d3}, forward operator A(\cdot): \mathbb{R}^{d1 \times d2} \to \mathbb{R}^{d1 \times d2}, pre-trained primary score model s{\theta^}, pre-trained auxiliary score model s{\phi^}, noise schedule \{\sigmai\}{i=0}^{10}, number of denoising steps N, integer hyperparameter K, and measurement consistency strength \lambda. Output: Reconstructed 3D volume X0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d1 \times d2 \times d3}. Data Structures: Xi: Tensor of shape d1 \times d2 \times d3 representing the volume at denoising step i. Y: Tensor of shape d1 \times d2 \times d3 representing the measurement data. s{\theta^}: Primary 2D diffusion model (score function). s{\phi^}: Auxiliary 2D diffusion model (score function). Parameters: K: Integer controlling the ratio of primary to auxiliary model usage. If K=4, the primary model is used 3 times and the auxiliary 1 time (ratio 3:1). \lambda: Hyperparameter controlling the strength of measurement consistency in the Data Consistency (DPS) step. N: Number of denoising steps. Typical value: 2000. \sigmat: Noise schedule parameter. Scheduled by a geometric sequence from \sigma0 = 0.01 to \sigma1 = 378. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the noisy volume XN by sampling from a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma1^2 I) with shape d1 \times d2 \times d3. 2. Iterate backwards from i = N-1 down to 0: a. Set time step t = i/N. b. Initialize an empty tensor Xi with the same shape as XN. c. Determine if the primary model is used. If K is an integer, use the condition mod(i, K) != 0. If true, use the primary model s{\theta^}; otherwise, use the auxiliary model s{\phi^}. (For non-integer K, sample from a Bernoulli distribution with probability p = 1 - 1/K). d. If using the primary model: i. Loop j from 1 to d3 (slicing along the Z-axis, or the axis perpendicular to the primary plane): 1. Extract current slice x = X{i+1}[:,:, j] and corresponding measurement slice y = Y[:,:, j]. 2. Compute the predicted clean sample \hat{x}0 = x + \sigmat^2 \cdot s{\theta^}(x, t). 3. Perform one step of the 2D Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DPM) using x, s{\theta^}, \sigmat, and t to get x'. 4. Apply data consistency correction: x'' = x' - \lambda \nablax \|A(\hat{x}0) - y\|2^2. 5. Assign the corrected slice to Xi[:,:, j] = x''. e. If using the auxiliary model: i. Loop j from 1 to d1 (slicing along the X-axis, or the axis perpendicular to the auxiliary plane): 1. Extract current slice x = X{i+1}[j,:,:]. 2. Perform one step of the 2D DPM using x, s{\phi^}, \sigmat, and t to get x'. 3. Assign the denoised slice to Xi[j,:,:] = x'. 3. Return X0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def tpdmsample(Y, A, sthetastar, sphistar, sigmaschedule, N, K, lambdaval): """ Solves 3D inverse problem using Two-Plane Diffusion Model. Args: Y: Observed 3D measurement data, shape (d1, d2, d3). A: Forward operator function. Takes a 2D slice and returns measurement. sthetastar: Primary 2D score model function. sphistar: Auxiliary 2D score model function. sigmaschedule: List of noise levels sigmat, descending from sigma1 to sigma0. N: Number of denoising steps. K: Integer controlling primary/auxiliary ratio. lambdaval: Strength of measurement consistency. Returns: X0: Reconstructed 3D volume. """ d1, d2, d3 = Y.shape sigma1 = sigmaschedule[0] # Initialize XN ~ N(0, sigma1^2 I) Xnext = [[[random.gauss(0, sigma1) for in range(d2)] for in range(d1)] for in range(d3)] for i in range(N - 1, -1, -1): t = i / N sigmat = sigmaschedule[i] sigmanext = sigmaschedule[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(sigmaschedule) else 0.0 Xcurr = [[[0.0 for in range(d2)] for in range(d1)] for in range(d3)] # Determine model usage: mod(i, K) != 0 for integer K useprimary = (i % K) != 0 if useprimary: for j in range(d3): x = Xnext[:,:, j] y = Y[:,:, j] score = sthetastar(x, t) x0hat = x + (sigmat 2) score xprime = step2ddpm(x, sthetastar, sigmat, sigmanext, t) gradx = computedataconsistencygradient(x, x0hat, y, A) xdoubleprime = xprime - lambdaval gradx Xcurr[:,:, j] = xdoubleprime else: for j in range(d1): x = Xnext[j,:,:] xprime = step2ddpm(x, sphistar, sigmat, sigmanext, t) Xcurr[j,:,:] = xprime Xnext = Xcurr return Xnext def step2ddpm(x, scoremodel, sigmat, sigmanext, t): # Euler-Maruyama step for VE-SDE noise = random.normal(size=x.shape) return x + (sigmanext 2 - sigmat 2) scoremodel(x, t) + math.sqrt(max(0, sigmanext 2 - sigmat 2)) noise def computedataconsistencygradient(x, x0hat, y, A): # Computes gradient of ||A(x0hat) - y||^2 w.r.t x residual = A(x0hat) - y return 2.0 residual # Simplified; general case uses adjoint of A Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: The slicing loops assume the volume dimensions d1, d2, d3 are accessible. If the volume is not cubic, the slicing logic must adapt to the chosen primary/auxiliary planes. Degenerate Input: The method assumes the forward operator A is differentiable to compute the gradient \nablax \|A(\hat{x}0) - y\|2^2. Time Complexity: The method iterates N times (typically 2000). In each step, it processes all slices of the volume. For the primary model, it processes d3 slices; for the auxiliary, d1 slices. The complexity is O(N \cdot (d1 + d3)) 2D DPM steps per volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D volume X and the measurement Y. The 2D models are loaded once. Memory is O(d1 \cdot d2 \cdot d3). Measured Performance: SV-CT (36-view): TPDM achieved PSNR 38.25 and SSIM (Axial) 0.947, outperforming DPS (38.20, 0.942) and score-CT (37.56, 0.951). CS-MRI (×48 acceleration): TPDM achieved PSNR 37.17 and SSIM (Axial) 0.966, outperforming DiffusionMBIR (34.83, 0.950) and DPS (35.30, 0.951). Strengths: Avoids artifacts in the batch direction that plague 2D solvers like DPS when applied to 3D. Works in an unsupervised manner without fine-tuning for individual inverse problems. Limitations: Performance on non-primary planes (e.g., Coronal/Sagittal in SV-CT) can be lower than the primary plane, though still competitive. Requires pre-training of two 2D models. TPDM was introduced in the paper "Improving 3D Imaging with Pre-Trained Perpendicular 2D Diffusion Models" (ICCV 2023). It addresses the limitations of 2D diffusion models (like DPS) when applied to 3D inverse problems, which suffer from artifacts in the batch direction. The method leverages the assumption that a 3D distribution can be approximated by the product of 2D distributions on perpendicular planes, allowing it to solve general 3D inverse problems (such as CS-MRI, SV-CT, and MRI ZSR) and generate 3D volumes without a 3D diffusion model. Improving 3D Imaging with Pre-Trained Perpendicular 2D Diffusion Models, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51070.2023.00983, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Score Distillation Loss Modifications
body: Score Distillation Loss Modifications are optimization objectives that adapt the gradient signal from a frozen 2D diffusion model to refine a 3D radiance field or latent representation. They solve the limitations of vanilla Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), such as oversaturation, poor composition, or lack of high-frequency detail, by altering how the diffusion model is conditioned, how noise is sampled, or how the loss is computed. This family is distinguished from its siblings by focusing specifically on the mathematical formulation of the loss function and its conditioning inputs, rather than the broader training loop architecture or sampling mechanisms. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable rendering loop defined in Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization. They share the following core mechanism: 1. Differentiable Rendering: A radiance field \Theta (or latent representation) is rendered to an image I (or latent z0) given a camera pose. 2. Diffusion Conditioning: The rendered image/latent is perturbed with noise to obtain xt (or zt) at timestep t. 3. Noise Prediction: A frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta (or \epsilon\phi) predicts the noise \hat{\epsilon} conditioned on xt, t, and additional context (prompts, masks, etc.). 4. Gradient Computation: The gradient \nabla\Theta L is computed by backpropagating the difference between the predicted noise and the actual noise (or a derived target) through the diffusion model and the differentiable renderer. 5. Optimization: The radiance field parameters \Theta are updated using the computed gradient. The specific modifications lie in the conditioning inputs (masks, background prompts), the noise sampling strategy (DDIM inversion, re-noising), or the loss target (reconstruction of noise estimates). Replaces the standard DDPM forward process with DDIM inversion to supervise multiple interval steps, reducing reconstruction error from single-step updates. Choose when high-fidelity geometry is required and single-step SDS fails. Uses a pre-trained inpainting diffusion model conditioned on a masked rendered image and binary mask to generate content that harmonizes with existing scene context. Choose when inserting objects into existing scenes to avoid isolated or misaligned geometry. Appends a background description to the text prompt while using a mask to restrict changes to the target object, preventing "black hole" artifacts in occluded regions. Choose when editing specific objects in a scene without collapsing the background. Optimizes latent residuals in intermediate timestep space to combine the sharpness of ancestral sampling with the consistency of SDS. Choose for super-resolution or refining latent vectors where standard SDS lacks detail. Enforces fidelity to a specific input image by comparing noise predictions of the rendered image against the input image. Choose when perceptual reconstruction of a reference image is required alongside generative guidance. A baseline method using per-scene text prompts to guide masked region generation via SDS. It improves quality by gradually and uniformly decreasing the maximum noise steps t{max} during fitting until it equals the minimum noise steps t{min} at the last iteration. This schedule leverages higher noise levels for global structure generation early on and lower noise levels for detail fixing later. Implementation typically uses Stable Diffusion as the underlying model. Iteratively updates initially generated voxels V by rendering viewpoints and applying SDS loss independently on each image. For latent diffusion models, noise prediction is applied after encoding the rendered view r(V, \kappa) into the LDM's latent space. The gradient is: \nablaV L{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{\epsilon, t, \kappa} \left[ w(\lambdat)(\epsilon - \hat{\epsilon}\theta(r(V, \kappa), t)) \frac{\partial r(V, \kappa)}{\partial V} \right] where \kappa is sampled uniformly in a 6m^2 region around the scene origin with random vertical rotation, and t \sim U[0.02T, 0.2T]. It employs LSDS with negative guidance using classifier-free guidance, replacing the unconditional embedding with artifact conditioning to sample from p(x|y)/p(x|y'), controlling the trade-off between dataset images and artifact-free samples. Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) was introduced in DreamFusion [Parent] as a method to optimize 3D structures from 2D diffusion models. Subsequent works identified limitations in SDS, such as oversaturation and poor composition, leading to modifications like Interval Score Matching (LucidDreamer), Inpainting SDS (LiSDS), and Renoised Score Distillation. The concept of post-optimizing neural fields with SDS was explored in NeuralField-LDM to refine hierarchical latent diffusion outputs. These modifications collectively form a family of techniques that adapt the diffusion prior to better suit 3D generation constraints. name: Interval Score Matching
head: LucidDreamer (ISM)
body: Interval Score Matching (ISM) is a modification to Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) that replaces the standard Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) forward process with Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) inversion. It introduces supervision from multiple interval steps of the diffusion process to mitigate the high error associated with one-step reconstruction. It is distinguished from siblings like Renoised Score Distillation (RSD) by its specific use of DDIM inversion to define the noise perturbation target rather than re-noising or standard DDPM sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A radiance field \Theta (e.g., NeRF, 3DGS), a frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta, a text prompt, and a set of interval steps \mathcal{T} = \{t1, t2, \dots, tk\} within the diffusion timeline. Output: Gradient \nabla\Theta L{ISM} for updating \Theta. Data Structures: \mathcal{T}: A list of integer timesteps t \in [1, T] where T is the total number of diffusion steps. The specific values of \mathcal{T} are not given in the sources. Method Steps: 1. Render: Render an image I from the radiance field \Theta using a camera pose. 2. Encode: Encode I into a latent space z0 if using a latent diffusion model, or use I directly if pixel-space. 3. DDIM Inversion: Instead of adding noise via the DDPM forward process, apply DDIM inversion to z0 to obtain a noisy latent zt at a specific timestep t. This step is crucial for defining the target noise. 4. Noise Prediction: For each interval step ti \in \mathcal{T}, pass z{ti}, ti, and the text prompt into the frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon}{ti}. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the loss by comparing the predicted noise \hat{\epsilon}{ti} with the actual noise added during the DDIM inversion process. The sources state that supervision is introduced from these interval steps to avoid large error in one-step reconstruction. The exact mathematical formulation of the loss function combining these interval steps is not given in the sources. 6. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the loss through the diffusion model and the differentiable renderer to compute \nabla\Theta L{ISM}. 7. Update: Update \Theta using the computed gradient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intervalscorematchingloss(theta, renderer, diffusionmodel, prompt, intervalsteps, camerapose): # 1. Render image from radiance field image = renderer.render(theta, camerapose) # 2. Encode to latent (if latent diffusion) # z0 = encoder(image) # For simplicity, assume z0 is available or image is used directly z0 = image totalloss = 0 # 3. Iterate over interval steps for t in intervalsteps: # 4. DDIM Inversion: Convert z0 to zt using DDIM inversion # This replaces the standard DDPM forward noise addition zt = ddiminvert(z0, t, diffusionmodel) # 5. Predict noise at timestep t # epsilontheta predicts the noise component predictednoise = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(zt, t, prompt) # 6. Compute loss against actual noise # The actual noise is derived from the inversion process # Exact formula not provided in sources # losst = MSE(predictednoise, actualnoiset) # Placeholder for the specific interval supervision loss losst = computeintervalloss(predictednoise, zt, t, diffusionmodel) totalloss += losst return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The choice of interval steps \mathcal{T} is critical but not specified in the sources. DDIM inversion requires the diffusion model to be consistent with the inversion algorithm. The primary method that introduced ISM. It uses ISM to replace DDPM in SDS with DDIM inversion to improve 3D asset generation quality. See LucidDreamer. The mathematical process used to invert the diffusion forward process, allowing for deterministic sampling from noise to data. See DDIM Inversion. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of interval steps |\mathcal{T}| and the cost of DDIM inversion. Each interval step requires a forward pass through the diffusion model. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard SDS, but may require storing intermediate latents for inversion. Strengths: Avoids high error in one-step reconstruction by leveraging multiple interval steps. Limitations: Requires implementing DDIM inversion, which is more complex than standard DDPM noise addition. When to use: When standard SDS suffers from reconstruction errors or when higher fidelity is needed from the diffusion prior. Interval Score Matching was proposed by LucidDreamer. It addresses the limitations of standard SDS which relies on DDPM forward process, aiming to reduce reconstruction errors by using DDIM inversion and interval supervision. It is used in 3D generation pipelines involving NeRF, 3DGS, and DMTet. name: Inpainting SDS Loss
head: LiSDS, Inpainting-based Score Distillation Sampling, SDS loss with scene context
body: Inpainting SDS Loss (LiSDS) is a score distillation method that uses a diffusion inpainting model to generate 3D content conditioned on both a text prompt and existing scene geometry. It solves the problem of incomplete object generation and poor compositional harmony found in vanilla SDS, which often produces isolated parts (e.g., only a head) that fail to integrate with the background. By conditioning the noise prediction on a binary mask M and the masked rendered image IM, LiSDS ensures the generated object maintains complete geometry and proper pose relative to the scene context. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Radiance field parameters \Theta, camera pose, text prompt y, binary mask M (defining the region to inpaint/generate), and the current rendered image I (or latent representation). Output: Gradient \nabla\Theta L for updating the radiance field. Data Structures: Mask M: A binary image of the same resolution as the rendered image, where 1 indicates the region to be inpainted/generated and 0 indicates the background/visible region. In, M is derived by projecting a 3D bounding box into the camera viewpoint. In, M defines the "in-boundary" (IB) and "out-of-boundary" (OB) regions. Masked Image IM: The rendered image where pixels outside the mask M are preserved, and pixels inside M are either zeroed, blurred, or left as the current NeRF prediction depending on the specific implementation variant. Numbered Steps: 1. Rendering: Render an image I from the current radiance field \Theta using the current camera pose. 2. Masking: Apply the binary mask M to I to create the masked image IM. 3. Noise Addition: Sample a timestep t and Gaussian noise \epsilon. Add noise to IM to obtain the noisy image xt. 4. Noise Prediction: Pass xt, timestep t, text embedding y, and mask M into a frozen inpainting diffusion model \epsilon\phi. The model predicts the noise \hat{\epsilon} = \epsilon\phi(xt; y, t, M). 5. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to \Theta by backpropagating through the diffusion model's noise prediction error and the differentiable renderer. Formulas: The core LiSDS loss is defined as: L{iSDS}(\phi, g(\theta)) = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} \left[ \| \epsilon\phi(xt; y, t, M) - \epsilont \|2^2 \right] where: y is the text embedding. M is the binary mask. \epsilont is the actual noise added at timestep t. xt is the noisy image at timestep t. \epsilon\phi is the inpainting diffusion model. The gradient computation for optimization is: \nabla\Theta L{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon,C} \left[ \omega(t) \cdot \left( \epsilon\phi(It; y, IM, M, t) - \epsilon \right) \frac{\partial It}{\partial \Theta} \right] where: \omega(t) is the weighting function (typically dependent on timestep t). It is the noisy image at timestep t. C represents the conditioning context (text, mask, masked image). Parameters: Mask M: Derived from projecting a 3D bounding box into the camera view or defined by IB/OB regions. Loss Weights: In, the total loss includes a reliability-guided loss LR and sparsity loss L{sp}: L{total} = \lambda{iSDS} L{iSDS} + \deltaR(\theta, \phi) LR + \lambda{sp} L{sp}. The weight \deltaR is 1 within the IB area and 0 otherwise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incomplete Generation: Vanilla SDS may generate only parts of an object (e.g., a cat's head) if not conditioned on scene context. LiSDS mitigates this by using the mask to guide the completion of the object. Texture Continuity: Standard LiSDS may result in discontinuities between the generated part and the existing image prior. A refinement step is used to address this. Saturation: Generated objects may exhibit over-saturation. Saturation loss is sometimes applied to regulate color values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inpaintingsdslossstep(radiancefield, camerapose, textprompt, mask, diffusionmodel, timestepsampler, noisesampler): """ Computes the gradient for Inpainting SDS Loss. Args: radiancefield: The NeRF or radiance field parameters theta. camerapose: Current camera extrinsics and intrinsics. textprompt: String text prompt for the diffusion model. mask: Binary mask M defining the inpainting region. diffusionmodel: Frozen inpainting diffusion model epsilonphi. timestepsampler: Sampler for timestep t. noisesampler: Sampler for Gaussian noise epsilon. Returns: gradient: Gradient of the loss with respect to radiancefield parameters. """ # 1. Render the current image from the radiance field # I is the rendered image, shape (H, W, 3) I = differentiablerender(radiancefield, camerapose) # 2. Create masked image IM # Pixels outside the mask are preserved, inside are masked (e.g., zeroed or blurred) # Implementation detail: The exact masking strategy (zeroing vs keeping NeRF prediction) # depends on the specific diffusion model implementation. IM = applymask(I, mask) # 3. Sample timestep and noise t = timestepsampler.sample() epsilon = noisesampler.sample(shape=IM.shape) # 4. Add noise to the masked image to get xt # alphat and sigmat are coefficients from the diffusion model's noise schedule alphat, sigmat = getdiffusioncoefficients(t) xt = alphat IM + sigmat epsilon # 5. Predict noise using the inpainting diffusion model # The model is conditioned on text y, timestep t, and mask M # Note: Some implementations may also pass IM or a version of it with masked regions # as context. Here we follow the formula from and. textembedding = encodetext(textprompt) predictednoise = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(xt, t, textembedding, mask) # 6. Compute the loss (Mean Squared Error between predicted and actual noise) loss = meansquarederror(predictednoise, epsilon) # 7. Compute gradient with respect to radiance field parameters # This requires backpropagation through the differentiable renderer and the diffusion model gradient = computegradient(loss, radiancefield) return gradient MVIP-NeRF is a diffusion-based method for multiview-consistent inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It solves the problem of reconstructing missing geometry and texture in masked regions of a scene while maintaining consistency across multiple camera views. Unlike prior approaches that rely on independent 2D inpainting per view—often resulting in inconsistencies and poor geometry—MVIP-NeRF jointly optimizes across views. It employs Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) with a text-conditioned diffusion model to guide inpainting in masked regions, alongside RGB reconstruction in visible areas. RefFusion inpaints one reference image using an inpainting Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) on both global and locally cropped versions of the reference view. It utilizes SDS loss to distill learned priors from the adapted LDM into the scene, incorporating a discriminator loss and depth loss to improve the quality of inpainting results. Quantitative results show RefFusion surpassed all baselines in LPIPSdir (0.4283) compared to NeRF-In (0.4884), SPIn-NeRF (SD) (0.5701), SPIn-NeRF (LaMa) (0.4654), Inpaint3D (0.5150), Reference-guided inpainting (SDV2) (0.4532), and Reference-guided inpainting (SDXL) (0.4453). A refinement step applied during the last 10% of training to improve texture and color continuity by masking foreground patches and optimizing them with LiSDS, excluding the Reliability-guided loss (LR). During the final 10% of training, if an in-boundary view is sampled, the Reliability-guided loss (LR) is excluded, and a random patch is given to the foreground to refine the corresponding part with the Inpainting SDS Loss (L{iSDS}). This process results in the color and texture of the generated 3D object becoming more similar to the part generated by the LiSDS, while maintaining the overall shape and content of the image prior. Time Complexity: Similar to vanilla SDS, as it involves one forward pass through the diffusion model per optimization step. However, the use of inpainting models may require additional conditioning steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the mask M and potentially the masked image IM. The diffusion model is frozen and loaded once. Performance: LiSDS generates complete objects with proper poses that seamlessly integrate with the scene, outperforming vanilla SDS which often generates incomplete parts. GO-NeRF using LiSDS achieved an average CLIP score of 74.6, significantly outperforming baselines like Blended-NeRF (63.0) and Spin-NeRF (60.8). Strengths: Ensures harmonized composition with existing scene context; generates complete objects; maintains texture continuity with refinement steps. Limitations: Requires a high-quality inpainting diffusion model; may require additional losses (sparsity, saturation) for optimal results; refinement step adds complexity to the training loop. When to use: When generating 3D objects that need to be composited into an existing scene or when inpainting missing regions in a NeRF. When not to use: When generating a standalone object without scene context (vanilla SDS may suffice); when computational resources are extremely limited (additional losses and refinement steps increase complexity). Inpainting SDS Loss was introduced to address the limitations of vanilla SDS in generating 3D objects that harmonize with existing scenes. Vanilla SDS often produces incomplete objects (e.g., only a cat's head) that fail to composite properly. LiSDS leverages the power of 2D inpainting diffusion models to guide 3D generation. The method was proposed in DITTO-NeRF and GO-NeRF. DITTO-NeRF introduced LiSDS with a refinement step for texture continuity. GO-NeRF applied LiSDS for generating objects in VR content creation, emphasizing scene context and geometry. RefFusion further adapted inpainting LDMs for 3D scene editing. name: MVIP-NeRF
head: MVIPNeRF
body: MVIP-NeRF is a diffusion-based method for multiview-consistent inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It solves the problem of reconstructing missing geometry and texture in masked regions of a scene while maintaining consistency across multiple camera views. Unlike prior approaches that rely on independent 2D inpainting per view—often resulting in inconsistencies and poor geometry—MVIP-NeRF jointly optimizes across views. It employs Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) with a text-conditioned diffusion model to guide inpainting in masked regions, alongside RGB reconstruction in visible areas. Inputs: An initial NeRF representation (implicitly or explicitly parameterized). An RGB sequence of images corresponding to the camera poses. Per-frame binary masks indicating visible (unmasked) and missing (masked) regions. A text description of the scene content. Outputs: An optimized NeRF model with inpainted geometry and texture in masked regions. Data Structures: NeRF: Standard volumetric representation storing density (\sigma) and color (c) at query points. Diffusion Model: A pre-trained 2D text-conditioned diffusion model used for score estimation. Normal Map: Distilled geometric consistency signal derived from the NeRF. Parameters: Text Prompt: Describes the semantic content to be inpainted. Mask: Binary mask per view distinguishing observed from unobserved pixels. Denoising Steps: Number of diffusion steps for SDS evaluation. Steps: 1. Rendering: For each view i, render the RGB image Ii and normal map Ni from the current NeRF using standard volume rendering. 2. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss as a combination of reconstruction and inpainting terms: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \mathcal{L}{inpaint} 3. Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{rec}): Compute the pixel-wise difference between the rendered image and the ground truth image only in the unmasked (visible) regions. 4. Inpainting Loss (\mathcal{L}{inpaint}): Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss in the masked regions. Sample noise \epsilon and add it to the rendered latent or image representation (depending on the specific diffusion pipeline, typically image space for 2D priors). Pass the noisy input through the text-conditioned diffusion model to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon}. Compute the SDS gradient based on the difference between predicted and sampled noise, weighted by the mask. 5. Multi-View Scoring: Incorporate a multi-view scoring mechanism to enhance consistency, particularly under large view variations. This involves aggregating scores or gradients from multiple views during the optimization step to ensure the inpainted content is geometrically and texturally consistent across viewpoints. 6. Geometric Distillation: Distill normal maps to enforce geometric consistency. This likely involves a loss term between rendered normals and normals predicted or implied by the diffusion prior or geometric consistency constraints. 7. Optimization: Update the NeRF parameters using the computed gradients. The optimization is performed jointly across all views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmvipnerf(nerf, images, masks, textprompt, numsteps): """ Optimizes NeRF for multiview-consistent inpainting. Args: nerf: Neural Radiance Field model. images: List of RGB images for each view. masks: List of binary masks for each view (1 for visible, 0 for masked). textprompt: String describing the scene. numsteps: Number of optimization steps. """ for step in range(numsteps): totalloss = 0 gradients = [] for viewidx in range(len(images)): # 1. Render current NeRF renderedrgb, renderednormals = nerf.render(viewidx) # 2. Compute Reconstruction Loss (visible regions) visiblemask = masks[viewidx] == 1 if visiblemask.any(): recloss = MSE(renderedrgb[visiblemask], images[viewidx][visiblemask]) gradients.append(grad(recloss, nerf)) totalloss += recloss # 3. Compute Inpainting Loss (masked regions) maskedmask = masks[viewidx] == 0 if maskedmask.any(): # Sample noise for SDS noise = samplenoise(renderedrgb.shape) noisyrgb = renderedrgb + noise # Get score from diffusion model # Note: Specific implementation of SDS with 2D diffusion on NeRF renders # varies, but generally involves predicting noise given text condition predictednoise = diffusionmodel.predict(noisyrgb, textprompt) # SDS Gradient # SDS = E{t, epsilon} [ w(t) (epsilon - predictednoise) d(noisyrgb)/d(nerf) ] sdsgrad = computesdsgradient(renderedrgb, predictednoise, noise) gradients.append(grad(sdsgrad, nerf)) totalloss += sdsgrad # 4. Multi-view consistency and normal distillation # Aggregate gradients or add consistency loss across views # Distill normals for geometric consistency normalloss = computenormalconsistencyloss(renderednormals, viewidx) gradients.append(grad(normalloss, nerf)) totalloss += normalloss # Update NeRF parameters nerf.update(gradients) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large View Variations: Inconsistencies may arise if the multi-view scoring mechanism is not robust to large angular differences. Mask Boundaries: Sharp transitions between masked and unmasked regions can cause artifacts if the diffusion prior does not align well with the visible geometry. Text Prompt Ambiguity: Incorrect or vague text prompts can lead to semantically incorrect inpainting. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of views, diffusion steps, and NeRF optimization iterations. Joint optimization across views increases per-step cost compared to independent view inpainting. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF representation, intermediate rendered images/normals, and the diffusion model state. Strengths: Ensures multiview consistency, handles large view variations better than independent 2D inpainting, produces high-fidelity results without high-resolution training data. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to joint optimization and diffusion model usage. Requires a text prompt. When to use: When multiview consistency is critical and the scene has significant missing regions. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or text prompts are unavailable. MVIP-NeRF was introduced in May 2024. It addresses limitations of prior NeRF inpainting methods that relied on independent 2D inpainting, which often resulted in inconsistencies and poor geometry. It builds on the concept of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) and extends it to a multi-view setting with a specific formulation for consistency. It is used for NeRF inpainting tasks. name: Mask+SDS with Background Prompt
head: Mask+SDS+BGT
body: Mask+SDS with Background Prompt is a score distillation loss modification for NeRF editing that explicitly conditions the diffusion model on the surrounding environment to prevent semantic inconsistencies in occluded regions. It solves the "black hole" artifact problem inherent in standard masked SDS, where previously occluded geometry collapses or generates undefined content due to lack of supervision. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Inpainting SDS Loss by integrating the background description directly into the diffusion model's text prompt rather than relying solely on geometric masking or external texture synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A radiance field \Theta (or latent representation), a camera pose, a semantic mask M identifying the region to be edited, an object text prompt P{obj}, and a background text prompt P{bg}. Output: Gradients \nabla\Theta L for updating the radiance field parameters. Data Structures: Mask M: A binary image of the same resolution as the rendered view, where M{ij}=1 indicates the region to be edited (masked) and M{ij}=0 indicates the background region. Text Prompts: Strings P{obj} and P{bg}. Steps: 1. Render: Render an image I from the radiance field \Theta using the current camera pose. 2. Combine Prompt: Construct the full text prompt P{full} by concatenating the object prompt and the background prompt. For example, if P{obj} is "a lego man head" and P{bg} is "leaves", then P{full} is "a lego man head in leaves". 3. Diffusion Conditioning: Pass the rendered image I and the full prompt P{full} to the frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta. 4. Noise Prediction: The diffusion model predicts the noise \hat{\epsilon} for the perturbed image xt at timestep t, conditioned on P{full}. 5. Gradient Computation: Compute the SDS gradient based on the difference between the predicted noise and the actual noise, backpropagating through the diffusion model and the differentiable renderer. 6. Optimization: Update \Theta using the computed gradient. Pitfalls: Black Holes: If only the background prompt is added to the diffusion model without additional supervision for the unmasked regions, the previously occluded or covered areas may develop into "black holes" (undefined or black regions) due to the lack of explicit supervision for those specific pixels. A variant that removes the background prompt from the diffusion model's text prompt and instead uses CLIP with a background prompt to fill occluded regions. It provides a view of the unmasked region to CLIP along with a background prompt to supervise and fill the black hole. While CLIP fills the black hole with reasonable texture, the generated shapes retain artifacts from the original occluded geometry (e.g., petal shapes). The final combined editing configuration that uses SDS with a full prompt (object + background) and CLIP with a background prompt on unmasked views. It sets the diffusion model text prompt to include both object and background (e.g., "object in background") and simultaneously feeds unmasked views to CLIP with the background prompt to supervise the surroundings. This produces normal shapes and fills black holes with appropriate background material (e.g., green leaves around a blue rose). Time Complexity: Standard SDS complexity, plus the cost of CLIP inference if the combined variant is used. Memory Complexity: Standard SDS memory usage. Strengths: Explicitly guides the diffusion model to generate semantically consistent background content, reducing semantic artifacts in the edited region. Limitations: Does not fully solve the black hole problem on its own; requires additional CLIP supervision for unmasked regions to prevent undefined content in previously occluded areas. When to use: When editing a specific object in a scene and ensuring the surrounding environment remains semantically coherent is critical. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and the combined Mask+SDS+BGT+CLIP variant is too expensive, or when the background is simple and does not require explicit prompting. Originated in the RePaint-NeRF paper, which introduced NeRF editing via semantic masks and diffusion models. The method was developed to address the limitations of standard SDS in editing tasks, where occluded regions often fail to generate plausible content. It builds on the idea that providing explicit context to the diffusion model improves generation quality.
