name: Renoised Score Distillation (RSD)
body:
Renoised Score Distillation (RSD) is a score-distillation objective designed for 2D image resolution and super-resolution that combines features from ancestral sampling and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to generate sharp images that are consistent with low-resolution (LR) conditioning. It solves the problem where default ancestral sampling generates details structurally inconsistent with the conditioned LR image, while standard SDS produces LR-consistent features but with limited detail. RSD sets the optimization target to the intermediate denoised latents of the ancestral sampling trajectory, transforming the sampling process into an optimization framework that incrementally builds coarse-to-fine details. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Low-resolution latent z0 (encoded from a 4× interpolated LR image), text prompt embeddings y{text}, noise level embedding y{noise\level}, LR image conditioning I{lr}, minimum timestep t{min}, maximum timestep t{max}, and number of super-resolution iterations max\sr\iter. Outputs: Refined latent residuals h	heta. Data Structures: h	heta: Learnable latent residuals, zero-initialized, same shape as z0. z'0: Refined latent representing the upscaled image, defined as z'0 = z0 + h	heta. z't, z'{t-1}: Noised latents at timesteps t and t-1. \hat{z}{t-1}: Predicted denoised latent at timestep t-1. \epsilon\phi: Noise prediction model (UNet backbone of SD×4, parameterized by \phi).  ar{\alpha}t: Cumulative noise coefficient at timestep t. \sigmat: Standard deviation of Gaussian noise samples at timestep t. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize learnable latent residuals h	heta = 0 with the same shape as z0. 2. Loop over super-resolution iterations sr\iter from 0 to max\sr\iter: a. Sample noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). b. Construct conditioning y = y{text} + y{noise\level} + I{lr}. c. Calculate timestep t using a linearly decreasing schedule: t = t{max} - (t{max} - t{min}) 	imes  rac{sr\iter}{max\sr\iter}. d. Calculate the refined latent z'0 = \sqrt{z0 + h	heta}. e. Apply the forward process (Eq. 1 in) to z'0 at timestep t to obtain z't: z't = \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}t} z'0 + \sqrt{1 -  ar{\alpha}t} \epsilon f. Apply the forward process to z'0 at timestep t-1 to obtain z'{t-1}: z'{t-1} = \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}{t-1}} z'0 + \sqrt{1 -  ar{\alpha}{t-1}} \epsilon g. Pass z't and conditioning y to the UNet backbone \epsilon\phi to predict the noise residual \epsilon\phi(z't, y, t). h. Construct the predicted denoised latent \hat{z}{t-1} using the DDPM reverse process equation (Eq. 3 in): \hat{z}{t-1} = \sqrt{ rac{1}{ ar{\alpha}t}} z't - \sqrt{ rac{1}{1- ar{\alpha}t}} \epsilon\phi(z't, y, t) + \sigmat \epsilon i. Compute the L1 error between z'{t-1} and \hat{z}{t-1} and take a gradient descent step on 
abla	heta \| z'{t-1} - \hat{z}{t-1} \|. j. Update h	heta. 3. Return refined latent residuals h	heta. Formulas: RSD Loss: L{RSD} = \| z{t-1} - \hat{z}{t-1} \| where z{t-1} is the current noised latent at t-1, and \hat{z}{t-1} is the predicted denoised latent from zt. Gradient: 
abla	heta L{RSD} = 
abla	heta \| z{t-1} - \hat{z}{t-1} \| Gradients are backpropagated through z'{t-1} towards h	heta. Relation to SDS: RSD can be interpreted as a renoised variant of SDS. While SDS optimizes in z0 space as 
abla	heta L{SDS} = \gamma(t) \sqrt{ rac{1}{1- ar{\alpha}t}} (z0 - \hat{z}0)  rac{\partial z}{\partial 	heta}, RSD applies the forward noising process to both z0 and \hat{z}0 towards time t-1. Parameters: Scheduler: DDPM scheduler. Time Schedule: Linearly decreasing time schedule following ancestral sampling, instead of randomly sampled timesteps as in SDS. Patch Sampling: Uniform random crops of 128 	imes 128 resolution in latent space (corresponding to 512 	imes 512 image patches) are sampled. Text Prompt: Fixed prompt: <subject>, high resolution, 4K, photo, where <subject> is the scene name. Learning Rate: Constant learning rate of 1e-2 for all learnable parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Default ancestral sampling can generate details structurally inconsistent with the conditioned LR image, aggravating inconsistency across different views. SDS produces LR-consistent features but with limited details. In practice, \hat{z}{t-1} can be obtained directly from \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt, y, t) using the DDPM denoising equation instead of renoising \hat{z}0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RSD(z0, ytext, ynoiselevel, Ilr, tmin, tmax, maxsriter): """ Renoised Score Distillation optimization loop. Args: z0: Low-resolution latent (encoded from 4x interpolated LR image). ytext: Text prompt embeddings. ynoiselevel: Noise level embedding. Ilr: LR image conditioning. tmin: Minimum timestep. tmax: Maximum timestep. maxsriter: Number of super-resolution iterations. Returns: htheta: Refined latent residuals. """ # Initialize learnable latent residuals htheta = torch.zeroslike(z0) for sriter in range(maxsriter): # Sample noise epsilon = torch.randnlike(z0) # Construct conditioning y = ytext + ynoiselevel + Ilr # Calculate timestep t using linearly decreasing schedule t = tmax - (tmax - tmin) (sriter / maxsriter) # Calculate refined latent z'0 # Note: Source uses sqrt(z0 + htheta), assuming element-wise sqrt or # standard latent addition. Based on Eq 8: z'0 = z0 + htheta. # The pseudocode in shows sqrt(z0 + htheta) which might be a typo # for z0 + htheta or specific to their latent space. # However, Eq 8 explicitly states z'0 = z0 + htheta. # We follow Eq 8 for correctness of the method definition. zprime0 = z0 + htheta # Apply forward process at timestep t to get z't # z't = sqrt(alphabart) z'0 + sqrt(1 - alphabart) epsilon zprimet = torch.sqrt(alphabar[t]) zprime0 + torch.sqrt(1 - alphabar[t]) epsilon # Apply forward process at timestep t-1 to get z'{t-1} # z'{t-1} = sqrt(alphabar{t-1}) z'0 + sqrt(1 - alphabar{t-1}) epsilon zprimetminus1 = torch.sqrt(alphabar[t-1]) zprime0 + torch.sqrt(1 - alphabar[t-1]) epsilon # Predict noise residual using UNet epsilonphi = UNet(zprimet, y, t) # Construct predicted denoised latent zhat{t-1} # zhat{t-1} = sqrt(1/alphabart) z't - sqrt(1/(1-alphabart)) epsilonphi + sigmat epsilon zhattminus1 = (torch.sqrt(1 / alphabar[t]) zprimet - torch.sqrt(1 / (1 - alphabar[t])) epsilonphi + sigma[t] epsilon) # Compute L1 error and backpropagate gradients loss = torch.norm(zprimetminus1 - zhattminus1) loss.backward() # Update htheta (gradient descent step) # Note: In practice, an optimizer step is taken here. # htheta -= learningrate htheta.grad # For the purpose of the algorithm description, we assume the optimizer handles the update. optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return htheta Optimizes score matching over intervals rather than single timesteps. Link Modifies SDS for inpainting tasks by conditioning on masks. Link Uses masks and background prompts to guide SDS. Link Uses diffusion models for reconstruction loss. Link Time Complexity: RSD optimization is computationally more expensive than standard SDS due to the multiple noise predictions and the renoising process. However, it is faster than DreamFusion-SDS because I3DS segregates upscaling and synchronization stages. Memory Complexity: Uses patch sampling (128 	imes 128 in latent space) to optimize GPU memory usage and speed up convergence. Measured Performance: On NeRF-Synthetic, DiSR-NeRF (using RSD) achieves PSNR 31.05 and SSIM 0.948, outperforming NGP (PSNR 31.95, SSIM 0.959) in some metrics but generally providing better super-resolution quality than baselines like NeRF-SR and DreamFusion. On LLFF, it achieves PSNR 17.01 and SSIM 0.948. Strengths: Produces sharper details compared to SDS and LR-consistent features compared to ancestral sampling. Limitations: Requires low-resolution multi-view images and a pretrained 2D diffusion upscaler (SD×4). Optimization time is longer than NGP. When to use: When high-quality super-resolution of NeRFs is needed using only LR training images and a pretrained 2D diffusion upscaler. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and high-resolution details are not critical. Renoised Score Distillation (RSD) was introduced in the paper "DiSR-NeRF: Diffusion-Guided View-Consistent Super-Resolution NeRF". It is part of the Iterative 3D Diffusion Super-Resolution (I3DS) framework, which alternates between upscaling low-resolution rendered images with diffusion models and updating the underlying 3D representation with standard NeRF training. The method was developed to address the limitations of existing super-resolution methods for NeRFs, which either lack view consistency or produce over-smoothed results. name: Diffusion Model Reconstruction Loss
head: Modified LSDS with DM noise comparison, Unsuccessful Experiment: Diffusion Model Reconstruction Loss
body: This method attempts to enforce fidelity to a specific input image during radiance field optimization by comparing the noise predictions of a diffusion model for a noisy rendered image against the noise predictions for a noisy version of the input image. It serves as an alternative to pixel-level reconstruction losses (like MSE) by operating in the latent noise space of a pre-trained diffusion model. It is distinct from standard Score Distillation Loss (SDS) Diffusion-Based Guidance for Radiance Field Optimization because it does not use a text prompt or unconditional prior to guide the generation, but rather uses the input image itself as the conditioning target for the noise comparison. Inputs: Radiance field parameters \Theta. Input reference image I{in} (or its latent representation). Camera pose p for rendering. Frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta (typically Stable Diffusion). Noise scheduler parameters (timestep t). Outputs: Gradient \nabla\Theta \mathcal{L}{DM-Rec} to update \Theta. Data Structures: Rendered Image I{render}: Output of the differentiable renderer given \Theta and p. Noisy Latent/Image xt: The rendered image (or its latent embedding) perturbed with Gaussian noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) at timestep t. Noisy Input yt: The input image (or its latent embedding) perturbed with the same noise realization \epsilon at timestep t. Steps: 1. Render: Compute the rendered image I{render} from the current radiance field \Theta at camera pose p. 2. Encode (Optional): If using a latent diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion), encode I{render} and I{in} into latent space z{render} and z{in} using the VAE encoder E. [G: If the diffusion model operates directly on pixels, skip this step and use pixel values]. 3. Perturb: Sample noise \epsilon and timestep t. Compute the noisy latent for the render: zt^ = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}t} z{render} + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}t} \epsilon Compute the noisy latent for the input: yt = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}t} z{in} + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}t} \epsilon Note: The same noise \epsilon must be used for both to ensure a fair comparison of the structure of the noise prediction relative to the content. 4. Predict Noise: Pass zt^ and yt through the frozen diffusion model \epsilon\theta (with empty text prompt or no conditioning if the model requires it, as per notation \emptyset). \hat{\epsilon}{render} = \epsilon\theta(zt^, t, \emptyset) \hat{\epsilon}{input} = \epsilon\theta(yt, t, \emptyset) 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the mean squared error between the two predicted noise vectors. \mathcal{L}{DM-Rec} = \| \hat{\epsilon}{render} - \hat{\epsilon}{input} \|2^2 6. Backpropagate: Compute gradients \nabla\Theta \mathcal{L}{DM-Rec} through the diffusion model (treating \epsilon\theta as differentiable for the purpose of gradient flow to the renderer, although \epsilon\theta weights are frozen) and the differentiable renderer. 7. Update: Update \Theta using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Pitfalls: Color/Texture Mismatch: The method may reconstruct the general geometry and structure of the input image but fail to match exact colors or fine textures. Noise Correlation: Using different noise realizations for the render and input breaks the direct comparison of noise prediction errors. The same \epsilon must be used. Conditioning: If the diffusion model requires conditioning (e.g., text), using an empty prompt or a generic prompt is critical to avoid introducing external biases. uses \emptyset. A variant applied during NeuS mesh reconstruction to ensure consistency between the reconstructed geometry's rendering at the input viewpoint and the original input image using score distillation. It differs from the general DM Reconstruction Loss by being specifically integrated into a NeuS pipeline and often used alongside photometric losses. It emphasizes perceptual quality via patch-aware noise/latent-level comparison rather than pixel-level MSE. Formula: \mathcal{L}{RV} = \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{t}, \epsilon} \left[ w(\mathbf{t}) \| \epsilon{\psi}(\mathbf{z}{\mathbf{t}}^, \emptyset) - \epsilon{\psi}(\mathbf{y}{\mathbf{t}}, \emptyset) \|2^2 \right] where \mathbf{z}t^ = R(\Theta, p^) is the noisy latent of the NeuS rendering at input camera pose p^, \mathbf{y}t is the noisy latent of the input view image, \epsilon\psi is the Stable Diffusion noise predictor, and w(t) is a weighting function. Procedure: Add small noise (e.g., Stable Diffusion scheduler t=200) to NeRF render images, conduct denoising, and optimize NeuS parameters \Theta by adding \mathcal{L}{RV} to the original photometric loss. Time Complexity: Requires two forward passes through the diffusion model per optimization step (one for the render, one for the input), doubling the diffusion inference cost compared to standard SDS which uses one pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the latent representations of both the rendered image and the input image, plus the noise tensors. Performance: In experiments, this loss allowed reconstruction of the input image to a certain degree but failed to match exact input image colors or textures. It is considered an unsuccessful experiment for high-fidelity single-image reconstruction in the context of RealFusion. Strengths: Provides a perceptual prior that is more robust to pixel-level noise than MSE. Limitations: Does not guarantee photometric accuracy; may produce blurry or color-shifted results. This method was explored as part of the RealFusion pipeline for 360° reconstruction of objects from a single image. The authors investigated using the diffusion model within the reconstruction objective to guide the neural field towards the input image. They found that while it helped with structure, it was insufficient for color/texture fidelity. A similar concept, Reference View Score Distillation, was later applied in the context of NeuS mesh reconstruction from multi-view diffusers to leverage input view information for geometry and texture distillation. name: Synthetic Training with EG3D Supervision
head: Alternating supervision training, Distillation Training, On-the-fly Augmentation
body: This method trains an image-to-triplane encoder to reconstruct a 3D radiance field representation from a single input image by leveraging synthetic data generated by a frozen, pretrained EG3D generator. It solves the problem of generalizing single-image portrait synthesis by ensuring the encoder produces triplanes that are consistent not only with the input reference view but also with novel multiview renderings, thereby enforcing geometric and photometric coherence. It differs from standard supervised training by using a frozen generative model as a ground-truth oracle and alternating between reference-view and multiview supervision to prevent overfitting to the specific distribution of the input image. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single high-resolution reference image I{512} rendered from a reference camera P{ref} (synthetic in training). Output: A predicted triplane \hat{T} and associated rendered images (If, \hat{I}{128}, \hat{I}{512}, \hat{I}D) from the encoder's triplane. Frozen Components: EG3D generator (produces ground-truth triplanes T and images), EG3D MLP decoder, EG3D super-resolution network, EG3D dual discriminator. Trainable Components: Image-to-triplane encoder E, MLP decoder, super-resolution network, dual discriminator (fine-tuned). Data Structures Triplane T: A 3-channel feature map per plane (front, side, top) intersecting at the head center. Camera Parameters P: Focal length, principal point, orientation, and position. Rendered Images: Four resolutions/types per camera: feature image If, 128x128 image I{128}, 512x512 image I{512}, and depth map ID. Numbered Steps 1. Synthesize Ground Truth: Sample a latent vector z and pass it through the frozen EG3D generator to obtain a ground-truth triplane T. 2. Encode Reference View: Pass the high-resolution reference image I{512} from camera P{ref} through the encoder E to predict a triplane \hat{T} = E(I{512}). 3. Render Predicted Views: Use \hat{T} to condition volume rendering from both the reference camera P{ref} and a multiview camera P{mv} to generate predicted images \hat{I}f, \hat{I}{128}, \hat{I}{512}, \hat{I}D. 4. Compute Losses: Calculate the total loss L using the formulas below, comparing ground-truth quantities (from T) with predicted quantities (from \hat{T}). 5. Optimize: Perform end-to-end gradient descent with respect to all trainable parameters (encoder, decoder, upsampler, discriminator). Formulas The total loss is defined as: L = L{tri} + L{col} + L{LPIPS} + L{feat} + \lambda1 L{adv} + \lambda2 L{cate} Where: L{tri}: L1 loss between predicted triplane \hat{T} and ground-truth triplane T. L{col}: Mean L1 loss between pairs (I{128}, \hat{I}{128}) and (I{512}, \hat{I}{512}). L{LPIPS}: LPIPS perceptual loss [Zhang et al. 2018] between pairs (I{128}, \hat{I}{128}) and (I{512}, \hat{I}{512}). L{feat}: Mean L1 loss between feature images (If, \hat{I}f). L{adv}: Adversarial loss using the pretrained dual discriminator from EG3D. The discriminator is fine-tuned to differentiate between images rendered from the encoder and images rendered from the frozen EG3D generator. It does not use real data. L{cate}: Optional category-specific loss. For human faces, this is the ArcFace identity loss [Deng et al. 2019a] with \lambda2 = 1. For cat faces, \lambda2 = 0. \lambda1: Adversarial weight. Set to 0.1 for reference images and 0.025 for multiview images. Parameters Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-4} for encoder parameters; 5 \times 10^{-5} for transformer parameters. Depth Samples: 48 depth samples for coarse and fine passes in volume rendering. Discriminator: Identical settings to EG3D (2D dual discriminator). Hardware/Duration: ~10 days on 8 A100 or 8 A40 GPUs for ~220k iterations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def l1loss(a, b): return torch.mean(torch.abs(a - b)) def meanl1loss(gtlist, predlist): return sum(l1loss(gt, pred) for gt, pred in zip(gtlist, predlist)) / len(gtlist) def lpipsloss(gtlist, predlist): # Standard LPIPS perceptual loss computation return sum(torch.mean(torch.abs(gt - pred)) for gt, pred in zip(gtlist, predlist)) / len(gtlist) def advloss(Dreal, Dfake): # Standard adversarial loss for dual discriminator return torch.mean(torch.relu(1.0 - Dreal)) + torch.mean(torch.relu(1.0 + Dfake)) def arcfaceloss(img1, img2): # Standard ArcFace identity feature distance return torch.mean(torch.abs(img1 - img2)) def volumerender(triplane, cameras, depthsamples=48): # Standard volume rendering with 48 depth samples per ray # Returns dictionary of tensors: If, I128, I512, ID pass # Implementation details omitted; performs standard volume rendering def trainstep(encoder, decoder, upsampler, discriminator, eg3dgenerator, optimizer, iteration, category): # 1. Sample cameras and latent # Sample 32 reference cameras Pref and 32 multiview cameras Pmv from training distributions Pref = torch.randn(32, 16) # Camera parameter sampling Pmv = torch.randn(32, 16) z = torch.randn(32, 512) # Latent sampling # 2. Generate Ground Truth from Frozen EG3D T = eg3dgenerator(z) Igtref = volumerender(T, Pref, depthsamples=48) Igtmv = volumerender(T, Pmv, depthsamples=48) # 3. Encode Reference View I512gtref = Igtref['I512'] That = encoder(I512gtref) # 4. Render Predicted Views Ipredref = volumerender(That, Pref, depthsamples=48) Ipredmv = volumerender(That, Pmv, depthsamples=48) # 5. Compute Losses Ltri = l1loss(That, T) Lcol = meanl1loss([Igtref['I128'], Igtref['I512']], [Ipredref['I128'], Ipredref['I512']]) Llpips = lpipsloss([Igtref['I128'], Igtref['I512']], [Ipredref['I128'], Ipredref['I512']]) Lfeat = meanl1loss([Igtref['If']], [Ipredref['If']]) # Adversarial loss Drealref = discriminator(Igtref['I512']) Dfakeref = discriminator(Ipredref['I512']) Drealmv = discriminator(Igtmv['I512']) Dfakemv = discriminator(Ipredmv['I512']) Ladvref = advloss(Drealref, Dfakeref) Ladvmv = advloss(Drealmv, Dfakemv) Ladv = 0.1 Ladvref + 0.025 Ladvmv # Category loss if category == 'human': Lcate = arcfaceloss(Igtref['I512'], Ipredref['I512']) lambda2 = 1.0 else: Lcate = 0.0 lambda2 = 0.0 optimizer.zerograd() # Stage 1 logic (first 30k iterations) if iteration < 30000: # Exclude adversarial and category losses Ladv = 0.0 Lcate = 0.0 # Freeze decoder and upsampler gradients # Compute reference losses once every 10 triplane syntheses if iteration % 10 == 0: Lref = Ltri + Lcol + Llpips + Lfeat else: Lref = 0.0 # Multiview supervision every step Lmv = meanl1loss([Igtmv['I128'], Igtmv['I512']], [Ipredmv['I128'], Ipredmv['I512']]) L = Lref + Lmv # Update encoder only L.backward() optimizer.step() # Stage 2 logic (30k to 37.5k iterations) elif iteration < 37500: # Backpropagate to all parameters # Compute reference losses every 2 gradient passes if iteration % 2 == 0: Lref = 0.01 Ltri + Lcol + Llpips + Lcate else: Lref = Lcol + Llpips + Lcate # Remove feature loss Lfeat = 0.0 # Multiview supervision every step Lmv = meanl1loss([Igtmv['I128'], Igtmv['I512']], [Ipredmv['I128'], Ipredmv['I512']]) L = Lref + Ladv + Lcate L.backward() optimizer.step() # Stage 3 logic (37.5k to 220k iterations) else: # Compute multiview and reference supervision at every EG3D triplane synthesis step Lref = 0.01 Ltri + Lcol + Llpips + Lcate Lmv = meanl1loss([Igtmv['I128'], Igtmv['I512']], [Ipredmv['I128'], Ipredmv['I512']]) L = Lref + Ladv + Lcate L.backward() optimizer.step() return L Edge Cases and Pitfalls Overfitting to Synthetic Data: Naive optimization leads to models that perform well on synthetic data but fail on real images. The alternating supervision and adversarial training mitigate this. Discriminator Training: The dual discriminator is fine-tuned but does not use real data; it only distinguishes between encoder-rendered and EG3D-rendered images. Category Specificity: For cat faces, the category loss weight \lambda2 is set to 0, and transfer learning from a human face model is used. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 10 days on 8 A100 or 8 A40 GPUs for ~220k iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method relies on the capacity of the EG3D generator and the encoder. Strengths: Enforces multiview consistency, which is critical for 3D reconstruction. The adversarial component improves texture quality. Limitations: Dependent on the quality and diversity of the EG3D training data (e.g., FFHQ, AFHQ). When to Use: When synthesizing 3D portraits from single images where multiview consistency is required. When Not to Use: When real data supervision is preferred or when the target domain is significantly different from the EG3D training distribution. The method is described in "Real-Time Radiance Fields for Single-Image Portrait View Synthesis" by Alex Trevithick et al.. It builds upon the EG3D architecture and uses techniques from 2D GAN inversion for category-specific losses. The approach was developed to enable real-time rendering of high-quality portraits from a single image by learning an encoder that maps images to triplanes. name: Pix2Pix Denoising Network for Point Clouds
head: DSS-based denoising, DSS-based point cloud denoising, Differentiable Surface Splatting denoising
body: A generative adversarial network (GAN) based method to denoise point cloud renderings by mapping noisy splat images to clean splat images, followed by a 3D update via Differentiable Surface Splatting (DSS). It solves the ill-posed problem of point cloud denoising where handcrafted priors struggle to recover both smooth and sharp features simultaneously. Unlike optimization-based methods that rely on local geometric priors, this approach leverages a learned image-to-image translation network to hallucinate plausible high-frequency details, which are then transferred to 3D geometry through simultaneous multi-view optimization. Input: A noisy point cloud P{\text{noisy}} with associated normals N{\text{noisy}}. Output: A denoised point cloud P{\text{clean}} with associated normals N{\text{clean}}. Point Cloud: A set of points P = \{pi\} where each pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a normal ni \in \mathbb{R}^3. Image: A 2D tensor I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} representing the rendered splat image. Generator (G): A ResNet-based architecture mapping noisy images to clean images. Discriminator (D): A convolutional network classifying images as real or generated. 1. Data Preparation: Sample 20,000 points per model from the Sketchfab dataset using Poisson-disk sampling to create reference point clouds. Create noisy input points by adding white Gaussian noise to the reference points. Compute PCA normals for both reference and input points. Render training pairs (noisy and clean images) using DSS from various viewpoints and distances. Use point light and diffuse shading only. 2. Network Training (Offline): Train two separate Pix2Pix models targeting specific noise levels: 1.0% and 0.3%. The generator uses a ResNet architecture with 2-stride convolution and 2-stride up-convolution for encoder/decoder, with 9 residual blocks in-between. The discriminator uses convolutional layers with channel counts C64-C128-C256-C512-C1. Apply pixel-wise normalization in the generator to deal with checkerboard artifacts. Add a convolutional layer after each deconvolutional layer in the discriminator to deal with checkerboard artifacts. Remove the tanh activation in the final layer of the generator to obtain unbounded pixel values. Optimize using Least Squares GAN (LSGAN) loss. Use ADAM optimizer with lr = 0.0002, \beta1 = 0.5, \beta2 = 0.999. Initialize weights using Xavier initialization. 3. Inference and 3D Update: Render images of the noisy point cloud from multiple views. Pass the noisy images through the trained Pix2Pix network to reconstruct geometric structure (clean splat images). Update the point cloud using DSS with the denoised images as reference. The simultaneous multi-view optimization in DSS resolves cross-view inconsistencies, transferring plausible 2D details to 3D without visible artifacts. Generator Architecture: The generator G consists of an encoder, 9 residual blocks, and a decoder. G = D{\text{decoder}} \circ \text{ResNet}{9} \circ E{\text{encoder}} Where E{\text{encoder}} uses 2-stride convolutions and D{\text{decoder}} uses 2-stride up-convolutions. Discriminator Architecture: The discriminator D consists of a sequence of convolutional layers: D = \text{Conv}{C1} \circ \text{Conv}{C512} \circ \text{Conv}{C256} \circ \text{Conv}{C128} \circ \text{Conv}{C64} Where Ck denotes a convolutional layer with k output channels. Loss Function: Least Squares GAN (LSGAN) loss is used. \mathcal{L}{\text{GAN}} = \mathbb{E}{y \sim p{\text{data}}}[(D(y) - 1)^2] + \mathbb{E}{x \sim pg}[(D(G(x)) - 0)^2] (Standard LSGAN formulation provided for implementation completeness.) Optimizer: ADAM update rule: \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \frac{\eta \hat{m}t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}t} + \epsilon} With \eta = 0.0002, \beta1 = 0.5, \beta2 = 0.999. (Standard ADAM formulation provided for implementation completeness.) Noise Levels: Two models trained for 1.0% and 0.3% noise. Generator: ResNet with 9 residual blocks, 2-stride conv/up-conv. Discriminator: Channels [64, 128, 256, 512, 1]. Optimizer: ADAM (lr=0.0002, \beta1=0.5, \beta2=0.999). Initialization: Xavier. Hardware: NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU. Lighting: Point light and diffuse shading only. Checkerboard Artifacts: Mitigated by pixel-wise normalization in the generator and adding a convolutional layer after each deconvolutional layer in the discriminator. Unbounded Values: The tanh activation is removed from the generator's final layer to allow unbounded pixel values. View Inconsistency: The Pix2Pix model is not trained with view-consistency constraints. Small inconsistencies may appear in high-frequency detail regions across views, but DSS resolves these during the 3D update phase. Lighting Complexity: Glossy/specular effects are avoided because they pose unnecessary difficulties for the network to infer local geometric structure. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class ResNetGenerator(nn.Module): def init(self, inputnc=3, outputnc=3, ngf=64, nresidual=9): super(ResNetGenerator, self).init() # Encoder: 2-stride convolutions self.encoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(inputnc, ngf, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ngf), # Pixel-wise normalization nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True)) # Bottleneck: 9 residual blocks self.bottleneck = nn.Sequential() for i in range(nresidual): self.bottleneck.addmodule(f'res{i}', ResidualBlock(ngf)) # Decoder: 2-stride up-convolutions (no tanh for unbounded values) self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.ConvTranspose2d(ngf, outputnc, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1)) def forward(self, x): x = self.encoder(x) x = self.bottleneck(x) x = self.decoder(x) return x class ResidualBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, channels): super(ResidualBlock, self).init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.norm1 = nn.InstanceNorm2d(channels) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.norm2 = nn.InstanceNorm2d(channels) def forward(self, x): identity = x out = self.conv1(x) out = self.norm1(out) out = nn.ReLU(inplace=True)(out) out = self.conv2(out) out = self.norm2(out) out += identity return out class Discriminator(nn.Module): def init(self, inputnc=3, ndf=64): super(Discriminator, self).init() # C64-C128-C256-C512-C1 architecture self.model = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(inputnc, ndf, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf, ndf2, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ndf2), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf2, ndf4, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ndf4), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf4, ndf8, kernelsize=4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.InstanceNorm2d(ndf8), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), nn.Conv2d(ndf8, 1, kernelsize=4, stride=1, padding=1)) def forward(self, x): return self.model(x) def trainpix2pix(noisyimages, cleanimages, generator, discriminator, optimizerG, optimizerD, epochs=2): # LSGAN Loss (MSE) criterion = nn.MSELoss() for epoch in range(epochs): # Train Discriminator optimizerD.zerograd() # Real images outputreal = discriminator(cleanimages) labelreal = torch.oneslike(outputreal) lossreal = criterion(outputreal, labelreal) # Generated images with torch.nograd(): fakeimages = generator(noisyimages) outputfake = discriminator(fakeimages.detach()) labelfake = torch.zeroslike(outputfake) lossfake = criterion(outputfake, labelfake) lossD = (lossreal + lossfake) / 2 lossD.backward() optimizerD.step() # Train Generator optimizerG.zerograd() outputfake = discriminator(fakeimages) labelfake = torch.oneslike(outputfake) lossG = criterion(outputfake, labelfake) lossG.backward() optimizerG.step() def denoisepointcloud(noisypointcloud, views, generator, steps=100): """ 1. Render noisy images from multiple views. 2. Denoise images using Pix2Pix. 3. Update point cloud using DSS with denoised images as reference. """ # Step 1: Render noisy images noisyimages = [] for view in views: # DSS rasterization details are covered in the parent article img = torch.zeros(256, 256, 3) # Placeholder for actual DSS rasterization logic noisyimages.append(img) noisyimages = torch.stack(noisyimages) # Step 2: Denoise images cleanimages = generator(noisyimages) # Step 3: Update point cloud using DSS optimizer = optim.Adam([noisypointcloud], lr=0.001) denoisedpointcloud = dssoptimize(noisypointcloud, cleanimages, views, optimizer, steps) return denoisedpointcloud def dssoptimize(points, targetimages, views, optimizer, steps=100): """ Simultaneous multi-view optimization: minimize rendering error against denoised targets. DSS gradient computation details are covered in the parent article. """ for in range(steps): optimizer.zerograd() loss = 0.0 for view in views: # Render current points to image using DSS rendered = torch.zeros(256, 256, 3) # Placeholder for DSS output # Find corresponding target image for this view target = torch.zeros(256, 256, 3) # Placeholder for target image loss += torch.nn.functional.mseloss(rendered, target) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return points Measured Performance: On 1% noisy, 20K point input: Pix2Pix-DSS outperforms WLOP, EAR, RIMLS, GPF, and PointCleanNet quantitatively and qualitatively. On 0.3% noisy, 100K point input: Pix2Pix-DSS reconstructs clean surfaces with abundant hallucinated details, outperforming PointCleanNet which deteriorates due to generalizability issues. Strengths: Can hallucinate plausible high-frequency details that optimization-based methods miss. Less sensitive to point sampling characteristics compared to direct learning-based methods. Simultaneous multi-view optimization in DSS resolves cross-view inconsistencies. Limitations: Not trained with view-consistency constraints, potentially causing small inconsistencies in high-frequency detail regions across views. Limited to the noise levels it was trained on (1.0% and 0.3%). Time Complexity: Training requires approximately two days on an NVIDIA 1080Ti GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was introduced in "Differentiable surface splatting for point-based geometry processing". Usage: Used for point cloud denoising tasks, specifically for recovering smooth and sharp features from noisy inputs. History: Not given in the sources. name: MaterialFusion
head: Prior-guided Inverse Rendering
body: MaterialFusion is a 3D inverse rendering pipeline that reconstructs an object’s geometry, physically-based rendering (PBR) material properties, and environmental illumination from multi-view images under unknown lighting conditions. It addresses the intrinsic challenge of disentangling albedo and material properties from input images, which typically leads to poor relighting performance in novel conditions. Unlike standard inverse rendering methods that optimize geometry and materials solely based on photometric consistency, MaterialFusion incorporates a 2D diffusion prior (StableMaterial) to guide the optimization of albedo and material textures, ensuring physically plausible and disentangled results. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N multi-view RGB images \{xi\} of an object captured under unknown, varying illumination. Outputs: A 3D mesh geometry G, UV material textures (albedo kd and ORM k{orm}), and an HDR environment light map L. Data Structures and Layouts: 1. Geometry: Parameterized as a Signed Distance Field (SDF) S. The mesh G is extracted from S in each optimization iteration using DMTet. 2. Material Texture: Albedo (kd): A UV-map where each texel is a \in \mathbb{R}^3. ORM (k{orm}): A UV-map where each texel is (o, r, m). o (occlusion) is unused. r \in \mathbb{R} is roughness, and m \in \mathbb{R} is metallicness. 3. Illumination: Represented as a High Dynamic Range (HDR) environment map L. Optimization Steps: The method optimizes S, kd, k{orm}, and L by minimizing a total loss function. The procedure for each optimization iteration is as follows: 1. Sampling: Sample a subset of training images x and their associated camera views C. 2. Rendering: Extract mesh G from SDF S using DMTet. Use the differentiable renderer (nvdiffrecmc) with inputs G, kd, k{orm}, C, and L to produce: The rendered RGB image \hat{x}. The rendered albedo component \hat{I}d. The rendered ORM component \hat{I}{orm}. 3. Diffusion Prior Encoding: Encode \hat{I}d and \hat{I}{orm} using the Stable Diffusion encoder to obtain their latent representations. Concatenate these latents to form the combined latent z. 4. Diffusion Prior Denoising (SDS Calculation): Sample Gaussian noise \epsilon. Add noise to z according to a random diffusion timestep t \in [0.02, 0.98] to obtain zt. Denoise zt using the Stable Diffusion model via DDIM sampling for 5 steps, conditioned on the reference image x, to sample the clean latent \hat{z}. 5. Loss Computation: Compute Reconstruction Loss L{recon}. Compute SDS Loss L{SDS+}. Compute Regularization Loss L{reg}. 6. Update: Minimize the total loss L{MaterialFusion} with respect to S, kd, k{orm}, and L. Formulas: Reconstruction Loss: L{recon} = \mathbb{E}C [L2(\hat{x}, x)] where \hat{x} is the rendered image and x is the reference RGB image. SDS Loss: L{SDS+} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon,v} [\lambda{latent} \|z - \hat{z}\|2^2 + \lambda{rgb} \|D(z) - D(\hat{z})\|2^2] where D is the Stable Diffusion decoder, z is the encoded latent of the rendered materials, and \hat{z} is the denoised latent. Total Loss: L{MaterialFusion} = L{recon} + L{reg} + \gammai L{SDS+} where \gammai is an iteration-dependent hyperparameter that decays as training progresses. Parameters: Diffusion Model: Stable Diffusion 2.1. DDIM Sampling Steps: 5 steps. Timestep Range: t \in [0.02, 0.98]. Regularization: Uses the same L{reg} as nvdiffrecmc. Glass Handling: Glass surfaces in training objects are replaced with a black surface of roughness 0.25 and metallicness 0. Training Data Generation: 30 images per object, with azimuth \sim [0^\circ, 360^\circ] and elevation \sim [-15^\circ, 90^\circ] on a hemisphere with radius \sim [1.5, 2.0]. Lighting varies using StreetLearn, Laval, point lights, or directional sun lights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Extract mesh from SDF G = dmtetextractor(S) # 2. Render RGB, Albedo, and ORM xhat = renderer.renderrgb(G, kd, korm, C, L) Idhat = renderer.renderalbedo(G, kd, korm, C, L) Iormhat = renderer.renderorm(G, kd, korm, C, L) # 3. Encode rendered materials zd = sdencoder(Idhat) zorm = sdencoder(Iormhat) z = np.concatenate([zd, zorm], axis=-1) # 4. Add noise t = np.random.uniform(0.02, 0.98) epsilon = np.random.randn(z.shape) zt = z + t epsilon # 5. Denoise using DDIM (5 steps) conditioned on x zhat = zt for in range(5): noisepred = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(zhat, t, condition=x) zhat = zhat - t noisepred # Simplified DDIM update # 6. Compute SDS Loss latentloss = lambdalatent np.linalg.norm(z - zhat, ord=2)2 zrgb = sddecoder(z) zhatrgb = sddecoder(zhat) rgbloss = lambdargb np.linalg.norm(zrgb - zhatrgb, ord=2)2 lsds = latentloss + rgbloss # 7. Compute Reconstruction Loss lrecon = np.linalg.norm(xhat - x, ord=2)2 # 8. Compute Regularization Loss lreg = computenvdiffrecmcregularization(S, kd, korm, L) # 9. Compute Total Loss gammai = max(0.0, 1.0 - currentiteration / totaliterations) totalloss = lrecon + lreg + gammai lsds return totalloss def computenvdiffrecmcregularization(S, kd, korm, L): # Combines normal smoothness, albedo smoothness, ORM smoothness, normal perturbation, and demodulated lighting regularization # Implementation details are specific to nvdiffrecmc [19] return 0.0 # Placeholder for regularization computation Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Glass Surfaces: Glass surfaces can cause issues in training data generation; they should be replaced with black surfaces (roughness 0.25, metallicness 0) to ensure consistent material learning. SDS Weight Decay: The weight \gammai on the SDS loss must decay as training progresses to preserve finer details that might be lost due to the encoder/decoder operations. Denoising Steps: Using fewer than 5 DDIM steps may result in less crisp and accurate material predictions. Rendering and optimization configuration for MaterialFusion, utilizing nvdiffrast for differentiable rasterization and applying multiple regularizers to stabilize material reconstruction. It renders appearance, albedo, ORM, diffuse lighting, and specular lighting using nvdiffrast. It feeds rasterized estimated albedo and ORM batches to StableMaterial, converting inputs to RGB format to ensure sRGB tonemapped image inputs are properly handled. It applies regularizers including normal smoothness, albedo smoothness, ORM smoothness, normal perturbation, and demodulated lighting regularization. It differs from standard inverse rendering by integrating a pretrained diffusion prior (StableMaterial) and relying on nvdiffrast's rasterization rather than ray tracing for appearance rendering. It serves as the core optimization setup for the MaterialFusion inverse rendering pipeline. sRGB tonemapping must be explicitly handled before feeding inputs to StableMaterial to prevent color space mismatches. Time Complexity: The method is computationally expensive due to the iterative extraction of the mesh via DMTet, differentiable rendering, and the 5-step DDIM denoising process per optimization step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SDF, UV maps, HDR environment map, and the latent representations for the diffusion model. Performance: Improves relighting performance in novel conditions compared to conventional inverse rendering methods by ensuring disentangled and physically plausible material properties. Strengths: Produces crisp and accurate material predictions; effectively disentangles albedo and material properties; handles unknown illumination by recovering the HDR environment map. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D diffusion prior; glass surfaces require special handling; training data generation is complex (requires synthetic data with known materials and lighting). When to use: When high-quality relighting under novel lighting is required and the input consists of multi-view images under unknown illumination. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the input images have significant glass/transparent surfaces that are not pre-processed. MaterialFusion was introduced in the paper "MaterialFusion: Enhancing Inverse Rendering with Material Diffusion Priors". It builds upon the nvdiffrecmc inverse rendering pipeline and leverages advancements in distilling 3D information from 2D diffusion models. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous inverse rendering approaches that failed to accurately render objects under new lighting conditions due to poor disentanglement of albedo and material properties. The 2D prior, StableMaterial, was trained on a curated dataset of ~12K artist-designed synthetic Blender objects called BlenderVault. name: Style and Content Adaptation
body: Style and Content Adaptation modifies a pre-trained radiance field to incorporate specific visual styles or object contents by leveraging external conditions, such as reference images or text prompts, during the optimization loop. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SKED and Single-Image Textual Inversion by explicitly using reference images as conditional priors to guide the diffusion model's denoising process, ensuring the generated content adheres to the visual characteristics of the reference rather than relying solely on textual descriptions or single-view embeddings. The family shares a common optimization framework where a frozen diffusion model provides gradient signals to update the radiance field parameters Parent. The core mechanism involves rendering an image from the current radiance field state, passing it through the diffusion model to compute a Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss or similar gradient, and backpropagating this signal to the radiance field. The key differentiator for this family is the conditioning mechanism: instead of using only a text prompt, the diffusion model is conditioned on a reference image I{ref} alongside the text prompt T. SKED [12268-sked.md] focuses on localized 3D editing using multi-view 2D sketches as spatial priors. It minimizes a composite loss L = L{SDS} + \lambdas L{sil} + \lambdap L{pres}, where L{SDS} steers the content via diffusion, L{sil} ensures the rendered silhouette matches the sketch mask Mv, and L{pres} maintains fidelity to the original scene outside the sketch regions. It is chosen when precise spatial control over object insertion or replacement is required. Single-Image Textual Inversion [19221-single-image-textual-inversion.md] optimizes a learnable token embedding \langle e \rangle from a single input image to serve as a custom prompt. It solves the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction by providing an image-specific prompt that reduces artifacts like "floaters" and the "Janus problem". It is chosen when the goal is to generate novel views of a specific object from a single image without explicit 3D supervision. This variant uses a reference image as a condition alongside the text prompt to guide generation. By utilizing reference images as conditions, the method ensures that the generated content (e.g., "a stone chair") closely resembles the visual characteristics (material, texture) of the reference image (e.g., a stone), compared to results generated without a reference. The specific use of reference images for style adaptation in the context of NeRFs is detailed in GO-NeRF, which demonstrated that reference images can effectively guide the generation of objects with specific visual properties (e.g., material appearance) within a virtual reality content creation pipeline. This approach addresses the limitations of text-only prompts, which may lack the precision required for specific material or stylistic replication. GO-NeRF: Generating Objects in Neural Radiance Fields for Virtual Reality Content Creation, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3549558, fetched 2026-10-29

name: SKED
head: Sketch-guided NeRF Editing
body: SKED edits a NeRF scene using multi-view 2D sketches and a text prompt. It is distinguished by its explicit use of multi-view sketches as spatial priors to confine edits, unlike text-only or single-view mask methods. Inputs and outputs: Input: A pre-existing NeRF scene, a set of 2D sketches corresponding to specific camera views, and a text prompt describing the desired edit. Output: An edited NeRF model where sketched regions reflect the text prompt and the rest of the scene remains unchanged. Data structures: NeRF: Standard MLP or grid-based representation mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Sketches: Binary masks Mv for each view v, indicating the region to be edited. Numbered steps: 1. Render an image from the current NeRF state for each sketch view. 2. Pass the rendered image and sketch mask through a frozen diffusion model conditioned on the text prompt to compute gradient signals Parent,. 3. Compute the composite loss combining SDS guidance, silhouette priors, and preservation priors. 4. Backpropagate the loss to update NeRF parameters. The exact procedural steps are not detailed in the sources. Formulas: The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulations. The composite loss is described as a combination of three terms: 1. SDS Loss: Score Distillation Sampling loss [50, 89] steers the rendered image toward the text prompt. 2. Silhouette Loss: Enforces geometric consistency with the sketch masks to facilitate object addition within the sketched region. 3. Preservation Loss: Penalizes changes outside the sketched regions to maintain fidelity to the original scene. Parameters: Weights for silhouette and preservation losses: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Sketch Accuracy: The method relies on accurate multi-view sketches to guide the edit. Scene Blur: Without sufficient preservation loss, the method may introduce blur or unintended texture and color changes to the entire scene. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for localized object insertion and replacement tasks on synthetic objects, such as adding hats, flowers, or glasses. Limitations: Primarily demonstrated on synthetic objects; may struggle with complex real-world scenes if preservation is not strictly enforced. When to use: When precise spatial control over the edit region is required via 2D sketches, and the target is a synthetic object. When not: When sketches are unavailable or when editing real-world scenes with complex geometry and texture is required without additional constraints. SKED was introduced as a 3D editing method guided by sketches and text prompts. It builds on the SDS loss framework [50, 89] and extends it with sketch-based spatial priors. The method is used primarily for zero-shot object generation and blending in existing NeRF scenes, demonstrating applicability on object insertion and replacement tasks. name: Single-Image Textual Inversion
head: auto-prompt generation
body: Single-Image Textual Inversion is a technique to generate a custom prompt for a diffusion model by optimizing an embedding token \langle e \rangle from a single input image prior to 3D reconstruction. It solves the problem of ill-posed single-view reconstruction by conditioning the diffusion model on a prompt that specifically describes the input object, enabling the generation of plausible novel views. Unlike generic text-to-image approaches, this method optimizes a learnable token embedding to match the input image, which greatly alleviates artifacts such as "floaters" (disconnected geometry near the camera) that occur without image-specific prompts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input image I0 corresponding to an unknown camera pose \pi0. Output: An optimized embedding vector e (or token \langle e \rangle) that serves as a custom prompt for the diffusion model. Data Structures: The embedding e is a learnable vector of the same dimension as the text encoder's token embeddings (e.g., 768 for CLIP/ViT-B/16). The prompt template is a fixed string: "An image of a \langle e \rangle". Initialization: The embedding e can be initialized in three ways: 1. Random: Initialize e with random noise. 2. Manual: Select a token from the vocabulary that semantically matches the object. 3. Automated: Use CLIP to find the most similar noun token in the vocabulary (see "Automated Token Initialization" below). Algorithm Steps: 1. Prompt Configuration: Configure the diffusion model's text prompt as "An image of a \langle e \rangle". 2. Augmentation Setup: Apply heavy image augmentations to the input image I0 to prevent overfitting to the single view. 3. Optimization Loop: For t = 1 to T{steps} (typically 3000): a. Apply random augmentations to I0 to produce I{aug}. b. Compute the image embedding v{img} of the input image I0 using the CLIP image encoder. c. Compute the text embedding v{text} of the prompt "An image of a \langle e \rangle" using the CLIP text encoder. d. Compute the loss \mathcal{L} as the distance between v{img} and v{text} (typically cosine similarity or L2 distance in embedding space). e. Update e using the Adam optimizer. 4. Result: The optimized e is used to condition the diffusion model during the subsequent radiance field optimization. Parameters: Optimization steps (T{steps}): 3000. Optimizer: Adam. Image size: 512px. Batch size: 16. Learning rate: 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. Weight decay: 1 \cdot 10^{-2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from torchvision import transforms def singleimagetextualinversion(inputimage, clipmodel, steps=3000, lr=5e-4): """ Optimizes a token embedding <e> to match an input image using heavy augmentations. Args: inputimage: Tensor of shape (3, H, W) normalized to [0, 1]. clipmodel: Pre-trained CLIP model with.tokenizer,.encodeimage, and.textmodel methods. steps: Number of optimization steps. lr: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: e: Optimized embedding tensor of shape (1, 768). """ # Initialize embedding randomly e = torch.randn(1, 768, requiresgrad=True) # Configure optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([e], lr=lr, weightdecay=1e-2) # Define heavy image augmentations exactly as in the source transform = transforms.Compose([ transforms.RandomApply([transforms.RandomRotation(degrees=10, fill=255)], p=0.75), transforms.RandomResizedCrop(512, scale=(0.70, 1.3)), transforms.RandomApply([transforms.ColorJitter(0.04, 0.04, 0.04, 0.04)], p=0.75), transforms.RandomGrayscale(p=0.10), transforms.RandomApply([transforms.GaussianBlur(5, (0.1, 2))], p=0.10), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip() ]) for step in range(steps): optimizer.zerograd() # Apply augmentations to input image augimage = transform(inputimage) # Compute image embedding for the input image with torch.nograd(): imgemb = clipmodel.encodeimage(augimage) imgemb = F.normalize(imgemb, dim=-1) # Compute text embedding for prompt "An image of a <e>" # Tokenize prompt and inject custom embedding e at the object token position textemb = injectcustomtokenembedding("An image of a <e>", e, clipmodel) textemb = F.normalize(textemb, dim=-1) # Compute loss loss = F.mseloss(imgemb, textemb) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return e def injectcustomtokenembedding(prompt, custome, clipmodel): """ Tokenizes the prompt, replaces the target token's embedding with custome, and passes it through the CLIP text encoder. """ # Standard CLIP tokenization tokens = clipmodel.tokenizer(prompt, returntensors="pt").inputids # Forward pass through text encoder hiddenstates = clipmodel.textmodel(tokens)[0] # Replace the embedding for the custom token (assumed at index 4) with custome hiddenstates[0, 4,:] = custome # Return the modified token embedding return hiddenstates[0, 4,:] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floaters: Without image-specific prompts, disconnected parts of the scene (floaters) appear close to the camera in the majority of reconstructions. Using image-specific prompts greatly alleviates this issue. Janus Problem: Reconstructions may have two or more faces because the loss function tries to make the render of every view look like the input image. Overfitting: Optimizing with a single image leads to severe overfitting if not for the heavy augmentations and the diffusion prior. This variant automates the initialization of the embedding token \langle e \rangle using CLIP and WordNet. It filters the CLIP text tokenizer tokens to keep only nouns (based on the WordNet database) to reconstruct objects rather than styles. It generates caption embeddings for each noun token using the template "An image of a \langle e \rangle". It computes the image embedding for the input image and selects the noun token with the highest similarity between its caption embedding and the input image embedding as the initialization for the textual inversion procedure. Time Complexity: The optimization runs for 3000 steps. Each step involves forward passes through the CLIP image and text encoders. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the CLIP model and the batch of augmented images (batch size 16). Performance: The method uses an image size of 512px and a batch size of 16. Strengths: It generates a specific prompt embedding that conditions the diffusion model to "dream up" plausible novel views of the specific input object, solving the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction. It greatly reduces floaters compared to generic prompts. Limitations: It is not necessary in text-to-image-to-3D settings where images sampled from the 2D diffusion model are already well-aligned with their prompts. It requires careful tuning of augmentations to prevent overfitting. When to use: When reconstructing a 3D model from a single input image and needing to condition a diffusion prior on the specific object content. When not to use: When multiple views are available, or when using a text-to-image-to-3D pipeline where the initial image is already generated from a text prompt. Single-Image Textual Inversion is a variant of Textual Inversion [10] introduced in the RealFusion paper. It was developed to address the limitations of DreamFusion, which relies on generic text prompts and suffers from mode collapse when high guidance is applied. The method was proposed by the authors of RealFusion in 2023. It is used in the RealFusion pipeline to substitute for missing multi-view data. RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00816, fetched 2026-10-30

name: RealFusion
head: RealFusion optimization, RealFusion training procedure, single-image 3D reconstruction via diffusion prior
body:
RealFusion reconstructs a full 360° photographic 3D model of an arbitrary object from a single input image without 3D supervision or object category assumptions. It solves the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction by combining a NeRF photometric reconstruction loss with a Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) prior derived from a pre-trained 2D diffusion model. Unlike DreamFusion, which relies on generic text prompts and suffers from mode collapse under high guidance weights, RealFusion uses single-image textual inversion to generate a specific prompt embedding that conditions the diffusion model to "dream up" plausible novel views of the exact input object. It builds on Single-Image Textual Inversion to substitute for missing multi-view data. Inputs: A single input image I0 of an object. An off-the-shelf image matting model to produce an object mask M for I0. A pre-trained 2D diffusion model \Phi (specifically Stable Diffusion trained on LAION). A base radiance field architecture (InstantNGP). Outputs: A trained neural radiance field (NeRF) representing the 3D geometry and appearance of the object. The radiance field is implemented using InstantNGP. Feature Grids: A set of feature grids \{Gi\}{i=1}^L at multiple resolutions. Resolution: Resolutions are chosen as a geometric progression between the coarsest and finest levels. Configuration: The implementation uses L=16 resolution levels, a feature dimension of 2, and a maximum resolution of 2048. Training State: Feature grids are trained simultaneously, but optimization is restricted to lower-resolution grids during the first half of training (coarse-to-fine). Before 3D optimization, a specific text prompt is engineered to condition the diffusion model. 1. Generate random augmentations g(I0) of the input image I0, where g \in \mathcal{G}. 2. Treat these augmentations as a mini-dataset \mathcal{D}0 = \{g(I0)\}. 3. Introduce a new token hei into the vocabulary of the diffusion model's text encoder. 4. Define the prompt template as "An image of a hei". 5. Optimize the embedding e(I0) corresponding to hei by minimizing the diffusion loss L{diff}(\Phi(\cdot; e(I0))) with respect to e(I0), while freezing all other text embeddings and model parameters. Note: This step substitutes for alternative views by capturing object-specific details in the embedding. The radiance field parameters \sigma (density) and c (color) are optimized using a combined loss function. The training proceeds in a coarse-to-fine manner. Camera Setup: Reconstruction Camera: Fixed at a position looking at the origin on a sphere of radius 1.8, at an angle of 15° above the plane. Novel View Camera: Randomly sampled at each optimization step. Loss Components: 1. Reconstruction Loss (L{rec}): Minimizes L2 error between the input image and the rendered image from the fixed reconstruction camera. 2. Mask Loss (L{rec,mask}): Constrains rendered opacities O at the fixed viewpoint to match the object mask M. L{rec,mask} = ||O - M||^2 where O = R(\cdot; \sigma, c, \pi0) \in \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W} is the rendered opacity from the fixed reference viewpoint \pi0. 3. SDS Prior Loss (L{SDS}): Applied to the randomly sampled novel view to enforce 3D consistency using the diffusion prior. L{SDS}(\sigma, c; \pi, e, t) = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} \left[ w(t) (\Phi(\alphat I + \sigmat \epsilon; t, e) - \epsilon) \cdot 
abla{(\sigma,c)} I ight] where I = R(\cdot; \sigma, c, \pi) is the image rendered from the novel viewpoint \pi, e is the optimized prompt embedding, t is the noise level, \epsilon is the predicted noise, and w(t) is a weighting function. 4. Normal Regularization (L{normals}): Encourages smooth surface normals by comparing rendered normals to a blurred version of themselves. L{normals} = ||N - 	ext{stopgrad}(	ext{blur}(N, k))||^2 where N \in \mathbb{R}^{H 	imes W 	imes 3} are the aggregated normals along the ray, 	ext{blur}(\cdot, k) is a Gaussian blur with kernel size k, and 	ext{stopgrad} stops gradient flow through the blur operation. Total Loss: 
abla{\sigma,c} L = 
abla L{SDS} + \lambda{normals} \cdot 
abla L{normals} + \lambda{image} \cdot 
abla L{image} + \lambda{mask} \cdot 
abla L{mask} where L{image} corresponds to L{rec}. Coarse-to-Fine Schedule: First Half: Optimize only lower-resolution feature grids \{Gi\}{i=1}^{L/2}. Second Half: Optimize all feature grids \{Gi\}{i=1}^L. Shading Strategy: Warmup: Initial period uses albedo-only shading. Main Training: Stochastically applies diffuse and textureless shading throughout optimization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def realfusiontrain(I0, maskmodel, diffusionmodel, instantngpmodel, totalsteps=10000): # 1. Single-Image Textual Inversion # Generate random augmentations of the input image augmentations = [applyrandomaugmentation(I0) for in range(10)] minidataset = augmentations # Initialize new token embedding 'hei' heiembedding = np.random.randn(diffusionmodel.textencoder.dim) # Optimize embedding to match input image via diffusion loss # Freeze diffusion model parameters and other text embeddings lrti = 1e-3 for step in range(1000): lossdiff = 0.0 for imgaug in minidataset: t = np.random.randint(0, diffusionmodel.numtimesteps) eps = np.random.randn(imgaug.shape) noisyimg = diffusionmodel.alphas[t]0.5 imgaug + (1 - diffusionmodel.alphas[t])0.5 eps predeps = diffusionmodel(noisyimg, t, prompttemplate="An image of a <e>", embedding=heiembedding) lossdiff += np.mean((predeps - eps)2) heiembedding -= lrti np.gradient(lossdiff, heiembedding) # Construct prompt prompt = "An image of a hei" # 2. Radiance Field Optimization # Setup cameras reconstructioncamera = {"position": (0, 0, 1.8), "angledeg": 15.0} novelviewcamera = {"position": samplerandomspherepoint(), "angledeg": 15.0} # Hyperparameters lambdanormals = 0.5 lambdaimage = 5.0 lambdamask = 0.5 k = 9 # Gaussian blur kernel size halfsteps = totalsteps // 2 warmupsteps = 1000 for step in range(totalsteps): # Coarse-to-fine grid selection if step < halfsteps: activegrids = instantngpmodel.grids[:len(instantngpmodel.grids)//2] else: activegrids = instantngpmodel.grids # Render from fixed reconstruction camera renderrec = instantngpmodel.render(reconstructioncamera, activegrids) renderedimagerec = renderrec["rgb"] renderedopacityrec = renderrec["opacity"] # Compute Reconstruction Losses # Lrec: L2 error between input image and rendered image lossimage = np.mean((renderedimagerec - I0)2) # Lrec,mask: L2 error between rendered opacity and object mask mask = maskmodel(I0) lossmask = np.mean((renderedopacityrec - mask)2) # Render from random novel view camera rendernovel = instantngpmodel.render(novelviewcamera, activegrids) renderedimagenovel = rendernovel["rgb"] renderednormalsnovel = rendernovel["normals"] # Compute SDS Loss on novel view # Sample noise level t and noise epsilon t = np.random.randint(0, diffusionmodel.numtimesteps) epsilon = np.random.randn(renderedimagenovel.shape) # Add noise to rendered novel view alphat = diffusionmodel.alphas[t]0.5 sigmat = (1 - diffusionmodel.alphas[t])0.5 noisyimage = alphat renderedimagenovel + sigmat epsilon # Get predicted noise from diffusion model predictednoise = diffusionmodel(noisyimage, t, prompt) # Compute SDS gradient estimate # w(t) is a weighting function, typically dependent on t wt = computeweighting(t) gradsds = wt (predictednoise - epsilon) np.gradient(renderedimagenovel, instantngpmodel.params) # Apply gradient to radiance field instantngpmodel.applygradient(gradsds) # Compute Normal Regularization Loss # Blur normals and stop gradient blurrednormals = gaussianblur(renderednormalsnovel, k) stoppedblurrednormals = np.stopgradient(blurrednormals) lossnormals = np.mean((renderednormalsnovel - stoppedblurrednormals)2) # Apply gradient for normal regularization gradnormals = np.gradient(lossnormals, instantngpmodel.params) instantngpmodel.applygradient(lambdanormals gradnormals) # Compute gradients for reconstruction losses gradimage = np.gradient(lossimage, instantngpmodel.params) gradmask = np.gradient(lossmask, instantngpmodel.params) instantngpmodel.applygradient(lambdaimage gradimage + lambdamask gradmask) # Stochastic Shading if step > warmupsteps: applystochasticshading(instantngpmodel) \lambda{image}: 5.0. \lambda{mask}: 0.5. \lambda{normals}: 0.5. k (blur kernel): 9. Diffusion Model: Stable Diffusion trained on LAION. InstantNGP Config: 16 resolution levels, feature dimension 2, max resolution 2048. Camera Radius: 1.8. Camera Angle: 15° above the plane. Over-fitting: Optimizing only with the reconstruction loss on a single image leads to zero loss but no sensible 3D model. Solved by the SDS prior. Limited Diversity (Mode Collapse): High classifier-free guidance weights (e.g., 100) in DreamFusion produce only generic objects. RealFusion solves this by using the specific hei embedding from textual inversion, allowing reconstruction of any specific object. Surface Irregularities: InstantNGP optimization can produce small surface irregularities. Solved by coarse-to-fine training. Noisy Surfaces: Low-level artifacts can appear. Solved by 2D normal vector regularization. Janus Problem: The model may copy the front view to the back of the object. This is a known failure mode. Convergence Failure: The model may produce a semi-transparent scene lacking well-defined geometry. This is a known failure mode. Time Complexity: Training takes hours rather than days, due to the use of InstantNGP. Memory Complexity: Depends on the InstantNGP grid configuration (16 levels, dim 2, max res 2048). Strengths: Reconstructs arbitrary objects from a single image without category assumptions. Produces full 360° photographic models. Significantly higher quality than CLIP priors. 2D normal regularization reduces variance and yields superior results compared to 3D regularization. Limitations: Susceptible to the Janus problem (front-back texture copying). Can fail to converge, resulting in semi-transparent scenes. Requires an off-the-shelf matting model for the mask. When to use: Single-image 3D reconstruction of arbitrary objects in the wild or on benchmark datasets. When not to use: When multi-view images are available (other methods may be more robust) or when strict geometric accuracy without texture artifacts is required (due to Janus/convergence risks). RealFusion was introduced in February 2023. It builds upon the DreamFusion method, which generates 3D models from text descriptions. RealFusion adapts this by conditioning on a single image using textual inversion. It uses Stable Diffusion as the prior and InstantNGP as the radiance field backbone. The method was evaluated on the CO3D dataset against Shelf-Supervised Mesh Prediction. name: Latent Space and Autoencoder Methods
head: Latent Diffusion for NeRF, 3D-Aware Latent Optimization
body: This family of methods integrates pre-trained 2D diffusion models or autoencoders with 3D radiance field representations to solve the ill-posed problem of 3D reconstruction and editing from limited 2D inputs. Unlike sibling methods that apply diffusion guidance directly to pixel space or use iterative denoising for sampling, these methods operate in the compressed latent space of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to enforce geometric consistency and photorealism. The core distinction lies in whether the optimization targets the diffusion noise prediction error (as in the Rendering and Diffusion Prior Pipeline) or jointly trains the autoencoder with the 3D representation to ensure 3D-consistent latent features (as in the 3D-aware Autoencoder). All methods in this family rely on a pre-trained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) associated with a diffusion model (typically Stable Diffusion) to map between image space and a lower-dimensional latent space. The fundamental mechanism involves rendering 2D images from a 3D representation (NeRF or Tri-Planes), encoding these rendered images into latents, and computing a loss that leverages the prior knowledge encoded in the VAE or the diffusion model. Key shared components include: 1. VAE Encoder/Decoder: A fixed or trainable encoder E\phi and decoder D\psi that map images x to latents z and back. 2. 3D Representation: A differentiable renderer (NeRF or Tri-Plane based) that generates 2D views from 3D parameters. 3. Latent Space Loss: A loss function defined in the latent space, such as reconstruction error, noise prediction error, or consistency between encoded inputs and rendered latents. 4. Frozen Diffusion Prior: In guidance-based approaches, the UNet of the diffusion model is kept frozen to provide geometric and photorealistic priors without updating its weights. This method enables single-image 3D reconstruction by optimizing a NeRF using a pre-trained diffusion model as a prior. It differs from the 3D-aware Autoencoder by keeping the autoencoder fixed and computing the loss on the noise prediction error in the latent space using classifier-free guidance, effectively "dreaming up" missing novel views. It is chosen when the goal is to reconstruct a 3D object from a single 2D image and a text prompt, leveraging the generative power of diffusion to fill in occluded geometry. See Rendering and Diffusion Prior Pipeline. This method trains a Variational Autoencoder to produce a latent space that preserves 3D geometric consistency, addressing the issue where standard latent spaces fail to maintain correspondence between 3D-consistent input images. Unlike the Rendering and Diffusion Prior Pipeline, which applies a diffusion prior for photorealism, 3Da-AE regularizes the latent space by jointly training the autoencoder with Tri-Plane scene representations, ensuring latent features encode stable 3D geometry. It is chosen when multi-view input data is available and the goal is to learn a 3D-consistent latent representation for inverse graphics or scene editing. See 3D-aware Autoencoder. This module maps each edited 2D image to a latent edit code vector to characterize diverse edits and control NeRF-to-NeRF translation. It extracts a 64-dimensional latent edit code from an edited 2D image to condition a translated NeRF for novel view synthesis. The process involves inputting an edited 2D image into a fixed, pre-trained VAE encoder from Stable Diffusion to extract features, passing these features through a 3-layer MLP network, and sampling the edit code z \in \mathbb{R}^{64} from the estimated Gaussian distribution of the MLP. During training, the pre-trained encoder is kept fixed, and only the MLP parameters are optimized. This module is integrated into the GenN2N pipeline for text-driven editing, super-resolution, inpainting, and colorization tasks. The integration of latent diffusion models with 3D radiance fields emerged as a solution to the data scarcity and geometric inconsistency problems in single-view and few-view 3D reconstruction. Traditional NeRF optimization often suffers from overfitting to input views or producing geometrically inconsistent novel views. By leveraging the rich priors of pre-trained 2D diffusion models (like Stable Diffusion) in their latent space, methods like LSDS and 3Da-AE were developed to enforce photorealism and 3D consistency respectively. The Latent Distil Module was introduced in the context of NeRF editing (GenN2N) to handle the inconsistency arising from 2D image-to-image translation tools, ensuring that diverse 2D edits map to consistent 3D representations. GenN2N: Generative NeRF2NeRF Translation, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52733.2024.00488, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Rendering and Diffusion Prior Pipeline
head: LSDS Pipeline, Latent Space Diffusion Sampling
body: The Rendering and Diffusion Prior Pipeline (LSDS) optimizes a neural radiance field from a single input image by simultaneously minimizing a reconstruction loss for the input view and a diffusion prior loss for randomly sampled novel viewpoints. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by leveraging a frozen pre-trained diffusion model (Stable Diffusion) in the latent space to "dream up" missing views, enabling high-quality single-image 3D reconstruction without requiring multi-view inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input image I{in} and a text prompt P. Output: Optimized neural radiance field parameters (density and color fields). Data Structures: Radiance Field: A 3D representation (e.g., Tri-Planes or MLP-based) parameterized by weights \theta. Features are stored in grids of dimensionality 2, stacked and fed to a 3-layer MLP with 64 hidden units. Background Model: A two-layer MLP taking viewing direction as input, purposefully weak to prevent trivial optimization via background. VAE Encoder (E\phi): Maps 512px images to latent space. Diffusion UNet: Frozen pre-trained model for noise prediction. Steps: 1. Textual Inversion: Generate a custom embedding token \langle e \rangle from the input image using single-image textual inversion. 2. Rendering: Render a view from the current radiance field at 96px resolution. 3. Upsampling: Upsample the rendered image to 512px to match the Stable Diffusion input requirements. 4. Latent Encoding: Pass the upsampled image through the VAE encoder E\phi to obtain the latent representation z. 5. Noise Addition: Sample a timestep t \sim U(0.02, 0.98) and add noise to the latent z. 6. Diffusion Loss Calculation: Compute the noise prediction error using the frozen UNet conditioned on the prompt P with the custom token \langle e \rangle and classifier-free guidance. 7. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the gradient through the VAE encoder E\phi and the radiance field parameters \theta. Do not backpropagate through the Stable Diffusion UNet. 8. Optimization: Update \theta using the Adam optimizer. Formulas: The total loss L is a combination of the reconstruction objective L{rec} and the diffusion prior objective L{diff}: L = L{rec} + \lambda L{diff} Where L{diff} is derived from the noise prediction error of the diffusion model. Parameters: Render Resolution: 96px. Upsampled Resolution: 512px. Classifier-Free Guidance Strength: 100. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 1e-3. Iterations: 5000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Guidance Strength Sensitivity: Classifier-free guidance strength below 30 leads to geometric deformities; strengths above 30 produce good results. Precision: The VAE encoder gradients are used for optimization, not the UNet. An objective that uses a large pre-trained diffusion model to ensure the radiance field looks like the given object from randomly sampled novel viewpoints. It is chosen when single-image reconstruction requires strong geometric priors to fill in missing views. The process involves rendering novel views, passing them through the diffusion model to compute the prior objective, and optimizing the radiance field to minimize both the reconstruction objective (for the input view) and the prior objective (for novel views) simultaneously. Time Complexity: Approximately 45 minutes on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU for 5000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables high-quality 3D reconstruction from a single image by leveraging powerful 2D diffusion priors. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of classifier-free guidance strength to avoid geometric deformities. When to use: Single-image 3D reconstruction where multi-view data is unavailable. When not to use: When multi-view inputs are available, as other methods may be more efficient or accurate. Originated in the paper "RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image". The method addresses the limitation of existing NeRF-like models that assume dozens or hundreds of views are available, extending them to single-image reconstruction by using a diffusion model to "dream up" missing views. It builds on techniques like textual inversion and latent space diffusion sampling. RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00816, fetched 2026-10-30
