name: Training Schedule
head: DCCVT Training Configuration, NeuS2 Training Details
body: Training schedules define the temporal progression of hyperparameters, loss functions, and structural updates during the optimization of differentiable volume rendering models. They solve the problem of unstable convergence, local minima, and slow training times inherent in high-dimensional radiance field optimization by decoupling coarse geometry learning from fine detail refinement. Unlike Learning Rate Scheduling, which focuses solely on step-size adaptation, this method encompasses the activation/deactivation of specific loss terms, structural densification/pruning cycles, and resolution scaling. The method comprises several distinct scheduling strategies applied to different aspects of the training loop. Implementers must select the appropriate schedule based on the scene type (static/dynamic) and representation (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting, etc.). For static scenes, the training is divided into a single continuous phase with specific iteration counts. 1. Initialization: Initialize point sizes with the average distance to the four nearest neighbors. 2. Optimization: Optimize point position, size, and features, camera model and poses, neural network weights, and tone mapper parameters. 3. Iteration Count: Train for 15,000 iterations. 4. Hardware: Typically executed on NVIDIA A100 GPU. Dynamic scenes use a multi-stage approach to handle temporal coherence and deformation. 1. First Frame Training: Train the first frame from scratch for 2,000 iterations (4,000 iterations for complex geometries like the Lego sequence). Optimize global transformation independently for the first 100 iterations. Fine-tune network parameters and global deformation together for the remaining iterations. 2. Subsequent Frame Training: Train each subsequent frame for 1,100 iterations. Optimize global transformation independently for the first 100 iterations. Fine-tune network parameters and global deformation together for the remaining iterations. This schedule manages the lifecycle of surfels (surface splats) through three distinct phases. 1. Warm-up Phase: Duration: 20 epochs. Losses: Activate only photometric and silhouette losses. Resolution: Train with half image resolutions. Purpose: Allow the surfel set to deform toward observed images under initial sparse coverage. 2. Densification Phase: Duration: Until 14–25% of the training process. Actions: Enable adaptive density control (splitting/pruning). Losses: Disable silhouette loss; activate geometric regularizers (L{cons}, L{nc}). Densification Frequency: Perform densification every 4 epochs. Optional Pruning: If ground-truth masks are available, periodically remove floater surfels that consistently project outside the foreground mask across a majority of training views. Random Zoom: Randomly zoom in and out each epoch to train all convolution weights (not shared) to contribute to the final result. 3. Refinement Phase: Actions: Freeze densification. Losses: Fine-tune with all remaining losses until convergence. Pruning: Structure-aware importance score pruning is applied at 42–50% of the training process. Final Pruning: Prune voxels/surfels once after the coarse stage and once after the fine stage. For BigBrain cerebellar chunks, prune three times: twice during densification at epochs 200 and 300 (ratio 0.8), and once after densification at epoch 800 (ratio 0.85). This schedule manages the transition from implicit MLP to explicit grid representations. 1. Coarse Stage: Duration: 1,000 epochs. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Voxel Grid Resolution: 256^3 for NeRF-synthetic, 320^3 for Tanks and Temples. Batch Size: 16,384 for NeRF-synthetic, 8,192 for Tanks and Temples. Sparsity Regularization: \lambdas = 1 \times 10^{-5}. Alpha Threshold for Pruning: \tau\alpha = 0.01. 2. Fine Stage: Duration: 1,000 epochs. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Rendering Threshold: \taut = 0.01. Pruning: Prune voxels after the coarse stage and after the fine stage. Used in photon field networks to improve convergence time by gradually increasing the KNN query radius. 1. Definition: Use a sequence of increasing KNN query radii ri approaching a target radius r. 2. Step: During training, determine the current step's sampling radius from the sequence. Query KNN with this radius. If radius is small, k < K samples are returned; as radius increases, k approaches K. 3. Loss: Relative Mean Square Error (rMSE) applied to each set of outputs individually. 4. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99, no L2 regularization. Learning Rate: 9 \times 10^{-4} with exponential decay of 0.92 starting at 70% of total steps, triggering every subsequent 25 steps. Duration: 2,000 to 3,000 steps. 5. Example Schedule (1M Photons): Steps 0–36%: Radius 25 Steps 37–63%: Radius 50 Steps 64–90%: Radius 50 Steps 91–100%: Radius 0 (target) Used to suppress floaters (unstable Gaussians) and improve temporal coherence in dynamic Gaussian Splatting. 1. Step: During sensitivity estimation, perturb the input timestamp t to the deformation field \mathcal{D} by adding noise. 2. Formula: (\mu + \Delta\mu, r + \Delta r, s + \Delta s) = \mathcal{D}(\mu, r, s, t + \mathcal{N}(0,1)\beta\Delta t(1 - i/\tau)) Where: \mathcal{D} is the deformation network. t is the current timestep. \mathcal{N}(0,1) is standard normal noise. \beta is a noise scaling factor. \Delta t is the timestep interval. i is the current training iteration. \tau is the total number of training iterations. 3. Pitfall: Floaters are unstable Gaussians that appear static in observed views but drift at unseen timestamps; TSS addresses this by revealing them early in training via timestamp jittering. Used in NeRF variants to manage the update frequency of proposal networks. 1. Definition: Clip the update frequency of proposal networks based on the training step. 2. Step: Interpolate the update frequency linearly from 0 to proposalupdateevery over the range [0, proposalwarmup]. 3. Formula: python updatefreq = clip(interpolate(step, [0, warmup], [0, maxfreq]), 1, maxfreq) Where: step is the current training step. warmup is proposalwarmup. maxfreq is proposalupdateevery. 4. Parameters: proposalwarmup: Number of initial steps during which proposal networks are not updated. proposalupdateevery: Maximum frequency (in steps) at which proposal networks are updated. Used to stabilize optimization by controlling the kernel parameter of the Gaussian kernel applied to the 3D radiance field. 1. Step: Exponentially reduce the kernel parameter \sigma to 0 over 10,000 iterations. 2. Effect: Stabilizes camera alignment and restricts the spectrum of the learned 3D scene. Used in LiTe-GS to dynamically select training views. 1. Static Scene (General): Initialize training with 3 images. Add K images at each acquisition step until reaching 15 total images. Each stage uses 300 training iterations. Total iterations: 15,000. 2. MipNeRF 360 (Garden) Variant: Initialize with 2 images. Add 3 images per step until 11 total. Each stage uses 300 training iterations. Total iterations: 78,000. Used for text-driven neural texture synthesis. 1. Data: Render 162 multi-view images using icosphere sampling. 2. Parameters: Learning rate for additional shading attributes and cpal: 0.01. Learning rate for texture attribute: 0.025. Learning rate for other attributes: Same as 2DGS. Optimizer: Adam. Multi-view image resolution for text-driven NPSE: 512x512. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX4090 GPU. Used for meta-learning signed distance functions. 1. Evaluation: Each model reconstructs each mesh twice because context points are randomly sampled; the better reconstruction is selected for computing chamfer distance. 2. Parameters: Composite loss function uses a learning rate decayed by a factor of 0.5 after 350 steps. Zero-level set MetaSDF and all other models use L1 loss for 2,000 epochs, with learning rate decayed by a factor of 0.5 every 500 steps. Batch size: 64 scenes. 3. Complexity: O(nm), where n is the number of query points and m is the number of inner gradient descent steps. 4. Performance: DeepSDF and PointNet Encoders train to 2,000 epochs in approximately 4 days on dual NVIDIA RTX 8000 GPUs; MetaSDF trains to 2,000 epochs in approximately 6 days on dual NVIDIA RTX 8000 GPUs. Standardized benchmark protocol for testing differentiable rendering optimization. 1. Scenes: Collect 8 scenes (Kitty, Buddha, Cube, Ginger, Box, Teapot, Stone, Joint) with varying parameters (translation, rotation, vertex position, camera pose, material, environment light, textures). 2. Initialization: For Kitty, Buddha, Cube, Box, Teapot: generate 10 random initial parameter groups. For Ginger, Stone, Joint: manually provide 1 initial group to avoid self-intersection or meaningless configurations. 3. Parameters: Rendering resolution: 128×128 for evaluation, 256×256 for furniture/face applications, 128×128 for pose fitting. Optimization iterations: 1,000 per run. 4. Metrics: 3D metric: MAE (Mean Absolute Error) between vertices of optimized and target meshes. 2D metrics: PSNR, SSIM, RMSE, and perceptual score LPIPS. Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization is a training schedule strategy that iteratively optimizes the scene representation by activating SH bands sequentially from a designated start band up to a target maximum band. It addresses the problem of optimizing high-frequency appearance details in radiance fields by decoupling the optimization of different frequency components, allowing the model to converge on coarse geometry and color before refining fine details. Unlike Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization, which adjusts the spatial resolution or density of the scene representation, this method specifically targets the frequency domain of the radiance field's color representation. Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization is a training protocol that initializes a high-resolution neural radiance field (or deformable voxel grid) using the optimized parameters from a lower-resolution counterpart. It solves the problem of unstable convergence and local minima in complex, high-dimensional loss landscapes by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency details. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. The NeuTex Training Schedule is a multi-stage optimization procedure for training the NeuTex neural texture mapping model. It solves the instability issues inherent in jointly optimizing geometry, texture, and mapping networks by decoupling the initialization of the UV-mapping components from the final high-fidelity texture synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF training loops by explicitly prioritizing geometric consistency via Chamfer loss and cycle consistency before transitioning to full volumetric rendering optimization, and by employing a final stage that freezes geometry and mapping networks to refine texture details. Time Complexity: Varies by method. Staggered KNN provides approximately 2–3× improvement in training speed compared to naïve training using the target radius directly. MetaSDF training takes approximately 6 days on dual NVIDIA RTX 8000 GPUs for 2,000 epochs. Memory Complexity: NeRFLight peak memory usage is approximately 40 GB on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Scaling: Total epochs for ESVR are scaled with volume size: 2,800 for small-medium, 1,600 for large, 800 for extremely large volumes. Strengths: Decoupling coarse and fine optimization stabilizes convergence. Staggered KNN reduces training time by avoiding expensive large-radius queries in early stages. TSS suppresses floaters and improves temporal coherence. Limitations: VGG-loss is slow to evaluate, increasing training times compared to MSE loss. Randomly initialized parameters may lead to meaningless configurations (e.g., self-intersection) in some scenes. When to Use: Use static schedules for non-deforming scenes. Use dynamic schedules for temporal data. Use staggered KNN for photon mapping training. Use TSS for dynamic Gaussian Splatting to reduce floaters. name: Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization
head: Band-by-band optimization, SH Band Strategy
body: Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization is a training schedule strategy that iteratively optimizes the scene representation by activating SH bands sequentially from a designated start band up to a target maximum band. It addresses the problem of optimizing high-frequency appearance details in radiance fields by decoupling the optimization of different frequency components, allowing the model to converge on coarse geometry and color before refining fine details. Unlike Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization, which adjusts the spatial resolution or density of the scene representation, this method specifically targets the frequency domain of the radiance field's color representation. The method implements a nested loop structure: an outer loop iterates through SH bands, and an inner loop performs standard training epochs and batches for the currently active band. Inputs: configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand: The maximum SH band index to optimize up to (integer). configs->hierarchyBandStrategy: Boolean flag determining if bands are optimized hierarchically or all at once. configs->SHsForTargetResoOnly: Boolean flag; if true and not at minimum hierarchy, resets startBand to 0. configs->initialFromFile: Boolean flag; if true and optimizingBand == availableSHBand+1, density is not re-initialized. configs->learningRate (rawLR): Base learning rate for general parameters. configs->shLearningRate (rawSHLR): Learning rate for SH coefficients. configs->batchSize: Number of rays per batch. configs->epochs: Number of epochs per band. configs->varianceLossInterval: Interval for applying variance loss. configs->varianceCoefficient, configs->shCoefficient: Weights for regularization losses. configs->vairanceType, configs->neighboorNums: Parameters for variance loss calculation. configs->maskLossCoefficient, configs->huberDelta: Parameters for RGB loss calculation. configs->saveIntervals: Frequency for saving model checkpoints. configs->justModel: Boolean; if false, saves results periodically. configs->solidStrategy: Boolean flag controlling sample offset application. this->ray.totalRays: Total number of rays in the dataset. this->scene: The scene representation object containing SH coefficients and density. this->sceneOptimizer: The optimizer object handling parameter updates. RenderUtils: Utility functions for rendering and loss calculation. Outputs: Updated scene representation with optimized SH coefficients for all bands up to configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand. Loss metrics per epoch stored in lossesPerEpochs. Scene Object (this->scene): optimizingBand: Integer field indicating the current SH band being optimized. sparse: Boolean flag indicating if the scene uses sparse storage. grayImage: Boolean flag indicating if the scene is grayscale. stepSize: Float value used for sample offset calculation. Losses Array (lossesPerEpochs): Array of size numbands epochs 4. Indices epoch4+0 to epoch4+3 store: minLoss, maxLoss, averageloss, gpuelapsedtime. 1. Determine Start Band: If hierarchyBandStrategy is false, set startBand = configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand. If SHsForTargetResoOnly is true and currentHierarchy is not minimumHierarchy, set startBand = 0. 2. Iterate Bands: Loop optimizingBand from startBand to configs->sphericalHarmonicsBand. 3. Set Current Band: Set this->scene->optimizingBand = optimizingBand. 4. Initialize Band Parameters: If hierarchyBandStrategy is true, or if (hierarchyBandStrategy is false AND SHsForTargetResoOnly is true AND currentHierarchy is not minimumHierarchy): determine densityInitialized as false if initialFromFile is true AND optimizingBand == availableSHBand+1, otherwise true; call this->sceneOptimizer.initialBand(optimizingBand, densityInitialized). Else, call this->sceneOptimizer.initialAll(). 5. Reset Learning Rates: Set configs->learningRate = rawLR and configs->shLearningRate = rawSHLR. 6. Iterate Epochs: Loop epoch from 0 to configs->epochs. 7. Calculate Batch Count: Compute batchCount = (this->ray.totalRays + configs->batchSize - 1) / configs->batchSize. 8. Iterate Batches: Loop batchIndex from 0 to batchCount. 9. Calculate Batch Indices: Compute startSampleIndex = batchIndex configs->batchSize. Compute actualBatchSize as configs->batchSize if startSampleIndex + configs->batchSize < this->ray.totalRays, else this->ray.totalRays - startSampleIndex. 10. Set Sample Offset: If !configs->solidStrategy, call this->scene->setSelfSampleOffset(this->scene->stepSize/2.). 11. Render Rays: Call RenderUtils::renderRays with ray, scene, sampleRaysIndexGPU, startSampleIndex, and actualBatchSize. 12. Compute Losses: If renderRes.grayImage is false, call RenderUtils::renderRayswithGradientsRGB with sceneOptimizer, ray, scene, lossesDevice, sampleRaysIndexGPU, startSampleIndex, actualBatchSize, configs->maskLossCoefficient, and configs->huberDelta. Copy losses from device to host using cudaMemcpy(lossesHost, lossesDevice, sizeof(double) actualBatchSize, cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost). Calculate loss = getMSEError(lossesHost, actualBatchSize). If isnan(loss), print error, free memory, and return. Update maxLoss and minLoss: if loss > maxLoss, set maxLoss = loss; if minLoss > loss, set minLoss = loss. Accumulate losses += loss. 13. Apply Regularization: If !scene->sparse or batchIndex % configs->varianceLossInterval == 0, call RenderUtils::addVarianceLoss with scene, sceneOptimizer, configs->varianceCoefficient, configs->shCoefficient, configs->vairanceType, and configs->neighboorNums. 14. Update RGB Scene: If scene->grayImage is false, call Optimizer::updateRGBScene with sceneOptimizer, scene, and timeStep. 15. Decay Learning Rates: Update configs->learningRate /= pow(2, 1. / batchCount / (epoch + 1.)) and configs->shLearningRate /= pow(2, 1. / batchCount / (epoch + 1.)). 16. Store Epoch Metrics: After the epoch loop, store minLoss, maxLoss, averageloss (losses/batchCount), and GPU elapsed time in lossesPerEpochs at indices epoch4+0 to epoch4+3. 17. Save Model: If !configs->justModel and (epoch + 1) % configs->saveIntervals == 0, save experiment results with directory name "Band%d". Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalshoptimization(configs, scene, sceneoptimizer, raydata, renderutils, optimizerutils): """Implements Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization.""" totalrays = raydata.totalrays maxband = configs.sphericalharmonicsband hierarchystrategy = configs.hierarchybandstrategy shsfortargetonly = configs.shsfortargetresoonly currenthierarchy = raydata.currenthierarchy minimumhierarchy = raydata.minimumhierarchy initialfromfile = configs.initialfromfile rawlr = configs.learningrate rawshlr = configs.shlearningrate batchsize = configs.batchsize numepochs = configs.epochs varianceinterval = configs.variancelossinterval variancecoeff = configs.variancecoefficient shcoeff = configs.shcoefficient variancetype = configs.variancetype neighbornums = configs.neighboornums maskcoeff = configs.masklosscoefficient huberdelta = configs.huberdelta saveinterval = configs.saveintervals justmodel = configs.justmodel solidstrategy = configs.solidstrategy grayimage = scene.grayimage # Helper definitions def getmseerror(losses, n): return sum(losses) / n def cudamemcpydevicetohost(devicedata, n): return devicedata[:n] def getgpuelapsedtime(): return 0.0 def saveexperimentresults(directoryname): pass def freememory(): pass # 1. Determine Start Band if not hierarchystrategy: startband = maxband if shsfortargetonly and currenthierarchy != minimumhierarchy: startband = 0 lossesperepochs = [] for optimizingband in range(startband, maxband + 1): # 3. Set Current Band scene.optimizingband = optimizingband # 4. Initialize Band Parameters cond1 = hierarchystrategy cond2 = (not hierarchystrategy) and shsfortargetonly and (currenthierarchy != minimumhierarchy) if cond1 or cond2: densityinitialized = not (initialfromfile and optimizingband == scene.availableshband + 1) sceneoptimizer.initialband(optimizingband, densityinitialized) else: sceneoptimizer.initialall() # 5. Reset Learning Rates configs.learningrate = rawlr configs.shlearningrate = rawshlr epochtotalloss = 0.0 minloss = float('inf') maxloss = float('-inf') # 6. Iterate Epochs for epoch in range(numepochs): # 7. Calculate Batch Count batchcount = (totalrays + batchsize - 1) // batchsize # 8. Iterate Batches for batchindex in range(batchcount): # 9. Calculate Batch Indices startsampleindex = batchindex batchsize actualbatchsize = min(batchsize, totalrays - startsampleindex) # 10. Set Sample Offset if not solidstrategy: scene.setselfsampleoffset(scene.stepsize / 2.0) # 11. Render Rays renderutils.renderrays( ray=raydata.rays, scene=scene, sampleraysindexgpu=raydata.sampleraysindexgpu, startsampleindex=startsampleindex, actualbatchsize=actualbatchsize) # 12. Compute Losses if not grayimage: renderutils.renderrayswithgradientsrgb( sceneoptimizer=sceneoptimizer, ray=raydata.rays, scene=scene, lossesdevice=raydata.lossesdevice, sampleraysindexgpu=raydata.sampleraysindexgpu, startsampleindex=startsampleindex, actualbatchsize=actualbatchsize, masklosscoefficient=maskcoeff, huberdelta=huberdelta) losseshost = cudamemcpydevicetohost(raydata.lossesdevice, actualbatchsize) loss = getmseerror(losseshost, actualbatchsize) if loss != loss: # NaN check print("Error: Loss is NaN") freememory() return if loss > maxloss: maxloss = loss if loss < minloss: minloss = loss epochtotalloss += loss # 13. Apply Regularization if not scene.sparse or (batchindex % varianceinterval == 0): renderutils.addvarianceloss( scene=scene, sceneoptimizer=sceneoptimizer, variancecoefficient=variancecoeff, shcoefficient=shcoeff, variancetype=variancetype, neighbornums=neighbornums) # 14. Update RGB Scene if not grayimage: optimizerutils.updatergbscene( sceneoptimizer=sceneoptimizer, scene=scene, timestep=epoch) # 15. Decay Learning Rates decayfactor = 2 (1.0 / batchcount / (epoch + 1.0)) configs.learningrate /= decayfactor configs.shlearningrate /= decayfactor # 16. Store Epoch Metrics avgloss = epochtotalloss / batchcount gpuelapsedtime = getgpuelapsedtime() lossesperepochs.append([minloss, maxloss, avgloss, gpuelapsedtime]) # 17. Save Model if not justmodel and (epoch + 1) % saveinterval == 0: saveexperimentresults(f"Band{optimizingband}") return lossesperepochs A curriculum training strategy that progressively increases the number of SH basis functions to prevent overfitting in sparse-view settings, starting with only isotropic (degree 0) components. It uses a mask \alpha\ell^m(t, T) to enable SH coefficients based on the current iteration t and a hyperparameter T. The mask is defined as \alpha\ell^m(t, T) = 1 if \ell=0 or \ell \leq \sqrt{t/T}(\ell{\max} + 1) - 1, and 0 otherwise. Unlike previous methods that constrain geometry and appearance, this method relies on depth-guided voxel pre-pruning for implicit geometry constraints, using SH regularization for secondary geometric refinement and artifact compensation. It is chosen when sparse views are available to mitigate high-frequency overfitting. A technique to reduce optimization cost by only updating non-DC spherical harmonic coefficients every T{\text{lazy}} iterations. If enabled, optimization steps for non-DC SH coefficients are performed only when the current iteration index is a multiple of T{\text{lazy}}. The default value for T{\text{lazy}} in Taming 3DGS is 12, but it is disabled by default in the referenced work. It is chosen when computational efficiency is prioritized and the visual impact of delayed non-DC updates is acceptable. Time Complexity: The method adds an outer loop over SH bands. If bands are optimized sequentially, the total training time is the sum of the time taken for each band. If optimized all at once (startBand = maxBand), it behaves like standard optimization but with specific initialization. The learning rate decay is per-batch, which can slow down convergence if not tuned correctly. Memory Complexity: No significant additional memory overhead compared to standard radiance field optimization, as it reuses the same scene representation and optimizer structures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the number of SH bands. Higher maximum bands increase the number of parameters and the complexity of the optimization landscape. Strengths: Allows for stable convergence of high-frequency details by optimizing lower frequencies first. Prevents overfitting in sparse settings when combined with SH Regularization. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rates and initialization strategies. May increase training time if many bands are optimized sequentially. When to use: When optimizing radiance fields with Spherical Harmonics, especially in scenarios where high-frequency details are important and stability is a concern. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and sequential band optimization is too slow. Hierarchical Spherical Harmonics Optimization is described in the context of Plenoxels and related radiance field methods. It is used to manage the optimization of Spherical Harmonics coefficients in different frequency bands. The method is implemented in the Clear-plenoxels repository. nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) F2Plenoxels: fast voxel radiance fields without neural networks for few-shot view synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1007/s44443-026-00491-2, fetched 2026-10-26 GRay: Ray Tracing 3D Gaussians Near the Speed of Splats, https://doi.org/10.1145/3804496, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization
head: Coarse-to-Fine Initialization, Progressive Scale Training
body: Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization is a training protocol that initializes a high-resolution neural radiance field (or deformable voxel grid) using the optimized parameters from a lower-resolution counterpart. It solves the problem of unstable convergence and local minima in complex, high-dimensional loss landscapes by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency details. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Inputs: 1. A trained coarse model consisting of: A deformation feature grid (voxel grid) optimized at resolution R{coarse}. A deformation MLP with weights W{deform}^{coarse}. 2. Target fine model architecture: A deformation feature grid at resolution R{fine} (where R{fine} > R{coarse}). A deformation MLP with identical architecture to the coarse model. Outputs: 1. Initialized fine model parameters ready for high-resolution optimization. Data Structures: Deformation Feature Grid: A 3D tensor of shape (D, H, W, C), where D, H, W are spatial dimensions and C is the feature dimension. Values are typically stored as 32-bit floats. Deformation MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron. For example, 4 fully connected layers with width 64, ReLU activations, input dimension 33 (3 pos + 1 time + 44 feat), output dimension 44. Steps: 1. Grid Interpolation: Initialize the fine model's deformation feature grid by interpolating the optimized coarse model's feature grid. If R{fine} = 2 \times R{coarse}, use trilinear interpolation or nearest-neighbor upscaling to map coarse grid values to the finer grid. This preserves the learned global structure at higher spatial fidelity. 2. Weight Transfer: Copy the trained weights W{deform}^{coarse} from the coarse deformation MLP to the fine deformation MLP. This is valid because the MLP architecture (layer count, width, activation functions) remains identical between coarse and fine models. 3. Progressive Scale Training (Optional/Variant): Instead of a single jump, apply progressive scale training. Start optimization at R{coarse}. After a fixed number of iterations, double the voxel resolution (R{next} = 2 \times R{current}). Re-initialize the new grid levels using interpolation from the previous resolution. Continue optimization at the new resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializefinemodel(coarsemodel, targetresolution): """ Initializes a fine-resolution model using a trained coarse model. Args: coarsemodel: Object containing: coarsegrid: 3D tensor (D, H, W, C) coarsemlpweights: List of numpy arrays for MLP layers targetresolution: Tuple (Dfine, Hfine, Wfine) Returns: finemodel: Initialized model structure """ # Step 1: Interpolate Feature Grid # Assuming trilinear interpolation for upscaling finegrid = interpolate3d(coarsemodel.coarsegrid, targetresolution) # Step 2: Transfer MLP Weights # Architecture is identical, so direct copy is valid finemlpweights = [w.copy() for w in coarsemodel.coarsemlpweights] # Step 3: Construct Fine Model finemodel = { 'grid': finegrid, 'mlpweights': finemlpweights, 'resolution': targetresolution } return finemodel def progressivescaletraining(model, maxresolution, stepiterations=10000): """ Doubles voxel resolution every stepiterations. """ currentres = model.resolution while currentres < maxresolution: # Double resolution newres = tuple(2 d for d in currentres) # Re-initialize grid via interpolation model.grid = interpolate3d(model.grid, newres) model.resolution = newres # Continue optimization for stepiterations optimize(model, iterations=stepiterations) currentres = newres Parameters: Interpolation Method: Trilinear or nearest-neighbor. Not given in the sources. Step Iterations: Number of iterations before doubling resolution. Not given in the sources. MLP Width: 64 for deformation module, 128 for color module. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Mismatch: If the fine resolution is not a power-of-two multiple of the coarse resolution, interpolation artifacts may occur. Not given in the sources. Feature Dimension Mismatch: The feature dimension C must remain constant between coarse and fine models for direct weight transfer to the MLP. If C changes, the MLP weights cannot be directly transferred. Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training is a strategy that gradually introduces finer levels of detail during optimization to ensure stable convergence and prevent overfitting. It solves the problem of complex loss landscapes and sparse initialization errors that occur when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. The NeRF Restarting Approach is an optimization protocol for jointly refining camera poses and neural radiance fields (NeRFs) from sparse, noisy initial poses. It solves the problem of artifacts persisting in the scene representation due to the coupling of pose and geometry optimization. Unlike Staged Training, which freezes poses after initial convergence but retains the learned network weights, this method re-initializes the network from scratch after pose convergence, thereby removing artifacts learned during the pose optimization phase. This pipeline defines the end-to-end training procedure for unconstrained neural radiance fields, specifically integrating pose estimation, transient artifact handling, and hierarchical sampling. It solves the problem of training NeRFs on unposed, internet-scale image collections where initial camera poses are unknown and images contain transient objects (e.g., people, vehicles). It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by jointly optimizing camera poses and scene representation using a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy, while explicitly decoupling transient artifacts via a dedicated transient network and depth-supervised scheduling. LiDAR Initialization is an initialization technique using LiDAR point clouds to provide prior information for the scene representation, helping to avoid local minima in optimization. On Argoverse2, the combination of Hybrid Scene Representation (HSR) and LiDAR Initialization (LI) yields more than 4 times boost in convergence speed compared with NGP. Without LI, the model cannot converge to NGP's PSNR, and training time is infinite ('Inf.') because it struggles to represent space sparsely. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The coarse-to-fine approach requires storing both the coarse and fine models during the transition phase if progressive training is used. The fine model's memory usage scales with R{fine}^3. Time: Initialization is fast (interpolation). However, the total training time is reduced compared to training from scratch at high resolution because the optimizer starts closer to the global optimum. Measured Performance: In, the combination of HSR and LI achieved a >4x speedup in convergence compared to NGP. Rendering speed was 10x faster due to reduced sample points per ray. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster convergence, better final PSNR, avoids local minima. Limitations: Requires a valid coarse model first. If the coarse model is poor, the fine model may inherit bad priors. When to Use: When training high-resolution NeRFs or voxel grids. When initial poses are noisy or unknown (combined with restarting). When LiDAR data is available for initialization. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and even the coarse model cannot be trained. When the scene is static and low-resolution is sufficient. Coarse-to-Fine Model Initialization originates from the need to stabilize the training of high-dimensional neural radiance fields. It was notably applied in Neural Deformable Voxel Grid for Fast Optimization of Dynamic View Synthesis and Lightning NeRF for Efficient Hybrid Scene Representation for Autonomous Driving. The method leverages the observation that global geometry converges faster than high-frequency details, allowing a hierarchical optimization strategy. name: Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training Strategy
head: Coarse-to-Fine Training
body: Progressive Coarse-to-Fine Training is a strategy that gradually introduces finer levels of detail during optimization to ensure stable convergence and prevent overfitting. It solves the problem of complex loss landscapes and sparse initialization errors that occur when training directly at high resolution by establishing a coherent global structure before fitting high-frequency features. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images (potentially with associated camera poses), a target scene geometry representation (octree or voxel grid), and hyperparameters controlling the progression schedule (initlevel, maxlevel, coarseintervals, progressive). Outputs: A trained radiance field model with optimized parameters for color, density, and geometry. Data Structures: Octree/Level Structure: A hierarchical representation where each level l corresponds to a specific spatial resolution. The base level is determined by scene dimensions, and higher levels provide finer granularity. Progressive Schedule: A set of coarseintervals that specify the training iteration at which each new octree level is introduced. Parameters: initlevel: The starting octree level for training. Typically set to the middle of the available range. progressive: A boolean flag to enable or disable progressive training. maxlevel: The highest octree level to be used in the final model. m: Interval frequency for sampling new training pixels; new pixels are added every m iterations. N: Total number of fine-stage optimization iterations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the octree structure based on scene dimensions and point cloud data. Determine the initlevel (typically the middle of the range). Calculate coarseintervals using a geometric progression of training steps to determine when to introduce each new level. Set the current maximum level currentmaxlevel to initlevel. Initialize the model parameters at initlevel. 2. Coarse Stage (Global Geometry): Train the model using only levels up to currentmaxlevel. In dynamic scene implementations, set color features to be the color itself, ignoring ray direction dependency, to simplify the initial optimization. Compute a smaller bounding box using proxy geometry learned during this stage to filter empty space. If incremental mapping is used, insert new observations into the training set every 50 iterations during the coarse stage. 3. Progressive Refinement: Iterate through training steps. At each step, check if the current iteration matches a value in coarseintervals. If a new level is due, increment currentmaxlevel by 1. Continue training with the extended set of levels (from initlevel to currentmaxlevel). This creates a continuous transition rather than a sudden switch between different LOD levels. 4. Fine Stage (High-Frequency Details): Once currentmaxlevel reaches maxlevel, the model includes all levels. Switch to high-dimensional features and model ray direction dependency explicitly (e.g., using a specific network branch F{\theta4}). Perform 20,000 refinement iterations to optimize the model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivecoarsefinetraining(scenepoints, scenedims, hyperparams): # 1. Initialization octree = [] for level in range(hyperparams.maxlevel + 1): voxelsize = scenedims / (2 level) octree.append(creategrid(voxelsize)) initlevel = hyperparams.initlevel maxlevel = hyperparams.maxlevel coarseintervals = [] stepsperlevel = hyperparams.totaliterations // (maxlevel - initlevel + 1) for i in range(initlevel, maxlevel + 1): coarseintervals.append(i stepsperlevel) currentmaxlevel = initlevel modelparams = initializeparameters(octree, currentmaxlevel) # 2. Training Loop for iteration in range(hyperparams.totaliterations): # Check if we need to increase resolution if iteration in coarseintervals and currentmaxlevel < maxlevel: currentmaxlevel += 1 # Sample rays based on current level constraints rays = sampleraysuniform(scenepoints, currentmaxlevel) # Forward pass and loss computation predictions = forwardpass(modelparams, rays) loss = computemseloss(predictions, rays.targets) # Backward pass and update modelparams = optimizerstep(modelparams, loss) # Incremental observation insertion (if applicable) if hyperparams.incremental and iteration % 50 == 0: scenepoints = addnewobservations(scenepoints) return modelparams Progressive training is a method that gradually increases the resolution of the rendered output during optimization to stabilize convergence and prevent geometric artifacts. It solves the problem of complex loss landscapes and sparse initialization errors that occur when training directly at high resolution. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. A method targeting issues caused by low-resolution diffusion images using a two-stage coarse-fine approach. Coarse stage: Instant-NGP is used as the NeRF model trained from images generated from text prompts using the image diffusion model eDiff-I. Fine stage: The coarse geometry extracted from Instant-NGP is placed on a mesh, which is optimized over in the fine stage using images generated with a latent diffusion model. Experiments over 397 prompts generated objects, each rated by three users, showed a preference toward Magic3D over DreamFusion. A variant where new observations are inserted into the training set incrementally during the coarse stage. Steps: Sample 8,192 rays from the input images to train the coarse models; train coarse models for 5,000 iterations; perform refinement for 20,000 iterations; insert new observations into the training set every 50 iterations during the coarse stage. Parameters: Ray sample count per optimization step: 8,192; Coarse training iterations: 5,000; Refinement iterations: 20,000; Observation insertion interval: every 50 iterations; Optimizer: Adam; Initial learning rate: 10^{-1}. A coarse-to-fine training procedure that smooths input images with a Gaussian kernel during NeRF training to improve pose estimation robustness. Steps: Smooth input images while training NeRFs using a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation \sigma = 4 \times (1 - \gammai). Apply a linear schedule to increase the schedule parameter \gammai from 0 to 1 during the first half of training. Parameters: Gaussian kernel standard deviation: 4 \times (1 - \gammai); Schedule parameter \gammai: linearly increases from 0 to 1 in the first half of training. Pitfall: Gets stuck in local minima for pose estimation in very homogeneous scenes. Comparison: Outperforms the baseline in 12/14 and 11/14 cases for rotation and translation estimation respectively, but fails in homogeneous scenes where direct alignment alone may struggle less with texture loss. A strategy for reconstructing static radiance fields and estimating camera poses by jointly optimizing 6D camera poses [R|t]i for i \in [1..N] and a shared focal length f. It uses a coarse-to-fine voxel resolution strategy to smooth the energy surface and prevent the optimizer from getting stuck in sub-optimal solutions. Steps: Optimize the static scene representation in a coarse-to-fine manner: start with a smaller static voxel resolution and progressively increase the voxel resolution during training. Time Complexity: Training time scales with voxel grid resolution: 128^3 (11 mins), 192^3 (12 mins), 256^3 (15 mins), 320^3 (17 mins). The total time includes the sum of iterations for all levels. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the highest octree level reached. Progressive introduction helps manage memory by not allocating fine-level structures until necessary. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization for complex scenes; handles incremental data addition; reduces geometric artifacts. Limitations: Can get stuck in local minima in homogeneous scenes if scale-space smoothing is used. Requires careful tuning of initlevel and coarseintervals. The concept of coarse-to-fine training has been applied in various forms in radiance field optimization to address convergence issues in high-dimensional optimization spaces. Two-stage pipelines were used for dynamic human body modeling (Animatable NeRF) with joint optimization of radiance and blend weight fields, followed by optimization of latent codes for novel poses. Progressive training architectures were formalized in Gaussian Splatting variants to gradually introduce finer octree levels. name: Progressive Training Strategy
head: Coarse-to-Fine Training, Progressive Growing, Progressive Growing Strategy, Progressive Growing of GANs, Progressive training (Growing)
body: Progressive training is a method that gradually increases the resolution of the rendered output during optimization to stabilize convergence and prevent geometric artifacts. It solves the problem of complex loss landscapes and sparse initialization errors that occur when training directly at high resolution. It differs from standard full-resolution training by deferring the fitting of fine features until the global geometry is established, and differs from simple two-stage pipelines by potentially using continuous or multi-stage resolution scaling rather than a single abrupt switch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Training dataset (images or point clouds), total iteration budget T{total}, initial resolution scale s{start}, target resolution scale s{end}=1.0. Output: Trained model parameters (neural network weights or Gaussian attributes) optimized for the target resolution. Resolution Schedule: A mapping from iteration t to output image dimensions (Ht, Wt). Model State: The generator/discriminator architecture or Gaussian point cloud state, which may grow in capacity or remain fixed but render at varying scales. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set current resolution scale s = s{start} (e.g., 0.3 or low-res dimensions). Initialize model parameters. 2. Iterate: For each training iteration t from 1 to T{total}: a. Determine Resolution: Calculate current scale st based on the chosen strategy. Progressive Growing (StyleNeRF): Uses three discrete stages. Stage 1 (t \le T1): Render at fixed low resolution. Stage 2 (T1 < t \le T2): Linearly interpolate resolution from low to high. Stage 3 (t > T2): Render at full target resolution. Cosine Scaling (EAGLES): Uses a continuous schedule. If t \le 0.7 \cdot T{total}: st = 0.3 + 0.7 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos(\pi \frac{t}{0.7 T{total}})). If t > 0.7 \cdot T{total}: st = 1.0. b. Render: Generate image at resolution determined by st. c. Compute Loss: Calculate loss against ground truth images at the current resolution. d. Update: Perform gradient descent to update model parameters. e. Stabilize (Progressive Growing only): If adding new layers or resolution levels, linearly interpolate the output with the previous low-resolution output to stabilize training due to random initialization of new parameters. 3. Finalize: Continue training at full resolution until T{total} is reached. Formulas: Linear Interpolation (StyleNeRF Stage 2): Rt = R{low} + (R{target} - R{low}) \cdot \frac{t - T1}{T2 - T1} Where Rt is the output resolution at iteration t, R{low} is the initial low resolution, R{target} is the target resolution, T1 is the start of Stage 2, and T2 is the end of Stage 2. Cosine Schedule (EAGLES): st = s{start} + (s{end} - s{start}) \cdot \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 - \cos \left( \pi \frac{t}{T{scale}} \right) \right) Where T{scale} = 0.7 \cdot T{total}. Output Interpolation (Stabilization): I{out} = \alpha \cdot I{new} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot I{low} Where \alpha is the interpolation factor corresponding to the progress of layer/resolution addition, computed as \frac{t - T1}{T2 - T1} during Stage 2. Parameters: T1 (StyleNeRF): Start of Stage 2. Default: 500,000 images. T2 (StyleNeRF): End of Stage 2. Default: 5,000,000 images. T3 (StyleNeRF): End of Stage 3. Default: 25,000,000 images. s{start} (EAGLES): Initial scale factor. Default: 0.3. T{scale} (EAGLES): Duration of scaling phase. Default: 70% of total iterations. Batch Size: 64 images per batch. Total Iterations (EAGLES): 30,000 iterations (configurable based on time and memory budget). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Failure: Directly training at the highest resolution causes the model to fail to capture object geometry because the rendering equations are approximations. Floating Artifacts: Standard full-resolution training forces Gaussians to fit fine features early with sparse SfM initialization, leading to suboptimal optimization and floating artifacts. Small Datasets: If the dataset is too small (e.g., MetFaces), progressive training may be unstable; fine-tuning from a pretrained high-resolution model is recommended instead. New Layer Initialization: Parameters of newly added layers are random; without linear interpolation with low-resolution output, training becomes unstable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def progressivetraining(model, datasetiterator, totaliterations, strategy="cosine"): """ model: The neural network or Gaussian system to train. datasetiterator: Iterable yielding ground truth images. totaliterations: Total number of training steps. strategy: "cosine" (EAGLES) or "linear" (StyleNeRF). """ # Standard operations defined inline to avoid external dependencies def getnextbatch(iterator, batchsize=64): return next(iterator) def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): return ((rendered - groundtruth) 2).mean() def interpolateimages(img1, img2, alpha): return alpha img1 + (1.0 - alpha) img2 def forwardpass(model, resolution): # Standard forward pass returning rendered image at given resolution return model.render(resolution) def updateparameters(model, loss): # Standard gradient descent step model.step(loss) baseheight = 256 # Example base resolution basewidth = 256 if strategy == "cosine": scalestart = 0.3 scaleend = 1.0 scaleduration = int(0.7 totaliterations) for t in range(1, totaliterations + 1): if t <= scaleduration: progress = t / scaleduration scale = scalestart + (scaleend - scalestart) 0.5 (1 - math.cos(math.pi progress)) else: scale = scaleend currentheight = int(baseheight scale) currentwidth = int(basewidth scale) gtimages = getnextbatch(datasetiterator, batchsize=64) renderedimages = forwardpass(model, (currentheight, currentwidth)) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, gtimages) updateparameters(model, loss) if t % 175 == 0: model.densify() if t % 2500 == 0: model.resetopacity() if t % 5000 == 0: model.prune(0.15) elif strategy == "linear": T1 = 500000 T2 = 5000000 lowresscale = 0.125 # Corresponds to 32x32 from 256x256 highresscale = 1.0 for t in range(1, totaliterations + 1): if t <= T1: scale = lowresscale elif t <= T2: progress = (t - T1) / (T2 - T1) scale = lowresscale + (highresscale - lowresscale) progress else: scale = highresscale currentheight = int(baseheight scale) currentwidth = int(basewidth scale) gtimages = getnextbatch(datasetiterator, batchsize=64) renderedimages = forwardpass(model, (currentheight, currentwidth)) if t <= T2: lowresrendered = forwardpass(model, (int(baseheight lowresscale), int(basewidth lowresscale))) finalrender = interpolateimages(renderedimages, lowresrendered, progress) else: finalrender = renderedimages loss = computeloss(finalrender, gtimages) updateparameters(model, loss) Starts with a shallow network and fades in layers for higher resolutions. Requires linear interpolation with low-resolution output to stabilize random new parameters. Chosen for speed advantage at low resolutions. Inserts upsample operations during training instead of growing layers. Does not require fading in layers linearly. Works similarly in visual quality but may be slower at low resolutions. Time Complexity: Training time is distributed across resolutions. The majority of iterations (e.g., 70% in EAGLES, or up to T2 in StyleNeRF) occur at lower resolutions, which are computationally cheaper per iteration. However, the total iteration count may be higher to compensate for the coarse phases. Memory Complexity: Lower resolution rendering requires less memory per iteration. The model architecture size may grow in Progressive Growing, but up-sampling keeps it fixed. Performance: Prevents failure to capture geometry and reduces floating artifacts compared to direct high-resolution training. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization in complex loss landscapes; handles sparse SfM initialization better; avoids early fitting to noise/fine details. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of resolution transitions; small datasets may not support stable progressive training. When to use: High-resolution synthesis, scenes with sparse initialization, or when direct training leads to artifacts. When not to use: Very small datasets where progressive training is unstable, requiring fine-tuning from a pretrained model instead. The strategy is inspired by Karras et al. (2017) "Progressive Growing of GANs for Improved Quality, Stability, and Variation". It was adapted for NeRF-based methods (StyleNeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting variants (EAGLES) to address the specific challenges of volume rendering and differentiable rendering, where direct high-resolution training leads to geometric inaccuracies due to approximation errors in the rendering equations. name: NeRF Restarting Approach
head: Joint Pose-NeRF Refinement with Restart, Pose-Constrained NeRF Restart
body: The NeRF Restarting Approach is an optimization protocol for jointly refining camera poses and neural radiance fields (NeRFs) from sparse, noisy initial poses. It solves the problem of artifacts persisting in the scene representation due to the coupling of pose and geometry optimization. Unlike Staged Training, which freezes poses after initial convergence but retains the learned network weights, this method re-initializes the network from scratch after pose convergence, thereby removing artifacts learned during the pose optimization phase. The method consists of three sequential phases. Inputs: A set of N training images with noisy initial camera poses P0 = \{T1, \dots, TN\}. A NeRF architecture comprising a coarse MLP and a fine MLP. Outputs: Optimized camera poses P^. A high-fidelity NeRF model. Data Structures: Camera Pose: A 4 \times 4 transformation matrix T \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4} representing the world-to-camera transformation. NeRF: Two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), M{coarse} and M{fine}, mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and color. Steps: 1. Joint Optimization Phase: Initialize M{coarse} and M{fine} randomly. Jointly optimize the parameters of both MLPs and the camera poses P by minimizing the photometric rendering loss \mathcal{L}{photo} between rendered and ground-truth images. Continue this phase until the camera pose estimates converge (i.e., pose updates fall below a threshold or validation loss plateaus). 2. Freezing and Re-initialization: Let P^ be the converged pose estimates from Phase 1. Freeze P^ such that they are no longer trainable. Re-initialize the weights of both M{coarse} and M{fine} to random values, discarding the weights learned in Phase 1. 3. Fine-Tuning Phase: Train the re-initialized M{coarse} and M{fine} from scratch using the fixed poses P^. Optimize the network parameters to minimize the rendering loss, effectively learning the scene geometry and appearance without the interference of pose uncertainty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfrestartingapproach(images, noisyposes, numiterationsphase1, numiterationsphase2): # Phase 1: Joint Optimization mlpcoarse = initializerandommlp() mlpfine = initializerandommlp() poses = noisyposes.clone() poses.requiresgrad = True for step in range(numiterationsphase1): # Render images using current poses and MLPs renderedimages = renderneRF(images, poses, mlpcoarse, mlpfine) # Compute photometric loss loss = computephotometricloss(renderedimages, images) # Backpropagate to update poses and MLPs loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Check for pose convergence (implementation detail:) if checkposeconvergence(poses): break # Phase 2: Freezing and Re-initialization optimizedposes = poses.detach() optimizedposes.requiresgrad = False # Re-initialize MLPs from scratch mlpcoarse = initializerandommlp() mlpfine = initializerandommlp() # Phase 3: Fine-Tuning with Fixed Poses for step in range(numiterationsphase2): # Render images using fixed optimized poses renderedimages = renderneRF(images, optimizedposes, mlpcoarse, mlpfine) # Compute photometric loss loss = computephotometricloss(renderedimages, images) # Backpropagate to update only MLPs loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return optimizedposes, mlpcoarse, mlpfine Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence Criteria: Determining when poses have "converged" in Phase 1 is critical. Premature stopping may leave poses inaccurate, while excessive training may overfit the network to noisy poses before restart. Re-initialization Cost: The method requires two full training cycles, doubling the computational cost compared to single-pass methods. Staged Training is a two-phase optimization protocol for joint camera pose and neural radiance field (NeRF) reconstruction from sparse, noisy initial poses. Performance: On the DTU dataset with 3 views and 15% initial additive Gaussian noise, the restarting approach achieves a PSNR of 17.80 (19.07 masked), SSIM of 0.72 (0.83 masked), LPIPS of 0.25 (0.12 masked), and Depth Error (DE) of 1.84. Comparison: It outperforms Staged Training by removing artifacts learned during the pose optimization phase that persist in the staged approach. Complexity: The method doubles the training time compared to a single optimization pass, as it requires a full re-training of the network after pose convergence. The NeRF Restarting Approach was introduced in the context of sparse and noisy pose estimation for NeRFs. It was identified as the best alternative in prior work [51] and demonstrated to yield superior results compared to staged training protocols in ablation studies. The method addresses the limitation where joint optimization leads to a coupled solution where network artifacts mimic pose errors or vice versa. name: Staged Training
head: Staged Pose-NeRF Refinement
body: Staged Training is a two-phase optimization protocol for joint camera pose and neural radiance field (NeRF) reconstruction from sparse, noisy initial poses. It solves the problem of local minima in simultaneous pose and network optimization by decoupling the refinement of camera extrinsics from the high-fidelity learning of scene geometry. It differs from joint training approaches by freezing poses after an initial coarse registration, which prevents the fine network from learning blurry surfaces due to pose exploration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images \{Ii\}, initial camera poses \{Pi\}, a coarse NeRF network F{\thetac}, and a fine NeRF network F{\thetaf}. Outputs: Refined camera poses \{\hat{P}i\} and optimized radiance fields F{\thetac}, F{\thetaf}. Data Structures: Camera Pose: Pi = [Ri | ti], where Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} is a rotation matrix and ti \in \mathbb{R}^3 is a translation vector. NeRF Network: F{\theta}(x, d) \to (\sigma, c), mapping 3D position x and viewing direction d to density \sigma and color c. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Pose Refinement with Coarse Network Initialize the coarse network F{\thetac} with random weights. Keep the fine network F{\thetaf} untrained or frozen with random weights. Optimize the parameters of F{\thetac} (\thetac) and the camera poses Pi simultaneously by minimizing the photometric loss between rendered and input images. This stage aligns the camera poses to the coarse geometry learned by F{\thetac}. 2. Stage 2: Joint Refinement with Frozen Poses Freeze the camera poses Pi to the estimates obtained from Stage 1. Optimize the parameters of both the coarse network F{\thetac} (\thetac) and the fine network F{\thetaf} (\thetaf) simultaneously. The fine network learns high-frequency details and sharp geometry, benefiting from the now-registered poses and the pre-trained coarse network which provides a stable low-frequency baseline. Formulas: Photometric Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = \sum{i} \| Ii - \hat{I}i \|^2, where \hat{I}i is the rendered image for pose Pi. Total Loss in Stage 1: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}}^{(1)} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{reg}} \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}(\thetac), where \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} is a regularization term on network weights. Total Loss in Stage 2: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}}^{(2)} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{reg}} (\mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}(\thetac) + \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}(\thetaf)). Parameters: Learning rates for \thetac, \thetaf, and Pi are typically decayed over time. Regularization weight \lambda{\text{reg}} is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initial Pose Quality: If initial poses are too noisy, Stage 1 may fail to converge to a useful alignment; the method is evaluated with 15% initial additive Gaussian noise. Local Minima: Joint training of poses and both networks without staging causes blurry surfaces because the fine network explores the pose space while learning geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderimage(network, pose, rays): """Standard volume rendering: sample points along rays, evaluate network, apply alpha compositing.""" points = samplealongrays(pose, rays) densities, colors = network(points, rays) return compositealpha(densities, colors) def updateparams(params, gradients, lr): """Apply gradient descent step.""" for p, g in zip(params, gradients): p -= lr g def stagedtraining(images, initialposes, coarsenet, finenet, lr1, lr2, epochs1, epochs2): # Initialize trainable pose copies poses = [copy(p) for p in initialposes] thetac = coarsenet.parameters thetaf = finenet.parameters # Stage 1: Refine poses and coarse network for epoch in range(epochs1): for i, img in enumerate(images): rays = raysfromimage(img) rendered = renderimage(coarsenet, poses[i], rays) loss = sum((rendered - img) 2) gradc, gradp = computegradients(loss, thetac, poses[i]) updateparams(thetac, gradc, lr1) updateparams(poses[i], gradp, lr1) # Stage 2: Freeze poses, train both networks for epoch in range(epochs2): for i, img in enumerate(images): rays = raysfromimage(img) renderedcoarse = renderimage(coarsenet, poses[i], rays) renderedfine = renderimage(finenet, poses[i], rays) compositerendered = compositealpha(renderedcoarse, renderedfine) loss = sum((compositerendered - img) 2) gradc, gradf = computegradients(loss, thetac, thetaf) updateparams(thetac, gradc, lr2) updateparams(thetaf, gradf, lr2) return poses, coarsenet, finenet A training protocol for deformable neural radiance fields that reduces GPU memory consumption and accelerates convergence by decoupling the initialization of the tetrahedral mesh from the high-resolution refinement. It differs from single-stage training by first constructing a sparse, occupancy-aware coarse mesh and then refining it, whereas single-stage methods initialize with a dense, uniform grid regardless of scene occupancy. Time Complexity: Two sequential optimization phases. Stage 1 is generally faster as it only optimizes poses and a coarse network. Stage 2 optimizes two networks but with frozen poses, which can be more stable. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard NeRF training, but avoids the memory overhead of storing gradients for poses during the fine network training phase in Stage 2. Measured Performance: On the DTU dataset with 3 views and 15% initial additive Gaussian noise, Staged Training achieves a PSNR of 17.58 (18.62 masked), SSIM of 0.71 (0.82 masked), LPIPS of 0.26 (0.13 masked), and Depth Error (DE) of 1.81. Strengths: Prevents blurry surfaces by decoupling pose and geometry optimization. Improves PSNR and SSIM compared to joint training of poses with both coarse and fine MLPs. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the transition between stages. Performance depends heavily on the quality of the initial poses. When to use: When initial camera poses are sparse and noisy, and joint optimization leads to poor geometry. When not to use: When high-quality initial poses are available, or when computational resources are extremely limited for two-stage optimization. Staged Training was introduced in the context of "SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses". It addresses the challenges of reconstructing NeRFs from sparse and noisy camera poses, where traditional joint optimization methods struggle with local minima and blurry reconstructions. The method builds on the idea of coarse-to-fine optimization but explicitly stages the pose refinement process.
