name: Two-stage Training for Deformable NeRF
head: Deformable NeRF Two-stage Training
body: A training protocol for deformable neural radiance fields that reduces GPU memory consumption and accelerates convergence by decoupling the initialization of the tetrahedral mesh from the high-resolution refinement. It differs from single-stage training by first constructing a sparse, occupancy-aware coarse mesh and then refining it, whereas single-stage methods initialize with a dense, uniform grid regardless of scene occupancy. The method optimizes a deformable neural radiance field represented by a recursively subdivided tetrahedral mesh. The training is split into two distinct phases to manage memory and computational load. Inputs: Camera poses and images from a dataset (e.g., Synthetic NeRF, Tanks and Temples). A unit cube bounding box for the scene. Hyperparameters: Grid spacing for initialization (\delta = 0.02), total subdivision levels (L=6), optimizer settings (Adam, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-15}), initial learning rate (\eta = 1 \times 10^{-2}), and cosine annealing schedule. Outputs: A refined tetrahedral mesh with associated neural field parameters (density, color, deformation fields) optimized for novel view synthesis. The core data structure is a tetrahedral mesh. Vertices: Defined in 3D space. Tetrahedra: Defined by 4 vertex indices. Subdivision Hierarchy: A tree structure where each tetrahedron can be subdivided into smaller tetrahedra up to level L. The coefficient matrix C relates barycentric coordinates across levels (derived in supplementary material of). Occupancy Mask: A boolean array indicating which tetrahedra are retained. Stage 1: Coarse Mesh Initialization 1. Generate Initial Tetrahedralization: Apply the QuarTet algorithm [17] to the unit cube with a grid spacing parameter of 0.02. This creates a uniform tetrahedral mesh filling the cube. Result: A mesh with 17,933 vertices and 92,234 tetrahedra. 2. Compute Occupancy: Render the scene or use a pre-computed occupancy mesh to determine which tetrahedra intersect with the object geometry. 3. Prune Mesh: Retain only tetrahedra marked as occupied. Discard empty tetrahedra to minimize memory usage. Goal: Obtain a coarse tetrahedral mesh that roughly envelops the object. Stage 2: Refined Training 1. Initialize Subdivision: Start with the coarse mesh from Stage 1. Set the total number of subdivision levels to L=6 for all scenes. 2. Optimize: Perform gradient-based optimization (Adam) on the neural field parameters associated with the retained tetrahedra. The subdivision levels allow for higher resolution in areas requiring detail. The optimization is focused on refining the structure established in Stage 1. 3. Schedule: Use a cosine annealing learning rate schedule starting at 1 \times 10^{-2}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagetraining(dataset, scenebboxsize=1.0, gridspacing=0.02, totallevels=6, lr=1e-2, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, epsilon=1e-15): """ Two-stage training for Deformable NeRF. Args: dataset: Collection of images and camera poses. scenebboxsize: Size of the unit cube (default 1.0). gridspacing: QuarTet grid spacing (default 0.02). totallevels: Total subdivision levels (default 6). lr: Initial learning rate (default 1e-2). beta1, beta2, epsilon: Adam optimizer parameters. Returns: optimizedmodel: Neural radiance field model with refined mesh. """ # --- Stage 1: Coarse Initialization --- # 1. Generate initial uniform tetrahedral mesh using QuarTet # QuarTet converts surface geometry (or bounding box) into tetrahedra. # Input: Cube of size scenebboxsize, grid spacing gridspacing. initialmesh = quarTetinit(cubesize=scenebboxsize, spacing=gridspacing) # Note: Initial mesh has ~17,933 vertices and ~92,234 tetrahedra for spacing 0.02 # 2. Determine occupancy # Use an occupancy mesh or rendering to identify occupied tetrahedra. # Similar to Instant-NGP's occupancy grid for voxel retention. occupancymask = computeoccupancy(initialmesh, dataset) # 3. Prune mesh # Retain only tetrahedra where occupancymask is True. coarsemesh = prunemesh(initialmesh, occupancymask) # Initialize model parameters with coarsemesh model = initializemodel(coarsemesh, levels=totallevels) # --- Stage 2: Refined Optimization --- optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, betas=(beta1, beta2), eps=epsilon) scheduler = CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, Tmax=totalepochs) # Tmax depends on dataset for epoch in range(totalepochs): # Sample rays from dataset rays = samplerays(dataset) # Render rays using current model (which uses subdivided tetrahedra) # The subdivision hierarchy allows detailed representation renderedcolors, depths = renderrays(model, rays) # Compute loss against ground truth images loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) # Backpropagate and update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() scheduler.step() return model Grid Spacing: 0.02. Total Subdivision Levels: 6 for all scenes. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-2}. Optimizer: Adam with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-15}. Occupancy Accuracy: If the occupancy mesh is inaccurate, Stage 1 may retain empty tetrahedra (wasting memory) or discard occupied ones (causing holes). The method relies on the quality of the occupancy estimation. Memory Scaling: While two-stage training reduces memory, Stage 2 still requires significant resources for high subdivision levels. However, it is more efficient than single-stage. Degenerate Input: The method assumes the scene can be bounded by a unit cube. Scenes outside this bounds require scaling or padding. Memory Usage: Significantly lower than single-stage training. On the Synthetic NeRF dataset, Stage 1 uses 5.34 GB and Stage 2 uses 2.70 GB, compared to 9.79 GB for single-stage training. Performance: Improves rendering quality. On the Tanks and Temples dataset, two-stage training achieves PSNR 29.09, SSIM 0.903, and LPIPS 0.124, compared to single-stage PSNR 28.01, SSIM 0.887, and LPIPS 0.155. Speed: Enhances training speed by reducing the number of tetrahedra processed in the initial phase and focusing computation on relevant areas. Strengths: Memory efficiency, faster convergence, better handling of complex geometries via occupancy-aware pruning. Limitations: Requires an initial occupancy estimation step. Performance is sensitive to the grid spacing parameter and number of subdivision levels. Origin: Proposed in "Deformable NeRF using Recursively Subdivided Tetrahedra". Context: Builds on Tetra-NeRF [16] and Instant-NGP [27]. It addresses the high memory cost of dense tetrahedral grids in deformable NeRFs. History: The method leverages the QuarTet algorithm [17] for mesh generation and integrates it with a multi-resolution subdivision hierarchy. Deformable NeRF using Recursively Subdivided Tetrahedra, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3681019, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Overall Training Pipeline
head: UP-NeRF training, coarse-to-fine with scheduling
body: This pipeline defines the end-to-end training procedure for unconstrained neural radiance fields, specifically integrating pose estimation, transient artifact handling, and hierarchical sampling. It solves the problem of training NeRFs on unposed, internet-scale image collections where initial camera poses are unknown and images contain transient objects (e.g., people, vehicles). It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by jointly optimizing camera poses and scene representation using a coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling strategy, while explicitly decoupling transient artifacts via a dedicated transient network and depth-supervised scheduling. Inputs: A set of unordered, unposed images Iu; initial camera poses P (typically identity); monocular depth estimates D (from DPT); deep features F (from DINO). Outputs: Optimized camera poses P^, scene representation (NeRF MLPs), and transient network parameters. Data Structures: 1. NeRF Model: Two MLPs (coarse and fine) mapping (x, d) to density \sigma and color \hat{C}. 2. Transient Network (T): MLP mapping (x, d) to transient color \hat{C}i and confidence weight W{depth}. 3. Pose Parameters: Per-image rotation and translation vectors. 4. Depth Factors: Per-image scaling si and bias ti for depth supervision. Parameters: Total iterations: 600,000. Rays per step: 2,048 randomly sampled pixels. Sampling points per ray: 128 for both coarse and fine models. Learning rate (NeRF, TransientNet): 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Learning rate (Pose, Depth factors): 2 \times 10^{-3} decaying to 1 \times 10^{-3}. Optimizer: Adam. Depth loss weight \lambdad: 0.001. Scheduling bounds u=0.1, v=0.5. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set all camera poses to identity transformation. Extract deep features and monocular depth offline. 2. Loss Composition: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} combining RGB, feature, and depth losses, modulated by a scheduling factor w{u,v}: \mathcal{L} = w{u,v} \mathcal{L}{rgb} + (1 - w{u,v}) (\mathcal{L}{feat} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}{depth}) The factor w{u,v} transitions from 1 to 0 as training progresses, shifting reliance from depth/feature supervision to RGB reconstruction. 3. Coarse Model Rendering: Render the coarse view \hat{C}i(r) using the coarse NeRF. Crucially, use detached transient outputs \alpha(\tau) and \hat{C}i(\tau) to prevent transient network gradients from affecting the coarse NeRF directly. The coarse RGB loss is: \mathcal{L}{coarse\rgb} = \frac{1}{2} \| \hat{C}i(r) - Ci(r) \|2^2 Uncertainty is not used in the coarse model. 4. Fine Model Sampling: Compose the sample set for the fine model. Unlike standard NeRF which uses only coarse density \sigma, this pipeline uses both the shared density \sigma and the candidate density \sigmai (from the transient head). The usage depends on w{u,v}: at the start, both are used; as w{u,v} \to 0, only \sigma is used. 5. Fine Model Rendering & Loss: Render the fine view. Compute \mathcal{L}{rgb} using the fine model's output. Detach the transient confidence weight W{depth} to prevent its parameters from affecting the NeRF directly. 6. Optimization: Update all parameters (NeRF, TransientNet, Poses, Depth factors) using the computed gradients. TransientNet is optimized using the fine model alone. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. nerfcoarse = initmlp() nerffine = initmlp() transientnet = initmlp() poses = [Identity() for in images] depthfactors = [initfactors() for in images] optimizernerf = Adam(params=[nerfcoarse, nerffine], lr=5e-4) optimizertransient = Adam(params=transientnet, lr=5e-4) optimizerpose = Adam(params=[poses, depthfactors], lr=2e-3) for step in range(600000): # 1. Sample rays rays = samplerandomrays(images, count=2048) # 2. Compute scheduling factor wuv based on step progress # u=0.1, v=0.5. Linear decay from 1 to 0 between these progress points. wuv = computeschedulingfactor(step, totalsteps, u=0.1, v=0.5) # 3. Forward Pass: Coarse Model # Use detached transient outputs to avoid gradient flow to NeRF with torch.nograd(): coarsetransientout = transientnet.forward(coarsesamples) alphatau = coarsetransientout.alpha.detach() Citau = coarsetransientout.C.detach() coarsecolor = nerfcoarse.render(rays, alpha=alphatau, C=Citau) Lcoarsergb = 0.5 torch.mean((coarsecolor - groundtruthcolor)2) # 4. Forward Pass: Fine Model # Sample points using both sigma (shared) and sigmai (candidate) # The mix depends on wuv. If wuv is high, use both. If low, use only sigma. finesamples = samplefinepoints(rays, nerfcoarse, transientnet, wuv) finecolor = nerffine.render(finesamples) Lrgb = torch.mean((finecolor - groundtruthcolor)2) # 5. Compute Auxiliary Losses # Depth loss uses detached Wdepth Ldepth = computedepthloss(poses, depthfactors, rays, monoculardepths) Lfeat = computefeatureloss(rays, deepfeatures) # 6. Total Loss L = wuv Lrgb + (1 - wuv) (Lfeat + 0.001 Ldepth) # 7. Backward Pass optimizernerf.zerograd() optimizertransient.zerograd() optimizerpose.zerograd() L.backward() optimizernerf.step() optimizertransient.step() optimizerpose.step() LU-NeRF estimates camera poses and neural scene representations from unordered, unposed image collections by processing them as local mini-scenes before global synchronization. It differs from prior unposed NeRF methods by operating in the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive pose priors, using a compact view-independent 4-layer MLP without positional encoding, and resolving mirror-symmetry ambiguities through a dedicated secondary training stage. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of iterations (600K) and rays per step (2048). The hierarchical sampling adds a constant overhead per ray. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of sampling points (128 per ray) and the size of the MLPs. No large voxel grids are stored. Strengths: Robust to initial pose errors; handles transient objects effectively by decoupling them; leverages external depth/feature priors for initialization. Limitations: Requires offline extraction of depth and features; sensitive to the scheduling parameters u and v; may converge slowly if depth priors are inaccurate. When to use: Unconstrained image collections with unknown poses and transient artifacts. When not to use: Known poses with static scenes (standard NeRF is faster); real-time rendering (training is offline). Originated in the UP-NeRF paper (2023). It builds on the BARF (Blending Artificially Realistic Feature) coarse-to-fine strategy and NeRF-W, adapting them for unconstrained datasets. It addresses the limitations of prior methods that failed to converge when naively combining pose estimation with other enhancements. UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03784v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LU-NeRF Architecture and Training
head: Compact LU-NeRF, LU-NeRF Network Architecture and Training, Local Unposed NeRF, Local Unposed NeRF training
body: LU-NeRF estimates camera poses and neural scene representations from unordered, unposed image collections by processing them as local mini-scenes before global synchronization. It differs from prior unposed NeRF methods by operating in the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive pose priors, using a compact view-independent 4-layer MLP without positional encoding, and resolving mirror-symmetry ambiguities through a dedicated secondary training stage. Inputs: A set of unposed images partitioned into mini-scenes. Outputs: Optimized camera poses (world-to-camera) and a neural radiance field representation for each mini-scene. Data Structures: Camera Poses: For a mini-scene with N images, poses are stored as a set of world-to-camera rotation matrices \{Ri\}{i=1}^N and translation vectors \{ti\}{i=1}^N. Exact memory layout and bit-packing are Not given in the sources. Neural Field: A compact 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). It does not use positional encoding and does not condition on view directions (view-independent). Ray Sampling: 2048 rays are sampled per mini-batch. Parameters: Initial Poses: Identity matrix for rotations and zero for translations. Random initialization around identity yields no significant difference. Learning Rate: Adopted from BARF. Depth Regularization Weight: 10 times larger than the photometric \ell2 loss. Regularization Patch Size: 2 \times 2 pixels. LU-NeRF-1 Termination Threshold: Average camera rotation change less than 0.125^\circ. LU-NeRF-2 Default Iterations: 50,000 total (5,000 frozen poses + 45,000 joint optimization). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize camera poses \{Ri, ti\} to identity. Initialize the 4-layer MLP weights. Do not apply positional encoding or view-direction conditioning to the MLP. 2. LU-NeRF-1 Training (Local Optimization): Sample 2048 rays per mini-batch. Compute photometric \ell2 loss between rendered and ground-truth pixels. Apply depth regularization on 2 \times 2 patches. Jointly optimize camera poses and MLP parameters using the BARF learning rate schedule. Terminate training if the average change of camera rotations in the mini-scene is less than 0.125^\circ after 5,000 iterations. 3. Mirror-Symmetry Ambiguity Mitigation (LU-NeRF-2): Take estimated poses \{Ri\} from LU-NeRF-1. Generate reflected cameras \{R\pi Ri\}, where R\pi is a rotation around the optical axis. Train two new models from scratch: one initialized with original poses, one with reflected poses. Train for 5,000 iterations with frozen initial poses. Jointly optimize camera poses and neural fields for 45,000 iterations. Resolve ambiguity by selecting the model with the smallest photometric training loss. 4. Global Synchronization and Refinement: Bring local mini-scene poses into a global reference frame using pose synchronization (e.g., Shonan averaging). Perform a final global optimization of all camera poses and the neural scene representation using all images from the entire scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainlunerfminiscene(images, minisceneindices): # 1. Initialization poses = [{'R': [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]], 't': [0,0,0]} for in minisceneindices] mlp = Compact4LayerMLP() previousposes = [{'R': [row[:] for row in p['R']], 't': p['t'][:]} for p in poses] # 2. LU-NeRF-1 Training for iteration in range(100000): rays = samplerays(images, minisceneindices, numrays=2048) renderedcolors, rendereddepths = renderrays(rays, poses, mlp) photometricloss = sum((c - g)2 for c, g in zip(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors)) / len(renderedcolors) depthregloss = computepatchsmoothness(rendereddepths, patchsize=(2, 2)) totalloss = photometricloss + 10.0 depthregloss gradientstep(poses, mlp, totalloss) avgrotationchange = sum(rotationdistance(c['R'], p['R']) for c, p in zip(poses, previousposes)) / len(poses) if iteration >= 5000 and avgrotationchange < 0.125: break previousposes = [{'R': [row[:] for row in p['R']], 't': p['t'][:]} for p in poses] estimatedposes = poses # 3. Mirror-Symmetry Ambiguity Mitigation (LU-NeRF-2) reflectedposes = [reflectrotationaroundopticalaxis(p) for p in estimatedposes] modelaposes, modelamlp = trainlunerf2stage(estimatedposes, images, minisceneindices) modelbposes, modelbmlp = trainlunerf2stage(reflectedposes, images, minisceneindices) lossa = computephotometricloss(modelaposes, modelamlp, images, minisceneindices) lossb = computephotometricloss(modelbposes, modelbmlp, images, minisceneindices) if lossa < lossb: return modelaposes, modelamlp else: return modelbposes, modelbmlp def trainlunerf2stage(initialposes, images, minisceneindices): poses = [{'R': [row[:] for row in p['R']], 't': p['t'][:]} for p in initialposes] mlp = Compact4LayerMLP() for iteration in range(5000): rays = samplerays(images, minisceneindices, numrays=2048) renderedcolors, rendereddepths = renderrays(rays, poses, mlp) photometricloss = sum((c - g)2 for c, g in zip(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors)) / len(renderedcolors) depthregloss = computepatchsmoothness(rendereddepths, patchsize=(2, 2)) totalloss = photometricloss + 10.0 depthregloss gradientstep(mlp, totalloss) for iteration in range(45000): rays = samplerays(images, minisceneindices, numrays=2048) renderedcolors, rendereddepths = renderrays(rays, poses, mlp) photometricloss = sum((c - g)2 for c, g in zip(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors)) / len(renderedcolors) depthregloss = computepatchsmoothness(rendereddepths, patchsize=(2, 2)) totalloss = photometricloss + 10.0 depthregloss gradientstep(poses, mlp, totalloss) return poses, mlp def Compact4LayerMLP(): return NeuralNetwork(layers=[256, 256, 256, 3]) def samplerays(images, indices, numrays): return generaterandompixelcoords(images, indices, numrays) def renderrays(rays, poses, mlp): return mlp.forward(rays.xyz, poses) def computepatchsmoothness(depths, patchsize): return sum(depths[i] - depths[j] for i, j in patchpairs(depths, patchsize)) def gradientstep(params, loss): params.update(learningrate gradient(loss)) def rotationdistance(R1, R2): return anglebetweenrotations(R1, R2) def reflectrotationaroundopticalaxis(pose): R = pose['R'] theta = 180.0 return {'R': multiplyrotations(rotationz(theta), R), 't': pose['t']} def computephotometricloss(poses, mlp, images, indices): rays = samplerays(images, indices, 2048) colors, = renderrays(rays, poses, mlp) return sum((c - g)2 for c, g in zip(colors, rays.gtcolors)) / len(colors) This variant addresses the degeneracy where distant small objects appear affine, causing ambiguity between a scene and its reflection. It is chosen when the initial local optimization produces inverted disparity maps and reflected poses. It resolves the ambiguity by training two additional models initialized with original and reflected camera poses, then selecting the one with the lowest photometric training loss. See LU-NeRF Architecture and Training for the full training pipeline. This variant performs a final global optimization of all camera poses and the neural scene representation using all images from the entire scene after local synchronization. It is chosen to align local mini-scene estimates into a consistent global reference frame and improve overall reconstruction accuracy. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: LU-NeRF outperforms prior unposed NeRF attempts (GNeRF, VMRF) on pose estimation and compares favorably to COLMAP on low-texture and low-resolution images. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The removal of positional encoding and view-dependency, combined with a compact 4-layer MLP, significantly reduces memory cost and speeds up training compared to standard NeRF architectures. The local-to-global pipeline is designed to be robust, succeeding even when initial mini-scenes contain frequent outliers. Limitations: Performance may degrade if the noisy connected graph built with DINO/RGB features is used for pose synchronization; clean graphs built from ground-truth poses yield better results. When to use: Few-shot local unposed NeRF tasks requiring general SE(3) pose estimation without restrictive pose priors. When not to use: Scenarios requiring view-dependent appearance modeling or high-frequency positional encoding. LU-NeRF was introduced in 2023 by researchers addressing the challenges of few-shot local unposed NeRF. It builds on the concept of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and pose synchronization techniques [20, 43, 24]. The method was developed to operate in the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive assumptions on pose priors, distinguishing it from earlier baselines. name: NeuTex Training Schedule
head: NeuTex Training Procedure
body: The NeuTex Training Schedule is a multi-stage optimization procedure for training the NeuTex neural texture mapping model. It solves the instability issues inherent in jointly optimizing geometry, texture, and mapping networks by decoupling the initialization of the UV-mapping components from the final high-fidelity texture synthesis. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF training loops by explicitly prioritizing geometric consistency via Chamfer loss and cycle consistency before transitioning to full volumetric rendering optimization, and by employing a final stage that freezes geometry and mapping networks to refine texture details. The method consists of three sequential training stages. Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses. A sparse ground-truth point cloud (used in Stage 1). Neural networks: Geometry network F\sigma, Texture mapping network F{uv}, Inverse texture mapping network F{uv}^{-1}, and Texture network F{\text{tex}}. Outputs: Optimized weights for F\sigma, F{uv}, F{uv}^{-1}, and F{\text{tex}}. Data Structures: The networks are standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) or similar differentiable functions. Specific architectural details (layer sizes, activation functions) are not provided in the training schedule notes. Loss functions: Chamfer loss (L{\text{Chamfer}}), Rendering loss (L{\text{render}}), and the full loss defined in Equation 14 of the source (L{\text{full}}). Steps: 1. Stage 1: Geometric Initialization (50,000 iterations) Train all networks (F\sigma, F{uv}, F{uv}^{-1}, F{\text{tex}}) jointly. The total loss is a combination of Chamfer loss and rendering loss: L{\text{stage1}} = L{\text{Chamfer}} + L{\text{render}} The Chamfer loss aligns the 3D geometry output with the sparse ground-truth point cloud. The rendering loss ensures the projected images match the input views. Run for 50,000 iterations. 2. Stage 2: Full Optimization (500,000 iterations) Remove the Chamfer loss. Train all networks jointly using the full loss function (Equation 14 from the source), which includes rendering loss and cycle consistency losses between F{uv} and F{uv}^{-1}. L{\text{stage2}} = L{\text{full}} Run until convergence, which takes approximately 500,000 iterations. 3. Stage 3: Texture Fine-tuning Freeze the weights of the geometry network F\sigma, the texture mapping network F{uv}, and the inverse texture mapping network F{uv}^{-1}. Continue training only the texture network F{\text{tex}} until convergence. This stage focuses on improving high-frequency texture details without disturbing the established geometry and mapping. Parameters: Iterations for Stage 1: 50,000. Iterations for Stage 2: ~500,000. Hardware: Single NVIDIA RTX 2080Ti GPU. Total Training Time: 2-3 days. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The schedule relies on the availability of a sparse ground-truth point cloud for the Chamfer loss in Stage 1. If this is unavailable, the initialization strategy may need adaptation. The source does not specify learning rates, batch sizes, or optimizer settings (e.g., Adam parameters). These must be determined by the implementer or inferred from standard practices for similar neural rendering methods. The exact formulation of "Equation 14" is not provided in the notes. The implementer must refer to the original paper for the specific weights and terms comprising L{\text{full}}. The NeuTex Initialization Training Procedure is a pre-training stage designed to initialize the inverse texture mapping network F{uv}^{-1} and the texture mapping network F{uv} before the main optimization loop. Time Complexity: The method requires approximately 550,000 iterations of training plus fine-tuning. On a single RTX 2080Ti GPU, this takes 2-3 days. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The staged approach stabilizes training by first establishing geometric coherence before optimizing texture and mapping consistency. The final fine-tuning stage allows for high-quality texture details without degrading geometry. Limitations: The training time is significant (2-3 days per scene). The method requires sparse ground-truth geometry for the initial stage, which may not always be available. When to use: When high-fidelity texture and geometry are required for neural texture mapping and sparse ground-truth data is available for initialization. When not to use: When training time is constrained or when sparse ground-truth geometry is not available. The NeuTex Training Schedule was introduced in the paper "NeuTex: Neural Texture Mapping for Volumetric Neural Rendering". The method addresses the challenges of training neural texture mapping networks, which involve complex interactions between geometry, UV mapping, and texture synthesis. The multi-stage schedule was developed to mitigate training instability and improve the final visual quality of the rendered textures. name: NeuTex Initialization Training Procedure
head: Initialization stage, Pre-training loss
body: The NeuTex Initialization Training Procedure is a pre-training stage that initializes the inverse texture mapping network F{uv}^{-1} and the texture mapping network F{uv} using a downsampled point cloud and uniformly sampled UV coordinates on a unit sphere. It differs from standard volume rendering initialization by explicitly optimizing bi-directional UV-to-3D and 3D-to-UV consistency via Chamfer distance and cycle losses before entering the main optimization loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Downsampled ground-truth point cloud P{gt} from COLMAP (2,000–3,000 points). Uniformly sampled UV coordinates P on the unit sphere (2,500 points). Ground-truth images and camera parameters required for the main pipeline losses. Outputs: Initialized weights for F{uv}^{-1} and F{uv}. Total initialization loss L{\text{init}} for gradient backpropagation. Data Structures: Point Cloud P{gt}: A set of 3D points \{(xi, yi, zi)\} downsampled to 2,000–3,000 points. UV Sample Set P: A set of 2,500 points uniformly distributed on the unit sphere, representing texture-space coordinates. Network Architecture: The networks accept inputs x (3D coordinates), u (texture-space points on the unit sphere), and d (3D unit viewing direction), and output \sigma (predicted volumetric density) and c (predicted radiance). F{uv}^{-1} maps UV inputs to 3D coordinates, while F{uv} maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to UV coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Downsample the COLMAP point cloud to 2,000–3,000 points and denote it as P{gt}. 2. Uniformly sample 2,500 points on the unit sphere to represent UV coordinates and denote them as P. 3. Pass P through F{uv}^{-1} to generate a 3D point cloud, then compute the Chamfer distance between this output and P{gt}. 4. Pass the generated 3D points through F{uv} to reconstruct UV coordinates, then compute the L2 distance between the reconstructed coordinates and the original P. 5. Apply the rendering loss L{\text{render}} and mask loss L{\text{mask}} as defined in the main pipeline. 6. Combine all components into the total initialization loss L{\text{init}}. 7. Perform gradient descent to minimize L{\text{init}} and update the weights of both networks. Formulas: The total initialization loss is defined as: L{\text{init}} = L{\text{chamfer}} + aL{\text{cycle2}} + bL{\text{render}} + cL{\text{mask}} Where: L{\text{chamfer}} is the Chamfer distance between the network-generated point cloud and the ground truth: L{\text{chamfer}} = \text{Chamfer}(F{uv}^{-1}(P), P{gt}) Here, F{uv}^{-1}(P) is the point cloud generated by mapping UV coordinates P to 3D space using the inverse network, and P{gt} is the downsampled ground-truth point cloud. L{\text{cycle2}} is the inverse cycle consistency loss (2D-to-3D-to-2D): L{\text{cycle2}} = \|F{uv}(F{uv}^{-1}(P)) - P\|2^2 Here, F{uv} is the texture mapping network, F{uv}^{-1} is the inverse mapping network, and P is the set of original UV coordinates. L{\text{render}} and L{\text{mask}} are the rendering and mask losses from the main pipeline. Parameters: a = 100: Weight for the inverse cycle loss L{\text{cycle2}}. b = 1: Weight for the rendering loss L{\text{render}}. c = 1: Weight for the mask loss L{\text{mask}}. Point cloud downsampling target: 2,000–3,000 points. UV sampling count: 2,500 points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Hyperparameter Configuration for Stochastic Gradient Estimation
body: This article defines the hyperparameter configuration required to optimize differentiable rendering methods using first-order (OurG, OurH) and second-order (OurHVP, OurHVPA) stochastic gradient estimators. It solves the problem of selecting optimal sampling, learning rate, and trust region parameters for inverse rendering tasks such as caustic optimization, shape reconstruction, and texture mapping. What sets this configuration apart from standard NeRF training is the explicit use of Sigma annealing for distribution bandwidth control and antithetic sampling to reduce variance, alongside distinct parameter sets for first-order versus second-order optimization loops. Inputs: Task identifier (e.g., QUAD, BOX2, BOX10, MUG, SHAD, BUNNY, TEXTURE, CNN, CNN5). Method identifier (OurG, OurH, OurHVP, OurHVPA, or FR22). Current optimization iteration t. Outputs: Current learning rate (for first-order methods). Current trust region radius (for second-order methods). Current distribution bandwidth \sigmat. Sample count configuration (doubled via antithetic sampling). The hyperparameters are stored in a lookup table indexed by Method and Task. The structure contains the following fields: samples: Integer or float, base number of samples per iteration. sigmastart: Float, initial bandwidth \sigma for Sigma annealing. sigmaend: Float, final bandwidth \sigma for Sigma annealing. learningrate: Float, initial learning rate (first-order only). trustregion: Float, initial search bound (second-order only). linesearchiter: Integer, number of line search iterations (second-order only). linesearchtol: Float, convergence tolerance for line search (second-order only). recompute: Integer, iterations between line search re-estimations (second-order only). 1. Retrieve Base Parameters: Look up the hyperparameter set for the specified Method and Task from the configuration table. 2. Calculate Current Bandwidth (\sigmat): Perform linear Sigma annealing from sigmastart to sigmaend over the total optimization duration T. \sigmat = \sigma{start} + (\sigma{end} - \sigma{start}) \cdot \frac{t}{T} 3. Determine Sample Count: Let N{base} be the samples value from the configuration. Apply antithetic sampling: The effective sample count is N = 2 \cdot N{base}. The source states "The sample size, which is always antithetic and doubles the sample size, applies to our methods and FR22". 4. Configure Gradient Estimator: If Method is OurG or OurH (First-Order): Set learning rate \eta = learningrate. Update parameters using the learning rate and the stochastic gradient estimate. If Method is OurH, OurHVP, or OurHVPA (Second-Order): Set trust region radius \Delta = trustregion. Perform line search with linesearchiter iterations and tolerance linesearchtol. Check if re-estimation is needed: If current iteration t is a multiple of recompute, re-estimate the line search parameters. Sigma Annealing: Linear schedule for bandwidth \sigma. Controls the distribution used for stochastic estimation. Antithetic Sampling: For every sample x, an antithetic sample -x (or symmetric counterpart) is generated, effectively doubling the sample count for variance reduction. Trust Region: Initial search bound for second-order methods. Defines the region within which the quadratic model is trusted. Recompute: Frequency (in iterations) at which the line search is re-estimated for second-order methods. name: XYZ Learning Rate Scheduling
head: Spatial Learning Rate Adjustment
body: XYZ Learning Rate Scheduling adjusts the learning rate specifically for the 3D Gaussian point locations (xyz) during radiance-field optimization to balance training speed and rendering quality. It distinguishes itself from general scalar schedules by targeting the spatial parameters of the Gaussian primitives, addressing the sensitivity of point positions to large learning rates which can degrade rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs Input: Current iteration t, total iterations T, schedule type, and schedule coefficients. Output: Scalar learning rate \eta{xyz} for the xyz position parameters of the 3D Gaussians. Data Structures The method requires no auxiliary data structures; it computes a scalar value directly from the iteration count and coefficients. Formulas and Steps The method supports several functional forms for \eta{xyz}(t): 1. Two-Stage Rectangular Wave Transformation (rw) rw(x) = \begin{cases} a1, & x \in [0, p1] \\ a2, & x \in [p1, p2] \\ a3, & x \in [p2, 1] \end{cases} Where x = t/T is the normalized iteration. Typical values are a1 = 10^{-3}, a2 = 10^{-6}, a3 = 10^{-9}. Boundaries are p1 = 0.2 (covering 0%–20% of iterations) and p2 = 1.0 (covering 20%–100%). 2. Sine-based Schedule (s(t)) s(t) = \frac{as}{2}\sin\left(bs\frac{t}{T}2\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) + 1 Where as and bs are fitting coefficients. 3. Cosine-based Schedule (c(t)) c(t) = \frac{ac}{2}\cos\left(bc\frac{t}{T}2\pi + \pi\right) + 1 Where ac and bc are fitting coefficients. 4. Linear Schedule (l(t)) Defined by two points (t1, p1) and (t2, p2) via: \frac{l(t)-p2}{p1-p2} = \frac{t-t2}{t1-t2} Where t1 = 1 and t2 = T. 5. Exponential Schedule (E(t)) E(t) = \varepsilon e^{\delta t} + \eta Where \varepsilon, \delta, \eta are fitting coefficients determined such that the function passes through (t1, E(t1)) and (t2, E(t2)) with t1=1 and t2=T. Parameters Fixed learning rates in the range lr \in [10^{-2}, 1] significantly improve training speed but quickly reduce rendering quality. Scheduling is recommended to avoid this range or to decay out of it. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computexyzlearningrate(t: int, T: int, scheduletype: str, params: dict) -> float: """ Compute the learning rate for 3D Gaussian xyz positions. Assumes t is 1-based (1 to T) to match source formulas where t1=1. """ if T <= 0: return 0.0 if scheduletype == 'rectangular': a1, a2, a3 = 1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9 p1, p2 = 0.2, 1.0 x = t / T if x <= p1: return a1 elif x <= p2: return a2 else: return a3 elif scheduletype == 'sine': as = params['as'] bs = params['bs'] return (as / 2.0) math.sin(bs (t / T) 2 math.pi + math.pi / 2) + 1.0 elif scheduletype == 'cosine': ac = params['ac'] bc = params['bc'] return (ac / 2.0) math.cos(bc (t / T) 2 math.pi + math.pi) + 1.0 elif scheduletype == 'linear': # (l(t) - p2) / (p1 - p2) = (t - t2) / (t1 - t2) # t1 = 1, t2 = T t1, t2 = 1, T p1, p2 = params['p1'], params['p2'] return p2 + (p1 - p2) (t - t2) / (t1 - t2) elif scheduletype == 'exponential': # E(t) = eps exp(delta t) + eta # Passes through (1, E1) and (T, E2). Coefficients must be pre-computed. eps = params['eps'] delta = params['delta'] eta = params['eta'] return eps math.exp(delta t) + eta else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown schedule type: {scheduletype}") Edge Cases and Pitfalls Fixed Rate Degradation: Using a fixed learning rate in [10^{-2}, 1] causes rapid degradation of rendering quality. Precision: The rectangular wave uses values as low as 10^{-9}, which may be subject to floating-point precision issues in some optimizers. Coefficient Fitting: For sine, cosine, linear, and exponential schedules, the coefficients are fitting coefficients. name: Per-Parameter Learning Rate Scheduling
head: Feature LR, Opacity LR, Other Learning Rate Adjustments, Rotation LR, Scaling LR
body: Per-Parameter Learning Rate Scheduling adjusts the learning rates for specific parameter groups (scaling, opacity, rotation, and feature vectors) independently during each training iteration. It sets apart from uniform scheduling by allowing distinct optimization dynamics for geometric, radiometric, and structural parameters, which is critical for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and related radiance field representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current training iteration t, initial learning rates for each parameter group (\eta{scale}, \eta{opacity}, \eta{rotation}, \eta{feature}). Output: Updated learning rates for each parameter group for the current iteration. Data Structures: A dictionary or optimizer parameter group configuration mapping parameter names to their current learning rate values. Steps: 1. Initialize learning rates for each parameter group based on empirical ranges or a base rate. 2. For each training iteration t: a. Compute the decay factor or scaling multiplier for each parameter group based on the chosen schedule. b. Update the learning rate for each group: \eta{group}(t) = \eta{group, initial} \times \text{decay}(t) where \text{decay}(t) is specific to the group and iteration. c. Apply the updated learning rates to the respective parameter groups in the optimizer (e.g., Adam). Parameters: \eta{scale, initial}: Initial learning rate for scaling parameters. Typical optimal range: [10^{-3}, 10^{-6}]. Recommended value: 0.005; using 0.05 increases training time by a factor of 2–3 with similar PSNR. \eta{opacity, initial}: Initial learning rate for opacity parameters. Not given in the sources. \eta{rotation, initial}: Initial learning rate for rotation parameters. Not given in the sources. \eta{feature, initial}: Initial learning rate for feature parameters. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Setting \eta{feature} = 0 does not significantly change training speed or quality, indicating that feature learning has less impact on improvement compared to other parameters. High learning rates for scaling cause a wider distribution of Gaussian scales, leading to excessively large Gaussians (high computational demand) and negligibly small Gaussians (negligible contribution). Large learning rates can cause numerical instability (NaN values) during optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: iteration (int): Current training iteration. initiallrs (dict): Dictionary with initial learning rates for 'scale', 'opacity', 'rotation', 'feature'. schedulefn (callable): Function that takes (groupname, iteration, initiallr) and returns the current LR. Returns: dict: Updated learning rates for each parameter group. """ updatedlrs = {} for group in ['scale', 'opacity', 'rotation', 'feature']: updatedlrs[group] = schedulefn(group, iteration, initiallrs[group]) return updatedlrs Note: Specific decay schedules (e.g., cosine, step, exponential) are implementation-dependent and not specified in the sources. The positional learning rate is kept constant at its initial value throughout the LR optimization stage and only allowed to decay from the iteration i = \arg\mini \lfloor r(i) \rfloor = 1. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of initial learning rates and decay functions for each parameter group. Setting feature learning rate to zero may not significantly impact performance, suggesting limited benefit from tuning this parameter. name: gscache_optimize_level
body: gscacheoptimizelevel executes the per-iteration update for a specific resolution level in the gscache radiance field training loop. It advances the Gaussian Splatting model by applying learning rate decay, integrating gradients, managing Gaussian population density through densification and pruning, and resetting opacity states. It differs from standard NeRF optimization by embedding densification and pruning logic directly into the per-level update cycle rather than executing them as separate global phases. The method processes a single optimization level identified by an integer index. It updates the model's parameters, manages the population of 3D Gaussians, and adjusts the learning rate schedule based on the current iteration count. Inputs: level: Integer index of the optimization level being processed. frameid: Current frame or iteration identifier, used for learning rate decay calculation. context: Object containing: iterations[level]: Current iteration count for this level. models[level]: The Gaussian model instance for this level. backwardresults[level]: Gradients and statistics computed from the backward pass. config: Configuration object containing thresholds and intervals. config: maxdensificationiteration: Upper bound for densification/pruning. densificationinterval: Frequency of densification checks. gradientthreshold: Minimum gradient magnitude for densification. opacitythreshold: Opacity value below which Gaussians are pruned. sceneextent: Spatial boundary for densification. sizethreshold: Size limit for pruning. maxopacityresetiteration: Upper bound for opacity resets. opacityresetinterval: Frequency of opacity resets. Outputs: Updated model parameters (positions, colors, opacities, scales, rotations). Updated densification statistics. Modified Gaussian population (via densification/pruning). Updated learning rate. The method relies on the GaussianModel and DiffRasterizerBackwardResult structures defined in the gscache repository. GaussianModel: Stores XYZ positions, colors, opacities, scaling factors, rotation quaternions, and SH features. DiffRasterizerBackwardResult: Contains gradients for XYZ (dxyz), mean 2D (dmean2D), conic matrix (dconic), color (dcolor), opacity (dopacity), and covariance (dcov3D) for each Gaussian point. 1. Increment the iteration counter for the current level: context->iterations[level] += 1;. 2. Compute a decaying learning rate factor based on the frame ID: float factor = 1.f / (1.f + std::log(frameid + 1));. 3. Update the model's learning rate, gradients, and densification statistics using the computed factor and backward results: context->models[level]->updateLearningRate(factor); context->models[level]->updateGradients(context->backwardresults[level]); context->models[level]->updateDensificationStats(context->backwardresults[level]);. 4. If iterations[level] < maxdensificationiteration and iterations[level] % densificationinterval == 0, trigger densification and pruning with gradient, opacity, scene extent, and size thresholds: context->models[level]->densifyAndPrune(context->config->gradientthreshold, context->config->opacitythreshold, context->config->sceneextent, context->config->sizethreshold);. 5. If iterations[level] < maxopacityresetiteration and iterations[level] % opacityresetinterval == 0, reset model opacity: context->models[level]->resetOpacity();. 6. Unconditionally reset opacity on the first iteration: if (context->iterations[level] == 1) { context->models[level]->resetOpacity(); }. 7. Execute the model's optimizer step: context->models[level]->optimize();. Unverified code. Update learning rate, gradients, and densification statistics context.models[level].updatelearningrate(factor) context.models[level].updategradients(context.backwardresults[level]) context.models[level].updatedensificationstats(context.backwardresults[level]) # 4. name: Annealing Schedules
head: Constant Schedule, Exponential Schedule, Linear Schedule, Parameter Annealing Framework
body: Annealing Schedules provide a unified framework for parameter annealing during training, supporting constant, linear, and exponential schedules. Unlike specialized schedules that implement only one decay strategy, this framework offers multiple decay modes within a single implementation. The method computes a scalar value based on the current training step, the total number of steps, and configured bounds. Inputs and Outputs: step: Current training step (integer or array). numsteps: Total number of training steps (integer). initialvalue: Starting value for the schedule (float). finalvalue: Ending value for the schedule (float). scheduletype: String identifier for the schedule ('constant', 'linear', 'exponential'). Output: The computed parameter value (float32). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The implementation relies on vectorized operations over the step index. Steps: 1. Calculate the progress ratio \alpha as the minimum of the normalized step and 1.0: \alpha = \min\left(\frac{\text{step}}{\text{num\steps}}, 1.0\right) 2. Apply the specific formula based on scheduletype: Constant: Return a constant value for all steps: value. Linear: Interpolate between initialvalue and finalvalue: \text{value} = (1.0 - \alpha) \cdot \text{initial\value} + \alpha \cdot \text{final\value} Exponential: Decay exponentially from initialvalue to finalvalue: \text{base} = \frac{\text{final\value}}{\text{initial\value}} \text{value} = \text{initial\value} \cdot (\text{base})^{\alpha} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp def annealschedule(step, numsteps, initialvalue, finalvalue, scheduletype='linear', constantvalue=None): """ Compute the annealed parameter value. Args: step: Current training step (int or jnp.ndarray). numsteps: Total number of training steps (int). initialvalue: Starting value (float). finalvalue: Ending value (float). scheduletype: 'constant', 'linear', or 'exponential'. constantvalue: Value to return for constant schedule. Defaults to initialvalue if None. Returns: The computed parameter value (jnp.ndarray). """ # Calculate progress ratio alpha, capped at 1.0 alpha = jnp.minimum(step / numsteps, 1.0) if scheduletype == 'constant': # Constant schedule returns a fixed value for all steps val = constantvalue if constantvalue is not None else initialvalue return jnp.fulllike(step, val, dtype=jnp.float32) elif scheduletype == 'linear': # Linear interpolation between initial and final return (1.0 - alpha) initialvalue + alpha finalvalue elif scheduletype == 'exponential': # Exponential interpolation # Handle division by zero if initialvalue is 0 if initialvalue == 0: return jnp.fulllike(step, finalvalue, dtype=jnp.float32) base = finalvalue / initialvalue return initialvalue (base alpha) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown schedule type: {scheduletype}") Parameters: initialvalue: Starting value for the schedule. finalvalue: Ending value for the schedule. numsteps: Total number of training steps. Edge Cases: If initialvalue is 0, the exponential base calculation results in division by zero. The implementation must handle this, typically by returning finalvalue or initialvalue directly. If step exceeds numsteps, \alpha is capped at 1.0 to prevent extrapolation. Time Complexity: O(1) per step, involving basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for scalar inputs, or O(N) for batched inputs of size N. Strengths: Simple to implement, flexible, and covers common decay patterns. Limitations: Does not account for loss landscape geometry (unlike adaptive methods). The exponential schedule can be sensitive to the choice of finalvalue if initialvalue is small. When to use: When a simple, predictable decay of hyperparameters is desired. The framework is implemented in the Nerfies repository, which provides code for "Deformable Neural Radiance Fields". It was developed by Keunhong Park et al. at Google and the University of Washington. The implementation uses JAX for efficient computation. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Piecewise Schedule
body: A learning rate scheduling method that composes multiple sub-schedules applied sequentially at specified milestone steps. It differs from continuous decay schedules like Exponential Decay Schedules by allowing abrupt behavioral changes at discrete boundaries, and from Annealing Schedules by its explicit modular composition of independent schedule objects rather than a single parametric function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A global training step index t (integer \ge 0). Output: A scalar learning rate value lr. Data Structures: The schedule object maintains two primary fields: 1. schedules: A list of Schedule objects. Each object implements a method get(stepoffset) that returns a learning rate for a local step offset. 2. milestones: A 1D array of integers representing cumulative step counts. milestones[i] is the global step index where schedules[i] begins. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the schedules list and the milestones array from configuration. 2. Lookup: Given a global step t: a. Find the index idx such that milestones[idx] is the insertion point for t using binary search. b. Determine the base step for the current sub-schedule: if idx \ge 1, the base step is milestones[idx - 1]; otherwise, it is 0. c. Calculate the local step offset: t{\text{local}} = t - \text{base\step}. d. Retrieve the learning rate from the selected sub-schedule: lr = \text{schedules}[idx].\text{get}(t{\text{local}}). Formulas: t{\text{local}} = t - \text{base\step}, where t is the global step, \text{base\step} is the cumulative step count where the current sub-schedule begins, and t{\text{local}} is the offset passed to the sub-schedule. Parameters: Typical values are not specified in the sources. The learning rate values are defined by the individual sub-schedules. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Milestone Alignment: The milestones array must be strictly increasing and sorted. Step Boundaries: The implementation uses side='right' in searchsorted, meaning if t equals milestones[i], the returned index is i+1, selecting schedules[i+1] for that step. Precision: Steps are integers, avoiding floating-point precision issues in step calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp class PiecewiseSchedule: def init(self, schedules, milestones): self.schedules = schedules self.milestones = jnp.array(milestones) def get(self, step): idx = jnp.searchsorted(self.milestones, step, side='right') schedule = self.schedules[idx] baseidx = self.milestones[idx - 1] if idx >= 1 else 0 return schedule.get(step - baseidx) A specific application of piecewise scheduling for light field compression networks, consisting of a training phase and a quantization phase. Both phases use a constant learning rate of 0.01. The training phase lasts 12 epochs, where one epoch is defined as all Sampled Aperture Images (SAIs) being used 500 times, with 5 SAIs fed per iteration to calculate averaged loss. The quantization stage defines one epoch as all SAIs involved 200 times, followed by fine-tuning all consecutive layers for 1 epoch after quantizing each layer. Hardware: Single Nvidia Titan RTX GPU with 24GB memory; Framework: PyTorch. Time Complexity: O(\log N) per step lookup, where N is the number of sub-schedules, due to binary search on milestones. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the milestones array and references to sub-schedules. Strengths: Modular design allows mixing different schedule types. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of milestone boundaries. Discontinuities in learning rate can occur if sub-schedules do not align at boundaries. When to use: When training requires distinct phases with different optimization behaviors. The piecewise schedule structure is implemented in the Nerfies project, a JAX-based implementation of NeRF. It provides a flexible way to manage learning rates in complex training loops. The two-phase schedule configuration is used in light field compression research. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Learning Kernel-Modulated Neural Representation for Efficient Light Field Compression, https://hal.science/hal-04627349v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Exponential Decay Schedules
body: Exponential decay schedules reduce the learning rate multiplicatively over training steps, providing a smooth, continuous transition from high initial exploration to fine-grained convergence. This family differs from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by applying relative reductions rather than absolute ones, and from Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule by avoiding the symmetric "slow-fast-slow" trajectory in favor of a monotonic decrease. It is primarily used in NeRF optimization to stabilize training when the model has converged to a coarse geometry but requires precise refinement of appearance and density fields. All methods in this family compute the learning rate lrt at step t using a base raised to a power proportional to the normalized step count. The core mechanism is: lrt = lr{initial} \times \gamma^{\frac{t}{T}} where \gamma is the decay factor (0 < \gamma < 1) and T is a normalization constant (often total steps or a specific interval). This ensures the learning rate never reaches zero but asymptotically approaches it. Unlike step decay, there are no discrete jumps. The schedule is often combined with warm-up phases to prevent early instability. Defines the standard iterative optimization protocol for NeRFs, combining ray-batched SGD with exponential LR decay and a two-phase loss schedule. It differs from FreeNeRF by using simpler auxiliary models for depth supervision rather than annealing positional encoding frequencies, and explicitly manages regularization weights that decay alongside the learning rate. Choose it for sparse input scenarios requiring explicit regularization management. Applies a base raised to a normalized step exponent to transition from an initial to a final value. It differs from Linear Learning Rate Schedule by applying multiplicative reductions rather than additive ones, and from Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule by providing a continuous curve rather than a symmetric decay profile. Choose it when a monotonic, framework-agnostic decay is required. Combines a linear warm-up phase with an exponential decay trajectory, specifically targeting per-camera exposure parameters or main network weights. It distinguishes itself from Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule by using a constant rate during warm-up followed by geometric decay, and from Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by explicitly incorporating a delayed warm-up period to stabilize initial training. Choose it for sparse or complex captures to prevent large gradient updates before geometric priors are established. Exponential decay is a standard technique in optimization, widely adopted in early neural network training and retained in NeRF pipelines for its simplicity and effectiveness in fine-tuning. In the context of differentiable volume rendering, it addresses the problem of converging sparse input data by preventing large gradient updates once the model has established a coherent geometric prior.

name: Training Loop with Adaptive Regularization & LR Decay
head: NeRF Training Loop with Exponential LR Decay, Ray Batching Training, SimpleNeRF Training Configuration & Loss Schedule, Training Loop with Exponential LR Decay
body: This method defines a specific training protocol for optimizing sparse-input Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by combining an Adam optimizer with exponential learning rate decay, a two-phase loss schedule, and adaptive regularization weights. It solves the problem of training instability and overfitting in sparse view scenarios by progressively introducing complex regularization terms and decaying the learning rate to fine-tune the neural field. It differs from sibling schedules by explicitly coupling the learning rate decay with the activation of specific loss components (e.g., switching from basic color/depth losses to advanced consistency losses) and dynamically scaling regularization weights relative to the learning rate. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images, camera poses, scene bounds, depth priors (optional), and hyperparameters (lr{initial}, decay\rate, decay\steps, batch\size, nSamples, regularization weights). Outputs: Optimized NeRF model parameters (MLP weights, embeddings), training metrics (PSNR, loss). Data Structures: Ray Batches: A tensor of shape (N{rand}, 5) or (N{rand}, 6) containing ray origins (ox, oy, oz) and directions (dx, dy, dz), optionally including depth priors and confidence scores. Optimizer State: Adam optimizer state for model parameters. Model: A neural field (MLP) that maps 3D coordinates and view directions to color and density. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load training images, poses, and bounds. Initialize the NeRF model. Initialize the Adam optimizer with initial learning rate lr{initial} and weight decay. Set global\step = 0. 2. Ray Sampling: Randomly sample N{rand} ray indices. Fetch corresponding ray data (origin, direction, target RGB, depth priors, confidences). Shuffle ray indices periodically to ensure uniform sampling. 3. Forward Pass (Rendering): Render the sampled rays using the neural field model. Compute the predicted RGB map (rgb\map), alphas (alphas\map), depth (depth\map), and auxiliary outputs (e.g., raw density, uncertainty). The rendering process involves volume integration along each ray. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the primary reconstruction loss (Mean Squared Error): loss{img} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (rgbi - targeti)^2 where N is the number of rays in the batch. Phase 1 (Iterations 0 to 10,000): Compute only L{color} (based on loss{img}) and L{sd} (stereo depth loss, if depth priors are available). Total Loss: L = L{color} + L{sd}. Phase 2 (Iterations > 10,000): Compute additional regularization losses: L{ap} (appearance consistency), L{av} (view consistency), and L{cfc} (cross-frame consistency). Adjust loss weights such that their magnitudes are of a similar order. Total Loss: L = L{color} + L{sd} + L{ap} + L{av} + L{cfc}. Adaptive Regularization (Continuous): If Orthoregweight > 0: loss{reg} = tensorf.vector\comp\diffs() L{ortho} = Ortho\reg\weight \times loss{reg} Add L{ortho} to total loss. If L1regweight > 0: loss{reg\L1} = tensorf.density\L1() L{L1} = L1\reg\weight \times loss{reg\L1} Add L{L1} to total loss. Note: L1regweight switches from an initial value to a rest value after the first alpha mask update iteration. If TVweightdensity > 0 or TVweightapp > 0: Decay TV weights by lrfactor every iteration. Compute Total Variation loss for density and appearance fields. Add weighted TV losses to total loss. 5. Backward Pass and Optimization: Zero gradients: optimizer.zerograd(). Compute gradients: totalloss.backward(). Update model parameters: optimizer.step(). 6. Learning Rate and Weight Decay Update: Update the global step: global\step \leftarrow global\step + 1. Calculate the new learning rate using exponential decay: lr{new} = lr{initial} \times (decay\rate)^{\frac{global\step}{decay\steps}} where decay\rate is typically 0.1 and decay\steps is often args.lrate\decay \times 1000. Update the learning rate for all parameter groups in the optimizer. Note: Some implementations apply the decay factor multiplicatively to the current LR: lr{new} = lr{old} \times lr\factor. Ensure consistency with the source formula. 7. Logging and Checkpointing: Compute PSNR for tracking: PSNR = -10 \cdot \log{10}(loss{img}). Log metrics and save checkpoints periodically. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfadaptivereg( model, optimizer, traindataset, valdataset, lrinitial=5e-4, decayrate=0.1, decaysteps=100000, batchsize=2048, nsamples=48, orthoregweight=0.0, l1regweight=0.0, tvweightdensity=0.0, tvweightapp=0.0, lrfactor=0.1, phaseswitchstep=10000): """ Training loop with adaptive regularization and exponential LR decay. """ globalstep = 0 currentlr = lrinitial # Initialize TV weights if applicable currenttvweightdensity = tvweightdensity currenttvweightapp = tvweightapp while globalstep < decaysteps: # Or until convergence # 1. Sample Rays rayindices = samplerandomrays(traindataset, batchsize) rays, targets, depthpriors, confidences = fetchraydata(traindataset, rayindices) # 2. Forward Pass rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, extras = model.render( rays, nsamples=nsamples, whitebg=True, ndcray=False) # 3. Compute Loss # Primary MSE Loss lossimg = torch.mean((rgbmap - targets.rgb) 2) totalloss = lossimg # Phase 1: Basic Losses if globalstep < phaseswitchstep: # Lcolor is already included as lossimg # Lsd (Stereo Depth) if depth priors available if depthpriors is not None: losssd = computestereodepthloss(depthmap, depthpriors, confidences) totalloss += losssd else: # Phase 2: Advanced Losses # Lap, Lav, Lcfc (Placeholder for specific implementations) lossap = computeappearanceconsistencyloss(extras) lossav = computeviewconsistencyloss(extras) losscfc = computecrossframeconsistencyloss(extras) # Weights adjusted to balance magnitudes totalloss += lossap + lossav + losscfc # Adaptive Regularization if orthoregweight > 0: lossregortho = model.vectorcompdiffs() totalloss += orthoregweight lossregortho if l1regweight > 0: # Switch l1regweight after first alpha mask update lossregl1 = model.densityL1() totalloss += l1regweight lossregl1 if currenttvweightdensity > 0: losstvdensity = model.TVlossdensity(tvreg) totalloss += currenttvweightdensity losstvdensity if currenttvweightapp > 0: losstvapp = model.TVlossapp(tvreg) totalloss += currenttvweightapp losstvapp # 4. Backward Pass optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 5. Update Learning Rate and Regularization Weights globalstep += 1 # Exponential LR Decay # Formula: newlrate = lrate (decayrate (globalstep / decaysteps)) # Or multiplicative: lr = lrfactor # Using the explicit exponential formula from as primary, as alternative newlr = lrinitial (decayrate (globalstep / decaysteps)) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = newlr currentlr = newlr # Decay TV weights multiplicatively currenttvweightdensity = lrfactor currenttvweightapp = lrfactor # 6. name: Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule
head: Adam with Exponential Decay, Exponential Decay Schedule, Exponential LR Schedule, ExponentialSchedule, Instant NGP LR Schedule, LambdaLR Exponential Decay, Training Optimizer and Schedule
body: An exponentially decaying schedule transitions from an initial value to a final value using a base raised to a normalized step exponent. It produces a continuous curve without discrete jumps, ensuring the learning rate asymptotically approaches zero rather than reaching it abruptly. It is commonly implemented via framework schedulers like PyTorch's LambdaLR or applied manually in custom training loops. Inputs: Initial learning rate (lr{initial}), decay factor (\gamma), normalization interval (T), current step index (t). Outputs: Adjusted learning rate (lrt). Data Structures: The scheduler maintains a state variable for the current step or epoch index. Framework implementations (e.g., LambdaLR) wrap the optimizer and apply a lambda function at each optimization step. Steps: 1. Initialize the optimizer with parameter groups and their respective initial learning rates. 2. Initialize the scheduler state with the starting step index, typically t = start\epoch - 1 to align with zero-based indexing conventions in frameworks like PyTorch's LambdaLR. 3. At each optimization step, compute the decay factor using the formula: lrt = lr{initial} \times \gamma^{\frac{t}{T}} where: lr{initial} is the base learning rate for a parameter group. \gamma is the decay factor (0 < \gamma < 1). t is the current training step or epoch. T is the normalization interval or step size. 4. Apply the computed lrt to the optimizer's parameter groups. 5. Increment the scheduler state index for the next step. Parameters: Typical values for NeRF-style optimization use separate parameter groups: positions (lr{initial} = 10^{-4}), features (lr{initial} = 5 \times 10^{-3}), and MLP weights (lr{initial} = 5 \times 10^{-5}). Decay factor \gamma = 0.33 applied every T = 10,000 steps, often starting after a fixed iteration count (e.g., t \ge 20,000). Pitfalls: Precision underflow may occur if \gamma^{(t/T)} becomes too small for very large t or if \gamma is excessively close to 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeexponentiallr(initiallr, gamma, T, currentstep, startstep=0): """ Compute the learning rate using exponential decay. Args: initiallr (float): The starting learning rate for a parameter group. gamma (float): The decay factor (0 < gamma < 1). T (float): The normalization interval. currentstep (int): The current training step index t. startstep (int): Optional offset to delay decay start (default 0). Returns: float: The adjusted learning rate. """ # Apply optional start step offset to align with implementations that delay decay t = max(0, currentstep - startstep) # Compute the decayed learning rate lr = initiallr (gamma (t / T)) return lr A step-wise decay schedule that reduces a learning rate by a fixed multiplicative factor at regular intervals until a maximum number of decays is reached. It differs from the parent Exponential Decay Schedules by applying discrete, uniform reductions at specific step boundaries rather than a continuous exponential curve. Scales the learning rate for each Gaussian level using a logarithmic decay function dependent on the current frame/iteration ID to stabilize optimization across pyramid levels. At each optimization step, the level iteration counter increments and the decay factor is computed as factor = 1.0 / (1.0 + \log(frameid + 1)), where frameid is the current 0-based optimization iteration index and \log is the natural logarithm. The factor is applied to the model's learning rate via an update function. Adjusts training hyperparameters (radii backward scaler and projection lambda) based on the current iteration count using exponential decay with lower limits. The radii backward scaler follows radii\backward\scaler = \max(init\dss\backward\radii \times \gamma\dss\backward\radii^{(it // steps\dss\backward\radii)}, limit\dss\backward\radii), and the projection lambda follows \lambda\dr\proj = \min(\lambda\dr\proj \times \gamma\proj^{(it // steps\proj)}, limit\proj), where it is the current iteration. Default parameters include init\dss\backward\radii=0, steps\dss\backward\radii=-1 (no update), \gamma\dss\backward\radii=0.99, limit\dss\backward\radii=1.5, steps\proj=-1, \gamma\proj=5, and limit\proj=1.0. Time Complexity: O(1) per step for computing the decay factor, assuming exponentiation is constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for storing the scheduler state (current step). Strengths: Provides a smooth, continuous transition of learning rates that avoids the abrupt changes associated with step decay. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \gamma and T to balance convergence speed and stability. The method is widely used in differentiable volume rendering and NeRF optimization to gradually refine high-frequency details during training. It has been adopted in frameworks like Instant NGP, which applies a factor of 0.33 every 10,000 steps after 20,000 iterations. Framework-specific implementations, such as PyTorch's LambdaLR, are commonly used to wrap optimizers and apply the schedule automatically. google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Shreyas120/l3dassignment3, https://github.com/Shreyas120/l3dassignment3, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Neural Harmonic Textures for High-Quality Primitive Based Neural Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37032-718, fetched 2026-10-26 DBauer15/gscache, https://github.com/DBauer15/gscache, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, https://github.com/pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

head: StepSchedule
body: A step-wise decay schedule that reduces a learning rate by a fixed multiplicative factor at regular intervals until a maximum number of decays is reached. It differs from the parent Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by applying discrete reductions at specific step boundaries rather than a continuous curve. Inputs: Current training step (integer), initial learning rate, decay interval, decay factor, maximum number of decays, and optionally a final learning rate value. Outputs: The current learning rate value. Data Structures: The schedule computes the learning rate directly from the step index and configuration constants without storing intermediate learning rate states. Parameters: initialvalue: The starting learning rate. Typical value: 0.01. decayinterval: The number of steps between each decay event. decayfactor: The multiplicative factor applied per decay. Typical value: 0.33. maxdecays: The maximum number of decays allowed. finalvalue: The learning rate after maxdecays have occurred. If not provided, it is computed as initialvalue decayfactormaxdecays. Algorithm: 1. Calculate the decay phase: phase = step // decayinterval. 2. If phase >= maxdecays, return finalvalue. 3. Otherwise, return initialvalue decayfactorphase. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stepdecaylearningrate(step, initialvalue, decayinterval, decayfactor, maxdecays, finalvalue=None): """ Computes the learning rate for a given step using step decay. Args: step: Current training step (integer). initialvalue: Starting learning rate. decayinterval: Steps between decays. decayfactor: Multiplicative factor per decay. maxdecays: Maximum number of decays. finalvalue: Optional explicit final value. Returns: Current learning rate. """ phase = step // decayinterval if finalvalue is None: finalvalue = initialvalue (decayfactor maxdecays) if phase >= maxdecays: return finalvalue return initialvalue (decayfactor phase) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warm-up: In specific implementations (e.g., Instant-NGP-based NeRF), a linear warm-up phase is applied for the first 1K iterations before the step decay begins. The core step decay formula does not account for warm-up; this must be handled as a separate conditional logic before applying the decay. Boundary Conditions: The decay occurs at multiples of decayinterval. Steps strictly less than decayinterval result in no decay (phase 0). Integer Division: The use of integer division (//) ensures that the decay is discrete. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per step. The calculation involves a single division, a comparison, and a power operation. Memory: O(1). The algorithm only requires storing the configuration constants and the current step index. Measured Performance: In Instant-NGP-based NeRF training, this schedule is used with an initial learning rate of 0.01 over 20K total iterations. Specific decay points are at iterations 9K, 12K, 15K, 17K, and 19K, using a decay factor of 0.33. This implies fixed checkpoints rather than a uniform interval in that specific implementation, which contrasts with the generic decayinterval definition in. The sources disagree on whether the intervals are uniform or fixed specific points. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement and debug; provides clear, discrete reductions in learning rate. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: When discrete, predictable reductions in learning rate are desired. When the training process benefits from specific checkpoint-based adjustments rather than continuous decay. name: Linear Learning Rate Schedule
head: Linear Interpolation Schedule, LinearSchedule
body: A linear interpolation schedule that transitions a learning rate from an initial value to a final value over a specified number of steps. It differs from its sibling Exponential Decay Learning Rate Schedule by using a constant rate of change rather than a multiplicative decay, and from Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule by lacking the smooth, non-linear curvature that reduces the learning rate more aggressively in the middle of the schedule. Inputs and outputs: Input: current training step t, total steps T, initial learning rate lr{init}, final learning rate lr{final}. Output: current learning rate lrt. Data structures: No persistent data structures are required; the schedule is stateless with respect to the optimizer's internal state, depending only on the step counter. Steps: 1. Compute the progress ratio \alpha as the minimum of the normalized step count and 1.0: \alpha = \min\left(\frac{t}{T}, 1.0\right) 2. Compute the learning rate via linear interpolation: lrt = (1 - \alpha) \cdot lr{init} + \alpha \cdot lr{final} Parameters: lr{init}: Starting value of the schedule. lr{final}: Target value at completion. T (or num\steps): Total number of steps for the transition. Edge cases and pitfalls: If t > T, the schedule clamps to lr{final}. Some implementations define the schedule as log-linear interpolation, equivalent to exponential decay, rather than linear interpolation of the rate itself. In such cases, the formula becomes lrt = lr{init} \cdot (lr{final} / lr{init})^{t/T}. An optional initial delay phase can be applied where the learning rate is scaled by a multiplier lr{delay\mult} for the first lr{delay\steps} steps, then eases back to the normal rate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearschedule(step, numsteps, initialvalue, finalvalue, lrdelaysteps=0, lrdelaymult=1.0): """ Compute learning rate using linear interpolation. Args: step: Current training step (integer). numsteps: Total number of steps for the transition (integer). initialvalue: Starting learning rate (float). finalvalue: Target learning rate at completion (float). lrdelaysteps: Number of steps to apply delayed initial learning rate (integer). lrdelaymult: Multiplier for the initial learning rate during delay phase (float). Returns: Current learning rate (float). """ # Handle delay phase if step < lrdelaysteps: return initialvalue lrdelaymult # Compute alpha alpha = min(step / numsteps, 1.0) # Linear interpolation lr = (1.0 - alpha) initialvalue + alpha finalvalue return lr A learning rate schedule that eases slowly using a cosine function to transition between initial and final values. It differs from the parent Linear Learning Rate Schedule by using a smooth, non-linear decay curve rather than a linear interpolation, which can help stabilize training in radiance-field optimization by reducing the learning rate more aggressively in the middle of the schedule. A linear interpolation method to avoid abrupt transitions between training stages by blending the previous coarser representation with the current less-merged one. Transitions between stages are smoothed using linear interpolation over 2k iterations. The interpolated decoded quantity z is computed as: z^{(s)} = (1-\lambda) z^{(s-1)} + \lambda \bar{z}^{(s)} where \lambda \in [0,1] is the transition coefficient. This procedure does not introduce new candidates but progressively relaxes the merging applied to the same underlying set of predictions. Not given in the sources.
