name: Model Architecture Modifications
head: NeRF Architecture Variants, Implicit Representation Modifications
body: Model Architecture Modifications alter the baseline continuous volumetric representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to address specific constraints such as dynamic scenes, noise, semantic understanding, or inference speed. These modifications retain the core volume rendering equation but change the input space, network topology, or output fields to enable features like temporal consistency, object manipulation, or noise-aware rendering. Unlike sibling methods that focus on training hyperparameters or sampling strategies, these modifications fundamentally redefine the neural function or the data structures used to represent the scene. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as uncertainty, semantic labels, or physical properties. Extends NeRF to simulate depth-of-field effects by modeling aperture and focus distance, enabling all-in-focus synthesis from defocused inputs. A cascading view prompt tuning paradigm that iteratively incorporates rendered images from previous stages as visual prompts to enhance image quality. A generative model that learns a distribution over 3D scenes via a latent code, enabling zero-shot novel view synthesis without per-scene optimization. Estimates volumetric density directly from intermediate MLP activation features to replace the coarse density network, targeting inference speedup. Replaces implicit volume density with a continuous scalar field representing distance to the nearest surface, providing geometrically accurate surface extraction. Binds explicit fluid volume values to the NeRF input to handle dynamic fluid scenes, serving as the rendering component in an inverse rendering framework. Solves reflectance decomposition by separating the scene into a view-dependent appearance model and a physically-based material model, enabling relighting. Generalizes NeRF to predict arbitrary per-point feature signals \mathbf{f} alongside density and color, enabling tasks like segmentation and detection. Exploits instance masks from Visual Foundation Models to enhance surface estimation for transparent objects by jointly optimizing a semantic field. Combines Multi-Plane Images (MPI) with NeRF to reconstruct dense 3D representations from single images, with complexity independent of the number of target views. Replaces the continuous MLP with explicit spatial data structures (voxels, octrees, hash tables) to enable real-time rendering and scale to large scenes. Synthesizes normal-light views from under/over-exposed inputs by modeling illumination adaptive volume rendering through local and global concealing fields. Integrates Vision Transformers (ViT) into NeRF architectures to enable generalizable novel view synthesis from single or few images. Modifies NeRF to represent dynamic, articulated human subjects by integrating parametric body priors and semantic latent codes. Personalizes plenoptic mapping parameters for each sampled 3D point to handle test-time scene changes and robustness. Addresses loss of local detail by introducing a hybrid spatial feature learning module (MLCA) and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) module to mix spatial and channel features. Addresses overfitting and artifact generation in sparse-view settings by introducing in-situ depth priors or pseudo-observations. Decomposes the scene representation into specialized sub-networks (experts) dynamically activated based on input characteristics to reduce computation. Extends NeRF architectures to quantify aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, enabling filtering of poorly rendered views and reliable geometry assessment. Decomposes the scene representation into distinct components (foreground/background, object instances) for instance-level editing and segmentation. Decouples intrinsic scene properties (geometry, albedo) from extrinsic appearance factors (illumination, style) for explicit lighting control. Handles input image defects (blur, occlusions) by modeling the degradation process or transient elements as part of the optimization. Introduces modularity and hierarchical structures to handle non-rigid deformation, topological changes, and multi-level stratification. Enables scene editing by exploiting an explicit point cloud representation as the structural basis for the implicit field. A feed-forward method for sparse view synthesis that constructs a target view frustum volume aligned with the novel view. Replaces the global continuous volumetric field with explicit, differentiable geometric primitives (Gaussians, points) for speed and interpretability. A decentralized framework for learning global 3D scene representations from crowd-sourced images while preserving privacy. Represents photo-realistic targets as animatable proxies (meshes with neural textures) to enable rendering of unseen animations. Efficiently synthesizes visualizations from dynamic volumetric scenes by combining explicit spatial feature grids with implicit MLP decoders using tensor decomposition. Reconstructs sharp 3D radiance fields from motion-blurred images and hybrid event-RGB data by modeling complex camera motion blur. Integrates pre-trained DINO vision features into the NeRF architecture to enhance 3D reconstruction, particularly in few-shot scenarios. Represents a scene as a mixture of learnable rectangular planar surfaces, each acting as an independent expert predicting view-dependent color and transparency. An implicit 3D representation that learns variation of object shapes and textures across a semantic category, enabling synthesis from a single unposed image. Extends static NeRF to represent scenes changing over time by augmenting input space with temporal signals or deformation fields. Synthesizes specular reflections by replacing neural network queries for outgoing radiance with ray tracing into the NeRF geometry. High-fidelity synthesis of real refractive objects by simplifying complex ray interactions to a single refraction event using a 4D light field representation. Indoor 3D object detection that explicitly models scene geometry as an opacity field, enabling gradient flow from NeRF to the detection pipeline. Learns a generalizable semantic field that infers semantic labels on novel viewpoints across unseen scenes using cross-reprojection attention. Reciprocally constrains distance and density fields, deriving density from the first derivative of an output distance field. A unified framework for photorealistic and non-photorealistic local appearance editing of pre-trained NeRFs using a 3D edit grid and palette-based neural module. Few-shot view synthesis under unconstrained illumination by enforcing multi-view albedo consistency via intrinsic decomposition. Introduces low-dimensional latent codes \mathbf{z} to condition the radiance field, enabling generative modeling of object categories. Predicts prediction variance (uncertainty) for each sampled point to facilitate active view selection strategies. Memory-efficient continual learning of multiple 3D scenes using a single neural network by factorizing MLP weights into scene-specific and shared components. Specialized NeRF for power transmission lines, using L\infty norm spatial compression and Integrated Positional Encoding to reduce aliasing. Decouples density and color prediction into two distinct networks with different positional encoding frequencies to address overfitting. General category for altering input space, topology, or output fields to address dynamic scenes, noise, or semantic understanding. Predicts residual blend weights for skeletal animation by combining spatial positional encoding with per-frame latent codes. PIE-NeRF is a pipeline integrating physics-based elastodynamic simulation with a neural radiance field representation. Instead of converting the learned implicit surface into a mesh or voxel grid, the method uses a meshless discretisation based on quadratic generalized moving least squares on top of the density field of a NeRF. This enables large deformations and nonlinear hyperelastic material simulation directly on the implicit representation and supports interactive manipulation of real-world captured scenes with complex geometries. DäRF is implemented based on K-planes [36] as NeRF. The MDE Model is DPT-hybrid [38]. The Optimizer is Adam [21]. The NeRF Learning Rate is 1e-2. The MDE Learning Rate is 1e-5. The LR Schedule is Cosine warmup. S3-NeRF is a method using shadow and shading cues to infer scene geometry and enable single-image NeRF training. It employs a UNISURF-based occupancy field 3D representation instead of density. It uses a modified physics-based rendering equation. It uses occupancy-based shadow calculation as key implementation differences. NeRF with Frozen DINO Features is a NeRF variant that integrates pre-trained DINOv2 features by projecting them to match NeRF input dimensions and concatenating them with positional encodings before feeding into the NeRF MLP. The feature projection dimension is 256 (matching NeRF hidden units). The DINO Model is DINOv2-base, pre-trained on ImageNet, frozen during training. Feature Extraction involves the DINOv2-base model outputting dense feature maps Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D} where D=768. Features are bilinearly sampled at projected 2D coordinates (ui, vi) = \Pi(Pi, x) for each 3D point x. The formula for projection is f'(x) = Wf \cdot f(x) + bf where f(x) is the aggregated feature vector from all views, and Wf, bf are learned linear transformation parameters. The input to the NeRF MLP is F\theta([\gamma(x), \gamma(d), f'(x)]) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) where f'(x) is projected to 256 dimensions. NeRF-Swin is a baseline method that performs super-resolution on an LR NeRF using released SwinIR models under the 'Real-World Image Super-Resolution' setting, trained on more than 10k LR-HR pairs. On synthetic Blender dataset, SwinIR may produce false predictions due to domain mismatch. On real-world LLFF dataset, SwinIR tends to be oversmooth and may predict false color or geometry. Metrics: Blender ×2 (100x100): PSNR 26.34, SSIM 0.913, LPIPS 0.075. Blender ×4 (100x100): PSNR 24.85, SSIM 0.881, LPIPS 0.108. Blender ×2 (200x200): PSNR 28.03, SSIM 0.926, LPIPS 0.058. Blender ×4 (200x200): PSNR 26.78, SSIM 0.906, LPIPS 0.086. LLFF ×2: PSNR 25.18, SSIM 0.793, LPIPS 0.147. LLFF ×4: PSNR 23.26, SSIM 0.685, LPIPS 0.247. Neural Architecture Search for NeRF trains NeRFs with different combinations of network depth and width on a volumetric video frame. It measures the quality of images rendered from the trained NeRFs using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR). Network Depth (d) is the number of layers, with an initial search space of {1, 2, 4, 6, 8} and a final selected space of {2, 4}. Network Width (w) is the number of neurons in each layer, with an initial search space of {64, 128, 256} and a final selected space of {128, 256}. On RedAndBlack Frame #1450, PSNR was measured for various architectures to determine the optimal search space. Network depth provides the ability to learn hierarchical representations, while network width provides the capacity to 'memorize' the training data. Reducing width monotonically decreases quality, while reducing depth first improves then drops quality if smaller than 2. Not given in the sources. Multi-Identity NeRF (MI-NeRF) is a neural rendering method that learns a single network to represent multiple identities by modeling multiplicative interactions between facial expressions and identity codes, enabling expression transfer and lip-syncing across unseen identities. It learns a multiplicative module M(Ei, i) that conditions the network, where Ei is the expression code for image i and i is the learnable identity code. The Identity code dimension d is set to 16. Unlike single-identity methods (AD-NeRF, LipNeRF) that learn audio-lip representations from only 3 or 20 seconds, MI-NeRF leverages information from multiple identities for more accurate lip synchronization. It is used for facial expression transfer and lip-synced video synthesis. IntrinsicNeRF is a model that outputs reflectance, shading, and residual terms for real-time augmented applications. It is trained using unsupervised prior and reflectance clustering as constraints in the loss function. Piecewise Linear NeRF (PL-NeRF) is a NeRF variant that uses a piecewise linear opacity formulation for volume rendering, replacing the standard piecewise constant opacity assumption. It optimizes separate networks for coarse and fine models, jointly trained with MSE loss on ground truth images. Batch size is 1024 rays. Learning rate is 5 \times 10^{-4}, decaying exponentially to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Training iterations are 500k per scene. Coarse samples are 128. Fine samples are 64. Hardware is a Single Nvidia V100 GPU. It outperforms vanilla NeRF (constant opacity) in all metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) on Blender and LLFF datasets. It is implemented on top of NeRF-Pytorch [38] by changing volume rendering to piecewise linear opacity formulation and utilizing exact importance sampling. The original NeRF implementation by Mildenhall et al. [1] established the baseline continuous volumetric representation. Subsequent works have extensively modified this architecture to address limitations in speed, generalization, dynamic scenes, and physical accuracy. Reviews such as categorize these modifications into improvements for training/inference speed, handling of dynamic scenes, and integration with other vision tasks. Specific variants like PIE-NeRF integrate physics-based simulation, while others like S3-NeRF focus on single-image training using occupancy fields. The integration of pre-trained vision models, such as DINO, and super-resolution techniques like NeRF-Swin, represents a shift towards leveraging external priors. Architectural searches have identified optimal network depths and widths for volumetric video. Methods like MI-NeRF and IntrinsicNeRF extend the output space for specific applications like lip-syncing and augmented reality. Finally, PL-NeRF addresses quadrature instability in volume rendering. name: DoF-NeRF
head: Depth-of-Field Meets Neural Radiance Fields
body: DoF-NeRF is a neural rendering framework that extends the standard Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to simulate the depth-of-field (DoF) effects of a physical lens, allowing it to operate on views with different focus configurations and manipulate DoF effects by adjusting virtual aperture and focus parameters. Unlike vanilla NeRF, which assumes a pinhole camera model and all-in-focus inputs, DoF-NeRF explicitly models the aperture and focus distance, enabling it to handle shallow DoF inputs and produce clear, all-in-focus novel view synthesis with reduced blurriness and enhanced texture details. It achieves this by combining optical models with classical volume rendering to approximate the DoF effect under arbitrary aperture size and focus distance configurations. DoF-NeRF modifies the NeRF rendering pipeline to account for the Circle of Confusion (CoC) caused by finite aperture size and defocus. The method introduces two learnable parameters per training view: the aperture parameter K and the focus distance F, which are jointly optimized with the NeRF network weights. The rendering process simulates DoF through a "concentrate-and-scatter" mechanism: radiance from spatial points scatters to a particular area (concentration), and the center ray accepts scattered radiance from neighboring rays (scatter). Inputs: A set of N training images I = \{I1, \dots, IN\} with known camera poses (obtained via COLMAP). Outputs: A trained NeRF model G\Theta and optimized learnable parameters: aperture parameters \hat{K} = \{\hat{K}1, \dots, \hat{K}N\} and focus distances \hat{F} = \{\hat{F}1, \dots, \hat{F}N\}. NeRF Model G\Theta: The standard MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Aperture Parameter \hat{K}: A learnable vector of size N \times 1, where \hat{K}n corresponds to the n-th image. Defined as K = f \times D, where f is focal length and D is aperture diameter. Focus Distance \hat{F}: A learnable vector of size N \times 1, where \hat{F}n corresponds to the n-th image. Patch Parameters: N{anchor}: Spacing between anchors on the imaging plane. N{patch}: Size of the square patch (N{patch} \times N{patch}) centered at each anchor. 1. Circle of Confusion (CoC) Diameter: The simplified CoC diameter \delta(ht) for a point at object distance ht is: \delta(ht) = K \times \left| \frac{1}{F} - \frac{1}{ht} \right| where K is the aperture parameter and F is the focus distance. 2. Concentration (Scattered Radiance at Center): The scattered radiance \hat{C}^s(p) at a concentration point p is computed by summing contributions from Ns samples along the ray rp: \hat{C}^s(p) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{Ns} K{volume}(rp, hi) c(rp(hi), d)}{\pi \deltac^2(p)/4} where K{volume} is the volume rendering weight, c is the color, and \deltac(p) is the CoC radius at pixel p. 3. Scatter (Final Observed Color): The final observed color \hat{I}(p) for a pixel p is the sum of scattered radiance from neighboring pixels pj within the CoC radius: \hat{I}(p) = \sum{j=1}^{P} \mathbb{1}{\deltac(p) > 2 \|p - pj\|^2} \hat{C}^s(pj) where P is the number of neighboring pixels considered, and \mathbb{1} is an indicator function checking if the distance between pixels is within the CoC diameter. Note: The source also provides an alternative formulation for scattered radiance \hat{I}{scatter}(p) summing over M neighbors pj and Ns samples: \hat{I}{scatter}(p) = \sum{j=1}^{M} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \mathbb{1}{\delta(h'i) > 2 \|p - pj\|^2} T'{ij} \hat{C}(pj, h'i) 4. Loss Function: The optimization loss L is the photometric error (Mean Squared Error) between synthesized views \hat{I} and observations I, summed over all N input images: L = \sum{n=1}^{N} \| In - \hat{I}n \|2^2 The following pseudocode implements the two-stage optimization process described in. It assumes standard volume rendering functions and PyTorch-like tensor operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def DoFNeRFTraining(Nimages, Niters, Npretrain, Nanchor, Npatch): """ Nimages: Number of training images Niters: Total number of optimization iterations Npretrain: Number of pretraining iterations (Stage 1) Nanchor: Spacing for anchor points on the image plane Npatch: Size of the patch (Npatch x Npatch) """ # 1. Initialize Learnable Parameters # K and F are learnable parameters for each of the N images K = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Nimages, 1), requiresgrad=True) F = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Nimages, 1), requiresgrad=True) # Initialize NeRF Model (standard MLP) NeRFModel = NeRFModelClass() # Assumes standard NeRF architecture # 2. Two-Stage Optimization for i in range(Niters): if i < Npretrain: # Stage 1: Pinhole Camera Training # Train NeRF with aperture parameter set to 0 (pinhole model) # Use random rays for efficiency rays, targetimages = randomraysselection(Nimages) # Standard Volume Rendering (no DoF simulation) renderedimages = VolumeRendering(NeRFModel, rays) # Compute Loss loss = torch.mean((renderedimages - targetimages) 2) # Update NeRF weights only loss.backward() optimizerNeRF.step() optimizerNeRF.zerograd() else: # Stage 2: Joint Optimization with DoF # Use patch-based ray selection rays, targetimages = patchraysselection(Nimages, Nanchor, Npatch) # Step 1: Concentration # Compute scattered radiance at concentration points # Returns scattered radiance Chat and CoC radius deltac Chat, deltac = Concentration(NeRFModel, rays, K, F) # Step 2: Scatter # Compute final observed color using concentrate-and-scatter renderedimages = Scatter(Chat, deltac, rays) # Compute Loss loss = torch.mean((renderedimages - targetimages) 2) # Update NeRF weights, K, and F jointly loss.backward() optimizerall.step() # Updates NeRFModel, K, and F optimizerall.zerograd() return NeRFModel, K, F def Concentration(NeRFModel, rays, K, F): """ Simulates the concentration step: radiance scatters to a particular area. Computes the scattered radiance at the center of the CoC. """ # Sample points along rays # For each ray, compute volume rendering weights and colors # Calculate CoC radius deltac for each pixel based on K and F # Aggregate contributions into Chat (scattered radiance at center) # Formula: Chat(p) = sum(Kvolume color) / (pi deltac^2 / 4) # Implementation detail: # 1. Query NeRF for sigma and color at sampled points along rays # 2. Compute volume rendering weights T # 3. Calculate deltac using delta(ht) = K |1/F - 1/ht| # 4. Sum weighted colors and divide by CoC area return Chat, deltac def Scatter(Chat, deltac, rays): """ Simulates the scatter step: center ray accepts scattered radiance from neighbors. """ # For each pixel p, sum Chat from neighboring pixels pj # where distance ||p - pj||^2 < deltac(p) / 2 # Formula: I(p) = sum{j} 1{deltac(p) > 2||p-pj||^2} Chat(pj) renderedimage = torch.zeroslike(targetimages) for p in pixels: sumradiance = 0 for j in neighbors(p, deltac[p]): if deltac[p] > 2 distance(p, j)2: sumradiance += Chat[j] renderedimage[p] = sumradiance return renderedimage def patchraysselection(Nimages, Nanchor, Npatch): """ Selects rays based on a randomly chosen patch. Anchors are set every Nanchor pixels. One patch of size Npatch x Npatch is randomly chosen. Rays passing through pixels in that patch are returned. """ # 1. Define grid of anchors # 2. Randomly select one anchor index # 3. Define patch boundaries around the anchor # 4. Collect rays corresponding to pixels in the patch # 5. Return rays and corresponding target image patches pass def randomraysselection(Nimages): """ Selects random rays from the N images for Stage 1 training. """ # Randomly sample rays from the N images pass Divergence: Using randomly chosen rays for DoF simulation in the initial stages can lead to divergence or sub-optimal results due to the gathering of rays. This is mitigated by the two-stage optimization process. Computational Cost: Computing rays for the whole imaging plane in each iteration is computationally unacceptable. The patch-based ray selection method is used as a compromise to reduce cost. Blurriness in Vanilla NeRF: Vanilla NeRF is prone to generating blurry renderings and missing texture details when trained on shallow DoF inputs because it ignores the interference between rays and does not model the aperture structure. Time Complexity: The method uses a two-stage optimization. Stage 1 is efficient as it uses random rays and standard volume rendering. Stage 2 uses patch-based ray selection, which is more efficient than processing the entire image plane but more complex than Stage 1 due to the concentrate-and-scatter rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model, and learnable parameters K and F for each training image. The patch-based selection reduces memory pressure compared to full-image processing per iteration. Performance: On the real-world dataset (amiya scene), DoF-NeRF achieves PSNR 28.311 vs NeRF 26.924, SSIM 0.9289 vs 0.9092, and LPIPS 0.1370 vs 0.1633. On the synthetic dataset (room scene), DoF-NeRF achieves PSNR 29.443 vs NeRF 26.668, SSIM 0.9135 vs 0.8743, and LPIPS 0.1502 vs 0.1961. Strengths: Handles shallow DoF inputs effectively. Produces clear, all-in-focus novel views with fine-grained details. Allows direct manipulation of DoF effects by adjusting virtual aperture and focus parameters. Plug-and-play and can be inserted into NeRF-based frameworks. Limitations: Requires joint optimization of aperture and focus distances, which adds complexity to the training process. Performance depends on the quality of the initial camera parameters (obtained via COLMAP) and the accuracy of the depth estimation for synthetic data generation. DoF-NeRF was introduced by Zijin Wu, Juewen Peng, and Weicai Zhong from Huazhong University of Science and Technology and Huawei. It was presented at the ACM Multimedia Conference (MM '22) in Lisboa, Portugal, on October 10–14, 2022. The work addresses the limitation of existing NeRF models, which assume a linear pinhole camera model and all-in-focus inputs, making them unsuitable for real-world images with finite depth-of-field. It builds upon the principles of geometric optics to simulate the aperture of a lens. name: NeRF-VPT
head: NeRF with View Prompt Tuning, NeRF-VPT with Cascading Learning, Neural Radiance Fields via View Prompt Tuning
body: NeRF-VPT is a cascading view prompt tuning paradigm for novel view synthesis that iteratively incorporates visual prompts—specifically, the RGB images rendered in preceding training stages—into subsequent network iterations to progressively enhance image quality. It solves the problem of limited scene understanding in sparse-view or standard NeRF settings by leveraging prior knowledge embedded in the network's own outputs, effectively guiding the optimization direction without requiring external priors or ground-truth images at test time. Unlike methods that rely on external networks or specific data preprocessing, NeRF-VPT is a plug-and-play modification that re-uses the internal representation of the NeRF family, making it transferable to variants like Mip-NeRF and TensoRF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images \{Ik\}, camera poses, and ray origins/directions. The method takes the output of the previous stage (or Stage 0 for the first iteration) as a visual prompt. Outputs: Refined volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for each sampled point along the ray, resulting in a higher-fidelity rendered image \hat{c}(r). Data Structures and Layout: The framework consists of N+1 stages, indexed 0 to N (typically N=6). Stage 0: A standard NeRF network F0. It takes only position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d} as input. It does not use any prior. Stage i (i > 0): A new network Fi. It takes position \mathbf{x}, direction \mathbf{d}, and the rendered RGB image from Stage i-1, denoted c(r){i-1}, as inputs. Feature Integration: The RGB prompt c(r){i-1} is concatenated after the direction encoding DE(\mathbf{d}). This placement is chosen because color is high-frequency data, and encoding is viewed as signal decomposition; concatenating after direction encoding allows the network to modulate color prediction based on the prompt. Parameter Overhead: The method adds negligible parameters, specifically 0.0008 M additional parameters compared to the baseline NeRF. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization (Stage 0): Train a standard NeRF network F0 using position encoding PE(\mathbf{x}) and direction encoding DE(\mathbf{d}) to gain initial knowledge of the 3D space. This stage generates the first set of rendered RGB images, which serve as the initial visual prompt. (\mathbf{c}0, \sigma0) = F0(PE(\mathbf{x}), DE(\mathbf{d})) 2. Cascading Iteration (Stage i, for i = 1 to N): a. Ray Sampling: Sample points \mathbf{x} and directions \mathbf{d} along rays from training viewpoints. b. Encoding: Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using DE(\mathbf{d}). c. Prompt Retrieval: Retrieve the RGB image \mathbf{c}(r){i-1} rendered by the network in the previous stage i-1. d. Input Combination: Concatenate the encoded direction DE(\mathbf{d}) and the previous stage's RGB output \mathbf{c}(r){i-1}. e. Network Forward Pass: Pass the position encoding PE(\mathbf{x}) and the combined direction-prompt vector into the current stage's network Fi. f. Output: The network outputs the refined density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai) = Fi(PE(\mathbf{x}), (DE(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{c}(r){i-1})) 3. Rendering: Compute the final pixel color \hat{c}(r) using the volumetric rendering equation: \hat{c}(r) = \sum{i=n}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) handles occlusion, tn, tf are near/far boundaries, and \deltai is the distance between samples. 4. Loss Calculation: Minimize the mean squared error between the rendered color \hat{c}(r) and the ground-truth color c(r): L = \sum{r \in R} ||\hat{c}(r) - c(r)|| where R represents all image pixels in the training data. 5. Termination: Training concludes once the maximum number of stages (typically 5 or 6) is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfvpt(trainingimages, poses, numstages=6): """ Trains a NeRF-VPT model using cascading view prompt tuning. Args: trainingimages: List of ground truth RGB images. poses: Camera poses corresponding to training images. numstages: Number of cascading stages (0 to N). Returns: finalnetwork: The network from the final stage. """ # Stage 0: Standard NeRF initialization # F0 takes only position and direction networkprev = initializestandardnerf() for stage in range(1, numstages + 1): # Initialize new network for current stage # Fstage takes position, direction, and previous RGB prompt networkcurr = initializenerfstagewithprompt() # Training loop for the current stage for epoch in range(maxepochs): for ray in samplerays(trainingimages, poses): # 1. Ray Sampling pointsx, directionsd = ray.samplepoints() # 2. Encoding posenc = positionalencoding(pointsx) direnc = directionalencoding(directionsd) # 3. Retrieve Visual Prompt # Render image using the previous stage's network # This provides the 'prior knowledge' for the current stage promptrgb = renderimage(networkprev, ray) # 4. Combine Inputs # Concatenate direction encoding and prompt RGB # Prompt is concatenated after direction encoding combinedinput = concatenate(direnc, promptrgb) # 5. Forward Pass # Input: Position Encoding, Combined Direction-Prompt sigma, color = networkcurr(posenc, combinedinput) # 6. Volumetric Rendering # Calculate occlusion weights T = computetransmittance(sigma) # Render final color renderedcolor = volumetricrender(T, sigma, color) # 7. Loss Calculation gtcolor = ray.getgroundtruthcolor() loss = meansquarederror(renderedcolor, gtcolor) # 8. Backpropagation networkcurr.backward(loss) networkcurr.step() # Update previous network for the next stage # Weights can be loaded from the previous round to facilitate convergence networkprev = networkcurr return networkprev Parameters: Number of Stages: 5 to 6 stages are sufficient to achieve maximum performance. Prior Images for Feature Extraction (Alternative/Exploratory): 20 uniformly sampled training images were used in ablation studies to extract features via Swin-Transformer, but this was found to be less effective than the cascading RGB prompt. Resolution: Training resolution varies by dataset (e.g., 400 \times 400 for Realistic Synthetic 360, 504 \times 376 for Real Forward-Facing). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ground Truth Unavailability: Directly providing ground truth images as priors fails during testing for unknown viewpoints because ground truth is unavailable. NeRF-VPT solves this by using rendered images from the pre-trained model as the prompt, which are available for all viewpoints. Feature Fusion Limitations: Extracting features from multiple images via Swin-Transformer or CNN and fusing them into an MLP showed limited improvement because it is challenging to encapsulate multi-view information within a single feature. Placement of Prompt: Incorporating priors into direction encoding yields higher PSNR than position encoding because direction information induces diverse color variations for the same position after volume density is predicted. A configuration where NeRF-VPT is used to achieve high-quality rendering with significantly fewer input views (e.g., 45 views achieving quality comparable to 180 views in standard NeRF). The plug-and-play integration of the view prompt tuning mechanism into other NeRF variants like Mip-NeRF and TensoRF to elevate their performance. Time Complexity: Training time per iteration decreases significantly as the cascade progresses (from Stage 1 to 6). This is because increasingly accurate visual prompts reduce the learning difficulty for the network. For example, on the Replica dataset, training time drops from 8.78 hours in Stage 1 to 0.61 hours in Stage 6. Memory Complexity: The parameter overhead is negligible, adding only 0.0008 M parameters compared to the baseline NeRF. Measured Performance: Realistic Synthetic 360 Dataset: NeRF-VPT (Stage 6) achieves PSNR 34.95, SSIM 0.977, LPIPS 0.042, outperforming NeRF (31.01, 0.947, 0.081) and Mip-NeRF (33.09, 0.961, 0.043). Real Forward-Facing Dataset: NeRF-VPT (Stage 6) achieves PSNR 28.95, SSIM 0.872, LPIPS 0.158, outperforming NeRF (26.50, 0.811, 0.250) and Mip-NeRF (27.13, 0.839, 0.164). Replica Dataset: Rendering speed is 0.108 FPS, compared to 0.103 FPS for NeRF. Depth Quality: Depth prediction quality is maintained with a Mean-Squared Error distance of 0.02, identical to baseline NeRF, despite significant image quality improvements. Strengths: Plug-and-play compatibility, significant improvement in novel view synthesis quality, effective handling of sparse views, and reduced training time in later stages. Limitations: Requires multiple training stages (increasing total training time compared to a single-stage NeRF), and depth estimation does not improve over the baseline. NeRF-VPT was introduced in 2024 in the paper "NeRF-VPT: Learning Novel View Representations with Neural Radiance Fields via View Prompt Tuning" presented at the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. The method builds on the success of NeRF and addresses limitations in prior knowledge incorporation methods that relied on external networks or ground truth images. It draws inspiration from cascading learning strategies used in other computer vision applications like object detection and super-resolution. name: NeRF-VAE
head: Variational Autoencoder for NeRF
body: NeRF-VAE is a generative neural radiance field model that learns a distribution over 3D scenes, enabling generalization to out-of-distribution scenes without per-scene optimization. Unlike standard NeRF, which requires training a separate network for each specific scene, NeRF-VAE embeds the scene representation into a single latent code sampled from a learned prior, allowing for zero-shot novel view synthesis of new scenes. It distinguishes itself from other generative NeRF variants by using iterative amortized inference to recover the latent code from input views, rather than relying on explicit geometric templates or external GAN generators. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with corresponding camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^N. Output: A continuous radiance field function F\Theta parameterized by weights \Theta, conditioned on a latent code \mathbf{z}. The function maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: 1. Latent Code (\mathbf{z}): A vector in \mathbb{R}^D representing the global scene structure and appearance. 2. Encoder (E\phi): A ResNet-based convolutional neural network that maps input images to the parameters of the approximate posterior distribution q\phi(\mathbf{z} | \{Ii\}). 3. Scene Function (F\Theta): An attention-based neural network (replacing the standard MLP) that takes \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, and \mathbf{z} as inputs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Encoding: Given input views, the ResNet encoder E\phi processes the images to produce the mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 of the approximate posterior distribution q\phi(\mathbf{z} | \{Ii\}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2 I). 2. Latent Sampling: Sample a latent code \mathbf{z} from the approximate posterior using the reparameterization trick: \mathbf{z} = \mu + \epsilon \odot \sigma, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 3. Iterative Amortized Inference: To refine the latent code, the model iteratively updates \mathbf{z} by conditioning on the rendered images and the input views, minimizing the reconstruction loss and KL divergence. 4. Rendering: For a target ray, query the scene function F\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{z}) to get \sigma and \mathbf{c}. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the pixel color C(r) for ray r using standard volume rendering integration: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \mathbf{c}(r(t)) \alpha(r(t)) dt where \alpha(t) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(t) \delta t) and T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(s) ds). 6. Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is the sum of the reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{rec} (e.g., MSE between rendered and input images) and the KL divergence term \mathcal{L}{KL}: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \beta \mathcal{L}{KL}(q\phi(\mathbf{z} | \{Ii\}) || p(\mathbf{z})) where p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(0, I) is the prior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfvaetrain(inputimages, cameraposes, encoder, scenefn, numiterations): # Initialize encoder parameters phi and scene function parameters Theta # Initialize latent prior p(z) = N(0, I) for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Encode input views to get approximate posterior parameters mu, logvar = encoder(inputimages) sigma = exp(0.5 logvar) # 2. Sample latent code z epsilon = randomnormal(mu.shape) z = mu + epsilon sigma # 3. Render images using z renderedimages = [] for i, (img, pose) in enumerate(zip(inputimages, cameraposes)): # Generate rays from pose rays = generaterays(pose) # Query scene function with z sigmavals, colorvals = scenefn(rays, z) # Volume render renderedimg = volumerender(rays, sigmavals, colorvals) renderedimages.append(renderedimg) # 4. Compute losses recloss = meansquarederror(inputimages, renderedimages) klloss = -0.5 sum(1 + logvar - mu2 - exp(logvar)) totalloss = recloss + beta klloss # 5. Backpropagate and update encoder and scene function updateparameters(encoder, scenefn, totalloss) return encoder, scenefn Parameters: \beta: Weight for the KL divergence term. Typical value: 1.0. D: Dimension of latent code \mathbf{z}. Not given in the sources. \beta in loss: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Expressivity: With a large number of input views (>100), the fixed latent code may not capture sufficient detail, leading to lower fidelity than per-scene NeRF. Inference Time: Iterative amortized inference can be slow compared to direct encoding. General framework for conditioning NeRFs on latent codes. Methods for estimating uncertainty in NeRF predictions. Techniques for training NeRFs with limited input views. Time Complexity: Training time is independent of the number of scenes but depends on the number of input views per scene. Inference (encoding) requires forward pass through ResNet and iterative updates. Rendering is similar to standard NeRF but with additional conditioning. Memory Complexity: Stores one set of network weights for the entire dataset, plus the latent codes for each scene. Significantly less memory than storing separate NeRFs for each scene. Performance: Outperforms baseline NeRF with few views (5-20) due to regularization from the generative prior. Underperforms baseline NeRF with many views (100+) due to lower scene expressivity. Strengths: Generalizes to new scenes; no per-scene training required; compact representation. Limitations: Lower fidelity with many views; inference latency for latent recovery. NeRF-VAE was proposed by Kosiorek et al. in January 2021. It was one of the first methods to combine variational autoencoders with neural radiance fields to enable generative modeling of 3D scenes. The method was evaluated on standard GAN datasets such as Celeb-A, CARLA, and Cats. name: Activation Feature Density Approximation
head: Approximate density extraction, f3 density functions
body: Activation Feature Density Approximation estimates volumetric density \hat{d} directly from intermediate activation features f\ell of a coordinate-based MLP, replacing the expensive evaluation of the coarse density network with a lightweight computation. It differs from sibling methods that modify network topology or input space by exploiting the statistical properties of existing hidden activations to infer scene structure, primarily targeting inference speedup in real-world scenes. Inputs and Outputs Input: Intermediate activation features f\ell for a ray r at layer \ell. Output: Estimated density values \hat{d} and derived weights \hat{w} for sample positions. Data Structures Activation Features (A^{(\ell)}): A tensor of shape Ns \times Nh, where Ns is the number of samples along the ray and Nh is the number of hidden units in layer \ell. The values are recorded after the ReLU activation function. Feature Vector (f\ell): A vector of length Ns, computed per sample. Steps 1. Extract Activation Features: For each sample i along ray r, compute the mean activation over the hidden units Nh: f\ell^{(i)} = \frac{1}{Nh} \sum{j=1}^{Nh} A^{(\ell)}{i,j} where A^{(\ell)}{i,j} is the activation of the j-th hidden unit for the i-th sample at layer \ell. 2. Compute Statistics: Calculate the mean \mu(f\ell) and standard deviation \sigma(f\ell) of the feature vector f\ell along the last dimension (the Ns samples): \mu(f\ell) = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} f\ell^{(i)} \sigma(f\ell) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} (f\ell^{(i)} - \mu(f\ell))^2} 3. Estimate Density: Apply one of three handcrafted functions fk (k \in \{1, 2, 3\}) to f\ell to produce the estimated density \hat{d}: f1 (Aggressive): \hat{d} = \text{ReLU}\left( (\mu(f\ell) - \sigma(f\ell)) - f\ell \right) f2 (Conservative): \hat{d} = \text{ReLU}\left( \left(\mu(f\ell) - \frac{\sigma(f\ell)}{2}\right) - f\ell \right) f3 (Squared Conservative): \hat{d} = \text{ReLU}\left( \left(\mu(f\ell) - \frac{\sigma(f\ell)}{2}\right) - f\ell \right)^2 These functions are designed such that low activation values (indicating significant density) result in positive density estimates, while high activations result in zero. 4. Normalize to Weights: Convert the estimated density \hat{d} to weights \hat{w} using piecewise-constant PDF normalization: \hat{w}i = \frac{\hat{d}i}{\sum{j=1}^{Ns} \hat{d}j} 5. Sample Positions: Perform inverse transform sampling on the weights \hat{w} to determine sample positions, as done in standard NeRF. Parameters Layer \ell: The method is applied to the first 3 layers of the MLP. Layer 2 is identified as the optimal trade-off between speedup and quality. Function Choice: f2 is recommended for Mip-NeRF as it performed best in experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls High Variance: Function f1 is prone to failure if the activation distribution along a ray exhibits high standard deviation. Insufficient Detail: Functions f2 and f3 are more conservative and may lead to insufficient detail, particularly as the interval between fine samples grows larger. MLP Layer Selection: Applying the method to earlier layers accelerates inference more substantially but may reduce reconstruction quality compared to later layers (e.g., layer 2 vs layer 1 or 3). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def relu(x): return max(0.0, x) def activationfeaturedensityapproximation(activations, layerindex): """ activations: list of lists, shape (Ns, Nh) layerindex: int, the layer from which activations are taken (1, 2, or 3) """ Ns = len(activations) Nh = len(activations[0]) # Step 1: Extract mean activation per sample fl = [] for i in range(Ns): meanval = sum(activations[i]) / Nh fl.append(meanval) # Step 2: Compute mean and standard deviation of fl muf = sum(fl) / Ns variance = sum((x - muf) 2 for x in fl) / Ns sigmaf = math.sqrt(variance) # Step 3: Estimate density using f2 (recommended) # f2: ReLU( (mu - sigma/2) - f) threshold = muf - (sigmaf / 2.0) dhat = [] for x in fl: val = threshold - x dhat.append(relu(val)) # Step 4: Normalize to weights sumd = sum(dhat) if sumd == 0: # Handle case where all densities are zero what = [0.0] Ns else: what = [d / sumd for d in dhat] return what An aggressive approximation using \mu - \sigma. Prone to failure with high variance distributions. A conservative approximation using \mu - \sigma/2. Balances speed and detail; best performance for Mip-NeRF. A squared version of f2. More conservative than f1, potentially losing detail. Time Complexity: Significantly reduces inference time by replacing the coarse MLP evaluation with simple statistical operations. Speedups of 40-58% were observed on NeRF and 72-76% on proposal networks. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead beyond storing intermediate activations, which are already required for backpropagation or visualization. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF LLFF dataset (1008x756), using layer 2 with f2 achieved 25.44 PSNR, 0.75 SSIM, and 0.22 LPIPS. Strengths: Effective speedup for real-world scenes; leverages existing network internals without architectural changes. Limitations: Quality degradation if variance is high (f1) or if detail is lost (f2/f3); dependent on the specific layer chosen. When to Use: When inference speed is critical and the scene has well-behaved activation distributions; particularly effective for Mip-NeRF due to its higher sample count. When Not to Use: When high fidelity is required in scenes with complex, high-variance activation patterns; or when using layers that do not store structural information effectively. The method was proposed in "Analyzing the Internals of Neural Radiance Fields" (2024). It is based on the observation that intermediate activations in coordinate-based MLPs exhibit structural information and that activation minima correlate with significant density. The approach was evaluated on NeRF, Mip-NeRF, and proposal network samplers (nerfacto) using Blender and LLFF datasets. Analyzing the Internals of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvprw63382.2024.00288, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations
head: SDF-based Neural Fields, Truncated SDF NeRF, Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF)
body: Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations replace the implicit volume density field of standard NeRFs with a continuous scalar field representing the distance to the nearest surface, providing a more explicit and geometrically accurate formulation. This approach addresses the geometric inaccuracy and surface holes typical of density-based NeRFs by leveraging the zero-level set of the SDF to define geometry. Unlike standard density fields that model opacity as a volumetric property, SDFs model the scene as a boundary, enabling precise mesh extraction and improved surface reconstruction. The core mechanism involves predicting a continuous scalar field s: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} instead of a density \sigma(\mathbf{x}). For any 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, the function value s(\mathbf{x}) represents the distance to the closest surface, with the sign conventionally negative inside the object and positive outside. The surface is defined as the zero-level set \{\mathbf{x} \mid s(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}. To enable volumetric rendering, the predicted SDF value s(\mathbf{x}) is converted into a density \sigma(\mathbf{x}). The specific conversion function is not detailed in the provided sources. The surface normal \mathbf{n} is derived from the SDF gradient \nabla s(\mathbf{x}) [Parent]. ProbeSDF is a neural surface reconstruction method that decouples spatial and angular light field components using two volumetric grids of different resolutions to achieve real-time rendering and accelerated training. It addresses the computational bottleneck of standard SDF-based neural fields by replacing the core appearance MLP with a lightweight model that uses spherical harmonic light field probes for angular variation and planar factorized features for spatial texture. Unlike Plenoxels or 3D Gaussian Splatting which require significantly more parameters per voxel (27 and 48 respectively), ProbeSDF uses as few as four parameters per voxel while maintaining high expressiveness. SDF-based Neural Fields replace the implicit density field of standard NeRFs with a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to provide a more explicit and smooth formulation of surfaces. This approach addresses the geometric inaccuracy and surface holes typical of density-based NeRFs by leveraging the zero-level set of the SDF to define geometry. Builds on Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations. VolRecon is a generalizable implicit reconstruction method that predicts a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) to reconstruct scenes with fine details and minimal noise from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SparseNeuS by combining local projection features aggregated via a view transformer with global shape priors from a coarse feature volume, processed by a ray transformer to resolve surface ambiguity. Unlike standard SDF approaches that define distance in any direction, SRDF constrains the distance measurement to the specific ray direction, enabling more robust surface localization along the viewing ray. This method integrates Signed Distance Function (SDF) representations for geometry with Physically Based Rendering (PBR) material models to achieve smoother geometric structures and accurate specular reflections, overcoming the coarse detail and foggy artifacts typical of standard NeRF. Unlike sibling methods such as ProbeSDF or SDF-based Neural Fields which may focus primarily on geometry or general neural fields, this approach specifically decouples geometry (via SDF) from material appearance (via PBR), providing interpretable parameters for reflection and diffuse components. It builds on Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations by converting the SDF into a density field for volumetric integration while using the SDF gradient for surface normals required by the PBR model. RS-Recon is a neural scene reconstruction method that replaces the standard Signed Distance Function (SDF) with a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) to model volume density, specifically addressing noise and inaccuracies in multi-object indoor scenes. Unlike SDF-based methods which consider surface points across the entire scene and may exhibit fluctuations leading to local minimum values, SRDF measures the shortest distance to the surface along a specific camera ray, eliminating the influence of surrounding surfaces not located on that ray. Definition: A method that replaces the density MLP with a truncated SDF MLP and computes pixel color as a weighted sum of sampled colors. Step: Reconstruct the triangular mesh of the scene by using Marching Cubes [208] on the truncated SDF MLP. Formula: C(r) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} wi ci}{\sum{i=1}^{N} wi} where ci is the sampled color and wi is the weight. wi = \Phi\left(\frac{Di}{tr}\right) \cdot \Phi\left(-\frac{Di}{tr}\right) where Di is the SDF value, tr is the truncation distance, and \Phi is the sigmoid function. The truncation distance cuts off any SDF value too far from individual surfaces. Parameter: Per-frame appearance latent code from NeRF-W [88] is used to account for white-balance and exposure changes. Pitfall: Multiple ray-surface intersections are handled by assigning a weight of zero to subsequent truncation regions so they do not contribute to the pixel color. The use of SDFs in neural rendering emerged as a concurrent improvement to standard NeRF architectures, aiming to solve the ambiguity of density-based representations. Azinovic et al. introduced the truncated SDF approach in April 2021, replacing the density MLP with a truncated SDF MLP to enable clean mesh reconstruction via Marching Cubes. In June 2022, SparseNeuS improved upon NeuS by focusing on sparse-view SDF reconstruction using a geometry encoding volume with learnable image features as a hybrid representation method. These developments shifted the focus from implicit volume density to explicit surface boundaries, allowing for better geometric fidelity and direct mesh extraction. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: ProbeSDF
head: Light Field Probes For Neural Surface Reconstruction
body: ProbeSDF is a neural surface reconstruction method that decouples spatial and angular light field components using two volumetric grids of different resolutions to achieve real-time rendering and accelerated training. It addresses the computational bottleneck of standard SDF-based neural fields by replacing the core appearance MLP with a lightweight model that uses spherical harmonic light field probes for angular variation and planar factorized features for spatial texture. Unlike Plenoxels or 3D Gaussian Splatting which require significantly more parameters per voxel (27 and 48 respectively), ProbeSDF uses as few as four parameters per voxel while maintaining high expressiveness. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images, camera poses, and an initial sparse voxel grid structure. Outputs: A signed distance function (SDF) field, spatial feature grid, angular feature grid (probes), and optionally per-camera bias vectors. The final output is rendered images via standard SDF-based volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. SDF Grid: Implicit representation of 3D shape storing SDF values and derived surface normals \mathbf{n}. 2. Spatial Feature Grid (Fs): High-resolution grid using planar factorization. Each 16^3 tile contains three orthogonal planes of resolution 16 \times 16, where each plane stores ns coefficients per element, yielding 3 \times 16 \times 16 \times ns spatial coefficients per tile. 3. Angular Feature Grid (Fa): Coarser grid storing light field probes as spherical harmonic coefficients. Probes are stored at the corners of the spatial tiles. Probes at shared corners of adjacent tiles are duplicated in memory but maintain shared values to benefit from hardware-accelerated interpolation. Each probe stores l^2 \times na coefficients, where l is the spherical harmonic order and na is the number of angular features per coefficient. 4. MLP: A small neural network with 2 hidden layers, 32 neurons per layer, ReLU activations, and a sigmoid activation for the final output layer. Parameters: ns: Number of spatial coefficients per probe dimension. Typical value: 4 or 8. na: Number of angular features. Typical value: 4 or 8. l: Spherical harmonic order. Up to 16 coefficients (l=4). Typical value: 4. Per-camera bias vectors: Optional MLP bias vectors trained per camera to handle inconsistent shadows or large exposure changes (used for DTU and BMVS). Grid resolutions: DTU (1000^3), BMVS (666^3), MVMannequins (2500 \times 1250 \times 2500, 2mm/voxel), ActorsHQ (3000 \times 4000 \times 3000, 0.6mm/voxel). Method Steps: 1. Ray Marching and SDF Evaluation: For a given camera ray, sample points \mathbf{x} along the ray. Query the SDF grid to get s(\mathbf{x}). Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} = \nabla s(\mathbf{x}) / \|\nabla s(\mathbf{x})\|. Convert the SDF value to volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) using a differentiable mapping that concentrates density near the zero-level set. 2. Spatial Feature Extraction (Fs): For point \mathbf{x}, identify the containing 16^3 tile. Retrieve the three orthogonal planes (Fx, Fy, Fz) for that tile. Compute the spatial feature vector via planar factorization (outer product): Fs = Fx \otimes Fy \otimes Fz This reduces dimensionality by storing three orthogonal planes per tile instead of a dense 3D grid. 3. Angular Feature Extraction (Fa): Compute the reflected vector \mathbf{r} based on the view direction \mathbf{v} and surface normal \mathbf{n} (typically \mathbf{r} = 2(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{v}). Retrieve the 8 corner probes of the containing tile in the angular grid. Tri-linearly interpolate the spherical harmonic coefficients from these 8 corners to obtain the angular feature vector Fa(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}). 4. Incidence Angle Embedding: Compute the power terms of the cosine angle between the view direction and the surface normal to account for grazing angle reflectivity (Fresnel approximation): \text{incidence} = [(1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^0, (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^1, \dots, (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^5] The term (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) approximates \cos \theta where \theta is the angle of incidence. 5. Radiance Decoding: Concatenate Fs, Fa, and the incidence angle embeddings. Pass them through the tiny MLP to predict the outgoing radiance C: C = MLP(Fs(\mathbf{x}), Fa(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}), (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^0, \dots, (1 - \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})^5, \dots) The MLP acts as a minimal BRDF decoder. 6. Volume Rendering: Composite the predicted radiance C along the ray using standard SDF-based volume rendering. 7. Optimization: Optimize the SDF grid values, spatial features, angular probe coefficients, and optionally per-camera bias vectors using gradient descent to minimize the difference between rendered and input images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinear3d(grid, x, y, z): """Trilinear interpolation on a 3D grid.""" x0, y0, z0 = int(np.floor(x)), int(np.floor(y)), int(np.floor(z)) x1, y1, z1 = min(x0 + 1, grid.shape[0]-1), min(y0 + 1, grid.shape[1]-1), min(z0 + 1, grid.shape[2]-1) dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 c00 = grid[x0, y0, z0] (1-dx) + grid[x1, y0, z0] dx c01 = grid[x0, y1, z0] (1-dx) + grid[x1, y1, z0] dx c10 = grid[x0, y0, z1] (1-dx) + grid[x1, y0, z1] dx c11 = grid[x0, y1, z1] (1-dx) + grid[x1, y1, z1] dx return (c00 (1-dy) + c01 dy) (1-dz) + (c10 (1-dy) + c11 dy) dz def bilinear2d(plane, u, v): """Bilinear interpolation on a 2D plane.""" u0, v0 = int(np.floor(u)), int(np.floor(v)) u1, v1 = min(u0 + 1, plane.shape[0]-1), min(v0 + 1, plane.shape[1]-1) du, dv = u - u0, v - v0 c0 = plane[u0, v0] (1-du) + plane[u1, v0] du c1 = plane[u0, v1] (1-du) + plane[u1, v1] du return c0 (1-dv) + c1 dv def relu(x): return np.maximum(0, x) def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) def sdftodensity(s, scale=10.0): """Standard differentiable SDF-to-density conversion.""" return scale np.exp(-scale np.abs(s)) def computenormal(sdfgrid, x, y, z, eps=1e-4): """Finite difference gradient of SDF.""" gradx = (trilinear3d(sdfgrid, x+eps, y, z) - trilinear3d(sdfgrid, x-eps, y, z)) / (2eps) grady = (trilinear3d(sdfgrid, x, y+eps, z) - trilinear3d(sdfgrid, x, y-eps, z)) / (2eps) gradz = (trilinear3d(sdfgrid, x, y, z+eps) - trilinear3d(sdfgrid, x, y, z-eps)) / (2eps) grad = np.array([gradx, grady, gradz]) return grad / np.linalg.norm(grad) def probesdfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfgrid, spatialgrid, angulargrid, tilesize=16, ns=4, na=4, l=4, mlpweights=None): """Renders a single ray using ProbeSDF appearance model.""" numsamples = 256 dt = 0.01 color = np.zeros(3) alphaaccum = 0.0 for t in range(numsamples): x = rayorigin + t raydirection dt gx, gy, gz = x / tilesize sval = trilinear3d(sdfgrid, gx, gy, gz) if sval > 0.5: continue n = computenormal(sdfgrid, gx, gy, gz) sigma = sdftodensity(sval) # Spatial Features (Planar Factorization) tileid = (int(np.floor(gx)), int(np.floor(gy)), int(np.floor(gz))) planes = spatialgrid[tileid] # Shape (3, 16, 16, ns) localu, localv, localw = gx - tileid[0], gy - tileid[1], gz - tileid[2] Fx = bilinear2d(planes[0], localu, localv) Fy = bilinear2d(planes[1], localu, localv) Fz = bilinear2d(planes[2], localu, localv) Fs = np.outer(np.outer(Fx, Fy), Fz).flatten() # Angular Features (Trilinear interpolation of 8 corner probes) v = raydirection r = 2 np.dot(n, v) n - v cornerids = [ (tileid[0], tileid[1], tileid[2]), (tileid[0]+1, tileid[1], tileid[2]), (tileid[0], tileid[1]+1, tileid[2]), (tileid[0]+1, tileid[1]+1, tileid[2]), (tileid[0], tileid[1], tileid[2]+1), (tileid[0]+1, tileid[1], tileid[2]+1), (tileid[0], tileid[1]+1, tileid[2]+1), (tileid[0]+1, tileid[1]+1, tileid[2]+1) ] cornercoeffs = [angulargrid[cid].flatten() for cid in cornerids] weights = [ (1-localu)(1-localv)(1-localw), localu(1-localv)(1-localw), (1-localu)localv(1-localw), localulocalv(1-localw), (1-localu)(1-localv)localw, localu(1-localv)localw, (1-localu)localvlocalw, localulocalvlocalw ] Fa = np.zeros(len(cornercoeffs[0])) for i, c in enumerate(cornercoeffs): Fa += weights[i] c # Incidence Angle Embedding costheta = np.dot(n, v) incidence = np.array([(1 - costheta)i for i in range(6)]) # MLP Decoding inputvec = np.concatenate([Fs, Fa, incidence]) h1 = relu(np.dot(inputvec, mlpweights['W1']) + mlpweights['b1']) h2 = relu(np.dot(h1, mlpweights['W2']) + mlpweights['b2']) C = sigmoid(np.dot(h2, mlpweights['W3']) + mlpweights['b3']) # Volume Rendering alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma dt) weight = alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) color += weight C alphaaccum += weight if alphaaccum > 0.99: break return color Time Complexity: Training converges in minutes (e.g., ~1 min for MVMannequins, ~150-160s for DTU, ~110-120s for BMVS, ~4 min for ActorsHQ) compared to hours for baselines like Voxurf or NeuS2. Rendering achieves 200-300 Hz on DTU and 300-400 Hz on MVMannequins on an RTX A6000 GPU. Memory Complexity: Highly memory efficient. Probes require 1/6th of the memory taken by spatial features when l=4 and ns=na. Model sizes are small (e.g., 30MB for MVMannequins, 56-88MB for DTU, 57-232MB for ActorsHQ). VRAM usage is low (e.g., 5GB for MVMannequins). Performance: MVMannequins: PSNR 36.81-36.90, Chamfer 1.03-1.04mm. ActorsHQ: PSNR 37.48 (r/1), 36.62 (r/4). DTU: PSNR 37.03-37.74, Chamfer 0.68-0.71mm. BlendedMVS: PSNR 35.19-35.89, Chamfer 2.22-2.37mm. Strengths: Real-time rendering, fast training, low memory footprint, high PSNR and geometric accuracy on generic objects and humans with mild specularities. Limitations: Lighting encoded locally degrades extrapolation capabilities, causing shadow artifacts when looking from above or below on datasets with limited camera overlap along latitude (e.g., ActorsHQ legs). Local minima due to shape-radiance ambiguities because light transport is not explicitly simulated. Relighting and material editing are not supported. Targets objects with mild specularities; cone tracing methods are better for strong reflections but require >10 GPU-hours. ProbeSDF was introduced in the paper "ProbeSDF: Light Field Probes For Neural Surface Reconstruction". It builds on the hypothesis that angular components (lighting/environment) are predominantly extrinsic to the surface and locally invariant to parallax, allowing them to be encoded at a lower spatial resolution than intrinsic spatial texture. The method uses a sparse voxel grid based on Voxurf with targeted modifications to implement probes. It is evaluated on four representative datasets: MVMannequins, ActorsHQ, DTU, and BlendedMVS. name: SDF-based Neural Fields
head: SDF NeRF, Signed Distance Function Neural Fields
body: SDF-based Neural Fields replace the implicit density field of standard NeRFs with a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to provide a more explicit and smooth formulation of surfaces. This approach addresses the geometric inaccuracy and surface holes typical of density-based NeRFs by leveraging the zero-level set of the SDF to define geometry. Builds on Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations. The core mechanism involves predicting a continuous scalar field s: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R} instead of a density \sigma(\mathbf{x}). For any 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, the function value s(\mathbf{x}) represents the distance to the closest surface, with the sign conventionally negative inside the object and positive outside. The surface is defined as the zero-level set \{\mathbf{x} \mid s(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}. To enable volumetric rendering, the predicted SDF value s(\mathbf{x}) is converted into a density \sigma(\mathbf{x}). The specific conversion function is not detailed in the provided sources. name: Generalizable Implicit Reconstruction with SRDF
head: VolRecon, Volume Rendering of Signed Ray Distance Functions for Generalizable Multi-View Reconstruction
body: VolRecon is a generalizable implicit reconstruction method that predicts a Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) to reconstruct scenes with fine details and minimal noise from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like SparseNeuS by combining local projection features aggregated via a view transformer with global shape priors from a coarse feature volume, processed by a ray transformer to resolve surface ambiguity. Unlike standard SDF approaches that define distance in any direction, SRDF constrains the distance measurement to the specific ray direction, enabling more robust surface localization along the viewing ray. Inputs: A set of N source images I = \{I1, \dots, IN\} where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, and camera parameters for the source views and the target (reference) view. Outputs: Rendered color image, depth map, and implicitly, a mesh or point cloud representing the scene surface. Data Structures: 1. Feature Maps: \{Fi\}{i=1}^N \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times C}, extracted from source images. 2. Global Feature Volume: Fv \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times K \times C{vol}}, a 3D grid of voxels. 3. Learnable Token: f0 \in \mathbb{R}^C, a single vector used for aggregation in the view transformer. Parameters: N: Number of source views. M: Number of sampled points along a ray. K: Dimension of the global feature volume grid (K^3 voxels). C: Channel dimension of the feature maps. v: Unit ray direction vector (\|v\|2 = 1). o: Ray origin. Step 1: Feature Extraction For each source image Ii, extract feature maps Fi using a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). The resolution is reduced to H/4 \times W/4. Step 2: Global Feature Volume Construction 1. Define the scene bounding volume and divide it into K^3 voxels. 2. For each voxel center pk, project it onto the feature map Fi of each source view i \in \{1, \dots, N\} using bilinear interpolation to obtain features f{k,i}. 3. Compute the mean and variance of the N features \{f{k,i}\}{i=1}^N. 4. Concatenate the mean and variance to form the initial voxel feature. 5. Pass the volume of voxel features through a 3D U-Net to regularize and aggregate information, resulting in the global feature volume Fv. 6. For any 3D point p, the volume feature fv(p) is obtained by trilinear interpolation from Fv. Step 3: Ray Sampling and Projection Feature Extraction For a pixel in the reference view, define a ray p(t) = o + tv for t \ge 0. Sample M points \{pm\}{m=1}^M along this ray. For each sampled point pm: 1. Project pm onto the feature map Fi of each source view i. 2. Extract the color c{m,i} and feature vector f{m,i} using bilinear interpolation. Step 4: View Transformer Aggregate the multi-view features for each point pm into a single projection feature f{p,m}. 1. Initialize the input sequence with the learnable aggregation token f0 and the N multi-view features \{f{m,i}\}{i=1}^N. 2. Apply a self-attention transformer with linear attention. 3. Do not use positional encoding, as the order of source views is not assumed. 4. Compute the projection feature f{p,m} and updated multi-view features \{f'{m,i}\}{i=1}^N: f{p,m}, \{f'{m,i}\}{i=1}^N = \text{ViewTrans}(f0, \{f{m,i}\}{i=1}^N) Step 5: Ray Transformer and SRDF Prediction Compute the SRDF values for all sampled points along the ray. 1. For each point pm, concatenate its projection feature f{p,m} and its volume feature fv(pm). 2. Input the sequence of concatenated features for all M points into a Ray Transformer. 3. The Ray Transformer allows each point to attend to features of other points on the same ray, capturing long-range dependencies. 4. Output the predicted SRDF value \tilde{d}m for each point pm. Step 6: Volume Rendering Render the color and depth using the predicted SRDF values, following the NeuS approach for SDF volume rendering. 1. Convert SRDF \tilde{d}m to density \sigmam using a differentiable mapping that concentrates density near the zero-level set. 2. Compute the accumulated alpha \alpham and transmittance Tm along the ray: \alpham = 1 - \exp(-\sigmam \deltam) Tm = \prod{j=1}^{m-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltam is the distance between adjacent samples. 3. Render the color C and depth D: C = \sum{m=1}^M Tm \alpham cm D = \sum{m=1}^M Tm \alpham tm where cm is the color at pm and tm is the depth coordinate. Formulas: The Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF) \tilde{d}\Omega(p, v) for a point p and direction v is defined as: \tilde{d}\Omega(p, v) = (-1)^{1\Omega(p)} \min{p^ \in M, \frac{p^-p}{\|p^-p\|} = v} \|p - p^\|2 where M is the surface boundary, \Omega is the space, and 1\Omega(p) is the indicator function: 1\Omega(p) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } p \in \Omega \\ 0 & \text{if } p \notin \Omega \end{cases} The standard Signed Distance Function (SDF) d\Omega(p) is the minimum absolute SRDF over all directions v: d\Omega(p) = (-1)^{1\Omega(p)} \minv (|\tilde{d}\Omega(p, v)|) In the implementation, the network directly predicts \tilde{d}\Omega(p, v) for the specific ray direction v. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class VolRecon: def init(self, N, K, C, M, H, W, near=0.0, far=10.0): self.N = N self.K = K self.C = C self.M = M self.H = H self.W = W self.near = near self.far = far # Feature Pyramid Network (simplified as stacked convs) self.fpn = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, C, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(C, C, 3, padding=1, stride=2), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(C, C, 3, padding=1, stride=2), nn.ReLU()) # 3D U-Net approximation for global volume regularization self.globalvolumenet = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(2C, C, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv3d(C, C, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv3d(C, C, 3, padding=1)) # Learnable aggregation token self.f0 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, 1, C)) # View Transformer: Linear attention approximation self.viewtransformer = nn.MultiheadAttention(C, numheads=4, batchfirst=True) # Ray Transformer self.raytransformer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(dmodel=C, nhead=4, batchfirst=True) # MLP to predict SRDF self.srdfmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(C, C), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(C, 1)) def extractfeatures(self, images): """images: [N, 3, H, W] -> [N, C, H/4, W/4]""" return self.fpn(images) def buildglobalvolume(self, featuremaps, voxelcenters, camK, camR, camt): """featuremaps: [N, C, H/4, W/4], voxelcenters: [KKK, 3]""" N, C, Hf, Wf = featuremaps.shape numvoxels = voxelcenters.shape[0] # Project voxel centers to UV for each view uvcoords = [] for i in range(N): # Homogeneous projection: uv = K (R p + t) ptsh = torch.cat([voxelcenters, torch.ones(numvoxels, 1, device=voxelcenters.device)], dim=1) ptscam = (camR[i] @ ptsh.t()).t() + camt[i] uv = (camK[i] @ ptscam.t()).t() uv = uv[:,:2] / uv[:, 2:].clamp(min=1e-6) # Normalize to [-1, 1] for gridsample uvnorm = 2.0 (uv / torch.tensor([Wf, Hf], device=uv.device)) - 1.0 uvnorm = uvnorm.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # [1, 1, V, 2] feat = F.gridsample(featuremaps[i].unsqueeze(0), uvnorm, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() uvcoords.append(feat.permute(0, 2, 1)) # [V, C] featurespervoxel = torch.stack(uvcoords, dim=1) # [V, N, C] # Compute mean and variance meanfeat = featurespervoxel.mean(dim=1) varfeat = featurespervoxel.var(dim=1) # Concatenate voxelfeatures = torch.cat([meanfeat, varfeat], dim=1) # [V, 2C] # Reshape for 3D U-Net voxelfeatures3d = voxelfeatures.view(K, K, K, 2C).permute(3, 0, 1, 2) # [2C, K, K, K] # Regularize out = self.globalvolumenet(voxelfeatures3d) # [C, K, K, K] out = out.permute(1, 2, 3, 0).view(-1, C) # [KKK, C] return out def getvolumefeature(self, volume, points): """volume: [KKK, C], points: [P, 3] -> [P, C]""" vol3d = volume.view(self.K, self.K, self.K, self.C).permute(3, 0, 1, 2) # [C, K, K, K] # Normalize points to [-1, 1] assuming scene bbox is [-1, 1]^3 normpoints = points.clamp(-1.0, 1.0) grid = normpoints.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # [1, 1, P, 1, 1, 3] feat = F.gridsample(vol3d.unsqueeze(0), grid, mode='trilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() return feat.permute(0, 2, 1).squeeze() # [P, C] def viewtransform(self, features): """features: [M, N, C] -> [M, C]""" M, N, C = features.shape f0expanded = self.f0.expand(M, 1, C) inputseq = torch.cat([f0expanded, features], dim=1) # [M, N+1, C] out, = self.viewtransformer(inputseq, inputseq, inputseq) return out[:, 0,:] # [M, C] def raytransform(self, projectionfeatures, volumefeatures): """projectionfeatures: [M, C], volumefeatures: [M, C] -> [M]""" combined = torch.cat([projectionfeatures, volumefeatures], dim=1) # [M, 2C] # Project back to C if needed, or let transformer handle it combined = nn.Linear(2C, self.C)(combined) out = self.raytransformer(combined) srdf = self.srdfmlp(out).squeeze(-1) # [M] return srdf def forward(self, images, rayorigins, raydirections, voxelcenters, camK, camR, camt): """images: [N, 3, H, W], rayorigins/directions: [H, W, 3]""" # 1. Feature Extraction featuremaps = self.extractfeatures(images) # [N, C, H/4, W/4] # 2. Global Feature Volume globalvol = self.buildglobalvolume(featuremaps, voxelcenters, camK, camR, camt) # [KKK, C] # 3. Ray Sampling tvals = torch.linspace(self.near, self.far, self.M, device=images.device) # [M] points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(2) + raydirections.unsqueeze(2) tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(3) # [H, W, M, 3] H, W, M, = points.shape pointsflat = points.view(-1, M, 3) # [HW, M, 3] # 4. Projection Feature Extraction multiviewfeatures = [] for i in range(self.N): ptsh = torch.cat([pointsflat, torch.ones(pointsflat.shape[0], 1, device=pointsflat.device)], dim=1) ptscam = (camR[i] @ ptsh.t()).t() + camt[i] uv = (camK[i] @ ptscam.t()).t() uv = uv[:,:2] / uv[:, 2:].clamp(min=1e-6) uvnorm = 2.0 (uv / torch.tensor([self.W/4, self.H/4], device=uv.device)) - 1.0 uvnorm = uvnorm.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # [1, 1, HWM, 2] feat = F.gridsample(featuremaps[i].unsqueeze(0), uvnorm, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() multiviewfeatures.append(feat.permute(0, 2, 1)) # [HWM, C] multiviewfeatures = torch.stack(multiviewfeatures, dim=1) # [HWM, N, C] # 5. View Transformer projectionfeatures = self.viewtransform(multiviewfeatures) # [HWM, C] # 6. Volume Feature Extraction volumefeatures = self.getvolumefeature(globalvol, pointsflat.view(-1, 3)).view(HW, M, C) # 7. Ray Transformer and SRDF Prediction srdfvalues = self.raytransform(projectionfeatures, volumefeatures) # [HWM] srdfvalues = srdfvalues.view(H, W, M) # 8. Volume Rendering # Convert SRDF to density sigma = torch.sigmoid(-srdfvalues 10.0) # Standard SDF-to-density mapping deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([0.0], device=tvals.device)]) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=2) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.ones(H, W, 1, device=transmittance.device), transmittance[:,:,:-1]], dim=2) # Sample colors from feature maps using projected UVs (reusing uvnorm from step 4) # Simplified: assume cm is interpolated similarly colors = torch.rand(H, W, M, 3, device=images.device) # Placeholder for actual color interpolation depth = torch.sum(transmittance alpha.unsqueeze(-1) tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(3), dim=2) color = torch.sum(transmittance.unsqueeze(-1) alpha.unsqueeze(-1) colors, dim=2) return color, depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: The view transformer aggregates multi-view features, which helps mitigate occlusion issues, but extreme occlusion may still lead to ambiguous features. Textureless Surfaces: The global feature volume provides shape priors, which is crucial for textureless regions where local projection features are unreliable. Large-Scale Scenes: The method is not suitable for very large-scale scenes due to the memory consumption of the global feature volume and the low resolution of the volume leading to decreased representation performance. Rendering Efficiency: The method is computationally expensive, taking approximately 30 seconds to render an 800x600 image and depth map. Time Complexity: Rendering is slow, taking ~30s for an 800x600 image. This is attributed to the volume rendering process and the transformer operations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the global feature volume size K^3 and the number of sampled points M. Performance: On the DTU dataset, VolRecon outperforms SparseNeuS by ~30% in sparse view (N=3) reconstruction and 22% in full view reconstruction. It achieves comparable accuracy to MVSNet in full view reconstruction and better depth evaluation. Strengths: Generalizable to new scenes without per-scene optimization; produces fine details and less noise compared to SparseNeuS; good generalization to large-scale scenes (ETH3D) without fine-tuning. Limitations: Slow rendering speed; not suitable for very large-scale scenes; reconstruction quality improves with more images but is limited by the global feature volume resolution. When to Use: Generalizable implicit reconstruction from multi-view images, especially in sparse view scenarios or when fine details are required. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. VolRecon was introduced in 2023 by researchers from the IVRL lab. It builds upon the concept of neural implicit reconstruction, which typically optimizes per-scene parameters, lacking generalizability. The method addresses this by using a generalizable architecture that incorporates multi-view features and a global feature volume. It is based on the Signed Ray Distance Function (SRDF), which defines distance along a ray direction, differing from standard SDF. The method is compared against SparseNeuS, which uses only global feature volumes and an MLP, leading to over-smoothed surfaces. VolRecon is available at https://github.com/IVRL/VolRecon/.
