name: NeRF2Points
head: Layered Perception and Integrated Modeling
body: NeRF2Points is a method for generating large-scale, geometrically consistent RGBD point clouds from street-view radiance fields. It solves the problem of "pavement collapse" and floating artifacts in point clouds generated by standard NeRF variants when applied to sparse, large-scale street-view data with weak textures. It sets itself apart by separating the scene into road and street components via a ray gate, modeling them with separate radiance fields, and merging them using rigid transformation derived from shared intersection rays. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of RGB images I from a street-view dataset; coarse initial camera poses from WIGO; refined camera poses and sparse point clouds from COLMAP; depth and normal estimations from Omnidata; road/scene masks from Mask2Former; SIFT features for temporal correspondence. Outputs: A merged RGBD point cloud PC \in \mathbb{R}^{(N1+N2) \times 3}; a trained radiance field representation. Data Structures Ray Gate M(I): A segmentation model (trained on Cityscapes) outputting a binary mask for each pixel, indicating road vs. non-road. An embedded morphological dilation operator ensures edge intersection. Ray Bundles: \mathbf{Ray}{i1}^r: Rays classified as road. \mathbf{Ray}{i2}^s: Rays classified as street scene. \mathbf{Ray}{i3}: Intersection of road and street rays (shared rays). \mathbf{Ray}i: Reconstructed original ray set: (\mathbf{Ray}{i1}^r - \mathbf{Ray}{i3}) \cup (\mathbf{Ray}{i2}^s - \mathbf{Ray}{i3}) \cup \mathbf{Ray}{i3}. Point Clouds: \mathbf{PC}r \in \mathbb{R}^{N1 \times 3}: Road surface point cloud. \mathbf{PC}s \in \mathbb{R}^{N2 \times 3}: Street scene point cloud. P \subset \mathbf{PC}r, Q \subset \mathbf{PC}s: Intersection points from shared rays \mathbf{Ray}{i3}, where |P|=|Q|=N' \ll N1, N2. Numbered Steps 1. Data Preparation: Collect street-view images (e.g., 180k images from 6 cameras). Obtain initial 6-DoF poses using Wheel-IMU-GNSS Odometry (WIGO). Refine poses and estimate sparse point cloud using COLMAP with Structure from Motion (SfM). Generate depth and normal maps using Omnidata. Generate road/scene masks using Mask2Former. Extract SIFT features from all images to identify correspondences between adjacent frames. 2. Layered Perception (Ray Splitting): For each image I, feed it to the ray gate M(\cdot) to obtain road rays \mathbf{Ray}{i1}^r and scene rays \mathbf{Ray}{i2}^s: \mathbf{Ray}{i1}^r = \mathbf{Ray}i(M(I)), \quad \mathbf{Ray}{i2}^s = \mathbf{Ray}i(1-M(I)) Compute intersection rays \mathbf{Ray}{i3} = \mathbf{Ray}{i1}^r \cap \mathbf{Ray}{i2}^s. Reconstruct the full ray set \mathbf{Ray}i ensuring no loss of information. 3. Radiance Field Training: Train separate radiance fields for road and street scenes. Compute Matching Cost for each ray bundle \mathbf{Ray}i' (either road or street) to identify hard samples: \mathbf{cos}i = \lambda1 \ell{depth}(\cdot) + \lambda2 \ell{rgb}(\cdot) + \lambda3 \ell{normal}(\cdot) Where losses are defined as: \ell{depth}(\mathbf{t}1', \mathbf{t}2') = \sum \| \textit{norm}(\mathbf{t}1') - \textit{norm}(\mathbf{t}2') \|2^2 \ell{rgb}(\mathbf{c}1', \mathbf{c}2') = \sum \| \mathbf{c}1' - \mathbf{c}2' \|2^2 \ell{normal}(\mathbf{n}1', \mathbf{n}2') = \sum \| \mathbf{n}1' - \mathbf{n}2' \|1 + \| 1 - \mathbf{n}1'^\top \mathbf{n}2' \|1 Here, \textit{norm}(\cdot) is max-min normalization, and \lambda1=0.1, \lambda2=1.0, \lambda3=0.05. Rank costs \mathbf{cos}i and select top-n rays \mathbf{Ray}{i,n}' as hard samples. Construct proposal regions R of size s \times s centered on pixel indices of hard samples. Randomly select consistent matching samples from R for each hard ray (selection varies per optimization step). Compute Spatial Dynamic Consistency Loss \ell{sdc} between hard rays and their neighbors in R: \ell{sdc} = \lambda1' \ell{jsd}(\phi(\mathbf{r}1'), \phi(\mathbf{r}2')) + \lambda2' \ell{rgb}(\cdot) + \lambda3' \ell{depth}(\cdot) Where \phi(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{xi}}{\sum{c=1}^C e^{xc}} is softmax, and \ell{jsd} is Jensen-Shannon Divergence: \ell{jsd}(\phi(\mathbf{r}1'), \phi(\mathbf{r}2')) = 0.5 \frac{\sum \phi(\mathbf{r}1') \ln(\phi(\mathbf{r}2')) + \sum \phi(\mathbf{r}2') \ln(\phi(\mathbf{r}1'))}{(\phi(\mathbf{r}1') + \phi(\mathbf{r}2'))/2} Compute Temporal Invariant Consistency Loss \ell{tic} between SIFT-matched rays \mathbf{Ray}{cur} and \mathbf{Ray}{next} from adjacent frames: \ell{tic} = \ell{jsd}(\phi(\mathbf{r}{cur}'), \phi(\mathbf{r}{next}')) Compute Reconstruction Loss \ell{rec}: \ell{rec} = \theta1 \ell{rgb}(\cdot) + \theta2 \ell{depth}(\cdot) + \theta3 \ell{normal}(\cdot) Compute Total Loss: \ell{total} = \ell{rec} + \beta \ell{sdc} + \gamma \ell{tic} Parameters: \theta1=1.0, \theta2=0.1, \theta3=0.005, \beta=0.01, \gamma=0.01. Optimize radiance fields using Adam optimizer, gradient clipping (threshold/norm 0.1), scene space annealing, and exponential learning rate decay with warm-up. 4. Integrated Modeling (Merging): Generate separate point clouds \mathbf{PC}r and \mathbf{PC}s from the trained fields: \mathbf{PC} = \text{origin} + \text{direction} \times \text{depth}. Identify intersection points P \subset \mathbf{PC}r and Q \subset \mathbf{PC}s from shared rays \mathbf{Ray}{i3}. Find rigid transformation (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}) by minimizing: \min{\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}} \sum{i=1}^{N'} (\textit{Dis}i(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}))^2 + \textit{I}{SO}(\mathbf{R}) Where \textit{Dis}i(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}) = \min{qj \in Q, pk \in P} \|\mathbf{R}pi + \mathbf{t} - qj\| and \textit{I}{SO}(\mathbf{R}) is an indicator function for SO(3) (0 if \mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{I} and \det(\mathbf{R})=1, else +\infty). Merge point clouds: \mathbf{PC} = \mathbf{PC}r \mathbf{R} + \mathbf{t} + \mathbf{PC}s. Parameters \lambda1=0.1, \lambda2=1.0, \lambda3=0.05 (Matching cost weights). \theta1=1.0, \theta2=0.1, \theta3=0.005 (Reconstruction loss weights). \beta=0.01, \gamma=0.01 (Consistency loss weights). Batch size: 2048. Iterations: 20,000. Hardware: Single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Pavement Collapse: Standard NeRF methods fail to optimize weak textures like road surfaces, leading to poor depth estimation and invisible details. Floaters: Sparse views and viewing angle shifts cause inconsistent geometry and floating artifacts above the road surface. Matching Overhead: Incorrect optimization of hard samples leads to significant artifacts; addressed by spatial dynamic consistency. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a proprietary street-view dataset (180k images, 20km span), NeRF2Points achieves PSNR 29.139, SSIM 0.831, and Chamfer Distance 1.876. Scaling: Designed for large-scale street-view data (20km span). Strengths: Outperforms NeRFacto, Instant-NPG, NeuS, Depth-NeRFacto, and Mip-NeRF in PSNR, SSIM, and Chamfer Distance on street-view data; generates clear RGBD point clouds with distinct features. Limitations: Relies on external priors (Omnidata, Mask2Former, SIFT); performance on non-street-view data is not detailed. When to use: Large-scale street-view point cloud generation from RGB sequences. When not to use: Small-scale or object-centered scenes where standard NeRF variants may suffice; scenes without road/structure distinction. NeRF2Points was introduced by Peng Tu et al. in 2024. It extends the NeRFacto framework within the NeRFSTUDIO ecosystem. The method addresses specific challenges in autonomous driving datasets, such as sparse views and weak textures, which are common in street-view data collection pipelines. name: GazeNeRF
head: GazeNeRF: 3D-Aware Gaze Redirection with Neural Radiance Fields
body: GazeNeRF is a 3D-aware method for gaze redirection that reformulates the task as a neural volume rendering problem, addressing the limitation of existing 2D methods that fail to generate 3D-consistent results. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like PI-NeRF and NeRF2Points by employing a two-stream MLP architecture that separately predicts volumetric features for the face and eye regions, allowing for explicit rigid 3D rotation of the eye features to achieve gaze redirection while preserving identity. Unlike HeadNeRF which uses a single MLP conditioned on gaze labels, GazeNeRF disentangles the eyes from the rest of the face to model their independent 3D movements. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A reference face image (resized to 512 \times 512 pixels), a target gaze label g (2D vector of pitch and yaw angles in radians), and learnable latent codes z^ for shape (z{sh}), expression (z{ex}), texture (z{te}), and illumination (z{il}) initialized from 3DMM parameters. Outputs: A rendered 2D image I{wf} of the whole face with redirected gaze, along with intermediate feature maps and images for the face-only region (I{fw/o}) and eyes region (Ie). Data Structures: Two-stream MLPs: Two separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons, h{\theta{fw/o}} for the face-only region and h{\theta{e}} for the eyes region, with learnable parameters \theta{fw/o} and \theta{e} respectively. Volume Feature Maps: Low-resolution feature maps F{fw/o} and Fe with dimensions \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 258} generated by volume rendering the MLP outputs. Rotated Eye Feature Map: Fe is reshaped to \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 86 \times 3} to facilitate 3D rotation matrix multiplication. Masks: Binary masks M{wf} (whole face), Mf (face-only), and Me (eyes) generated via face parsing models to supervise specific regions. Numbered Steps: 1. Encode Inputs: Apply positional encoding \gamma to the 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d}. Concatenate \gamma(\mathbf{x}) with the latent codes z{sh}, z{ex}, z{te}, z{il} and the gaze label g. 2. Face Stream Processing: Pass the encoded inputs through the face-only MLP h{\theta{fw/o}} to predict volume density \sigma and feature vector \mathbf{f} for the face region (excluding eyes). h{\theta{fw/o}}: (\gamma(\mathbf{x}), z{sh}, z{ex}, z{te}, z{il}, g) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{f}) 3. Eye Stream Processing: Pass the encoded inputs through the eye MLP h{\theta{e}} to predict volume density \sigma and feature vector \mathbf{f} for the eye region. h{\theta{e}}: (\gamma(\mathbf{x}), z{sh}, z{ex}, z{te}, z{il}, g) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{f}) 4. Volume Rendering: Use differentiable volume rendering on the outputs of both MLPs to generate low-resolution volume feature maps F{fw/o} and Fe \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 258}. 5. 3D Rotation: Reshape the eye feature map Fe from \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 258} to \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 86 \times 3}. Calculate a 3D rotation matrix R based on the target gaze direction g. Apply this rotation matrix to the eye feature map to rigidly rotate the eyeball features: F{e-rot} = R Fe 6. Feature Composition: Map the rotated eye feature map F{e-rot} to the segmented eyes region and the face feature map F{fw/o} to the segmented face-only region. Merge them using element-wise maximum to create the whole-face feature map F{wf}: F{wf} = \max(F{fw/o}, F{e-rot}) 7. Final Rendering: Composite the mapped features and render the final 2D images using a neural rendering module with shared weights \pi\omega. This produces the face-only image I{fw/o} from F{fw/o}, the eyes image Ie from F{e-rot}, and the whole face image I{wf} from F{wf}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GazeNeRF: def init(self, latentcodesinit, gazelabel, faceparsingmasks): """ Initialize GazeNeRF. Args: latentcodesinit: Dict with keys 'sh', 'ex', 'te', 'il' containing initial latent codes from 3DMM. gazelabel: Tensor of shape (2,) containing pitch and yaw in radians. faceparsingmasks: Dict with keys 'wf', 'f', 'e' containing binary masks for whole face, face-only, and eyes regions. """ # Two-stream MLPs self.mlpface = FaceMLP() # hthetafw/o self.mlpeye = EyeMLP() # hthetae # Neural rendering module with shared weights self.renderer = NeuralRenderer() # piomega # Learnable latent codes initialized from 3DMM self.latentcodes = {k: nn.Parameter(v.clone()) for k, v in latentcodesinit.items()} # Masks self.masks = faceparsingmasks # Gaze label self.gazelabel = gazelabel # Loss coefficients self.lambdaR = 1.0 self.lambdaP = 1.0 self.lambdaFcontent = 1e-3 self.lambdaD = 1.0 # Disentanglement weights self.wsh = 1e-3 self.wte = 1e-3 self.wil = 1e-3 self.wex = 1.0 # Initial latent codes for disentanglement loss self.latentcodesinit = latentcodesinit def computerotationmatrix(self, gazelabel): """ Compute 3D rotation matrix R from gaze label (pitch, yaw). Note: Exact rotation matrix construction from pitch/yaw is not detailed in sources. Assuming standard rotation matrix composition from pitch (y-axis) and yaw (z-axis) angles. """ pitch, yaw = gazelabel # Placeholder for actual rotation matrix computation from pitch/yaw # R = Ry(pitch) @ Rz(yaw) return torch.eye(3) # Placeholder def forward(self): """ Forward pass to generate redirected gaze image. """ # 1. Encode Inputs # x and d are sampled along rays. For simplicity, assume we have batch of x, d. # In practice, this is done per-ray during volume rendering. # Here we show the MLP input preparation. zsh = self.latentcodes['sh'] zex = self.latentcodes['ex'] zte = self.latentcodes['te'] zil = self.latentcodes['il'] g = self.gazelabel # 2. Face Stream Processing # hthetafw/o: (gamma(x), zsh, zex, zte, zil, g) -> (sigma, f) # Note: gamma(x) and gamma(d) are applied inside the MLP or before. # The source says inputs are gamma(x) and gamma(d) concatenated with latent codes. # We assume the MLP handles the positional encoding or it's passed in. # For volume rendering, we need sigma and f for many x, d. # 3. Eye Stream Processing # hthetae: (gamma(x), zsh, zex, zte, zil, g) -> (sigma, f) # 4. Volume Rendering # Render Ffw/o and Fe from the two streams. # Ffw/o, Fe in R^{64x64x258} Ffw/o = volumerender(self.mlpface, zsh, zex, zte, zil, g) Fe = volumerender(self.mlpeye, zsh, zex, zte, zil, g) # 5. 3D Rotation R = self.computerotationmatrix(g) # Reshape Fe to R^{64x64x86x3} Fereshaped = Fe.view(64, 64, 86, 3) # Apply rotation: Fe-rot = R Fe # Matrix multiplication over the last dimension Ferot = torch.einsum('ij,bhwj->bihw', R, Fereshaped) # Reshape back to R^{64x64x258} if needed for subsequent operations, # but source says Fe-rot is used for rendering Ie and merging. # The merge operation is element-wise max, so dimensions must match. # Ffw/o is R^{64x64x258}. Ferot is R^{64x64x86x3}. # Wait, source says: "Map the rotated eye feature map Fe to the segmented eyes region... # Merge... using element-wise maximum". # This implies Ferot must be compatible with Ffw/o. # Source: "reshape the Fe... to R^{64x64x86x3} and explicitly apply... Fe-rot = R Fe". # Then "Merge face-only features (Ffw/o) and rotated eye features (Fe-rot) using element-wise maximum". # This suggests Fe-rot is reshaped back or the max is applied on the 3D volume representation. # Given Ffw/o is 258, and 863=258, it's likely Fe-rot is reshaped back to 258 channels. Ferotfinal = Ferot.view(64, 64, 258) # 6. Feature Composition Fwf = torch.max(Ffw/o, Ferotfinal) # 7. Final Rendering Ifw/o = self.renderer.render(Ffw/o) Ie = self.renderer.render(Ferotfinal) Iwf = self.renderer.render(Fwf) return Iwf, Ifw/o, Ie def computeloss(self, Iwf, Ifw/o, Ie, Igt): """ Compute the total loss. """ # Reconstruction Loss LRwhole = self.maskedl1loss(Iwf, Igt, self.masks['wf']) LRface = self.maskedl1loss(Ifw/o, Igt, self.masks['f']) LReyes = self.maskedl1loss(Ie, Igt, self.masks['e']) LR = LRwhole + LRface + LReyes # Perceptual Loss (VGG16) LPwhole = self.perceptualloss(Iwf, Igt) LPface = self.perceptualloss(Ifw/o, Igt) LPeyes = self.perceptualloss(Ie, Igt) LP = LPwhole + LPface + LPeyes # Functional Loss (Gaze Estimator) # thetag is a gaze estimator network # Eang is angular error LFcontent = self.functionalcontentloss(Iwf, Igt) LF = self.lambdaFcontent LFcontent # Disentanglement Loss LD = 0 for key, w in [('sh', self.wsh), ('ex', self.wex), ('te', self.wte), ('il', self.wil)]: zstar = self.latentcodes[key] zstar0 = self.latentcodesinit[key] LD += w self.disentanglementterm(zstar, zstar0) LD = self.lambdaD LD LOverall = self.lambdaR LR + self.lambdaP LP + LF + LD return LOverall def maskedl1loss(self, Ipred, Igt, mask): """ Compute masked L1 loss. LR = (1/|M|) ||M (Ipred - Igt)||1 """ maskeddiff = mask (Ipred - Igt) loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(maskeddiff)) # Note: Source divides by |M|, which is the number of pixels in mask. # If mask is binary 0/1, torch.mean(abs(maskeddiff)) effectively divides by total pixels, # but we want average over masked pixels. # Correct implementation: numpixels = torch.sum(mask) if numpixels > 0: loss = torch.sum(torch.abs(maskeddiff)) / numpixels else: loss = torch.tensor(0.0) return loss def perceptualloss(self, Ipred, Igt): """ Compute perceptual loss using VGG16. LP = sumi (1/|phii(Igt)|) ||phii(Ipred) - phii(Igt)||1 """ # phii is the i-th layer of VGG16 # Sum over layers i loss = 0 # Placeholder for VGG16 feature extraction # featurespred = vgg(Ipred) # featuresgt = vgg(Igt) # for fp, fg in zip(featurespred, featuresgt): # loss += torch.mean(torch.abs(fp - fg)) / torch.mean(torch.abs(fg)) return loss # Placeholder def functionalcontentloss(self, Ipred, Igt): """ Compute functional content loss. LFcontent = Eang(thetag(Ipred), thetag(Igt)) Eang(v, vhat) = arccos( (v. vhat) / (|v| |vhat|)) """ # thetag is gaze estimator network # gpred = gazeestimator(Ipred) # ggt = gazeestimator(Igt) # angularerror = arccos(dot(gpred, ggt) / (norm(gpred) norm(ggt))) return 0.0 # Placeholder def disentanglementterm(self, zstar, zstar0): """ Compute disentanglement term. LDterm = (1/|z0|) ||zstar - zstar0||2^2 """ numparams = zstar0.numel() loss = torch.sum((zstar - zstar0) 2) / numparams return loss Parameters: Gaze label g: A 2D vector consisting of pitch and yaw angles of the gaze vector in radians. Feature map dimensions: The volume feature maps F{fw/o} and Fe have dimensions \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 258}. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 1 \times 10^{-4}. Loss coefficients: \lambdaR = \lambdaP = \lambdaF = \lambdaD = 1. Disentanglement weights: w{sh} = w{te} = w{il} = 1 \times 10^{-3} and w{ex} = 1.0. Functional loss coefficient \lambda{F{content}}: Starts at 1 \times 10^{-3} and increases by 1 \times 10^{-3} after each epoch. Input resolution: Face images resized to 512 \times 512 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mask Accuracy: The method relies on face parsing models to generate masks for the face-only and eyes regions. Inaccurate masks can lead to incorrect disentanglement and blending artifacts. Rotation Matrix Computation: The exact method for computing the 3D rotation matrix R from the 2D gaze label (pitch/yaw) is not detailed in the sources, relying on external references [24, 44]. Feature Map Reshaping: The eye feature map must be correctly reshaped to \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 86 \times 3} for rotation and then back to \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 258} for merging. Incorrect reshaping will break the rotation or the element-wise maximum operation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the ETH-XGaze dataset. GazeNeRF achieves better results than STED and HeadNeRF in terms of gaze and head redirection errors (degrees), as well as image quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, FID) and identity similarity. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly models the 3D nature of eyeball rotation and face deformation via separate volumetric streams, providing fine-grained control over gaze angle and preserving identity better than 2D methods. Limitations: Requires face parsing masks for disentanglement. The method is specific to gaze redirection and may not be as general as other NeRF variants. When to use it: When 3D-consistent gaze redirection is required, especially for applications where identity preservation and accurate gaze angle are critical. When not: When high-fidelity rendering and relighting quality are the primary goals (use EyeNeRF instead) or when computational resources are limited and 2D methods are sufficient. GazeNeRF was proposed in 2023 by authors who contributed equally to the work, published in the CVPR proceedings. It builds on the intuition that the face region and eyeballs are separate 3D structures that move in a coordinated yet independent fashion. The method leverages advancements in conditional image-based neural radiance fields and proposes a two-stream architecture to predict volumetric features for the face and eye regions separately. It differs from 2D methods like STED and FAZE, which apply weak rotation priors to mixed 2D latent features, and from EyeNeRF, which focuses on high-fidelity rendering rather than gaze redirection accuracy. name: NeRF for Object Segmentation
head: Area Encoding NeRF, Object Segmentation Component in NeRF, Semantic NeRF Segmentation
body: This method extends the standard NeRF formulation to perform object segmentation by simultaneously estimating scene geometry and predicting semantic occlusion masks. It introduces "area encoding" to represent the probability that a sampling point belongs to an occluded area, leveraging the correlation between geometry estimation and semantic label prediction. Unlike sibling methods that predict semantic labels directly as a feature vector [Siblings], this approach treats segmentation as a volumetric integration problem, ensuring view-consistent results by jointly optimizing color, depth, and area encoding losses. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images Io, corresponding camera poses, and ground truth semantic masks P(r) for the target object. Optionally, ground truth depth D(r) and 2D inpainted color priors Cl(r) for occluded regions. Outputs: A continuous volumetric field F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma, p), where \mathbf{c} is color, \sigma is density, and p is the area encoding probability (probability of being occluded). Data Structures: The network F\Theta is a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A tuple (\mathbf{c}, \sigma, p). \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3: RGB color. \sigma \in \mathbb{R}: Volume density (opacity). p \in [0, 1]: Area encoding probability. Rendering Process: For a ray r passing through the scene, N sample points \mathbf{x}i are sampled along the ray. The predicted mask value \hat{P}(r) is computed via volumetric rendering integration of the area encoding probabilities pi, weighted by transmittance and opacity: \hat{P}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) pi where: \deltai is the distance between sample points i and i+1. Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) is the transmittance up to point i, representing the probability that the ray travels from the camera to \mathbf{x}i without being occluded by density. \hat{C}(r) and \hat{D}(r) are similarly rendered using standard volume rendering equations for color and depth, respectively. Loss Functions: The total loss is a weighted sum of three components: 1. Color Loss (L{rgb}): Applied only to rays where the predicted mask is zero (non-occluded areas) to ensure correct modeling of visible geometry and appearance: L{rgb} = \sum{r \in R \land \hat{P}(r)=0} \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|2^2 where R is the set of all rays in the input views and C(r) is the ground truth color. 2. Area Encoding Loss (L{area-encoding}): Minimizes the difference between the predicted mask and the actual semantic mask for the specific view: L{area-encoding} = \sum{r \in Ro} \|\hat{P}(r) - P(r)\|2^2 where Ro is the set of rays in view o and P(r) is the ground truth binary mask. 3. Depth Loss (L{depth}): Guides the geometric modeling of occluded areas by comparing rendered depth with ground truth depth, addressing the issue where geometric errors in occluded areas propagate to non-occluded areas due to NeRF's entangled representation: L{depth} = \sum{r \in R} \|\hat{D}(r) - D(r)\|2^2 where D(r) is the ground truth depth. Total Loss: L = \lambda1 L{area-encoding} + \lambda2 L{rgb} + \lambda3 L{depth} where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are hyperparameter weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forward(x, d, network): """ Forward pass of the NeRF segmentation network. x: (N, 3) tensor of 3D sample points along rays. d: (N, 3) tensor of viewing directions. network: The MLP model FTheta. Returns: c (N, 3), sigma (N,), p (N,) """ # Concatenate position and direction for positional encoding if used # Note: Standard NeRF uses positional encoding; assuming network handles input mapping c, sigma, p = network(x, d) return c, sigma, p def renderray(xi, di, sigmai, ci, pi, deltai): """ Renders mask, color, and depth for a single ray given N samples. xi: (N, 3) di: (N, 3) sigmai: (N,) ci: (N, 3) pi: (N,) deltai: (N,) distance between samples Returns: Phat, Chat, Dhat """ N = len(sigmai) # Compute transmittance Ti # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # Using cumulative sum for efficiency alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmai deltai) # Opacity at each point T = torch.cumsum(sigmai deltai, dim=0) T = torch.exp(-T) # Shift T to align with samples (T1 = 1.0 effectively, or exp(0)) # Standard definition: Ti is transmittance BEFORE sample i # T[0] should be 1.0 (or exp(0)) Tshifted = torch.cat([torch.tensor([1.0]).to(T.device), T[:-1]]) # Weight for each sample: Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) weight = Tshifted alpha # Render Mask Phat = torch.sum(weight pi) # Render Color Chat = torch.sum(weight.unsqueeze(1) ci, dim=0) # Render Depth (assuming zi is depth along ray, e.g., distance from camera) # zi needs to be computed from xi and camera origin/direction # For simplicity, assuming zi is provided or computed externally # Dhat = sum(weight zi) return Phat, Chat def computelosses(Phat, Chat, Dhat, Pgt, Cgt, Dgt, maskvalid): """ Computes the three loss components. maskvalid: boolean mask for rays where Phat == 0 (non-occluded) """ # Lrgb: Only for non-occluded rays if maskvalid.any(): Lrgb = torch.mean((Chat[maskvalid] - Cgt[maskvalid])2) else: Lrgb = torch.tensor(0.0) # Lareaencoding: For all rays in the view (or specific view Ro) Larea = torch.mean((Phat - Pgt)2) # Ldepth: For all rays Ldepth = torch.mean((Dhat - Dgt)2) return Lrgb, Larea, Ldepth Parameters: \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: Loss weights. Specific values are not given in the sources. N: Number of sample points per ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Propagation Errors: Errors in modeling occluded areas can propagate to non-occluded areas due to the entangled nature of NeRF's scene representation, breaking multi-view consistency and causing inaccurate mask predictions. This is mitigated by the inclusion of the depth loss. Occluded Regions: Areas occluded in all views lack supplementary information. The method may use 2D inpainting priors Cl(r) for these regions, though the specific integration of this prior into the main loss formula in the notes is described as L{Occ} in the source text, distinct from the primary L{rgb} definition provided in the summary notes. Time Complexity: Determined by the number of samples N per ray and the depth of the MLP F\Theta. Rendering requires O(N) evaluations per ray. Memory Complexity: Depends on the MLP size and the number of rays processed per batch. Strengths: Provides view-consistent segmentation by integrating semantic probabilities volumetrically. Jointly optimizes geometry and semantics, reducing artifacts in occluded regions. Limitations: Relies on the availability of ground truth masks and depth maps for supervision. Performance may degrade if the correlation between geometry and semantic labels is weak. When to use: When view-consistent object segmentation is required in complex scenes with occlusions, and ground truth masks/depth are available. When not to use: For open-world semantic segmentation without ground truth masks, or when computational resources are severely limited for training deep volumetric networks. The method was introduced in the paper "3D Scene De-occlusion in Neural Radiance Fields: A Framework for Obstacle Removal and Realistic Inpainting". It addresses the challenge of segmenting objects in scenes where parts of the object are occluded by other geometry, a common issue in standard NeRF training which can lead to incomplete or inconsistent semantic predictions. The approach builds on the observation that geometry estimation and semantic label prediction are strongly correlated. 3D Scene De-occlusion in Neural Radiance Fields: A Framework for Obstacle Removal and Realistic Inpainting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3681429, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Semantic-NeRF
body: Semantic-NeRF is a method for synthesizing semantic labels for novel views by extending the standard NeRF formulation with an additional direction-independent MLP branch. It solves the problem of 3D semantic understanding and label propagation by ensuring multi-view consistency between rendered semantic labels and ground-truth 2D annotations. It sets itself apart from siblings like Multi-Space Neural Radiance Field (MS-NeRF) and Semantic and Feature Branches by being the first work to integrate semantic information directly into the NeRF architecture using a specific branch that consumes position and density features, rather than relying on separate scene/object branches or multi-space embeddings. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: RGB images \mathbf{I} and corresponding semantic label maps \mathbf{L} for a set of known camera poses. Outputs: Rendered RGB images and rendered semantic label maps for novel camera poses. Data Structures: The model consists of two primary neural network components, building on the baseline NeRF architecture Parent: 1. Base NeRF Network: Takes 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input. It outputs density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. It also produces intermediate features (typically from the feature vector before the final color prediction layer) which are used by the semantic branch. 2. Semantic Branch: A direction-independent MLP. It takes the position \mathbf{x} and the intermediate features from the Base NeRF network as input. It outputs a semantic label vector \mathbf{s} (logits or probabilities for K classes). Rendering Process: Semantic labels are rendered along a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} using standard volume rendering integration. For each sample point ti along the ray, the semantic branch predicts a label distribution \mathbf{s}i. The final rendered semantic label S(\mathbf{r}) is computed as a weighted sum of these predictions, where the weights are the alpha values \alphai from the volume rendering equation: S(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{s}i where: N is the number of samples along the ray. \alphai = (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance weight for sample i, derived from density \sigmai and step size \deltai. Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. \mathbf{s}i is the semantic label vector (e.g., one-hot encoded or logits) predicted by the semantic branch at point \mathbf{x}i. Training Procedure: 1. Forward Pass: For each training image, render RGB and semantic labels using the Base NeRF and Semantic Branch networks. 2. Loss Calculation: Color Loss: Standard photometric loss (e.g., MSE) between rendered RGB and input RGB. Semantic Loss: Categorical cross-entropy loss between the rendered semantic labels S(\mathbf{r}) and the ground-truth semantic labels \mathbf{L}. 3. Optimization: Minimize the combined loss using stochastic gradient descent (or Adam) to update the weights of both the Base NeRF and the Semantic Branch. Parameters: Number of semantic classes K: Depends on the dataset (e.g., 19 for NYUv2, 40 for SUN RGB-D). Sampling strategy: Uniform or stratified sampling along rays. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Labels: The method is robust to sparse semantic label data (e.g., 10% labeled pixels) and can recover semantic labels from pixel-wise noise. Direction Independence: The semantic branch is direction-independent, meaning it predicts the same semantic label for a point regardless of the viewing angle, ensuring multi-view consistency. Feature Input: The semantic branch relies on the intermediate features from the Base NeRF. If the Base NeRF fails to encode sufficient geometric or appearance information, the semantic branch may perform poorly. This variant refers to a specific training strategy where a Semantic-NeRF network is trained for each scene by fusing predictions from an external segmentation model. Instead of relying solely on ground-truth semantic labels, it uses view-consistent rendered semantic labels as pseudo-labels for model adaptation. This approach simultaneously trains a frame-level semantic network and a scene-level NeRF, ensuring that semantic forecasts and NeRF renderings remain aligned. This strategy is particularly useful for real-world deployment scenarios involving covariate shift across different scenes or when revisiting previously observed scenes. Time Complexity: Training time is proportional to the number of training images and the number of samples per ray, similar to standard NeRF. The additional semantic branch adds minimal computational overhead during the forward pass. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is slightly higher than standard NeRF due to the additional parameters in the semantic branch. Performance: The method achieves good label super-resolution results and label propagation from sparse point-wise annotation. It outperforms non-deep learning methods in multi-view semantic fusion. Strengths: Handles sparse and noisy labels effectively; ensures multi-view consistency; enables semantic understanding of scenes. Limitations: Requires semantic labels for training (though sparse labels are sufficient); performance depends on the quality of the Base NeRF's feature encoding. When to use: When semantic understanding of a scene is required, and ground-truth or pseudo-labels are available. When not to use: When only RGB data is available and no semantic labels or segmentation models can be used for pseudo-labeling. Semantic-NeRF was introduced in March 2021. It is the first work to integrate semantic information into NeRF, utilizing RGB images alongside corresponding semantic labels to train the NeRF network. The method was developed to enhance semantic understanding of scenes and enable tasks such as multi-view semantic fusion and label propagation. It builds upon the foundational NeRF architecture Parent and has influenced subsequent works such as Panoptic NeRF and Fig-NeRF. name: Augmented Features (Avg, Var, Color)
head: Augmented Cost Volume Features, Mean-Variance-Color Augmentation
body: This method augments the volumetric representation in NeRF-based 3D detection by explicitly encoding mean (average), variance, and color features into the cost volume or feature field. It solves the problem of insufficient geometric priors in standard NeRF formulations for 3D object detection by leveraging statistical moments of the radiance field and low-level color information as explicit geometry cues. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Semantic-NeRF by focusing on statistical variance and color intensity rather than semantic class labels or latent descriptors, providing a lightweight geometric prior for detection heads. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images, camera poses, and a base NeRF or cost volume representation. Outputs: An augmented feature volume containing mean, variance, and color channels, used to supervise or guide the 3D detection branch. Data Structures: The method augments the standard feature volume (or cost volume) with three specific channels: 1. Mean Volume (\mathbf{V}{avg}): The expected value of the radiance/opacity field along the ray. 2. Variance Volume (\mathbf{V}{var}): The variance of the radiance/opacity field along the ray, serving as a geometry prior. 3. Color Volume (\mathbf{V}{color}): The integrated color information along the ray. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, sample points along the viewing ray. 2. Feature Prediction: At each sample point, predict the raw features (e.g., opacity \sigma, color \mathbf{c}) using the network. 3. Volume Integration: Integrate these predictions along the ray to compute the aggregated features: Compute the Mean feature by integrating the weighted sum of features. Compute the Variance feature by calculating the second moment minus the square of the first moment, weighted by opacity. Compute the Color feature by standard volume rendering of the RGB channels. 4. Augmentation: Concatenate or fuse \mathbf{V}{avg}, \mathbf{V}{var}, and \mathbf{V}{color} into the final feature representation used by the detection head. 5. Supervision: Use these augmented features to supervise the 3D detection task, leveraging the geometric cues from variance and color. Formulas: Let wi = Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) be the weight for sample i, where Ti is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the distance between samples. Mean: \mathbf{V}{avg} = \sumi wi \mathbf{f}i Variance: \mathbf{V}{var} = \sumi wi (\mathbf{f}i - \mathbf{V}{avg})^2 (Note: Exact formula for variance in NeRF context is derived from second moment E[\mathbf{f}^2] - E[\mathbf{f}]^2). Color: \mathbf{V}{color} = \sumi wi \mathbf{c}i Parameters: Number of samples per ray: Not given in the sources. Weighting scheme: Standard NeRF opacity weighting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Variance calculation involves subtraction of squared terms, which may suffer from numerical instability if not handled carefully. Boundaries: The variance feature is zero in empty space, providing a strong prior for object boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeaugmentedfeatures(rayorigins, raydirections, network, numsamples): """ Computes mean, variance, and color features for a batch of rays. """ # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples) zvals = rayorigins + raydirections tvals.unsqueeze(-1) # Shape: [B, N, 3] # Query network for density and features # network returns sigma (density) and f (raw features, e.g., color or latent) sigma, f = network(zvals) # Shape: [B, N, 1], [B, N, C] # Compute weights # Assuming uniform spacing for simplicity, delta is constant delta = 1.0 / numsamples weights = torch.exp(-sigma torch.cumsum(sigma, dim=1) delta) (1 - torch.exp(-sigma delta)) weights = weights / (weights.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) # Normalize # Compute Mean meanfeat = (weights.unsqueeze(-1) f).sum(dim=1) # Compute Variance # Variance = E[f^2] - E[f]^2 fsq = f f secondmoment = (weights.unsqueeze(-1) fsq).sum(dim=1) variancefeat = secondmoment - meanfeat meanfeat # Compute Color (assuming f includes color or separate color query) # If f is color, then colorfeat is meanfeat. If separate, query color separately. # Assuming f is color for this example colorfeat = meanfeat return meanfeat, variancefeat, colorfeat Uses semantic labels and latent features for classification and segmentation. Choose when semantic understanding is required. Link Encodes semantic class probabilities into the NeRF. Choose for semantic segmentation tasks. Link Focuses on segmenting objects using NeRF. Choose for instance segmentation. Link Uses neural radiance fields for feature fusion. Choose for multi-view feature aggregation. Link Uses multiple coordinate spaces. Choose for large-scale scenes. Link Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead to the standard NeRF rendering process, as mean, variance, and color are computed during the same ray marching loop. Memory Complexity: Increases memory usage by storing three additional feature channels per ray/sample. Measured Performance: On the Waymo Open Dataset, the method achieves 50.1 mAP@.25 and 50.1 mAP@.50 with Avg+Var+Color. Strengths: Variance features provide strong geometric priors, improving 3D detection accuracy. Color features add low-level geometric cues. Limitations: The ablation study shows that adding variance to average features alone slightly decreases performance (49.7 vs 50.1), and adding color further decreases it (49.0), but the full combination (Avg+Var+Color) recovers to 50.1, suggesting complex interactions. The text claims variance improves performance significantly over "only average features," which contradicts the table if "Avg" is the baseline, indicating a potential comparison with a different baseline or a specific configuration not fully detailed. When to use: When 3D object detection performance is critical and geometric priors are needed. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of computing variance is prohibitive. The method was introduced in "NeRF-Det: Learning Geometry-Aware Volumetric Representation for Multi-View 3D Object Detection". It builds on the observation that standard NeRFs lack explicit geometric priors for detection tasks. By augmenting the feature volume with mean, variance, and color, the method leverages the statistical properties of the radiance field to improve 3D object detection. The work demonstrates that variance features act as effective geometry priors, while color features provide additional low-level cues. name: SAID-NeRF
head: Segmentation-AIDed NeRF
body: SAID-NeRF is a semantic radiance field method that exploits instance masks generated by Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) to enhance the estimation of surfaces for transparent objects, which are otherwise ambiguous when relying purely on RGB data. It differs from standard NeRFs and other inverse rendering methods by jointly optimizing a semantic field to enforce view-independent surface densities, thereby producing sharper depth estimates and diffuse color components suitable for robotic grasping, while maintaining the fast reconstruction times of hash-encoded architectures like Instant-NGP. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N RGB images \{Ii\}, their corresponding camera poses \{Pi\}, and optional depth maps from an RGB-D camera. Semantic target masks are generated externally using a Visual Foundation Model (specifically Light-HQ SAM). Outputs: A continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta that outputs volume density \sigma, view-independent diffuse color \mathbf{c}d, view-dependent specular color \mathbf{c}s, and semantic logits \mathbf{s} for a given 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Data Structures: The architecture is built upon Multiresolution Hash Encoding. Position Encoding: A frequency embedding is concatenated with the features of the multiresolution hash encoding to avoid floaters and warped geometry on patternless surfaces. MLP Layers: Density MLP: Single layer, width 16. Diffuse Color MLP: Shallow MLP, width 32. Specular Color MLP: Shallow MLP, width 32. Segmentation MLP: Two layers, width 32. Direction Encoding: Viewing direction \mathbf{d} is projected using Spherical Harmonics (SH) basis functions before being appended to the feature vector for the specular component. Algorithm Steps: 1. Mask Generation and Hierarchical Grouping: Use Light-HQ SAM to generate instance masks for the scene. Group masks into a hierarchical set of non-overlapping scene masks using Algorithm 1 to ensure consistency across views. The number of semantic classes C is kept low (empirically \le 3). 2. Network Forward Pass: For a ray \mathbf{r} sampled at points \mathbf{x}i along the ray: Compute hash-encoded features for \mathbf{x}i. Concatenate with frequency embedding. Pass through Density MLP to get \sigmai. Pass through Diffuse MLP to get \mathbf{c}{d,i}. Pass through Specular MLP (using \mathbf{x}i features and SH-encoded \mathbf{d}) to get \mathbf{c}{s,i}. Pass through Segmentation MLP to get semantic logits \mathbf{s}i of length C. Compute final color \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{c}{d,i} + \mathbf{c}{s,i}. 3. Volume Rendering: Render the expected color \hat{C} and expected depth \hat{D} using numerical quadrature: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i \hat{D} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ti Where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), \deltai = t{i+1} - ti, and ti is the distance along the ray. 4. Semantic Rendering: Render the expected semantic distribution S(\mathbf{r}) by integrating the semantic logits weighted by transmittance and density: S(\mathbf{r}) = \int{t{near}}^{t{far}} T(t) \sigma(t) \mathbf{s}(t) dt Approximated discretely as: \hat{S} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{s}i This leverages density assignments from the semantic head to enforce higher surface densities for transparent objects, despite their low contribution to color components. 5. Loss Computation and Optimization: RGB Loss: L1 loss between rendered color \hat{C} and ground truth RGB. Semantic Loss: Binary cross-entropy loss between rendered semantic distribution \hat{S} and target masks. Depth Loss: L2 loss between rendered depth \hat{D} and ground truth depth from RGB-D camera (vital for scenes without significant background patterns). Specular Penalty: A small L2 penalty applied to the specular term \mathbf{c}s to encourage diffuse color components. Optimization runs for a fixed time limit T (e.g., 20 seconds for robotic experiments, 60 seconds for ClearPose dataset) rather than a fixed number of steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SAIDNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, numsemanticclasses=3): super().init() # Architecture components as per self.hashencoding = MultiresolutionHashEncoding() # From Instant-NGP self.freqembedding = FrequencyEmbedding() # MLPs with specified widths self.densitymlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(self.hashencoding.outdim + self.freqembedding.outdim, 16), nn.ReLU()) self.diffusemlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(self.hashencoding.outdim + self.freqembedding.outdim, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 3) # RGB) self.specularmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(self.hashencoding.outdim + self.freqembedding.outdim + 16, 32), # 16 for SH nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 3) # RGB) self.segmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(self.hashencoding.outdim + self.freqembedding.outdim, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, numsemanticclasses)) self.shencoder = SphericalHarmonicsEncoder(basis=4) # Standard SH basis def forward(self, positions, directions): """ positions: (N, 3) directions: (N, 3) """ # 1. Position Encoding hashfeat = self.hashencoding(positions) freqfeat = self.freqembedding(positions) posfeat = torch.cat([hashfeat, freqfeat], dim=-1) # 2. Density sigma = self.densitymlp(posfeat).squeeze(-1) # 3. Diffuse Color cdiffuse = self.diffusemlp(posfeat) # 4. Specular Color dirfeat = self.shencoder(directions) specinput = torch.cat([posfeat, dirfeat], dim=-1) cspecular = self.specularmlp(specinput) # 5. Semantic Logits slogits = self.segmlp(posfeat) # Final Color c = cdiffuse + cspecular return sigma, c, slogits def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, numsamples, nerfmodel): """ Renders a single ray using volume rendering equations. """ # Sample points along ray tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples) positions = rayorigin + raydirection.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(1) # Forward pass sigma, c, slogits = nerfmodel(positions, raydirection) # Compute deltas deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltainf = torch.tensor(1e10) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], dim=0) # Compute transmittance alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha], dim=1), dim=1)[:,:-1] # Render Color weights = alpha T renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=0) # Render Depth rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights tvals, dim=0) # Render Semantic renderedsemantic = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) slogits, dim=0) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, renderedsemantic def computeloss(renderedcolor, rendereddepth, renderedsemantic, gtcolor, gtdepth, gtsemanticmasks, sigmaspecular): """ Computes the total loss for SAID-NeRF. """ # RGB Loss: L1 rgbloss = F.l1loss(renderedcolor, gtcolor) # Depth Loss: L2 depthloss = F.mseloss(rendereddepth, gtdepth) # Semantic Loss: Binary Cross-Entropy # gtsemanticmasks should be binary masks for each class segloss = F.binarycrossentropywithlogits(renderedsemantic, gtsemanticmasks) # Specular Penalty: Small L2 penalty specularpenalty = torch.mean(sigmaspecular 2) totalloss = rgbloss + depthloss + segloss + specularpenalty return totalloss Parameters: Number of semantic classes (C): Empirically kept low (\le 3). Training Time Limit (T): 20 seconds for robotic experiments; 60 seconds for ClearPose dataset. Mask Generation: Light-HQ SAM variant. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX4000 Ada (robotic experiments), NVIDIA Tesla V100 (ClearPose dataset). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Patternless Backgrounds: Without frequency embedding, hash-encoded NeRFs suffer from "floaters" and warped geometry on unremarkable backgrounds, which confuses grasp generation. Transparent Objects: Standard NeRFs fail to recover underlying geometry for transparent objects because specular effects dominate color, leading to diffuse density assignments and inaccurate depth. Mask Consistency: The hierarchical mask grouping algorithm (Algorithm 1) is imprecise but compensates for faulty assignments across multiple views if the number of classes is low. Time Complexity: Reconstruction time is measured in seconds (e.g., <10 seconds for 4 images) due to the use of Multiresolution Hash Encoding and fixed time-limit training, significantly faster than hour-long training times of methods like Dex-NeRF. Memory Complexity: Depends on the hash grid size of Instant-NGP and the number of semantic classes. Not explicitly quantified in sources, but described as efficient enough for robotic real-time constraints. Performance: Outperforms vanilla Instant-NGP on depth completion for transparent objects using as few as four images. Strengths: Robust depth estimation for transparent objects; fast reconstruction; label-free segmentation guidance; suitable for robotic grasping pipelines. Limitations: Relies on external VFM (SAM) for masks; hierarchical mask grouping is imprecise; depth supervision requires RGB-D data which may be noisy for transparent objects. When to use: Robotic grasping of transparent objects; depth completion where few views are available; scenarios requiring fast reconstruction. When not to use: Opaque objects where standard NeRFs suffice; scenarios with significant background patterns where depth supervision is less critical; scenarios requiring high-fidelity specular rendering (as specular is penalized). SAID-NeRF was proposed in 2024 by researchers addressing the challenge of acquiring accurate 3D information of transparent objects for robotics. It builds upon Instant-NGP [8] and leverages Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) like SAM. The method was developed to overcome the limitations of previous NeRF-based grasping methods like Dex-NeRF, which required hours of computation, and implicit surface methods like NeUS, which were too slow for robotic applications. It is used in robotic grasping systems with adaptive fingers and GraspNet for grasp candidate generation. SAID-NeRF: Segmentation-AIDed NeRF for Depth Completion of Transparent Objects, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros58592.2024.10801979, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MINE
head: Continuous Depth MPI, MINE (Continuous Depth MPI), MINE: Towards Continuous Depth MPI with NeRF for Novel View Synthesis, Multi-Plane Image NeRF, Multiplane Image with Neural Radiance Fields
body: MINE is a hybrid method that combines Multi-Plane Images (MPI) with Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to reconstruct dense 3D representations from single color images for novel view synthesis. Unlike pixelNeRF and GRF, which model the entire 3D space per ray, MINE models the frustum of the source camera using continuous depth MPIs. This architectural difference allows MINE to be significantly more efficient, as its complexity is independent of the number of target views, whereas pixelNeRF and GRF scale with the number of novel views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single source image I{src} and camera intrinsics. Output: A rendered image I{target} for a target viewpoint, generated via homography warping of the reconstructed frustum. Data Structures: The method uses a continuous depth MPI representation. The scene is represented as a set of N{\text{planes}} planes. Each plane contains: RGB: View-independent color (3 channels). \sigma: Opacity/density (1 channel). Disparity: Continuous depth information associated with the plane. The network outputs a 4-channel RGB-\sigma image for each plane. Network Architecture: 1. Encoder: A standard ResNet50. Feature maps are extracted from layers: conv1, layer1, layer2, layer3, and layer4. 2. Decoder: A fully convolutional depth decoder. It consists of downsampling and upsampling blocks with skip connections from the encoder. The decoder is based on the architecture in [12], augmented with two additional downsampling blocks and two upsampling blocks to increase receptive fields. The final output is a 4-channel tensor. The first 3 channels are passed through a Sigmoid activation to produce RGB. The 4th channel is passed through an absolute value function to produce \sigma. Decoder Layer Layout: The decoder processes features through the following sequence: | Layer | Input Channels | Output Channels | Input Composition | Activation | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | downconv1 | 2048 | 512 | Encoder output | ELU | | downconv2 | 512 | 256 | downconv1 output | ELU | | upconv1extra | 256 | 256 | downconv2 output | ELU | | upconv2extra | 256 | 2048 | upconv1extra output | ELU | | upconv5 | 2048 + 21 | 256 | cat(upconv2extra, disparityencoding) | ELU | | iconv5 | 256 + 1024 + 21 | 256 | cat(upconv5, encoderlayer3, disparityencoding) | ELU | | output4 | 256 | 4 | iconv5 | Sigmoid (RGB), Abs (\sigma) | | upconv4 | 256 | 128 | output4 features | ELU | | iconv4 | 128 + 512 + 21 | 128 | cat(upconv4, encoderlayer2, disparityencoding) | ELU | | output3 | 128 | 4 | iconv4 | Sigmoid (RGB), Abs (\sigma) | | upconv3 | 128 | 64 | output3 features | ELU | | iconv3 | 64 + 256 + 21 | 64 | cat(upconv3, encoderlayer1, disparityencoding) | ELU | | output2 | 64 | 4 | iconv3 | Sigmoid (RGB), Abs (\sigma) | | upconv2 | 64 | 32 | output2 features | ELU | | iconv2 | 32 + 64 + 21 | 32 | cat(upconv2, encoderconv1, disparityencoding) | ELU | | output1 | 32 | 4 | iconv2 | Sigmoid (RGB), Abs (\sigma) | | upconv1 | 32 | 16 | output1 features | ELU | | iconv1 | 16 | 16 | upconv1 output | ELU | Note: upconv blocks consist of convolution, batch normalization, activation, followed by 2x nearest neighbor upsampling. downconv blocks consist of max pooling (stride 2), convolution, activation. Number of Planes (N{\text{planes}}): The number of planes is a hyperparameter. The specific value is not given in the sources, but it determines the depth resolution of the MPI. Rendering Process: 1. Encoder Pass: The source image is passed through the ResNet50 encoder once. 2. Decoder Passes: The encoder features are passed through the decoder N{\text{planes}} times to reconstruct the frustum. Each pass produces one plane of the MPI (RGB and \sigma). 3. Homography Warping: To render a target view, the reconstructed frustum (the set of N{\text{planes}} planes) is warped using homography transformations corresponding to the target camera pose. 4. Compositing: The warped planes are composited using standard alpha compositing (volume rendering equation) to produce the final image. View-Dependent Color: By default, MINE does not take viewing direction as input. To support view-dependent effects, per-ray viewing directions can be concatenated with the output feature maps at the target view (after warping), and a lightweight fully convolutional network can predict the view-dependent radiance. Training Strategy: Loss Functions: MINE uses multiscale training losses. L{L1} and L{SSIM} are applied only to output1. L{smooth} (edge-aware smoothness loss) is applied to all outputs (output1, output2, output3, output4). Dense Supervision: Because MINE renders the full target image and disparity map during training, it can utilize dense supervision signals like SSIM and edge-aware smoothness, which are infeasible for NeRF-like methods due to their inefficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MINE: def init(self, nplanes, encoder, decoder): """ Initialize MINE. Args: nplanes (int): Number of planes in the MPI representation. encoder: ResNet50 encoder model. decoder: Fully convolutional depth decoder model. """ self.nplanes = nplanes self.encoder = encoder self.decoder = decoder def encode(self, image): """ Encode the source image into feature maps. Args: image (torch.Tensor): Input image of shape (B, 3, H, W). Returns: list: Feature maps from encoder layers [conv1, layer1, layer2, layer3, layer4]. """ # Standard ResNet50 forward pass # Extract features from specific layers features = [] x = self.encoder.conv1(image) features.append(x) # conv1 x = self.encoder.layer1(x) features.append(x) # layer1 x = self.encoder.layer2(x) features.append(x) # layer2 x = self.encoder.layer3(x) features.append(x) # layer3 x = self.encoder.layer4(x) features.append(x) # layer4 return features def decode(self, features, disparityencoding): """ Decode features into MPI planes. The table structure implies # output1 is the result of iconv1 or a subsequent layer. # Based on "output1 (16->4, Sigmoid/abs)" and "iconv1 (16->16, ELU)", # it seems output1 is generated from iconv1. # Re-evaluating Table 5 order: # upconv1 -> iconv1 -> output1 # So: x = F.elu(self.decoder.upconv1(out2)) # Wait, table says upconv1 input is output2? # Table: upconv1 (32->16), iconv1 (16->16), output1 (16->4). # Input to upconv1 is output2? No, upconv2 takes output3? # Let's look at channels: # output3 is 4 channels? No, output3 is 4 channels. # upconv3 takes output3? No, upconv3 takes output4? # Table: upconv3 (128->64). Input must be 128. output4 is 4. iconv4 is 128. # So upconv3 takes iconv4? No, upconv3 takes output4? No. # The table lists: # output4 -> upconv3 -> iconv3 -> output3 # output3 -> upconv2 -> iconv2 -> output2 # output2 -> upconv1 -> iconv1 -> output1 # This matches the channel flow if we assume the "output" layers are just the final projection # and the upconv layers take the previous output's features? # Actually, the table says: # upconv3 (128->64). Input: output3? No, output3 is 4. # Input to upconv3 is output3? No. # Let's look at "iconv3 (64+256+21->64)". Args: mpiplanes (list): List of (RGB, sigma) tuples for each plane. targethomography (torch.Tensor): Homography matrix for the target view. Returns: torch.Tensor: Rendered image. """ # Warp each plane using the homography warpedplanes = [] for rgb, sigma in mpiplanes: # Warp RGB and Sigma separately warpedrgb = F.affinegrid(targethomography, rgb.shape) # Simplified warpedrgb = F.gridsample(rgb, warpedrgb) warpedsigma = F.affinegrid(targethomography, sigma.shape) warpedsigma = F.gridsample(sigma, warpedsigma) warpedplanes.append((warpedrgb, warpedsigma)) # Composite the warped planes # Standard alpha compositing finalrgb = torch.zeroslike(warpedplanes[0][0]) accumulatedsigma = torch.zeroslike(warpedplanes[0][1]) for rgb, sigma in reversed(warpedplanes): # Alpha compositing # C = Cprev (1 - alpha) + Cnew alpha # alpha = sigma (1 - accumulatedsigma) alpha = sigma (1 - accumulatedsigma) finalrgb = finalrgb (1 - alpha) + rgb alpha accumulatedsigma = accumulatedsigma + alpha (1 - accumulatedsigma) return finalrgb def forward(self, image, targethomography): """ Full forward pass. Args: image (torch.Tensor): Source image. targethomography (torch.Tensor): Homography for target view. Returns: torch.Tensor: Rendered target image. """ features = self.encode(image) # Disparity encoding is assumed to be generated or passed disparityencoding = self.generatedisparityencoding() mpiplanes = self.decode(features, disparityencoding) renderedimage = self.render(mpiplanes, targethomography) return renderedimage Parameters: N{\text{planes}}: The number of planes in the MPI representation. Not given in the sources. Disparity Range: For Flowers Light Fields, the disparity range is set to [3.0, 0.03]. Grid Distance: For Flowers Light Fields, the distance between adjacent grids is set to 0.00128. Camera Intrinsics (Flowers Light Fields): fx = 0.868056 fy = 1.250000 c{xij} = 0.5 + 0.002667 \times i c{yij} = 0.5 + 0.002667 \times j where [i, j] is the index in the extracted 8 \times 8 grid and [0, 0] is the top-left view. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Principle Point Shift: The Flowers Light Fields dataset, captured with a Lytro Illum camera, has a shift in the principle point between different views. Since there is no metadata for the shift amount, it is set to a constant value based on the grid index [i, j]. View-Dependent Color: MINE does not take viewing direction as input by default. If view-dependent effects are required, a lightweight fully convolutional network must be added after warping, which adds N{\text{views}} network inferences. Time Complexity: The number of network forward passes P for MINE is P{\text{MINE}} = 1 + N{\text{planes}}. This is independent of the number of target views N{\text{targets}}. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Comparison: pixelNeRF: P{\text{pixelNerF}} = 1 + N{\text{targets}} \times N{\text{points}} \times H \times W. GRF: P{\text{GRF}} = N{\text{views}} + N{\text{targets}} \times N{\text{points}} \times H \times W. MINE is significantly more efficient than pixelNeRF and GRF because its complexity does not scale with N{\text{targets}}. Strengths: Efficient novel view synthesis from a single image. Allows for dense supervision signals (SSIM, edge-aware smoothness) during training. Generalizes well to large-scale real-world datasets (KITTI, NYU-V2, RealEstate10k, Flowers Light Fields, iBims-1). Limitations: Does not natively support view-dependent color without additional network layers. Requires careful handling of camera intrinsics for datasets with principle point shifts (e.g., Flowers Light Fields). MINE was proposed by Liu et al. in 2021. It is a hybrid between Multi-Plane Images (MPI) and NeRF. The method was verified on datasets including KITTI, NYU-V2, RealEstate10k, Flowers Light Fields, and iBims-1. It addresses the inefficiency of NeRF-like methods in novel view synthesis by reconstructing the camera frustum per plane rather than the entire 3D space per ray. name: Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations
head: Grid-based NeRF, Explicit Radiance Fields, Hash Encoding, Triplane NeRF
body: Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations replace the continuous multi-layer perceptron (MLP) of standard NeRF with explicit spatial data structures—such as dense voxel grids, sparse octrees, hash tables, or triplanes—to store scene features. This substitution eliminates heavy feed-forward neural computations during rendering, enabling real-time volume rendering and scaling to large-scale scenes that exceed single-GPU memory limits. Unlike sibling methods that modify network topology or output spaces while retaining implicit coordinate-based functions, this family fundamentally alters the Representation Basis by substituting the implicit function with explicit structures Parent. The family shares the mechanism of mapping 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} to feature vectors \mathbf{f} via discrete spatial indexing, rather than continuous neural transformation. 1. Spatial Discretization: The scene volume is partitioned into a structured grid (dense or sparse). A query point \mathbf{x} is mapped to grid indices (i, j, k) or hash keys. 2. Feature Retrieval: Features are retrieved from the grid via interpolation (e.g., trilinear or bilinear) or direct lookup. 3. Feature Aggregation: For multi-resolution grids (e.g., hash encoding), features from multiple resolution levels are aggregated (summed or concatenated) to form a high-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{F}. 4. Decoding: The aggregated feature vector \mathbf{F} is passed to a lightweight decoder (often a small MLP or linear layer) to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, or view-dependent coefficients. Replaces the MLP with explicit voxel grids for density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. It limits learnable parameters strictly to grid values, enabling memory-efficient training via coarse-to-fine sparse voxel reconstruction and pruning. Choose this for real-time rendering where explicit control over spatial resolution and pruning is required. Combines a hash-encoded geometry network with a separate light field MLP. It uses a hierarchical hash grid for spatial features and a specific initialization strategy. Choose this for high-frequency geometric detail reconstruction from multi-view images, addressing noise in density-based methods and textureless area failures in SDF-based baselines. Predicts ray color directly without point-wise volume density modeling. It represents a ray as a sequence of spatial-aware features from a hash-based multi-resolution tri-plane, decoded by an LSTM. Choose this to overcome training difficulties of previous NeLF methods that required synthesizing thousands of pseudo-views, enabling training with 100 or fewer original views. A coarse-to-fine framework for scalable large-scale neural scene reconstruction. It decomposes expansive scenes into manageable blocks, trains a shared decoder from a coarse global model, and fuses local results using the global model. Choose this to avoid the 'foggy' issue in Block-NeRF and enable training on a single GPU for large scenes. A hybrid explicit–implicit 3D representation for few-shot novel view synthesis. It decouples scene representation into explicit triplanes for high-frequency color prediction and implicit continuous density fields for volume density. Choose this for remote sensing or few-shot scenarios (e.g., 3 views) where overfitting and slow convergence are critical issues. An out-of-core method that scales NeRFs to large-scale Earth observation scenes by partitioning the region into non-overlapping 3D tiles, each trained with its own independent NeRF. Choose this for terabyte-scale satellite imagery where standard NeRFs fail due to memory bottlenecks, ensuring scalability with a fixed memory budget. Definition: A real-time rendering pipeline that stores a NeRF model in a sparse 3D voxel grid, using an indirection grid to skip empty regions and a deferred MLP to compute view-dependent color from accumulated diffuse and specular features. Step: Raymarch along r(t) = o + td. For occupied voxels, set step size \deltai equal to the voxel width. Concatenate accumulated diffuse color Cd, accumulated specular feature Fs, and positional encoding PE(\mathbf{d}) of the ray's view direction \mathbf{d}. Pass through a lightweight deferred MLP \Phi to produce a view-dependent residual color. Formula: wi = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alphai, where wi is the accumulated weight for sample i. The final color is C(\mathbf{r}) = Cd + \Phi(Cd, Fs, PE(\mathbf{d})). Definition: Distills a large teacher NeRF into a spatially partitioned grid of tiny MLPs to enable fast, adaptive evaluation by mapping 3D positions to local student networks. Step: Initialize a dictionary mapping 3D grid cell indices (i,j,k) to TinyMLP instances. For each training iteration, sample a random ray and generate numsamples stratified samples along it. Compute the grid cell index for each sample by normalizing its position within the bounding box and scaling by grid resolution. Accumulate L2 loss between student and teacher outputs across all samples. Update all grid MLPs using the accumulated loss and the configured learning rate. Parameter: gridresolution: 3D tuple defining the number of cells per axis, e.g., (16,16,16). numdistilliterations: Number of distillation optimization steps, e.g., 1000. numsamples: Number of stratified samples per ray, e.g., 384. learningrate: Optimization step size for grid MLP updates, e.g., 1e^{-3}. bmin, bmax: Axis-aligned bounding box defining the scene bounds, e.g., [0,0,0] and [1,1,1]. The shift from implicit MLPs to explicit grids was driven by the need for real-time rendering and scalability. SNeRG and MERF set benchmarks for real-time rendering by using sparse voxel grids and hybrid low-resolution sparse voxels with 2D high-resolution triplanes, respectively. Hash encoding, popularized by Instant-NGP, introduced multi-resolution hash tables to balance memory and detail. Large-scale extensions like City-on-Web and Snake-NeRF addressed the memory limits of single-GPU training by partitioning scenes into blocks or tiles. name: Voxel-based Radiance Fields
head: Voxel NeRF, Voxel Radiance Fields
body: Voxel-based Radiance Fields replace the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) decoder of standard Neural Radiance Fields with structured voxel grids to store volume density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, enabling real-time volume rendering by eliminating heavy feed-forward neural computations. Unlike MLP-based NeRF which requires evaluating fully-connected layers for every sample point, this method computes color directly from interpolated grid values, offering a memory-efficient framework that limits learnable parameters to the voxel grid values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D spatial location \mathbf{X}k and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} for the k-th sample point on a ray. Output: Volume density \sigmak and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}k. Data Structures: The representation consists of two distinct voxel grids: 1. Density Grid (G\sigma): Maps \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}. Stores scalar volume density values. 2. SH Coefficient Grid (G{sh}): Maps \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{9 \times 3}. Stores degree 2 spherical harmonic coefficients for RGB color. Each spatial location holds a vector of 9 coefficients per color channel (R, G, B), totaling 27 values per voxel. Method Steps: 1. Density Retrieval: For a query point \mathbf{X}k, perform trilinear interpolation using the values from the nearest 8 voxels in G\sigma to obtain the volume density \sigmak. 2. SH Coefficient Retrieval: For the same query point \mathbf{X}k, perform trilinear interpolation using the values from the nearest 8 voxels in G{sh} to obtain a vector of SH coefficients \mathbf{v}k. 3. Direction Mapping: Map the viewing direction \mathbf{d} to a 9-dimensional vector \mathbf{s}(\mathbf{d}) using the degree 2 spherical harmonic basis functions. 4. Color Computation: Compute the color \mathbf{c}k by taking the dot product of the SH direction vector and the interpolated coefficients. Formulas: The volume density \sigmak at sample point \mathbf{X}k is defined as: \sigmak = \mathcal{G}\sigma(\mathbf{X}k) where \mathcal{G}\sigma denotes trilinear interpolation from the nearest 8 voxels in G\sigma. The color \mathbf{c}k is defined as: \mathbf{c}k = S(\mathbf{d})^\intercal \cdot \mathcal{G}{sh}(\mathbf{X}k) where: \mathbf{c}k is the resulting RGB color vector. \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. S(\mathbf{d}) is the SH function mapping direction \mathbf{d} to \mathbb{R}^9. \mathcal{G}{sh}(\mathbf{X}k) is the trilinearly interpolated vector of SH coefficients from the nearest 8 voxels in G{sh}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelradiancefieldquery(Xk, d, Gsigma, Gsh): """ Query voxel-based radiance field for density and color. Args: Xk: 3D spatial coordinate (float32[3]) d: Viewing direction vector (float32[3]) Gsigma: Density grid, shape [D, D, D], stores scalar density Gsh: SH coefficient grid, shape [D, D, D, 27], stores degree-2 SH coeffs for RGB Returns: sigma: Volume density (float32) c: RGB color (float32[3]) """ # 1. Retrieve density via trilinear interpolation # Gsigma is a 3D grid. Trilinear interpolation uses the 8 nearest neighbors. sigma = trilinearinterpolate(Gsigma, Xk) # 2. Retrieve SH coefficients via trilinear interpolation # Gsh is a 4D grid (3D space + 27 channels). shcoeffs = trilinearinterpolate(Gsh, Xk) # Returns vector of size 27 # 3. Map direction to SH basis vector # S(d) maps direction to R^9. For degree 2, there are 9 basis functions. # The coefficients are stored as 9 per channel (R, G, B). # We assume a standard degree-2 SH basis evaluation. shbasis = evaluateshbasis(d, degree=2) # Returns vector of size 9 # 4. Compute color # shcoeffs layout: [R0..R8, G0..G8, B0..B8] # We split coefficients into R, G, B components shcoeffsr = shcoeffs[0:9] shcoeffsg = shcoeffs[9:18] shcoeffsb = shcoeffs[18:27] # Dot product of SH basis and coefficients for each channel r = dotproduct(shbasis, shcoeffsr) g = dotproduct(shbasis, shcoeffsg) b = dotproduct(shbasis, shcoeffsb) c = np.array([r, g, b]) return sigma, c def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point): """ Perform trilinear interpolation on a 3D grid. grid: 3D array (or 4D for SH grid) point: 3D coordinate in continuous space """ # Normalize point to grid coordinates if necessary, assuming grid covers [-1, 1]^3 or similar # Find integer indices of the corner voxel x, y, z = point ix = floor(x) iy = floor(y) iz = floor(z) # Fractional parts fx = x - ix fy = y - iy fz = z - iz # Get values from 8 corners # Handle boundary checks v000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] v100 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz] v010 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz] v110 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz] v001 = grid[ix, iy, iz+1] v101 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz+1] v011 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz+1] v111 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] # Interpolate along x v00 = lerp(v000, v100, fx) v01 = lerp(v010, v110, fx) v10 = lerp(v001, v101, fx) v11 = lerp(v011, v111, fx) # Interpolate along y v0 = lerp(v00, v01, fy) v1 = lerp(v10, v11, fy) # Interpolate along z result = lerp(v0, v1, fz) return result def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def evaluateshbasis(d, degree): """ Evaluate spherical harmonic basis functions for a direction d. Returns a vector of size (degree+1)^2. For degree 2, size is 9. """ # Normalize direction d = d / np.linalg.norm(d) x, y, z = d # Degree 0 y0 = 0.282096 # Degree 1 y1 = 0.488603 y y2 = 0.488603 z y3 = 0.488603 x # Degree 2 y4 = 1.092548 x y y5 = 1.092548 y z y6 = 0.315392 (3 z2 - 1) y7 = 1.092548 x z y8 = 0.546274 (x2 - y2) return np.array([y0, y1, y2, y3, y4, y5, y6, y7, y8]) Parameters: Grid Resolution: Not given in the sources. SH Degree: 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Trilinear interpolation requires handling points outside the grid bounds. Standard practice clamps coordinates or uses padding, but specific boundary handling is not detailed in the source. Precision: Trilinear interpolation is differentiable, allowing gradient flow through the grid for training. Uses coarse-to-fine sparse voxel reconstruction combined with pruning strategies to further enhance memory efficiency during training. Neural Multi-View Image Reconstruction with Hash Encoding uses hash tables instead of structured grids for spatial indexing, offering a trade-off between memory locality and storage density. G-NeLF incorporates geometric constraints into the radiance field optimization, differing in its regularization strategy rather than its spatial representation. SCALAR-NeRF focuses on scalar field representations for specific optimization properties, distinct from the explicit voxel grid storage of Voxel NeRF. TriDF utilizes tri-plane representations, which are a compressed form of 3D feature storage, differing from the full 3D voxel grid. Tile and Slide Framework processes the scene in tiles to manage memory, whereas Voxel NeRF typically loads the entire grid or sparse structure into memory. Time Complexity: Rendering is significantly faster than MLP-based NeRF because it eliminates the feed-forward neural network computation. Color is computed via direct interpolation and dot product. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of voxels. The density grid requires 1 value per voxel, and the SH grid requires 27 values per voxel (degree 2, 3 channels). Performance: Achieves real-time volume rendering. Strengths: Memory-efficient framework; limits learnable parameters to grid values; enables real-time rendering by avoiding heavy MLP computations. Limitations: Resolution is limited by grid size; aliasing may occur at high frequencies if grid resolution is insufficient; not given in the sources. When to use: When real-time rendering is required and memory efficiency is critical, such as in dynamic scenes or mobile applications. When not to use: When high-frequency detail is required beyond the grid resolution, or when the scene geometry is highly complex and sparse, requiring adaptive resolution not provided by a uniform grid. Voxel-based Radiance Fields were introduced as an optimization of NeRF [29] to address the computational bottleneck of MLP-based decoders. The method was notably applied in ExBluRF for efficient radiance field optimization in the presence of extreme motion blur. By replacing the MLP with voxel grids, the approach leverages differentiable volume rendering while achieving real-time performance through direct grid lookups and interpolation.
