name: Transformer and Vision Model Integration
head: Vision-Transformer NeRF, Generalizable NeRF with Vision Backbones
body: This family integrates Vision Transformers (ViT) and other vision models into NeRF architectures to replace or augment the standard coordinate-based MLP, enabling generalizable novel view synthesis from single or few images without per-scene optimization. It solves the limitation of standard NeRF, which requires expensive per-scene training, by leveraging global semantic and local appearance features extracted from pre-trained vision backbones to condition the radiance field. Unlike sibling methods that rely on latent codes or explicit voxel grids, this approach directly maps 2D image features to 3D spatial queries via attention or interpolation mechanisms. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as surface normals \mathbf{n}, semantic logits \mathbf{s}, uncertainty variance \nu, or blend weights \Delta w. 4. Representation Basis: Substituting the coordinate-based implicit function with explicit structures like voxel grids, hash tables, Gaussian primitives, or planar surfaces, which change how features are stored and interpolated. ViT-NeRF combines a Vision Transformer (ViT) to encode global shape information and a 2D CNN to extract local appearance features, conditioning volume rendering on hybrid per-pixel features. It addresses the limitation of using only global features, which compromises rendering quality for views close to the input view, by fusing them with local CNN features. Unlike CodeNeRF and DISN, it does not require a canonical coordinate system to utilize global features. See ViT-NeRF. VisionNeRF infers a 3D radiance field from a single unposed input image by combining global features learned from a ViT and local appearance features extracted from a 2D CNN. It solves the problem of rendering quality degradation in occluded regions, where standard image-conditioned models incorrectly query features from visible surfaces that do not correspond to the target view's geometry. Unlike sibling methods that rely on per-scene optimization or latent codes, VisionNeRF uses an explicit mapping between input image pixels and 3D point queries, enabling generalization across object categories without requiring camera pose information. See VisionNeRF. TransNeRF is a generalizable neural radiance field method that learns a generic scene representation for novel view synthesis using an encoder-decoder Transformer framework, avoiding per-scene optimization. Unlike standard NeRF which optimizes a scene-specific MLP, TransNeRF aggregates multi-view information from source images into a coordinate-based representation via attention mechanisms, enabling generalization to unseen scenes without fine-tuning. It differs from previous pooling-based multi-view representations by exploring deep relationships amongst multiple views and aggregating them into the radiance field via a single Transformer-based architecture. See TransNeRF. NeRF Analogies transfers visual attributes (appearance) from a source NeRF to a target NeRF by establishing dense semantic correspondences using Vision Transformer (ViT) features. It solves the problem of appearance editing in 3D by creating a "NeRF analogy" where the target object adopts the texture and material properties of the source object based on semantic similarity rather than geometric proximity. It is distinguished from sibling methods like ViT-NeRF and VisionNeRF by its explicit use of cross-scene semantic matching to drive a differentiable loss function, rather than using vision features solely for conditioning a single-scene reconstruction. See NeRF Analogies. Definition: A modification to the GNT view transformer where dense MLP layers are replaced with sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers to specialize different components for specific rendering properties (e.g., diffuse vs. specular reflection). Step: Replace the dense MLP layer in the view transformer with a sparsely activated MoE layer composed of a set of half-sized MLP experts \{fe\}{e=1}^E. Formula: The routing weights are computed as R(x) = \text{softmax}(\text{TopK}(G(x), K)), where G is the learnable network within the router. The output is the weighted summation of the selected experts. A diversity regularizer L{div} = \text{CV}(\mathbb{E}{r \sim R} \mathbb{E}{x \in r} R(x)) is applied, where \text{CV}(g) = \text{mean}(g)/\text{var}(g), to encourage different views to exploit the expert space and different experts to capture nuances. Parameters: K=2 (number of top experts selected), E=4 (total expert candidates), Expert Size is half the dense MLP size, and \lambda{div} = 1 \times 10^{-3}. The integration of vision transformers into NeRFs emerged to address the computational cost of per-scene optimization in standard NeRF. Early methods like ViT-NeRF and VisionNeRF demonstrated that pre-trained vision backbones could provide robust global and local features for single-image novel view synthesis. TransNeRF extended this by using transformer decoders to aggregate multi-view information without per-scene tuning. NeRF Analogies later applied these semantic features for cross-scene appearance transfer. The use of Mixture-of-Experts in generalizable NeRFs (GNT) further refined this by specializing transformer layers for different material properties. Enhancing NeRF akin to Enhancing LLMs: Generalizable NeRF Transformer with Mixture-of-View-Experts, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.00296, fetched 2026-10-26

name: ViT-NeRF
head: Global-Local Feature NeRF, Hybrid ViT-CNN NeRF, Vision Transformer for NeRF (ViT-NeRF)
body: ViT-NeRF is a view synthesis method that combines a Vision Transformer (ViT) to encode global shape information and a 2D CNN to extract local appearance features, conditioning volume rendering on hybrid per-pixel features. It addresses the limitation of pure global feature methods, which compromise rendering quality for views close to the input view, by fusing long-range dependencies with local appearance consistency. Unlike CodeNeRF and DISN, it does not require a canonical coordinate system to utilize global features, and compared to SRN and PixelNeRF, it produces sharper edges and clearer structures on invisible parts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single source image Is \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, where H and W are height and width. Output: A rendered 2D image for a target viewpoint defined by ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Data Structures: Image Tokens: Sequence of flattened 2D patches P \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times P^2 \times 3}, where N = \frac{HW}{P^2} is the number of patches and P is the patch size. Latent Features: Set of latent features \mathbf{f} extracted by the ViT encoder. Global Feature Maps: Multi-level feature maps W^0G,..., W^JG, where W^jG \in \mathbb{R}^{Hj \times Wj \times Dj}. Local Feature Map: WL \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{2} \times \frac{W}{2} \times DL}. Hybrid Feature Map: W \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}, the fused result. Positional Encoding: \gamma(\mathbf{p}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2M}, where M=10. Numbered Steps: 1. Global Feature Extraction: a. Reshape Is into a sequence of flattened 2D patches P. b. Linearly project each patch to an image token. c. Input image tokens and learnable positional embeddings into the Transformer Encoder to extract latent features \mathbf{f}. d. Drop the class token from \mathbf{f}. The class token is useful during self-attention but has no physical meaning when unflattened. e. Unflatten the remaining tokens into feature patches \mathbf{P}f. f. Generate multi-level global feature maps W^jG using a convolutional decoder D for each level j \in \{0,..., J\}: W^jG = (D \circ U \circ O)(\mathbf{f}j) where O: \mathbb{R}^{(N+1) \times D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} drops the class token, U: \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{P} \times \frac{W}{P} \times D} unflattens, and D consists of a 1 \times 1 convolution, strided/transposed convolution for resizing, and a 3 \times 3 convolution. 2. Local Feature Extraction: a. Pass Is through a 2D CNN module GL consisting of three ResBlocks to extract local image features: WL = GL(Is) where GL: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{2} \times \frac{W}{2} \times DL}. 3. Feature Fusion: a. Fuse the global maps W^0G,..., W^JG and the local map WL using a convolutional layer G to produce the hybrid feature map W: W = G(W^0G, W^1G,..., W^JG; WL). 4. Volumetric Rendering: a. For a target ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} bounded by t{near} and t{far}, sample equally distributed 3D locations \mathbf{x}c along the ray. b. Project \mathbf{x}c to the 2D image plane to find the corresponding pixel \pi(\mathbf{x}c) in the source image. c. Extract the per-pixel hybrid feature \mathbf{w} = W(\pi(\mathbf{x}c)). d. Encode the 3D location \mathbf{x}c using positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}c) with M=10 frequency bases: \gamma(\mathbf{p}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{p}),..., \sin(2^{M-1} \pi \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^{M-1} \pi \mathbf{p})). e. Input \gamma(\mathbf{x}c), viewing direction \mathbf{d}c, and feature \mathbf{w} into an MLP to output density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \text{MLP}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}c); \mathbf{d}c; \mathbf{w}). f. Render the image using standard volume rendering: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) \mathbf{c}(t) dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds) is the accumulated transmittance. Parameters: Frequency bases (M): 10. Learning Rate: 10^{-4} for the NeRF MLP; 10^{-5} for the ViT and CNN modules. Batch Size: 8 instances, with 512 rays per instance. Training Iterations: Converges at 500K iterations. Warm-up: Linear warm-up from 0 learning rate for the first 10k steps. ViT Initialization: Initialized from pretrained weights of reference [55] and fine-tuned. Local CNN: GL consists of three ResBlocks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Class Token: The class token in ViT must be dropped before decoding into spatial feature maps, as it has no physical meaning in that context. Global-Only Limitation: Using only global ViT features compromises rendering quality for views close to the input view (inconsistent color/appearance). This is solved by adding the local CNN branch. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On ShapeNet Chairs, ViT-NeRF achieves PSNR 24.48, SSIM 0.93, LPIPS 0.077. On ShapeNet Cars, it achieves PSNR 22.88, SSIM 0.91, LPIPS 0.084. Hardware: Trained on 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Strengths: Produces sharper edges and clearer structures than SRN and PixelNeRF, especially on invisible parts like chair legs. Combines the advantage of 2D-based methods (local appearance) and 1D-based methods (global information). Limitations: Volume-based methods are more computationally intensive and require more memory when increasing the grid size. ViT-NeRF was introduced in "Vision Transformer for NeRF-Based View Synthesis from a Single Input Image". It builds on the success of Vision Transformers in learning long-range dependencies between features. Unlike CodeNeRF and DISN, it does not require a canonical coordinate system to utilize global features. name: VisionNeRF
head: Vision Transformer for NeRF
body: VisionNeRF is a novel view synthesis method that infers a 3D representation from a single unposed input image by combining global features learned from a Vision Transformer (ViT) and local appearance features extracted from a 2D CNN, rendered via a NeRF-based MLP. Unlike sibling methods such as ViT-NeRF which may focus on different architectural integrations, VisionNeRF specifically addresses the degradation of rendering quality in occluded regions by using self-attention to retrieve relevant features from distant parts of the source view, rather than querying features along the ray corresponding to the visible surface. It differs from TransNeRF by adopting a radiance field representation with per-pixel information from feature maps, providing an explicit mapping between the input image and 3D point queries, whereas SRT learns 3D scene information as a set of latent codes decoded by a transformer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single unposed image Is at camera s. No camera pose information is required. Output: A rendered image for a target viewpoint defined by a ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Data Structures: 1. Feature Tokens: A sequence of vectors obtained by lifting the input image into patches and processing them through the ViT. 2. Multi-level Feature Maps: 2D tensor grids at multiple resolutions, derived from unflattened and resampled ViT tokens, capturing global information in a coarse-to-fine manner. 3. Local Feature Maps: 2D tensor grids extracted from a 2D CNN, capturing local details and appearance. Numbered Steps: 1. Global Feature Extraction: Lift the input 2D image Is into feature tokens and apply a Vision Transformer (ViT) to learn global information. 2. Feature Map Resampling: Unflatten the ViT feature tokens and resample them into multi-level feature maps to capture global information in a coarse-to-fine manner. 3. Local Feature Extraction: Extract local features from the input image Is using a 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) to capture details and appearance. 4. 3D Representation Conditioning: For a query 3D point \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}, condition a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) on the learned 3D representation. This representation is formed by combining the global features (from the multi-level feature maps) and local features (from the CNN). 5. Volume Rendering: Use the MLP to predict volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for the query point, then integrate these values along the ray using standard volume rendering equations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def visionnerfrender(inputimage, rayorigin, raydirection): """ Renders a novel view from a single unposed image using VisionNeRF. Args: inputimage: 2D tensor of shape (H, W, 3) representing the single input image Is. rayorigin: 3D vector o for the target viewpoint ray. raydirection: 3D vector d for the target viewpoint ray. Returns: color: Rendered color value for the ray. depth: Integrated depth value for the ray. """ # Step 1: Global Feature Extraction via Vision Transformer # Lift image to tokens and apply ViT # Note: Specific ViT architecture (e.g., patch size, number of layers) # is not detailed in the source notes. tokens = visiontransformerforward(inputimage) # Step 2: Resample to Multi-level Feature Maps # Unflatten tokens and resample into coarse-to-fine feature maps # Note: The specific resampling mechanism (e.g., bilinear, nearest) # and number of levels are not detailed in the source notes. globalfeaturemaps = unflattenandresample(tokens) # Step 3: Local Feature Extraction via CNN # Extract local features capturing details and appearance # Note: Specific CNN architecture (e.g., ResNet, EfficientNet) # is not detailed in the source notes. localfeaturemaps = cnnforward(inputimage) # Step 4: Sample Features for Query Point # Query the global and local feature maps at the 3D point's projection # Note: The method uses an explicit mapping between input image and 3D point. # Since no camera pose is provided, the projection of x onto the input image # plane must be inferred or handled implicitly by the conditioning network. # The source states it does not enforce symmetry or canonical coordinate systems. # globalfeatures = samplefeatures(globalfeaturemaps, rayorigin, raydirection) localfeatures = samplefeatures(localfeaturemaps, rayorigin, raydirection) # Step 5: MLP Conditioning and Volume Rendering # Condition MLP on global and local features # The MLP takes (globalfeatures, localfeatures, raydirection) as input # to predict density and color. # Note: The exact MLP input concatenation and structure are not detailed. density, color = mlpforward(globalfeatures, localfeatures, raydirection) # Standard Volume Rendering Integration along the ray # Note: Standard NeRF integration is assumed. color, depth = volumerender(rayorigin, raydirection, density, color) return color, depth Parameters and Typical Values: Dataset: ShapeNet (13 object categories) and real-world images. Performance (ShapeNet): LPIPS: 0.09, PSNR: 21.03. Comparison Baseline (PixelNeRF on ShapeNet): LPIPS: 0.20, PSNR: 21.85. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-occlusion: In standard image-conditioned models, when a target view pixel is invisible from the input view, the model incorrectly uses features from other visible surfaces (e.g., using window features to render a wheel). VisionNeRF mitigates this by using self-attention to find long-range dependencies, allowing it to retrieve relevant features from distant parts of the source view for occluded regions. Coordinate System: The method uses a viewer-centered coordinate system and does not enforce constraints like symmetry or canonical coordinate systems. Strengths: Renders richer details and more accurate structure in occluded regions compared to existing approaches like PixelNeRF. Generalizes across multiple object categories using a single model. Limitations: Performance on PSNR is slightly lower than PixelNeRF on ShapeNet (21.03 vs 21.85), though LPIPS is significantly better (0.09 vs 0.20), indicating superior perceptual quality. When to use: When novel view synthesis from a single unposed image is required, particularly when occluded regions need to be rendered with high fidelity. When not to use: When camera pose information is available and precise PSNR is prioritized over perceptual quality in non-occluded regions, as PixelNeRF may offer higher PSNR. VisionNeRF was introduced to address the problem of novel view synthesis from a single unposed image, where existing approaches using local image features often render blurry predictions at viewpoints distant from the source view due to self-occlusion. The method leverages advances in Vision Transformers (ViT) and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to learn a better 3D representation by integrating global and local information. It was trained and evaluated on the ShapeNet dataset including 13 object categories, as well as real-world images. The work was done while the authors were interning at Google or at Google. name: TransNeRF
head: Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields for Novel View Synthesis with Transformer
body: TransNeRF is a generalizable neural radiance field method that learns a generic scene representation for novel view synthesis using an encoder-decoder Transformer framework, eliminating the need for per-scene optimization. Unlike standard NeRF which optimizes a scene-specific MLP, TransNeRF aggregates multi-view information from a set of source images into a coordinate-based representation via attention mechanisms, allowing it to generalize to unseen scenes without finetuning. It differs from previous pooling-based multi-view methods by exploring deep relationships among multiple views and preserving local consistency of the 5D radiance field through ray-cast space processing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A query 3D point location (x, y, z), a unit-length viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and a set of M source views \{Im, \Thetam\}{m=1}^M, where Im is the image and \Thetam contains camera poses, intrinsic parameters, and scene bounds. Outputs: Differential volumetric density \sigma and directional emitted color \mathbf{c} for the query point. Data Structures and Layouts: The method uses four decoders: Density-ViewDecoder, Density-RayDecoder, Color-ViewDecoder, and Color-RayDecoder. 1. Density-ViewDecoder Input X0: Concatenation of a learnable query density embedding \mathbf{x}\sigma^0 and initial source-view embeddings \mathbf{x}1^0, \dots, \mathbf{x}M^0: X0 = [\mathbf{x}\sigma^0; \mathbf{x}1^0; \mathbf{x}2^0; \dots; \mathbf{x}M^0] The initial source-view embeddings \mathbf{x}m^0 are retrieved spatial-aligned 2D-pixel features from a pre-trained U-Net feature volume for the query point projected onto source view m. 2. Density-ViewDecoder Output XL: Concatenation of final query density embedding \mathbf{x}\sigma^L and final source-view embeddings \mathbf{x}1^L, \dots, \mathbf{x}M^L: XL = [\mathbf{x}\sigma^L; \mathbf{x}1^L; \mathbf{x}2^L; \dots; \mathbf{x}M^L] The final query density representation is computed as \mathbf{x}\sigma^L concatenated with (x, y, z). 3. Density-RayDecoder Input D0: Initial density representations of 2n+1 neighboring points along the target-view ray plus positional encodings \mathbf{E}{pos}: D0 = [\sigma{i-n}^0; \dots; \sigma{i-1}^0; \sigmai^0; \sigma{i+1}^0; \dots; \sigma{i+n}^0] + \mathbf{E}{pos} The initial density representation \sigmai^0 for a point is a linear function of the Density-ViewDecoder output: \sigmai^0 = FC(\mathbf{x}\sigma^L(x, y, z)), where FC is a linear projection and \oplus denotes concatenation. Positional encodings use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies. 4. Color-ViewDecoder Keys X{src} and Values C{src}: Keys: Concatenation of linearly projected final source-view embeddings and their source viewing directions \mathbf{d}m^{src}: X{src} = [FC(\mathbf{x}1^L) \oplus \mathbf{d}1^{src}; \dots; FC(\mathbf{x}M^L) \oplus \mathbf{d}M^{src}] Values: Concatenation of embedding functions of source view RGB colors \mathbf{c}m^{src}: C{src} = [\gamma(\mathbf{c}1^{src}); \gamma(\mathbf{c}2^{src}); \dots; \gamma(\mathbf{c}M^{src})] where \gamma(\cdot) is an embedding function. 5. Color-RayDecoder Input Z0: Initial color embeddings of neighboring points plus positional encodings: Z0 = [\mathbf{z}{i-n}^0; \dots; \mathbf{z}{i-1}^0; \mathbf{z}i^0; \mathbf{z}{i+1}^0; \dots; \mathbf{z}{i+n}^0] + \mathbf{E}{pos} The latent color representation \mathbf{y}i^L from Color-ViewDecoder is assigned to \mathbf{z}i^0. Parameters: Nq: Number of queries stacked in Q. N{kv}: Number of key-value pairs stacked in K. dv: Dimension of V. H: Number of attention heads. dh: Feature dimension in each head, such that H \times dh = dk. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each observed source view m, extract a feature volume from a pre-trained U-Net. Retrieve spatial-aligned 2D-pixel features for the query 3D point projected onto view m to form the initial source-view feature \mathbf{x}m^0. 2. Density View Decoding: Decode the initial features for source views into latent density representations using Density-ViewDecoder. The decoder applies self-attention across views: \tilde{X}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Density-ViAttn}(X{l-1}) + X{l-1}) Xl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{X}l) + \tilde{X}l) where \text{Density-ViAttn}(X) = \text{MH-Attn}(X, X, X). 3. Density Ray Decoding: Enhance the latent density representation by considering neighboring points along the target-view ray using Density-RayDecoder. The decoder applies self-attention along the ray: \tilde{D}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Density-Attn}(D{l-1}) + D{l-1}) Dl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{D}l) + D{l-1}) where \text{Density-Attn}(D) = \text{MH-Attn}(D, D, D). The output density \sigmai^L is projected to a scalar density value. 4. Color View Decoding: Fuse latent source-view features from Density-ViewDecoder and the query-point density representation from Density-RayDecoder into a latent color representation using Color-ViewDecoder. The initial query color embedding is \mathbf{Y}0 = FC(\sigmai^L) \oplus \mathbf{d}{tgt}, where \mathbf{d}{tgt} is the target viewing direction. The decoder applies cross-attention: \tilde{Y}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Color-ViAttn}(Y{l-1}, X{src}, C{src}) + Y{l-1}) Yl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{Y}l) + \tilde{Y}l) where \text{Color-ViAttn}(Y, X{src}, C{src}) = \text{MH-Attn}(Y, X{src}, C{src}). 5. Color Ray Decoding: Decode the query color by integrating color information of 3D points along the target-viewing ray using Color-RayDecoder. The decoder applies self-attention along the ray: \tilde{Z}l = \text{Norm}(\text{Color-Attn}(Z{l-1}) + Z{l-1}) Zl = \text{Norm}(\text{FFN}(\tilde{Z}l) + Z{l-1}) where \text{Color-Attn}(Z) = \text{MH-Attn}(Z, Z, Z). The final color embedding \mathbf{z}i^L is projected to the predicted color \mathbf{c}. Rendering: Classical volume rendering computes the rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) of a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} with near/far bounds [tn, tf]: C(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t)\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t); Im, \Thetam)\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}; Im, \Thetam)dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s); Im, \Thetam)ds). Multi-Head Attention Definition: \text{MH-Attn}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(A1, \dots, AH)W Ah = \text{Attention}(Qh, Kh, Vh) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Qh Kh^T}{\sqrt{dh}}\right)Vh where Qh = QWh^q, Kh = KWh^k, Vh = VWh^v. Training: The model is trained end-to-end by minimizing the rendering loss between rendered and ground truth pixel colors for all camera rays of the target view: \mathcal{L} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R(\Theta)} \|\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 where R(\Theta) is the set of all camera rays of the desired virtual camera with pose \Theta. Pitfalls: Pooling-based fusion models in previous methods can barely explore complex relationships across multiple views and ignore local consistency of the 5D radiance field. The method requires a large dataset of diverse scenes for training to generalize effectively; it does not perform well on single-scene generalization without sufficient prior data. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, the use of attention mechanisms over M source views and 2n+1 neighboring points along the ray suggests complexity dependent on O(M^2) or O((2n+1)^2) for attention computations, plus the cost of U-Net feature extraction. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the number of source views M, the number of ray neighbors n, and the Transformer depth L. Performance: TransNeRF effectively generalizes to unseen scenes even without per-scene finetuning after being trained on a large dataset containing diverse scenes. Strengths: Explores deep relationships amongst multiple views; aggregates multi-view information into coordinate-based scene representation via attention; learns local geometry consistency of shape and appearance by considering information in ray-cast and surrounding-view spaces. Limitations: Requires training on a large dataset of diverse scenes; inference requires access to multiple source views and their camera parameters; attention mechanisms may be computationally expensive for high numbers of views or ray samples. When to use: Novel view synthesis for unseen scenes where per-scene optimization is prohibitive or impossible, and a pre-trained general model is available. When not to use: Single-scene reconstruction where per-scene optimization is feasible and desired for maximum fidelity; scenes significantly different from the training distribution. TransNeRF was proposed in the paper "Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields for Novel View Synthesis with Transformer". It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which requires per-scene optimization, by introducing a Transformer-based architecture that learns a generic radiance field representation. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and multi-view geometry, integrating concepts from computer vision Transformers. Generalizable Neural Radiance Fields for Novel View Synthesis with Transformer, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2206.05375, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeRF Analogies
head: Example-Based Visual Attribute Transfer, NeRF Analogies: Example-Based Visual Attribute Transfer
body: NeRF Analogies is a method for transferring visual appearance attributes from a source NeRF to a target NeRF by establishing dense semantic correspondences using Vision Transformer (ViT) features. It solves the problem of style or texture transfer in 3D scenes by mapping semantically similar regions between two distinct objects, creating a "NeRF analogy" where the target object adopts the appearance of the source. Unlike sibling methods that modify architecture for general feature integration, this method specifically leverages the semantic depth of DiNO-ViT features to guide the optimization of the target NeRF's color output, distinguishing itself from simpler feature-matching approaches like SIFT which fail to capture semantic similarity. The method optimizes a target NeRF to match the appearance of a source NeRF by enforcing consistency between their respective ViT feature representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source NeRF (with known geometry and appearance) and a target NeRF (initialized with geometry, typically from a standard reconstruction or template). Both are represented by images captured from specific viewpoints. Output: An optimized target NeRF whose color output \mathbf{c} reflects the visual attributes of the source NeRF, guided by semantic correspondences. Data Structures: NeRF Model: A fully-connected Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Architecture: 8 hidden layers with 256 neurons each, followed by 1 hidden layer with 128 neurons, and an output layer. Activation: The output layer uses a Sigmoid activation function. Output: Standard NeRF outputs (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \sigma is density and \mathbf{c} \in [0, 1]^3 is color. ViT Features: Extracted using DiNO-ViT. Backbone: ViT-8B. Patch Size: 8 pixels. Stride: 4 pixels. Feature Dimension: 384 features per pixel. Layer Used: The key-component of the attention maps from the deepest (11th) attention layer. Feature Maps: High-resolution feature maps generated by querying the ViT on translated versions of the input image. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 512. Total Iterations: 60,000. DoG Loss Weight (\lambda): Starts at 0 for the first 20,000 iterations, then gradually increases up to 50. Image Resolution: Evaluated on 400p images, resulting in feature maps of resolution 392 \times 392. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each input image I of the source and target scenes, extract dense semantic features \mathbf{F} using DiNO-ViT. To achieve pixel-granularity and smoother feature maps, query the ViT on four subsequent translations of the image by one pixel in the -x and -y directions. This increases the spatial resolution of the feature maps. 2. Ray Sampling and Rendering: For a given camera pose, sample points \mathbf{x}i along rays. Query the target NeRF MLP to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. Render the target image \mathbf{C}{target} using standard volume rendering. Similarly, render the source image \mathbf{C}{source} using the source NeRF. 3. Correspondence Mapping: Map pixels from the target image to the source image based on semantic similarity of their ViT features. Let \mathbf{F}{target}(\mathbf{u}) and \mathbf{F}{source}(\mathbf{v}) be the feature vectors at pixel coordinates \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}. Find the correspondence \mathbf{v} = \mathcal{M}(\mathbf{u}) that maximizes the cosine similarity between \mathbf{F}{target}(\mathbf{u}) and \mathbf{F}{source}(\mathbf{v}). Note: The sources mention that noisy correspondences may occur where two points on the target mesh map to different points in the source NeRF. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted combination of the color loss \mathcal{L}c and the Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) loss \mathcal{L}G: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \lambda \, \mathcal{L}G \mathcal{L}c: Standard color reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 or L2) between the rendered target color and the source color at corresponding pixels. The use of L1 loss is explicitly noted to encourage sparsity in handling noisy correspondences. \mathcal{L}G: A DoG loss term applied to the feature maps or rendered outputs to preserve edges and structural details during transfer. \lambda: The weight for the DoG loss, scheduled as described in Parameters. 5. Optimization: Update the target NeRF parameters \Theta using the Adam optimizer to minimize \mathcal{L}. Repeat for 60,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim from torchvision import transforms class NeRFMLP(nn.Module): def init(self): super(NeRFMLP, self).init() layers = [] # 8 layers of 256 neurons for in range(8): layers.append(nn.Linear(256, 256)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # 1 layer of 128 neurons layers.append(nn.Linear(256, 128)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Output layer with Sigmoid layers.append(nn.Linear(128, 4)) # 1 for sigma, 3 for color self.net = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x): # x: (N, 3) h = self.net(x) sigma = h[..., 0:1] color = torch.sigmoid(h[..., 1:4]) return sigma, color def extractvitfeatures(image, vitmodel): """ Extracts features using DiNO-ViT with ViT-8B backbone. Handles overlapping patches by querying translations. Returns feature map of shape (H, W, 384). """ # Implementation details for translation and patching are omitted # as they depend on specific ViT library internals. # The source specifies: patch size 8, stride 4, 11th layer keys. pass def computedogloss(img1, img2): """ Computes Difference-of-Gaussians loss between two images. """ # Gaussian blur kernels with different sigmas # LG = || Blur(img1, sigma1) - Blur(img2, sigma2) || # Exact kernel sizes and sigmas not specified in sources. pass def trainnerfanalogy(sourcenerf, targetnerf, sourceimages, targetimages, vitmodel): optimizer = optim.Adam(targetnerf.parameters(), lr=1e-4) totaliterations = 60000 warmupiterations = 20000 maxlambda = 50 for i in range(totaliterations): optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Sample rays and render # Assume getraybatch() returns rayso, raysd, and ground truth colors rayso, raysd, gtcolor = getraybatch(targetimages) # Render target sigmat, colort = renderrays(targetnerf, rayso, raysd) # Render source (using fixed sourcenerf) # Note: Source rendering might use same rays or mapped rays sigmas, colors = renderrays(sourcenerf, rayso, raysd) # 2. Extract ViT Features # Features are extracted from the 2D images, not 3D points directly # We need to map 3D points to 2D pixels for feature lookup # This step assumes a projection or pre-computed correspondence map featt = extractvitfeatures(targetimages, vitmodel) feats = extractvitfeatures(sourceimages, vitmodel) # 3. Compute Correspondences # Find pixel u in target that corresponds to pixel v in source # based on max cosine similarity of featt[u] and feats[v] # This is computationally expensive and done per batch or precomputed correspondencemap = findsemanticcorrespondence(featt, feats) # 4. Compute Losses # Color Loss (L1 as per source) # Map target rendered color to source color via correspondence mappedsourcecolor = gathercolors(colors, correspondencemap) Lc = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(colort, mappedsourcecolor) # DoG Loss # Applied to feature maps or rendered images to preserve edges LG = computedogloss(featt, feats) # Or on rendered images # Schedule lambda if i < warmupiterations: lambdaval = 0 else: # Gradually fade in up to 50 progress = (i - warmupiterations) / (totaliterations - warmupiterations) lambdaval = progress maxlambda loss = Lc + lambdaval LG loss.backward() optimizer.step() if i % 1000 == 0: print(f"Iter {i}, Loss: {loss.item()}, Lambda: {lambdaval}") Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Correspondences: DiNO features can produce noisy correspondences where multiple target points map to different source points. The method mitigates this by using L1 loss, which encourages sparsity. Feature Granularity: Using coarser features (e.g., DiNO-v2 with larger patch sizes) reduces correspondence quality. The method requires high-resolution features (patch size 8, stride 4). Computational Cost: Using diffusion features doubles computation time without significant quality improvement compared to DiNO. SIFT features perform poorly due to lack of semantic understanding. Time Complexity: Training takes less than two hours on a single GPU, including feature extraction. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of high-resolution feature maps (384 features per pixel for 400p images) and the ViT model weights (ViT-8B). Strengths: Effective transfer of complex visual attributes using semantic understanding; fast training time; works with standard NeRF architectures. Limitations: Relies on the quality of semantic correspondences; may struggle with semantically unrelated but similarly shaped objects (though plausible results can be achieved); sensitive to feature extraction resolution. When to Use: When the goal is to transfer appearance/style between two 3D objects with semantic similarities. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is required (training is offline); when semantic correspondence is not available or reliable; when computational resources are extremely limited (ViT extraction is heavy). NeRF Analogies was introduced by Michael Fischer, Zhengqin Li, Thu Nguyen-Phuoc, Aljaž Božič, Zhao Dong, Carl Marshall, and Tobias Ritschel from University College London and Meta Reality Labs. The method was presented at CVPR 2024. It builds on the standard NeRF architecture [Parent] and leverages advances in Vision Transformers (ViT), specifically DiNO, for dense semantic correspondence. The work addresses the limitation of previous methods that either lacked semantic understanding (e.g., SIFT) or were computationally prohibitive (e.g., diffusion features). name: Human and Specific Subject Modeling
head: Human NeRF, Dynamic Human NeRF, Volumetric Avatar
body: This family modifies the NeRF architecture to represent dynamic, articulated human subjects, addressing the high-frequency geometry, non-rigid deformation, and pose-dependent appearance that static scene NeRFs cannot capture. Unlike general scene modeling, these methods integrate parametric body priors (e.g., SMPL, MANO) or semantic latent codes to disentangle rigid skeletal motion from non-rigid clothing deformation and identity-specific appearance. They distinguish themselves by conditioning the radiance field on pose, shape, and semantic information, enabling novel view synthesis for unseen poses and generalizing across subjects without per-scene optimization. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as surface normals \mathbf{n}, semantic logits \mathbf{s}, uncertainty variance \nu, or blend weights \Delta w. 4. Representation Basis: Substituting the coordinate-based implicit function with explicit structures like voxel grids, hash tables, Gaussian primitives, or planar surfaces, which change how features are stored and interpolated. LISA is a part-based implicit neural representation method specifically designed for modeling human hands. It addresses the complexity of hand geometry by approximating the hand as a collection of rigid parts, leveraging the MANO model for structural priors. Unlike general body avatars, LISA distinguishes itself by using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for shape description and implicitly encoding MANO shape parameters via skeletal posture, while simultaneously learning a color field for realistic appearance. Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA) is a neural volumetric representation for human avatars that enables local and independent editing of both geometry and texture while supporting novel view and pose synthesis. It distinguishes itself from methods relying on pre-defined UV mapping or two-stage distillation by anchoring separate neural fields for geometry and appearance to a deformable mesh in canonical space, allowing direct manipulation of latent codes and end-to-end training from scratch. HumanNeRF is a generalizable neural radiance field method for high-fidelity free-view synthesis of dynamic humans from sparse multi-view inputs, designed to generalize to unseen subjects and camera settings without per-scene training. It distinguishes itself from prior generalizable methods by combining aggregated pixel-alignment features with a pose-embedded non-rigid deformation field and a neural appearance blending scheme, addressing the blur artifacts and geometric discontinuities common in implicit texture representations. Unlike per-scene methods that require hours of optimization per subject, HumanNeRF provides reasonable results immediately and achieves state-of-the-art quality with only ~1 hour of fine-tuning. HumanNeRF-SE is a method for synthesizing novel pose images of humans from monocular video inputs by combining explicit SMPL shape priors with an implicit NeRF representation. It solves the problem of overfitting and high computational complexity inherent in previous NeRF-based human avatars by using frozen SMPL blending weights for rigid deformation and a sparse voxel volume to filter irrelevant sampling points. Unlike sibling methods that rely on learnable neural blend weights or frame-level features, HumanNeRF-SE uses only point-level spatial-aware features to ensure pose generalization, reducing learnable parameters to less than 1% of previous methods. Dynamic Semantic Human NeRF extends the NeRF framework to model dynamic human motion by learning a consistent continuous function for geometry and appearance variations across frames. It solves the problem of rendering humans in motion by warping observations into a canonical reference frame using the imGHUM prior, allowing a single radiance field to represent articulated human bodies. It differs from static human NeRF variants by conditioning the network on semantic latent codes (shape \beta, pose \theta, and root transformation T) to generalize to novel poses and shapes, and by using a residual Signed Distance Field (SDF) to capture fine-grained details like clothing deformation. Definition: A NeRF architecture consisting of a coarse sub-model and a fine sub-model for the scene, and a single sub-model for the human NeRF model, leveraging SMPL geometry priors. Layout: Architecture visualization (Fig. 10): Blue boxes are raw inputs, green boxes are positional encoded values, black boxes are hidden layers, pink boxes are final outputs. Numbers indicate feature dimensions. '+' indicates concatenation. ReLU is applied after each hidden layer. Comparison: Unlike NeuralBody which overfits to training observations and produces poor rendering on the back of the subject, NeuMan generalizes better and faithfully renders the back. Definition: A method showing how to train a neural radiance field for a specific actor based on monocular input data. Origin: The application of NeRF to human modeling emerged shortly after the initial NeRF publication. Early works like NeuMan and NeuralBody demonstrated the feasibility of using SMPL priors to guide human NeRF training from monocular or sparse multi-view video. Subsequent developments, such as HumanNeRF, shifted focus toward generalizable models that do not require per-subject optimization, while methods like UVA and LISA introduced more sophisticated representations for geometry and appearance decoupling. These methods are primarily used in virtual production, digital avatars, and motion capture visualization. name: LISA
head: LISA (April 2022)
body: LISA is a part-based implicit neural representation method specifically designed for modeling human hands. It approximates the hand structure as a collection of rigid parts, leveraging the MANO (Modeling of the HAND) parametric model to define the underlying skeletal and shape topology. Unlike monolithic NeRF approaches, LISA decouples geometry and appearance by using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for shape description and a separate color field for realistic rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D query points \mathbf{q}, MANO skeletal posture parameters (joint angles), and MANO shape parameters (implicitly derived from posture). Outputs: Signed Distance Field value d(\mathbf{q}) representing geometry, and color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) representing appearance. Data Structures: MANO Model: A parametric hand model providing a skeletal hierarchy and mesh topology. The shape parameters \beta are not learned directly as independent variables but are implicitly described by the current skeletal posture. MLPs: Two distinct Multi-Layer Perceptrons (or a shared backbone with separate heads) are employed. One network predicts the SDF value, and the other predicts the RGB color. Steps: 1. Pose-Driven Shape Definition: Given a specific hand pose, the MANO model defines the spatial configuration of the hand's rigid parts (bones and fingers). The shape parameters \beta are implicitly determined by this skeletal posture, ensuring the geometry adheres to anatomical constraints. 2. Query Processing: For each 3D query point \mathbf{q} in the scene: a. Determine the local coordinate system or feature representation relative to the nearest rigid part or bone defined by the MANO skeleton. b. Input \mathbf{q} and relevant pose-dependent features into the geometry MLP. c. Input \mathbf{q} and relevant pose-dependent features into the color MLP. 3. Geometry Prediction: The geometry MLP outputs the Signed Distance Field value d(\mathbf{q}), which represents the distance from \mathbf{q} to the hand surface. This SDF representation allows for precise boundary definition and avoids the "fuzzy" density fields of standard NeRFs. 4. Color Prediction: The color MLP outputs the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}). 5. Rendering: Standard volume rendering or ray marching is performed using the SDF to determine surface intersections and the color field to shade the surface. Physical constraints may be introduced to prevent hand-object penetration if interacting objects are present. Formulas: Geometry: d = \text{MLP}{geo}(\mathbf{q}, \text{pose}) Color: \mathbf{c} = \text{MLP}{color}(\mathbf{q}, \text{pose}) Shape Constraint: \beta = f(\text{pose}) (Implicitly described by skeletal posture). Parameters: MANO model parameters (joint angles, shape coefficients). MLP hyperparameters (layers, hidden dimensions). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Penetration: Without explicit physical constraints, the hand mesh may intersect with other objects. LISA addresses this by introducing physical constraints during optimization. Part Boundaries: Since the hand is modeled as rigid parts, discontinuities may occur at joint boundaries if not handled smoothly by the MLPs. Focuses on full-body avatars with unified volumetric representation, whereas LISA is specialized for hands using part-based SDFs Link. Uses a standard NeRF architecture for full-body humans, lacking the explicit part-based SDF structure of LISA Link. Extends HumanNeRF with semantic embeddings, but does not use the MANO-based part decomposition Link. Incorporates semantic labels and dynamics for full-body, whereas LISA is static/part-based for hands Link. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of query points and MLP depth. SDF evaluation is generally faster than density integration for surface extraction. Memory Complexity: Lower than dense voxel grids due to implicit representation, but requires storing MANO model data. Strengths: High-fidelity hand geometry via SDF; realistic appearance via learned color field; anatomical plausibility via MANO. Limitations: Limited to hand modeling; requires accurate pose estimation for MANO parameters. When to use: When high-quality, animatable hand avatars are needed from image sequences. When not to use: For full-body avatars or non-hand objects. LISA was introduced in April 2022 as a method specifically targeting the modeling of human hands. It emerged from the broader research area of neural radiance fields for 3D avatars, distinguishing itself by approximating hands as a collection of rigid parts rather than a continuous volume. It builds upon the MANO parametric hand model, using it to implicitly describe shape parameters via skeletal posture. This approach addresses the complexity of hand topology and the need for realistic appearance in hand avatars. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 Human 3D Avatar Modeling with Implicit Neural Representation: A Brief Survey, https://doi.org/10.1109/icsps58776.2022.00148, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA)
body: Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA) is a neural radiance field representation for dynamic human avatars that enables local and independent editing of both geometry and texture while supporting novel view and pose synthesis. It distinguishes itself from UV-mapping-based methods by anchoring structured latent codes to a deformable mesh in canonical space, thereby avoiding the 3D-to-2D directionality limitation that hinders local texture editing, and from two-stage distillation methods by being end-to-end trainable with joint optimization of the skinning field. Inputs: Target space observation points \mathbf{x}t sampled along rays. A deformable canonical mesh \mathcal{M} with anchor nodes. Skeleton pose parameters defining the target pose. Top-K parameter for nearest-neighbor search. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}) for each ray \mathbf{r}. Volume density \sigma and base color \mathbf{c}0 for volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Deformable Canonical Mesh \mathcal{M}: A mesh in canonical space with N anchor nodes. Each node i stores: Position \mathbf{p}i in canonical space. Geometry latent code \mathbf{l}{geo}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d{geo}}. Appearance latent code \mathbf{l}{rgb}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d{rgb}}. UV coordinates (ui, vi) on the canonical surface. 2. Neural Deformation Field: An MLP \phi{def} that predicts non-rigid deformation offsets \Delta \mathbf{x} given a canonical point and pose. 3. Geometry MLP: \phi{geo} takes interpolated latent codes and signed height indicator to predict \sigma. 4. Color MLP: \phi{rgb} takes interpolated latent codes and signed height indicator to predict base color \mathbf{c}0. 5. Shading MLP: \phi{shade} takes pose parameters and view direction to predict shading factor s. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute LBS Weights: For a target point \mathbf{x}t, find the Top-K nearest neighbor anchor nodes on the current posed mesh. Interpolate their pre-defined Linear Blending Skinning (LBS) weights to obtain the blending weights \mathbf{w}b for \mathbf{x}t. 2. Transform to Canonical Space: Apply the inverse skinning motion to \mathbf{x}t to find its canonical position \mathbf{x}c. This combines the LBS transformation (using \mathbf{w}b) with a neural deformation field correction \Delta \mathbf{x}: \mathbf{x}c = \text{LBS}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}t, \mathbf{w}b) + \Delta \mathbf{x} where \Delta \mathbf{x} = \phi{def}(\mathbf{x}c, \text{pose}) [G: Note that \mathbf{x}c appears on both sides; in practice, this is solved via iterative refinement or by defining the deformation field on the target space and adding to the LBS result, but the source describes it as transforming \mathbf{x}t to \mathbf{x}c using the combined field]. 3. Interpolate Latent Codes: In the canonical space, find the Top-K nearest neighbor anchor nodes to \mathbf{x}c. Interpolate their latent codes using the same weights \mathbf{w}b (or NN weights derived from \mathbf{x}c) to obtain the local latent codes \mathbf{l}{geo} and \mathbf{l}{rgb}: \mathbf{l}{geo} = \sum{i \in \text{Top-}K} wi \mathbf{l}{geo}^{(i)}, \quad \mathbf{l}{rgb} = \sum{i \in \text{Top-}K} wi \mathbf{l}{rgb}^{(i)} 4. Compute Signed Height Indicator: Calculate the local signed height indicator \tilde{h} for \mathbf{x}c relative to the canonical mesh \mathcal{M}: \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}] where (u, v) are the UV coordinates of the closest point on the canonical mesh surface to \mathbf{x}c, and \bar{d} is the signed point-to-surface distance. 5. Predict Density and Base Color: Pass the interpolated latent codes and the signed height indicator through separate MLPs: \sigma = \phi{geo}(\mathbf{l}{geo}, \tilde{h}) \mathbf{c}0 = \phi{rgb}(\mathbf{l}{rgb}, \tilde{h}) 6. Modulate Color with Shading: Compute a pose-dependent shading factor s using the current pose and view direction. Modulate the base color \mathbf{c}0 to get the final radiance color \mathbf{c}: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}0 \otimes s where \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication or a specific shading modulation operation defined by \phi{shade} [G: The source uses \otimes, implying a multiplicative modulation]. 7. Volume Rendering: Integrate the modulated colors \mathbf{c} and densities \sigma along the ray \mathbf{r} using standard volume rendering equations to produce the final pixel color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}). Parameters: Top-K: The number of nearest neighbors used for interpolating LBS weights and latent codes. Typical values are not explicitly given in the abstract, but Table 1 in the source lists "Local Tex." and "Local Geo." with values like 8, 4, 8, 4, 4, suggesting K may vary or be a hyperparameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spatial Ambiguity: Using discrete latent codes defined on mesh nodes and diffusing them via nearest-neighbor interpolation can lead to spatial query indistinguishability, where points in different regions might map to the same latent code if they share the same nearest neighbors. This is mitigated by the signed height indicator \tilde{h}, which provides continuous local context. Boundary Conditions: The accuracy of the signed height indicator \bar{d} and UV coordinates (u, v) depends on the quality of the canonical mesh \mathcal{M}. Degenerate mesh regions may lead to inaccurate \tilde{h} values. Time Complexity: Dominated by the nearest-neighbor searches for LBS weights and latent codes, and the MLP evaluations. The complexity is O(N \log N) for preprocessing and O(K) per query point for interpolation, where N is the number of mesh nodes and K is Top-K. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot (d{geo} + d{rgb})) to store the latent codes on the mesh nodes, plus the memory for the mesh structure and MLP parameters. Strengths: Enables local and independent editing of geometry and texture by allowing direct manipulation of latent codes on specific mesh nodes. Supports novel view and pose synthesis. End-to-end trainable. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the canonical mesh and the skinning motion field. Spatial ambiguity from NN interpolation requires the signed height indicator for resolution. Not suitable for static objects only; designed for dynamic avatars. When to use: When local editing of geometry and texture is required for dynamic human avatars, and novel view/pose synthesis is needed. When not to use: For static scenes where simpler methods suffice, or when high-fidelity global illumination is required without pose-dependent shading approximations. Unified Volumetric Avatar (UVA) was proposed in the paper "UVA: Towards Unified Volumetric Avatar for View Synthesis, Pose rendering, Geometry and Texture Editing". It addresses the limitations of previous neural field methods for humans, which either relied on pre-defined UV mapping (making local texture editing difficult) or two-stage distillation (requiring manual tuning and being suitable only for static objects). The method builds on the baseline NeRF architecture Parent by augmenting the input space with structured latent codes anchored to a mesh and modifying the output space to include pose-dependent shading. UVA: Towards Unified Volumetric Avatar for View Synthesis, Pose rendering, Geometry and Texture Editing, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2304.06969, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: HumanNeRF
head: HumanNeRF (Generalized)
body: HumanNeRF is a generalizable neural radiance field method designed for high-fidelity free-view synthesis of dynamic humans from sparse multi-view inputs. It enables rendering of unseen subjects and camera settings without per-scene training by aggregating pixel-aligned features from source images and using a pose-embedded non-rigid deformation field. Unlike methods that rely solely on implicit texture representation or suffer from geometric discontinuity, HumanNeRF combines image-based rendering with NeRF-based volume rendering via a neural appearance blending scheme to preserve high-frequency details. HumanNeRF takes K synchronized videos of a performer captured at different viewpoints (preferably 360°) with T frames, denoted as I = \{I{k,t}\}, as input. The goal is to synthesize free-viewpoint videos and generalize motion to an arbitrary person. The method consists of three main components: a generalizable neural radiance field, an optional fast per-scene fine-tuning scheme, and a neural appearance blending field. 1. Feature Extractor Network U A U-Net architecture extracts 2D image feature maps representing local image appearance. Input: Image I^k \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 4} (RGB + mask as the last channel). Output: 2D feature map f^k \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}. Layers: 8 layers of CRB2D (ConvBnReLU2D). Kernel size k=3, stride s=1, dilation d=1 for all layers. Channel mappings: Down0: 4/32 Down1: 32/64 Down2: 64/128 Down3: 128/256 Up1: 256/256 Up2: 256/128 Up3: 128/64 Final: 64/32 2. Feature Blending Network MLPB Estimates blending weights for aggregating features from multiple views. Input: Viewing direction \vec{v}, angle \theta^kq (angle of viewing direction relative to the query ray of source view k), positional encoding PE0, and features f. Layers: PE0: 6/54 (for \vec{v}), 3/27 (for \theta). LR0: Input channels 54 + 27 + 32 \times 6 to 256. LR1-4: 256/256. LR5: 256/128. LR6: 128/6. 3. Deformation Network MLPd Learns subtle non-rigid displacements of the human body on top of a parametric model. Input: Rd \in \mathbb{R}^{24}: Distances between sample point p and the 24 joints of the SMPL skeleton. Rv \in \mathbb{R}^{72}: Directions between p and the 24 SMPL joints. PE0: Positional encoding of Rd (24/216). Fp: Aggregated pixel alignment feature. Layers: PE0: 24/216. LR0: Input channels 216 + 72 + 32 to 256. LR1-4: 256/256. LR5: 256/128. LR6: 128/3. 4. Generalizable Dynamic Neural Radiance Field \Phi Regresss volume density and RGB radiance in canonical space. Input: Position x, view direction d, positional encodings PE0, PE1, and blended feature F. Layers: PE0: 3/63. LR0: 63/256. LR1-4: 256/256. LR5: Input channels 27 + 256 to 256. LR6: 256/256. Density \sigma: 256/1. PE1: 3/27. LR7: Input channels 256 + 27 + 32 to 256. LR8: 256/128. Color c: 128/3. 5. Appearance Blending Network MLPA Refines texture details by aggregating colors from neighboring views. Input: Two adjacent image features and occlusion maps f{r,0}^r, f{l,0}^l. Layers: LR0: Input channels (32 + 3) \times 2 to 256. LR1-5: 256/256. LR6: 256/128. Blending weights W: 128/3. 1. Feature Extraction: For each input image I^k, extract the feature map f^k using the U-Net network U: f^k = U(I^k) 2. Aggregated Pixel Alignment Feature: For a spatial point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, project it into view k at q^k \in \mathbb{R}^2 and fetch the feature vector fq^k. Compute the aggregated feature Fp as a weighted summation: Fp = \sum{k=1}^{K} wq^k fq^k where the blending weights wq^k are estimated by MLPB: wq^k = MLPB(\vec{v}, \thetaq^k, fq^k) 3. Deformation: Estimate the motion \mathcal{M} using the SMPL parametric model. Compute the deformed point p' in canonical space using the deformation network MLPd: p' = \mathcal{S}(p, \mathcal{M}, w^s) + MLPd(Rd, Rv, Fp) where \mathcal{S} is the skinning function, w^s are skinning weights, Rd and Rv are distances and directions to the 24 SMPL joints. 4. Radiance Field Query: Query the neural radiance field \Phi at p' with viewing direction d and feature Fp to obtain volume density \sigma and color c. 5. Appearance Blending (Optional Fine-tuning): To refine high-frequency details, use the appearance blending network MLPA to compute blending weights W from adjacent image features and occlusion maps, aggregating colors from neighboring views. 6. Rendering: Render the final image using standard volume rendering integration of \sigma and c along the rays. SMPL Joints: The deformation network uses 24 joints for computing distances and directions. Fine-tuning: The method supports an optional fast per-scene fine-tuning scheme. Fine-tuning duration is approximately 300 frames for a specific performer, taking about one hour. Pitfalls: Multi-person/Interaction: The method relies on a regressed parametric human model, limiting it to single-person setups and failing on multi-person or human-object interactions. Lighting: No explicit lighting model is used. Significant brightness or color changes between views cause severe artifacts. Switching nearest views during appearance blending causes jumping artifacts, especially with high brightness variance. Generalization Limits: Capability is limited because human dataset distributions only cover a small portion of human dynamics and appearances. Efficiency: HumanNeRF requires significantly less fine-tuning time than per-scene methods. On the 'batman' video (300 frames), HumanNeRF full fine-tuning takes 1.2 hours, compared to Neural Body (6.7h), Neural Volumes (8.4h), and ST-NeRF (9.5h). Performance: With six input views, HumanNeRF achieves PSNR 32.59, SSIM 0.9817, and LPIPS 0.0304. Ablation Times: Removing the feature aggregation (F) reduces training time to 22.44 min; removing the deformation network (MLPd) reduces it to 25.88 min; removing the appearance blending (MLPA) increases it to 1.2h (same as full, suggesting MLPA is part of the fine-tuning or post-processing step that doesn't change the core NeRF training time significantly, or the table implies the full method including blending is 1.2h). Note: The source table lists "Ours full" as 1.2h and "w/o MLPA" as 1.2h, while "w/o F" and "w/o MLPd" are much faster, indicating that the generalizable pre-training is fast, but the full pipeline including fine-tuning/blending takes 1.2h. Strengths: Efficient generalization to unseen identities and poses; high-fidelity rendering from sparse inputs; avoids per-scene training for initial synthesis. Limitations: Limited to single-person setups; sensitive to lighting variations; generalization is bounded by the distribution of training datasets. HumanNeRF was introduced by Zhang et al. [ZYZ∗ 21] as a method for efficiently generated human radiance fields from sparse inputs. It builds upon the generalizable neural rendering paradigm, analogous to how IBRNet assists NeRF by avoiding per-scene training. The method addresses the limitations of previous approaches that require dense multi-view inputs and costly training, which are infeasible for dynamic models. It was published in CVPR 2022. Advances in Neural Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2111.05849, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) HumanNeRF: Efficiently Generated Human Radiance Field from Sparse Inputs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00759, fetched 2026-10-26

name: HumanNeRF-SE
head: HumanNeRF with Sparse Encoding
body: HumanNeRF-SE is a method for synthesizing novel pose images of humans from monocular video inputs by combining explicit SMPL shape priors with an implicit NeRF representation. It solves the problems of overfitting and high computational complexity inherent in previous monocular human NeRF methods. Unlike sibling methods that rely on frame-level features or learnable blend weights, HumanNeRF-SE uses frozen SMPL blending weights for rigid deformation and point-level spatial-aware features for non-rigid refinement, ensuring pose generalization without pose leakage. Inputs: Monocular video frames \{In\}, corresponding SMPL mesh vertices v and pose parameters J (rotation/translation of joints relative to T-pose). Outputs: Rendered image color C(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: Voxel Volume V: A sparse 3D grid. Each voxel containing SMPL vertices stores a tuple (nv, w1, \dots, w{24}), where nv is the vertex count (occupancy) and wj are the 24 Linear Blending Skinning (LBS) weights from SMPL. Empty voxels store (0, 0, \dots, 0). Spatial-Aware Features Fs: The result of channel-by-channel convolution on V. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxelization: Calculate the bounding box of SMPL vertices v (min/max coordinates). Scale the bounding box to a set voxel size vs. Find the least common multiple of the axes dimensions and 32. Scale vertices down by vs after subtracting the minimum. Construct the voxel volume V using Sparse Convolution Sp: V = Sp(v, vs, W) 2. Conv-Filter (Feature Extraction & Point Filtering): Initialize a convolution kernel to one. Perform channel-by-channel convolution on V to obtain spatially-aware features Fs. For a voxel at position (h, w, d) with kernel size k: F{s,i} = \sum{m=h-k}^{h'-k} \sum{n=w-k}^{w'-k} \sum{t=d-k}^{d'-k} \nu{m,n,t,i} \cdot \vartheta{m,n,t,i} where \nu is the voxel value and \vartheta is the kernel weight. Query the occupancy of Fs at sampling point \mathbf{x}: \text{if } Fs(\mathbf{x}) = 0: \quad \mathbf{x}o \text{ (filtered out)}, \sigma(\mathbf{x}o) = 0 \text{if } Fs(\mathbf{x}) > 0: \quad \mathbf{x}r \text{ (kept, human-related)} 3. Point Canonicalization (Deformation): Rigid Deformation (D): Query the nearest neighbor SMPL weights W{smpl} = K(\mathbf{x}r, v). Compute rigid deformation \mathbf{x}{rcnl} using the frozen SMPL blending weights wj and joint transformations (Rj, Tj) relative to the T-pose: \mathbf{x}{rcnl} = \sum{j \in J} wj ((\mathbf{x}r \cdot Rj) + Tj) where J is the set of joints. Non-Rigid Refinement (P): Refine the coarse coordinates using a network P conditioned on the point-level spatial-aware features Fs and the kept points \mathbf{x}r: \mathbf{x}{cnl} = \mathbf{x}{rcnl} + P(Fs, \mathbf{x}r) 4. Appearance Net: Encode \mathbf{x}{cnl} using positional encoding (standard NeRF). Pass through an MLP M\sigma to output color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma: \mathbf{c}, \sigma = M\sigma(\mathbf{x}{cnl}) 5. Rendering: Render the image using differentiable volume rendering. For ray \mathbf{r} with Ns samples: \tilde{C}t(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{Ns} \alphai \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i) \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \Delta ti). Loss Function: L = L{LPIPS} + \lambda L{MSE} L{MSE} = \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{R}\|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbf{R}} \|\tilde{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|^2 L{LPIPS} = l{pips}(\Theta{fore}(\tilde{I}i), \Theta{fore}(Ii)) where \Theta{fore} is the foreground mask derived from density, and \lambda is the MSE weight. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for MSE loss term. vs: Voxel size for bounding box scaling. Rigid deformation uses frozen SMPL blending weights (no fine-tuning). Non-rigid deformation is conditioned on point-level features Fs, not frame-level features. Pitfalls: Using nearest SMPL vertex blending weights directly fills the space with incorrect colors because training deforms irrelevant points onto the body. Learning blending weights from scratch or fine-tuning SMPL weights leads to overfitting on restricted poses. Direct nearest weight rigid deformation ignores non-rigid clothing deformation; solved by adding P(Fs, \mathbf{x}r). Pose leakage in datasets like ZJU-MOCAP due to action repetition; mitigated by few-shot training and diverse evaluation videos. Complexity: Reduces required sampling points from ~300K to <100K. Uses <1% of learnable parameters compared to previous methods. Performance: Reduces training time by 95% (1/20 of previous methods). Increases rendering speed by 15x without acceleration modules. Metrics (ZJU-MOCAP Few-Shot): PSNR=31.09, SSIM=0.974, LPIPS=24.085. Outperforms HumanNeRF (PSNR 30.10) and MonoHuman (PSNR 30.11). Strengths: Generalizes to novel poses without overfitting; works with monocular input; fast training/inference. Limitations: Relies on SMPL accuracy; performance depends on the quality of the initial SMPL fit. HumanNeRF-SE was introduced in 2024 by Miles et al.. It addresses the limitations of prior monocular human NeRF methods that required large numbers of optimizable parameters and multi-camera data. It builds on the SMPL model [29] and Sparse Convolution [7] techniques. name: Dynamic Semantic Human NeRF
head: H-NeRF (dynamic)
body: Dynamic Semantic Human NeRF (H-NeRF) models dynamic human motion and appearance in a scene by learning a continuous function that maps spatial positions to canonical geometric and appearance descriptors, conditioned on semantic latent codes. It solves the problem of rendering humans in arbitrary poses and shapes from sparse or dynamic video inputs by warping observations into a canonical reference frame using a pre-trained human model, allowing a single NeRF to represent the human across time. It differs from static NeRFs by incorporating semantic latent codes for shape and pose, and from other dynamic human NeRFs by using imGHUM to provide explicit spatial-temporal correspondences and residual Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for fine-grained deformation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D spatial point \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{v}, shape latent code \beta, pose latent code \theta, root transformation T. Outputs: Volume density \sigma, view-dependent color \mathbf{c}, residual SDF \Delta d. Data Structures: imGHUM: A pre-trained implicit human model that takes (\beta, \theta, T) and outputs a 4D point descriptor (s, d), where s is semantic information and d is signed distance. NeRF Function F\omega: An MLP conditioned on (s, d, \theta, T) outputting (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Residual SDF Function \Delta H\omega: An MLP conditioned on (s, d, \theta) outputting \Delta d. Bounding Box \mathcal{B}: Defines the region where human motion warping is applied; background is assumed invariant. Steps: 1. Canonical Warping: For a spatial point \mathbf{x} inside bounding box \mathcal{B}, compute the canonical descriptor (s, d) using the fixed imGHUM model conditioned on (\beta, \theta, T): (s, d) = H\omega(T^{-1}\mathbf{x}, \beta, \theta) Points outside \mathcal{B} are treated as static background and do not undergo warping. 2. NeRF Conditioning: Input the canonical descriptor (s, d), pose code \theta, and root transformation T into the NeRF function F\omega to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = F\omega(s, d, \theta, T) Note that \mathbf{c} is conditioned on T to account for illumination changes due to relative position/rotation, while \sigma is primarily conditioned on \theta for geometric deformation. 3. Residual SDF Prediction: Input (s, d, \theta) into the residual SDF function \Delta H\omega to predict the residual distance \Delta d: \Delta d = \Delta H\omega(s, d, \theta) This residual models personalized geometric details on top of the imGHUM skin surface. 4. Regularization: Apply a regularization term L{reg} to constrain \Delta d to be non-positive, ensuring imGHUM remains within the predicted geometry: L{reg} = \max(0, \Delta d). 5. Inference with Novel Poses/Shapes: To render a novel pose or shape, assign new (\beta, \theta) values. Add Gaussian noise to the input codes (\theta, T) to prevent overfitting to training-specific deformations and appearance effects. If views are sparse, add noise to the viewing direction \mathbf{v} as well. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicsemantichumannerf(x, v, beta, theta, T, boundingbox): """ x: 3D spatial point v: viewing direction beta: shape latent code theta: pose latent code T: root transformation boundingbox: region where warping is applied """ # Step 1: Canonical Warping if isinsideboundingbox(x, boundingbox): # Apply inverse root transformation xcanonical = transforminverse(T, x) # Get canonical descriptor from fixed imGHUM s, d = imghumforward(xcanonical, beta, theta) else: # Background: no warping, assume static # Placeholder for background handling logic s, d = getbackgrounddescriptor(x) # Step 2: NeRF Conditioning # Condition density on pose, color on pose and root transformation sigma, color = nerfforward(s, d, theta, T) # Step 3: Residual SDF Prediction deltad = residualsdfforward(s, d, theta) # Step 4: Regularization (applied during training) # Lreg = max(0, deltad) return sigma, color, deltad def inferencewithnoise(x, v, beta, theta, T, noisestd=0.01): """ Add Gaussian noise to latent codes for generalization """ thetanoisy = theta + GaussianNoise(noisestd) Tnoisy = T + GaussianNoise(noisestd) vnoisy = v + GaussianNoise(noisestd) # For sparse views return dynamicsemantichumannerf(x, vnoisy, beta, thetanoisy, Tnoisy) Parameters: Noise Standard Deviation: Not given in the sources. Typical values for Gaussian noise in latent spaces range from 0.01 to 0.1. Bounding Box \mathcal{B}: Not given in the sources. Should tightly enclose the human subject. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: imGHUM Fitting Errors: imGHUM fitting can introduce errors in dynamic sequences. Fine-tuning imGHUM pose and shape parameters is suggested but not detailed in the core method. Background Handling: Background is assumed invariant. If the background moves, the method fails as warping is only applied inside \mathcal{B}. Overfitting: Without noise, the network may overfit to specific pose-dependent deformations and appearance effects. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the depth of the MLPs and the cost of imGHUM evaluation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the size of the MLPs and the number of parameters in imGHUM. Strengths: Generalizes to novel poses and shapes; leverages semantic latent codes for interpolation; reduces computation by warping only the human region. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of imGHUM; background must be static; requires pre-trained imGHUM. When to Use: Dynamic human rendering with sparse views or novel poses/shapes. When Not to Use: Scenes with significant background motion or non-human subjects. Dynamic Semantic Human NeRF (H-NeRF) was introduced in "H-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Rendering and Temporal Reconstruction of Humans in Motion". It builds on prior work in dynamic NeRFs [36, 38] and integrates the imGHUM model for semantic human representation.
