name: Mixture-of-Experts Implicit Neural Representation
head: MoE-INR
body: Mixture-of-Experts Implicit Neural Representation (MoE-INR) is an architecture for time-varying volumetric data compression that automates the subdivision of spatiotemporal fields and dynamically assigns input coordinates to specialized expert networks. It solves the limitations of conventional INRs (which struggle with complex features using a single network) and grid-based INRs (which suffer from boundary discontinuity artifacts due to manual decomposition) by using a shared encoder to maintain cross-boundary continuity while allowing experts to specialize in distinct subdomains. Unlike siblings like MIMO-NeRF-self-R2 which may use different routing or ensemble strategies, MoE-INR specifically targets scientific visualization datasets with a unified framework that can emulate conventional, grid-based, or ensemble INRs by adjusting the number of experts and pre-training schemes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A spatiotemporal coordinate \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z, t) and a set of ground truth voxel values v for training. Output: A predicted scalar voxel value \hat{v} and a probability distribution over k experts. Data Structures and Layout: The architecture consists of three components defined by the number of initial neurons M and the number of experts k. 1. Policy Network: Structure: Fully connected (FC) layers with \sin(\cdot) activation, followed by a final FC layer with Softmax activation. Parameters: 4M + M + M^2 + M + 9M \times k + k. Function: Outputs a probability vector \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^k. 2. Shared Encoder: Structure: Positional encoding (learnable Fourier transformation) \rightarrow FC layers with \sin(\cdot) activation \rightarrow Residual block with bottleneck. Parameters: 4M + M + 8M^2 + 4M + 32M^2 + 8M + 36M^2 + 12M. Function: Maps \mathbf{x} to a high-dimensional compact representation \mathbf{h}. 3. Expert Decoders: Structure: k parallel networks. Each consists of FC layers with \sin(\cdot) activation, followed by a final FC layer with no activation. Parameters per expert: 8M + 1. Total: k \times (8M + 1). Function: Maps \mathbf{h} to a scalar value. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-training (Initialization): Optimize only the Policy Network and Shared Encoder. Supervised Pre-training: Generate ground truth assignments yc for coordinates using one of four methods: Random partition: Random expert assignment. Spatial partition: k non-overlapping spatial blocks. Temporal partition: k non-overlapping time intervals. Voxel clustering: k-means clustering on voxels. Loss: Cross-entropy \mathcal{L}{pre} = -\frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^k \log \left( \frac{e^{pi}}{\sum{j=1}^k e^{pj}} \right) where pi is the logit for expert i. Unsupervised Pre-training (Load Balancing): Loss: \mathcal{L}{lb} = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum{j=1}^k cj sj, where cj is the count of coordinates assigned to expert j, sj is the sum of assignment probabilities for expert j, and N is total coordinates. Note: Voxel clustering yields the best results; random partition and load balancing perform worse than no pre-training. 2. Training (Joint Optimization): Optimize Policy Network, Shared Encoder, and all Expert Decoders jointly. Forward Pass: 1. Compute \mathbf{p} = \text{Softmax}(G(\mathbf{x})) using the Policy Network. 2. Compute \mathbf{h} = E{shared}(\mathbf{x}) using the Shared Encoder. 3. Compute \hat{v}j = Ej(\mathbf{h}) for all j=1 \dots k using Expert Decoders. Loss Calculation: Weighted MSE: \mathcal{L}{train} = \sum{j=1}^k pj ||\hat{v}j - v||^2, where v is the ground truth voxel value. Inference: Select expert j^ = \arg\maxj pj. Output \hat{v} = E{j^}(\mathbf{h}). Parameters: M: Number of initial neurons (user-specified). k: Number of experts. Optimal value is 7 for tested datasets (e.g., Ionization PD, Vortex). Parameter Allocation: The "Larger Encoder" strategy is optimal, allocating ~96.9% of parameters to the shared encoder, ~0.8% to experts, and ~2.3% to the policy network (for Vortex dataset, CR 5,065). Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Too many experts: Setting k > 7 degrades performance (e.g., PSNR drops) because the policy network struggles to correctly classify coordinates, leading to misclassifications. Bad Pre-training: Random partition and load balancing pre-training fail to produce meaningful assignments, resulting in inferior performance compared to no pre-training. Boundary Discontinuity: Avoided by using a shared encoder; grid-based INRs without shared encoders suffer from block artifacts. Complexity: Memory: Scales linearly with the number of experts k. Memory Usage (MU) for Ionization (PD) dataset (CR 10,078) ranges from 8,177 MB (k=2) to 21,745 MB (k=9). Time: Compression Time (CT) increases with k. For Ionization (PD), CT ranges from 11.83 hours (k=2) to 25.36 hours (k=9). Performance: Outperforms conventional INRs (single network) and grid-based INRs (manual decomposition) in PSNR and LPIPS across various compression ratios (CR). On Vortex dataset (CR 5,065, k=7, Larger Encoder): Best PSNR/LPIPS achieved. On Ionization (PD) dataset (CR 10,078, k=7): PSNR 58.76 dB, LPIPS 0.024. On Ionization (T) dataset (CR 5,033, k=7, Voxel Clustering Pre-training): PSNR 56.71 dB, LPIPS 0.047. Strengths: Automates irregular subdivisions without explicit storage of mapping. Shared encoder ensures boundary continuity. Unified framework accommodating conventional, grid-based, and ensemble INR types. Limitations: Conventional INRs (single encoder/decoder) have lower computational cost for visualization than MoE-INR with k>1 due to fewer matrix multiplications, but MoE-INR with k=1 reduces to conventional INR. Ensemble INRs (e.g., RMDSRN) decode a single coordinate using multiple experts and average results; MoE-INR typically uses single expert selection but can function as an ensemble INR if configured to average. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) paradigm was originally proposed by Nowlan and Hinton [26], applying supervision to a system of separate networks where each handles a subset of training samples and specializes in a different part of the data space. MoE-INR was developed to address the limitations of existing INRs for scientific data compression, specifically the inability of conventional INRs to preserve complex features and the boundary discontinuity issues of grid-based INRs. It is designed for time-varying volumetric data compression and representation in scientific visualization, tested on datasets including argon bubble, combustion, ionization, Tangaroa, and vortex. MoE-INR: Implicit Neural Representation with Mixture-of-Experts for..., https://academicweb.nd.edu/~cwang11/papers/vis25-moeinr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Uncertainty and Reliability
body: Uncertainty and Reliability methods extend NeRF architectures to quantify the confidence of their predictions, addressing artifacts, redundancy, and geometric inaccuracies inherent in standard deterministic rendering. Unlike standard NeRF which outputs fixed values, these methods model aleatoric (data) and epistemic (model) uncertainty, enabling the filtering of poorly rendered views, weighting of training samples based on information gain, and the generation of conformal prediction intervals for reliable geometry assessment. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as surface normals \mathbf{n}, semantic logits \mathbf{s}, uncertainty variance \nu, or blend weights \Delta w. 4. Representation Basis: Substituting the coordinate-based implicit function with explicit structures like voxel grids, hash tables, Gaussian primitives, or planar surfaces, which change how features are stored and interpolated. Uncertainty-aware NeRF (U-NeRF) separately predicts uncertainties for rendered color and depth images to reveal data reliability at the pixel level, addressing artifacts and redundancy in synthetic data for Scene Coordinate Regression (SCR). It renders pixel color and depth as Gaussian distributions, providing mean and variance estimates for uncertainty-aware visual localization. Unlike standard NeRF which outputs deterministic values, U-NeRF models the aleatoric uncertainty of the scene representation, allowing for the filtering of poorly rendered views and the weighting of training samples based on information gain. UA-PlantNeRF is a unified framework for reconstructing volumetric radiance fields from sparse, unstructured video footage of plants, addressing degraded geometry and the absence of calibrated uncertainty estimates. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by jointly predicting density, color, and decomposed uncertainty (aleatoric and epistemic) via a dual-head architecture with Monte Carlo Dropout, enabling conformal prediction intervals for reliable geometry assessment. Definition: The use of an error correction network and conditioning on a scene NeRF to prevent the canonical NeRF from hallucinating clothing dynamics or background colors. Pitfall: Training only the human NeRF in isolation leads to worse performance because the human NeRF model may encode background pixels into its radiance fields due to segmentation errors. Without error correction or scene conditioning, the canonical NeRF creates fogs around the human to hallucinate clothing dynamics or background colors. The concept of modeling uncertainty in neural radiance fields emerged to address the limitations of deterministic implicit representations, particularly in sparse-view or noisy data regimes. U-NeRF introduced the formulation of rendering color and depth as Gaussian distributions to handle Scene Coordinate Regression tasks. UA-PlantNeRF extended this to biological structures, combining aleatoric uncertainty estimation with epistemic uncertainty via Monte Carlo Dropout to provide conformal prediction guarantees for plant phenotyping. NeuMan introduced error correction and scene conditioning to mitigate hallucinations in human radiance fields. NeuMan: Neural Human Radiance Field from a Single Video, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-324, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Uncertainty-aware NeRF
head: U-NeRF
body: Uncertainty-aware NeRF (U-NeRF) is a NeRF variant that separately predicts uncertainties for rendered color and depth images to reveal data reliability at the pixel level, addressing artifacts and redundancy in synthetic data for Scene Coordinate Regression (SCR). It renders pixel color and depth as Gaussian distributions, providing mean and variance estimates for uncertainty-aware visual localization. Unlike standard NeRF which outputs deterministic values, U-NeRF extends the output space to include variance fields, allowing the model to quantify aleatoric uncertainty inherent in the scene representation and rendering process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Volume density \tau, mean view-dependent RGB color \bar{\mathbf{c}}, and pre-activation color variance \bar{\sigma}c^2 for each sampled point along the ray. Data Structures: The core data structure is a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) F\Theta. Input Layer: Concatenated positional encoding \phi(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}). Hidden Layers: Standard MLP layers. Output Layer: A tuple (\tau, \bar{\mathbf{c}}, \bar{\sigma}c^2). \tau: Scalar volume density. \bar{\mathbf{c}}: Vector of size 3 (RGB). \bar{\sigma}c^2: Scalar pre-Softplus variance prediction. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} traversing range [tn, tf], partition the range into N bins and sample N points \{ti\}{i=1}^N uniformly within each bin. 2. Network Forward Pass: For each sample point ti, compute position \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{r}(ti). Pass \mathbf{x}i and \mathbf{d} through the MLP: (\taui, \bar{\mathbf{c}}i, \bar{\sigma}{c,i}^2) = \text{MLP}(\phi(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d})) Apply Softplus activation to \bar{\sigma}{c,i}^2 to ensure valid variance: \sigma{c,i}^2 = \text{Softplus}(\bar{\sigma}{c,i}^2) 3. Volume Rendering (Color): Compute the expected color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and its variance \bar{\sigma}C^2(\mathbf{r}) by integrating along the ray. Compute weights wi: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\taui \deltai)) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \tauj \deltaj\right) \deltai = t{i+1} - ti Compute mean color \bar{C}: \bar{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi \bar{\mathbf{c}}i Compute color variance \bar{\sigma}C^2: \bar{\sigma}C^2(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi^2 \sigma{c,i}^2 Assumption: The distributions of different sampled scene points on one ray are independent, so the rendered pixel color follows a Gaussian distribution \hat{C} \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar{C}, \bar{\sigma}C^2). 4. Volume Rendering (Depth): Compute expected depth \hat{z}(\mathbf{r}) and its variance \hat{\sigma}z^2(\mathbf{r}). Expected depth: \hat{z}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti Depth variance: \hat{\sigma}z^2(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi (ti - \hat{z}(\mathbf{r}))^2 Assumption: The ray termination distribution is Gaussian. 5. Loss Computation: Color Loss (L{color}): Uses a \zeta-NLL loss to address hard-to-fit regions. L{color} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \lfloor \hat{\sigma}C(\mathbf{r}) \rfloor^{-2\zeta} L(\mathbf{r}) Where L(\mathbf{r}) is the standard Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) for color: L(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\|\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) - \bar{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2}{2\hat{\sigma}C^2(\mathbf{r})} + \log \hat{\sigma}C(\mathbf{r}) Here, \lfloor \cdot \rfloor denotes the stop-gradient operation, preventing the gradient from flowing through the variance term, effectively making it an adaptive learning rate. Depth Loss (L{depth}): Standard NLL on depth. L{depth} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left( \frac{\|\hat{z}(\mathbf{r}) - z(\mathbf{r})\|2^2}{2\hat{\sigma}z^2(\mathbf{r})} + \log \hat{\sigma}z(\mathbf{r}) \right) Where z(\mathbf{r}) is the target depth. Overall Loss: L{overall} = L{color} + \lambda L{depth} Parameters: \zeta: Interpolation parameter for the color loss weighting. \zeta=0 corresponds to standard NLL, \zeta=1 corresponds to MSE. It acts as a factor on the gradient to address ignorance of hard-to-fit regions. Typical value not explicitly stated in sources, but used to balance uncertainty estimation and fit quality. \lambda: Weight for the depth loss term in the overall objective function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premature Convergence: Standard NLL optimization leads to sub-optimal mean fits and premature convergence because badly-fit regions receive increasingly less weights as their uncertainty decreases. This is addressed by the variance-weighting term \hat{\sigma}C^{-2\zeta} with stop-gradient. Theoretical Grounding: NeRF-W applies volume rendering over \sigmaC (standard deviation) instead of \sigmaC^2 (variance), which is not theoretically grounded. U-NeRF uses \sigmaC^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class UncertaintyNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, D=8, W=256, inputch=3, inputchdir=3, outputch=4, skips=[4], useviewdirs=True): """ D: Number of layers in the main MLP. W: Dimensionality of hidden layers. inputch: Dimensionality of position encoding. inputchdir: Dimensionality of direction encoding. outputch: 1 (density) + 3 (color) + 1 (variance). skips: Indices where skip connections are added. useviewdirs: Whether to use view directions in the network. """ super(UncertaintyNeRF, self).init() self.D = D self.W = W self.inputch = inputch self.inputchdir = inputchdir self.useviewdirs = useviewdirs # First layer self.basenet = nn.Linear(inputch, W) # Hidden layers self.hiddenlayers = nn.ModuleList() for i in range(D - 1): if i in skips: self.hiddenlayers.append(nn.Linear(W + inputch, W)) else: self.hiddenlayers.append(nn.Linear(W, W)) # View direction layers (if using viewdirs) if useviewdirs: self.dirnet = nn.Linear(inputchdir, W // 4) self.colorlayer = nn.Linear(W, 3) # Mean color self.varlayer = nn.Linear(W, 1) # Variance self.densitylayer = nn.Linear(W, 1) # Density else: self.colorlayer = nn.Linear(W, 3) self.varlayer = nn.Linear(W, 1) self.densitylayer = nn.Linear(W, 1) def forward(self, x, d): """ x: (N, 3) 3D positions d: (N, 3) viewing directions Returns: (N, 1) density, (N, 3) mean color, (N, 1) pre-softplus variance """ # Positional encoding is assumed to be applied before calling this function # xencoded: (N, inputch) # dencoded: (N, inputchdir) h = F.relu(self.basenet(x)) for i, layer in enumerate(self.hiddenlayers): if i in [4, 5, 6, 7]: # Assuming skips at 4 based on typical NeRF, adjust as needed h = torch.cat([h, x], dim=-1) h = F.relu(layer(h)) if self.useviewdirs: # Branch for density density = self.densitylayer(h) # Branch for color and variance hdir = F.relu(self.dirnet(d)) hcombined = torch.cat([h, hdir], dim=-1) meancolor = self.colorlayer(hcombined) varpre = self.varlayer(hcombined) return density, meancolor, varpre else: density = self.densitylayer(h) meancolor = self.colorlayer(h) varpre = self.varlayer(h) return density, meancolor, varpre def renderray(rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, Nsamples, nerfmodel, useviewdirs=True, zeta=0.0, lambdadepth=1.0, gtcolor=None, gtdepth=None): """ Renders a single ray with uncertainty estimation. """ # 1. Sampling tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, Nsamples) # Hierarchical stratified sampling can be implemented here, # but for simplicity we use uniform sampling as per basic description # In practice, NeRF uses hierarchical sampling. # 2. Network Forward Pass # x: (Nsamples, 3) x = rayo.unsqueeze(0) + tvals.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2) rayd.unsqueeze(0) x = x.view(-1, 3) # d: (Nsamples, 3) - same direction for all samples on the ray d = rayd.unsqueeze(0).expandas(x) # Apply positional encoding phi(x, d) here if not done in model init # For this pseudocode, we assume the model handles raw inputs or # the caller passes encoded inputs. Let's assume raw inputs for clarity # and that the model's forward pass handles encoding or expects it. # To be strictly self-contained, we assume phi is applied externally or # the model expects encoded inputs. Let's assume the model expects # encoded inputs for the 'inputch' dimension. # Placeholder for positional encoding application # xenc = positionalencoding(x) # denc = positionalencoding(d) # density: (Nsamples, 1) # meancolor: (Nsamples, 3) # varpre: (Nsamples, 1) density, meancolor, varpre = nerfmodel(x, d) # 3. Compute Variances # Softplus to ensure positive variance varcolor = F.softplus(varpre) # 4. Volume Rendering # Compute deltas deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # Add a small epsilon to avoid division by zero or log(0) issues if needed # But here we use deltas for integration # Compute alphas and weights # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # weight = alpha Tprev # Tprev = exp(-sum(sigma delta)) # density: (Nsamples, 1) # deltas: (Nsamples - 1,) -> need to pad or handle last sample # NeRF usually samples N bins, so N-1 deltas? Or N samples with N-1 intervals? # Standard NeRF: N samples, N-1 intervals. # Let's assume tvals has N elements, so N-1 deltas. # To match the formula wi = Ti (1 - exp(-taui deltai)) # We need to handle the last sample carefully. Usually, the last sample # has delta = infinity or is handled by a termination probability. # For simplicity, we assume N samples and N-1 deltas, and the last sample # is treated as the background or has delta=0? # Actually, standard NeRF uses N samples for N bins. # Let's stick to the formula provided: sum{i=1}^N. # This implies N weights. # Re-sampling to match N weights: # If we have N samples, we have N-1 intervals. # The formula uses deltai = t{i+1} - ti. # So for i=1 to N-1, deltai is defined. What about i=N? # Usually, the last sample is at tf, and deltaN is effectively infinity # or the ray terminates. # Let's assume we have N samples and we compute weights for all N. # For the last sample, deltaN is often set to a large value or handled # by the termination term. # Let's implement the standard NeRF weighting logic: # tvals: (N,) # deltas: (N-1,) # We need to pad deltas to N? Or handle the last term separately? # The formula wi = Ti (1 - exp(-taui deltai)) # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} tauj deltaj) # Let's assume N samples and N deltas, where the last delta is large. # Or, more commonly, N samples, N-1 deltas, and the last weight is # TN (1 - exp(-tauN infinity)) = TN. # Let's use N samples and N-1 deltas for the first N-1 weights, # and the N-th weight is TN. # Compute alphas # density: (N, 1) # deltas: (N-1,) # We need to align dimensions. # Let's assume we have N samples. # deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # (N-1,) # To make it N weights, we can append a large delta for the last sample. deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=deltas.device)]) # (N,) # Compute alpha # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-density.squeeze(-1) deltas) # (N,) # Compute T # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # cumsum of sigma delta sigmadelta = density.squeeze(-1) deltas cumsumsigmadelta = torch.cumsum(sigmadelta, dim=0) # Ti corresponds to exp(-cumsum up to i-1) # T1 = exp(0) = 1 # T2 = exp(-sigma1 delta1) # Shift cumsum to get T # T = exp(-cumsumsigmadelta.shift(1, fillvalue=0)) # In PyTorch: T = torch.exp(-torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, device=deltas.device), cumsumsigmadelta[:-1]])) # (N,) # Weights w = T alpha # (N,) # 5. Compute Rendered Color and Variance # meancolor: (N, 3) # varcolor: (N, 1) -> squeeze to (N,) # Expected Color renderedcolor = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) meancolor, dim=0) # (3,) # Expected Variance # sigmaC^2 = sum(wi^2 sigmaci^2) renderedvarcolor = torch.sum(w2 varcolor.squeeze(-1), dim=0) # () # 6. Compute Rendered Depth and Variance # Expected Depth rendereddepth = torch.sum(w tvals, dim=0) # () # Depth Variance # sigmaz^2 = sum(wi (ti - zhat)^2) renderedvardepth = torch.sum(w (tvals - rendereddepth)2, dim=0) # () # 7. Compute Losses losses = {} if gtcolor is not None: # NLL for color # L(r) = ||C - Chat||^2 / (2 sigmaC^2) + log sigmaC # Note: renderedvarcolor is sigmaC^2 # We need to handle zero variance to avoid division by zero eps = 1e-6 sigmaC = torch.sqrt(renderedvarcolor + eps) colornll = (torch.norm(gtcolor - renderedcolor)2) / (2 renderedvarcolor + eps) + torch.log(sigmaC) # Variance weighting term # Lcolor = sum( sigmaC^{-2zeta} L(r)) # Here we have one ray, so sum is just the term. # Stop gradient on sigmaC sigmaCsg = sigmaC.detach() weightterm = sigmaCsg (-2 zeta) losses['color'] = weightterm colornll if gtdepth is not None: # NLL for depth sigmaz = torch.sqrt(renderedvardepth + eps) depthnll = (gtdepth - rendereddepth)2 / (2 renderedvardepth + eps) + torch.log(sigmaz) losses['depth'] = depthnll return renderedcolor, renderedvarcolor, rendereddepth, renderedvardepth, losses A semi-automatic process to mark background regions, moving occluders, saturated highlights, and strongly reflective areas as low-reliability regions, converting them into binary masks to reduce viewpoint-dependent artifacts. It involves creating binary masks for low-reliability regions, propagating these masks into the cross-view weighting term so that inconsistent evidence contributes less to the optimization, and using masks to constrain the influence of occluded and high-reflectivity regions. Standard NeRF baseline excludes reliability masks and cross-view consistency regularization, whereas the proposed method uses them to reduce artifacts from viewpoint imbalance and material-dependent reflections. Time Complexity: The method adds a small constant overhead to the standard NeRF forward pass due to the additional variance output and the computation of variance-weighted losses. The rendering process itself remains O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: The MLP output size increases by 1 scalar (variance) per sample point, which is negligible compared to the color and density outputs. Measured Performance: The method is used to render RGB-D images with uncertainty estimation for novel view synthesis in visual localization pipelines. It allows for filtering out poorly rendered images and weighing pixels in regression learning losses, requiring only a small portion of the training set while delivering comparable or better performance. Strengths: Provides pixel-level reliability metrics, addresses artifacts and redundancy in synthetic data, and improves scene coordinate regression by filtering low-quality samples. Limitations: Standard NLL optimization can lead to sub-optimal mean fits and premature convergence if not for the variance-weighting term. The method assumes Gaussian distributions for color and depth, which may not hold for all scenes. When to use: When uncertainty estimation is required for downstream tasks like visual localization or scene coordinate regression, and when dealing with synthetic data that may contain redundancy or artifacts. When not to use: When deterministic rendering is sufficient and computational overhead for uncertainty estimation is not justified. Uncertainty-aware NeRF (U-NeRF) was introduced to address challenges in Scene Coordinate Regression (SCR), specifically the high cost of obtaining 2D-3D ground truth and the inefficiency of learning accurate mappings with large amounts of samples. The method leverages NeRF's ability to synthesize novel views with uncertainty estimation to generate synthetic training data for SCR networks, using the uncertainties to filter out poorly rendered images and weigh pixels in regression learning losses. The approach is similar to ActiveNeRF but adopts a \zeta-NLL loss to cope with sub-optimal performance in hard-to-fit regions. name: UA-PlantNeRF Architecture
head: Dual-Head NeRF
body: UA-PlantNeRF is a unified framework for reconstructing volumetric radiance fields from sparse, unstructured video footage of plants, addressing degraded geometry and the absence of calibrated uncertainty estimates. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by jointly predicting density, color, and decomposed uncertainty (aleatoric and epistemic) via a dual-head architecture trained with a heteroscedastic negative log-likelihood objective, followed by split conformal prediction for provable coverage guarantees. Unlike Uncertainty-aware NeRF, which focuses on general scene uncertainty, UA-PlantNeRF is specifically tailored for botanical phenotyping, incorporating semantic consistency constraints to prevent geometry collapse in occluded leaf regions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of sparse, unstructured 2D images (typically 15 frames) of plants. Outputs: A continuous volumetric radiance field R predicting density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, a spatially varying uncertainty field U providing aleatoric (U{al}) and epistemic (U{ep}) uncertainty estimates, and conformal prediction intervals for reliability. Data Structures: Backbone: A hierarchical NeRF structure using positional encoding with L=10 frequency levels. Network Topology: Two parallel Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), each with 8 layers and a width of 256 neurons. Skip connections are inserted at layer 4. Head 1 (Standard): Predicts volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Head 2 (Dual Head): Predicts the log-variance \log \beta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) for aleatoric uncertainty. Dropout: Monte Carlo Dropout is applied after every hidden layer of the fine network with probability p=0.1. Training Steps: 1. Frame Selection: Identify maximally informative, non-redundant viewpoints from raw footage using the VISAR strategy (weights \alpha1=0.4, \alpha2=0.3, \alpha3=0.3) to select top-N frames after temporal non-maximum suppression (\omega=5). 2. Forward Pass: For each ray r, sample points \mathbf{x}i and directions \mathbf{d}. Pass through the backbone to get \sigmai, \mathbf{c}i. 3. Uncertainty Prediction: Compute aleatoric uncertainty variance \betai from the dual head: \betai = \exp(\log \beta(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d})). During training, dropout is active. During inference, perform K=20 stochastic passes with dropout active to estimate epistemic uncertainty. 4. Volume Rendering: Render color \hat{c}(r) and accumulated density using standard volume rendering equations, weighted by \betai for the likelihood model. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} (see Formulas). 6. Optimization: Update network parameters \Theta to minimize \mathcal{L}. 7. Conformal Calibration: Construct a calibration set D{cal} from held-out plants (excluded from training) to ensure exchangeability. Compute residuals and determine quantiles for prediction intervals. Formulas: Aleatoric Uncertainty: The variance \beta(r) is predicted by the parallel head. The contribution to the rendering is weighted by this variance in the likelihood. U{al}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{M} Ti \alphai \beta(\mathbf{x}i) (Note: The source formula (3) in defines U{al} as a sum involving transmission Ti, alpha \alphai, and variance \beta. However, standard heteroscedastic regression typically uses \beta directly in the loss. The text states "predicts log-variance \log \beta(x, d) of a heteroscedastic likelihood". We cite the source's definition of U{al} as given in Eq 3, but note that \beta is the predicted variance parameter.) Epistemic Uncertainty: Estimated via Monte Carlo Dropout variance over K passes: U{ep}(r) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \|\hat{\mathbf{c}}k - \bar{\mathbf{c}}\|^2 where \hat{\mathbf{c}}k is the color prediction of the k-th stochastic pass and \bar{\mathbf{c}} is the mean prediction. Total Uncertainty: U{total}(r) = U{ep}(r) + U{al}(r) Training Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{NLL} + \lambda{reg} \mathcal{L}{reg} + \lambda{sem} \mathcal{L}{sem} where \lambda{reg} = 0.01 and \lambda{sem} = 0.1. Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL): \mathcal{L}{NLL} = \frac{1}{|B|} \sum{r \in B} \left[ \frac{\|\hat{\mathbf{c}}(r) - \mathbf{c}(r)\|^2}{2\beta(r)} + \frac{1}{2} \log \beta(r) \right] where \beta(r) is the predicted variance for ray r. Regularization Terms: \mathcal{L}{reg}: Mip-NeRF 360 distortion regularizer. \mathcal{L}{sem}: CLIP semantic-consistency term to prevent geometry collapse in occluded leaf regions. Parameters: Dropout probability p = 0.1. Number of stochastic passes K = 20. Positional encoding levels L = 10. MLP layers = 8, width = 256. Skip connections at layer 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Calibration Set Construction: Calibration must be performed on held-out plants, not held-out views of the same plants, to preserve exchangeability with future test-plant rays. Sparse Views: The method is designed for as few as 15 frames; performance may degrade if frame selection fails to capture informative viewpoints. Occlusion: Without the semantic consistency term \mathcal{L}{sem}, geometry may collapse in occluded leaf regions. A preprocessing step that selects non-redundant viewpoints using homography differences and temporal non-maximum suppression. It is chosen when input data is sparse and unstructured video. See VISAR. A post-processing step that provides distribution-free coverage guarantees. It is chosen when calibrated reliability intervals are required. See Conformal Prediction. Time Complexity: Training involves standard NeRF optimization plus the overhead of the dual head and dropout sampling. Inference requires K=20 stochastic passes for epistemic uncertainty, increasing inference time by a factor of 20 compared to a deterministic NeRF. Memory Complexity: The dual-head architecture doubles the output dimension of the final MLP layer (predicting \sigma, \mathbf{c}, \log \beta). Memory usage is comparable to standard NeRF with minor overhead for the additional head. Performance: Evaluated on Pheno4D, ROSE-X, and UA-Field benchmarks. It addresses degraded geometry under sparse views and provides calibrated uncertainty. Strengths: Handles sparse, unstructured input; provides decomposed uncertainty; prevents geometry collapse in occlusions via semantic consistency. Limitations: Requires careful calibration set construction (held-out plants); inference is slower due to MC Dropout sampling. UA-PlantNeRF was introduced to address limitations in 3D plant reconstruction from sparse video, specifically degraded geometry and lack of uncertainty estimates. It builds on the VISAR frame-selection strategy and integrates concepts from heteroscedastic regression and conformal prediction. The method is part of a broader effort to apply differentiable rendering to agricultural phenotyping. Uncertainty-Aware 3D Plant Reconstruction from Sparse Video Frames Using Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9904108/v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Object Decomposition and Composition
head: Scene Decomposition, Compositional NeRF, Object-Centric NeRF
body: Object Decomposition and Composition methods address the limitation of monolithic NeRFs in handling individual objects within a scene, enabling instance-level editing, segmentation, and interpolation. Unlike standard NeRFs that treat the scene as a single continuous field, these methods decompose the representation into distinct components (foreground/background, object instances, or articulated parts) and compose them for rendering. This family is distinguished from sibling methods like Feature Fields or Conditional and Latent Representations by its explicit focus on structural separation of scene entities rather than just feature augmentation or conditional generation. The family shares the core principle of splitting the scene representation into multiple, distinct radiance fields or latent codes that correspond to semantic or geometric entities. 1. Decomposition: The scene is partitioned into K object instances and a background component. This can be achieved via: Explicit Fields: Separate NeRFs or MLP heads for each entity. Latent Codes: Learnable vectors \mathbf{z}i associated with each instance, concatenated with shared features. Object Codes: One-hot or soft assignment vectors predicting instance membership for each 3D point. 2. Composition: The final radiance (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) is computed by combining the outputs of the decomposed components. Common strategies include: Weighted Sum: Using softmax or Gumbel-Softmax weights based on density or learned probabilities. Dominant Selection: Selecting the component with the highest density or probability. Residual Addition: Adding a global background field to local object fields. 3. Supervision: Training often relies on 2D object masks or semantic labels to supervise the decomposition, as 3D ground truth for object boundaries is rarely available. Fig-NeRF decomposes the scene into a foreground object and a background, modeling the object as a deformable template conditioned on a latent code z. It enables shape interpolation and amodal segmentation by learning a deformation field T(x, z) that maps a template shape to the observed instance. It is chosen when shape variation explanation and object-background separation are required. DM-NeRF introduces an explicit "object field" that predicts a one-hot object code for every 3D point, enabling instance-level decomposition and manipulation (translation, rotation, scaling) from 2D images alone. It distinguishes itself by supporting simultaneous reconstruction, decomposition, and manipulation of objects, including handling occlusions during editing. It is chosen when interactive object editing is a primary goal. UDC-NeRF unites global synthesis and local editing in a single pipeline using a coarse global field to guide sampling for a fine-grained stage that decomposes the scene into distinct object and background components. It uses Gumbel-Softmax for composition and 3D one-hot density regularization to separate objects from the background. It is chosen when joint novel view synthesis and object editing are needed without separate training stages. This method decomposes a scene into multiple NeRFs based on the detail frequency of detected objects, assigning high-frequency objects to dedicated NeRFs and low-frequency objects to a joint NeRF. It reduces the learning burden by scaling up high-frequency objects during training. It is chosen when computational efficiency for complex scenes with varying object detail levels is prioritized. NARF models articulated objects by decomposing them into rigid parts, each represented by a separate RT-NeRF, and combines them using a differentiable softmax weighting scheme based on density. It solves part dependency by explicitly estimating rigid transformations via forward kinematics. It is chosen for modeling articulated objects with known kinematic structures. A division of NeRF into a dual-pathway architecture comprising a scene (background) branch for encoding scene geometry/appearance and an object (foreground) branch for individual object encoding. It eliminates the need for separate training per object by assigning activation codes to training rays for each object. For view generation with manipulation, it renders transformed objects using the conditioned object branch and the background from the scene branch together, using an object manipulator to handle collisions and occlusions. Methods that address guidance collapse in scene-level editing by representing scenes as compositions of multiple locally optimized NeRFs integrated globally. They decompose and reassemble scenes through proxy manipulation for editing without additional fine-tuning, ensuring entity distinctiveness while maintaining scene coherence. The concept of decomposing NeRFs emerged from the need to edit individual objects within a scene, a task difficult for monolithic representations. Early works like Fig-NeRF focused on figure-ground separation and shape deformation. Subsequent research, including works cited in (e.g., [204, 248, 257, 8]), developed dual-pathway architectures for simultaneous object encoding. More recent methods like DM-NeRF and UDC-NeRF have refined this by introducing explicit object fields and unified decomposition-composition pipelines. Methods like CompoNeRF and Set-the-Scene address guidance collapse in text-guided editing by composing multiple local NeRFs. Semantically-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Visual Scene Understanding: A Comprehensive Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-025-02663-5, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Fig-NeRF
head: FigNeRF
body: Fig-NeRF is a scene composition model designed for object interpolation and amodal segmentation by partitioning the scene into distinct foreground and background components. It differs from monolithic NeRFs by using two separate models: a deformable NeRF for the foreground object and a latent-conditioned appearance NeRF for the background, enabling explicit manipulation of object shape and appearance. Inputs: A set of multi-view images of an object category, potentially with associated 2D masks or semantic labels for supervision. Outputs: Two radiance fields: a foreground field representing the deformable object and a background field representing the scene context. Data Structures: 1. Foreground Model: A deformable NeRF architecture (specifically the Nerfies model). It maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density and color, incorporating a deformation field. 2. Background Model: An appearance NeRF conditioned on a latent code. It maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density and color, with appearance variations controlled by the latent vector. 3. Latent Code: A learnable vector \mathbf{z} that conditions both the object's template shape and its deformation. Steps: 1. Latent Encoding: For a given object instance, encode its shape and appearance variations into a latent code \mathbf{z}. 2. Foreground Deformation: Use \mathbf{z} to condition a template shape of the object category. Apply a deformation field, also conditioned on \mathbf{z}, to map canonical 3D coordinates to the observed object geometry. This allows the network to explain shape variations as intuitive deformations. 3. Background Conditioning: Condition the background appearance NeRF on the same latent code \mathbf{z} (or a separate background-specific latent) to capture scene context and appearance variations. 4. Rendering: Render the foreground and background components separately using volume rendering. 5. Supervision: Compute two separate photometric losses: one for the foreground object and one for the background. Use a learnable background model to assist in segmenting the object from the background. Formulas: Foreground Radiance: \mathbf{C}f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \text{DeformableNeRF}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{z}) Background Radiance: \mathbf{C}b(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \text{AppearanceNeRF}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{z}) Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photometric}^{foreground} + \mathcal{L}{photometric}^{background} Parameters: Latent dimension: Not given in the sources. Deformation field complexity: Based on Nerfies. Edge Cases: Amodal segmentation requires handling occluded parts of the object, which the deformable model must infer from visible parts. Separation between foreground and background relies on the distinct conditioning and loss functions; ambiguity in boundary regions may require additional mask supervision. Time Complexity: Training involves optimizing two NeRFs and a latent code, likely slower than a single NeRF due to the dual-model structure and deformation field. Memory Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to storing parameters for both foreground and background models. Strengths: Enables object interpolation and amodal segmentation; disentangles object shape/appearance from background. Limitations: Requires careful balancing of two photometric losses; deformation field may be sensitive to initialization. When to use: When object-level manipulation, interpolation, or segmentation is required. When not to use: For simple novel view synthesis without object-level control, where a single NeRF is more efficient. Fig-NeRF was introduced in April 2021. It focuses on scene composition for object interpolation and amodal segmentation. It builds on the Nerfies deformable NeRF model for the foreground. It was evaluated on datasets such as ShapeNet, Gelato, and Objectron. The approach models an object category as a template shape conditioned on a latent code, with deformation also conditioned on the same latent variable. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 Advances in Neural Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2111.05849, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: DM-NeRF
body: DM-NeRF is a method that simultaneously reconstructs continuous 3D scene geometry, decomposes all individual objects in 3D space, and supports flexible object shape manipulation (translation, rotation, size adjustment, deformation) from 2D images only. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by introducing an explicit "object field" that predicts a one-hot object code for every 3D point, enabling instance-level decomposition without 3D ground truth, and an "object manipulator" that handles occlusions during editing. Unlike Fig-NeRF which focuses on image-guided generation, or Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF which uses unified latent codes, DM-NeRF explicitly learns per-point object assignments via a dedicated MLP branch supervised by 2D masks. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of L images for a static scene with known camera poses and intrinsics, denoted as \{(I1, \xi1, K1) \cdots (IL, \xiL, KL)\}. Input: 2D object masks for the L images, denoted as \{\bar{I}1 \cdots \bar{I}L\}, where \bar{I}l \in \mathbb{R}^{U \times V \times T}. U, V are spatial width and height; T is the number of ground truth objects. Output: Volume density \sigma, object code \mathbf{o}, and color \mathbf{c} for any query 3D point \mathbf{p} and viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Data Structures Object Code \mathbf{o}: A one-hot vector of size H+1, where H is the predefined number of object channels. The first H channels correspond to specific objects, and the (H+1)-th channel corresponds to empty/background space. Network Architecture: A single MLP with the following layer dimensions: Input: Positional Encoded location + Positional Encoded direction. Hidden Layers: 128 \to 256 \to 256 \to 256 \to 256 \to 256 \to 256 \to 256 \to 256 \to 256 \to 128. Output Heads: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^1 (function of location only). Object Code \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^{H+1} (function of location only). Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (function of location and viewing direction). Algorithm Steps 1. Positional Encoding: Compute positional encoding \text{PE}(\mathbf{p}) for 3D location \mathbf{p}=(x,y,z) and \text{PE}(\mathbf{v}) for viewing direction \mathbf{v}=(\theta, \phi). 2. Forward Pass: Feed \text{PE}(\mathbf{p}) and \text{PE}(\mathbf{v}) into the MLP. The network outputs raw density \sigma, raw object code logits \mathbf{o}{raw}, and color \mathbf{c}. Apply sigmoid to \sigma{raw} to get \sigma \in [0, 1] (standard NeRF practice, implied by "volume density"). Apply softmax to \mathbf{o}{raw} to get the object code probability distribution \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^{H+1}. 3. Volume Rendering: Render the 2D image using standard volumetric rendering equation: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \left( 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) \right) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right), \deltai is the distance between samples, and \mathbf{r} is the camera ray (standard NeRF rendering, assumed from "leveraging vanilla NeRF as backbone"). 4. 2D Object Matching (Supervision): Render 2D object prediction images \{I1 \cdots IL\} where Il \in \mathbb{R}^{U \times V \times (H+1)}. Reshape predicted object channels M \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times H} and ground truth labels \bar{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times T}, where N = U \times V. Compute cost matrices using Soft Intersection-over-Union (sIoU) and Cross-Entropy Score (CES). Use the Hungarian algorithm to associate each ground truth 2D object mask with a unique predicted 2D object mask. 5. Loss Computation: Compute standard photometric loss between rendered color and ground truth color. Compute object supervision losses \ell{3d}^{empty} and \ell{3d}^{obj} based on the matched 2D masks and the rendered object codes. 6. Optimization: Minimize the total loss to update MLP weights. 7. Object Manipulation: To edit an object, identify the 3D points belonging to the target object code. Apply transformation (translation, rotation, scale, deformation) to these points. Tackle Visual Occlusions: Use a lightweight inverse query algorithm to handle occlusions and collisions without evaluating dense 3D points explicitly. Note: The specific steps of the inverse query algorithm are not detailed in the provided text, only that it is "lightweight" and "automatically edits the scene geometry". Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.optimize import linearsumassignment def positionalencoding(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, appendidentity=True): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = np.array([2i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg + 1)]) xb = np.reshape((x[..., None,:] scales[:, None]), (x.shape[0], -1)) fb = np.sin(xb np.pi) if appendidentity: fb = np.concatenate([x, fb], axis=-1) return fb def forwardpass(p, v, mlpweights): """ p: (N, 3) query points v: (N, 2) viewing directions Returns: sigma (N,), o (N, H+1), c (N, 3) """ pep = positionalencoding(p) pev = positionalencoding(v) # Concatenate PE of position and direction inputvec = np.concatenate([pep, pev], axis=-1) # Pass through MLP defined by mlpweights # Architecture: 128 -> 256 (x9) -> 128 -> Heads # Note: Specific weight loading omitted for brevity, assuming standard MLP forward hidden = mlpforward(inputvec, mlpweights) # Split outputs sigmaraw, oraw, c = splitheads(hidden) sigma = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-sigmaraw)) # Sigmoid o = np.exp(oraw) / np.sum(np.exp(oraw), axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Softmax return sigma, o, c def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, numsamples, mlpweights): """Standard volumetric rendering for a single ray.""" tvals = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = np.append(deltas, np.finfo(float).eps) xyz = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, None] sigma, o, c = forwardpass(xyz, raydirection, mlpweights) # Alpha values alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltas) T = np.cumprod(np.concatenate([np.ones((1,)), 1.0 - alpha + np.finfo(float).eps], axis=0))[:-1] weights = alpha T[:, None] color = np.sum(weights c, axis=0) # Render object channels objchannels = np.sum(weights o, axis=0) # Shape (H+1,) return color, objchannels def match2dmasks(predobjchannels, gtmasks, H, T): """ predobjchannels: (N, H+1) rendered object probs for one image gtmasks: (N, T) ground truth one-hot masks Returns: matched indices """ # Reshape to (N, H) and (N, T) pred = predobjchannels[:,:H] gt = gtmasks # Compute cost matrix using sIoU and CES # Note: Exact formula for sIoU/CES cost matrix construction is complex, # simplified here as a placeholder for the Hungarian algorithm input costmatrix = computecostmatrix(pred, gt) rowind, colind = linearsumassignment(costmatrix) return rowind, colind def trainstep(images, masks, poses, intrinsics, mlpweights): """Single training step.""" totalloss = 0 for i in range(len(images)): # Setup ray rayorigins, raydirections = getrays(poses[i], intrinsics[i], images[i].shape) # Render colors, objchannels = renderbatch(rayorigins, raydirections, mlpweights) # Compute photometric loss photometricloss = np.mean((colors - images[i])2) # Match 2D masks # Flatten objchannels for matching N = images[i].shape[0] images[i].shape[1] predflat = objchannels.reshape(-1, H + 1) gtflat = masks[i].reshape(-1, T) rowind, colind = match2dmasks(predflat, gtflat, H, T) # Compute object loss based on matched indices # This involves mapping 2D matched masks back to 3D points along the ray # and comparing with the 3D object codes o objectloss = computeobjectloss(objchannels, gtflat, rowind, colind) # Add empty space regularization loss emptyloss = computeemptyloss(objchannels, gtflat) totalloss += photometricloss + objectloss + emptyloss return totalloss def manipulateobject(scenepoints, objectcodeindex, transformation): """ scenepoints: (N, 3) objectcodeindex: int, index of the object to manipulate transformation: function or matrix to apply """ # Identify points belonging to the object # This requires querying the object field for all points in the scene # or using the inverse query algorithm mentioned in the paper mask = getobjectmask(scenepoints, objectcodeindex) # Apply transformation manipulatedpoints = scenepoints[mask].copy() manipulatedpoints = transformation(manipulatedpoints) # Tackle visual occlusions # The paper mentions a lightweight inverse query algorithm for this # Implementation detail not fully specified in sources manipulatedpoints = tackleocclusions(manipulatedpoints, scenepoints) return manipulatedpoints Parameters H: Predefined number of objects, determines the channel dimension of 2D object prediction tensors. T: Number of ground truth objects, determines the channel dimension of 2D ground truth label tensors. L: Number of generated 2D images used for 2D object matching and supervision. U, V: Spatial width and height dimensions of the 2D object prediction and ground truth label images. Typical values for H and T are not explicitly given in the sources, but H must be \ge T. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No 3D Ground Truth: Learning the object code faces the critical issue that no ground truth 3D object codes are available for full supervision. Variable Object Count: The number of total objects is variable and there is no fixed order for objects. Empty Space: Non-occupied (empty) 3D space must be taken into account, but there are no labels for supervision as well. This is addressed by jointly learning correct codes for empty 3D points using \ell{3d}^{empty}. Occlusion Artifacts: Manipulating originally occluded objects or parts may produce artifacts due to inaccuracies in the learned radiance fields. Lighting Discrepancies: Lighting factors are not decomposed, causing illumination discrepancies on edited objects compared to non-manipulated scenes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method uses a standard NeRF backbone, implying similar training time to NeRF, plus the overhead of 2D mask matching (Hungarian algorithm) per image per step. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the MLP weights and rendering object channels for all rays. Measured Performance: Novel view rendering quality is clearly better than PointNeRF, though it decreases after manipulation compared to non-manipulation baselines. Strengths: Simultaneously reconstructs, decomposes, manipulates, and renders complex 3D scenes in a single pipeline from 2D images. Robust object decomposition from 2D views. Limitations: Lighting factors are not decomposed. Manipulation of occluded objects may produce artifacts. When to use: When 3D object-level manipulation and decomposition are required from 2D images only, and 3D ground truth is unavailable. When not to use: When high-fidelity lighting manipulation is required, or when the scene contains many occluded objects that need precise editing. DM-NeRF was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023. It addresses the problem of 3D scene geometry decomposition and manipulation from 2D images. It builds on the success of NeRF by adding an object field component. The method was developed to enable users to virtually manipulate objects in 3D scenes (e.g., moving a chair) in applications like mixed reality. DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07227v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF
head: Joint decomposition and composition framework, Two-stage NeRF for joint decomposition and composition, UDC-NeRF, Unifed decompositional and compositional NeRF
body: Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF (UDC-NeRF) is a two-stage framework that jointly learns disentangled object-level representations and a global scene representation to enable both novel view synthesis and semantic scene editing. Unlike sibling methods that treat decomposition and composition as separate or loosely coupled tasks, UDC-NeRF unites them in a single pipeline where a coarse global field guides sampling for a fine-grained stage that enforces one-hot object activation and residual composition. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N multi-view posed images \{xi \mid i \in [1, N]\} and their corresponding instance semantic masks \{s{ij} \mid i \in [1, N], j \in [1, K+1]\} for a static scene. K is the number of object instances; the background is treated as instance index 1. Outputs: A composited radiance field (c{comp}, \sigma{comp}) for novel view synthesis, and individual object/background radiance fields (c^k{object}, \sigma^k{object}) for editing. Data Structures Shared Backbone: A 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input: 3D point coordinate p=(x,y,z) and view direction d. Output: Generic implicit scene feature vector f with dimension 256. Guidance Head: Several MLPs following the backbone. Output: Global RGB color c{guidance} and volume density \sigma{guidance}. Object/Background Heads: Two separate 3-layer MLPs (color and density prediction layers). Input: Generic feature f concatenated with learnable object codes (vectors representing specific objects or background). Output: RGB color c^i{object} and volume density \sigma^i{object} for instance i. Learnable Codes: A set of vectors, one for each of the K objects and the background. Positional Encoding: 10 levels for coordinates, 4 levels for ray directions. Algorithm Steps The method operates in two stages: Coarse Stage and Fine Stage. 1. Coarse Stage (Global Guidance): Sample points along camera rays. Pass points and directions through the Shared Backbone to get f. Pass f through the Guidance Head to predict global color c{guidance} and density \sigma{guidance}. Use the distribution of \sigma{guidance} to guide point sampling for the Fine Stage (coarse-to-fine sampling). 2. Fine Stage (Decomposition): Sample points along rays using the guidance from Stage 1. Pass points and directions through the Shared Backbone to get generic feature f. For each instance i \in [1, K+1]: Concatenate f with the learnable code for instance i. Pass to the corresponding Head (Background Head for i=1, Object Head for i>1) to predict c^i{object} and \sigma^i{object}. 3D One-Hot Density Regularization: Determine if foreground objects dominate at a point by checking if any object density exceeds 1: Mc = [\arg\max([\sigma^1{object}, \sigma^2{object},..., \sigma^{K+1}{object}]) > 1] where Mc is a binary mask. Apply regularization to the background branch (index 1) at these points to suppress its density: L{one-hot} = Mc \|\sigma^1{object} - \sigma0\|^22 Set \sigma0 = -0.01. Note: ReLU is applied to \sigma during rendering to ensure positivity, so negative raw predictions do not contribute to rendering. 3. Fine Stage (Composition): One-Hot Activation: Compute soft probability pi for the i-th object using Gumbel-Softmax on densities: pi = \frac{\exp((\sigma^i{object} + gi)/\tau)}{\sumj \exp((\sigma^j{object} + gj)/\tau)} where gi \sim \text{Gumbel}(0,1) and temperature \tau = 0.1. Compute one-hot composition weights M{obj} using stop-gradient (f{sp}) and one-hot function (fh): M{obj} = fh(\arg\max[gi + \log \sigma^i{object}]) - f{sp}(P) + P where P is the tensor of soft probabilities pi. Composite the radiance fields: (c{comp}, \sigma{comp}) = \sum{i=1}^{K+1} M{obj}^i \cdot (c^i{object}, \sigma^i{object}). Residual Composition: Combine the composited field (c{comp}, \sigma{comp}) with the coarse stage residual (c{guidance}, \sigma{guidance}) using point-wise average pooling: c{final} = \text{AvgPool}(c{comp}, c{guidance}) \sigma{final} = \text{AvgPool}(\sigma{comp}, \sigma{guidance}). Rendering: Render final color \hat{C}(r) and opacity \hat{O}(r) using standard volume rendering equations with \sigma{final} and c{final}. Loss Functions The total loss is: L{overall} = L{comp} + \lambda1 L{object} + \lambda2 L{color pseudo} + \lambda3 L{one-hot} where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are balancing weights. 1. Object Loss (L{object}): Enforces color and opacity consistency using semantic masks Mo(r)^k (foreground) and Mb(r)^1 (background). Render intermediate local object color and opacity: \hat{C}^k{object}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N T^ki (1 - \exp(-\sigma^k{object} \deltai)) c^k{object} \hat{O}^k{object}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N T^ki (1 - \exp(-\sigma^k{object} \deltai)) T^ki = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma^k{object} \deltaj) where N is the number of sampled points and \deltai is the distance between adjacent points. Calculate loss: L{object} = \sum{k=1}^{K+1} Mo(r)^k \|\hat{C}^k{object}(r) - C(r)\|^22 + \lambdab Mb(r)^1 \|\hat{O}^1{object}(r) - Mo(r)^1\|^22. 2. In-Painting Pseudo Supervision (L{color pseudo}): Handles occluded background regions using a pre-trained Lama inpainting model to generate pseudo-color C^1{pseudo}(r) for uncertain background regions. Calculate loss: L{color pseudo} = M^1b(r) \|\hat{C}^1{object}(r) - C^1{pseudo}(r)\|^22 where M^1b(r) is a 2D spatial weight map with value 0.05 for uncertain background regions. 3. One-Hot Regularization (L{one-hot}): Defined in Step 2 above. 4. Composition Loss (L{comp}): Standard color loss on the final rendered pixels \hat{C}(r) against ground truth C(r). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class UDCNeRF: def init(self, numobjects, hiddendim=256, numcoarsesamples=64, numfinesamples=48): """ numobjects: K, number of foreground objects. Background is index 1, objects are 2..K+1. Limitations: Relies on semantic masks for supervision. Performance depends on the quality of the pre-trained in-painting model for background regions. When to use: When both high-fidelity novel view synthesis and semantic object-level editing are required. When not to use: If only novel view synthesis is needed without editing, or if semantic masks are unavailable. The method was proposed in "Learning Unified Decompositional and Compositional NeRF for Editable Novel View Synthesis" (2023). It addresses the limitation of prior works like ObjectNeRF, which learn separate networks for global scene branch and local object branch without modeling interactions. UDC-NeRF unites decomposition and composition to model these interactions. name: Detail-based Segmentation
head: Detail-based NeRF Segmentation, Frequency-based Object Segmentation
body: Detail-based Segmentation is a preprocessing technique for NeRF training that partitions a scene into multiple radiance fields based on the spatial frequency of detected objects. It solves the problem of single-NeRF networks struggling to learn high-frequency details by assigning high-frequency objects to dedicated NeRFs while grouping low-frequency objects into a shared NeRF. Unlike sibling methods that rely on semantic labels or explicit geometric decomposition, this method uses image-domain frequency analysis to determine object importance, ensuring that complex visual features are handled by specialized networks. Inputs: A set of training images I = \{I1, I2,..., IN\} and a user-defined frequency threshold \tau. Outputs: A set of segmented image datasets \{D1, D2,..., DK\}, where each dataset Dj corresponds to a specific NeRF instance (either a dedicated high-frequency object or a shared low-frequency background group). Data Structures: Object Metadata: For each detected object o in image In, store: mask: Binary mask M{n,o} of size H \times W. maxfreq: Scalar value representing the maximum detail frequency of object o across all images. Segmented Images: New images I'{n,o} of size H \times W containing only the scaled object o on a transparent or black background. Steps: 1. Object Detection: Apply an object detection algorithm to all training images In to identify objects and generate binary masks M{n,o} covering the pixels occupied by each object o. 2. Frequency Calculation: For each detected object o in each image In, calculate the detail frequency f{n,o}. Note: The specific formula for f{n,o} is not provided in the sources. It is assumed to be a measure of high-frequency content (e.g., gradient magnitude or Laplacian variance) within the masked region. 3. Max Frequency Aggregation: Determine the maximum frequency recorded for each object o across all images in the dataset: Fo = \max{n} (f{n,o}) This metric is chosen over average frequency because the maximum frequency better reflects the object's importance to the user's viewing experience, particularly when users focus on complex or high-frequency regions. 4. Segmentation Decision: Compare Fo against the threshold \tau: If Fo > \tau, object o is assigned to a dedicated NeRF. If Fo \le \tau, object o is assigned to the shared NeRF group (along with other low-frequency objects). 5. Image Extraction and Scaling: For each object o assigned to a dedicated NeRF: Extract the object from each image In using the mask M{n,o}, using the outermost pixels of the mask as boundaries. Apply interpolation scaling to enlarge the segmented object within the H \times W frame. This reduces the spatial frequency of details the network must learn, improving rendering quality for high-frequency regions. Store the resulting scaled image as part of the training set for the dedicated NeRF. 6. Shared Group Processing: For objects in the shared NeRF group, the original images (or cropped versions if necessary) are used for training the single shared NeRF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def detailbasedsegmentation(images, thresholdtau): """ images: List of training images. thresholdtau: User-defined frequency threshold. Returns: List of datasets for each NeRF. """ # Step 1: Object Detection # Returns list of (imageindex, objectid, mask) detections = detectobjects(images) # Step 2 & 3: Frequency Calculation and Aggregation # Object max frequencies objectmaxfreqs = {} for imgidx, objid, mask in detections: # Calculate detail frequency for this object in this image # Note: Specific frequency metric implementation is source-dependent freq = calculatedetailfrequency(images[imgidx], mask) if objid not in objectmaxfreqs: objectmaxfreqs[objid] = freq else: # Update maximum frequency objectmaxfreqs[objid] = max(objectmaxfreqs[objid], freq) # Step 4: Segmentation Decision dedicatedobjects = [] sharedobjects = [] for objid, maxfreq in objectmaxfreqs.items(): if maxfreq > thresholdtau: dedicatedobjects.append(objid) else: sharedobjects.append(objid) # Step 5 & 6: Image Extraction and Scaling dedicateddatasets = [] for objid in dedicatedobjects: dataset = [] for imgidx, objidcurr, mask in detections: if objidcurr == objid: # Extract object using outermost pixels as boundaries cropped = extractobject(images[imgidx], mask) # Scale up to retain image size but enlarge object scaled = interpolatescale(cropped, targetsize=images[imgidx].shape) dataset.append(scaled) dedicateddatasets.append(dataset) # Shared dataset uses original images or combined low-freq objects # Implementation detail for shared group not fully specified in sources shareddataset = prepareshareddataset(images, sharedobjects) return dedicateddatasets + [shareddataset] Parameters: \tau (Threshold frequency): A user-adjustable threshold used to decide which objects warrant individual NeRF representations. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of the segmentation depends heavily on the object detection quality and the robustness of the frequency calculation metric. Boundaries: The extraction process uses the "outermost pixels" of the mask as boundaries, which may lead to jagged edges if the mask is not smooth. Degenerate Input: If no objects exceed the threshold, all objects are grouped into a single NeRF, effectively reverting to standard NeRF training. Uses maximum frequency rather than average frequency to prioritize objects with complex details that impact user experience. Interpolation scaling is used to enlarge objects in dedicated datasets, reducing the frequency of details the network needs to learn. Time Complexity: The method adds a preprocessing overhead proportional to the number of images and detected objects, involving detection, frequency calculation, and image scaling. Memory Complexity: Increases memory usage during training due to the storage of multiple NeRF models and their associated datasets. Performance: Improves rendering quality for high-frequency details by allowing dedicated networks to focus on specific objects. Strengths: Abstracts away network details, allowing direct application to any NeRF variant without modification. Reduces the learning burden for high-frequency regions. Limitations: Requires object detection as a prerequisite. The threshold \tau must be tuned manually. When to use: When rendering complex scenes with distinct high-frequency objects on resource-constrained devices (e.g., mobile) where single NeRFs fail to capture details. Detail-based Segmentation was introduced in the NeRFlex framework, designed for resource-aware, real-time, high-quality rendering of complex scenes on mobile devices. The method leverages domain knowledge that single NeRFs have weak learning ability for high-frequency details, resulting in lower rendering quality in those regions. By segmenting objects based on frequency, NeRFlex can allocate computational resources more effectively. name: Neural Articulated Radiance Field (NARF)
head: NARFP, Part-Wise NARF
body: Neural Articulated Radiance Field (NARF) models articulated objects by decomposing them into P rigid parts, each represented by a separate Rigidly Transformed Neural Radiance Field (RT-NeRF). Unlike implicit methods that learn pose-dependent deformations within a single network, NARF explicitly computes global rigid transformations via forward kinematics and combines part-wise outputs using a differentiable softmax weighting scheme. This approach avoids the "part dependency" issue found in earlier methods like P-NeRF, where a single network might learn erroneous correlations between unrelated parts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray \mathbf{r}, articulated object pose configuration \{\mathbf{T}0, \boldsymbol{\zeta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}\} (root transform, global shape variations, joint angles), and number of parts P. Outputs: Rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), optional foreground mask \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}), and optional segmentation mask \mathbf{S}^i(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: RT-NeRF Models: P separate neural networks F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}} for i=1 \dots P. Each network maps local coordinates to density \sigma and feature/color \mathbf{h}, \mathbf{c}. Pose Parameters: \mathbf{T}0: Global root transformation. \boldsymbol{\zeta: Global shape variation parameters (e.g., limb length). \boldsymbol{\theta}: Joint angles. Transformation: Rigid transformation li = \{\mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{t}i\} for each part i, derived from forward kinematics. Steps: 1. Compute Global Rigid Transformations: For each part i \in \{1, \dots, P\}, compute the global rigid transformation li = \{\mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{t}i\} from the pose configuration \{\mathbf{T}0, \boldsymbol{\zeta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}\} using forward kinematics. 2. Transform Ray and Position: For a query 3D point \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} along ray \mathbf{r}, transform them into the local coordinate system of each part i: \mathbf{x}^i = \mathbf{R}i^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}i) \mathbf{d}^i = \mathbf{R}i^{-1}\mathbf{d} 3. Query Part-Wise RT-NeRFs: For each part i, query the corresponding RT-NeRF F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}} to obtain density \sigma^i and color \mathbf{c}^i. The input to the network includes the encoded local position \gamma(\mathbf{x}^i), encoded local direction \gamma(\mathbf{d}^i), encoded shape parameters \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i) (if applicable), and encoded global shape variations \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta}): (\mathbf{c}^i, \sigma^i) = F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}^i), \gamma(\mathbf{d}^i), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta})) 4. Combine Densities and Colors: Combine the outputs from all P parts into a global density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using a differentiable weighted sum via softmax over the densities, controlled by a temperature parameter \tau: \sigma = \frac{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)\sigma^i}{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)} \mathbf{c} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)\mathbf{c}^i}{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)} Note: The softmax ensures differentiability, allowing gradients to flow to all RT-NeRF models during training, unlike a non-differentiable max operation. 5. Volume Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering using the combined density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} to generate the rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}): \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^N Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) \mathbf{c}j where Tj = \exp(-\sum{k=1}^{j-1} \sigmak \deltak) is the accumulated transmittance, \deltaj is the distance between samples, and \sigmaj, \mathbf{c}j are the density and color at sample j. 6. Optional: Foreground Mask and Segmentation: Foreground Mask: Estimate the foreground mask \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}) as the integral of opacity along the ray: \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^N Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) Segmentation Mask: Render a segmentation image indicating which part i contributed most to each pixel. First, determine the part index with the highest density at each sample j: sj(\mathbf{r}) = \arg \max{i \in \{1, \dots, P\}} \{\sigmaj^i\} Then, accumulate the opacity weighted by the indicator function for part i: \mathbf{S}^i(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^N Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) \cdot \mathbb{I}(sj(\mathbf{r}) == i) Parameters: \tau: Temperature parameter for the softmax function in Eq. 15. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density Problem: Training is dominated by zero-density samples because a surface point belongs to only one part, resulting in zero density for all other parts. This can make training inefficient as parts with small densities do not significantly affect the final value but still require computation. Non-Differentiable Max: Using a max operation to select the highest density is not differentiable, preventing gradient flow to all RT-NeRF models. The softmax approximation is required for effective training. Computational Cost: The computational cost is proportional to the number of object parts P, which limits the representation capacity for complex articulated objects with many parts. Holistic NARF (NARFH) combines the inputs of the RT-NeRF models from Part-Wise NARF and feeds them as a whole into a single NeRF model for direct regression of final density and color. Unlike Part-Wise NARF, NARFH does not satisfy Part Dependency because all parameters are considered for each 3D location, and object part segmentation masks cannot be generated using Eq. 18. However, NARFH has computational cost almost constant to the number of object parts and naturally avoids the zero density problem. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of object parts P in Part-Wise NARF (NARFP), as each part requires a separate RT-NeRF query. Holistic NARF (NARFH) has computational cost almost constant to the number of object parts. Memory Complexity: Proportional to P for NARFP, as it stores P separate RT-NeRF models. NARFH uses a single model, reducing memory overhead relative to P. Strengths: Avoids part dependency issues by explicitly modeling rigid transformations via forward kinematics. Allows for novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and body part segmentation. Differentiable combination allows gradient flow to all parts. Limitations: NARFP suffers from high computational cost for complex objects with many parts and inefficient training due to zero-density samples. NARFH loses the ability to generate explicit part segmentation masks based on density dominance. When to Use: Use NARFP when explicit part segmentation and strict part dependency avoidance are required, and the number of parts is small. Use NARFH when computational efficiency is critical and part-specific segmentation is not needed. NARF was introduced in 2021 by [NSLH21]. It builds on the concept of RT-NeRF, which models rigidly transformed object parts. The method addresses limitations in previous approaches like P-NeRF, which suffered from part dependency issues where the network learned erroneous dependencies between parts. NARF is trained using pose-annotated images, decomposing the articulated object into rigid parts with local coordinate systems and global shape variations. The converged NARF can be used for novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and body part segmentation.
