name: Lighting and Appearance Models
head: Relighting NeRF, Appearance-Aware NeRF, Stylized NeRF
body: Lighting and Appearance Models extend the standard NeRF representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) by decoupling intrinsic scene properties (geometry, albedo) from extrinsic appearance factors (illumination, artistic style) [Parent]. This separation enables explicit control over lighting conditions or global stylistic transformations while maintaining 3D geometric consistency, addressing the limitations of implicit view-dependent color prediction in standard NeRFs. The family modifies the baseline NeRF architecture Parent primarily through Input Space augmentation and Output Space extension. 1. Input Augmentation: The input tuple (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) is augmented with additional signals to condition appearance. Common augmentations include: Illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l representing light source parameters or environment maps. Roughness scalars br for material properties. Latent codes \mathbf{z} for style or identity. 2. Output Decoupling: The output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) is modified to predict intermediate physical quantities rather than final color. Albedo/Geometry: Networks predict accumulated albedo \mathbf{A} and surface normals \mathbf{N} derived from density gradients, which are then shaded by a separate lighting model. Pre-integrated Light: Networks predict pre-integrated radiance \tilde{L}i to approximate the rendering equation without numerical integration. 3. Joint Optimization: In appearance editing tasks, the 3D radiance field is optimized jointly with a 2D appearance network (e.g., style transfer or lighting estimation) to enforce consistency between the 3D structure and the 2D appearance target. Replaces numerical light integration with a neural network query predicting pre-integrated light \tilde{L}i from illumination embedding, direction, and roughness. Chosen when fine-grained illumination details are required without the memory cost of Spherical Harmonics. Replaces view-dependent color prediction with an explicit 2nd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) illumination model. Chosen when explicit relighting via learnable SH coefficients is needed, separating albedo/geometry from lighting. Applies artistic styles to 3D scenes using a mutual learning strategy between a 3D NeRF and a 2D stylization network with latent codes. Chosen for global artistic style transfer while maintaining geometric consistency, unlike region-specific or view-inconsistent methods. Originating from the need to control appearance in Neural Radiance Fields, these methods evolved from implicit view-dependent modeling to explicit physical or stylistic decomposition. Spherical Harmonics NeRF introduced explicit lighting control, while Neural-PIL addressed the computational cost of light integration. StylizedNeRF extended this to non-photorealistic rendering by jointly optimizing 3D and 2D networks. These approaches are used in relighting, virtual production, and artistic content creation.

name: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting (Neural-PIL)
head: Neural-PIL
body: Neural-PIL replaces the costly numerical integration of incoming light in physically-based rendering with a direct neural network query, predicting pre-integrated light \tilde{L}i from illumination embeddings, view direction, and material roughness. Unlike spherical harmonic or spherical Gaussian light representations which suffer from a lack of fine illumination details or high memory costs, Neural-PIL uses a coordinate-based MLP to represent finer details in illumination efficiently. It builds on Lighting and Appearance Models by decoupling the output space to predict intermediate physical quantities (pre-integrated radiance) rather than final color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l \in \mathbb{R}^{128}, incoming light direction (mirrored view direction) \omegar \in \mathbb{R}^3, and roughness scalar br. Output: Pre-integrated light \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br). Data Structures: The method employs a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture based on SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Networks) enhanced with FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) layers. FiLM-SIREN Layer: A layer that modulates the output of a linear transformation followed by a sine activation. It takes modulating parameters: a scalar \lambda0 and vectors \beta, \gamma. Mapping Networks: Two separate networks predict the modulating parameters for the FiLM-SIREN layers. 1. Light Mapping Network: Takes \mathbf{z}l as input and generates parameters (\gamma, \beta) for the first few layers to decode illumination information for the given direction. 2. Roughness Mapping Network: Takes br as input and generates parameters for the penultimate layer to perform light integration conditioned on roughness. Mathematical Formulation: The rendering equation is approximated by splitting the specular term, allowing the light integral to be pre-integrated into the neural network. The final radiance Lo is computed as: Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao) \approx \frac{bd}{\pi}\tilde{L}i(\mathbf{n}, 1) + bs \left( F0(\omegao, \mathbf{n}) B0(\omegao \cdot \mathbf{n}, br) + B1(\omegao \cdot \mathbf{n}, br) \right) \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br) Where: bd, bs are diffuse and specular albedo components. \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br) = \int{\Omega} D(br, \omegai, \omegar) Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) d\omegai is the pre-integrated light, dependent on the microfacet distribution D. F0(\omegao, \mathbf{n}) = (1 - \omegao \cdot \mathbf{h})^5 is the Fresnel term at normal incidence, with \mathbf{h} = \frac{\omegai + \omegao}{\|\omegai + \omegao\|}. B0, B1 are 2D lookup textures indexed by (\omegao \cdot \mathbf{n}) and roughness br. Note: The diffuse part queries \tilde{L}i with normal \mathbf{n} and fixed diffuse roughness 1, while the specular part queries \tilde{L}i with \omegar and material roughness br. The Neural Network Activation: The core activation function in the FiLM-SIREN layers is defined as: \phi(\mathbf{y}) = \sin(\lambda0 \gamma \odot \mathbf{y} + \beta) Where \odot denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product, and \mathbf{y} is the output of the preceding linear layer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Encode Illumination: Pass the illumination embedding \mathbf{z}l through the first mapping network to generate modulating parameters (\gamma{light}, \beta{light}). 2. Encode Roughness: Pass the roughness scalar br through the second mapping network to generate modulating parameters (\gamma{rough}, \beta{rough}) for the penultimate layer. 3. Forward Pass: a. Input the direction \omegar into the first layer of the MLP. b. For the first few layers, apply the FiLM modulation using (\gamma{light}, \beta{light}) and the sine activation \phi(\mathbf{y}). c. Propagate through intermediate layers. d. For the penultimate layer, apply the FiLM modulation using (\gamma{rough}, \beta{rough}). e. Output the final value \tilde{L}i(\omegar, br). 4. Rendering: Use the predicted \tilde{L}i in the split-sum approximation formula to compute pixel color. Parameters: Illumination embedding dimension: 128. Direction dimension: 3. Roughness: Scalar. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Stability: The method separates the training of the Light-SMAE (Smooth Manifold Autoencoder) and the Neural-PIL to ease memory requirements. The Light-SMAE is trained on a dataset of environment maps to map 2D environment maps to the 128-dimensional latent space \mathbf{z}l, which is then frozen during Neural-PIL training. Differentiability: The approach is designed for differentiable rendering engines, avoiding costly numerical accumulation or convolution on complete environment maps. A baseline approximation method that splits the specular term of the rendering equation into two factors: one involving the light integral and one involving the BRDF terms (D, G, F), allowing the light integral to be pre-integrated into a neural network. The specular term is split as \int{\Omega+} L(\hat{x}, l)(\hat{n} \cdot l) dl \int{\Omega+} \frac{DGF}{4(\hat{n} \cdot v)(\hat{n} \cdot l)} (\hat{n} \cdot l) dl. The rendering equation becomes \tilde{L}\hat{\mathbf{c}}b + (\pi\tilde{L}) \int{\Omega+} \frac{DGF}{4(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{v})(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l})} (\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \mathbf{l}) d\mathbf{l}, where \tilde{L} is the pre-integrated neural network representing the light integral factor divided by \pi. This allows the forward rendering model to be expressed as \widehat{Lcb} + (\pi\widehat{L}) \int{\Omega+} \frac{DGF}{4(\hat{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})(\hat{n} \cdot \mathbf{l})} (\hat{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) d\mathbf{l}. Time Complexity: Replaces numerical integration with a single MLP query, which is significantly faster than Monte Carlo integration or spherical harmonic evaluation for high-frequency details. Memory Complexity: Lower than spherical harmonic representations which require high memory costs for fine details. The MLP size is determined by the number of FiLM-SIREN layers and mapping networks. Strengths: Capable of representing finer details in illumination compared to SG or SH representations without prohibitive memory costs. Suitable for differentiable rendering engines. Limitations: Requires training of auxiliary networks (Light-SMAE, BRDF-SMAE) and careful handling of the computation graph to avoid large memory footprints from naive implementation of voxel grid features. When to use: When high-fidelity illumination details are required in differentiable inverse rendering or neural radiance field optimization, and spherical harmonics are insufficient or too expensive. Neural-PIL was introduced in the paper "Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition". It addresses the limitations of existing differentiable rendering frameworks that rely on spherical Gaussian (SG) or spherical harmonic (SH) light representations, which lack fine details or are computationally expensive. The method leverages a pi-GAN-like architecture with FiLM-SIREN layers. It is used in the context of reflectance decomposition and inverse rendering, where separating geometry, lighting, and material properties is required. The approach is also referenced in the context of Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering (NDJIR) as a baseline for split-sum and PIL approximation. Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.14373, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NDJIR: Neural Direct and Joint Inverse Rendering for Geometry, Lights, and Materials of Real Object, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2302.00675, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics NeRF
head: NeRF with Spherical Harmonics, SH-NeRF
body: Spherical Harmonics NeRF replaces the view-dependent color prediction of the baseline NeRF Parent with an explicit 2nd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) illumination model, enabling explicit relighting by varying learnable SH coefficients. Unlike siblings that predict pre-integrated light or use latent style codes, this method decouples the scene's intrinsic albedo and geometry from the illumination, allowing the lighting to be modified post-training. The method modifies the standard volume rendering pipeline by accumulating albedo and surface normals in screen space, then applying a Lambertian shading model driven by per-image SH coefficients. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray samples \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^{N{\mathrm{depth}}}, density \sigma(\mathbf{x}i), albedo MLP outputs, and per-image SH coefficients \mathbf{L}. Outputs: Final color \mathbf{C}. Data Structures \mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{9 \times 3}: Per-image learnable SH coefficients. The 9 coefficients correspond to the 2nd-order SH basis (1 DC + 8 directional), and 3 channels correspond to RGB. \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{n}) \in \mathbb{R}^9: The SH basis vector evaluated at normal \mathbf{n}. \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Accumulated screen-space albedo. \mathbf{N} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Accumulated screen-space surface normal. Numbered Steps 1. Accumulate Albedo and Density Gradients: For each ray, iterate through N{\mathrm{depth}} samples. Compute the opacity weight for sample i: wi = T(ti) \alpha(\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai), where T(ti) is the transmittance up to sample i, \alpha is the opacity function, and \deltai is the distance between samples. Accumulate the albedo \mathbf{A} by summing the albedo MLP output \mathbf{c}i weighted by wi: \mathbf{A} = \sum{i=1}^{N{\mathrm{depth}}} wi \mathbf{c}i Compute the unnormalized normal \mathbf{\hat{N}} by summing the gradient of the density \frac{\partial \sigma(\mathbf{x}i)}{\partial \mathbf{x}i} weighted by wi: \mathbf{\hat{N}} = \sum{i=1}^{N{\mathrm{depth}}} \left( \frac{\partial \sigma(\mathbf{x}i)}{\partial \mathbf{x}i} \right) wi The gradient \frac{\partial \sigma(\mathbf{x}i)}{\partial \mathbf{x}i} is computed via automatic differentiation of the density network with respect to the spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}i. 2. Normalize Normal: Normalize the accumulated unnormalized normal \mathbf{\hat{N}} to obtain the unit surface normal \mathbf{N}: \mathbf{N} = \frac{\mathbf{\hat{N}}}{\|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|} Note: The source formula (3) divides by \|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|^2, but the text explicitly states "normalise the resulting vector to a unit sphere," which implies division by the L2 norm \|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\|. The standard normalization is used here. If \|\mathbf{\hat{N}}\| \approx 0, \mathbf{N} defaults to (0,0,1) or similar arbitrary normal. 3. Evaluate SH Basis: Compute the SH basis vector \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}) for the 2nd-order (9 coefficients) basis using the normal \mathbf{N}. 4. Compute Illumination: Compute the illumination color \mathbf{I} by multiplying the SH coefficients \mathbf{L} with the basis vector \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}): \mathbf{I} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}) This is a matrix-vector multiplication where \mathbf{L} is 9 \times 3 and \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{N}) is 9 \times 1, resulting in a 3 \times 1 RGB vector. 5. Render Color: Compute the final color \mathbf{C} by elementwise multiplying the accumulated albedo \mathbf{A} with the illumination \mathbf{I}: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{A} \odot \mathbf{I} This rendering happens in screen space using the accumulated albedo and normals. Formulas Rendering Equation: \mathbf{C}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}},\textbf {L}\right)= \mathbf {A}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)\odot \mathbf {L}\mathbf {b}\left (\mathbf {N}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)\right) Normal Extraction: \mathbf {N}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right) = \frac {\mathbf {\hat {N}}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)}{\left \|\mathbf {\hat {N}}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right)\right \|} (Textual description overrides potential typo in source formula denominator power). Unnormalized Normal: \mathbf {\hat {N}}\left (\{\mathbf {x}i\}{i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\right) = \sum {i=1}^{N\mathrm {depth}}\left (\frac {\partial }{\partial \mathbf {x}i}\sigma (\mathbf {x}i)\right)\odot T(ti)\alpha (\sigma (\mathbf {x}i)\delta i) Parameters \mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{9 \times 3}: Per-image learnable SH coefficients for illumination. Order of SH: 2nd-order (9 coefficients). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Shadowing: The model lacks direct shadow generation, which is crucial for outdoor scenes and accurate relighting. Normal Degeneracy: If the accumulated density gradient \mathbf{\hat{N}} is near zero (e.g., in empty space or uniform density regions), normalization fails. Screen Space Accumulation: Accumulating albedo and normals in screen space reduces noise and aids convergence compared to per-sample shading, but ties the shading calculation to the specific ray sampling strategy. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def shbasis2nd(n): """ Computes the 2nd-order Spherical Harmonics basis vector for normal n. n: (3,) tensor, normalized surface normal. Returns: (9,) tensor. """ x, y, z = n.unbind(dim=0) # 2nd order SH basis (9 coefficients) # Order 0: Y00 # Order 1: Y1-1, Y10, Y11 # Order 2: Y2-2, Y2-1, Y20, Y21, Y22 # Constants for normalization are omitted for brevity as they are fixed. # Standard 2nd order SH basis evaluation: b = torch.zeros(9, device=n.device) b[0] = 0.282095 # sqrt(1/pi) b[1] = 0.488603 y b[2] = 0.488603 z b[3] = 0.488603 x b[4] = 1.092548 x y b[5] = 0.315392 (3 z2 - 1) b[6] = 1.092548 y z b[7] = 0.546274 (x2 - y2) b[8] = 1.092548 x z return b class SHNeRFRenderer: def init(self, densitynet, albedonet, numimages): self.densitynet = densitynet self.albedonet = albedonet # L: (numimages, 9, 3) -> (numimages, 27) flattened or kept as (9,3) self.L = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numimages, 9, 3)) def render(self, rayso, raysd, tnear, tfar, numsamples, imageidx): """ Renders a single image given rays and SH coefficients. """ # 1. Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples) tsamples = tnear + tvals (tfar - tnear) points = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tsamples.unsqueeze(2) # points: (numrays, numsamples, 3) # 2. Compute density and albedo # densitynet expects (N, 3) density = self.densitynet(points.reshape(-1, 3)).reshape(points.shape[:2]) albedo = self.albedonet(points.reshape(-1, 3)).reshape(points.shape[:2], 3) # 3. Compute weights # delta = distance between samples deltas = tsamples[:, 1:] - tsamples[:,:-1] # Add zero for the last sample to match dimensions if needed, # but standard NeRF uses deltas for opacity calculation. # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-density deltas) # Transmittance T(ti) # T(ti) = prod{j<i} (1 - alphaj) # We need T for each sample i. # Accumulate product of (1-alpha) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=1) # Prepend 1.0 for the first sample's transmittance (before any absorption) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) # Weights wi = T(ti) alphai weights = T alpha.unsqueeze(2) # (numrays, numsamples, 1) # 4. Accumulate Albedo A and Unnormalized Normal Nhat # Albedo accumulation A = torch.sum(weights albedo, dim=1) # (numrays, 3) # Normal accumulation # Compute gradient of density w.r.t x, y, z points.requiresgrad(True) densitysum = density.sum() densitysum.backward(torch.oneslike(densitysum), retaingraph=True) graddensity = points.grad # (numrays, numsamples, 3) # Nhat = sum( graddensityi weightsi) Nhat = torch.sum(graddensity weights, dim=1) # (numrays, 3) # 5. Normalize Normal Nnorm = torch.norm(Nhat, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Guard against division by zero Nnorm = torch.clamp(Nnorm, min=1e-8) N = Nhat / Nnorm # (numrays, 3) # 6. Compute SH Basis and Illumination # Get SH coefficients for this image Limg = self.L[imageidx] # (9, 3) # Compute basis for all normals # b(N) shape: (numrays, 9) bN = torch.stack([shbasis2nd(N[i]) for i in range(N.shape[0])], dim=0) # Illumination I = L b(N) # L: (9, 3), b(N): (numrays, 9) -> I: (numrays, 3) # Matrix mult: (numrays, 9) @ (9, 3).T -> (numrays, 3) # Or: torch.einsum('ij,ik->jk', bN, Limg) -> (3, numrays) then transpose I = torch.einsum('ij,ij->i', bN, Limg.T) # This is wrong, L is (9,3), b is (9,) # Correct: Ir = sumj Ljr bj # I = bN @ Limg.T -> (numrays, 9) @ (9, 3) -> (numrays, 3) I = torch.matmul(bN, Limg.T) # 7. Final Color C = A I # Elementwise multiplication return C An extension that introduces a dedicated shadow model S to handle shadows, which the basic SH model lacks. A sibling method that predicts pre-integrated radiance to approximate the rendering equation without numerical integration. Sibling A sibling method that uses latent codes for style or identity rather than explicit physical lighting models. Sibling Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the density and albedo network evaluations and the accumulation steps. The SH evaluation is O(1) per ray (fixed 9 coefficients). Memory Complexity: Requires storing per-image SH coefficients \mathbf{L} (9 \times 3 floats per image). Strengths: Allows explicit relighting by modifying \mathbf{L} after training. Screen-space accumulation reduces noise. Limitations: Lacks direct shadow generation, making it unsuitable for outdoor scenes without extensions. When to use: When explicit relighting is required and shadows are not critical or can be handled by a separate network. When not to use: For outdoor scenes requiring realistic shadows. Spherical Harmonics NeRF was introduced by V. Rudnev et al. in "NeRF for Outdoor Scene Relighting" (2022). It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which lacks semantic meaning of scene intrinsics and direct control over lighting. The method builds on the baseline NeRF architecture Parent by modifying the output space to decouple albedo and geometry from illumination. name: StylizedNeRF
head: Stylized Neural Radiance Fields
body: StylizedNeRF is a method for non-photorealistic rendering that synthesizes 3D-consistent stylized images by jointly optimizing a 3D radiance field and a 2D stylization network. It solves the problem of view-inconsistent stylization and the ambiguity of 2D style transfer in 3D space by using a mutual learning strategy where the 2D stylization network provides style guidance to the 3D model, while the 3D model enforces geometric consistency. It differs from its siblings, such as Non-Photorealistic Style Editing which allows region-specific styles, and StyleRF-VolVis which supports both photorealistic and non-photorealistic editing, by focusing on a global style transfer that ensures 3D consistency through learnable latent codes. StylizedNeRF extends the baseline NeRF architecture Parent by integrating a 2D stylization network into the training loop. The method relies on the Shared principles of the parent family, specifically Joint Optimization and Input/Output Augmentation [Parent]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses (\mathbf{c}), viewing directions (\mathbf{d}), 3D positions (\mathbf{x}), and a target style image \mathbf{I}{style}. Outputs: Stylized color \mathbf{c}{stylized} for each ray. Data Structures: 1. Stylized NeRF (\mathcal{N}): A standard MLP-based radiance field predicting density \sigma and base color \mathbf{c}{base}. 2. 2D Stylization Network (\mathcal{S}): A 2D convolutional network (e.g., based on WCT or AdaIN) that maps base images to stylized images. 3. Learnable Latent Codes (\mathbf{z}): A set of latent vectors used to resolve ambiguities in the 2D stylization process, ensuring 3D consistency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each camera view, sample points \mathbf{x}i along rays. Query \mathcal{N} to get density \sigmai and base color \mathbf{c}{base, i}. 2. Volume Rendering: Compute the rendered base image \mathbf{I}{base} using standard volume rendering integration [Parent]. 3. Stylization: Pass \mathbf{I}{base} through the 2D stylization network \mathcal{S} conditioned on the target style and latent codes \mathbf{z} to produce the stylized image \mathbf{I}{stylized}. 4. Loss Computation: Stylization Loss (\mathcal{L}{style}): Measures the difference between \mathbf{I}{stylized} and the target style image \mathbf{I}{style} (e.g., using Gram matrices or perceptual loss). Geometric Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{geo}): Ensures that the underlying geometry (density \sigma) remains consistent across views, preventing style-induced geometric distortions. Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{rec}): Standard photometric loss between \mathbf{I}{base} and the input view (optional, depending on implementation). 5. Mutual Learning Update: Update \mathcal{N} to minimize \mathcal{L}{geo} and \mathcal{L}{rec}, preserving geometry. Update \mathcal{S} and latent codes \mathbf{z} to minimize \mathcal{L}{style}. The latent codes \mathbf{z} are optimized to handle ambiguities in the 2D stylization, ensuring that the stylized output is consistent with the 3D structure. Formulas: The total loss is typically a weighted sum: \mathcal{L}{total} = \lambda{style} \mathcal{L}{style} + \lambda{geo} \mathcal{L}{geo} + \lambda{rec} \mathcal{L}{rec} Where \lambda are hyperparameters. The latent codes \mathbf{z} are updated via gradient descent on \mathcal{L}{style}. Parameters: \lambda{style}, \lambda{geo}, \lambda{rec}: Weights for the respective losses. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but mutual learning implies balanced weighting. Number of latent codes: One per view or per scene, depending on implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Style Bleeding: If \mathcal{L}{geo} is too weak, the style may distort the geometry. Ambiguity: Without latent codes \mathbf{z}, the 2D stylization may produce inconsistent results for the same 3D point viewed from different angles. A variant that integrates a Phong reflection model into the NeRF optimization. It uses MLPs to predict tint, roughness, modeled normal vectors, and diffuse/specular colors from integrated average features. The modeled normal vectors are trained with regularization losses from RefNeRF and optimized towards estimated normal vectors via a confidence-weighted loss. This drives outlier points with abnormal normals to zero confidence and uses estimated normals to supervise point features. Time Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to the joint optimization of the 2D stylization network and the 3D radiance field. Memory Complexity: Increased memory usage due to the storage of latent codes and the 2D stylization network parameters. Strengths: Produces 3D-consistent stylized images; handles 2D style transfer ambiguities via latent codes. Limitations: Requires careful balancing of style and geometry losses; may be slower to converge than single-network approaches. When to use: When 3D-consistent stylization is required for novel view synthesis. When not to use: When region-specific stylization is needed (use Non-Photorealistic Style Editing) or when photorealistic editing is also required (use StyleRF-VolVis). StylizedNeRF was introduced as part of the broader effort to extend NeRF for non-photorealistic rendering. It builds on the Shared principles of the parent family, specifically the joint optimization of 3D and 2D networks [Parent]. The method addresses the limitations of previous approaches that either discarded view directions (leading to inconsistency) or failed to enforce 3D consistency. It is cited in surveys on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28 NeuralEditor: Editing Neural Radiance Fields via Manipulating Point Clouds, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01197, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Physical Imaging Model with Spherical Harmonics
head: Lambertian reflectance-based physical imaging model
body:
This method integrates a physically constrained imaging model into the NeRF optimization loop to decompose illumination into direct sunlight and ambient skylight, using spherical harmonics to model the latter. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly separating albedo, surface normals, and lighting to provide auxiliary supervision, thereby reducing lighting ambiguity and improving reconstruction fidelity in shadowed or radiometrically inconsistent regions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Density field \sigma(P) and its gradient 
abla\sigma(P) at a 3D point P=(x,y,z). Camera origin op for the current view. Surface albedo hoi (RGB) at point i. Illumination coefficients Lk for k=0..8. Outputs: Synthesized image intensity I{p2}^i at point i. Data Structures Illumination Coefficients: A vector of 9 coefficients L = [L0, L1,..., L8] representing the second-order spherical harmonic expansion of the ambient skylight field. Basis Functions: A vector of 9 values b = [b0,..., b8] computed from the surface normal components. Steps 1. Extract Density Gradient: Calculate the gradient of the density field \sigma at point P: 
abla\sigma(P) = \left[  rac{\partial\sigma}{\partial x},  rac{\partial\sigma}{\partial y},  rac{\partial\sigma}{\partial z} ight] 2. Normalize Gradient: Compute the unit normal vector n(P): n(P) =  rac{
abla\sigma(P)}{\|
abla\sigma(P)\|} 3. Constrain Normal Direction: Calculate the ray direction from the surface point P to the camera origin op: d{obs} = 	ext{normalize}(P - op) Compute the inner product n(P) \cdot d{obs}. If n(P) \cdot d{obs} < 0, reverse the normal vector: n(P) \leftarrow -n(P). Otherwise, retain n(P). This ensures the normal faces the camera (angle < 90^\circ). 4. Compute Spherical Harmonic Basis Functions: Evaluate the second-order basis functions bk using the components nx, ny, nz of the constrained unit normal n(P): b0 = \sqrt{ rac{1}{4\pi}} b1 = \sqrt{ rac{3}{4\pi}} nz b2 = \sqrt{ rac{3}{4\pi}} nx b3 = \sqrt{ rac{3}{4\pi}} ny b4 = \sqrt{ rac{5}{12\pi}} (3nz^2 - 1) b5 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} nx nz b6 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} ny nz b7 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} (nx^2 - ny^2) b8 = \sqrt{ rac{15}{4\pi}} nx ny 5. Synthesize Intensity: Compute the intensity I{p2}^i for each RGB channel: I{p2}^i = hoi \sum{k=0}^{8} Lk bk Here, hoi is the surface albedo (RGB), Lk are the illumination coefficients, and bk are the basis functions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computephysicalimagingintensity(densitygradient, cameraorigin, pointp, albedo, illuminationcoeffs): """ Computes synthesized intensity using physical imaging model with spherical harmonics. Args: densitygradient: Array [dx, dy, dz] representing nabla sigma(P). cameraorigin: Array [ox, oy, oz] representing op. pointp: Array [x, y, z] representing P. albedo: Array [r, g, b] representing rhoi. illuminationcoeffs: Array [L0,..., L8] of length 9. Returns: intensity: Array [r, g, b] representing Ip2^i. """ PI = 3.141592653589793 # Step 1 & 2: Normalize gradient to get unit normal normmagnitude = (densitygradient[0]2 + densitygradient[1]2 + densitygradient[2]2) 0.5 if normmagnitude == 0: # Guard against zero gradient; return zero intensity or handle as degenerate case. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] nx = densitygradient[0] / normmagnitude ny = densitygradient[1] / normmagnitude nz = densitygradient[2] / normmagnitude # Step 3: Constrain normal direction # Calculate ray direction from surface point to camera origin dx = pointp[0] - cameraorigin[0] dy = pointp[1] - cameraorigin[1] dz = pointp[2] - cameraorigin[2] raylen = (dx2 + dy2 + dz2) 0.5 if raylen == 0: # Guard against point coincident with camera origin return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dobsx = dx / raylen dobsy = dy / raylen dobsz = dz / raylen # Inner product dotproduct = nx dobsx + ny dobsy + nz dobsz # If negative, reverse normal if dotproduct < 0: nx = -nx ny = -ny nz = -nz # Step 4: Compute Spherical Harmonic Basis Functions (Second Order, k=0..8) b0 = (1 / (4 PI)) 0.5 b1 = (3 / (4 PI)) 0.5 nz b2 = (3 / (4 PI)) 0.5 nx b3 = (3 / (4 PI)) 0.5 ny b4 = (5 / (12 PI)) 0.5 (3 nz2 - 1) b5 = (15 / (4 PI)) 0.5 nx nz b6 = (15 / (4 PI)) 0.5 ny nz b7 = (15 / (4 PI)) 0.5 (nx2 - ny2) b8 = (15 / (4 PI)) 0.5 nx ny basisfunctions = [b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7, b8] # Step 5: Synthesize Intensity # Sum over k=0 to 8 of Lk bk totalirradiance = 0.0 for k in range(9): totalirradiance += illuminationcoeffs[k] basisfunctions[k] # Apply albedo intensity = [albedo[0] totalirradiance, albedo[1] totalirradiance, albedo[2] totalirradiance] return intensity Parameters Spherical Harmonic Order: Second-order, resulting in 9 coefficients (k=0 to 8). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Gradient: If 
abla\sigma(P) is zero, the normal cannot be normalized. Camera Coincidence: If P = op, the ray direction is undefined. Normal Ambiguity: Without the camera-view constraint, NeRF-predicted density gradients may point in the opposite direction of the actual surface normal. The inner product check constrains the normal direction to face the camera, providing stable geometric information for the physical imaging model. Time Complexity: The computation involves a constant number of operations (gradient, normalization, 9 basis evaluations, dot product, and sum) per sample point, making it O(1) per sample relative to scene size, but adds overhead to the per-point shading calculation during training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 9 illumination coefficients Lk per view or globally, and the basis functions are computed on the fly. Strengths: Reduces lighting ambiguity and improves reconstruction fidelity in shadowed or radiometrically inconsistent regions by separating illumination from albedo. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the density gradient for normal estimation; assumes distant illumination sources (sunlight and skylight). When to Use: Satellite imaging conditions with complex lighting where radiometric decomposition is needed for accurate 3D reconstruction. When Not to Use: Scenes with complex local lighting or non-distant light sources where spherical harmonics may not adequately capture the illumination field. This method was introduced in the context of NeRF reconstruction for multi-view satellite images, specifically to handle radiometric decomposition under complex satellite imaging conditions. It was proposed by researchers publishing in Remote Sensing in 2026. The approach integrates the physical imaging module directly into the NeRF optimization process rather than applying it post-reconstruction. name: StyleRF-VolVis
body: StyleRF-VolVis is a framework for editing the style (appearance) of a DVR scene represented by a NeRF model without losing original content (geometry) information. It supports both photorealistic (PSE) and non-photorealistic (NPSE) editing in a single pipeline by separating content and appearance, allowing explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions via a Palette Color Network (PCN) and an Unrestricted Color Network (UCN), while preserving view-dependent lighting. It differs from prior works by supporting both photorealistic and non-photorealistic editing in a single framework, whereas others focus on one or the other. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of the scene, an initial Transfer Function (TF) defining opacity ranges, and optionally reference images for style transfer. Outputs: A stylized DVR scene represented by the optimized networks, allowing for interactive PSE and NPSE. Data Structures: 1. Base NeRF Model: Uses Instant-NGP architecture. Density MLP: Takes position x and hash-grid encoded features; outputs density \sigma(x). Hash-grid Encoder: Multiresolution hash-grid encoding for efficient optimization. Note: Parameters are frozen after Stage 1. 2. Palette Color Network (PCN): Composed of two branches. Specular Branch (Lighting MLP): Inputs: Geometry features (from density MLP) and spherical harmonics (SH) encoded view direction d. Output: Grayscale specular color cs(x, d). Diffuse Branch (Palette MLP): Inputs: Features from palette hash-grid encoder Ep. Outputs: Intensity I(x), weights \omegai(x) for NP palette colors, and color offsets \deltai(x). Palette Colors: P = \{P1,..., P{NP}\}, extracted and refined from input images. 3. Unrestricted Color Network (UCN): Architecture: Similar to the diffuse branch but without palette constraints. Inputs: Geometry features (no view direction d during optimization to ensure cross-view consistency). Output: Diffuse color cd(x). Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Base NeRF Optimization Optimize the base NeRF model (Instant-NGP) to reconstruct scene geometry using the loss L{BASE}: L{BASE} = ||c(r) - \hat{c}(r)||2^2 where c(r) is ground-truth color and \hat{c}(r) is predicted color. Freeze all parameters of the base NeRF (density MLP and hash-grid encoder) to prevent style editing from affecting geometry. 2. Palette Refinement Extract initial palette colors P{CONVEX} using the RGB convex hull method from multi-view images. Refine the palette by removing similar colors. Calculate the distance between colors in HSB space using only the hue component. If the distance is below a threshold, remove the color. Determine the final number of palette colors NP. 3. Stage 2: PCN Optimization (PSE) Initialize the PCN. Initialize shallow layers of the palette MLP with hidden parameters from the base NeRF’s color function. Optimize PCN parameters and palette colors P using the loss L{PALETTE}: L{PALETTE} = ||c(r) - \hat{c}(r)||2^2 + \lambda\delta \sum{i=1}^{M} \sum{j=1}^{NP} ||\deltaj(xi)||2^2 where \lambda\delta = 0.1 is the regularization strength. The predicted color c(x, d) is computed as: c(x, d) = cs(x, d) + I(x) \sum{i=1}^{NP} \omegai(x)(Pi + \deltai(x)) Render \hat{c}(r) using the standard NeRF volume rendering equation: \hat{c}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{M} \alphai (1 - \omegai) c(xi, d) where \omegai = \exp(-(ti - t{i-1})\sigma(xi)) is transmittance, \alphai = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \omegaj is attenuation, and r=(o,d) is the ray. 4. Photorealistic Style Editing (PSE) Setup For PSE, compute the difference \Delta P between the original palette P and target palette P' in HSB space. Add \Delta Pi to Pi + \deltai(x) in the color equation. For opacity/lighting editing, multiply \sigma(x{Pi}) or cs(x{Pi}, d) by a scalar. 5. Stage 3: UCN Optimization (NPSE) via Knowledge Distillation (KD) Initialization: Perform color transfer in the PCN (teacher) to match target style colors. This ensures the UCN (student) color representation matches selected styles before NPSE. Optimization: Optimize the UCN using KD to transfer color knowledge from the PCN. Remove view direction input in UCN optimization to ensure cross-view consistency during NPSE. Optimize on a single camera view by rendering different regions independently to map a style to a region. Utilize the additional lighting MLP (optimized in Stage 2) to preserve DVR lighting during NPSE, keeping view directions for lighting calculation. 6. Inference For partial stylization, combine color representations: regions preserving original appearance use colors from PCN; stylized regions use UCN. Perform additional feedforward steps of the lighting MLP to provide lighting information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def optimizeparams(params, lossfn, lr, steps): """Standard parameter update loop.""" for in range(steps): loss = lossfn() loss.backward() for p in params: if p.grad is not None: p -= lr p.grad p.grad.zero() def extractconvexhullcolors(images): """Extract initial palette using RGB convex hull method.""" # Flatten all pixel RGB values from multi-view images allcolors = [pixel.rgb for img in images for pixel in img.pixels] # Compute convex hull vertices in RGB space return convexhullvertices(allcolors) def refinepalette(P, huethreshold): """Remove similar colors based on hue distance in HSB space.""" refined = [] for color in P: h, s, b = rgbtohsb(color) issimilar = False for existing in refined: hex,, = rgbtohsb(existing) if abs(h - hex) < huethreshold: issimilar = True break if not issimilar: refined.append(color) return refined def transferstylecolors(P, targetpalette): """Compute delta P in HSB space and add to original palette.""" newP = [] for i, (porig, ptarget) in enumerate(zip(P, targetpalette)): ho, so, bo = rgbtohsb(porig) ht, st, bt = rgbtohsb(ptarget) deltah = ht - ho deltas = st - so deltab = bt - bo newcolor = hsbtorgb(ho + deltah, so + deltas, bo + deltab) newP.append(newcolor) return newP def rendervolume(rayo, rayd, densityfn, colorfn, M=128): """Standard volume rendering with M samples.""" tstart, tend = 0.0, 1.0 dt = (tend - tstart) / M transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(M): t = tstart + i dt x = rayo + t rayd sigma = densityfn(x) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma dt) c = colorfn(x, rayd) accumulatedcolor += alpha transmittance c transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor def trainbasenerf(images, tf, lr=0.01, steps=10000): densitymlp, hashgrid = initinstantngp() def lossfn(): rayo, rayd = sampleraysfromimage(images[0]) points, depths = samplepointsalongray(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, M=128) sigma = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) cpred = rendervolume(rayo, rayd, lambda x: densitymlp(x, hashgrid), lambda x, d: basecolorfn(x, d, hashgrid)) cgt = images[0].color return mse(cgt, cpred) optimizeparams([densitymlp.parameters(), hashgrid.parameters()], lossfn, lr, steps) return densitymlp, hashgrid def trainpcn(densitymlp, hashgrid, images, refimages, lr=0.001, steps=5000): Pconvex = extractconvexhullcolors(refimages) P = refinepalette(Pconvex, huethreshold=0.15) NP = len(P) lightingmlp = initlightingmlp() palettemlp = initpalettemlp() initpalettemlpshallow(palettemlp, densitymlp) def lossfn(): rayo, rayd = sampleraysfromimage(images[0]) points, depths = samplepointsalongray(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, M=128) geofeatures = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) viewdirsh = encodesphericalharmonics(rayd, degree=3) cs = lightingmlp(geofeatures, viewdirsh) palettefeatures = palettemlp(points, hashgrid) I = intensity(palettefeatures) weights = softmax(paletteweights(palettefeatures), dim=-1) delta = coloroffsets(palettefeatures) cd = I sum(weights[i] (P[i] + delta[i]) for i in range(NP)) c = cs + cd cpred = rendervolume(rayo, rayd, lambda x: densitymlp(x, hashgrid), lambda x, d: c) cgt = images[0].color mseloss = mse(cgt, cpred) regloss = 0.1 sum(norm(delta[i])2 for i in range(NP)) return mseloss + regloss optimizeparams([lightingmlp.parameters(), palettemlp.parameters(), P], lossfn, lr, steps) return lightingmlp, palettemlp, P def trainucn(lightingmlp, palettemlp, P, images, targetstyleref, lr=0.001, steps=3000): P = transferstylecolors(P, targetstyleref) NP = len(P) ucn = initucn() def lossfn(): rayo, rayd = sampleraysfromimage(images[0]) points, depths = samplepointsalongray(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, M=128) geofeatures = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) viewdirsh = encodesphericalharmonics(rayd, degree=3) csteacher = lightingmlp(geofeatures, viewdirsh) palettefeatures = palettemlp(points, hashgrid) It = intensity(palettefeatures) wt = softmax(paletteweights(palettefeatures), dim=-1) dt = coloroffsets(palettefeatures) cdteacher = It sum(wt[i] (P[i] + dt[i]) for i in range(NP)) cteacher = csteacher + cdteacher ucnfeatures = ucn(points, hashgrid) cdstudent = ucnoutput(ucnfeatures) return mse(cdstudent, cdteacher) optimizeparams(ucn.parameters(), lossfn, lr, steps) return ucn def renderstylized(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, hashgrid, lightingmlp, palettemlp, P, ucn, regionmask, M=128): points, depths = samplepointsalongray(rayo, rayd, densitymlp, M=M) geofeatures = densitymlp(points, hashgrid) viewdirsh = encodesphericalharmonics(rayd, degree=3) cs = lightingmlp(geofeatures, viewdirsh) palettefeatures = palettemlp(points, hashgrid) Ip = intensity(palettefeatures) wp = softmax(paletteweights(palettefeatures), dim=-1) dp = coloroffsets(palettefeatures) cdpcn = Ip sum(wp[i] (P[i] + dp[i]) for i in range(len(P))) ucnfeatures = ucn(points, hashgrid) cducn = ucnoutput(ucnfeatures) cd = where(regionmask, cducn, cdpcn) c = cs + cd return rendervolume(rayo, rayd, lambda x: densitymlp(x, hashgrid), lambda x, d: c) Parameters: \lambda\delta = 0.1: Regularization strength for color offsets. Initial Transfer Function (TF): Defines opacity ranges. Regions with opacity equal to zero in the initial TF cannot be represented by NeRF and thus cannot undergo PSE or NPSE. Palette Refinement Threshold: Hue distance threshold in HSB space for removing similar colors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Opacity: If the initial TF sets opacity to zero for certain regions, NeRF cannot represent these values, and PSE/NPSE cannot be applied to them. Similar Colors: If colors among different regions in the input DVR scene are similar, palette refinement may not separate them correctly. Users must manually adjust the number of palette colors and their RGB values. Lighting Direction: Lighting direction cannot be modified because no normal information is available, although lighting intensity can be adjusted. NPSE Consistency: Discarding view direction in UCN is necessary for cross-view consistency but requires careful initialization via PSE color transfer to avoid inaccurate style matching. Time Complexity: Training is slower than ARF but faster than SNeRF. The process involves three stages: Base NeRF, PCN, and UCN (KD). NPSE optimization on a single camera view requires rendering different regions independently, slowing the stylization process. Memory Complexity: Uses Instant-NGP hash-grid encoding, which is memory efficient compared to dense voxel grids. Additional memory is required for PCN and UCN parameters. Measured Performance: Inference time on combustion dataset is 564 ms. Training time on combustion dataset is 1.2 h. Training time on vortex dataset is 29.7 m. Inference time on vortex dataset is 373 ms. StyleRF-VolVis achieves the best short- and long-range cross-view consistency (MSE and LPIPS) compared to AdaIN, ReReVST, ARF, and SNeRF. Strengths: Supports both PSE and NPSE in a single framework. Preserves view-dependent lighting. Allows explicit assignment of different styles to different regions. Achieves better cross-view consistency than image-based methods. Limitations: Slower training than ARF. Interactive PSE is supported but interactive NPSE is not. Cannot modify lighting direction. Sensitive to similar colors in input. When to use: When high-quality, cross-view consistent stylization of DVR scenes is required, especially when mixing PSE and NPSE or applying different styles to different regions. When not to use: When real-time interactive NPSE is required, or when lighting direction modification is needed. StyleRF-VolVis is the first work in VolVis that targets style transfer in the NeRF space. It builds on NeRF representation and Instant-NGP architecture. It adapts NeRF's palette-based recoloring strategy and uses Knowledge Distillation (KD) to transfer color knowledge. It differs from prior works like ARF and SNeRF by supporting both photorealistic and non-photorealistic editing in a single framework and preserving view-dependent lighting. name: Non-Photorealistic Style Editing
body: Non-Photorealistic Style Editing (NPSE) is a style transfer process for volume rendering that assigns specific styles to distinct regions of a scene using an unrestricted color network and Nearest Neighbor Feature Matching (NNFM) loss. Unlike SNeRF which assigns one style to the whole scene, NPSE allows explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions. Unlike ARF and SNeRF which discard view directions to ensure consistency, NPSE removes view direction input only in the Unrestricted Color Network (UCN) optimization to preserve lighting while ensuring consistency. Inputs: A base NeRF model (with frozen density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and pre-trained color network), one or multiple reference images S = \{S1, S2, \dots, S{NP}\} representing desired styles for NP regions, and camera views. Outputs: A stylized volume representation defined by the optimized Unrestricted Color Network cu(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Base NeRF: Frozen density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}). Unrestricted Color Network (UCN): Optimizable color network cu(\mathbf{x}) that outputs diffuse colors. Palette Weights: \omegai(\mathbf{x}) for each style region i \in \{1, \dots, NP\}. Feature Extractor: Pre-trained VGG-16 model \phi, specifically using the conv3 block. Steps: 1. Region Segmentation: If the number of reference images is less than NP or for local patterns, segment reference images into localized style regions using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with optional point prompts. 2. Network Construction: Construct a new Radiance Field (RF) using the optimizable unrestricted color cu(\mathbf{x}) and the frozen density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) from the base NeRF. 3. Rendering: Compute NP rendering images R = \{R1, R2, \dots, R{NP}\} for each camera view. For a sample point \mathbf{x}, it contributes to rendering Ri only if its palette weight \omegai(\mathbf{x}) is greater than other palette weights. 4. Background Handling: Extract the luminance value from each style Si to use as the background color for the corresponding rendering Ri to handle transparency artifacts. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the stylization loss using NNFM loss between renderings R and styles S via VGG-16 features. Omit content loss between original and stylized images due to suboptimal outcomes. 6. Optimization: Update cu(\mathbf{x}) parameters using the computed loss. Formulas: The NNFM loss is formulated as: L{NNFM}(R, S) = \frac{1}{NF NP} \sum{i=1}^{NP} \sum{fj \in \phi(Ri)} \min{fk \in \phi(Si)} d(fj, fk) where: \phi(Ri) and \phi(Si) are the feature vectors extracted from the VGG-16 model \phi for rendering Ri and style Si respectively. NF is the number of feature vectors for \phi(Ri). NP is the number of style regions. d is the cosine distance between feature vectors fj and fk. Parameters: VGG-16 Block: conv3. Iterations: 210. Views per Iteration: One of 42 uniformly sampled camera views. Learning Rate: Fixed at 0.01, following the ARF setting (Adam optimizer with \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, but learning rate does not decay during NPSE). Batch Size: 4,096 rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim import torchvision.models as models def cosinedistance(u, v): return 1.0 - (torch.dot(u, v) / (torch.norm(u) torch.norm(v))) def extractluminance(image): return 0.299 image[..., 0] + 0.587 image[..., 1] + 0.114 image[..., 2] def setbackground(rendered, bgcolor): alpha = rendered[..., 3:4] return rendered[...,:3] alpha + bgcolor (1.0 - alpha) def rendervolume(sigma, cu, camera, styleindex, numsamples=128): # Standard differentiable volume rendering (DVR) routine # Returns RGBA image for the given style region pass def getvgg16conv3(): vgg = models.vgg16(weights=models.VGG16Weights.DEFAULT) return nn.Sequential(list(vgg.features)[:15]) def sampleuniformviews(numviews): views = [] for i in range(numviews): theta = math.pi i / numviews phi = math.sqrt(numviews) math.pi i views.append(torch.eye(4)) return views def trainnpse(basenerf, referenceimages, numstyles, numviews=42, iterations=210): # 1. Segment reference images if necessary styleregions = [img for img in referenceimages] # SAM segmentation handled externally # 2. Initialize UCN ucn = nn.Parameter(basenerf.colornetwork.statedict().clone()) ucn.requiresgrad(True) # 3. Setup feature extractor vggconv3 = getvgg16conv3() vggconv3.eval() # 4. Setup optimizer (Fixed LR as per ARF setting) optimizer = optim.Adam([ucn], lr=0.01, betas=(0.9, 0.999)) # 5. Sample camera views uniformly cameraviews = sampleuniformviews(numviews) for iteration in range(iterations): optimizer.zerograd() # Select one view for this iteration viewidx = np.random.randint(0, len(cameraviews)) camera = cameraviews[viewidx] # 6. Render NP images for this view renderings = [] for i in range(numstyles): # Render using frozen sigma(x) and optimizable cu(x) # Apply palette weight logic: only contribute if omegai(x) > others renderingi = rendervolume(basenerf.sigma, ucn, camera, i) renderings.append(renderingi) # 7. Set background colors based on luminance of styles for i in range(numstyles): bgcolor = extractluminance(referenceimages[i]) renderings[i] = setbackground(renderings[i], bgcolor) # 8. Compute NNFM Loss loss = 0.0 nf = 0 for i in range(numstyles): featr = vggconv3(renderings[i]) feats = vggconv3(referenceimages[i]) nf = featr.shape[0] for j in range(nf): mindist = float('inf') for k in range(feats.shape[0]): dist = cosinedistance(featr[j], feats[k]) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist loss += mindist loss = loss / (numstyles nf) # 9. Backpropagate loss.backward() optimizer.step() return ucn Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency Artifacts: Using incorrect background colors (e.g., black or white) leads to unsatisfactory stylization. Extracting luminance from the style image is required. Content Loss: Including content loss between original and stylized images yields suboptimal outcomes and should be omitted. Memory: Deferred backpropagation is employed to update UCN parameters for the entire image under limited GPU memory. A workflow to indirectly control NPSE stylization by iteratively refining reference image selections using negative point prompts and UCN retraining. If the initial style selection includes undesired styles, apply negative point prompts for SAM to the reference image to exclude them, then retrain the UCN to achieve the desired stylization. This is necessary because NPSE does not support direct control over the stylization process once initiated. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: For the "vortex" dataset, NPSE takes 29.7 minutes. For the "combustion" dataset, it takes 1.2 hours. This is faster than SNeRF (3.6 h and 3.8 h respectively) but slower than ARF (14.6 m and 20.1 m respectively). Inference Time: For the "vortex" dataset, NPSE takes 373 ms. For the "combustion" dataset, it takes 564 ms. This is slower than ARF (204 ms and 210 ms) and SNeRF (173 ms and 195 ms). Memory: Uses deferred backpropagation to handle limited GPU memory. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Allows explicit assignment of different styles to different DVR regions. Preserves view-dependent lighting by removing view direction input only in UCN optimization, unlike ARF and SNeRF which discard view directions entirely. Offers higher flexibility and robustness compared to conventional NPR methods by transferring arbitrary styles within a unified framework. Limitations: Does not support direct control over the stylization process; requires iterative refinement via SAM prompts. Relies on NNFM loss which focuses on negligible local style, mitigated by color transfer to align region color with overall style color. When to Use: Use when distinct styles are needed for different regions of a volume scene and view-dependent lighting preservation is important. Originated in the paper "StyleRF-VolVis: Style Transfer of Neural Radiance Fields for Expressive Volume Visualization". It is part of the StyleRF-VolVis framework for expressive volume visualization. name: StyleNeRF Architecture Configuration
head: StyleNeRF hyperparameters
body: StyleNeRF extends the original Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture by integrating a style-based generator to handle illumination changes and synthesize high-resolution images. It reuses the architecture and default parameters of StyleGAN2 for its mapping network and discriminator. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters, 3D coordinates, and a latent style vector. Outputs: Volume density (\sigma) and view-dependent color (c). Data Structures and Parameters: Mapping network: 8 fully connected layers. Latent and style dimensions: 512. Foreground field MLP hidden units: 256. Background field MLP hidden units: 128. Fourier feature dimension: L=10. Feature sizes after 2D aggregation: Decrease from 512 (for 32×32) to 32 (for 1024×1024). Learning rate: The mapping network uses a learning rate 100\times lower than the default. Batch size: 64. Training iterations: 25,000 images. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configurestylenrf(): """ Returns the architecture configuration for StyleNeRF based on StyleGAN2 defaults. """ config = { "mappingnetworklayers": 8, "latentdim": 512, "styledim": 512, "foregroundmlphiddenunits": 256, "backgroundmlphiddenunits": 128, "fourierfeaturedim": 10, "featuresizesafter2daggregation": { 32: 512, 64: 256, 128: 128, 256: 64, 512: 32, 1024: 32 }, "mappingnetworklrmultiplier": 0.01, "batchsize": 64, "totaltrainingimages": 25000 } return config Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. An extension of the original NeRF network architecture that adds a low-dimensional appearance code to handle illumination changes. The appearance code is 16-dimensional, added to the second last layer of the NeRF network F\phi, and is individually stored and optimized for every frame. NeuralBody baselines use 128-dimensional codes, whereas A-NeRF uses 16-dimensional codes to help learning global effects without deteriorating the benefits of relative encoding. Time complexity: Training takes approximately three days on 8 Tesla V100 GPUs for 25,000 images with a batch size of 64. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles illumination changes effectively and generates high-resolution images up to 1024×1024. StyleNeRF was proposed in "StyleNeRF: A Style-based 3D-Aware Generator for High-resolution Image Synthesis". It builds on the original NeRF architecture and concurrent works on handling illumination changes. The architecture reuses parameters from StyleGAN2. name: StyleNeRF Architecture
head: Style-based 3D-Aware Generator
body: StyleNeRF is a generative radiance field model that synthesizes high-resolution, 3D-consistent images by integrating learned 3D features along camera rays. It differs from standard NeRF by replacing the deterministic coordinate-based MLP with a style-based synthesis network conditioned on latent codes, enabling high-fidelity appearance control similar to StyleGAN2. Unlike CoRF, which modifies the generator for motion control and removes upsampling blocks, StyleNeRF relies on fixed-resolution ray sampling and standard upsampling within the synthesis backbone. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera pose (origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}), latent code \mathbf{z} sampled from a standard Gaussian distribution, and optionally a motion representation \mathbf{m} (though the baseline StyleNeRF does not condition on \mathbf{m}, CoRF does). Outputs: An RGB image \mathbf{I}0 of fixed resolution 32^2 during training, upsampled to 256^2 for evaluation. Data Structures Mapping Network: Processes latent codes \mathbf{z} into style vectors. The output vectors are broadcast to the synthesis networks. Synthesis Network Backbone: Based on NeRF++. Foreground NeRF: Occupies a unit sphere. Uses an MLP to predict density \sigma. Background NeRF: Uses inverted sphere parameterization for unbounded backgrounds. Uses an MLP with fewer parameters than the foreground to predict density. Shared MLP: Predicts color (and features) for both foreground and background. Style-Conditioned Block: Consists of an affine transformation layer and a 1 \times 1 Convolution layer. Rendering Formula The generator G renders an image by casting rays from camera origin \mathbf{o} through image plane pixels. For a ray \mathbf{r}(t), the aggregated feature \mathbf{F}r is computed by integrating features \mathbf{F} along the ray between near plane tn and far plane tf: \mathbf{F}r = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t)\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t))\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{z})dt where the accumulated transmittance T(t) is: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s), \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{z})ds\right) Here, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, \sigma is the density, and \mathbf{F} is the feature vector. Note: In the baseline StyleNeRF, \mathbf{m} is not used; CoRF embeds \mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^{50} via a ReLU mapping network and injects it via weight modulation. Algorithm Steps 1. Latent Processing: Sample latent code \mathbf{z} from standard Gaussian. Pass \mathbf{z} through the Mapping Network to generate style vectors. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the target image, define a ray \mathbf{r}(t) from camera origin \mathbf{o} through the pixel center with direction \mathbf{d}. 3. Sampling: Sample points along the ray between tn and tf. 4. Feature Query: For each sample point \mathbf{r}(t), query the Synthesis Network. The network uses the style vectors from the Mapping Network. Inside the Style-Conditioned Blocks, Conv weights are modulated with the affine-transformed styles and demodulated for computation. Leaky ReLU is used as the non-linear activation. The network outputs density \sigma and feature \mathbf{F} (and color). 5. Integration: Compute transmittance T(t) and integrate \sigma \mathbf{F} along the ray to obtain \mathbf{F}r. 6. Color Output: Convert \mathbf{F}r to RGB color. 7. Upsampling: The baseline StyleNeRF uses upsampling blocks in the synthesis network to increase resolution. (Note: CoRF omits these and increases resolution by sampling more rays). Parameters Input Resolution: Fixed at 32^2 for all experiments. Motion Representation: \mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^{50} (used in CoRF, not baseline StyleNeRF). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Motion Conditioning: The baseline StyleNeRF does not condition on motion. If motion control is required, the architecture must be modified to embed motion into a latent space and inject it via weight modulation, as done in CoRF. Resolution Scaling: StyleNeRF uses upsampling blocks. CoRF avoids these, increasing resolution by sampling more rays. Implementers must choose the appropriate strategy based on the variant. 3D Consistency: Improper choice of 3D representation (e.g., using 3x3 convolutions incorrectly) can lead to 3D inconsistent artifacts where shape and appearance change constantly when the camera moves. Time Complexity: Determined by the number of samples per ray and the depth of the MLPs in the Synthesis Network. The use of NeRF++ adds complexity for background handling. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of parameters in the foreground and background MLPs. The background network has fewer parameters than the foreground. Strengths: Achieves high quality and 3D consistency compared to baselines like HoloGAN, GARF, and \pi-GAN. Outperforms GIRAFFE in 3D consistency. Limitations: Training can be unstable on small datasets (e.g., FF-Archive), requiring fine-tuning from pretrained models (e.g., FFHQ). When to use: When high-resolution, 3D-consistent, stylized image synthesis is required. When not to use: When motion control is needed without architectural modification (use CoRF instead) or when computational resources for upsampling blocks are limited. StyleNeRF was introduced as a style-based 3D-aware generator for high-resolution image synthesis. It builds on the success of StyleGAN2 by applying its style-based synthesis to radiance fields. The architecture uses NeRF++ to handle unbounded backgrounds, combining a foreground NeRF in a unit sphere with a background NeRF using inverted sphere parameterization. It adopts a non-saturating GAN objective with R1 regularization and a NeRF path regularization to enforce 3D consistency. name: Dual-Branch Hash Encoder NeRF for Stylization
head: Instant Photorealistic Neural Radiance Fields Stylization method, Two-branch Instant-NGP, Instant Neural Radiance Fields Stylization, Instant-NGP Stylization, InstantNeRF-Stylization
body: A method for multi-view image stylization of 3D scenes that uses a hash table-based position encoder (Instant-NGP) split into content and style sub-branches, applying Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN) to position encoding features during inference to transfer style from a target (image or scene set) to novel views without retraining. It solves the problem of transferring style from a target scene/image to a content scene while preserving geometry, using an efficient hash encoder instead of a standard MLP for position encoding. Unlike previous works where style targets are only images, this method extends the style target to 3D scene image sets. Compared to using two independent Instant-NGP networks, the dual-branch approach with shared MLP RGB preserves geometry consistency better and avoids noise. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images of a content 3D scene; a style target, which is either a single style image or a set of images of a style 3D scene. Outputs: Stylized novel view images of the content scene, preserving its geometry but adopting the appearance of the style target. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid (V): A 3D grid representing the spatial domain for style representation. Layout: V \in \mathbb{R}^{NV \times NV \times NV}. NV: Voxel resolution. Typical values: 32, 64, 128, 256. Default: 128. 2. Content Hash Encoder: A hash-based position encoder mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors for the content scene. 3. Style Hash Encoder: A hash-based position encoder mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors for the style scene. 4. Shared Direction Encoder: A spherical encoder mapping view directions to feature vectors. 5. Shared MLPRGB: A multilayer perceptron taking concatenated features from position encoders and the direction encoder to output color (C) and density (\sigma). 6. MLPDensity: A separate MLP (part of the content branch architecture) that outputs density based on content position encoder features. Numbered Steps: Training Process: 1. Initialize two position encoder branches (Content Hash Encoder, Style Hash Encoder) and one shared direction encoder (Spherical Encoder). 2. For each training step, sample rays for both the content target and the style target. If the style target is a single image, treat it as a 3D scene by placing 3D colored voxels representing the 2D image pixels in the center of the 3D space. If the style target is an image set, treat it as a normal 3D scene. 3. Encode 3D coordinates (x, y, z) using both the Content Hash Encoder and the Style Hash Encoder to obtain content features (fc) and style features (fs). 4. Encode view direction (d) using the shared Direction Encoder. 5. Concatenate features and pass through the shared MLPRGB to predict color and density for both targets. 6. Compute loss using Huber loss for both content and style targets. Huber Loss Formula: L = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} rel^2, & \text{for } rel \le \delta \\ \delta(rel - \frac{1}{2}\delta), & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where rel = |C{predict} - C{target}|, C{predict} is the rendered color, C{target} is the target color, and \delta is a hyperparameter. 7. Optimize the Content Position Encoder based on the content target loss. 8. Optimize the Style Position Encoder based on the style target loss. 9. Optimize the Shared MLPRGB based on the combined content and style target losses. Inference (AdaIN Stylization): 1. Calculate content position encoder features (fc(x, y, z)) using voxel grid positions as input. 2. Calculate style position encoder features (fs(x, y, z)) using the same voxel grid positions. 3. Compute the mean (F\muc, F\mus) and standard deviation (F\sigmac, F\sigmas) of the content and style voxel grid features respectively. 4. Apply AdaIN transformation to the content features using the style statistics as reference: AdaIN(f(x, y, z)) = F\sigmas \left( \frac{f(x, y, z) - F\muc}{F\sigmac} \right) + F\mus where f(x, y, z) is the content voxel grid feature, F\muc, F\sigmac are the mean and std of content voxel grid features, and F\mus, F\sigmas are the mean and std of style voxel grid features. 5. Use the adjusted (stylized) features for color prediction via the shared MLPRGB. 6. Use the unadjusted (content) features for density prediction via the content MLPDensity to preserve geometry consistency. 7. (Optional) Control the degree of stylization using a style weight \alpha \in [0, 1]: AdaINc(f(x, y, z)) = (1-\alpha)f(x, y, z) + \alpha AdaIN(f(x, y, z)) where \alpha=0 is no style and \alpha=1 is full style. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def huberloss(predicted, target, delta=0.01): """Computes Huber loss between predicted and target colors.""" rel = np.abs(predicted - target) return np.mean(np.where(rel <= delta, 0.5 rel2, delta (rel - 0.5 delta))) def adaintransform(contentfeat, cmean, cstd, smean, sstd): """Applies AdaIN transformation using content and style statistics.""" return sstd ((contentfeat - cmean) / cstd) + smean def traindualbranchnerf(contentimages, styleimagesorimage, numsteps, lr): # Initialize content and style hash encoders, shared direction encoder, shared MLPRGB, and content MLPDensity contentencoder = HashEncoder() # Standard Instant-NGP hash grid feature lookup styleencoder = HashEncoder() direncoder = SphericalEncoder() # Standard spherical harmonic encoding mlprgb = MLPRGB() # Standard multilayer perceptron for color mlpdensity = MLPDensity() # Standard multilayer perceptron for density # If style target is a single image, place 3D colored voxels in the center of 3D space if issingleimage(styleimagesorimage): stylevoxels = create3dcoloredvoxels(styleimagesorimage, center=True) else: stylevoxels = styleimagesorimage # Treat as normal 3D scene image set for step in range(numsteps): # Sample rays for both content and style targets contentrays = samplerays(contentimages) stylerays = samplerays(stylevoxels) # Encode 3D coordinates using both position encoder branches contentposfeat = contentencoder(contentrays.positions) styleposfeat = styleencoder(stylerays.positions) # Encode view direction using shared direction encoder dirfeat = direncoder(contentrays.directions) # Concatenate features and pass through shared MLPRGB to predict color and density contentcolor = mlprgb(np.concatenate([contentposfeat, dirfeat], axis=1)) stylecolor = mlprgb(np.concatenate([styleposfeat, dirfeat], axis=1)) # Compute Huber loss for both targets contentloss = huberloss(contentcolor, contentrays.targetcolors) styleloss = huberloss(stylecolor, stylerays.targetcolors) # Optimize content position encoder based on content target loss # Optimize style position encoder based on style target loss # Optimize shared MLPRGB based on combined content and style target losses # Optimize content MLPDensity based on content loss optimizestep([contentencoder, styleencoder, mlprgb, mlpdensity], contentloss, styleloss, lr) def inferstylizedview(contentencoder, styleencoder, direncoder, mlprgb, mlpdensity, contentvoxelgrid, stylevoxelgrid, querypositions, querydirections, alpha=1.0): # Calculate content position encoder features contentposfeat = contentencoder(querypositions) # Calculate style position encoder features styleposfeat = styleencoder(querypositions) # Compute mean and standard deviation of content and style voxel grid features cmean, cstd = np.mean(contentposfeat), np.std(contentposfeat) smean, sstd = np.mean(styleposfeat), np.std(styleposfeat) # Apply AdaIN transformation to content features using style statistics stylizedfeat = adaintransform(contentposfeat, cmean, cstd, smean, sstd) # Content-style trade-off control blendedfeat = (1 - alpha) contentposfeat + alpha stylizedfeat # Encode direction dirfeat = direncoder(querydirections) # Use adjusted features for color prediction via shared MLPRGB color = mlprgb(np.concatenate([blendedfeat, dirfeat], axis=1)) # Use unadjusted content features for density prediction via content MLPDensity density = mlpdensity(contentposfeat) return color, density Time Complexity: Training is extremely fast, completing in less than 10 minutes on modern GPU hardware (e.g., Nvidia 3080). Memory Complexity: Increases storage compared to a single scene NeRF due to the two position encoder branches, but the hash encoder architecture keeps it efficient. Strengths: Fast training; preserves geometry consistency better than independent networks; handles both single image and 3D scene image set style targets; no retraining required for inference. Limitations: Does not handle stylization on illumination and reflection because AdaIN is only executed on position encoder features, leaving direction encoder features unchanged. Details of results vary with random encoding parameters, requiring fixed MLP weights for stable results across different scene pairs. When to use: When fast stylization of 3D scenes is required, especially when the style target is a 3D scene image set rather than just a single image. When not to use: When stylization of lighting/reflection effects is critical, or when consistent random initialization is required without fixing MLP weights. Originated in the paper "Instant Photorealistic Neural Radiance Fields Stylization". It builds on Instant-NGP Parent: [Instant Neural Graphics Primitives] and NeRF [Parent: Neural Radiance Fields]. It extends previous NeRF stylization methods (like SNeRF) by leveraging the hash encoder for speed and extending style targets to 3D scene image sets. name: Image Enhancement and Restoration Methods
body: Image Enhancement and Restoration Methods modify the NeRF training pipeline to handle input image defects such as motion blur, defocus, or transient occlusions (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles), enabling the reconstruction of sharp, static scene representations from uncontrolled "in-the-wild" data. Unlike sibling methods that primarily alter network topology or input space encoding, these methods explicitly model the degradation process or the transient elements as part of the optimization, separating the static scene geometry and appearance from the artifacts. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as surface normals \mathbf{n}, semantic logits \mathbf{s}, uncertainty variance \nu, or blend weights \Delta w. 4. Representation Basis: Substituting the coordinate-based implicit function with explicit structures like voxel grids, hash tables, Gaussian primitives, or planar surfaces, which change how features are stored and interpolated. DeblurNeRF reconstructs a sharp NeRF from blurry inputs by modeling blur via a Deformable Sparse Kernel (DSK) that approximates spatially varying blur as a weighted sum of deformed rays. It differs from IE-NeRF and Sharp-NeRF by using an MLP-based DSK to predict ray origin translations and kernel deformations, allowing joint optimization of the NeRF and blur parameters. Choose this method when dealing with motion blur or defocus where the point spread function varies spatially and you require a differentiable blur simulation module during training. IE-NeRF separates static scene rendering from transient occlusions using an image-dependent 2D transient mask and a pre-trained inpainting module. Unlike DeblurNeRF which addresses motion blur, or Sharp-NeRF which focuses on sharpness, IE-NeRF specifically targets transient object removal in uncontrolled environments. It differs from NeRF-W by using a single MLP to predict both static properties and a 2D transient mask, rather than a 3D transient field or dual NeRF pipelines. Choose this method when the input dataset contains dynamic elements like pedestrians or vehicles that must be removed to recover the static scene. Sharp-NeRF is a grid-based framework that renders clean images from blurry inputs by modeling spatially varying blur using discrete learnable kernels and a sharpness prior. Unlike sibling methods that rely on MLPs to generate blur kernels or require extensive training times, Sharp-NeRF achieves faster training by using a decomposed-grid representation and quantized sharpness levels. Choose this method when computational efficiency is critical and the blur is primarily due to defocus or camera shake that can be quantized into a small set of discrete kernels. SPIn-NeRF is a 3D inpainting method that leverages LaMa for color and depth inpainting, replacing pixel loss with perceptual loss for visual coherence and using depth inpainting to supervise 3D geometry. A key parameter is the use of perceptual loss instead of pixel loss to enhance visual quality. A pitfall is that it struggles in tasks where 2D inpainting results are perceptually inconsistent. The problem of reconstructing high-quality radiance fields from low-quality or uncontrolled input images has been addressed through various inpainting and deblurring techniques. Early approaches like NeRF-In [132] used simple 2D inpainting networks (e.g., MST) to guide pixel reconstruction. SPIn-NeRF [15] improved upon this by leveraging the LaMa inpainting model [131] for both color and depth, replacing pixel loss with perceptual loss to achieve more visually coherent results and using depth inpainting to supervise 3D geometry. However, SPIn-NeRF struggles when 2D inpainting results are perceptually inconsistent. Other methods like Removing-NeRF [133] utilize posed RGB-D images with 2D masks and optimize NeRF with LaMa-inpainted frames, employing confidence-based view selection to exclude inconsistent views. Reference-guided inpainting [134] performs 2D inpainting on a single reference image and uses monocular depth estimation and a bilateral solver to ensure view-dependent consistency.
