name: DeblurNeRF
head: Deblur-NeRF, Deblur-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields from Blurry Images
body: DeblurNeRF is a framework that reconstructs a sharp Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) from blurry input images by explicitly modeling the blurring process via an analysis-by-synthesis approach. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes sharp inputs, DeblurNeRF jointly optimizes the NeRF parameters and a Deformable Sparse Kernel (DSK) module to simulate how a sharp scene would appear blurry, allowing the network to learn the underlying sharp geometry and appearance. It sets itself apart from siblings like IE-NeRF and Sharp-NeRF by introducing a learnable, spatially-varying blur kernel parameterized by an MLP, rather than relying on fixed priors or post-processing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of blurry multi-view images B. Camera poses (origin o, direction d) are assumed known or estimated (e.g., via COLMAP). Outputs: A sharp NeRF representation F\Theta and optimized DSK parameters \Phi. At inference, the output is sharp novel views rendered from F\Theta without the DSK module. Data Structures: 1. NeRF (F\Theta): An MLP mapping positional encoded 3D position \mathbf{x} and 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d} to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Input: \gammaL(\mathbf{x}), \gammaL(\mathbf{d}). Output: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma). 2. Deformable Sparse Kernel (DSK) Module (G\Phi): An MLP parameterized by \Phi that predicts blur kernel deformations and weights for each pixel. Structure: 4 fully-connected hidden layers, each with 64 channels and ReLU activations. Includes a shortcut connection from the first layer to the last layer. Inputs: Pixel coordinate \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Canonical kernel location \mathbf{q}^0 \in \mathbb{R}^2 (fixed for a given pixel). View embedding \mathbf{l} \in \mathbb{R}^{32} (learned per view). Outputs: For each of the N sparse locations, a tuple (\Delta \mathbf{o}q, \Delta \mathbf{v}T, wq). \Delta \mathbf{o}q \in \mathbb{R}^3: Ray origin translation. \Delta \mathbf{v}T \in \mathbb{R}^2: Direction deformation (applied to pixel coordinates to derive new direction). wq \in \mathbb{R}: Composition weight. 3. Canonical Kernel: A set of N fixed 2D locations N^0(\mathbf{p}) = \{\mathbf{q}^0i\}{i=0}^{N-1} distributed around pixel \mathbf{p}. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation (Standard NeRF): For a pixel \mathbf{p}, generate a primary ray \mathbf{r}p(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}p from camera origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}p. 2. Coarse Sampling: Divide the ray interval [tn, tf] into Ns intervals (default 64) using stratified sampling to generate coarse samples \mathbf{r}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}p. 3. Coarse Rendering: Query F\Theta at each sample to get (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai). Compute transmittance Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) and color \hat{\mathbf{C}}c = \sum{i=1}^{Ns} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i, where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 4. Hierarchical Sampling: Compute normalized weights \hat{w}i = wi / \sumj wj where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)). Use \hat{w}i as a PDF to sample Ns additional fine samples. 5. Fine Rendering: Query F\Theta at fine samples and compute fine color \hat{\mathbf{C}}f using the same volume rendering equation. 6. DSK Prediction: For the target pixel \mathbf{p}, iterate over each canonical location \mathbf{q}^0 \in N^0(\mathbf{p}). Input (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}^0, \mathbf{l}) into G\Phi to predict (\Delta \mathbf{o}q, \Delta \mathbf{v}T, wq). 7. Ray Deformation: Compute the deformed kernel location \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}^0 + \Delta \mathbf{v}T (Note: Source uses \Delta \mathbf{q} for location deformation, Source uses \Delta \mathbf{v}T for direction/coordinate transformation. We follow 's notation for location: \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}^0 + \Delta \mathbf{q}). Derive the new direction \mathbf{d}q from the deformed location \mathbf{q} relative to the camera center (or as defined by the transformation). Generate the optimized ray \mathbf{r}q(t) = (\mathbf{o} + \Delta \mathbf{o}q) + t \mathbf{d}q. 8. Blurred Color Synthesis: Render each deformed ray \mathbf{r}q using F\Theta to obtain color \mathbf{c}^0q. Compute the final blurry pixel color \hat{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{p} by blending the rendered colors with weights wq, applying gamma correction to handle non-linear Camera Response Function (CRF): \hat{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{p} = \left( \sum{q \in N(\mathbf{p})} wq \mathbf{c}^0q \right)^{1/2.2} where \sum{q \in N(\mathbf{p})} wq = 1. 9. Loss Computation: Compute the reconstruction loss against the ground truth blurry image \mathbf{b}^{gt}\mathbf{p} and the alignment loss: L{reconstruct} = \| \hat{\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{b}^{gt}\mathbf{p} \|2^2 L{align} = \| \mathbf{q}^0 - \mathbf{p} \|2^2 + \lambdao \| \Delta \mathbf{o}{q^0} \|2^2 where \mathbf{q}^0 is a fixed element in N(\mathbf{p}) (typically the center). Total Loss: L = L{reconstruct} + \lambdaa L{align}. 10. Optimization: Jointly update F\Theta and G\Phi using Adam optimizer. 11. Inference: Render rays from the trained F\Theta directly without DSK deformation to produce sharp novel views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class DeblurNeRF: def init(self, nerfmodel, dskmlp, numkernelpoints=5, viewembeddingdim=32): self.nerf = nerfmodel self.dsk = dskmlp self.N = numkernelpoints self.viewembeddingdim = viewembeddingdim self.lambdao = 10.0 self.lambdaa = 0.1 self.epsilon = 0.1 # Initialize DSK outputs to be small to keep rays close to original # This is a heuristic initialization strategy mentioned in # In practice, weights are initialized to be uniform or small, # and deformations are scaled by epsilon. def positionalencoding(self, x, L=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding """ scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(L)], dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) xb = torch.reshape((x scales[:, None]), (len(x), -1)) freqbands = torch.cat([torch.sin(xb), torch.cos(xb)], dim=-1) return freqbands def renderray(self, rayorigins, raydirections, numsamples=128): """Render a single ray using the NeRF """ # Stratified sampling tn, tf = 0.1, 100.0 # Typical bounds, not given in sources, assumed standard tvals = torch.linspace(tn, tf, numsamples) tvals = tvals + torch.randlike(tvals) (tf - tn) / numsamples points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) # Query NeRF # Assuming nerfmodel takes (x, d) and returns (c, sigma) # x and d need positional encoding xenc = self.positionalencoding(points.view(-1, 3)).view(points.shape + (-1,)) denc = self.positionalencoding(raydirections).view(raydirections.shape + (-1,)) # Flatten for MLP xflat = xenc.view(-1, xenc.shape[-1]) dflat = denc.view(-1, denc.shape[-1]) csigma = self.nerf(xflat, dflat) c = csigma[:,:3].view(points.shape[:-1] + (3,)) sigma = csigma[:, 3:].view(points.shape[:-1]) # Volume Rendering deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltainf = 1e10 deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], dim=-1) alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[...,:1]), 1 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=-1), dim=-1)[...,:-1] weights = alpha transmittance color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=-2) return color def forward(self, pixelcoords, rayorigins, raydirections, viewembedding, gtimage): """ pixelcoords: (B, 2) rayorigins: (B, 3) raydirections: (B, 3) viewembedding: (B, 32) gtimage: (B, 3) """ B = pixelcoords.shape[0] # 1. Generate Canonical Kernel Locations # N^0(p) are fixed relative to p. # For simplicity, assume they are offsets. In implementation, these are broadcasted. # Let's assume canonicaloffsets is (N, 2) canonicaloffsets = torch.zeros(self.N, 2, device=pixelcoords.device) # In reality, these would be spread out, e.g., grid around p. # Source says "sparsely distributed around p". q0 = pixelcoords.unsqueeze(1) + canonicaloffsets # (B, N, 2) # 2. DSK Prediction # Inputs: p (B, 2), q0 (B, N, 2), l (B, 32) # Reshape for MLP: (BN, 2+2+32) pinput = pixelcoords.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.N, -1).reshape(-1, 2) q0input = q0.reshape(-1, 2) linput = viewembedding.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.N, -1).reshape(-1, self.viewembeddingdim) dskinput = torch.cat([pinput, q0input, linput], dim=-1) # MLP Forward dskoutput = self.dsk(dskinput) # (BN, 3 + 2 + 1) = (BN, 6) # Parse outputs deltao = dskoutput[:,:3].reshape(B, self.N, 3) deltavT = dskoutput[:, 3:5].reshape(B, self.N, 2) # Direction/Location deformation weights = dskoutput[:, 5:].reshape(B, self.N, 1) # Initialize with small gain epsilon deltao = deltao self.epsilon deltavT = deltavT self.epsilon # Weights need to sum to 1. Source says "roughly the same weights at beginning". # We normalize here. weights = F.softmax(weights, dim=1) # 3. Deform Rays # New locations q = q0 + deltavT (using deltavT as location shift per notation q=q0+Delta q) # Note: calls deltavT direction transform. calls deltaq location transform. # We follow logic: q is location on image plane. q = q0 + deltavT # (B, N, 2) # New directions dq derived from q. # If q is a pixel coordinate, direction is from camera center to q. # This requires camera intrinsics. Assuming standard pinhole: # dq = normalize(cameracenter -> pixelatq) # For implementation simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume raydirections # can be recomputed or passed. Here we approximate direction change. # A robust implementation would use camera matrix K. # dq = K^{-1} [q, 1] # New origins oq = o + deltao oq = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + deltao # (B, N, 3) # 4. Render Deformed Rays # We need dq. Let's assume a helper to get direction from pixel coord. # dq = getdirectionfrompixel(q, cameraintrinsics) # For this pseudocode, we assume raydirections are updated or passed. # Let's assume we have a function getrayfrompixel dq = self.getraydirectionsfrompixelcoords(q, rayorigins) # (B, N, 3) # Flatten for rendering oqflat = oq.reshape(-1, 3) dqflat = dq.reshape(-1, 3) colorsq = self.renderray(oqflat, dqflat) # (BN, 3) colorsq = colorsq.reshape(B, self.N, 3) # 5. Blend # Gamma correction: (sum w c)^(1/2.2) blended = torch.sum(weights colorsq, dim=1) # (B, 3) blurredpred = torch.pow(blended, 1/2.2) # 6. Loss Lrecon = torch.mean((blurredpred - gtimage)2) # Alignment Loss: q0 (center) should be close to p, and deltao for center should be small # Assume index 0 is the center Lalign = torch.mean((q0[:, 0,:] - pixelcoords)2) + \ self.lambdao torch.mean((deltao[:, 0,:])2) Ltotal = Lrecon + self.lambdaa Lalign return blurredpred, Ltotal, Lrecon, Lalign def getraydirectionsfrompixelcoords(self, pixelcoords, origins): """ Approximate direction calculation from pixel coordinates. Assumes origins are camera centers. In a real implementation, this uses camera intrinsics K. d = K^{-1} [x, y, 1] """ # Placeholder for actual camera matrix logic # For the sake of the article, we note that direction is derived from the deformed pixel location # relative to the camera center. # Since we don't have K in the class, we return a dummy direction or assume # the direction change is handled by the DSK's deltavT if interpreted as direction. # However, explicitly says q is location and d is derived. # We will return the original directions for now, noting this is a simplification. # A correct implementation would transform the ray direction based on the pixel shift. return origins.newzeroslike(origins) # Placeholder Parameters: N (Number of sparse locations): 5. Improves quality as N increases, but diminishing returns after 5. View Embedding Length: 32. MLP Hidden Layers: 4 layers, 64 channels each, ReLU activation. Learning Rate: Starts at 5 \times 10^{-4}, decays exponentially to 8 \times 10^{-5}. Batch Size: 1024 rays. Samples: 64 coarse, 64 fine. Alignment Loss Weight (\lambdao): 10. Reconstruction Loss Weight (\lambdaa): 0.1. Initialization Gain (\epsilon): 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-rigid Distortion: If all components (NeRF and DSK) are freely optimized, the NeRF may undergo non-rigid distortion to compensate for blur errors. This is mitigated by the alignment loss L{align}. Positional Encoding: Using positional encoding on the input pixel coordinate \mathbf{p} of the DSK MLP G\Phi was tested but found not to help, likely because the spatially-varying kernel changes gradually without high-frequency variation. 3D Inconsistency: Pixel-wise independent optimization of the blur kernel (as in DeblurNeRF) can incur inconsistency in 3D geometry and appearance compared to scene-wise shared transformations (like in DP-NeRF). Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive due to the joint optimization of the NeRF and the DSK module, requiring rendering multiple rays per pixel (N=5) during training. Inference is comparable to standard NeRF as the DSK is bypassed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF MLP and the DSK MLP. The DSK MLP is small (4 layers, 64 channels). Performance: On synthetic scenes, DeblurNeRF achieves higher PSNR/SSIM and lower LPIPS compared to ablations without gamma correction, alignment loss, or origin optimization. It handles both camera motion blur and defocus blur. Hardware: Tested on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. Scaling: The method scales with the number of kernel points N, but N=5 is sufficient for most cases. Strengths: Can recover sharp NeRF from blurry inputs without needing sharp reference images. Handles spatially-varying blur. Limitations: May suffer from 3D inconsistency due to pixel-wise independent blur modeling. Less effective for severe motion blur compared to physically grounded methods like BAD-NeRF. DeblurNeRF was introduced by Xiaoyu Li et al. in 2021/2022. It is the first method to recover a sharp NeRF from blurry input images using an analysis-by-synthesis approach. It builds on the standard NeRF architecture Parent and addresses the degradation of reconstruction quality caused by defocus or motion blur in real-world captures. It differs from DP-NeRF by using pixel-wise independent transformations (DSK) instead of scene-wise shared rigid transformations. name: IE-NeRF
head: IE-NeRF Pipeline, Image-dependent NeRF with transient mask inpainting, Inpainting Enhanced NeRF
body: IE-NeRF is a Neural Radiance Field variant designed to enhance novel view synthesis in uncontrolled, "in-the-wild" environments by separating static scene rendering from transient occlusions (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) using an image-dependent transient mask and an inpainting module. Unlike sibling methods such as DeblurNeRF or Sharp-NeRF which focus on resolution or blur, IE-NeRF specifically addresses dynamic occlusions. It differs from NeRF-W by using a single MLP to predict both static properties and a 2D transient mask, rather than a 3D transient field, and avoids the need for external semantic segmentation priors by learning the mask end-to-end. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of uncontrolled images \{Ii\} with corresponding camera poses. Each image Ii is pre-filtered (NIMA score > 3, transient objects < 80% area) and downsampled by a factor of 2. Outputs: A continuous volumetric representation of the static scene, producing static color \mathbf{c}s and density \sigmas for novel view synthesis, and a transient mask M{ij} for each pixel j in image i. Data Structures and Layout: 1. CNN Encoder (EE): Encodes input image Ii into a feature latent vector \boldsymbol{\ell}i \in \mathbb{R}^d. 2. NeRF MLPs: MLP{\theta1}: 8 fully connected layers, 256 hidden units. Input: Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) of ray position \gammax(\mathbf{r}(t)). Output: Density \sigma(t) and intermediate feature \mathbf{z}i(t). MLP{\theta2}: Input: Directional encoding \gammad(\mathbf{d}), intermediate feature \mathbf{z}i(t), and original position (x,y,z). Output: Image-dependent radiance \mathbf{c}i(t) and transient mask embedding \boldsymbol{\ell}t. Transient Mask Head: A fully connected layer with 128 channels and Sigmoid activation. Input: \boldsymbol{\ell}t and 2D pixel location \mathbf{l}{ij}. Output: Transient mask probability M{ij}. Static Color Head: A fully connected layer with 128 channels and Sigmoid activation. Input: \mathbf{c}i(t). Output: Static RGB color \mathbf{c}s. 3. Inpainting Module (G\Delta): Uses the LaMa model. Architecture: ResNet-like with 3 downsampling blocks, 12 residual blocks using Fast Fourier Convolution (FFC), and 3 upsampling blocks. Input: Four-channel tensor \mathbf{x}' = \text{stack}(\mathbf{x} \odot \mathbf{m}, \mathbf{m}), where \mathbf{x} is the masked image and \mathbf{m} is the binary thresholded mask. Output: Restored static image \hat{I}{ri} and repaired depth map \hat{D}{ri}. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: For each input image Ii, encode it into a latent vector \boldsymbol{\ell}i using EE. Discard images with NIMA score < 3 or transient occupancy > 80%. 2. Ray Sampling: For each pixel, sample points tk along the camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Apply Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE). 3. Static Feature Extraction: Compute \sigma(t) and \mathbf{z}i(t) via \text{MLP}{\theta1}[\gammax(\mathbf{r}(t))]. 4. Radiance and Mask Prediction: Compute image-dependent radiance \mathbf{c}i(t) and transient embedding \boldsymbol{\ell}t via \text{MLP}{\theta2}[\gammad(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{z}i(t)]. 5. Transient Mask Generation: Generate pixel-wise transient mask probability M{ij} using linear layers E\phi mapping \mathbf{l}{ij} and \boldsymbol{\ell}t: M{ij} = E\phi(\mathbf{l}{ij}, \boldsymbol{\ell}t). 6. Volumetric Rendering: Render the static scene image \hat{C}i(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{D}s(\mathbf{r}) using the static density \sigma(t) and radiance \mathbf{c}i(t): \hat{C}i(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^K T(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) \mathbf{c}i(tk) where T(tk) = \exp\left(-\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(t{k'})\delta{k'}\right). 7. Inpainting: Threshold M{ij} to create a binary mask. Apply this mask to the original image Ii and the rendered depth. Feed the masked image and mask into G\Delta to produce the restored static image \hat{I}{ri} and repaired depth \hat{D}{ri}. 8. Optimization: Minimize the total loss L (defined below) to update \theta and EE. Formulas: NeRF Preliminary: [\sigma(t), \mathbf{z}i(t)] = \text{MLP}{\theta1}[\gammax(\mathbf{r}(t))] \mathbf{c}i(t) = \text{MLP}{\theta2}[\gammad(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{z}i(t)] where \theta = [\theta1, \theta2] are learnable weights. Transient Loss (Lt): Balances occlusion and reconstruction errors: Lt = \sum{ij} (1 - M{ij}) \|\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}{ij}) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}s(\mathbf{r}{ij})\|^2 + \lambda M{ij} \|\mathbf{C}s(\mathbf{r}{ij}) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}s(\mathbf{r}{ij})\|^2 where \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}{ij}) is the observed color, \hat{\mathbf{C}}s is the rendered static color, and \lambda balances static/transient components. Depth Loss (L{depth}): L{depth} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\hat{D}s(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{D}r(\mathbf{r})\|^2 where \hat{D}s is rendered static depth and \hat{D}r is inpainted depth. Total Loss: L = \alpha \sum{ij} Ls + \beta \sum{ij} Lt + \gamma \sumi L{LPIPS} + \rho \sumi L{depth} where \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \rho are weights. Frequency Regularization (RegFre-IPE): \gamma'L(t, T; \mathbf{x}) = \gammaL(\mathbf{x}) \odot \omega(t, T, L) where \omega^i(t, T, L) is a linearly increasing frequency mask based on current iteration t, max iteration T, max frequency L, and transient mask factor r (ratio of transient pixels): \omega^i(t, T, L) = \begin{cases} \left(1 - \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor \right) \cdot r & \text{if } i \le \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor + 3 \\ 0 & \text{if } i > \lfloor \frac{t \cdot L}{T} \rfloor + 6 \end{cases} (Note: The source provides a piecewise definition with a gap; the implementation should follow the source's specific bit-wise logic for \omega). Parameters: MLP Architecture: 8 layers, 256 hidden units for \sigma; 128 units for color/mask heads. IPE: Integrated Positional Encoding used instead of single-ray point encoding. \lambda: Balances static/transient components in Lt. \alpha, \beta, \gamma, \rho: Weights for static, transient, perceptual (LPIPS), and depth losses. L: Maximum encoded frequency in positional encoding. r: Transient mask factor (ratio of transient pixels to total image area). Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Small Datasets: The method struggles with sparse inputs because the transient mask lacks sufficient information to guarantee accurate inpainting. Blurry Results: Inpainting modules may produce blurry results or view inconsistencies. Mitigated by using LPIPS loss inside the mask and depth supervision. High-Frequency Instability: High-frequency signals cause instability in transient separation. Mitigated by starting training without positional encoding and incrementally boosting frequency via RegFre-IPE. Time and Memory Complexity: Uses mip-NeRF cone casting, which is more computationally expensive than single-ray sampling but handles multiscale representations better. The dual MLP strategy (coarse and fine) adds overhead. Measured Performance: On the Phototourism dataset (Brandenburg Gate), IE-NeRF achieved PSNR 25.33, SSIM 0.898, and LPIPS 0.158, outperforming NeRF (18.90/0.816/0.232), NeRF-W (24.17/0.891/0.167), and Ha-NeRF (24.04/0.877/0.139). Scaling: Performance degrades with sparse inputs or small datasets. Strengths: Effectively separates static and transient components in uncontrolled environments without requiring 3D transient fields or external semantic segmentation models. Limitations: Struggles with small datasets; inpainting artifacts may persist if the mask is inaccurate; camera pose inaccuracies affect performance. IE-NeRF was proposed by Wang et al. from Sun Yat-sen University and Pengcheng Laboratory, published in 2024. It builds on the NeRF architecture Parent and addresses the limitations of NeRF-W, which uses a 3D transient field, and prior-assisted methods like SF-NeRF, which rely on semantic segmentation. It is evaluated on the Phototourism dataset, including scenes like Brandenburg Gate, Sacre Coeur, Trevi Fountain, and Taj Mahal. IE-NeRF: Exploring transient mask inpainting to enhance neural radiance fields in the wild, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2024.129112, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Sharp-NeRF
head: Grid-based Fast Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields using Sharpness Prior
body: Sharp-NeRF is a grid-based NeRF framework designed to render clean, sharp images from input blurry images by utilizing discrete learnable kernels and a sharpness prior. It addresses the high computational cost and long training times associated with MLP-based deblurring methods (such as Deblur-NeRF and DP-NeRF) by replacing neural kernel generators with a decomposed-grid representation and a fixed set of discrete blur kernels. Unlike sibling methods that rely on MLPs to predict blur parameters or require all-in-focus training data, Sharp-NeRF quantizes spatial sharpness levels to index a small set of learned kernels, enabling training completion in approximately half an hour. Inputs and Outputs: Training Inputs: Blurry images of the scene; precomputed per-pixel sharpness level maps L for each training view. Training Outputs: Blurred image patches Ib that match the input blurry images. Inference Output: Sharp novel view images Ic. Data Structures: 1. Grid-based Neural Field (Backbone): A decomposed-grid representation storing density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. This replaces the monolithic MLP used in prior works. 2. Discrete Blur Kernel Set (B): A set of Nk learnable 2D convolution kernels. The size of each kernel is determined by the patch size K \times K. 3. Sharpness Level Map (L): A quantized map where each pixel value corresponds to an index in B. Values are integers in the range [0, Nk - 1]. Parameters: Nk: The number of discrete blur kernels used to quantize sharpness levels. K: The spatial dimension of the ray patches (patch size is K \times K). Typical values: Nk is small (e.g., 5–10, exact value not specified in sources). K is small (e.g., 5 or 6, matching the "5 or 6 neighboring pixels" mentioned in pitfalls). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Sharpness Quantization): For each training view, compute a defocus map (sharpness level) for every pixel using a sharpness measure operator. Quantize this continuous map into Nk discrete values to create the sharpness level map L. This step is performed once before training and is not part of the forward pass. 2. Patch Sampling: During training, sample ray patches with stride 1. Each patch has a spatial size of K \times K. 3. Backbone Rendering (Sharp Image): Feed the ray patch inputs into the grid-based backbone neural fields. Render a sharp and clean image patch Ic' from these inputs. 4. Kernel Indexing: Use the preprocessed sharpness level map L corresponding to the input ray patch to index into the set of learned discrete blur kernels B. For each pixel in the patch, retrieve the specific kernel b{idx} where idx = L(x,y). This yields per-pixel weights wx (the kernel values). 5. Blurring Synthesis: Perform a weighted sum (convolution) of the rendered sharp patch Ic' and the indexed discrete kernels to produce the final blurred image patch Ib. Mathematically, for a pixel p in the patch: Ib(p) = (Ic' b{L(p)})(p) where denotes convolution with the discrete kernel b{L(p)} selected by the sharpness level at p. 6. Loss Calculation: Compare the synthesized blurred patch Ib with the ground-truth blurry input patch using a standard reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 or L2). 7. Inference: At inference time, the blur kernel module is bypassed. The grid-based backbone renders the sharp image Ic directly, which is used as the final output. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sharpnerfforward(viewparams, Lmap): """ viewparams: Camera parameters and ray origins/directions for the current view. Lmap: Sharpness level map for the current view. """ # 1. Sample ray patches # Sample patches with stride 1. Each patch covers K x K pixels. # Let patchcoords be the set of top-left coordinates of these patches. patchcoords = samplepatcheswithstride1(viewparams, K=K) renderedsharppatches = [] blurredpatches = [] for coords in patchcoords: # 2. Render sharp patch # Extract rays for the K x K patch defined by coords rays = getraysforpatch(coords, viewparams) # Render using grid-based backbone # Returns a tensor of shape (K, K, 3) for color Icprime = gridmodel.render(rays) # 3. Kernel Indexing # Get sharpness levels for this patch from Lmap # Lpatch shape: (K, K) Lpatch = Lmap[coords.y: coords.y + K, coords.x: coords.x + K] # 4. Blurring Synthesis # For each pixel in the patch, select the kernel based on Lpatch # and convolve Icprime with that kernel. # Since kernels are discrete and small, this can be implemented as: Ib = torch.zeroslike(Icprime) for k in range(Nk): # Mask of pixels in this patch with sharpness level k mask = (Lpatch == k) if mask.any(): # Get the k-th kernel kernelk = B[k] # Convolve the sharp patch with the kernel # Note: Standard convolution might add padding; # Sharp-NeRF likely uses 'same' padding or crops to match input size. # Given the "weighted sum" description, it implies a local operation. blurredk = conv2d(Icprime, kernelk, padding='same') # Add to result where mask is true # Using scatter or masked assignment Ib[mask] = blurredk[mask] renderedsharppatches.append(Icprime) blurredpatches.append(Ib) return blurredpatches def sharpnerfinference(viewparams): """ Inference only renders the sharp image. """ rays = getallrays(viewparams) Ic = gridmodel.render(rays) return Ic Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Retaining a unique blur kernel for every individual pixel is impractical for high-resolution and multi-view images due to memory constraints. Sharp-NeRF mitigates this by quantizing sharpness levels into a small number Nk of discrete kernels. Training Time: Rendering multiple neighboring pixels (e.g., 5 or 6) to synthesize one pixel's blur increases training time proportionally to the number of rays per pixel. Sharp-NeRF handles this by rendering a K \times K patch and applying the convolution operation over the entire patch, rather than ray-by-ray. Training Time: Approximately half an hour. This is significantly faster than MLP-based methods like Deblur-NeRF and DP-NeRF. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to MLP-based kernel generators. The grid-based representation is more memory-efficient than large MLPs, and the discrete kernel set B is small (Nk kernels). Strengths: Fast training; handles spatially varying blur (defocus) effectively; does not require all-in-focus training data (unlike DoF-NeRF). Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the precomputed sharpness measure operator; quantization of sharpness levels may introduce discretization artifacts if Nk is too small. When to use: When training time is a critical constraint and the input data consists of blurry images with spatially varying defocus blur. When not to use: When the blur is motion blur with a fixed kernel (Hybrid Neural Rendering Model handles this with fixed kernels, but Sharp-NeRF is designed for spatially varying defocus) or when all-in-focus reference images are available (DoF-NeRF might be an alternative). Sharp-NeRF was proposed to overcome the computational bottlenecks of MLP-based NeRF deblurring methods. Previous approaches like Deblur-NeRF and DP-NeRF used MLPs to generate blur kernels, which resulted in long training times and potential bias from the neural network's capacity limits. PDRF also used grid-based representations but relied on two MLPs (one for density, one for blur kernels). Sharp-NeRF introduces a grid-based model with discrete learnable kernels and a sharpness prior, achieving high-quality results with significantly reduced training time. The method was presented in a paper published in 2024. Sharp-NeRF: Grid-based Fast Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields using Sharpness Prior, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv57701.2024.00367, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Modular, Hierarchical, and Latent Architectures
head: Conditional NeRFs, Latent NeRFs, Hierarchical NeRFs
body: This family extends the baseline NeRF architecture Parent by introducing modularity, hierarchical structures, and latent conditioning to handle complex scene properties such as non-rigid deformation, topological changes, and multi-level stratification. Unlike monolithic NeRFs, these methods decouple scene representation into specialized components (e.g., deformation fields, latent routers, or ambient slicing surfaces) or condition the radiance field on external latent codes, enabling the modeling of dynamic, stratified, or semantically rich environments that standard continuous implicit functions cannot capture. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as surface normals \mathbf{n}, semantic logits \mathbf{s}, uncertainty variance \nu, or blend weights \Delta w. 4. Representation Basis: Substituting the coordinate-based implicit function with explicit structures like voxel grids, hash tables, Gaussian primitives, or planar surfaces, which change how features are stored and interpolated. HyperNeRF models non-rigidly deforming scenes with topological variations by embedding the scene in a higher-dimensional ambient space. It treats each observation frame as a non-planar slice through a hyperdimensional "template" NeRF, allowing it to capture topology changes (e.g., openings/closings) that continuous deformation fields cannot. It combines deformation with latent conditioning in higher dimensions, sacrificing hard spatial correspondences for topological flexibility. See HyperNeRF for implementation details. Strata-NeRF models "stratified scenes" with distinct hierarchical levels (e.g., building exterior/interior) using Vector Quantized (VQ) latent representations. It conditions a single radiance field network on discrete latent codes generated from 3D positions, enabling seamless switching between levels and avoiding the cloudy artifacts of standard NeRFs trained jointly on hierarchical data. See Strata-NeRF for implementation details. Comparison: Using two parallel dense layers in the Latent Router outperforms individual dense layers. The full Latent Router architecture is superior to direct concatenation or VAE substitution. Ablation: Disabling the second router (D1), disabling the first router (D2), removing the Latent Router to directly concatenate embeddings (D3), or replacing VQ-VAE with VAE (D4) all result in inferior performance compared to the full design. Definition: A generalized model representing faces under different views, expressions, and illumination by conditioning the NeRF MLP on parameters controlling shape, expression, albedo, and illumination. Step: Requires a refinement network (2D network) to improve the coarse results of volumetric rendering based on the conditioned NeRF MLP. Step: Introduces a global-local attribute consistency loss and a swapped-attribute classification loss to enhance disentanglement. Step: Applies a GAN-based stage-wise training approach to elevate performance. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as surface normals \mathbf{n}, semantic logits \mathbf{s}, uncertainty variance \nu, or blend weights \Delta w. 4. Representation Basis: Substituting the coordinate-based implicit function with explicit structures like voxel grids, hash tables, Gaussian primitives, or planar surfaces, which change how features are stored and interpolated. name: HyperNeRF
head: Hyper-Space Template, Hyper-space Neural Radiance Fields, HyperNeRF (2021), HyperNeRF Template
body: HyperNeRF is a method for modeling non-rigidly deforming scenes with topological variations (e.g., mouth opening/closing) by extending NeRF’s 3D input coordinate space to include higher-dimensional coordinates. It addresses the limitation of continuous deformation fields, which cannot model discontinuities required for topological changes. Unlike its sibling Strata-NeRF which focuses on stratified sampling for efficiency, HyperNeRF focuses on representational capacity for topology, achieving lower error rates than deformation-only baselines like Nerfies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images with known camera poses, viewing directions \mathbf{d}, and spatial positions \mathbf{x}. Per-frame latent codes for deformation \boldsymbol{\omega}i and appearance \boldsymbol{\psi}i. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for ray marching. Data Structures: 1. Template NeRF (F): An MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{d}, \boldsymbol{\psi}i) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma). \mathbf{x}' \in \mathbb{R}^3: Canonical spatial coordinates. \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^W: Ambient (hyper) coordinates. \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3: View direction. \boldsymbol{\psi}i \in \mathbb{R}^{D\psi}: Appearance embedding for frame i. 2. Deformation Field (T): An MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) \rightarrow \mathbf{x}'. \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Observation-space spatial coordinates. \boldsymbol{\omega}i \in \mathbb{R}^{D\omega}: Deformation latent code for frame i. Output: Canonical spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}'. 3. Slicing Surface Field (H): An MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) \rightarrow \mathbf{w}. \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Observation-space spatial coordinates. \boldsymbol{\omega}i \in \mathbb{R}^{D\omega}: Deformation latent code for frame i. Output: Ambient coordinates \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^W. Parameters: W: Number of ambient dimensions. Typical value: 2. m: Number of sinusoids in positional encoding. m=1 for \mathbf{w}, m=6 for \mathbf{x} in H. \alpha: Window function parameter for coarse-to-fine optimization. Algorithm: The method combines deformation-based and modulation-based approaches. It retains a deformation field T to model motion and fuse information, but extends the input space to handle topology changes via ambient dimensions. 1. Positional Encoding: Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma to inputs. \gamma(\mathbf{z}) = [\sin(\mathbf{z}), \cos(\mathbf{z}), \dots, \sin(2^{m-1}\mathbf{z}), \cos(2^{m-1}\mathbf{z})]^T For optimization, use windowed positional encoding \gamma\alpha to control Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) bandwidth: \gamma\alpha(\mathbf{z}) = [w0(\alpha)\sin(\mathbf{z}), \dots, w{m-1}(\alpha)\cos(2^{m-1}\mathbf{z})]^T where wj(\alpha) = \frac{1 - \cos(\pi \cdot \text{clamp}(\alpha - j, 0, 1))}{2} and \alpha increases from 0 to m. 2. Compute Canonical Coordinates: For a pixel at observation space \mathbf{x} in frame i: \mathbf{x}' = T(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) \mathbf{w} = H(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) The pair (\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{w}) represents the point in the canonical hyper-space. 3. Evaluate Radiance Field: Query the template NeRF F with the canonical coordinates, ambient coordinates, view direction, and appearance code: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = F(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{d}, \boldsymbol{\psi}i) 4. Volume Rendering: Integrate \sigma and \mathbf{c} along the ray using standard volume rendering equations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import grad, jit def positionalencoding(x, m): """Standard sinusoidal positional encoding.""" freqbands = 2.0 jnp.arange(m) x = jnp.expanddims(x, axis=-1) freqbands return jnp.concatenate([jnp.sin(x), jnp.cos(x)], axis=-1) def windowedpositionalencoding(x, m, alpha): """Windowed positional encoding for coarse-to-fine optimization.""" freqbands = 2.0 jnp.arange(m) x = jnp.expanddims(x, axis=-1) freqbands # Window function wj(alpha) jindices = jnp.arange(m) # clamp(alpha - j, 0, 1) clamped = jnp.clip(alpha - jindices, 0.0, 1.0) # (1 - cos(pi clamped)) / 2 weights = (1.0 - jnp.cos(jnp.pi clamped)) / 2.0 sinx = jnp.sin(x) cosx = jnp.cos(x) # Apply weights to frequency bands # weights shape: (m,), sinx shape: (..., m) # Broadcast weights to match sinx/cosx dimensions weightsexpanded = jnp.expanddims(weights, axis=0) encodedsin = weightsexpanded sinx encodedcos = weightsexpanded cosx return jnp.concatenate([encodedsin, encodedcos], axis=-1) def hypernerfforward(xobs, d, omegai, psii, Tparams, Hparams, Fparams, mw, mx, alpha): """ Forward pass for HyperNeRF. Args: xobs: (3,) Spatial position in observation space. d: (3,) View direction. omegai: (Domega,) Deformation latent code for frame i. psii: (Dpsi,) Appearance latent code for frame i. Tparams: Parameters for deformation MLP T. Hparams: Parameters for slicing surface MLP H. Fparams: Parameters for template NeRF MLP F. mw: Number of frequency bands for ambient coord w. mx: Number of frequency bands for spatial coord x. alpha: Current optimization bandwidth parameter. Returns: sigma: Volume density. c: View-dependent color. """ # 1. Compute canonical spatial coordinates x' # T: (x, omegai) -> x' # Assuming T is a standard MLP (e.g., MLP with ReLU) xprime = mlpT(xobs, omegai, Tparams) # 2. Compute ambient coordinates w # H: (x, omegai) -> w # Assuming H is a standard MLP w = mlpH(xobs, omegai, Hparams) # 3. Positional Encoding # Encode w with mw bands, x with mx bands # Note: The paper specifies m=1 for w and m=6 for x in H, # but F takes the raw w or encoded w? # Paper says: "We use m=1 for the hyper-coordinate input w to the template T" # and "m=6 for the spatial position input x to the slicing surface field H". # It implies F takes encoded inputs. # Encode w for F wenc = positionalencoding(w, mw) # Encode xprime for F? # Paper: "F: (x, w, d, psii) -> (c, sigma)" # Usually x in F is the canonical spatial coordinate x'. # We need to encode xprime. The paper doesn't explicitly state m for x' in F, # but standard NeRF uses m=10. However, H uses m=6 for x. # Let's assume standard positional encoding for x' in F with a default mxf. # Given the constraint "No placeholders", and source S3 says "m=6 for... x to... H", # it's ambiguous for F. However, S3 says "F: (x, w, d, psii)". # Let's assume x' is encoded similarly to standard NeRF or as specified. # To be safe and implementable, we use a standard mxf. # But wait, S3 says "We use m=6 for the spatial position input x to the slicing surface field H". # It does not specify m for x' in F. # Let's look at S3 again: "F: (x, w, d, psii) -> (c, sigma)". # And "We use m=1 for the hyper-coordinate input w to the template T". # This phrasing is slightly confusing. "template T" likely refers to the NeRF F. # So mw=1 for w in F. # For x' in F, standard NeRF uses m=10. Let's assume mxf=10. xprimeenc = positionalencoding(xprime, 10) # Standard NeRF m # Encode d for F denc = positionalencoding(d, 10) # Standard NeRF m # 4. Query Template NeRF F # F takes encoded x', w, d and latent psii # Concatenate encoded features inputtoF = jnp.concatenate([xprimeenc, wenc, denc, psii]) sigma, c = mlpF(inputtoF, Fparams) return sigma, c def mlpT(x, omega, params): """Deformation MLP T.""" # Simple MLP implementation h = jnp.concatenate([x, omega]) for i, (W, b) in enumerate(params): h = jnp.dot(h, W) + b if i < len(params) - 1: h = jnp.relu(h) # Output is 3D canonical position return h def mlpH(x, omega, params): """Slicing Surface MLP H.""" h = jnp.concatenate([x, omega]) for i, (W, b) in enumerate(params): h = jnp.dot(h, W) + b if i < len(params) - 1: h = jnp.relu(h) # Output is W-dimensional ambient position return h def mlpF(xenc, params): """Template NeRF MLP F.""" h = xenc for i, (W, b) in enumerate(params): h = jnp.dot(h, W) + b if i < len(params) - 2: h = jnp.relu(h) elif i == len(params) - 2: # Density layer sigma = jnp.exp(h) # Ensure positive density h = h[:-1] # Remove last element for color # Color layer c = jnp.sigmoid(h) # Ensure color in [0,1] return sigma, c Uses a single canonical frame and a deformation field T conditioned on a latent code. It assumes rigid or smooth non-rigid deformations and cannot handle topological changes. Choose HyperNeRF when topology changes are present. Uses a rigidity flag to distinguish rigid and non-rigid regions. It handles small non-rigid deformations without topological changes. Choose HyperNeRF for topological variations. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive. Full-HD training takes roughly 64 hours on 4 TPU v4s for 1M iterations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the MLPs for F, T, and H. The addition of ambient dimensions W increases the input size to F slightly. Performance: Reduces average error rates by 4.1% for interpolation and 8.6% for novel-view synthesis compared to Nerfies, measured by LPIPS. Strengths: Handles topological changes (e.g., mouth opening, banana peeling) that deformation-only methods cannot. Limitations: Dependent on accurate camera registration; poor registration leads to artifacts. Limited to observed data; cannot reconstruct rapid motion or occluded regions faithfully. Fails on real-world photos with varying illumination and transient occluders. The elastic regularization from Nerfies is ill-suited for these scenes. HyperNeRF was introduced by Park et al. in June 2021. It is inspired by level set methods pioneered in the late 1980s by Osher and Sethian, which model moving scenes as static objects in a higher-dimensional ambient space. The method extends Deformable NeRF (Nerfies) by embedding the template NeRF in a higher-dimensional space (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) \in \mathbb{R}^{3+W}, where a slice taken by an intersecting high-dimensional slicing surface yields a full 3D NeRF.
