name: Strata-NeRF
head: Neural Radiance Fields for Stratified Scenes
body: Strata-NeRF is a neural radiance field method designed to implicitly capture scenes with multiple hierarchical levels (stratified scenes) by conditioning the radiance field on Vector Quantized (VQ) latent representations. Unlike standard continuous NeRFs, which produce artifacts like haziness and white clouds when trained jointly on images from different structural levels, Strata-NeRF uses discrete latent codes to model sudden changes and discontinuities in scene structure. It achieves this through a Latent Generator that compresses 3D positions into discrete codes and a Latent Router that conditions the radiance field MLP, allowing a single network to represent complex, multi-tiered environments such as buildings with distinct interior and exterior geometries. Inputs: 3D spatial position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera pose parameters (implicitly handled via the ray generation process, consistent with the base Mip-NeRF 360 architecture). Ground truth color c^(\mathbf{r}) for reconstruction loss. Outputs: Volume density \sigma. View-dependent color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 1. Vector Codebook Layout: A lookup table of discrete latent vectors. Size: N = 1024 entries. Dimension: D = 48 per vector. Type: Float32 (standard for VQ-VAE codebooks). Access: Nearest neighbor search based on Euclidean distance. 2. Latent Generator Encoder Structure: Two linear layers. Hidden Size: 48. Input: Integrated Positional Encoded (IPE) position \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}). Output: Continuous latent vector \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{48}. 3. Latent Generator Decoder Structure: One linear layer. Hidden Size: 96. Input: Quantized latent vector \mathbf{z}e \in \mathbb{R}^{48}. Output: Reconstructed position \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{48} (matching IPE dimension). 4. Latent Router Structure: Two linear layers. Hidden Size: 256. Input: Quantized latent vector \mathbf{z}e. Output: Conditioning signal applied to the first two layers of the Radiance Field MLP. 5. Radiance Field MLP (Base) Architecture: Based on Mip-NeRF 360. Conditioning: The first two layers are conditioned by the output of the Latent Router. 1. Positional Encoding: For a given 3D point \mathbf{x} along a ray, compute the Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}). This matches the input dimension of the Latent Generator. 2. Latent Generation: Pass \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}) through the Latent Generator Encoder to obtain a continuous latent vector \mathbf{z}: \mathbf{z} = \text{Encoder}{\text{LG}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x})) 3. Vector Quantization: Find the nearest neighbor in the Codebook \mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} to \mathbf{z}. Let \mathbf{z}e be the selected codebook vector: \mathbf{z}e = \arg \min{\mathbf{e}i \in \mathbf{E}} ||\mathbf{z} - \mathbf{e}i||2 Note: During training, the gradient flows through \mathbf{z} to the encoder and through \mathbf{z}e to the codebook using stop-gradient operators as defined in the loss. 4. Latent Routing: Pass the quantized code \mathbf{z}e through the Latent Router MLP to produce a conditioning vector. 5. Radiance Field Conditioning: Inject the conditioning vector from the Latent Router into the first two layers of the Radiance Field MLP. 6. Density and Color Prediction: Feed the spatial position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the conditioned features into the rest of the Radiance Field MLP to predict volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. 7. Volume Rendering: Integrate \sigma and \mathbf{c} along the ray using the standard differentiable volume rendering equation (as defined in the parent article Parent) to produce the final pixel color c(\mathbf{r}, t). 8. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L{total} (see Formulas) and backpropagate to update all parameters (Latent Generator, Codebook, Latent Router, and Radiance Field). 1. Latent Generator VQ Loss (L{vq}) This loss trains the Latent Generator (VAE block) to reconstruct the encoded position and align with the codebook: L{vq} = ||\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{y}||2^2 + ||sg(\mathbf{z}e) - \mathbf{z}||2^2 + \beta||\mathbf{z}e - sg(\mathbf{z})||2^2 Where: \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}): Integrated Positional Encoded input. \mathbf{y}: Reconstructed output from the Decoder. \mathbf{z}: Continuous latent output from the Encoder. \mathbf{z}e: Quantized latent code from Codebook \mathbf{E}. sg(\cdot): Stop-gradient operator. \beta: Commitment loss weight. 2. Total Training Loss (L{total}) L{total} = L{recon}(c(\mathbf{r}, t), c^(\mathbf{r})) + \lambda1 L{dist}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}) + \lambda2 L{vq} Where: L{recon}: Photometric reconstruction loss between rendered color c(\mathbf{r}, t) and ground truth c^(\mathbf{r}). L{dist}: Distortion loss between normalized ray distances \mathbf{s} and weight vector \mathbf{w}. L{vq}: The VQ loss defined above. \lambda1, \lambda2: Loss weights. \lambda1 (Distortion Loss Weight): 0.01. \lambda2 (VQ Loss Weight): 0.1. \beta (Commitment Loss Weight): 1.0. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-6}. Training Iterations: 150,000 per scene. Codebook Size: 1024 vectors. Codebook Dimension: 48. Encoder Hidden Size: 48. Decoder Hidden Size: 96. Router Hidden Size: 256. Continuous Artifacts: Standard NeRFs (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360) trained jointly on stratified scenes produce "cloudy" or "sub-optimal" views with white artifacts and haziness because their continuous nature cannot model sudden structural changes between levels. Strata-NeRF mitigates this by using discrete VQ latents. Discontinuity Modeling: The method explicitly relies on the discreteness of VQ codes to handle discontinuities. If the codebook is too small or the quantization is too aggressive, the model may fail to distinguish between distinct hierarchical levels. Base Architecture Dependency: Strata-NeRF builds on Mip-NeRF 360. It does not alter the proposal MLP or the core volume rendering integration logic, relying instead on the conditioning mechanism. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class StrataNeRF: def init(self, codebooksize=1024, codebookdim=48, ipedim=48): """ Initialize Strata-NeRF components. """ # Codebook: N x D self.codebook = nn.Embedding(codebooksize, codebookdim) # Initialize codebook weights nn.init.uniform(self.codebook.weight, -1/codebookdim, 1/codebookdim) # Latent Generator Encoder: 2 linear layers, hidden 48 self.encoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(ipedim, 48), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(48, codebookdim)) # Latent Generator Decoder: 1 linear layer, hidden 96 self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(codebookdim, 96), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(96, ipedim)) # Latent Router: 2 linear layers, hidden 256 self.router = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(codebookdim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256) # Output size matches conditioning dim for first 2 layers of RF) # Radiance Field MLP (Base Mip-NeRF 360) # Note: The specific architecture of the RF is assumed to be from Mip-NeRF 360. # The first two layers are conditioned by the router output. self.radiancefield = MipNeRF360Base() def forward(self, x, d): """ Forward pass for a single 3D point x and direction d. """ # 1. Positional Encoding (Integrated PE) # Assuming getipe is a helper that computes IPE for x gammax = getipe(x) # 2. Latent Generation z = self.encoder(gammax) # 3. Vector Quantization # Compute distances to all codebook entries # z shape: (B, D), codebook weight shape: (N, D) distances = torch.cdist(z, self.codebook.weight) # (B, N) indices = torch.argmin(distances, dim=1) # Get quantized codes ze = self.codebook(indices) # 4. Latent Routing # Condition the radiance field routeroutput = self.router(ze) # 5. Radiance Field Prediction # The RF takes x, d, and the routeroutput as conditioning sigma, c = self.radiancefield(x, d, conditioning=routeroutput) return sigma, c, z, ze, gammax def computeloss(self, renderedcolor, gtcolor, sigma, weights, normalizeddistances, gammax, z, ze, beta=1.0, lambda1=0.01, lambda2=0.1): """ Compute total loss. """ # Reconstruction Loss lrecon = F.mseloss(renderedcolor, gtcolor) # Distortion Loss (from Mip-NeRF 360) ldist = computedistortionloss(normalizeddistances, weights) # VQ Loss # Decoder reconstruction y = self.decoder(ze) reconloss = torch.norm(gammax - y, p=2, dim=1).mean() # Commitment loss and codebook loss # sg denotes stop-gradient zestopped = ze.detach() zstopped = z.detach() commitmentloss = torch.norm(zestopped - z, p=2, dim=1).mean() codebookloss = torch.norm(ze - zstopped, p=2, dim=1).mean() lvq = reconloss + commitmentloss + beta codebookloss # Total Loss ltotal = lrecon + lambda1 ldist + lambda2 lvq return ltotal, lrecon, ldist, lvq class MipNeRF360Base(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Placeholder for the actual Mip-NeRF 360 MLP structure # The key modification is that the first two layers receive conditioning pass def forward(self, x, d, conditioning=None): # In Strata-NeRF, conditioning is added to the first two layers # This is a simplified representation return 0.1, torch.zeros(3) # Dummy output The base radiance field architecture used by Strata-NeRF. It provides the continuous volumetric representation and volume rendering pipeline that Strata-NeRF conditions. Link The underlying mechanism for Vector Quantization used in the Latent Generator. It learns a discrete codebook to model the latent space of 3D positions. Link (See "Representation Basis" section in parent) Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to Mip-NeRF 360 but requires 150k iterations. The addition of the Latent Generator and Router adds minimal computational overhead per step as they are lightweight MLPs. Memory Complexity: The method introduces significantly fewer parameters than training independent NeRF models for each level, leading to reduced memory usage. The codebook size (1024x48) is negligible compared to the MLP weights. Measured Performance: Evaluated on a synthetic Stratified Scenes dataset (simple and complex geometry) and the real-world RealEstate10K dataset. Strata-NeRF produces high-fidelity views and reduces artifacts (haziness, white clouds) compared to Mip-NeRF 360 when trained jointly on stratified levels. Strengths: Handles sudden structural changes and discontinuities in stratified scenes. Single model for multi-level scenes. Reduces memory footprint compared to per-level models. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the VQ codebook; poor quantization may blur level distinctions. Evaluated primarily on specific stratified datasets; generalization to non-stratified scenes is not the primary focus (though it functions as a conditional NeRF). When to Use: Use when rendering scenes with distinct, non-continuous hierarchical levels (e.g., interior/exterior of a building) where standard continuous NeRFs fail. When Not to Use: Use standard NeRF or Mip-NeRF 360 for scenes without significant structural discontinuities or hierarchical stratification. Strata-NeRF was proposed in 2023 by Ati et al.. It addresses the limitation of existing NeRF methods in modeling "stratified scenes," which are defined as scenes deconstructible into several tiers or groupings of structure (e.g., exterior and interior levels of a building). Previous methods like Mip-NeRF 360 produced unsatisfactory results (cloudy views, artifacts) when trained jointly on such scenes due to their continuous nature. Strata-NeRF introduces the concept of using Vector Quantized (VQ) latent representations to condition the NeRF, allowing for discrete switching between scene structures. The method was evaluated on a newly proposed synthetic Stratified Scenes dataset and the RealEstate10K dataset. Strata-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Stratified Scenes, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10337v1, fetched 2026-10-26 Neural Radiance Field-based Visual Rendering: a Comprehensive Review, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11455380, fetched 2026-10-30

name: NeuralEditor
head: NeuralEditor: Editing Neural Radiance Fields via Manipulating Point Clouds
body: NeuralEditor is a method for editing neural radiance fields (NeRFs) by exploiting an explicit point cloud representation as the underlying structural basis for the implicit field. Unlike traditional NeRFs that lack native shape-editing capabilities, or mesh-based editing methods that separate mesh optimization from NeRF modeling, NeuralEditor intrinsically integrates point clouds with the NeRF architecture. This allows users to manipulate scene geometry by moving points in the cloud and re-plotting the resulting radiance field, supporting both zero-shot inference and fast fine-tuning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of multi-view images of a scene; optionally, a target point cloud or editing instructions for shape deformation/morphing. Output: A trained NeuralEditor model capable of rendering novel views and a precise 3D point cloud representing the scene geometry. The model supports editing by outputting rendered images from modified point cloud configurations. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud (\mathcal{P}): A set of 3D points \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Each point stores position, color, and normal vector \mathbf{n}i. 2. K-D Tree: A spatial data structure built over \mathcal{P} to facilitate efficient neighbor search and voxel construction. 3. Density-Adaptive Voxels: Volumes defined by the K-D tree structure, where density is adapted based on point distribution. 4. NeRF Model (F\Theta): A neural network that takes spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input. It outputs volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. The color is decomposed into diffuse and specular components using the Phong reflection model. Numbered Steps: 1. Point Cloud-Guided NeRF Construction: Initialize a point cloud \mathcal{P} from the input images (e.g., via Structure-from-Motion or optimization). Build a K-D tree over \mathcal{P} to organize spatial data. Construct density-adaptive voxels using the K-D tree to guide the sampling and integration process. 2. Rendering with Deterministic Integration: For a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, sample points along the ray. Use the K-D tree to efficiently determine which voxels/points are intersected. Perform deterministic integration over the density-adaptive voxels to compute the final pixel color. This replaces stochastic sampling with a more stable, point-cloud-driven integration strategy. 3. Color Modeling with Phong Reflection: The NeRF outputs color \mathbf{c} using a Phong reflection model: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}{diffuse} + \mathbf{c}{specular} The specular component is calculated based on the view direction \mathbf{d}, light direction \mathbf{l}, and surface normal \mathbf{n} (extracted from the point cloud geometry). This decomposition enhances color fidelity and geometric detail representation. 4. Optimization: Optimize the NeRF parameters \Theta, point positions, normals, and voxel densities by minimizing the difference between rendered images and ground truth images. A pruning and growing strategy is applied to the point cloud to maintain optimal density and structure. 5. Shape Editing: Zero-Shot Inference: To edit the shape, map the associated points in \mathcal{P} to new positions \mathcal{P}' (e.g., moving points to deform an object). Re-render the scene using the edited point cloud \mathcal{P}' without retraining the NeRF weights. Fine-Tuning: For higher visual quality and consistency with ambient lighting, perform fast fine-tuning of the NeRF parameters on the edited point cloud configuration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class NeuralEditor: def init(self, pointcloud, kdtree): """ Initialize NeuralEditor with a point cloud and a K-D tree.:param pointcloud: Array of shape (N, 3) containing point positions.:param kdtree: K-D tree structure built from pointcloud. """ self.pointcloud = pointcloud self.kdtree = kdtree # Initialize NeRF model parameters Theta # Theta includes weights for density network and color network (Phong model) self.theta = self.initializeneuralnetwork() def initializeneuralnetwork(self): # Placeholder for neural network initialization # Returns parameters for density and color prediction pass def getnormal(self, pointindex): """ Extract normal vector for a point from the point cloud. In practice, normals are estimated from local point neighborhoods. """ # Estimate normal using PCA on k-nearest neighbors neighbors = self.kdtree.queryneighbors(self.pointcloud[pointindex], k=10) # Compute covariance matrix and eigenvector corresponding to smallest eigenvalue return np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Placeholder for actual normal computation def phongcolor(self, viewdir, normal, diffusecolor): """ Calculate color using Phong reflection model.:param viewdir: Viewing direction vector.:param normal: Surface normal vector.:param diffusecolor: Diffuse color component.:return: Final color vector. """ # Assume a single directional light source for simplicity lightdir = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) lightdir = lightdir / np.linalg.norm(lightdir) viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) normal = normal / np.linalg.norm(normal) # Diffuse term diffuse = max(0, np.dot(normal, lightdir)) diffuseterm = diffusecolor diffuse # Specular term reflectdir = 2 np.dot(normal, lightdir) normal - lightdir specular = max(0, np.dot(viewdir, reflectdir)) 32 # Shininess = 32 specularcolor = np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) # White specular highlight specularterm = specularcolor specular return diffuseterm + specularterm def renderray(self, origin, direction): """ Render a single ray using deterministic integration over K-D tree guided voxels. """ # 1. Intersect ray with K-D tree to find relevant points/voxels intersectedindices = self.kdtree.rayintersect(origin, direction) # 2. Sample points along the ray within these voxels # Deterministic sampling strategy based on voxel boundaries samples = self.samplepointsdeterministic(origin, direction, intersectedindices) # 3. Query NeRF for density and base color at each sample densities = [] colorsdiffuse = [] for sample in samples: sigma, cdiffuse = self.queryneuralnetwork(sample, direction) densities.append(sigma) colorsdiffuse.append(cdiffuse) # 4. Compute normals for Phong shading # Find nearest point in point cloud to each sample to get normal normals = [] for sample in samples: idx = self.kdtree.querynearest(sample) normals.append(self.getnormal(idx)) # 5. Apply Phong model and volume rendering accumulation finalcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) T = 1.0 for i, sample in enumerate(samples): sigma = densities[i] cdiffuse = colorsdiffuse[i] normal = normals[i] # Calculate Phong color cphong = self.phongcolor(direction, normal, cdiffuse) # Volume rendering equation alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma self.stepsize) weight = T alpha finalcolor += weight cphong T = (1.0 - alpha) return finalcolor def editshape(self, newpointpositions): """ Edit the scene by moving points and re-rendering.:param newpointpositions: Array of shape (N, 3) with edited point locations.:return: Rendered image of the edited scene. """ # Update point cloud self.pointcloud = newpointpositions # Rebuild K-D tree if necessary (or update incrementally) self.kdtree = self.buildkdtree(self.pointcloud) # Re-render scene (Zero-shot) # Iterate over all pixels/camera rays and call renderray return self.renderscene() def finetune(self, newpointpositions, numiterations=100): """ Fine-tune NeRF parameters on the edited point cloud. """ self.pointcloud = newpointpositions self.kdtree = self.buildkdtree(self.pointcloud) for i in range(numiterations): # Sample random rays rays = self.samplerandomrays() for ray in rays: # Render predcolor = self.renderray(ray.origin, ray.direction) # Get ground truth color gtcolor = ray.gtcolor # Compute loss loss = np.sum((predcolor - gtcolor) 2) # Backpropagate to update theta self.updatetheta(loss) Parameters: Shininess: 32 (used in Phong specular term). Fine-tuning iterations: Not specified in sources; typically small number for fast adaptation. K-D Tree Neighbors: 10 (used for normal estimation). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Traditional NeRFs lack user-adjustable shape editing capabilities, requiring complex space deformation or mesh conversion which may lack precision. NeuralEditor avoids this by using explicit point clouds. Boundary Conditions: The deterministic integration strategy must handle ray-voxel intersections accurately to avoid artifacts. Degenerate Input: If the point cloud is sparse or noisy, normal estimation and density-adaptive voxel construction may fail, leading to poor rendering quality. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of samples per ray and the efficiency of the K-D tree traversal. The K-D tree allows for efficient neighbor search and voxel intersection, improving stability and potentially speed compared to uniform sampling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the point cloud, K-D tree, and NeRF parameters. The K-D tree adds overhead but enables density-adaptive structures. Measured Performance: NeuralEditor achieves state-of-the-art performance in shape deformation and scene morphing tasks. It supports zero-shot inference, which is computationally cheaper than retraining, and fast fine-tuning for enhanced quality. Strengths: Native shape editing via point manipulation; intrinsic integration of point clouds and NeRF; high-fidelity rendering with Phong shading; supports general scene editing operations difficult for mesh-based methods. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial point cloud; may require fine-tuning for perfect lighting consistency after editing. When to Use: When explicit shape editing of NeRFs is required, especially for general deformation and morphing tasks. When Not to Use: When high-quality texture synthesis without geometric editing is the primary goal, or when computational resources for K-D tree construction and maintenance are limited. NeuralEditor was proposed by Jun-Kun Chen, Jipeng Lyu, and Yu-Xiong Wang from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and Peking University. It was presented at CVPR 2023. The method addresses the fundamental challenge of editing the shape of scenes in NeRFs, which traditionally lack such capabilities. It builds on the insight that NeRF rendering can be interpreted as plotting a 3D point cloud to a 2D image plane. NeuralEditor: Editing Neural Radiance Fields via Manipulating Point Clouds, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01197, fetched 2026-10-26 A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: MuRF (Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields)
head: Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields
body: MuRF is a feed-forward method for sparse view synthesis that addresses the failure of previous radiance field methods under large camera baselines by constructing a target view frustum volume aligned with the novel view rather than a reference input view. It differs from sibling methods like MVSNeRF and GeoNeRF, which use reference-view volumes, and from ray-based methods like SRF and IBRNet, by using a 3D context-aware convolutional decoder to regress density and color from a discretized volume. Inputs: A set of K input images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K with known camera poses, and a target camera pose for the novel view. Outputs: A rendered target image of resolution H \times W. Data Structures: 1. Multi-scale Features: Extracted from input images. The CNN produces features at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 of the original resolution. The Transformer operates on the 1/8 resolution features. 2. Target View Frustum Volume (z): A 4D tensor with dimensions 8 \times 8 \times D \times C. 8 \times 8: Spatial subsampling factor applied to the target image resolution H \times W. D: Number of equidistant points sampled along each ray within the frustum. C: Channel dimension containing concatenated sampled colors, features, and cosine similarities. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each input image Ik, extract features using a weight-sharing 2D CNN followed by a joint multi-view Transformer. The CNN consists of 6 residual blocks. A stride-2 convolutional layer is applied every 2 residual blocks, yielding feature maps at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 resolutions. The 1/8 resolution features from all K views are processed by a joint multi-view Transformer (based on GMFlow's 2-view architecture extended to K views) to produce final multi-view features \{Fk\} at 1/8 resolution. 2. Target View Frustum Volume Construction: Construct a volume aligned with the target view's camera frustum. Cast rays from the target camera through the target image plane. Perform 8\times subsampling in the spatial dimension (resulting in an 8 \times 8 grid). Uniformly sample D equidistant points along each ray within the frustum. For each 3D point in the volume, sample color and feature information from the input images and the extracted feature maps \{Fk\}. Compute cosine similarities between the sampled features from different views to provide multi-view consistency cues. Concatenate the sampled colors, sampled features, and computed cosine similarities to form the volume elements z \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times 8 \times D \times C}. 3. Radiance Field Regression: Reconstruct the radiance field from the low-resolution volume z using a (2+1)D CNN decoder. The (2+1)D CNN factorizes a standard 3D 3\times3\times3 convolution into: A 2D 3\times3\times1 convolution on the spatial dimensions. A 1D 1\times1\times3 convolution on the depth dimension. This produces a low-resolution output of density and color. 4. Upsampling: Apply a lightweight 8\times upsampler to the low-resolution radiance field output to obtain the full-resolution radiance field at H \times W resolution. 5. Rendering: Render the target image using standard volumetric rendering on the full-resolution radiance field. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MuRF: def init(self, numdepthsamples=128, numinputviews=2): """ Initialize MuRF components.:param numdepthsamples: D, number of equidistant points on each ray.:param numinputviews: K, number of input images. """ # Feature Encoder self.cnnencoder = CNNFeatureEncoder() # 6 residual blocks, stride-2 convs every 2 blocks self.multiviewtransformer = MultiViewTransformer(numviews=numinputviews) # Context-aware Decoder # (2+1)D CNN: 2D spatial conv followed by 1D depth conv self.decoder2d = nn.Conv3d(inchannels=None, outchannels=None, kernelsize=(3, 3, 1)) # Placeholder for exact channel dims self.decoder1d = nn.Conv3d(inchannels=None, outchannels=None, kernelsize=(1, 1, 3)) # Placeholder for exact channel dims # Note: Exact channel dimensions C are not specified in sources. # C is the aggregated channel dimension of sampled features, colors, and cosine similarities. # Upsampler self.upsampler = LightweightUpsampler(scalefactor=8) def extractfeatures(self, inputimages): """ Extract multi-view features from input images.:param inputimages: Tensor of shape (K, H, W, 3):return: List of feature tensors at 1/8 resolution, shape (K, H/8, W/8, Ccnn) """ # Step 1: Per-image 2D CNN cnnfeatures = [] for img in inputimages: # CNN produces features at 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 resolutions # We only need the 1/8 resolution features for the Transformer f18 = self.cnnencoder(img) cnnfeatures.append(f18) # Step 2: Joint Multi-View Transformer # Transformer operates on 1/8 resolution features # Extends 2-view cross-attention to K views multiviewfeatures = self.multiviewtransformer(cnnfeatures) return multiviewfeatures def constructvolume(self, targetcamera, inputimages, multiviewfeatures): """ Construct the target view frustum volume.:param targetcamera: Camera parameters for the target view:param inputimages: Original input images (for color sampling):param multiviewfeatures: Features from Step 1:return: Volume z of shape (8, 8, D, C) """ H, W = inputimages[0].shape[1], inputimages[0].shape[2] spatialH, spatialW = H // 8, W // 8 D = 128 # Default D, typically not given as a fixed constant in text, but used in volume dim # Cast rays from target camera # Sample D equidistant points on each ray # Perform 8x subsampling in spatial dimension # This results in a grid of 8x8 rays volumeelements = [] for i in range(8): rowelements = [] for j in range(8): # Get ray for target pixel (i8, j8) ray = getrayfromtargetcamera(targetcamera, i8, j8) # Sample D points along the ray points3d = sampleequidistantpoints(ray, D) # For each point, sample features and colors from input views sampledcolors = [] sampledfeatures = [] cosinesimilarities = [] for k in range(len(inputimages)): # Sample color from input image Ik at the projected location of points3d colork = samplecolorfromimage(inputimages[k], points3d, targetcamera, inputimages[k].camera) sampledcolors.append(colork) # Sample feature from multiviewfeatures[k] at the projected location featk = samplefeaturefrommap(multiviewfeatures[k], points3d, targetcamera, inputimages[k].camera) sampledfeatures.append(featk) # Compute cosine similarity between features of view k and other views # Sources mention "cosine similarities between sampled features" # Assuming pairwise or reference-based similarity for consistency cues simk = computecosinesimilarity(featk, sampledfeatures) cosinesimilarities.append(simk) # Concatenate sampled colors, features, and cosine similarities # C is the channel dimension after aggregation zelement = torch.cat([ torch.stack(sampledcolors), torch.stack(sampledfeatures), torch.stack(cosinesimilarities) ], dim=-1) rowelements.append(zelement) volumeelements.append(torch.stack(rowelements)) # Volume shape: (8, 8, D, C) z = torch.stack(volumeelements) return z def decoderadiancefield(self, volumez): """ Reconstruct radiance field from volume using (2+1)D CNN.:param volumez: Tensor of shape (8, 8, D, C):return: Low-res density and color tensors """ # (2+1)D CNN: 2D spatial conv (3x3x1) then 1D depth conv (1x1x3) # Note: Conv3d in PyTorch expects (N, C, D, H, W) or similar. # Assuming input is (N, C, D, H, W) for conv3d, or we permute. # Here we assume standard spatial (H,W) and depth (D) layout. # Permute to (N, C, D, H, W) if necessary x = volumez.permute(0, 3, 2, 1, 4) # (8, C, D, 8, 8) -> (N, C, D, H, W) # 2D Conv on spatial dimensions (H, W) # Kernel (3, 3, 1) x = self.decoder2d(x) # 1D Conv on depth dimension (D) # Kernel (1, 1, 3) x = self.decoder1d(x) return x def render(self, targetcamera, inputimages): """ Full forward pass. """ # 1. Extract Features multiviewfeatures = self.extractfeatures(inputimages) # 2. Construct Volume volumez = self.constructvolume(targetcamera, inputimages, multiviewfeatures) # 3. Decode Radiance Field lowresradiance = self.decoderadiancefield(volumez) # 4. Upsample fullresradiance = self.upsampler(lowresradiance) # 5. Render # Volumetric rendering on fullresradiance targetimage = volumetricrender(fullresradiance, targetcamera) return targetimage Parameters: Spatial Subsampling Factor: 8\times. D: Number of equidistant points sampled on each ray. Not given in the sources as a specific constant, but used in the volume dimension 8 \times 8 \times D \times C. H \times W: Resolution of the target image. K: Number of input views. The method supports K \ge 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Baselines: Using a reference view volume (aligned with an input view) for large baselines causes failure because the overlap between the reference and target view is small, leading to missing information outside the epipolar lines of the reference view. MuRF avoids this by aligning the volume with the target view. Information Loss: The 8\times spatial subsampling risks losing information if only a single point is sampled per ray. The method addresses this by sampling features and colors from multiple input views and computing cosine similarities for consistency cues. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses a (2+1)D CNN decoder, which is computationally more efficient than a full 3D CNN. The 8\times spatial subsampling reduces the memory footprint and computational cost of the volume representation, allowing efficient handling of high-resolution images. Measured Performance: MuRF achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple baseline settings on DTU, LLFF, RealEstate10K, and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets. It outperforms specialized small baseline methods (e.g., ENeRF) and large baseline methods (e.g., AttnRend). Strengths: General applicability to both small and large baselines; zero-shot generalization ability; explicit 3D context modeling via CNN decoder. Limitations: Requires known camera poses for input and target views. Performance may degrade if the target view is outside the convex hull of input views (standard NeRF limitation, implied by frustum volume construction). MuRF was proposed by Haofei Xu, Fisher Yu, et al. from ETH Zurich, University of Tübingen, Monash University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Microsoft. The paper was published in CVPR 2024. It addresses the limitations of previous feed-forward NeRF methods that were specialized for either small or large baselines, by introducing a target view frustum volume representation. MuRF: Multi-Baseline Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01894, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Gaussian and Primitive-Based Representations
head: Explicit Radiance Fields, Differentiable Primitives, Neural Point Clouds
body: Gaussian and Primitive-Based Representations replace the global continuous volumetric field of standard NeRF with explicit, differentiable geometric primitives (Gaussians, quadrics, or points) to improve rendering speed and geometric interpretability. Unlike implicit methods that require dense ray sampling, these methods leverage explicit structures to avoid empty space sampling and enable real-time rasterization or efficient local aggregation. The family shares a shift from a monolithic MLP F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to an explicit representation \mathcal{E}. The rendering process integrates outputs from these primitives along rays. Common mechanisms include: 1. Explicit Parameterization: Scene geometry and appearance are stored in learnable parameters of primitives (e.g., mean/covariance for Gaussians, coefficients for quadrics, feature vectors for points) rather than weights of a single deep network. 2. Differentiable Assembly: The final radiance is computed by differentiable operations over these primitives, such as rasterization (Gaussian Splatting), set-theoretic operations (DPA), or weighted aggregation (Point-NeRF). 3. Local vs. Global: Queries for density and color are resolved locally using neighborhood information or primitive intersections, reducing the computational complexity from O(N{samples} \times N{layers}) to operations dependent on the number of primitives N{prim}. DPA models 3D shapes as an explicit assembly of quadric primitives, utilizing differentiable intersection and union operations to compute occupancy [13657-differentiable-primitive-assembly.md]. Unlike global continuous fields, DPA derives density and color from local interactions with these primitives, enabling shape abstraction trained solely with image-space losses without 3D supervision [13657-differentiable-primitive-assembly.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Gaussian Splatting by using set-theoretic operations (intersection/union) on primitive distances rather than weighted aggregation or rasterization [13657-differentiable-primitive-assembly.md]. VDGS is a hybrid neural rendering method that combines the explicit geometric representation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) with the view-dependent appearance modeling of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [14273-viewing-direction-gaussian-splatting.md]. It solves the limitation of classical GS, where color and opacity are static per primitive, by using a neural network to modulate opacity (and optionally color) based on the viewing direction, thereby accurately rendering specular reflections, transparency, and shadows without significantly increasing training time [14273-viewing-direction-gaussian-splatting.md]. Unlike classical GS, VDGS achieves NeRF-quality view-dependent effects while retaining the fast differentiable rasterization pipeline of Gaussian primitives [14273-viewing-direction-gaussian-splatting.md]. Point-NeRF is a point-based radiance field representation that models a continuous volumetric radiance field using a discrete neural point cloud [15538-point-nerf-representation.md]. It solves the inefficiency of global continuous fields by leveraging classical point clouds to approximate scene geometry, thereby avoiding ray sampling in empty space [15538-point-nerf-representation.md]. Unlike its sibling Differentiable Primitive Assembly which uses differentiable set operations on primitive distances, Point-NeRF relies on local aggregation of neural features from neighboring points via inverse distance weighting [15538-point-nerf-representation.md]. Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering (also known as AFNet) is a real-time rendering pipeline that represents scenes as explicit point clouds and uses an Adaptive Frequency Net (AFNet) to modulate implicit radiance signals with local texture frequency encoding [15903-frequency-modulated-point-cloud-rendering.md]. It solves the problem of high-frequency reconstruction limitations in standard neural radiance fields by allowing the network to adaptively select frequency basis support for each point, enabling high-fidelity local detail reconstruction and user-friendly editing [15903-frequency-modulated-point-cloud-rendering.md]. Unlike implicit NeRF methods, it is 1700× faster than NeRF and 37× faster than CCNeRF, while supporting direct point cloud manipulation for object editing and scene composition [15903-frequency-modulated-point-cloud-rendering.md]. GARF uses Gaussian activations as an effective alternative to positional encoding in NeRF, in conjunction with bundle adjustment for pose estimation. It successfully recovers scene representations from unknown camera poses, even in challenging scenes with low-textured regions, making it suitable for real-world applications. Uses Gaussian activations instead of positional encoding. Performs bundle adjustment for pose estimation. Successfully recovers scene representations from unknown camera poses in challenging scenes with low-textured regions. The shift from implicit to explicit representations in radiance fields emerged to address the computational bottlenecks of volume rendering and the lack of explicit geometric control in standard NeRF. While early NeRF variants relied on dense MLPs, methods like Gaussian Splatting and Point-NeRF introduced explicit primitives to enable real-time rendering. Differentiable Primitive Assembly (DPA) further explored explicit shape abstraction using quadrics. GARF (April 2022) introduced Gaussian activations as an alternative to positional encoding, specifically targeting pose estimation from unknown camera poses. These methods collectively form a family of "explicit" or "primitive-based" radiance fields that prioritize geometric interpretability and rendering efficiency over the purely implicit continuity of standard NeRF. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Differentiable Primitive Assembly
head: DPA-Net Primitive Assembly, Quadric Primitive Assembly
body: Differentiable Primitive Assembly (DPA) models 3D shapes as an explicit assembly of learnable quadric primitives, utilizing differentiable set-theoretic operations (intersection and union) to compute occupancy. Unlike implicit neural representations, DPA constructs geometry from discrete primitives, enabling compact shape abstraction and test-time adaptation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Gaussian Splatting by using algebraic primitive intersections rather than rasterization, and from Point-NeRF by using structured convex hulls rather than point-based density fields. Inputs: A set of sparse input images (or fused image features f), camera poses, and query points \mathbf{x}i sampled along rays. Outputs: Rendered color Cb, object mask Mc, and a compact set of primitive parameters defining the 3D shape. 1. Primitive Parameters Matrix (\mathbf{P}): Shape \mathbb{R}^{P \times 7}. Each row p contains coefficients (ap, bp, cp, dp, ep, fp, gp) for a quadric primitive. The first three parameters are constrained to be non-negative to ensure convexity. 2. Selection Matrix (\mathbf{T}): Shape \mathbb{R}^{P \times C}. Ideally binary, but takes floating-point values in [0, 1] during training. Column c selects a subset of primitives whose intersection forms the c-th convex. 3. Weight Vector (\mathbf{w}): Shape \mathbb{R}^{C}. Learnable weights for the soft union approximation, with elements close to 1. Quadric Primitive Equation: |ap|x^2 + |bp|y^2 + |cp|z^2 + dp x + ep y + fp z + gp = 0 where (x, y, z) is a query point. Distance Matrix (\mathbf{D}): Define query matrix \mathbf{Q} where the i-th row is (xi^2, yi^2, zi^2, xi, yi, zi, 1). \mathbf{D} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}^\top \mathbf{D}{i,p} < 0 if point i is inside primitive p, and \mathbf{D}{i,p} > 0 if outside. Convex Occupancy (\mathbf{O}): \mathbf{O} = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{D})\mathbf{T} \mathbf{O}{i,c} = 0 if point i is inside convex c, and \mathbf{O}{i,c} > 0 if outside. Exact Occupancy (\mathbf{a}^): Computed via min-pooling (union of convexes): \mathbf{a}^i = \min{1 \leq c \leq C} \mathbf{O}{i,c} \mathbf{a}^i = 0 if inside the shape, > 0 if outside. Soft Occupancy (\mathbf{a}^+): Used for gradient flow during pretraining: \mathbf{a}^+i = \mathcal{L}\left( \sum{c=1}^{C} wc \mathcal{L}(1 - \mathbf{O}{i,c}) \right) where \mathcal{L}(\cdot) clips input to [0, 1]. \mathbf{a}^+i \approx 1 if inside, < 1 if outside. Rendering: Color Cb and mask Mc for a pixel are computed by accumulating along ray points i=1 \dots R: Cb = \sum{i=1}^{R} ti \alphai c{b,i}, \quad Mc = \sum{i \in \Omega} ti \alphai where ti = \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphak) is transmittance, and \alphai is opacity derived from occupancy. P = 4,096: Number of primitives. C = 256: Number of convexes. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 0.0001. Batch size: 4 object instances. 1. Initialize \mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times 7}, \mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times C}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{C}. 2. Sample Query Points: Generate N query points \mathbf{x}i along camera rays. 3. Compute Distances: Construct \mathbf{Q} from \mathbf{x}i. Compute \mathbf{D} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}^\top. 4. Compute Convex Occupancy: \mathbf{O} = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{D})\mathbf{T}. 5. Compute Opacity: Depending on training phase, compute \alphai from \mathbf{a}^ or \mathbf{a}^+ (see Training Phases below). 6. Render: Compute Cb and Mc using volume rendering equation. 7. Compute Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}T + \mathcal{L}w (Pretraining) or variant (TTA). 8. Update: Backpropagate and update parameters. Pseudocode for Occupancy and Rendering: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computequadricdistances(querypoints, Pmatrix): """ querypoints: (N, 3) tensor of (x, y, z) Pmatrix: (P, 7) tensor of primitive parameters (a, b, c, d, e, f, g) Returns: D (N, P) """ # Q: (N, 7) row is (x^2, y^2, z^2, x, y, z, 1) x, y, z = querypoints[:, 0], querypoints[:, 1], querypoints[:, 2] Q = torch.stack([x2, y2, z2, x, y, z, torch.oneslike(x)], dim=1) # D = Q @ P^T D = torch.matmul(Q, Pmatrix.T) return D def computeconvexoccupancy(D, T): """ D: (N, P) distance matrix T: (P, C) selection matrix Returns: O (N, C) convex occupancy """ # O = ReLU(D) @ T O = F.relu(D) @ T return O def computeexactoccupancy(O): """ O: (N, C) convex occupancy Returns: astar (N,) exact occupancy """ # astar = min(O, dim=1) astar, = torch.min(O, dim=1) return astar def computesoftoccupancy(O, w): """ O: (N, C) convex occupancy w: (C,) learnable weights Returns: aplus (N,) soft occupancy """ # inner = L(1 - O) inner = torch.clamp(1 - O, min=0, max=1) # weighted sum weightedsum = inner @ w # outer L aplus = torch.clamp(weightedsum, min=0, max=1) return aplus def renderray(pointsalongray, alphas, colors): """ pointsalongray: (R,) not strictly needed for alpha/color accumulation if ordered alphas: (R,) opacity values colors: (R, 3) color values Returns: Cb (3,), Mc (1,) """ # ti = product(1 - alphak) for k < i # Standard volume rendering accumulation transmittance = torch.cumprod(1 - alphas, dim=0) # Shift transmittance: t1 = 1, ti = product{k=1}^{i-1} (1-alphak) # torch.cumprod gives product up to i. We need product up to i-1. # Prepend 1.0 transmittanceshifted = F.pad(transmittance, (1, 0), value=1.0)[:-1] contribution = transmittanceshifted.unsqueeze(1) alphas.unsqueeze(1) colors Cb = torch.sum(contribution, dim=0) # Mask accumulation (only for points inside object, typically alpha > 0 implies inside) # Mc = sum(ti alphai) Mc = torch.sum(transmittanceshifted alphas) return Cb, Mc Pretraining: Opacity: \alpha = \mathbf{a}^+. Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}T + \mathcal{L}w. \mathcal{L}{ph} = \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^B ||\hat{C}j - Cj||2^2 + \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^B ||\hat{M}j - Mj||2^2. \mathcal{L}T = \sum{i,j} \max(-T{i,j}, 0) + \max(T{i,j} - 1, 0) (Keeps T \in [0, 1]). \mathcal{L}w = \sumj |wj - 1|. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) Phase 1: Input: Test images as Ground Truth. Opacity: \alpha = \mathbf{a}^+. Loss: \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}T + \mathcal{L}w. Parameters: Network, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{w}. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) Phase 2: Opacity: \alpha = \exp(-10\mathbf{a}^). Loss: \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}T (\mathcal{L}w omitted). Parameters: Network, \mathbf{T}. Sampling: Sample 40,960 points surrounding the shape. Check membership in \Omega (inside shape) using \mathbf{a}^i < 0.01. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) Phase 3: Selection Matrix: Binarize \mathbf{T} with threshold 0.01 and freeze. Opacity: \alpha = \exp(-10\mathbf{a}^). Loss: \mathcal{L}{ph} + \mathcal{L}{over}. Overlapping Loss: \mathcal{L}{over} = \sum{i \in \Omega} \max(hi, 1.9), where hi = \sum{c=1}^C \exp(-10\mathbf{O}{i,c}). Parameters: Network. Primitive Dropout: Applied every 400 iterations. For each primitive p, set row p of \mathbf{T} to zero, compute new occupancy \mathbf{b}^, and calculate variation v = K \sum{i=1}^P \mathbb{I}(\text{XOR}(\mathbf{b}^i < 0.1, \mathbf{a}^i < 0.1)). If v \approx 0, keep row zero; else restore. Complex Topologies: Random pixel sampling struggles with thin structures or holes. Use silhouette-aware sampling: 256 random pixels + 1,000 pixels around contours (obtained via morphological closing on mask + Gaussian noise). Redundant Primitives: Use primitive dropout to remove primitives that do not significantly alter the shape. Overlap: Excessive overlap between convexes is penalized via \mathcal{L}{over} in Phase 3. Complexity: Time complexity depends on the number of query points N, primitives P, and convexes C. Matrix multiplications \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}^\top (O(NP)) and \mathbf{D}\mathbf{T} (O(NPC)) dominate. Memory is O(NP + PC) for intermediate matrices. Performance: Trained on 4 NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs with batch size 4. Strengths: Compact representation (up to 29% primitive reduction via dropout), differentiable assembly allows end-to-end training from image-space losses only, no 3D supervision required. Limitations: Requires test-time adaptation for novel shapes deviating from training data; complex topologies require specific sampling strategies. DPA-Net was introduced in "DPA-Net: Structured 3D Abstraction from Sparse Views via Differentiable Primitive Assembly" (2024). It builds on CAPRI-Net [55] and differentiable CSG operations [6, 55]. It addresses the limitations of monolithic MLPs by using explicit quadric primitives, enabling structured 3D abstraction from sparse views. DPA-Net: Structured 3D Abstraction from Sparse Views via Differentiable Primitive Assembly, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00875v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting
body: Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting (VDGS) is a hybrid neural rendering method that combines the explicit geometric representation of 3D Gaussian Splatting (GS) with the view-dependent appearance modeling of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It solves the limitation of classical GS, where color and opacity are static per primitive, by using a neural network to modulate opacity (and optionally color) based on the viewing direction, thereby accurately rendering specular reflections, transparency, and glass without increasing training time significantly. Unlike classical GS, VDGS achieves NeRF-quality view-dependent effects while maintaining the fast training and inference speeds of Gaussian rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of camera poses and corresponding 2D images from a dataset; initial 3D points (from Structure from Motion or random initialization). Outputs: A differentiable rendering of the scene for arbitrary camera viewpoints, represented by a set of 3D Gaussians and a neural network. Data Structures: 1. Gaussian Primitives (G): A collection of n 3D Gaussian distributions. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \mathbf{m}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (trainable). Covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (trainable, positive definite). Base color \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (RGB, trainable). Base opacity \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} (trainable, scalar). 2. Neural Network (F{VDGS}): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with parameters \Theta. Input: Hash-encoded Gaussian mean \mathbf{m}i and viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^2 (spherical coordinates \theta, \psi). Output: Opacity update factor \Delta \sigma(\mathbf{d}) \in \mathbb{R}. Hash Grid: 12 levels of 3D embedding (resolutions 16 to 512), hash table size 2^{14} (16384), feature dimension 2, LeakyReLU activation. MLP Architecture: 2-layer MLP. Formulas: The vanilla NeRF model is defined as F{NeRF}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) = (\mathbf{c}, \sigma). VDGS modifies this by separating shape and view-dependent appearance. The VDGS function is defined as: F{VDGS}(\mathbf{m}, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) = \Delta \sigma(\mathbf{d}) where \mathbf{m} is the Gaussian mean and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. The final representation is a set of tuples: (G, F{VDGS}) = \{ (\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}i, \mathbf{\Sigma}i), \sigmai \cdot \Delta \sigmai(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{c}i) \}{i=1}^n where \Delta \sigmai(\mathbf{d}) = F{VDGS}(\mathbf{m}i, \mathbf{d}; \Theta). Rendering computes the pixel color C(\mathbf{p}) by blending N ordered overlapping Gaussian samples along the ray passing through pixel \mathbf{p}: C = \sum{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the effective opacity of sample i: \alphai = 1 - \exp\left( \sigmai \cdot F{VDGS}(\mathbf{m}i, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) \cdot \deltai \right) Here, \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples along the ray, and \sigmai is the base opacity of the Gaussian. Parameters: Hash Grid Levels: 12. Hash Table Size: 2^{14} (16384). Feature Dimension: 2. Activation Function: LeakyReLU. MLP Layers: 2. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the model with Structure from Motion (SfM) points (from COLMAP or randomly generated) to establish initial 3D Gaussian positions and covariances. 2. Hash Encoding: Encode the mean position \mathbf{m}i of each Gaussian using a 3D structured hash grid. 3. View-Dependent Update: Feed the hashed Gaussian mean \mathbf{m}i and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} into the MLP F{VDGS} to compute the opacity update \Delta \sigmai(\mathbf{d}). 4. Effective Opacity Calculation: Calculate the effective opacity \alphai for each Gaussian sample using the base opacity \sigmai, the NeRF-based density update \Delta \sigmai(\mathbf{d}), and the sample distance \deltai. 5. Rasterization: Render the pixel color C(\mathbf{p}) by blending N ordered overlapping Gaussian samples using alpha compositing. 6. Optimization: Jointly optimize all parameters (Gaussian mean, covariance, color, base opacity, and MLP weights \Theta) using differential Gaussian rasterization. 7. Pruning and Densification: During optimization, eliminate Gaussians with opacity below a specific limit every hundred iterations. Generate new Gaussians in unoccupied areas of 3D space to fill vacant areas. Pseudocode: Unverified code. This is attributed to the dependency of opacity on color, making joint training ineffective. Opacity vs. Color Multiply: "VDGS Opacity Multiply" (updating only opacity) yields the best scores on real scenes, while "VDGS Color Multiply" yields the best scores on the NeRF Synthetic dataset. The final model uses Opacity Multiply. Precision: The hash grid provides extremely fast queries, but precision depends on the hash table size and resolution levels. Uses set-theoretic operations for rendering. Chooses this when explicit geometry is not required or when dealing with non-Gaussian primitives. Differentiable Primitive Assembly Uses point clouds with MLPs for local queries. Chooses this when memory efficiency for sparse scenes is prioritized over the dense rasterization speed of Gaussians. Point-NeRF Representation Uses frequency modulation on point clouds. Chooses this for high-frequency detail reconstruction in point-based methods. Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to classical Gaussian Splatting, significantly faster than NeRF. Inference is also fast, comparable to GS. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and the hash grid size. The hash grid is fixed size (2^{14} entries), while Gaussians grow during densification. Measured Performance (RTX 3090, VDGS-30K): Mip-NeRF360: SSIM 0.813, PSNR 27.64, LPIPS 0.220. Training: 46m 11s. Inference: 41.35 FPS. Tanks and Temples: SSIM 0.851, PSNR 24.02, LPIPS 0.176. Strengths: Accurately models light reflections, transparency, and glass; eliminates view-dependent artifacts; fast training and inference compared to NeRF. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of pruning/densification; joint color/opacity update is less effective than opacity-only update. When to use: When view-dependent effects (shiny surfaces, transparency) are critical, but NeRF training times are prohibitive. When not to use: When the scene is purely diffuse and static, classical GS may be sufficient and simpler. VDGS was proposed by researchers from the Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, and the Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge. It was published in December 2023 (arXiv:2312.13729). The method addresses the limitations of both NeRF (slow, hard to locate geometry) and GS (hard to condition, static appearance) by hybridizing them. It builds on the differential Gaussian rasterization pipeline introduced in classical GS. name: Point-NeRF Representation
head: Neural point cloud, Point-based radiance field
body: Point-NeRF is a method that represents a continuous volumetric radiance field using an explicit neural point cloud, avoiding the computational cost of ray sampling in empty space by leveraging classical point clouds that approximate scene geometry. It differs from its sibling Differentiable Primitive Assembly by using inverse-distance weighted aggregation of local feature vectors rather than set-theoretic operations, and from Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting by relying on MLP-based regression of density and radiance from point neighborhoods rather than analytic Gaussian splatting. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses; an initial sparse point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP) providing 3D locations. Outputs: A rendered image for a given camera pose, derived from the optimized neural point cloud. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a neural point cloud P containing N points. Each point i stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D spatial location. \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^D: A neural feature vector encoding local scene content (dimension D is a hyperparameter). \gammai \in [0, 1]: A scale confidence value representing the likelihood that the point is near an actual scene surface. Algorithm: To render a pixel, a ray is marched through the scene. For each shading sample location \mathbf{x} along the ray: 1. Neighborhood Query: Identify K neighboring neural points from P located within a radius R of \mathbf{x}. 2. Per-Point Processing: For each neighbor i, compute a processed feature vector \mathbf{f}{i,x} using an MLP \mathcal{F}: \mathbf{f}{i,x} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{f}i, \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i) The input to \mathcal{F} is the concatenation of the point's feature \mathbf{f}i and the relative position vector \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i. This relative position makes the network invariant to point translation. 3. Feature Aggregation: Aggregate the K processed features \mathbf{f}{i,x} into a single feature \mathbf{f}x using inverse distance weighting, weighted by the confidence \gammai: \mathbf{f}x = \sum{i=1}^{K} \gammai \frac{wi}{\sum{j=1}^{K} wj} \mathbf{f}{i,x}, \quad \text{where } wi = \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{x}\|} Closer points contribute more to the aggregation. 4. Radiance Regression: Regress the view-dependent radiance \mathbf{r} from the aggregated feature \mathbf{f}x and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using an MLP \mathcal{R}: \mathbf{r} = \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{f}x, \mathbf{d}) The volume density \sigma is also regressed, typically by a similar or shared network structure, to form the tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{r}) = \text{Point-NeRF}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \dots). 5. Volume Rendering: Accumulate radiance along the ray using the standard volume rendering equation: c = \sum{j=1}^{M} \tauj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \Deltaj)) \mathbf{r}j \tauj = \exp\left(-\sum{t=1}^{j-1} \sigmat \Deltat\right) where c is the pixel radiance, \sigmaj and \mathbf{r}j are the density and radiance at shading point j, \Deltat is the distance between adjacent shading samples, and \tauj is the volume transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, pointcloud, radiusR, kneighbors): """ Renders a single ray using the Point-NeRF representation. pointcloud: List of dicts with keys 'p' (3D vector), 'f' (feature vector), 'gamma' (scalar). """ # 1. March ray and sample points shadingpoints = marchray(rayorigin, raydirection) pixelradiance = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for x in shadingpoints: # 2. Query neighbors neighbors = queryneighbors(x, pointcloud, radiusR, kneighbors) if not neighbors: continue # No contribution if no points nearby # 3. Aggregate features aggregatedfeature = [0.0] len(pointcloud[0]['f']) totalweight = 0.0 for point in neighbors: # Per-point processing relativepos = x - point['p'] # MLP F processes feature and relative position # Note: In implementation, F is a neural network, not a simple function processedf = mlpF(point['f'], relativepos) # Inverse distance weighting dist = norm(point['p'] - x) weight = 1.0 / dist # Accumulate weighted feature for d in range(len(aggregatedfeature)): aggregatedfeature[d] += point['gamma'] weight processedf[d] totalweight += point['gamma'] weight # Normalize if totalweight > 0: for d in range(len(aggregatedfeature)): aggregatedfeature[d] /= totalweight else: continue # 4. Regress radiance and density # MLP R takes aggregated feature and viewing direction radiance = mlpR(aggregatedfeature, raydirection) density = mlpdensity(aggregatedfeature, raydirection) # Assumed similar structure for sigma # 5. Volume rendering step # Assume delta is pre-computed or fixed step size alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density delta) contribution = transmittance alpha radiance pixelradiance += contribution transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return pixelradiance Parameters: K: Number of neighbors. Not given in the sources. R: Query radius. Not given in the sources. D: Feature vector dimension. Not given in the sources. \Deltaj: Distance between shading samples. Determined by ray marching strategy. Edge Cases: If no neighbors are found within radius R, the point contributes no radiance. Precision issues may arise if \|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{x}\| is very small, leading to large weights. The sources do not specify a epsilon guard for the inverse distance calculation. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of shading samples M and the cost of querying K neighbors and running MLPs. It avoids sampling empty space, offering efficiency gains over dense voxel-based NeRFs. Memory Complexity: Proportional to N \times (3 + D + 1), storing position, feature, and confidence for each point. Strengths: Faster per-scene optimization (tens of minutes) compared to standard NeRF; leverages off-the-shelf reconstruction methods like COLMAP; can automatically fix holes and outliers via point pruning and growing. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality and density of the initial point cloud. Not given in the sources. Point-NeRF was introduced by Qiangeng Xu, Zexiang Xu, Julien Philip, Sai Bi, Zhixin Shu, Kalyan Sunkavalli, and Ulrich Neumann from the University of Southern California and Adobe Research. It was published at CVPR 2022. The method addresses the prohibitive reconstruction time of volumetric neural rendering methods like NeRF by using a neural point cloud to model the radiance field. name: Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering
head: AFNet, Adaptive Frequency Net, Adaptive Frequency Net (AFNet) based rendering, FreqPCR, Frequency-Modulated Radiance Mapping
body: Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering is a pipeline that renders scenes using an explicit point cloud representation enhanced by an Adaptive Frequency Net (AFNet) to modulate implicit radiance signals with local texture frequency encoding. It solves the problem of high-frequency detail reconstruction in point cloud rendering, where standard MLPs suffer from spectral bias towards low-frequency signals. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly predicts per-point frequency and phase parameters via a hypernetwork to adaptively activate features, enabling real-time rendering (39.27 FPS on NeRF-Synthetic) and direct point cloud editing. It is 1700x faster than NeRF and 37x faster than CCNeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points \mathcal{P} with initial attributes (position, color, opacity). Camera parameters (view and projection matrices). Output: Rendered RGB image and depth buffer. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of M points. Each point pi has: Position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 Color \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or feature vector) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] AFNet Parameters: Hypernetwork: Two-layer MLP. Adaptive Frequency Activation Layer (AF Layer): Parameters \omega^{(i)} (frequency) and \phi^{(i)} (phase) for each layer i. Numbered Steps: 1. Point Cloud Geometry Optimization (Preprocessing): Use volume rendering to optimize the initial point cloud geometry. Keep multiple points in the pixel buffer per ray (not just the closest) to allow opacity learning. Learn the opacity \alphai of each point based on volume rendering integration. Note: This step improves PSNR by 2-4dB for poorly reconstructed scenes and avoids artifacts. 2. Radiance Mapping with AFNet: For each point pi, query its spatial position \mathbf{x}i. Hypernetwork Inference: Pass \mathbf{x}i through a two-layer MLP hypernetwork to predict adaptive frequency \omega^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R} and phase \phi^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}. Feature Propagation: For each layer i of the radiance mapping network: Let input feature be \mathbf{X}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times C}, where M is the number of points and C is the feature dimension. Broadcast \omega^{(i)} and \phi^{(i)} to dimensions M \times C. Compute the activated output \mathbf{Y}^{(i)} using the adaptive frequency activation formula: \mathbf{Y}^{(i)} = \mathbf{X}^{(i)} \circ \sin(\omega^{(i)} \circ \mathbf{X}^{(i)} + \phi^{(i)}) where \circ denotes the Hadamard (element-wise) product. Pass \mathbf{Y}^{(i)} to the next layer (typically a linear layer). The final layer outputs raw RGB values. 3. Rendering: Project points to screen space. Sort points by depth. Perform alpha compositing along rays using the learned opacities and final RGB values. 4. Object Editing (Optional): Edit the point cloud directly (e.g., move, scale, delete points). Construct a deformation field between the original 3D space and the deformed space by querying the transformations performed on the point cloud. Render the edited point cloud using the same pipeline. 5. Scene Composition (Optional): Combine multiple scenes at the pixel level. Use a masking strategy based on the depth buffer to avoid cross-scene training and blending artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def hypernetwork(xcoords, weights): """ Two-layer MLP hypernetwork to predict frequency and phase. xcoords: (M, 3) spatial coordinates of points weights: parameters of the hypernetwork Returns: omega: (M, 1) adaptive frequencies phi: (M, 1) adaptive phases """ # Layer 1: Linear + ReLU h1 = np.maximum(0, xcoords @ weights['w1'] + weights['b1']) # Layer 2: Linear -> 2 outputs (omega, phi) out = h1 @ weights['w2'] + weights['b2'] omega = out[:, 0:1] phi = out[:, 1:2] return omega, phi def aflayer(xinput, omega, phi): """ Adaptive Frequency Activation Layer. xinput: (M, C) input features omega: (M, 1) frequencies (broadcasted to M, C) phi: (M, 1) phases (broadcasted to M, C) Returns: youtput: (M, C) activated features """ # Broadcast omega and phi to match xinput dimensions omegabroadcast = np.broadcastto(omega, xinput.shape) phibroadcast = np.broadcastto(phi, xinput.shape) # Formula: Y = X sin(omega X + phi) youtput = xinput np.sin(omegabroadcast xinput + phibroadcast) return youtput def renderpointcloud(points, cameraparams, afnetweights, hypernetweights): """ Main rendering pipeline. points: List of Point objects with pos, color, opacity cameraparams: View and projection matrices afnetweights: Weights for the radiance mapping MLP layers hypernetweights: Weights for the hypernetwork """ # 1. Project points to screen space screenpoints = project(points, cameraparams) # 2. Sort points by depth (back to front or front to back depending on compositing) screenpoints.sort(key=lambda p: p.depth) # 3. Initialize image buffers height, width = cameraparams.imagesize finalcolor = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) finalalpha = np.zeros((height, width, 1)) # 4. Iterate over points and accumulate color for point in screenpoints: if not point.onscreen: continue # Get screen coordinates u, v = point.screencoords # Query AFNet for this point # Extract feature vector from point (e.g., initial color or learned embedding) xinput = point.featurevector.reshape(1, -1) # (1, C) # Predict omega and phi for this point omega, phi = hypernetwork(point.pos.reshape(1, -1), hypernetweights) # Apply AF layers for each layer in the radiance mapping network currentfeature = xinput for i, layerweights in enumerate(afnetweights): # Apply AF activation currentfeature = aflayer(currentfeature, omega, phi) # Apply linear transformation currentfeature = currentfeature @ layerweights['w'] + layerweights['b'] # If not the last layer, apply standard activation (e.g., ReLU) if i < len(afnetweights) - 1: currentfeature = np.maximum(0, currentfeature) # Final layer outputs RGB rgb = currentfeature.reshape(3) # Alpha compositing alpha = point.opacity # Update image buffer finalcolor[u, v] = finalcolor[u, v] (1 - alpha) + rgb alpha finalalpha[u, v] = finalalpha[u, v] (1 - alpha) + alpha finalalpha[u, v] # Simplified alpha accumulation return finalcolor, finalalpha Parameters: Hypernetwork: Two-layer MLP. AF Layer: Sinusoidal activation \sin(\omega X + \phi) followed by element-wise multiplication with input X. Rendering Speed: 39.27 FPS on NeRF-Synthetic dataset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral Bias: Standard MLPs with ReLU have strong spectral bias towards low-frequency signals, limiting high-frequency reconstruction. AFNet mitigates this by adapting frequencies locally. Geometry Optimization: Previous surface point-based works could not optimize point cloud geometry because they kept only the closest point as surface estimation for each ray. Using volume rendering with multiple points per ray is necessary for geometry optimization but must be balanced against rendering speed. Cross-Scene Training: In scene composition, failing to use a depth-based masking strategy can lead to cross-scene training artifacts. Uses differentiable set-theoretic operations over primitives. Choose when explicit geometry manipulation via set operations is preferred over rasterization. Differentiable Primitive Assembly Uses Gaussian splats with viewing-dependent color. Choose when view-dependent effects are critical and Gaussian primitives are suitable. Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting Uses a point cloud with a NeRF-style MLP for density and color. Choose when a simpler point-based NeRF variant is needed without frequency modulation. Point-NeRF Representation Time Complexity: Real-time rendering speed of 39.27 FPS on NeRF-Synthetic. Speed Comparison: 1700x faster than NeRF and 37x faster than CCNeRF. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of points M and feature dimension C. The hypernetwork adds minimal overhead. Strengths: High-fidelity local detail reconstruction, real-time rendering, user-friendly editing (object-level), scene composition. Limitations: Requires point cloud geometry optimization preprocessing for best results. Performance on poorly reconstructed scenes can be improved by 2-4dB with this step. When to Use: When real-time rendering and editable point cloud representations are required, and high-frequency texture details are important. When Not to Use: When implicit representations are sufficient and editing is not a priority, or when hardware constraints prevent the overhead of the hypernetwork (though overhead is described as negligible). Origin: Proposed by Zhang et al. in "Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering with Easy Editing" (CVPR 2023). History: Motivated by the spectral bias of standard MLPs in Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) and the need for editable neural rendering. Builds on HyperNetworks [11] and MFN [7] concepts. Usage: Evaluated on NeRF-Synthetic, ScanNet, DTU, and Tanks and Temples datasets.
