name: Decentralized Federated NeRF
head: DecentNeRF, Decentralized Neural Radiance Fields from Crowdsourced Images
body: DecentNeRF is a decentralized framework for learning global 3D scene representations from crowd-sourced images by distributing training computation to users and aggregating only global radiance field models to minimize server compute and personal data leakage. It solves the problem of achieving photorealistic 3D reconstruction of global scene content while preventing the server from reconstructing transient personal content (e.g., users, objects) present in crowdsourced images taken at different times. Unlike centralized approaches like NeRF-W which require all personal user images to be transferred to a central server, or existing federated learning NeRF techniques which assume static scenes devoid of personal information, DecentNeRF handles personal content and uses secure aggregation. It differs from standard federated learning by employing a Personal MLP, appearance embedding, secure aggregation, and learned weighted averaging instead of standard FedAvg aggregation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K users, each possessing a local dataset of images \mathcal{I}k with known camera poses. The images contain both static global content (e.g., monuments) and dynamic personal content (e.g., people, transient objects). Outputs: A globally aggregated global MLP \mathbf{G} held by the server and distributed to users, and locally held personal MLPs \mathbf{P}k for each user. Data Structures: Each user k maintains two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Global MLP: Weights \mathbf{g}k. Captures shared global content. These weights are federated to the server. 2. Personal MLP: Weights \mathbf{p}k. Captures user-specific transient content. These weights remain local to the user device and are never sent to the server. Both MLPs follow the NeRF backbone architecture: Input: A 5D vector consisting of 3D spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and viewing direction parameters pitch \theta and yaw \phi. Output: Scalar density \sigma and RGB color vector \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b). Parameters: \alphak: A per-user weighting factor applied to local weights/gradients during obfuscation and aggregation. It is learned via gradient descent to maximize visual fidelity, implicitly handling user importance based on factors like occlusion levels. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Randomly initialize global MLP weights \mathbf{G}^{(0)} and personal MLP weights \mathbf{P}^{(0)} at all K users. 2. Local Training (User Side): For each training round m: a. Each user k trains their local Global MLP (\mathbf{g}k) and Personal MLP (\mathbf{p}k) on their local images \mathcal{I}k. b. The rendering process synthesizes images via volume rendering by sampling predicted color and density at many points along rays traversing the scene. c. The final rendered image is an alpha-composite of the output images from both the global and personal MLPs. d. The user calculates the loss Lk by comparing the predicted color with ground truth RGB values. e. The user computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the global MLP weights: \frac{\partial Lk}{\partial \mathbf{g}^{(m-1)}}. f. The user updates the weighting factor \alphak based on the gradient updates. 3. Obfuscation (User Side): a. Weight Obfuscation (sendwts): Each user obfuscates their local global weights \mathbf{g}k by multiplying with \alphak and applying a random mask or encrypting with additively homomorphic encryption. This ensures original values cannot be recovered during aggregation while enabling accurate weighted averaging. b. Gradient Obfuscation (sendgrads): Each user communicates local gradients by performing randomized obfuscation similar to the weight obfuscation process. 4. Secure Aggregation (Server Side): a. The server receives the obfuscated weights and gradients from all users. b. The server uses a Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) protocol to securely aggregate the weights and previous rounds' gradients. c. The function weightavg(g) executes the computation of the weighted average of the obfuscated weights sent by the users. d. The server distributes the updated global MLP back to each user. 5. Update (User Side): a. Each user receives the updated global MLP. b. Each user calculates the update step for \alphak and updates \alphak accordingly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. K = number of users M = number of federation rounds alpha = [1.0] K # Initial per-user weighting factors def usertrainandobfuscate(userid, localimages, globalmlpweights, personalmlpweights, alphak): """ Trains local MLPs and obfuscates global weights for transmission. """ # 1. Local Training # Train globalmlp and personalmlp on localimages # Loss is computed on alpha-composite of global and personal outputs # Compare rendered color with ground truth RGB globalmlpweights, personalmlpweights = trainlocalmlp( localimages, globalmlpweights, personalmlpweights) # 2. Compute Gradients for alpha update # Calculate loss Lk and gradient w.r.t global weights lossk, gradglobal = computelossandgradient( globalmlpweights, personalmlpweights, localimages) # 3. Update alphak # Update alphak based on gradient updates (Eq 2 in source) alphak = updatealpha(alphak, gradglobal) # 4. Obfuscate Weights for Server # Multiply weights by alphak and apply random mask or homomorphic encryption obfuscatedweights = obfuscate(globalmlpweights, alphak) # 5. Obfuscate Gradients for Server obfuscatedgrads = obfuscate(gradglobal, alphak) return obfuscatedweights, obfuscatedgrads, alphak, globalmlpweights, personalmlpweights def serveraggregate(obfuscatedweightslist, obfuscatedgradslist): """ Securely aggregates obfuscated weights and gradients from all users. """ # Use SMPC protocol to compute weighted average # The server does not see individual user weights aggregatedglobalmlp = secureweightedaverage(obfuscatedweightslist) # Aggregate gradients similarly if needed for further updates aggregatedgrads = secureweightedaverage(obfuscatedgradslist) return aggregatedglobalmlp def decernettraining(K, M, localdatasets): # Initialization globalmlpweights = initializemlp() personalmlpweights = [initializemlp() for in range(K)] for m in range(M): # Parallel user training results = [] for k in range(K): obfw, obfg, newalpha, gw, pw = usertrainandobfuscate( k, localdatasets[k], globalmlpweights, personalmlpweights[k], alpha[k]) results.append((obfw, obfg, newalpha, gw, pw)) # Server aggregation obfwlist = [r[0] for r in results] obfglist = [r[1] for r in results] newglobalmlp = serveraggregate(obfwlist, obfglist) # Update global state and user alphas globalmlpweights = newglobalmlp for k in range(K): alpha[k] = results[k][2] personalmlpweights[k] = results[k][4] return globalmlpweights, personalmlpweights Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initial Rounds: During initial rounds of federation, users’ global MLPs contain personal content, leading to undesired reconstruction of personal content by the server. However, secure aggregation minimizes this leakage compared to non-secure methods. View Overlap: If two users have no overlapping views (entirely separate scene areas), the server's ability to reconstruct personal content increases considerably. The method assumes sufficient overlap in views such that no single user has views that don’t overlap with another user. Standard Averaging: Standard federated learning uniformly averages user weights, which does not maximize visual fidelity for global scene reconstruction. DecentNeRF uses learned weighted averaging to address this. Server Compute: DecentNeRF requires \sim 10^4 times less server computing for a scene than a centralized approach. FLOPs: DecentNeRF FLOPs are \sim 0.6B (for specific setups mentioned in Fig 1b labels, though context implies comparative metrics) or \approx 5B server FLOPs on the Phototourism dataset, compared to \approx 200T FLOPs for NeRF-W. Performance: On the Phototourism dataset, DecentNeRF achieves PSNR 24.62, SSIM 0.8802, LPIPS 0.2571. Personal Content Leakage: Personal content reconstruction by the server is reduced by 10 dB compared to FedNeRF. In the first federation round, server-rendered global image PSNR is 14.2 dB and server-rendered personal content PSNR is 14.9 dB. In the final federation round, server-rendered global image PSNR is 27.2 dB and server-rendered personal content PSNR is 9.3 dB. Strengths: Minimizes server compute, prevents personal data leakage, handles dynamic personal content, photorealistic global reconstruction. Limitations: Requires known camera poses (assumed known, not derived decentralisedly in this work), assumes sufficient view overlap, honest-but-curious server model. DecentNeRF was introduced by Z. Tasneem et al. in the paper "DecentNeRFs: Decentralized Neural Radiance Fields from Crowdsourced Images". It is the first work to analyze the decentralization aspects of radiance fields for real-world crowd-sourced images. It builds on NeRF and NeRF-W, addressing their limitations regarding personal data access and server compute costs. It is used for decentralized NeRF training on crowdsourced datasets including the Novel Blender Dataset and Phototourism Dataset (Brandenburg Gate, Trevi Fountain, Sacre Couer). DecentNeRFs: Decentralized Neural Radiance Fields from Crowdsourced Images, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-73202-79, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Neural Proxy
head: Neural Proxy Model
body: Neural Proxy is a neural rendering method that represents photo-realistic targets as animatable proxies to enable the rendering of unseen animations without temporal learning. It combines neural volume rendering with neural texture techniques, injecting a proxy into a scene such that each proxy represents its photo-realistic counterpart, mimicking the typical CG pipeline of a 3D mesh for placement and a texture for appearance. Unlike NeRF, which ties content to continuous Cartesian coordinates making animation difficult, Neural Proxy uses an animatable mesh proxy allowing particles to move with the animation. Unlike Neural Texture, which requires animated training samples to render unseen animations, Neural Proxy renders unseen animations without temporal learning by animating the proxy geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference geometry (mesh \bar{M}), UV coordinates for the mesh, offset parameters for shell extrusion (\epsilon{\rightarrow}, \epsilon{\leftarrow}), and a neural texture \Omega{Tex}. Outputs: Rendered image I for a given camera pose and animation state. Data Structures: 1. Coarse Geometry (\bar{M}): A mesh defined by vertices \mathbf{v}i and smoothed normals \mathbf{n}i for i=1 \dots Nv. 2. Proxy Shell: A volume enclosing the target, constructed by extruding \bar{M} along normals. It consists of an outward surface M{\rightarrow} and an inward surface M{\leftarrow}. Outward vertices: \overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}i = \mathbf{v}i + \mathbf{n}i \cdot \epsilon{\rightarrow} Inward vertices: \overleftarrow{\mathbf{v}}i = \mathbf{v}i - \mathbf{n}i \cdot \epsilon{\leftarrow} Constraints: \epsilon{\rightarrow}, \epsilon{\leftarrow} \ge 0 and \epsilon{\rightarrow} + \epsilon{\leftarrow} > 0. 3. UV Coordinates: Original mesh: \mathbf{u}{2D} for each vertex. Extruded surfaces: Lifted to 3D with a depth component w. Outward: \overrightarrow{\mathbf{u}}i = (\mathbf{u}{2D}, \overrightarrow{w}) where \overrightarrow{w}=1. Inward: \overleftarrow{\mathbf{u}}i = (\mathbf{u}{2D}, \overleftarrow{w}) where \overleftarrow{w}=0. The proxy volume includes vertices from both surfaces: \{\overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}i\} \cup \{\overleftarrow{\mathbf{v}}i\}. 4. Neural Texture (\Omega{Tex}): A learnable feature map wrapped around the proxy. Steps: 1. Proxy Construction: Retrieve reference geometry \bar{M} (e.g., via COLMAP or manual low-res mesh). 2. Shell Extrusion: Compute outward and inward surfaces M{\rightarrow} and M{\leftarrow} using the offset parameters. 3. UV Lifting: Assign 3D UV coordinates to the shell vertices using the depth labels w=1 (outward) and w=0 (inward). 4. Tetrahedralization: Break the prisms formed by the extrusion of triangles into three tetrahedra using the method from [PBFJ05] to enable Barycentric coordinate sampling. 5. Neural Texture Wrapping: Wrap the neural texture \Omega{Tex} around the proxy shell. 6. Particle Sampling: For a ray r, determine intersection with the proxy shell. Convert the Cartesian intersection point \mathbf{x} to Barycentric coordinates within the tetrahedra. Map Barycentric coordinates to UV coordinates on the neural texture. Use a bilinear sampler f{Bi} to sample features from \Omega{Tex} based on UV coordinates. Feed sampled features into a neural proxy sampler Sp to produce color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Note: The view direction \mathbf{d} is dropped for simplicity in the proxy sampler definition, or handled implicitly by the texture. Formula: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = Sp(\mathbf{x}) where the input to Sp is derived from the texture sample. 7. Rendering: Use a mixture of a neural proxy sampler (for animatable targets) and a static sampler (for static surroundings) for particle sampling. Render the image using standard volume rendering integration over the sampled particles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderneuralproxy(ray, proxyshell, neuraltexture, staticsampler): """ Renders a single ray using the Neural Proxy method. Args: ray: Ray origin and direction. proxyshell: Object containing mesh vertices, normals, UVs, and tetrahedra. neuraltexture: The learnable texture map OmegaTex. staticsampler: Sampler for static background/surroundings. Returns: Rendered color and density. """ # 1. Intersect ray with proxy shell intersection = intersectraywithshell(ray, proxyshell) if intersection is not None: # 2. Convert Cartesian intersection point to Barycentric coordinates # This requires identifying the specific tetrahedron in the proxy shell barycentriccoords = cartesiantobarycentric(intersection.point, proxyshell.tetrahedra) # 3. Map Barycentric coordinates to UV coordinates # The UVs are pre-computed for the shell vertices uvcoords = barycentrictouv(barycentriccoords, proxyshell.uvmap) # 4. Sample features from the neural texture using bilinear sampling # fBi is the bilinear sampler features = bilinearsampler(neuraltexture, uvcoords) # 5. Generate color and density using the neural proxy sampler # Sp takes the sampled features (and potentially the Cartesian point x) # Note: View direction d is dropped in the simplified definition color, density = neuralproxysampler(features, intersection.point) return color, density else: # 6. If no intersection with proxy, use static sampler for surroundings return staticsampler(ray) def buildproxyshell(mesh, normals, epsilonout, epsilonin): """ Constructs the proxy shell from a coarse mesh. Args: mesh: List of vertices vi. normals: List of smoothed normals ni. epsilonout: Offset for outward surface. epsilonin: Offset for inward surface. Returns: ProxyShell object containing extruded vertices, UVs, and tetrahedra. """ Nv = len(mesh) outwardvertices = [] inwardvertices = [] for i in range(Nv): v = mesh[i] n = normals[i] # Extrude vertices vout = v + n epsilonout vin = v - n epsilonin outwardvertices.append(vout) inwardvertices.append(vin) # Lift UV coordinates to 3D # Original UVs are assumed to be available for the coarse mesh outwarduvs = [(uv, 1.0) for uv in originalmeshuvs] inwarduvs = [(uv, 0.0) for uv in originalmeshuvs] # Combine vertices for the shell allshellvertices = outwardvertices + inwardvertices allshelluvs = outwarduvs + inwarduvs # Break prisms into tetrahedra for Barycentric sampling # Method from [PBFJ05] tetrahedra = decomposeprismsintotetrahedra(mesh, outwardvertices, inwardvertices) return ProxyShell(allshellvertices, allshelluvs, tetrahedra) Parameters: \epsilon{\rightarrow}, \epsilon{\leftarrow}: Offset parameters for shell extrusion. Must be non-negative and sum to >0. Set such that the shell encloses the target object. w: Depth component for UV lifting. \overrightarrow{w}=1 for outward, \overleftarrow{w}=0 for inward. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on accurate intersection detection with the proxy shell. Degenerate tetrahedra or poor mesh quality in the reference geometry can lead to sampling errors. Boundaries: The shell must fully enclose the photo-realistic target to ensure relevant particles are contained. Animation: The proxy geometry is animated. If the animation causes self-intersection or extreme deformation, the Barycentric mapping may fail or produce artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The proposed model significantly outperforms current neural rendering works in rendering unseen animations. Strengths: Enables animation of neural rendering targets without temporal learning; combines the localization of neural texture with the volumetric nature of NeRF. Limitations: Requires a reference geometry proxy; limited to animatable targets that can be represented by a mesh proxy. Neural Proxy was proposed to address the lack of discussion on enabling neural rendering for synthesizing frames for unseen animations. It builds on Neural Volume Rendering [LSS19] and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [MST20], while incorporating ideas from Neural Texture [TZN19]. The method mimics the typical computer graphics pipeline by using a 3D mesh for placement and a texture for appearance. Neural Proxy: Empowering Neural Volume Rendering for Animation, https://doi.org/10.2312/pg.20211384, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: ViSNeRF
head: ViSNeRF (Vector-matrix and Tensor factorization for Neural Radiance Fields)
body: ViSNeRF is a hybrid neural radiance field method designed for the efficient synthesis of visualizations from dynamic volumetric scenes with arbitrary adjustable parameters (e.g., time, isovalue, transfer functions). It solves the scalability problem of high-dimensional radiance fields by combining explicit spatial feature grids with implicit MLP decoders, utilizing block-term tensor decomposition for the 3D spatial volume and CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) decomposition for the K-dimensional parameter space. Unlike sibling methods that rely solely on fully implicit networks or fully explicit grids, ViSNeRF achieves a balance of memory efficiency and visual quality by factorizing the (3+K)-D representation into compact components, reducing complexity from O(N^3 M^K) to O(N^2 M). Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of training images (DVR or IR) with known camera poses, ray origins, directions, RGB values, and scene parameters (p0, p1, \dots) defining the specific frame. Outputs: Synthesized visualization images (DVR or IR) for novel viewpoints and interpolated parameter values. Data Structures The model maintains three primary explicit feature structures and two implicit decoders: 1. Spatial Feature Grid (T^3): Layout: Factorized into vector-matrix pairs. Density Components: R\sigma components. Each component consists of a spatial matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} (or X \times Y, etc.) and a spatial vector v \in \mathbb{R}^{L} (where L is the remaining dimension length). Color Components: Rc components. Same structure as density. Total Spatial Components: Rs = R\sigma + Rc. Resolution: Initialized at N \times N \times N (e.g., 128^3), potentially increasing to 300^3 for complex scenes. The grid is not necessarily cubic; dimensions match the bounding box aspect ratio. 2. Parameter Feature Grid (T^K): Layout: Factorized into K vectors per component. Dimensions: M^K, where M is the number of distinct values for each parameter in the training set. Components: Rp one-rank components. Each component is the outer product of K vectors, one for each parameter dimension. 3. Implicit Decoders: Color MLP (gc): One hidden layer, 128 channels. Density MLP (g\sigma): One hidden layer, 128 channels. Both are fully connected networks. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Casting: Cast rays from screen pixels toward the scene from camera locations. For each pixel, define the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and associate the specific scene parameters \mathbf{p} = (p0, p1, \dots) for the target frame. 2. Sampling: Estimate the integral along the ray using stratified sampling. Select n sample points ti along the ray segment [tn, tf]. Calculate step size \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 3. Feature Retrieval (Spatial): For a sample point \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}: Retrieve features from the spatial factorization T^3. For each component r \in \{1, \dots, Rs\}, perform element-wise multiplication between the sampled spatial matrix M and the sampled spatial vector v corresponding to the coordinates of \mathbf{x}i. Concatenate the outcomes of these multiplications to form the spatial feature vector f{\text{spatial}}. 4. Feature Retrieval (Parameter): Retrieve features from the parameter factorization T^K. For each component r \in \{1, \dots, Rp\}, perform element-wise multiplication between the sampled parameter vectors v^1r, v^2r, \dots, v^Kr corresponding to the parameters \mathbf{p}. Concatenate these products to form the parameter feature vector f{\text{param}}. 5. Feature Combination: Combine f{\text{spatial}} and f{\text{param}}. The source describes concatenating the outcomes of spatial and parameter multiplications. Specifically, the final feature input to the decoders integrates the products from the three spatial pairs (XY, XZ, YZ) and the parameter vector product. Let f\sigma be the density feature and fc be the color feature derived from this combination. 6. Decoding: Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using Spherical Harmonics (SH): E{SH}(\mathbf{d}). Encode the spatial position \mathbf{x}i using Positional Encoding (PE): EP(\mathbf{x}i). Compute density: \sigmai = g\sigma(f\sigma, EP(\mathbf{x}i)). Compute color: \mathbf{c}i = gc(fc, E{SH}(\mathbf{d})). 7. Volume Rendering: Compute transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Compute ray color: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i 8. Loss Computation: Compute Reconstruction Loss (L{REC}): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between \hat{C}(r) and ground truth color. Compute L1 Norm Loss (L{L1}): L{L1} = \begin{cases} \sum ||1 - w|| & \text{if } W \in vp \text{ (parameter vectors)} \\ \sum \frac{||w||1}{|W|} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where W are weights in vectors/matrices. Parameter vector weights are initialized/regularized to 1. Compute Total Variation Loss (L{TV}): L{TV} = L{TV1} + L{TV2} L{TV1} = \frac{1}{|V||Q|l} \sum{v,q,i} ||v{i,q} - v{i-1,q}||2 L{TV2} = \frac{1}{|M||Q|hw} \sum{M,q,i,j} \left( ||M{q,i,j} - M{q,i-1,j}||2^2 + ||M{q,i,j} - M{q,i,j-1}||2^2 \right) where v are vectors, M are matrices, Q is channels, l is vector length, h,w are matrix dimensions. Total Loss: L = L{REC} + \lambda1 L{L1} + \lambda2 L{TV}. 9. Optimization: Update matrices, vectors, and MLPs using Adam optimizer (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99). Apply dynamic bounding box shrinking and voxel skipping starting at iteration 2,000. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ViSNeRF: def init(self, spatialres, paramdims, Rsigma, Rcolor, Rparam, hiddendim=128): """ spatialres: tuple (X, Y, Z) for spatial grid dimensions paramdims: tuple of lengths for each parameter dimension (M1, M2,...) Rsigma: number of low-rank components for density Rcolor: number of low-rank components for color Rparam: number of low-rank components for parameter space """ super().init() self.Rsigma = Rsigma self.Rcolor = Rcolor self.Rparam = Rparam self.spatialres = spatialres # Spatial Feature Grid Factorization (Block-term) # Density: Rsigma components of (Matrix x Vector) # Matrices: MXY, MXZ, MYZ. Vectors: vX, vY, vZ # Dimensions depend on spatialres. Simplified for one component r: # MXY: (X, Y), vZ: (Z,) -> Outer product shape (X, Y, Z) # MXZ: (X, Z), vY: (Y,) # MYZ: (Y, Z), vX: (X,) # Initialize Spatial Matrices and Vectors for Density self.densityMXY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[0], spatialres[1])) self.densityMXZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[0], spatialres[2])) self.densityMYZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[1], spatialres[2])) self.densityvX = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[0])) self.densityvY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[1])) self.densityvZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rsigma, spatialres[2])) # Initialize Spatial Matrices and Vectors for Color self.colorMXY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[0], spatialres[1])) self.colorMXZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[0], spatialres[2])) self.colorMYZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[1], spatialres[2])) self.colorvX = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[0])) self.colorvY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[1])) self.colorvZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rcolor, spatialres[2])) # Parameter Feature Grid Factorization (CP) # T^K = sumr (v^1r o v^2r o... o v^Kr) # paramdims is a tuple (M1, M2,...) self.paramvectors = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.randn(Rparam, M)) for M in paramdims ]) # Implicit Decoders # Density MLP: Input is combined spatial+param features + PE(x) # Color MLP: Input is combined spatial+param features + SH(d) # Note: The paper states inputs are fsigma/fc (from grid) and EP(x)/ESH(d). # The combination of grid features is done before the MLP. # Density MLP self.gsigma = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) # Output sigma) # Color MLP self.gc = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) # Output RGB) # SH Encoding for view direction (simplified to fixed order for implementation) # Standard SH encoding function would be called here. def getspatialfeatures(self, xcoords, componenttype='density'): """ xcoords: tensor of shape (N, 3) containing (x, y, z) indices normalized to grid size Returns feature vector of shape (N, R) """ if componenttype == 'density': MXY = self.densityMXY MXZ = self.densityMXZ MYZ = self.densityMYZ vX = self.densityvX vY = self.densityvY vZ = self.densityvZ R = self.Rsigma else: MXY = self.colorMXY MXZ = self.colorMXZ MYZ = self.colorMYZ vX = self.colorvX vY = self.colorvY vZ = self.colorvZ R = self.Rcolor # Extract indices xidx = xcoords[:, 0].long() yidx = xcoords[:, 1].long() zidx = xcoords[:, 2].long() # Gather vectors # vX shape: (R, X) -> gather -> (N, R) vXgathered = vX[:, xidx].transpose(0, 1) # (N, R) vYgathered = vY[:, yidx].transpose(0, 1) # (N, R) vZgathered = vZ[:, zidx].transpose(0, 1) # (N, R) # Gather matrices # MXY shape: (R, X, Y) -> gather x -> (R, N, Y) -> gather y -> (R, N, N) -> transpose -> (N, N, R) # This is complex. Element-wise multiplication implies we sum over R. # Feature for point i is sumr ( MXY[r, xi, yi] vZ[r, zi] +...) # This results in a scalar per component type? # The paper says "concatenate the outcomes... to construct the final feature". # If R is the depth, we need to preserve R. # Let's assume the "feature" is the vector of length R formed by the contributions of each rank. # Contribution from XY plane + Z vector # MXY[r, x, y] vZ[r, z] MXYvals = MXY[:, xidx, yidx] # (R, N) vZvals = vZgathered # (N, R) termXY = MXYvals vZvals # (N, R) # Contribution from XZ plane + Y vector MXZvals = MXZ[:, xidx, zidx] # (R, N) vYvals = vYgathered # (N, R) termXZ = MXZvals vYvals # (N, R) # Contribution from YZ plane + X vector MYZvals = MYZ[:, yidx, zidx] # (R, N) vXvals = vXgathered # (N, R) termYZ = MYZvals vXvals # (N, R) # Combine spatial features (sum over the three planes for each rank) spatialfeat = termXY + termXZ + termYZ # (N, R) return spatialfeat def getparamfeatures(self, paramindices): """ paramindices: list of tensors, one for each parameter dimension. Each tensor shape (N,) containing indices into the parameter grid. Returns feature vector of shape (N, Rparam) """ # T^K = sumr (v^1r o... o v^Kr) # For a point with parameter indices p1, p2,..., pK # Feature[r] = v^1r[p1] v^2r[p2]... v^Kr[pK] # Initialize with ones paramfeat = torch.ones(paramindices[0].shape[0], self.Rparam, device=paramindices[0].device) for k, idx in enumerate(paramindices): # v^k shape: (R, Mk) # Gather: (R, N) -> transpose to (N, R) vk = self.paramvectors[k][:, idx].transpose(0, 1) paramfeat = paramfeat vk return paramfeat def forward(self, xcoords, paramindices, viewdirs): """ xcoords: (N, 3) spatial coordinates (indices) paramindices: list of (N,) tensors for each parameter viewdirs: (N, 3) viewing directions """ # 1. Get Spatial Features fsigmaspatial = self.getspatialfeatures(xcoords, 'density') fcolorspatial = self.getspatialfeatures(xcoords, 'color') # 2. Get Parameter Features fparam = self.getparamfeatures(paramindices) # 3. Combine Features # The paper implies concatenating spatial and param products. # However, the decoders take fsigma and fc. # Let's assume fsigma = fsigmaspatial + fparam (or concat) # Given the dimensions, if Rsigma != Rparam, we might need projection. # The paper says "concatenate the outcomes... to construct the final feature". # Let's assume the final feature vector is the concatenation of spatial and param contributions. # But the decoders have fixed input size (hiddendim). # We must project or assume R matches hiddendim. # In the paper, hiddendim is 128. Rsigma=16, Rcolor=48, Rparam=4. # This suggests the "feature" passed to MLP is not just the raw grid output. # Re-reading: "decode the retrieved features...". # "concatenate the outcomes... to construct the final feature". # It is likely that the grid outputs are summed or projected. # For implementation, we will assume the grid outputs are summed to form a vector of size Rmax, # then projected to hiddendim. Or, more likely, the "feature" is the result of the element-wise ops # which results in a scalar per rank, and these scalars are the input. # Let's assume the input to the MLP is the concatenated vector of all rank contributions. # Simplified: Input to MLP is the spatial feature vector (size R) concatenated with param feature vector (size Rparam). # We need to align dimensions. Let's assume a linear projection to hiddendim. # Density Input # fsigmaspatial (N, Rsigma) and fparam (N, Rparam) # Concatenate fsigmainput = torch.cat([fsigmaspatial, fparam], dim=1) # Project to hiddendim # Note: The paper doesn't explicitly state a projection layer, but MLP input dim must match. # We'll assume a linear layer is part of the decoder or implicit. # For this pseudocode, we pass the concatenated vector to the MLP. # If dimensions don't match, the MLP weights must be initialized accordingly. # Color Input fcolorinput = torch.cat([fcolorspatial, fparam], dim=1) # 4. Encode Inputs # PE(x) and SH(d) are added to the features or concatenated. # Paper: sigma(x) = gsigma(fsigma(x), EP(x)) # This implies concatenation or addition. # We will concatenate. # Placeholder for PE and SH encoding functions pex = positionalencoding(xcoords) # (N, Dpe) shd = sphericalharmonicsencoding(viewdirs) # (N, Dsh) # 5. Decode # Density # Input to gsigma: fsigmainput concatenated with PE(x) # We need to ensure fsigmainput is projected to match MLP input size if necessary. # Assuming gsigma handles the dimensionality. sigma = self.gsigma(torch.cat([fsigmainput, pex], dim=1)) # Color # Input to gc: fcolorinput concatenated with SH(d) color = self.gc(torch.cat([fcolorinput, shd], dim=1)) return sigma.squeeze(-1), color def computeloss(self, sigma, color, gtcolor, rays): # LREC lrec = F.mseloss(color, gtcolor) # LL1 # Apply to all parameters in the model (matrices, vectors) l1loss = 0.0 for name, param in self.namedparameters(): if 'paramvectors' in name: # Parameter vectors: sum ||1 - w|| l1loss += torch.sum(torch.abs(1 - param)) else: # Matrices/Vectors: sum ||w||1 / |W| l1loss += torch.sum(torch.abs(param)) / param.numel() # LTV # Simplified TV loss calculation on spatial matrices # LTV1 on vectors tv1 = 0.0 for v in [self.densityvX, self.densityvY, self.densityvZ, self.colorvX, self.colorvY, self.colorvZ]: # Diff along first dim diff = v[:, 1:] - v[:,:-1] tv1 += torch.sum(torch.norm(diff, dim=0)) / (v.shape[0] v.shape[1]) # LTV2 on matrices tv2 = 0.0 for M in [self.densityMXY, self.densityMXZ, self.densityMYZ, self.colorMXY, self.colorMXZ, self.colorMYZ]: # Diff along rows and cols diffh = M[:, 1:,:] - M[:,:-1,:] diffw = M[:,:, 1:] - M[:,:,:-1] tv2 += torch.sum(diffh2) / (M.shape[0] M.shape[1] M.shape[2]) tv2 += torch.sum(diffw2) / (M.shape[0] M.shape[1] M.shape[2]) ltv = tv1 + tv2 # Total Loss lambda1 = 1e-4 # Initial lambda2 = 1.0 return lrec + lambda1 l1loss + lambda2 ltv Parameters Spatial Resolution (N): Initial 128^3. Can increase to 300^3 for complex scenes. Low-rank Components (R): R\sigma = 16 (density), Rc = 48 (color), Rp = 4 (parameter). MLP Hidden Dim: 128 channels. Batch Size: 4096. Samples per Ray: 192 (initial), 512 (if grid is 300^3). Optimizer: Adam (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99). Learning Rate: 0.02 for matrices/vectors, 0.001 for MLPs. L1 Weight (\lambda1): 10^{-4} initially, 10^{-5} after 2,000 iterations. TV Weight (\lambda2): 1.0. Training Iterations: 30,000 for static, 90,000 for dynamic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noise: Without L1 and TV regularization, excessive noise and film grains appear in spatial matrices and images. Memory: High-resolution datasets (e.g., 1024x1024) require significant RAM (~29 GB for ray storage alone). ViSNeRF filters rays not intersecting the bounding box to reduce runtime RAM. Hardware: Minimum 32 GB RAM and 10 GB VRAM recommended; 64 GB RAM and 16 GB VRAM ideal. Bounding Box: Empty voxels must be handled. A mask volume is created at iteration 2,000 to shrink the bounding box and enable voxel skipping. Time Complexity: Factorization reduces spatial complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2) and parameter complexity from O(M^K) to O(M), resulting in overall O(N^2 M). Memory Complexity: Reduced from O(N^3 M^K) to O(N^2 M). Performance: ViSNeRF is the fastest among compared methods (InSituNet, CoordNet, StyleGAN2, EG3D) for training time. It is the slowest for inference time, with frame rates dropping substantially for 1024x1024 images (at least 1.86 FPS for 256x256). Strengths: High visualization quality (PSNR/SSIM) with significantly reduced training data (95% less than InSituNet) and smaller model size than most baselines. Supports super-resolution synthesis. Limitations: High VRAM/RAM requirements compared to traditional DVR/IR. Slow inference speed for high resolutions. ViSNeRF was introduced in the paper "ViSNeRF: Efficient Multidimensional Neural Radiance Field Representation for Visualization Synthesis of Dynamic Volumetric Scenes". It addresses the need for efficient visualization of dynamic volumetric scenes (e.g., scientific simulations) by extending the NeRF framework with tensor factorization techniques (TensoRF, K-Planes) to handle arbitrary parameters. ViSNeRF: Efficient Multidimensional Neural Radiance Field Representation for Visualization Synthesis of Dynamic Volumetric Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/pacificvis64226.2025.00029, fetched 2026-10-26

name: EBAD-NeRF
head: Event-driven Bundle Adjustment for Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields
body: EBAD-NeRF is a method for reconstructing sharp 3D radiance fields and accurate camera trajectories from motion-blurred images and hybrid event-RGB data. It solves the problem of modeling complex camera motion blur during exposure time, which standard NeRF methods fail to capture accurately. Unlike BAD-NeRF, which uses linear interpolation between start and end poses, EBAD-NeRF models the motion trajectory using multiple learnable poses, and unlike E2 NeRF, it jointly optimizes these poses and NeRF parameters rather than relying on fixed poses from pre-deblurred images. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Blurry RGB images B, corresponding event data (intensity changes), and exposure start/end times t{start}, t{end} for each view. Outputs: A sharp NeRF model F\Theta (mapping 3D coordinates and view directions to color and density) and a set of learnable camera poses modeling the motion trajectory during exposure. Data Structures: NeRF MLP (F\Theta): A multi-layer perceptron taking encoded 3D position \mathbf{o} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input, outputting volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Learnable Poses: For each view, a set of p poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^p in SE(3) space, sampled evenly over the exposure interval [t{start}, t{end}]. Ray Sampling: Rays are divided into N equal parts between l{near} and l{far}. One point is sampled per part. Numbered Steps: 1. Trajectory Modeling: For each view, define p learnable camera poses \{Pi\}{i=1}^p distributed evenly across the exposure time [t{start}, t{end}]. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel \mathbf{x} in the blurry image, generate a ray \mathbf{r} based on the camera projection. Divide the ray segment [l{near}, l{far}] into N equal intervals. 3. Sampling: Sample N points along the ray. For each point i, determine its 3D world coordinate \mathbf{o}i and view direction \mathbf{d}. 4. Positional Encoding: Encode the 3D coordinate \mathbf{o}i and view direction \mathbf{d} using positional encoding \gammaK(\cdot): \gammaK(\mathbf{x}) = \{\sin(2^k \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^k \pi \mathbf{x})\}{k=0}^K where K is the number of frequency bands. 5. NeRF Query: Pass the encoded coordinates and directions into the NeRF MLP F\Theta to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for each sampled point. 6. Volume Rendering (Sharpness): Compute the sharp color C(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{x}) for the ray using volume rendering: C(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \deltai = l{i+1} - li is the distance between adjacent points, and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transparency. 7. Blur Simulation: Model the motion blur by averaging the rendered sharp colors from the p poses in the trajectory: \hat{B}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{p} \sum{i=1}^p C(P(ti), \mathbf{x}) where P(ti) is the pose at time ti. 8. Loss Computation: Photo-metric Blur Loss: Compare the simulated blurry image \hat{B} with the observed blurry image B. Intensity-change-metric Event Loss: Supervise the pose changes during exposure using event data to ensure the modeled trajectory matches the intensity changes captured by the event camera. 9. Optimization: Jointly optimize the NeRF parameters \Theta and the learnable poses \{Pi\} using the combined losses. Parameters: N: Number of stratified samples per ray (Not given in the sources). p: Number of learnable poses per view to model the trajectory (Not given in the sources). K: Number of frequency bands in positional encoding (Not given in the sources). l{near}, l{far}: Near and far clipping planes for ray sampling (Not given in the sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The integration of light intensity over time requires accurate temporal sampling of poses. Insufficient p may fail to model complex non-linear motion. Boundaries: The method assumes a static 3D scene; dynamic scenes are not explicitly handled by the core formulation. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive due to the joint optimization of NeRF parameters and multiple camera poses per view, requiring multiple forward passes through the NeRF for each pixel to simulate blur. Memory Complexity: Requires storing p poses per view in addition to the NeRF parameters. Strengths: Capable of recovering accurate camera trajectories and sharper 3D representations from blurry images by leveraging event data for explicit motion supervision. Limitations: Requires hybrid event-RGB data; performance depends on the quality and synchronization of event data. When to use: When reconstructing scenes from motion-blurred images where event camera data is available and accurate camera trajectory estimation is required. When not: When only RGB data is available (use BAD-NeRF or E2 NeRF) or when the scene is dynamic. EBAD-NeRF was proposed by Yunshan Qi, Lin Zhu, Yifan Zhao, Nan Bao, and Jia Li. It addresses limitations in prior works like BAD-NeRF (linear interpolation of poses) and E2 NeRF (fixed poses from pre-deblurred images) by introducing event-driven bundle adjustment. The method was published in 2024. Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields with Event-driven Bundle Adjustment, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3680569, fetched 2026-10-27

name: DINO-enhanced NeRF
head: DINO variants, NeRF with DINO features
body: DINO-enhanced NeRF refers to a family of radiance field optimization methods that integrate pre-trained DINO (Distillation of Knowledge without Labels) vision features into the NeRF architecture to enhance 3D reconstruction, particularly in few-shot scenarios. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on positional encodings and view-dependent color/density predictions, these variants augment the input space with semantic or structural priors extracted from a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone. The defining characteristic of this family is the investigation of how self-supervised visual representations align with geometric constraints; however, empirical evidence suggests that for extreme few-shot reconstruction (e.g., 5 views), these enhancements often degrade performance compared to the baseline due to feature-task mismatch and overfitting. The DINO-enhanced NeRF family modifies the baseline NeRF input space by injecting external feature vectors \mathbf{f} derived from a frozen or fine-tuned DINO model. The core volume rendering equation remains unchanged, but the neural field F\Theta accepts an augmented input tuple: F\Theta([\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \gamma(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})]) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) where \gamma denotes positional encoding. The shared principles across all variants in this family include: 1. Feature Extraction Source: Features are extracted from a pre-trained DINOv2-base model. The base model is typically frozen, or adapted via low-rank mechanisms, to provide semantic context. 2. Dimensionality Projection: DINO features are high-dimensional (e.g., 768 dimensions for DINOv2-base) and must be projected to match the NeRF MLP's hidden dimensionality (typically 256) before fusion. 3. Unified Backbone: All variants share a unified NeRF backbone to ensure fair comparison: an 8-layer MLP with 256 hidden units, ReLU activations, a skip connection at layer 4, and 10 frequency bands for position encoding and 4 for direction encoding. 4. Training Configuration: Models are trained using the Adam optimizer (lr = 2 \times 10^{-4}) for 200 epochs with cosine learning rate annealing, gradient clipping (max norm 1.0), and dropout (p=0.1). Early stopping is applied based on validation PSNR with a patience of 20. 5. Rendering: Stratified sampling with 32 samples per ray is used for rendering. This method adapts frozen DINO vision features to the geometric objectives of NeRF by applying Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to the attention layers of the Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone. It addresses the misalignment between semantic DINO features and NeRF’s geometric requirements, which frozen features alone may not satisfy. Unlike frozen feature baselines, this approach makes only low-rank matrices trainable, allowing the model to adapt to few-shot 3D reconstruction while preserving pre-trained knowledge. A mechanism used to fuse DINO features with NeRF's positional encoding, optimized to handle the large number of 3D points sampled during training. The cross-attention mechanism utilizes 8 attention heads and a dropout rate of 0.1 to prevent overfitting. A technique that extracts DINO features at multiple input resolutions to capture complementary information (fine details from shallow layers/resolutions, semantic context from deeper ones) and fuses them using a learnable weighting mechanism. The fused representation is calculated as: f{fused}(x) = \sum{s=1}^{S} ws f^{(s)}(x) where f^{(s)}(x) is the feature vector at scale s, ws are learnable weights such that \sum ws = 1, and S is the number of scales. Input resolutions for feature extraction are 224x224, 448x448, and 896x896. The fused representation is projected to match the NeRF MLP input dimensions (256). The DINO-enhanced NeRF family originates from a systematic investigation into the limitations of combining pre-trained vision features with NeRF for few-shot 3D reconstruction. The work was published as a preprint in 2026. The study was motivated by the common assumption that pre-trained vision features should improve few-shot 3D reconstruction by providing strong semantic priors. However, the authors found counterintuitive results: all DINO variants performed worse than the baseline NeRF, achieving PSNR values around 12.9-13.0 compared to the baseline's 14.71 on the Lego dataset with 5 training views. This represents a degradation of approximately 1.7 PSNR points. The study evaluated four approaches: baseline NeRF, frozen DINO features, LoRA-fine-tuned features, and multi-scale features. The findings suggest that for few-shot scenarios, simpler architectures focusing on geometric consistency may be more effective than complex feature fusion approaches, due to issues such as feature-task mismatch, overfitting to limited data, and integration challenges. Limitations of NERF with pre-trained Vision Features for Few-Shot 3D Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18208v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LoRA Fine-Tuning of DINO
head: LoRA-NeRF, NeRF with LoRA-fine-tuned DINO features
body: LoRA Fine-Tuning of DINO adapts frozen DINOv2 features to the geometric objectives of NeRF by applying Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to the attention layers of the Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone. It addresses the misalignment between semantic features and geometric reconstruction by making only low-rank matrices trainable while keeping pre-trained weights frozen. Unlike frozen feature baselines, it allows the model to adapt DINO features to few-shot 3D reconstruction requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Pre-trained DINOv2-base model weights W0, training images, camera poses, and scene geometry. Output: Fine-tuned DINO feature extractor with LoRA matrices (A, B), and the NeRF field F\Theta parameters. Data Structures: LoRA Matrices: A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}: Down-projection matrix. B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}: Up-projection matrix. r: LoRA rank (default 16). d: Dimension of the attention layer weights. Feature Projection: DINO features (768-dim) are projected to 256-dim to match the NeRF MLP hidden dimension. Steps: 1. Initialize LoRA: For each attention layer in the DINOv2 ViT backbone, initialize trainable matrices A and B. The pre-trained weights W0 remain frozen. 2. Forward Pass (Feature Extraction): Compute the attention output using the adapted weight matrix: W = W0 + BA where W is the effective weight matrix. Extract features \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) from the ViT. 3. Project Features: Project \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) from 768 dimensions to 256 dimensions. 4. NeRF Forward Pass: Feed positional encodings \gamma(\mathbf{x}), \gamma(\mathbf{d}), and projected features \mathbf{f}'(\mathbf{x}) into the NeRF MLP F\Theta: F\Theta([\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \gamma(\mathbf{d}), \mathbf{f}'(\mathbf{x})]) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) 5. Optimization: Update only A and B (and NeRF parameters) using the Adam optimizer (lr = 2 \times 10^{-4}) for 200 epochs with cosine annealing. Gradient clipping (max norm 1.0) and dropout (p=0.1) are applied. Parameters: LoRA rank r = 16. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 2 \times 10^{-4}. Epochs: 200. Edge Cases: LoRA is applied selectively to attention layers only. DINO features are computed once and cached for efficiency. A technique that fine-tunes the diffusion model with minimal computational overhead, making it adaptable to new tasks by modifying a few parameters within the model. Time Complexity: Training typically takes 2-4 hours per experiment. Memory: Mixed-precision training is used to accelerate experiments. Performance: On the Lego dataset with 5 training views, LoRA-NeRF achieves a PSNR of 12.97, SSIM of 0.45, and LPIPS of 0.54. This is slightly worse than Baseline NeRF (PSNR 14.71) but comparable to Frozen DINO-NeRF (PSNR 12.99). Strengths: Parameter-efficient adaptation of semantic features to geometric tasks. Limitations: All DINO variants performed worse than Baseline NeRF on the tested dataset. Originated in the study of limitations of NeRF with pre-trained vision features for few-shot 3D reconstruction. It leverages LoRA [10] to adapt DINOv2-base features. The implementation is based on PyTorch [27] and uses Weights & Biases [28] for tracking. Limitations of NERF with pre-trained Vision Features for Few-Shot 3D Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18208v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: NeurMiPs
head: NeurMiPs (Neural Mixture of Planar Experts), Neural Mixture of Planar Experts, Neural Mixture of Planar Experts for View Synthesis
body: NeurMiPs represents a 3D scene as a mixture of K learnable rectangular planar surfaces, where each surface acts as an independent "expert" predicting view-dependent color and transparency via a local neural radiance field. It solves the frontal-parallel limitation of traditional Multi-Plane Imagery (MPI) and the blurring artifacts of large-scale NeRFs by combining explicit geometric priors with implicit appearance modeling, offering superior extrapolation capabilities and real-time rendering speeds. Unlike voxel-based methods that prune unseen regions, NeurMiPs maintains a continuous representation on planes, allowing it to generalize better to novel viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse 3D point cloud \{xi\} from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); a set of training images with known camera poses. Outputs: Rendered pixel color c(\mathbf{r}) and expected depth d(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: 1. Planar Expert Geometry (sk): A tuple for each expert k \in \{1, \dots, K\} containing: pk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center coordinate of the rectangle. nk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Normalized 3D normal vector of the plane. uk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Normalized up vector defining the y-axis direction of the plane's local coordinate system. wk, hk \in \mathbb{R}: Width and height of the rectangle. 2. Student Radiance Field (fk): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for each expert k. Architecture: Three fully-connected hidden layers with ReLU activation; final output layer with sigmoid activation. Input: 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}k on the plane and normalized ray direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2. The direction \mathbf{d} is transformed into a higher-dimensional space using high-frequency positional encoding before entering the network. Output: Color \mathbf{c}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 and transparency \alphak \in \mathbb{R}. 3. Alpha Textures (Ai): Optional pre-baked textures of size w \times h for each plane i, storing view-independent alpha values for accelerated inference. Numbered Steps: 1. Plane Initialization: Initialize plane parameters \{sk\} using the coarse 3D point cloud \{xi\} from SfM. Plane centers pk are selected via farthest point sampling. Orientations nk, uk are initialized as normals estimated from local point sets around pk. Optimize the geometry parameters by minimizing the geometry loss \mathcal{L}g: \mathcal{L}g = \sumi \mink d(xi, sk) + \lambda \sumk (wk hk)^2 where d(xi, sk) is the distance from point xi to the closest rectangular surface sk, and (wk hk)^2 is an area regularization term to prevent arbitrarily large rectangles. \lambda is a weighting factor. 2. Teacher Model Training: Train a large-capacity standard NeRF (the "teacher") to serve as a knowledge source. Point sampling for the teacher is conducted through the NeurMiPs ray-plane intersection mechanism. Jointly optimize the planar experts' geometric parameters and the teacher's weights using the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}g + \mathcal{L}c where \mathcal{L}c is the photometric loss. 3. Distillation: Distill knowledge from the teacher to the student experts (fk). For each planar expert, draw random points uniformly from its rectangle and random view directions from the half unit sphere. Update the student network parameters by minimizing the L2 loss between the teacher's output (\mathbf{c}{teacher}, \alpha{teacher}) and the student's output (\mathbf{c}k, \alphak) for both color and alpha values. 4. Fine-Tuning: Fix the plane parameters \{sk\}. Fine-tune the student radiance field models fk to improve rendering quality by minimizing the L2-photometric loss \mathcal{L}c between the rendered pixel color and the ground-truth color: \mathcal{L}c = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \|c(\mathbf{r}) - c{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2. 5. Ray-Plane Intersection: For a ray r = \{o, d\} (origin o, direction d) and plane k (normal nk, center pk), compute the intersection point xk: xk = o + \frac{(pk - o) \cdot nk}{d \cdot nk} d Only keep rectangles that are actually intersected by the ray. 6. Radiance Evaluation: For each intersecting planar expert k, evaluate the neural radiance function fk using the intersection point coordinate x{p,k} (projected onto the plane's local 2D coordinates) and ray direction d to output transparency \alphak and color ck. Note: If Alpha Baking is enabled, retrieve \alphak by bilinear interpolation from the baked texture Ak instead of evaluating the network for alpha. 7. Alpha Composition: Collect the set of point samples \{xj, cj, \alphaj\} from all intersecting experts. Sort the points from closest to furthest relative to the eye o. Compute the final ray color: c(\mathbf{r}) = \sumj \left( \prod{i}^{j-1} (1 - \alphai) \right) \alphaj cj. 8. Early Ray Termination (Optional): If the accumulated transmittance \prod (1 - \alphai) is close to zero, stop evaluating further intersecting rectangles to save computation. If the sum of alpha values is smaller than 1, re-normalize the alphas. 9. Depth Estimation (Optional): Estimate expected depth d(\mathbf{r}) along the ray using alpha composition: d(\mathbf{r}) = \sumj \left( \prod{i}^{j-1} (1 - \alphai) \right) \alphaj tj where tj is the depth (distance from origin) of sampled point j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rayplaneintersection(rayorigin, raydir, planecenter, planenormal): """ Computes intersection of ray with infinite plane. Returns distance t along ray, or None if parallel/no intersection. """ denom = np.dot(raydir, planenormal) if np.isclose(denom, 0.0): return None t = np.dot(planecenter - rayorigin, planenormal) / denom if t < 1e-6: # Intersection behind ray origin return None return t def projecttoplane(point, planecenter, planenormal, planeup): """ Projects 3D point to 2D coordinates on the plane. Assumes planeup is orthogonal to planenormal. """ # Construct local basis # planeright = cross(planenormal, planeup) # Not strictly needed if up is fixed # However, standard projection uses two orthogonal vectors in the plane. # Let's assume planeup defines Y, and we derive X. planeright = np.cross(planenormal, planeup) planeright = planeright / np.linalg.norm(planeright) v = point - planecenter xcoord = np.dot(v, planeright) ycoord = np.dot(v, planeup) return np.array([xcoord, ycoord]) def renderrayneurmiips(rayorigin, raydir, planes, studentnetworks, usealphabaking, alphatextures): """ Renders a single ray using NeurMiPs. planes: List of dicts with keys 'center', 'normal', 'up', 'width', 'height' studentnetworks: List of MLP functions fk usealphabaking: Boolean alphatextures: List of 2D arrays (w x h) for baked alpha values """ intersections = [] # Step 5: Ray-Plane Intersection for k, plane in enumerate(planes): t = rayplaneintersection(rayorigin, raydir, plane['center'], plane['normal']) if t is not None: # Check if intersection point is within the rectangle bounds intersectionpoint = rayorigin + t raydir localcoords = projecttoplane(intersectionpoint, plane['center'], plane['normal'], plane['up']) # Check bounds [-w/2, w/2] and [-h/2, h/2] halfw = plane['width'] / 2.0 halfh = plane['height'] / 2.0 if -halfw <= localcoords[0] <= halfw and -halfh <= localcoords[1] <= halfh: intersections.append({ 'k': k, 't': t, 'localcoords': localcoords, 'point': intersectionpoint }) # Sort by distance (closest to furthest) intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x['t']) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = np.zeros(3) # Step 6 & 7: Radiance Evaluation and Alpha Composition for item in intersections: k = item['k'] localcoords = item['localcoords'] # Evaluate Radiance # Input to network: localcoords (2D) and raydir (3D) # Note: The paper says input is xk (3D space coordinate on plane) and d. # Usually, for planar experts, the 3D coordinate is mapped to 2D or used directly. # The paper states: "evaluate... using intersection point coordinate x{p,k}". # We assume the network takes the 2D local coordinates or the 3D point. # Given "xk (3D space coordinate on the plane)" in formula 1, we pass the 3D point. # However, standard practice for planar sprites often uses 2D. # The paper says: "The function takes the 3D space coordinate xk... as input". # So we pass the 3D intersection point. inputcoord = item['point'] inputdir = raydir # High-frequency encoding for direction (standard NeRF practice mentioned in paper) # Assuming a standard positional encoding function exists encodeddir = positionalencoding(inputdir) # Student Network Evaluation # fk takes (xk, d) # We need to implement the MLP structure: 3 hidden layers (ReLU), 1 output (Sigmoid) # For brevity, assume studentnetworks[k] is a callable that handles this color, alpha = studentnetworksk # Alpha Baking (Optional Optimization) if usealphabaking: # Retrieve alpha from texture via bilinear interpolation # Map localcoords to texture coordinates [0, 1] h, w = alphatextures[k].shape u = (localcoords[0] + planes[k]['width']/2) / planes[k]['width'] v = (localcoords[1] + planes[k]['height']/2) / planes[k]['height'] # Bilinear interpolation logic would go here alpha = bilinearinterpolate(alphatextures[k], u, v) # Early Ray Termination if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break # Alpha Composition weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha finalcolor += weight color accumulatedtransmittance = (1 - alpha) return finalcolor def trainneurmiips(planes, studentnetworks, teachernetwork, pointcloud, trainingimages, optimizer): """ Training loop for NeurMiPs. """ # Hyperparameters teacherepochs = 6000 distillepochs = 1500 finetuneepochs = 2500 lr = 5e-4 # Step 1: Plane Initialization # Optimize plane geometry parameters {sk} using point cloud # Loss: Lg = sum(mink d(xi, sk)) + lambda sum((wk hk)^2) optimizegeometry(planes, pointcloud) # Step 2: Teacher Model Training # Train teacher NeRF. Sampling points via NeurMiPs ray-plane intersection. # Jointly optimize plane geometry and teacher weights. for epoch in range(teacherepochs): for image in trainingimages: # Render using current planes and teacher # Loss: Ltotal = Lg + Lc loss = computelossteacher(planes, teachernetwork, image) optimizer.step(loss) # Step 3: Distillation # Fix teacher? No, distill from teacher to students. # Draw random points from rectangles and random directions. for epoch in range(distillepochs): for k in range(len(planes)): # Sample points uniformly from rectangle k # Sample directions from half unit sphere # Minimize L2 loss between teacher output and student output (color + alpha) lossdistill = computedistillationloss(planes[k], studentnetworks[k], teachernetwork) optimizer.step(lossdistill) # Step 4: Fine-Tuning # Fix plane parameters for epoch in range(finetuneepochs): for image in trainingimages: # Render using students # Minimize Lc (photometric loss) lossfinetune = computephotometricloss(planes, studentnetworks, image) optimizer.step(lossfinetune) Parameters: K: Number of planar experts. Typical values: 500 for Replica dataset, 1000 for Tanks & Temples dataset. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}. Training Epochs: Teacher model: 6,000 epochs; Distillation: 1,500 epochs; Fine-tuning: 2,500 epochs. \lambda: Weighting factor for area regularization in \mathcal{L}g. Value not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Finite Plane Size: Planes may not cover all regions in extreme viewpoints, inducing higher depth error for scenes modeled by the background. This can be resolved by adopting multiple-layer boxes or incorporating techniques from NeRF++ for unbounded scenes. SfM Dependency: The method relies heavily on SfM point clouds for plane initialization. If sparse point clouds are noisy or unavailable, performance degrades significantly. Unbounded Scenes: NeurMiPs currently cannot handle unbounded scenes natively. A solution involves modeling background texture with non-Euclidean coordinates. Alpha Baking Artifacts: Applying alpha baking directly during inference might bring a minor rendering performance drop or quality drop due to discretization of the continuous radiance field. Time Complexity: Rendering is efficient due to closed-form ray-plane intersection and the fact that each ray hits only a handful of planes. Custom CUDA kernels fuse network evaluation, allowing parallel rendering of all experts. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower memory footprint compared to voxel-based approaches (e.g., PlenOctrees, KiloNeRF) because it uses compact planar parameters and small MLPs. Alpha baking increases memory usage for textures. Measured Performance: Replica Dataset: Achieves 19.16 frames per second (FPS) on a single TITAN RTX using customized CUDA kernels. Tanks & Temples (Truck Scene): Achieves 976 FPS at 1920x1080 resolution on a single RTX 3090 desktop using texture baking. Quality (Tanks & Temples): PSNR 28.46, SSIM 0.908, LPIPS 0.089. Quality (Replica): PSNR 30.80, SSIM 0.900, LPIPS 0.088. Strengths: More sample-efficient than volume rendering; better extrapolation than voxel-based methods; captures detailed textures on planar surfaces with sharp boundaries; avoids "fog-like" artifacts of NeRF and "stack-of-cards" effects of MPI. Limitations: Cannot handle unbounded scenes without modification; performance degrades with poor/no SfM data; finite plane size causes depth errors in extreme viewpoints. NeurMiPs (Neural Mixture of Planar Experts) was introduced in the paper "NeurMiPs: Neural Mixture of Planar Experts for View Synthesis". It builds upon the success of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and multi-plane imagery (MPI), aiming to combine the geometric flexibility of neural rendering with the efficiency of explicit planar representations. The method was developed to address the limitations of existing approaches in large-scale scenes and view extrapolation. NeurMiPs: Neural Mixture of Planar Experts for View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01525, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dynamic Scene and Temporal Modeling
head: Dynamic NeRF, 4D Radiance Fields, Time-Conditioned NeRF
body: Dynamic Scene and Temporal Modeling extends the static Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture Parent to represent scenes that change over time, solving the "ghosting" and blurriness artifacts that occur when static NeRFs are applied to video sequences. It differs from sibling methods by augmenting the input space with temporal signals or by explicitly modeling deformation fields, rather than treating the scene as a fixed 3D volume. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as uncertainty, semantic logits, or physical properties like albedo and normals. Gear-NeRF is a method for free-viewpoint rendering and tracking of dynamic scenes that leverages semantic information from image segmentation models to stratify the scene into motion-based 'gears', allowing for region-specific spatio-temporal sampling resolution. It addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling in dynamic scenes by assigning higher-resolution feature volumes to regions with larger motion scales. Unlike sibling methods that use a single unified 4D volume or explicit time-parameterized MLPs, Gear-NeRF maintains a series of parallel 4D feature volumes, one for each gear level, enabling adaptive resource allocation based on local motion intensity. This method adapts the static Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture Parent to represent dynamic scenes by introducing a temporal dimension. It solves the problem of "ghosting" and blurry predictions in static NeRFs when applied to video sequences by allowing the scene representation to vary over time. It differs from sibling methods like ST-NeRF or KFD-NeRF by using a minimal modification: simply concatenating a positional encoding of time to the spatial input, rather than employing complex warping fields, latent codes, or separate temporal modules. Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis is a method for rendering dynamic scenes by modeling a static scene at a canonical time step and forward warping the entire canonical field to other time steps. It addresses the many-to-one and one-to-many mapping difficulties inherent in dynamic scene reconstruction using differentiable forward warping with average splatting and an inpaint network. Unlike backward flow methods such as NDVG, this approach leverages a canonical representation to simplify the deformation field, achieving state-of-the-art performance on public datasets, particularly for canonical frames. Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field (DAP-NeRF) is a method for novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes using monocular video input. It solves the problem of modeling temporal dynamics without requiring multi-view data or prior geometric knowledge of moving objects. Unlike ParticleNeRF, which encodes the entire scene with particles and requires multiple camera views per frame, DAP-NeRF applies appearance particles only to dynamic elements while maintaining a static grid-based field for the background, enabling efficient linear interpolation and monocular training. KFD-NeRF is a dynamic neural radiance field method that models the 4D radiance field as a dynamic system with temporally varying states, estimated using a Kalman filter to combine observations from input data and predictions based on local linear motion equations. It differs from sibling methods like Gear-NeRF and NeRF with Time Parameter by explicitly separating motion estimation into an observer branch (direct observation) and a predictor branch (history-based prediction), weighted by a learnable Kalman gain, rather than relying solely on time-conditioned feature interpolation or rigid deformation priors. SLS4D is a method for 4D novel view synthesis that represents dynamic scenes using a sparse, compact, and informative latent feature space, significantly reducing the number of network parameters compared to previous state-of-the-art methods like V4D. It distinguishes itself by abandoning direct coordinate-based feature determination in favor of relative relationships in a latent space, utilizing dense learnable time slots for temporal continuity and an attention-based interpolator decoder for spatial feature aggregation. ST-NeRF is a layered radiance field representation designed for editable free-viewpoint videos of dynamic scenes containing independently moving or articulated objects. It solves the problem of spatial and temporal consistency in dynamic neural rendering by disentangling the position, deformation, and appearance of each entity into separate continuous functions spanning space and time. Unlike monolithic dynamic NeRFs that model the entire scene as a single time-dependent field, ST-NeRF uses a layered architecture where each object is a distinct entity, enabling specific editing operations such as rescaling, shifting, duplication, removal, and re-timing. ER-NeRF is a Conditional NeRF framework for effective, high-accuracy dynamic portrait creation, producing dynamic portrait videos synchronized with audio. It utilizes spatial regions’ distinct contributions to steer dynamic head modeling and develops a concise and articulate Tri-Plane Hash Representation. It introduces rapid and straightforward Adaptive Pose Encoding to enhance the separation of the head and torso. ER-NeRF attains instantaneous rendering and rapid convergence using a compact model size. Additional fine-tuning might be necessary to sustain superior rendering outcomes for poses that exceed the scope of the training dataset. NeRF-MS is a method that diminishes vagueness in visual alterations by implementing a ternary loss to standardize the spread of visual codes across each image. It suggests a temporary decomposition unit to more effectively distinguish still scenes from dynamic objects. Trials using both real-life outdoor and artificial datasets reveal that NeRF-MS attains cutting-edge results in multi-sequence scenarios, markedly enhancing rendering efficiency through the reconstruction of 3D-consistent visuals and minimizing ghost effects. The technique might encounter difficulties in managing significant sequence discrepancies, like severe alterations in the visual aspect of scenes caused by the activation of lights. DCT-NeRF is a method that learns smooth and stable trajectories for each point in space in an input video sequence using Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) parameterization, allowing for high-quality reconstruction and consistent motion extrapolation beyond the last available frame. It parameterizes trajectories with the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to model motion. The method handles temporal occlusions and reflects changes in reflectance over time. The concept of extending NeRF to dynamic scenes emerged shortly after the initial publication of static NeRF Parent. Early approaches focused on simple time concatenation, while later methods introduced complex deformation fields, canonical spaces, and hybrid representations to handle non-rigid motion and occlusions. These methods are widely used in free-viewpoint video synthesis, digital humans, and 4D scene reconstruction.
