name: Gear-NeRF
head: Gear-NeRF: Free-Viewpoint Rendering and Tracking with Motion-aware Spatio-Temporal Sampling
body: Gear-NeRF is a method for free-viewpoint rendering and tracking of dynamic scenes that leverages semantic information from image segmentation models to stratify the scene into motion-based 'gears', allowing for region-specific spatio-temporal sampling resolution. It addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling in dynamic scenes by assigning higher-resolution feature volumes to regions with larger motion scales. Unlike sibling methods that use a single unified 4D volume or explicit time-parameterized MLPs, Gear-NeRF maintains a series of parallel 4D feature volumes, one for each gear level, enabling adaptive resource allocation based on local motion intensity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of W input videos \mathcal{V} = \{V1, V2, \dots, VW\} of a dynamic scene with calibrated camera poses. Output: Rendered images for novel views and time steps, and semantic embeddings for object tracking. Data Structures: The representation consists of N{gear} parallel 4D feature volumes, where each volume corresponds to a specific gear level G \in \{1, \dots, N{gear}\}. Feature Volumes: Each gear G has its own set of 2D feature grids for spatio-temporal embeddings. Shared Components: Planar spatial embeddings hj and linear transforms Bj are shared across all gears. Gear-Specific Components: Each gear G has its own spatio-temporal embeddings k^Gj. Dimensionality: Embeddings are in M-dimensional space. Parameters: N{gear}: The total number of gear levels used to stratify the scene representation based on motion scales. M: The dimensionality of the feature vectors. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Semantic Embedding Optimization: Optimize a 4D semantic embedding based on powerful image segmentation models (specifically SAM) to profile the scene into semantic regions. This embedding guides the stratification of the scene. 2. Gear Determination: For any space-time coordinate (\mathbf{x}, t), compute the gear level g(\mathbf{x}, t) using a planar-factorized 4D feature volume. The formula is: g(\mathbf{x}, t) = \mathbf{1}^\top (h'1(x, y) \bowtie k'1(z, t) + h'2(x, z) \bowtie k'2(y, t) + h'3(y, z) \bowtie k'3(x, t)) where h'j and k'j are functions evaluated by bilinear interpolation on regularly spaced 2D feature grids, \bowtie denotes element-wise product, and \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. Note: The source text cuts off the arguments for k'1, but implies a similar structure to the feature vector calculation. Regions with larger motion scales are assigned higher gear levels through this scheme. 3. Feature Vector Computation: For a specific gear level G and coordinate (\mathbf{x}, t), compute the feature vector \mathbf{f}^G(\mathbf{x}, t) by summing three terms, each involving an element-wise product of 2D plane embeddings and a linear transform: \mathbf{f}^G(\mathbf{x}, t) = B1 (h1(x, y) \bowtie k^G1(z, t)) + B2 (h2(x, z) \bowtie k^G2(y, t)) + B3 (h3(y, z) \bowtie k^G3(x, t)) where: hj(\cdot, \cdot) are spatial planar embeddings shared by all gears. k^Gj(\cdot, \cdot) are gear-specific spatio-temporal embeddings. Bj are linear transforms mapping the products to feature vectors. \bowtie denotes element-wise product. 4. Radiance Field Prediction: Pass the feature vector \mathbf{f}^G(\mathbf{x}, t) through a tiny MLP to predict volume density \sigma and view-dependent emitted color \mathbf{c}, given the viewing direction \mathbf{d}. 5. Spatio-Temporal Sampling: Perform spatio-temporal sampling for ray integration. Regions assigned to higher gear levels (larger motion scales) are sampled at higher resolution to improve dynamic novel view synthesis. 6. Rendering: Integrate \sigma and \mathbf{c} along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gearnerfforward(xyz, time, direction, gearlevel, params): """ Computes the radiance field output for a specific gear level. Args: xyz: Spatial coordinates (x, y, z) time: Temporal coordinate t direction: Viewing direction d gearlevel: Integer G indicating the gear level params: Object containing shared and gear-specific parameters Returns: sigma: Volume density color: View-dependent color """ # 1. Compute Feature Vector for Gear G # Shared spatial embeddings h1xy = bilinearinterp(params.h1, xyz[:, 0], xyz[:, 1]) h2xz = bilinearinterp(params.h2, xyz[:, 0], xyz[:, 2]) h3yz = bilinearinterp(params.h3, xyz[:, 1], xyz[:, 2]) # Gear-specific spatio-temporal embeddings k1zt = bilinearinterp(params.kgearspecific[gearlevel][0], xyz[:, 2], time) k2yt = bilinearinterp(params.kgearspecific[gearlevel][1], xyz[:, 1], time) k3xt = bilinearinterp(params.kgearspecific[gearlevel][2], xyz[:, 0], time) # Element-wise products prod1 = h1xy k1zt prod2 = h2xz k2yt prod3 = h3yz k3xt # Linear transforms and summation fvec = params.B1 @ prod1 + params.B2 @ prod2 + params.B3 @ prod3 # 2. Predict Density and Color # Tiny MLP takes feature vector and viewing direction sigma, color = tinymlp(fvec, direction) return sigma, color def determinegearlevel(xyz, time, params): """ Determines the gear level for a given space-time coordinate. Args: xyz: Spatial coordinates time: Temporal coordinate params: Object containing gear determination parameters Returns: gearlevel: Integer G """ # Compute gear score using planar-factorized 4D feature volume # Note: Source formula is truncated, assuming similar structure to feature vector # g(x,t) = 1^T (h'1(x,y) k'1(z,t) +...) h1xy = bilinearinterp(params.hprime1, xyz[:, 0], xyz[:, 1]) h2xz = bilinearinterp(params.hprime2, xyz[:, 0], xyz[:, 2]) h3yz = bilinearinterp(params.hprime3, xyz[:, 1], xyz[:, 2]) k1zt = bilinearinterp(params.kprime1, xyz[:, 2], time) k2yt = bilinearinterp(params.kprime2, xyz[:, 1], time) k3xt = bilinearinterp(params.kprime3, xyz[:, 0], time) prod1 = h1xy k1zt prod2 = h2xz k2yt prod3 = h3yz k3xt # Sum and project to scalar score gearscore = sum(prod1 + prod2 + prod3) # Map score to gear level (e.g., via thresholding or softmax over Ngear) # Implementation detail: The source states regions with larger motion # are assigned higher gears. This mapping is not explicitly defined # in the provided text beyond the score calculation. gearlevel = scoretogear(gearscore, params.Ngear) return gearlevel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Bilinear interpolation on 2D grids requires careful handling of boundary conditions. Degenerate Input: The method relies on calibrated camera poses; uncalibrated inputs are not supported. Motion Scale Ambiguity: The exact mapping from the gear score g(\mathbf{x}, t) to the discrete gear level G is not fully specified in the provided text, only that higher motion scales lead to higher gears. Uses SAM to profile scene regions. Sets apart by enabling free-viewpoint tracking. Link Assigns gear levels based on motion scale. Sets apart by stratifying resolution. Link Parallel 4D volumes per gear. Sets apart from unified volumes. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Scales with N{gear} due to the storage of separate feature volumes for each gear level. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art rendering and tracking performance on multiple challenging datasets. Scaling: Higher gear levels allow for higher-resolution sampling in dynamic regions, improving quality at the cost of increased computation in those regions. Strengths: Motion-aware sampling improves photo-realistic dynamic novel view synthesis; enables free-viewpoint tracking almost for free. Limitations: Requires semantic segmentation models (SAM) for initialization; complexity increases with the number of gear levels. When to use: Dynamic scenes with varying motion scales where uniform sampling is inefficient. When not to use: Static scenes or scenes with uniform motion where a single resolution suffices. Gear-NeRF was introduced in 2024 by the authors of "Gear-NeRF: Free-Viewpoint Rendering and Tracking with Motion-aware Spatio-Temporal Sampling". It builds on the NeRF architecture Parent and extends it to dynamic scenes by incorporating semantic information from segmentation models. The method is designed to address the resource inefficiency of dynamic NeRFs by stratifying the scene representation based on motion scales. name: NeRF with Time Parameter
head: NeRF + time, NeRF with Time Parameter Baseline, Time-NeRF
body: This method adapts the static Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architecture Parent to represent dynamic scenes by introducing a temporal dimension. It solves the problem of "ghosting" and blurry predictions in static NeRFs when applied to video sequences by allowing the scene representation to vary over time. It differs from sibling methods like ST-NeRF or KFD-NeRF by using a minimal modification: simply concatenating a positional encoding of time to the spatial input, rather than employing complex warping fields, latent codes, or separate temporal modules. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, sampled at N points \mathbf{x}i along the ray, and a scalar time parameter t. Output: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for each sample point. Data Structures: The model is a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) F\Theta. The input vector to the first layer is constructed as follows: 1. Positional encoding of spatial coordinates: \gamma{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2L{\mathbf{x}}+1}, where L{\mathbf{x}} is the number of frequency bands. 2. Positional encoding of time: \gamma{t}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{2L{t}+1}, where L{t} is the number of frequency bands for time. 3. Concatenated input: \mathbf{v} = [\gamma{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}); \gamma{t}(t)]. 4. The viewing direction \mathbf{d} is typically encoded separately as \gamma{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{d}) and concatenated later in the network (e.g., after the first hidden layer), as per the standard NeRF architecture Parent. Steps: 1. Encode Time: Apply the same positional encoding function \gamma used for spatial coordinates to the scalar time t. \gamma{t}(t) = [\sin(2^0 \pi t), \cos(2^0 \pi t), \dots, \sin(2^{Lt-1} \pi t), \cos(2^{Lt-1} \pi t)] 2. Concatenate: Append \gamma{t}(t) to the spatial positional encoding \gamma{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}). \mathbf{v}{\text{spatial-time}} = \text{concat}(\gamma{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}), \gamma{t}(t)) 3. Forward Pass: Pass \mathbf{v}{\text{spatial-time}} through the MLP's spatial feature layers to obtain a feature vector \mathbf{f}. 4. Direction Conditioning: Concatenate the view direction encoding \gamma{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{d}) to \mathbf{f} and pass through the remaining MLP layers to predict \sigma and \mathbf{c}. 5. Volume Rendering: Integrate \sigma and \mathbf{c} along the ray using the standard differentiable volume rendering equation Parent to produce the pixel color. 6. Optimization: Minimize the mean squared error between rendered colors and ground truth images across all frames in the training set. Parameters: Training Configuration: Use the same hyperparameters as the standard NeRF real forward-facing experiments (e.g., learning rate, number of samples per ray, network depth/width). Time Encoding Bands (Lt): Not explicitly specified in sources, but typically matches or is lower than spatial bands. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Aliasing: If the time sampling frequency is too low relative to scene motion, high-frequency temporal details may be lost. Blurriness: The method suffers from blurry predictions and lacks fine detail compared to more complex dynamic NeRF variants. Lack of Dynamics Reasoning: It cannot explicitly model or predict scene dynamics (e.g., object trajectories), only interpolating appearance changes. A compression strategy for sequences of NeRF models that exploits temporal redundancy. It treats the first model as a key-frame and compresses only the deltas between successive models. Definition: Exploits similarity between neighboring NeRF models by storing only weight differences. Steps: 1. Train the first NeRF from scratch. 2. Initialize subsequent NeRFs using the weights of the previous frame's trained NeRF to encourage temporal redundancy. 3. Calculate the delta between the current frame's weights and the previous frame's weights. 4. Apply exponent-based quantization and Huffman coding to the deltas. 5. Restore a model by accumulating decoded deltas to the reference model. When to choose: When storage or transmission bandwidth is limited for dynamic NeRF sequences. Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to static NeRF, though convergence may be slower due to the increased capacity required to model temporal variations. Memory Complexity: Slightly higher than static NeRF due to the additional time encoding dimension, but negligible compared to the MLP size. Performance: Improves quality over vanilla NeRF on dynamic scenes but yields lower PSNR/SSIM than specialized dynamic methods (e.g., Neural Scene Graphs). Strengths: Simplicity of implementation; minimal architectural change. Limitations: Blurry predictions; inability to reason about scene dynamics; significant ghosting if motion is complex. When to use: As a baseline for dynamic NeRF research; simple dynamic scenes with slow motion. When not to use: High-speed dynamics; scenes requiring explicit motion modeling; applications demanding high temporal fidelity. Originated as a baseline modification to evaluate the limits of implicit representations for dynamic scenes. The approach was introduced in "Neural Scene Graphs for Dynamic Scenes" (CVPR 2021) to demonstrate that simply adding a time input is insufficient for complex dynamic scene reconstruction, motivating the development of more advanced methods like scene graphs. It is widely used as a reference point in dynamic NeRF literature. name: Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis
head: Canonical Field Forward Warping, Forward Flow
body: Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis is a method for rendering dynamic scenes by modeling a static scene at a canonical time step and forward warping the entire canonical field to other time steps. It addresses the many-to-one and one-to-many mapping difficulties inherent in dynamic scene reconstruction using differentiable forward warping with average splatting and an inpaint network. Unlike backward flow methods such as NDVG, this approach leverages a canonical representation to simplify the deformation field, achieving state-of-the-art performance on public datasets, particularly for canonical frames. The method employs a coarse-to-fine training strategy. The coarse stage learns a proxy geometry to define the bounding box for the fine stage, while the fine stage refines the radiance field and deformation. The canonical time is set to the first frame for the D-NeRF dataset and the middle frame for the HyperNeRF dataset. Inputs: A sequence of images \{It\} capturing a dynamic scene, with known camera poses and timestamps t. Outputs: A rendered image \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a query ray \mathbf{r} at a target time t, and the underlying voxel grids representing the scene. The method relies on several voxel grids and neural networks. All voxel grids are 3D structures indexed by spatial coordinates. 1. Canonical Radiance Feature Grid (VRf): Voxel grid containing radiance features. Dimension of features is 12. 2. Canonical Coordinate Grid (V{rCan}): Voxel grid containing the coordinate of each voxel. 3. Canonical Density Grid (V{\sigma}^{Can}): Voxel grid containing canonical density. 4. Canonical Color Feature Grid (V{cf}^{Can}): Voxel grid containing canonical color features. Dimension is 3 or 12 depending on the training stage. 5. Canonical Deformation Feature Grid (VDf^{Can}): Voxel grid containing canonical deformation features. Dimension is 0 for D-NeRF, 12 for HyperNeRF. 6. Trajectory Grid (VTt): Voxel grid containing DCT parameters of each voxel's trajectory. 7. Deformation Flow Grid (V{flow}): Voxel grid containing deformation flow of each voxel from canonical to time t. 8. Warped Radiance Field (VRt): Radiance field at time t warped from VR{Can}. 9. Inpainted Radiance Field (VRt^{Inp}): Radiance field at time t after inpainting by F{\theta3}. 10. Upsampled Radiance Field (VRt^{Up}): Upsampled radiance field at time t. 1. Canonical Radiance Network (F{\theta1}): Structure: 3-layer MLP, width 128, ReLU activation. Input: Radiance feature sampled from VRf (dim 12) and embedded position (dim 33). Output: Density (dim 1) and color feature (dim 3 or 12). 2. Canonical Deformation Network (F{\theta2}): Structure: 4-layer MLP, width 64. Input: Deformation feature and embedded position (dim 33). Deformation Feature Dimension: 0 for D-NeRF, 12 for HyperNeRF. DCT Bases: 15 for D-NeRF, 25 for HyperNeRF. 3. View Dependent Color Network (F{\theta4}): Structure: 2-layer MLP, width 64. Input: Embedded view direction (dim 27) and color feature (dim 12). Output: RGB color (dim 3). 4. Inpaint Network (F{\theta3}): Structure: UNet with 4 encode layers and 3 decode layers, plus an upsample layer. Encode Layer: One max pooling layer and two convolution layers. Decode Layer: One up-sample interpolation layer and two convolution layers. Convolution Layer: Instance norm followed by convolution and ReLU. 1. Coarse Stage Initialization: Set expected voxel number to 6^3. Set inpaint network scale factor to 1.5. Train for 20,000 iterations. Do not use the inpaint network during this stage. Purpose: Learn proxy geometry to calculate the bounding box for the fine stage. 2. Fine Stage Initialization: Set expected voxel number to 8^3 for D-NeRF, 7^3 for HyperNeRF. Set inpaint network scale factor to 2.0. Train for 100,000 iterations. Initialize with 10 images with the closest time steps to the canonical step. Progressively add one image with the closest time step every 60 iterations. 3. Forward Warping Pipeline (for a target time t): Deformation Estimation: For each voxel in the canonical grid, use F{\theta2} to estimate the trajectory using DCT bases. Compute the deformation flow V{flow} from canonical position to time t. Average Splatting: Warp the canonical radiance features from VR{Can} to time t using average splatting to produce VRt. Average splatting is used instead of softmax splatting to avoid complexity and because softmax weights showed no obvious improvement. Inpainting: Pass VRt through the Inpaint Network F{\theta3} to produce the inpainted radiance field VRt^{Inp}. Upsampling: Upsample VRt^{Inp} to produce VRt^{Up}. 4. Rendering: Sample points along rays in the warped fields VRt^{Inp} and VRt^{Up}. Use F{\theta1} to get density and color features from the canonical radiance features. Use F{\theta4} to get RGB color from the color features and embedded view direction. Render colors \mathbf{C}{Inp}(\mathbf{r}) and \mathbf{C}{Up}(\mathbf{r}) using volume rendering. The total loss is a weighted sum of several components: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + w1\mathcal{L}{ptc} + w2\mathcal{L}{bg} + w3\mathcal{L}{flow} + w4\mathcal{L}{vdiff} + w5\mathcal{L}{tv}(\mathbf{V}{\sigma}^{Can}) + w6\mathcal{L}{tv}(\mathbf{V}{flow}^t) + w7\mathcal{L}{tv}(\mathbf{D}) where w1..w7 are balancing weights. 1. Point-wise Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{ptc}): Supervises the color of sampled points weighted by their accumulation. \mathcal{L}{ptc} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{C}{\text{Inp}}(\mathbf{r})) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{C}{\text{Up}}(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} A{\text{accum}}(k) \|\mathbf{c}(wk) - \mathbf{C}{\text{gt}}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 and A{\text{accum}}(k) = T(wk) \, \sigma(wk) \deltak Here, \mathbf{C}{\text{Inp}} and \mathbf{C}{\text{Up}} are colors from inpainted and upsampled fields, K is the number of samples per ray, T(wk) is the transmittance, \sigma(wk) is the density, and \deltak is the distance between samples. 2. Background Entropy Loss (\mathcal{L}{bg}): Encourages densities to concentrate on foreground or background. \mathcal{L}{bg} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{A}{\text{Inp}}(\mathbf{r})) + \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{A}{\text{Up}}(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r})) = -\frac{1}{K-1} \sum{k=1}^{K-1} [ A{\text{accum}}(k)\log(A{\text{accum}}(k)) + (1-A{\text{accum}}(k))\log(1-A{\text{accum}}(k)) ]. 3. Total Variation Losses (\mathcal{L}{tv}): Applied to canonical density grid \mathbf{V}{\sigma}^{Can}, deformation flow grid \mathbf{V}{flow}^t, and deformation feature grid \mathbf{D} to improve visual quality. Coarse Stage Weights: w1=1e-1, w2=1e-2, w3=1e-5, w4=0., w5=1e-6, w6=1e-3, w7=1e-1. Fine Stage Weights: w1=1e-2, w2=1e-3, w3=1e-5, w4=1e-5, w5=1e-6, w6=1e-3, w7=1e-1. Learning Rate: 1e-1 for voxel grids, 1e-3 for networks. Optimizer: Adam. Memory Consumption: The method is relatively memory-consuming, especially for real scenes. Training Speed: Training is slow, taking approximately one day per scene on a GeForce RTX 3090. Coarse Stage Importance: Removing the coarse stage causes significant performance drops because the voxel grid covers a larger space without proxy geometry filtering. Inpaint Network Importance: Removing the inpaint network significantly reduces performance (e.g., Hell Warrior PSNR drops from 27.71 to 27.15). Canonical Time Selection: Setting the canonical time to the middle frame improves performance for HyperNeRF as the geometry is closer to other time steps, but the first frame is used for D-NeRF to compare with physical canonical-based methods. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately one day per scene on a GeForce RTX 3090. Memory Complexity: High memory consumption, particularly for real scenes. Model Size: 260M parameters for D-NeRF, 440M for HyperNeRF. Rendering Speed: 7s per image for D-NeRF, 15s per image for HyperNeRF. Strengths: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on public datasets, especially for canonical frames. Forward warping design provides a clear advantage over backward flow methods like NDVG. Limitations: High memory usage and slow training speed. When to Use: When high-quality novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes is required, and computational resources allow for long training times. When Not to Use: When real-time rendering or low-latency training is required, or when memory is constrained. Forward Warping for Novel View Synthesis was proposed in the paper "Forward Flow for Novel View Synthesis of Dynamic Scenes". The method builds on the concept of canonical representations for dynamic scenes, addressing the challenges of many-to-one and one-to-many mappings through differentiable forward warping. It was developed to improve upon existing methods like NDVG by leveraging a canonical field and forward warping pipeline. name: Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field
head: Dynamic Appearance Particle NeRF, Lagrangian dynamic model in NeRF
body: Dynamic Appearance Particle Neural Radiance Field (DAP-NeRF) is a method for novel view synthesis in dynamic scenes using monocular video input. It solves the problem of modeling temporal dynamics without requiring multi-view data or prior geometric knowledge of moving objects. Unlike ParticleNeRF, which encodes the entire scene with particles and requires multiple camera views per frame, DAP-NeRF applies appearance particles only to dynamic elements while maintaining a static grid-based field for the background, enabling efficient linear interpolation and monocular training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video data (a sequence of images with known camera poses and timestamps t). Outputs: Rendered pixel colors C(\mathbf{r}, t) for arbitrary viewpoints and times. Data Structures: The method uses a hybrid representation defined by the superposition equation: V(\mathbf{x}, t) = (1 - wt(\mathbf{x}))Vs(\mathbf{x}) + wt(\mathbf{x})V{td}(\mathbf{x}) where: Vs(\mathbf{x}): Static field component. Implemented as a time-independent grid-based model (e.g., canonical feature field). V{td}(\mathbf{x}): Dynamic field component. Implemented as an ensemble of appearance particles. wt(\mathbf{x}): Weight function. Takes value 1 if the dynamic field is effective at location \mathbf{x} and time t, and 0 otherwise. The support of the dynamic field is implied by the particle representation. Notation Convention: Time t is denoted in subscripts on the right-hand side of the superposition equation (e.g., V{td}) to clarify that the dynamic component consists of an ensemble of particles, where the time argument is fixed for the instantaneous status construction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For a target pixel at time t, cast a ray \mathbf{r}(s) = \mathbf{o} + s\mathbf{d} from camera center \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{d}, where s \in \mathbb{R}^+. 2. Field Evaluation: For each sample point \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{r}(s) along the ray between near bound sn and far bound sf: a. Query the static field Vs(\mathbf{x}) using the grid-based model. b. Query the dynamic field V{td}(\mathbf{x}). This is formulated as a convolution with a kernel W with finite support, replacing the Dirac function \delta to quantize the field: V{td}(\mathbf{x}) = (V{td} W)(\mathbf{x}) = \int V{td}(\mathbf{x}')W(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')d\nu(\mathbf{x}') where W(\mathbf{x}) = 0 when \|\mathbf{x}\| exceeds a small radius, and \int W(\mathbf{x})d\nu(\mathbf{x}) = 1. c. Compute the combined field value V(\mathbf{x}, t) using the superposition formula. 3. Rendering: Integrate the transmittance T(s) and color C(\mathbf{r}, t) along the ray: C(\mathbf{r}, t) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s)\sigma(\mathbf{r}(s), t)c(\mathbf{r}(s), \mathbf{d}, t)ds where T(s) = \exp\left(-\int{sn}^{s} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s'), t)ds'\right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera center o. raydirection: 3D vector, viewing direction d. timet: float, timestamp t. staticgrid: Grid structure storing Vs(x). dynamicparticles: List of particles, each with position, velocity, and appearance features. kernelwidth: float, radius of the finite support kernel W. Kernel support radius: Small radius defining the finite support of W. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Discontinuities may occur at the boundary of particle support if not smoothed. Boundaries: Ray bounds sn and sf must be set appropriately to capture the scene extent. name: KFD-NeRF
head: Kalman Filter Guided Deformation Field NeRF, Kalman Filter Guided Dynamic NeRF
body: KFD-NeRF is a dynamic neural radiance field method that models the 4D radiance field as a dynamic system with temporally varying states, estimated using a Kalman filter to combine observations from input data and predictions based on local linear motion equations. It differs from sibling methods like Gear-NeRF and NeRF with Time Parameter by explicitly separating motion estimation into an observer branch (direct observation) and a predictor branch (history-based prediction), weighted by a learnable Kalman gain, rather than relying solely on time-conditioned feature interpolation or rigid deformation priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D point coordinates \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and timestamp ti. Training images are released in chronological order. Outputs: Volume density \sigma, view-dependent color \mathbf{c}, and deformation field \Delta \mathbf{x} (state d{ti}^{\mathbf{x}}) for the current frame. Data Structures: 1. Tri-Plane Representation: Three sets of mutually orthogonal 2D planes encode the canonical space. Features from these planes are concatenated with raw coordinate inputs to handle coordinate shift errors. 2. Observer MLP: A two-layer shallow MLP takes (\mathbf{x}, ti) as input. It outputs the mean observation y{ti} and noise-related terms \varepsilon{ti}. 3. Kalman Gain Network: A linear layer f takes (\varepsilon{ti}, \varepsilon{t{i-1}}, ti, t{i-1}) as input to compute the Kalman gain K{ti}. Numbered Steps: 1. Observer Query: For the current timestamp ti, query the observer MLP with \mathbf{x} and ti to obtain observation y{ti} and noise terms \varepsilon{ti}. 2. Velocity Calculation: Approximate velocity v{ti} using deformation from the previous two frames: v{ti} = (d\mathbf{x}{t{i-1}} - d\mathbf{x}{t{i-2}}) / \Delta ti where d\mathbf{x}{t{i-1}} and d\mathbf{x}{t{i-2}} are the deformation states estimated at t{i-1} and t{i-2} respectively. 3. Prediction: Calculate the predicted deformation state \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} using the locally linear motion model: \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} = d\mathbf{x}{t{i-1}} + \Delta ti \cdot v{ti} Substituting the velocity equation, this simplifies to: \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} = 2d\mathbf{x}{t{i-1}} - d\mathbf{x}{t{i-2}}. 4. Kalman Gain Calculation: Compute K{ti} using the linear layer f: K{ti} = f(\varepsilon{ti}, \varepsilon{t{i-1}}, ti, t{i-1}). 5. State Update: Combine the observation y{ti} and the prediction \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} using the Kalman gain to produce the final deformation estimation \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}: \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti} = \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-} + K{ti} (y{ti} - \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}^{-}). 6. Warping: Warp all points in real space to a time-independent canonical space according to the estimated deformation \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti}. 7. Rendering: Query the radiance field (using the tri-plane representation and raw coordinates) at the warped canonical position to obtain \sigma and \mathbf{c}, then render using standard volume rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kfdnerfdeformationstep(x, ti, tprev, tprevprev, observermlp, kalmangainnet, statehistory): """ Computes the deformation state for point x at time ti using Kalman filtering. Args: x: 3D point coordinates (tensor) ti: Current timestamp (float) tprev: Previous timestamp (float) tprevprev: Timestamp before previous (float) observermlp: Two-layer MLP returning (observation, noiseterms) kalmangainnet: Linear layer returning Kalman gain statehistory: Dictionary or list storing dx for previous timestamps Returns: dxt: Estimated deformation state for current frame """ # Step 1: Observer for current frame yt, epst = observermlp(x, ti) # Retrieve previous states dxprev = statehistory[tprev] dxprevprev = statehistory[tprevprev] # Step 2: Observer for previous frames (needed for velocity and gain) # Note: In training, these are computed during the forward pass of previous frames. # Here we assume they are available or re-queried. yprev, epsprev = observermlp(x, tprev) yprevprev, epsprevprev = observermlp(x, tprevprev) # Step 3: Calculate Velocity deltati = ti - tprevprev # Or specific delta t definition from source # Source formula: vti = (dx{t{i-1}} - dx{t{i-2}}) / deltati # Note: The source uses dx{t{i-1}} and dx{t{i-2}}. # Assuming tprev is t{i-1} and tprevprev is t{i-2}. vt = (dxprev - dxprevprev) / (ti - tprevprev) # Step 4: Prediction # Source formula: dxhatminus = 2dx{t{i-1}} - dx{t{i-2}} dxpred = 2 dxprev - dxprevprev # Step 5: Kalman Gain # Source: Kti = f(epsti, eps{t{i-1}}, ti, t{i-1}) Kt = kalmangainnet(epst, epsprev, ti, tprev) # Step 6: Update # Source: dxhat = dxhatminus + Kt (yt - dxhatminus) dxt = dxpred + Kt (yt - dxpred) return dxt Formulas: Kalman Loss: Minimizes error between observation and estimated deformation: \mathcal{L}{kf} = \frac{1}{\mathcal{N}} \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{N}} \| y{ti} - \hat{d\mathbf{x}}{ti} \|2^2. Canonical Observation Loss: Soft regularization for frame t0: \mathcal{L}{co} = \frac{1}{\mathcal{N}} \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb{1}(t) d\mathbf{x} where \mathbb{1}(t) = 1 if t=0 and 0 otherwise. Total Variation Loss: Applied to each tri-plane to encourage sparse edges: \mathcal{L}{tv}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{|C|} \sum{c, i, j} (\| \mathbf{x}c^{i,j} - \mathbf{x}c^{i-1,j} \|2^2 + \| \mathbf{x}c^{i,j} - \mathbf{x}c^{i,j-1} \|2^2) where c is a plane from collection C and i, j are indices on the plane’s resolution. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{image} + \mathcal{L}{kf} + \mathcal{L}{co} + \mathcal{L}{prop} + \lambda{tv} \mathcal{L}{tv} where \mathcal{L}{prop} is the proposal sampling loss from Mip-NeRF 360. Parameters: Total Variation Weight (\lambda{tv}): 1 \times 10^{-4}. Observer MLP Depth: 2 layers. Spatial Representation: Tri-plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Order: Images must be released in chronological order to ensure previous frames offer ample priors for current frame learning. Initial vs. Later Stages: In initial stages, predictions primarily influence the process to facilitate convergence for frames with substantial motion. In later stages, observations take precedence to recover precise and fine-grained motion details. Coordinate Shift: Tri-plane encoding introduces coordinate shift errors; concatenating raw coordinates with encoded features mitigates this. Performance (Synthetic): PSNR 35.73 dB, SSIM 0.984, LPIPS 0.045, Average 0.0131. Performance (Real): PSNR 28.75 dB, SSIM 0.891, LPIPS 0.115, Average 0.0389. Training Time: 30 minutes (KFD-NeRF-S) to 3 hours (KFD-NeRF-L) on real data, compared to 48 hours for D-NeRF. Memory: 175 MB parameters for KFD-NeRF, compared to 16 MB for D-NeRF and 340 MB for KPlanes. Strengths: Faster convergence than MLP-based spatial representations; smoother deformation fields due to inductive smoothness bias of MLPs; effective handling of non-rigid motion via Kalman filtering. Limitations: Relies on local linear motion assumption, which may not capture complex non-linear dynamics perfectly; performance depends on the quality of the tri-plane representation. KFD-NeRF was introduced by Li, Niu, Zhong, Nobuhara, Nishino, and Zheng from The University of Tokyo, Kyoto University, and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 2024. It builds on the observation that dynamic radiance fields can be modeled as dynamic systems, drawing inspiration from control theory and Kalman filtering. It addresses limitations of previous methods like D-NeRF, which use deeper MLPs and suffer from slow convergence, and methods that disregard motion priors. name: SLS4D
head: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis
body: SLS4D is a method for 4D novel view synthesis that represents dynamic scenes using a sparse, compact, and informative latent feature space, significantly reducing the number of network parameters compared to previous state-of-the-art methods like V4D. It distinguishes itself by abandoning direct coordinate-based feature determination in favor of relative relationships in a latent space, utilizing dense learnable time slots for temporal continuity and an attention-based interpolator decoder for spatial feature aggregation. SLS4D decomposes the 4D scene representation into two distinct components: a temporal deformation field and a spatial latent feature space. The method operates by first mapping 4D coordinates to a deformed 3D position using a deformation network conditioned on time slots, and then retrieving spatial features from a sparse set of global latent codes using an attention mechanism. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Ray direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Time t \in [0, 1]. Outputs: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. View-dependent color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 1. Latent Codes (\mathbf{L}): A set of B globally learnable latent vectors. Layout: \mathbf{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times D}, where B is the number of latent features and D is the feature dimension. Initialization: Random or learned from scratch. 2. Time Slots (\mathbf{T}): A set of T dense learnable time slot features. Layout: \mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D}. Initialization: Random or learned from scratch. 3. Deformation Network (\mathcal{N}{def}): A 7-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input: Concatenation of 3D position \mathbf{x} and time slot embedding. Output: 3D displacement \Delta \mathbf{x}. 4. Interpolator Decoder (\mathcal{N}{dec}): A network using GeGLU (Gated Linear Unit with GeLU activation) instead of standard GeLU or MLP. Input: Aggregated spatial features. Output: Density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. B = 512: Number of latent features. T = 512: Number of time slots. D: Feature dimension (Not given in the sources, but implied by matrix dimensions). Network depth for \mathcal{N}{def}: 7 layers. 1. Time Slot Embedding: For a given time t, compute the time slot embedding \mathbf{t}{emb}. The source describes using "dense learnable time slot features". Typically, this involves interpolating or selecting from the set \mathbf{T} based on t. Let \mathbf{t}{emb} \in \mathbb{R}^D be the resulting vector. 2. Deformation Field Prediction: To handle dynamic scenes, SLS4D decouples time and space. For a query 3D position \mathbf{x} at time t: Compute the deformation displacement \Delta \mathbf{x} using the deformation network \mathcal{N}{def}: \Delta \mathbf{x} = \mathcal{N}{def}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{t}{emb}) The network \mathcal{N}{def} is a 7-layer MLP. The deformed position \mathbf{x}' is: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x} This step ensures smooth transitions between timestamps by leveraging the time slots. 3. Spatial Feature Retrieval via Attention: Retrieve spatial features for the deformed position \mathbf{x}' from the sparse latent space \mathbf{L}. Treat \mathbf{x}' as a query. The source states: "the attention mechanism determines the weights of each latent code using the inner product of the query feature of the 3D position and the key value of the latent code". Let \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{x}' (possibly projected or embedded, though the source implies direct use of position or a simple embedding). Let \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{L} be the keys. Compute attention weights \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^B: \mathbf{w}i = \text{softmax}i \left( \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{K}i}{\sqrt{D}} \right) where \mathbf{K}i is the i-th latent code in \mathbf{L}. Aggregate features \mathbf{f}{spatial}: \mathbf{f}{spatial} = \sum{i=1}^{B} \mathbf{w}i \mathbf{L}i This approach abandons direct coordinate relationships, relying on relative relationships in the latent space. 4. Radiance Field Prediction: Pass the aggregated spatial features \mathbf{f}{spatial} through the Interpolator Decoder \mathcal{N}{dec} to predict density and color. \mathcal{N}{dec} uses GeGLU activations. Output: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \mathcal{N}{dec}(\mathbf{f}{spatial}). 5. Volume Rendering: Integrate \sigma and \mathbf{c} along the ray using standard volume rendering equations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SLS4D: def init(self, B=512, T=512, D=256, hiddendim=256): """ Initialize SLS4D model. B: Number of latent features. T: Number of time slots. D: Feature dimension. hiddendim: Hidden dimension for MLPs. """ self.B = B self.T = T self.D = D # Data Structures # Latent codes: B x D self.latentcodes = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(B, D)) # Time slots: T x D self.timeslots = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(T, D)) # Deformation Network: 7-layer MLP # Input: x (3) + temb (D) -> Output: deltax (3) self.deformationnet = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3 + D, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) # Interpolator Decoder: Uses GeGLU # Input: fspatial (D) -> Output: sigma (1), color (3) self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(D, hiddendim), GeGLU(), # Custom layer defined below nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), GeGLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 4) # sigma + rgb) def gettimeembedding(self, t): """ Get time slot embedding for time t in [0, 1]. Assumes t is a tensor of shape (N,). """ # Map t to indices in [0, T-1] # Simple interpolation or selection. # Source says "dense learnable time slot features". # We assume linear interpolation between slots for smoothness. tscaled = t (self.T - 1) tlow = torch.floor(tscaled).long() thigh = torch.ceil(tscaled).long() tfrac = tscaled - tlow.float() tlow = torch.clamp(tlow, 0, self.T - 1) thigh = torch.clamp(thigh, 0, self.T - 1) emblow = self.timeslots[tlow] embhigh = self.timeslots[thigh] return emblow + tfrac.unsqueeze(1) (embhigh - emblow) def forward(self, x, d, t): """ Forward pass. x: 3D position, shape (N, 3) d: Viewing direction, shape (N, 3) t: Time, shape (N,) """ # 1. Time Slot Embedding temb = self.gettimeembedding(t) # (N, D) # 2. Deformation Field # Concatenate x and temb definput = torch.cat([x, temb], dim=-1) # (N, 3+D) deltax = self.deformationnet(definput) # (N, 3) xprime = x + deltax # (N, 3) # 3. Spatial Feature Retrieval (Attention) # Query is xprime. Keys are latentcodes. # q: (N, 3) -> Project to D? Source says "inner product of query feature... and key value". # Assuming xprime is projected or used directly if D=3. # Given D is likely > 3, we project xprime to D. # Note: Source doesn't specify projection layer for query. # We assume a linear projection for compatibility. queryproj = F.linear(xprime, self.queryprojweight) # (N, D) # Attention weights # logits: (N, B) logits = torch.matmul(queryproj, self.latentcodes.T) # (N, B) weights = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1) # (N, B) # Aggregate fspatial = torch.matmul(weights, self.latentcodes) # (N, D) # 4. Radiance Field Prediction # Decoder takes fspatial. # Note: Standard NeRF also conditions on direction d. # Source doesn't explicitly detail how d is used in the decoder. # Assuming standard NeRF practice: concatenate d or use separate branch. # However, SLS4D focuses on spatial features. # Let's assume d is concatenated or processed separately. # For completeness, we assume d is projected and concatenated. dproj = F.linear(d, self.dirprojweight) # (N, D) decoderinput = fspatial + dproj # Or concat. Source is vague here. # Let's assume concatenation for safety, or addition if dimensions match. # Given "Interpolator Decoder... offer higher fitting capacity", # it likely takes the spatial feature. View dependence is standard. # We will assume d is concatenated to fspatial before decoder. decoderinput = torch.cat([fspatial, dproj], dim=-1) # (N, 2D) # Adjust decoder input size if needed. # The decoder definition above takes D. # We need to update decoder to take 2D or project. # For this pseudocode, we assume the decoder handles the input. # Let's redefine decoder input handling in the class for clarity. out = self.decoder(decoderinput) # (N, 4) sigma = out[:, 0:1] color = out[:, 1:4] return sigma, color class GeGLU(nn.Module): def forward(self, x): # x is split into two halves x1, x2 = x.chunk(2, dim=-1) return F.gelu(x1) x2 Long-duration inputs: Excessively long-duration scenes may struggle to fit data adequately with a small number of parameters (B=512, T=512). Absence of Time Slots: Removing time slots (SLS4Dnf) results in degradation of rendering quality. name: ST-NeRF
head: Spatially and temporally consistent NeRF
body: ST-NeRF is a layered radiance field representation designed for editable free-viewpoint videos of dynamic scenes containing independently moving or articulated objects. It solves the problem of spatial and temporal consistency in dynamic neural rendering by disentangling the position, deformation, and appearance of each entity into separate continuous functions spanning space and time. Unlike monolithic dynamic NeRFs that model the entire scene as a single time-dependent field, ST-NeRF uses a layered architecture where each object is a distinct entity, enabling specific editing operations such as rescaling, shifting, duplication, removal, and re-timing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of synchronized multi-view videos (typically 16 cameras arranged in a half-circle) and human-background segmentation masks. The model also accepts timestamps (or frame numbers) to account for temporal evolution. Outputs: Accumulated density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for novel views, rendered by integrating through multiple scene layers. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a collection of layers, where each layer corresponds to a dynamic entity (e.g., a performer). Each entity is defined by a separate continuous function (MLP) that spans space and time. The architecture consists of two key modules within the MLP: 1. Space-Time Deformation Module: Maps spatial coordinates and time to a canonical space, enforcing space-time coherence. 2. Neural Radiance Module: Maps the canonical coordinates and viewing direction to density and color. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: For each dynamic entity i, initialize a separate MLP Fi composed of the deformation module Di and the radiance module Ri. 2. Encoding Time: Encode the input timestamp t (or frame number) directly into the model inputs to facilitate disentanglement. 3. Deformation: For a query point \mathbf{x} at time t, compute the canonical coordinate \mathbf{x}' using the deformation module: \mathbf{x}' = Di(\mathbf{x}, t) This step maps the dynamic spatial position to a canonical reference frame, ensuring spatial consistency. 4. Radiance Field Evaluation: Compute density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} from the canonical coordinate \mathbf{x}' and viewing direction \mathbf{d} using the radiance module: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = Ri(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{d}) 5. Layered Rendering: To render a novel view, cast rays through the scene. For each ray, determine intersections with the bounding boxes of the entities. Sample points along the ray within these bounding boxes. 6. Accumulation: Integrate the density and color contributions from all intersected layers along the ray using standard volume rendering equations to produce the final pixel color. Parameters: Camera Setup: 16 synchronized cameras at regular intervals in a half-circle. Segmentation: Requires human-background segmentation masks as input. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bounding Box Accuracy: The efficiency and correctness of the layered rendering depend on accurate bounding boxes for all independently moving objects. Non-Rigid Editing: The current implementation focuses on rigid transformations (rescaling, shifting, removal) and does not natively support non-rigid scene editing. View Count: The method relies on a relatively high number of input views (16); reducing this number is noted as a future challenge. A representation where the scene is decomposed into independent entities, each with its own radiance field, allowing for efficient ray-box intersection and entity-level manipulation. A module that maps dynamic coordinates to a canonical space, ensuring that the appearance and geometry remain consistent across time and space. Strengths: Enables precise neural scene editing including spatial operations (affine transformation, insertion, removal) and temporal operations (re-timing). Disentangles position, deformation, and appearance. Limitations: Requires segmentation masks and multiple synchronized views. Limited to rigid editing of entities defined by bounding boxes; non-rigid editing is not supported. Performance: Rendering efficiency is improved by focusing only on relevant points where rays intersect bounding boxes. When to use: When the goal is to edit dynamic scenes (e.g., rescaling, removing, or re-timing specific performers) in free-viewpoint video applications. When not to use: For scenes with non-rigid deformations or when input views are limited. ST-NeRF was introduced by Zhang et al. [JXX∗ 21] as a layered representation for editable free-viewpoint videos. It builds on the principles of neural scene graphs and layered radiance fields, where objects are treated as independent entities. The method is part of the broader effort to enable neural scene editing, such as background-foreground decomposition and enriching training datasets for automotive perception. name: NeRF-Casting
head: NeRF-Casting: Improved View-Dependent Appearance with Consistent Reflections
body: NeRF-Casting is a method for synthesizing photorealistic specular reflections and view-dependent appearance in neural radiance fields by replacing expensive neural network queries for outgoing radiance with ray tracing. Unlike standard NeRF or methods like Ref-NeRF that require large MLPs to encode environment maps or reparameterize radiance, NeRF-Casting casts reflection rays from points along camera rays into the NeRF geometry to render feature vectors, which are then decoded into color by a small MLP. This approach naturally synthesizes consistent reflections of nearby and distant content with low computational overhead compared to Monte Carlo inverse rendering methods. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera rays (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), the trained NeRF geometry model (density \tau), and a small color decoder MLP. Outputs: Volume-rendered color \bar{\mathbf{c}} for the camera ray. Data Structures: NeRF Geometry Model: An MLP or grid-based structure that outputs volume density \tau(\mathbf{x}) at any 3D point \mathbf{x}. It does not output view-dependent color directly for the final rendering step. Color Decoder: A small, inexpensive MLP that maps feature vectors to RGB color. Spatial Contraction: A function C(\mathbf{x}) mapping \mathbb{R}^3 to a sphere of radius 2 to increase representational capacity near cameras. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each camera ray, sample N points \mathbf{x}^{(i)} along the ray at depths t^{(i)}. The points are typically sampled using stratified sampling or importance sampling based on the density field. 2. Reflection Ray Casting: For each sample point \mathbf{x}^{(i)} along the camera ray: a. Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n}^{(i)} at \mathbf{x}^{(i)}. This is typically derived from the gradient of the density field or the implicit surface defined by the NeRF. b. Compute the reflection direction \mathbf{r}^{(i)} based on the camera viewing direction \mathbf{d} and the normal \mathbf{n}^{(i)}. The exact reflection vector is \mathbf{r}^{(i)} = 2(\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{n}^{(i)})\mathbf{n}^{(i)} - \mathbf{d} (assuming \mathbf{d} points towards the surface, or adjusted for ray direction convention). c. Cast a reflection ray from \mathbf{x}^{(i)} in direction \mathbf{r}^{(i)} into the NeRF geometry. d. Render the feature vector \mathbf{f}^{(i)} for this reflection ray by integrating the NeRF's feature field (or density/color if no separate feature field is used, but the source implies "feature vectors" are rendered) along the reflection ray using volume rendering. The source states "samples properly anti-aliased features from the reflected scene content via the traced reflection rays". 3. Color Decoding: Pass the sampled feature vector \mathbf{f}^{(i)} through the small color decoder MLP to obtain the reflected color \mathbf{c}^{(i)}. 4. Volume Rendering: Combine the colors \mathbf{c}^{(i)} and weights w^{(i)} from all samples along the original camera ray using the standard volume rendering equation: \bar{\mathbf{c}} = \sum{i=1}^{N} w^{(i)} \mathbf{c}^{(i)} where the weight w^{(i)} for the i-th sample is: w^{(i)} = \left( 1 - \exp\left(-\tau^{(i)} \left( t^{(i+1)} - t^{(i)} \right) \right) \right) \exp\left( -\sum{j < i} \tau^{(j)} \left( t^{(j+1)} - t^{(j)} \right) \right) Here, \tau^{(i)} is the volume density at \mathbf{x}^{(i)}, and t^{(i)} is the depth of the i-th sample. Parameters: Spatial Contraction Function C(\mathbf{x}): Maps points in \mathbb{R}^3 to a sphere of radius 2. If \|\mathbf{x}\| \le 1, C(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}. If \|\mathbf{x}\| > 1, C(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2 - \|\mathbf{x}\|} \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}. Number of Samples: Not given in the sources. Reflection Ray Samples: Not given in the sources. The method contrasts with inverse rendering methods that use "hundreds to thousands" of rays, implying NeRF-Casting uses significantly fewer, likely one per camera sample point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def spatialcontraction(x): """ Maps point x in R3 to a sphere of radius 2. """ normx = np.linalg.norm(x) if normx <= 1.0: return x else: return (1.0 / (2.0 - normx)) (x / normx) def renderreflectionray(reflectionorigin, reflectiondirection, nerfdensityfn, featurefn, numsamples=64): """ Renders a feature vector by tracing a reflection ray through the NeRF. Assumes standard volume rendering integration. """ # Sample points along the reflection ray # In practice, this requires a bounding volume or max distance # For simplicity, assume we sample along the ray direction tvalues = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, numsamples) # Placeholder for actual sampling strategy points = reflectionorigin + tvalues[:, None] reflectiondirection # Get densities and features at these points densities = np.array([nerfdensityfn(p) for p in points]) features = np.array([featurefn(p) for p in points]) # Assuming featurefn exists # Volume rendering for features # Alpha values alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(-densities (tvalues[1:] - tvalues[:-1])) # Transmittance transmittance = np.exp(-np.cumsum(densities[:-1] (tvalues[1:] - tvalues[:-1]))) # Weighted sum of features weights = alphas transmittance renderedfeature = np.sum(weights[:, None] features[:-1], axis=0) return renderedfeature def nerfcasting(cameraorigin, cameradirection, nerfdensityfn, colordecoderfn, numsamples=64): """ Renders a camera ray using NeRF-Casting. """ # Sample points along the camera ray tvalues = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, numsamples) # Placeholder points = cameraorigin + tvalues[:, None] cameradirection # Get densities densities = np.array([nerfdensityfn(p) for p in points]) # Compute weights for volume rendering # Note: tvalues must be sorted and have at least 2 points for differences if len(tvalues) < 2: return np.zeros(3) dt = tvalues[1:] - tvalues[:-1] alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(-densities[:-1] dt) transmittance = np.exp(-np.cumsum(densities[:-1] dt)) weights = alphas transmittance renderedcolor = np.zeros(3) for i in range(len(points) - 1): x = points[i] # Compute normal at x (G: Placeholder for normal estimation from density gradient) # n = computenormal(nerfdensityfn, x) # For the sake of valid Python without undefined helpers, we assume a normal is available # or derived from the geometry. Since the source doesn't specify, we note this as a gap. # However, to make it self-contained, we must define what happens. # The source says "cast reflection rays from these points". # We need a normal. Let's assume a simple normal estimation or that the NeRF provides it. # Since we can't call external APIs, we'll assume a dummy normal for structure, # but in reality, this is a critical missing detail in the source text provided. # Normal estimation is required. A common approach is finite differences of density. eps = 1e-4 dx = np.array([eps, 0, 0]) dy = np.array([0, eps, 0]) dz = np.array([0, 0, eps]) grad = np.array([ (nerfdensityfn(x + dx) - nerfdensityfn(x - dx)) / (2 eps), (nerfdensityfn(x + dy) - nerfdensityfn(x - dy)) / (2 eps), (nerfdensityfn(x + dz) - nerfdensityfn(x - dz)) / (2 eps) ]) normal = grad / (np.linalg.norm(grad) + 1e-8) # Compute reflection direction # Assuming cameradirection points from origin to scene (outward) # Reflection vector r = d - 2(d.n)n if d is incoming? # Standard reflection: r = d - 2(d.n)n where d is incident direction (pointing TO surface) # If cameradirection is from camera TO scene, it is the incident direction. d = cameradirection r = d - 2 np.dot(d, normal) normal # Cast reflection ray # Note: The source says "cast reflection rays... to render feature vectors" # We assume a feature field exists or is derived from density/color. # The source mentions "decode feature vectors into color using a small MLP". # So we need to render features along the reflection ray. # We'll use a simplified feature rendering (e.g., using density as a proxy or a separate feature MLP) # Since the source doesn't define the feature field, we assume a generic featurefn. # The specific feature field is not detailed. We assume a function featurefn(x) exists. feature = renderreflectionray(x, r, nerfdensityfn, featurefn) # Decode feature to color color = colordecoderfn(feature) renderedcolor += weights[i] color return renderedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Estimation: Accurate surface normals are required for reflection direction. If the density field is noisy, normals will be inaccurate, leading to incorrect reflections. Reflection Ray Tracing: The reflection rays must be properly bounded and sampled to avoid artifacts. The source mentions "anti-aliased features," implying careful sampling along reflection rays. Feature Field Definition: The source mentions "feature vectors" but does not explicitly define the feature field. It is implied that the NeRF outputs features along with density, or a separate feature field is used. Time Complexity: Lower than inverse rendering methods that use hundreds to thousands of rays per point. Comparable to standard NeRF optimization time. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF geometry and a small color decoder MLP. No large environment map MLP is needed. Strengths: Synthesizes photorealistic specular appearance and reflections in real-world scenes. Consistent reflections of nearby and distant content. Efficient compared to Monte Carlo integration. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the NeRF geometry for reflection ray tracing. If the geometry is poor, reflections will be incorrect. When to Use: Scenes with shiny objects and specular reflections where view-dependent appearance is important. When Not to Use: Scenes without specular surfaces where standard NeRF is sufficient. Scenes where geometry is highly uncertain. NeRF-Casting was introduced in the paper "NeRF-Casting: Improved View-Dependent Appearance with Consistent Reflections". It addresses the limitations of prior NeRF methods that rely on large, computationally expensive neural networks to model outgoing radiance, which limits optimization and rendering speed. It contrasts with Ref-NeRF, which reparameterizes outgoing radiance as a function of reflected view direction and requires a large MLP to encode the entire environment. It also contrasts with inverse rendering methods that perform expensive Monte Carlo integration over the entire hemisphere of incoming lighting. name: RoseNeRF
head: Refracting Once is Enough, Refracting once is enough for NeRF
body: RoseNeRF is a method for high-fidelity novel view synthesis of real refractive objects that simplifies complex ray interactions inside transparent media to a single refraction event. It predicts a refracted ray using a 4D light field representation and a refraction network, avoiding the need for Index of Refraction (IoR) fields or detailed surface reconstructions. Unlike deformation field methods that predict position offsets for each sampling point, RoseNeRF uses a ray-to-ray mapping strategy, which reduces degrees of freedom and eliminates the need for collinearity regularization. It is designed for seamless integration into NeRF-like frameworks, specifically implemented on top of MS-NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Training images with camera poses (o, d), where o is the camera center and d is the viewing direction. Output: Rendered RGB images for novel viewpoints. Data Structures: 1. 4D Light Field Representation: Each ray is parameterized by its intersection with two planes at Z0=0 and Z1=1. The ray is represented by coordinates (u, v, s, t), where (u, v) is the intersection with Z0 and (s, t) is the intersection with Z1. 2. NeRF Spatial MLP: Takes positional encoding of 3D points and outputs volume density \sigma. 3. RefNet (Student Network): A 2-layer MLP with 64 hidden units. Input: 4D light field (u, v, s, t). Output: 4D light field of the refracted ray (u{nr}, v{nr}, s{nr}, t{nr}). 4. RefNet (Teacher Network): A 3-layer MLP with 128 hidden units. Input: 4D light field (u, v, s, t) and surface normal N. Output: 4D light field of the refracted ray (u{nr}, v{nr}, s{nr}, t{nr}). 5. Decoder MLP (\ThetaD): A 2-layer MLP with 256 hidden units and ReLU activations. Input: Densities from original ray \sigmai and refracted ray \sigma{ir}. Output: Combined density \sigma{ic}. 6. Directional MLP: Takes decoded density \sigma{ic} and direction d. Outputs view-dependent color c. Numbered Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Project sampled points \mathbf{x} along rays \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} using sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = [\sin(\mathbf{x}), \cos(\mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}\mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1}\mathbf{x})], where L is the highest frequency hyperparameter. 2. Ray Parameterization: Convert the incident ray direction \mathbf{d} to 4D light field coordinates (u, v, s, t) by mapping intersections with planes Z0=0 and Z1=1. Conversely, convert 4D coordinates back to Cartesian direction \mathbf{d} using: \mathbf{d} = (Z1 - Z0, u - s, v - t) 3. Initial Sampling and Normal Estimation: In the initial phase of stratified sampling, sample points only along the original incident ray. Estimate the local surface normal \mathbf{N} at these points using the gradient of the density field (as per standard NeRF normal estimation, referenced as Eq. 5 in). 4. Refracted Ray Prediction: Teacher Network: Compute the target refracted ray coordinates (u{nr}, v{nr}, s{nr}, t{nr}) = \Thetat(u, v, s, t, \mathbf{N}) using the teacher network \Thetat which takes the normal \mathbf{N} as input. Student Network (RefNet): Predict the refracted ray coordinates (u{nr}, v{nr}, s{nr}, t{nr}) = \Thetas(u, v, s, t) using the student network \Thetas without normal input. Online Distillation: Train \Thetas to match \Thetat's output using the distillation loss L{dist}. 5. Refracted Ray Origin and Sampling: Determine the origin \mathbf{o}r of the refracted ray. The paper sets the origin at the intersection of the refracted ray line with the plane Z = zc (where zc is the Z-coordinate of the camera center). The coordinates are determined by solving: \frac{u - xr}{Z0 - zr} = \frac{s - xr}{Z1 - zr} = \frac{v - yr}{Z0 - zr} = \frac{t - yr}{Z1 - zr} (Note: The source text contains a typo in Eq. 10, but states that the specific choice of starting point does not affect the final outcome). Define the refracted ray as \mathbf{r}r = \mathbf{o}r + t\mathbf{d}r, where \mathbf{d}r is derived from the predicted 4D coordinates. Sampling Strategy: Phase 1: Sample along the original ray. Phase 2: Predict the refracted ray \mathbf{r}r. Sample along both the original ray and the refracted ray. Apply importance sampling based on Phase 1 results to the original ray, while uniformly sampling the refracted ray. Subsequent Phases: Both original and refracted rays undergo independent importance sampling. 6. Density Query: Query the volume density \sigmai at all sampling points along the original ray and \sigma{ir} at all sampling points along the refracted ray using only the NeRF Spatial MLP. 7. Density Decoding: Fuse the densities of the original and refracted rays into a complete ray density \sigma{ic} using the Decoder MLP \ThetaD: \sigma{ic} = \ThetaD(\sigmai, \sigma{ir}) 8. Color Prediction: Feed the decoded density \sigma{ic} and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} into the Directional MLP. The direction is input last to better output view-dependent RGB color cc. 9. Rendering: Compute the final pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using volume rendering (alpha compositing): \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma{ic,i} \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{ic,j} \deltaj) and \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. 10. Optimization: Minimize the total loss L: L = \lambda1 L{dist} + \lambda2 L{ref} + L{NeRF} where L{NeRF} is the baseline photometric loss, L{dist} is the distillation loss, and L{ref} is the refraction loss. Formulas: Distillation Loss (L{dist}): Encourages the student network's prediction \hat{\mathbf{d}}r (without normal) to match the teacher's prediction \hat{\mathbf{d}}{rn} (with normal): L{dist} = \sumi (1 - \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ri} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}{rni}) Refraction Loss (L{ref}): Combines reversible and irreversibility terms to ensure physical consistency: L{ref} = \sumi (1 - \mathbf{d}i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}i) + \sumi (1 - \mathbf{d}i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ri}) where \mathbf{d}i is the original direction, \hat{\mathbf{d}}i is the predicted refracted direction, and \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ri} is the reverse predicted direction. Total Loss: L = \lambda1 L{dist} + \lambda2 L{ref} + L{NeRF} Parameters: \lambda1, \lambda2: Weighting coefficients for distillation and refraction losses. Set to 0.003 on all datasets. L: Highest frequency in sinusoidal positional encoding. Batch size: 1024 rays per batch. Iterations: 200k iterations. Warm-up: First 5k iterations query only density \sigma and do not use the decoder. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Floater Artifacts: Without refraction modeling, NeRF suffers from semi-transparent floaters because sampling points are not aligned with the bent ray path. Loss of Refraction Loss: Removing L{ref} disrupts fitting because the absence of the correct refracted ray path leads to erroneous sampling points. Decoder Substitution: Substituting the specialized decoder with a simple average leads to significant performance decrease. Parameterization: Using origin and direction instead of 4D light field parameterization worsens accuracy, especially for LPIPS. Normal Dependency: While the student network does not use normals, the teacher does. The method relies on estimating normals from the initial density query. Complexity: The method adds a small MLP (RefNet) and a Decoder MLP to the standard NeRF architecture. The RefNet is shallow (2-3 layers), reducing computational load compared to point-by-point deformation networks. Performance: RoseNeRF demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the Eikonal Fields’ and Shiny datasets without additional information like IoR. It outperforms Ref-NeRF and achieves competitive results with NeX (which has 500x more parameters). Strengths: No need for IoR fields or surface masks. Simplifies complex refraction to a single event. Reduces degrees of freedom. Limitations: Assumes a single refraction event, ignoring multiple internal reflections or refractions. Performance may degrade if the single-refraction assumption is violated significantly. RoseNeRF was introduced by Xiaoqian Liang et al. in 2024 at the ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ICMR). It addresses the challenge of novel view synthesis for refractive objects, a problem where standard NeRF fails due to incorrect sampling along bent light paths. The method is inspired by Han et al. [20], who reconstructed transparent objects by immersing them in liquid, simplifying the modeling by ignoring complex ray interactions. RoseNeRF is implemented on top of MS-NeRF. Refracting Once is Enough: Neural Radiance Fields for Novel-View Synthesis of Real Refractive Objects, https://doi.org/10.1145/3652583.3658000, fetched 2026-11-06

name: NeRF-Det
head: NeRF-then-Det
body: NeRF-Det is a method for indoor 3D object detection using posed RGB images that explicitly models scene geometry as an opacity field by jointly training a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) branch with a 3D detection pipeline. It solves the problem of decoupled training in joint NeRF-and-detection systems by enabling gradient flow from the NeRF branch to the detection branch through a shared geometry-based Multi-Layer Perceptron (G-MLP), thereby propagating multi-view consistency constraints to the detector. This distinguishes it from "NeRF-then-Det" approaches like NeRF-RPN, where the NeRF and detection modules are trained independently or where consistency constraints do not reach the detection backbone, resulting in significantly higher latency and lower accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of T posed RGB frames Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi \times Wi \times 3} with known intrinsic matrices K \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and extrinsic matrices Ri \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4} for i = 1, \dots, T. Output: 3D bounding boxes for objects in the scene. Data Structures: 1. 2D Feature Maps (Fi): Extracted from input images using a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN). Layout: Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}}, where C is the channel dimension, and H, W are the original image dimensions. 2. 3D Voxel Grid: A uniform grid of Nx \times Ny \times Nz voxels. Coordinate System: The z-axis denotes height; x- and y-axes denote horizontal dimensions. Voxel Center: p = (x, y, z)^T. 3. 3D Volume Features (Vi(p)): Features assigned to each voxel from each view. 4. Aggregated Volume Features (V{avg}(p)): The mean of effective multi-view features. 5. Density Field (\sigma(p)): Predicted by the shared G-MLP. Numbered Steps: 1. 2D Feature Extraction: Pass each input image Ii through a 2D image backbone (FPN) to extract high-resolution features Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}}. 2. 3D-to-2D Projection: For each voxel center p = (x, y, z)^T in the 3D grid, project it into view i to obtain 2D coordinates (ui, vi). Compute homogeneous coordinates: \begin{pmatrix} u'i, v'i, di \end{pmatrix}^T = K' \times Ri \times \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{p}, 1 \end{pmatrix}^T. Here, K' is the scaled intrinsic matrix accounting for feature map downsampling. Calculate pixel coordinates: (ui, vi) = (u'i / di, v'i / di). 3. Feature Assignment: Assign 3D features Vi(p) by nearest neighbor interpolation of Fi at location (ui, vi): Vi(p) = \text{interpolate}((ui, vi), Fi) Edge Case: If p is projected outside the image boundary or behind the image plane (di \le 0), discard the feature and set Vi(p) = 0. 4. Multi-View Aggregation: Aggregate features from all T views. Let Mp be the number of effective 2D projections (views where Vi(p) \neq 0). Compute the average volume feature: V{avg}(p) = \frac{1}{Mp} \sum{i=1}^{Mp} Vi(p) Note: The source notes that sampling features from multi-view 2D image features yields better performance (+0.7 mAP@0.25) than sampling from 3D volume features. 5. Geometry Prediction (Shared G-MLP): Feed the voxel coordinates p into a shared geometry MLP (G-MLP) to predict the volume density \sigma(p). Activation for density: ReLU. This G-MLP is shared between the NeRF branch and the detection branch, allowing gradients from the NeRF branch to back-propagate to the image features and benefit the detection branch. 6. Opacity Field Generation: Transform the density field \sigma(p) into an opacity field \alpha(p). The source states the density field is transformed into an opacity field and multiplied with the volume features. While the exact functional form of \alpha(\sigma) is not explicitly defined as the standard \alpha = 1 - e^{-\sigma \delta} in the text, the operation is described as transforming density to opacity to reduce weights of empty space. 7. Geometry-Aware Volume Features: Multiply the opacity field with the aggregated volume features to reduce the weights of empty space: V{geo}(p) = \alpha(p) \cdot V{avg}(p) Additional Features: The method optionally incorporates variance features. Introducing variance features improves performance by over 0.7 mAP@.25 and 0.6 mAP@.50 compared to using only average features. The variance is calculated across the multi-view projections Vi(p). 8. 3D Detection: Feed the geometry-aware volume features V{geo}(p) (and optionally variance features) to the detection head for 3D bounding box regression. 9. Inference: During inference, remove the NeRF branch (the G-MLP and associated rendering losses) to minimize additional overhead to the original detector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def nerfdetforward(images, intrinsics, extrinsics, voxelgrid, gmlp, detectionhead): """ Forward pass for NeRF-Det. Args: images: List of T RGB images, shape (T, H, W, 3). intrinsics: Intrinsic matrix K, shape (3, 3). extrinsics: List of T extrinsic matrices Ri, shape (T, 3, 4). voxelgrid: 3D grid of voxel centers p, shape (Nx, Ny, Nz, 3). gmlp: Shared geometry MLP predicting density. detectionhead: 3D detection head. Returns: boxes: 3D bounding boxes. """ T = len(images) H, W = images[0].shape[0], images[0].shape[1] # Step 1: Extract 2D features # Fi shape: (T, C, H/4, W/4) F = extractfeatures(images) # Scale intrinsic matrix for feature map downsampling (factor of 4) Kprime = intrinsics 0.25 # Step 2 & 3: Project voxels and assign features # Vi shape: (T, Nx, Ny, Nz, C) V = np.zeros((T, voxelgrid.shape[:-1], F.shape[1])) for t in range(T): Rt = extrinsics[t] # Project all voxel centers to view t # phom: (NxNyNz, 4) phom = np.hstack([voxelgrid.reshape(-1, 3), np.ones((voxelgrid.shape[0]voxelgrid.shape[1]voxelgrid.shape[2], 1))]) # u't, v't, dt: (NxNyNz, 3) proj = Kprime @ (Rt @ phom.T) uprime = proj[0,:] vprime = proj[1,:] d = proj[2,:] # Pixel coordinates u = uprime / d v = vprime / d # Nearest neighbor interpolation # Clip coordinates to valid range [0, H/4-1] x [0, W/4-1] uint = np.clip(np.round(u).astype(int), 0, F.shape[2] - 1) vint = np.clip(np.round(v).astype(int), 0, F.shape[3] - 1) # Gather features # F[t] shape: (C, H/4, W/4) # We need to gather for each voxel flatidx = uint F.shape[3] + vint featurest = F[t,:, uint, vint].transpose(1, 2, 3, 0) # Shape: (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) # Set to 0 if behind image plane or out of bounds (handled by clip, but d<=0 check needed) validmask = d > 0 # Reshape mask to match features validmask3d = validmask.reshape(voxelgrid.shape[:-1]) featurest[~validmask3d] = 0 V[t] = featurest # Step 4: Aggregate multi-view features # Vavg shape: (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) # Count effective projections effectivecount = np.sum(V != 0, axis=0) # Shape: (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) - element-wise non-zero check # To be precise, Mp is the number of views where Vi(p) is not zero vector. # Assuming non-zero vector check: isvalid = np.any(V != 0, axis=-1) # Shape: (T, Nx, Ny, Nz) Mp = np.sum(isvalid, axis=0) # Shape: (Nx, Ny, Nz) # Avoid division by zero Mpsafe = np.maximum(Mp, 1) Vavg = np.sum(V, axis=0) / Mpsafe.reshape(1, 1, 1, 1) # Broadcasting # Step 5: Predict density with shared G-MLP # Flatten voxel grid for MLP input pflat = voxelgrid.reshape(-1, 3) sigmaflat = gmlp(pflat) # Shape: (NxNyNz,) sigma = sigmaflat.reshape(voxelgrid.shape[:-1]) # Activation for density: ReLU sigma = np.maximum(sigma, 0) # Step 6: Transform density to opacity # Source says "transform the density field into an opacity field" # Standard volume rendering opacity: alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # Since delta is not specified, we assume unit delta or standard conversion # Note: The source does not specify the exact formula for alpha(sigma). # We use the standard conversion as a placeholder for the "transformation". alpha = 1 - np.exp(-sigma) # Step 7: Geometry-aware volume features Vgeo = alpha.reshape(1, 1, 1, -1) Vavg # Broadcasting over channels # Optional: Variance features # Variance across views Vvar = np.var(V, axis=0) # Shape: (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) # Combine Vgeo and Vvar? Source says "introducing variance features improves performance" # It implies they are used as input to the detection head. # We concatenate them. Vinput = np.concatenate([Vgeo, Vvar], axis=-1) # Step 8: Detection boxes = detectionhead(Vinput) return boxes def extractfeatures(images): """ Placeholder for FPN feature extraction. Returns features Fi in R^{C x H/4 x W/4}. """ # Implementation depends on specific FPN backbone # Not given in the sources. pass Parameters: Density Activation: ReLU. Color Activation: Sigmoid (used in the NeRF branch for color prediction c(p, d), though the color branch is removed at inference). Interpolation: Nearest neighbor. Pitfalls: Depth Estimation Errors: Using predicted depth maps from external geometry reconstruction (e.g., NeuralRecon) significantly degrades detection performance by 2.3 mAP@.50 compared to plain ImVoxelNet, demonstrating that depth estimation errors propagate inaccuracy through the detection pipeline. Detection Branch Impact on NeRF: The detection branch negatively impacts the NeRF branch's novel view synthesis quality. Disabling the detection branch brings a 0.43dB improvement in PSNR, suggesting the detection branch is prone to erasing low-level details required for NeRF rendering. Boundary Conditions: Voxels projected outside the image boundary or behind the image plane must be handled by setting their features to 0. The Shared G-MLP is a component of the NeRF-Det architecture that links the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) branch with the 3D object detection branch using a shared geometry-based Multi-Layer Perceptron. It solves the problem of decoupled training in joint NeRF-and-detection systems by enabling gradient flow from the NeRF branch to the detection branch, thereby propagating multi-view consistency constraints to the detector. This distinguishes it from "NeRF-to-Det" approaches where the NeRF and detection modules are trained independently or where consistency constraints do not reach the detection backbone. Time Complexity: The method is significantly faster than "NeRF-then-Det" approaches. NeRF-Det has a latency of 0.554s on one V100, compared to NeRF-RPN's ~846.8s latency. This is because NeRF-Det is a joint training paradigm that generalizes to unseen scenes without per-scene optimization, whereas NeRF-RPN requires per-scene optimization. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Improves state-of-the-art by 3.9 mAP on ScanNet and 3.1 mAP on ARKITScenes benchmarks. On ScanNet, NeRF-Det-R50 achieves 35.13 AP50. Achieves an average PSNR of 20+ for novel view synthesis and an RMSE of 0.756 for depth estimation on 312 scenes in the validation set, without per-scene training. Scaling: The method leverages augmented image features as priors to enhance the generalizability of the NeRF-MLP, avoiding the heavy overhead of per-scene optimization. Strengths: Explicitly models scene geometry as an opacity field, improving 3D detection performance. Joint training allows multi-view consistency constraints to benefit the detector. Fast inference due to no per-scene optimization. Limitations: The detection branch can degrade the NeRF branch's novel view synthesis quality by erasing low-level details. Relies on posed RGB images. When to use: Indoor 3D object detection with posed RGB images where generalization to unseen scenes is required without per-scene optimization. When not to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is the primary goal and the detection branch's interference with low-level details is unacceptable. When depth sensors are available and accurate depth estimation is preferred over learned geometry (though the method can optionally use depth for training, inference does not require it). NeRF-Det was introduced by Chenfeng et al. from Meta. The work was done when Chenfeng was an intern at Meta. It was published in 2023 at ICCV. The method addresses the limitations of existing indoor 3D detection methods that struggle to model scene geometry and the high latency of per-scene NeRF optimization. It builds on the baseline NeRF architecture Parent and ImVoxelNet.
