name: Shared G-MLP
head: NeRF-Det
body: The Shared G-MLP is a component of the NeRF-Det architecture that links the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) branch with the 3D object detection branch using a shared geometry-based Multi-Layer Perceptron. It enables gradient flow from the NeRF branch to the detection branch, propagating multi-view consistency constraints to the detector. This joint training setup improves upon NeRF-to-Det approaches by directly integrating the branches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D spatial coordinates (x, y, z) sampled along rays or within the voxel grid. Output: A geometry-aware feature representation used by both the volume rendering loss and the detection head. Data Structures: Shared G-MLP: A standard Multi-Layer Perceptron. The specific layer dimensions, activation functions, and weight initialization are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Coordinate Sampling: Sample 3D points along rays or within the 3D volume feature grid. 2. Geometry Encoding: Pass the 3D coordinates through the Shared G-MLP to obtain a geometry-aware feature or density value. 3. Joint Optimization: The geometry output is used by the NeRF branch to compute volume rendering losses. The same output is used by the detection branch to estimate opacity fields for 3D bounding box regression. Gradients from both losses flow back through the Shared G-MLP weights. 4. Free Space Masking: The shared geometry signal effectively masks out free space in the feature volume, reducing ambiguity for the detection head. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: MLP Depth/Width: Not given in the sources. Activation Function: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance Degradation: Removing the shared G-MLP causes a drastic performance drop in 3D object detection. Specifically, mAP@.25 decreases from 50.1 to 48.1. This occurs because the influence of multi-view consistency is restricted to the image backbone rather than the volumetric representation. The parent method that utilizes the Shared G-MLP for joint NeRF and detection training. It explicitly models scene geometry as an opacity field to improve indoor 3D object detection from posed RGB images. Link Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In the ablation study, the method achieves an mAP@.25 of 50.1 and mAP@.50 of 24.4 when using the Shared G-MLP with multi-view 2D feature sampling. Without the Shared G-MLP, performance drops to 48.1 mAP@.25 and 23.8 mAP@.50. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables direct gradient flow from NeRF to the detection branch, effectively masking free space and reducing feature volume ambiguity. Propagates multi-view consistency constraints to the detection module. Limitations: Requires joint training of NeRF and detection branches. When to Use: Use when performing joint NeRF-and-detection tasks where multi-view consistency is critical for accurate 3D bounding box regression and free-space suppression. The Shared G-MLP was introduced in the NeRF-Det paper. It addresses limitations in previous NeRF-to-Det approaches by ensuring the NeRF branch sufficiently influences the detection branch. The method builds on the concept of using neural volumetric features for direct 3D bounding box regression. name: Semantic Ray (S-Ray)
head: S-Ray
body: Semantic Ray (S-Ray) is a method for learning a generalizable semantic field that infers semantic labels on novel viewpoints across unseen scenes, addressing the overfitting and lack of generalization inherent in single-scene semantic NeRFs like Semantic-NeRF. It distinguishes itself by training a unified model on multiple scenes and utilizing a Cross-Reprojection Attention module to exploit semantic context from multiple views, rather than estimating semantics from a single ray. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of m input views with known camera poses and semantic labels; a query ray \mathbf{r} from a novel viewpoint. Outputs: A rendered semantic map (logits or probabilities) and color image for the novel view. Data Structures: Contextual Space (\mathbf{M}): A matrix of shape m \times N \times C, where m is the number of input views, N is the number of sampled points along the reprojected ray, and C is the channel dimension. \mathbf{M} = [\mathbf{F}1, \mathbf{F}2, \dots, \mathbf{F}m]^T. Radial Feature (\mathbf{F}i): A matrix of shape N \times C representing the features for the i-th view along the reprojected ray. \mathbf{F}i = [\mathbf{f}i(r^(z1)), \mathbf{f}i(r^(z2)), \dots, \mathbf{f}i(r^(zN))], where r^(zk) denotes the reprojected position of the k-th sample point. Parameters: N: Number of random quadrature points between near plane tn and far plane tf used to approximate continuous integration. H: Number of heads in the intra-view radial attention module. C: Channel dimension of the feature vectors. Steps: 1. Build Initial 3D Contextual Space: For each input view i \in \{1, \dots, m\}, reproject the query ray \mathbf{r} to the view. Since the emitted ray is virtual, the network models the uncertainty of reprojection, obtaining a reprojected ray showing possible positions rather than exact points. Apply a CNN-based module to extract contextual features for sampled points along this reprojected ray, forming \mathbf{F}i. Assemble these into \mathbf{M}. 2. Cross-Reprojection Attention: Decompose the dense attention over \mathbf{M} into two lightweight modules to reduce computational cost: Intra-view Radial Attention: Learns relations among sampled points within each view. For each \mathbf{F}i \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}, compute attention with H heads: \text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^T}{\sqrt{dk}}\right)\mathbf{V} where \mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} are derived from \mathbf{F}i. Cross-view Sparse Attention: Distinguishes the same point across different viewpoints and scores the semantic contribution of each view. The output is a refined contextual space \mathbf{M}'. 3. Semantic Ray Construction: Adopt a Semantic-Aware Weight Net to learn the significance of each view. This net assigns weights to the views in \mathbf{M}' to construct the semantic ray, effectively aggregating the refined contextual information. 4. Geometry-Aware Rendering: Leverage a Geometry-Aware Net to predict volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Render the semantics along the query ray using the weighted semantic features from Step 3 and the density/color from Step 4. The color rendering follows the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}; \theta) = \sum{k=1}^{N} T(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk) \deltak) \mathbf{c}(tk) where T(tk) = \exp\left(-\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(t{k'}) \delta{k'}\right), \alpha(x) = 1 - \exp(-x), and \deltak = t{k+1} - tk. The semantic output is rendered similarly, using the aggregated semantic features instead of \mathbf{c}(tk). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def semanticrayrendering(inputviews, queryray, cameraposes): """ inputviews: List of m images with semantic labels. queryray: Ray origin and direction for the novel view. cameraposes: Poses of the input views. """ m = len(inputviews) N = 128 # Number of quadrature points C = 256 # Channel dimension # Step 1: Build Initial 3D Contextual Space M = [] for i in range(m): # Reproject query ray to view i # Model uncertainty by sampling points along the reprojected ray reprojectedray = reprojectray(queryray, cameraposes[i]) samples = samplealongray(reprojectedray, N) # Extract features using CNN # Note: The source mentions a CNN-based module but does not specify architecture details # Assuming a standard CNN feature extractor Fcnn Fi = extractfeatures(inputviews[i], samples) M.append(Fi) M = stack(M) # Shape: (m, N, C) # Step 2: Cross-Reprojection Attention # Intra-view Radial Attention Mrefined = [] for i in range(m): Fi = M[i] # Shape: (N, C) # Standard Multi-Head Attention Q, K, V = linearheads(Fi, H=8) # H is number of heads attnoutput = multiheadattention(Q, K, V) Mrefined.append(attnoutput) Mrefined = stack(Mrefined) # Shape: (m, N, C) # Cross-view Sparse Attention # The source describes the function (distinguishing points across views, scoring contribution) # but does not provide the exact mathematical formulation for the cross-view module. # We assume a sparse attention mechanism over the view dimension m. Mfinal = crossviewsparseattention(Mrefined) # Step 3: Semantic Ray Construction # Semantic-Aware Weight Net weights = semanticweightnet(Mfinal) # Shape: (m, 1) or (m,) # Aggregate features weighted by view significance semanticrayfeatures = aggregatefeatures(Mfinal, weights) # Step 4: Geometry-Aware Rendering # Geometry-Aware Net # The source mentions a "Geometry-Aware Net" but does not specify its inputs/outputs beyond density/color. # We assume it takes the query ray and possibly the semantic features to predict sigma and color. sigma, color = geometryawarenet(queryray, semanticrayfeatures) # Render Color colorrendered = volumerendercolor(queryray, sigma, color, N) # Render Semantics # The source states semantics are rendered along the query ray using the semantic ray features. # The exact weighting function for semantic rendering is not explicitly detailed beyond the weight net. # We assume a similar volume rendering process using the aggregated semantic features. semanticrendered = volumerendersemantic(queryray, sigma, semanticrayfeatures, N) return colorrendered, semanticrendered Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Directly performing dense attention over sampled points on each reprojected ray of multiple views suffers from heavy computational costs. The decomposition into intra-view and cross-view attention is critical to mitigate this. Reprojection Uncertainty: Since the emitted ray from the query point is virtual, the network cannot obtain the exact reprojected point on each view, but a reprojected ray showing possible positions. The network must model this uncertainty. Overfitting: Unlike Semantic-NeRF, which relies on positional encoding and is prone to overfitting the current scene, S-Ray is designed to generalize. SegNeRF addresses generalization by learning a semantic field and performing reconstruction and segmentation in a self-supervised fashion from a single view, allowing for semantic object/scene completion. Time Complexity: The decomposition of dense attention into intra-view radial and cross-view sparse attention reduces computational costs compared to dense multi-view attention. Memory Complexity: Storing the contextual space \mathbf{M} requires O(m \cdot N \cdot C) memory. Performance: S-Ray achieves comparable quality to Semantic-NeRF's result for 100k iterations per-scene optimization by fine-tuning on more images for only 10 min (2k iterations). Strengths: Generalizes to unseen scenes; exploits rich semantic context from multiple views; efficient attention mechanism. Limitations: Requires multiple input views for the cross-reprojection attention; relies on the quality of the CNN feature extractor for the initial contextual space. When to use: When generalizing semantic understanding across diverse, unseen scenes is required, and multiple input views are available. When not to use: When only a single view is available (consider SegNeRF) or when per-scene optimization is feasible and generalization is not needed (Semantic-NeRF). Semantic Ray (S-Ray) was introduced by Fangfu Liu, Chubin Zhang, Yu Zheng, and Yueqi Duan from Tsinghua University in March 2023. It was proposed to address the limitations of Semantic-NeRF, which trains one specific model for each scene and relies on positional encoding prone to overfitting. S-Ray trains one unified model on multiple scenes and generalizes to unseen scenes. It was evaluated on synthetic scenes from the Replica dataset and real-world scenes from the ScanNet dataset. name: Neural Density-Distance Fields
head: NeDDF (Neural Density-Distance Fields), Neural Density-Distance Fields (NeDDF) Architecture
body:
Neural Density-Distance Fields (NeDDF) is a method that reciprocally constrains distance and density fields, extending the distance field formulation to adapt to any density field. It allows for boundaryless scenes and complex shapes by deriving density from the first derivative of an output distance field D. Unlike standard NeRF which optimizes density \sigma directly, NeDDF optimizes a distance field D and computes \sigma via 
abla D, requiring careful setup of Positional Encoding (PE) and activation functions to handle second derivatives. It provides competitive novel view synthesis quality, more stable meshes, and a broader range of valid camera poses than NeRF, while handling transparency and thin surfaces better than NeuS by interpreting occupancy as lower density. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D spatial position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Distance field value D(\mathbf{p}) \in \mathbb{R}. Color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Auxiliary gradient component  rac{\partial D}{\partial w} (internal to the network for cusp handling). Data Structures and Layout: The network consists of two parallel branches sharing the same input processing: 1. Distance Branch: Input: Concatenated PE vectors (see Input Processing). Layers: Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation. Output: D(\mathbf{p}). 2. Color Branch: Input: Concatenated PE vectors. Layers: Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(256) ightarrow Activation ightarrow Dense(128) ightarrow Activation. Output: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) (size 3). Input Processing: The input to the MLPs is a concatenation of three Positional Encoding (PE) vectors: 1. Standard PE \gamma(\mathbf{p}) (size 60). 2. Distance PE \gamma(d) (size 24). 3. Damped PE \gamma'(\mathbf{p}) (size 60). Standard PE \gamma(\mathbf{p}) for position \mathbf{p} with frequency bands L: \gamma(\mathbf{p}) = [\sin(\mathbf{p}), \cos(\mathbf{p}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p}), \cos(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p})]^T Damped PE \gamma'(\mathbf{p}) dampens high-frequency terms by 1/2^{L-1} to keep the scale in the single-differentiation hierarchy same as original PE: \gamma'(\mathbf{p}) = [\sin(\mathbf{p}), \cos(\mathbf{p}), \dots,  rac{1}{2^{L-1}}\sin(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p}),  rac{1}{2^{L-1}}\cos(2^{L-1}\mathbf{p})]^T Density Calculation: Density \sigma(\mathbf{p}) is derived from the distance field D(\mathbf{p}) and its gradient 
abla D(\mathbf{p}). The view-independent distance field is defined as the minimum volumetric depth over all viewing directions \mathbf{v} \in S^2: D(\mathbf{p}):= \min{\mathbf{v} \in S^2} [d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v})] where volumetric depth is: d(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}):= tn + \int{tn}^{tf} t T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt and transmission T(t) = \exp \left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s))ds ight). The optimal view direction \mathbf{v}n is recovered from the gradient: \mathbf{v}n = - rac{
abla D(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla D(\mathbf{p})\|2} The density is obtained from the directional derivative of the distance field along the gradient direction. The derivative is expressed as:  rac{\partial D(\mathbf{r}(t))}{\partial t} = 
abla D(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = -\|
abla D(\mathbf{p})\|2 Combining this with the definition of the derivative via depth limits yields the exact density formula: \sigma(\mathbf{p}) =  rac{1 - \|
abla D(\mathbf{p} - tn \mathbf{v})\|2}{D(\mathbf{p} - tn \mathbf{v}) - tn} Assuming tn is small and D(\mathbf{p} - tn \mathbf{v}) \simeq D(\mathbf{p}) + tn, the approximated density calculation is: \sigma(\mathbf{p}) \simeq  rac{1 - \|
abla D(\mathbf{p})\|2}{D(\mathbf{p})} Cusp Handling (Auxiliary Gradient): Distance fields are not differentiable at cusps where the minimum distance direction switches, causing small gradient values to convert to false densities. To handle this, the distance field domain is extended from 3D [x,y,z] to 4D hyperspace [x,y,z,w] with an auxiliary gradient axis w. The slice at w=0 is the distance field. Gradient components  rac{\partial D}{\partial w} are distributed to suppress spurious densities near cusps. A heuristic constraint is applied when  rac{\partial D}{\partial t} > 0:  rac{\partial^2 D}{\partial t \partial w} = \alpha  rac{1}{D}  rac{\partial D}{\partial w} where \alpha is a hyperparameter determining the scale of the auxiliary gradient. To handle instability around D=0 and  rac{\partial D}{\partial w}=0, a weight coefficient  eta is introduced:  eta = D \left( rac{\partial D}{\partial t}ight)^2  rac{\partial D}{\partial w} Note:  eta is separated from the calculation graph during training (stop-gradient). The shape constraint objective function L{const} over M sampling points \mathcal{P} is: L{const} =  rac{\lambda{const}}{M} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}}  eta \left[ rac{\partial^2 D}{\partial t \partial w} -  rac{\alpha}{D(\mathbf{p})}  rac{\partial D}{\partial w}ight]^2 Reprojection Error and Localization: For camera pose estimation, pseudo-correspondence points are calculated. For each ray, points closer to observed color C(\mathbf{q}) than estimated \hat{C}(\mathbf{q}) are selected. The near-surface point is \mathbf{p}i - Di(
abla Di). The weight gi for sampling point \mathbf{p}i is: gi = \mathrm{softmax}\left(-\lambdaD  rac{Di \|
abla Di 	imes \mathbf{v}\|2}{ti} - \lambdac \|\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}) - \mathbf{c}i\|2ight) where \lambdaD and \lambdac are hyperparameters. The reprojection error measures the distance \|\mathbf{q} - \hat{\mathbf{q}}\|2 between pixel coordinates of ray \mathbf{q} and projected pseudo-correspondence point \hat{\mathbf{q}}. Blank Region Penalty: To constrain the color field in regions outside the object (where \|

L is number of frequency bands. # Standard PE size: 2 L 3 = 60 for 3D pos. # Damped PE size: 60. # Distance PE size: 24 (Not given in sources exactly, assumed based on note). # Total input dim: 60 + 24 + 60 = 144. self.L = L self.numfreqs = numfreqs # Distance Branch: 3 hidden layers of 256 self.distmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(144, 256), nn.TanhExp(), # Custom activation nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.TanhExp(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.TanhExp(), nn.Linear(256, 1) # Output D) # Color Branch: 4 hidden layers (256, 256, 256, 128) self.colormlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(144, 256), nn.TanhExp(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.TanhExp(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.TanhExp(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.TanhExp(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # Output Color) def positionalencoding(self, x, L=10): """Standard PE""" # x shape: (..., 3) freqbands = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, L-1, L).to(x.device) # sin(2^0 x), cos(2^0 x),..., sin(2^(L-1) x), cos(2^(L-1) x) pe = [] for freq in freqbands: pe.append(torch.sin(x freq)) pe.append(torch.cos(x freq)) return torch.cat(pe, dim=-1) def dampedpositionalencoding(self, x, L=10): """Damped PE: high freq terms scaled by 1/2^(L-1)""" freqbands = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, L-1, L).to(x.device) pe = [] for i, freq in enumerate(freqbands): scale = 1.0 / (2.0 (L-1)) if i == L-1 else 1.0 # Note: Source says dampens high-freq by 1/2^(L-1). # Actually source eq 20: 1/2^(L-1) applied to the highest freq term sin(2^(L-1)p). # Let's implement strictly: last term scaled. pe.append(torch.sin(x freq)) pe.append(torch.cos(x freq)) # Apply damping to the last pair (highest frequency) # The source equation shows 1/2^(L-1) on the last sin/cos. # pe[-2] is sin(2^(L-1)x), pe[-1] is cos(2^(L-1)x) dampingfactor = 1.0 / (2.0 (L-1)) pe[-2] = pe[-2] dampingfactor pe[-1] = pe[-1] dampingfactor return torch.cat(pe, dim=-1) def forward(self, x): # x: (N, 3) pestd = self.positionalencoding(x, self.L) pedamp = self.dampedpositionalencoding(x, self.L) # Distance PE is noted as size 24. Assuming similar structure to standard PE but for distance scalar? # Source says "distance PE gamma(d) (size 24)". # If d is scalar, 24 dims implies 12 freq bands? Or 3D distance? # Given the ambiguity, we assume a placeholder or standard PE of a scalar d. # However, to be implementable, we need a definition. # Let's assume gamma(d) is PE of the scalar distance value d, with 12 bands (24 dims). # But d is not an input to the network, it's derived or sampled. # In NeDDF, the input is just p. The "distance PE" might refer to encoding the sampled t or similar? # Re-reading: "Concatenate standard PE gamma(p)... distance PE gamma(d)... and damped PE gamma'(p)". # This implies d is an input. In volume rendering, we sample points along rays. # Perhaps d is the depth t? Or the distance field value D? # Given the architecture diagram description, it's an intermediate input. # Let's assume d is the sampled depth t along the ray, or a placeholder for now. # Since the source doesn't define d's origin in the forward pass explicitly as a network input variable # other than "intermediate inputs", and standard NeRF takes (x, dview), # here d might be the viewing direction? No, "distance PE". # Let's assume d is the scalar depth t for the sampled point. # We will pass t as an additional input or compute it. # For the sake of the method definition, we assume the network takes (p, t) or similar. # But the source says "Input processing: Concatenate...". # Let's assume the caller provides 'd' (depth) along with 'p'. # Note: The source does not specify how 'd' is obtained. # In volume rendering, we sample t. Let's assume d=t. # If d is not provided, this step is incomplete. # However, looking at Eq 1, D(p) is min depth. # The network outputs D(p). # The input to the network is p. # Why is there a distance PE? # Maybe d is the viewing direction encoded? No, "distance PE". # Let's assume d is a scalar depth value associated with the point p in the context of a ray. # We will define a helper to encode a scalar depth. # Re-evaluating: The source lists "distance PE gamma(d) (size 24)". # If d is a scalar, 24 dims = 12 freq bands. # We need to pass 'd' to the network. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the network input is (p, d). # d is the depth along the ray. ped = self.positionalencoding(d.unsqueeze(-1), L=12) # 12 bands 2 = 24 dims inputconcat = torch.cat([pestd, ped, pedamp], dim=-1) D = self.distmlp(inputconcat) c = self.colormlp(inputconcat) return D, c def computedensity(self, D, gradD, tn=0.0): """ Compute density from Distance and Gradient. D: (N, 1) gradD: (N, 3) tn: near clip plane (scalar) """ # Approximated formula: sigma = (1 - ||gradD||) / D # Guard against D ~ 0 normgrad = torch.norm(gradD, dim=-1, keepdim=True) sigma = (1.0 - normgrad) / (D + 1e-6) return sigma def computeauxiliarygradientpenalty(self, D, gradD, gradDw, gradDt, alpha, lambdaconst, points): """ Compute Lconst for auxiliary gradient shape constraint. """ # beta = D (dD/dt)^2 (dD/dw) # Note: beta is detached from graph beta = D (gradDt 2) gradDw beta = beta.detach() # Constraint: d2D / dt dw = alpha / D dD/dw # Lconst = lambdaconst / M sum( beta [ d2D/dt/dw - alpha/D dD/dw ]^2) # d2D/dt/dw is the mixed partial derivative. # In practice, this requires higher order autodiff. # We assume gradDtw is computed via torch.autograd.grad(gradDw, t, creategraph=True) or similar. # But t is not a direct input to D(p). D is function of p. # The source extends domain to 4D [x,y,z,w]. # So D is function of (x,y,z,w). # gradDt corresponds to gradient in the viewing direction? # The source says "slice at w=0". # This implementation detail is complex. # We will note the formula. term = gradDtw - (alpha / (D + 1e-6)) gradDw loss = (lambdaconst / len(points)) torch.sum(beta term2) return loss Parameters: \alpha: Hyperparameter for auxiliary gradient shape. Values \le 1 make gradient active in narrower range; larger values concentrate gradient near cusps. \lambda{const}: Hyperparameter for shape constraint objective. \lambdaD: Hyperparameter for distance component in reprojection weight. \lambdac: Hyperparameter for color component in reprojection weight. MLP Width: 256 neurons per hidden layer. Activation: tanhExp (second derivative is continuous). Optimizer: Adam with exponential decay for camera pose (6D SE(3) parameter). Sampling: 256 rays per iteration for interest region sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cusps: Distance fields are not differentiable at cusps, causing false densities. Mitigated by auxiliary gradient in 4D hyperspace. Interior Objects: Lack of distance field information inside objects. NeDDF is based on UDF, so it cannot provide helpful gradient directions in the interior object region. Discontinuities: View direction \mathbf{v}n has discontinuities, making gradient-based calculation difficult. Numerical Stability: Density is undefined for D \sim 0. Also, from tn > 0, density is limited to \sigma(\mathbf{p}) < 1/tn. PE Instability: Standard PE amplifies high-frequency elements in the density derivative hierarchy by a scale difference of 2^{L-1}, making learning unstable. Damped PE is used to mitigate this. Color Quality: Color field reconstruction performance is worse than NeRF for the same network size because damped PE neglects high-frequency components in the non-derivative hierarchy. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, it retains the same formulation as NeRF, implying similar complexity to standard NeRF, which is time-consuming for optimization and rendering. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the NeRF synthetic dataset (Lego, Drums, Ficus, Hotdog, Chair, Materials, Mic, Ship). PSNR results are competitive with NeRF and NeuS but slightly inferior to state-of-the-art methods. Lego: 32.91 (NeDDF) vs 32.54 (NeRF) vs 27.18 (NeuS). Chair: 29.11 (NeDDF) vs 33.00 (NeRF) vs 27.69 (NeuS). Hotdog: 30.85 (NeDDF) vs 36.18 (NeRF) vs 32.14 (NeuS). Strengths: More stable meshes, broader range of valid camera poses for localization, handles transparency and thin surfaces better than NeuS. Limitations: Slightly inferior PSNR to SOTA, worse color reconstruction than NeRF for same size, lack of interior distance info, time-consuming optimization. When to use: When stable mesh extraction and camera pose localization are required, or when dealing with thin surfaces/transparency. When not to use: When maximum PSNR is the primary goal and computational resources are limited. Neural Density-Distance Fields (NeDDF) was proposed to represent reciprocally constrained distance and density fields. It extends the distance field formulation to adapt to any density field, allowing for boundaryless scenes and complex shapes. The method was evaluated on the NeRF synthetic dataset for novel view synthesis and camera pose localization. It builds on the principles of NeRF [14] and NeuS [24], addressing limitations of boundary-based distance fields like NeuS. name: LAENeRF
head: Local Appearance Editing for Neural Radiance Fields
body:
LAENeRF is a unified framework for the photorealistic and non-photorealistic local appearance editing of pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It solves the problem of recoloring or stylizing arbitrary 3D regions while minimizing background artifacts and maintaining interactivity. Unlike methods that rely on semantic segmentation masks or global style transfer, LAENeRF uses a 3D edit grid for content selection and a palette-based neural module to learn a mapping from estimated ray terminations to output colors. It is distinguished by its ability to model smooth transitions between the edited region and the original scene content using a growing queue mechanism, and by its efficient distillation step that transfers edits back to the original radiance field parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model \Theta{NeRF} (typically Instant-NGP based), a set of training rays R, a user-defined 2D mask on a reference view, and optionally a style image s for stylization. Output: An edited NeRF model \Theta{NeRF}' and/or a set of learned palette parameters \hat{P} for interactive recoloring. Data Structures: 1. Edit Grid (E): A 3D voxel grid of resolution 128^3 (matching Instant-NGP's occupancy grid resolution). It is a bitfield where bits are set to 1 for voxels belonging to the selected region. 2. Growing Queue (G): A queue storing direct neighbors of voxels in E to facilitate region growing and smooth transitions. 3. Growing Grid (\mathcal{G}): A 3D grid constructed from the growing queue G, used to compute transition weights. 4. LAENeRF Module Parameters (\Theta{LAENeRF}): Color Palette (\hat{P}): A learnable tensor of shape N{\hat{P}} 	imes 3, where N{\hat{P}} is the number of base colors (initialized to 8). Hash Grid: A trainable multi-resolution hash grid (from Instant-NGP) for featurizing input positions. MLPs: Shallow multi-layer perceptrons that map featurized positions to weights and offsets. Numbered Steps: 1. Region Selection: The user scribbles on a 2D projection of the scene. For each selected pixel, a ray is cast through the pre-trained NeRF \Theta{NeRF} to compute the estimated ray termination x{term}. Compute estimated depth \zeta along the ray: \zeta = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) t{i+1} where Ti is transmittance, \sigmai is density, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti, and t{i+1} is the next sample position. Compute termination point: x{term} = o + \zeta d where o is the camera position and d is the viewing direction. Map x{term} to the nearest voxel in the edit grid E and set the corresponding bit to 1. 2. Region Growing: To ensure smooth transitions, a growing queue G is initialized with neighbors of the selected voxels. While G is not empty: Pop a voxel v from G. If the occupancy grid O at v is set (O=1): Add v to E. Add direct neighbors of v to G. Construct the growing grid \mathcal{G} from the final state of G. 3. Featurization and Prediction: For each ray r \in R intersecting E: Check if the accumulated alpha inside the edit grid T\alpha exceeds the edit threshold 	au{edit} = 0.5 to handle occlusions and resolution errors: T\alpha = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbbm{1}(o + ti d \in E) Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) If T\alpha > 	au{edit}: Featurize x{term} using the trainable hash grid to get \xi(x{term}). Featurize the viewing direction d using spherical harmonics encoding. Pass \xi(x{term}) and encoded d through shallow MLPs to predict: Per-ray barycentric weights \hat{w} \in [0, 1]^{N{\hat{P}}}. View-dependent offsets \hat{\delta} \in [-1, 1]^3. Compose the predicted color \hat{c}: \hat{c} = 	ext{clamp}(\hat{w}^T \hat{P} + \hat{\delta}) where 	ext{clamp} restricts values to [0, 1]. 4. Optimization: Optimize \Theta{LAENeRF} by minimizing the total loss \mathcal{L} over the set of rays R: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{content} + \mathcal{L}{style} + \mathcal{L}{TV} + \mathcal{L}{depth-disc} + \mathcal{L}{weight} + \mathcal{L}{offset} + \mathcal{L}{palette} + \mathcal{L}{smooth} Content Loss: \mathcal{L}{content} = \|\hat{c} - \mathcal{C}(r)\|2^2 where \mathcal{C}(r) is the ground truth color. Style Loss (optional): \mathcal{L}{style} = \lambda{style} \|G(s) - G(\hat{c})\|2^2 where G(\cdot) is the Gram matrix of features from a semantic encoder (e.g., VGG19 conv5, conv6, conv7). Total Variation Loss (geometry-aware): \mathcal{L}{TV} = \lambda{TV} \|
abla \hat{c} \cdot (1 - 	ext{depth\guide})\|2^2 where 
abla \hat{c} denotes image gradients in x/y directions, and 	ext{depth\guide}{i,j} = (|	ext{depth}{i,j+1} - 	ext{depth}{i,j}|, |	ext{depth}{i+1,j} - 	ext{depth}{i,j}|) restricts the loss to regions without depth discontinuities. Depth Discontinuity Loss: \mathcal{L}{depth-disc} = -\lambda{depth-disc} \|
abla \hat{c} \cdot 	ext{depth\guide}\|2^2 This encourages gradients to be placed in regions of depth discontinuities. Weight Loss (sparsity): \mathcal{L}{weight} = \lambda{weight} (1 - \|\hat{w}\|\infty) Encourages sparse per-pixel predictions. Offset Loss: \mathcal{L}{offset} = \lambda{offset} \|\hat{\delta}\|2^2 Prevents extreme high-frequency offset solutions. Palette Regularization: \mathcal{L}{palette} = \|\lfloor \hat{P} floor \cdot \hat{P}\|2^2 Guarantees valid colors in RGB space (\hat{P}{i,j} \in [0, 1]). Smooth Transition Loss (optional): \mathcal{L}{smooth} = \lambda{smooth} \|(\hat{c} - c)^2 \cdot d{trans}\|1 Adds to content loss when d{trans} \in (0, 1] for stylization. 5. Distillation/Transfer: After training \Theta{LAENeRF}, transfer changes to \Theta{NeRF} via fine-tuning. Compute per-ray transition weights d{trans} for smooth blending at boundaries: Raymarch through \mathcal{G} and O to obtain estimated ray terminations for rays intersecting \mathcal{G}, resulting in point cloud \mathcal{Z}. For each x{term} from E, compute minimum distance to \mathcal{Z}: d{min} = \min{y \in \mathcal{Z}} \|x{term} - y\|2 Compute transition weight: d{trans} = 1 -  rac{\min(d{min}, 	au{dist})}{	au{dist}} where 	au{dist} controls transition size (typically 1 	imes 10^{-2}). Construct modified training dataset: For rays intersecting E: Target color C{target} = T\alpha \hat{c} + (1 - T\alpha) \mathcal{C}(r). For rays not intersecting E: Target color C{target} = \mathcal{C}(r). Fine-tune \Theta{NeRF} using the modified dataset for 7 	imes 10^4 iterations. For interactive recoloring, interpolate the learned palette \hat{P} and a user-modified palette \hat{P}{mod} based on d{trans}. Parameters and Typical Values: Edit grid resolution: 128^3. Edit threshold 	au{edit}: 0.5. Initial palette size N{\hat{P}}: 8. Learning rate: 1 	imes 10^{-3} for all components, except \hat{P} which is 1 	imes 10^{-2}. Training iterations for LAENeRF: 1 	imes 10^5. Distillation iterations: 7 	imes 10^4. Style weight \lambda{style}: 1.3 	imes 10^2 for stylization, 0 for recoloring. \lambda{TV}: 1 	imes 10^{-4}. \lambda{depth-disc}: 5 	imes 10^{-4}. \lambda{weight}: 1 	imes 10^{-7}. \lambda{offset}: 5 	imes 10^{-5}. \lambda{smooth}: 1 	imes 10^{-3}. 	au{dist}: 1 	imes 10^{-2} (scene-dependent). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Structures: Naive stylization using only \mathcal{L}{content} and \mathcal{L}{style} often eliminates small structures. Geometry-aware losses (\mathcal{L}{TV}, \mathcal{L}{depth-disc}) are required to preserve them. Noise in x{term}: Imperfect geometry reconstruction in the pre-trained NeRF leads to noise in x{term}, requiring regularization via \mathcal{L}{offset} and \mathcal{L}{TV}. Sharp Discontinuities: Recoloring produces sharp discontinuities on the boundary of E if adjacent cells are occupied. The growing queue mechanism and \mathcal{L}{smooth} mitigate this. Palette Contribution: Color palettes that do not contribute significantly should be removed after 1.5 	imes 10^3 iterations to maintain sparsity and efficiency. Geometry-Aware Stylization Initialization: For geometry-aware stylization, train without \mathcal{L}{style}, \mathcal{L}{offset}, \mathcal{L}{TV} for the first 1000 iterations to achieve a well-initialized palette \hat{P}. A stylization technique that respects the learned geometry of the pre-trained NeRF by performing depth estimation to counteract the removal of small structures common in naive 2D style transfer. It utilizes depth-guided total variation and depth discontinuity losses to preserve geometric details while applying style. Time Complexity: The optimization of the LAENeRF module is lightweight as it operates on a sparse point cloud of ray terminations rather than the full volume. Training takes \sim 20 seconds for previews and 1 	imes 10^5 iterations total. Distillation takes no longer than 5 minutes on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the Instant-NGP hash grid and the edit grid (128^3), which is significantly lower than full-volume optimization methods. Performance: LAENeRF reduces background MSE error rates by 59% compared to PaletteNeRF with semantic guidance on the LLFF dataset. It introduces fewer background artifacts than Ref-NPR and models smooth transitions between original and edited content, a capability unique among compared methods. Strengths: Interactive local editing, photorealistic recoloring, non-photorealistic stylization, smooth transitions, low background artifacts, efficient computation. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained NeRF's geometry (noise in x{term} if geometry is poor). Requires user input for region selection. When to use: When local appearance editing (recoloring or stylization) is required with minimal background artifacts and smooth transitions. When not to use: When global scene editing is needed, or when the pre-trained NeRF has poor geometry reconstruction. LAENeRF was proposed by Lukas Radl, Michael Steiner, Andreas Kurz, and Markus Steinberger from Graz University of Technology. The method was published in arXiv:2312.09913v2 on March 25, 2024, and later in CVPR 2024. It builds upon Instant-NGP for efficient rendering and NeRFShop for region selection. It is implemented on torch-ngp and evaluated on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and mip-NeRF 360 datasets. name: ExtremeNeRF
head: Few-shot NeRF under varying-illumination, NeRF Extreme
body: ExtremeNeRF is a few-shot view synthesis framework designed to generate novel views from sparse multi-view images captured under unconstrained, varying illumination. It solves the problem of illumination-induced geometry distortion in standard NeRF by enforcing multi-view albedo consistency, assuming albedo is an intrinsic, illumination-invariant property of the scene. Unlike methods requiring massive image collections (e.g., NeRF-W) or those that fail with limited data (e.g., RegNeRF, FreeNeRF), ExtremeNeRF uses a two-stage intrinsic decomposition pipeline: an offline Full-image Intrinsic Decomposition Network (FIDNet) to generate pseudo-albedo ground truths, and an online Patch-wise Intrinsic Decomposition Network (PIDNet) to guide NeRF optimization via albedo consistency losses. ExtremeNeRF builds on the baseline NeRF architecture Parent but augments the training objective with intrinsic decomposition constraints. The method consists of an offline stage to prepare ground truths and an online stage where NeRF and PIDNet are optimized jointly. Inputs: A set of N input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with known camera poses (Ki, Ti) and intrinsics Ki. N is small (few-shot, e.g., 3 views). Outputs: A trained NeRF MLP F\Theta mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). A trained PIDNet F{PID} mapping color patches to intrinsic components. 1. NeRF MLP (F\Theta): Standard coordinate-based MLP. Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}, view-dependent color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. FIDNet: Pre-trained intrinsic decomposition network (based on IIDWW). Input: Full input image Ii. Output: Pseudo-albedo map Ai^{pseudo} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. 3. PIDNet (F{PID}): Patch-wise intrinsic decomposition network. Input: Color patch \hat{c}(x) of size S{patch} \times S{patch}. Output: Extracted albedo \hat{a}(x) and shading \hat{s}(x). Stage 1: Offline Pseudo-Albedo Generation 1. For each input image Ii in the training set: Pass Ii through the pre-trained FIDNet. Store the output as the pseudo-albedo ground truth Ai^{pseudo}. Note: FIDNet is not fine-tuned during this stage. Stage 2: Joint NeRF and PIDNet Optimization For each training iteration: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays from the input views and novel view candidates. 2. NeRF Rendering: For each ray, sample points \mathbf{x}t along the ray. Query NeRF F\Theta(\mathbf{x}t, \mathbf{d}) to get \sigmat, \mathbf{c}t. Render color \hat{c}(x) and depth \hat{d}(x) using standard volume rendering equations: \hat{c}(x) = \sum{t=1}^T Tt (1 - \alphat) \mathbf{c}t, \quad \alphat = 1 - e^{-\sigmat \deltat} \hat{d}(x) = \sum{t=1}^T Tt (1 - \alphat) t 3. Geometric Alignment (Pixel Correspondence): For a pixel x in the novel view with rendered depth \hat{d}(x), map it to the corresponding pixel x' in an input view i: \bar{x} = [x^T, 1]^T \mathbf{x}w = Ti \hat{d}(x) Ki^{-1} \bar{x} x' = Ki Ti^{-1} \mathbf{x}w where Ti is the camera-to-world transformation and Ki is the intrinsic matrix. 4. Projection Error Calculation: Calculate the projected depth d(x') from the input view's geometry (or use the input view's depth if available, otherwise use the NeRF's depth at x' projected back). The source defines projection error E{proj} as: E{proj}(x') = (\hat{d}(x') - \tilde{d}(x'))^2 where \hat{d}(x') is the rendered depth at the projected location and \tilde{d}(x') is the projected depth from the novel view. Pitfall: Direct minimization of E{proj} is counterproductive due to occlusions smoothing unrelated surface depths. 5. Visibility Mask Weight: Compute weight \omega(x) to handle projection errors and occlusions: \omega(x) = re \left( 1 - \frac{E{proj}(x')}{M{proj}} \right) where re is an error rate coefficient that diminishes toward the end of training, and M{proj} is the maximum projection error. 6. PIDNet Intrinsic Decomposition: Extract a color patch \hat{c}(x) of size S{patch} \times S{patch} centered at x from the rendered novel view. Pass \hat{c}(x) through PIDNet to get extracted albedo \hat{a}(x) and shading \hat{s}(x). 7. Loss Computation: Color Loss: Mean squared error between rendered color and ground truth. L{color} = \sum{x \in S} \|\hat{c}(x) - c{gt}(x)\|2^2 Albedo Consistency Loss (L{ac}): Enforce that the albedo extracted from the novel view matches the pseudo-albedo from the corresponding input view pixel x'. L{ac} = \sum{x \in P} \omega(x) \|\hat{a}(x) - A{x'}^{pseudo}\|2^2 where P is the set of pixels in the novel view. Depth Consistency Loss (L{dc}): Regularize projection error between adjacent pixels to prevent geometry smoothing errors. L{dc} = \sum{x' \in P'} \sum{y \in N(x')} (E{proj}(y) - E{proj}(x'))^2 where N(x') are the 4-neighbor adjacent pixels of x' in the input view. Additional Regularization: Depth smoothness (L{ds}), edge-preserving (L{edge}), intrinsic smoothness (L{pid}), chromaticity consistency (L{chrom}), and frequency regularization. Total Loss: L{total} = L{color} + \lambda{ac} L{ac} + \lambda{dc} L{dc} + \dots 8. Update: Backpropagate gradients to update NeRF parameters \Theta and PIDNet parameters. Intrinsic Decomposition (Lambertian): \log c(x) = \log a(x) + \log s(x). Intrinsic Decomposition (Real-world): \log c(x) = \log a(x) + \log s(x) + l + R, where l is light color vector and R is non-Lambertian residuals. Pixel Correspondence: x' = (K' T'^{-1} T) \hat{d}(x) K^{-1} \bar{x}. 3D Point Projection: \mathbf{x}w = T \hat{d}(x) K^{-1} \bar{x}. Inverse Projection: x = K T^{-1} \mathbf{x}w. S{patch}: Patch size for PIDNet input/output. Value: 32 \times 32. Training Resolution: Image size. Value: 300 \times 400. Training Duration: 70,000 iterations per scene. Hardware: 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. re: Error rate coefficient. Diminishes toward end of training. M{proj}: Maximum projection error. Not given in the sources. Projection Errors: Incorrect synthesized depth leads to projection errors. If x' falls outside the field of view or corresponds to an occluded region, \omega(x) should be 0 or low. Occlusion Handling: Direct minimization of E{proj} causes smoothing of unrelated surfaces. L{dc} and \omega(x) mitigate this. Geometry Rectification: As geometry improves, re diminishes, reducing the weight of cross-view consistency for pairs with high projection error, allowing occlusions to persist without forcing consistency. FIDNet Substitution: Replacing FIDNet with other intrinsic decomposition models (e.g., Das et al. 2022) degrades performance. Training Time: 1.5 hours for 3 views on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. This is significantly faster than most other few-shot NeRF methods (e.g., RegNeRF: 2.4 hours, FreeNeRF: 2 hours) and much faster than methods requiring 10-20 hours. Memory: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Works with few-shot inputs (sparse multi-view images) under unconstrained illumination. Faster training than comparable methods. FIDNet provides global context-aware guidance, outperforming MLP-based albedo synthesis. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained FIDNet (IIDWW). Performance degrades if FIDNet is replaced with less suitable intrinsic decomposition models. Requires careful tuning of visibility mask weights and projection error thresholds. When to use: Few-shot view synthesis with varying illumination where computational efficiency is important. When not to use: When high-quality intrinsic decomposition models are unavailable or when dense multi-view inputs are available (other methods may be more robust). ExtremeNeRF was introduced in 2024 by authors from the AAAI conference. It addresses the limitations of NeRF, which requires constrained illumination and extensive multi-view images, and previous few-shot methods that rely on large datasets or yield sub-optimal results with limited data. The method builds on the concept of intrinsic image decomposition, separating albedo and shading, and applies it to NeRF optimization via a two-stage pipeline. It was evaluated on the Phototourism F3 and the newly created NeRF Extreme benchmark, the first in-the-wild benchmark for novel view synthesis under varying illumination. Few-Shot Neural Radiance Fields under Unconstrained Illumination, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i4.28075, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Conditional and Latent Representations
head: Conditional NeRF, Latent NeRF, Disentangled Conditional NeRF
body: Conditional and Latent Representations extend the standard NeRF architecture by introducing low-dimensional latent codes \mathbf{z} that condition the radiance field, enabling generative modeling of object categories rather than single-scene reconstruction. Unlike standard NeRF which maps (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), these methods map (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{z}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), allowing for the manipulation of shape, appearance, identity, or expression through the latent space. This family is distinguished from siblings like Feature Fields by its focus on generative control via learned latent distributions (often trained within GAN frameworks) and disentangled control mechanisms that prevent cross-talk between geometric and photometric attributes. The core mechanism involves augmenting the input space of the implicit function F\Theta with latent vectors \mathbf{z} that represent semantic attributes (e.g., shape, appearance, identity). 1. Latent Conditioning: The network input is augmented with \mathbf{z}. A trivial concatenation F{\theta'}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a): \Gamma(\mathbf{x}) \oplus \mathbf{z}s, \Gamma(\mathbf{v}) \oplus \mathbf{z}a \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) often leads to mutual intervention, where shape changes affect color. 2. Disentanglement Strategy: To achieve independent control, methods typically separate the influence of \mathbf{z}s (shape) and \mathbf{z}a (appearance). Shape Conditioning: Often implemented via explicit volumetric deformation. A deformation network T maps (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}s) \rightarrow \Delta \mathbf{x}, where \Delta \mathbf{x} are displacement vectors applied to the positional encoding bands. Appearance Conditioning: Often deferred to the color prediction branch. The appearance code \mathbf{z}a is concatenated with the view direction \mathbf{v} or intermediate feature vectors, ensuring it does not influence the density prediction \sigma. 3. Generative Training: Many conditional NeRFs are trained as generative models using adversarial losses (GANs) to ensure photorealism and consistency across the latent space. 4. Latent Space Manipulation: Once trained, the latent codes can be manipulated directly (e.g., scaling, interpolation) or via feed-forward mappers (e.g., CLIP-driven) to edit the rendered output without per-sample optimization. A generative radiance field architecture that achieves individual control over the shape and appearance of 3D objects by isolating their conditioning mechanisms. Unlike standard conditional NeRFs where concatenating latent codes to position features causes mutual intervention (e.g., shape changes altering color), this method uses explicit volumetric deformation for shape conditioning and direct latent injection for appearance, preventing cross-talk between the two attributes. It is typically trained in two stages: first, a GAN-based training of the generator and deformation network, and second, the training of CLIP-driven mappers for text-based manipulation. HeadNeRF is a NeRF-based parametric head model that integrates neural radiance fields into the parametric representation of the human head to render high-fidelity head images in real-time while supporting direct control over rendering pose and semantic attributes (identity, expression, albedo, illumination). It differs from standard NeRF by conditioning the implicit function on low-dimensional latent codes rather than just spatial coordinates and view directions, and it accelerates rendering by combining volumetric rendering with a 2D neural refinement network. This approach allows for the generation of novel views and semantic editing (e.g., changing expression or identity) without the computational cost of full volumetric integration for the final high-resolution image. A feed-forward approach using shape mapper Ms and appearance mapper Ma to update initial shape/appearance codes (z{s0}, z{a0}) based on a text prompt t, avoiding per-sample optimization. The updated shape code zs is calculated as zs = Ms(\hat{E}t(t)) + z{s0}, and the appearance code za as za = Ma(\hat{E}t(t)) + z{a0}, where \hat{E}t is the pre-trained CLIP text encoder. The disentangled conditional NeRF F\theta maps deformed position and view/appearance codes to color and density: F\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, zs, za): \Gamma^(\mathbf{x}, zs), \Gamma(\mathbf{v}) \oplus za \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma). The cross-modal CLIP distance D{CLIP}(\mathbf{I}, t) measures similarity between image patch \mathbf{I} and text t: D{CLIP}(\mathbf{I}, t) = 1 - \langle \hat{E}i(\mathbf{I}), \hat{E}t(t) \rangle. A technique to achieve gradual editing of shape and appearance by scaling the editing direction vectors in the latent space using a scalar factor s. The codes are updated as zs = s \times \Delta zs + z{s0} and za = s \times \Delta za + z{a0}, where \Delta zs and \Delta za are the manipulation directions provided by the code mappers. The scalar s controls the intensity of the edit, with a typical range of 0 to 1.6 with step 0.2; manipulation strength increases as s increases. This is used for continuous editing of both shape and appearance given a single text prompt or exemplar, allowing users to adjust the degree of change. A method that differs from optimization-based editing (e.g., EditNeRF) by using learned feed-forward networks mapping user edits to latent codes, enabling fast inference for interactive editing instead of slow iterative optimization per sample. The steps are: 1. Extract CLIP feature embedding from input text prompt or exemplar image. 2. Feed embedding into two separate feed-forward code mappers (shape mapper and appearance mapper). 3. Mappers output local displacements in the latent space to update zs and za. 4. Render image with updated codes. 5. Train mappers using a CLIP-based matching loss to enforce CLIP space consistency between input constraint and output renderings. A technique where appearance conditioning is deferred to concatenate the appearance code with the view direction as input to the radiance prediction network, allowing appearance manipulation without affecting shape/density. In NeRF, density is predicted first as a function of position; by deferring appearance conditioning, the method ensures that changes to the appearance code do not alter the underlying geometry. The first approach to leverage a conditional NeRF in the GAN framework, achieving significant improvements in photorealism for 3D scene generation given only 2D images. This framework enables learning a 3D generative model of shape and appearance, building upon earlier voxel-grid parameterizations. The concept of conditional NeRFs emerged as a solution to the limitation of standard NeRF, which requires per-scene optimization and cannot generalize across object categories. The foundational work on conditional NeRFs within a GAN framework was proposed by GRAF (cited in), which demonstrated significant improvements in photorealism over voxel-based generative models. Subsequent works, such as CLIP-NeRF (Wang et al., 2022), introduced disentangled latent codes for shape and appearance, enabling text-and-image driven manipulation via CLIP embeddings. HeadNerf extended this to parametric head modeling, integrating latent codes for identity, expression, albedo, and illumination. These methods are widely used in 3D content generation, virtual try-on, and interactive editing of neural radiance fields. name: Disentangled Conditional NeRF
head: Disentangled Conditional NeRF Training
body: Disentangled Conditional NeRF is a generative radiance field architecture that achieves independent control over the shape and appearance of 3D objects by isolating their conditioning mechanisms. Unlike trivial conditional NeRF formulations where concatenating latent codes leads to mutual intervention (e.g., shape changes affecting color), this method uses explicit volumetric deformation for shape and deferred color conditioning for appearance. It is built upon Conditional and Latent Representations and differs from HeadNerf by its specific two-stage training pipeline involving CLIP-driven mappers for text-based manipulation. The method consists of two distinct phases: training the disentangled generator and training the CLIP-driven manipulation mappers. Inputs: Spatial position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, view direction \mathbf{v}, shape latent code \mathbf{z}s, appearance latent code \mathbf{z}a, and optionally a text prompt \mathbf{t}. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. 1. Deformation Network T: A neural network mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}s) \rightarrow \Delta \mathbf{x}. Input: Position \mathbf{x} and shape code \mathbf{z}s. Output: Displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2m}, where m is the number of frequency bands in the positional encoding. 2. Generator F\Theta: The main NeRF MLP. Input: Deformed positional encoding \Gamma^(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}s), view direction \mathbf{v}, and appearance code \mathbf{z}a. Output: Density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. 3. Discriminator D: A standard GAN discriminator evaluating image realism. 4. CLIP Mappers: Shape Mapper Ms: Maps CLIP text embedding to shape code adjustment. Appearance Mapper Ma: Maps CLIP text embedding to appearance code adjustment. 5. Positional Encoding \Gamma(\mathbf{x}): Standard sine/cosine encoding with m bands. The generator F\Theta and deformation network T are trained jointly using a non-saturating GAN objective. 1. Sampling: Randomly sample \mathbf{z}s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \mathbf{z}a \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), and camera pose \mathbf{v} from the upper hemisphere \mathcal{Z}v. Sample real image \mathbf{I} from the training distribution \mathcal{D}. 2. Deformation: Compute displacement \Delta \mathbf{x} = T(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}s). 3. Deformed Encoding: Apply displacement to the positional encoding bands. The deformed encoding \Gamma^(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}s) is computed by adding \Delta \mathbf{x} to the standard positional encoding components. Specifically, if \Gamma(\mathbf{x}) consists of bands \gammai(\mathbf{x}), the deformed band is \gamma^i(\mathbf{x}, \Delta \mathbf{x}i) = \gammai(\mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x}i). 4. Rendering: Feed \Gamma^(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}s), \mathbf{v}, and \mathbf{z}a into F\Theta to predict \sigma and \mathbf{c}. Render the image \mathbf{I}{gen} = F\Theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a). 5. Discriminator Update: Update D to distinguish real images \mathbf{I} from generated images \mathbf{I}{gen}. 6. Generator Update: Update F\Theta and T to fool D. The GAN loss is defined as: L{GAN} = \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{z}s \sim \mathcal{Z}s, \mathbf{z}a \sim \mathcal{Z}a, \mathbf{v} \sim \mathcal{Z}v} [f(D(F\Theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a)))] + \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{I} \sim \mathcal{D}} [f(-D(\mathbf{I}))] + \lambdar \|\nabla{\mathbf{I}} D(\mathbf{I})\|^2 where f(x) = -\log(1 + \exp(-x)) and \lambdar is the gradient penalty regularization weight. The generator weights are fixed (\hat{F}\Theta, \hat{D}), and the mappers Ms and Ma are trained. 1. Sampling: Sample \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a, \mathbf{v} as in Stage 1. Sample text prompt \mathbf{t} from a pre-defined library \mathcal{T}. 2. CLIP Encoding: Encode text \mathbf{t} using CLIP text encoder \hat{E}t to get embedding \mathbf{e}t = \hat{E}t(\mathbf{t}). 3. Mapper Application: Shape adjustment: \mathbf{z}'s = Ms(\mathbf{e}t) + \mathbf{z}s. Appearance adjustment: \mathbf{z}'a = Ma(\mathbf{e}t) + \mathbf{z}a. 4. Rendering: Render image using fixed generator: \mathbf{I}{clip} = \hat{F}\Theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}'s, \mathbf{z}'a). 5. Loss Calculation: Shape Mapper Loss: L{shape} = f(\hat{D}(\hat{F}\Theta(\mathbf{v}, Ms(\hat{E}t(\mathbf{t})) + \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a))) + \lambdac D{CLIP}(\hat{F}\Theta(\mathbf{v}, Ms(\hat{E}t(\mathbf{t})) + \mathbf{z}s, \mathbf{z}a), \mathbf{t}) Appearance Mapper Loss: L{appear} = f(\hat{D}(\hat{F}\Theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, Ma(\hat{E}t(\mathbf{t})) + \mathbf{z}a))) + \lambdac D{CLIP}(\hat{F}\Theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{z}s, Ma(\hat{E}t(\mathbf{t})) + \mathbf{z}a), \mathbf{t}) where \lambdac is the weight for the CLIP distance term. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def positionalencoding(x, numbands): """ Computes standard positional encoding for x. Returns tensor of shape (..., 2 numbands 3) """ # Implementation details of standard NeRF PE pass class DeformationNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim, outputdim): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim)) def forward(self, x, zs): # x: (B, 3), zs: (B, Zdim) # Output: deltax (B, 3 2 m) return self.net(torch.cat([x, zs], dim=-1)) class NeRFGenerator(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim, hiddendim, outputdim): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim)) def forward(self, encodedpos, v, za): # encodedpos: (B, 6m), v: (B, 3), za: (B, Zdim) # Output: sigma (B, 1), color (B, 3) x = torch.cat([encodedpos, v, za], dim=-1) out = self.net(x) sigma = out[:,:1] color = out[:, 1:] return sigma, color class Discriminator(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, 512), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Linear(512, 256), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Linear(256, 1)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class CLIPMapper(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim, outputdim): super().init() self.net = nn.Linear(inputdim, outputdim) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) def applydeformation(pe, deltax, numbands): """ Applies displacement deltax to the positional encoding pe. pe: (B, 6m), deltax: (B, 6m) """ return pe + deltax def ganloss(reallogits, fakelogits, lambdar, discriminator): """ Computes the non-saturating GAN loss with gradient penalty. """ f = lambda x: -torch.log(1 + torch.exp(-x)) # Generator loss (fooling discriminator) genloss = torch.mean(f(fakelogits)) # Discriminator loss realloss = torch.mean(f(-reallogits)) # Gradient penalty realimages =... # Placeholder for real image tensor # Compute gradient of D(I) w.r.t I grad = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=reallogits.sum(), inputs=realimages, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] gradpenalty = lambdar torch.mean((grad.norm(2, dim=1) - 1) 2) discloss = realloss + gradpenalty return genloss, discloss def trainstage1(generator, deformationnet, discriminator, optimizergen, optimizerdisc, batchsize, numbands, lambdar, device): """ Stage 1: Train disentangled conditional NeRF generator and deformation network. """ generator.train() deformationnet.train() discriminator.train() # Sample latents zs = torch.randn(batchsize, zsdim, device=device) za = torch.randn(batchsize, zadim, device=device) v = samplecamerapose(batchsize, device=device) # Upper hemisphere # Sample real images realimages = samplerealimages(batchsize, device=device) # Forward pass # 1. Deformation # x is sampled from scene geometry or random points x = samplepoints(batchsize, device=device) deltax = deformationnet(x, zs) # 2. Positional Encoding and Deformation pe = positionalencoding(x, numbands) deformedpe = applydeformation(pe, deltax, numbands) # 3. Rendering sigma, color = generator(deformedpe, v, za) # Render image from sigma and color (standard volume rendering) fakeimages = volumerender(sigma, color, v) # 4. Discriminator reallogits = discriminator(realimages) fakelogits = discriminator(fakeimages.detach()) genloss, discloss = ganloss(reallogits, fakelogits, lambdar, discriminator) # Update Discriminator optimizerdisc.zerograd() discloss.backward() optimizerdisc.step() # Update Generator optimizergen.zerograd() genloss.backward() optimizergen.step() def trainstage2(generator, deformationnet, discriminator, shapemapper, appearancemapper, optimizermappers, lambdac, device): """ Stage 2: Train CLIP-driven mappers. Generator weights are fixed. """ generator.eval() deformationnet.eval() discriminator.eval() shapemapper.train() appearancemapper.train() # Sample inputs zs = torch.randn(batchsize, zsdim, device=device) za = torch.randn(batchsize, zadim, device=device) v = samplecamerapose(batchsize, device=device) textprompts = sampletextprompts(batchsize, device=device) # CLIP Encoding # Assuming pre-trained CLIP text encoder is available textembeddings = cliptextencoder(textprompts) # Mapper Outputs zsadj = shapemapper(textembeddings) + zs zaadj = appearancemapper(textembeddings) + za # Rendering with fixed generator x = samplepoints(batchsize, device=device) deltax = deformationnet(x, zs) # Use fixed deformation net pe = positionalencoding(x, numbands) deformedpe = applydeformation(pe, deltax, numbands) sigma, color = generator(deformedpe, v, zaadj) fakeimages = volumerender(sigma, color, v) # Discriminator Loss (using fixed discriminator) fakelogits = discriminator(fakeimages) # Note: In Stage 2, we typically only update mappers to fool D and match CLIP # The GAN loss term is included in Lshape and Lappear as per source f = lambda x: -torch.log(1 + torch.exp(-x)) # Shape Mapper Loss # Lshape = f(D(F(v, Ms(et) + zs, za))) + lambdac DCLIP(F(...), t) # Note: Source formula uses Ms(et) + zs for shape, but za is passed as is. # However, the generator input is (v, zsadj, za). # The source formula for Lshape uses: F(v, Ms(et) + zs, za) # This implies za is NOT adjusted in shape loss calculation? # Re-reading source: "Lshape =... D(F(v, Ms(et) + zs, za))" # It seems za is the original sampled za, not adjusted. # Let's stick strictly to the source formulas. # For Lshape: zs is adjusted, za is original. # For Lappear: zs is original, za is adjusted. # Re-render for specific losses if needed, or use the same fakeimages if zaadj was used for both? # The source defines Lshape and Lappear separately. # Lshape uses zsadj and za. # Lappear uses zs and zaadj. # Render for Shape Loss sigmas, colors = generator(deformedpe, v, za) # za is original fakeimagesshape = volumerender(sigmas, colors, v) logitsshape = discriminator(fakeimagesshape) lossganshape = f(logitsshape) lossclipshape = clipdistance(fakeimagesshape, textprompts) Lshape = lossganshape + lambdac lossclipshape # Render for Appearance Loss # Need to re-compute deformed PE with original zs? # Deformation depends on zs. If we use original zs, deltax is original. peorig = positionalencoding(x, numbands) deltaxorig = deformationnet(x, zs) deformedpeorig = applydeformation(peorig, deltaxorig, numbands) sigmaa, colora = generator(deformedpeorig, v, zaadj) fakeimagesappear = volumerender(sigmaa, colora, v) logitsappear = discriminator(fakeimagesappear) lossganappear = f(logitsappear) lossclipappear = clipdistance(fakeimagesappear, textprompts) Lappear = lossganappear + lambdac lossclipappear # Update Mappers optimizermappers.zerograd() (Lshape + Lappear).backward() optimizermappers.step() A variant training phase where the pre-trained generator is fixed, and specific mappers (Ms, Ma) are trained to map CLIP text embeddings to latent code adjustments. It is chosen when text-driven editing is required without retraining the entire NeRF. It differs from Stage 1 by freezing the generator and discriminator and optimizing only the mappers using a combination of GAN loss and CLIP distance. Time Complexity: Training is computationally expensive due to the GAN objective and the two-stage process. Stage 1 requires training the deformation network and generator jointly. Stage 2 requires additional forward passes for CLIP distance computation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the generator, deformation network, discriminator, and CLIP encoders. The deformation network adds memory overhead proportional to the number of positional encoding bands. Strengths: Achieves clean disentanglement where shape changes do not affect color, and vice versa. Allows for text-driven manipulation via CLIP mappers. Limitations: Requires a GAN discriminator, which can be unstable to train. The deformation network must be carefully regularized to avoid unrealistic deformations. When to use: When independent control over shape and appearance is critical, and text-based editing is desired. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or when simple per-scene optimization suffices. Disentangled Conditional NeRF was introduced in "CLIP-NeRF: Text-and-Image Driven Manipulation of Neural Radiance Fields" (CVPR 2022). It addresses the mutual intervention problem found in earlier conditional NeRF models where latent codes for shape and appearance were concatenated directly, leading to entangled outputs. The method builds on the principles of conditional latent representations. name: HeadNerf
head: NeRF-based parametric head model
body: HeadNeRF is a NeRF-based parametric head model that integrates neural radiance fields into the parametric representation of the human head to render high-fidelity head images in real-time while supporting direct control over rendering pose and semantic attributes (identity, expression, albedo, illumination). It differs from standard NeRF by conditioning the implicit function on disentangled latent codes for shape and appearance, and by employing a 2D neural rendering module to accelerate the volumetric rendering process from seconds per frame to milliseconds. It builds on Conditional and Latent Representations by explicitly separating shape conditioning (identity, expression) from appearance conditioning (albedo, illumination) to prevent mutual intervention. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Latent codes: z{id} (identity), z{exp} (expression), z{alb} (albedo), z{ill} (illumination). Camera parameters P: Extrinsic and intrinsic matrices. 3D points x \in \mathbb{R}^3 sampled along rays r(t) emitted from the camera center. Outputs: Final rendered image I \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 256 \times 256}. Data Structures: Implicit Function h\theta: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Positional Encoding \gamma(\cdot): Pre-defined NeRF positional encoding applied to input coordinates. Feature Vector F(x): High-dimensional vector, F(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{256}. Low-Resolution Feature Map IF: Tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32 \times 32}. 2D Neural Rendering Module \pi\psi: Composed of 1x1 Conv2D layers and Leaky ReLU activations, followed by upsampling layers to increase resolution from 32 \times 32 to 256 \times 256. Method Steps: 1. Latent Code Extraction: Extract four types of latent codes from the input image: identity, expression, texture (albedo), and illumination. 2. Density and Feature Prediction: For each 3D point x sampled along a ray, compute the positional encoding \gamma(x). Concatenate \gamma(x) with the shape latent codes z{id} and z{exp}. Pass this concatenation through the implicit function h\theta to predict the density \sigma and an intermediate feature vector. h\theta: (\gamma(x), z{id}, z{exp}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \text{feature}) 3. Appearance Conditioning: Concatenate the intermediate feature from Step 2 with the appearance latent codes z{alb} and z{ill}. Pass this through h\theta (or a subsequent branch, as implied by the separation of density and feature prediction) to predict the final high-dimensional feature vector F(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{256}. Note: The viewing direction is removed from the input to avoid capturing dataset bias inconsistencies. F(x) = h\theta(\text{intermediate feature}, z{alb}, z{ill}) 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the low-resolution 2D feature map IF \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 32 \times 32} by integrating the feature vectors along the rays. The weight w(t) is defined as: w(t) = \exp\left(-\intt^\infty \sigma(r(s)) ds\right) \sigma(r(t)) The feature map is calculated as: IF(r) = \frac{\int0^\infty w(t) F(r(t)) dt}{\int0^\infty w(t) dt} 5. 2D Neural Rendering: Map the low-resolution feature map IF to the final high-resolution image I \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 256 \times 256} using the 2D neural rendering module \pi\psi. This module uses 1x1 Conv2D layers and Leaky ReLU activations, with upsampling layers to increase resolution, to alleviate multi-view inconsistent artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class HeadNeRF: def init(self, hiddendim=256, numlayers=8): # Implicit function htheta # Input: gamma(x) + zid + zexp -> sigma, intermediatefeature # Input: intermediatefeature + zalb + zill -> F # Note: Source implies a single MLP structure or two stages. # We implement a single MLP for the core prediction, # but logically separate the inputs as described. self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim + 2 64 + 2 64, hiddendim), # Simplified dim assumption nn.ReLU(), #... additional layers as per source Fig 2 (not detailed in text) nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1 + hiddendim) # sigma (1) + F (hiddendim)) # 2D Neural Rendering Module pipsi self.renderer = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(hiddendim, hiddendim, 1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), #... upsampling layers to 256x256 nn.Upsample(scalefactor=8, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False), nn.Conv2d(hiddendim, 3, 1),) def positionalencoding(self, x, numbands=10): # Standard NeRF positional encoding # x: [N, 3] scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numbands)]) xb = torch.reshape((x scales[:, None]), (x.shape[0], -1)) pe = torch.cat((torch.sin(xb), torch.cos(xb)), dim=1) return pe def forward(self, x, zid, zexp, zalb, zill, P): """ x: [N, 3] 3D points sampled along rays zid, zexp, zalb, zill: latent codes [B, D] P: Camera parameters (used for ray generation, not passed to MLP) """ # 1. Positional Encoding gammax = self.positionalencoding(x) # 2. Density and Intermediate Feature Prediction # Concatenate gamma(x), zid, zexp # Assuming latent codes are projected to match MLP input dim if necessary shapeinput = torch.cat([gammax, zid, zexp], dim=-1) sigmaandfeat = self.mlp(shapeinput) sigma = sigmaandfeat[:,:1] intermediatefeature = sigmaandfeat[:, 1:] # 3. Appearance Conditioning # Concatenate intermediatefeature, zalb, zill appearanceinput = torch.cat([intermediatefeature, zalb, zill], dim=-1) F = self.mlp(appearanceinput) # Or a separate branch as implied by separation # 4. Volume Rendering (Simplified for feature map generation) # In practice, this is done per-ray during sampling. # Here we assume sigma and F are already weighted/integrated into IF # by the rendering engine. We return the raw predictions for the engine. return sigma, F def render(self, rays, zid, zexp, zalb, zill): """ rays: [B, N, 3] (origin, direction) or similar structure """ # Sample points along rays # Compute sigma and F for all points # Perform volume rendering to get IF [B, 256, 32, 32] IF = volumerender(rays, self.forward, zid, zexp, zalb, zill) # 2D Neural Rendering I = self.renderer(IF) return I Parameters: Latent code dimension: Not given in the sources. Feature vector dimension: 256. Low-resolution feature map size: 32 \times 32. Final image size: 256 \times 256. Activation: Leaky ReLU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewing Direction: The viewing direction is explicitly removed from the input to avoid capturing undesired inconsistencies caused by dataset bias. Multi-view Inconsistency: The 2D neural rendering module is specifically designed to alleviate multi-view inconsistent artifacts. Focuses on independent control of shape and appearance using explicit volumetric deformation for shape and deferred conditioning for appearance [16793-disentangled-conditional-nerf.md]. HeadNeRF uses a similar disentanglement but relies on a 2D refinement network for speed. The parent framework providing the principles of latent conditioning and disentanglement [15989-conditional-and-latent-representations.md]. Time Complexity: Rendering time is significantly accelerated compared to standard NeRF. One frame rendering time is reduced from 5s to 25ms. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Can exceed 40fps without sacrificing rendering quality. Strengths: Real-time rendering, high-fidelity details (teeth gaps, wrinkles, beards), direct control over semantic attributes (identity, expression, albedo, illumination). Limitations: Relies on a 2D refinement network which may introduce slight accuracy loss compared to pure volumetric rendering. Not applicable to highly non-rigid deformations or articulated body motion. When to use: When real-time, high-fidelity head rendering with semantic control is required. When not to use: For general non-rigid body animation or when pure volumetric accuracy is prioritized over speed. HeadNeRF was proposed in 2021/2022 by. It integrates neural radiance fields into the parametric representation of the human head, moving away from traditional 3D textured meshes to generate high-fidelity images. It addresses the computational expense of original NeRF by integrating 2D neural rendering. The model is trained on datasets like FaceSEIP, FaceScape, and FFHQ. It is available at https://github.com/CrisHY1995/headnerf. name: ActiveNeRF Model Architecture
head: ActiveNeRF MLP structure, Uncertainty-aware NeRF network
body:
ActiveNeRF extends the standard NeRF architecture by predicting not only volume density and view-dependent color but also a prediction variance (uncertainty) for each sampled point. This modification allows the rendering pipeline to weigh contributions based on the model's confidence, facilitating active view selection strategies where new camera poses are chosen to minimize uncertainty in poorly observed regions. Unlike sibling architectures that modify input spaces or use explicit primitives, ActiveNeRF retains the coordinate-based implicit representation but augments the output space with a scalar uncertainty field. The model is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that maps 3D spatial coordinates and viewing directions to density, color, and variance. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: 3D position \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and viewing direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz). Outputs: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}, RGB color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and prediction variance 
u \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures and Layout The network consists of a shared feature encoder and specialized output heads: 1. Positional Encoding: Separate encoding functions for coordinates and directions. 2. Feature Encoder: An 8-layer fully connected (FC) MLP with a residual connection applied to the 4th layer. 3. Density Head: A single FC layer taking the encoder's output to predict \sigma. 4. Variance Head: A single FC layer with a softplus activation function taking the encoder's output to predict 
u. 5. Color Head: A single FC layer taking the concatenation of the latent feature vector and the encoded viewing direction to predict \mathbf{c}. Positional Encoding The positional encoding function \gamma(p) maps a scalar input p to a vector of sinusoidal frequencies: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0\pi p), \cos(2^0\pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}\pi p), \cos(2^{L-1}\pi p)) where L is the number of frequency bands. Parameters L=10: Number of frequency bands for 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}. L=4: Number of frequency bands for viewing directions \mathbf{d}. Algorithm Steps 1. Encode the 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} using \gamma with L=10. 2. Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using \gamma with L=4. 3. Pass the encoded coordinates through the 8-layer MLP encoder. Let the output of the i-th layer be hi. For i=4, apply the residual connection: h4 = 	ext{MLP}(h3) + h3. 4. Extract the latent feature vector \mathbf{z} from the final layer of the encoder. 5. Compute volume density: \sigma = 	ext{FC}{\sigma}(\mathbf{z}). 6. Compute variance: 
u = 	ext{softplus}(	ext{FC}{

Encode coordinates (L=10) xenc = self.positionalencoding(x, L=10) # 2. Encode directions (L=4) denc = self.positionalencoding(d, L=4) # 3. Predict density sigma = self.fcsigma(h) # 5. Predict variance with softplus varraw = self.fcvar(h) variance = F.softplus(varraw) # 6. The source specifies using a softplus activation function for the variance head to ensure this. Residual Connection: The residual connection is explicitly applied only to the 4th layer of the 8-layer encoder. Encoding Separation: Coordinates and directions are encoded separately with different numbers of bands (L=10 vs L=4) before being processed by their respective branches. Strengths: Provides a per-point uncertainty estimate that can be used for active learning and view selection, potentially improving reconstruction quality in sparse-view scenarios. Limitations: The uncertainty is a prediction variance from a single forward pass, which may not capture all sources of epistemic uncertainty compared to ensemble methods.
