name: SCARF
head: Scalable Continual Learning Framework, Scalable Continual Learning Framework for Memory-efficient Multiple Neural Radiance Fields
body: SCARF is a method for memory-efficient continual learning of multiple 3D scenes using a single neural network, addressing catastrophic forgetting when training on a sequence of scenes with access to only one scene at a time and training data accessible only once. It sets itself apart from siblings like DoF-NeRF or NeRF-VPT by factorizing the NeRF MLP weights into scene-specific and cross-scene shared components generated by a hypernetwork, rather than augmenting inputs or modifying topology for single-scene enhancement. Unlike MINE or Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations which focus on spatial efficiency, SCARF focuses on parameter efficiency across scene sequences. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of scenes \{Si\}{i=1}^N. For each scene Si, training data consists of rays \mathbf{r} with associated ground truth colors C(\mathbf{r}). Position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} are encoded using positional encoding. Outputs: A unified model F\Theta capable of rendering any scene Si given its specific scene identifier (implicitly handled via the generated weights) and ray \mathbf{r}. The output is the RGB radiance \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma. Data Structures: 1. Cross-Scene Weight Matrix (CSWM): C{Ml} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times c{out}} for each encoder layer l \in \{1, \dots, L\}. Shared across all scenes. 2. Cross-Scene Decoder: D. Shared across all scenes. 3. Hypernetwork: Gl. Generates scene-specific weight matrices. 4. Scene-Specific Weight Matrix (SSWM): S{Ml}^i \in \mathbb{R}^{c{in} \times K} for scene i at layer l. Generated by Gl. 5. Coefficient Matrix: C{li} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K} for scene i at layer l. Learnable per scene. 6. Random Noise: z{il} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Input to Gl for scene i at layer l. 7. Occupancy Grid: Explicit density grid for each learned scene to guide sampling during distillation. Neural Network Structure: The NeRF MLP is divided into an encoder and a decoder: Encoder: 8 fully-connected layers (plus an output layer for density/feature), each with 256 channels. Input is 10-degree positional encoding of position \mathbf{x}. A skip connection is added at the 5th layer. Output is density \sigma and a 256-dim feature vector. Decoder: 128 channels, then 3 channels. Input is 4-degree positional encoding of viewing direction \mathbf{d} concatenated with the encoder's feature vector. Output is RGB radiance \mathbf{c}. Weight Factorization: For an encoder layer E{li} (input dim c{in}, output dim c{out}) of scene i: 1. The layer is factorized into a scene-specific matrix S{Ml}^i and a cross-scene matrix C{Ml}: E{li} = S{Ml}^i \times C{Ml} 2. The SSWM is generated by a hypernetwork Gl from random noise z{il}: S{Ml}^i = Gl(z{il}) 3. A scene-dependent linear transformation is applied to the CSWM using a learnable coefficient matrix C{li}: C{Mli} = C{li} \times C{Ml} 4. The final encoder layer weights are: E{li} = Gl(z{il}) \times C{Mli} The decoder D is global and shared across all scenes. Continual Learning Procedure: When the t-th scene St arrives: 1. Initialization: Initialize model Mt with parameters from M{t-1}: shared CSWM \{C{Ml}\}, shared hypernetwork \{Gl\}, and existing coefficient matrices \{C{li}\} and noises \{z{il}\} for i=1 \dots t-1. 2. New Parameters: Add only new parameters for scene t: L layers of random noise \{z{tl}\} and L layers of coefficient matrices \{C{tl}\}. 3. Uncertain Surface Radiance field Distillation (USD): To prevent catastrophic forgetting, distill knowledge from M{t-1} to Mt for all previous scenes i=1 \dots t-1. Pre-extraction: Extract an explicit density occupancy grid for each learned scene. Resolution is 50 \times 50 \times 50. Divide each cell into a 5 \times 5 \times 5 subgrid. A cell is considered "surface" if any subgrid point has density \sigma > \tau (where \tau=3). Only sample radiance field points on these surfaces for distillation to avoid blank regions. Loss Functions: Density-Radiance Distillation Loss (L{ic\sigma}^i): L{ic\sigma}^i = ||\hat{c}i^{Mt} - ci^{M{t-1}}||^2 + \alpha ||\hat{\sigma}i^{Mt} - \sigmai^{M{t-1}}||^2 where \hat{c}i^{Mt}, \hat{\sigma}i^{Mt} are sampled from Mt in scene Si, and ci^{M{t-1}}, \sigmai^{M{t-1}} are from M{t-1} in scene Si. \alpha balances the terms. Rendered Pixel Distillation Loss (L{C(r)}^i): L{C(r)}^i = ||\hat{C(r)}i^{Mt} - C(r)i^{M{t-1}}||^2 where \hat{C(r)}i^{Mt} is the rendered pixel from Mt in scene Si, and C(r)i^{M{t-1}} is from M{t-1} in scene Si. Uncertain Loss (L{dis}^i): L{dis}^i = \beta1 \mathbb{I}(\sigmai > \tau) L{ic\sigma}^i + \beta2 L{C(r)}^i + \log(\beta1) + \log(\beta2) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function, \tau is the density threshold, and \beta1, \beta2 are learnable self-balancing parameters. Total Loss: L = \sum{i=1}^{t-1} L{dis}^i + \gamma L{C(r)}^t where \gamma balances distillation for previous scenes and learning for the new scene St. L{C(r)}^t is the standard photometric loss for the new scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class SCARF: def init(self, numencoderlayers=9, encoderdim=256, decoderdims=[128, 3], latentdimK=21, noisedimZ=256, densitythresholdtau=3): """ Initialize SCARF model. """ self.L = numencoderlayers self.cin = encoderdim self.cout = encoderdim self.K = latentdimK self.Z = noisedimZ self.tau = densitythresholdtau # Shared parameters (Cross-Scene) # CSWM: L layers, shape (K, cout) self.CM = [np.random.randn(self.K, self.cout) for in range(self.L)] # Hypernetwork Gl: Simple MLP to generate SSWM from noise # Input: Z, Output: cin K self.G = [self.inithypernetwork() for in range(self.L)] # Decoder D self.D = self.initdecoder(decoderdims) # Scene-specific parameters (initialized when scene arrives) self.sceneparams = {} # Key: sceneid, Value: {Cli, zil, occupancygrid} def inithypernetwork(self): """ Initialize a simple hypernetwork Gl. Input: noise (Z), Output: latent feature (Z), Resized to (cin, K), then multiplied by CM to get final weights? Note: Source says Gl outputs latent feature resized to 256x21, then multiplied by Cli, then by CM. Actually, source says: Gl(zil) generates SSWM SMli. But then it says: SMli = Gl(zil). And Eli = SMli CMli. And CMli = Cli CMl. So Gl outputs SMli directly? Source Appendix B: "Input random noise... output a latent feature. After resizing the feature to 256x21, A learnable coefficient matrix is multiplied by the feature. Finally, by multiplying the cross-scene share weight matrix... the parameter of fully-connected layer is generated." This implies Gl outputs a latent vector, which is reshaped and transformed. Let's follow the formula: Eli = Gl(zil) CMli. And CMli = Cli CMl. So Gl(zil) must produce SMli (cin x K). """ # Simplified Hypernetwork: Linear projection from Z to cinK # In practice, Gl is a small MLP. Here we use a linear layer for simplicity. return lambda z: np.dot(z, np.random.randn(self.Z, self.cin self.K)) def initdecoder(self, dims): """Initialize shared decoder.""" return lambda x: np.dot(x, np.random.randn(dims[0], dims[1])) def generateencoderweights(self, sceneid, layeridx): """ Generate encoder weights for a specific scene and layer. """ if sceneid not in self.sceneparams: raise ValueError("Scene parameters not initialized.") params = self.sceneparams[sceneid] zil = params['zil'][layeridx] Cli = params['Cli'][layeridx] # 1. Generate SSWM from Hypernetwork # Gl(zil) -> SMli (cin x K) SMli = self.Glayeridx.reshape(self.cin, self.K) # 2. Transform CSWM with Coefficient Matrix # CMli = Cli CMl (K x K K x cout -> K x cout) CMl = self.CM[layeridx] CMli = np.dot(Cli, CMl) # 3. Final Encoder Layer Weights # Eli = SMli CMli (cin x K K x cout -> cin x cout) Eli = np.dot(SMli, CMli) return Eli def forward(self, xencoded, dencoded, sceneid): """ Forward pass for a ray. xencoded: (cin,) positional encoding of position dencoded: (4,) positional encoding of direction sceneid: identifier for the scene """ # Encoder h = xencoded for l in range(self.L): Eli = self.generateencoderweights(sceneid, l) h = np.dot(h, Eli) if l == 4: # Skip connection at 5th layer (index 4) hskip = h if l < 7: # First 8 layers are encoder hidden h = np.maximum(0, h) # ReLU else: # Last encoder layer outputs density and feature pass # Output density and feature vector # Assuming the last layer of encoder produces sigma and feature # The source says: "An additional layer outputs the density sigma and a 256-dimensional feature vector." # This implies the 9th layer (index 8) is special. # For simplicity, we assume the last encoder output is split. sigma = h[0] # Placeholder for density feature = h[1:] # 256-dim feature # Decoder # Concatenate feature with dencoded decoderinput = np.concatenate([feature, dencoded]) rgb = self.D(decoderinput) return sigma, rgb def trainscene(self, sceneid, rays, gtcolors, optimizer, numsteps): """ Train the model on a new scene or update for continual learning. """ if sceneid not in self.sceneparams: # Initialize new scene parameters self.sceneparams[sceneid] = { 'zil': [np.random.randn(self.Z) for in range(self.L)], 'Cli': [np.random.randn(self.K, self.K) for in range(self.L)], 'occupancygrid': None # To be filled by pre-extraction } # Pre-extract occupancy grid for this scene if new if self.sceneparams[sceneid]['occupancygrid'] is None: self.sceneparams[sceneid]['occupancygrid'] = self.extractoccupancygrid(sceneid) for step in range(numsteps): # Sample rays batchrays, batchcolors = self.samplebatch(rays, gtcolors) # Forward pass for new scene sigmas, rgbs = [], [] for ray in batchrays: sigma, rgb = self.forward(ray.xencoded, ray.dencoded, sceneid) sigmas.append(sigma) rgbs.append(rgb) # Loss for new scene lossnew = self.computephotometricloss(rgbs, batchcolors) # Distillation loss for previous scenes lossdistill = 0 for previd in self.sceneparams.keys(): if previd == sceneid: continue # Sample rays from previous scene using its occupancy grid prevrays = self.samplefromoccupancygrid(previd) prevgt = self.getgtforscene(previd, prevrays) prevsigmas, prevrgbs = [], [] for ray in prevrays: sigma, rgb = self.forward(ray.xencoded, ray.dencoded, previd) prevsigmas.append(sigma) prevrgbs.append(rgb) # Compute distillation loss # Note: In practice, we need to compare Mt and Mt-1 outputs. # Here, we assume we have access to Mt-1 outputs or re-render with old weights. # For implementation, we would store Mt-1 weights or re-render. # Simplified: Assume we have prevsigmasmt1, prevrgbsmt1 # lossdistill += self.computedistillationloss(prevsigmas, prevrgbs, prevsigmasmt1, prevrgbsmt1) pass totalloss = lossdistill + lossnew optimizer.step(totalloss) def extractoccupancygrid(self, sceneid): """ Extract explicit density occupancy grid for a scene. Resolution 50x50x50. Subgrid 5x5x5. """ # Placeholder for grid extraction logic return np.zeros((50, 50, 50)) def computephotometricloss(self, rgbs, gtcolors): return np.mean((np.array(rgbs) - np.array(gtcolors))2) def computedistillationloss(self, sigmasmt, rgbsmt, sigmasmt1, rgbsmt1, alpha=1.0, beta1=1.0, beta2=1.0): # Licsigma licsigma = np.mean((np.array(rgbsmt) - np.array(rgbsmt1))2) + \ alpha np.mean((np.array(sigmasmt) - np.array(sigmasmt1))2) # LC(r) lcr = np.mean((np.array(rgbsmt) - np.array(rgbsmt1))2) # Simplified, should be rendered pixels # Ldis # Indicator function I(sigma > tau) indicator = (np.array(sigmasmt) > self.tau).astype(float) ldis = beta1 indicator licsigma + beta2 lcr + np.log(beta1) + np.log(beta2) return np.mean(ldis) Time Complexity: Training is approximately 1.2x slower than vanilla NeRF due to the Uncertain Surface Distillation (USD) strategy. Rendering speed is equivalent to vanilla NeRF because weights are pre-generated. Memory Complexity: Parameters depend most on the number of layers L rather than the number of scenes N. For N scenes, vanilla NeRF parameters grow linearly with N. SCARF achieves a 16.4% compression rate for 8 scenes and 0.03% for 50 scenes compared to vanilla NeRF. Strengths: Memory-efficient continual learning across multiple 3D scenes with vast domain gaps. No catastrophic forgetting. Orthogonal to single-scene NeRF extensions. Limitations: Requires pre-extraction of occupancy grids. Hyperparameter tuning for \alpha, \beta1, \beta2, \tau, \gamma is required. Performance degradation is minor but present (e.g., Lego PSNR dropped by 0.31 in M3). When to use: When learning a sequence of distinct 3D scenes with limited memory and single-pass access to training data. When not to use: When only a single scene is needed, or when real-time weight generation during rendering is required (though pre-generation mitigates this). SCARF (Scalable Continual Learning Framework) was proposed by Y. Wang et al. in a preprint submitted in 2024. It addresses the problem of catastrophic forgetting in NeRF when training on a sequence of scenes. It builds on HyperNetworks [HDL16] and contrasts with methods like Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) [FXW23], MEIL-NeRF [CLBL22], and CL-NeRF [unofficial], which either focus on single scenes with multiple sequences or are multi-stage/overfitting. name: PL-NeRF
head: Power Line NeRF
body: PL-NeRF is a specialized Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) method designed for the 3D reconstruction of power transmission lines (PTLs) from progressive motion sequence images captured by inspection robots. It addresses the specific challenges of unbounded, thin, and low-texture scenes by replacing standard NeRF's Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) contraction with an L\infty norm spatial compression to align with hash encoding, and by substituting standard positional encoding with Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) and Hash Encoding (HE) to reduce aliasing and ghosting artifacts. Unlike general-purpose NeRF variants, PL-NeRF prioritizes reconstruction fidelity for long, narrow structures over real-time rendering speed, outperforming methods like Volinga in visual quality while maintaining competitive metrics against Instant-NGP and F2-NeRF. PL-NeRF modifies the standard NeRF pipeline through four key architectural and sampling improvements: spatial compression, dual encoding (HE/IPE), a proposal network sampler, and appearance embedding. The method assumes a dataset of close-distance, continuous images of PTLs. Inputs: A set of calibrated camera poses and images from a Flying–walking Power Line Inspection Robot (FPLIR). Outputs: Rendered RGB images, volume density \sigma, view-dependent color \mathbf{c}, and predicted surface normals \mathbf{n}. 1. Spatial Compression Map The unbounded scene is compressed into a fixed bounded volume. PL-NeRF uses the L\infty norm to map coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to a cube [-1, 1]^3. Let \|\mathbf{x}\|\infty = \max(|x|, |y|, |z|). The compressed coordinate \mathbf{x}' is defined as: \mathbf{x}' = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|\infty \le 1 \\ \text{sgn}(\mathbf{x}) \left( 2 - \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}\|\infty} \right) & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|\infty > 1 \end{cases} This creates a cube-shaped bounded space, distinct from the sphere-shaped space created by the L2 norm used in Mip-NeRF 360. 2. Hash Encoding (HE) Table A hash table stores feature vectors for spatial positions. Structure: A hash table with N buckets. Initialization: The scene space is normalized using the L\infty contraction. Coordinates are quantized to small vertices. Hash Function: A hash function H maps a quantized vertex coordinate to an index in the table. Interpolation: For a given input point, the 8 surrounding vertices in the hash grid are identified. Their feature vectors are retrieved via H and combined using trilinear (cubic) interpolation. 3. Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) Representation Instead of discrete sine/cosine bases, IPE represents the direction \mathbf{d} as a multivariate Gaussian distribution derived from the truncated frustum of the viewing cone. Representation: A mean vector \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma} representing the expected position and variance of the encoding within the frustum. 4. MLP Networks Two separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) process the encoded features: Position MLP: Input: Interpolated features from Hash Encoding. Architecture: 8 layers, 256 hidden units per layer. Output: Volume density \sigma and intermediate features for color. Color MLP: Input: Intermediate features from Position MLP + Direction Encoding (IPE) + Appearance Embedding. Architecture: 4 layers, 256 hidden units per layer. Output: View-dependent color \mathbf{c}. 5. Appearance Embedding A per-image embedding vector \mathbf{z}i is appended to the input of the Color MLP to account for exposure differences between training images. 1. Ray Generation and Frustum Construction: For each pixel in the input image, emit a cone beam from the camera center. Divide the ray bundle into frustums perpendicular to the ray axis. 2. Spatial Compression: Apply the L\infty norm contraction to all sample points \mathbf{x} along the ray to map them into the bounded cube [-1, 1]^3. 3. Hash Encoding (Position): Quantize the compressed coordinates of the sample points. Use the Hash Function to locate the indices of the 8 surrounding vertices in the Hash Table. Retrieve the feature vectors and perform trilinear interpolation to obtain the position feature vector \mathbf{f}{pos}. 4. Integrated Positional Encoding (Direction): Identify the truncated frustum region corresponding to the sample interval. Compute the Gaussian representation (mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}) of the positional encoding over this frustum. Truncate the frustum's encoding to calculate the expected encoding vector \mathbf{f}{dir}. 5. Proposal Network Sampling: Use a proposal network to sample additional points concentrated in the region where the first surface intersects (high density), contributing most to the final rendering. This merges sampling positions into the effective area. 6. Feature Aggregation: Pass \mathbf{f}{pos} into the Position MLP. Pass \mathbf{f}{dir} and the image-specific appearance embedding \mathbf{z}i into the Color MLP, along with the output features from the Position MLP. 7. Rendering and Normal Prediction: The Color MLP outputs color \mathbf{c}. The Position MLP outputs density \sigma. Use a volume renderer incorporating techniques from Ref-NeRF to predict surface normals \mathbf{n}. Render the final RGB image using standard volume rendering integration. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def linfinitycontraction(x): """ Compresses unbounded 3D coordinates into a cube [-1, 1]^3 using L-infinity norm. Inspired by Mip-NeRF 360 but uses Linf for cube alignment with Hash Encoding. """ norminf = np.max(np.abs(x), axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Avoid division by zero norminf = np.maximum(norminf, 1e-8) # If norm <= 1, return x. If norm > 1, apply contraction formula. # Formula: sgn(x) (2 - 1/||x||inf) # Note: The source describes this as twisting space into a fixed volume. # Standard Linf contraction maps ||x||inf > 1 to the boundary. mask = norminf > 1.0 xcontracted = np.where(mask, np.sign(x) (2.0 - 1.0 / norminf), x) return xcontracted def hashencode(xcontracted, hashtable, numlevels=16, leveldim=2): """ Hash Encoding for position. Quantizes coordinates, finds 8 neighbors, retrieves values, and interpolates. """ # 1. Quantize coordinates to grid vertices # Assuming a grid resolution determined by hashtable levels # This is a simplified representation of the "small vertex" quantization gridcoords = np.floor(xcontracted (2numlevels - 1)).astype(int) # 2. Determine 8 surrounding vertices # In practice, this involves bitwise operations on the integer coordinates # to generate the 8 corner indices in the hash grid. vertexindices = get8neighbors(gridcoords) # 3. Hash function to map vertex indices to hash table buckets # H(vertexindex) -> bucketindex bucketindices = hashfunction(vertexindices) # 4. Retrieve feature vectors from hash table # hashtable shape: (numbuckets, featuredim) features = hashtable[bucketindices] # 5. Trilinear interpolation # Calculate weights based on fractional part of gridcoords weights = calculatetrilinearweights(xcontracted, gridcoords) interpolatedfeature = np.sum(features weights, axis=0) return interpolatedfeature def integratedpositionalencoding(raydirection, frustumparams): """ Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) for direction. Approximates integration of PE over a truncated frustum using multivariate Gaussian. """ # 1. Find truncated frustum region for the ray segment # frustumparams contains the start and end points of the segment along the ray # 2. Compute Gaussian representation (mean and covariance) # The source states: "approximate the integration using a multivariate Gaussian approach" # and "compute the Gaussian representation of the truncated frustum" # This results in a mean vector mu and covariance Sigma representing the # expected encoding and variance within the cone region. mu, sigma = computegaussianrepresentation(frustumparams) # 3. Truncate and calculate expected encoding # The encoding is transmitted as this Gaussian representation to the MLP return mu, sigma def plnerfforward(image, camerapose, hashtable, posmlp, colormlp, appearanceembeddings): """ Main forward pass for PL-NeRF. """ # 1. Generate ray bundles rays = generateraysfromimage(image, camerapose) # 2. Sample points along rays # Use proposal network sampler to focus on high-density areas samplepoints = proposalnetworksampling(rays) # 3. Spatial Compression compressedpoints = linfinitycontraction(samplepoints) # 4. Hash Encoding (Position) posfeatures = hashencode(compressedpoints, hashtable) # 5. Integrated Positional Encoding (Direction) # For each sample point, determine its frustum segment frustums = getfrustums(rays, samplepoints) dirmeans, dircovs = integratedpositionalencoding(rays.direction, frustums) # 6. Appearance Embedding # Get image-specific embedding imgid = getimageid(camerapose) appemb = appearanceembeddings[imgid] # 7. Position MLP # Input: posfeatures # Output: sigma (density) and intermediate features sigma, intermediatefeatures = posmlp(posfeatures) # 8. Color MLP # Input: intermediatefeatures, dirmeans (or derived encoding from mu/sigma), appemb # Output: color c color = colormlp(intermediatefeatures, dirmeans, appemb) # 9. Volume Rendering # Integrate sigma and color along the ray # Also predict normals using Ref-NeRF technique renderedcolor, normals = volumerender(rays, sigma, color) return renderedcolor, normals def get8neighbors(gridcoords): """ Helper to get 8 corner indices for trilinear interpolation. """ # Implementation detail: generate 8 combinations of floor/ceil for x, y, z # This is a standard grid neighbor lookup pass def hashfunction(vertexindices): """ Helper to map vertex indices to hash table buckets. """ # Standard hash function (e.g., XOR folding) pass def calculatetrilinearweights(x, gridcoords): """ Helper to calculate interpolation weights. """ # Fractional part of coordinates frac = x - gridcoords # Weights are products of (1-frac) and frac for each dimension pass def computegaussianrepresentation(frustumparams): """ Helper to compute mean and covariance of PE over a frustum. """ # Mathematical integration of sinusoidal functions over the frustum volume # Resulting in a Gaussian approximation pass def volumerender(rays, sigma, color): """ Standard volume rendering integration. """ # Alpha compositing: C = sum(Ti alphai ci) # where Ti is transmittance, alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltai) pass Position MLP: 8 layers, 256 hidden units per layer. Color MLP: 4 layers, 256 hidden units per layer. Spatial Compression: L\infty norm, resulting in a cube-shaped bounded volume. Reconstruction Metrics (on PTL dataset): PSNR = 29, SSIM = 0.871, LPIPS = 0.087. Unbounded Scenes: Standard NDC contraction is ill-defined for unbounded PTL scenes where near/far boundaries are not clear. PL-NeRF mitigates this by using L\infty contraction to a fixed cube. Thin Structures: Power lines are thin and low-texture, causing discontinuity and jagged edges in standard NeRF. The combination of IPE and HE reduces sample counts and generates anti-aliasing features to address ghosting. Exposure Differences: Training cameras may have varying exposure. PL-NeRF uses per-image appearance embeddings to handle this; failing to include this may result in inconsistent color rendering across images. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses Hash Encoding (Instant-NGP style), which offers fast lookup and interpolation, reducing the memory footprint compared to dense voxel grids. However, the source notes that PL-NeRF prioritizes reconstruction quality over rendering smoothness and real-time capabilities. It is slower than Volinga (which focuses on speed) but provides higher fidelity. Measured Performance: On the PTL dataset, PL-NeRF achieved PSNR = 29, SSIM = 0.871, and LPIPS = 0.087. It outperformed F2-NeRF, Instant-NGP, and Volinga in reconstruction metrics, except for FPS (where Volinga was faster). Strengths: High reconstruction fidelity for thin, long structures; effective handling of unbounded scenes via L\infty compression; reduced aliasing via IPE/HE. Limitations: Not optimized for real-time rendering; performance is specific to the structured, thin geometry of power lines; requires progressive motion sequence images for optimal continuity. When to Use: 3D reconstruction of power transmission lines or similar thin, unbounded structures from close-range, continuous image sequences. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring high FPS; scenes with dense, complex textures where hash encoding collisions might degrade quality; bounded scenes where NDC is sufficient. PL-NeRF was developed to address the difficulties of 3D reconstruction of power transmission lines (PTLs) using image-based methods. The method was inspired by Mip-NeRF 360 for spatial compression and Ref-NeRF for normal prediction. It was applied to data captured by a Flying–walking Power Line Inspection Robot (FPLIR). The method was published in Sensors in 2023. name: Separate Modeling of Colors and Volume Density
head: Color Branch and Density Branch, Dual-Branch NeRF, Separate MLP for Color and Density
body: This method addresses the overfitting and artifact issues in few-shot view synthesis by decoupling the prediction of volume density (geometry) and color (appearance) into two distinct neural networks. Unlike the baseline NeRF architecture Parent which uses a single monolithic MLP to predict both outputs synchronously, this approach employs separate branches with different positional encoding frequencies, prioritizing low-frequency information for geometry and high-frequency information for appearance. The method replaces the single output head of the baseline NeRF with two specialized Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a Density Branch D\theta and a Color Branch C\theta. The core innovation is the use of distinct positional encoding frequencies for the inputs of each branch, based on the assumption that geometry is smoother (lower frequency) than appearance (higher frequency). Inputs: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D spatial coordinate. \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Viewing direction vector. Outputs: \sigma \in \mathbb{R}: Volume density. \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3: View-dependent color. The network parameters \theta are split into \thetaD for the Density Branch and \thetaC for the Color Branch. Hyperparameters: L1, L2, L3: Integers controlling the number of frequency bands in the positional encoding. Constraint: L3 \le L1 \le L2. L1: Frequency for Density Branch spatial input. L2: Frequency for Color Branch spatial input. L3: Frequency for Color Branch directional input. \gammaL(\mathbf{v}): Positional encoding function applied to vector \mathbf{v} with L frequency bands. 1. Density Branch (D\theta) The Density Branch estimates \sigma using only the spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} with low-frequency encoding L1. It incorporates inputs into every layer (similar to mi-MLP) to improve few-shot performance. For layer i (where i \ge 1): f1^D = \phi1^D(\gamma{L1}(\mathbf{x})) fi^D = \phii^D(f{i-1}^D, \gamma{L1}(\mathbf{x})) \quad \text{for } i \ge 2 Where: \phii^D is the i-th layer of the Density Branch MLP (linear transformation + activation). fi^D is the output feature of layer i. The final volume density is \sigma = f{ND}^D (assuming ND layers). 2. Color Branch (C\theta) The Color Branch estimates \mathbf{c} using the spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} with high-frequency encoding L2 and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} with frequency L3. It includes a residual interaction mechanism with the Density Branch features to aid geometry recovery. For layer i (where i \ge 1): f1^C = \phi1^C(\gamma{L2}(\mathbf{x})) For i \ge 2: f{i-1}^C = \phi{i-1}^C(f{i-2}^C, \gamma{L3}(\mathbf{d})) + f{i-1}^C fi^C = \phii^C(f{i-1}^C, \gamma{L3}(\mathbf{d})) Note: The source formula for the interaction step f{i-1}^C = \dots + f{i-1}^C implies a residual connection where the previous layer's output is added to the result of the current layer's transformation. The exact implementation of the "interaction" described as "beneficial to better geometry recovery" is defined by these equations. Where: \phii^C is the i-th layer of the Color Branch MLP. fi^C is the output feature of layer i. The final color is \mathbf{c} = f{NC}^C (assuming NC layers). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): """ Standard positional encoding with L frequency bands. Input v: (..., 3) Output: (..., 6L) """ def init(self, L): super().init() self.L = L def forward(self, v): # v shape: (..., 3) # Create frequencies # freqbands = 2^0, 2^1,..., 2^(L-1) freqbands = torch.tensor([2.0 i for i in range(self.L)], device=v.device, dtype=v.dtype) # Expand v to match freqbands shape for broadcasting # v: (..., 3) -> (..., 1, 3) # freqbands: (L,) -> (1, L, 1) # result: (..., L, 3) scaledv = v.unsqueeze(-2) freqbands.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1) # Apply sin and cos sinvals = torch.sin(scaledv) cosvals = torch.cos(scaledv) # Concatenate along the last dimension # (..., L, 3) -> (..., L3) encoded = torch.cat([sinvals, cosvals], dim=-1) return encoded class DensityBranch(nn.Module): def init(self, indim, hiddendim, outdim, numlayers, L1): super().init() self.L1 = L1 self.pe = PositionalEncoding(L1) self.layers = nn.ModuleList() # First layer self.layers.append(nn.Linear(indim + self.pe.L 6, hiddendim)) self.layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Hidden layers for in range(numlayers - 2): self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim + self.pe.L 6, hiddendim)) self.layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Output layer self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim + self.pe.L 6, outdim)) def forward(self, x): # x: (..., 3) pex = self.pe(x) # Concatenate original x and PE? # Source says input is gammaL1(x). Usually PE replaces or augments. # NeRF standard PE augments. Let's assume augmentation for compatibility with standard NeRF pipelines mentioned in S1. # However, S1 says "reduce dimensions of input embeddings". # Let's assume the input to the MLP is the PE vector itself or PE + x. # Standard NeRF uses PE. S1 says "dimensions of encoded input embeddings... decide how detailed". # We will use the PE vector as the primary feature, potentially concatenated with x if needed, # but strictly following S1 formula: input is gammaL1(x). h = pex for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): if i % 2 == 0: # Linear layer # Concatenate input x (or its PE) at every layer # S1: "incorporate inputs into each layer" # Input to layer i is (prevh, gammaL1(x)) h = torch.cat([h, pex], dim=-1) h = layer(h) else: # Activation h = layer(h) return h class ColorBranch(nn.Module): def init(self, indimx, indimd, hiddendim, outdim, numlayers, L2, L3): super().init() self.L2 = L2 self.L3 = L3 self.pex = PositionalEncoding(L2) self.ped = PositionalEncoding(L3) self.layers = nn.ModuleList() # First layer takes only spatial input self.layers.append(nn.Linear(indimx + self.pex.L 6, hiddendim)) self.layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Hidden layers take previous feature and direction for in range(numlayers - 2): self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim + self.ped.L 6, hiddendim)) self.layers.append(nn.ReLU()) # Output layer self.layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim + self.ped.L 6, outdim)) def forward(self, x, d): pex = self.pex(x) ped = self.ped(d) h = pex for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): if i == 0: # First layer: input is gammaL2(x) h = layer(h) else: # Subsequent layers: interaction with density branch features is mentioned in text, # but formula 10 shows interaction between color branch layers themselves via residual. # Formula: f{i-1}^C = phi(f{i-2}, d) + f{i-1} # This implies a residual connection. # Calculate new feature from previous feature and direction hinput = torch.cat([h, ped], dim=-1) hnew = layer(hinput) # Residual connection: add previous h to new h # Note: S1 formula: f{i-1}^C = phi(...) + f{i-1}^C # This notation is slightly ambiguous. It likely means: # temp = phi(prev, d) # curr = temp + prev # But the variable names in S1 are f{i-1} on both sides. # Let's interpret as: h = layer(h, d) + h h = hnew + h return h class SeparateModel(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim, numlayersdensity, numlayerscolor, L1, L2, L3): super().init() # Assuming input dim 3 for x and d self.densitybranch = DensityBranch(3, hiddendim, 1, numlayersdensity, L1) self.colorbranch = ColorBranch(3, 3, hiddendim, 3, numlayerscolor, L2, L3) def forward(self, x, d): # x: (N, 3), d: (N, 3) sigma = self.densitybranch(x) c = self.colorbranch(x, d) return sigma, c Frequency Selection: The constraint L3 \le L1 \le L2 is critical. If L1 is too high, the density branch may overfit to noise, creating artifacts. If L2 is too low, fine appearance details are lost. Interaction Implementation: The residual interaction in the Color Branch (f{i-1}^C = \dots + f{i-1}^C) must be implemented carefully to ensure gradient flow. The source notes this interaction is "beneficial to better geometry recovery". Few-Shot Overfitting: While this method reduces artifacts, it is specifically designed for few-shot scenarios. In dense-view settings, the standard shared MLP might still be competitive or superior due to parameter efficiency. Complexity: The method increases the number of parameters compared to a single shared MLP because two separate networks are trained. However, the Density Branch uses lower-dimensional embeddings (L1), partially offsetting the cost. Performance: It significantly reduces artifacts in few-shot view synthesis compared to vanilla NeRF. Strengths: Better geometry recovery in object-centric scenes; reduced overfitting in few-shot settings. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of L1, L2, L3. May not provide significant benefits in dense-view scenarios where the shared MLP is sufficient. This method was introduced in the paper "Is Vanilla MLP in Neural Radiance Field Enough for Few-Shot View Synthesis?" (CVPR 2024). It was developed to address the limitations of the standard NeRF architecture when applied to few-shot view synthesis, where the shared MLP tends to overfit and produce geometric artifacts. The design is motivated by the observation that geometry is typically smoother than appearance. body: Network Structure Modifications alter the baseline continuous volumetric representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to address specific constraints such as dynamic scenes, noise, semantic understanding, or inference speed. These modifications retain the core volume rendering equation but change the input space, network topology, or output fields to enable features like temporal consistency, object manipulation, or noise-aware rendering. The baseline NeRF architecture Parent defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as uncertainty, semantic logits, or physical properties like albedo and normals. These architectures alter the network topology, input space, or output fields to enable features like temporal consistency, object manipulation, or noise-aware rendering. The multi-input MLP (mi-MLP) is a network architecture modification for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that incorporates the raw input embeddings (3D location and viewing direction) into every layer of the network to prevent overfitting in few-shot view synthesis without reducing model capacity. Unlike the vanilla NeRF architecture Parent, which relies on deep hierarchical mappings where each layer only sees the output of the previous one, mi-MLP ensures that every layer is explicitly aware of the input embeddings, creating shorter paths between inputs and outputs. This structural change alleviates overfitting by balancing gradient amplitudes across layers, allowing the model to synthesize high-frequency details with fewer effective parameters. Default is 8. inputchviews: The number of input channels for view directions. Default is 3. outputch: The number of output channels. name: Network Architectures
head: NeRF Network Architectures
body: Network architectures in neural radiance fields modify the baseline continuous volumetric representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to address specific constraints such as dynamic scenes, noise, semantic understanding, or inference speed. These architectures alter the network topology, input space, or output fields to enable features like temporal consistency, object manipulation, or noise-aware rendering. The baseline NeRF architecture defines a continuous volumetric scene representation F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial position, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction, \sigma is the volume density, and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color. The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations. Most modifications in this family retain the core volume rendering equation but alter one or more of the following components: 1. Input Space: Augmenting \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} with additional signals such as latent codes \mathbf{z}, time t, illumination embeddings \mathbf{z}l, or external feature vectors \mathbf{f} from vision models. 2. Network Topology: Replacing the monolithic MLP with specialized branches (e.g., separate density and color networks), modular experts, or hybrid structures combining MLPs with convolutional or transformer backbones. 3. Output Space: Extending the output tuple (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) to include additional fields such as uncertainty, semantic logits, or physical properties like albedo and normals. MIMO-DONeRF is a method that applies the Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) neural rendering concept to the DONeRF architecture. It modifies the shading network to accept multiple spatial inputs and view directions simultaneously, producing multiple color and density outputs per forward pass. This approach improves inference speed compared to increasing the number of samples in standard DONeRF, while maintaining or improving image quality by allowing the network to accumulate neighbor information through grouped samples. It differs from standard DONeRF by processing Np samples in parallel rather than sequentially, and from MIMO-NeRF by being specifically adapted to the two-network structure (depth oracle and shading) of DONeRF. This method adapts the Point-NeRF architecture to enable 3D scene geometry decomposition and manipulation from 2D images. It solves the problem of editing specific objects within a complex scene by replacing the standard Multi-View Stereo (MVS) point cloud generation with ground-truth dense data during training and using a diffusion model to infer object codes for manipulation. It differs from standard Point-NeRF by integrating a DM-NeRF module to map spatial locations to object codes and modifying the rendering pipeline to support point transformation. SLS4D is a method for 4D novel-view synthesis that represents dynamic radiance fields using a learnable sparse latent space, reducing network parameters compared to dense grid discretizations while maintaining high-frequency detail via attention-based interpolation. It differs from dense grid methods (like TiNeuVox) by avoiding the O(N^3TF) space complexity of 4D grids, and from per-image latent code methods by offering better generalization across time through continuous temporal interpolation. Neural Feature Fusion Fields (N3F) is a method that distills dense 2D image features from a pre-trained teacher network into a 3D neural field (student) via differentiable volumetric rendering, enabling 3D-aware feature representation. Unlike Semantic NeRF or Panoptic NeRF which fuse discrete semantic labels, N3F fuses continuous dense feature vectors, allowing for open-world applications without manual labels. It differs from standard feature distillation because the student operates in 3D world space (ensuring spatial consistency) while the teacher operates in 2D image space. CLNeRF is a model architecture modification for NeRF that enables continual learning by incorporating scene changes (appearance and geometry) over time within a single model, preventing model size growth as new scans are added. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like MIMO-DONeRF and SLS4D by using explicit, trainable per-scan embedding vectors rather than latent space compression or multi-instance networks, allowing for efficient updates and low overhead for generative replay. Mutual Information Gradient Shaping (MIGS), implemented as JacobiNeRF, is a training regularization technique that shapes the tangent space of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to encode semantic correlations between scene entities. Unlike first-order approaches that distill 2D features into 3D radiance channels or treat labels as separate output channels, MIGS aligns the Jacobians of correlated entities to maximize their mutual information under random weight perturbations, enabling efficient sparse label propagation and semantic consensus. Multi-Level Neural Scene Graph (NSG) is a scene representation that decomposes an environment into a graph of static, dynamic, and temporal nodes to model urban environments with moving objects and appearance variations. It distinguishes itself from sibling architectures by explicitly separating the radiance field into a static component \phi and a dynamic component \psi, conditioned on sequence-level and object-level latent vectors respectively, enabling the disentanglement of scene-dependent appearance from object texture. NAN is a burst-denoising method that extends the IBRNet architecture to handle degraded noisy images, such as those captured in low-light conditions, by modifying feature extraction, aggregation, and color blending to be noise-aware. Unlike standard NeRFs that synthesize novel views, NAN fixes an existing view image by leveraging multiple noisy inputs of the same scene. It distinguishes itself from its sibling MIMO-DONeRF and Point-NeRF Adaptation for Object Manipulation by explicitly modeling spatial noise statistics through 3D blending kernels and cross-view variance features, rather than relying solely on single-pixel cross-view consistency. The Multiplicative Interaction Module (MIM) is a neural component that generates conditional inputs for a NeRF by computing multiplicative interactions between expression, identity, and optional latent codes to improve facial disentanglement and rendering quality. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like MIMO-DONeRF or Point-NeRF Adaptation for Object Manipulation by explicitly modeling higher-order (second and third) multiplicative dependencies between semantic codes rather than relying on linear concatenation or simple additive fusion. Part-Wise NARF (NARFP) is a neural articulated radiance field method that models an articulated object by training a separate Ray-Traced NeRF (RT-NeRF) for each rigid part, combining their outputs to estimate global density and color. It differs from holistic approaches by explicitly computing rigid transformations via forward kinematics, thereby avoiding implicit transformation issues and part dependency problems inherent in other methods. This architecture divides dynamic scenes into static and dynamic parts modeled by two separate MLPs. Inputs: Static Network F{\Theta}^{st} takes positional encoding of position \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and direction \gamma(\mathbf{d}). Dynamic Network F{\Theta}^{dy} takes positional encoding of position \gamma(\mathbf{x}), direction \gamma(\mathbf{d}), and time \gamma(t). Outputs: Static Network outputs color \mathbf{c}, density \sigma, and blending weight v. Dynamic Network outputs color \mathbf{c}t, density \sigmat, scene flow \mathcal{F}t, and disocclusion weights \mathcal{W}t. Formulas: (\mathbf{c}t, \sigmat, \mathcal{F}t, \mathcal{W}t) = F{\Theta}^{dy}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \gamma(\mathbf{d}), \gamma(t)) \quad (22) (\mathbf{c}, \sigma, v) = F{\Theta}^{st}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \gamma(\mathbf{d})) \quad (23) where \gamma(\cdot) denotes the positional encoding. Steps: Use equidistant sampling to obtain spatial points along rays, instead of hierarchical sampling. Use predicted scene flow to establish inter-frame relationship for time consistency. Jointly optimize camera parameters \Delta f, \Delta P along with the MLPs F{\Theta}^{dy}, F{\Theta}^{st}. This architecture extends the radiance field with a blend weight field F{\Delta w} to handle dynamic human bodies. Parameters: Sampling uses single-level NeRF with 64 points along each camera ray. Appearance code and blend weight field code dimensions are both 128. Network Layout: Radiance fields F\sigma, Fc follow the original NeRF architecture. Blend weight field F{\Delta w} is almost identical to F\sigma, except the final output layer has 24 channels and applies \exp(\cdot) to the output. Steps: Train parameters of F\sigma, Fc, F{\Delta w}, appearance codes \{\mathbf{l}i\} and blend weight field codes \{\boldsymbol{\psi}i\} jointly over the input video. Learn neural blend weight fields under novel human poses using equation (9) from the source. Use Adam optimizer with learning rate starting from 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying exponentially to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Occupancy Networks is a single-level version of NeRF that does not leverage positional encodings. Performance: 2D Images: 13.90 PSNR / 0.437 SSIM. Performance on Radiance Field: 20.60 PSNR / 0.849 SSIM. Training Time: 02:17 / 100:23 (2D / RF). Model Size: 0.38 / 0.43 (2D / RF). An ablation variant of Residual-NeRF where background and residual NeRFs are merged by simply adding their outputs before activation, instead of using a Mixnet. Formulas: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-(\sigma{bg} + \sigma{res})i \deltai)) (\mathbf{c}{bg+res})i \quad (8) with \mathbf{c}{bg+res} = S(\mathbf{c}'{bg} + \mathbf{c}'{res}) (\mathbf{c}'{bg}, \sigma{bg}) = \Phi{bg}(h(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}, \theta, \phi)) (\mathbf{c}'{res}, \sigma{res}) = \Phi{res}(h(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}, \theta, \phi)) S(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{x}}} where S(\cdot) is the sigmoid activation. Comparison: Residual-NeRF-S produces worse depth and view reconstruction compared to Residual-NeRF with Mixnet, especially for partially opaque objects. Pyramid NeRF accomplishes rapid NeRF training and inference through the application of an image pyramid and a strategy based on frequency optimization. This technique utilizes a "low-frequency-first, high-frequency-second" approach, substituting large MLPs with thousands of smaller ones via progressive segmentation, markedly enhancing both training and inference efficiency. Furthermore, the introduction of a sampling approach that is aware of depth aims to enhance the quality of rendering and hasten the convergence of training. The experimental findings reveal that Pyramid NeRF enhances training and inference speeds by 15x and 805x, respectively, and notably betters structural and perceptual resemblance relative to the original NeRF. Dynamic Scene Network: Uses equidistant sampling instead of hierarchical sampling, which may affect convergence speed but simplifies the training pipeline for dynamic scenes. Pyramid NeRF: Enhances training speed by 15x and inference speed by 805x relative to the original NeRF. OccNet: Performance on 2D Images: 13.90 PSNR / 0.437 SSIM. Performance on Radiance Field: 20.60 PSNR / 0.849 SSIM. Training Time: 02:17 / 100:23. Model Size: 0.38 / 0.43. Residual-NeRF-S: Produces worse depth and view reconstruction compared to Residual-NeRF with Mixnet, especially for partially opaque objects. Blend Weight Field: Training takes around 200k iterations (about 12 hours) for a three-view video of 300 frames on four 2080 Ti GPUs. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) were introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020, establishing the baseline continuous volumetric representation. Subsequent research has modified this architecture to handle specific challenges such as dynamic scenes, noise, semantic understanding, and efficient inference. The modifications described here represent the evolution of the NeRF architecture from a static, monolithic MLP to specialized, multi-component systems. name: MIMO-DONeRF
head: MIMO-NeRF applied to DONeRF
body: MIMO-DONeRF applies the Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) neural rendering concept to the DONeRF architecture. It modifies the shading network to accept multiple spatial inputs and view directions simultaneously, producing multiple color and density outputs per forward pass. This approach improves inference speed compared to increasing the number of samples in standard DONeRF, while maintaining or improving image quality by allowing the network to accumulate neighbor information through grouped samples. It differs from standard DONeRF by processing Np samples in parallel rather than sequentially, and from MIMO-NeRF by being specifically adapted to the two-network structure (depth oracle and shading) of DONeRF. Inputs and Outputs: For each ray, a depth oracle network selects Ns samples. The MIMO shading network takes these Ns samples, grouped into batches of size Np, as input. It outputs colors and densities for all grouped samples. Data Structures: The shading network accepts a batch of inputs. For a group of Np samples, the input consists of positions (xi, \dots, xj) and a single view direction d, where j = i + Np - 1. The output consists of colors (ci, \dots, cj) and densities (\sigmai, \dots, \sigmaj) for the same indices. The network architecture (hidden unit dimensions, number of layers, activation functions) remains identical to the original DONeRF shading network. Number of Runs: The total number of forward passes (# Run) required to process all Ns samples is calculated as: \text{\# Run} = 1 + \frac{Ns}{Np} where Ns is the number of samples selected by the depth oracle and Np is the number of grouped samples processed in parallel. In standard DONeRF, Np=1, so # Run equals Ns. Parameters: Ns: Number of samples selected by the depth oracle network. Typical values: 4, 5, 11, 16. Np: Number of grouped samples (parallel inputs) processed by the shading network. Typical values: 1, 4. \lambda: Hyperparameter for the MIMO loss function. Set to 0.001. Training and Loss: The depth oracle and shading networks are trained separately for 300,000 iterations using the Adam optimizer. The learning rate is 5 \times 10^{-4} with momentum terms \beta1=0.9 and \beta2=0.999. The batch size is 4096 rays. MIMO-DONeRF uses a specific loss function L{\text{MIMO}} (Equation 10 in the source) instead of the standard pixel loss L{\text{pixel}} (Equation 3 in the source). The implementation is based on the official DONeRF source code. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def positionalencoding(x, mindeg, maxdeg): # Standard NeRF positional encoding: concat(x, sin(2^l pi x), cos(...)) scales = [2i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg)] scaledx = torch.einsum('bij,k->bkij', x, torch.tensor(scales)) encoded = torch.cat([x] + [torch.sin(scaledx), torch.cos(scaledx)], dim=-1) return encoded.view(x.shape[0], -1) class MIMODONeRFShadingNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim=256, numlayers=8, outdim=4): super().init() # Output layer produces Np colors and Np densities. out = self.outputlayer(x) # (Np, 4) colors = out[:,:3] densities = out[:, 3] return colors, densities def computemimoloss(predictedcolors, groundtruthcolors, lambdaparam): # Not given in the sources. The source notes that DONeRF-4 sometimes yields artifacts (e.g., belt in 'Bulldozer', hair in 'Forest'), which are mitigated by increasing samples to 16 or using MIMO-DONeRF. Time and Memory Complexity: MIMO-DONeRF reduces the number of forward passes (# Run) compared to standard DONeRF. For Ns=16 and Np=4, # Run is 1 + 16/4 = 5, whereas standard DONeRF requires 16 passes. This results in a significant speedup. DONeRF-16 increases inference time approximately three times compared to DONeRF-4, while MIMO-DONeRF-16/4-naive and MIMO-DONeRF-16/4-self only increase inference time 1.1 times compared to DONeRF-4. Measured Performance: PSNR: MIMO-DONeRF-16/4-self achieves an average PSNR of 36.27, comparable to DONeRF-16 (36.98) and better than DONeRF-4 (31.14). FLIP: MIMO-DONeRF-16/4-self achieves an average FLIP of 0.061, comparable to DONeRF-16 (0.062) and better than DONeRF-4 (0.070). Scene Specifics: MIMO-DONeRF-16/4-naive and MIMO-DONeRF-16/4-self succeed in representing lotus leaves in the 'Pavillon' scene, whereas DONeRF-16 and DONeRF-4 fail. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Faster inference than increasing Ns in standard DONeRF; better handling of fine details (e.g., lotus leaves) due to neighbor information accumulation; maintains high image quality (PSNR/FLIP) comparable to high-sample DONeRF. Limitations: Requires modification of the shading network to handle multiple inputs/outputs; relies on the MIMO loss function which may require careful tuning (though \lambda=0.001 is suggested). When to Use: Use MIMO-DONeRF when inference speed is critical but high image quality (comparable to high-sample DONeRF) is required, particularly for scenes with fine details that suffer from artifacts in low-sample DONeRF. MIMO-DONeRF was introduced in the paper "MIMO-NeRF: Fast Neural Rendering with Multi-input Multi-output Neural Radiance Fields". It is an application of the MIMO-NeRF concept to the DONeRF architecture. The method was implemented based on the official DONeRF source code. The authors note that the depth oracle network in DONeRF is already fast and runs only once per ray, so the MIMO concept is applied to the shading network to improve efficiency. name: Point-NeRF Adaptation for Object Manipulation
head: Point-NeRF Object Manipulation
body: This method adapts the Point-NeRF architecture to enable 3D scene geometry decomposition and manipulation from 2D images. It solves the problem of editing specific objects within a complex scene by replacing standard Multi-View Stereo point cloud generation with ground-truth dense data during training and using a diffusion model to infer object codes for manipulation. It differs from standard Point-NeRF by integrating a DM-NeRF module to map spatial locations to object codes and modifying the rendering pipeline to support point transformation. Inputs and Outputs: Training Input: Ground truth dense point cloud (400 million points per scene). Inference Input: Spatial locations of all neural points, manipulation information (target locations), and a camera view. Output: Rendered image with manipulated objects. Data Structures: Neural Point Cloud: A set of points \{pi\} where each point pi has a 3D spatial location \mathbf{x}i and an associated object code \mathbf{c}i inferred by DM-NeRF. DM-NeRF: A network that maps spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} to object codes \mathbf{c}. Steps: 1. Training Phase: Generate the neural point cloud using the ground truth dense point cloud instead of MVSNet-generated points. The source specifies 400 million points per scene. 2. Inference - Code Inference: Feed the spatial locations \mathbf{x}i of all neural points into DM-NeRF to infer the corresponding object codes \mathbf{c}i. 3. Inference - Manipulation: Identify points to be edited based on manipulation information. Transform the spatial locations of these points to desired new locations \mathbf{x}'i. 4. Rendering: Use the modified neural point cloud (with transformed points \mathbf{x}'i) to render an image from a given view using point-based volume rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainandgenerateneuralcloud(scenegtpoints): # Use ground truth dense point cloud instead of MVSNet neuralpoints = [] for pt in scenegtpoints: neuralpoints.append({'location': pt.position, 'code': None}) return neuralpoints def manipulateandrender(neuralpoints, dmnerfmodel, viewcamera, manipulationinfo): # 1. Infer object codes from spatial locations locations = [p['location'] for p in neuralpoints] # DM-NeRF network forward pass to infer object codes codes = [None] len(locations) # Network implementation details not provided in sources for i, p in enumerate(neuralpoints): p['code'] = codes[i] # 2. Apply manipulation: determine points to edit and transform them for p in neuralpoints: if p in manipulationinfo.targetpoints: p['location'] = manipulationinfo.getnewlocation(p) # 3. Render with new neural point cloud # Standard point-based volume rendering rays = viewcamera.generaterays() image = [] for ray in rays: # Find points along ray, sort by distance hits = sorted([p for p in neuralpoints if ray.intersects(p['location'])], key=lambda p: ray.distanceto(p['location'])) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for p in hits: c = p['code'] a = 1.0 # Simplified opacity for point cloud rendering accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] (1 - a) + c[j] a for j in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += a (1 - accumulatedalpha) if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break image.append(accumulatedcolor) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Quality: Using MVSNet-generated points during training may degrade quality; ground truth is required for the DM-SR dataset. Scale: The dataset scenes are approximately 12 \times 12 \times 3 meters. Renders foreground features by sampling points along rays from a dense point cloud and aggregating local geometric structure from neighboring neural points. It differs from standard Point-NeRF by replacing the original feature encoding with a redesigned per-point aggregate module that perceives local geometry, necessary because the upstream diffusion module generates coordinates without color information. Choose it when local geometric perception is required for diffusion-generated coordinates. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables geometry manipulation in complex indoor rooms with complicated geometry. Limitations: Requires ground truth dense point clouds for training, which may not be available in real-world scenarios. Originated in DM-NeRF, presented at ICLR 2023. The method is part of a pipeline for 3D scene geometry decomposition and manipulation from 2D images, utilizing a synthetic dataset called DM-SR based on Hypersim and NeRF synthetic datasets. name: Foreground Rendering with Point-NeRF
head: Per-point Aggregate Module, Point-based Radiance Field
body: This method renders foreground features by sampling points along rays from a dense point cloud and aggregating local geometric structure from neighboring neural points. It differs from standard Point-NeRF by replacing the original feature encoding with a redesigned per-point aggregate module that perceives local geometry, which is necessary because the upstream diffusion module generates coordinates without color information. Inputs: Dense point cloud coordinates x0. Ray direction d. Sampling points pi along the rays. Outputs: Volume density \sigma. View-dependent radiance r. Local geometric features fi for each sampling point. Data Structures: Neural points: Stored as coordinates c. Neighborhood points kpi: A set of K points queried within radius R. Geometric differences kgi: Encoded vector representation of local geometry. Parameters: Number of neighbors K=8. Neighborhood geometric feature dimension expanded to 8. Euclidean distance radius R. Steps: 1. Query Neighbors: For each sampling point pi, query K neighboring neural points kpi = \{kp{1i}, kp{2i},..., kp{Ki}\} within a Euclidean distance radius R. 2. Encode Geometric Differences: For each neighborhood point kpj (with coordinate cj) relative to the sampling point pi (with coordinate ci), encode the geometric differences kgi using an MLP: kgi = \text{MLP}(ci \oplus cj \oplus (ci - cj) \oplus d(ci, cj)) where \oplus is concatenation, d(\cdot, \cdot) is Euclidean distance, and ci, cj are coordinates. 3. Compute Local Geometric Features: Obtain the local geometric feature fi by weighted summation of the neighborhood points' encoded differences: fi = \text{SUM}(\text{softmax}(\text{MLP}(kgi)) \odot kgi) where \text{softmax} is performed on each dimension, \odot is the Hadamard product, and \text{SUM} aggregates the weighted features. 4. Regress Density and Radiance: Regress volume density \sigma and view-dependent radiance r from the coordinates c, local geometric features f, and ray direction d using the Point-NeRF module: (\sigma, r) = \text{Point-NeRF}(c, d, f). 5. Synthesize Feature: Synthesize the foreground feature by combining the outputs from each neural sampling point along the sampling ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def queryneighbors(pointcloud, querypoint, radius, k): """Query K nearest neighbors within radius R.""" diffs = pointcloud - querypoint dists = np.linalg.norm(diffs, axis=1) mask = dists <= radius validindices = np.where(mask)[0] validdists = dists[validindices] sortedindices = np.argsort(validdists) selectedindices = validindices[sortedindices[:k]] return pointcloud[selectedindices] def encodegeometricdiff(ci, cj): """Encode geometric differences kgi per neighbor.""" diff = ci - cj dist = np.linalg.norm(diff) inputvec = np.concatenate([ci, cj, diff, [dist]]) # MLP is a learnable neural network layer; sources do not specify architecture. # Represented here as a linear projection for syntactic validity. return inputvec @ np.eye(inputvec.shape[0])[:8] def computelocalfeature(neighborcoords, ci): """Compute local geometric feature fi via weighted summation.""" K = neighborcoords.shape[0] kgvectors = [] for j in range(K): cj = neighborcoords[j] kg = encodegeometricdiff(ci, cj) kgvectors.append(kg) kgmatrix = np.array(kgvectors) # Shape (K, Dkg) # Apply MLP to kgi mlpoutput = kgmatrix @ np.eye(kgmatrix.shape[1])[:kgmatrix.shape[1]] # Softmax on each dimension (across neighbors, axis=0) expvals = np.exp(mlpoutput - np.max(mlpoutput, axis=0, keepdims=True)) weights = expvals / np.sum(expvals, axis=0, keepdims=True) # Hadamard product and Sum weightedkg = weights kgmatrix fi = np.sum(weightedkg, axis=0) return fi def pointnerfrender(c, d, f): """Regress density and radiance.""" inputvec = np.concatenate([c, d, f]) # MLP is a learnable neural network layer; sources do not specify architecture. out = inputvec @ np.eye(inputvec.shape[0])[:2] sigma = np.exp(out[0]) r = out[1:] return sigma, r def renderforeground(pointcloud, rays, K=8, R=1.0): """Main rendering function.""" renderedfeatures = [] for origin, direction in rays: # Sampling strategy along ray is not detailed in sources. tvals = np.linspace(0, 10, 10) pilist = origin + tvals[:, None] direction rayfeatures = [] for pi in pilist: neighbors = queryneighbors(pointcloud, pi, R, K) fi = computelocalfeature(neighbors, pi) sigma, r = pointnerfrender(pi, direction, fi) rayfeatures.append((sigma, r)) renderedfeatures.append(rayfeatures) return renderedfeatures Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sampling points, the number of neighbors K, and the cost of the MLPs. Querying neighbors requires distance calculations. Memory Complexity: Stores the point cloud coordinates and the MLP parameters. Performance: Trained on 4 A100 GPUs for around one day in the first stage, and 20 hours on a single A100 GPU in the second stage. Strengths: Preserves detail from dense surface points; handles foreground effectively. Limitations: Point clouds cannot handle unbounded backgrounds, requiring a separate background module (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360). This method is part of a point diffusion implicit function for large-scale scene neural representation. It builds on Point-NeRF and Mip-NeRF 360. The specific adaptation addresses the lack of color information in point clouds generated by a point super-resolution diffusion module.
