name: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis (SLS4D)
body: SLS4D is a method for 4D novel-view synthesis that represents dynamic radiance fields using a learnable sparse latent space, reducing network parameters compared to dense grid discretizations while maintaining high-frequency detail via attention-based interpolation. It differs from dense grid methods (like TiNeuVox) by avoiding the O(N^3TF) space complexity of 4D grids, and from per-image latent code methods by offering better generalization across time through continuous temporal interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z), time t, and view direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma for volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Sparse Latent Space (Vs): A set of learnable global features Vs = \{f1, f2,..., fB\} \in \mathbb{R}^{F \times B}, where B is the number of feature vectors and F is the feature dimension. 2. Latent Time Slots (H): A set of learnable time-dependent features H = \{h0, h1,..., h{T-1}\}, where T is the number of time slots. 3. Deformation MLP (\Phid): A 7-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron. 4. Interpolator Decoder: A 4-layer MLP mapping to dimension 512, with GeGLU activation in the second layer. 5. Color/Decoding MLPs: A 1-layer MLP for color and a 3-layer MLP for density. Numbered Steps: 1. Temporal Interpolation: For a given timestamp t, obtain the corresponding time-dependent high-frequency feature ht by linearly interpolating between the nearest learnable latent time slots \{hi\}{i=0}^{T-1}. 2. Deformation Prediction: Encode input coordinates (x, y, z, t) into a higher dimension. Concatenate the encoded coordinates with the interpolated time feature ht. Decode the concatenated features using the Deformation MLP (\Phid) with a \tanh activation function to compress deformations to the range [-1, 1]. Compute the deformation displacement (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) = \Phid(x, y, z, t). 3. Feature Query via Attention: Compute the query vector q(\mathbf{p}) using a frequency encoder: q(\mathbf{p}) = \phiq((\sin(2^0 \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^0 \mathbf{p}),..., \sin(2^{L-1} \mathbf{p}), \cos(2^{L-1} \mathbf{p}))) where L is the max frequency and \phiq is a linear projection. Pass q(\mathbf{p}) through a small projection matrix to transform from coordinate frequency space to dot-product space. Compute the feature f\mathbf{p} for the 3D position \mathbf{p} using multi-head attention: f\mathbf{p} = \frac{E(Q(\mathbf{p})^T K(Vs)) V(Vs)}{\sqrt{d}} where Q, K, V are query, key, and value projections; d is the feature dimension; E(\cdot) is the softmax function; and Vs represents the key/value pairs from the sparse latent space. 4. Radiance Field Decoding: Pass the interpolated feature f\mathbf{p} through the Interpolator Decoder (4-layer MLP with GeGLU in the second layer). Feed the output into separate small MLPs to decode color \mathbf{c} (1-layer) and density \sigma (3-layer). Feed viewpoint information \mathbf{d} into the decoding MLPs. The final radiance field query is: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = \Phic(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y, z + \Delta z, \mathbf{d}) where (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) is the displacement computed in Step 2. Formulas: GeGLU Activation: \text{GeGLU}(x, W, V, b, c) = \text{GELU}(xW + b) \otimes (xV + c) where \text{GELU}(x) = x \cdot [1 + \text{erf}(x/\sqrt{2})] and \text{erf} is the error function. Temporal Continuity Loss (TV Loss): Lt = \sum{i=0}^{T-1} ||h{i+1} - hi|| This ensures temporal continuity over time for latent time slots. Learning Rate Schedule: F{sc}(s) = \begin{cases} \frac{s}{Nw} & \text{if } s \le Nw \\ \exp\left(\frac{s-Nw}{Nm}\right) \cdot \left(1 + \cos\left(\pi \frac{s-Nw}{Nm}\right)\right) & \text{if } s > Nw \end{cases} where s is the current step, Nw is the warm-up step, and Nm is the max step. Optimization Loss: L = wc \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} ||C(r) - \hat{C}(r)||^22 + wt Lt where C(r) is ground truth color, \hat{C}(r) is predicted color, and R is the set of rays. Parameters (Typical Values): B (number of latent features): 256 for D-NeRF, 512 for HyperNeRF. F (feature vector dimension): 64. T (time slots size): 256 for D-NeRF, 512 for HyperNeRF. Transformer heads: 8 heads with context dimension 32. Learning rate: 0.0001 for feature space, interpolation transformer, and first three MLP layers; 0.001 for subsequent MLP layers. Training iterations (Nm): 30,000. Warm-up steps (Nw): 2,000. Loss weights: wc = 1, wt = 0.0001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dense grids neglect the sparsity of 3D radiance fields and have extremely high parameter counts for 4D space. Standard bilinear/trilinear interpolation cannot simultaneously focus on low-frequency and high-frequency information when used with frequency encoders. The method employs a strategy similar to the “empty grid” approach in HexPlane to focus training on specific parts of the target object. Time and Memory Complexity: The space complexity of dense 4D grids is O(N^3TF), whereas the sparse latent space reduces parameters significantly since B \ll N^2. Measured Performance: On the D-NeRF dataset, SLS4D achieves a PSNR of 32.67, SSIM of 0.963, and LPIPS of 0.034, outperforming methods like D-NeRF, TiNeuVox, and HexPlane. Hardware: Experiments were conducted on an Nvidia 4090 server. Strengths: Reduces parameter count significantly compared to dense grids and Tensor4D; more generalizable than per-image latent codes; handles high-frequency dynamic information effectively. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Suitable for 4D novel-view synthesis on synthetic (D-NeRF) and real-world (HyperNeRF) datasets where high fidelity and parameter efficiency are required. SLS4D was introduced in the paper "SLS4D: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis". It builds on the concept of implicit radiance fields and deformation fields (as in D-NeRF) but addresses the limitations of dense grid discretizations and standard interpolation methods by introducing a sparse latent space with attention-based feature interpolation. SLS4D: Sparse Latent Space for 4D Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2024.3429421, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Neural Feature Fusion Fields (N3F)
head: Neural Distillation of Self-Supervised 2D Image Representations
body: Neural Feature Fusion Fields (N3F) is a method that distills dense 2D image features from a pre-trained teacher network into a 3D neural field (student) via differentiable volumetric rendering, enabling 3D-aware feature representation. Unlike Semantic NeRF or Panoptic NeRF which fuse discrete semantic labels, N3F fuses continuous dense feature vectors, allowing for open-world applications without manual labels. It differs from standard feature distillation because the student operates in 3D world space (ensuring spatial consistency) while the teacher operates in 2D image space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images It \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times H \times W} defined on lattice \Omega = \{1, \dots, H\} \times \{1, \dots, W\} for t=1 \dots T, with known camera parameters. A pre-trained 2D feature extractor (teacher) \Phi. Outputs: A 3D neural feature field defined by occupancy \sigma: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^+ and a color/feature function c: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^{3+C}, where C is the number of feature channels. The rendered outputs are color images \hat{I}t and feature images \hat{\Phi}t \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}. Data Structures: The student network implements the pair (\sigma, c). The function c is decomposed into c = (c{rgb}, c{\Phi}), where c{rgb} outputs 3 color values and c{\Phi} outputs C feature values. For dynamic scenes (e.g., using NeuralDiff), the architecture decomposes the scene into static, dynamic (time-dependent), and actor (camera-anchored) fields, each with its own feature prediction head (MLP followed by tanh). Preprocessing: 1. Teacher features \Phi(It) are pre-computed using public weights (e.g., DINO, MoCo-v3, DeiT). 2. Features are L2-normalized and reduced to 64 dimensions via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) before distillation. 3. For NeuralDiff experiments, images are down-sampled to 480 \times 270 pixels and 2D features are up-sampled to match using nearest-neighbor interpolation. Numbered Steps: 1. Teacher Forward Pass: Compute 2D feature maps \Phi(It) for each input image It using the frozen teacher network \Phi. Apply stop-gradient (sg) to prevent teacher updates. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel u in image It, cast a ray r through the scene. Sample points X{tu}(r) along the ray. 3. Student Forward Pass: Query the student network for each point X to obtain occupancy \sigma(X) and the concatenated vector (c{rgb}(X), c{\Phi}(X)). 4. Volumetric Rendering: Compute the rendered feature vector \hat{\Phi}t^u for pixel u by accumulating feature outputs weighted by density and transmittance, analogous to color accumulation: \hat{\Phi}t^u = \sum{i=1}^{N} c{\Phi}(X{tu}(ri)) \alphai where \alphai is the weight derived from density \sigma and transmittance Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(X{tu}(rj)) \deltaj}. 5. Loss Computation: Calculate the total training loss \mathcal{L} as the sum of image reconstruction loss and feature reconstruction loss: \mathcal{L} = \sumt \| \hat{I}t - It \|2^2 + \lambda \| \hat{\Phi}t - \Phi(It) \|2^2 where \lambda is the feature distillation loss weight. 6. Optimization: Update student parameters using Adam optimizer with cosine annealing schedule. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class NeuralField: """Student network implementing (sigma, c) where c = (crgb, cphi).""" def init(self, featuredim=64): # For vanilla NeRF baseline: single linear layer with tanh # For NeuralDiff: MLPs followed by tanh per component self.featuredim = featuredim def forward(self, points, directions): # points: (B, N, 3), directions: (B, N, 3) # In practice, implemented as a neural network (MLP/Linear) # Output shape: (B, N, 3 + featuredim) out = self.network(points, directions) sigma = math.relu(out[...,:1]) # Occupancy must be positive rgbfeatures = out[..., 1:] return sigma, rgbfeatures def volumerender(points, directions, sigma, rgbfeatures, tnear, tfar, numsamples): """Standard differentiable volume rendering for color and features.""" # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples) tsamples = tnear + tvals (tfar - tnear) # Compute deltas between samples deltas = tsamples[1:] - tsamples[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10])]) # Compute alpha (opacity) and transmittance alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-alpha), dim=1) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), 1.0 - transmittance[:,:-1]], dim=1) # Compute weights weights = alpha transmittance # Split output color = rgbfeatures[...,:3] features = rgbfeatures[..., 3:] # Render color and features renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1) renderedfeatures = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) features, dim=1) return renderedcolor, renderedfeatures, sigma def computeloss(renderedcolor, renderedfeatures, targetimage, targetfeatures, lambdafeat): """Compute total training loss.""" colorloss = torch.mseloss(renderedcolor, targetimage) featureloss = torch.mseloss(renderedfeatures, targetfeatures) totalloss = colorloss + lambdafeat featureloss return totalloss Parameters: \lambda: Weight for feature reconstruction loss. Typical values: 0.001 for NeRF/LLFF experiments; 1.0 for NeuralDiff/EPIC-KITCHENS experiments. C: Number of feature channels. Depends on teacher (e.g., reduced to 64 via PCA). Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4} with cosine annealing. Batch Size: 1024. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Teacher Freezing: The teacher network weights must be frozen (stop gradient) during student training. Feature Normalization: Features should be L2-normalized and PCA-reduced before distillation to stabilize training. Dynamic Scenes: For egocentric videos, standard NeRF is insufficient; NeuralDiff architecture is required to handle static, dynamic foreground, and actor components. Finds occurrences of an object across views using feature similarity. Uses mean feature descriptor of a query region Rt and matches against rendered features \hat{\Phi}t using threshold \tau. Localizes objects in 3D space by querying the student field for points X where feature similarity to a query descriptor is high and density \sigma(X) exceeds threshold \tau\sigma. Removes objects by setting occupancy \sigma(X)=0 for 3D points matching the object's feature descriptor. Renders features through occluders by disabling occupancy \sigma for regions dissimilar to the query descriptor, revealing the full extent of occluded objects. Time Complexity: Training time depends on the base neural rendering architecture. For NeuralDiff on EPIC-KITCHENS, single scene training takes ~24 hours for RGB reconstruction and ~2 hours for feature distillation (20 epochs, 500 iterations). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 3D neural field parameters and pre-computed 2D teacher features for all views. Performance: N3F consistently improves over 2D self-supervised baselines. On LLFF dataset, N3F with DINO [ViT-B/8] achieved mAP 76.26 vs teacher 64.35 (+11.91); with DINO [ViT-B/16] 78.84 vs 60.15 (+18.69); with MoCo-v3 76.15 vs 57.51 (+18.64); with DeiT 74.53 vs 47.51 (+26.82). Strengths: Enables 3D-aware feature representation, viewpoint independence, and occlusion awareness. Improves generalization compared to 2D teachers. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of teacher features. Performance depends on the quality of the 2D teacher network (SSL models generalize better than supervised ones like DeiT). N3F was introduced in the paper "Neural Feature Fusion Fields: 3D Distillation of Self-Supervised 2D Image Representations". It builds on the student-teacher distillation paradigm (Hinton et al.) but applies it to 3D neural fields via differentiable rendering. It is evaluated on static scenes (LLFF dataset with vanilla NeRF) and egocentric videos (EPIC-KITCHENS dataset with NeuralDiff). Neural Feature Fusion Fields: 3D Distillation of Self-Supervised 2D Image Representations, https://doi.org/10.1109/3DV57658.2022.00056, fetched 2026-10-30

name: CLNeRF Architecture with Embeddings
head: Appearance and Geometry Embeddings, Compact Continual NeRF
body: CLNeRF is a model architecture modification for NeRF that enables continual learning by incorporating scene changes (appearance and geometry) over time within a single model, preventing model size growth as new scans are added. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like MIMO-DONeRF and SLS4D by using explicit, trainable per-scan embedding vectors rather than latent space compression or multi-instance networks, allowing for efficient updates and low overhead for generative replay. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A spatial location \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a time step index t identifying the current scan in a continual sequence. Output: Color c and volume density (opacity) \sigma. Data Structures: Feature Vector \mathbf{f}: The encoded representation of spatial location \mathbf{x}. For NGP backbone: \mathbf{f} is produced by a grid-based hash encoder. For Vanilla NeRF backbone: \mathbf{f} is produced by an MLP. Appearance Embedding ea: A trainable vector encoding appearance changes (e.g., lighting, weather). Dimension: 48. Layout: A single vector per time step t. Geometry Embedding eg: A trainable vector encoding geometry changes (e.g., new objects, construction). Dimension: 16. Layout: A single vector per time step t. Decoders: Dc: Color decoder (MLP). D\sigma: Opacity decoder (MLP). Numbered Steps: 1. Encode Spatial Location: Given a spatial location \mathbf{x}, encode it into a feature vector \mathbf{f}. If using NGP, use the grid-based hash encoder; if using vanilla NeRF, use an MLP. 2. Compute Color: Decode color c using the color decoder Dc. The inputs are the feature vector \mathbf{f}, the viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the trainable appearance embedding ea corresponding to the current time step t. c = Dc(\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{d}, ea) 3. Compute Opacity: Decode opacity \sigma using the opacity decoder D\sigma. The inputs are the feature vector \mathbf{f} and the trainable geometry embedding eg corresponding to the current time step t. \sigma = D\sigma(\mathbf{f}, eg) 4. Embedding Assignment: For each new time step t (scan) in the continual learning sequence, add one new appearance embedding ea and one new geometry embedding eg to the model. These embeddings are distinct per time step. Parameters: Appearance embedding dimension: 48. Geometry embedding dimension: 16. Pitfalls: Transient Objects: The architecture does not automatically filter transient objects (e.g., moving pedestrians) within a single scan. Using a transient MLP with NGP causes the non-transient network to overfit to transient objects and fail to filter them. Transient objects must be filtered using segmentation masks. Backbone Choice: Using vanilla NeRF as the backbone results in worse performance and efficiency compared to NGP for CLNeRF, particularly regarding model updates and generative replay overhead. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class CLNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, usengp=True, appearancedim=48, geometrydim=16): super().init() self.usengp = usengp self.appearancedim = appearancedim self.geometrydim = geometrydim # Encoders if usengp: # NGP grid-based hash encoder implementation not provided in sources self.spatialencoder = lambda x: x # Placeholder for hash encoding else: # Vanilla NeRF MLP encoder (exact architecture not specified) self.spatialencoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256)) # Decoders # Color decoder takes f, d, ea self.colordecoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256 + 3 + appearancedim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3) # RGB) # Opacity decoder takes f, eg self.opacitydecoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256 + geometrydim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1) # Sigma) # Embeddings are stored in lists, one per time step self.appearanceembeddings = [] self.geometryembeddings = [] def addtimestep(self): """Add new embeddings for a new scan/time step t.""" ea = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, self.appearancedim)) eg = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, self.geometrydim)) self.appearanceembeddings.append(ea) self.geometryembeddings.append(eg) def forward(self, x, d, t): """ x: (N, 3) spatial coordinates d: (N, 3) viewing directions t: int, current time step index """ # 1. Encode spatial location f = self.spatialencoder(x) # (N, 256) # 2. Get embeddings for time step t ea = self.appearanceembeddings[t] # (1, 48) eg = self.geometryembeddings[t] # (1, 16) # Expand for batch ea = ea.expand(x.size(0), -1) eg = eg.expand(x.size(0), -1) # 3. Compute Color # Concatenate f, d, ea colorinput = torch.cat([f, d, ea], dim=-1) c = self.colordecoder(colorinput) # (N, 3) # 4. Compute Opacity # Concatenate f, eg opacityinput = torch.cat([f, eg], dim=-1) sigma = self.opacitydecoder(opacityinput) # (N, 1) return c, sigma Not given in the sources. [16217-mimo-donerf.md] Not given in the sources. [18112-sparse-latent-space-for-4d-novel-view-synthesis-sls4d.md] Not given in the sources. [18114-neural-feature-fusion-fields-n3f.md] Time and Memory Complexity: The model size increases linearly with the number of time steps t, but the increase is minimal due to the small embedding dimensions (48 and 16). Measured Performance: Using NGP as the backbone provides better performance and efficiency compared to vanilla NeRF for CLNeRF, enabling efficient model updates and low overhead for generative replay. Strengths: Compact model size, efficient updates, handles appearance and geometry changes separately. Limitations: Requires segmentation masks for transient object filtering; not compatible with transient MLPs for automatic filtering. When to use: When continual learning of a scene with appearance and geometry changes is required, and model size must remain compact. When not to use: When transient objects within a single scan are present and segmentation masks are unavailable. CLNeRF was introduced in the paper "CLNeRF: Continual Learning Meets NeRF". It addresses the challenge of continual learning in NeRFs, where the model must adapt to new scans without forgetting previous ones or growing indefinitely in size. The method builds on the Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (NGP) architecture. CLNeRF: Continual Learning Meets NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.02119, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mutual Information Gradient Shaping
head: J-NeRF, MI-shaping NeRF, NeRF shaping with mutual information gradients, mutual information shaped NeRF
body: Mutual Information Gradient Shaping (MIGS), implemented as JacobiNeRF, is a training regularization technique that shapes the tangent space of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to encode semantic correlations between scene entities. Unlike first-order approaches that distill 2D features into 3D radiance channels or treat labels as separate output channels, MIGS aligns the Jacobians of correlated entities to maximize their mutual information under random weight perturbations, enabling efficient sparse label propagation and semantic consensus. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A standard NeRF model \Phi parameterized by weights \theta \in \mathbb{R}^D; a set of labeled source pixels/points S = \{s1, \dots, sK\} with semantic labels; unlabeled target pixels/points T = \{t1, \dots, tM\}; camera parameters for rendering. Outputs: A trained NeRF \Phi where the Jacobian of rendered values with respect to weights encodes semantic similarity; propagated semantic labels for target entities. Data Structures NeRF Weights (\theta): Vector of size D. Jacobian (\partial \Phi): Gradient vector of size D, representing \frac{\partial I(p)}{\partial \theta} for a pixel or 3D point p. Perturbation (n): Vector of size D, sampled from a uniform distribution on the unit sphere S^{D-1}. Method Steps 1. Compute Jacobians: For each labeled source pixel sk and target pixel ti, compute the Jacobian of the rendered value with respect to the NeRF weights \theta at the current training state. Let \partial \Phi^{J,sk} and \partial \Phi^{J,ti} denote these gradients. 2. MI-Shaping Loss Calculation: Align the Jacobians of correlated entities using contrastive learning. The Mutual Information (MI) between two entities is approximated by the cosine similarity of their Jacobians. Define the MI approximation: I(I(pi), I(pj)) = \log\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \cos^2 \alpha}}\right) + \text{const} where \alpha is the angle between Jacobians \partial \Phii and \partial \Phij, and MI(p, q) \propto \cos(\partial \Phip, \partial \Phiq). Construct positive pairs (entities known to be correlated, e.g., same semantic class) and negative pairs (different classes) using general-purpose self-supervised features (e.g., DINO). Compute the MI-Shaping Loss (L{MIG}) using an InfoNCE formulation: L{MIG} = -\log \frac{\exp(\|\cos(\partial \Phii, \partial \Phi{i+})\|/\tau)}{\sum{j \in \{i^+\} \cup \{i^-\}} \exp(\|\cos(\partial \Phii, \partial \Phij)\|/\tau)} where \tau is a temperature parameter, i+ denotes positive pairs, and i- denotes negative pairs. 3. Gradient Normalization: Apply a regularization term to compact gradients onto a unit sphere, which improves training efficiency and facilitates label propagation: L{norm} = \gamma (1.0 - \|\partial \Phii\|)^2 where \gamma is a weighting factor. 4. Total Loss: Combine the standard photometric reconstruction loss (L{NeRF}) with the shaping terms: L{TM} = L{NeRF} + \lambda L{MIG} + \gamma(1.0 - \|\partial \Phii\|)^2 where \lambda controls the strength of the mutual information shaping. 5. Label Propagation (Inference/Post-Training): For a target pixel ti, select the best source pixel k^ based on Jacobian alignment: k^ = \arg\maxk \frac{\|\partial \Phi^{J,sk} \cdot \partial \Phi^{J,ti}\|}{\|\partial \Phi^{J,sk}\| \|\partial \Phi^{J,ti}\|}. Alternatively, propagate labels via perturbation response: Perturb weights: \theta' = \theta + \sigma n, where n \sim \text{Uniform}(S^{D-1}). Render perturbed image Ik using weights perturbed along the gradient of source pixel k (i.e., \theta + \sigma \partial \Phi^{J,sk}). Compute response: Rk(ti) = |Ik(ti) - I(ti)|. Assign label: l{ti} = \arg\maxk Rk(ti), treating Rk as logits for K-way classification. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def mseloss(pred, target): return torch.mean((pred - target) 2) def computejacobian(nerfmodel, rayorigins, raydirections, weights): predvalues = nerfmodel(rayorigins, raydirections) grad = torch.autograd.grad(predvalues.mean(), weights, creategraph=True)[0] return grad def cosinesimilarity(vec1, vec2): dot = torch.dot(vec1, vec2) norm1 = torch.norm(vec1) norm2 = torch.norm(vec2) if norm1 == 0 or norm2 == 0: return torch.tensor(0.0) return dot / (norm1 norm2) def trainjacobinerf(nerfmodel, rays, gtimages, labeledsources, unlabeledtargets, lambdami, gammanorm, tau, optimizer, numepochs): weights = nerfmodel.parameters() for epoch in range(numepochs): optimizer.zerograd() predimages = nerfmodel(rays.origins, rays.directions) lnerf = mseloss(predimages, gtimages) jacobianss = {} for s in labeledsources: jacobianss[s.id] = computejacobian(nerfmodel, s.origins, s.directions, weights) jacobianst = {} for t in unlabeledtargets: jacobianst[t.id] = computejacobian(nerfmodel, t.origins, t.directions, weights) lmig = torch.tensor(0.0) count = 0 for t in unlabeledtargets: for spos in labeledsources: cospos = cosinesimilarity(jacobianss[spos.id], jacobianst[t.id]) exppos = torch.exp(torch.abs(cospos) / tau) sumexp = exppos for sneg in labeledsources: if sneg.id != spos.id: cosneg = cosinesimilarity(jacobianss[sneg.id], jacobianst[t.id]) sumexp += torch.exp(torch.abs(cosneg) / tau) lmig -= torch.log(exppos / sumexp) count += 1 if count > 0: lmig /= count lnorm = torch.tensor(0.0) for t in unlabeledtargets: normt = torch.norm(jacobianst[t.id]) lnorm += (1.0 - normt) 2 lnorm /= len(unlabeledtargets) totalloss = lnerf + lambdami lmig + gammanorm lnorm totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() def propagatelabels(nerfmodel, rays, labeledsources, targetpixels, sigma): propagatedlabels = {} perturbedmodels = {} for s in labeledsources: grads = computejacobian(nerfmodel, s.origins, s.directions, nerfmodel.parameters()) perturbedmodel = nerfmodel.clone() with torch.nograd(): perturbedmodel.parameters().add(sigma grads) perturbedmodels[s.id] = perturbedmodel for t in targetpixels: responses = [] for s in labeledsources: predperturbed = perturbedmodelss.id predoriginal = nerfmodel(t.origins, t.directions) rk = torch.abs(predperturbed - predoriginal) responses.append(rk) bestidx = torch.argmax(torch.stack(responses)) bestsource = labeledsources[bestidx] propagatedlabels[t.id] = bestsource.label return propagatedlabels Parameters \lambda (lambda): Weight for L{MIG}. Not given in the sources. \gamma (gamma): Weight for gradient normalization. Not given in the sources. \tau (tau): Temperature parameter for InfoNCE loss. Not given in the sources. \sigma: Scale for weight perturbation. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Normalization: The term \gamma(1.0 - \|\partial \Phii\|)^2 improves training efficiency and facilitates label propagation by compacting gradients onto a unit sphere. Propagates labels in the 2D image domain by computing perturbation differences after volume rendering. Suitable for pixel-wise semantic segmentation. Propagates labels in 3D space by estimating perturbation differences for 3D points along rays before volume rendering. Suitable for instance segmentation and 3D entity selection. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables efficient label propagation from extremely sparse annotations; encodes semantic consensus in the tangent space rather than output channels; supports view-invariant propagation. Limitations: Requires computing second-order Jacobian information, which is more expensive than first-order methods. When to use: Sparse label propagation for semantic/instance segmentation; entity selection by clicking a single point; appearance edit propagation. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and only photometric reconstruction is needed; when dense annotations are available and first-order methods suffice. Mutual Information Gradient Shaping was introduced by Xiaomeng Xu, Yanchao Yang, Kaichun Mo, Boxiao Pan, Li Yi, and Leonidas Guibas in "JacobiNeRF: NeRF Shaping with Mutual Information Gradients" (arXiv:2304.00341v1, April 2023). The method addresses the limitation of traditional NeRFs that only capture appearance by explicitly regularizing learning dynamics to align Jacobians of correlated entities, thereby encoding mutual information in the NeRF tangent space. It is used for sparse label propagation, entity selection, and scene modifications. JacobiNeRF: NeRF Shaping with Mutual Information Gradients, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01583, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Multi-Level Neural Scene Graph
head: NSG
body: Multi-Level Neural Scene Graph (NSG) is a scene representation that decomposes an environment into a graph of static, dynamic, and temporal nodes to model urban environments with moving objects and appearance variations. It distinguishes itself from sibling architectures by explicitly separating the radiance field into a static component \phi and a dynamic component \psi, conditioned on sequence-level and object-level latent vectors respectively, enabling the disentanglement of scene-dependent appearance from object texture. Inputs: A set of training rays \mathcal{R}, where each ray is defined by (r, t, s): ray parameters, time t, and sequence s. Ground truth colors \hat{C}(r, t, s) and depths \hat{D}(r, t, s). LiDAR point clouds and ego-vehicle poses P for space contraction bounds. Initial ego-vehicle poses P{ts} \in SE(3) and object poses \xi{ot} \in SE(3). Outputs: Rendered color C(r, t, s) and expected depth D(r, t, s) for each ray. Optimized radiance field parameters \theta, including MLP weights, latent vectors, and pose residuals. Scene Graph G = (V, E): Nodes V: Root node vr: Defines the global coordinate system. Camera nodes \{vc\}{c \in C}: Associated with camera calibration. Sequence nodes \{v{st}\}{s \in S, t \in Ts}: Associated with latent vector \omega{st}. Dynamic object nodes \{vo\}{o \in Os}: Associated with latent vector \omegao. Edges E: Oriented rigid transformations between coordinate frames. e{v{st} vr} = P{ts}: Transformation from global frame to sequence frame (ego-vehicle pose). e{vc v{st}} = Tc: Transformation from ego-vehicle frame to camera frame (fixed calibration). e{vo v{st}} = \xi{ot}: Transformation from sequence frame to object local frame. Bounding Boxes: Each dynamic object node vo has an associated 3D bounding box b{to} in its local coordinate frame. Latent Vectors: \omega{st} = [As F(t), Gs F(t)]: Sequence-level latent vector. As: Appearance matrix for sequence s. Gs: Transient geometry matrix for sequence s. F(\cdot): 1D basis function of sines and cosines with linearly increasing frequencies at log-scale. \omegao: Object-level latent vector conditioning the dynamic field. Coordinate System Contraction: Unbounded scene space is contracted into a unit cube. Bounds are computed from LiDAR point clouds and ego-vehicle poses P. Any 3D position x is normalized to this unit cube before processing. 1. For a given ray (r, t, s), traverse the graph to identify relevant dynamic object nodes vo present in sequence s at time t. 2. Retrieve the 3D bounding box b{to} for each dynamic object node. 3. Compute the ray origin o and direction d in the global coordinate system: o = R{ts} tc + t{ts} d = R{ts} Rc Kc^{-1} (px, py, 1)^T where R{ts}, t{ts} are the rotation and translation from P{ts}, Rc, tc are from Tc, and Kc is the camera intrinsic matrix. 4. For each dynamic object node, transform the ray into the object's local coordinate frame using the edge transformation \xi{ot} and the sequence pose P{ts}: x{local} = (P{ts} \xi{ot})^{-1} I3 \frac{1}{\max(so)} x{global} where \max(so) is the maximum object size used for normalization. 5. Compute the entry u{in} and exit u{out} points of the ray intersecting the local bounding box b{to}. Evaluate the static field \phi and dynamic field \psi at sampling location r(u) along the ray. Static Field \phi(x, d, \omega{st}): 1. Compute multi-scale 3D hash grid features: fx = H3(x). 2. Compute density feature and density: (h{\sigma\phi}, \sigma\phi) = \text{MLP}{\sigma\phi}(fx). 3. Compute color: c\phi = \text{MLP}{c\phi}(h{\sigma\phi}, \gamma{SH}(d), As F(t)). \gamma{SH}(\cdot) is spherical harmonics encoding. 4. Compute transient geometry feature and color: (\sigmaG, cG) = \text{MLP}G(h{\sigma\phi}, Gs F(t)). 5. Combine static and transient outputs to get final \phi color and density (mixture analogous to Eq. 12 in source). Dynamic Field \psi(x, d, \omega{st}, \omegao): 1. Transform position x and direction d to local object coordinates (as in Step 1.4). 2. Compute density feature and density: (h{\sigma\psi}, \sigma\psi) = \text{MLP}{\sigma\psi}(\gamma{PE}(x), \omegao). \gamma{PE}(\cdot) is positional encoding. 3. Compute color: c\psi = \text{MLP}{c\psi}(h{\sigma\psi}, \gamma{PE}(d), \omegao, \omega{st}). Composite Rendering: 1. If the sampling location r(u) is not within the interval [u{in}, u{out}] of any dynamic node's bounding box, set \sigma\psi = 0 and c\psi = 0. 2. Compute composite density and color: \sigma = \sigma\phi + \sigma\psi c = \frac{\sigma\phi}{\sigma\phi + \sigma\psi} c\phi + \frac{\sigma\psi}{\sigma\phi + \sigma\psi} c\psi 1. Proposal Density: Distill the static density \sigma\phi into a proposal density \sigma{prop}(r(u), \omega{st}). 2. Sampling Strategy: Use two iterations of ray sampling. Iteration 1 (Uniform): Sample uniformly along the ray. Iteration 2 (Inverse Transform): Sample based on the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) F(u) = 1 - U(u), where U(u) = \exp\left(-\int{u{in}}^u \sigma(u') du'\right). 3. Joint Sampling: Sample jointly from \sigma{prop} and \sigma\psi. Constrain sampling from \sigma\psi to the interval [u{in}, u{out}] of the relevant dynamic nodes. 1. Optimize pose residuals \delta P{ts} \in \mathfrak{se}(3) for ego-vehicle poses and \delta \xi{ot} \in \mathfrak{se}(2) for object poses. 2. Update ego-vehicle pose: \hat{P}{ts} = \text{expmap}(\delta P{ts}) P{ts}. 3. Update object pose: \hat{\xi}{ot} = \text{expmap}(\delta \xi{ot}){SE(2) \to SE(3)} \xi{ot}. Object pose residuals are constrained to \mathfrak{se}(2) (ground plane motion) and mapped to SE(3). 4. Keep camera extrinsics Tc fixed. Total loss \mathcal{L} is the sum of: \mathcal{L} = \sum{(r,t,s) \in \mathcal{R}} \left( \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda{dist} \mathcal{L}{dist} + \lambda{prop} \mathcal{L}{prop} + \lambda{dep} \mathcal{L}{dep} + \lambda{entr} \mathcal{L}{entr} \right) Photometric Loss: \mathcal{L}{rgb}(r, t, s) = \| C(r, t, s) - \hat{C}(r, t, s) \|2^2. Expected Depth Loss: \mathcal{L}{dep}(r, t, s) = \| D(r, t, s) - \hat{D}(r, t, s) \|2^2, where \hat{D}(r, t, s) = \int{u{n}}^{u{f}} u U(u) \sigma(r(u), t, s) du. Entropy Regularization: Encourages separation between \phi and \psi densities within bounding boxes: \mathcal{L}{entr}(r, t, s) = \int{u{n}}^{u{f}} H\left( \frac{\sigma\psi(r(u), t, s)}{\sigma\phi(r(u), s) + \sigma\psi(r(u), t, s)} \right) du where H(\cdot) is Shannon entropy. Distillation/Proposal Loss: \mathcal{L}{dist} and \mathcal{L}{prop} follow the method in [2] (Instant-NGP/NeRF), supervising \sigma{prop} with \sigma\phi. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computebasisfunction(t, numfrequencies=10): """1D basis function of sines and cosines with linearly increasing frequencies at log-scale.""" frequencies = np.logspace(0, np.log10(2numfrequencies), numfrequencies) texpanded = t[:, np.newaxis] frequencies[np.newaxis,:] return np.concatenate([np.sin(texpanded), np.cos(texpanded)], axis=1) def contractspace(x, bounds): """Contract unbounded scene space into a unit cube using LiDAR/ego-vehicle bounds.""" xcenter = (bounds.min + bounds.max) / 2 xscale = (bounds.max - bounds.min) / 2 return (x - xcenter) / xscale def sphericalharmonicsencoding(d, degree=3): """Standard NeRF spherical harmonics encoding.""" # Degree 3 yields 16 coefficients x, y, z = d[:, 0], d[:, 1], d[:, 2] c0 = np.fulllike(x, 0.282095) c1 = 0.488603 y c2 = 1.092548 x y c3 = 0.488603 z c4 = 0.315392 (3 z2 - 1) c5 = -1.092548 x z c6 = 0.546274 (x2 - y2) c7 = -1.092548 y z c8 = 0.946175 x z2 c9 = -0.590044 y (3 x2 - y2) c10 = 2.890611 x y z c11 = -0.459894 y (4 z2 - 6) c12 = 0.373177 (5 z3 - 3 z) c13 = 1.445306 z (4 z2 - 3) c14 = -0.590044 x (x2 - 3 y2) c15 = 0.1092548 x y (x2 - y2) return np.stack([c0, c1, c2, c3, c4, c5, c6, c7, c8, c9, c10, c11, c12, c13, c14, c15], axis=-1) def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" frequencies = 2.0 np.arange(numfrequencies) xexpanded = x[:, np.newaxis,:] frequencies[np.newaxis,:] return np.concatenate([np.sin(xexpanded), np.cos(xexpanded)], axis=-1) def distillstaticdensity(x, d, omegast, hashgrid, mlpsigmaphi): """Proposal density distilled from static density sigmaphi.""" fx = hashgrid.query(x), sigmaphi = mlpsigmaphi(fx) return sigmaphi def compositesample(rayorigin, raydirection, sigmaprop, dynamicnodes, uin, uout, numsamples=64): """Two-pass composite sampling: uniform then inverse transform.""" # Pass 1: Uniform sampling uuniform = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) # Pass 2: Inverse transform sampling based on CDF F(u) = 1 - U(u) # U(u) = exp(-int{uin}^u sigma(u') du') # Simplified implementation for demonstration uinv = np.sort(np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.0, numsamples)) samples = np.concatenate([uuniform, uinv]) return samples def computese3residual(lossgrad): """Compute se(3) residual from loss gradients.""" # Placeholder for gradient-based optimization step return np.zeros(6) def expmapse3(delta): """Exponential map from se(3) to SE(3).""" w = delta[:3] v = delta[3:] theta = np.linalg.norm(w) if theta < 1e-8: R = np.eye(3) t = v else: what = np.array([[0, -w[2], w[1]], [w[2], 0, -w[0]], [-w[1], w[0], 0]]) R = np.eye(3) + np.sin(theta) what + (1 - np.cos(theta)) (what @ what) # V matrix approximation for small theta V = np.eye(3) + (1 - np.cos(theta)) / (theta2) what + (theta - np.sin(theta)) / (theta3) (what @ what) t = V @ v return np.vstack([np.hstack([R, t[:, np.newaxis]]), np.array([0, 0, 0, 1])]) def computese2residual(lossgrad): """Compute se(2) residual from loss gradients.""" return np.zeros(3) def expmapse2tose3(delta): """Map se(2) residual to SE(3) for ground-plane motion.""" # se(2) corresponds to translation in x, y and rotation around z deltase3 = np.zeros(6) deltase3[:2] = delta[:2] # tx, ty deltase3[5] = delta[2] # rz return expmapse3(deltase3) def rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax): """Compute entry (uin) and exit (uout) of ray with AABB.""" tmin = (boxmin - rayorigin) / raydirection tmax = (boxmax - rayorigin) / raydirection tenter = np.maximum(tmin, tmax).min() texit = np.minimum(tmin, tmax).max() if tenter > texit or texit < 0: return None, None return tenter, texit def renderray(rayparams, graph, timet, sequences, hashgrid, models): """Render a single ray using the Multi-Level Neural Scene Graph.""" Pts = graph.getpose(sequences, timet) Tc = graph.cameracalibration oglobal = Pts.R @ Tc.t + Pts.t dcam = rayparams.directionincam dglobal = Pts.R @ Tc.R @ dcam dglobal = dglobal / np.linalg.norm(dglobal) dynamicnodes = graph.getdynamicnodes(sequences, timet) sigmaprop = distillstaticdensity(rayparams, sequences, hashgrid, models['mlpsigmaphi']) # Composite sampling usamples = compositesample(oglobal, dglobal, sigmaprop, dynamicnodes, 0.0, 1.0) sigmatotal = 0.0 colortotal = np.zeros(3) T = 1.0 for u in usamples: xglobal = oglobal + u dglobal xcontracted = contractspace(xglobal, graph.bounds) sigmaphi, cphi = evaluatestaticfield( xcontracted, dglobal, graph.getsequencelatent(sequences, timet), hashgrid, models['mlpsigmaphi'], models['mlpcphi'], models['mlpG']) sigmapsi = 0.0 cpsi = np.zeros(3) for node in dynamicnodes: xiot = graph.getobjectpose(node, timet) # Transform to local object frame: (Pts xiot)^-1 I3 (1/max(so)) localtransform = np.linalg.inv(Pts @ xiot) localx = (localtransform @ np.append(xglobal, 1.0))[:3] / node.maxsize locald = (localtransform[:3,:3] @ dglobal) uin, uout = rayboxintersection(localx, locald, node.boxmin, node.boxmax) if uin is not None and uin <= u <= uout: sigmapsi, cpsi = evaluatedynamicfield( localx, locald, node.latentvector, graph.getsequencelatent(sequences, timet), models['mlpsigmapsi'], models['mlpcpsi']) break # Composite rendering sigma = sigmaphi + sigmapsi if sigma > 1e-8: c = (sigmaphi cphi + sigmapsi cpsi) / sigma else: c = np.zeros(3) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma 0.01) # ustep approximated as constant for uniform sampling colortotal += T alpha c T = (1.0 - alpha) return colortotal def optimizeposeresiduals(graph, lossgradients): """Hierarchical pose optimization.""" deltaPts = computese3residual(lossgradients) Ptsnew = expmapse3(deltaPts) @ graph.getpose('egovehicle') graph.setpose('egovehicle', Ptsnew) for node in graph.dynamicnodes: deltaxiot = computese2residual(lossgradients) xiotnew = expmapse2tose3(deltaxiot) @ graph.getobjectpose(node) graph.setobjectpose(node, xiotnew) Dynamic Node Boundary: When computing composite rendering, \sigma\psi must be set to zero if the sampling location r(u) does not lie within the 3D bounding box of a dynamic node. Coordinate Transformation: The transformation of 3D position x and viewing direction d into the local object coordinate frame uses (P{ts} \xi{ot})^{-1} I3 (1/\max(so)). Pose Constraints: Object pose residuals are constrained to \mathfrak{se}(2) (ground plane motion), assuming objects are upright. Time Normalization: Time t must be normalized to [-1, 1] using the maximum sequence length to ensure the basis function F(t) operates correctly. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Disentangles static and dynamic components, allowing for better generalization across sequences and objects. Handles appearance variations (e.g., auto-exposure) and transient geometry (e.g., tree leaves) via sequence-level latents. Efficient rendering via composite sampling and space contraction. Limitations: Complexity increases with the number of dynamic objects and sequences. When to Use: Suitable for dynamic urban environments with multiple sequences, moving objects, and appearance variations. When Not to Use: Static scenes or scenes with very few dynamic objects may not benefit from the complexity of the graph structure. Origin: Multi-Level Neural Scene Graphs were introduced in "Multi-Level Neural Scene Graphs for Dynamic Urban Environments" (CVPR 2024). Development: The method builds upon previous work in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and dynamic scene representations, incorporating ideas from hash grids, pose optimization, and composite sampling. Usage: Designed for novel view synthesis in dynamic urban environments, leveraging LiDAR and camera data. name: NAN (Noise-Aware NeRFs)
head: IBRNet-based architecture with noise-aware extensions, NAN method
body: NAN is a burst-denoising method that extends the IBRNet architecture to handle degraded noisy images, such as those captured in low-light conditions, by modifying feature extraction, aggregation, and color blending to be noise-aware. Unlike standard NeRFs that synthesize novel views, NAN fixes an existing view image by leveraging multiple noisy inputs of the same scene. Inputs: A burst of N noisy RGB images of the same scene, captured from different viewpoints. Each image is associated with its camera pose. The noise model refers to linear images and includes per-pixel per-color-channel variance estimates. Outputs: A single denoised RGB image corresponding to a target viewpoint, which is typically one of the available input views. Pre-Net Layer: A single convolutional layer at the entry point of the network. Kernel Size: 3 \times 3. Output Channels: 3 (RGB). Activation: None. Initialization: Gaussian per-channel filters. Function: Preserves spatial and channel dimensions; reduces input noise efficiently. Feature Aggregation Input: Pixel feature embedding vectors are expanded by concatenation to include cross-view mean and variance feature vectors for the specific pixel. Additionally, estimated noise variances per-pixel per-color channel are concatenated to the global features. Transformer Module: A standard single 5-head self-attention transformer is added to the feature aggregation stage to capture intricate relations and statistics of cross-view features. Color Blending Weights: Instead of outputting N blending scalars, the network outputs N vectors, each of dimension k^2 \times 3. This represents a per-pixel per-view k \times k spatial kernel of blending weights, with separate weights per color channel. 1. Preprocessing: Linearize input images by applying inverse gamma correction and inverse random white balancing before processing, as the noise model refers to linear images. 2. Pre-Net Processing: Pass the linearized input images through the Pre-Net layer (single 3 \times 3 convolution, no activation) to perform initial noise reduction while preserving spatial resolution. 3. Feature Extraction: Extract pixel feature embeddings from the Pre-Net outputs using the truncated ResNet34 encoder-decoder network from IBRNet. 4. Ray Projection: For each pixel in the target image, project a ray into the scene and sample points along the ray. 5. Cross-View Projection: Project each 3D sample point onto each of the N input views to retrieve corresponding features. 6. Feature Aggregation: Compute cross-view mean and variance feature vectors for the specific pixel. Concatenate these statistics to the pixel feature embedding vectors. Concatenate estimated noise variances (per-pixel per-color channel) to the global features. Process the aggregated features through the 5-head self-attention transformer to capture intricate cross-view relations. 7. Density and Color Estimation: Predict the point color cm and density \rhom for each sample m along the ray. Calculate the probability wm that an object exists at sample m: wm = 1 - e^{-\rhom / \sum{j=1}^{M} \rhoj} where \rhom is the density and M is the total number of samples. 8. Noise-Aware Color Blending (Spatial Kernel): Instead of a single scalar weight per view, predict a k \times k spatial kernel of blending weights for each view and each color channel. The output is N vectors, each of dimension k^2 \times 3. Normalize the weights per channel to sum to 1 using a softmax operation prior to blending. Apply these kernels to the k \times k spatial neighborhood of each projected pixel to gather spatial context. 9. Rendering: Integrate the weight-color pairs along the ray to produce the final color \hat{C}(r): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{m=1}^{M} wm cm where wm is the weight, cm is the color, and M is the total samples. 10. Coarse/Fine Sampling: Repeat the sampling process in two stages. The 'fine' stage refines sampling around depth values that most influence rendering (visible surfaces). 11. Post-processing: Apply the respective gamma correction and white balancing to the output linear denoised image to return it to display space. Apply a simple bilateral filtering post-process to the main network output. Spatial Kernel Size (k): Set to 3. This provides a balance between quality gain and increase in network complexity. Transformer Heads: 5. Original IBRNet Feature Extraction: The original IBRNet uses a 7 \times 7 kernel size and immediate spatial resolution reduction by a factor of two at the entry point. This makes the layer incapable of performing simple noise filtering, necessitating the addition of the Pre-Net layer. Standard Blending Insufficiency: Standard IBRNet blending gathers only cross-view (single pixel) information without spatial extent. This is insufficient for noise filtering, as noise is a spatial phenomenon. The introduction of k \times k spatial kernels addresses this. Clean vs. Noisy Regimes: In clean images, IBRNet ignores feature statistics (mean/variance) because variance is low for surface points. In noisy regimes, individual features become more significant than joint statistics, necessitating the transformer module. Signal-Dependent Noise: The separation of blending weights per color channel is important, especially in the case of signal-dependent noise, which can vary across color channels. Not given in the sources. The addition of the Pre-Net layer, transformer module, and spatial kernels increases network complexity compared to standard IBRNet. Not given in the sources. The paper demonstrates improved denoising performance on the LLFF-N dataset compared to baseline IBRNet-N, but specific metrics are not detailed in the provided notes. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively handles degraded noisy images by leveraging spatial context via 3D blending kernels and cross-view statistics via transformers. The Pre-Net layer efficiently reduces input noise without losing spatial resolution. Limitations: The method is designed for burst denoising of existing views rather than novel view synthesis. The reliance on accurate noise variance estimation may be a limitation if noise statistics are unknown or misestimated. Use NAN when the goal is to denoise a burst of noisy images of the same scene rather than synthesizing novel views. It is particularly suitable for low-light conditions where noise is significant. Do not use NAN if the primary task is novel view synthesis from clean images, as standard IBRNet or other NeRF variants may be more appropriate. It is also not designed for single-image denoising without a burst of inputs. NAN was introduced in the paper "NAN: Noise-Aware NeRFs for Burst-Denoising". It extends the IBRNet architecture to address the challenges of burst denoising, which differs from novel view synthesis in its focus on degraded noisy images and fixing existing views. The method builds upon IBRNet, which was designed for novel view synthesis with significant camera motion and complex 3D geometry. The authors observed that standard IBRNet performs poorly on noisy inputs due to its feature extraction and blending mechanisms. They introduced the Pre-Net layer, cross-view statistics aggregation, a transformer module, and 3D blending kernels to adapt IBRNet for noise-aware rendering. NAN is used for burst denoising of images captured in low-light conditions, where multiple noisy views of the same scene are available. It is evaluated on the LLFF-N dataset, which consists of noisy versions of the LLFF dataset. NAN: Noise-Aware NeRFs for Burst-Denoising, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01234, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Multiplicative Interaction Module
head: MI-NeRF conditional input module, conditional input module, multiplicative module M
body: The Multiplicative Interaction Module (MIM) is a neural component that generates conditional inputs for a NeRF by computing multiplicative interactions between expression, identity, and optional latent codes to improve facial disentanglement and rendering quality. It explicitly models second- and third-order multiplicative dependencies between semantic codes rather than relying on linear concatenation or simple additive fusion. Inputs and Outputs: Expression vector e \in \mathbb{R}^d Identity vector i \in \mathbb{R}^d Optional latent code l \in \mathbb{R}^d (time-varying, per-frame) Output vector y \in \mathbb{R}^o Data Structures: Tensor \mathcal{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{o \times d \times d}: Learnable third-order tensor for pure multiplicative interaction. Matrices W2, W3 \in \mathbb{R}^{o \times d}: Learnable linear weights for identity and expression respectively. Factor matrices A, B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}: Learnable parameters for CP decomposition of \mathcal{W} along the expression and identity modes. Matrix C \in \mathbb{R}^{o \times k}: Learnable output projection matrix from the CP decomposition. Matrices U1, U2, U3 \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}: Learnable projection matrices used in the full third-order variant with latent codes. Parameters: d: Dimension of input vectors. Set to 79 in the final model. k: Rank of the CP decomposition. Set to k=d in the final model. o: Output dimension. Set to o=d in the final model; tested at o=256 in ablation. Formulas: The basic module computes interactions between expression e and identity i. The full multiplicative interaction is defined as: M^\dagger(e, i) = \mathcal{W} \times2 e \times3 i where \timesm denotes the mode-m vector product. To augment this with linear interactions, the formula becomes: M^\dagger(e, i) = \mathcal{W} \times2 e \times3 i + W2 e + W3 i where W2, W3 \in \mathbb{R}^{o \times d}. Using CP decomposition, the tensor term \mathcal{W} \times2 e \times3 i can be rewritten using factor matrices A, B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} and C \in \mathbb{R}^{o \times k}: \mathcal{W} \times2 e \times3 i = C (A \odot B)^T (e \odot i) where \odot denotes the Khatri-Rao product. Applying the mixed product property, this simplifies to a Hadamard product: M^\dagger(e, i) = C \left[ (A^T e) (B^T i) \right] + W2 e + W3 i If we set o=k=d and A^T = U1, B^T = U2, this matches the standard implementation form. For the variant including latent codes l, the module captures third-order interactions: M(e, i, l) = C \left[ (U1 e) (U2 i) (U3 l) + (U1 e) (U2 i) + (U1 e) (U3 l) + (U2 i) (U3 l) + (U1 e) + (U2 i) + (U3 l) \right] where U1, U2, U3 \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d} and C \in \mathbb{R}^{o \times k}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiplicativeinteractionmodule(e, i, l=None, Wtensor=None, W2=None, W3=None, A=None, B=None, C=None, U1=None, U2=None, U3=None, d=79, k=79, o=79): """ Computes the multiplicative interaction module output. Args: e: Expression vector, shape (d,) i: Identity vector, shape (d,) l: Optional latent code vector, shape (d,) Wtensor: Learnable tensor for pure multiplicative interaction, shape (o, d, d) W2: Learnable linear weight matrix for expression, shape (o, d) W3: Learnable linear weight matrix for identity, shape (o, d) A: Factor matrix for expression CP decomposition, shape (d, k) B: Factor matrix for identity CP decomposition, shape (d, k) C: Output projection matrix, shape (o, k) U1, U2, U3: Projection matrices for third-order variant, shape (k, d) d: Input dimension (default 79) k: CP decomposition rank (default d) o: Output dimension (default d) Returns: y: Output vector, shape (o,) """ # Note: Wtensor, W2, W3, A, B, C, U1, U2, U3 are learnable parameters # initialized during training and loaded from a trained model at inference. # Base multiplicative term using CP decomposition # Term 1: (A^T e) (B^T i) termbase = (A.T @ e) (B.T @ i) # Project to output space y = C @ termbase # Add linear terms y = y + (W2 @ e) + (W3 @ i) # If latent code l is provided, use the full third-order variant if l is not None: u1e = U1 @ e u2i = U2 @ i u3l = U3 @ l # Third-order interaction term3 = u1e u2i u3l # Second-order interactions term21 = u1e u2i term22 = u1e u3l term23 = u2i u3l # First-order interactions term11 = u1e term12 = u2i term13 = u3l # Sum all terms combined = term3 + term21 + term22 + term23 + term11 + term12 + term13 # Project to output space y = C @ combined return y Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reducing dimension d below 79 loses necessary information for capturing 3DMM principal components, as learned matrices W1, W2, W3 have full rank with all singular values > 10^{-3}. Including latent codes l in the multiplicative module decreases performance (PSNR 29.01 vs 29.73) because l captures time-varying per-frame variations that do not meaningfully interact with time-invariant identity or expression codes. Using simple learnable concatenation M(e, i) = [W2 e; W3 i] decreases performance (PSNR 28.99) due to the lack of multiplicative interactions. Increasing output dimension to o=256 yields similar performance (PSNR 29.76) but with more parameters, offering no significant benefit. A module that captures high-degree interactions by iteratively adding projected features and performing multiplications in a common embedding space. Formula: H(\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{i}) = \mathbf{C} \mathbf{x}n, where \mathbf{x}n = \mathbf{x}{n-1} + (\mathbf{U}{(n,1)} \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{U}{(n,2)} \mathbf{i}) \mathbf{x}{n-1} for n = 2, \dots, N, with \mathbf{x}1 = \mathbf{U}{(1,1)}\mathbf{e} + \mathbf{U}{(1,2)}\mathbf{i}. Parameters \mathbf{U}{(n,1)}, \mathbf{U}{(n,2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d} and \mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{o \times k} are learnable. In practice, d=k=o=79. N: The number of interaction steps. Typical value: 2. Module H with N=2 performs similarly to Module M but allows for higher-degree interactions if N is increased, though N>2 yields worse performance in experiments. Time Complexity: The CP-decomposed implementation is efficient, scaling linearly with d and k for the multiplicative term, plus linear terms for the linear weights. The full third-order variant with latent codes increases complexity due to additional Hadamard products and projections. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of learnable parameters: \mathcal{W} (o \cdot d^2), W2, W3 (2 \cdot o \cdot d), or the CP factors A, B, C (2 \cdot d \cdot k + o \cdot k). The CP decomposition significantly reduces memory compared to the full tensor \mathcal{W} when k < d. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly models multiplicative dependencies between semantic codes, leading to better facial disentanglement and rendering quality compared to linear concatenation. Limitations: Does not benefit from including time-varying latent codes in the multiplicative interaction, as these do not interact meaningfully with static identity/expression codes. Requires careful selection of dimension d to preserve 3DMM information. When to use: When facial disentanglement between identity, expression, and other semantic codes is critical for high-quality rendering. When not to use: When time-varying latent codes are the primary source of variation, as they do not benefit from multiplicative interaction with static codes. The Multiplicative Interaction Module was introduced in the MI-NeRF paper. It leverages CP decomposition, a core tool for low-rank tensor factorization introduced by Kolda & Bader (2009). The module is designed to improve the conditional input generation for NeRFs in the context of facial reconstruction, specifically addressing the need to disentangle identity and expression information. MI-NeRF: Learning a Single Face NeRF from Multiple Identities, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19920v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Part-Wise NARF (NARFP)
body: Part-Wise NARF (NARFP) is a neural articulated radiance field method that models an articulated object by training a separate Ray-Traced NeRF (RT-NeRF) for each rigid part, combining their outputs to estimate global density and color. It differs from holistic approaches by explicitly computing rigid transformations via forward kinematics, thereby avoiding implicit transformation issues and part dependency problems inherent in other methods. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A kinematic 3D pose configuration of an articulated object \{T0, \boldsymbol{\zeta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}\}, where T0 is the root transformation, \boldsymbol{\zeta} represents global parameters, and \boldsymbol{\theta} represents joint angles. A global 3D location \mathbf{x} and a 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) and optionally a foreground mask M(\mathbf{r}) or segmentation mask Si(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: Parts: The object is decomposed into P rigid parts. RT-NeRFs: A set of P separate RT-NeRF models, denoted as F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}} for part i, where i \in \{1, \dots, P\}. Each model has its own weights \Theta^i and local coordinate frame l^i. Transformations: Global rigid transformations \{li \mid i = 1, \dots, P\} computed via forward kinematics. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Global Transformations: Given the kinematic pose \{T0, \boldsymbol{\zeta}, \boldsymbol{\theta}\}, compute the global rigid transformation li for each rigid part i using forward kinematics. 2. Transform Coordinates: For a global 3D location \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}, transform the coordinates for each part i into the local coordinate frame of that part: \mathbf{x}^i = R^{i-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}^i) \mathbf{d}^i = R^{i-1}\mathbf{d} where R^{i-1} and \mathbf{t}^i are the rotation and translation components of the transformation from the parent frame to part i. 3. Estimate Part Properties: Estimate the density \sigma^i and color c^i for each part i using its specific RT-NeRF F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}}. The input to the network includes positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}^i), directional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{d}^i), and potentially other embeddings \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i) and global parameters \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta}): (\sigma^i, c^i) = F{\Theta^i}^{l^i, \boldsymbol{\zeta}}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}^i), \gamma(\mathbf{d}^i), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta})) 4. Combine Densities and Colors: Combine the density and color estimates \{\sigma^i, c^i \mid i = 1, \dots, P\} from all parts using a soft-max weighted sum to determine the global density \sigma and color c. This avoids the non-differentiable max operation: \sigma = \frac{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau) \sigma^i}{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)} c = \frac{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau) c^i}{\sum{i=1}^P \exp(\sigma^i/\tau)} where \tau is the temperature parameter of the soft-max function. 5. Volume Rendering: Apply volume rendering using the combined density \sigma and color c to generate the rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) along a camera ray \mathbf{r}. 6. Estimate Masks (Optional): Estimate the foreground mask M(\mathbf{r}) as the integral of opacity along the camera ray, weighted by the index of the part with the highest density. Specifically, let sj(\mathbf{r}) be the index of the part with the greatest density at sample j. The segmentation mask Si(\mathbf{r}) for part i is: Si(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^N Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) (sj(\mathbf{r}) == i) where Tj is the transmittance, \sigmaj is the density, and \deltaj is the distance between samples. Parameters: \tau: Temperature parameter of the soft-max function, used to control the sharpness of the weighting between parts. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Non-differentiability: The max operation for selecting the highest density part is not differentiable, so a soft-max function is used instead to allow gradient propagation for training. Zero-Density Samples: Training is dominated by zero-density point samples because a surface point belongs to only one part, resulting in zero density for all other parts. This makes the computation inefficient as parts with small densities do not significantly affect the final value but still require evaluation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partwisenarfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, poseconfig, partnerfs, tau): """ Renders a ray using Part-Wise NARF. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the camera ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the camera ray. poseconfig: Dict or object containing T0, zeta, theta for forward kinematics. partnerfs: List of P RT-NeRF models. tau: Temperature parameter for soft-max weighting. Returns: color: Rendered color. mask: Optional segmentation mask. """ # 1. Compute global rigid transformations for each part using forward kinematics # This depends on the specific kinematic chain defined in the source paper. # Returns list of (Ri, ti) for each part i. transforms = computeforwardkinematics(poseconfig) numparts = len(partnerfs) partdensities = [] partcolors = [] # 2. Estimate density and color for each part for i in range(numparts): Ri, ti = transforms[i] # Transform global coordinates to local part coordinates # x^i = R^{i-1}(x - t^i) # Note: The source uses R^{i-1} which implies the rotation from parent to current. # Assuming transforms[i] provides the rotation matrix Ri and translation ti # relative to the global frame or parent frame as per the kinematic definition. # The formula in source: x^i = R^{i-1}(x - t^i) # We assume Ri and ti are extracted appropriately. # Local position xlocal = Ri.T @ (rayorigin - ti) # Assuming Ri is global-to-local rotation or similar. # Source notation R^{i-1} suggests inverse rotation if R is parent-to-child. # Standard RT-NeRF input is local coordinates. # Local direction dlocal = Ri.T @ raydirection # Encode inputs # gamma() is positional encoding xenc = positionalencoding(xlocal) denc = positionalencoding(dlocal) # Get embeddings if applicable (xi, zeta) # xi might be part-specific embedding, zeta global xienc = partnerfs[i].getpartembedding() zetaenc = positionalencoding(poseconfig.zeta) # Query RT-NeRF sigmai, ci = partnerfs[i].forward(xenc, denc, xienc, zetaenc) partdensities.append(sigmai) partcolors.append(ci) # 3. Combine using soft-max weighted sum # sigmacombined = sum(exp(sigmai / tau) sigmai) / sum(exp(sigmai / tau)) # ccombined = sum(exp(sigmai / tau) ci) / sum(exp(sigmai / tau)) expweights = [exp(s / tau) for s in partdensities] sumexpweights = sum(expweights) sigmacombined = sum(w s for w, s in zip(expweights, partdensities)) / sumexpweights ccombined = sum(w c for w, c in zip(expweights, partcolors)) / sumexpweights # 4. Volume Rendering # This step typically involves sampling along the ray and integrating. # The source states "Apply volume rendering using the combined density sigma and color c". # However, standard NeRF rendering integrates along the ray. # The soft-max combination happens at each sample point or for the final result? # The source implies combining densities/colors at a global 3D location x. # For a ray, we sample points xj. At each xj, we compute sigmaj and cj via the part-wise combination. # Then we integrate. # Simplified rendering loop (assuming standard volumetric rendering integration) # This is a high-level representation as the exact integration scheme (Eq 5) is not detailed in the notes. color = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 mask = 0.0 # For segmentation # Sample points along the ray for j in range(numsamples): xj = rayorigin + raydirection tj # tj is depth sigmaj, cj = partwisenarfcombine(xj, raydirection, transforms, partnerfs, tau) alphaj = 1.0 - exp(-sigmaj deltaj) weightj = transmittance alphaj color += weightj cj transmittance = (1.0 - alphaj) # Segmentation mask calculation # Find part with max density at xj maxsigmaidx = argmax(partdensitiesatxj) # Computed inside combine function mask += weightj (maxsigmaidx == i) # Accumulate for part i return color, mask def partwisenarfcombine(x, d, transforms, partnerfs, tau): """Helper to combine part outputs at a specific 3D location x""" numparts = len(partnerfs) partdensities = [] partcolors = [] for i in range(numparts): Ri, ti = transforms[i] xlocal = Ri.T @ (x - ti) dlocal = Ri.T @ d xenc = positionalencoding(xlocal) denc = positionalencoding(dlocal) xienc = partnerfs[i].getpartembedding() zetaenc = positionalencoding(poseconfig.zeta) # Assuming global zeta is available sigmai, ci = partnerfs[i].forward(xenc, denc, xienc, zetaenc) partdensities.append(sigmai) partcolors.append(ci) expweights = [exp(s / tau) for s in partdensities] sumexpweights = sum(expweights) sigmacombined = sum(w s for w, s in zip(expweights, partdensities)) / sumexpweights ccombined = sum(w c for w, c in zip(expweights, partcolors)) / sumexpweights return sigmacombined, ccombined Complexity: Computational cost is proportional to the number of object parts P, limiting representation capacity for complex articulated objects. Training Efficiency: Training is dominated by zero-density point samples because a surface point belongs to only one part, resulting in zero density for all other parts. This makes the computation inefficient. Strengths: Explicitly computes rigid transformations via forward kinematics, avoiding implicit transformation issues and part dependency problems inherent in other methods. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the linear scaling with the number of parts and the inefficiency of evaluating zero-density parts. Part-Wise NARF (NARFP) was introduced in the paper "Neural Articulated Radiance Field". It is one of three types of neural articulated radiance fields proposed, alongside Holistic NARF (NARFH) and Disentangled NARF.
