name: UE4-NeRF
body: UE4-NeRF is a neural rendering system designed for the real-time interactive rendering of large-scale 3D scenes by integrating Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with the Unreal Engine 4 (UE4) rasterization pipeline. It partitions large environments into sub-NeRFs, representing each block using textured polygonal meshes initialized from regular octahedra, and utilizes a Level of Detail (LOD) hierarchy to maintain high frame rates at varying observation heights. Unlike Block-NeRF, which is limited to grid structures, UE4-NeRF supports diverse terrains including mountainous areas, and unlike Mobile-NeRF, it handles tilted surfaces and semi-transparent objects more effectively. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of posed camera images (typically drone-captured) with GPS metadata; camera intrinsics and extrinsics; a large-scale scene bounding box. Outputs: A set of textured polygonal meshes (shading meshes) for each scene block at multiple Levels of Detail (LOD); a neural shader (HLSL fragment shader) deployed in UE4; real-time rendered RGB images. Data Structures 1. Scene Partitioning: The large scene is divided into overlapping blocks. Each training area is slightly larger than the corresponding scene area to ensure smooth transitions at boundaries. 2. Mesh Representation: Each block is represented by a textured polygonal mesh. The mesh is initialized from a grid and optimized during training. The texture atlas stores feature vectors and opacity information. 3. Coordinate System: X-axis points east, Y-axis points south, Z-axis points up. The world scale is 100:1 (UE4 units to real-world units). 4. Network Architecture: The Encoder is a 4-layer MLP with dimensions 32 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 8. It takes multi-resolution hash-encoded position features and outputs an opacity scalar \alpha and an 8-dimensional feature vector \mathbf{m}. The Decoder is a 3-layer MLP with dimensions 17 \times 16, 16 \times 16, 16 \times 3. It takes the feature vector \mathbf{m} and spherical harmonics coefficients of the view direction to predict the final RGB color \mathbf{c}. Method Steps 1. Preprocessing and Coordinate Transformation: Convert GPS-captured drone imagery coordinates to the UE4 coordinate system (X=East, Y=South, Z=Up) and apply the 100:1 scale conversion. 2. Block Partitioning: Partition the large-scale scene into multiple blocks (sub-NeRFs). Train a coarse model for sub-region segmentation to capture overall terrain and building outlines. Filter images associated with each sub-region and apply a mask to exclude pixels outside the specific scene area. 3. Mesh Initialization: Initialize a 128 \times 128 \times 128 grid for each block. Select the center point of each grid cell along with its six neighboring grids (front, back, left, right, top, bottom) to form the initial polygonal mesh structure. Use regular octahedra with 20 faces (8 exterior, 12 interior) instead of the Mobile-NeRF approach to address slow/unstable convergence on tilted surfaces. 4. Training (Optimization): For each block, optimize the Encoder-Decoder network parameters and the vertex positions of the meshes simultaneously. Use multi-resolution hash encoding (from Instant-NGP) for the position input pi to accelerate training. Represent the viewing direction d using spherical harmonics SH(d). Compute opacity and feature vector via \mathbf{m}i, \alphai = E(\text{hash}(pi); \thetaE). Compute color via \mathbf{c}i = D(\mathbf{m}i, SH(di); \thetaD). Minimize the difference between rendered colors and ground truth images using PSNR/SSIM and LPIPS metrics. Implement computationally intensive portions using CUDA on NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., RTX 3090). Train for 80,000 epochs per block to achieve convergence. 5. Shading Mesh Extraction: Extract coarse polygonal meshes without textures during training. Apply vertex optimization results. Encode texture maps (feature vectors and opacity) into the network outputs. 6. Level of Detail (LOD) Generation: Train meshes with varying levels of detail for different observation heights. Coarser meshes are used for higher observation heights to ensure real-time performance. Extract pre-rendered polygonal meshes at different LODs for the final rendering module. 7. Rendering in UE4: Deploy the Encoder-Decoder network as an HLSL fragment shader in UE4. The shader takes feature vectors (from the texture atlas) as input and outputs colors. Combine the extracted LOD meshes with the UE4 rasterization pipeline. UE4 handles occlusion automatically; if traditional 3D models (e.g.,.obj,.fbx) are imported, the neural shader computation is skipped for occluded regions. Pseudocode Unverified code. Spherical harmonics degree 3 yields 9 coefficients x, y, z = direction return np.array([ 0.282095, -0.488603y, 0.488603z, -0.488603x, 1.092548xy, -1.092548yz, 0.315392(3z2-1), -1.092548xz, 0.546274(x2-y2) ]) def hashencode(position, grid): # Multi-resolution hash encoding from Instant-NGP # Maps 3D position to a 32-dim feature vector via hash table lookups. return np.random.rand(32) # Standard hash grid lookup implementation def mlpforward(x, weights): for w, b in weights: x = np.dot(x, w) + b x = np.maximum(0, x) # ReLU activation return x def intersectmesh(origin, direction, vertices, faces): # Ray-triangle intersection for all faces # Returns closest intersection point and normal, or None. return None # Standard ray-mesh intersection logic class UE4NeRFBlock: def init(self, scenebounds, gridsize=128): self.scenebounds = scenebounds self.gridsize = gridsize # Initialize mesh vertices from 128x128x128 grid neighbors self.vertices = np.random.rand(gridsize3, 3) # Simplified initialization # 20 faces: 8 exterior, 12 interior self.faces = np.random.randint(0, gridsize3, (20, 3)) # Simplified face indices # Network Parameters # Encoder: 4-layer MLP (32->64->64->64->8) self.encoderweights = [(np.random.randn(32, 64)np.sqrt(2/32), np.zeros(64)), (np.random.randn(64, 64)np.sqrt(2/64), np.zeros(64)), (np.random.randn(64, 64)np.sqrt(2/64), np.zeros(64)), (np.random.randn(64, 8), np.zeros(8))] # Decoder: 3-layer MLP (17->16->16->3) self.decoderweights = [(np.random.randn(17, 16)np.sqrt(2/17), np.zeros(16)), (np.random.randn(16, 16)np.sqrt(2/16), np.zeros(16)), (np.random.randn(16, 3), np.zeros(3))] # Multi-resolution hash grid (from Instant-NGP) self.hashgrid = {} # Hash table structure def forwardencoder(self, hashedpos): # E(hash(pi); thetaE) -> Mi, alphai x = mlpforward(hashedpos, self.encoderweights) featurevector = x[:,:8] opacity = sigmoid(x[:, 8]) return featurevector, opacity def forwarddecoder(self, featurevector, shcoeffs): # D(Mi, SH(di); thetaD) -> ci inputvec = concat(featurevector, shcoeffs) color = mlpforward(inputvec, self.decoderweights) return sigmoid(color) def renderray(self, rayorigin, raydirection): intersectionpoint, normal = intersectmesh(rayorigin, raydirection, self.vertices, self.faces) if intersectionpoint is None: return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) hashedpos = hashencode(intersectionpoint, self.hashgrid) shcoeffs = computeshcoefficients(raydirection) featurevector, opacity = self.forwardencoder(hashedpos) color = self.forwarddecoder(featurevector, shcoeffs) return color def trainstep(self, images, poses, optimizer): # Filter images for this block using mask blockimages, blockposes = [], [] for img, pose in zip(images, poses): if self.isinbounds(pose): blockimages.append(img) blockposes.append(pose) for image, pose in zip(blockimages, blockposes): rays = generaterays(pose, image.shape) renderedcolors = [self.renderray(r.origin, r.direction) for r in rays] loss = np.mean((np.array(renderedcolors) - image)2) optimizer.step(loss) updatemeshvertices(self.vertices, self.faces, loss) def isinbounds(self, pose): return True # Placeholder for mask logic def generaterays(pose, shape): return [] # Standard camera ray generation def updatemeshvertices(vertices, faces, gradients): pass # Vertex optimization step def selectlod(cameraheight, mesheslod): return max(0, min(len(mesheslod)-1, int(cameraheight))) # Simple LOD selection def rasterizewithneuralshader(mesh, texture, camerapose): return np.zeros((1080, 1920, 3)) # Standard rasterization calling HLSL shader def handleocclusion(renderedimage, importedmodels): return renderedimage # UE4 depth buffer handles occlusion Parameters Grid Initialization Size: 128 \times 128 \times 128. Octahedron Faces: 20 total (8 exterior, 12 interior). Encoder MLP Dimensions: 32 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 64, 64 \times 8. Decoder MLP Dimensions: 17 \times 16, 16 \times 16, 16 \times 3. Training Hardware: 1 Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU. Training Iterations: 80,000 epochs per block. Coordinate System: X=East, Y=South, Z=Up. World Scale: 100:1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Tilted Surfaces: Mobile-NeRF suffers from slow/unstable convergence on tilted surfaces; UE4-NeRF addresses this by using regular octahedra. Semi-transparent Objects: Mobile-NeRF cannot handle transparent/semi-transparent objects (water, glass, plastic) due to opacity binarization. UE4-NeRF stores opacity in texture maps to mitigate this, though semi-transparent objects (e.g., vegetation) increase computational overhead and reduce frame rates. Pre-rendering Gaps: Pre-rendering cannot capture rays from all viewing angles, potentially resulting in gaps or holes in the final rendered scene. Exposure Matching: Consistent exposure matching with original images is difficult in UE4, causing evaluation metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) to underestimate actual reconstruction quality. Memory Overhead: Rendering large scenes (square kilometers) incurs significant memory overhead, especially when using CUDA and NVIDIA GPUs. Increasing accuracy further amplifies memory consumption. Training Speed: 1000× faster than Mobile-NeRF. Training time per block is 40 minutes on 1×RTX 3090. Training time for a full scene of n blocks is 1 hour + (40 minutes × n/4) on 1×RTX 3090. Rendering Performance: Real-time rendering at 4K resolution achieves up to 43 FPS. Full scene rendering at 2K resolution achieves 50 FPS. Individual block rendering at 2K resolution achieves ≥70 FPS. Memory: Significant memory overhead for large scenes (square kilometers). Requires NVIDIA GPUs and CUDA. Strengths: Real-time interactive rendering of large-scale scenes. Handles tilted surfaces and semi-transparent objects better than Mobile-NeRF. Supports scene editing with traditional 3D models. Suitable for diverse terrains (mountainous, farmland) unlike Block-NeRF. Limitations: Pre-rendering gaps/holes. Exposure matching issues in UE4. High memory consumption. Semi-transparent objects reduce frame rates. Requires NVIDIA GPUs. When to Use: Real-time interactive rendering of large-scale outdoor scenes (e.g., digital twins, VR, games) where high fidelity and editability are required. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring perfect ray-casting from all angles without pre-rendering artifacts; environments with extremely high densities of semi-transparent objects where frame rate is critical; hardware without NVIDIA GPUs/CUDA support. UE4-NeRF was introduced in the paper "UE4-NeRF: Neural Radiance Field for Real-Time Rendering of Large-Scale Scene". It was developed to address the limitations of existing NeRF methods in real-time rendering of large-scale scenes, such as high training costs, slow rendering speeds, and lack of editability. The method combines NeRF with the Unreal Engine 4 (UE4) rasterization pipeline, leveraging LOD techniques and multi-resolution hash encoding to achieve real-time performance. It is used in UE4 for real-time interactive rendering and scene editing/manipulation, particularly for drone-captured large-scale scenes like farmlands, construction sites, and industrial parks, and has been evaluated on the Mega-NeRF public dataset. name: Multi-view Aggregation with Skeletal Features
head: Multi-view aggregation of skeletal and query features
body: This method integrates geometric priors from a parametric human model (SMPL) with multi-view image features to improve the quality of neural radiance fields for human performance rendering. It solves the problem of ambiguous geometry and texture in single-view or poorly constrained multi-view setups by using skeletal features as a robust, time-augmented geometric backbone. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on positional encoding of 3D coordinates, this approach explicitly retrieves features from a learned skeletal volume and aggregates them with pixel-aligned image features using a cross-attention mechanism. It differs from SUDS by using a parametric model prior rather than unsupervised depth, and from Rip-NeRF by focusing on articulated human performance rather than static geometry. The method processes a query 3D point \mathbf{x} and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} at a specific time t across C camera views. It retrieves skeletal and image features, aggregates them via attention, and predicts density and color. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, time t, camera poses for C views. Outputs: Volume density \tilde{\sigma}t(\mathbf{x}) and RGB color \tilde{r}^g{bt}(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures Skeletal Features: A 3D volume S learned via SparseConvNet, representing time-augmented features in SMPL space. Image Features: A 2D feature map I{c,t} for each view c and time t. Attention Weights: Matrix mv\att^x \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C}. Meta Representation: Vector z^xt \in \mathbb{R}^d. Steps 1. Retrieve Skeletal Feature: Retrieve the time-augmented skeletal feature s^0{c,t} at query location \mathbf{x} via trilinear interpolation in the SMPL space using SparseConvNet. This feature is consistent across views for the same \mathbf{x} and t. 2. Sample Pixel-Aligned Feature: Sample the pixel-aligned image feature p^x{c,t} by directly projecting \mathbf{x} onto the image plane of view c at time t (\mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2). This feature is view-specific and time-specific. 3. Construct Attention Weights: Compute multi-view cross-attention weights mv\att^x using keys derived from skeletal and pixel-aligned features: mv\att^x = \psi \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} K(s^0{1:C,t}) \cdot K(p^x{1:C,t})^T \right) where \psi is the softmax operator applied along the second axis (columns), K(\cdot) is a learnable linear projection to keys, and d is the feature dimension. 4. Compute View-wise Representation: Compute the view-wise representation z^x{1:C,t} by combining weighted pixel-aligned values and skeletal values: z^x{1:C,t} = mv\att^x \cdot V(p^x{1:C,t}) + V(s^0{1:C,t}) where V(\cdot) is a learnable linear projection to values. 5. Compute Meta Representation: Compute the meta-time and meta-view representation z^xt by averaging the view-wise representations across all C views: z^xt = \frac{1}{C} \sum{c=1}^C z^x{c,t} 6. Predict Density: Compute the final density \tilde{\sigma}t(\mathbf{x}) using a Multi-Layer Perceptron MLP\sigma with four linear layers applied to z^xt: \tilde{\sigma}t(\mathbf{x}) = MLP\sigma(z^xt) 7. Predict Color: Compute the final color \tilde{r}^g{bt}(\mathbf{x}) using a Multi-Layer Perceptron MLP{rgb} with two linear layers. The input is the concatenation of the mean of pixel-aligned values and the positional encoding of the viewing direction: \tilde{r}^g{bt}(\mathbf{x}) = MLP{rgb} \left( \frac{1}{C} \sum{c=1}^C V(p^x{c,t}); \gammad(\mathbf{d}) \right) where \gammad(\mathbf{d}) is the positional encoding of \mathbf{d} as defined in the parent article. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiviewaggregation(x, d, t, cameras, sparseconvnet, imagefeatures, kskel, kimg, vskel, vimg, mlpsigma, mlprgb): """ x: Query 3D point (3,) d: Viewing direction (3,) t: Time step cameras: List of camera parameters for C views sparseconvnet: SparseConvNet model for skeletal features imagefeatures: Dict of image feature maps for each view and time kskel, kimg: Linear layers for key projections vskel, vimg: Linear layers for value projections mlpsigma: MLP for density (4 linear layers) mlprgb: MLP for color (2 linear layers) """ C = len(cameras) dfeat = imagefeatures[0].shape[-1] # Feature dimension # Step 1: Retrieve skeletal feature (same for all views) # Trilinear interpolation in SMPL space via SparseConvNet s0 = sparseconvnet.interpolate(x, t) # Shape: (d,) # Step 2: Sample pixel-aligned features for each view plist = [] for c in range(C): # Project x to 2D image coordinates for view c uv = project3dto2d(x, cameras[c]) # Sample feature from image feature map at uv p = sampleimagefeature(imagefeatures[c], uv) plist.append(p) ptensor = torch.stack(plist) # Shape: (C, d) # Step 3: Compute attention weights # Keys for skeletal features: broadcast s0 to C views kskeltensor = kskel(s0).unsqueeze(0).repeat(C, 1) # Shape: (C, d) kimgtensor = kimg(ptensor) # Shape: (C, d) # Dot product scaled by 1/sqrt(d) scores = torch.matmul(kskeltensor, kimgtensor.T) / math.sqrt(dfeat) # Shape: (C, C) # Softmax along second axis mvatt = softmax(scores, dim=1) # Shape: (C, C) # Step 4: Compute view-wise representation vskeltensor = vskel(s0).unsqueeze(0).repeat(C, 1) # Shape: (C, d) vimgtensor = vimg(ptensor) # Shape: (C, d) # Weighted sum of image values + skeletal values zview = torch.matmul(mvatt, vimgtensor) + vskeltensor # Shape: (C, d) # Step 5: Compute meta representation (mean across views) zmeta = torch.mean(zview, dim=0) # Shape: (d,) # Step 6: Predict density sigma = mlpsigma(zmeta) # Shape: (1,) # Step 7: Predict color # Mean of pixel-aligned values pmean = torch.mean(vimgtensor, dim=0) # Shape: (d,) # Positional encoding of direction denc = positionalencoding(d) # Shape: (6L,) # Concatenate and pass through MLP colorinput = torch.cat([pmean, denc], dim=0) color = mlprgb(colorinput) # Shape: (3,) return sigma, color Parameters C: Number of views. d: Feature dimension. L: Number of frequency bands in positional encoding (from parent article). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Occlusion: Pixel-aligned features may be occluded. The attention mechanism helps mitigate this by weighting skeletal features (which are geometrically consistent) higher when image features are unreliable. SMPL Space Alignment: Accurate trilinear interpolation requires the query point \mathbf{x} to be correctly mapped to the SMPL space. Misalignment leads to incorrect skeletal features. Time Augmentation: Skeletal features are time-augmented, meaning they capture temporal dynamics. Ensure t is consistent between skeletal and image feature retrieval. This method samples time-augmented skeletal features at arbitrary 3D query points by diffusing discrete skeletal features into a continuous 3D volume using sparse convolutions, enabling spatially aware feature retrieval for NeRF input. It differs from dense voxelization by using sparse convolutions to process only occupied voxels, improving efficiency for large 3D spaces. A technique to improve pose refinement by incorporating multi-view constraints when motion is captured from multiple cameras, averaging joint rotation estimates without requiring camera calibration. Rotations are relative to the parent and root, allowing averaging without calibrating cameras. Only global position and orientation remain view-specific. Step: Initialize \thetak by averaging individual joint rotation estimates from all V views v \in [1,..., V]. Formula: Multi-view loss function: L{MV}(\theta, \phi) = \sumv \sumk \left( d(C\phi(\thetak, \omega{k,0}^{(v)}, \omega{k,1}^{(v)}), Ik) + \lambda\theta \|\thetak - \hat{\theta}k\|^2 + \lambdat \|\frac{\partial^2 \thetak}{\partial t^2}\|^2 \right) where \thetak is shared across all views v, except for \omega{k,0} and \omega{k,1} which are estimated independently per camera view v since the relative camera position and orientation is unknown. Time Complexity: Dominated by the attention mechanism O(C^2 \cdot d) and the MLPs O(d \cdot L{mlp}). SparseConvNet interpolation is efficient for sparse data. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the SparseConvNet volume and image features for all views and times. Strengths: Robust to occlusions and ambiguous geometry due to skeletal prior. Effective for human performance rendering. Limitations: Requires a parametric human model (SMPL). Performance depends on the accuracy of the SMPL fit and camera poses. When to Use: Human-centric scenes with articulated motion. When Not to Use: Static scenes or scenes without a parametric model prior. Originated in "Neural Human Performer" and "A-NeRF". It builds on the idea of using parametric models to regularize neural radiance fields for humans. The method was developed to address the challenges of rendering high-fidelity human performances from multi-view videos. name: SparseConvNet-based Skeletal Feature Sampling
head: 3D sparse convolution feature diffusion, SparseConvNet sampling
body: This method samples time-augmented skeletal features at arbitrary 3D query points by diffusing discrete skeletal features into a continuous 3D volume using sparse convolutions, enabling spatially aware feature retrieval for NeRF input. It differs from dense voxelization by using sparse convolutions to process only occupied voxels, improving efficiency for large 3D spaces. Inputs: SMPL parameters defining the human body pose and shape. Discrete skeletal features initialized on a voxel grid. A 3D query point x in world coordinates. Outputs: A sampled skeletal feature vector s^x \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times 128}. Data Structures: Input Volume: A 3D grid of dimensions D0 \times H0 \times W0 representing the 3D bounding box of the human body. SparseConvNet Architecture: A sequence of sparse convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU activation. The architecture is defined as follows: Layer 1: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 2 Layer 2: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 3: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 2 Layer 4: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 5: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 6: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 64 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 7: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 8: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 9: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 10: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 11: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layer 12: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 2) Layer 13: (3 \times 3 \times 3 \text{ conv}, 128 \text{ features}, \text{stride } 1) \times 3 Layers 14-17: Resize and concatenate outputs of layers 5, 9, 13, and 17. Steps: 1. Compute the 3D bounding box of the human body based on the SMPL parameters. 2. Divide the 3D bounding box into voxels of size 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm}, resulting in a volume of dimensions D0 \times H0 \times W0. 3. Transform skeletal feature locations and the query location x to the SMPL coordinate system to ensure invariance to world position and orientation. 4. Pass the input volume through the SparseConvNet architecture, which consists of 3D sparse convolutions that diffuse the skeletal features into the nearby 3D space. 5. Resize and concatenate the multi-scale outputs from layers 5, 9, 13, and 17 to form the output feature. 6. Sample the corresponding skeletal feature at query location x via trilinear interpolation from the concatenated output volume. 7. Pass the sampled feature through a fully-connected layer to reduce the channel size to 128. Formulas: Input volume dimensions: D0 \times H0 \times W0. Output feature dimensions before reduction: D'/16 \times H'/16 \times W'/16 \times 384, where D', H', W' correspond to the spatial dimensions after the respective strided convolutions. Parameters: Voxel size: 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm} \times 5\text{mm}. Output channel size after reduction: 128. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method relies on the accuracy of the SMPL parameters to define the bounding box and coordinate transformation. Sparse convolutions require efficient data structures to handle sparsity. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves efficiency for large 3D spaces by processing only occupied voxels. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When spatially aware feature retrieval for NeRF input is required, and efficiency in large 3D spaces is a concern. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in "Neural Human Performer: Learning Generalizable Radiance Fields for Human Performance Rendering". name: Residual-NeRF
head: Residual-NeRF-S (ablation variant)
body: Residual-NeRF is a method for improving depth perception and training speed for transparent objects in mostly static scenes by leveraging a static scene prior. It solves the ambiguity of depth estimation for transparent objects, where standard NeRFs struggle due to multiple surfaces radiating light along a ray, leading to noisy depth maps and perceived holes that hinder robotic grasp planning. Unlike methods that require pre-defined spatial areas for fusion (e.g., Block-NeRF, NeRFusion), Residual-NeRF learns to mix a pre-trained background NeRF and a residual NeRF at every point in space using a learned Mixnet, resulting in fewer holes and less noise in depth maps. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: I{bg}: Set of images of the scene without transparent objects (used to train the background NeRF). I{res}: Set of images of the scene with transparent objects present (used to train the residual NeRF and Mixnet). Camera poses P for I{bg} and I{res}. Ray parameters r(\lambda) = o + \lambda d for rendering. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}(r) for a given ray. Depth map \hat{D}(r) for the scene. Data Structures The method utilizes three Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Background NeRF (\Phi{bg}): Input: Encoded position and view direction h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi). Output: Pre-activation color \mathbf{c}'{bg} and volume density \sigma{bg}. 2. Residual NeRF (\Phi{res}): Input: Encoded position and view direction h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi). Output: Pre-activation color \mathbf{c}'{res} and volume density \sigma{res}. 3. Mixnet (\Phi{mix}): Input: Encoded position h(x, y, z) using a location-dependent multi-resolution hash encoding. Output: Mixing weight \beta \in [0, 1]. Numbered Steps 1. Train Background NeRF: Train \Phi{bg} on images I{bg} (scene without transparent objects) to infer \sigma{bg} and \mathbf{c}'{bg}. 2. Train Residual NeRF and Mixnet: Train \Phi{res} and \Phi{mix} on images I{res} (scene with transparent objects). The background NeRF \Phi{bg} is frozen and not updated during this phase. 3. Compute Mixing Weight: For each point along a ray, the Mixnet infers \beta using the encoded position. 4. Render Color: Combine the outputs of \Phi{bg} and \Phi{res} using \beta in the volumetric rendering equation to render the final color. 5. Compute Depth: Estimate depth using a density threshold m. Formulas The rendering process combines the background and residual fields. The final color \hat{C}(r) is computed by integrating along the ray: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-((1 - \beta)\sigma{bg} + \beta\sigma{res})i \deltai)) (\mathbf{c}{bg} + \mathbf{c}{res})i Where: Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the segment length between samples. \sigma{bg} and \sigma{res} are the densities from the background and residual NeRFs, respectively. \beta is the mixing weight from the Mixnet. (\mathbf{c}{bg} + \mathbf{c}{res})i is the combined color at sample i. The combined color is a sigmoid-weighted sum of the pre-activation colors: \mathbf{c}{bg+res} = S((1.0 - \beta)\mathbf{c}'{bg} + \beta\mathbf{c}'{res}) The mixing weight \beta is the sigmoid output of the Mixnet MLP applied to the encoded position: \beta = S(\Phi{mix}(h(x, y, z))) The sigmoid function is defined as S(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}. The individual network outputs are defined as: (\mathbf{c}'{bg}, \sigma{bg}) = \Phi{bg}(h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)) (\mathbf{c}'{res}, \sigma{res}) = \Phi{res}(h(x, y, z, \theta, \phi)) Depth Estimation Standard depth estimation using the expected distance is inaccurate for transparent objects because multiple surfaces radiate light along the ray. Instead, the method finds the point closest to the camera where the density exceeds a threshold m: \hat{D}(r) = tn \quad \text{where} \quad \sigman \ge m \quad \text{and} \quad \forall j < n, \sigmaj < m Parameters m: A tunable parameter for depth estimation threshold. It is used to find the closest point to the camera where density \sigmai \ge m. A single tuned value is reused across scenes. Typical value: 3.0 for Blender scenes; tuned per real environment. \beta: The mixing weight inferred by the Mixnet, constrained to [0, 1] via sigmoid activation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class ResidualNeRF: def init(self, bgmlp, resmlp, mixmlp, mthreshold=3.0, numfreqbands=10): """ Initialize Residual-NeRF. Args: bgmlp: Background NeRF MLP (Phibg). resmlp: Residual NeRF MLP (Phires). mixmlp: Mixnet MLP (Phimix). mthreshold: Density threshold for depth estimation (m). numfreqbands: Number of frequency bands for positional encoding. """ self.bgmlp = bgmlp self.resmlp = resmlp self.mixmlp = mixmlp self.mthreshold = mthreshold self.numfreqbands = numfreqbands def positionalencoding(self, x, numfreqbands): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numfreqbands)]) xb = torch.reshape((x scales), (x.shape, numfreqbands, 1)) fb = torch.stack((torch.sin(xb), torch.cos(xb)), dim=-1) return torch.reshape(fb, (x.shape, -1)) def forward(self, rayorigins, raydirections, numsamples, near, far): """ Render a batch of rays. Args: rayorigins: Tensor of shape (..., 3). raydirections: Tensor of shape (..., 3). numsamples: Number of samples per ray. near: Near plane distance. far: Far plane distance. Returns: color: Rendered color tensor. depth: Estimated depth tensor. """ # 1. Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples) zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(-2) + raydirections.unsqueeze(-2) zvals.unsqueeze(-1) # 2. Encode inputs posenc = self.positionalencoding(points, self.numfreqbands) direnc = self.positionalencoding(raydirections, self.numfreqbands) # Mixnet uses location-dependent multi-resolution hash encoding # Hash grid lookup is implementation-specific; standard positional encoding shown for structure. mixposenc = self.positionalencoding(points, self.numfreqbands) # 3. Query Background and Residual NeRFs bginput = torch.cat([posenc, direnc], dim=-1) resinput = torch.cat([posenc, direnc], dim=-1) bgoutput = self.bgmlp(bginput) resoutput = self.resmlp(resinput) cprimebg, sigmabg = bgoutput[...,:3], bgoutput[..., 3] cprimeres, sigmares = resoutput[...,:3], resoutput[..., 3] # 4. Query Mixnet beta = torch.sigmoid(self.mixmlp(mixposenc)) # 5. Compute combined density and color sigmacombined = (1.0 - beta) sigmabg + beta sigmares ccombined = torch.sigmoid((1.0 - beta) cprimebg + beta cprimeres) # 6. Volumetric Rendering deltas = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] deltainf = 1e10 torch.oneslike(deltas[...,:1]) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], -1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmacombined deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-alpha), dim=-2) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[...,:1]), T], -1) weights = alpha T[...,:-1] color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) ccombined, dim=-2) # 7. Depth Estimation # Find closest point where sigmacombined >= mthreshold mask = sigmacombined[...,:-1] >= self.mthreshold indices = torch.argmax(mask.float(), dim=-1) anymask = torch.any(mask, dim=-1) depths = zvals[torch.arange(zvals.shape[0]), indices] depths = torch.where(anymask, depths, zvals[..., -1]) return color, depths Edge Cases and Pitfalls Transparent Objects: Standard depth estimation (expected distance) is inaccurate for transparent objects because multiple surfaces radiate light along the ray. Mixnet Necessity: Without the Mixnet (using simple addition, referred to as Residual-NeRF-S), the residual NeRF must deduce the background NeRF's predictions in previously empty regions. Depth Map Holes: Perceived holes in depth maps can lead to robot collisions, while hallucinating non-existent surfaces may lead to no available grasp location. Threshold Tuning: The parameter m must be tuned. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses three MLPs (\Phi{bg}, \Phi{res}, \Phi{mix}). Measured Performance: On synthetic data, Residual-NeRF achieves 46.1% lower RMSE and 29.5% lower MAE compared to baselines (NeRF, Dex-NeRF). RMSE on 'Bowl' scene: NeRF 0.1900, Dex-NeRF 0.1065, Residual-NeRF 0.0699. MAE on 'Bowl' scene: NeRF 0.1453, Dex-NeRF 0.0195, Residual-NeRF 0.0140. Scaling: The method is designed for mostly static scenes where the background can be extensively observed (e.g., 100 images) while the foreground (transparent objects) is observed with fewer viewpoints (e.g., 50 images). Strengths: Improves depth perception of transparent objects, reduces holes and noise in depth maps, speeds up training compared to training a single NeRF on the complex scene, and facilitates robust grasp planning for robots. Limitations: Requires a static background scene. Performance depends on the quality of the background NeRF prior. The threshold m requires tuning. When to use: When depth perception of transparent objects is required in a mostly static environment, particularly for robotic manipulation tasks. When not to use: In highly dynamic scenes where the background changes significantly, or when transparent objects are not the primary focus of depth estimation. Residual-NeRF was proposed by Ichnowski et al. in 2024. It addresses the challenge of dexterous manipulation of transparent objects, where common depth sensors struggle. The method builds on the observation that robot work areas (kitchens, shelves) are mostly static and opaque, allowing a background NeRF to serve as a strong prior. It is implemented using Torch-NGP (PyTorch version of InstantNGP) with multi-resolution hash grids, running on hardware such as RTX 4090 and AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 5965WX. The method is compatible with grasp planners like Dex-Net. name: MZEN (Multi-zoom Enhanced NeRF)
head: Multi-zoom Enhanced NeRF
body: MZEN is a framework for 3-D reconstruction from images with unknown camera poses that explicitly models optical zoom as a learnable intrinsic parameter and uses cross-zoom pose registration to align non-overlapping zoomed-in and zoomed-out views. It solves the problem of stable training across multiple zoom levels without requiring high-resolution images or external pose initialization. Unlike CamP which perturbs focal length per view, or Mip-NeRF and Zip-NeRF which rely on image pyramids, MZEN keeps every frame at native resolution and assumes a single base focal length shared by all views, scaling it via a per-view zoom parameter. Inputs: A set of N images \mathcal{I} = \{Ik\}{k=1}^N. The set is partitioned into N{out} zoomed-out images (indices i=1 \dots N{out}) and N{in} zoomed-in images (indices j=N{out}+1 \dots N). Initial rough estimates of zoom parameters \xik (e.g., from camera dial readings or apparent size comparison). Base focal length f = (fx, fy) and principal point c = (cx, cy). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta (radiance field MLP weights). Optimized camera poses \Pi = \{Rk, tk, \xik\}{k=1}^N (rotation, translation, zoom). The camera pose for image k is defined as \Pik = (Rk, tk, f, c, \xik). Rk \in SO(3): Rotation matrix. tk \in \mathbb{R}^3: Translation vector. f \in \mathbb{R}^2: Shared base focal length (fx, fy). c \in \mathbb{R}^2: Principal point (cx, cy). \xik \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 1}: Learnable zoom parameter for view k. The effective intrinsic matrix is: K{eff}^k = \text{diag}(\xik fx, \xik fy, 1) The training proceeds in three distinct phases to ensure stability. Phase A: Global Pose Bootstrap 1. Initialize zoom parameters for the N{out} most zoomed-out images: \xii = 1 for i=1 \dots N{out}. 2. Randomly initialize NeRF parameters \Theta^{(A)}, rotations Ri, translations ti, and focal lengths f^{(A)}. 3. Withhold all zoomed-in images (j > N{out}) from the loss calculation. 4. Minimize the coarse loss L{coarse} over the N{out} images to obtain coarse NeRF parameters and globally consistent poses. Phase B: Cross-Zoom Pose Registration 1. Freeze NeRF parameters at \Theta^{(A)}. 2. For each zoomed-in image Ij (j > N{out}): a. Find the best matching zoomed-out image g^(j) from the set of N{out} images by minimizing the RGB mean-squared error between Ij and a surrogate view \tilde{I}{g \to j}. b. The surrogate view \tilde{I}{g \to j} is created by extracting the central 1/\xij crop from the zoomed-out image Ig and bilinearly resizing it to the native resolution of Ij. c. Initialize the pose \Pij for image j using the parameters (Rg, tg, f, c) from the matched zoomed-out image g^(j) and the zoom parameter \xij. This is "pose priming". 3. Optimize only the rotation Rj, translation tj, and zoom parameter \xij for each zoomed-in image j by minimizing L{pose}. Intrinsics f, c remain fixed from the surrogate. 4. The output is the provisional full pose set \Pi^{(B)} = \{\Pii^{(A)}\}{i=1}^{N{out}} \cup \{\Pij^{(B)}\}{j=N{out}+1}^{N}. Phase C: Joint Refinement 1. Initialize \Theta^{(C)} = \Theta^{(A)}. 2. Unfreeze NeRF parameters and all camera pose parameters (including all \xik). 3. Optimize \Theta^{(C)} and \Pi^{(B)} jointly for all N images by minimizing L{fine}. 4. This step sharpens fine details and yields pixel-accurate poses. Rendering: The rendered image \hat{I}k for camera k is computed using the differentiable volume renderer F\Theta: \hat{I}k = F\Theta(\Theta, \Pik) Loss Functions: Phase A Loss: L{coarse} = \sum{i=1}^{N{out}} \| F{\Theta^{(A)}}(\Theta^{(A)}, \Pi^{(A)}) - Ii \|2^2 Phase B Loss: L{pose} = \sum{j=N{out}+1}^{N} \| F{\Theta^{(A)}}(\Theta^{(A)}, \Pi^{(B)}) - Ij \|2^2 Phase C Loss: L{fine} = \sum{k=1}^{N} \| F{\Theta^{(C)}}(\Theta^{(C)}, \Pi^{(B)}) - Ik \|2^2 General Photometric Loss: L(\Theta, \Pi) = \sum{k=1}^{N} \| F\Theta(\Theta, \Pik) - Ik \|2^2 Convergence Analysis (Phase B): Under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition and L-smoothness, full-batch gradient descent with step size \eta converges linearly: e^{(t+1)} \leq (1 - \eta\mu) e^{(t)} where e^{(t)} = Lj(\Pij^{(t)}) - L^j is the excess loss, \mu > 0 is the PL constant, and \eta \in (0, 1/L] where L is the Lipschitz constant of the gradients. Zoom parameter \xik: Learnable intrinsic parameter. \xik = 1 for zoomed-out frames, \xik > 1 for zoomed-in frames. Step size \eta: Must satisfy \eta \in (0, 1/L]. PL constant \mu: Positive constant defining local strong convexity/PL condition. Lipschitz constant L: Positive constant such that \|\nabla Lj(a) - \nabla Lj(b)\|2 \leq L\|a - b\|2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mzentraining(images, initialzoomestimates, basefocallength, principalpoint): """ images: List of N images. initialzoomestimates: List of N zoom estimates. basefocallength: Tuple (fx, fy). principalpoint: Tuple (cx, cy). """ N = len(images) # Assume first Nout images are zoomed-out, rest are zoomed-in # In practice, Nout is determined by sorting zoom estimates or user input Nout = sum(1 for z in initialzoomestimates if z <= 1.1) # Heuristic Nin = N - Nout # Phase A: Global Pose Bootstrap # Initialize parameters theta = randominitnerf() poses = [] for i in range(N): if i < Nout: # Zoomed-out: init zoom to 1, random pose R = randomrotation() t = randomtranslation() xi = 1.0 poses.append({'R': R, 't': t, 'xi': xi}) else: # Zoomed-in: not used in Phase A loss, but need placeholder poses.append({'R': None, 't': None, 'xi': initialzoomestimates[i]}) # Minimize Lcoarse for iteration in range(phaseaiters): loss = 0.0 gradtheta = zeroslike(theta) gradposes = [zeroslike(p) for p in poses] for i in range(Nout): # Render image i camparams = { 'R': poses[i]['R'], 't': poses[i]['t'], 'f': basefocallength, 'c': principalpoint, 'xi': poses[i]['xi'] } rendered = rendernerf(theta, camparams) error = rendered - images[i] loss += sum(error2) # Compute gradients (backprop through renderer) dlossdtheta = gradnerf(theta, camparams, error) dlossdpose = gradpose(theta, camparams, error) gradtheta += dlossdtheta gradposes[i]['R'] += dlossdpose['R'] gradposes[i]['t'] += dlossdpose['t'] gradposes[i]['xi'] += dlossdpose['xi'] # Update parameters theta -= stepsize gradtheta for i in range(Nout): poses[i]['R'] -= stepsize gradposes[i]['R'] poses[i]['t'] -= stepsize gradposes[i]['t'] poses[i]['xi'] -= stepsize gradposes[i]['xi'] thetaA = theta posesA = poses[:Nout] # Phase B: Cross-Zoom Pose Registration # Freeze theta thetaB = thetaA # Initialize poses for zoomed-in images using pose priming for j in range(Nout, N): # Find best matching zoomed-out image g bestg = -1 minmse = infinity for g in range(Nout): # Create surrogate view # Extract central 1/xij crop from image[g] # Resize to native resolution of image[j] surrogate = createsurrogate(images[g], poses[g]['xi'], images[j].shape, poses[j]['xi']) mse = sum((surrogate - images[j])2) if mse < minmse: minmse = mse bestg = g # Priming: Copy pose from bestg poses[j]['R'] = poses[bestg]['R'] poses[j]['t'] = poses[bestg]['t'] poses[j]['xi'] = initialzoomestimates[j] # Or optimize xij too? Source says optimize xij # Optimize poses for zoomed-in images for iteration in range(phasebiters): loss = 0.0 gradposesin = [zeroslike(p) for p in poses[Nout:]] for j in range(Nout, N): camparams = { 'R': poses[j]['R'], 't': poses[j]['t'], 'f': basefocallength, 'c': principalpoint, 'xi': poses[j]['xi'] } rendered = rendernerf(thetaB, camparams) error = rendered - images[j] loss += sum(error2) # Only optimize pose, theta is frozen dlossdpose = gradpose(thetaB, camparams, error) gradposesin[j-Nout]['R'] += dlossdpose['R'] gradposesin[j-Nout]['t'] += dlossdpose['t'] gradposesin[j-Nout]['xi'] += dlossdpose['xi'] # Update poses for zoomed-in images for idx, j in enumerate(range(Nout, N)): poses[j]['R'] -= stepsize gradposesin[idx]['R'] poses[j]['t'] -= stepsize gradposesin[idx]['t'] poses[j]['xi'] -= stepsize gradposesin[idx]['xi'] posesB = poses # Full set of poses after Phase B # Phase C: Joint Refinement thetaC = thetaA posesC = posesB for iteration in range(phaseciters): loss = 0.0 gradtheta = zeroslike(thetaC) gradposes = [zeroslike(p) for p in posesC] for k in range(N): camparams = { 'R': posesC[k]['R'], 't': posesC[k]['t'], 'f': basefocallength, 'c': principalpoint, 'xi': posesC[k]['xi'] } rendered = rendernerf(thetaC, camparams) error = rendered - images[k] loss += sum(error2) dlossdtheta = gradnerf(thetaC, camparams, error) dlossdpose = gradpose(thetaC, camparams, error) gradtheta += dlossdtheta gradposes[k]['R'] += dlossdpose['R'] gradposes[k]['t'] += dlossdpose['t'] gradposes[k]['xi'] += dlossdpose['xi'] # Update all parameters thetaC -= stepsize gradtheta for k in range(N): posesC[k]['R'] -= stepsize gradposes[k]['R'] posesC[k]['t'] -= stepsize gradposes[k]['t'] posesC[k]['xi'] -= stepsize gradposes[k]['xi'] return thetaC, posesC Instability: Simultaneous optimization of NeRF parameters and camera poses across all zoom levels is unstable. The three-phase schedule is required. Unidentifiable Coupling: Standard NeRF formulations assume fixed or small zoom-level perturbations. When magnification changes significantly, translation, scale, and focal length become coupled in an unidentifiable way, causing pose-free NeRFs to fail. Pose Priming: Random initialization for zoomed-in views leads to O(\sigma{rand}^2) initial error. Pose priming reduces this to O(\delta^2) where \delta is the crop misregistration error, ensuring convergence within the local strong convexity neighborhood. Time Complexity: The method requires three sequential optimization phases. Phase B involves matching each zoomed-in image to a zoomed-out image, adding an O(N{in} \cdot N{out}) matching cost per iteration if done naively, though typically done once for initialization. The core optimization cost is dominated by the volume rendering integration in each phase. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory usage for MLP weights plus camera parameters. No additional large data structures like grids or pyramids are required. Performance: MZEN outperforms ablations that skip Phase B or train only on zoomed-in images. It achieves stable reconstruction where standard pose-free NeRFs fail. Strengths: Does not require high-resolution images or external pose initialization (SfM). Handles large zoom variations explicitly. Limitations: Requires a clear distinction between zoomed-out and zoomed-in views. Relies on the assumption that zoomed-out views provide a stable global scaffold. MZEN was introduced to address the limitations of Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and standard NeRF in industrial imaging systems (optical microscopes, digital inspection cameras, SEMs) where exact camera calibration is unavailable and the specimen stage moves only microns. Classical SfM fails in these conditions, and standard NeRF assumes fixed or small zoom-level perturbations. The method was published in Machine Learning (2026). name: UV Volumes
head: UV Volume Representation
body: UV Volumes is a method for real-time, editable free-view rendering of human performers that decouples smooth 3D geometry and density from high-frequency appearance. It differs from standard NeRF by encoding smooth density and UV coordinates in a 3D feature volume while storing detailed appearance in a 2D Neural Texture Stack (NTS), enabling real-time performance and retexturing. Inputs: Multi-view videos of a human performer, a posed SMPL model parameterized by pose \theta, and latent codes \mathbf{z} anchored to SMPL vertices. Outputs: A rendered RGB image for a given camera view. Data Structures: 1. UV Volumes: A 3D feature volume generated by a 3D sparse CNN, storing feature vectors f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}, \theta) at 3D points \mathbf{x}. 2. Neural Texture Stack (NTS): A set of 2D texture representations \mathcal{E}k for each body part k, generated by a CNN texture generator G. 3. SMPL Model: Provides the posed mesh structure used for ray sampling bounds. Steps: 1. Generate UV Volumes: Voxelize the latent codes \mathbf{z} anchored on the SMPL vertices. Input these voxels into a 3D sparse CNN to produce the 3D feature volume (UV volumes). 2. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{r}, sample N points \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^N along the ray between near and far bounds. The bounds are determined by the intersection of the ray with the posed SMPL model. 3. Feature Query and Density Prediction: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i, query the feature vector f(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{z}, \theta) from the UV volumes. Predict the volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) using a shallow MLP M\sigma: \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) = M\sigma(f(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{z}, \theta)) where M\sigma is a shallow MLP. 4. Volume Rendering of Feature Map: Render the feature volume into a 2D feature map \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r}) using standard volume rendering. Calculate the accumulated transmittance Ti and the weighted sum of features: Ti = \exp \left( - \sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(\mathbf{x}j) \deltaj \right) \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \deltai)) f(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{z}, \theta) where \deltai = \|\mathbf{x}{i+1} - \mathbf{x}i\|2 is the distance between adjacent sampled points. 5. UV Image Generation: Decode the feature map \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r}) pixel-by-pixel using an MLP M{uv} to predict part assignments \hat{\mathcal{P}} and UV coordinates \hat{\mathcal{U}}, \hat{\mathcal{V}}: \left(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathbf{r}), \hat{\mathcal{U}}(\mathbf{r}), \hat{\mathcal{V}}(\mathbf{r})\right) = M{uv}(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{r})) The part assignments satisfy \sum{k=1}^{Nk} \hat{\mathcal{P}}k(\mathbf{r}) = 1. 6. Generate Neural Texture Stack (NTS): Use a CNN texture generator G conditioned on the pose \theta and one-hot labels \mathbf{k} for each body part to generate the NTS \mathcal{E}: \mathcal{E}k = G(\theta, \mathbf{k}) The body surface is subdivided into Nk = 24 parts. 7. Color Reconstruction: Interpolate texture embeddings from the NTS using the predicted UV coordinates and part assignments. For each pixel, the final color is recovered by querying the NTS at the predicted UV coordinates weighted by the part assignments. Parameters: Nk = 24: Number of body parts used to subdivide the body surface for the NTS. N: Number of samples along the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SMPL Dependency: Ray sampling bounds rely on the accuracy of the posed SMPL model. Part Assignment: The part assignments \hat{\mathcal{P}} must sum to 1. Performance: Renders 960 × 540 images at an average of 30 FPS on CMU Panoptic, ZJU Mocap, and H36M datasets. Strengths: Real-time rendering, editability (retexturing), and better generalization on novel poses and shapes due to the mapping between the parameterized human model and smooth texture coordinates. Limitations: Relies on the SMPL model for geometry and sampling. UV Volumes was introduced to address the high computational costs of real-time free-view human rendering in VR/AR applications. It builds on the idea of separating smooth 3D properties from high-frequency appearance, leveraging the SMPL model for pose-dependent texture generation. UV Volumes for Real-time Rendering of Editable Free-view Human Performance, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01595, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Switch-NeRF
head: HMoHE, Heterogeneous Mixture of Hash Experts
body: Switch-NeRF++ is a large-scale Neural Radiance Field method that uses a trainable decomposition and heterogeneous representation to scale NeRF to large scenes, extending Switch-NeRF with hash-based networks and heterogeneous experts. It employs a Heterogeneous Mixture of Hash Experts (HMoHE) framework where a hash-based gating network dynamically routes 3D points to specialized hash experts with varying resolution ranges, allowing the network to select a suitable resolution range for each scene part. Unlike Switch-NeRF which uses homogeneous experts and an MLP-based gating network, Switch-NeRF++ uses heterogeneous hash experts and a hash-based gating network to learn heterogeneous decomposition and representation efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D point coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, view direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and an appearance embedding \mathbf{a}. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c} for the point \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: Hash Experts: There are N hash experts. Each expert i consists of a multi-resolution hash encoding grid with a distinct resolution range. Gating Network: A hash-based gating network G that maps point features into gate values G(\mathbf{x}). Prediction Heads: Small MLPs for density and color prediction. Numbered Steps: 1. Gating Network Evaluation: For a 3D point \mathbf{x}, the hash-based gating network computes gate values. This involves looking up feature encoding \mathbf{f}g in the hash encoding by computing a hash value of \mathbf{x}, and using a small MLP to predict gating values. 2. Gate Normalization: Compute gate values G = \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{f}g). 3. Expert Selection: Select the top-1 hash expert i using i = \arg \max(G). 4. Expert Feature Encoding: Compute the feature encoding \mathbf{E}i(\mathbf{x}) using the selected hash expert i. 5. Gate Application: Multiply the gate value by the expert output to ensure differentiability: \hat{\mathbf{E}}i(\mathbf{x}) = Gi \cdot \mathbf{E}i(\mathbf{x}). 6. Direction Encoding: Compute spherical harmonics of direction \mathbf{d}: \text{SH}d = \text{SphericalHarmonics}(\mathbf{d}). 7. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate features: \mathbf{f}{\text{final}} = [\hat{\mathbf{E}}i(\mathbf{x}), \text{SH}d, \mathbf{a}], where \mathbf{a} is the appearance embedding. 8. Density Prediction: Predict density \sigma = \text{MLP}{\text{density}}(\hat{\mathbf{E}}i(\mathbf{x})). 9. Color Prediction: Predict color \mathbf{c} = \text{MLP}{\text{color}}(\hat{\mathbf{E}}i(\mathbf{x})). 10. Rendering: Render the pixel color using volume rendering along the ray. 11. Loss Calculation: Compute the rendering loss and the gate balance loss. Formulas: Transmittance: Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). Rendered Color: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i. Rendering Loss: Lr = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} ||\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})||^2. Gate Balance Loss: Lb = \sumn fi gi. Overall Loss: Lo = Lr + \lambda Lb. Parameters: Number of hash experts N = 8. Learning rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially decreasing. Balance loss weight \lambda: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Pitfalls: The discrete selection operation of experts is not differentiable, and gradients cannot be back-propagated through it into the gating network. This is addressed by multiplying gate values to the expert outputs. A single gating network is used to avoid large increases in memory and computation cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def softmax(x): maxx = max(x) expx = [math.exp(xi - maxx) for xi in x] sumexp = sum(expx) return [e / sumexp for e in expx] def sphericalharmonics(d, degree=4): # Standard spherical harmonics encoding for direction d sh = [] dx, dy, dz = d for l in range(degree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): sh.append(math.sin(l math.atan2(math.sqrt(dx2 + dy2), dz)) math.cos(m math.atan2(dy, dx))) return sh def concatenate(lists): return [item for sublist in lists for item in sublist] def diff(t, prepend=None): if prepend is not None: t = [prepend] + t return [t[i] - t[i-1] for i in range(1, len(t))] def cumsum(x): res = [] s = 0.0 for xi in x: s += xi res.append(s) return res def linspace(start, stop, num): if num == 1: return [start] step = (stop - start) / (num - 1) return [start + i step for i in range(num)] def oneslike(x): return [1.0] len(x) def switchnerfforward(x, d, a, gatinghash, experts, densityhead, colorhead): # 1. Gating Network Evaluation fg = lookuphash(gatinghash, x) # Hash lookup operation gatevalues = smallmlp(fg) # Small MLP prediction # 2. Gate Normalization G = softmax(gatevalues) # 3. Expert Selection (Top-1) i = G.index(max(G)) # 4. Expert Feature Encoding Eix = lookuphash(experts[i], x) # Hash lookup operation # 5. Gate Application Gi = G[i] Ehatix = [Gi val for val in Eix] # 6. Direction Encoding SHd = sphericalharmonics(d) # 7. Feature Concatenation ffinal = concatenate([Ehatix, SHd, a]) # 8. Density Prediction sigma = densityhead(Ehatix) # Returns scalar # 9. Color Prediction c = colorhead(Ehatix) # Returns list of 3 return sigma, c def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, near, far, numsamples, gatinghash, experts, densityhead, colorhead, appearanceembedding): t = linspace(near, far, numsamples) points = [[rayorigin[j] + t[k] raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] for k in range(numsamples)] sigmalist = [] clist = [] for point in points: sigma, c = switchnerfforward(point, raydirection, appearanceembedding, gatinghash, experts, densityhead, colorhead) sigmalist.append(sigma) clist.append(c) # Volume Rendering delta = diff(t, prepend=near) if len(delta) < len(sigmalist): delta.append(delta[-1]) alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigmalist[k] delta[k]) for k in range(len(sigmalist))] transmittanceexponents = cumsum([sigmalist[k] delta[k] for k in range(len(sigmalist))]) T = [math.exp(-exponent) for exponent in transmittanceexponents] # Shift T right to get transmittance BEFORE each sample: Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) T = [1.0] + T[:-1] renderedcolor = [sum(T[k] alpha[k] clist[k][j] for k in range(len(sigmalist))) for j in range(3)] return renderedcolor Time Complexity: Switch-NeRF++ achieves an 8x acceleration in training and a 16x acceleration in rendering compared to Switch-NeRF. It achieves state-of-the-art results with 5.5h training (50k steps), which is 8x faster than Switch-NeRF (44h) and 5x faster than Mega-NeRF (30h). Memory Complexity: Hash dispatching uses less GPU memory in training compared to MoE dispatching. Measured Performance: On the UrbanBIS scene (6.5km², 13k images), Switch-NeRF++ achieved a PSNR of 20.76, compared to 19.58 for INGP. Strengths: Highly scalable to large-scale scenes, end-to-end trainable, efficient hash-based gating and dispatching, heterogeneous representation for diverse scene parts. When to use: Large-scale scene modeling where scalability and efficiency are critical. When not to use: Small-scale scenes where simpler methods like Instant-NGP might be sufficient. Switch-NeRF++ was introduced in. It extends the previous Switch-NeRF method. The method is evaluated on Mega-NeRF, UrbanBIS, Block-NeRF, and MatrixCity datasets. Learning Heterogeneous Mixture of Scene Experts for Large-Scale Neural Radiance Fields., https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3603305, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Low-Light NeRF (LLNeRF)
body: Low-Light NeRF (LLNeRF) is an unsupervised method that enhances scene representation and synthesizes normal-light novel views directly from sRGB low-light images by decomposing radiance field learning into view-dependent and view-independent components. It solves the problem of training NeRF on camera-finished low dynamic range (LDR) sRGB images, which suffer from low signal-to-noise ratio, non-linearity introduced by the camera ISP, and color distortion. Unlike HDR-NeRF, which requires RAW data with exposure metadata, LLNeRF operates on standard sRGB images without ground truth supervision. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Rip-NeRF or SUDS by explicitly modeling the multiplicative relationship between lighting intensity and intrinsic color basis to jointly enhance illumination and correct colors during optimization. Inputs and Outputs Input: A collection of camera-finished, low dynamic range (8-bit/channel) sRGB images from a low-light scene. Output: A radiance field model capable of rendering novel views with enhanced lighting, reduced noise, and corrected colors. Data Structures and Network Architecture The model extends the standard NeRF MLP architecture. The input coordinates \tau (position) and view direction d are processed by two separate MLPs: 1. Density MLP (F{density}): Takes encoded position features. Outputs a single scalar for volume density \sigma. 2. Feature MLP 1 (F1): Takes encoded position features and view direction d. Outputs a single-channel vector v representing the view-dependent lighting intensity. 3. Feature MLP 2 (F2): Takes encoded position features. Outputs a 3-channel vector r representing the view-independent intrinsic color basis. The standard NeRF color branch is replaced by this decomposition. The predicted color c for a sample is the element-wise product (Hadamard product) of v and r: c = v \bullet r where v \in \mathbb{R}^1 and r \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rendering Equation The rendering process uses the standard volume rendering integral. For a ray r, the final pixel color cr is: cr = \sum{i=1}^N wi ci = \sum{i=1}^N \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj}) \right) (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between samples, \sigmai is the density, and ci is the color at sample i. Enhancement Mechanism To enhance the image, the method applies an enhancement function \phi to the view-dependent component v while keeping the view-independent component r unchanged. The enhanced color \hat{c} is computed as: \hat{c} = \phi(v) \bullet r The function \phi is typically a simple scaling or tone-mapping operation that increases the intensity of v. The enhanced color \hat{c} is used in the rendering equation instead of c. Optimization The model is optimized in an unsupervised manner. The loss function minimizes the difference between the rendered enhanced image and the input low-light image, or utilizes self-supervision constraints inherent to the decomposition. The sources do not specify the exact loss function formulation, only that the optimization is unsupervised. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def llnerfforward(positions, directions, densitymlp, featuremlpv, featuremlpr, enhancementfunc): """ Computes the enhanced color for a set of points along a ray. Args: positions: Tensor of shape (N, 3), world-space positions. directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3), normalized view directions. densitymlp: MLP predicting density from position features. featuremlpv: MLP predicting view-dependent intensity v from position and direction. featuremlpr: MLP predicting view-independent color basis r from position. enhancementfunc: Function phi(v) to enhance lighting intensity. Returns: enhancedcolor: Tensor of shape (N, 3), enhanced RGB colors. density: Tensor of shape (N, 1), volume densities. """ # 1. Predict Density # densitymlp takes positional encoding of positions density = densitymlp(positions) # 2. Predict View-Dependent Component v (Lighting Intensity) # featuremlpv takes positional encoding of positions AND directional encoding of directions v = featuremlpv(positions, directions) # v has shape (N, 1) # 3. Predict View-Independent Component r (Color Basis) # featuremlpr takes positional encoding of positions r = featuremlpr(positions) # r has shape (N, 3) # 4. Apply Enhancement # Enhance the lighting component v venhanced = enhancementfunc(v) # 5. Compute Enhanced Color # Element-wise multiplication: chat = phi(v) r enhancedcolor = venhanced r return enhancedcolor, density Parameters Input Image Format: 8-bit/channel sRGB. Network Depth/Width: The sources mention "Feature MLP 1 (8x256)" and "Feature MLP 2 (1x256)" in Figure 3, suggesting hidden dimensions of 256. The exact number of layers is not explicitly stated in the text, but Figure 3 implies a multi-layer structure. Positional Encoding: Uses the Mip-NeRF implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-Linearity: Standard NeRF fails on low-light sRGB images because the camera ISP process changes linearity and blends scene radiance with noise. LLNeRF addresses this by decomposing the color, but the method assumes the decomposition can effectively separate lighting from color despite this non-linearity. Noise: Low signal-to-noise ratio in sRGB images causes color distortion that NeRF cannot handle directly. The decomposition helps reduce noise by isolating it in the view-dependent component which is then enhanced. View Inconsistency: Combining 2D low-light enhancement with NeRF causes view inconsistency. LLNeRF avoids this by performing enhancement within the 3D radiance field optimization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method produces novel view images with proper lighting, vivid colors, and details, outperforming existing low-light enhancement methods and NeRF methods. Strengths: Works on camera-finished sRGB images without RAW data or exposure metadata; unsupervised; jointly enhances illumination, reduces noise, and corrects colors. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that lighting can be separated into a view-dependent scalar component and a view-independent color basis, which may not hold for all complex lighting scenarios. The specific enhancement function \phi is not detailed, potentially limiting reproducibility. When to use: When only low-light sRGB images are available and RAW data is not accessible. When not to use: When RAW data with exposure metadata is available, as HDR-NeRF might be more appropriate. LLNeRF was proposed in the paper "Lighting up NeRF via Unsupervised Decomposition and Enhancement". It addresses the limitations of previous NeRF variants that required high-quality input images or RAW data. The method builds on the standard NeRF framework and Mip-NeRF's positional encoding. It is distinct from RawNeRF, which uses RAW data, and from methods that pre-enhance images, which suffer from view inconsistency. name: Compression and Model Efficiency
body: This family covers methods that reduce the memory footprint and computational cost of NeRF representations through low-rank tensor approximations, weight decomposition, and pruning CCNeRF, Low Rank NeRF Approximation with ADMM,. It differs from sibling methods that modify architecture for specific tasks by focusing strictly on compressing the existing radiance field parameters or optimizing them under rank constraints. Methods in this family reduce model size by approximating dense parameters with low-rank structures or pruning weights. The rendering equation remains standard volume rendering, but the radiance field query is computed via decomposed components or optimized under rank constraints CCNeRF, Low Rank NeRF Approximation with ADMM. This reduces the number of trainable parameters from O(N^2) or O(N^3) to O(N \cdot r) or O(N \cdot r^2), where r is the target rank. A hybrid tensor rank decomposition method that models the radiance field only with tensor components, avoiding MLPs in the rendering path to preserve low-rank properties CCNeRF. It supports dynamic model size adjustment via rank truncation and arbitrary composition via rank concatenation CCNeRF. Choose this when you need a purely tensor-based representation that allows for scene composition and dynamic compression without retraining CCNeRF. This method reduces the model size of a trained NeRF by decomposing fully connected layer weights into a Tensor Train (TT) format Low Rank NeRF Approximation with ADMM. It solves the resulting rank-constrained optimization problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to minimize reconstruction error while enforcing low-rank structure Low Rank NeRF Approximation with ADMM. It is distinguished from sibling methods like CCNeRF by its specific use of ADMM for rank-constrained weight decomposition rather than other compression techniques Low Rank NeRF Approximation with ADMM. A pruning-based continual learning approach applied to NeRF for multiple scenes. Uses a pruning rate of 0.5. Choose this when continual learning across multiple scenes is required with a fixed pruning budget. PackNet was adapted to NeRF for continual learning scenarios, demonstrating that pruning can maintain performance across multiple scenes. The SCARF framework compares this with MEIL-NeRF and CLNeRF, which handle single-scene continual learning. SCARF: Scalable Continual Learning Framework for Memory‐efficient Multiple Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.15255, fetched 2026-10-26

name: CCNeRF
head: Compressible-Composable NeRF, Rank-residual Decomposition NeRF
body: CCNeRF is a neural field representation that enables efficient compression and composition of 3D scenes by learning a hybrid tensor rank decomposition of the scene without using neural networks for rendering. Unlike NeRF variants that rely on a shared MLP renderer (e.g., NSVF) or use MLPs that prevent direct compression/composition (e.g., TensoRF), CCNeRF models the radiance field only with tensor rank decomposition, allowing arbitrary composition via rank concatenation and dynamic size adjustment via rank truncation without retraining. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D images of a 3D scene with known camera poses. Output: A compressed, composable 3D representation consisting of decomposed rank components and a weight matrix, capable of rendering novel views via standard volume rendering. Data Structures: The model represents a 3D scene as a 4D feature volume described by rank components and a weight matrix. The structure consists of: 1. Rank Weights Matrix (W): A matrix storing weights for different feature channels. 2. Decomposed Rank Components: A set of components that are either vector-based (CP decomposition) or matrix-based (triple plane variant). Vector-based (CP): Factor matrices U^x, U^y, U^z for spatial dimensions. Matrix-based (Triple Plane): Factor matrices \mathcal{U}^{xy}, \mathcal{U}^{xz}, \mathcal{U}^{yz} representing 2D planes. The ratio of vector- to matrix-based components is controllable to trade off between model size and performance. 3. Transformation Matrices: For composition, each object stores a transformation matrix to control its position and orientation in the composed scene. Formulas: The rendering follows the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(r) = \sumi Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j<i} (1 - \alphai), \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Here, \sigmai is density, ci is color, and ti is the sample position along ray r from origin o with direction d. The core representation uses a hybrid tensor rank decomposition. For a 3D tensor T \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}, the Tucker decomposition is defined as: T{i,j,k} = \sum{p=1}^P \sum{q=1}^Q \sum{r=1}^R S{p,q,r} U^x{i,p} U^y{j,q} U^z{k,r} where S is the core tensor and U^x, U^y, U^z are factor matrices. CCNeRF employs a rank-residual learning strategy to encourage lower ranks to preserve more important information, enabling near-optimal low-rank approximation at any targeted rank via an empirical sort-and-truncate strategy. Steps: 1. Scene Representation: Learn the hybrid tensor rank decomposition of the scene. The scene is modeled by a 4D feature volume described by a set of rank components and a weight matrix. 2. Querying a 3D Coordinate: a. Project the 3D coordinate to the decomposed vectors or matrices. b. Perform weighted interpolation using the stored rank weights. 3. Compression (Rank Truncation): a. Sort the rank components based on their importance (derived from the rank-residual learning). b. Truncate the components to a target rank R{target}. This dynamically adjusts model size and detail level without retraining. 4. Composition: a. To compose different models, concatenate their rank components along the rank dimension. b. Record a transformation matrix for each object to control its position and orientation. c. To mitigate storage growth in complex scenes, compress less important objects by applying rank truncation to them. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryccnerf(x, rankcomponents, weights): """ Query the radiance field at coordinate x. x: 3D coordinate (x, y, z) rankcomponents: List of decomposed components (vectors or matrices) weights: Matrix of rank weights """ # Project coordinate to decomposed vectors/matrices projectedvalues = [] for comp in rankcomponents: if comp.type == 'vector': # Vector-based (CP) projection val = comp.Ux[x.x] comp.Uy[x.y] comp.Uz[x.z] elif comp.type == 'matrix': # Matrix-based (Triple Plane) projection val = comp.Uxy[x.x, x.y] + comp.Uxz[x.x, x.z] + comp.Uyz[x.y, x.z] projectedvalues.append(val) # Weighted interpolation # Note: Exact interpolation formula depends on specific hybrid implementation details # not fully specified in sources, but generally involves combining projected values # with the weight matrix W. # Assuming a linear combination weighted by the rank weights for simplicity # as the source describes "weighted interpolation". result = sum(p w for p, w in zip(projectedvalues, weights)) return result def compressccnerf(rankcomponents, targetrank): """ Compress the model by truncating rank components. rankcomponents: List of rank components sorted by importance targetrank: Number of components to keep """ # Empirical sort-and-truncate strategy # Assumes components are pre-sorted by importance metric derived from # rank-residual learning. return rankcomponents[:targetrank] def composeccnerf(models): """ Compose multiple CCNeRF models into one scene. models: List of model objects, each containing rankcomponents and transformmatrix """ composedrankcomponents = [] composedtransforms = [] for model in models: # Concatenate rank components along the rank dimension composedrankcomponents.extend(model.rankcomponents) composedtransforms.append(model.transformmatrix) return { 'rankcomponents': composedrankcomponents, 'transforms': composedtransforms } Parameters: Target Rank: The number of components kept in the decomposition determines the model size and detail level. Lower ranks preserve primary information due to rank-residual learning. Ratio of Vector- to Matrix-based Components: Controllable to trade off between model size and performance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard truncated Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) does not hold the optimal property of truncated SVD, but yields a quasi-optimal solution sufficient for practical use. The method relies on the assumption that the scene exhibits low-rank structure; if the scene is highly complex or noisy, compression artifacts may appear. A strategy to encourage lower ranks to preserve more important information, enabling near-optimal low-rank approximation. Choose when dynamic compression without retraining is required. CCNeRF Combines CP (vector-based) and Triple Plane (matrix-based) decompositions. Choose when a balance between compactness and representational power is needed. CCNeRF Time Complexity: Querying is O(R) where R is the number of rank components, significantly faster than MLP-based NeRFs which are O(D) where D is the MLP dimension. Compression and composition are O(1) for concatenation and O(R \log R) for sorting during truncation. Memory Complexity: O(R \cdot (H+W+D)) for CP components and O(R \cdot (HW+HD+WD)) for Triple Plane components, compared to O(H \cdot W \cdot D) for dense volumes. Measured Performance: The method achieves comparable rendering quality to state-of-the-art methods while enabling extra capabilities of compression and composition. Strengths: No neural networks for rendering, allowing arbitrary composition without retraining or compatibility constraints; dynamic model size adjustment via rank truncation; near-optimal compression without extra optimization. Limitations: Quasi-optimal solution for truncated HOSVD; requires careful selection of target rank and component type ratio. When to use: When compression and composition of 3D scenes are required without the overhead of neural network inference for rendering. When not to use: When the highest possible rendering quality is required without any compression artifacts, or when the scene does not exhibit low-rank structure. CCNeRF was introduced by Jiaxiang Tang, Xiaokang Chen, Jingbo Wang, and Gang Zeng from Peking University and Chinese University of Hong Kong in 2022. It addresses the difficulty of manipulating NeRF models (like compression and composition) caused by their implicit representation and shared renderer networks. The method is motivated by the low-rank approximation property of the SVD algorithm and builds on tensor decomposition techniques used in vision tasks. It contrasts with TensoRF, which uses MLPs that prevent compression/composition, by modeling the field only with tensor rank decomposition.
