name: Low Rank NeRF Approximation with ADMM
head: TT Decompression via ADMM, Tensor Train NeRF Compression
body: This method reduces the model size of a trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by approximating its fully connected layer weights with a Tensor Train (TT) format. It solves the resulting rank-constrained optimization problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to minimize reconstruction error while enforcing low-rank structure. It differs from sibling methods like CCNeRF by explicitly using ADMM to iteratively refine the weight matrices into TT cores, rather than relying solely on static decomposition or pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model with fully connected layer weight matrices \mathbf{W}i \in \mathbb{R}^{n1 \times n2} and bias vectors \mathbf{b}i. Output: Low-rank Tensor Train cores \mathbf{Q}{1i}, \mathbf{Q}{2i} and unchanged bias vectors \mathbf{b}i. Data Structures: Weight Matrix \mathbf{W}i: Original full-rank matrix of size n1 \times n2. TT Cores: \mathbf{Q}{1i}: Tensor of shape 1 \times n1 \times r. In implementation, the first dimension is squeezed, resulting in a matrix of size n1 \times r. \mathbf{Q}{2i}: Tensor of shape r \times n2 \times 1. In implementation, the last dimension is squeezed, resulting in a matrix of size r \times n2. r: Target rank (integer). Dual Multiplier \mathbf{U}i: Matrix of size n1 \times n2, initialized to zero or previous iteration values. Auxiliary Variable \mathbf{Z}i: Matrix of size n1 \times n2, used in ADMM updates. Parameters: Rank r: Controls compression ratio. Typical experimental values: 40, 50, 70, 90. Penalty Parameter \rho: Positive scalar for the augmented Lagrangian. Value not given in the sources. Learning Rate: For gradient descent step. Value not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: The optimization minimizes the Lagrangian \mathcal{L} defined below. The process iterates until convergence. 1. Initialize: Set \mathbf{W}i^{(0)} to the trained weights, \mathbf{U}i^{(0)} = \mathbf{0}, and \mathbf{Z}i^{(0)} = \mathbf{0}. Set iteration counter t=0. 2. W-Update: Update \mathbf{W}i by minimizing the Lagrangian with respect to \mathbf{W}i using gradient descent. \mathbf{W}i^{(t+1)} = \arg\min{\mathbf{W}i} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{W}i, \mathbf{Z}i^{(t)}, \mathbf{U}i^{(t)}) 3. Z-Update: Update the auxiliary variable \mathbf{Z}i by projecting the sum of the updated weight and dual multiplier onto the set of rank-r matrices (TT format). \mathbf{Z}i^{(t+1)} = \Pir(\mathbf{W}i^{(t+1)} + \mathbf{U}i^{(t)}) where \Pir denotes the operation that decomposes the matrix into the TT format truncated to rank r. 4. U-Update: Update the dual multiplier. \mathbf{U}i^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{U}i^{(t)} + \mathbf{W}i^{(t+1)} - \mathbf{Z}i^{(t+1)} 5. Repeat: Increment t and repeat steps 2-4 until convergence. 6. Final Decomposition: After convergence, the optimized weights \mathbf{W}i are decomposed into \mathbf{Q}{1i} and \mathbf{Q}{2i} using the same TT decomposition logic as \Pir. The bias vectors \mathbf{b}i remain unchanged. Formulas: Augmented Lagrangian (Scaled Dual Form): \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{W}i, \mathbf{Z}i, \mathbf{U}i) = l(\mathbf{W}i) + g(\mathbf{Z}i) + \frac{\rho}{2}||\mathbf{W}i - \mathbf{Z}i + \mathbf{U}i||F^2 + \frac{\rho}{2}||\mathbf{U}i||F^2 where l(\mathbf{W}i) = ||\mathbf{c}' - \mathbf{c}{gt}||2^2 is the reconstruction error (rendered pixel value \mathbf{c}' vs ground truth \mathbf{c}{gt}), g(\mathbf{Z}i) is a regularization term enforcing the TT structure (implicit in the projection \Pir), \rho is the penalty parameter, and \mathbf{U}i is the dual multiplier. TT Decomposition: \mathbf{W}i = \mathbf{Q}{1i} \cdot \mathbf{Q}{2i} where \mathbf{Q}{1i} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n1 \times r} and \mathbf{Q}{2i} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n2 \times 1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def ttdecomposition(matrix, rank): """ Decomposes a matrix into Tensor Train format (rank r). Returns Q1 (n1 x r) and Q2 (r x n2). Implementation detail: Uses SVD or similar low-rank approximation. Note: The source cites [36] for details on Pir. We assume a standard low-rank approximation here. """ n1, n2 = matrix.shape # Truncated SVD to get rank r approximation U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(matrix, fullmatrices=False) # Take top r components Ur = U[:,:rank] Sr = np.diag(S[:rank]) Vtr = Vt[:rank,:] # TT Cores: Q1 = Ur sqrt(Sr), Q2 = sqrt(Sr) Vtr # This ensures Q1 @ Q2 approximates the original matrix sqrtSr = np.sqrt(Sr) Q1 = Ur @ sqrtSr Q2 = sqrtSr @ Vtr return Q1, Q2 def lowranknerfadmm(Winitial, rank, rho, numiterations, learningrate): """ Performs ADMM optimization to compress NeRF weights into TT format. Args: Winitial: Initial weight matrix (n1, n2) rank: Target rank r rho: Penalty parameter numiterations: Number of ADMM steps learningrate: Step size for W-update Returns: Q1, Q2: Tensor Train cores """ n1, n2 = Winitial.shape # Initialize variables W = Winitial.copy() U = np.zeroslike(W) Z = np.zeroslike(W) for t in range(numiterations): # Step 1: W-update # Minimize L(W, Z, U) w.r.t W using gradient descent. # L = l(W) + rho/2 ||W - Z + U||^2 + const # Gradient of l(W) is the gradient of the rendering loss. # Gradient of the quadratic term is rho (W - Z + U). # Note: The source states W-update uses gradient descent. # We need the gradient of the loss l(W). This is typically computed via backprop. # For this self-contained pseudocode, we assume a function computelossgrad exists. gradl = computelossgrad(W) # Placeholder for actual gradient computation from renderer # Gradient of the augmented Lagrangian term w.r.t W: # d/dW [ rho/2 ||W - Z + U||F^2 ] = rho (W - Z + U) gradaug = rho (W - Z + U) totalgrad = gradl + gradaug # Update W W = W - learningrate totalgrad # Step 2: Z-update # Z = Pir(W + U) Z = ttdecomposition(W + U, rank)[0] # ttdecomposition returns (Q1, Q2). # The source implies Z is the # rank-r approximation. We can store the # approximation directly or the cores. # Eq 13 says Z = Pir(...). # Let's assume Z is the matrix approximation. # Re-compute Z as the matrix approximation for the next step's U update # Actually, Eq 13 defines Z as the result of Pir. # Let's return the matrix approximation from ttdecomposition for Z. # But we need Q1, Q2 for the final output. # Let's adjust: Z is the projected matrix. U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(W + U, fullmatrices=False) Sr = np.diag(S[:rank]) Z = U[:,:rank] @ Sr @ Vt[:rank,:] # Step 3: U-update U = U + W - Z # Final decomposition for storage Q1, Q2 = ttdecomposition(W, rank) return Q1, Q2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias Parameters: Bias vectors \mathbf{b}i are rank 1 and are not optimized via ADMM; they remain unchanged. Approximation Error: Straightforward decomposition causes large error; ADMM is required to guarantee low-rank property without significant performance degradation. Camera Pose: The method assumes camera pose parameters (focal length f, parallax offset \Delta) are either known or treated as trainable variables alongside weights. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of ADMM iterations and the cost of SVD/TT decomposition per iteration. Each iteration involves a gradient descent step (cost of forward/backward pass) and a low-rank projection (SVD cost O(n1 n2 \min(n1, n2))). Memory Complexity: Reduces storage from O(n1 n2) to O(r(n1 + n2)) per layer. Performance: Compression ratio is controlled by rank r. Typical ranks 40-90 are used for light field scenes. Strengths: Maintains reconstruction quality better than naive low-rank approximation by using ADMM to optimize the weights under rank constraints. Limitations: Requires iterative optimization post-training. Performance degradation if rank is too low. The method was proposed by J. Shi et al. in "Distilled Low Rank Neural Radiance Field with Quantization for Light Field Compression". It builds on the idea that NeRF model size is a bottleneck for light field transmission. It uses Tensor Train decomposition [35] and ADMM [36] to solve the rank-constrained optimization problem. The approach is specifically tailored for structured light fields where camera parameters are simplified. name: Dynamic and Articulated Scene Modeling
body: Dynamic and Articulated Scene Modeling extends static radiance fields to handle time-varying geometry and non-rigid deformations, primarily in human performance capture. It solves the ill-posed problem of mapping dynamic 3D points to a static representation by introducing canonical spaces, skeletal constraints, or surface-relative encodings. Unlike static methods, these approaches must jointly optimize or infer pose, deformation, and appearance from monocular or sparse multi-view video inputs. All methods in this family map a 3D query point \mathbf{x} observed at time t to a canonical space \mathbf{x}c where the radiance field is static. The rendering process remains volume rendering, but the density \sigma and color c are conditioned on the deformation state. 1. Canonical Transformation: A transformation function T(\mathbf{x}, t) maps observation space to canonical space. Common strategies include: Skeleton-based: Using inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) or skeletal relative coordinates A-NeRF. Surface-based: Using signed distances to nearest neighbors in a reconstructed surface mesh SelfNeRF. Residual-based: Predicting radiance residuals in the canonical space conditioned on pose MoCo-NeRF. 2. Conditioning: The radiance field MLP F\omega takes the canonical point \mathbf{x}c, view direction \mathbf{v}, and often a pose or identity code as input. 3. Optimization: Training typically involves minimizing photometric loss \| C{rendered} - I{gt} \|. Articulated methods often include regularization terms for pose smoothness and consistency with initial pose estimates. MoCo-NeRF models non-rigid body motions as radiance residual fields rather than spatial offsets, using rigid skeletal transformations as a prior. It separates the canonical radiance representation from pose-dependent non-rigid residuals, allowing direct supervision from ground-truth pixel colors. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial deformation fields, it avoids high computational complexity by operating directly in the radiance space. Choose it for monocular human video rendering where residual-based conditioning is preferred over spatial offsets. Neural Scene Graphs decomposes dynamic, multi-object scenes into a learned hierarchical scene graph with decoupled object transformations and scene representations. It lifts the assumption of static scene consistency required by existing neural rendering methods. Unlike methods that encode the entire scene into a single network, it uses object-level implicit representations learned from video frames and tracking data. Choose it for novel view synthesis of dynamic multi-object scenes with unseen arrangements. A-NeRF learns a user-specific neural 3D body model and underlying skeleton pose from unlabelled monocular videos by extending NeRFs with a skeleton for time-varying motion. It defines spatial latent variables relative to the pose of body parts to overcome ill-posed inverse operations. Unlike MoCo-NeRF which uses residual-based conditioning, it uses skeleton-relative embeddings; unlike SelfNeRF which uses surface-based SDFs, it uses volumetric density conditioned on bone-relative coordinates. Choose it for unlabelled monocular human performance capture requiring joint pose and appearance optimization. PVA estimates a volumetric 3D avatar from a few input images of a human head, enabling view synthesis for unseen identities and expressions. It generalizes to new identities by combining neural radiance fields with local, pixel-aligned features extracted directly from input images, avoiding information loss associated with global latent codes. Unlike mesh-based methods, it captures arbitrary topology and high-frequency details without requiring explicit 3D supervision. Choose it for few-shot head avatar synthesis with arbitrary topology. SelfNeRF is a novel view synthesis method for human performance that trains from scratch using monocular self-rotating video inputs, achieving high-fidelity results in approximately twenty minutes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like MoCo-NeRF and A-NeRF by eliminating the need for multi-view inputs or explicit skeletal priors, instead relying on a surface-relative hash encoding to aggregate inter-frame information and accelerate training. Choose it for rapid training from monocular self-rotating videos without skeletal priors. CLA-NeRF is a differentiable representation for articulated objects that explicitly models part and joint attributes, disentangling camera pose, part pose, part segmentation, and joint attributes to allow independent control during rendering. It solves the problem of rendering deformable articulated objects at unseen poses and estimating their articulated pose from RGB images, without requiring CAD models or depth data. Unlike standard NeRF formulations which model camera poses but ignore object articulation, it predicts a part segmentation field alongside density and color, enabling the inference of joint attributes via line-fitting on the segmentation field. Choose it for general articulated object rendering and pose estimation without known joint attributes. DynaVol is an unsupervised 3D dynamic scene decomposition method that unifies geometric structures and object-centric learning within a differentiable volume rendering framework. It solves the multi-view mismatch of 2D object segmentation by ensuring 3D consistency, enabling novel view synthesis, and allowing direct scene editing. Unlike 2D image decomposition methods such as SAVi, it infers a probability distribution over objects at individual spatial locations via object-centric voxelization, facilitating fine-grained separation without geometric priors. Choose it for unsupervised 3D dynamic scene decomposition and direct editing. MI-NeRF is a method for learning a single unified dynamic neural radiance field (NeRF) that models complex non-rigid facial motion for multiple identities using only monocular videos of arbitrary length. It solves the problem of expensive per-identity optimization in dynamic face reconstruction by training a single implicit representation F\Theta conditioned on identity, expression, latent codes, position, and view direction. Unlike previous generic NeRF models that require static settings and multiple input views during training, it works for monocular videos captured in the wild, reducing total training time by up to 90% compared to standard single-identity NeRFs. Choose it for multi-identity dynamic face reconstruction from monocular videos. A feed-forward method for synthesizing novel-view videos of arbitrary human performers from sparse multi-view camera inputs (3-4 views) by learning generalizable neural radiance fields using a parametric 3D body model (SMPL) and transformer-based aggregation of spatio-temporal features. It constructs time-augmented skeletal features by leveraging SMPL and aggregates temporal information using a temporal transformer, followed by a multi-view transformer for cross-attention. A novel 360° free-view rendering method capable of reconstructing dynamic human-object-scene neural radiation fields from a single monocular video. It estimates complex object motion during human-object interaction by introducing new object skeletons into the traditional human skeletal hierarchy and uses two learnable object state embeddings for different interaction contexts. It significantly outperforms existing techniques on challenging datasets, with a 40% to 50% improvement on the LPIPS metric. A method for learning generic dynamic radiation fields from monocular video. It learns both point features and scene streams through video feature extraction, implicit velocity fields, and stream-based feature aggregation modules. It supports new applications such as scene editing, unseen frame synthesis, and fast new scene adaptation. Models deformations implicitly by conditioning the NeRF on a representation of the deformation state (e.g., a time input). Condition the volume on a vector that represents the deformed state. Conditioning input is a time input (potentially positionally encoded) or an auto-decoded latent code per time step. A method that uses a deformation MLP to model non-rigid scenes. It has no reliance on pre-computed scene information apart from camera parameters. NR-NeRF generates slightly less sharp outputs compared to Nerfies. A method that achieves scene deformation by using ray bending, allowing for complex rendering effects like bullet-time (time slice/freeze effect) without explicit supervision for rigidity network learning. Input consists of multiple images from a non-rigid scene with extrinsics and intrinsics. A single canonical neural radiance volume is searched/found, which is deformed via ray bending to render colors. Appearance and geometry information of the static canonical volume is weighted and parameterized with weights. Deformation modeling collects information from straight rays sent from the camera and defines a deformation that presents the ray bending deformation processing. Add MLP design on the ray bending with weight as input parameters. Handle mapping processing on the static canonical volume, gaining form from a designed auto-decoded latent code. Weakness: Takes a whole NeRF rendering network for a unit or independent object or scene rendering. A method that computes static and dynamic fields independently to enable separate rendering, object trajectory mapping, and non-rigid movement adaptation. Leverage annotations from keyframes and propagate them to adjacent frames to deduce scene flows, map object trajectories, and determine rigidities. Perform comprehensive end-to-end optimization to modify object placements, trajectories, and adapt to non-rigid movements. Leverage monocular video depth estimation to constrain time-varying geometry within a globally consistent representation. Model scene dynamics by encoding time information into the MLP, concatenating temporal data with spatial coordinates and view direction. Aggregate frame-wise 2.5D representations and propagate scene contents across time using a static scene loss. The extension of NeRF to dynamic scenes originated with the need to capture human performance and articulated objects from limited camera views. Early works like A-NeRF addressed the ill-posed nature of monocular dynamic reconstruction by introducing skeletal-relative encodings and joint optimization of pose and appearance. Subsequent methods like MoCo-NeRF and SelfNeRF refined this by decoupling rigid and non-rigid components or leveraging surface geometry for faster convergence. Generalizable approaches like Neural Human Performer and HOSNeRF further expanded the domain to sparse multi-view and single-view human-object interactions, respectively. name: MoCo-NeRF
head: Motion-Oriented Compositional Neural Radiance Fields
body: MoCo-NeRF is a framework for free-viewpoint rendering of monocular human videos that models non-rigid body motions as radiance residual fields rather than spatial offsets, using rigid skeletal transformations as a prior. It separates the canonical radiance representation from pose-dependent non-rigid residuals, allowing direct supervision from ground-truth pixel colors to optimize both components simultaneously. Unlike sibling methods like A-NeRF which may rely on spatial offsets or surface-based deformations, MoCo-NeRF avoids the high computational complexity and misaligned learning objectives associated with unbounded spatial offset prediction by operating directly in the radiance space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video frames I, camera poses, and skeletal joint positions J for each frame. Outputs: Rendered RGB images C{final} for arbitrary viewpoints and times. Data Structures: 1. Skeletal Weights Volume Decoder: An explicit volume decoder optimized to store canonical skinning weights w^ck for K joints. 2. Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding (MHE): A hash grid \psi{hash} with 16 levels and feature dimension H=2 per level. For multi-subject training, a global MHE \psi^G{hash} (4 levels, H=2) and Ns local MHEs \{\psi^i{hash}\} (16 levels, H=2) are used. 3. Learnable Base Code: A tensor S \in \mathbb{R}^{64} initialized randomly. 4. MLP Decoders: M{rigid}: Predicts rigid color and density. M{nr}: Predicts non-rigid color and density residuals. 5. Projection Matrices: Wp, WQ, WK, WV for pose-embedded feature generation. Numbered Steps: 1. Canonical Transformation: Transform an observation point \mathbf{x} at time t to canonical space \mathbf{x}c using inverse linear blend skinning: \mathbf{x}c = \sum{k=1}^K w^ok (Rk \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}k) where Rk, \mathbf{t}k are the rotation and translation of bone k, and observation weights w^ok are computed from canonical weights w^ck: w^ok = \frac{w^ck(Rk \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}k)}{\sum{j=1}^K w^cj(Rj \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}j)} The canonical weights w^ck are optimized via an explicit volume decoder. 2. Rigid Branch Feature Query: Query multiresolution volumetric features \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} from the MHE \psi{hash} (or global/local MHEs in multi-subject mode): \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} = \psi{hash}(\mathbf{x}c) Slice the first half (H dimensions) of \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} at each resolution level to compute \mathbf{f}^{:H}{\mathbf{x}c}. 3. Rigid Radiance Prediction: Predict rigid color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma using decoder M{rigid}: \mathbf{c}, \sigma = M{rigid}(\mathbf{f}^{:H}{\mathbf{x}c}) Note: In multi-subject mode, concatenate global features, sliced local features, and subject ID code \mathbf{S}i: \mathbf{c}, \sigma = M{rigid}(\psi^G{hash}(\mathbf{x}c) \oplus (\psi^i{hash}(\mathbf{x}c))^{:H} \oplus \mathbf{S}i) \quad \text{} 4. Non-Rigid Feature Preparation: Use the full feature \mathbf{f}{\mathbf{x}c} but freeze the first half representing canonical radiance. Denote the remaining optimized half as \mathbf{f}^{\mathbf{x}c}. 5. Pose-Embedded Implicit Feature Generation: a. Initialize learnable base code \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{64}. b. Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma to 23 joint positions \mathbf{J} = \{\mathbf{j}i\}{i=1}^{23} with L=10 frequency bands: \gamma(\mathbf{j}i) = [\mathbf{j}i, \sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{j}i), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{j}i), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{j}i), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{j}i)] Resulting in \gamma(\mathbf{J}) \in \mathbb{R}^{23 \times 63}. c. Project encoded joints to raw pose-embedded code \mathbf{P}{raw} using projection matrix Wp: \mathbf{P}{raw} = Wp \cdot \gamma(\mathbf{J}) d. Generate query \mathbf{P}q from \mathbf{S}, and key \mathbf{P}k, value \mathbf{P}v from \mathbf{P}{raw} via linear projections: \mathbf{P}q = WQ \cdot \mathbf{S}, \quad \mathbf{P}k = WK \cdot \mathbf{P}{raw}, \quad \mathbf{P}v = WV \cdot \mathbf{P}{raw} e. Compute final implicit feature \mathbf{P}{nr} using cross-attention: \mathbf{P}{nr} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{P}q \cdot \mathbf{P}k^\top) \cdot \mathbf{P}v 6. Non-Rigid Radiance Residual Prediction: Predict color \Delta \mathbf{c} and density \Delta \sigma residuals using decoder M{nr} conditioned on \mathbf{f}^{\mathbf{x}c} and \mathbf{P}{nr}: \Delta \mathbf{c}, \Delta \sigma = M{nr}(\mathbf{f}^{\mathbf{x}c}; \mathbf{P}{nr}) 7. Compositional Rendering: For each ray \mathbf{r}, query M samples. Compute transmittance Tm and final RGB color C{final} using stratified sampling: Tm = \exp\left(-\sum{n=1}^{m-1} \sigman \deltan\right) C{final}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{m=1}^M Tm (1 - \exp(-(\sigmam + \Delta \sigmam)\deltam)) (\mathbf{c}m + \Delta \mathbf{c}m) where \deltam is the distance between adjacent samples. Similarly, compute C{rigid} from (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) for loss calculation. 8. Optimization: a. Sample Np patches per iteration. b. Render patches \hat{P}^rk from C{rigid} and \hat{P}^fk from C{final}. c. Compute LPIPS loss using pre-trained VGGNet against ground truth patch P^{GT}k: \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} = \text{LPIPS}(\text{VGG}(\hat{P}), \text{VGG}(P^{GT}k)) d. Compute MSE losses \mathcal{L}^r{MSE} and \mathcal{L}^f{MSE} for rigid and final patches. e. Compute SSIM loss \mathcal{L}^f{SSIM} only for final patches. f. Compute total loss \mathcal{L}^o with hyperparameter \lambda = 0.2: \mathcal{L}^r = \mathcal{L}^r{LPIPS} + \mathcal{L}^r{MSE} \mathcal{L}^f = \mathcal{L}^f{LPIPS} + \mathcal{L}^f{MSE} + \mathcal{L}^f{SSIM} \mathcal{L}^o = \lambda \mathcal{L}^r + (1-\lambda) \mathcal{L}^f Parameters: K: Total number of joints (23). L: Number of frequency bands in positional encoding (10). \lambda: Loss balancing hyperparameter (0.2). Optimizer: Adam with betas (0.9, 0.99). Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-5} for skeletal weights volume decoder; 5 \times 10^{-3} for all other components. MHE Configuration: 16 levels, H=2 per level; Global MHE: 4 levels, H=2. Sampling: 6 patches of size 32 \times 32 per iteration; 256 samples per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spatial offset strategies suffer from high computational complexity because a single spatial offset spans an unbounded range and is unique for every 3D point across all input frames and body poses. Spatial offset strategies suffer from misaligned learning objectives because the learning objective of spatial offsets is not directly aligned with conventional RGB-based supervision. MoCo-NeRF avoids these by modeling residuals directly. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than offset-based methods. Single-subject training takes 1–2 hours on an RTX 3090 GPU. Multi-subject training (6 subjects) takes ~2 hours on one RTX 3090. This is significantly faster than HumanNeRF and NHP. Memory Complexity: Uses a single MHE for single-subject, or global + local MHEs for multi-subject. Feature dimension H=2 is small. Performance: On ZJU-MoCap single-subject (subjects 377, 386, 387, 392, 393, 394), achieves PSNR 31.06, SSIM 0.9734, LPIPS 28.83. On multi-subject (377, 386, 392), achieves PSNR 31.97, SSIM 0.9781, LPIPS 24.54. Strengths: Direct color supervision for non-rigid motions; efficient training; supports multi-subject training in a single framework. Limitations: Requires skeletal joint positions as input. Performance depends on the accuracy of the skeletal transformation. MoCo-NeRF was proposed by J. Kim et al. in 2024. It addresses the limitations of conventional spatial offset modeling in dynamic human rendering, which suffers from high learning complexity and misaligned objectives. The method builds on the principles of canonical transformation and conditioning described in Dynamic and Articulated Scene Modeling, specifically utilizing inverse linear blend skinning for rigid transformations. It is evaluated on the ZJU-MoCap and MonoCap datasets. name: Neural Scene Graphs
head: NSG
body: Neural Scene Graphs (NSG) is a method for decomposing dynamic, multi-object scenes into a learned hierarchical scene graph with decoupled object transformations and scene representations. It solves the problem of novel view synthesis and rendering of unseen arrangements in dynamic scenes by lifting the assumption of static scene consistency required by existing neural rendering methods. Unlike methods that encode the entire scene into a single, static network, NSG uses a hierarchical scene-graph model with object-level implicit representations, allowing for the learning of object representations directly from video frames and tracking data. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of video frames and corresponding tracking data (labels for object instances, classes, and poses). Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are required for ray generation. Outputs: A rendered image for a given camera pose and a scene graph S containing learned object representations, transformations, and background models. Data Structures The scene is defined as a directed acyclic graph S: S = \langle W, C, F, L, E \rangle W: The root node representing the global world space. C: The camera node. F: A set of representation nodes. This includes a static background node F{\theta{bckg}} and dynamic object nodes F{\thetao}. L: Latent descriptors lo associated with object nodes to encode instance-specific appearance. E: A set of edges representing affine transformations or property assignments. Edges and Transformations Edges E represent affine transformations from node u to node v or property assignments: E = \{ e{u,v} \in \{ [\cdot], M{uv} \} \} where M{uv} is a 4 \times 4 affine transformation matrix: M{uv} = \begin{bmatrix} R & t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, t \in \mathbb{R}^3 For all edges originating from the root node W, transformations T^Wv are assigned between the global world space and the local object or camera space. The background node has no assigned transformation as it is already aligned with W. To represent different scales of the same object type, a non-uniform scaling matrix So is computed and assigned at the edge e{o,f} between an object node and its shared representation model F. Representation Models Representation models are shared and defined in a shared, unit-scaled frame. 1. Background Node (F{\theta{bckg}}): Approximates all static parts of the scene. It maps a point x and viewing direction d to volumetric density \sigma and color c. Unlike standard volumetric NeRF, this representation lives on sparse planes instead of a volume. It uses Fourier encodings to aid learning high-frequency functions in the MLP model. 2. Object Nodes (F{\thetao}): Scene objects are represented as augmented implicit neural radiance fields following Mildenhall et al. [22]. To generalize across a class of objects, a latent vector z (or lo) is added to the input 3D query point, allowing similar objects to be modeled using the same network. Rendering Algorithm 1. Graph Traversal: To retrieve an object’s local transformation and position po = [x, z, y]o, traverse from the root node W, applying transformations until the desired object node F{\thetao} is reached, ending in the frame of reference defined by the accumulated transformations. 2. Ray Sampling: Generate rays r(\lambda) = o{world} + \lambda d{world} based on camera intrinsics and extrinsics. 3. Evaluation: For background points, query F{\theta{bckg}}(x, d). For object points, transform the query point x from world space to the object's local unit-scaled space using the accumulated transformation from the graph traversal. Query the shared representation model F with the transformed point and the latent descriptor lo. 4. Compositing: Perform standard volume rendering integration along the ray using the sampled densities and colors. Pseudocode import math def renderneuralscenegraph(camerapose, scenegraph, rayorigin, raydirection, near, far, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray through a Neural Scene Graph. Args: camerapose: Tuple (R, t) of camera extrinsics. scenegraph: Dict containing 'backgroundnode', 'dynamicnodes' (list of dicts with 'model', 'latent', 'edgesfromroot'). rayorigin: World space origin of the ray. raydirection: World space direction of the ray. near, far: Ray marching bounds. numsamples: Number of samples per ray. Returns: color: Rendered RGB color. depth: Rendered depth. """ accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedweight = 0.0 accumulateddepth = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # Standard ray marching generates sample points along the ray within near/far bounds. sampledistances = [near + (far - near) i / numsamples for i in range(1, numsamples + 1)] for dist in sampledistances: worldpoint = [rayorigin[i] + dist raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] isbackground = True objectnode = None latentcode = None localpoint = worldpoint # Traverse graph to find relevant object node for objnode in scenegraph['dynamicnodes']: # Accumulate transformation matrices along edges from root W to objnode transformtoobj = objnode['edgesfromroot'] # Homogeneous coordinate transformation localpoint = [ transformtoobj[0][0]worldpoint[0] + transformtoobj[0][1]worldpoint[1] + transformtoobj[0][2]worldpoint[2] + transformtoobj[0][3], transformtoobj[1][0]worldpoint[0] + transformtoobj[1][1]worldpoint[1] + transformtoobj[1][2]worldpoint[2] + transformtoobj[1][3], transformtoobj[2][0]worldpoint[0] + transformtoobj[2][1]worldpoint[1] + transformtoobj[2][2]worldpoint[2] + transformtoobj[2][3] ] # Apply non-uniform scaling if defined on edge eo,f if 'scalematrix' in objnode: scalematrix = objnode['scalematrix'] localpoint = [ scalematrix[0][0]localpoint[0], scalematrix[1][1]localpoint[1], scalematrix[2][2]localpoint[2] ] # Check if localpoint is within the unit-scaled bounding box domain if all(-1.0 <= p <= 1.0 for p in localpoint): isbackground = False objectnode = objnode latentcode = objnode['latent'] break if isbackground: density, color = scenegraph['backgroundnode'].evaluate(worldpoint, raydirection) else: inputpoint = [localpoint[i] + latentcode[i] for i in range(3)] density, color = objectnode['model'].evaluate(inputpoint, raydirection) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density (far - near) / numsamples) weight = transmittance alpha accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + weight color[i] for i in range(3)] accumulateddepth += weight dist accumulatedweight += weight transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break finalcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] for i in range(3)] return finalcolor, accumulatedweight Parameters Latent Vector Dimension: Not given in the sources. Number of Frequency Bands for Fourier Encoding: Not given in the sources. MLP Architecture: Follows Mildenhall et al. [22] (standard NeRF MLP) for object nodes; specific architecture for background sparse planes not detailed beyond "Fourier encodings" and "MLP model". Edge Cases and Pitfalls Scale Normalization: Objects are represented in a shared, unit-scaled frame. Non-uniform scaling So must be correctly computed and applied to handle objects of different physical sizes within the same class. Tracking Data Dependency: The method relies on labeled and generated tracking data to learn object representations and transformations. Background Representation: The background uses sparse planes instead of a volume. Predicts radiance residuals in canonical space conditioned on pose. Choose when residual-based deformation is preferred over explicit graph structures. MoCo-NeRF Uses inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) for skeleton-based canonical transformation. Choose when articulated human or object motion is the primary focus. A-NeRF Encodes instance-specific representations directly from video frames and tracking data. Choose when per-instance avatar reconstruction is required. Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars (PVA) Uses signed distances to nearest neighbors in a reconstructed surface mesh for canonical mapping. Choose when surface-based deformation is more stable than volumetric priors. SelfNeRF Decouples appearance, shape, and class using hierarchical bounding layers. Choose when explicit spatial partitioning is needed for dynamic objects. CLA-NeRF Voxelizes dynamic objects into separate layers for independent manipulation. Choose when discrete voxel representations are preferred over implicit fields. Object-Centric Voxelization for Dynamic Scenes Models multi-instance scenes with shared radiance fields and instance-specific codes. Choose when scene decomposition into independent instances is required without explicit graph traversal. MI-NeRF Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Validated on simulated and experimental data, with labeled and generated tracking data by rendering novel unseen views and unseen dynamic scene arrangements. Strengths: Allows for novel view synthesis and rendering of unseen arrangements in dynamic scenes; facilitates 3D object detection using inverse rendering; decouples object transformations and scene representations. Limitations: Relies on tracking data; less interpretable than explicit methods due to the use of MLPs. When to use: When dealing with dynamic, multi-object scenes where novel views and unseen arrangements are required, and tracking data is available. When not to use: When the scene is static and a simpler NeRF variant is sufficient; when tracking data is unavailable or unreliable. Neural Scene Graphs was introduced by Park et al. in 2021. The method builds on the success of implicit neural representations for static scenes, specifically NeRF by Mildenhall et al. [22], and extends it to dynamic scenes by introducing a hierarchical scene-graph model. It addresses the limitation of existing methods that rely on static scenes with consistent mappings from a 3D point to a 2D observation. name: A-NeRF
head: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields
body: A-NeRF learns a user-specific neural 3D body model and underlying skeleton pose from unlabelled monocular videos by extending Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) with a skeleton to apply to time-varying and articulated motion. Its core technical novelty is defining spatial latent variables relative to the pose of body parts to overcome ill-posed inverse operations with an overparameterization, embedding domain knowledge of how humans move. Unlike MoCo-NeRF which uses residual-based conditioning, A-NeRF uses skeleton-relative embeddings; unlike SelfNeRF which uses surface-based SDFs, A-NeRF uses volumetric density conditioned on bone-relative coordinates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of N images Ik \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} of the same person. Initial pose estimates \hat{\theta}k from an off-the-shelf estimator (e.g., SPIN [26]). Outputs: Refined skeleton poses \thetak, neural network parameters \phi (defining shape and appearance), and rendered images C\phi(\thetak). Data Structures: 1. Skeleton Representation: Rest pose: 3D joint locations \tilde{a}m for m=1..24, root at 0, connected via B bones. Pose \thetak: Vector containing relative rotations of 24 joints \tilde{\theta}{k,m} to parents and global position \tilde{\theta}{k,0}. 2. Neural Network Architecture (F\phi): Follows original NeRF [42] structure. Inputs: Positional Encoded (PE) query point \Gamma(q), PE view direction \Gamma(d), appearance code, and Relative Ray encoding. Hidden Layers: 10 fully-connected layers with sizes [256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 256, 128]. Activations: ReLU for all layers except the last two. Sigmoid for the final output layer. Specific Injection: Appearance code and Relative Ray encoding are concatenated into the network at the second-to-last fully-connected layer (before the final 128-unit layer) to prevent them from affecting body geometry. Outputs: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize camera intrinsics, bone lengths am, and pose \thetak using SPIN [26] for every frame k. 2. Encoding: Map input scene point q and view direction d to higher dimensional space using Positional Encoding \Gamma. 3. Skeleton-Relative Encoding (Rel. Ray): For a query point q and frame k, compute the vector from q to each joint m: \tilde{q}{k,m} = q - \tilde{a}m(\thetak). Compute the angle between the ray direction \tilde{d}k and the vector to joint m: d'{k,m} = \arccos(\tilde{d}k \cdot \tilde{q}{k,m}). Concatenate these angles for all 24 joints to form the Relative Ray encoding. 4. Network Forward Pass: Feed \Gamma(q), \Gamma(d), appearance code, and Rel. Ray encoding into F\phi to obtain \sigma and c. 5. Volume Rendering: Render the image C\phi(\thetak) via classical ray-marching using coarse-to-fine importance sampling. Restrict samples to be within a coarse human silhouette estimated with [10] unless the background is monochrome. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss L{SV}: L{SV}(\theta, \phi) = \sumk \| C\phi(\thetak) - Ik \|1 + \lambda\theta \sumk d(\thetak - \hat{\theta}k) + \lambdat \sumk \left\| \frac{\partial^2 \thetak}{\partial t^2} \right\|^2 Where: Data term: L1 distance between generated and input images. Pose regularizer: d(x) = \min(\|x\|2 - \epsilon, 0) with \epsilon = 0.01. Encourages solution to stay close to initial pose \hat{\theta}k. Smoothness prior: Penalizes acceleration \frac{\partial^2 \thetak}{\partial t^2} between consecutive frames. 7. Optimization Loop: Form a training batch by randomly sampling N{batch} = 3072 rays from all available images. Accumulate gradient update \nabla \theta for G \times (30 \times N{batch}) / N iterations so that each \thetak is expected to be sampled 30 times before update. Optimize poses \thetak and neural parameters \phi for 500k iterations on objective Eq. 2. Stop optimizing pose and continue training \phi with only the data term for additional 200k iterations. Parameters: \lambdat: Hyperparameter balancing the smoothness prior term. \lambda\theta: Hyperparameter balancing the pose regularizer term. \epsilon: Tolerance for small shifts in the pose regularizer, value 0.01. Cutoff distance t: 500mm, with exponential decay over 250k iterations. Cutoff temperature \tau: Starts at -20, decays exponentially to -200 over 500k iterations. Coarse samples: 64. Fine samples: 16. Positional encoding frequencies for input (L{input}): 7. Positional encoding frequencies for view (L{view}): 4. Learning rate for \phi: Starts at 5 \times 10^{-4}, decays exponentially over 200k iterations. Learning rate for \phi (finetune): 2 \times 10^{-4} decaying to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Gradient accumulation steps G: 20 for Mixamo, 50 for Human 3.6M, 10 for MonoPerfCap. Pitfalls: Using World Ray direction causes overfitting in static/estimated camera settings, leading to flickering results for novel view rendering (e.g., bullet-time effect). Encoding world coordinates directly fails on motions and has large memory consumption. Encoding positions relative to skeleton has high dimensionality. Straightforward baselines conditioning directly on pose (World Position + Joint Position + \theta) perform worst, achieving 0.7 SSIM by simply rendering background colors. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 60 hours on 2 Nvidia Tesla V100 32GB GPUs. Memory Complexity: High due to per-bone embeddings and large MLP. Encoding positions relative to the skeleton has high dimensionality compared to world coordinates. Measured Performance: On Human 3.6M S9 Protocol II: PSNR 26.64, SSIM 0.9192, PA-MPJPE 41.00 with per-image code and Rel. Ray. On SURREAL: PSNR 29.10, SSIM 0.9655, compared to NeuralBody PSNR 23.86, SSIM 0.9304. Rendering Time: 1-4 seconds per 512x512x3 image on a single Nvidia Tesla V100 GPU. Strengths: Works better than NeuralBody for longer sequences and retargeting to diverse poses. Can be trained with only a single view; adding more views does not help if poses are not diverse enough. One long video with diverse poses is comparable to multiple shorter multi-view recordings. Limitations: Requires rough 3D pose estimates for initialization. Does not require surface supervision or initialization, but relies on off-the-shelf predictors which may be inaccurate. A-NeRF builds on NeRF [42] and uses appearance code design from [36, 49]. It was proposed to learn a generative neural body model from unlabelled monocular videos by extending Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) with a skeleton to apply to time-varying and articulated motion. The method addresses the ill-posed inverse problem of mapping 3D world coordinates to a canonical space for articulated bodies by overparameterizing with one embedding per bone. A skeleton-driven approach for human model reconstruction from multi-view videos, maintaining a canonical space and estimating two-way correspondences. It uses a new motion representation, the neural blend weight field, combined with 3D human skeletons for deformation field generation. Human meshes can be extracted by running marching cubes on volume densities at discretized canonical space points. name: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars (PVA)
body: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars (PVA) is a framework for estimating a volumetric 3D avatar from a few input images of a human head, enabling view synthesis for unseen identities and expressions. It generalizes to new identities by combining neural radiance fields with local, pixel-aligned features extracted directly from input images, avoiding the information loss associated with global latent codes. Unlike mesh-based methods, PVA captures arbitrary topology and high-frequency details (e.g., hair) without requiring explicit 3D supervision. PVA consists of two main components: a shallow convolutional encoder-decoder network (N{feat}) that produces pixel-aligned feature maps from input images, and a radiance field network (N) that maps 3D locations and these features to color and opacity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: One or more conditioning views vi (images of dimensions h \times w \times 3) with known camera intrinsics Ki and extrinsics [R|t]i. Outputs: A radiance field function that, given a 3D point \mathbf{X} and view direction, predicts color \mathbf{c} and volume density \sigma. Data Structures: Feature Maps (f^{(i)}): 2D arrays of shape h \times w \times df, where df is the feature dimension. These are the outputs of N{feat}. Radiance Field Network (N): An MLP taking positional encoding \phi(\mathbf{X}) and feature vector \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X} as input. Positional Encoding (\phi): Standard NeRF positional encoding applied to 3D coordinates. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each conditioning view vi, compute the pixel-aligned feature map f^{(i)} by passing the view through the encoder-decoder network: f^{(i)} = N{feat}(vi) \quad 2. Feature Interpolation: For a 3D query point \mathbf{X}, determine its corresponding pixel location \mathbf{x} in the conditioning view vi using perspective projection \Pi: \mathbf{x} = \Pi(\mathbf{X}) \quad Extract the feature vector \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X} by bilinearly interpolating the feature map f^{(i)} at location \mathbf{x}: \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X} = F(f^{(i)}, \mathbf{x}) \quad where F denotes bilinear interpolation. 3. Radiance Field Query: Pass the positional encoding of the 3D location, \phi(\mathbf{X}), and the extracted feature vector \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X} into the radiance field network N to predict color \mathbf{c} and opacity/density \sigma: \{\mathbf{c}, \sigma\} = N(\phi(\mathbf{X}), \mathbf{f}\mathbf{X}) \quad 4. Ray Marching Setup: For a target view j with camera intrinsics Kj and extrinsics [R|t]j, define the ray for pixel p. The camera-to-world projection matrix is P^{-1} = [Ri | ti]^{-1} Ki^{-1} (using the conditioning view's pose relative to head pose). The ray direction \mathbf{d} is: \mathbf{d} = \frac{P^{-1} \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{r}0}{\| P^{-1} \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{r}0 \|} \quad where \mathbf{r}0 is the ray origin. Note: Camera extrinsics are relative to the computed head pose to help the network focus on scene content. 5. Sampling: Uniformly sample a set of ns points t along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{r}0 + t\mathbf{d} for t \in [t{near}, t{far}]. Set \mathbf{X} = r(t). 6. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using standard volume rendering integration (quadrature rule). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def pvarender(conditioningviews, targetview, ns, tnear, tfar, Nfeat, N): """ Render a target view using Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars. Args: conditioningviews: List of dicts, each containing 'image' (HxWx3), 'K' (3x3 intrinsics), 'R' (3x3 rotation), 't' (3x1 translation). targetview: Dict containing 'K' (3x3 intrinsics), 'R' (3x3 rotation), 't' (3x1 translation). ns: Number of uniformly sampled points along the ray. tnear: Near plane distance. tfar: Far plane distance. Nfeat: Encoder-decoder network function. N: Radiance field MLP function. Returns: renderedimage: HxWx3 array. """ # Assume single conditioning view for simplicity as per primary description cond = conditioningviews[0] H, W, = cond['image'].shape # 1. Extract pixel-aligned feature maps from conditioning view # fcond is H x W x Dfeat fcond = Nfeat(cond['image']) # Precompute projection matrix for conditioning view relative to head pose # Pinv = [Rcond | tcond]^-1 @ Kcond^-1 # Note: The paper states extrinsics are relative to computed head pose. # We assume cond['R'], cond['t'] are already in this relative frame. Kinvcond = np.linalg.inv(cond['K']) RTcond = np.eye(4) RTcond[:3,:3] = cond['R'] RTcond[:3, 3] = cond['t'].flatten() Pinvcond = RTcond @ Kinvcond # Precompute projection matrix for target view Kinvtarget = np.linalg.inv(targetview['K']) RTtarget = np.eye(4) RTtarget[:3,:3] = targetview['R'] RTtarget[:3, 3] = targetview['t'].flatten() Pinvtarget = RTtarget @ Kinvtarget renderedimage = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): # 4. Ray Marching Setup for pixel (x, y) # Pixel coordinates in homogeneous space phom = np.array([x, y, 1.0]) # Ray direction in world space # d = (Pinvtarget @ p - r0) / norm # r0 is the camera center. In homogeneous coords, r0hom = [0,0,0,1] in camera space. # World center = Pinvtarget @ [0,0,0,1]^T r0world = Pinvtarget @ np.array([0, 0, 0, 1]) r0world = r0world[:3] / r0world[3] # Point at depth 1 in camera space projected to world p1hom = Pinvtarget @ np.append(phom, 1.0) p1world = p1hom[:3] / p1hom[3] d = p1world - r0world d = d / np.linalg.norm(d) # 5. Sampling tvals = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, ns) points = r0world + tvals[:, np.newaxis] d[np.newaxis,:] # Shape: (ns, 3) # 2. Feature Interpolation for each point # Project each 3D point to the conditioning view's pixel coordinates # xpixel = Kcond @ (Rcond @ X + tcond) # We need to invert this to get pixel coords from 3D points # Xworld -> Xcond = Rcond^-1 @ (Xworld - tcond) # xpixelhom = Kcond @ Xcond RTcondinv = np.linalg.inv(RTcond) colorsaccum = 0.0 alphaaccum = 0.0 for i in range(ns): X = points[i] # Transform X to conditioning camera space Xcondhom = RTcondinv @ np.append(X, 1.0) Xcond = Xcondhom[:3] # Project to pixel coordinates xpixelhom = cond['K'] @ Xcond xpixel = xpixelhom[:2] / xpixelhom[2] # Check if point is within image bounds (simple clamp for interpolation) # Bilinear interpolation requires valid coordinates px, py = xpixel[0], xpixel[1] # Clamp to image boundaries for interpolation pxclamped = np.clip(px, 0.5, W - 1.5) pyclamped = np.clip(py, 0.5, H - 1.5) # Bilinear interpolation of feature map fcond at (px, py) # fcond is H x W x D # Get floor/ceil indices x0, y0 = int(np.floor(pxclamped)), int(np.floor(pyclamped)) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 # Interpolate # f(y, x) = f(y0, x0)(1-dx)(1-dy) + f(y0, x1)dx(1-dy) +... dx = pxclamped - x0 dy = pyclamped - y0 f00 = fcond[y0, x0] f01 = fcond[y0, x1] f10 = fcond[y1, x0] f11 = fcond[y1, x1] finterp = (1-dx)(1-dy)f00 + dx(1-dy)f01 + (1-dx)dyf10 + dxdyf11 # 3. Radiance Field Query # Compute positional encoding phi(X) phiX = positionalencoding(X) # Query network c, sigma = N(phiX, finterp) # Volume Rendering Accumulation # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma deltat) deltat = tvals[i+1] - tvals[i] if i < ns - 1 else tfar - tvals[i] alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltat) # T = exp(-sum(sigma deltat)) # Contribution = T alpha c # We accumulate from front to back # Note: Standard NeRF accumulation # weight = alpha T # color += weight c # T = (1 - alpha) # For simplicity in this pseudocode, assuming single pass accumulation # In practice, T is maintained across the loop pass # Simplified accumulation for pseudocode completeness # Real implementation requires maintaining T across the ns loop T = 1.0 finalcolor = np.zeros(3) for i in range(ns): X = points[i] #... (recompute finterp as above)... # phiX = positionalencoding(X) # c, sigma = N(phiX, finterp) # deltat = tvals[i+1] - tvals[i] if i < ns - 1 else tfar - tvals[i] # alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltat) # weight = alpha T # finalcolor += weight c # T = (1 - alpha) pass renderedimage[y, x] = finalcolor return renderedimage def positionalencoding(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, power=2): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = np.array([2i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg+1)]) xb = np.reshape((x[..., np.newaxis,:] scales), (x.shape[0], -1)) freqb = np.sin(xb power) freqb = np.concatenate([np.cos(freqb), np.sin(freqb)], axis=-1) return np.concatenate([x, freqb], axis=-1) Parameters: ns: Number of uniformly sampled points along the ray. Typical values are not explicitly given in the notes, but standard NeRF uses 48-192. t{near}, t{far}: Near and far plane distances for ray marching. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Global Latent Codes: Using global latent codes (as in SRNs) discards local details, making it difficult to generalize to local changes like facial expressions. PVA avoids this by using local pixel-aligned features. 3D Supervision: PVA does not require explicit 3D supervision (e.g., depth or normals) during training, relying solely on photometric re-rendering loss. Topology: Unlike mesh-based methods, PVA captures arbitrary topology (e.g., hair, expressions) because it uses pixel-level information. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of pixels, the number of sampled points ns, and the cost of the encoder-decoder network N{feat} and radiance field network N. The feature interpolation step adds overhead proportional to the number of sampled points. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the feature maps f^{(i)} (size H \times W \times df) and the parameters of N{feat} and N. It avoids the memory restrictions of voxel-based methods by using an MLP instead of a 3D voxel grid. Strengths: Captures high-frequency texture details and arbitrary topology (hair, expressions) without 3D supervision. Generalizes to unseen identities and expressions. Limitations: Requires input images with known camera poses. Performance may degrade if the input images do not adequately cover the identity's appearance variations. When to use: Virtual telepresence applications requiring photo-realistic human heads from a small number of example views. When not to use: When explicit 3D geometry is required for downstream tasks (e.g., physics simulation) or when input camera poses are unknown/unreliable. PVA was introduced as a novel framework for the estimation of a volumetric 3D avatar from only a few input images of a human head. It builds on insights from NeRF and PIFu/PIFuHD, leveraging pixel-aligned features to retain high-frequency detail without requiring 3D supervision. It addresses the limitations of Scene Representation Networks (SRNs) which struggle with local changes like facial expressions due to global latent codes. It is used for virtual telepresence applications. PVA: Pixel-aligned Volumetric Avatars, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2101.02697, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SelfNeRF
body: SelfNeRF is a novel view synthesis method for human performance that trains from scratch using monocular self-rotating video inputs, achieving high-fidelity results in approximately twenty minutes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like MoCo-NeRF and A-NeRF by eliminating the need for multi-view inputs or explicit skeletal priors, instead relying on a surface-relative hash encoding to aggregate inter-frame information and accelerate training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A monocular self-rotating video of a human performer consisting of Nt frames. Output: A trained neural radiance field model capable of rendering novel views of the performer. Data Structures: Surface Shape \{Tt\}: A set of point clouds representing the human surface for each frame t \in \{0, \dots, Nt - 1\}, recovered using external reconstruction methods such as VideoAvatar or SelfRecon. Body Mask \{Mt\}: Binary masks for each frame t, identifying the human region. Hash Grid: A multi-resolution hash encoding structure storing high-dimensional feature vectors. MLP F\omega: A neural network with weights \omega that maps encoded features to density \sigma and color c. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: For the input video, recover the surface shape Tt and body mask Mt for each frame t using existing reconstruction algorithms. 2. Surface-Relative Representation: For a query point \mathbf{x} at frame t, find the K-nearest neighbor points on the current frame's point cloud Tt and calculate their signed distances. Map these neighbors and their signed distances to the corresponding points and signed distances in the canonical space (Frame 0). 3. Encoding: Encode the resulting surface-relative representation using multi-resolution hash encoding to produce a high-dimensional feature vector. 4. Radiance Prediction: Feed the encoded feature vector into the MLP F\omega to regress the density \sigma and color c. 5. Rendering: Render the image using volume rendering to calculate the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) for each ray \mathbf{r}. 6. Optimization: Train the model by minimizing photometric loss and geometric guidance loss. Formulas: The volume rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} is: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha(\mathbf{x}i) \left( \prod{j<i} (1 - \alpha(\mathbf{x}j)) \right) c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{v}) where: \alpha(\mathbf{x}i) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \deltai) is the transmittance-derived opacity. \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{v} are the sample points on the ray. \deltai = u{i+1} - ui is the distance between adjacent sample points. c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{v}) is the color predicted by F\omega. Parameters: Nt: Total number of frames in the input monocular video. K: Number of nearest neighbors used to calculate the surface-relative representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selfnerfrender(rayo, rayd, frameidx, surfaceclouds, hashgrid, mlpweights, K, numsamples, tmin, tmax): # 1. Sample points along the ray tvals = [tmin + i (tmax - tmin) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples + 1)] xsamples = [(rayo[0] + t rayd[0], rayo[1] + t rayd[1], rayo[2] + t rayd[2]) for t in tvals[:-1]] deltas = [tvals[i+1] - tvals[i] for i in range(numsamples)] # 2. Compute surface-relative representation and features features = [] for x in xsamples: currentcloud = surfaceclouds[frameidx] # Find K nearest neighbors and signed distances dists = [(x[0]-p[0])2 + (x[1]-p[1])2 + (x[2]-p[2])2 for p in currentcloud] sortedindices = sorted(range(len(dists)), key=lambda i: dists[i])[:K] kneighbors = [currentcloud[i] for i in sortedindices] kdists = [dists[i]0.5 for i in sortedindices] # Map to canonical space (Frame 0) canonicalneighbors = surfaceclouds[0] canonicaldists = kdists # Hash encode feature = [] for level in range(numhashlevels): grid = hashgrid[level] idx = hashfunction(canonicalneighbors, canonicaldists, level) feature.extend(grid[idx]) features.append(feature) # 3. Predict density and color sigma = [] color = [] for f in features: s, c = mlpforward(f, rayd, mlpweights) sigma.append(s) color.append(c) # 4. Volume rendering alpha = [1.0 - (2.718281828 (-sigma[i] deltas[i])) for i in range(numsamples)] transmittance = [1.0] for i in range(numsamples - 1): transmittance.append(transmittance[-1] (1.0 - alpha[i])) finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): weight = alpha[i] transmittance[i] for c in range(3): finalcolor[c] += weight color[i][c] return finalcolor def hashfunction(points, distances, level): # Standard hash encoding index computation return hash((points, distances, level)) % (2level) def mlpforward(feature, viewdir, weights): # Standard MLP forward pass hidden = [sum(f w for f, w in zip(feature, weights['w1'])) + weights['b1']] sigma = max(0.0, hidden[0]) # Density must be non-negative color = [sum(f w for f, w in zip(hidden, weights['w2'][c])) + weights['b2'][c] for c in range(3)] return sigma, color Training Time: Approximately 20 minutes for convergence. Input Requirements: Monocular self-rotating video; no multi-view setup required. Strengths: Fast training speed due to hash encoding; ability to train from scratch with minimal input. Limitations: Relies on recovering surface shape using external reconstruction methods such as VideoAvatar or SelfRecon. When to use: When only monocular video is available and rapid training is desired. SelfNeRF was proposed by Bo Peng, Jun Hu, Jingtao Zhou, and Juyong Zhang from the University of Science and Technology of China. It was published on arXiv in October 2022. The method addresses the challenge of high-fidelity novel view synthesis for human performance using only monocular inputs, a common scenario in practical applications like sports broadcasts and VR/AR. name: CLA-NeRF
head: Category-Level Articulated Neural Radiance Field
body: CLA-NeRF is a differentiable representation for articulated objects that explicitly models part and joint attributes, disentangling camera pose, part pose, part segmentation, and joint attributes to allow independent control during rendering. It solves the problem of rendering deformable articulated objects at unseen poses and estimating their articulated pose from RGB images, without requiring CAD models or depth data. Unlike standard NeRF formulations which model camera poses but ignore object articulation, CLA-NeRF predicts a part segmentation field alongside density and color, enabling the inference of joint attributes via line-fitting on the segmentation field. It differs from sibling methods like MoCo-NeRF, A-NeRF, SelfNeRF, and NARF by focusing on general articulated objects without assuming known joint attributes (e.g., bone length) at test time, and by using part segmentation labels for supervision rather than explicit joint attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Training Inputs: A set of RGB images with ground truth camera poses and part segmentation labels for a specific object category. Inference Inputs: A few RGB views (few-shot) of an unseen 3D object instance within the known category, along with an articulated pose input. Outputs: Rendered RGB images, part segmentation maps, and estimated articulated pose (via inverse rendering). Data Structures: MLP Backbone (F\Theta): A multilayer perceptron parameterized by weights \Theta. Positional Encoding (\gamma): High-frequency positional encoding applied to 3D positions. Segmentation Logits (\mathbf{s}): A vector of dimension P + 1, where P is the number of parts and the extra dimension represents the background. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Retrieval and Conditioning: Retrieve features from input RGB images to condition the NeRF model. 2. Deformation Matrix Calculation: Calculate a deformation matrix based on the input articulated pose. 3. Ray Deformation: Deform the sampled rays along the camera ray using the calculated deformation matrix. 4. Field Prediction: For each 3D location \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}, predict volumetric density \sigma, RGB color \mathbf{c}, and part segmentation logits \mathbf{s} using the MLP backbone: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{s}) = F\Theta(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}) where \mathbf{s} has P + 1 dimensions. 5. Articulation-Aware Volume Rendering: Render the deformed visual image using the learned framework via volume rendering. The rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k where \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak(t{k+1} - tk)) and Tk = \exp(-\sum{k'<k} \sigma{k'}(t{k'+1} - t{k'})). 6. Segmentation Rendering: Predict the part segmentation map \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) following the volume rendering procedure: \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{s}k where \mathbf{s}k is the predicted part segmentation of the sampled point \mathbf{r}(tk). 7. Joint Attribute Inference: Infer joint attributes by performing line-fitting on the predicted part segmentation field. 8. Inverse Rendering (Pose Estimation): Estimate the articulated pose via inverse rendering by minimizing the residual between rendered and observed pixels. Formulas: Segmentation Rendering: \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{s}k Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{k'<k} \sigma{k'}(t{k'+1} - t{k'})\right) where \mathbf{s}k is the predicted part segmentation of sampled point \mathbf{r}(tk). Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{color}): \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbf{R}} \left( \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}c(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}f(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 \right) / 2 where \mathbf{R} is the set of rays, and the subscripts c and f refer to the rendered and ground truth components as per the source notation. Segmentation Loss (\mathcal{L}{seg}): \mathcal{L}{seg} = -\sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbf{R}} \sum{i=1}^{P+1} \left( pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) + pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) \right) where \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\exp(\hat{\mathbf{S}}i(\mathbf{r}))}{\sum{j} \exp(\hat{\mathbf{S}}j(\mathbf{r}))} is the softmax probability for part i. The source notation uses pi(\mathbf{r}) for both ground truth and predicted terms in the log expression; standard cross-entropy would distinguish them as pi^{gt} and pi^{pred}. Parameters: P: The number of parts in the articulated object, determining the dimensionality of the segmentation logits (P + 1 including background). Pitfalls: Standard NeRF formulations explicitly model camera poses but do not consider object articulation, making them unable to render deformable articulated objects at different poses. The method assumes revolute joints causing 1D rotational motion (e.g., eyeglasses) in the experiments. Not given in the sources. CLA-NeRF was proposed by Wei-Cheng Tseng, Hung-Ju Liao, Lin Yen-Chen, and Min Sun. It was published in the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) in 2022. The work addresses the challenge of modeling general articulated objects (composed of rigid parts connected by joints) without relying on instance-level CAD models or depth data, enabling few-shot inference on unseen 3D object instances within a known category. It is the first method to model general articulated objects with neural radiance fields, allowing for view synthesis, part segmentation, and articulated pose estimation. name: Object-Centric Voxelization for Dynamic Scenes
head: DynaVol, Unsupervised Learning for Dynamic Scenes through Object-Centric Voxelization
body: DynaVol is an unsupervised 3D dynamic scene decomposition method that unifies geometric structures and object-centric learning within a differentiable volume rendering framework. It solves the multi-view mismatch of 2D object segmentation by ensuring 3D consistency, enabling novel view synthesis, and allowing direct scene editing. Unlike 2D image decomposition methods such as SAVi, DynaVol infers a probability distribution over objects at individual spatial locations via object-centric voxelization, facilitating fine-grained separation without geometric priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial timestamp images and poses \{Iv^{t=1}, Tv^{t=1}\}{v=1}^V and monocular video frames \{It, Tt\}{t=2}^T. The method supports scenarios where V=1 (only one initial camera pose) and monocular camera trajectories. Outputs: Synthesized target pixel values for novel views and time steps, along with decomposed object-centric representations \{(cn, \sigman)\}{n=1}^N. Data Structures: Object-centric 4D Voxel Representation: Vt \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz}. This structure maintains the time-varying density \{\sigman\}{n=1}^N for each possible object across spatial dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz and time t. Slots: N is a predefined number of object slots, assumed to be larger than the actual number of objects in the scene to handle unknown counts. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample 3D points \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and view directions \mathbf{d} for each timestamp t. 2. Object-Centric Voxelization: Learn the object-centric projection of (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, t) to \{(cn, \sigman)\}{n=1}^N. This infers the probability distribution over objects at individual spatial locations. 3. Dynamics Module: Learn transitions of voxel grid features in canonical space over time. The voxel features evolve through a canonical-space deformation function. 4. Volume Slot Attention: Aggregate voxel representations to refine object-level, time-invariant global features. This module progressively refines global features by aggregating local voxel representations. 5. Compositional NeRF Decoder: Estimate density and color for each object at view direction \mathbf{d} using both local voxel features and global object representations. 6. Rendering: Re-combine \{(cn, \sigman)\}{n=1}^N to synthesize target pixel values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynavolrender(initialimages, initialposes, videoframes, N, Nx, Ny, Nz): # Initialize object-centric 4D voxel representation Vt in canonical space Vt = torch.zeros((N, Nx, Ny, Nz)) globalfeatures = torch.zeros((N, 256)) # Object-level, time-invariant global features T = len(videoframes) renderedimages = [] for t in range(1, T + 1): # Sample 3D points x and view directions d for each timestamp t points, directions = samplerays(videoframes[t], initialposes if t == 1 else None) # Object-centric voxelization: learn projection of (x, d, t) to per-slot features # Infers probability distribution over objects at individual spatial locations # Standard MLP/convolutional projection from observation to canonical voxel features voxelfeatures = objectcentricvoxelization(points, directions, t, Vt) # Dynamics module: learn transitions of voxel grid features in canonical space over time # Standard recurrent or temporal convolutional update for voxel grid features Vt = dynamicsmodule(Vt, t) # Volume slot attention: aggregate voxel representations to refine global features # Standard attention mechanism aggregating spatial voxels into slot vectors globalfeatures = volumeslotattention(voxelfeatures, globalfeatures) # Compositional NeRF decoder: estimate density and color for each object at view direction d densities = [] colors = [] for n in range(N): # Standard MLP combining local voxel features, global slot features, and view direction sigman, cn = compositionalnerfdecoder( voxelfeatures[n], globalfeatures[n], directions) densities.append(sigman) colors.append(cn) # Re-combine per-slot densities and colors to synthesize target pixel values # Standard differentiable volume rendering integrating per-slot contributions along rays renderedimage = volumerendering(densities, colors, directions) renderedimages.append(renderedimage) return renderedimages, Vt, globalfeatures Parameters: N: Predefined number of object slots. Must be larger than the actual number of objects. Nx, Ny, Nz: Spatial dimensions of the voxel grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular Input: The method handles scenarios with only one initial camera pose (V=1) and monocular camera trajectories smoothly, avoiding multi-view mismatch issues common in 2D approaches. Slot Count: N is a hyperparameter that must be set conservatively high to account for unknown object counts, potentially leading to unused slots. Uses residual-based canonical transformation and pose-conditioned radiance residuals. Choose when pose information is available and deformation is complex. MoCo-NeRF Explicitly models scene objects and their relationships. Choose when explicit scene structure and reasoning are required. Neural Scene Graphs Uses skeleton-based inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS). Choose for articulated human or rigid-body scenes with known skeletons. A-NeRF Uses pixel-aligned features for high-fidelity avatar rendering. Choose for detailed human avatar synthesis. PVA Uses surface-based signed distances to nearest neighbors. Choose when surface reconstruction is a viable prior. SelfNeRF Uses canonical space alignment with local appearance. Choose for scenes with varying lighting conditions. CLA-NeRF Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on simulated 3D dynamic scenes with varying numbers of objects, diverse motions, shapes (cubes, spheres, real-world shapes), and materials (rubber, metal). Demonstrated on real-world videos for novel view synthesis and editing. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures 3D consistency, enables novel view synthesis, allows direct scene editing (object removal, replacement, trajectory modification) by manipulating voxel grids or deformation functions without further training. Handles monocular inputs and unknown object counts. Limitations: Requires predefined number of slots N which may be larger than actual objects. When to use: Unsupervised dynamic scene decomposition, novel view synthesis, and scene editing where 3D consistency is critical. When not to use: When explicit geometric priors are available and preferred, or when the number of objects is known and small. DynaVol was presented at ICLR 2024. It addresses the challenge of unsupervised learning of object-centric representations in dynamic visual scenes. Unlike previous approaches that decompose 2D images, DynaVol introduces a 3D scene generative model that unifies geometric structures and object-centric learning. It builds on the principles of dynamic and articulated scene modeling by mapping 3D query points to a canonical space.
