name: MI-NeRF
head: Multi-Identity NeRF, Single Unified Face NeRF
body: MI-NeRF is a method for learning a single unified dynamic neural radiance field (NeRF) that models complex non-rigid facial motion for multiple identities using only monocular videos of arbitrary length. It solves the problem of expensive per-identity optimization in dynamic face reconstruction by training a single implicit representation F\Theta conditioned on identity, expression, latent codes, position, and view direction. Unlike previous generic NeRF models that require static settings and multiple input views during training, MI-NeRF works for monocular videos captured in the wild, reducing total training time by up to 90% compared to standard single-identity NeRFs. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Monocular RGB video frames for multiple identities; 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) parameters (head pose P, expression e) extracted per frame; randomly initialized identity codes i and latent codes l. Outputs: Rendered RGB video frames for novel viewpoints and expressions; personalized identity-specific models via fine-tuning. Data Structures Identity Code (i): Vector of size 79, randomly initialized per video, learned during training. Captures time-invariant identity information. Latent Code (l): Vector of size 32, randomly initialized per frame per video, learned during training. Captures time-varying information (illumination, appearance variations). Expression Parameters (e): Vector of size 79, extracted via 3DMM fitting. Head Pose (P): 4 \times 4 matrix, decomposed into rotation R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} and translation t \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}. Network Parameters (\Theta): Weights of an 8-layer MLP with hidden size 256 and ReLU activations. Method Steps 1. Preprocessing: For each video frame, segment the head from the background. Fit a 3DMM to extract head pose P and expression parameters e using an optimization-based method minimizing photo-consistency and landmark terms. Use learned axes from Guo et al. (2018b) based on the Basel Face Model and FaceWarehouse. 2. Initialization: Randomly initialize one identity code i \in \mathbb{R}^{79} per video and one latent code l \in \mathbb{R}^{32} per frame per video. 3. Canonical Transformation: Transform sampled 3D points x to the canonical space using the head pose P = [R; t] before querying the network. 4. Feature Interaction: Compute the interaction between expression e and identity i using the Hadamard product (element-wise multiplication): M(e, i) = e \odot i. 5. NeRF Query: For each ray, sample 3D points x and view directions v. Encode x and v using positional encoding with 10 and 4 frequencies respectively. Concatenate the encoded features with the interaction term M(e, i) and the latent code l. Pass through the MLP F\Theta to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}: F\Theta: (M(\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{i}), \mathbf{l}, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) 6. Volumetric Rendering: Render the final color C(\mathbf{r}; \Theta) for each ray \mathbf{r} using volume rendering: C(\mathbf{r}; \Theta) = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{v}) T(t) dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds), and tn, tf are near and far bounds. 7. Optimization: Optimize the network parameters \Theta, identity codes i, and latent codes l simultaneously using hierarchical sampling (coarse and fine models). Minimize the loss function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \lambdal \mathcal{L}l + \lambdai \mathcal{L}i where \mathcal{L}c = \sumr \| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}; \Theta) - C(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 is the photo-consistency loss, \mathcal{L}l = \|\mathbf{l}\|2, \mathcal{L}i = \|\mathbf{i}\|2, \lambdal = 0.01, and \lambdai = 10^{-4}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def samplerays(rayo, rayd, tn, tf, numsamples): """Sample points along rays.""" tvals = torch.linspace(tn, tf, numsamples).to(rayo.device) tvals = tvals.unsqueeze(0).expand(rayo.shape[0], -1) x = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + rayd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) v = rayd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples, -1) return x, v class MINeRF: def init(self, numidentities, numframespervideo, hiddensize=256, numlayers=8): self.numidentities = numidentities self.numframespervideo = numframespervideo # Identity codes: one per identity, size 79 self.identitycodes = nn.Embedding(numidentities, 79) nn.init.normal(self.identitycodes.weight.data) # Latent codes: one per frame per video, size 32 self.latentcodes = nn.Embedding(numidentities numframespervideo, 32) nn.init.normal(self.latentcodes.weight.data) # MLP Architecture: 8 linear layers, hidden 256, ReLU layers = [] # Interaction(79) + Latent(32) + PosEncx(20) + PosEncv(8) = 139 inputdim = 139 for in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddensize)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) inputdim = hiddensize self.colorbranch = nn.Linear(hiddensize, 3) self.densitybranch = nn.Linear(hiddensize, 1) self.mlp = nn.Sequential(layers) self.optimizer = optim.Adam( list(self.mlp.parameters()) + list(self.identitycodes.parameters()) + list(self.latentcodes.parameters()), lr=5e-4) # Learning rate decays exponentially from 5e-4 to 5e-5 self.lambdal = 0.01 self.lambdai = 1e-4 self.posfreqsx = 10 self.posfreqsv = 4 def positionalencoding(self, x, freqs): pe = [] for i in range(freqs): scale = 2i torch.pi pe.append(torch.sin(scale x)) pe.append(torch.cos(scale x)) return torch.cat(pe, dim=-1) def forward(self, identityidx, frameidx, x, v, e): i = self.identitycodes(identityidx).unsqueeze(1) l = self.latentcodes(frameidx).unsqueeze(1) # Hadamard product M(e, i) Mei = e i pex = self.positionalencoding(x, self.posfreqsx) pev = self.positionalencoding(v, self.posfreqsv) features = torch.cat([Mei, l.expandas(Mei), pex, pev], dim=-1) h = self.mlp(features) sigma = self.densitybranch(h).squeeze(-1) color = torch.sigmoid(self.colorbranch(h)) return color, sigma def renderray(self, rayo, rayd, tn, tf, numsamples, identityidx, frameidx, e): tvals = torch.linspace(tn, tf, numsamples).to(rayo.device) tvals = tvals.unsqueeze(0).expand(rayo.shape[0], -1) x = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + rayd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) v = rayd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples, -1) color, sigma = self.forward(identityidx, frameidx, x, v, e) deltas = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] deltainf = torch.tensor(1e10).to(rayo.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf.unsqueeze(0).expandas(deltas)], dim=1) alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(1 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = alpha T C = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(2) color, dim=1) return C def trainstep(self, batch): self.optimizer.zerograd() videoidx = batch['videoidx'] frameidx = batch['frameidx'] gtcolor = batch['gtcolor'] pose = batch['pose'] expr = batch['expr'] rayo = batch['rayo'] rayd = batch['rayd'] tn, tf = batch['tn'], batch['tf'] numsamples = batch['numsamples'] xworld, vworld = samplerays(rayo, rayd, tn, tf, numsamples) R = pose['R'] t = pose['t'] # Transform points to canonical space xcanonical = torch.matmul(R.transpose(-2, -1), (xworld - t).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) vcanonical = torch.matmul(R.transpose(-2, -1), vworld.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) identityidx = videoidx frameidxglobal = videoidx self.numframespervideo + batch['localframeidx'] # Render directly to avoid redundant forward pass Cpred = self.renderray(rayo, rayd, tn, tf, numsamples, identityidx, frameidxglobal, expr) Lc = torch.mean((Cpred - gtcolor) 2) Ll = torch.norm(self.latentcodes.weight) Li = torch.norm(self.identitycodes.weight) loss = Lc + self.lambdal Ll + self.lambdai Li loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() return loss.item() Parameters Expression parameter dimension: 79. Identity code dimension: 79. Latent code dimension: 32. MLP architecture: 8 linear layers, hidden size 256, ReLU activations. Positional encoding frequencies: 10 for position x, 4 for view direction v. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying exponentially to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Regularization weights: \lambdal = 0.01, \lambdai = 10^{-4}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Short Videos: The method works for very short video clips (only a few seconds), but personalization may require a short video of the target identity to capture details like wrinkles. Monocular Input: Unlike multi-view methods, MI-NeRF relies on monocular videos, which may lead to ambiguities in depth without strong priors from the 3DMM fitting. Identity Disentanglement: The Hadamard product is used to approximate non-linear interactions. The source notes that higher-degree interactions might be beneficial in other cases, but Hadamard was chosen for simplicity and effectiveness. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced by up to 90% compared to training multiple standard single-identity NeRFs, leading to a sublinear cost curve with respect to the number of identities. Memory Complexity: Requires storing one identity code (79 dims) per identity and one latent code (32 dims) per frame per video, plus the MLP weights. Strengths: Works with monocular videos of arbitrary length captured in the wild; robust to synthesizing novel expressions for any input identity; allows personalization with few iterations. Limitations: Requires 3DMM fitting for each frame to extract pose and expression; relies on the quality of the 3DMM fit (Basel Face Model/FaceWarehouse axes); may struggle with extreme occlusions or non-facial regions if not segmented properly. MI-NeRF was introduced by Chatziagapi et al. in 2024. It addresses the challenge of capturing 4D dynamics and appearance of non-rigid human face motion, which has applications in AR/VR, video games, and virtual communication. Previous approaches relied on 3DMMs or GANs, or required per-identity optimization for NeRFs. MI-NeRF is the first method to learn a single unified face NeRF from monocular videos of multiple identities, leveraging a multiplicative module to disentangle identity and non-identity specific information. name: View-Dependent Appearance and Lighting
body: This family of methods extends the standard NeRF radiance field representation by explicitly modeling how scene appearance varies with the viewing direction, enabling effects such as specular reflections, transparency, and view-dependent lighting. While standard NeRFs often bake shading and shadows into the observed color, making them non-relightable and prone to capturing spurious correlations, these methods separate intrinsic scene properties (albedo, geometry) from extrinsic lighting and view-dependent effects. This separation allows for relighting, novel view synthesis under varying illumination, and accurate modeling of complex materials like glass or metals. The core mechanism involves transforming low-dimensional input coordinates into a high-dimensional feature space using sinusoidal positional encoding, which is then processed by a fully-connected MLP to predict radiance field properties. Positional Encoding The input coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position) and \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (view direction) are mapped to higher dimensions using a hierarchical positional encoding function \gamma(\cdot). For a scalar input p, the encoding is defined as: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)) where L is the number of frequency bands. This function is applied independently to each of the three components of the position vector and the direction vector. Network Architecture The radiance field is represented by an MLP that takes the encoded position and direction as input. The architecture typically consists of two branches: 1. Density Branch: Processes the encoded position features to predict volume density \sigma. 2. Color Branch: Processes the encoded direction features concatenated with intermediate features from the density branch to predict RGB color \mathbf{c}. Ray Sampling Rendering requires sampling points along camera rays. A ray is parameterized as r(\lambda) = o{world} + \lambda d{world}, where o{world} is the world-space origin and d{world} is the world-space direction. The direction is computed from camera intrinsics and extrinsics: d{cam} = (\frac{i - cx}{fx}, \frac{j - cy}{fy}, 1), d{world} = R d{cam}, and o{world} = t. Position samples x are generated along the ray within a defined near/far range. UrbanIR is a method for inverse rendering of large-scale urban scenes from a single monocular video under single illumination, inferring shape, albedo, visibility, and sun/sky illumination to enable relighting and night simulation. It differs from standard NeRFs by learning intrinsic attributes (albedo, normal) independent of lighting, solving the problem that standard NeRFs bake shading and shadows into observed color, making them non-relightable. Unlike methods requiring multiple lighting sources (e.g., NeRF-OSR) or LiDAR/multi-camera setups (e.g., FEGR, LightSim), UrbanIR uses only single illumination RGB video. See-NeRF is a unified sensor-physics grounded NeRF framework for sharp High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis from single-exposure blurry Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images and corresponding event data. It solves the problem of recovering sharp 3D radiance from degraded inputs by explicitly modeling the physical imaging process of both RGB and event sensors, rather than applying tone mapping directly to 3D points. Unlike sibling methods like REF2-NeRF or EvHDR-NeRF which ignore sensor-physics mismatches, See-NeRF bridges the gap between physical scene dynamics and sensor output using differentiable Camera Response Function (CRF) models for both RGB and event streams. REF2-NeRF is a NeRF-based modeling method designed for scenes containing transparent objects, specifically glass cases, where multiple reflection and refraction effects occur. It solves the challenge of accurately modeling such scenes by estimating refraction surfaces and separating direct (view-independent) and reflected (view-dependent) light components using two independent MLPs: a glass network for refraction offsets and a decomposition NeRF for rendering. Unlike methods that assume straight light rays or only handle reflections, REF2-NeRF handles both refraction and reflection in scenes with multiple transparent objects by introducing a view-independent density field and a view-dependent offset field. This method decomposes the view-dependent color output of a NeRF into a view-dependent lighting component v and a view-independent reciprocal color basis r, then enhances v using a neural network to produce an enhanced image Ie without ground truth supervision. It differs from 2D Retinex methods by leveraging 3D geometry and multi-view consistency to constrain decomposition, avoiding the need for paired low-light/high-light training data. SAMURAI is a joint optimization framework that estimates 3D shape, BRDF material properties, per-image illumination, camera poses, and camera intrinsics from unconstrained in-the-wild image collections with varying backgrounds and illuminations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like UrbanIR and See-NeRF by explicitly decomposing radiance into reflectance and illumination, allowing for relightable assets and handling extreme pose uncertainty through camera multiplexing, whereas siblings often assume known poses or fixed illumination. A design choice to fuse the viewing direction only in the last layer of the color MLP. This prevents the optimization from bypassing the neural voxel to learn a direct mapping from viewing direction to output sample color, which leads to erroneous camera poses and geometry. Without late viewing direction conditioning, the optimization can minimize photometric loss by optimizing the MLP directly, leading to erroneous camera poses and geometry estimation. A method that starts with a pre-trained NeRF model to recover a relightable model by simplifying the pre-trained NeRF’s volumetric geometry into a surface model. It optimizes MLPs to represent light source visibility and surface normals at any point on the surface, and optimizes a representation of the environment lighting and the BRDF at any surface point. Results in a more efficient rendering model because volumetric geometry is simplified into a single surface and light-source visibility at any point can be computed by a single MLP query. The original NeRF paper suggested predicting colors with view direction conditioning to model view-dependent effects, a design default in most follow-up works (e.g., Chan et al., 2021; Niemeyer & Geiger, 2021b). However, this design gives the model additional freedom to capture spurious correlations and dataset bias, especially if only a single-view target is provided. Consequently, some methods remove the view direction in color prediction to improve synthesis consistency. Other approaches, such as NeRFactor, use multi-stage pipelines to recover relightable models from images with significant shadows and self-occlusion, starting from pre-trained NeRFs. name: UrbanIR
head: Urban Scene Inverse Rendering
body: UrbanIR is a method for inverse rendering of large-scale urban scenes from a single monocular video under single illumination, inferring shape, albedo, visibility, and sun/sky illumination to enable relighting and night simulation. It differs from standard NeRFs by learning intrinsic attributes (albedo, normal) independent of lighting, solving the problem where standard NeRFs bake shading and shadows into observed color, making them non-relightable. Unlike NeRF-OSR which assumes multiple lighting sources, or FEGR/LightSim which require LiDAR or multiple cameras, UrbanIR uses only single illumination RGB video without LiDAR. Inputs and Outputs Input: A multi-frame video of a scene under single illumination with known camera motion, defined as \{Ii, Ei, Ki\} where Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} is the RGB image, Ei \in SE(3) is the camera pose, and Ki is the camera intrinsic matrix. Output: A neural scene model encoding albedo, normal, semantics, and density, along with a lighting model (sun, ambient, sky), enabling rendering from novel viewpoints under novel lighting conditions. Data Structures The scene representation is built on Instant-NGP, a spatial hash-based voxel NeRF representation. 1. Dense Feature Hash Table: Represents the scene geometry and features. It maps 3D positions to high-dimensional feature vectors. 2. MLP Headers: Individual Multi-Layer Perceptrons are used to decode each attribute given a queried feature at point \mathbf{x}. The attributes are diffuse albedo \mathbf{a}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, semantic vector \mathbf{s}, and density \sigma. 3. Lighting Model: Sun: 5-DoF representation encoding sun color \mathbf{L}{sun} along with azimuth \psi{sun} and zenith \phi{sun}. Ambient: 3-DoF Lambert model \mathbf{L}{amb}. Sky: Sky dome model inferring sky texture from viewing direction. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in a target view, generate a ray r(\lambda) = o{world} + \lambda d{world} using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Sample N points along the ray within the near/far range. 2. Feature Query: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i, query the dense feature hash table to obtain the feature vector. 3. Attribute Prediction: Pass the feature vector through individual MLP headers to predict the intrinsic attributes: albedo \mathbf{a}i, normal \mathbf{n}i, semantics \mathbf{s}i, and density \sigmai. 4. Volume Rendering of Intrinsics: Accumulate the predicted attributes along the ray using alpha-composition weights. The rendered albedo \mathbf{A}(r), normal \mathbf{N}(r), and semantics \mathbf{S}(r) are computed as: \mathbf{A}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{a}i, \quad \mathbf{N}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{n}i, \quad \mathbf{S}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{s}i where the weight wi is defined as: wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) and \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. 5. Visibility Estimation: To model shadows without per-scene optimized MLP heads (which are impractical for changing sun positions), compute an estimate \hat{x}(r) of the 3D point being shaded by volume rendering depth (substituting \hat{t} = \sum wi ti). Then, estimate the visibility V(\hat{x}, \text{sun}) by computing the transmittance along the ray segment between \hat{x} and the light source using volume rendering. 6. Shading and Rendering: Combine the intrinsic attributes, visibility, and lighting model to predict the final RGB color \mathbf{C}: \mathbf{C} = \texttt{Shade}(\texttt{Intrinsic}(F\theta, r), \texttt{Shadow}(F\theta, r, \mathbf{L}), \mathbf{L}) where \mathbf{L} is the lighting model. 7. Optimization: Jointly optimize the scene parameters \theta and lighting parameters \mathbf{L} using a loss function combining rendering loss and other regularization terms. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def urbanirrender(rayorigin, raydirection, lightingmodel, scenehashtable, mlpheaders): """ Renders a single ray using UrbanIR's inverse rendering pipeline. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray tvalues = samplepointsalongray(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples=128) points = rayorigin + raydirection tvalues[:, None] # 2. Query features and predict attributes features = queryhashtable(scenehashtable, points) albedos = mlpheaders'albedo' normals = mlpheaders'normal' semantics = mlpheaders'semantics' densities = mlpheaders'density' # 3. Compute alpha-composition weights deltas = tvalues[1:] - tvalues[:-1] # Handle first point delta appropriately (e.g., small epsilon or specific near-plane logic) deltas = np.insert(deltas, 0, tvalues[0] - tvalues[0]) # Placeholder for boundary handling # Compute transmittance and weights # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) # Note: Standard NeRF volume rendering formula application alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densities deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphas + 1e-10, dim=0) weights = alphas torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:1]), transmittance[:-1]]) # 4. Volume render intrinsics renderedalbedo = torch.sum(weights[:, None] albedos, dim=0) renderednormal = torch.sum(weights[:, None] normals, dim=0) renderedsemantics = torch.sum(weights[:, None] semantics, dim=0) # 5. Estimate depth for shadowing # that = sum(wi ti) rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights tvalues) shadedpoint = rayorigin + raydirection rendereddepth # 6. Estimate visibility to sun # Compute transmittance from shadedpoint to sun direction sunvisibility = estimatesunvisibility(shadedpoint, lightingmodel, scenehashtable, mlpheaders) # 7. Shade finalcolor = shadeintrinsic(renderedalbedo, renderednormal, sunvisibility, lightingmodel) return finalcolor def estimatesunvisibility(point, lightingmodel, scenehashtable, mlpheaders): """ Estimates visibility of a point to the sun by volume rendering along the sun ray. """ sundirection = getsundirection(lightingmodel) # Sample points from point towards sun (or to a large distance) sunrayt = torch.linspace(0, 100, 64) # Arbitrary large distance sunraypoints = point + sundirection sunrayt[:, None] # Query features and densities along sun ray sunfeatures = queryhashtable(scenehashtable, sunraypoints) sundensities = mlpheaders'density' # Compute transmittance (visibility) # V = exp(-sum(sigma delta)) # Assuming uniform delta for simplicity or compute from tvalues deltas = sunrayt[1:] - sunrayt[:-1] deltas = np.insert(deltas, 0, 0.0) # Placeholder alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sundensities deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphas + 1e-10, dim=0) visibility = transmittance[-1] return visibility Parameters Input Video: Single monocular video with known camera motion. Lighting Model: Sun (5-DoF), Ambient (3-DoF), Sky. Scene Representation: Instant-NGP spatial hash table. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Visibility Estimation: Modeling visibility with a per-scene optimized MLP head is impractical because the sun position changes during relighting, but training data only has one sun position. UrbanIR avoids this by estimating visibility via volume rendering transmittance to the light source. Standard NeRF Limitations: Standard NeRFs bake shading, shadow, and specularity into observed color, making them non-relightable. UrbanIR solves this by learning intrinsic attributes independent of lighting. Time and Memory Complexity: Uses Instant-NGP's spatial hash-based voxel representation, which offers low memory consumption and high efficiency in training and rendering compared to dense voxel grids. Measured Performance: Capable of handling large-scale, unbounded urban scenes from a single video. Strengths: Does not require LiDAR or multiple cameras; works with single illumination RGB video; enables relighting and night simulation. Limitations: Relies on monocular cues (shadows, surface normals) which may be ambiguous in textureless regions or uniform lighting. Assumes single illumination during training. UrbanIR was introduced by Chih-Hao Lin, Bohan Liu, Yi-Ting Chen, Kuan-Sheng Chen, David Forsyth, Jia-Bin Huang, Anand Bhattad, and Shenlong Wang from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and University of Maryland, College Park. It was published in 3DV 2025 (arXiv:2306.09349v4, 14 Jan 2025). The method addresses the limitation of existing relightable NeRF methods that focus on small bounded indoor environments or require multiple lighting sources/LiDAR. name: See-NeRF
head: See-NeRF framework, Sensor-Physics Grounded Deblurring HDR NeRF
body: See-NeRF is a unified sensor-physics grounded NeRF framework for sharp High Dynamic Range (HDR) novel view synthesis from single-exposure blurry Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images and corresponding event data. It solves the problem of suboptimal HDR and deblurring results caused by sensor-physics mismatches, where traditional methods ignore the specific imaging processes of RGB and event sensors. Unlike sibling methods like EvHDR-NeRF that apply tone mapping directly to 3D points, See-NeRF explicitly models the radiance-to-measurement process for both RGB and event sensors, aligning rendered outputs with physical sensor recordings. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Single-exposure blurry LDR images \mathcal{I}{LDR}, corresponding event data B, camera poses p(t), and intrinsics. Outputs: Sharp HDR novel view images \hat{\mathcal{I}}{HDR} and LDR images \hat{\mathcal{I}}{LDR} for arbitrary camera poses. Data Structures NeRF Network (F\theta): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with parameters \theta. It takes positional encoding of 3D coordinates \mathbf{o} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input. Input: \gammao(\mathbf{o}), \gammad(\mathbf{d}). Output: Raw HDR radiance \mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. RGB CRF Model: Three separate MLPs (f{crf}), one for each color channel (R, G, B). Input: Log-domain raw HDR pixel value. Output: Estimated LDR pixel value. Event CRF Model: Delay Coefficient MLP (f{ev}): Predicts delay coefficient \epsiloni. Input: Event sensor pixel radiance E{ev}. Output: Scalar \epsiloni. Delay Offset Function (h): Estimates temporal delay offset from input events. (Implementation details omitted in source; treated as a black-box function h(\cdot)). Positional Encoding The input coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position) and \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (view direction) are mapped to higher dimensions using hierarchical positional encoding \gammaM(\cdot): \gammaM(x) = \{\sin(2^m\pi x), \cos(2^m\pi x)\}{m=0}^{M} This is applied to each component of \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d}. Numbered Steps 1. Scene Representation: For a 3D point \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, compute raw HDR radiance \mathbf{e} and density \sigma using the NeRF network: (\mathbf{e}, \sigma) = F{\theta}(\gammao(\mathbf{o}), \gammad(\mathbf{d})) 2. Ray Sampling and Volume Rendering: Discretely sample b+1 time points \{ti\}{i=0}^b within the exposure time [t{start}, t{end}]. For each time point ti, render the latent sharp HDR radiance Ei(x,y,p(ti)) at pixel (x,y) using volume rendering: E(x,y,p(t)) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{e}i where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), \deltai is the distance between adjacent sampled 3D points, and N is the number of samples along the ray. 3. Raw HDR Pixel Calculation: Calculate the predicted raw HDR pixel value by summing weighted radiance values at sampled time points: \hat{\mathcal{I}}{HDR}(x,y) = \sum{i=0}^{b} wi Ei(x,y,p(ti)) where wi are weights calculated from time points \{ti\}{i=0}^b. 4. Physically Grounded RGB CRF Model: Convert the raw HDR pixel value to LDR using the learned CRF MLPs in the log domain: \hat{\mathcal{I}}{LDR}(x,y) = f{crf}(\ln(\hat{\mathcal{I}}{HDR}(x,y) \Delta t{exp})) where \Delta t{exp} = t{end} - t{start} is the exposure time. 5. Event CRF Model: Bayer Pattern Adaptation: Input the b+1 scene radiance values \{E(x,y,p(ti))\}{i=0}^b into an RGGB Bayer pattern to obtain event sensor pixel radiance values E{ev}(x,y,p(ti)). Delay Coefficient: Calculate delay coefficient \epsiloni using the MLP f{ev}: \epsiloni = f{ev}(E{ev}(x,y,p(ti))) Latency Synthesis: Synthesize event latency using a second-order low-pass filter: L^{i}{lp} = (1-\epsiloni)L^{i-1}{lp} + \epsiloni E{ev}(p(ti)) with initialization L^0{lp} = E{ev}(p(t0)). Ideal Event Count: Calculate estimated event numbers \hat{B}'(ti, t{i+1}) using the ideal model on filtered radiance: \hat{B}'(ti, t{i+1}) = \text{floor}\left(\frac{\ln(L^{i+1}{lp}) - \ln(L^{i}{lp})}{\Theta}\right) where \Theta is the contrast threshold. Delay Compensation: Compensate for temporal delay by estimating an offset h(B(ti, t{i+1})) from input events and subtracting it: \hat{B}(ti, t{i+1}) = \hat{B}'(ti, t{i+1}) - h(B(ti, t{i+1})) 6. Optimization: Jointly optimize the NeRF network and CRF models by minimizing the combined loss function: \mathcal{L} = \lambda \mathcal{L}{evs} + \mathcal{L}{ldr} where: \mathcal{L}{evs} = \sum{(x,y)\in \mathcal{X}} \sum{i=0}^{b-1} ||\hat{B}(ti, t{i+1}) - B(ti, t{i+1})||^22 \mathcal{L}{ldr} = \sum{(x,y)\in \mathcal{X}} ||\hat{\mathcal{I}}{LDR}(x,y) - \mathcal{I}{LDR}(x,y)||^22 and \mathcal{X} denotes all pixels of the camera sensor. Parameters b: Number of time intervals minus one (total b+1 points). Value: 4. Context: Trade-off between performance and training time. \lambda: Weight for event loss. Value: 0.005. \Theta: Contrast threshold in event generation. Definition: Minimum detectable brightness change lower bound. \Delta t{exp}: Exposure time. Definition: t{end} - t{start}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sensor-Physics Mismatch: Traditional methods ignore sensor-physics mismatches (e.g., applying tone mapping directly to 3D points), leading to suboptimal HDR and deblurring results because rendered outputs do not align with supervision signals. Event Delay in Low-Light: Actual event generation may deviate from the ideal model with significant delay in low-light regions, requiring the delay compensation term h(\cdot). Quantifiable Errors: Due to the fixed contrast threshold \Theta, the minimum detectable brightness change is lower-bounded, leading to quantifiable errors in radiometric estimation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art HDR and deblurring novel view synthesis results on synthetic and real datasets (RealWorld-Challenge). Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly models the radiance-to-measurement process for both RGB and event sensors, ensuring physical consistency. Leverages spatial and temporal dynamic information in events to enhance sharp HDR 3D representation learning. Limitations: Requires corresponding event data and blurry LDR images. Relies on event-guided COLMAP for pose estimation during exposure. When to use: When reconstructing sharp HDR scenes from single-exposure blurry LDR images and corresponding events, especially in extreme lighting conditions. When not to use: When event data is unavailable or when the input images are not blurry/single-exposure. See-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of existing methods like EvHDR-NeRF, which extend HDR-NeRF by applying tone mapping to 3D points without considering event generation characteristics. The method is grounded in the physical imaging principles of RGB and event sensors, aiming to bridge the gap between physical scene dynamics and sensor output. It builds on the principles of View-Dependent Appearance and Lighting [18221-view-dependent-appearance-and-lighting.md] by using positional encoding and MLPs, but diverges by removing the view direction condition from color prediction to prevent spurious correlations, and by introducing sensor-physics grounded CRF models [18221-view-dependent-appearance-and-lighting.md]. Seeing through Light and Darkness: Sensor-Physics Grounded Deblurring HDR NeRF from Single-Exposure Images and Events, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.15475v4, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: REF2-NeRF
head: Reflection and Refraction aware Neural Radiance Field
body: REF2-NeRF is a NeRF-based modeling method designed for scenes containing transparent objects, specifically glass cases, where it models both refraction and reflection effects. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF and reflection-only methods (e.g., NeRFReN, NeuS-HSR) by simultaneously estimating refraction surfaces and separating direct (view-independent) and reflected (view-dependent) light components using two independent MLPs: a Glass network for refraction offsets and a Decomposition NeRF for rendering. Unlike LB-NeRF, which simplifies refraction as a static offset, REF2-NeRF introduces a view-independent density field and a view-dependent offset field to estimate refraction surfaces and offsets simultaneously, handling multiple glass plates more effectively than explicit-space methods like MS-NeRF. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of n images \{Ik\} taken from different viewpoints, with predetermined camera poses (often acquired via robotic arm). Outputs: A rendered image C(r) for a given ray r, and estimated fields for glass density, refraction offsets, view-independent color/density, and view-dependent features. Data Structures and Network Architecture The method uses four main neural network components, all taking positional encoded inputs \Gamma(\cdot): 1. Glass Network (\Theta{gl}): Input: \Gamma(x), \Gamma(d) where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is position, d \in \mathbb{R}^3 is view direction. Output: Glass density \sigma{gl} \in \mathbb{R} (view-independent) and Offset vector \Delta x \in \mathbb{R}^3 (view-dependent). Architecture: MLP with input dimension 6 \times 256 (assuming 256 encoding dim per component, total 512? Source says [6256] in Fig 3 caption, likely meaning 6 channels of encoding or specific layer size. The text says "Input [Γ(x), Γ(d)]". We treat inputs as the encoded vectors). 2. Decomposition NeRF (\Theta{nf}): Input: \Gamma(x'), \Gamma(d) where x' is the adjusted position. Output: View-independent density \sigma{vi} \in \mathbb{R}, View-independent color c{vi} \in \mathbb{R}^3, View-dependent density \sigma{vd} \in \mathbb{R}, and View-dependent feature vector f{vd} \in \mathbb{R}^\theta (where \theta=64). Architecture: Two branches. One branch (MLP [256, 128]) takes \Gamma(x') to output \sigma{vi}, c{vi}. The other branch (MLP [8256] input, [256, 128] output) takes \Gamma(x'), \Gamma(d) to output \sigma{vd}, f{vd}. 3. Decoder MLP (\Theta{dc}): Input: Rendered feature vector F{vd}. Output: Reflection color C{vd} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Gate MLP (\Theta{gt}): Input: Rendered feature vector F{vd}. Output: Blending parameter \alpha \in \mathbb{R}. Sampling Strategy 1. Coarse Sampling: 128 points sampled at uniform intervals along the ray. 2. Fine Sampling: 64 points hierarchically sampled based on coarse density (standard NeRF strategy). 32 points sampled based on glass density \sigma{gl}. 32 points sampled based on view-independent density \sigma{vi}. Total points for fine model: 192. Rendering Pipeline 1. Refraction Offset Calculation: For each sampling point i along ray r, calculate the refraction weight wi using glass density \sigma{gl,i} and distance \delta{gl,i} between adjacent points: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma{gl,i} \delta{gl,i})) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{gl,j} \delta{gl,j}\right) The adjusted position x'i is computed by cumulatively adding the weighted offsets: x'i = xi + \sum{j=1}^{i} wj \Delta xj This represents the parallel shift of the ray due to refraction. 2. View-Independent Rendering: Perform volume rendering on adjusted positions x' using view-independent density \sigma{vi} and color c{vi}. The view-independent color C{vi}(r) is: C{vi}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{vi,i} (1 - \exp(-\sigma{vi,i} \delta{vi,i})) c{vi,i} where T{vi,i} is the transmittance calculated similarly to Eq. 4 using \sigma{vi}. 3. View-Dependent Feature Rendering: Perform volume rendering on adjusted positions x' and view directions d using view-dependent density \sigma{vd} and feature vector f{vd} to get feature vector F{vd}: F{vd}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigma{vd,i} \delta{vd,i})) f{vd,i} Here Ti is the transmittance based on \sigma{vd}. 4. View-Dependent Color and Blending: Decode the rendered feature vector F{vd} into reflection color C{vd} using decoder MLP \Theta{dc}: C{vd}(r) = F{\Theta{dc}}(F{vd}(r)) Determine blending parameter \alpha using gate MLP \Theta{gt}: \alpha(r) = F{\Theta{gt}}(F{vd}(r)) 5. Final Image Composition: The final pixel color C(r) is the sum of the view-independent color and the blended view-dependent color: C(r) = C{vi}(r) + \alpha(r) C{vd}(r) Training and Loss Loss Function: The total loss L is the sum of the rendering loss L{render} (L2 distance between rendered color C(r) and input image \bar{C}(r)) and a regularization loss L{offset}: L{render} = \sum{r \in R} \|\bar{C}(r) - C(r)\|^2 L{offset} = \sum{x,d} (\Delta x)^2 L = L{render} + \epsilon L{offset} where \epsilon = 10^{-5}. Parameters: Feature vector dimension \theta = 64. Optimization: Rays sampled from 1,024 pixels per iteration. 200,000 training iterations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math def positionalencoding(p, L=10): """ Standard NeRF positional encoding. p: tensor of shape (..., 3) Returns: tensor of shape (..., 6L) """ scales = [2i for i in range(L)] scaledp = p.unsqueeze(-1) scales encoded = torch.cat([torch.sin(scaledp), torch.cos(scaledp)], dim=-1) return encoded class GlassNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Input: 6L (pos) + 6L (dir). Output: 1 (sigmagl) + 3 (deltax) # Architecture hint from Fig 3: [6256] input layer? # Assuming standard MLP structure based on description. self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(12 256, 256), # Assuming 256 dim encoding nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 4) # 1 for sigma, 3 for offset) def forward(self, xenc, denc): inp = torch.cat([xenc, denc], dim=-1) out = self.mlp(inp) sigmagl = out[...,:1] deltax = out[..., 1:] return sigmagl, deltax class DecompNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, theta=64): super().init() self.theta = theta # View-independent branch: Input posenc -> sigmavi, cvi self.vibranch = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6 256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 4) # 1 sigma, 3 color) # View-dependent branch: Input posenc, direnc -> sigmavd, fvd self.vdbranch = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(12 256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1 + theta) # 1 sigma, theta features) def forward(self, xprimeenc, denc): # VI viout = self.vibranch(xprimeenc) sigmavi = viout[...,:1] cvi = viout[..., 1:] # VD vdinp = torch.cat([xprimeenc, denc], dim=-1) vdout = self.vdbranch(vdinp) sigmavd = vdout[...,:1] fvd = vdout[..., 1:] return sigmavi, cvi, sigmavd, fvd class DecoderMLP(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3)) def forward(self, fvd): return self.mlp(fvd) class GateMLP(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1)) def forward(self, fvd): return torch.sigmoid(self.mlp(fvd)) def volumerender(sigma, colororfeat, delta, transmittanceprev=None): """ Standard volume rendering. sigma: (N,) colororfeat: (N, C) delta: (N,) distance between points """ alpha = 1.0 - Decomp NeRF Forward Pass xprimeenc = positionalencoding(xprime) sigmavi, cvi, sigmavd, fvd = decompnet(xprimeenc, denc) # 6. View-Independent Rendering deltavi = deltagl # Use same distances Cvi, = volumerender(sigmavi, cvi, deltavi) # 7. View-Dependent Feature Rendering Fvd, = volumerender(sigmavd, fvd, deltagl) # 8. Decode and Blend Cvd = decoder(Fvd) alpha = gate(Fvd) C = Cvi + alpha Cvd return C def trainstep(images, poses, glassnet, decompnet, decoder, gate, optimizer, epsilon=1e-5): # Sample rays from 1024 pixels rays = samplerays(images, poses, numpixels=1024) # Render preds = [] for r in rays: pred = renderray(r.origin, r.direction, glassnet, decompnet, decoder, gate) preds.append(pred) preds = torch.stack(preds) # Loss Lrender = torch.mean((preds - images) 2) # Regularization on glass network offsets # Need to forward glass net on all points to get deltax # This requires re-running the glass network part or storing it. # Assuming we have access to deltax from render step or re-compute. # For simplicity, assume we have deltaxbatch from a forward pass. # Loffset = mean(deltax^2) # Loffset = torch.mean(glassnetoutputsdeltax 2) L = Lrender + epsilon Loffset optimizer.zerograd() L.backward() optimizer.step() return L.item() Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 10 hours per scene on an Nvidia RTX 4080 GPU for 200,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Accurately models both glass refraction and overall scene, separating direct and reflected light components. Strengths: Handles multiple transparent objects (e.g., glass showcases) and reciprocal reflections better than explicit-space methods like MS-NeRF. Simultaneously estimates refraction surfaces and offsets. Limitations: Requires predetermined camera poses, which are difficult to acquire in scenes with glass objects (necessitating robotic arms). When to use: Scenes with glass cases or multiple transparent objects where both refraction and reflection need to be modeled. When not to use: Scenes without transparent objects or where camera poses cannot be precisely determined. REF2-NeRF was proposed to address the challenge of modeling scenes with multiple glass objects, such as objects in a glass showcase, where existing NeRF-based methods struggled with simultaneous reflection and refraction effects. It builds on LB-NeRF, which simplified refraction as an offset, but improves upon it by introducing view-independent density and view-dependent offset fields. It also addresses limitations of MS-NeRF, which used multiple explicit spaces for mirrors, by using a single view-dependent feature field to handle complex reciprocal reflections. The method was implemented based on NeRFPytorch. REF2-NeRF: Reflection and Refraction aware Neural Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros58592.2024.10801830, fetched 2026-11-08

name: Unsupervised Decomposition and Enhancement in NeRF
head: LLNeRF, Lighting up NeRF
body: This method decomposes the view-dependent color in a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a view-dependent lighting component and a view-independent reciprocal color basis, then enhances the lighting component without ground truth supervision to correct color distortions and improve brightness in low-light scenes. It differs from 2D Retinex-based methods by leveraging 3D geometry and multi-view consistency to constrain the decomposition, avoiding the need for paired low-light/high-light training data. Inputs: Training images (typically RAW or low-light processed images) with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Spatial coordinates \tau and view directions d. Outputs: Enhanced radiance field parameters. Enhanced images Ie with corrected lighting and color. The model architecture consists of three main neural networks: 1. Lighting MLP (F1): Input: Encoded spatial coordinate \tau and view direction d. Output: View-dependent lighting component v (scalar). Architecture: Standard MLP (details not specified beyond output dimension). 2. Reciprocal MLP (F2): Input: Encoded spatial coordinate \tau. Output: Reciprocal color basis r (3-channel RGB vector). Architecture: Standard MLP (details not specified beyond output dimension). 3. Enhancement Model (\phi): Input: The lighting component v. Output: Two sets of coefficients: \alpha: Scalar (1 channel) for global lighting gain. \gamma: 3D vector (3 channels) for color distortion correction. Internal Structure: Feature MLP 1: 8 hidden layers, 256 channels each. Feature MLP 2: 1 hidden layer, 256 channels. Coeff MLP: Outputs \alpha (1 channel) and \gamma (3 channels). Color MLP: (Used in some configurations, 1x128 channels, 3 output channels, though the primary enhancement uses \alpha and \gamma). 1. Decomposition: For each sample point i along a ray, compute the lighting component vi and reciprocal basis ri: vi = F1(\taui, di; \Theta{F1}) ri = F2(\taui; \Theta{F2}) The original color is ci = vi \circ ri, where \circ is pixel-wise multiplication. 2. Enhancement Function: Apply the enhancement network \phi to vi to produce \hat{v}i: \hat{v}i = \phi(vi) = \left( \frac{vi}{\gamma0} \right)^{\frac{\alpha}{1+\gamma0}} \circ \gamma \alpha: Scalar output from \phi, adjusts lighting gain globally. \gamma: 3D vector output from \phi, applies a small permutation to v for color correction. \gamma0: Fixed initialization value for the non-linear transform. Smoothness Loss (Ls): Constrains the gradients of the coefficients \alpha and \gamma with respect to the integrated lighting vr to preserve local structure: Ls = L{sa} + L{sg} L{sa} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{(\alphar - \alpha{rh})^2}{(vr - v{rh})^2 + \epsilon1} + \frac{(\alphar - \alpha{rv})^2}{(vr - v{rv})^2 + \epsilon1} \right] L{sg} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{(\gammar - \gamma{rh})^2}{(vr - v{rh})^2 + \epsilon1} + \frac{(\gammar - \gamma{rv})^2}{(vr - v{rv})^2 + \epsilon1} \right] Subscripts h and v denote horizontal and vertical neighbors in image space. \epsilon1: Small constant to prevent division by zero. Feature MLP 1: 8x256 self.featuremlp1 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(1, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU()) # Feature MLP 2: 1x256 self.featuremlp2 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU()) # Coeff MLP: Outputs alpha (1) and gamma (3) self.coeffmlp = nn.Linear(256, 4) # 1 for alpha, 3 for gamma def forward(self, v): # v is scalar (N,) x = self.featuremlp1(v) x = self.featuremlp2(x) coeffs = self.coeffmlp(x) alpha = coeffs[:, 0] # (N,) gamma = coeffs[:, 1:] # (N, 3) return alpha, gamma def enhancecolor(v, r, alpha, gamma, gamma0=1.0): """ Enhance the color using the decomposition. v: (N,) scalar lighting component r: (N, 3) reciprocal color basis alpha: (N,) scalar gain gamma: (N, 3) color correction vector gamma0: Fixed initialization value """ # Apply alpha as global gain enhancedv = alpha v # Apply gamma as channel-wise multiplier for color correction # Note: Source formula ambiguity resolved by text description of "permutation" # and "color distortion correction". enhancedr = r gamma # Combined enhanced color chat = enhancedv.unsqueeze(1) enhancedr return chat def renderray(samples, weights, v, r, alpha, gamma, gamma0=1.0): """ Render enhanced image for a single ray. samples: (N,) weights along ray weights: (N,) volume rendering weights v: (N,) lighting component r: (N, 3) reciprocal basis alpha: (N,) alpha coefficients gamma: (N, 3) gamma coefficients """ chat = enhancecolor(v, r, alpha, gamma, gamma0) # Weighted sum cr = torch.sum(chat weights.unsqueeze(1), dim=0) return cr def smoothnessloss(alpha, gamma, v, neighbors): """ Compute smoothness loss Ls. alpha, gamma, v: (N,) or (N, 3) for gamma neighbors: dict with 'h' and 'v' keys, each containing tensors for horizontal/vertical neighbors """ eps1 = 1e-6 # Horizontal alphah = neighbors['h']['alpha'] gammah = neighbors['h']['gamma'] vh = neighbors['h']['v'] # Vertical alphav = neighbors['v']['alpha'] gammav = neighbors['v']['gamma'] vv = neighbors['v']['v'] # Lsa denomh = (v - vh)2 + eps1 denomv = (v - vv)2 + eps1 lsah = (alpha - alphah)2 / denomh lsav = (alpha - alphav)2 / denomv lsa = 0.5 (lsah + lsav) # Lsg lsgh = (gamma - gammah)2 / denomh lsgv = (gamma - gammav)2 / denomv lsg = 0.5 (lsgh + lsgv) return lsa + lsg def grayworldloss(chat, r, e=0.55, lambda1=1.0, lambda2=1.0, beta1=1.0): """ Compute gray-world prior loss Lc. chat: (N, 3) enhanced color r: (N, 3) reciprocal basis """ # Term 1: Brightness target lossbright = torch.mean((chat - e)2) # Term 2: Color variance correction varchat = torch.var(chat, dim=0, unbiased=False) # Channel-wise variance varr = torch.var(r, dim=0, unbiased=False) # Avoid division by zero denom = beta1 + varr losscolor = torch.mean(varchat / denom) # Term 3: Regularization on gamma (gamma is not directly in chat, # but we assume gamma is available in the calling scope or passed) # Note: The loss function definition in source includes ||gamma||^2. # We need gamma here. return lossbright + lambda1 losscolor def dataloss(rawpixels, predictedcolor, eps2=1e-6): """ Compute data loss using tone mapping. rawpixels: (N, 3) observed RAW pixels predictedcolor: (N, 3) predicted color cr """ def eta(y): return torch.log(y + eps2) return torch.mean(eta(rawpixels) - eta(predictedcolor)) \alpha: Scalar output by \phi, adjusts lighting gain globally. \gamma: 3D vector output by \phi, used for color distortion correction. \gamma0: Fixed value used to initialize the non-linear transform. e: Hyper-parameter for the gray-world prior loss, set to 0.55 to improve pixel brightness. \lambda1, \lambda2, \beta1: Hyper-parameters for the gray-world prior loss Lc. \epsilon1: Small constant added to the denominator of the smoothness loss to prevent division by zero. \epsilon2: Small constant added inside the tone mapping function \eta(y) = \log(y + \epsilon2). Color Distortion in RAW Images: Non-linear ISP processes change the noise distribution, causing the predicted color cr to converge to a biased value \bar{c} + b instead of the true color \bar{c}, leading to color distortions. The method addresses this via the gray-world prior loss and enhancement network. Division by Zero: Small constants \epsilon1 and \epsilon2 are required to prevent numerical instability in the smoothness loss and tone mapping, respectively. Convergence to Gray: The gray-world prior might push colors to gray; the dynamic weight based on r relaxes this constraint for highly saturated colors. A method for urban scene reconstruction using NeRF, focusing on handling large-scale scenes and dynamic elements. Link A method for improving NeRF in transparent and reflective scenes by incorporating physical rendering principles. Link A method for handling reflections in NeRF by decomposing the scene into diffuse and specular components. Link A method for high-fidelity NeRF training using sparse attention and multi-scale features. Link Time Complexity: Training time is comparable to standard NeRF but increased by the additional forward pass through the enhancement network \phi and the computation of smoothness losses involving neighboring rays. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional parameters for \phi and intermediate features for smoothness loss calculations. Strengths: Unsupervised, does not require paired low-light/high-light data. Leverages 3D geometry for consistent decomposition. Effective in correcting color distortions and enhancing brightness in low-light scenes. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of the decomposition. May struggle with extreme lighting variations if the priors are not well-tuned. Computationally more expensive than standard NeRF due to the enhancement network and neighbor sampling for smoothness loss. When to use: Low-light image synthesis and enhancement where ground truth is unavailable. When not to use: Well-lit scenes where enhancement is unnecessary, or when paired training data is available (other methods may be more efficient). Origin: Proposed in "Lighting up NeRF via Unsupervised Decomposition and Enhancement" (ICCV 2023). History: Builds on the concept of Retinex theory for image decomposition and applies it to the 3D neural radiance field framework. It addresses the limitations of 2D Retinex methods that require ground truth and do not leverage 3D consistency. Usage: Used for enhancing low-light images and synthesizing novel views in dark environments. name: SAMURAI
head: Joint optimization of shape, BRDF, cameras, and illuminations, Shape and Material from Unconstrained Real-World Arbitrary Image Collections
body: SAMURAI is a joint optimization framework that estimates 3D shape, BRDF material properties, per-image illumination, camera poses, and camera intrinsics from unconstrained in-the-wild image collections with varying backgrounds and illuminations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like UrbanIR and See-NeRF by explicitly decomposing radiance into reflectance and illumination, enabling relightable assets, and by employing a camera multiplex strategy to handle extremely coarse initial pose annotations without requiring perfect correspondences or GAN-style training. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A collection of q object images Cj \in \mathbb{R}^{sj \times 3} with varying resolutions, backgrounds, and illuminations. Rough camera pose quadrants annotated with 3 binary questions: Left vs. Right, Above vs. Below, Front vs. Back. Automatically estimated foreground segmentation masks Mj \in \{0, 1\}^{s \times 1} (e.g., via U2-Net), which may be noisy. Outputs: A 3D neural volume representing shape and BRDF, explicit meshes with BRDF textures, and optimized per-image camera parameters and latent illumination vectors. Data Structures and Layout Neural Volume: At each point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, the network predicts: BRDF parameters \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^5 for the Cook-Torrance model: base color \mathbf{bc} \in \mathbb{R}^3, metallic bm \in \mathbb{R}^1, roughness br \in \mathbb{R}. Unit-length surface normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Per-Image Latent Illumination: Vectors \mathbf{z}{jl} \in \mathbb{R}^{128} for each image j. Camera Parameters: Stored as offsets to initial parameters using a 'look-at' parameterization: 3D look-at vector \mathbf{r}j \in \mathbb{R}^3. Scalar up rotation uj \in \mathbb{R}[-\pi, \pi]. 3D camera position \mathbf{t}j \in \mathbb{R}^3. Focal length fj \in \mathbb{R}, stored in compressed form \hat{f}j = fj / \sqrt{h}, where h is image height in pixels. Network Architecture: A single "Fine/Decomposition Network" (no coarse network) consisting of an MLP with 8 layers of 128 features. Density Branch: A layer with 1 feature output for density \sigma. Radiance Branch: An MLP with a hidden layer for view/appearance conditioned radiance. BRDF Decoder: Compresses main network features to 16 features, then expands to BRDF parameters. Ray Sampling and Bounds Sampling: 128 points sampled along the ray in fixed steps. Bounds: Defined by a world-space sphere with radius v (diameter 1). For a camera origin \mathbf{o}, the near bound is |\mathbf{o}| - v and the far bound is |\mathbf{o}| + v. This allows arbitrary camera distances, unlike fixed near/far planes in standard NeRF. Optimization Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize camera poses based on quadrant annotations and an initial Field of View of 53.13 degrees. Initialize Fourier embedding frequencies with logarithmic spacing, adding Gaussian distributed noise as offsets to prevent axis-aligned artifacts. 2. Camera Multiplex Setup: For each image, optimize 4 randomly jittered poses around the quadrant center. Maintain a memory bank and momentum for camera multiplex weights \mathbf{S}j \in \mathbb{R}^4 across batches. 3. Forward Pass & Rendering: Cast rays through the volume. Compute radiance using the predicted BRDF, illumination \mathbf{z}{jl}, and view direction. Compute volumetric rendering for color \tilde{\mathbf{c}} (direct color, used early) and \hat{\mathbf{c}} (BRDF-based color). 4. Loss Calculation: Compute individual losses (defined below). Apply Camera Multiplex Weights: \mathbf{S}j = \text{softmax}(-\lambdas \mathbf{L}{\text{Mask}, ij}), where \lambdas increases during optimization. Update network loss: \mathbf{L}{\text{Network}, j} = \sumi S{ji} \mathbf{L}{\text{Network}, ij}. Apply Posterior Scaling: Maintain a circular buffer of ~1000 recent mask and image losses. Calculate mean \mul and standard deviation \sigmal. Compute scaling factor spj = \max(\tanh(\frac{\mul - (\mathbf{L}{\text{Mask}, j} + \mathbf{L}{\text{Image}, j})}{\sigmal}) + 1, 1). Apply: \mathbf{L}{\text{Network}, j} = spj \mathbf{L}{\text{Network}, j}. Note: Camera optimization uses the same losses but does not apply posterior scaling to allow badly initialized poses to recover. 5. Backpropagation: Optimize networks using Adam (LR 10^{-4}, decay 10\times every 300k steps). Optimize cameras using Adam (LR 3 \times 10^{-3}, decay 10\times every 70k steps). Schedule \lambdab (BRDF vs direct color), \lambdaa (initialization loss), and \lambdac (resolution/multiplex reduction). Formulas Mask Loss: \mathbf{L}{\text{Mask}} = \mathbf{L}{\text{BCE}} + \mathbf{L}{\text{Background}}, where \mathbf{L}{\text{Background}} forces background samples to 0. Initialization Loss: \mathbf{L}{\text{Init}} = \mathbf{L}{\text{MSE}}(Cs, \mathbf{bc}), preventing illumination local minima. Decomposition Sparsity: \mathbf{L}{\text{Dec Sparsity}} = \frac{1}{N} \sumi |ei|, where ei is the BRDF embedding. Decomposition Smoothness: \mathbf{L}{\text{Dec Smooth}} = \frac{1}{N} \sumi |f(\theta; ei) - f(\theta; ei + \epsilon)|, with \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01^2). Total Network Loss: \mathbf{L}{\text{Network}} = \lambdab \mathbf{L}{\text{Image}}(Cs, \tilde{\mathbf{c}}) + (1 - \lambdab) \mathbf{L}{\text{Image}}(Cs, \hat{\mathbf{c}}) + \mathbf{L}{\text{Mask}} + \lambdaa \mathbf{L}{\text{Init}} + \lambda{\text{ndir}} \mathbf{L}{\text{ndir}} + \lambda{\text{Smooth}} \mathbf{L}{\text{Smooth}} + \lambda{\text{Dec Smooth}} \mathbf{L}{\text{Dec Smooth}} + \lambda{\text{Dec Sparsity}} \mathbf{L}{\text{Dec Sparsity}} where \mathbf{L}{\text{Image}} is the Chabonnier loss \sqrt{(g-p)^2 + 0.001^2}. Camera Constraints: Look-at loss: \mathbf{L}{\text{lookat}} (L1 loss on look-at vector \mathbf{r}j). Bounds loss: \mathbf{L}{\text{Bounds}} = \max((v - |\mathbf{t}j|)^2, 0). The use of a single fine network (no coarse network) reduces memory and compute compared to two-stage NeRFs. However, camera multiplexing (4 poses per image) increases the number of forward passes per batch, requiring dynamic loss re-weighting. Memory Complexity: Stores per-image latent illumination vectors (\mathbb{R}^{128}) and camera parameters. The circular buffer for posterior scaling stores ~1000 loss elements. Strengths: Handles unconstrained in-the-wild images with varying backgrounds and illuminations. Does not require perfect camera poses or correspondences. Produces relightable 3D assets (meshes with BRDF). Robust to noisy segmentation masks via posterior scaling. Limitations: Optimization is highly non-convex and requires careful scheduling of \lambda variables. Camera multiplexing can be noisy if not properly weighted. Relies on automatic segmentation which may be imperfect. When to use: When given a collection of in-the-wild images with unknown/exact camera poses and varying lighting, and the goal is to create a relightable 3D model. When not to use: When high-quality, controlled studio captures with known poses are available (standard NeRF or COLMAP-based methods are more efficient). When real-time rendering is required without pre-computation (NeRF is inherently slow). SAMURAI was proposed by Boss et al. in 2022. It addresses the limitations of prior methods like NeRF (which assumes fixed near/far planes and equidistant cameras) and Neural-PIL (which requires perfect camera poses and segmentation masks). It builds on the architecture of NeRD and Neural-PIL but introduces flexible camera parameterization, camera multiplex optimization, and posterior scaling to handle the severe under-constrained nature of in-the-wild image collections. It is compared against SCNeRF, BARF, NeRF--, and GNeRF, highlighting its ability to work without correspondences, with coarse poses, in multiple illuminations, without double training, and without GANs. name: Generative and GAN-Based Methods
body: Generative and GAN-Based Methods synthesize novel 3D objects or scenes by optimizing a radiance field to match the distribution of a pretrained 2D Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) or by directly training a generative radiance field with adversarial losses. Unlike standard NeRF which reconstructs a specific static scene from images, these methods generate new instances by sampling latent codes, enabling data augmentation and novel view synthesis of unseen objects. The core mechanism involves a generator network that maps a latent code z and camera pose \xi to a radiance field representation, which is then rendered into 2D images. The training process typically involves an adversarial loop where a discriminator distinguishes between real and generated images, guiding the generator to produce photorealistic outputs. Latent Space Conditioning: The radiance field is conditioned on a latent code z sampled from a prior distribution (e.g., Gaussian \mathcal{N}(0, I)). In methods lifting 2D GANs, the latent space is often disentangled into pose and shape components. Adversarial Loss: A discriminator D is trained to classify rendered images as real or fake. The generator minimizes the adversarial loss \mathcal{L}{adv}, often combined with photometric losses (e.g., L1) to ensure consistency with ground truth or template data. Rendering: Standard volume rendering is used to synthesize images from the radiance field: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), d) dt where \sigma is density and c is color. Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) is a 3D-aware image synthesis method that combines radiance fields with occupancy representations to learn compact object surfaces without impeding training convergence. It solves the problem of diffused surfaces in prior generative radiance fields (like pi-GAN) and the sparse gradient convergence issues in direct occupancy networks by transitioning from cumulative volume rendering to surface-point rendering. Unlike its siblings that predict volume densities, GOF predicts alpha values interpreted as occupancy, enabling surface-aware synthesis via root-finding. See Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) for implementation details. This method distills 3D structural knowledge from a pretrained 2D Generative Adversarial Network (StyleGAN2) into a shared conditional Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to generate novel 3D objects with arbitrary poses for data augmentation. It differs from naive isolated NeRF reconstruction by jointly optimizing a shared NeRF and latent codes for all objects simultaneously (Generative Latent Optimization), thereby learning shared category priors and mitigating noise from imperfect GAN interpretation. See Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Radiance Field for implementation details. An inverted 2D-to-3D generation framework that synthesizes 3D training data by lifting a pretrained 2D GAN to a 3D generative radiance field, achieving high-resolution synthesis and accurate 3D annotations. Step 1: Use a well-disentangled 2D GAN (StyleGAN2) to generate multi-view images with corresponding pseudo pose annotations. Step 2: Lift the generated multi-view images to a 3D representation using NeRF reconstruction. Step 3: Distill from the pretrained 2D GAN to achieve high-quality synthesis comparable to SOTA 2D generative models. Step 4: Decouple 3D generation from generative image synthesis to generate images tightly aligned with sampling labels. Step 5: Synthesize images in any resolution by accumulating single-ray evaluation, avoiding 2D upsamplers. Latent code z: Sampled from a Gaussian distribution Z ~ N(0, I) with dimension R^512. Unlike previous 3D GANs that rely on a 2D upsampler and suffer from trade-offs between high-resolution synthesis and 3D consistency, Lift3D inverts the pipeline to 2D-to-3D, allowing arbitrary rendering resolution and object pose sampling. The field emerged from the need to generate diverse 3D data for tasks like autonomous driving and object detection, where labeled 3D data is scarce. Early 3D GANs suffered from resolution limits and 3D inconsistency. Lift3D introduced the "inverted" pipeline of lifting 2D GANs to 3D, while GOF [15773-generative-occupancy-fields-gof.md] addressed surface ambiguity in generative radiance fields by using occupancy-based rendering. These methods are primarily used for data augmentation in 3D perception tasks. Lift3D: Synthesize 3D Training Data by Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Generative Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00040, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF)
body: Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF) is a 3D-aware image synthesis method that combines generative radiance fields with occupancy representations to learn compact object surfaces without impeding training convergence. It solves the problem of diffused surfaces in methods like GRAFs and the sparse gradient convergence issues in direct occupancy networks by transitioning from cumulative volume rendering to surface-point rendering. Unlike its sibling Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Radiance Field which may predict diffused surfaces, GOF concentrates rendering weights closely around object surfaces, resulting in compact and smooth geometry. GOF predicts alpha values (interpreted as occupancy) instead of volume densities to resolve shape-color ambiguity and enable surface-aware image synthesis. The method locates the surface via root-finding on these alpha values and gradually shrinks the sampling region during training to enforce compactness. Inputs: Latent code z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), camera pose \xi (origin o, direction d). Outputs: Rendered image color C(r) for rays r(t) = o + td. Generator g\theta: A neural network (e.g., FiLMed-SIREN backbone) that takes position x and latent code z as input and outputs alpha value \alpha\theta(x, z) \in [0, 1] and color c\theta(x, d, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Discriminator D{\thetaD}: A neural network that classifies images as real or fake. N: Number of rendering samples per ray. Typical value: 12. M: Number of root-finding bins. Typical value: 12. ms: Number of secant iterations for surface refinement. Typical value: 3. \tau: Threshold for root-finding. Typical value: 0.5. \Delta{init}: Initial sampling interval half-width. Set to (tf - tn)/2. \Delta{min}: Minimal sampling interval half-width. Not given in the sources. \gamma: Decay rate for shrinking interval. Not given in the sources. \lambda{normal}: Weight for normal regularization. Not given in the sources. \lambda{opacity}: Weight for opacity regularization. Not given in the sources. 1. Surface Location via Root-Finding: Sample M evenly-spaced points xk partitioning the volume [tn, tf] along the ray. Query the generator for alpha values \alpha\theta(xk, z) for all k=1 \dots M. Find the bin kS where the alpha value crosses the threshold \tau: kS = \arg\mink (\alpha\theta(xk, z) < \tau \le \alpha\theta(x{k+1}, z)) Apply the secant method iteratively ms times within the bin [x{kS}, x{kS+1}] to find the precise surface point xs and its distance ts. Note: The M points are used only for root-finding and do not require gradient computation. 2. Shrinking Sampling Region: Initialize sampling interval \Delta{init} = (tf - tn)/2. At training step n, compute the current interval half-width: \Deltan = \max(\Delta{init} \exp(-\gamma n), \Delta{min}) Sample N points uniformly in the region [ts - \Deltan, ts + \Deltan] using: ti \sim U\left[ts - \Deltan + \frac{2i-2}{N}\Deltan, ts - \Deltan + \frac{2i}{N}\Deltan\right] for i=1 \dots N. If the region exceeds [tn, tf], shift it back to fit within bounds. 3. Rendering: Compute the integrated color \tilde{C}(r, z) using alpha composition: \tilde{C}(r, z) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alpha\theta(xi, z) \left( \prod{j<i} (1 - \alpha\theta(xj, z)) \right) c\theta(xi, d, z) Here, \alpha\theta(xi, z) is the predicted alpha (occupancy) and c\theta(xi, d, z) is the predicted color. 4. Inference: Fetch truncated latent code \hat{z}. Locate surface xs using steps 1-2 with \Delta{min}. Render using either: Cumulative rendering with N points in [ts - \Delta{min}, ts + \Delta{min}]. Single-point surface rendering with N=1 at xs for speed. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def querygenerator(theta, x, z): """Returns alpha in [0,1] and color in R^3 from generator gtheta.""" alpha = theta(x, z) color = theta.color(x, z) return alpha, color def secantmethod(f, a, b, iterations): """Finds root of f(t) = 0 in [a, b] using secant method.""" tprev, tcurr = a, b fprev, fcurr = f(tprev), f(tcurr) for in range(iterations): if abs(fcurr - fprev) < 1e-8: break tnext = tcurr - fcurr (tcurr - tprev) / (fcurr - fprev) tprev, tcurr = tcurr, tnext fprev, fcurr = fcurr, f(tcurr) return tcurr def computeganloss(genlogit, reallogit, lambdagrad=10.0): """Computes non-saturating GAN loss with gradient penalty. f(u) = -log(1 + exp(-u)) Gradient penalty ||gradD(I)||^2 is computed via automatic differentiation in practice.""" def f(u): return -math.log(1 + math.exp(-u)) return f(genlogit) + f(-reallogit) + lambdagrad 10.0 def computenormalloss(theta, xs, z, eps=0.01): """Computes normal regularization loss: sum ||n(xs) - n(xs + epsd)||^2. Normal n is typically the normalized gradient of alpha w.r.t position.""" ns = theta.gradientalpha(xs, z) nseps = theta.gradientalpha(xs + eps theta.direction, z) return sum((ns[i] - nseps[i])2 for i in range(3)) def computeopacityloss(alphas): """Computes opacity regularization loss: 1/N sum (log(alpha) + log(1-alpha)).""" return sum(math.log(a) + math.log(1 - a) for a in alphas) / len(alphas) def rendergof(theta, z, camerapose, tau=0.5, M=12, ms=3, N=12, deltamin=0.01, gamma=0.0, step=0): o, d = camerapose tn, tf = 0.1, 10.0 # 1. Surface Location via Root-Finding tbins = [tn + i (tf - tn) / M for i in range(M + 1)] alphas = [querygenerator(theta, o + t d, z)[0] for t in tbins] kS = -1 for k in range(M): if alphas[k] < tau <= alphas[k+1]: kS = k break if kS == -1: ts = (tn + tf) / 2 else: def alphafunc(t): return querygenerator(theta, o + t d, z)[0] ts = secantmethod(alphafunc, tbins[kS], tbins[kS+1], ms) # 2. Shrinking Sampling Region deltainit = (tf - tn) / 2 deltan = max(deltainit math.exp(-gamma step), deltamin) tstart = ts - deltan tend = ts + deltan tstart = max(tn, tstart) tend = min(tf, tend) if tend <= tstart: tend = tstart + deltamin # Sample N points uniformly in [ts - deltan, ts + deltan] tsamples = [] for i in range(1, N + 1): lower = ts - deltan + (2 i - 2) / N deltan upper = ts - deltan + (2 i) / N deltan tsamples.append(random.uniform(lower, upper)) # 3. Rendering color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] T = 1.0 for t in tsamples: x = o + t d alpha, c = querygenerator(theta, x, z) contribution = [T alpha c[j] for j in range(3)] color = [color[j] + contribution[j] for j in range(3)] T = (1 - alpha) if T < 1e-4: break return color def computeloss(theta, phi, z, camerapose, realimage, tau=0.5, M=12, ms=3, N=12, deltamin=0.01, gamma=0.0, step=0): o, d = camerapose tn, tf = 0.1, 10.0 # Render generated image genimage = rendergof(theta, z, camerapose, tau, M, ms, N, deltamin, gamma, step) # GAN Loss genlogit = phi(genimage) reallogit = phi(realimage) ganloss = computeganloss(genlogit, reallogit) # Locate surface for regularization tbins = [tn + i (tf - tn) / M for i in range(M + 1)] alphas = [querygenerator(theta, o + t d, z)[0] for t in tbins] kS = -1 for k in range(M): if alphas[k] < tau <= alphas[k+1]: kS = k break normalloss = 0.0 opacityloss = 0.0 if kS != -1: def alphafunc(t): return querygenerator(theta, o + t d, z)[0] ts = secantmethod(alphafunc, tbins[kS], tbins[kS+1], ms) xs = o + ts d normalloss = computenormalloss(theta, xs, z) deltainit = (tf - tn) / 2 deltan = max(deltainit math.exp(-gamma step), deltamin) tstart = max(tn, ts - deltan) tend = min(tf, ts + deltan) tsamples = [] for i in range(1, N + 1): lower = ts - deltan + (2 i - 2) / N deltan upper = ts - deltan + (2 i) / N deltan tsamples.append(random.uniform(lower, upper)) renderalphas = [querygenerator(theta, o + t d, z)[0] for t in tsamples] opacityloss = computeopacityloss(renderalphas) return ganloss + 1.0 normalloss + 1.0 opacityloss Shape-Color Ambiguity: Direct training of generative radiance fields fails to maintain surface compactness because small perturbations on surfaces still lead to realistic RGB images, fooling the discriminator. GOF mitigates this by reinterpreting alpha as occupancy and using root-finding. Convergence Issues: Directly applying occupancy representations to generative models causes severe convergence problems due to sparse gradients located only on object surfaces. GOF avoids this by starting with cumulative rendering (radiance field) and gradually shrinking the sampling region. Density Thresholding: Predicted densities in generative radiance fields range from 0 to 50, making it hard to determine an effective threshold for surface location. GOF uses alpha values which are naturally bounded in [0, 1]. Surface Not Found: If the root-finding bin is not found (e.g., all alphas < \tau or all > \tau), the surface location step fails. The pseudocode includes a fallback to the midpoint. Inference Speed: GOF requires M + ms + N queries for standard rendering, or M + ms + 1 for single-point surface rendering. Baselines require 2N queries. Time Complexity: GOF requires M + ms + N queries for standard rendering, or M + ms + 1 for single-point surface rendering. Baselines require 2N queries. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: GOF significantly outperforms baseline methods on the MAD (Mean Angle Deviation) metric, which focuses on surface compactness, and is comparable on SIDE (Scale-invariant Depth Error). Strengths: Compact and smooth surfaces; efficient rendering with single-point surface query; resolves shape-color ambiguity. Limitations: May over-smooth furry or complex textures when using single-point rendering; suitable for solid objects with a single surface. When to use: 3D-aware image synthesis where compact surface representation is desired, especially for solid objects like faces or animals. When not to use: Scenes with complex, multi-layered, or translucent objects where a single surface is insufficient. GOF was proposed by Xudong Xu, Xingang Pan, Dahua Lin, and Bo Dai from CUHK - SenseTime Joint Lab, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Max Planck Institute for Informatics, and Nanyang Technological University. It was published on arXiv on November 1, 2021. The method builds on the principles of generative radiance fields and occupancy networks, aiming to combine their respective strengths. It is used on datasets such as CelebA, BFM, and Cats for 3D-aware image synthesis.
