name: Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Radiance Field
head: GAN-to-NeRF Lifting, Lift3D
body: This method distills 3D structural knowledge from a pretrained 2D Generative Adversarial Network (specifically StyleGAN2) into a shared conditional Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It solves the problem of generating photorealistic 3D objects with arbitrary poses for training data augmentation in downstream tasks by jointly optimizing the NeRF parameters and latent codes. Unlike naive isolated NeRF reconstruction which fails to capture category priors and is hindered by noisy GAN sampling, this approach uses Generative Latent Optimization (GLO) to learn shared shape and appearance priors across all objects simultaneously. Inputs: 1. Pretrained 2D GAN: StyleGAN2 trained on a specific category (e.g., LSUN Car). 2. Template Data: A set of 3D models (e.g., from ShapeNet) rendered under 200 viewpoints to establish pose-latent mappings. 3. Ground Truth Masks: Binary masks for objects, extracted using a segmentation network like PointRend. 4. Environment Layout: 2D images with drivable area annotations, processed via HRNet and Inverse Perspective Mapping (IPM). Outputs: 1. Shared Conditional NeRF (\Phi\theta): A 3D radiance field representation conditioned on latent codes. 2. Optimized Latent Codes (\hat{Z}): A set of latent vectors for each object in the asset bank. 3. Synthetic 3D Assets: Novel views of generated objects with consistent geometry and appearance. 1. Disentangled Latent Space (w^): The StyleGAN2 latent code z is mapped to an intermediate space w^ = (w1^,..., w{16}^) via 16 affine transformations. Pose Latents (wp): The first 8 layers (w1^... w8^) control camera viewpoint/pose. Shape/Appearance Latents (ws): The remaining 8 layers (w9^... w{16}^) control shape, texture, and background. 2. Tri-Plane NeRF Representation (\Phi\theta): The NeRF is represented using three axis-aligned orthogonal feature planes (XY, YZ, XZ). Feature Planes: Generated by a 2D CNN mapping a constant input conditioned on latent code z. Point Query: For a 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, features are retrieved by projecting x onto the three planes and performing bilinear interpolation. MLP Head: The summed feature vector is fed into a single-layer SIREN-based MLP conditioned on z to output density \sigma and color c. 3. Pose Label (P): Defined by azimuth \alpha \in 0, 360^\circ) and elevation \beta \in [0, 20^\circ), representing a unit sphere looking at the origin. 1. Disentangle StyleGAN2: Map the input latent code z to w^ using the StyleGAN2 [generator's affine layers. Separate w^ into pose latents wp (first 8 layers) and shape/appearance latents ws (remaining 8 layers). 2. Obtain Latent-Label Pairs: Select a 3D model (e.g., from ShapeNet). Render the model under 200 different viewpoints P. Use optimization-based GAN inversion to find the template latent code corresponding to the rendered image. Associate the first 8 layers of this template latent with the pose label P. 3. Generate 2D Training Data: Sample pose latents wp from the obtained pose-latent pairs. Sample shape/appearance latents ws randomly from a Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). Combine wp and ws to generate 2D images I with associated pose labels P. Filter out generated objects that fall outside drivable areas by projecting 2D drivable area masks (from HRNet) to Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) via IPM. 4. Joint Optimization (GLO): Initialize a shared NeRF \Phi\theta and a set of latent codes Z for all objects in the asset bank. Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L} with respect to \theta and Z simultaneously. 5. Volumetric Rendering: For a camera ray r(t) = o + td, compute the expected color C(r): C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), d) dt Compute transmittance T(t): T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s)) ds\right) tn and tf are the nearest and furthest sampling bounds. 6. Shadow Generation: Cast a pre-computed shadow map at the bottom of each object to simulate lighting interactions. 7. Binary Mask Prediction: Extract the foreground mask \hat{M} based on accumulated transmittance at the furthest bound tf: \hat{M} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } T(tf) \geq 0.5 \\ 0 & \text{if } T(tf) < 0.5 \end{cases} 8. Composition: Alpha blend the foreground image I2 and background image I1 using the smoothed mask M (smoothed via Gaussian filter): I{out} = I1 \cdot M + I2 \cdot (1 - M) Optimization Objective: \hat{Z}, \hat{\theta} = \arg \min{z, \theta} \mathcal{L}(I, \Phi{\theta}(z, P)) where \hat{Z} is the concatenation of all latent codes, P is the pose label, and \mathcal{L} is the total loss. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i=1}^{N} (\mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda{IoU}\mathcal{L}{IoU} + \lambda{perc}\mathcal{L}{perc}) where N is the number of image pairs, and \lambda{IoU}, \lambda{perc} are loss weights. Photometric Loss (L1): \mathcal{L}{RGB} = \frac{1}{CHW} |Ii - \Phi{\theta}(zi, Pi)| where C, H, W are channel, height, and width dimensions. Perceptual Loss: \mathcal{L}{perc} = \frac{1}{CHW} |VGG(Ii) - VGG(\hat{I}i)| where VGG is a 16-layer network pretrained on ImageNet. IoU Loss: \mathcal{L}{IoU} = 1 - \frac{\hat{M} \cap M^}{\hat{M} \cup M^} where \hat{M} is the predicted mask and M^ is the ground truth mask from PointRend. Pose Latent Layers: First 8 layers of w^. Shape/Appearance Latent Layers: Remaining 8 layers of w^. Mask Threshold: 0.5 (for binary mask prediction). Segmentation Confidence Filter: 0.5 (during inference, PointRend segmentation confidence < 0.5 filters noisy objects). Pose Sampling Range: Azimuth 0-360^\circ, Elevation 0-20^\circ. Viewpoints per Model: 200. Asset Bank Size: 1000 different vehicles (each with 200 multi-view images). Loss Weights: \lambda{IoU}, \lambda{perc} are hyperparameters; exact values not specified in sources. Noisy GAN Sampling: Generated images and pose labels can be noisy or corrupted. This is mitigated by filtering low-confidence images and using GLO to learn shared priors rather than isolated reconstruction. Drivable Area Constraints: Objects must be filtered if they fall outside drivable areas to maintain environmental consistency (e.g., vehicles not appearing inside buildings). Boundary Artifacts: Alpha blending with a Gaussian-filtered mask is required to smooth edges when composing foreground and background. Unverified code. z: (B, latentdim, 1, 1) -> feature planes: (B, featuredim3, H, W) return self.conv(z).chunk(3, dim=1) class SIRENMLP(nn.Module): """Single-layer SIREN-based MLP conditioned on z.""" def init(self, indim, hiddendim): super().init() self.linear = nn.Linear(indim, hiddendim) self.sigma = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(30.0)) def forward(self, x, z): # (N, 1, 2) feat = F.gridsample(plane, coords, aligncorners=False).squeeze(2) # (N, featuredim) return feat fxy = sampleplane(planes[0], 2) fyz = sampleplane(planes[1], 0) fxz = sampleplane(planes[2], 1) combined = fxy + fyz + fxz out = self.mlp(combined, z) return torch.split(self.outlayer(out), [1, 3], dim=1) def computevolumetricrendering(rayo, rayd, nerfmodel, z, tn, tf, numsamples=256): """Renders a single ray using standard discrete volume rendering.""" tvals = torch.linspace(tn, tf, numsamples) xyz = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + rayd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) density, color = nerfmodel(xyz, z) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] if deltas.numel() == 0: return torch.zeroslike(rayo), torch.oneslike(rayo) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-density[:,:-1] deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-density[:,:-1] deltas), dim=0) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), transmittance], dim=0) weights = alpha transmittance[:,:-1] colorrendered = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color[:,:-1], dim=0) Ttf = transmittance[-1] return colorrendered, Ttf def computeloss(renderedimg, gtimg, renderedmask, gtmask, vggmodel): lrgb = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimg - gtimg)) intersection = torch.sum(renderedmask gtmask) union = torch.sum(renderedmask + gtmask) + 1e-6 liou = 1.0 - (intersection / union) lperc = torch.mean(torch.abs(vggmodel(renderedimg) - vggmodel(gtimg))) return lrgb + liou + lperc def trainlifting3d(stylegan2model, gtmasks, drivableareas, assetbanksize=1000): # 1. Disentangle StyleGAN2 poselatentpairs = [sampleposelatent(stylegan2model.mapping) for in range(200)] # 2. Generate 2D Training Data images, poses = [], [] for in range(assetbanksize 200): wp = sampleposelatent(poselatentpairs) ws = torch.randn(8) wfull = torch.cat([wp, ws], dim=0) img = stylegan2model.synthesis(wfull) azimuth = torch.rand(1) 360 elevation = torch.rand(1) 20 images.append(img) poses.append((azimuth.item(), elevation.item())) validindices = filterbydrivablearea(images, drivableareas) images = [images[i] for i in validindices] poses = [poses[i] for i in validindices] gtmasks = [gtmasks[i] for i in validindices] # 3. Initialize Shared NeRF and Latent Codes nerf = TriPlaneNeRF(latentdim=512, featuredim=64, hiddendim=256) latentcodes = [torch.randn(512) for in range(len(images))] optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(nerf.parameters()) + [nn.Parameter(code) for code in latentcodes], lr=1e-4) vggmodel = nn.Sequential(list(torchvision.models.vgg16(pretrained=True).features.children())[:30]) # 4. Joint Optimization (GLO) numepochs = 100 # Not given in the sources. for epoch in range(numepochs): for img, pose, mask in zip(images, poses, gtmasks): rayo, rayd = sampleraysfrompose(pose) renderedcolor, Ttf = computevolumetricrendering(rayo, rayd, nerf, latentcodes[0], tn=0.0, tf=10.0) renderedmask = (Ttf >= 0.5).float() loss = computeloss(renderedcolor, img, renderedmask, mask, vggmodel) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerf, latentcodes Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method uses a Tri-Plane representation, which is more memory-efficient than voxel grids or dense point clouds for high-resolution scenes. The memory usage scales with the number of feature planes and the resolution of the 2D CNN output. Time: The joint optimization (GLO) requires simultaneous updates of the NeRF parameters and all latent codes, which can be computationally intensive compared to isolated NeRF reconstruction. However, the Tri-Plane representation allows for efficient feature querying. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated on KITTI and nuScenes datasets for 3D object detection tasks. Generates novel 3D objects with arbitrary poses for training data augmentation. Qualitative comparisons show superior visual quality compared to GIRAFFE and GIRAFFE HD, especially when increasing depth magnitude. Strengths: Data Augmentation: Enables the generation of novel 3D objects with arbitrary poses for training data augmentation. Shared Priors: Learns shared shape and appearance priors within a category, mitigating the noise from GAN sampling. Efficiency: Uses Tri-Plane representation for efficient 3D feature encoding. High Quality: Produces photorealistic images with consistent geometry and appearance. Limitations: Dependency on 2D GAN: Relies on the quality of the pretrained 2D GAN (StyleGAN2). Noisy Inputs: Generated images and pose labels can be noisy, requiring filtering and robust optimization. Environment Constraints: Requires accurate drivable area annotations to filter out invalid objects. When to Use: When generating large-scale synthetic 3D datasets for training perception models in autonomous driving or robotics. When high-quality, diverse 3D objects with consistent appearance are needed. When Not to Use: When precise geometric accuracy is more important than photorealism. When computational resources are limited for joint optimization. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Lift3D: Synthesize 3D Training Data by Lifting 2D GAN to 3D Generative Radiance Field". History and Development: The method builds on the success of StyleGAN2 in generating high-quality 2D images. It leverages the concept of GANSpace to disentangle pose and shape latents. It addresses the limitations of naive NeRF reconstruction by incorporating Generative Latent Optimization (GLO). The method was applied to the LSUN Car dataset and evaluated on KITTI and nuScenes datasets. Applications: Autonomous driving perception (3D object detection). Robotics simulation. name: Training Configuration and Optimization
head: NeRF Training Hyperparameters, Optimization Settings
body: This article defines the hyperparameter configurations, optimization schedules, and loss function variants required to train Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models effectively. It addresses the problem of converging implicit neural representations from sparse or unconstrained 2D image collections by specifying learning rates, sampling strategies, and architectural regularizations. What sets this family apart from the underlying Model Architecture and Encoding is the focus on the training dynamics—such as learning rate schedules, loss weighting, and specific regularization techniques—rather than the network topology or positional encoding functions themselves. The training process for NeRF variants generally follows a stochastic gradient descent loop using the Adam optimizer. The core mechanism involves minimizing a photometric reconstruction loss between rendered pixels and ground-truth images. Key shared principles include: Ray Sampling: Rays are sampled through the scene, and points are queried along these rays using stratified or importance sampling to estimate the volume rendering integral. Optimization: The Adam optimizer is the standard choice, often with a learning rate decay schedule. Loss Function: The primary loss is typically Mean Squared Error (MSE) or L1 loss between rendered and target colors. This configuration extends standard NeRF training by incorporating explicit depth supervision to improve geometric accuracy, particularly in sparse settings. It distinguishes itself by using an Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) based depth loss and architectural regularization (dropout) to handle depth uncertainty. It is chosen when ground-truth depth maps are available or when high-fidelity geometry is required over pure photometric fidelity. See Depth-Guided NeRF Training Configuration. This configuration enables text-guided stylization of NeRFs by replacing photometric loss with semantic constraints in the CLIP embedding space. It distinguishes itself by minimizing the negative cosine similarity between rendered image patches and text prompts, allowing for style transfer without paired 3D data. It is chosen for artistic stylization or semantic editing tasks. See CLIPNeRF Training Configuration. This configuration addresses the reconstruction of unconstrained, "in-the-wild" photo collections containing transient objects (pedestrians, vehicles) and varying lighting. It distinguishes itself by decomposing the scene into static geometry and transient appearance components using a multi-branch MLP, preventing transient artifacts from corrupting the static structure. It is chosen for large-scale, uncontrolled scene capture. See NeRF-W Hyperparameter Configuration. The original NeRF paper established the baseline training configuration, using Adam with a learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-4}, 500,000 total steps, and a learning rate decay to 5 \times 10^{-5} after 80% of training. Subsequent works have adapted these configurations to handle specific challenges: depth guidance for accuracy, CLIP for semantic control, and NeRF-W for in-the-wild robustness.

name: Depth-Guided NeRF Training Configuration
head: DäRF Training Configuration, Earth Mover’s Distance Depth-Guided NeRF
body: This configuration defines the training protocol for a NeRF variant that incorporates depth priors to improve reconstruction quality, specifically utilizing an Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) based depth loss. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by integrating explicit depth supervision and architectural regularization (dropout) to handle uncertainty in depth estimation. It builds on Training Configuration and Optimization. Inputs: Camera poses and intrinsics. RGB images. Ground truth depth maps (optional, used for loss calculation and thresholding). Scene-specific depth bounds (min\depth, max\depth). Outputs: Trained NeRF model parameters (MLP weights, embedding tables). Data Structures: NeRF MLP: Standard NeRF architecture with positional encoding. Dropout Layers: Added after the first 8 fully connected ReLU layers. Depth Loss Weight (\lambda): Scalar hyperparameter. Uncertainty Weight (\gamma): Scalar hyperparameter. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Initial Learning Rate (lr): 5 \times 10^{-4}. LR Schedule: Reduce to 5 \times 10^{-5} after 80% of total steps. Weight Decay: 1 \times 10^{-6}. Total Steps: 500,000. Depth Scale Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-7}. Depth Loss Weight (\lambda): 0.007 for most scenes; 0.02 for Scene 710. Uncertainty Weight (\gamma): 1.0. Dropout Probability: 0.1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the NeRF model based on the original NeRF architecture. 2. Modify Architecture: Insert dropout layers with probability p=0.1 after each of the first eight fully connected ReLU-activated layers that encode the positional encoding. 3. Configure Optimizer: Initialize Adam optimizer with lr = 5 \times 10^{-4} and weight decay 1 \times 10^{-6}. 4. Set Depth Scale LR: Assign a learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-7} specifically for the depth scale parameter. 5. Compute Threshold: For depth evaluation and uncertainty, compute a threshold \tau using the scene's depth bounds: \tau = (max\depth - min\depth) \cdot 0.0001 For ScanNet, typical values are max\depth = 10 and min\depth = 0.001. 6. Training Loop: a. Sample rays and points using stratified sampling (as per shared principles). b. Render color and depth. c. Compute photometric loss (MSE/L1) between rendered and ground-truth colors. d. Compute depth loss using the configured weight \lambda. e. Compute uncertainty loss using weight \gamma = 1. f. Backpropagate and update weights. g. Apply LR schedule: reduce lr to 5 \times 10^{-5} after 80% of 500,000 steps. 7. Evaluate: Compute metrics on valid pixels (K) where ground truth depth exists: RMSE(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} (dk - \hat{d}k)^2} RMSE{log}(d, \hat{d}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} (\log dk - \log \hat{d}k)^2} AbsRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \frac{|dk - \hat{d}k|}{dk} SqRel(d, \hat{d}) = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \frac{(dk - \hat{d}k)^2}{dk} Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene 710: Requires a higher depth loss weight (\lambda = 0.02) compared to other scenes (\lambda = 0.007). Depth Bounds: The threshold \tau depends on max\depth and min\depth. Incorrect bounds lead to incorrect uncertainty evaluation. Overfitting: The dropout layers are critical for preventing overfitting, especially in sparse settings. Integrates the depth loss implementation from the official DS-NeRF code base into the training pipeline. This variant is used when re-training on specific splits (e.g., LLFF) because original publication results used different splits or unreleased configurations. For DTU, official results are reported directly as reproduction failed due to missing config files, suggesting potential undocumented architectural tricks (e.g., reduced PE frequency) were used in the original work. Time Complexity: Standard NeRF training complexity, scaled by 500,000 steps. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory usage plus overhead for depth map storage and dropout states. Strengths: Improved depth accuracy and structural consistency through explicit depth supervision and uncertainty modeling. Limitations: Requires ground truth depth maps for training (or reliable pseudo-labels); sensitive to depth scale learning rate. When to Use: When depth accuracy is critical and ground truth depth is available or can be reliably estimated. When Not to Use: When depth supervision is unavailable or unreliable. Originated from the DäRF (Depth-guided NeRF) method, which introduces Earth Mover’s Distance for depth guidance. The configuration details were provided in the supplementary material of the DäRF paper. It is used in datasets like ScanNet and LLFF. name: CLIPNeRF Training Configuration
head: Absolute Directional CLIP Loss, CLIPNeRF Hyperparameters, CLIPNeRF Implementation, Directional CLIP Loss, Relative Directional CLIP Loss, StyleGAN-NADA CLIP Loss
body: CLIPNeRF training configuration defines the optimization procedure for text-guided stylization of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by minimizing the negative cosine similarity between rendered images and text prompts in the CLIP embedding space. It distinguishes itself from standard photometric NeRF training by replacing pixel-wise MSE loss with directional constraints in the semantic embedding space, enabling style transfer without requiring paired 3D data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model (MLP parameters), a source image I{src}, a target text prompt t{tgt}, and optionally a source text prompt t{src}. Outputs: Stylized NeRF parameters that render images matching the semantic direction of t{tgt} relative to I{src}. Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP encoding position and view direction. Parameters are split into density-related and color-related sub-parameters. CLIP Encoder: ViT-B/32 architecture, frozen during training. Patch Data: A 128 \times 128 pixel patch is rendered per iteration. Parameters: Iterations: 500. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.0001. Patch Size: 128 \times 128 pixels. Ray Sampling Stride: 5 within the patch, creating a receptive field of 640 \times 640 on the original image scale. Importance Sampling Points: 16 per ray during patch rendering. Fine MLP Samples: 80 total (64 coarse + 16 fine). Method Steps: 1. Freeze Density: Freeze sub-parameters related to density in the NeRF MLP to prevent structural collapse during stylization. 2. Sample View: Randomly sample a camera pose from the training dataset. 3. Render Patch: Render a 128 \times 128 patch from the sampled view. Rays are sampled with a stride of 5 to cover a wider area. 4. Resize: Apply bilinear interpolation to resize the rendered patch to the input resolution required by the CLIP encoder (typically 224 \times 224). 5. Encode: Pass the resized patch through the frozen CLIP image encoder \mathcal{E}i to get embedding \hat{v}i = \mathcal{E}i(I{tgt}). 6. Encode Text: Pass the target text prompt t{tgt} through the CLIP text encoder \mathcal{E}t to get embedding \hat{v}t = \mathcal{E}t(t{tgt}). 7. Compute Loss: Calculate the loss based on the chosen directional strategy (see Formulas). 8. Backpropagate: Compute gradients with respect to the unfrozen NeRF parameters and update using Adam. Formulas: Two variants of directional CLIP loss are used: 1. Absolute Directional CLIP Loss: Measures cosine similarity between the rendered image embedding and the target text embedding. \mathcal{L}{dir} = 1 - \langle \hat{v}i, \hat{v}t \rangle Where \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle denotes the dot product of normalized vectors. This guides the NeRF with a global direction but may cause mode collapse. 2. Relative Directional CLIP Loss: Measures the similarity between the difference in image embeddings and the difference in text embeddings. This transfers the style from a source image I{src} to the target domain. \mathcal{L}{dir} = 1 - \langle \hat{v}i(I{tgt}) - \hat{v}i(I{src}), \hat{v}t(t{tgt}) - \hat{v}t(t{src}) \rangle This approach enforces the correct stylization trajectory while ignoring magnitude differences, though it may struggle to reach sufficient stylization magnitude. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. iterations = 500 learningrate = 0.0001 patchsize = 128 raystride = 5 samplesperray = 16 coarsesamples = 64 finesamples = 16 nerfmodel = loadnerf() clipencoder = loadclipvitb32() # Frozen optimizer = Adam(nerfmodel.parameters(), lr=learningrate) freezedensityparams(nerfmodel) for step in range(iterations): # 1. Sample random view camerapose = randomsampletrainingview() # 2. Render patch # Rays are sampled with stride 5 within the 128x128 patch renderedpatch = rendernerfpatch( nerfmodel, camerapose, patchsize=patchsize, raystride=raystride, samplesperray=samplesperray, coarsesamples=coarsesamples, finesamples=finesamples) # 3. Resize for CLIP resizedpatch = bilinearresize(renderedpatch, targetsize=224) # 4. Encode Image imageembedding = clipencoder.encodeimage(resizedpatch) # 5. Encode Text (Target) textembedding = clipencoder.encodetext(targetprompt) # 6. Compute Loss (Absolute Directional) # Normalize embeddings imageembedding = normalize(imageembedding) textembedding = normalize(textembedding) # Cosine similarity similarity = dotproduct(imageembedding, textembedding) loss = 1.0 - similarity # 7. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: Naive differentiable rendering of high-resolution images is intractable due to memory limits. The patch-based approach mitigates this. Mode Collapse: Absolute directional CLIP loss can cause mode collapse of the generator and hurt generation diversity. Insufficient Magnitude: Directional loss alone may struggle to reach sufficient stylization magnitude, resulting in weak style transfer. Relative loss or additional contrastive losses may be needed to enforce magnitude. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of iterations (500) and the number of rays sampled per patch. The patch-based rendering reduces per-step cost compared to full-image rendering. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to full-resolution rendering due to the 128 \times 128 patch size and reduced sampling points (16 importance samples). Strengths: Enables text-driven stylization without 3D ground truth; efficient memory usage via patch rendering. Limitations: May suffer from mode collapse (absolute loss) or insufficient stylization magnitude (directional loss alone). Quality depends heavily on the CLIP model's ability to align 3D geometry with 2D text embeddings. CLIPNeRF was introduced by Wang et al. in 2021 as an extension of StyleCLIP [Patashnik et al. 2021] to 3D neural radiance fields. It utilizes the directional CLIP loss originally designed for StyleGAN-NADA [Gal et al. 2021] to guide NeRF stylization. The method addresses the lack of 3D paired data for style transfer by leveraging the semantic alignment capabilities of CLIP. name: NeRF-W Hyperparameter Configuration
head: NeRF-W Training Parameters
body: NeRF-W (NeRF in the Wild) is a method for reconstructing 3D scenes from unconstrained, in-the-wild photo collections, specifically addressing the presence of transient objects (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles) and varying lighting conditions. It solves the problem of geometric reconstruction in dynamic environments by decomposing the scene representation into static geometry and transient appearance components. What sets it apart from standard NeRF is the explicit modeling of transient effects via a separate neural head and appearance embeddings, allowing the static geometry MLP to converge on the underlying scene structure rather than being dominated by view-dependent transient artifacts. The method employs a multi-branch MLP architecture to separate static scene geometry from transient, view-dependent effects. The training process minimizes photometric error while regularizing the transient components to prevent them from absorbing static geometry. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of uncalibrated or weakly calibrated images from an unconstrained collection; optional segmentation masks for transient objects. Outputs: A static signed distance field (SDF) or density field representing the static scene geometry, and a transient field representing dynamic objects and lighting variations. Data Structures The model consists of three distinct MLPs: 1. Base MLP: 8 layers, 512 hidden units. Encodes the static scene density and base radiance. 2. Static MLP: 4 layers, 128 hidden units. Refines the static radiance. 3. Transient/Uncertainty MLP: 4 layers, 128 hidden units. Encodes transient appearance and uncertainty. Positional Encoding Position: 15 frequencies. Viewing direction: 4 frequencies. Latent Embeddings Appearance embedding dimension n(a) = 48. Transient object embedding dimension n(\tau) = 16. Sampling Training: 512 points per ray per model (coarse and fine), totaling 1024 points per ray. Evaluation: 2048 points per ray. Optimization Parameters Optimizer: Adam. Batch size: 2048. Initial learning rate: 0.001. Learning rate schedule: Decays ten-fold every 150,000 iterations. Total iterations: 300,000. L1 regularizer multiplier for transient uncertainty: \lambdau = 0.01. Minimum importance threshold: \beta{min} = 0.03. Algorithm Steps 1. Preprocessing: Filter input images to remove low-quality images (e.g., NIMA score < 3) and images where transient objects occupy >80% of the area. 2. Initialization: Initialize the Base, Static, and Transient MLPs. Initialize appearance embeddings for each image and transient embeddings for detected dynamic objects. 3. Ray Sampling: For each training batch, sample 512 points along each ray for the coarse network and 512 for the fine network. 4. Forward Pass: Encode position and viewing direction using positional encodings. Pass through Base MLP to get static density and base color. Pass through Static MLP to refine static color. Pass through Transient MLP, conditioned on the transient embedding, to get transient color and uncertainty. 5. Rendering: Composite the static and transient contributions along the ray to produce the final pixel color. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute photometric loss (MSE or L1) between rendered and ground-truth colors. Apply L1 regularization on the transient uncertainty term weighted by \lambdau = 0.01. If segmentation masks are available, exclude rays belonging to dynamic objects from the static geometry supervision to prevent the transient head from dominating the geometry. 7. Update: Update weights using Adam optimizer with the specified learning rate schedule. 8. Evaluation: During evaluation, double the number of samples per ray to 2048. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Transient Dominance: If the transient NeRF head is not properly regularized or if segmentation masks are not used, the transient head may converge faster than the geometry MLP, causing the network to model static scene structures as view-dependent transient effects. Sky Reconstruction: Textureless sky regions lack motion parallax. Using a background NeRF for foreground-background separation can lead to reconstructions in spherical shells. Background rays should be labeled with semantic masks and penalized as free space. A method to handle dynamic objects in Internet photo collections by using segmentation masks to exclude rays belonging to dynamic objects during training. This prevents the transient NeRF head from dominating the rendered color, which occurs because the transient head converges faster than the geometry MLP, leading the network to model scene structures as view-dependent transient effects rather than static geometry. Time Complexity: Training requires 300,000 iterations with a batch size of 2048. The use of multiple MLPs (Base, Static, Transient) increases computational cost compared to standard NeRF. Memory Complexity: The model stores three MLPs and latent embeddings for appearance (n(a)=48) and transient objects (n(\tau)=16) per image. Performance: The hyperparameters were optimized for the Brandenburg Gate scene of the Phototourism dataset and reused for remaining scenes, suggesting potential sensitivity to scene characteristics. Strengths: Effectively handles unconstrained photo collections with transient objects and varying lighting. Limitations: Requires careful handling of transient objects to avoid geometric artifacts; performance may degrade if segmentation masks are inaccurate or unavailable. NeRF-W was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2021. It extends the original NeRF framework to handle "in-the-wild" photo collections, which are characterized by uncontrolled capture conditions, transient objects, and varying illumination. The method was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF, which assumes a static scene and controlled lighting. The hyperparameters were determined via grid search on the Brandenburg Gate scene from the Phototourism dataset. name: Surface and SDF-Based Representations
body: This family replaces the standard volume density \sigma output of canonical NeRF with a Signed Distance Function (SDF) or occupancy field to represent geometry. By modeling the scene as an implicit surface, these methods achieve sharper geometry extraction and better surface definition than density-based approaches, which often suffer from "fuzzy" boundaries. The core mechanism involves predicting a scalar field f(\mathbf{x}) that represents the signed distance to the nearest surface (or occupancy) at position \mathbf{x}, rather than volume density. This scalar field is transformed into opacity \alpha or density \sigma for volume rendering integration. SDF to Opacity/Density Transformation The SDF value s(\mathbf{x}) is converted into a probability of occupancy or density using a distribution parameterized by a variance or sparsity term \beta. 1. Laplacian CDF (Standard SDF): Used in SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF. The opacity \sigma is derived from the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Laplacian distribution: \sigma = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s \le 0 \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(-\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s > 0 \end{cases} where \beta controls the tightness of the surface representation SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF. 2. Piecewise Exponential (I2-SDF): Used in I2-SDF. The density \sigma is defined as: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\beta}(1 - \exp(d(\mathbf{x})/\beta)) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) < 0 \\ \frac{1}{2\beta}\exp(-d(\mathbf{x})/2\beta) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \end{cases} where d(\mathbf{x}) is the SDF value and \beta is a learnable sparsity parameter I2-SDF. Inverse CDF Sampling To sample points efficiently near the surface, methods like SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF use inverse CDF sampling. Random numbers ui \in [0, 1] are generated and transformed to sample distances ti using the inverse of the CDF \Phi^{-1}(ui), concentrating samples near the zero-crossing of the SDF SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF. Stratification is applied by dividing the unit interval into bins SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF. Occupancy Fields As seen in Explicit Mesh and Surface Reconstruction, an occupancy field acts as an indicator of surface presence. For solid objects, the occupancy at the i^{th} sample corresponds to an indicator of whether the sample is inside the surface Explicit Mesh and Surface Reconstruction. I2-SDF is a neural implicit framework for complex indoor scenes that jointly recovers underlying shape, radiance, and material fields from multi-view images I2-SDF. It distinguishes itself by decomposing the radiance field into spatially-varying material and emission components using surface-based, differentiable Monte Carlo raytracing, enabling physically based scene relighting and editing I2-SDF. Unlike standard NeRF approaches that treat radiance as a monolithic field, I2-SDF employs a two-stage training scheme and error-guided adaptive sampling to resolve ambiguities and improve reconstruction quality on fine-grained small objects I2-SDF. This method renders geometry by outputting a Signed Distance Function (SDF) value s and a variance parameter \beta from a neural network, then transforming s into opacity \sigma using a Laplacian Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF. It builds on Model Architecture and Encoding by integrating triplane features and SDF-based sampling. Unlike standard NeRF which outputs density directly, this approach enables tight surface extraction and inverse CDF sampling for more accurate depth estimation SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF. This family encompasses methods that convert implicit neural radiance fields (NeRFs) or signed distance fields (SDFs) into explicit polygonal mesh representations or duplex surface structures Explicit Mesh and Surface Reconstruction. It solves the problem of high computational cost and lack of explicit geometric topology in volumetric NeRFs by replacing dense ray sampling with surface intersections or deformable anchor grids. It differs from sibling methods like I2-SDF and SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF by prioritizing explicit mesh extraction or duplex surface approximation for real-time rendering, rather than optimizing a continuous SDF field for volume rendering integration Explicit Mesh and Surface Reconstruction. NeuralUDF is a method for multi-view surface reconstruction that uses Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) and volume rendering to recover surfaces with arbitrary topologies, including open surfaces, without requiring 3D ground truth shapes NeuralUDF. Unlike SDF-based methods that are limited to closed shapes, NeuralUDF avoids the sign ambiguity of SDFs by modeling the distance to the nearest surface as a strictly positive value, using probabilistic models to locate surface intersections and enforce color consistency NeuralUDF. IDR is a method for learning a neural Signed Distance Function (SDF) and camera parameters simultaneously from uncalibrated images IDR (Implicit Differentiable Renderer). It disentangles geometry and appearance by combining a DVR-like implicit surface MLP with a NeRF-like view-dependent branch IDR (Implicit Differentiable Renderer). Unlike standard NeRF which models volume density, IDR represents geometry as the zero-level set of an MLP and uses a neural renderer to approximate light reflection IDR (Implicit Differentiable Renderer). Uses an SDF representation instead of volume densities to reconstruct scenes from RGB-D data, converting sdf values to densities for the NeRF formulation. A scene representation using two neural implicit functions encoded by MLPs to model accurate surface geometry and appearance from unconstrained Internet photos with varying lighting. d = \text{MLP}{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}), where \mathbf{x} is a point in \mathbb{R}^3. d approximates the signed distance to the true surface S. Azinovic et al. [AMBG∗ 21] propose to use an SDF representation instead of volume densities to reconstruct scenes from RGB-D data. NeuS [WLL∗ 21] ties the volume density to an SDF and reparameterizes the transmittance function such that it achieves its maximal slope precisely at the zero-crossing of this SDF, allowing an unbiased estimate of the corresponding surface. VolSDF [YGKL21b] uses an alternate mapping from SDF to volume density, which allows them to devise a new resampling strategy to achieve provably bounded error on the approximated opacity in the volume rendering quadrature equation. name: I2-SDF
head: Intrinsic Indoor Scene Reconstruction and Editing via Raytracing in Neural SDFs
body: I2-SDF is a neural implicit framework that jointly reconstructs the geometry, material, and incident radiance of complex indoor scenes from multi-view images. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF approaches by modeling geometry as a Signed Distance Field (SDF) and decomposing the radiance field into spatially-varying material and emission components via surface-based, differentiable Monte Carlo raytracing. This decomposition enables physically based scene relighting and editing, which standard volume rendering cannot achieve directly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of an indoor scene, optionally with geometry priors such as depth maps and surface normals. Outputs: Neural fields for geometry (Fd), radiance (Fc), material (Fa, F\rho), and emission (Fe, L[\cdot]); rendered novel views; and decomposed intrinsic maps. Data Structures: The method uses four Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) to represent implicit fields: 1. Fd: Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} to SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) and its gradient (normal). 2. Fc: Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{v} to radiance \hat{c}. 3. Fa, F\rho: Map \mathbf{x} to material parameters (e.g., albedo, roughness). 4. Fe: Maps \mathbf{x} to emitter semantic probability (identifying light sources). SDF to Density Transformation: The SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) is converted to volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) using a learnable sparsity parameter \beta: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\beta}(1 - \exp(d(\mathbf{x})/\beta)) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) < 0 \\ \frac{1}{2\beta}\exp(-d(\mathbf{x})/2\beta) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \end{cases} Rendering: To render a pixel, a ray \mathbf{r} is cast from camera origin \mathbf{o} along direction \mathbf{v}. M points \mathbf{x}{ir} = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{v} are sampled along the ray and fed into Fd and Fc to predict SDF values and radiance. The pixel color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is computed via numerical integration: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{M} T{ri} \alpha{ri} \hat{c}{ir} where: \hat{c}{ir} = Fc(\mathbf{x}{ir}, \mathbf{v}) is the predicted radiance. \alpha{ri} = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{ri} \delta{ri}) is the opacity, with \sigma{ri} = \sigma(\mathbf{x}{ir}) and \delta{ri} the distance to the next sample. T{ri} = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{rj}) is the accumulated transmittance. Training Strategy: I2-SDF employs a two-stage training scheme to resolve ambiguities between geometry, material, and lighting: 1. Stage 1 (Geometry & Radiance): Train Fd, Fc, and the emitter semantic field Fe. The network learns the SDF and the total incident radiance (lighting + material). 2. Stage 2 (Material & Emission): Train the material fields (Fa, F\rho) and the emission field L[\cdot]. During this stage, Fd, Fc, and Fe are fixed and detached from gradient descent. The radiance field is decomposed using surface-based, differentiable Monte Carlo raytracing. Adaptive Sampling and Loss: To handle fine-grained small objects, I2-SDF introduces an error-guided adaptive sampling scheme and a "bubble loss". Standard uniform sampling often fails to capture high-frequency details of small objects because low-frequency large objects converge faster. The adaptive scheme concentrates samples where rendering error is high, and the bubble loss penalizes deviations from the expected SDF structure near small surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computedensity(sdfvalues, beta): """Converts SDF values to volume density using the piecewise exponential function.""" density = [] for d in sdfvalues: if d < 0: density.append((1.0 / beta) (1.0 - math.exp(d / beta))) else: density.append((1.0 / (2.0 beta)) math.exp(-d / (2.0 beta))) return density def volumerender(rayorigin, raydirection, tvalues, Fd, Fc, beta): """Renders a single ray using volume rendering integration.""" points = [rayorigin + t raydirection for t in tvalues] sdfvalues = Fd(points) density = computedensity(sdfvalues, beta) radiance = [Fc(p, raydirection) for p in points] deltas = [tvalues[i] - tvalues[i-1] if i > 0 else 0.0 for i in range(len(tvalues))] opacity = [1.0 - math.exp(-density[i] deltas[i]) for i in range(len(tvalues))] transmittance = [1.0] for i in range(1, len(opacity)): transmittance.append(transmittance[-1] (1.0 - opacity[i-1])) color = sum(transmittance[i] opacity[i] radiance[i] for i in range(len(tvalues))) return color, density, opacity def trainstage1(model, images, depths, normals): """Stage 1: Train Geometry (Fd), Radiance (Fc), and Emitter Semantic (Fe).""" for image, depth, normal in zip(images, depths, normals): renderedimage = [] for ray in image.rays: # Error-guided adaptive sampling concentrates points near high-error regions tvals = [ray.origin + t ray.direction for t in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]] color,, = volumerender(ray.origin, ray.direction, tvals, model.Fd, model.Fc, model.beta) renderedimage.append(color) lossrgb = sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(renderedimage, image.rgb)) / len(renderedimage) losssdf = sum((model.Fd(p) - d)2 for p, d in zip(depth.points, depth.values)) lossemitter = sum((model.Fe(p) - e)2 for p, e in zip(image.emitterpoints, image.emittertargets)) totalloss = lossrgb + losssdf + lossemitter model.updategradients(totalloss) def trainstage2(model, images): """Stage 2: Train Material (Fa, Frho) and Emission (L). Fd, Fc, Fe are frozen.""" for image in images: # Decompose radiance using surface-based Monte Carlo raytracing on fixed fields materialmap = [model.Fa(p) for p in image.surfacepoints] emissionmap = [model.L(p) for p in image.surfacepoints] lossmaterial = sum((m - target)2 for m, target in zip(materialmap, image.materialtargets)) lossemission = sum((e - target)2 for e, target in zip(emissionmap, image.emissiontargets)) totalloss = lossmaterial + lossemission model.updategradients(totalloss) Complexity: Training is iterative and requires multiple passes over the dataset. Stage 1 follows standard differentiable volume rendering, while Stage 2 incorporates surface-based Monte Carlo raytracing for intrinsic decomposition. Strengths: Superior reconstruction quality for complex indoor scenes with fine-grained small objects due to adaptive sampling and bubble loss. Enables intrinsic decomposition (relighting, editing) which standard NeRF lacks. Limitations: Requires a two-stage training process, increasing implementation complexity. The second stage depends entirely on the accuracy of the fixed geometry and emitter semantic fields from the first stage. When to use: When the goal is not just novel view synthesis but also scene editing, relighting, or when the scene contains many small, high-frequency details that standard NeRF struggles to reconstruct. I2-SDF is a neural implicit framework developed by Zhu et al.. It builds upon differentiable volume rendering and neural SDF representations to address limitations in handling complex indoor scenes and intrinsic decomposition. The method was developed to enable physically based scene editing and relighting, which are difficult with standard volume rendering approaches. name: SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF
head: Laplacian opacity transformation, VolSDF variant
body: This method renders geometry by predicting a Signed Distance Function (SDF) value s and a variance parameter \beta from a neural network, then transforming s into volume opacity \sigma using the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of a Laplacian distribution. It builds on Surface and SDF-Based Representations by providing a differentiable mechanism to extract tight surfaces while enabling efficient inverse CDF sampling. Unlike I2-SDF, which uses a piecewise exponential density definition, this approach explicitly models the opacity via the Laplacian CDF, allowing \beta to vary spatially to control surface tightness locally. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Output: Opacity \sigma \in [0, 1], radiance color \mathbf{c}, and geometry features \mathbf{f}{geo}. Data Structures Triplane Features (\mathbf{T}x): Three aligned 2D feature grids (e.g., resolution 512 \times 512, feature size 32). For a point \mathbf{x}, features are gathered by projecting \mathbf{x} onto the three axis-aligned planes and taking the Hadamard product of the resulting vectors. MLP Architecture: MLPSDF: Takes positional encoding of \mathbf{x} and triplane features \mathbf{T}x. Outputs scalar SDF s, scalar variance \beta, and geometry feature vector \mathbf{f}{geo}. MLPc: Takes positional encoding of viewing direction \mathbf{v} and geometry features \mathbf{f}{geo}. Outputs radiance \mathbf{c}. Parameters \beta: The variance of the Laplacian distribution, governing the "tightness" of the surface representation. It is a learnable output of MLPSDF and varies spatially across the volume. N: Number of samples per ray. Step-by-Step Method 1. Positional Encoding: Compute the positional encoding \text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{x}) for the input point \mathbf{x}. 2. Feature Gathering: Retrieve triplane features \mathbf{T}x by projecting \mathbf{x} to the three axis-aligned planes and computing the Hadamard product of the three resultant vectors. 3. SDF Prediction: Pass (\text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{T}x) to MLPSDF to obtain the SDF value s, variance \beta, and geometry features \mathbf{f}{geo}: (s, \beta, \mathbf{f}{geo}) = \text{MLPSDF}(\text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{T}x) Initialize the ReLU activations in MLPSDF as in SAL to ensure an approximately spherical SDF in early training. 4. Opacity Transformation: Transform s and \beta into opacity \sigma using the Laplacian CDF: \sigma = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s \le 0 \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2} \exp\left(-\frac{s}{\beta}\right) & \text{if } s > 0 \end{cases} where s is the SDF value and \beta is the variance. 5. Radiance Prediction: Compute radiance \mathbf{c} using the geometry features and viewing direction: \mathbf{c} = \text{MLP}c(\text{PosEnc}(\mathbf{v}), \mathbf{f}{geo}) 6. Inverse CDF Sampling: To sample points near the surface, generate random numbers ui \in [0, 1] and transform them to sample distances ti using the inverse CDF \Phi^{-1}: ti = \Phi^{-1}(ui) where \Phi is the CDF derived from the Laplacian distribution defined by s and \beta, and ui is sorted in increasing order. 7. Rendering: Approximate the volumetric rendering integral for a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} by summing the contributions of samples: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance, \alphai is the opacity \sigma at sample i, and \mathbf{c}i is the radiance. Stratification During training, stratify the random numbers ui by dividing the unit interval into bins and taking a sample from each bin to lower rendering variance, especially at low sample counts N. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch def positionalencoding(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, power=2): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg + 1)], dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) scaledx = (math.pi x.unsqueeze(-1)) scales return torch.cat([torch.sin(scaledx), torch.cos(scaledx)], dim=-1) def gathertriplanefeatures(triplanes, x): """Project x to three axis-aligned planes and take Hadamard product.""" features = [] for plane in triplanes: # Extract 2D coordinates for each axis-aligned plane coords = torch.stack([x[:2], x[1:], x[2:]], dim=1) # Bilinear interpolation at projected coordinates feat = torch.nn.functional.gridsample(plane.unsqueeze(0), coords.unsqueeze(0), aligncorners=False).squeeze() features.append(feat) return torch.prod(torch.stack(features), dim=0) def laplaciancdf(s, beta): """Transform SDF s and variance beta into opacity sigma.""" beta = torch.clamp(beta, min=1e-6) return torch.where(s <= 0, 0.5 torch.exp(s / beta), 1.0 - 0.5 torch.exp(-s / beta)) def inverselaplaciancdf(u, beta): """Compute sample distance t from random u using inverse Laplacian CDF.""" # Inverse of the CDF: if u <= 0.5, t = beta ln(2u); else t = -beta ln(2(1-u)) return torch.where(u <= 0.5, beta torch.log(2 u), -beta torch.log(2 (1 - u))) def renderray(rayo, rayd, triplanes, mlpsdf, mlpc, numsamples): """Render a single ray using SDF-based volume rendering with Laplacian CDF.""" # 1. Stratified sampling: divide unit interval into bins and sample from each indices = torch.arange(numsamples) u = (indices + torch.rand(numsamples)) / numsamples u = torch.sort(u).values # Ensure increasing order # 2. Initialize sample distances and points tsamples = torch.zeros(numsamples) points = rayo.unsqueeze(0) + tsamples.unsqueeze(1) rayd.unsqueeze(0) # 3. Query network at sample points posencx = positionalencoding(points) trifeat = gathertriplanefeatures(triplanes, points) s, beta, fgeo = mlpsdf(posencx, trifeat) # 4. Transform to opacity and predict radiance sigma = laplaciancdf(s, beta) posencv = positionalencoding(rayd) c = mlpc(posencv, fgeo) # 5. Inverse CDF sampling to refine distances near surface tsamples = inverselaplaciancdf(u, beta) # 6. Volume rendering integral alpha = sigma transmittance = torch.oneslike(alpha) transmittance[1:] = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha[:-1], dim=0) color = torch.sum(transmittance.unsqueeze(-1) alpha.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=0) return color, sigma, s, beta Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples N and the cost of the MLP evaluations. The use of inverse CDF sampling concentrates samples near the surface, potentially reducing the number of samples needed for high-fidelity geometry compared to uniform sampling. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the triplane features (e.g., 3 \times 512 \times 512 \times 32 floats) and the MLP weights. Strengths: Tight surface extraction due to the SDF representation; efficient sampling near the surface via inverse CDF; lower rendering variance with stratification. Limitations: Requires careful initialization (e.g., SAL initialization) to avoid degenerate SDFs early in training. The spatially varying \beta requires regularization to prevent instability. When to use: When high-fidelity geometry extraction is prioritized over texture, and when training a 3D GAN or differentiable renderer. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and simple uniform sampling suffices, or when the scene does not have well-defined surfaces. This method is described in "What You See is What You GAN: Rendering Every Pixel for High-Fidelity Geometry in 3D GANs". It builds upon VolSDF and StyleSDF, improving upon NeRF and EG3D by incorporating stratified sampling and a triplane-based SDF representation. The use of the Laplacian CDF for opacity transformation was previously explored in VolSDF, but this method extends it by allowing \beta to vary spatially and integrating it into a GAN framework with triplane conditioning. name: Explicit Mesh and Surface Reconstruction
body: This family extracts explicit polygonal meshes or duplex surface structures from implicit neural radiance fields (NeRFs) or signed distance fields (SDFs). It solves the high computational cost and lack of explicit geometric topology in volumetric NeRFs by replacing dense ray sampling with surface intersections or deformable anchor grids. It differs from sibling methods like I2-SDF and SDF-based Volume Rendering with Laplacian CDF by prioritizing explicit mesh extraction or duplex surface approximation for real-time rendering, rather than optimizing a continuous SDF field for volume rendering integration. Subsequent developments like Neural Deformable Anchor (NeuDA) and Neural Duplex Radiance Fields (NDRF) extended these principles to address specific limitations in spatial encoding efficiency and rendering speed, respectively. NeuDA is a neural implicit representation for high-fidelity surface reconstruction that replaces learnable feature vectors at voxel vertices with optimized 3D positions (anchors) to adaptively encode local geometry [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. It solves the limitation of standard voxel grids where uniformly distributed features fail to capture small structures with complicated topologies [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Unlike Instant-NGP which uses multi-resolution hash encoding and may suffer from hash collision, NeuDA uses hierarchical voxel grids with deformable anchors [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Inputs are camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}) and a hierarchical voxel grid structure G [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. The output is the rendered color \hat{C} [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. The grid consists of deformable anchors \{ \mathbf{p}v, \Delta \mathbf{p}v \mid v \in G \}, where \mathbf{p}v is the base position and \Delta \mathbf{p}v is a learnable offset, initially uniformly distributed at voxel vertices [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. A 4-layer MLP F takes geometric features to output SDF f(\mathbf{x}) and a 256-dimensional geometric feature vector \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}) [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. A 4-layer MLP M takes view direction \mathbf{d}, normal \mathbf{n}, and \hat{\mathbf{z}} to output color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Frequency encoding uses Hierarchical Positional Encoding (HPE): \gamma(\mathbf{p}l) = (\sin(2^l \pi \mathbf{p}l), \cos(2^l \pi \mathbf{p}l)), returning a 6-dimensional embedding per anchor [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Feature interpolation for a sample point \mathbf{p} sums the encoded deformable positions of 8 adjacent anchors: \phi(\mathbf{p}, \psi(G)) = \sum{v \in \mathcal{V}} w(\mathbf{p}v) \cdot \gamma(\mathbf{p}v + \Delta \mathbf{p}v) [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Weights are normalized cosine similarities: \hat{w}(\mathbf{p}n) = \frac{\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{p}n}{\|\mathbf{p}\| \|\mathbf{p}n\|} [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Opacity \alphai is derived from consecutive SDF values f(\mathbf{p}(ti)) and f(\mathbf{p}(t{i+1})) using a trainable parameter s: \alphai = \max\left( \frac{\Phis(f(\mathbf{p}(ti))) - \Phis(f(\mathbf{p}(t{i+1})))}{\Phis(f(\mathbf{p}(ti)))}, 0 \right), where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. As optimization converges, 1/s approaches zero [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Rendering accumulates color: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, with Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Edge cases include avoiding hash collisions via hierarchical grids and managing numerical stability for s [18140-neural-deformable-anchor-neuda.md]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def hierarchicalpositionalencoding(pl, level): freq = 2level math.pi return np.concatenate([np.sin(freq pl), np.cos(freq pl)]) def computeanchorweights(p, anchorpositions): pnorm = np.linalg.norm(p) if pnorm == 0: return np.ones(8) / 8.0 rawweights = np.zeros(8) for i in range(8): pn = anchorpositions[i] pnnorm = np.linalg.norm(pn) rawweights[i] = np.dot(p, pn) / (pnorm pnnorm) if pnnorm > 0 else 0 sumweights = np.sum(rawweights) return rawweights / sumweights if sumweights > 0 else np.ones(8) / 8.0 def getfeatureatpoint(p, gridlevel, gridsize, anchorparams): x = p gridsize minidx = np.floor(x).astype(int) corners = [] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): corners.append(np.array([minidx[0] + i, minidx[1] + j, minidx[2] + k])) corners = np.array(corners) # Grid-to-anchor index mapping is implementation-specific anchorpositions = np.array([anchorparams['positions'][getvertexindex(c, gridsize)] for c in corners]) anchoroffsets = np.array([anchorparams['offsets'][getvertexindex(c, gridsize)] for c in corners]) weights = computeanchorweights(p, anchorpositions) feature = np.zeros(6) for i in range(8): deformablepos = anchorpositions[i] + anchoroffsets[i] feature += weights[i] hierarchicalpositionalencoding(deformablepos, gridlevel) return feature def getvertexindex(corner, gridsize): return corner[0] gridsize gridsize + corner[1] gridsize + corner[2] def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, gridlevels, gridsizes, anchorparamslist, sdfnet, colornet, numsamples): tnear, tfar = 0.0, 10.0 # Not given in sources tvalues = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples) samplepoints = rayorigin + raydirection tvalues[:, np.newaxis] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) sparam = 100.0 # The process feeds the center coordinates of a 256^3 voxel grid to the CodeNeRF MLP to obtain volume density values \sigma. Marching cubes is then applied to the volume density values \sigma to find mesh vertices. Finally, rays are cast along the vertex normals of the generated mesh to associate colors to the vertices. The concept of extracting explicit meshes from neural fields was introduced by CodeNeRF (2021), which disentangles shape and appearance to allow 3D reconstruction from a single image. The method leverages texture priors learned by CodeNeRF to complete object shape and texture information not present in the input image. Subsequent developments like Neural Deformable Anchor (NeuDA) and Neural Duplex Radiance Fields (NDRF) extended these principles to address specific limitations in spatial encoding efficiency and rendering speed, respectively. name: Neural Deformable Anchor (NeuDA)
body: NeuDA is a neural implicit representation for high-fidelity surface reconstruction that replaces learnable feature vectors at voxel vertices with optimized 3D positions, called anchors, to adaptively encode local geometry. It solves the limitation of standard voxel grids where uniformly distributed features fail to capture small structures with complicated topologies or sharp local details. Unlike Instant-NGP which uses multi-resolution hash encoding and may suffer from hash collision, NeuDA uses hierarchical voxel grids with deformable anchors to better exploit spatial context. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of multi-view images, camera poses, and a hierarchical voxel grid structure G. Output: A rendered color image \hat{C} and a reconstructed surface mesh (extracted from the SDF). Data Structures: Hierarchical Anchor Grid (G): A set of levels. Each level consists of a grid where vertices store deformable anchors. Deformable Anchor (\psi(G)): A set of parameters \{pv, \Delta pv \mid v \in G\}, where pv is the base position (initially uniform voxel vertex) and \Delta pv is the learnable offset. SDF Network (F): A 4-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) taking geometric features and outputting signed distance f(x) and geometric feature vector z(x). Color Network (M): A 4-layer MLP taking view direction d, normal n, and geometric feature \hat{z} to output color c. Numbered Steps: 1. Coordinate Normalization: For a sample point p along a ray, normalize its coordinate to the grid's scale, denoted as x. 2. Voxel Mapping: Map the normalized coordinate x to a specific voxel V in the grid using the formula: V = \{v \mid \lfloor x \cdot N \rfloor \le v < \lceil x \cdot N \rceil \} where N is the grid size. The anchors are stored at the eight vertices of this voxel. 3. Feature Interpolation: Compute the input feature \phi(p, \psi(G)) by interpolating the frequency-encoded positions of the eight adjacent anchors: \phi(p, \psi(G)) = \sum{v \in V} w(pv) \cdot \gamma(pv + \Delta pv) where \psi(G) = \{pv, \Delta pv \mid v \in G\} is the set of deformable anchors, and \gamma is the frequency encoding function. 4. Frequency Encoding: The frequency encoding function \gamma is applied to the three coordinate values of the anchor position individually. For a hierarchical positional encoding (HPE) at level l, the function is: \gamma(pl) = (\sin(2^l \pi pl), \cos(2^l \pi pl)) This returns a small 6-dimensional embedding for each anchor grid level. Multi-level embeddings are concatenated. 5. Weight Calculation: The weight w(pn) for each anchor pn is calculated using cosine similarity to measure the contribution of different anchors: w(pn) = \frac{\hat{w}(pn)}{\sumn \hat{w}(pn)}, \quad \hat{w}(pn) = \frac{p \cdot pn}{\|p\| \|pn\|} where p is the sample point and pn is the anchor position. 6. SDF and Feature Prediction: Feed the interpolated feature into the SDF network F to obtain the signed distance f(p) and geometric feature z(p). 7. Opacity Calculation: Compute the discrete opacity \alphai for the sample point ti along the ray based on the SDF f(p(t)) and a trainable parameter s: \alphai = \max\left( \frac{\Phis(f(p(ti))) - \Phis(f(p(t{i+1})))}{\Phis(f(p(ti)))}, 0 \right) where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1}. 8. Color Prediction: Compute the surface normal from the SDF gradient. Feed the view direction d, normal n, and geometric feature \hat{z} = z(x; \theta) into the color network M to get color ci. 9. Volume Rendering: Accumulate the rendered color \hat{C} along the ray with N discrete sampled points: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance. 1: pnext = points[i+1] xnext = normalizetogrid(pnext, gridsize) voxelindicesnext = getvoxelvertices(xnext, gridsize) basepos8next = anchorbasepositions[voxelindicesnext] offset8next = anchoroffsets[voxelindicesnext] deformablepos8next = basepos8next + offset8next # Re-calculate weights for next point pnextnorm = torch.norm(pnext) if pnextnorm < 1e-8: weightsnext = torch.ones(8) / 8.0 else: dotproductsnext = torch.sum(pnext deformablepos8next, dim=1) anchornormsnext = torch.norm(deformablepos8next, dim=1) safeanchornormsnext = torch.where(anchornormsnext < 1e-8, torch.oneslike(anchornormsnext), anchornormsnext) rawweightsnext = dotproductsnext / (pnextnorm safeanchornormsnext) weightsnext = rawweightsnext / (torch.sum(rawweightsnext) + 1e-8) encodedanchorsnext = frequencyencode(deformablepos8next) featurenext = torch.sum(weightsnext.unsqueeze(1) encodedanchorsnext, dim=0) sdfvalnext, = sdfmlp(featurenext) # Phis function phiscurr = 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-s sdfval)) phisnext = 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-s sdfvalnext)) # Alpha calculation numerator = phiscurr - phisnext denominator = phiscurr alpha = torch.clamp(numerator / (denominator + 1e-8), min=0.0) else: # Last sample, assume full opacity if inside surface or handle differently # Standard volume rendering often sets alpha=1 for the last sample to ensure convergence alpha = 1.0 # Step 8: Color Prediction # Compute normal from SDF gradient (not shown in formula, but required for color network) # In practice, this requires backpropagation or finite differences. # For forward pass pseudocode, we assume a computenormal function exists. normal = computenormal(sdfmlp, feature, p) # Color network inputs: view direction d, normal n, geometric feature z # z is geofeature from SDF network color = colormlp(raydirections[b], normal, geofeature) # Step 9: Accumulate accumulatedcolor += transmittance alpha color transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break renderedcolors[b] = accumulatedcolor return renderedcolors def normalizetogrid(point, gridsize): """ Normalizes a 3D point to the grid scale [0, 1] assuming the grid spans [-1, 1]. This is a placeholder for the specific normalization used in the paper. """ # Assuming point is in [-1, 1] return (point + 1.0) / 2.0 def getvoxelvertices(normalizedpoint, gridsize): """ Returns the indices of the 8 vertices of the voxel containing the normalized point. """ # normalizedpoint is in [0, 1] # Grid indices are 0 to gridsize-1 coords = normalizedpoint gridsize floorcoords = torch.floor(coords).long() ceilcoords = torch.ceil(coords).long() # Clamp to grid boundaries floorcoords = torch.clamp(floorcoords, 0, gridsize - 1) ceilcoords = torch.clamp(ceilcoords, 0, gridsize - 1) # Generate 8 combinations vertices = [] for x in [floorcoords[0], ceilcoords[0]]: for y in [floorcoords[1], ceilcoords[1]]: for z in [floorcoords[2], ceilcoords[2]]: vertices.append(x gridsize gridsize + y gridsize + z) return torch.tensor(vertices, dtype=torch.long) def frequencyencode(positions): """ Applies frequency encoding to positions. gamma(pl) = (sin(2^l pi pl), cos(2^l pi pl)) Assuming single level l=0 for basic implementation. MLP Layers: The SDF network F is a 4-layer MLP. The color network M is a 4-layer MLP. Trainable Parameter (s): Used in the sigmoid approximation \Phis. 1/s approaches zero as optimization converges. Frequency Encoding: Uses hierarchical positional encoding (HPE) where higher frequency bands are applied to finer grid levels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uniform Distribution Limitation: Standard voxel grids store uniformly distributed features which may fail to capture small structures with complicated topologies. NeuDA solves this by optimizing anchor positions to move from corners to the vicinity of abrupt geometry-changing areas. Hash Collision: Unlike Instant-NGP which uses multi-resolution hash encoding and may suffer from hash collision, NeuDA uses hierarchical voxel grids with deformable anchors. Precision: The weight calculation involves division by norms. Care must be taken to avoid division by zero if the sample point or anchor position is at the origin. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: NeuDA employs a shallower MLP (4 layers vs. 8 layers for NeuS and volSDF) to achieve better surface reconstruction performance due to the promising scene representation capability of the hierarchical deformable anchor structure. Strengths: Improves flexibility of voxel grid representation, better exploits spatial context in 3D space, and captures sharp local topologies such as small holes and structures. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When high-fidelity surface reconstruction is required, especially for scenes with small structures and complicated topologies, and when avoiding hash collisions associated with hash-based encodings is desired. When not to use: Not given in the sources. NeuDA was introduced by Bowen Cai, Jinchi Huang, Rongfei Jia, Chengfei Lv, and Huan Fu from Alibaba Group. The method builds on NeuS but replaces the fixed feature vectors with deformable anchors to address the limitation of overlooking spatial context in 3D space. name: Neural Duplex Radiance Fields (NDRF)
body: Neural Duplex Radiance Fields (NDRF) is a method to distill a pretrained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a mesh-based representation that enables real-time view synthesis. It overcomes inaccuracies in 3D surface reconstruction by learning aggregated radiance information from a reliable interval of ray-surface intersections (a 'duplex' interval) rather than a single surface point. Unlike NeRF, which uses a deep MLP for every sample, NDRF uses a shallow CNN to exploit local geometric relationships of nearby pixels, achieving high-quality appearance with lower computational cost. Unlike MobileNeRF, which requires complex multi-stage optimization or retraining from scratch, NDRF serves as a post-processing step for any existing NeRFs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pretrained NeRF model (MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (c, \sigma)) and a set of training views (camera poses and ground-truth images). Output: A two-layer duplex mesh with baked neural radiance features, and a shallow CNN for view-dependent color prediction. The final output is the rendered RGB color for a given camera ray. Data Structures: 1. Duplex Mesh: Two layers of geometry extracted from the pretrained NeRF's density field. Vertices: 3D coordinates \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Faces: Triangular connectivity defining the surface. Radiance Features: A feature vector \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^k (where k is the feature dimension, typically determined by the CNN input size) stored at each vertex. These features encode appearance and geometry information. 2. Shallow CNN: A convolutional network that takes local image patches (derived from the features of the two intersection points) and outputs the final color. Numbered Steps: 1. Geometry Proxy Extraction: Extract a geometry proxy (mesh) from the pretrained NeRF model using marching cubes. This defines the reliable interval of the density field. The method uses a two-layer mesh to approximate the reliable interval covering the true underlying geometry, addressing artifacts inherent in single-surface extraction. 2. Ray-Surface Intersection: For each target camera ray with view direction \mathbf{d}, find the two intersection points where the ray intersects the two layers of the duplex mesh. Let these points be \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2. These points represent the under- and over-estimation boundaries of the surface interval. 3. Feature Interpolation: Derive radiance features at the intersection points \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2 using barycentric interpolation on the mesh triangles. Let \mathbf{f}1 and \mathbf{f}2 be the interpolated feature vectors. 4. Color Prediction: Use a shallow convolutional network (CNN) to aggregate the local geometric and appearance information from \mathbf{f}1 and \mathbf{f}2 and produce view-dependent colors. The CNN replaces the deep MLP used in NeRF. The input to the CNN is constructed from the features \mathbf{f}1 and \mathbf{f}2 and potentially local neighborhood information in screen space. 5. Optimization: Optimize the representation (mesh features and CNN weights) by comparing the output color directly with pixels of rendered or ground-truth views. This is done via a multi-view distillation optimization strategy. Formulas: Ray Intersection: For a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, find t1, t2 such that r(t1) and r(t2) lie on the two mesh layers. Barycentric Interpolation: For a point \mathbf{p} on a triangle with vertices \mathbf{v}i and features \mathbf{f}i, the feature \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}) is computed as \sumi \lambdai \mathbf{f}i, where \lambdai are the barycentric coordinates of \mathbf{p} with respect to the triangle. Rendering Loss: The optimization minimizes the difference between the predicted color \hat{C} and the ground-truth color C{gt}: \mathcal{L} = \| \hat{C} - C{gt} \|^2 where \hat{C} is the output of the shallow CNN. Parameters: Number of sampled 3D locations per ray: Reduced from hundreds (in NeRF) to two (in NDRF). CNN Depth: Shallow (specific depth not given in sources, but described as "shallow" compared to NeRF's deep MLP). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Direct Training Artifacts: Directly training the neural duplex radiance field from scratch leads to noticeable artifacts. This is mitigated by using a multi-view distillation optimization strategy. Mesh Inaccuracies: The extracted mesh may not faithfully represent the true underlying geometry and can contain artifacts due to inaccuracies in the density field around surfaces. The duplex approach helps alleviate this by covering a reliable interval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ndrfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, duplexmesh, cnn, pretrainednerf): """ Renders a single ray using the Neural Duplex Radiance Field. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera origin. raydirection: 3D vector, camera direction. duplexmesh: Object containing two mesh layers (vertices, faces, features). cnn: Shallow convolutional network. pretrainednerf: Pretrained NeRF model (used for initial mesh extraction, not during rendering). Returns: color: 3D vector, predicted RGB color. """ # Step 1: Find intersection points with the two mesh layers # This assumes a function to intersect a ray with a mesh and return the first two hits # on the two distinct layers. p1, p2 = findduplexintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, duplexmesh) # Step 2: Interpolate features at intersection points # Barycentric interpolation based on which triangle the point falls on f1 = interpolatefeatures(p1, duplexmesh.layer1) f2 = interpolatefeatures(p2, duplexmesh.layer2) # Step 3: Aggregate features using shallow CNN # The CNN takes the features from the two points and possibly local neighborhood info # to predict the final color. color = cnn(f1, f2) return color def trainndrf(duplexmesh, cnn, trainingviews, pretrainednerf, numepochs): """ Trains the NDRF by distilling from a pretrained NeRF. Args: duplexmesh: The duplex mesh structure. cnn: The shallow CNN. trainingviews: List of (camerapose, groundtruthimage) pairs. pretrainednerf: The source NeRF for distillation. numepochs: Number of training iterations. """ # Step 1: Extract initial mesh from pretrained NeRF using marching cubes # This is done once before training. initialmesh = marchingcubes(pretrainednerf) duplexmesh.initialize(initialmesh) # Step 2: Multi-view distillation optimization for epoch in range(numepochs): for camerapose, gtimage in trainingviews: # Render the image using the current NDRF renderedimage = renderimage(camerapose, duplexmesh, cnn) # Compute loss against ground truth loss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, gtimage) # Backpropagate to update CNN weights and mesh features updateparameters(cnn, duplexmesh, loss) Time Complexity: Significantly faster than NeRF. The number of sampled 3D locations per ray is reduced from hundreds to two. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the duplex mesh and the CNN parameters. The mesh stores features per vertex, and the CNN is shallow. Measured Performance: Improves run-time performance by 10,000 times compared to the original NeRF while maintaining high-quality rendering. NeRF requires about 30 seconds to render a single 800x800 image, whereas NDRF achieves real-time performance. Strengths: Real-time view synthesis, high-quality appearance, post-processing compatibility with existing NeRFs, exploitation of local geometric relationships via CNN. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial mesh extraction; direct training from scratch causes artifacts. When to use: When real-time rendering of a pretrained NeRF is required, and the scene geometry can be approximated by a duplex mesh. When not to use: When the scene geometry is too complex or ambiguous for a mesh proxy to capture reliably, or when the highest possible fidelity is needed over speed. Origin: Proposed in "Learning Neural Duplex Radiance Fields for Real-Time View Synthesis" (CVPR 2023). History: Developed to address the high computational cost of NeRF rendering, which prevents its use for real-time applications. It builds on the concept of distilling NeRFs into efficient representations, similar to MobileNeRF, but without the need for complex multi-stage optimization. Usage: Used for real-time novel-view synthesis of complex scenes.
