name: Ray-Space Embedding Network with Local Affine Transformation
head: Local affine transformation-based embedding, Ours (no subdivision)
body: This method is a neural light field representation that uses a ray-space embedding network to predict local affine transformations for color computation, enabling view-dependent effects and multi-view consistency without explicit geometry. It differs from standard NeRF by parameterizing the radiance field locally within a voxel grid (for sparse inputs) or globally (for dense inputs), using an embedding network to infer affine parameters that linearize color level sets, thereby improving interpolation quality. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera ray r, defined by origin and direction. For subdivided models, the ray intersects a regular voxel grid covering NDC space. Output: Final color c for the ray. Data Structures 1. Voxel Grid: For sparse light fields (e.g., Real Forward-Facing, Shiny): A regular grid covering NDC space. Default resolution is 32^3. For specific Shiny sequences (CD, Lab), a coarser 4^3 grid is used. For dense/small-baseline light fields (e.g., Stanford): No subdivision; a single global model is used. Each voxel i has a center point pi. 2. Networks: Embedding Network (E\phi): An 8-layer MLP with 256 hidden units and one skip connection. Color Network (F\theta): An 8-layer MLP with 256 hidden units and one skip connection. A single network is shared for all local light fields for both E\phi and F\theta in the subdivided representation, indexed by voxel center points pi. 3. Parameters: Embedding space dimension N = 32. Local affine transformation parameters: 32 \times 4 matrices A and 32-dimensional bias vectors b. Positional Encoding The input coordinates \mathbf{x} (position) and \mathbf{d} (view direction) are mapped to higher dimensions using hierarchical positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). For a scalar input p: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)) where L is the number of frequency bands. L=8 for the subdivided model and L=10 for the one-evaluation model. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Voxel Intersection: For each ray r, intersect it with the voxel grid. Identify the sequence of voxels V(r) intersected by the ray. For each voxel i \in V(r), compute the local ray coordinates ri within that voxel. 2. Embedding Network Forward Pass: For each voxel i, compute the local affine transformation parameters (Ai, bi) using the embedding network: (Ai, bi) = E\phi(ri, \gamma(i)) where i represents the voxel index or center point. 3. Normalization: Feature Normalization: If using feature-based embedding (ablation), normalize the embedded feature f with L2 normalization and multiply by \sqrt{32} so the average square value is close to one. Matrix Normalization: Normalize the matrix Ai with its Frobenius norm and multiply by \sqrt{32} \cdot 4. Bias Activation: Apply \tanh activation to the predicted bias vectors bi. 4. Color and Alpha Prediction: For each sample point ri in voxel i, compute color ci and alpha \alphai using the color network: (ci, \alphai) = F\theta(\gamma(Ai ri + bi), \gamma(i)) Here, the input to the color network is the affine-transformed local ray coordinate Ai ri + bi, encoded via \gamma, concatenated with the global positional encoding \gamma(i). 5. Volume Rendering: Sort the samples by distance from the ray origin. Compute the final color c by over-compositing: c = \sum{i \in V(r)} \alphai ci \prod{j \in V(r), j < i} (1 - \alphaj). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def positionalencoding(p, L): """ Hierarchical positional encoding. p: scalar input. L: number of frequency bands. Returns: array of size 2L. """ out = [] for l in range(L): freq = 2l math.pi out.append(math.sin(freq p)) out.append(math.cos(freq p)) return np.array(out) def rayspaceembeddingnetwork(xlocal, voxelindex, Lenc): """ Placeholder for the 8-layer MLP Ephi. In implementation, this network takes the local ray coordinates and the voxel index (encoded) to output A and b. """ # Note: The actual MLP weights are learned during training. # This function represents the forward pass of Ephi. # Input: xlocal (4D vector in voxel space), voxelindex (scalar or encoded) # Output: A (32x4 matrix), b (32D vector) pass def colornetwork(encodedtransformedray, encodedvoxel): """ Placeholder for the 8-layer MLP Ftheta. Input: Concatenation of encoded affine-transformed ray and encoded voxel. Output: color (3D), alpha (scalar) """ pass def normalizematrix(A): """ Normalize matrix A with Frobenius norm and scale by sqrt(32)4. """ frobnorm = np.linalg.norm(A, 'fro') if frobnorm == 0: return A return A (math.sqrt(32) 4) / frobnorm def normalizefeature(f): """ L2 normalize feature f and multiply by sqrt(32). """ norm = np.linalg.norm(f) if norm == 0: return f return f math.sqrt(32) / norm def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, Lenc): """ Renders a single ray using the ray-space embedding method. """ # 1. Intersect ray with voxel grid to get list of intersected voxels V(r) # and local coordinates ri for each voxel. intersectedvoxels = voxelgrid.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) samples = [] for voxel in intersectedvoxels: # 2. Get local ray coordinates ri ri = voxel.getlocalraycoords(rayorigin, raydirection) # 3. Compute affine parameters (Ai, bi) # Note: In the paper, Ephi takes ri and gamma(i). # We assume ri is a 4D vector (x,y,z,w) or similar local coord system. Ai, bi = rayspaceembeddingnetwork(ri, voxel.index, Lenc) # 4. Normalize Ai Ai = normalizematrix(Ai) # 5. Apply tanh to bi bi = np.tanh(bi) # 6. Transform local ray coordinate # ri is typically 4D (x,y,z,1) or similar. Ai is 32x4. transformedray = np.dot(Ai, ri) + bi # 7. Encode transformed ray and voxel index # gamma is applied to each component of the transformed ray and voxel index encodedtransformedray = [] for val in transformedray: encodedtransformedray.extend(positionalencoding(val, Lenc)) encodedvoxel = positionalencoding(voxel.index, Lenc) # Simplified indexing # 8. Predict color and alpha ci, alphai = colornetwork(encodedtransformedray, encodedvoxel) # 9. Store sample with depth depth = voxel.getdepth(rayorigin, raydirection) samples.append({'c': ci, 'alpha': alphai, 'depth': depth}) # 10. Sort samples by depth samples.sort(key=lambda s: s['depth']) # 11. Over-compositing accumulatedalpha = 0.0 finalcolor = np.zeros(3) for sample in samples: alpha = sample['alpha'] c = sample['c'] weight = (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha finalcolor += weight c accumulatedalpha += weight if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break return finalcolor Parameters Embedding Dimension: N=32. Frequency Bands (L): 8 for subdivided model, 10 for one-evaluation model. Batch Size: 4,096 for subdivided model, 8,192 for one-evaluation model. Training Iterations: 50,000 with subdivision, 80,000 without. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Plücker Coordinates: Color level sets for Plücker coordinates are no longer affine, limiting the method's effectiveness for 360-degree scenes parameterized this way. Subdivision Cost: Subdivision increases render time and training time linearly with grid resolution N. Small-Baseline: For small-baseline light fields (Stanford), subdivision is not used; a single-evaluation per ray model is employed. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is competitive. On Stanford dataset (512x512), it takes ~0.11 seconds per frame (9.14 FPS). On Real Forward-Facing, it is >4.5x faster than NeRF. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint is 5.4 MB, compared to 4.6 MB for NeRF and 38.4 MB for NeX. Training Time: ~20 hours for Real Forward-Facing and Shiny datasets at 32^3 resolution; ~10 hours for Stanford. Strengths: Better reconstruction of view dependence than baselines; outperforms AutoInt in quality (~2 dB) and speed (~30%) on Real Forward-Facing; competitive with NeRF on PSNR/SSIM; outperforms NeX on PSNR for Shiny dataset. Limitations: Requires subdivision for sparse light fields, increasing training and render time; less effective for 360-degree scenes using Plücker coordinates. Origin: The method was introduced in "Learning Neural Light Fields with Ray-Space Embedding Networks". History: It was developed to address the limitations of existing neural light field methods in handling sparse input views and complex view-dependent effects. It builds on the idea of local affine transformations to implicitly encourage color level sets to be locally linear, facilitating multi-view consistency. Usage: Evaluated on Real Forward-Facing, Shiny, and Stanford Light Field datasets. name: Skeleton-Relative Encoding
head: A-NeRF Skeleton-Relative Encoding, Relative Encoding, Skeleton-Relative Input Encoding
body: Skeleton-Relative Encoding transforms 3D query positions and view directions into local bone-relative coordinate systems before processing them through a neural radiance field, explicitly incorporating domain knowledge of human body part linkage. Unlike standard NeRF which treats space as continuous and unstructured, this method reparameterizes the input space to respect the piece-wise rigidity of articulated motion, making it suitable for dynamic human avatars where global coordinate systems are insufficient. Inputs: World-space query position q \in \mathbb{R}^3. World-space view direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Skeleton pose parameters \thetak for frame k, defining bone transformations T(\thetak, m) for each bone m. Outputs: Combined encoding vector ek \in \mathbb{R}^D, which serves as the input to the density/color MLP F\phi. Skeleton Representation: A set of M bones (typically M=24 for a standard human skeleton, indices 1 to 24). Bone Transformation: T(\thetak, m) is a 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix mapping local bone coordinates to world coordinates for bone m at pose \thetak. Encoding Components: Relative Distance \tilde{v}k \in \mathbb{R}^M: Scalar distance from q to each bone. Relative Direction \tilde{r}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3M}: Unit vector from q to each bone. Relative Ray Direction \tilde{d}k \in \mathbb{R}^{3M}: View direction rotated to local bone frame. 1. Compute Bone-relative Position: For each bone m \in \{1, \dots, M\}, transform the world query q into the local coordinate system of bone m using the inverse transformation: \tilde{q}{k,m} = T^{-1}(\thetak, m) q where \tilde{q}{k,m} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Compute Relative Distance: Calculate the L2 norm of the bone-relative position to obtain the radial distance: \tilde{v}{k,m} = \| \tilde{q}{k,m} \|2 \in \mathbb{R} The vector of distances for all bones is \tilde{v}k = [\tilde{v}{k,1}, \dots, \tilde{v}{k,M}]. 3. Compute Relative Direction: Normalize the bone-relative position to capture orientation information: \tilde{r}{k,m} = \frac{\tilde{q}{k,m}}{\| \tilde{q}{k,m} \|2} \in \mathbb{R}^3 The vector of directions is \tilde{r}k = [\tilde{r}{k,1}, \dots, \tilde{r}{k,M}]. 4. Compute Relative Ray Direction: Rotate the incoming world-space view direction d by the rotational part of the inverse bone-to-world transformation: \tilde{d}{k,m} = [T^{-1}(\thetak, m)]{3\times3} d \in \mathbb{R}^3 where [T^{-1}(\thetak, m)]{3\times3} is the upper-left 3 \times 3 rotation submatrix. The vector of ray directions is \tilde{d}k = [\tilde{d}{k,1}, \dots, \tilde{d}{k,M}]. 5. Apply Cutoff Function: To prevent distant bones from influencing the prediction, apply a sigmoid-based cutoff function h(\cdot) to the distance and ray direction encodings: h(\tilde{v}{k,m}) = 1 - S(\tau (\tilde{v}{k,m} - t)) where S(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, t is the cutoff threshold, and \tau controls the sharpness of the cutoff. 6. Construct Final Encoding: Combine the components into the final input vector ek. Positional Encoding \Gamma(\cdot) is applied to the relative distance and relative ray direction, but not to the relative direction \tilde{r}k. ek = [h(\tilde{v}k) \odot \Gamma(\tilde{v}k), \quad \tilde{r}k, \quad h(\tilde{v}k) \odot \Gamma(\tilde{d}k)] Here, \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. \Gamma(\cdot) is the hierarchical sinusoidal positional encoding defined in the parent article Model Architecture and Encoding. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def skeletonrelativeencoding(q, d, bonetransformsinv, t=1.0, tau=10.0, L=10): """ Computes the skeleton-relative encoding for a query point and view direction. Args: q: np.array, shape (3,), world-space query position. d: np.array, shape (3,), world-space view direction. bonetransformsinv: list of np.array, shape (4, 4), inverse bone-to-world transforms for M bones. t: float, cutoff threshold for the sigmoid function. tau: float, sharpness of the cutoff. L: int, number of frequency bands for positional encoding. Returns: ek: np.array, the combined encoding vector. """ M = len(bonetransformsinv) # Lists to store components for each bone reldistances = [] reldirections = [] relraydirections = [] for m in range(M): # Step 1: Bone-relative position qhomogeneous = np.append(q, 1.0) qlocalhomogeneous = bonetransformsinv[m] @ qhomogeneous qlocal = qlocalhomogeneous[:3] # Step 2: Relative Distance vm = np.linalg.norm(qlocal) reldistances.append(vm) # Step 3: Relative Direction if vm < 1e-8: rm = np.zeros(3) else: rm = qlocal / vm reldirections.append(rm) # Step 4: Relative Ray Direction Rinv = bonetransformsinv[m][:3,:3] dlocal = Rinv @ d relraydirections.append(dlocal) # Convert to arrays vk = np.array(reldistances) # Shape (M,) rk = np.array(reldirections) # Shape (M, 3) dk = np.array(relraydirections) # Shape (M, 3) # Step 5: Cutoff Function sigmoidinput = tau (vk - t) h = 1.0 - (1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-sigmoidinput))) # Step 6: Positional Encoding and Combination vpe = positionalencoding(vk, L) # Shape (M, 2L) # Apply PE to each component of dk dpeflat = positionalencoding(dk.flatten(), L) # Shape (3M, 2L) dpe = dpeflat.reshape(M, 3 2 L) # Shape (M, 6L) # Apply cutoff h to the PE outputs vpecropped = vpe h[:, np.newaxis] dpecropped = dpe h[:, np.newaxis] # Concatenate: [h(v)Gamma(v), r, h(d)Gamma(d)] ek = np.concatenate([vpecropped, rk, dpecropped], axis=1) return ek def positionalencoding(values, L): """ Applies hierarchical sinusoidal positional encoding to a 1D array of values. Args: values: np.array, shape (N,), scalar values to encode. L: int, number of frequency bands. Returns: encoded: np.array, shape (N, 2L). """ N = len(values) encoded = np.zeros((N, 2 L)) for i in range(L): freq = 2i np.pi encoded[:, 2i] = np.sin(values freq) encoded[:, 2i+1] = np.cos(values freq) return encoded Number of Bones (M): 24, corresponding to indices 1 to 24 of the human skeleton. Cutoff Threshold (t): Not given in the sources. Sharpness (\tau): Not given in the sources. Frequency Bands (L): Not given in the sources (inherited from parent Model Architecture and Encoding). Dimensionality Explosion: Using bone-relative position (\tilde{q}{k,m}) instead of relative distance (\tilde{v}{k,m}) increases the input dimensionality by an order of magnitude, which can hinder learning. The method prefers relative distance for lower dimensionality and better reconstruction accuracy. Relative Direction Encoding: The relative direction \tilde{r}k is passed directly into the final encoding ek without subsequent positional encoding (PE). Applying PE to direction vectors is not beneficial in this context. Ambiguity: While bone-relative position removes ambiguities of assigning a query to a single part, the radial distance encoding naturally captures spherically shaped limbs and is robust to the ill-posed association to a single part. Maps the query q to local coordinates of each bone. Sets itself apart by preserving full 3D local structure but suffers from high dimensionality. Computes the L2 norm from q to each bone. Sets itself apart by being lower-dimensional and capturing radial symmetry of limbs. This is the preferred encoding in the final A-NeRF model. Normalizes the bone-relative position vector. Sets itself apart by providing orientation information without PE. Always used in conjunction with distance encoding. Rotates the view direction into the local bone frame. Sets itself apart by enabling view-dependent appearance modeling relative to the body part. A sigmoid-based weighting mechanism. Sets itself apart by localizing the influence of each bone, preventing distant bones from affecting the prediction. Time Complexity: O(M \cdot L) per query point, where M is the number of bones and L is the number of frequency bands. The transformation T^{-1} is O(1) per bone. Memory Complexity: O(M \cdot L) for the encoding vector. The skeleton transforms must be stored or computed on the fly. Strengths: Incorporates explicit domain knowledge of human articulation. Invariant to global shift and rotation of the person. Preserves piece-wise rigidity of articulated motion. Lower dimensionality compared to full bone-relative position encoding. Limitations: Requires a skeleton pose estimator for initialization and runtime. Performance depends on the accuracy of the skeleton tracking. Does not model complex soft-tissue deformation (muscle bulging) as explicitly as parametric surface models, though it approximates it via the neural field. When to use: Dynamic human avatar rendering where pose information is available or can be estimated. When not to use: Static scenes, scenes without articulated structures, or when skeleton tracking is unreliable. Skeleton-Relative Encoding was introduced in A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose by Gkioxari et al. (2021). The method was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF in modeling dynamic humans, where global coordinates fail to capture the rigid motion of body parts. It inverts the approach of parametric models like SMPL: instead of deforming a surface, it deforms the query space. The work builds on the foundational NeRF architecture Model Architecture and Encoding and integrates it with articulated skeleton data. name: Position Encoding
head: Frequency Position Encoding, Sine/Cosine Encoding
body: Position Encoding (PE) is a feature mapping technique that transforms low-frequency coordinate representations into high-frequency information using sine and cosine functions, thereby increasing dimensionality to help deep networks approximate high-frequency functions and prevent the loss of high-frequency spatial information. It sets itself apart from its siblings by serving as the foundational explicit encoding scheme for NeRF, whereas alternatives like Frequency-Modulated Position Encoding or Random Offset Annealed Fourier Encoding introduce stochasticity, modulation, or local affine transformations to address specific limitations such as spectral bias or domain shift. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a query point coordinate vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position) and a camera viewing direction vector \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 as input. It outputs a high-dimensional encoded vector resulting from the application of the encoding function \gamma(\cdot) to \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}, which is then concatenated and passed to a fully-connected MLP. Data Structures: The encoding relies on an encoding level parameter L, representing the number of frequency bands. In the standard NeRF configuration, L=10 for position \mathbf{x} and L=4 for direction \mathbf{d}. Formulas: The encoding function \gamma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{2L} is defined as: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)) The final encoded feature vector is computed by applying \gamma separately to each of the three components of \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}, and then feeding the result into a regular MLP F{\Theta'}: F\Theta = F{\Theta'} \circ \gamma where \circ denotes the composition of the mapping \gamma with the MLP F{\Theta'}. The MLP architecture typically consists of two branches: a density branch that processes the encoded position features to predict volume density \sigma, and a color branch that processes the encoded direction features concatenated with intermediate features from the density branch to predict RGB color \mathbf{c}. Parameters: Lx = 10: Encoding levels for position. Ld = 4: Encoding levels for direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the frequency scaling factors 2^l \pi for l = 0, \dots, L-1. 2. For each coordinate component p \in \{x1, x2, x3, d1, d2, d3\}, evaluate \sin(2^l \pi p) and \cos(2^l \pi p) for all l. 3. Concatenate the resulting 2L values for each component to form the encoded vectors for position and direction. 4. Concatenate the position and direction encoded vectors and pass them to the MLP branches (density for position, color for direction). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def positionencoding(p, L): """ Applies the standard NeRF position encoding to a scalar or vector p. Args: p (float or list of floats): Input coordinate(s). L (int): Number of frequency bands. Returns: list: Encoded vector of size 2 L len(p). """ encoded = [] if isinstance(p, (int, float)): p = [p] for coord in p: for l in range(L): freq = (2 l) math.pi encoded.append(math.sin(freq coord)) encoded.append(math.cos(freq coord)) return encoded def nerfencode(x, d, Lx=10, Ld=4): """ Encodes position x and direction d for NeRF. Args: x (list of 3 floats): 3D position coordinates. d (list of 3 floats): 3D viewing direction vector. Lx (int): Encoding levels for position. Ld (int): Encoding levels for direction. Returns: list: Concatenated encoded vector for x and d. """ encx = positionencoding(x, Lx) encd = positionencoding(d, Ld) return encx + encd Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Spectral Bias: Deep networks tend to focus on learning low-frequency functions while losing high-frequency information; PE explicitly injects high frequencies to mitigate this. Precision: High-frequency components 2^{L-1} can cause numerical instability or overflow if input coordinates are not normalized, requiring careful scaling or clamping. Degenerate Input: Zero or near-zero direction vectors should be normalized before encoding to avoid undefined behavior in downstream ray sampling. A specialized hardware accelerator designed to compute feature mapping functions for neural radiance fields by performing inner product operations with vector sizes R=3 and R=6. It differs from software-based implementations by offloading the matrix multiplication and trigonometric evaluation to dedicated logic, supporting isotropic and anisotropic random Fourier features. Choose when hardware acceleration is required for NeRF training and rendering. Positional Encoding Unit (PEU) Time Complexity: The encoding step is O(L \cdot D), where L is the number of frequency bands and D is the dimensionality of the input (3 for position, 3 for direction). This is negligible compared to the MLP evaluation. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint for the encoding parameters is minimal, as the frequencies are fixed constants. The output vector size is 2 \cdot L \cdot D, which for standard NeRF (Lx=10, Ld=4, D=3) results in a vector of size 72. Strengths: Simple to implement, fully differentiable, and effective at mitigating spectral bias in MLPs by expanding the frequency spectrum. Limitations: Fixed frequency bands may not be optimal for all scenes; high frequencies can be difficult to optimize without careful initialization or optimization strategies. When to Use: Standard NeRF training and rendering where high-frequency spatial details must be preserved. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. NeRF employs PE as a specialized mapping technique to transform low-frequency coordinate representations into high-frequency information, addressing the tendency of deep networks to learn low-frequency functions and lose high-frequency spatial information. The technique maps coordinates to a higher-dimensional space using multi-period sine and cosine functions with exponentially increasing frequencies. Neural Radiance Fields-Based 3D Reconstruction of Power Transmission Lines Using Progressive Motion Sequence Images., https://doi.org/10.3390/s23239537, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Positional Encoding Unit (PEU)
head: Hardware Positional Encoding Unit
body: The Positional Encoding Unit (PEU) is a specialized hardware accelerator designed to compute feature mapping functions for neural radiance fields (NeRF) by performing inner product operations with vector sizes R=3 and R=6. It differs from software-based implementations by offloading the matrix multiplication and trigonometric evaluation to dedicated logic, supporting isotropic and anisotropic random Fourier features. It builds on Position Encoding by providing a fixed-function pipeline for the specific frequency transformations required in NeRF training and rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Position vectors \mathbf{x} (dimension 3) or direction vectors \mathbf{d} (dimension 3), and a frequency matrix \mathbf{F} (dimensions R \times N, where R \in \{3, 6\} and N is the number of frequency bands, typically 128). Output: Transformed feature vectors containing \sin(\mathbf{z}) and \cos(\mathbf{z}) components, where \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{F} or \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{F}. Data Structures: Frequency Matrix Memory: For R=3: A single memory block of size 3 \times 128 stores the frequency matrix \mathbf{F}. For R=6: Two separate memory blocks, each of size 3 \times 128. The first block stores the first half of the 6 \times 128 matrix, and the second block stores the second half. MAC Unit: A cascaded Multiply-Accumulate unit. For R=3: A 3-stage cascaded MAC unit performs 3 multiplications and 2 additions in serial. For R=6: The same hardware structure is used but operates through all 6 stages. Steps: 1. Load Frequency Matrix: Store the frequency matrix \mathbf{F} in local memory. This matrix is constant for all sample points in a particular rendering task. 2. Stream Coordinates: Stream position \mathbf{x} or direction \mathbf{d} vectors into the matrix multiplication unit. 3. Matrix Multiplication: Multiply the streamed coordinates with the frequency matrix \mathbf{F} in a pipelined manner to generate the intermediate vector \mathbf{z}. For R=3: Access one memory block. Process through the first 3 stages of the MAC unit. The later 3 stages are bypassed. For R=6: Access both memory blocks simultaneously. Process through all 6 stages of the cascaded MAC unit. 4. Trigonometric Transformation: Feed the intermediate vector \mathbf{z} to a Coordinate Rotation Digital Computer (CORDIC) array to generate the final transformed features \sin(\mathbf{z}) and \cos(\mathbf{z}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def peucompute(coordinates, frequencymatrix, mode): """ Simulates the PEU hardware logic. coordinates: list of 3 floats (x or d) frequencymatrix: list of lists, shape (R, N) mode: 'R3' or 'R6' """ R = 3 if mode == 'R3' else 6 N = len(frequencymatrix[0]) # Step 1 & 2: Memory access and streaming # In hardware, F is pre-loaded. Coordinates are streamed. # Step 3: Matrix Multiplication via MAC unit # z = coordinates. F.T z = [0.0] N for i in range(R): for j in range(N): z[j] += coordinates[i] frequencymatrix[i][j] # Step 4: CORDIC array for sin/cos # Hardware uses CORDIC for efficiency sinz = [math.sin(val) for val in z] cosz = [math.cos(val) for val in z] return sinz, cosz Parameters: Frequency Matrix Dimension R: Supports R=3 (for 3-dimensional data) and R=6 (for 6-dimensional data, likely combining position and direction or higher-order features). Memory Size: 3 \times 128 per block. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Power Management: In R=3 mode, the second memory block is set to sleep mode to reduce power consumption. Bypassing: In R=3 mode, the later 3 stages of the MAC unit are bypassed, not disabled, to maintain pipeline integrity. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of frequency bands N and the dimension R. The pipelined nature allows for high throughput per sample point. Memory Complexity: Fixed memory footprint of 2 \times (3 \times 128) elements for the frequency matrix storage, regardless of the number of sample points. Performance: Designed to accelerate the MLP component of NeRF, which is the most computation-intensive part due to tens of millions of MLP queries. Strengths: Hardware efficiency for inner product operations; power reduction in R=3 mode; support for both isotropic and anisotropic random Fourier features. Limitations: Fixed support for R=3 and R=6; requires pre-loading of frequency matrix; specific to NeRF rendering tasks. The PEU was developed as part of the ICARUS architecture, a specialized hardware system for Neural Radiance Fields rendering. It addresses the computational bottleneck of MLP queries in NeRF pipelines. The design supports various positional encoding algorithms, including isotropic random Fourier features [Tancik et al. 2020] and anisotropic random Fourier features [Yu et al. 2022], as cited in. ICARUS: A Specialized Architecture for Neural Radiance Fields Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2203.01414, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Random Offset Annealed Fourier Encoding
head: ROAFE
body: Random Offset Annealed Fourier Encoding (ROAFE) is a positional encoding scheme for radiance fields that modifies standard Fourier encoding by introducing random Gaussian offsets to frequency basis functions and applying an annealing schedule to the frequencies. It solves the problem of axis-aligned frequency artifacts (striping) inherent in standard NeRF encoding while maintaining the optimization stability provided by frequency annealing. It is distinguished from standard NeRF encoding by the addition of random offsets and from BARF/Nerfies by the specific handling of these offsets within the annealing window. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D coordinate vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: L: Number of frequency bands. Default: 10. \alpha: Annealing parameter, ranging from 0 to L. Annealed over 50,000 steps. \mathbf{R}: Random offset matrix of size L \times 3, sampled from \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1). Output: An encoded vector \gamma(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 + 6L}. Data Structures \mathbf{R}: A static matrix of shape (L, 3) containing Gaussian random values. \alpha: A scalar integer or float representing the current training step normalized to the frequency range. Formulas The encoding is defined as: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x}, \Gamma1, \dots, \Gamma{L-1}) where each frequency component \Gammak for k \in \{1, \dots, L-1\} is computed as: \Gammak(\mathbf{x}; \alpha) = wk(\alpha) \left[ \sin(2^k \mathbf{x} + 2^k \mathbf{R}k), \cos(2^k \mathbf{x} + 2^k \mathbf{R}k) \right] The annealing weight wk(\alpha) acts as a truncated Hann window: wk(\alpha) = \frac{1 - \cos(\pi \cdot \text{clamp}(\alpha - k, 0, 1))}{2} where \text{clamp}(v, 0, 1) restricts v to the interval [0, 1]. Direction Encoding View directions \mathbf{d} are encoded separately using 4 non-annealed and non-offset Fourier frequencies. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def roafeencode(x, L=10, alpha=0, R=None): """ Encode a 3D coordinate using Random Offset Annealed Fourier Encoding. Args: x: numpy array of shape (3,), the 3D coordinate. L: int, number of frequency bands. alpha: float, annealing parameter (0 to L). R: numpy array of shape (L, 3), random offsets. If None, generated deterministically for reproducibility in this example. Returns: numpy array of shape (3 + 6(L-1),), the encoded vector. """ if R is None: # Deterministic seed for reproducibility in implementation example rng = np.random.RandomState(42) R = rng.normal(0, 0.1, size=(L, 3)) # Initialize output with raw coordinates # Note: The source defines gamma(x) = (x, Gamma1,..., Gamma{L-1}) # This implies the raw x is included, and frequencies start from index 1 to L-1. # However, standard NeRF often uses 0 to L-1. The source explicitly writes Gamma1 to Gamma{L-1}. # We follow the source notation strictly. encodedparts = [x] for k in range(1, L): # Calculate base frequency scaling factor 2^k # Source text has garbled '2k' but context implies 2^k or similar scaling. # The formula block shows 2^k. freqscale = 2 k # Get random offset for this frequency band # Rk is the k-th row of R. Note: R is size Lx3. # If k goes 1..L-1, we access R[1]..R[L-1]. # The source says R is sampled from N(0, 0.1). offset = R[k] # Compute the argument for sin/cos: 2^k x + 2^k Rk # This is equivalent to 2^k (x + Rk) arg = freqscale (x + offset) # Compute sine and cosine components sincomp = np.sin(arg) coscomp = np.cos(arg) # Concatenate sin and cos for this band bandoutput = np.concatenate([sincomp, coscomp]) # Compute annealing weight wk(alpha) # clamp(alpha - k, 0, 1) clampval = max(0.0, min(1.0, alpha - k)) weight = (1.0 - math.cos(math.pi clampval)) / 2.0 # Apply weight weightedband = weight bandoutput encodedparts.append(weightedband) return np.concatenate(encodedparts) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Annealing Boundary: When \alpha < k, the weight wk(\alpha) is 0, effectively disabling higher frequencies early in training. When \alpha \ge k+1, the weight is 1. The transition occurs between \alpha=k and \alpha=k+1. Direction Encoding: Directions use a fixed 4-band encoding without annealing or offsets, distinct from position encoding. Offset Initialization: Offsets are sampled from \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1). These should be fixed after initialization to avoid non-deterministic behavior during training. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of frequency bands L and the number of samples. Memory complexity is O(L \cdot D) for storing the offset matrix \mathbf{R}, where D=3 is the input dimension. Performance: Improves optimization landscape by breaking axis-alignment, reducing striping artifacts compared to standard NeRF. Strengths: Combines the benefits of random frequency rotation (reducing artifacts) with annealing (stabilizing optimization). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the annealing schedule (50,000 steps in SAMURAI) and offset variance (0.1). ROAFE was introduced in the SAMURAI paper (2022). It builds upon the Fourier encoding used in NeRF, the annealing technique from BARF and Nerfies, and the concept of random frequency offsets demonstrated by Tancik et al.. It was developed to handle unconstrained real-world image collections where axis-aligned artifacts are more pronounced. SAMURAI: Shape and Material from Unconstrained Real-World Arbitrary Image Collections, https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1914, fetched 2026-10-29

name: NeuRay
head: Neural Rays
body: NeuRay is an occlusion-aware image-based rendering method that represents a scene by estimating occlusion probabilities (hitting probabilities) from input views to arbitrary 3D points, enabling efficient novel view synthesis. Unlike standard radiance field methods that treat volume density as a continuous scalar, NeuRay explicitly models visibility to handle feature inconsistency caused by occlusions, particularly in sparse or 360-degree captures. It differs from sibling methods like IBRNet by integrating a visibility encoder and using spherical harmonics to fit anisotropic colors, allowing it to outperform baselines in generalization and fine-tuning settings where occlusions are prevalent. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of N input images with known camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). For rendering a test view, a subset of Nw neighboring input images (working views) is selected. Outputs: A synthesized RGB image for the test view, and optionally depth maps. Data Structures 1. Cost Volume: Constructed using Ns=3 neighboring source views. Dimensions are H/4 \times W/4 \times D, where D=64 is the number of disparity planes. 2. Visibility Feature: A feature map of size H/4 \times W/4 \times 32 generated by the Initialization Network and refined by the Visibility Encoder. 3. Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: For each sample point, a vector \boldsymbol{\theta}i \in \mathbb{R}^{16} representing SH coefficients up to degree 3. 4. Hitting Probability: A scalar \hat{h}i representing the probability that a point pi is visible from the test view, derived from a mixture of logistics distributions. Network Architecture The model consists of shared encoders and task-specific decoders for coarse and fine stages. 1. Image Encoder: A ResNet with 13 residual blocks, outputting a feature map with 32 channels. Convolution layers use ReLU; batch normalization is replaced by instance normalization. 2. Initialization Network: Inputs: Image feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 64), Depth regression (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32), Cost Volume (H/4 \times W/4 \times 1). Structure: Conv3x3(32) \rightarrow ResBlock(32) \rightarrow Conv1x1(32). Output: Visibility Feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32). 3. Visibility Encoder: Inputs: Visibility Feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32), Image feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 96). Structure: Conv3x3(32) \rightarrow ResBlock(32) \rightarrow Conv1x1(32). Output: Refined Visibility Feature (H/4 \times W/4 \times 32). 4. Decoder F (Distribution): Contains 5 sub-networks, each with 3 fully-connected layers. Predicts \mu1, \mu2, \sigma1, \sigma2 and mixing weight w0 (where w1 = 1 - w0). Uses ReLU for hidden layers, SoftPlus/Sigmoid for output. 5. Aggregation Networks (Coarse/Fine): Network \mathcal{M} (Feature Aggregation): Inputs are Visibility features (N \times K \times 32), View directions (N \times K \times 3), Image features (N \times K \times 3). Process: MLP(1,32,32) on visibility, MLP(3,32,32) on directions, MLP(32,32,1) on image features. Element-wise product. MLP(32,32,32). Element-wise plus. MLP(192,64,32). Transformer. MLP(16,1). Output: Aggregated feature. Network \mathcal{A} (Alpha): Inputs are Mean (N \times 1 \times 32) and Var (N \times 1 \times 32). MLP(35,16,8,1) followed by Softmax. Output: Alpha value \alphai \in [0,1]. Network \mathcal{B} (Blending): Inputs are Mean (N \times 1 \times 32) and Var (N \times 1 \times 32). MLP(64,32,16) followed by sigmoid. Output: Blending weights (N \times K \times 1). Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Construct a cost volume using COLMAP patch-match stereo and Ns=3 source views. Pass image features through the Image Encoder, Initialization Network, and Visibility Encoder to obtain the Refined Visibility Feature. 2. Ray Sampling: For a test ray r(\lambda) = o + \lambda d, sample K{t,1} points for the coarse stage and K{t,2} points for the fine stage. Default values are K{t,1}=64, K{t,2}=64. Use the coarse model to estimate hitting probabilities \hat{h}i for all coarse points. Perform coarse-to-fine sampling: select fine points based on the distribution defined by the coarse hitting probabilities. 3. Visibility and Alpha Computation: For each sample point pi, compute the hitting probability \hat{h}i using the mixture of Nl=2 logistics distributions parameterized by the Decoder F. Compute the alpha value \alphai = \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{f}i), where \mathbf{f}i is the aggregated feature. The network \mathcal{A} assigns large \alphai when features from visible input views are consistent. 4. Color Computation (Radiance Field Rendering): Compute the color \mathbf{c}i for point pi using the color blending network \mathcal{B}: \mathbf{c}i = \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{f}i, \{\mathbf{f}{i,j}; \mathbf{r}{i,j} - \mathbf{r}; \mathbf{c}{i,j}; v{i,j}\}) where \mathbf{r}{i,j} is the view direction from the j-th input view to pi, \mathbf{c}{i,j} is the projected color, and v{i,j} is the visibility. Render the final pixel color \hat{c} using alpha compositing weighted by hitting probabilities: \hat{c} = \sumi \mathbf{c}i \hat{h}i. 5. Spherical Harmonics Fitting (Direct Rendering / Anisotropic Color): To represent anisotropic colors, fit a function R(\mathbf{r}; \boldsymbol{\theta}i) on the sphere for each point pi using spherical harmonics. Solve the linear least squares problem for coefficients \boldsymbol{\theta}i: \min{\boldsymbol{\theta}i} \sumj \tilde{h}{i,j}(z{i,j}, z{i,j}+li) \|R(\mathbf{r}{i,j}; \boldsymbol{\theta}i) - \mathbf{c}{i,j}\|^2 + \boldsymbol{\theta}i^\intercal \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{\theta}i where \tilde{h}{i,j} is the hitting probability, \boldsymbol{\Lambda} is a diagonal regularization matrix with elements (0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01) for degrees 0 to 3, and R is the SH basis function. The color is then computed as \mathbf{c}i = R(\mathbf{r}; \boldsymbol{\theta}i). 6. Training and Loss: Depth loss is \ell{depth} = \sum \|\mu1 - z{in}\|^2, where \mu1 is the mean of the first logistics distribution and z{in} is input depth from the cost volume. The color difference is weighted by hitting probabilities in the loss function to ensure occluded input rays do not interfere with output colors. During training, predicted hitting probabilities hi are memorized. If a point is invisible to view A, this is used to refine visibility predictions for other views (e.g., view D) in subsequent steps. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def neurayrender(inputimages, cameraposes, testviewpose, numworkingviews=8): """Renders a test view using NeuRay.""" # 1. Select Working Views workingviews = selectnearestviews(testviewpose, cameraposes, numworkingviews) # 2. Construct Cost Volume costvolume = constructcostvolume(workingviews, depthplanes=64) # 3. Encode Features imagefeatures = imageencoder(workingviews) depthregression = getdepthfromcostvolume(costvolume) visibilityfeature = initializationnetwork(imagefeatures, depthregression, costvolume) refinedvisibility = visibilityencoder(visibilityfeature, imagefeatures) # 4. Sample Points along Test Ray coarsepoints = sampleray(testviewpose, numsamples=64) coarseparams = distributiondecoder(refinedvisibility, coarsepoints) coarsehittingprobs = computelogisticsmixture(coarseparams) finepoints = samplefine(coarsepoints, coarsehittingprobs, numsamples=64) # 5. Compute Alpha and Color for Fine Points aggregatedfeatures = featureaggregationnetwork(refinedvisibility, finepoints, workingviews) alphavalues = alphanetwork(aggregatedfeatures) colors = colorblendingnetwork(aggregatedfeatures, workingviews, finepoints) # 6. Render finalcolor = np.zeros(3) for i, point in enumerate(finepoints): hi = coarsehittingprobs[i] ci = colors[i] finalcolor += ci hi return finalcolor def selectnearestviews(testpose, allposes, k): """Selects k nearest camera poses based on translation distance.""" distances = np.linalg.norm(allposes[:,:3, 3] - testpose[:3, 3], axis=1) return np.argsort(distances)[:k] def constructcostvolume(views, depthplanes): """Constructs a cost volume using correlation over depth planes.""" # Standard MVS cost volume construction return np.zeros((views[0].height//4, views[0].width//4, depthplanes)) def imageencoder(views): """ResNet-13 with instance normalization, outputs 32 channels.""" # Standard ResNet-13 forward pass return np.zeros((views[0].height//4, views[0].width//4, 32)) def getdepthfromcostvolume(costvolume): """Extracts depth map via argmax over cost volume depth dimension.""" return np.argmax(costvolume, axis=2) def initializationnetwork(imagefeat, depthreg, costvol): """Conv3x3(32) -> ResBlock(32) -> Conv1x1(32).""" x = conv3x3(imagefeat, 32) x = resblock(x, 32) return conv1x1(x, 32) def visibilityencoder(visfeat, imagefeat): """Conv3x3(32) -> ResBlock(32) -> Conv1x1(32).""" x = conv3x3(visfeat, 32) x = resblock(x, 32) return conv1x1(x, 32) def sampleray(viewpose, numsamples): """Samples points linearly along the camera ray.""" origins = viewpose[:3, 3] directions = viewpose[:3, 3] # Simplified for ray direction t = np.linspace(0.1, 10.0, numsamples) return origins + t[:, None] directions def distributiondecoder(refinedvis, points): """Predicts 5 parameters: mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2, w0.""" # MLP predicting 5 values per point return np.random.randn(len(points), 5) def computelogisticsmixture(params): """Computes CDF of mixture of 2 logistics distributions.""" mu1, mu2, s1, s2, w0 = np.split(params, 5, axis=1) s1, s2 = np.maximum(s1, 1e-6), np.maximum(s2, 1e-6) cdf1 = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(params[:, 0] - mu1) / s1)) cdf2 = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(params[:, 1] - mu2) / s2)) return w0 cdf1 + (1 - w0) cdf2 def samplefine(coarsepoints, coarseprobs, numsamples): """Stratified sampling based on coarse hitting probabilities.""" # Simple uniform resampling for demonstration return coarsepoints[:numsamples] def featureaggregationnetwork(visfeat, points, views): """MLP(1,32,32) -> MLP(3,32,32) -> MLP(32,32,1) -> prod -> MLP(32,32,32) -> + -> MLP(192,64,32) -> Transformer -> MLP(16,1).""" # Standard aggregation pipeline return np.random.randn(len(points), 32) def alphanetwork(aggregatedfeat): """MLP(35,16,8,1) + Softmax.""" return np.ones(len(aggregatedfeat)) / len(aggregatedfeat) def colorblendingnetwork(aggregatedfeat, views, points): """MLP(64,32,16) + sigmoid.""" return np.random.rand(len(points), 3) def sphericalharmonicsfit(point, workingviews, hittingprobs): """Fits spherical harmonics to anisotropic color at a point.""" lambdadiag = np.array([0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01]) Amatrix = [] bvector = [] for j, view in enumerate(workingviews): hij = hittingprobs[j] rij = viewdirection(view, point) cij = projectcolor(view, point) basis = evaluateshbasis(rij, degree=3) Amatrix.append(hij basis) bvector.append(hij cij) Amat = np.array(Amatrix) bvec = np.array(bvector) Lambda = np.diag(lambdadiag) ATA = Amat.T @ Amat ATb = Amat.T @ bvec theta = np.linalg.solve(ATA + Lambda, ATb) return theta def evaluateshbasis(direction, degree): """Evaluates spherical harmonics basis functions up to given degree.""" # Standard SH basis evaluation x, y, z = direction if degree == 0: return np.array([1.0]) if degree == 1: return np.array([y, z, x]) if degree == 2: return np.array([xy, yz, 2z2 - x2 - y2, xz, x2 - y2]) # Degree 3 omitted for brevity, follows standard spherical harmonic definitions return np.zeros(16) def viewdirection(view, point): return point - view[:3, 3] def projectcolor(view, point): return np.random.rand(3) Parameters D=64: Number of planes in cost volume. Nl=2: Number of logistics distributions. K{t,1}=64, K{t,2}=64: Sample points in coarse/fine stages. Ns=3: Neighboring source views for cost volume. SH Degree: 3, resulting in \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^{16}. Regularization \boldsymbol{\Lambda}: Diagonal elements (0, 0.001, 0.005, 0.01). Optimizer: Adam (\beta1=0.999, \beta2=0.9). Batch Size: 512 rays per step. Learning Rate: Generalization 2 \times 10^{-4} (decay half every 100k steps); Finetuning 1 \times 10^{-4} (decay half every 100k steps). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Invisible Regions: NeuRay cannot render regions invisible to all working views, even if visible in other input views, because it is image-based. Textureless/Cluttered Regions: Feature matching struggles in textureless or cluttered complex regions (e.g., Ficus), leading to view inconsistency and artifacts. Generalization Speed: In generalization settings, predicted visibility is often inaccurate, preventing high-quality rendering with very few sample points. Speeding up rendering requires accurate surface location estimation, which is only reliable in finetuned models. Direct Rendering Artifacts: Direct rendering produces meaningful results but artifacts occur on edges. Time Complexity: Rendering time is significantly reduced compared to NeRF. On the DTU 'birds' dataset, using 4-8 fine sample points speeds up rendering from 30s to ~3s (10x speedup). Memory Complexity: Uses a cost volume of size H/4 \times W/4 \times 64 and feature maps of size H/4 \times W/4 \times 32. The image encoder is lighter than IBRNet. Performance: NeRF Synthetic (Lego): NeuRay-Ft achieves 30.63 PSNR in ~32 minutes, comparable to NeRF's 30.27 PSNR in ~9.5 hours. LLFF (Nw=8): NeuRay 27.06 PSNR vs IBRNet 26.87 PSNR. LLFF (Nw=2): NeuRay 24.86 PSNR vs IBRNet 21.72 PSNR. Generalization (Lego, N=100): NeuRay 28.41 PSNR vs IBRNet 25.64 PSNR. Strengths: Occlusion-aware, handles sparse 360-degree captures better than IBRNet, recovers details more clearly than NeRF with fewer training steps, fast finetuning. Limitations: Fails on regions invisible to all working views, struggles with textureless regions, generalization mode requires more samples for high quality. When to Use: Novel view synthesis with sparse or 360-degree input views, especially where occlusions are present. Suitable for scenarios requiring fast finetuning. When Not to Use: Scenes with large invisible regions relative to working views, or highly textureless environments. NeuRay was introduced in the paper "Neural Rays for Occlusion-aware Image-based Rendering". It addresses the limitations of existing image-based rendering methods like IBRNet, which suffer from feature inconsistency due to occlusions in sparse captures. By explicitly modeling occlusion probabilities, NeuRay refines scene representation and provides better occlusion inference during finetuning. It is used on datasets such as LLFF, NeRF synthetic (Lego), and DTU. Neural Rays for Occlusion-aware Image-based Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00767, fetched 2026-10-26

name: AReT (Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF)
head: AReT NeRF, AReT framework, AReT model, Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF, Prior TensoRF v2, proposed AReT model
body: AReT is a scene-specific (patient-specific) inverse solver that reconstructs 3D lung nodule volumes from only three orthogonal Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs: coronal, sagittal, axial) using a Tensorial Radiance Field (TensoRF) representation. It solves the problem of sparse-view medical reconstruction where standard TensoRF fails due to a density-parameterization dead zone that suppresses gradients. Unlike generative-prior approaches like MedNeRF, AReT is prior-free during training, relying instead on a corrected density initialization and anatomy-aware regularization (\ell1 sparsity and Total Variation smoothness) to enforce physiologically plausible attenuation distributions in the air-dominated thoracic cavity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Three orthogonal DRRs (coronal, sagittal, axial) generated from a patient's ground-truth CT volume via Beer-Lambert forward projection. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D density field (linear attenuation coefficient \mu) and a segmented nodule volume. Data Structures: TensoRF Representation: A VM-rank-16 TensoRF model decomposes the scene into low-rank tensor factors. Grid Resolution: A 64^3 grid is used for density queries, with voxel spacing approximately [3.75, 1.875, 2.1875] mm. Memory: A 64^3 VM-rank-16 TensoRF requires approximately 14 GB VRAM (including gradient buffers) on an NVIDIA T4. Parameters: Density Shift (\Delta): Set to 0 (default in standard TensoRF is -10). Scale (s): Set to 1 (default in standard TensoRF is 25). Regularization Weights: \lambda1 = 1 \times 10^{-4} (sparsity), \lambda2 = 1 \times 10^{-5} (TV smoothness). Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 0.02 for grid parameters and 0.002 for MLP. Batch Size: 2048 rays per iteration. Iterations: 3000 total iterations. Alpha Mask Updates: Deterministic updates at iterations 1500 and 2500 to prune near-empty voxels. Random Seeds: torch.manualseed(0) and numpy.random.seed(0). Numbered Steps: 1. CT Preprocessing and HU Calibration: Load DICOM slices and sort by ImagePositionPatient Z-coordinate. Convert Hounsfield Units (HU) using RescaleSlope and RescaleIntercept. Apply lung-window clipping and linear normalization: v{norm} = \frac{HU - (-1000)}{400 - (-1000)} 2. DRR Simulation and Camera Pose Assignment: Generate three orthogonal DRRs (coronal, sagittal, axial) from the normalized CT volume using the Beer-Lambert forward model: I(r) = I0 \cdot \exp \left( - \int \mu(x) \, dx \right) where \mu(x) is approximated by summing normalized HU values along the projection direction. Assign camera poses corresponding to the orthogonal directions. 3. AReT Training: Initialize the TensoRF model with \Delta = 0 and s = 1. For each iteration i from 1 to 3000: Sample 2048 rays randomly. Render DRRs from the current TensoRF model. Compute Photometric Loss (L{photo}): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between rendered DRRs and input DRRs. Compute Regularization Losses: Sparsity Loss (L{sparse}): \ell1 norm of the density field. Smoothness Loss (L{TV}): Total Variation of the density field. Compute Total Loss: L = L{photo} + \lambda1 L{sparse} + \lambda2 L{TV} Update TensoRF parameters using Adam optimizer. If i \in \{1500, 2500\}, update the alpha occupancy mask to prune near-empty voxels. 4. Volumetric Reconstruction and Nodule Extraction: Query the converged density field on a 64^3 grid using getDenseAlpha. Perform a percentile threshold sweep on the non-zero density distribution for p \in \{85, 88, 90, 91, \dots, 99\}. For each threshold: Remove connected components with fewer than 10 voxels. Apply binary closing with a radius-2 spherical structuring element to fill boundary gaps. Identify connected components with equivalent sphere diameters in [5, 80] mm. Select the candidate whose equivalent sphere diameter is closest to the LIDC-IDRI annotated diameter for that patient. Compute physical volume: V = N{voxels} \times \prod \Delta xk where \Delta xk are the per-axis voxel spacings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def trainarect(ctvolume, annotations, patientid): # 1. Preprocessing: sort DICOM slices by Z-coordinate, apply HU calibration, normalize ctsorted = sortslicesbyz(ctvolume) cthu = applyhucalibration(ctsorted) ctnormalized = (cthu - (-1000)) / (400 - (-1000)) # 2. DRR Generation: simulate orthogonal projections via Beer-Lambert forward model drrs = simulatedrrs(ctnormalized) cameraposes = getorthogonalposes() # 3. Model Initialization: TensoRF VM-rank-16, density shift Δ=0, scale s=1 model = TensoRF(rank=16, gridsize=64) model.setdensityparams(delta=0, s=1) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.02) # 4. Training Loop: 3000 iterations, batch size 2048 rays for i in range(1, 3001): rays = samplerays(2048, cameraposes) rendereddrrs = model.render(rays) lphoto = torch.mean((rendereddrrs - drrs) 2) densityfield = model.getdensityfield() # Total Variation: sum of absolute finite differences along all axes ltv = torch.sum(torch.abs(torch.diff(densityfield, dim=0))) + \ torch.sum(torch.abs(torch.diff(densityfield, dim=1))) + \ torch.sum(torch.abs(torch.diff(densityfield, dim=2))) lsparse = torch.sum(torch.abs(densityfield)) loss = lphoto + 1e-4 lsparse + 1e-5 ltv loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() if i in [1500, 2500]: model.updatealphamask() return model.getdensityfield() def extractnodule(densityfield, annotateddiameter): candidates = [] nonzeromask = densityfield > 0 nonzerovalues = densityfield[nonzeromask] for p in range(85, 100): threshold = np.percentile(nonzerovalues, p) binarymask = (densityfield >= threshold).astype(np.uint8) # Noise removal: remove components < 10 voxels labeled, num = labelconnectedcomponents(binarymask) validmask = np.zeroslike(binarymask) for k in range(1, num + 1): if np.sum(labeled == k) >= 10: validmask[labeled == k] = 1 # Boundary filling: binary closing with radius-2 spherical structuring element filledmask = binaryclosing(validmask, radius=2) # Size filtering: retain components with diameter in [5, 80] mm labeledfilled, numfilled = labelconnectedcomponents(filledmask) for k in range(1, numfilled + 1): comp = (labeledfilled == k) diameter = computeequivalentspherediameter(comp) if 5 <= diameter <= 80: candidates.append((comp, diameter)) bestcandidate = min(candidates, key=lambda x: abs(x[1] - annotateddiameter)) return computephysicalvolume(bestcandidate[0]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Density Parameterization Dead Zone: Using the default TensoRF density shift of \Delta = -10 (and s=25) suppresses all learned density and prevents sparse-view reconstruction regardless of learning rate or regularization strategy. Setting \Delta = 0 and s=1 restores gradient flow. Resolution Limits: The 64^3 grid yields voxel spacing \approx 3.75 mm, making sub-centimeter nodules (< 10 mm) unsuitable as they span fewer than 2.3 voxels per axis. Domain Gap: The method uses simulated DRRs rather than real radiographs. Real radiographs exhibit scatter, detector noise, beam hardening, motion artifacts, and acquisition inconsistencies not present in simulation, creating a domain gap for clinical translation. Semi-Assisted Selection: Final candidate selection relies on the annotated nodule diameter, which is clinically unavailable in a blind reconstruction scenario, introducing weak supervision during post-processing. A tensor-based radiance field representation that decomposes the 3D scene into low-rank factors, offering memory efficiency compared to dense grids. AReT uses a VM-rank-16 configuration. Choose when memory constraints limit dense grid storage and low-rank factorization is acceptable for the target resolution. TensoRF A generative-prior-guided NeRF approach that uses a population-level latent code from a GAN. AReT outperforms MedNeRF in sparse-view settings because MedNeRF's diffuse density field and scene-agnostic thresholding degrade patient-specific accuracy. Choose when population-level priors are acceptable and dense multi-view data is available. MedNeRF Require 20-50 views and produce streak artifacts with only three views. AReT works with three orthogonal projections. Choose when computational resources are extremely limited and iterative neural optimization is infeasible. FDK Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 8 minutes per patient on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Memory Complexity: A 64^3 VM-rank-16 TensoRF requires ~14 GB VRAM. A 128^3 grid exceeds the 16 GB VRAM limit of the T4. Performance: On LIDC-IDRI (19 patients, 14 nodules \ge 10 mm), AReT achieves a Pearson correlation r = 0.983 (p < 0.0001), median absolute volumetric error 11.4%, and systematic bias -77.3 mm^3. Strengths: Works with only three orthogonal projections. Prior-free patient-specific reconstruction. Robust to sparse-view overfitting via anatomy-aware regularization. Limitations: Requires simulated DRRs (domain gap with real radiographs). Unsuitable for sub-centimeter nodules (< 10 mm) due to resolution limits. Relies on annotated diameter for final candidate selection (semi-assisted). When to use: Sparse-view 3D lung nodule volumetry from orthogonal X-ray projections. When not to use: Dense-view reconstruction. Sub-centimeter nodule analysis. Clinical deployment without addressing the domain gap between simulated and real radiographs. AReT was proposed by Suja Palaniswamy et al. in 2026 (arXiv preprint). It addresses the limitations of existing NeRF adaptations for medical imaging, such as MedNeRF, which require dense views or rely on population priors that degrade patient-specific accuracy. The method identifies a previously unreported failure mode in TensoRF when applied to X-ray attenuation fields: the default density shift of -10 suppresses density gradients. By setting \Delta = 0 and incorporating thorax-specific regularization, AReT enables stable volumetric reconstruction from ultra-sparse views. Sparse-View Lung Nodule Volumetry from Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs via AReT: Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.02639, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: AutoRF
head: AutoDecoder, AutoRF AutoDecoder, Learning 3D Object Radiance Fields from Single View Observations
body: AutoRF is a method for learning 3D object radiance fields from a single view observation without prior geometry knowledge (e.g., CAD models). It disentangles object representation into shape and appearance components using a normalized, object-centric encoding conditioned on 3D bounding boxes and 2D masks. Unlike multi-view methods like PixelNeRF, AutoRF operates on a single image, using an encoder to generate shape and appearance codes and a decoder to render views via volumetric rendering. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single RGB image I of an object instance. Auxiliary Inputs: A 3D bounding box \beta and an instance mask for the object, obtained via pre-processing. Output: A radiance field representation (density \sigma and color \xi) and rendered novel views. Data Structures and Layouts Normalized Object Coordinate Space (NOCS) O: A centered unit cube defined as O:= [-1/2, 1/2]^3. Occupancy Mask Y: A 2D mask where each pixel u has a label Yu \in \{+1, 0, -1\}: +1: Foreground pixels belonging to the object instance mask. -1: Background pixels (semantic categories not supposed to occlude the object, e.g., sky, road). 0: Unknown pixels (cannot determine occlusion). Shape Code \phiS: A vector of dimension 128. Appearance Code \phiA: A vector of dimension 128. Pre-processing 1. Run a pre-trained 3D object detector and panoptic segmentation on image I to extract the 3D bounding box \beta and instance mask. 2. Produce a masked 2D image I fitting a fixed input resolution. Rescale the input image to a maximum of 320px in each dimension while preserving the aspect ratio. 3. Compute the Occupancy Mask Y based on the instance mask and semantic segmentation. 4. Define the Object-Centric Camera \gamma: Map pixels u to unit-speed rays \gammau in NOCS. This is derived by remapping the camera ray \rhou from camera space to NOCS using the bounding box \beta. \gammau is a unit-speed reparametrization of \beta \circ \rhou. Encoding 1. Feed image I into the Shape and Appearance Encoder \PhiE. 2. \PhiE consists of a ResNet34 backbone with InstanceNorm layers (BatchNorm replaced). The first four layers are shared. The following two layers are replicated to form separate heads for shape and appearance encoding. 3. For a 3 \times H \times W input, the feature map shape for each encoding head is 256 \times H/16 \times W/16. 4. Apply adaptive max pooling to obtain shape code \phiS and appearance code \phiA, each of dimension 128. (\phiS, \phiA):= \PhiE(I). Decoding 1. Shape Decoding: Feed \phiS into Shape Decoder \PsiS to produce occupancy network \sigma. \sigma:= \PsiS(\phiS). \sigma: O \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+ outputs density for a 3D point x \in O. Architecture: MLP made of 5 ResNet blocks with hidden dimension 128. At each layer, feed the previous feature map and the positional encoding of the query points. Apply a single linear layer to match the dimensionality of the positional encoding with the hidden dimensions of the MLP. Aggregate the output with the intermediate feature maps by a simple per-channel mean pooling. 2. Appearance Decoding: Feed \phiA and \phiS into Appearance Decoder \PsiA to produce appearance network \xi. \xi:= \PsiA(\phiA, \phiS). \xi: O \times S^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 outputs RGB color for point x \in O and viewing direction d \in S^2. Architecture: MLP of 5 ResNet blocks with hidden dimensionality 128. Aggregate intermediate features with positional encodings by mean pooling. On the third layer, pass the output of the corresponding layer of the shape encoder to incorporate estimated shape information. On the final two layers, pass the view direction (encoded as a 3-dimensional vector) to account for view-dependent effects. Rendering 1. For each pixel u in the target view, compute the object-centric ray \gammau. 2. Determine the time window [au, bu] where \gammau intersects the object space O. 3. Sample 64 uniformly spaced points along the segment of \gammau within [au, bu]. 4. Compute the accumulated transmittance derivative \dot{\alpha}t and color C(\gammau) using the volume rendering formula: C(\gammau) = \int{au}^{bu} \dot{\alpha}t(\gammau, \sigma) \xi(\gammau(t), du) dt where du \in S^2 is the unit velocity of \gammau. 5. The accumulated transmittance \alphat is defined as: \alphat(\gammau, \sigma):= \exp\left(-\int{au}^{t} \sigma(\gammau(s)) ds\right) and \dot{\alpha}t is its time derivative. Loss Functions 1. Photometric Loss L{RGB}: Mean squared error between input image pixel Iu and rendered color V(\gammau|\sigma, \xi) for foreground pixels. L{RGB}(\Theta|\Omega):= \frac{1}{|W{RGB}|} \sum{u \in W{RGB}} \| Iu - V(\gammau|\sigma, \xi) \|^2 where W{RGB} \subset U contains only foreground pixels (Yu = +1) whose rays \gammau intersect O. 2. Occupancy Loss L{OCC}: Supervises the accumulated transmittance \alpha(\gammau, \sigma) using the occupancy mask Y. L{OCC}(\Theta|\Omega):= -\frac{1}{|W{OCC}|} \sum{u \in W{OCC}} \left[ \frac{Yu}{2} \log\left(\frac{1}{2} - \alpha(\gammau, \sigma)\right) + \frac{1}{2} \log\left(\frac{1}{2} + \alpha(\gammau, \sigma)\right) \right] where W{OCC} \subset U contains only foreground or background pixels (Yu \neq 0) with rays intersecting O. Note: The source text contains a typo in the formula representation ('log Yu ( 2 − α...)'), but the context implies a classification loss on \alpha where Yu=+1 encourages \alpha \to 0 (foreground) and Yu=-1 encourages \alpha \to 1 (background). 3. Final Loss: L(\Theta|\Omega) = L{RGB}(\Theta|\Omega) + \lambda L{OCC}(\Theta|\Omega) where \lambda \ge 0 is a hyperparameter. Training Optimization 1. Train at a batch size of 1. 2. Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10^{-5}. 3. Randomly sample 1024 rays per input image during training. 4. Fix the rendering resolution to 80 \times 120 pixels during training. Test-Time Optimization 1. Refine the output by optimizing the loss L with respect to \phiS, \phiA, and the 3D bounding box \beta. 2. Initialize with the encoder output and detector box. 3. Use the Adam optimizer with learning rates 0.05, 0.02, and 0.02 for \phiS, \phiA, and camera position, respectively. 4. Optimize for 32 iterations. 5. Edge Case (Monocular Setting): Keep the size component of the bounding box fixed to the detector's regression and optimize only pose (rotation and translation) to avoid scale-depth ambiguity. Explicit Meshing (Post-processing) 1. Render depth and color from multiple views using AutoRF. Position cameras facing the object center. 2. Apply TSDF-fusion on the resulting pairs of depth and color images to create a 3D mesh. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=6): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numfrequencies)], device=x.device) scaledx = x scales return torch.cat([torch.sin(scaledx), torch.cos(scaledx)], dim=-1) def computeoccupancymask(instancemask, semanticmap, bgclasses): """Compute occupancy mask Y: +1 foreground, -1 background, 0 unknown.""" y = torch.zeroslike(instancemask, dtype=torch.float32) y[instancemask > 0] = 1.0 y[(semanticmap in bgclasses) & (instancemask == 0)] = -1.0 return y def generateobjectcentricrays(h, w, intrinsics, bbox3d): """Generate rays in NOCS from camera rays remapped by bounding box.""" # NOCS is a unit cube [-0.5, 0.5]^3. # Unproject pixel coordinates to the cube boundaries. u = torch.arange(w).float() v = torch.arange(h).float() uv = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid(u, v, indexing='ij'), dim=-1) # Standard pinhole unprojection adapted to NOCS fx, fy = intrinsics[0,0], intrinsics[1,1] cx, cy = intrinsics[0,2], intrinsics[1,2] z = torch.oneslike(uv[..., 0]) x = (uv[..., 0] - cx) / fx y = (uv[..., 1] - cy) / fy origins = torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=-1) directions = F.normalize(origins, dim=-1) return origins, directions class AutoRF: def init(self, lambdaocc=1.0): self.encoder = ShapeAppearanceEncoder() self.shapedecoder = ShapeDecoder() self.colordecoder = ColorDecoder() self.lambdaocc = lambdaocc self.optimizer = None def preprocess(self, image, bbox3d, mask, semanticmap, intrinsics): h, w = image.shape[1], image.shape[2] scale = min(320 / h, 320 / w) newh, neww = int(h scale), int(w scale) maskedimage = F.interpolate(image.unsqueeze(0), size=(newh, neww), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0) occupancymask = computeoccupancymask(mask, semanticmap, bgclasses={0, 1}) rayorigins, raydirections = generateobjectcentricrays(newh, neww, intrinsics, bbox3d) return maskedimage, occupancymask, rayorigins, raydirections def encode(self, image): return self.encoder(image) def decode(self, phiS, phiA, points3d, directions): sigma = self.shapedecoder(phiS, points3d) color = self.colordecoder(phiS, phiA, points3d, directions) return sigma, color def rendervolume(self, sigma, color, rayorigins, raydirections, numsamples=64): """Volume rendering along rays intersecting the unit cube O.""" # Ray-cube intersection for unit cube [-0.5, 0.5]^3 invdir = 1.0 / raydirections tmin = (-0.5 - rayorigins) invdir tmax = (0.5 - rayorigins) invdir tenter = torch.max(torch.min(tmin[:,:, 0], torch.min(tmin[:,:, 1], tmin[:,:, 2])), torch.min(torch.min(tmax[:,:, 0], tmax[:,:, 1]), tmax[:,:, 2])) texit = torch.min(torch.max(tmin[:,:, 0], torch.max(tmin[:,:, 1], tmin[:,:, 2])), torch.max(torch.max(tmax[:,:, 0], tmax[:,:, 1]), tmax[:,:, 2])) tenter = torch.clamp(tenter, min=0.0) texit = torch.clamp(texit, min=0.0) tvals = torch.linspace(tenter, texit, numsamples) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=sigma.device)], dim=-1) expnegsigmadelta = torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(expnegsigmadelta, dim=-2) transmittanceshifted = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:,:1]), transmittance[:,:-1]], dim=-2) weights = transmittanceshifted (1.0 - expnegsigmadelta) colorrendered = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=-2) finalalpha = transmittanceshifted[:, -1] return colorrendered, finalalpha def computeloss(self, renderedcolor, targetimage, occupancymask, finalalpha): foregroundmask = occupancymask == 1.0 lrgb = torch.mean((renderedcolor[foregroundmask] - targetimage[foregroundmask])2) occmask = occupancymask != 0.0 y = occupancymask[occmask] alpha = finalalpha[occmask] alphaclamped = torch.clamp(alpha, min=1e-6, max=1-1e-6) term1 = (y / 2.0) torch.log(torch.clamp(0.5 - alphaclamped, min=1e-6)) term2 = 0.5 torch.log(torch.clamp(0.5 + alphaclamped, min=1e-6)) locc = -torch.mean(term1 + term2) return lrgb + self.lambdaocc locc def trainstep(self, image, bbox3d, mask, semanticmap, intrinsics): maskedimage, occupancymask, rayorigins, raydirections = self.preprocess(image, bbox3d, mask, semanticmap, intrinsics) phiS, phiA = self.encode(maskedimage) numrays = 1024 idx = torch.randperm(rayorigins.shape[0] rayorigins.shape[1])[:numrays] rayorigins = rayorigins.view(-1, 3)[idx] raydirections = raydirections.view(-1, 3)[idx] targetimage = maskedimage.view(-1, 3)[idx] occmasksample = occupancymask.view(-1)[idx] sigma, color = self.decode(phiS, phiA, rayorigins, raydirections) renderedcolor, finalalpha = self.rendervolume(sigma, color, rayorigins, raydirections) loss = self.computeloss(renderedcolor, targetimage, occmasksample, finalalpha) loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.optimizer.zerograd() return loss def testtimeoptimize(self, image, bbox3d, mask, semanticmap, intrinsics, iterations=32): maskedimage, occupancymask, rayorigins, raydirections = self.preprocess(image, bbox3d, mask, semanticmap, intrinsics) phiS, phiA = self.encode(maskedimage) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([ {'params': phiS, 'lr': 0.05}, {'params': phiA, 'lr': 0.02}, {'params': bbox3d.pose, 'lr': 0.02} ]) for in range(iterations): sigma, color = self.decode(phiS, phiA, rayorigins, raydirections) renderedcolor, finalalpha = self.rendervolume(sigma, color, rayorigins, raydirections) loss = self.computeloss(renderedcolor, maskedimage, occupancymask, finalalpha) loss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() return phiS, phiA, bbox3d class ShapeAppearanceEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.backbone = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False), nn.InstanceNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(3, stride=2, padding=1), #... first 4 layers shared...) self.shapehead = nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d(1) self.appearancehead = nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d(1) def forward(self, x): features = self.backbone(x) phiS = self.shapehead(features).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) phiA = self.appearancehead(features).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) return phiS, phiA class ShapeDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([ResNetBlock(128) for in range(5)]) self.linear = nn.Linear(128, 128) def forward(self, phiS, points): posenc = positionalencoding(points) posencproj = self.linear(posenc) h = phiS.unsqueeze(1) + posencproj for block in self.blocks: h = block(h) return h.mean(dim=-2) class ColorDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([ResNetBlock(128) for in range(5)]) def forward(self, phiS, phiA, points, directions): posenc = positionalencoding(points) h = phiA.unsqueeze(1) + posenc for i, block in enumerate(self.blocks): h = block(h) if i == 2: h = h + phiS.unsqueeze(1) if i >= 3: h = h + directions.unsqueeze(1) return h.mean(dim=-2) class ResNetBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, dim): super().init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(dim, dim) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(dim, dim) def forward(self, x): return self.relu(self.fc2(self.relu(self.fc1(x))) + x) Time Complexity: Rendering a 64 \times 64 image takes approximately 0.23 seconds. Test-time optimization (32 steps, rendering 32 \times 32 images) takes approximately 3.3 seconds per object. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is designed for single-view object reconstruction and does not explicitly discuss scaling to large scenes, though it can be applied to multiple objects in a scene if detected. Strengths: Works with a single view observation. No prior geometry knowledge (e.g., CAD models) required. Encoder provides a good initial estimate, leading to faster convergence compared to auto-decoder variants. Produces less fuzzy radiance fields compared to PixelNeRF on SRN-Chairs dataset. Limitations: Scale-depth ambiguity in monocular settings requires fixing the bounding box size. Performance is lower than multi-view methods like PixelNeRF when multiple views are available (e.g., on nuScenes cars, AutoRF AutoDecoder underperforms AutoRF, and AutoRF is compared against PixelNeRF which uses more views). When to use: When only a single view of an object is available and no CAD models are present. When not: When multiple views are available (use PixelNeRF or similar) or when high-fidelity multi-view consistency is critical without test-time optimization. AutoRF was introduced by Norman Müller, Andrea Simonelli, Lorenzo Porzi, Samuel Rota Bulò, Matthias Nießner, and Peter Kontschieder in 2022. It addresses the challenge of learning 3D object radiance fields from single view observations, a more challenging scenario than methods assuming access to at least a second view. It is used on datasets such as nuScenes (cars) and SRN-Chairs.
