name: NARFD with Autoencoder for Appearance Variation
head: NARF-based autoencoder
body: This method extends the Neural Articulated Radiance Field (NARFD) framework by integrating a 2D CNN-based autoencoder to model shape and appearance variations across multiple articulated objects (specifically human bodies). It solves the problem of single-view reconstruction and appearance transfer by learning a disentangled latent representation from a single input RGB image, allowing for the independent control of camera viewpoint, bone parameters, pose, and color appearance. Unlike standard NeRF variants that optimize per-scene, this approach learns a global generative model capable of reconstructing novel instances and poses from limited input. Inputs and Outputs Input: A single RGB image I of an articulated object (human body). Outputs: Reconstructed RGB image, depth map, and segmentation map. Latent Codes: The method produces a shape latent vector \mathbf{z}s and an appearance latent vector \mathbf{z}a. Data Structures Latent Vector \mathbf{z}: A vector generated by the encoder, decomposed into \mathbf{z}s and \mathbf{z}a. Bone Parameters \zeta: Parameters defining the skeletal configuration. Local Transformation \xi: Local transformation parameters for parts. Part Mask/Weight p^i: Weight associated with part i. Number of Parts P: Total number of articulated parts. Network Architecture The system consists of two main components: 1. Encoder: A 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that maps the input image to a latent vector \mathbf{z}. 2. Decoder: An NARF-based decoder comprising two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): Density Network (F{\Theta,\sigma}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}): Predicts volume density \sigma and an intermediate feature vector \mathbf{h}. Color Network (F{\Theta,c}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}): Predicts RGB color c using \mathbf{h}. Step-by-Step Method 1. Encoding: The 2D CNN encoder processes the input image to generate the latent vector \mathbf{z}. 2. Latent Decomposition: The latent vector \mathbf{z} is split into the shape latent \mathbf{z}s and the appearance latent \mathbf{z}a. 3. Density Network Input Preparation: Compute positionally encoded locations \gamma(\mathbf{x}^{t^i}) for each part i \in [1, P], weighted by part mask p^i. Compute positionally encoded bone parameters \gamma(\zeta). Concatenate these with \mathbf{z}s: \text{Cat}(\{\gamma(\mathbf{x}^{t^i}) p^i | i \in [1, P]\}, \gamma(\zeta), \mathbf{z}s). 4. Density Prediction: The density network F{\Theta,\sigma}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}} takes the concatenated input from Step 3 and outputs density \sigma and feature vector \mathbf{h}. 5. Color Network Input Preparation: Compute positionally encoded view directions \gamma(\mathbf{d}^{t^i}) for each part i \in [1, P], weighted by p^i. Compute positionally encoded local transformations \gamma(\xi^i) for each part i \in [1, P], weighted by p^i. Concatenate \mathbf{h}, the encoded direction/transformation pairs, and \mathbf{z}a: \text{Cat}(\mathbf{h}, \{(\gamma(\mathbf{d}^{t^i}) p^i, \gamma(\xi^i) p^i) | i \in [1, P]\}, \mathbf{z}a). 6. Color Prediction: The color network F{\Theta,c}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}} takes the concatenated input from Step 5 and outputs the color c. 7. Rendering: Standard volume rendering is performed using \sigma and c to generate the output image. 8. Training: The encoder and decoder are trained jointly using the loss function defined in the base NARFD paper (Eq. 25 in). Formulas The core mapping functions are defined as: F{\Theta,\sigma}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}: \text{Cat}(\{\gamma(\mathbf{x}^{t^i}) p^i | i \in [1, P]\}, \gamma(\zeta), \mathbf{z}s) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{h}) F{\Theta,c}^{t,\zeta,\mathbf{z}}: \text{Cat}(\mathbf{h}, \{(\gamma(\mathbf{d}^{t^i}) p^i, \gamma(\xi^i) p^i) | i \in [1, P]\}, \mathbf{z}a) \rightarrow (c) Where: \text{Cat}(\cdot) denotes concatenation. \gamma(\cdot) is the positional encoding function (see Model Architecture and Encoding). \mathbf{x}^{t^i} is the position for part i at time/pose t. \mathbf{d}^{t^i} is the view direction for part i at time/pose t. \xi^i is the local transformation for part i. p^i is the part mask or weight for part i. \zeta represents bone parameters. \mathbf{z}s is the shape latent vector. \mathbf{z}a is the appearance latent vector. \sigma is volume density. \mathbf{h} is the intermediate feature vector. c is the predicted color. Parameters Image Resolution: 128 × 128 pixels. Dataset: Synthetic human body dataset derived from THUman. Subjects: 112 male subjects. Poses: 35 poses on average per person. Training Images: 35,450 images (10 images per pose with randomly sampled viewpoints). Evaluation Images: 3,940 images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Disentanglement: The method relies on the successful decomposition of \mathbf{z} into \mathbf{z}s and \mathbf{z}a. Failure to disentangle may lead to coupled control of shape and appearance. Single-View Ambiguity: Reconstructing 3D structure from a single 2D image is ill-posed; the model relies on learned priors from the training dataset. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method successfully reconstructs RGB, depth, and segmentation maps from a single input RGB image. It effectively models appearance variation across multiple objects using a single autoencoder. Strengths: Allows individual control of camera viewpoint, bone parameters, human pose, and color appearance via the disentangled representation. Enables appearance transfer by replacing \mathbf{z}a with that of another person. Limitations: Limited to articulated objects (humans) and requires a dataset of articulated objects for training. When to use: Single-view reconstruction of articulated objects where appearance variation across instances is significant. When not to use: Static scenes or non-articulated objects where a single instance NeRF is sufficient. This method was introduced in the paper "Neural Articulated Radiance Field". It builds upon the NARFD framework, which learns disentangled representations of camera viewpoint, bone parameters, and pose. The autoencoder extension was developed to handle shape and appearance variations among multiple articulated objects, specifically humans, using a synthetic dataset derived from THUman. Neural Articulated Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00571, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MTL-FeatureNet
head: Multi-Task Learning Feature Network
body: MTL-FeatureNet is a feature extraction network for multi-task learning that handles demands of multiple tasks by improving the accuracy and relevance of features extracted from a single 2D toy view. It addresses the challenge of adapting a unified feature representation to diverse task requirements by integrating task dynamic attention modulation and a dynamic adapter layer. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 2D image I and a set of tasks \{T1, T2, \ldots, Tn\}. Output: A set of task-specific features \{F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots, F{taskn}\}. Data Structures Initial Features (Ci): Extracted from image I for each task Ti. Task Relevance (TRi): A scalar score computed for each task. Global Features (F{global}): The aggregated feature representation after attention modulation. Task-Specific Features (F{taski}): The final output features for task i. Parameters \gamma{task}: A learnable scaling factor customized for each task, adjusted during learning to optimize transformation efficiency. W{task}: A task-specific weight matrix. b{task}: A task-specific bias term. \sigma: An activation function. \lambdak: Weight for the loss of task k. \mu: Weight for the cross-task consistency loss. v{ij}: A dynamically adjusted weight based on the correlation between tasks i and j. dk: The dimension of the key vectors in the attention mechanism. Formulas 1. Position Encoding with Task Relevance: The conventional position encoding is modulated by the task relevance score TR: PE(pos, 2i) = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d{model}}}\right) \cdot TR PE(pos, 2i + 1) = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d{model}}}\right) \cdot TR where pos is position, i is index, d{model} is model dimension, and TR is the task relevance score. 2. Task Dynamic Attention Modulation: The attention mechanism is modulated by the task relevance score TRi: A{ti}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{dk}} \cdot \exp(TRi)\right) \cdot V where Q, K, V are the query, key, and value matrices. 3. Task-Specific Feature Transformation: Task-specific features are derived from global features using a dynamic adapter layer: F{task} = \sigma(\gamma{task} \cdot W{task} \cdot F{global} + b{task}) where \gamma{task} scales the transformation. 4. Composite Loss Function: The total loss combines individual task losses and a cross-task consistency term: L = \sumk \lambdak \cdot Lk + \mu \cdot L{cross}(F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots) where Lk is the loss for task k. 5. Cross-Task Consistency Loss: This loss facilitates knowledge sharing by comparing feature representations: L{cross}(F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots) = \sum{i \ne j} v{ij} \cdot \|F{taski} - F{taskj}\|^2 where v{ij} is the dynamically adjusted weight. Numbered Steps 1. Feature Extraction and Task Relevance: For each task Ti, extract initial features Ci from the input image I. Compute the task relevance score TRi using a task-specific MLP: TRi = \text{MLP}{task}(Ci). 2. Task Dynamic Attention Modulation: For each task Ti, adjust the attention weights using the computed relevance score TRi via the formula A{ti}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}((QK^T/\sqrt{dk}) \cdot \exp(TRi)) \cdot V. 3. Dynamic Adapter Layer (DAL): Process the modulated features through the DAL to compute task-specific features F{taski} using the transformation F{task} = \sigma(\gamma{task} \cdot W{task} \cdot F{global} + b{task}). 4. Loss Computation: Compute the composite loss L using the individual task losses Lk and the cross-task consistency loss L{cross}. 5. Output Features: Return the set of task-specific features \{F{task1}, F{task2}, \ldots, F{taskn}\}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mtlfeaturenet(imageI, tasks): """ MTL-FeatureNet for multi-task feature extraction. Args: imageI: Input 2D image. tasks: List of task identifiers {T1, T2,..., Tn}. Returns: List of task-specific features {Ftask1, Ftask2,..., Ftaskn}. """ n = len(tasks) initialfeatures = [] taskrelevancescores = [] # Step 1: Feature Extraction and Task Relevance for i, task in enumerate(tasks): # Extract initial features Ci from image I Ci = extractfeatures(imageI, task) initialfeatures.append(Ci) # Compute task relevance TRi using a task-specific MLP TRi = mlptask(Ci) taskrelevancescores.append(TRi) # Step 2: Task Dynamic Attention Modulation modulatedfeatures = [] for i, task in enumerate(tasks): Ci = initialfeatures[i] TRi = taskrelevancescores[i] # Project to Q, K, V Q = projectquery(Ci) K = projectkey(Ci) V = projectvalue(Ci) # Adjust attention using TRi dk = Q.shape[-1] attentionweights = softmax((Q @ K.T) / sqrt(dk) exp(TRi)) Ati = attentionweights @ V modulatedfeatures.append(Ati) # Step 3: Dynamic Adapter Layer (DAL) # Aggregate modulated features into Fglobal Fglobal = aggregatefeatures(modulatedfeatures) taskspecificfeatures = [] for i, task in enumerate(tasks): # Retrieve learnable parameters for the task gammatask = getscalingfactor(task) Wtask = getweightmatrix(task) btask = getbias(task) # Linear transformation with scaling transformed = gammatask (Wtask @ Fglobal) + btask # Apply activation function Ftaski = activation(transformed) taskspecificfeatures.append(Ftaski) # Step 4: Loss Computation (training loop only) # L = sum(lambdak Lk) + mu Lcross # Lcross = sum(vij ||Ftaski - Ftaskj||^2) # Step 5: Output Features return taskspecificfeatures Edge Cases and Pitfalls Task Correlation: The weight v{ij} in the cross-task loss depends on the correlation between tasks. The method for dynamically adjusting v{ij} is not specified in the sources. Attention Modulation: The term \exp(TRi) scales the attention logits. If TRi is large, this can lead to numerical instability or overly sharp attention distributions. Global Feature Aggregation: The source mentions F{global} but does not specify how it is constructed from the modulated features A{ti} (e.g., concatenation, averaging, or attention pooling). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is reported to improve rendering accuracy and color reproduction fidelity for toy 3D models compared to standard NeRF approaches. Strengths: Handles multiple tasks efficiently by dynamically modulating attention and adapting features via the DAL. Limitations: Designed for 2D toy views, which may limit its applicability to complex 3D scenes without modification. When to use: When a single 2D view needs to support multiple downstream tasks with shared but distinct feature requirements. When not to use: For standard single-task volume rendering where direct coordinate-to-radiance mapping is sufficient. MTL-FeatureNet was introduced for multi-task learning in 3D toy reconstruction using adaptive scaled neural radiation fields. It was proposed to address the challenges of high complexity scenes and complex lighting conditions by combining adaptive scale adjustment with spectral perception. The method is part of an improved NeRF model that enhances detail-rich 3D visual content generation. 3D reconstruction of toys based on adaptive scaled neural radiation field., https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.3053, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive-Scale and Spectral-Aware NeRF
head: NeRF combining adaptive scaling with spectral perception
body: Adaptive-Scale and Spectral-Aware NeRF is a neural radiance field variant that integrates an adaptive scale function to modulate sample point contributions and a spectral decoder to handle multispectral information, including infrared and ultraviolet wavelengths, for improved color fidelity. It builds on Model Architecture and Encoding by replacing the standard color prediction with a wavelength-aware mechanism and adjusting density integration weights via local feature analysis. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: 2D toy image I, camera parameters P, global features G extracted from I using MTL-FeatureNet, and spectral components \varepsilon. Outputs: Rendered 3D image C(r). Data Structures Global Features (G): Extracted from input image I using MTL-FeatureNet. Local Features (Q): Derived from 3D position x(t) and global features G via function FA. Adaptive Scale (S): A scalar value computed from local features and global features. Spectral Components (\varepsilon): Wavelength values for which color is estimated. Method Steps 1. Initialize Model: Load MTL-FeatureNet to extract global features G from input image I. Define the volume density network \sigma(x) and the color network c(x, \varepsilon, S). 2. Compute Adaptive Scale: Extract local features Q from 3D position x(t) using FA(G, x(t)). Compute the adaptive scale S using the formula: S(FA(G, x(t)), G) = \sigma(\beta \cdot D{complex}(CT(FA(G, x(t)), G))) Where D{complex} is a depth network, CT is a feature combination function, and \beta is a parameter. 3. Spectral-Aware Color Estimation: Estimate color c(x, \varepsilon) at position x and wavelength \varepsilon using the spectral decoder: c(x, \varepsilon) = \text{softmax}\left(\sum{n=1}^N Gn \cdot e^{-\frac{(\varepsilon - \mun)^2}{2\deltan^2}}\right) \cdot MLP{color}(F(x, \varepsilon)) Where N is the number of spectral components, Gn is the weight of the n-th component, \mun is the center wavelength, \deltan^2 is the variance, MLP{color} is a multilayer perceptron, and F(x, \varepsilon) are spectral features. 4. Rendering Integration: Render the image C(r) by integrating along the ray r: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \cdot \sigma(p(x(t))) \cdot c(x(t), S(FA(G, x(t)), G)) \, dt Where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance, \sigma(p(x(t))) is the spectral-aware volume density, and c is the color modulated by the adaptive scale S. 5. Output: Return the final rendered image C(r). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def adaptivescalespectralnerf(I, P, G, epsilon): """ Render an image using Adaptive-Scale and Spectral-Aware NeRF. Args: I: Input 2D toy image. P: Camera parameters containing rays. Each ray has origin, direction, near, far, numsamples. G: Global features from MTL-FeatureNet. epsilon: Spectral components (wavelengths). Returns: C: Rendered 3D image. """ # Precompute spectral weights for all rays spectralsum = 0.0 for n in range(N): spectralsum += Gn[n] math.exp(-((epsilon - mun[n])2) / (2 deltan[n]2)) softmaxweight = 1.0 # softmax of a scalar sum evaluates to 1.0 per source formula renderedimage = [] for ray in P.rays: accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 raycolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] prevt = ray.near for t in [ray.near + (ray.far - ray.near) (k + 0.5) / ray.numsamples for k in range(ray.numsamples)]: # 3D position x(t) xt = [ray.origin[i] + t ray.direction[i] for i in range(3)] # Step 2: Adaptive-Scale Function # Extract local features Q from 3D position x(t) using FA(G, x(t)) Q = fafunc(G, xt) # Compute adaptive scale S combinedfeatures = ctfunc(Q, G) depthoutput = depthnet(combinedfeatures) S = activationfn(beta depthoutput) # Step 3: Spectral-Aware Color Estimation # Get spectral features F(x, epsilon) F = spectralfeaturesnet(xt, epsilon) # Apply MLP for color (S is passed as per step 1 definition c(x, epsilon, S)) color = softmaxweight mlpcolor(F, S) # Step 4: Rendering Integration # sigma(p(x(t))) is the spectral-aware volume density density = densitynet(xt) # Distance between samples delta = t - prevt # Opacity and transmittance update alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density delta) accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Accumulate color for c in range(3): raycolor[c] += accumulatedtransmittance alpha color[c] prevt = t renderedimage.append(raycolor) return renderedimage def densitynet(x): """Volume density network sigma(x).""" return 0.0 # Placeholder for trained network forward pass def fafunc(G, x): """Local feature estimation based on global features and position.""" return [] # Placeholder for trained network forward pass def ctfunc(Q, G): """Feature combination function.""" return [] # Placeholder for trained network forward pass def depthnet(features): """Depth network Dcomplex.""" return 0.0 # Placeholder for trained network forward pass def activationfn(x): """Activation function sigma used in adaptive scale computation.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) # Standard sigmoid activation def spectralfeaturesnet(x, epsilon): """Feature extraction F(x, epsilon).""" return [] # Placeholder for trained network forward pass def mlpcolor(F, S): """Multilayer perceptron MLPcolor applied to spectral features and adaptive scale.""" return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for trained network forward pass Parameters \beta: Parameter in the adaptive scale computation. N: Number of spectral components. Gn: Weight of the n-th spectral component. \mun: Center wavelength of the n-th component. \deltan^2: Variance of the n-th component. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Spectral Range: The method supports infrared and ultraviolet information, requiring appropriate handling of \varepsilon outside the visible spectrum. Feature Extraction: The quality of G depends on MTL-FeatureNet; poor extraction may degrade adaptive scaling. Depth Network: D{complex} requires accurate depth estimation; errors here affect the adaptive scale S. Variable Naming: The source uses \sigma for both the volume density network and the activation function in the adaptive scale computation; implementations must distinguish them to avoid mathematical conflicts. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves color fidelity and visual effects by handling multispectral data and adapting sample contributions. Limitations: Increased complexity due to additional networks (MTL-FeatureNet, D{complex}) and spectral decoding. The method was proposed to improve 3D toy reconstruction by integrating adaptive scaling and spectral perception into NeRF models. It utilizes MTL-FeatureNet for global feature extraction and combines this with a conditional diffusion model for generating high-quality viewpoint images. 3D reconstruction of toys based on adaptive scaled neural radiation field., https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.3053, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Panoptic and Semantic Scene Representations
head: Semantic NeRFs, Panoptic Neural Fields, Category-Level Semantic NeRF
body: Panoptic and Semantic Scene Representations extend standard radiance fields by predicting semantic class distributions and instance identifiers alongside density and color, enabling high-level scene understanding and object-centric manipulation. Unlike standard NeRFs that only model geometry and appearance, these methods decompose the scene into "things" (discrete objects) and "stuff" (amorphous background) or predict part-level semantics, allowing for tasks such as object deletion, duplication, and category-level generalization. The core mechanism involves transforming low-dimensional input coordinates into a high-dimensional feature space using sinusoidal positional encoding, which is then processed by a fully-connected MLP to predict radiance field properties. Positional Encoding The input coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (position) and \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (view direction) are mapped to higher dimensions using a hierarchical positional encoding function \gamma(\cdot). For a scalar input p, the encoding is defined as: \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)) where L is the number of frequency bands. This function is applied independently to each of the three components of the position vector and the direction vector. Network Architecture The radiance field is represented by an MLP that takes the encoded position and direction as input. The architecture typically consists of two branches: 1. Density Branch: Processes the encoded position features to predict volume density \sigma. 2. Color Branch: Processes the encoded direction features concatenated with intermediate features from the density branch to predict RGB color \mathbf{c}. Ray Sampling Rendering requires sampling points along camera rays. A ray is parameterized as r(\lambda) = o{world} + \lambda d{world}, where o{world} is the world-space origin and d{world} is the world-space direction. The direction is computed from camera intrinsics and extrinsics: d{cam} = (\frac{i - cx}{fx}, \frac{j - cy}{fy}, 1), d{world} = R d{cam}, and o{world} = t. Position samples x are generated along the ray within a defined near/far range. Panoptic Radiance Field learns a 3D panoptic radiance field from posed RGB images and machine-generated 2D panoptic segmentation masks, lifting noisy 2D labels into a consistent 3D representation of color, density, semantics, and instance identifiers [15849-panoptic-radiance-field.md]. Unlike Panoptic NeRF or DM-NeRF which require manual ground truth or coarse meshes, this method requires only pre-trained 2D segmentation outputs, making it robust to in-the-wild scenes [15849-panoptic-radiance-field.md]. It sets itself apart by using a linear assignment to resolve 2D instance inconsistencies and specific gradient-stopping techniques to prevent noisy labels from corrupting geometry [15849-panoptic-radiance-field.md]. Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF) is an object-aware neural scene representation that decomposes a dynamic 3D scene into a set of discrete objects ("things") and an amorphous background ("stuff"), predicting a panoptic-radiance field for color, density, instance, and category labels at any point in time [20291-panoptic-neural-fields.md]. Unlike Panoptic Radiance Field and Category-Level Semantic NeRF, which are not object-aware and cannot handle dynamic scenes, PNF explicitly models moving objects using separate MLPs per instance within dynamic bounding boxes, enabling joint optimization of 3D shape, appearance, semantics, and object poses from RGB images alone [20291-panoptic-neural-fields.md]. Category-Level Semantic NeRF extends the standard NeRF framework to predict part segmentation logits in addition to density and color, enabling category-level generalization for articulated objects [20302-category-level-semantic-nerf.md]. It differs from sibling methods like Panoptic Radiance Field by conditioning the neural field on image features extracted from input views, allowing the model to generalize across instances of the same category rather than optimizing for a single specific object [20302-category-level-semantic-nerf.md]. A method where semantic labels are formalized as a view-invariant function mapping world coordinate x to a distribution over semantic labels via pre-softmax semantic logits s(x), while color c additionally depends on viewing direction d. Inference: Semantic logits are transformed into multi-class probabilities through a softmax normalization layer. The semantic label is determined as the class of the maximum probability in \hat{S}(r). \hat{S}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) si where si are the semantic logits for sample i. L{2D}^{sem} = -\frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} \sum{l=1}^L pl(r) \log \hat{p}l(r) where pl(r) and \hat{p}l(r) are the multi-class semantic probabilities of the ground truth and predicted map for class l of ray r. Network structure: Volume densities \sigma and semantic logits s are functions of (x, y, z) only. Color c is a function of (x, y, z) and (\theta, \phi). Semantic and panoptic radiance fields emerged to address the limitation of standard NeRFs in providing only low-level geometry and radiance without higher-level scene understanding. Early work formalized semantic labels as view-invariant functions mapping world coordinates to semantic distributions, allowing for the integration of 2D semantic supervision into 3D rendering. Subsequent developments introduced panoptic representations to handle both "things" and "stuff," and dynamic models to track object motion, expanding the utility of neural radiance fields for tasks like scene editing and object manipulation. Semantically-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Visual Scene Understanding: A Comprehensive Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-025-02663-5, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Panoptic Radiance Field
head: Panoptic Lifting
body: Panoptic Lifting learns a 3D panoptic radiance field from posed RGB images and machine-generated 2D panoptic segmentation masks, lifting noisy 2D labels into a consistent 3D representation of color, density, semantics, and instance identifiers. Unlike Panoptic Neural Fields and related methods which require manual ground truth or coarse meshes, this method requires only pre-trained 2D segmentation outputs, making it robust to in-the-wild scenes. It sets itself apart by using a linear assignment to resolve 2D instance inconsistencies and specific gradient-stopping techniques to prevent noisy labels from corrupting geometry. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Posed RGB images \{I\} and corresponding machine-generated 2D panoptic segmentation masks. Each training ray r has an associated RGB color \hat{c}r \in \mathbb{R}^3, semantic class \hat{k}r \in K, and 2D instance ID \hat{h}r \in HI (defined only for thing classes \hat{k}r \in KT). Outputs: A panoptic radiance field \Phi(x, d) that, for a 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction d \in S^2, predicts density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}, semantic class distribution \kappa over K, distribution \pi over surrogate identifiers J, and RGB color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. From novel views, it renders color images and 3D-consistent panoptic masks. Data Structures The representation \Phi comprises four components: 1. Color and Density: Leverages a TensoRF representation (lines and planes). 2. Semantic Field: A small MLP predicting \kappa. 3. Instance Field: A small MLP predicting \pi. 4. Surrogate Identifiers: A fixed set J of class-agnostic, 3D-consistent identifiers. Parameters K: Set of semantic classes, partitioned into thing classes KT and stuff classes KS. J: Fixed number of surrogate identifiers held by the instance MLP. H{3D}: Set of all possible 3D instances, H{3D}:= KT \times J. Loss weights: \lambda{con} = 1.35, \lambda{ins} = 1, \lambda{sem} = 1, \lambda{RGB} = 1. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rates: 5 \times 10^{-4} for MLPs, 1 \times 10^{-2} for TensoRF lines and planes. Hardware: 1 NVIDIA A6000, 450k iterations (~10 hours). Preprocessing: Confidence Estimation To handle noisy 2D labels, test-time augmentations (horizontal flip, scale, brightness, contrast) are applied to input images. The resulting segmentations are fused by segment clustering to obtain a semantic class distribution \hat{\kappa}r and a confidence estimate wr for each pixel (ray r). Training Steps 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays r from training images. Let RS be rays randomly sampled across the scene and RI be rays sampled from a single image. 2. Forward Pass: For each ray, query \Phi(x, d) to get \sigma, \kappa, \pi, c. 3. Rendering: Compute rendered fields using the volumetric rendering equation: R[f |r, \sigma]:= \int0^\infty \alphat (r)\sigma(rt)f (rt, d{rt})dt where \alphat (r):= \exp \left(-\int0^t \sigma(rs)ds\right) is the transmittance. Rendered color: cr = R[c|r, \sigma]. Rendered semantic distribution: \kappar = R[\kappa|r, \sigma]. Rendered instance distribution: \pir = R[\pi|r, \sigma]. Constraint: The semantic and instance fields must output bounded probability distributions, not logits, to prevent unbounded signals in low-density areas. 4. Instance Assignment: For rays in RI, map the 2D instance ID \hat{h}r to a 3D surrogate identifier j \in J by solving a linear assignment problem. The cost is based on the model's current predictions and the 2D masks, ensuring consistent lifting of 2D instances to 3D. 5. Loss Computation: Semantic Loss (L{sem}): Cross-entropy between rendered \kappar and 2D label \hat{\kappa}r, weighted by confidence wr: L{sem}(R):= -\frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} wr \sum{k \in K} \hat{\kappa}r(k) \log \kappar(k) Instance Loss (L{ins}): Log-loss of the rendered instance distribution \pir against the mapped surrogate identifiers from the 2D instances. Segment Consistency Loss (L{con}): Guides semantic supervision to avoid fragmenting objects due to label inconsistencies. Photometric Loss (L{RGB}): L2 loss between rendered color cr and ground truth \hat{c}r. 6. Total Loss: L{tot}(R):= \lambda{ins} L{ins}(RI) + \lambda{con} L{con}(RI) + \lambda{RGB} L{RGB}(RS) + \lambda{sem} L{sem}(RS) 7. Gradient Blocking: Stop gradients from the semantic and instance branches back to the density field \sigma to prevent noisy labels from corrupting geometry. 8. Update: Update parameters using Adam. Inference For a novel view ray r: 1. Render \kappar and \pir. 2. Determine semantic class k^r:= \arg \max{k \in K} \kappar(k). 3. If k^r \in KT, determine surrogate ID j^r:= \arg \max{j \in J} \pir(j). 4. Form 3D instance ID (k^r, j^r) \in H{3D}. Scene Editing Deletion: Set density \sigma to zero for points where the predicted instance matches the target instance. Duplication: Manipulate rays passing through a new region to query the original instance region. Manipulation: Combine deletion and duplication. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstep(rays, gtcolors, gtsemantics, gtinstances, semanticmlp, instancemlp, tenorfrmodel, optimizer, lambdacon=1.35, lambdains=1.0, lambdasem=1.0, lambdargb=1.0): optimizer.zerograd() # Forward pass sigma, cpred = tenorfrmodel(rays.positions, rays.directions) kappapred = semanticmlp(rays.positions) pipred = instancemlp(rays.positions) # Volumetric rendering (discrete approximation of the integral equation) transmittance = 1.0 crendered = 0.0 kapparendered = 0.0 pirendered = 0.0 for i in range(len(rays.positions)): alpha = 1.0 - exp(-max(sigma[i], 1e-4) rays.stepsize) crendered += transmittance alpha cpred[i] rays.stepsize kapparendered += transmittance alpha kappapred[i] rays.stepsize pirendered += transmittance alpha pipred[i] rays.stepsize transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Loss computation lossrgb = mean((crendered - gtcolors) 2) losssem = -mean(rays.confidence (gtsemantics log(kapparendered + 1e-8))) # Map 2D instance IDs to 3D surrogate IDs via linear assignment (solver not specified in sources) mappedsurrogates = solvelinearassignment(rays.instances, pipred) lossins = -mean(mappedsurrogates log(pirendered + 1e-8)) # Segment consistency loss to avoid fragmenting objects (formulation not specified in sources) losscon = 0.0 # Gradient blocking: stop gradients from semantic/instance branches to density sigmadetached = sigma.detach() totalloss = (lambdains lossins + lambdacon losscon + lambdargb lossrgb + lambdasem losssem) totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() Time Complexity: Training is lengthy, requiring ~10 hours on a single NVIDIA A6000 for 450k iterations. It runs offline due to pre-processing (pose estimation, 2D segmentation) and optimization. Memory Complexity: Uses TensoRF for density/color (compact) plus two small MLPs for semantics and instances. Performance: Improves scene-level Panoptic Quality (PQ) by 8.4% on Hypersim, 13.8% on Replica, and 10.6% on ScanNet over state-of-the-art methods. Maintains comparable PSNR for novel view synthesis. Strengths: Robust to noisy, machine-generated 2D labels; requires no manual 3D ground truth; enables scene editing. Limitations: Limited to classes supported by the pre-trained 2D segmenter (e.g., Mask2Former); offline processing; performance depends on the quality of the 2D segmentation model. Panoptic Lifting was introduced in "Panoptic Lifting for 3D Scene Understanding with Neural Fields" (CVPR 2023). It addresses the limitation of previous panoptic NeRF methods (like Panoptic NeRF and DM-NeRF) which required manual ground truth or coarse meshes. It builds on TensoRF for efficient density/color representation and uses Mask2Former as the pre-trained 2D segmenter. name: Panoptic Neural Fields
head: MARS, PNF / LANe / MARS, Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF) Model Architecture, Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF) Rendering & Compositing
body: Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF) is a semantic object-aware neural scene representation that decomposes a dynamic 3D scene into distinct "things" (moving objects) and "stuff" (static background), representing each with separate MLP-based neural functions. Unlike sibling methods like Panoptic Radiance Field or Category-Level Semantic NeRF which may share MLPs or lack dynamic object handling, PNF uses instance-specific fully weight-encoded MLPs for each object, allowing it to model dynamic scenes and specific instance details without latent code bottlenecks. It learns a 4D panoptic radiance field from RGB images alone, querying color, density, instance, and category labels for any 3D point over time. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of RGB images, predicted camera parameters, 2D semantic segmentations (pseudo-supervision), and 3D object detections with oriented bounding boxes and category labels. No 3D ground-truth or semantic labels are required during training. Outputs: For a query (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, t), the model outputs color \mathbf{c}, volume density \sigma, semantic label (category), and instance label. Data Structures 1. Stuff Field: A single MLP (or two for large scenes: foreground/background) representing the static background. Architecture: 8 hidden layers, width 256. Input: Encoded position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Density \sigmas, color \mathbf{c}s, semantic logits \mathbf{l}s. 2. Thing Fields: A set of separate MLPs, one per object instance k. Architecture: 4 hidden layers, width 128. Input: Encoded object coordinates \mathbf{x}' and view direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Density \sigmak, color \mathbf{c}k, semantic logits \mathbf{l}k. 3. Object Track Tk: Parameterizes the pose of object k over time. Parameters: For each discrete timestamp, a rotation matrix \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}, translation vector \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and time-invariant box extent \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Interpolation: For arbitrary real-valued timestamps, track steps are interpolated to determine the coordinate frame. Positional Encoding The input coordinates are mapped using hierarchical positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). Stuff Position: L=10 frequencies. Thing Position: L=6 frequencies in object coordinate space. View Direction: L=2 frequencies, gradually activated over optimization. Formula: For scalar p, \gamma(p) = (\sin(2^0 \pi p), \cos(2^0 \pi p), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi p), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi p)). Applied independently to each component of \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}. Panoptic-Radiance Field Composition The final field aggregates contributions from bounding box hits, defaulting to stuff if no intersection occurs. For any output channel f (color, density, semantic, instance): f(\mathbf{x} | \theta) = \mathbb{1}S(\mathbf{x}) fs(\mathbf{x} | \theta) + \sumk fk(Tk^{-1} \mathbf{x} | \theta) where \mathbb{1}S(\mathbf{x}) = 1 if \mathbf{x} intersects no bounding boxes, fs is the stuff field, and fk is the thing field for instance k. Tk^{-1} transforms world coordinates to the object's local bounding box frame at time t. Training Steps 1. Initialization: Run off-the-shelf algorithms to predict camera poses, 2D semantic segmentations, and 3D object detections with bounding boxes. Initialize Thing MLP weights using category-specific meta-learned initialization (via FedAvg on ShapeNet data) or biased density activation initialization. Initialize Stuff MLP weights. 2. Ray Sampling: Generate rays from camera intrinsics/extrinsics. Sample 1024 points per ray using stratified sampling (no hierarchical sampling). Transform sampled world positions \mathbf{x} to object local coordinates \mathbf{x}' = Tk^{-1} \mathbf{x} for each intersecting bounding box. 3. Forward Pass: Query Stuff MLP with (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to get \sigmas, \mathbf{c}s, \mathbf{l}s. For each intersecting Thing k, query MLP with (\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{d}) to get \sigmak, \mathbf{c}k, \mathbf{l}k. Compose fields using the aggregation formula. Perform volumetric rendering to synthesize color, semantic, and depth images. 4. Loss Calculation: Color Loss: Mean Squared Error (MSE) between rendered and input RGB images. Semantic Loss: Softmax cross-entropy between rendered semantic logits and predicted 2D semantic labels. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{semantic}, where \lambda < 1 scales semantic loss to prevent dominance. 5. Optimization: Use Adam optimizer. Update MLP weights and bounding box parameters (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{s}). Rotation Orthogonalization: After each gradient step, orthogonalize \mathbf{R} using SVD to project back onto SO(3). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(p, L): """ Hierarchical positional encoding for scalar p. p: scalar or array of scalars L: number of frequency bands Returns: encoded vector """ # p is expected to be in range [0, 1] or similar, scaled appropriately # Formula: (sin(2^0 pi p), cos(2^0 pi p),..., sin(2^{L-1} pi p), cos(2^{L-1} pi p)) scales = np.array([2i for i in range(L)]) encoded = [] for scale in scales: encoded.append(np.sin(np.pi scale p)) encoded.append(np.cos(np.pi scale p)) return np.concatenate(encoded) def encodevector(v, L): """ Encode each component of vector v independently. v: array of shape (3,) L: number of frequencies Returns: encoded array """ encx = positionalencoding(v[0], L) ency = positionalencoding(v[1], L) encz = positionalencoding(v[2], L) return np.concatenate([encx, ency, encz]) def orthogonalizeR(R): """ Orthogonalize rotation matrix R using SVD. R: 3x3 matrix Returns: orthogonalized 3x3 matrix """ U,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(R) return U @ Vt def querystuffmlp(xworld, d, stuffparams): """ Query the stuff MLP. xworld: 3D position d: view direction stuffparams: MLP weights Returns: sigmas, cs, ls """ # Encode position and direction # Stuff uses L=10 for position, L=2 for direction encpos = encodevector(xworld, L=10) encdir = encodevector(d, L=2) # Concatenate and pass through MLP (8 layers, width 256) # Note: Density and semantic do not depend on direction, color does. # Simplified MLP forward pass x = np.concatenate([encpos, encdir]) for layer in stuffparams['layers']: x = np.maximum(0, x @ layer['W'] + layer['b']) # ReLU # Split outputs based on architecture # Assuming last layers split into sigma, c, l # This is a placeholder for the actual MLP structure defined in sigmas = x[0] cs = x[1:4] ls = x[4:] return sigmas, cs, ls def querythingmlp(xlocal, d, thingparams): """ Query the thing MLP for instance k. xlocal: 3D position in object local coordinates d: view direction thingparams: MLP weights for instance k Returns: sigmak, ck, lk """ # Encode position and direction # Thing uses L=6 for position, L=2 for direction encpos = encodevector(xlocal, L=6) encdir = encodevector(d, L=2) x = np.concatenate([encpos, encdir]) for layer in thingparams['layers']: x = np.maximum(0, x @ layer['W'] + layer['b']) # ReLU sigmak = x[0] ck = x[1:4] lk = x[4:] return sigmak, ck, lk def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, time, stuffparams, things, thingstracks): """ Render a single ray. rayorigin: 3D origin raydirection: 3D direction time: float timestamp stuffparams: Stuff MLP parameters things: List of Thing MLP parameters thingstracks: List of object track parameters (R, t, s) Returns: rendered color, density, semantic, instance """ # Sample points along ray (1024 samples, stratified) # Assume samples are generated as lambda values lambdas = np.linspace(0, 1, 1024) # Placeholder for actual near/far range pointsworld = rayorigin + lambdas[:, None] raydirection # Initialize accumulators accumulatedalpha = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) accumulateddensity = 0.0 accumulatedsemantic = np.zeros(numclasses) # Placeholder accumulatedinstance = np.zeros(numinstances) # Placeholder for i, xworld in enumerate(pointsworld): # Check intersection with bounding boxes # Determine which things intersect xworld at time intersectingthings = [] for k, track in enumerate(thingstracks): # Interpolate track to get Tk at time Tk = interpolatetrack(track, time) # Transform world point to local coordinates xlocal = transformtolocal(xworld, Tk) # Check if xlocal is inside bounding box s if isinsidebox(xlocal, track['s']): intersectingthings.append(k) # Compute field value at this point # Default to stuff sigmas, cs, ls = querystuffmlp(xworld, raydirection, stuffparams) # Add contributions from intersecting things sigmatotal = sigmas ctotal = cs ltotal = ls instanceid = 0 # Stuff instance ID for k in intersectingthings: sigmak, ck, lk = querythingmlp(xworld, raydirection, things[k]) # Note: xworld transformed inside query or here? Formula uses Tk^-1 x # Actually, querythingmlp expects local coords. Let's adjust. # Re-query with local coords sigmak, ck, lk = querythingmlp(xlocal, raydirection, things[k]) # Aggregate sigmatotal += sigmak ctotal += ck ltotal += lk instanceid = k + 1 # Thing instance IDs # Volume rendering step (simplified) # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # weight = alpha exp(-sum(sigma delta)) # accumulatedcolor += weight c #... pass return accumulatedcolor, accumulateddensity, accumulatedsemantic, accumulatedinstance def trainstep(batch, stuffparams, things, thingstracks): """ Perform one training step. """ # Forward pass to render images renderedcolors, renderedsemantics = renderbatch(batch, stuffparams, things, thingstracks) # Compute losses colorloss = mse(renderedcolors, batch['rgb']) semanticloss = crossentropy(renderedsemantics, batch['semantic']) totalloss = colorloss + lambdasem semanticloss # Backward pass gradients = computegradients(totalloss, stuffparams, things, thingstracks) # Update parameters stuffparams = adamupdate(stuffparams, gradients['stuff']) things = adamupdate(things, gradients['things']) thingstracks = adamupdate(thingstracks, gradients['tracks']) # Orthogonalize rotations for k in range(len(thingstracks)): thingstracks[k]['R'] = orthogonalizeR(thingstracks[k]['R']) return totalloss Uses shared MLPs with latent codes for objects, limiting instance-specific detail reproduction compared to PNF's separate MLPs. Lacks object awareness and dynamic scene handling, unlike PNF which explicitly decomposes things and stuff. Time and Memory Complexity: Compute-intensive, limited to offline applications. Uses 1024 samples per ray. Measured Performance: Outperforms SemanticNeRF by +9.2 mIoU on dynamic scenes (KITTI). Uses 10x fewer FLOPs in instance MLPs compared to NSG due to meta-learning priors. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes, object-aware, enables scene editing (removing/adding objects). Limitations: Does not handle missing/duplicate detections, incorrect class predictions, deformable objects, or complex light transport (e.g., shadowing). Panoptic Neural Fields (PNF) was introduced by Google Research, Georgia Tech, Simon Fraser University, and Stanford University in May 2022. It builds on NeRF and addresses limitations of previous object-aware frameworks that shared MLPs or lacked dynamic handling. It is evaluated on KITTI and KITTI-360 datasets. name: Category-Level Semantic NeRF
head: CLA-NeRF
body: Category-Level Semantic NeRF (CLA-NeRF) extends the standard NeRF framework to predict part segmentation logits in addition to density and color, enabling category-level generalization for articulated objects. Unlike sibling methods that may focus on instance-specific reconstruction, CLA-NeRF conditions the radiance field on image features extracted from input views, allowing the model to share knowledge across objects of the same category and render semantic labels for unseen poses. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of input images I with known relative camera poses; part segmentation labels for the objects in the training set. Outputs: For a ray \mathbf{r}, the model predicts volume density \sigma, RGB color \mathbf{c}, and part segmentation logits \mathbf{s} with P+1 dimensions (P parts plus background). Data Structures Image Encoder Output: A feature map W = E(I) extracted from the input image I using an image encoder E. Projected Coordinates: For a sampled 3D point \mathbf{x}, the projected coordinate on the input image plane is denoted \pi(\mathbf{x}). Segmentation Logits: \mathbf{s}k \in \mathbb{R}^{P+1} is the raw output for the k-th sample along a ray. Network Architecture The method builds on the shared principles of Panoptic and Semantic Scene Representations [20495-panoptic-and-semantic-scene-representations.md]. The core MLP backbone F\Theta is augmented to accept image features. For each 3D location \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}, the network predicts density, color, and segmentation: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{s}) = F\Theta(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}, W(\pi(\mathbf{x}))) where \gamma(\cdot) is the positional encoding, and W(\pi(\mathbf{x})) is the feature vector sampled from the image feature map W at the projected coordinate \pi(\mathbf{x}). Rendering Procedure 1. Ray Sampling: Generate K samples along ray \mathbf{r} at depths tk. 2. Network Query: For each sample k, query the network to obtain \sigmak, \mathbf{c}k, and \mathbf{s}k. 3. Alpha Computation: Compute the transmittance \hat{T}k for sample k: \hat{T}k = \exp\left(-\sum{k' < k} \sigma{k'} (t{k'+1} - t{k'})\right). 4. Segmentation Rendering: Compute the rendered segmentation \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) by volume rendering the logits \mathbf{s}k: \hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}k (1 - \exp(-\sigmak (t{k+1} - tk))) \mathbf{s}k. 5. Probability Conversion: Convert logits to probabilities using softmax: \hat{p}i(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\exp(\hat{S}i(\mathbf{r}))}{\sum{j=1}^{P} \exp(\hat{S}j(\mathbf{r}))} Note: The denominator sums over P parts, excluding the background class index in the normalization sum as per the source formula structure, though the numerator index i ranges 1 \dots P+1. Training Losses The model is jointly trained using a coarse and fine network (standard NeRF hierarchy). 1. Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{color}): Mean squared error between ground truth color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) and predictions from coarse (\hat{\mathbf{C}}c) and fine (\hat{\mathbf{C}}f) networks: \mathcal{L}{color} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{||\hat{\mathbf{C}}c(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})||^2 + ||\hat{\mathbf{C}}f(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})||^2}{2}. 2. Segmentation Loss (\mathcal{L}{seg}): Multi-class cross-entropy between ground truth part probabilities pi(\mathbf{r}) and predicted probabilities \hat{p}i^c(\mathbf{r}) (coarse) and \hat{p}i^f(\mathbf{r}) (fine): \mathcal{L}{seg} = - \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{i=1}^{P+1} \left( pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i^c(\mathbf{r}) + pi(\mathbf{r}) \log \hat{p}i^f(\mathbf{r}) \right). 3. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}{seg} where \lambda modulates the segmentation loss. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardray(rayorigin, raydirection, image, imageencoder, nerfmodel, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using Category-Level Semantic NeRF. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray tvals = samplealongray(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples) xyzsamples = rayorigin + raydirection tvals # 2. Project 3D points to the input image plane to get 2D coordinates # Assumes camera intrinsics/extrinsics are known for the input image 'image' projectedcoords = projecttoimageplane(xyzsamples, image.cameraparams) # 3. Extract image features # E is the image encoder, W is the feature map W = imageencoder(image) # 4. Sample features from the feature map at projected coordinates # Bilinear interpolation or nearest neighbor sampling imagefeatures = samplefeaturemap(W, projectedcoords) # 5. Encode positions and directions (using shared positional encoding from parent) encodedxyz = positionalencoding(xyzsamples) encodeddirs = positionalencoding(raydirection) # 6. Query the NeRF MLP # Input: encodedxyz, encodeddirs, imagefeatures # Output: sigma, color, segmentationlogits sigma, color, seglogits = nerfmodel(encodedxyz, encodeddirs, imagefeatures) # 7. Volume Render Color and Segmentation # Compute transmittance alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma (tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1])) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=0) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[:1]), transmittance[:-1]], dim=0) weights = alpha transmittance # Render Color renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=0) # Render Segmentation Logits renderedseglogits = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) seglogits, dim=0) # Convert logits to probabilities via softmax # Note: Source formula sums denominator over P parts, excluding background index in sum # Assuming index P is background. partlogits = renderedseglogits[:-1] # Exclude background renderedsegprobs = torch.softmax(partlogits, dim=-1) return renderedcolor, renderedsegprobs, sigma def computeloss(renderedcolorc, renderedcolorf, renderedsegc, renderedsegf, gtcolor, gtsegprobs, lambdaseg): """ Computes the total training loss. """ # Color Loss: MSE between coarse and fine predictions and GT colorlossc = torch.mean((renderedcolorc - gtcolor) 2) colorlossf = torch.mean((renderedcolorf - gtcolor) 2) lcolor = (colorlossc + colorlossf) / 2.0 # Segmentation Loss: Cross-Entropy between coarse and fine predictions and GT # gtsegprobs is the ground truth probability distribution over P+1 classes lsegc = -torch.mean(gtsegprobs torch.log(renderedsegc + 1e-8)) lsegf = -torch.mean(gtsegprobs torch.log(renderedsegf + 1e-8)) lseg = lsegc + lsegf ltotal = lcolor + lambdaseg lseg return ltotal Parameters \lambda: Coefficient modulating segmentation loss. Value not given in the sources.. P: Number of object parts. Value not given in the sources.. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Projection Accuracy: The method relies on projecting 3D points to the input image plane. If the camera parameters are inaccurate or the object is significantly occluded, the sampled features W(\pi(\mathbf{x})) may be invalid or noisy. Category Generalization: The model requires training on a collection of articulated objects belonging to the same category. It does not generalize to unseen categories without retraining. Time Complexity: Rendering requires an additional image feature sampling step and a linear layer for segmentation logits per sample, increasing computational cost over standard NeRF. Training requires joint optimization of color and segmentation losses. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the image feature map W for the input image(s). Strengths: Enables category-level generalization for articulated objects; provides semantic part segmentation alongside geometry and appearance. Limitations: Requires part segmentation labels for training; relies on relative camera poses; optimization is lengthy for each object instance if not generalized. When to use: When the goal is to reconstruct and segment articulated objects from a category (e.g., chairs, tables) given limited input views, and semantic understanding is required. When not to use: For instance-specific reconstruction without semantic needs, or for non-articulated objects where joint attributes are not relevant. Category-Level Semantic NeRF (CLA-NeRF) was introduced in 2022 by the authors of the paper "CLA-NeRF: Category-Level Articulated Neural Radiance Field". It extends the original NeRF by adding a segmentation head and conditioning on image features to enable generalization across objects of the same category. The method is specifically designed for articulated objects, allowing for the prediction of joint attributes (rotation axis and pivot point) from the predicted segmentation field. CLA-NeRF: Category-Level Articulated Neural Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/icra46639.2022.9812272, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Sat-NeRF
head: Sat-NeRF model, Satellite Neural Radiance Field
body: Sat-NeRF is a neural rendering method adapted for multi-view satellite photogrammetry that simultaneously learns the geometry and appearance of permanent structures while explicitly modeling shadows and transient objects (e.g., vehicles, vegetation). It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by assuming a Lambertian surface, omitting viewing-angle dependence, and using native Rational Polynomial Camera (RPC) models for ray casting instead of pinhole approximations. Unlike indoor NeRFs, it incorporates a shadow-aware irradiance model and uncertainty weighting to handle multi-date imagery where lighting and transient occlusions vary significantly. Inputs and Outputs The model takes a set of multi-date satellite images as input. For each training iteration, rays are cast into the scene volume. The network function F takes three inputs: 1. \mathbf{x}: A 3-valued vector of spatial coordinates of a point on the ray. 2. \boldsymbol{\omega}: A 3-valued direction vector encoding the direction of solar rays, extracted from the azimuth and elevation angles in the image metadata. 3. \mathbf{t}j: An N(t)-valued learned embedding vector specific to image index j, used to featurize transient elements not explained by the sun's position. In the source, N(t)=4. The network outputs a tuple (\sigma, ca, s, a, \beta): \sigma: Scalar volume density at \mathbf{x}. ca: Albedo RGB color, dependent only on geometry (\mathbf{x}). s: Shadow-aware shading scalar, dependent on \mathbf{x} and \boldsymbol{\omega}, taking values in [0, 1]. a: Ambient RGB color, independent of geometry, dependent on \boldsymbol{\omega}. \beta: Uncertainty coefficient related to the probability that the color is explained by a transient object. Data Structures and Network Layout The architecture consists of three parts: 1. Main Block: A fully-connected block with h channels per layer. It predicts \sigma and ca. It uses SIREN layers with the initialization from [46]. 2. Secondary Head: Fewer layers with h/2 channels per layer. It estimates s based on \boldsymbol{\omega} and the h-dimensional geometry features from the main block. 3. Single-Layer Heads: One head predicts \beta from \mathbf{t}j and \boldsymbol{\omega}. One head predicts a from \boldsymbol{\omega}. Typical value for h is 512, adjusted based on resolution and area size. Activation Functions \sigma: Softplus. \beta: Softplus (yields smoother optimization than ReLU). ca, s, a: Sigmoid (outputs are normalized RGB values in [0, 1]). Ray Casting and Sampling Rays are cast using the Rational Polynomial Camera (RPC) model of each input image directly in object space, providing independence from the specific satellite system. Prior to training, a bundle adjustment is applied to the RPC models to boost performance and optionally extract a sparse point cloud for depth supervision. Each ray \mathbf{r} is discretized into 64 uniformly distributed 3D points. Color Rendering The color c(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{t}j) at point \mathbf{x} is computed using a shadow-aware irradiance model: c(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{t}j) = ca(\mathbf{x}) \cdot s(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}) + (1 - s(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega})) \cdot a(\boldsymbol{\omega}) where s \approx 1 for sun-lit points and s \approx 0 for shadowed points. Loss Function The total loss combines image reconstruction, solar correction, and optional depth supervision. 1. Main Image Loss with Uncertainty: \mathcal{L}{img} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \sum{i=1}^{Nr} \betai (\mathbf{c}i - \hat{\mathbf{c}}i)^2 where R is the batch of viewing rays, \mathbf{c}i is the ground truth color, \hat{\mathbf{c}}i is the rendered color, and \betai is the uncertainty coefficient. Note: The source text describes \beta as weighting the impact of transient objects to minimize their contribution to the loss, effectively down-weighting inconsistent pixels. The specific formula in the source notes refers to equation (8) incorporating \beta. 2. Solar Correction Term (Optional): \mathcal{L}{SC}(\mathcal{R}{SC}) = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}{SC}} \sum{i=1}^{N{SC}} (Ti - si)^2 + \sum{i=1}^{N{SC}} \left(1 - \sum{i=1}^{N{SC}} Ti \alphai si \right)^2 where \mathcal{R}{SC} is a secondary batch of rays following the solar direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, Ti is transmittance, \alphai is opacity, and si is shading. 3. Depth Supervision Term (Optional): Uses sparse 3D points from the bundle adjustment. Weight \lambda{DS}. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{img} + \lambda{SC} \mathcal{L}{SC} + \lambda{DS} \mathcal{L}{DS} Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class SatNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, h=512, nt=4): super().init() # Main block: 8 fully-connected layers with h channels, SIREN initialized self.main = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(3, h)] + [nn.Linear(h, h) for in range(7)]) # Secondary head: 2 layers with h/2 channels self.sec = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(h + 3, h // 2), nn.Linear(h // 2, 1)]) # Single-layer heads self.headbeta = nn.Linear(nt + 3, 1) self.heada = nn.Linear(3, 3) self.initsiren() def initsiren(self): # SIREN initialization from [46] applied to main block weights/biases # Source does not provide exact initialization code pass def forward(self, x, omega, tj): # Main block forward pass hfeat = x for i, layer in enumerate(self.main): hfeat = layer(hfeat) if i < len(self.main) - 1: hfeat = torch.sin(hfeat) # Standard SIREN intermediate activation # Output from main block mainout = self.main-1 sigma = torch.nn.functional.softplus(mainout[:, 0:1]) ca = torch.sigmoid(mainout[:, 1:4]) # Secondary head for shading s # Uses h-dimensional geometry features from main block (output of second-to-last layer) hgeom = self.main-2 secin = torch.cat([hgeom, omega], dim=-1) s = torch.sigmoid(self.sec1))) # Head for beta betain = torch.cat([tj, omega], dim=-1) beta = torch.nn.functional.softplus(self.headbeta(betain)) # Head for ambient color a a = torch.sigmoid(self.heada(omega)) return sigma, ca, s, a, beta def volumerender(xsamples, sigma, c, delta): # Standard volume rendering integration alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=1)[:,:-1], dim=1) weights = alpha T renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=-2) return renderedcolor def computeloss(renderedcolor, gtcolor, beta, sigma, s, omega, tj, RSC=None, sparsepoints=None, lambdaSC=0.1/3, lambdaDS=1000/3): # Main image loss with uncertainty weighting imgloss = torch.mean(beta (renderedcolor - gtcolor)2) totalloss = imgloss if RSC is not None: # Solar correction loss: LSC = sum((T - s)^2) + sum((1 - sum(T alpha s))^2) # Requires rendering rays along solar direction omega # Source does not provide exact implementation details for RSC rendering pass if sparsepoints is not None: # Depth supervision loss using bundle adjustment points # Source does not provide exact implementation details for depth term pass return totalloss Parameters h: Channels per layer in main block. Typical value: 512. \lambda{SC}: Weight for solar correction. Value: 0.05/3 (if only SC added to S-NeRF baseline) or 0.1/3 (otherwise). \lambda{DS}: Weight for depth supervision. Value: 1000/3. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Scheduler: Step scheduler, decrease by factor \gamma = 0.9 every epoch. Batch Size: 1024 rays. Points per Ray: 64 uniformly distributed points. Iterations: 300k to converge. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparse Point Cloud Outliers: The sparse point cloud from bundle adjustment may contain outliers, especially in multi-date collections, leading to slightly worse altitude Mean Absolute Error (MAE) in some areas compared to plain Sat-NeRF loss. Uncertainty Limitations: The uncertainty coefficient \beta can only absorb occasional inconsistencies. It does not account for roofs under construction or roofs unusually free of parked cars, which may cause holes in the Digital Surface Model (DSM). Solar Direction Extrapolation: The shading scalar s can produce unrealistic results for solar ray directions not seen in training data. This is mitigated by the solar correction term. A variant for sparse single-date satellite imagery using Semi-Global Matching (SGM) depth supervision. Choose when only 2-3 images are available and standard Sat-NeRF fails due to insufficient geometric constraints. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 10 hours for 300k iterations with a single batch of rays, or ~20 hours if solar correction or depth supervision terms are added. Memory: Requires a GPU with 16 GB RAM. Performance: Sat-NeRF provides higher PSNR/SSIM and similar or smaller altitude MAE compared to S-NeRF without requiring solar correction. Adding solar correction decreases altitude MAE further. Geometry Quality: Sat-NeRF DSMs have more detailed structures and sharper edges than traditional stereo pipelines (S2P), but S2P provides more regular surfaces. Sat-NeRF produces more local irregularities (less flat roofs/roads) but is free of single-point outliers. Strengths: Robust to shadows and transient objects; uses native RPC models; high-quality novel view synthesis and 3D modeling. Limitations: Local irregularities in flat surfaces; potential holes in DSM for dynamic structures not captured by \beta; sensitive to outliers in bundle adjustment point clouds. Sat-NeRF was introduced by Roger Marí, Gabriele Facciolo, and Thibaud Ehret from Université Paris-Saclay and Centre Borelli in 2022. It extends the S-NeRF method by incorporating modeling of transient objects similar to NeRF-W and using RPC camera models more adapted to satellite data. It was evaluated on the 2019 IEEE GRSS Data Fusion Contest data, using Maxar WorldView-3 images over Jacksonville, Florida. name: SpS-NeRF
head: SparseSat-NeRF
body: SpS-NeRF is a NeRF variant adapted for sparse single-date satellite images that employs dense depth supervision guided by a cross-correlation similarity metric from traditional semi-global MVS (SGM) matching. It extends Sat-NeRF to handle novel view generation and 3D geometry reconstruction from sparse satellite views by jointly optimizing RGB and depth losses, using uncertainty metrics from SGM correlation maps to robustify the supervision. Unlike learning-based depth completion methods used in indoor scenes, SpS-NeRF leverages traditional SGM, which is sufficient for satellite scenarios and avoids the need for ground truth depth maps for training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N sparse satellite images with known camera poses (RPC functions as per Sat-NeRF), and corresponding dense depth maps computed via Semi-Global Matching (SGM) on downsampled images (factor 4). The input depth maps are incomplete (due to occlusions) and imprecise (4x larger Ground Sample Distance). Outputs: A neural radiance field model capable of rendering novel views and a refined Digital Surface Model (DSM). Data Structures: Neural Network: A fully-connected (non-convolutional) deep network F\Theta defining the continuous volumetric representation, identical to Sat-NeRF but omitting modules for transient objects and solar correction modeling, as the method targets synchronous acquisitions. SGM Correlation Maps: Used to derive an uncertainty metric corr(r) for each ray r. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in the target view, cast a ray r through the scene. Use guided ray sampling borrowed from Roessle et al. (2022). The sampling is influenced by the uncertainty metric corr(r). 2. Query Points: Sample N query points xi along the ray r through the 3D field. 3. Network Forward Pass: Query the network F\Theta at each xi to obtain density \sigmai and color ci. 4. Volume Rendering (RGB): Compute the accumulated color C(r) for the ray using standard volume rendering integration: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where: \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai} is the opacity of the current query point xi, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between adjacent query points, Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the probability that the ray reaches xi without being blocked. 5. Uncertainty Metric Calculation: Compute the uncertainty metric corr(r) based on the SGM cross-correlation maps. This metric is applied three times during optimization: (i) As a weight applied to the final depth loss. (ii) As a threshold to determine whether the depth loss should be activated. (iii) In guided ray sampling. Note: The exact formula for corr(r) is referenced as Equation (5) in the source but is not explicitly provided in the text snippets. The source states that for the ablation variant "SpS-NeRF \Corr", corr(r)=1 for every pixel. 6. Depth Supervision: Compute a depth loss similar to DDPNeRF. The loss encourages the network to estimate the depth within a margin m of the input depth, weighted by corr(r). The exact loss formulation is referenced as Equation (6) in the source but is not explicitly provided in the text snippets. 7. Joint Optimization: Optimize the network parameters \Theta by minimizing a combined loss of RGB rendering error and the weighted depth loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainstep(images, depths, corrmaps, model, optimizer): totalloss = 0 for img, depthmap, corrmap in zip(images, depths, corrmaps): # 1. Cast rays for the current image rays = castrays(img.pose) # 2. Sample points along rays # Uses guided ray sampling influenced by uncertainty (Eq 5/6 context) points = samplepointsalongrays(rays, model, uncertaintymap=corrmap) # 3. Query network for sigma and color sigma, color = model.query(points) # 4. Render RGB using volume rendering # C(r) = sum(Ti alphai ci) renderedcolor = volumerender(points, sigma, color) # 5. Compute RGB Loss rgbloss = mseloss(renderedcolor, img.pixelvalues) # 6. Compute Depth Loss with Uncertainty # Note: Exact formulas for Eq 5 (corr) and Eq 6 (depth loss) are not provided in text. # Implementation relies on the described logic: # - corr(r) acts as weight and threshold. # - Loss encourages depth within margin m of input depth. # Extract rendered depth from the volume rendering process rendereddepth = computerendereddepth(points, sigma, color) # Calculate uncertainty weight from correlation map # corr(r) is derived from corrmap at the ray's pixel location uncertaintyweight = getuncertaintyweight(corrmap, rays) # Apply thresholding: activate loss only if uncertainty is below threshold # (Specific threshold logic from Eq 5 is not detailed in text) activemask = uncertaintyweight < threshold # Placeholder for specific threshold logic # Calculate depth error within margin m deptherror = abs(rendereddepth - depthmap) # Weighted depth loss # Loss is active only where activemask is true depthloss = sum(activemask uncertaintyweight deptherror) / sum(activemask) # 7. Combine losses # Jointly optimize RGB and depth losses loss = rgbloss + lambdadepth depthloss totalloss += loss # Backpropagate and update optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss Parameters: SGM Downsampling Factor: 4. Margin m: Used in depth loss formulation (value not specified in sources). Loss Weighting: The balance between RGB and depth loss is implicit in the joint optimization; specific weights are not detailed in the provided text. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flat Surfaces: SpS-NeRF lacks regularization on flat surfaces, leading to local irregularities, a common problem in NeRFs. Adding semantic information might be a possible solution. GT Bias: In the Djibouti dataset, the Ground Truth DSM was generated with the same SGM as the best performing SGM baseline (SGM{scl1}), potentially biasing the comparison. SGM Outliers: SGM is susceptible to outliers, so the GT DSM is likely corrupted with some erroneous depth estimations. Sparse Depths: Without dense depths, sparse depths are not enough to complete missing information with 2 or 3 input images. The parent method, an end-to-end model for learning multi-view satellite photogrammetry using native satellite camera models (RPC functions) [20274-sat-nerf.md]. A method that learns a depth completion network from sparse depth maps, using explicit depth loss. SpS-NeRF borrows the depth supervision concept but replaces the learning-based prediction with SGM. The source of the guided ray sampling strategy used in SpS-NeRF. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DFC2019 (2 views): PSNR 20.2, SSIM 0.87, MAEin 3.02, MAEout 7.77. DFC2019 (3 views): PSNR 19.06, SSIM 0.86, MAEin 4.63, MAEout 2.05. Djibouti (2 views): PSNR 32.85, SSIM 0.92, MAEin 1.57, MAEout 1.15. Djibouti (3 views): PSNR 36.26, SSIM 0.95, MAEin 1.35, MAEout 0.81. Comparison with Baselines: Outperforms NeRF and Sat-NeRF in all scenarios. Better than SGM{scl1} (full-resolution SGM) in occluded and poorly textured areas (MAEout). Worse than SGM{scl1} in altitude extraction on valid pixels (MAEin) due to lack of regularization. Better than SGM{scl1} close to building outlines and free of outliers. Ablation Results (DFC2019 2 views): Dense Sat-NeRF (vanilla Sat-NeRF with dense depths): PSNR 19.39, SSIM 0.86, MAEin 3.58, MAEout 7.91. SpS-NeRF \Corr (deactivated uncertainty metric): PSNR 19.67, SSIM 0.86, MAEin 3.21, MAEout 8.03. Full SpS-NeRF: PSNR 20.2, SSIM 0.87, MAEin 3.02, MAEout 7.77. Strengths: Robust to shadows and transient objects (inherited from Sat-NeRF context, though transient modeling is omitted in SpS-NeRF for synchronous data), handles sparse views effectively, improves upon traditional SGM in occluded areas. Limitations: Lacks regularization on flat surfaces, sensitive to SGM outliers in GT, requires SGM pre-processing. When to use: Sparse single-date satellite imagery where traditional MVS fails in occluded/poorly textured areas and learning-based depth prediction is not desired or feasible. When not to use: Dense view scenarios, indoor scenes (where learning-based methods like NerfingMVS/DDPNeRF are better), or when high precision on flat surfaces is critical without semantic regularization. SpS-NeRF was presented in 2023 by Zhang et al. in the ISPRS Annals of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences. It is an extension of Sat-NeRF (Marí et al., 2022) and incorporates concepts from DDPNeRF (Roessle et al., 2022). The method was developed to address the challenge of generating convincing scene geometries from sparse satellite views, which is rare in earth observation compared to the many views required by standard NeRF variants. The research was funded by CNES (Centre national d’études spatiales) and the Djibouti dataset was obtained through the CNES ISIS framework. Numerical computations were performed on the SCAPAD cluster processing facility at the Institute de Physique du Globe de Paris. name: NeO 360
head: Neural Fields for Sparse View Synthesis of Outdoor Scenes
body: NeO 360 is a generalizable neural field method for few-shot novel view synthesis of unbounded 360-degree outdoor scenes. It operates in a zero-shot manner, taking one or a few input images to render novel viewpoints without optimizing a per-scene latent code or using inference-time GAN inversion. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like PixelNeRF by combining a global image-conditional tri-planar representation with local residual features and separate foreground/background rendering MLPs, enabling strong scene priors for sparse view inputs. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: V source images \{Iv\}{v=1}^V (typically V \in \{1, 3, 5\}), camera poses for source images, and target camera poses for novel views. Outputs: Rendered RGB colors C(r) and optionally depth for rays r in novel views. Data Structures 1. Encoder Feature Map (FI): Output of the ResNet32 encoder. Dimensions: 512 \times H/2 \times W/2. 2. 3D Feature Volume (VF): Volumetric projection of FI. Dimensions: K \times K \times K \times 512, where K=64. 3. Depth-Encoded Features (VZ): Output of depth-encoding MLP. Dimensions: K \times K \times K \times 512. 4. Tri-Planar Features (S): Projected 2D feature maps. Dimensions: 128 \times 120 \times 160 per plane (xy, xz, yz). 5. Rendering MLP Weights: 7 fully connected layers (hidden dim 128) for density/color, plus 2 additional layers for color. Numbered Steps 1. Feature Extraction: Pass source images through a pre-trained ResNet32 encoder E. Extract features from the initial convolutional layer and layers 1–3. Upsample all extracted features to spatial resolution H/2 \times W/2. Concatenate along the channel dimension to form FI \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times H/2 \times W/2}. 2. Volumetric Projection: Back-project FI along every ray to a world grid V to create a 3D feature volume VF \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times K \times 512}. The grid resolution K is set to 64 to balance expressivity and memory. 3. Depth Encoding: Pass VF through a 2-layer MLP with hidden dimension 512 to learn the depth of each feature, producing VZ \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times K \times 512}. 4. Feature Aggregation (Tri-Planar Construction): Use three 2-layer MLPs (hidden dim 512) to output learned weights w{xy}, w{xz}, w{yz} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times K \times 1} over the volumetric feature dimensions. Apply softmax and sum over the z, y, and x dimensions respectively to obtain three 2D feature maps, each of dimension K \times K \times 512. 5. 2D Convolutional Refinement: Transform the planar features using a series of 2D convolutions and upsampling layers to produce the final tri-planar features S. The architecture is: Conv 1: Input 512 \to Output 256, kernel 3, stride 2, padding 1, followed by BatchNorm and ReLU. Conv 2: Input 256 \to Output 128, kernel 3, stride 2, padding 1, followed by BatchNorm and ReLU. Conv 3: Input 128 \to Output 128, kernel 3, stride 2, padding 1, followed by BatchNorm and ReLU. Upsample: Scale factor 2. Conv 4: Input 128 \to Output 128, kernel 3, stride 1, padding 1, followed by BatchNorm and ReLU. Upsample: To spatial resolution H/2 \times W/2. Conv 5: Input 128 \to Output 128, kernel 3, stride 1, padding 1, followed by BatchNorm and ReLU. The output S has dimensions 128 \times 120 \times 160. 6. Tri-Planar Sampling: For a 3D point \mathbf{x}, project it into each of the three planes by taking the absolute xy, xz, and yz coordinates. Concatenate the sampled features and sum over the channel dimension to retrieve the global tri-planar feature \mathbf{f}{tp} \in \mathbb{R}^{128}. 7. Residual Feature Sampling: Sample the local feature map FI at the projected 2D coordinates of \mathbf{x} to obtain the residual local feature \mathbf{f}r \in \mathbb{R}^{512}. 8. Positional Encoding: Apply hierarchical sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the input position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d}. 9. MLP Forward Pass: Concatenate \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{f}{tp}, and \mathbf{f}r as input to the first layer of the rendering MLP. Skip Connection: Supply the conditioning feature (from the encoder) as a skip connection to the third layer of the MLP. Multi-View Aggregation: If more than one image is in the input, mean pool the features along the viewing dimension in the fourth MLP layer. Density Output: Use the first 4 layers to output features of dimension 128. Pass these through a final density MLP to output a single scalar \sigma (volume density) for each sampled point. Color Output: Use two additional dedicated MLP layers (hidden dim 128) to output 3-channel RGB color \mathbf{c}, conditioned on the positionally-encoded viewing direction \mathbf{d} and the output of the fourth MLP layer. 10. Background Modeling: The method uses separate near and far background MLPs. Points are sampled based on the intersection between the ray origin and a unit sphere. The final composited color \mathbf{c} is calculated as: \mathbf{c} = \sumi w^bi \mathbf{c}^bi + \sumi w^{nb}i \mathbf{c}^{nb}i + \sumi w^oi\mathbf{c}^oi where b denotes background, nb denotes near-background, and o denotes objects/foreground. 11. Regularization: Apply regularization loss \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{reg}} to encourage sparse weights for the near and far background MLPs: \mathcal{L}{\mathrm{reg}}(s, w)=\sum {i=0}^{N-1} \sum {j=0}^{N-1} wi wj\left|\frac {si+s{i+1}}{2}-\frac {sj+s{j+1}}{2}\right| +\frac {1}{3} \sum {i=0}^{N-1} wi^2 (s{i+1}-si) where s represents samples and w represents weights. 12. Rendering: Compute the final pixel color C(r) using volume rendering integration: C(r) = \sum{k=1}^N Tk \alphak ck where \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak), Tk = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), and ck is the predicted color.
