Encoder: Pre-trained ResNet32 (frozen during training) self.encoder = ResNet32() # Volumetric Projection: Back-projection logic handled in forward self.K = K # Depth Encoding MLP: 2 layers, hidden enchidden self.depthmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(enchidden, enchidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(enchidden, enchidden)) # Feature Aggregation MLPs: 3 MLPs for xy, xz, yz weights self.weightmlpxy = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(enchidden, enchidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(enchidden, 1)) self.weightmlpxz = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(enchidden, enchidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(enchidden, 1)) self.weightmlpyz = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(enchidden, enchidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(enchidden, 1)) # 2D Convolutional Blocks for Tri-Planar Features # Input: KK512 -> Output: H/2W/2128 self.triplanarconv = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(512, 256, kernelsize=3, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(256, 128, kernelsize=3, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(128, 128, kernelsize=3, stride=2, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2), nn.Conv2d(128, 128, kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Upsample(scalefactor=2), # To H/2, W/2 nn.Conv2d(128, 128, kernelsize=3, stride=1, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU()) # Rendering MLPs # First 4 layers shared for density and color features self.rendermlpshared = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3 + 128 + 512, hiddendim), # x(3) + ftp(128) + fr(512) nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) # Density MLP: Final layer from shared features self.densitymlp = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) # Color MLP: 2 additional layers self.colormlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim + 3, hiddendim), # Features + d(3) nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) # Background MLPs (Near and Far) self.nearbgmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) self.farbgmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) # Background Weight MLPs (for regularization) self.nearbgweightmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) self.farbgweightmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) def positionalencoding(self, x, L=10): # Standard NeRF positional encoding # x: (N, 3) scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(L)], dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) xb = torch.reshape((x scales[:, None]), (x.shape[0], -1)) pe = torch.cat((torch.sin(xb), torch.cos(xb)), dim=1) return pe def forward(self, sourceimages, targetcameras, Nsamples=128): # 1. Feature Extraction # sourceimages: (V, 3, H, W) # Extract features from ResNet32 layers 0, 1, 2, 3 featl0 = self.encoder.conv1(sourceimages) # (V, 64, H/2, W/2) approx featl1 = self.encoder.layer1(sourceimages) featl2 = self.encoder.layer2(sourceimages) featl3 = self.encoder.layer3(sourceimages) # Upsample all to H/2 x W/2 and concatenate # Note: ResNet32 layer outputs might have different strides, # assuming upsampling logic from notes: upsample all to H/2 x W/2 featl0 = F.interpolate(featl0, size=(sourceimages.shape[2]//2, sourceimages.shape[3]//2), mode='bilinear') featl1 = F.interpolate(featl1, size=(sourceimages.shape[2]//2, sourceimages.shape[3]//2), mode='bilinear') featl2 = F.interpolate(featl2, size=(sourceimages.shape[2]//2, sourceimages.shape[3]//2), mode='bilinear') featl3 = F.interpolate(featl3, size=(sourceimages.shape[2]//2, sourceimages.shape[3]//2), mode='bilinear') FI = torch.cat([featl0, featl1, featl2, featl3], dim=1) # (V, 512, H/2, W/2) # 2. Volumetric Projection # Back-project FI to 3D grid VF (K, K, K, 512) # This step involves ray casting from source cameras into the world grid # VF = volumetricprojection(FI, sourcecameras, K) # For implementation, this is a complex operation. # We assume VF is computed as KxKxKx512 tensor. VF = self.volumetricproject(FI, sourcecameras, self.K) # 3. Depth Encoding VFflat = VF.view(-1, 512) VZflat = self.depthmlp(VFflat) VZ = VZflat.view(self.K, self.K, self.K, 512) # 4. Feature Aggregation # Compute weights for xy, xz, yz VZflat = VZ.view(-1, 512) wxyflat = self.weightmlpxy(VZflat).view(self.K, self.K, self.K, 1) wxzflat = self.weightmlpxz(VZflat).view(self.K, self.K, self.K, 1) wyzflat = self.weightmlpyz(VZflat).view(self.K, self.K, self.K, 1) # Softmax and sum wxy = F.softmax(wxyflat, dim=2) # Sum over z wxz = F.softmax(wxzflat, dim=1) # Sum over x wyz = F.softmax(wyzflat, dim=0) # Sum over y # Weighted sum to get 2D planes # Plane XY: Sum over Z planexy = torch.sum(VF wxy, dim=2) # (K, K, 512) # Plane XZ: Sum over X planexz = torch.sum(VF wxz, dim=1) # (K, K, 512) # Plane YZ: Sum over Y planeyz = torch.sum(VF wyz, dim=0) # (K, K, 512) # 5. 2D Convolution # Apply convs to each plane planexy = self.triplanarconv(planexy.permute(2, 0, 1)).permute(1, 2, 0) # (H/2, W/2, 128) planexz = self.triplanarconv(planexz.permute(2, 0, 1)).permute(1, 2, 0) planeyz = self.triplanarconv(planeyz.permute(2, 0, 1)).permute(1, 2, 0) # 6. Ray Casting and Sampling # Cast rays from targetcameras # x: (N, 3), d: (N, 3) x, d = self.castrays(targetcameras, Nsamples) # 7. Tri-Planar Sampling # Project x to xy, xz, yz xxy = torch.stack([x[:, 0], x[:, 1]], dim=1) # (N, 2) xxz = torch.stack([x[:, 0], x[:, 2]], dim=1) xyz = torch.stack([x[:, 1], x[:, 2]], dim=1) # Sample from planes # Note: Coordinates need to be normalized to [-1, 1] for gridsample ftpxy = F.gridsample(planexy.unsqueeze(0), xxy.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') ftpxz = F.gridsample(planexz.unsqueeze(0), xxz.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') ftpyz = F.gridsample(planeyz.unsqueeze(0), xyz.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') # Concatenate and sum ftp = ftpxy + ftpxz + ftpyz # (N, 128) # 8. Residual Feature Sampling # Sample FI at projected 2D coords of x # This requires projecting 3D points x back to 2D image coordinates for each source view frlist = [] for v in range(sourceimages.shape[0]): # Project x to view v's image plane # Get 2D coords (u, v) coordsv = self.projecttoimage(x, sourcecameras[v]) frv = F.gridsample(FI[v:v+1], coordsv.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') frlist.append(frv) fr = torch.cat(frlist, dim=1) # (N, 512) # 9. Rendering # Compute alpha, T, and final color # delta = distance between samples # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) # T = exp(-sum(sigma delta)) # C = sum(T alpha color) return C def volumetricproject(self, FI, cameras, K): # Placeholder for complex back-projection logic # Returns KxKxKx512 tensor return torch.zeros(K, K, K, 512) def castrays(self, cameras, N): # Placeholder for ray casting # Returns x (N, 3), d (N, 3) return torch.zeros(N, 3), torch.zeros(N, 3) def projecttoimage(self, x, camera): # Placeholder for 3D to 2D projection return torch.zeros(x.shape[0], 2) def getconditioningfeature(self, FI): # Placeholder for computing conditioning feature return torch.zeros(FI.shape[0], 512) Parameters Grid Resolution (K): 64. Near Clipping Plane: 0.02. Far Clipping Plane: 3.0. Coarse Samples per Ray: 64. Fine Samples per Ray: 64. Perceptual Loss Lambda: 0.3. Initial Learning Rate: 5.0 \times 10^{-4}. Final Learning Rate: 5.0 \times 10^{-6}. Total Training Epochs: 100. Epochs before Perceptual Loss: 30. Fine-tuning Learning Rate: 5.0 \times 10^{-6}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls OOM: Large grid sizes cause out-of-memory issues. Mitigation: Use K=64. Pooling Strategy: Pooling features along the viewing dimension too early (during tri-planar construction) hurts performance. Mitigation: Mean pool in the fourth MLP layer if multiple images are input. Naive Triplanes: Using triplanes without generative losses or proper training degrades performance. Time Complexity: Training requires approximately 1 day on 8 A-100 GPUs. Memory Complexity: Model size is 17M parameters, significantly larger than vanilla NeRF (1.2M rendering MLP) due to the ResNet encoder (~10M) and convolutional blocks. Performance: On the NeRDS 360 dataset (Single Map, 3 views, zero-shot), NeO 360 achieves PSNR 19.35, SSIM 0.59, LPIPS 0.50. It outperforms PixelNeRF and MVSNeRF in zero-shot and fine-tuning scenarios. Strengths: Zero-shot generalization to novel scenes and objects; strong scene priors for unbounded 360-degree outdoor scenes; effective few-shot synthesis. Limitations: Larger model size compared to vanilla NeRF; requires careful tuning of grid resolution to avoid OOM. When to Use: Sparse view synthesis of outdoor 360-degree scenes where zero-shot generalization is required. When Not to Use: Dense view synthesis where per-scene optimization is feasible and memory is constrained. NeO 360 was introduced in 2023 by the authors of the paper "NeO 360: Neural Fields for Sparse View Synthesis of Outdoor Scenes". It was developed to address the challenges of novel view synthesis in unbounded 360-degree outdoor environments, where traditional NeRF methods struggle with generalization to novel scenes and sparse inputs. The method builds on the NeRF framework but introduces image-conditional tri-planar representations and local residual features to learn strong scene priors from large-scale datasets like NeRDS 360. It is used for novel-view synthesis, scene decomposition, and 360-degree predictions. name: SCADE
head: Space Carving with Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates
body: SCADE is a NeRF reconstruction approach that regularizes optimization with multimodal depth estimates from an ambiguity-aware prior, resolving ambiguities via a space carving loss that fuses estimates across views to achieve globally consistent 3D reconstruction. Unlike Dense Depth Prior (DDP) which uses a unimodal Gaussian prior and 2D supervision on moments, SCADE uses a multimodal prior and 3D supervision on the full distribution. This allows it to clear "dust" in space by supervising the full distribution of ray termination distances rather than just moments. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images with known camera poses (obtained via SfM), and a pretrained ambiguity-aware depth estimation prior. Outputs: A NeRF model predicting volume density \sigma and RGB color c, optimized to minimize the space carving loss and photometric error. Data Structures: Ambiguity-Aware Prior: A neural network that outputs M depth estimates for a given input image. The prior is trained on the Taskonomy dataset using cIMLE to model multimodal distributions from inconsistently labeled data. Depth Estimates: A set of M depth values \{d1, d2, \dots, dM\} for each pixel, representing possible depth modes (e.g., through glass, on glass). Ray Samples: Standard NeRF ray sampling along the ray r, producing positions xk and distances \lambdak. Parameters: M: Number of depth estimates used in the prior, set to 20 in experiments. Initialization: Weights initialized with the pretrained LeReS model. Algorithm: The method integrates the ambiguity-aware prior into the NeRF training loop. For each ray r cast from a camera view: 1. Depth Estimation: Pass the input image through the ambiguity-aware prior to obtain M depth estimates \{d1, \dots, dM\} for the corresponding pixel. 2. Ray Sampling: Sample points xk along the ray r at distances \lambdak from the camera origin. 3. Space Carving Loss Calculation: The core innovation is the space carving loss, which supervises the full distribution of ray termination distances. For each depth estimate dm from the prior, the method computes a loss that encourages the NeRF's predicted depth distribution to align with dm while carving out space in front of it. Let T(\lambda) be the accumulated transmission at distance \lambda along the ray, defined as T(\lambda) = \exp(-\int0^\lambda \sigma(s) ds). The probability density of ray termination at \lambda is p(\lambda) = \sigma(\lambda) T(\lambda). The space carving loss for a single depth estimate d is designed such that to move a sample from the ray termination distance distribution farther in depth, the loss decreases the probability density of all points in front of it. This effectively clears "dust" (incorrect density predictions) in space. The total loss combines the space carving loss over all M depth estimates and the standard photometric rendering loss. \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda{sc} \sum{m=1}^M \mathcal{L}{sc}(dm) Where \mathcal{L}{photo} is the mean squared error between rendered and ground truth colors, and \mathcal{L}{sc} is the space carving loss for depth estimate dm. The specific formulation of \mathcal{L}{sc} ensures 3D supervision by operating on the distribution rather than moments. 4. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters using gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-opaque Surfaces: Reflective or transparent surfaces (e.g., glass, mirrors) create ambiguous depth estimates with multiple modes. The ambiguity-aware prior handles this by modeling multimodal distributions. Sparsity: The method is robust to sparse views, outperforming DDP even with as few as 18 views. Domain Gap: The prior is trained on Taskonomy, which may differ from the target domain (e.g., ScanNet, in-the-wild), but SCADE remains robust. Performance: On ScanNet, SCADE achieves PSNR 21.54, SSIM 0.732, LPIPS 0.292, outperforming Vanilla NeRF (19.03, 0.670, 0.398) and DDP (19.29, 0.695, 0.368). On in-the-wild iPhoneX data, SCADE achieves PSNR 22.82, SSIM 0.743, LPIPS 0.347, outperforming Vanilla NeRF (20.46, 0.713, 0.398) and DDP (21.28, 0.727, 0.366). Ablation: MonoSDF supervision yields PSNR 20.13; DDP prior single sample yields 20.85; DDP prior multiple samples yields 21.00; SCADE prior single sample yields 21.22; SCADE (Ours) yields 21.54. Sparsity: With 18 views (1.87 avg visible), DDP/SCADE PSNR is 19.35/21.66. With 24 views (2.2 avg visible), DDP/SCADE PSNR is 23.56/24.84. Strengths: Handles non-opaque surfaces better than baselines; robust to sparse views; resolves ambiguities via 3D supervision. Limitations: Requires a pretrained depth prior; computational overhead from evaluating M depth estimates and the space carving loss. SCADE was introduced in the paper "SCADE: NeRFs from Space Carving with Ambiguity-Aware Depth Estimates". It addresses the underconstrained nature of NeRF reconstruction with modest numbers of in-the-wild views by regularizing optimization with multimodal depth estimates. The method builds on the concept of using depth priors but extends it to handle ambiguity via multimodal modeling and 3D supervision. name: PBR-NeRF
head: Inverse Rendering with Physics-Based Neural Fields, Physics-Based Neural Fields
body: PBR-NeRF is an inverse rendering model that jointly estimates scene geometry, materials, and illumination by extending the NeILF/NeILF++ neural fields framework with two novel physics-based priors: Conservation of Energy and NDF-weighted Specular Losses. It solves the material-lighting ambiguity inherent in standard NeRF approaches by enforcing physical validity on the estimated BRDF, preventing issues such as specular highlights being "baked in" to the diffuse albedo. Unlike NeILF/NeILF++, which use a Lambertian prior that assumes perfectly rough, non-metallic materials and suppresses the specular lobe, PBR-NeRF uses physics-based losses that enhance physical validity without sacrificing expressiveness. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics), RGB images, and optionally ground-truth geometry (for evaluation). Outputs: Estimated outgoing radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) for novel view synthesis, and spatially varying material fields: albedo \mathbf{b} \in [0, 1]^3, metallicness m \in [0, 1], and roughness r \in [0, 1]. Data Structures The framework consists of three implicit neural networks (MLPs): 1. NeRF SDF: Predicts volume density \sigma (geometry) and color \mathbf{c} (estimating outgoing radiance Lo). 2. BRDF MLP: Predicts the Disney BRDF parameters: albedo \mathbf{b}, roughness r, and metallicness m. 3. NeILF MLP: Predicts incident radiance Li(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i). Rendering Integral Approximation The outgoing radiance is approximated using a fixed set SL of incident directions \boldsymbol{\omega}i generated by Fibonacci sampling: Lo(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \frac{2\pi}{|SL|} \sum{\boldsymbol{\omega}i \in SL} fr(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) Li(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) (\boldsymbol{\omega}i \cdot \mathbf{n}) where |SL| = 256, \mathbf{n} is the surface normal, and fr is the BRDF. BRDF Model The model uses a simplified Disney BRDF [11] decomposed into diffuse and specular lobes: fr(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = fd(\mathbf{x}) + fs(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) 1. Diffuse Lobe: fd(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1-m(\mathbf{x})}{\pi} \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}) 2. Specular Lobe (Microfacet Model): fs(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) = \frac{D(\boldsymbol{\omega}h) F(\boldsymbol{\omega}o, \boldsymbol{\omega}h) G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \mathbf{n})}{4(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i)(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o)} where \boldsymbol{\omega}h = \frac{\boldsymbol{\omega}o + \boldsymbol{\omega}i}{||\boldsymbol{\omega}o + \boldsymbol{\omega}i||} is the normalized halfway vector. 3. Normal Distribution Function (NDF): Uses a Spherical Gaussian approximation controlled by roughness r: D(\boldsymbol{\omega}h) = \frac{1}{\pi r^4} \exp \left( \frac{2}{r^4}(\boldsymbol{\omega}h \cdot \mathbf{n} - 1) \right) Physics-Based Losses Two novel losses constrain the BRDF: 1. Conservation of Energy Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{cons}}): Enforces that reflected radiance weights do not exceed unity: \mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} = \max \left( \left( \frac{2\pi}{|SL|} \sum{\boldsymbol{\omega}i \in SL} fr (\boldsymbol{\omega}i \cdot \mathbf{n}) \right) - 1, 0 \right) This penalizes physically invalid BRDFs that reflect more energy than received. 2. NDF-weighted Specular Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{spec}}): Promotes separation of specular and diffuse lobes by penalizing the diffuse lobe’s magnitude in specular regions: \mathcal{L}{\text{spec}} = \frac{1}{|SL|} \sum{\boldsymbol{\omega}i \in SL} \operatorname{softmax} \left( \frac{\operatorname{detach}(D(\boldsymbol{\omega}h))}{T{\text{spec}}} \right) fd where T{\text{spec}} is a temperature parameter. The NDF term D(\boldsymbol{\omega}h) is detached from the computation graph to prevent gradient flow through it, ensuring only diffuse contributions update weights. Optimization Phases Optimization proceeds in three phases: 1. Geometry: Train only NeRF SDF with geometry loss \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}}. 2. Material: Train NeILF and BRDF MLPs while freezing NeRF SDF with material loss \mathcal{L}{\text{mat}}. 3. Joint Optimization: Train all fields with total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{mat}}. The material loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{mat}} = \lambda{\text{pbr}}\mathcal{L}{\text{pbr}} + \lambda{\text{ref}}\mathcal{L}{\text{ref}} + \lambda{\text{smth}}\mathcal{L}{\text{smth}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{mat,physics}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{mat,physics}} = \lambda{\text{cons}}\mathcal{L}{\text{cons}} + \lambda{\text{spec}}\mathcal{L}{\text{spec}}. \mathcal{L}{\text{pbr}} is the standard RGB rendering loss, \mathcal{L}{\text{ref}} is the NeILF++ reflection loss, and \mathcal{L}{\text{smth}} is the BRDF smoothness loss. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math NUMLIGHTSAMPLES = 256 def fibonaccisphere(samples=NUMLIGHTSAMPLES): """Generate incident directions using Fibonacci sampling.""" points = [] phi = math.pi (3.0 - math.sqrt(5.0)) for i in range(samples): y = 1.0 - (i / float(samples - 1)) 2.0 radius = math.sqrt(max(1.0 - y y, 0.0)) theta = phi i x = math.cos(theta) radius z = math.sin(theta) radius points.append(torch.tensor([x, y, z])) return torch.stack(points) def sphericalgaussianndf(roughness, costhetah): """Compute NDF D(omegah) using Spherical Gaussian approximation.""" r4 = roughness 4 return (1.0 / (math.pi r4)) torch.exp((2.0 / r4) (costhetah - 1.0)) def computediffusebrdf(albedo, metallicness): """Compute diffuse lobe fd.""" return ((1.0 - metallicness) / math.pi) albedo def computespecularbrdf(roughness, normal, omegai, omegao): """Compute specular lobe fs using microfacet model.""" h = omegao + omegai h = h / torch.norm(h, dim=-1, keepdim=True) costhetah = torch.sum(h normal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) D = sphericalgaussianndf(roughness, costhetah) # Schlick Fresnel approximation F0 = 0.04 + (1.0 - 0.04) torch.clamp(torch.sum(normal normal, dim=-1, keepdim=True), max=1.0) costhetao = torch.sum(omegao normal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) torch.pow(1.0 - costhetao, 5.0) # Schlick-GGX Geometric Occlusion k = (roughness + 1.0) 2 / 8.0 costhetai = torch.sum(omegai normal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) G = 1.0 / (1.0 + k (1.0 / torch.clamp(costhetai, min=1e-8) + 1.0 / torch.clamp(costhetao, min=1e-8) - 2.0)) denom = 4.0 torch.clamp(costhetai, min=1e-8) torch.clamp(costhetao, min=1e-8) return (D F G) / denom def computebrdf(albedo, metallicness, roughness, normal, omegai, omegao): """Compute total BRDF fr.""" fd = computediffusebrdf(albedo, metallicness) fs = computespecularbrdf(roughness, normal, omegai, omegao) return fd + fs def computeenergyconservationloss(brdfvalues, omegai, normal, numsamples): """Compute Conservation of Energy Loss.""" cosi = torch.sum(omegai normal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) sumweights = (2.0 math.pi / numsamples) torch.sum(brdfvalues cosi, dim=0) return torch.relu(sumweights - 1.0) def computespecularloss(roughness, normal, omegai, omegao, albedo, metallicness, numsamples, tempspec): """Compute NDF-weighted Specular Loss.""" h = omegao + omegai h = h / torch.norm(h, dim=-1, keepdim=True) costhetah = torch.sum(h normal, dim=-1, keepdim=True) D = sphericalgaussianndf(roughness, costhetah) Ddetached = D.detach() weights = torch.softmax(Ddetached / tempspec, dim=0) fd = computediffusebrdf(albedo, metallicness) return torch.mean(weights fd) def trainpbrnerf(scenedata, geometrymlp, brdfmlp, neilfmlp, optimizer, numiterations): """Training loop for PBR-NeRF.""" incidentdirections = fibonaccisphere(NUMLIGHTSAMPLES) # Phase 1: Geometry (5K iterations) for i in range(5000): # Ray sampling and forward pass through geometrymlp # Compute geometry loss Lgeo optimizer.zerograd() lossgeo.backward() optimizer.step() # Phase 2: Material (1K iterations) geometrymlp.eval() for i in range(1000): # Ray sampling, forward pass through frozen geometrymlp # Predict materials from brdfmlp, lighting from neilfmlp # Compute rendering Lo and material loss Lmat optimizer.zerograd() lossmat.backward() optimizer.step() # Phase 3: Joint Optimization (30K iterations) lrscheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.StepLR(optimizer, stepsize=10000, gamma=0.2) for i in range(30000): lrscheduler.step() # Ray sampling, forward pass through all MLPs # Compute total loss L = Lgeo + Lmat optimizer.zerograd() losstotal.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters Batch Size: 8192 rays. Learning Rate: 0.002. Fixed for Geometry and Material phases. Decreases by a factor of 5 every 10K iterations during Joint Optimization. Phase Durations: Geometry: 5K iterations; Material: 1K iterations; Joint Optimization: 30K iterations. Loss Weights (NeILF++ Dataset): \lambda{\text{cons}} = 0.01, \lambda{\text{spec}} = 0.5, \lambda{\text{pbr}} = 1. Loss Weights (DTU Dataset): \lambda{\text{cons}} = 0.01, \lambda{\text{spec}} = 0.01. Light Samples: |SL| = 256. Edge Cases and Pitfalls NDF Detachment: In the NDF-weighted Specular Loss, the NDF term D(\boldsymbol{\omega}h) must be detached from the computation graph to prevent gradient flow through it during backpropagation. Lambertian Prior Limitation: Standard NeILF/NeILF++ use a Lambertian prior that suppresses the specular lobe, causing specular effects to appear in the diffuse albedo. Energy Conservation: The Conservation of Energy Loss uses a ReLU-style formulation, allowing reflected irradiance to vary freely as long as it does not exceed incident irradiance. Time Complexity: Training runtime is 3 to 7.5 hours on a single NVIDIA A6000. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the NeILF++ dataset, PBR-NeRF achieves a mean PSNR of 31.27 and SSIM of 87.05 for RGB, outperforming NeILF++ (30.51 PSNR, 86.59 SSIM). It outperforms baselines by 1-3 PSNR on average across albedo, metallicness, and roughness estimation. Strengths: State-of-the-art material estimation without compromising novel view synthesis quality. Faithful albedo estimates consistent across diverse illuminations. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the three-phase optimization and physics-based losses. PBR-NeRF was introduced in the paper "PBR-NeRF: Inverse Rendering with Physics-Based Neural Fields". It builds upon the NeILF/NeILF++ neural fields framework and addresses the limitation of existing NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting approaches that estimate view-dependent appearance without modeling scene materials and illumination. The method introduces two novel physics-based priors: Conservation of Energy and NDF-weighted Specular Losses, to better constrain the inverse rendering estimation. name: Static Semantic Human NeRF
head: H-NeRF (static)
body: Static Semantic Human NeRF (H-NeRF) is a neural rendering method that co-learns a volumetric radiance field for free-viewpoint rendering and a signed distance function (SDF) for 3D geometric reconstruction of a static human subject. It solves the problem of poor generalization and ambiguous opacity fields in standard NeRF when trained on sparse multi-view images of humans, by leveraging an implicit parametric human model (imGHUM) as a geometric prior. Unlike standard NeRF, which relies solely on photometric consistency, H-NeRF couples the radiance field with an SDF to ensure the learned geometry aligns with human anatomy, using a residual SDF network to capture details like clothing and hair that the parametric model misses. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A video sequence of a human in motion captured by Nc calibrated cameras. For each frame t and camera c, the input is the image I{t}^{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h \times 3} and a binary foreground human mask M{t}^{c} \in \{0, 1\}^{w \times h} obtained via a segmentation algorithm. Temporally consistent latent shape \beta and pose codes (\thetat, Tt) for the imGHUM model are also required. Outputs: A radiance field function F\omega predicting color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha, and a signed distance field function \hat{H}\omega predicting distance \hat{d}. Data Structures 1. 3D Bounding Box (\mathcal{B}): Defined by minimal and maximal coordinates [\mathbf{S}-, \mathbf{S}+] of the human body surface \mathcal{S} plus a spatial margin. An indicator function b(\mathbf{x}i) is used: b(\mathbf{x}i) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{B} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 2. imGHUM SDF (H\omega): An implicit articulated 3D human body model where the surface is the zero-isosurface of the signed distance field d(\mathbf{x}|\beta, \theta, T). 3. Residual SDF Network (\Delta H\omega): A lightweight MLP mapping \mathbf{x} \to \Delta d. 4. Composite SDF (\hat{H}\omega): The final SDF is the sum of the imGHUM SDF and the residual: \hat{d}(\mathbf{x}i) = d(\mathbf{x}i|\beta, \theta, T) + \Delta d(\mathbf{x}i) Numbered Steps 1. Preprocessing: For each training image, obtain the binary human mask M{t}^{c} and optimize the imGHUM latent codes (\beta, \thetat, Tt) using multi-view keypoint and body segmentation losses. 2. Define Bounding Box: Compute the 3D bounding box \mathcal{B} enclosing the human body surface \mathcal{S} derived from the imGHUM fit, including a margin for non-modeled geometry. 3. Define Pseudo Alpha: Calculate a pseudo alpha value \dot{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}i) based on the composite SDF \hat{d}(\mathbf{x}i): \dot{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}i) = \phi(\gamma \hat{d}(\mathbf{x}i)) where \phi is the Sigmoid function and \gamma controls boundary sharpness. 4. Render with Masked Points: Compute a rendered color \tilde{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) that only considers points inside the bounding box \mathcal{B}: \tilde{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N b(\mathbf{x}i) \alpha(\mathbf{x}i) \prod{j < i} (1 - b(\mathbf{x}j) \alpha(\mathbf{x}j)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{v}) 5. Render with Blended Alpha: Compute a rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) using the pseudo alpha \dot{\alpha} for points inside \mathcal{B} and the learned NeRF alpha \alpha for points outside \mathcal{B} (or blended as per the specific implementation of \hat{\alpha} described in the source, where \hat{\alpha} replaces \alpha inside \mathcal{B}). Note: The source defines \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) generally as the sum using \hat{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}i), where \hat{\alpha} is the blended alpha value. 6. Optimize: Minimize the total loss function (defined below) with respect to the radiance field parameters \omega and the residual SDF parameters. 7. Test Time Rendering: Use the standard volumetric radiance rendering with the learned NeRF alpha values \alpha (not the pseudo alpha \dot{\alpha}) to support transparency effects and complex geometry like hair. Formulas The total loss is a combination of the following terms: 1. Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{rec}}): Standard L1 loss between observed color \bar{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{L}{\text{rec}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\bar{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|1 2. Mask Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{mask}}): Ensures points outside the bounding box do not contribute to the human mask region: \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r})(\bar{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \tilde{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}))\|1 3. Blend Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{blend}}): Couples the radiance field with the SDF-based pseudo alpha. It forces the rendered color to match the observed color within the human mask using the blended alpha, and matches the background outside the mask: \mathcal{L}{\text{blend}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left( \|\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r})(\bar{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}))\|1 + \eta \|(1 - \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}))(\bar{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}))\|1 \right) Here, \eta is a weight for the background term. 4. Geometry Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{geom}}): Couples the NeRF surface boundary (defined by volume density \sigma) with the SDF zero-isosurface using Binary Cross Entropy (BCE): \mathcal{L}{\text{geom}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N b(\mathbf{x}i) \text{BCE}(\phi(\lambda(\sigmah - \sigma(\mathbf{x}i))), \dot{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}i)) \sigmah is a density threshold, \lambda controls sharpness. 5. Segmentation Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{seg}}): Ensures that if a pixel is inside the human mask, at least one sampled ray point has a non-positive signed distance: \mathcal{L}{\text{seg}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \text{BCE}(\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}), \hat{d}{\min}(\mathbf{r})) \hat{d}{\min}(\mathbf{r}) is the minimal signed distance for all sampled ray points on ray \mathbf{r}. 6. Eikonal Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{eik}}): Enforces the composite SDF \hat{d} to be a valid signed distance function by penalizing deviations of the gradient magnitude from 1: \mathcal{L}{\text{eik}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N b(\mathbf{x}i) (\|\nabla{\mathbf{x}i} \hat{d}(\mathbf{x}i)\|2 - 1)^2 7. Regularization Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}): Regularizes the residual distance \Delta d to be non-positive, ensuring the imGHUM surface remains inside the final geometry and details are added on top: \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \|\psi(\Delta d)\|1 \psi is the ReLU activation. Parameters \eta: Weight for the background term in \mathcal{L}{\text{blend}}. Set to 1 when no other geometry than the person is inside \mathcal{B}. Tune down if the assumption is violated (e.g., person standing on a floor). \gamma: Controls the sharpness of the pseudo alpha boundary. \lambda: Controls the sharpness of the geometry loss coupling. \sigmah: Density threshold for the geometry loss. Typical values for \gamma, \lambda, \sigmah, \eta are not explicitly given in the sources beyond the description of \eta's behavior. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparse Views: Standard NeRF fails to separate the person from the background under sparse training views. H-NeRF addresses this with the bounding box and SDF priors. Complex Geometry: Structures like hair are not well-represented by the parametric imGHUM model. The residual SDF network \Delta H\omega is used to capture these details. Transparency: At test time, the learned NeRF alpha \alpha is used instead of the pseudo alpha \dot{\alpha} to support transparency effects. Background Assumption: The \mathcal{L}{\text{blend}} loss assumes that all background color is formed from ray samples outside \mathcal{B}. If other geometry (like a floor) is inside \mathcal{B}, \eta must be tuned down. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Accurate 3D geometric reconstruction and volume rendering of humans; handles complex geometry like hair via residual SDF; robust to sparse views; co-learns radiance field and SDF for consistent geometry. Limitations: Requires calibrated cameras and initial imGHUM fitting; relies on binary human masks; assumes static human (though the paper title mentions motion, the method described is for the static case with temporally consistent codes). When to use: When accurate geometric reconstruction and high-quality rendering of a human subject is required from sparse multi-view images. When not to use: For dynamic scenes with significant non-human geometry changes within the bounding box without adjusting \eta; for scenes where the human is not the primary subject or is heavily occluded by other geometry inside \mathcal{B}. H-NeRF was introduced in the paper "H-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Rendering and Temporal Reconstruction of Humans in Motion". It builds upon the original NeRF method and integrates the implicit articulated human model imGHUM. The method addresses the limitations of standard NeRF in human reconstruction, specifically the lack of geometric regularization and poor generalization under sparse views. H-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Rendering and Temporal Reconstruction of Humans in Motion, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.13746, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Attention-Based Volumetric Rendering
head: AB Transformer, ABLE-NeRF, Attention-Based Rendering With Learnable Embeddings for Neural Radiance Field, Attention-based Neural Radiance Fields
body: Attention-Based Volumetric Rendering (ABLE-NeRF) replaces the physics-based volumetric rendering (VR) equation with a self-attention mechanism to handle view-dependent effects, glossy surfaces, and translucent objects. Unlike standard NeRF which assigns weights based on density \sigma and interval \delta, ABLE-NeRF uses Transformer attention to determine point importance, and unlike Ref-NeRF which relies on normal prediction, it avoids the ill-posed nature of predicting normals in an object's interior. It sets itself apart from other transformer-based methods (e.g., IBRNet, SRT) by applying transformers directly to model the volumetric rendering approach rather than just for feature aggregation or point proposal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray r(t) = o + td (origin o, direction d), camera pose. Output: Predicted RGB color \mathbf{y} for the ray. Data Structures: Volume Embedding (vi): Latent vector of dimension D. Generated by passing a conic frustum through an embedding block. Ray Token (R): Latent vector of dimension D. Prepended to the sequence of volume embeddings. Learnable Embeddings (LE): Static memory tokens of dimension D. Stored in latent space to capture scene lighting. View Token (V): Latent vector of dimension D. Derived from camera pose. Parameters: N: Number of conic frustum volumes sampled along the ray. Typical value: 96 per network (coarse/fine). L: Number of transformer layers. Typical value: 2 for coarse network, 6 for fine network. D: Latent dimensional size. Typical value: 192. Camera pose encoding: 16-band Fourier features. Steps: 1. Ray Casting and Sampling: Cast a camera ray r(t) = o + td into the scene. Sample N conic frustum volumes along the ray using Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) from mip-NeRF. 2. Volume Embedding: Pass each conic volume through a volume embedding block consisting of four MLP layers (hidden units D, ReLU activation) to generate volume embeddings vi, where i denotes the position along the ray starting from the camera. 3. Sequence Construction: Prepend a Ray token R (dimension D) to the sequence of volume embeddings to form the input sequence Z0 = \{R, v1, v2,..., vN\}. 4. AB Transformer (Direct Lighting): Apply masked self-attention for volume embeddings. A volume embedding vi can only attend to itself, the ray token R, and other volume embeddings lying in front of it (indices < i). Implement masking by setting scaled-dot product attention scores to -\infty in the input of softmax for illegal connections (rear points). Do not apply masking to the ray token R, allowing it to attend to all volume embeddings. Update equations for layer l: v^li = \text{Att}(Z^{l-1} \setminus \{v^{l-1}{i+1},..., v^{l-1}N\}) R^l = \text{Att}(Z^{l-1}) After the final encoder layer L, attach a single MLP classification head to the final ray token RL to predict the color of the ray. 5. Learnable Embeddings (LE) Integration: Incorporate Learnable Embeddings (LE) as learnable memory tokens in latent space to store scene information. Use cross-attention where the LE attends to points sampled during ray casting (volume embeddings) to memorize scene information. During inference, map volume embeddings to latent space via Cross Attention with LE. 6. View-Dependent Decoding (LE Transformer): Decode view-dependent effects using a directional view token V comprising the camera pose. The view token V is a linear mapping of the camera pose encoded with 16-band Fourier features to the LE dimension. The view token queries the Learnable Embeddings to capture view-dependent lighting. 7. Final Output: Separate output into AB Transformer (direct lighting) and LE Transformer (view-dependent lighting). Apply a fixed mapping function to convert to sRGB for final output. Sample N conic frustums along the ray # Assuming tvals are pre-computed based on near/far and IPE tvals = gettvals(rayorigins, raydirections, self.N) xyz = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + tvals.unsqueeze(2) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # 2. Encode with IPE (Integrated Positional Encoding) # Note: IPE encoding is applied to the frustum bounds, resulting in D-dim features # For simplicity, assume xyz is already encoded to D dimensions by an external IPE module volumefeatures = encodewithipe(xyz) # Shape: (B, N, D) # 3. Generate Volume Embeddings vi = self.volumeembedder(volumefeatures) # Shape: (B, N, D) # 4. Construct Sequence Z0 = {R, v1,..., vN} batchsize = xyz.shape[0] R = self.raytoken.expand(batchsize, -1, -1) # Shape: (B, 1, D) Z0 = torch.cat([R, vi], dim=1) # Shape: (B, N+1, D) # 5. AB Transformer (Self-Attention with Mask) # Create causal mask for volume embeddings, but not for Ray Token # Mask shape: (N+1, N+1). # Ray token (index 0) attends to all. # Volume embedding i attends to 0..i. mask = createattentionmask(N+1) Zab = Z0 for layer in self.abtransformer: Zab = layer(Zab, mask=mask) RL = Zab[:, 0,:] # Extract final Ray Token # 6. the sequence being processed as Query. # Let's follow the description: "LE cross-attend to the embedded volumes" # We need to implement Cross Attention manually or via nn.MultiheadAttention # Q: LE, K: vi, V: vi leattnoutput = F.scaleddotproductattention( leinput, vi, vi, attnmask=None # No mask specified for LE cross-attention in text) # Combine LE output with Ray Token output? # The paper says "Separate output into AB Transformer (direct lighting) and LE Transformer (view-dependent lighting)" # And "Apply a fixed mapping function to convert to sRGB for final output" # Final Prediction # The paper states: "After the final encoder layer L, attach a single MLP classification head to the final ray token RL to predict the color" # This suggests the AB Transformer output RL is the primary predictor, potentially enhanced by LE. # However, it also mentions LE Transformer. # Let's assume RL is combined with LE information or RL is the final input to MLP. # Given the ambiguity, we use RL as the primary signal, potentially modified by LE. # A common interpretation in such architectures is that LE refines the representation. # Let's assume RL is passed through the MLP head. color = self.mlphead(RL) # Apply sRGB mapping color = srgbmapping(color) return color class TransformerLayer(nn.Module): def init(self, D, numheads=4, mask=False): super().init() self.numheads = numheads self.mask = mask self.selfattn = nn.MultiheadAttention(D, numheads, batchfirst=True) self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(D) self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(D) self.ffn = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(D, D 3), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(D 3, D)) def forward(self, x, mask=None): # Self Attention attnoutput, = self.selfattn(x, x, x, attnmask=mask) x = self.norm1(x + attnoutput) # Feed Forward ffnoutput = self.ffn(x) x = self.norm2(x + ffnoutput) return x def createattentionmask(N): # N is the sequence length (N+1 including Ray Token) # Ray token (index 0) attends to all. # Volume embedding i (index i+1) attends to 0..i+1. mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(N, N), diagonal=1) mask = mask.bool() # Invert mask for attention (True means mask out) # But PyTorch attnmask expects True to mask out. # We want lower triangular including diagonal. # So upper triangular (excluding diagonal) should be masked. # However, Ray token (0) should attend to all. # So row 0 should be all False (no mask). # Rows 1..N-1 should have mask for columns > rowindex. # Create a mask where True means "do not attend" mask = torch.zeros(N, N, dtype=torch.bool) for i in range(1, N): mask[i, i+1:] = True return mask def encodecameraposefourier(pose, bands=16): # Simplified Fourier encoding for camera pose # Pose is typically (B, 3) or (B, 4) # Apply sin/cos at frequencies 2^0 to 2^(bands-1) freqbands = torch.pow(2, torch.arange(bands, device=pose.device).float()) # Expand pose to (B, 3, 1) and freq to (1, 1, bands) # Result (B, 3, bands) encoded = torch.sin(pose.unsqueeze(2) freqbands torch.pi) # Concatenate sin and cos? The formula in parent says sin and cos. # Here we just use sin for simplicity, or add cos encoded = torch.cat([encoded, torch.cos(pose.unsqueeze(2) freqbands torch.pi)], dim=2) return encoded.flatten(startdim=1) def srgbmapping(color): # Fixed mapping to sRGB # Standard sRGB gamma correction color = torch.clamp(color, 0, 1) return torch.where(color <= 0.0031308, 12.92 color, 1.055 torch.pow(color, 1/2.4) - 0.055) Slot-guided Feature Lifting is a method for learning object-centric radiance fields that encodes scene representations from source views using Slot-Attention, lifts 2D features to 3D to capture fine-grained details, and uses a point-slot mapping to decode 3D representations for rendering color and segmentation masks. It differs from sibling methods like uORF, uOCF, and sVORF by computing only a single radiance field rather than K fields (one per slot), which significantly reduces training time and memory overhead. Time Complexity: High computational cost due to repeated Attention calculations for AB and LE Transformers, leading to long training times. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Learnable Embeddings (LE) and volume embeddings for all sampled points. Measured Performance: On A100 GPU x8 (rendering on A100 x1): 'mic' train 25h, render 59s, PSNR 36.84; 'drums' train 25h, render 59s, PSNR 26.87; 'materials' train 25h, render 59s, PSNR 35.46. Strengths: Significantly reduces 'blurry' glossy surfaces and produces realistic translucent surfaces compared to Ref-NeRF and standard NeRF. Achieves SOTA results on the Blender dataset. Limitations: Long training times due to attention calculations. When to use: When rendering glossy and translucent objects with view-dependent effects is critical. When not to use: When training time is a constraint or when the scene does not exhibit complex view-dependent lighting. Attention-Based Volumetric Rendering (ABLE-NeRF) was introduced by Zhe Jun Tang, Tat-Jen Cham, and Haiyu Zhao in the paper 'ABLE-NeRF: Attention-Based Rendering with Learnable Embeddings for Neural Radiance Field' (arXiv:2303.13817v1, March 2023). It was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF in rendering glossy and transparent surfaces, which often appear murky due to the inherent usage of volumetric rendering (VR) where features are accumulated in the color space. The method draws inspiration from modern game engines that use Light Probes to store local lighting, incorporating Learnable Embeddings to capture view-dependent effects within the scene.
