name: Slot-guided Feature Lifting
head: SlotLifter
body: Slot-guided Feature Lifting is a method for learning object-centric radiance fields that encodes scene representations from source views using Slot-Attention, lifts 2D features to 3D to capture fine-grained details, and uses a point-slot mapping to decode 3D representations for rendering color and segmentation masks. It differs from sibling methods like uORF, uOCF, and sVORF by computing only a single radiance field rather than K fields (one per slot), which significantly reduces training time and memory overhead. Inputs: A set of L source views \{Il\}{l=1}^L (typically L=1 for single-view input) and their associated camera parameters. Outputs: Rendered color images \hat{C}(r) and segmentation masks for a target view. Data Structures: F^{2D}l \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times Df}: 2D feature maps extracted from source view l. S \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times Ds}: Object-centric scene features (slots), where K is the number of objects. P \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}: 3D points sampled along rays in the target view. Ep \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times Dp}: Positional embeddings for 3D points. F{lift} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times L \times Df}: Lifted feature field containing 2D features projected from all source views. Fp \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times Dp}: Final 3D point features. Ap \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}: Attention weights used for density estimation. Wp \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times (K+1)}: Point-slot mapping weights. Steps: 1. Extract 2D Features: Extract feature maps F^{2D}l from each source view Il using a shared encoder network. 2. Slot-Attention Encoding: Obtain object-centric scene features S = \{s1, \dots, sK\} from the 2D features \{F^{2D}l\} using Slot-Attention. The slots are initialized with learnable parameters rather than random sampling to improve optimization. 3. Ray Sampling: For a target view, sample N points P = \{p1, \dots, pN\} along each ray r. 4. Feature Lifting: Project each 3D point p onto the image coordinates \pi(p) of each source view to retrieve corresponding 2D features. Construct the lifted feature field F{lift}: F{lift}(p) = \left[ F^{2D}1[\pi(p)], \dots, F^{2D}L[\pi(p)] \right] where F^{2D}l[\pi(p)] denotes the feature vector at pixel coordinates \pi(p) in view l. 5. Feature Fusion: Pool the multi-view lifted features to obtain 3D point features Fp. For multi-view input: Fp = \text{MLP}\left( \left[ \text{Mean}(F{lift}), \text{Var}(F{lift}) \right] \right) + Ep For single-view input (L=1), ignore the variance term: Fp = \text{MLP}(F{lift}) + Ep Here, Ep preserves spatial information. 6. Random Masking (Training Only): To prevent degenerate reliance on lifted features, randomly mask Fp using only Ep. The masking ratio follows a cosine annealing schedule from 0.99 to 0 over 30,000 steps. 7. Point-Slot Mapping: Calculate point-slot mapping weights Wp using a cross-attention-based allocation transformer between Fp and S. 8. Density Estimation: Compute attention weights Ap for density prediction: Ap = q(Fp) \cdot k(S1)^T where S1 refers to the K object slots (ignoring the empty slot). Estimate density \sigmai for the i-th point: \sigmai = \sum{j=1}^{K+1} Wp^{i,j} \odot \text{ReLU}(Ap^{i,j}) where \odot is the Hadamard product, and the sum includes the empty slot (index K+1). 9. Color Prediction: Add Fp with Ep and pass through an MLP to predict color ci. 10. Volume Rendering: Render the final color \hat{C}(r) using standard volume rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti [1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)] ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) and \deltai is the distance between adjacent volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SlotGuidedFeatureLifting: def init(self, numslots, featuredim, hiddendim): self.K = numslots self.Df = featuredim self.Dp = hiddendim # MLP for feature fusion and color prediction self.fusionmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(2 featuredim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) self.colormlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) # RGB) # Learnable slot initialization self.slots = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(self.K, hiddendim)) # Positional embedding generator (e.g., sine/cosine) self.posembed = PositionalEmbedding(hiddendim) # Masking schedule parameters self.maxmaskratio = 0.99 self.masksteps = 30000 self.currentstep = 0 def extract2dfeatures(self, views): # views: [B, L, H, W, 3] # Returns F2D: [B, L, H, W, Df] # Implementation depends on specific encoder (e.g., ResNet) # Placeholder for encoder logic pass def slotattention(self, f2d): # f2d: [B, L, H, W, Df] # Flatten spatial dims B, L, H, W, Df = f2d.shape fflat = f2d.view(B, L H W, Df) # Slot-Attention mechanism # Standard Slot-Attention implementation: # 1. Initialize slots with self.slots # 2. Attention: q=slots, k=fflat, v=fflat # 3. Update slots with mean-pooled attended values # 4. Return updated slots S: [B, K, Ds] slots = self.slots.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1) # Simplified attention logic for brevity # In practice, use the specific Slot-Attention module from the paper return slots def liftfeatures(self, f2d, points3d, cameraparams): # f2d: [B, L, H, W, Df] # points3d: [B, N, 3] # cameraparams: projection matrices # Returns Flift: [B, N, L, Df] B, N, = points3d.shape L = f2d.shape[1] # Project 3D points to 2D coordinates for each view # Implement projection using camera intrinsics/extrinsics # pi(p) -> (u, v) normalized to [-1, 1] or [0, 1] coords = projectto2d(points3d, cameraparams) # [B, N, 2] # Sample features from F2D using bilinear interpolation # Flift[b, n, l,:] = F2D[b, l, pi(pn)] Flift = torch.zeros(B, N, L, self.Df, device=points3d.device) for l in range(L): # Grid sample F2D[:, l,:,:,:] at coords Flift[:,:, l,:] = gridsample(f2d[:, l,:,:,:], coords) return Flift def fusefeatures(self, Flift, points3d, issingleview=False): # Flift: [B, N, L, Df] # Returns Fp: [B, N, Dp] B, N, L, Df = Flift.shape # Mean pooling over views meanfeat = Flift.mean(dim=2) # [B, N, Df] if not issingleview: # Variance pooling over views varfeat = Flift.var(dim=2) # [B, N, Df] fused = torch.cat([meanfeat, varfeat], dim=-1) # [B, N, 2Df] else: fused = meanfeat # [B, N, Df] # MLP Fp = self.fusionmlp(fused) # [B, N, Dp] # Add positional embeddings Ep = self.posembed(points3d) # [B, N, Dp] Fp = Fp + Ep return Fp def getmaskratio(self): # Cosine annealing from 0.99 to 0 over 30k steps progress = min(self.currentstep / self.masksteps, 1.0) return self.maxmaskratio 0.5 (1 + torch.cos(torch.tensor(progress torch.pi))) def forward(self, views, points3d, cameraparams, issingleview=False): # 1. Extract 2D features F2D = self.extract2dfeatures(views) # 2. Slot-Attention S = self.slotattention(F2D) # [B, K, Ds] # 3. Lift features Flift = self.liftfeatures(F2D, points3d, cameraparams) # 4. Fuse features Fp = self.fusefeatures(Flift, points3d, issingleview) # 5. Random Masking maskratio = self.getmaskratio() if self.training and maskratio > 0: mask = torch.rand(Fp.shape, device=Fp.device) < maskratio # Replace masked features with positional embeddings only Ep = self.posembed(points3d) Fp = torch.where(mask.unsqueeze(-1), Ep, Fp) # 6. Point-Slot Mapping (Simplified) # Implement cross-attention between Fp and S # Ap = q(Fp) @ k(S)^T # Assume q and k are linear projections qfp = Fp @ self.qproj # [B, N, K] ks = S @ self.kproj # [B, K, K] Ap = torch.bmm(qfp, ks.transpose(1, 2)) # [B, N, K] # 7. Density Estimation # sigmai = sum(Wp^{i, 1:K+1} o ReLU(Ap^{i, 1:K+1})) # Wp is obtained from another MLP/Attention # For simplicity, assume Wp is learned or derived from Ap # The paper uses Wp from point-slot mapping module # Here we approximate with softmax of Ap for demonstration Wp = F.softmax(Ap, dim=-1) # [B, N, K] # ReLU on attention weights Aprelu = F.relu(Ap) # Density calculation # Note: Paper sums over K+1 slots (including empty). # Assuming Wp has shape [B, N, K+1] and Ap has [B, N, K+1] # For this implementation, we assume K slots + 1 empty slot # Extend Ap and Wp to K+1 Apext = torch.cat([Aprelu, torch.zeroslike(Ap[:,:,:1])], dim=-1) Wpext = torch.cat([Wp, torch.zeroslike(Wp[:,:,:1])], dim=-1) sigma = torch.sum(Wpext Apext, dim=-1) # [B, N] # 8. Color Prediction # Add Fp with Ep (already done in fusefeatures, but re-add if masked) # Pass into MLP c = self.colormlp(Fp) # [B, N, 3] # 9. Volume Rendering # Standard volume rendering loop # Ti = exp(-sum(sigmaj deltaj)) # C = sum(Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci) # deltai is distance between points # Implement volume rendering pass def step(self): self.currentstep += 1 Parameters: Optimizer: Lion. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-5}. Iterations: 250,000. Batch Size: 4. Sampled Rays: 1,024 rays per scene. Masking Schedule: Cosine annealing from 0.99 to 0 over 30,000 steps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single-View Input: When L=1, the variance term in feature fusion is ignored. The model must handle this branch explicitly. Empty Slot: The density calculation includes an "empty slot" (index K+1) to account for background or unassigned points. This slot is ignored in the slot-attention output S1 but included in the density summation. Degenerate Reliance: Without random masking, the model may rely too heavily on lifted features, ignoring slots. The masking schedule is critical to enforce alignment between slots and 3D point grids. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 30 hours on a single Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU for the Room-Diverse dataset, which is 5x faster than uORF (6 days). Memory Complexity: Uses a single radiance field, whereas uORF, uOCF, and sVORF compute K fields (one per slot), leading to lower memory usage. Strengths: Faster convergence due to feature lifting providing detailed information; efficient rendering with fewer sampled rays (1,024 or even 256) due to no auxiliary losses on fully rendered images. Limitations: Requires Slot-Attention, which may be sensitive to initialization (mitigated by learnable slot initialization). SlotLifter was introduced to improve object-centric radiance field learning by combining Slot-Attention with feature lifting. It addresses the limitations of NeRF, which lacks generalization and requires per-scene optimization. The method builds on Attention-Based Volumetric Rendering by incorporating learnable embeddings and attention mechanisms. It was evaluated on synthetic (CLEVR-567, Room-Chair, Room-Diverse, Room-Texture) and real-world (Kitchen-Shiny, Kitchen-Matte) datasets. SlotLifter: Slot-Guided Feature Lifting for Learning Object-Centric Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72673-615, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Deferred NeRF
head: Def-NeRF, Deferred NeRF Variant (Def-NeRF†)
body: Deferred NeRF is a radiance field optimization method that decouples view-independent geometry and diffuse color from view-dependent specular effects to enable real-time rendering via voxel grid baking. Unlike standard NeRF which predicts final color directly from position and direction, Deferred NeRF separates the rendering equation into an accumulated diffuse component and a residual specular component predicted by a secondary network, allowing the diffuse properties to be stored in a dense 3D grid. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera rays parameterized by origin o and direction d; a pre-trained MLP backbone \Theta (initialized from a non-converged NeRF); background regularization target. Outputs: Final pixel color \hat{C}(r); baked voxel grid containing volume density \sigma, diffuse color c, and specular feature vector v. Data Structures The method utilizes two primary data structures during the training phase: 1. MLP Backbone (\Theta): A fully connected network taking encoded position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d} as input. It outputs three values: diffuse color c, volume density \sigma, and a feature vector v. 2. Tiny MLP (\Phi): A small network taking the accumulated feature vector V(r) and viewing direction d as input to predict the specular color residual. During the baking phase (Def-NeRF†), the outputs are stored in a 3D voxel grid. Each voxel stores: Volume density \sigma (scalar). Diffuse color c (RGB vector). Specular feature vector v (3-dimensional vector). Note: The base SNeRG formulation uses a 4-dimensional vector, but Def-NeRF† reduces this to 3 dimensions to preserve high-frequency lighting details while reducing memory. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the opacity/density prediction MLP from a non-converged NeRF model. Fix the parameters of this backbone MLP (\Theta) to serve as a geometry and diffuse color prior. 2. Feature Extraction: For each sample point i along a ray r at location \mathbf{x}i with viewing direction \mathbf{d}, query the fixed backbone MLP to obtain: ci, \sigmai, vi = \text{MLP}{\Theta}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) where ci is the diffuse color, \sigmai is the volume density, and vi is the feature vector. 3. Accumulation: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti and the accumulated diffuse color \hat{C}d(r) and accumulated feature vector V(r) along the ray using standard volume rendering integration: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) \hat{C}d(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci V(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) vi where \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples. 4. Specular Prediction: Pass the accumulated feature vector V(r) and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} to the tiny MLP \Phi to predict the specular color residual: \hat{C}{spec}(r) = \text{MLP}{\Phi}(V(r), \mathbf{d}) 5. Final Color Composition: Combine the diffuse and specular components to produce the final rendered color: \hat{C}(r) = \hat{C}{spec}(r) + \hat{C}d(r) \hat{C}(r) = \text{MLP}{\Phi}(V(r), \mathbf{d}) + \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci 6. Regularization: Incorporate a background regularization term \mathcal{L}{BG} to ensure the reconstruction focuses on the object of interest and not the background: \mathcal{L}{BG} = - \sum (\log(T{BG}) + \log(1 - T{BG})) where T{BG} is the background transmittance. 7. Optimization: Train the parameters of the tiny MLP \Phi and the feature vectors v (if not baked) using the combined loss. In the Def-NeRF† variant, the backbone \Theta is fixed, and only c, \sigma, and v are learned/updated in the subsequent grid optimization stage. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class DeferredNeRF: def init(self, backbonemlp, tinymlp, numsamples=128): """ backbonemlp: Fixed MLP predicting (c, sigma, v) from (x, d) tinymlp: Trainable MLP predicting specular residual from (V, d) numsamples: Number of samples per ray """ self.backbone = backbonemlp self.tinymlp = tinymlp self.numsamples = numsamples # Freeze backbone parameters for param in self.backbone.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False def forward(self, rayorigins, raydirections, near, far): """ rayorigins: (B, 3) raydirections: (B, 3) near: scalar far: scalar Returns: finalcolor (B, 3), losscomponents """ B = rayorigins.shape[0] device = rayorigins.device # 1. Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., self.numsamples, device=device) zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals # Add noise for anti-aliasing (standard NeRF practice, implied by sampling) midz = 0.5 (zvals[..., 1:] + zvals[...,:-1]) deltaz = midz - zvals[...,:-1] # Expand for batch zvals = zvals.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1) midz = midz.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1) deltaz = deltaz.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1) # 2. Query Backbone for c, sigma, v # x = o + d z points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(1) midz.unsqueeze(2) # points shape: (B, N, 3) # directions shape: (B, 3) -> expand to (B, N, 3) dirs = raydirections.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.numsamples, -1) # Backbone outputs: c (B,N,3), sigma (B,N,1), v (B,N,3) [using 3D v for Def-NeRF†] # Note: Backbone input requires positional encoding if not handled internally. # Assuming backbone handles encoding or inputs are already encoded. backboneout = self.backbone(points, dirs) c = backboneout[...,:3] sigma = backboneout[..., 3:4] v = backboneout[..., 4:7] # 3 dimensions for Def-NeRF† # 3. Volume Rendering Accumulation # Alpha: 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltaz) # Transmittance: Ti = exp(-sum{j<i} sigmaj deltaj) # Compute cumulative sum of sigma delta sigmadelta = sigma deltaz cumsum = torch.cumsum(sigmadelta, dim=1) # Ti = exp(-cumsum{i-1}) # T shape (B, N). T0 = 1.0 T = torch.cat([torch.ones(B, 1, device=device), torch.exp(-cumsum[...,:-1])], dim=1) # Weight: wi = Ti alphai weights = T alpha # Accumulated Diffuse Color: Cd = sum(wi ci) Cd = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=1) # Accumulated Feature Vector: V = sum(wi vi) V = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) v, dim=1) # 4. Predict Specular Residual # tinymlp takes V and d Cspec = self.tinymlp(V, raydirections) # 5. Final Color finalcolor = Cspec + Cd # 6. Background Regularization # TBG is the transmittance after the last sample (background transmittance) TBG = T[:, -1:] LBG = -torch.mean(torch.log(TBG) + torch.log(1.0 - TBG)) return finalcolor, LBG Parameters Feature Vector Dimension: 3 dimensions are used in Def-NeRF† to preserve high-frequency lighting details, reducing memory compared to the 4-dimensional vector in the base SNeRG formulation. Training Duration: Training Def-NeRF† for several epochs is sufficient, as the subsequent Hierarchical Sparse Radiance Grid (HrSRG) optimization stage is robust to imperfect initialization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Initialization: The method relies on a non-converged NeRF initialization for the backbone. Poor geometry initialization can lead to suboptimal results, although the specular features can sometimes be learned from scratch if geometry is good. Background Artifacts: Without the \mathcal{L}{BG} term, the model may fail to reconstruct the object of interest, blending it with the background. The base formulation that introduced the deferred architecture with a 4-dimensional feature vector. Def-NeRF† is a variant that optimizes this for real-time baking. The data structure used to bake the Deferred NeRF outputs for real-time rendering. It exploits hierarchical voxel spaces to store \sigma, c, and v. Time Complexity: Training involves two stages: initial MLP training (fixed backbone) and subsequent optimization of the tiny MLP and grid parameters. The baking process requires querying the MLP for every voxel, which is computationally intensive but performed once. Memory Complexity: The baked representation stores \sigma, c, and a 3D feature vector v per voxel. This is significantly more memory-efficient than storing full NeRF weights for real-time inference, but requires a dense or sparse voxel grid. Strengths: Enables real-time rendering by baking view-independent properties into a grid; separates geometry/diffuse from specular effects for better detail preservation. Limitations: Requires a pre-training step; the quality of the baked grid depends on the accuracy of the initial NeRF geometry. When to use: When real-time view synthesis is required and the scene can be represented by a voxel grid, particularly when high-frequency lighting details need to be preserved. Deferred NeRF, specifically the SNeRG formulation, was introduced to address the difficulty of baking view-dependent colors into a voxel grid, which is non-trivial because standard NeRF relies on viewing direction (\theta, \phi) to encode view-dependent effects. The method was developed to enable real-time rendering by separating the radiance field into deferred components. The Def-NeRF† variant was proposed in the context of the "Digging into Radiance Grid for Real-Time View Synthesis with Detail Preservation" paper to optimize this architecture for hierarchical sparse voxel grids. Digging into Radiance Grid for Real-Time View Synthesis with Detail Preservation, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19784-042, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Surface Reconstruction and Rendering for LiDAR-Visual Systems
head: M2Mapping
body: M2Mapping is a method that integrates LiDAR-derived occupancy maps with neural radiance fields (NeRF) and signed distance fields (SDF) to reconstruct geometry and render appearance for LiDAR-visual systems. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF approaches by using visible-aware occupancy classification to handle unknown spaces and structure-aware sampling to adaptively capture sharp geometric details, particularly for slim objects. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: LiDAR point clouds (used to build the occupancy map), camera images, camera intrinsics, and extrinsics. Outputs: Reconstructed 3D mesh (geometry) and rendered RGB images (appearance). Data Structures Occupancy Map: A 3D grid representing the environment with states: free, occupied, and unknown. The unknown state is further classified into visible unknown and invisible unknown based on visibility from camera viewpoints. Neural Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architecture. SDF Network (fS): Takes 3D position \mathbf{x} as input and outputs a signed distance value \hat{s} and a scale parameter \hat{\beta}. Color Network (fC): Takes encoded position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input and outputs view-dependent color \hat{\mathbf{c}}. Encoding The method uses two distinct encoding strategies for the input coordinates: 1. Hash Encoding: Applied to the 3D position \mathbf{x} for multi-resolution feature encoding. 2. Spherical Harmonics Encoding: Applied to the viewing direction \mathbf{d} for directional encoding. These encodings are concatenated before being fed into the respective MLPs. Numbered Steps 1. Classify unknown grid states in the occupancy map into visible unknown and invisible unknown via pixel ray casting from camera images. A grid is visible unknown if it is visible from the camera without any occupied grid in between. 2. Sample points along a pixel ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} from the camera origin \mathbf{o} in direction \mathbf{d} using structure-aware sampling. 3. Encode sample positions and view directions using hash and spherical harmonics encodings, respectively. 4. Query the SDF network to obtain \hat{s}k and \hat{\beta}k at each sample point \mathbf{x}k. 5. Compute volume density \hat{\sigma}k from the SDF output and ray direction. 6. Query the color network with concatenated encoded features to obtain \hat{\mathbf{c}}k. 7. Render the pixel color \hat{\mathbf{C}} by volume rendering blending the samples' colors and densities. Formulas The volume rendering equation blending colors and densities is: \hat{\mathbf{C}} = \sum{k} \left( \prod{j<k} \exp(-\hat{\sigma}j \deltaj) \right) (1 - \exp(-\hat{\sigma}k \deltak)) \hat{\mathbf{c}}k where \deltak = t{k+1} - tk is the distance between adjacent samples, and \hat{\sigma}k is the density. This abbreviates to \hat{\mathbf{C}} = \sum{k} Tk \alphak \hat{\mathbf{c}}k, where \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\hat{\sigma}k \deltak) is the opacity and Tk = \prod{j<k} \exp(-\hat{\sigma}j \deltaj) is the transmittance. Density is derived from the SDF output using the gradient of the signed distance value along the ray direction (slope): \hat{\sigma}k = \max \left( - \frac{\Phi(-\hat{s}k, \hat{\beta}k) \frac{\partial \hat{s}k}{\partial \mathbf{x}k} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\hat{\beta}k}, 0 \right) where \frac{\partial \hat{s}k}{\partial \mathbf{x}k} is the gradient of the SDF at \mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, and \Phi is the derivative of the cumulative distribution function used for SDF rendering (Gaussian PDF). Parameters Number of samples per ray: Not given in the sources. Hash encoding levels and grid resolutions: Not given in the sources. Spherical harmonics degree: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The density computation involves exponentials and gradients; numerical stability requires clamping \hat{\beta}k away from zero and handling negative slopes correctly. Boundaries: The last sample's delta must be large enough to ensure full ray coverage, otherwise transmittance will not decay to zero. Degenerate Input: If the ray direction \mathbf{d} is zero or unnormalized, the slope calculation fails; rays must be normalized before rendering. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gaussianpdf(x): """Standard Gaussian probability density function.""" return np.exp(-0.5 x2) / np.sqrt(2 np.pi) def computedensityfromsdf(sdfvalue, sdfscale, sdfgradient, raydirection): """Computes volume density from SDF output using the source formula.""" slope = np.dot(sdfgradient, raydirection) # Phi is the derivative of the Gaussian CDF, i.e., the Gaussian PDF phifactor = gaussianpdf(-sdfvalue / sdfscale) / sdfscale density = max(- (phifactor slope) / sdfscale, 0.0) return density def computesdfgradients(sdfnetwork, points): """Computes SDF gradients via finite differences for self-containment.""" eps = 1e-4 grad = np.zeroslike(points) for i in range(3): pplus = points.copy() pplus[:, i] += eps pminus = points.copy() pminus[:, i] -= eps grad[:, i] = (sdfnetwork(pplus)[:, 0] - sdfnetwork(pminus)[:, 0]) / (2 eps) return grad def renderpixel(cameraorigin, cameradirection, occupancymap, sdfnetwork, colornetwork, hashencoder, shencoder, numsamples, near, far): """Renders a single pixel using M2Mapping.""" # 1. Structure-aware sampling (linear spacing as placeholder for occupancy-guided strategy) sampledistances = np.linspace(near, far, numsamples) # 2. Get sample points samplepoints = cameraorigin + sampledistances[:, np.newaxis] cameradirection # 3. Encode inputs posfeatures = hashencoder(samplepoints) dirfeatures = shencoder(cameradirection) # 4. Predict SDF and Color sdfoutputs = sdfnetwork(posfeatures) sdfvalues = sdfoutputs[:, 0] sdfscales = sdfoutputs[:, 1] sdfgradients = computesdfgradients(sdfnetwork, posfeatures, samplepoints) colorinput = np.concatenate([posfeatures, dirfeatures], axis=-1) colors = colornetwork(colorinput) # 5. Compute densities densities = np.zeros(numsamples) for k in range(numsamples): densities[k] = computedensityfromsdf(sdfvalues[k], sdfscales[k], sdfgradients[k], cameradirection) # 6. Volume Rendering deltas = np.diff(sampledistances) deltas = np.append(deltas, 1e10) # Ensure last delta covers remaining ray alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(-densities deltas) transmittances = np.ones(numsamples + 1) for k in range(numsamples): transmittances[k+1] = transmittances[k] np.exp(-densities[k] deltas[k]) transmittances = transmittances[:-1] weights = alphas transmittances renderedcolor = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colors, axis=0) return renderedcolor Strengths: Captures more precise geometric details in slim objects compared to standard NeRF. Retains both structure and texture in extrapolation rendering. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the LiDAR-derived occupancy map. The specific implementation details of "structure-aware sampling" and the exact SDF-to-density conversion function \Phi are not fully detailed in the provided notes, requiring reference to the original paper. Performance: Not given in the sources. M2Mapping was introduced in the paper "Neural Surface Reconstruction and Rendering for LiDAR-Visual Systems". It is designed for generalized LiDAR-visual systems, leveraging the strong geometric priors from LiDAR point clouds (occupied, free, unknown spaces) to improve NeRF training. The method was developed by researchers associated with HKU-MARS. Neural Surface Reconstruction and Rendering for LiDAR-Visual Systems, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05310v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: CRAYM
head: Neural Field Optimization via Camera RAY Matching
body: CRAYM is a method for 3D neural field optimization that jointly optimizes camera poses and an implicit field to handle noisy camera poses. It constructs a 3D feature volume V and optimizes it by matching rays across different images, using key rays for structural constraints and auxiliary rays for local context. Unlike standard NeRF approaches that assume known poses, CRAYM parameterizes transformation matrices as variables in the joint optimization, allowing it to recover geometry and appearance even when initial pose estimates are inaccurate. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of input images, initial camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics), and initial sparse keypoint matches between image pairs. Outputs: A 3D feature volume V, optimized camera poses, and a trained geometry network \Phig and texture network \Phit for novel view synthesis or 3D reconstruction. Data Structures 1. Feature Volume V: Represented using multi-resolution hash encoding. It stores features for 3D points. 2. Progressive Feature Mask M: A mask used to filter out fine-level features during early iterations of coarse-to-fine training. 3. Key Rays \{rk\}: Rays issued from cameras through pixel centers associated with surface points having rich textures and sharp features. Obtained by detecting keypoints using SuperPoint and performing point-to-point matching using SuperGlue. 4. Auxiliary Rays \{ra\}: Rays sampled around keypoints to provide contextual or local structural information. 5. Geometry Network \Phig: Takes a 3D point p and its feature as input to produce an SDF value and opaque density \sigma. 6. Texture Network \Phit: Takes output features from \Phig, ray directions, and normal at p as inputs to predict color \mathbf{c}(p). Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the feature volume V using multi-resolution hash encoding. Initialize camera poses as variables for joint optimization. Initialize networks \Phig and \Phit. 2. Ray Selection: Detect keypoints on input images using SuperPoint and match them using SuperGlue to obtain key rays \{rk\}. Sample auxiliary rays \{ra\} around the keypoints. 3. Feature Extraction: For a 3D point p, extract its feature f(p) from the volume: f(p) = M(V(p)) where V(p) is the value in the feature volume at p and M is the progressive feature mask. 4. Key Rays Enrichment (KRE): For each point pk along a key ray rk: Sample points qj around pk along the j-th auxiliary ray. Fuse features using function g to get the enriched feature f'(pk): f'(pk) = \sumj g(f(pk), f(qj)) where g fuses the feature of the key ray point and the auxiliary ray points. 5. Geometry Prediction: Pass the enriched feature f'(pk) and point pk to the geometry network \Phig to predict the SDF value and feature vector f''(pk), from which opaque density \sigma is derived. 6. Color Prediction: Pass the output features from \Phig, ray direction, and normal at pk to the texture network \Phit to predict color \mathbf{c}(pk). 7. Joint Optimization: Optimize the feature volume V, camera poses, and networks \Phig, \Phit end-to-end. The Matched Rays Coherency (MRC) module is used to enhance rendering quality by maintaining coherency between matched key rays and disambiguating imprecise matchings. Parameters Multi-resolution hash encoding: Used for V. Progressive feature mask M: Filters fine-level features in early training. Camera poses: Parameterized as variables. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def craysmstep(images, initialposes, superpointmatches): # 1. Initialize structures V = MultiResolutionHashEncoding() M = ProgressiveFeatureMask() Phig = GeometryNetwork() Phit = TextureNetwork() poses = Parameterize(initialposes) # Variables for joint optimization # 2. Ray Selection keypoints = SuperPoint(images) keyraymatches = SuperGlue(keypoints) keyrays = [Ray(origin=pose.o, direction=pose.d) for pose, match in keyraymatches] auxrays = SampleAuxiliaryRays(keyrays) # 3. Joint Optimization Loop (simplified) for iteration in range(numiterations): loss = 0 for rk in keyrays: # Sample points along key ray pk = SamplePointAlongRay(rk) # Feature Extraction fpk = M(V(pk)) # Key Rays Enrichment faux = [] for ra in auxraysaround(rk, pk): qj = SamplePointAlongRay(ra) fqj = M(V(qj)) faux.append(fqj) # Fuse features (g is a fusion function, e.g., concatenation + MLP) fprimepk = FuseFeatures(fpk, faux) # Geometry Prediction sdf, fdoubleprimepk = Phig(pk, fprimepk) sigma = DensityFromSDF(sdf) # Color Prediction normal = NormalFromSDF(sdf) color = Phit(fdoubleprimepk, rk.direction, normal) # Compute loss (rendering loss + coherency loss + pose regularization) loss += ComputeLoss(color, gtcolor) # Update all parameters Update(poses, V, Phig, Phit, loss) return V, poses, Phig, Phit Strengths: Robust to noisy camera poses; handles occlusion and unreliable matching better than methods assuming perfect poses. Limitations: Requires keypoint detection and matching (SuperPoint/SuperGlue), which may fail in textureless regions. Joint optimization increases computational complexity and training time compared to fixed-pose NeRF. Performance: Not given in the sources. When to use: When camera poses are noisy or unknown, and the scene has sufficient texture for keypoint matching. When not to use: When poses are known with high accuracy, or the scene is textureless. CRAYM was proposed to address the failure of existing approaches at high noise levels in camera poses. It builds on the idea of mapping rays to density and color implicitly but introduces ray matching across images to formulate geometric priors. The method uses multi-resolution hash encoding for the feature volume and joint optimization of poses and the implicit field. CRAYM: Neural Field Optimization via Camera RAY Matching, https://core.ac.uk/works/318675119, fetched 2026-10-31

name: ColNeRF
head: Collaboration for Generalizable Sparse Input Neural Radiance Field, Collaborative Neural Radiance Fields
body: ColNeRF is a generalizable sparse-input neural radiance field method that achieves accurate 3D modeling with color and geometric consistency without auxiliary supervision. It sets itself apart from siblings like PixelNeRF by replacing direct pixel feature averaging with Collaborative Cross-View Volume Integration (CCVI) to implicitly correct occluded regions, and from methods like DS-NeRF by using self-supervised ray regularization instead of inaccurate depth labels. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sparse set of source images Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} and their corresponding camera extrinsics Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4} for i=1 \dots N. Outputs: Predicted volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c} for points along rays, rendered into novel view images. Data Structures 1. Feature Pyramid: Extracted from a pre-trained ResNet34 encoder. Feature maps are taken before the first pooling operation and after the first three ResNet stages. These are upsampled to H/2 \times W/2 and concatenated. The resulting feature volume has dimensions 512 \times H/2 \times W/2. 2. Affined Feature Volume (Ff): The output of the CCVI module, with dimensions Hv \times Wv \times d (where d=512). 3. Neural Radiance Network: A fully connected ResNet architecture with 5 blocks and width 512. Positional Encoding The input 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) are encoded using \gamma(\mathbf{x}). The view direction \mathbf{d} is not position encoded. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \omega \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \omega \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \omega \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \omega \mathbf{x})) Parameters: L=6, \omega=1.5. The output is a 39-dimensional vector. Numbered Steps 1. Feature Extraction: Extract feature volumes Fv \in \mathbb{R}^{Hv \times Wv \times d} from each source view Ii using the ResNet34 encoder. 2. Collaborative Cross-View Volume Integration (CCVI): For each anchor view i, compute the affined feature volume F{fi}: Define anchor F{anc} = F{iv} and auxiliary sum F{aux} = \sum{j \neq i} F{jv}. Concatenate [F{anc}, F{aux}] and apply a convolutional layer to reduce dimensions to 512, yielding \hat{F}{aux}. Patch Expansion: To allow information exchange between adjacent blocks, expand the Query (Q) and Key (K) volumes. Block size becomes (s + 2a) \times (s + 2a). Band pixels are copied from neighboring blocks if they exist, otherwise zero-padded. Expansion is not applied to Value (V). DTU parameters: patch size s=5, band width a=3. LLFF parameters: patch size s=9, band width a=3. Compute Attention: Q = WQ(\hat{F}{aux}), \quad K = WK(\hat{F}{aux}), \quad V = WV(F{anc}) \text{AVGI}(F{anc}, \hat{F}{aux}) = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{dk}}\right) V where dk is the feature channel dimension. Compute Feed-Forward Network (FFN) output: \hat{F}{anc} = \text{AVGI}(F{anc}, \hat{F}{aux}) + F{anc} F{fi} = \text{FFN}(\hat{F}{anc}) + \hat{F}{anc} The FFN consists of two convolutional layers. 3. Ray Sampling: Coarse Stage: Partition the ray range [tn, tf] into 64 evenly-spaced bins. Draw one sample uniformly at random from within each bin: tn + \frac{i}{N}(tf - tn). Fine Stage: Use the outcomes of the coarse network to determine sampling probability density for refinement. Training Ray Selection: Sample 128 rays per iteration. 112 are randomly emitted. The remaining 16 are reference rays. Additionally, 16 adjacent rays are sampled with up to 7 pixel offset from reference rays for regularization. 4. Feature Interpolation: For each sampled point \mathbf{x} on a target ray, project it onto the affined feature volumes F{fi} of all N source views using camera parameters \pi. Extract local features via bilinear interpolation: f{pi} = \text{Interpolate}(F{fi}(\pi(\mathbf{x}))) Average the local features: \rho = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N f{pi}. 5. Radiance Prediction: Feed the encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}), direction \mathbf{d}, and averaged features \rho into the Neural Radiance Network F\theta: F\theta(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}, \rho) = (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) The network fuses pixel features with coordinates/directions in the first three ResNet blocks, averages across the N views after the third block, and fuses further in the final two blocks. 6. Ray Regularization: Compute loss components for geometry and appearance consistency. Geometry Regularization (L{geo}): Pair adjacent target rays ri and \hat{r}i. Minimize L1 loss of predicted depths D(r), masked by cumulative density Q(r): L{geo} = \sum{i=1}^{N{pairs}} M(ri) \odot |D(ri) - D(\hat{r}i)| D(ri) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t)\sigma(ri(t))t dt, \quad T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^t \sigma(ri(s))ds\right) Mask M(ri) = 1 if Q(ri) \ge \tau and Q(\hat{r}i) \ge \tau, else 0. \tau = 0.1. Appearance Regularization (L{app}): Minimize KL-divergence between color distributions of target rays and pseudo-label rays \hat{r}i (derived from epipolar line averaging): L{app} = \sum{i=1}^{Nr} \sum{j=1}^{Np} \frac{pc(M'(c(r{i,j})))}{pc(M(c(r{i,j})))} \log \frac{pc(M'(c(r{i,j})))}{pc(M'(c(\hat{r}{i,j})))} Mask M' excludes points where homography coordinate \epsilon(r{i,j}) > \epsilon{max}. 7. Volume Rendering: Aggregate final RGB values C(r) using classical volume rendering principles. 8. Loss Computation: L{total} = L{rec} + \lambda1 L{geo} + \lambda2 L{app} \lambda1 = 10^{-4}, \lambda2 = 2 \times 10^{-4}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ColNeRF: def init(self, encoder, nerfnet, patchsizes, bandwidtha, tau=0.1): self.encoder = encoder # ResNet34 self.nerfnet = nerfnet # 5-block ResNet MLP self.s = patchsizes self.a = bandwidtha self.tau = tau self.L = 6 self.omega = 1.5 self.lambdageo = 1e-4 self.lambdaapp = 2e-4 def positionalencoding(self, x): # x shape: (batch, 3) # Only encode spatial coordinates, not direction freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(self.L, device=x.device).float() scaledx = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands self.omega s = torch.sin(scaledx) c = torch.cos(scaledx) # Concatenate sin/cos for each band encoded = torch.cat([s, c], dim=-1) # (batch, 3 2 L) = (batch, 36) # Note: Source says 39-dim. 3 coords 12 freqs = 36. # Source states "39 dimension coordinate vector". # PixelNeRF usually uses 3 + 32L = 39 if original coords are concatenated. return torch.cat([x, encoded], dim=-1) def extractfeatures(self, images): # images: (N, 3, H, W) # ResNet34 feature pyramid extraction # Take features before first pool and after first 3 stages # Upsample to H/2 x W/2 and concatenate -> (N, 512, H/2, W/2) features = self.encoder(images) return features def ccvi(self, anchorfeatures, auxfeatures): # anchorfeatures: (B, 512, H, W) # auxfeatures: (B, 512, H, W) summed from other views # 1. Concat and reduce dim concat = torch.cat([anchorfeatures, auxfeatures], dim=1) # (B, 1024, H, W) auxreduced = self.convreduce(concat) # (B, 512, H, W) # 2. Prepare Q, K, V # Q, K from auxreduced, V from anchor Q = self.WQ(auxreduced) K = self.WK(auxreduced) V = self.WV(anchorfeatures) # 3. Patch Expansion for Q and K # Expand patch size from s to s+2a Qexpanded = self.expandpatches(Q, self.s, self.a) Kexpanded = self.expandpatches(K, self.s, self.a) # V is not expanded # 4. Attention # Compute attention at patch level attn = F.softmax(torch.matmul(Qexpanded, Kexpanded.transpose(-2, -1)) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(Qexpanded.shape[-1])), dim=-1) out = torch.matmul(attn, V) # 5. Residual and FFN # Note: Dimensions must be handled carefully in implementation # Simplified representation of the residual connection and FFN Fhat = out + anchorfeatures Faffined = self.ffn(Fhat) + Fhat return Faffined def expandpatches(self, volume, s, a): # Expand each patch by band 'a' # If neighbor exists, copy; else zero-pad # Implementation detail: Pad volume, then select patches pass def samplerays(self, numrays=128): # Random scene selection # 112 random rays, 16 reference rays # 16 adjacent rays with offset <= 7 pixels rays = [] #... logic to generate origins and directions return rays def render(self, rays, affinedvolumes): # 1. Sample points along rays (Coarse: 64 bins stratified) # 2. Project points to source views # 3. Interpolate features from affinedvolumes # 4. Average features # 5. Encode position, pass through NERF net # 6. Volume render pass def computeloss(self, renderedrgb, gtrgb, rays, affinedvolumes): Lrec = F.mseloss(renderedrgb, gtrgb) # Geometry Regularization # Pair adjacent rays Lgeo = 0 for ri, rhati in pairedrays: # Compute cumulative density Q Qi = computecumulativedensity(ri) Qhat = computecumulativedensity(rhati) mask = (Qi >= self.tau) & (Qhat >= self.tau) depthi = computeexpecteddepth(ri) depthhat = computeexpecteddepth(rhati) Lgeo += torch.sum(mask torch.abs(depthi - depthhat)) # Appearance Regularization Lapp = 0 for ri, rhati in pairedrays: # Pseudo-label from epipolar lines # KL divergence between color distributions pass Ltotal = Lrec + self.lambdageo Lgeo + self.lambdaapp Lapp return Ltotal Time Complexity: Training requires no more than 15K fine-tuning iterations per scene, compared to FreeNeRF's 250K iterations. Memory Complexity: Uses a single model for all scenes, reducing storage overhead compared to per-scene optimization methods. Performance: On DTU 3-view, achieves PSNR 19.55, SSIM 0.716, LPIPS 0.362. On LLFF 3-view, achieves PSNR 20.97, SSIM 0.587, LPIPS 0.447. Data Efficiency: Requires 51% fewer images than NeRF and 35% fewer images than PixelNeRF to achieve similar performance on DTU. Strengths: Handles sparse inputs effectively; corrects blurriness and shape distortion common in direct averaging methods; ensures multi-view consistency without auxiliary depth/semantic data. Limitations: Performance may degrade if ray casting is too concentrated, leading to overfitting (mitigated by random sampling). ColNeRF was introduced as a generalizable sparse input neural radiance field method. It builds on the experimental settings of PixelNeRF (Yu et al. 2021). The DTU dataset is from Jensen et al. 2014, and LLFF scenes are from Mildenhall et al. 2019 and 2021. It addresses limitations in methods like PixelNeRF (blurriness from direct averaging) and DS-NeRF (inaccuracy of COLMAP depth labels). ColNeRF: Collaboration for Generalizable Sparse Input Neural Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.09095, fetched 2026-10-29

name: VolSDF Model Architecture
head: VolSDF Training, Volume Rendering of Neural Implicit Surfaces, Volume Rendering of Neural Implicit Surfaces training
body: VolSDF is a volume rendering framework for neural implicit surfaces that represents volume density as a transformed version of the signed distance function (SDF) to the learned surface geometry, allowing disentanglement of geometry (density) and radiance field. Unlike IDR, which requires object masks and sets pixel color based on a single intersection point leading to extraneous surface parts, VolSDF does not require masks and uses the volume rendering integral to avoid this issue. It builds on Model Architecture and Encoding by replacing the standard density prediction with an SDF-based density transformation. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of images with camera parameters. For each pixel p, the input triplet is (Ip, \mathbf{c}p, \mathbf{v}p), where Ip \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the intensity (RGB), \mathbf{c}p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the camera location, and \mathbf{v}p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the viewing direction (from camera to pixel). Outputs: Rendered RGB images and a reconstructed 3D surface geometry defined by the SDF. Data Structures The model consists of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) and two scalar parameters: 1. Geometry MLP (f\varphi): Approximates the SDF d(\mathbf{x}) and a global geometry feature vector \mathbf{z}. Input: Position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Tuple (d(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x})) \in \mathbb{R}^{1+256}. The feature vector \mathbf{z} has dimension 256. Parameters: \varphi. 2. Radiance Field MLP (L\psi): Represents the scene's radiance field. Input: Position \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, viewing direction \mathbf{v}, and geometry feature \mathbf{z}. Output: RGB color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: \psi. 3. Scalar Parameters: Two learnable scalars \alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}. In implementation, \alpha = \beta^{-1} is enforced. 4. Total Parameters: \theta = (\varphi, \psi, \beta). Positional Encoding Positional encoding [25] is exploited for the position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{v} in both the geometry and radiance field MLPs, following the shared principles of the parent article. Density Transformation The volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) is derived from the SDF d(\mathbf{x}) predicted by f\varphi. The specific transformation formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided text, but it is defined as a "transformed version of the signed distance function". The scalar parameter \beta (and \alpha) controls this transformation. Rendering Rendering follows the standard volume rendering integral using samples along the ray. The radiance Li at sample point si is computed as: Li = L\psi(\mathbf{x}(si), \mathbf{n}(si), \mathbf{v}p, \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}(si))) where \mathbf{n}(si) is the normal derived from the gradient of the SDF. Training Procedure The model is trained using a batch size of 1024 pixels. The loss function includes: 1. Photometric Loss: Comparing rendered images to ground truth Ip. 2. SDF Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{SDF}}): An Eikonal loss encouraging d to approximate a signed distance function. 3. Sampling Strategy: Samples \mathbf{z} for the Eikonal loss are taken from a combination of a single random uniform space point and a single point from the set \mathcal{S} (samples along the ray) for each pixel p. 4. Hyperparameters: The weight \lambda for the SDF loss is set to 0.1. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainvolsdf(images, cameras, numepochs=1000, batchsize=1024, lambdasdf=0.1): # Initialize models fphi = GeometryMLP() # Outputs (d, z) Lpsi = RadianceMLP() # Outputs color beta = Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0)) # Scalar parameter alpha = 1.0 / beta # Enforce alpha = beta^-1 optimizer = Adam([fphi.parameters(), Lpsi.parameters(), beta]) for epoch in range(numepochs): # Sample batch of pixels batchpixels = samplepixels(images, batchsize) totalloss = 0 for pixel in batchpixels: Igt = pixel.intensity ccam = pixel.cameralocation vview = pixel.viewingdirection # Generate ray and sample points rayo, rayd = generateray(ccam, vview) samplesx, samplest = samplealongray(rayo, rayd) # Forward pass through Geometry MLP # Note: Positional encoding is applied to samplesx and vview dvals, zvals = fphi(samplesx) # Compute normals from SDF gradient (not shown in detail,) normals = computesdfgradient(dvals, samplesx) # Compute density from SDF using beta # Formula not explicitly given, but d is transformed sigmas = transformsdftodensity(dvals, beta) # Forward pass through Radiance MLP colors = Lpsi(samplesx, normals, vview, zvals) # Volume rendering to get rendered color Irender = volumerender(samplest, sigmas, colors) # Photometric loss lossphoto = mse(Irender, Igt) # SDF Loss (Eikonal) # Requires combining random uniform point and ray sample randompoint = sampleuniforminbounds() drandom, zrandom = fphi(randompoint) gradrandom = computesdfgradient(drandom, randompoint) losseikonal = mse(norm(gradrandom), 1.0) # Combine losses loss = lossphoto + lambdasdf losseikonal totalloss += loss # Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Complexity: Time complexity is dominated by the two MLP evaluations per sample point along the ray. Memory complexity is proportional to the number of parameters in the two MLPs and the stored features. Performance: On the DTU dataset, VolSDF is on par with IDR (which uses object masks) and outperforms NeRF and COLMAP in reconstruction accuracy. Rendering quality is comparable to NeRF. On BlendedMVS, it provides more faithful results than IDR without requiring ground truth masks. Strengths: Disentangles geometry and appearance; does not require object masks for training; avoids extraneous surface parts common in mask-based methods like IDR. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the SDF approximation; performance depends on the choice of positional encoding. VolSDF was introduced in the paper "Volume Rendering of Neural Implicit Surfaces". It addresses the limitations of previous implicit surface methods like IDR, which required segmentation masks and suffered from extraneous geometry. The method leverages the properties of Signed Distance Functions to regularize the neural network's output, ensuring the predicted density corresponds to a valid surface geometry. It is used for multi-view 3D surface reconstruction on datasets like DTU and BlendedMVS. name: Hierarchical and Sparse Grid Representations
head: Grid-based NeRF, Voxel-based NeRF, Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) in NeRF
body: Hierarchical and Sparse Grid Representations discretize 3D space into learnable structures (grids, octrees, or hash tables) to store density and feature vectors, enabling efficient differentiable querying via interpolation. Unlike coordinate-based MLPs that map coordinates to color directly, this family decouples spatial storage from decoding, allowing for faster rendering and explicit scene manipulation. It distinguishes itself from sibling planar representations (e.g., Triplanes) by maintaining full 3D spatial coherence and from pure neural implicit methods by providing an explicit, queryable data structure that can be sparsified or binarized for efficiency. The family shares a mechanism of discretizing 3D space into learnable structures and querying them via differentiable interpolation. Discretization The 3D scene space is divided into voxels organized in a hierarchy (e.g., coarse-to-fine levels, octrees) or a regular tensor \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}. Feature Storage Each voxel (or octree node) stores learnable parameters, which may include: Volume density \sigma. Latent feature vectors f or e used to decode color or SDF. Binary values \{-1, +1\} for compressed storage. Differentiable Query For a query point \mathbf{x}, values are retrieved via interpolation. Standard trilinear interpolation is used for 3D grids: f(\mathbf{x}) = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}) where \mathbf{V} is the feature grid. This operation is differentiable, allowing gradients to flow back to the grid values during optimization. Decoding Interpolated features are passed to a small decoder network (typically an MLP) S\Theta to predict final outputs like color \mathbf{c} or SDF s: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) = S\Theta(\text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}a)). Voxel and Grid Representations discretize 3D space into learnable structures (grids, octrees, or hash tables) to store density and feature vectors, enabling efficient differentiable querying via interpolation. Unlike coordinate-based MLPs that map coordinates to color directly, this family decouples spatial storage from decoding, allowing for faster rendering and explicit scene manipulation. It distinguishes itself from sibling planar representations (e.g., Triplanes) by maintaining full 3D spatial coherence and from pure neural implicit methods by providing an explicit, queryable data structure that can be sparsified or binarized for efficiency. Voxel and Grid Representations Triplane and Planar Representations encode 3D scenes using a set of learnable 2D feature grids (planes) aligned with the canonical coordinate axes, rather than a 3D voxel grid. This approach reduces memory complexity from cubic to linear relative to resolution while maintaining high fidelity. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D voxel grids by leveraging 2D convolutions for efficient feature aggregation and from pure MLPs by avoiding local minima issues associated with high-resolution spatial queries. It serves as a generative backbone for state-of-the-art 3D-aware GANs and efficient neural rendering of dynamic or outdoor scenes. Triplane and Planar Representations HIVE is a hierarchical volume encoding module for neural implicit surface reconstruction that explicitly encodes spatial information using multi-scale feature volumes to capture high-frequency details while enforcing spatial consistency. It replaces or augments the implicit encoding of MLPs by concatenating trilinearly interpolated features from low-to-medium resolution volumes with sparsified high-resolution volumes. Unlike single high-resolution volumes that suffer from global incoherence due to isolated voxel updates, or hash-table encodings that suffer from collisions, HIVE uses low-resolution volumes to enforce smoothness and high-resolution volumes for detail, reducing memory consumption via sparsification. HIVE (HIerarchical Volume Encoding) This method represents a 3D scene using an adaptive octree structure where leaf nodes store learnable property values, specifically Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for color and Signed Distance Function (SDF) values for geometry. It solves the trade-off between the high quality of continuous neural fields and the computational cost of trilinear interpolation by using constant property values at leaf nodes for rendering, achieving over 30x speedup while maintaining visual fidelity through fine-tuning. Unlike standard grid-based methods that rely on interpolation for continuity, this approach explicitly optimizes the discrete leaf node values to approximate the continuous field, allowing for real-time rendering speeds comparable to or exceeding point-based methods like 3DGS. Octree-based Implicit Surface Representation with SH and SDF Optimization Handles large-scale scenes by decomposing the scene on different scales, including a progressive training scheme. Decompose the scene on different scales. Use a progressive training scheme. A representation introduced by Reiser et al. that allows for fast rendering of large-scale scenes. Utilizes a sparse feature grid and high-resolution 2D feature planes. The shift from pure MLP-based NeRFs to grid-based representations was driven by the need to scale to large environments and improve rendering speed. Early work by Mildenhall et al. [M+20] established the coordinate-based MLP approach. Subsequent research introduced voxel grids to accelerate training and rendering. For large-scale scenes, methods like URF [RLS+21] and those by Xu et al. [XXP+21] and Tang et al. [TRS21] utilized localized NeRFs, decomposing the scene into spatial cells or different scales with progressive training schemes. Reiser et al. [68] introduced MERF, which combines sparse feature grids with 2D planes for efficient large-scale rendering. The use of hierarchical volumes (HIVE) and octrees with SH/SDF optimization further refined the balance between memory efficiency and geometric detail. name: Voxel and Grid Representations
head: Grid-based Radiance Fields, Feature Volumes, Sparse Feature Volumes
body: Voxel and Grid Representations store scene information in discretized 3D structures rather than relying solely on coordinate-based MLPs. This family decouples spatial storage from decoding, enabling efficient querying and explicit scene manipulation. It maintains full 3D spatial coherence compared to planar representations, and provides an explicit, queryable data structure that can be sparsified or binarized for efficiency. The family shares a mechanism of discretizing 3D space into learnable structures and querying them via differentiable interpolation. Discretization The 3D scene space is divided into voxels organized in a hierarchy (e.g., coarse-to-fine levels, octrees) or a regular tensor \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}. Feature Storage Each voxel (or octree node) stores learnable parameters, which may include: Volume density \sigma. Latent feature vectors f or e used to decode color or SDF. Binary values \{-1, +1\} for compressed storage or \{0, 1\} for occupancy. Differentiable Query For a query point \mathbf{x}, values are retrieved via interpolation. Standard trilinear interpolation is used for 3D grids: f(\mathbf{x}) = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}) where \mathbf{V} is the feature grid. This operation is differentiable, allowing gradients to flow back to the grid values during optimization. Decoding Interpolated features are passed to a small decoder network (typically an MLP) S\Theta to predict final outputs like color \mathbf{c} or SDF s: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) = S\Theta(\text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}a)). Binary Radiance Fields (BiRF) is a storage-efficient radiance field representation that constrains learnable feature grid parameters to binary values \{-1, +1\}, reducing model size by orders of magnitude compared to real-valued floating-point grids. It distinguishes itself from post-processing compression methods (e.g., PlenOctrees, Re:NeRF) by performing binarization directly during training via a straight-through estimator, avoiding additional optimization steps and pre-trained model performance bounds. It further employs a 2D-3D hybrid multi-resolution architecture to mitigate hash collisions inherent in 3D grids while maintaining high reconstruction quality. See Binary Radiance Fields. Adaptive Differentiable Grids (ADG) is a learning-based representation for cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) reconstruction that replaces the fully connected MLPs of traditional neural fields with an adaptive octree structure, where each node stores a learnable 3D density grid. It solves the challenge of reconstructing high-noise, low-signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) cryo-ET data by combining differentiable image formation with regularization terms (Total Variation, boundary consistency, and cross-nodes non-local constraints) to separate noise from signal while preserving fine features. Unlike coordinate-based neural networks which suffer from long training times and slow rendering, ADG uses trilinear interpolation for faster querying and allows better detail recovery in complex regions while denoising uniform areas. See Adaptive Differentiable Grids for Cryo-ET. Vox-Surf is a voxel-based neural implicit surface representation that combines explicit sparse voxel structures with neural implicit surface representations to enable efficient surface reconstruction and realistic rendering from multi-view posed images. It differs from dense neural implicit methods (like NeRF or NeuS) by dividing the scene into bounded voxels, thereby reducing sampling and learning in empty areas, and from traditional voxel-based methods by storing only trainable embeddings at voxel corners rather than explicit SDF or color values in every voxel. This approach allows for finer surface representation with larger voxels and a lightweight network, while the resulting explicit voxel structure serves as efficient bounding volumes for collision detection and scene editing. See Vox-Surf. This method addresses novel-view synthesis from sparse input views by treating the radiance field as an explicit voxel grid of features, constructing per-view point clouds, and fusing them to refine depth inaccuracies. Unlike sibling methods that either ignore depth errors (DSNeRF) or introduce noise via completion networks (DDP-NeRF), this approach directly refines sparse depth by referencing a fused point cloud from all views, achieving faster reconstruction and greater compactness than hierarchical or dense grid alternatives. See Depth-Guided Robust and Fast Point Cloud Fusion NeRF. Sparse Feature Volume is a method for representing 3D scenes as a sparse grid of learnable latent vectors, where each voxel stores features decoded into a continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) and radiance field. It solves the problem of high-fidelity surface reconstruction and online monocular 3D reconstruction by combining the efficiency of sparse voxel structures with the detail-preserving power of SDFs, distinguishing itself from dense occupancy fields and standard color-only radiance fields. See Sparse Feature Volume. PAC-NeRF is a method for geometry-agnostic system identification that estimates both the unknown 3D geometry and physical parameters (e.g., Young’s modulus, viscosity) of highly dynamic objects from multi-view videos. It differs from standard dynamic NeRFs by not learning dynamics from scratch; instead, it enforces continuum mechanics conservation laws using a differentiable Material Point Method (MPM). This hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian approach allows for robust handling of topology changes and frictional contacts, which are difficult for mesh-based methods. See PAC-NeRF. Spatially Encoded Radiance Fields (SERF) simplify the implicit radiance function by spatially decomposing it into smaller functions to reduce the computational complexity load on the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). By storing feature vectors in a 3D voxel grid, the method divides volumetric model information into local batches, allowing equal or higher rendering quality than coordinate-based NeRF with a smaller or faster-decoding MLP. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by replacing the heavy coordinate-to-color mapping with a lookup-and-decode pipeline, and from sibling sparse methods by explicitly defining the grid-based feature storage mechanism that enables this acceleration. See Spatially Encoded Radiance Fields. A strategy to distill knowledge of previously learned 3D scenes by querying density on a subdivided occupancy grid. Divide each occupancy grid cell into a 5x5x5 subgrid. Query the density of each subgrid point. Consider a volume cell as a surface for distillation if any subgrid point has density above threshold τ. USD occupancy grid resolution: 50x50x50. Subgrid division per cell: 5x5x5. Density threshold τ: 3. A NeRF variant that jointly learns volumetric density (σ), RGB color (c), and a binary occupancy value (o) for a 3D point x and viewing direction d, enabling O(1) collision queries via a cached 3D array. At inference, the occupancy grid is cached as a regular 3D array at resolution Δ to enable O(1) collision queries. f\theta(x, d) = (\sigma, c, o), where \sigma is volumetric density, c \in \mathbb{R}^3 is RGB color, and o \in \{0, 1\} is binary occupancy. L = L{rgb} + \lambdad L{depth} + \lambdao BCE(\hat{o}, o^), where L{rgb} is photometric loss, L{depth} is depth supervision, o^ is derived from depth observations via volumetric carving, and BCE is binary cross-entropy. \gamma(x) = \Pi{l=1}^{L} hl(\lfloor x \cdot sl \rfloor), where hl are learned hash tables at L resolution levels, sl are per-level scales, and \Pi denotes concatenation. Network architecture: A shared hash-grid backbone (from Instant-NGP [4]) feeds into a separate two-layer MLP head with sigmoid activation for the occupancy branch. A method that builds and dynamically updates an octree structure while the MLP is optimized to allow aggressive empty space skipping and early ray termination. Build and dynamically update an octree structure during MLP optimization. Perform aggressive empty space skipping. Perform early ray termination when the transmittance along the ray approaches zero. A method querying the MLP to produce a sparse voxel octree of volume density and spherical harmonic coefficients, finetuned using a rendering loss. Query the MLP to produce a sparse voxel octree of volume density and spherical harmonic coefficients. Finetune this octree representation using a rendering loss to improve output image quality. Voxel and grid representations emerged to address the computational bottlenecks of coordinate-based neural radiance fields, which relied on dense MLPs mapping coordinates to color, resulting in slow rendering and high memory usage. The introduction of sparse voxel structures (e.g., Neural Sparse Voxel Fields) and hash-encoded grids (e.g., Instant-NGP, referenced in) enabled efficient spatial indexing and interpolation. This family supports applications including robotics navigation, scientific imaging like cryo-ET, and dynamic scene reconstruction.
