name: Binary Radiance Fields
head: BRF, BiRF, Binarized Radiance Fields
body: Binary Radiance Fields (BiRF) is a storage-efficient radiance field representation that constrains learnable feature grid parameters to binary values \{-1, +1\}, reducing model size by orders of magnitude compared to real-valued floating-point grids. It distinguishes itself from post-processing compression methods (e.g., PlenOctrees, Re:NeRF) by performing binarization directly during training via a straight-through estimator, avoiding additional optimization steps and pre-trained model performance bounds. It further employs a 2D-3D hybrid multi-resolution architecture to mitigate hash collisions inherent in 3D grids while maintaining high reconstruction quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images (poses and RGB), 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}, viewing directions \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Volume density \sigma, color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: The representation consists of four multi-resolution feature grids implemented using hash encoding: 1. 3D Voxel Grid (\Phi{\theta{xyz}}): L levels with resolutions ranging from 16 to 1024. Each level stores up to T{3D} feature vectors. 2. 2D Plane Grids (\Phi{\theta{xy}}, \Phi{\theta{xz}}, \Phi{\theta{yz}}): M levels with resolutions ranging from 64 to 512. Each level stores up to T{2D} feature vectors. 3. Feature Values: All grid parameters are constrained to \{-1, +1\}, stored as 1-bit values. 4. MLPs: Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 128 channels, ReLU activation. Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 128 channels, ReLU activation. Parameters: L: Number of 3D grid levels. M: Number of 2D grid levels. T{3D}: Max feature vectors per 3D level. T{2D}: Max feature vectors per 2D level. F: Feature dimension per level. Variants use F \in \{2, 4, 8\}. \lambda{\text{sparsity}}: Sparsity loss weight, typically 2.0 \times 10^{-5}. Model Variants: Small (Ours-S): \log2(T{3D}) = 17, \log2(T{2D}) = 15. Base (Ours-B): \log2(T{3D}) = 19, \log2(T{2D}) = 17. Numbered Steps: 1. Binarization (Training): Maintain real-valued parameters \theta. During the forward pass, binarize them using the sign function: \theta' = \text{sign}(\theta) = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } \theta \ge 0 \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} During backpropagation, use the Straight-Through Estimator (STE) to pass gradients: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta'} \cdot \mathbb{I}(|\theta| \le 1) This constrains \theta to \{-1, 1\} and prevents scale divergence. 2. 3D Feature Encoding: For input coordinate \mathbf{x}, compute features from the 3D grid by linearly interpolating the binary parameters across L resolution levels and concatenating them: \mathbf{f}{xyz} = \left\{ \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \text{sign}(\Phi^l{\theta{xyz}})) \right\}{l=1}^L where \text{interp} denotes tri-linear interpolation. 3. 2D Feature Encoding: Project \mathbf{x}=(x,y,z) to 2D coordinates: \mathbf{x}{xy}=(x,y), \mathbf{x}{xz}=(x,z), \mathbf{x}{yz}=(y,z). For each axis, interpolate binary parameters across M resolution levels and concatenate: \mathbf{f}{xy} = \left\{ \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}{xy}, \text{sign}(\Phi^m{\theta{xy}})) \right\}{m=1}^M Repeat for \mathbf{f}{xz} and \mathbf{f}{yz} using bi-linear interpolation. 4. Feature Concatenation: Combine all encoded features: \mathbf{f} = \{ \mathbf{f}{xyz}, \mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, \mathbf{f}{yz} \} 5. Density Prediction: Apply positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) to the input coordinate. Feed \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{f} into the density MLP: (\sigma, \mathbf{e}) = \text{MLP}{\text{density}}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{f}) where \sigma is volume density and \mathbf{e} is the embedded feature vector. 6. Color Prediction: Encode the viewing direction \mathbf{d} using spherical harmonics \mathbf{d}{\text{enc}}. Feed \mathbf{e} and \mathbf{d}{\text{enc}} into the color MLP: \mathbf{c} = \text{MLP}{\text{color}}(\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{d}{\text{enc}}) 7. Loss Calculation: Compute reconstruction loss L{\text{recon}} (MSE between rendered and ground truth colors) and sparsity loss L{\text{sparsity}}: L{\text{sparsity}} = \sum{i,k} \log(1 + 2\sigma(\mathbf{r}i(tk))^2) Total loss: L = L{\text{recon}} + \lambda{\text{sparsity}} L{\text{sparsity}} Optimize using Adam. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class BinaryRadianceField: def init(self, L=4, M=4, T3D=217, T2D=215, F=2, hashsize=219): """ Initialize BiRF. L: Number of 3D grid levels. M: Number of 2D grid levels. T3D: Max feature vectors per 3D level. T2D: Max feature vectors per 2D level. F: Feature dimension per level. hashsize: Hash table size for Instant-NGP style encoding. """ self.L = L self.M = M self.F = F self.hashsize = hashsize # Initialize hash tables for 3D grid (L levels) # Each level has resolution 16^3 to 1024^3, mapped to hash table self.grid3d = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Embedding(hashsize, F) for in range(L) ]) # Initialize hash tables for 2D grids (3 planes M levels) # Each level has resolution 64^2 to 512^2 self.grid2dxy = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Embedding(hashsize, F) for in range(M) ]) self.grid2dxz = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Embedding(hashsize, F) for in range(M) ]) self.grid2dyz = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Embedding(hashsize, F) for in range(M) ]) # Initialize MLPs # Density MLP: Input dim = LF + M3F, Hidden=128, Output=1+128 (sigma + e) inputdimdensity = L F + 3 M F self.mlpdensity = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdimdensity + 10, 128), # +10 for positional encoding of x nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 129) # 1 for sigma, 128 for e) # Color MLP: Input dim = 128 + 27 (SH), Hidden=128, Output=3 self.mlpcolor = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(128 + 27, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3)) # Initialize weights self.initweights() def initweights(self): for layer in self.grid3d + self.grid2dxy + self.grid2dxz + self.grid2dyz: nn.init.uniform(layer.weight, -1, 1) for m in self.mlpdensity.modules(): if isinstance(m, nn.Linear): nn.init.kaimingnormal(m.weight, mode='fanin', nonlinearity='relu') for m in self.mlpcolor.modules(): if isinstance(m, nn.Linear): nn.init.kaimingnormal(m.weight, mode='fanin', nonlinearity='relu') def binarize(self, x): """ Binarize real-valued parameters to {-1, 1} using STE. """ # Forward: sign function # Backward: identity if |x| <= 1, else 0 return (x.sign() (x.abs() <= 1).float()).detach() + x - x.detach() def gethashindices(self, coords, resolution): """ Compute hash indices for coordinates at a given resolution. Simplified hash function based on Instant-NGP. """ # coords: (N, 3) # resolution: int # Returns: (N,) indices # Note: In practice, this involves bit manipulation and hashing. # Here we assume a placeholder hash function that maps coords to indices. # For implementation, one would use the specific hash function from Instant-NGP. # We simulate it here by returning random indices for demonstration of structure. # In real code, use torch.ops.nvrtc or similar for efficient hashing. N = coords.shape[0] # Placeholder: In reality, this is a deterministic hash based on coords and resolution return torch.randint(0, self.hashsize, (N,)) def query3d(self, x, levels): """ Query 3D grid features. x: (N, 3) levels: list of resolution levels [16, 32,..., 1024] Returns: (N, LF) """ features = [] for l, res in enumerate(levels): # Get hash indices for this resolution indices = self.gethashindices(x, res) # Get embeddings emb = self.grid3dl # (N, F) # Interpolate? Instant-NGP uses hash lookup directly, but BiRF uses interpolation. # BiRF paper says "linearly interpolating binary parameters". # However, hash encoding typically skips explicit interpolation by hashing neighbors. # The paper states: "all feature grids are implemented using a hash encoding [20]". # And: "tri-linearly interpolating binary parameters". # This implies the hash encoding is used to store the grid, but interpolation is performed on the grid values. # For a pure hash implementation (Instant-NGP), interpolation is over the hash table entries of the 8 neighbors. # We will implement the interpolation logic assuming we have the grid values. # Since hash encoding maps coords to indices, we need the 8 neighbors. # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume gethashindices returns the index of the cell, # and we need to fetch neighbors. # Given the complexity of implementing Instant-NGP hash interpolation from scratch, # we will use a simplified lookup that assumes the hash function handles the neighbor fetching or # we approximate it by just fetching the primary index if exact interpolation is too verbose. # However, the paper explicitly mentions interpolation. # Let's assume a helper interpolatehash exists which takes coords, resolution, and grid embedding. feat = interpolatehash(x, res, self.grid3d[l], self.hashsize) features.append(feat) return torch.cat(features, dim=-1) def query2d(self, x, levels, planetype): """ Query 2D grid features. planetype: 'xy', 'xz', 'yz' """ features = [] for m, res in enumerate(levels): if planetype == 'xy': coords2d = x[:,:2] grid = self.grid2dxy[m] elif planetype == 'xz': coords2d = x[:, [0, 2]] grid = self.grid2dxz[m] elif planetype == 'yz': coords2d = x[:, 1:] grid = self.grid2dyz[m] feat = interpolatehash(coords2d, res, grid, self.hashsize) features.append(feat) return torch.cat(features, dim=-1) def forward(self, x, d): """ Forward pass. x: (N, 3) 3D coordinates d: (N, 3) viewing directions Returns: sigma (N,), color (N, 3) """ # 1. Binarize grid weights # Note: In PyTorch, we usually binarize the weights in the forward pass of the embedding or manually. # We will binarize the embeddings retrieved. # 3D Features # Resolutions: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024 (7 levels? Paper says L levels, 16 to 1024) # Assuming L=4 for small model, resolutions might be 16, 32, 64, 128? # Paper says "resolutions from 16 to 1024". Let's assume geometric progression. res3d = [16 (2i) for i in range(self.L)] fxyz = self.query3d(x, res3d) # 2D Features res2d = [64 (2i) for i in range(self.M)] fxy = self.query2d(x, res2d, 'xy') fxz = self.query2d(x, res2d, 'xz') fyz = self.query2d(x, res2d, 'yz') # Concatenate f = torch.cat([fxyz, fxy, fxz, fyz], dim=-1) # Positional Encoding for x gammax = positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10) # Density MLP densityinput = torch.cat([gammax, f], dim=-1) densityout = self.mlpdensity(densityinput) sigma = densityout[:, 0:1] e = densityout[:, 1:] # Directional Encoding (Spherical Harmonics) denc = sphericalharmonicencoding(d, degree=4) # 27 coefficients for degree 4 # Color MLP colorinput = torch.cat([e, denc], dim=-1) color = self.mlpcolor(colorinput) return sigma, color def loss(self, sigma, color, gtcolor, gtsigma=None): """ Compute loss. """ Lrecon = F.mseloss(color, gtcolor) # Sparsity loss # Lsparsity = sum(log(1 + 2 sigma^2)) Lsparsity = torch.mean(torch.log(1 + 2 sigma2)) lambdasparsity = 2.0e-5 L = Lrecon + lambdasparsity Lsparsity return L def interpolatehash(coords, resolution, embeddinglayer, hashsize): """ Interpolate features from hash grid. This is a simplified placeholder for the complex hash interpolation logic. In Instant-NGP, this involves finding the 8 neighbors in the hash table and interpolating. """ # Get indices for the 8 corners of the voxel containing coords # This requires a specific hash function implementation. # For the purpose of this article, we assume this function correctly retrieves # and interpolates the binary features. # The features are binarized inside the embedding lookup or immediately after. # Get raw embeddings for the 8 neighbors # indices = get8neighborindices(coords, resolution, hashsize) # embs = embeddinglayer(indices) # (8, F) # Binarize # embsbin = binarize(embs) # Interpolate # weights = gettrilinearweights(coords, resolution) # feat = sum(weights embsbin) # Placeholder return return embeddinglayer.weight.mean(dim=0).unsqueeze(0).expand(coords.shape[0], -1) def binarize(x): return (x.sign() (x.abs() <= 1).float()).detach() + x - x.detach() def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies): # Standard NeRF positional encoding scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numfrequencies)], device=x.device) shaped = x.shape[:-1] + (numfrequencies,) + x.shape[-1:] x = torch.reshape(x, shaped) x = x scales return torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1) def sphericalharmonicencoding(d, degree): # Simplified SH encoding # Returns 27 coefficients for degree 4 # Implementation details omitted for brevity, standard library available return torch.randn(d.shape[0], 27) Storage: Extremely compact. Ours-S2 requires < 0.5 MB, outperforming TensoRF-CP (3.7 MB) and Instant-NGP (24.5 MB) on the mic scene. Training Time: Approximately 6, 9, and 14 minutes for Synthetic-NeRF scenes using Ours-B2 to Ours-B8 models on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000. Performance: PSNR of 32.03 dB on Synthetic-NeRF, 34.48 dB on Synthetic-NSVF, and 28.20 dB on Tanks and Temples. Strengths: Significant reduction in storage overhead (1-bit parameters); no post-optimization required; competitive reconstruction quality. Limitations: Hash collisions in 3D grids at high resolutions can limit performance; mitigated by 2D grids but adds complexity. When to use: When storage is a critical bottleneck and real-time or fast training is desired. When not to use: When maximum possible reconstruction quality is required over storage constraints, or when hardware does not support efficient hash table operations. Binary Radiance Fields (BiRF) was proposed by Seungjoo Shin and Jaesik Park in 2023. It builds on the Instant-NGP architecture [20] and NerfAcc [42] for efficient ray sampling. The method addresses the storage burden of implicit feature embeddings in NeRFs by introducing binarization during training. It is used for static scene reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. name: Adaptive Differentiable Grids for Cryo-ET
head: Adaptive density grid optimization, Adaptive density grids based on an octree structure, Adaptive differentiable grids, Coordinate-based representation with adaptive octree
body: Adaptive Differentiable Grids (ADG) is a learning-based representation for cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) reconstruction that replaces the fully connected MLPs of traditional neural fields with an adaptive octree structure, where each node stores a learnable 3D density grid. It solves the challenge of reconstructing high-noise, low-signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) cryo-ET data by combining differentiable image formation with regularization terms (Total Variation, boundary consistency, and cross-nodes non-local constraints) to separate noise from signal while preserving fine features. Unlike coordinate-based neural networks which suffer from long training times and slow rendering, ADG uses trilinear interpolation for faster querying and allows better detail recovery in complex regions while denoising uniform areas. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Noisy 2D projection images b (preprocessed with motion and intensity correction), acquisition geometry (tilt angles), and a Region of Interest (ROI) mask. Outputs: A continuous 3D density field \hat{x} reconstructed within the ROI, obtained by querying the optimized octree structure. Data Structures: 1. Octree: A hierarchical tree structure where each node represents a sub-volume of the ROI. Node State: Each node is either enabled (active), disabled (outside ROI or empty), or leaf (contains a density grid). Density Grid: Each enabled leaf node stores a 3D tensor of learnable density values. The grid dimensions are Nx \times Ny \times Nz. In the source implementation, Nx = Ny = Nz for all nodes. 2. Ray Sampling State: For each ray, a list of 3D sample positions is generated based on the current octree structure. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the octree to cover the ROI. Disable all nodes outside the ROI. Initialize the density values in the enabled nodes (e.g., to zero or small random values). 2. Octree Update (Coarse Phase): Use down-sampled projections to update the octree structure. Uniformly sample each octant (node) and compute the standard deviation (SD) of the densities inside each node. If the SD is significant, the node has a higher chance of being divided into eight child octants. Solve a mixed-integer program to divide, merge, or keep octants, ensuring the total number of nodes remains below a fixed limit. Note: This step prioritizes regions with more features and accelerates computation. 3. Freeze Structure and Optimize Grids (Fine Phase): Freeze the octree structure (no further division/merging). Optimize the density grid values in each enabled node using the original noisy projections. Apply a binary mask M to exclude rays intersecting fiducial markers or padded gray regions at the borders. 4. Ray Sampling: For each ray, determine the intersection with the current octree nodes. For each octree node oc crossed by the ray, calculate the number of samples N{oc} using stratified random sampling: N{oc} = N{max} \frac{loc}{doc} where N{max} is a hyperparameter (maximum samples per node), loc is the length of the ray segment inside node oc, and doc is the diagonal length of node oc. Generate N{oc} 3D positions along the ray segment within node oc. 5. Density Query: For a query point p, identify the containing octree node. Perform trilinear interpolation from the eight vertices of the density grid stored in that node to obtain the density f\phi(p). Formula: f\phi(p) = \text{trilinear\interp}(p, \text{Grid}{node(p)}) where \text{Grid}{node(p)} is the Nx \times Ny \times Nz tensor of the node containing p. 6. Loss Computation: Data Fidelity Loss (L{data}): Discretize the image formation model bi = Ai xi + ni, where Ai is the Radon transform along ray i, xi is the vector of sampled densities, and bi is the measured intensity. L{data}(\phi) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} || M (A f\phi(pi) - bi) ||2^2 where N is the batch size (number of sampling points), M is the binary mask excluding fiducial markers, and f\phi(pi) is the density at sample point pi. Total Variation Loss (L{tv}): Spatial regularizer to smooth the reconstruction. (Formula not explicitly detailed in the provided text, but cited as a standard prior). Cross-Nodes Non-Local Constraint Loss (L{cnlc}): To reduce noise and enforce consistency between different nodes: 1. Randomly select two enabled nodes m and n inside the ROI at each iteration. 2. Sample densities f\phi(pi^m) from node m and f\phi(pj^n) from node n. 3. Compute the loss: L{cnlc} = \sum || \text{softmax}(f\phi(pi^m)^T f\phi(pj^n)) f\phi(pj^n) - f\phi(pi^m) ||2^2 The softmax operation estimates similarities between density vectors in different nodes. Boundary Consistency Loss (L{bc}): Minimizes density differences between neighboring grids at their shared boundaries to handle discontinuity artifacts caused by independent optimization of octree nodes. Total Loss: L{total} = L{data} + k{tv} L{tv} + k{cnlc} L{cnlc} + k{bc} L{bc} where k{tv}, k{cnlc}, k{bc} are weighting parameters. 7. Optimization Loop: Compute gradients of L{total} with respect to the density grid values using backpropagation through the differentiable image formation model and trilinear interpolation. Update the density grid values using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Repeat steps 2-6 until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinearinterp(x, y, z, grid): """ Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D grid. grid: numpy array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) x, y, z: float coordinates normalized to [0, 1] relative to the grid bounds Returns: interpolated density value """ # Scale to grid indices ix = x (grid.shape[0] - 1) iy = y (grid.shape[1] - 1) iz = z (grid.shape[2] - 1) # Floor and ceil indices x0, x1 = int(np.floor(ix)), int(np.ceil(ix)) y0, y1 = int(np.floor(iy)), int(np.ceil(iy)) z0, z1 = int(np.floor(iz)), int(np.ceil(iz)) # Clamp indices to grid bounds x0 = np.clip(x0, 0, grid.shape[0] - 1) x1 = np.clip(x1, 0, grid.shape[0] - 1) y0 = np.clip(y0, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) y1 = np.clip(y1, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) z0 = np.clip(z0, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) z1 = np.clip(z1, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) # Interpolation weights wx = ix - x0 wy = iy - y0 wz = iz - z0 # Trilinear interpolation c00 = grid[x0, y0, z0] (1 - wx) + grid[x1, y0, z0] wx c01 = grid[x0, y1, z0] (1 - wx) + grid[x1, y1, z0] wx c10 = grid[x0, y0, z1] (1 - wx) + grid[x1, y0, z1] wx c11 = grid[x0, y1, z1] (1 - wx) + grid[x1, y1, z1] wx v0 = c00 (1 - wy) + c01 wy v1 = c10 (1 - wy) + c11 wy return v0 (1 - wz) + v1 wz def computeradontransform(samples, densities, raydirection, origin): """ Approximates the Radon transform (line integral) for a set of samples along a ray. samples: list of 3D points along the ray densities: array of density values at those points raydirection: unit vector of the ray origin: starting point of the ray Returns: projected intensity """ # Calculate distances between consecutive samples distances = [] for i in range(len(samples) - 1): p1 = np.array(samples[i]) p2 = np.array(samples[i+1]) dist = np.linalg.norm(p2 - p1) distances.append(dist) # Simple Riemann sum approximation of the integral # Note: The source defines Ai as the Radon transform operation. # In practice, this involves integrating density along the ray path. # For implementation, we sum density stepsize. # Assuming uniform sampling for simplicity in this placeholder, # but source uses stratified sampling. totalintegral = 0.0 for i in range(len(densities)): # Step size can be approximated by distance to next sample or half-distance step = distances[i] if i < len(distances) else distances[-1] totalintegral += densities[i] step return totalintegral def updateoctreestructure(octree, projectionsdownsampled): """ Updates the octree structure based on density variance. """ for node in octree.enablednodes: # Sample densities uniformly within the node's grid densities = sampleuniformly(node.grid) sd = np.std(densities) # If SD is significant, mark for division if sd > threshold: node.markfordivision() # Solve mixed-integer program to divide, merge, or keep nodes # ensuring total nodes < maxnodes octree.solvemip() def trainadg(projections, mask, roi, maxiterations): """ Main training loop for Adaptive Differentiable Grids. """ # 1. Initialize Octree octree = Octree(roi) octree.disableoutsidenodes() # 2. Coarse Phase: Update Octree Structure # Use down-sampled projections projectionscoarse = downsample(projections) for in range(coarseiterations): updateoctreestructure(octree, projectionscoarse) # 3. Fine Phase: Optimize Density Grids # Freeze octree structure octree.freezestructure() for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Ray Sampling rays = generaterays(projections) allsamples = [] alldensities = [] for ray in rays: # Determine intersection with octree nodes intersections = octree.intersectray(ray) raysamples = [] raydensities = [] for node, startpoint, endpoint in intersections: # Calculate number of samples for this node loc = np.linalg.norm(endpoint - startpoint) doc = node.diagonallength Noc = max(1, int(Nmax loc / doc)) # Stratified random sampling along the segment points = stratifiedsample(startpoint, endpoint, Noc) # Query densities for p in points: density = trilinearinterp(p, node.grid) raysamples.append(p) raydensities.append(density) allsamples.extend(raysamples) alldensities.extend(raydensities) # Compute Data Fidelity Loss # A is the Radon transform operator # b is the measured intensity # M is the mask projected = computeradontransform(allsamples, alldensities,...) lossdata = 0.5 np.sum(mask (projected - projections) 2) / len(allsamples) # Compute Regularization Losses losstv = computetvloss(octree) lossbc = computeboundaryconsistencyloss(octree) # Compute CNLC Loss # Randomly select two enabled nodes nodem, noden = randomselecttwoenablednodes(octree) samplesm = randomsamplefromgrid(nodem.grid) samplesn = randomsamplefromgrid(noden.grid) densitiesm = [trilinearinterp(s, nodem.grid) for s in samplesm] densitiesn = [trilinearinterp(s, noden.grid) for s in samplesn] # Lcnlc formula # Lcnlc = sum || softmax(fm^T fn) fn - fm ||^2 # Note: The source formula implies vector operations. # Assuming densities are scalars per point, this might be a typo in source # or implies feature vectors. Given "density grids", densities are scalars. # If densities are scalars, softmax of scalar product is just sigmoid-like. # We implement the formula as written, assuming f is scalar. # If f is scalar, f^T f is just product. cnlcloss = 0.0 for i in range(len(samplesm)): # Assuming single density value per point fm = densitiesm[i] fn = densitiesn[i] # Assuming paired sampling or similar indices # Softmax of scalar product? # Source: softmax(fphi(pi^m)^T fphi(pj^n)) # If these are scalars, softmax is exp(x)/sum(exp). # With one term, it's 1. This suggests f might be a vector or the formula # implies a sum over neighbors. # However, source says "sample densities fphi(p)". # We will implement the scalar version as a placeholder for the exact vector logic # which is not fully detailed in the text provided. # Assuming the source implies a non-local operation on feature vectors, # but only density is mentioned. We stick to the scalar density interpretation # and note the ambiguity. # Placeholder for CNLC calculation based on scalar densities # This part is ambiguous in the source text regarding vector vs scalar. # We will skip detailed implementation of CNLC as the source # does not provide the full vector definition or how pi and pj are paired. pass losscnlc = 0.0 # Placeholder losstotal = lossdata + ktv losstv + kcnlc losscnlc + kbc lossbc # Backpropagate and update grid values gradients = computegradients(losstotal, octree) updategrids(octree, gradients) return octree Parameters: Nx, Ny, Nz: Grid size in x, y, z dimensions for each density grid. Typically Nx = Ny = Nz. N{max}: Hyperparameter for the maximum number of samples per node in ray sampling. k{tv}, k{cnlc}, k{bc}: Weighting parameters for Total Variation, Cross-Nodes Non-Local Constraint, and Boundary Consistency losses, respectively. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Raw cryo-ET data follows a Poisson noise model, but preprocessing (motion/intensity correction) makes it approximately Gaussian. The method assumes Gaussian noise for simplicity. Discontinuities: Independent optimization of octree nodes causes discontinuity artifacts at grid edges. This is mitigated by the boundary consistency loss L{bc}. Fiducial Markers: Fiducial markers and padded gray regions interfere with reconstruction. A binary mask M is applied to the data-fidelity loss to exclude rays intersecting these regions. Inadequacy of Standard Neural Fields: Standard MLP-based neural fields either learn noise as signal or oversmooth the signal, losing main features. ADG addresses this by using adaptive grids and specific regularizations. Time Complexity: Faster than traditional MLP-based neural fields because querying density uses trilinear interpolation instead of evaluating a neural network at each sample point. The octree structure accelerates computation by prioritizing regions with features. Memory Complexity: Lower memory requirement than classical tomographic reconstruction techniques as it does not store the entire 3D volume during optimization, only the active octree nodes and their density grids. Performance: Evaluated on datasets EMPIAR 10643, EMPIAR 10453, and EMPIAR 11462. Outperforms SART+TV, Kniesel et al., and NeAT in reconstruction quality and denoising. Strengths: Better detail preservation in complex regions, effective denoising in uniform regions, faster optimization and rendering than MLP-based methods. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization weights (k{tv}, k{cnlc}, k{bc}) and octree update constraints. The mixed-integer program for octree updates may be computationally intensive. Origin: Proposed by Wang et al. in the paper "Adaptive differentiable grids for cryo-electron tomography reconstruction and denoising". History: Inspired by recent advances in neural representations (NeRFs) and adaptive octree structures (ACORN, NeAT). Addresses specific challenges in cryo-ET: missing-wedge acquisition, sample misalignment, motion, large data processing, and low SNR. Usage: Used for cryo-electron tomography reconstruction and denoising. name: Vox-Surf
head: Voxel-based Implicit Surface Representation
body: Vox-Surf is a voxel-based neural implicit surface representation that combines explicit sparse voxel structures with neural implicit surface representations to enable efficient surface reconstruction and realistic rendering from multi-view posed images. It differs from dense neural implicit methods (like NeRF or NeuS) by dividing the scene into bounded voxels, thereby reducing sampling and learning in empty areas, and from traditional voxel-based methods by storing only trainable embeddings at voxel corners rather than explicit SDF or color values in every voxel. This approach allows for finer surface representation with larger voxels and a lightweight network, while the resulting explicit voxel structure serves as efficient bounding volumes for collision detection and scene editing. Inputs: Multiple-view posed images (RGB), camera poses, and an approximate bounding box of the scene. Optional depth sensor data (e.g., from LiDAR or ToF). Outputs: Rendered images, a signed distance field (SDF) surface, and a sparse octree of optimized voxels. Data Structures: 1. Sparse Hierarchical Octree: The scene space is divided into uniformly spaced coarse voxels V = \{V1,..., Vk\}, which form the leaf nodes of a sparse octree. 2. Vertex Embeddings: Each voxel has eight corner vertices. Each vertex stores a fixed-length trainable embedding vector e \in \mathbb{R}^{Le} containing encoded geometry and appearance information. Adjacent voxels share 4 vertices and their corresponding embeddings. 3. Geometry Extractor (F\sigma): An MLP mapping F\sigma: \mathbb{R}^{Le} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{1+Lf}. It takes an embedding e and outputs a signed distance value \sigma \in \mathbb{R} (the first element, index [0]) and a geometry feature vector f \in \mathbb{R}^{Lf} (the remaining elements, index [1:]). 4. Appearance Extractor (Fc): An MLP mapping color based on concatenated features. Parameters: Le: Dimension of vertex embeddings. Lf: Dimension of geometry features. \tau: Distance threshold for voxel pruning. \delta t: Small noise tolerance depth range for depth loss intervals, dependent on sensor confidence. s: Scale parameter for the S-density function. Np: Number of uniform sample points inside each voxel for pruning checks. Positional Encoding: Applied to embedding e and view direction d before feeding into networks, as in NeRF. Steps: 1. Initialization: Divide the bounding area into uniformly spaced coarse voxels. Build a sparse hierarchical octree with these voxels as leaf nodes. Assign each vertex a random initial embedding e \in \mathbb{R}^{Le}. 2. Ray Generation and Culling: Generate rays r=(o,d) from camera centers. Perform an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) intersection test between each ray and the octree. Cull rays that do not intersect any voxels. For remaining rays, calculate the distance m{Vi} inside each intersected voxel Vi. 3. Surface-Aware Sampling: Step 1 (Uniform Voxel Sampling): Uniformly sample points p on rays inside the intersected voxels. Step 2 (Cross-Surface Voxel Searching): Compute SDF values using F\sigma(\Gamma(p)). Find points pi, p{i+1} where the SDF changes sign (positive to negative) along the ray. Mark the voxels containing these points as "important voxels". Step 3 (Resampling): Increase sampling probability in important voxels. Normalize probabilities along the ray. Resample rays with a fixed total point count. Two variants exist: 'full' (all important voxels) for unstable shapes, and 'first' (only the first important voxel) for fine details on stable shapes. Boundary Handling: To prevent cross-voxel accumulation (where sampling spacing exceeds voxel boundaries due to independent interpolation), cut off intervals near voxel boundaries and recalculate sample points ti and tj. 4. Point Retrieval and Extraction: For any 3D point p within a voxel, retrieve its embedding e via the retrieval function \Gamma: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{Le}, which maps p to an embedding vector using trilinear interpolation of the eight voxel corner embeddings. Geometry Extraction: Pass e to F\sigma to get \sigma = F\sigma(e)[0] and f = F\sigma(e)[1:]. Normal Calculation: Compute normal n via automatic differentiation (double backpropagation) on the SDF output: n = \frac{d F\sigma(\Gamma(p))[0]}{dp}. Appearance Extraction: Concatenate geometry feature f, ray direction d, and point embedding e. Feed into Fc to obtain color c = Fc(\text{concat}(f, d, e)). 5. Volume Rendering: Define the S-density function: \phis(\sigma) = \frac{s e^{-s\sigma}}{(1 + e^{-s\sigma})^2}, which is the derivative of the Sigmoid \Phis(\sigma) = (1 + e^{-s\sigma})^{-1}. Calculate discrete volume density weight: \alpha(ti) = \text{ReLU}\left( \frac{\Phis(F\sigma(\Gamma(r(ti)))[0]) - \Phis(F\sigma(\Gamma(r(t{i+1})))[0])}{\Phis(F\sigma(\Gamma(r(ti)))[0])} \right). Calculate discrete accumulated transmittance: T(ti) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(tj)). Rendered color: C(r) = \sumi T(ti)\alpha(ti)ci. 6. Progressive Training (Pruning and Splitting): Voxel Pruning: Uniformly sample Np points inside each voxel. Compute SDF values. If any point p inside voxel Vi has |F\sigma(\Gamma(p))[0]| < \tau, keep the voxel (K=1); otherwise, prune it (K=0) from the octree. Voxel Splitting: Periodically split existing voxels into 8 sub-voxels and insert them into the octree. Compute initial embeddings for new vertices using \Gamma. Optimize these embeddings independently of parent nodes. 7. Loss Functions: Color Loss: L{color} = \sumr ||\hat{C}(r) - C(r)||1, where \hat{C}(r) is the ground truth color. Eikonal Loss: L{eikonal} = \sumi (||\nabla F\sigma(\Gamma(pi))[0]||2 - 1)^2, applied to sampled points to constrain SDF gradient magnitude to 1. Depth Loss (if depth data available): Occupancy function: \text{occ}(t) = \text{Sigmoid}(-\text{scale} \cdot F\sigma(\Gamma(r(t)))[0]). L{outside} = \sum{t < \hat{t} - \delta t} ||1 - \text{occ}(t)||2^2. L{near} = \sum{\hat{t} - \delta t \le t \le \hat{t} + \delta t} ||F\sigma(\Gamma(r(t)))[0]||2^2. L{inside} = \sum{t > \hat{t} + \delta t} ||\text{occ}(t)||2^2. Total Depth Loss: L{depth} = L{outside} + L{near} + L{inside}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ self.embeddingdim = embeddingdim self.featuredim = featuredim self.octree = octree # Initialize embeddings for all vertices in the octree # Each vertex has a trainable embedding e in R^Le self.vertexembeddings = self.initvertexembeddings(octree) # Define MLPs self.geometryextractor = GeometryExtractorMLP(embeddingdim, 1 + featuredim) self.appearanceextractor = AppearanceExtractorMLP(1 + featuredim + embeddingdim) # Parameters self.pruningthreshold = 0.01 # tau self.depthnoisetol = 0.05 # deltat self.sdensityscale = 10.0 # s def initvertexembeddings(self, octree): # Initialize random embeddings for each unique vertex in the octree # Adjacent voxels share vertices, so we map vertex coordinates to embeddings uniquevertices = octree.getuniquevertices() embeddings = torch.randn(len(uniquevertices), self.embeddingdim, requiresgrad=True) return embeddings def retrieveembedding(self, points, octree): """ Retrieve embedding for points via trilinear interpolation of voxel corner embeddings.:param points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates.:param octree: The current octree structure.:return: Tensor of shape (N, Le) containing interpolated embeddings. name: Depth-Guided Robust and Fast Point Cloud Fusion NeRF
head: Ours, Point Cloud Fusion NeRF
body: This method addresses novel-view synthesis from sparse input views by treating the radiance field as an explicit voxel grid of features, constructing per-view point clouds, and fusing them to refine depth inaccuracies. Unlike sibling methods that either ignore depth errors (DSNeRF) or introduce noise via completion networks (DDP-NeRF), this approach directly refines sparse depth by referencing a fused point cloud from all views, achieving faster reconstruction and greater compactness than hierarchical or dense grid alternatives. Inputs: Sparse set of RGB-D images \{Ii, Di\} with known camera parameters. Outputs: A rendered RGB image and depth map for a target view. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a standard 3D feature grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K}, where I, J, K are the resolutions along the X, Y, and Z axes. This grid is segregated into two distinct components: 1. Geometry Grid (G\sigma): A single-channel grid G\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K} where values directly represent volume density \sigma. 2. Appearance Grid (Gc): A multi-channel grid Gc \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K \times P}, where P is the number of appearance feature channels. This grid stores neural features and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Algorithm: 1. Per-View Point Cloud Construction: For each input view i, map the 2D pixels to 3D space using the sparse RGB-D image Di and camera parameters to generate a point cloud PCi. 2. Voxel Encoding: Convert the depth values from PCi into densities. Encode both depth and color information from PCi into the voxel grid G using distinct sets of matrices and vectors. 3. Point Cloud Fusion: Aggregate the point clouds from all input views (PCi) to assemble a fused point cloud PC{fused} representing the entire scene. 4. Voxel Query and Density/Appearance Determination: For a shading location \mathbf{x}w = (x, y, z), determine its density and appearance by referencing PC{fused}. Specifically, use sampled values from the vectors and matrices associated with the grid to compute the corresponding tensor components for the voxel at \mathbf{x}w. 5. Color Decoding: Send the appearance feature values retrieved from Gc at \mathbf{x}w to a decoding MLP S. The MLP S transforms the appearance feature vector combined with the viewing direction \mathbf{d} into the final color \mathbf{c}. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the loss function composed of an RGB loss (between rendered and ground truth color) and a depth loss (between rendered and ground truth depth). 7. Optimization: Iteratively refine the matrices, vectors, and grid values. As these are refined, the PC{fused} is updated, allowing inaccuracies in depth values from individual views to be refined or substituted by accurate depth from other views in the fused cloud. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodepointcloudintogrid(pointcloud, gridsigma, gridc, matrices, vectors): """ Encodes a single view's point cloud into the voxel grid. pointcloud: List of 3D points (x,y,z) and colors (r,g,b). """ for point in pointcloud: # Map 3D point to grid coordinates gx, gy, gz = maptogridindices(point.xyz, griddimensions) # Convert depth to density and encode into geometry grid density = depthtodensity(point.depth) gridsigma[gx, gy, gz] = density # Encode color and features into appearance grid using matrices/vectors features = encodecolorwithmatrices(point.color, matrices, vectors) gridc[gx, gy, gz] = features def queryradiancefield(xw, gridsigma, gridc, viewingdirection): """ Queries the radiance field at a 3D location. """ # Interpolate density from geometry grid sigma = interpolate3d(gridsigma, xw) # Interpolate appearance features from appearance grid appearancefeatures = interpolate3d(gridc, xw) # Decode color using MLP S color = decodecolor(appearancefeatures, viewingdirection) return sigma, color def trainstep(inputviews, targetview): # 1. Construct per-view point clouds perviewpointclouds = [] for view in inputviews: pc = mappixelsto3d(view.rgb, view.depth, view.cameraparams) perviewpointclouds.append(pc) # 2. Encode initial point clouds into grid for pc in perviewpointclouds: encodepointcloudintogrid(pc, Gsigma, Gc, currentmatrices, currentvectors) # 3. Fuse point clouds fusedpointcloud = aggregatepointclouds(perviewpointclouds) # 4. Render target view # Cast rays for target view rays = generaterays(targetview.cameraparams, targetview.resolution) renderedcolors = [] rendereddepths = [] for ray in rays: # Sample points along ray points = samplepointsalongray(ray, gridbounds) # Query radiance field for each point sigmas = [] colors = [] for p in points: sigma, color = queryradiancefield(p, Gsigma, Gc, ray.direction) sigmas.append(sigma) colors.append(color) # Volume rendering to get final pixel color and depth finalcolor, finaldepth = volumerender(sigmas, colors, ray) renderedcolors.append(finalcolor) rendereddepths.append(finaldepth) # 5. Compute Loss rgbloss = computergbloss(renderedcolors, targetview.rgb) depthloss = computedepthloss(rendereddepths, targetview.depth) totalloss = rgbloss + depthloss # 6. Backpropagate and update # Gradients flow back to Gsigma, Gc, and the encoding matrices/vectors optimize(totalloss) # Note: The fused point cloud is implicitly updated via the refined grid/matrix values # in subsequent iterations, refining depth inaccuracies. Parameters: P: Number of appearance feature channels in the appearance grid Gc. S: A small MLP that transforms an appearance feature vector in combination with a viewing direction \mathbf{d} into a color \mathbf{c}. It comprises neural features and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Inaccuracies: The method specifically targets inaccuracies in sparse depth maps. If the initial depth is severely erroneous (e.g., holes or artifacts), the fusion process relies on other views to substitute these values. If all views have similar errors, the fusion may propagate them. Sparse Input Overfitting: Like other NeRFs, sparse inputs risk overfitting. The explicit voxel grid and point cloud fusion act as regularizers, but extreme sparsity may still lead to inconsistencies. Model Size: Significantly smaller than hierarchical or dense alternatives. On the LLFF dataset, the model size is much smaller than PlenOctrees (1750 MB), SNeRG (1500 MB), Plenovels (1250 MB), DVGO (1000 MB), RegNeRF (750 MB), ViP-NeRF (300 MB), and DSNeRF (250 MB). Training Time: Significantly faster than PlenOctrees, SNeRG, Plenovels, DVGO, RegNeRF, ViP-NeRF, and DSNeRF on the LLFF dataset. Strengths: Robustness to inaccurate depth via fusion; fast reconstruction; high compactness. Limitations: Performance depends on the quality of the initial sparse depth; if depth is missing in critical areas, fusion may not recover geometry as effectively as dense depth methods. This method was proposed to address the limitations of existing depth-aware NeRFs for sparse input views, which often overlook depth map inaccuracies (holes, artifacts) and suffer from low time efficiency. It is the first NeRF framework integrated with point cloud fusion, offering a novel scene representation that boosts time efficiency and delivers superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods like DSNeRF, DDP-NeRF, and SparseNeRF. name: Sparse Feature Volume
head: Neural Implicit Scene Representation
body: Sparse Feature Volume is a method for representing 3D scenes as a sparse grid of learnable latent vectors, where each voxel stores features decoded into a continuous Signed Distance Function (SDF) and radiance field. It solves the problem of high-fidelity surface reconstruction and online monocular 3D reconstruction by combining the efficiency of sparse voxel structures with the detail-preserving power of SDFs, distinguishing itself from dense occupancy fields and standard color-only radiance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of multi-view images (or a single monocular image sequence for online reconstruction). Output: A sparse feature volume data structure F{\theta} containing latent vectors for each active voxel, and a decoder network capable of querying SDF s and color \mathbf{c} at any 3D point \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Sparse Feature Volume. Structure: The 3D space is divided into a hierarchy of sparse voxels organized in coarse-to-fine levels. Levels: Three levels are defined: coarse (c), middle (m), and fine (f). Voxel Content: Each active voxel v at level l stores a feature latent vector F{\theta}^l. Storage: The sparsity is managed using the data structure from NeuralRecon, which efficiently stores only non-empty or relevant voxels. Parameters: Levels: l \in \{c, m, f\}. Sampling Points: N points sampled along a ray for volume rendering. Steps: 1. Sparse Voxel Division: Divide the 3D scene space into a set of sparse voxels. 2. Feature Fusion (2D CNN): Encode input multi-view images using a 2D CNN-based image encoder to extract 2D features. 3. Spatial-Aware Fusion: Fuse features from multiple views into the voxel space using a transformer module. This replaces the channel-wise average fusion used in prior works (e.g., NeuralRecon) to build more expressive latent vectors. 4. Temporal/Global Update: Merge the newly fused feature latent vectors with previous latent vectors using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) module, preceded by a sparse 3D CNN, to form global feature latent vectors F{\theta}^l. 5. Hierarchical Construction: Construct the sparse feature volumes F{\theta}^l for l \in \{c, m, f\} in a coarse-to-fine fashion. 6. Querying (Interpolation): For a query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, retrieve the feature vector by trilinearly interpolating the latent vectors from the eight corners of the containing voxel in the fine-level volume F{\theta}^f. 7. Decoding: SDF: Decode the signed distance s using an MLP decoder f\theta. Color: Decode the color \mathbf{c} using a separate MLP decoder f\omega and the radiance field latent vector F\omega. Formulas: The SDF decoder predicts the signed distance s for a query point \mathbf{x}: s = f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \text{interp}(F{\theta}^f, \mathbf{x})) where f\theta is an MLP-based decoder, \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the query point, and \text{interp} denotes trilinear interpolation in the fine-level sparse feature volume F{\theta}^f. The radiance decoder predicts the color \mathbf{c}: \mathbf{c} = f\omega(\mathbf{x}, \text{interp}(F{\omega}, \mathbf{x})) where f\omega is an MLP-based radiance decoder and F{\omega} is the radiance field latent vector. Args: querypoint (np.array): 3D coordinates [x, y, z]. sparsevolume (dict): Dictionary mapping voxel coordinates to latent vectors. Keys are voxel indices, values are feature vectors. decodersdf (nn.Module): MLP decoder for SDF. decodercolor (nn.Module): MLP decoder for color. Returns: s (float): Signed distance. c (np.array): Color vector. """ # 1. Identify the containing voxel # In a sparse grid, we must find the voxel containing querypoint. # This typically involves hashing or spatial indexing. voxelcoords = getcontainingvoxel(querypoint, sparsevolume.gridparams) # 2. Trilinear Interpolation # Calculate interpolation weights based on querypoint's position within the voxel weights = calculatetrilinearweights(querypoint, voxelcoords) # Interpolate the latent vector latentvector = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) cornerfeatures, dim=0) # 4. Decode Color # Note: The paper uses Fomega for color. Assuming Fomega is stored similarly # or derived from Ftheta. For this implementation, we assume a separate lookup # or the same latent vector is used if Fomega == Ftheta in simplified setups. # The paper distinguishes Ftheta (SDF) and Fomega (Radiance). # We assume Fomega is retrieved similarly or is the same structure. # If Fomega is distinct, replace sparsevolume with radiancevolume. radiancelatent = latentvector # Placeholder if Fomega == Ftheta, else lookup Fomega colorinput = torch.cat([querypoint, radiancelatent], dim=-1) c = decodercolor(colorinput) return s, c def constructsparsefeaturevolume(images, initialvolume): """ Construct and update the sparse feature volume from multi-view images. """ # 1. Encode images using 2D CNN imagefeatures = imageencoder(images) # 2. Spatial-aware feature fusion using Transformer # Fuse multi-view features into voxel space fusedfeatures = transformerfusion(imagefeatures, initialvolume) # 3. Merge with previous features using GRU after Sparse 3D CNN # This step updates the global feature latent vectors updatedvolume = sparse3dcnn(fusedfeatures) globalfeatures = gruupdate(updatedvolume, initialvolume) return globalfeatures Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Boundary: If a query point falls into a region with no voxels in the sparse volume, interpolation requires a fallback strategy (e.g., zero padding, nearest neighbor, or expanding the sparse volume). The use of sparse voxels reduces the number of queries compared to dense grids, but transformer-based fusion adds computational overhead per frame/update. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active voxels in the sparse volume, significantly less than dense H \times W \times D grids for large scenes. Strengths: Efficient geometry learning via volume rendering optimization in the space of latent vectors; suitable for online reconstruction; continuous SDF provides stronger detail expression than occupancy fields. Limitations: Requires multi-view inputs for optimal fusion (though adapted for monocular online); sparsity management adds complexity compared to dense grids. When to use: High-fidelity surface reconstruction, online monocular 3D reconstruction, scenes with large empty spaces where sparse representation is beneficial. When not to use: Scenes with uniform density where dense grids might be simpler; real-time applications where transformer fusion overhead is prohibitive. Origin: The Sparse Feature Volume, also known as Neural Implicit Scene Representation (NISR), was introduced in "MonoNeuralFusion: Online Monocular Neural 3D Reconstruction with Geometric Priors". History: It builds upon the sparse voxel structure from NeuralRecon and improves upon it by using transformer-based spatial-aware feature fusion instead of channel-wise average fusion, and by using SDFs for geometry representation instead of continuous occupancy fields. Usage: Used in online monocular neural 3D reconstruction, leveraging geometric priors for high-fidelity surface reconstruction. name: PAC-NeRF
head: Physics Augmented Continuum Neural Radiance Fields
body: PAC-NeRF is a method for geometry-agnostic system identification that estimates both the unknown 3D geometry and physical parameters (e.g., Young’s modulus, viscosity) of highly dynamic objects from multi-view videos. It differs from standard dynamic NeRFs by not learning dynamics from scratch; instead, it enforces continuum mechanics conservation laws using a differentiable Material Point Method (MPM). This hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian approach allows for robust handling of topology changes and frictional contacts, which are difficult for mesh-based methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of posed multi-view video frames \{\hat{C}(r, ti)\} of a dynamic scene, where r is a ray and ti is time. Output: An explicit geometric representation (volume density \sigma) and physical parameters (e.g., material constants) that minimize the difference between rendered and observed images. Data Structures: The method uses a hybrid Eulerian-Lagrangian representation: 1. Eulerian Grid: A voxel grid stores the view-independent volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}, t) and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}, t). This grid is discretized using the efficient voxel representation from Sun et al. (2022). 2. Lagrangian Particles: A set of particles advects the field quantities. Each particle carries state information used in the MPM simulation. 3. Physical Parameters: Learnable parameters characterizing the material, such as Young’s modulus, fluid viscosity, and friction angles. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Eulerian voxel NeRF for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Initialize Lagrangian particles and physical parameters. 2. Particle Binding: Bind renderable quantities (density and color) from the Eulerian grid to Lagrangian particles using a sampling scheme. 3. Physics Simulation: Simulate particle dynamics using a differentiable Material Point Method (MPM). The velocity field \mathbf{v} evolves according to momentum conservation: \frac{D\mathbf{v}}{Dt} = \frac{1}{\rho}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T} + \mathbf{g} where \rho is physical density, \mathbf{T} is the internal Cauchy stress tensor, and \mathbf{g} is gravity. 4. Grid Update (G2P): Convert particle states back to the Eulerian grid via Grid-to-Particle (G2P) transforms. This step enforces the conservation laws for density and color: \frac{D\sigma}{Dt} = 0, \quad \frac{D\mathbf{c}}{Dt} = 0 where \frac{D\phi}{Dt} = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \phi is the material derivative. 5. Rendering: Render images from the updated Eulerian voxel NeRF. For a ray r(s) with s \in [s{min}, s{max}], the pixel color C(r, t) is: C(r, t) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s, t) \sigma(r(s), t) \mathbf{c}(r(s), \boldsymbol{\omega}, t) ds + \mathbf{c}{bg} T(sf, t) where T(s, t) = \exp\left(-\int{sn}^{s} \sigma(r(\bar{s}), t) d\bar{s}\right). 6. Loss Computation: Compute the rendering loss against ground truth video frames: L{render} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| C(r, ti) - \hat{C}(r, ti) \|^2 where N is the number of frames and \mathcal{R} is the set of rays. 7. Optimization: Optimize geometry (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) and physical parameters via gradient-based optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pacnerftrain(videoframes, initialparams): # 1. Initialize Eulerian Grid and Lagrangian Particles voxelgrid = initvoxelnerf() particles = initparticles(voxelgrid) physicalparams = initphysicalparams(initialparams) for step in range(numtrainingsteps): # 2. Bind Grid to Particles (Sampling) particles.bindfromgrid(voxelgrid) # 3. Differentiable MPM Simulation # Evolve velocity using momentum conservation velocity = simulatempm(particles, physicalparams) # 4. Grid-to-Particle (G2P) / Particle-to-Grid (P2G) # Advect fields using material derivative conservation voxelgrid.updatefromparticles(particles, velocity) # 5. Render Images renderedframes = [] for frameidx, rayset in enumerate(videoframes.rays): color = volumerender(voxelgrid, rayset) renderedframes.append(color) # 6. Compute Loss loss = computemseloss(renderedframes, videoframes.gtcolors) # 7. Backpropagate and Optimize gradients = computegradients(loss, [voxelgrid, physicalparams]) updateparameters(gradients) return voxelgrid, physicalparams Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Changes: Standard mesh-based methods fail here. PAC-NeRF uses MPM, which naturally handles topology changes and frictional contacts. Unknown Geometry: The method does not require watertight mesh representations or known object geometries, unlike many system identification methods. Performance: PAC-NeRF accelerates NeRF rendering by two orders of magnitude compared to standard dynamic NeRFs due to the Eulerian voxel representation. Data Efficiency: By using a prescriptive physics model (MPM) rather than learning dynamics from scratch, it is more data-efficient and generalizable. Applicability: Validated on elastic bodies, plasticine, sand, and Newtonian/non-Newtonian fluids. Limitations: Requires multi-view video input. The complexity of the MPM simulation adds computational overhead per step compared to pure neural dynamics, though rendering is faster. PAC-NeRF was introduced to address the challenge of inferring geometric and physical properties from visual observations without assuming object geometry or topology. It builds on the concept of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and the Material Point Method (MPM) for differentiable physics simulation. Previous dynamic NeRF variants (e.g., D-NeRF) learned dynamics from scratch, requiring significant data and lacking interpretability. PAC-NeRF integrates these fields to enable system identification for a wide range of continuum materials. name: Spatially Encoded Radiance Fields
head: Sparse Radiance Fields, Voxel-based NeRF
body: Spatially Encoded Radiance Fields (SERF) simplify the implicit radiance function by spatially decomposing it into smaller functions to reduce the computational complexity load on the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). By storing feature vectors in a 3D voxel grid, the method divides volumetric model information into local batches, allowing equal or higher rendering quality than coordinate-based NeRF with a smaller or faster-decoding MLP. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by replacing the heavy coordinate-to-color mapping with a lookup-and-decode pipeline, and from sibling sparse methods by explicitly defining the grid-based feature storage mechanism that enables this acceleration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses; optionally, time t for dynamic scenes. Output: A rendered image (color \mathbf{c}) and depth, derived from the radiance field parameters. Data Structures: 1. Density Volume Grid (\mathbf{V}\sigma): A 3D tensor \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D} storing volume density \sigma. In sparse implementations, this may be stored in a hash table or octree structure to save memory. 2. Feature Volume Grid (\mathbf{V}a): A 3D tensor \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D \times F} storing latent feature vectors f of dimension F. These features encode appearance and geometry information. 3. Decoder Network (S\Theta): A small MLP that takes the interpolated feature vector as input and outputs the final color \mathbf{c}. Steps: 1. Grid Initialization: Initialize \mathbf{V}\sigma and \mathbf{V}a with learnable parameters. For sparse variants, initialize the hash map or octree structure. 2. Query Point Sampling: For a ray passing through the scene, sample points \mathbf{x} along the ray. 3. Feature Interpolation: Retrieve the feature vector f and density \sigma at \mathbf{x} from the grids using trilinear interpolation: f(\mathbf{x}) = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}a) \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}\sigma). 4. Color Decoding: Pass the interpolated feature vector f(\mathbf{x}) through the decoder MLP S\Theta to predict the view-dependent color \mathbf{c}: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}) = S\Theta(f(\mathbf{x})). 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the final pixel color using standard volume rendering integration over the sampled points, combining \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}). 6. Optimization: Update \mathbf{V}\sigma, \mathbf{V}a, and S\Theta parameters via gradient descent to minimize the difference between rendered and ground-truth images. Parameters: Grid Resolution (H, W, D): Not given in the sources. Feature Dimension (F): Not given in the sources. Decoder Size: Typically smaller than standard NeRF MLPs due to the pre-computed features. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Dense grids scale cubically with resolution. Sparse representations (e.g., hash grids) are required for high resolutions to avoid out-of-memory errors. Interpolation Artifacts: Trilinear interpolation may introduce blurring compared to nearest-neighbor or higher-order methods, potentially affecting high-frequency detail. Boundary Conditions: Points outside the grid bounds must be handled (e.g., clamping or treating as transparent). A voxel-grids-based scene representation that replaces coordinate-based MLPs with explicit density and feature volume grids to accelerate optimization, combined with a canonical field and time-dependent deformation field for dynamic surgical scenes. It differs from static SERF by modeling dynamic scenes via warping a canonical radiance field with a time-dependent deformation field. Choose this for dynamic endoscopic/surgical video reconstruction. Time Complexity: Faster inference and optimization than coordinate-based NeRF because the MLP is smaller and operates on lower-dimensional feature vectors rather than raw coordinates. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of voxels. Dense grids are O(H \times W \times D), while sparse grids reduce this significantly. Strengths: Faster optimization convergence; reduced MLP complexity; suitable for real-time or near-real-time rendering with sufficient grid resolution. Limitations: Memory intensive for high-resolution dense grids; interpolation may smooth out fine details compared to pure MLP representations. When to use: When training speed and inference latency are critical, and the scene can be adequately represented by a voxel grid. When not to use: For scenes with extremely high-frequency details that cannot be captured by the grid resolution, or when memory is severely constrained and sparse structures are not feasible. The concept of spatially decomposing the radiance function to reduce MLP complexity was demonstrated by Yu et al.. Müller et al. developed Instant-NeRF, a multi-resolution feature voxel grid implementation. The approach addresses the slow inference speed of standard NeRF MLPs. Efficient EndoNeRF extends this to dynamic surgical scenes using canonical fields and deformation fields. ADVANCEMENTS IN RADIANCE FIELD TECHNIQUES FOR VOLUMETRIC VIDEO GENERATION: A TECHNICAL OVERVIEW, https://hal.science/hal-05049100v1, fetched 2026-10-26 Efficient EndoNeRF reconstruction and its application for data-driven surgical simulation., https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-024-03114-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Coarse-Fine Dynamic Radiance Field
head: Compositional Radiance Field with Coarse Voxel and Fine MLP, Hybrid Encoder-Decoder Radiance Field
body: The Coarse-Fine Dynamic Radiance Field is a method for novel view synthesis of dynamic human heads that combines a discrete 3D voxel grid for efficient geometry estimation with a continuous MLP for high-frequency radiance modeling. It differs from standard NeRF by conditioning the continuous scene function on spatially-varying local animation codes retrieved from the voxel grid, and from Neural Volumes by using a hybrid coarse-fine representation to avoid the cubic memory complexity of a single high-resolution warped voxel grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse set of camera views (typically 3 concatenated RGB images) and camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics). Output: A rendered RGB image Ir and accumulated opacity Ar for a given viewpoint. Data Structures: 1. Global Animation Code (z): A latent vector z \in \mathbb{R}^{256} sampled from a Gaussian distribution. 2. Coarse Voxel Grid (G): A discrete 3D grid of dimensions D \times D \times D \times F, where D=64 and F=68. Each voxel at position p stores: Coarse color e{cp} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Differential opacity \sigma{ep} \in \mathbb{R}. View-independent local animation code fp \in \mathbb{R}^{32}. View-dependent local animation code f{vp} \in \mathbb{R}^{32}. Note: Values at continuous locations are obtained via trilinear interpolation. 3. Continuous Scene Function (f): An MLP that takes positional encoded coordinates, view vector, and local animation codes to output fine color cp \in \mathbb{R}^3 and differential opacity \sigmap \in \mathbb{R}. Numbered Steps: 1. Encoder (Global Code Generation): Concatenate N{views} input images (e.g., 3) along the channel axis. Pass through a 2D convolutional network to predict parameters \mu, \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{256} of a diagonal Gaussian distribution. Sample the global animation code z \in \mathbb{R}^{256} using the reparameterization trick: z = \mu + \epsilon \odot \sigma, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 2. Decoder (Coarse Grid Generation): The decoder consists of two 3D convolutional branches conditioned on z: Branch 1 (View-Independent): Predicts \sigma{ep} and fp. Conditioned only on z. Branch 2 (View-Dependent): Predicts e{cp} and f{vp}. Conditioned on z and the viewpoint vector v \in \mathbb{R}^3. Viewpoint v is computed as the normalized difference between the camera location and the center of the scene. The output is the coarse voxel grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{64 \times 64 \times 64 \times 68}. 3. Coarse Volumetric Rendering: For a ray r from camera center o, sample N points pi = o + di \cdot r, where di are uniformly sampled between near plane d{min} and far plane d{max}. Retrieve \sigma{ep} and e{cp} at pi via trilinear interpolation from G. Compute accumulated opacity Ae and color I{e0}: Ae = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai I{e0} = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai e{cpi} where: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{epj} \deltaj\right) \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{epi} \deltai) \deltai = |d{i+1} - di| Compute final coarse rendering Ie: Ie = I{e0} + (1 - Ae) I{bg} where I{bg} is the background color. 4. Efficient Sampling (Fine Depth Estimation): Compute coarse depth estimate de: de = \frac{1}{Ae} \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai di Sample fine depths d from a uniform distribution centered at de with range \Delta d: d \sim \mathcal{U}[de - \Delta d, de + \Delta d] where \Delta d = \frac{d{max} - d{min}}{k} and k=10. 5. Fine Volumetric Rendering: For each fine sample point p, retrieve local animation codes fp and f{vp} from G via trilinear interpolation. Apply positional encoding \phi(\cdot) to position p and view vector v. Evaluate the continuous scene function f: cp, \sigmap = f(\phi(p), \phi(v), fp, f{vp}) Compute fine accumulated opacity Af and color If using the same compositing equations as the coarse level (Eq. 2-3 in), substituting \sigmap for \sigma{ep} and cp for e{cp}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class CoarseFineDynamicRadianceField: def init(self, D=64, F=68, latentdim=256, numviews=3, k=10): self.D = D self.F = F self.latentdim = latentdim self.numviews = numviews self.k = k # Encoder: 2D CNN to predict mu and sigma self.encoder = Encoder2D(latentdim) # Decoder: Two 3D CNN branches # Branch 1: View-independent (sigmaep, fp) self.decoderbranch1 = Decoder3DViewIndep(F=68) # Outputs sigmaep and fp # Branch 2: View-dependent (ecp, fvp) self.decoderbranch2 = Decoder3DViewDep(F=68) # Outputs ecp and fvp # Continuous Scene Function: MLP self.scenemlp = MLPSceneFunction() # Positional Encoding function self.posenc = PositionalEncoding() def encode(self, images): """ images: Tensor of shape (B, numviews, C, H, W) Returns: z (B, latentdim), mu (B, latentdim), sigma (B, latentdim) """ # Concatenate views along channel axis x = images.view(images.size(0), -1, images.size(3), images.size(4)) mu, sigma = self.encoder(x) # Reparameterization trick epsilon = torch.randnlike(sigma) z = mu + epsilon sigma return z, mu, sigma def decode(self, z, viewpoint): """ z: Global animation code (B, latentdim) viewpoint: Normalized camera direction (B, 3) Returns: Voxel grid G (B, D, D, D, F) """ # Branch 1: View-independent # Note: In practice, decoder branches might share weights or be separate modules # conditioned on z. The output is a 3D volume. out1 = self.decoderbranch1(z) # out1 contains sigmaep and fp. Assuming layout: [sigmaep, fp] # sigmaep: (B, D, D, D, 1) # fp: (B, D, D, D, 32) # Branch 2: View-dependent out2 = self.decoderbranch2(z, viewpoint) # out2 contains ecp and fvp. # ecp: (B, D, D, D, 3) # fvp: (B, D, D, D, 32) # Concatenate to form G: [ecp, sigmaep, fp, fvp] -> F=3+1+32+32=68 G = torch.cat([out2['ecp'], out1['sigmaep'], out1['fp'], out2['fvp']], dim=-1) return G def rendercoarse(self, G, rayso, raysd, dmin, dmax, Nsamples): """ G: Voxel grid (B, D, D, D, F) rayso: Ray origins (B, 3) raysd: Ray directions (B, 3) Returns: Icoarse, Acoarse, dcoarse """ # Sample depths uniformly tvals = torch.linspace(dmin, dmax, Nsamples) # Add noise for anti-aliasing (optional, standard in NeRF-like methods) # For simplicity, using uniform samples as per source description zvals = tvals.expandas(raysd[..., 0]) # (B, N) # Compute points points = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) # (B, N, 3) # Interpolate voxel values at points # G is (B, D, D, D, F). Need to normalize points to [-1, 1] for gridsample or similar # Assuming helper function to interpolate from 3D grid sigmaep, ecp = interpolatevoxel(G, points) # (B, N, 1), (B, N, 3) # Compute deltas deltas = zvals[:, 1:] - zvals[:,:-1] deltainf = torch.tensor(1e10).expandas(deltas) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], dim=1) # Compute alphas and transmittance alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaep.squeeze(-1) deltas) # (B, N) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=1), dim=1)[:,:-1] # (B, N) # Accumulate weights = T alpha # (B, N) Acoarse = torch.sum(weights, dim=1) # (B,) Icoarse = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) ecp, dim=1) # (B, 3) # Coarse depth estimate dcoarse = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=1) / (Acoarse + 1e-10) # (B,) return Icoarse, Acoarse, dcoarse def renderfine(self, G, rayso, raysd, dmin, dmax, Nsamplescoarse, Nsamplesfine, dcoarse, Acoarse): """ Renders fine detail using efficient sampling around dcoarse. """ # Efficient Sampling deltad = (dmax - dmin) / self.k # Sample Nfine points uniformly in [dcoarse - deltad, dcoarse + deltad] # zvalsfine = torch.rand(B, Nfine) 2 deltad + (dcoarse - deltad) # For deterministic implementation, use linspace or fixed samples tvals = torch.linspace(-deltad, deltad, Nsamplesfine) zvalsfine = dcoarse.unsqueeze(1) + tvals.expandas(dcoarse) # (B, Nfine) # Compute points points = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvalsfine.unsqueeze(2) # (B, Nfine, 3) # Interpolate local animation codes fp, fvp = interpolatelocalcodes(G, points) # (B, Nfine, 32), (B, Nfine, 32) # Positional Encoding posencp = self.posenc(points) # View vector v is raysd (normalized) posencv = self.posenc(raysd.unsqueeze(1).expandas(points)) # MLP Evaluation # Concatenate features: posencp, posencv, fp, fvp inputfeatures = torch.cat([posencp, posencv, fp, fvp], dim=-1) sigmaf, cf = self.scenemlp(inputfeatures) # (B, Nfine, 1), (B, Nfine, 3) # Compute deltas for fine samples deltasfine = zvalsfine[:, 1:] - zvalsfine[:,:-1] deltainf = torch.tensor(1e10).expandas(deltasfine) deltasfine = torch.cat([deltasfine, deltainf], dim=1) # Compute alphas and transmittance alphaf = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaf.squeeze(-1) deltasfine) # (B, Nfine) Tf = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alphaf[:,:1]), 1.0 - alphaf + 1e-10], dim=1), dim=1)[:,:-1] # (B, Nfine) # Accumulate weightsf = Tf alphaf # (B, Nfine) Afine = torch.sum(weightsf, dim=1) # (B,) Ifine = torch.sum(weightsf.unsqueeze(-1) cf, dim=1) # (B, 3) return Ifine, Afine def forward(self, images, rayso, raysd, dmin, dmax, Ncoarse, Nfine): # 1. Encode z, mu, sigma = self.encode(images) # 2. Decode # Viewpoint v is derived from raysd or camera params. # Source says v is normalized difference between camera location and center. # Assuming raysd is normalized direction. viewpoint = raysd # Simplified, usually requires camera center G = self.decode(z, viewpoint) # 3. Coarse Render Icoarse, Acoarse, dcoarse = self.rendercoarse(G, rayso, raysd, dmin, dmax, Ncoarse) # 4. Fine Render Ifine, Afine = self.renderfine(G, rayso, raysd, dmin, dmax, Ncoarse, Nfine, dcoarse, Acoarse) # 5. Background Compositing (for coarse) # Icoarsefinal = Icoarse + (1 - Acoarse) Ibg # Ifinefinal = Ifine + (1 - Afine) Ibg return Ifine, Afine, Icoarse, Acoarse, mu, sigma def computeloss(self, Ifine, Afine, Icoarse, Acoarse, mu, sigma, Igt, Ibg): # Fine Rendering Loss Lr = torch.mean((Ifine - Igt) 2) # Coarse Rendering Loss Icoarsefinal = Icoarse + (1 - Acoarse.unsqueeze(-1)) Ibg Ler = torch.mean((Icoarsefinal - Igt) 2) # Opacity Prior Loss (for both fine and coarse) # Lbeta = sum(log(A) + log(1-A)) # Applied to accumulated opacities Lbetafine = torch.mean(torch.log(Afine) + torch.log(1 - Afine)) Lbetacoarse = torch.mean(torch.log(Acoarse) + torch.log(1 - Acoarse)) # KL Divergence Loss # LKL = 0.5 sum(exp(sigma) + mu^2 - 1 - sigma) LKL = torch.mean(0.5 torch.sum(torch.exp(sigma) + mu2 - 1 - sigma, dim=1)) # Total Loss # Lambda values not specified in source, assume placeholders or standard values lambdaf = 1.0 lambdac = 1.0 lambdaKL = 1.0 L = Lr + Ler + lambdaf Lbetafine + lambdac Lbetacoarse + lambdaKL LKL return L Parameters: D=64: Spatial dimension of the voxel grid. F=68: Dimensionality of the field (3 color + 1 opacity + 32 view-indep local code + 32 view-dep local code). k=10: Factor for fine sampling range reduction (\Delta d = (d{max}-d{min})/k). Training Data: Multi-camera system with ~100 cameras, 2048x1334 resolution at 30Hz, downsampled to 1024x667. Dataset Split: Trained on m=93 cameras, tested on q=33 frames from p=7 other cameras. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The reparameterization trick requires stable gradients through the sampling of z. Boundaries: The efficient sampling range \Delta d must be chosen carefully; if too small, fine details outside the coarse depth estimate are missed. If too large, computational cost increases. Degenerate Input: The encoder requires a sparse set of views (e.g., 3). Performance may degrade with fewer views or highly occluded scenes not covered by the input views. Time Complexity: Rendering involves two passes: coarse ray-marching on a 64^3 grid and fine ray-marching on an MLP. The efficient sampling reduces the number of MLP queries compared to uniform sampling over the entire depth range. Memory Complexity: The voxel grid is 64^3 \times 68 floats, which is significantly smaller than a high-resolution single grid (e.g., 128^3 or 256^3) used in methods like Neural Volumes. The MLP memory footprint is independent of scene resolution. Strengths: Captures fine-level detail better than pure voxel methods (like NV) while avoiding their memory constraints. Better generalization for dynamic scenes than pure MLP methods (like NeRF) due to the structured prior from the voxel grid. Limitations: Requires a multi-camera setup for training. The coarse grid resolution is fixed (64^3), limiting the maximum geometric detail that can be explicitly stored. When to use: Dynamic human head capture with multi-camera rigs where high-frequency detail (skin, hair) and animation are required. When not to use: Static scenes (NeRF is simpler), scenes with very large scale variations (voxel grid may not cover the volume efficiently), or single-view setups. The method was introduced in "Learning Compositional Radiance Fields of Dynamic Human Heads". It builds upon the concept of compositional representations, combining the strengths of discrete voxel-based methods (like Neural Volumes) and continuous neural rendering (like NeRF). The key innovation is the use of a hybrid coarse-fine structure conditioned on a global latent code and spatially-varying local animation codes, enabling efficient and high-quality rendering of dynamic human heads.
