name: Triplane and Planar Representations
head: Triplanar Representation, Feature Planes
body: Triplane and Planar Representations encode 3D scenes using a set of learnable 2D feature grids (planes) aligned with the canonical coordinate axes, rather than a 3D voxel grid. This approach reduces memory complexity from cubic to linear relative to resolution while maintaining high fidelity. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D voxel grids by leveraging 2D convolutions for efficient feature aggregation and is specifically optimized for integration into Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for 3D-aware image synthesis. It serves as a generative backbone for state-of-the-art 3D-aware GANs and efficient neural rendering of dynamic or outdoor scenes [18169-image-conditional-triplanar-representation.md]. The family builds on Hierarchical and Sparse Grid Representations, sharing the mechanism of discretizing 3D space into learnable structures and querying them via differentiable interpolation. Specifically: Discretization The 3D scene space is represented by a tensor \mathbf{T} of shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D}. The first dimension (size 3) indexes the three orthogonal canonical planes: xy, xz, and yz. Feature Storage Each plane stores learnable feature vectors [13901-eg3d-triplane-representation.md]. The channel dimension C varies by method (e.g., C=32 in EG3D Triplane Representation, or C transformed to G=C/4 in Image-Conditional Triplanar Representation). The spatial resolution D \times D is typically square. Differentiable Query For a query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, features are gathered by projecting \mathbf{x} onto each canonical plane and bilinearly interpolating the nearby features [13901-eg3d-triplane-representation.md]. Let \mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, \mathbf{f}{yz} be the features gathered from the respective planes. These are combined using an aggregation operator \Phi (e.g., mean in EG3D Triplane Representation) and passed to a lightweight MLP to predict radiance field properties [13901-eg3d-triplane-representation.md]: (\mathbf{f}, c, \sigma) = \text{MLP}(\Phi(\mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, \mathbf{f}{yz})) The output values, including color c, are independent of viewing direction and depend only on \mathbf{x} in the static case [13901-eg3d-triplane-representation.md]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def querytriplane(T, x): # T: shape (3, C, D, D) # x: shape (3,) query point in world coordinates # Project x to each plane and bilinearly interpolate fxy = bilinearinterp(T[0], x[0], x[1]) fxz = bilinearinterp(T[1], x[0], x[2]) fyz = bilinearinterp(T[2], x[1], x[2]) # Aggregate features fagg = (fxy + fxz + fyz) / 3.0 # Decode to radiance field properties f, c, sigma = mlpdecode(fagg) return f, c, sigma A 3D scene encoding method that uses three orthogonal 2D feature grids to model volumetric properties for differentiable rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D voxel grids by reducing memory footprint through 2D convolutions and is specifically optimized for integration into Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for 3D-aware image synthesis. It serves as the generative backbone for state-of-the-art 3D-aware GANs, enabling high-fidelity image synthesis from unposed inputs via a distillation pipeline. A 3D scene representation that constructs axis-aligned orthogonal feature planes from input images, enabling efficient neural rendering of outdoor scenes without the cubic complexity of voxel-based methods. It differs from standard static triplane representations (e.g., EG3D Triplane Representation) by explicitly conditioning the feature grid on camera poses and depth, allowing the planes to encode appearance information derived from multiple viewpoints rather than representing a fixed canonical volume. This variant uses a triplane NeRF representation where scene codes are optimized jointly with a diffusion prior to handle sparse-view data and ensure end-to-end coherence. The scene code xi has shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}, representing a triplane NeRF representation. The denoising network is a U-Net with 122M parameters, taking noisy and denoised triplane features as input/output, with channels of all three planes stacked together. For prediction format, it adopts the v-parameterization \hat{v}\phi(x^{(t)}, t) from [43], such that \hat{x} = \alpha(t)x^{(t)} - \sigma(t)\hat{v}. Regarding the weighting function w(t) in the diffusion loss, it uses SNR-based weighting w(t) = (\alpha(t)/\sigma(t))^2\omega from Eq. (5), instead of LSGM mechanisms, which are found unstable with NeRF auto-decoders. On the D-NeRF dataset, DoublePlane achieves PSNR 30.370, SSIM 0.961, LPIPS 0.054, and Training Time 8m 04s. Triplane representations originated in the context of 3D-aware generative models, specifically EG3D Triplane Representation, which utilized them for high-fidelity image synthesis [13901-eg3d-triplane-representation.md]. They have since been adapted for inverse rendering and reconstruction, including image-conditional variants for outdoor scenes [18169-image-conditional-triplanar-representation.md] and diffusion-based priors for sparse-view reconstruction. name: EG3D Triplane Representation
head: ConvONet / EG3D (Tri-plane), EG3D Triplane-Based 3D GAN, Hybrid Triplane Representation, Tri-plane Features, Tri-plane representation
body: The EG3D Triplane Representation is a 3D scene encoding method that stores learnable features in three orthogonal 2D planes (xy, xz, yz) to enable efficient neural volumetric rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard 3D grids by reducing memory footprint through 2D convolution operations while maintaining high-resolution detail, and it is specifically optimized for integration into Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for 3D-aware image synthesis. Inputs and Outputs Input: A noise vector z and camera pose parameters. Output: A triplane tensor \mathbf{T}, which is queried to produce feature vectors, color, and density for volume rendering. Data Structures The core data structure is the triplane tensor \mathbf{T}: Shape: \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256 \times 96}. Layout: This tensor comprises 3 axis-aligned planes (xy, xz, yz). Channels: Each plane has 32 channels (C=32). Resolution: Each plane has a spatial resolution of 256 \times 256. Querying and Rendering To render an image, the system performs the following steps: 1. Feature Gathering: For a query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, project \mathbf{x} onto each of the three canonical planes (xy, xz, yz). 2. Interpolation: Bilinearly interpolate the features at the projected coordinates on each plane to obtain feature vectors \mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, and \mathbf{f}{yz}. 3. Aggregation: Combine the three feature vectors using the mean operator \Phi: \mathbf{f}{agg} = \Phi(\mathbf{f}{xy}, \mathbf{f}{xz}, \mathbf{f}{yz}) = \frac{\mathbf{f}{xy} + \mathbf{f}{xz} + \mathbf{f}{yz}}{3} 4. Decoding: Pass the aggregated feature vector through a lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict the feature vector \mathbf{f}, color c, and volume density \sigma: (\mathbf{f}, c, \sigma) = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{f}{agg}) Note that the output values, including color, are independent of viewing direction and depend only on \mathbf{x}. 5. Volume Rendering: Accumulate points along rays using the predicted \sigma and c to perform volume rendering [Max 1995]. This produces a raw neural rendering RGB image \mathbf{I}{128} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 128 \times 128} and a feature image \mathbf{I}f \in \mathbb{R}^{32 \times 128 \times 128}. The first three channels of \mathbf{I}f correspond to \mathbf{I}{128}. 6. Depth Extraction: Extract a dense depth map \mathbf{I}D \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 128} from the volume rendering. 7. Super-Resolution: Feed the feature image \mathbf{I}f and the raw RGB image \mathbf{I}{128} into a 2D super-resolution network to yield the final output \mathbf{I}{512} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 512 \times 512}: \text{SuperRes}(\mathbf{I}f, \mathbf{I}{128}) = \mathbf{I}{512} Parameters Image Resolution: Input images and final output are 512 \times 512. Intermediate Resolution: Neural rendering occurs at 128 \times 128. Pitfalls Axis-Aligned Bias: The orthogonal coordinate transformation can be challenging to handle complicated structures due to the axis-aligned bias of the representation. Local Minima: Optimization is more easily affected by local minima compared to MLP representations, which benefit from inductive smoothness bias. Memory: While efficient compared to 3D grids, it still requires high spatial resolution to represent fine details, leading to a large memory footprint relative to sparse methods. Performance: The efficient design allows rendering from a triplane at 42 fps on an RTX 3090. Quality: Provides quality comparable to state-of-the-art 2D GANs in terms of Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). Limitations: The axis-aligned nature limits its ability to model complex, non-axis-aligned structures without high resolution. The EG3D Triplane Representation was introduced in EG3D [Chan et al. 2022] as a method for learning unconditional 3D-aware image generation from single-view images. It builds upon the ConvONet approach [43] which first utilized a tri-plane representation to model 3D scenes. In the context of Factor Fields, this representation corresponds to N=1, with an orthogonal 2D coordinate transformation \gamma1(\mathbf{x}), 2D map basis f1(\mathbf{x}), and MLP projection P(\mathbf{x}). name: Image-Conditional Triplanar Representation
head: Tri-plane Features
body: Image-Conditional Triplanar Representation is a 3D scene representation that constructs learnable triplanes directly from input images, enabling efficient modeling of complex scenes without the cubic complexity of voxel-based methods. It differs from static triplane methods like EG3D Triplane Representation by conditioning the feature grid on camera poses and intrinsic parameters, allowing the representation to adapt to specific viewpoints and handle sparse-view outdoor scenes effectively. Inputs and Outputs Input: An input image I \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi \times Wi \times 3}, camera pose \gammai, and camera intrinsic matrix Ki. Output: A triplanar feature tensor \mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times G \times D \times D}, where G = C/4 is the output channel dimension, and D \times D is the spatial resolution of each plane. Data Structures Feature Map (FI): A 2D feature map of shape \mathbb{R}^{Hi/2 \times Wi/2 \times C} extracted from the input image. 3D Feature Volume (VF): A volumetric representation where features are projected from FI. Depth-Encoded Features (VZ): Features enhanced with depth information via an MLP. Triplane (\mathbf{S}): A tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times C \times D \times D} initially, transformed to \mathbb{R}^{3 \times G \times D \times D}. Steps 1. Image Encoding: Extract low-resolution spatial features from the input image I using an ImageNet pre-trained ConvNet backbone E. This transforms I into a 2D feature map FI \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi/2 \times Wi/2 \times C}. 2. Back-Projection: Project local features from FI backwards along every ray to construct a 3D feature volume VF. This projection uses the camera pose \gammai and intrinsic matrix Ki. 3. Depth Encoding: Encode the depth of individual features in the grid using an MLP Z. The MLP takes as input the concatenated features in the grid VF, the positions of the grid in the camera frame xc, and the directions from the world frame positions xw to the camera frame. The output is depth-encoded features VZ = Z(VF, xc, d). 4. Triplane Aggregation: Obtain triplane features \mathbf{S}{xy}, \mathbf{S}{xz}, \mathbf{S}{yz} by summing weighted depth-encoded features VZ. The weights are softmax scores from aggregation MLPs A{xy}, A{xz}, A{yz} conditioned on VZ and world coordinates. 5. Channel Transformation and Upsampling: Transform the built image-conditional triplanes into a new G-channel output using learned 2D convolutions, where G = C/4. This step also upsamples the spatial dimension of the planes from D \times D to the image feature space resolution (H/2 \times W/2). Formulas The triplane features are computed as: \mathbf{S}{xy} = \sumi w{xyi} \mathbf{V}{Zi}, \quad w{xy} = A{xy}(V{Zi}, x{wz}) \mathbf{S}{xz} = \sumi w{xzi} \mathbf{V}{Zi}, \quad w{xz} = A{xz}(V{Zj}, x{wy}) \mathbf{S}{yz} = \sumi w{yzi} \mathbf{V}{Zi}, \quad w{yz} = A{yz}(V{Zj}, x{wx}) where A{xy}, A{xz}, A{yz} are feature aggregation MLPs, and w{xy}, w{xz}, w{yz} are softmax scores obtained after summing over the z, y, and x dimensions respectively. Parameters C: Feature dimension of the initial triplane. G = C/4: Output channel dimension after 2D convolution. D \times D: Spatial resolution of each plane, upsampled to H/2 \times W/2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparse Views: The method is designed for sparse-view synthesis; performance may degrade if input views are insufficient to cover the scene geometry. Depth Ambiguity: The depth encoding MLP Z must accurately resolve depth ambiguities from 2D features; incorrect depth encoding can lead to artifacts in the triplane. Complexity: Avoids the cubic complexity of 3D CNNs and voxel-based representations, offering linear scaling with respect to the number of voxels/features. Expressiveness: More expressive than BEV or 2D feature representations by maintaining full 3D dimensionality without omitting any axis. Performance: Efficient for outdoor scenes with sparse views, leveraging 2D convolutions for feature aggregation and upsampling. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial image encoder and camera poses; errors in pose estimation can propagate to the triplane. Originated in the NeO 360 paper, which introduced neural fields for sparse view synthesis of outdoor scenes. The method builds on prior works involving volumetric reconstruction but adapts them for appearance estimation and neural rendering. It addresses the limitations of 2D/BEV representations and the computational cost of voxel-based methods. NeO 360: Neural Fields for Sparse View Synthesis of Outdoor Scenes, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.00843, fetched 2026-10-26

name: HIVE (HIerarchical Volume Encoding)
body: HIVE is a hierarchical volume encoding module for neural implicit surface reconstruction that explicitly encodes spatial information using multi-scale feature volumes to capture high-frequency details while enforcing spatial consistency. It replaces or augments the implicit encoding of MLPs by concatenating trilinearly interpolated features from low-to-medium resolution volumes with sparsified high-resolution volumes. Unlike single high-resolution volumes that suffer from global incoherence due to isolated voxel updates, or hash-table encodings that suffer from collisions, HIVE uses low-resolution volumes to enforce smoothness and high-resolution volumes for detail, reducing memory consumption via sparsification. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Multi-view images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, camera poses, and a query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 with viewing direction \mathbf{v} \in S^2. Outputs: Signed Distance Field (SDF) value s(\mathbf{x}) and color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}). Data Structures The method employs K=8 feature volumes \mathcal{V} = \{V1, \dots, VK\}. Resolutions: The volumes increase in resolution. The text specifies a basic setting with resolutions increasing from 2 \times 2 \times 2 up to 256 \times 256 \times 256. Figure 3 indicates the sequence includes 2, 8, 32, 128, 512, 1024. Feature Dimension: Each voxel stores a feature vector. The text notes "small-feature-channel" volumes compared to octree-based methods. The specific channel count is not explicitly defined in the text, but Figure 3 labels the volumes with a dimension of 4 (e.g., 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 4). Sparse High-Resolution Volumes: Volumes with resolution 512 or 1024 are sparsified. Only voxels near the preliminary surface reconstruction are retained. Algorithm Steps The optimization is performed in two stages: 1. Stage 1 (Coarse Reconstruction): Compute an initial result using features from low-to-medium resolution volumes (resolutions 2 to 256). For a query point \mathbf{x}, retrieve features fi(\mathbf{x}) from each volume Vi via trilinear interpolation. Concatenate these features to form the input feature vector \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}): \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \text{concat}(f1(\mathbf{x}), \dots, fK(\mathbf{x})) Input \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) into the SDF network S\Theta and Color network C\Theta. The SDF network outputs s(\mathbf{x}) = S\Theta(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x})). 2. Stage 2 (Fine Reconstruction): Sparsification: Based on the preliminary surface from Stage 1, sparsify the high-resolution volumes (512 or 1024). Keep only voxels nearby the surface. Finalization: Finalize the result using features from the sparsified high-resolution volumes. The same interpolation and concatenation logic applies, but now including the sparse high-res volumes. Decoding and Rendering SDF Network: s(\mathbf{x}) = S\Theta(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x})). Color Network: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = C\Theta(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{v}). Volume Rendering: Images are rendered by integrating along rays \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{d}) = \int{tn}^{tf} w(t) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}(t), \mathbf{v}) dt where the weighting function is w(t) = T(t)\rho(t). Transmittance: T(t) = e^{-\int{tn}^{t} \rho(u) du} Density: Derived from the SDF using the derivative of a sigmoid function \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1}: \rho(t) = \max\left(-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}(\text{sdf}(\mathbf{p}(t))), 0\right) = \max\left(\frac{s e^{-s \cdot \text{sdf}(\mathbf{p}(t))}}{(1 + e^{-s \cdot \text{sdf}(\mathbf{p}(t))})^2}, 0\right) where s is the sharpness parameter of the sigmoid. Optimization Minimize the difference between rendered images and input images. Add two regularization terms for smoothness. The specific formulas for these terms are not provided in the text. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point): """ Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D grid at a given point. grid: numpy array of shape (D, H, W, C) point: numpy array of shape (3,) with coordinates in [0, 1] Returns: feature vector of shape (C,) """ # Scale point to grid dimensions coords = point np.array(grid.shape[:3]) # Get integer and fractional parts x0, y0, z0 = np.floor(coords).astype(int) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 # Handle boundary conditions x0 = np.clip(x0, 0, grid.shape[0] - 1) x1 = np.clip(x1, 0, grid.shape[0] - 1) y0 = np.clip(y0, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) y1 = np.clip(y1, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) z0 = np.clip(z0, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) z1 = np.clip(z1, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) # Fractional weights fx, fy, fz = coords - np.floor(coords) # Interpolate c00 = grid[x0, y0, z0] (1 - fx) (1 - fy) (1 - fz) + \ grid[x1, y0, z0] fx (1 - fy) (1 - fz) + \ grid[x0, y1, z0] (1 - fx) fy (1 - fz) + \ grid[x1, y1, z0] fx fy (1 - fz) c10 = grid[x0, y0, z1] (1 - fx) (1 - fy) fz + \ grid[x1, y0, z1] fx (1 - fy) fz + \ grid[x0, y1, z1] (1 - fx) fy fz + \ grid[x1, y1, z1] fx fy fz return c00 (1 - fz) + c10 fz def hiveencode(point, volumes): """ Concatenates features from hierarchical volumes. point: numpy array (3,) volumes: list of numpy arrays (grids) Returns: concatenated feature vector """ features = [] for vol in volumes: features.append(trilinearinterpolate(vol, point)) return np.concatenate(features) def sigmoidderivative(sdfval, sharpness): """ Computes density from SDF using sigmoid derivative. sdfval: float sharpness: float (s) Returns: density """ # Phis(x) = (1 + exp(-sx))^-1 # dPhi/dx = s exp(-sx) / (1 + exp(-sx))^2 expterm = np.exp(-sharpness sdfval) denom = (1 + expterm) 2 dPhi = (sharpness expterm) / denom return max(-dPhi, 0) def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfnet, colornet, volumes, tnear, tfar, sharpness): """ Renders a single ray using neural volume rendering. """ # Sample points along the ray tvals = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, 128) points = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, np.newaxis] # Get features features = np.array([hiveencode(p, volumes) for p in points]) # Get SDF and Color sdfvals = sdfnet(features) colors = colornet(features, raydirection) # Compute density densities = np.array([sigmoidderivative(s, sharpness) for s in sdfvals]) # Compute transmittance and weights # T(t) = exp(-int rho du) # Approximate integral using trapezoidal rule or simple sum dt = tvals[1] - tvals[0] alpha = 1 - np.exp(-densities dt) T = np.oneslike(alpha) T[1:] = np.cumprod(1 - alpha[:-1]) weights = T alpha # Composite color color = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colors, axis=0) return color Parameters Number of Volumes: 8 in the basic setting. Resolutions: 2, 8, 32, 128, 256 (dense), 512, 1024 (sparse). Sharpness (s): Parameter for the sigmoid function \Phis. Value not specified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Memory Consumption: High-resolution dense volumes consume significant memory. Sparsification is required for resolutions 512 and 1024. Sparsification Threshold: The method keeps voxels "nearby the surface" but does not specify the exact distance threshold for sparsification. Hash Collisions: Avoided by using hierarchical volumes instead of hash tables. Uses regular 3D grids for feature storage. HIVE differs by using a hierarchy of grids and sparsification. Voxel and Grid Representations Uses 2D planes for feature storage. HIVE uses 3D volumes, capturing volumetric information directly. Triplane and Planar Representations Uses octrees with summed features. HIVE uses concatenated features from multiple small-channel volumes, consuming less memory. Octree-based Implicit Surface Representation with SH and SDF Optimization Time Complexity: Query time is proportional to the number of volumes (K=8) and the cost of trilinear interpolation. Sparsification reduces the number of active high-resolution voxels, potentially speeding up memory access but adding overhead for sparsification logic. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to a single dense high-resolution volume due to sparsification and the use of small feature channels. The text states it consumes less memory than octree-based methods with large feature channels. Performance: On the DTU dataset, HIVE reduced error by 25% for NeuS (0.84 mm to 0.63 mm), 23% for VolSDF (0.86 mm to 0.66 mm), and 10% for NeuralWarp (0.68 mm to 0.61 mm). On EPFL, NeuralWarp error reduced by 31%. Strengths: Captures high-frequency details, enforces spatial consistency, avoids hash collisions, reduces memory via sparsification. Limitations: Requires multi-stage optimization. Sparsification threshold is not specified. HIVE was introduced in the paper "HIVE: HIerarchical Volume Encoding for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction". It addresses limitations in existing volume encoding methods (global incoherence) and hash-table encoding (collisions). It is demonstrated on DTU, EPFL, and BlendedMVS datasets. name: Octree-based Implicit Surface Representation with SH and SDF Optimization
head: Octree-NeRF, Octree-SDF
body:
This method represents a 3D scene using an adaptive octree structure where leaf nodes store learnable property values, specifically Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for color and Signed Distance Function (SDF) values for geometry. It solves the trade-off between the high quality of continuous neural fields and the computational cost of trilinear interpolation by using constant property values at leaf nodes for rendering, achieving over 30x speedup while maintaining visual fidelity through fine-tuning. Unlike standard grid-based methods that rely on interpolation for continuity, this approach explicitly optimizes the discrete leaf node values to approximate the continuous field, allowing for real-time rendering speeds comparable to or exceeding point-based methods like 3DGS. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Multi-view images of a scene, camera poses, and an initial octree structure (often initialized from a pre-trained neural field like VolSDF). Outputs: An optimized octree where each leaf node stores an SDF value S and a set of SH coefficients \mathbf{c} (degree 2, 9 coefficients per node). Data Structures The scene is represented by an octree. Each node in the octree contains: isleaf: Boolean flag. If isleaf is true: sdf: Float value representing the signed distance to the surface. shcoeffs: Array of 9 floats (degree 2 SH basis coefficients for RGB). If isleaf is false: children: Array of 8 child nodes. Subdivision Strategy The octree is built using a fine-to-coarse strategy guided by SDF values: 1. Initialize a coarse grid or use a pre-trained network (e.g., VolSDF) to query SDF values at grid points. 2. Evaluate SDF values at the center of each potential leaf node. 3. Subdivide a node if the SDF variation within it exceeds a threshold or to reach a target maximum resolution level l. 4. Continue subdivision until the target resolution is achieved. Property Storage and Decoding Instead of storing values at all grid points and interpolating, values are stored only at leaf nodes. SDF Query: For a query point \mathbf{x}, find the containing leaf node. The SDF value S(\mathbf{x}) is the constant value stored in that leaf node. Color Query: The SH coefficients \mathbf{c} are retrieved from the containing leaf node. The view direction \mathbf{v} is used to compute the color \mathbf{C} using SH basis functions Y(\mathbf{v}): \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{m=0}^{8} \mathbf{c}m Ym(\mathbf{v}) where \mathbf{c}m are the SH coefficients stored in the leaf node. Rendering Volume rendering is performed by sampling points along rays. For each sample point, the SDF determines the density/opacity (via a standard SDF-to-density conversion, e.g., \sigma = \alpha / \epsilon or similar differentiable mapping, though the specific mapping function is not detailed in the source, the SDF is used for geometry) and the SH coefficients determine the color. The use of constant leaf node values avoids the computational cost of trilinear interpolation. Optimization Loop The octree properties (SDF and SH coefficients) are optimized using a loss function composed of three terms: 1. Color Loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{col}}): Mean squared error between rendered pixel colors \hat{\mathbf{C}}n and ground truth \mathbf{C}n: \mathcal{L}{	ext{col}} =  rac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N \|\mathbf{C}n - \hat{\mathbf{C}}n\|2^2 where N is the total number of pixels. 2. Total Variation Loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{TV}}): Applied to SH coefficients to preserve geometric continuity and stability, especially at low resolutions: \mathcal{L}{	ext{TV}} =  rac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{V}} \sqrt{(D{\mathbf{p}}^x)^2 + (D{\mathbf{p}}^x)^2 + (D{\mathbf{p}}^z)^2} Note: The source text contains a typo in the formula, repeating (D{\mathbf{p}}^x)^2 instead of (D{\mathbf{p}}^y)^2. The intent is likely the gradient magnitude in 3D space. \mathcal{V} is the set of grid points. Only 1% of points from \mathcal{V} are randomly selected to calculate this loss to speed up training. The SH TV term is turned off when subdivision level l > 8 to prevent excessive smoothness and ensure detail recovery. 3. SDF Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}}): Encourages a smooth surface by regularizing the gradient of the SDF: \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}} =  rac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{V}} \|\mathcal{G}(
abla S(\mathbf{p})) - 
abla S(\mathbf{p})\|2^2 where \mathcal{G} is a Gaussian filter applied to the gradient 
abla S. The set of points \mathcal{V} is defined as \{\mathbf{p} \mid -0.1 \le S(\mathbf{p}) \le 0.1\} when subdivision level l \le 8. When l > 8, only 10% of points from \mathcal{V} are selected for fast training. Total Loss: \min{\Theta} \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{	ext{col}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{	ext{TV}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{	ext{smooth}} where \lambda1 and \lambda2 are weights. Parameters: \lambda1 (TV weight): Default 10^{-5}. Increased to (10^{-5}, 10^{-3}] for bright scenes (metallic/transparent materials or intense light). \lambda2 (Smoothness weight): 2 	imes 10^{-4}. SH Degree: 2. Fine-tuning: After achieving the target resolution, the property values of leaf nodes are fine-tuned to mitigate quality loss from using constant values instead of interpolation, making rendering quality comparable to trilinear interpolation. Pitfalls: Small \lambda1 results in coarse shapes with holes at low octree resolution, which are difficult to patch as resolution increases. Methods like Voxurf and BakedSDF are sensitive to lighting, exhibiting holes in areas with high specular highlights or intense lighting, whereas this method consistently produces satisfactory geometry. Speed: Using constant property values at leaf nodes with fine-tuning achieves a speed increase of over 30 times compared to trilinear interpolation on grid points. NeRF-Synthetic (Chair, l=9, Constant): 288.62 FPS (vs 18.51 FPS for Trilinear l=9). NeRF-Synthetic (Mic, l=9, Constant): 692.03 FPS (vs 18.35 FPS for Trilinear l=9). DTU (ID 24, l=10, Constant): 146.27 FPS (vs 5.59 FPS for Trilinear l=10). Training Time: Level l=9: 75k iterations in 40 minutes on NVIDIA Tesla V100. Level l=10: 100k iterations in 60 minutes on NVIDIA Tesla V100. Quality: PSNR on NeRF-Synthetic (Chair, l=10, Trilinear): 34.62 (VolSDF: 30.75, Plenoxels: 33.87). Chamfer Distance (CD) on NeRF-Synthetic (Chair, l=10, Trilinear): 1.39 (VolSDF: 1.57, Voxurf: 1.27). Strengths: Real-time rendering capability, consistent geometry even in intense lighting conditions where other methods fail, efficient memory usage via sparse octree. Limitations: May struggle to recover specular highlights in intense lighting compared to some neural methods, though geometry remains robust. This method was introduced in the paper "Real-time volume rendering with octree-based implicit surface representation". It builds on the principles of neural implicit surfaces (like VolSDF) and adaptive octree representations, aiming to bridge the gap between high-quality neural rendering and real-time performance. The integration with VolSDF (VolSDF-SH) demonstrates its extensibility to pre-trained network-based methods. name: LiveScene
head: Language Embedding Interactive Radiance Fields for Physical Scene Rendering and Control
body: LiveScene is a scene-level language-embedded interactive radiance field that reconstructs and controls multiple articulated objects in complex physical scenes from monocular video. It solves the challenge of high-dimensional interaction space modeling by decomposing the scene into local deformable fields, allowing independent control of individual objects and handling topology changes induced by interactions. Unlike joint modeling approaches like CoNeRF or static language fields like LERF, LiveScene projects high-dimensional (3+\alpha)-dimensional interaction features into compact 4D local fields using multi-scale ray sampling. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Monocular video frames, camera poses, and control variables \kappa = [\kappa1, \dots, \kappa\alpha] indicating the motion states of \alpha interactive objects. Outputs: Rendered RGB images, interaction probabilities, and language embeddings for spatial points. Data Structures Local Deformable Fields: A set of disjoint regions, each containing a local 4D deformable field representing an individual object or interaction region. Multi-scale Feature Planes: The 4D fields are compressed into multi-scale feature planes for storage. Model Parameters: The total model size is constant at 39M parameters. Method Steps 1. Define Interactive Space: Model the scene as a function y = \rho(x, \kappa, H; \theta), where y is the scene property (color, probability, or language embedding), x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial coordinate, \kappa \in \mathbb{R}^\alpha are the control variables, H are optional parameters (e.g., view direction), and \theta stores scene information. 2. Ray Definition: Define a ray in the (3+\alpha)-dimensional interactive space: r(t) = [ox | o\kappa] + t [dx | d\kappa] where ox \in \mathbb{R}^3 and dx \in \mathbb{R}^3 are the spatial origin and direction, and o\kappa \in \mathbb{R}^\alpha and d\kappa \in \mathbb{R}^\alpha are the control variable origin and direction. 3. Intersection: Determine the intersection point p = [x | \kappa] \in \mathbb{R}^{3+\alpha} where the ray intersects the interaction region. 4. Multi-scale Interaction Probability Sampling: For a given intersection point, retrieve deformable features from the corresponding local 4D deformable field by maximizing the sampling probability Pi: u = \arg \maxi \{Pi\} where P = \Theta(\kappa, \theta) is the probability feature function. The projected sample is pu = [x | \kappa(u)]. 5. Feature Retrieval: Retrieve the features from the selected local 4D deformable field for the projected sample pu. 6. Interaction-Aware Language Embedding: Generate varying language embeddings to localize and control objects under arbitrary states using natural language. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlivescene(rayoriginspatial, raydirectionspatial, rayorigincontrol, raydirectioncontrol, controlvariableskappa, modeltheta): """ Renders a point along a ray in the interactive space using LiveScene. Args: rayoriginspatial: 3D vector (ox) raydirectionspatial: 3D vector (dx) rayorigincontrol: Alpha-dimensional vector (okappa) raydirectioncontrol: Alpha-dimensional vector (dkappa) controlvariableskappa: Alpha-dimensional vector (kappa) representing current object states modeltheta: Model parameters containing local deformable fields and probability function Returns: sceneproperty: Color, probability, or language embedding """ # Step 2: Determine intersection point p = [x | kappa] # x is the 3D spatial position, kappa is the interaction variable # This step involves finding the t where the ray intersects the object's interaction region. # Or derived from ray control params # Step 3: Multi-scale Interaction Probability Sampling # Calculate probability Pi for each local deformable field i probabilities = [] for i in range(numlocalfields): # Step 4: Project to compact 4D space and retrieve features # The features are retrieved from the corresponding local 4D deformable field # The specific projection to 4D is handled by the local field's internal structure features = retrievefeaturesfromlocalfield( spatialpos=intersectionpointspatial, controlvar=intersectionpointcontrol, fieldindex=bestfieldindex, modeltheta=modeltheta) # Step 5: Decode scene property (color, probability, or language embedding) # The decoding depends on the target output type sceneproperty = decodefeatures(features) return sceneproperty Parameters \alpha: The number of interactive articulated objects. \kappa: Control variable vector [\kappa1, \dots, \kappa\alpha] indicating object motion states. Model size: 39M parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Topology Changes: Static language embeddings (e.g., LERF, OpenNeRF) fail when scene topology changes (e.g., a cabinet opening). LiveScene handles this via interaction-aware language embedding. Memory Consumption: Joint modeling of all interaction variables leads to high memory usage. LiveScene's decomposition mitigates this. Decomposes the scene into disjoint regions, each modeled by a 4D deformable field, enabling independent object control. A strategy to project high-dimensional features into compact 4D space by selecting the most relevant local field based on interaction probability. Generates dynamic language embeddings that adapt to object states, enabling natural language control of interactive objects. Time and Memory Complexity: Maintains a constant model parameter size of 39M, scaling well with increasing scene complexity. Strengths: Handles complex physical scenes with multiple interactive objects; supports natural language control; robust to topology changes; memory efficient. Limitations: Requires monocular video input; evaluation limited to specific datasets (OmniSim, InterReal). When to Use: When reconstructing and controlling multiple interactive objects in complex scenes with natural language interface is required. When Not to Use: For static scenes or scenes with single-object interactions where simpler methods (CoNeRF, K-Planes) suffice. LiveScene was introduced as a preprint in 2024. It addresses the limitations of prior interactive scene modeling methods like CoNeRF and K-Planes, which use joint modeling and struggle with memory and topology changes. It also improves upon language-embedded NeRFs like LERF and OpenNeRF, which fail with dynamic topology. The authors constructed two new datasets, OmniSim and InterReal, featuring 28 scenes with 70 interactive objects for evaluation. name: NeuTex
head: Neural Texture Mapping
body: NeuTex is a neural scene representation that explicitly disentangles scene geometry from appearance by representing geometry as a continuous 3D volume and appearance as a continuous 2D texture map in an automatically discovered UV space. Unlike standard NeRF, which uses a single MLP to bake both density and radiance into a 3D volume, NeuTex uses three separate MLPs for geometry, texture mapping, and texture, enabling disentangled modeling and texture editing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a scene, camera poses, and optionally a coarse point cloud for initialization. Outputs: A rendered image for a given camera pose, and a 2D neural texture map representing the scene's appearance. Data Structures: The method relies on four Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Geometry Network (F\sigma): Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} to volume density \sigma. 2. Texture Mapping Network (F{\mathbf{uv}}): Maps 3D position \mathbf{x} to 2D UV coordinates \mathbf{u}. 3. Texture Network (F{\text{tex}}): Maps 2D UV coordinates \mathbf{u} and view direction \mathbf{d} to radiance \mathbf{c}. 4. Inverse Texture Mapping Network (F{\mathbf{uv}}^{-1}): Maps 2D UV coordinates \mathbf{u} back to 3D position \mathbf{x}. Positional Encoding: Following the parent article Model Architecture and Encoding, inputs to the geometry and texture networks use hierarchical sinusoidal positional encoding. However, the texture mapping networks (F{\mathbf{uv}} and F{\mathbf{uv}}^{-1}) do not use positional encoding, as the mapping is expected to be smooth and uniform. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Normalize the scene space to a unit box. Initialize the inverse mapping network F{\mathbf{uv}}^{-1} using a coarse point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP) by minimizing a Chamfer loss. Initialize other networks randomly or with standard NeRF weights. 2. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in a batch, generate a ray r(\lambda) = o + \lambda d. Sample N=256 shading points along the ray within the unit box using stratified sampling. 3. Forward Pass (Rendering): For each shading point \mathbf{x}i on the ray: Compute density: \sigmai = F\sigma(\mathbf{x}i). Compute UV coordinate: \mathbf{u}i = F{\mathbf{uv}}(\mathbf{x}i). Compute radiance: \mathbf{c}i = F{\text{tex}}(\mathbf{u}i, \mathbf{d}). Compute transmittance Ti and contribution weights wi: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) Render pixel color: \mathbf{I} = \sumi wi \mathbf{c}i 4. Cycle Consistency Check: For shading points with high contribution weights (near the surface), map their UV coordinates back to 3D space: \mathbf{x}'i = F{\mathbf{uv}}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}i) = F{\mathbf{uv}}^{-1}(F{\mathbf{uv}}(\mathbf{x}i)) 5. Loss Calculation: Rendering Loss: L{\text{render}} = \|\mathbf{I}{\text{gt}} - \mathbf{I}\|2^2. Cycle Loss: Weighted by radiance contribution to focus on surface points: L{\text{cycle}} = \sumi wi \| \mathbf{x}'i - \mathbf{x}i \|2^2 Mask Loss: Supervises foreground/background using the transmittance of the last point TN: L{\text{mask}} = \| M{\text{gt}} - (1 - TN) \|2^2 Total Loss: L = L{\text{render}} + a1 L{\text{cycle}} + a2 L{\text{mask}} Where a1 = 1 and a2 = 1 (or 0 if view coverage is dense). 6. Optimization: Phase 1: Train with Chamfer loss (on F{\mathbf{uv}}^{-1}) and Rendering loss for 50,000 iterations. Phase 2: Remove Chamfer loss. Train with full loss (L{\text{render}} + L{\text{cycle}} + L{\text{mask}}) for ~500,000 iterations. Phase 3: Fine-tune F{\text{tex}} while freezing F\sigma, F{\mathbf{uv}}, and F{\mathbf{uv}}^{-1} to improve texture details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class NeuTex: def init(self, config): # Initialize the four MLPs self.Fsigma = GeometryMLP() self.Fuv = TextureMappingMLP() self.Ftex = TextureMLP() self.Fuvinv = InverseTextureMappingMLP() # Hyperparameters self.a1 = 1.0 self.a2 = 1.0 # Set to 0 if view coverage is dense self.numsamples = 256 self.batchsize = 600 # Pixels per batch def positionalencoding(self, x, L=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" # Implementation details from parent article Model Architecture and Encoding pass def forward(self, rayso, raysd, gtimages, gtmasks=None): """ rayso: [B, 3] ray origins raysd: [B, 3] ray directions gtimages: [B, H, W, 3] ground truth images gtmasks: [B, H, W] ground truth masks (optional) """ B, H, W = gtimages.shape[:3] # Flatten rays to batch of pixels rayso = rayso.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, H, W, -1).reshape(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, H, W, -1).reshape(-1, 3) # Stratified sampling along rays within unit box # Returns points [BHW, N, 3] points = stratifiedsample(rayso, raysd, self.numsamples) # 1. Geometry # Apply positional encoding to 3D points pointspe = self.positionalencoding(points) sigma = self.Fsigma(pointspe) # [BHW, N, 1] # 2. Texture Mapping # No positional encoding for UV mapping uv = self.Fuv(points) # [BHW, N, 2] # 3. Texture # View direction is constant per ray, broadcast to points raysdexpanded = raysd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.numsamples, -1) # Apply positional encoding to view direction raysdpe = self.positionalencoding(raysdexpanded, L=4) # Concatenate UV and view direction features? # Note: Ftex takes (u, d). The source says Ftex(u, d). # Usually d is also encoded. c = self.Ftex(uv, raysdpe) # [BHW, N, 3] # 4. Rendering # Compute transmittance and weights # delta is distance between samples. Assume uniform or compute from points. # For simplicity, assume uniform delta or compute from points. # Let's assume points are sorted and we can compute deltas. # Standard NeRF ray marching logic. deltas = computedeltas(points) # [BHW, N] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) # [BHW, N] T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) # [BHW, N] T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) # Shift for Ti weights = T alpha # [BHW, N] renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=1) # [BHW, 3] # Reshape to image renderedimage = renderedcolor.reshape(B, H, W, 3) # 5. Cycle Loss # Map UV back to 3D pointsinv = self.Fuvinv(uv) # [BHW, N, 3] # Weighted cycle loss # Only consider points with significant contribution cycleloss = torch.mean(weights torch.sum((pointsinv - points)2, dim=-1)) # 6. Mask Loss maskloss = 0.0 if gtmasks is not None: # Transmittance of the last point indicates background Tlast = T[:, -1] # [BHW] # (1 - TN) is the foreground mask foregroundpred = 1.0 - Tlast foregroundpred = foregroundpred.reshape(B, H, W) maskloss = torch.mean((gtmasks - foregroundpred)2) # 7. Rendering Loss renderloss = torch.mean((gtimages - renderedimage)2) totalloss = renderloss + self.a1 cycleloss + self.a2 maskloss return renderedimage, totalloss, cycleloss, maskloss def trainstep(self, rayso, raysd, gtimages, gtmasks): self.optimizer.zerograd() renderedimage, totalloss, cycleloss, maskloss = self.forward(rayso, raysd, gtimages, gtmasks) totalloss.backward() self.optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() Parameters: a1 (Cycle loss weight): 1. a2 (Mask loss weight): 1 for most scenes, 0 for scenes with good view coverage. Number of shading points per ray: 256. Batch size: 600-800 pixels. Training iterations: 50,000 (Chamfer + Render) + 500,000 (Full loss) + Fine-tuning. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Mapping: Naively adding a texture mapping network and supervising only with rendering loss leads to a degenerate texture mapping that does not unwrap the surface. Empty Space Cycle Loss: Enforcing cycle mapping in empty space is meaningless; it must be weighted by radiance contribution. Mask Loss Necessity: Mask loss is necessary when viewpoints do not cover the object entirely to prevent the network from faking shading effects via volume density. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive, taking 2-3 days on a single RTX 2080Ti GPU for convergence. Memory Complexity: Depends on batch size (600-800 pixels) and number of samples (256). Four MLPs must be stored in memory. Performance: On DTU scenes, NeuTex achieves a PSNR of 28.23 and SSIM of 0.894, which is lower than NeRF (30.73 PSNR, 0.938 SSIM) but enables texture editing. Strengths: Disentangled geometry and appearance; enables 2D texture editing; discovers more uniform surface parameterization than AtlasNet. Limitations: Lower rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM) compared to standard NeRF; requires careful initialization of the inverse mapping network. NeuTex was introduced by Xiang et al. in 2021. It builds on the NeRF framework to address the limitation of "black-box" volumetric representations that cannot be edited. The method was developed while F. Xiang was an intern at Adobe Research. name: Sampling and Rendering Pipeline Configuration
body: This configuration defines the parameters and logic for generating rays and querying the neural radiance field during training and inference. It solves the problem of balancing rendering fidelity with computational cost by controlling sample density, noise injection, and multi-resolution strategies. It differs from sibling configurations by focusing specifically on the ray-sampling mechanics and the structure of the rendering kwargs dictionary, rather than initialization weights, architecture, or regularization terms. The core mechanism involves constructing a renderkwargs dictionary that is passed to the volumetric rendering function. This dictionary controls how rays are discretized into samples and how the network outputs are processed. Key shared concepts include: Ray Discretization: Rays are sampled at discrete points along their length. The number of samples (N{samples}) and the distribution (linear vs. inverse depth) determine the spatial resolution of the query. Noise Regularization: Random noise is added to the sampled depths or the network's raw density output (\sigma) to prevent the network from memorizing the training views and to encourage smoothness. Multi-Stage Rendering: High-fidelity rendering often involves a coarse network for initial sampling and a fine network for denser sampling in promising regions. Determinism vs. Stochasticity: Training typically uses stochastic sampling (perturbation, noise) to improve generalization, while testing uses deterministic sampling to ensure consistent evaluation metrics. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configurerenderkwargs(datasettype='llff', nondc=False, lindisp=True, perturb=1.0, rawnoisestd=0.0, Nsamples=64, Nimportance=0): renderkwargstrain = { 'perturb': perturb, 'rawnoisestd': rawnoisestd, 'Nsamples': Nsamples, 'Nimportance': Nimportance, 'ndc': not (datasettype != 'llff' or nondc), 'lindisp': lindisp } renderkwargstest = renderkwargstrain.copy() renderkwargstest['perturb'] = False renderkwargstest['rawnoisestd'] = 0.0 return renderkwargstrain, renderkwargstest Definition: Configures the rendering kwargs to support multi-resolution sampling (coarse and fine networks) and noise regularization for sigma. Step: 1. Create renderkwargstrain dict with networkqueryfn, perturb, Nimportance, networkfine, Nsamples, networkfn, useviewdirs, whitebkgd, rawnoisestd. 2. If args.datasettype != 'llff' or args.nondc, set ndc=False and lindisp=args.lindisp. 3. Copy train kwargs to renderkwargstest, overriding perturb=False and rawnoisestd=0.. Parameter: Nsamples: number of coarse samples per ray, default 64. Nimportance: number of additional fine samples per ray, default 0. perturb: jitter factor for sampling, default 1.0. rawnoisestd: std dev of noise added to sigma output, default 0.0. Code: renderkwargstest['perturb'] = False and renderkwargstest['rawnoisestd'] = 0.. Pitfall: Test rendering disables perturbation and raw noise to ensure deterministic output. Definition: A training strategy divided into warm-up and finetuning phases to optimize efficiency, accelerate convergence, minimize early overfitting artifacts, and learn intricate details via denser sampling in high-complexity areas. Step: Divide training into two phases: warm-up and finetuning. During the finetuning phase, set the base number of samples per ray to match the final count of the warm-up phase. Add an additional small number of sample points to the finetuning count. Sample the additional points using an importance sampling technique. Parameter: Initial warm-up samples per ray: 64. Additional finetuning samples: 64. Definition: A ray sampling strategy that excludes rays passing through the black outer areas of laparoscopic images to prevent artifacts caused by overlapping images where black areas intersect with valid color regions of other views. Step: Create a single circular mask centered on the image. Calculate the radius of the circular mask based on the circular view of the laparoscope. Sample rays only from pixels that fall within the mask (i.e., pixels with color values), excluding rays from the black peripheral areas. Allow the NeRF model to infer the content of the masked black areas based on color information from overlapping regions in other images. Parameter: Mask shape: Circular. Mask position: Centered on the image. Pitfall: Artifacts occur at intersections between valid color lines of one image and black area lines of overlapping images if rays are sampled from the black areas. This configuration family defines the hyperparameters and logic for ray generation and network querying during NeRF training and inference. It builds on NeRF Hyperparameters to control sample density, noise injection, and multi-resolution strategies. Specific implementations target distinct constraints: VR headsets require optimized hash grids and compact models for real-time inference, dynamic volumetric scenes benefit from two-phase progressive sampling to accelerate convergence and reduce overfitting, and laparoscopic medical imaging requires mask-based sampling to prevent artifacts from black peripheral regions. name: VR NeRF Rendering Configuration
head: Meta Quest Pro NeRF Config
body: This configuration defines the hyperparameters and rendering pipeline settings for training and rendering room-scale Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) specifically for native execution on the Meta Quest Pro headset. It addresses the constraints of high-resolution (dual 2K×2K), high-frame-rate (72 FPS), and low-latency rendering in virtual reality. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF configurations by targeting iNGP-style hash grid networks with specific MLP depths and a fixed sampling strategy optimized for VR hardware, rather than general-purpose desktop rendering. The method configures the training loop and rendering parameters to balance visual fidelity with the strict performance budgets of standalone VR headsets. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Training images (1K or 2K resolution), camera poses, and scene bounds. Outputs: Trained hash grid embeddings and MLP weights for the density and color fields. Data Structures Hash Grid: L=16 levels, base resolution T0=128, scaling factor s=1.4. Density MLP: 1 hidden layer, 64 neurons. Color MLP: 2 hidden layers, 64 neurons. Optimizer State: Adam state for hash grids and remaining modules. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize Networks: Initialize the hash grid embeddings and the two MLPs (density and color) as specified. 2. Configure Sampling: Set the number of samples per ray to N{samples} = 1024. Use exponential distance sampling for integration along the ray. 3. Set Learning Rates: Assign a learning rate of \eta{grid} = 0.01 for the hash grid embeddings and \eta{mlp} = 0.005 for the density and color MLPs. 4. Configure Optimizer: Use the Adam optimizer with parameters \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99, and \epsilon = 10^{-15}. 5. Batch Construction: For each training step, sample a batch of 12,800 rays. This is achieved by selecting 256 random rays from 50 random training images. 6. Training Loop: Iterate for the specified number of steps (110K for ablation, >200K for demo videos). 7. Rendering: During inference, render to dual 2K×2K eyebuffers at 72 FPS using a custom multi-GPU CUDA renderer. Formulas Hash Grid Resolution: The resolution at level l is Tl = T0 \cdot s^l. Batch Ray Count: N{batch} = N{rays\per\img} \times N{imgs} = 256 \times 50 = 12,800. Parameters Target Resolution: Dual 2K×2K eyebuffers. Target Frame Rate: 72 FPS. Hash Grid Levels (L): 16. Base Resolution (T0): 128. Scaling Factor (s): 1.4. Samples per Ray (N{samples}): 1024. Batch Size: 12,800 rays. Learning Rate (Hash Grids): 0.01. Learning Rate (MLPs): 0.005. Adam \beta1: 0.9. Adam \beta2: 0.99. Adam \epsilon: 10^{-15}. Training Iterations (Ablation): 110K. Training Iterations (Demo): >200K. Dataset Resolution (Ablation): 1K. Dataset Resolution (Demo): 2K. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Unbounded Scenes: For unbounded scenes, far-field contraction must be applied. HDR: The configuration supports HDR modeling, potentially using PQ color space and weighted loss to prevent bright areas from dominating. Pruning: A coarse occupancy grid of 128^3 resolution is used, upsampled at predefined iteration milestones to prune scenes. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configurevrnerftraining(): # Hyperparameters from L = 16 T0 = 128 s = 1.4 Nsamples = 1024 Nbatch = 12800 Nraysperimg = 256 Nimgs = 50 lrgrid = 0.01 lrmlp = 0.005 beta1 = 0.9 beta2 = 0.99 eps = 1e-15 # Network architecture densitymlp = MLP(hiddenlayers=1, neurons=64) colormlp = MLP(hiddenlayers=2, neurons=64) hashgrid = HashGrid(levels=L, baseresolution=T0, scalingfactor=s) # Optimizer setup optimizer = Adam( params=[{'params': hashgrid.parameters(), 'lr': lrgrid}, {'params': list(densitymlp.parameters()) + list(colormlp.parameters()), 'lr': lrmlp}], betas=(beta1, beta2), eps=eps) # Training loop configuration # For ablation: 110K iterations on 1K resolution images # For demo: >200K iterations on 2K resolution images # Standard training loop structure assumed return { 'hashgrid': hashgrid, 'densitymlp': densitymlp, 'colormlp': colormlp, 'optimizer': optimizer, 'Nsamples': Nsamples, 'Nbatch': Nbatch, 'Nraysperimg': Nraysperimg, 'Nimgs': Nimgs } A holistic pipeline for capturing and rendering high-fidelity walkable spaces in VR, targeting native rendering on Meta Quest Pro with strict latency and resolution constraints, utilizing specific training configurations and pruning strategies to maintain smoothness via Asynchronous Spacewarp (ASW). Time Complexity: The most computationally expensive portion is MLP evaluation, which is optimized by evaluating all layers within registers using Nvidia Tensor Cores. Memory Complexity: Uses a hash grid with 16 levels, base resolution 128, and scaling factor 1.4. Measured Performance: Tested on a 20-GPU workstation (20 Nvidia A40 GPUs). Dynamic work distribution across GPUs achieves 49% higher FPS compared to static splits. Strengths: High resolution (dual 2K×2K), high frame rate (72 FPS), and low latency suitable for VR. Limitations: Requires significant hardware resources (20-GPU workstation) for training. When to use: When rendering room-scale NeRF models for native VR headsets like Meta Quest Pro. When not to use: For general-purpose desktop rendering or when hardware resources are limited. VR-NeRF was introduced to address the challenges of rendering room-scale NeRF models in virtual reality, specifically targeting the Meta Quest Pro headset. The work combines hardware, software, and model optimizations to achieve high resolution, high frame rates, and low latency. It builds on iNGP for efficient hash grid-based NeRF representation and incorporates techniques for HDR modeling and LOD. name: VR-NeRF
head: Virtualized Walkable Spaces
body: VR-NeRF is a holistic pipeline for the capture, reconstruction, and rendering of high-fidelity walkable spaces in virtual reality, designed to achieve higher resolution, frame rate, and visual fidelity than standard NeRF. It distinguishes itself by targeting native rendering on headsets like the Meta Quest Pro with strict latency and resolution constraints, utilizing specific training configurations and pruning strategies to maintain smoothness via Asynchronous Spacewarp (ASW). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Thousands of uniformly distributed HDR photos of a scene captured via a custom multi-camera rig. Output: A reconstructed neural radiance field optimized for VR rendering, capable of generating stereoscopic eyebuffers at high frame rates. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D grid storing features and density, with resolutions such as 1024^3 used for aggressive pruning. Pruning Mask: A binary structure determining occupied versus free voxels based on a density threshold. Method Steps: 1. Capture: Acquire HDR images using a custom multi-camera rig that captures thousands of uniformly distributed photos. 2. Optimization: Optimize the neural radiance field using a novel perceptual color space for HDR model optimization. 3. Feature Weighting: Apply level-of-detail feature weighting to allow the model to reproduce distance-dependent appearance, such as varying level of detail or rig shadows. 4. Pruning: Threshold density to determine if a voxel is occupied; for bounded scenes with solid surfaces, a higher threshold (e.g., \alpha = 0.3) and finer grid resolution (e.g., 1024^3) accelerate rendering. 5. Free-Space Management: To mitigate extrapolation failures caused by distance-aware features, prune as much free-space as possible so density cannot suddenly appear when moving through previously unseen free-space regions. Parameters: Density Threshold (\alpha): 0.3 for aggressive pruning in bounded scenes. Grid Resolution: 1024^3 for aggressive pruning. Native VR Resolution: Two 2064 \times 2096 eyebuffers for Meta Quest Pro. Target Frame Rate: 72 FPS. ASW Critical Threshold: 36 FPS (half of native 72 FPS). Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Aggressive Pruning Artifacts: Using a high density threshold (> 0.3) and fine grid resolution (1024^3) causes box-like artifacts in VR for complex scenes (reflective/transparent surfaces, unbounded scenes), which are less visible in 2D renders. Extrapolation Failure: Distance-aware features reduce the model's ability to extrapolate to unseen viewpoints or distances because feature vectors with unseen weighting may be used, causing density to vary with distance. This is mitigated by extensive free-space pruning. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configurevrrendering(headset="Meta Quest Pro"): """Configure rendering parameters for VR-NeRF.""" if headset == "Meta Quest Pro": return { "eyebufferresolution": (2064, 2096), "stereo": True, "targetfps": 72, "aswthresholdfps": 36 } raise ValueError("Unsupported headset configuration") def applypruning(voxelgrid, densitythreshold=0.3, gridres=10243): """Prune free-space voxels to prevent density extrapolation artifacts.""" occupiedmask = voxelgrid.density > densitythreshold prunedgrid = voxelgrid.copy() prunedgrid.density[~occupiedmask] = 0.0 return prunedgrid def computep99fps(frametimes): """Compute the 99th percentile FPS to evaluate VR experience quality.""" sortedtimes = sorted(frametimes) idx = int(0.99 len(sortedtimes)) return sortedtimes[idx] def checkpruningartifacts(scenetype, threshold, resolution): """Warn about potential artifacts based on scene complexity.""" if threshold > 0.3 and resolution == 10243: if scenetype in ["reflective", "transparent", "unbounded"]: return "Warning: Aggressive pruning may cause box-like artifacts in VR." return "Pruning configuration appears safe for scene type." Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in terms of Big-O, but performance is measured in FPS. Halving the resolution (from full to half) only approximately doubles the FPS, despite rendering 1/4 the pixels, indicating substantial per-frame overhead (e.g., kernel launches, VR compositor, OpenGL display pipeline) or insufficient parallelism at lower resolutions. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly defined, but grid resolution affects memory usage (e.g., 1024^3 grid). Measured Performance: Tested on an off-the-shelf 3-GPU workstation and a custom 20-GPU rendering workstation. Half-Resolution (2064 \times 2096): The 3-GPU workstation achieved 36 FPS for half the scenes. The 20-GPU workstation achieved a p99 of 72 FPS for all scenes but one, providing a smooth experience even without ASW. Full-Resolution: The 20-GPU workstation achieved a p99 exceeding the critical ASW threshold of 36 FPS for 4 out of 6 scenes. Strengths: Achieves higher resolution, frame rate, and visual fidelity than standard NeRF, suitable for comfortable VR viewing of neural radiance fields. Limitations: Aggressive pruning causes artifacts in complex scenes, distance-aware features hinder extrapolation, and significant per-frame overhead limits scaling benefits from resolution reduction. When to Use: When high-fidelity, walkable space reconstruction is required for VR headsets like Meta Quest Pro, and sufficient GPU resources (e.g., 20-GPU workstation) are available. When Not to Use: For complex scenes with reflective/transparent surfaces or unbounded environments if aggressive pruning is necessary for performance, as this leads to visible artifacts. VR-NeRF was presented as the first holistic approach for capture, reconstruction, and rendering of high-fidelity walkable spaces in virtual reality. It integrates a custom multi-camera rig, a novel perceptual color space for HDR optimization, and efficient feature mip-mapping. The work addresses the specific challenges of VR rendering, such as the need for high frame rates to avoid motion sickness and the limitations of standard NeRF in this context. name: Method-Specific Training Pipelines
body: This family covers specialized training configurations and optimization loops for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that deviate from standard baselines to handle specific input conditions or scene structures. Unlike generic NeRF training, these pipelines integrate domain-specific constraints—such as physical exposure models for motion blur, generative adversarial frameworks for single-image synthesis, or coordinate contraction for large-scale stratified environments—directly into the optimization loop BAD-NeRF, Pix2NeRF Training Configuration, and Strata-NeRF Training Configuration. All methods in this family optimize NeRF parameters via gradient descent using the Adam optimizer. They rely on differentiable volume rendering to backpropagate gradients from image space to the scene representation, and sample points along camera rays to query density and color fields. The number of samples and sampling strategy are hyperparameters tuned per method. Each pipeline defines a specific loss function and optimizes auxiliary variables alongside the NeRF. BAD-NeRF reconstructs 3D scenes and recovers camera poses from motion-blurred images by explicitly modeling the physical image formation process during the camera's exposure time BAD-NeRF. It differs from its siblings by jointly optimizing the NeRF parameters and the continuous camera motion trajectory (start and end poses) for each image, synthesizing blurred images by averaging interpolated sharp intermediate views BAD-NeRF. Choose this method when inputs are motion-blurred and accurate pose estimation is required. Pix2NeRF is an unsupervised method for translating a single image into a NeRF by leveraging a pre-trained \pi-GAN Pix2NeRF Training Configuration. It differs from its siblings by relying on a generative adversarial framework with a discriminator and encoder, rather than explicit geometric constraints or multi-view consistency losses Pix2NeRF Training Configuration. It achieves a super-resolution effect by training at 64×64 resolution while rendering at 128×128 Pix2NeRF Training Configuration. Choose this method for single-image 3D reconstruction where multi-view data is unavailable. Strata-NeRF optimizes NeRFs for stratified scenes (e.g., multi-level buildings) using a specific configuration derived from Mip-NeRF 360. It uses the "360.gin" configuration file, which employs a contract function to map input coordinates onto a ball of radius 2, handling large scenes better than the "blender 256.gin" configuration. It uses a vector codebook in a "Latent Generator" network. Choose this method for large-scale, multi-level synthetic or real-world scenes where standard NeRF configurations fail to capture global structure. step: Learning rate schedule uses log-linear interpolation from 0.002 down to 0.00002 at maximum steps, with 512 warmup steps. parameter: Adam optimizer hyperparameters are \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, \epsilon = 10^{-6}, and initial learning rate = 0.002. Loss weighting for the Latent Generator is \lambda2 = 0.1. Codebook sizes tested are 512, 1024, and 4096, with size 1024 yielding the best overall PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS across Coffee Shop, Bhutanese House, and Buddhist Temple datasets. pitfall: Distortion loss from Mip-NeRF 360 is disabled for Blender datasets to prevent artifacts, following the original authors' recommendation. comparison: The method uses the “360.gin” configuration instead of “blender 256.gin” because the contract function handles large scenes better, yielding higher PSNR/SSIM and lower LPIPS. Increasing codebook size to 4096 does not improve metrics and may slightly degrade performance, while 512 underfits, making 1024 the optimal balance between capacity and generalization. Method-specific training pipelines were developed to address limitations of standard NeRF training when applied to non-ideal inputs or complex scene geometries. BAD-NeRF was introduced to handle the physical reality of camera exposure times, which standard NeRF ignores BAD-NeRF. Pix2NeRF was developed to enable single-image 3D reconstruction without multi-view supervision Pix2NeRF Training Configuration. Strata-NeRF adapted Mip-NeRF 360's architecture to handle large-scale stratified environments using a coordinate contraction function. Strata-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Stratified Scenes, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10337v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: BAD-NeRF
head: Bundle Adjusted Deblur Neural Radiance Fields
body: BAD-NeRF is a method for reconstructing 3D scenes and synthesizing sharp novel views from a collection of motion-blurred images. It solves the problem that standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) assume infinitesimal exposure times and require accurate, sharp camera poses, both of which are violated by severe motion blur. Unlike methods that fix camera poses or estimate single timestamps, BAD-NeRF jointly optimizes the NeRF parameters and the continuous camera motion trajectory (start and end poses) for each image, explicitly modeling the physical image formation process of motion blur by averaging virtual sharp images rendered along the trajectory. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M motion-blurred images \{Bm\}{m=1}^M, their initial camera poses (typically initialized via COLMAP), and camera intrinsic parameters K. Outputs: A trained NeRF model F\theta representing the 3D scene, and the optimized camera motion trajectories for each input image. Data Structures: NeRF (F\theta): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) parameterized by \theta, taking a 3D point Xw and viewing direction as input, outputting volume density \sigma and view-dependent color c. Camera Pose Trajectory: For each image m, the trajectory is parameterized by two poses in SE(3): T{start}^{(m)} and T{end}^{(m)}. These are represented as 6D vectors corresponding to their Lie algebras. Ray Sampling: Points are sampled along rays defined by the camera poses. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Definition: For a pixel location x in image m, compute the ray direction dc in the camera coordinate frame using the inverse intrinsic matrix K^{-1}: dc = K^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} The ray origin and direction in the world frame are determined by the current camera pose Tt (see Step 3). 2. Trajectory Interpolation: BAD-NeRF assumes linear motion in the Lie algebra of SE(3) during the exposure time \tau. For a given image m, the virtual camera pose Tt at time t \in [0, \tau] is interpolated between T{start}^{(m)} and T{end}^{(m)}: Tt = T{start}^{(m)} \cdot \exp\left( \frac{t}{\tau} \cdot \log\left( (T{start}^{(m)})^{-1} \cdot T{end}^{(m)} \right) \right) where \exp and \log are the exponential and logarithmic maps on SE(3). 3. Virtual Sharp Image Rendering: Render n virtual sharp images \{Ii(x)\}{i=0}^{n-1} along the trajectory. The time ti for the i-th sample is ti = \frac{i}{n-1} \tau (or uniformly spaced within [0, \tau]). For each virtual pose Ti, render Ii(x) using standard volume rendering: Ii(x) = \sum{k=1}^{ns} Ti^k (1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak)) ck where ns is the number of 3D points sampled along the ray (typically 128), \sigmak and ck are the density and color predicted by F\theta at the k-th point, \deltak is the distance between adjacent points, and Ti^k = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance. 4. Blur Synthesis: Synthesize the blurred image B(x) by averaging the n virtual sharp images: B(x) \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} Ii(x) where n is the number of interpolated virtual poses (typically 7). 5. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss L between the synthesized blurred image B(x) and the observed blurred image B{obs}(x). 6. Gradient Backpropagation: Compute gradients with respect to NeRF parameters \theta, start pose T{start}, and end pose T{end}: \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \frac{\partial L}{\partial Bk(x)} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{\partial Bk(x)}{\partial Ii(x)} \cdot \frac{\partial Ii(x)}{\partial \theta} \frac{\partial L}{\partial T{start}} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \frac{\partial L}{\partial Bk(x)} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{\partial Bk(x)}{\partial Ii(x)} \cdot \frac{\partial Ii(x)}{\partial T{start}} \frac{\partial L}{\partial T{end}} = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \frac{\partial L}{\partial Bk(x)} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{\partial Bk(x)}{\partial Ii(x)} \cdot \frac{\partial Ii(x)}{\partial T{end}} where K is the number of pixels (or batch size). The derivatives \frac{\partial Ii(x)}{\partial T{start}} and \frac{\partial Ii(x)}{\partial T{end}} are derived via the chain rule through the interpolation formula. 7. Optimization: Update \theta, T{start}, and T{end} using the Adam optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import numpy as np def se3exp(logtransform): """ Exponential map from se3 (6D vector) to SE3 (4x4 matrix). logtransform: [6] vector [omega, v] Returns: 4x4 matrix """ # Implementation of SE3 exponential map # This is a standard mathematical operation, assumed available or implemented # via scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation or custom Lie algebra code. pass def se3log(matrix): """ Logarithmic map from SE3 (4x4 matrix) to se3 (6D vector). matrix: 4x4 matrix Returns: [6] vector """ # Implementation of SE3 logarithmic map pass def interpolatese3(Tstart, Tend, t, tau): """ Linearly interpolate camera pose in SE3 Lie algebra. Tstart: 4x4 matrix Tend: 4x4 matrix t: float, current time in [0, tau] tau: float, exposure time Returns: 4x4 matrix Tt """ # Tt = Tstart exp( (t/tau) log(Tstart^-1 Tend)) delta = torch.matmul(torch.inverse(Tstart), Tend) logdelta = se3log(delta) scaledlog = (t / tau) logdelta expscaled = se3exp(scaledlog) Tt = torch.matmul(Tstart, expscaled) return Tt def rendersharpimage(rayorigins, raydirections, nerfmodel, K): """ Standard NeRF volume rendering for a single sharp image. rayorigins: [H, W, 3] raydirections: [H, W, 3] in camera frame nerfmodel: NeRF MLP K: 3x3 intrinsic matrix Returns: [H, W, 3] color image """ # Convert ray directions to world frame if necessary, or assume they are already # in the coordinate system expected by the NeRF query. # Standard NeRF rendering loop pass def badnerfstep(blurryimages, nerfmodel, K, Tstarts, Tends, exposuretimes, nsamples=7, npoints=128): """ One training step for BAD-NeRF. blurryimages: [B, H, W, 3] Tstarts: [B, 4, 4] Tends: [B, 4, 4] exposuretimes: [B] Returns: loss, gradients """ B, H, W, = blurryimages.shape totalloss = 0 # Precompute ray origins and directions for each image based on initial poses? # BAD-NeRF optimizes Tstart and Tend, so rays change. # However, standard NeRF rays are defined by camera pose. # We need to generate rays for each virtual pose. for b in range(B): Tstart = Tstarts[b] Tend = Tends[b] tau = exposuretimes[b] # Generate nsamples virtual poses virtualposes = [] for i in range(nsamples): t = (i / (nsamples - 1)) tau if nsamples > 1 else 0 Tt = interpolatese3(Tstart, Tend, t, tau) virtualposes.append(Tt) # Render virtual sharp images virtualimages = [] for Tt in virtualposes: # Get ray origins and directions for this pose # This depends on the specific ray generation implementation # Assuming a function getrays(T, K, H, W) exists origins, directions = getrays(Tt, K, H, W) # Render sharp image sharpimg = rendersharpimage(origins, directions, nerfmodel, K) virtualimages.append(sharpimg) # Average to get blurred image synthesizedblur = torch.mean(torch.stack(virtualimages), dim=0) # Compute loss loss = torch.mean((synthesizedblur - blurryimages[b])2) totalloss += loss totalloss = totalloss / B totalloss.backward() return totalloss Parameters: n: Number of interpolated virtual poses/samples. Typical value: 7. \tau: Exposure time of the captured image. ns: Number of points sampled per ray. Typical value: 128. Learning rate for NeRF optimizer: Exponentially decays from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Learning rate for pose optimizer: Exponentially decays from 1 \times 10^{-3} to 1 \times 10^{-5}. Training iterations: 200K. Optimizer: Adam. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NeRF assumes infinitesimal exposure time, which is violated by motion blur. Accurate camera poses are difficult to obtain from blurred images because they encode motion trajectory information. Directly optimizing N individual camera poses loses ordering information and performs worse than trajectory-based methods (linear or spline). Linear interpolation is chosen for simplicity and slightly better performance on Deblur-NeRF datasets compared to cubic B-Spline, though both perform comparably for short exposure times. Vanilla RS-NeRF is a method that reconstructs a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) from rolling shutter (RS) images by explicitly modeling the camera's motion trajectory during exposure and jointly optimizing NeRF parameters and camera extrinsics for each image row. It differs from standard NeRF training by replacing the single static camera pose per image with a row-wise continuous pose trajectory, allowing it to handle severe motion blur and geometric distortions inherent to RS sensors. Time Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to the rendering of n virtual sharp images per pixel per training step. With n=7 and 128 points per ray, the computational cost is roughly 7 \times that of a single NeRF forward pass per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing n virtual poses and intermediate rendered images for backpropagation, increasing memory usage. Measured Performance: Evaluated on synthetic datasets from Deblur-NeRF (Cozy2room, Factory, Pool, Tanabata, Trolley) and MBA-VO (ArchViz-low, ArchViz-high). BAD-NeRF surpasses earlier studies in artificial and actual datasets, particularly in intense motion blur cases. It achieves superior performance compared to prior state-of-the-art works like SRN-Deblur and Deblur-NeRF. Scaling: Training takes 200K iterations on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Explicitly models the physical image formation process of motion blur, leading to sharper results and improved pose accuracy under severe motion blur compared to compact approximations like DeblurNeRF. Robust to inaccurate initialized camera poses. Limitations: Higher computational complexity than methods that do not model blur explicitly. Relies on the assumption of linear motion in SE(3) during exposure, which may not hold for very complex motions or long exposure times (though linear interpolation performs comparably to cubic B-Spline for short exposures). BAD-NeRF was introduced in 2023, citing [75] in later reviews, with the original paper published in November 2022. It addresses the limitations of standard NeRF training pipelines when applied to motion-blurred images, which violate the assumption of sharp images and accurate poses. It builds on the concept of bundle adjustment by jointly optimizing scene representation and camera motion trajectories. It is used on synthetic datasets from Deblur-NeRF and MBA-VO.
