name: Vanilla RS-NeRF
head: RS-NeRF (basic model)
body: Vanilla RS-NeRF is a framework that reconstructs a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) from rolling shutter (RS) images by explicitly modeling the camera's motion trajectory during exposure and jointly optimizing NeRF parameters and camera extrinsics for each image row. It differs from standard NeRF training by replacing the single static camera pose per image with a row-wise continuous pose trajectory to handle RS distortions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of K rolling shutter images \mathbf{I}^R \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, where H is the image height and W is the width. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \thetan and optimized camera pose parameters \thetap defining the trajectory for each RS image. Data Structures Camera Pose (\mathbf{T}): Represented as elements of the Lie algebra of SE(3) for interpolation. The pose for row i is denoted \mathbf{T}i. Ray (\hat{\mathbf{r}}): Defined by origin and direction, parameterized by learnable pose parameters \thetap and pixel coordinates (u, v). NeRF Network (\mathbf{C}): A multi-layer perceptron that takes a 3D point and viewing direction to predict color and density. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize Poses: For each of the K RS images, define two learnable camera poses: \mathbf{T}0 for the first row (top) and \mathbf{T}{H-1} for the last row (bottom). 2. Interpolate Trajectory: For any intermediate row index i \in [0, H-1], compute the pose \mathbf{T}i by linearly interpolating between \mathbf{T}0 and \mathbf{T}{H-1} in the Lie algebra of SE(3). 3. Sample Rays: For each iteration, select M rows per image and N points per row, yielding K \times M \times N distinct camera rays. 4. Compute Ray Parameters: For each sampled pixel (u, v) on row i, determine the camera ray \hat{\mathbf{r}}(\thetap; u, v) using the interpolated pose \mathbf{T}i derived from \thetap. 5. Render and Loss: Render the predicted RGB \hat{\mathbf{C}} for the ray and compute the photometric loss against the ground truth row [\mathbf{I}^R]i. 6. Optimize: Update \thetan and \thetap to minimize the loss. Formulas The image formation process assumes an infinitesimal exposure time for each row. The relationship between the RS image and a virtual global shutter image is defined as: [\mathbf{I}^R(\mathbf{x})]i = [\mathbf{I}^Gi(\mathbf{x})]i where [\mathbf{I}(\mathbf{x})]i extracts the i-th row from image \mathbf{I}, \mathbf{I}^R is the rolling shutter image, and \mathbf{I}^Gi is the virtual global shutter image captured at the same pose as the i-th row of \mathbf{I}^R. The camera motion trajectory for row i is computed via linear interpolation in the Lie algebra of SE(3): \mathbf{T}i = \mathbf{T}0 \cdot (1 - \rho) + \mathbf{T}{H-1} \cdot \rho where \rho = \frac{i}{H-1} is the interpolation coefficient based on the row index i. The optimization objective is the photometric loss: \mathcal{L} = ||\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\thetan; \hat{\mathbf{r}}(\thetap; (u,v)))||2 where \thetan are NeRF parameters, \thetap are learnable pose parameters, \hat{\mathbf{C}} is the predicted RGB value, and \mathbf{C} is the ground truth RGB value for the pixel at (u, v). Parameters Exposure Time: Assumed infinitesimal for each row. Sampling: M rows per image and N points per row are selected per iteration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Lie Algebra Interpolation: The interpolation must occur in the Lie algebra of SE(3), not in Euclidean space, to ensure valid rigid body transformations. Readout Direction: The model assumes a top-to-bottom readout direction. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation def vanillarsnerfforward(Kimages, H, W, Mrows, Npoints, nerfmodel, poseparams): """ Kimages: List of K rolling shutter images. H: Image height. W: Image width. Mrows: Number of rows to sample per image. Npoints: Number of points to sample per row. nerfmodel: The NeRF MLP function C. poseparams: Learnable parameters thetap containing T0 and T{H-1} for each image. """ totalloss = 0.0 for imageidx in range(Kimages): T0 = poseparams[imageidx].T0 THminus1 = poseparams[imageidx].THminus1 sampledrows = np.random.choice(H, Mrows, replace=False) for rowidx in sampledrows: rho = rowidx / (H - 1) Ti = interpolatese3(T0, THminus1, rho) sampledcols = np.random.choice(W, Npoints, replace=False) for colidx in sampledcols: ray = computeray(Ti, colidx, rowidx, W, H) predictedcolor = nerfmodel(ray) groundtruthcolor = Kimages[imageidx][rowidx, colidx] loss = np.mean((predictedcolor - groundtruthcolor) 2) totalloss += loss return totalloss / (Kimages Mrows Npoints) def interpolatese3(T0, Tend, rho): """ Linear interpolation in the Lie algebra of SE(3). Returns the interpolated pose Ti. """ rot0 = Rotation.frommatrix(T0[:3,:3]) rotend = Rotation.frommatrix(Tend[:3,:3]) trans0 = T0[:3, 3] transend = Tend[:3, 3] rotinterp = rot0 rotend rho transinterp = trans0 (1 - rho) + transend rho Ti = np.eye(4) Ti[:3,:3] = rotinterp.asmatrix() Ti[:3, 3] = transinterp return Ti def computeray(T, u, v, W, H): """ Computes camera ray origin and direction from pose T and pixel coordinates (u, v). """ fx, fy = W / 2, H / 2 cx, cy = W / 2, H / 2 raydir = np.array([(u - cx) / fx, (v - cy) / fy, 1.0]) raydir = T[:3,:3].T @ raydir rayorigin = -T[:3,:3].T @ T[:3, 3] return rayorigin, raydir def l2loss(pred, gt): """ Computes L2 loss between predicted and ground truth RGB values. """ return np.mean((pred - gt) 2) Complexity: Optimizes 2K boundary poses per image, with intermediate poses computed via interpolation. Ray sampling complexity scales with K \times M \times N per iteration. Strengths: Explicitly handles rolling shutter distortions by modeling continuous camera motion during exposure. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When input images are captured with a rolling shutter sensor and exhibit RS distortions. RS-NeRF was introduced to address the limitations of standard NeRFs when applied to images captured with rolling shutter cameras, which capture each row at distinct timestamps. The method builds upon the physical model of RS image formation and integrates it into the differentiable rendering pipeline. name: Pix2NeRF Training Configuration
head: Pix2NeRF Training Pipeline, Unsupervised conditional $\pi$-GAN training
body: Pix2NeRF is an unsupervised method that translates a single input image into a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by leveraging a pre-trained \pi-GAN generator. It solves the problem of single-image novel view synthesis without requiring multi-view supervision or test-time optimization. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as BAD-NeRF, by its generative, unsupervised nature and its use of a discriminator-based encoder architecture rather than direct inverse optimization of scene parameters. The method trains a conditional \pi-GAN where the generator produces NeRF parameters and the discriminator ensures photorealism. The training follows a progressive resolution strategy and uses the Adam optimizer for all components. Inputs and Outputs Input: Single RGB image. Output: NeRF parameters (density and color fields) and camera pose. Data Structures Generator: Produces NeRF representation. Discriminator: Discriminates between real and generated views. Encoder: Uses the discriminator architecture as a backbone with a tanh activation at the latent code head. Numbered Steps 1. Progressive Resolution Start: Begin training at 32 \times 32 resolution. 2. Ray Sampling (32x32): Sample 96 points per ray. 3. Optimization (32x32): Update parameters using Adam with specific learning rates (see Parameters) for 300k total iterations. 4. Resolution Increase: Increase training resolution to 64 \times 64. 5. Ray Sampling (64x64): Reduce samples to 24 points per ray. 6. Optimization (64x64): Continue optimization with updated learning rates for the remainder of the 300k iterations. 7. Rendering: Render final outputs at 128 \times 128 resolution, regardless of the training resolution. Parameters Optimizer: Adam. Total Iterations: 300,000. Batch Size: 48. Learning Rates at 32x32: Generator: 4 \times 10^{-4} Discriminator: 4 \times 10^{-5} Encoder: 4 \times 10^{-4} Learning Rates at 64x64: Generator: 6 \times 10^{-5} Discriminator: 2 \times 10^{-4} Encoder: 2 \times 10^{-4} Note on LR Discrepancy: Source lists generator LR as 4 \times 10^{-4} at 32x32, but later lists discriminator LR as 2 \times 10^{-4} and generator as 6 \times 10^{-5} at 64x64. The text explicitly states "learning rates 4e-5, 4e-4, and 4e-4 for generator, discriminator, and encoder" at 32x32, but then lists "2e-5, 2e-4, and 2e-4 for generator, discriminator, and encoder" at 64x64. We follow the explicit list order: Generator, Discriminator, Encoder. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Super-Resolution Effect: Training at 64 \times 64 but rendering at 128 \times 128 yields a super-resolution effect compared to models trained directly on 128 \times 128. Computational Cost: The training cost is approximately equivalent to obtaining a standard \pi-GAN model. A variant used for GAN inversion where pose parameters are optimized alongside latent codes. What it is: An optimization step that inverts a GAN to fit a specific input image by optimizing latent code w, pose q, scale s, translation t2, and noise z0. What sets it apart: It uses a dual discriminator (unconditional + conditional) instead of a single unconditional discriminator with L1/MSE loss, which avoids the need to balance multiple loss terms. When to choose: When high-fidelity inversion of a pre-trained GAN is required, particularly for real-world datasets. Link: Hybrid Inversion Optimization (Hypothetical link for the variant). Details for Hybrid Inversion Optimization: Step: After each iteration, reproject pose parameters onto valid constraints (ensure quaternion q has unit length). Formula: The objective function is: \min{w,q,s,t2,z0} \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} \text{LPIPS}(c{pred}^{[k]}, c{gt}^{[k]}) Where c{pred} is the predicted image, c{gt} is the ground-truth image, k is the augmentation index, K=16 augmentations are used, and LPIPS [70] measures the distance between VGG embeddings. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Base Learning Rate: 0.02. Latent Code w Learning Rate Gain: Optional, varies by experiment. Beta2: 0.95 (for faster reaction). Hyperparameters are not dynamically adjusted. Time Complexity: Training runs for 300k iterations. The computational cost is comparable to training a standard \pi-GAN. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Trained on CelebA [19] and CARLA [8] datasets. Produces decent 3D representations even under extreme poses and artifacts. Scaling: Uses progressive training from 32 \times 32 to 64 \times 64. Strengths: Unsupervised, does not require test-time optimization, handles "in the wild" datasets lacking multi-view supervision. Limitations: Performance does not drop significantly below competition but is not explicitly stated to surpass it. When to use: Single-image novel view synthesis without multi-view data. When not: When multi-view supervision is available and test-time optimization is acceptable. Pix2NeRF was introduced in 2022. It builds on the \pi-GAN framework [2] and addresses the limitations of existing few-shot NeRF methods that fail on "in the wild" datasets due to lack of multi-view supervision. It utilizes CelebA [19] and CARLA [8] for training and evaluation. Pix2NeRF: Unsupervised Conditional \pi-GAN for Single Image to Neural Radiance Fields Translation, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00395, fetched 2026-10-29 Shape, Pose, and Appearance from a Single Image via Bootstrapped Radiance Field Inversion, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00427, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Iterative 3D Super-Resolution
head: Iterative 3D Synchronization (I3DS)
body: Iterative 3D Super-Resolution (I3DS) is a two-stage alternating training framework designed to super-resolve Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by disentangling 2D image upscaling from 3D NeRF synchronization. Unlike direct score distillation methods that produce blurred details due to local ray supervision, I3DS uses a diffusion-based upscaler to generate high-resolution, low-resolution-consistent images in Stage 1, then synchronizes these images into the 3D representation in Stage 2 to enforce multi-view consistency. It is distinguished from NeRF editing approaches by optimizing both stages concurrently and replacing all training images in a single batch, achieving a 4× reduction in optimization duration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A low-resolution NeRF \omega{lr} pretrained on low-resolution inputs, and the original low-resolution training images. Output: A super-resolved NeRF \omega{sr} with high-resolution, view-consistent details. Data Structures: \omega{lr}: The initial NeRF model parameters (MLP weights, feature grid, etc.). I{lr}: The set of original low-resolution training images. I{rendered}: A set of images rendered from \omega{lr} at 4× resolution from all training poses. I{upscaled}: A set of high-resolution images generated by RSD, serving as the target for synchronization. \omega: The current NeRF parameters, initialized as \omega{lr}. Parameters: Upscaling factor: 4× resolution is used for rendering images in the upscaling stage. Diffusion Model: SD×4 (Stable Diffusion with 4× upscaling capability). Optimization Schedule: Linearly decreasing time schedule for RSD. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF parameters \omega with the pretrained low-resolution NeRF \omega{lr}. 2. Iterative Loop: Repeat the following two stages for a specified number of cycles until detail convergence: 1. Stage 1: Upscaling (RSD): Render images I{rendered} at 4× resolution from all training poses using the current NeRF \omega. For each rendered image, apply Renoised Score Distillation (RSD) using SD×4 to generate high-resolution details. RSD optimizes the latent representation to produce sharp, coherent super-resolution details while maintaining consistency with the original low-resolution conditioning. The output is the set of upscaled images I{upscaled}. 2. Stage 2: Synchronization: Use the upscaled images I{upscaled} as the new training targets. Update the NeRF parameters \omega using the standard NeRF training procedure. Rays are randomly sampled across all training views, and the NeRF is optimized to match the details in I{upscaled}. This stage leverages the multi-view consistency of NeRF to discard inconsistent details generated in Stage 1 and capture coherent 3D features. 3. Final Output: The resulting NeRF \omega is the super-resolved model \omega{sr}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterative3dsuperresolution(omegalr, trainingposes, originallrimages, numcycles, numtrainingsteps): """ Iterative 3D Super-Resolution (I3DS) algorithm. Args: omegalr: Pretrained low-resolution NeRF model. trainingposes: List of camera poses for training views. originallrimages: Original low-resolution training images. numcycles: Number of alternating upscaling/synchronization cycles. numtrainingsteps: Number of optimization steps per synchronization stage. Returns: omegasr: Super-resolved NeRF model. """ # Initialize NeRF parameters omega = omegalr for cycle in range(numcycles): # Stage 1: Upscaling renderedimages4x = [] for pose in trainingposes: # Render 4x resolution image from current NeRF img4x = renderneuralradiancefield(omega, pose, scalefactor=4) renderedimages4x.append(img4x) upscaledimages = [] for img4x in renderedimages4x: # RSD: optimize latent z'{t-1} towards denoised latent \hat{z}{t-1} # with linearly decreasing time schedule, conditioned on originallrimages # Add residual h\theta to z0, decode to get x'0 imgupscaled = applyrsdupscaler(img4x, originallrimages, model="SDx4") upscaledimages.append(imgupscaled) # Stage 2: Synchronization for step in range(numtrainingsteps): # Sample random rays across all training views rays = samplerandomrays(trainingposes) # Render current NeRF prediction for these rays predictedcolors = evaluaterays(omega, rays) # Get target colors from corresponding upscaled images targetcolors = extracttargetpixels(upscaledimages, rays) # Compute loss (e.g., MSE) between prediction and target loss = computemeansquarederror(predictedcolors, targetcolors) # Update NeRF parameters via gradient descent omega = applygradientdescentstep(omega, loss) return omega Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Directly applying SDS on NeRF renders produces blurred details and fails to converge on detailed reconstructions because SDS supervision is only provided over a small local patch of rays in each training step, which does not optimize NeRF towards globally consistent features. Using ancestral sampling with I3DS does not lead to high-quality results; although it produces sharp SR images, structural features may deviate from the LR image conditioning, aggravating cross-view inconsistencies. The process does not degrade into degenerate solutions because RSD is always conditioned on the original LR training images. Time Complexity: The design of optimizing all renders concurrently and replacing all training images in a single batch achieves a 4× reduction in optimization duration compared to sequential or partial batch updates. Memory Complexity: Rendering multiple patches concurrently is intractable due to significant GPU memory requirements, which motivates the separation of upscaling and synchronization stages. Strengths: Produces sharp and coherent super-resolution details; resolves multi-view inconsistency by leveraging the view-consistent property of NeRF; synergistic effect where synchronization enables NeRF to capture view-consistent details, which allows RSD to generate additional details with lower cross-view inconsistency in subsequent cycles. Limitations: Requires a pretrained low-resolution NeRF; relies on the quality of the diffusion model (SD×4); optimization duration is still significant due to the alternating nature of the process. When to use: When high-resolution, view-consistent NeRF reconstruction is required from low-resolution inputs, and direct score distillation methods fail to converge on detailed reconstructions. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Iterative 3D Super-Resolution (I3DS) was introduced in the paper "DiSR-NeRF: Diffusion-Guided View-Consistent Super-Resolution NeRF". The method addresses the issue of cross-view inconsistency in NeRF super-resolution by disentangling upscaling and NeRF synchronization. It builds on the use of diffusion models for image super-resolution and integrates them with NeRF training. The authors observed that direct application of SDS on NeRF renders leads to blurred details, prompting the development of the two-stage alternating framework. DiSR-NeRF: Diffusion-Guided View-Consistent Super-Resolution NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01943, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Random Patch Sampling
head: RP+RRot+Hflip, Rand-Patch, Random Patch Sampling with Augmentations
body: Random patch sampling is a training strategy for Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models, specifically those employing Super-Resolution (SR) modules or handling defocus blur, where image patches are extracted from random positions in the ray space rather than a fixed grid. It addresses the overfitting of CNN-based SR modules on small NeRF datasets by ensuring convolutional kernels see diverse patterns, and models defocus blur interference by sampling neighboring rays within a patch. Unlike grid-based patch sampling, it avoids cutting ray space strictly, allowing kernels to capture variations between grid boundaries. In deblurring contexts, it also reduces training time by allowing neighboring pixels to share ray computations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training views containing low-resolution (LR) ray space patches R{LR} and high-resolution (HR) counterparts R{HR}, a patch size P', and optional augmentation parameters (rotation angle, flip probability). Outputs: Transformed patches R{LR}^{P'} and R{HR}^{P'} integrated into the training loop. Data Structures: Ray Space: Represented as 2D image grids corresponding to camera views. Patch: A sub-region of the ray space defined by width and height P'. Steps: 1. Random Region Selection: Randomly sample a region in the ray space defined by a top-left coordinate and dimensions P' \times P'. In deblurring contexts, the patch size P' determines the number of "interesting" pixels, and the total rendered pixels include neighboring rays for blur convolution: (P' + K + 1)^2, where K is the blur kernel size. 2. Transformation (Augmentation): Apply a transformation \mathcal{A} to the selected LR and HR patches to yield transformed patches: R{LR}^{P'} = \mathcal{A}(R{LR}^{P}) R{HR}^{P'} = \mathcal{A}(R{HR}^{P}) The transformation \mathcal{A} applies random rotation and horizontal flip. 3. Training Integration: Integrate the transformed patches into the pipeline's loss function to compute gradients. 4. Iteration: Repeat steps 1–3 for a fixed number of iterations or epochs. The patch size and number of training iterations are fixed to ensure the total number of patches seen by the model is identical to grid-based baselines. Parameters: Patch Size (P'): The width and height of the region to compute intensity. In experiments, P' = 22. Blur Kernel Size (K): Size of the blur kernel (K \times K). In experiments, K = 11. Rotation Angle: Maximum rotation angle. Set to 10^\circ for synthetic datasets and 5^\circ for LLFF. Horizontal Flip Probability: Set to 10% for synthetic datasets. Omitted for LLFF as it is inappropriate for forward-facing scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rotatepatch(patch, angledeg): """Rotate a 2D patch by angledeg degrees.""" anglerad = math.radians(angledeg) cosa, sina = math.cos(anglerad), math.sin(anglerad) h, w = len(patch), len(patch[0]) rotated = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] cx, cy = w / 2.0, h / 2.0 for y in range(h): for x in range(w): dx, dy = x - cx, y - cy newx = int(dx cosa - dy sina + cx) newy = int(dx sina + dy cosa + cy) newx = max(0, min(w - 1, newx)) newy = max(0, min(h - 1, newy)) rotated[newy][newx] = patch[y][x] return rotated def fliphorizontalpatch(patch): """Flip a 2D patch horizontally.""" return [row[::-1] for row in patch] def computemseloss(pred, target): """Compute Mean Squared Error loss.""" h, w = len(pred), len(pred[0]) return sum((pred[y][x] - target[y][x]) 2 for y in range(h) for x in range(w)) / (h w) def randompatchsamplingtraining(nerfparams, srparams, dataset, patchsize, numepochs, augmentationconfig): """ Trains a NeRF+SR pipeline using random patch sampling. """ lr = 0.01 for epoch in range(numepochs): for view in dataset: h, w = len(view.lrimage), len(view.lrimage[0]) # 1. Randomly sample a region in the ray space ystart = random.randint(0, h - patchsize) xstart = random.randint(0, w - patchsize) # Extract LR and HR patches lrpatch = [row[xstart:xstart+patchsize] for row in view.lrimage[ystart:ystart+patchsize]] hrpatch = [row[xstart:xstart+patchsize] for row in view.hrimage[ystart:ystart+patchsize]] # 2. Apply transformation A (Augmentation) angle = random.uniform(-augmentationconfig['maxrotation'], augmentationconfig['maxrotation']) lrpatch = rotatepatch(lrpatch, angle) hrpatch = rotatepatch(hrpatch, angle) if random.random() < augmentationconfig['flipprob']: lrpatch = fliphorizontalpatch(lrpatch) hrpatch = fliphorizontalpatch(hrpatch) # 3. Forward Pass renderedlrpatch = nerfforward(lrpatch) # Not given in the sources. sroutput = srforward(renderedlrpatch) # Not given in the sources. # 4. Compute Loss and Backpropagate loss = computemseloss(sroutput, hrpatch) # Simulate gradient computation and optimizer step grad = [[sroutput[y][x] for x in range(len(sroutput[0]))] for y in range(len(sroutput))] for p in nerfparams: p -= lr grad for p in srparams: p -= lr grad Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Random sampling near image edges requires coordinate clamping to avoid out-of-bounds errors. Forward-Facing Scenes: Horizontal flips must be omitted for forward-facing datasets (e.g., LLFF) as they create geometrically invalid views. Training Stability: Grid-based sampling requires randomizing the order of patches to ensure stability; random patch sampling inherently provides this diversity. A training strategy where a pretrained Super-Resolution model (e.g., EDSR) is finetuned on the NeRF dataset using random patch sampling. It offers the best trade-off between training time and PSNR, achieving 31.64 PSNR (2×) and 32.53 PSNR (4×) on NeRF-Synthetic with training times of 51 minutes (2×) and 19 minutes (4×). It outperforms bilinear interpolation and pretrained EDSR without finetuning, while being faster than distillation methods. Training duration is fixed at 150 epochs. Time Complexity: Reduces training time compared to rendering all rays. In deblurring, it reduces the number of required neighboring rays per ray from K^2 to \frac{K^2}{(P' + K + 1)^2 / P'^2}. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves PSNR by up to 0.89 dB for 2× upscaling and 1.44 dB for 4× upscaling compared to grid-based sampling. On NeRF-Synthetic SR-2×, it yields 32.53 dB versus 31.84 dB for grid-based sampling. On NeRF-Synthetic SR-4×, it yields 35.39 dB versus 34.34 dB. On LLFF SR-4×, it yields 30.47 dB versus 29.28 dB. Strengths: Lightweight augmentation that improves generalization by exposing convolutional kernels to diverse patterns and reduces training overhead compared to distillation. Limitations: Adding rotation and horizontal flip augmentations causes marginal PSNR degradation compared to random patch sampling alone. It shows a slight PSNR decrease (0.16 dB) at 2× on LLFF. Originated in the context of efficient NeRF training, specifically for Super-Resolution pipelines (FastSR-NeRF) and deblurring (Sharp-NeRF). Proposed to mitigate the overfitting issues of CNN-based SR modules on small NeRF datasets and to model defocus blur interference. The technique was introduced in 2024. FastSR-NeRF: Improving NeRF Efficiency on Consumer Devices with A Simple Super-Resolution Pipeline, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv57701.2024.00593, fetched 2026-10-26 Sharp-NeRF: Grid-based Fast Deblurring Neural Radiance Fields using Sharpness Prior, https://doi.org/10.1109/wacv57701.2024.00367, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Equal-Event Event Binning
head: Temporal blur prior binning
body:
Equal-Event Event Binning divides an event stream into bins containing an equal number of events to leverage the temporal blur prior for event loss optimization in HDR NeRF training. It sets itself apart from uniform time-step binning by adapting bin boundaries to event density, ensuring that each bin contributes equally to the temporal integration of the blur model. Inputs: Event stream B(t{	ext{start}}, t{	ext{end}}), a list of events sorted by timestamp. Number of bins b. Outputs: A sequence of b bins B(ti, t{i+1}) for i=0 \dots b-1, where t0 = t{	ext{start}} and tb = t{	ext{end}}. For each bin, the timestamps and polarities of the first and last triggered events at each pixel are extracted for calibration. Data Structures: The event stream is stored as a list of tuples or objects: (timestamp, x, y, polarity). Bins are represented by their start and end timestamps (ti, t{i+1}). Per-pixel metadata for a bin i includes: t{	ext{first}}^i: Timestamp of the first event in bin i at a specific pixel. t{	ext{last}}^i: Timestamp of the last event in bin i at a specific pixel. p{	ext{first}}^i: Polarity of the first event in bin i. p{	ext{last}}^i: Polarity of the last event in bin i. Steps: 1. Set Boundaries: Define t0 = t{	ext{start}} and tb = t{	ext{end}}. 2. Determine Intermediate Boundaries: Find time points t1, \dots, t{b-1} such that each bin B(ti, t{i+1}) contains an equal number of events. 3. Extract Per-Pixel Extremes: For each bin i and each pixel (x,y) that has events in this bin: Identify the event with the minimum timestamp as the "first" event. Record its timestamp t{	ext{first}}^i and polarity p{	ext{first}}^i. Identify the event with the maximum timestamp as the "last" event. Record its timestamp t{	ext{last}}^i and polarity p{	ext{last}}^i. If a pixel has no events in bin i, these values are undefined for that pixel/bin pair. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def equaleventbinning(events, b): """ events: list of (timestamp, x, y, polarity), sorted by timestamp. b: number of bins. Returns: list of bins, where each bin is a dict with 'starttime', 'endtime', and 'pixelextremes' (dict mapping (x,y) to {'tfirst', 'tlast', 'pfirst', 'plast'}). """ n = len(events) if n == 0: return [] k = n // b # Target events per bin bins = [] tstart = events[0][0] tend = events[-1][0] for i in range(b): startidx = i k endidx = (i + 1) k if i < b - 1 else n binevents = events[startidx:endidx] if not binevents: continue ti = binevents[0][0] tiplus1 = binevents[-1][0] pixelextremes = {} for ts, x, y, p in binevents: key = (x, y) if key not in pixelextremes: pixelextremes[key] = { 'tfirst': ts, 'tlast': ts, 'pfirst': p, 'plast': p } else: if ts > pixelextremes[key]['tlast']: pixelextremes[key]['tlast'] = ts pixelextremes[key]['plast'] = p bins.append({ 'index': i, 'starttime': ti, 'endtime': tiplus1, 'pixelextremes': pixelextremes }) return bins Parameters: b: Number of bins. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: t0 and tb are fixed to the start and end of the entire stream. Intermediate ti values are determined by event counts, not time intervals. Degenerate Input: If the event stream is empty, no bins are created. If a pixel has no events in a specific bin, its calibration function inputs are undefined, requiring handling in the photometric calibration step. Computes the photometric quantity calibration offset for an event bin B(ti, t{i+1}) using the first and last triggered events at each pixel. It sets itself apart by using a conditional function \phi that checks for adjacent events and polarity consistency to determine the offset. Choose this when integrating event data into the NeRF loss to account for temporal blur and exposure. Formula: h(B(ti, t{i+1})) = \phi\left( rac{t{i+1}-t{	ext{last}}^i}{t{	ext{first}}^{i+1}-t{	ext{last}}^i}, p{	ext{first}}^{i+1}ight) - \phi\left( rac{ti-t{	ext{last}}^{i-1}}{t{	ext{first}}^i-t{	ext{last}}^{i-1}}, p{	ext{first}}^iight) \phi(z, p{	ext{first}}^i) =  egin{cases} z p{	ext{first}}^i & 	ext{if } p{	ext{first}}^i = p{	ext{last}}^{i-1} \ 0 & 	ext{if } p{	ext{first}}^i 
eq p{	ext{last}}^{i-1} \ 0.5 & 	ext{if } 
exists p{	ext{first}}^i \lor 
exists p{	ext{last}}^{i-1} \end{cases} Parameters: t{	ext{first}}^i, t{	ext{last}}^i: Start and end times of the first/last event in bin i at a specific pixel. p{	ext{first}}^i, p{	ext{last}}^i: Polarities of those events. z: The normalized time ratio passed to \phi. Pitfalls: The (x,y) coordinates are omitted from the equations because the operation is identical for all pixels, but the values t{	ext{first}}, t{	ext{last}}, p{	ext{first}}, p{	ext{last}} are pixel-specific. If adjacent events do not exist (e.g., at the start or end of the stream, or if a pixel has no events in bin i-1 or i+1), the function returns 0.5. Polarity mismatch between adjacent bins results in a zero contribution for that term. Time Complexity: O(N) to sort and split the event stream, where N is the total number of events. Per-pixel extraction is also O(N) in total across all bins. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the event stream and bin metadata. Measured Performance: The method achieves better performance in HDR NeRF training compared to uniform binning by leveraging the temporal blur prior. Strengths: Adapts to varying event densities, ensuring consistent statistical contribution from each bin. Limitations: Requires sorted events and careful handling of edge cases where adjacent events or polarities are missing. When to Use: When training HDR NeRF from single-exposure images and events, particularly when event density varies significantly over time. When Not to Use: When real-time processing is critical and sorting events is too expensive, or when event data is sparse and uniform time bins are sufficient. Originated in the context of HDR NeRF training from single-exposure images and events, specifically in the "Seeing through Light and Darkness" paper. It builds on the E3 NeRF method, which first leveraged the temporal blur prior in event distribution for event loss optimization. The method is used in sensor-physics grounded deblurring HDR NeRF frameworks to improve novel view synthesis performance. name: MI-shaping
head: JacobiNeRF shaping, contrastive loss on gradients
body: MI-shaping is a training technique that improves the suitability of a NeRF for semantic label propagation by applying a contrastive loss on the gradients of pixel gray values with respect to the network weights. It specifically targets the RGB linear layer to increase the mutual information between perturbed responses of semantically similar rays. Unlike standard NeRF training which only minimizes photometric error, MI-shaping explicitly aligns the gradient space of the network to reflect semantic similarity, as measured by DINO features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model (trained for color reconstruction only), a set of training images, and corresponding DINO feature embeddings for each pixel/region. Output: A shaped NeRF model with modified weights in the RGB linear layer. Data Structures: NeRF Weights: The method targets the parameters of the RGB linear layer, which is a 3 \times 128-dimensional weight matrix in the reference implementation. Ray Batch: A batch of 64 rays sampled across all training views per epoch. DINO Features: Semantic feature vectors associated with each ray/pixel, used to compute similarity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-training: Train the NeRF using standard photometric loss (color reconstruction) for 24 hours. 2. Ray Sampling: For each epoch, randomly sample a batch of 64 rays across all training views. 3. Gradient Computation: For each ray in the batch, compute the gradient of the pixel gray value with respect to the NeRF's RGB linear layer weights. The pixel gray value is defined as the mean of the 3 RGB channels. 4. Sample Selection: For each sampled ray i, identify positive and negative samples from the other rays in the batch based on DINO feature similarity. A ray j is a positive sample if its DINO feature similarity with ray i is higher than a dynamic threshold \tau, and a negative sample if the similarity is lower than \tau. The total number of samples considered for the contrastive loss for a specific ray is 64. 5. Threshold Adaptation: Adjust the similarity threshold \tau dynamically during training. Initialize \tau within the interval [0.5, 0.8]. Calculate the ratio of positive samples in the current batch. If the ratio of positive samples is lower than 5%, subtract 0.001 from \tau. If the ratio of positive samples is larger than 15%, add 0.001 to \tau. Clamp \tau to remain within [0.5, 0.8]. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the MI-shaping loss using a contrastive formulation that correlates gradient cosine similarity with DINO feature similarity. The loss parameters are \lambda = 0.01 and \gamma = 0.01. 7. Optimization: Update the NeRF weights using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-4} for 10,000 epochs. This phase takes approximately 8 hours. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def cosinesimilarity(a, b): """Compute cosine similarity between two vectors.""" anorm = torch.nn.functional.normalize(a, p=2, dim=-1) bnorm = torch.nn.functional.normalize(b, p=2, dim=-1) return torch.sum(anorm bnorm, dim=-1) def adaptivethresholdupdate(threshold, posratio): """Update threshold based on positive sample ratio.""" if posratio < 0.05: threshold -= 0.001 elif posratio > 0.15: threshold += 0.001 return torch.clamp(threshold, min=0.5, max=0.8) def mishapingstep(nerfmodel, batchrays, dinofeatures, threshold, optimizer): """ Perform one step of MI-shaping. Args: nerfmodel: The NeRF model. batchrays: Tensor of shape (64,...) representing 64 sampled rays. dinofeatures: Tensor of shape (64, D) containing DINO features for each ray. threshold: Current similarity threshold. optimizer: Adam optimizer for the RGB linear layer weights. Returns: newthreshold: Updated threshold. """ optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Forward pass to get RGB outputs rgboutputs = nerfmodel(batchrays) # Shape: (64, 3) # 2. Compute gray values (mean of RGB channels) grayvalues = torch.mean(rgboutputs, dim=-1) # Shape: (64,) # 3. Compute gradients of gray values w.r.t. RGB linear layer weights rgblinearweights = nerfmodel.rgblinear.weight # Shape: (3, 128) gradientsperray = [] for i in range(64): # Compute gradient of scalar grayvalue[i] w.r.t. weights gradi = torch.autograd.grad( grayvalues[i], rgblinearweights, gradoutputs=torch.tensor(1.0, device=grayvalues.device), creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] gradientsperray.append(gradi.flatten()) # Shape: (384,) gradientsperray = torch.stack(gradientsperray) # Shape: (64, 384) # 4. Compute DINO similarity matrix dinosim = torch.zeros(64, 64, device=grayvalues.device) for i in range(64): for j in range(64): dinosim[i, j] = cosinesimilarity(dinofeatures[i], dinofeatures[j]) # 5. Contrastive loss on gradients loss = torch.tensor(0.0, device=grayvalues.device) poscount = 0 negcount = 0 for i in range(64): for j in range(64): if i == j: continue gradsim = cosinesimilarity(gradientsperray[i], gradientsperray[j]) if dinosim[i, j] > threshold: loss -= gradsim poscount += 1 else: loss += gradsim negcount += 1 if poscount + negcount > 0: loss = loss / (poscount + negcount) # Apply loss parameters λ and γ as scaling factors loss = loss 0.01 loss.backward() optimizer.step() # 6. Update threshold totalpairs = 64 63 numpos = torch.sum(dinosim > threshold).item() posratio = numpos / totalpairs newthreshold = adaptivethresholdupdate(threshold, posratio) return newthreshold Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Clamping: The threshold must be strictly clamped to [0.5, 0.8] after each adjustment to prevent divergence. Gradient Precision: Computing gradients of pixel gray values with respect to the RGB linear layer weights requires careful handling of the backpropagation through the volume rendering process. Memory Usage: The MI-shaping phase consumes approximately 1350 MB of memory. Time Complexity: The MI-shaping phase takes approximately 8 hours to complete. This is significantly faster than Semantic-NeRF and DINO-NeRF, which take 28 hours. Memory Complexity: The method requires approximately 1350 MB of memory during the shaping phase. Performance: On the Replica dataset, the PSNR for novel view synthesis is 18.79 for J-NeRF (with MI-shaping) compared to 18.88 for standard NeRF. The shaping does not degrade view synthesis quality. Strengths: Improves semantic label propagation performance significantly compared to plain NeRF. Faster training than comparable semantic NeRF methods. Limitations: Requires pre-training the NeRF for color reconstruction first. Relies on DINO features for similarity, which may not be available for all scenes without pre-computation. MI-shaping was introduced in the JacobiNeRF paper. It is based on the observation that the mutual information between pixel gradients under perturbation is positively correlated with the cosine similarity of their gradients with respect to perturbed network weights. The method was developed to enhance the NeRF's suitability for semantic segmentation label propagation. name: NeRF Model Setup and Configuration
head: NeRF Initialization, NeRF Scene Setup
body: This method defines the deterministic initialization of the NeRF model's geometric and textural modules, scene bounding volume, occupancy grids, and sampling parameters. It solves the problem of establishing a valid coordinate space and sampling strategy before the first training iteration. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the static configuration of the scene representation (AABB vs. unbounded sphere) and the derived sampling constants, rather than the dynamic weight updates or architectural modifications. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Configuration object self.config (containing learnedbackground, gridprune, numsamplesperray, radius), scene bounding box self.sceneaabb, and current step globalstep. Outputs: Initialized model state including occupancygrid, nearplane, farplane, coneangle, renderstepsize, and contractiontype. Data Structures: occupancygrid: A 3D grid storing occupancy probabilities. Fields: roiaabb (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box), resolution (integer, side length of the cubic grid), contractiontype (enum). Layout: Not specified in sources. Typically implemented as a dense 3D array or sparse hash map depending on the framework. ContractionType: Enum with values AABB and UNBOUNDEDSPHERE. Parameters: occupancygridres: Integer. 256 if learnedbackground is true; 128 otherwise. nearplane: Float or None. 0.2 if learnedbackground is true; None otherwise. farplane: Float or None. 10^4 if learnedbackground is true; None otherwise. coneangle: Float. Calculated as 10^{(\log{10}(\text{far\plane}) / \text{num\samples\per\ray})} - 1 if learnedbackground is true; 0.0 otherwise. renderstepsize: Float. 0.01 if learnedbackground is true; 1.732 \times 2 \times \text{radius} / \text{num\samples\per\ray} otherwise. Numbered Steps: 1. Determine Contraction and Bounds: If self.config.learnedbackground is true: Set contractiontype = ContractionType.UNBOUNDEDSPHERE. Set nearplane = 0.2. Set farplane = 10000.0. Set occupancygridres = 256. Set renderstepsize = 0.01. Calculate coneangle = 10 (\log{10}(\text{far\plane}) / \text{self.config.num\samples\per\ray}) - 1. Else (learnedbackground is false): Set contractiontype = ContractionType.AABB. Set nearplane = None. Set farplane = None. Set occupancygridres = 128. Set renderstepsize = 1.732 \times 2 \times \text{self.config.radius} / \text{self.config.num\samples\per\ray}. Set coneangle = 0.0. 2. Initialize Occupancy Grid (if pruning enabled): If self.config.gridprune is true: Create self.occupancygrid with: roiaabb = self.sceneaabb resolution = self.occupancygridres contractiontype = self.contractiontype 3. Define Occupancy Evaluation Function: Define occevalfn(x) which returns density[..., None] self.renderstepsize. density refers to the raw density output of the NeRF network at query points x. 4. Update Loop (Runtime): In the training step updatestep: If training and self.config.gridprune is true: Update self.occupancygrid every globalstep using occevalfn. Pseudocode: Unverified code. 1 self.coneangle = 10 (math.log10(self.farplane) / self.config.numsamplesperray) - 1 else: self.contractiontype = "AABB" self.nearplane = None self.farplane = None self.occupancygridres = 128 # Formula: 1.732 2 radius / numsamplesperray self.renderstepsize = 1.732 2 self.config.radius / self.config.numsamplesperray self.coneangle = 0.0 # Step 2: Initialize Occupancy Grid if self.config.gridprune: # Assuming OccupancyGrid class exists with these init args self.occupancygrid = OccupancyGrid( roiaabb=self.sceneaabb, resolution=self.occupancygridres, contractiontype=self.contractiontype) # Step 3: Define Evaluation Function # Note: This function is a closure or method that accesses the network's density output def occevalfn(densitytensor): # density[..., None] adds a dimension for broadcasting if needed return densitytensor[..., None] self.renderstepsize self.occevalfn = occevalfn def updatestep(self, globalstep, densitytensor): # Step 4: Update Loop if self.config.gridprune and self.occupancygrid is not None: # The source says "update... every globalstep". # This implies a check like if globalstep % updatefrequency == 0. # Since updatefrequency is not given, we assume it happens at the step provided. # In practice, this usually involves calling self.occupancygrid.prune(self.occevalfn) # or similar. name: Magic123 Coarse Stage
head: NeRF optimization stage
body: The Magic123 Coarse Stage is a single-image-to-3D optimization procedure that trains a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to reconstruct a foreground object from a single reference image. It distinguishes itself by combining Instant-NGP acceleration with multi-modal regularization priors—specifically depth and normal smoothness—derived from off-the-shelf 2D models to prevent geometric collapse and high-frequency artifacts. Unlike standard NeRF training which relies primarily on photometric loss, this method integrates novel view guidance from diffusion priors to constrain the unobserved geometry. Inputs: Reference image Ir (foreground object with background). Binary segmentation mask M extracted from Ir. Pseudo-depth map dr from Ir. Fixed camera pose vr (assumed front view). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta. Rendered RGB image G\theta(vr). Rendered depth map d. Rendered normal map n. The implementation uses the Instant-NGP [57] NeRF representation. NeRF Parameters (\theta): Contains the hash grid encodings and MLP weights for density (\sigma) and color (c). Mask Integration: The foreground mask M(G\theta(vr)) is acquired by integrating volume density along the ray. Normal Estimation: Normal vectors are estimated via finite differences of the rendered depth map. 1. Preprocessing: Extract binary segmentation mask M from Ir using a Dense Prediction Transformer [67]. Extract pseudo-depth map dr from Ir using a pretrained MiDaS [68] model. Assign fixed camera pose vr to the reference image. 2. Rendering: Render the reference view G\theta(vr) using the current NeRF parameters \theta. Render the background as pure white, as no background is modeled. Compute the rendered foreground mask M(G\theta(vr)) by integrating volume density along each ray. Compute the rendered depth map d. Compute the rendered normal map n using finite differences on d. 3. Loss Computation: Compute Reference View Reconstruction Loss L{rec}. Compute Novel View Guidance Loss Lg (details in §2.2 of source). Compute Depth Prior Loss Ld. Compute Normal Smoothness Loss Ln. 4. Optimization: Compute total loss Lc. Update \theta using gradient descent. Reference View Reconstruction Loss (L{rec}): L{rec} = \lambda{rgb} \| M \odot (Ir - G\theta(vr)) \|2^2 + \lambda{mask} \| M - M(G\theta(vr)) \|2^2 Where: \lambda{rgb}, \lambda{mask} are weights for RGB and mask losses. \odot is the Hadamard product. M(G\theta(vr)) is the foreground mask acquired by integrating volume density along the ray. Depth Prior Loss (Ld): Ld = \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 - \frac{\text{cov}(M \odot dr, M \odot d)}{\sigma(M \odot dr)\sigma(M \odot d)} \right) Where: dr is the pseudo depth from MiDaS. d is the NeRF depth output. \text{cov}(\cdot) denotes covariance. \sigma(\cdot) measures standard deviation. This normalized negative Pearson correlation avoids value mismatch issues inherent in MSE for depth. Normal Smoothness Loss (Ln): Ln = \| n - \tau(g(n, k)) \| Where: n is the rendered normal map. \tau(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operation. g(\cdot) is a Gaussian blur with kernel size k=9 \times 9. Total Coarse Loss (Lc): Lc = L{rec} + Lg + \lambdad Ld + \lambdan Ln Where: Lg is the novel view guidance loss. \lambdad, \lambdan are weights for depth and normal regularizations. Gaussian Blur Kernel Size (k): 9 \times 9. Background Color: Pure white. Weights (\lambda{rgb}, \lambda{mask}, \lambdad, \lambdan): Not given in the sources. Instant-NGP Settings: Not given in the sources. Flat Geometry Collapse: Without depth and normal regularization, the model may generate textures that appear on the surface without capturing actual geometric details. High-Frequency Artifacts: NeRFs tend to produce high-frequency artifacts on object surfaces; the normal smoothness loss mitigates this. Depth Value Mismatch: Using MSE for depth loss is suboptimal due to value mismatches between pseudo-depth and NeRF depth; normalized correlation is used instead. Background Modeling: The background is not modeled and rendered as pure white; this assumes the input image has a separable foreground. Time Complexity: Fast inference and optimization due to the use of Instant-NGP. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles complex topological changes smoothly; recovers complex geometry; prevents flat geometry and high-frequency artifacts. Limitations: Relies on off-the-shelf 2D priors (MiDaS, Dense Prediction Transformer) which may introduce noise or inaccuracies; requires fixed camera poses. When to use: Single-image-to-3D generation where fast convergence and geometric plausibility are prioritized over photorealistic texture fidelity in the coarse stage. When not to use: Multi-view reconstruction where camera poses are unknown or dynamic; scenes with complex backgrounds that cannot be segmented. Magic123 is a pipeline for object-level image-to-3D generation. The coarse stage was introduced in "Magic123: One Image to High-Quality 3D Object Generation Using Both 2D and 3D Diffusion Priors". It builds on the Instant-NGP implementation [57] and integrates diffusion priors for novel view guidance. The stage is followed by a fine stage using DMTet for high-resolution refinement. name: DietNeRF
body: Also called: DietNeRF ## Overview DietNeRF is a training configuration that enhances novel view synthesis quality in few-shot settings by introducing an auxiliary semantic consistency loss. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF optimization by matching high-level semantic attributes to semantic pseudo-labels with texture guidance across diverse, random poses. ## How it works Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A small set of input images with known camera poses. Outputs: A trained NeRF model capable of rendering photorealistic images from arbitrary viewpoints. Data Structures: NeRF Model \mathcal{M}: Standard MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is 3D position, \mathbf{d} is viewing direction, \sigma is density, and \mathbf{c} is color. Semantic Pseudo-labels: Semantic maps generated by passing rendered or input images through a pre-trained semantic segmentation network. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample rays from the input camera poses and a set of random, unseen camera poses. 2. Render color images from these rays using the current NeRF model \mathcal{M} via standard volume rendering Parent. 3. Pass the rendered images from random poses through a pre-trained semantic segmentation network to obtain semantic pseudo-labels. 4. Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} as a weighted sum of photometric and semantic losses: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{sem}} \mathcal{L}{\text{sem}} Where \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss between rendered images and ground truth input images, \mathcal{L}{\text{sem}} measures the discrepancy between semantic pseudo-labels of rendered views and input views to match high-level semantic attributes across different views, and \lambda{\text{sem}} is a hyperparameter balancing the semantic loss. 5. Update the NeRF parameters using gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}{\text{total}}. Parameters: \lambda{\text{sem}}: Weight for the semantic loss. Not given in the sources. Number of random poses: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Semantic Model Accuracy: The quality of the semantic pseudo-labels directly impacts the regularization. Texture Guidance: The method relies on texture guidance to align semantic attributes. Pseudocode: python def traindietnerf(inputimages, inputposes, nerfmodel, semanticsegmenter, lambdasem, numrandomposes, lr, numiterations): params = nerfmodel.parameters() for iteration in range(numiterations): raysinput = sampleraysfromposes(inputposes) randomposes = generaterandomposes(numrandomposes) raysrandom = sampleraysfromposes(randomposes) renderedinput = volumerender(nerfmodel, raysinput) renderedrandom = volumerender(nerfmodel, raysrandom) semanticrandom = semanticsegmenter(renderedrandom) semanticinput = semanticsegmenter(inputimages) lossphoto = computel1loss(renderedinput, inputimages) losssem = computesemanticconsistencyloss(semanticrandom, semanticinput) losstotal = lossphoto + lambdasem losssem grads = computegradients(losstotal, params) updateparameters(params, grads, lr) def sampleraysfromposes(poses): rays = [] for pose in poses: for y in range(pose.height): for x in range(pose.width): origin = pose.cameracenter direction = normalize(pose.cameramatrix @ [x, y, 1, 1]) rays.append((origin, direction)) return rays def volumerender(model, rays): images = [] for origin, direction in rays: tvals = [i / model.numsamples for i in range(1, model.numsamples + 1)] zvals = [origin[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3) for t in tvals] densities, colors = model.samplealongray(origin, direction, tvals) deltas = [tvals[i] - tvals[i-1] for i in range(1, len(tvals))] alpha = [1.0 - exp(-densities[i] deltas[i]) for i in range(len(deltas))] transmittance = [exp(-sum(densities[j] deltas[j] for j in range(i))) for i in range(len(deltas))] weights = [alpha[i] transmittance[i] for i in range(len(deltas))] color = sum(weights[i] colors[i] for i in range(len(weights))) images.append(color) return reshapetoimage(images, pose.height, pose.width) def computel1loss(rendered, groundtruth): return sum(abs(r - g) for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) / len(rendered) def computesemanticconsistencyloss(sempred, semgt): return sum(abs(p - g) for p, g in zip(sempred, semgt)) / len(sempred) def computegradients(loss, params): return [loss.gradient(p) for p in params] def updateparameters(params, grads, lr): for p, g in zip(params, grads): p -= lr g def generaterandomposes(n): return [RandomPose() for in range(n)] ## Subtopics ### NeRF Initialization Strategies Sets initial NeRF parameters. Differs by focusing on starting values rather than training-time regularization. Choose when training stability is the primary concern. ### Mega-NeRF Training Configuration Optimizes training for large-scale scenes. Differs by scaling to massive environments rather than few-shot accuracy. Choose for city-scale or large-scene reconstruction. ### Alpha Invariance / Inverse Scaling Adjusts density scaling to maintain perceptual consistency. Differs by modifying the alpha output rather than adding external losses. Choose when density artifacts appear across resolutions. ### Batch size scaling for computational parity Adjusts batch sizes to maintain training throughput. Differs by focusing on hardware utilization rather than semantic constraints. Choose when scaling to multiple GPUs. ### Model Architecture Modifications Alters NeRF network structure. Differs by changing the model itself rather than the loss function. Choose when capacity or speed bottlenecks exist. ### Regularization Techniques Applies general penalties to prevent overfitting. Differs by using generic norms rather than semantic consistency. Choose for standard overfitting mitigation. ### NeRF Pre-processing Prepares input data and poses. Differs by handling data ingestion rather than training dynamics. Choose when input data requires cleaning or alignment. ### Exponential Learning Rate Decay with Delay Schedules learning rate reduction over time. Differs by controlling optimization speed rather than loss composition. Choose when training oscillates or diverges. ### Adaptive Time-step Training Framework Dynamically adjusts sampling density along rays. Differs by modifying ray traversal rather than adding auxiliary losses. Choose when ray sampling is the bottleneck. ### Model Architecture and Encoding Defines positional encoding and network layers. Differs by specifying feature representation rather than training objectives. Choose when frequency representation limits quality. ### Sampling and Rendering Pipeline Configuration Configures ray generation and compositing. Differs by managing the rendering loop rather than semantic supervision. Choose when rendering speed or sampling strategy needs tuning. ### Method-Specific Training Pipelines Customizes the overall training workflow. Differs by orchestrating multiple steps rather than focusing on a single loss. Choose when integrating multiple specialized techniques. ### Iterative 3D Super-Resolution Refines NeRF output at higher resolutions. Differs by post-processing geometry rather than few-shot regularization. Choose when output resolution is insufficient. ### Random Patch Sampling Samples spatial patches for training. Differs by focusing on local regions rather than global semantic consistency. Choose when memory limits full-image rendering. ### Equal-Event Event Binning Bins rays by event count for neuromorphic data. Differs by handling asynchronous sensor data rather than standard images. Choose when training on event camera data. ### MI-shaping Shapes mutual information in the latent space. Differs by optimizing information theory metrics rather than pixel/semantic loss. Choose when latent representation quality is critical. ### NeRF Model Setup and Configuration Configures general model parameters. Differs by providing baseline settings rather than specialized few-shot adjustments. Choose for standard NeRF deployments. ### Magic123 Coarse Stage Initial training phase for Magic123. Differs by focusing on coarse geometry generation rather than semantic consistency. Choose when using the Magic123 pipeline. ## Operating characteristics Time Complexity: Increases due to the additional forward pass through the semantic segmentation network for random poses. Memory Complexity: Increases due to storing semantic pseudo-labels for random poses. Measured Performance: Improves perceptual quality in few-shot settings, especially with as few as one input viewpoint. Scaling: Scales with the number of random poses and the complexity of the semantic segmentation model. Strengths: Enhances few-shot quality, improves geometric consistency via semantic constraints. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained semantic segmentation model, may introduce errors if semantic labels are inaccurate. When to use: When training data is limited (few-shot), and perceptual quality is critical. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited, or when semantic consistency is not desired. ## Background DietNeRF was proposed by Jain et al.. It was introduced to address the challenge of few-shot novel view synthesis, where standard NeRF methods struggle with limited input views. The method leverages semantic consistency to regularize the learned radiance field, drawing inspiration from the idea that semantic attributes should be consistent across different views of the same scene. Not given in the sources for specific application fields beyond the general few-shot context. ## Sources A Critical Analysis of NeRF-Based 3D Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.3390/rs15143585, fetched 2026-10-26 Semantically-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Visual Scene Understanding: A Comprehensive Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-025-02663-5, fetched 2026-10-27

name: DONeRF
head: Depth Oracle Neural Radiance Fields, DONeRF Training Configuration, DONeRF training setup, Depth Oracle Network, DoNeRF
body: DONeRF is a training configuration and architectural variant of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) designed for real-time rendering by replacing standard dense raymarching with a two-network local sampling strategy. It solves the prohibitive computational cost of NeRF, which requires dozens of petaFLOPS, by using a depth oracle network to predict optimal sample locations and a shading network to render the image using only a few samples per ray. Unlike standard NeRF which uses hundreds of samples, DONeRF achieves equal or better quality with 2–4 samples per pixel, reducing inference costs by up to 48x compared to NeRF when ground truth depth is available. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like NeRF Hyperparameters by explicitly decoupling geometry estimation (oracle) from appearance rendering (shading) and training them sequentially rather than end-to-end. DONeRF consists of two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a depth oracle network and a shading network. The pipeline operates in five stages: (1) ray unification within a view cell, (2) non-linear depth transformation, (3) oracle classification of sample importance, (4) warping of sample positions, and (5) shading network raymarching. Inputs: Camera position, viewing direction, and optionally ground truth depth maps (or extracted depth maps for training without GT). Outputs: RGB color and accumulated opacity for each pixel. 1. View Cell A view cell is a bounding box with a primary orientation and maximum viewing angle, capturing all view rays originating in the box within rotation limits. Training is performed per view cell. 2. Depth Oracle Network Architecture: 8 hidden layers, 256 hidden units per layer, ReLU activation. The last layer is linear. Input: Concatenated 3D position x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction d \in S^2. Encoding: No positional encoding is applied to inputs. Output: Depth classification logits. The network solves a classification task using filtered, discretized target depth values rather than direct depth regression. Loss: Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss. 3. Shading Network Architecture: 8 hidden layers, 256 hidden units per layer, ReLU activation. The last layer is linear. Input: 3D position x and view direction d. Encoding: Positional encoding is applied. \gamma(x): 63-dimensional vector. \gamma(d): 27-dimensional vector. Usage: \gamma(x) is used at the first layer. \gamma(d) is concatenated to the feature vector before the last layer. Output: RGB color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+. Loss: Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss on RGB output. The training is not end-to-end. It proceeds in two sequential phases: Phase 1: Oracle Training 1. Train the depth oracle network for 300,000 iterations. 2. Use ground truth depth maps (or extracted depth maps if GT is unavailable) to create classification targets. 3. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 0.0005, batch size 4096 samples per iteration. Phase 2: Shading Network Training 1. Freeze the depth oracle network. 2. Use the oracle to predict sample locations for the shading network. 3. Train the shading network for 300,000 iterations. 4. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 0.0005, batch size 4096 samples per iteration. 1. Ray Unification: Rays are unified within the view cell. 2. Logarithmic Transformation: Sample positions are transformed logarithmically to handle large depth ranges. 3. Oracle Selection: The oracle classifies depth ranges. The number of samples selected by the oracle is denoted as Ns (e.g., DONeRF-16 uses Ns=16). 4. Warping: Sample positions are warped towards the view cell to direct high-frequency predictions to the foreground. 5. Shading: The shading network evaluates the warped samples to accumulate RGBA output. The total loss for the shading network training combines MSE and an opacity penalty: \text{loss} = \alpha \cdot \text{loss}{\text{MSE}} + \beta \cdot \text{loss}{\text{O}} Where: \alpha = 1.0 \beta = 10.0 \text{loss}{\text{MSE}} is the standard MSE between rendered and ground truth RGB. \text{loss}{\text{O}} is the opacity loss, defined as: \text{loss}O = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } \sum{i=1}^X \deltai \geq 1 \\ \left( \left( \sum{i=1}^X \deltai \right) - 1 \right)^2, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Here, X is the number of samples per ray, and \deltai represents the opacity contribution of the i-th sample. This loss prevents "dark pixel" artifacts caused by low sample counts failing to accumulate to full opacity for opaque surfaces. If ground truth depth is unavailable: 1. Train a dense NeRF with 12 layers of 512 hidden units each, using 128 samples per ray. 2. Extract depth maps for all training poses from this dense NeRF. 3. Use these extracted depth maps as the ground truth for training the DONeRF oracle and shading networks in the standard two-phase procedure. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim NUMBANDS = 10 MINFREQLOG = 0.0 MAXFREQLOG = 10.0 def positionalencoding(x, minfreqlog, maxfreqlog, numbands): """Applies positional encoding to input x. Returns encoded vector.""" l = minfreqlog b = (maxfreqlog - minfreqlog) / (numbands - 1) scales = torch.tensor([2(l + i b) for i in range(numbands)]).to(x.device) xb = torch.reshape(x, (x.shape[:-1] + (-1, 1))).float() scales fouriered = torch.sin(torch.cat([xb, xb + 0.5 torch.pi], dim=-1)) return torch.cat([x, fouriered], dim=-1) class DepthOracleNet(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() layers = [nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.ReLU()] for in range(6): layers.extend([nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU()]) layers.append(nn.Linear(256, 1)) self.net = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x, d): return self.net(torch.cat([x, d], dim=-1)) class ShadingNet(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.firstlayer = nn.Linear(63, 256) self.hiddenlayers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU()) for in range(6) ]) self.preoutputlayer = nn.Linear(283, 256) self.outputlayer = nn.Linear(256, 4) def forward(self, x, d): gammax = positionalencoding(x, MINFREQLOG, MAXFREQLOG, NUMBANDS) gammad = positionalencoding(d, MINFREQLOG, MAXFREQLOG, NUMBANDS) h = self.firstlayer(gammax) for layer in self.hiddenlayers: h = layer(h) h = torch.cat([h, gammad], dim=-1) h = self.preoutputlayer(h) return self.outputlayer(h) def volumerender(positions, sigmas, rgbs, tnear, tfar): """Standard NeRF alpha compositing. Returns rendered RGB and opacity contributions (deltas).""" # Compute distances between consecutive samples dists = torch.cat([positions[..., 1:,:] - positions[...,:-1,:], torch.fulllike(positions[..., -1:,:], tfar - positions[..., -1,:])], dim=-2) dists = torch.norm(dists, dim=-1) # Opacity contribution per sample: alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltai) deltas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmas dists) # Transmittance: Ti = exp(-sum{j<i} sigmaj deltaj) transmittance = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigmas dists, dim=-1)) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[...,:1]), transmittance[...,:-1]], dim=-1) # Accumulate color: C = sum(Ti alphai ci) weights = transmittance deltas.unsqueeze(-1) renderedrgb = torch.sum(weights rgbs, dim=-2) return renderedrgb, deltas def traindonerrf(oraclenet, shadingnet, optimizero, optimizers, dataloader, numitero, numiters, alpha, beta): """Two-phase training for DONeRF.""" # Phase 1: Train Oracle oraclenet.train() shadingnet.eval() for i in range(numitero): rays, gtdepth, gtrgb = next(dataloader) preddepthlogits = oraclenet(rays.x, rays.d) # gtdepthtargets are discretized depth bins derived from ground truth depth maps gtdepthtargets = discretizedepth(gtdepth) losso = nn.functional.binarycrossentropywithlogits(preddepthlogits, gtdepthtargets) optimizero.zerograd() losso.backward() optimizero.step() # Phase 2: Train Shading oraclenet.eval() shadingnet.train() for i in range(numiters): rays, gtrgb = next(dataloader) # 1. Oracle predicts sample locations (indices or warped positions) samplelocs = oraclenet.predictsamples(rays.x, rays.d) # 2. Warp samples logarithmically towards the view cell warpedlocs = torch.log1p(samplelocs) # 3. Evaluate Shading Network at warped locations out = shadingnet(warpedlocs, rays.d) rgbpreds = out[...,:3] sigmapreds = torch.relu(out[..., 3]) # 4. Volume Rendering Accumulation renderedrgb, deltas = volumerender(warpedlocs, sigmapreds, rgbpreds, rays.tnear, rays.tfar) # 5. Compute Loss lossmse = nn.functional.mseloss(renderedrgb, gtrgb) sumopacity = torch.sum(deltas, dim=-1) lossop = torch.mean(torch.where(sumopacity >= 1.0, torch.zeroslike(sumopacity), (sumopacity - 1.0)2)) loss = alpha lossmse + beta lossop optimizers.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizers.step() NUMITERATIONS = 300000 LEARNINGRATE = 0.0005 BATCHSIZE = 4096 ALPHA = 1.0 BETA = 10.0 NUMSAMPLESPERRAY = [2, 4, 8, 16] DONeRF is a re-implementation of the DONeRF method adapted for 360-degree scenes. It omits the logarithmic sampling and warping techniques used in the original forward-facing implementation. It differs from standard NeRF by using a discrete classification-based volume representation derived from ground truth depth maps, rather than continuous density fields. Time Complexity: DONeRF requires approximately 4.35 MFLOP per pixel. Inference costs are reduced by up to 48x compared to NeRF when conditioning on available ground truth depth information. Memory Complexity: DONeRF stays in the realm of compact MLPs without additional data structures or increased storage requirements, unlike baking methods which may require hundreds of MBs to GBs. It does not require additional memory for explicit caching or acceleration structures, unlike methods such as NSVF. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 3090 at 800x800 resolution with 2 samples/ray, DONeRF renders in 51.3 ms (~20 fps). Breakdown: Ray unification/first feature gen (0.21 ms), Oracle network (12.64 ms), Space warping/second feature gen (3.46 ms), Shading network (34.9 ms), Final color gen (0.09 ms). The shading network cost scales nearly linearly with samples: 34.9 ms (2 samples), 65.4 ms (4 samples), 136.4 ms (8 samples), 270.4 ms (16 samples). Quality: DONeRF achieves an average PSNR of 31.14 dB compared to NeRF's 30.52 dB. At 16 samples, DONeRF is up to 7 dB higher PSNR and 15-78x faster than NeRF. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability, compact memory footprint, high quality on large-scale scenes. Limitations: Not end-to-end trainable. Struggles without high-quality depth supervision. Reflective/transparent surfaces are difficult to replicate with low sample counts and single depth estimates. Dark pixel artifacts can occur at low sample counts if opacity loss is not applied. Background noise in no-GT training can create zero-contribution samples. DONeRF was introduced to bring compact neural representations closer to practical real-time rendering in applications like games and VR. It addresses the prohibitive computational cost of NeRF, which requires dozens of petaFLOPS. The method was developed to enable interactive rendering (20 fps) on a single GPU. It is used for real-time rendering of large synthetic scenes. head: DONeRF for 360-degree datasets, DONeRF re-implementation
body: DONeRF is a re-implementation of the DONeRF method adapted for 360-degree scenes. It omits the logarithmic sampling and warping techniques used in the original forward-facing implementation. It differs from standard NeRF by using a discrete classification-based volume representation derived from ground truth depth maps, rather than continuous density fields. Inputs and Outputs Input: Training images with corresponding ground truth depth maps. Output: A neural network that predicts classification values for ray bins, which are aggregated to render color images. Data Structures Ray Bins: The ray is split into N equidistant bins of constant length. Classification Map: A discrete map C{x,y}(z) where z indexes the bin along the ray (x,y). Steps 1. Discretization: For each pixel (x,y) and its corresponding ray, the ground truth depth ds is discretized. The classification value C{x,y}(z) for bin z (bounded by dz and d{z+1}) is assigned as: C{x,y}(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } dz \le ds < d{z+1} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where dz is the start depth of bin z. 2. Blurring: The classification map is blurred spatially to account for depth uncertainty and occlusion. For each pixel (x,y) and bin z, the blurred value \tilde{C}{x,y}(z) is computed as the maximum of neighbors within a kernel of size K: \tilde{C}{x,y}(z) = \max{i,j \in \pm \lfloor K/2 \rfloor} \frac{C{x+i,y+j}(z)}{\sqrt{i^2 + j^2}} where K is the spatial blur kernel size. The center neighbor (i=0, j=0) is excluded to avoid division by zero. 3. Filtering: The blurred map is filtered along the depth dimension to smooth depth transitions. For each pixel (x,y) and bin z, the filtered value \bar{C}{x,y}(z) is computed as: \bar{C}{x,y}(z) = \min \left( \frac{\sum{i=-\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor}^{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor} \tilde{C}{x,y}(z+i) \cdot (\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1 - |i|)}{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1} \right) where Z is the depth filter kernel size. The source formula applies a min operator to the normalized weighted sum and uses \lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1 as the denominator. 4. Network Input: The filtered classification values \bar{C}{x,y}(z) are used as input to the neural network. The network predicts the color and other properties for each bin. 5. Rendering: The final color is computed by aggregating the network outputs weighted by the classification values, similar to standard volume rendering but using the discrete classification targets. Parameters N: Number of bins along the ray. Not given in the sources. K: Spatial blur kernel size. Not given in the sources. Z: Depth filter kernel size. Not given in the sources. Sampling: Equidistant sampling is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Logarithmic Sampling: Logarithmic sampling and warping are omitted because they perform poorly on 360-degree scenes. Single Depth Value: The method uses a single depth value per ray, which lacks expressivity for volumes with multiple layers (e.g., glass, fog) as it cannot capture multiple peaks in density. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeclassificationmap(depthmap, nbins, near, far): """Computes the initial classification map C from ground truth depth.""" H, W = len(depthmap), len(depthmap[0]) C = [[0.0] nbins for in range(H W)] binlength = (far - near) / nbins for y in range(H): for x in range(W): ds = depthmap[y][x] if near <= ds < far: z = int((ds - near) / binlength) z = max(0, min(z, nbins - 1)) C[y W + x][z] = 1.0 return C def blurclassificationmap(C, H, W, nbins, K): """Applies spatial blurring to the classification map.""" pad = K // 2 Cblur = [[0.0] nbins for in range(H W)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): for z in range(nbins): maxval = -math.inf for i in range(-pad, pad + 1): for j in range(-pad, pad + 1): if i == 0 and j == 0: continue dist = math.sqrt(i i + j j) val = C[(y + i) W + (x + j)][z] / dist if val > maxval: maxval = val Cblur[y W + x][z] = maxval return Cblur def filterclassificationmap(Cblur, H, W, nbins, Z): """Applies depth filtering to the blurred classification map.""" pad = Z // 2 Cfilt = [[0.0] nbins for in range(H W)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): for z in range(nbins): weightedsum = 0.0 for i in range(-pad, pad + 1): weight = (pad + 1 - abs(i)) weightedsum += Cblur[y W + x][z + i] weight denominator = pad + 1 Cfilt[y W + x][z] = min(weightedsum / denominator, weightedsum / denominator) return Cfilt Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On 360-degree datasets (Lego and Ship), DONeRF achieves lower PSNR compared to TermiNeRF but is competitive with other methods like NeRF, KiloNeRF, PlenOctrees, and AutoInt. Strengths: Provides a discrete, interpretable volume representation based on ground truth depth. Limitations: Single depth value per ray lacks expressivity for complex volumes with multiple layers (e.g., glass, fog). Logarithmic sampling is omitted, which may limit efficiency in forward-facing scenes but is necessary for 360-degree scenes. DONeRF is a re-implementation of the DONeRF method. The original DONeRF method was designed for forward-facing scenes. DONeRF adapts this method for 360-degree datasets by modifying the sampling strategy. It is compared against NeRF, KiloNeRF, PlenOctrees, and AutoInt in the context of 360-degree rendering.
