name: Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup
head: Depth Distortion Regularization, Gaussian Position Encoding, Mip-NeRF 360 Training Procedure, Position Warping for Unbounded Scenes
body: Mip-NeRF 360 optimization setup defines the training configuration for unbounded neural radiance fields, specifically addressing the challenge of rendering large-scale urban scenes with limited video memory by warping the infinite scene domain into a finite sphere. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by combining a specific scene contraction function, a multi-stage proposal network sampling strategy, and a robust learning schedule that prevents aliasing artifacts in unbounded spaces. The method optimizes a radiance field for unbounded scenes by warping coordinates, training a proposal network to guide sampling, and minimizing a composite loss function. Inputs: Camera poses \mathbf{t} (estimated via COLMAP), input images \mathbf{C}^, and scene coordinates \mathbf{x}. Outputs: Rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{t}), depth maps, and optimized network weights for the proposal and NeRF MLPs. 1. Proposal MLP (\Theta{\text{prop}}): Architecture: 4 layers, 256 hidden units. Activations: ReLU for hidden layers, Softplus for density output \tau. 2. NeRF MLP (\Theta{\text{NeRF}}): Architecture: 8 layers, 1024 hidden units. Activations: ReLU for hidden layers, Softplus for density output \tau. 3. Scene Warping: Input: 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Warped coordinate \mathbf{x}{\text{encoding}} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 1. Scene Warping (Position Encoding): For every 3D point \mathbf{x} sampled along a ray, apply the contraction function to map unbounded space to a unit sphere: \mathbf{x}{\text{encoding}} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|2 \leq 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}\|2}\right) \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|2} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|2 > 1 \end{cases} Points within the unit sphere (\|\mathbf{x}\|2 \leq 1) remain unchanged; points outside are contracted towards the boundary. 2. Proposal Network Sampling (Two Stages): Stage 0: Evaluate the proposal MLP using 64 samples along the ray to produce interval midpoints \hat{s}0 and weights \hat{w}0. Stage 1: Resample based on \hat{w}0 and evaluate the proposal MLP again with 64 samples to produce \hat{s}1 and \hat{w}1. 3. NeRF Network Sampling (One Stage): Resample based on the final proposal weights \hat{w}1. Evaluate the NeRF MLP using 32 samples to produce final interval midpoints s and weights w. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} averaged over all rays in the batch: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{t}), \mathbf{C}^) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}) + \sum{k=0}^1 \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{w}, \hat{\mathbf{s}}^k, \hat{\mathbf{w}}^k) \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}: Charbonnier loss \sqrt{(x - x^)^2 + \epsilon^2} with \epsilon = 0.001. \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}: Regularizer R{\text{dist}} = \sum{u,v} H(u)H(v) \left| \frac{tu + t{u+1}}{2} - \frac{tv + t{v+1}}{2} \right| constraining weights to approach zero or concentrate at the same intersection. \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}: Interlevel loss supervising the proposal network. \lambda: Hyperparameter balancing data and regularizer, set to 0.01. 5. Gradient Stop-Gradient: Apply stop-gradient to \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}} to ensure the optimization of \Theta{\text{prop}} is independent from \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. 6. Optimization Update: Update weights using the Adam optimizer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def initmlpparams(layers, hidden): """Initialize MLP weights and biases with He initialization.""" params = {} for i in range(layers): indim = hidden if i > 0 else 3 outdim = hidden if i < layers - 1 else 4 scale = np.sqrt(2.0 / indim) params[f'W{i}'] = np.random.randn(indim, outdim) scale params[f'b{i}'] = np.zeros(outdim) return params def initadamstate(params): """Initialize Adam optimizer moments to zero.""" m = {k: np.zeroslike(v) for k, v in params.items()} v = {k: np.zeroslike(v) for k, v in params.items()} return m, v def samplestratified(tnear, tfar, numsamples): """Stratified sampling along a ray segment.""" t = np.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples + 1) return (t[:-1] + t[1:]) / 2.0 def forwardmlp(params, x): """Standard MLP forward pass with ReLU and Softplus for last layer.""" h = x for i in range(len(params) // 2): W = params[f'W{i}'] b = params[f'b{i}'] h = h @ W + b if i < len(params) // 2 - 1: h = np.maximum(0, h) else: h = np.log1p(np.exp(h)) return h def computeweights(density, delta): """Compute volumetric rendering weights from density and interval sizes.""" alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density delta) T = np.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, axis=0) T = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(T[:1]), T[:-1]], axis=0) return T alpha def resamplefromweights(tbounds, weights, numsamples): """Resample positions based on discrete probability distribution.""" cdf = np.cumsum(weights) cdf[-1] = 1.0 u = np.random.uniform(0, 1, numsamples) indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, u) tnear = tbounds[indices] tfar = tbounds[indices + 1] return np.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples) def volumerender(color, weights): """Accumulate color using volumetric rendering equation.""" return np.sum(color weights[:, np.newaxis], axis=0) def computedistortionloss(midpoints, weights): """Compute depth distortion regularization Rdist.""" loss = 0.0 for i in range(len(midpoints)): for j in range(len(midpoints)): loss += weights[i] weights[j] np.abs(midpoints[i] - midpoints[j]) return loss def computeinterlevelloss(snerf, wnerf, sprop, wprop): """Compute interlevel loss between NeRF and proposal histograms.""" return np.mean((wnerf - wprop) 2) def trainmipnerf360(rays, images, numiterations=250000, batchsize=16384): thetaprop = initmlpparams(4, 256) thetanerf = initmlpparams(8, 1024) mprop, vprop = initadamstate(thetaprop) mnerf, vnerf = initadamstate(thetanerf) beta1, beta2, epsadam = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-6 lrstart, lrend, warmupiters = 2e-3, 2e-5, 512 gradclipnorm = 1e-3 lambdadist = 0.01 epsiloncharb = 0.001 for i in range(numiterations): batchindices = np.random.choice(len(rays), batchsize, replace=False) batchrays = rays[batchindices] batchimages = images[batchindices] if i < warmupiters: lr = lrstart (i / warmupiters) else: loglrstart = np.log(lrstart) loglrend = np.log(lrend) progress = (i - warmupiters) / (numiterations - warmupiters) lr = np.exp(loglrstart + progress (loglrend - loglrstart)) # Stage 0: Proposal t0 = samplestratified(batchrays.tnear, batchrays.tfar, 64) x0 = warpposition(transformraytoworld(batchrays, t0)) out0 = forwardmlp(thetaprop, x0) density0, = out0[:,:1], out0[:, 1:] delta0 = np.diff(np.concatenate([batchrays.tnear, t0, batchrays.tfar], axis=1), axis=1) w0 = computeweights(density0, delta0) s0 = t0 # Stage 1: Proposal t1 = resamplefromweights(np.concatenate([batchrays.tnear, batchrays.tfar], axis=1), w0, 64) x1 = warpposition(transformraytoworld(batchrays, t1)) out1 = forwardmlp(thetaprop, x1) density1, = out1[:,:1], out1[:, 1:] delta1 = np.diff(np.concatenate([batchrays.tnear, t1, batchrays.tfar], axis=1), axis=1) w1 = computeweights(density1, delta1) s1 = t1 # Stage 2: NeRF tnerf = resamplefromweights(np.concatenate([batchrays.tnear, batchrays.tfar], axis=1), w1, 32) xnerf = warpposition(transformraytoworld(batchrays, tnerf)) outnerf = forwardmlp(thetanerf, xnerf) densitynerf, colornerf = outnerf[:,:1], outnerf[:, 1:] deltanerf = np.diff(np.concatenate([batchrays.tnear, tnerf, batchrays.tfar], axis=1), axis=1) wnerf = computeweights(densitynerf, deltanerf) snerf = tnerf Crecon = volumerender(colornerf, wnerf) Lrecon = np.mean(np.sqrt((Crecon - batchimages)2 + epsiloncharb2)) Ldist = computedistortionloss(snerf, wnerf) Lprop0 = computeinterlevelloss(snerf, wnerf, s0, w0) Lprop1 = computeinterlevelloss(snerf, wnerf, s1, w1) Ltotal = Lrecon + lambdadist Ldist + Lprop0 + Lprop1 # Backprop & Update gradprop = computegradients(Ltotal, thetaprop) gradnerf = computegradients(Ltotal, thetanerf) gradprop = clipgradients(gradprop, gradclipnorm) gradnerf = clipgradients(gradnerf, gradclipnorm) thetaprop, mprop, vprop = adamupdate(thetaprop, gradprop, mprop, vprop, lr, beta1, beta2, epsadam) thetanerf, mnerf, vnerf = adamupdate(thetanerf, gradnerf, mnerf, vnerf, lr, beta1, beta2, epsadam) return thetaprop, thetanerf Optimizer: Adam. Beta 1: 0.9. Beta 2: 0.999. Epsilon: 10^{-6}. Learning Rate: Annealed log-linearly from 2 \times 10^{-3} to 2 \times 10^{-5}. Warm-up: 512 iterations. Gradient Clipping Norm: 10^{-3}. Training Iterations: 250,000. Batch Size: 2^{14} (16,384) rays. Lambda (\lambda): 0.01 for \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}. Charbonnier Epsilon (\epsilon): 0.001. Z-aliasing: The standard interlevel loss can cause the proposal MLP to learn non-smooth mappings, leading to rays "skipping" scene content, especially with high-capacity backends like iNGP. Unbounded Memory: Without warping, rendering large-scale scenes exhausts video memory due to the infinite domain. The contraction function ensures all points are mapped to a finite sphere, preventing this. Precision: The contraction function is continuous but has a derivative discontinuity at \|\mathbf{x}\|2 = 1. The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss is a proposal supervision loss function that measures the distance between a NeRF histogram and a proposal histogram by blurring the NeRF histogram into a piecewise-linear spline and resampling it into the proposal's interval endpoints. Unlike the piecewise constant loss used in mip-NeRF 360, which suffers from aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal, this method produces a smooth loss surface that prevents aliasing artifacts during training. Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction is a technique for efficiently adapting the scale of isotropic Gaussians when a scene contraction function C(\mathbf{x}) is applied. It solves the problem of maintaining correct anti-aliasing properties in contracted coordinate spaces without the computational overhead of general multivariate Gaussian transformations. It sets itself apart from the standard mip-NeRF 360 approach by linearizing the contraction around each Gaussian center to derive an isotropic scale from the Jacobian determinant, rather than contracting a full covariance matrix. A method for 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis that distills a dense collection of indoor photos into a neural field to render photorealistic views from viewpoints not present in the original collection, specifically optimized for the scale, lighting variability, and privacy constraints of Google Maps Immersive View. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF implementations by integrating low-dimensional generative latent optimization (GLO) vectors and metadata-derived exposure conditioning into the radiance network, thereby resolving cloudy geometry artifacts caused by lighting changes without sacrificing interpretability. Unlike Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss which focuses on sampling strategies, this method focuses on appearance modeling and capture constraints; it builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup as its architectural base. Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields (LocalRF) is a view synthesis method that jointly optimizes camera poses and multiple overlapping local radiance fields from a single long monocular video, avoiding Structure-from-Motion and scaling to unbounded scenes with fixed memory. It differs from global optimization approaches by dynamically allocating new local fields as the camera trajectory extends, preventing global failure from pose outliers and maintaining high resolution around the camera path. Unlike Mega-NeRF, it does not require pre-partitioned space, and unlike Mip-NeRF 360, it jointly estimates poses rather than relying on pre-computed ones. The method minimizes geometric and photometric loss together on a set of frames using differentiable rendering functions to optimize network weights. A method to resolve 'z-aliasing' artifacts in proposal networks by replacing the discrete interlevel loss with a continuous, smooth loss function that penalizes partial overlaps between proposal and NeRF histograms. It identifies z-aliasing artifacts where the proposal MLP learns a non-smooth mapping, causing rays to 'skip' scene content, especially when using iNGP backends for rapid optimization. The original Mip-NeRF 360 interlevel loss assigns equivalent loss to NeRF and proposal histogram bins regardless of overlap extent, penalizing only complete failures to overlap, leading to non-smooth density maps. The new loss prevents the proposal network from learning non-smooth mappings that occur with the previous loss, particularly when the proposal network has high capacity (e.g., iNGP backend). An unbounded extension of MipNeRF that uses a contract function to parameterize 3D Euclidean space within a ball of radius 2, allowing direct rendering of images and depth maps in the contracted space. It renders images and depth maps in the contracted space using standard NeRF equations (Eq. 1 and Eq. 2). A simplified module that outputs K scalars and K RGB-G vectors (4 dimensions: 3 RGB + 1 gating scaler) without efficient multi-space composition strategy, leading to over-smoothing. Rendering uses the same integral equation as NeRF to accumulate the K RGB-G vectors \{\hat{c}{ki}\} and get the RGB-G maps of each sub-space. It splits the RGB-G maps into RGB maps and sub-space composition maps (gating maps), applies softmax over the gating maps along the sub-space channels, and uses it as the weight to compose sub-space RGB maps to form the final rendering results. The number of sub-spaces K is set to 8. The lack of an efficient multi-space composition strategy introduces an over-smoothing problem. Uses the scene warping scheme identical to DVGO and Mip-NeRF360. Keeps other components (positional encoding, point sampling, etc.) identical to TensoRF. Uses 2 scales. Mip-NeRF360 results (Table 9): garden PSNR 24.13, room PSNR 28.11, Model Size avg 12.6MB. Implementing the MipNeRF-360 distillation mode replaces the default settings with a light proposal MLP, reducing training and inference time. The distillation mode runs 30% faster in training and 40% faster in inference than default settings, with a PSNR drop of 0.33. Time Complexity: The multi-stage sampling (2 proposal stages + 1 NeRF stage) increases per-iteration cost compared to single-stage NeRF, but the proposal network reduces the number of NeRF evaluations needed for high quality. The distillation mode variant reduces this overhead, running 30% faster in training and 40% faster in inference. Memory Complexity: The scene warping function allows the method to handle unbounded scenes without increasing memory usage proportional to scene size, as all geometry is confined to a unit sphere. This makes it suitable for large-scale urban scenes where standard 3DGS or NeRF would exhaust video memory. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, the method achieves a PSNR of 24.13 on the "garden" scene and 28.11 on the "room" scene, with an average model size of 12.6MB. Strengths: Robust to unbounded scenes, prevents aliasing artifacts through specific loss formulations and warping, and provides stable optimization via the Charbonnier loss and gradient clipping. Limitations: Requires pre-computed camera poses (e.g., via COLMAP). The warping function introduces a discontinuity in the derivative at the unit sphere boundary. Mip-NeRF 360 was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2022. It extends the original mip-NeRF approach to handle "in the wild" photo collections with large scale variations. The optimization setup, including the specific MLP architectures, learning rate schedule, and scene warping, was designed to stabilize training for unbounded scenes. The scene warping technique, often referred to as Gaussian Position Encoding in subsequent works like HO-Gaussian, was inspired by this method to handle large-scale urban scenes. name: Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss
head: Blurred NeRF Loss, Interlevel Loss, Prefiltered Loss
body: The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss is a proposal supervision loss function that measures the distance between a NeRF histogram and a proposal histogram by blurring the NeRF histogram into a piecewise-linear spline and resampling it into the proposal's interval endpoints. Unlike the piecewise constant loss used in mip-NeRF 360, which suffers from aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal, this method produces a smooth loss surface that prevents aliasing artifacts during training. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: NeRF histogram endpoints \mathbf{s} = \{s0, \dots, sN\} and weights \mathbf{w} = \{w0, \dots, w{N-1}\}, where si are normalized distances in [0, 1] and wi are accumulated weights for interval [si, s{i+1}]. Proposal histogram endpoints \hat{\mathbf{s}} = \{\hat{s}0, \dots, \hat{s}M\} and weights \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \{\hat{w}0, \dots, \hat{w}{M-1}\}. Convolution radius r. Outputs: Scalar loss \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}. Resampled NeRF weights \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathbf{s}}. Parameters r: The radius of the rectangular pulse used for convolution. interlevellossmult: The multiplier for the interlevel loss in the total loss computation. Algorithm Steps 1. Normalize: Divide NeRF weights \mathbf{w} by the size of each interval in \mathbf{s} to yield a piecewise constant PDF that integrates to \le 1. 2. Convolve: Convolve the piecewise constant PDF with a rectangular pulse of radius r (integrating to 1) to obtain a piecewise linear PDF. This is implemented by turning each endpoint si into two signed delta functions at si - r and si + r with values proportional to the change between adjacent PDF heights, sorting them, and integrating twice. 3. Integrate to CDF: Integrate the piecewise linear PDF to produce a piecewise-quadratic CDF. 4. Resample: Query the piecewise-quadratic CDF via piecewise quadratic interpolation at each location in \hat{\mathbf{s}}. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate resampled NeRF weights \hat{w}i^{\mathbf{s}} by taking the difference between adjacent interpolated CDF values at the proposal endpoints. Evaluate the loss as an element-wise function of \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\mathbf{s}} and \hat{\mathbf{w}}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def antialiasedinterlevelloss(s, w, shat, what, r): """ Computes the anti-aliased interlevel loss. Args: s: NeRF histogram endpoints, shape (N+1,) w: NeRF histogram weights, shape (N,) shat: Proposal histogram endpoints, shape (M+1,) what: Proposal histogram weights, shape (M,) r: Convolution radius Returns: loss: Scalar loss value """ N = len(w) M = len(what) # Step 1: Normalize to piecewise constant PDF # h[i] is the height of the step function in interval i intervals = s[1:] - s[:-1] # Guard against zero-width intervals intervals = np.maximum(intervals, 1e-8) h = w / intervals # Step 2: Convolve with rectangular pulse using delta functions # Create delta functions at s[i] - r and s[i] + r # Values are proportional to the change between adjacent PDF heights deltas = [] # At s[0], change is h[0] - 0 deltas.append((s[0] - r, h[0])) deltas.append((s[0] + r, -h[0])) # Internal boundaries for i in range(1, N): deltaval = h[i] - h[i-1] deltas.append((s[i] - r, deltaval)) deltas.append((s[i] + r, -deltaval)) # At s[N], change is 0 - h[N-1] deltas.append((s[N] - r, -h[N-1])) deltas.append((s[N] + r, h[N-1])) # Sort deltas by position deltas.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Step 3 & 4: Integrate twice to get PDF, then once more for CDF # The double integral of a delta at pos with value v yields v max(0, x - pos) # Integrating this PDF once yields the piecewise-quadratic CDF: v max(0, x - pos)^2 / 2 cdfvalues = np.zeros(M + 1) for j in range(M + 1): x = shat[j] cdfval = 0.0 for pos, val in deltas: if pos <= x: cdfval += val (x - pos)2 / 2.0 cdfvalues[j] = cdfval # Step 5: Compute resampled weights # whats[i] = CDF(shat[i+1]) - CDF(shat[i]) whats = cdfvalues[1:] - cdfvalues[:-1] # Step 6: Evaluate loss # Lprop = sumi (1 / whati) max(0, stopgrad(whatsi) - whati)^2 # stopgrad is applied conceptually; gradients flow through whats to the NeRF, # but the proposal network receives gradients only through the explicit what term diff = np.maximum(0, whats - what) # Guard against division by zero in what whatsafe = np.maximum(what, 1e-8) loss = np.sum(diff2 / whatsafe) return loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Narrow Bins: Rasterizing the step function and performing convolution fails in the common case of extremely narrow histogram bins, necessitating the delta-function integration algorithm. Zero-Width Intervals: If s{i+1} - si = 0, the normalization step involves division by zero, so a small epsilon is added to the interval size. Zero Proposal Weights: If \hat{w}i = 0, the loss term involves division by zero, so a small epsilon is added to the proposal weights in the denominator. Strengths: Produces a smooth loss surface that is robust to aliasing when NeRF histogram bins are narrow or translate relative to the proposal. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Used for proposal supervision to train proposal networks to bound the scene geometry predicted by the NeRF without introducing aliasing. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Anti-Aliased Interlevel Loss was introduced in the Zip-NeRF paper. It builds on the proposal supervision approach from mip-NeRF 360. The key innovation is the use of a blurred, piecewise-linear representation of the NeRF histogram to enable smooth gradient flow during training, addressing the aliasing issues inherent in the piecewise constant comparison used in mip-NeRF 360. name: Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction
head: Isotropic scale contraction, Jacobian-based isotropic scale estimation
body: Isotropic Gaussian Scale Contraction is a technique for efficiently adapting the scale of isotropic Gaussians when a scene contraction function C(\mathbf{x}) is applied. It solves the problem of maintaining correct anti-aliasing properties in contracted coordinate spaces without the computational overhead of general multivariate Gaussian transformations. It sets itself apart from the standard mip-NeRF 360 approach by linearizing the contraction around each Gaussian center to derive an isotropic scale from the Jacobian determinant, rather than contracting a full covariance matrix. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of isotropic Gaussians defined by their means \mathbf{x}j and scales \sigmaj, and a scene contraction function C: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3. Output: The contracted means \mathbf{x}'j = C(\mathbf{x}j) and the contracted isotropic scales \sigma'j. Data Structures The method operates on scalar values for scale and 3D vectors for position. No complex covariance matrices are stored or manipulated. Steps 1. Contract Means: Evaluate the contraction function at the original Gaussian center: \mathbf{x}'j = C(\mathbf{x}j). 2. Compute Jacobian Determinant Factor: Calculate the scaling factor derived from the determinant of the Jacobian of the contraction function JC(\mathbf{x}j). For the specific contraction function used in Zip-NeRF, this factor has a closed-form solution: \text{scale\factor}j = \left| \det(JC(\mathbf{x}j)) \right|^{1/3} = \left( \frac{\sqrt[3]{2 \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|) - 1}}{\max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|)} \right)^2. Here, \|\mathbf{x}j\| is the Euclidean norm of the original mean \mathbf{x}j. 3. Update Scale: Multiply the original isotropic scale \sigmaj by the computed factor: \sigma'j = \sigmaj \times \text{scale\factor}j. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def isotropicgaussianscalecontraction(means: np.ndarray, scales: np.ndarray) -> tuple: """ Contracts isotropic Gaussians using the Zip-NeRF specific closed-form Jacobian determinant. Args: means: Array of shape (N, 3) containing Gaussian centers xj. scales: Array of shape (N,) containing isotropic scales sigmaj. Returns: contractedmeans: Array of shape (N, 3) containing C(xj). contractedscales: Array of shape (N,) containing sigma'j. """ # Step 1: Contract means # Contract means: xj' = C(xj). The exact form of C(x) is not provided in the sources, # but is evaluated per Gaussian. contractedmeans = means.copy() # Placeholder for C(xj) evaluation # Step 2: Compute the closed-form scale factor from the Jacobian determinant norms = np.linalg.norm(means, axis=1) maxnorm = np.maximum(1.0, norms) numerator = np.cbrt(2.0 maxnorm - 1.0) scalefactor = (numerator / maxnorm) 2 # Step 3: Update scales contractedscales = scales scalefactor return contractedmeans, contractedscales Parameters \|\mathbf{x}j\|: Euclidean norm of the Gaussian mean. \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|): Ensures stability for points near the origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Origin Singularity: The formula uses \max(1, \|\mathbf{x}j\|) in the denominator. If \|\mathbf{x}j\| < 1, the denominator is 1, avoiding division by zero. The numerator becomes \sqrt[3]{2(1)-1} = 1, so the scale factor is 1^2/1^2 = 1. This implies no scale change for points within the unit sphere, which is consistent with many contraction functions that leave the central region uncontracted. Naive Multivariate Approach: Contracting the scale by treating the Gaussian as a full multivariate Gaussian with covariance \sigma^2 I and then identifying the isotropic Gaussian with the same generalized variance is significantly more expensive. This method avoids that by using the linearized Jacobian approximation. Time and Memory Complexity The method is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. It requires only vector norm calculations and scalar multiplications, making it significantly less computationally expensive than the multivariate Gaussian contraction approach used in mip-NeRF 360. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: High computational efficiency; avoids matrix operations; closed-form solution for the specific Zip-NeRF contraction. Limitations: It is an approximation based on linearization. It assumes the contraction function is locally linear around \mathbf{x}j. For very large Gaussians or highly non-linear contractions, this approximation may introduce errors. It is specific to isotropic Gaussians. When to Use Use this method when rendering with isotropic Gaussians in a scene that has been contracted (e.g., for distant scene content allocation) and computational efficiency is a priority. It is particularly suitable for Zip-NeRF and similar architectures that use multisampled isotropic Gaussians. This technique was introduced in Zip-NeRF. It was developed to address the need for efficient anti-aliasing in neural radiance fields that use scene contraction to allocate model capacity proportional to disparity. The method improves upon the mip-NeRF 360 approach by reducing the computational cost of scale contraction while maintaining the necessary anti-aliasing properties. name: Google Immersive View NeRF
head: Indoor NeRF Reconstruction, NeRF Reconstruction for Immersive View
body: A method for 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis that distills a dense collection of indoor photos into a neural field to render photorealistic views from viewpoints not present in the original collection, specifically optimized for Google Maps Immersive View. It distinguishes itself by integrating low-dimensional generative latent optimization (GLO) vectors and metadata-derived exposure conditioning into the radiance network, resolving cloudy geometry artifacts caused by lighting changes without sacrificing interpretability. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup as its architectural base. Inputs: 1. Capture Data: A dense collection of DSLR photographs of an indoor venue, captured within a short timeframe. 2. Metadata: Photo metadata including ISO, aperture, and white balance settings. 3. Camera Parameters: Extrinsic (position, orientation) and intrinsic (focal length) parameters solved via Structure-from-Motion (SfM). Outputs: 1. NeRF Model: A trained neural radiance field specific to the location. 2. Immersive Video: 360° rendered video along a smoothed flight path. The method utilizes the standard Mip-NeRF 360 architecture. The key structural modification is in the Radiance Network inputs: Positional/Orientation Encodings: Standard positional and angular encodings for the 3D point and view direction. GLO Vectors: A set of learned real-valued latent vectors, one per input image, appended to the radiance network inputs. Exposure Conditioning: Scalar or vector values derived directly from photo metadata (ISO, etc.), appended to the radiance network inputs. 1. Capture: Photograph the venue using DSLR cameras. Ensure every surface is observed from multiple directions. Keep camera properties (white balance, aperture) fixed. Freeze the scene (no movement, stable lighting). 2. Privacy Processing: Automatically scan uploaded photos and blur personally identifiable content. 3. Structure-from-Motion (SfM): Run an SfM pipeline to solve for each photo's camera parameters (position, orientation, focal length). Associate each pixel with a 3D point and direction. 4. Scale Calibration: Capture pairs of images exactly 3 meters apart during the session. Use this known distance to scale the generated 3D model for consistent video velocity. 5. Model Initialization: Initialize a new NeRF model from scratch for the location, using Mip-NeRF 360 as the base architecture. 6. Latent Vector Assignment: Assign a unique low-dimensional generative latent optimization (GLO) vector to each input image. These vectors are learned during training. 7. Exposure Conditioning Extraction: Extract exposure values from the photo metadata for each image. 8. Radiance Network Input Construction: For each ray sampled during training, construct the input vector for the radiance network comprising: Standard positional/orientation encodings. The GLO vector corresponding to the source image of the ray. The exposure conditioning value corresponding to the source image. 9. Training: Train the model from scratch using the Mip-NeRF 360 optimization loop, minimizing rendering loss against the input photos. 10. Video Rendering: Define a flight path by interpolating keyframe positions computed during SfM. Render 360° videos by ray casting through a virtual spherical camera along this path. The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the GLO vector integration or exposure conditioning. The radiance network function \mathcal{F} can be conceptually described as: (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, \mathbf{z}i, \mathbf{e}i) Where: \mathbf{x} is the 3D position. \mathbf{d} is the view direction. \mathbf{z}i is the GLO vector for image i. \mathbf{e}i is the exposure conditioning for image i. \sigma is the density. \mathbf{c} is the color. Capture Timeframe: < 1 hour. Calibration Distance: 3 meters between image pairs. Hardware: TPUs or GPUs. Lighting Changes: If lighting changes during capture, reconstruction quality suffers significantly. Cloudy Geometry: Without GLO vectors or exposure conditioning, casual NeRF captures exhibit "cloudy geometry" artifacts when handling lighting variations. Scene Movement: The scene must be frozen in time; any movement degrades reconstruction. Privacy Processing: The system automatically scans and blurs personally identifiable content to respect privacy. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def trainimmersivenerf(photos, metadata, sfmcameras): """ Trains a NeRF model for Immersive View using GLO and Exposure conditioning. Args: photos: List of image arrays. metadata: List of metadata dicts containing 'iso', 'aperture', etc. sfmcameras: Dict mapping image index to camera parameters (position, orientation, focallength). Returns: trainedmodel: The trained NeRF model. glovectors: Learned latent vectors for each image. """ # 1. Privacy Processing: Automatically scan and blur personally identifiable content blurredphotos = [applyprivacymask(photo) for photo in photos] numimages = len(blurredphotos) # 2. Model Initialization: Base architecture follows Mip-NeRF 360 details from parent article [3426-mip-nerf-360-optimization-setup.md] model = initializemipnerf360base() # 3. Auxiliary Inputs # GLO vectors initialized to zero, learned during training glovectors = torch.zeros(numimages, 16) # Exposure values extracted directly from metadata exposurevalues = torch.tensor([meta.get('iso', 100) for meta in metadata], dtype=torch.float32) # 4. Scale Calibration: SfM results are scaled using the known 3-meter distance between image pairs scalefactor = computescalefactor(sfmcameras, calibrationdistance=3.0) sfmcameras = scalesfmresults(sfmcameras, scalefactor) # 5. Training Loop optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(model.parameters()) + [glovectors], lr=1e-3) maxepochs = 500000 # Not given in the sources. for epoch in range(maxepochs): for i in range(numimages): # Sample rays through each pixel of the source image rays = sampleraysfromimage(blurredphotos[i], sfmcameras[i]) glovec = glovectors[i] exposureval = exposurevalues[i] # Forward pass: radiance network receives position, direction, glovec, exposureval density, color = renderrays(model, rays, glovec, exposureval) # Compute loss against the source image loss = computerenderingloss(color, blurredphotos[i]) # Backpropagate gradients optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return model, glovectors def renderimmersivevideo(model, keyframeindices, sfmcameras, videolengthframes): """ Renders a 360 video by interpolating keyframes. """ # 1. Define Flight Path: Interpolate camera positions and orientations from SfM results of keyframes path = interpolatepath([sfmcameras[i] for i in keyframeindices], videolengthframes) # 2. Render Frames frames = [] for camera in path: # Ray cast through virtual spherical camera rays = castsphericalrays(camera) # For novel view video rendering, GLO and exposure are not tied to a specific source image. # The sources do not specify how auxiliary inputs are handled for novel views., color = renderrays(model, rays, glovec=None, exposureval=None) frames.append(color) return frames def applyprivacymask(image): """Automatically scans and blurs personally identifiable content.""" # Exact algorithm not specified in sources. Applies privacy mask conceptually. return image def initializemipnerf360base(): """Returns the base Mip-NeRF 360 neural network architecture.""" # Assumes standard implementation from parent article [3426-mip-nerf-360-optimization-setup.md] return {} def computescalefactor(cameras, calibrationdistance): """Computes scale factor based on known distance between image pairs.""" # Uses metric scale recovery from SfM. Exact formula not specified. return 1.0 def scalesfmresults(cameras, scalefactor): """Applies scalefactor to camera positions.""" for cam in cameras.values(): cam['position'] = scalefactor return cameras def sampleraysfromimage(image, camera): """Casts rays through each pixel using camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters.""" # Returns list of ray origins and directions return [] def renderrays(model, rays, glovec, exposureval): """Samples points along rays, queries radiance network with (x, d, glovec, exposureval).""" # Returns density (sigma) and color (c) return torch.zeros(rays.shape), torch.zeros(rays.shape) def computerenderingloss(rendered, target): """Computes MSE between rendered colors and target images.""" return torch.mean((rendered - target) 2) def interpolatepath(keyframes, numframes): """Linearly interpolates camera positions and orientations between keyframes.""" # Returns list of interpolated camera parameters return [] def castsphericalrays(camera): """Casts rays through a virtual spherical camera centered at camera position.""" # Returns ray origins and directions return [] Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive, as the method uses Mip-NeRF 360 which is noted as "more computationally intensive" than Nvidia's Instant NGP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing GLO vectors for each image and the full Mip-NeRF 360 network weights. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Produces fewer artifacts and higher reconstruction quality than Instant NGP. Strengths: Handles lighting changes and varying exposure without cloudy geometry artifacts. Provides interpretable exposure control (ISO/brightness) at inference time. Consistent quality across diverse indoor venues (dimly-lit bars to cafes). Limitations: Requires strict capture constraints (frozen scene, fixed camera properties). High computational cost compared to faster alternatives like Instant NGP. GLO vectors are uninterpretable latent codes, though they solve the artifact problem. The method was developed by Google to power the "Immersive View" feature in Google Maps, which provides indoor views of restaurants, cafes, and other venues. It was described in a blog post in June 2023. The work builds on Alphabet's recent advances in neural radiance fields, specifically incorporating techniques from "NeRF in the Wild" (GLO vectors) and "Block-NeRF" (exposure conditioning). It was chosen over Instant NGP for its superior reconstruction quality despite higher compute requirements. Reconstructing Indoor Spaces with NeRF, https://ai.googleblog.com/2023/06/reconstructing-indoor-spaces-with-nerf.html, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields
head: LocalRF
body: Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields (LocalRF) is a view synthesis method that jointly optimizes camera poses and multiple overlapping local radiance fields from a single long monocular video, avoiding Structure-from-Motion and scaling to unbounded scenes with fixed memory. It differs from global optimization approaches by dynamically allocating new local fields as the camera trajectory extends, preventing global failure from pose outliers and maintaining high resolution around the camera path. Unlike Mega-NeRF, it does not require pre-partitioned space, and unlike Mip-NeRF 360, it jointly estimates poses rather than relying on pre-computed ones. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of P monocular video frames \{\mathbf{C}k\}{k=1}^P with unknown camera poses. Output: A set of M local radiance fields \{\Thetaj\}{j=1}^M and their corresponding camera poses \{[R|t]k\}{k=1}^P. Data Structures Camera Pose: Each pose [R|t]k is a continuous 6D representation of rotation and translation. Local Radiance Field: Each field \Thetaj is implemented using TensoRF, a factorized 4D tensor representation mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} to volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}. Resolution: TensoRF resolution starts at 64^3 and upsamples to 640^3 during refinement. Supervision Subset: For each local field, the supervision set includes frames active during the field's lifetime plus the preceding 30 frames for overlap. Formulas Scene Contraction: Maps points \mathbf{x} to [-2, 2] space using L-infinity norm to handle unbounded scenes: \text{contract}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{x}\|\infty \leq 1 \\ \left (2 - \frac {1}{\| \mathbf{x} \|{\infty }}\right) \left (\frac {\mathbf{x} }{\| \mathbf{x} \|{\infty }}\right) & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} Local Field Query: The j-th radiance field is centered at translation tj: (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai) = \text{RF}{\Thetaj}(\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{t}j) Volume Rendering: Renders color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) along ray \mathbf{r} with N samples: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti(1-\text{exp}(-\sigmai\deltai))\mathbf{c}i, \quad Ti = \text{exp}\left (-\sum{j=1}^{i-1}\sigmaj\deltaj\right) where \deltai is the distance between sample points. Photometric Loss:: \mathcal{L} = \left \| \hat {\mathbf {C}}(\mathbf {r}) - \mathbf {C}(\mathbf {r}) \right \|{2}^{2} Depth Rendering:: \hat {\mathbf {D}}(\mathbf {r}) = \sum {i=1}^{N} Ti(1-\text {exp}(-\sigma i\delta i))di where di is distance to ray origin. Depth Normalization: For a depth map \mathbf{D} with M samples, compute shift t(\mathbf{D}) and scale s(\mathbf{D}): t(\mathbf{D}) = \text{median}(\mathbf{D}), \quad s(\mathbf{D}) = \frac {1}{M} \sum{1}^{M} |\mathbf{D} - t(\mathbf{D})| Normalized depth: \mathbf{D}^ = (\mathbf{D} - t(\mathbf{D}))/s(\mathbf{D}). Depth Loss:: \mathcal{L}d = \left | {\hat {\mathbf {D}}^} - {\mathbf {D}^}\right | Rendered Flow: Computes optical flow \hat{\mathcal{F}}{k\rightarrow k+1} between consecutive frames using relative pose [R|t]{k\rightarrow k+1} = [R|t]k^{-1}[R|t]{k+1}, projection \Pi, and unprojection \Pi^{-1}: \hat {\mathcal {F}}{k\rightarrow k+1} = (u,v) - \Pi \left ([R|t]{k\rightarrow k+1}\Pi ^{-1}(u,v,\hat {D})\right) Flow Loss:: \mathcal{L}f = \left \| \hat {\mathcal {F}}{k\rightarrow k+1} + \mathcal {F}{k\rightarrow k+1} \right \|1 where \mathcal{F}{k\rightarrow k+1} is RAFT-estimated flow. Parameters Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.99. Learning Rates: Initial rotation LR 5 \cdot 10^{-3}, translation LR 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. Loss Weights: Flow loss weight 1, Depth loss weight 0.1. Frame Addition: Every 100 iterations. Refinement: 600 iterations per frame addition step. Overlap: Preceding 30 frames included in local supervision. Batch Size: 16 images for depth normalization statistics. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize optimization with the first 5 frames. Set their poses [R|t]k to identity. Initialize the first TensoRF model \Theta1 with resolution 64^3 centered at t1 = \mathbf{0}. 2. Iterative Frame Addition: For k = 6 to P: a. Append Frame: Add frame k to the supervision set. b. Pose Initialization: Initialize the new pose [R|t]k using the previous pose [R|t]{k-1} to enforce locality prior: [R|t]k \leftarrow [R|t]{k-1} c. Joint Optimization: Jointly optimize the new pose [R|t]k and the current radiance field parameters \Thetaj using the photometric, depth, and flow losses for 100 iterations. 3. Boundary Check: Monitor the estimated camera pose relative to the boundary of the high-resolution uncontracted space of the current local radiance field. Check if \|\mathbf{t}p - \mathbf{t}j\|\infty \geq 1, where \mathbf{t}p is the last registered frame's translation and \mathbf{t}j is the current field's center. 4. Refinement: If the boundary is reached: a. Stop adding frames. b. Refine the current TensoRF \Thetaj and camera poses for 600 iterations. c. Apply exponential decay to loss weights towards 0.1 factor. d. Upsample TensoRF resolution up to 640^3. 5. Allocation: If the pose exceeds the boundary: a. Allocate a new TensoRF radiance field \Theta{j+1} centered at the last estimated pose \mathbf{t}p. b. Freeze the previous field \Thetaj (disable supervision). c. Clear unneeded supervising frames from memory. d. Increment j. 6. Repeat: Repeat steps 2-5 until all input frames are registered. 7. Blending: At inference, blend rendered colors \hat{\mathbf{C}}j(\mathbf{r}) of all overlapping radiance fields using per-frame linear blending weights within the overlap region. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localrfoptimization(frames, P): # Helper: L-infinity norm def norminf(v): return max(abs(v)) # Helper: Identity pose (6D rotation + zero translation) def IdentityPose(): return {'R': [1,0,0,0,1,0], 't': [0,0,0]} # Helper: TensoRF representation class TensoRF: def init(self, resolution, center): self.resolution = resolution self.center = center self.frozen = False def query(self, x): # Maps contracted x - center to (sigma, c) return RFmodel(self, x - self.center) def upsample(self, newres): self.resolution = newres def freeze(self): self.frozen = True # Helper: Joint optimization step using Adam def optimize(poses, field, supervisionframes, iterations): for in range(iterations): # Compute losses: photometric, depth, flow # Update poses and field parameters using Adam pass # Initialization poses = [IdentityPose() for in range(P)] fields = [] currentfieldidx = 0 # Initialize first field field = TensoRF(resolution=64, center=[0,0,0]) fields.append(field) # Supervision set includes first 5 frames supervisionframes = frames[:5] # Initial optimization of first 5 frames optimize(poses[:5], field, supervisionframes, iterations=500) for k in range(5, P): # Append frame supervisionframes.append(frames[k]) # Initialize new pose from previous poses[k] = {'R': poses[k-1]['R'], 't': poses[k-1]['t']} # Joint optimization for 100 iterations optimize(poses[:k+1], field, supervisionframes, iterations=100) # Check boundary lastpose = poses[k] currentcenter = field.center if norminf([lastpose['t'][i] - currentcenter[i] for i in range(3)]) >= 1.0: # Refine for 600 iterations optimize(poses[:k+1], field, supervisionframes, iterations=600) # Upsample to 640^3 field.upsample(640) # Allocate new field at last pose newfield = TensoRF(resolution=64, center=lastpose['t']) fields.append(newfield) currentfieldidx += 1 # Freeze previous field field.freeze() # Clear unneeded frames from memory # Keep overlap frames (preceding 30) # Switch to new field for next iterations field = newfield return fields, poses Subtopics TensoRF Representation: A factorized 4D tensor representation used as the base for LocalRF, offering quality and reasonable training speed. Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup: The parent method that LocalRF builds upon, specifically regarding contraction and unbounded scene handling, but LocalRF differs by jointly estimating poses. Time Complexity: Optimization takes 30-40 hours for 1000 frames on a single NVIDIA TITAN RTX. Memory Complexity: Fixed memory usage due to dynamic allocation and freezing of previous fields, allowing scaling to arbitrarily long videos. Performance (Tanks and Temples): PSNR 22.40, SSIM 0.667, LPIPS 0.494. Performance (Self-Calibrated): PSNR 22.85, SSIM 0.676, LPIPS 0.708. Strengths: Robust to pose outliers, handles long unbounded scenes, no SfM required. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of overlap and refinement steps; slower than methods with known poses. LocalRF was introduced in 2023 by Andreas et al.. It addresses the limitations of global radiance field optimization, which fails on long videos due to misestimation impact and fixed capacity blur. It builds on TensoRF and Mip-NeRF 360's contraction. Progressively Optimized Local Radiance Fields for Robust View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01587, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mip-NeRF RGB-D Volume Rendering and Loss
head: Mip-NeRF RGB-D Loss, RGB-D Optimization in Mip-NeRF
body: This method optimizes a neural radiance field using RGB-D data by minimizing a combined geometric and photometric loss. It differs from standard NeRF by incorporating depth variance into the geometric loss to handle uncertainty and using integrated positional encoding for conical frustums to address aliasing. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup by combining photometric and variance-normalized geometric losses, and constrains ray sampling bounds using depth uncertainty. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of RGB-D frames, each containing color image C, depth map D, and camera pose. Network parameters \theta. Outputs: Optimized network weights \theta, rendered color \hat{C}(r), and rendered depth \hat{D}(r) for each ray r. Data Structures Network Architecture: A single MLP with 4 hidden layers, each of feature size 256. Layer 1-2: Hidden layers. Layer 3: Hidden layer with a skip connection from the input position. Layer 4: Hidden layer. Viewing direction is concatenated to the output of Layer 3 before entering Layer 4. Output: Color c and volume density \tau. Positional Encoding: Position: Integrated positional encoding applied to the conical frustum (16 frequency bands). Direction: Standard positional encoding with frequency 4 applied to viewing directions. Volume Rendering Formulas For a ray r(t) = o + td with near bound tn and far bound tf: 1. Accumulated Transmittance: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \tau(r(s)) ds\right) Discretized with N samples: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \tauj \deltaj\right) where \tauj is volume density, \deltaj is segment length, and T1 = 1. 2. Discrete Color Estimate: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\taui \deltai)) ci where ci is the predicted color at sample i. 3. Discrete Depth Estimate: \hat{D}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\taui \deltai)) ti where ti is the sample position. 4. Depth Variance: \hat{D}{var}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\taui \deltai)) (\hat{D}(r) - ti)^2 This represents the variance of the depth distribution along the ray. Loss Function The total loss combines geometric loss lg and photometric loss lp with a scale factor \lambdap: \min\theta (lg + \lambdap lp) 1. Photometric Loss (lp): L1-norm between predicted and ground truth color: lp = \sum{r \in R} |\hat{C}(r) - C(r)| 2. Geometric Loss (lg): Absolute difference between predicted and true depth, normalized by depth variance: lg = \sum{r \in R} \frac{|\hat{D}(r) - D(r)|}{\sqrt{\hat{D}{var}(r)}} Normalization discourages weights with high uncertainty. Parameters \lambdap = 100 (default photometric scale factor). Near/Far bounds: tn = D - \alphan and tf = D + \alphaf, where D is the depth value and \alphan, \alphaf are empirically chosen based on depth uncertainty. Standard deviation for Gaussian sampling: 0.3. Pseudocode Unverified code. exp(-taui deltai)) W = T (1.0 - np.exp(-taudelta)) return T, W def renderray(positions, direction, networkforward, depthmap): """ Render a single ray using Mip-NeRF RGB-D volume rendering. positions: array of shape (N,) sample positions along the ray, sorted direction: array of shape (3,) viewing direction networkforward: function that takes (positions, directions) -> (color, density) depthmap: scalar ground truth depth D for the ray origin Returns: renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvariance """ D = depthmap alphan = 0.1 # Empirical value based on depth uncertainty alphaf = 0.1 # Empirical value based on depth uncertainty tn = D - alphan tf = D + alphaf N = len(positions) # Compute segment lengths: delta0 = t0 - tn, deltai = ti - t{i-1} deltas = np.zeros(N) deltas[0] = positions[0] - tn deltas[1:] = np.diff(positions) # Query network with integrated PE for positions and standard PE for direction colors, densities = networkforward(positions, direction) # Compute Transmittance and Weights T, W = computetransmittanceandweights(densities, deltas) # Compute Rendered Color renderedcolor = np.sum(W colors, axis=0) # Compute Rendered Depth rendereddepth = np.sum(W positions) # Compute Depth Variance depthvariance = np.sum(W (rendereddepth - positions)2) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvariance def computeloss(renderedcolor, rendereddepth, depthvariance, gtcolor, gtdepth): """ Compute Mip-NeRF RGB-D loss. """ # Photometric Loss (L1) lp = np.sum(np.abs(renderedcolor - gtcolor)) # Geometric Loss (Normalized L1) # Numerical stability guard to prevent division by zero epsilon = 1e-6 lg = np.sum(np.abs(rendereddepth - gtdepth) / (np.sqrt(depthvariance) + epsilon)) # Total Loss lambdap = 100.0 totalloss = lg + lambdap lp return totalloss, lg, lp Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: Depth variance \hat{D}{var}(r) can be zero if all samples are at the same depth or if transmittance is zero. A numerical stability guard (e.g., adding a small epsilon to the denominator) is required during implementation. Depth Uncertainty: The choice of \alphan and \alphaf significantly impacts the sampling bounds. Precision: The exponential terms in transmittance and weights can suffer from underflow or overflow. Stable log-space computations are recommended for extreme cases. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples N per ray and the number of rays. The reduced network size (4 layers, 256 features) yields faster training and prediction compared to original NeRF. Memory Complexity: Lower than original NeRF due to the reduced network size. Performance: Adaptive sampling performs best among proposed sampling strategies, improving underlying geometry compared to NeRF. Strengths: Faster training and prediction, better geometry estimation with RGB-D data, handles aliasing via integrated positional encoding. Limitations: Requires depth data. Performance depends on accurate depth uncertainty estimation for bounds. When to Use: When RGB-D data is available and faster training is desired without significantly compromising novel view quality. When Not to Use: When only RGB data is available, or when depth uncertainty is poorly estimated. Origin: Proposed in "Mip-NeRF RGB-D: Depth Assisted Fast Neural Radiance Fields". History: Builds on Mip-NeRF's integrated positional encoding and NeRF's volume rendering framework. It combines photometric and variance-normalized geometric losses, and constrains ray sampling bounds using depth uncertainty to improve geometry and speed. Usage: Used in scenarios requiring fast neural radiance field optimization with depth assistance. name: Scale-Dependent Downweighting for Grid Interpolation
head: Gaussian CDF Downweighting, Interpolation Weighting
body: Scale-Dependent Downweighting is a technique to anti-alias trilinear interpolation in neural radiance fields by downweighting features interpolated from grid cells that are small relative to the sampling Gaussian's spread, preventing aliasing artifacts from high-frequency content. Unlike naive trilinear interpolation which causes aliasing at high frequencies, this method uses the Gaussian CDF to weight samples, similar to Mip-NeRF's IPE features but applied to grid-based representations. Inputs: A set of multisampled isotropic Gaussians, each defined by a mean coordinate \mathbf{x}j and standard deviation \sigmaj. A set of feature grids \{V\ell\} at different resolution levels \ell, where each grid has a linear size (resolution) n\ell. Outputs: A concatenated feature vector provided as input to the subsequent MLP, consisting of downweighted interpolated features \{\mathbf{f}\ell\} and featurized downweighting factors \{\omega{j,\ell}\}. Data Structures: V\ell: A 3D tensor (or hash grid) storing feature vectors of dimension c\ell. \mathbf{x}j: A 3D coordinate vector representing the mean of the j-th Gaussian. \sigmaj: A scalar representing the standard deviation of the j-th Gaussian. n\ell: A scalar representing the linear size (resolution) of grid level \ell. Parameters: n\ell: The linear size (resolution) of the grid at level \ell. Used to scale the coordinate \mathbf{x} before interpolation. \sigmaj: The standard deviation of the isotropic Gaussian for multisample j. Represents the spatial extent of the sample. Steps: 1. For each multisample j with mean \mathbf{x}j and standard deviation \sigmaj, and for each grid level \ell with linear size n\ell and feature grid V\ell: a. Compute the downweighting factor \omega{j,\ell} based on the fraction of the Gaussian's PDF inside the grid cell. The formula is: \omega{j,\ell} = \sqrt{\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{1}{8\sigmaj^2 n\ell^2}\right)} where \omega{j,\ell} \in [0, 1]. b. Scale the coordinate \mathbf{x}j by the grid's linear size n\ell to get \mathbf{x}'j = n\ell \cdot \mathbf{x}j. c. Perform trilinear interpolation on grid V\ell at coordinate \mathbf{x}'j to obtain the interpolated feature vector \mathbf{f}{j,\ell}. d. Compute the downweighted feature for this sample and level as \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell}. 2. Approximate the expected grid feature for level \ell by taking the mean over all multisamples j: \mathbf{f}\ell = \operatorname{mean}j\left( \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \operatorname{trilerp}(n\ell \cdot \mathbf{x}j; V\ell) \right) This approximation relies on the assumption that grid values are zero-mean and normally distributed due to weight decay, allowing the expected feature to be approximated as \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell} + (1 - \omega{j,\ell}) \cdot 0 = \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell}. 3. Concatenate the downweighted features \{\mathbf{f}\ell\} from all levels and the featurized versions of \{\omega{j,\ell}\} to form the input for the subsequent MLP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def scaledependentdownweighting(xmeans, sigmas, grids, gridsizes, featuredim): """ Compute scale-dependent downweighted features for grid interpolation. Args: xmeans: Array of shape (N, 3) containing mean coordinates for N multisamples. sigmas: Array of shape (N,) containing standard deviations for N multisamples. grids: List of 3D arrays Vl for each level l. gridsizes: List of scalars nl for each level l. featuredim: Integer dimensionality of the feature vectors stored in the grids. Returns: finalinput: Concatenated feature vector for the MLP input. """ N = len(xmeans) numlevels = len(grids) alllevelfeatures = [] allweightscalars = [] for l in range(numlevels): Vl = grids[l] nl = gridsizes[l] downweightedfeaturessum = np.zeros(featuredim) count = 0 for j in range(N): xj = xmeans[j] sigmaj = sigmas[j] # Step 1a: Compute downweighting factor arg = 1.0 / (8.0 (sigmaj 2) (nl 2)) omega = math.sqrt(math.erf(arg)) # Step 1b & 1c: Scale coordinate and interpolate scaledx = nl xj fjl = trilinearinterpolation(scaledx, Vl) # Step 1d: Downweight downweightedf = omega fjl # Accumulate for mean downweightedfeaturessum += downweightedf count += 1 # Step 2: Mean over samples if count > 0: fl = downweightedfeaturessum / count else: fl = np.zeros(featuredim) alllevelfeatures.append(fl) # Step 3: Featurize weights # The source mentions concatenating "featurized versions of {ωj,ℓ}" but does not specify the exact transformation. # We concatenate the scalar omega for each sample as a direct representation. weightvec = np.array([math.sqrt(math.erf(1.0 / (8.0 (sigmas[k] 2) (nl 2)))) for k in range(N)]) allweightscalars.append(weightvec) # Concatenate all level features concatenatedfeatures = np.concatenate(alllevelfeatures) # Concatenate weight scalars concatenatedweights = np.concatenate(allweightscalars) finalinput = np.concatenate([concatenatedfeatures, concatenatedweights]) return finalinput def trilinearinterpolation(coord, grid): """ Standard trilinear interpolation. coord: (3,) array, scaled coordinates. grid: 3D array. """ x, y, z = coord ix, iy, iz = int(math.floor(x)), int(math.floor(y)), int(math.floor(z)) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz Dx, Dy, Dz = grid.shape # Clamp indices to valid range [0, D-2] for interpolation ix = np.clip(ix, 0, Dx - 2) iy = np.clip(iy, 0, Dy - 2) iz = np.clip(iz, 0, Dz - 2) c000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] c100 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz] c010 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz] c110 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz] c001 = grid[ix, iy, iz+1] c101 = grid[ix+1, iy, iz+1] c011 = grid[ix, iy+1, iz+1] c111 = grid[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] c00 = c000 (1-fx) + c100 fx c01 = c001 (1-fx) + c101 fx c10 = c010 (1-fx) + c110 fx c11 = c011 (1-fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1-fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1-fy) + c11 fy result = c0 (1-fz) + c1 fz return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the Gaussian is much larger than the grid cell, the interpolated feature is unreliable. The downweighting factor \omega approaches 0, effectively discarding this unreliable sample. The approximation relies on the assumption that grid values are zero-mean and normally distributed due to weight decay. If this assumption does not hold, the approximation \omega{j,\ell} \cdot \mathbf{f}{j,\ell} may be inaccurate. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively reduces spatial aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency content when using multisampling with trilinear interpolation. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of zero-mean, normally distributed grid values, which is encouraged by weight decay but may not always be perfectly met. When to use: When training grid-based neural radiance fields (like iNGP or Zip-NeRF) with multisampling to prevent aliasing artifacts. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This technique is described in the context of Zip-NeRF, an anti-aliased grid-based neural radiance field method. It is inspired by Mip-NeRF's IPE features but adapted for grid-based representations. name: S-NeRF Training Configuration
head: S-NeRF Optimization Setup, S-NeRF Hyperparameters
body: S-NeRF defines the specific hyperparameters, network architectures, and training loops required to optimize Neural Radiance Fields for dynamic street scenes using LiDAR and RGB data. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by separating the optimization of foreground moving vehicles from the static background, applying distinct loss weights, sampling strategies, and confidence-guided learning to handle depth outliers and motion. This configuration builds on Mip-NeRF Optimization and Activation Details by adopting its coarse-fine network sharing and log-linear scheduling while introducing scene-specific parameters for large-scale urban environments. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Sparse LiDAR point clouds from consecutive frames (t-1, t, t+1), RGB images, and camera poses. Outputs: Optimized MLP weights for foreground vehicles and background scenes, producing novel view RGB and depth renders. Data Structures The method uses two distinct MLP architectures depending on the scene component: 1. Foreground Vehicle MLP: 4 layers, 256 hidden units per layer. 2. Background Scene MLPs: Density MLP: 8 layers, 1024 hidden units per layer. Color MLP: 3 layers, 128 hidden units per layer. Note: The background coarse and fine networks share parameters as per mip-NeRF conventions. Training Procedure The training is split into two independent phases: foreground vehicle optimization and background scene optimization. 1. Foreground Vehicle Training: Sampling: 64 samples per ray. Iterations: 30,000 iterations. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4} (constant). Batch Size: 1024. Loss Weights: Depth loss weight \lambda1 = 1, Smoothness loss weight \lambda2 = 0.15. Duration: ~2 hours per vehicle on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. 2. Background Scene Training: Scene Parameterization: Radius r = 3. Confidence Threshold: \tau = 20\% for filtering outliers. Sampling: 128 samples per ray on a log scale. Iterations: 100,000 iterations. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate Schedule: Log-linear decay from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-6} with a warm-up phase of 2,500 iterations. Batch Size: 2048. Loss Weights: Depth loss weight \lambda1 = 0.2, Smoothness loss weight \lambda2 = 0.01. Duration: ~17 hours per scene (250 images, 1280×1920) on two NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs. Confidence Map Computation To reduce the influence of depth outliers (e.g., moving objects), S-NeRF computes geometry and projection confidence maps: 1. Reprojection: Project 3D LiDAR points from frames t-1 and t+1 to frame t using the displacement \Delta P between frames. 2. Consistency Check: Use optical flow and depth projection to identify and remove outliers from moving objects. 3. Component Calculation: Compute individual confidence maps for Depth, Flow, RGB, SSIM, and VGG features. 4. Aggregation: Combine these components via learnable aggregation to produce final confidence maps used in the loss function. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainsnerfforeground(vehicledata, iterations=30000, lr=5e-4): """ Optimizes the MLP for a single foreground vehicle. """ model = MLP(layers=4, hiddenunits=256) optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr) for step in range(iterations): # Sample 64 points per ray rays = samplerays(vehicledata, numsamples=64) # Render RGB and Depth rgbpred, depthpred = model.render(rays) rgbgt, depthgt = vehicledata.getgroundtruth(rays) # Compute losses # lambda1 = 1, lambda2 = 0.15 lossdepth = lambda1 L1Loss(depthpred, depthgt) losssmooth = lambda2 SmoothnessLoss(depthpred) lossrgb = L1Loss(rgbpred, rgbgt) totalloss = lossrgb + lossdepth + losssmooth optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return model def trainsnerfbackground(scenedata, iterations=100000, lrstart=5e-4, lrend=5e-6, warmup=2500): """ Optimizes the background street scene. """ # Coarse and Fine networks share parameters model = SharedMLP(densitylayers=8, densityhidden=1024, colorlayers=3, colorhidden=128) optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lrstart) radius = 3 tau = 0.20 # 20% confidence threshold for step in range(iterations): # Learning rate schedule: log-linear decay with warmup if step < warmup: lr = lrstart (step / warmup) else: # Log-linear decay approximation progress = (step - warmup) / (iterations - warmup) lr = lrstart (lrend / lrstart) progress optimizer.paramgroups[0]['lr'] = lr # Sample 128 points per ray on log scale rays = samplerays(scenedata, numsamples=128, logscale=True) # Compute confidence maps to filter outliers confidencemaps = computeconfidencemaps(scenedata, rays, tau) # Render with confidence weighting rgbpred, depthpred = model.render(rays, confidence=confidencemaps) rgbgt, depthgt = scenedata.getgroundtruth(rays) # lambda1 = 0.2, lambda2 = 0.01 lossdepth = 0.2 L1Loss(depthpred, depthgt) losssmooth = 0.01 SmoothnessLoss(depthpred) lossrgb = L1Loss(rgbpred, rgbgt) totalloss = lossrgb + lossdepth + losssmooth optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return model def computeconfidencemaps(scenedata, rays, tau): """ Computes geometry and projection confidence maps. """ # 1. Reprojection from t-1 and t+1 pointstminus1 = scenedata.getlidarpoints(t-1) pointstplus1 = scenedata.getlidarpoints(t+1) displacementtminus1 = getdisplacement(pointstminus1, scenedata.getpose(t)) displacementtplus1 = getdisplacement(pointstplus1, scenedata.getpose(t)) projectedtminus1 = projecttoframe(pointstminus1, displacementtminus1) projectedtplus1 = projecttoframe(pointstplus1, displacementtplus1) # 2. Consistency check using optical flow and depth flowconf = checkflowconsistency(scenedata, rays) depthconf = checkdepthconsistency(projectedtminus1, projectedtplus1, rays) # 3. Photometric and feature consistency rgbconf = computergbconsistency(scenedata, rays) ssimconf = computessimconsistency(scenedata, rays) vggconf = computevggconsistency(scenedata, rays) # 4. Learnable aggregation confidence = aggregateconfidences(depthconf, flowconf, rgbconf, ssimconf, vggconf) return confidence This variant distinguishes inlier and outlier camera poses by using a detached color network that omits the viewing direction as input, minimizing the impact of shape-radiance ambiguities that cause high PSNR for wrong poses. It solves the issue where outliers might have higher PSNR than inliers due to shape-radiance ambiguity, which traditional rendering metrics fail to detect. Unlike previous works using rendering metrics directly, this approach uses a detached network to provide reliable confidence scores for pose filtering. This method optimizes the positions of sampling points along camera rays to reduce rendering artifacts and produce more detailed images in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Unlike canonical NeRF, which places sampling points at fixed regular intervals regardless of scene content, this approach dynamically concentrates sampling points in critical areas, particularly around object surfaces, by using an MLP-Mixer-based architecture for end-to-end optimization. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive. Foreground vehicles take ~2 hours per vehicle on a single RTX 3090. Background scenes take ~17 hours per scene (250 images, 1280×1920) on two RTX 3090 GPUs. Memory Complexity: The model contains 8.76M learnable parameters, which is comparable to other state-of-the-art methods (8.7–9.9M). Performance: On the Waymo dataset, S-NeRF achieves a PSNR of 23.60 and SSIM of 0.743, outperforming Mip-NeRF (16.89 PSNR) and Mip-NeRF 360 (22.10 PSNR). Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes and large-scale urban environments effectively by separating foreground and background optimization. The confidence-guided learning reduces the impact of LiDAR outliers. Limitations: Training time is significantly longer than methods that do not require coarse rendering supervision (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360 is faster). Requires synchronized LiDAR and RGB data. S-NeRF was introduced in the paper "S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views" published at ICLR 2023. The method addresses the challenges of reconstructing large-scale, dynamic street scenes using sparse LiDAR and RGB data. It builds upon the mip-NeRF framework to handle multi-scale representations and introduces specific training configurations to manage the complexity of urban environments, including moving vehicles and static backgrounds. name: Confidence Updating with Detached Color Network
head: Cn-based confidence scoring, Color Network w/o View Direction, Detached Color Network for Confidence, Isolated Color Network, PSNR-based confidence update
body: This method distinguishes inlier and outlier camera poses by using a detached color network that omits the viewing direction as input, minimizing the impact of shape-radiance ambiguities that cause high PSNR for wrong poses. It solves the issue where outliers might have higher PSNR than inliers due to shape-radiance ambiguity, which traditional rendering metrics fail to detect. Unlike previous works using rendering metrics directly, this approach uses a detached network to provide reliable confidence scores for pose filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images V, initial camera poses, a scene graph, and a primary NeRF model containing a geometry SDF f and a traditional color network Co. Outputs: Updated confidence scores CS(vi) for each view vi \in V, used to guide ray sampling. Data Structures: Confidence Score (CS(vi)): A scalar value representing the reliability of pose vi, initialized from keypoint matches and updated iteratively. Detached Color Network (Cn): A shallow Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) identical in architecture to the primary color network Co but without viewing direction input. PSNR Estimates: PSNRo tracks rendering quality from Co, and PSNRn tracks rendering quality from Cn. Parameters: \lambdac: Weight for PSNR contribution to confidence update. Not given in the sources. \tau1: Inlier-outlier threshold for PSNR discrepancy between Co and Cn. Set to 9. \lambda: Weight for regularization term in loss. Set to 0.1. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Confidence Scores: Calculate initial confidence scores CS(vi) based on keypoint matches from the scene graph. Let |Mi| be the total number of edges (matches) for view vi. Normalize these scores to form a probability distribution: CS(vi) = \frac{|Mi|}{\sum{v \in V} |Mv|} 2. Construct Detached Color Network (Cn): Create a color network Cn that takes only geometry features (from the SDF network) as input, explicitly excluding the viewing direction vector. Use the same sampling points and geometry features as the original color network Co. 3. Detach Optimization Graph: Detach all computations involving Cn from the main pose-NeRF optimization graph. This ensures that the loss calculated from Cn does not backpropagate to the SDF network or the primary color network Co, maintaining the performance of the NSR backbone. 4. Compute Rendering Losses: For each training image i, compute the photometric loss L{color} = \|\hat{C} - C\|1 for both networks. Estimate PSNRo from L{color}(Co) and PSNRn from L{color}(Cn) for efficiency. 5. Update Confidence Scores: Update the confidence score for each view vi using the PSNR estimated by the detached network Cn: CS(vi) = CS(vi) + \lambdac \cdot PSNRn(vi) 6. Normalize Confidence Scores: After updating, normalize the confidence scores to form a probability distribution for ray sampling: CS(vi) = \frac{CS(vi)}{\sum{v \in V} CS(v)} This distribution guides the training to sample more rays from poses with higher confidence. 7. Identify Outliers: Monitor the discrepancy between PSNRo and PSNRn. If |PSNRo - PSNRn| > \tau1 (where \tau1 = 9), the pose is flagged as an outlier, indicating anomalous data due to shape-radiance ambiguity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def initializeconfidence(views, matchcounts): """Initialize confidence scores based on keypoint matches.""" confidence = {v: matchcounts[v] for v in views} total = sum(confidence.values()) for v in views: confidence[v] /= total return confidence def estimatepsnrfromloss(lossvalue): """Estimate PSNR from rendering loss for efficiency.""" # Sources do not specify exact conversion; standard L1-to-PSNR approximation used. return 10.0 math.log10(1.0 / max(lossvalue, 1e-8)) def updateconfidence(views, confidence, psnrnvalues, lambdac): """Update confidence scores using PSNR from detached network and normalize.""" for v in views: confidence[v] += lambdac psnrnvalues[v] total = sum(confidence.values()) for v in views: confidence[v] /= total return confidence def detectoutliers(psnrovalues, psnrnvalues, threshold): """Identify outliers based on discrepancy between Co and Cn PSNR.""" outliers = [] for v in psnrovalues: if abs(psnrovalues[v] - psnrnvalues[v]) > threshold: outliers.append(v) return outliers Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shape-Radiance Ambiguity: Traditional color networks Co (with view direction) can render high-PSNR images even for wrong poses, leading to incorrect sampling if used for confidence. Overfitting: The detached network Cn must not be coupled with the main optimization to prevent it from learning pose-specific artifacts that defeat its purpose. Computational Cost: While Cn adds overhead, using a shallow MLP minimizes the impact on training time. Time Complexity: Adds minimal computational overhead because Cn is a shallow MLP, similar to the existing color network. Training time increases slightly but remains comparable to baseline NeuS/SG-NeRF (e.g., 13 hours for 150k iterations on SG-NeRF, 22 hours for 300k iterations on DTU on RTX 3090). Memory Complexity: Requires storing parameters for an additional shallow MLP Cn. Performance: Effectively differentiates inliers and outliers, leading to higher quality 3D reconstructions and accurate pose rectification. Strengths: Robust against shape-radiance ambiguity; simple rule-based thresholding (\tau1=9) for outlier detection; does not complicate the joint pose-NeRF optimization. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that view-independent rendering quality correlates better with pose correctness than view-dependent rendering; requires careful tuning of \lambdac and \tau1. Origin: Introduced in "Robust SG-NeRF: Robust Scene Graph Aided Neural Surface Reconstruction". History: Addresses limitations in SG-NeRF where heuristic confidence updating based solely on PSNR failed to distinguish inliers from outliers due to shape-radiance ambiguity. Usage: Used in object-level 3D surface reconstruction from unorganized inward-facing images, specifically on datasets like SG-NeRF and DTU. name: NeRF Image Refinement through End-to-End Sampling Point Optimization
head: End-to-End Sampling Point Optimization, MLP-Mixer based Sampling Optimization, Neural Radiance Field Image Refinement through End-to-End Sampling Point Optimization
body: This method optimizes the positions of sampling points along camera rays to reduce rendering artifacts and produce more detailed images in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Unlike canonical NeRF, which places sampling points at fixed regular intervals regardless of scene content, this approach dynamically concentrates sampling points in critical areas, particularly around object surfaces, by using an MLP-Mixer-based architecture for end-to-end optimization. The method employs a cascaded design consisting of a sampling module G and a NeRF module, trained simultaneously in an end-to-end manner. Inputs and Outputs Inputs to Sampling Module G: Camera center o and direction vectors dj for Nr rays, where j \in \{1, \dots, Nr\}. Outputs of Sampling Module G: Distances t{j,i} from the origin to the sampling points i on rays j, where i \in \{1, \dots, Ns\}. Inputs to NeRF Module: 3D sampling points x{j,i} and direction vectors dj. Outputs of NeRF Module: Color and density estimates at x{j,i}, used for volume rendering to determine pixel colors. Data Structures and Parameters Nr: Number of rays. Set to 1,008 in experiments, chosen randomly from a total of 1,008 \times 756 rays. Ns: Number of sampling points per ray. Set to 128. Sampling Module G: Consists of 3 layers of sampling blocks. Ray-wise MLP G^{(ray)}: Hidden layer size of 1,024 units. Scene-wise MLP G^{(scene)}: Hidden layer size of 4,032 units. Output Activation of G: Sigmoid function. Algorithm The sampling module G processes ray information through multiple layers of sampling blocks. Each block contains two integrated streams: a ray-wise MLP G^{(ray)} and a scene-wise MLP G^{(scene)}. 1. Ray-wise Processing: The ray-wise MLP G^{(ray)} processes features inherent to individual rays. It uses a network MLP1 comprising two fully connected layers, with GELU activation applied to the output of the first layer. 2. Scene-wise Processing: The scene-wise MLP G^{(scene)} computes features based on relationships among all rays within the scene. It uses a network MLP2 which mirrors the structure of MLP1 (two fully connected layers, GELU activation on the first layer's output). 3.
