name: Mip-Grid
head: Mip-TensoRF, Mip-K-Planes
body: Mip-Grid is a method for integrating anti-aliasing techniques into grid-based radiance field representations, mitigating aliasing artifacts that occur when rendering scenes at varying camera distances or resolutions. Unlike methods that store distinct grids for each scale or rely on heavy multisampling, Mip-Grid generates multi-scale grid representations from a single shared base grid using learnable depth-wise convolutions, allowing features to vary with camera distance while maintaining fast training times and minimal storage overhead. It sets itself apart from siblings like Mip-NeRF 360 Optimization Setup by operating directly on the grid structure rather than just the ray integration, and from Scale-Dependent Downweighting for Grid Interpolation by explicitly generating hierarchical feature grids rather than downweighting interpolation weights. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A shared single-scale grid representation (density G\sigma and appearance Gc), camera parameters (ray origin, direction, and pixel dimensions), and a scale-aware coordinate s. Outputs: Density \sigma and color c for each sampled point along a ray, derived from the generated multi-scale grids. Data Structures and Layouts: The method modifies standard grid-based representations (such as TensoRF or K-Planes) by adding a scale dimension S to the grids. Multi-scale Density Grid: \tilde{G}\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times L \times S \times C\sigma} Multi-scale Appearance Grid: \tilde{G}c \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times L \times S \times Cc} H, W, L: Spatial resolutions along axes X, Y, Z. S: Number of generated scales (typically 4). C\sigma, Cc: Number of density and appearance feature channels. Convolution Kernels: Learnable filters applied to the base grid factors. For Mip-TensoRF (VM factorization): Vector filters: k{i,vX}^v \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times R} for vector vr^X. Matrix rank filters: k{i,r}^{M{YZ}} \in \mathbb{R}^K for rank r of matrix Mr^{YZ}. Matrix filters: k{i,M{YZ}} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times R} for matrix Mr^{YZ}. Separate kernels exist for each rank, axis, and scale i. For Mip-K-Planes (Plane factorization): Plane filters: ki^{YZ} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times K \times K \times R}, ki^{XZ} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times 1 \times K \times R}, ki^{XY} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times 1 \times R}. K: Kernel size (typically 3). R: Tensor rank. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Shared Grids: Train the base single-scale grids G\sigma and Gc (or their factorized components) using standard grid-based NeRF optimization. 2. Generate Multi-Scale Grids: Apply learnable depth-wise convolutions to the shared grid factors to generate S scales of multi-scale grids. This is done during the rendering process to minimize storage costs. For Mip-TensoRF, the i-th scale of the multi-scale grid \tilde{G}i is computed as: \tilde{G}i = \sum{r=1}^{R} \left( (vr^X k{i,vX}^v) \circ (Mr^{YZ} k{i,r}^{M{YZ}}) + (vr^Y k{i,vY}^v) \circ (Mr^{XZ} k{i,r}^{M{XZ}}) + (vr^Z k{i,vZ}^v) \circ (Mr^{XY} k{i,r}^{M{XY}}) \right) Where denotes convolution, \circ denotes tensor product, and k are the learnable depth-wise convolution filters. For Mip-K-Planes, the i-th scale \tilde{G}{ik} is computed as: \tilde{G}{ik} = (M^{YZ} ki^{YZ}) \odot (M^{XZ} ki^{XZ}) \odot (M^{XY} ki^{XY}) Where \odot is broadcast element-wise multiplication. 3. Compute Scale-Aware Coordinate: Calculate the scale coordinate s based on the camera and ray properties. Three variants are defined: Discrete Scale Coordinate: Defined as the mean of the pixel width and height in world coordinates scaled by 2/\sqrt{12}. This value is unique for each image scale and used for all sampled points within that image. Continuous Scale Coordinate: The discrete scale coordinate scaled by the distance from the ray origin to the sampled point. This provides distinct scale values for each point, allowing smooth interpolation across broader ranges of scales. 2-Dimensional Scale Coordinate: Consists of the continuous scale coordinate and the distance from the ray origin to the sampled point. 4. Feature Extraction: Interpolate features from the generated multi-scale grids \tilde{G}\sigma and \tilde{G}c using the scale-aware coordinate s and the spatial coordinate x. Features are extracted from each of the S scales independently. The feature sets from all scales are averaged to produce the final features. 5. Decode Density and Color: Density: \sigma = f\sigma(x, s; \tilde{G}\sigma) Color: c = fc(x, s, d; \theta, \tilde{G}c) Where d is the viewing direction and \theta are MLP parameters. 6. Volume Rendering: Perform differentiable volume rendering using the computed \sigma and c to generate the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mipgridrender(rayorigin, raydirection, pixelwidth, pixelheight, basegridfactors, kernels, scalecoordtype): """ Renders a single ray using Mip-Grid. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. pixelwidth: float, width of the pixel in world coordinates. pixelheight: float, height of the pixel in world coordinates. basegridfactors: Dictionary containing base grid factors (e.g., vectors and matrices for TensoRF). kernels: Dictionary containing learnable convolution kernels for each scale and factor. scalecoordtype: str, one of 'discrete', 'continuous', or '2d'. Returns: color: float, rendered RGB color. """ # 1. Compute Scale-Aware Coordinate # Mean of pixel width and height scaled by 2/sqrt(12) basescale = (pixelwidth + pixelheight) / 2 (2 / (12 0.5)) # Sample points along the ray (standard volume rendering sampling) # Assume samples is a list of distances t from rayorigin samples = getraysamples(rayorigin, raydirection) # 2. Generate Multi-Scale Grids and Extract Features # Note: In practice, grids are generated on-the-fly or cached. # Here we simulate the feature extraction for each sample. finaldensityfeatures = [] finalcolorfeatures = [] numscales = len(kernels) # Typically 4 for i in range(numscales): # Generate i-th scale grid factors using convolutions # This step is equivalent to applying 3D convolutions to the 3D tensor # due to the linearity of convolution and factorization structure. # Example for Mip-TensoRF VM factorization: # Gi = sumr ( (vX kivX) o (MYZ kirMYZ) +...) # We assume a helper function that applies the specific convolution logic # for the chosen grid representation (TensoRF or K-Planes) scalegridfactors = generatescalegrid(basegridfactors, kernels[i]) # 3. Determine Scale Coordinate for this sample if scalecoordtype == 'discrete': s = basescale elif scalecoordtype == 'continuous': # Scale by distance from ray origin to sampled point # Note: 'samples' contains distances t # We need to iterate over samples here, but for pseudocode clarity, # we assume we process one sample at a time or vectorize. # Let's assume we are processing a single sample with distance t t = getsampledistance() # Placeholder for current sample distance s = basescale t elif scalecoordtype == '2d': t = getsampledistance() scontinuous = basescale t s = (scontinuous, t) # 4. Interpolate Features from Multi-Scale Grid # Interpolate density and color features from scalegridfactors using spatial coord x and scale s # x = rayorigin + t raydirection x = rayorigin + getsampledistance() raydirection densityfeat = interpolatefeatures(scalegridfactors['density'], x, s) colorfeat = interpolatefeatures(scalegridfactors['appearance'], x, s) finaldensityfeatures.append(densityfeat) finalcolorfeatures.append(colorfeat) # 5. Average Features from all scales avgdensityfeat = average(finaldensityfeatures) avgcolorfeat = average(finalcolorfeatures) # 6. Decode Density and Color # fsigma and fcolor are typically small MLPs sigma = decodedensity(avgdensityfeat) color = decodecolor(avgcolorfeat, raydirection) # 7. Return for volume rendering accumulation return sigma, color def generatescalegrid(basefactors, kernels): """ Generates multi-scale grid factors by applying depth-wise convolutions. Implementation depends on whether using Mip-TensoRF or Mip-K-Planes. """ # Placeholder for the specific convolution logic described in the formulas # For Mip-TensoRF: # Apply 1D/2D depth-wise convolutions to vectors and matrices # Return the resulting factorized representation pass def interpolatefeatures(gridfactors, x, s): """ Interpolates features from the grid at spatial coordinate x and scale s. """ # Standard trilinear or higher-order interpolation # The grid is effectively 4D (H, W, L, S) or factorized equivalent pass Parameters and Typical Values: Kernel Size (K): 3. Number of Scales (S): 4. Training Iterations: Mip-TensoRF: 40k iterations on multi-scale Blender dataset, 25k on multi-scale LLFF dataset. Mip-K-Planes: 30k iterations. Kernel Training Start: Mip-TensoRF: Kernel training begins after grid upsampling is completed. Mip-K-Planes: Kernels are optimized from the beginning. Loss Scaling: Pixel loss is scaled following mip-NeRF to account for scale differences. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting to Scales: Using only the discrete scale coordinate can lead to overfitting to the specific scales present in the training dataset, making it difficult to render images at unseen scales. The continuous scale coordinate mitigates this by providing distinct scale values for each sampled point, enabling smoother interpolation across a broader range of scales. Storage Complexity: While Mip-Grid avoids the dramatic increase in space complexity associated with storing distinct grids for each scale, it still introduces additional parameters for the convolution kernels. However, this is significantly less than storing full multi-resolution grids. Time Complexity: Rendering involves generating multi-scale grids via convolutions and interpolating from S scales. The convolutions operate on reduced dimensions (1D or 2D instead of 3D), minimizing computational costs compared to full 3D convolutions. Memory Complexity: Uses a single shared base grid plus learnable kernels. This avoids the storage overhead of maintaining distinct grids for each scale, which would dramatically increase space complexity. Performance: Mip-TensoRF on Full Res Blender: PSNR 34.77, SSIM 0.9786, LPIPS 0.0168. Training Time: Mip-TensoRF training time on RTX 4090 is not explicitly listed in the source table but is noted to be significantly faster than mip-NeRF (>30 hours). Mip-TensoRF training took 0.27 hours for the multi-scale Blender dataset in the provided table, compared to 0.16 hours for original TensoRF. Strengths: Mitigates aliasing artifacts effectively. Fast training time compared to MLP-based methods like mip-NeRF. Easily integrated into existing grid-based methods (TensoRF, K-Planes) with minimal modifications. Single-sampling approach, unlike Zip-NeRF which requires ~50 samplings. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of scale coordinates to avoid overfitting. Performance depends on the quality of the learned convolution kernels. When to Use: Use when anti-aliasing is critical for grid-based NeRFs and fast training is desired, especially when dealing with multi-scale datasets or varying camera distances. When Not to Use: Avoid if storage for kernels is prohibitive (though it is low) or if the scene does not exhibit significant aliasing issues at the target resolutions. Mip-Grid was introduced in the paper "Mip-Grid: Anti-aliased Grid Representations for Neural Radiance Fields". It builds upon the concept of mipmapping in computer graphics to address aliasing in grid representations. The method was developed to combine the anti-aliasing benefits of mip-NeRF with the fast training speeds of grid-based methods like TensoRF and K-Planes. It was tested on multi-scale Blender and LLFF datasets, demonstrating superior performance over original grid-based methods and competitive performance with mip-NeRF. name: Tri-MipRF Training Configuration
head: Tri-MipRF Training
body: Tri-MipRF Training optimizes a tri-plane based radiance field representation to achieve anti-aliased novel view synthesis by explicitly modeling multi-scale features. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by replacing the single-resolution MLP coordinate encoding with a learnable tri-plane mipmap structure, allowing the network to adaptively select the appropriate frequency detail based on the ray's footprint. This approach builds on Multi-scale and Mip-aware Representations by using differentiable texture sampling to approximate cone integrals, addressing the aliasing artifacts common in high-frequency scene reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of calibrated multi-view 2D images with known camera poses. Outputs: A trained Tri-MipRF representation consisting of three learnable tri-planes (XY, YZ, XZ) organized as mipmaps, and a small MLP mapping sampled features to color and density. Data Structures: Tri-Mip Encoding: Three 3D tensors representing the tri-planes. Each tri-plane is structured as a mipmap pyramid. Base Level (M{l0}): The highest resolution level. Dimensions are Height H=512, Width W=512, and Channels C=16. Mipmap Levels: Lower resolution levels are generated by downsampling the base level, following standard texture mipmap generation principles. MLP: A small Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes the aggregated features from the tri-plane queries and outputs volume density (\sigma) and view-dependent color (c). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the target image, cast a ray through the scene volume. 2. Ray Cone Approximation: Determine the footprint of the pixel on the image plane to approximate the ray as a cone, following the MipNeRF approach. 3. Tri-Plane Query: Sample the ray's 3D coordinates against the three tri-planes (XY, YZ, XZ). Use differentiable bilinear interpolation to query features from the tri-planes. Select the appropriate mipmap level based on the ray's footprint size to ensure anti-aliasing. The nvdiffrast library is used to perform these mipmap queries efficiently. Aggregate the features from the three planes (e.g., via concatenation or addition) to form a feature vector. 4. MLP Forward Pass: Pass the aggregated feature vector and the viewing direction into the small MLP to predict density and color. 5. Volume Rendering: Perform standard differentiable volume rendering (alpha compositing) along the ray to compute the final pixel color. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss between the rendered pixel color and the ground truth image pixel. 7. Optimization: Update the Tri-Mip encoding parameters and MLP weights using gradient descent. Formulas: Area Loss: The pixel loss is scaled by the area of its footprint on the image plane, denoted as L{area}. L{total} = \sum{p \in \text{pixels}} \text{Area}(p) \cdot \| C{rendered}(p) - C{ground\truth}(p) \|^2 Where \text{Area}(p) is the footprint area of pixel p. Parameters: Base Mipmap Shape: H=512, W=512, C=16. Optimizer: AdamW. Weight Decay: 1 \times 10^{-5}. Learning Rate (MLP): 2 \times 10^{-3}. Learning Rate (Tri-Mip Encoding): 2 \times 10^{-2} (scaled up 10x relative to the MLP). Learning Rate Schedule: MultiStepLR. Iterations: 25,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of tiny-cuda-nn and nvdiffrast requires careful handling of GPU memory and precision settings to ensure stable gradient flow during mipmap sampling. Boundary Conditions: The tri-plane representation assumes the scene fits within the defined coordinate space. Out-of-bounds queries must be handled via padding or clamping in the texture sampling operation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Project 3D ray points to 2D UV coordinates for each plane uvxy, uvyz, uvxz = projecttoplanes(rays.points) # 2. Determine mipmap level based on ray footprint area mipmaplevel = computemipmaplevel(rays.footprintarea) # 3. Sample features using nvdiffrast for differentiable bilinear interpolation # Note: nvdiffrast handles the mipmap selection internally if configured featuresxy = nvdiffrast.texture.trilinear( trimipparams[0], uvxy.unsqueeze(0), mipmaplevel) featuresyz = nvdiffrast.texture.trilinear( trimipparams[1], uvyz.unsqueeze(0), mipmaplevel) featuresxz = nvdiffrast.texture.trilinear( trimipparams[2], uvxz.unsqueeze(0), mipmaplevel) # Aggregate features (e.g., concatenate or sum) aggregatedfeatures = aggregatefeatures(featuresxy, featuresyz, featuresxz) # MLP forward pass density, color = mlp(aggregatedfeatures, rays.directions) # Volume rendering renderedcolors = volumerender(rays, density, color) # Compute Area Loss pixelareas = computepixelfootprintareas(rays) loss = torch.mean(pixelareas (renderedcolors - images[rays.pixelindices])2) # Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() scheduler.step() def projecttoplanes(points): # Extract 2D coordinates for XY, YZ, XZ planes # points shape: [N, 3] uvxy = points[:,:2] uvyz = points[:, 1:] uvxz = torch.stack([points[:, 0], points[:, 2]], dim=1) return uvxy, uvyz, uvxz def computemipmaplevel(footprintarea): # Map footprint area to a discrete mipmap level index # Larger area -> higher level (lower resolution) # Implementation detail: Not given in the sources. pass def aggregatefeatures(f1, f2, f3): # Concatenate features along channel dimension return torch.cat([f1, f2, f3], dim=-1) LoD-NeuS is a neural implicit surface reconstruction method that encodes features with a continuous level of detail (LoD) from a tri-plane-based representation to adaptively reconstruct high-fidelity geometry and address aliasing concerns. It builds on Tri-MipRF Training Configuration by introducing multi-scale tri-plane position encoding and multi-convolved featurization to approximate ray integrals within a cone, distinguishing itself from standard NeuS by reducing MLP queries while maintaining high-frequency detail. Time Complexity: Training time is dominated by the differentiable texture sampling operations. The use of tiny-cuda-nn and nvdiffrast optimizes these queries, making them comparable to standard texture lookups. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is determined by the base mipmap size. With H=512, W=512, C=16 for three planes, the base memory is 3 \times 16 \times 512 \times 512 \times 4 bytes \approx 24 MB. Mipmap levels add negligible overhead. This is significantly more compact than high-resolution 3D voxel grids. Measured Performance: The method is evaluated on the multi-scale Blender dataset, which includes downscaling factors of 2, 4, and 8 to test anti-aliasing capabilities. Strengths: Efficient memory usage due to the compact tri-plane representation; effective anti-aliasing through mipmap-based feature selection; fast training due to optimized texture sampling libraries. Limitations: The representation is limited to the 2D plane projections, which may struggle with complex 3D structures that do not align well with the XY, YZ, or XZ planes. The choice of base resolution (512x512) is empirical and may not be optimal for all scene scales. When to use: Suitable for novel view synthesis tasks where anti-aliasing is critical and memory constraints prevent the use of large 3D voxel grids or high-resolution NeRF MLPs. When not to use: Not ideal for scenes with highly complex 3D geometry that cannot be well-approximated by tri-plane projections. Tri-MipRF was introduced in the paper "Tri-MipRF: Tri-Mip Representation for Efficient Anti-Aliasing Neural Radiance Fields". The method was developed to address the aliasing artifacts present in standard NeRF representations, particularly when rendering scenes at multiple resolutions. It builds upon the MipNeRF concept of approximating rays as cones but replaces the positional encoding with a learnable tri-plane mipmap structure. The implementation relies on PyTorch, tiny-cuda-nn, and nvdiffrast to achieve efficient differentiable rendering. body: LoD-NeuS is a neural implicit surface reconstruction method that encodes features with a continuous level of detail (LoD) from a tri-plane-based representation to adaptively reconstruct high-fidelity geometry and address aliasing concerns. It builds on Tri-MipRF Training Configuration by introducing multi-scale tri-plane position encoding and multi-convolved featurization to approximate ray integrals within a cone, distinguishing itself from standard NeuS by reducing MLP queries while maintaining high-frequency detail. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images, camera parameters, and an initial set of sparse points or volume (for initialization). Outputs: A signed distance function (SDF) field and a color field, defining the 3D geometry and appearance. Data Structures: Tri-Planes: Three 2D feature planes (xy, yz, zx) representing the 3D space. Each plane has a specific resolution and number of channels. The features are initialized using a Gaussian distribution derived from the spatial coordinates. Geometry Network: An MLP with 8 hidden layers, hidden size 256, and weight normalization. Color Network: An MLP taking features, position, view direction, and normal to predict color. Numbered Steps: 1. Multi-Scale Tri-Plane Position Encoding: For a 3D point \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z), encode it into multiple scales. The tri-planes are initialized such that the variance \sigma^2 for each plane is proportional to the squared distance of the coordinates in that plane's subspace. Specifically, for n scales, the initialization is: \sigma{xy}^2 = \frac{1}{2n}(x^2 + y^2), \quad \sigma{yz}^2 = \frac{1}{2n}(y^2 + z^2), \quad \sigma{zx}^2 = \frac{1}{2n}(z^2 + x^2) This ensures that higher frequencies are captured at finer scales. 2. Multi-Convolved Featurization (Cone Discrete Sampling): To approximate the ray integral within a cone and reduce aliasing, the method aggregates LoD features from multi-convolved multi-scale features of vertices within a conical frustum along a ray. This replaces standard point sampling with a cone-tracing approximation. Compared to 4x super-sampling, this requires only 1/4 of the MLP queries. 3. SDF and Color Prediction: The aggregated features are passed to the geometry network to predict the SDF value \hat{d} and feature vector \mathbf{f}. The geometry network uses a skip connection: the input is concatenated with the output of the 4th hidden layer. The color network takes \mathbf{f}, the 3D position, view direction, and surface normal (derived from the SDF gradient) to predict the color \hat{c}. 4. SDF Growth Refinement (Optional/For Thin Surfaces): For thin surfaces, an SDF growth refinement is applied based on SDF sphere tracing to improve reconstruction. This involves rendering rays around error maps and refining the SDF values. 5. Loss Computation and Optimization: Compute photometric loss between rendered and input images. Compute SDF loss (e.g., Eikonal loss, consistency loss). Update network weights using the ADAM optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Initialize Tri-Planes with Gaussian distribution based on spatial coordinates # See Eq. 11 in for initialization logic self.triplanes = nn.ParameterList([ nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, numscales, hiddensize, triplaneres[0], triplaneres[1])) ]) # Geometry Network: 8 hidden layers, size 256, skip connection at layer 4 self.geometrynet = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddensize + 3, hiddensize), # Input: features + xyz nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), # Layer 4 output nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, hiddensize), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddensize, 1 + hiddensize) # Output: SDF + features) # Apply Weight Normalization to stabilize training for m in self.geometrynet.modules(): if isinstance(m, nn.Linear): nn.utils.weightnorm(m) # Color Network (simplified) self.colornet = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(hiddensize + 3 + 3, 128), # Features + xyz + viewdir nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # Output: RGB) self.optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(self.parameters(), lr=5e-4) self.scheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(self.optimizer, Tmax=300000) def encodeposition(self, xyz, triplanes): """ Multi-scale tri-plane position encoding.:param xyz: (N, 3) coordinates:param triplanes: List of 3 tensors (xy, yz, zx) for each scale:return: Aggregated features (N, hiddensize) """ # Extract xy, yz, zx coordinates x, y, z = xyz[:, 0:1], xyz[:, 1:2], xyz[:, 2:3] features = [] for scale in range(self.numscales): # Get tri-planes for this scale # triplanes[scale] is a list of 3 tensors: [xy, yz, zx] xyplane, yzplane, zxplane = triplanes[scale] # Sample features from tri-planes using bilinear interpolation # Normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] for sampling xycoords = torch.cat([x, y], dim=1) yzcoords = torch.cat([y, z], dim=1) zxcoords = torch.cat([z, x], dim=1) # Sample from planes (pseudo-code for gridsample) xyfeat = F.gridsample(xyplane.unsqueeze(0), xycoords.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() yzfeat = F.gridsample(yzplane.unsqueeze(0), yzcoords.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() zxfeat = F.gridsample(zxplane.unsqueeze(0), zxcoords.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze() # Aggregate features from the three planes scalefeat = (xyfeat + yzfeat + zxfeat) / 3.0 features.append(scalefeat) # Concatenate features from all scales aggregatedfeat = torch.cat(features, dim=1) return aggregatedfeat def forward(self, xyz, viewdir, triplanes): """ Forward pass.:param xyz: (N, 3) 3D points:param viewdir: (N, 3) view directions:param triplanes: List of tri-planes for each scale:return: SDF, color, normal """ # Step 1: Encode position with multi-scale tri-planes features = self.encodeposition(xyz, triplanes) # Step 2: Predict SDF and features using geometry network # Concatenate features with xyz for the first layer geoinput = torch.cat([features, xyz], dim=1) geooutput = self.geometrynet(geoinput) sdf = geooutput[:, 0:1] geofeatures = geooutput[:, 1:] # Step 3: Compute normal from SDF gradient (numerical or analytical) # Normal is typically computed via finite differences or automatic differentiation normal = self.computenormal(xyz, sdf) # Step 4: Predict color using color network colorinput = torch.cat([geofeatures, xyz, viewdir], dim=1) color = self.colornet(colorinput) return sdf, color, normal def computenormal(self, xyz, sdf): """ Compute surface normal from SDF. """ # Standard finite difference or autograd method eps = 1e-4 dx = torch.zeroslike(xyz) dx[:, 0] = eps sdfdx = self.forward(xyz + dx, None, None)[0] dy = torch.zeroslike(xyz) dy[:, 1] = eps sdfdy = self.forward(xyz + dy, None, None)[0] dz = torch.zeroslike(xyz) dz[:, 2] = eps sdfdz = self.forward(xyz + dz, None, None)[0] normal = torch.cat([sdfdx - sdf, sdfdy - sdf, sdfdz - sdf], dim=1) normal = F.normalize(normal, dim=1) return normal def trainstep(self, rays, triplanes): """ Single training step.:param rays: Batch of rays (origin, direction, color):param triplanes: Current tri-planes:return: Loss """ self.optimizer.zerograd() # Sample points along rays xyz, viewdir, targetcolor = self.samplerays(rays) # Forward pass sdf, color, normal = self.forward(xyz, viewdir, triplanes) # Compute losses # Photometric loss, SDF loss, Eikonal loss, etc. loss = self.computeloss(sdf, color, targetcolor, normal) loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.scheduler.step() return loss.item() def samplerays(self, rays): """ Sample points along rays using hierarchical sampling and cone discrete sampling. """ # Implementation of hierarchical sampling from [Wang et al. 2021] # and cone discrete sampling as described in pass def computeloss(self, sdf, color, targetcolor, normal): """ Compute total loss. """ # Photometric loss photometricloss = F.mseloss(color, targetcolor) # SDF loss (e.g., Eikonal loss) eikonalloss = torch.mean((torch.norm(normal, dim=1) - 1.0) 2) # Other losses (consistency, etc.) totalloss = photometricloss + eikonalloss return totalloss Parameters: Geometry Network: 8 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Skip Connection: Concatenates input with output of the 4th layer. Optimizer: ADAM. Learning Rate: Linearly warmed up from 0 to 5 \times 10^{-4} in the first 5k iterations, then cosine decay to a minimum of 2.5 \times 10^{-5}. Ray Batch Size: 512. Total Training Iterations: 300k. Hierarchical Sampling: Follows [Wang et al. 2021]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NGP Encoding Artifacts: Using Neural Graphics Primitives (NGP) encoding can cause performance degradation due to hash collisions, leading to artifacts in areas with scarce textures or observations, as spatial points record surface distance. Thin Surfaces: Standard sampling may fail for thin surfaces; the SDF growth refinement module is recommended for such cases. Time Complexity: Training takes around 9 hours for 300k iterations on a single Nvidia A100 GPU. Inference time is approximately 160 seconds for a 1600x1200 image. Memory Complexity: GPU memory usage is 13G. Performance: Compared to 4x super-sampling, the method requires 1/4 of MLP queries. Training time is nearly half that of HF-NeuS. Accuracy: Achieves an average Chamfer distance of 0.72 on the DTU dataset. On a specific comparison table (Table 4), it achieves a Chamfer Distance of 0.114. Strengths: High-fidelity geometry reconstruction, reduced computational burden compared to super-sampling, faster training than HF-NeuS. Limitations: May require additional regularization or refinement for thin surfaces or areas with scarce textures if using hash-based encodings like NGP. LoD-NeuS was introduced in the paper "Anti-Aliased Neural Implicit Surfaces with Encoding Level of Detail". It addresses the issue of aliasing in neural surface reconstruction by introducing a continuous level of detail in the encoding process. The method builds upon the NeuS framework [Wang et al. 2021] and incorporates ideas from tri-plane representations. It was evaluated on the DTU dataset without mask supervision. name: NeRF-SR Training Configuration
head: NeRF-Supersampling, Ours-SS, Ours-Refine
body: NeRF-SR is a training configuration that enhances the resolution of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by integrating a supersampling strategy directly into the volume rendering process, allowing the network to learn high-frequency details from low-resolution inputs without requiring high-resolution ground truth. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by explicitly modeling the camera's point spread function (PSF) during training to prevent aliasing, and from post-hoc upsampling methods (like NeRF-Bi) by maintaining 3D consistency through differentiable rendering at multiple scales. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Low-resolution (LR) images of a scene, camera intrinsics (K) and extrinsics (T), and estimated depth maps (d) for the input views. Outputs: High-resolution (HR) novel view images rendered from the trained NeRF model. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard NeRF MLP architecture mapping 5D coordinates (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) to density \sigma and color c. No new data structures are introduced for the core supersampling mechanism; it modifies the sampling and loss computation steps. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a standard NeRF MLP. Set the optimizer to Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. Set the batch size to 2048 rays. Initialize the learning rate to 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. 2. Ray Sampling: For each batch, sample 2048 rays. For each ray, perform hierarchical sampling: Generate 64 coarse samples along the ray using a uniform distribution. Query the coarse MLP to obtain densities. Use the densities to compute a probability distribution for sampling 64 fine samples. 3. Supersampling Loss Computation: Unlike standard NeRF which minimizes pixel-wise MSE between rendered and ground truth images, NeRF-SR computes the loss by simulating the camera's integration process. For each pixel in the input LR image, render the color C{rendered} using the fine samples. The ground truth color C{GT} for that pixel is the average of the high-resolution pixels that map to it. The loss is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between C{rendered} and C{GT}. Note: The sources describe the method as "supersampling" where the network is trained to predict values at a higher resolution grid, effectively learning the continuous function that, when integrated over the pixel footprint, matches the LR observation. This prevents the network from overfitting to high-frequency noise present in LR inputs. 4. Optimization: Update the MLP weights using the computed loss. Decay the learning rate exponentially from 5 \cdot 10^{-4} to 5 \cdot 10^{-6} over the course of training. 5. Inference (Standard): To render an HR image, sample rays through the HR pixel grid and query the trained NeRF. The output is denoted as "Ours-SS". Refinement Network (Ours-Refine): For real-world datasets (LLFF) where supersampling alone yields blurry textures, a refinement network is applied post-rendering. 1. Patch Extraction: Divide the input HR image into non-overlapping patches of size 64 \times 64. 2. Reference Patch Selection: Select K=8 reference patches from the training set (typically the first image in the dataset). 3. Patch Refinement: For each patch P{i,j} in the rendered image: Compute the 3D world coordinate of the patch center using the estimated depth d{i,j} and camera parameters Kn, Tn of the current view In. Backproject this 3D coordinate to the reference view I{REF} using K{REF} and T{REF} to find the corresponding location. Extract the corresponding patch from I{REF} as P^{REF}. The refinement network takes the rendered patch P{i,j} and the set of reference patches \{P^{REF}k\}{k=1}^K as input to predict the refined texture details. Formula: The transformation involves computing the 3D world coordinate from depth and camera matrices, then backprojecting to the reference image plane. Points falling outside I{REF} are discarded. 4. Stitching: Stitch the refined patches together to form the final HR image. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 2048 rays. Learning Rate: Exponential decay from 5 \cdot 10^{-4} to 5 \cdot 10^{-6}. Samples: 64 coarse, 64 fine. Epochs: 20 for Blender dataset, 30 for LLFF dataset. Refinement Patches: K=8, size 64 \times 64. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Estimation: The refinement step relies on accurate depth estimates. Poor depth estimation leads to incorrect backprojection and artifacts. Arbitrary Scale: NeRF-SR does not support arbitrary-scale super-resolution; it is trained for specific scale factors (e.g., \times 2, \times 4). Real-world Blur: Supersampling alone is insufficient for real-world images with complex structures; the refinement network is necessary for LLFF but adds inference time. Super-NeRF is a method for NeRF super-resolution that generates plausible, 3D-consistent high-resolution (HR) details using only low-resolution (LR) observations, without requiring HR ground truth. It distinguishes itself from NeRF-SR by coupling the NeRF with a GAN-based 2D super-resolution backbone and per-view latent codes to explicitly search the latent space of a powerful SR prior, rather than relying on simple linear formulations or HR refinement via per-patch warping. The method employs a Consistency Controlling Super Resolution (CCSR) module and mutual learning between a fixed LR NeRF and a learnable HR NeRF to ensure view consistency. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: Comparable to training a standard HR NeRF. The supersampling strategy introduces negligible additional computational overhead during training compared to standard NeRF. Inference Time: The base NeRF rendering time dominates. For a 1008 \times 756 image, NeRF's MLP takes ~48 seconds on a single 1080Ti. The refinement stage adds ~1.3 seconds. Measured Performance: Hardware: NVIDIA 1080Ti. Datasets: Blender (synthetic), LLFF (real-world). Metrics: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS. LLFF Results (Scale \times 4): Ours-SS: PSNR 25.13, SSIM 0.730, LPIPS 0.244. Ours-Refine: PSNR 25.59, SSIM 0.759, LPIPS 0.165. LLFF Results (Scale \times 2): Ours-SS: PSNR 26.81, SSIM 0.823, LPIPS 0.145. Ours-Refine: PSNR 27.34, SSIM 0.842, LPIPS 0.103. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Achieves photorealistic HR novel view synthesis from LR inputs without external HR data. Maintains 3D consistency. Improves LPIPS significantly, indicating better perceptual quality. Limitations: Does not support arbitrary-scale super-resolution. Introduces extra computation during inference if refinement is used. Requires accurate depth estimation for the refinement step. NeRF-SR was introduced by Wang et al. in 2021 as the first pipeline for high-resolution novel view synthesis using mostly low-resolution inputs. It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which often produces blurry results when trained on LR images due to the inability to resolve high-frequency details. The method builds on the differentiable volume rendering framework of NeRF. NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01759v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Super-NeRF
body: Super-NeRF is a method for NeRF super-resolution that generates plausible, 3D-consistent high-resolution (HR) details using only low-resolution (LR) observations, without requiring HR ground truth. It distinguishes itself from NeRF-SR by coupling the NeRF with a GAN-based 2D super-resolution backbone and per-view latent codes to explicitly search the latent space of a powerful SR prior, rather than relying on simple linear formulations or HR refinement via per-patch warping. The method employs a Consistency Controlling Super Resolution (CCSR) module and mutual learning between a fixed LR NeRF and a learnable HR NeRF to ensure view consistency. Inputs: A set of low-resolution (LR) images C{LR,i} with corresponding camera poses. A pre-trained LR NeRF (fixed during Super-NeRF training). A pre-trained 2D SR backbone (ESRGAN). Outputs: A high-resolution (HR) NeRF model capable of rendering novel views at super-resolved resolution. A Consistency Controlling Latent Code (CCLC) for each view, which guides the 2D SR module. 1. LR NeRF: Lightweight MLP structure, approximately 1/4 the size of the HR NeRF. Uses lower-dimensional positional encoding to capture coarse details. Pre-trained on LR images and kept fixed during Super-NeRF optimization. 2. HR NeRF: Standard NeRF structure with higher-dimensional positional encoding to capture fine details. Learnable parameters optimized during training. 3. CCSR Module Components: CCLC (Consistency Controlling Latent Code): A learnable latent code for each view. For an LR image of size H \times W, the CCLC is a tensor of dimensions 3 \times (sH) \times (sW), where 3 corresponds to the image channels and s is the super-resolution multiplier. 2D SR Module: A pre-trained ESRGAN backbone. CEM (Consistency Enforcing Module): A post-processing step that enforces consistency with the LR input. 4. Parameters: s: Super-resolution multiplier. Set to 4 for the 4x SR backbone. 1. Pre-training: Train the LR NeRF on LR images for approximately 30 minutes. Pre-train the ESRGAN backbone. 2. Initialization: Initialize the HR NeRF and the CCLC for each training view. 3. Training Iteration: For each iteration: a. Randomly select a training viewpoint i. b. SR Generation: Concatenate the LR input C{LR,i} to a random CCLC and pass it to the ESRGAN backbone to generate an initial super-resolved image \tilde{C}{HR,i}. c. Consistency Enforcement: Apply the Consistency Enforcing Module (CEM) to \tilde{C}{HR,i} to produce the final CCSR output C{HR,i}, ensuring it matches the LR input after blurring. d. Ray Sampling: Upsample rays for viewpoint i to match the HR resolution. e. LR Rendering: Query the fixed LR NeRF with the upsampled rays to obtain the rendered image C{LN,i}. f. HR Rendering: Query the learnable HR NeRF with the same rays to obtain the rendered image C{HN,i}. g. Loss Computation: Calculate the total loss L using C{HR,i}, C{LN,i}, and C{HN,i}. h. Optimization: Update the HR NeRF parameters and the CCLC for view i using gradient descent. 1. Consistency Enforcing Module (CEM) Objective: Find a solution C{HR,i} that minimizes the distance to the SR output \tilde{C}{HR,i} while satisfying the constraint that blurring H yields the LR image C{LR,i}: \arg \min | \tilde{C}{HR,i} - C{HR,i} |, \quad \text{s.t.} \quad H C{HR,i} = C{LR,i} where H is the blur/downsampling kernel. 2. CEM Output Adjustment: The final CCSR output C{HR,i} is calculated by mapping LR content via orthogonal projection and ESRGAN output via the remainder matrix: C{HR,i} = (I - H^T (H H^{-1} H)) \tilde{C}{HR,i} + H^T (H H^{-1}) C{LR,i} where H^{-1} denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse for numerical stability. The term H^T (H H^{-1}) maps the LR content to the HR space. 3. Mutual Learning Loss (L{SR}): Combines constraints from the LR NeRF (C{LN,i}) and HR NeRF (C{HN,i}) against the CCSR output (C{HR,i}) using a trade-off function \alpha(t): L{SR} = \alpha(t) | C{LN,i} - C{HR,i} | + (1 - \alpha(t)) | C{HN,i} - C{HR,i} | where t is the iteration time, \alpha(0) = 1, and \lim{t\to\infty} \alpha(t) = 0. This gradually shifts supervision from the LR NeRF (view consistency) to the HR NeRF (detail generation). 4. Range Penalty Loss (L{range}): Penalizes CCSR output colors exceeding the valid range [0, 1]: L{range} = \frac{1}{N} \sumx | \hat{x} - \text{truncate}{0,1}(\hat{x}) |1 where N is the number of pixels, and \text{truncate}{0,1}(\hat{x}) is defined as: \text{truncate}{0,1}(\hat{x}) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \hat{x} < 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } \hat{x} > 1 \\ \hat{x} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. 5. Total Loss: L = L{SR} + L{range}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SimpleNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, dimin, dimhidden, dimout): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dimin, dimhidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(dimhidden, dimhidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(dimhidden, dimout)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class ESRGANBackbone(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Placeholder for pre-trained ESRGAN architecture self.model = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(6, 64, 3, 1, 1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 3, 3, 1, 1)) def forward(self, lrimg, cclc): x = torch.cat([lrimg, cclc], dim=1) return self.model(x) def applycem(sroutput, lrinput, blurkernel): # CEM Output Adjustment Formula: # CHR = (I - H^T (H H^-1 H)) CtildeHR + H^T (H H^-1) CLR # H^-1 denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse for numerical stability. H = blurkernel Hpinv = torch.linalg.pinv(H) projlr = H.T @ (H @ Hpinv) projsr = torch.eye(H.shape[0]) - H.T @ (H @ Hpinv @ H) # Flatten images to vectors for matrix multiplication, then reshape B, C, Hh, Ww = sroutput.shape srflat = sroutput.view(B, C Hh Ww) lrflat = lrinput.view(B, C Hh Ww) outflat = projsr @ srflat.T + projlr @ lrflat.T return outflat.T.view(B, C, Hh, Ww) def truncate01(x): return torch.clamp(x, 0.0, 1.0) def computerangepenalty(pred): # Lrange = 1/N sum |x - truncate(x)|1 truncated = truncate01(pred) diff = pred - truncated return torch.mean(torch.abs(diff)) def computel1loss(pred, target): return torch.mean(torch.abs(pred - target)) def alphaschedule(t, totaliters): # alpha(0) = 1, lim t->inf alpha(t) = 0 # Linear decay as a standard implementation of the trade-off function. return 1.0 - (t / totaliters) def trainsupernerf(lrimages, poses, lrnerf, esrgan, cem, hrnerf, cclcs, numiters, blurkernel): """ lrimages: List of LR images, shape (N, 3, H, W) poses: List of camera poses for each view lrnerf: Pre-trained LR NeRF (fixed) esrgan: Pre-trained ESRGAN backbone cem: Consistency Enforcing Module hrnerf: HR NeRF (learnable) cclcs: List of CCLC tensors, shape (N, 3, sH, sW) numiters: Total training iterations blurkernel: Blur kernel H """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(hrnerf.parameters()) + [cclcs], lr=1e-4) for t in range(numiters): # 1. Randomly choose training viewpoint i i = torch.randint(0, len(lrimages), (1,)).item() lrimg = lrimages[i] # (3, H, W) pose = poses[i] cclc = cclcs[i] # (3, sH, sW) # 2. Super-resolve LR image with CCSR (ESRGAN) lrimghr = F.interpolate(lrimg.unsqueeze(0), size=(cclc.shape[1], cclc.shape[2]), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0) cclcexpanded = cclc.unsqueeze(0) esrganinput = torch.cat([lrimghr, cclcexpanded], dim=1) tildeCHR = esrgan(esrganinput).squeeze(0) # 3. Refine tildeCHR by CEM to get CHR CHR = applycem(tildeCHR.unsqueeze(0), lrimg.unsqueeze(0), blurkernel).squeeze(0) # 4. Upsample rays for viewpoint i and query LR NeRF # Standard volume rendering: generate rays from pose, sample points, # query MLP for color/density, perform alpha compositing to return (3, sH, sW) CLN = rendernerf(lrnerf, pose, resolution=(cclc.shape[1], cclc.shape[2])) # 5. Query HR NeRF with same rays CHN = rendernerf(hrnerf, pose, resolution=(cclc.shape[1], cclc.shape[2])) # 6. Compute loss alpha = alphaschedule(t, numiters) losssr = alpha computel1loss(CLN, CHR) + (1 - alpha) computel1loss(CHN, CHR) lossrange = computerangepenalty(CHR) loss = losssr + lossrange # 7. Train HR NeRF and CCLC optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() if t % 100 == 0: print(f"Iter {t}, Loss: {loss.item()}, Alpha: {alpha}") def rendernerf(nerfmodel, pose, resolution): # Standard volume rendering implementation omitted for brevity. # Generates rays from pose, samples points, queries MLP, composites colors. pass Precision: The CEM formula involves matrix operations (H^T (H H^{-1} H)) which may be sensitive to the properties of the blur kernel H. Boundaries: The range penalty loss handles colors outside [0, 1], but the CEM assumes the LR input is within a valid range. Degenerate Input: If the LR images are extremely noisy or have severe artifacts, the ESRGAN may generate inconsistent details, which the CEM may not fully correct if the LR constraint is weak. Training Time: The method requires significant training time (10 hours for Super-NeRF on a single RTX 3090). Time Complexity: Training involves iterative optimization of the HR NeRF and CCLC. The average training time for Super-NeRF is 10 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Pre-training the LR NeRF takes 30 minutes. Memory Complexity: The method requires storing the LR NeRF, HR NeRF, and CCLC for each view. The LR NeRF is lightweight (1/4 size of HR NeRF). Measured Performance: Super-NeRF achieves 4x super-resolution of NeRFs on various datasets (LLFF, Synthesis360, Blender, FaceScape). Scaling: The method is designed for 4x super-resolution (s=4). Strengths: Generates plausible 3D-consistent HR details without HR ground truth; explores the SR solution space using CCLC for better view consistency compared to NeRF-SR. Limitations: Relies on a pre-trained 2D SR prior (ESRGAN); training time is longer than standard NeRF training. When to use: When HR ground truth is unavailable and high-quality, view-consistent super-resolution of NeRFs is required. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or real-time training is required. Super-NeRF was proposed in the paper "Super-NeRF: View-Consistent Detail Generation for NeRF Super-Resolution". It addresses the limitations of NeRF-SR, which uses a simple linear formulation from LR to HR causing aliasing at edges and relies on HR refinement via per-patch warping. Super-NeRF focuses on generating plausible 3D-consistent HR details based on LR observations only, exploring the SR solution space using CCLC. It was published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence in 2024. name: NARF Training
head: NARF Optimization
body: NARF (Neural Articulated Radiance Field) training optimizes a neural network to represent the radiance field of articulated 3D objects by minimizing photometric and mask errors between rendered images and ground truth inputs. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by incorporating known kinematic pose configurations \{T0, \zeta, \theta\} into the rendering pipeline, allowing the model to disentangle geometry from articulation. Among its variants, Disentangled NARF (NARFD) is preferred for its balance of computational efficiency and ability to generate segmentation masks, outperforming Part-Wise and Holistic variants in novel pose/view settings. Inputs: Set of training images with known camera poses. Kinematic 3D pose configuration for the articulated object: global rigid transformation T0, bone parameters \zeta, and joint angles \theta. Ground truth pixel colors \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) and foreground masks \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r}). Outputs: Rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and mask \hat{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{r}) for each ray \mathbf{r}. Optimized network parameters \Theta. Data Structures: NARF Model: A single Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) mapping spatial coordinates and viewing directions to density \sigma, feature vector \mathbf{h}, and color C. Selector S (NARFD only): A set of P lightweight sub-networks, one for each object part. Each sub-network O\Gamma^i is a two-layer MLP with 10 hidden nodes. Input: Local 3D position \mathbf{x}^i and bone parameter \zeta. Output: Logit o^i, normalized to probability p^i via softmax. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Randomly sample a batch of camera rays \mathcal{R} from all pixels. 2. Hierarchical Sampling: For each ray, query N samples using the hierarchical volume sampling strategy from original NeRF. 3. Coordinate Transformation: For each sample at global position \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{d}, compute local coordinates for each part i using the known kinematic pose \{T0, \zeta, \theta\}: \mathbf{x}^i = R^{i-1}(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}^i), \quad \mathbf{d}^i = R^{i-1}\mathbf{d} where R^{i-1} and \mathbf{t}^i are the rotation and translation of part i. 4. Positional Encoding: Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to inputs. Dimensions are set to 10 for 3D location \mathbf{x} and 4 for other parameters (directions, bone parameters). 5. Selector Probability (NARFD only): For each part i, compute the probability p^i that \mathbf{x} belongs to part i: O\Gamma^i: (\gamma(\mathbf{x}^i), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta})) \rightarrow (o^i), \quad p^i = \frac{\exp(o^i)}{\sum{k=1}^P \exp(o^k)}. 6. Network Forward Pass: Construct the input vector by concatenating the masked local features. For each part i, mask the encoded local position and direction with the selector probability p^i: \text{Input}\sigma = \text{Cat}(\{\gamma(\mathbf{x}^i) p^i \mid i \in [1, P]\}, \gamma(\zeta)) \text{Input}c = \text{Cat}(\mathbf{h}, \{(\gamma(\mathbf{d}^i) p^i, \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}^i) p^i) \mid i \in [1, P]\}) where \mathbf{h} is the intermediate feature vector from the density network. Query the NARF model to obtain density \sigma, feature \mathbf{h}, and color C. 7. Volume Rendering: Render the color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and mask \hat{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray using standard volume rendering equations (Eq. 5 and Eq. 16 in). 8. Loss Computation: Compute the total squared error loss: \mathcal{L} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + \|\hat{\mathbf{M}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 where \mathbf{C} and \mathbf{M} are ground truth color and foreground mask. 9. Optimization: Update network parameters using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def posenc(x, dim): # Standard positional encoding expanding x to dim dimensions return x # Conceptual representation; actual implementation uses sin/cos frequencies def concatenate(vectors): return [val for vec in vectors for val in vec] def transformtolocalpart(xglobal, partidx, poses): R = poses.rotation(partidx) t = poses.translation(partidx) return [sum(R[j][k] (xglobal[k] - t[k]) for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] def transformdirection(dglobal, partidx, poses): R = poses.rotation(partidx) return [sum(R[j][k] dglobal[k] for k in range(3)) for j in range(3)] def softmax(logits): m = max(logits) exps = [math.exp(l - m) for l in logits] s = sum(exps) return [e / s for e in exps] def volumerender(tvals, sigma, color, mask): T = 1.0 renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] renderedmask = 0.0 for i in range(len(tvals)): ti = tvals[i] tprev = tvals[i-1] if i > 0 else tvals[0] - 0.5 dist = ti - tprev alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[i] dist) weight = T alpha renderedcolor = [renderedcolor[j] + weight color[i][j] for j in range(3)] renderedmask += weight mask[i] T = (1.0 - alpha) return renderedcolor, renderedmask def trainnarf(batchrays, poses, gtcolors, gtmasks, nerfmodel, selector=None, numsamples=64): totalloss = 0.0 numparts = len(poses.parts) if hasattr(poses, 'parts') else (len(selector) if selector else 1) for ray, gtcolor, gtmask in zip(batchrays, gtcolors, gtmasks): # 1. Hierarchical sampling (standard NeRF strategy) tvals = [ray.originnorm + i 0.5 for i in range(numsamples)] samples = [(t, [ray.origin[j] + t ray.direction[j] for j in range(3)]) for t in tvals] # 2. Transform coordinates & compute selector probabilities probs = [] if selector is not None: for i in range(numparts): xlocal = transformtolocalpart(samples[0][1], i, poses) logit = selector[i].forward(posenc(xlocal, 10), posenc(poses.zeta, 4)) probs.append(logit) probs = softmax(probs) sigmalist, colorlist, masklist = [], [], [] for t, xglobal in samples: sigmainputs = [] colorinputs = [] for i in range(numparts): xlocal = transformtolocalpart(xglobal, i, poses) dlocal = transformdirection(ray.direction, i, poses) # Masked inputs per Eq 22 & 23 sigmainputs.append([v probs[i] for v in posenc(xlocal, 10)]) colorinputs.append([v probs[i] for v in posenc(dlocal, 4)]) sigmainputvec = concatenate(sigmainputs + [posenc(poses.zeta, 4)]) sigma, h = nerfmodel.forwardsigma(sigmainputvec) colorinputvec = [h] + colorinputs color = nerfmodel.forwardcolor(concatenate(colorinputvec)) sigmalist.append(sigma) colorlist.append(color) masklist.append(1.0) # Standard foreground mask assumption # 3. Volume Rendering renderedcolor, renderedmask = volumerender(tvals, sigmalist, colorlist, masklist) # 4. Loss colorloss = sum((c - g)2 for c, g in zip(renderedcolor, gtcolor)) maskloss = (renderedmask - gtmask)2 totalloss += colorloss + maskloss return totalloss / len(batchrays) Parameters: Positional encoding dimension for 3D location \mathbf{x}: 10. Positional encoding dimension for other parameters (directions, bone parameters): 4. Number of samples per ray N: Not given in the sources. Selector network architecture: Two-layer MLP with 10 hidden nodes per part. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Input Concatenation: Although irrelevant parts are masked, the input remains a concatenation of all parts. This is intentional to allow the single NeRF to distinguish different bones via the dimensions of the concatenated vector, similar to part identity encoding. Selector Output: The selector outputs probabilities for all parts, even if a location belongs to only one. The softmax ensures normalization. An approach that shares the merits of both Part-Wise NARF (NARFP) and Holistic NARF (NARFH) while avoiding their weaknesses by introducing a selector S to identify which object part a global 3D location belongs to. It uses lightweight sub-networks to output part probabilities, which mask the concatenated inputs to the main NeRF. It outperforms other methods under all evaluation metrics and test data settings, exhibiting high performance under novel pose and/or novel view settings with low computational cost close to a single NeRF model. Time Complexity: Computational cost is close to a single NeRF model, as it uses one unified network rather than separate networks per part. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of elements to preserve during forward propagation per ray, which is similar to a single NeRF. Performance: NARFD outperforms NARFP and NARFH under all evaluation metrics and test data settings. It shows slight performance drop on SSIM (within 4%) in novel pose/view settings but maintains high performance. Strengths: Avoids the zero density problem of NARFH; satisfies Part Dependency unlike NARFH; generates segmentation masks; low computational cost. Limitations: Requires known kinematic 3D pose configuration \{T0, \zeta, \theta\}. When to use: When reconstructing articulated 3D objects with known kinematics and requiring efficient training with segmentation capabilities. When not to use: When kinematic poses are unknown or when the object is not articulated. NARF was introduced in the paper "Neural Articulated Radiance Field". It addresses the challenge of representing articulated 3D objects by combining neural radiance fields with kinematic models. The method was developed to overcome the limitations of Part-Wise and Holistic NARF approaches, offering a disentangled representation that is both efficient and accurate. name: Regularization and Priors
body: Regularization and Priors augment the training objective with auxiliary constraints to enforce physical plausibility, stabilize optimization, and mitigate geometric ambiguities in neural radiance fields. This family addresses issues such as scale ambiguity in material decomposition, instability in dynamically growing networks, and overfitting to noisy observations. It modifies the loss landscape or network outputs directly, contrasting with sibling methods like Learning Rate Scheduling or Adam Optimisation with Adaptive Scaling that adjust the optimization trajectory. Not given in the sources. Balances photometric and uncertainty losses across multiple training stages to stabilize dynamically growing networks. Sets itself apart by tying loss weights to a multi-resolution progression rather than applying static priors. Choose when training adaptive, multi-stage radiance fields. Enforces physical plausibility by decoupling rendered color into material reflectance and shading. Solves unstable material properties in novel view synthesis and object insertion. Distinguishes itself by regularizing intermediate decomposition components to mitigate scale ambiguity. Choose when handling complex lighting or inserted objects. Imposes piece-wise smoothness constraints on rendered depth from unobserved rays to stabilize joint optimization of blur kernels and radiance fields in sparse-view DeRF. Integrates "hidden rays" from estimated blur kernels alongside unseen rays, targeting coupled defocus and geometry uncertainty. Choose for sparse-view deblurring scenarios. Transfers texture information from 2D pre-deblurred priors to the implicit 3D radiance field via feature-space matching to address 3D geometric inconsistency in sparse-view deblurring. Operates on high-level perceptual features rather than pixel values or geometric derivatives. Choose when deblurring NeRFs trained on sparse views. Applies constraints to rendering weights and volume densities to correct inaccurate geometry caused by small camera motion, operating without SfM point clouds. Designed for minimal camera movement regimes where traditional multi-view stereo fails. Choose when camera motion is small and SfM is unreliable. Optimizes neural fields for high-resolution 3D reconstruction from sparse-view measurements (e.g., X-ray CT) by integrating a learned regularizer directly into the optimization loop. Leverages the RED framework to decouple the conditioning network from optimization, using pre-trained denoisers as implicit priors. Choose for sparse-view tomography or ill-posed inverse reconstruction. A technique to anneal proposal weights by raising them to a power that increases from 0 to 1 over training steps, encouraging exploration by presenting a wider range of proposal intervals early in training. The annealed weight \hat{\mathbf{w}}n at step n (out of N total steps) is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{w}}n \propto \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\frac{bn/N}{(b-1)n/N+1}} where b is the bias hyperparameter. In experiments, b=10 is used. Ablating this annealing causes SSIM on the bicycle scene to decrease from 0.687 to 0.679. Approximates the posterior distribution of network parameters as a multivariate Gaussian centered at the optimal weights \omega^, using the inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior as the covariance matrix. The covariance is derived as \Sigma = -H(\omega^)^{-1}. Directly applying this to NeRF parameters is impracticable due to high parameter correlation, making accurate covariance estimation challenging, and the expensive sampling overhead. A self-supervised regularization technique that shifts the grouping of samples along the ray to assess each point in multiple ways using different groups, imposing consistency on the results. The head index k of the first group is shifted by s towards the camera, where s is randomly sampled from \{1, \dots, Np-1\} during training. Padding samples are added before the front sample to handle indices exceeding the original range (i' < 1 or j' > N). The shifted MIMO function maps shifted group positions to outputs: f{\text{MIMO}}^{\text{shift}}: (\mathbb{R}^3)^{Np} \times \mathbb{S}^2 \rightarrow (\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^+)^{Np}, where (\mathbf{x}{i'}, \dots, \mathbf{x}{j'}, \mathbf{d}) \mapsto (\mathbf{c}{i'}, \dots, \mathbf{c}{j'}, \sigma{i'}, \dots, \sigma{j'}). Choose when implementing MIMO-NeRF to reduce ambiguity in sample grouping. Weight annealing was introduced in mip-NeRF 360 to improve proposal network training stability. Intrinsic decomposition priors (reflectance/shading) were developed to handle lighting variations and object insertion. Uncertainty-aware losses in multi-scale training address the instability of dynamically growing architectures. Bayesian approaches using Laplace approximation have been explored for uncertainty quantification but face scalability issues. Group shift was proposed in MIMO-NeRF to reduce ambiguity in sample grouping. name: Multi-scale Joint Training Parameters
head: Multi-scale joint training loss weights
body: Multi-scale joint training parameters define the weighting scheme for combining losses across different spatial resolutions or training stages in radiance field optimization. This method addresses the instability of optimizing high-frequency details before coarse geometry is established by balancing mean squared error (MSE) and uncertainty-based losses with specific coefficients. It is distinct from single-scale training by explicitly decoupling the contribution of fidelity and uncertainty metrics across a hierarchy of network depths or image pyramids. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Per-stage output images, per-stage uncertainty maps, and hyperparameters \beta1, \beta2. Outputs: A scalar total loss value \mathcal{L} for the current training iteration. Data Structures: Loss Components: For each stage i (where i \in \{1, \dots, D\}), the method requires: \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i: The Mean Squared Error between the rendered image and the ground truth image at stage i. \mathcal{L}{unct}^i: The uncertainty loss at stage i, derived from the network's predicted uncertainty volume. Parameters: D: The current number of stages or network growth levels. \beta1: Weight for the MSE loss. \beta2: Weight for the uncertainty loss. Steps: 1. Initialize the total loss \mathcal{L} = 0. 2. Iterate through each stage i from 1 to D: a. Compute \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i for the rendered output of stage i. b. Compute \mathcal{L}{unct}^i for the uncertainty output of stage i. c. Accumulate the weighted loss: \mathcal{L} \leftarrow \mathcal{L} + \beta1 \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i + \beta2 \mathcal{L}{unct}^i. 3. Return \mathcal{L}. Formulas: The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \sum{i=1}^D \left( \beta1 \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i + \beta2 \mathcal{L}{unct}^i \right) Where: D is the current number of stages (also equal to D-1 times the network growth count). \mathcal{L}{MSE}^i is the MSE loss of the output image of layer i. \mathcal{L}{unct}^i is the uncertainty loss of the output image of layer i. \beta1 and \beta2 are the joint training weights. Parameters: \beta1 = 1.0 \beta2 = 0.1 The uncertainty loss \mathcal{L}{unct} typically corresponds to a probabilistic formulation such as -\log \sigma or a similar divergence term depending on the specific implementation of the uncertainty volume, though the exact functional form is not specified in the source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stage Count: The number of stages D is dynamic in Recursive-NeRF, growing as the network densifies. The loss summation must adapt to the current D. Uncertainty Definition: The source does not specify the exact mathematical definition of \mathcal{L}{unct}^i beyond it being an "uncertainty loss". Implementers must refer to the specific uncertainty modeling technique used in the parent method (e.g., aleatoric or epistemic uncertainty estimation). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemultiscalejointloss(renderedimages, uncertaintymaps, beta1=1.0, beta2=0.1): """ Computes the multi-scale joint training loss. Args: renderedimages: List of rendered images for each stage i=1..D. uncertaintymaps: List of uncertainty maps for each stage i=1..D. beta1: Weight for MSE loss. beta2: Weight for uncertainty loss. Returns: Total scalar loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 numstages = len(renderedimages) for i in range(numstages): # Compute MSE loss for stage i # Assuming ground truth images are available via a global reference or passed separately # For the purpose of this self-contained function, we assume a helper exists or # the caller computes the difference. Here we denote the MSE calculation. mselossi = computemse(renderedimages[i], groundtruthimages[i]) # Compute uncertainty loss for stage i # The specific formula for uncertainty loss is not detailed in # Placeholder for the specific uncertainty loss function (e.g., negative log likelihood) unctlossi = computeuncertaintyloss(uncertaintymaps[i]) # Accumulate weighted loss stageloss = beta1 mselossi + beta2 unctlossi totalloss += stageloss return totalloss def computemse(rendered, groundtruth): return torch.mean((rendered - groundtruth) 2) def computeuncertaintyloss(uncertaintymap): # Generic placeholder. In Recursive-NeRF, this likely involves the predicted # variance or uncertainty volume. The exact formulation is not in. # A common implementation for uncertainty loss is -log(sigma) or similar. # Since the source does not specify, this function must be implemented # according to the specific uncertainty model used in the broader context. raise NotImplementedError("Uncertainty loss formula not specified in source ") A coarse-to-fine training scheme that uses different camera intrinsic parameters to construct an image pyramid, enhancing multi-scale feature learning. It sets itself apart by reconfiguring the intrinsic matrix K for each layer of the pyramid rather than just downsampling the image. Choose this when multi-view consistency is critical and the scene requires stable gradient-based optimization across scales. Definition: Constructs a 4-layer image pyramid with downsampling factors S = \{2^{k-1} \mid k = 4, 3, 2, 1\} by reconfiguring the focal length f and principal point c in the intrinsic matrix K. Steps: 1. Construct the pyramid with downsampling factors S = \{1, 2, 4, 8\}. 2. For each layer s \in S, reconfigure the intrinsic matrix K's as: K's = \begin{bmatrix} f/s & 0 & cx/s \\ 0 & f/s & cy/s \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} 3. Assign matched multi-view settings Ms = \{M4, M3, M2, M1\} to each layer, where larger downsampling factors use more views for stronger constraints. 4. Run only a few thousand iterations per stage for the first three coarse stages (s=8, 4, 2). 5. Start fine training (s=1) to refine details. Parameters: S: Set of downsampling factors \{1, 2, 4, 8\}. The largest factor s=8 is empirically sufficient. Pitfalls: Excessively large downsampling factors lead to blurry ground truth, decreasing fidelity and increasing refinement difficulty. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of stages D and the number of pixels in the rendered images. The cross-intrinsic variant adds overhead for intrinsic matrix reconfiguration and multiple training stages. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the storage of intermediate rendered images and uncertainty maps for all active stages. Performance: In Recursive-NeRF, this weighting scheme supports dynamic network growth, allowing efficient resource allocation by focusing uncertainty on complex regions. In MVGS, it stabilizes multi-view optimization by enforcing constraints at coarser scales first. Strengths: Prevents overfitting to high-frequency noise in early training stages; balances fidelity and uncertainty modeling. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \beta1 and \beta2; the cross-intrinsic method requires managing multiple camera setups and image pyramids. When to use: When training radiance fields or Gaussian splats that involve multi-scale representations or dynamic network growth. When not to use: For single-scale, static networks where multi-view consistency is not a primary concern or where uncertainty modeling is not employed. The concept of multi-scale joint training parameters originates from Recursive-NeRF, which introduced a dynamically growing NeRF architecture. The specific weights \beta1=1.0 and \beta2=0.1 were established to balance MSE and uncertainty losses in this recursive framework. The related cross-intrinsic guidance scheme was proposed in MVGS (Multi-view-regulated Gaussian Splatting) to address multi-view consistency issues in 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging image pyramids and intrinsic parameter adjustments. name: Multi-stage Training Protocol
head: Pretrain and Joint Train Strategy
body: Multi-stage training protocols decompose complex inverse rendering or radiance field optimization into sequential phases to stabilize convergence and ensure logical dependency between network components. Unlike single-stage end-to-end training, which can suffer from gradient conflicts or poor initialization in coupled systems, this method isolates the learning of geometric priors (albedo, normals, depth) before introducing appearance or lighting variables. It is distinct from standard NeRF training by enforcing a strict hierarchy of feature learning, ensuring that coarse geometry is established before high-frequency details or complex lighting models are optimized. The protocol consists of a sequence of optimization phases. The specific steps depend on the architectural variant (e.g., inverse rendering vs. UV-volume human modeling), but the general logic follows a "Pretrain -> Joint -> Refine" pattern. Inputs: Training images (LDR or HDR), camera poses, and optionally semantic or geometric priors (e.g., SMPL bounds, visible surface volumes). Outputs: Optimized network weights for all modules (Direct Prediction, Lighting, Re-prediction, UV volumes, NTS) and the final rendered images or inverse rendering results (albedo, normals, depth, lighting). The data structures vary by variant. 1. Inverse Rendering Variant: Direct Prediction Module (h{DP}): Predicts intermediate outputs (\tilde{A}, \tilde{N}, \tilde{D}) for albedo, normal, and depth. Lighting Joint Prediction Module: Predicts lighting \hat{L} based on inputs from h{DP}. Joint Re-prediction Module: Refines (\tilde{A}, \tilde{N}, \tilde{D}). Final Outputs: Joint predictions (\hat{A}, \hat{N}, \hat{D}, \hat{L}) and intermediate outputs (\tilde{A}, \tilde{N}, \tilde{D}). 2. UV Volume Variant: UV Volumes: Coarse geometry representation. Neural Texture Stack (NTS): High-frequency detail representation. Ray Sampling: 64 points sampled along each camera ray between near/far bounds estimated by SMPL. The following steps describe the general progression, with specific details for each variant in the Subtopics section. 1. Pretrain Geometric Priors: Train the modules responsible for coarse geometry (albedo, normal, depth) independently or with a subset of the loss. This ensures reasonable initial values for subsequent modules that depend on these properties. 2. Joint Train Core Modules: Unfreeze and jointly train the geometric modules and the primary appearance/lighting modules using a multi-task loss function. 3. Refine/Re-predict: Freeze the weights of the previously trained modules and train a dedicated refinement module (e.g., Joint Re-prediction) to correct errors in the geometric outputs. 4. End-to-End Finetune: Jointly finetune all modules end-to-end using the full multi-task loss on both intermediate and final outputs to resolve any inconsistencies introduced by freezing. Multi-task Loss for Inverse Rendering: L = \lambdaA L{albedo} + \lambdaN L{normal} + \lambdaD L{depth} + \lambdaL L{light} + \lambda{visible} L{visible} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambda{rerender} L{rerender} Where \lambda are hyperparameters balancing the different loss terms. Learning Rate Decay for UV Volume Variant: The learning rates for UV volumes and NTS decay exponentially over epochs: l{uv} = 1 \times 10^{-3} \gamma{250}^{\text{epoch}} l{nts} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \gamma{1000}^{\text{epoch}} Where \gamma = 1 \times 10^{-1} is the decay rate. Note: The sources specify different base epochs for the decay start or normalization (250 vs 1000) in the exponents, implying a piecewise or distinct decay schedule for each branch. Optimizer: Adam. Ray Sampling: 64 points per ray. Volume Resolution: 128^3 for initialized visible surface volume and predicted VSG lighting. Hardware: Single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Training Duration: ~200k iterations (~20 hours) for 26-view videos of 100 frames at 960x540 resolution. Dependency Violation: In the inverse rendering variant, the Lighting Joint Prediction Module depends on the albedo/normal/depth outputs. Training them simultaneously from scratch can lead to poor convergence if the geometric priors are not reasonable. UV Volume Warm-start: In the UV volume variant, NTS optimization is ineffective if UV volumes are not warmed up first, as NTS relies on a coarse geometry to fit high-frequency signals. Precision: The sources do not specify floating-point precision requirements, but standard practice suggests FP32 for training stability. MobileNeRF Staged Training is a three-stage optimization protocol that sequentially trains the geometry, acceleration structures, and appearance networks of the MobileNeRF representation. It decouples joint optimization into phases with adaptive ray marching to stabilize convergence. Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train is a method that constructs a multi-resolution ground feature plane representation for large urban scenes, capturing density and appearance separately to reduce memory footprint and guide subsequent NeRF sampling. It differs from standard NeRF training by decoupling the initial scene representation into a compact, low-rank tensor factorization (the grid branch) that is pre-trained before joint optimization with a full 3D NeRF branch. This approach leverages the planar nature of urban environments to achieve robust performance with sparse view data. The UV Volume Training Strategy uses two distinct optimization strategies for UV volumes and the Neural Texture Stack (NTS) branch. UV volumes are learned primarily in early stages to warm-start coarse geometry, while NTS is optimized later to fit high-frequency signals. The learning rates decay exponentially: l{uv} = 1 \times 10^{-3} \gamma{250}^{\text{epoch}} and l{nts} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \gamma{1000}^{\text{epoch}}, with \gamma = 1 \times 10^{-1}. Ray sampling uses 64 points along camera rays between SMPL-estimated bounds. Training takes approximately 20 hours (200k iterations) on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU for 26-view videos of 100 frames at 960x540 resolution. Time Complexity: The multi-stage approach increases total training time due to sequential phases, but reduces the risk of divergence and the need for extensive hyperparameter tuning for joint optimization. Memory Complexity: Depends on the variant. The inverse rendering variant uses a 128^3 volume. The UV volume variant uses UV volumes and NTS, with memory optimized for real-time rendering. Strengths: Stabilizes convergence for complex, coupled models (e.g., lighting + geometry); ensures geometric priors are reasonable before appearance optimization; allows for specialized learning rates for different components. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of when to freeze/unfreeze modules; may not be necessary for simpler radiance field models that do not have strong inter-component dependencies. When to Use: When training inverse rendering models with separate lighting and geometry predictors, or when using UV-based representations where coarse geometry must precede fine detail. When Not to Use: For standard NeRF training without explicit inverse rendering components or UV mappings, where end-to-end training is sufficient. The Multi-stage Training Protocol originates from research in inverse rendering and human performance modeling. The inverse rendering variant was introduced in "Learning Indoor Inverse Rendering with 3D Spatially-Varying Lighting" (2021) to handle the coupling between albedo, normal, depth, and lighting predictions. The UV volume variant was introduced in "UV Volumes for Real-time Rendering of Editable Free-view Human Performance" (2023) to address the challenges of rendering editable human performances with high-frequency details. These methods address the instability of jointly optimizing geometric and photometric properties in complex neural representations.
