name: MobileNeRF Staged Training
head: MobileNeRF Training Stages
body: MobileNeRF Staged Training is a three-stage optimization protocol that sequentially trains the geometry, acceleration structures, and appearance networks of the MobileNeRF representation. It decouples joint optimization into phases with adaptive ray marching to stabilize convergence. The method optimizes the MobileNeRF representation through three distinct training stages, interleaved with specific acceleration grid optimization steps. The representation consists of a regular-grid mesh \mathbf{M} defined by vertices \mathbf{V}, an acceleration grid \mathbf{G}, and three Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): an opacity MLP with parameters \theta{OpacityMLP} (also denoted \thetaA), a features MLP with parameters \theta{FeaturesMLP}, and a shader MLP with parameters \theta{ShaderMLP}. Inputs: Training images, camera poses, initial vertex positions \mathbf{V}, initial acceleration grid \mathbf{G}, initial MLP parameters, and scene type (synthetic 360°, forward-facing, or unbounded 360°). Outputs: Optimized vertices \mathbf{V}, acceleration grid \mathbf{G}, and MLP parameters \theta{OpacityMLP}, \theta{FeaturesMLP}, \theta{ShaderMLP}. Vertices (\mathbf{V}): Defines the geometry of the regular-grid mesh \mathbf{M}. Acceleration Grid (\mathbf{G}): A 3D grid of size P \times P \times P used to prune voxels during ray marching. MLPs: Three separate networks for opacity, features, and shading. wd: Weight for the distance loss \mathcal{L}{dist}. Synthetic 360° scenes: 0.0. Forward-facing scenes: 0.01. Unbounded 360° scenes: 0.001. w{g1}, w{g2}: Weights for sparse and smooth grid losses. Value is 10^{-5} for both. \tauG: Threshold for pruning voxels in the acceleration grid. Value is 0.1. P: Grid dimension for the P \times P \times P acceleration grid and mesh intersections. 1. Initialization: Initialize vertices \mathbf{V}, acceleration grid \mathbf{G}, and MLP parameters \theta{OpacityMLP}, \theta{FeaturesMLP}, \theta{ShaderMLP} using standard initialization. 2. Stage 1 (First Quarter): Optimize \mathbf{V}, \theta{OpacityMLP}, \theta{FeaturesMLP}, and \theta{ShaderMLP} to minimize \mathcal{L}{Color} + wd \mathcal{L}{dist} + \mathcal{L}{v}. Concurrently optimize \mathbf{G} to minimize \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{bnd} + w{g1} \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{sparse} + w{g2} \mathcal{L}{Grid}^{smooth}. During ray marching, \mathbf{G} is inaccurate, so the algorithm keeps all 3P intersected voxels and intersection points regardless of \tauG. 3. Stage 2 (Next Quarter): Optimize \mathbf{V}, \theta{OpacityMLP}, \theta{FeaturesMLP}, and \theta{ShaderMLP} to minimize \mathcal{L}{Color}^{stage2} + wd \mathcal{L}{dist} + \mathcal{L}{v}. Optimize \mathbf{G} using the same grid loss as Stage 1. During ray marching, use \mathbf{G} with threshold \tauG=0.1 to prune empty voxels, keeping at most 3P/2 non-empty voxels and the 3P/2 intersection points closest to the camera. Double the training batch size. 4. Stage 3 (Rest of Training): When the loss converges, fix \mathbf{V}, \theta{OpacityMLP} (\thetaA), and \mathbf{G}. Optimize only \theta{FeaturesMLP} and \theta{ShaderMLP} to minimize \mathcal{L}{Color}^{bin}. During ray marching, keep at most 3P/4 non-empty voxels and intersection points. Double the training batch size again. For unbounded 360° scenes, compute intersections for concentric boxes and keep all of them throughout the process. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mobilenrfstagedtraining(images, poses, P, tauG, scenetype): # Initialize parameters using standard initialization (e.g., small random values) V =... G =... thetaOpacityMLP =... thetaFeaturesMLP =... thetaShaderMLP =... # Set distance loss weight based on scene type if scenetype == "synthetic360": wd = 0.0 elif scenetype == "forwardfacing": wd = 0.01 elif scenetype == "unbounded360": wd = 0.001 else: wd = 0.0 wg1 = 1e-5 wg2 = 1e-5 totaliterations =... # Not given in the sources. quarter = totaliterations // 4 batchsize =... # Not given in the sources. for iteration in range(totaliterations): # Determine ray marching strategy based on training progress if iteration < quarter: # Stage 1: First quarter. G is inaccurate. maxvoxels = 3 P maxintersections = 3 P usegridpruning = False elif iteration < 2 quarter: # Stage 2: Next quarter. Use G to prune. maxvoxels = 3 P // 2 maxintersections = 3 P // 2 usegridpruning = True batchsize = batchsize 2 else: # Stage 3: Rest of training. maxvoxels = 3 P // 4 maxintersections = 3 P // 4 usegridpruning = True batchsize = batchsize 2 # Unbounded scenes exception: keep all intersections if scenetype == "unbounded360": maxvoxels = None maxintersections = None usegridpruning = False # Sample rays from images and poses for the current batch rays =... # Standard ray sampling from camera poses # Render colors and depths using MobileNeRF forward pass colors, depths =... # Standard volume rendering or rasterization forward pass # Compute losses based on stage if iteration < 2 quarter: if iteration < quarter: # Stage 1 loss loss =... # Standard color loss (e.g., MSE) + wd distance loss + volume loss else: # Stage 2 loss loss =... # Modified color loss + wd distance loss + volume loss # Update all parameters using gradient descent V, thetaOpacityMLP, thetaFeaturesMLP, thetaShaderMLP =... # Standard optimizer step # Optimize Grid G lossgrid =... # Boundary loss + wg1 sparse loss + wg2 smooth loss G =... # Standard optimizer step for G else: # Stage 3: Post-convergence. Fix V, thetaOpacityMLP, G loss =... # Binarized color loss # Update only features and shader MLPs using gradient descent thetaFeaturesMLP, thetaShaderMLP =... # Standard optimizer step return V, G, thetaOpacityMLP, thetaFeaturesMLP, thetaShaderMLP Inaccurate Grid Early On: In the first quarter, the acceleration grid \mathbf{G} is not reliable. Failing to disable pruning or keep all 3P intersections will lead to missing geometry and poor convergence. Batch Size Scaling: The batch size must be doubled when the number of kept intersections is halved to maintain stable gradient statistics. Unbounded Scenes: Standard pruning logic fails for concentric boxes in unbounded 360° scenes; all intersections must be retained. Texture Constraints: Mobile hardware requires texture sizes to be powers of 2 and at most 4096 \times 4096. Large texture images must be split into multiple tiles. The core training objective minimizes \mathcal{L}{Color} + wd \mathcal{L}{dist} + \mathcal{L}{v} with respect to vertices \mathbf{V}, opacity MLP parameters \theta{OpacityMLP}, features MLP parameters \theta{FeaturesMLP}, and shader MLP parameters \theta{ShaderMLP}. This objective is used in the first stage. The distance loss weight wd varies by scene type, and the loss terms include color, distance, and volume components. Time Complexity: The regular-grid mesh \mathbf{M} provides an efficient way for computing intersections between a ray and the mesh of size P \times P \times P in O(P) complexity. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Stabilizes training by decoupling geometry/acceleration from appearance refinement. Adapts ray marching efficiency based on training progress. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of stage transitions and batch size scaling. The acceleration grid optimization adds complexity. When to Use: When training MobileNeRF and standard joint optimization fails to converge due to geometry/acceleration instability. MobileNeRF was introduced in the MobileNeRF paper. The staged training protocol is part of its optimization procedure. name: Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train
head: Grid Branch Pre-training, Stage 1 Training
body: Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train is a method that constructs a multi-resolution ground feature plane representation for large urban scenes, capturing density and appearance separately to reduce memory footprint and guide subsequent NeRF sampling. It differs from standard NeRF training by decoupling the initial scene representation into a compact, low-rank tensor factorization (the grid branch) that is pre-trained before joint optimization with a full 3D NeRF branch. This approach leverages the planar nature of urban environments to achieve robust performance with sparse view data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of calibrated images and camera poses for a large urban scene. Outputs: Pre-trained multi-resolution density and appearance feature grids (\mathcal{G}\sigma, \mathcal{G}c) used to initialize the joint training stage. Data Structures: The method uses a multi-resolution feature grid composed of density and appearance tensors at various resolutions n. For a specific resolution n, the tensors are constructed from low-rank components: \mathbf{v}{\sigma, r}^{z}: A vector along the z-axis for density component r. \mathbf{M}{\sigma, r}^{xy}: A matrix in the xy-plane for density component r. \mathbf{v}{c, r}^{z}: A vector along the z-axis for appearance component r. \mathbf{M}{c, r}^{xy}: A matrix in the xy-plane for appearance component r. R\sigma: Number of density components. Rc: Number of appearance components. Formulas: The density and appearance tensors at resolution n are obtained by concatenating outer products of z-axis vectors and xy-plane matrices: \mathcal {G}{\sigma }^n = \oplus [ (\mathbf {v}{\sigma, r}^{z} \circ \mathbf {M}{\sigma,r}^{xy})]{R\sigma }, \quad \mathcal {G}{c}^n = \oplus [(\mathbf {v}{c, r}^{z} \circ \mathbf {M}{c,r}^{xy})]{Rc} where \circ denotes the outer product and \oplus denotes concatenation over the R\sigma and Rc dimensions. Positional Encoding (PE) uses Fourier features: \text{PE}(x) = (\sin(x), \cos(x), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1}x), \cos(2^{L-1}x)) Parameters: Positional Encoding Frequency: The highest frequency is set to 2^{15}. Components: 8 components for density and 16 for appearance. Resolutions: The method uses a highest resolution feature plane plus downsampled resolutions at \times 4 and \times 16. MLP Head: A small MLP with 2 fully connected layers of 128 hidden units and ReLU activation is used as the output head for the grid branch. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Initial learning rate of 0.02 for tensor factors and 0.01 for MLP layers. Batch Size: 4096 rays. Pre-training Iterations: 10,000 iterations. Steps: 1. Scene Capture: Construct a pyramid of feature planes at the pre-train stage. 2. Coarse Sampling: Perform coarse sampling of ray points (64 samples per ray). 3. Feature Interpolation: Interpolate features from the multi-resolution feature grids at sampled point locations. 4. Prediction: Predict radiance values (density \sigma and color c) through a shallow MLP renderer (grid branch) using interpolated features and positional encoding. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute MSE loss between predicted volumetrically integrated pixel colors and ground truth. 6. Optimization: Update tensor factors and MLP weights to minimize loss using Adam optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pretraingridbranch(images, poses, numiterations=10000): # Initialize multi-resolution feature grids # Resolutions: base, base/4, base/16 # Density: 8 components, Appearance: 16 components Gsigma = initmultiresgrid(resolutions=[1.0, 0.25, 0.0625], numcomponents=8, type='density') Gc = initmultiresgrid(resolutions=[1.0, 0.25, 0.0625], numcomponents=16, type='appearance') # Initialize shallow MLP for grid branch (2 FC layers, 128 hidden, ReLU) gridmlp = initmlp(inputdim=158, hiddendim=128, numlayers=2) # Optimizer groups: tensor factors lr=0.02, MLP layers lr=0.01 optimizer = Adam([ {'params': list(Gsigma.values()) + list(Gc.values()), 'lr': 0.02}, {'params': gridmlp.parameters(), 'lr': 0.01} ]) for iteration in range(numiterations): rays = samplerays(images, poses, numrays=4096, coarsesamples=64) points = rays.origin + rays.direction rays.sampledistances featuressigma = interpolatefeatures(Gsigma, points) featuresc = interpolatefeatures(Gc, points) pepos = fourierpositionalencoding(points, maxfreq=15) inputtomlp = np.concatenate([featuressigma, featuresc, pepos], axis=-1) sigmapred, cpred = gridmlp.forward(inputtomlp) colorpred = volumetricrender(rays, sigmapred, cpred) gtcolors = getpixelcolors(rays, images) loss = mseloss(colorpred, gtcolors) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return Gsigma, Gc def initmultiresgrid(resolutions, numcomponents, type): grids = {} for res in resolutions: v = np.random.randn(numcomponents, 1, 128) M = np.random.randn(numcomponents, 1, 1, 128) grids[res] = {'v': v, 'M': M} return grids def interpolatefeatures(grid, points): features = [] for res, factors in grid.items(): vz = factors['v'] Mxy = factors['M'] xycoords = points[:,:2] res zcoords = points[:, 2] Minterp = bilinearinterpolate(Mxy, xycoords) vinterp = linearinterpolate(vz, zcoords) compfeatures = [] for r in range(vz.shape[0]): feat = np.outer(vinterp[r], Minterp[r]) compfeatures.append(feat) features.append(np.concatenate(compfeatures, axis=-1)) return np.concatenate(features, axis=-1) def initmlp(inputdim, hiddendim, numlayers): layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): ind = inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim w = np.random.randn(ind, hiddendim) 0.01 b = np.zeros(hiddendim) layers.append({'w': w, 'b': b}) return {'layers': layers} def samplerays(images, poses, numrays, coarsesamples): # Standard ray generation from camera poses and image grid origins = np.random.rand(numrays, 3) directions = np.random.rand(numrays, 3) directions /= np.linalg.norm(directions, axis=1, keepdims=True) sampledistances = np.random.rand(numrays, coarsesamples) return type('Rays', (), {'origin': origins, 'direction': directions, 'sampledistances': sampledistances})() def fourierpositionalencoding(points, maxfreq): scales = [2i for i in range(maxfreq)] encoded = [] for scale in scales: encoded.append(np.sin(points scale)) encoded.append(np.cos(points scale)) return np.concatenate(encoded, axis=-1) def volumetricrender(rays, sigma, c): alphas = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma rays.sampledistances) transmittance = np.cumprod(1.0 - alphas, axis=1) weights = alphas transmittance return np.sum(weights[..., np.newaxis] c, axis=1) def getpixelcolors(rays, images): # Standard image sampling at ray pixel coordinates return np.random.rand(rays.origin.shape[0], 3) def mseloss(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target) 2) def bilinearinterpolate(grid, coords): # Standard bilinear interpolation implementation return np.random.rand(coords.shape[0], grid.shape[1], grid.shape[2]) def linearinterpolate(grid, coords): # Standard linear interpolation implementation return np.random.rand(coords.shape[0], grid.shape[1]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Urban Scene Assumption: The method relies on the assumption that large urban scenes are grounded on the xy-plane. Precision: The use of Fourier features with high frequencies (2^{15}) requires careful handling of numerical precision during optimization. A staged training approach for mobile devices, focusing on efficiency and quantization, whereas Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train focuses on large-scale urban scenes and tensor factorization. The parent method that encompasses Multi-resolution Feature Grid Pre-train as its first stage. Time Complexity: The pre-training stage takes approximately 10,000 iterations, which is roughly 1/5 of the total training time (100k iterations for joint optimization). Memory Complexity: The low-rank tensor factorization significantly reduces the memory footprint compared to full 3D grids. For example, using 8/16 components for density/appearance with multi-resolution planes is more compact than the 16/48 components used in the TensoRF baseline. Performance: The method achieves robust performance on large urban scenes with sparse view data. Strengths: Reduced memory footprint, robustness to sparse views, suitability for large urban scenes. Limitations: Assumption of planar scene structure. The method was introduced in "Grid-guided Neural Radiance Fields for Large Urban Scenes". It builds on the observation that large urban scenes are primarily grounded on the xy-plane, allowing for efficient representation using 2D feature planes and 1D vectors. The approach is inspired by tensor factorization techniques like those used in TensoRF. name: Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors
head: Intrinsic Priors, Mean Reflectance Regularization, Shading Smoothness
body: Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors enforce physical plausibility in neural radiance fields by decoupling the rendered color into material reflectance (intrinsic to the surface) and shading (dependent on illumination and viewpoint). This method solves the problem of unstable or physically inconsistent material properties in novel view synthesis, particularly when inserting objects into scenes or handling complex lighting. It distinguishes itself from standard photometric priors by explicitly regularizing the intermediate decomposition components—reflectance and shading—rather than just the final pixel values, thereby mitigating scale ambiguity and ensuring consistent brightness levels across different scenes or inserted objects. The method augments the primary photometric reconstruction loss with specific regularization terms targeting the decomposed reflectance \mathbf{R} and shading \mathbf{S} fields. Inputs: \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}): Reflectance vector at ray \mathbf{r} (typically RGB). \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}): Shading scalar or vector at ray \mathbf{r}. \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}): Surface normal at ray \mathbf{r}. \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{r}): 3D position of the sample point on ray \mathbf{r}. \beta{avg,r}: Target mean reflectance hyperparameter. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{mean,r}: Mean reflectance regularization loss. \mathcal{L}s: Shading smoothness loss. \mathcal{L}{sn}: Shading-Normal consistency loss. The network outputs two primary channels per sample point: 1. Reflectance \mathbf{R}: A 3-channel vector (RGB) representing the material albedo. 2. Shading \mathbf{S}: A scalar or 3-channel vector representing the illumination factor. In the context of the mean reflectance loss, \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max refers to the maximum value among the three RGB channels of the reflectance vector. 1. Mean Reflectance Regularization (\mathcal{L}{mean,r}) This term constrains the reflectance magnitude to prevent unreasonable brightness changes, ensuring that inserted objects match the scene's brightness level. \mathcal{L}{mean,r} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left| (\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max) - \beta{avg,r} \right| \mathcal{R}: The set of sampled rays in the current batch. \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}).max: The maximum value across the RGB channels of the reflectance vector \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{r}). \beta{avg,r}: A hyperparameter representing the target average reflectance. The source sets this to 0.6 for most scenes. |\mathcal{R}|: The number of rays in the batch. 2. Shading Smoothness Loss (\mathcal{L}s) This term enforces spatial coherence in the shading field, reducing noise in the estimated illumination. \mathcal{L}s = \text{Var}(\{\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}) \mid \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}\}) Defined as the variance of shading values for all pixels (or sampled points) in a single batch. 3. Shading-Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{sn}) This term leverages the correlation between shading and surface normals to enforce local smoothness, weighted by geometric proximity and orientation. \mathcal{L}{sn} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \omegan(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') \cdot |\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{r}')| \cdot (1 - \tanh(\text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'))) \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}': Rays/samples. The summation iterates over \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R} and aggregates contributions from neighboring samples \mathbf{r}'. \omegan(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'): A weight measuring the cosine similarity between the surface normals \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}) and \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}'). \text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'): The Euclidean distance between the 3D points associated with rays \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{r}'. The term (1 - \tanh(\text{Dis}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}'))) acts as a distance decay factor, giving higher weight to closer points. 4. Total Training Loss The priors are combined with other intrinsic priors (chromaticity \mathcal{L}{chro}, sparsity \mathcal{L}{rs}, non-local sparsity \mathcal{L}{nrs}) and the base photometric loss \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L}{train} = \lambda0 \mathcal{L} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}d + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{mean,r} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{chro} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{rs} + \lambda5 \mathcal{L}{nrs} + \lambda6 \mathcal{L}s + \lambda7 \mathcal{L}{sn} \lambdai: Adjustable weights for each loss term. \mathcal{L}d: A decomposition loss term. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeintrinsicpriors(reflectancebatch, shadingbatch, normalsbatch, positionsbatch, betaavgr=0.6): """ Computes the Reflectance and Shading Decomposition Priors losses. Args: reflectancebatch: list of [r, g, b] floats for N rays. shadingbatch: list of floats for N rays. normalsbatch: list of [nx, ny, nz] floats for N rays. positionsbatch: list of [x, y, z] floats for N rays. betaavgr: Float, target mean reflectance (default 0.6). Returns: dict: Loss values for mean reflectance, shading smoothness, and shading-normal consistency. """ N = len(reflectancebatch) # 1. Mean Reflectance Regularization # R(r).max is the max value across the RGB channels for each ray maxreflectance = [max(rgb) for rgb in reflectancebatch] lmeanr = sum(abs(m - betaavgr) for m in maxreflectance) / N # 2. Shading Smoothness Loss # Variance of shading for all pixels in the batch means = sum(shadingbatch) / N ls = sum((s - means) 2 for s in shadingbatch) / N # 3. Shading-Normal Consistency Loss # Sum over rays r in R, comparing with neighbors r' lsn = 0.0 for i in range(N): r = positionsbatch[i] rnorm = normalsbatch[i] si = shadingbatch[i] pairsum = 0.0 for j in range(N): if i == j: continue rprime = positionsbatch[j] rprimenorm = normalsbatch[j] sj = shadingbatch[j] # Dis(r, r') is Euclidean distance dist = math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(r, rprime))) # omegan measures cosine similarity of normals dotprod = sum(a b for a, b in zip(rnorm, rprimenorm)) normi = math.sqrt(sum(a 2 for a in rnorm)) normj = math.sqrt(sum(a 2 for a in rprimenorm)) cossim = dotprod / (normi normj) if (normi normj) > 1e-8 else 0.0 # Shading difference sdiff = abs(si - sj) # Distance decay factor: (1 - tanh(Dis(r, r'))) decay = 1.0 - math.tanh(dist) pairsum += cossim sdiff decay lsn += pairsum lsn /= N return { "lmeanr": lmeanr, "ls": ls, "lsn": lsn } Scale Ambiguity: There is an inherent scale ambiguity between shading and reflectance; scaling reflectance by k and shading by 1/k yields the same observed image. The mean reflectance regularization helps constrain this by fixing the brightness level of reflectance, ensuring inserted objects match the scene's shading brightness. Sampling Sparsity: In scenes with large backgrounds and small objects, sampling points on objects may be sparse, leading to missing details or artifacts if not handled by specialized sampling strategies (e.g., segmented sampling). Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The value of \beta{avg,r} is critical. The source recommends 0.6 for most scenes, but this may need adjustment for scenes with significantly different average brightness. Strengths: Produces smoother normal maps and more physically plausible material properties, especially in complex scenes. Enables consistent object insertion by aligning shading levels. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of estimated normals and sampling density. Sparse sampling on small objects can degrade performance. This method originates from the work on "Relighting Scenes With Object Insertions in Neural Radiance Fields". It adapts traditional intrinsic image decomposition constraints (chromaticity, sparsity, non-local sparsity) into the NeRF backbone to improve the quality of rendered images and enable novel view synthesis with inserted objects. name: Surface Smoothness Regularization
head: Depth Smoothness Regularization, Surface Smoothness on Integrated Unobserved Rays
body: Surface Smoothness Regularization imposes piece-wise smoothness constraints on rendered depth from unobserved rays to alleviate spatial ambiguity and stabilize the joint optimization of blur kernels and radiance fields in sparse-view DeRF. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF regularization by integrating "hidden rays" derived from the estimated blur kernel alongside standard "unseen rays," specifically targeting the coupled uncertainty of defocus and geometry. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of target camera poses \{Pi^{\text{target}}\}, an estimated blur kernel h, and the current radiance field parameters. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{ss} added to the total training objective. Data Structures Target Poses: Pi^{\text{target}} = [Ri^{\text{target}} | ti^{\text{target}}] \in \text{SE}(3). Sampled Poses: SP, a set of camera poses [R|t]. Integrated Unobserved Rays: r{iu}, a union of hidden rays rq and unseen rays r{us}. Depth Map: \hat{d}, computed per ray. Color Map: \hat{C}, computed per ray. Step-by-Step Method 1. Define Sample Space for Unseen Rays: Determine the bounding box for camera translation t based on target poses: t{\min} = \min(\{ti^{\text{target}}\}), \quad t{\max} = \max(\{ti^{\text{target}}\}) Sample translation t within [t{\min}, t{\max}]. 2. Compute Mean Focus Point: Calculate the mean focus point \bar{p}f by solving a least squares problem to find the central point of the scene. 3. Sample Camera Rotation: Calculate the normalized mean over the up axes of all target poses, denoted \bar{p}u. Sample a rotation matrix R using: SR|t = \{R(\bar{p}u, \bar{p}f + \epsilon, t) \mid \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.125)\} where \epsilon is a small jitter value added to the focus point to ensure the camera roughly focuses on the scene center. 4. Generate Unseen Rays (r{us}): Form the set of sampled camera poses: SP = \{[R|t] \mid R \sim SR|t, t \sim St\} Generate rays r{us} from these poses. 5. Generate Hidden Rays (rq): Derive rays rq from the estimated blur kernel h. The kernel transforms rays to approximate the color composition process of the blur. These rays are defined as: rq \sim h(r) where r represents the main rays. These hidden rays provide supplementary information exclusively present in blurry inputs. 6. Form Integrated Unobserved Rays: Combine the two sets: r{iu} = \{rq, r{us}\} Note that r{us} remains unchanged during training, while rq changes as the blur kernel h is optimized. 7. Compute Expected Depth and Color: For each ray r \in r{iu}, compute the expected depth \hat{d} and color \hat{C}: \hat{d} = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t))t \, dt \hat{C} = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(r(t))c(r(t)) \, dt where \sigma is density and c is color. 8. Calculate Weighted Depth Differences: For a patch of size S{ptc} \times S{ptc} centered at ray r{i,j}, compute horizontal and vertical weighted depth differences: \Delta \hat{d}x(r{i,j}) = \omega{i+1,j} (\hat{d}(r{i+1,j}) - \hat{d}(r{i,j}))^2 \Delta \hat{d}y(r{i,j}) = \omega{i,j+1} (\hat{d}(r{i,j+1}) - \hat{d}(r{i,j}))^2 The weights \omega are based on pixel-wise color difference: \omega{i+k,j+l} = \exp(-|\hat{C}(r{i,j}) - \hat{C}(r{i+k,j+l})|) This ensures smoothness is enforced where colors are similar, preserving edges. 9. Compute Loss: Sum the differences over all rays in r{iu} and all positions in the patch: \mathcal{L}{ss}\{r{iu}\} = \sum{r \in r{iu}} \sum{i,j=1}^{S{ptc}-1} (\Delta \hat{d}x(r{i,j}) + \Delta \hat{d}y(r{i,j})) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def computesurfacesmoothnessloss(targetposes, blurkernel, radiancefield, patchsize): """ Computes the Surface Smoothness Regularization loss. Args: targetposes: List of SE(3) poses [R|t] used for training. blurkernel: The current estimated blur kernel h. radiancefield: The radiance field model (NeRF/DeRF). patchsize: Integer size of the depth patch for smoothness calculation. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # 1. Define sample space for translations tmin = min(t for, t in targetposes) tmax = max(t for, t in targetposes) # 2. Compute mean focus point # Standard least-squares fit to scene center is used. pf = solveleastsquaresfocus(targetposes) # 3. Compute mean up axis upaxes = [R[:, 2] for R, in targetposes] # Third column of rotation matrix pu = [sum(axis) / len(axis) for axis in zip(upaxes)] norm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in pu)) pu = [x / norm for x in pu] # 4. Generate unseen rays unseenrays = [] numunseensamples = 100 # Sample count not specified in sources for in range(numunseensamples): t = [random.uniform(tmin[k], tmax[k]) for k in range(3)] epsilon = random.gauss(0, 0.125) R = computerotation(pu, [pf[k] + epsilon for k in range(3)], t) unseenrays.append((R, t)) # 5. Generate hidden rays hiddenrays = [] for R, t in targetposes: rq = transformbyblurkernel((R, t), blurkernel) hiddenrays.append(rq) # 6. Integrated unobserved rays integratedrays = hiddenrays + unseenrays # 7-9. Compute loss over patches totalloss = 0.0 # Assume rays are projected to a 2D grid of size patchsize x patchsize for i in range(1, patchsize - 1): for j in range(1, patchsize - 1): idx = i patchsize + j raycurr = integratedrays[idx] dcurr, ccurr = radiancefield.integrate(raycurr) # Horizontal neighbor (i+1, j) idxh = (i + 1) patchsize + j rayh = integratedrays[idxh] dh, ch = radiancefield.integrate(rayh) wh = math.exp(-abs(ccurr - ch)) totalloss += wh (dh - dcurr)2 # Vertical neighbor (i, j+1) idxv = i patchsize + (j + 1) rayv = integratedrays[idxv] dv, cv = radiancefield.integrate(rayv) wv = math.exp(-abs(ccurr - cv)) totalloss += wv (dv - dcurr)2 return totalloss def solveleastsquaresfocus(poses): # Implementation depends on scene geometry; typically returns mean of target positions. return [sum(t[k] for, t in poses) / len(poses) for k in range(3)] def computerotation(upaxis, focuspoint, cameracenter): # Standard look-at matrix construction forward = [focuspoint[k] - cameracenter[k] for k in range(3)] norm = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in forward)) forward = [x / norm for x in forward] right = [upaxis[1]forward[2] - upaxis[2]forward[1], upaxis[2]forward[0] - upaxis[0]forward[2], upaxis[0]forward[1] - upaxis[1]forward[0]] normr = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in right)) right = [x / normr for x in right] up = [right[1]forward[2] - right[2]forward[1], right[2]forward[0] - right[0]forward[2], right[0]forward[1] - right[1]forward[0]] return [[right[0], up[0], -forward[0]], [right[1], up[1], -forward[1]], [right[2], up[2], -forward[2]]] def transformbyblurkernel(ray, kernel): # Applies kernel-induced perturbation to ray origin/direction return ray Parameters Jitter Standard Deviation: 0.125 for the normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 0.125). Patch Size (S{ptc}): Not given in the sources. Number of Unseen Ray Samples: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Blur Kernel Convergence: Hidden rays rq depend on the blur kernel h and change during training. Boundary Conditions: The summation limits i,j=1 to S{ptc}-1 imply that boundary rays in the patch do not contribute to the loss in the same way, or require padding. Precision: Computing depth integrals and exponential weights requires stable numerical integration to avoid gradient instability during backpropagation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Stabilizes joint optimization of blur and geometry in sparse-view DeRF; alleviates spatial ambiguity by leveraging unobserved rays. Limitations: Relies on accurate estimation of the blur kernel for hidden rays; requires careful sampling of the camera pose space. When to Use: Sparse-view DeRF training where spatial ambiguity is high and blur kernel optimization is coupled with radiance field optimization. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of Deblurred Neural Radiance Fields (DeRF) from sparse views. The method was introduced in "Sparse-DeRF: Deblurred Neural Radiance Fields From Sparse View" (2025) to address the difficulty of regularizing complex joint optimization in DeRF, where standard NeRF regularization fails. It builds on the concept of using unseen rays for regularization as seen in RegNeRF [6], but extends it with blur-kernel-derived hidden rays. name: Perceptual Distillation Module
head: Perceptual Loss for Deblurred Radiance Fields
body: The Perceptual Distillation Module (PDM) is a regularization technique for deblurring Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) trained on sparse views. It addresses the 3D geometric inconsistency inherent in independently deblurred multi-view images by using pre-deblurred images as a perceptual prior. The module transfers texture information from 2D deblurred priors to the implicit 3D radiance field via feature-space matching. The module augments the training loss by comparing features extracted from rendered patches against features extracted from pre-deblurred versions of the input blurry images. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Blurry training images I, camera poses, the current NeRF model (MLPs for color and density), a pre-trained image deblurring network \ThetaD, and a pre-trained feature extractor E. Outputs: A scalar perceptual loss value \mathcal{L}{pd} used for backpropagation. Data Structures Patch Rays (r{pd}^{ptc}): A set of rays sampled from the training view frustum corresponding to a specific image patch. Deblurred Image Patch (\bar{C}{ptc}): A 2D image patch of size S{ptc}^{pd} \times S{ptc} extracted from the pre-deblurred image \bar{I}. Rendered Color Patch (\hat{C}{ptc}): A 2D image patch rendered from the NeRF using rays r{pd}^{ptc}. This rendering is performed without the blur kernel to produce "clean" radiance. Feature Maps (\hat{\phi}{ptc}, \bar{\phi}{ptc}): Multi-channel feature tensors extracted from \hat{C}{ptc} and \bar{C}{ptc} respectively. Numbered Steps 1. Generate Pre-deblurred Images: For each blurry training image I, compute the deblurred image \bar{I} using the pre-trained deblurring network \ThetaD: \bar{I} = \ThetaD(I) \quad 2. Sample Patch Rays: On the training views, sample a set of rays r{pd}^{ptc} that correspond to a patch of size S{ptc}^{pd} \times S{ptc} in the image plane. 3. Render Clean Patch: Render the color patch \hat{C}{ptc} from the sampled rays r{pd}^{ptc} using the NeRF MLPs. Crucially, this rendering does not apply the blur kernel, producing a "patch radiance". 4. Extract Features: Pass both the rendered patch \hat{C}{ptc} and the corresponding deblurred image patch \bar{C}{ptc} (extracted from \bar{I}) through the shared pre-trained feature extractor E: \hat{\phi}{ptc} = E(\hat{C}{ptc}) \quad \bar{\phi}{ptc} = E(\bar{C}{ptc}) \quad Here, E denotes the deterministic feature extractor network, not a statistical expectation operator. 5. Compute Perceptual Loss: Calculate the L2 norm between the extracted feature maps: \mathcal{L}{pd} = ||\hat{\phi}{ptc} - \bar{\phi}{ptc}||2^2 \quad Parameters Patch Dimensions: The source specifies S{ptc}^{pd} = 8 and S{ptc} = 64, yielding 8 \times 64 patches. Perceptual Loss Weight (\lambda{pd}): The weight applied to \mathcal{L}{pd} in the total loss function. Set to 0.01. Deblurring Network (\ThetaD): MPRNet. Feature Extractor (E): VGG19. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perceptualdistillationloss( blurryimage: Tensor, rays: List[Ray], nerfmodel: NeRFModel, deblurringnet: Module, featureextractor: Module, patchdims: tuple = (8, 64), lambdapd: float = 0.01) -> Tensor: # Step 1: Generate deblurred image Ibar = ThetaD(I) deblurredimage = deblurringnet(blurryimage) # Step 2 & 3: Render clean patch Chatptc from rays using NeRF MLPs without blur kernel renderedpatch = nerfmodel.render(rays) # Returns tensor of shape (patchheight, patchwidth, 3) # Step 2 (continued): Extract corresponding deblurred image patch Cbarptc from Ibar # Ray origins map to pixel coordinates; we slice the deblurred image accordingly h, w = patchdims origin = rays[0].origin x, y = int(origin.x), int(origin.y) deblurredpatch = deblurredimage[y:y+h, x:x+w,:] # Step 4: Extract features phihatptc = E(Chatptc) and phibarptc = E(Cbarptc) # VGG19 requires input normalization (mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]) renderedfeatures = featureextractor(renderedpatch) deblurredfeatures = featureextractor(deblurredpatch) # Step 5: Compute perceptual loss Lpd = ||phihatptc - phibarptc||2^2 perceptualloss = sum((renderedfeatures - deblurredfeatures) 2) # Return weighted loss return lambdapd perceptualloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Geometric Inconsistency: The method relies on the assumption that the 2D deblurred image \bar{I} contains valid texture information consistent with the 3D scene. Patch Alignment: The rays r{pd}^{ptc} must precisely correspond to the spatial location of \bar{C}{ptc} in \bar{I}. Feature Normalization: VGG19 requires specific input normalization (mean/std). Failure to normalize \hat{C}{ptc} and \bar{C}{ptc} identically will result in meaningless feature differences. Time Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of patch rays sampled per iteration. Requires forward passes through \ThetaD and E per patch. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-deblurred images \bar{I} or computing them on the fly. The feature extractor E (VGG19) is large, but only features for small patches are computed. Strengths: Effectively transfers high-frequency texture details from 2D priors to 3D fields, mitigating the blurriness and artifacts common in sparse-view deblurring. Limitations: Depends heavily on the quality of the pre-trained deblurring network \ThetaD and the feature extractor E. When to use: Sparse-view deblurring scenarios where geometric consistency is compromised by independent 2D deblurring. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Perceptual Distillation Module was introduced in the context of Sparse-DeRF (Deblurred Neural Radiance Fields From Sparse View). It addresses the problem of camera motion blur in sparse view settings, where traditional NeRF optimization fails to recover sharp details due to insufficient angular coverage and blur. The method is described as a "first attempt" at utilizing pre-deblurred images as an additional prior in deblurring radiance fields. It builds upon the observation that independently deblurred multi-view images suffer from 3D geometric inconsistency, which can be alleviated by distilling texture information from these 2D priors into the 3D field. The implementation uses MPRNet for deblurring and VGG19 for feature extraction, standard choices in perceptual loss literature. name: NeRF Training with Depth Distribution Regularization
head: DDR for NeRF
body: Depth Distribution Regularization (DDR) is a constraint applied to rendering weights and volume densities to correct inaccurate scene geometry representation caused by small camera motion. Unlike methods such as DS-NeRF that rely on Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds, DDR operates without point cloud data, avoiding geometric errors when SfM fails on small camera motion inputs. It is specifically designed for scenarios where camera movement is minimal, a regime where traditional multi-view stereo often fails to produce reliable depth priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of images with small camera motion; initial camera poses (optional, if optimizing); volume density and color fields (NeRF). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters and camera poses; novel views with corrected geometry. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard NeRF representation: \sigma(x, t): Volume density at position x and time t. c(x, t, d): View-dependent color at position x, time t, and viewing direction d. wi: Rendering weight for sample i, defined as wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)), where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the distance between samples. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF network and camera parameters. If initial poses are unknown, they are treated as trainable parameters. 2. Rendering: For each training image, render the color using standard volume rendering integration along rays. 3. Weight Distribution Analysis: Compute the rendering weights wi for all samples along each ray. The distribution of these weights indicates the perceived depth and opacity of the scene. 4. Regularization Application: Apply the Depth Distribution Regularization loss \mathcal{L}{DDR} to constrain the rendering weights and volume densities. The specific mathematical formulation of \mathcal{L}{DDR} is not explicitly detailed in the provided sources, but it acts as a prior to ensure the weight distribution aligns with expected geometric consistency for small motion baselines. 5. Joint Optimization: Simultaneously optimize the NeRF network parameters and the camera parameters to improve robustness against small camera motion inputs. 6. Visualization (Optional): A dedicated visualization method is applied during training to monitor the spatial distribution of rendering weights, allowing for diagnostic inspection of the regularization effect. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainneRFwithDDR(images, initialposes, numiterations): # Initialize NeRF network and camera parameters nerfmodel = InitializeNeRF() cameraparams = initialposes.clone().requiresgrad(True) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Select a batch of images and corresponding poses batchimages, batchposes = SampleBatch(images, cameraparams) # Render images using current NeRF and poses renderedimages, renderingweights = Render(batchimages, batchposes, nerfmodel) # Compute photometric loss lossphoto = ComputePhotometricLoss(renderedimages, batchimages) # Compute Depth Distribution Regularization loss # The exact formula for LDDR is not provided in the source text # It constrains rendering weights and volume densities lossddr = ComputeDDRLoss(renderingweights, nerfmodel.densities) # Total loss loss = lossphoto + lambdaddr lossddr # Backpropagate and update loss.backward() Optimizer.step() Optimizer.zerograd() # Optional: Visualize weight distribution for debugging if iteration % debuginterval == 0: VisualizeWeightDistribution(renderingweights) return nerfmodel, cameraparams Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Significant Occlusions: Scenes with significant occlusions where foreground objects move minimally leave background areas unobserved, causing artifacts or gaps in novel views. Mitigation: hierarchical scene representations or generative models. Non-opaque Objects: Large regions of non-opaque objects (e.g., flames) cause inaccurate rendering weight distributions, producing artifacts in novel views. Densely Thin Geometry: Densely thin geometry causes depth maps to lack accuracy, resulting in artifacts in novel views. Mitigation: a more accurate depth prediction network. Motion Blur: Fast-moving objects introduce motion blur into input frames, causing blurry artifacts around moving parts in novel views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Experimental results on the NVIDIA dataset show the proposed depth constraint method outperforms alternative depth constraint methods when handling small camera motion inputs. Strengths: Does not rely on SfM point clouds, which often fail or contain significant errors with small camera motion. Effective at capturing and representing scene geometry information effectively even when SfM fails. Limitations: Performs poorly in extreme scenarios: significant occlusions with minimal foreground movement, large regions of non-opaque objects, densely thin geometry, and scenes with motion blur from fast-moving objects. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Dynamic View Synthesis From Small Camera Motion Videos". History: It addresses the specific problem of space-time novel view synthesis from small camera motion inputs, where traditional methods relying on SfM point clouds (like DS-NeRF) suffer from inaccurate scene geometry representation. Usage: Evaluated on the NVIDIA dataset to simulate small camera motion; point clouds from this dataset are used to compute depth constraints for comparative methods like DS-NeRF. name: Neural Field Regularization by Denoising (NEF-RED)
head: NeF-RED, RED-based neural field optimization
body:
NEF-RED is a method for optimizing neural fields to reconstruct high-resolution 3D volumes from sparse-view measurements, specifically targeting X-ray Computed Tomography (CT). It solves the problem of ill-posed inverse reconstruction by integrating a learned regularizer directly into the neural field optimization loop, avoiding the computational overhead of two-stage approaches that generate synthetic projections before pixel-basis reconstruction. Unlike sibling methods that rely on explicit smoothness priors or perceptual distillation, NEF-RED leverages the Regularization by Denoising (RED) framework to decouple the conditioning network from the neural field optimization, allowing the use of pre-trained denoisers as implicit priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of measurements b \in \mathbb{R}^m (where m \ll n), a forward operator A (e.g., Radon Transform for CT), and a pre-trained denoiser network D	heta. Outputs: Optimized neural field parameters \hat{\Phi} representing the reconstructed volume. Data Structures: Neural Field F\Phi: A function mapping 3D coordinates to scalar values. In this implementation, it uses the Instant-NGP architecture. Domain: X \subset \mathbb{R}^3 (positions within the projection area). Range: \mathbb{R} (attenuation value). Formula: F\Phi: X ightarrow \mathbb{R}. Reconstruction Grid X{grid}: A finite set of voxel coordinates in the reconstruction grid, size n 	imes 3. Denoiser D	heta: A convolutional neural network (CNN) trained for artifact removal or denoising. Blocks: A set S = \{fk\} of all possibly overlapping regular blocks of size p (where p \ll n) within the volume. Formulas: 1. Data Fidelity Term: L(f) =  rac{1}{2} \|Af - b\|2^2 where A is the forward operator, f is the object representation, and b is the measurement. 2. Regularization Term (RED): The regularization potential ho(f) is defined such that its gradient is approximated by the denoiser residual: 
abla ho(f) = f - D(f) This holds if D is differentiable with a symmetric Jacobian and locally homogeneous, or converges if D is nonexpansive. 3. Optimization Objective: \hat{\Phi} = \arg \min\Phi L(F\Phi(X{grid})) + \lambda R(F\Phi(X{grid})) where \lambda > 0 is the relaxation weight. 4. Update Step: f^{(k+1)} = f^{(k)} - 	au 
abla L(f^{(k)}) - \lambda H(f^{(k)}) where H(f) = f - D	heta(f) and 	au > 0 is the step size parameter. Parameters: \eta: Learning rate for the Adam optimizer (\eta > 0). \lambda: Relaxation weight for the regularization term (\lambda > 0). 	au: Step size parameter for the gradient descent update (	au > 0). l: Number of rays sampled per step (l \ll m). p: Size of the regular block sampled for regularization (p \ll n). Algorithm Steps: The optimization uses a randomized coordinate gradient procedure to handle high-resolution grids (e.g., 1024^3) where full gradient computation is infeasible. 1. Initialization: Set learning rate \eta > 0, relaxation weight \lambda > 0, and initialize neural field parameters \Phi0 randomly. 2. Iteration Loop: For each step j = 1, 2, \dots: a. Sample Rays: Sample l rays uniformly at random from the total m rays. b. Sample Block: Sample a block of coordinates Xk uniformly at random from the set of all possible overlapping blocks S. c. Data Fidelity Gradient: Compute the gradient of the data fidelity term with respect to \Phij using the sampled rays. Since the forward operator A can be separated into m single ray-integration operators, the gradient is estimated stochastically: 
abla{\Phij} L(F{\Phij}(X{grid})) \approx  rac{1}{l} \sum{s=1}^l 
abla{\Phij} L{is}(F{\Phij}(X{grid})) where L{is}(f) = \|A{is} f - bi\|2^2. d. Regularization Step: Compute the RED update step on the sampled block fk (where fk corresponds to F{\Phij}(Xk)): Hj(F{\Phij}(Xk)) = fk - D	heta(fk) Note: This computes the residual on the block rather than the full volume. e. Update Parameters: Update \Phi using the Adam optimizer with the computed gradients and the regularization residual: \Phi{j+1} \leftarrow 	ext{Adam}(
abla L(F{\Phij}(X{grid})), Hj(F{\Phij}(Xk)), \Phij, \eta, \lambda). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: measurementsb: Array of sparse measurements (size m). forwardoperatorA: Function or object representing the forward operator (e.g., Radon Transform). denoiserDtheta: Pre-trained denoiser network Dtheta. neuralfieldF: Instant-NGP neural field instance with parameters Phi. gridcoordsXgrid: Array of voxel coordinates (n x 3). numraysm: Total number of available rays. numsampledraysl: Number of rays to sample per step (l << m). blocksizep: Size of the block for regularization (p << n). learningrateeta: Learning rate for Adam. relaxationlambda: Weight for the regularization term. numiterations: Total number of optimization steps. Returns: Optimized neural field parameters Phi. """ # Initialize parameters randomly Phi = randominitializeparameters() for j in range(1, numiterations + 1): # 1. Sample l rays at random # Assuming rays are indexed 0 to m-1 sampledrayindices = randomsample(range(numraysm), numsampledraysl) # 2. Sample a block of coordinates Xk at random # Generate all possible blocks of size p from the grid allblocks = generatealloverlappingblocks(gridcoordsXgrid, blocksizep) sampledblockindices = randomsample(range(len(allblocks)), 1)[0] Xk = allblocks[sampledblockindices] # 3. Compute Data Fidelity Gradient # Extract measurements corresponding to sampled rays bsampled = measurementsb[sampledrayindices] # Compute gradient of L(FPhi(Xgrid)) w.r.t Phi # L(f) = 0.5 ||Af - b||^2 # Gradient estimation: (1/l) sum( gradLis) gradL = computestochasticdatafidelitygradient( Phi, neuralfieldF, forwardoperatorA, sampledrayindices, bsampled, gridcoordsXgrid) # 4. Compute Regularization Step Hj # Extract values for the sampled block fk = neuralfieldF.evaluate(Xk, Phi) # Apply denoiser to the block denoisedfk = denoiserDtheta(fk) # H(f) = f - D(f) Hj = fk - denoisedfk # 5. Update Phi using Adam # Note: Hj is computed on a block, but needs to be integrated into the # parameter update. In the source, it is passed to Adam alongside gradL. # The source implies Hj acts as a gradient-like term for the regularization. Phi = adamupdate(Phi, gradL, Hj, learningrateeta, relaxationlambda) return Phi def computestochasticdatafidelitygradient(Phi, F, A, rayindices, bsampled, Xgrid): """ Computes the stochastic gradient of the data fidelity term. L(f) = 0.5 ||Af - b||^2 """ # Evaluate neural field on the full grid to get f ffull = F.evaluate(Xgrid, Phi) # Initialize gradient accumulator gradaccum = zeroslike(Phi) # Sum gradients for each sampled ray for i, rayidx in enumerate(rayindices): # Get the specific ray operator Ais and measurement bi # Ais is the projection of f along ray 'rayidx' # In practice, this involves ray marching through the neural field fray = raymarch(F, rayidx, Phi) # Returns scalar projection value bi = bsampled[i] # Loss for this ray: Lis = 0.5 (fray - bi)^2 # Gradient dLis/dPhi = (fray - bi) d(fray)/dPhi error = fray - bi gradray = raygradient(F, rayidx, Phi) # Gradient of ray projection w.r.t Phi gradaccum += error gradray # Average over l rays gradL = gradaccum / len(rayindices) return gradL def adamupdate(Phi, gradL, Hj, eta, lambdareg): """ Performs Adam update. Note: Hj is a block-level residual. The source algorithm passes it directly to the optimizer step. In a strict implementation, Hj must be mapped back to the full parameter space or the optimizer must support block-wise updates. The source pseudocode implies a direct update: Phi{i+1} <- Adam(gradL, Hj, Phii, eta, lambda) Since Hj is defined on a block, this implies the regularization gradient is applied only to the parameters influencing that block, or Hj is zero-padded. Given the disjoint coordinate estimation, we assume Hj contributes to the gradient for the parameters associated with Xk. """ # Construct full regularization gradient from block residual # This is a simplification; the source states "disjoint coordinate estimation" # meaning we update based on the sampled block. # For the purpose of this self-contained pseudocode, we assume # the optimizer handles the combination of the full gradient and the # block-specific regularization term. # Combined gradient for Adam # The source uses lambda in the update step. # Standard RED update: f - tau gradL - lambda H # Here, we use Adam which adapts the step size. # We approximate the full regularization gradient by zero-padding Hj # to the size of Phi, assuming Hj only affects parameters in Xk. gradreg = zeropadtophisize(Hj, Xk, Phi) combinedgrad = gradL + lambdareg gradreg # Standard Adam step Phi = adamstep(Phi, combinedgrad, eta) return Phi Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cone-Beam Geometry: Unlike parallel-beam geometries, cone-beam rays intersect the object non-axially, preventing independent evaluation of the forward model on different slices. This prevents coordinate-friendly partitioning of the problem. Theoretical Convergence: Because of the cone-beam geometry and the non-linearity of the neural field w.r.t \Phi, the method deviates from Block Coordinate RED conditions. Theoretical convergence guarantees are lost, but empirical convergence to a fixed point is observed. Denoiser Assumptions: The gradient formula 
abla ho(f) = f - D(f) assumes D is differentiable with a symmetric Jacobian and locally homogeneous. While CNNs often do not strictly respect the symmetric Jacobian assumption, convergence is still observed if the denoiser is nonexpansive. Time Complexity: The method uses stochastic sampling for both data fidelity (l rays) and regularization (1 block), making each iteration significantly faster than full-grid updates. However, the neural field evaluation (Instant-NGP) and ray marching are computationally intensive per sample. Memory Complexity: NEF-RED is memory-efficient compared to two-stage methods (like IntraTomo or CoIL) because it avoids storing synthetic projections and performing pixel-basis reconstruction. It allows the entire pipeline to run on a single GPU, even for high-resolution volumes (1024^3). Performance: Quantitatively, NEF-RED is either better or on par with state-of-the-art methods regarding reconstruction quality on sparse-view CT datasets (e.g., Cork-CBCT). Strengths: Decouples conditioning from optimization; leverages pre-trained denoisers; single-stage optimization; memory efficient. Limitations: Loss of theoretical convergence guarantees due to non-linear neural field and cone-beam geometry; requires a pre-trained denoiser D	heta. When to use: Sparse-view X-ray CT reconstruction, particularly in industrial inspection with Cone-Beam geometries. When not to use: When theoretical convergence guarantees are required; when parallel-beam geometry allows for simpler block-coordinate updates. NEF-RED was introduced by Romain Vo, Etienne Decencière, and colleagues from Mines Paris, PSL University, and CEA. The method was presented in 2024 at the International Conference on 3D Vision (3DV). It builds upon the Regularization by Denoising (RED) framework proposed by Romano et al. and extends it to neural fields. The work addresses limitations in previous neural field applications for CT, such as IntraTomo and CoIL, which used two-stage approaches. The authors note that leveraging the neural field solution as a prior in a second stage is inefficient, and directly regularizing its optimization yields better results with a lower computation budget. The specific neural field architecture used is Instant-NGP by Müller et al.. name: Warm-start Encoding
head: Temporal Coherency Encoding, Temporal warm-start, Temporally-Coherent Warm-Start Encoder, Warm-start Encoder
body: Warm-start encoding accelerates the training of neural volume representations for animated sparse volumes by initializing the network weights for each frame with the converged weights from the previous frame. It solves the problem of flickering artifacts caused by weight discontinuities in high-frequency details (e.g., thin smoke layers) when using naive cold-start training, while simultaneously reducing encoding time by a factor of 1.5–2.5 compared to independent frame training. Unlike standard cold-start methods, it leverages temporal coherency to preserve smooth transitions across frames. Inputs: A sequence of animated sparse volumes V1, V2, \dots, VN; a target learning rate \eta{\text{target}}; a neural network architecture. Outputs: A sequence of trained neural networks W1, W2, \dots, WN, where Wi encodes volume Vi. Data Structures: W{\text{prev}}: The converged network weights from the previous frame. For the first frame, W{\text{prev}} is initialized using standard random initialization. \eta{\text{current}}: The active learning rate for the current training phase. L1: The final loss of the first frame, used as a stopping threshold for subsequent frames. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set W{\text{prev}} \leftarrow \text{RandomInit}(). Set \eta{\text{current}} \leftarrow \eta{\text{target}}. 2. Iterate Frames: For each frame i from 1 to N: a. Warm-Start Initialization: Initialize the current network weights W{\text{curr}} with W{\text{prev}}. b. First Frame Special Handling: If i == 1: i. Train W{\text{curr}} on V1 using learning rate \eta{\text{target}} until convergence, recording the final loss as L1. ii. Save W1 \leftarrow W{\text{curr}}. iii. Re-process frame 1: Set \eta{\text{fine}} \leftarrow \eta{\text{target}} / 100 (or smaller). Train W1 on V1 using \eta{\text{fine}} until convergence. iv. Update \eta{\text{current}} \leftarrow \eta{\text{fine}}. c. Subsequent Frames: If i > 1: i. Train W{\text{curr}} on Vi using \eta{\text{current}} for a single pass, stopping training iterations when the loss becomes lower than L1. ii. Save Wi \leftarrow W{\text{curr}}. d. Update Previous: Set W{\text{prev}} \leftarrow Wi. 3. Domain Decomposition Exception: If a new domain is added mid-sequence (e.g., via domain decomposition), repeat the "First Frame Special Handling" process for that new domain using \eta{\text{target}} followed by \eta{\text{fine}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def warmstartencode(volumes, targetlr, networkclass): prevweights = None currentlr = targetlr firstframefinalloss = None savednetworks = [] for i, volume in enumerate(volumes): # 1. Initialize network with previous frame's weights if prevweights is None: net = networkclass() net.weights = standardrandominit() # else: net = networkclass() net.weights = prevweights.copy() if i == 0: # 2. First frame: Train with target LR until convergence net.train(volume, lr=targetlr) # Standard training loop firstframefinalloss = net.getloss() # 3. First frame: Re-process with smaller LR to fix flickering finelr = targetlr / 100.0 net.train(volume, lr=finelr) # Standard training loop currentlr = finelr savednetworks.append(net) else: # 4. Subsequent frames: Train once with reduced LR # Stop when loss is lower than first frame's final loss net.train(volume, lr=currentlr, stoploss=firstframefinalloss) savednetworks.append(net) prevweights = net.getweights() return savednetworks Parameters: \eta{\text{target}}: Target learning rate for initial convergence. Typical value: Not given in the sources. \eta{\text{fine}}: Reduced learning rate for re-processing. Value: Up to 100 times smaller than \eta{\text{target}}. Stop Condition: Training iterations stop when loss becomes lower than the first frame's final loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flickering: Naive cold-start encoding with a fixed learning rate causes discontinuities in network weights across frames, leading to flickering, especially in high-frequency details like thin smoke layers. Domain Decomposition: If new domains are added mid-sequence, the warm-start logic must be reset for that domain, re-running the target LR then fine LR process. Defines the basic iteration structure for training. It sets apart from warm-start by handling generic loop control rather than temporal weight initialization. Choose it for standard single-pass or multi-pass training pipelines. Provides mechanisms for dynamic learning rate adjustment and regularization. It sets apart from warm-start by focusing on per-step optimization dynamics rather than frame-to-frame weight coupling. Choose it when training stability requires adaptive scaling. General strategies for adjusting learning rates over time. It sets apart from warm-start by applying global schedules rather than sequence-dependent initialization. Choose it for standard curriculum or decay-based training. Optimizes memory and compute by using lower-precision data types. It sets apart from warm-start by targeting hardware efficiency rather than temporal coherence. Choose it for memory-constrained or high-throughput training. An adaptive optimizer that adjusts step sizes per parameter. It sets apart from warm-start by focusing on gradient normalization rather than initialization state. Choose it for non-convex optimization with sparse gradients. Defines the overall timeline and phase transitions of training. It sets apart from warm-start by managing macro-level phases rather than micro-level weight transfers. Choose it for complex multi-stage training pipelines. Specifies loss functions for high-fidelity reconstruction. It sets apart from warm-start by defining the optimization target rather than the initialization strategy. Choose it when detail preservation is the primary goal. A collection of tailored settings for specific neural volume methods. It sets apart from warm-start by being a category header rather than a specific temporal technique. Choose it for method-specific tuning. Techniques to constrain the solution space and prevent overfitting. It sets apart from warm-start by applying explicit penalties rather than implicit temporal continuity. Choose it when model complexity needs control. A view-based neural rendering method using pixel-aligned implicit functions. It sets apart from warm-start by operating on image-space features rather than volume-space weights. Choose it for novel view synthesis from sparse images. Time Complexity: Accelerates encoding by a factor of 1.5–2.5 compared to cold-start training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the network weights for each frame during sequential processing. Measured Performance: Tested on NVIDIA RTX A40 GPUs and AMD EPYC 7502 CPU. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Ensures temporal coherence; reduces flickering in high-frequency details; speeds up training. Limitations: Sequential dependency (frame i depends on i-1); requires careful LR tuning for the fine step. When to Use: Animated sparse volumes with high-frequency details (e.g., smoke, fire) where temporal coherence is critical. When Not to Use: Static volumes or sequences with no temporal coherence. Introduced in the NeuralVDB paper for encoding time-sequences of animated sparse volumes. It is similar to fine-tuning in transfer learning [Zhou et al. 2017], adapting to a new target without drifting too much from the old one. The method leverages the temporal coherency of input volumes to preserve coherency in output volumes. name: Training Setup and Baselines
body: This family defines reference training protocols for differentiable volume rendering, establishing hyperparameters, optimization strategies, and architectural configurations for radiance field models. It differs from its siblings by covering diverse representations including HDR tone-mapped NeRF [11349-nerf-gt-baseline-training-setup.md], GAN-based radiance fields [12972-stylegan2-training-configuration.md], feature-volume NeRF [13271-nerf-training-setup.md], and light-field baselines [15254-nlr-baseline.md]. All children build on the core differentiable volume rendering pipeline defined in NeRF Training Loop. Establishes a reference protocol for NeRF using HDR inputs, serving as an upper-bound for methods synthesizing HDR from LDR. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly handling dynamic range mismatch via tone-mapping during loss computation. Choose this when evaluating HDR reconstruction capabilities. Defines the training protocol for StyleGAN2-based radiance fields (e.g., StyleNeRF, VoxGRAF). It solves GAN instability in 3D by enforcing R1 regularization, specific learning rate scaling, and removing 2D noise injection to preserve 3D consistency. Choose this for generative 3D-aware models. Describes the configuration for NeRF-based models using Nerfstudio/Instant-NGP, focusing on fast convergence for static scenes. It details Control-NeRF's use of feature volumes instead of raw coordinates for the fine network. Choose this for efficient static scene reconstruction. Implements the Neural Lumigraph Representation (NLR) as a foundational reference for differentiable volume rendering. It differs from standard NeRF by using an architecture optimized for light fields rather than a static MLP. Choose this for meta-learning or light field baselines. Configures training for sparse volume representations using hierarchical neural networks. It addresses the trade-off between noise reduction and computational efficiency in VDB-based rendering. Choose this when high-resolution sparse volume reconstruction is required. Step: Batch sampling strategy is either drawing 2^{16} random samples per epoch, or resampling a subset of input voxels at fixed intervals (100 or 500) and drawing 2^{12} batches per epoch. The resampled subset size equals the resampling intervals multiplied by the batch size. Resampling is used when fine details with thin structures are critical. Parameter: Subdomain size must be a multiple of 512. Too large wastes compute on empty subdomains; too small increases dispatch overhead and causes dominant overlapping halo regions leading to redundant computation. Network width: Level-1 networks use half the width of level-0 networks. Default starting point: level-0 width 128, depth 3. Use 4 layers for volumes requiring more detail capture. Optimizer: Adam with default learning rate 0.001. Decay: 0.975 every 100 epochs (no resampling) or 0.75 every 1,000 epochs (with resampling). Max epochs: 2,500 for non-resampled; more for resampled cases. Comparison: Dense grid training produces the highest noise. Block grid (dense leaf nodes without active masks) reduces noise but still shows visible fog artifacts. Sparse VDB with active voxel masks yields the best visual quality and low noise reconstruction. Configures training for compact real-time radiance fields using a Neural Codebook (NCB). It focuses on efficient storage and fast inference through codebook quantization. Choose this for real-time applications requiring compact representation. Step: Multiply learning rate by 0.3 for every 5,000 iterations. Cast the trained Neural Codebook (NCB) to float16 after training. Parameter: Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.999. Weight decay: 1e-5. Initial learning rate: 5e-3. Total training iterations: 20,000. Batch size: 100,000 voxels. Not given in the sources. name: NeRF-GT Baseline Training Setup
head: NeRF-GT
body: The NeRF-GT baseline establishes a reference training protocol for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) using High Dynamic Range (HDR) inputs, serving as an upper-bound comparison for methods designed to synthesize HDR views from Low Dynamic Range (LDR) inputs. It differs from standard NeRF implementations by explicitly addressing the dynamic range mismatch between HDR scene representations and LDR ground truth observations, utilizing a tone-mapping strategy during loss computation. Unlike the standard NeRF Training Setup which typically assumes consistent exposure, this setup handles the high dynamic range challenges that can lead to poor encoding of scene areas if not managed correctly. The method extends the standard differentiable volume rendering pipeline defined in NeRF Training Loop by modifying the loss computation stage to accommodate HDR-to-LDR comparisons. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of camera poses and corresponding HDR images (or consistently exposed LDR images) representing the scene. Output: A trained NeRF model (MLP) capable of rendering novel views. Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP taking 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input, outputting volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Ray Samples: N points sampled along each ray, with parameters defined below. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Generate rays from the camera poses and sample points along each ray within the scene bounds using the coarse and fine sampling strategies. 2. Network Query: Evaluate the NeRF MLP at each sampled point to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. 3. Volume Rendering: Compute the predicted HDR pixel color for each ray using the discretized volume rendering equation. 4. Tone Mapping: Apply a tone-mapping operator f{TM}(\cdot) to the predicted HDR pixel values to convert them into LDR space. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss (typically Mean Squared Error) between the tone-mapped predicted LDR values and the tone-mapped ground truth LDR views. 6. Optimization: Update the NeRF model parameters using gradient descent. Formulas: The predicted HDR pixel color \hat{\mathbf{C}}{HDR}(\mathbf{r}) is computed as \hat{\mathbf{C}}{HDR}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i. The accumulated transmittance is defined as Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). The tone-mapped prediction is \hat{\mathbf{C}}{LDR} = f{TM}(\hat{\mathbf{C}}{HDR}). The loss is \mathcal{L} = \| \hat{\mathbf{C}}{LDR} - \mathbf{C}{GT, LDR} \|^2. In these formulas, \mathbf{r} is the ray, N is the number of samples, \sigmai is the volume density at sample i, \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples, and \mathbf{c}i is the color at sample i. Parameters: Coarse samples (Nc): 64 samples per ray. Fine samples (Nf): 128 samples per ray. Batch size: 2,048 rays per batch. Resolution: 800 × 600 pixels. Max iterations: 200,000 solver steps. Pitfalls: Training directly on HDR views can fail to encode all areas of a scene well due to the high dynamic range, even when tone-mapped colors are used for loss calculation. This is a critical limitation of the baseline compared to methods that explicitly model exposure or use LDR inputs directly. The standard NeRF baseline serves as the foundational comparison for the NeRF-GT setup. It typically uses LDR inputs with consistent exposure and does not incorporate the HDR-specific tone-mapping loss strategy described in the NeRF-GT baseline. Time Complexity: The training time is approximately 0.40 seconds per iteration. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Rendering time is approximately 32 seconds per frame. Scaling: The method processes 2,048 rays per batch at 800 × 600 resolution. Strengths: Provides an upper-bound performance metric for HDR synthesis tasks by training directly on HDR data. Limitations: Struggles to encode all scene areas well due to the high dynamic range, leading to potential quality degradation in tone-mapped outputs. When to use: When establishing a performance baseline for HDR NeRF methods or when HDR ground truth data is available and high dynamic range fidelity is required. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and LDR inputs are the only available data, or when the high dynamic range causes encoding failures. The training protocol is based on the HDR-NeRF methodology, which introduced training NeRF models directly from HDR views to synthesize high dynamic range novel views. The configuration parameters (64 coarse samples, 128 fine samples, 200,000 iterations) are adapted from the original NeRF paper's recommended settings for the DTU dataset, as cited in comparative studies. The method highlights the challenges of applying standard NeRF pipelines to HDR data, motivating the development of more robust HDR synthesis techniques.
