name: Model Architecture and Representation
head: Neural Radiance Field Representations, Implicit Scene Representations
body: This article defines the neural network architectures and data structures used to represent 3D scenes in differentiable volume rendering. It solves the problem of mapping continuous 3D coordinates and viewing directions to radiance and density (or attenuation) values, enabling the synthesis of novel views from sparse or dense input imagery. Unlike explicit voxel grids or mesh-based representations, these methods use coordinate-based networks (MLPs) or tensor decompositions to store scene information implicitly, allowing for high-frequency detail and differentiable optimization. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of querying a neural network with 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} to predict scene properties. 1. Coordinate Query: The input to the representation is a 3D point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. In standard NeRF variants, the viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is also included to model view-dependent effects (specularity). 2. Positional Encoding: Raw coordinates are often mapped to higher dimensions using positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) to help the network learn high-frequency details. 3. Neural Mapping: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) or tensor factorization maps the encoded coordinates to: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} (or attenuation \mu). Color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or intensity I). 4. Volume Rendering: The predicted values are integrated along rays using the volume rendering equation to produce pixel colors. PixelNeRF is a neural radiance field method that synthesizes novel views from one or a few input images by conditioning a standard NeRF renderer on image features extracted via a pretrained CNN. Unlike vanilla NeRF, which requires many views for training and relies solely on positional encoding, PixelNeRF projects camera rays onto the source image plane to extract spatial features for each query point, enabling sparse-view reconstruction. It differs from sibling methods like MVSNeRF by operating in view-space with direct ray-to-pixel feature extraction rather than canonical-space voxelization. The Attenuation Field method maps 3D coordinates \mathbf{X} to attenuation coefficients \mu rather than color values, modeling X-ray beam decay through diverse structures to a flat-panel detector. It solves transmission-based imaging reconstruction by adhering to the Beer–Lambert Law, differing from natural-image NeRFs that model emitted radiance. This configuration defines the training protocol for the TensoRF representation in the context of sparse-view lung nodule volumetry from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs). It addresses the instability of standard TensoRF density parameterization, which causes zero gradient flow during early training, and introduces anatomy-aware regularization to prevent overfitting in highly under-constrained settings (18:1 parameter-to-ray ratio). It sets itself apart from standard NeRF variants by using vector-matrix (VM) tensor factorization for the density field and specific initialization shifts to ensure non-zero density gradients. The concept of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. This work established the paradigm of using MLPs to represent continuous 3D scenes for novel view synthesis. Subsequent works extended this to sparse-view settings by incorporating CNN-extracted features, as detailed in PixelNeRF. The Attenuation Field approach adapts this implicit representation for medical X-ray imaging, replacing the radiance model with the Beer–Lambert law. Not given in the sources.

name: PixelNeRF
head: Pixel-aligned Neural Radiance Field, pixelNeRF, spatial CNN feature
body: PixelNeRF is a neural radiance field method that synthesizes novel views from one or a few input images by conditioning a standard NeRF renderer on image features extracted via a pretrained CNN. Unlike vanilla NeRF, which requires many views for training and relies solely on positional encoding, PixelNeRF projects camera rays onto the source image plane to extract spatial features for each query point, enabling sparse-view reconstruction. It differs from sibling methods like MVSNeRF by operating in view-space with direct ray-to-pixel feature extraction rather than canonical-space voxelization. Inputs: Reference images: A set of N input images (typically 1–3) with known camera poses. Query rays: For each pixel in the target view, a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Sampling depths: Near (near) and far (far) bounds for the ray segment. Outputs: RGB color and opacity (density) for each sample point along the ray. Final rendered image (RGB) and depth map. Ray Tensor: Shape (B, 8), where B is the batch size. The last two elements are near and far distances. Feature Maps: Extracted from reference images using a CNN backbone. Feature map size is adjusted from 64 to 128 channels. MLP: A 3-layer network with skip connections to the second layer. 1. Feature Extraction: For each query point \mathbf{x} on a ray, project the point onto the image planes of the reference images. Extract 2D features using a pretrained CNN (ResNet-34) and bilinear interpolation. 2. Feature Aggregation: If multiple reference views are used, aggregate the features from all views via average pooling. 3. Sampling: Generate sample positions along the ray using stratified sampling. Calculate step size: step = 1.0 / n{coarse}. Generate normalized depths: z{steps} = \text{linspace}(0, 1 - step, n{coarse}). Add uniform noise: z{steps} += \text{rand\like}(z{steps}) \times step. Compute physical positions z based on near and far: If lindisp is False: z = near \cdot (1 - z{steps}) + far \cdot z{steps}. If lindisp is True: z = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{near} \cdot (1 - z{steps}) + \frac{1}{far} \cdot z{steps}}. 4. NeRF Query: Pass the query point \mathbf{x}, view direction \mathbf{d}, and the aggregated CNN features into the NeRF MLP. 5. Output Prediction: The MLP outputs density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for each sample. 6. Volume Rendering: Composite the samples into final RGB and depth using standard volume rendering equations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def extractcnnfeatures(rayorigins, raydirections, referenceimages, cameraposes, cnnbackbone): # Projects 3D query points onto 2D image planes of reference images. # Uses bilinear interpolation on pretrained CNN feature maps. features = [] for img, pose in zip(referenceimages, cameraposes): # Standard perspective projection to get 2D coordinates (u, v) u, v = project3dto2d(rayorigins, raydirections, pose) # Sample features from CNN backbone feat = F.gridsample(cnnbackbone(img), torch.stack([u, v], dim=-1).unsqueeze(1)) features.append(feat) # Aggregate via average pooling if multiple views if len(features) > 1: return torch.mean(torch.stack(features, dim=0), dim=0) return features[0] def project3dto2d(origins, directions, pose): # Computes 2D image coordinates from 3D ray points using camera pose and intrinsics # Returns normalized coordinates in [-1, 1] # Not given in the sources. Standard pinhole projection. def samplecoarse(rays, ncoarse=128, lindisp=False): near = rays[:, -2:-1] # Shape (B, 1) far = rays[:, -1:] # Shape (B, 1) step = 1.0 / ncoarse zsteps = torch.linspace(0, 1 - step, ncoarse, device=rays.device) zsteps = zsteps.repeat(rays.shape[0], 1) # Shape (B, Kc) zsteps += torch.randlike(zsteps) step if not lindisp: z = near (1 - zsteps) + far zsteps else: z = 1.0 / (1.0 / near (1 - zsteps) + 1.0 / far zsteps) return z def mlpforward(positions, directions, features): # 3-layer MLP with skip connections to the second layer # Input: [positions, directions, features] # Output: density (sigma) and color (c) # Not given in the sources. Standard MLP forward pass. def computeweights(sigma, z): delta = z[:, 1:] - z[:,:-1] delta = torch.cat([delta, delta[:, -1:]], dim=1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha[:,:-1]], dim=1), dim=1) weights = alpha T return weights def importancesample(z, weights, nfine): # Samples nfine points based on coarse weights # Standard stratified sampling from discrete distribution # Not given in the sources. Standard importance sampling. def volumerender(sigma, color, z): weights = computeweights(sigma, z) rgb = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1) depth = torch.sum(weights z, dim=1) return rgb, depth def render(rays, ncoarse=128, nfine=0, cnnbackbone=None, referenceimages=None, cameraposes=None): if rays.shape[0] == 0: return torch.zeros((0, 3), device=rays.device), torch.zeros((0,), device=rays.device) rayorigins = rays[:,:3] raydirections = rays[:, 3:6] cnnfeatures = extractcnnfeatures(rayorigins, raydirections, referenceimages, cameraposes, cnnbackbone) zcoarse = samplecoarse(rays, ncoarse) sigmacoarse, colorcoarse = mlpforward(zcoarse, raydirections, cnnfeatures) rgbcoarse, depthcoarse = volumerender(sigmacoarse, colorcoarse, zcoarse) if nfine > 0: weights = computeweights(sigmacoarse, zcoarse) zfine = importancesample(zcoarse, weights, nfine) sigmafine, colorfine = mlpforward(zfine, raydirections, cnnfeatures) rgbfine, depthfine = volumerender(sigmafine, colorfine, zfine) return rgbfine, depthfine return rgbcoarse, depthcoarse ncoarse: Number of coarse samples. Default: 128. nfine: Number of fine samples. Default: 0. evalbatchsize: Ray batch size for evaluation. Default: 100,000. R: Batch size of rendered rays per object. Default: 50,000 (eval), 128 (train). whitebkgd: If true, background is white; else black. Default: False. lindisp: If true, sample in disparity space. Default: False. noisestd: Noise added to sigma. Not used in this implementation. depthstd: Noise for depth samples. Default: 0.01. P: Source-view specification string (e.g., '64' for 1-view). L: Path to viewlist file. DTU Overfitting: The model overfits significantly to the training set on the DTU dataset. Use only train/val sets, with val used for testing. SRN View Sampling: Training with random 1/2 views per batch degrades performance, especially for 1-view. Use a fixed number of views. Memory: Reduce R if running out of memory; can increase to 100,000 on large-memory GPUs. Time Complexity: Rendering time is higher than vanilla NeRF due to CNN feature extraction. For example, 2.189 s for Feet dataset and 5.493 s for Chest dataset. Memory Complexity: Depends on batch size R and feature map size. Feature map size adjusted from 64 to 128. Performance: Outperforms vanilla NeRF but has smaller margins than Instant-NGP (e.g., 0.031 vs 0.058 in 3D SSIM in Chest dataset). Strengths: Enhances reconstruction of internal small structures (e.g., teeth in Jaw dataset). Limitations: Relies on frequency-based encoding, which may not capture high-frequency details as well as hash encoding. PixelNeRF was introduced by Alex Yu, Vickie Ye, Matthew Tancik, and Angjoo Kanazawa from UC Berkeley in December 2020. It extends vanilla NeRF by leveraging pretrained CNN features to enable sparse-view reconstruction. It is used for ShapeNet (NMR, SRN), DTU, and real car images. name: Attenuation Field
head: Beer-Lambert NeRF, X-ray NeRF
body: The Attenuation Field method maps 3D coordinates \mathbf{X} to attenuation coefficients \mu rather than color values, modeling X-ray beam decay through diverse structures to a flat-panel detector. It solves transmission-based imaging reconstruction by adhering to the Beer–Lambert Law, differing from natural-image NeRFs that model emitted radiance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D spatial coordinates \mathbf{X}, initial beam intensity I0, and sampling step size \delta. Output: Attenuated intensity I at the detector plane. Data Structures: Neural Network: A coordinate-based network (e.g., MLP) that takes \mathbf{X} as input and outputs a scalar attenuation coefficient \mu. Sampling: Uniform sampling is used along the ray path. Stratified or importance sampling is explicitly avoided because, in medical volume reconstruction, every region contributes equally, and uniform distribution ensures no regions are overlooked or over-represented. Formulas: The rendering equation follows the Beer–Lambert Law: I = I0 e^{-\sumi \mui \deltai} Where: I: Resultant attenuated intensity at the detector. I0: Initial intensity of the X-ray source. \mui: Attenuation coefficient at the i-th sample point. \deltai: Sampling step size (distance between samples). Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast a ray from the X-ray source through the volume to the flat-panel detector. 2. Uniform Sampling: Sample points \mathbf{X}i uniformly along the ray path within the volume bounds. 3. Query Attenuation: Pass each \mathbf{X}i through the neural network to obtain the local attenuation coefficient \mui. 4. Integration: Compute the total optical depth \tau = \sumi \mui \deltai. 5. Attenuation: Calculate the final intensity I = I0 e^{-\tau}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderattenuationfield(rayorigin, raydirection, network, I0, numsamples, stepsize): # 1. Ray Casting & 2. Uniform Sampling points = rayorigin + raydirection (stepsize torch.arange(numsamples)) # 3. Query Attenuation muvalues = network(points) # Returns scalar attenuation coefficient μ for each point # 4. Integration opticaldepth = torch.sum(muvalues stepsize) # 5. Attenuation intensity = I0 torch.exp(-opticaldepth) return intensity Parameters: Sampling Strategy: Uniform sampling is the standard configuration for this method. Initial Intensity (I0): Treated as a known constant or calibrated parameter of the X-ray source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Attenuation: Attenuation coefficients must be non-negative to maintain physical interpretation. If the network outputs negative values, truncation or non-negative activation functions are required (see Trainable Flat Field). Empty Space: Rays passing through air (empty space) should ideally not contribute to attenuation. Standard networks may predict false density in empty regions if background attenuation is not decoupled. A technique to decouple the attenuation path into material and air components using a trainable parameter for background attenuation, preventing false density in empty space. It addresses the issue where rays passing through empty space (air) get incorrectly attenuated, leading to inaccurate density fields. Definition: The method introduces a trainable scalar parameter ff representing the flat field (background) attenuation. Steps: 1. Define a trainable parameter ff. 2. Derive the air attenuation coefficient \muA using truncation to ensure non-negativity: \muA = \max(0, ff). 3. Assume the path through air is approximately constant for all rays. 4. Compute intensity by separating the integral into material (M) and air (A) components: I = I0 \exp \left( - \intM \mu(s) ds - \intA \mu(s) ds \right) = I0 \exp(-\muA) \exp \left( - \intM \mu(s) ds \right) When to choose: Use this variant when training on data with significant empty space or when a "white background" assumption (no air attenuation) leads to inaccurate density representations. It allows the network to learn the true material density by decoupling it from the background air attenuation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Physically grounded for transmission imaging (X-ray, CT); handles diverse structures by modeling absorption directly. Limitations: Uniform sampling is computationally less efficient than importance sampling but is chosen because medical volumes require every region to contribute equally. Sensitive to background attenuation assumptions without variants like Trainable Flat Field. When to use: Specifically for medical imaging, X-ray, or any scenario where the input data represents beam attenuation rather than emitted radiance. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Attenuation Field formulation was introduced to adapt Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for high-fidelity volume reconstruction in medical images, specifically X-ray modalities. It maps 3D coordinates to attenuation coefficients \mu rather than color values, based on the Beer–Lambert Law. The approach recognizes that X-ray sources emit cone-shaped beams that undergo attenuation as they pass through diverse structures before being received by a flat-panel detector. The use of uniform sampling was specifically justified for medical volumes where every region equally contributes to reconstruction, unlike natural images where surface regions are prioritized. name: TensoRF Training Configuration
head: Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF, AReT Configuration
body: This configuration defines the training protocol for the TensoRF representation in the context of sparse-view lung nodule volumetry from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs). It addresses the instability of standard TensoRF density parameterization, which causes zero gradient flow during early training, and introduces anatomy-aware regularization to prevent overfitting in highly under-constrained settings (18:1 parameter-to-ray ratio). It sets itself apart from standard NeRF variants by using vector-matrix (VM) tensor factorization for the density field and specific initialization shifts to ensure non-zero density gradients. Inputs: Sparse set of DRR images (e.g., 72 views from MedNeRF-rendered data). Camera poses corresponding to the input views. Scene bounding box (AABB): x \in [-2.5, 3.5], y \in [-1.5, 1.5], z \in [-2.0, 1.5]. Outputs: Optimized density grid parameters and appearance MLP weights. A volumetric density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) suitable for Marching Cubes extraction. Data Structures: 1. Density Grid (VM Decomposition): Layout: Vector-Matrix decomposition with rank 16 per axis. Dimensions: 16 \times 16 \times 16 voxel grid, resulting in 64^3 voxels. Voxel spacing: Approximately 3.75 mm per voxel (anisotropic: [3.75, 1.875, 2.1875] mm). Parameters: Density feature planes Pi and lines Li. 2. Appearance MLP: Hidden layers: 2 layers with 128 units each. Activation: ReLU. Input features: 27-dimensional appearance features. 3. Positional Encoding: Frequencies: 6. Training Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize density feature planes/lines such that f\theta(\mathbf{x}) \in [-1, 1]. Set density shift \Delta = 0 and scale s = 1. Note: The default parameterization (\Delta = -10, s = 25) is avoided because it results in f\theta(\mathbf{x}) + \Delta \in (-\infty, 0), causing the ReLU in the density equation to be identically zero, yielding zero density and zero photometric gradient flow. 2. Density Computation: Compute raw density output f\theta(\mathbf{x}) from the VM decomposition. Apply the corrected density parameterization: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(\mathbf{x}) + \Delta) \cdot s With \Delta=0, s=1, this simplifies to \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(\mathbf{x})). 3. Rendering: Sample rays (batch size 2048). Query \sigma(\mathbf{x}) along rays. Compute photometric loss against target views. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute photometric loss: L{photo} = \text{MSE}(\hat{I}, I). Compute sparsity loss (L1 penalty on density planes): L{sparse} = \sumi \| Pi \|1 Encodes domain knowledge that the thoracic cavity is predominantly air. Compute Total Variation (TV) regularization on density planes: L{TV} = \sumi \left( \| \Deltah Pi \|1 + \| \Deltav Pi \|1 \right) where \Deltah, \Deltav are horizontal and vertical finite differences. Total loss: L = L{photo} + \lambda1 L{sparse} + \lambda2 L{TV} With \lambda1 = 1 \times 10^{-4} and \lambda2 = 1 \times 10^{-5}. 5. Optimization: Use Adam optimizer. Learning rates: 0.02 for grid parameters, 0.002 for MLP parameters. Iterate for 3000 iterations. 6. Alpha Mask Updates: Update alpha masks at iterations 1500 and 2500. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traintensorfaert(views, poses, iterations=3000, batchsize=2048): # 1. Initialize Density Grid (VM Rank-16) # P: density feature planes (16x16x16), L: density feature lines (16x16) P = [[[0.0 for in range(16)] for in range(16)] for in range(16)] L = [[[0.0 for in range(16)] for in range(16)] for in range(16)] # Appearance MLP (2x128 ReLU) W = [np.random.randn(27, 128), np.random.randn(128, 128), np.random.randn(128, 3)] # Adam state mP, vP = np.zeroslike(P), np.zeroslike(P) mL, vL = np.zeroslike(L), np.zeroslike(L) mW, vW = [np.zeroslike(w) for w in W], [np.zeroslike(w) for w in W] for step in range(iterations): rays = samplerays(views, poses, batchsize) # Query Density via VM decomposition ftheta = vmdecompose(rays.x, P, L) sigma = relu(ftheta) # Query Appearance Features and MLP features = getappearancefeatures(rays.x, rays.d, P, L) c = mlpforward(features, W) # Render predicted image Ihat = volumerender(rays, sigma, c) # Compute Losses Lphoto = mse(Ihat, rays.I) Lsparse = sum(np.sum(np.abs(plane)) for plane in P) LTV = sum(np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(plane, axis=0))) + np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(plane, axis=1))) for plane in P) L = Lphoto + 1e-4 Lsparse + 1e-5 LTV # Backpropagate (conceptual) gP, gL, gW = computegradients(L, rays, sigma, c, P, L, W) # Adam update adamstep(P, mP, vP, gP, lr=0.02, step=step) adamstep(L, mL, vL, gL, lr=0.02, step=step) for i in range(3): adamstep(W[i], mW[i], vW[i], gW[i], lr=0.002, step=step) if step in [1500, 2500]: updatealphamasks(rays, sigma) def vmdecompose(x, P, L): # ftheta(x) = sumi (Pi(x) Li(x)) return sum(P[i][int(x[0]16)][int(x[1]16)] L[i][int(x[1]16)][int(x[2]16)] for i in range(16)) def relu(x): return max(0.0, x) def getappearancefeatures(x, d, P, L): # Not given in sources return np.zeros(27) def mlpforward(features, W): h1 = relu(features @ W[0]) h2 = relu(h1 @ W[1]) return h2 @ W[2] def volumerender(rays, sigma, c): # Not given in sources return np.mean(c) def mse(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target)2) def computegradients(loss, rays, sigma, c, P, L, W): # Conceptual gradient computation return np.zeroslike(P), np.zeroslike(L), [np.zeroslike(w) for w in W] def adamstep(params, m, v, grad, lr, step): beta1, beta2, eps = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8 m[:] = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) grad v[:] = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) grad2 mhat = m / (1 - beta1(step+1)) vhat = v / (1 - beta2(step+1)) params -= lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + eps) def updatealphamasks(rays, sigma): # Not given in sources pass def samplerays(views, poses, batchsize): # Not given in sources return type('Rays', (), {'x': np.zeros((batchsize, 3)), 'd': np.zeros((batchsize, 3)), 'I': np.zeros((batchsize, 3))})() Uses the original TensoRF density parameterization with \Delta = -10 and s = 25. Trained on 72 MedNeRF-rendered views. Achieves a training PSNR of 32.0 dB, confirming the model learns to reproduce projected views. However, the Marching Cubes sweep remains unstable (e.g., 204% error at p=97), revealing that high photometric fidelity does not imply geometrically consistent volumetric structure. This variant serves as a baseline to demonstrate the necessity of the density-shift correction. Time Complexity: Converges in approximately 8 minutes per patient on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Memory Complexity: The density grid is 16^3 voxels with rank-16 VM decomposition; the appearance MLP is small (2x128). Strengths: The corrected parameterization (\Delta=0, s=1) ensures stable gradient flow and geometric consistency, reducing Marching Cubes error to ~13.8-14.3% compared to >200% with default parameters. Explicit regularization is essential to prevent overfitting in sparse-view scenarios. Limitations: Highly sensitive to threshold selection during Marching Cubes extraction if not properly regularized; default parameterization leads to complete training failure (zero density). When to use: Sparse-view volumetric reconstruction where geometric consistency is critical and standard NeRF/TensoRF fails to produce stable isosurfaces. Originated from the AReT (Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF) method for sparse-view lung nodule volumetry from DRRs. The work highlights that standard TensoRF density parameterization (\Delta=-10, s=25) causes the ReLU to be identically zero at initialization, halting gradient flow. The proposed correction (\Delta=0, s=1) and anatomy-aware regularization (L1 sparsity and TV smoothness) are tailored to the thoracic cavity's air-filled nature and nodule morphology. name: Distributed NeRF Optimization
head: Auxiliary Variable Method in Di-NeRF, Centralized ADMM for Di-NeRF, Consensus ADMM for NeRF, Di-NeRF, Di-NeRF Distributed Optimization
body: Distributed NeRF Optimization (Di-NeRF) is a collaborative learning framework that enables multiple robots to jointly reconstruct a global Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and refine their relative camera poses without sharing raw sensor data. It distinguishes itself from centralized training by using Consensus Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (C-ADMM) to enforce agreement on global network parameters across a network of agents, while simultaneously optimizing local pose and depth distortion parameters. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: For each robot i \in V, a set of images Ii, initial camera poses \pii, and an off-the-shelf monocular depth network (e.g., DPT). Outputs: Global NeRF parameters \theta^, relative camera pose transformations T{ig}^ for each robot, and mono-depth distortion parameters \psi^{i}. Data Structures \thetai: Local copy of the global NeRF network parameters for robot i. T{ig}: Relative camera pose transformation matrix from robot i to the global reference coordinate system Rg. Represented as an element of SE(3), decomposed into rotation \phi = \alpha\omega (axis-angle, \omega \in \mathbb{R}^3 normalized, \alpha \in \mathbb{R}) and translation tg \in \mathbb{R}^3. \psi^i: Set of mono-depth distortion parameters for robot i, specifically scale \alphai^m and shift \betai^m for each image m. yi: Dual variable (Lagrangian multiplier) for robot i. z{ij}: Auxiliary variable (complicating variable) representing the consensus value between neighbors i and j. \Gammai: Combined local variable set \{\thetai, T{ig}, \psi^i\}. Ni: Set of neighboring robots that robot i communicates with. Local Loss Function The local loss Li for robot i combines RGB rendering loss and a depth consistency loss: Li = \sum{m=0}^{Mi-1} \| Ii^m - \hat{I}i^m \|^2 + \gamma \sum{m=0}^{Mi-1} \| Di^{m} - \hat{D}i^m \|^2 where: Ii^m is the input image. \hat{I}i^m is the NeRF-rendered RGB image. Di^m is the raw mono-depth map from DPT. Di^{m} = \tilde{\alpha}i^m Di^m + \tilde{\beta}i^m is the corrected mono-depth map, where \tilde{\alpha}i^m, \tilde{\beta}i^m are the scale and shift parameters optimized during training. \hat{D}i^m is the NeRF-rendered depth image. \gamma is a weighting factor for the depth loss term. Algorithm Steps The optimization solves the constrained problem: \theta^, T^, \psi^ = \arg\min{\theta, T, \psi} \sum{i \in V} Li(\thetai, T{ig}, \psi^i) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \thetai = z{ij}, \forall j \in Ni using the augmented Lagrangian: \mathcal{L}i(\Gammai) = Li(\Gammai) + \thetai^\top yi + \frac{\rho}{2} \sum{j \in Ni} \| \thetai - z{ij} \|^2 where \rho is the penalty factor. 1. Initialization: Initialize \thetai, T{ig}, \psi^i, yi, z{ij} for all i \in V, j \in Ni. Set iteration counter k=0. 2. Local Subproblem Update: Each robot i updates its local variables \Gammai^{(k+1)} by minimizing the augmented Lagrangian. This involves gradient descent on Li(\Gammai) plus the ADMM penalty terms: \Gammai^{(k+1)} = \arg\min{\Gamma} \left\{ Li(\Gammai) + \thetai^\top yi^{(k)} + \frac{\rho}{2} \sum{j \in Ni} \| \thetai - z{ij}^{(k)} \|^2 \right\} Specifically, \thetai^{(k+1)} is updated via gradient descent on the NeRF loss, while T{ig} and \psi^i are updated jointly with \thetai. 3. Dual Variable Update: Each robot i updates its dual variable yi using the central collector's output: yi^{(k+1)} = yi^{(k)} + \rho (\thetai^{(k+1)} - z{ij}^{(k+1)}) 4. Auxiliary Variable Update (Central Collector): A central fusion center computes the auxiliary variable z{ij}^{(k+1)} by averaging the local parameters and dual variables of the neighbors: z{ij}^{(k+1)} = \frac{1}{|Ni|} \sum{i \in Ni} \left( \thetai^{(k+1)} + \frac{1}{\rho} yi^{(k)} \right) This simplifies to the average local parameter plus the scaled average dual variable: z{ij}^{(k+1)} = \bar{\theta}^{(k+1)} + \frac{\bar{y}^{(k)}}{\rho} where \bar{\theta}^{(k+1)} is the average of \thetai^{(k+1)} over neighbors and \bar{y}^{(k)} is the average of yi^{(k)}. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 until convergence. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distributednerfoptimization(robots, neighbors, images, depthnet, gamma, rho, maxiters): """ robots: List of Robot objects. Each has attributes: id: int images: List of image tensors initpose: SE(3) matrix theta: NeRF parameters (tensor) Tig: Relative pose (SE(3)) psi: Depth distortion params (scale, shift) y: Dual variable (tensor, same shape as theta) neighbors: Dict mapping robotid -> List of neighbor robotids images: Dict mapping robotid -> List of image tensors depthnet: Function to compute raw mono-depth from image gamma: Weight for depth loss rho: Penalty factor maxiters: Maximum number of ADMM iterations """ # Initialization for robot in robots: robot.theta = initializenerfparams() robot.Tig = robot.initpose robot.psi = initializedepthdistortion() robot.y = zeroslike(robot.theta) # Initialize auxiliary variables zij for all edges z = {} for robot in robots: for neighborid in neighbors[robot.id]: z[(robot.id, neighborid)] = zeroslike(robot.theta) for k in range(maxiters): # Step 1: Local Subproblem Update (Parallel on each robot) localupdates = {} for robot in robots: # Compute raw mono-depth rawdepths = [depthnet(img) for img in images[robot.id]] # Compute corrected mono-depth using current psi correcteddepths = [psi.scale d + psi.shift for d, psi in zip(rawdepths, robot.psi)] # Define local augmented loss def localloss(theta, Tig, psi): # Render RGB and Depth from NeRF defined by theta, Tig renderedrgb, rendereddepth = nerfrender(theta, Tig, images[robot.id]) # RGB Loss rgbloss = sum((img - rrgb)2 for img, rrgb in zip(images[robot.id], renderedrgb)) # Depth Loss depthloss = sum((cd - rd)2 for cd, rd in zip(correcteddepths, rendereddepth)) baseloss = rgbloss + gamma depthloss # ADMM Penalty Terms penalty = 0 for neighborid in neighbors[robot.id]: zval = z[(robot.id, neighborid)] penalty += rho 0.5 sum((theta - zval)2) # Dual Term dualterm = sum(theta robot.y) return baseloss + dualterm + penalty # Minimize localloss w.r.t theta, Tig, psi # Note: In practice, this involves gradient descent steps # Here we assume a generic optimizer step newtheta, newTig, newpsi = minimize(localloss, robot.theta, robot.Tig, robot.psi) localupdates[robot.id] = { 'theta': newtheta, 'Tig': newTig, 'psi': newpsi } # Update local variables for robot in robots: robot.theta = localupdates[robot.id]['theta'] robot.Tig = localupdates[robot.id]['Tig'] robot.psi = localupdates[robot.id]['psi'] # Step 2 & 3: Dual and Auxiliary Updates (Centralized) # Calculate averages over neighbors for each robot # Note: The source describes a central collector computing zij based on neighbors. # We iterate over each robot to update its duals and the z variables associated with it. for robot in robots: # Update Dual Variable yi # yi^{(k+1)} = yi^{(k)} + rho (thetai^{(k+1)} - zij^{(k+1)}) # However, zij is updated centrally. The source says y update uses zij^{(k+1)}. # We must compute zij first or simultaneously. # Step 3: Auxiliary Variable Update (Central) # zij^{(k+1)} = mean(thetai^{(k+1)} + yi^{(k)}/rho) for i in Nj? # Source Eq 16: z{ij}^{(k+1)} = (1/N) sum{i in Ni} (thetai^{(k+1)} + yi^{(k)}/rho) # This implies z is computed for the edge (i,j) based on the neighbors of i? # Actually, Eq 16 sums over i in Ni. This suggests z{ij} is determined by the # neighborhood of i. But z{ij} is shared between i and j. # Standard C-ADMM: z{ij} is the average of thetai and thetaj? # Source Eq 16: z{ij} = mean{i in Ni} (thetai + yi/rho). # This formula calculates a single value for the group Ni? # Let's follow the source strictly: z{ij} is computed by the central collector. # To implement Eq 16: # For each edge (i, j), we need z{ij}. # The source says "z{ij}^{(k+1)} = 1/N sum{i in Ni}...". # This notation is slightly ambiguous. Usually, z{ij} is associated with the constraint between i and j. # If the graph is undirected, Ni is the set of neighbors of i. # The central collector computes z{ij} for all edges. # Let's assume the standard consensus: z{ij} is the average of the variables of the nodes connected by the edge? # No, Eq 16 sums over Ni. This implies z{ij} might be specific to the "center" i? # Let's look at Eq 17: z{ij} = thetabar + ybar/rho. # thetabar is average of thetai for i in Ni. # This suggests z{ij} is a consensus value for the neighborhood of i. # But z{ij} is used in the constraint thetai = z{ij}. # If z{ij} depends only on Ni, then for neighbor j, the constraint is thetaj = z{ji}. # Are z{ij} and z{ji} the same? In symmetric consensus, yes. # If z{ij} = mean(Ni), then z{ji} = mean(Nj). These are different if degrees differ. # However, Eq 18 shows thetabar = mean(thetai). # Let's stick to the explicit formula in Eq 16/17 for the central collector. # We need to compute z for all edges. # The source implies a central entity computes z{ij}. # Let's compute z{ij} for each robot i and its neighbors j. # Compute local averages for robot i's neighborhood thetavals = [localupdates[nid]['theta'] for nid in neighbors[robot.id]] yvals = [robotsbyid[nid].y for nid in neighbors[robot.id]] avgtheta = mean(thetavals) avgy = mean(yvals) # Compute z{ij} for all j in Ni # Note: The source uses z{ij} in the dual update for i. # So we compute z{ij} based on Ni. for neighborid in neighbors[robot.id]: z[(robot.id, neighborid)] = avgtheta + avgy / rho # Now update dual variables using the newly computed z for robot in robots: for neighborid in neighbors[robot.id]: zval = z[(robot.id, neighborid)] robot.y = robot.y + rho (robot.theta - zval) return robots Edge Cases and Pitfalls Pose Optimization: Camera rotation is in SO(3) space, requiring axis-angle representation to avoid singularities. Depth Consistency: Mono-depth maps from off-the-shelf networks (like DPT) are scale-ambiguous. The optimization jointly learns scale and shift parameters \psi^i to align rendered depth with corrected mono-depth. Communication: The method assumes a connected communication graph among robots. Disconnected components will converge to separate local NeRFs. Convergence: The penalty factor \rho affects convergence speed. A value not specified in the sources is used. Time Complexity: Each iteration requires local gradient descent on the NeRF loss (expensive) and a central averaging step (lightweight). The number of iterations depends on the convergence of ADMM, which is generally slower per iteration than centralized SGD but allows parallel local computation. Memory Complexity: Each robot stores its own copy of the NeRF parameters \thetai, poses T{ig}, and depth parameters \psi^i. No raw images are stored or transmitted, only gradients or parameters (depending on implementation, here parameters are exchanged via the central collector). Strengths: Enables collaborative mapping in challenging environments where broad communication is not feasible (only local neighbor communication required for the graph structure, though a central collector is used for the auxiliary variable update, implying a star topology or a central server). Preserves data privacy as raw data is not shared. Limitations: Requires a central fusion center for the auxiliary variable update, which can be a bottleneck. Convergence depends on the choice of \rho and the connectivity of the robot network. Di-NeRF was introduced in a 2024 paper published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters by Asadi et al.. It addresses the challenge of multi-robot simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) and collaborative scene reconstruction, where robots must learn a global representation without sharing raw sensor data, which is often impractical due to bandwidth constraints or privacy concerns. The method builds on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) and specifically uses Consensus ADMM (C-ADMM) to handle the distributed nature of the optimization problem. name: Domain-Specific and Advanced Configurations
body: This family encompasses training configurations tailored to specific domains (e.g., humans, objects), advanced physical properties (PBR, HDR), or specific optimization stages (fine representation). It solves the problem of applying generic NeRF training loops to complex inverse rendering tasks where standard assumptions (e.g., Lambertian surfaces, static scenes, LDR inputs) fail. It differs from generic Training Configuration by introducing domain-specific loss terms, physical constraints, and specialized data handling. All configurations in this family extend the standard volume rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rec} by adding domain-specific regularization or physical constraints. They typically involve: 1. Specialized Loss Terms: Adding losses \mathcal{L}{domain} (e.g., PBR energy conservation, Eikonal, geometric priors) to the total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \sum \lambdai \mathcal{L}i. 2. Multi-Stage or Joint Optimization: Decoupling geometry, material, and illumination estimation into sequential phases or optimizing them jointly with specific freezing/unfreezing strategies. 3. Domain-Specific Data Handling: Modifying ray sampling or query points to handle dynamic bodies, HDR inputs, or specific object categories. Defines the loss for the high-resolution radiance field after coarse convergence. It reduces regularization weights to prevent over-smoothing of high-frequency details. Decouples geometry, material, and illumination into three phases (Geometry, Material, Joint) before final refinement. It optimizes for material parameters (roughness, metallicness) and incident lighting using physics-based losses (energy conservation, inter-reflection). Specifies hyperparameters for training humans in motion using the imGHUM parametric model. It addresses memory limitations by limiting query points and distinguishes between dynamic human regions and static backgrounds. Step: Randomly flip input scenes along x and y axes with probability 0.5. Randomly rotate input scenes along z-axis by \pi/2 with probability 0.5. Randomly rotate scenes along z-axis by an angle \alpha \in [-\pi/18, \pi/18] with probability 0.5. Parameter: Optimizer: AdamW with initial learning rate 0.0003 and weight decay 0.001. Loss weight \lambda = 5.0 for Eq. (3) and \lambda = 1.0 for Eq. (6). Definition: A variant of NeRF trained with 32-bit HDR images to produce 3-channel radiance in linear color space, reconciling the color space difference between NeRF (sRGB) and path tracing (linear). Step: Train the NeRF using 32-bit HDR images as ground truth supervision instead of standard 8-bit images. Parameter: Color depth: 32-bit per channel for HDR NeRF, 8-bit per channel for standard LDR NeRF. Comparison: HDR NeRF achieves higher lighting realism compared to 8-bit LDR NeRF, as shown in Figure 5. Definition: A procedure to enhance visual quality for a specific subject or adapt to an unseen identity by fine-tuning the network. Step: 1. Fine-tune network with learning rate 10^{-5} for few iterations. 2. Keep weights of multiplicative module frozen. 3. Learn identity and latent codes for the target subject. Parameter: Learning rate for personalization: 10^{-5}. The need for domain-specific configurations arises from the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering. Standard NeRF assumes Lambertian surfaces and static scenes, which fails for dynamic humans, physically based materials, or high-dynamic-range lighting. The concept of multi-stage optimization (coarse-to-fine) is standard in NeRF, while joint optimization of geometry and material is introduced by PBR-NeRF. HDR NeRF addresses the color space mismatch between neural rendering and physical simulation. Personalization techniques leverage few-shot fine-tuning to adapt general models to specific identities. name: Training Objective for Fine Representation
head: Fine Representation Training Objective, Fine-stage Training Configuration
body: The training objective for the fine representation specifies the loss configuration for the second optimization phase, using the same loss types as the coarse stage but with modified regularization weights. It differs from the coarse stage objective primarily by reducing the weight of regularization terms, a modification empirically shown to yield slightly better visual quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images, camera poses, and the fine representation parameters. Outputs: Updated fine representation parameters and the computed training loss scalar. Data Structures: The fine representation mirrors the coarse structure but is optimized with the adjusted loss configuration. Steps: 1. Sample points along rays using the same sampling strategy as the coarse stage. 2. Query the fine representation to obtain density and color values at the sampled points. 3. Compute the rendered image color for each training ray using volume rendering. 4. Calculate the reconstruction loss between the rendered image and the ground truth image. 5. Calculate the regularization loss terms using the same definitions as the coarse stage. 6. Combine the reconstruction loss and regularization loss using a reduced regularization weight. 7. Backpropagate the combined loss and update the fine representation parameters. Formulas: The total training loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{fine} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda{reg} \mathcal{L}{reg} Where: \mathcal{L}{rec} is the reconstruction loss between the rendered image and the ground truth image. \mathcal{L}{reg} represents the regularization losses applied to the fine representation parameters. \lambda{reg} is the regularization weight. Parameters: Regularization Weight (\lambda{reg}): The key difference from the coarse stage is that \lambda{reg} is set to a smaller value in the fine stage. The exact numerical value is not given in the sources; it is a hyperparameter tuned relative to the coarse stage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainfinestage(finereprparams, dataset, optimizer, lambdaregfine): """ Optimizes the fine representation using a reduced regularization weight. Args: finereprparams: Parameters of the fine representation (e.g., voxel grid or MLP weights). dataset: Iterable of (image, camerapose) pairs. optimizer: Optimizer instance for finereprparams. lambdaregfine: The reduced regularization weight for the fine stage. Returns: finereprparams: The updated fine representation parameters. """ for image, camerapose in dataset: # 1. Sample points along rays using the coarse stage strategy rayorigins, raydirections, samplepoints = samplerays(camerapose) # 2. Query fine representation for density and color densities, colors = finereprparams.query(samplepoints) # 3. Volume render the image renderedimage = volumerender(rayorigins, raydirections, densities, colors) # 4. Compute reconstruction loss (MSE) lossrec = sum((renderedimage - image) 2) / len(renderedimage) # 5. Compute regularization loss (L2 norm of parameters) lossreg = sum(p 2 for p in finereprparams) / len(finereprparams) # 6. Compute total loss with reduced regularization weight loss = lossrec + lambdaregfine lossreg # 7. Backpropagate and update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return finereprparams def samplerays(camerapose): # Standard ray generation from camera pose and image grid; not detailed in sources return rayorigins, raydirections, samplepoints def volumerender(rayorigins, raydirections, densities, colors): # Standard alpha compositing over sample points; not detailed in sources return renderedimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. This method adapts a StyleGAN2 discriminator to evaluate NeRF-rendered images, configured for 64×64 RGB inputs. It differs from sibling methods such as Test-Time Finetuning by integrating adversarial evaluation directly into the training loop rather than applying post-processing. Choose this method when perceptual sharpness and photorealistic texture synthesis are prioritized over pure pixel-wise fidelity. Test-Time Finetuning is a post-sampling optimization step that refines a sampled scene code by minimizing a combined loss of rendering fidelity and a diffusion prior, while keeping the model parameters frozen. It addresses the limitation where reconstruction guidance alone cannot strictly enforce rendering constraints towards faithful reconstruction. It sets itself apart from two-stage generative neural field methods by retaining the prior term during the optimization of the scene code, avoiding the biased and noisy scene codes that result from ignoring this term. Choose this method when refining a fixed model for specific novel views without retraining the network weights. A learnable module combining spatial (pixel) and geometric (camera) attention to regulate contributions from neighbours and reduce ghosting artifacts from remaining misalignments. It computes pixel attention weights \psi{pix}^i \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h} using a module \mathcal{A}{pix} with two convolutional layers and sigmoid activation, and camera attention weights \psi{cam}^i \in \mathbb{R}^1 using a module \mathcal{A}{cam} with two fully connected layers and sigmoid activation. The final attention-regulated features are computed as H{i \rightarrow k}^{f^a} = \psi{cam}^i \times \psi{pix}^i \times H{i \rightarrow k}^{f'}, where H{i \rightarrow k}^{f'} are the input neighbour features. A loss function enforcing consistency between hitting probabilities derived from the constructed radiance field and those decoded from the NeuRay visibility feature map. It samples points pi on a pseudo test ray and computes hitting probability hi from the constructed radiance field, then decodes the distribution t(z) from the NeuRay representation for the pseudo test ray. It computes a new hitting probability \tilde{h}i = t(z{i+1}) - t(zi) and minimizes the cross entropy between \tilde{h}i and hi via \ell{consist}=\frac{1}{Kt}\sum{i=1}^{Kt} CE(\tilde{h}i,hi), where CE is the cross entropy loss function. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Empirically leads to slightly better visual quality compared to using the same regularization weights as the coarse stage. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method was highlighted in the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization paper. The concept of multi-stage training with adjusted objectives is central to modern radiance field optimization. name: StyleGAN2-based Discriminator Integration
head: GANeRF Discriminator, StyleGAN2 Discriminator
body: This method adapts a StyleGAN2 discriminator to evaluate NeRF-rendered images, configured for 64×64 RGB inputs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Rendered RGB image X of resolution 64 \times 64 with 3 channels. Output: A scalar logit indicating whether the image is real or generated. Data Structures: The discriminator is configured with the following parameters: basechannels: 16384 maxchannels: 512 fp16resolutions: 4 (number of resolution steps using FP16 precision) convclamp: 256 (maximum absolute value for convolution outputs) mbstdgroupsize: 4 (group size for the minibatch standard deviation layer) blockkwargs: Empty dictionary mappingkwargs: Empty dictionary imagechannels: 3 classconditioningdim: 0 resolution: 64 Numbered Steps: 1. Instantiation: Check if the adversarial loss multiplier advlossmult is greater than 0.0. If true, instantiate the discriminator with the configuration above. If false, skip instantiation. 2. Forward Pass: Pass the rendered image X through the discriminator D\phi to obtain the prediction score D\phi(X). 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the adversarial loss scaled by advlossmult. For generated images, the target label is 0 (fake). Formulas: Let D\phi(X) be the discriminator output for image X. The adversarial loss for generated images X{gen} is: L{adv} = \text{adv\loss\mult} \cdot \mathbb{E}{X{gen}} [\ell(D\phi(X{gen}), 0)] where \ell is a standard GAN loss function (e.g., binary cross-entropy or least-squares). Parameters: advlossmult: Multiplier for the adversarial loss. If 0.0, the discriminator is not instantiated. mbstdgroupsize: Default 4. Controls the group size for the minibatch standard deviation layer. convclamp: Default 256. Clamps convolution outputs to [-256, 256] to stabilize training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If advlossmult is 0.0, the discriminator must not be instantiated to avoid unnecessary computation. FP16 precision is applied to 4 resolution steps; gradient scaling must be handled appropriately for mixed-precision training. The discriminator is fixed to 64×64 resolution; inputs must be resized or cropped to match this dimension. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def bceloss(logits, target): p = sigmoid(logits) return -(target math.log(p + 1e-8) + (1 - target) math.log(1 - p + 1e-8)) def instantiatediscriminator(advlossmult, basechannels=16384, maxchannels=512, fp16resolutions=4, convclamp=256, mbstdgroupsize=4): if advlossmult <= 0.0: return None config = { 'basechannels': basechannels, 'maxchannels': maxchannels, 'fp16resolutions': fp16resolutions, 'convclamp': convclamp, 'mbstdgroupsize': mbstdgroupsize, 'blockkwargs': {}, 'mappingkwargs': {}, 'imagechannels': 3, 'classconditioningdim': 0, 'resolution': 64 } return {'config': config, 'initialized': True} def forwardpass(image, config): # The sources do not specify the framework-specific forward pass implementation return 0.5 def computeadversarialloss(discriminator, renderedimages, advlossmult): if discriminator is None: return 0.0 config = discriminator['config'] Doutput = forwardpass(renderedimages, config) target = 0.0 loss = bceloss(Doutput, target) return advlossmult loss A variant where the discriminator takes an image and a normalized depth map as input. It includes a small decoder to enforce a reconstruction penalty, preventing overfitting and encouraging the learning of relevant features. The input is the concatenation of the RGB image and the depth map (normalized to [0, 1]). The discriminator output D\phi(X) is passed through a decoder C to reconstruct the input image X. The method adapts the convolutional discriminator architecture from StyleGAN2 for NeRF training. The specific configuration (64×64 resolution, channel scaling, FP16 steps, and clamping) is derived from the GANeRF implementation. A variant incorporating a reconstruction penalty via a small decoder was introduced to stabilize training and improve feature learning. barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.01404, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Test-Time Finetuning
head: Code Finetuning, Guidance-Finetuning
body: Test-Time Finetuning is a post-sampling optimization step that refines a sampled scene code by minimizing a combined loss of rendering fidelity and a diffusion prior, while keeping the model parameters frozen. It addresses the limitation where reconstruction guidance alone cannot strictly enforce rendering constraints towards faithful reconstruction. It sets itself apart from two-stage generative neural field methods by retaining the prior term during the optimization of the scene code, avoiding the biased and noisy scene codes that result from ignoring this term. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sampled scene code x initialized from the sampling process (e.g., DDIM step). Output: An optimized scene code x that balances rendering accuracy and diffusion prior consistency. Frozen Parameters: The diffusion model parameters and the decoder parameters are kept fixed during this step. Data Structures: Scene Code (x): The latent representation of the scene being optimized. The specific layout of x depends on the underlying representation (e.g., triplane, voxel grid), but it is treated as a tensor of learnable parameters for this optimization step. Steps: 1. Initialize the scene code x from the sampling process. 2. Optimize x using the Adam optimizer to minimize the combined loss function. 3. The optimization minimizes the following objective: \minx \lambda{\text{rend}} L{\text{rend}}(x) + \lambda'{\text{diff}} L{\text{diff}}(x) where: L{\text{rend}}(x) is the rendering loss, measuring the difference between rendered images and ground truth. L{\text{diff}}(x) is the diffusion prior loss, enforcing consistency with the learned data distribution. \lambda{\text{rend}} is the rendering loss weight. \lambda'{\text{diff}} is the test-time prior weight. Parameters: \lambda'{\text{diff}}: The test-time prior weight. It should be lower than the training weight \lambda{\text{diff}} because the prior learned from the training dataset is less reliable when transferred to a different testing dataset. The exact value is not specified in the sources. Optimizer: Adam. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Frozen Parameters: If the decoder or diffusion model parameters are not properly frozen, the optimization may inadvertently update the model, leading to incorrect results. A training phase that prevents the model from overfitting to the input view and ensures fine details are captured during distillation by temporarily freezing or adjusting objectives before full joint training. It serves as a stabilization mechanism for radiance-field optimization, particularly when introducing perceptual or adversarial losses that might otherwise cause mode collapse or weak distillation if applied immediately. Frozen Latent Code is a finetuning variant in differentiable volume rendering where the per-identity latent code is kept fixed while only the model parameters are optimized. It solves the problem of adapting a pretrained volumetric prior to a target identity by reducing the optimization degrees of freedom compared to joint optimization. Unlike Model Fitting (Fine-tuning), which jointly optimizes the latent code and model weights, this method optimizes only the model parameters, yielding visually similar results but with different quantitative metrics. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations and the cost of computing the rendering and diffusion losses per iteration. The sources do not provide specific complexity measures. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the scene code x and the gradients during optimization. The frozen model parameters also consume memory but are not updated. Performance: Improves reconstruction fidelity by enforcing the diffusion prior during the test phase. Strengths: Addresses the issue of reconstruction guidance alone not strictly enforcing rendering constraints. Avoids the biased and noisy scene codes associated with two-stage methods that ignore the prior term. Limitations: The reliability of the diffusion prior decreases when transferred to different testing datasets, necessitating a lower test-time prior weight. When to Use: When faithful reconstruction is required and the scene code has been sampled from a diffusion process. Test-Time Finetuning is introduced in the context of Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF, a unified approach to 3D generation and reconstruction. It builds upon the observation that previous two-stage methods often ignore the prior term during the training of auto-decoders, leading to biased scene codes. The method was proposed to address these limitations by integrating the prior term into the test-time optimization of the scene code. name: Warm-up Strategy
head: Encoder-freezing Warm-up, Warm-up
body: A training phase that prevents the model from overfitting to the input view and ensures fine details are captured during distillation by temporarily freezing or adjusting objectives before full joint training. It builds on Test-Time Finetuning and serves as a stabilization mechanism for radiance-field optimization, particularly when introducing perceptual or adversarial losses that might otherwise cause mode collapse or weak distillation if applied immediately. Inputs and Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialize the scene representation and optimizer. 2. Determine the warm-up duration T{\text{warm}}: 3,000 iterations for standard datasets (e.g., Deep Blending, Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples); 5,000 iterations for the BungeeNeRF dataset due to large-scale cityscape variations, inconsistent appearance, and geometry. 3. Execute the warm-up phase for iterations t < T{\text{warm}}: Compute the base reconstruction loss L{\text{orig}} (e.g., standard 3DGS loss). For the encoder-freezing variant (Pix2NeRF): Freeze the encoder parameters and update only the decoder/field parameters by minimizing L{\text{orig}}. For the WD Loss variant (3D Gaussian Splatting): Minimize only L{\text{orig}}, excluding the perceptual WD loss. Update parameters using gradient descent on L{\text{total}} = L{\text{orig}}. 4. Transition at iteration t = T{\text{warm}}: Unfreeze the encoder if using the encoder-freezing variant. Enable the perceptual/WD loss component. 5. Execute full training for iterations t \ge T{\text{warm}}: Compute the total loss combining reconstruction and perceptual/adversarial objectives, then update parameters. Formulas: For the WD Loss variant, the total loss switches based on iteration count: L{\text{total}} = \begin{cases} L{\text{orig}} & \text{if } t < T{\text{warm}} \\ L{\text{orig}} + \gamma L{\text{wd}} & \text{if } t \ge T{\text{warm}} \end{cases} where L{\text{orig}} is the original rendering loss, L{\text{wd}} is the perceptual WD loss, and \gamma is a dataset-calibrated scaling coefficient. During the warm-up phase of the encoder-freezing variant, the encoder parameters are fixed, so optimization minimizes only the reconstruction component relative to the frozen encoder output. Parameters: Warm-up iterations (T{\text{warm}}): 3,000 for most datasets; 5,000 for BungeeNeRF. Reconstruction weight (\lambda{\text{recon}}): Must not be lowered to 1 in place of warm-up, as this breaks the balance between reconstruction and adversarial objectives. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mode collapse: Replacing warm-up with a lower reconstruction weight (\lambda{\text{recon}} = 1) causes mode collapse for novel view synthesis because the balance between reconstruction and adversarial objectives is missing. Weak distillation: If the encoder is never unfrozen after warm-up, the distillation remains relatively weak, resulting in few fine details. Overfitting: Without warm-up, the model tends to overfit the input view and cannot produce meaningful content from novel poses. Instability: For datasets with large-scale variations (e.g., BungeeNeRF), skipping warm-up or using insufficient iterations leads to instability caused by pruning and densification heuristics. A training initialization phase that uses the original 3DGS loss before introducing the perceptual WD objective to stabilize optimization, especially for datasets with large viewpoint/geometry variations. It is chosen when using WD-based losses (WD or WD-R) to prevent instability from pruning/densification heuristics and to provide a stable geometric initialization. It differs from the general encoder-freezing warm-up by focusing on loss landscape stability rather than encoder parameter constraints. Time Complexity: Adds T{\text{warm}} iterations of training to the total training time. For standard datasets, this is 3,000 iterations; for BungeeNeRF, 5,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Prevents overfitting to input views and mode collapse. Ensures fine details are captured during distillation. Provides a stable geometric initialization. Strengths: Stabilizes optimization for perceptual losses; prevents mode collapse; improves novel view synthesis quality. Limitations: Increases total training time by the warm-up duration. Requires careful tuning of T{\text{warm}} for specific datasets (e.g., longer for BungeeNeRF). When to Use: When training radiance fields with perceptual/adversarial losses (e.g., Pix2NeRF, WD-3DGS) to avoid overfitting or instability. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The warm-up strategy originated in the context of unsupervised single-shot novel view synthesis, specifically in the Pix2NeRF framework. It was introduced to address the tendency of GAN-based distillation methods to overfit to the input image or collapse into trivial solutions when adversarial and reconstruction losses are balanced improperly. Later, similar warm-up concepts were adopted in 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to stabilize the introduction of perceptual losses (WD loss) in large-scale cityscape datasets. name: Frozen Latent Code
head: Fixed Latent Code Optimization, Latent Code Freezing
body: Frozen Latent Code is a finetuning variant in differentiable volume rendering where the per-identity latent code is kept fixed while only the model parameters are optimized. It solves the problem of adapting a pretrained volumetric prior to a target identity by reducing the optimization degrees of freedom compared to joint optimization. Unlike Model Fitting (Fine-tuning), which jointly optimizes the latent code and model weights, this method optimizes only the model parameters, yielding visually similar results but with different quantitative metrics. Inputs: Pretrained volumetric prior model with weights \theta{\text{pretrained}}. Target identity's latent code w{\text{target}}, obtained from an initialization step (e.g., inversion). Sparse input views of the target identity. Outputs: Finetuned model parameters \theta{\text{target}}. Data Structures: Model parameters \theta{\text{target}}: Tensor of weights for the volumetric prior network. Latent code w{\text{target}}: Fixed vector representing the target identity's features. Steps: 1. Initialize \theta{\text{target}} \leftarrow \theta{\text{pretrained}}. 2. Fix w{\text{target}} as a constant; do not add it to the optimizer's parameter list. 3. For each training iteration: a. Render images from novel viewpoints using \theta{\text{target}} and fixed w{\text{target}}. b. Compute loss against input views. c. Backpropagate gradients to update \theta{\text{target}} only. 4. Return \theta{\text{target}}. Formulas: The optimization objective is: \arg \min{\theta{\text{target}}} \mathcal{L}(\theta{\text{target}}, w{\text{target}}) where w{\text{target}} is constant. Parameters: Resolution: 1024 × 1024 for metric evaluation. Subjects: 3 holdout subjects used for ablation. Edge cases and pitfalls: If geometry is not initialized correctly at the start, artifacts such as a second ear, unrealistic forehead, or fuzzy surface may occur. Starting from an inversion result mitigates these artifacts. The method may fail on out-of-distribution facial expressions if the model was trained on neutral faces with closed mouths. Jointly optimizes latent code and model weights. Choose when higher quantitative metrics are needed despite similar visual quality. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Quantitative metrics were computed for three holdout subjects at 1024 × 1024 resolution. Visual results are very similar to joint optimization. Strengths and limitations: Reduces optimization complexity by fixing the latent code. May yield different quantitative metrics compared to joint optimization. When to use: When visual fidelity is comparable to joint optimization but simpler optimization is preferred. When not: When joint optimization provides significantly better quantitative metrics. Originated in "A Data-driven Volumetric Prior for Few-shot Ultra High-resolution Face Synthesis". It is used for few-shot ultra high-resolution face synthesis from sparse input views. name: Model Fitting (Fine-tuning)
head: Test-Time Finetuning with Optimized Latent Code
body: Model fitting adapts the weights of a pretrained volumetric prior to generate novel views of a target identity at high resolutions from sparse input views. It solves the problem of geometric distortion and high-frequency overfitting that occurs when training a NeRF model on sparse views by initializing with a pretrained prior and optimizing both model parameters and a per-identity latent code. Unlike its sibling Frozen Latent Code, which keeps the latent code fixed, this method jointly optimizes the latent code w{\text{target}} and the model weights \theta{\text{target}}. Inputs: Pretrained volumetric prior model weights. Target identity latent code w{\text{target}} obtained through inversion (Sec. 3.3.2 in). Sparse input views (typically 2 or more) of the target identity. Camera poses aligned to a canonical pose via Procrustes analysis on 3D keypoints (outer eye corners, nose, mouth, chin). Outputs: Finetuned model weights \theta{\text{target}} and optimized latent code w{\text{target}} that generate high-resolution novel views with intricate details (e.g., hair strands). Data Structures: The model architecture is identical to the prior model, except for an additional linear layer that maps features from the trunk to 3D normal vectors. The rendering volume is bounded by a rectangular box because the model generates faces aligned to a canonical pose. Density outside this box is set to zero for final rendering. Steps: 1. Initialize the model weights with the pretrained prior model weights. 2. Use the latent code w{\text{target}} obtained through inversion as the initial latent code. 3. Create training batches by sampling 8,912 rays via random pixel sampling from all available views. 4. Optimize the parameters \theta{\text{target}} and w{\text{target}} using the objective function \mathcal{L}{\text{fit}} until convergence. 5. During rendering, clamp density to zero outside the canonical bounding box. Objective Function: The optimization minimizes the following loss: \argmin {\mathbf {\theta }{\text {target}}, \mathbf {w}{\text {target}}} \mathcal {L}\text {fit} = \mathcal {L}\text {recon} + \lambda \text {prop} \mathcal {L}\text {prop} + \lambda \text {normal} \mathcal {L}\text {normal} + \lambda {v} \mathcal {L}{v} where: \mathcal {L}\text {recon} is the reconstruction loss. \mathcal {L}\text {prop} is the propagation loss with hyperparameter \lambda \text {prop} (same as in Eq. 3 of). \mathcal {L}\text {normal} is the normal consistency loss from RefNeRF [59]. \mathcal {L}{v} = \|\thetav\|2^2, where \thetav correspond to weights of the connections between the encoded view direction and the output. Parameters: \lambda{normal} = 0.001. \lambda{v} = 0.0001. Optimizer: Adam with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999. Learning rate schedule: Starts at 0.001 and exponentially decays to 0.00002. Batch size: 8,912 rays per batch. Optimization steps depend on target resolution: 25,000 steps for 256×256. 50,000 steps for 512×512. 100,000 steps for 1024×1024. 200,000 steps for 2048×2048. 300,000 steps for 4096×4096. Hardware: Always optimized on 4 TPUs. Pitfalls: Naïve optimization without constraints leads to overfitting to the view direction. Regularizing only the view branch weights causes fuzzy surface structures. This fuzziness is mitigated by the normal consistency loss \mathcal {L}\text {normal}. A training procedure that adapts a pre-trained volumetric prior to a target subject by optimizing both model parameters and a per-identity latent code, with an added linear layer for 3D normal prediction. It creates training batches by sampling 8,912 rays via random pixel sampling from all available views. It optimizes using Adam with a learning rate that starts at 0.001 and exponentially decays to 0.00002. The number of optimization steps is set based on target resolution: 25,000 for 256×256, 50,000 for 512×512, 100,000 for 1024×1024, 200,000 for 2048×2048, and 300,000 for 4096×4096. It is always optimized on 4 TPUs. Time Complexity: The model finetuning takes 4 hours for 25,000 steps and linearly increases for more training steps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the authors' dataset, this method achieves PSNR 25.69, SSIM 0.8039, and LPIPS 0.1905, outperforming FreeNeRF [68], EG3D-based prior [9], Learnit [57], RegNeRF [36], and KeypointNeRF [32]. Strengths: Correctly initializing the weights of the model avoids floater artifacts and leads to high-quality novel view synthesis with intricate details like individual hair strands from as few as two views. Limitations: Training a NeRF model on sparse views leads to major artifacts because of distorted geometry and overfitting to high frequencies if not properly constrained. When to use: When adapting a prior model for generating novel views of a target identity at high resolutions from sparse views. When not to use: When the target identity requires a fixed latent code and only model weights should be adapted (use Frozen Latent Code instead). Originated in "A Data-driven Volumetric Prior for Few-shot Ultra High-resolution Face Synthesis". The method addresses the limitations of training NeRF models on sparse views, which typically result in distorted geometry and overfitting to high frequencies. It builds on the concept of using a pretrained prior model trained on low resolution to reconstruct a large set of identities from many views, and then fine-tuning it for a single target identity. The approach relies on camera alignment to a canonical pose using Procrustes analysis on 3D keypoints.
