name: Occlusion-Eliminating NeRF Variant
head: Occlusion-Eliminating NeRF, Zhu et al. NeRF
body: This method addresses novel view synthesis degradation caused by foreground occlusions obscuring background features during training. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by explicitly modeling the scene and the occluding background as separate components, allowing for the recovery of occlusion-free background information. Unlike siblings that rely on generic regularization or diffusion priors, this variant uses a dual-MLP architecture with specific cost volume and depth inconsistency losses to disentangle foreground objects from background artifacts. The method employs a neural network architecture composed of two distinct Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a Scene MLP and a Background MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters (position, orientation), 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}, and viewing directions \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Volume density and color predictions for both the scene and background components, which are combined during rendering. Data Structures: Scene MLP: A standard NeRF-style MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigmas, \mathbf{c}s). Background MLP: A separate MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigmab, \mathbf{c}b). Cost Volume: A 3D structure used to guide the joint optimization of scene parameters and camera poses. Training Procedure: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Scene MLP and Background MLP with random weights. 2. Cost Volume Loss: Construct a cost volume to guide the joint optimization of the Scene MLP parameters and the camera parameters. 3. Depth Bidirectional Inconsistency Prior: Apply a depth bidirectional inconsistency prior within the Background MLP to restore occlusion-free backgrounds via depth distance supervision. 4. Mask Learning: Train the background MLP and remove occlusions from aggregated information from the scene MLP to determine if the output of the background NeRF matches the observed color, learning a mask from the ray's weights. 5. Depth Constraint: Include a depth constraint for probing occluded areas by comparing the depth of occlusion and background, based on the assumption that occlusions are foreground objects at a closer distance. 6. Total Loss: Minimize the sum of the photometric loss and the regularization terms derived from the cost volume and depth priors. Formulas: Exact loss formulas are not given in the sources. Parameters: Typical parameter values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparent Occluders: When the occluding object is a light-loss transparent glass body, reflection artifacts introduce noise pollution into the training images. This prevents the model from generalizing effectively, as the background MLP struggles to distinguish between true background geometry and reflection artifacts. Strengths: Capable of recovering background information that is occluded in training views, improving synthesis quality in cluttered scenes. Limitations: Performance degrades significantly in the presence of transparent or reflective occluders (e.g., glass) due to reflection artifacts. Complexity: Requires maintaining and optimizing two separate MLPs and additional depth-based loss computations, increasing memory and computational overhead compared to single-MLP NeRF. The method was proposed by Zhu et al. in 2023. It was developed to solve the problem of feature damage in NeRF synthesis caused by foreground occlusions. It is part of the broader effort to improve NeRF robustness in real-world scenarios where perfect unobstructed views are unavailable. A follow-up model, NeRFReN by Guo et al., addresses the glass reflection limitation by utilizing geometric priors for depth smoothness and bidirectional depth consistency losses to separate reflection artifacts from physical entities. name: Depth and Geometry Supervision
head: Geometric Regularization, Depth Priors
body: Depth and Geometry Supervision refers to a family of regularization techniques in differentiable volume rendering that incorporate geometric constraints—typically derived from sparse 3D points, monocular depth priors, or multi-view consistency—to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). Unlike pure photometric methods that rely solely on RGB reconstruction, these methods enforce that the rendered depth distribution aligns with external geometric signals, preventing blur and artifacts such as "floaters" or translucent geometry in empty space. The family is distinguished by its direct manipulation of the ray termination distribution or the expected depth via explicit loss terms. Builds on the differentiable volume rendering framework [8586-regularization-and-loss-functions.md], where gradients flow from the loss \mathcal{L} back through the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) to the network parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). The rendering process computes expected color and depth along rays r(t) = o + td using sample points ti with weights wi = T(ti)\rho(ti), where \rho(ti) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(ti))(t{i+1} - ti)) and T(ti) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). The rendering weights wi serve as the probability distribution of absorption along the ray, often denoted as h(t) = T(t)\sigma(t), which is used in distributional geometric losses. The rendered depth is typically the expected distance along the ray: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights, ti are sample depths, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Gradients are backpropagated through the differentiable volume rendering process to update the density and color field parameters. Geometric Baseline Regularization is a composite loss function designed to prevent degenerate solutions in NeRF optimization, particularly in few-view settings where the network might collapse to copying training images [7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. It serves as a strong baseline by combining photometric reconstruction with geometric priors that enforce compact depth distributions, full absorption, and multi-view consistency [7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on external depth supervision or complex structural constraints, this method derives regularization directly from the probabilistic interpretation of the volume rendering weights [7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. Guided Optimization of NeRF mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor scenes by constraining the sampling range of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) using adapted monocular depth priors [7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md]. Unlike standard NeRF, which samples uniformly between near and far bounds derived from sparse reconstruction, this method calculates adaptive bounds based on multi-view consistency errors of the depth priors, ensuring samples concentrate around plausible geometry even in textureless regions [7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md]. It sets itself apart from Depth and Geometry Supervision methods that apply explicit geometric losses by instead guiding the sampling distribution itself, thereby preventing the network from exploring degenerate geometric solutions that still fit the RGB data [7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md]. Depth-Supervised NeRF (DS-NeRF) is a training procedure for Neural Radiance Fields that incorporates sparse 3D depth supervision from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds to accelerate convergence and improve reconstruction quality with fewer input views [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Unlike methods relying on category-specific priors or dense multi-view stereo (MVS) initialization, DS-NeRF treats the sparse keypoints generated during standard SfM preprocessing as "free" geometric constraints, enforcing that the rendered ray termination distribution aligns with these surface priors [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. This approach reduces overfitting in sparse-view settings and typically achieves target quality in 2–3× fewer training iterations than standard NeRF [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Robust Depth Loss is a geometry supervision function designed to mitigate the degradation of extrapolation performance caused by inaccurate or noisy pseudo-depth maps in differentiable volume rendering [9368-robust-depth-loss.md]. It addresses the problem where standard L2 losses are overly sensitive to outliers, forcing the neural radiance field (NeRF) to fit erroneous geometry [9368-robust-depth-loss.md]. By using a loss function that is less sensitive to large errors than L2, it encourages the network to terminate rays near the pseudo-depth while retaining freedom to ignore inaccurate geometry when the error is very large or very small [9368-robust-depth-loss.md]. It is distinct from Geometric Baseline Regularization which focuses on baseline consistency, and Depth-Supervised NeRF which typically uses standard L1/L2 losses without this specific robust formulation. Depth Structural Consistency Regularization (RDSC) is a geometric regularization technique applied during Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training to enforce continuity constraints on rendered depth maps, leveraging external depth priors such as those from DepthAnythingV2 [9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Patch-Based Depth Regularization by explicitly modeling structural consistency through k-nearest neighbor (KNN) relationships in depth space rather than spatial proximity alone, ensuring that neighboring pixels in the prior map exhibit similar continuity in the rendered output [9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md]. Indirect Depth Supervision treats the volume-rendering weights along a ray as a discrete probability distribution and minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between this rendered distribution and a unimodal target distribution centered at a measured LiDAR range [10481-indirect-depth-supervision-kl-loss.md]. It differs from direct depth supervision (e.g., Direct Depth Supervision) by enforcing geometric consistency through distribution alignment rather than penalizing the difference between expected depth values [10481-indirect-depth-supervision-kl-loss.md]. Novel View Regularization mitigates the shape-radiance ambiguity in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by incorporating rays from unobserved viewpoints into the training loop [10806-novel-view-regularization.md]. Unlike methods that rely solely on observed image supervision, this approach adds geometric guidance to prevent overfitting to sparse input views [10806-novel-view-regularization.md]. It sets itself apart by explicitly sampling and rendering novel views during optimization to enforce geometric consistency, whereas siblings like Depth and Geometry Supervision may rely on external depth priors or structural constraints without necessarily synthesizing new viewpoints [10806-novel-view-regularization.md]. Volumetric Supervision is a training strategy that leverages high-quality volumetric reconstructions from conventional tomography to supervise neural network training at intermediate time steps where only sparse projection data is available [11100-volumetric-supervision.md]. It solves the problem of temporal interpolation in dynamic tomography by using dense ground-truth volumes at the start and end of an experiment to regularize the learning of the canonical model and deformation field [11100-volumetric-supervision.md]. Unlike sibling methods that primarily enforce geometric consistency via depth or gradient losses, this method directly minimizes the discrepancy between the predicted 3D volume and a physically reconstructed 3D volume [11100-volumetric-supervision.md]. Direct Depth Supervision is a regularization technique in differentiable volume rendering that minimizes the pixel-wise discrepancy between the depth map rendered by the neural radiance field and a provided ground truth depth prior [11396-direct-depth-supervision.md]. It explicitly constrains the geometric structure of the scene, distinguishing it from photometric losses that enforce color consistency. Unlike indirect methods that enforce geometric consistency through other signals, this approach directly penalizes errors in the expected depth value [11396-direct-depth-supervision.md]. This method minimizes the Euclidean distance between 3D points backprojected from rendered depth and ground-truth 3D points to enforce global geometric consistency during NeRF optimization [12693-3d-point-supervision-loss.md]. Unlike direct depth regression, which often fails to register camera poses in sparse-view regimes by favoring per-image local geometry, this loss explicitly connects training images to the underlying scene structure, enabling robust pose refinement [12693-3d-point-supervision-loss.md]. Generalized Ray Supervision is a framework for optimizing neural scene representations by treating arbitrary rays in a scene as "ray sensors" that record incoming radiance, extending the standard NeRF approach which only supervises camera rays [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md]. It solves the problem of limited geometric and photometric constraints in standard multi-view optimization by allowing supervision signals from non-camera perspectives, such as shadow rays or rays from unseen viewpoints, to guide the learning of density and color fields [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md]. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes light emission from scene particles, this generalization allows for physically correct modeling where the scene absorbs light from known sources or enforces semantic consistency across views [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md]. Not given in the sources. S-NeRF Confidence Components is a selective confidence weighting mechanism for differentiable volume rendering that adapts the reliability of supervision signals based on scene content, specifically distinguishing between static background environments and dynamic foreground objects like vehicles [15152-s-nerf-confidence-components.md]. It sets itself apart from standard geometric regularization by decoupling confidence metrics per object class: it employs geometry and reprojection measurements for background learning, while restricting foreground vehicle learning to RGB and SSIM confidences, leveraging the higher quality of LiDAR depth maps available for foreground objects [15152-s-nerf-confidence-components.md]. Not given in the sources. A loss function that enforces consistency between depth estimates of the coarse and fine NeRF models to prevent ineffective hierarchical sampling and blur. The loss is defined as L{cfc} = \mathbb{1}{\{mf=1\}} \odot \|zc - \hat{\nabla}(zf)\|^2 + \mathbb{1}{\{mc=1\}} \odot \|\hat{\nabla}(zc) - zf\|^2, where zc and zf are coarse and fine depths, and mc/mf are reliability masks determined by reprojection. An approach that uses data augmentation by rendering new training images with new noisy camera poses using DSNeRF as a baseline and using depth as regularization. A supervision technique that incorporates off-the-shelf Multi-View Stereo (MVS) features into Gaussian primitives to prevent geometric degradation under sparse views, where color alone overfits. It extracts feature maps from an MVS network (e.g., CLMVSNet), samples both RGB color and MVS features into each Gaussian primitive, and fixes these values during optimization to enforce learning specifically for geometry. The rendered feature is computed via alpha compositing over M primitives: \hat{f} = \sum{m=1}^{M} fm \cdot \alpham \prod{o=1}^{m-1} (1 - \alpham), where \alpham is opacity. A pitfall is that simultaneous learning of appearance and feature with geometry causes geometric degradation under sparse views. An analysis characterizing the strength with which photometric supervision constrains geometric parameters by decomposing the Gaussian-center gradient over observations. Not given in the sources. name: Geometric Baseline Regularization
head: Geometric Baseline, Geometric Loss
body: Geometric Baseline Regularization is a composite loss function designed to prevent degenerate solutions in Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization, particularly in few-view settings where the network might collapse to copying training images. It serves as a strong baseline by combining photometric reconstruction with geometric priors that enforce compact depth distributions, full absorption, and multi-view consistency. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on external depth supervision or complex structural constraints, this method derives regularization directly from the volume rendering process. The method optimizes the density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} fields by minimizing a total loss \mathcal{L}{\text{geom}} that combines a photometric term with three geometric regularizers. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Training images \mathcal{I}, camera poses, ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d}, sample depths ti along rays, and hyperparameters \lambda{\text{fg}}, \lambda{\text{fr}}, \lambda{\text{dist}}. Outputs: Updated network parameters \theta = (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Data Structures Rendering Weights: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)), where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rhoj) is the accumulated transmittance, \rhoi = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the opacity, and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Expected Depth: \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N wi ti}{\sum{i=1}^N wi}. Formulas The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{geom}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda{\text{fg}} \mathcal{L}{\text{fg}} + \lambda{\text{fr}} \mathcal{L}{\text{fr}} + \lambda{\text{dist}} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} 1. Photometric Loss: L2 difference between input image Ii and rendered color \mathbf{C}i: \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}(\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = \sum{i=1}^{\mathcal{I}} ||Ii - \mathbf{C}i||2 2. Foreground Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{fg}}): Encourages weights to sum to unity, ensuring rays are fully absorbed by scene geometry: \mathcal{L}{\text{fg}} = \left( 1 - \sum{i=1}^N wi \right)^2 3. Frustum Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{fr}}): Penalizes density placed in only one view frustum to prevent "image plane" collapse: \mathcal{L}{\text{fr}} = \sumi wi \mathbf{1}(ni \le 1) where ni is the number of training view frustums containing the point \mathbf{r}(ti), and \mathbf{1}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 4. Distribution Loss (\mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}): Regularizes weights to have a compact distribution, deviating from the original formulation by dividing by expected depth to increase strength for geometry close to the camera: \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r})} \left( \sum{i,j} wi wj \left| \frac{ti + t{i+1}}{2} - \frac{tj + t{j+1}}{2} \right| + \frac{1}{3} \sum{i=1}^N wi^2 (t{i+1} - ti) \right) Note: The source text contains a typo using wk in the pairwise sum; it is corrected here to wj to match the summation indices. Parameters \lambda{\text{fg}}, \lambda{\text{fr}}: Coefficients for foreground and frustum losses. Values not explicitly given in the sources. \lambda{\text{dist}}: Weight for the distribution regularizer. It is 0 for the first 3000 steps, then linearly increases to 1 \times 10^{-4} for the DTU dataset and 1.5 \times 10^{-5} for the LLFF dataset at 8000 steps. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometricbaselineloss(renderedcolors, targetimages, weights, depths, frustumcounts, lambdafg, lambdafr, lambdadist, step, maxsteps=8000, dataset='DTU'): """ Computes the Geometric Baseline Loss. weights: list of lists, shape [numrays, N] depths: list of lists, shape [numrays, N+1] (N sample depths + ray end) frustumcounts: list of lists, shape [numrays, N] """ # 1. Photometric Loss photoloss = 0.0 for img, pred in zip(targetimages, renderedcolors): photoloss += sum((x - y) 2 for x, y in zip(img, pred)) 0.5 # 2. Foreground Loss: Encourage sum of weights to be 1 fgloss = 0.0 for w in weights: fgloss += (1.0 - sum(w)) 2 # 3. Frustum Loss: Penalize weights in only one frustum frloss = 0.0 for w, n in zip(weights, frustumcounts): for wi, count in zip(w, n): if count <= 1: frloss += wi # 4. Distribution Loss distloss = 0.0 for w, d in zip(weights, depths): numerator = sum(wi di for wi, di in zip(w, d[:-1])) denominator = sum(w) # Avoid division by zero if denominator > 1e-8: D = numerator / denominator else: D = 1.0 # Fallback if D < 1e-8: continue # Term 1: Sum over pairs i, j of |midi - midj| wi wj pairsum = 0.0 numsamples = len(w) for i in range(numsamples): midi = (d[i] + d[i + 1]) / 2.0 for j in range(numsamples): midj = (d[j] + d[j + 1]) / 2.0 pairsum += w[i] w[j] abs(midi - midj) # Term 2: 1/3 sum(wi^2 deltai) deltasum = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): delta = d[i + 1] - d[i] deltasum += (w[i] 2) delta raydist = (pairsum + (1.0 / 3.0) deltasum) / D distloss += raydist # Schedule lambdadist: starts at 3000 steps per source if step < 3000: currentlambdadist = 0.0 else: progress = (step - 3000) / (maxsteps - 3000) maxval = 1e-4 if dataset == 'DTU' else 1.5e-5 currentlambdadist = progress maxval totalloss = photoloss + lambdafg fgloss + lambdafr frloss + currentlambdadist distloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls Division by Zero: The distribution loss divides by expected depth \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}). If a ray has no absorption (sum of weights \approx 0), depth is undefined. Few-View Collapse: Without \mathcal{L}{\text{fr}}, NeRFs may collapse to copying training images. Depth Scaling: The division by \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{r}) in \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} increases the regularizer's strength for geometry close to the camera, which is a deviation from the original formulation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a robust baseline for few-view reconstruction without requiring external depth maps or point clouds. It effectively prevents degenerate solutions. Limitations: The effectiveness depends on careful tuning of \lambda{\text{dist}} schedule. The Geometric Baseline Regularization is a loss combination used as a strong baseline for NeRF optimization, detailed in the DiffusioNeRF paper. It addresses degenerate solutions in few-view settings by regularizing the density and color fields through derived ray metrics. name: Guided Optimization of NeRF
head: Confidence-Based Depth Filtering
body: Guided Optimization of NeRF mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor scenes by restricting the sampling range of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) along camera rays using adapted monocular depth priors. Unlike standard NeRF, which samples uniformly between near and far bounds derived from sparse reconstruction, this method computes adaptive bounds based on multi-view geometric consistency errors, ensuring samples concentrate around plausible geometry. It sets itself apart from siblings like Depth-Supervised NeRF by not requiring ground-truth depth labels during training, instead using the rendered RGB reconstruction error to derive confidence scores for post-processing depth refinement. Inputs: N input views with RGB images and camera intrinsics K. Initial adapted monocular depth priors \{D^i\}{i=1}^N for each view i, obtained from a finetuned monocular depth network. Relative poses T^{i \rightarrow j} between views. Parameters: K=4 (number of cross-view errors for consistency), \alphal = 0.05 (lower bound factor), \alphah = 0.15 (upper bound factor), M (number of samples per ray). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). Refined depth maps for all views. Data Structures: Error Map e^i: A 2D array per view i, where each pixel value represents the average of the K minimum cross-view reprojection errors. Confidence Map S^i: A 2D array per view i, where each pixel value S^ij \in [0, 1] represents the confidence of the depth prediction at pixel j. Steps: 1. Acquire Adapted Depth Priors: Initialize depth priors \{D^i\}{i=1}^N using a pre-trained monocular depth network finetuned on the target scene. 2. Compute Geometric Consistency Error Maps: For each view i, project its depth map D^i to all other views j \neq i. Calculate the projected depth D^{i \rightarrow j} at 2D coordinates p^{i \rightarrow j} in view j: p^{i \rightarrow j}, D^{i \rightarrow j} = \text{proj}(K, T^{i \rightarrow j}, D^i) D^{j'} = D^j(p^{i \rightarrow j}) Compute the relative reprojection error for overlapping pixels. For each pixel in view i, calculate the error map value e^i as the average of the K minimum cross-view depth projection errors. 3. Calculate Adaptive Sample Ranges: For each ray \mathbf{r} corresponding to a pixel in view i, determine the near bound tn and far bound tf using the adapted depth prior D (the value of D^i at that pixel) and the error map value e (the value of e^i at that pixel): tn = D(1 - \text{clamp}(e, \alphal, \alphah)) tf = D(1 + \text{clamp}(e, \alphal, \alphah)) Here, \text{clamp}(x, a, b) restricts x to the interval [a, b]. 4. Stratified Sampling: Partition the interval [tn, tf] into M bins. For each bin k \in [1, M], sample a point tk uniformly from the bin interval: tk \sim \mathcal{U} \left[ tn + \frac{k-1}{M}(tf - tn), \,\, tn + \frac{k}{M}(tf - tn) \right] Query the NeRF at positions xk = o + tk d to obtain color \mathbf{c}k and density \sigmak. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the accumulated transmittance Tk = \exp \left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right), where \deltaj = t{j+1} - tj. Render the color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{M} Tk (1 - e^{-\sigmak \deltak}) \mathbf{c}k \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{M} Tk (1 - e^{-\sigmak \deltak}) tk 6. Compute Confidence Scores: After rendering, compute the confidence score S^ij for pixel j in view i based on the L1 difference between the ground truth RGB image \mathbf{C}{gt}^i(j) and the rendered RGB image \hat{\mathbf{C}}^i(j) (values normalized to [0, 1] by dividing by 255): S^ij = 1 - \frac{1}{3} \|\mathbf{C}{gt}^i(j) - \hat{\mathbf{C}}^i(j)\|1 7. Depth Refinement: Apply plane bilateral filtering to the rendered depth map \hat{D}^i, weighted by the confidence scores S^i, to produce the final refined depth map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Standard NeRF sampling fails here because sampled points predict similar RGB values with confidence concentrated in a limited range, leading to depth deviation from ground truth. Correspondence-based optimization degradation: Applying existing correspondence-based neural optimization (like CVD) to adapted depth priors degrades quality due to unreliable flow correspondences in poorly textured regions. Integrates pixel-region and depth-boundary-guided ray sampling into ENeRF to reduce GPU memory and improve sampling efficiency using monocular depth priors. Uses a discrete feature grid to guide NeRF sampling toward the scene surface, resolving shape-radiance ambiguity in large-scale urban scenes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method adds overhead to the standard NeRF training loop due to the initial multi-view consistency check (projection of depth maps) and the final bilateral filtering. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing N depth maps and N error maps during the consistency check phase. Performance: Outperforms original NeRF and other state-of-the-art methods on indoor datasets like ScanNet in terms of depth estimation accuracy (e.g., AbsRel, SqRel) and view synthesis quality (PSNR). Strengths: Effectively mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in poorly textured indoor areas (e.g., walls) where standard NeRF fails. Does not require ground-truth depth supervision during training. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial monocular depth priors. The method assumes sufficient multi-view overlap for the consistency check. When to use: Indoor multi-view stereo and depth estimation where texture is sparse and ground-truth depth is unavailable. The method was introduced in "Depth-Guided Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields for Indoor Multi-View Stereo". It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which suffers from shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor environments, particularly in texture-less regions like walls. While NeRF can synthesize high-quality RGB images, the underlying geometry (depth) often deviates significantly from the ground truth. The authors observed that applying correspondence-based optimization directly to monocular depth priors degrades quality, motivating the guided optimization approach that uses the priors to constrain sampling rather than as direct supervision. name: ENeRF with Guided Sampling Training
head: ENeRF Depth-Guided Training, ENeRF Guided Sampling
body: ENeRF with Guided Sampling Training is a training procedure that integrates pixel-region and depth-boundary-guided ray sampling into the Efficient Neural Radiance Field (ENeRF) framework. It reduces GPU memory consumption and improves sampling efficiency by using fewer rays per iteration while maintaining or improving rendering performance. It builds on Guided Optimization of NeRF by actively guiding sampling locations using adapted monocular depth priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained ENeRF model (generalized from the DTU dataset), input images, and estimated depth maps for the input views. Outputs: Optimized radiance field parameters and rendered images for novel views. Data Structures: Ray Sampling Set: A subset of camera rays selected based on pixel region importance and depth boundary locations. Sampling Points: Points along the selected rays where the neural network is evaluated. The default configuration uses 8 points for the coarse stage and 2 points for the fine stage in a 2-stage NeRF setup. Training Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the ENeRF model pre-trained on the DTU dataset. 2. Ray Selection: Sample a reduced number of rays (Nr) per iteration. The selection is guided by prioritizing regions with high gradient or error, and prioritizing rays passing through depth discontinuities derived from monocular depth estimates. 3. Point Sampling: For each selected ray, sample points along the ray. The number of points is typically 8 for the coarse network and 2 for the fine network. 4. Rendering: Render the color \hat{C}i for each ray using volume rendering. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} using the following components: MSE Loss: \mathcal{L}{mse} = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{i=1}^{Nr} \| \hat{C}i - Ci \|^2 where Nr is the number of sampled rays, \hat{C}i is the rendered color, and Ci is the ground-truth color. Perceptual Loss: \mathcal{L}{perc} = \frac{1}{Ni} \sum{i=1}^{Ni} \| \Phi(\hat{I}i) - \Phi(Ii) \| where Ni is the number of image blocks, \Phi is the perceptual function defined in the original ENeRF paper, \hat{I}i is the rendered image block, and Ii is the ground-truth image block. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{mse} + \lambda' \mathcal{L}{perc} where \lambda' is the weight for perceptual loss. 6. Optimization: Update the ENeRF model parameters using gradient descent on \mathcal{L}. 7. Fine-tuning: After pre-training on DTU, fine-tune the model on the target novel scenes for a few epochs. Parameters: \lambda': Weight for perceptual loss. Default value: 0.01. Sampling Points: 8 (coarse) and 2 (fine) for standard settings; 16 (coarse) and 4 (fine) for large-baseline adaptations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Estimation Quality: In large baseline settings with sparse view overlap, monocular depth estimation quality degrades, which negatively affects the NeRF rendering process. Memory Usage: While the method reduces GPU memory usage compared to standard ENeRF by sampling fewer rays, insufficient sampling points in low-quality depth scenarios can lead to poor results. Args: model: Pre-trained ENeRF model. images: List of input images. depths: List of estimated depth maps. numepochs: Number of fine-tuning epochs. lambdaprime: Weight for perceptual loss. numcoarse: Number of coarse sampling points per ray. numfine: Number of fine sampling points per ray. """ # Standard gradient-based optimizer (e.g., Adam) optimizer = Optimizer(model.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, depth in zip(images, depths): # 1. It sets itself apart from the standard ENeRF guided sampling by doubling the number of sampling points on each ray from 8 and 2 to 16 and 4 for 2-stage NeRFs. Choose this variant when input views have small overlap, leading to lower depth estimation quality that negatively affects the rendering process. Time and Memory Complexity: The method reduces GPU memory usage compared to standard ENeRF by sampling fewer rays per iteration. Measured Performance: Achieves improved performance on the DTU dataset (pre-training) and fine-tuned on novel scenes. Tested on Real Forward-facing, NeRF Synthetic, ZJU-MoCap, and digital human datasets. Scaling: Performance degrades in large baseline settings if sampling density is not increased. Strengths: Lower GPU memory footprint, improved performance with fewer rays, effective generalization to novel scenes. Limitations: Relies on the quality of monocular depth estimates; performance drops if depth estimation is poor (e.g., large baselines). When to Use: When GPU memory is constrained and high-quality monocular depth estimates are available. When Not to Use: In large baseline settings with sparse view overlap unless sampling density is increased. ENeRF with Guided Sampling Training was introduced in the context of efficient radiance field reconstruction. It builds on the ENeRF framework, which focuses on rapid generalization for novel scenes. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of standard ray sampling in NeRFs, particularly in generalizable settings. It has been used in experiments on the DTU dataset for pre-training and fine-tuned on various other datasets including Real Forward-facing, NeRF Synthetic, ZJU-MoCap, and digital human datasets. The large-baseline adaptation was proposed in the MuRF paper to handle sparse view scenarios. name: Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training
head: Grid Pretrain, Grid branch, Grid-guided Neural Radiance Fields, NeRF Branch, Ours, Stage 2 Joint Learning
body: Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training is a two-stage optimization procedure for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that integrates a discrete feature grid with a continuous MLP branch to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in large-scale urban scene reconstruction. Unlike pure grid-based methods (e.g., TensoRF) that suffer from noise in continuous regions or pure NeRF methods that struggle with high-frequency details, this method uses a pre-trained grid to guide NeRF sampling toward the scene surface while the NeRF branch provides high-frequency regularization and detail recovery. It sets itself apart from siblings like ENeRF with Guided Sampling Training by explicitly coupling the grid's density/appearance features with the NeRF's positional encoding in a joint optimization loop, rather than using the grid solely for sampling density. Inputs: A set of calibrated camera poses and corresponding RGB images for a large-scale scene. A pre-trained multi-resolution feature grid (see Data Structures). Outputs: A refined feature grid and a NeRF branch network (MLP) that jointly predict volume density and color for any 3D point and viewing direction. Multi-Resolution Feature Grid: The 3D feature grid is stored as a plane-vector representation to reduce memory usage compared to a full 3D voxel grid. It consists of: 1. Ground Feature Planes: 2D planes representing the xy-plane. For each resolution level r, there are separate planes for density (R{\sigma}) and appearance (R{c}). 2. Z-Axis Encoding: Globally encoded feature vectors for the z-axis. 3. Resolution Levels: The grid uses multiple resolutions. The highest resolution is denoted as H^2 (e.g., 4096^2). Additional lower resolutions are included at downsampled scales of \times 4 and \times 16 relative to the highest resolution. 4. Channel Allocation: The highest resolution plane uses 8 components for density and 8 for appearance. Lower resolutions follow similar allocations scaled by the resolution factor. 5. Parameter Count: The total parameter count for this representation is approximately 3 \times 10^8, which is fewer than TensoRF's 4 \times 10^8 parameters. NeRF Branch Network: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with D=3 hidden layers (4 layers total) and no skip connections. Hidden width W=256. Input dimension depends on the concatenation of grid features and positional encodings. 1. Stage 1: Grid Pretraining Train the feature grid branch independently for the first 10,000 iterations. Sample N points along each ray using a coarse sampling strategy (e.g., uniform or stratified sampling). For each sampled point X, retrieve grid features \mathcal{G}\sigma(X) and \mathcal{G}c(X) via bilinear interpolation on the multi-resolution feature planes. Predict volume density \sigma and color c using a small MLP head (same architecture as TensoRF's renderer). Render pixel colors via volumetric integration. Optimize the grid parameters using the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between rendered and ground truth pixel colors. 2. Stage 2: Joint Optimization Initialize the NeRF branch network. Optimize both the grid branch and the NeRF branch jointly for 100,000 iterations. Sampling Guidance: Use the density predictions from the pre-trained grid branch to guide the sampling of points along camera rays. The sampling concentrates on the scene surface approximated by the grid, allowing for denser sampling in relevant regions. Feature Extraction: For each sampled point X, infer grid features \mathcal{G}\sigma(X) and \mathcal{G}c(X) by bilinear interpolation on the multi-resolution feature planes. NeRF Input Construction: Concatenate the inferred grid features with positional encodings of the point coordinates X and viewing direction d. \text{Input} = [\mathcal{G}\sigma(X), \mathcal{G}c(X), \operatorname{PE}(X), \operatorname{PE}(d)] NeRF Prediction: Feed the concatenated input into the NeRF branch network F' to predict refined volume density \sigma' and color c': (\sigma', c') = F'(\mathcal{G}\sigma(X), \mathcal{G}c(X), \operatorname{PE}(X), \operatorname{PE}(d)) Rendering: Render fine-resolution pixel colors using the NeRF branch's density and color predictions via volumetric integration. Loss Calculation: Compute the reconstruction loss (MSE) for both the grid branch outputs and the NeRF branch outputs. Joint Update: Update both the grid parameters and the NeRF branch parameters using the combined loss. The loss weighting between the two branches is set to 1:1. Grid Feature Interpolation: For a point X = (x, y, z), the grid features are obtained by projecting X onto the ground feature planes and interpolating. Let P{xy} be the 2D coordinates on the ground plane. The feature F(X) at resolution r is: F(X) = \text{BilinearInterpolate}(P{xy}, \text{Plane}r) This is performed for each resolution level and combined (e.g., via summation or concatenation as per the specific implementation, though the text implies retrieval from the multi-resolution set). NeRF Branch Forward Pass: (\sigma', c') = F'(\mathcal{G}\sigma(X), \mathcal{G}c(X), \operatorname{PE}(X), \operatorname{PE}(d)) Where: \sigma' is the predicted volume density. c' is the predicted view-dependent color. F' is the 4-layer MLP without skip connections. \operatorname{PE}(\cdot) is the positional encoding function. Loss Function: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{grid}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{nerf}} Where \mathcal{L}{\text{grid}} is the MSE loss between the grid branch's rendered image and the ground truth, and \mathcal{L}{\text{nerf}} is the MSE loss between the NeRF branch's rendered image and the ground truth. The weights are equal (1:1). Pretraining Iterations: 10,000. Joint Optimization Iterations: 100,000. Time Fraction: Roughly 1:4 between pretraining and joint optimization stages. Loss Weighting: 1:1 between grid branch and NeRF branch during joint training. Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.02 for tensor factors (grid parameters), 0.01 for MLP layers (NeRF branch). Batch Size: 4096 rays. NeRF MLP Architecture: Depth D=3 hidden layers (4 layers total), Width W=256, no skip connections. Positional Encoding (PE) Frequency: Standard configuration bandwidth ranges from 20 to 22. Ablation tests used up to 216. Grid Resolutions: Tested at 512^2, 2048^2, and 4096^2. Low-Resolution Grids: Using a low-resolution grid (e.g., 512^2) during pretraining results in blurry artifacts. While the NeRF branch can recover some details, the overall result lacks sharpness. High-Resolution Grids without NeRF: High-resolution grids (e.g., 2048^2) pre-trained without NeRF supervision produce fuzzy and noisy results in continuous regions (e.g., roads, walls) due to grid variation artifacts. Small NeRF Capacity: A NeRF branch with insufficient capacity (e.g., D=3, W=32) is unable to effectively translate grid features, leading to inaccurate geometry and scene contents. Training Speed: The joint optimization stage suffers from slow training times. Shuffled ray batch sampling is highly ineffective for large scenes without distributed training infrastructure. PE Frequency: Increasing PE frequency bandwidth beyond the standard range (20-22) provides little benefit if the NeRF model capacity is not sufficiently large (e.g., W=256). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def gridguidednerftraining(scenedata, gridconfig, nerfconfig): """ Main training loop for Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training. Args: scenedata: Object containing camera poses and RGB images. gridconfig: Configuration for the feature grid (resolutions, channels). nerfconfig: Configuration for the NeRF branch (MLP layers, PE frequency). Returns: Trained grid parameters and NeRF branch weights. """ # Initialize Grid Branch grid = FeatureGrid(gridconfig) gridoptimizer = Adam(grid.parameters(), lr=0.02) # Initialize NeRF Branch nerfmlp = MLP(layers=[256, 256, 256, 1], skipconnections=False) nerfoptimizer = Adam(nerfmlp.parameters(), lr=0.01) # Stage 1: Grid Pretraining (10,000 iterations) for iteration in range(10000): rays = samplerays(scenedata, batchsize=4096) points = samplepointsuniform(rays, numsamples=64) gridfeaturessigma = grid.interpolatedensity(points) gridfeaturescolor = grid.interpolateappearance(points) sigma, color = gridrenderer(gridfeaturessigma, gridfeaturescolor) renderedimage = volumerender(points, sigma, color, rays) gtimage = getgroundtruth(rays, scenedata) loss = mseloss(renderedimage, gtimage) gridoptimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() gridoptimizer.step() # Stage 2: Joint Optimization (100,000 iterations) for iteration in range(100000): rays = samplerays(scenedata, batchsize=4096) coarsepoints = samplepointsuniform(rays, numsamples=32) coarsegridsigma = grid.interpolatedensity(coarsepoints) coarsesigma, = gridrenderer(coarsegridsigma, grid.interpolateappearance(coarsepoints)) finepoints = samplepointsguided(rays, coarsesigma, numsamples=128) finegridsigma = grid.interpolatedensity(finepoints) finegridcolor = grid.interpolateappearance(finepoints) pepoints = positionalencoding(finepoints, freqmin=20, freqmax=22) pedirs = positionalencoding(rays.directions, freqmin=20, freqmax=22) nerfinput = concatenate([finegridsigma, finegridcolor, pepoints, pedirs]) sigmanerf, colornerf = nerfmlp(nerfinput) renderedimagenerf = volumerender(finepoints, sigmanerf, colornerf, rays) gtimage = getgroundtruth(rays, scenedata) lossnerf = mseloss(renderedimagenerf, gtimage) gridsigma, gridcolor = gridrenderer(finegridsigma, finegridcolor) renderedimagegrid = volumerender(finepoints, gridsigma, gridcolor, rays) lossgrid = mseloss(renderedimagegrid, gtimage) totalloss = lossnerf + lossgrid gridoptimizer.zerograd() nerfoptimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() gridoptimizer.step() nerfoptimizer.step() return grid, nerfmlp def positionalencoding(x, freqmin, freqmax): """Standard positional encoding.""" scales = np.array([2i for i in range(freqmin, freqmax)]) scaledx = np.outer(x.flatten(), scales) return np.sin(scaledx).reshape(-1, 3 2 (freqmax - freqmin)) def concatenate(tensors): """Concatenate tensors along the last dimension.""" return np.concatenate(tensors, axis=-1) def mseloss(pred, target): """Mean squared error loss.""" return np.mean((pred - target) 2) def getgroundtruth(rays, scenedata): """Fetch ground truth image for the given rays.""" return scenedata.images[rays.cameraids] def volumerender(points, sigma, color, rays): """Standard alpha compositing volume rendering.""" tvals = points[:, 2] # Assuming z is depth along ray deltas = np.diff(np.concatenate([np.zeroslike(tvals[:1]), tvals])) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma deltas) weights = alpha np.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10)[:-1] return np.sum(weights[:, None] color, axis=0) def gridrenderer(gridsigma, gridcolor): """Small MLP renderer for grid features (TensoRF style).""" # Simplified: direct pass-through for pseudocode clarity return gridsigma, gridcolor def samplepointsguided(rays, coarsesigma, numsamples): """Sample points using inverse CDF of coarse density.""" tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) # Inverse CDF sampling based on coarsesigma cdf = np.cumsum(coarsesigma) cdf /= cdf[-1] indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, tvals) return rays.origin + tvals[:, None] rays.direction def samplepointsuniform(rays, numsamples): """Uniformly sample points along rays.""" tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) return rays.origin + tvals[:, None] rays.direction def samplerays(scenedata, batchsize): """Generate random rays from camera poses.""" idx = np.random.choice(len(scenedata.poses), batchsize) rays = type('Rays', (), {})() rays.origin = scenedata.poses[idx,:3, 3] rays.direction = scenedata.poses[idx,:3,:3] @ np.array([0, 0, -1]) rays.cameraids = idx return rays class MLP: """Simple Multi-Layer Perceptron.""" def init(self, layers, skipconnections=False): self.layers = layers self.weights = [np.random.randn(layers[i], layers[i+1]) for i in range(len(layers)-1)] self.skipconnections = skipconnections def call(self, x): for i, w in enumerate(self.weights): x = np.dot(x, w) if i < len(self.weights) - 1: x = np.maximum(0, x) # ReLU return x[:,:1], x[:, 1:] # Split for sigma and color class Adam: """Standard Adam optimizer.""" def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.m = {id(p): np.zeroslike(p) for p in params} self.v = {id(p): np.zeroslike(p) for p in params} self.t = 0 def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = np.zeroslike(p) def step(self): self.t += 1 for p in self.params: g = p.grad self.m[id(p)] = 0.9 self.m[id(p)] + 0.1 g self.v[id(p)] = 0.999 self.v[id(p)] + 0.001 (g 2) mhat = self.m[id(p)] / (1 - 0.9 self.t) vhat = self.v[id(p)] / (1 - 0.999 self.t) p -= self.lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + 1e-8) class FeatureGrid: """Plane-vector feature grid.""" def init(self, config): self.resolutions = config['resolutions'] self.planes = {r: {'sigma': np.random.randn(config['channels'], r, r), 'color': np.random.randn(config['channels'], r, r)} for r in self.resolutions} self.zvec = np.random.randn(config['channels']) def interpolatedensity(self, points): features = [] for r in self.resolutions: plane = self.planes[r]['sigma'] # Bilinear interpolation on xy x, y = points[:, 0], points[:, 1] ix = np.clip(x r, 0, r-1).astype(int) iy = np.clip(y r, 0, r-1).astype(int) features.append(plane[:, iy, ix]) return np.sum(np.stack(features, axis=0), axis=0) def interpolateappearance(self, points): features = [] for r in self.resolutions: plane = self.planes[r]['color'] x, y = points[:, 0], points[:, 1] ix = np.clip(x r, 0, r-1).astype(int) iy = np.clip(y r, 0, r-1).astype(int) features.append(plane[:, iy, ix]) return np.sum(np.stack(features, axis=0), axis=0) The initial phase where only the feature grid is trained using coarse sampling and a small renderer. It provides a coarse approximation of the scene density and appearance. It is chosen when a strong geometric prior is needed before refining with a complex MLP. Link: Grid Pretrain (conceptual link within the parent article). The continuous MLP component that takes grid features and positional encodings as input. It is chosen for its ability to recover high-frequency details and regularize the grid features. Link: NeRF Branch. Time Complexity: The joint optimization stage is computationally expensive. Training time is dominated by the 100,000 iterations of joint optimization, with a time fraction of roughly 1:4 compared to the pretraining stage. Memory Complexity: The plane-vector representation uses approximately 3 \times 10^8 parameters, which is memory-efficient compared to full 3D voxel grids and slightly better than TensoRF's 4 \times 10^8 parameters. Measured Performance: On large urban scenes, the method achieves a PSNR of 20.915, comparable to TensoRF's 21.075, but with fewer parameters. Scaling: The method is designed for extremely large-scale environments (e.g., urban scenes). However, shuffled ray batch sampling is ineffective for large scenes without distributed training, limiting scalability on single machines. Strengths: Mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity by guiding sampling to the scene surface. Reduces noise in continuous regions (roads, walls) through NeRF's implicit regularization. Achieves photorealistic quality with high visual fidelity. Limitations: Slow training times in the joint optimization stage. Ineffective batch sampling for large scenes without distributed training. Sensitive to grid resolution; low resolution causes blurriness, high resolution causes noise without NeRF supervision. When to Use: Large urban scene rendering where high visual fidelity is required and computational resources allow for long training times. When Not to Use: Scenarios requiring real-time inference or lacking distributed training infrastructure, as shuffled ray batch sampling is highly ineffective for large scenes. Grid-Guided NeRF Branch Training was proposed in the paper "Grid-guided Neural Radiance Fields for Large Urban Scenes". The work addresses the limitations of existing NeRF and grid-based methods when applied to large-scale urban environments. Pure NeRF methods suffer from blurry artifacts and slow convergence due to the difficulty of learning low-frequency functions in large scenes. Grid-based methods like TensoRF offer better performance but can produce noisy appearance and inaccurate shapes in continuous regions. The authors introduced this two-branch framework to combine the global structure capture of feature grids with the local detail recovery of NeRF, specifically targeting large urban scene rendering. name: Depth-Supervised NeRF
body: Depth-Supervised NeRF (DS-NeRF) is a training procedure for Neural Radiance Fields that incorporates sparse 3D depth supervision from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) point clouds to accelerate convergence and improve reconstruction quality with fewer input views. Unlike methods relying on category-specific priors or dense multi-view stereo initialization, DS-NeRF treats the sparse keypoints generated during standard SfM preprocessing as free geometric constraints, enforcing that the rendered ray termination distribution aligns with these surface priors. This approach reduces overfitting in sparse-view settings and typically achieves target quality in 2–3× fewer training iterations than standard NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N training images \{Ij\} with known camera poses \{Pj\} (estimated via SfM, e.g., COLMAP); sparse 3D keypoints \{X\} and their visibility flags from the SfM pipeline; near and far clipping bounds tn, tf for ray marching. Outputs: A trained NeRF model (MLP parameters \theta for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) capable of rendering novel views. Data Structures: Keypoints: A set X = \{xi\} where each xi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Visibility: For each image j, a subset Xj \subset X of keypoints visible from camera Pj. Depth Estimates: For each visible keypoint xi \in Xj, a scalar depth D{ij} and uncertainty \hat{\sigma}i. Ray Termination Distribution: Discretized values hk = h(tk) computed during volume rendering. Step-by-Step Method: 1. SfM Preprocessing: Run an SfM solver (e.g., COLMAP) on the input images to estimate camera poses Pj and reconstruct a sparse 3D point cloud X. 2. Depth and Uncertainty Estimation: For each image Ij and camera Pj, identify visible keypoints Xj. Compute the projected depth D{ij} for each xi \in Xj by projecting xi with Pj and taking the re-projected z-value (depth along the camera axis). Compute the depth uncertainty \hat{\sigma}i for each keypoint xi as the average reprojection error across all views where xi was detected. Model the true depth of the first surface as a random variable D{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(D{ij}, \hat{\sigma}i). 3. Ray Generation for Supervision: For each detected keypoint xi \in Xj, define a ray \mathbf{r} originating from the camera center oj with direction \mathbf{d} pointing towards the projection of xi on the image plane. In local camera coordinates, the ray direction is derived from the keypoint's image coordinates (u, v) and -1 in the camera axis. To combine color and depth supervision efficiently, the method exploits the continuity of image coordinates. Rays corresponding to keypoints are sampled within the same ray marching procedure used for standard pixel rays, interpolating RGB supervision values for these specific rays. 4. Volume Rendering: Shoot rays \mathbf{r} into the scene using standard NeRF sampling between tn and tf. Compute the ray termination distribution h(t) = T(t)\sigma(t), where T(t) = \exp(-\int0^t \sigma(s)ds) is the transmittance. Discretize this distribution at sample points tk with step size \Delta tk: hk = h(tk). Compute the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and rendered depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}). 5. Loss Computation: Color Loss: Standard photometric loss L{Color} = \|\hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{I}[u, v]\|2^2. Depth Loss: Minimize the KL divergence between the rendered ray termination distribution h(t) and the noisy depth distribution \mathcal{N}(D{ij}, \hat{\sigma}i). The loss is approximated as: L{Depth} = \mathbb{E}{xi \in Xj} \left[ \sumk -\log hk \exp \left( -\frac{(tk - D{ij})^2}{2\hat{\sigma}i^2} \right) \Delta tk \right] where tk are the sample depths along the ray. Alternative: An MSE loss between rendered depth and D{ij} can be used, but KL divergence yields fewer artifacts. Total Loss: L = L{Color} + \lambdaD L{Depth} where \lambdaD is a hyperparameter balancing the terms. 6. Optimization: Update network parameters \theta using gradients backpropagated through the differentiable volume rendering process. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computerayterminationdistribution(sigma, tstarts, tends): """ Computes the ray termination distribution h(t) = T(t) sigma(t). Args: sigma: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples), differential density. tstarts: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples), start depths. tends: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples), end depths. Returns: h: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples), termination distribution values. T: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples), accumulated transmittance. """ hlist = [] Tlist = [] for raysigma, raytstarts, raytends in zip(sigma, tstarts, tends): numsamples = len(raysigma) T = [] h = [] cumsigmadelta = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): delta = raytends[i] - raytstarts[i] sigmadelta = raysigma[i] delta Ti = math.exp(-cumsigmadelta) T.append(Ti) hi = Ti raysigma[i] h.append(hi) cumsigmadelta += sigmadelta hlist.append(h) Tlist.append(T) return hlist, Tlist def depthsupervisednerfloss(sigma, tstarts, tends, keypointsdepths, keypointuncertainties, renderedcolors, gtcolors, rayindicesforkeypoints): """ Computes the combined loss for DS-NeRF. Args: sigma: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples) tstarts: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples) tends: List of lists, shape (numrays, numsamples) keypointsdepths: List of scalars, depth Dij from SfM keypointuncertainties: List of scalars, uncertainty sigmahati renderedcolors: List of lists, shape (numrays, 3) gtcolors: List of lists, shape (numrays, 3) rayindicesforkeypoints: List of indices in the batch corresponding to keypoint rays Returns: totalloss: float """ # 1. Color Loss for all rays colorloss = 0.0 for rc, gc in zip(renderedcolors, gtcolors): colorloss += sum((r - g) 2 for r, g in zip(rc, gc)) colorloss /= len(renderedcolors) # 2. Depth Loss for keypoint rays if not rayindicesforkeypoints: return colorloss # Extract sigma and t for keypoint rays sigmak = [sigma[i] for i in rayindicesforkeypoints] tstartsk = [tstarts[i] for i in rayindicesforkeypoints] tendsk = [tends[i] for i in rayindicesforkeypoints] # Compute h(t) for keypoint rays hk, = computerayterminationdistribution(sigmak, tstartsk, tendsk) # Discretization step size deltask = [[tendsk[i][j] - tstartsk[i][j] for j in range(len(tstartsk[i]))] for i in range(len(tstartsk))] # Sample points tk (using midpoints as standard approximation) tsamplesk = [[tstartsk[i][j] + deltask[i][j] / 2.0 for j in range(len(tstartsk[i]))] for i in range(len(tstartsk))] # KL Divergence approximation: # Ldepth = sumk -log(hk) exp(-(tk - Dij)^2 / (2 sigmahati^2)) deltatk depthsk = [keypointsdepths[i] for i in rayindicesforkeypoints] uncertaintiesk = [keypointuncertainties[i] for i in rayindicesforkeypoints] depthlosssum = 0.0 numkeypointrays = len(rayindicesforkeypoints) for i in range(numkeypointrays): rayloss = 0.0 for j in range(len(hk[i])): hval = hk[i][j] # Clamp to avoid log(0) hval = max(hval, 1e-6) gaussianterm = math.exp(-((tsamplesk[i][j] - depthsk[i]) 2) / (2 (uncertaintiesk[i] 2))) rayloss += -math.log(hval) gaussianterm deltask[i][j] depthlosssum += rayloss depthloss = depthlosssum / numkeypointrays # Total Loss lambdad = 1.0 # Empirically set to 1 totalloss = colorloss + lambdad depthloss return totalloss Parameters: \lambdaD: Depth loss weight. Empirically set to 1. tn, tf: Near and far clipping planes. tf is often treated as an opaque wall to ensure \int h(t)dt = 1. Training Iterations: Typically 10,000 - 100,000. Image Resolution: 400 \times 300 in standard experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SfM Failure: Optimization fails if SfM produces poor depth estimates or inaccurate depth measurements. Gaussian Assumption: The method assumes a Gaussian distribution models keypoint uncertainty, which may not hold for depth from non-SfM sources (e.g., noisy sensors). Domain Gap: While DS-NeRF itself generalizes, combining it with other methods (like pixelNeRF) may suffer if there is a domain gap between pre-training data and test data. MVSNeRF Compatibility: Adding depth supervision did not improve MVSNeRF because it already possesses a strong geometry prior via PSV initialization. Time Complexity: Training iterations are reduced by 2–3× compared to standard NeRF. Wall-clock time per iteration is comparable (\sim 362.4 ms vs \sim 359.8 ms on RTX A5000). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the NeRF Real dataset with 5 input views, DS-NeRF achieves a test PSNR of 22.6 (vs 18.2 for NeRF). It reaches target PSNR significantly faster, e.g., 13 hours faster in the 5-view case. Strengths: Accelerates training, improves quality with few views, compatible with other NeRF variants, and uses "free" SfM data. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of SfM keypoints; does not improve methods that already have strong geometric priors (like MVSNeRF). DS-NeRF was introduced by Deng et al. in 2022. It addresses the failure mode of NeRF when trained on insufficient input views, where the model fits incorrect geometries due to the lack of constraints enforcing empty space and opaque surfaces. The method leverages the fact that SfM pipelines (like COLMAP), which are standard prerequisites for NeRF training, already produce sparse 3D keypoints. name: Robust Depth Loss
body: Robust Depth Loss is a geometry supervision function designed to mitigate the degradation of extrapolation performance caused by inaccurate or noisy pseudo-depth maps in differentiable volume rendering. It addresses the problem where standard L2 losses are overly sensitive to outliers, forcing the neural radiance field (NeRF) to fit erroneous geometry. By using a loss function that is less sensitive to large errors than L2, it encourages the network to terminate rays near the pseudo-depth while retaining freedom to ignore inaccurate geometry when the error is very large or very small. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The rendered depth expectation \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r}, and a target depth value D(\mathbf{r}) (typically from a geometry scaffold or pseudo-depth map). Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{robust}}(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond the scalar depth values and the hyperparameter \beta. Parameters: \beta: A constant threshold controlling the transition between the quadratic and logarithmic regimes. The source sets \beta = 0.1 throughout experiments. Formula: The loss is defined as a piecewise function based on the absolute depth difference \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) = |\hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) - D(\mathbf{r})|: \mathcal {L}{\text {robust}}(\mathbf {r}) = \begin {cases} 0.5\Delta {D}(\mathbf {r})^{2}, &\text {if } \Delta {D}(\mathbf {r}) < \beta \\ \beta ^ {2} \left(0.5 + \log \left(\frac {\Delta {D}(\mathbf {r})}{\beta }\right)\right), &\text {otherwise } \end {cases} Steps: 1. Compute the rendered depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard differentiable volume rendering equation for expected distance along the ray. 2. Retrieve the target depth D(\mathbf{r}) from the provided geometry scaffold or depth map. 3. Calculate the absolute difference \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) = |\hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) - D(\mathbf{r})|. 4. Compare \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) with the threshold \beta (0.1). 5. If \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) < \beta, compute the loss as 0.5 \Delta D(\mathbf{r})^2. 6. If \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) \ge \beta, compute the loss as \beta^2 (0.5 + \log(\Delta D(\mathbf{r}) / \beta)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def robustdepthloss(rendereddepth: float, targetdepth: float, beta: float = 0.1) -> float: """ Computes the Robust Depth Loss as defined in NeRFVS. Args: rendereddepth: The expected depth along the ray, Dhat(r). targetdepth: The target depth from the geometry scaffold, D(r). beta: The threshold constant, default 0.1. Returns: The scalar loss value. """ # Calculate absolute depth difference deltad = abs(rendereddepth - targetdepth) if deltad < beta: # Quadratic regime for small errors return 0.5 (deltad 2) else: # Logarithmic regime for large errors, reducing sensitivity to outliers return (beta 2) (0.5 + math.log(deltad / beta)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The logarithmic term \log(\Delta D(\mathbf{r}) / \beta) requires \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) > 0. If \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) = 0, the first branch (0 < \beta) is taken, returning 0, which is safe. Boundary: The transition at \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) = \beta is continuous. At \beta, the quadratic form gives 0.5\beta^2 and the logarithmic form gives \beta^2(0.5 + \log(1)) = 0.5\beta^2. This variant, associated with S-NeRF, focuses on the robustness of the training process to noisy depth inputs rather than just the loss function shape. It involves adding random Gaussian noise to original depth map inputs to simulate errors and computing outlier rates using a threshold of 1 compared to original depth inputs. The method employs a confidence strategy to locate and measure depth outliers accurately, avoiding their negative influence during training. Training with strong depth noise causes only a slight drop in PSNR and SSIM (0.05–0.5%), demonstrating robustness. Using only sparse depth improves PSNR by 5% over RGB-only baselines but is 2% worse in PSNR and 8% worse in LPIPS than dense depth with confidence. The method does not rely on high-quality depth completion (e.g., NLSPN); replacing it with traditional methods like Ku et al. (2018) yields similar rendering quality (24.41 vs 24.40 PSNR). Time Complexity: The computation is O(1) per ray, involving basic arithmetic and a logarithm. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray for the loss calculation. Performance: The loss is designed to improve extrapolation performance when using inaccurate geometry scaffolds. Strengths: Less sensitive to outliers than L2 loss; encourages termination around pseudo-depth while retaining freedom for inaccurate geometry. Limitations: Requires a geometry scaffold or pseudo-depth map as input. The choice of \beta (0.1) is fixed in the source; optimal values for different scales may vary. When to use: When training NeRFs with dense but inaccurate depth maps or geometry scaffolds where standard L2 losses lead to geometry error degradation. When not to use: When high-precision, clean depth maps are available, or when the primary goal is not geometry regularization but color fidelity alone. The Robust Depth Loss was introduced in the paper "NeRFVS: Neural Radiance Fields for Free View Synthesis via Geometry Scaffolds". It was proposed to address the issue that combining NeRF with geometry scaffolds could degrade extrapolation performance if the geometry error was not handled properly. The method draws inspiration from previous works [8,10] (not cited in the provided text, but referenced in the source) to create a loss that is less sensitive to outliers than L2. name: Depth Structural Consistency Regularization
head: RDSC
body: Depth Structural Consistency Regularization (RDSC) is a geometric regularization technique applied during Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training to enforce continuity constraints on rendered depth maps, leveraging external depth priors such as those from DepthAnythingV2. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Patch-Based Depth Regularization by explicitly modeling structural consistency through k-nearest neighbor (KNN) relationships in depth space rather than spatial proximity alone, ensuring that neighboring pixels in the prior map exhibit similar continuity in the rendered output. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{\mathbf{D}} from the NeRF model, where \hat{d}{k} is the depth value at pixel index k. Prior depth map \mathbf{D}^{V2} (e.g., from DepthAnythingV2), where d^{V2}{k} is the prior depth value at pixel index k. Hyperparameter m{ar'}: a small boundary value accounting for minor depth variations between neighboring pixels. Hyperparameter K: the number of nearest neighbors to consider. Outputs: Scalar regularization loss R{DSC}. Data Structures Depth maps are treated as 2D grids of floating-point values. The KNN search operates on the values within \mathbf{D}^{V2} within a local spatial region. Algorithm 1. For each pixel k1 in the rendered depth map \hat{\mathbf{D}}: a. Identify the corresponding pixel location in the prior depth map \mathbf{D}^{V2}. b. Define a small spatial region around this location in \mathbf{D}^{V2}. c. Compute the k-nearest neighbors (KNN) of the prior depth value d^{V2}{k1} based on depth values within this region. d. For each neighbor k2 in the KNN set: i. Retrieve the rendered depth value d^{r}{k1} at pixel k1 and d^{r}{k2} at pixel k2. ii. Compute the absolute difference |d^{r}{k1} - d^{r}{k2}|. iii. Apply the hinge-like penalty: \max(|d^{r}{k1} - d^{r}{k2}| - m{ar'}, 0). e. Sum the penalties for all neighbors of k1. 2. Sum the results over all pixels k1 to obtain the total loss. Formula The regularization term is defined as: R{DSC} = \sum{k1} \sum{k2 \in \text{KNN}(k1)} \max(|d^{r}{k1} - d^{r}{k2}| - m{ar'}, 0) Where: k1 indexes the pixels in the rendered depth map. \text{KNN}(k1) returns the set of K nearest neighbors based on depth values within a small region of the prior depth map \mathbf{D}^{V2}. d^{r}{k1} and d^{r}{k2} are the rendered depth values at pixels k1 and k2 respectively. m{ar'} is the small boundary value for minor depth variations. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computerdscloss(rendereddepth, priordepth, kneighbors=5, margin=0.01, regionradius=2): """ Computes the Depth Structural Consistency Regularization loss. Args: rendereddepth (np.ndarray): 2D array of rendered depths d^r. priordepth (np.ndarray): 2D array of prior depths d^V2. kneighbors (int): Number of KNN to consider. margin (float): Boundary value mar' for minor variations. regionradius (int): Half-side length of the square spatial region for KNN search. Returns: float: The RDSC loss value. """ loss = 0.0 h, w = rendereddepth.shape for r in range(h): for c in range(w): currentrenderedval = rendereddepth[r, c] currentpriorval = priordepth[r, c] neighbors = [] for dr in range(-regionradius, regionradius + 1): for dc in range(-regionradius, regionradius + 1): nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc if 0 <= nr < h and 0 <= nc < w: if dr == 0 and dc == 0: continue neighbors.append((priordepth[nr, nc], nr, nc)) neighbors.sort(key=lambda x: abs(x[0] - currentpriorval)) selectedneighbors = neighbors[:kneighbors] for, nr, nc in selectedneighbors: neighborrenderedval = rendereddepth[nr, nc] diff = abs(currentrenderedval - neighborrenderedval) penalty = max(diff - margin, 0.0) loss += penalty return loss Parameters m{ar'}: Small boundary value. Typical value not given in the sources. K: Number of nearest neighbors. Typical value not given in the sources. region\radius: Spatial extent for KNN candidate selection. Typical value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Pixels: Pixels at the image boundary have fewer neighbors. Out-of-bounds handling: The implementation must handle out-of-bounds checks. Depth Scale: The margin m{ar'} must be scaled appropriately to the depth units of \mathbf{D}^{V2} and \hat{\mathbf{D}}. KNN Definition: The phrase "based on depth values within a small region" requires careful implementation. It implies a spatial constraint (small region) followed by a value-based sort (KNN on depth). Uses bilateral filters to smooth depth while preserving edges. Choose when spatial continuity is more important than structural depth-value consistency. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enhances overall scene reconstruction quality by clarifying depth information for both neighboring and distant pixels. Effective in sparse-view scenarios where depth ambiguity is high. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the external depth prior (e.g., DepthAnythingV2). Computationally more expensive than simple pairwise smoothness terms due to KNN search. When to Use: Sparse-view 3D reconstruction where standard depth supervision is insufficient. Origin: Introduced in DASNeRF. History: Developed to address the loss of structure in sparse-view 3D reconstruction by leveraging latest depth models (like DepthAnythingV2) to standardize depth regularization. Usage: Used in sparse-view neural radiance fields training. name: Patch-Based Depth Regularization
head: Bilateral Depth Regularization, Bilateral filter regularization, Joint Bilateral Depth Regularization, Joint bilateral filter regularization
body: Patch-Based Depth Regularization is a technique applied during Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training to enforce geometric consistency by smoothing rendered depth maps while preserving sharp structural edges. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like RegNeRF’s patch similarity constraints by utilizing bilateral or joint bilateral filters, which explicitly account for spatial proximity and intensity/depth similarity to reduce noise without blurring boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of rendered depth patches P extracted from the NeRF’s depth output \hat{D}. Output: A scalar regularization loss L{reg} added to the total training loss. Data Structures Depth Patch \hat{D}(p): A 2D tensor of shape (Hp, Wp) containing depth values for a specific patch p. Set P: The collection of all patches sampled from the rendered depth map during a training step. Filter Kernel: Defined by spatial sigma \sigma{space} and range sigma \sigma{color}. Parameters Patch Size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Larger sizes (32, 64) cause undertraining and excessive compute time. Kernel Size: 9 \times 9. Spatial Sigma (\sigma{space}): 75 \times 75 (defines spatial extent). Range Sigma (\sigma{color}): 10 (controls intensity/depth similarity). Weight (\lambda{reg}): 10^{-7}. Color Weight (\lambda{color}): 1 (used in joint bilateral filter). Algorithm Steps 1. Pre-training: Train the NeRF model to convergence using only photometric (RGB) loss. 2. Patch Sampling: Extract patches p \in P from the rendered depth map \hat{D}. 3. Filtering: Apply a bilateral or joint bilateral filter F to each patch \hat{D}(p) to produce a filtered patch F(\hat{D}(p)). Bilateral Filter: Weights pixels based on spatial distance and depth difference. Joint Bilateral Filter: Weights pixels based on spatial distance, depth difference, and RGB intensity similarity in the corresponding view. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the original depth patch and the filtered patch for all pixels in the patch, then average over all patches. Formula The regularization loss is defined as: L{reg} = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{p \in P} \frac{1}{|p|} \sum{i,j} \| \hat{D}(p{ij}) - F(\hat{D}(p)){ij} \|^2 Where: |P| is the number of patches. |p| is the number of pixels in patch p. \hat{D}(p{ij}) is the original depth value at pixel (i,j) in patch p. F(\hat{D}(p)){ij} is the filtered depth value at pixel (i,j) in patch p. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def patchbaseddepthregularization(depthmap, patches, lambdareg, sigmaspace=75.0, sigmacolor=10.0, usejoint=False, rgbmap=None): """ Computes the patch-based depth regularization loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 numpatches = len(patches) for p in patches: if usejoint and rgbmap is not None: rgbp = extractrgbpatch(rgbmap, p.coords) filteredp = jointbilateralfilter(p.values, rgbp, sigmaspace, sigmacolor) else: filteredp = bilateralfilter(p.values, sigmaspace, sigmacolor) mse = 0.0 h, w = len(p.values), len(p.values[0]) for i in range(h): for j in range(w): diff = p.values[i][j] - filteredp[i][j] mse += diff diff mse /= (h w) totalloss += mse return (totalloss / numpatches) lambdareg def extractrgbpatch(rgbmap, coords): # Returns the RGB tensor corresponding to the patch coordinates return rgbmap[coords.y1:coords.y2, coords.x1:coords.x2] def bilateralfilter(depthpatch, sigmaspace, sigmacolor): h, w = len(depthpatch), len(depthpatch[0]) filtered = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] kernelradius = 4 # 9x9 kernel for y in range(h): for x in range(w): numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for dy in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): for dx in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < h and 0 <= nx < w: spatialdist = dy2 + dx2 depthdiff = (depthpatch[y][x] - depthpatch[ny][nx])2 # Standard bilateral weight calculation weight = math.exp(-(spatialdist / (2 sigmaspace2)) - (depthdiff / (2 sigmacolor2))) numerator += weight depthpatch[ny][nx] denominator += weight filtered[y][x] = numerator / denominator if denominator > 0 else depthpatch[y][x] return filtered def jointbilateralfilter(depthpatch, rgbpatch, sigmaspace, sigmacolor): h, w = len(depthpatch), len(depthpatch[0]) filtered = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] kernelradius = 4 for y in range(h): for x in range(w): numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for dy in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): for dx in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < h and 0 <= nx < w: spatialdist = dy2 + dx2 depthdiff = (depthpatch[y][x] - depthpatch[ny][nx])2 # RGB intensity difference for joint range weighting rgbdiff = sum((rgbpatch[y][x][c] - rgbpatch[ny][nx][c])2 for c in range(3)) weight = math.exp(-(spatialdist / (2 sigmaspace2)) - (depthdiff / (2 sigmacolor2)) - (rgbdiff / (2 sigmacolor2))) numerator += weight depthpatch[ny][nx] denominator += weight filtered[y][x] = numerator / denominator if denominator > 0 else depthpatch[y][x] return filtered Edge Cases and Pitfalls Training Time: Adding patch-based regularization significantly increases training time. Models using this method converged in 280,000 iterations, compared to 200,000 for photometric-only training. Patch Size Sensitivity: Larger patches (32x32, 64x64) remain undertrained even after 400,000 iterations and drastically increase compute cost. Occlusion: Performance may degrade in scenes with significant occlusions (e.g., large furniture) where ray coverage is limited. Implementation: The method relies on open-source libraries like Kornia for filter implementation. Time Complexity: Significantly higher than standard NeRF training due to the additional filtering step per patch and the need for longer training durations (280,000 iterations vs 200,000). Memory Complexity: Increases with the number of patches and patch size. Larger patches require more memory for intermediate filter computations. Performance: Outperforms RegNeRF’s depth patch regularization in indoor scenes by reducing noise while preserving sharp edges. Joint bilateral filtering provides additional gains over standard bilateral filtering. Strengths: Effective at mitigating rendering irregularities beyond planar architectural surfaces while preserving structural details. Limitations: Computationally expensive; sensitive to patch size; less effective in highly occluded areas. When to Use: Indoor scenes with planar architectural surfaces where geometric consistency is critical and computational resources allow for extended training. The method was proposed in "Improving Geometric Consistency for 360-Degree Neural Radiance Fields in Indoor Scenarios" (2025). It builds on the concept of depth regularization introduced in RegNeRF (Niemeyer et al., 2022) but replaces simple patch similarity constraints with bilateral and joint bilateral filters. The bilateral filter was originally introduced by Tomasi and Manduchi (1998), and the joint bilateral filter by He et al. (2012). The implementation was tested using Instant-NGP within the Nerfstudio framework.
