name: Indirect Depth Supervision (KL Loss)
head: DS-NeRF loss, Depth supervision via KL-divergence, KL-Divergence Depth Loss, LiDAR depth loss
body: Indirect Depth Supervision treats the volume-rendering weights along a ray as a discrete probability distribution and minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between this rendered distribution and a unimodal target distribution centered at a measured LiDAR range. It differs from direct depth supervision (e.g., Direct Depth Supervision) by enforcing geometric consistency through distribution alignment rather than penalizing the difference between expected depth values. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of LiDAR rays \mathcal{R}{\text{LiDAR}}. For each ray r, the measured range dr^ (ground truth depth). The neural network parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} to be minimized. Data Structures: Ray Samples: For each ray r, a list of N sample points ti (depths) and their associated rendering weights wi. Rendering Weights: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)), where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)) is the accumulated transmittance, \rho(ti) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(ti))\deltai) is the opacity, and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between samples. Target Distribution Parameters: dr^: The measured LiDAR range for ray r. v{si}: The size of the voxel containing sample i. \hat{\sigma}: A variance parameter controlling the spread of the target distribution. \epsilon: A kernel parameter/bound. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Weights: For each LiDAR ray r \in \mathcal{R}{\text{LiDAR}}, compute the rendering weights wi for all sample points ti along the ray using the current network parameters \theta. 2. Construct Target Distribution qr(di): For each sample i on ray r, compute the unnormalized target probability qr(di) based on the distance to the measured range dr^. Using the formulation from: qr(di) \propto \Delta ti \exp\left(-\frac{(ti - dr^)^2}{2v{si}^2}\right) where \Delta ti is the sample spacing (often \deltai or a fixed step) and v{si} is the voxel size. Using the formulation from: qr(di) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{(ti - D(ri))^2}{2\hat{\sigma}^2}\right) where D(ri) is the ground truth depth and \hat{\sigma} is a variance parameter. Note: The sources provide slightly different normalizations and parameters (v{si} vs \hat{\sigma}). explicitly states the target sharpens as the map refines via v{si}. uses a fixed variance \hat{\sigma} and a kernel \epsilon. Implementers should choose one formulation or average them if the specific variant is not mandated. The standard DS-NeRF approach is cited as the representative for indirect supervision. 3. Normalize Target Distribution: Normalize qr(di) such that \sumi qr(di) = 1. 4. Compute KL Divergence: Calculate the KL divergence between the target distribution qr and the rendered distribution pr (where pr(di) = wi): D{\text{KL}}(qr \parallel pr) = \sumi qr(di) \log \frac{qr(di)}{pr(di)} = \sumi qr(di) \log qr(di) - \sumi qr(di) \log wi Since \sumi qr(di) \log qr(di) is constant with respect to \theta, the loss simplifies to: \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} = - \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}{\text{LiDAR}}} \sumi qr(di) \log(wi) 5. Aggregate: Sum the KL divergence over all LiDAR rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computekldepthloss(lidarrays, network, voxelsizes): """ Computes the Indirect Depth Supervision (KL Loss). Args: lidarrays: List of Ray objects, each containing: origin: (3,) float array direction: (3,) float array measuredrange: float (dr^) samples: List of sample depths ti network: A function or object that returns (sigma, color) for a batch of points. voxelsizes: A function or lookup that returns v{si} for a sample at depth ti. Returns: loss: Scalar tensor. """ totalloss = 0.0 for ray in lidarrays: # 1. Get sample points along the ray tsamples = ray.samples # List of floats ti # 2. Query network for density sigma at sample points # Assuming network takes (points, directions) and returns sigma points = ray.origin + tsamples ray.direction sigmas = network(points, ray.direction) # Shape: (N,) # 3. Compute rendering weights wi # deltat is the distance between consecutive samples # For the last sample, deltat might be 0 or handled via truncation deltat = np.diff(tsamples, prepend=tsamples[0]) # Shape: (N,) # Opacity alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltati) alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmas deltat) # Transmittance Ti = product(1 - alphaj) for j < i # T1 = 1.0 transmittances = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphas, dim=0) transmittances = torch.cat([torch.tensor([1.0]), transmittances[:-1]]) # Weights wi = Ti alphai weights = transmittances alphas # 4. Construct target distribution qr(di) # Using formulation from: qr(di) proportional to deltati exp(-(ti - dr^)^2 / (2 v{si}^2)) dstar = ray.measuredrange # Get voxel sizes for each sample vs = torch.tensor([voxelsizes(t) for t in tsamples]) # Shape: (N,) # Exponent term exponent = -((tsamples - dstar) 2) / (2.0 vs 2) # Unnormalized q qunnorm = deltat torch.exp(exponent) # Normalize q q = qunnorm / qunnorm.sum() # 5. Compute KL Divergence term: - sum(qi log(wi)) # Add epsilon to weights to avoid log(0) weightsclamped = weights + 1e-8 lossray = -torch.sum(q torch.log(weightsclamped)) totalloss += lossray return totalloss Parameters with Typical Values: v{si}: Voxel size, varies by spatial location. \hat{\sigma}: Variance parameter, not given in the sources. \epsilon: Kernel parameter, not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: If wi = 0, \log(wi) is undefined. Clamp weights with a small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-8}) before taking the logarithm. Voxel Size Definition: The definition of v{si} (voxel size containing sample i) requires access to the underlying voxel grid structure. If using a continuous coordinate network without explicit voxels, this parameter may need approximation or substitution with \hat{\sigma}. Distribution Normalization: The target distribution qr must be normalized to sum to 1. Failure to normalize leads to incorrect KL divergence values. LiDAR Ray Availability: This loss only applies to rays that have corresponding LiDAR measurements. Rays without LiDAR data do not contribute to this specific loss term. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of samples per ray and R is the number of LiDAR rays. The computation involves forward passes for density, weight calculation, and a summation over samples. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot R) to store intermediate weights and target distributions for all LiDAR rays during the backward pass. Strengths: Enforces geometric consistency by aligning the entire depth distribution with the LiDAR measurement, rather than just the mean. It is robust to noise in the LiDAR data due to the probabilistic nature of the KL divergence. Limitations: Requires LiDAR data; cannot be used with image-only supervision. The target distribution's sharpness depends on voxel size, which may require careful tuning as the map refines. When to Use: When LiDAR data is available and geometric consistency is critical, such as in outdoor mapping or SLAM applications. When Not to Use: When only RGB images are available, or when computational resources are severely limited and the overhead of computing the target distribution is prohibitive. Origin: The method was introduced in DS-NeRF. It treats rendering weights as a probability distribution and uses KL divergence to align it with LiDAR measurements. History: It is part of the broader effort to integrate geometric priors into NeRF training. The URF loss from Urban-NeRF is another variant of indirect supervision, but it lacks an open-source implementation, making the KL loss the representative for this category. Usage: Commonly used in LiDAR-Visual SLAM and mapping systems where geometric accuracy is paramount. SpaRV: Sparse Radiance Voxels for Scalable Geometrically Consistent LiDAR-Visual Mapping and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.25665, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Digging into Depth Priors for Outdoor Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3581783.3612306, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Novel View Regularization
head: Novel view rays regularization, Novel view supervision
body: Novel View Regularization mitigates the shape-radiance ambiguity in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by incorporating rays from unobserved viewpoints into the training loop. Unlike methods that rely solely on observed image supervision, this approach adds geometric guidance to prevent overfitting to sparse input views. It sets itself apart by explicitly sampling and rendering novel views during optimization to enforce geometric consistency, whereas siblings like Depth and Geometry Supervision may rely on external depth priors or structural constraints without necessarily synthesizing new viewpoints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current NeRF parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}), observed camera rays, and novel view rays \mathbf{r}{novel}. Outputs: Updated parameters \theta' after gradient descent. Data Structures: Ray Set: A collection of rays \mathbf{r} = (o, d) combining observed and novel view rays. Sample Points: Along each ray, points ti are sampled using the primary rendering strategy. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Construct a batch of rays including observed rays and novel view rays \mathbf{r}{novel}. 2. Volume Rendering: For each ray \mathbf{r}, compute rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) using differentiable volume rendering. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}, which combines standard supervision with geometric adaptation loss \mathcal{L}{geo} to guide geometry. 4. Backpropagation: Compute gradients \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} flowing back through the rendered outputs to the network parameters. 5. Update: Update \theta using gradient descent. Formulas: The rendering process computes expected color and depth along rays r(t) = o + td using sample points ti with weights wi = T(ti)\rho(ti), where \rho(ti) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(ti))(t{i+1} - ti)) and T(ti) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). The rendered depth is typically the expected distance along the ray: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights, ti are sample depths, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Parameters: Number of Novel Views: Not given in the sources. Sampling Strategy: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Omitting novel view rays risks converging to local minima, causing incorrect geometry. Overfitting: Without novel view supervision, the model may overfit to the observed views, leading to poor generalization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cumprod(arr): res = [1.0] for x in arr: res.append(res[-1] x) return res[1:] def samplerays(cameras): rays = [] for cam in cameras: for u in range(cam.width): for v in range(cam.height): origin = cam.origin + u cam.dx + v cam.dy rays.append((origin, cam.direction)) return rays def volumerender(rays, model, numsamples=128): Chat, Dhat = [], [] for o, d in rays: t = [o + d (i 0.1) for i in range(1, numsamples + 1)] sigma, c = model(o, d, t) delta = [t[i+1] - t[i] for i in range(len(t)-1)] alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-s dt) for s, dt in zip(sigma, delta)] T = cumprod([1.0 - a for a in alpha]) w = [T[i] alpha[i] for i in range(len(alpha))] Chat.append(sum(wi ci for wi, ci in zip(w, c))) Dhat.append(sum(wi ti for wi, ti in zip(w, t))) return Chat, Dhat def novelviewregularizationstep(model, obscameras, novelcameras, gtcolorsobs, optimizer): raysobs = samplerays(obscameras) raysnovel = samplerays(novelcameras) Chatobs, Dhatobs = volumerender(raysobs, model) Chatnovel, Dhatnovel = volumerender(raysnovel, model) lossobs = sum((chat - cgt) 2 for chat, cgt in zip(Chatobs, gtcolorsobs)) / len(Chatobs) # Geometric loss Lgeo exact form not given in sources lossgeo = sum(abs(dhat) for dhat in Dhatnovel) / len(Dhatnovel) totalloss = lossobs + lossgeo optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss Few-View Reconstruction via Regularization: A family of approaches that mitigate shape-radiance ambiguity in sparse-input settings by applying geometric or semantic priors to prevent overfitting and reduce floaters. Choose it when supervision from multiple viewpoints is limited and explicit regularization is preferred over progressive capacity restraint. Few-View Reconstruction via Regularization NGP-ERGAS: A regularization strategy for Instant Neural Graphics Primitives that improves fine detail reconstruction by incorporating nonlocal structural information via thread-based global error computation. Choose it when training Instant-NGP and standard per-pixel losses fail to capture fine structural details. NGP-ERGAS Performance: Reduces overfitting and enhances geometry accuracy compared to training without novel view supervision. It significantly reduces floaters and improves cross-scale geometric adaptation. Strengths: Improves rendering quality and geometric consistency in few-shot scenarios. Limitations: Omitting novel view rays risks converging to local minima, causing incorrect geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Novel View Regularization is used in the context of FrugalNeRF, a method for fast convergence in extreme few-shot novel view synthesis. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing 3D scenes from very limited input views by leveraging geometric priors through novel view supervision. FrugalNeRF: Fast Convergence for Extreme Few-shot Novel View Synthesis without Learned Priors, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52734.2025.01049, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Few-View Reconstruction via Regularization
body: Few-View Reconstruction via Regularization is a family of approaches designed to mitigate the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) when supervision from multiple viewpoints is sparse. By applying geometric or semantic priors, these methods prevent overfitting to observed views and improve generalization to unseen ones. This family addresses artifacts like "floaters" and "background collapse" common in sparse-input settings. Unlike progressive reconstruction methods that restrain model capacity over time, this family relies on explicit regularization terms to guide the optimization toward geometrically plausible solutions. The core mechanism involves augmenting the standard photometric loss with auxiliary constraints that enforce consistency across views or adherence to prior knowledge about scene geometry. Geometric priors stabilize the learned density field or Gaussian distribution by applying smoothness or normal consistency constraints. Semantic regularization enforces cross-view consistency by leveraging high-level scene structure to align reconstructions with expected object layouts. Unseen Viewpoint Regularization is a module designed to mitigate background collapse and overfitting in sparse-input settings by regularizing 3DGS training at viewpoints different from the input views. It is chosen when training data is extremely sparse and standard photometric loss leads to artifacts like floaters or empty backgrounds. The method splits regularization based on the distance of the novel view from training cameras. For viewpoints distant from training cameras, it incorporates a Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss to provide geometric priors. For viewpoints close to training cameras, it incorporates a depth warping loss, which uses traditional transformations to re-render depth and color from novel view points and enforces consistency. The challenge of reconstructing scenes from sparse views is critical in real-world settings where dense multi-view captures are impractical. Early solutions focused on constraining variation between views, such as DietNeRF, which added constraints to ensure high-level semantic features remained the same across views. More recently, with the advent of 3D Gaussian Splatting, methods like SparseGS have introduced specific modules like Unseen Viewpoint Regularization to address the unique artifacts of Gaussian representations, such as floaters, by combining SDS losses with depth-based constraints. The broader family of regularization approaches contrasts with progressive reconstruction techniques like FreeNeRF and Nerfies, which restrain model complexity over time rather than adding explicit loss terms. From reconstruction to reasoning: neural radiance fields for comprehensive 3D scene understanding, https://theses.hal.science/tel-05693528v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Sparsegs: Sparse View Synthesis Using 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00100, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NGP-ERGAS
head: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with ERGAS
body: NGP-ERGAS is a regularization and loss function strategy for Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (Instant-NGP) that improves fine detail reconstruction in novel view synthesis by incorporating nonlocal structural information. Unlike standard Instant-NGP, which computes loss per-pixel independently, NGP-ERGAS groups GPU threads into custom blocks to compute the Relative Dimensionless Global Error (ERGAS) loss, addressing the inability of previous nonlocal methods like S3IM to run on Instant-NGP's tile-independent parallel architecture. It sets itself apart by using a thread-based strategy to efficiently collect global structure information with lower computational overhead than patch-based SSIM methods. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Initial NeRF network parameters \Theta, a batch of rays (pixels), ground truth image colors C, and hyperparameters M1 (thread block size), \lambda1 (ERGAS weight), \lambda2 (SSIM weight). Outputs: Updated network parameters \Theta. Data Structures Custom Thread Block: A set of M1 threads. Defined by an index range [m{min}, m{max}] centered on a dominant thread index \hat{m}. m{min} = \lceil \hat{m} - M1/2 \rceil m{max} = \lfloor \hat{m} + M1/2 \rfloor The thread with index \hat{m} is the dominant thread. Other threads in the block are auxiliary threads. If an auxiliary thread index is 0 or out of the valid image range, it is skipped. Color Vectors: For each thread m, C(m) is the ground truth RGB color vector, and \hat{C}(m) is the rendered RGB color vector. Parameters M1: Number of threads in a custom thread block. Adjustable. Typical values are not explicitly stated, but it defines the minibatch size for the ERGAS calculation. \lambda1: Weight parameter for the ERGAS term. Determined experimentally. \lambda2: Weight coefficient for the SSIM loss term. Determined experimentally after fixing \lambda1. Training steps: 4000 steps (as used in reported experiments). Formulas 1. ERGAS for a Thread Block: For RGB images, the number of bands K=3. The spatial resolution ratio h/l=1. The ERGAS for a specific thread block is computed as: \text{ERGAS} = 100 \sqrt{\frac{1}{3} \sum{k=1}^{3} \left( \frac{\frac{1}{M1} \sum{m=1}^{M1} (Ck^m - \hat{C}k^m)^2}{\left(\frac{1}{M1} \sum{m=1}^{M1} Ck^m\right)^2} \right)} Where Ck^m is the ground truth color value of the k-th band (channel) for the pixel corresponding to the m-th thread, and \hat{C}k^m is the rendered color value. 2. Average ERGAS Error (E): The average ERGAS value over all threads \hat{m} in the block is: E(\hat{m}, M1) = \frac{1}{M1} \sum{\hat{m}=1}^{M1} \text{ERGAS}(\hat{C}(\hat{m}) - C(\hat{m})) Where \hat{C}(\hat{m}) and C(\hat{m}) denote the sets of rendered and ground truth colors for the threads in the block. 3. ERGAS Loss Term (L{ERGAS}): Since ERGAS itself does not directly yield a differentiable gradient suitable for standard backpropagation in this context, it is merged with the original color loss (MSE) of the dominant thread: L{ERGAS}(\Theta) = \frac{1}{|\Omega|} \sum{\hat{m} \in \Omega} \| C(\hat{m}) - \hat{C}(\hat{m}) + \lambda1 E(\hat{m}, M1) \|^2 Where \Omega is the set of pixels in the batch and |\Omega| is the number of pixels. 4. SSIM Loss (L{SSIM}): L{SSIM} = 1 - \text{SSIM} Where SSIM is the Structural Similarity Index. 5. Total Loss (L{all}): L{all} = L{ERGAS} + \lambda2 L{SSIM} Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize NeRF network parameters \Theta. 2. While stopping criterion is not met: 3. Select a current pixel as the dominant thread \hat{m}. 4. Randomly select M1 - 1 other pixels to form a data minibatch of rays. The threads corresponding to these M1 pixels form a custom thread block. 5. Retrieve the ground truth color C(\hat{m}) for the dominant thread. 6. Compute the rendered colors \hat{C}(m) for all threads m in the custom thread block using the current network parameters \Theta. 7. Calculate the ERGAS value for the thread block using the formula above. 8. Compute the average error E(\hat{m}, M1) for the block. 9. Calculate L{ERGAS}(\Theta) by adding \lambda1 E(\hat{m}, M1) to the color difference term for the dominant thread and averaging over the batch. 10. Calculate L{SSIM} for the batch. 11. Compute the total loss L{all} = L{ERGAS} + \lambda2 L{SSIM}. 12. Compute the gradient \nabla L{all}(\Theta). 13. Update \Theta using a gradient descent optimizer (e.g., Adam). 14. End While. 15. Return updated \Theta. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainngpergas(network, groundtruthimages, rays, M1, lambda1, lambda2, optimizer, maxsteps): """ Trains an Instant-NGP style network using the NGP-ERGAS loss function. Args: network: The NeRF network function taking rays and parameters, returning RGB colors. groundtruthimages: Dictionary or array mapping ray indices to ground truth RGB vectors. rays: List of ray objects or indices to render. M1: Number of threads (pixels) in a custom thread block. lambda1: Weight for the ERGAS term. lambda2: Weight for the SSIM term. optimizer: Gradient descent optimizer with step() method. maxsteps: Maximum number of training iterations. Returns: network: Trained network parameters. """ # Initialize network parameters theta = network.getparameters() for step in range(maxsteps): # 1. Sample a batch of rays # In Instant-NGP, rays are typically batched for GPU processing. # Here we simulate the "custom thread block" logic. batchrays = samplerays(rays, batchsize=M1) # 2. Render the batch # network(rays, theta) returns rendered RGB colors for the batch renderedcolors = network(batchrays, theta) # 3. Get ground truth for the batch groundtruthcolors = getgroundtruth(groundtruthimages, batchrays) # 4. Compute ERGAS Loss # ERGAS is computed over the entire block (M1 threads) # Formula: 100 sqrt( (1/3) sumk( RMSEk / meank)^2) # Where RMSEk and meank are computed over the M1 pixels in the block for channel k ergasvalue = 0.0 for k in range(3): # RGB channels gtchannel = groundtruthcolors[:, k] predchannel = renderedcolors[:, k] # Mean of ground truth for this channel in the block meangt = torch.mean(gtchannel) # RMSE for this channel in the block rmse = torch.sqrt(torch.mean((gtchannel - predchannel) 2)) # Avoid division by zero if meangt > 1e-6: ergasvalue += (rmse / meangt) 2 ergasvalue = 100.0 torch.sqrt(ergasvalue / 3.0) # Average ERGAS error E(mhat, M1) is just the ERGAS value itself # as it is a scalar for the block in this implementation context. # The loss formulation adds this scalar to the per-pixel error. # LERGAS = (1/|Omega|) sum || C - Chat + lambda1 E ||^2 # Note: The source describes adding E to the color difference of the dominant thread. # In a batched implementation, we apply this regularization term. # Calculate per-pixel MSE component colordiff = groundtruthcolors - renderedcolors # Add the ERGAS regularization term to the color difference # The source implies E is added to the residual. # Since E is a scalar for the block, it acts as a global bias correction for the block's error. regularizeddiff = colordiff + lambda1 ergasvalue lergas = torch.mean(regularizeddiff 2) # 5. Compute SSIM Loss # LSSIM = 1 - SSIM # SSIM is typically computed over local windows. # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume a standard SSIM function. ssimvalue = computessim(renderedcolors, groundtruthcolors) lssim = 1.0 - ssimvalue # 6. Total Loss lall = lergas + lambda2 lssim # 7. Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() lall.backward() optimizer.step() # Update network parameters (handled by optimizer.step() in most frameworks) # network.setparameters(optimizer.getparameters()) return network Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Conditions: If an auxiliary thread index in the custom thread block is 0 or out of the valid image range, it must be skipped during ERGAS calculation. Gradient Computation: ERGAS itself does not directly calculate gradients in the standard sense used by the loss function formulation; it is averaged and merged with the original color loss to enable backpropagation. Computational Cost: Unlike S3IM, which requires M times random patch forming and SSIM computing per pixel (heavy cost), NGP-ERGAS uses a thread-based strategy to reduce cost. However, the mutual influence between pixels in the thread block introduces a slight decrease in rendering and reconstruction efficiency compared to standard Instant-NGP. Hardware Constraints: DVGO-S3IM requires an L40 GPU with 48 GB memory, whereas NGP-ERGAS runs on an RTX 4060, making direct time comparisons with DVGO-S3IM potentially misleading due to hardware differences. Time Complexity: Slightly higher than standard Instant-NGP due to the centralized consideration of the custom thread block and the mutual influence between pixels. Memory Complexity: Approximately 10K network parameters, similar to Instant-NGP, and significantly lower than DVGO-S3IM (~22K parameters). Measured Performance: NeRFsynthetic Lego: PSNR 34.093 (vs 34.203 Standard), SSIM 0.99910 (vs 0.99907 Standard), Time 51s (vs 51s Standard). NeRFsynthetic Drums: PSNR 25.515 (vs 25.507 Standard), SSIM 0.99240 (vs 0.99211 Standard), Time 51s (vs 49s Standard). NeRFsynthetic Ship: PSNR 29.175 (vs 28.901 Standard), SSIM 0.99854 (vs 0.99843 Standard), Time 50s (vs 48s Standard). Tanks & Temple Family: PSNR 29.639 (vs 26.902 Instant-NGP), SSIM 0.91487 (vs 0.91068 Instant-NGP), Time 62s (vs 76s Instant-NGP). Ship with Gaussian Noise: PSNR 19.545 (vs 19.384 Standard), SSIM 0.98992 (vs 0.98899 Standard), Time 44s (vs 40s Standard). Scaling: Improves PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and UQI compared to standard Instant-NGP. Strengths: Significantly improves visual effect of fine details and structural integrity with fewer iterations; robust to Gaussian noise; lower parameter count than DVGO-S3IM; runs on consumer hardware (RTX 4060). Limitations: Slightly inferior running times compared to standard Instant-NGP due to pixel mutual influence. When to Use: When fine detail reconstruction and structural integrity are prioritized over raw training speed, and when running on hardware with limited memory (e.g., RTX 4060 vs L40). Origin: Introduced in the paper "NGP-ERGAS: Revisit Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with the Relative Dimensionless Global Error in Synthesis" published in Comput Mater Contin in 2025. History: Developed to address the limitation that S3IM (which uses random patch forming and SSIM) could not be applied to Instant-NGP due to its parallel programming technique (one thread per pixel) and inapplicability of tiles-based rendering. NGP-ERGAS transforms the pixel-based strategy into a thread-based strategy using custom thread blocks and ERGAS loss to incorporate nonlocal structural information efficiently. Usage: Evaluated on NeRFsynthetic, Tanks & Temple, and DL3DV datasets. name: Volumetric Supervision
head: CT-Guided Training, Hybrid Supervision
body: Volumetric Supervision is a training strategy that leverages high-quality volumetric reconstructions from conventional tomography to supervise neural network training at intermediate time steps where only sparse projection data is available. It solves the problem of temporal interpolation in dynamic tomography by using dense ground-truth volumes at the start and end of an experiment to regularize the learning of the canonical model and deformation field. Unlike sibling methods that primarily enforce geometric consistency via depth or gradient losses, this method directly minimizes the discrepancy between the predicted 3D volume and a physically reconstructed 3D volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse projection data for intermediate time steps t \in (0, 1). Dense projection data at boundary time steps t=0 and t=1. Conventional tomography reconstructions (ground truth volumes) \mathbf{y} at t=0 and t=1. Neural network parameters \theta defining the canonical volume and deformation field. Outputs: Updated network parameters \theta. Predicted volume \hat{\mathbf{y}} at intermediate times. Data Structures: Target Volume \mathbf{y}: A 3D voxel grid representing the ground-truth density/attenuation field reconstructed via conventional tomography at t=0 or t=1. Predicted Volume \hat{\mathbf{y}}: A 3D voxel grid sampled from the neural network's canonical representation, warped by the deformation field to match the intermediate time step. Note: The exact resolution and bit-depth of these volumes are not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Boundary Reconstruction: Obtain rich projection data at the start (t=0) and end (t=1) of the experiment. Reconstruct the 3D volumetric data \mathbf{y}0 and \mathbf{y}1 using conventional tomography algorithms. 2. Intermediate Prediction: For an intermediate time step t \in (0, 1) with sparse projections, query the neural network to predict the volume \hat{\mathbf{y}}t. This involves evaluating the canonical volume and applying the learned deformation field to account for temporal changes. 3. Correlation Calculation: Compute the normalized correlation coefficient C{cor} between the target volume \mathbf{y} (interpolated or selected from t=0 or t=1 based on temporal proximity or specific protocol) and the predicted volume \hat{\mathbf{y}}t. 4. Loss Computation: Calculate the volumetric loss \mathcal{L}{vol} as the negative normalized correlation coefficient: \mathcal{L}{vol} = -C{cor}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}t) 5. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L}{vol} along with other task-specific losses (e.g., projection consistency) using gradient descent to update \theta. Formula: The volumetric loss is defined as the negative normalized correlation coefficient between the target CT volume \mathbf{y} and the predicted volume \hat{\mathbf{y}}: \mathcal{L}{vol} = -C{cor}(\mathbf{y}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}) The normalized correlation coefficient is used because density level scales may differ between the canonical volume and the CT-reconstructed volume. Parameters: Time Steps: t=0 and t=1 denote the start and end of the experiment. Intermediate t values are not given specific typical values. Correlation Metric: Normalized correlation coefficient is used to handle scale differences in density levels between the canonical volume and the CT-reconstructed volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Mismatch: Density levels may differ between the canonical volume and the CT-reconstructed volume, which the normalized correlation coefficient mitigates. Sparse Data: The method is specifically designed for the "sparse few-projection regime" at intermediate times. Temporal Alignment: The method assumes that the deformation field can accurately warp the canonical volume to match the physical state at time t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevolumetricloss(targetvolume, predictedvolume): """Computes the volumetric loss as the negative normalized correlation coefficient.""" n = len(targetvolume) meantarget = sum(targetvolume) / n meanpred = sum(predictedvolume) / n devtarget = [x - meantarget for x in targetvolume] devpred = [x - meanpred for x in predictedvolume] numerator = sum(dt dp for dt, dp in zip(devtarget, devpred)) denomtarget = sum(dt 2 for dt in devtarget) 0.5 denompred = sum(dp 2 for dp in devpred) 0.5 if denomtarget == 0 or denompred == 0: correlation = 0.0 else: correlation = numerator / (denomtarget denompred) return -correlation def trainstep(sparseprojections, targetvolume, network, optimizer, t): """Single training step for Volumetric Supervision.""" optimizer.zerograd() # Evaluate canonical volume and apply deformation field to match time t predictedvolume = network.predictvolumeattime(t) lossvol = computevolumetricloss(targetvolume, predictedvolume) totalloss = lossvol totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() An optimization strategy that approximates the dense voxel objective using a subset of voxels while preserving consistency with the full-volume optimization. It uses importance-weighted Monte Carlo estimation to approximate dense reconstruction objectives from sparse voxel subsets. Instead of computing the reconstruction loss over the full voxel grid, it uses the Monte Carlo estimator to approximate the objective. Importance-weighted sampling improves coverage of informative regions. This updates Gaussian parameters using more representative voxel samples and stabilizes optimization. However, without slice supervision, the model lacks structured planar constraints and shows lower performance in rendered views than methods combining sparse voxel sampling with slice-based sampling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Directly supervises the 3D structure, which can improve the accuracy of the canonical model and deformation field in dynamic tomography. Handles scale differences between canonical and CT volumes via normalized correlation. Limitations: Requires high-quality volumetric reconstructions at the start and end of the experiment, which may not always be available. Relies on the quality of the conventional tomography reconstruction. When to Use: When dense volumetric ground truth is available at boundary time steps and sparse projections are available at intermediate times. Volumetric Supervision was introduced in the context of dynamic tomography, where the goal is to reconstruct 4D (3D + time) volumes from sparse projections. The method builds on the idea that while intermediate time steps may have sparse data, the start and end states often have rich data that can be reconstructed using conventional tomography. This approach was proposed to improve the training of neural networks for dynamic tomography by providing strong volumetric constraints. name: Direct Depth Supervision
head: Direct supervision, L1 depth loss, MSE depth loss
body: Direct Depth Supervision is a regularization technique in differentiable volume rendering that minimizes the pixel-wise discrepancy between the depth map rendered by a neural radiance field and a provided ground truth depth prior. It directly penalizes errors in the expected depth value, distinguishing it from indirect geometric methods that enforce consistency through other signals. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of Nr camera rays \{ri\}{i=1}^{Nr}, where each ray ri is defined by origin oi and direction di. Ground truth depth values \{D(ri)\}{i=1}^{Nr} corresponding to these rays. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}d used for backpropagation to update network parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). Data Structures: Rendered Depth: For each ray ri, the rendered depth \hat{D}(ri) is computed as the expected distance along the ray using the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{D}(ri) = \sum{k=1}^N w{i,k} t{i,k} where t{i,k} is the sample depth along ray i at index k, and w{i,k} is the rendering weight: w{i,k} = T{i,k} (1 - \exp(-\sigma{i,k} \delta{i,k})) with accumulated transmittance T{i,k} = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \rho{i,j}) and opacity \rho{i,k} = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{i,k} \delta{i,k}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Sample a batch of Nr rays from the training camera poses. 2. For each ray ri, query the neural network for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} at sample points t{i,k}. 3. Compute rendering weights w{i,k} and accumulated transmittance T{i,k}. 4. Calculate the rendered depth \hat{D}(ri) for each ray. 5. Retrieve the ground truth depth D(ri) for each ray from the depth prior. 6. Compute the loss using either Mean Squared Error (MSE) or L1 norm. Formulas: The loss function \mathcal{L}d is defined as: For MSE Loss: \mathcal{L}d^{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{i=1}^{Nr} \| D(ri) - \hat{D}(ri) \|^2 \quad For L1 Loss: \mathcal{L}d^{\text{L1}} = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{i=1}^{Nr} | D(ri) - \hat{D}(ri) | \quad where D(ri) is the ground truth depth and \hat{D}(ri) is the rendered depth for ray ri. Variations exist: some implementations use the L1 norm over sparse LiDAR projections \|D - D{\text{LiDAR}}\|1, while others normalize by the number of pixels with valid depth S1 as \frac{1}{S1} \sum |\hat{D}s - Ds|. Parameters: Nr: Batch size of rays. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Loss Type: Either MSE or L1. Both are included in experimental setups. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Prior Quality: The method relies on the accuracy of the ground truth depth prior. Ambiguity: In regions with low texture or transparency, the rendered depth may be ambiguous, leading to high loss values even if the color is correct. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed for the summation in the depth calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def directdepthsupervision(rays, gtdepths, near, far, numsamples): """ Computes direct depth supervision loss. Args: rays: List of tuples (origin, direction). gtdepths: Ground truth depth values for each ray. near: Near plane distance. far: Far plane distance. numsamples: Number of samples per ray. Returns: loss: Scalar loss value. """ rendereddepths = [] for (origin, direction), gt in zip(rays, gtdepths): # Sample points along the ray tvals = [near + (far - near) (i + 0.5) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] # Query network for density (standard MLP forward pass) sigmavals = [networkforward(origin + t direction) for t in tvals] # Compute rendering weights and transmittance weights = [] transmittance = 1.0 for i, sigma in enumerate(sigmavals): delta = tvals[i+1] - tvals[i] if i < len(tvals) - 1 else (far - tvals[-1]) opacity = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) weight = transmittance opacity weights.append(weight) transmittance = (1.0 - opacity) # Compute rendered depth rendereddepth = sum(w t for w, t in zip(weights, tvals)) rendereddepths.append(rendereddepth) # Compute L1 loss (MSE can be used similarly) loss = sum(abs(gt - pred) for gt, pred in zip(gtdepths, rendereddepths)) / len(rays) return loss def networkforward(point): # Standard 2-layer MLP forward pass for density # In practice, this is the trained neural network evaluating density at point return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual network evaluation Extends direct depth supervision by adding gradient terms to the L1 loss on inverse depths: \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} = \alpha |D{\text{pred}} - D{\text{gt}}| + \beta |\partialx D{\text{pred}} - \partialx D{\text{gt}}| + \beta |\partialy D{\text{pred}} - \partialy D{\text{gt}}|. The weights are \alpha=20 and \beta=20. Choose this when preserving local depth structure and edges is critical. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays Nr and samples per ray N. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to Nr \times N to store intermediate values (weights, transmittances) for backpropagation. Strengths: Directly enforces geometric accuracy; simple to implement; differentiable. Limitations: Sensitive to the quality of the depth prior; may struggle with sparse or noisy depth data if not regularized. When to use: When high-quality depth priors (e.g., from LiDAR or stereo matching) are available and geometric accuracy is prioritized over photometric consistency. When not to use: When depth priors are unreliable or absent. Direct Depth Supervision was introduced as part of the broader effort to integrate depth priors into neural radiance fields for outdoor scenes. The method leverages the differentiability of volume rendering to backpropagate gradients from depth errors to the network parameters, enabling joint optimization of color and geometry. It is a foundational technique in depth-supervised neural radiance field frameworks.
