name: 3D Point Supervision Loss
head: 3D Point Supervision, Point-based Pose Registration Loss
body: This method minimizes the Euclidean distance between 3D points backprojected from rendered depth and ground-truth 3D points to enforce global geometric consistency during NeRF optimization. Unlike direct depth regression, which often fails to register camera poses in sparse-view regimes by favoring per-image local geometry, this loss explicitly connects training images to the underlying scene structure, enabling robust pose refinement. Inputs: Neural Radiance Field parameters \theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). Camera poses Pk (view-to-world matrices) for each training view k. Ground-truth 3D points \mathbf{X}{gt} corresponding to the scene geometry. Intrinsics K (used for backprojection). Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{3D} used for gradient descent. Data Structures: Rendered depth map \hat{D}k(u,v) for each pixel (u,v) in view k, computed via differentiable volume rendering. World-frame 3D point \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) derived from \hat{D}k(u,v) and Pk. Steps: 1. Render Depth: For each training view k, render the expected depth \hat{D}k(\mathbf{r}) along rays \mathbf{r} using the current NeRF parameters \theta. The depth is the weighted sum of sample distances ti: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights. 2. Backproject to 3D: Convert the rendered depth \hat{D}k(u,v) into a 3D point \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) in the world coordinate frame using the camera pose Pk and intrinsic matrix K. Let \mathbf{p}{uv} = K^{-1} [u, v, 1]^T. The ray direction in world coordinates is \mathbf{d}k = Pk^{-1} \mathbf{p}{uv} (normalized). The 3D point is: \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) = \mathbf{o}k + \hat{D}k(u,v) \cdot \mathbf{d}k where \mathbf{o}k is the camera center in world coordinates. 3. Compute Distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance between the backprojected point \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) and the ground-truth 3D point corresponding to pixel (u,v). 4. Minimize: Optimize \theta and camera poses Pk to minimize the mean distance: \mathcal{L}{3D} = \frac{1}{N{valid}} \sum{k} \sum{(u,v) \in \text{valid}} \| \hat{\mathbf{X}}k(u,v) - \mathbf{X}{gt,k}(u,v) \|2 where \mathbf{X}{gt,k}(u,v) is the ground-truth 3D point corresponding to pixel (u,v) in view k, and N{valid} is the count of valid pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute3dpointloss(nerfmodel, poses, intrinsics, gt3dpoints, H, W): """ Computes the mean Euclidean distance between backprojected rendered depth and GT 3D points. Args: nerfmodel: Differentiable NeRF model. poses: List of camera-to-world matrices (N, 4, 4). intrinsics: Camera intrinsic matrix K (3, 3). gt3dpoints: Ground truth 3D points for each view. List of (H, W, 3) arrays. H, W: Image height and width. Returns: loss: Scalar tensor representing the mean Euclidean distance. """ Kinv = invert3x3(intrinsics) totalloss = 0.0 count = 0 for k, pose in enumerate(poses): # Render depth map using differentiable volume rendering depthmap = renderdepth(nerfmodel, pose, intrinsics, H, W) R = [[pose[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] t = [pose[i][3] for i in range(3)] # Camera center in world: -R^T @ t camcx = -(R[0][0]t[0] + R[1][0]t[1] + R[2][0]t[2]) camcy = -(R[0][1]t[0] + R[1][1]t[1] + R[2][1]t[2]) camcz = -(R[0][2]t[0] + R[1][2]t[1] + R[2][2]t[2]) for u in range(H): for v in range(W): d = depthmap[u][v] if d <= 0.0: continue # Ray in camera space: K^-1 @ [u, v, 1] rx = Kinv[0][0]u + Kinv[0][1]v + Kinv[0][2] ry = Kinv[1][0]u + Kinv[1][1]v + Kinv[1][2] rz = Kinv[2][0]u + Kinv[2][1]v + Kinv[2][2] norm = (rxrx + ryry + rzrz)0.5 rx, ry, rz = rx/norm, ry/norm, rz/norm # Ray in world space: R @ raycam wx = R[0][0]rx + R[0][1]ry + R[0][2]rz wy = R[1][0]rx + R[1][1]ry + R[1][2]rz wz = R[2][0]rx + R[2][1]ry + R[2][2]rz # 3D point: o + d dworld px = camcx + d wx py = camcy + d wy pz = camcz + d wz # Distance to GT point gx, gy, gz = gt3dpoints[k][u][v] dist = ((px-gx)2 + (py-gy)2 + (pz-gz)2)0.5 totalloss += dist count += 1 return totalloss / count if count > 0 else 0.0 Parameters: Weighting: The loss is typically applied as a primary term or combined with photometric loss. In SPARF, it is combined with photometric loss. Point Matching: The specific method for finding the "nearest" ground-truth point is not detailed in the primary text, but implies a correspondence exists per pixel. Edge Cases: Sparse Views: The method is specifically designed for sparse-view regimes (e.g., 3 views) where standard depth loss fails. Noisy Poses: It is effective when initial poses are noisy (e.g., perturbed by 15% Gaussian noise). Overfitting: Standard NeRF with high-frequency positional encoding overfits immediately; this loss helps mitigate degenerate geometry. A training loss that enforces geometric consistency across multiple training views by minimizing the re-projection error of corresponding rays. Performance: On DTU with 3 views and noisy poses, Photo + L1 GT 3D points yields PSNR 18.8 (20.3 masked), SSIM 0.75 (0.84 masked), LPIPS 0.21 (0.11 masked), and DE 0.07. This significantly outperforms Photo + L1 GT depth (PSNR 13.8, SSIM 0.54, LPIPS 0.46, DE 0.17). Strengths: Enforces global geometric connection between training images, successfully registering poses in sparse-view regimes. Comparison: Unlike L1 loss on rendered depth vs ground-truth depth, which struggles to refine poses and leads to disjoint local solutions, 3D point supervision results in drastically better novel-view rendering. Origin: Introduced in SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses. Context: Developed to address the failure of standard NeRF training in sparse-view settings with noisy poses, where photometric loss alone leads to degenerate geometry. Usage: Used in joint pose-NeRF refinement pipelines. SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00408, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-view correspondence loss
head: MV-Corr
body: A training loss that enforces geometric consistency across multiple training views by minimizing the re-projection error of corresponding rays. It acts on both camera pose estimates and the learned neural field to prevent overfitting to sparse input views. Unlike photometric loss [7], which fails to register poses in sparse regimes, MV-Corr provides strong supervision on rendered depth, implicitly encouraging it to be close to the true surface and favoring a solution consistent across all training images. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: A set of N training images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, their initial (potentially noisy) camera poses Pi, and a differentiable volume renderer that produces rendered depth Di and color Ci for each view. Outputs: A scalar loss value L{MV} used for gradient backpropagation to update poses and network weights. Data structures: Correspondences: A set of pixel coordinates representing corresponding points across views. Not given in the sources. Ray representation: A ray is defined by an origin and direction. Not given in the sources. Numbered steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a reference view i and a target view k, sample a pixel (u, v) in view i. 2. Back-projection: Construct the ray for pixel (u, v) in view i using the current pose Pi. 3. Depth Query: Query the rendered depth Di(u, v) from the neural field along the ray. 4. 3D Point Estimation: Compute the 3D point X in the world frame using the ray origin, direction, and sampled depth. 5. Re-projection: Transform X into the coordinate system of the target view k using the current pose Pk and project it onto the image plane of view k to obtain predicted pixel coordinates (u', v'). 6. Depth Sampling: Sample the rendered depth Dk(u', v') from the neural field at the predicted pixel location in view k. 7. Consistency Check: Compute the loss by penalizing the discrepancy between the depth implied by the correspondence and the actual rendered depth in the target view, minimizing the rays' intersection re-projection error. Formulas: The core intuition is minimizing the intersection re-projection error. The exact mathematical formulation is not explicitly expanded in the provided text. In practice, this involves a symmetric loss between views i and k that penalizes the reprojection discrepancy. Parameters: Number of views: The method is designed for sparse regimes, e.g., N=3 views. Pose Noise: Evaluated with 15% additive Gaussian noise on initial poses. Edge cases and pitfalls: Sparse Views: Photometric loss alone fails in sparse regimes; MV-Corr is specifically required to register poses in these conditions. Disconnected Solutions: Without multi-view constraints, the NeRF/poses can converge to disconnected solutions for each training image. Background: DTU scenes have black backgrounds, which can impact PSNR values if color prediction is wrong, though MV-Corr focuses on geometry. A loss objective that directly enforces the learned scene to be consistent from any viewpoint, boosting performance when combined with multi-view correspondences. It works best in collaboration with multi-view correspondences loss (8) because the latter is needed to learn an accurate geometry first; on its own or without (8), it yields lower performance. On DTU with 3 views and fixed GT poses, adding DCons to the baseline yields PSNR 18.30 (21.01), SSIM 0.78 (0.87), LPIPS 0.21 (0.10), DE 0.08, compared to no DCons which yields PSNR 18.13 (20.81), SSIM 0.77 (0.87), LPIPS 0.22 (0.10), DE 0.10. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: On DTU with 3 views and noisy poses, combining Photo + MVCorr yields PSNR 16.0 (17.8), SSIM 0.68 (0.81), LPIPS 0.28 (0.14), DE 0.13, outperforming Photo alone which yields PSNR 10.7 (9.8), SSIM 0.43 (0.62), LPIPS 0.59 (0.36), DE 1.9. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Strengths: Drastically outperforms photometric loss in terms of pose and learned geometry (depth error) in sparse regimes. Favors a NeRF/pose solution consistent across all training images. Limitations: Requires accurate geometry learning first to be effective when combined with other consistency modules. When to use it and when not: Use it when training NeRFs from sparse views with noisy poses where photometric loss fails to register poses. It is particularly effective when combined with photometric loss for the best overall performance. Originated in SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses. The method was developed to address the failure of existing regularization approaches in joint pose-NeRF training in the sparse regime. SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00408, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Generalized Ray Supervision
body: Generalized Ray Supervision is a framework for optimizing neural scene representations by treating arbitrary rays in a scene as "ray sensors" that record incoming radiance, extending the standard NeRF approach which only supervises camera rays. It solves the problem of limited geometric and photometric constraints in standard multi-view optimization by allowing supervision signals from non-camera perspectives, such as shadow rays or rays from unseen viewpoints, to guide the learning of density and color fields. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes light emission from scene particles, this generalization allows for physically correct modeling where the scene absorbs light from known sources or enforces semantic consistency across views. The method operates within the differentiable volume rendering framework. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A neural scene representation (mapping 3D coordinates to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}), a set of arbitrary rays \mathbf{r} (defined by origin o and direction d), and target radiance values C{\text{target}} recorded by the "ray sensors". Outputs: Updated neural field parameters \theta that minimize the difference between simulated radiance and target radiance. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). Sample Points: Along each ray, N sample points ti are selected. Rendering Weights: Computed via standard volume rendering quadrature wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)), where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti and Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Define a set of rays \mathbf{r} that are not necessarily camera rays. These can be shadow rays (connecting scene to light source) or rays from virtual/unseen viewpoints. 2. Radiance Simulation: For each ray \mathbf{r}, compute the simulated incoming radiance \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using volume rendering quadrature. If modeling shadow rays with a known light source and no self-emission: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \taui C{\text{light}} where Ti is the light transmittance, \taui is the discrete opacity, and C{\text{light}} is the incident radiance from the light source. If modeling general radiance (including emission): standard volume rendering quadrature is applied. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the loss between the simulated radiance \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the target radiance C{\text{target}} recorded by the ray sensor. For Multi-view Consistency, the loss is weighted by a confidence function \Gamma(\mathbf{r}i, D{\text{pgt}}): \mathcal{L}v = \sum{\mathbf{r}i \in Ii} \Gamma(\mathbf{r}i, D{\text{pgt}}) \| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}'i) - C{\text{pgt}}(\mathbf{r}i) \|2^2 where \Gamma(\mathbf{r}i, Di) = \exp\left( -\frac{\| Di - D{\text{pgt}} \|1}{2\epsilon} \right). 4. Backpropagation: Compute gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} and update the neural network parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Parameters: \epsilon: Uncertainty parameter for confidence weighting. \delta: Random perturbation vector for ray origins in unseen view generation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Rays from unseen views may pass through occluded regions, requiring careful ray sampling or filtering to avoid invalid supervision. Lighting Assumptions: Shadow ray supervision assumes the scene does not emit light. If the scene has emissive materials, this assumption leads to incorrect radiance simulation. Precision: The confidence function \Gamma is sensitive to the depth difference \| Di - D{\text{pgt}} \|1. Large errors result in near-zero weights, potentially stalling learning if \epsilon is not tuned appropriately. A specific application of generalized ray supervision using shadow rays (connecting scene points to a light source) to reconstruct neural scenes. It differs from standard NeRF by assuming the scene does not emit light, modeling only absorption from a known directional light source, which is more physically correct for non-emissive scenes. Choose this when accurate lighting interaction and shadow modeling are required, and the scene is known to be non-emissive. Link: ShadowNeuS. A supervision signal that ensures semantic consistency (e.g., road lanes look consistent from any view) by generating rays from unseen views and supervising their color against pseudo-ground truth, weighted by a confidence function. It differs from standard depth supervision by focusing on semantic consistency across views rather than just geometric depth accuracy. Choose this for driving scenes or structured environments where semantic priors (like map data) are available. Link: MapNeRF. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and samples per ray. Shadow ray supervision adds the cost of simulating light transport along additional rays. Multi-view consistency adds the cost of generating unseen rays and supervising their rendered colors. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the neural field parameters and intermediate rendering values for all active rays (camera + auxiliary). Strengths: Improves geometric accuracy and semantic consistency by providing additional constraints beyond camera rays. Shadow ray supervision enables physically correct lighting modeling. Limitations: Requires additional assumptions (e.g., known light source for shadow rays, map priors for multi-view consistency). Sensitive to noise in pseudo-labels or depth priors if confidence weighting is not properly tuned. When to use: When standard NeRF optimization results in poor geometry or inconsistent semantics, and auxiliary information (light sources, map data) is available. Generalized Ray Supervision was introduced in ShadowNeuS (2023) as a generalization of the NeRF training paradigm, revealing that NeRF essentially supervises camera rays and that this can be extended to arbitrary rays like shadow rays. The method builds on the differentiable volume rendering framework established by NeRF. ShadowNeuS: Neural SDF Reconstruction by Shadow Ray Supervision, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00025, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-view Consistency Supervision
body: Multi-view Consistency Supervision is a regularization technique for neural radiance fields that enforces semantic and geometric consistency across different viewpoints by generating rays from unseen views and supervising their rendered colors against pseudo-ground truth. It differs from standard color loss by using uncertainty-weighted pseudo-labels derived from map priors or depth estimates, ensuring that semantic structures (e.g., road lanes) appear consistent regardless of the viewing angle. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input images I, a ground depth map D{pgt} from map priors, an uncertainty parameter \epsilon, and a random perturbation vector norm \|\delta\| = 0.1. Outputs: A scalar loss value Lv. Data Structures: D{pgt}: 2D tensor of ground truth depth values. \Gamma(ri, Di): Confidence function returning a scalar weight. Steps: 1. Ray Origin Perturbation: For each input ray ri = oi + t \cdot di from image I, perturb the origin oi by a random 3D vector \delta with norm 0.1 to obtain a new origin o'i = oi + \delta. 2. Ray Construction: Retrieve the 3D point pi corresponding to the ray termination in the global coordinate system using the ground depth D{pgt}. Construct a new sampled ray r'i connecting the perturbed origin o'i to the point pi: r'i = o'i + t \cdot \frac{pi - o'i}{\|pi - o'i\|2} 3. Optional Occlusion Filtering: Optionally filter occluded regions on D{pgt} using DPT [47] and least squares fitting [48] to ensure D{pgt} represents visible surfaces. 4. Lane Enlargement (Optional): If the original ray ri passes near rendered vector lanes, enlarge the supervision area according to the minimal distance to the lane. 5. Confidence Weighting: Compute the confidence \Gamma(ri, Di) that the ray ri terminates on the surface of the ground: \Gamma(ri, Di) = \exp\left( -\frac{\|D(ri) - D{pgt}\|1}{2\epsilon} \right) where \epsilon is the uncertainty parameter. 6. Loss Calculation: Compute the multi-view consistency loss Lv by comparing the rendered color C(r'i) against the pseudo-ground truth color C{pgt}(r'i), weighted by the confidence \Gamma: Lv = \sum{r \in Ii} \Gamma(ri, D{pgt}) \| C(r'i) - C{pgt}(r'i) \|2^2 Parameters: \delta: Randomly sampled 3D vector with norm 0.1. \epsilon: Uncertainty parameter (same as used in ground density supervision). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Prior online pseudo-labels [7] are insufficient due to imprecise ray termination; this method explicitly uses D{pgt} to stabilize training. If D{pgt} contains occluded regions, the supervision may be incorrect unless filtered. A constraint enforcement mechanism that uses sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points to validate multi-view consistency during training. It selects context views based on three thresholds: spatial overlap \taus = 0.25, scale consistency \taur = 1.3, and a minimum point count N \ge \taun = 5 across context views. This ensures that only geometrically valid and sufficiently overlapping views contribute to the multi-view constraints. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves PSNR and SSIM while reducing LPIPS compared to baseline NeRF. Strengths: Enforces semantic consistency (e.g., lanes look like lanes from any view). Limitations: Relies on the quality of D{pgt} and map priors; requires careful tuning of \epsilon. Originated in MapNeRF, which incorporates map priors into neural radiance fields for driving view simulation. The method addresses the limitation of online pseudo-labels [7] by using explicit ground depth and uncertainty weighting to stabilize training. MapNeRF: Incorporating Map Priors into Neural Radiance Fields for Driving View Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1109/iros55552.2023.10341681, fetched 2026-10-26 WildSplat: Feedforward Gaussian Splatting from Unposed In-the-Wild Images, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37324-32, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Statistical Depth Refinement
head: Corrupt Depth Patching, Underfitting Depth Smoothing
body: Statistical Depth Refinement is a post-processing step applied during the training of radiance fields to mitigate artifacts caused by corrupt stereo depth inputs, such as those arising from fuzzy pixels or specular highlights in surgical scenes. It prevents the model from overfitting to these noisy depth values by replacing them with smoother depth estimates from an underfitting model state. Unlike direct depth supervision which may lock in errors, this method statistically identifies outliers in the residual between the current model's depth and the noisy input, replacing them with the "averaged" output of the early-stage model. Inputs: Di: The noisy stereo depth map for the i-th frame. Db^Ki: The depth map rendered by the radiance field after K iterations of training. \alpha: A threshold parameter in [0, 1] defining the quantile of largest residuals to treat as corrupt. Outputs: \widehat{D}i: The patched depth map used for subsequent optimization. Data Structures: Residual Map R: A 2D array of the same spatial dimensions as Di and Db^Ki, where each element R[u,v] stores the absolute difference between the depth values at pixel (u,v). Steps: 1. Render Underfitting Depth: After K iterations of training, render the depth map Db^Ki for the current frame i. At this early stage, the model tends to average learned colors and occupancy, producing smoother depth estimates. 2. Compute Residuals: Calculate the absolute difference between the underfitting depth and the noisy stereo depth to form the residual map R: R[u,v] = | Db^Ki[u,v] - Di[u,v] | where (u,v) is the pixel coordinate. 3. Compute Probabilistic Distribution: Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) or rank order of the values in R. 4. Identify Corrupt Pixels: Determine the threshold value corresponding to the (1-\alpha)-quantile of the residual distribution. Identify all pixels (u,v) where R[u,v] exceeds this threshold. These pixels are statistically identified as having large residuals and are classified as corrupt depth. 5. Patch Depth: Replace the depth values of the identified corrupt pixels in the noisy depth map Di with the corresponding values from the smoother underfitting depth map Db^Ki. The resulting map is \widehat{D}i. 6. Optimize: Use the patched depth map \widehat{D}i for depth supervision in subsequent training iterations. Parameters: K: The number of training iterations after which the underfitting depth is sampled. Typical value: 4000. \alpha: The fraction of pixels with the largest residuals to patch. Typical value: 0.1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def statisticaldepthrefinement(noisydepthDi, model, K, alpha): """ Refines noisy stereo depth by patching outliers with underfitting model output. Args: noisydepthDi: 2D array, noisy stereo depth map for current frame. model: Radiance field model. K: Number of training iterations to wait for underfitting state. alpha: Quantile threshold for identifying corrupt pixels (e.g., 0.1). Returns: patcheddepth: 2D array, depth map with corrupt pixels replaced. """ # Step 1: Obtain underfitting depth after K iterations # Note: In practice, this requires pausing optimization or maintaining a snapshot # of the model state at iteration K. underfittingdepthDb = model.renderdepth(iteration=K) # Step 2: Compute residual map residualmapR = abs(underfittingdepthDb - noisydepthDi) # Step 3 & 4: Identify pixels with largest residuals (top alpha quantile) # Flatten residuals to find the threshold value flatresiduals = residualmapR.flatten() thresholdvalue = np.percentile(flatresiduals, 100 (1 - alpha)) # Create mask for corrupt pixels corruptmask = residualmapR > thresholdvalue # Step 5: Patch corrupt pixels # Replace noisy depth with underfitting depth where mask is True patcheddepth = np.where(corruptmask, underfittingdepthDb, noisydepthDi) return patcheddepth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the assumption that the underfitting model is smoother than the noisy input. If the model has already overfit by iteration K, the "smooth" reference may also contain artifacts. Boundary Conditions: The residual calculation is per-pixel. Discontinuities at object boundaries may be treated as corrupt if the stereo depth is noisy there, potentially leading to over-smoothing of valid geometry. Degenerate Input: If the stereo depth is uniformly corrupt or the model fails to converge, the statistical distribution may not separate "normal" from "corrupt" effectively. A technique that transfers deblurred texture information from pre-deblurred images to the NeRF using perceptual loss on rendered patches, overcoming the geometric inconsistency of pre-deblurred images. It uses an off-the-shelf deep learning-based image deblurring network to generate pre-deblurred images from blurred inputs. It renders color patches \hat{C}{ptc} from the NeRF using patch-wise sampled rays r{ptc}^{pd} at the same pixel locations as the pre-deblurred color patches \bar{C}{ptc}. Perceptual loss is applied by extracting features from both the pre-deblurred color patch and the rendered color patch using a shared pre-trained image feature extractor. Pre-deblurred images cannot be used as direct pixel-wise color supervision due to lack of 3D consistency caused by the ill-posed property of image deblurring and independent processing across multi-view images. A local, per-pixel geometry supervision method that generates refined depth candidates via spatial neighbors and multiplicative perturbations, scored by normalized cross-correlation (NCC). For training camera C and pixel p, it forms a candidate set D(p) = \{ \hat{D}t(C)(p), \hat{D}t(C)(p+ex), \hat{D}t(C)(p+ey) \} \cup \{ \hat{D}t(C)(p)(1+\epsilonk) \mid k=1..n{rand} \}, where \epsilonk \sim \text{Unif}(-2s, 2s), s \ll 1. Each candidate is backprojected from C and reprojected into K nearest views N(C). Each candidate is scored by NCC between fixed-size, bilinear-sampled patches. The candidate with the highest score is selected as refined depth Dt^(p). Refined depths are rejected if reprojection error exceeds a small threshold. Time Complexity: The method adds a one-time cost per refinement step (every K iterations) proportional to the number of pixels N in the depth map, primarily for residual calculation and sorting/quantile determination O(N \log N) or O(N) with selection algorithms. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the residual map and the mask, O(N) additional memory. Measured Performance: Evaluated on robotic surgery stereo videos (DaVinci robotic prostatectomy data), 6 cases, 807 frames, 15 fps. Metrics include PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Strengths: Effectively handles corrupt stereo depth caused by fuzzy pixels and specular highlights. Prevents overfitting to corrupt depth which leads to abrupt artifacts. Limitations: Relies on the availability of stereo depth inputs. Requires careful tuning of K and \alpha. When to use: When training radiance fields with noisy stereo depth supervision, particularly in scenes with specular highlights or fuzzy pixels. When not to use: When high-quality, clean depth supervision is available, or when computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of maintaining an underfitting snapshot is prohibitive. Statistical Depth Refinement was proposed in the context of neural rendering for stereo 3D reconstruction of deformable tissues in robotic surgery. The method addresses the challenge of using stereo depth from surgical cameras, which often suffer from noise due to specular highlights and fuzzy pixels. The authors observed that early-stage (underfitting) radiance fields produce smoother depth estimates, which can be used to identify and patch corrupt depth values in the noisy stereo input. The method was implemented with K=4000 iterations and \alpha=0.1. Neural Rendering for Stereo 3D Reconstruction of Deformable Tissues in Robotic Surgery, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-16449-141, fetched 2026-10-26 Sparse-DeRF: Deblurred Neural Radiance Fields From Sparse View, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3563398, fetched 2026-10-27 Advancing Structured Priors for Sparse-Voxel Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2601.17720, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: S-NeRF Confidence Components
head: S-NeRF Confidence
body: S-NeRF Confidence Components is a selective confidence weighting mechanism for differentiable volume rendering that adapts supervision reliability based on scene content, distinguishing between static background environments and dynamic foreground objects like vehicles. It sets itself apart from standard geometric regularization by decoupling confidence metrics per object class: it employs geometry and reprojection measurements for background learning, while restricting foreground vehicle learning to RGB and SSIM confidences, leveraging the higher quality of LiDAR depth maps available for foreground objects. The method operates within the S-NeRF framework. It computes a composite loss where individual components are weighted by confidence scores derived from specific measurements. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}, rendered depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}, ground-truth color \mathbf{C}, ground-truth depth \mathbf{D}, SSIM maps, and region classification flags indicating background or foreground vehicle regions. Outputs: Confidence weights for background (geometry, reprojection) and foreground (RGB, SSIM) which modulate the loss gradients. Data Structures: Confidence Flags: Boolean or categorical indicators for each ray/sample point determining if it belongs to "background" or "foreground vehicle" regions. Threshold \tau: A scalar parameter for geometry confidence calculation. Steps: 1. Classify Region: Determine if the current ray sample or pixel corresponds to a background element or a foreground vehicle. 2. Compute Background Confidence: If background, calculate geometry confidence and reprojection confidence. Geometry confidence is derived from the consistency between the rendered depth and the LiDAR depth, modulated by threshold \tau. Reprojection confidence is derived from multi-view consistency checks. 3. Compute Foreground Confidence: If foreground vehicle, calculate RGB confidence and SSIM confidence. Geometry and reprojection confidences are explicitly excluded for foregrounds because the training depth maps for vehicles are of higher quality, making strong geometric constraints redundant. 4. Apply Weights: Use the computed confidences to weight the respective loss terms in the optimization loop. Formulas: Geometry Confidence: The geometry confidence module uses a threshold \tau. The paper notes that geometry confidence is not sensitive to \tau, with a reasonable range of [10\%, 40\%]. The exact mathematical expression is referenced as Eq. (7) in the source paper, but the specific formula is not provided in the extracted notes. Loss Balance: The confidence components interact with loss balance weights \lambda1 and \lambda2. For background views, the source only specifies \lambda2 \in (0.02). For foreground vehicles, reasonable ranges are \lambda1 \in [0.5, 2] and \lambda2 \in (0.075, 0.015). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeconfidenceweights(rendereddepth, lidardepth, renderedcolor, gtcolor, ssimmap, isvehicle, tau=0.2): """ Computes confidence weights for S-NeRF loss components. Args: rendereddepth: Array of rendered depth values. lidardepth: Array of ground-truth LiDAR depth values. renderedcolor: Array of rendered RGB colors. gtcolor: Array of ground-truth RGB colors. ssimmap: Array of SSIM values between rendered and ground truth. isvehicle: Boolean mask indicating foreground vehicle regions. tau: Threshold for geometry confidence (default 20%). Returns: backgroundweights: Dict with 'geometry' and 'reprojection' weights. foregroundweights: Dict with 'rgb' and 'ssim' weights. """ # Initialize weights backgroundweights = {'geometry': 1.0, 'reprojection': 1.0} foregroundweights = {'rgb': 1.0, 'ssim': 1.0} # Background Confidence Calculation # Geometry confidence depends on depth consistency and threshold tau # Note: The sources do not provide the exact formula for geometry confidence (referenced as Eq. 7) deptherror = abs(rendereddepth - lidardepth) geometryconfidence = 1.0 if deptherror < tau else 0.0 # Reprojection confidence is derived from multi-view consistency # Note: The sources do not provide the exact formula for reprojection confidence reprojectionconfidence = 1.0 backgroundweights['geometry'] = geometryconfidence backgroundweights['reprojection'] = reprojectionconfidence # Foreground Confidence Calculation # For vehicles, only RGB and SSIM confidences are used # RGB confidence is typically based on pixel-wise error rgberror = abs(renderedcolor - gtcolor) rgbconfidence = math.exp(-rgberror) # SSIM confidence is derived from the SSIM map ssimconfidence = ssimmap foregroundweights['rgb'] = rgbconfidence foregroundweights['ssim'] = ssimconfidence return backgroundweights, foregroundweights Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Sensitivity: While the geometry confidence is not highly sensitive to \tau, values outside [10\%, 40\%] may degrade performance. Foreground Depth Quality: The exclusion of geometry confidence for vehicles relies on the assumption that training depth maps for vehicles are "relatively better" than backgrounds. Metric Trade-offs: Using only RGB or SSIM confidence for vehicles yields a 1–2% PSNR increase but a 6.6–11% LPIPS decrease compared to using both. Therefore, using both is recommended for balanced performance. S-NeRF Loss Balance Weights are hyperparameters (\lambda1, \lambda2) used to scale the depth and smoothness components of the composite loss function in S-NeRF, balancing geometric supervision against the primary RGB reconstruction loss. They are distinct from the learnable confidence weights (\omegai) that adaptively weight individual confidence metrics; these balance weights are fixed user-defined constants. They set S-NeRF apart from standard NeRF by explicitly incorporating depth and edge-aware smoothness constraints, requiring careful tuning of \lambda1 and \lambda2 to handle the disparity between static background scenes and dynamic foreground vehicles. Performance Impact: Removing the reprojection confidence module drops PSNR by 0.4%. Training without geometry confidence drops PSNR and SSIM by about 0.7%. Foreground Optimization: For foreground vehicles, using both RGB and SSIM confidences provides better overall performance (considering PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS) than using either alone, despite a slight PSNR trade-off. Depth Error Rate: The method predicts high confidence for accurate depths, encouraging NeRF geometry to be consistent with LiDAR signals. S-NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views) was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023. It addresses the challenges of novel view synthesis in street scenes, which contain both static backgrounds and dynamic foreground objects. The confidence components method was introduced to handle the differing reliability of depth and color supervision signals between these two types of objects. S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.00749, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: S-NeRF Loss Balance Weights
head: S-NeRF λ1 and λ2 weights
body: S-NeRF Loss Balance Weights are fixed user-defined hyperparameters (\lambda1, \lambda2) that scale the depth and edge-aware smoothness components of the composite loss function in S-NeRF, balancing geometric supervision against the primary RGB reconstruction loss. They operate within a loss structure that explicitly incorporates depth and smoothness constraints, distinguishing S-NeRF from standard NeRF which relies primarily on RGB photometric loss. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training rays \mathcal{R}, ground truth RGB images I, predicted RGB images \hat{I}, ground truth depth/disparity D, predicted depth/disparity \hat{D}, image gradients |\partial I|, confidence metrics \tilde{C}, and balance weights \lambda1, \lambda2. Outputs: Total loss scalar L{total} for gradient descent. Data Structures: \lambda1: Scalar float, balance weight for depth loss. \lambda2: Scalar float, balance weight for smoothness loss. L{color}: Scalar float, RGB photometric loss. L{depth}: Scalar float, confidence-conditioned depth loss. L{smooth}: Scalar float, edge-aware smoothness loss. Formulas: The total loss is a linear combination of three terms: L{total} = L{color} + \lambda1 L{depth} + \lambda2 L{smooth} 1. RGB Loss (L{color}): Sum of squared errors over all training rays: L{color} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \| I(r) - \hat{I}(r) \|^2 2. Depth Loss (L{depth}): Sum of absolute differences between ground truth and predicted depth/disparity, normalized by a factor of 6: L{depth} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{|D - \hat{D}|}{6} Note: For background street scenes, D represents disparity (inverse depth) to focus on close objects; for foreground vehicles, D represents depth. 3. Smoothness Loss (L{smooth}): Edge-aware constraint penalizing large depth variances relative to image gradients, weighted by confidence \tilde{C}: L{smooth} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{\tilde{C} \cdot |D - \hat{D}|}{|\partialx \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialx I|} + |\partialy \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialy I|}} Note: \partialx and \partialy denote spatial derivatives. Parameters and Typical Values: \lambda1 and \lambda2 are user-defined constants. Reasonable ranges depend on the scene type: Street Background Views: \lambda1 \in [0.1, 0.4], \lambda2 \in (0.005, 0.02). Typical values: \lambda1 = 0.2, \lambda2 = 0.01. Foreground Vehicles: \lambda1 \in [0.5, 2], \lambda2 \in (0.075, 0.015). Typical values: \lambda1 = 1, \lambda2 = 0.15. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesnerfloss(Igt, Ipred, Dgt, Dpred, Iimage, Csmoothconf, lambda1, lambda2): """ Computes the total S-NeRF loss. Args: Igt: Ground truth RGB image tensor (H, W, 3). Ipred: Predicted RGB image tensor (H, W, 3). Dgt: Ground truth depth (vehicles) or disparity (background) tensor (H, W). Dpred: Predicted depth/disparity tensor (H, W). Iimage: Original RGB image tensor for gradient computation (H, W, 3). Csmoothconf: Confidence metric tensor for smoothness loss (H, W). lambda1: Balance weight for depth loss. lambda2: Balance weight for smoothness loss. Returns: Total loss scalar. """ # 1. RGB Loss (Lcolor) lcolor = torch.sum((Igt - Ipred) 2) # 2. Depth Loss (Ldepth) depthdiff = torch.abs(Dgt - Dpred) ldepth = torch.sum(depthdiff) / 6.0 # 3. Smoothness Loss (Lsmooth) # Compute image gradients |∂I| on grayscale to match source notation Igray = torch.mean(Iimage, dim=-1) Ix = torch.abs(Igray[:, 1:,:] - Igray[:,:-1,:]) Iy = torch.abs(Igray[:,:, 1:] - Igray[:,:,:-1]) # Compute predicted depth/disparity gradients |∂D̂| Dx = torch.abs(Dpred[:, 1:,:] - Dpred[:,:-1,:]) Dy = torch.abs(Dpred[:,:, 1:] - Dpred[:,:,:-1]) # Denominator: |∂x D̂| exp^−|∂x I| + |∂y D̂| exp^−|∂y I| denom = Dx torch.exp(-Ix) + Dy torch.exp(-Iy) denom = torch.clamp(denom, min=1e-8) # Numerator: C̃ · |D − D̂| # Crop depthdiff and confidence to match gradient dimensions (H-1, W-1) depthdiffcrop = depthdiff[:, 1:,:] confcrop = Csmoothconf[:, 1:,:] smoothnessnum = confcrop depthdiffcrop lsmooth = torch.sum(smoothnessnum / denom) # 4. Total Loss ltotal = lcolor + lambda1 ldepth + lambda2 lsmooth return ltotal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sensitivity: The method is robust to parameter variation; varying \lambda1 or \lambda2 outside reasonable ranges reduces PSNR and SSIM by only 0.2–1% on background novel view rendering. Disparity vs Depth: For background scenes, D must be disparity (inverse depth) to focus on close objects; for vehicles, it is depth. Using the wrong interpretation breaks the loss semantics. Confidence Metrics: The confidence \tilde{C} is derived from geometry and reprojection measurements for background, and RGB/SSIM for foreground [Parent]. Incorrect confidence calculation leads to incorrect weighting. The composite loss function consists of RGB loss, confidence-conditioned depth loss, and edge-aware smoothness constraints, defining the structure within which \lambda1 and \lambda2 operate. The total loss is L{total} = L{color} + \lambda1 L{depth} + \lambda2 L{smooth}. The smoothness loss penalizes large depth variances according to image gradients: L{smooth} = \sum (\tilde{C} \cdot |D - \hat{D}|) / (|\partialx \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialx I|} + |\partialy \hat{D}| \exp^{-|\partialy I|}). Typical values are \lambda1=1, \lambda2=0.15 for vehicles and \lambda1=0.2, \lambda2=0.01 for background. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Training Duration: Ablation experiments are trained for 30k iterations. Robustness: The method is robust to parameter variation. Deviating from optimal \lambda1, \lambda2 ranges results in only minor performance drops (0.2–1% PSNR/SSIM reduction) on background novel view rendering. Scene Specificity: Optimal weights differ significantly between static background (low \lambda) and dynamic foreground (high \lambda), requiring scene-specific tuning or separate training pipelines. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Improves geometric consistency and depth accuracy, especially for foreground objects where standard NeRF fails due to lack of structure. Robust to hyperparameter tuning. Limitations: Requires ground truth depth/disparity for supervision. Performance degrades if confidence metrics are inaccurate. Not suitable for scenes without reliable depth cues or where disparity/depth interpretation is ambiguous. When to Use: Use when geometric accuracy is critical (e.g., autonomous driving scenarios) and ground truth depth is available. Use separate weights for background and foreground if training jointly. When Not to Use: Avoid if depth supervision is unavailable or unreliable. Avoid if computational resources are extremely limited and standard NeRF suffices. S-NeRF was introduced in 2023 by the authors of "S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views". It extends NeRF to handle large-scale street scenes with dynamic foreground vehicles. The loss balance weights \lambda1 and \lambda2 were introduced to incorporate depth and smoothness constraints, addressing the limitations of NeRF in reconstructing dynamic objects and ensuring geometric consistency in autonomous driving datasets like nuScenes and Waymo. S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.00749, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Depth Priors and Initialization
body: This family of methods addresses the ill-posed nature of single-view or sparse-view NeRF optimization by initializing or regularizing geometry using external depth estimates. It sets itself apart from siblings like Geometric Baseline Regularization by fusing perspective depth maps into a canonical panorama map via deformable alignment before training [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md], and distinguishes itself from Depth-Supervised NeRF by refining radiance-field optimizations through external geometric priors rather than relying on multi-view consistency [14220-depth-supervision.md]. All methods in this family integrate external depth estimates into the differentiable volume rendering framework Parent. Gradients flow from the depth loss \mathcal{L}{\text{depth}} back through the rendered depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) to update the network parameters. The rendered depth is computed as the expected distance along the ray: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights, ti are sample depths, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. This expected depth serves as the differentiable geometric target for the supervision losses. This method initializes the geometry of visible regions in a single-view NeRF using a 360-degree depth estimation pipeline, addressing the under-constrained optimization problem inherent to single-view reconstruction [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly fusing perspective depth maps into a canonical panorama depth map via deformable alignment before NeRF training, rather than relying solely on RGB consistency or post-hoc inpainting [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. Choose it when reconstructing scenes from a single panorama where standard monocular estimators fail on 360-degree inputs [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. Depth supervision is a training technique that improves reconstructed geometry and reduces floating artifacts by providing depth priors derived from off-the-shelf monocular depth estimation models [14220-depth-supervision.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map by focusing on refining existing radiance-field optimizations through external geometric priors rather than relying solely on multi-view consistency or specific single-view architectures [14220-depth-supervision.md]. Choose it when training multi-view datasets where off-the-shelf depth models provide useful scale-consistent priors [14220-depth-supervision.md]. Definition: Incorporates precomputed depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls into NeRF training to enforce geometric constraints on textureless planar surfaces. Steps: 1. Compute depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls using semantic segmentation. 2. Incorporate these priors into training with MSE and BoundL losses alongside photometric loss. 3. Train until convergence. Parameters: \delta (BoundL tolerance): 1 mm. \lambda{\text{color}}: 10 (bedroom), 1 (living room). \lambda{\text{depth}}: 10 (bedroom), 1 (living room). Metrics: RMSE of priors vs ground truth: 2.786 mm (bedroom), 3.201 mm (living room). Converged in 120,000 iterations. Comparison: Faster convergence than photometric-only (120k vs 200k) and patch-regularization (120k vs 280k) methods due to depth supervision enabling quick identification of empty spaces, concentrating sampling on occupied regions, and providing a stronger optimization signal. The method originates from the challenge of improving geometric consistency for 360-degree neural radiance fields in indoor scenarios. It is used to address textureless surfaces like walls, floors, and ceilings, where photometric loss alone leads to "floaters" and cloudy artifacts. The approach incorporates precomputed architectural depth priors to enforce geometric constraints and accelerate convergence. name: Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map
head: Depth-guided Single-view NeRF, Single-view NeRF with Depth Initialization
body: This method addresses the under-constrained optimization problem of single-view NeRF reconstruction by initializing the geometry of visible regions using a 360-degree depth estimation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Depth Supervision by explicitly constructing a canonical panorama depth map from multiple perspective projections via deformable alignment before integrating it into the NeRF training loop, rather than applying depth loss directly to raw perspective estimates or using multi-view consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input panorama I{\text{rgb}}. Output: A trained NeRF network f{\text{nerf}} parameterized by \theta, representing the geometry and appearance of visible regions. Data Structures: Perspective Projections: A set of K perspective images \{\bar{I}{\text{rgb}}^k\}{k=1}^K and their corresponding estimated depth maps \{\bar{I}d^k\}{k=1}^K. Canonical Panorama Depth Map: A learnable depth map Id defined on the same coordinate system as I{\text{rgb}}. Alignment Parameters: For each perspective view k, a global scale factor wk and a local bias field \{b{k,i,j}\} for each pixel (i,j). Numbered Steps: 1. Perspective Projection: Project the single input panorama I{\text{rgb}} into K perspective images \{\bar{I}{\text{rgb}}^k\}{k=1}^K using different viewing directions. The number of projections is set to K=20. This is necessary because existing monocular depth estimators are trained on limited field-of-view images and do not handle 360-degree panoramas directly. 2. Monocular Depth Estimation: Pass each perspective image \bar{I}{\text{rgb}}^k through a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model (referenced as [52] in the source) to obtain depth maps \{\bar{I}d^k\}{k=1}^K. Note that due to scale ambiguity in single-view depth estimation, depth values in overlapped regions between different perspectives may differ significantly. 3. Deformable Alignment: Align the perspective depth maps \{\bar{I}d^k\} to a canonical learnable panorama depth map Id by optimizing the alignment objective. This step resolves scale and bias inconsistencies across views. For each perspective map k, assign a scale wk and local bias \{b{k,i,j}\}. Optimize the following objective function (Eq. 2 in): \sum{k,i,j} \left\| \bar{v}{i,j}^k wk + b{k,i,j} - v{M(i,j)} \right\| + \lambdas \left( Ls(b{i,j+1}, b{i,j}) + Ls(b{i+1,j}, b{i,j}) \right) where: \bar{v}{i,j}^k is the pixel value of depth map \bar{I}d^k at coordinates (i,j). v{M(i,j)} is the pixel value of the canonical panorama depth map Id at the coordinate mapped from (i,j) via the projective operation M (mapping perspective image coordinates to panorama image coordinates). Ls is the smooth L1 loss. The second term is a total variation regularization term on the bias field to ensure spatial smoothness. \lambdas is a weighting factor for the regularization term (Not given in the sources). 4. NeRF Training: Train the single-view NeRF using the RGB panorama I{\text{rgb}} and the aligned canonical depth map Id. The NeRF is optimized to minimize the combined color and depth reconstruction loss (Eq. 3 in): \mathcal{L}{\text{nerf}}' = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \left( \left\| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r}) \right\|^2 + \left\| \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) - \bar{D}(\mathbf{r}) \right\|^2 \right) where: \mathcal{R} is the set of rays sampled from the panorama. \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is the expected pixel color rendered by the NeRF. C(\mathbf{r}) is the ground-truth pixel color from I{\text{rgb}}. \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) is the expected depth value rendered by the NeRF, computed as \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti (as per Parent). \bar{D}(\mathbf{r}) is the corresponding depth pixel value from the canonical depth map Id at the ray's intersection point. Parameters: K: Number of perspective projections. Set to 20. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth estimation suffers from scale ambiguity, leading to inconsistent depth values in overlapping regions of different perspective projections. The deformable alignment step is critical to resolve this. Visible Regions Only: Since only a single panorama is available, the trained NeRF f{\text{nerf}} is only accurate for visible regions. Invisible regions require separate completion methods (e.g., collaborative RGBD inpainting). Time Complexity: The method requires an initial depth estimation pass for K views and an optimization step for deformable alignment before the main NeRF training loop. The alignment optimization involves solving for scale and bias parameters for all pixels across K views. Memory Complexity: Requires storing K perspective depth maps and the canonical panorama depth map Id. The alignment parameters (wk, b{k,i,j}) add memory overhead proportional to the resolution of the depth maps. Strengths: Provides accurate geometry initialization for visible regions, addressing the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction. The deformable alignment effectively handles scale inconsistencies from monocular estimators. Limitations: The method is limited to visible regions; invisible regions are not reconstructed by this step alone. Performance depends on the accuracy of the underlying monocular depth estimator [52] and the quality of the perspective projections. When to use: When reconstructing a scene from a single panoramic image and accurate geometry of visible parts is required. When not to use: When the scene has significant occlusions or invisible regions that need to be filled, or when multi-view inputs are available. This method was introduced in the paper "PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama". It addresses the limitation of previous single-view NeRF methods that did not fully ensure geometry consistency. By leveraging 360-degree depth estimation and deformable alignment, it enables photo-realistic panoramic NeRF reconstruction from a single input. PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2024.3387307, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Depth Supervision
head: Depth Prior Supervision, Monocular Depth Supervision
body: Depth Supervision is a training technique that improves reconstructed geometry by providing depth priors using off-the-shelf depth estimation models, resulting in better geometry and reduced number of floaters. It differs from Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map by explicitly integrating external monocular depth priors rather than relying solely on photometric consistency, and builds on Depth Priors and Initialization shared principles. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset containing images and corresponding depth maps stored in <dataset-root>/depths/<FILENAME>.png, where FILENAME matches the dataset image name. A boolean parameter usedepthloss in OptimizationParams enables the feature. Outputs: Updated neural network parameters (or Gaussian attributes) that minimize the depth discrepancy. Data Structures: Depth maps are stored as PNG files in a subdirectory depths/ relative to the dataset root. The implementation must handle a boolean flag usedepthloss to toggle the loss calculation. Steps: 1. Load: Retrieve depth maps from the dataset directory. 2. Refit: Since depth estimates from off-the-shelf models may vary in scale between frames, all depth maps are refitted against a prior point cloud to a common scale. 3. Discard: Depth maps that fail the refitting process against the prior point cloud are discarded and not used for supervision. 4. Render: Compute the rendered depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti using the differentiable volume rendering framework. 5. Loss: Enforce that the rendered depth matches the depth predicted by a pre-trained monocular depth network (e.g., MiDaS [37]) for the input image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import statistics def computedepthloss(rendereddepth, monoculardepth, priorpointclouddepths, usedepthloss): """ Computes the depth supervision loss. Args: rendereddepth: List of floats representing the rendered depth map. monoculardepth: List of floats representing the depth predicted by a monocular network. priorpointclouddepths: List of floats representing depths from the prior point cloud. usedepthloss: Boolean flag to enable/disable depth supervision. Returns: loss: Scalar float representing the depth loss. """ if not usedepthloss: return 0.0 # Filter valid depth values (positive and finite) validmono = [d for d in monoculardepth if d > 0 and math.isfinite(d)] validprior = [d for d in priorpointclouddepths if d > 0 and math.isfinite(d)] # Discard invalid maps that fail refitting preparation if not validmono or not validprior: return 0.0 # Refit: estimate scale factor s using median ratio for robustness against outliers ratios = [p / m for p, m in zip(validprior, validmono)] scalefactor = statistics.median(ratios) # Sources do not specify a quality threshold or exact refitting algorithm. # We proceed with the estimated scale factor. refitteddepth = [d scalefactor for d in monoculardepth] # Compute L1 loss between rendered and refitted depth errors = [abs(r - rd) for r, rd in zip(rendereddepth, refitteddepth)] loss = sum(errors) / len(errors) if errors else 0.0 return loss Parameters: usedepthloss: A boolean parameter in OptimizationParams that enables depth supervision during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Refitting Failure: Depth maps that fail the refitting process against the prior point cloud are discarded. Harmful Effects: In some cases, monocular depth supervision was found to be harmful to reconstruction quality. Noise: Regularization terms involving depth can be noisy. Refined Depth for Geometry Supervision is a lightweight depth-regularization objective used during per-scene training to refine reconstructed geometry, specifically improving local sharpness and depth consistency without sacrificing efficiency. It sets itself apart from standard photometric losses by explicitly leveraging rendered depths and input images to derive a geometry-supervision loss (L{refD}), which is combined with the original training loss to yield more geometrically faithful surfaces with fast convergence. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for monocular depth inference and refitting per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for depth maps in the dataset directory. Measured Performance: Sources report mixed results; one notes better geometry and reduced floaters, while another found it did not noticeably improve quality and was sometimes harmful. Strengths: Can reduce floaters and improve geometric fidelity when successful. Limitations: Can be harmful to reconstruction quality in some cases. Results are not conclusive. When to use: When floaters are a significant issue and other methods are not available. When not to use: When reconstruction quality is already high and depth supervision introduces noise or harm. Origin: The technique is discussed in the context of Gaussian Splatting optimization and RealFusion. History: It was explored as a way to improve geometry in single-view or multi-view reconstruction pipelines by leveraging pre-trained monocular depth networks like MiDaS [37]. Usage: Used in 3D reconstruction pipelines to constrain the location of surfaces. name: Refined Depth for Geometry Supervision
head: Depth-regularization objective
body: Refined Depth for Geometry Supervision is a lightweight depth-regularization objective used during per-scene training to refine reconstructed geometry, specifically improving local sharpness and depth consistency without sacrificing efficiency. It sets itself apart from standard photometric losses by explicitly leveraging rendered depths and input images to derive a geometry-supervision loss (L{refD}), which is combined with the original training loss to yield more geometrically faithful surfaces with fast convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depths \{Di\} for each camera view i, and the associated input images for each view. Outputs: A scalar loss value L{refD} used to update the scene representation (e.g., Sparse Voxel Octree) during optimization. Data Structures: Rendered Depths \{Di\}: A set of depth maps, one per camera view, generated by the current state of the volume rendering pipeline. Steps: 1. Derive Refined Depths: For each camera view i, derive refined depth information by advancing the geometry supervision from the rendered depths Di and the associated input images. 2. Compute Loss: Calculate the geometry-supervision loss L{refD} based on the derived refined depths. 3. Combine Losses: Combine L{refD} with the original SVRaster training loss to form the total loss for the per-scene optimization stage. 4. Optimize: Update the scene parameters (e.g., voxel properties) using the combined loss to improve geometric accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ lrefd = computerefineddepthloss(rendereddepths, inputimages) loriginal = originallossfn(model, inputimages) # Combine losses # The source states: "This geometry-supervision loss, when combined # with the original SVRaster training loss, improves the geometric # accuracy." # The weighting factor is not specified. totalloss = loriginal + lrefd # Update model parameters via gradient descent updateparameters(model, totalloss) Parameters: Weighting of L{refD}: Not given in the sources. It differs from Refined Depth for Geometry Supervision by relying on ground truth depth priors rather than derived refined depths from rendered outputs, and targets 3DGS primitives rather than sparse-voxel structures. Choose this when high reconstruction accuracy and local sharpness are needed for indoor scenes with available ground truth depth, and shorter training times are critical. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves local sharpness and depth consistency; lightweight; does not sacrifice efficiency; bridges efficient initialization and high-fidelity surface reconstruction. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the paper "Advancing Structured Priors for Sparse-Voxel Surface Reconstruction". It is part of a broader framework that includes a topology-aligned multi-view fusion mechanism and level-of-detail unprojection to integrate sparse octrees from different camera views into a globally consistent structure. name: Depth-Regularized Fine-Tuning
head: Regularized Fine-Tuning
body: Depth-Regularized Fine-Tuning is a per-scene optimization procedure that refines 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives using dense, multi-view consistent ground truth depth maps as geometric priors. It addresses the limitation of feed-forward generalizable 3DGS methods in reconstructing whole indoor scenes by enhancing local sharpness and depth consistency. Unlike vanilla 3DGS which relies solely on photometric and structural similarity losses, this method explicitly minimizes the discrepancy between rendered and ground truth depth, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy with significantly shorter training times. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input views with corresponding dense, multi-view consistent ground truth depth images \{D^n\}{n=1}^N and color images. The initial 3DGS primitives (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) are obtained from a feed-forward prediction phase. Outputs: Refined 3DGS primitives that preserve geometric accuracy and improve rendering quality. Data Structures: D^nr: Rendered depth map for view n, generated by differentiable rendering of the current 3DGS primitives. D^n: Ground truth depth map for view n. L{fcolor}: Photometric loss (e.g., MSE) between rendered and input color images. L{fssim}: Structural Similarity (SSIM) loss between rendered and input color images. L{fdepth}: Depth regularization loss. Parameters: \lambda1: Weight for SSIM loss in fine-tuning. Typical value: 0.2. \lambda2: Weight for depth regularization loss in fine-tuning. Typical value: 0.1. Steps: 1. Render Depth: For each view n \in \{1, \dots, N\}, render the depth map D^nr from the current 3DGS primitives using the standard differentiable rasterization pipeline. 2. Compute Depth Loss: Calculate the L1 norm difference between the rendered depth D^nr and the ground truth depth D^n for all views: L{fdepth} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N \| D^nr - D^n \|1 3. Compute Color Losses: Calculate the photometric loss L{fcolor} (typically MSE) and the SSIM loss L{fssim} between the rendered color images and the input color images. 4. Compute Total Loss: Combine the losses using the weighted formula: L{rft} = (1 - \lambda1) L{fcolor} + \lambda1 L{fssim} + \lambda2 L{fdepth} 5. Optimize: Perform gradient descent to update the 3DGS primitives (positions, scales, rotations, opacities, colors) to minimize L{rft}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthregularizedfinetuning(primitives, views, lambda1=0.2, lambda2=0.1, numiterations=100, optimizer=None): """ Refines 3DGS primitives using depth priors. Args: primitives: Current 3D Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, etc.) views: List of view dictionaries containing 'colorimage', 'depthimage', 'cameraparams' lambda1: Weight for SSIM loss lambda2: Weight for depth loss numiterations: Number of optimization steps optimizer: Optimizer for primitive parameters Returns: Refined primitives """ N = len(views) for iteration in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() lcolor = 0.0 lssim = 0.0 ldepth = 0.0 for n in range(N): view = views[n] colorgt = view['colorimage'] depthgt = view['depthimage'] camera = view['cameraparams'] # Differentiable rendering of 3DGS primitives to obtain color and depth maps colorrendered, depthrendered = renderprimitives(primitives, camera) # Compute photometric loss (MSE) lcolor += mseloss(colorrendered, colorgt) # Compute SSIM loss lssim += ssimloss(colorrendered, colorgt) # Compute depth regularization loss (L1) ldepth += l1loss(depthrendered, depthgt) # Average losses over number of views lcolor /= N lssim /= N ldepth /= N # Combine losses: Lrft = (1 - lambda1) Lfcolor + lambda1 Lfssim + lambda2 Lfdepth loss = (1 - lambda1) lcolor + lambda1 lssim + lambda2 ldepth # Backpropagate and update loss.backward() optimizer.step() return primitives def mseloss(rendered, gt): return sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered.flatten(), gt.flatten())) / len(rendered.flatten()) def l1loss(rendered, gt): return sum(abs(r - g) for r, g in zip(rendered.flatten(), gt.flatten())) / len(rendered.flatten()) def ssimloss(rendered, gt): # Standard SSIM computation return 1.0 - computessim(rendered, gt) def renderprimitives(prims, cam): # Standard differentiable alpha-blending rasterizer pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Mismatch: The method supervises the output on full resolution even if lower resolution maps are used for uninitialization, to encourage high-resolution renderings. Depth Consistency: The ground truth depth maps must be dense and multi-view consistent to serve as effective priors without harming rendering quality. This variant refers to the specific application of the depth-regularized fine-tuning step after the feed-forward 3DGS prediction phase. It leverages the efficient and geometrically accurate initialization from the feed-forward pipeline to refine the entire scene’s 3DGS primitives. It is chosen when a competitive alternative to vanilla 3DGS is needed, offering significant improvement in reconstruction accuracy within considerably shorter training time. Time Complexity: Significantly shorter training time compared to conventional per-scene optimized 3DGS approaches. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Outperforms existing generalizable 3DGS methods (e.g., pixelSplat, MVSplat, PixelGaussian) and provides a competitive alternative to vanilla 3DGS in whole-scene reconstructions, especially for indoor scenes. Strengths: Enhances rendering quality while preserving geometric accuracy; removes floaters effectively. Limitations: Relies on the availability of dense, multi-view consistent ground truth depth maps. Originated in the FreeSplat++ method, which is tailored for generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting for efficient indoor scene reconstruction. The approach was introduced to address challenges in reconstructing whole indoor scenes where previous fusion modules could not adequately remove floaters or redundancy. It builds on the feed-forward reconstruction of 3DGS primitives and adds a depth-regularized per-scene fine-tuning step to leverage geometric constraints. name: Multi-view SDS
head: BoostDream
body: Multi-view SDS is a plug-and-play regularization method that addresses the Janus problem caused by one-by-one view sampling in standard Score Distillation Sampling (SDS). Unlike single-view approaches, it stitches rendered images from four sampled views into a single 2 \times 2 composite image and computes gradients conditioned on a multi-view normal map to enforce geometric consistency across the 3D asset. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A differentiable 3D representation (NeRF, 3DGS, or DMTet), a text prompt, a diffusion model, and a set of N=4 camera viewpoints. Outputs: Optimized 3D representation parameters. Data Structures: Composite Image: A 2 \times 2 grid formed by stitching N rendered views. Multi-view Normal Map: A composite image of normal vectors corresponding to the stitched views, used to condition the gradient calculation. Steps: 1. Sample N=4 distinct camera viewpoints for the current optimization step. 2. Render the current 3D representation from each viewpoint to produce individual color images \mathbf{I}1, \dots, \mathbf{I}4 and normal maps \mathbf{N}1, \dots, \mathbf{N}4. 3. Construct a composite image \mathbf{I}{\text{multi}} by stitching \mathbf{I}1, \dots, \mathbf{I}4 into a 2 \times 2 grid. 4. Construct a composite normal map \mathbf{N}{\text{multi}} from \mathbf{N}1, \dots, \mathbf{N}4. 5. Compute the SDS gradients conditioned on \mathbf{N}{\text{multi}} using the diffusion model. 6. Backpropagate the gradients through the differentiable rendering process to update the 3D representation parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiviewsdsstep(nerfmodel, diffusionmodel, textprompt, cameras): N = len(cameras) assert N == 4, "Multi-view SDS uses 4 views." colorimgs, normalimgs = [], [] for cam in cameras: c, n = nerfmodel.render(cam) colorimgs.append(c) normalimgs.append(n) # Stitch 4 views into 2x2 grid h, w = colorimgs[0].shape[:2] compcolor = np.zeros((2h, 2w, 3), dtype=np.float32) compnormal = np.zeros((2h, 2w, 3), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(4): r, c = divmod(i, 2) compcolor[rh:(r+1)h, cw:(c+1)w] = colorimgs[i] compnormal[rh:(r+1)h, cw:(c+1)w] = normalimgs[i] # Compute SDS gradients conditioned on multi-view normal map # Standard SDS gradient: grad = w (E[epsilon0] - epsilontheta) # Conditioned on composite normal map; exact diffusion conditioning omitted as not in sources grad = diffusionmodel.computesdsgradient(compcolor, compnormal, textprompt) return grad Parameters: Number of views (N): Typically 4. Grid Layout: 2 \times 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Map Alignment: The multi-view normal map must be correctly aligned with the color images to provide valid geometric conditioning. Precision: Standard volume rendering precision and boundary handling apply as defined in the parent article. The specific implementation of Multi-view SDS that introduced the 2x2 stitching technique. It sets itself apart by explicit multi-view conditioning via normal maps. Choose it when geometric consistency across asymmetric objects is critical. Link: BoostDream. A related method that incorporates structured noise from multiple viewpoints to alleviate the Janus problem using variational 3DGS. It sets itself apart by noise injection rather than image stitching. Choose it when mitigating floaters is prioritized. Link: GaussianDiffusion. Time Complexity: Increases optimization time compared to single-view SDS due to rendering and processing N views per step. Memory Complexity: Higher memory usage due to storing intermediate renders for N views and the composite image. Strengths: Effectively reduces the Janus problem and improves geometric coherence while remaining plug-and-play with various 3D representations. Limitations: Increased computational cost relative to single-view baselines. When to use: When generating 3D assets with distinct front/back asymmetry where single-view SDS fails to maintain consistency. Multi-view SDS was proposed by BoostDream. It addresses limitations in standard SDS optimization where views are sampled one by one, leading to inconsistencies. The method leverages the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting in some implementations, replacing MipNeRF as used in DreamGaussian, to render high-resolution images with high FPS and small memory. It is part of a broader trend of improving 3D generation by incorporating multi-view supervision.
