name: CLIP Distillation for Semantic NeRFs
head: Kobayashi et al. (CLIP Distillation)
body: A method that distills knowledge from an off-the-shelf 2D feature extractor (CLIP-based) into 3D feature fields, optimized in conjunction with in-scene radiance fields to produce a NeRF model with semantic understanding. It sets itself apart from standard photometric NeRFs by enabling zero-shot segmentation from an open set of text labels or queries, and from direct supervision methods by using image features as a teacher signal rather than ground-truth labels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input images with known camera poses, an off-the-shelf CLIP-based 2D feature extractor, and a set of text queries or labels for segmentation. Outputs: A NeRF model that outputs color and semantic feature vectors for any 3D point and viewing direction. Data Structures: 3D Feature Field: A continuous function mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to semantic feature vectors. The specific network architecture and feature dimensionality are not given in the sources. Teacher Features: 2D semantic features extracted from input images using the CLIP-based feature extractor. Steps: 1. Initialize Fields: Initialize the standard radiance field and the 3D feature field. 2. Render Features: For each training view, sample points along camera rays and query the 3D feature field to obtain per-point semantic features. 3. Aggregate Features: Aggregate the per-point features along each ray using standard volume rendering to produce a rendered 2D feature map. 4. Extract Teacher Features: Extract corresponding 2D features from the input images using the off-the-shelf CLIP-based feature extractor. 5. Compute Distillation Loss: Calculate the distillation loss between the rendered 3D features and the extracted 2D teacher features. The exact loss function formulation is not given in the sources. 6. Optimize: Update the radiance field and feature field parameters jointly to minimize the distillation loss alongside standard photometric losses. 7. Inference: Render semantic feature maps for novel views and perform zero-shot segmentation by comparing the rendered features to text embeddings from the CLIP text encoder. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Feature dimension: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Teacher Signal Source: The method relies on features extracted from input training images as the teacher signal. The source does not specify a fallback mechanism if novel views are unavailable during training. Precision: Not given in the sources. The 2D Semantic Distillation Loss is a regularization term used in semantic-aware NeRF training to enhance the discrimination and semantic consistency of rendered features. It addresses the problem of weak semantic understanding in standard radiance fields by distilling knowledge from an off-the-shelf 2D feature extractor (specifically CLIP-based features from novel views) into the 3D feature field. It sets itself apart from standard color losses by operating in the semantic feature space rather than RGB space, and from direct supervision by using novel-view features as a teacher signal rather than ground-truth labels. It builds on CLIP Distillation for Semantic NeRFs. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables zero-shot segmentation from an open set of text labels or queries. Allows for scene editing via manipulating object-specific MLPs. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When semantic understanding and zero-shot segmentation are required without ground-truth semantic labels. When not: When only photometric accuracy is needed. Originated by Kobayashi et al. in May 2022. The work demonstrated that distilling CLIP-based features into 3D fields allows for semantic segmentation synthesis, instance segmentation synthesis, and scene editing. It is part of the broader effort to add semantic capabilities to NeRFs, following related works like SS-NeRF (June 2022) which employed separate encoding and decoding MLPs for semantics. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: 2D Semantic Distillation Loss
body: The 2D Semantic Distillation Loss distills aggregated 3D semantic features using novel-view 2D features as a teacher to minimize differences between them, addressing weak semantic understanding in radiance fields. It builds on CLIP Distillation for Semantic NeRFs and operates by aligning rendered features with teacher features rather than ground-truth labels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of sampled rays \mathcal{R}, the aggregated semantic features \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{sem} for each ray, and the teacher semantic features \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{novel} extracted from novel-view images. Output: A scalar loss value L{S.D}. Data Structures: \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{sem}(r): The aggregated semantic feature vector for ray r, produced by the 3D model's aggregation process. \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{novel}(r): The teacher semantic feature vector for ray r, extracted directly from novel-view images. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each ray r \in \mathcal{R}, obtain the aggregated 3D semantic feature \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{sem}(r) from the model. 2. Teacher Extraction: Extract the corresponding 2D teacher feature \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{novel}(r) from novel-view images using a ResNet-34 encoder. 3. Gradient Blocking: Apply a gradient block immediately after the ResNet-34 encoder to ensure the loss supervises the aggregation process of the Transformer modules, preventing the extractor from learning less discriminative features to minimize the loss without improving semantics. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss by summing 1 - \cos(\boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{sem}(r), \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{novel}(r)) over all rays in \mathcal{R}. Formula: The loss is defined as: L{S.D} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left[ 1 - \cos\left(\boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{sem}(r), \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{novel}(r)\right) \right] where \cos(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\|\mathbf{a}\| \|\mathbf{b}\|} is the cosine similarity between vectors \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b}, and \mathcal{R} denotes the sampled rays in a training batch. Parameters: Gradient Block: Applied immediately after the ResNet-34 encoder. Pitfalls: Cheating via Feature Degradation: Without the gradient block after the ResNet-34 encoder, the 2D feature extractor may adapt during training to produce less discriminative features that match the poorly trained 3D features, thereby minimizing the loss without improving semantic understanding. Geometry Corruption: Using L{S.D} alone can corrupt the geometry representation of the model, as the loss can be minimized by misguiding point features instead of optimizing the attention weights that define geometry. Restores semantic consistency with geometry constraints by performing per-point semantic distillation, preventing the model from misguiding features instead of optimizing attention weights. It is chosen when geometry preservation is critical alongside semantic accuracy. The loss is defined as: L{D.G} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{i=1}^{N{pts}} L{sim}(xi, \boldsymbol{f}^{sem}{i}, \boldsymbol{S}^{2D}{novel}(r)) where xi is the i-th sampled point on ray r, \boldsymbol{f}^{sem}{i} is its semantic feature, and N{pts} is the number of sampled points per ray. The similarity term L{sim} is defined as: L{sim}(xi, f1, f2) = \begin{cases} 1 - \cos(f1, f2) & \text{if } |xi - xd| < Np \\ \max(0, \cos(f1, f2)) & \text{if } |xi - xd| > Np \end{cases} where xd is the sampled point projected by ground-truth depth, and Np is a depth proximity threshold set to 2 in implementation. This formulation encourages similarity for points near the GT surface and anti-similarity for distant points, aligning semantics with geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Adds overhead proportional to the 2D feature extraction cost (ResNet-34). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significantly boosts the discrimination and semantic-aware ability of rendered features for semantic-driven tasks. Limitations: Can corrupt geometry representation if used without geometry-consistent losses. When to use: When training semantic-aware NeRFs where accurate semantic features are required and ground-truth 3D labels are unavailable. When not to use: When geometry fidelity is the sole priority and semantic understanding is not needed. The 2D Semantic Distillation Loss was introduced in the context of Generalized Perception NeRF (GP-NeRF) for context-aware 3D scene understanding, leveraging pre-trained 2D vision model priors to enrich 3D radiance fields. name: CLIP Direction Consistency
head: CLIP Direction Score, CLIP directional similarity loss, Consistency Score
body: CLIP Direction Consistency is a quantitative metric used to evaluate the temporal or spatial coherence of edits in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by comparing the semantic trajectory of changes between adjacent views. It solves the problem of verifying that an edited scene evolves smoothly relative to the original scene, ensuring that the direction of semantic change in the edited views matches the direction of change in the original views. It is distinct from the CLIP Direction Similarity metric, which measures the alignment between the text prompt and the image features; instead, this metric focuses on the consistency of the delta (change) between consecutive frames. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of rendered images from the original NeRF (I^o) and a sequence of rendered images from the edited NeRF (I^e). The sequences must consist of consecutive views (e.g., adjacent camera poses). Outputs: A scalar score representing the average cosine similarity between the change vectors of the original and edited scenes across the selected views. Data Structures: Images are treated as tensors or arrays of pixel values. CLIP embeddings are vectors in the CLIP image feature space. Steps: 1. Select View Pairs: Identify N pairs of consecutive views with indices i and i+1. 2. Encode Images: Pass the original images I^oi, I^o{i+1} and edited images I^ei, I^e{i+1} through the CLIP image encoder EI (or \mathbf{C}I) to obtain embeddings. 3. Compute Change Vectors: Calculate the difference between the embeddings of consecutive views for both the original and edited sequences. Original change: \Delta I^oi = EI(I^o{i+1}) - EI(I^oi). Edited change: \Delta I^ei = EI(I^e{i+1}) - EI(I^ei). 4. Compute Cosine Similarity: Calculate the cosine similarity between the original change vector and the edited change vector for each pair. L{direction, i} = \frac{\Delta I^oi \cdot \Delta I^ei}{\|\Delta I^oi\| \|\Delta I^ei\|} Where \cdot denotes the dot product and \|\cdot\| denotes the L2 norm. 5. Average: Compute the final score by averaging the similarity scores over the selected consecutive view pairs. \text{Score} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} L{direction, i} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def clipdirectionconsistency(originalimages, editedimages, clipencoder): """ Computes the CLIP Direction Consistency score. Args: originalimages (Tensor): Shape (N, C, H, W), consecutive original views. editedimages (Tensor): Shape (N, C, H, W), consecutive edited views. clipencoder (Module): CLIP image encoder returning embeddings. Returns: float: Average cosine similarity of change vectors. """ # Encode all frames to embeddings of shape (N, D) embo = clipencoder(originalimages) embe = clipencoder(editedimages) # Compute change vectors (deltas) between consecutive frames # deltao[i] = embo[i+1] - embo[i] for i in 0..N-2 deltao = embo[1:] - embo[:-1] deltae = embe[1:] - embe[:-1] similarities = [] for i in range(len(deltao)): do = deltao[i] de = deltae[i] # Compute L2 norms normo = torch.norm(do) norme = torch.norm(de) # Guard against zero vectors (degenerate case where no change occurred) if normo < 1e-8 or norme < 1e-8: sim = 0.0 else: dotproduct = torch.dot(do, de) sim = dotproduct / (normo norme) similarities.append(sim) if not similarities: return 0.0 finalscore = sum(similarities) / len(similarities) return finalscore Parameters: Number of views: The sources specify computing the score on six consecutive views and averaging the results. This implies 5 pairs of consecutive frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Change: If the original or edited scene does not change between two views, the delta vector is zero and the cosine similarity is undefined. The implementation must handle this by skipping the pair or assigning a neutral value. View Ordering: The views must be temporally or spatially ordered such that i and i+1 are adjacent in the camera trajectory. Random pairs will yield meaningless results. Resolution: The CLIP encoder expects specific input resolutions (e.g., 224x224). Images must be resized or cropped accordingly before encoding. A regularization strategy for text-driven NeRF stylization that controls stylization strength by combining global and local contrastive terms in CLIP space. It ensures uniform stylization across the entire scene, overcoming the directional-only limitation of standard CLIP losses and the non-uniformity of global-only approaches. It builds on CLIP Direction Consistency by adding magnitude control and local balance. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In simple settings (5 edits on face scene), ViCA-NeRF achieved a score of 0.9035 compared to Instruct-NeRF2NeRF's 0.9004. In difficult settings (10 edits on real-world scenes), ViCA-NeRF achieved 0.6498 compared to Instruct-NeRF2NeRF's 0.5161. Higher scores indicate better consistency between the direction of change in the original and edited scenes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a semantic measure of edit consistency that correlates with human perception of smoothness. Limitations: It is a post-hoc evaluation metric, not a loss function used during training. When to Use: Use for evaluating the quality of NeRF editing methods, specifically when assessing the smoothness and coherence of semantic changes across views. The CLIP Direction Consistency metric was introduced in the context of evaluating neural radiance field editing methods. It appears in ViCA-NeRF and Blended-NeRF for evaluation purposes. name: Global-Local Contrastive Learning
head: Global-Local Contrastive Loss Strategy, Glocal Contrastive Loss
body: Global-Local Contrastive Learning is a regularization strategy for text-driven NeRF stylization that controls stylization strength by combining global and local contrastive terms in CLIP space. It ensures uniform stylization across the entire scene, overcoming the directional-only limitation of standard CLIP losses and the non-uniformity of global-only approaches. It builds on CLIP Direction Consistency by adding magnitude control and local balance. Inputs: Rendered image I{tgt}, target text prompt t{tgt}, set of negative text prompts \mathcal{T}{neg}, patch size p. Outputs: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{glocal}. Data Structures: E{img}(\cdot): CLIP image encoder. E{text}(\cdot): CLIP text encoder. \mathcal{P}: Set of non-overlapping patches extracted from I{tgt}, each of size p \times p. Steps: 1. Global Contrastive Loss (\mathcal{L}{gc}): Compute global image embedding: v = E{img}(I{tgt}). Compute target text embedding: v^+ = E{text}(t{tgt}). Sample N negative text prompts from \mathcal{T}{neg} and compute their embeddings: v^-i = E{text}(t^-i) for i=1 \dots N. Calculate \mathcal{L}{gc} using the InfoNCE-like formula: \mathcal{L}{gc} = -\log \frac{\exp(v \cdot v^+ / \tau)}{\exp(v \cdot v^+ / \tau) + \sum{i=1}^{N} \exp(v \cdot v^-i / \tau)} where \cdot denotes dot product and \tau is the temperature parameter. 2. Local Contrastive Loss (\mathcal{L}{lc}): Extract patches \{Pj\} from I{tgt} using patch size p. For each patch Pj: Compute patch embedding: vj = E{img}(Pj). Compute target text embedding: v^+ = E{text}(t{tgt}). Use the same negative text embeddings v^-i as in the global loss. Compute local loss for patch j: \mathcal{L}{lc}^{(j)} = -\log \frac{\exp(vj \cdot v^+ / \tau)}{\exp(vj \cdot v^+ / \tau) + \sum{i=1}^{N} \exp(vj \cdot v^-i / \tau)}. Aggregate local loss: \mathcal{L}{lc} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|} \sum{j} \mathcal{L}{lc}^{(j)}. 3. Combine: Total loss: \mathcal{L}{glocal} = \mathcal{L}{gc} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{lc}, where \lambda is a weighting factor. Parameters: Temperature \tau = 0.07. Patch size p = \frac{1}{10} \times \text{original image dimension} (both width and height). Number of negative samples N \approx 200 (collected from external sources like Pinterest). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Global-only failure: Using only \mathcal{L}{gc} leads to excessive stylization on parts with distinguishable features and insufficient stylization elsewhere, as CLIP focuses on local distinct features. Local-only failure: Using only \mathcal{L}{lc} may produce hallucinated attributes (e.g., extra eyes or ears) because local patches lack sufficient semantic context. Regularizes latent codes for 3D content invariance across viewpoints, building on this method by targeting latent representation stability rather than just stylization uniformity. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot |\mathcal{P}|) per iteration, where N is the number of negative samples and |\mathcal{P}| is the number of patches. High due to multiple forward passes through CLIP encoders. Memory Complexity: Stores embeddings for N negatives and all patches. Strengths: Ensures uniform stylization magnitude and distribution across the scene. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple CLIP evaluations. When to use: Text-driven NeRF stylization requiring uniform style application. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in "NeRF-Art: Text-Driven Neural Radiance Fields Stylization" (2023). Developed to address limitations of directional CLIP losses in preserving stylization strength and uniformity. Inspired by PatchNCE loss [Park et al. 2020] for local attention. NeRF-Art: Text-Driven Neural Radiance Fields Stylization, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2023.3283400, fetched 2026-10-26

name: View-invariant Contrastive Loss
head: Contrastive Learning Framework, Contrastive Loss, Latent Contrastive Loss
body: This method regularizes the latent code of a generative NeRF to ensure it reflects 3D content variations without depending on 2D viewpoints, effectively disentangling 3D edits from camera views. It prevents optimization instability caused by latent codes that vary violently when input images are similar in appearance but differ in viewpoint. Inputs: N: Number of input views. M: Number of edited styles/images per view. zi^j: Edit code (latent vector) extracted from the i-th input view's j-th edited image Si^j. \mathcal{N}{\theta}: The translated NeRF conditioned on the edit code. \mathcal{E}: Encoder used to extract edit codes from images. Outputs: \mathcal{L}{\textrm {contr}}: The scalar contrastive loss value. Data Structures: Edit codes are vectors in \mathbb{R}^{64}. Images are 2D tensors. Steps: 1. Render Multi-View Images: Given edit code zi^j from input view i at edited image Si^j, render multi-view images \{Cj^l\}{l=0}^{N-1} using the translated NeRF conditioned on zi^j. 2. Extract Positive Codes: Extract edit codes \{zj^l\}{l=0}^{N-1} from \{Cj^l\}{l=0}^{N-1} using the encoder. 3. Extract Negative Codes: Extract edit codes \{zi^k\}{k=0}^{M-1} from \{Si^k\}{k=0}^{M-1} where k \neq j. 4. Compute Loss: Calculate the contrastive loss \mathcal{L}{\textrm {contr}} by minimizing the distance between the original code zi^j and the rendered codes \{zj^l\}, while maximizing the distance between zi^j and the alternative edit codes \{zi^k\}. Formula: The total contrastive loss is the sum of an attraction term (\mathcal{L}{\textrm {contr}}^{\textrm {att}}) and a repulsion term (\mathcal{L}{\textrm {contr}}^{\textrm {rep}}): \mathcal {L}{\textrm {contr}} = \mathcal {L}{\textrm {contr}}^{\textrm {att}} + \mathcal {L}{\textrm {contr}}^{\textrm {rep}} = \sum {l=0}^{N-1}||{\mathbf {z}}^j{i}-{\mathbf {z}}^j{l}||2^2 + \sum {k=0}^{M-1}\max(0,\alpha -||{\mathbf {z}}^j{i}-{\mathbf {z}}{i}^k||2^2) Where: ||\cdot||2^2 is the squared Euclidean distance. \alpha is the margin hyperparameter. k \neq j. Parameters: \alpha (Margin): A hyperparameter that encourages the difference in features between distinct edits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extracteditcode(image): """Placeholder for the encoder E that maps an image to a 64-dimensional vector.""" # In practice, this is the trained encoder network. return [0.0] 64 def viewinvariantcontrastiveloss(zij, renderedimages, editedimagessameview, alpha): """ Computes the view-invariant contrastive loss. Args: zij: List of 64 floats, the edit code from the i-th view, j-th edit. renderedimages: List of N images, rendered from translated NeRF conditioned on zij. editedimagessameview: List of M images, other edited images for the i-th view. alpha: Float, margin for the repulsion term. Returns: loss: Float, the computed loss value. """ # Step 2: Extract edit codes from rendered images (positives) zjllist = [extracteditcode(img) for img in renderedimages] # Step 3: Extract edit codes from other edited images of the same view (negatives) ziklist = [extracteditcode(img) for img in editedimagessameview] # Step 4a: Attraction term - minimize distance to same-edit, different-view codes attractionloss = 0.0 for zjl in zjllist: dist = sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(zij, zjl)) attractionloss += dist # Step 4b: Repulsion term - maximize distance to different-edit, same-view codes repulsionloss = 0.0 for zik in ziklist: dist = sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(zij, zik)) # hinge loss: max(0, alpha - dist) repulsionloss += max(0.0, alpha - dist) return attractionloss + repulsionloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Encoder Consistency: The encoder \mathcal{E} must be consistent across the original edited images and the rendered images to ensure the latent space comparison is valid. Margin Selection: If \alpha is too small, the repulsion term may vanish; if too large, it may dominate the attraction term, leading to unstable training. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is used in the GenN2N framework for universal NeRF editing tasks including text-driven editing, colorization, super-resolution, and inpainting. It ensures multi-view consistency of the edited NeRF. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Disentangles 3D content variations from camera viewpoints, preventing instability when input images are similar in appearance but different in viewpoints. Enables high-quality, multi-view consistent 3D scene generation from 2D edits. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D image-to-image translation and the encoder. When to use it: Use when training a generative NeRF that needs to support diverse editing tasks while maintaining multi-view consistency. Origin: Introduced in "GenN2N: Generative NeRF2NeRF Translation". The paper proposes a 3D VAE-GAN framework that incorporates a differentiable volume renderer to connect 3D content creation with 2D GAN losses. History and Development: The method addresses the issue that edit codes obtained from a Latent Distill Module may contain viewpoint-related effects, which causes instability in the translated NeRF. It is part of a larger set of four loss functions used to optimize GenN2N, including KL loss, reconstruction loss, and adversarial loss. Where it is used: Used in the GenN2N framework for NeRF-to-NeRF translation. GenN2N: Generative NeRF2NeRF Translation, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52733.2024.00488, fetched 2026-10-29

name: CLIP Similarity Loss
head: CLIP Loss, Image-Text CLIP Loss
body: A loss function that quantifies the similarity between a rendered image I and a text prompt T in the CLIP embedding space. Inputs and outputs: Input: Rendered image I and text prompt T. Output: Scalar loss value L{CLIP}. Data structures: E{img}: Pre-trained CLIP image encoder. E{txt}: Pre-trained CLIP text encoder. Embeddings: Feature vectors in \mathbb{R}^d output by the encoders. Steps: 1. Encode the rendered image I using E{img}. 2. Encode the text prompt T using E{txt}. 3. Compute the cosine similarity between the resulting feature vectors. 4. Compute the loss as one minus the similarity. Formula: L{CLIP}(I, T) = 1 - \text{sim}(E{img}(I), E{txt}(T)) Where: E{img} and E{txt} are the pre-trained CLIP image and text encoders, respectively. \text{sim}(A, B) is the cosine similarity between two feature vectors A and B, defined as \text{sim}(A, B) = \frac{A \cdot B}{\|A\| \|B\|}. I is the rendered image. T is the text prompt. Parameters: CLIP model variant: Not given in the sources. Image preprocessing: Standard CLIP normalization (resize to 224x224, normalize). Edge cases and pitfalls: Resolution sensitivity: CLIP encoders expect fixed input sizes; resizing rendered images may introduce artifacts. Semantic ambiguity: Text prompts may be ambiguous, leading to suboptimal semantic alignments. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clipsimilarityloss(renderedimage: Tensor, textprompt: str, clipimgencoder: Module, cliptxtencoder: Module) -> Tensor: """ Compute CLIP similarity loss between a rendered image and a text prompt. Args: renderedimage: Tensor of shape (C, H, W) or (B, C, H, W), normalized to [-1, 1]. textprompt: String text prompt. clipimgencoder: Pre-trained CLIP image encoder. cliptxtencoder: Pre-trained CLIP text encoder. Returns: Scalar loss tensor. """ # Encode image and text imgembedding = clipimgencoder(renderedimage) txtembedding = cliptxtencoder(textprompt) # Normalize embeddings to unit length for cosine similarity imgembedding = imgembedding / imgembedding.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) txtembedding = txtembedding / txtembedding.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Compute cosine similarity similarity = (imgembedding txtembedding).sum(dim=-1) # Compute loss as one minus similarity loss = 1.0 - similarity return loss.mean() Uses CLIP semantic distance to control the appearance of a 3D scene via text prompts while maintaining multi-view consistency. It builds on CLIP Similarity Loss by introducing appearance embeddings and specific network architecture modifications to ProLiF. Not given in the sources. Originated from the CLIP model, which trains image and text encoders using contrastive learning. It was adapted for 3D editing in methods like CLIP-NeRF, which introduced disentangled conditional NeRFs for text-guided editing. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Text-guided Scene Style Editing
head: CLIP Loss for Text-Guided Style Editing, CLIP loss training
body: Text-guided scene style editing uses CLIP semantic distance to control the appearance of a 3D scene via text prompts while maintaining multi-view consistency. Unlike previous style editing methods that target single images, this method edits the entire scene, producing multi-view consistent images of the same style. It builds on CLIP Similarity Loss by introducing appearance embeddings and specific network architecture modifications to ProLiF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference images of the scene, text prompts describing the desired style, and a pre-trained CLIP model. Outputs: Rendered images with the edited style, maintaining the original scene structure. Data Structures: Appearance Embeddings: Feature codes concatenated to intermediate features of the ProLiF network. Two distinct appearance embeddings are used per training step: one for L{render} and one for L{CLIP}. ProLiF Network: A progressively-connected light field network. The architecture is modified for style editing to include appearance embeddings. Parameters: \lambda{CLIP}: Weight for the CLIP loss, set to 0.05. Pixel Sampling: 16,384 pixels for L{render}. A 224 \times 224 patch for L{CLIP}. 4,096 extra pixels for L{reg}. Steps: 1. Network Forward Pass: Generate rendered images using the ProLiF network with appearance embeddings concatenated to intermediate features. 2. Loss Calculation: Compute L{render} as the MSE loss between rendered pixels and reference image pixels using one appearance embedding. Compute L{CLIP} using a 224 \times 224 patch and a second, different appearance embedding. Compute L{reg} using 4,096 extra pixels. 3. Stop-Gradient Application: When calculating L{CLIP}, apply stop-gradient operators to the output densities and a hidden feature of the appearance network. This regularizes the rendered results to preserve the original intrinsic structure of the scene. 4. Total Loss: Combine losses: L = L{render} + L{reg} + \lambda{CLIP} L{CLIP}. Formulas: Total Loss: L = L{render} + L{reg} + \lambda{CLIP} L{CLIP} CLIP Loss: L{CLIP} = 1 - \frac{f{image} \cdot f{text}}{\|f{image}\| \cdot \|f{text}\|} Where f{image} and f{text} are the extracted features of the rendered image patch and the given text respectively by the CLIP model. Pitfalls: L{CLIP} and L{render} must be calculated from two different appearance embeddings to avoid conflicting optimization signals. The method is built on a near-far-plane setting and cannot be used for 360° scenes. Training is time-consuming compared to inference. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestyleeditingloss(renderedimage, referenceimage, textprompt, appearanceembedding1, appearanceembedding2, lambdaclip=0.05): # 1. Sample pixels for Lrender (16384 pixels) renderpixels = randomsample(renderedimage, count=16384) refpixels = randomsample(referenceimage, count=16384) lrender = meansquarederror(renderpixels, refpixels) # 2. Sample patch for Lclip (224x224) clippatch = extractpatch(renderedimage, size=(224, 224)) # 3. Get CLIP features fimage = clipimageencoder(clippatch) ftext = cliptextencoder(textprompt) # 4. Compute CLIP loss cosinesim = dotproduct(fimage, ftext) / (norm(fimage) norm(ftext)) lclip = 1.0 - cosinesim # 5. Sample pixels for Lreg (extra 4096 pixels) regpixels = randomsample(renderedimage, count=4096, offset=16384) lreg = computeregularizationloss(regpixels) # Implementation details not specified in source # 6. Total loss totalloss = lrender + lreg + lambdaclip lclip # Note: Stop-gradient operators are applied to output densities and hidden appearance features # when calculating Lclip in the actual backpropagation graph. return totalloss def randomsample(tensor, count, offset=0): return tensor.flatten()[offset:offset+count] def meansquarederror(a, b): return sum((x - y) 2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) / len(a) def extractpatch(tensor, size): return tensor[:size[0],:size[1]] def clipimageencoder(image): # Standard CLIP image encoder return [0.0] 512 def cliptextencoder(text): # Standard CLIP text encoder return [0.0] 512 def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def norm(v): return sum(x 2 for x in v) 0.5 def computeregularizationloss(pixels): # Implementation details not specified in source return 0.0 Time Complexity: Training is time-consuming, requiring network optimization for each scene. Inference is fast. Memory Complexity: Model size is 11.0MB for ProLiF, compared to 5.0MB for NeuLF. Performance: Achieves faster rendering in inference stage. Quantitative comparisons show better rendering quality than NeuLF on the Shiny Object dataset. Strengths: Produces multi-view consistent images of the same style for the whole scene. Limitations: Cannot be used for 360° scenes due to near-far-plane setting. The method was introduced in the paper "Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis". It extends the ProLiF architecture to support text-guided style editing using CLIP loss. Previous style editing methods targeted single images, whereas this approach targets the entire 3D scene. Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2207.04465, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeRF-Det Training Objectives
head: Joint NeRF-Detection Training Loss, Loss Functions for NeRF Branch, Photo-metric and Depth Loss for NeRF-Det
body: NeRF-Det Training Objectives define the loss functions used to jointly optimize a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) branch and a 3D object detection branch in a single end-to-end framework. The method solves the problem of ambiguous volumetric representations in multi-view 3D object detection by leveraging the NeRF branch to learn a geometry-aware opacity field, which provides superior scene geometry modeling compared to explicit depth estimation or cost volumes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like KNN-NeRF or Progressive and Dynamic Scene Growth by explicitly coupling the photometric/depth supervision of the radiance field with the detection head's classification and localization losses, ensuring that better NeRF optimization directly improves detection results. The method jointly trains the detection and NeRF branches end-to-end. No per-scene optimization is performed for the NeRF branch at test time; the network is generalizable to unseen scenes. Inputs: Multi-view RGB images. Ground truth 3D bounding boxes for the detection branch. Optional ground truth depth maps for the NeRF branch (not required at inference). Outputs: Detection predictions (categories, 3D locations, centerness). Rendered RGB colors \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and expected depth D(\mathbf{r}) for rays \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: The detection branch follows the ImVoxelNet architecture. It uses a voxel feature grid and a detection head with three convolutional layers to predict: 1. Object categories (27 location candidates per object). 2. 3D locations (localization). 3. Centerness scores. Loss Formulas: The total loss L is the sum of detection losses and NeRF branch losses: L = L{cls} + L{cntr} + L{loc} + Lc + Ld Where: L{cls}: Focal loss for classification. L{cntr}: Centerness loss. L{loc}: Localization loss. Lc: Photo-metric loss for the NeRF branch: Lc = ||\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}{gt}(\mathbf{r})||^2 where \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is the rendered color and \hat{C}{gt}(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth color for ray \mathbf{r}. Ld: Optional depth supervision loss (used only if depth ground truth is available during training): Ld = ||D(\mathbf{r}) - D{gt}(\mathbf{r})|| where D(\mathbf{r}) is the expected depth computed via volume rendering integration (Eq. 5 in) and D{gt}(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mean(x): return sum(x) / len(x) def computenerfdetloss(renderedcolor, rendereddepth, gtcolor, gtdepth, clslogits, bboxpred, centerness, gtboxes): """ Computes the joint loss for NeRF-Det. """ # Detection losses follow ImVoxelNet; exact formulations are not given in the sources. lcls = 0.0 # Focal loss for classification lcntr = 0.0 # Centerness loss lloc = 0.0 # Localization loss # NeRF photo-metric loss (MSE) lc = mean((renderedcolor - gtcolor) 2) # NeRF depth supervision loss (L1) if gtdepth is not None: ld = mean(abs(rendereddepth - gtdepth)) else: ld = 0.0 # Total Loss totalloss = lcls + lcntr + lloc + lc + ld return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Availability: Depth supervision is optional. If depth ground truth is not available, Ld is omitted. The method remains effective without it, though performance is slightly lower than when depth is used. Loss Balance: The ablation study indicates that photo-metric loss alone provides sufficient geometry cues, performing close to depth supervision alone. However, combining both yields the best results. No NeRF Optimization at Test Time: The NeRF branch is not optimized per scene during inference. The model relies on the learned generalizable representation. StegaNeRF is a training procedure that embeds invisible, recoverable information (such as images or identity markers) into a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by jointly optimizing the radiance field and a detector network. It differs from standard NeRF training by adding steganographic loss terms that force the rendered images to carry hidden data while maintaining photometric fidelity to the original scene. It builds on NeRF-Det Training Objectives. A method to mitigate volume representation ambiguity by learning an opacity field using NeRF, which estimates scene geometry more effectively than explicit depth estimation or cost volumes. Depth supervision is used as a loss term to improve the NeRF branch's geometry modeling. After using depth supervision, NeRF-Det achieves an improvement of +3.7 mAP@.50. Using NeRF to model scene geometry improves performance by +3.6 mAP@.25 and +2.5 mAP@.50 compared to the baseline, which is more effective than using predicted depth or cost volume. Performance: Using NeRF to model scene geometry improves performance by +3.6 mAP@.25 and +2.5 mAP@.50 compared to the baseline. With depth supervision, it achieves +3.7 mAP@.50. Loss Impact: With only photo-metric loss, performance is close to purely using depth supervision in terms of mAP@.50. Using both photo-metric loss and depth loss improves performance further. When neither is used, performance falls back to that of a cost-volume based method, dropping by 1.2 mAP@.25 and 0.5 mAP@.50. Inference: The method does not require per-scene optimization at test time, making it efficient for inference on unseen scenes. Comparison: The joint NeRF-and-Det paradigm is more effective than NeRF-then-Det methods like NeRF-RPN. NeRF-Det was introduced to address the ambiguity of volume representations in multi-view 3D object detection. It leverages the simplicity and effectiveness of NeRF-style rendering to learn an opacity field for scene geometry, which is more effective than explicit depth estimation or cost volumes. The method is implemented based on MMDetection3D and is the first to implement NeRF in this framework. name: StegaNeRF Training Algorithm
head: StegaNeRF Training Loop
body: StegaNeRF is a training procedure that embeds invisible, recoverable information (such as images or text) into a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by jointly optimizing the radiance field and a detector network. It solves the problem of copyright protection and attribution in 3D content by allowing a hidden signal to be decoded from rendered views without degrading visual quality. Unlike standard NeRF training which only minimizes photometric error, StegaNeRF introduces steganographic losses to enforce the presence of a specific hidden signal, distinguishing it from NeRF-Det Training Objectives by providing the specific optimization loop and loss combination required to achieve this embedding. Inputs: Training images \{Yi\} with corresponding camera poses \{Pi\}. Hidden information I to be embedded (e.g., an image). Initial NeRF model parameters \theta0 (after pre-training). Detector network parameters \psi. Learning rates \eta = [\eta0, \eta1] for the NeRF and detector respectively. Loss weights \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3. Outputs: Steganographic NeRF model \theta. Detector network F\psi. Data Structures: NeRF \theta: Standard MLP-based radiance field representation. Detector F\psi: A network that takes a rendered view x and the classifier output F{\psic}(x) as input, defined as F\psi(x) = F\psi(x, F{\psic}(x)). Classifier F{\psic}: A sub-network or branch used to classify the presence of the hidden signal. Importance Mask m: A scalar mask computed per pixel to guide gradient flow. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF model \theta0 and the detector network F\psi. 2. Pre-training: Optimize \theta0 on the training images \{Yi\} with poses \{Pi\} using standard NeRF training (minimizing photometric loss only) to obtain a high-quality initial model. 3. Mask Computation: Compute the importance mask m for \theta0 using Equation (3): w = \frac{|\theta0|^\alpha}{\sum |\theta0|^\alpha}, \quad m = w where \alpha = 3. This mask highlights regions with significant radiance contributions. 4. Optimization Loop: For each training iteration t: a. Sampling: Randomly sample a training pose Pi. b. Rendering: Render the current NeRF view \theta(Pi). c. Steganographic Losses: Compute the losses defined in Equations (1) and (2): L{cdec}: Classifier loss. L{dec}^+: Positive detection loss (when the hidden signal is present). L{dec}^-: Negative detection loss (when the hidden signal is absent). d. Photometric Loss: Compute the standard reconstruction loss L{rgb} using Equation (4): L{rgb} = \|\theta(Pi) - Yi\| where Yi is the ground truth training image. e. Total Loss: Combine the losses as in Equation (5): L = \lambda0 L{cdec} + \lambda1 L{dec}^+ + \lambda2 L{dec}^- + \lambda3 L{rgb} f. Update Detector: Update detector parameters \psi using gradient descent: \psi \leftarrow \psi - \eta1 \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \psi} g. Update NeRF: Update NeRF parameters \theta using the masked gradient: \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta0 \cdot \left( m \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainsteganerf(images, poses, hiddeninfo, eta0, eta1, lam0, lam1, lam2, lam3, alpha=3, pretrainepochs=1000, jointepochs=5000): theta = initializenerf() Fpsi = initializedetector() # Step 2: Pre-training for epoch in range(pretrainepochs): for i in range(len(images)): render = theta(poses[i]) loss = Lrgb(render, images[i]) theta.update(loss, eta0) # Step 3: Mask Computation w = abs(theta) alpha / sum(abs(theta) alpha) m = w # Step 4: Joint Optimization Loop for t in range(jointepochs): i = random.randint(0, len(images) - 1) P = poses[i] Y = images[i] render = theta(P) # Step 4c: Steganographic Losses (Eq 1, 2) Lcdec = computeclassifierloss(render, hiddeninfo) Lplusdec = computepositivedetectionloss(render, hiddeninfo) Ldec = computenegativedetectionloss(render, hiddeninfo) # Step 4d: Photometric Loss (Eq 4) Lrgb = norm(render - Y) # Step 4e: Total Loss (Eq 5) L = lam0 Lcdec + lam1 Lplusdec + lam2 Ldec + lam3 Lrgb # Step 4f: Update Detector Fpsi.update(grad(L, Fpsi), eta1) # Step 4g: Update NeRF theta.update(grad(L, theta) m, eta0) return theta, Fpsi Parameters: \alpha = 3 for the importance mask calculation. \eta = [\eta0, \eta1] are the learning rates for the NeRF and detector, respectively. \lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are the loss weights. Specific values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-Scene Scaling: When handling multiple scenes, the data amount increases, requiring an increase in training epochs until convergence. Per-Scene Fitting: Multi-scene training may result in noticeable performance drops compared to single-scene training due to the inherent requirement of per-scene fitting in the NeRF framework. Modality Extension: The framework can embed modalities other than images (e.g., strings, text, audio) by modifying the detector architecture to have a 1D prediction branch. Multi-Identity Embedding identifies contributing users in collaborative NeRF training by embedding customized hidden information about specific clusters of training views. It solves scalable attribution in multi-user scenarios by allowing a single NeRF model to hide distinct identities for different spatial regions without requiring model retraining for each new watermark. Unlike prior approaches that embed only a single global watermark, this method isolates identity information to specific clusters of anchor views, maintaining high visual quality by preventing false positives for unmarked identities. Choose this variant when attributing contributions from multiple distinct users in a shared cultural landmark reconstruction pipeline. See Multi-Identity Embedding. This setting extends the StegaNeRF scheme to embed information within multiple scenes simultaneously. It operates in two sub-settings: 1. One-for-All: Embeds a common hidden image across multiple scenes using a single detector F\psi and classifier F{\psic}. 2. One-for-One: Embeds scene-specific hidden images across multiple scenes using a single detector F\psi and classifier F{\psic}. In both cases, the difference lies in the number of hidden images the detector needs to identify and recover. The training procedure samples one scene for every training epoch. Due to the increased data volume, training epochs are increased until convergence. Choose this setting when protecting multiple distinct 3D assets with a unified detection pipeline. Complexity: The method adds the computational cost of the detector network F\psi and classifier F{\psic} to the standard NeRF rendering pipeline. Performance: Multi-scene settings show a noticeable performance drop compared to single-scene training, attributed to the inherent requirement of per-scene fitting in NeRF frameworks. Strengths: Allows for copyright protection and attribution. Can embed various modalities (images, text, audio). Limitations: Multi-scene training requires more epochs and may suffer from quality degradation compared to single-scene training. StegaNeRF was introduced in the paper "StegaNeRF: Embedding Invisible Information within Neural Radiance Fields". The method builds on the concept of differentiable volume rendering and extends it with steganographic objectives to hide information within the radiance field parameters. It is applicable to scenarios such as protecting cultural landmark reconstructions formed by community contributions. name: Multi-Identity Embedding
body: Multi-Identity Embedding is a method for identifying contributing users in collaborative Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training by embedding customized hidden information about specific clusters of training views. It solves the problem of scalable attribution in multi-user scenarios by allowing a single NeRF model to hide distinct identities for different spatial regions without requiring model retraining for each new watermark. Unlike prior approaches that embed only a single global watermark, this method assigns identity information to specific clusters of anchor views, preventing false positives for unmarked identities. It builds on StegaNeRF Training Algorithm. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A collection of user-uploaded training images with associated camera poses. Output: A trained NeRF model with a modified classifier network capable of recovering specific contributor identities conditioned on the rendering viewpoint. Data Structures: Classifier Network (F{\phic}): A neural network component that outputs a probability distribution over M+1 classes: M classes corresponding to specific contributor clusters, and one additional class for "unmarked" identities. Steps: 1. Anchor Selection: Select M anchor views with distinct viewing positions from the training set. 2. Cluster Formation: For each anchor view, find the K nearest neighbor views based on viewing position to form a cluster. Each cluster is assumed to share a common contributor identity. 3. Network Modification: Modify the classifier network F{\phic} to output M-class cluster predictions plus one class for identities outside the M clusters. 4. Loss Computation for Unmarked Views: For poses outside the M clusters, compute the decoding loss L{dec} and the reconstruction loss L^{-dec} to ensure no information is recovered for unmarked identities, thereby preventing false positives. Formulas: L{dec}: Classification loss applied to unmarked poses to force the classifier to predict the "unmarked" class. L^{-dec}: Reconstruction loss applied to unmarked poses to ensure no hidden identity information is recoverable. Parameters: M: Number of anchor views/clusters. Typical value: 3. K: Number of nearest neighbours per anchor. Typical value: 20. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def euclideandistance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def multiidentityembedding(trainingviews, M=3, K=20): # Step 1: Select M anchor views with different viewing positions # Sources specify random selection from the training set anchors = random.sample(trainingviews, M) # Step 2: Find K nearest neighbour views to each anchor to form clusters clusters = [] for anchor in anchors: distances = [euclideandistance(anchor['pose'], view['pose']) for view in trainingviews] sortedindices = sorted(range(len(distances)), key=lambda i: distances[i]) neighbors = [trainingviews[i] for i in sortedindices[:K]] clusters.append(neighbors) # Step 3: Modify classifier network Fphic to output M+1 classes # M classes for clusters, 1 class for unmarked identities # Standard neural network classification head implementation classifier = ClassifierNetwork(numoutputclasses=M + 1) # Step 4: Compute losses for unmarked views to prevent false positives def computelosses(batch): totalloss = 0.0 unmarkedviews = [] for view in batch: ismarked = any(view in cluster for cluster in clusters) if not ismarked: unmarkedviews.append(view) if unmarkedviews: # Ldec ensures the classifier predicts the 'unmarked' class correctly # Standard categorical cross-entropy computation lossdec = crossentropy(classifier(unmarkedviews), targetclass=M) # L^-dec ensures no hidden information is recoverable for unmarked views # Standard reconstruction loss computation lossminusdec = reconstructionloss(classifier(unmarkedviews), target=None) totalloss += lossdec + lossminusdec return totalloss return classifier, computelosses A 3D watermarking method that embeds multiple uniquely keyed watermarks within images rendered by a single NeRF model, specifically extending the TensoRF architecture. It solves the problem of scalable, robust digital watermarking in 3D scenes by allowing distinct messages to be identified by unique integer IDs at rendering time, without requiring model retraining for each new watermark. Unlike prior approaches that embed only a single watermark, MultiNeRF accommodates multiple distinct messages as an additional model input, maintaining high visual quality by isolating watermark features in a dedicated grid rather than entangling them with scene appearance. Choose it when scalable multi-message watermarking is required without retraining. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated on the NeRF-W dataset using a network backbone similar to NeRFW. Qualitative results show successful recovery of User A, User B, and User C identities within their respective clusters, with low recovery scores for unmarked identities (e.g., 0.2368 for User A's identity in an unmarked region). Strengths: Allows scalable, robust digital watermarking in 3D scenes by accommodating multiple distinct messages as an additional model input. Limitations: Requires careful selection of anchor views and nearest neighbours to ensure cluster separation. When to use: When identifying contributing users in collaborative NeRF projects is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Multi-Identity Embedding was introduced in the paper "StegaNeRF: Embedding Invisible Information within Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the scenario where a collection of user-uploaded training images is used to generate a NeRF, and it is meaningful to identify the contributing users in the rendered output. The method extends the StegaNeRF framework to handle multiple identities simultaneously. name: MultiNeRF
head: MultiNeRF-Noised
body: MultiNeRF is a 3D watermarking method that embeds multiple uniquely keyed watermarks within images rendered by a single Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model, specifically extending the TensoRF architecture. It solves the problem of scalable, robust digital watermarking in 3D scenes by allowing distinct messages to be identified by unique integer IDs at rendering time, without requiring model retraining for each new watermark. Unlike prior approaches that embed only a single watermark, MultiNeRF accommodates multiple distinct messages as an additional model input, maintaining high visual quality by isolating watermark features in a dedicated grid rather than entangling them with scene appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D position x, view direction d, and a watermark integer ID I(n) corresponding to a distinct message M(n). Outputs: Rendered image color C and decoded message m'n (during training). Data Structures: The model extends TensoRF's decomposition into three explicit 3D grids: 1. Geometry Grid (A\sigma): Stores density features. Layout: \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K}. 2. Appearance Grid (Ac): Stores appearance features. Layout: \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K \times P}. 3. Watermark Grid (Aw): Stores watermark-specific features. Layout: \mathbb{R}^{I \times J \times K \times Cw}, where Cw is the number of watermark feature channels. The spatial resolution (I \times J \times K) is identical to the geometry and appearance grids. Parameters: Embedding Dimension: The learnable embedding layer maps integer IDs to a 16-dimensional message vector en. Grid Resolution: I \times J \times K for all three grids. Numbered Steps: 1. Input Embedding: Map the integer ID I(n) to a 16-dimensional message vector en using a learnable small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) Emb(): en = Emb(I(n)) 2. Modulation Parameter Generation: Pass the embedding en through a learnable linear layer Mod() to output scale \gamman and shift \betan parameters: [\gamman, \betan] = Mod(en) 3. Feature Sampling: Sample the watermark features w(x) from the watermark grid Aw at position x: w(x) = Aw(x) 4. Feature Modulation: Apply the Hadamard product to scale and shift the sampled watermark features w(x) to produce modulated features w'(x) specific to ID I(n): w'(x) = \gamman \odot w(x) + \betan where \odot is the element-wise (Hadamard) product. 5. Color Decoding: Pass the appearance grid features Gc(x) (sampled from Ac), the modulated watermark features w'(x), and the view direction d to the color decoding function S (an MLP) to compute the final watermark color \tilde{c}(x): \tilde{c}(x) = S(Gc(x), w'(x), d) 6. Volume Rendering: Perform differentiable volume rendering using the computed density \sigma (from A\sigma) and color \tilde{c}(x) along rays. For a ray passing through the scene, sampling Q points xq, the final pixel color C is computed as: C = \sum{q=1}^{Q} \tauq (1 - \exp(-\sigmaq \Deltaq)) \tilde{c}q where \sigmaq and \tilde{c}q are the density and color of the sampled point xq, \Deltaq is the step size along the ray, and \tauq is the transmittance: \tauq = \exp \left( -\sum{p=1}^{q-1} \sigmap \Deltap \right) 7. Training Augmentation (Differentiable): To promote robustness, apply differentiable noise sources and image augmentations to the fully rendered image \tilde{I} before passing it to the watermark decoder. The set of augmentations \mathcal{A} includes brightness, contrast, color jiggle, Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, hue, posterize, RGB shift, saturation, median blur, box blur, motion blur, sharpness, and differentiable JPEG compression. A random pair of augmentations is applied: \hat{I} = \mathcal{A}(\tilde{I}) 8. Watermark Extraction (Training Phase 1): Freeze the watermark decoder D. Generate a random watermark ID I(n) with ground truth message mn. Render full-resolution image I. Apply a level 2 Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) decomposition to I. Use the LL2 sub-band (denoted I{LL2}) as it retains the majority of energy and broad structural features. Pass I{LL2} to decoder D to obtain decoded message m'n. Calculate Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) loss between mn and m'n: L{secret} = BCE(mn, m'n) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MultiNeRF: def init(self, gridres, appearancechannels, watermarkchannels): """ Initialize MultiNeRF extending TensoRF.:param gridres: Tuple (I, J, K) for grid dimensions.:param appearancechannels: P, number of appearance feature channels.:param watermarkchannels: Cw, number of watermark feature channels. """ super().init() # TensoRF Grids self.Asigma = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(gridres)) # Geometry grid self.Ac = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(gridres + (appearancechannels,))) # Appearance grid self.Aw = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(gridres + (watermarkchannels,))) # Watermark grid # Embedding Layer: Maps ID to 16-dim vector self.embdim = 16 self.Emb = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(1, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, self.embdim)) # Modulation Layer: Linear layer to produce scale and shift self.Mod = nn.Linear(self.embdim, 2 watermarkchannels) # Color Decoder MLP (S) # Input: Appearance features + Modulated Watermark features + View direction self.S = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(appearancechannels + watermarkchannels + 3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # Output RGB) # Watermark Decoder D self.Decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 gridres[0] gridres[1], 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1) # Output probability for binary message) def samplegrid(self, grid, coords): """ Sample from a 3D grid using trilinear interpolation.:param grid: Tensor of shape (I, J, K,...) or (I, J, K):param coords: Tensor of shape (..., 3) with values in [0, 1]:return: Sampled features """ # Normalize coords to [-1, 1] for gridsample coordsnorm = 2.0 coords - 1.0 # Add batch and channel dims if necessary for gridsample # Assuming grid is (I, J, K, C) or (I, J, K) if grid.dim() == 4: # gridsample expects (N, C, H, W) for 2D or (N, C, D, H, W) for 3D # Here we assume a simplified sampling or use torch.nn.functional.gridsample # For 3D, we might need to permute or use a specific 3D interpolation function # This is a placeholder for the actual tensor decomposition sampling logic of TensoRF pass # In a real implementation, this would use the specific tensor decomposition # reconstruction logic of TensoRF (e.g., CP or VM decomposition) to retrieve # features at continuous coordinates. Here we assume a direct grid lookup # for conceptual clarity, but TensoRF uses factorized grids. # For the purpose of this article, we assume samplegrid returns the # feature vector at coords from the grid. return F.gridsample(grid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), coordsnorm.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=True).squeeze() def forward(self, x, d, idn): """ Render a pixel with watermark embedding.:param x: 3D position (..., 3):param d: View direction (..., 3):param idn: Integer ID for watermark:return: Rendered color, modulated features (for debugging/training) """ # 1. Input Embedding # idn is an integer, convert to tensor idtensor = torch.tensor([idn], dtype=torch.float32).view(1, 1) en = self.Emb(idtensor) # (1, 16) # 2. Modulation Parameters gammabeta = self.Mod(en) # (1, 2 Cw) gamman = gammabeta[:,:self.Aw.shape[-1]] # (1, Cw) betan = gammabeta[:, self.Aw.shape[-1]:] # (1, Cw) # 3. Feature Sampling # Sample from grids at position x # Note: In TensoRF, x is used to index into the factorized grids. # Here we simulate the feature retrieval. wx = self.samplegrid(self.Aw, x) # (..., Cw) Gcx = self.samplegrid(self.Ac, x) # (..., P) # 4. Feature Modulation # w'(x) = gamman w(x) + betan # Broadcasting gamman and betan to match wx dimensions wprimex = gamman wx + betan # 5. Color Decoding # Concatenate appearance, modulated watermark, and view direction # d needs to be broadcasted or sampled if it varies per ray # Assuming d is aligned with x for a single ray inputfeatures = torch.cat([Gcx, wprimex, d], dim=-1) ctilde = self.S(inputfeatures) # (..., 3) # 6. Volume Rendering (Simplified for single point) # In full rendering, this integrates along the ray. # Here we return the color contribution for the point. sigma = self.samplegrid(self.Asigma, x) # (..., 1) # Transmittance and integration would happen in a ray marching loop # For this function, we return the color and features for extraction return ctilde, wprimex def trainstep(self, x, d, idn, groundtruthmessage): """ Perform one training step. """ # Render image (simplified to single pixel for logic) color, = self.forward(x, d, idn) # 7. Augmentation # Apply random augmentations to the rendered image # Implementing full differentiable augmentations requires specific libraries. # We assume a function applyaugmentations that returns the augmented image. augmentedimage = applyaugmentations(color) # 8. Watermark Extraction # Apply DWT level 2 and take LL2 sub-band # DWT implementation is assumed. ll2band = getll2subband(augmentedimage) # Decode message decodedmessage = self.Decoder(ll2band) # Calculate BCE loss loss = F.binarycrossentropy(decodedmessage, groundtruthmessage) return loss def applyaugmentations(image): """ Apply differentiable augmentations. """ # This is a placeholder for the specific augmentation pipeline. # It should include brightness, contrast, blur, noise, JPEG, etc. return image def getll2subband(image): """ Apply level 2 DWT and return LL2 sub-band. """ # This is a placeholder for the DWT implementation. return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Entanglement: Directly embedding the watermark into the existing appearance grid Gc risks entangling watermark features with scene color, potentially degrading both capacity and quality. Precision: The use of differentiable augmentations and DWT requires careful handling of numerical precision to ensure the gradient flow remains stable during training. Boundary Conditions: The grid sampling must handle coordinates outside the valid range [0, 1] appropriately, typically by clamping or using periodic boundary conditions depending on the TensoRF implementation. Time Complexity: Training time is increased due to the additional grid Aw, the modulation network, and the differentiable augmentation pipeline. Rendering time is slightly increased due to the additional feature sampling and modulation operations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases by the size of the watermark grid Aw, which has the same spatial resolution as the geometry and appearance grids. Measured Performance: MultiNeRF maintains high visual quality while embedding multiple watermarks. It is robust against various image attacks due to the differentiable augmentation layer. Scaling: The method scales to multiple watermarks by simply adding more IDs, as the modulation mechanism allows for independent activation of watermark features. Strengths: High capacity for multiple watermarks, no need for model retraining for new watermarks, robustness to image attacks. Limitations: Requires training with a dedicated watermark grid and decoder, which adds complexity to the training pipeline. When to use: When multiple distinct watermarks need to be embedded in a single NeRF model for different users or contexts. When not to use: When only a single watermark is needed, or when computational resources are severely limited. MultiNeRF was introduced in the paper "MultiNeRF: Multiple Watermark Embedding for Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the TensoRF architecture, which decomposes a scene into geometry and appearance grids. The method was developed to address the limitations of prior single-watermark embedding approaches, which were vulnerable to entanglement and lacked scalability. The use of FiLM-based modulation allows for conditional activation of watermarks based on input identifiers. name: Gaussian Splatting Specific Regularization
head: 3DGS Regularization, Gaussian Primitive Regularization
body: Gaussian Splatting Specific Regularization refers to a family of loss functions and training strategies designed to constrain the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) radiance fields. Unlike generic NeRF regularization, these methods address the unique discrete, point-based nature of Gaussians, targeting issues such as opacity collapse, geometric instability under sparse views, high-frequency detail loss, and aliasing artifacts. They set themselves apart from sibling methods like RegNeRF by operating directly on Gaussian parameters (opacity, scale, rotation, position) rather than continuous density fields, and from Diffusion-regularized NeRF by leveraging explicit geometric priors or structural constraints specific to splatting rather than implicit generative priors. All methods in this family operate within the differentiable volume rendering framework where gradients flow from the loss \mathcal{L} back through the rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}) and depth \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) to the Gaussian parameters \theta (position \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, color \mathbf{c}) [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md, unofficial]. The rendering process computes expected color and depth along rays r(t) = o + td using sample points ti with weights wi = T(ti)\rho(ti), where \rho(ti) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{r}(ti))(t{i+1} - ti)) and T(ti) = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \rho(tj)). The rendering weights wi serve as the probability distribution of absorption along the ray, often denoted as h(t) = T(t)\sigma(t), which is used in distributional geometric losses. The rendered depth is typically the expected distance along the ray: \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N wi ti where wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) are the rendering weights, ti are sample depths, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Gradients are backpropagated through the differentiable volume rendering process to update the density and color field parameters. A geometric constraint strategy applied during the optimization of point-based radiance fields to prevent the point cloud from collapsing into local minima and to enforce manifold structure. It addresses the lack of inherent connectivity in point clouds by combining a denoising stage, which optimizes point geometry and opacity via volume rendering, and a completion stage, which fills gaps in the point cloud. Unlike mesh-based regularization, it operates directly on unstructured points using weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to estimate local geometry. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing point density through an iterative add/remove cycle driven by a specific sparsity-inducing loss function. A training-time loss term applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to enforce local smoothness on the 2D attribute grids of sorted Gaussians, thereby improving compressibility without significantly degrading rendering quality. Unlike post-processing compression methods that apply sorting and encoding after training, this method integrates smoothing during the optimization process, encouraging the renderer to prefer Gaussian configurations that exhibit spatial coherence in their 2D grid representation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Adaptive Gaussian Refinement and Selective Densification by focusing on the statistical properties of the attribute distribution rather than geometric density or pruning thresholds. A method that applies frequency-domain regularization to the rendered 2D image to encourage recovery of high-frequency detail, resolving blurring issues. A regularization method that aligns 2D Gaussian primitives (orientation R, scale S, position p) with latent scene surfaces using multi-view consistency on sampled points. Step: Sample K points Z = \{zk\} from the standard Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I) on each disk-shaped primitive. Project the transformed 3D points Z to source and target views to obtain 2D positions q^{src} and q^{tar}. Query MVS features F{src}(q^{src}) and F{tar}(q^{tar}) at the projected 2D positions. Formula: Compute point position loss L{df} via cosine similarity over K points: L{df} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^{K} (1 - \frac{F{src}(qk^{src}) \cdot F{tar}(qk^{tar})}{\|F{src}(qk^{src})\| \|F{tar}(qk^{tar})\|}). Compute normal loss L{dn} to supervise the normal vector R[..., 2] using rendered normal n: L{dn} = 1 - R[..., 2]^\top n. Combine losses for final primitive regularization: L{dr} = L{df} + L{dn}. Pitfall: The last scale value of 2D Gaussian primitives is zero, making it difficult to optimize the normal vector R[..., 2] in the last dimension. Formula: Total loss L is the weighted sum of image reconstruction loss L{rgb}, depth distortion loss Ld, depth-normal consistency loss Ln, direct Gaussian primitive regularization loss L{dr}, and feature splatting loss L{fea}: L = L{rgb} + \lambda1 Ld + \lambda2 Ln + \lambda3 L{dr} + \lambda4 L{fea}. Parameter: Hyperparameter \lambda1 (weight for Ld) is 1000. Hyperparameter \lambda2 (weight for Ln) is 0.05. Hyperparameter \lambda3 (weight for L{dr}) is 1. Hyperparameter \lambda4 (weight for L{fea}) is 0.2. A plug-in approach that combines Random Dropout Regularization (RDR) and Edge-guided Splitting Strategy (ESS) to improve the generalization performance of existing 3DGS methods under sparse views. Step: First, employ RDR to alleviate the overfitting issue. Then, adopt ESS to split large Gaussians to better capture high-frequency details. Parameter: The method is compatible with diverse 3DGS-based methods. Regularization applied to semantic embeddings of neighboring Gaussians to encourage regional smoothness, prevent high-frequency noise, and ensure continuous surfaces have homogeneous semantic representations. Parameter: Target: Semantic embeddings of neighboring Gaussians. A physically-grounded regularization framework for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting that mitigates aliasing artifacts (flickering textures, jagged edges) and optimization instability in high-resolution (e.g., 4K) urban environments by enforcing cross-scale consistency and geometric stability. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) was introduced as a real-time radiance field representation method. However, standard 3DGS suffers from issues such as blurring, sensitivity to initialization, and degradation under sparse views. Various regularization techniques have been developed to address these specific weaknesses. Frequency-domain regularization (FreGS) was proposed to resolve blurring. Geometrically enhanced supervision (Sparse2DGS) was introduced to handle sparse-view degradation by incorporating MVS features. DropoutGS was developed to alleviate overfitting in sparse views. Spatial total variation regularization was applied to semantic embeddings for vision-language tasks. PrismGS was proposed to address aliasing and instability in large-scale urban environments. These methods collectively form the family of Gaussian Splatting Specific Regularization, evolving from the base 3DGS framework to improve robustness, fidelity, and generalization.
