name: Sparse Regularization for Point Cloud Opacity
head: Denoising and Completion, Point Cloud Geometry Optimization, Sparse Opacity Optimization
body: Sparse regularization for point cloud opacity is an optimization strategy applied during the training of point-based radiance fields to manage point density and geometry. It operates through an alternating loop of denoising and completion stages. Unlike sibling methods that focus on smoothness, it explicitly manages opacity parameters via a sparsity-inducing loss function and iteratively adds points to fill rendering gaps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points P = \{pi\}, each with an associated optimizable opacity parameter \alphai, and a set of training views with ground truth images. Output: An optimized point cloud with refined geometry and opacity values, where low-opacity points are removed based on a threshold \mu. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of points pi. Each point has an opacity parameter \alphai. Depth Buffer: For each pixel, a buffer storing the depths of k points along the ray, explicitly not restricted to the single nearest point. Rectified Coordinates: Computed from the depth buffer values using a transformation defined in the source (Eqn. 1 in), which maps points to a deformed space suitable for radiance mapping. Parameters: k: Number of points maintained in the depth buffer per pixel. \mu: Threshold used to remove low-opacity points after training convergence. Typical values for k and \mu are not given in the sources. Steps: The method operates in an alternating loop of Denoising and Completion until convergence. 1. Denoising: 1. Rasterization: For each training view, rasterize the point cloud. Maintain a depth buffer of k points for each pixel. 2. Coordinate Transformation: Compute rectified coordinates for the points in the depth buffer using the depth values and the transformation equation (Eqn. 1 in). 3. Radiance Mapping: Feed the rectified coordinates and the ray directions into a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to estimate colors. 4. Volume Rendering: Assign an optimizable opacity parameter \alphai to each point pi. Compute the pixel RGB values using the volume rendering equation. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the sparse regularization loss \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}}: \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N [\log(\alphai) + \log(1 - \alphai)] where N is the number of points and \alphai is the opacity parameter. 6. Optimization: Optimize the point positions and opacity parameters \alphai using the computed loss. 2. Completion: 1. Masking: Rasterize the current point cloud to get a mask. Identify pixels where the ground truth image indicates an occupied surface, but the rasterization buffer is empty (i.e., no points were rendered). 2. Point Addition: For each such pixel, add a set of new points with opacity parameters along the pixel ray. 3. Depth Range Determination: Determine the depth range for the added points by referring to the depth range of adjacent pixel buffers. 4. Note: The completion step may introduce noise, which is expected to be removed in the subsequent denoising stage. 3. Convergence Check: Repeat the Denoising and Completion steps alternatively until convergence. After convergence, remove all points with opacity \alphai < \mu. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def sparseregularizationoptimization(points, trainingviews, thresholdmu, k): """ Optimizes point cloud geometry and opacity using sparse regularization. Args: points: List of dicts with 'pos' (3D array) and 'alpha' (float). trainingviews: List of dicts with 'camera' (dict with pose) and 'gtimage' (HxWx3 array). thresholdmu: Threshold for removing low-opacity points. k: Number of points to keep in the depth buffer per pixel. Returns: Optimized list of points. """ while True: # --- Denoising Step --- for view in trainingviews: # 1. Rasterize and maintain depth buffer of k points depthbuffer = {} for p in points: u, v, z = projectpoint(p['pos'], view['camera']) pixel = (int(u), int(v)) if pixel not in depthbuffer: depthbuffer[pixel] = [] depthbuffer[pixel].append(z) depthbuffer[pixel].sort() if len(depthbuffer[pixel]) > k: depthbuffer[pixel] = depthbuffer[pixel][:k] # 2. Compute rectified coordinates using depth buffer (Eqn 1 in) # Source defines rectified coordinates via Eqn. 1; exact formula not provided here. rectifiedcoords = {pix: applyrectificationformula(depths, view['camera']) for pix, depths in depthbuffer.items()} # 3. Estimate colors using MLP raydirs = {pix: normalize(computeraydirection(pix, view['camera'])) for pix in rectifiedcoords} colors = {pix: mlpforward(rectifiedcoords[pix], raydirs[pix]) for pix in rectifiedcoords} # 4. Compute pixel RGB using volume rendering equation renderedimages = volumerenderequation(points, colors, view['camera']) # 5. Compute sparse regularization loss losssparse = computesparseloss(points) # 6. Optimize points and opacities # Standard gradient descent update using computed gradients. points = optimizeparameters(points, losssparse) # --- Completion Step --- for view in trainingviews: # 1. Rasterize to get mask mask = rasterizeoccupancy(points, view['camera']) gtimage = view['gtimage'] # 2. Identify empty pixels where GT is occupied emptyoccupiedpixels = [] for y in range(gtimage.shape[0]): for x in range(gtimage.shape[1]): if mask[y, x] == 0 and np.linalg.norm(gtimage[y, x]) > 0.0: emptyoccupiedpixels.append((x, y)) # 3. Add points for empty pixels for pixel in emptyoccupiedpixels: # Determine depth range from adjacent pixels depthrange = getadjacentdepthrange(pixel, depthbuffer) # Add points along the ray within the depth range newpoints = addpointsalongray(pixel, view['camera'], depthrange) points.extend(newpoints) # Check convergence criteria (e.g., loss change, max iterations) # Source states to run until convergence; specific criterion not given. if checkconvergence(points): break # --- Post-processing --- # Remove low-opacity points finalpoints = [p for p in points if p['alpha'] >= thresholdmu] return finalpoints def applyrectificationformula(depths, camera): # Applies coordinate transformation defined in source Eqn. 1 return [transformdepth(d, camera) for d in depths] def computeraydirection(pixel, camera): # Computes ray direction from camera pose and pixel coordinates return camera['direction'][:, pixel[1], pixel[0]] def mlpforward(coords, dirs): # Standard MLP forward pass return np.tanh(coords + dirs) # Simplified activation for pseudocode def volumerenderequation(points, colors, camera): # Standard alpha compositing: C = sum(wi ci), wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) pass # Standard implementation per volume rendering framework def computesparseloss(points): N = len(points) if N == 0: return 0.0 total = 0.0 for p in points: a = p['alpha'] a = max(min(a, 1.0 - 1e-6), 1e-6) # Guard against log(0) total += math.log(a) + math.log(1 - a) return total / N def optimizeparameters(points, loss): # Standard gradient descent update return [updatepoint(p, loss) for p in points] def rasterizeoccupancy(points, camera): mask = np.zeros((camera['height'], camera['width']), dtype=bool) for p in points: u, v, z = projectpoint(p['pos'], camera) if 0 <= u < camera['width'] and 0 <= v < camera['height']: mask[int(v), int(u)] = True return mask def getadjacentdepthrange(pixel, depthbuffer): x, y = pixel neighbors = [(x-1, y), (x+1, y), (x, y-1), (x, y+1)] depths = [d for nx, ny in neighbors if (nx, ny) in depthbuffer for d in depthbuffer[(nx, ny)]] return (min(depths) if depths else 0.0, max(depths) if depths else 1.0) def addpointsalongray(pixel, camera, depthrange): x, y = pixel rayo = camera['origin'] rayd = normalize(camera['direction'][:, y, x]) newpts = [] for z in np.linspace(depthrange[0], depthrange[1], 5): newpts.append({'pos': rayo + z rayd, 'alpha': 0.5}) return newpts def checkconvergence(points): # Checks if training has stabilized return False # Placeholder for convergence logic Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Logarithm Domain: The loss function involves \log(\alphai) and \log(1 - \alphai). If \alphai is exactly 0 or 1, the log is undefined. A guard clamping \alphai to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon] is necessary. Noise in Completion: The completion step introduces noise, which must be handled by the subsequent denoising step. Depth Buffer Size: The choice of k affects the smoothness of the rendering and the accuracy of the rectified coordinates. Not given in the sources. Threshold Selection: The threshold \mu determines the final sparsity. Not given in the sources. Surface Regularization is a geometric constraint strategy applied during the optimization of point-based radiance fields to prevent the point cloud from collapsing into local minima and to enforce manifold structure. It addresses the lack of inherent connectivity in point clouds by combining a repulsion term, which encourages uniform point distribution on local tangent planes, and a projection term, which forces points to lie on those planes. Unlike mesh-based regularization, it operates directly on unstructured points using weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to estimate local geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Prevents point cloud collapse, enforces manifold structure, handles gaps in point clouds via completion. Limitations: Introduces noise during completion, requires iterative optimization, sensitive to threshold \mu. When to Use: When optimizing point-based radiance fields and needing to enforce geometric structure and handle incomplete point clouds. When Not to Use: When a mesh-based representation is preferred or when real-time performance is critical and iterative optimization is too slow. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering with Easy Editing". History: The paper proposes a frequency-modulated point cloud rendering approach with easy editing capabilities, including object-level editing and scene composition. Usage: Used in point-based radiance field optimization for novel view synthesis and editing. name: Surface Regularization
head: Point Cloud Surface Regularization, Repulsion and Projection Regularization
body: Surface Regularization is a geometric constraint strategy applied during the optimization of point-based radiance fields to prevent the point cloud from collapsing into local minima and to enforce manifold structure. It addresses the lack of inherent connectivity in point clouds by combining a repulsion term, which encourages uniform point distribution on local tangent planes, and a projection term, which forces points to lie on those planes. Unlike mesh-based regularization, it operates directly on unstructured points using weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to estimate local geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of points P = \{pi\} with associated normals N = \{ni\}, a neighborhood radius D, and an occlusion counter O = \{ok\} for each point. Outputs: Gradient updates for point positions pi and normals ni derived from the regularization losses Lr and Lp. Data Structures: Point: 3D position vector pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Normal: 3D unit vector ni \in \mathbb{R}^3. Occlusion Counter: Integer ok \ge 0 tracking how many times point pk is occluded across all camera views. Algorithm: The method computes two loss terms based on local surface estimation via weighted PCA. 1. Compute Weights: For a target point pi and each neighbor pk within distance D (i.e., \|pi - pk\| \le D), compute three weights: Spatial Weight (\psi{ik}): Penalizes distance. \psi{ik} = \exp \left( - \frac{\|pi - pk\|^2}{D^2} \right) Normal Similarity Weight (\theta{ik}): Penalizes normal divergence. \theta{ik} = \exp \left( - \frac{(1 - nk^\top ni)^2}{\max(10^{-5}, 1 - \cos(\Theta))} \right) The denominator uses a constant floor of 10^{-5} or a threshold \cos(\Theta) to prevent division by zero when normals are identical. Visibility Weight (\phi{ik}): Penalizes occluded points, treating them as potential outliers. \phi{ik} = \frac{1}{ok + 1} Combined Weight (w{ik}): w{ik} = \frac{\psi{ik} \theta{ik} \phi{ik}}{\sum{k \in \mathcal{N}i} \psi{ik} \theta{ik} \phi{ik}} where \mathcal{N}i is the set of neighbors of pi. 2. Estimate Local Tangent Plane: Compute the weighted centroid \mui = \sum{k \in \mathcal{N}i} w{ik} pk. Perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the matrix of weighted centered vectors \sqrt{w{ik}}(pk - \mui) to find the principal components. Let V be the matrix of eigenvectors (principal components) sorted by eigenvalue magnitude. \tilde{V} contains the first 2 principal components (spanning the tangent plane). Vn is the 3rd principal component (the surface normal). 3. Compute Repulsion Loss (Lr): Calculate projected point-to-point distances on the tangent plane: d{ik} = \tilde{V}^\top (pi - pk) This represents the 2D vector of distances in the tangent space. The loss encourages points to spread out uniformly: Lr = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i} \sum{k \in \mathcal{N}i} \frac{\psi{ik}}{N} (d{ik}^\top d{ik} + 10^{-4}) The term 10^{-4} is added to the squared distance as specified in the source. 4. Compute Projection Loss (Lp): Calculate point-to-plane distances (distance to the tangent plane): d{ik} = Vn^\top (pi - pk) This is the scalar projection of the vector (pi - pk) onto the normal Vn. The loss forces points to lie on the surface: Lp = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i} \sum{k \in \mathcal{N}i} w{ik} d{ik}^2 The method minimizes this together with the per-pixel image loss. 5. Total Objective: The total loss for optimization is: L = \sum{v=0}^{V} L(Iv, Iv^) + \gammap Lp + \gammar Lr where L(Iv, Iv^) is the image reconstruction loss for view v, \gammap = 0.02, and \gammar = 0.05. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def surfaceregularization(points, normals, occlusioncounts, neighbors, D, gammap=0.02, gammar=0.05): """ Computes regularization gradients for point positions based on Surface Regularization. Normals and points are updated alternately during optimization. """ N = points.shape[0] gradp = np.zeroslike(points) for i in range(N): pi = points[i] ni = normals[i] kindices = neighbors[i] K = len(kindices) if K == 0: continue pk = points[kindices] nk = normals[kindices] # 1. Compute Weights distsq = np.sum((pi - pk) 2, axis=1) psi = np.exp(-distsq / (D 2)) dot = np.sum(ni nk, axis=1) oneminuscos = 1.0 - dot theta = np.exp(-(1.0 - dot) 2 / np.maximum(1e-5, oneminuscos)) phi = 1.0 / (occlusioncounts[kindices] + 1.0) raww = psi theta phi w = raww / np.sum(raww) # 2. Weighted PCA for tangent plane mu = np.sum(w[:, np.newaxis] pk, axis=0) centered = pk - mu sqrtw = np.sqrt(w)[:, np.newaxis] A = sqrtw centered,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, fullmatrices=False) Vtilde = Vt[:2,:] # Tangent plane basis (2x3) Vn = Vt[2,:] # Normal (3,) # 3. Repulsion Loss & Gradient diff = (pi - pk).T # (3, K) drep = Vtilde @ diff # (2, K) drepsq = np.sum(drep 2, axis=0) # (K,) # Gradient of (drep^2 + 1e-4) w.r.t pi: 2 Vtilde^T @ drep gradrepk = 2.0 Vtilde.T @ drep # (3, K) gradp[i] += gammar np.sum((psi / (N N))[:, np.newaxis] gradrepk, axis=1) # 4. Projection Loss & Gradient dproj = Vn @ diff # (K,) # Gradient of dproj^2 w.r.t pi: 2 dproj Vn gradprojk = 2.0 dproj Vn # (K, 3) gradp[i] += gammap np.sum((w / N)[:, np.newaxis] gradprojk, axis=0) # Note: Normal gradients are computed similarly but omitted for brevity. return gradp Parameters: \gammap = 0.02: Weight for the projection loss. \gammar = 0.05: Weight for the repulsion loss. D: Neighborhood radius. Not given in the sources. \Theta: Numerical floor constant. The source uses \max(10^{-5}, 1 - \cos(\Theta)) as a stability floor to prevent division by zero. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion Counters: Points with high occlusion counts receive low visibility weights, reducing their influence on the local plane estimation. This prevents outliers inside the model from distorting the surface. Normal Similarity: The term \max(10^{-5}, 1 - \cos(\Theta)) prevents division by zero when normals are parallel. If normals are identical, the weight \theta{ik} becomes \exp(0) = 1. Alternating Updates: Normals and points are updated alternately because the gradient for positions depends on normals and vice versa. The source suggests optimizing normals for Tn steps, then points for Tp steps. The parent method that provides the opacity constraints. Surface regularization adds geometric constraints to the point positions and normals. Sparse Regularization for Point Cloud Opacity Time Complexity: The method requires computing weights and PCA for each point's neighborhood. If K is the average number of neighbors, the complexity per point is O(K) for weight computation and O(K \cdot 3^2) for the SVD. Total complexity is O(N \cdot K). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot K) to store neighbor weights and intermediate vectors. Strengths: Effectively prevents point clustering in local minima and enforces clean manifold surfaces. It is robust to noise due to the weighted PCA and visibility filtering. Limitations: Requires maintaining and updating normals for each point, which adds computational overhead compared to position-only optimization. The method is sensitive to the choice of neighborhood radius D. When to Use: Use when optimizing point-based radiance fields or implicit surfaces where geometric smoothness and uniformity are required, and mesh structures are not available. Surface Regularization was introduced by Wang Yifan, Serena Felice, Shihao Wu, Cengiz Öztireli, and Olga Sorkine-Hornung in their paper "Differentiable Surface Splatting for Point-based Geometry Processing" (2020). It is inspired by earlier works on point cloud denoising and surface reconstruction by Huang et al. (2009) and Öztireli et al. (2009). The method is used in differentiable rendering pipelines that optimize point clouds to match target images, ensuring that the resulting geometry is well-structured and manifold-like. name: Smoothness Regularization
head: neighbor loss
body: Smoothness Regularization is a training-time loss term applied to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to enforce local smoothness on the 2D attribute grids of sorted Gaussians, thereby improving compressibility without significantly degrading rendering quality. Unlike post-processing compression methods that apply sorting and encoding after training, this method integrates smoothing during the optimization process, encouraging the renderer to prefer Gaussian configurations that exhibit spatial coherence in their 2D grid representation. The method operates on the 2D grid of Gaussians, which are sorted based on their depth or spatial proximity to form a structured representation. The goal is to minimize the deviation between the original attribute values and a smoothed version of these attributes, using a loss function that is robust to outliers to facilitate better compression. Inputs: The current 2D attribute grids for all active Gaussians, containing five attribute channels: position, color (spherical harmonics coefficients), opacity, scaling, and rotation. Hyperparameters include the overall multiplier \lambda, per-grid multipliers, blur kernel size K, and blur standard deviation \sigma. Outputs: A scalar loss value L{smooth} added to the total training loss, and gradients propagated back through the Gaussian renderer to update the 3D Gaussian parameters. The method operates on 2D grids for each attribute type, where each cell corresponds to a Gaussian's attribute value at its sorted position. The grid dimensions are fixed per scene (e.g., a side length of 2091 for the Garden scene with 4.37M Gaussians). 1. Apply a 2D Gaussian filter to each of the five attribute grids to create smoothed versions. 2. Compute the element-wise difference between the original grid and the smoothed grid for each attribute channel. 3. Calculate the Huber loss for the error term of each attribute grid. 4. Scale the Huber loss for each grid by its respective separate multiplier, sum them, and scale the total by the overall multiplier \lambda. 5. Add the resulting smoothness loss to the standard 3DGS training loss. 6. Propagate the gradient of the smoothness loss through the Gaussian renderer to update the 3D Gaussian parameters during optimization. Let A be an attribute grid (e.g., color). Let A' be the blurred version of A. The error term E is: E = A - A' The Huber loss L{Huber}(E, \delta) for a given error E and threshold \delta is: L{Huber}(E, \delta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}E^2 & \text{if } |E| \le \delta \\ \delta(|E| - \frac{1}{2}\delta) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The total smoothness loss L{smooth} is: L{smooth} = \lambda \sum{i \in \{pos, color, opacity, scale, rot\}} wi \cdot \text{Mean}(L{Huber}(Ei, \delta)) Where: \lambda is the overall multiplier. wi is the separate multiplier for attribute i. \text{Mean}(\cdot) computes the average loss over all elements in the grid. \delta is the Huber threshold (Not given in the sources.). \lambda (Overall Multiplier): Scales the entire smoothness regularization loss. Typical values range from 0.01 to 1.5. Higher \lambda results in smaller storage size but potentially lower rendering quality (PSNR). Separate Multipliers: Individual scalars applied to each of the five 2D attribute grids (position, color, opacity, scaling, rotation). Kernel Size (K): Integer size of the Gaussian blur filter. Higher values produce smoother target images. Sigma (\sigma): Standard deviation of the Gaussian blur filter. Huber Threshold (\delta): Not given in the sources. Precision: The method relies on the differentiability of the Gaussian blur and the Huber loss. Boundaries: The 2D grid may have empty cells or boundaries where sorting is incomplete. Degenerate Input: If the grid is too small or the blur kernel is too large relative to the grid size, the smoothing may over-smooth, leading to significant loss of detail. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothnessregularizationloss( grids: dict, lambdaval: float, multipliers: dict, kernelsize: int, sigma: float, delta: float) -> float: """ Computes the smoothness regularization loss for 3D Gaussian Splatting. Args: grids: Dictionary mapping attribute names ('pos', 'color', 'opacity', 'scale', 'rot') to 2D list of lists representing the grid values. lambdaval: Overall multiplier for the smoothness loss. multipliers: Dictionary mapping attribute names to their specific loss multipliers. kernelsize: Integer size of the Gaussian blur filter. sigma: Standard deviation of the Gaussian blur filter. delta: Huber loss threshold (Not given in the sources, standard default is 1.0). Returns: Scalar float representing the smoothness loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 for attrname, grid in grids.items(): # Step 1: Apply 2D Gaussian filter to blur the grid blurredgrid = gaussianblur2d(grid, kernelsize, sigma) # Step 2: Compute error term error = [[grid[i][j] - blurredgrid[i][j] for j in range(len(grid[0]))] for i in range(len(grid))] # Step 3: Calculate Huber loss huberlossgrid = huberloss(error, delta) # Step 4: Average the loss over the grid meanloss = sum(sum(row) for row in huberlossgrid) / (len(grid) len(grid[0])) # Step 5: Scale by separate multiplier scaledloss = meanloss multipliers.get(attrname, 1.0) totalloss += scaledloss # Step 6: Scale by overall multiplier lambda finalloss = lambdaval totalloss return finalloss def gaussianblur2d(grid: list, kernelsize: int, sigma: float) -> list: """ Applies a 2D Gaussian blur to a grid. """ h = len(grid) w = len(grid[0]) halfk = kernelsize // 2 blurred = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] # Precompute kernel kernel = [] for i in range(kernelsize): row = [] for j in range(kernelsize): x = i - halfk y = j - halfk row.append(math.exp(-(x2 + y2) / (2 sigma2))) kernel.append(row) kernelsum = sum(sum(row) for row in kernel) kernel = [[k / kernelsum for k in row] for row in kernel] for i in range(h): for j in range(w): acc = 0.0 for ki in range(kernelsize): for kj in range(kernelsize): ni = i + ki - halfk nj = j + kj - halfk if 0 <= ni < h and 0 <= nj < w: acc += grid[ni][nj] kernel[ki][kj] blurred[i][j] = acc return blurred def huberloss(errorgrid: list, delta: float) -> list: """ Computes Huber loss element-wise. """ lossgrid = [] for row in errorgrid: lossrow = [] for e in row: abse = abs(e) if abse <= delta: lossrow.append(0.5 e2) else: lossrow.append(delta (abse - 0.5 delta)) lossgrid.append(lossrow) return lossgrid The prerequisite step that organizes Gaussians into 2D grids, enabling the smoothness regularization to be effective. It differs from smoothness regularization by being a structural organization step rather than a loss term. Sorting An additional exponential activation for coordinates used during training to allow for more relative precision, often used in conjunction with sorting and smoothing. Coordinate Space Contraction Time Complexity: The blurring step adds a convolutional cost proportional to the number of Gaussians and the kernel size. Sorting is performed periodically after densification, and smoothing is applied every training step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 2D attribute grids and their blurred versions during the forward pass. Measured Performance: On the Truck dataset, \lambda=0.01 yields PSNR 24.39 and Size 18.02 MB, while \lambda=1.5 yields PSNR 24.02 and Size 10.73 MB. The method achieves significantly higher PSNR compared to compressing vanilla 3DGS after training (e.g., 25.37 PSNR vs 21.98 PSNR for compressed vanilla 3DGS on the Truck scene). Strengths: Improves compressibility by creating local smoothness in attribute grids, allowing for better performance with standard image compression algorithms. Limitations: Higher \lambda values reduce rendering quality (PSNR). The method requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (\lambda, kernel size, sigma). When to Use: When the goal is to reduce the storage size of 3DGS models while maintaining high visual quality, especially when combined with sorting and compression. When Not to Use: When maximum rendering quality is prioritized over storage size, or when computational resources for the additional loss computation are limited. The concept of self-organizing grids relates to Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) introduced by Kohonen in 1982 and 2013. The method was introduced in the paper "Compact 3D Scene Representation via Self-Organizing Gaussian Grids". It differentiates from previous compression methods by integrating smoothing during training rather than as a post-processing step. name: KNN-NeRF
head: KNN approach to training NeRF on point cloud, NeRFs trained on point clouds with KNN color assignment
body: KNN-NeRF is a baseline method for training Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using sparse 3D point clouds as supervision instead of multi-view images. It solves the problem of generating ground-truth color labels for rays that do not pass through existing points by assigning the color of the nearest point in the cloud to the ray. Unlike standard NeRF which relies on pixel colors from images, KNN-NeRF constructs a dense training signal from sparse geometry, though it struggles with sharp object borders due to the low-frequency bias of neural networks and the sparsity of the input. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D point cloud X \subset \mathbb{R}^6 where each element x \in X contains position xp \in \mathbb{R}^3 and RGB color xc \in \mathbb{R}^3. Input: A set of rays \mathcal{R}, where each ray is defined by origin o \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A trained NeRF model that predicts color \hat{C}(r) for any ray r. Data Structures Point Cloud X: A list or array of tuples/objects. Each entry has fields: pos (3D vector (x, y, z)) and color (3D vector (r, g, b)). Ray r: Defined by origin o \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Direction is normalized. Algorithm Steps 1. Define Point Cloud: Let X be the input set where x = (xp, xc) for xp \in \mathbb{R}^3 and xc \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Generate Rays: Produce many rays not restricted to passing through points in X. 3. KNN Selection (Front Surface): For a given ray origin o, find the k nearest neighbors in X based on Euclidean distance to o. Let this subset be KN{o,k}(X). This step approximates the front surface of the object relative to the camera origin. 4. Nearest Point to Ray: Within the subset KN{o,k}(X), find the point \bar{x} that minimizes the geometric distance to the ray r. The distance d(xp, r) from a point xp to a line defined by o and d is calculated as the length of the perpendicular vector from xp to the line. Formally: C(X, r) = \bar{x} \in KN{o,k}(X): d(\bar{x}p, r) \leq d(xp, r) \quad \forall x \in KN{o,k}(X) The ground truth color for the ray is C{gt} = \bar{x}c. 5. Training: Train the NeRF to minimize the squared error between the predicted ray color \hat{C}(r) and the assigned ground truth color C{gt}. Formulas Point-to-Line Distance: d(xp, r) = \| (xp - o) \times d \| where \times denotes the cross product and d is normalized. Ground Truth Assignment: C{gt} = Cc(X, r) = \bar{x}c where \bar{x} is the point in KN{o,k}(X) minimizing d(\bar{x}p, r). Loss Function: L = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \|\hat{C}(r) - C{gt}\|^22. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def distancepointtoline(pointpos, lineorigin, linedir): """ Calculates the perpendicular distance from a point to a line. linedir is assumed to be normalized. """ op = pointpos - lineorigin return np.linalg.norm(np.cross(op, linedir)) def getgroundtruthcolorknn(pointcloud, rayorigin, raydir, k): """ pointcloud: List of tuples (pos, color) Returns the color of the nearest point in the k-nearest neighbors to the origin. """ # Step 1: Find k nearest neighbors to the origin based on Euclidean distance distancestoorigin = [] for i, (pos, color) in enumerate(pointcloud): dist = np.linalg.norm(pos - rayorigin) distancestoorigin.append((dist, i)) # Sort by distance and take top k distancestoorigin.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) kindices = [idx for, idx in distancestoorigin[:k]] # Subset of points kneighbors = [pointcloud[i] for i in kindices] # Step 2: Find the point in kneighbors closest to the ray line mindist = float('inf') bestcolor = None for pos, color in kneighbors: dist = distancepointtoline(pos, rayorigin, raydir) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestcolor = color return bestcolor def trainknnnerf(pointcloud, rays, k, model): """ Iterative training step. rays: List of (origin, direction) tuples. """ totalloss = 0.0 for rayorigin, raydir in rays: # Get ground truth color using KNN logic gtcolor = getgroundtruthcolorknn(pointcloud, rayorigin, raydir, k) # Predict color from NeRF predcolor = model(rayorigin, raydir) # Calculate Loss: L = sum ||Chat(r) - Cc(X, r)||^22 loss = np.sum((predcolor - gtcolor) 2) totalloss += loss # Update model parameters via backpropagation # (Standard optimizer step: optimizer.zerograd(), loss.backward(), optimizer.step()) Parameters k: The number of nearest neighbors to consider from the origin. It is a hyperparameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sparsity: The method fails to reconstruct sharp object borders because the input point clouds are highly sparse. Frequency Bias: NeRFs are biased towards learning lower-frequency functions, making them unable to represent high-frequency variations in color and geometry present in sparse data. Extrapolation: If rays are generated in regions where no points exist nearby, the KNN selection may fail or pick distant, incorrect points, leading to artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard KNN search requires O(N) per ray without spatial indexing. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the point cloud X and the KNN subset for each ray during training. Strengths: Provides a direct way to train NeRFs on 3D point clouds without requiring multi-view image alignment or depth maps. Limitations: Cannot reconstruct sharp object borders; suffers from the low-frequency bias of neural networks when dealing with sparse data. When to use: As a baseline for training NeRFs on 3D point clouds. When not to use: When high-frequency detail or sharp geometry is required from sparse input data. KNN-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Points2NeRF: Generating Neural Radiance Fields from 3D point cloud". It serves as a baseline method for adapting NeRF architectures to work with 3D point cloud data, addressing the need for ground-truth color assignment when rays do not intersect existing points. The authors note that while this approach is simple, it is insufficient for high-quality reconstruction due to sparsity and network bias, motivating their subsequent auto-encoder-based proposal. name: Progressive and Dynamic Scene Growth
body: Progressive and Dynamic Scene Growth refers to training procedures that adaptively increase model capacity or expand the training dataset during optimization, rather than using a fixed architecture and static data subset. This family solves the problem of balancing computational resources with reconstruction fidelity in complex, large-scale, or continuously changing scenes. It sets itself apart from static NeRF training by dynamically allocating representational power (via network branches, octree leaves, or block attachments) to regions of high uncertainty or novelty, and by incrementally incorporating new observations to prevent catastrophic forgetting or to handle unbounded data streams. The core mechanism across this family is the conditional expansion of the scene representation or training scope based on a metric of insufficiency (e.g., uncertainty, novelty, or temporal progression). 1. Metric Computation: A scalar metric is computed for spatial regions or training samples. 2. Expansion Trigger: When the metric exceeds a predefined threshold, a growth event is triggered. Network Growth: New sub-networks (branches) are initialized at cluster centers of high-uncertainty points. Structural Growth: New octree leaves are spawned when the ratio of unmodeled visible voxels |V{new} \setminus V{covered}| / |V{new}| exceeds \tau{spawn}. Data Growth: New camera views are added to the training buffer, often with specific initialization strategies for their poses. 3. Re-optimization: The expanded system (new branches, leaves, or data points) is jointly optimized with the existing parameters. 4. Pruning/Frozen State: To bound memory and computational cost, regions or parameters that are no longer active or have exceeded a temporal threshold are frozen or pruned. Dynamic Growth Parameters is a training procedure that adaptively increases model capacity by adding network branches in regions of high reconstruction uncertainty. Unlike static architectures, it clusters high-error query points and spawns child networks to refine predictions locally, enabling efficient coarse-to-fine scene representation. It is chosen when a single global MLP cannot capture high-frequency details in complex scenes without excessive memory usage. See Dynamic Growth Parameters. Progressive View Synthesis Training (PERF) is a training strategy for Panoramic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that synthesizes novel views from a single input panorama by progressively adding reference views to improve geometry and semantic coherence in occluded regions. Unlike methods that rely on semantic regularization via CLIP or DINO features on perspective patches, PERF uses collaborative RGBD inpainting and an inpainting-and-erasing strategy to generate high-quality pseudo-ground truth for unseen areas, avoiding the "foggy effects" and redundant geometry common in other few-shot NeRF approaches. It is chosen for single-view or few-shot panoramic reconstruction. See Progressive View Synthesis Training. Incremental Registration is a training strategy that registers camera poses sequentially following the temporal order of input images, leveraging the intuition that adjacent camera motions in videos are smooth. It solves the problem of non-convex pose optimization and local minima in joint pose and radiance field optimization by providing good initializations for new frames based on previously registered ones. Unlike global registration methods that optimize all poses simultaneously, this method builds the trajectory incrementally, freezing older parameters to prevent catastrophic forgetting and reduce computational cost. It is chosen for large-scale or video-based NeRF training where global optimization is intractable. See Incremental Registration. Online Incremental NeRF Optimization addresses the problem of reconstructing 3D scenes from a continuous stream of incoming camera views, rather than a fixed, pre-collected dataset. It differs from offline methods like DVGO by updating the scene representation \Phi dynamically as new observations arrive, enabling active exploration and real-time adaptation. This approach is essential for robotics and large-scale mapping where data volume is unbounded and memory constraints require discarding older frames. See Online Incremental NeRF Optimization. CityNeRF is a progressive learning paradigm that synchronously grows the NeRF model and training set. It starts by fitting distant views with shallow basic blocks. New blocks are continuously attached as training iterates to adapt to details in far-near views. This method effectively activates high-frequency channels in position encoding and unfolds more complex details as training progresses. It is chosen for large-scale urban scene reconstruction where multi-scale details are critical. The concept of hierarchical and progressive scene representation originated from the need to scale NeRF to large environments. NeRF-Nav introduced a hierarchical NeRF allocation using an octree structure, where the root maintains a coarse global representation and leaves represent high-resolution local fields, spawned based on exploration frontiers. This approach reduced memory usage by 3.8× compared to a single global NeRF while maintaining rendering quality (PSNR within 0.3 dB). The spawning condition is defined as Spawn(L{new}) \Leftarrow |V{new} \setminus V{covered}| / |V{new}| > \tau{spawn}, where \tau{spawn} = 0.3 is the novelty threshold. Leaves whose last observation exceeds a temporal threshold are frozen and optionally pruned to bound memory. In the context of urban scenes, Xiangli et al. proposed CityNeRF in 2021, a progressive learning paradigm that synchronously grows the NeRF model and training set. It starts by fitting distant views with shallow basic blocks, and new blocks are continuously attached as training iterates to adapt to details in far-near views. These methods address the limitations of monolithic NeRF structures in handling large-scale, multi-scale data. Incremental registration strategies were developed to handle the non-convexity of joint pose and NeRF optimization. By registering frames sequentially and freezing older parameters, these methods mitigate local minima associated with global optimization. Online incremental methods extend this to continuous streams, crucial for robotics applications where real-time adaptation and memory management are required. name: Dynamic Growth Parameters
head: NeRF Growth Steps, Recursive NeRF Growth
body: Dynamic Growth Parameters configure the iterative expansion of a neural radiance field's network architecture during training. It sets apart from static NeRF variants by using k-means clustering of uncertain query points to spawn new network branches, and from other growth methods by strictly limiting the total number of growth iterations and the branching factor k per step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current network branch, training dataset, current iteration count, total allowed growth steps N{grow}, branching factor k, iterations per stage I1, and an uncertainty threshold. Outputs: Updated network architecture with new child branches and optimized parameters. Data Structures: Network Branch: A multi-layer perceptron defined as F{\Phii}: (y{pi}, d) \rightarrow (ci, \sigmai, \deltai, yi), taking parent output y{pi} and viewing direction d as input, and predicting color ci, density \sigmai, uncertainty \deltai, and latent vector yi. Cluster Centers: k vectors representing the mean position/latent space of high-uncertainty points. Numbered Steps: 1. Training Phase: Train the current network branch for a fixed number of iterations I1. 2. Uncertainty Estimation: Compute the uncertainty metric \deltai for all sampled query points in the scene. 3. Clustering: Identify points where \deltai exceeds a predefined threshold and cluster them using k-means with parameter k \in [2, 4]. 4. Branch Initialization: Grow k new child network branches initialized at the corresponding cluster centers. 5. Growth Check: If the total number of growth steps performed is less than N{grow}, repeat from Step 1 with the expanded network. Parameters: N{grow}: Total number of growth iterations. Default value is 3. k: Number of branches spawned per growth step. Default value is 2, with a range of [2, 4]. I1: Iterations per growth stage. Not given in the sources. Threshold: Uncertainty threshold for clustering. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Termination: The method uses early termination to finalize predictions when uncertainty is low enough, avoiding unnecessary calculations and speeding up rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def dynamicgrowthparameters(network, dataset, Ngrow=3, k=2, I1=1000, threshold=0.0): currentnetwork = network growthstep = 0 while growthstep < Ngrow: # Step 1: Train current network for I1 iterations currentnetwork = trainstep(currentnetwork, dataset, I1) # Step 2: Compute uncertainty for sampled query points points = samplepoints(dataset) uncertainties = computeuncertainties(currentnetwork, points) # Step 3: Cluster high uncertainty points highuncpoints = [p for p, u in zip(points, uncertainties) if u > threshold] if not highuncpoints: break centers = kmeans(highuncpoints, k) # Step 4: Initialize and attach k new child branches for center in centers: child = initchildbranch(center) currentnetwork.addchild(child) growthstep += 1 return currentnetwork def trainstep(net, data, iters): for in range(iters): batch = samplebatch(data) net.updategradients(batch) return net def samplepoints(data): return data.points def computeuncertainties(net, points): return [net.predict(p).uncertainty for p in points] def kmeans(points, k): centers = random.sample(points, k) for in range(10): assignments = [min(range(k), key=lambda c: math.dist(p, centers[c])) for p in points] newcenters = [sum(points[i] for i, a in enumerate(assignments) if a == idx) / max(1, sum(1 for a in assignments if a == idx)) for idx in range(k)] if newcenters == centers: break centers = newcenters return centers def initchildbranch(center): # Initialize new branch network parameters based on cluster center # The exact initialization logic is not specified in the sources return NetworkBranch(initialstate=center) An adaptive strategy that clusters uncertain queries at the current stage and grows deeper networks according to the clustering result. After I1 iterations, points with uncertainty higher than a threshold are clustered using k-means with k \in [2, 4]. The network grows k branches according to the cluster centers. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Increases linearly with the number of growth steps and k, as each step adds k new network branches. Time: Training time increases due to iterative clustering and re-training phases, but is bounded by the default limit of 3 growth steps. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with scene complexity by allocating capacity to high-uncertainty regions, while early termination speeds up rendering for low-uncertainty points. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficiently represents complex scenes by focusing capacity where needed and accelerates rendering via early termination. Limitations: Introduces overhead from iterative clustering and re-training phases. When to use it and when not: Use when representing scenes with varying levels of detail and when iterative training is feasible. Origin: Recursive NeRF was introduced in "Recursive-NeRF: An Efficient and Dynamically Growing NeRF". History and Development: The method was developed to address the limitations of single-branch NeRFs by introducing a recursive structure that grows dynamically based on uncertainty metrics. Where it is used: It is used in neural radiance field optimization for view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. Recursive-NeRF: An Efficient and Dynamically Growing NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2022.3204608, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Progressive View Synthesis Training
head: PERF training loop, collaborative RGBD inpainting and progressive inpainting-and-erasing
body: Progressive View Synthesis Training (PERF) is a training strategy for Panoramic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that synthesizes novel views from a single input panorama by progressively adding reference views to improve geometry and semantic coherence in occluded regions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly integrating a collaborative RGBD inpainting and progressive inpainting-and-erasing mechanism to resolve geometry conflicts and semantic inconsistencies that arise when expanding the view set. The method trains a NeRF representation (specifically using Instant-NGP) by starting with a single panorama and iteratively introducing new synthetic reference views. Each iteration involves inpainting missing content, erasing conflicting geometry, and re-optimizing the network with a staged learning rate and supervision schedule. Input: A single input RGB-D panorama (color and depth maps). Output: A trained NeRF model capable of rendering novel views (RGB and depth) from arbitrary camera poses sampled around the scene. The implementation relies on the Instant-NGP representation via the NeRFAcc framework. Hash Grid: A hash table of size 2^{19} with 16 levels of feature vectors, each with a channel size of 2. Ray Buffer: At each iteration, 2048 rays are randomly sampled, each associated with a ground-truth or inpainted color value and a depth value for supervision. Initial Training Iterations: 10,000 iterations on the single input panorama. Progressive Views: 32 new positions are sampled with gradually increased distance from the original reference view position. Iterations per New View: 2,000 iterations. Supervision Schedule: First 100 iterations use only the new reference view; remaining 1,900 iterations use all reference views (original + newly added). Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: Initial 10^{-3}, decaying to 10^{-4} using cosine annealing for each new view stage. Distortion Loss Weight (\lambda{dist}): 1. Inpainting Model: Pre-trained Stable Diffusion 2. 1. Initial Training: Train the NeRF model using the single input panorama for 10,000 iterations. 2. View Sampling: Progressively sample 32 new camera positions with approximately gradually increased distance from the original reference panorama view position. 3. Iterative Expansion Loop: For each newly added reference view position: a. Collaborative RGBD Inpainting: Generate a synthetic reference view. Since the inpainting model is trained on perspective FOV and cannot handle panoramic distortion directly, masked regions are projected to perspective views, inpainted, and projected back to the panoramic coordinate system. b. Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing: Apply an erasing strategy to remove conflicting geometry from previous views that contradicts the new inpainted content, preventing wrong redundant geometry and degraded RGB quality. c. NeRF Re-optimization: Continue training the NeRF for 2,000 iterations. i. Phase 1 (Iterations 1–100): Use only the new reference view (color and depth) for supervision. ii. Phase 2 (Iterations 101–2000): Use all accumulated reference views (original + all newly added) for supervision. iii. At each iteration, randomly sample 2048 rays. The supervision targets are the ground-truth or inpainted colors and depth values for these rays. iv. Optimize NeRF parameters using Adam with the learning rate schedule (10^{-3} \to 10^{-4} via cosine annealing). v. Apply distortion loss with weight \lambda{dist} = 1 to encourage volume densities to converge to valid surfaces, avoiding "foggy effects" or "floating" densities. 4. Completion: Repeat Step 3 for all 32 sampled positions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim from torch.optim.lrscheduler import CosineAnnealingLR def progressiveviewsynthesistraining(singlepanoramargb, singlepanoramadepth): """ Trains a NeRF from a single panorama using progressive view synthesis. Args: singlepanoramargb: Tensor, RGB panorama image. singlepanoramadepth: Tensor, Depth panorama image. Returns: nerf: The trained Instant-NGP model. """ # 1. Initialize NeRF (Instant-NGP) # Hash table size 2^19, 16 levels, channel size 2 nerf = InstantNGP(hashsize=219, numlevels=16, channelsize=2) # 2. Initial Training on Single Panorama optimizer = optim.Adam(nerf.parameters(), lr=1e-3) for iteration in range(10000): rays = samplerays(2048) # Randomly sample 2048 rays renderedcolors, rendereddepths = renderrays(nerf, rays) gtcolors, gtdepths = getgtforrays(rays, singlepanoramargb, singlepanoramadepth) loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, gtcolors) + \ computeloss(rendereddepths, gtdepths) + \ 1.0 computedistortionloss(nerf, rays) # lambdadist = 1 optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # 3. Progressive View Sampling # Sample 32 new positions with gradually increased distance newviewpositions = samplepositions(32, initialpose=singlepanoramapose) # Store all reference views for supervision allreferenceviews = [singlepanoramargb] allreferencedepths = [singlepanoramadepth] inpainter = StableDiffusionInpaint() # Pre-trained Stable Diffusion 2 for viewidx, newpos in enumerate(newviewpositions): # Learning rate schedule for this stage scheduler = CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, Tmax=2000, etamin=1e-4) # Generate synthetic reference view for the new position # This involves collaborative RGBD inpainting and erasing syntheticrgb, syntheticdepth = generatesyntheticview( nerf, newpos, inpainter, allreferenceviews, allreferencedepths) # Add to reference set allreferenceviews.append(syntheticrgb) allreferencedepths.append(syntheticdepth) # Re-optimization for 2000 iterations for iterinstage in range(2000): rays = samplerays(2048) # Sample 2048 rays # Determine supervision source based on iteration count if iterinstage < 100: # First 100 iterations: only new view targetrgb = syntheticrgb targetdepth = syntheticdepth else: # Remaining 1900 iterations: all views # Aggregate losses from all views for the sampled rays targetrgb, targetdepth = getmultiviewtargets(rays, allreferenceviews, allreferencedepths) renderedcolors, rendereddepths = renderrays(nerf, rays) loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, targetrgb) + \ computeloss(rendereddepths, targetdepth) + \ 1.0 computedistortionloss(nerf, rays) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() scheduler.step() return nerf def generatesyntheticview(nerf, camerapose, inpainter, refrgbs, refdepths): # Render initial guess from NeRF initialrender = renderview(nerf, camerapose) # Identify masked/occluded regions (e.g., using depth consistency or visibility) mask = identifyoccludedregions(initialrender, refrgbs, refdepths) # Project masked regions to perspective views perspectivepatches = projecttoperspective(mask, initialrender) # Inpaint perspective patches inpaintedpatches = inpainter.inpaint(perspectivepatches) # Project back to panorama inpaintedpanorama = projectbacktoperspective(inpaintedpatches, mask) # Apply progressive inpainting-and-erasing to resolve conflicts finalrgb, finaldepth = applyerasingstrategy(inpaintedpanorama, initialrender) return finalrgb, finaldepth def computedistortionloss(nerf, rays): # Encourages volume densities to converge to a valid surface # Standard distortion loss implementation weights = nerf.getweights(rays) depths = nerf.getdepths(rays) meandepth = torch.sum(weights depths, dim=-1) / (torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) + 1e-8) distloss = torch.sum(weights (depths - meandepth) 2, dim=-1) return torch.mean(distloss) def samplerays(numrays): return torch.randn(numrays, 3) def renderrays(nerf, rays): return torch.randn(rays.shape[0], 3), torch.randn(rays.shape[0], 1) def getgtforrays(rays, rgb, depth): return rgb, depth def computeloss(pred, target): return torch.nn.functional.mseloss(pred, target) def samplepositions(n, initialpose): return [initialpose + i 0.1 for i in range(n)] def identifyoccludedregions(render, refrgbs, refdepths): return torch.zeroslike(render[:,:1]) def projecttoperspective(mask, render): return render def projectbacktoperspective(inpainted, mask): return inpainted def applyerasingstrategy(inpainted, initial): return inpainted, initial def getmultiviewtargets(rays, refrgbs, refdepths): # Aggregate targets from all reference views return refrgbs[0], refdepths[0] Panoramic Distortion: Inpainting models trained on perspective FOV (like Stable Diffusion 2) cannot be directly applied to panoramas due to distortion. The method must project masked regions to perspective views, inpaint, and project back. Foggy Effects/Floating Densities: NeRF can produce invalid surfaces ("foggy effects") if not regularized. This is mitigated by using distortion loss with weight \lambda{dist} = 1. Geometry Conflicts: Without the inpainting-and-erasing strategy, geometry conflicts arise from different views, leading to wrong redundant geometry and degraded RGB quality. Time Complexity: Training a scene takes approximately 2 hours on a single Nvidia V100 GPU with 32G memory. The complexity is dominated by the iterative inpainting and re-optimization steps for each of the 32 views. Memory Complexity: Depends on the Instant-NGP hash grid size (2^{19} entries) and the storage of reference views. The V100 with 32G memory is sufficient for the reported scenes. Performance: On the Replica dataset, PERF achieves the best performance in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS compared to DS-NeRF, DietNeRF, SinNeRF, 360FusionNeRF, and Omni-NeRF. Specifically, it shows significant improvement in masked PSNR, indicating better inpainting of invisible regions. Strengths: Superior semantic coherence in occluded regions compared to methods using CLIP or DINO regularization (DietNeRF, SinNeRF). Better visual quality than Omni-NeRF which relies on pseudo ground truth from point clouds. Limitations: Relies on a heavy pre-trained inpainting model (Stable Diffusion 2), which may limit real-time applicability. When to Use: Single panorama novel view synthesis, 3D virtual tours, VR games/conferences, filmmaking, text-to-3D, and 3D scene stylization. When Not to Use: When real-time training is required, or when high-quality perspective multi-view inputs are available (other methods may be more efficient). Origin: Proposed in the paper "PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama". History: Developed to address the limitations of existing NeRF methods in handling single panorama inputs, specifically the lack of semantic coherence and geometric validity in occluded regions. It builds on Instant-NGP [40] and integrates Stable Diffusion 2 [61] for content completion. Usage: Used for single panorama novel view synthesis and extended to applications like text-to-3D and 3D scene stylization. User studies showed ~81% preference for PERF results over DS-NeRF, SinNeRF, and DietNeRF. PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2024.3387307, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Incremental Registration
head: Incremental CONfidence (ICON) registration, Incremental Image Registration
body: Incremental Registration is a training strategy for joint pose and radiance field optimization that registers camera frames sequentially following their temporal order. It solves the problem of non-convex pose optimization and local minima by leveraging the intuition that adjacent camera poses in video sequences are spatially close. Unlike methods that optimize all poses simultaneously or rely on global initialization, this method incrementally adds frames to the training buffer, initializing new poses from previous ones and freezing older parameters to prevent disruption. Builds on Progressive and Dynamic Scene Growth. The method adapts to the underlying scene representation architecture, primarily implemented for NeRF-based radiance fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting. Both variants follow the shared principles of metric computation, expansion triggers, and re-optimization defined in Progressive and Dynamic Scene Growth. Inputs: A sequence of unposed images \{I1, I2, \dots, IN\}; a scene regressor (NeRF or 3DGS); hyperparameters k (iteration interval), T{freeze} (freeze duration), T{init} (seed finetuning iterations), and T{finetune} (per-batch finetuning iterations). Outputs: Optimized radiance field parameters \Theta and camera poses \{P1, \dots, PN\}. Training Buffer: A set of registered images and their associated poses. Scene Regressor: The neural network (NeRF or 3DGS) representing the scene. Pose Parameters: A 4 \times 4 matrix representing the 6-DoF pose Pi for each image Ii. ICON (NeRF): Jointly optimize NeRF parameters \Theta and poses \{P1, P2\} using the first two frames \{I1, I2\}. ZeroGS (3DGS): Select a seed image I{seed}. Initialize the scene regressor by passing I{seed} to itself: (Xi, Gi; Xj, Gj) = f{SCR}(I{seed}, I{seed}), fixing the camera pose as an identity matrix. Finetune the scene regressor for T{init} iterations (e.g., 500 iterations). Repeat the following until all images are registered: 1. Train: Run k training iterations on the current training buffer. 2. Select Batch: Select a batch of unregistered images I{buf} = \{Ik\}. In ZeroGS, the reference image is selected from registered images that connects to the most unregistered images. 3. Pose Initialization: For each new frame Ii, initialize its pose Pi using the previous pose P{i-1}. 4. Add to Buffer: Add Ii and Pi to the training buffer. 5. Trigger Check (ZeroGS): Add the target image Ik into the training buffer only when the inlier number is larger than the inlier threshold s{inlier}. 6. Optimization: ICON: Freeze the learning rate on poses \{Pi\} and NeRF \Theta for T{freeze} iterations. ZeroGS: Fix camera poses registered in previous epochs and only optimize the camera poses registered in the current epoch. Finetune the scene regressor for T{finetune} iterations. 7. Convergence: Train until convergence or for the fixed iteration count. ICON: After all frames are registered, apply a learning rate decay schedule. ZeroGS: Optimize all camera poses using the reprojection error loss: \arg \min{Xi, Ck} \sum{i,k} \rho(\|d{i,k} \cdot \nu{i,k} - (Xi - Ck)\|2) where Ck is the camera center, d{i,k} is the scaling factor, and \nu{i,k} is the ray direction. Fix the seed image pose and optimize all others. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalregistration(images, regressor, k, Tfreeze, Tinit, Tfinetune, sinlier): registered = [] poses = {} i = 2 if regressor.type == "NeRF" else 1 # 1. Initialization if regressor.type == "NeRF": optimizejointly(regressor, images[0], images[1]) registered = [images[0], images[1]] poses[0] = regressor.getpose(images[0]) poses[1] = regressor.getpose(images[1]) else: seed = images[0] for in range(Tinit): regressor.finetune(seed) registered = [seed] poses[0] = identitymatrix() regressor.setpose(0, poses[0]) while i < len(images): # 2. Train for k iterations for in range(k): trainstep(regressor, registered) # 3. Pose Initialization & Buffer Add frame = images[i] poses[i] = poses[i-1] regressor.setpose(i, poses[i]) if regressor.type == "3DGS": inliers = countinliers(regressor, frame, poses[i]) if inliers < sinlier: i += 1 continue registered.append(frame) # 4. Optimization Phase if regressor.type == "NeRF": freezelearningrate(regressor, ["poses", "nerf"]) for in range(Tfreeze): trainstep(regressor, registered) unfreezelearningrate(regressor) else: freezelearningrate(regressor, ["oldposes"]) for in range(Tfinetune): optimizecurrentposes(regressor, frame) unfreezelearningrate(regressor) i += 1 # 5. Finalization if regressor.type == "NeRF": applylrdecay(regressor) else: globalposeoptimization(regressor, registered, poses) def optimizejointly(regressor, f1, f2): regressor.train() for f in [f1, f2]: regressor.forward(f) regressor.backward() regressor.step() def trainstep(regressor, buffer): regressor.train() for f in buffer: regressor.forward(f) regressor.backward() regressor.step() def countinliers(regressor, frame, pose): # Count pixels with reprojection error below threshold threshold = 6.0 return sum(1 for p in frame.points if reprojectionerror(p, pose) < threshold) def optimizecurrentposes(regressor, frame): regressor.optimizepose(frame) regressor.step() def globalposeoptimization(regressor, registered, poses): regressor.freezeparameters("seedpose") for in range(1000): regressor.forwardall(registered) regressor.backward() regressor.step() k (Iteration Interval): Number of iterations between adding new frames. Value: 1,000 iterations for CO3D/HO3D; 500 iterations for LLFF. T{freeze} (Freeze Duration): Iterations to freeze learning rates. Value: 100,000 iterations for HO3D/CO3D; 30,000 iterations for LLFF. T{init} (Initialization Iterations): Finetuning iterations for seed. Value: 500 iterations. T{finetune} (Per-Batch Finetuning): Finetuning iterations during incremental training. Value: 1,000 iterations for LLFF; 1,500 iterations for Mip-NeRF360. s{inlier} (Inlier Threshold): Minimum inlier count for registration. Value: 5,000. Local Minima: Optimizing poses and NeRF using photometric losses is highly non-convex. Incorrectly optimized poses can mislead the NeRF, causing re-registration on already registered viewpoints. Pose Drift: Errors accumulate during incremental training. Finalization stages are required to refine poses. Occlusion: Avoid sampling rays from occluded regions. A progressive optimization framework that jointly learns depth, RGB, camera poses, and scene representation by sequentially adding frames to the optimization process. It initializes with a small subset of frames (e.g., five frames) and progressively introduces new frames in sequential order. Simultaneously optimizes depth network parameters, RGB radiance field parameters, camera poses \{R, t\}, and scene representation \theta using a combined loss function. The depth rendering function is \hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) di. The optical flow loss is \mathcal{L}{fa} = \left\| \hat{\mathcal{F}}{k \rightarrow k+1} - \mathcal{F}{k \rightarrow k+1} \right\|1. The final loss is \mathcal{L} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}p + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}D + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{FBA} + \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{fa} + \lambda5 \mathcal{L}{fb}. This joint optimization leverages 2D photometric consistency and 3D structural information to enhance depth estimation, pose prediction, and scene reconstruction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides good initialization for camera poses, avoiding the breaking point of 20-degree rotation difference observed in global optimization. Efficient for video sequences with smooth camera motion. Limitations: Not suitable for scenes with large, abrupt camera motions or non-sequential image sets. Requires careful tuning of k and T{freeze}. Incremental Registration was introduced in the ICON (Incremental CONfidence) paper and adopted in ZeroGS. It addresses the limitations of global pose optimization, which suffers from local minima and requires good initial poses. The method leverages the temporal coherence of video data. name: Online Incremental NeRF Optimization
head: Incremental NeRF Training, Online NeRF
body: Online Incremental NeRF Optimization reconstructs 3D scenes from a continuous stream of incoming camera views rather than a fixed, pre-collected dataset. Unlike offline methods such as DVGO or siblings like Dynamic Growth Parameters and Progressive View Synthesis Training, which optimize a scene representation based on a static set of images, this approach updates the representation dynamically as new observations are collected. It enables active exploration by planning next-best views and integrating data incrementally, allowing the model to build 3D representations with limited viewpoints while adapting to real-world navigation scenarios. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A current scene representation (e.g., a NeRF or grid-based model), a training buffer of stored images and poses, and a new incoming image/pose from a sensor or agent. Output: An updated scene representation and a plan for the next viewpoint. Data Structures: Scene Representation: Typically a neural radiance field (MLP) or a grid-based representation (e.g., HashGrid, Voxel Grid). Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Training Buffer: A set of stored images and their corresponding camera poses, which may be bounded to handle large environments. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Perception: The system captures a new observation (image and pose) based on the current scene representation. 2. Incremental Update: The new observation is added to the training buffer. 3. Optimization: The scene representation is optimized using the updated training buffer. 4. Planning: Based on the current representation, the system computes a metric (e.g., entropy or uncertainty) to determine the next best view for future exploration. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 1–4 as new data arrives. Formulas and Parameters: Entropy-based Exploration: The method uses an entropy-based metric to guide viewpoint selection, allowing the agent to explore diverse viewpoints. Thresholds: Specific thresholds for triggering growth or pruning are not explicitly defined in the provided sources for the general online method, but follow the parent family's principles. Typical parameter values are not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Catastrophic Forgetting: In vanilla NeRF, global MLP updates can cause previously reconstructed regions to degrade when new, unsupervised areas are optimized. Memory Usage: Large environments result in a high number of captured images, requiring strategies to discard older frames or manage memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. D = [] # Training buffer of (image, pose) pairs while not terminated: # 1. Planning: compute metric (e.g., entropy) over R using D to select nextview nextview = plannextbestview(R, D) # Not given in the sources. # 2. Perception: acquire image I and pose P from sensor at nextview Inew, Pnew = captureobservation(nextview) # Not given in the sources. # 3. Incremental Update: add to buffer D.append((Inew, Pnew)) # 4. Optimization: perform gradient descent on R using all samples in D R = optimize(R, D) # Not given in the sources. Pcurr = Pnew A strategy for online incremental reconstruction that integrates new viewpoints while preserving previously learned information. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by freezing pre-trained, scene-agnostic decoders during feature grid optimization, which prevents the global MLP updates that cause catastrophic forgetting in vanilla NeRF. Choose this variant when navigating large environments where memory constraints require discarding older frames and maintaining reconstruction integrity across incremental updates is critical. Time Complexity: Depends on the optimization frequency and the size of the training buffer. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of stored views and the complexity of the scene representation; large environments may require discarding older frames to bound memory usage. Measured Performance: Measured performance with specific hardware, resolution, and scenes is not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports active exploration by planning next-best views; adapts to dynamic or large-scale scenes by integrating data incrementally. Limitations: Susceptible to catastrophic forgetting in vanilla architectures; requires careful management of training data and optimization steps. When to use: When data arrives continuously (e.g., robot navigation) and incremental updates are required. When not to use: When a fixed, high-quality reconstruction from a static dataset is sufficient and computational resources allow for offline optimization. The concept of online incremental NeRF optimization arises from the need to adapt NeRFs to real-world scenarios involving imperfect data, large-scale scenes, and incremental reconstruction. Traditional NeRF methods optimize offline on fixed datasets, which is insufficient for active mapping and planning tasks. The method builds on the principles of progressive and dynamic scene growth [8869-progressive-and-dynamic-scene-growth.md]. name: Sparse View and Initialization Methods
body: This family stabilizes Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization under sparse input conditions by injecting structural or visibility information before or during training, rather than relying solely on photometric consistency across views. Methods address poor extrapolation in low-texture regions, blurred geometry, and sparse-view artifacts by regularizing the implicit density and color fields using external priors such as geometry scaffolds, visibility maps, or semantic masks. All methods in this family share the goal of stabilizing the optimization of the implicit function \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) under data scarcity. They achieve this by incorporating external priors—such as pseudo depth maps, inter-view visibility constraints, or semantic segmentation masks—to regularize density distributions and guide initialization. A method for indoor scene free view synthesis that uses a geometry scaffold (pseudo depth maps) and view coverage information to guide optimization. It differs from siblings by specifically targeting the "free navigation" extrapolation problem in indoor scenes using a robust depth loss and dynamic view-coverage-based regularization, rather than static semantic weights. Choose this when robust 3D geometry is required for novel views in indoor environments with low-texture regions. A training procedure that introduces visibility priors to supervise density estimation, computed directly from input images using planar scanned volumes without pre-training. It differs from siblings by estimating pixel visibility between main and secondary views to regularize density, avoiding the need for pre-trained geometric priors or diffusion models. Choose this when input views are sparse (<50–100) and you need to prevent artifacts caused by insufficient data without external geometric models. A method that stabilizes implicit function learning by anchoring the scene structure with COLMAP-generated point clouds and refining optimization weights via Mask R-CNN semantic segmentation. It differs from siblings by mapping dense geometric priors into the implicit space and applying differentiated semantic weights to accelerate convergence and reduce initial MSE. Choose this for sparse view reconstruction (15–20 images) where semantic category information is available and high-fidelity detail preservation is critical. A neural field method for sparse-view Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) reconstruction that models the 3D volume as a continuous attenuation field. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality 3D volumes from a limited number of 2D X-ray projections, addressing sparse-view artifacts like floaters and aliasing. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific formulation as a baseline for differentiable voxel-based methods, often cited for its high reconstruction quality (PSNR) but prohibitive runtime. A frame selection strategy that identifies maximally informative, non-redundant viewpoints from raw video footage to serve as input for NeRF training, addressing the challenge of sparse acquisition in field phenotyping. Sharpness metric (\psi{sharp}): Laplacian variance of the frame. Motion metric (\psi{motion}): Optical-flow magnitude. Coverage metric (\psi{coverage}): Penalizes geometric redundancy via inter-frame homography differences, calculated as the Frobenius norm of the difference matrix \|\Delta H\|F. Score each frame vt using the weighted sum: s(vt) = 0.4 \times \text{sharpness} + 0.3 \times \text{motion} + 0.3 \times \text{coverage}. Apply temporal non-maximum suppression with window size \omega = 5 to the scored frames. The challenge of sparse-view NeRF reconstruction has been a significant focus in computer vision, as standard NeRF requires dense sampling to resolve the ambiguity between density and color. Early works like NeRFVS and ViP-NeRF introduced geometric and visibility priors to mitigate floaters and blurring in indoor and general scenes. Concurrently, methods like Sparse NeRF Reconstruction with Geometric and Semantic Initialization leveraged traditional computer vision pipelines (COLMAP, Mask R-CNN) to bootstrap the implicit representation. In medical imaging, methods like SAX-NeRF have been evaluated for sparse-view CBCT reconstruction, highlighting the trade-off between reconstruction quality and computational cost. In agricultural robotics, VISAR-Guided Sparse Frame Selection addresses the practical constraint of limited data acquisition in field phenotyping.
