name: CLIP-NeRF
body: CLIP-NeRF is a neural radiance field method that enables text- or image-guided editing of 3D scenes by extracting latent space displacements from user input via the CLIP model. It differs from prior editing methods like Edit-NeRF by bypassing per-edit latent code optimization, achieving significant speedups (8–60x) through a disentangled conditional architecture that maps semantic input directly to shape and appearance modifications. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF representation (initial weights and base latent codes), a user-provided text prompt or reference image, and camera parameters for the target view. Outputs: A modified radiance field capable of rendering the scene according to the semantic guidance, and the rendered image. Data Structures: The method relies on a disentangled conditional NeRF architecture. Key components include: 1. Base NeRF: Standard MLPs for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, conditioned on latent codes. 2. Shape Latent Code (zs): A vector controlling geometric deformation. 3. Appearance Latent Code (za or zc): A vector controlling texture and color. 4. Shape Mapper Network: A neural network that takes the CLIP embedding of the input text/image and outputs the displacement for zs. 5. Appearance Mapper Network: A neural network that takes the CLIP embedding and outputs the displacement for za. 6. Deformation Network (Instance-Specific Network): An MLP that takes the encoded position and the shape latent code to produce a deformation vector, modifying the input position before it enters the density network. Steps: 1. CLIP Embedding: Encode the user input (text or image) into a latent vector using the pre-trained CLIP model. 2. Latent Displacement Extraction: Pass the CLIP embedding through the Shape Mapper and Appearance Mapper networks to compute displacements \Delta zs and \Delta za. 3. Latent Code Update: Add the computed displacements to the base latent codes to form the updated scene representation: zs^{\text{new}} = zs^{\text{base}} + \Delta zs and za^{\text{new}} = za^{\text{base}} + \Delta za. 4. Deformation: For a ray point \mathbf{x}, encode it with positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Pass \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and zs^{\text{new}} through the Deformation Network to get a deformation vector \mathbf{d}{\text{def}}. Compute the deformed position \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{d}{\text{def}}. 5. Radiance Field Query: Query the Density Network with \gamma(\mathbf{x}') and zs^{\text{new}} to get density \sigma. Query the Color Network with \gamma(\mathbf{x}'), viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and za^{\text{new}} to get color \mathbf{c}. 6. Volume Rendering: Render the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volumetric rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def positionalencoding(x, L): # x: (N, 3), returns (N, 2L3) encoded = [] for i in range(L): freq = 2.0 i 3.141592653589793 encoded.append(x freq) sinvals = [v.sin() for v in encoded] cosvals = [v.cos() for v in encoded] return torch.cat(sinvals + cosvals, dim=-1) def clipnerfrender(rayorigin, raydirection, clipinput, basezs, baseza, shapemapper, appearancemapper, deformationnet, densitynet, colornet, L=10, numsamples=128, near=0.0, far=1.0): # 1. CLIP embedding (assumed pre-computed or passed as tensor) clipemb = clipinput # 2. Latent displacements deltazs = shapemapper(clipemb) deltaza = appearancemapper(clipemb) # 3. Update latent codes zs = basezs + deltazs za = baseza + deltaza # 4. Sample points along ray tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) tdiffs = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] tdiffs = torch.cat([tdiffs, torch.tensor([1e10], device=tvals.device)]) points = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + raydirection.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(1) # 5. Encode & Deform xenc = positionalencoding(points, L) defvec = deformationnet(xenc, zs) deformedpoints = points + defvec deformedenc = positionalencoding(deformedpoints, L) # 6. Query networks densities = densitynet(deformedenc, zs).squeeze(-1) # (N,) colors = colornet(deformedenc, raydirection, za) # (N, 3) # 7. Volume rendering alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densities tdiffs) transmittances = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-alphas[:-1]), dim=0) transmittances = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittances[:1]), transmittances]) weights = alphas transmittances renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) colors, dim=0) return renderedcolor Parameters: Number of frequency bands (L): Not given in the sources. Deformation Network Depth/Width: Not given in the sources. Mapper Network Architecture: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision and Boundaries: The deformation network modifies spatial coordinates before density evaluation, requiring careful handling of out-of-bounds or degenerate deformations to prevent NaN values in the exponential term. Semantic Alignment: The quality of the edit depends on how well the CLIP embedding aligns with the underlying 3D geometry, which may require careful prompt engineering or reference image selection. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than Edit-NeRF during the editing phase because it avoids iterative optimization of latent codes for each edit. The speedup is reported as a factor of ~8–60 depending on the task. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the base NeRF weights, the mapper networks, and the deformation network. Strengths: Enables global deformation and shape operations with high freedom; fast editing without per-edit optimization. Limitations: Not given in the sources. CLIP-NeRF was proposed by Wang et al. in 2022. It builds upon the latent-conditioned NeRF framework and Edit-NeRF, aiming to overcome the slow editing speed of iterative latent optimization by leveraging the pre-trained multimodal capabilities of CLIP. It is used for text- or image-guided 3D scene editing and generation. name: NeRF-RPN
head: NeRF Region Proposal Network
body: NeRF-RPN is a general framework for 3D object detection within neural radiance fields that regresses bounding boxes directly from the scene representation without rendering intermediate views. It solves the problem of identifying and localizing discrete objects in a continuous radiance field by treating detection as a dense prediction task on a voxelized feature volume. It sets itself apart from instance-level segmentation methods like NeRF-RCNN by generating proposals without refining them into discrete masks or class labels, whereas NeRF-RCNN appends prediction heads to refine these proposals into final instances. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model representing the scene, defined by its density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} fields. Output: A set of 3D Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) with associated objectness scores. Data Structures: The method employs a multi-scale Object-NeRF architecture. This consists of two coupled branches: 1. Scene Branch: Encodes the global geometry and appearance of the scene using a voxel representation of 3D neural volume features. 2. Object Branch: Encodes features for each independent object candidate. Network Topology: The core detection head is built upon a feature extraction backbone (e.g., VGG19, ResNet-50, Swin-S) applied to the voxelized features. The head architecture varies between two main variants: 1. Anchor-based: Predicts offsets relative to predefined 3D anchor boxes. 2. Anchor-free: Predicts bounding box dimensions and center offsets directly, augmented by a centerness prediction to suppress low-quality off-center proposals. Rendering Integration: Unlike traditional 2D detectors, NeRF-RPN operates directly on the implicit 3D representation without rendering images from multiple viewpoints. Training Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: The voxel representation of 3D neural volume features from the Scene Branch is passed through a feature extraction backbone to generate multi-scale feature volumes. 2. Proposal Generation: The RPN head processes these feature volumes to predict objectness scores and bounding box coordinates. For anchor-free models, all output proposals are used to compute the loss. For anchor-based models, a ratio of positive to negative anchors of 1:1 is maintained during loss computation. 3. Loss Computation: The model is optimized using a combination of classification/objectness loss and bounding box regression loss. Common regression losses include IoU loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfrpnforward(scenenerf, voxelfeatures, backbone, rpnhead): """ Forward pass for NeRF-RPN. scenenerf: Pre-trained NeRF model (provides density/color fields). voxelfeatures: 3D voxel grid of neural volume features from Scene Branch. backbone: Feature extractor (e.g., VGG19, ResNet-50, Swin-S). rpnhead: Region Proposal Network head (Anchor-based or Anchor-free). """ # 1. Extract multi-scale features from the voxelized scene representation featurevolumes = backbone(voxelfeatures) # 2. Generate proposals using the RPN head proposals, scores = rpnhead(featurevolumes) return proposals, scores def nerfrpntest(proposals, scores, sceneboundary, nmsiouthreshold=0.1, topk=2500): """ Testing and proposal filtering pipeline for NeRF-RPN. """ validproposals = [] validscores = [] for box, score in zip(proposals, scores): if isinsidesceneboundary(box.center, sceneboundary): validproposals.append(box) validscores.append(score) # Select top proposals on each level of feature volumes independently filteredproposals = [] filteredscores = [] for levelboxes, levelscores in zip(validproposals, validscores): indices = argsortdesc(levelscores) filteredproposals.extend([levelboxes[i] for i in indices[:topk]]) filteredscores.extend([levelscores[i] for i in indices[:topk]]) # Apply Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) based on rotated-IoU to aggregated boxes finalboxes, finalscores = nms(filteredproposals, filteredscores, nmsiouthreshold, userotatediou=True) # Select the top 2,500 boxes with the highest objectness scores sortedindices = argsortdesc(finalscores) selectedboxes = finalboxes[sortedindices[:topk]] selectedscores = finalscores[sortedindices[:topk]] return selectedboxes, selectedscores def isinsidesceneboundary(center, boundary): """Returns True if center is within the scene's spatial bounds.""" return (boundary.minx <= center.x <= boundary.maxx and boundary.miny <= center.y <= boundary.maxy and boundary.minz <= center.z <= boundary.maxz) def nms(boxes, scores, iouthreshold, userotatediou=False): """Standard Non-Maximum Suppression.""" if len(scores) == 0: return [], [] keep = [] indices = argsortdesc(scores) while len(indices) > 0: currentidx = indices[0] keep.append(currentidx) currentbox = boxes[currentidx] remainingindices = indices[1:] remainingboxes = [boxes[i] for i in remainingindices] if userotatediou: ious = computerotatediou(currentbox, remainingboxes) else: ious = computeaabbiou(currentbox, remainingboxes) mask = [iou < iouthreshold for iou in ious] indices = [remainingindices[i] for i in range(len(remainingindices)) if mask[i]] return [boxes[i] for i in keep], [scores[i] for i in keep] def argsortdesc(scores): """Returns indices that would sort scores in descending order.""" return sorted(range(len(scores)), key=lambda k: scores[k], reverse=True) def computerotatediou(box1, boxes2): """Standard geometric computation for rotated 3D bounding boxes.""" return [0.0] len(boxes2) def computeaabbiou(box1, boxes2): """Standard geometric computation for axis-aligned 3D bounding boxes.""" return [0.0] len(boxes2) Parameters: NMS Threshold: Rotated-IoU threshold of 0.1. Top-K Proposals: 2,500 proposals selected per feature level and after NMS. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy NeRF Input: Noisy NeRF inputs can cause misalignment between bounding box centers and mass centers, though anchor-free heads with centerness prediction mitigate this. Tiny Objects: The method may fail to generate proposals for tiny or second-level objects. Rotation Errors: Incorrect rotation predictions can occur in complex scenes. Merging/Missing: Proposals may merge distinct objects or miss objects entirely in cluttered scenes. The performance of NeRF-RPN is sensitive to the choice of backbone and head type. Head Type: Anchor-free models generally achieve higher Average Precision (AP) than anchor-based models across datasets (3D-FRONT, ScanNet, Hypersim) when backbones are fixed. This is attributed to centerness prediction suppressing off-center proposals and the flexibility to handle varying 3D object sizes without limited anchor aspect ratios. Backbone Choice: VGG19 generally achieves better recall and AP compared to ResNet-50 and Swin-S. However, on the Hypersim dataset, which contains noisier NeRF results and complex scenes, Swin-S demonstrates superior recall and AP for anchor-based models due to its larger receptive fields, shifted windows, and attention mechanisms. The inference pipeline filters raw proposals to ensure spatial validity and remove redundancy. Boundary Filtering: ROIs whose geometry centers fall outside the defined scene boundary are discarded. Per-Level Selection: The top 2,500 proposals are selected independently on each level of the feature volumes. Aggregation and NMS: Proposals are aggregated and filtered using Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) based on rotated-IoU with a threshold of 0.1. Final Selection: The 2,500 boxes with the highest objectness scores after NMS are retained for downstream processing. NeRF-RCNN is a proposal-based 3D instance segmentation model that takes a pre-trained NeRF as input. It extends NeRF-RPN by appending a box prediction head and a mask prediction head to refine proposals into final instances. Unlike NeRF-RPN, which outputs bounding boxes, NeRF-RCNN outputs discrete 3D masks and class labels. It is chosen when instance-level segmentation is required rather than just detection. NeRF-MAE is a self-supervised pretraining architecture for 3D radiance fields that utilizes Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to learn robust scene representations from unlabeled data. It sets itself apart from supervised baselines like NeRF-RPN by enabling efficient transfer learning for downstream tasks such as 3D object detection and voxel super-resolution, achieving significant performance gains with fewer labeled annotations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On Hypersim, VGG19 (Anchor-free) achieves Recall@25 of 66.7 and AP@25 of 27.7. Swin-S (Anchor-based) achieves Recall@25 of 69.8 and AP@25 of 13.0. On 3D-FRONT, VGG19 (Anchor-free) achieves Recall@25 of 96.3 and AP@25 of 69.9. On ScanNet, VGG19 (Anchor-free) achieves Recall@25 of 89.2 and AP@25 of 42.9. Strengths: General framework for unlabelled object detection; does not require rendering views; anchor-free variant handles varying object sizes well. Limitations: May miss tiny or second-level objects. Noisy NeRF inputs can cause misalignment between bounding box centers and mass centers, though anchor-free heads with centerness prediction mitigate this. Rotation errors can occur in complex scenes. Proposals may merge distinct objects or miss objects entirely in cluttered scenes. When to use: When detecting objects in a NeRF scene without instance masks or when using a general detection framework. When not to use: When instance-level segmentation masks are required (use NeRF-RCNN) or when self-supervised pretraining is needed for downstream tasks (use NeRF-MAE). NeRF-RPN was proposed by Hu et al. in 2023. It was introduced to enable the detection of all objects' bounding boxes in a scene using a multi-scale Object-NeRF architecture. The method leverages the voxel representation of 3D neural volume features to regress 3D bounding boxes directly, avoiding the need for rendering from any viewpoint. It serves as a general framework applicable to unlabelled objects. name: NeRF-RCNN
head: Instance-NeRF RCNN stage
body: NeRF-RCNN is a proposal-based 3D instance segmentation model that takes a pre-trained NeRF as input and outputs 3D Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABB), class labels, and discrete 3D masks of detected objects. It extends NeRF-RPN by appending a box prediction head (MLP) and a mask prediction head (3D CNN) to refine coarse proposals into precise instance-level geometry. Unlike Semantic-NeRF, which produces only semantic labels, NeRF-RCNN generates discrete instance masks and bounding boxes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained Instance-NeRF model (providing radiance and density fields), and Region of Interest (RoI) proposals generated by NeRF-RPN. Output: For each proposal, class logits, AABB regression offsets, and discrete 3D masks. Data Structures: Sampled Grid: A 3D grid covering the full traceable volume of the Instance-NeRF, uniformly sampled for appearance and density. RoI Features: Extracted via 3D RoIAlign, ensuring consistent feature dimensions across proposals. Box Offsets (t{i,k}): A 6-dimensional vector per class k for each RoI i: (tx{i,k}, ty{i,k}, tz{i,k}, tw{i,k}, tl{i,k}, th{i,k}). Masks (m{i,k}): A 3D binary mask of size m \times m \times m for each class k. Parameters: m=5 for the box head resolution. m=10 for the mask head resolution. \lambda1, \lambda2: Hyper-parameters weighting regression and mask losses. NMS threshold for NeRF-RCNN: 0.15. Score threshold for detection: 0.5. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampling: Uniformly sample appearance and density on a grid covering the full traceable volume of the pre-trained Instance-NeRF model. 2. Proposal Generation: Pass the sampled grid to NeRF-RPN to output proposals and a feature pyramid. 3. Feature Extraction: Extract features using a backbone identical to NeRF-RPN. 4. RoI Alignment: Use 3D RoIAlign to obtain features within the RoI of each output proposal. This extends standard RoIAlign with an additional dimension to ensure consistent feature extraction for each RoI on the feature map. 5. Ground Truth Assignment: For each RoI, set the ground truth box with the largest Intersection over Union (IoU) as its regression target. 6. Box Head Processing: Flatten the aligned RoI features. Pass through a fully connected layer for encoding. Split into a box branch and a classification branch. The box branch regresses the RoI to a more accurate bounding box per class. The classification branch predicts classification scores. 7. Mask Head Processing: Feed aligned features into a 3D CNN (Mask Head). Output L binary masks of size m \times m \times m for each RoI, where L is the number of classes including background. Apply sigmoid activation. 8. 2D Mask Refinement (Post-Processing/Refinement Stage): Apply 2D mask refinement using CascadePSP on the Instance-NeRF results to improve segmentation quality on object boundaries. Compose the refined masks into a single segmentation map to further optimize the instance field. Formulas: Box Offsets: The output t{i,k} relates to bounding box parameters as follows: \begin{aligned} tx{i,k} &= (xk - xa)/wa \\ ty{i,k} &= (yk - ya)/la \\ tz{i,k} &= (zk - za)/ha \\ tw{i,k} &= \log(wk/wa) \\ tl{i,k} &= \log(lk/la) \\ th{i,k} &= \log(hk/ha) \end{aligned} Where xk, yk, zk are center coordinates, wk, lk, hk are side lengths, and xa, ya, za, wa, la, ha are the corresponding RoI parameters. Box Regression Loss (L{reg}): L{reg} = \frac{1}{|Np|} \sum{i \in Np} \sum{k=1}^L p{i,k} L{smooth}(t{i,k}, t^i) Where Np is the set of positive samples, L is the number of classes including background, p{i,k} is the k-th dimension of the predicted score vector pi, t{i,k} is the box offset of class k, and t^i is the ground-truth target. L{smooth} is the smooth L1 loss. Note: For an RoI associated with ground truth class c, only the c-th box regression loss contributes. Mask Loss (L{mask}): L{mask} = \frac{\lambda2}{|Np|} \sum{i \in Np} \sum{k=1}^L p{i,k} Lp(m{i,k}, m^i) Where m{i,k} is the predicted mask of class k, m^i is the ground truth mask, and Lp is the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss. Only the mask BCE loss corresponding to the ground truth label contributes. Classification Loss (L{cls}): L{cls} = \frac{1}{|N|} \sum{i \in N} L{BCE}(pi, p^i) Where N is the set of sampled RoIs, pi is the predicted classification score vector after sigmoid, and p^i is the ground truth target. Total Loss: L = L{cls} + \lambda1 L{reg} + \lambda2 L{mask} Where \lambda1, \lambda2 are hyper-parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfrcnnforward(pretrainednerf, rpnproposals): """ Forward pass for NeRF-RCNN. Args: pretrainednerf: Pre-trained Instance-NeRF model. rpnproposals: List of RoI proposals from NeRF-RPN. Returns: boxes: Refined 3D bounding boxes. scores: Classification scores. masks: Discrete 3D masks. """ # 1. Sample grid from NeRF grid = sampleappearanceanddensity(pretrainednerf) # 2. Extract features using backbone (same as NeRF-RPN) featurepyramid = extractfeatures(grid) # 3. RoI Align roifeatures = [] for proposal in rpnproposals: # Extend RoIAlign with 3rd dimension feat = roialign3d(featurepyramid, proposal.roibox) roifeatures.append(feat) roifeatures = stack(roifeatures) # 4. Box Head (MLP) # Flatten and encode encoded = flatten(roifeatures) encoded = fullyconnected(encoded, hiddendim) # Split into branches boxbranchoutput = fullyconnected(encoded, boxbranchdim) clsbranchoutput = fullyconnected(encoded, clsbranchdim) # Regress boxes # Output is 6 values per class: tx, ty, tz, tw, tl, th rawoffsets = boxbranchoutput boxes = decodeboxes(rawoffsets, rpnproposals.roiboxes) # Classify scores = sigmoid(clsbranchoutput) # 5. Mask Head (3D CNN) # Input: roifeatures masks = maskhead3dcnn(roifeatures) # Output: L binary masks of size m x m x m masks = sigmoid(masks) return boxes, scores, masks def computeloss(predictions, groundtruth): """ Compute total training loss. Args: predictions: (boxes, scores, masks) groundtruth: (gtboxes, gtlabels, gtmasks) Returns: totalloss """ boxes, scores, masks = predictions gtboxes, gtlabels, gtmasks = groundtruth # Identify positive samples (RoIs with largest IoU with GT) positiveindices = assigngtboxes(boxes, gtboxes) # Classification Loss (BCE) # Apply to all RoIs or just positive? Source says N is set of sampled RoIs. # Standard RCNN applies cls loss to all, but reg/mask only to positive. # Source Eq 13 sums over N (all RoIs). lcls = mean(binarycrossentropy(scores, gtlabels)) # Box Regression Loss (Smooth L1) # Only for positive samples lreg = 0 if len(positiveindices) > 0: posboxes = boxes[positiveindices] posgtboxes = gtboxes[positiveindices] posscores = scores[positiveindices] # Smooth L1 loss lreg = smoothl1loss(posboxes, posgtboxes) # Weight by score? Source formula includes pi,k. # Assuming pi,k is the score for the specific class k. # Implementation detail: usually masked by class. lreg = weightedsmoothl1(posscores, posboxes, posgtboxes) # Mask Loss (BCE) # Only for positive samples lmask = 0 if len(positiveindices) > 0: posmasks = masks[positiveindices] posgtmasks = gtmasks[positiveindices] posscores = scores[positiveindices] # BCE loss lmask = binarycrossentropy(posmasks, posgtmasks) # Weighted by score lmask = weightedbce(posscores, posmasks, posgtmasks) # Total Loss totalloss = lcls + lambda1 lreg + lambda2 lmask return totalloss Panoptic NeRF is a method for 3D-to-2D label propagation in urban environments, designed to extend autonomous driving datasets with semantic annotations. It distinguishes itself by using a dual semantic field architecture: one field is rigidly defined by 3D bounding boxes to enforce geometric correctness, while the other is learned to capture semantic distribution. This approach outperforms non-deep learning methods and prior semantic label transfer techniques on the KITTI-360 dataset. Complexity: The method relies on a pre-trained NeRF and a proposal network (NeRF-RPN). The RCNN stage adds a 3D CNN mask head and an MLP box head. The complexity is dominated by the 3D feature extraction and the 3D RoIAlign operation on the sampled grid. Performance: Benchmarked on the NeRF-RPN dataset (1015 scenes from 3D-FRONT) with multi-view images, camera poses, 3D bounding boxes, and 2D/3D ground truth instance segmentation. Strengths: It is one of the first methods to propose 3D instance segmentation for NeRF without utilizing ground-truth information at test time, generalizing to different kinds of scenes requiring only a pre-trained NeRF during inference. It produces discrete instance masks and bounding boxes, unlike Semantic-NeRF. Limitations: Instance label regularization can smooth out detailed structures like thin chair legs or lamp stands, degrading segmentation quality on object silhouettes. The method requires a large NeRF segmentation dataset (e.g., 3D-FRONT) for training. When to use: When 3D instance segmentation is required for a pre-trained NeRF scene, particularly in indoor environments like those in the 3D-FRONT dataset. When not to use: When instance-level information is not needed (use Semantic-NeRF instead) or when computational resources for 3D CNNs and 3D RoIAlign are insufficient. NeRF-RCNN was introduced in the paper "Instance Neural Radiance Field". It builds on NeRF-RPN [23] and imitates the architecture of Mask R-CNN [19]. The method was trained on a large NeRF segmentation dataset built on 3D-FRONT, a large-scale synthetic indoor scene dataset. The authors note that they are among the first to propose 3D instance segmentation for NeRF without utilizing ground-truth information at test time. name: Panoptic NeRF
body: Panoptic NeRF is a method for 3D-to-2D label propagation in urban environments, designed to extend autonomous driving datasets with semantic annotations. It distinguishes itself by using a dual semantic field architecture: one field is rigidly defined by 3D bounding boxes to enforce geometric correctness, while the other is learned to capture semantic distribution. This approach outperforms non-deep learning methods and prior semantic label transfer techniques on the KITTI-360 dataset. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse point-wise annotations, multi-view images, and 3D bounding box primitives. Outputs: A radiance field model that outputs color, density, and semantic logits, enabling 3D-to-2D label propagation. Data Structures: The method utilizes two distinct semantic fields: 1. Fixed Semantic Field: Defined by 3D bounding primitives. It is rigid and guides the underlying density. 2. Learned Semantic Field: A semantic head that learns semantic distribution and improves semantic understanding. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a NeRF-based radiance field. Define 3D bounding box primitives for objects in the scene. 2. Dual Field Construction: Construct the Fixed Semantic Field based on the 3D bounding boxes to guide underlying density estimation. Construct the Learned Semantic Field via a semantic head to capture semantic distribution. 3. Optimization: Perform optimization guided by semantics, where the fixed field enforces geometric constraints and the learned head refines semantic accuracy. 4. Label Propagation: Use the trained model to propagate 3D labels to 2D views. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The sources describe the conceptual dual of semantic fields but do not provide explicit mathematical formulations for the density guidance or the semantic head loss. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Label Noise: The method is designed to handle label noise, low-resolution dense or sparse labeling, and partial labeling. Imperfect Segmentation: It can utilize output from imperfect segmentation models. Domain Specificity: Specialized for urban environments; performance in other domains is not specified. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the KITTI-360 dataset. Outperforms previous methods of semantic label transfer. Strengths: Forces correct geometry learning via rigid bounding boxes; improves semantic understanding via learned head; handles sparse and noisy annotations. Limitations: Specialized for urban environments; relies on 3D bounding box primitives. When to use: When 3D-to-2D label propagation is required for urban autonomous driving datasets with sparse annotations. When not to use: Not specified in the sources. Panoptic NeRF was introduced in March 2022. It specializes in urban environments for 3D-to-2D label propagation, a key task in extending urban autonomous driving datasets. It builds on the concept of using 3D geometry to resolve label uncertainties. The method was evaluated on the KITTI-360 dataset. name: NeRF-MAE Pretraining Architecture
head: NeRF-MAE
body: NeRF-MAE is a self-supervised pretraining method for Neural Radiance Fields that applies Masked Autoencoder principles to 3D radiance and density grids. It differs from supervised baselines like NeRF-RPN by training an encoder-decoder architecture on randomly masked input volumes, which forces the model to learn general-purpose scene understanding rather than task-specific features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D radiance and density grid representing a scene. Output: Reconstructed color and density values for the masked patches, and latent features for the unmasked patches that are passed to downstream heads. Data Structures: Encoder: Swin-S Transformer backbone with four sequential Swin blocks. Block 1 has depth 2 and 3 heads, Block 2 has depth 2 and 6 heads, Block 3 has depth 18 and 12 heads, and Block 4 has depth 2 and 24 heads. Decoder: Lightweight reconstruction network that processes latent features and mask tokens. It incorporates feature pyramids and skip connections from the encoder to preserve spatial information. Numbered Steps: 1. Apply online data augmentation to the input grid using random flip, rotation, and scaling with a 50% probability. 2. Partition the augmented grid into patches and randomly select 75% of them to be masked. 3. Pass the unmasked patches through the Swin-S encoder to extract latent features. 4. Concatenate the latent features with learnable mask tokens and feed them into the lightweight decoder. 5. Compute the masked color reconstruction loss by comparing the decoder output against the ground-truth upsampled grid values at the masked patch locations. 6. Update all network weights using the Adam optimizer. 7. Repeat the process for 1200 epochs. Formulas: The exact mathematical formulation of the reconstruction loss is not given in the sources. The method enforces a masked color reconstruction loss against the ground-truth upsampled grid. Parameters: Total parameter count: 70 million. Masking ratio: 75% of input patches. Ablation studies comparing 65%, 75%, and 85% confirm 75% yields optimal downstream performance. Pretraining batch size: 32. Transfer learning batch size: 8. Optimizer: Adam. Maximum learning rate: 3 \times 10^{-4}. Weight decay: 1 \times 10^{-3}. Learning rate schedule: One-cycle scheduling. Gradient clipping: Maximum normal gradient clip value of 0.1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Changing the learning rate or schedule during the transfer learning phase decreases performance for both NeRF-MAE and the NeRF-RPN baseline. The pretraining learning rate and strategy must be preserved during fine-tuning. Convergence determination is task-dependent: AP50 for 3D OBB prediction, accuracy for 3D semantic voxel labeling, and PSNR for voxel super-resolution. Early stopping is applied based on the hold-out validation set using these metrics. A task to predict 3D Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) by regressing bounding box offsets, objectness scores, and objectness probabilities for each voxel, functioning as an anchor-free Region Proposal Network (RPN). It differs from standard RPN implementations by utilizing the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder rather than training from scratch or using other baselines like NeRF-RPN. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: On the HM3D test set, NeRF-MAE improves voxel super-resolution PSNR from 14.65 to 15.20 and reduces MSE from 0.035 to 0.030 compared to NeRF-RPN. For 3D OBB prediction on HM3D, it increases AP@25 from 0.30 to 0.37 and Recall@50 from 0.31 to 0.40. Strengths: The 70 million parameter network efficiently trains on diverse scenes, and the pretraining weights capture general-purpose semantic and spatial structure that transfers effectively to downstream tasks. Skip connections in the decoder further improve representation learning. Limitations: Performance degrades if the learning rate strategy is altered during transfer learning. When to use it: Use when large amounts of unlabeled 3D data (e.g., Front3D, Habitat-Matterport3D, HyperSim) are available and the goal is to learn robust scene representations for downstream 3D tasks. When not to use it: Avoid when strict computational budgets prevent training a 70 million parameter Transformer-based architecture, or when labeled data is abundant enough to train a supervised baseline directly. NeRF-MAE was introduced by M.Z. Irshad et al. in 2024. It adapts the original 2D Masked Autoencoder framework to 3D radiance fields. The method is designed to leverage large-scale unlabeled datasets, specifically Front3D, Habitat-Matterport3D, and HyperSim, to learn better scene representations for downstream 3D tasks. NeRF-MAE: Masked AutoEncoders for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01300v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Downstream 3D Object Detection in NeRF
head: 3D OBB prediction, NeRF-MAE for 3D Object Detection
body: A task to predict 3D Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) by regressing bounding box offsets, objectness scores, and objectness probabilities for each voxel, functioning as an anchor-free Region Proposal Network (RPN). It differs from standard RPN implementations by utilizing the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder rather than training from scratch or using other baselines like NeRF-RPN. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid representation of the scene, processed through the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder. Output: For each voxel, a prediction vector t, an objectness score c, and a single objectness probability p. Data Structures: The prediction for each voxel is a vector t containing 8 components: t = (x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, \Delta\alpha, \Delta\beta) Where: (x0, y0, z0) and (x1, y1, z1) represent the bounding box offsets (likely defining the center and dimensions or corners relative to the voxel). \Delta\alpha, \Delta\beta represent orientation offsets. c is the objectness score. p is the single objectness probability. Steps: 1. Encode the input voxel grid using the NeRF-MAE pre-trained encoder. 2. For each voxel in the grid, regress the bounding box offset vector t. 3. Simultaneously predict the objectness score c and the single objectness probability p for each voxel. 4. Aggregate these voxel-level predictions to form 3D OBB proposals, similar to an anchor-free RPN mechanism. Parameters: Voxel grid resolution: Not given in the sources. Encoder: NeRF-MAE pre-trained weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The quality of the initial 3D object detector bounding boxes can be inaccurate. Inaccurate poses may require refinement, guided by depth supervision and visual multiview constraints, to ensure robust training. A variant or subsequent step where inaccurate initial 3D object detector bounding boxes are corrected. It improves inaccurate poses by being guided by depth supervision and visual multiview constraints during the training of the scene representation (e.g., S-NeRF). It is chosen when the initial detection quality is insufficient for high-fidelity rendering or when robustness to detection errors is required. The quality of the 3D object detector does not significantly influence the final rendering quality if pose refinement is employed. The method is robust to varying detection qualities; bounding boxes with an Intersection over Union (IoU) greater than 0.5 are sufficient for training. Measured performance impacts on rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM) relative to ground truth bounding boxes when using different detector qualities (mIoU): mIoU 0.79 (default detector): PSNR drops by 0.23, SSIM drops by 0.04, LPIPS does not change. mIoU 0.67: PSNR drops by 0.49. mIoU 0.55: PSNR drops by 0.97. Strengths include robustness to imperfect detection inputs, allowing the use of existing 3D object detectors without strict accuracy requirements. Limitations include the dependency on the effectiveness of the pose refinement stage to mitigate initial detection errors. The task is defined in the context of NeRF-MAE, which applies masked autoencoder pre-training to 3D representation learning for Neural Radiance Fields. It builds on the concept of anchor-free Region Proposal Networks (RPN). The robustness of this approach to detection errors is further explored in S-NeRF, which focuses on neural radiance fields for street views. NeRF-MAE: Masked AutoEncoders for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01300v3, fetched 2026-10-26 S-NeRF: Neural Radiance Fields for Street Views, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.00749, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: RefSR-NeRF
head: Reference-guided super-resolution neural radiation field
body: RefSR-NeRF is a framework that combines a standard NeRF backbone with a Reference-guided Super-Resolution CNN (RefSR-CNN) to synthesize high-quality novel views from low-resolution inputs. It solves the parameter explosion and memory constraints of training NeRF directly on high-resolution data by decoupling 3D field optimization from high-frequency detail reconstruction. Unlike methods that modify the NeRF architecture directly or use generative priors, RefSR-NeRF preserves the standard radiance field while using a separate CNN to inject details guided by a single high-resolution reference image. Inputs: 1. Low-resolution input images with known camera poses. 2. A single high-resolution reference image of the scene. 3. Ray origins and directions for the target viewpoint. Outputs: 1. A high-resolution rendered image for the target viewpoint. 2. Optimized NeRF parameters (density and color networks). Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP mapping 6D coordinates (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, as defined in Specific Model Architectures. RefSR-CNN: Convolutional network containing a detail-dominant information module, a degradation-dominant information module, and a feature fusion layer. Algorithm: The method operates in two distinct stages. Stage 1: Low-Resolution NeRF Training. The NeRF is trained using a modified sampling strategy to reduce memory usage and computational cost. 1. Patch Ray Sampling: Rays are sampled in patches corresponding to the high-resolution input image grid instead of independent batch sampling. This generates a low-resolution image from the NeRF. 2. Optimization: NeRF parameters are optimized by minimizing the difference between the rendered low-resolution image and the ground-truth low-resolution input images. The rendering equation remains: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. Stage 2: Reference-Guided Super-Resolution. The low-resolution image rendered by the NeRF and the high-resolution reference image are processed by the RefSR-CNN. 1. Feature Extraction: The RefSR-CNN extracts features from both inputs. The detail-dominant module captures high-frequency textures and fine details from the reference image. The degradation-dominant module captures structural and low-frequency information from the NeRF-rendered image. 2. Feature Fusion: The feature maps from both modules are fused to reconstruct a high-resolution image. 3. Reconstruction: The fused features are upsampled and decoded to produce the final high-resolution output. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfstage1(inputimages, cameraposes, patchsize): nerfmodel = MLP(numlayers=8, hiddendim=256) optimizer = Optimizer(nerfmodel.parameters(), lr=1e-4) for epoch in range(1000): for patch in extractpatches(inputimages, patchsize): rays = generaterays(patch, cameraposes) sigma, color = nerfmodel(rays) rendered = volumetricrender(sigma, color, rays.stepsize) loss = meansquarederror(rendered, patch) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfmodel def superresolvestage2(nerfmodel, lowrestargetview, refhighresimage, cameraposes, patchsize): rays = generaterays(lowrestargetview, cameraposes) sigma, color = nerfmodel(rays) lowresoutput = volumetricrender(sigma, color, rays.stepsize) refsrcnn = RefSRCNN() featdegradation = refsrcnn.degradationmodule(lowresoutput) featdetail = refsrcnn.detailmodule(refhighresimage) fusedfeat = concatenate(featdegradation, featdetail, dim=1) highresresult = refsrcnn.reconstructionhead(fusedfeat) return highresresult def volumetricrender(sigma, color, stepsize): alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma stepsize) T = cumprod(1.0 - alpha) return sum(T alpha color) def extractpatches(images, size): patches = [] for img in images: H, W = img.shape for i in range(0, H, size): for j in range(0, W, size): patches.append(img[i:i+size, j:j+size]) return patches def generaterays(patch, poses): rays = [] for pixelidx in range(patch.shape[0] patch.shape[1]): origin, direction = poses[pixelidx] rays.append((origin, direction)) rays.stepsize = 0.05 return rays def concatenate(a, b, dim): return stack([a, b], axis=dim) class Optimizer: def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params; self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = None def step(self): for p in self.params: p -= self.lr p.grad Parameters: Patch Size: Not given in the sources. Reference Image: Must be high-resolution and semantically aligned with the scene. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Distortion Rectification: The method adapts the Inverse Degradation Process (IDP) from NeRF rendering to high-resolution images to rectify distortions caused by pretrained models. Memory Explosion: The primary motivation for this method is the "explosion of parameters and computational complexity" when training NeRF on high-resolution data directly. A deterministic supersampling method that enforces sub-pixel multi-view consistency and uses a depth-guided patch warp network. It differs from RefSR-NeRF by not relying on an external CNN reference model but rather on 3D consistency and patch-based refinement. Memory Efficiency: Significantly reduces memory storage requirements compared to training NeRF directly on high-resolution images by using patch ray sampling in Stage 1. Speed: Improves training speed by lowering the resolution of the NeRF optimization phase, achieving a 52 times speed increase compared to standard NeRF and derivatives. Quality: On the NeRF-LLFF dataset, the PSNR is nearly one point higher than the best competing paper at the time of publication. Limitations: Relies on the availability of a high-quality reference image; performance degrades if the reference lacks detail or is poorly aligned. RefSR-NeRF was introduced in 2023 to address the challenges of high-resolution processing in Neural Radiance Fields, specifically the trade-off between image quality and computational resources. It builds on the standard NeRF framework Specific Model Architectures and integrates concepts from Reference-based Super-Resolution (RefSR) CNNs. The method adapts the Inverse Degradation Process (IDP) from NeRF rendering to high-resolution images to rectify distortions caused by pretrained models. It is part of a broader trend of improving novel view synthesis quality through high-resolution processing techniques. Neural Radiance Field-based Visual Rendering: a Comprehensive Review, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11455380, fetched 2026-10-30 Methods and Strategies for Improving the Novel View Synthesis Quality of Neural Radiation Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3382997, fetched 2026-10-30

name: NeRF-SR
head: NeRF-SR Refinement, NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling, Patch-Based Refinement
body: NeRF-SR is a super-resolution method that attacks the problem by deterministic supersampling that enforces sub-pixel multi-view consistency and by a depth guided patch warp and refine network that reuses one high-resolution reference image. It solves the problem of generating high-resolution novel views from mostly low-resolution inputs by exploiting the 3D consistency of NeRF, where an observed pixel absorbs information from nearby views. Unlike Super-NeRF which couples NeRF with a GAN based 2D super-resolution backbone, NeRF-SR stays closer to classical supersampling and patch based refinement. Unlike Mip-NeRF which only considers rendering with downsampled resolutions, NeRF-SR studies how to increase the resolution of NeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Posed multi-view low-resolution images of the target scene; one high-resolution reference image (I{REF}). Outputs: High-resolution synthesized images (In) and depth maps for novel viewpoints. Data Structures: NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) predicting per-point density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and color c(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = (r, g, b) given 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Refinement Network: A U-Net based convolutional network. Encoder: Consists of seven convolutional layers followed by ReLU activation. Decoder: Takes as input the nearest-neighbor upsampled features from previous layers concatenated with both the encoded features of Pe and max-pooled features of \{P{REF}^k\}. All convolutional layers are followed by a ReLU activation. Parameters: Supersampling Rays: Multiple rays are shot per pixel. Not given in the sources. Reference Patches (K): Number of reference patches sampled within a fixed window around the projected location. Not given in the sources. Loss Weights (\lambdal): Reciprocal of the number of neurons in layer l of the pretrained VGG-19 network. Numbered Steps: 1. NeRF Training with Supersampling: Train the base NeRF using the low-resolution input images. During rendering for supervision, shoot multiple rays at each image pixel to enforce multi-view constraints at a sub-pixel level. Supervision: Compare the average color of sub-pixels, referred to as 'average kernel'. Note: The sources mention that while the method assumes an "average kernel" degradation, the actual Blender dataset uses Lanczos downsampling, which is asymmetric. Using a symmetric average kernel for degradation simulation improves results (e.g., PSNR 30.94 vs 29.77 for Blender \times 2 at 100x100). 2. Depth Estimation: Render the estimated depth map d{i,j} for the target view using the trained NeRF. 3. Reference Patch Extraction (Testing/Inference): For each pixel (i,j) in the synthesized SR patch Pe: a. Compute its 3D world coordinate using the estimated depth d{i,j} and camera parameters. b. Backproject this 3D coordinate to the high-resolution reference image I{REF} to find the corresponding pixel location. c. Extract patches around this location to form a set of reference patches \{P{REF}^k\}{k=1}^K. d. Points falling out of I{REF} are discarded. 4. Patch Refinement: For each SR patch Pe: a. Encode Pe and each reference patch P{REF}^k respectively using the encoder (7 conv layers + ReLU). b. The decoder takes as input the nearest-neighbor upsampled features from previous layers concatenated with both the encoded features of Pe and max-pooled features of \{P{REF}^k\}. c. The refinement stage is efficient and introduces negligible running time compared with NeRF rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class RefinementEncoder(nn.Module): """Encoder: 7 convolutional layers followed by ReLU.""" def init(self): super().init() # Channel dimensions not specified in sources [G: Standard U-Net encoder assumed] self.convs = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Conv2d(3 if i == 0 else 256, 256, 3, padding=1) for i in range(7) ]) def forward(self, x): for conv in self.convs: x = F.relu(conv(x)) return x class RefinementDecoder(nn.Module): """Decoder: takes concatenated features, outputs refined patch.""" def init(self): super().init() self.convout = nn.Conv2d(256, 3, 3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): return F.relu(self.convout(x)) class RefinementNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.encoder = RefinementEncoder() self.decoder = RefinementDecoder() def forward(self, Pe, PREFlist): feate = self.encoder(Pe) reffeats = [self.encoder(p) for p in PREFlist] # Max pool at same spatial resolution pooledrefs = [F.maxpool2d(f, f.shape[2]) for f in reffeats] # Concatenate encoded Pe and pooled reference features combined = torch.cat([feate] + pooledrefs, dim=1) return self.decoder(combined) def trainrefinementstep(model, Pe, P, K, window): """Single training step for the refinement network.""" # Sample K reference patches within a fixed window around P # Not given in sources [G: Random crop within window] PREFlist = [torch.randlike(P) for in range(K)] # Apply perspective transformations to account for different camera poses # Not given in sources [G: Standard homography transformation] Pet = Pe Pt = P # Forward pass Prefined = model(Pet, PREFlist) # Reconstruction loss lossrec = F.l1loss(Prefined, Pt) # Perceptual loss using pretrained VGG-19 lossper = 0 vgglayers = getvgg19features() for l, phil in enumerate(vgglayers): lambdal = 1.0 / phil.numneurons # Reciprocal of neurons in layer l lossper += lambdal F.l1loss(phil(Prefined), phil(Pt)) return lossrec + lossper def rendersupersampled(nerf, cameraparams, numraysperpixel): """Render NeRF with deterministic supersampling.""" # Shoot multiple rays at each image pixel # Not given in sources [G: Stratified or jittered sampling per pixel] rays = generaterays(cameraparams, numraysperpixel) # Query NeRF for density and color sigma, c = nerf.query(rays) # Volume render to get pixel color pixelcolor = volumerender(sigma, c) # Supervision compares average color of sub-pixels (average kernel) return pixelcolor def extractreferencepatches(depthmap, cameraparams, IREF, patchcoords): """Extract reference patches using estimated depth and backprojection.""" patches = [] for i, j in patchcoords: # Compute 3D world coordinate from estimated depth and camera parameters # Not given in sources [G: Standard pinhole camera backprojection] x3d = backproject(depthmap[i, j], cameraparams) # Backproject to IREF to find corresponding pixel # Not given in sources [G: Standard projection with reference camera params] uvref = projecttoreference(x3d, cameraparams, IREF) # Extract patch, discarding points out of bounds if iswithinbounds(uvref, IREF.shape): patches.append(extractpatch(IREF, uvref)) return patches Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Arbitrary Scale: The method does not support arbitrary-scale super-resolution. Reference Out of Bounds: Points falling out of I{REF} during backprojection are discarded. Degradation Kernel: The method assumes an "average kernel" degradation for supervision, but real datasets (like Blender) use Lanczos. Training Data: Training data for the refinement network is only available at the camera pose of I{REF}, requiring perspective transformations during training to generalize to other views. Time Complexity: The refinement stage is efficient and introduces negligible running time compared with NeRF rendering. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Blender \times 2 (100x100): PSNR 29.77, SSIM 0.946, LPIPS 0.045. Blender \times 4 (100x100): PSNR 28.07, SSIM 0.921, LPIPS 0.071. Blender \times 2 (200x200): PSNR 31.00, SSIM 0.952, LPIPS 0.038. Blender \times 4 (200x200): PSNR 28.46, SSIM 0.921, LPIPS 0.076. LLFF \times 2: PSNR 27.31, SSIM 0.838, LPIPS 0.139. LLFF \times 4: PSNR 25.13, SSIM 0.730, LPIPS 0.244. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Generates high-quality results for novel view synthesis at HR on both synthetic and real-world datasets without any external information. Outperforms baselines that require LR-HR pairs for training. Works even with only one HR reference. Limitations: Does not enjoy the nice arbitrary-scale property. Requires at least one HR reference image. Origin: NeRF-SR was presented by Wang et al. from Tsinghua University and Kuaishou Technology. Paper: "NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling" published in ACM Multimedia (MM '22), October 10–14, 2022, Lisboa, Portugal. History: It is the first framework that produces decent multi-view super-resolution results with mostly LR input images. Usage: Used for high-resolution novel view synthesis, particularly in VR and AR applications. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 NeRF-SR: High-Quality Neural Radiance Fields using Supersampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01759v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: AligNeRF
body: AligNeRF is a training strategy and architectural modification for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) designed to improve high-frequency detail recovery and mitigate artifacts caused by misalignment from moving objects or camera calibration errors. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF implementations by combining a convolution-augmented architecture with a staged, alignment-aware fine-tuning procedure that utilizes patch-based sampling and explicit spatial alignment matching. Unlike sibling methods that primarily focus on sparse representations or differentiable rendering integrals, AligNeRF explicitly addresses the spatial coherence of high-resolution features through local neighborhood encoding and robust alignment matching. AligNeRF builds on the standard NeRF representation [Parent] but modifies the architecture and training loop to support local spatial reasoning and misalignment correction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D coordinates \mathbf{x}, viewing directions \mathbf{d}, and ground truth image patches. Outputs: Rendered RGB color images. Internally, the model outputs high-dimensional feature vectors during the pre-training stage. Data Structures and Layout: 1. Positional Encoding: As per [Parent], coordinates \mathbf{x} and directions \mathbf{d} are encoded using \gamma(\cdot) with L frequency bands. 2. MLP Backbone: Two coupled MLPs (density F\sigma and color Fc) with skip connections [Parent]. Modification: The output channel count of the final layer in the MLPs is changed from 3 (RGB) to a larger number N (feature space). 3. Convolutional Network: A 3-layer CNN with ReLU activations and 3 \times 3 kernels follows the volumetric rendering step. Padding: "Reflectance" padding is used for inputs to prevent checkerboard artifacts; padding values are removed from outputs. 4. Feed-Forward Perceptron: A final layer converts the CNN feature representation back to RGB space. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-training (Normal Stage): Train the modified MLPs (outputting N-dimensional features) using standard volumetric rendering in the feature space. Use random ray sampling during this initial phase to establish a baseline density and feature field. 2. Architecture Augmentation: After pre-training, append the 3-layer CNN to the rendering pipeline. The CNN takes the rendered feature map (from the N-channel output) as input. The CNN output is passed to the feed-forward perceptron to produce the final RGB color. 3. Alignment-Aware Fine-Tuning: Sampling Switch: Change from random ray sampling to patch-based sampling. Gather a local image region (patch) during each iteration. Ground Truth Patch Size: Sample a larger ground truth patch G of size 48 \times 48 pixels. Rendered Patch Size: Render a smaller patch R of size 32 \times 32 pixels. Alignment Search: Search over every possible subpatch Gi within the larger ground truth patch G to find the best match with the rendered patch R. Loss Function: Minimize the alignment-aware loss L{PM}: L{PM}(G, R) = \min{i=1,...,N} \left( D(Gi, R) + \lambda \cdot D{coord}(Gi, R) \right) where: D(Gi, R) = \|Gi - R\|2^2 is the Euclidean distance between the subpatch and rendered patch. D{coord}(Gi, R) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2} is the coordinate offset penalty, where \Delta x and \Delta y are the horizontal and vertical offsets between Gi and R. \lambda is a regularization weight, empirically set to 0.01. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alignerftraining(gtimage, numepochspre, numepochsfine, batchsize, N): # Helper: Standard volumetric rendering formula [Parent] def volumetricrendering(samples, sigmas, features): deltas = [samples[i+1] - samples[i] for i in range(len(samples)-1)] alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-s d) for s, d in zip(sigmas, deltas)] transmittances = [math.prod(1.0 - a for a in alphas[:i]) for i in range(len(alphas))] rendered = [t a f for t, a, f in zip(transmittances, alphas, features)] return sum(rendered) # Helper: Feed-forward perceptron for feature-to-RGB conversion def featuretorgb(features): return [sum(f w for f, w in zip(feature, weights)) for feature in features] # 1. Initialize MLPs with N-channel output mlpdensity = MLP(outputdim=1) mlpcolor = MLP(outputdim=N) # 2. Pre-training: Standard volumetric rendering in feature space for in range(numepochspre): rays = samplerandomrays(batchsize) renderedfeatures = [] for ray in rays: samples = samplepointsalongray(ray) sigmas = mlpdensity(samples) features = mlpcolor(samples) renderedfeatures.append(volumetricrendering(samples, sigmas, features)) rgb = featuretorgb(renderedfeatures) loss = mseloss(rgb, gtimage) updateparameters(mlpdensity, mlpcolor, loss) # 3. Append CNN and Perceptron cnn = ConvNet(layers=3, kernelsize=3, padding='reflect') perceptron = LinearLayer(infeatures=N, outfeatures=3) # 4. Alignment-Aware Fine-Tuning for in range(numepochsfine): # Patch-based sampling gtpatch = gtimage.crop(size=(48, 48)) renderedpatch = renderpatch(mlpdensity, mlpcolor, cnn, perceptron, size=(32, 32)) bestloss = float('inf') bestoffset = (0, 0) # Search over all possible subpatches in the larger GT patch for i in range(gtpatch.height - renderedpatch.height + 1): for j in range(gtpatch.width - renderedpatch.width + 1): subpatch = gtpatch.crop(i, j, renderedpatch.height, renderedpatch.width) # Euclidean distance dist = sum((subpatch - renderedpatch) 2) # Coordinate offset penalty coordpenalty = math.sqrt(i2 + j2) # Total loss with lambda currentloss = dist + 0.01 coordpenalty if currentloss < bestloss: bestloss = currentloss bestoffset = (i, j) loss = bestloss updateparameters(mlpdensity, mlpcolor, cnn, perceptron, loss) Parameters: Patch size (rendered): 32 \times 32 pixels. Patch size (ground truth): 48 \times 48 pixels. Regularization weight \lambda: 0.01. CNN Kernel size: 3 \times 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Checkerboard Artifacts: Mitigated by using "reflectance" padding and removing padding values in CNN outputs. Multiview Inconsistency: The shallow CNN does not perform upsampling, which helps avoid introducing multiview inconsistencies. Blurry Renderings: If the rendered patch R is too blurry, it may match multiple subpatches equally well. The coordinate penalty D{coord} regularizes this by penalizing large offsets. Time Complexity: The alignment-aware fine-tuning stage involves searching over all possible subpatches, which adds a computational overhead proportional to the number of subpatches in the ground truth patch relative to the rendered patch. However, the CNN is shallow, and the method does not significantly increase training time compared to baseline NeRF. Memory Complexity: The modification increases memory usage slightly due to the larger output channel count N in the MLP and the storage of the CNN weights, but it reduces the total number of parameters compared to a pure high-resolution MLP approach by leveraging convolutional efficiency. Performance: On outdoor datasets, AligNeRF achieves a PSNR more than 3 points higher than standard NeRF and outperforms the best mip-NeRF results. It is particularly effective for high-resolution images and scenes with moving objects. Strengths: Improves high-frequency detail recovery; handles misalignment from moving objects; easy to plug into existing NeRF-like models (point-sampling or frustum-based). Limitations: Requires staged training (pre-training then fine-tuning); relies on patch-based sampling which increases memory bandwidth usage per iteration. AligNeRF was introduced by Yifan Jiang, Peter Hedman, Ben Mildenhall, Dejia Xu, Jonathan T. Barron, Zhangyang Wang, and Tianfan Xue in 2022. It was published at CVPR 2023. The method addresses limitations in training NeRF on high-resolution images, specifically the degradation of quality due to misalignment and the inability of standard MLPs to capture high-frequency details efficiently. It builds upon the mip-NeRF 360 baseline. name: DiffusioNeRF
body: DiffusioNeRF is a method that integrates a denoising diffusion model (DDM) as an initial learning factor to standardize the training of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It utilizes the DDM to learn priors for scene geometry and color, normalizing these fields to achieve higher quality reconstruction, particularly under sparse input views. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on photometric consistency, DiffusioNeRF steers the optimization by backpropagating gradients derived from the diffusion model's likelihood estimates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view RGB images, camera poses, and a pre-trained denoising diffusion model trained on synthetic RGBD data (e.g., Hypersim). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters and rendered novel views. Data Structures: The method builds on the standard NeRF architecture Specific Model Architectures. 1. NeRF MLPs: Two coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (F\sigma for density, Fc for color) taking positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input. 2. Diffusion Model: A denoising network D\theta trained on synthetic RGBD patches to predict noise and estimate gradients of the log-likelihood of the joint probability distribution of color and depth. Algorithm Steps: 1. Diffusion Prior Training: Train the DDM on a large synthetic dataset (e.g., Hypersim) consisting of RGBD patches. The model learns the joint distribution P(\text{RGB}, \text{Depth}). 2. Ray Sampling: During NeRF training, sample points \mathbf{x}i along rays \mathbf{r} using standard stratified sampling. 3. NeRF Prediction: Query the NeRF MLPs to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i for each sample point. 4. Patch Rendering: Render random RGBD patches from the current NeRF state by aggregating the sampled \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i into a depth map and color image. 5. Gradient Estimation: Compute the estimated gradients of the log-likelihood of the rendered RGBD patches with respect to the NeRF parameters using the pre-trained DDM. Specifically, the DDM provides the gradient of the log-prior \nabla{\text{NeRF}} \log P{\text{diff}}(\text{RGBD}{\text{rendered}}). 6. Backpropagation: Backpropagate these estimated gradients to the NeRF's color and density fields to normalize the geometry and color of the scene. 7. Optimization Update: Update NeRF parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) with the combined loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photometric}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{diffusion}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{photometric}} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss, \lambda is the diffusion prior weight, and \mathcal{L}{\text{diffusion}} is derived from the diffusion model's gradient guidance. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for the diffusion prior loss. Not given in the sources. Patch Size: Size of the RGBD patches rendered for diffusion guidance. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Views: The method is specifically designed to handle sparse views (e.g., 3 views) where standard NeRF fails due to ambiguity. Synthetic Bias: The diffusion prior is trained on synthetic data (Hypersim), which may cause a domain gap when applied to real-world scenes. SSDNeRF is a unified framework that jointly optimizes a NeRF auto-decoder and a latent diffusion model in a single training stage to learn generalizable 3D priors from multi-view images. Unlike two-stage approaches that pretrain auto-decoders without diffusion models, SSDNeRF blends generative and rendering biases coherently, enabling robust training on sparse-view data (as few as three views) and avoiding the noisy latent manifolds induced by inverse rendering uncertainty. It supports flexible test-time sampling for both unconditional 3D generation and reconstruction from arbitrary view counts. Time Complexity: Training time is increased due to the additional gradient computation from the diffusion model and the need to render RGBD patches for prior evaluation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF parameters and the diffusion model parameters. Not given in the sources. Performance: On the LLFF dataset, DiffusioNeRF achieves PSNR improvements of 1-2 points over SOTA methods for 3, 6, and 9 input views. Specifically, with 3 input views, it is nearly 1 point higher than ViP-NeRF. It outperforms current methods on the DTU dataset as well. Strengths: Improved geometry and color quality in sparse-view scenarios; reduced artifacts in stratified scenes. Limitations: Reliance on synthetic data for prior training; potential domain gap; increased training complexity. DiffusioNeRF was introduced in 2023. It addresses the limitations of NeRF in handling sparse input views and complex geometries by incorporating generative priors from diffusion models. The method leverages the ability of diffusion models to capture complex data distributions, using them to guide the NeRF optimization process. It has been evaluated on the LLFF and DTU datasets. name: SSDNeRF
head: Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF
body: SSDNeRF is a unified framework that jointly optimizes a NeRF auto-decoder and a latent diffusion model in a single training stage to learn generalizable 3D priors from multi-view images. Unlike two-stage approaches that pretrain auto-decoders without diffusion models, SSDNeRF blends generative and rendering biases coherently, enabling robust training on sparse-view data (as few as three views) and avoiding the noisy latent manifolds induced by inverse rendering uncertainty. It supports flexible test-time sampling for both unconditional 3D generation and reconstruction from arbitrary view counts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of multi-view images \{y{ij}\} and corresponding camera poses \{r{ij}\} for scenes indexed by i and rays/pixels indexed by j. Outputs: Optimized decoder parameters \psi, diffusion prior parameters \phi, and scene latent codes xi. Data Structures: Scene Code (xi): A latent representation for scene i using a triplane NeRF format with shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}. NeRF Decoder (p\psi): A network mapping xi and ray parameters r{ij} to predicted RGB color y{ij}. It applies spherical harmonic (SH) encoding to position features, passes them through Linear layers with SiLU activations, and applies Sigmoid/Exp activations for the final RGB output. Diffusion Prior (p\phi): A U-Net denoising network conditioned on time step t and scene code xi. It takes a noisy code xi^{(t)} and outputs a denoised estimate \hat{x}\phi(xi, t). Parameters: Time Step (t): Sampled uniformly from U(0, T). Weighting Function (w(t)): An empirical time-dependent weighting function applied to the diffusion loss. Minimum Views: Training requires at least 3 views per scene. Formulas: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a simplified variational upper bound on the negative log-likelihood (NLL), ignoring uncertainty in latent codes: \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}i [-\log p\psi(\{y{ij}\}|xi, \{r{ij}\})] + \mathbb{E}i [-\log p\phi(xi)] Where: The first term is the rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rend}, measuring the negative log-likelihood of the observed data given the scene code and ray parameters. The second term is the prior term, measuring the negative log-likelihood of the scene code under the diffusion prior. The diffusion loss approximates the prior term as: \mathcal{L}{diff} = \mathbb{E}{t, xi} [w(t) \| xi^{(t)} - \hat{x}\phi(xi, t) \|^2] where xi^{(t)} is the noisy code at step t and \hat{x}\phi(xi, t) is the denoised prediction. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize NeRF decoder parameters \psi, diffusion prior parameters \phi, and scene latent codes xi for all scenes in the dataset. 2. Batch Sampling: Sample a batch of scene indices, rays, ground-truth images, and camera poses. 3. Rendering Forward Pass: For each scene i and ray j, encode position features using SH, pass xi and r{ij} through p\psi to predict RGB color \hat{y}{ij}, and compute rendering loss \mathcal{L}{rend} against y{ij}. 4. Diffusion Forward Pass: Sample t \sim U(0, T) and apply the standard Gaussian forward diffusion process to xi to obtain the noisy code xi^{(t)}. 5. Denoising Prediction: Pass xi^{(t)} and t through the U-Net prior p\phi to predict the denoised code \hat{x}\phi(xi, t). 6. Diffusion Loss: Compute \mathcal{L}{diff} using w(t) and the squared error between xi^{(t)} and \hat{x}\phi(xi, t). 7. Joint Optimization: Compute total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rend} + \mathcal{L}{diff} and update \psi, \phi, and xi simultaneously via gradient descent. 8. Test-Time Unconditional Sampling: Draw random Gaussian noise x^{(T)} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), recursively denoise to x^{(0)} using a solver like DDIM, then decode x^{(0)} with p\psi to generate a 3D scene. 9. Test-Time Guided Reconstruction: Guide the reverse diffusion sampling by backpropagating gradients of the rendering loss through p\psi to update xi against known observations, enabling reconstruction from arbitrary view counts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def forwarddiffusion(x, t, alphasbar): """Standard Gaussian diffusion forward process [G: Standard DDPM formulation].""" sqrtalphabar = torch.sqrt(alphasbar[t]) sqrtoneminusalphabar = torch.sqrt(1 - alphasbar[t]) epsilon = torch.randnlike(x) return sqrtalphabar x + sqrtoneminusalphabar epsilon def ddimstep(xt, xhat, t, alphas, alphasbar): """Standard DDIM reverse sampling update [G: Standard DDIM formulation].""" alpha = alphas[t] alphabar = alphasbar[t] alphabarprev = alphasbar[t-1] if t > 0 else 1.0 c = torch.sqrt((1 - alphabarprev) / (1 - alphabar) (1 - alpha)) xprev = torch.sqrt(alphabarprev) xhat + c torch.randnlike(xt) return xprev class SSDNeRF: def init(self, numscenes, T=1000, lr=1e-4): """Initialize SSDNeRF model.""" self.numscenes = numscenes self.T = T self.lr = lr # NeRF Decoder: SH encoding -> Linear -> SiLU -> Linear -> Sigmoid/Exp # Architecture details not fully specified in sources self.decoder = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(64, 256), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3), nn.Sigmoid()) self.psi = self.decoder.parameters() # Diffusion Prior: U-Net conditioned on t and xi # Architecture details not fully specified in sources self.diffusionmodel = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(36128128 + 1, 512), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(512, 36128128)) self.phi = self.diffusionmodel.parameters() # Scene latent codes xi self.x = torch.randn(numscenes, 3, 6, 128, 128) # Optimizer for joint optimization self.optimizer = optim.Adam(list(self.psi) + list(self.phi) + [self.x], lr=lr) # Diffusion schedule and weighting function w(t) self.alphas = torch.linspace(1.0, 0.0001, T) self.alphasbar = torch.cumprod(self.alphas, dim=0) self.wt = torch.ones(T) # Empirical time-dependent weighting def render(self, xi, rays): """Render RGB from scene code and rays.""" # SH encoding and ray processing [G: Standard NeRF SH encoding] posfeats = torch.sin(rays) # Placeholder for SH encoding xflat = xi.view(1, -1) yhat = self.decoder(torch.cat([xflat, posfeats], dim=-1)) return yhat def computerenderingloss(self, yhat, ygt): """Compute rendering loss Lrend.""" return torch.mean((yhat - ygt) 2) def computepriorloss(self, xi, xit, t): """Compute diffusion loss Ldiff.""" xhat = self.diffusionmodel(torch.cat([xit.view(1, -1), torch.tensor([t])], dim=-1)) weight = self.wt[t] return torch.mean(weight (xit - xhat) 2) def trainstep(self, batchdata): """Single training step.""" self.optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for i, sceneidx in enumerate(batchdata['sceneindices']): xi = self.x[sceneidx] rays = batchdata['rays'][i] ygt = batchdata['images'][i] # Rendering loss yhat = self.render(xi, rays) lrend = self.computerenderingloss(yhat, ygt) # Prior loss t = torch.randint(0, self.T, (1,)).item() xit = forwarddiffusion(xi, t, self.alphasbar) lprior = self.computepriorloss(xi, xit, t) # Joint update ltotal = lrend + lprior ltotal.backward() totalloss += ltotal.item() self.optimizer.step() return totalloss / len(batchdata['sceneindices']) def sampleunconditional(self, numsamples=1): """Unconditional 3D generation.""" samples = [] for in range(numsamples): xt = torch.randn(3, 6, 128, 128) for t in reversed(range(self.T)): xhat = self.diffusionmodel(torch.cat([xt.view(1, -1), torch.tensor([t])], dim=-1)) xt = ddimstep(xt, xhat, t, self.alphas, self.alphasbar) samples.append(xt) return samples def reconstructguided(self, observations, rays, guidancescale=1.0): """Guided reconstruction from arbitrary observations.""" xt = torch.randn(3, 6, 128, 128) for t in reversed(range(self.T)): xt.requiresgrad = True yhat = self.render(xt, rays) lrend = self.computerenderingloss(yhat, observations) grad = torch.autograd.grad(lrend, xt)[0] xt = xt - guidancescale grad xt.requiresgrad = False xhat = self.diffusionmodel(torch.cat([xt.view(1, -1), torch.tensor([t])], dim=-1)) xt = ddimstep(xt, xhat, t, self.alphas, self.alphasbar) return xt A method that utilizes a denoising diffusion model to learn priors for scene geometry and color, normalizing the geometry and color of the scene to achieve better quality in reconstructed geometry under sparse input views. Sets apart by focusing on geometry normalization rather than joint auto-decoder/diffusion optimization. Choose when geometry regularization is the primary goal. DiffusioNeRF Approaches that pretrain auto-decoders or VAEs without diffusion models, then train diffusion models on the resulting latent codes. Sets apart by separating representation learning from prior learning, which induces noisy latent manifolds with sparse views. Choose when computational budget allows separate pretraining phases or when dense views are available. Time and Memory Complexity: Joint optimization of \psi, \phi, and xi increases memory usage compared to single-stage NeRF due to storing latent codes for all scenes and the diffusion model. Training time is longer than standard NeRF but avoids the separate pretraining phase of two-stage methods. Measured Performance: Demonstrates robust results comparable to or better than leading task-specific methods in unconditional generation and single/sparse-view 3D reconstruction. Scaling: Enables training on as sparse as three views per scene, which is previously infeasible for two-stage methods. Strengths: Blends generative and rendering biases coherently; supports flexible test-time sampling (unconditional and guided); robust to sparse-view input. Limitations: Requires joint optimization which may be computationally intensive; sensitive to the choice of weighting function w(t) and guidance scale in reconstruction. When to use: When generalizable 3D priors are needed from sparse multi-view data, or for unconditional 3D generation. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction from dense views is the only goal and computational resources are limited, as standard NeRF may be more efficient. SSDNeRF was proposed in April 2023. It addresses the issue that previous two-stage approaches (pretraining auto-decoders/VAEs then training diffusion models) induce noisy patterns and artifacts in the latent code due to the uncertain nature of inverse rendering, particularly with sparse-view data. The method was developed during a remote internship with UCSD. It advances the field of 3D learning by providing a general-purpose framework for both generation and reconstruction.
