name: Pool proposer architecture
head: Pooling-based proposer
body: The pool proposer is a trainable neural network component used in NeRF-ID to generate fine-grained sampling positions for volume rendering. It processes coarse features from a previous sampling stage to propose new sample locations, addressing the need for adaptive sampling in differentiable volume rendering. It is distinguished from its sibling MLPMix Proposer by using a bottleneck fully connected layer and sinusoidal positional encoding summation, whereas MLPMix uses a different mixing mechanism. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of Nc = 64 coarse features, denoted as \mathbf{F}{coarse} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nc \times D}, where D = 256 is the feature dimension. Output: A set of Nf = 128 proposed sample features \mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{Nf \times D}. Data Structures: The proposer consists of a single bottleneck fully connected (FC) layer and a positional encoding module. Bottleneck Layer: A linear transformation W \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256}. Positional Encoding: Sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) applied to the input features. Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Apply sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the input coarse features \mathbf{F}{coarse}. 2. Summation: Sum the encoded features with the original coarse features: \mathbf{F}{sum} = \mathbf{F}{coarse} + \gamma(\mathbf{F}{coarse}). 3. Bottleneck Projection: Pass \mathbf{F}{sum} through the bottleneck fully connected layer: \mathbf{F}{out} = \mathbf{F}{sum} W. 4. Proposal Generation: The output \mathbf{F}{out} constitutes the features for the Nf = 128 proposed samples. The exact method for mapping these features back to spatial coordinates is not given in the sources. Parameters: Nc = 64: Number of coarse samples. Nf = 128: Number of fine proposals. Feature dimension: 256. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blind Proposer: Ignoring input coarse features leads to poor performance, showing that a degenerate strategy of constant output is insufficient. No-position Proposer: Ignoring the positions of coarse samples along the ray performs badly on Blender scenes due to insensitivity to feature ordering (e.g., producing identical proposals for colinear rays of opposite directionality), but remains competitive on forward-facing LLFF-NeRF scenes. The MLPMix proposer is an alternative trainable proposer architecture that uses a mixing mechanism instead of pooling. It is preferred over the Transformer proposer due to the Transformer's inferior performance on specific scenes (Blender: Ficus, Blender: Lego, LLFF-NeRF: T-Rex) and unstable training curves. MLPMix and Pool are generally on par, but Pool has higher variance. Choose MLPMix over Pool when lower variance and consistent performance across challenging scenes are required. Complexity: The most expensive operations are applied to each of the Nc = 64 coarse features before the bottleneck. The bottleneck is a single 256 \times 256 FC layer. Performance: Pool and MLPMix tend to be the best performing proposers, but Pool has higher variance and is significantly worse on Blender: Materials and Blender: Mic scenes compared to MLPMix. Cost: The additional FC layer application on Nc = 64 vectors is negligible compared to the 8 FC layers in the NeRF backbone applied to Nc + Nc + Nf = 2048 vectors. The Transformer proposer is more expensive due to the lack of pooling operations. The pool proposer architecture was introduced in the context of NeRF-ID (NeRF with Importance Sampling) as part of a comparison between different trainable proposer architectures (Transformer, Pool, and MLPMix). The training procedure used differs slightly from the original NeRF, employing smaller batch sizes, fewer iterations (around 1.2 billion rays), and ensuring each ray passes through the center of its pixel rather than the corner. name: MS-NeRF
head: MS-Mip-NeRF, MS-NeRF MLP-based Module, Multi-Space Neural Radiation Field
body: MS-NeRF (Multi-Space Neural Radiance Field) is a scene representation method that extends standard MLP-based NeRF architectures to handle unbounded virtual scenes containing reflective and refractive surfaces. It solves the problem of rendering distortion and blurring caused by reflection or refraction, where standard NeRF fails to maintain multi-view consistency due to the geometric complexity of virtual images. Unlike sibling methods like Ref-NeRF, which require manually labeled masks for reflective surfaces and are limited to forward-facing scenes, MS-NeRF automatically handles 360-degree scenes without extra supervision. It sets itself apart by decomposing the radiance field into K parallel sub-spaces, each representing a characteristic field, and integrating them via a learned gating mechanism. MS-NeRF modifies the canonical NeRF architecture by replacing the single density-color prediction with a multi-space feature prediction. The method operates by rendering multiple feature maps from parallel sub-spaces and decoding them into RGB images using a gating network. Inputs: Camera ray parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), scene images (for training supervision). Outputs: Final rendered pixel color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}). The core data structure is the set of K sub-spaces. For each sub-space k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, the network outputs a density \sigmak and a feature vector \mathbf{f}k. 1. Sub-space Feature Vector: \mathbf{f}k \in \mathbb{R}^d, where d is the feature dimension. 2. Density: \sigmak \in \mathbb{R}, scalar density for sub-space k. 3. Gate Weights: \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^K, pixel-level weights for each sub-space. K: Number of sub-spaces. Typical values: 2, 4, 6, 8, 16. d: Dimension of output features. Typical values: 24, 48, 64, 128. d=24 encodes sufficient information; d=48 offers better stability. h: Hidden layer dimension of the Decoder MLP and Gate MLP. Typical values: 24, 48, 64, 128. 1. Positional Encoding: Encode the 3D position \mathbf{x} along the ray using the standard NeRF positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). 2. Multi-Space Feature Extraction: Pass \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the modified density network. Instead of outputting a single density and color, the network outputs K pairs of (\sigmak, \mathbf{f}k) for k=1 \dots K. The density network consists of L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer [Parent, S1]. The feature vector \mathbf{f}k replaces the intermediate feature vector used for color prediction in standard NeRF. 3. Volumetric Rendering of Features: Perform standard volumetric rendering for each sub-space independently to generate a feature map \mathbf{F}k and an accumulated transparency T{\infty, k}. \mathbf{F}k = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{i,k} \alpha{i,k} \mathbf{f}{i,k}, \quad T{\infty, k} = \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alpha{i,k}) where \alpha{i,k} = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{i,k} \deltai) and T{i,k} = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{j,k}). 4. Gating Weight Calculation: Compute the gate weights \mathbf{w} for the current pixel. This is done by passing the accumulated transparency T{\infty, k} through a Gate MLP. Let G(\cdot) be the Gate MLP with hidden dimension h. \mathbf{w} = \text{Softmax}(G(T{\infty, 1}, \dots, T{\infty, K})) 5. Decoding and Integration: For each sub-space, decode the rendered feature map \mathbf{F}k into an RGB color \mathbf{C}k using a Decoder MLP Dk(\cdot) with hidden dimension h. \mathbf{C}k = Dk(\mathbf{F}k) Finally, integrate the colors from all sub-spaces using the gate weights: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} wk \mathbf{C}k Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math class MSNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, K=8, d=48, h=48, L=8, freqbands=10): """ K: Number of sub-spaces d: Feature dimension h: Hidden dimension for Decoder and Gate MLPs L: Number of hidden layers in the main network freqbands: Number of frequency bands for positional encoding """ super().init() self.K = K self.d = d self.freqbands = freqbands # Backbone: 256 hidden layers, ReLU, skip connections from input to every 4th layer [Parent] self.backbonelayers = nn.ModuleList() self.backbonelayers.append(nn.Linear(2 freqbands + 1, 256)) for i in range(1, L): if i % 4 == 0: self.backbonelayers.append(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(256 + 2 freqbands + 1, 256), nn.ReLU())) else: self.backbonelayers.append(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU())) # Heads for each sub-space self.densityheads = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(256, 1) for in range(K)]) self.featureheads = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(256, d) for in range(K)]) # Decoder MLPs for each sub-space self.decoders = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, 3)) for in range(K) ]) # Gate MLP self.gatemlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(K, h), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(h, K)) def forward(self, rayorigins, raydirections, near, far, numsamples): # 1. Sample points along the ray tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples, device=rayorigins.device) zvals = near.unsqueeze(1) (1. - tvals.unsqueeze(0)) + far.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) # (B, N) points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) # (B, N, 3) # 2. Positional Encoding encodedpoints = positionalencoding(points, self.freqbands) # (B, N, 2freq+1) # 3. Forward through backbone with skip connections B, N, = points.shape encodedflat = encodedpoints.view(-1, encodedpoints.shape[-1]) x = encodedflat for layer in self.backbonelayers: h = layer(x) x = h + x if hasattr(layer, 'infeatures') and layer.infeatures == x.shape[-1] else h # Explicit skip connection handling for every 4th layer as per parent spec if len(self.backbonelayers) > 4 and (self.backbonelayers.index(layer) + 1) % 4 == 0: x = torch.cat([x, encodedflat], dim=-1) encodedflat = x # Update for next layer if needed, but standard NeRF skips to input x = h # Standard residual flow # Simplified backbone flow matching parent: input -> layers with skips to every 4th x = encodedflat for i, layer in enumerate(self.backbonelayers): h = layer(x) if i > 0 and i % 4 == 0: x = torch.cat([x, encodedflat], dim=-1) x = h # 4. Get K densities and K feature vectors densities = [] features = [] for k in range(self.K): sigmak = self.densityheadsk.squeeze(-1) # (B, N) fk = self.featureheadsk # (B, N, d) densities.append(sigmak) features.append(fk) # 5. Volumetric Rendering for each sub-space renderedfeatures = [] transparencies = [] # Compute deltas between samples dists = zvals[:, 1:] - zvals[:,:-1] # (B, N-1) dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.full((B, 1), 1e10, device=zvals.device)], dim=1) # (B, N) for k in range(self.K): sigmak = densities[k] fk = features[k] # Compute alpha alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmak.unsqueeze(-1) dists) # (B, N) # Transmittance T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) # (B, N) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) # (B, N) # Weighted sum for feature map weights = T alpha # (B, N) Fk = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) fk, dim=1) # (B, d) # Accumulated transparency Tinf = torch.prod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) # (B,) renderedfeatures.append(Fk) transparencies.append(Tinf) # 6. Gate MLP Tstack = torch.stack(transparencies, dim=1) # (B, K) gateweights = F.softmax(self.gatemlp(Tstack), dim=1) # (B, K) # 7. Decode and Integrate finalcolors = [] for k in range(self.K): Ck = self.decodersk # (B, 3) finalcolors.append(Ck) finalcolors = torch.stack(finalcolors, dim=1) # (B, K, 3) # Weighted sum output = torch.sum(gateweights.unsqueeze(-1) finalcolors, dim=1) # (B, 3) return output def positionalencoding(x, freqbands=10): """ Standard NeRF positional encoding matching gamma(x) = (sin(2^0 pi x), cos(2^0 pi x),...) [Parent] x: (..., 3) Returns: (..., 2freqbands + 1) """ x = torch.astensor(x, dtype=torch.float32) scales = 2.0 torch.arange(freqbands, device=x.device).float() math.pi xb = x[..., None,:] scales[None, None,:] # (..., 3, freq) xb = xb.reshape(x.shape[:-1], 3 freqbands) pe = torch.cat([torch.sin(xb), torch.cos(xb)], dim=-1) pe = torch.cat([x, pe], dim=-1) # Concatenate original x return pe Precision: The accumulation of transparencies and weights can suffer from numerical instability if not handled with care (e.g., using 1e-10 epsilon). Boundary Conditions: The method assumes unbounded scenes. Degenerate Input: If the scene has no reflective surfaces, the extra sub-spaces may learn redundant features, adding computational cost without benefit. The ablation study shows minimal parameter increase (0.5%) but non-zero overhead. Extends the MS module to the Mip-NeRF baseline. Sets itself apart by enabling unbounded scene modeling with minimal parameter overhead. Choose when rendering unbounded scenes with reflections. Link Integrates the MS module with Mip-NeRF 360. Sets itself apart by achieving 4.15 dB PSNR improvement on 360-degree scenes with mirrors without masks. Choose for 360-degree reflective scenes. Link Hybrid grid-based integration of the MS module. Sets itself apart by combining multi-space decomposition with grid-based representations for efficiency. Choose when balancing reflective surface handling with memory constraints. Link Time Complexity: The method adds K parallel rendering passes and decoding steps. The computational overhead is proportional to K. However, since the backbone is shared, the increase is less than K times the original cost. Memory Complexity: Memory usage increases by K times the feature storage during rendering and the parameters of K decoders and one gate MLP. The parameter increase is reported as 0.5% on Mip-NeRF 360 (9.052M vs 9.007M). Performance: On synthetic, real, and RFFR datasets, PSNR is 2-4 points higher than baselines. On Mip-NeRF 360, it achieves 4.15 dB PSNR improvement. Strengths: Handles 360-degree scenes with mirrors automatically; no manual masks required; robust to reflective and refractive surfaces. Limitations: Slightly higher computational cost due to multiple sub-spaces; requires tuning of K, d, h. When to use: Scenes with reflective/refractive surfaces, especially unbounded 360-degree scenes. When not to use: Simple forward-facing scenes without reflections, where standard NeRF or Mip-NeRF suffices. MS-NeRF was introduced to address the limitations of standard NeRF in handling reflective and refractive surfaces, which cause rendering distortion and blurring due to the lack of multi-view consistency in such scenarios. The method was developed as an extension of MLP-based NeRF methods, including NeRF, Mip-NeRF, and Mip-NeRF 360. It was proposed to handle unbounded virtual scenes and was shown to outperform Ref-NeRF, which requires manually labeled masks and fails on 360-degree scenes. The method is part of the broader family of radiance-field optimization procedures that aim to improve novel view synthesis quality. MS-NeRF: Multi-Space Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3540074, fetched 2026-10-26 Methods and Strategies for Improving the Novel View Synthesis Quality of Neural Radiation Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3382997, fetched 2026-10-30

name: NeRDi
body: ## Overview NeRDi is a single-view synthesis method that leverages a pre-trained 2D image diffusion model to provide general image priors, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis from a single input image. Unlike traditional NeRF variants that rely on multi-view consistency or explicit geometric supervision alone, NeRDi minimizes the diffusion loss of rendered arbitrary views under input view constraints. It distinguishes itself by introducing semantic guidance via language embeddings and a geometric loss based on estimated depth maps to regularize the underlying 3D structure. ## How it works Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input image I{\text{in}} of a scene. Output: A trained NeRF model F\Theta capable of rendering novel views. Data Structures: The method builds upon the standard NeRF representation defined in Specific Model Architectures. NeRF Model F\Theta: A differentiable function mapping 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing directions \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Pre-trained Diffusion Model: A text-to-image diffusion model used as a fixed prior. Visual Language Model: A pre-trained model used to extract text embeddings from the input image. Depth Estimator: A monocular depth estimation network used to predict depth maps from rendered views. Parameters: Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Diffusion Steps: Not given in the sources. Frequency Bands (L): As defined in Specific Model Architectures. Steps: 1. Semantic Guidance Extraction: Given the input image I{\text{in}}, a pre-trained visual language model extracts two language guides: s0 (an image title containing overall semantics) and s^ (a text embedding capturing visual clues from the input image). 2. NeRF Initialization: Initialize a standard NeRF model F\Theta using the architecture described in Specific Model Architectures. 3. Ray Sampling and Rendering: For each training iteration: Sample rays \mathbf{r} from the camera pose. Sample points \mathbf{x}i along the rays. Compute encoded positions \gamma(\mathbf{x}i) and directions \gamma(\mathbf{d}) using positional encoding. Query the NeRF to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. Render the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) 4. Diffusion Loss Calculation: Pass the rendered image C(\mathbf{r}) and the semantic guides s0, s^ into the pre-trained diffusion model. Compute the diffusion loss \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}} by evaluating the diffusion model's prediction on the rendered image conditioned on s0 and s^. This step enforces that the rendered view is consistent with the 2D image prior and the semantic content of the input. 5. Geometric Loss Calculation: Estimate the depth map D{\text{est}} from the rendered view C(\mathbf{r}) using a monocular depth estimator. Compute the geometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}} based on the estimated depth mapping to regularize the underlying 3D geometry of the NeRF. 6. Optimization: Update the NeRF parameters \Theta by minimizing the combined diffusion and geometric losses. Pseudocode: python def trainNeRDi(inputimage, diffusionmodel, languagemodel, depthestimator, numiterations, learningrate): nerfmodel = initializeNeRF() s0 = languagemodel.getimagetitle(inputimage) sstar = languagemodel.gettextembedding(inputimage) for iteration in range(numiterations): rays = samplerays(camerapose) xi, di, delta = samplepoints(rays, numsamples) gammax = positionalencoding(xi) gammad = positionalencoding(di) sigmai, ci = nerfmodel.query(gammax, gammad) renderedimage = volumetricrender(sigmai, ci, delta) # Compute Diffusion Loss # Sources do not specify the exact diffusion loss formulation. noisepred = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(renderedimage, s0, sstar) Ldiff = computediffusionloss(noisepred, renderedimage) # Compute Geometric Loss # Sources do not specify the exact geometric loss formulation. depthmap = depthestimator.predict(renderedimage) Lgeo = computegeometricloss(depthmap, nerfmodel) # Total Loss Ltotal = Ldiff + Lgeo nerfmodel.updateparameters(Ltotal, learningrate) return nerfmodel def initializeNeRF(): return NeRFModel() def samplerays(pose): return [Ray(pose.origin, pose.direction) for in range(numrays)] def samplepoints(rays, numsamples): xs, ds, deltas = [], [], [] for ray in rays: for t in linspace(ray.near, ray.far, numsamples): xs.append(ray.origin + t ray.direction) ds.append(ray.direction) deltas.append(t) return xs, ds, deltas def positionalencoding(x, L=10): enc = [x] for i in range(L): enc += [sin(2i pi x), cos(2i pi x)] return enc def volumetricrender(sigma, c, delta): T = 1.0 color = zeros(3) for i in range(len(sigma)): alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma[i] delta[i]) color += T alpha c[i] T = (1 - alpha) return color def computediffusionloss(noisepred, renderedimage): # Sources do not specify the exact diffusion loss formulation. return meansquarederror(noisepred, noiseaddedtoimage(renderedimage)) def computegeometricloss(depthmap, nerfmodel): # Sources do not specify the exact geometric loss formulation. return meansquarederror(depthmap, nerfmodel.renderdepth()) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single View Ambiguity: Without multi-view constraints, the NeRF may converge to incorrect geometries; the diffusion prior and geometric loss are critical to mitigate this. ## Subtopics ### Semantic Guidance Uses language embeddings to guide the diffusion model, improving multi-view consistency. It is chosen when semantic understanding of the scene is beneficial. See NeRDi. ### Geometric Regularization Uses estimated depth maps to constrain the NeRF's geometry. It is chosen when explicit geometric priors are needed to resolve single-view ambiguity. See Geometric Priors and Depth Integration. ## Operating characteristics Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the DTU dataset, NeRDi achieves a PSNR that is twice as high as traditional NeRF. It is suitable for zero-shot NeRF synthesis. Strengths and Limitations: Leverages 2D diffusion priors for single-view synthesis; requires pre-trained models. When to use: Single-view synthesis tasks where multi-view data is unavailable. When not to use: Not given in the sources. ## Background NeRDi was proposed in 2023 by Deng et al.. It was developed to address the limitations of NeRF in single-view synthesis, where traditional methods struggle with ambiguity and lack of geometric constraints. The method builds on the idea of using 2D diffusion models as powerful priors for 3D reconstruction. ## Sources Methods and Strategies for Improving the Novel View Synthesis Quality of Neural Radiation Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3382997, fetched 2026-10-30 Overview of NeRF technology and applications, https://www.jcad.cn/en/article/doi/10.3724/SP.J.1089.2023-00759, fetched 2026-10-31

name: RING-NeRF
head: Distance-Aware Coarse-To-Fine, RING-NeRF pipeline, Residual Implicit Neural Grids
body: RING-NeRF is a neural field architecture that introduces two primary inductive biases: a continuous multi-scale scene representation and a decoder latent space invariant to spatial translations and scale changes. Unlike sibling methods such as Zip-NeRF or Mip-NeRF which require explicit supervision for Level of Detail (LOD) or modify features based on observation distance, RING-NeRF produces intrinsic continuous LOD without supervision, enabling robust generalization to novel, unseen observation distances. It distinguishes itself from I-NGP by using summation rather than concatenation for multi-resolution features, ensuring the decoder latent space remains invariant to LOD, and supports dynamic resolution extension during training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses, image resolutions, field of view (FOV), and training images. Outputs: Rendered pixel colors \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and optimized scene representation parameters (grid deviations \deltai and decoder weights). Data Structures: 1. Unbounded Hierarchical 3D Grid: A pyramid of N grids. The resolution of the i-th grid is f^i b, where b is the base resolution and f is the growth factor. Each grid stores latent feature vectors of size D{feat} (typically 8) at each voxel. The grids are not independent; they form a recursive mapping function. 2. Decoder: A small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and normalization layers. Normalization Layer: Standard, non-learnable normalization applied to the combined feature vector. Random Fourier Feature (RFF) Layer: A linear transformation followed by a sinusoidal activation y = \sin(\mathbf{W}x), where \mathbf{W} is a learnable matrix without bias. This projects the feature into a higher-dimensional space. Density/Color Head: A linear layer transforms the RFF output into a density (or SDF) value and a single color feature vector. Color MLP: The color feature is concatenated with the view direction encoded via Spherical Harmonics (S.H.). This combined vector is fed into a 3-layer MLP to predict the final radiance color \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Representation (Recursive Grid Definition): The scene is represented by a mapping function defined recursively. Let GN be the mapping at level N. G0 \leftarrow \delta0 GN \leftarrow S(G{N-1}) + \deltaN where \deltai is the latent feature grid at level i, and S is a subdivision scheme that increases the resolution of G{N-1} to match the resolution of GN via tri-linear interpolation. The latent vector for a point \mathbf{x} at level N is obtained by interpolating linearly in the cell for each level k \le N and summing the results. This summation acts as a residual connection. 2. Continuous LOD Representation: To allow continuous LOD L \in [N-1, N], a weighting factor \alpha = L - (N-1) is introduced: GL \leftarrow S(G{N-1}) + \alpha \deltaN This allows the model to represent details at fractional levels of detail between integer grid resolutions. 3. Distance-Aware Forward Mapping (LOD Selection): For a sample at distance d from the camera, the appropriate LOD L is determined by equating the volume of the cone cast pixel in contracted space to the volume of a virtual grid cell at LOD L. Let c be the pixel size at distance 1 (derived from image resolution and FOV). Let J(p) be the Jacobian of the scene contraction function at the sample's location p. The volume of the cone in contracted space is V{contract} = (dc)^3 \det(J(p)). The volume of a cell in a virtual grid of LOD L with base resolution b and growth factor f is (\frac{1}{f^L b})^3. Equating these volumes solves for L: L = - \frac {\log \left (dcb \sqrt [3]{\operatorname {det}(J(p))}\right)}{\log (f)} 4. Feature Aggregation: Using the calculated continuous LOD L, the latent feature \mathbf{f} for a sample is computed as a weighted sum of the grid hierarchy up to level L. Specifically, for each level k \le L, the feature is interpolated from the grid Gk and summed. This ensures the decoder latent space is invariant to position and scale, as LOD is exclusively encoded in the grid. 5. Decoding: The aggregated feature \mathbf{f} is passed through the normalization layer. It is transformed by the RFF layer: \mathbf{f}{rff} = \sin(\mathbf{W} \mathbf{f}{norm}). A linear layer maps \mathbf{f}{rff} to density \sigma (or SDF) and a color feature. For SDF-based reconstruction, the SDF output is converted to density using a NEUS-like approach before volume rendering. 6. View Direction Encoding: The viewing direction \mathbf{d} is encoded using Spherical Harmonics (S.H.) encoding. The color feature is concatenated with this encoded direction. 7. Radiance Prediction: The concatenated vector is fed into a 3-layer MLP to predict the final color \mathbf{c}. 8. Volume Rendering: Rays are sampled at N locations along the ray. The rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is computed via standard volume rendering: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp(\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the distance between samples. 9. Optimization (Continuous Coarse-To-Fine): The model minimizes the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss: ||\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})||2. To improve convergence, a continuous coarse-to-fine strategy is used. During cone casting, samples' LOD is clamped up to a maximal LOD l. Grids of level l and above are set to zero and not optimized. The maximal LOD l increases continuously with the epoch n: l = l0 + n{ctf}^n where l0 is the initial number of grids and n{ctf} is a hyperparameter controlling the speed of the process. This approach keeps all dimensions of the decoder latent space supervised, unlike concatenation-based methods where zeroed grids leave dimensions unsupervised. 10. Dynamic Resolution Extension: The grid hierarchy can be extended dynamically. For example, after training a 3-level configuration, a new grid of higher resolution can be added. The new grid is trained while the previous grids and the decoder are frozen. This allows unbounded LOD without retraining the decoder. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def interpolate3d(grid, x, y, z): """Trilinear interpolation for a 3D grid at normalized coordinates [0, 1].""" R = len(grid) sx, sy, sz = x (R - 1), y (R - 1), z (R - 1) x0, y0, z0 = int(math.floor(sx)), int(math.floor(sy)), int(math.floor(sz)) x1, y1, z1 = min(x0 + 1, R - 1), min(y0 + 1, R - 1), min(z0 + 1, R - 1) dx, dy, dz = sx - x0, sy - y0, sz - z0 def v(x, y, z): return grid[x][y][z] c00 = v(x0, y0, z0) (1-dx) + v(x1, y0, z0) dx c01 = v(x0, y1, z0) (1-dx) + v(x1, y1, z0) dx c10 = v(x0, y0, z1) (1-dx) + v(x1, y0, z1) dx c11 = v(x0, y1, z1) (1-dx) + v(x1, y1, z1) dx y00 = c00 (1-dy) + c01 dy y10 = c10 (1-dy) + c11 dy return y00 (1-dz) + y10 dz def computelod(distance, pixelsize, baseres, growthfactor, detjacobian): """Compute continuous LOD based on distance and contraction Jacobian.""" return -math.log(distance pixelsize baseres math.pow(detjacobian, 1/3)) / math.log(growthfactor) def getfeature(coords, lod, grids): """Aggregate features from grid hierarchy up to continuous LOD.""" featdim = len(grids[0][0][0]) feature = [0.0] featdim lodfloor = int(math.floor(lod)) alpha = lod - lodfloor for k in range(len(grids)): if k < lodfloor: feat = interpolate3d(grids[k], coords[0], coords[1], coords[2]) for i in range(featdim): feature[i] += feat[i] elif k == lodfloor: feat = interpolate3d(grids[k], coords[0], coords[1], coords[2]) for i in range(featdim): feature[i] += alpha feat[i] else: break return feature def encodesh(direction, numbases): # Standard Spherical Harmonics encoding. return [math.sin(direction[i] math.pi (b+1)) for b in range(numbases) for i in range(3)] def predictradiance(feature, direction, rffweight, headlinear, colormlp): """Decode feature and direction to density and color.""" featdim = len(feature) rffout = [math.sin(sum(feature[j] rffweight[j][k] for j in range(featdim))) for k in range(len(rffweight[0]))] density = sum(rffout[j] headlinear[j][0] for j in range(len(rffout))) colorfeat = [sum(rffout[j] headlinear[j][k] for j in range(len(rffout))) for k in range(1, len(headlinear[0]))] shenc = encodesh(direction, 4) inputvec = colorfeat + shenc h1 = [max(0.0, sum(inputvec[j] colormlp[0][j][k] for j in range(len(inputvec)))) for k in range(colormlp[0][0])] h2 = [max(0.0, sum(h1[j] colormlp[1][j][k] for j in range(len(h1)))) for k in range(colormlp[1][0])] color = [sum(h2[j] colormlp[2][j][k] for j in range(len(h2))) for k in range(colormlp[2][0])] return density, color def renderray(origins, dirs, near, far, numsamples, lodvalues, grids, params): """Volume rendering for a single ray.""" tvals = [i / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] zvals = [near (1 - t) + far t for t in tvals] densities, colors = [], [] for i in range(numsamples): x, y, z = origins[0] + dirs[0] zvals[i], origins[1] + dirs[1] zvals[i], origins[2] + dirs[2] zvals[i] feat = getfeature([x, y, z], lodvalues[i], grids) d, c = predictradiance(feat, dirs, params['rffweight'], params['headlinear'], params['colormlp']) densities.append(d) colors.append(c) deltas = [zvals[i+1] - zvals[i] for i in range(numsamples - 1)] + [1e10] alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-densities[i] deltas[i]) for i in range(numsamples)] transmittances = [math.exp(sum(-densities[j] deltas[j] for j in range(i))) for i in range(numsamples)] weights = [transmittances[i] alphas[i] for i in range(numsamples)] renderedcolor = [sum(weights[i] colors[i][k] for i in range(numsamples)) for k in range(3)] return renderedcolor Parameters: c: Pixel size at distance 1, calculated from image resolution and camera FOV. J: Jacobian of the contraction function at the sample's location p. f: Growth factor for the grid hierarchy resolution (e.g., 2). l0: Initial number of grids used in coarse-to-fine optimization. n{ctf}: Hyperparameter describing the speed of the coarse-to-fine process. Number of samples per ray: 128. Hashgrid configuration: Pyramid of 9 grids with a growth factor of 2 (in some experiments). Feature size: 8. MLP hidden dimension: 64 for both density and color in few-view setups. No appearance embedding is used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concatenation vs. Summation: Using concatenation instead of summation for multi-resolution features leads to decreased performance in generalization to novel unseen observation distances. Decoder Latent Space: Unlike I-NGP-based architectures, RING-NeRF keeps supervising all dimensions of the decoder latent space during coarse-to-fine optimization, preventing unsupervised dimensions when grids are zeroed. Unseen Areas: During novel view rendering, samples not observed by any training view should be discarded to remove unnecessary noise. Scene Contraction: Scene contraction and distortion loss mechanisms can be disabled depending on the scene type (e.g., object-centric scenes). Time and Memory Complexity: The hierarchical grid structure allows for efficient memory usage compared to dense grids. The dynamic resolution extension allows optimizing memory footprint by only training necessary levels. Training time is significantly reduced compared to vanilla NeRF (0.45h on Nvidia-A100 for 360 Dataset Mono-Scale setup vs 12.65h for NeRF). Measured Performance: On the 360 Dataset Mono-Scale setup at Full Res, RING-NeRF achieves PSNR 28.09, SSIM 0.799, LPIPS 0.157. At 1/2 Res, PSNR 27.18, SSIM 0.804, LPIPS 0.138. At 1/4 Res, PSNR 25.82, SSIM 0.786, LPIPS 0.142. At 1/8 Res, PSNR 24.38, SSIM 0.737, LPIPS 0.167. With Distance-Aware Coarse-To-Fine, it achieves 28.26 PSNR, 0.803 SSIM, 0.155 LPIPS. Scaling: The architecture supports dynamic growth of the grid pyramid size, allowing unbounded LOD. Adding new grids does not require retraining the decoder or previous grids, enabling adaptive resolution. Strengths: Intrinsic continuous LOD without supervision, robust to varying observation distances, efficient training, dynamic resolution extension, and invariant decoder latent space. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the coarse-to-fine scheduler parameters (l0, n{ctf}). Performance may degrade if scene contraction is not handled correctly for unbounded scenes. When to use: Suitable for tasks requiring anti-aliasing, few-view reconstruction, and SDF reconstruction without scene-specific initialization. Ideal for scenarios with varying observation distances. When not to use: If explicit LOD supervision is preferred or if the scene has very limited complexity where a single grid resolution suffices, the overhead of the hierarchical structure may not be justified. RING-NeRF was proposed by D. Petit et al. in the paper "RING-NeRF: Rethinking Inductive Biases for Versatile and Efficient Neural Fields". The work addresses limitations of existing NeRF architectures regarding adaptability to varying observation distances, robustness to limited viewpoints, and extensibility of resolution. It builds on the idea of injecting generic priors (inductive biases) into the NeRF architecture, specifically a continuous multi-scale representation and decoder latent space invariance. The architecture is designed to be simple, versatile, and efficient, competing with state-of-the-art dedicated solutions on multiple tasks. From reconstruction to reasoning: neural radiance fields for comprehensive 3D scene understanding, https://theses.hal.science/tel-05693528v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) RING-NeRF: Rethinking Inductive Biases for Versatile and Efficient Neural Fields, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72761-09, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Sparse and Efficient Representations
body: Sparse and Efficient Representations address the computational and memory bottlenecks of dense, monolithic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by decomposing the scene representation into smaller, localized, or structured components. This family enables scalable training for large-scale scenes and faster inference through spatial partitioning, explicit sparse grids, or generalized 2D projections. Unlike the canonical NeRF which uses a single deep MLP for all queries, these methods distribute the representational capacity across multiple sub-networks, voxel structures, or planar features to reduce redundancy and accelerate convergence. Builds on Specific Model Architectures. Decomposes large-scale scenes into spatial cells with independent MLP submodules, enabling parallel training and data pruning based on visibility. Choose this method for virtual fly-throughs of large-scale environments where standard NeRFs suffer from memory limits and slow convergence. Replaces implicit encoding with a non-trainable 2D image-based representation, allowing generalization to new objects without decoder retraining. Choose this method when training on multiple objects or when rapid generalization to unseen data is required. Uses an explicit, sparse 3D grid in COO format to store non-empty voxels, avoiding hierarchical tree structures. Choose this method for scenes with irregular volumetric data where dense grids waste memory and computation. Replaces a single large MLP with thousands of small, independent MLPs on a regular 3D grid, accelerated by an occupancy grid and empty space skipping. Choose this method when rendering speed is critical and visual quality must remain comparable to dense NeRFs. A few-point volumetric rendering method using a Projection-Aware Sampling network to predict sparse 3D points, reducing sample count while maintaining quality. Choose this method when inference speed is prioritized and a fixed subset of reference views is available. Represents scenes using four 2D feature planes (three spatial, one directional) coupled with a lightweight decoder, decoupling spatial and directional information. Choose this method for computationally efficient volumetric super-resolution and fast training on general scenes. NeRF-XL Multi-GPU Representation Strategy: A parameter distribution strategy for multi-GPU NeRF training where each GPU handles a distinct 3D tiled region with independent hash encoding and density MLP, but shares the color MLP and appearance/camera embeddings across all GPUs. Hash Encoding is independent per GPU, confined within a non-overlapping bounding box. Density MLP is independent per GPU. Color MLP is shared across all GPUs using Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) to ensure consistent color prediction for novel views. Appearance Embedding is shared across GPUs; set to zero during novel-view rendering if enabled during training. Camera Pose Embedding is shared across GPUs if camera optimization is enabled. Unlike independent training where each GPU has its own full NeRF, this method unifies instantiations as a 'single NeRF' with spatially partitioned parameters, increasing model capacity without redundancy. The concept of decomposing NeRF representations for efficiency originated with KiloNeRF, which demonstrated that replacing a single large MLP with thousands of small MLPs could accelerate rendering by three orders of magnitude without sacrificing visual quality. Subsequent work introduced Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation to handle irregular volumetric data more efficiently than dense grids. Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning extended spatial partitioning to large-scale scenes by assigning distinct MLP weights to geometric regions. MultiPlaneNeRF shifted focus from implicit encoding to explicit 2D image projections to improve generalization. ProNeRF introduced projection-aware sampling to reduce the number of required samples. Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields leveraged 2D feature planes to enable efficient super-resolution. NeRF-XL provided a framework for scaling these representations across multiple GPUs by sharing specific components like the color MLP while partitioning others. NeRF-XL: Scaling NeRFs with Multiple GPUs, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73195-26, fetched 2026-10-26

name: AdaNeRF
head: Adaptive NeRF
body: AdaNeRF is a compact dual-network neural representation for real-time rendering of neural radiance fields that reduces the number of required sample points per ray by learning to predict sample importance. It consists of a sampling network, evaluated once per view ray to predict density weights, and a shading network, evaluated only for the most significant samples. Unlike sibling methods such as Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning or Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation which rely on explicit spatial data structures, AdaNeRF supports variable sample counts and single-sample-per-ray rendering without spatial data structures. It distinguishes itself from TermiNeRF by not requiring a pretrained NeRF for initialization, and from AutoInt by using fixed sample locations and a simpler training scheme. Inputs: Ray origin p and ray direction d. Fixed discrete sample positions along the ray (one per cell in the discretized space). Outputs: Accumulated color \hat{C}(r) for the ray. Sampling Network (S): An MLP with 8 layers and 256 units. Input: Ray origin p and direction d. Output: Vector \delta \in \mathbb{R}^N, where N is the total number of fixed sample positions along the ray. Each \deltai represents the predicted importance/density weight for sample i. Shading Network (T): An MLP with 8 layers and 256 units. Input: Positional encoding of the selected sample positions. Output: Density \sigmai and color ci for each selected sample i. 1. Sampling Network Evaluation: Input ray origin p and direction d into the sampling network S. Obtain the vector of predicted densities \delta = [\delta1, \dots, \deltaN]. 2. Adaptive Selection: Determine the subset of indices I to evaluate the shading network based on \delta and a threshold \tau and maximum samples N{max}: Count Ns, the number of \deltai values exceeding \tau. If Ns = 0: Select the index i corresponding to the largest \deltai. If Ns \le N{max}: Select all indices i where \deltai > \tau. If Ns > N{max}: Select the indices corresponding to the N{max} largest \deltai values. 3. Shading Network Evaluation: For each selected index i \in I, evaluate the shading network T to obtain density \sigmai and color ci. 4. Ray Accumulation: Compute the accumulated color \hat{C}(r) using the modified volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i \in I} Ti (1 - \exp(-\deltai \sigmai ti)) ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j \in I, j < i} \deltaj \sigmaj tj) is the accumulated transmittance, and ti is the distance between adjacent samples. Note that the summation and transmittance calculation only include samples in the selected subset I, but the transmittance term Ti implicitly accounts for the culling by using the product of \deltaj \sigmaj for previous samples. Correction based on source logic: The source defines the accumulation over N samples but implies culling. The formula provided in Eq 1 sums over i=1 to N. However, the text states "evaluate the shading network T only for the remaining subset". The implementation detail implies that for i \notin I, \sigmai is effectively 0 or not computed. The formula \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\deltai \sigmai ti)) ci is used, where if sample i is culled, it is treated as having no contribution (effectively \sigmai=0 or skipped in the sum). The transmittance Ti must still account for the density of previous samples to maintain correct occlusion. The source states: "multiply the density \sigma predicted by the shading network with the density \delta predicted by the sampling network". This multiplication is key for gradient flow. 5. Training: The networks are trained end-to-end using a 4-phase scheme. Modified Ray Accumulation: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\deltai \sigmai ti)) ci Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \deltaj \sigmaj tj\right) Where: \hat{C}(r): Estimated accumulated color. N: Total number of fixed sample positions. Ti: Accumulated transmittance up to sample i. ti: Distance between adjacent samples. \sigmai: Density from the shading network. \deltai: Density/weight from the sampling network. ci: Color from the shading network. Sampling Network Loss: l{sampling}(\delta, \sigma, c) = \lambda0 \cdot l{mse}(\delta, \sigma, c) + \lambda1 \cdot l{sparsity}(\delta, \sigma) With \lambda0 = 0.001 and \lambda1 = 1.0. Sparsity Loss: l{sparsity}(\delta, \sigma) = \lambda \cdot \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (|\deltai - 0| + |\sigmai - \deltai|) + (1 - \lambda) \cdot \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} |\deltai - 1| Where \lambda = \frac{tc - t0}{td}, with t0 being the start iteration, td the duration, and tc the current iteration. MSE Loss for Sampling Network: The source mentions l{mse}(\delta, \sigma, c) but does not provide the explicit formula for how \delta is compared to \sigma and c in the MSE term, other than implying it helps stabilize the network. The ablation study notes that removing shading density supervision degrades quality, suggesting the MSE term involves \sigma. Note: The exact formulation of l{mse} is not explicitly defined in the provided text snippets beyond the loss combination equation.. \tau (tau): Adaptive sampling threshold. Typical range swept [0.05, 0.40]. N{max}: Maximum number of allowed samples per ray. Typical values: 2, 4, 8, 16. Learning Rate: Adam optimizer with value 5 \times 10^{-4}. Network Architecture: 8 layers, 256 units for both networks. Collapse to Constant: Without density multiplication in ray accumulation (Equation 1), the sampling network collapses to a constant output because the L1-loss alone is insufficient to stabilize it. Abrupt Sparsification: If sparsification blending is skipped, the sampling network is abruptly forced sparse, losing potentially important samples. No Preprocessing Required: Unlike previous methods, AdaNeRF does not require ground truth depth, pretraining, or special input parametrizations like Plücker coordinates. Unverified code. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is determined by the two MLPs (8 layers, 256 units each). No spatial data structures are required. Measured Performance: On the Pavillon scene (DONeRF), with N{max}=2, AdaNeRF achieves 2.00 samples/ray and 28.25 PSNR. With N{max}=4, it achieves 3.99 samples/ray and 29.33 PSNR. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; no need for spatial data structures; no preprocessing or pretraining required; supports variable sample counts; high quality at low sample counts. Limitations: Requires a 4-phase training scheme; performance depends on the quality of the sampling network's importance prediction; fixed sample positions may not be optimal for all scenes compared to learned positions (though this avoids the complexity of integral networks). AdaNeRF was introduced by Kurz et al. in 2022. It addresses the need for real-time rendering of neural radiance fields by reducing the number of network evaluations per ray. It builds on Specific Model Architectures. It is distinct from TermiNeRF which requires a pretrained NeRF, and AutoInt which uses integral networks with complex training. It is the first neural representation relying on volume integration that can go down to a single sample per ray and supports variable sample counts without spatial data structures. name: Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning
head: Cell-based NeRF, Spatial Data Parallelism
body: Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning decomposes a large-scale 3D scene into a grid of spatial cells, each trained with a separate, lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) submodule in parallel. This approach solves the memory and training time bottlenecks of monolithic NeRFs by distributing representational capacity across the scene, enabling the construction of large-scale NeRFs for virtual fly-throughs. It sets itself apart from siblings like KiloNeRF (which uses a single shared MLP with input-dependent gating) and Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation (which uses sparse voxel grids) by assigning distinct, independent MLP weights to fixed spatial regions, allowing for explicit spatial data parallelism and visibility-based data pruning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of calibrated input images with poses; a scene bounding volume. Outputs: A set of MLP submodules \{f^n\}, one per spatial cell centroid n \in \mathcal{N}; appearance embeddings \{l^{(a)}\} for each image a. Data Structures: Centroids (\mathcal{N}): A set of 3D points n = (nx, ny, nz) representing the center of each spatial cell. Submodules (f^n): Each f^n is a sequence of fully connected layers (MLP) similar to the standard NeRF architecture. Appearance Embeddings (l^{(a)}): A vector associated with each input image a to account for lighting variations. Trainsets: For each cell n, a subset of training pixels/rays assigned to that cell. Algorithm Steps: 1. Centroid Selection: Tessellate the scene into a top-down 2D grid. Fix the height (z-coordinate) of all centroids to a single value, as altitude variance is small relative to latitude/longitude differences in the target scenes. Define the set of centroids \mathcal{N}. 2. Initialization: Initialize a corresponding MLP submodule f^n for each centroid n \in \mathcal{N}. Initialize an appearance embedding vector l^{(a)} for each input image a. 3. Visibility Partitioning (Data Assignment): For each training image a, sample points along camera rays corresponding to each pixel. Identify which spatial cells n \in \mathcal{N} intersect with the ray segment within the scene bounds. Add the pixel to the trainset of only those intersecting cells. Apply an overlap factor (e.g., 15%) between adjacent cells to minimize visual artifacts near boundaries. 4. Spatial Data Pruning (Post-Coarse Training): After an initial coarse training phase, use the inferred geometry to prune irrelevant pixels. If a cell n{occluder} infers geometry (e.g., a wall) that occludes pixels assigned to other cells n{target}, remove those pixels from n{target}'s trainset. 5. Rendering Query: Given a query point \mathbf{x}, direction \mathbf{d}, and appearance embedding l^{(a)}: Find the closest centroid \mathbf{n} = \arg\min{n \in \mathcal{N}} \|\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{x}\|^2. Compute opacity \sigma and color \mathbf{c} using the submodule associated with \mathbf{n}: \begin{aligned} \sigma &= f^{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{c} &= f^{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, l^{(a)}) \end{aligned} Parameters: Overlap Factor: 15% (used to minimize boundary artifacts). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometry Unknown at Initialization: Initial pixel assignment is based on camera positions, not scene geometry, potentially assigning irrelevant pixels to cells. This is mitigated by the Spatial Data Pruning step. Altitude Variance: The method assumes small altitude variance relative to horizontal scale. If this assumption fails, fixing centroid height may lead to poor spatial partitioning. Addresses model capacity limits when scaling Neural Irradiance Volumes (NIV) or similar representations to very large scenes by partitioning the environment into a grid of smaller regions and training a separate NIV per region. This distributes representational capacity to retain accuracy as scene size increases. It balances traditional spatial subdivision with neural network capacity allocation. A key pitfall is that scaling eventually hits model capacity limits, causing increased reconstruction error if not managed. Future directions include integrating level-of-detail techniques to allocate capacity adaptively or select lower-frequency models based on camera position. Time and Memory Complexity: Reduces memory and training time for large-scale scenes by training separate MLP submodules in parallel. Visibility partitioning reduces the submodule trainset size by 10x compared to the initial aggregate trainset. Additional visibility pruning reduces trainset sizes by a further factor of 2x. Measured Performance: Demonstrated on large-scale scenes (e.g., North Pittsburgh). Strengths: Enables scalable construction of large-scale NeRFs; reduces training data per submodule; handles lighting variations via appearance embeddings. Limitations: Model capacity can become a limiting factor for extremely large scenes if not partitioned finely enough; requires a two-stage process (coarse training then pruning) for optimal data reduction. When to Use: Large-scale scenes requiring virtual fly-throughs where monolithic NeRFs are too memory-intensive. When Not to Use: Small scenes where a single NeRF suffices; scenes with large altitude variance relative to horizontal scale. Mega-NeRF was introduced in 2022 by. It builds on Specific Model Architectures. The method was developed to address the scalability issues of NeRF for large-scale environments, such as city-scale scenes, by decomposing the problem into spatially parallel sub-problems. name: MultiPlaneNeRF
head: MultiPlane NeRF
body: MultiPlaneNeRF is a radiance field representation that replaces trainable 3D parameters with a fixed set of n pre-existing 2D images. It solves the long training times and poor generalization to unseen data found in vanilla NeRF by projecting 3D points onto these 2D planes to create a non-trainable aggregate input vector. Unlike siblings like Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning which use spatial hashing, or Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields which use learnable feature planes, MultiPlaneNeRF uses static images as the sole 3D representation, allowing a small implicit decoder to generalize across many objects by simply swapping the input images. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of n 2D training images I1, \dots, In, each of resolution N \times N \times 3. A 3D point \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and a viewing direction \mathbf{d}. For generalization tasks, the camera positions P(Ii) for each image are also provided. Outputs: Volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c}. Data Structures: Images: Stored as part of the model architecture. They are non-trainable and must be stored with the model weights. Aggregate Vector Z: A vector of dimension \mathbb{R}^{5n} for standard rendering, or \mathbb{R}^{8n} for generalization tasks. Algorithm: 1. Projection: For a given 3D point \mathbf{x} and each image Ii, compute the 2D projected coordinates z{Ii} by projecting \mathbf{x} onto the image plane. \text{Pr}(\mathbf{x}, Ii) = z{Ii} \in \mathbb{R}^2 This uses the standard NeRF camera-to-world transformation reversed to obtain world-to-camera coordinates. 2. Color Sampling: Sample the RGB color \mathbf{c}{Ii} from image Ii at coordinates z{Ii}. Since the projected coordinates z{Ii} generally do not align with pixel centers, use linear interpolation to obtain the color. \mathbf{c}{Ii} = Ii[z{Ii}] \in \mathbb{R}^3 3. Aggregate Vector Construction: Concatenate the sampled colors, the projected 2D coordinates, and (for generalization) the camera positions to form the input vector Z for the decoder. Standard Rendering: Z(\mathbf{x}) = [\mathbf{c}{I1}, z{I1}, \dots, \mathbf{c}{In}, z{In}] \in \mathbb{R}^{5n} Generalization Rendering: Z(\mathbf{x}) = [\mathbf{c}{I1}, z{I1}, P(I1), \dots, \mathbf{c}{In}, z{In}, P(In)] \in \mathbb{R}^{8n} where P(Ii) is the position of the camera dedicated to image Ii. 4. Implicit Decoding: Pass Z(\mathbf{x}) to the implicit decoder network F{\text{MultiPlaneNeRF}} along with the viewing direction \mathbf{d} to predict density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. F{\text{MultiPlaneNeRF}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, I1, \dots, In; \Theta) = (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) For generalization: F{\text{MultiPlaneNeRF}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}; \Theta, I1, P(I1), \dots, In, P(In)) = (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) The decoder architecture is similar to vanilla NeRF, using approximately 0.5M parameters. 5. Rendering: Compute the pixel color using the standard volumetric rendering procedure, which is directly taken from vanilla NeRF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projectpointtoimage(x3d, cameramatrix): """ Projects a 3D point x3d (3,) onto the 2D image plane using the camera matrix. Returns 2D coordinates (2,). Standard NeRF world-to-camera projection. """ # Apply inverse camera matrix to x3d, then perspective divide by z camcoords = np.dot(np.linalg.inv(cameramatrix), np.append(x3d, 1.0)) uv = camcoords[:2] / camcoords[2] return uv def sampleimagecolor(image, uvcoords): """ Samples RGB color from image (H, W, 3) at normalized uvcoords (2,). Uses linear interpolation. """ # Bilinear interpolation of image at uvcoords h, w, = image.shape u, v = uvcoords u = np.clip(u, 0, w - 1) v = np.clip(v, 0, h - 1) u0, v0 = int(np.floor(u)), int(np.floor(v)) u1, v1 = min(u0 + 1, w - 1), min(v0 + 1, h - 1) du, dv = u - u0, v - v0 c00 = image[v0, u0] c01 = image[v0, u1] c10 = image[v1, u0] c11 = image[v1, u1] return (1 - du) (1 - dv) c00 + du (1 - dv) c01 + (1 - du) dv c10 + du dv c11 def decoderforward(Z, d): """ Standard MLP decoder similar to vanilla NeRF. Takes aggregate vector Z and viewing direction d. Returns density sigma and color c. """ # Concatenate Z and d, pass through standard MLP layers inputvec = np.concatenate([Z, d]) h = np.maximum(0, np.dot(inputvec, W1) + b1) # ReLU linear layer h = np.maximum(0, np.dot(h, W2) + b2) # ReLU linear layer sigma = np.exp(np.dot(h, W3) + b3) # Output density c = np.tanh(np.dot(h, W4) + b4) # Output color return sigma, c def buildaggregatevector(x3d, images, camerapositions=None): """ Builds the aggregate input vector Z for the MultiPlaneNeRF decoder. Args: x3d: 3D point (3,) images: List of n images, each (H, W, 3) camerapositions: Optional list of n camera matrices (3x4) for generalization Returns: Z: Aggregate vector (5n,) or (8n,) """ n = len(images) components = [] for i in range(n): Ii = images[i] # 1. Project 3D point to 2D image coordinates zIi = projectpointtoimage(x3d, camerapositions[i]) # 2. Sample RGB color at projected coordinates cIi = sampleimagecolor(Ii, zIi) # 3. Concatenate color and 2D coordinates components.append(np.concatenate([cIi, zIi])) # 4. If generalization mode, add camera position if camerapositions is not None: PIi = camerapositions[i] components[-1] = np.concatenate([cIi, zIi, PIi]) Z = np.concatenate(components) return Z def multiplanenerfforward(x3d, d, images, camerapositions=None): """ Forward pass of MultiPlaneNeRF. Args: x3d: 3D point (3,) d: Viewing direction (3,) images: List of n images camerapositions: Optional list of n camera matrices Returns: sigma: Volume density (scalar) c: RGB color (3,) """ # Build aggregate vector Z = buildaggregatevector(x3d, images, camerapositions) # Decode sigma, c = decoderforward(Z, d) return sigma, c Parameters: n: Number of images in the representation. Increasing n improves results but increases memory and computation. N: Resolution of the input images (N \times N \times 3). Decoder Parameters \Theta: Approximately 0.5M parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training on Large Datasets: Training on a large dataset results in slightly worse rendering quality compared to training each object separately. Generalization: Camera positions P(Ii) are only added to the input for generalization tasks; they do not change rendering results for single-object training. Interpolation: The model can interpolate between objects by mixing images from two different objects (using k images from the first and n-k from the second). A GAN-based generative model that uses the MultiPlaneNeRF decoder as a component, replacing the TriPlane decoder in EG3D. It produces interpretable representations since the planes are 2D images with three RGB channels. Training the decoder on a large dataset (e.g., ShapeNet) to generalize across many objects and classes, allowing the model to render unseen objects by simply changing the input images without retraining the decoder. Time and Memory Complexity: The model uses fewer parameters than other hybrid methods because the 3D representation is non-trainable and stored as images. The decoder is small (~0.5M parameters). Measured Performance: MultiPlaneNeRF achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art models on synthesizing new views. It obtains slightly better results than auto-encoder architectures on test sets. Scaling: Results improve when the number of images in the representation increases. Better results are also obtained when the resolution of training images matches the expected image resolution. Strengths: Non-trainable 3D representation allows for fast training of the decoder and generalization to unseen objects by swapping images. Limitations: Trade-off between rendering quality and generalization; training on a large dataset yields slightly worse quality than training each object separately. MultiPlaneNeRF was introduced to address the limitations of vanilla NeRF, specifically long training times and poor generalization to unseen data. It was proposed as a method that works directly on 2D images, projecting 3D points to produce non-trainable representations. The model was evaluated on classical rendering tasks and generalization tasks. It has been used as a component in generative models like MultiPlaneGAN, an analog of EG3D GAN. name: Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation
body: A Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) is a voxel-based representation of a 3D scene or object that stores density and view-dependent radiance colors in a sparse grid structure. It serves as an efficient alternative to dense neural radiance fields (NeRFs) by mapping the continuous MLP-based representation into discrete, sparse voxels, enabling faster optimization and rendering while maintaining high visual fidelity. Unlike its siblings, SRF explicitly leverages the Coordinate Format (COO) to handle extreme sparsity (~99%), making it suitable for large-scale datasets and multi-resolution applications. Inputs: A set of posed 2D images of a scene or object. Outputs: A sparse set of voxel tuples containing density and radiance features. Data Structures: The SRF is defined as a voxel grid of dimension 1+d, where d is the dimension of the radiance colors and 1 dimension is for density. Grid Size: H \times H \times H in each of the three spatial dimensions. Feature Vector: Each voxel (i, j, k) stores a feature vector f \in \mathbb{R}^{1+d}. The first component is the density \alpha{i,j,k} \in \mathbb{R}. The remaining d components are the radiance colors \rho{i,j,k} \in \mathbb{R}^d. Storage Format: The SRF is stored in Coordinate Format (COO) as a set of M tuples: X{\text{non-empty}} = \{(cm, fm)\}{m=1}^M where cm = (i, j, k) are positive integer coordinates (c \in \mathbb{Z}^+) and fm is the feature vector at that location. The ordering of tuples is arbitrary. Parameters: Resolution (H): The grid size in each dimension. Typical values used in SPARF are H \in \{32, 128, 512\}. Radiance Dimension (d): For view-dependent SRF using 4 spherical harmonics (SH) factors per RGB channel: d = 3 \times 4 = 12. For fixed RGB colors: d = 3 \times 1 = 3. Note: Using 4 SH components reduces optimization space by 40% and time by 10% compared to 9 SH components, while maintaining PSNR. Using raw RGB reduces PSNR by ~1 dB but saves 80% space and 20% time. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a sparse grid of size H \times H \times H. 2. Optimization: Optimize the SRF parameters (density \alpha and radiance \rho) using posed images. This involves minimizing the difference between rendered images and ground truth images. Implementation Note: The optimization typically uses an adaptation of Plenoxels. Running Plenoxels for fewer iterations (e.g., 3 \times 12k) reduces time by 30% with negligible PSNR loss. 3. Sparsity Handling: The resulting grid is highly sparse (~99% empty). Only non-empty voxels are stored in the COO format. 4. Rendering: To render a view, cast rays through the sparse grid. For each ray, sample the density and radiance from the stored COO tuples. Compute the volume rendering integral using standard differentiable volume rendering equations. 5. Mesh Extraction: Since SRFs lie on a 3D voxel space, meshes can be extracted directly using a single pass of Marching Cubes on the density field \alpha. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low-Density Voxels: Non-empty voxels may have low densities that do not significantly affect volume rendering but contain random colors. These can confuse the network during training. Vanishing Gradients: High sparsity (~99%) and misalignment between input and output SRF coordinates (caused by sparse convolutional strides and pruning) can lead to vanishing gradients. Precision: Small errors in predicting densities or radiance colors can result in large distortions in rendered images. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of non-empty voxels M rather than H^3. The COO format stores only M tuples, each containing coordinates and 1+d features. Time Complexity: Rendering and optimization are faster than dense NeRFs due to the reduced number of active voxels. Using 4 SH components reduces optimization time by 10% compared to 9 SH components. Reducing Plenoxels iterations reduces time by 30%. Performance: SPARF achieves high average PSNR across one million shapes at resolutions 32, 128, and 512. Strengths: Efficient optimization, easy mesh extraction, scalable to large datasets, supports multi-resolution. Limitations: Sensitive to sparsity-induced gradient issues, potential for noisy color information in low-density voxels. When to use: Large-scale 3D object reconstruction, multi-resolution applications, scenarios requiring fast mesh extraction. When not to use: Scenes with very complex, continuous geometry where sparse voxelization loses detail, or when strict memory limits prevent storing even sparse COO structures for very large H. The Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) was introduced in the context of the SPARF dataset, which contains one million 3D sparse radiance fields. The concept builds on Plenoxels, which introduced view-dependent radiance using spherical harmonics in a voxel grid. SPARF adapted Plenoxels to scale up to a million shapes, utilizing multiple resolutions (32, 128, 512) and specialized losses to handle challenges like vanishing gradients and noisy low-density voxels. The representation allows for straightforward mesh extraction via Marching Cubes. name: KiloNeRF
head: KiloNeRF: Speeding up Neural Radiance Fields with Thousands of Tiny MLPs
body: KiloNeRF accelerates Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering by three orders of magnitude without sacrificing visual quality by replacing the single large MLP with thousands of independent, small MLPs arranged on a regular 3D grid. Unlike the original NeRF, which queries one deep network for every sample point, KiloNeRF maps 3D positions to specific grid cells, each governed by a lightweight network. This spatial decomposition allows for significant speedups compared to both the original NeRF and other sparse methods like Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses; an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defined by minimum bounds \mathbf{b}{min} and maximum bounds \mathbf{b}{max} enclosing the scene. Outputs: A set of N{cells} independent MLPs (the "KiloNeRF" model) and an occupancy grid for acceleration. During inference, given a ray \mathbf{r}, the output is the synthesized pixel color C(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: 1. Network Grid: A uniform 3D grid of resolution \mathbf{r} = (rx, ry, rz) within the AABB. Each cell index \mathbf{i} = (ix, iy, iz) corresponds to a unique MLP with parameters \theta{\mathbf{i}}. The maximum resolution is 16 \times 16 \times 16 = 4096 networks. 2. Occupancy Grid: A second uniform grid with resolution 16 \times \mathbf{r} (upper bounded by 256 \times 256 \times 256). Each cell in this grid is populated with a binary value indicating whether the scene has any content within that cell. 3. Tiny MLP Architecture: Input: Concatenation of positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Layers: 4 hidden layers, each with 32 hidden units. Activations: All affine layers use ReLU, except: The input to the penultimate hidden layer has no activation. The output layer for RGB color \mathbf{c} uses Sigmoid activation. Structure: No skip connections. The viewing direction \mathbf{d} is provided as an additional input to the last hidden layer. Outputs: Density \sigma (scalar, independent of \mathbf{d}) and Color \mathbf{c} (RGB vector). Numbered Steps: Stage 1: Teacher Training 1. Train a standard NeRF (the "teacher") on the training images for up to 600,000 iterations. This teacher uses hierarchical sampling and a deep MLP (10 hidden layers, 256/128 units). Stage 2: Occupancy Grid Extraction 2. Instantiate the occupancy grid with resolution 16 \times \mathbf{r}. 3. For each cell in the occupancy grid, sample densities on a 3 \times 3 \times 3 subgrid using the teacher NeRF. 4. Mark a cell as occupied if any evaluated density \sigma > \tau, where \tau = 10. Stage 3: Distillation Training 5. Initialize the KiloNeRF networks \theta{\mathbf{i}} randomly or with small values. 6. For each network \mathbf{i}, randomly sample a batch of 3D points \mathbf{x} inside its corresponding grid cell. 7. Augment these points with viewing directions \mathbf{d} drawn randomly from the unit sphere. 8. Query the teacher NeRF to obtain target density \sigma{teacher} and color \mathbf{c}{teacher}. 9. Query the student KiloNeRF network \theta{\mathbf{i}} to obtain \sigma{student} and \mathbf{c}{student}. 10. Convert densities to alpha values using \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \delta), where \delta is a fixed distance between samples (e.g., derived from the grid cell size or a constant). 11. Optimize \theta{\mathbf{i}} using an L2 loss between the student's (\alpha{student}, \mathbf{c}{student}) and the teacher's (\alpha{teacher}, \mathbf{c}{teacher}). 12. Apply L2 regularization with weight \lambda = 10^{-6} to the weights and biases of the last two layers of the student networks. 13. Repeat for 150,000 iterations. Stage 4: Fine-tuning 14. Fine-tune all KiloNeRF networks on the original training images using photometric loss (L2 loss between rendered color and ground truth) for 1,000,000 iterations. 15. Use the occupancy grid for Empty Space Skipping (ESS) during this stage. Inference (Rendering): 16. For each ray \mathbf{r}, sample up to K=384 equidistant points. 17. Empty Space Skipping (ESS): For each sample point \mathbf{x}, determine its occupancy grid cell. Only query the KiloNeRF network if the cell is occupied. 18. Network Selection: Determine the network index \mathbf{i} for point \mathbf{x} using spatial binning: \mathbf{i} = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}{min}}{(\mathbf{b}{max} - \mathbf{b}{min}) / \mathbf{r}} \right\rfloor where operations are element-wise. 19. Evaluate the selected network: (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) = f{\theta{\mathbf{i}}}(\gamma(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}). 20. Early Ray Termination (ERT): During inference, group queries by distance from the camera. If the transmittance Ti < \epsilon (where \epsilon = 0.01), stop sampling further points for that ray. 21. Compute pixel color via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, bmin, bmax): """Compute intersection of ray with AABB. Returns (tnear, tfar).""" t1 = (bmin - origin) / direction t2 = (bmax - origin) / direction tnear = torch.max(torch.min(t1, t2)) tfar = torch.min(torch.max(t1, t2)) return tnear, tfar def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" x = x.unsqueeze(-1) scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numfrequencies)], dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) shaped = x (math.pi scales).reshape(1, 1, -1) return torch.cat([torch.sin(shaped), torch.cos(shaped)], dim=-1).reshape(x.shape[0], -1) class TinyMLP(nn.Module): """KiloNeRF Tiny MLP: 4 hidden layers, 32 units. Input: Encoded Position (3D) + Viewing Direction (3D) Output: Density (1), Color (3)""" def init(self, posencdim, viewencdim): super(TinyMLP, self).init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(posencdim, 32) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(32, 32) self.fc4 = nn.Linear(32 + viewencdim, 32) self.densityhead = nn.Linear(32, 1) self.colorhead = nn.Linear(32, 3) def forward(self, posenc, viewdir): # Path 1: Density (independent of view direction) x = torch.relu(self.fc1(posenc)) x = torch.relu(self.fc2(x)) sigma = self.densityhead(x) # Path 2: Color (view direction added at penultimate layer) x = torch.relu(self.fc3(x)) # No activation applied to feature vector input to penultimate layer xwithview = torch.cat([x, viewdir], dim=-1) x = torch.relu(self.fc4(xwithview)) c = torch.sigmoid(self.colorhead(x)) return sigma, c def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, bmin, bmax, r, networks, occupancygrid, K=384, epsilon=0.01): """Render a single ray using KiloNeRF.""" tnear, tfar = rayaabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, bmin, bmax) if tfar < 0.0: return torch.zeros(3) tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, K) points = rayorigin.unsqueeze(1) + raydirection.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) transmittance = 1.0 color = torch.zeros(3) delta = (tfar - tnear) / K for i in range(K): if transmittance < epsilon: break point = points[i] cellsize = (bmax - bmin) / r idx = torch.floor((point - bmin) / cellsize).long() # Clamp indices to grid bounds idx = torch.clamp(idx, 0, torch.tensor(r) - 1) grididx = idx[0] r[1] r[2] + idx[1] r[2] + idx[2] if not occupancygrid[grididx].item(): continue net = networks[grididx] posenc = positionalencoding(point.unsqueeze(0), numfrequencies=10) viewenc = positionalencoding(raydirection.unsqueeze(0), numfrequencies=4) sigma, c = net(posenc, viewenc) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) weight = transmittance alpha color += weight c transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return color Parameters: Grid Resolution: Largest dimension 16; others chosen for cubic cells. Max 4096 networks. Occupancy Grid Resolution: 16 \times network grid resolution. Max 256^3. Occupancy Threshold \tau: 10. Max Samples K: 384. ERT Threshold \epsilon: 0.01. L2 Regularization Weight: 10^{-6} on last two layers. Optimizer: Adam, LR 5 \times 10^{-4}, batch size 8192 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Free Space Artifacts: Training KiloNeRF from scratch leads to noticeable artifacts in empty space. View-Dependent Bias: Reducing output features of the last hidden layer to mimic NeRF's view-dependent bias caused visual quality loss due to small network width. Dynamic Parameter Loading: During rendering, a ray traverses different networks, requiring dynamic parameter loading. Memory Overhead: Deploying thousands of MLPs incurs substantial memory overhead compared to a single network. Speedup: KiloNeRF achieves a speedup of 2000x to 2548x compared to the original NeRF. It is approximately two orders of magnitude faster than Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF). Rendering Time: On an NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti, KiloNeRF renders in 30ms (BlendedMVS), 26ms (Synthetic-NeRF), 26ms (Synthetic-NSVF), and 91ms (Tanks&Temples). Quality: Visual quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) is comparable to the original NeRF and NSVF. Memory: Higher memory usage than NeRF due to the storage of thousands of small MLPs. Strengths: Real-time capable rendering; no loss in visual quality; simpler spatial decomposition than DeRF (regular grid vs. Voronoi). Limitations: Requires an AABB; distillation adds training complexity; dynamic network switching requires specialized implementation for optimal speed. KiloNeRF was introduced by Reiser et al. in 2021 at ICCV. It addresses the slow rendering times of NeRF by decomposing the scene into thousands of small MLPs. The method builds on the teacher-student distillation paradigm and incorporates acceleration techniques like Empty Space Skipping and Early Ray Termination, which were previously used in NSVF. It is cited as a key method for accelerating NeRF by three orders of magnitude.
