name: ProNeRF
head: ProNeRF-12, ProNeRF-32, ProNeRF-8, Projection-Aware Ray Sampling for Fine-Grained Implicit Neural Radiance Fields
body: ProNeRF is a few-point volumetric rendering method that uses a Projection-Aware Sampling (PAS) network to predict sparse 3D sampling points and opacity adjustments, allowing high-quality rendering with significantly fewer samples than standard NeRF. It achieves faster inference than vanilla NeRF with higher quality than HyperReel. Unlike generalizable radiance fields (e.g., IBRNet, NeuRay) that store all training input images for epipolar feature projection, ProNeRF uses a fixed subset of reference views, eliminating the need for nearest-neighbor projection among all available training views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target ray \mathbf{r} defined by origin \mathbf{r}o and direction \mathbf{r}d, near/far bounds tn, tf, and a fixed set of Nn neighboring reference view camera centers and colors. Output: Rendered ray color \hat{c}(\mathbf{r}). Data Structures: Plucker Ray-Point Encoding: A vector of size N{pr} (typically 48) representing the ray. MLP Heads: F{\thetac} (Coarse Sampler): 6 fully connected layers, 256 neurons, ELU activation. F{\thetaf} (Fine Sampler): 6 fully connected layers, 256 neurons, ELU activation. F{\thetas} (Shading Network): 8 fully connected layers, 256 neurons (based on DoNeRF). F{\thetam} (Pruning Head, optional): Same complexity as F{\thetac}. Reference Views: A small, fixed subset of Nn views from the training set. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Encoding: Compute the Plucker ray-point representation \mathbf{r}{pr} for the target ray \mathbf{r}: \mathbf{r}{pr} = [\mathbf{r}d, \mathbf{r}o + \mathbf{r}d \odot \mathbf{t}{nf}, (\mathbf{r}o + \mathbf{r}d \odot \mathbf{t}{nf}) \odot \mathbf{r}d] where \mathbf{t}{nf} is a vector of N{pr} elements evenly spaced between near tn and far tf bounds, and \odot is the Hadamard product. 2. Coarse Sampling: Pass \mathbf{r}{pr} through F{\thetac} to obtain coarse sampling distances \mathbf{T}' = \{t'1, \dots, t'{Ns}\}, opacity shifts At, scales Bt, and auxiliary light-field outputs \hat{c}c, \hat{c}f: [ \mathbf{T}', At, Bt, \hat{\mathbf{c}}c, \hat{\mathbf{c}}f ] = F{\thetac}(\mathbf{r}{pr}) 3. Color-to-Ray Projection: For each coarse point pi = \mathbf{r}(t'i), trace lines from pi to the camera centers of Nn neighboring reference views. Collect the colors at these intersection points to form projection vectors \mathbf{f}{pi} = [c^1{pi}, c^2{pi}, \dots, c^{Nn}{pi}]. 4. Refined Sampling: Concatenate the encoded ray \mathbf{r}'{pr} with the projected features \mathbf{f}{p1}, \dots, \mathbf{f}{p{Ns}} and pass through F{\thetaf} to obtain refinement weights \DeltaT, weights W, and mixing coefficients M: [\DeltaT, W, M] = F{\thetaf}([\mathbf{r}'{pr}, \mathbf{f}{p1}, \dots, \mathbf{f}{p{Ns}}]) 5. Distance Interpolation: Compute refined ray distances \mathbf{T} by linear interpolation between consecutive elements of the expanded set \dot{\mathbf{T}} = \{tn, t'1, \dots, t'{Ns}, tf\} using \DeltaT: \mathbf{T} = \left\{ \frac{1}{2} \left( (\dot{\mathbf{T}}i + \dot{\mathbf{T}}{i+1}) + \Delta{Ti}(\dot{\mathbf{T}}{i+2} - \dot{\mathbf{T}}i) \right) \right\}{i=1}^{Ns} 6. Volumetric Rendering: Query the shading network F{\thetas} at points \mathbf{r}(t) for t \in \mathbf{T} to get densities \sigmai and colors ci. Compute opacity \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai(t{i+1} - ti)}. Adjust opacities using At and Bt (as per Eq. 5 in, typically \hat{\alpha}i = 1 - e^{-(\sigmai + At) \Delta t} \cdot Bt or similar adjustment to compensate for sparse sampling, though the exact formula for At, Bt application is referenced as Eq. 5 in the source). Render color \hat{c}(\mathbf{r}) using alpha compositing: \hat{c}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} 1 - \hat{\alpha}j \right) \hat{\alpha}i ci Training Strategy (Exploration-Exploitation): Training alternates between two passes: Exploration Pass (Every other iteration, first 4 \times 10^5 iterations): 1. Sample a random number of samples N^+s uniformly between Ns and N (max 64). 2. Sample N^+s distances T^+ randomly around the estimated coarse points \mathbf{T} and add Gaussian noise. 3. Query F{\thetas} at T^+ to get \{ci, \sigmai\}. 4. Compute loss using standard VRE (Eq. 1). 5. Update only F{\thetas} parameters. Exploitation Pass (Every other iteration, all iterations): 1. Query F{\thetas} at the sparse points \mathbf{T} predicted by PAS. 2. Compute loss using PAS-guided VRE (Eq. 5 in). 3. If iteration < 4 \times 10^5, add auxiliary losses for coarse color \hat{c}c and fine color \hat{c}f. 4. Update all MLP heads (F{\thetac}, F{\thetaf}, F{\thetas}). Auxiliary Losses: Primary loss: l = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{Nr} \|\hat{c}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r})\|2. Auxiliary loss: la = \frac{1}{Nr} \sum{Nr} \|\hat{\mathbf{c}}c(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r})\|2 + \|\hat{\mathbf{c}}f(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r})\|2. Note: The source text for Eq. 13 contains identical terms, but describes the structure of combining coarse and fine light-field outputs. Total loss: lT = l + \lambda la, where \lambda = 1 for the first 60% of training (4 \times 10^5 iterations) and 0 afterward. Pruning (ProNeRF-8 prune): Train a complementary MLP head F{\thetam} (same complexity as F{\thetac}) to predict the error between the fast output \hat{c}f and the full output \hat{c}. During inference, if the predicted error is low, render using \hat{c}f (AVR); otherwise, run F{\thetas}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ProNeRF: def init(self, Ns=8, Npr=48, Nn=5, Nmaxexplore=64, lr=5e-4, totaliters=700000, auxiters=400000): self.Ns = Ns self.Npr = Npr self.Nn = Nn self.Nmaxexplore = Nmaxexplore self.totaliters = totaliters self.auxiters = auxiters # Define MLPs self.Fc = CoarseMLP(Npr) self.Ff = FineMLP(Npr + Nn Ns) self.Fs = ShadingMLP() self.Fm = PruningMLP(Npr) # Optional # Optimizers self.opts = torch.optim.Adam(self.Fs.parameters(), lr=lr) self.optcfs = torch.optim.Adam(list(self.Fc.parameters()) + list(self.Ff.parameters()) + list(self.Fs.parameters()), lr=lr) # Reference views data (colors and camera centers) # self.refcolors: [Nn, H, W, 3] # self.refcameras: [Nn, 4, 4] transformation matrices def encoderay(self, ro, rd, tn, tf): # ro: [B, 3], rd: [B, 3] tnf = torch.linspace(tn, tf, self.Npr).to(ro.device) # Expand dims for broadcasting tnf = tnf.unsqueeze(0).expand(ro.shape[0], -1) # [B, Npr] # Plucker encoding components # rd: [B, 3] # ro + rd tnf: [B, Npr, 3] term1 = rd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.Npr, -1) term2 = ro.unsqueeze(1) + rd.unsqueeze(1) tnf.unsqueeze(2) # Concatenate [rd, ro + rd tnf, (ro + rd tnf) rd] # Note: Source says Hadamard product for last term term3 = term2 rd.unsqueeze(1) rpr = torch.cat([term1, term2, term3], dim=-1) # [B, Npr, 9] return rpr.flatten(1) # [B, Npr 9] def getprojections(self, ro, rd, tcoarse, refcameras, refcolors): # tcoarse: [B, Ns] # Points pi = ro + rd tcoarse points = ro.unsqueeze(1) + rd.unsqueeze(1) tcoarse.unsqueeze(2) # [B, Ns, 3] # For each point, project to Nn reference views # This requires ray-plane intersection or similar. # Simplified: Assume we have precomputed colors at these projected locations # In practice, this involves tracing rays from points to camera centers # and sampling the reference images. # fpi shape: [B, Ns, Nn, 3] fpi = self.samplereferenceviews(points, refcameras, refcolors) return fpi def samplereferenceviews(self, points, refcameras, refcolors): # Placeholder for actual ray-triangle/intersection logic # Returns colors at the intersection of rays (point -> camcenter) with reference planes # B, Ns, Nn, 3 B, Ns, = points.shape # Initialize with zeros colors = torch.zeros(B, Ns, self.Nn, 3, device=points.device) #... Implementation of color-to-ray projection... return colors def forward(self, ro, rd, tn, tf, refcameras, refcolors): rpr = self.encoderay(ro, rd, tn, tf) # Step 2: Coarse Sampling outc = self.Fc(rpr) # Split output: T', At, Bt, chatc, chatf # Assuming specific split based on layer output size # T' shape: [B, Ns] # At, Bt: [B, Ns] or scalars? Source implies per-point or global adjustment # Let's assume At, Bt are [B, Ns] for opacity adjustment Tprime = outc[:,:self.Ns] At = outc[:, self.Ns: 2self.Ns] Bt = outc[:, 2self.Ns: 3self.Ns] chatc = outc[:, 3self.Ns: 3self.Ns + 3] # [B, 3] chatf = outc[:, 3self.Ns + 3: 3self.Ns + 6] # [B, 3] # Step 3: Projections fpi = self.getprojections(ro, rd, Tprime, refcameras, refcolors) # [B, Ns, Nn, 3] # Step 4: Refined Sampling # Concatenate rpr and flattened fpi fpiflat = fpi.view(fpi.shape[0], -1) # [B, Ns Nn 3] inputf = torch.cat([rpr, fpiflat], dim=-1) outf = self.Ff(inputf) # Split: DeltaT, W, M # DeltaT: [B, Ns] # W: [B, Ns] # M: [B, Nn] DeltaT = outf[:,:self.Ns] W = outf[:, self.Ns: 2self.Ns] M = outf[:, 2self.Ns: 2self.Ns + self.Nn] # Step 5: Interpolation # Expand Tprime to include tn and tf tnexp = torch.fulllike(Tprime[:,:1], tn) tfexp = torch.fulllike(Tprime[:,:1], tf) Tdot = torch.cat([tnexp, Tprime, tfexp], dim=1) # [B, Ns + 2] # T = 0.5 ( (Tdoti + Tdot{i+1}) + DeltaTi (Tdot{i+2} - Tdoti)) # Indices: i from 0 to Ns-1 # Tdoti, Tdot{i+1}, Tdot{i+2} Ti = Tdot[:,:-2] Tip1 = Tdot[:, 1:-1] Tip2 = Tdot[:, 2:] Trefined = 0.5 ((Ti + Tip1) + DeltaT (Tip2 - Ti)) # Step 6: Rendering # Query Fs at Trefined pointsrefined = ro.unsqueeze(1) + rd.unsqueeze(1) Trefined.unsqueeze(2) # [B, Ns, 3] sigma, color = self.Fs(pointsrefined) # [B, Ns], [B, Ns, 3] # Opacity calculation # Delta t dt = torch.diff(Trefined, dim=1, prepend=torch.zeros(B, 1, device=Trefined.device)) # Standard opacity alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma dt) # Adjust opacity with At, Bt # Source Eq 5 reference. Assuming: alphaadj = 1 - exp(-(sigma + At) dt) Bt # Or similar. Let's use a generic adjustment placeholder if exact formula is ambiguous # However, source says "adjusting alphai in Eq. 4 is needed... At and Bt" # Let's assume: alphaadj = (1 - exp(-sigma dt)) Bt + At ? # Given ambiguity, we stick to the structure: alphaadj = alpha Bt.unsqueeze(-1) + At.unsqueeze(-1) # [B, Ns, 1] alphaadj = torch.clamp(alphaadj, 0, 1) # Alpha compositing # Transmittance Ti = prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) ones = torch.oneslike(alphaadj) oneminusalpha = ones - alphaadj transmittance = torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha, dim=1) transmittance = torch.cat([ones[:,:1,:], transmittance[:,:-1,:]], dim=1) contribution = transmittance alphaadj color chat = torch.sum(contribution, dim=1) # [B, 3] return chat, chatc, chatf, Trefined, alphaadj def trainstep(self, batch, it): ro, rd, cgt, tn, tf, refcameras, refcolors = batch # Get PAS outputs chat, chatc, chatf, Trefined, alphaadj = self.forward(ro, rd, tn, tf, refcameras, refcolors) isexploration = (it % 2 == 0) and (it < self.auxiters) if isexploration: # Exploration: Dense sampling around T Nsplus = torch.randint(self.Ns, self.Nmaxexplore, (1,)).item() # Sample Nsplus points around Trefined # Add noise # Query Fs # Compute VRE loss # Update Fs only pass else: # Exploitation: Sparse sampling Trefined # Compute VRE loss with adjusted opacities loss = F.mseloss(chat, cgt) if it < self.auxiters: lossc = F.mseloss(chatc, cgt) lossf = F.mseloss(chatf, cgt) loss = loss + lossc + lossf # Update all pass Speed: ProNeRF is 15-23× faster than vanilla NeRF. ProNeRF-8 is >20× faster, ProNeRF-12 is ~15× faster. ProNeRF-8 prune is 23% faster than standard ProNeRF-8. Quality: ProNeRF-12 achieves 0.65dB higher PSNR than vanilla NeRF and 0.95dB higher PSNR than HyperReel on LLFF. ProNeRF-8 achieves 26.78 dB PSNR on LLFF, outperforming vanilla NeRF (26.50 dB) by 0.28 dB. Memory: Memory footprint is similar to NeRF. Pruning adds 3.3 MB of memory overhead. Scaling: Uses a fixed subset of reference views (Nn) regardless of the total number of training views (Nt), ensuring consistent memory footprint. Strengths: Optimal trade-off between memory, speed, and quality. Better quality than explicit methods like K-Planes and HyperReel. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the exploration-exploitation balance. Removing auxiliary loss causes ~1 dB PSNR drop; removing Plucker encoding causes ~0.5 dB drop. ProNeRF was proposed in 2024. It builds on Specific Model Architectures. It is evaluated on LLFF (Mildenhall et al. 2019) and Blender (Mildenhall et al. 2020) datasets. name: Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields
head: 4-Plane Representation, Quadri-Plane Model
body: Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields represent a 3D scene using four multi-channel 2D feature planes coupled with a decoder MLP, designed to allow computationally efficient volumetric super-resolution by leveraging 2D image super-resolution techniques. It diverges from typical volumetric schemes by using explicit feature vectors arranged in planes rather than a dense 3D grid or hash table, allowing the scene to be viewed as a pair of 3D fields for density and radiance. It sets itself apart from siblings like Mega-NeRF Spatial Partitioning and Sparse Radiance Field (SRF) Representation by relying on fixed, axis-aligned 2D planes for positional data and a dedicated view-direction plane, rather than spatial hashing or octrees. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction defined by azimuth \thetap and elevation \phip. Output: Volume density \sigma and RGB radiance \{r, g, b\} for the point. Data Structures The scene representation Ps consists of four planes: 1. Three positional planes: P{xy}, P{xz}, P{yz}. 2. One view-direction plane: P{dir}. Layout and Dimensions: Positional planes P{xy}, P{xz}, P{yz}: Dimensions N \times N \times C. View-direction plane P{dir}: Dimensions N{dir} \times N{dir} \times C. Typical values: N=200, N{dir}=32, C=48. Decoders Two fully-connected MLPs are used: 1. Coarse Decoder (Dc): 128 channels, 4 layers. 2. Fine Decoder (Df): 128 channels, 4 layers. 3. Radiance Decoder: Identical characteristics to density MLPs (128 channels, 4 layers). Algorithm Steps 1. Positional Feature Retrieval: For point p, retrieve feature vectors from the three positional planes via bilinear interpolation. v{p,xy} = \text{BilinearInterpolate}(P{xy}, px, py) v{p,xz} = \text{BilinearInterpolate}(P{xz}, px, pz) v{p,yz} = \text{BilinearInterpolate}(P{yz}, py, pz) 2. Positional Aggregation: Compute the average of the positional feature vectors to form vp. vp = \frac{1}{3} (v{p,xy} + v{p,xz} + v{p,yz}) 3. View-Direction Feature Retrieval: Determine the viewing direction (\thetap, \phip) for the ray passing through p. Retrieve a complementary feature vector v{pdir} from P{dir} via bilinear interpolation at coordinates (\thetap, \phip). v{pdir} = \text{BilinearInterpolate}(P{dir}, \thetap, \phip) 4. Density Computation: Compute density \sigma using the coarse decoder Dc and fine decoder Df. \sigmac = Dc(vp) \sigmaf = Df(vp) The final density \sigma is derived from these outputs (typically via volume rendering integration, though the specific combination of \sigmac and \sigmaf for the final \sigma value is not explicitly defined in the source text beyond their use in rendering). 5. Radiance Computation: Compute radiance \{r, g, b\} using the radiance decoder MLP. Concatenate all four feature vectors: v{concat} = [v{p,xy}, v{p,xz}, v{p,yz}, v{pdir}]. \{r, g, b\} = \text{RadianceDecoder}(v{concat}) Note: The view-direction plane P{dir} affects only radiance, not density, as volume density does not vary with viewing direction in the real world. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def bilinearinterpolate(plane, u, v): """ Performs bilinear interpolation on a 2D plane at coordinates (u, v). plane: numpy array of shape (H, W, C) u, v: float coordinates in [0, 1] range (normalized to plane dimensions) Returns: numpy array of shape (C,) """ H, W, C = plane.shape # Normalize coordinates to pixel indices uidx = u (W - 1) vidx = v (H - 1) # Floor and ceil indices u0, v0 = int(np.floor(uidx)), int(np.floor(vidx)) u1, v1 = min(u0 + 1, W - 1), min(v0 + 1, H - 1) # Interpolation weights du = uidx - u0 dv = vidx - v0 # Get corner values q00 = plane[v0, u0,:] q01 = plane[v0, u1,:] q10 = plane[v1, u0,:] q11 = plane[v1, u1,:] # Bilinear interpolation top = q00 (1 - du) + q01 du bottom = q10 (1 - du) + q11 du result = top (1 - dv) + bottom dv return result def quadriplanequery(p, theta, phi, Pxy, Pxz, Pyz, Pdir, Dc, Df, Drad): """ Queries the Quadri-Plane Radiance Field for density and radiance. p: numpy array (3,) - 3D point coordinates theta: float - viewing azimuth phi: float - viewing elevation Pxy, Pxz, Pyz: numpy arrays (N, N, C) - positional planes Pdir: numpy array (Ndir, Ndir, C) - view-direction plane Dc, Df, Drad: callable MLPs - decoders """ # 1. Retrieve positional features vpxy = bilinearinterpolate(Pxy, p[0], p[1]) vpxz = bilinearinterpolate(Pxz, p[0], p[2]) vpyz = bilinearinterpolate(Pyz, p[1], p[2]) # 2. Aggregate positional features vp = (vpxy + vpxz + vpyz) / 3.0 # 3. Retrieve view-direction feature # Note: theta and phi must be normalized to [0, 1] for interpolation vpdir = bilinearinterpolate(Pdir, theta, phi) # 4. Compute density sigmac = Dc(vp) sigmaf = Df(vp) # The source does not specify the exact formula combining sigmac and sigmaf # into the final sigma used for rendering. Assuming standard NeRF # coarse-to-fine integration or direct usage as per implementation. sigma = sigmac # Placeholder for exact combination logic not in source # 5. Compute radiance vconcat = np.concatenate([vpxy, vpxz, vpyz, vpdir]) radiance = Drad(vconcat) return sigma, radiance Parameters N: Plane resolution for positional planes. Determines visual frequency representation. Too small prohibits high frequencies; too large causes artifacts due to insufficient information in LR training images. Typical value for LR: N=200 (learned from 100px images). N{dir}: View-direction plane resolution. Set smaller than positional planes (N{dir} < N) because each pixel's information is relevant to only one point on P{dir} (same viewing direction for all points on a ray), whereas it is relevant to many points on positional planes. Typical value: N{dir}=32. C: Number of channels. Typical value: C=48. Edge Cases and Pitfalls View-direction dependency: Without P{dir}, reconstruction performance drops significantly, especially for shiny/reflective objects with non-uniform lighting. Using P{dir} improves PSNR (e.g., 29.6 dB vs 23.7 dB in the source context). Resolution trade-off: Using planes that are too small prohibits the representation of high visual frequencies. Using too large planes results in some plane regions having too little relevant information in the captured scene images, manifested as visual artifacts when rendering novel scene views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, training uses Adam optimizers with learning rates of 0.0005 for the decoder and feature planes and 0.00005 for the SR model F. 4096 rays are sampled per step. Strengths: Allows computationally efficient volumetric super-resolution by leveraging 2D image SR techniques. The fixed plane structure simplifies the representation compared to dense 3D grids. Limitations: The resolution N must be carefully chosen relative to the training image resolution. Too small N limits frequency, too large N causes artifacts. The method relies on the assumption that density is view-independent, which may not hold for participating media or complex lighting effects not captured by the view-direction plane. When to use: When volumetric super-resolution is required and 2D SR techniques can be effectively adapted to 3D plane representations. Suitable for scenes where view-dependent effects are primarily due to lighting and reflectance, captured by the P{dir} plane. When not to use: For scenes with complex view-dependent density (e.g., smoke, fog) or when high-frequency details require resolutions that exceed the memory budget for the planes. Quadri-Plane Radiance Fields were proposed in "Neural Volume Super-Resolution". The work builds on the idea of using feature planes for scene representation, initially proposed by Chan et al. [9] for human faces, and extends it to general scenes. It diverges from typical neural rendering methods [32] by using explicit feature vectors arranged in planes. The introduction of the fourth plane P{dir} addresses the limitation of positional planes alone in capturing non-uniform lighting and reflective effects. The method is designed to be trained end-to-end, leveraging advances in 2D image super-resolution (e.g., EDSR [25]) for the super-resolution component. name: Non-Baked Models
head: Hybrid Representations, Learning separate scene features from MLP parameters
body: Non-baked models are scene representations that decouple the learning of geometric/appearance features from the neural network parameters, typically using a hybrid approach where features are stored in explicit data structures and queried by a smaller MLP. This approach solves the trade-off between model capacity and inference speed by enabling smaller MLPs, which improves both training and inference speed at the cost of increased memory usage. Unlike baked models, which pre-compute and store the final output in accessible data structures to speed up inference without affecting training time, non-baked models retain the neural network for the final mapping step. The core mechanism of non-baked models is the separation of scene representation into two distinct components: an explicit feature storage structure and a compact neural network (MLP). 1. Explicit Feature Storage: The scene is represented by a data structure (e.g., hash tables, grids, or other spatial partitions) that stores intermediate features (such as color, density, or embeddings) at specific spatial locations or along rays. These features are learned during training. 2. Compact MLP: A smaller, parameter-efficient MLP takes the queried features as input and predicts the final radiance and density values. The MLP parameters are shared across the scene or spatial regions, while the features are location-specific. 3. Hybrid Nature: The term "hybrid" refers to the combination of explicit, learnable feature storage (like a lookup table) and implicit neural representation (the MLP). This contrasts with purely implicit models (like original NeRF, which uses only an MLP) and purely explicit models (which omit neural networks entirely). 4. Performance Trade-off: The primary benefit is improved inference speed due to the smaller MLP, and potentially faster training due to reduced computational load per sample. The cost is increased memory consumption due to the storage of explicit features. Methods that omit neural networks entirely and use only explicit scene representations. While not strictly NeRF models, they are included in this family due to their relevance and similarity. The standard non-baked approach where separate scene features are learned and stored explicitly, while a smaller MLP processes these features. This is the most common form of non-baked models. The concept of non-baked models emerged as an optimization strategy to address the computational bottlenecks of standard NeRF architectures. The original NeRF paper utilized hierarchical sampling and coarse/fine MLPs, which are often combined with per-paper innovations in non-baked approaches. The distinction between "baked" and "non-baked" models was formalized in comprehensive reviews of Neural Radiance Fields, where baked models were defined as those storing final outputs in accessible data structures, while non-baked models included innovations like hybrid representations. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Edit-NeRF
head: EditNeRF
body: Edit-NeRF is a method for user-controlled 3D scene editing that formulates the problem as a joint optimization of NeRF network parameters and latent codes. It solves the limitation of standard NeRFs, which are static and cannot be easily modified by external features, by introducing a modular network architecture with conditional radiance fields. It differs from its siblings by being the first method to execute user-controlled deformation models on NeRF using a shared shape network and instance-specific latent codes, whereas methods like CLIP-NeRF later introduced text/image guidance via CLIP embeddings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User-provided image conditioning (2D image or sketch) representing the desired edit; initial NeRF weights; category-specific shared shape network parameters. Output: Edited 3D radiance field (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) consistent with the user's edit. Data Structures: The shape representation is composed of two networks: 1. Shared Shape Network (F{share}): Category-specific, not conditioned on latent codes. It behaves as a deformation field. 2. Instance-Specific Shape Network (F{inst}): Conditioned on a shape latent code zs. The color network is conditioned on an appearance latent code za (or zc in some notations). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Train the model on multiple instances of the same category to learn underlying part features in an unsupervised manner. 2. Latent Code Optimization: Optimize the latent codes zs and za to minimize the NeRF photometric loss against the user-provided image conditioning. 3. Network Weight Optimization: Optimize the MLP weights of the NeRF networks. 4. Joint Optimization: Optimize both the latent codes (zs, za) and the MLP weights jointly to refine the edit. Formulas: The rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}, zs, zc) for a ray \mathbf{r} is computed via volumetric rendering: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}, zs, zc) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc-1} ci \alphai \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right) where: Nc is the number of samples along the ray. ci is the color at sample i. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is the transmittance-derived alpha. \sigmaj is the density at sample j. \deltaj is the distance between samples. Parameters: zs: Shape latent code. za (or zc): Appearance/Color latent code. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Limited Shape Operations: The method only supports adding or deleting local parts of an object; it does not support complex global deformations. Slow Convergence: The editing process is slow due to its iterative optimization nature. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF is a diffusion-based method for editing a NeRF scene guided by text instructions, utilizing InstructPix2Pix. It solves the problem of 3D scene modification by iteratively updating the training dataset with edited images and retraining the NeRF. It differs from its sibling Edit-NeRF by bypassing explicit 3D deformation fields or conditional radiance field architectures, instead relying on 2D image-level diffusion editing to drive 3D consistency. SINE is a method for editing a NeRF scene by editing a single view and applying the edit to the entire scene. It encodes changes in geometry and texture over the original NeRF scene by learning a prior-guided editing field. This field is used to render modified object geometry and color, and a color compositing layer supervised by the single edited view applies the edit on novel views. It is applied on real and synthetic scenes by changing geometry and texture of objects. Time Complexity: Slow due to its iterative optimization nature. Memory Complexity: Requires storing latent codes zs and za per instance/edit. Strengths: Allows user-controlled deformation; modular architecture separates shape and appearance. Limitations: Limited to local part addition/deletion; slow convergence. When to Use: When user-controlled local edits on a category of objects are required and computational time is not the primary constraint. When Not to Use: For global deformations, real-time editing, or when high geometric consistency is critical without additional constraints. Edit-NeRF was proposed by Liu et al. in 2021. It was the first method to execute user-controlled deformation models on NeRF, proposing a modular network's conditional radiance field to guide model editing. It builds on the standard latent-conditioned NeRF architecture but introduces a shared shape network and instance-specific latent codes to enable editing. It was innovated upon by CLIP-NeRF in December 2021, which introduced text/image guidance via CLIP. name: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF
head: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF Baseline
body: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF (IN2N) is a diffusion-based method for editing a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene guided by text instructions, utilizing InstructPix2Pix. It solves the problem of 3D scene modification by iteratively updating the training dataset with edited images and retraining the NeRF. It differs from its sibling Edit-NeRF by bypassing explicit 3D deformation fields or conditional radiance field architectures, instead relying on 2D image-level diffusion editing to drive 3D consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model representing the original scene, a set of original training images \{Ii\}, and a text instruction T. Output: An edited NeRF model that renders scenes consistent with instruction T. Data Structures: The method operates on the existing NeRF representation and the 2D image dataset. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Load the original NeRF model and the original training image dataset. 2. Iterative Editing Loop: a. For each image Ii in the training dataset: i. Pass Ii and the text instruction T to the InstructPix2Pix (IP2P) model. ii. Generate the edited image I'i = \text{IP2P}(Ii, T). b. Replace the original dataset \{Ii\} with the edited dataset \{I'i\}. c. Re-train the NeRF model using the edited dataset \{I'i\}. 3. Convergence: Repeat steps 2a-2c until the edited NeRF converges or a fixed number of iterations is reached. Parameters: Text Instruction T: A natural language string describing the desired edit. Example: "Make it look like it was taken at night.". InstructPix2Pix Model: A fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model capable of following text instructions to edit images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lack of Localization: The method applies edits to entire 2D images, lacking the ability to perform precise, localized modifications. Scene Preservation: It sometimes fails to preserve the rest of the scene, resulting in a blurrier scene compared to the original. Global Changes: It may introduce unintended texture and color changes to the entire scene rather than just the target object. Time Complexity: High. Requires iterative retraining of the NeRF after each round of 2D image editing. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Demonstrates high-quality local edit results on real scenes. Slower than methods like Depth-Guided Sequential Editing which avoid integrating a diffusion model into the training loop. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation leveraging existing 2D editing models; intuitive text-based control. Limitations: Applies edits to entire 2D images, lacking precise localization. Sometimes fails to preserve the rest of the scene, resulting in a blurrier output and unintended texture/color changes across the entire scene. When to use: When intuitive text-based editing is prioritized over strict multi-view consistency or speed. When not to use: When precise, localized modifications or strict multi-view consistency are required. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF was presented at ICCV 2023. It is the first work to edit a NeRF by iteratively updating the training dataset with edited images generated by a text-based image editing model, specifically InstructPix2Pix. It builds on the capability of generative models to edit 2D images according to text instructions. name: Depth-Guided Sequential Editing
head: ViCA-NeRF, ViCA-NeRF Sequential Editing, View-Consistency-Aware 3D Editing of Neural Radiance Fields, View-Consistency-Aware NeRF
body: Depth-Guided Sequential Editing (ViCA-NeRF) is a two-stage method for editing Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using text instructions, which ensures multi-view consistency by sequentially editing key 2D views and propagating those edits to the rest of the scene via geometric projection and learned regularization. It differs from Instruct-NeRF2NeRF by explicitly enforcing consistency through depth-guided pixel projection and latent code alignment, avoiding the need to integrate a diffusion model into the NeRF training loop, resulting in editing speeds approximately 3 times faster. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model (specifically nerfacto from NeRFStudio), a set of input views (images, camera poses, and coarse depth maps rendered from the source NeRF), and a text editing instruction. Outputs: A refined NeRF model representing the edited 3D scene, and a corresponding set of edited 2D images. Data Structures: View Data: Each view i consists of an RGB image Ii, a coarse depth map Di, a camera intrinsic matrix Ki, and a camera pose \xii. Key View Sequence: An ordered list of view indices selected for sequential editing. Modified Mask: A binary mask per view tracking which pixels have already been overwritten by previous projections to prevent overwriting. Parameters: \phi: Maximum desired modified ratio for key view selection, set to \phi = 0.3. lr{thresh}: Reprojection error threshold for valid correspondences, set to 5 pixels. T{warmup}: Warm-up iterations for the diffusion model; 10 for face-centric scenes, 30 for outdoor scenes. T{fine}: Fine-tuning iterations for the NeRF; 10,000 for general scenes, \approx 5,000 for small scenes. T{train}: Initial training iterations for the source NeRF; 30,000. Steps: 1. Source NeRF Training: Train a pre-trained NeRF (e.g., nerfacto) on the original unedited data for T{train} = 30,000 iterations. 2. Depth Extraction: Render coarse depth maps Di for all input views i from the trained source NeRF. 3. Key View Selection: Select a sequence of key views starting from a random view. 4. Sequential Editing and Projection: Iterate through the selected key views in order. Edit Key View: Apply Instruct-Pix2Pix to the current key view j using the text prompt to generate an edited image I'j. A warm-up procedure is applied: run the diffusion process for T{warmup} iterations to shift the main distribution of 2D edits. Geometric Projection: Project the edited pixels from I'j to all other views i (including non-key views and subsequent key views) using the depth maps and camera poses. Calculate 3D points for view i: pi = P^{-1}(Di, Ki, \xii). Reproject pi to view j to find corresponding pixel coordinates. Calculate reprojection error lr. If lr < lr{thresh} (5px), the correspondence is valid. Copy the pixel value from I'j to the corresponding location in view i, but only if that pixel has not yet been modified (checked via the Modified Mask). This creates a "mixup" dataset where edits are mixed but not overwritten. 5. Blending Refinement (Learned Regularization): The projected mixup images may contain noise due to depth inaccuracies. Run the diffusion process (Instruct-Pix2Pix) multiple times on each mixup image. Average the resulting latent codes from these runs. Decode the averaged latent code into a single final image. This corrects noisy depth correspondences and stabilizes the edit, accepting slight image smoothness. 6. NeRF Fine-Tuning: Train the source NeRF on the fully refined, view-consistent edited dataset for T{fine} iterations (10,000 for general, 5,000 for small scenes). 7. Optional Post-Refinement: Re-render images from the fine-tuned NeRF. Apply the blending refinement model (Step 5) again to further improve consistency. Skip this step for large-scale outdoor scenes (e.g., 'campsite', 'farm') as high complexity prevents further consistency improvement. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def depthguidedsequentialediting(sourceneurf, views, textprompt): # Step 1: Train source NeRF on original data for 30,000 iterations # sourceneurf.train(views, iterations=30000) # Step 2: Extract coarse depth maps for all input views depthmaps = {v.id: sourceneurf.renderdepth(v) for v in views} # Step 3: Select a sequence of key views starting from a random view randomstart = random.randint(0, len(views) - 1) keyviewids = [views[i].id for i in range(randomstart, len(views))] + \ [views[i].id for i in range(randomstart)] # Initialize storage for edited images and modification masks editedimages = {v.id: v.image.copy() for v in views} modifiedmasks = {v.id: [[False] v.width for in range(v.height)] for v in views} for keyvid in keyviewids: # Step 4: Edit Key View with warm-up to shift 2D edit distribution warmupiters = 30 if isoutdoorscene(keyvid) else 10 editedkeyimg = ip2pixedit(editedimages[keyvid], textprompt, warmupiters=warmupiters) # Step 4: Geometric Projection to all other views for targetvid in [v.id for v in views if v.id != keyvid]: Dtarget = depthmaps[targetvid] Ktarget = viewsbyid[targetvid].intrinsics xitarget = viewsbyid[targetvid].pose Kkey = viewsbyid[keyvid].intrinsics xikey = viewsbyid[keyvid].pose for y in range(Dtarget.height): for x in range(Dtarget.width): if not modifiedmasks[targetvid][y][x]: # Unproject target pixel to 3D point z = Dtarget[y][x] xcam = (x - Ktarget[0][2]) z / Ktarget[0][0] ycam = (y - Ktarget[1][2]) z / Ktarget[1][1] p = transformpoint([xcam, ycam, z], xitarget) # Reproject 3D point to key view pcam = transformpoint(p, inversepose(xikey)) uk = pcam[0] Kkey[0][0] / pcam[2] + Kkey[0][2] vk = pcam[1] Kkey[1][1] / pcam[2] + Kkey[1][2] lr = math.sqrt((uk - x)2 + (vk - y)2) if lr < 5.0: # Correspondence matching valid threshold if 0 <= uk < editedkeyimg.width and 0 <= vk < editedkeyimg.height: editedimages[targetvid][y][x] = editedkeyimg[vk][uk] modifiedmasks[targetvid][y][x] = True # Blending refinement for the edited key view editedimages[keyvid] = blendrefine(editedkeyimg, textprompt) # Step 5: Blending Refinement for all views to correct noisy depth correspondences refinedimages = {} for vid, img in editedimages.items(): refinedimages[vid] = blendrefine(img, textprompt) # Step 6: Train NeRF on fully refined dataset for 10,000 iterations (5,000 for small scenes) dataset = builddataset(refinedimages, views) sourceneurf.finetune(dataset, iterations=10000) # Step 7: Optional Post-Refinement if not islargeoutdoorscene(): rerendered = sourceneurf.renderall() finalrefined = blendrefineall(rerendered, textprompt) sourceneurf.finetune(finalrefined, iterations=10000) return sourceneurf def transformpoint(p, pose): return pose.R @ p + pose.t def inversepose(pose): return Pose(R=pose.R.T, t=-pose.R.T @ pose.t) def isoutdoorscene(viewid): # Scene classification logic not specified in sources. return False def viewsbyid: # Dictionary mapping view IDs to view objects. pass def builddataset(images, views): # Standard dataset construction. pass def islargeoutdoorscene(): # Scene classification logic not specified in sources. return False def ip2pixedit(image, prompt, warmupiters): # Calls Instruct-Pix2Pix with warm-up steps. pass def blendrefine(image, prompt): # Runs diffusion multiple times, averages latent codes, decodes final image. pass def blendrefineall(images, prompt): # Applies blendrefine to all images. pass Pitfalls: Depth estimation from NeRF is often noisy, yielding incorrect pixel correspondences during projection. Inability to perform large spatial changes (e.g., manipulating existing objects or adding/removing large objects) due to inherited Instruct-Pix2Pix limitations. Blurry results caused by high-frequency information loss (texture on face, beard, hair) when the mixup image passes through the diffusion model, which attempts to reduce introduced noise. Time Complexity: The method is significantly faster than joint training approaches, achieving approximately 3 times faster editing speed compared to Instruct-NeRF2NeRF. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth maps for all views and the modified masks. The blending refinement step requires multiple passes through the diffusion model's latent space, increasing VRAM usage during the refinement stage. Performance: Evaluated on scenes ranging from faces to outdoor environments, providing higher levels of consistency and detail compared to the state of the art. Strengths: Explicitly enforces multi-view consistency via geometric projection and latent code alignment. Offers improved controllability (by editing key views) and efficiency (less GPU time). Limitations: Inherits limitations from Instruct-Pix2Pix: inability to perform large spatial changes (e.g., adding/removing large objects) and difficulty with highly detailed instructions involving interactions between parts. Blurry results due to high-frequency information loss (texture on face, beard, hair) when the mixup image passes through the diffusion model, which attempts to reduce noise introduced during projection. Post-refinement is ineffective for large-scale outdoor scenes due to high complexity. When to use: Suitable for 3D scene editing and AR applications where multi-view consistency is critical and computational efficiency is desired. Best for scenes where the user can define key views that capture the desired edit. When not to use: Avoid for large-scale outdoor scenes if post-refinement is expected to improve results. Avoid if large spatial manipulations (adding/removing objects) are required. Origin: ViCA-NeRF was introduced as the first view-consistency-aware method for 3D editing with text instructions. History: It builds upon the limitations of Instruct-NeRF2NeRF, which suffers from convergence problems and slower speeds due to iterative diffusion model updates during NeRF training. ViCA-NeRF decouples the editing from the training loop by using geometric and learned regularization in a pre-processing stage. Usage: Evaluated on various scenes and text prompts, ranging from faces to outdoor scenes. Code is available at https://dongjiahua.github.io/VICA-NeRF. name: SINE
head: Semantic Editing with Inpainting and Normal Editing
body: SINE is a method for editing a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene by modifying a single view and propagating those changes to the entire 3D scene. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by introducing cyclic constraints, a proxy mesh for geometric accuracy, color compositing for texture fidelity, and feature cluster regularization to preserve unedited content. Inputs: An original NeRF scene representation, a single edited view (containing user-defined geometry and texture changes), and potentially text prompts for semantic guidance. Outputs: A modified NeRF scene where the edited object's geometry and texture are updated in all novel views. Data Structures: The method utilizes a "prior-guided editing field" to encode changes in geometry and texture relative to the original NeRF. This field is used to render modified object geometry and color. A proxy mesh is maintained to guide geometric modifications. Steps: 1. Learn Editing Field: Encode the desired changes in geometry and texture over the original NeRF scene by learning a prior-guided editing field. 2. Render Modified Geometry and Color: Use the learned editing field to render the modified object geometry and color. 3. Color Compositing: Present a color compositing layer supervised by the single edited view to apply the edit on novel views. This ensures better texture editing. 4. Geometric Refinement: Utilize a proxy mesh and cyclic constraints to achieve accurate geometric modifications. 5. Regularization: Apply feature cluster-based regularization to manage the edited areas while maintaining the integrity of content that is not being edited. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method is applied on real and synthetic scenes. Specific edge cases regarding precision or degenerate input are not detailed in the provided sources. A sibling method for NeRF editing. SINE focuses on single-view editing with specific geometric and texture constraints, whereas Instruct-NeRF2NeRF uses natural language instructions. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method is applied on real and synthetic scenes by changing the geometry and texture of objects in the scene. It has been demonstrated on object insertion and replacement tasks such as hats, flowers, and glasses. Strengths and Limitations: SINE enhances semantic editing by introducing advanced methods for accurate geometric and texture modifications. It facilitates compatibility with off-the-shelf text-prompt editing methods, enabling modifications to an object's appearance and geometry, and the inpainting of missing parts of an object based on textual cues. When to Use: Use SINE when you need to edit a NeRF scene based on a single edited view with a focus on accurate geometric and texture modifications. SINE was introduced as a method for editing NeRF scenes by only editing a single view and then applying the edit to the entire scene. It enhances semantic editing by introducing advanced methods such as cyclic constraints, a proxy mesh, color compositing, and feature cluster regularization. name: Geometric Priors and Depth Integration
body: Geometric Priors and Depth Integration methods enhance standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by incorporating explicit geometric constraints—such as depth maps, surface normals, or Structure-from-Motion (SfM) features—into the optimization loop. Unlike standard NeRF, which relies solely on implicit photometric consistency and often suffers from ambiguous geometry in sparse-view or textureless scenarios, these methods enforce hard boundaries, metric scale, or structural consistency to improve reconstruction fidelity. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods like AdaNeRF or SinNeRF by explicitly modeling the scene's 3D structure (via SDFs, cost volumes, or depth priors) rather than just refining the radiance field's appearance or frequency representation. All methods in this family build on Specific Model Architectures but diverge in how the geometric information is integrated into the optimization loop. The shared mechanism involves augmenting the standard photometric loss with geometric terms or modifying the ray sampling process to respect geometric boundaries. Geometric Loss Functions: Many methods introduce explicit loss terms that penalize deviations from geometric priors. Common forms include: 1. Depth Consistency Loss: Minimizes the difference between the rendered depth (computed as the expected depth along the ray) and a prior depth map D{prior}: L{depth} = \| D{rendered} - D{prior} \|1 2. Normal Smoothness: Encourages surface normals derived from the density field to be smooth or aligned with estimated normals. 3. Epipolar Constraints: Enforces that 3D points reconstructed from matched features in different views lie on the corresponding epipolar lines. Depth-Guided Sampling: Instead of uniform or hierarchical sampling along the entire ray, these methods use depth priors to concentrate samples near the estimated surface. This reduces computational cost and mitigates the "transparent" artifacts common in standard NeRF when geometry is ambiguous. For example, samples are clustered around the depth value predicted by a monocular depth estimator. Signed Distance Fields (SDF): Some variants replace the volumetric density \sigma with a Signed Distance Field (SDF). The rendering integral is modified to integrate weights based on the SDF value relative to a truncation distance tr, effectively creating a thin shell around the surface rather than a volumetric blob. The weight for a sample at distance d is often computed as: w = \sigma\left(\frac{d}{tr}\right) \cdot \sigma\left(-\frac{d}{tr}\right) This allows for direct mesh extraction via Marching Cubes. Integrates explicit SfM constraints (matched features, epipolar geometry) into the NeRF loss to improve geometric accuracy under sparse inputs. It uses sub-pixel rendering and a pyramidal optimization strategy to avoid local minima. Uses monocular depth priors (DepthAnythingV2) to guide learning via Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss and Depth Structural Consistency Regularization. It employs dynamic optimal sampling to handle varying depth levels. Addresses sparse-view ambiguity by modeling geometry through a cascaded 3D cost volume and Transformer-based attention. It extracts view-independent and view-dependent tokens to predict density and color, enabling robust generalization. Replaces density with a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) for geometry and a radiance field for appearance. It enforces hard boundaries, allowing direct mesh extraction and solving the issue of semi-transparent artifacts. Solves high-disparity synthesis artifacts by using dense depth priors to guide feature fusion and sampling. It leverages predicted depth maps to align features from sparse input views, improving correspondence search. Replaces handcrafted UDF-to-density mappings with a learnable neural network fw that considers 3D context from neighboring points. It learns a robust mapping from local geometric structures to rendering weights, reducing bias and outlier sensitivity. Integrates explicit geometric priors (normal smoothness, bilateral edge-aware constraints) directly into the optimization loop. It unifies physical imaging and geometric constraints for accurate 3D reconstruction under complex imaging conditions. The integration of geometric priors into NeRF-based reconstruction emerged to address the inherent ambiguity of implicit volumetric representations, particularly in sparse-view settings or scenes with low texture. Early NeRF implementations relied on photometric consistency alone, which often resulted in "floaters" or incorrect geometry in unobserved regions. Subsequent works introduced explicit geometric signals such as SfM features, monocular depth estimators, and SDFs to regularize the optimization landscape. This family represents the convergence of traditional multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques with differentiable rendering, allowing for metric-scale reconstruction and direct mesh extraction.

name: SfMNeRF
head: SfM-NeRF
body: SfMNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis and 3D-scene geometry reconstruction using Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) under sparse input conditions. It improves geometric accuracy and avoids local minima by integrating Structure-from-Motion (SfM) constraints—specifically matched feature positions, epipolar geometry, and multi-view photometric consistency—into the view synthesis training loop. Unlike standard NeRF, which relies solely on implicit photometric consistency, SfMNeRF explicitly constrains the 3D-scene structure using sparse feature matches and epipolar lines, while employing sub-pixel rendering to increase sample density and generalization. SfMNeRF builds on Specific Model Architectures by augmenting the standard NeRF optimization with explicit geometric losses derived from sparse features and multi-view geometry. Inputs: A set of m training images with known camera intrinsics K and global poses [\mathbf{r}i, \mathbf{t}i]. Matched Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) correspondences between image pairs. A pyramidal representation of the input images for coarse-to-fine optimization. Outputs: A trained NeRF model (MLP parameters \theta) representing volume density \sigma\theta and color c\theta. Synthesized novel views and depth maps. Camera Intrinsic Matrix (K): 3 \times 3 matrix mapping 3D world coordinates to 2D image coordinates. Relative Pose (T{r \to t}): Transformation matrix from reference image r to target image t, composed of rotation \mathbf{r} and translation \mathbf{t}. SIFT Features: A set of 2D pixel coordinates in reference and target images, matched across views. Mask Map (M): A binary mask where M(p(k))=1 if point p(k) lies within the minimum bounding rectangle of all matched SIFT features in the reference image, else 0. Depth Map (D): Estimated depth for each pixel, computed via volume rendering integration. 1. Pyramidal Construction: Construct an L-level pyramid for the reference image Ir and target image It. Let I^0r = Ir and I^0t = It. For level n > 0, I^nr and I^nt are downsampled versions of I^{n-1}r and I^{n-1}t with half the resolution. 2. Initialization: Start optimization at the lowest pyramid level L-1. 3. Sub-pixel Sampling: For a selected patch \Omegap in the reference image, generate sub-pixel coordinates p = (x + x{off}, y + y{off}) where x{off}, y{off} \in (0, 1). 4. Ground Truth Interpolation: Compute the ground-truth color \hat{I}(p) for each sub-pixel using bilinear interpolation of the four nearest integer-pixel neighbors in the reference image. 5. Volume Rendering: Input sub-pixel coordinates and viewing directions into the NeRF to render color \tilde{I}(p) and depth D(p). 6. Feature Extraction: Extract SIFT features from the reference and target images and obtain matched correspondences. 7. 3D Coordinate Estimation: For each matched SIFT feature k, compute its 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}s^k in the reference and target views using weighted volume rendering integration. 8. Loss Computation: Calculate the following loss terms: rendering loss (L{ren}), position-of-matches loss (L{3D}), epipolar loss (L{epi}), photometric consistency loss (L{pr}), SSIM loss (L{SSIM}), depth smoothness loss (L{ds}), and depth prior loss (L{depth}). 9. Optimization: Minimize the total loss L{total}. 10. Pyramidal Progression: Recursively move to level n-2, using the depth map from level n-1 as a prior via L{depth}, until the "zeroth" level is reached. Rendering Loss: L{ren} = \frac{1}{m} \sum{pi \in \Omegap} \left\| \hat{I}(pi) - \tilde{I}(pi) \right\|2^2 where \hat{I}(pi) is the ground-truth color from interpolation and \tilde{I}(pi) is the synthesized color from NeRF. Position-of-Matched Features Loss: L{3D} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{k=1}^n \|\mathbf{x}s^k - \mathbf{x}{s'}^k\|2^2 where \mathbf{x}s^k and \mathbf{x}{s'}^k are the estimated 3D coordinates of matched SIFT feature k in the reference and target images, respectively. Epipolar Constraint Loss: L{epi} = \mint \left\{ \left\| \mathbf{d}{pr} - \mathbf{d}{pt} \right\|2^2 \right\} where \mathbf{d}{pr} is the 3D coordinate of the point in the reference image, and \mathbf{d}{pt} are the 3D coordinates of points on the epipolar line in the target image. Implausible points on the epipolar line are filtered by color similarity threshold. Warped Pixel Coordinate: \hat{p}t = K T{r \to t} \mathbf{x}p where \mathbf{x}p is the 3D coordinate of pixel p in the reference image, K is the intrinsic matrix, and T{r \to t} = [\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}] is the relative pose. Relative Pose Definition: \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}t^{-1}, \quad \mathbf{t} = -\mathbf{r}t^{-1}\mathbf{t}t where [\mathbf{r}t, \mathbf{t}t] is the global pose of the target image. Photometric Reconstruction Loss: L{pr} = \sum{p(k) \in \Omegap} M(p(k)) \left| \hat{I}r(p(k)) - \hat{I}t(\hat{p}t(k)) \right| where \hat{I}r is the reference patch color, \hat{I}t(\hat{p}t(k)) is the interpolated color of the warped point in the target image, and M is the binary mask. SSIM Loss: L{SSIM} = M \left( \frac{1 - SSIM{r \to t}}{2} \right) where SSIM{r \to t} is the structural similarity between the reference and target patches. Depth Smooth Loss: L{ds} = \sum{p(k) \in \Omegap} \left| \nabla D ( p(k)) \cdot \left( e^{-|\hat{I}(p(k))|} \right) \right| where \nabla is the 2D differential operator and D(p(k)) is the estimated depth. Depth Prior Loss (Pyramidal): L{depth} = \sum{p(k) \in \Omegap} |D(p(k)) - Dr^{L-1}(p(k)/2)| where Dr^{L-1}(p(k)/2) is the depth value sampled via bilinear interpolation from the lower-resolution depth map Dr^{L-1}. Total Loss: L{total} = \lambda{ren} L{ren} + \lambda{3D} L{3D} + \lambda{pr} L{pr} + \lambda{epi} L{epi} + \lambda{SSIM} L{SSIM} + \lambda{ds} L{ds} + \lambda{depth} L{depth} where \lambda terms are loss weights. Loss Weights: Not given in the sources. Patch Size: Not given in the sources. Optimizer: Not given in the sources. Sampling: Not given in the sources. Epipolar Point Filtering: The large number of points on an epipolar line causes computational inefficiency, and occluded points may lack corresponding points on the epipolar line. SfMNeRF filters implausible epipolar points by checking if the color difference between the point on the epipolar line and the reference point is below a threshold. Local Minima: Large pixel motions can cause the photometric consistency loss to get stuck in local minima. This is mitigated by the pyramidal strategy, which starts from low-resolution images and progressively moves to higher resolutions. Masking: The mask M(p(k)) ensures that only pixels within the minimum bounding rectangle of matched SIFT features are used for photometric consistency, filtering out regions without reliable feature correspondences. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F import numpy as np def bilinearinterpolate(image, coords): """Bilinear interpolation at float coordinates. image: [C, H, W] tensor coords: [N, 2] tensor of (x, y) in pixel space [0, W-1], [0, H-1] """ h, w = image.shape[-2], image.shape[-1] xnorm = 2 (coords[:, 0] / (w - 1)) - 1 ynorm = 2 (coords[:, 1] / (h - 1)) - 1 grid = torch.stack([xnorm, ynorm], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # gridsample expects [N, C, H, W] and grid [N, Hout, Wout, 2] # We reshape to interpolate at N points out = F.gridsample(image.unsqueeze(0), grid, aligncorners=False, mode='bilinear') return out.squeeze(0).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) def computeweighteddepth(samplesz, samplessigma, origin, direction): """Compute 3D coordinate of a feature using volume rendering integration. samplesz: [N] depth values along ray samplessigma: [N] volume densities origin: [3] ray origin direction: [3] ray direction """ delta = torch.diff(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, device=samplesz.device), samplesz])) transmittance = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(samplessigma[:-1] delta[:-1], dim=0)) weights = transmittance (1 - torch.exp(-samplessigma delta)) samplepositions = origin.unsqueeze(0) + samplesz.unsqueeze(1) direction.unsqueeze(0) weightedpos = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) samplepositions, dim=0) return weightedpos def constructpyramid(images, levels=4): """Construct L-level pyramid by halving resolution each level.""" pyr = [images] curr = images for in range(levels - 1): curr = F.interpolate(curr, scalefactor=0.5, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) pyr.append(curr) return pyr def computerelativepose(poser, poset): """Compute relative pose T{r->t} from global poses.""" Rt, tt = poset[:3,:3], poset[:3, 3] Rr, tr = poser[:3,:3], poser[:3, 3] Rinv = Rt.inverse() r = Rinv @ Rr t = -Rinv @ tt + Rinv @ Rr @ tr Trel = torch.eye(4, device=poser.device) Trel[:3,:3] = r Trel[:3, 3] = t return Trel def projecttoimage(points3d, K, Trel): """Project 3D points to 2D image coordinates.""" pointsh = torch.cat([points3d, torch.oneslike(points3d[:,:1])], dim=1) pointscam = (Trel @ pointsh.t()).t()[:,:3] points2d = (K @ pointscam.t()).t()[:,:2] return points2d def computesiftmask(coords, matches, imgshape): """Compute binary mask M(p(k)) based on SIFT bounding box.""" h, w = imgshape[-2], imgshape[-1] if len(matches) == 0: return torch.zeros(h, w, dtype=torch.float32, device=coords.device) refcoords = torch.stack([m.refx, m.refy] for m in matches) minx, maxx = refcoords[:, 0].min(), refcoords[:, 0].max() miny, maxy = refcoords[:, 1].min(), refcoords[:, 1].max() mask = torch.zeros(h, w, dtype=torch.float32, device=coords.device) yidx, xidx = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(h), torch.arange(w), indexing='ij') mask[(xidx >= minx) & (xidx <= maxx) & (yidx >= miny) & (yidx <= maxy)] = 1.0 return mask def computedepthgradient(depthmap): """Compute L1 norm of 2D depth gradient.""" dy = torch.abs(depthmap[:, 1:,:] - depthmap[:,:-1,:]) dx = torch.abs(depthmap[:,:, 1:] - depthmap[:,:,:-1]) return torch.cat([dy, dx], dim=1) def getraysfromcoords(coords, K, pose): """Generate ray origins and directions from 2D coordinates.""" h, w = coords.shape[0], coords.shape[1] y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(h), torch.arange(w), indexing='ij') xy = torch.stack([x.float(), y.float()], dim=-1).view(-1, 2) xyh = torch.cat([xy, torch.oneslike(xy[:,:1])], dim=1) invK = K.inverse() camdirs = (invK @ xyh.t()).t()[:,:3] camdirs = camdirs / torch.norm(camdirs, dim=1, keepdim=True) R = pose[:3,:3] dirs = (R @ camdirs.t()).t() origins = pose[:3, 3].unsqueeze(0).expand(h w, -1) return origins.view(h, w, 3), dirs.view(h, w, 3) def renderneurf(rayso, raysd, nerfmodel, numsamples=64): """Simplified NeRF rendering returning color and depth.""" # Standard hierarchical sampling would occur here z = torch.linspace(0.2, 6.0, numsamples, device=rayso.device).view(1, 1, numsamples).expandas(rayso[...,:1]) pts = rayso + raysd z sigma, color = nerfmodel(pts, raysd) # Alpha compositing delta = 0.1 alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-2) weights = alpha T[...,:-1,:] renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights color, dim=-2) rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights z[..., 0], dim=-2) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth def sfmnerfstep(referenceimage, targetimage, nerfmodel, kmatrix, poser, poset, siftmatches, prevdepthmap=None): """One optimization step for a specific pyramid level.""" h, w = referenceimage.shape[-2], referenceimage.shape[-1] # 1. Sub-pixel Sampling xoff = torch.rand(h, w, device=referenceimage.device) yoff = torch.rand(h, w, device=referenceimage.device) basex, basey = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(w), torch.arange(h), indexing='ij') subpixelcoords = torch.stack([basex.float() + xoff, basey.float() + yoff], dim=-1) # 2. Ground Truth Interpolation gtcolors = bilinearinterpolate(referenceimage, subpixelcoords.view(-1, 2)).view(h, w, 3) # 3. Volume Rendering rayso, raysd = getraysfromcoords(subpixelcoords, kmatrix, poser) renderedcolors, rendereddepths = renderneurf(rayso, raysd, nerfmodel) # 4. Loss Computation lren = torch.mean((gtcolors - renderedcolors) 2) l3d = 0.0 lepi = 0.0 for match in siftmatches: rayrefo, rayrefd = getraysfromcoords(match.refcoord.unsqueeze(0), kmatrix, poser) raytgto, raytgtd = getraysfromcoords(match.tgtcoord.unsqueeze(0), kmatrix, poset) zref, sigmaref = nerfmodel.sample(rayrefo, rayrefd) xsref = computeweighteddepth(zref, sigmaref, rayrefo[0], rayrefd[0]) ztgt, sigmatgt = nerfmodel.sample(raytgto, raytgtd) xstgt = computeweighteddepth(ztgt, sigmatgt, raytgto[0], raytgtd[0]) l3d += torch.norm(xsref - dpt) 2 if dist < mindist: mindist = dist lepi += mindist l3d /= max(len(siftmatches), 1) lepi /= max(len(siftmatches), 1) # Photometric consistency patchrayso, patchraysd = getraysfromcoords(subpixelcoords, kmatrix, poser), zpatch = nerfmodel.sample(patchrayso, patchraysd) patch3d = patchrayso + patchraysd zpatch relativepose = computerelativepose(poser, poset) warpedcoords2d = projecttoimage(patch3d.view(-1, 3), kmatrix, relativepose).view(h, w, 2) warpedcolors = bilinearinterpolate(targetimage, warpedcoords2d.view(-1, 2)).view(h, w, 3) mask = computesiftmask(subpixelcoords, siftmatches, referenceimage.shape) lpr = torch.mean(mask torch.abs(referenceimage - warpedcolors)) lssim = torch.mean(mask (1.0 - ssimindex(referenceimage, warpedcolors)) / 2.0) # Depth smoothness depthgrad = computedepthgradient(rendereddepths) intensityweight = torch.exp(-torch.abs(renderedcolors)) lds = torch.mean(depthgrad intensityweight) # Depth prior ldepth = 0.0 if prevdepthmap is not None: lowrescoords = subpixelcoords / 2.0 prevdepthvals = bilinearinterpolate(prevdepthmap, lowrescoords.view(-1, 2)).view(h, w) ldepth = torch.mean(torch.abs(rendereddepths - prevdepthvals)) totalloss = (1.0 lren + 1.0 l3d + 0.001 lpr + 0.0001 lepi + 0.008 lssim + 0.01 lds + 1.0 ldepth) return totalloss def trainsfmnerf(images, poses, kmatrix, siftmatches): """Main training loop with pyramidal strategy.""" levels = constructpyramid(images) model = NeRFModel() prevdepthmap = None for level in reversed(range(len(levels))): refimg = levels[level] tgtimg = levels[level] # Simplified: same image pair for demo optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) for iteration in range(1000): optimizer.zerograd() loss = sfmnerfstep(refimg, tgtimg, model, kmatrix, poses[0], poses[1], siftmatches, prevdepthmap) loss.backward() optimizer.step() with torch.nograd(): rayso, raysd = getraysfromcoords(torch.zeros(1, 1, 2, device=refimg.device), kmatrix, poses[0]), prevdepthmap = renderneurf(rayso, raysd, model) return model Time Complexity: The method is computationally intensive due to the additional geometric losses. The epipolar constraint requires searching for the minimum distance along the epipolar line for each feature match, which can be optimized by filtering implausible points via color similarity. The pyramidal strategy reduces the computational burden at higher resolutions by initializing from coarse estimates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model, intermediate depth maps for the pyramidal strategy, and SIFT feature matches. Performance: Evaluated on three public datasets, SfMNeRF surpasses state-of-the-art approaches given sparse inputs. It improves novel view synthesis quality and 3D-scene geometry reconstruction compared to standard NeRF, which suffers from inaccurate 3D structures under sparse conditions. Strengths: Explicitly constrains geometry using SfM priors, reducing shape-radiance ambiguity. Sub-pixel rendering improves generalization. Pyramidal strategy prevents local minima. Limitations: Relies on the quality of SIFT feature matches. Large occlusions or textureless regions may lack sufficient features. The epipolar constraint can be computationally expensive if not filtered properly. SfMNeRF was proposed to address the limitations of existing NeRF-based methods in obtaining moderate 3D structures under sparse input conditions, where novel view synthesis quality drops dramatically due to implicitly reconstructed inaccurate 3D-scene structures. The method leverages knowledge from self-supervised depth estimation and Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to explicitly constrain the 3D-scene geometry during view synthesis training. It was evaluated on three public datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/XTU-PR-LAB/SfMNeRF. name: DASNeRF
head: Depth consistency optimization, adaptive sampling, and hierarchical structural fusion for sparse view neural radiance fields
body: DASNeRF is a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization method designed for sparse-view 3D reconstruction that integrates accurate monocular depth priors to guide learning and reduce lighting artifacts. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF and other geometric priors by combining a dynamic optimal sampling mechanism with two specific depth regularization terms: Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss and Depth Structural Consistency Regularization. Unlike methods that rely on uniform sampling or simple depth consistency, DASNeRF uses a pre-trained depth estimator (DepthAnythingV2) to extract relative depth ordering and structural continuity constraints, which are enforced via a dynamic boundary adjustment strategy to handle varying depth levels in complex scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of M input images I = \{I1,..., IM\} with corresponding camera poses P = \{p1,..., pM\}. Outputs: A trained implicit radiance field model (MLP) that predicts volumetric density \sigma and color c, and rendered images/depth maps for novel views. Data Structures: Scene Representation: An MLP f\Theta mapping 3D position x and viewing direction d to density \sigma and color c. The input to the MLP is enhanced with position encoding \gamma and a five-dimensional vector containing coordinate and ray information. Depth Prior: A depth map D{V2} estimated by the DepthAnythingV2 model. Sampling Points: A set of N points along a ray, obtained via 3D cone frustum sampling (Mip-NeRF) and a three-layer dynamic sampling mechanism. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss. Default: 0.2. \gamma: Weight for Depth Structural Consistency Regularization. Default: 0.02. \alpha: Hyperparameter for dynamic boundary adjustment. Value: Not given in the sources. m{ar}: Dynamic boundary margin, calculated per pixel pair. m'{ar}: Small boundary value for structural consistency. Value: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Depth Prior Estimation: For each input image Ii, use the pre-trained DepthAnythingV2 model to estimate the depth map D{V2}^i. DepthAnythingV2 is preferred over MiDaS for its ability to handle transparent/reflective objects and its 10x faster inference speed. The depth data is processed using relative inverse depth. 2. Dynamic Optimal Sampling: For a ray r originating from camera center o with direction d, defined by near tn and far tf boundaries: Employ 3D cone frustum sampling from Mip-NeRF to account for pixel footprint size. Apply a three-layer dynamic sampling mechanism to obtain N sample points t1,..., tN along the ray. For each sample point ti, compute the 3D position xi = o + ti d and the viewing direction d. Construct a five-dimensional input vector for the MLP containing the coordinates and ray information of the sampled points. 3. NeRF Forward Pass: Feed the five-dimensional input vector into the MLP with per-layer input fusion. Each MLP layer l takes two inputs: the features from the previous layer h{l-1} and the processed five-dimensional input information v. The MLP outputs volumetric density \sigmai and color ci for each sample point. 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the transmittance Ti and opacity \alphai for each sample: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the interval between samples. Compute the rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \omegai ci, \quad \text{where } \omegai = Ti \alphai Compute the rendered depth dr for the ray: dr = \sum{i=1}^{N} \omegai ti This depth dr corresponds to a local region P of the RGB image I. 5. Loss Calculation: The total loss is L = L{nerf} + \lambda L{DOF} + \gamma R{DSC}. Photometric Loss (L{nerf}): L{nerf} = \sum{r \in R} \| C(r) - \hat{C}(r) \|2^2 where C(r) is the ground truth pixel color and R is the set of all rays. Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss (L{DOF}): This loss enforces relative depth ordering consistency between the rendered depth dr and the prior depth D{V2}. 1. Identify pairs of 2D pixel coordinates (k1, k2) in the local region such that D{V2}^{k1} \leq D{V2}^{k2} (pixel k1 is closer or equal depth to k2 in the prior). 2. Calculate the dynamic boundary margin m{ar}: m{ar} = \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} |dr^{k1}[i] - dr^{k2}[i]| where dr^{k1}[i] and dr^{k2}[i] denote the depth values of the i-th pixel at different sampling layers for pixels k1 and k2. 3. Compute the loss: L{DOF} = \sum{D{V2}^{k1} \leq D{V2}^{k2}} \max(dr^{k1} - dr^{k2} + m{ar}, 0) This penalizes cases where the rendered depth order contradicts the prior, with a margin that adapts to the local depth variance. Depth Structural Consistency Regularization (R{DSC}): This loss enforces continuity of depth values between neighboring pixels if they are continuous in the prior. 1. For each pixel k1, identify neighboring pixels k2 such that d{V2}^{k2} \in KNN(d{V2}^{k2}) based on depth values within a small region. 2. Compute the loss: R{DSC} = \sum{k1} \sum{d{V2}^{k2} \in KNN(d{V2}^{k2})} \max(|dr^{k1} - dr^{k2}| - m'{ar}, 0) where m'{ar} is a small boundary value accounting for minor depth variations. 6. Optimization: Minimize L with respect to the MLP parameters using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DASNeRF: def init(self, mlp, depthestimator, alpha=1.0, lambdadof=0.2, gammadsc=0.02): self.mlp = mlp self.depthestimator = depthestimator self.alpha = alpha self.lambdadof = lambdadof self.gammadsc = gammadsc def getdepthprior(self, image): """Estimate depth map using DepthAnythingV2.""" # DepthAnythingV2 returns relative inverse depth or normalized depth depthprior = self.depthestimator(image) return depthprior def sampleray(self, rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, nsamples): """ Sample points along a ray using 3D cone frustum and dynamic sampling. Returns: positions (N, 3), directions (N, 3), tvalues (N,) """ # 1. 3D cone frustum sampling from Mip-NeRF tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, nsamples) # 2. Dynamic sampling mechanism (three-layer) # Standard perturbation for anti-aliasing and dynamic spacing tvals = tvals + torch.randlike(tvals) (tfar - tnear) / nsamples # Compute 3D positions positions = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1) rayd.unsqueeze(1) # Directions are constant for straight rays directions = rayd.unsqueeze(1).expandas(positions) return positions, directions, tvals def forwardmlp(self, positions, directions): """ MLP with per-layer input fusion. Input: 5D vector (coords + ray info) fused with layer features. """ # Position encoding gamma is applied to positions and directions # Each layer takes previous features and the 5D input sigma, color = self.mlp(positions, directions) return sigma, color def volumerender(self, sigma, color, tvals): """ Standard volume rendering. Returns: renderedcolor, rendereddepth, weights """ deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # Handle last delta if needed, usually zero or negligible deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.zeroslike(deltas[:1])], dim=-1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:1]), 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10], dim=-1), dim=-1)[:,:-1] weights = alpha transmittance renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1) rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights tvals, dim=1) return renderedcolor, rendereddepth, weights def computedepthorderingloss(self, rendereddepth, depthprior, alpha): """ Compute Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss (LDOF). """ # Identify pixel pairs (k1, k2) where depthprior[k1] <= depthprior[k2] # Standard grid iteration to find valid pairs pairs = [] H, W = depthprior.shape for y1 in range(H): for x1 in range(W): for y2 in range(H): for x2 in range(W): if depthprior[y1, x1] <= depthprior[y2, x2]: pairs.append(((y1, x1), (y2, x2))) loss = 0.0 for (y1, x1), (y2, x2) in pairs: drk1 = rendereddepth[y1, x1] drk2 = rendereddepth[y2, x2] # Dynamic margin calculation # mar = alpha mean(|dr^k1[i] - dr^k2[i]|) over samples # Using sample positions tvals as proxy for sample depths mar = alpha torch.mean(torch.abs(tvals[y1, x1] - tvals[y2, x2])) loss += torch.clamp(drk1 - drk2 + mar, min=0) return loss def computestructuralconsistencyloss(self, rendereddepth, depthprior, kneighbors=3): """ Compute Depth Structural Consistency Regularization (RDSC). """ # Find k-nearest neighbors in depth space for each pixel in depthprior # Standard grid-based KNN on depth values loss = 0.0 H, W = depthprior.shape for y1 in range(H): for x1 in range(W): # Compute distances to all other pixels in a small region neighbors = [] for dy in range(-2, 3): for dx in range(-2, 3): ny, nx = y1 + dy, x1 + dx if 0 <= ny < H and 0 <= nx < W and (ny != y1 or nx != x1): neighbors.append((ny, nx)) # Sort by depth difference and pick k nearest neighbors.sort(key=lambda p: torch.abs(depthprior[p[0], p[1]] - depthprior[y1, x1])) selectedneighbors = neighbors[:kneighbors] for y2, x2 in selectedneighbors: drk1 = rendereddepth[y1, x1] drk2 = rendereddepth[y2, x2] # Small boundary value m'ar marprime = 1e-3 loss += torch.clamp(torch.abs(drk1 - drk2) - marprime, min=0) return loss def trainstep(self, images, poses, tnear, tfar, nsamples): """ Single training step. """ self.mlp.train() totalloss = 0.0 for i, (image, pose) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # 1. Get Depth Prior depthprior = self.getdepthprior(image) # 2. Sample Rays Generate rays from camera pose rayo, rayd = self.generaterays(pose, image.shape) # 3. Sample Points positions, directions, tvals = self.sampleray(rayo, rayd, tnear, tfar, nsamples) # 4. MLP Forward sigma, color = self.forwardmlp(positions, directions) # 5. Volume Render renderedcolor, rendereddepth, weights = self.volumerender(sigma, color, tvals) # 6. Compute Losses # Photometric Loss gtcolor = image.permute(2, 0, 1) # Assuming HWC to CHW lnerf = torch.mean((renderedcolor - gtcolor) 2) # Depth Ordering Fidelity Loss ldof = self.computedepthorderingloss(rendereddepth, depthprior, self.alpha) # Depth Structural Consistency Loss rdsc = self.computestructuralconsistencyloss(rendereddepth, depthprior) # Total Loss loss = lnerf + self.lambdadof ldof + self.gammadsc rdsc totalloss += loss return totalloss / len(images) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Prior Accuracy: If the monocular depth estimator (DepthAnythingV2) fails on transparent or reflective surfaces, the regularization may introduce artifacts. Dynamic Margin Calculation: The dynamic boundary adjustment m{ar} depends on the depth differences at different sampling layers. Sparse Views: The method is designed for sparse inputs. Time Complexity: The method involves an additional forward pass through the DepthAnythingV2 model for each input image during training (or pre-computed). The dynamic sampling and per-layer input fusion add computational overhead to the standard NeRF forward pass. DepthAnythingV2 is 10 times faster than MiDaS, reducing this overhead. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard NeRF, plus storage for the depth priors. The five-dimensional input fusion does not significantly increase memory usage. Performance: DASNeRF outperforms existing methods in sparse reconstruction details. It is particularly effective in scenes with complex geometries, transparent objects, and intricate details where standard NeRF struggles. Strengths: Improved detail preservation in sparse views. Robustness to lighting variations via dynamic sampling. Effective handling of depth discontinuities and noise through dynamic boundary adjustment. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the monocular depth estimator. Computational cost is higher than standard NeRF due to depth estimation and additional loss calculations. Hyperparameters \alpha, m'{ar} are not specified in the sources, requiring tuning. DASNeRF is an optimized Neural Radiance Field approach for sparse inputs that improves sparse reconstruction details. It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF, which typically requires hundreds of images for high-fidelity reconstruction, by enabling sparse-view 3D reconstruction. The method builds on the Neural Radiance Field framework [8] and integrates recent advances in monocular depth estimation (DepthAnythingV2) and Mip-NeRF sampling. It is used in applications requiring rapid depth map generation and practical deployment in fields such as autonomous driving and augmented reality, leveraging the speed and accuracy of DepthAnythingV2.
