A: (nchannels, k), B: (k, 3) # Layer i: nchannels -> nchannels. A: (nchannels, k), B: (k, nchannels) # Layer last-1: nchannels -> 1. A: (1, k), B: (k, nchannels) # Layer last: nchannels -> 3. A: (3, k), B: (k, nchannels) # Simplified: Generate a large vector and reshape # Total params = sum(nout k + k nin) for all layers # Let's assume a simpler approach: Generate A and B for each layer sequentially self.numfmm = nlayers + 3 # Input + Hidden + 2 Heads # Calculate total output size totalparams = 0 # Input layer totalparams += nchannels k + k 3 # Hidden layers for in range(nlayers): totalparams += nchannels k + k nchannels # Output layers totalparams += 1 k + k nchannels # Sigma totalparams += 3 k + k nchannels # Color self.outputlayer = nn.Linear(512, totalparams) def forward(self, z): style = self.mapping(z) style = self.synthesis(style) params = self.outputlayer(style) # Reshape params into A and B matrices for each layer Alist = [] Blist = [] idx = 0 # Input layer: 3 -> nchannels nout = self.nchannels nin = 3 A = params[:, idx:idx + nout self.k].view(-1, nout, self.k) B = params[:, idx + nout self.k:idx + nout self.k + self.k nin].view(-1, self.k, nin) Alist.append(A) Blist.append(B) idx += nout self.k + self.k nin # Hidden layers for in range(self.nlayers): nout = self.nchannels nin = self.nchannels A = params[:, idx:idx + nout self.k].view(-1, nout, self.k) B = params[:, idx + nout self.k:idx + nout self.k + self.k nin].view(-1, self.k, nin) Alist.append(A) Blist.append(B) idx += nout self.k + self.k nin # Sigma head: nchannels -> 1 nout = 1 nin = self.nchannels A = params[:, idx:idx + nout self.k].view(-1, nout, self.k) B = params[:, idx + nout self.k:idx + nout self.k + self.k nin].view(-1, self.k, nin) Alist.append(A) Blist.append(B) idx += nout self.k + self.k nin # Color head: nchannels -> 3 nout = 3 nin = self.nchannels A = params[:, idx:idx + nout self.k].view(-1, nout, self.k) B = params[:, idx + nout self.k:idx + nout self.k + self.k nin].view(-1, self.k, nin) Alist.append(A) Blist.append(B) return Alist, Blist class Discriminator(nn.Module): """ Standard 2D Discriminator (e.g., StyleGAN2 discriminator). Hidden layer channels: 128. Network depth: 4 to 8 layers. Input noise vector: Gaussian distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewing Directions: Standard NeRF requires viewing directions. HyperNeRFGAN omits them, which is suitable for datasets lacking view-dependent characteristics (e.g., reflections). Fine Network: HyperNeRFGAN rejects the "fine" network used in standard NeRF for multi-scale rendering, using only the "coarse" network to reduce training cost. Computational Expense: Reducing channels from 256 to 128 and layers from 8 to 4 reduces computational expense. Uses style-based generators to control NeRF attributes. Choose when explicit style control is needed. StyleNeRF Encodes scenes into a latent code. Choose when compact scene representation is prioritized. Latent-NeRF Uses SIREN with conditioning. Choose when high-quality 3D-aware generation is needed with view dependence. pi-GAN Uses attention-based latent codes. Choose for complex scene synthesis. GIRAFFE Optimizes latent codes for fixed networks. Choose for image editing. Generative Latent Optimization General GAN framework. Choose for general generative modeling. Adversarial Training (GAN) Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to standard NeRF due to the omission of the fine network and reduced network size (128 channels, 4-8 layers). Memory Complexity: Controlled by the rank k of the modulation matrices. Higher k increases expressiveness but also memory usage. Measured Performance: ShapeNet Car: FID 29.6 (vs. Point2NeRF 82.1). CARLA: FID 20.5, KID 0.78, IS 4.20 (outperforming HoloGAN, GRAF, π-GAN). CelebA: FID 15.04, KID 0.66, IS 2.63 (comparable to π-GAN). Strengths: Does not require camera position information; suitable for medical data and datasets with few views; superior performance on datasets where camera estimation is challenging. Limitations: Cannot model view-dependent effects (e.g., reflections) as viewing directions are omitted. When to Use: When camera poses are unknown/unreliable, or for medical imaging (DRR). When Not to Use: When view-dependent effects are critical. HyperNeRFGAN was introduced in 2023 by authors who proposed using a hypernetwork to generate NeRF weights, trained with a StyleGAN2 objective. It addresses the limitation of NeRF training requiring camera positions, which is often unavailable in medical data or datasets with few views. name: Latent-NeRF
body: Latent-NeRF optimizes a Neural Radiance Field to render 2D feature maps directly in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder (specifically Stable Diffusion), rather than in RGB space. This avoids the computational burden of encoding rendered RGB images to latent space at each guidance step. Unlike standard NeRF, which predicts RGB colors directly, it predicts pseudo-color channels corresponding to latent features, allowing the use of powerful 2D image priors for 3D consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, text prompt T, and optional Sketch-Shape geometry. Output: Volume density \sigma and a 4-channel latent feature map \mathbf{z}. Data Structures: NeRF MLP: A multi-layer perceptron with ReLU activations and skip connections that takes positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and direction \mathbf{d} as input. Latent Space: The MLP outputs \sigma and \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 64 \times 64}, matching the channel depth and resolution of Stable Diffusion's latent space. Diffusion Model: A pre-trained Stable Diffusion UNet used for conditional denoising. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling & MLP Query: Sample points \mathbf{x}i along rays and directions \mathbf{d}i. Query the NeRF MLP to predict density \sigmai and latent features \mathbf{z}i. 2. Volumetric Rendering: Integrate \sigmai and \mathbf{z}i along the ray to produce a 2D latent feature map \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{r}) for the current viewpoint. 3. Noise Addition: Add Gaussian noise \epsilon to \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{r}) at a randomly sampled diffusion timestep t to obtain \mathbf{z}t. 4. Conditional Denoising: Pass \mathbf{z}t to the Stable Diffusion model conditioned on T to predict the noise component \hat{\epsilon}\phi. 5. Gradient Approximation: Approximate the score distillation gradient by subtracting the input noise from the predicted noise: \nabla{\mathbf{z}} \approx \hat{\epsilon}\phi - \epsilon. 6. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the gradient through the rendering equation to update the NeRF MLP weights. 7. Auxiliary Losses: Optionally apply sparsity and Sketch-Shape guidance losses to constrain geometry and prevent floating artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainlatentnerf(nerfmlp, diffusionmodel, textprompt, sketchshape=None): for iteration in range(maxiterations): # 1. Sample rays and query NeRF rays = samplerandomviewpoints() sigma, z = nerfmlp(rays.positions, rays.directions) # 2. Volumetric render latent feature map zrendered = volumerender(z, sigma, rays) # 3. Add noise at random diffusion step t epsilon = torch.randnlike(zrendered) zt = addnoise(zrendered, epsilon, t) # 4. Denoise with Stable Diffusion conditioned on text predictednoise = diffusionmodel(zt, t, textprompt) # 5. Approximate SDS gradient and backprop grad = predictednoise - epsilon grad = computerenderinggradient(grad, zrendered, sigma) nerfmlp.backward(grad) # 6. Apply auxiliary losses if enabled if sketchshape is not None: losssketch = computesketchshapeloss(nerfmlp, sketchshape) losssketch.backward() if enablesparsity: losssparse = computesparsityloss(nerfmlp) losssparse.backward() optimizer.step() Formulas: Latent Rendering: \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{z}i, where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) and Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Sparsity Loss: L{\text{sparse}} = \text{BE}(w{\text{blend}}), where \text{BE} is binary entropy and w{\text{blend}} is the binary mask for blending object and background NeRFs. Sketch-Shape Loss: L{\text{Sketch-Shape}} = \text{CE}(\alpha{\text{NeRF}}(p), \alpha{\text{GT}}(p)) \cdot (1 - e^{-\frac{d^2}{2\sigmaS}}), where \text{CE} is cross-entropy, \alpha is occupancy, d is distance to the surface, and \sigmaS controls constraint leniency. Total Loss: L = \lambda{\text{SDS}} L{\text{SDS}} + \lambda{\text{sparse}} L{\text{sparse}} + \lambda{\text{sketch}} L{\text{Sketch-Shape}}. Parameters: Latent Channels: 4 channels are used to match the input of the diffusion model. Resolution: The NeRF outputs 64×64 latent features, which are decoded by the diffusion model to 512×512 RGB images. Sketch-Shape Leniency (\sigmaS): Typical values range from 0.05 (tight constraint) to 1.5 (loose/no resemblance). Loss Weights (\lambda{\text{SDS}}, \lambda{\text{sparse}}): Weights for Score-Distillation and sparsity losses; exact values not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sketch-Shape Tuning: If \sigmaS is too low (e.g., 0.05), the generated mesh strictly takes the form of the conditioning shape with no new details; if too high (e.g., 1.5), little resemblance to the shape remains. RGB Refinement Speed: Converting to RGB via a linear layer and fine-tuning takes approximately 2× longer per iteration, increasing total runtime to >30 minutes. View Inconsistency: Naive 2D super-resolution leads to inconsistent details across views; operating in the latent space before diffusion decoding mitigates this. Points2NeRF generates NeRF representations directly from 3D point clouds using a hypernetwork-based auto-encoder. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality radiance fields from sparse 3D input data by learning a mapping from point clouds to NeRF network weights, rather than optimizing a NeRF for each object individually. Unlike standard NeRF training which optimizes per-object parameters, Points2NeRF trains a single hypernetwork to produce weights for any input point cloud, enabling the generation of various NeRF functions at test time. NeRF as an Auto-Decoder generalizes single-scene NeRF fitting to multi-scene optimization by sharing network parameters across all scenes while maintaining per-scene latent codes. It treats the plenoptic function as a decoder and the scene-specific codes as latent variables with Gaussian priors, enabling joint learning of a code bank and shared weights. This approach distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by allowing unconditional 3D generation and single-view reconstruction through the latent space, rather than requiring per-scene optimization for every new input. DLR-NeRF Construction is a network distillation method that transforms a low-rank NeRF (LR-NeRF) into a distilled, slimmer network (DLR-NeRF) by decomposing its weight tensors into Tensor Train (TT) components. It solves the problem of preserving low-rank properties during subsequent weight quantization, which would otherwise break the rank constraint during fine-tuning. Unlike its siblings, it acts as a bridge between low-rank approximation and quantization, ensuring the distilled network maintains the structural benefits of low-rank optimization while enabling efficient compression. DiSR-NeRF generates high-fidelity, super-resolved NeRFs without requiring high-resolution training data. It differs from naive 2D super-resolution, which leads to inconsistent details across views. It introduces Iterative 3D Synchronization (I3DS), which alternates between 2D diffusion-based super-resolution and NeRF training to progressively align details in 3D space. It also uses Renoised Score Distillation (RSD), which refines the diffusion process by optimizing over intermediate denoised latents to produce sharper and more consistent results. Pix2NeRF uses a loss function that includes the \pi-GAN loss plus: 1) Reconstruction loss comparing predicted and sampled latent features z to ensure latent space consistency, 2) Reconstruction loss ensuring image reconstruction quality between real images I{\text{real}} and reconstructed images I{\text{reconstructed}} (generated from predicted z{\text{pred}}, d{\text{pred}}), and 3) A conditional adversarial objective to prevent mode collapse towards trivial poses. These are adaptations of single-scene continual learning NeRF methods for multiple scenes by adding a scene-specific latent code. The scene-specific latent code dimension is 32. Sketch-Shape Guidance is a technique using a coarse alignment of 3D primitives to constrain the NeRF's occupancy, allowing new details near surfaces. It computes the loss over the entire point set p used by the NeRF's volumetric rendering, leveraging existing point evaluations for efficiency. It applies L{\text{Sketch-Shape}} in addition to the standard Latent-NeRF loss. RGB Refinement is a post-training fine-tuning step that converts a Latent-NeRF (4 latent channels) to an RGB-NeRF (3 RGB channels) to improve texture detail and color fidelity. It adds a linear layer to the NeRF MLP initialized with weights from the linear approximation equation, then fine-tunes the entire model using RGB supervision. RGB refinement iterations are approximately 2× slower than latent space iterations, increasing total runtime to >30 minutes. It is most useful for complex objects or regions with detailed textures, whereas latent optimization is faster for initial shape convergence. Latent-NeRF Text Guidance is a text-guided 3D generation method using a NeRF to represent a latent space Z, optimized via score distillation from a diffusion model and a sparsity loss to prevent floating artifacts. It uses the loss L = \lambda{\text{SDS}} L{\text{SDS}} + \lambda{\text{sparse}} L{\text{sparse}}, where L{\text{sparse}} = \text{BE}(w{\text{blend}}) prevents floating radiance clouds. Textual Inversion for Latent-NeRF is a technique to condition Latent-NeRF generation on specific objects or styles defined by input images, using learned tokens from Textual Inversion. It is used to generate variations of specific objects (e.g., 'a backpack that looks like ') or styles. SNeRL is a NeRF integrated with semantic and distilled feature fields for reinforcement learning applications. It employs a NeRF-based autoencoder trained as a feature extractor for fine-tuning in multi-view RL tasks. Time Complexity: Training is slower than standard NeRF due to the iterative denoising steps and backpropagation through the diffusion model. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-trained diffusion model weights in addition to the NeRF parameters. Performance: Achieves high-fidelity, 512×512 RGB images from 64×64 latent features. Outperforms DS-NeRF, PixelNeRF, and DietNeRF on NeRF Synthetic, DTU, and LLFF datasets. Strengths: Enables text-guided and shape-guided 3D generation; produces high-frequency details not present in low-resolution training data. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to diffusion model usage; requires careful tuning of guidance strength and Sketch-Shape leniency parameters. Latent-NeRF was introduced in November 2022. It was inspired by advances in generative 2D computer vision, specifically the use of latent diffusion models like Stable Diffusion. It is the first approach to allow coloring of a grid under the guidance of a pre-trained diffusion model, achieving impressive results in novel view synthesis. It builds upon the concept of score distillation sampling (SDS) introduced in DreamFusion. body: Points2NeRF is a method that generates Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations directly from 3D point clouds using a hypernetwork-based auto-encoder architecture. It solves the problem of reconstructing continuous, view-dependent (or view-independent) implicit scenes from sparse or incomplete discrete point inputs, enabling generalizable reconstruction without per-scene optimization. Unlike sibling methods that either optimize NeRF weights per scene or use point-based sampling that cannot generalize, Points2NeRF learns a mapping from point clouds to NeRF parameters, allowing a single trained model to produce NeRFs for unseen objects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D colored point cloud X \subset \mathbb{R}^6, where each point xi contains 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and RGB color (r, g, b). Output: The parameters (weights) \phi of a NeRF network \Phi\phi. Optionally, a rendered image or mesh representation derived from \Phi\phi. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud X: A set of n points. Each point is a vector in \mathbb{R}^6. 2. Latent Code Z: A vector in a lower-dimensional latent space Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^D. 3. NeRF Parameters \phi: A vector containing the weights of the target NeRF network. 4. Voxel Grid (Optional/Implicit): The method may utilize a voxelized 3D representation for feature extraction, decoded by 3D UNet networks. Components: 1. Encoder \varepsilon: A PointNet-like permutation-invariant encoder that maps the input point cloud X to the latent code Z. 2. Decoder Hypernetwork \Psi\psi: A fully-connected network (decoder) that maps the latent code Z to the NeRF weights \phi. 3. Target NeRF \Phi\phi: A neural network that maps 3D coordinates to color and density. It does not use viewing direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Encode Point Cloud: Pass the input point cloud X through the encoder \varepsilon to obtain the latent code Z. Z = \varepsilon(X) 2. Generate NeRF Weights: Pass the latent code Z through the decoder hypernetwork \Psi\psi to generate the weight vector \phi for the NeRF. \phi = \Psi\psi(Z) Note: The hypernetwork H\Phi is effectively the composition D(E(X)). 3. Define NeRF Function: The NeRF \Phi\phi is defined as a function mapping 3D location to color and density. \Phi\phi: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^4 Given location (x, y, z), it returns color c=(r, g, b) and volume density \sigma. Note: One source defines the target network as F\Theta: \mathbb{R}^5 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^4 including viewing direction (\theta, \psi), but the primary "Generation Framework" description explicitly states viewing direction is not used because training images lack view-dependent features. The implementation follows the view-independent definition. 4. Render Scene: Render the scene using the generated NeRF \Phi\phi. The method adopts NeRFAcc with occupancy grid-based sampling from Instant-NGP to sample rays. Voxelize the original point cloud into a 3D representation. Utilize three 3D UNet networks to decode the voxelized representation into a feature representation. Use the feature extractor/aggregator combined with occupancy grid sampling to render rays. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the training loss L as the sum of the L2 rendering loss and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. L = L{color} + D{KL}(\varepsilon(X), \mathcal{N}(0, I)) Where L{color} is the L2 rendering loss over the set of rays R: L{color} = \sum{r \in R} || \Phi\phi(r) - C(r) ||^2 Here, \Phi\phi(r) is the predicted ray color and C(r) is the ground truth color. 6. Optimize: Train the hypernetwork parameters \psi (and encoder/decoder weights) by minimizing L over a training set of point cloud and 2D image pairs. The NeRF \Phi\phi is not trained directly; only the hypernetwork is trained. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class PointNetEncoder(nn.Module): """ Permutation-invariant encoder based on PointNet. Maps point cloud X (N, 6) to latent vector Z (D). """ def init(self, inputdim=6, latentdim=256): super().init() # Simplified PointNet structure self.mlp1 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, 64), nn.BatchNorm1d(64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.BatchNorm1d(128), nn.ReLU()) self.mlp2 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(128, 256), nn.BatchNorm1d(256), nn.ReLU()) self.latentdim = latentdim def forward(self, x): # x shape: (batchsize, numpoints, 6) features = self.mlp1(x) # Global max pooling features = torch.max(features, dim=1, keepdim=True)[0] z = self.mlp2(features).squeeze(1) return z class HyperNetworkDecoder(nn.Module): """ Decoder hypernetwork. Maps latent vector Z (D) to NeRF weights phi. """ def init(self, latentdim=256, numneurfparams=10000): # numneurfparams is example size super().init() self.fc = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(latentdim, 512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, numneurfparams)) def forward(self, z): phi = self.fc(z) return phi class NeRFNetwork(nn.Module): """ Target NeRF network. Maps 3D coordinates to color (RGB) and density (sigma). Does NOT use viewing direction. """ def init(self, inputdim=3, hiddendim=256, outputdim=4): super().init() self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, outputdim) # RGB + sigma) def forward(self, x): # x shape: (batchsize, numsamples, 3) out = self.layers(x) return out class Points2NeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, latentdim=256, numneurfparams=10000): super().init() self.encoder = PointNetEncoder(inputdim=6, latentdim=latentdim) self.decoder = HyperNetworkDecoder(latentdim=latentdim, numneurfparams=numneurfparams) # Note: NeRF weights are generated dynamically, so we don't store a single NeRF instance # We instantiate NeRFNetwork with the generated weights or use a functional approach. # For simplicity in this pseudocode, we assume a fixed architecture for NeRFNetwork # and we reshape phi to match its weight tensors. self.neurfarch = NeRFNetwork() def getneurfweights(self, phi): """ Reshape phi vector into the weight tensors of NeRFNetwork. This is a placeholder for the actual weight reshaping logic. """ # In a real implementation, phi would be split and reshaped into # weight matrices and bias vectors for each layer of NeRFNetwork. # Here we assume phi is already compatible or we use a functional call. return phi def forward(self, x, rays=None, gtcolors=None): """ x: Point cloud (batchsize, numpoints, 6) rays: Ray origins and directions for rendering (optional, for loss calculation) gtcolors: Ground truth colors for rays (optional, for loss calculation) """ # 1. Encode z = self.encoder(x) # 2. Generate Weights phi = self.decoder(z) # 3. Render (if rays and gtcolors provided) if rays is not None and gtcolors is not None: # Render using NeRF with weights phi # This requires a renderer that can apply dynamic weights phi to NeRFNetwork # For pseudocode, we assume a function rendernerf that takes weights and rays predcolors = rendernerfwithweights(self.neurfarch, phi, rays) # 4. Compute Loss lcolor = torch.mean((predcolors - gtcolors) 2) # 5. KL Divergence # Assume encoder outputs mean and logvar for VAE, or we approximate # The source specifies DKL(z, N(0, I)) # Assuming z is the mean of the distribution, and we need logvar # For simplicity, assuming z is sampled from N(0, I) or we have logvar # The source says: DKL(epsilon(X), N(0, I)) # This implies z ~ N(mu, sigma^2) and we compute KL(mu, sigma^2 || 0, 1) # We need to modify encoder to output mu and logvar pass return lcolor else: return phi def trainpoints2nerf(model, dataloader, optimizer, numepochs=100): model.train() for epoch in range(numepochs): for pointclouds, images in dataloader: # pointclouds: (B, N, 6) # images: (B, H, W, 3) optimizer.zerograd() # Generate NeRF weights phi = model(pointclouds) # Render images from point cloud using generated NeRF # This involves ray marching with occupancy grid sampling (NeRFAcc) # and 3D UNet feature extraction (as per source) # For pseudocode, we assume a render function exists renderedimages = renderwithoccgridandunet(pointclouds, phi, images.shape) # Compute L2 Loss lcolor = torch.mean((renderedimages - images) 2) # Compute KL Divergence # Assuming encoder outputs mu and logvar mu, logvar = model.encoder(pointclouds) # Modified encoder output klloss = -0.5 torch.mean(1 + logvar - mu2 - torch.exp(logvar)) loss = lcolor + klloss loss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: Latent Dimension D: Not specified in sources. [Not given in the sources.] NeRF Architecture: Fully connected network. Number of layers and hidden units not specified. [Not given in the sources.] Voxel Grid Resolution: Not specified. [Not given in the sources.] Sampling: Occupancy grid-based sampling from Instant-NGP. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View-Dependent Features: The method does not use viewing direction in the NeRF because the training images do not have view-dependent features like reflections. If view-dependent effects are present, this model may fail to capture them. Sparse Input: The method is designed to mitigate problems with sparse input data by generating a continuous implicit representation. Generalization: Unlike point-based sampling methods where geometry/color are determined uniquely by points and cannot be trained for generalization, this method uses voxel-based sampling which is learning-based and allows generalization. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to per-scene NeRF optimization because the hypernetwork is trained once for a dataset. Rendering time depends on the occupancy grid sampling and 3D UNet feature extraction. Memory Complexity: The method stores the hypernetwork weights, not per-scene NeRF weights. This allows producing various NeRFs at test time with minimal memory overhead per scene. Performance: The method significantly decreases generalization training time and GPU memory compared to vanilla NeRF. Strengths: Generalizable reconstruction from point clouds; single model produces multiple NeRFs; handles sparse data; enables mesh extraction via Marching Cubes. Limitations: Does not support view-dependent effects (reflections, specularities); requires 3D point clouds as input. When to use: When you have 3D point clouds and want to generate generalizable NeRFs for novel views or mesh extraction without per-scene optimization. When not to use: When view-dependent effects are important; when only 2D images are available without 3D point clouds. Points2NeRF was introduced in the paper "Points2NeRF: Generating Neural Radiance Fields from 3D point cloud" and further developed in "GPN: Generative Point-Based NeRF". It builds on the concept of hypernetworks, which generate weights for a separate target network. The method leverages PointNet for encoding point clouds and Instant-NGP's occupancy grid sampling for efficient rendering. It is used for reconstructing and repairing incomplete point clouds, and for generating complete NeRF implicit scenes from partial inputs. name: NeRF as an Auto-Decoder
body: NeRF as an Auto-Decoder generalizes single-scene NeRF fitting to multi-scene optimization by sharing network parameters across all scenes while maintaining per-scene latent codes. It treats the plenoptic function as a decoder and the scene-specific codes as latent variables with Gaussian priors, enabling joint learning of a code bank and shared weights. This approach distinguishes itself from standard NeRF by allowing unconditional 3D generation and single-view reconstruction through the latent space, rather than requiring per-scene optimization for every new input. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of multi-view images for multiple scenes, where each scene i provides a set of input views. Outputs: A shared neural network decoder \psi and a set of per-scene latent codes \{xi\}. Data Structures: Shared Decoder \psi: A neural network (e.g., MLP or triplane-based) that maps a latent code x and a 3D coordinate/ray to color and density. Parameters \psi are shared across all scenes. Per-scene Latent Codes \{xi\}: A vector xi for each scene i, treated as a latent variable optimized during training. Method: The model is trained as an auto-decoder. The plenoptic function is modeled as a probabilistic decoder assuming independent Gaussians for pixel colors: p\psi(\{yj\}|x, \{rj\}):= \prodj \mathcal{N}(yj | y\psi(x, rj), I) where yj is the rendered color, rj is the ray, and I is the identity covariance matrix. The optimization minimizes the L2 rendering loss over all scenes i and pixels j: \mathcal{L}{rend}(\{xi\}, \psi) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sumi \sumj \frac{1}{2} \| y{ij}^{gt} - y\psi(xi, r{ij}^{gt}) \|^2 \right] where y{ij}^{gt} is the ground truth pixel RGB and r{ij}^{gt} is the corresponding ray. Steps: 1. Initialize shared decoder parameters \psi and per-scene latent codes xi. 2. For each training iteration: a. Sample a scene i and a set of rays \{r{ij}\} from its input views. b. Decode the latent code xi and ray positions to predict colors y\psi(xi, r{ij}). c. Compute the L2 loss between predicted colors and ground truth y{ij}^{gt}. d. Update \psi and xi using gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}{rend}. 3. After training, xi can be sampled from the Gaussian prior for unconditional generation, or optimized for single-view reconstruction. Parameters: Latent Dimension: Not given in the sources. Prior: Gaussian prior for latent codes xi Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimization Difficulty: Ensuring continuity in generation requires a low-dimensional latent space and a complex decoder, which makes optimizing the latent code to faithfully reconstruct any given views difficult. Expressiveness: Vanilla auto-decoders may not be expressive enough for faithful reconstruction of detailed objects. A method for training an encoder and decoder pair to reconstruct images from latent codes embedded in a 3D representation like the RNR-Map. It resembles an autoencoder but is adapted for 3D environments where neural radiance fields are conditioned on these latent codes. Unlike standard NeRF optimization which directly optimizes voxel or coordinate-based fields, this approach generalizes to unseen environments by learning a mapping from 2D image features to 3D latent codes. Choose it when reconstructing or generating novel scenes from sparse or single views without per-scene optimization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables multi-scene fitting, unconditional 3D generation, and single-view reconstruction by leveraging shared parameters and latent codes. Limitations: Vanilla auto-decoders lack expressiveness for detailed objects; optimizing latent codes for faithful reconstruction is challenging due to the need for low-dimensional latents and complex decoders. When to use: When generating or reconstructing 3D scenes from limited views or unconditionally, especially in a multi-scene setting. When not to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of highly detailed single objects is required without additional priors (e.g., diffusion). The concept of treating NeRF as an auto-decoder was introduced to generalize single-scene fitting to multi-scene scenarios by sharing network parameters. This approach allows scene codes to be treated as latents with Gaussian priors, facilitating 3D completion and generation. While early methods trained auto-decoders and diffusion models in two separate stages, recent unified approaches like SSDNeRF integrate them to overcome limitations in 3D tasks. name: Encoder-Decoder Training
head: Reconstruction Framework
body: Encoder-Decoder Training is a method for training a pair of encoder \theta{enc} and decoder \theta{dec} to reconstruct images from latent codes embedded in a 3D representation, such as the RNR-Map. It generalizes to unseen environments by learning a mapping from 2D image features to 3D latent codes, unlike standard NeRF optimization which directly optimizes voxel or coordinate-based fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An RGBD image It and its relative pose \Delta pt = (\Delta xt, \Delta yt, \Delta \alphat) from the previous pose. Output: Reconstructed images at query poses. Data Structures: RNR-Map (m): A grid-form map containing latent codes. Latent Code (Ct): A feature map of size H \times W \times D, where H, W are image height/width and D is the channel size. Encoder Parameters (\theta{enc}): Network parameters for the encoder. Decoder Parameters (\theta{dec}): Network parameters for the decoder. Steps: 1. Encode: The encoder \theta{enc} encodes the input RGBD image It into a same-sized feature map Ct \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}. 2. Register (Embed): The latent codes are embedded into the RNR-Map m via a registration function F{reg}. Mapping each pixel feature c{h,w} \in Ct to a 3D world position [qx, qy, qz]^T using inverse camera projection based on camera intrinsic K, extrinsic matrix [R|t], and depth d{h,w}. Aggregating features into grid cells. X{(u,v)} = \left\{ c{h,w} \in Ct \mid u = \left\lfloor \frac{qx(h,w)}{s} \right\rceil, v = \left\lfloor \frac{qy(h,w)}{s} \right\rceil \right\} where s is the grid scale. The value m(u,v) is the mean of features in X{(u,v)}: m(u,v) = \frac{1}{n(u,v)} \sum{ci \in X{(u,v)}} ci, \quad n(u,v) = |X{(u,v)}| where n(u,v) is the count of features in the cell. 3. Decode: At a query pose, the decoder \theta{dec} samples latent codes from the RNR-Map m along each camera ray corresponding to each pixel and renders the corresponding images. 4. Update: The parameters \theta{enc} and \theta{dec} are updated to minimize the L1 loss between the rendered image and the target image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def invertmatrix(M): # Standard 3x3 matrix inversion inv = [[0.0]3 for in range(3)] det = (M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])) inv[0][0] = (M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])/det inv[0][1] = (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])/det inv[0][2] = (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])/det inv[1][0] = (M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])/det inv[1][1] = (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])/det inv[1][2] = (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])/det inv[2][0] = (M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])/det inv[2][1] = (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])/det inv[2][2] = (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])/det return inv def vectoradd(a, b): return [a[i]+b[i] for i in range(len(a))] def vectorscale(v, s): return [v[i]s for i in range(len(v))] def encoderdecodertrainingstep(It, pt, K, Rt, tt, deptht, s, thetaenc, thetadec, m, querypose, targetimage, lr): # Step 1: Encode image to latent features Ct = thetaenc(It) # [H, W, D] # Step 2: Register (Embed) features into RNR-Map H, W = len(deptht), len(deptht[0]) Kinv = invertmatrix(K) Rinv = invertmatrix(Rt) # Compute 3D world positions for each pixel using inverse camera projection qxyz = [[None]3 for in range(H)] for h in range(H): for w in range(W): p = [w, h, 1.0] cam = [sum(Kinv[i][j]p[j] for j in range(3)) deptht[h][w] for i in range(3)] qxyz[h][w] = vectoradd(vectorscale([sum(Rinv[i][j]cam[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)], 1.0), vectorscale(tt, -1.0)) # Aggregate features into grid cells according to formula (2) m = registerfeatures(Ct, qxyz, s) # Step 3: Decode latent codes to render image at query pose renderedimage = thetadec(m, querypose) # [H, W, 3] # Step 4: Compute Loss and Update parameters loss = computeloss(renderedimage, targetimage) thetaenc, thetadec = applygradients(thetaenc, thetadec, loss, lr) return renderedimage, m def registerfeatures(Ct, qxyz, s): # Aggregates features Ct into grid m based on world coordinates qxyz H, W, D = len(Ct), len(Ct[0]), len(Ct[0][0]) gridbuckets = {} for h in range(H): for w in range(W): c = Ct[h][w] qx, qy = qxyz[h][w][0], qxyz[h][w][1] u = int(round(qx / s)) v = int(round(qy / s)) key = (u, v) if key not in gridbuckets: gridbuckets[key] = [] gridbuckets[key].append(c) m = {} for key, features in gridbuckets.items(): n = len(features) if n > 0: m[key] = [sum(c[i] for c in features)/n for i in range(D)] else: m[key] = [0.0] D # Handle empty cells by zero-initialization return m def computeloss(rendered, target): return sum(abs(rendered[h][w][c] - target[h][w][c]) for h in range(len(rendered)) for w in range(len(rendered[0])) for c in range(3)) / (len(rendered)len(rendered[0])3) def applygradients(thetaenc, thetadec, loss, lr): # Standard gradient descent update gradenc = gradient(loss, thetaenc) graddec = gradient(loss, thetadec) thetaenc = {k: v - lrgradenc[k] for k, v in thetaenc.items()} thetadec = {k: v - lrgraddec[k] for k, v in thetadec.items()} return thetaenc, thetadec Parameters: Grid Scale (s): Determines the resolution of the RNR-Map grid. Loss Function: L1 loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Grid Cells: If no features map to a grid cell (u,v), n(u,v)=0. Pose Accumulation: The agent determines its absolute pose pt by cumulating relative pose differences \Delta pt from a start pose p0 = (0,0,0). Errors in relative pose estimation can lead to misalignment in the RNR-Map. A method where the NeRF is trained in latent space but supervised by a photometric loss computed in the RGB space after decoding the rendered latent images. It uses the decoder and supervises the pipeline with RGB images while keeping the NeRF in 3D latent space. The loss is defined as: \min{\alpha, T} LD(\alpha, T) \triangleq \mathbb{E}p \| xp - D(R\alpha(T, p)) \| where D represents the decoder, R\alpha is the rendering operation in latent space, and xp is the target RGB image. This ensures high-fidelity color output supervision. A hybrid training method that uses a weighted combination of the Encode-Scene loss (LE) and Decode-Scene loss (LD) to train the latent NeRF, ensuring both latent consistency and high-fidelity RGB reconstruction. It utilizes both the encoder and decoder modules of a 3D-aware autoencoder. The steps are: 1. Encode input images to latent space. 2. Train Tri-Planes in latent space. 3. Decode rendered latent images. 4. Compute loss in RGB space or latent space, or a combination. The optimization objective is: \min{\alpha, T} (1-t)LD(\alpha, T) + tLE(\alpha, T) where t \in (0, 1) is a mixing coefficient. This method combines the accelerated training of Encode-Scene with the high-fidelity color output supervision of Decode-Scene. A method for training an encoder to predict latent codes and canonical maps using data generated from an unconditional generator, avoiding the need for ground-truth 3D meshes or hand-modeled synthetic meshes required by NOCS. The steps are: 1. Sample a minibatch of priors z \sim N(0, I). 2. Feed priors through a mapping network to obtain latent codes w \in W. 3. Train the network (e.g., SegFormer with a custom regression head) to predict the canonical map and latent code w from the RGB image. A key pitfall in related methods like NOCS is the requirement for ground-truth 3D meshes or hand-modeled synthetic meshes representative of the training dataset, which are not available on real datasets. Time Complexity: The method is designed to be real-time capable, avoiding the significant time required for inference in other NeRF-based navigation methods that require rendering-based optimization. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the RNR-Map grid and the dimensionality of the latent codes D. Strengths: Enables generalization to unseen environments using pretrained encoder and decoder. Real-time capability for visual navigation. Limitations: Autoencoding a 3D environment is not trivial compared to 2D images. Pose accumulation errors can degrade map alignment. When to use: Multi-scene visual navigation where real-time performance and generalization are required. When not to use: Single-scene high-fidelity rendering without latent constraints, or when precise absolute pose is available without accumulation. The method was proposed in the context of visual navigation using a Renderable Neural Radiance Map (RNR-Map). It addresses the challenge of generalizing NeRF-based methods to unseen environments by treating the plenoptic function as a decoder and scene codes as latent codes with Gaussian priors, building on the NeRF as an Auto-Decoder framework. The RNR-Map is designed to contain the overall visual information of a 3D environment in a grid form. name: Decode-Scene
body: Decode-Scene is a method for training neural radiance fields (NeRFs) in a latent space by supervising the pipeline with RGB images directly, rendering in the latent space and then decoding to RGB for the loss computation. It differs from its sibling Encode-Scene by computing the photometric loss in RGB space after decoding, rather than encoding target images into latent space first. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input RGB images xp with corresponding camera poses p, and a decoder network D\phi with trainable parameters \phi that maps latent images to RGB space. Outputs: Optimized latent scene representation parameters \alpha and T that minimize the decoding loss. Data Structures: Latent NeRF (R\alpha): A neural radiance field that outputs a latent vector instead of RGB color. Decoder (D\phi): A neural network mapping rendered latent images to RGB space. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Latent Image: For a given camera pose p and latent scene representation (\alpha, T), render a latent image L = R\alpha(T, p). 2. Decode to RGB: Pass the rendered latent image L through the decoder network to obtain the predicted RGB image: \hat{x} = D\phi(L). 3. Compute Loss: Calculate the photometric loss between the decoded RGB image \hat{x} and the ground truth input image xp. Formula: The optimization objective is defined as: \min{\alpha, T} LD(\alpha, T) \triangleq \mathbb{E}{x, p} \| xp - D(R\alpha(T, p)) \| where: LD(\alpha, T) is the Decode-Scene loss. xp is the input RGB image for pose p. D is the decoder network. R\alpha(T, p) is the rendered latent image from the latent NeRF. The norm \| \cdot \| is generic in the source, typically representing L1 or L2. Parameters: \phi: Trainable parameters of the decoder network D\phi. \alpha, T: Parameters of the latent NeRF (e.g., Tri-Planes). Pitfalls: Performance: This method is generally slower than Encode-Scene because no latent images can be cached, and a gradient step requires differentiation through all parameters of the decoder for every training step. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mse(a, b): """Mean squared error between two tensors.""" return ((a - b) 2).mean() def decodescenestep(inputrgb, camerapose, latentnerf, decoder, alpha, T, phi): """One training step for Decode-Scene.""" # Step 1: Render latent image from the latent NeRF latentimage = latentnerf(alpha, T, camerapose) # Step 2: Decode the latent image to RGB space decodedrgb = decoder(latentimage, phi) # Step 3: Compute photometric loss in RGB space loss = mse(decodedrgb, inputrgb) return loss Encode-Scene is a method for training 3D-aware latent scene representations by first encoding input RGB images into a lower-dimensional latent space and then optimizing a neural radiance field (NeRF) to render latent images that match these pre-computed encodings. Time Complexity: Slower than Encode-Scene because the decoder must be evaluated and differentiated for every training step. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supervises the pipeline with RGB images directly, ensuring high-fidelity color images in the output space. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the lack of caching and the need to backpropagate through the decoder. Decode-Scene is a method for training NeRFs in a latent space described in. It is part of a family of latent-space training methods that contrasts with Encode-Scene and Encode-Decode-Scene. name: Encode-Scene
head: Encoder-Scene
body: Encode-Scene is a method for training 3D-aware latent scene representations by first encoding input RGB images into a lower-dimensional latent space and then optimizing a neural radiance field (NeRF) to render latent images that match these pre-computed encodings. It differs from its sibling Decode-Scene by caching latent representations, which avoids differentiating through the decoder during training and significantly accelerates the optimization process. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of training images \{xp\} with corresponding camera poses \{p\}, a 3D-aware autoencoder with encoder E\psi, and a scene representation structure (e.g., Tri-Planes T) parameterized by \alpha. Outputs: Optimized scene representation parameters (\alpha, T) that encode the 3D structure of the scene in latent space. Data Structures Latent Images (z): Cached representations of input images, stored once before training. The sources note that these latent images are 64 times smaller in resolution than the original RGB images. Scene Representation (T): A 3D-aware structure (specifically Tri-Planes in the cited work) that maps 3D coordinates to latent features. Steps 1. Encoding: For each training image xp with pose p, compute its latent representation zp = E\psi(xp) using the pre-trained encoder. 2. Caching: Store all computed latent images zp in memory. 3. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between the cached latent images and the images rendered from the latent NeRF. The objective function is: \min{\alpha, T} \mathcal{L}E(\alpha, T) \triangleq \mathbb{E}p \| E\psi(xp) - R\alpha(T, p) \| where R\alpha(T, p) is the rendered latent image from the Tri-Plane T queried at pose p. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def encodescene(trainingdata, encoder, sceneparams, numepochs, learningrate): # Step 1 & 2: Encoding and Caching latentcache = {} for image, pose in trainingdata: latentcache[pose] = encoder(image) # Step 3: Optimization for epoch in range(numepochs): for pose in trainingdata.poses: # Render latent image from current scene representation renderedlatent = renderscene(sceneparams, pose) # Get cached target latent image targetlatent = latentcache[pose] # Compute photometric loss in latent space (L2 norm) loss = sum((renderedlatent[i] - targetlatent[i]) 2 for i in range(len(renderedlatent))) / len(renderedlatent) # Backpropagate to update scene representation parameters gradients = computegradients(loss, sceneparams) sceneparams = sceneparams - learningrate gradients def computegradients(loss, params): # Standard automatic differentiation or manual gradient computation return gradientof(loss, params) Parameters Resolution Scaling: The latent space resolution is typically 64 times smaller than the RGB input resolution. Loss Function: Mean squared error (or similar L2 norm) between rendered and encoded latent images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The significant reduction in resolution (64x smaller) requires the rendering algorithm to query fewer pixels, which accelerates training but may lose high-frequency details if the latent space is too compressed. Time Complexity: Faster than Decode-Scene because the encoder is only used once during the caching phase. Gradients do not need to pass through the decoder during training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing cached latent images for all training views. However, since latent images are 64 times smaller in resolution than RGB images, the memory footprint is significantly reduced compared to storing RGB images. Performance: The reduction in rendering resolution (64x fewer pixels) greatly accelerates both rendering and training times. Strengths: Accelerated training and rendering; efficient memory usage due to latent space compression. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained 3D-aware encoder; potential loss of high-frequency details due to resolution reduction. Encode-Scene was introduced in the context of exploring 3D-aware latent spaces for efficiently learning numerous scenes. It is part of a family of methods that include Decode-Scene and Encode-Decode-Scene, designed to leverage the efficiency of latent space representations while maintaining 3D consistency. The method builds on the concept of training NeRFs in latent space, as proposed in earlier works on latent NeRFs. name: DLR-NeRF Construction
head: DLR-NeRF, DLR-NeRF Initialization, Distilled Low Rank Neural Radiance Field, Network Distillation for DLR-NeRF, Network Distillation via Tensor Train (TT) Decomposition
body: DLR-NeRF Construction is a network distillation method that transforms a low-rank NeRF (LR-NeRF) into a distilled, slimmer network (DLR-NeRF) by decomposing its weight tensors into Tensor Train (TT) components. It solves the problem of preserving low-rank properties during subsequent weight quantization, which would otherwise break the rank constraint during fine-tuning. Unlike its siblings, it acts as a bridge between low-rank approximation and quantization, ensuring the distilled network maintains the structural benefits of low-rank optimization while enabling efficient compression. Inputs and Outputs Input: The weight matrices \mathbf{W}r^i and biases \mathbf{b}i of each layer Li in a pre-trained LR-NeRF, where \mathbf{W}r^i \in \mathbb{R}^{n1 \times n2} has been reduced to rank r. Output: A DLR-NeRF model consisting of layers initialized with TT components, ready for fine-tuning. Data Structures TT Components: Each weight matrix \mathbf{W}r^i is decomposed into two tensors \mathbf{Q}{1i} and \mathbf{Q}{2i} such that \mathbf{W}r^i = \mathbf{Q}{1i} \cdot \mathbf{Q}{2i}. \mathbf{Q}{1i} \in \mathbb{R}^{n1 \times r}. \mathbf{Q}{2i} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n2}. DLR-NeRF Layers: If parameter reduction is achieved, the layer is split into two cascaded fully-connected layers: L'{i1} with weights \mathbf{Q}{1i} and L'{i2} with weights \mathbf{Q}{2i} and bias \mathbf{b}i. If parameter reduction is not achieved, the layer remains a single fully-connected layer L'i with weights \mathbf{W}r^i and bias \mathbf{b}i. Steps 1. Decomposition: For each layer i in the LR-NeRF, decompose the low-rank weight matrix \mathbf{W}r^i into TT components \mathbf{Q}{1i} and \mathbf{Q}{2i}. 2. Parameter Count Check: Calculate the number of parameters in the TT components versus the original weight matrix. TT parameters: (n1 + n2) \times r. Original parameters: n1 \times n2. 3. Layer Initialization: Case 1 (Split): If (n1 + n2) \times r < n1 \times n2, initialize two cascaded fully-connected layers L'{i1} and L'{i2} in the DLR-NeRF. Set the weights of L'{i1} to \mathbf{Q}{1i} and the weights of L'{i2} to \mathbf{Q}{2i} with bias \mathbf{b}i. Case 2 (Keep): If (n1 + n2) \times r \ge n1 \times n2, initialize one layer L'i in the DLR-NeRF with the original weight matrix \mathbf{W}r^i and bias \mathbf{b}i. 4. Fine-tuning: Fine-tune the DLR-NeRF using the same loss function as the original LR-NeRF training (Eq. 2 in) to update its parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructdlrnerf(lrnerflayers): """ Constructs DLR-NeRF from LR-NeRF by decomposing weights into TT components. Args: lrnerflayers: List of dicts with keys 'weight' (shape n1 x n2), 'bias' (shape n2,), and 'rank' (r). Returns: dlrnerflayers: List of layer dicts for DLR-NeRF. """ dlrnerflayers = [] for layer in lrnerflayers: W = layer['weight'] b = layer['bias'] n1, n2 = W.shape r = layer['rank'] # Decompose W into TT components Q1 and Q2 such that W = Q1 @ Q2 Q1, Q2 = decomposett(W, r) # Check parameter count ttparams = (n1 + n2) r origparams = n1 n2 if ttparams < origparams: # Split into two cascaded layers # Layer 1: weights Q1, no bias dlrnerflayers.append({'weight': Q1, 'bias': None}) # Layer 2: weights Q2, bias b dlrnerflayers.append({'weight': Q2, 'bias': b}) else: # Keep as single layer with original low-rank weights dlrnerflayers.append({'weight': W, 'bias': b}) return dlrnerflayers def decomposett(W, r): """ Decomposes matrix W into Q1 and Q2 using standard SVD. W = U @ S @ V^T -> Q1 = U[:,:r] @ sqrt(diag(S[:r])), Q2 = sqrt(diag(S[:r])) @ V^T[:r,:] """ import numpy as np U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(W, fullmatrices=False) Sr = np.diag(S[:r]) sqrtSr = np.sqrt(Sr) Q1 = U[:,:r] @ sqrtSr Q2 = sqrtSr @ Vt[:r,:] return Q1, Q2 Parameters Rank r: The target rank for the low-rank approximation. Loss Function: The same loss function used in the LR-NeRF training (Eq. 2 in). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Training from Scratch: Training a distilled NeRF from scratch with random weights yields poor reconstruction quality because the weight distribution differs from low-rank weights. Parameter Count Threshold: If the TT decomposition does not reduce the parameter count (i.e., (n1 + n2) \times r \ge n1 \times n2), the layer is kept as is to avoid unnecessary complexity. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The DLR-NeRF has fewer parameters than the original LR-NeRF if the TT decomposition condition is met, reducing memory footprint. Strengths: Preserves low-rank properties during quantization, enabling efficient compression without degrading reconstruction quality. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained LR-NeRF; not suitable for direct training from scratch. When to Use: When compressing NeRFs via quantization while maintaining low-rank structure is required. When Not to Use: When high-quality reconstruction is needed without compression constraints, or when training from scratch is preferred. DLR-NeRF Construction was introduced by J. Shi et al. in "Distilled Low Rank Neural Radiance Field with Quantization for Light Field Compression". It is part of the QDLR-NeRF pipeline, which combines low-rank approximation, network distillation, and quantization for light field compression. The method bridges the gap between low-rank optimization and quantization, ensuring that the distilled network retains the benefits of low-rank representation. name: pi-GAN
head: 3D Generative Adversarial Models (GANs), GRAF / pi-GAN, Periodic Implicit Generative Adversarial Networks
body: pi-GAN is a generative adversarial network (GAN) that learns an unconditional 3D-aware image synthesis model by embedding a conditional neural radiance field (NeRF) into the generator. Unlike standard 2D GANs, it produces a 5D spatio-angular radiance field parameterized by a SIREN network, conditioned on a latent noise vector via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM). It distinguishes itself from its sibling GRAF by replacing concatenation-based conditioning with FiLM, using a SIREN backbone instead of ReLU MLPs, and employing a global discriminator rather than a patch-based one to avoid local overfitting. Input: A latent noise vector \mathbf{z} \sim pz (typically standard normal) and a camera pose \boldsymbol{\xi} (defining the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}). Output: A 2D image I rendered from the camera pose \boldsymbol{\xi}. 1. Mapping Network (M) Type: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with ReLU activations. Input: Latent vector \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{dz}. Output: A set of frequency parameters \{\gammai\}{i=0}^{n-1} and phase shift parameters \{\betai\}{i=0}^{n-1}, one pair per layer of the SIREN backbone. Layout: The output is a flat vector of size 2 \times n \times N{hidden}, where n is the number of SIREN layers and N{hidden} is the hidden dimension of the SIREN. 2. SIREN Backbone (\Phi) Type: MLP with periodic sine activations. Input: 3D spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Layers: n hidden layers. Each layer i applies an affine transformation followed by a sine non-linearity. Parameters: \mathbf{W}i \in \mathbb{R}^{Ni \times Mi}: Weight matrix for layer i. \mathbf{b}i \in \mathbb{R}^{Ni}: Bias vector for layer i. \gammai \in \mathbb{R}^{Ni}: Frequency scaling factor for layer i (from Mapping Network). \betai \in \mathbb{R}^{Ni}: Phase shift for layer i (from Mapping Network). Activation Function for layer i: \phii(\mathbf{x}i) = \sin(\gammai \cdot (\mathbf{W}i \mathbf{x}i + \mathbf{b}i) + \betai) where \cdot denotes element-wise multiplication. 3. Density Head Input: Output of the final SIREN layer \Phi(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{Nn}. Parameters: \mathbf{W}\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times Nn}, \mathbf{b}\sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Output: Density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}. 4. Color Head Input: Concatenation of the SIREN output \Phi(\mathbf{x}) and the viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Parameters: \mathbf{W}c \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times (Nn + 3)}, \mathbf{b}c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Activation: \phic is typically a linear or ReLU layer (source specifies \phic generally, but standard NeRF uses ReLU; pi-GAN paper implies a final linear projection for RGB). Output: Color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \in \mathbb{R}^3. 5. Discriminator Type: Traditional convolutional neural network (CNN). Input: 2D rendered image. Output: Scalar logits for real/fake classification. 1. Latent Sampling: Sample a noise vector \mathbf{z} from the prior distribution pz. 2. Mapping: Pass \mathbf{z} through the Mapping Network M to obtain frequencies \{\gammai\} and phase shifts \{\betai\}. 3. Radiance Field Construction: Define the implicit radiance field using the SIREN backbone \Phi conditioned by \{\gammai, \betai\}. Compute the backbone output for a 3D point \mathbf{x}: \Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \phi{n-1}(\dots \phi0(\mathbf{x}) \dots) where \phii(\mathbf{x}i) = \sin(\gammai \cdot (\mathbf{W}i \mathbf{x}i + \mathbf{b}i) + \betai). 4. Density Prediction: Compute density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) using the density head: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{W}\sigma \Phi(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{b}\sigma. 5. Color Prediction: Compute view-dependent color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) using the color head: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \mathbf{W}c \phic \left( [\Phi(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{d}]^T \right) + \mathbf{b}c where [\cdot, \cdot]^T denotes concatenation. 6. Volume Rendering: Cast rays from camera origin \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{d} defined by pose \boldsymbol{\xi}. Sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. Compute pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using the standard volumetric rendering equation: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. 7. Adversarial Training: Generator Loss: The rendered image is passed to the Discriminator. The generator is trained to minimize the adversarial loss (e.g., non-saturating GAN loss) by fooling the discriminator. Discriminator Loss: The discriminator is trained to maximize the likelihood of correctly classifying real images (from the dataset) and generated images (from the generator). 8. Progressive Growing: During training, the resolution of the rendered images and the discriminator is progressively increased to accelerate convergence and stabilize training. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class MappingNetwork(nn.Module): """ Maps latent vector z to SIREN parameters (frequencies and phase shifts). """ def init(self, zdim, nlayers, hiddendim): super().init() self.nlayers = nlayers self.hiddendim = hiddendim # Simple ReLU MLP as described in layers = [] layers.append(nn.Linear(zdim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) for in range(nlayers - 1): layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) self.mlp = nn.Sequential(layers) # Output 2 nlayers hiddendim values self.paramhead = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 2 nlayers hiddendim) def forward(self, z): h = self.mlp(z) params = self.paramhead(h) # Reshape to (nlayers, 2, hiddendim) -> (nlayers, hiddendim) for gamma and beta params = params.view(self.nlayers, 2, self.hiddendim) gammas = params[:, 0,:] betas = params[:, 1,:] return gammas, betas class SIRENLayer(nn.Module): def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures, gamma, beta): super().init() self.linear = nn.Linear(infeatures, outfeatures, bias=True) # Initialize weights for sine activation stability self.linear.weight.data.uniform(-1 / infeatures, 1 / infeatures) self.linear.bias.data.uniform(-1 / infeatures, 1 / infeatures) self.gamma = gamma self.beta = beta def forward(self, x): # phii(xi) = sin(gammai (Wi xi + bi) + betai) affine = self.linear(x) return torch.sin(self.gamma affine + self.beta) class SIRENBackbone(nn.Module): def init(self, indim, nlayers, hiddendim, gammas, betas): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList() for i in range(nlayers): inf = indim if i == 0 else hiddendim outf = hiddendim # gammas and betas are tensors of shape (nlayers, hiddendim) self.layers.append(SIRENLayer(inf, outf, gammas[i], betas[i])) def forward(self, x): h = x for layer in self.layers: h = layer(h) return h class PiGANGenerator(nn.Module): def init(self, zdim, nlayers, hiddendim, nsamples): super().init() self.mapping = MappingNetwork(zdim, nlayers, hiddendim) self.nlayers = nlayers self.hiddendim = hiddendim self.nsamples = nsamples # Density head self.densityhead = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) # Color head self.colorhead = nn.Linear(hiddendim + 3, 3) # [Phi(x), d] -> RGB def forward(self, z, cameraposes): """ z: (B, zdim) cameraposes: (B, 6) or similar structure defining rays Returns: rendered images (B, H, W, 3) """ # 1. Map z to SIREN parameters gammas, betas = self.mapping(z) # (B, nlayers, hiddendim) # 2. Sample points along rays # Assuming cameraposes provides ray origins o and directions d # For simplicity, assume we have sampled points xsamples (B, N, 3) # and directions dsamples (B, N, 3) corresponding to these points # In a real implementation, this involves ray casting logic xsamples, dsamples = self.samplerays(cameraposes) # 3. Compute SIREN output for all points # Expand gammas/betas to match batch and sample dimensions # gammas: (B, nlayers, hiddendim) -> (B, N, nlayers, hiddendim) gammasexp = gammas.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.nsamples, -1, -1) betasexp = betas.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.nsamples, -1, -1) # We need to process each layer sequentially for the SIREN # However, to vectorize, we can compute the full forward pass # Note: The SIREN backbone definition in is sequential composition. # We will implement a helper that processes the batch of points through the SIREN phioutput = self.computesirenoutput(xsamples, gammasexp, betasexp) # 4. Predict Density # phioutput shape: (B, N, hiddendim) sigma = self.densityhead(phioutput).squeeze(-1) # (B, N) # 5. Predict Color # Concatenate phioutput and dsamples # dsamples shape: (B, N, 3) colorinput = torch.cat([phioutput, dsamples], dim=-1) # (B, N, hiddendim + 3) color = self.colorhead(colorinput) # (B, N, 3) # 6. Volume Rendering images = self.volumerender(xsamples, sigma, color, cameraposes) return images def computesirenoutput(self, x, gammas, betas): """ Computes the output of the SIREN backbone for a batch of points. x: (B, N, 3) gammas: (B, nlayers, hiddendim) betas: (B, nlayers, hiddendim) Returns: (B, N, hiddendim) """ B, N, = x.shape nlayers = self.nlayers hiddendim = self.hiddendim h = x # (B, N, 3) for i in range(nlayers): W = self.mapping.layers[i].linear.weight # (hiddendim, indim) b = self.mapping.layers[i].linear.bias # (hiddendim,) gammai = gammas[:, i,:] # (B, hiddendim) betai = betas[:, i,:] # (B, hiddendim) # Affine transform: W @ x.T + b # h: (B, N, indim) -> (B, N, hiddendim) h = torch.matmul(h, W.T) + b # Sine activation: sin(gamma h + beta) # gamma and beta are broadcasted over N h = torch.sin(gammai.unsqueeze(1) h + betai.unsqueeze(1)) return h def samplerays(self, cameraposes): # Placeholder for ray sampling logic # Returns xsamples (B, N, 3) and dsamples (B, N, 3) pass def volumerender(self, xsamples, sigma, color, cameraposes): # Placeholder for volumetric rendering logic # Uses the formula: C(r) = sum Ti alphai ci pass class Discriminator(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Traditional CNN discriminator self.conv = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 4, stride=2, padding=1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2, inplace=True), #... more layers nn.Conv2d(64, 1, 4, stride=1, padding=0), nn.Sigmoid() # Or linear logits depending on loss function) def forward(self, x): return self.conv(x) Latent Dimension (dz): Not given in the sources. SIREN Layers (n): Not given in the sources. Hidden Dimension (N{hidden}): Not given in the sources. Number of Samples (N): Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Local Overfitting: SIREN networks are prone to local overfitting to the last batch if sufficient coverage of the space is not maintained. This is the primary reason pi-GAN avoids the patch-based discriminator used in GRAF, opting instead for a global convolutional discriminator. Spectral Bias: While SIREN mitigates spectral bias compared to ReLU MLPs, proper initialization of weights (uniform distribution scaled by input dimension) is critical for stable training. The predecessor to pi-GAN. Uses concatenation-based conditioning of a ReLU MLP. pi-GAN improves upon it with FiLM conditioning and SIREN. GRAF Uses style-based generation but focuses on style transfer rather than unconditional 3D-aware synthesis from unposed images. StyleNeRF Uses hypernetworks to generate NeRF weights, differing from pi-GAN's direct FiLM conditioning of a SIREN. HyperNeRFGAN Infers latent codes from observations for conditional reconstruction, whereas pi-GAN is unconditional. Latent-NeRF Extends the generative NeRF framework to compositional scenes with multiple objects, using a more complex feature field representation. GIRAFFE Jointly optimizes latent codes with the scene model for reconstruction, not generative synthesis. Generative Latent Optimization The general framework used by pi-GAN. Adversarial Training (GAN) Time Complexity: Training is computationally expensive due to the 3D nature of the representation and the need for volume rendering per image. Progressive growing helps mitigate this. Memory Complexity: High, as the SIREN network must be evaluated for many samples along each ray during rendering. The global discriminator also consumes significant memory at high resolutions. Measured Performance: Achieved state-of-the-art results on CelebA, Cats, and CARLA datasets at the time of publication. Outperformed GRAF. Strengths: High-quality, photorealistic 3D-aware image synthesis. View-consistent rendering from arbitrary camera poses. Extractable 3D proxy shapes via marching cubes. Limitations: Prone to local overfitting if training coverage is insufficient. Computational cost of 3D GANs is higher than 2D GANs. Proxy shapes may not be as high quality as explicit supervision methods. When to Use: When high-quality 3D-aware image synthesis is required from unposed 2D images, and computational resources allow for 3D GAN training. When Not to Use: When explicit 3D geometry is required with high fidelity (consider surface representations) or when computational resources are limited. Origin: pi-GAN was developed by Chan et al. in December 2020, approximately three months after GRAF. Paper: "pi-GAN: Periodic Implicit Generative Adversarial Networks for 3D-Aware Image Synthesis". History: It was proposed as an improvement over GRAF, addressing its limitations in conditioning and network architecture. It leverages SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Networks). Usage: Used for 3D-aware image synthesis on datasets like CelebA, Cats, and CARLA. name: GIRAFFE
head: Compositional Generative Neural Feature Fields, GIRAFFE Object Representation, GIRAFFE Scene Composition, Generative Inverse Radiance Fields, Generative Neural Feature Fields
body: GIRAFFE represents scenes as compositions of N entities (typically N-1 foreground objects and 1 background), where each entity possesses a separate generative neural feature field and an affine transformation. This architecture allows for the disentanglement of individual objects' shapes, appearances, and poses from the background without explicit supervision. It extends the generative NeRF paradigm by enabling the synthesis of complex multi-object scenes through a composition operator that aggregates densities and features from multiple latent-coded NeRFs. Inputs: Camera pose \xi (extrinsics). Number of entities N (sampled from distribution pN or fixed). For each entity i \in \{1, \dots, N\}: Shape latent code \mathbf{z}s^i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). Appearance latent code \mathbf{z}a^i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). Transformation parameters \mathbf{T}i = \{\mathbf{s}i, \mathbf{t}i, \mathbf{R}i\} (scale, translation, rotation), sampled from pT. 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: Synthesized RGB image \hat{\mathbf{I}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. (Implicitly) Feature image \mathbf{I}V \in \mathbb{R}^{HV \times WV \times Mf}. 1. Feature Field MLP (h\theta): All object feature fields share weights. The background field h\theta^N uses half the layers and hidden dimension. Input: Concatenated positional encoding of transformed position \gamma(k^{-1}(\mathbf{x})), directional encoding \gamma(k^{-1}(\mathbf{d})), shape latent \mathbf{z}s, appearance latent \mathbf{z}a. Positional Encoding: Position: Lx = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 10 = 60 dimensions. Direction: Ld = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24 dimensions. Architecture: 8 hidden layers (objects) / 4 hidden layers (background). Hidden dimension: 128 (objects) / 64 (background). Activation: ReLU. Skip connections: From input to every 4th layer (standard NeRF architecture implied by "8 layers... ReLU" and standard practice, though specific skip connection details are inherited from the parent). Output Heads: Density head: 1 unit (\sigma). Feature head: Mf units (\mathbf{f}). Mf = 128 for 64x64 output, Mf = 256 for 256x256 output. 2. Transformation Parameters (\mathbf{T}i): Scale \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Translation \mathbf{t}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation \mathbf{R}i \in SO(3). Background Constraint: For the background entity (i=N), \mathbf{s}N and \mathbf{t}N are fixed to span the entire scene and be centered at the origin. \mathbf{R}N is typically identity or fixed. 3. 2D Neural Renderer (\pi\theta^{\text{neural}}): Input: Feature image \mathbf{I}V of resolution HV \times WV (typically 16x16). Architecture: 2D CNN with Leaky ReLU. Upsampling: Combines nearest neighbor upsampling with 3x3 convolutions. Skip Connections: Maps feature image to RGB at every spatial resolution via 3x3 conv, adds to previous output via bilinear upsampling. Output: Final RGB image \hat{\mathbf{I}} of resolution H \times W (64x64 or 256x256). Sigmoid activation on final layer. 1. Sample Latents and Transforms: For a given scene, sample N \sim pN. For each entity i, sample \mathbf{z}s^i, \mathbf{z}a^i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and \mathbf{T}i \sim pT. 2. Ray Sampling: For each pixel in the target image, generate a ray \mathbf{d} from camera pose \xi. Sample Ns = 64 points \mathbf{x}j along the ray. 3. Transform to Canonical Space: For each sample point \mathbf{x}j and direction \mathbf{d}, compute the inverse transformation ki^{-1} for each entity i to map to canonical object space. ki(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{R}i \begin{bmatrix} s{i,1} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s{i,2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & s{i,3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & s{i,3} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t}i ki^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{R}i^{-1} \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1/s{i,1} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/s{i,2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1/s{i,3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1/s{i,3} \end{bmatrix} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}i) \right) [Note: The source matrix for k(\mathbf{x}) has a typo in the last row/column index in the text snippet, but standard affine transformation implies the last row is [0,0,0,1] for homogeneous coordinates. The inverse operation applies the inverse scale and rotation.] 4. Evaluate Feature Fields: For each entity i, input \gamma(ki^{-1}(\mathbf{x}j)), \gamma(ki^{-1}(\mathbf{d})), \mathbf{z}s^i, \mathbf{z}a^i into h\theta to obtain density \sigma{i,j} and feature vector \mathbf{f}{i,j}. 5. Compose Entities (Composition Operator): Combine the outputs from all N entities at point \mathbf{x}j using the density-weighted mean: \sigmaj = \sum{i=1}^N \sigma{i,j} \mathbf{f}j = \frac{1}{\sigmaj} \sum{i=1}^N \sigma{i,j} \mathbf{f}{i,j} \quad \text{if } \sigmaj > 0, \text{ else } \mathbf{0} 6. Volume Render Features: Compute the final feature vector \mathbf{f} for the pixel by integrating along the ray: \alphaj = 1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj) \tauj = \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) \mathbf{f} = \sum{j=1}^{Ns} \tauj \alphaj \mathbf{f}j where \deltaj = \|\mathbf{x}{j+1} - \mathbf{x}j\|2. 7. 2D Neural Rendering: Upsample the low-resolution feature image \mathbf{I}V (containing \mathbf{f} for all pixels) to high-resolution RGB using \pi\theta^{\text{neural}}. Transformation: k(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{R} \cdot \text{diag}(s1, s2, s3, s3) \cdot \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{t} Composition: C(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \left( \sigma, \frac{1}{\sigma} \sum{i=1}^N \sigmai \mathbf{f}i \right), \quad \sigma = \sum{i=1}^N \sigmai Feature Rendering: \mathbf{f} = \sum{j=1}^{Ns} \tauj \alphaj \mathbf{f}j, \quad \tauj = \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak), \quad \alphaj = 1 - e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj} GAN Objective: \mathcal{V}(\theta, \phi) = \mathbb{E}[f(D\phi(G\theta(\{\mathbf{z}s^i, \mathbf{z}a^i, \mathbf{T}i\}i, \xi)))] + \mathbb{E}[f(-D\phi(\mathbf{I})) - \lambda \|\nabla\phi(\mathbf{I})\|^2] where f(t) = -\log(1 + \exp(-t)) and \lambda = 10. Ns (Samples per ray): 64. Feature Image Resolution (HV \times WV): 16x16. Output Resolution (H \times W): 64x64 or 256x256. Feature Dimension (Mf): 128 (for 64x64), 256 (for 256x256). Generator MLP Layers: 8 (objects), 4 (background). Hidden Dimension: 128 (objects), 64 (background). Positional Encoding Bands: Lx = 60, Ld = 24. Optimizer: RMSprop. Learning Rates: Generator 1 \times 10^{-4} (or 2.5 \times 10^{-4} for 256x256), Discriminator 5 \times 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 32. EMA Decay: 0.999. Latent Distribution: \mathcal{N}(0, I). Camera Pose Distribution (p\xi): Uniform over dataset-dependent elevation angles. Transformation Distribution (pT): Uniform over valid object transformations. Zero Density: If \sigmaj = 0 for all entities at a point, the feature vector \mathbf{f}j is undefined in the composition operator. The implementation must handle this, typically by setting \mathbf{f}j = \mathbf{0}. Computational Cost: Training and rendering at high resolutions (e.g., 256x256) requires considerable computational power, although it uses less memory than voxel-based techniques. Background Handling: The background entity must be fixed to span the scene. Incorrectly allowing background transformation parameters to vary can lead to artifacts or incorrect scene composition. Time Complexity: Rendering is dominated by the MLP evaluations for Ns \times N entities per pixel. The 2D neural renderer adds overhead proportional to the upsampling steps. Memory Complexity: Lower than voxel-based techniques. Memory is dominated by the MLP weights and the latent codes. The feature image is small (16x16), reducing VRAM usage during the volume rendering step. Strengths: Disentangles object shape, appearance, and pose without explicit supervision. Allows for compositional scene generation (adding/removing objects). Limitations: High computational cost for training and high-resolution rendering. Limited to scenes with a manageable number of objects (N). Performance depends on the quality of the learned transformation distributions. When to Use: When generative control over multiple distinct objects in a scene is required, and explicit 3D annotations are unavailable. When Not to Use: For real-time rendering of complex scenes with many objects, or when high-fidelity texture is required without the 2D upsampling step (though GIRAFFE HD addresses this). GIRAFFE was introduced by Nagano et al. in 2021. It builds upon GRAF by extending the generative NeRF framework from single-object synthesis to compositional scenes. The method addresses the limitation of previous generative models that could only synthesize simple, single-object scenes. It is used in research for unsupervised scene decomposition, generative modeling of multi-object datasets (e.g., Chairs, Cats, CelebA), and as a foundation for higher-resolution variants like GIRAFFE HD and UrbanGIRAFFE.
