name: Generative Latent Optimization
body: Generative Latent Optimization (GLO) is a training procedure for generative radiance fields where a set of latent codes is jointly optimized with the generator network parameters to minimize a reconstruction loss against input images. It is distinguished from standard Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) by the absence of a discriminator, effectively functioning as a discriminator-less GAN. Unlike methods that use latent codes merely for conditioning (e.g., NeRF-W), GLO explicitly treats the latent codes as learnable parameters to account for scene variability or to enable inversion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of N images \{I1, \dots, IN\} and a generator network G (which maps latent codes and optional auxiliary inputs to radiance field predictions or rendered images). Outputs: Optimized generator parameters \thetaG and a set of latent codes \{z1, \dots, zN\}. Data Structures: Latent Codes: A set of vectors Z = \{z1, \dots, zN\}. Each zi is typically sampled from a prior distribution (e.g., standard normal \mathcal{N}(0, I)) at initialization. Generator Parameters: \thetaG, representing the weights of the neural network (e.g., MLPs for density and color). Algorithm: The optimization minimizes the reconstruction error between the generated output and the target image for each pair. The objective function is: \min{G, z1, \dots, zN} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{L}(G(zi, ui), Ii) where: \mathcal{L} is a reconstruction loss, such as L2 or L1. G(zi, ui) is the output of the generator given latent code zi and auxiliary inputs ui. ui represents other inputs not optimized over (e.g., camera poses, viewing directions, or positional encodings required by the specific radiance field architecture). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generativelatentoptimization(images, generator, lossfn, optimizerconfig): """ Jointly optimizes generator parameters and latent codes. Args: images: List of N target images {I1,..., IN}. generator: Function G(z, u) that generates output from latent z and inputs u. lossfn: Reconstruction loss function (e.g., L2). optimizerconfig: Configuration for the optimizer (e.g., Adam). Returns: generatorparams: Optimized parameters of G. latentcodes: Optimized latent codes {z1,..., zN}. """ N = len(images) # Initialize latent codes from a prior distribution (e.g., standard normal) # Standard practice for GLO initialization. latentcodes = [torch.randnlike(generator.latentdim) for in range(N)] # Initialize generator parameters generatorparams = generator.getparameters() # Create optimizer that updates both generator parameters and latent codes # The optimizer must treat latentcodes as parameters to be updated. optimizer = Adam([generatorparams] + latentcodes, optimizerconfig) # Optimization loop for step in range(maxsteps): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Get auxiliary inputs for image i (e.g., camera pose, viewing direction) # ui is specific to the scene representation (e.g., NeRF requires ray origins/directions). ui = getauxiliaryinputs(images[i]) # Generate output generatedoutput = generator(latentcodes[i], ui) # Compute reconstruction loss loss = lossfn(generatedoutput, images[i]) totalloss += loss # Backpropagate and update totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return generatorparams, latentcodes Parameters: Loss Function: Typically L2 or L1. Optimizer: Adam is commonly used. Initialization: Latent codes are usually sampled from a normal distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Auxiliary Inputs: In NeRF-based GLO, ui must include ray sampling information (positions and directions). Failure to provide these leads to incorrect rendering. Optimization Stability: Without a discriminator, the model may collapse to a single mode if not regularized. Joint optimization can be sensitive to learning rates for zi vs. \thetaG. An optimization-based initialization procedure used to find a good starting latent code for finetuning a generative radiance field. It solves the problem of poor convergence by initializing latent codes via patch reconstruction rather than random sampling. Definition: Optimizes a latent code to reconstruct random image patches from input views. Steps: 1. Sample 8 random patches of size 32 \times 32 from all available input views. 2. Initialize the new latent code vector with zeros. 3. Optimize the latent code using Adam (\beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, learning rate 0.001) for 1,500 steps. When to choose: When finetuning a pre-trained prior model (e.g., for few-shot face synthesis) to ensure the latent code is in a valid region of the latent space. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot T \cdot C), where N is the number of images, T is the number of optimization steps, and C is the cost of one forward/backward pass through the generator. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D + M), where D is the latent dimension and M is the memory for generator parameters. Performance: GLO can be computationally expensive due to the joint optimization of N latent codes. For example, inversion on a prior model may take 10 minutes on 4 TPUs for 1,500 steps. Strengths: Simple to implement (no discriminator); effective for view synthesis and scene editing when latent codes are explicitly optimized. Limitations: Lacks the stability guarantees of GANs; may suffer from mode collapse or poor generalization if not regularized. Generative Latent Optimization was introduced by Salimans et al.. It is described as a "Discriminator-less GAN". In the context of NeRF, GLO has been used in models like NeRF-W and Edit-NeRF to optimize latent codes for appearance and scene editing. The method is particularly relevant in the 2020–2023 era for models that use latent codes to account for changeable aspects of a scene. name: GAN Inversion Encoder and Optimization
head: GSN Inversion Encoder and Optimization
body: This method enables view synthesis and scene completion by inverting a trained generative radiance field (specifically a Generative Scene Network, GSN) into a latent code grid. It solves the problem of generating unseen parts of a scene or editing scenes by optimizing local latent codes rather than sampling from the prior distribution. To handle scenes that do not share a canonical orientation, the method predicts an initial latent grid at multiple rotation angles about the y-axis to find the generator's preferred orientation, which is then used during optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed source views S = \{(X, T)i\}{i=t-5}^t, where X represents the image data and T represents the camera pose transformations. Outputs: An optimized latent code grid \hat{W} that conditions the radiance field to synthesize new views. Data Structures: Encoder Parameters (\thetaE): Weights of the neural network encoder E{\thetaE}. Feature Volume (V): A 3D volume with layout V \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s \times s}, where c is the channel dimension and s is the spatial resolution. Latent Code Grid (W0): The initial grid of latent codes with layout W0 \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}, derived from V. Radiance Field (f): The trained generator function that maps latent codes and camera poses to images. Numbered Steps: 1. Encoder Architecture Setup: Construct an encoder E{\thetaE} consisting of a UNet backbone [47] with a ResNet-50 encoder. The encoder maps input views and poses to a feature volume: E{\thetaE}: \mathbb{R}^{3 \times w \times h} \times SE(3) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s \times s}. 2. Feature Extraction and Back-projection: Process the input views \hat{X} through the backbone to obtain feature maps. Back-project these feature maps using the camera poses T into the shared feature volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s \times s}. 3. Latent Grid Initialization: Perform average pooling over the height dimension of V to produce the initial latent code grid W0 \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}. 4. Orientation Selection: Since scenes do not share a canonical orientation, predict W0 at multiple rotation angles about the y-axis for the source views \{Ti\}{i=t-5}^t. Define the preferred orientation as the one that minimizes an auto-encoding LPIPS loss. Use this orientation during the subsequent optimization. 5. Optimization: Optimize the initial grid W0 via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for 1000 iterations to obtain the final grid \hat{W}. The radiance field parameters are frozen during this process. Formulas: The encoder is trained by minimizing the reconstruction loss: L(\hat{X}, T, W; \thetaE) = \|W - E{\thetaE}(\hat{X}, T)\|2^2 + \|\hat{X} - f(E{\thetaE}(\hat{X}, T), T)\|2^2 Where: The first term \|W - E{\thetaE}(\hat{X}, T)\|2^2 encourages the reconstruction of the local latent grid. The second term \|\hat{X} - f(E{\thetaE}(\hat{X}, T), T)\|2^2 encourages samples from the locally conditioned radiance field f to match the original input views. Parameters: Optimization Iterations: 1000 iterations. Optimizer: SGD. Source View Window: 6 views (i=t-5 to t). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mixed Precision: Mixed precision training is not applied to the discriminator (if present in the base GSN) as training stability decreases in that case. Orientation Ambiguity: Failure to select the generator's preferred orientation via LPIPS minimization may result in suboptimal reconstruction due to lack of canonical alignment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ganinversionencoderoptimization(sourceviews, cameraposes, encoder, radiancefield, numiterations=1000): # Step 1: Find preferred orientation by testing rotations about the y-axis bestangle = 0.0 minlpips = float('inf') # Test multiple rotation angles about the y-axis for angle in [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5]: # Angles in radians; exact set not specified in sources # Apply y-axis rotation to poses; implementation details not specified in sources rotatedposes = [applyyrotation(T, angle) for T in cameraposes] W0candidate = encoder(sourceviews, rotatedposes) renderedviews = radiancefield(W0candidate, rotatedposes) # Auto-encoding LPIPS loss; specific architecture not detailed in sources lpips = perceptualloss(sourceviews, renderedviews) if lpips < minlpips: minlpips = lpips bestangle = angle # Apply preferred orientation finalposes = [applyyrotation(T, bestangle) for T in cameraposes] # Step 2: Initialize W0 using the encoder with preferred orientation W0 = encoder(sourceviews, finalposes) # Step 3: Optimize W0 via SGD for 1000 iterations Wopt = W0.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) lr = 0.01 # Learning rate not specified in sources for in range(numiterations): rendered = radiancefield(Wopt, finalposes) # Reconstruction loss for optimization: image matching term loss = sum((r - s)2 for r, s in zip(rendered, sourceviews)) loss.backward() # Manual SGD step Wopt -= lr Wopt.grad Wopt.grad.zero() return Wopt GSN Inversion is a method for view synthesis and scene completion that inverts source views into a latent code grid to locally condition a trained radiance field. It solves the problem of generating unseen parts of a scene or editing scenes by optimizing latent codes rather than sampling from the prior. Unlike methods relying on global coordinate systems, GSN uses a local coordinate system that is robust to rearrangements of latent codes, such as 2D rotations, whereas global systems suffer rendering quality degradation as rotation angles increase. A hybrid inversion scheme where an encoder produces an initial guess of the latent code and pose, which are then refined for a small number of iterations. Feed a real image into the encoder E to predict an initial latent code w and a canonical map. Convert the predicted canonical map to a point cloud. Run a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solver on the point cloud to recover all pose parameters (view matrix and focal length). Split the initial latent code w into a different vector for each layer, referred to as w^+ \in W^+. For a fixed number of steps N, update w^+ and the pose to minimize reconstruction error between rendered and input images. N: Number of optimization steps, typically as few as 10. Unlike methods initializing from average/random latent codes requiring hundreds of steps, this method accelerates convergence. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles scenes without a canonical orientation by searching for a preferred y-axis rotation. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained GSN and encoder. Sensitive to the choice of canonical orientation. When to use: When view synthesis or scene completion is required for a scene generated by a GSN, particularly when the scene orientation is unknown or variable. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the work on Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields. It adapts common practices for GAN inversion [57] to the context of Generative Scene Networks (GSN). The encoder architecture is conceptually similar to prior works [22, 36]. name: GSN Inversion
head: Inversion of Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields, Latent Code Optimization
body: GSN Inversion is a method for view synthesis and scene completion that inverts source views into a latent code grid to locally condition a trained radiance field. It solves the problem of generating unseen parts of a scene or editing scenes by optimizing latent codes rather than sampling from the prior. Unlike methods relying on global coordinate systems, GSN uses a local coordinate system that is robust to rearrangements of latent codes, such as 2D rotations, whereas global systems suffer rendering quality degradation as rotation angles increase. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of source views S = \{(X, T)i\}{i=t-5}^{t} (5 previous frames, where X is the image and T is the camera pose) and target views T = \{(X, T)i\}{i=t}^{t+5} (camera poses for target views). Outputs: An optimized latent code grid \hat{W} and rendered images \hat{S} (reconstruction of source views) and \hat{T} (prediction of target views). Data Structures: Encoder Output (W0): A latent code grid of shape \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s}, derived from a shared feature volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{c \times s \times s \times s} via average pooling over the height dimension. Radiance Field (f{\thetaf}): A locally conditioned radiance field with frozen weights \thetaf. Parameters: Optimization Iterations: 1000 SGD iterations. Source Window: 5 previous frames (i=t-5 to t). Loss Metric: LPIPS loss [60] for orientation selection. Steps: 1. Initialization: Feed the source views S through the trained encoder E{\thetaE} to predict an initial latent code grid W0. 2. Canonical Orientation Selection: Since scenes do not share a canonical orientation and the generator may prefer a specific one, predict W0 at multiple rotation angles of the source camera poses \{Ti\}{i=t-5}^{t} about the y-axis. Select the orientation that minimizes an auto-encoding LPIPS loss as the 'preferred orientation'. Use this preferred orientation for subsequent optimization. 3. Latent Code Optimization: Optimize W0 via SGD for 1000 iterations to obtain \hat{W}, while freezing the weights of the radiance field f{\thetaf}. Compute a reconstruction loss w.r.t. S during optimization. 4. Reconstruction and Prediction: Render observations using the camera poses of S to produce \hat{S} (reconstruction). Render from the camera poses of target views T to produce \hat{T} (prediction of unseen parts). Training Loss (for Encoder): The encoder is trained by minimizing the following reconstruction loss: L(\hat{X}, T, W; \thetaE) = \|W - E{\thetaE}(\hat{X}, T)\|^2 + \|\hat{X} - f(E{\thetaE}(\hat{X}, T), T)\|^2 where the first term encourages the reconstruction of the local latent grid, and the second term encourages samples from the locally conditioned radiance field f to match the original input views \hat{X}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gsninversion(sourceviewsS, targetposesT, encoderE, radiancefieldf): # sourceviewsS: list of (image, pose) tuples for i=t-5 to t # targetposesT: list of camera poses for target views # encoderE: trained encoder EthetaE # radiancefieldf: trained radiance field fthetaf (weights frozen) # Step 1: Find preferred orientation # Not given in the sources. candidateyaxisrotations = [0.0, 10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0, 50.0, 60.0, 70.0, 80.0, 90.0, 100.0, 110.0, 120.0, 130.0, 140.0, 150.0, 160.0, 170.0, 180.0, 190.0, 200.0, 210.0, 220.0, 230.0, 240.0, 250.0, 260.0, 270.0, 280.0, 290.0, 300.0, 310.0, 320.0, 330.0, 340.0, 350.0] bestorientation = None minlpipsloss = float('inf') bestW0 = None bestsourceposes = None for angle in candidateyaxisrotations: rotatedposes = rotateposesyaxis(sourceviewsS, angle) W0 = encoderE(sourceviewsS, rotatedposes) reconstructedimages = radiancefieldf(W0, rotatedposes) lpipsloss = computelpipsloss(sourceviewsS, reconstructedimages) if lpipsloss < minlpipsloss: minlpipsloss = lpipsloss bestorientation = angle bestW0 = W0 bestsourceposes = rotatedposes # Step 2: Optimize latent code grid # Not given in the sources. learningrate = 0.01 Wopt = bestW0.clone() Wopt.requiresgrad = True for iteration in range(1000): reconstructedimages = radiancefieldf(Wopt, bestsourceposes) loss = computereconstructionloss(sourceviewsS, reconstructedimages) grad = computegradient(loss, Wopt) Wopt = Wopt - learningrate grad What = Wopt.detach() # Step 3: Render outputs Shat = radiancefieldf(What, bestsourceposes) That = radiancefieldf(What, targetposesT) return What, Shat, That def rotateposesyaxis(sourceviewsS, angledegrees): cosa = math.cos(math.radians(angledegrees)) sina = math.sin(math.radians(angledegrees)) Ry = [[cosa, 0, sina], [0, 1, 0], [-sina, 0, cosa]] rotated = [] for, pose in sourceviewsS: newpose = [row[:] for row in pose] for i in range(3): newpose[i] = [Ry[i][0]newpose[0][j] + Ry[i][1]newpose[1][j] + Ry[i][2]newpose[2][j] for j in range(3)] rotated.append(newpose) return rotated def computelpipsloss(sourceviewsS, reconstructedimages): # Standard LPIPS perceptual loss [60] # Computes perceptual distance between source images and reconstructions return sum(abs(srcimg - reconimg) for srcimg, reconimg in zip(sourceviewsS, reconstructedimages)) / len(sourceviewsS) def computereconstructionloss(sourceviewsS, reconstructedimages): # Standard L1 reconstruction loss return sum(abs(srcimg - reconimg) for srcimg, reconimg in zip(sourceviewsS, reconstructedimages)) / len(sourceviewsS) def computegradient(loss, variable): # Standard operation: computes partial derivatives of loss w.r.t. variable return gradient(loss, variable) A method for view synthesis where source views are inverted into the prior to obtain a latent code, which is then used to locally condition the radiance field to render target views. Given source views S = \{(X, T)i\}{i=t-5}^{t} and target views T = \{(X, T)i\}{i=t}^{t+5}, the source views S are inverted into the prior to obtain a latent code. The resulting latent code is used to locally condition the radiance field, and observations are rendered using the camera poses of the target views T. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: GSN improves view synthesis quality on Vizdoom and AVD datasets compared to GTM-SM and ISS, outperforming them in both Memorization (reconstruction) and Hallucination (scene completion) metrics (L1 and SSIM). Strengths: Robust to rearrangements of latent codes (e.g., 2D rotation of W) due to the local coordinate system. Limitations: Scenes do not share a canonical orientation, requiring multiple rotations to find the generator's preferred orientation. The optimization process freezes the radiance field weights, limiting joint optimization. GSN Inversion is based on "Unconstrained Scene Generation with Locally Conditioned Radiance Fields". It builds on standard practices for GAN inversion [57] to handle the task of view synthesis and scene completion. The method was evaluated on Vizdoom and AVD datasets. name: Adversarial Training (GAN)
head: Discriminator Training, GAN Loss, Joint Adversarial-Rasterization Training, LSGAN Adversarial Training
body: Adversarial Training integrates a discriminator network into the optimization loop of a generative volume rendering model to distinguish between real ground-truth images and synthesized renders, using the discriminator's feedback to refine the generator's output. Unlike standard supervised training that relies solely on pixel-wise reconstruction losses, this method enforces perceptual realism and reduces artifacts by learning the distribution of real data, making it distinct from sibling methods like StyleNeRF which focus on style transfer, or HyperNeRFGAN which may use different generative priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Real ground-truth images I{gt}, generated/fake images G(z) or R\theta(\cdot), camera parameters \theta, and latent codes z. Outputs: Updated network parameters for the generator (synthesizer) \theta and discriminator \phi. Data Structures: Generator/Synthesizer (G or R\theta): A neural network that maps inputs to rendered images. Discriminator (D or D\phi): A neural network that outputs a scalar score indicating the likelihood of an image being real, optionally equipped with multi-scale branches or a pose estimation branch. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize generator parameters \theta and discriminator parameters \phi. If using multi-scale discrimination, initialize Ns branches. 2. Forward Pass (Generator): Sample latent codes z and camera parameters \theta. Compute the generated image I{fake} = G(z, \theta) (or R\theta(St^{(i)})). 3. Discriminator Update: Compute discriminator scores for real images D(I{gt}) and fake images D(I{fake}). Calculate Discriminator Loss L{GAN,D} based on the specific GAN variant (e.g., LSGAN or non-saturating with R1). Update \phi by minimizing L{GAN,D}. 4. Generator Update: Compute discriminator scores for fake images D(I{fake}). Calculate Generator Loss L{GAN,G}. If using contrastive pose learning, compute pose embeddings pI from I{fake} and p\theta from \theta, then calculate L{pose}. If using 3D Gaussian regularization, compute L{center} and L{knn} based on anchor Gaussian positions \mu^0A. Calculate total Generator Loss LG = L{GAN,G} + \lambda{pose} L{pose} + \lambda{center} L{center} + \lambda{knn} L{knn}. Update \theta by minimizing LG. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for the desired number of epochs. 6. Inference: Remove the discriminator D\phi to avoid inference overhead; use only R\theta. Formulas: LSGAN Adversarial Loss (Synthesizer/Discriminator Joint): L{adv}^\phi = \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \left[ \sum{t=1}^{T} D\phi(R\theta(St^{(i)}))^2 + (D\phi(I{gt}^{(i)}) - 1)^2 \right] Where Ns is the total number of discriminator scales, I{gt}^{(i)} is the scale-adjusted ground-truth image, and St^{(i)} is the rasterized raw image at resolution level t and scale i. Non-Saturating Adversarial Loss with R1 Regularization: L{adv} = \mathbb{E}{z \sim Pz, \theta \sim P\theta} [f(d(g(z, \theta)))] + \mathbb{E}{Ir \sim P{Ir}} [f(-d(Ir)) + \lambda \|\nabla d(Ir)\|^2] Where f(t) = -\log(1 + \exp(-t)) is the softplus function, d(\cdot) is the discriminator, g(\cdot) is the generator, and \lambda is the R1 regularization strength. Standard Log-Loss (Alternative Formulation): L{GAN,D} = - \log(D(x)) - \log(1 - D(G(z))) L{GAN,G} = - \log(D(G(z))) Where x is real data, G(z) is generated data, and D(\cdot) is the discriminator score. Contrastive Pose Loss: L{pose} = -\log \left( \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(pI, p\theta^+) / \tau)}{\sum{b=1}^{B} \exp(\text{sim}(pI, p\theta^{(b)}) / \tau)} \right) Where \text{sim}(\cdot, \cdot) is cosine similarity, \tau is temperature, pI is the pose embedding from the image, p\theta^+ is the positive pose embedding from parameters, and B is batch size. 3D Gaussian Regularization Losses: L{center} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^N \|\mu^0{A,j}\|^2 L{knn} = \frac{1}{NK} \sum{j=1}^N \sum{k=1}^K \|\mu^0{A,j} - \text{KNN}(\mu^0{A,j}, k)\|^2 Where \mu^0{A,j} is the position of the j-th anchor Gaussian at the coarsest level, and \text{KNN}(\cdot, k) returns the position of the k-th nearest neighbor. Total Loss: L = L{adv} + \lambda{pose} L{pose} + \lambda{center} L{center} + \lambda{knn} L{knn} Parameters: Ns: Total number of discriminator scales. Typical value: 5. \lambda: R1 regularization strength. \tau: Temperature scaling parameter in contrastive loss. K: Number of nearest neighbors for L{knn}. \lambda{pose}, \lambda{center}, \lambda{knn}: Strengths of corresponding objectives. L: Number of frequency bands in positional encoding (inherited from parent). T: Number of resolution levels in the synthesizer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inference Overhead: The discriminator must be removed at test time to avoid adding computational complexity. Precision: The softplus function f(t) is used to avoid saturation in the non-saturating loss formulation. Data Augmentation: Adaptive data augmentation is recommended for limited datasets (e.g., AFHQ-Cat) to prevent overfitting. Degenerate Input: If point cloud information is insufficient, the synthesizer may produce artifacts; adversarial supervision helps generalize to unseen inputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softplus(t): return -math.log(1 + math.exp(-t)) def cosinesimilarity(a, b): return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) np.linalg.norm(b)) def computeknndistances(points, k): # Returns distances to k nearest neighbors for each point n = len(points) dists = np.zeros((n, n)) for i in range(n): for j in range(n): dists[i, j] = np.linalg.norm(points[i] - points[j]) knndists = np.sort(dists, axis=1)[:, 1:k+1] return knndists def trainadversarialvolumerendering(generator, discriminator, realimages, latentsampler, poseencoder, config): """ Trains a volume rendering generator with adversarial supervision. Args: generator: Synthesizer network Rtheta. discriminator: Discriminator network Dphi. realimages: Iterator of ground-truth image batches. latentsampler: Sampler for latent codes z and camera parameters theta. poseencoder: MLP encoding camera parameters theta to pose embeddings. config: Dictionary containing hyperparameters. """ optimizerG = GradientDescent(generator.parameters(), lr=config.lrG) optimizerD = GradientDescent(discriminator.parameters(), lr=config.lrD) lambdar1 = config.lambdar1 lambdapose = config.lambdapose lambdacenter = config.lambdacenter lambdaknn = config.lambdaknn tau = config.tau Ns = config.Ns K = config.K for epoch in range(config.epochs): for realbatch in realimages: # 1. Sample latent codes and camera parameters z, theta = latentsampler.sample(batchsize=len(realbatch)) # 2. Generate fake images fakebatch = generator(z, theta) # 3. Discriminator Update optimizerD.zerograd() if Ns > 1: # LSGAN style loss for multi-scale drealscales = discriminator.multiscale(realbatch) dfakescales = discriminator.multiscale(fakebatch) lossd = 0 for i in range(Ns): lossd += np.sum(dfakescales[i]2) + np.sum((drealscales[i] - 1)2) else: # Non-saturating with R1 regularization dreal = discriminator(realbatch) dfake = discriminator(fakebatch) # R1 Regularization: lambda ||grad D(real)||^2 gradreal = gradient(dreal, realbatch) r1reg = lambdar1 0.5 np.sum(gradreal2) lossd = np.mean(softplus(-dreal)) + np.mean(softplus(dfake)) + r1reg lossd.backward() optimizerD.step() # 4. name: Lighting Prediction Network Training
head: Hybrid Loss Training for Lighting Prediction
body: A training strategy for predicting lighting conditions in street scenes that addresses depth rendering ambiguity and encourages photorealism through adversarial supervision. It distinguishes itself from standard differentiable rendering pipelines by combining a multi-term hybrid loss (including sky regression, reconstruction, and regularization) with a PatchGAN discriminator, trained in a two-stage process (pre-training followed by joint adversarial training) to stabilize convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth lighting parameters (direction f{dir}, intensity f{intensity}), real-world images \{I{real}\} from nuScenes and HoliCity street views, and HDR panoramas. Outputs: Predicted lighting parameters and rendered images \hat{I}{edit}. Data Structures: Discriminator (D): A 5-layer PatchGAN network with spectral normalization applied to each weight matrix. Generator: The lighting prediction network that outputs latent codes and radiance/depth volumes. Loss Weights: \lambda{sky}=1, \lambda{recon}=1, \lambda{transmit}=1, \lambda{reg}=10^{-4}, \lambda{adv}=3 \times 10^{-3}. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-training: Train the generator without the adversarial loss term L{adv} for 50 epochs. 2. Joint Training: Train the generator with all loss terms for an additional 50 epochs. 3. Sky Regression Loss (L{sky}): Compute the L1 loss for the latent code and linearly fade it out during the first 50 epochs of training. 4. Adversarial Training: Sample real images I{real} and generated images \hat{I}{edit}. Compute the discriminator loss LD using hinge loss. Update the discriminator D. Compute the generator adversarial loss L{adv} based on D(\hat{I}{edit}). 5. Optimization: Update the generator parameters using the total hybrid loss L{hybrid}. Formulas: The final hybrid loss is defined as: L{hybrid} = \lambda{sky} L{sky} + \lambda{recon} L{recon} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambda{transmit} L{transmit} + \lambda{adv} L{adv} where: L{sky}: Sky regression loss (L1 loss on latent code, faded in the first 50 epochs). L{recon}: Radiance and depth reconstruction loss. L{reg}: Regularization loss encouraging the alpha channel of the volume to be binary (0 or 1) to address depth rendering ambiguity. L{transmit}: Sky separation loss. L{adv}: Adversarial supervision loss. The discriminator uses hinge loss: LD = \max(0, 1 - D(I{real})) + \max(0, 1 + D(\hat{I}{edit})) Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 3 \times 10^{-4}, decaying by a factor of 0.3 every 30 epochs. Discriminator Batch Size: 1. Total GPU Memory: 20G (8G for network inference, 12G for rendering). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: The regularization loss L{reg} is critical to prevent the volume alpha channel from converging to intermediate values, which causes depth rendering ambiguity. Training Stability: The two-stage training (pre-training then joint) is necessary to stabilize the adversarial training. Memory Constraints: The method requires significant GPU memory (20G total), with rendering consuming the majority (12G). Pseudocode: Unverified code. a) for a in alpha) / len(alpha) class AdamOptimizer: def init(self, params, lr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.m = {id(p): 0.0 for p in params} self.v = {id(p): 0.0 for p in params} self.t = 0 def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = 0.0 def step(self): self.t += 1 for p in self.params: g = p.grad self.m[id(p)] = 0.9 self.m[id(p)] + 0.1 g self.v[id(p)] = 0.999 self.v[id(p)] + 0.001 (g 2) mhat = self.m[id(p)] / (1 - 0.9 self.t) vhat = self.v[id(p)] / (1 - 0.999 self.t) p -= self.lr mhat / (math.sqrt(vhat) + 1e-8) class PatchGAN5LayerSpectralNorm: # 5-layer convolutional network with spectral normalization on each weight matrix def init(self): pass def forward(self, x): pass model = LightingPredictionNetwork() discriminator = PatchGAN5LayerSpectralNorm() optimizer = AdamOptimizer(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4) discoptimizer = AdamOptimizer(discriminator.parameters(), lr=3e-4) epochspretrain = 50 epochsjoint = 50 totalepochs = epochspretrain + epochsjoint decayfactor = 0.3 decaystep = 30 lambdasky = 1.0 lambdarecon = 1.0 lambdareg = 1e-4 lambdatransmit = 1.0 lambdaadv = 3e-3 for epoch in range(1, totalepochs + 1): # Learning rate decay: 3e-4, decaying by 0.3 every 30 epochs currentlr = 3e-4 (decayfactor ((epoch - 1) // decaystep)) optimizer.lr = currentlr discoptimizer.lr = currentlr for batch in trainingdata: # Forward pass latentpred, renderedimage = model(batch.input) targetlighting = batch.targetlighting targetimage = batch.targetimage # Loss computation lrecon = meanabserror(renderedimage, targetimage) lreg = alpharegularization(renderedimage.alpha) ltransmit = 0.0 # Sky separation loss: Not defined in the sources. if epoch <= epochspretrain: # Pre-training phase: no adversarial loss lsky = meanabserror(latentpred, targetlighting) ladv = 0.0 else: # Joint training phase # Linearly fade out L1 loss for latent code in the first 50 epochs fadefactor = max(0.0, 1.0 - (epoch - 1) / 50.0) lsky = meanabserror(latentpred, targetlighting) fadefactor # Adversarial training dreal = discriminator(targetimage) dfake = discriminator(renderedimage.detach()) # Discriminator hinge loss ld = max(0, 1 - dreal) + max(0, 1 + dfake) # Update Discriminator (batch size 1) discoptimizer.zerograd() ld.backward() discoptimizer.step() # Generator adversarial loss (hinge GAN standard) dfakegen = discriminator(renderedimage) ladv = max(0, 1 - dfakegen) # Total hybrid loss lhybrid = (lambdasky lsky + lambdarecon lrecon + lambdareg lreg + lambdatransmit ltransmit + lambdaadv ladv) # Update Generator optimizer.zerograd() lhybrid.backward() optimizer.step() Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but training involves 4000 epochs in the main paper context. The specific hybrid loss strategy details 100 epochs (50 pre-training + 50 joint). Memory Complexity: 20G GPU memory usage (8G for network inference, 12G for rendering). Strengths: Addresses depth rendering ambiguity via regularization; encourages photorealism via adversarial supervision; handles sky regression ambiguity via fading loss. Limitations: High GPU memory requirement; requires careful tuning of loss weights and learning rate decay. When to use: When generating photorealistic street scene lighting with differentiable rendering and depth ambiguity is a concern. When not to use: When GPU memory is limited (<20G) or when adversarial training instability is unacceptable without careful tuning. Originated in the context of "Neural Light Field Estimation for Street Scenes with Differentiable Virtual Object Insertion". The method combines techniques from differentiable rendering (sky regression, depth reconstruction) with GAN-based adversarial training (PatchGAN discriminator) to improve the realism of predicted lighting in street scenes. It builds on prior work addressing depth rendering ambiguity. name: IRON
head: IRON, Inverse Rendering by Optimizing Neural SDFs and Materials, PIR (Photometric Inverse Rendering), Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization
body: IRON is a neural inverse rendering pipeline that reconstructs high-quality 3D geometry and spatially varying materials from photometric images (multi-view images captured with a collocated flashlight and moving camera). It outputs triangle meshes and material textures compatible with standard graphics pipelines. Unlike standard NeRF variants that optimize density and color directly, IRON uses Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for geometry and separate neural networks for diffuse, specular, and roughness parameters. It employs a hybrid optimization scheme: a first stage using volumetric radiance field rendering to recover correct topology, followed by a second stage using edge-aware physics-based surface rendering to refine geometry and disentangle materials from lighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of photometric images captured with a flashlight co-located with the camera. Assumptions include opaque objects, no ambient light, and ignored shadows/inter-reflections. Output: A triangle mesh and material textures (diffuse albedo, specular albedo, roughness). Data Structures: The method uses four Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). 1. Neural SDF (F{\Thetas}): Input: 3D position \mathbf{x}. Output: Tuple (S, \mathbf{f}), where S \in \mathbb{R} is the SDF value and \mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^{256} is a local geometric feature descriptor. 2. Neural Diffuse Albedo (F{\Theta\beta}): Input: Position \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{v} (or normal \mathbf{n} in Stage 2), and feature descriptor \mathbf{f}. Output: Diffuse albedo \beta \in \mathbb{R}^3. 3. Neural Specular Albedo (F{\Theta\kappa}): Input: Position \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, and feature descriptor \mathbf{f}. Output: Specular albedo \kappa \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Neural Roughness (F{\Theta\alpha}): Input: Position \mathbf{x}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, and feature descriptor \mathbf{f}. Output: Roughness \alpha \in \mathbb{R} (small values indicate shiny surfaces, large values indicate matte surfaces). Optimization Stages: Stage 1: Volumetric Radiance Field Rendering This stage initializes the topology (number and location of holes). 1. Treat the neural diffuse albedo network F{\Theta\beta}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{f}) as a view-dependent neural radiance field by substituting the view direction -\mathbf{d} for the second normal argument. 2. Optimize F{\Thetas} and F{\Theta\beta} using volumetric rendering. 3. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via the standard volumetric rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Here, \sigmai is derived from the SDF S, \mathbf{c}i = F{\Theta\beta}(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{n}i, -\mathbf{d}i, \mathbf{f}i), and \deltai is the step size. 4. If this stage is skipped, optimization frequently diverges or gets stuck in local minima with incorrect topology. Stage 2: Edge-aware Physics-based Surface Rendering This stage refines geometric details and factorizes materials from lighting. 1. Jointly optimize F{\Thetas}, F{\Theta\beta}, F{\Theta\kappa}, F{\Theta\alpha}, and light intensity L. 2. Use physics-based surface rendering. The light is modeled as a point source: Li(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{L}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{o}\|^2} where L is light intensity, \mathbf{x} is the surface location, and \mathbf{o} is the light/camera position. 3. Edge Sampling: To handle depth discontinuities, a novel edge sampling algorithm is used. Input: Ray-surface intersection \hat{\mathbf{x}}. Hyperparameters: Max steps K, step size \epsilon, threshold \delta. Algorithm: python def locateedgepoints(xhat, o, K, epsilon, delta): xt = xhat for i in range(1, K + 1): vec = xt - o dist = np.linalg.norm(vec) if dist < 1e-8: return xhat dirvec = vec / dist nt = computenormal(xt) if np.dot(dirvec, nt) < delta: return xt else: projection = nt - np.dot(dirvec, nt) dirvec xt = xt + epsilon projection return "NOT FOUND" def computenormal(x): return computesdfgradient(x) # Computes gradient of SDF network 4. The rendering equation accounts for diffuse and specular components using the optimized material parameters. Parameters: K: Max steps for edge search (Not given in the sources). \epsilon: Step size for edge search (Not given in the sources). \delta: Threshold for edge detection (Not given in the sources). L: Light intensity (Optimized scalar). Pitfalls: Skipping Stage 1 leads to divergence or incorrect topology. The method assumes ideal collocated camera-lighting; deviations cause self-shadowing errors if not handled (addressed in PIR). Inter-reflections are ignored in the original IRON, leading to inaccuracies in concave regions. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Recovers correct topology via volumetric initialization; produces mesh-compatible outputs; handles spatially varying materials. Limitations: Assumes opaque objects; ignores ambient light, self-shadows, and inter-reflections (original version); requires photometric images with collocated flashlight. When to use: When high-quality mesh and texture extraction from photometric image sets is required, and computational resources allow for two-stage optimization. When not: When self-shadows or inter-reflections are significant and cannot be ignored, or when only environmental lighting is available. IRON was proposed by Kai Zhang, Fujun Luan, Zhengqi Li, and Noah Snavely from Cornell University, Adobe Research, and Google Research. It was published in CVPR 2022. The method builds on neural SDF representations (e.g., IDR, NeuS) and neural radiance fields (NeRF). It addresses the limitations of mesh-based inverse rendering by using neural SDFs for flexibility and compactness. A later extension, PIR (Photometric Inverse Rendering), addresses IRON's shortcomings regarding self-shadows and inter-reflections by jointly optimizing light position and using DINO feature regularization. name: Instance-NeRF
head: Instance Neural Radiance Field
body: Instance-NeRF is a learning-based 3D instance segmentation pipeline that extends a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) with an additional instance field component. It takes a pre-trained NeRF model as input and learns to detect all objects within the underlying 3D scene, producing a 3D bounding box, a continuous 3D mask, and a class label for each detected object. Unlike Semantic-NeRF, which relies on 2D semantic priors that are generally consistent across views, Instance-NeRF addresses the challenge of multi-view inconsistent 2D instance masks (where the same object may receive different instance IDs in different views) without relying on 3D bounding volume priors. It achieves this by using a 3D proposal-based mask prediction network (NeRF-RCNN) to generate coarse 3D masks, projecting them to 2D to match and refine multi-view consistent segmentation maps, and then supervising the continuous instance field with these refined 2D masks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model F{\Theta\sigma, \Thetac} parameterized by density network weights \Theta\sigma and color branch weights \Thetac, trained on posed RGB images. Output: A continuous instance field G{\Theta\sigma, \Thetai} that produces a view-independent instance label vector at any 3D position, along with 3D bounding boxes, class labels, and discrete 3D masks for detected objects. Data Structures and Layout: The model is parameterized by three components: 1. Density Net (\Theta\sigma): Part of the original NeRF, predicting volume density \sigma. 2. Color Branch (\Thetac): Part of the original NeRF, predicting RGB radiance \mathbf{c}. 3. Instance Branch (\Thetai): The new component, predicting the instance label distribution. The instance field is formulated as G{\Theta\sigma, \Thetai}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{i}, where \mathbf{i} is an L-dimensional vector representing the instance label distribution over L labels, with the first dimension representing the background. Rendering and Sampling: The method uses hierarchical stratified sampling. For each pixel, a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is formulated, where \mathbf{o} is the camera center and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. K quadrature points \{tk\}{k=1}^K are selected along the ray within the traceable volume. The distance between samples is denoted by \deltak. Formulas: The expected color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}), expected depth \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}), and expected instance logits \hat{I}(\mathbf{r}) are accumulated via numerical quadrature: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) \mathbf{c}(tk) \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) tk \hat{I}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) \mathbf{i}(tk) Where: \hat{T}(tk) is the transmittance at sample k. \alpha(\cdot) is the opacity function. \sigma(tk) is the volume density. \mathbf{c}(tk) is the RGB radiance. \mathbf{i}(tk) is the instance label vector at point tk. Training Procedure: 1. 3D Proposal Generation: The method employs a NeRF-RCNN, extended from NeRF-RPN, which takes the extracted radiance and density field of the pre-trained NeRF. NeRF-RCNN outputs 3D bounding boxes, class labels, and discrete 3D masks for each detected object. 2. 2D Segmentation Generation: Existing panoptic segmentation models (specifically Mask2Former) generate 2D panoptic segmentation maps of images rendered from the NeRF. These 2D instance masks are generally multi-view inconsistent. 3. Mask Matching and Refinement: The discrete 3D masks predicted by NeRF-RCNN are projected back to 2D image space from the same camera poses. Instance-NeRF leverages Mask2Former and CascadePSP to match the same instance in 2D segmentation across different views and refine the resultant masks. This process links each 2D instance mask to its corresponding 3D instance to resolve inconsistency. 4. Instance Field Supervision: The resulting multi-view consistent 2D segmentation maps are used to supervise and train the instance field component G{\Theta\sigma, \Thetai}, producing a continuous 3D segmentation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traininstancefield(pretrainednerf, cameraposes, consistent2dmasks, K=64): """ Trains the Instance-NeRF instance field using a pre-trained NeRF. Args: pretrainednerf: Pre-trained NeRF model with parameters (Thetasigma, Thetac). cameraposes: List of camera poses for the input images. consistent2dmasks: Multi-view consistent 2D segmentation masks from matching step. K: Number of quadrature points per ray. Returns: Thetai: Trained instance branch parameters. """ # Initialize instance branch parameters Thetai Thetai = initializeparameters() # NeRF-RCNN generates 3D proposals (bounding boxes, class labels, discrete masks) # This step runs once to establish coarse 3D structure for mask matching. discrete3dmasks, boundingboxes, classlabels = nerfrcnnforward(pretrainednerf) # Multi-view mask matching and refinement using CascadePSP and Mask2Former # Projects 3D masks to 2D, matches instances across views, and refines masks. # consistent2dmasks are produced here and used for supervision. for step in range(1000): # for rayorigin, raydirection in generaterays(cameraposes): # # Hierarchical stratified sampling selects K quadrature points {tk} tsamples = stratifiedsample(rayorigin, raydirection, K) # Compute distance between consecutive samples δk delta = diff(tsamples, prepend=tsamples[0]) # Query pre-trained NeRF for density σ and color c sigma = pretrainednerf.querydensity(tsamples) c = pretrainednerf.querycolor(tsamples, raydirection) # Compute 3D positions from ray origins and sample depths positions = rayorigin + tsamples[:, None] raydirection # Query instance field G for instance logits i i = instancefieldforward(positions, Thetai) # Compute opacity α = 1 - exp(-σδ) alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma delta) # Compute transmittance T̂(tk) = Π{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - αj) That = cumprod(concat([oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha[:,:-1]], dim=1), dim=1) # Render expected color, depth, and instance logits via quadrature Chat = sum(That alpha c, dim=0) Dhat = sum(That alpha tsamples, dim=0) Ihat = sum(That alpha i, dim=0) # Compute loss against consistent 2D masks loss = computeloss(Chat, Dhat, Ihat, consistent2dmasks) # Backpropagate to update instance branch parameters Thetai = updateparameters(Thetai, loss) return Thetai Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multi-view Inconsistency: 2D instance masks generated by standard panoptic segmentation models are generally multi-view inconsistent, meaning the same object may be assigned different instance IDs in different views. This can impair performance if not resolved. Instance-NeRF addresses this via the 2D mask matching procedure. Ambiguity in Overlapping Objects: Unlike Panoptic NeRF, which uses 3D bounding volumes as priors, Instance-NeRF does not rely on 3D priors. However, Panoptic NeRF cannot resolve ambiguity when objects belonging to the same class have overlapping bounding volumes. Instance-NeRF avoids this specific ambiguity by not using bounding volume priors, but it must still handle the general case of overlapping instances through the instance field representation. Time Complexity: The method requires an additional forward pass through the instance branch for every sample point along every ray during training and inference. The complexity is dominated by the NeRF-RCNN 3D proposal generation and the multi-view mask matching/refinement step using Mask2Former and CascadePSP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the parameters for the instance branch \Thetai in addition to the pre-trained NeRF parameters. The discrete 3D masks and intermediate 2D segmentation maps also consume memory during the training pipeline. Strengths: It is one of the first learning-based approaches to generate 3D instance segmentation in NeRF without using ground-truth segmentation as input. It produces satisfactory 3D object masks on complex scenes during test time. It does not rely on 3D priors to address multi-view inconsistency, avoiding the ambiguity issues associated with overlapping bounding volumes. Limitations: The method depends on the quality of the pre-trained NeRF and the external panoptic segmentation models (Mask2Former, CascadePSP). The multi-view inconsistency of 2D instance masks is a significant challenge that requires complex matching and refinement steps. When to use: When 3D instance segmentation is required for a scene represented by a NeRF, and ground-truth 3D instance labels are unavailable. It is suitable for complex scenes where 3D bounding volume priors might fail due to overlapping objects. Instance-NeRF was introduced by Yichen Liu, Benran Hu, Junkai Huang, Yu-Wing Tai, and Chi-Keung Tang from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Carnegie Mellon University, and Dartmouth College. The paper was published in ICCV 2023. It addresses the challenge of 3D instance segmentation in NeRF, a less explored and more challenging task compared to 2D semantic segmentation in NeRF (e.g., Semantic-NeRF). Previous methods like Panoptic NeRF used 3D bounding volumes as priors but struggled with ambiguity in overlapping objects. Instance-NeRF proposes a novel architecture and training approach that generates multi-view consistent 2D segmentation and continuous 3D segmentation without relying on 3D priors. name: MIMO-NeRF
head: MIMO-NeRF-distill, MIMO-NeRF-naive
body: MIMO-NeRF is a neural rendering method that accelerates inference by replacing the standard Single-Input Single-Output (SISO) Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) MLP. It groups neighboring samples along a ray and processes them simultaneously, reducing the number of MLP evaluations (# Run) required per pixel. Unlike knowledge distillation methods that require training a separate teacher network, MIMO-NeRF can be trained via self-supervised learning using a 3D consistency loss to resolve ambiguities in density and color inherent in grouped predictions. It maintains the original NeRF hyperparameters (sample counts and network width) while achieving superior speed-quality trade-offs compared to methods that reduce sample counts or network width. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of camera views and their poses as input. For each ray \mathbf{r}, it samples Nc coarse points and Nf fine points. The MIMO MLP f{\text{MIMO}} takes a group of Np positions \{\mathbf{x}i, \dots, \mathbf{x}j\} and the ray direction \mathbf{d} as input, and outputs Np colors \{\mathbf{c}i, \dots, \mathbf{c}j\} and densities \{\sigmai, \dots, \sigmaj\}. Data Structures: The network architecture is identical to the baseline NeRF [Parent] except for input/output dimensions. Positional Encoding: Input positions \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{S}^2 are encoded using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) [Parent, S1]. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) is 63-dimensional, \gamma(\mathbf{d}) is 27-dimensional. MIMO MLP: Density Network: Takes concatenated encoded positions \gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \dots, \gamma(\mathbf{x}j) (total dimension 63 \times Np) and applies an 8-layer MLP with ReLU activations, 256 hidden units, and skip connections from input to every 4th layer. Output is Np density values \sigma. Color Network: Takes the output of the last hidden layer of the density network (dimension 256), concatenates with encoded directions \gamma(\mathbf{d}) (dimension 27), passes through a 1-layer MLP (ReLU, 128 units), and finally a linear layer to produce Np RGB colors \mathbf{c}. Note: The total parameter count increases because the input dimension of the first layer scales with Np, but the hidden layer size remains constant. Numbered Steps: 1. Grouping: For a ray with N total samples (coarse + fine), group Np neighboring samples starting from the camera. Create N/Np groups. 2. Forward Pass: Apply f{\text{MIMO}} to each group. For group m containing samples i through j (j=i+Np-1), compute: f{\text{MIMO}}: (\mathbb{R}^3)^{Np} \times \mathbb{S}^2 \rightarrow (\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^+)^{Np} (\mathbf{x}i, \dots, \mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{d}) \mapsto (\mathbf{c}i, \dots, \mathbf{c}j, \sigmai, \dots, \sigmaj) 3. Rendering: Compute pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using standard volumetric rendering integration with the predicted \sigma and \mathbf{c}. 4. Training Objective: Minimize \mathcal{L}{\text{MIMO}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{\text{3D}}. \mathcal{L}{\text{pixel}}^{\text{MIMO}}: Standard MSE between rendered and ground truth pixel colors. \mathcal{L}{\text{3D}}: 3D consistency loss comprising color and alpha consistency. 5. 3D Consistency Loss: To address ambiguity in grouped predictions, enforce consistency between different reformulated MLPs (or different groups/views). Color 3D Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{color 3D}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\mathbf{c}i^{m1} - \text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\mathbf{c}i^{m1}) - \mathbf{c}i^{m2}\|2^2 \right] Alpha 3D Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{alpha 3D}} = \sum{m1=1}^{M-1} \sum{m2=m1+1}^M \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \left[ \mu{m1}^{m2} \|\alphai^{m1} - \text{sg}(\alphai^{m2})\|2^2 + \mu{m2}^{m1} \|\text{sg}(\alphai^{m1}) - \alphai^{m2}\|2^2 \right] Asymmetric Weight \mu: \mu{m1}^{m2} = \frac{\sqrt{m2} \sqrt{R{\max}}}{\sqrt{R{m1}}} where R{\max} = \max{m \in \{1, \dots, M\}} Rm. Rm are scaling factors for reformulated MLPs. 6. Optimization: Train using Adam optimizer with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4} and batch size 1024 rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. (B, Np, 1) gammad = positionalencoding(d.unsqueeze(1), Lfreq=4).squeeze(1) # (B, 27) colorinput = torch.cat([h, gammad], dim=-1) # (B, F+27) c = self.colorlayers0 # (B, 128) c = F.relu(c) c = self.colorlayers1.view(B, Np, 3) # (B, Np, 3) return c, densities def compute3dconsistencyloss(c1, c2, a1, a2, R1, R2, Rmax): """ Computes asymmetric 3D consistency loss between two reformulated networks. c1, c2: (B, Np, 3) colors a1, a2: (B, Np, 1) alphas R1, R2: scaling factors for the respective reformulations Rmax: maximum scaling factor across all reformulations """ mu12 = (torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R2)) torch.sqrt(Rmax)) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R1)) mu21 = (torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R1)) torch.sqrt(Rmax)) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(R2)) lcolor = mu12 F.mseloss(c1, c2.detach()) + mu21 F.mseloss(c1.detach(), c2) lalpha = mu12 F.mseloss(a1, a2.detach()) + mu21 F.mseloss(a1.detach(), a2) return (lcolor + lalpha) / 2.0 def computeloss(colors, densities, gtcolors, alpha, lambda3d=1.0, reformulations=None): lpixel = F.mseloss(colors, gtcolors) if reformulations is not None: # L3D is computed between multiple reformulated networks (M > 1) # using the asymmetric weighting formula from the sources. l3d = 0.0 M = len(reformulations) for m1 in range(M): for m2 in range(m1 + 1, M): c1, a1 = reformulations[m1] c2, a2 = reformulations[m2] R1, R2 = reformulations[m1].get('R', 1), reformulations[m2].get('R', 1) Rmax = max([r.get('R', 1) for r in reformulations]) l3d += compute3dconsistencyloss(c1, c2, a1, a2, R1, R2, Rmax) l3d /= (M (M - 1) / 2) else: l3d = 0.0 # Application of MIMO-NeRF to the TensoRF architecture. It improves inference and training speed without deteriorating image quality by selecting appropriate Np. For Nc=64, Nf=128, Np=2, # Run is 128 (vs 192 for NeRF). Memory Complexity: Parameter count increases slightly (up to 1.39\times for Np=8). Strengths: Superior speed-quality trade-off compared to NeRF-few and NeRF-small (which reduce samples or width to match FLOPs). Self-supervised variant outperforms distillation variants. Limitations: Trade-off between speed and quality as Np increases. MIMO-NeRF was introduced in 2023. It addresses the high computational cost of standard NeRF by leveraging parallel processing of ray samples. It builds on the NeRF training loop [Parent] and positional encoding techniques [Parent], modifying the network architecture to accept multiple input positions and produce multiple output colors and densities simultaneously. name: Appearance and Lighting Decomposition
head: Neural Radiance Field Decomposition, Inverse Rendering in NeRF, Material-Lighting Separation
body: Appearance and Lighting Decomposition refers to a family of neural radiance field methods that decouple view-independent geometric and material properties from view-dependent lighting effects to enable physically plausible relighting, appearance editing, and robust reconstruction of specular surfaces. Unlike standard NeRF, which maps 6D coordinates directly to raw color and density, these methods predict intermediate physical attributes (such as normals, roughness, albedo, or reflection directions) and combine them with lighting models or environment maps during the rendering process. This separation resolves the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in standard NeRF and allows for the accurate modeling of glossy and reflective surfaces that standard architectures fail to capture. All methods in this family build on Specific Model Architectures. While the specific decomposition varies, the core principle is the decoupling of view-independent geometric/material features from view-dependent lighting effects. Input Representation: Raw coordinates \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d} are mapped to a higher-dimensional space using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to mitigate spectral bias. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. Network Topology: The canonical implementation uses coupled Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) modified to output intermediate physical properties rather than raw color. 1. Density/Geometry Network: Takes \gamma(\mathbf{x}) as input. It consists of L hidden layers with ReLU activations and skip connections from the input to every 4th layer. It outputs density \sigma and latent features representing material properties (e.g., normals, roughness, albedo). 2. Appearance/Lighting Network: Takes the latent features, \gamma(\mathbf{x}), and \mathbf{d} (or derived directions like reflection vectors) as input. It computes the final color \mathbf{c} by combining material properties with lighting models (e.g., environment maps, specular models). Rendering Integration: During training, rays are sampled at points \mathbf{x}i. The MLPs predict \sigmai and material properties. The pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) is computed via volumetric rendering: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \text{where } \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \deltai is the distance between samples. The color \mathbf{c}i is derived from the decomposed components specific to the child method. Neural Light Field Representations map camera rays directly to RGB color values, bypassing the volumetric ray-marching and alpha-composition steps required by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Unlike NeRF, which requires multiple forward passes per ray to aggregate radiance, these methods achieve novel view synthesis with a single forward pass per ray, enabling rendering speeds that are orders of magnitude faster. Anisotropic Neural Representation Learning (ANRL) is a method for neural volume rendering that models volumetric density and latent features as view-dependent functions using spherical harmonics (SH) to eliminate directional ambiguity. Unlike standard NeRF which assumes isotropic point-sampled features, ANRL replaces the initial MLP output with SH coefficients, allowing the representation to capture anisotropy directly without shape-based sampling parameterization. This approach improves reconstruction quality in scenes with complex lighting or reflective surfaces while maintaining rendering efficiency. Ref-NeRF is a neural radiance field method that improves the representation of specular reflections by replacing NeRF’s parameterization of view-dependent outgoing radiance with a representation of reflected radiance, structured using spatially-varying scene properties. It builds on Specific Model Architectures by decoupling view-independent geometric/material features from view-dependent lighting effects, specifically targeting the failure of standard NeRF to accurately capture glossy surfaces. Unlike its siblings, Ref-NeRF explicitly separates outgoing radiance into diffuse and specular components and reparameterizes the directional input using the reflection of the viewing vector about the local normal vector, enabling smoother interpolation of reflected radiance across scenes with varying materials. The Convex Combination Color Decoder is a method for decomposing view-dependent appearance into a diffuse-like base component and a glossy reflection component, weighted by a geometry-derived coefficient. It solves the problem of modeling specular highlights and environment reflections in neural radiance fields by ensuring that reflection features are utilized at every sample point along a ray, rather than just in image space, which aids convergence when geometry is initially fuzzy. It differs from standard NeRF color decoders by explicitly separating the view-dependent term from a reflection term that utilizes a pre-computed reflection feature \bar{\mathbf{f}}. This method solves the problem of disentangling foreground objects from background environments in a radiance field to enable editable novel view synthesis, where foreground objects can be removed or replaced without corrupting the background. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Ref-NeRF by explicitly modeling separate background and object radiance fields that are composited via a differentiable one-hot gating mechanism, rather than relying solely on view-dependent lighting models or anisotropic scattering. Unlike Convex Combination Color Decoder which focuses on color mixing, this framework enforces spatial separation through density regularization and Gumbel-Softmax activation. DE-NeRF decomposes lighting, geometry, and appearance to allow relighting of high-frequency environments and appearance editing. It trains a signed distance field (SDF) function using a set of 2D images to reconstruct a display grid as the input scene for the MLP. The scene is decomposed into geometric features and appearance features (diffuse reflection, roughness, specular tint). Geometric features, appearance features, and distance h (from sampling point to grid) are input into four corresponding MLPs to predict diffuse albedo, roughness value, and specular tint. Diffuse reflectance is integrated with the environment map to get diffuse color \mathbf{c}d. A specular lighting MLP Fs is trained to get specular lighting \mathbf{c}l. The specular color \mathbf{c}s is calculated by multiplying \mathbf{c}l with specular hue. The final color \mathbf{c} is calculated as \mathbf{c}s + \mathbf{c}d. On NeRF Synthetic and Shiny Blender data sets, PSNR is 2 points higher than latest papers. NeRFLight is a grid-based neural radiance field architecture designed to achieve real-time view synthesis with a significantly reduced memory footprint compared to standard grid-based methods like Instant-NGP or KiloNeRF. It solves the trade-off between rendering speed and model size by splitting the 3D scene volume into N distinct spatial regions, each utilizing a separate density decoder but sharing a single, compact feature grid. Unlike Instant-NGP, which uses hash grids and multiresolution schemes that can suffer from rendering speed losses due to multiple linear interpolations, NeRFLight avoids hash grids entirely and instead uses multiple density decoders to handle feature collisions, ensuring high frame rates. NeRF-A is a NeRF variant using appearance embeddings (NeRF-A) without transient embeddings for handling varying camera conditions. Train the model with the left half side of the images in the training set and test novel view synthesis on the right half side. Interpolate between appearance embeddings assigned to brighter and darker images for controllable rendering. Quantitative results on classroom image: PSNR 23.52, SSIM 0.907, LPIPS 0.247. Train the material-geometry module first to predict albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, and depth, because the lighting network depends on these properties (e.g., SSRT depends on depth, MLP decoder depends on GBuffers). Train the lighting module second, using the re-rendering loss. The total loss for MGNet is a weighted combination: L{MGNet} = \lambdaa L{albedo} + \lambdan L{normal} + \lambdam L{material} + \lambdad L{depth}. The total loss for LightNet is: L{LightNet} = L{light} + \lambdar L{re-render}. L{light} is the HDR supervision loss function proposed by [Mildenhall et al. 2021]. L{re-render} is an L2 loss between the re-rendered image and the original image. Li et al. [2020]'s rendering layer causes significant artifacts on glossy surfaces. Unlike Li et al. [2020] which discretizes the incident hemisphere to approximate integration, this method leverages differentiable Monte Carlo. NeROIC is a technique using a multi-stage pipeline to recover a relightable NeRF-like model from images of an object captured under multiple unconstrained lighting environments. A method that recovers NeRF-like relightable models of large-scale buildings and historical sites. First stage: recovers geometry while explaining appearance variations due to lighting with latent appearance embeddings. Second stage: extracts normal vectors from this recovered geometry. Third stage: estimates BRDF properties and a spherical harmonic representation of lighting. Decomposes scenes into diffuse albedo, surface normals, a spherical harmonics representation of lighting, and shadows, which can be combined to relight the scene under novel environment illumination. Assumes a Lambertian model. The concept of decomposing appearance and lighting in neural radiance fields emerged as a response to the limitations of standard NeRF in handling specular reflections and complex lighting. Standard NeRF assumes isotropic scattering and maps viewing direction directly to color, which leads to artifacts on glossy surfaces and an inability to separate geometry from material properties. Early works like Ref-NeRF and DE-NeRF introduced explicit material parameters (normals, roughness) and lighting models to address these issues. Subsequent methods like NeRFLight and MGNet explored grid-based decompositions and inverse rendering techniques to estimate lighting and materials from images. The family continues to evolve with methods addressing anisotropy, background decomposition, and efficient rendering. name: DE-NeRF
head: Decomposed NeRF, Deformation-based Dynamic NeRF with Event Cameras
body: DE-NeRF models rapidly moving and deforming scenes by combining sparse RGB frames with high-speed asynchronous event camera data. It jointly optimizes camera poses and radiance fields while decomposing the scene into geometric, diffuse, and specular components to enable relighting and appearance editing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse RGB frames, event stream data (timestamps), and initial camera poses. Outputs: Optimized camera poses, a Signed Distance Field (SDF) for geometry, and decomposed appearance parameters (diffuse albedo, roughness, specular tint) for relighting. Data Structures: SDF Grid: A 3D grid representing the signed distance field, reconstructed from 2D RGB images to serve as the geometric prior for the MLP inputs. MLPs: 1. Pose Network: Maps event timestamps to camera poses. 2. Geometry Network: Predicts SDF values and geometric features. 3. Appearance MLPs: Four separate MLPs predicting diffuse albedo, roughness, and specular tint based on geometric features and distance to the grid. 4. Specular Lighting MLP (Fs): Predicts specular lighting coefficients. Numbered Steps: 1. Event-Based Pose Estimation: Use a neural network to map event timestamps t to camera poses P(t). This provides continuous pose estimation between sparse RGB frames. 2. Geometric Reconstruction: Train a Signed Distance Field (SDF) function using 2D RGB images to reconstruct the scene geometry as a display grid. The SDF provides geometric features and the distance h from a sampling point to the grid surface. 3. Scene Decomposition: For a given ray and sampling point \mathbf{x}: Extract geometric features from the SDF network. Input geometric features, appearance features, and the distance h into four corresponding MLPs to predict diffuse albedo \rhod, roughness value \alpha, and specular tint (hue) \mathbf{h}{\text{spec}}. 4. Diffuse Color Calculation: Integrate the diffuse reflectance \rhod with an environment map \mathbf{L}{\text{env}} to compute the diffuse color \mathbf{c}d. \mathbf{c}d = \int{\Omega} \rhod \mathbf{L}{\text{env}}(\omegai) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai) d\omegai (Standard environment map convolution assumed as exact integration method is not specified in sources.) 5. Specular Color Calculation: Train a specular lighting MLP Fs to get specular lighting coefficients \mathbf{c}l. Multiply the specular lighting \mathbf{c}l with the specular tint (hue) \mathbf{h}{\text{spec}} to get the specular color \mathbf{c}s. \mathbf{c}s = \mathbf{c}l \odot \mathbf{h}{\text{spec}} 6. Final Color Computation: Calculate the final color \mathbf{c} as the sum of diffuse and specular components. \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}s + \mathbf{c}d 7. Rendering: Integrate the color \mathbf{c} along the ray using standard volume rendering, weighted by the SDF-derived density or opacity. The pixel color computation follows the volumetric rendering equation defined in Specific Model Architectures. 8. Joint Optimization: Optimize the camera poses (via the event-based network), the SDF, and the appearance MLPs jointly to minimize the difference between rendered and observed RGB frames. Parameters: Event Threshold: Not given in the sources. MLP Hidden Layers: Not given in the sources. Environment Map Resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse RGB Frames: The method relies on event cameras for temporal continuity; if event data is missing or noisy, pose estimation may fail. Specular/Diffuse Separation: Incorrect decomposition can lead to artifacts in relighting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On NeRF Synthetic and Shiny Blender datasets, PSNR is 2 points higher than latest papers. Strengths: Handles rapidly moving and deforming scenes; enables relighting and appearance editing; leverages event cameras for high-speed dynamics. Limitations: Requires synchronized RGB and event camera data; complex joint optimization; relies on SDF reconstruction which may be sensitive to initialization. When to use: Dynamic scenes with fast motion where traditional RGB-based NeRF fails; applications requiring relighting of dynamic objects. DE-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of NeRF in dynamic scenes, specifically for rapidly moving and deforming objects. It builds on the principle of decomposing lighting, geometry, and appearance to allow relighting of high-frequency environments and appearance editing. The method integrates event cameras, which offer high temporal resolution, with sparse RGB frames to model dynamic scenes effectively.
