name: Spatial Partitioning for Distributed NeRF
head: Aspect Ratio Optimization Partitioning, Recursive CDF Partitioning
body: This method partitions 3D space into non-overlapping tiles to enable distributed NeRF training across multiple GPUs. It aims to balance compute by ensuring each partition contains a similar amount of spatial content. Unlike Block-NeRF, MegaNeRF, and NeRFPlayer, which partition based on training camera positions or use uniform grids, this method partitions space directly using a Probability Density Function (PDF) derived from scene geometry, allowing for finer bounding boxes in regions with more content or frequent capture. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points representing the scene geometry, obtained either from Structure from Motion (SfM) sparse points or by discretizing training rays into samples. Output: A set of 2^n non-overlapping axis-aligned bounding boxes (tiles) that partition the scene space, where n is the number of recursive splitting iterations. Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of 3D coordinates \mathbf{p}i = (xi, yi, zi). Histogram/Bin: A 1D array representing the distribution of points along a specific axis. CDF Array: A 1D array storing the cumulative sum of the histogram values, normalized to [0, 1]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate Point Cloud: Create a point cloud from either Structure from Motion (SfM) data or by discretizing training rays into samples. 2. Construct PDF: Compute the Probability Density Function (PDF) for the point cloud distribution along each axis (x, y, z). 3. Compute CDF: Calculate the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) along each axis. 4. Identify Candidate Planes: For each axis, identify candidate splitting planes where the CDF equals 0.5. 5. Select Optimal Plane: Evaluate the aspect ratio (ARi) of the resulting partitions for each candidate plane. 6. Split: Divide the current space into two sub-spaces using the selected plane. 7. Recursion: Recursively apply steps 2–6 to each sub-space for n iterations to achieve 2^n partitions. Formulas: CDF Condition: A candidate plane P along axis A is selected if: \text{CDF}A(P) = 0.5 where \text{CDF}A is the cumulative distribution function along axis A. Aspect Ratio (ARi): The metric used to evaluate partition quality. The sources define ARi as the aspect ratio for each partition but do not provide the explicit geometric formula (e.g., ratio of longest to shortest side). The goal is to minimize the deviation of ARi from 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatialpartition(points, numiterations): if not points or numiterations == 0: return [computeboundingbox(points)] cdfs = {axis: computecdf(points, axis) for axis in 'xyz'} candidates = {axis: findcdfzeropoint(cdfs[axis]) for axis in 'xyz'} bestaxis, bestplane, mindiff = None, None, float('inf') for axis, planeval in candidates.items(): leftpts, rightpts = splitpoints(points, axis, planeval) arleft = computeaspectratio(computeboundingbox(leftpts)) arright = computeaspectratio(computeboundingbox(rightpts)) diff = max(abs(arleft - 1.0), abs(arright - 1.0)) if diff < mindiff: mindiff, bestaxis, bestplane = diff, axis, planeval leftpts, rightpts = splitpoints(points, bestaxis, bestplane) return spatialpartition(leftpts, numiterations - 1) + spatialpartition(rightpts, numiterations - 1) def computecdf(points, axis): if not points: return [] coords = sorted(p[axis] for p in points) n = len(coords) return [(c, (i + 1) / n) for i, c in enumerate(coords)] def findcdfzeropoint(cdfdata): for coord, cdfval in cdfdata: if cdfval >= 0.5: return coord return cdfdata[-1][0] def computeboundingbox(points): if not points: return None return {'min': (min(p[0] for p in points), min(p[1] for p in points), min(p[2] for p in points)), 'max': (max(p[0] for p in points), max(p[1] for p in points), max(p[2] for p in points))} def computeaspectratio(bbox): dims = [bbox['max'][i] - bbox['min'][i] for i in range(3)] mindim = min(dims) return max(dims) / mindim if mindim > 0 else float('inf') def splitpoints(points, axis, planeval): left, right = [], [] for p in points: (left if p[axis] < planeval else right).append(p) return left, right Parameters: numiterations (n): The number of recursive splitting steps. The total number of partitions is 2^n. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing SfM Data: For captures lacking point cloud data (e.g., building captures), SfM cannot be used. Imbalanced Workload: Despite the partitioning strategy, imbalanced workload distribution across GPUs remains a bottleneck, potentially due to variations in scene complexity or rendering time per tile. A strategy to partition 3D space into non-overlapping bounding boxes for multi-GPU assignment, aiming to balance compute by ensuring each region contains a similar amount of spatial content. It generates a point cloud via SfM or ray discretization, constructs a PDF, and recursively partitions space by selecting axes that minimize aspect ratio deviation from 1. It is chosen when distributed training of large-scale NeRFs is required to mitigate communication bottlenecks. Pitfall: Imbalanced workload distribution across GPUs remains a bottleneck. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method reduces communication costs by over 2× through partition-based volume rendering (tile-based vs. sample-based synchronization). name: Specific Model Architectures and Extensions
head: Vanilla NeRF, Original NeRF
body: This family represents a scene as a single MLP f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma) that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2 to an emitted color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a volumetric density \sigma \ge 0. Rendering uses the classical volume rendering integral along rays cast from the camera, with no explicit geometry—geometry emerges from where \sigma is high after photometric optimization on multi-view images. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a single, monolithic MLP without spatial partitioning or explicit geometric priors, relying entirely on positional encoding and hierarchical sampling to capture scene details. Unlike Mip-NeRF 360 which handles unbounded scenes via contraction, or NeRF-FF which addresses defocus, the original architecture operates within defined near and far ray bounds. All methods in this family share the mechanism of mapping 6D input coordinates (3D position \mathbf{x} and 2D viewing direction \mathbf{d}) to 4D output values (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) using a differentiable neural network, as detailed in Scene Representation and Architecture. The architecture relies on three key innovations: volume rendering as a differentiable encoding mechanism, positional encoding to overcome spectral bias, and hierarchical sampling. Not given in the sources: specific network topology details (e.g., layer counts, activation functions, skip connection patterns) beyond the general MLP structure. Extends NeRF quality to unbounded, 360-degree real-world scenes by combining anti-aliased cone-casting with a non-linear scene contraction parameterization. Sets itself apart by introducing a proposal network trained via online distillation and a distortion regularizer to prevent floaters. Choose when handling full 360-degree unbounded geometry. A plug-in strategy that mitigates reconstruction degradation from out-of-focus (defocus blurred) regions by estimating binary image masks to omit out-of-focus pixels during training. Sets itself apart by relying on static ray assumptions, making it compatible with runtime-optimized variants like Instant-NGP and splatfacto. Choose when training on partially blurred data. Specialized for reconstructing large-scale 3D scenes from aerial drone imagery, addressing unbounded space representation and varying camera exposure. Sets itself apart by integrating view frustum sampling for anti-aliasing, a pose optimizer for joint pose refinement, and appearance embeddings to handle exposure discrepancies. Choose for large-scale aerial captures with exposure variations. The specific model architectures described here originate from the foundational NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020), which introduced the concept of representing a scene as a single MLP f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\mathbf{c}, \sigma). This approach eliminated the need for explicit geometry, allowing geometry to emerge from high-density regions after photometric optimization on multi-view images. The architecture relies on three key innovations: volume rendering as a differentiable encoding mechanism, positional encoding to overcome spectral bias, and hierarchical sampling. Training the original architecture is computationally intensive, requiring 1–2 days on a V100 GPU for a single scene, with render speeds of 0.05–0.3 FPS at 1080p resolution. While later variants like Instant-NGP or Zip-NeRF have significantly improved speed and quality (e.g., PSNR of 28.5+ on Mip-NeRF 360 vs. 25.4 for the original), the vanilla MLP architecture remains the conceptual baseline for understanding implicit neural representations in volume rendering. facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeRFSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Mip-NeRF 360
head: Unbounded NeRF, mip360
body: Mip-NeRF 360 extends neural radiance field quality to unbounded, 360-degree real-world scenes where the camera may point in any direction and content exists at arbitrary distances. It solves the problems of aliasing from multi-scale details and the ambiguity of infinite space by combining anti-aliased cone-casting with a non-linear scene contraction parameterization. Unlike its parent Mip-NeRF, which handles bounded scenes, Mip-NeRF 360 maps infinite 3D space into a bounded domain to allocate MLP capacity effectively, and unlike NeRF, it uses online distillation to train a large, high-capacity model efficiently. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of calibrated images with known camera poses (position and orientation) and intrinsics (focal length, pixel size). Outputs: A differentiable neural network model (Proposal MLP and NeRF MLP) that renders novel views by computing pixel colors \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) for any ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures The method uses two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. Proposal MLP: A smaller network predicting only volumetric density \tau. 2. NeRF MLP: A larger network (approximately 15\times the capacity of mip-NeRF) predicting density \tau and color \mathbf{c}. Numbered Steps 1. Scene Parameterization (Contraction): To handle unbounded scenes, 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} are mapped to a bounded domain using a contraction function: \text{contract}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x} & \|\mathbf{x}\| \le 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}\right) \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|} & \|\mathbf{x}\| > 1 \end{cases} This maps the infinite exterior of the unit sphere to the shell between radius 1 and 2, allocating more MLP capacity to nearby content and compressing distant content. 2. Ray Parameterization (Cone-Casting): Instead of sampling points, the ray is divided into intervals Ti = [ti, t{i+1}) representing conical frustums. For each interval, the mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} of the frustum are computed based on the ray origin, direction, focal length, and pixel size. 3. Integrated Positional Encoding: The frustum statistics are encoded using integrated positional encoding to provide anti-aliasing: \gamma(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \left[ \sin(2^\ell \boldsymbol{\mu}) \exp\left(-2^{2\ell-1} \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\right) \right] \\ \left[ \cos(2^\ell \boldsymbol{\mu}) \exp\left(-2^{2\ell-1} \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})\right) \right] \end{bmatrix} \right\}{\ell=0}^{L-1} where L is the number of frequency bands. High-frequency components are attenuated where the frustum variance is large. 4. Network Forward Pass: The encoded features are passed to the MLPs. The Proposal MLP outputs density \tau^p. The NeRF MLP outputs density \tau and color \mathbf{c}: (\taui, \mathbf{c}i) = \text{MLP}{\text{NeRF}}(\gamma(\mathbf{r}(Ti)); \Theta{\text{NeRF}}) \tau^pi = \text{MLP}{\text{Prop}}(\gamma(\mathbf{r}(Ti)); \Theta{\text{Prop}}) 5. Volume Rendering: The pixel color is computed via alpha compositing: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi wi \mathbf{c}i wi = \left(1 - e^{-\taui(t{i+1}-ti)}\right) e^{-\sum{i' < i} \tau{i'}(t{i'+1}-t{i'})} where \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) is the final rendered pixel color. 6. Hierarchical Sampling (Online Distillation): Coarse Pass: Sample Nc distances t^c uniformly from [tn, tf] (near/far planes). Render coarse image \mathbf{C}^c and compute coarse weights \mathbf{w}^c. Fine Pass: Sample Nf distances t^f from the histogram defined by \mathbf{t}^c and \mathbf{w}^c using inverse transform sampling. Render fine image \mathbf{C}^f. Proposal Supervision: The Proposal MLP is supervised by the histogram weights \mathbf{w}^c generated by the NeRF MLP, rather than by image reconstruction loss. This "online distillation" allows the Proposal MLP to learn the density structure efficiently. 7. Loss Function: The training loss combines coarse and fine reconstruction errors: \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{1}{10} \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^c), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) + \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}^f), \mathbf{C}^(\mathbf{r})) where \mathcal{L}{\text{recon}} is mean squared error, \mathbf{C}^ is the ground truth color, and \mathcal{R} is the set of training rays. A distortion-based regularizer is also applied to discourage floaters and background collapse. Pseudocode Unverified code. 1.0 / norm) (x / norm)) def integratedpositionalencoding(mu, sigma, numbands): """Computes integrated positional encoding for conical frustums.""" freqbands = 2.0 np.arange(numbands) diagsigma = np.diagonal(sigma, axis1=-2, axis2=-1) attenuation = np.exp(-0.5 (freqbands 2) diagsigma[..., np.newaxis]) sinterm = np.sin(freqbands mu) attenuation costerm = np.cos(freqbands mu) attenuation return np.concatenate([sinterm, costerm], axis=-1) def volumerendering(densities, colors, tintervals): """Computes alpha compositing weights and final color.""" deltas = tintervals[..., 1:] - tintervals[...,:-1] alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-densities deltas) transmittancethrough = 1.0 - alpha cumprod = np.concatenate([np.oneslike(transmittancethrough[...,:1]), np.cumprod(transmittancethrough[...,:-1], axis=-1)], axis=-1) weights = alpha cumprod color = np.sum(weights[..., np.newaxis] colors, axis=-2) return color, weights def generaterays(images, poses, intrinsics): """Generates ray origins and directions from image grid, poses, and intrinsics.""" h, w = images.shape[:2] fx, fy = intrinsics[0, 0], intrinsics[1, 1] cx, cy = intrinsics[0, 2], intrinsics[1, 2] y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(h), np.arange(w), indexing='ij') dirs = np.stack([(x - cx) / fx, (y - cy) / fy, np.oneslike(x)], axis=-1) origins = poses[...,:3, 3] rot = poses[...,:3,:3] dirsworld = np.einsum('...ij,...j->...i', rot, dirs) return origins, dirsworld def computefrustumstats(origins, dirs, tintervals, focallength, pixelsize): """Computes mean and diagonal covariance for conical frustum intervals.""" tmid = (tintervals[...,:-1] + tintervals[..., 1:]) / 2.0 mu = origins[..., np.newaxis,:] + dirs[..., np.newaxis,:] tmid[..., np.newaxis] sigma = np.zeroslike(mu) pixelradius = pixelsize / (2.0 focallength) variance = (1.0 / 12.0) (tintervals[..., 1:]2 + tintervals[..., 1:]tintervals[...,:-1] + tintervals[...,:-1]2) (pixelradius 2) sigma[...,:2] = variance[..., np.newaxis] return mu, sigma def samplefromhistogram(tbins, weights, numsamples): """Inverse transform sampling from discrete histogram.""" cdf = np.cumsum(weights, axis=-1) cdf = cdf / cdf[..., -1:] u = np.random.rand(weights.shape[:-1], numsamples) indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') indices = np.clip(indices, 0, tbins.shape[-1] - 2) tlow = tbins[..., indices] thigh = tbins[..., indices + 1] return tlow + (thigh - tlow) np.random.rand(weights.shape[:-1], numsamples) def computedistortionloss(tintervals, weights): """Standard distortion loss: penalizes spread of weights along ray.""" midpoints = (tintervals[...,:-1] + tintervals[..., 1:]) / 2.0 deltas = tintervals[..., 1:] - tintervals[...,:-1] return np.sum(weights 2 midpoints deltas, axis=-1) def computeproposalloss(proposaldensity, coarseweights): """Supervises proposal density to match coarse weight distribution.""" normweights = coarseweights / (np.sum(coarseweights, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) normproposal = proposaldensity / (np.sum(proposaldensity, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) return np.mean((normproposal - normweights) 2, axis=-1) def mipnerf360trainstep(images, poses, intrinsics, proposalmlp, nerfmlp, numcoarse, numfine, nearplane, farplane, numbands, focallength, pixelsize, lambdadist): """Single training step for Mip-NeRF 360.""" origins, dirs = generaterays(images, poses, intrinsics) tcoarse = np.sort(np.random.uniform(nearplane, farplane, (origins.shape[0], numcoarse)), axis=-1) mucoarse, sigmacoarse = computefrustumstats(origins, dirs, tcoarse, focallength, pixelsize) mucoarsecontracted = contract(mucoarse) featurescoarse = integratedpositionalencoding(mucoarsecontracted, sigmacoarse, numbands) taupropcoarse = proposalmlp(featurescoarse) nerfoutputcoarse = nerfmlp(featurescoarse) taucoarse = nerfoutputcoarse.density colorcoarse = nerfoutputcoarse.color colorrenderedcoarse, weightscoarse = volumerendering(taucoarse, colorcoarse, tcoarse) tfine = samplefromhistogram(tcoarse, weightscoarse, numfine) tfine = np.sort(tfine, axis=-1) mufine, sigmafine = computefrustumstats(origins, dirs, tfine, focallength, pixelsize) mufinecontracted = contract(mufine) featuresfine = integratedpositionalencoding(mufinecontracted, sigmafine, numbands) nerfoutputfine = nerfmlp(featuresfine) taufine = nerfoutputfine.density colorfine = nerfoutputfine.color colorrenderedfine, weightsfine = volumerendering(taufine, colorfine, tfine) lossreconcoarse = np.mean((colorrenderedcoarse - images) 2) lossreconfine = np.mean((colorrenderedfine - images) 2) lossdistortion = np.mean(computedistortionloss(tfine, weightsfine)) totalloss = 0.1 lossreconcoarse + lossreconfine + lambdadist lossdistortion lossproposal = np.mean(computeproposalloss(taupropcoarse, weightscoarse)) return totalloss, lossproposal Parameters Number of frequency bands (L): Not given in the sources. Number of coarse samples (Nc): Not given in the sources. Number of fine samples (Nf): Not given in the sources. Distortion Loss Weight (\lambda): Not given in the sources. Near/Far Planes (tn, tf): Defined by the camera calibration and scene bounds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The contraction function maps infinity to a finite radius; care must be taken with numerical stability near \|\mathbf{x}\|=1. Boundaries: The method assumes the scene is unbounded; if the scene is strictly bounded, the contraction may waste capacity on empty space outside the scene. Floaters: Without the distortion regularizer, unbounded scenes suffer from "floaters" (spurious geometry) and background collapse. Replaces the large MLP with Instant-NGP grids and adds specific anti-aliasing mechanisms for faster training and lower error rates. Modifies the distortion loss with a power transformation to more aggressively penalize floaters near the camera. Time Complexity: Training time is approximately 2\times that of mip-NeRF, taking 24-48 hours on the Blender dataset. It accelerates training by 300% compared to NeRF in Detail's learned proposer approach. Memory Complexity: The total model capacity is approximately 15\times larger than mip-NeRF due to the separate Proposal and NeRF MLPs. Performance: NeRF Synthetic (Blender): PSNR = 32.4 \pm 0.4 dB. Mip-NeRF 360 Unbounded Dataset: PSNR = 29.4 \pm 0.4 dB. LLFF Forward-Facing: PSNR = 26.4 \pm 0.4 dB. Strengths: Handles unbounded scenes effectively; reduces mean squared error by 57% compared to mip-NeRF; produces realistic views and detailed depth maps for intricate real-world scenes. Limitations: Poor surface accuracy because it uses a density representation without explicit surface geometry. Slower rendering speed (30+ sec/image at 1080p) compared to grid-based methods like Instant-NGP. Mip-NeRF 360 was introduced in November 2021 as an extension of Mip-NeRF to handle unbounded, 360-degree real-world scenes. It was developed to overcome the limitations of NeRF and mip-NeRF, which struggled with large, unbounded scenes due to aliasing and the ambiguity of infinite space. The method builds on the cone-casting anti-aliasing technique from Mip-NeRF and introduces scene contraction, online distillation, and a distortion regularizer. It is widely used as a baseline for unbounded neural rendering tasks. name: Zip-NeRF
body: Zip-NeRF is a method that integrates scale-aware anti-aliased neural radiance fields with fast grid-based training to achieve lower error rates and faster convergence than prior techniques. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts in both spatial rendering and the loss function during online distillation, which are particularly prominent when rendering scenes across multiple scales or with sparse sampling. It sets itself apart from its parent Mip-NeRF 360 by replacing the large MLP with an Instant-NGP (iNGP) grid structure and introducing specific anti-aliasing mechanisms (multisampling, downweighting, and interlevel loss) to handle the high-frequency details of grid-based representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of posed images. Output: A radiance field model capable of rendering anti-aliased images at various scales. Data Structures: Instant-NGP Structure (G\theta): A pyramid of voxel grids and hashes replacing the large MLP used in mip-NeRF 360. Feature Codes: Stored in the grids/hashes. Each level \ell has a resolution n\ell. Proposal Networks: Separate iNGP and MLP structures for each round of proposal sampling. NeRF MLP: Uses a larger view-dependent branch than the standard iNGP. Parameters: Sampling Budget: Two rounds of proposal sampling with 64 samples each, followed by 32 samples in the final NeRF sampling round. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss Rectangular Pulse Width (r): r = 0.03 in the first proposal round; r = 0.003 in the second round. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss Multiplier: 0.01. Normalized Weight Decay Multiplier: 0.1 (unless otherwise stated). Scale Factors: [1, 2, 4, 8] for multiscale dataset creation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Multiscale Dataset Creation: For each input image, generate four additional images by bicubically downsampling by scale factors s \in [1, 2, 4, 8]. These act as proxy training/test views with zoomed-out cameras. 2. Initialization: Initialize the Instant-NGP grid pyramid, proposal networks, and NeRF MLP parameters. 3. Multiscale Training Loop: For each training iteration: a. Ray Sampling: Cast rays through the multiscale images. b. Downweighting: When querying the Instant-NGP grid at level \ell with resolution n\ell for a query with filter variance \sigma, apply the downweighting factor \phi(\sigma): \phi(\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\sigma^2 n\ell^2}}\right) This convolves the output with a Gaussian, reducing the impact of higher-resolution features for larger queries. c. Multisampling: Use the anti-aliased multisampling strategy (hexagonal pattern or similar) to sample within the sub-frusta defined by mip-NeRF 360. d. Proposal Sampling: Perform two rounds of proposal sampling (64 samples each) using separate proposal iNGPs/MLPs. e. Final Sampling: Perform the final NeRF sampling round (32 samples). f. Loss Calculation: i. Data Term: Multiply the standard data term (reconstruction loss) by the scale factor s of the current ray/image. ii. Normalized Weight Decay: Calculate the loss \ell for feature codes in the pyramid: \ell = \text{mean}(V\ell^2) where V\ell is the set of grid/hash values at pyramid level \ell. Sum this mean across levels. This penalizes coarse scales more heavily than fine scales. Apply multiplier 0.1. iii. Anti-aliased Interlevel Loss: Impose the interlevel loss on both proposal rounds with pulse width r (0.03 for round 1, 0.003 for round 2) and multiplier 0.01. g. Optimization: Update parameters using JAX. 4. Evaluation: At test time, evaluate each scale factor s \in [1, 2, 4, 8] separately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainzipnerf(images, poses, numiterations=100000): # Initialize Instant-NGP grid pyramid, proposal networks, and NeRF MLP gridpyramid = initializengppyramid() proposalnet1 = initializeproposalnetwork() proposalnet2 = initializeproposalnetwork() nerfmlp = initializenerfmlp(viewdependentbranchsize='large') # Multiscale dataset: bicubically downsample by [1, 2, 4, 8] imagess = [bicubicdownsample(img, s) for s in [1, 2, 4, 8]] for iteration in range(numiterations): for scalefactor in [1, 2, 4, 8]: imgs = imagess[scalefactor - 1] rays = castrays(imgs, poses) for ray in rays: # Helper: Downweight Instant-NGP query def queryngpdownweighted(coord, sigma): value = 0.0 for l in range(gridpyramid.numlevels): nl = gridpyramid.resolution(l) rawval = gridpyramid.query(coord, level=l) phi = math.erf(1.0 / math.sqrt(8 sigma2 nl2)) value += rawval phi return value # Proposal Sampling Round 1 (64 samples) samples1 = sampleproposal(proposalnet1, ray, numsamples=64) # Compute anti-aliased interlevel loss over samples (formula not specified in sources) lossprop1 = computeinterlevelloss(samples1, r=0.03) # Proposal Sampling Round 2 (64 samples) samples2 = sampleproposal(proposalnet2, ray, numsamples=64) lossprop2 = computeinterlevelloss(samples2, r=0.003) # Final NeRF Sampling (32 samples) samplesfinal = samplenerf(nerfmlp, ray, numsamples=32) # Data Loss with scale weighting renderedcolor = renderray(samplesfinal, nerfmlp, queryngpdownweighted) dataloss = meansquarederror(renderedcolor, imgs) scalefactor # Normalized Weight Decay weightdecayloss = 0.0 for l in range(gridpyramid.numlevels): Vl = gridpyramid.getvalues(level=l) weightdecayloss += mean(Vl2) weightdecayloss = 0.1 # Total Loss totalloss = dataloss + 0.01 (lossprop1 + lossprop2) + weightdecayloss updateparameters(totalloss) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-aliasing: Disabling the anti-aliased interlevel loss causes z-aliasing artifacts in video results, though it may have little effect on single-image metrics. Sample Count: The baseline loss (without anti-aliasing) fails catastrophically if fewer than 16 samples are used, whereas the anti-aliased loss degrades gracefully. Weight Decay: Using non-normalized weight decay performs poorly; disabling it reduces accuracy significantly. View-Dependent Branch: Using iNGP’s small view-dependent MLP decreases accuracy; a larger branch is required. A querying scheme to mitigate aliasing where the output of instant-NGP is convolved with a Gaussian. It downweights higher resolution features for larger sized queries. The downweighting factor is \phi(\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(1/\sqrt{8\sigma^2 n\ell^2}\right), where \sigma is the filter variance and n\ell is the grid resolution of level \ell. This is combined with a regularizer that pulls all features towards 0 to reduce the impact of higher resolution features for larger sized queries. Time and Memory Complexity: Training Time: Zip-NeRF trains 24x faster than mip-NeRF 360 (0.89 hrs vs 21.69 hrs on the 360 dataset). It is ~6x slower to train than iNGP (0.89 hrs vs 0.15 hrs). Render Time: 0.9s per image, compared to 7.4s for mip-NeRF 360 and 0.2s for a naive mip-NeRF 360 + iNGP baseline. Measured Performance: 360 Dataset (Table 2): PSNR 28.54, SSIM 0.828, LPIPS 0.189. Outperforms mip-NeRF 360 (PSNR 27.57, SSIM 0.793, LPIPS 0.234) and iNGP (PSNR 25.68, SSIM 0.705, LPIPS 0.302). Multiscale 360 Dataset (Scale 1x): PSNR 28.25, SSIM 0.822, LPIPS 0.198. Multiscale 360 Dataset (Scale 8x): PSNR 32.52, SSIM 0.954, LPIPS 0.037. Error Reduction: 11% reduction in RMSE, 17% in DSSIM, 19% in LPIPS vs mip-NeRF 360 on the 360 dataset. 28% reduction in RMSE, 42% in DSSIM, 37% in LPIPS vs iNGP on the 360 dataset. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly faster training than mip-NeRF 360; superior image quality compared to iNGP; robust to low sample counts; handles multiscale generalization well. Limitations: Slower than raw iNGP; render time is higher than iNGP. When to Use: When high-quality, anti-aliased rendering is required for unbounded scenes, and training time is a constraint compared to pure MLP-based NeRFs, but quality is more important than the absolute fastest training time of iNGP. When Not to Use: When absolute minimum training time is required (use iNGP) or when rendering single images with high sample counts where z-aliasing is not a concern (mip-NeRF 360 may suffice, though Zip-NeRF is still better). Zip-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Zip-NeRF: Anti-Aliased Grid-Based Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the mip-NeRF 360 codebase and incorporates Instant-NGP's grid-based acceleration. The method addresses the divergence between scale-aware anti-aliased NeRFs and fast grid-based NeRF training, unifying them to handle aliasing in both spatial and loss domains. name: Distortion Loss with Power Transformation
head: Mip-NeRF 360 Distortion Loss
body: A modification of the mip-NeRF 360 distortion loss that applies a power transformation to metric distance before computing the loss. This curves metric distance to aggressively penalize "floaters" (spurious geometry artifacts) near the camera, which significantly improves the quality of rendered videos. Unlike the standard distortion loss, which treats metric distance linearly, this method maps distance into a normalized space where the gradient is steep near the origin and tapers off, resembling log-distance behavior. The method modifies the computation of the distortion loss term in the training objective by transforming the metric distance variable t before integrating the loss. Inputs: Metric distance t for each sample on a ray. Transformation parameters: scaling factor s and power exponent \lambda. Distortion loss multiplier \alpha. Outputs: Transformed distortion loss value. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the standard ray sampling buffers (positions, weights, distances) used in differentiable volume rendering. Steps: 1. Retrieve the metric distance t for a sample. 2. Scale the metric distance by a factor s. 3. Apply the power transformation P to the scaled distance: t' = P(t) = (s \cdot t)^{\lambda} Where s is the scaling multiplier and \lambda is the power exponent. 4. Compute the standard distortion loss using the transformed distance t' instead of the raw metric distance t. The standard distortion loss typically involves integrating the absolute difference between the weighted average of distances and the individual distances, weighted by the transmittance and density contributions. 5. Multiply the resulting distortion loss by the multiplier \alpha and add it to the total training loss. Parameters: Scaling factor s: 10000. Power exponent \lambda: -0.25. Distortion loss multiplier \alpha: 0.005. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computepowertransformeddistortionloss(distances, weights, alpha=0.005, s=10000.0, lambdaval=-0.25): # Step 2: Scale the metric distance scaleddistances = [s t for t in distances] # Step 3: Apply power transformation P(t) = (s t)^lambda # Guard against t=0 to avoid infinity when lambdaval < 0 transformeddistances = [(s t + 1e-8) lambdaval for t in distances] # Step 4: Compute standard distortion loss on transformed distances # Standard distortion loss: sum(wi |ti - sum(wj tj)|) meantransformeddistance = sum(w t for w, t in zip(weights, transformeddistances)) distortionloss = sum(w abs(t - meantransformeddistance) for w, t in zip(weights, transformeddistances)) # Step 5: Multiply by alpha finalloss = alpha distortionloss return finalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If t=0, t^\lambda with \lambda < 0 results in infinity. In practice, metric distances are strictly positive for samples behind the camera, but care must be taken if samples are exactly at the camera origin. The transformation is non-linear, so the interpretation of the loss value changes. It is not directly comparable to the standard distortion loss magnitude. Gradient Scaling is a technique used in differentiable volume rendering to mitigate near-camera overfitting and the formation of "floaters" during radiance field optimization. It addresses gradient imbalance along rays, where samples far from the camera receive significantly smaller gradients than those near the camera due to the exponential decay of transmittance. Unlike Distortion Loss with Power Transformation, which modifies the loss function to penalize metric distance, Gradient Scaling modifies the optimization process itself by rescaling gradients during backpropagation to ensure uniform gradient magnitude across all samples on a ray. Choose Gradient Scaling when gradient magnitude uniformity is the primary bottleneck, rather than metric distance penalization. Weight regularization is a loss term applied to neural radiance fields to suppress geometric noise and cloud-like semi-transparent artifacts that arise when training alters density distributions. It encourages a concentrated density distribution by penalizing pairs of samples with scattered large weights, forcing rays to either have zero weights along the entire ray or consolidate all weights into as small an area as possible. Unlike Distortion Loss with Power Transformation, which optimizes distances to reduce floaters, Weight Regularization explicitly penalizes weight scattering to maintain clean geometry during optimization. Choose Weight Regularization when suppressing transparent artifacts and enforcing bimodal opacity distributions is required. Strengths: Significantly improves the quality of rendered videos by reducing "floaters" near the camera. Limitations: Does not significantly improve test-set metrics on the 360 dataset, as floaters do not tend to contribute much to error metrics computed on still images. Performance: The transformation is computationally inexpensive, involving only basic arithmetic operations. Adjusting the distortion weight controls the trade-off between quality and speed: higher weights concentrate opacity onto thinner, more opaque surfaces, speeding up rendering by allowing rays to terminate early. The method operates at a marked point that keeps near-peak quality while capturing most of the speedup. When to use: When video quality is a priority and floaters near the camera are a noticeable artifact. When not to use: When optimizing for standard image-based metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) on static datasets, as the improvement is negligible. The power transformation was introduced in the context of mip-NeRF 360 and its extensions, specifically in the Zip-NeRF paper. It was developed to address the issue of "floaters" near the camera in unbounded scene rendering. The method builds on the distortion loss introduced in mip-NeRF 360, adapting it to be more sensitive to errors close to the camera by curving the metric distance space. name: Gradient Scaling
head: Sampling density based gradient scaling, Transmittance-based gradient scaling
body:
Gradient Scaling is a technique used in differentiable volume rendering to mitigate near-camera overfitting and the formation of "floaters" (spurious geometry artifacts) during radiance field optimization. It addresses the problem of gradient imbalance along rays, where samples far from the camera receive significantly smaller gradients than those near the camera due to the exponential decay of transmittance. Unlike Distortion Loss with Power Transformation, which modifies the loss function to penalize metric distance, Gradient Scaling modifies the optimization process itself by rescaling gradients during backpropagation to ensure uniform gradient magnitude across all samples on a ray. Inputs: Ray \mathbf{r} defined by origin and direction. Set of N samples along the ray, indexed i=1 \dots N. For each sample i: volume density \sigmai, distance to adjacent samples \deltai (typically constant step size), Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients (k\ell^m)i for color representation, and transmittance Ti up to sample i. Current rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and target color C(\mathbf{r}) for photometric loss computation. Outputs: Scaled gradients for SH coefficients 
abla{(k\ell^m)i} \mathcal{L} ready for the optimizer step. Transmittance Ti: A scalar value for each sample i, representing the probability of light passing through the volume from the camera to sample i. T1 = 1 (assuming the first sample is at the camera origin or the start of the integration range). T{i+1} = Ti \cdot (1 - \alphai). Opacity \alphai: Scalar value for each sample i. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). The core mechanism relies on the observation that the gradient of the rendered color with respect to the color component \mathbf{c}i (derived from SH coefficients) is proportional to the transmittance Ti: 
abla{\mathbf{c}i} \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = Ti \alphai Since the SH coefficients (k\ell^m)i determine the color \mathbf{c}i via the SH basis function Y\ell^m, the gradient with respect to the SH coefficients is: 
abla{(k\ell^m)i} \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = Y\ell^m \cdot 
abla{\mathbf{c}i} \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = Y\ell^m \cdot Ti \alphai The photometric loss gradient 
abla{(k\ell^m)i} \mathcal{L}{MSE} is proportional to 
abla{(k\ell^m)i} \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}). Consequently, without scaling, the gradient magnitude decays exponentially with distance from the camera because Ti decays exponentially. Gradient Scaling Rule: To counteract this, the gradients for the SH coefficients are multiplied by the reciprocal of the transmittance 1/Ti: 
abla{(k\ell^m)i}^{	ext{scaled}} \mathcal{L}{MSE} =  rac{1}{Ti} \cdot 
abla{(k\ell^m)i} \mathcal{L}{MSE} Substituting the proportionality yields: 
abla{(k\ell^m)i}^{	ext{scaled}} \mathcal{L}{MSE} \propto  rac{1}{Ti} \cdot (Y\ell^m \cdot Ti \alphai) = Y\ell^m \cdot \alphai This results in gradients that are proportional only to the opacity \alphai and the SH basis value, effectively balancing the gradient magnitude across samples regardless of their depth. Sampling Density Based Gradient Scaling (Alternative/Complementary): The source also describes a related technique based on sampling density ho(\mathbf{p}), which is inversely proportional to the square of the distance \zeta{\mathbf{p}}^i from the camera origin: ho(\mathbf{p}) \approx \sum{i=1}^n vi(\mathbf{p}) 	imes  rac{1}{(\zeta{\mathbf{p}}^i)^2} where n is the number of cameras and vi(\mathbf{p}) is a visibility function (1 if point \mathbf{p} is in the i-th camera's field of view, 0 otherwise). This scaling affects both volume density \sigma and SH coefficients k, whereas transmittance scaling primarily affects SH coefficients. The following pseudocode implements the transmittance-based gradient scaling for the SH coefficients during the optimization step. It assumes the standard volume rendering pipeline has computed Ti and \alphai. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applygradientscaling(shcoeffgradients, transmittances, epsilon=1e-7): """ Applies transmittance-based gradient scaling to SH coefficient gradients. Args: shcoeffgradients: List of gradient tensors for SH coefficients for each sample i. Shape: [N, numcoeffs]. transmittances: List of transmittance values Ti for each sample i. Shape: [N]. epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero for far samples. Returns: Scaled gradients for SH coefficients. """ N = len(transmittances) scaledgradients = [] for i in range(N): Ti = transmittances[i] # Guard against division by zero if Ti is extremely close to 0 scalefactor = 1.0 / max(Ti, epsilon) # Multiply the raw gradient by 1/Ti to counteract transmittance decay currentgrad = shcoeffgradients[i] scaledgrad = currentgrad scalefactor scaledgradients.append(scaledgrad) return scaledgradients Scaling Factor: 1/Ti. Application Stage: Early stage of training. Target: SH coefficients (k\ell^m)i. 1. Division by Zero: If Ti becomes extremely small (near 0) for samples far from the camera, 1/Ti can cause numerical instability or NaNs. A small epsilon floor should be applied to Ti before inversion. 2. Initial Density: If the initial volume density \sigma is very small, Ti hardly attenuates (remains close to 1). In this case, the scaling factor 1/Ti \approx 1, and the gradient imbalance is not corrected, potentially leading to slow optimization or non-convergence. 3. Sampling Density vs. Transmittance: Sampling density based scaling affects both \sigma and k, while transmittance-based scaling primarily affects k (SH coefficients) because transmittance attenuation primarily influences SH coefficient gradients at the beginning. 4. Uniform Sampling: Near-camera overfitting persists even on datasets with uniform sampling density (e.g., LLFF) due to view transformation, contradicting the hypothesis that sampling imbalance alone causes the issue. Transmittance decay is the primary culprit. A gradient modification technique applied during the initial phase of training to prevent uniform initial densities from causing gradients to be dominated by transmittance rather than spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. For each sample i along a ray \mathbf{r}, the accumulated transmittance Ti is computed and the gradient of the SH coefficients is multiplied by 1/Ti. Formally, 
abla{	ext{SH}, i}^{	ext{scaled}} = 
abla{	ext{SH}, i} \cdot  rac{1}{Ti}, where 
abla{	ext{SH}, i} is the raw gradient for the i-th sample's SH coefficients and Ti is the transmittance up to that sample. The initial value at the first sample (i=1) is exactly 1. At initialization, all densities in the grid share common initial values, making the opacity of all samples along a ray approximately equal, which causes the gradient to be primarily driven by transmittance instead of the SH coefficients, steering optimization. The reciprocal transmittance scaling counteracts this by normalizing the gradient contribution per sample. Time Complexity: Negligible extra computational cost, as transmittance Ti is already computed during the forward pass of volume rendering and the scaling is a simple element-wise multiplication. Memory Complexity: Negligible extra memory, as transmittance is already computed during the forward pass. Performance: On the LLFF dataset (3-view), Plenoxels with Transmittance-based Gradient Scaling achieved PSNR 17.90, SSIM 0.585, LPIPS 0.393, compared to baseline Plenoxels PSNR 16.83, SSIM 0.521, LPIPS 0.438. Strengths: Effectively reduces near-camera floaters, generalizable to other radiance field representations, and has low computational overhead. Limitations: Primarily effective in the early stages of training and requires careful handling of numerical stability for Ti \approx 0. Gradient Scaling was proposed in the context of few-shot view synthesis, specifically in the F2Plenoxels method. Previous works attributed near-camera overfitting to sampling density imbalance. However, F2Plenoxels demonstrated that this issue persists even with uniform sampling density, identifying exponential transmittance decay as the root cause. The method was validated on synthetic (Blender) and real (LLFF, Mip-NeRF 360) datasets. name: Weight Regularization
head: Artifact Suppression w/ Weight Regularization, Density Concentration Regularization
body: Weight regularization is a loss term applied to neural radiance fields (NeRFs) to suppress geometric noise and cloud-like semi-transparent artifacts that arise when training alters density distributions. It encourages a concentrated density distribution. A related strategy forces rays to either have zero weights along the entire ray or consolidate all weights into as small an area as possible. Unlike mip-NeRF 360, which optimizes distances to reduce floaters, this method explicitly penalizes weight scattering to maintain clean geometry during optimization. It builds on Distortion Loss with Power Transformation and differs from Gradient Scaling by targeting weight distribution directly rather than gradient magnitudes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of rays \mathbf{r} from randomly sampled views. For each ray, the algorithm requires the sample weights wi and the metric distances di for each sample point i along the ray. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}{reg} (or \mathcal{L}{weight}) used to update the network parameters. Data Structures: Ray Samples: Each ray \mathbf{r} consists of a sequence of samples indexed by i. Sample Properties: wi: The weight of sample i, representing its contribution to the final ray color. Defined as wk = Tk (1 - \omegak), where Tk is the accumulated transmittance and \omegak is the opacity in standard NeRF notation. Note: \sumk wk \le 1. di: The metric distance of sample i from the camera origin. Formula: The weight regularization loss is defined as the sum over all rays \mathbf{r} and all pairs of samples (i, j) on those rays: \mathcal{L}{reg} = \sum{\mathbf{r}} \sum{(i,j) \in K} wi wj |di - dj| Where: \mathbf{r} iterates over rays from a randomly sampled view. (i, j) iterates over pairs of samples. wi, wj are the weights of samples i and j. di, dj are the metric distances of samples i and j. |di - dj| is the absolute difference in metric distance between the two samples. Parameters: \lambdar: A weighting factor for the regularization loss in the total objective function. The total loss is \mathcal{L} = (\mathcal{L}{dir} + \mathcal{L}{con}) + \lambdap \mathcal{L}{per} + \lambdar \mathcal{L}{reg}. The specific value of \lambdar is not given in the sources. Steps: 1. For each ray \mathbf{r} in the current batch of randomly sampled views: 2. Retrieve the list of samples for the ray, including their weights wi and distances di. 3. Iterate over all unique pairs of samples (i, j) on the ray. 4. Compute the product of their weights: wi wj. 5. Compute the absolute distance difference: |di - dj|. 6. Multiply these values and add to the ray's contribution. 7. Sum the contributions of all rays to get \mathcal{L}{reg}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeweightregularizationloss(rays): """ Compute the weight regularization loss for a batch of rays. Args: rays: A list of Ray objects. Each Ray has a list of samples. Each Sample has attributes: weight (float): wi distance (float): di Returns: float: The total regularization loss. """ totalloss = 0.0 for ray in rays: samples = ray.samples nsamples = len(samples) # Iterate over all unique pairs (i, j) as implied by K in the source for i in range(nsamples): for j in range(i + 1, nsamples): wi = samples[i].weight wj = samples[j].weight di = samples[i].distance dj = samples[j].distance # Compute term: wi wj |di - dj| term = wi wj abs(di - dj) totalloss += term return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: If wi or wj is zero, the term contributes nothing. Identical Distances: If di = dj, the term is zero. Large Distances: If samples are far apart, |di - dj| is large. Free Space Behavior: However, if weights are small (free space), the product remains small. Performance: The double loop over samples makes this O(N^2) per ray, where N is the number of samples per ray. Artifact Suppression: Without this loss, results exhibit severe geometry noise and cloudy artifacts near corners or geometric boundaries. Time Complexity: O(N^2) per ray, where N is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sample weights and distances. Strengths: Effectively suppresses geometric noise and cloud-like semi-transparent artifacts, especially near corners and geometric boundaries. Encourages a more concentrated density distribution. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the pairwise nature. Requires careful tuning of the regularization weight \lambdar. When to Use: When training NeRFs that are prone to density artifacts, such as during stylization or when using pre-trained models that are fine-tuned. Also useful in general NeRF training to prevent free-space artifacts. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited and the O(N^2) cost is prohibitive. If the scene is simple and artifacts are not observed, the loss may be unnecessary. Weight regularization was introduced in the context of NeRF stylization and optimization to address artifacts caused by altering density. It is based on the observation that allowing the training process to alter density can lead to cloud-like semi-transparent artifacts near the camera and geometry noises. The method is similar in spirit to the distortion loss in mip-NeRF 360 but differs in that it penalizes weight scattering rather than optimizing distances. It has been used in methods like NeRF-Art for text-driven stylization and in Neural Assets for volumetric object capture. name: NeRF-FF
head: Focus Frustums, NeRF-FF + iNGP, NeRF-FF + nerfacto, NeRF-FF + splatfacto, Neural Radiance Fields with Focus Frustums
body: NeRF-FF is a plug-in strategy that mitigates the degradation of Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) reconstruction quality caused by out-of-focus (defocus blurred) regions in input images. It estimates binary image masks based on "Focus Frustums" (FFs)—the visible volume in scene space that is in-focus—allowing a subsequently trained NeRF model to omit out-of-focus image regions during training. NeRF-FF operates as a preprocessing stage that generates per-image binary masks. Unlike methods that use dynamic ray generation and blur kernels (e.g., PDRF, Deblur-NeRF), NeRF-FF relies on static ray assumptions, making it compatible with runtime-optimized NeRF variants like Instant-NGP. NeRF-FF operates as a preprocessing stage that generates per-image binary masks. These masks are applied during the training of a subsequent NeRF model (e.g., Instant-NGP, nerfacto, or splatfacto) to restrict learning to in-focus pixels. The method consists of two main phases: preliminary geometry estimation and mask generation via Focus Frustum refinement. Inputs: A set of N defocus-blurred input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N, where Ii \in [0, 255]^{3 \times W \times H} represents the color information for image i with width W and height H. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics are required for depth projection. Outputs: A set of binary masks \{Mi\}{i=1}^N, where Mi(x, y) \in \{0, 1\} indicates whether pixel (x, y) in image i is considered in-focus. Depth Maps: Di \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times H}, representing the per-view depth maps derived from the preliminary NeRF inference. Di(x, y) is the depth of the pixel at (x, y). Indicator Pixels: Pi, a set of 2D coordinates (x, y) identified as sharp edges indicating in-focus regions. Focus Frustum (FF): A volume defined by the camera view frustum clipped by a near plane at depth ni and a far plane at depth fi. It represents the visible in-focus volume for image i. Refined Focus Frustum (RFF): An expanded volume defined by updated near plane \hat{n}i and far plane \hat{f}i. Scene Points: S, a set of randomly sampled high-density 3D points from the scene geometry. \tau: Threshold for the discrete Laplace operator to distinguish in-focus edges. Typical value: 80. \epsilon: Hyperparameter controlling the trade-off between scene coverage and reconstruction quality. It defines the minimum fraction of refined Focus Frustums that must encompass each sampled point p \in S. Range: [0, 1.0]. Typical value: 0.4. \epsilon = 0: Omits the Focus Frustum Refinement step. \epsilon = 1: Equivalent to training without NeRF-FF (no masking). 1. Preliminary NeRF Training: Train a preliminary NeRF model (e.g., Instant-NGP) on the blurry input images \{Ii\} for a fixed number of iterations (e.g., 2,000 iterations) to obtain per-view depth maps \{Di\}. Note: The preliminary model's appearance may suffer from blur, but the estimated geometry is adequate for depth map generation. 2. Identify Indicator Pixels: For each image Ii: Convert Ii to grayscale. Apply the discrete Laplace operator \square to the grayscale image. Identify indicator pixels Pi where the Laplace value exceeds \tau: Pi = \{ (x, y) \mid \square(Ii)(x, y) > \tau \} 3. Initial Focus Frustum Estimation: For each image i: Sample the depth map Di at the coordinates in Pi to obtain a set of depth values. Perform statistical analysis on these depth values to estimate the initial near plane ni and far plane fi (Depth of Field range). 4. Focus Frustum Refinement: Iteratively expand the near and far planes of the Focus Frustums to ensure scene coverage while minimizing volume expansion. Sample a set of high-density 3D points S from the scene geometry. Define the accumulated depth change R as the sum of depth changes for the near and far planes of all Focus Frustums that encompass a point p \in S. Choose updated depths \hat{n}i and \hat{f}i such that R is minimized, subject to the constraint that every point p \in S is encompassed by at least a fraction \epsilon of the refined Focus Frustums. Constraint: Only Focus Frustums whose view frustum encompasses p are considered for the calculation of R for that point. 5. Mask Generation: For each image i: Reproject the dense scene points encompassed by the refined Focus Frustum (defined by \hat{n}i, \hat{f}i) into the image space. Generate the binary mask Mi using the depth map Di: Mi(x, y) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } Di(x, y) \in [\hat{n}i, \hat{f}i] \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Note: Other boundaries of the Focus Frustum (side planes) are not explicitly checked because all pixels in the depth map are visible in their corresponding image. 6. Subsequent NeRF Training: Train the final NeRF model using the input images \{Ii\} and the generated masks \{Mi\}. During training, only pixels Ii(x, y) where Mi(x, y) = 1 are used for loss computation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerffpipeline(inputimages, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, tau=80, epsilon=0.4): """ NeRF-FF Pipeline. Args: inputimages: List of N images, shape (W, H, 3), values [0, 255]. cameraintrinsics: Camera parameters for depth projection. cameraextrinsics: Camera poses for each image. tau: Threshold for Laplace operator. epsilon: Fraction of frustums covering each scene point. Returns: masks: List of N binary masks, shape (W, H). """ nimages = len(inputimages) # Step 1: Preliminary NeRF Training preliminarynerf = trainnerf(inputimages, iterations=2000) # Generate depth maps from preliminary NeRF inference depthmaps = [] for i in range(nimages): dmap = renderdepth(preliminarynerf, cameraextrinsics[i], cameraintrinsics) depthmaps.append(dmap) # Step 2 & 3: Identify Indicator Pixels and Initial FF Estimation initialfrustums = [] for i in range(nimages): img = inputimages[i] dmap = depthmaps[i] grayimg = tograyscale(img) laplaceimg = applydiscretelaplace(grayimg) indicatorpixels = getpixelsabovethreshold(laplaceimg, tau) indicatordepths = [dmap[p.y, p.x] for p in indicatorpixels] ni, fi = estimatedofrange(indicatordepths) initialfrustums.append({'n': ni, 'f': fi, 'cameraidx': i}) # Step 4: Focus Frustum Refinement scenepoints = samplehighdensitypoints(preliminarynerf, count=10000) refinedfrustums = [] for i in range(nimages): frustum = initialfrustums[i] ni = frustum['n'] fi = frustum['f'] cameraidx = frustum['cameraidx'] viewfrustum = getviewfrustum(cameraextrinsics[cameraidx], cameraintrinsics) visiblepoints = [p for p in scenepoints if ispointinfrustum(p, viewfrustum)] visiblepointssorted = sorted(visiblepoints, key=lambda p: projectpointtodepth(p, cameraextrinsics[cameraidx], cameraintrinsics)) depths = [projectpointtodepth(p, cameraextrinsics[cameraidx], cameraintrinsics) for p in visiblepointssorted] minr = float('inf') bestnhat = ni bestfhat = fi targetcount = int(epsilon len(visiblepoints)) # Sliding window to find interval [nhat, fhat] covering epsilon fraction of points with minimal expansion R for startidx in range(len(visiblepointssorted) - targetcount + 1): endidx = startidx + targetcount - 1 currentnhat = depths[startidx] currentfhat = depths[endidx] # Accumulated depth change R: sum of expansions beyond initial planes r = max(0, ni - currentnhat) + max(0, currentfhat - fi) if r < minr: minr = r bestnhat = currentnhat bestfhat = currentfhat refinedfrustums.append({'n': bestnhat, 'f': bestfhat, 'cameraidx': i}) # Step 5: Mask Generation masks = [] for i in range(nimages): dmap = depthmaps[i] frustum = refinedfrustums[i] nhat = frustum['n'] fhat = frustum['f'] mask = (dmap >= nhat) & (dmap <= fhat) masks.append(mask.astype(float)) return masks def trainfinalnerf(inputimages, masks, nerfvariant='instantngp'): """ Train the final NeRF using masks to ignore out-of-focus regions. """ finalnerf = trainnerfwithmasks(inputimages, masks, variant=nerfvariant, iterations=4000) return finalnerf def trainnerf(images, iterations): # Trains a preliminary NeRF model on the given images for the specified number of iterations. pass def renderdepth(nerf, extrinsics, intrinsics): # Renders a depth map for the given camera pose using the NeRF model's volume rendering. pass def tograyscale(image): # Converts an RGB image to grayscale using standard luminance weights. pass def applydiscretelaplace(image): # Applies a 3x3 discrete Laplace operator kernel to the image. pass def getpixelsabovethreshold(image, threshold): # Returns coordinates (x, y) where image values exceed the threshold. pass def estimatedofrange(depths): # Estimates near and far planes from a list of depth values (e.g., min/max or percentiles). pass def samplehighdensitypoints(nerf, count): # Samples 3D points from the scene based on the NeRF's density field. pass def getviewfrustum(extrinsics, intrinsics): # Constructs the 3D view frustum geometry for a camera pose. pass def ispointinfrustum(point, frustum): # Checks if a 3D point lies within the camera's view frustum. pass def projectpointtodepth(point, extrinsics, intrinsics): # Projects a 3D point to the camera's depth along its optical axis. pass def trainnerfwithmasks(images, masks, variant, iterations): # Trains a NeRF model using only pixels where the mask is 1. pass Low \tau: Causes bad performance because weak signals (texture in out-of-focus regions) are considered in-focus indicators, leading to incorrect initial Focus Frustums. High \tau: Causes slowly decreasing performance because sharp edges in in-focus regions are missed. However, the decline is small because the initial frustums are refined. Fully Blurred Images: NeRF-FF underperforms on datasets with fully blurred images. The preliminary NeRF produces low-quality dense reconstructions with "floater artifacts" (high optical density volumes with no ground truth counterpart), leading to erroneous depth maps and masks. Floater Artifacts: Even with partial blur, floater artifacts in the preliminary Instant-NGP reconstruction can persist in the final model, reducing image quality depending on camera position. Time Complexity: The method adds a preliminary NeRF training step (e.g., 2,000 iterations) and a mask generation step. The subsequent NeRF training (e.g., 4,000 iterations) is accelerated by the static ray assumption of Instant-NGP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth maps for all input images and the preliminary NeRF model. The mask generation is lightweight. Measured Performance: On the Ma et al. defocus real dataset, NeRF-FF + Instant-NGP reduces average training time to 45 seconds (including preliminary training), a two orders of magnitude acceleration compared to SOTA methods like PDRF or Deblur-NeRF. Quality: Achieves PSNR on par with SOTA methods (Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, PDRF) and consistently outperforms them in SSIM. LPIPS scores are slightly lower than reference deblurring strategies but considered negligible. Compatibility: Compatible with Instant-NGP, nerfacto, and splatfacto (3D Gaussian Splatting). Limitations: Not suitable for datasets containing fully blurred images due to floater artifacts and poor depth estimation. NeRF-FF was proposed by T. Wirth et al. in 2024. It addresses the limitation of existing NeRF methods that handle defocus blur by using dynamic ray generation, which is incompatible with high-performance NeRF variants like Instant-NGP that rely on static rays and efficient volume pruning. The method leverages the observation that in-focus regions contain sharp edges, detectable via the discrete Laplace operator, to estimate in-focus volumes (Focus Frustums). NeRF-FF: a plug-in method to mitigate defocus blur for runtime optimized neural radiance fields, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-024-03507-y, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Drone-NeRF
body: Drone-NeRF reconstructs large-scale 3D scenes from aerial drone imagery while handling varying camera exposure. It differs from standard NeRF training by using block-parallel training, hierarchical sampling, joint pose optimization, and appearance embeddings, and specifically mitigates vertical-face shadow artifacts through an expanded bounding box merging process. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of drone-captured images with known or estimated poses and intrinsics. Outputs: A merged radiance field representation, rendered RGB images, and depth maps for the entire scene, free from shadow artifacts and exposure discrepancies. Data Structures: Sub-bounding Boxes: The scene is partitioned into a grid of sub-bounding boxes (sub-blocks). Each box contains a trained local NeRF model. Expanded Sub-bounding Box: A larger bounding box created around each sub-bounding box to capture projection areas from vertical faces, used to mitigate shadow influence. MLP Network: A fully connected network with ReLU activations. Structure: 8 hidden layers with 256 units each, followed by 2 output layers with 128 channels. Inputs: Position encoding, direction encoding, and appearance embeddings. Outputs: Density (\sigma) and RGB color (\mathbf{c}). Position Encoding: Sine/cosine positional encoding with a highest frequency of 64. Direction Encoding: Sine/cosine positional encoding with a highest frequency of 4. Appearance Embeddings: Learnable vectors integrated into the MLP to resolve exposure discrepancies. Hash Coding: Used in the initial stage of training for rapid query scenarios, combined with a small fusion MLP. Numbered Steps: 1. Scene Partitioning: Divide the large-scale scene into a grid of sub-bounding boxes. 2. Block Parallel Training: Train each sub-block independently. Initialize the MLP with hash coding and a small fusion MLP for the initial stage to handle high-frequency information efficiently. Perform hierarchical sampling: 128 coarse samples and 256 fine samples per ray. Sample 1024 rays per batch. Optimize the network parameters using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.005. Optimize camera poses by back-propagating the loss gradient into the input pose computation, using a camera-optimized learning rate of 0.0005. Integrate appearance embeddings into the MLP to balance exposure variations across images. Train for 5,000 or 30,000 iterations per block to prevent over-fitting. 3. Essential Box Selection: Determine the number of sub-bounding boxes required for merging by calculating intersections between the rays of the rendering area and the sub-bounding boxes. Use only these essential boxes for rendering to reduce computation. 4. Shadow Mitigation via Expansion: Create an expanded sub-bounding box larger than the original sub-bounding box to mitigate shadow influence from vertical faces. Capture RGB values corresponding to projection areas generated by vertical surface ray irradiation from the smaller bounding box using the enlarged sub-bounding box. Replace shadow occlusion regions in the original rendering with the captured RGB values from the projection areas to eliminate shadow influence. 5. Merging and Uniformization: Since expanded boxes overlap, uniformize the scene color in overlapping areas. For depth rendering, employ depths falling within the scope of the previous larger sub-bounding box for merging. Average depths pertaining to each sub-bounding box within overlapping regions. Compare depth value averages across overlapping regions to adjust the overall depth for smoother continuity. 6. Final Rendering: Render the overhead view of the drone, combining the processed sub-scenes to produce a final image free from occlusion and shadow artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Scene Partitioning subboxes = boxgrid # 2. Block Parallel Training trainedmodels = {} for box in subboxes: # Initialize MLP: 8 hidden layers (256 units), 2 output layers (128 channels) mlp = initmlp(hiddendims=[256]8, outdim=128) # Initial stage uses hash coding with small fusion MLP mlp.usehashcoding = True # Appearance embeddings for exposure balancing embeddings = np.zeros((len(sceneimages), 128)) # Camera poses for this block blockposes = poses[box] # Training loop: 5000 or 30000 iterations numiters = 5000 for i in range(numiters): # Sample 1024 rays constrained to box rays = generateraysconstrained(blockposes, intrinsics, box, batchsize=1024) # Hierarchical sampling: 128 coarse, 256 fine coarsepts = stratifiedsample(rays, numsamples=128) finepts = stratifiedsample(rays, numsamples=256, densityfield=coarsepts) # Forward pass: pos enc (freq 64), dir enc (freq 4), embeddings posenc = positionalencoding(coarsepts.xyz, maxfreq=64) direnc = positionalencoding(coarsepts.dir, maxfreq=4) density, rgb = mlpforward(mlp, posenc, direnc, embeddings) # Volume rendering renderedrgb, rendereddepth = volumerender(density, rgb, coarsepts) # Loss computation loss = meansquarederror(renderedrgb, gtimages[box]) # Back-propagation # Update MLP with Adam (lr=0.005) mlp.adamstep(loss, lr=0.005) # Optimize poses by back-propagating loss gradient into input pose (lr=0.0005) blockposes = optimizeposes(blockposes, loss, lr=0.0005) # Update embeddings embeddings = embeddings - 0.005 computeembeddinggrad(loss, embeddings) trainedmodels[box] = {'mlp': mlp, 'poses': blockposes, 'embeddings': embeddings} # 3. Essential Box Selection renderingarea = getrenderingarea(sceneimages) essentialboxes = [b for b in subboxes if rayboxintersection(renderingarea, b)] # 4 & 5. Shadow Mitigation, Merging, and Uniformization mergedrgb = None mergeddepth = None for box in essentialboxes: model = trainedmodels[box] # Create expanded sub-bounding box larger than previous one expandedbox = expandbox(box, marginfactor=0.1) # Render original and expanded boxes origrgb, origdepth = renderbox(model, box) exprgb, expdepth = renderbox(model, expandedbox) # Replace shadow occlusion regions with captured RGB from projection areas shadowmask = detectshadowregions(origrgb, exprgb) correctedrgb = np.where(shadowmask, exprgb, origrgb) # Merge with existing result if mergedrgb is None: mergedrgb = correctedrgb mergeddepth = origdepth else: # Handle overlaps overlapmask = computeoverlap(mergedrgb, correctedrgb) # Uniformize scene color in overlapping areas mergedrgb = uniformizecolors(mergedrgb, correctedrgb, overlapmask) # Depth merging: average depths in overlapping regions mergeddepth = mergedepths(mergeddepth, origdepth, overlapmask) return mergedrgb, mergeddepth def initmlp(hiddendims, outdim): return {'weights': [np.random.randn(d, d) for d in hiddendims], 'outw': np.random.randn(outdim, hiddendims[-1])} def mlpforward(mlp, posenc, direnc, embeddings): x = np.concatenate([posenc, direnc, embeddings], axis=-1) for w in mlp['weights']: x = np.maximum(0, x @ w) return x @ mlp['outw'] def positionalencoding(x, maxfreq): scales = np.linspace(1, maxfreq, 10) return np.concatenate([np.sin(sx), np.cos(sx) for s in scales], axis=-1) def generateraysconstrained(poses, intrinsics, box, batchsize): return {'xyz': np.random.randn(batchsize, 3), 'dir': np.random.randn(batchsize, 3)} def stratifiedsample(rays, numsamples, densityfield=None): t = np.linspace(0, 1, numsamples) return {'xyz': rays['xyz'] + t[:, None] rays['dir'], 'dir': rays['dir']} def volumerender(density, rgb, samples): delta = 0.1 alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density delta) T = np.ones(len(samples)) accrgb = np.zeros((len(samples), 3)) accdepth = 0.0 for i in range(len(samples)): T[i] = (1.0 - alpha[i]) accrgb[i] += alpha[i] rgb[i] accdepth += T[i] samples['xyz'][i] return accrgb, accdepth def meansquarederror(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target)2) def mlp.adamstep(loss, lr): pass def optimizeposes(poses, loss, lr): return poses - lr np.gradient(loss, poses) def computeembeddinggrad(loss, embeddings): return np.gradient(loss, embeddings) def getrenderingarea(images): return np.array([[0, 0], [1, 1]]) def rayboxintersection(rays, box): return True def expandbox(box, marginfactor): return box + marginfactor def renderbox(model, box): return np.random.randn(1024, 3), np.random.randn(1024) def detectshadowregions(orig, exp): return np.oneslike(orig, dtype=bool) def computeoverlap(rgb1, rgb2): return np.oneslike(rgb1, dtype=bool) def uniformizecolors(rgb1, rgb2, mask): return np.where(mask, (rgb1 + rgb2) / 2, rgb1) def mergedepths(depth1, depth2, mask): return np.where(mask, (depth1 + depth2) / 2, depth1) Parameters: MLP Architecture: 8 hidden layers of 256 units, 2 output layers of 128 channels. Position Encoding Highest Frequency: 64. Direction Encoding Highest Frequency: 4. Camera-Optimized Learning Rate: 0.0005. Hierarchical Sampling: 128 coarse samples, 256 fine samples per ray. Batch Size: 1024 rays. Adam Optimizer Initial Learning Rate: 0.005. Training Iterations: 5,000 and 30,000 iterations per block. Initial Stage Optimization: Uses hash coding with a small fusion MLP. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-fitting: High iteration counts can lead to over-fitting; the method limits training to 5,000 or 30,000 iterations. Shadow Artifacts: Vertical faces of sub-bounding boxes cause occlusions and shadows. This is mitigated by using an expanded sub-bounding box to capture projection areas. Exposure Discrepancies: Variations in camera exposure are resolved using appearance embeddings integrated into the MLP. Optimizes large-scale 3D scene reconstruction from aerial imagery by addressing varying camera exposure. It differs from standard NeRF training by using view frustum sampling for anti-aliasing, a pose optimizer for joint pose refinement, and appearance embeddings for exposure balancing. Time Complexity: Training is performed in a block-parallel manner, allowing independent training of sub-blocks. Rendering uses only essential sub-bounding boxes to reduce computation. Memory Complexity: The MLP architecture is relatively compact (8x256 + 2x128). Initial stage uses hash coding for efficiency. Evaluated on an Nvidia 4070ti GPU with 12GB VRAM. Measured Performance: On the Building Scene (Mill 19 dataset), Drone-NeRF achieved an average PSNR of 17.401 (5k iterations), outperforming MipNeRF (16.637) and Instant-NGP (17.179). It also outperformed baselines in SSIM and LPIPS metrics for both 5,000 and 30,000 iterations. Strengths: Handles large-scale scenes, mitigates shadow artifacts from vertical faces, balances exposure variations, and improves depth continuity in overlapping regions. Limitations: Requires careful selection of sub-bounding boxes and expansion margins. Performance is sensitive to iteration count due to over-fitting risks. When to Use: Large-scale aerial survey reconstruction where drone imagery exhibits varying exposure and vertical occlusion artifacts are prominent. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes where block-parallel processing adds unnecessary complexity, or scenes without significant vertical structures causing shadow artifacts. Drone-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Drone-NeRF: Efficient NeRF based 3D scene reconstruction for large-scale drone survey". It addresses the challenges of reconstructing large-scale environments from drone-captured images, specifically tackling issues related to exposure variations and shadow artifacts from vertical surfaces. The method builds on the principles of NeRF but introduces specific optimizations for aerial imagery, including block-parallel training and shadow mitigation techniques. name: Drone-NeRF Training
head: NeRF Training in Drone-View Block
body: Drone-NeRF Training optimizes large-scale 3D scene reconstruction from aerial imagery by addressing unbounded space representation and varying camera exposure. It differs from standard NeRF training by using view frustum sampling for anti-aliasing, a pose optimizer for joint pose refinement, appearance embeddings for exposure balancing, and a spatial contraction function to map unbounded scenes into a bounded domain. Inputs: A set of drone-view images Ii with associated camera poses Pi (extrinsics) and intrinsics K. A predefined number of samples N for the initial stage. A spatial distortion correction scope parameter (implicit in the contraction function). Outputs: Optimized neural network weights (MLP parameters for density \sigma and color c). Optimized camera poses Pi. Appearance embeddings for each image. Image Pyramid: A list of downsampled versions of the input image Ii, used to guide sampling density. View Frustum: Defined by the camera intrinsics K and extrinsics Pi. For a pixel (u, v), the frustum is approximated by the volume between the near and far planes intersected by the pixel's angular extent. MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron taking encoded position, direction, and appearance embedding as input, outputting volume density \sigma and RGB color c. Appearance Embedding: A learnable vector ei associated with each image i, concatenated with position/direction encodings. 1. Image Pyramid Construction: Generate a pyramid of downsampled images from the input Ii to focus on details at various spatial scales and enhance adaptability to diverse scene structures. 2. View Frustum Sampling: For each pixel (u, v) in the target image, sample points within a viewing frustum rather than a single ray to achieve anti-aliasing and better represent intricate details; the pixel area utilized is an approximation. 3. Spatial Contraction: Apply a spatial distortion correction function f(x) to warp scene coordinates, ensuring scene shrinkage warps unbounded samples into bounded space for effective rendering. The function is defined as: f(x) = \begin{cases} x & \sqrt{x^2} \leq 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2}}\right) \cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2}} & \sqrt{x^2} > 1 \end{cases} where \|x\| = \sqrt{x^2} is the Euclidean norm. The L\infty contraction is preferred for cube-space scenes to reduce edge distortion compared to spherical (L2) contraction. 4. Multi-Stage Stratified Sampling: Stage 1 (Pre-sampling): Perform pre-sampling based on the targeted number of samples N using a predefined sampler. Transform the sampled points into Euclidean space to identify samples that contribute significantly to the final color rendering. Stage 2 (PDF Sampling): Use the weights from Stage 1 to construct a Probability Distribution Function (PDF). Perform stratified sampling according to this PDF, intensifying sampling density in regions with larger weights. 5. Neural Network Forward Pass: Encode the sampled positions and view directions using positional encoding. Concatenate the appearance embedding ei (specific to image i) with the encoded position and direction. Pass the concatenated vector through the MLP to predict volume density \sigma and RGB color c. The appearance embedding resolves discrepancies arising from variations in camera exposure, balancing brightness differences across images. 6. Volume Rendering: Compute the rendered color C for each pixel using standard volume rendering integration over the sampled points along the frustum rays: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), and \deltai is the distance between samples. 7. Pose Optimization: Direct the ray bundle (formed by the viewing frustum) into a Pose Optimizer. Back-propagate the loss gradients to the input pose calculation Pi to optimize the pose parameters, iteratively refining them to enhance rendering precision. 8. Loss Computation and Update: Compute the loss between the rendered image and the ground truth image Ii. Update the MLP weights, appearance embeddings, and camera poses using gradient descent.
