1.0 / normx) (v / normx) for v in x] def encodepositionsanddirections(positions, directions): """Applies standard positional encoding to positions and view directions.""" return positions, directions def concat(arrays): """Concatenates multiple vectors along the last dimension.""" return [val for arr in arrays for val in arr] def computesampleweights(densities, samples): """Computes weights based on density to identify significant samples.""" return [math.exp(-d) for d in densities] def stratifiedpdfsampling(pdf, numsamples): """Intensifies sampling density in high-weight regions using PDF.""" # Standard inverse CDF sampling cdf = [sum(pdf[:i+1]) for i in range(len(pdf))] samples = [] for j in range(numsamples): u = (j + random.random()) / numsamples idx = next(i for i, c in enumerate(cdf) if c >= u) samples.append(idx) return samples def mlpforward(encodedpos, encodeddir, embedding, weights): """Multi-Layer Perceptron predicting density and color.""" # Standard MLP forward pass return [0.5], [[1.0, 1.0, 1.0]] def volumerendering(samples, sigmas, colors): """Standard volume rendering integration.""" rendered = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] T = 1.0 for sigma, color in zip(sigmas, colors): alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma) rendered = [rendered[i] + T alpha color[i] for i in range(3)] T = (1.0 - alpha) return rendered def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): """Mean squared error loss.""" return sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) / len(groundtruth) def dronenerftraining(images, poses, intrinsics, numstages=2, numsamplesstage1=64, numsamplesstage2=128, epochs=100): """Main training loop for Drone-NeRF.""" imagepyramids = buildimagepyramid(images) embeddings = {i: [0.0] 16 for i in range(len(images))} modelweights = [] # Placeholder for MLP parameters for epoch in range(epochs): for i, img in enumerate(images): # 1. View Frustum Sampling frustumsamples = samplefrustum(img.shape, poses[i], intrinsics, numsamplesstage1) # 2. Spatial Contraction contractedsamples = [spatialcontraction(p) for p in frustumsamples] # 3. Stage 1: Pre-sampling and Euclidean Transformation posenc, direnc = encodepositionsanddirections(contractedsamples, poses[i].direction) appemb = embeddings[i] inputs = concat(posenc, direnc, appemb) sigmastage1, colorstage1 = mlpforward(inputs, modelweights) weightsstage1 = computesampleweights(sigmastage1, contractedsamples) # 4. Stage 2: PDF Sampling pdf = [w / sum(weightsstage1) for w in weightsstage1] finalsamples = stratifiedpdfsampling(pdf, numsamplesstage2) posencfinal, direncfinal = encodepositionsanddirections(finalsamples, poses[i].direction) inputsfinal = concat(posencfinal, direncfinal, appemb) # 5. Neural Network Forward Pass sigmafinal, colorfinal = mlpforward(inputsfinal, modelweights) # 6. Volume Rendering renderedcolor = volumerendering(finalsamples, sigmafinal, colorfinal) # 7. Loss Computation loss = computeloss(renderedcolor, img) # 8. Pose Optimization & Update # Back-propagate loss gradients to optimize pose and model parameters # Gradient descent step pass return modelweights, poses, embeddings Number of Samples (Stage 1): Predefined, e.g., 64. Number of Samples (Stage 2): Determined by PDF, e.g., 128. Contraction Type: L\infty is preferred for cube-space scenes to reduce edge distortion. Appearance Embedding Dimension: Not given in the sources. Spatial Distortion Scope: If the space warp scope is not suitable for the scene, the scene within the original reasonable field of view will be distorted and deformed. Frustum Approximation: The pixel area utilized in frustum sampling is an approximation. Exposure Discrepancies: Without appearance embeddings, variations in camera exposure will cause rendering artifacts. Time: Higher than standard NeRF due to multi-stage sampling and pose optimization. The frustum sampling adds overhead per pixel compared to single-ray sampling. Memory: Increased memory usage due to storing appearance embeddings for each image and maintaining image pyramids. Not given in the sources. The method is designed for large-scale drone surveys by dividing the scene into sub-scenes (blocks). Strengths: Handles unbounded scenes effectively via spatial contraction; improves rendering quality for intricate details via frustum sampling and anti-aliasing; robust to exposure variations via appearance embeddings; improves pose accuracy via joint optimization. Limitations: Sensitive to the choice of spatial warp scope; computational cost of multi-stage sampling and pose optimization is higher than standard NeRF. Drone-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Drone-NeRF: Efficient NeRF based 3D scene reconstruction for large-scale drone survey". The method builds upon NeRF and addresses specific challenges in aerial photogrammetry, such as unbounded scene representation and exposure variations. It integrates techniques from differentiable rendering and pose optimization. Used for 3D scene reconstruction from drone-captured images, particularly in large-scale surveying applications. name: NeRFReN
head: Reflective NeRF
body: NeRFReN addresses the failure of standard Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to render reflective surfaces, such as glass and mirrors, by separating the radiance field into transmitted and reflected components. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the reflection fraction \beta derived from the transmitted geometry, allowing for the separation of reflection artifacts from physical entities. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and ray parameters. Outputs: Final pixel intensity I. Data Structures: The method separates the radiance field into two coupled components: a transmitted field with parameters (\sigmat, \mathbf{c}t) representing physical geometry and direct lighting, and a reflected field with parameters (\sigmar, \mathbf{c}r) representing virtual geometry and reflected lighting. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sample Transmitted Field: For a given ray, sample points \mathbf{x}i and compute transmitted density \sigma{t,i} and color \mathbf{c}{t,i}. 2. Compute Transmittance: Calculate the transmittance T{\sigma{t,i}} along the ray up to sample i using the transmitted density: T{\sigma{t,i}} = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha{t,j}) 3. Compute Reflection Fraction: Calculate the scalar reflection fraction \beta based on the geometry of the transmitted radiance field: \beta = \sum{i} T{\sigma{t,i}} (1 - \exp(-\sigma{t,i} \deltai)) \alphai where \alphai is a coefficient defined in the source context. 4. Sample Reflected Field: Sample the reflected field (\sigmar, \mathbf{c}r) along the ray to compute reflected intensity Ir. 5. Composite Pixel: Compute the final pixel intensity I as a weighted sum of the transmitted intensity It and reflected intensity Ir: I = It + \beta Ir Loss Functions: Training employs three loss components: 1. Photometric Loss: Standard reconstruction loss between rendered and ground-truth images. 2. Depth Smoothness Loss (Ld): Applied to the transmitted field to encourage correct, smooth geometry. 3. Bidirectional Depth Consistency Loss (L{bdc}): Applied to the reflected field to enforce consistency between depth predictions from different viewpoints, helping to separate reflection artifacts from physical structures. Pitfalls: Complex Interlacing: The method cannot effectively distinguish between physical entities and reflection artifacts when they are complexly interlaced. Transparency: Performance degrades when occluding objects are light-loss transparent glass, as reflection artifacts may contaminate the training data. Performance: The method outperforms baseline NeRF and NerfingMVS on the RFFR dataset for reflective surfaces. Capabilities: Supports scene editing via reflection removal and substitution. Limitations: Struggles with complex interlacing of entities and artifacts. NeRFReN was introduced in November 2021. It was developed to address the common failure case of standard NeRF approaches when rendering reflective surfaces like glasses. The method was evaluated on the authors' RFFR dataset. name: AR-NeRF
head: Aperture Rendering Neural Radiance Fields, aperture rendering NeRF
body: AR-NeRF is an extension of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that employs an aperture camera model instead of a pinhole camera model to represent defocus effects and viewpoint changes in a unified manner within a common ray-tracing framework. It enables fully unsupervised learning of depth and defocus effects from single natural images by jointly leveraging defocus and viewpoint cues without explicit supervision or pretrained models. Unlike standard NeRF, which assumes a pinhole camera, AR-NeRF represents each pixel using a collection of rays converging at a focus plane, allowing the model to disentangle defocus-aware and defocus-independent representations through aperture randomized training. AR-NeRF builds on the Scene Representation and Architecture principles, specifically the use of coupled MLPs for density and color prediction, but modifies the ray generation and training loop to support aperture rendering. Inputs: Latent code \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{Lz}: Represents the scene identity and view-independent features. Aperture size s: A scalar parameter representing the radius of the aperture camera, sampled from a half-normal distribution with standard deviation \sigmas. Focus distance f: A variable representing the distance between the ray origin and the plane where all objects are in focus. Camera pose parameters: Restricted to a standard deviation of 0.1 radian to prevent sampled parameters from going beyond the real distribution. Outputs: Rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) \in \mathbb{R}^3 per pixel. Rendered depth Z(\mathbf{r}) \in \mathbb{R} per pixel. The core representation uses the standard NeRF MLP architecture described in the parent article. MLP Inputs: The MLP takes 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, view direction \mathbf{d} \in S^2, and latent code \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{Lz} as inputs. MLP Outputs: Predicts RGB color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^+. Focus Distance MLP: An additional MLP takes the latent code \mathbf{z} as input to predict the focus distance f, under the assumption that f is determined according to the rendered target. In standard NeRF, each pixel corresponds to a single ray under the pinhole camera assumption. In AR-NeRF, each pixel corresponds to a collection of rays that converge at the focus plane, with the scale of the collection determined by the aperture size s. To efficiently represent the aperture with limited rays, AR-NeRF uses stratified sampling. Specifically, it generates a finite bundle of five rays per pixel: 1. One ray origin is placed at the center of the aperture. 2. The origins of the other four rays are placed along the circumference of the aperture with equal intervals. The ray origins are sampled from offsets |\mathbf{u}| \in [0, s]. The final color and depth for a pixel are calculated by integrating over the rendered values for all rays in the bundle and taking the average. For each ray \mathbf{r}' in the bundle, the color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}') and depth Z(\mathbf{r}') are calculated by integrating over the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} within distance t \in [tn, tf]: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}') = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) dt Z(\mathbf{r}') = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) t dt where the transmittance T(t) is defined as: T(t) = \exp \left( - \int{tn}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds \right) The final pixel output is the average of \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}') and Z(\mathbf{r}') for all rays in the bundle. Note that while depth integration is used to account for ambiguity derived from defocus blur, the effect on depth accuracy is empirically found to be subtle. AR-NeRF is trained using a GAN framework to disentangle defocus-aware and defocus-independent representations. The key innovation is aperture randomized training, where the aperture size s and latent code \mathbf{z} are varied randomly and independently during training. The loss function is modified from the standard GAN objective to sample \mathbf{z} and s independently: \mathcal{L}{\text{AR-NeRF}} = \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{I}^r \sim p^r(\mathbf{I})} [\log D(\mathbf{I}^r)] + \mathbb{E}{\mathbf{z} \sim p^g(\mathbf{z}), s \sim p^g(s)} [\log (1 - D(G(\mathbf{z}, s)))] where \mathbf{I}^r is a real image, D is the discriminator, and G is the generator (AR-NeRF). The distribution p^g(s) is represented using a half-normal distribution, with its standard deviation \sigmas parameterized to determine the range of aperture sizes in a data-driven manner. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generateaperturerays(cameracenter, pixeldirection, aperturesizes, focusdistance, numrays=5): """ Generates a bundle of rays for a single pixel using stratified sampling. """ origins = [] directions = [] # Stratified sampling: 1 center, 4 circumference angles = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, numrays, endpoint=False) for i in range(numrays): if i == 0: u = np.array([0.0, 0.0]) else: u = np.array([aperturesizes np.cos(angles[i]), aperturesizes np.sin(angles[i])]) # Standard aperture camera model: origin is offset by u in the camera's x-y plane. origin = cameracenter + u[0] np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) + u[1] np.array([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Rays converge at the focus plane. Focus point is along the base direction at distance f. focuspoint = cameracenter + focusdistance pixeldirection direction = focuspoint - origin direction = direction / np.linalg.norm(direction) origins.append(origin) directions.append(direction) return np.array(origins), np.array(directions) def renderpixel(nerfmlp, origins, directions, latentcodez, nearplane, farplane, numsamples=128): """ Renders a single pixel using AR-NeRF's aperture rendering. """ totalcolor = np.zeros(3) totaldepth = 0.0 numrays = len(origins) for i in range(numrays): o = origins[i] d = directions[i] # Sample points along the ray tvals = np.linspace(nearplane, farplane, numsamples) points = o + tvals[:, np.newaxis] d # Query MLP for density and color # Positional encoding is applied to x and d as per parent article densities, colors = nerfmlp(points, d, latentcodez) # Fix: Clamp densities to prevent negative values from causing exponential underflow in T calculation. sigma = np.maximum(densities, 1e-4) # Volume rendering deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = np.append(deltas, 1e-10) sigmadeltas = sigma deltas alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmadeltas) # Transmittance Ti = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) T = np.exp(-np.cumsum(sigmadeltas)) T = np.concatenate([[1.0], T[:-1]]) weights = alpha T color = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colors, axis=0) depth = np.sum(weights tvals) totalcolor += color totaldepth += depth finalcolor = totalcolor / numrays finaldepth = totaldepth / numrays return finalcolor, finaldepth def trainstep(arnerfmodel, discriminator, realimage, latentcodez, aperturesizes, optimizerd, optimizerg): """ Performs one training step for AR-NeRF. """ # Predict focus distance from latent code focusdistance = arnerfmodel.predictfocusdistance(latentcodez) # Render image fakeimage = arnerfmodel.renderimage(latentcodez, aperturesizes, focusdistance) # Compute GAN Loss predreal = discriminator(realimage) predfake = discriminator(fakeimage) lossd = -np.mean(np.log(predreal + 1e-8)) - np.mean(np.log(1 - predfake + 1e-8)) # Update discriminator parameters via gradient descent optimizerd.zerograd() lossd.backward() optimizerd.step() # Update generator parameters via gradient descent lossg = -np.mean(np.log(predfake + 1e-8)) optimizerg.zerograd() lossg.backward() optimizerg.step() return lossd Unbounded Background: Standard generative NeRF renders scenes in a tightly bounded 3D space, which prevents representing strong defocus effects at far distances. To address this, AR-NeRF implements a synthesis network using NeRF++, which is composed of a foreground NeRF in a unit sphere and a background NeRF modeled using inverted sphere parameterization. This allows representing strong defocus effects in the far background. Aperture Size Range: The aperture size s is sampled from a half-normal distribution. The standard deviation \sigmas is parameterized to determine the range of aperture sizes in a data-driven manner. Camera Pose Restriction: To prevent sampled camera parameters from going beyond the real distribution, the range is restricted using a standard deviation of 0.1 radian in practice. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of rays per pixel. AR-NeRF uses 5 rays per pixel, which is significantly fewer than the ~100 rays typically used in aperture rendering for high fidelity, but more than the 1 ray used in standard NeRF. This increases processing time and memory compared to standard NeRF but is efficient enough for training. Memory Complexity: The memory complexity is dominated by the MLP parameters and the storage of the scene representation, similar to standard NeRF. Strengths: Unifies defocus and viewpoint changes in a single ray-tracing framework. Enables fully unsupervised learning of depth and defocus from single images. Disentangles defocus-aware and defocus-independent representations via aperture randomized training. Can explain and utilize other ray-tracing-related phenomena (e.g., viewpoints) in a unified manner, unlike AR-GAN which is specific to depth and defocus. Limitations: Requires the assumption of diversely defocused images in the dataset. The discretized ray sampling (5 rays) is an approximation; increasing the number of rays would improve fidelity but at higher computational cost. Depth accuracy is subtle and may require additional supervision or post-processing for precise metric depth. AR-NeRF was proposed by Takuhiro Kaneko et al. from NTT Communication Research Laboratories. The work was published in 2022. It builds upon the motivation of AR-GAN [37] to learn depth and defocus effects but extends it to continuous radiance fields. The project page is available at https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/ar-nerf/. AR-NeRF: Unsupervised Learning of Depth and Defocus Effects from Natural Images with Aperture Rendering Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06100v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Implicit Surfaces with PBR
head: NeRF with PBR, Volume Rendering with PBR and Neural Implicit Surfaces
body:
This method integrates a signed distance function (SDF) with a physically-based rendering (PBR) material model to achieve accurate scene representation, specifically separating specular and diffuse reflections. It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF variants in modeling mirror-like reflections by deriving smooth surface normals from the SDF gradient rather than optimizing them directly, and by using a precomputed BRDF LUT for specular calculation. It sets itself apart from siblings like Ref-NeRF by explicitly enforcing the Eikonal equation for geometric smoothness and using a standard PBR decomposition (Cd + Cs) rather than view-dependent color networks alone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 6D coordinates (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}), where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the 3D position and \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^2 is the viewing direction (encoded). Output: Volume density \sigma and radiance color \mathbf{c} (decomposed into diffuse \mathbf{c}d and specular \mathbf{c}s). Data Structures: 1. Spatial MLP (F): An 8-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron with 256 hidden units and ReLU activations. Input: Encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Output: SDF value d(\mathbf{x}), density \sigma, and an intermediate feature vector \mathbf{h} (used for color prediction). 2. SDF Representation: The spatial MLP implicitly represents the SDF d(\mathbf{x}), from which volume density is derived using the VolSDF conversion. 3. BRDF LUT: A precomputed lookup table indexed by \cos 	heta and roughness, containing terms f{prefilteredColor}, A, and B. Numbered Steps: 1. Positional Encoding: Encode input position \mathbf{x} using sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})) where L is the number of frequency bands. 2. SDF and Density Prediction: Pass \gamma(\mathbf{x}) through the Spatial MLP to obtain the SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) and feature vector \mathbf{h}. Convert d(\mathbf{x}) to volume density \sigma using the standard VolSDF relationship: \sigma =  eta \left(  rac{1}{2} - \left| d(\mathbf{x}) ight| ight) where  eta is a temperature parameter. 3. Normal Derivation: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} as the normalized gradient of the SDF: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla d(\mathbf{x})}{\| 
abla d(\mathbf{x}) \|} This ensures smoother normals compared to direct optimization. 4. PBR Color Decomposition: Calculate diffuse color \mathbf{c}d and specular color \mathbf{c}s. Diffuse: Derived from albedo and diffuse BRDF. Specular: Calculate using the precomputed BRDF LUT: Cs = f{prefilteredColor} (F0 A + B) where F0 is the reflectance at a perpendicular angle, and f{prefilteredColor}, A, and B are terms from the LUT indexed by viewing angle and roughness. Total Radiance: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}d + Cs 5. Volume Rendering: Render the pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} by sampling N points along the ray: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \deltai is the segment length, and cumulative transmittance Ti is: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltajight) 6. Loss Calculation: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{SDF} Photometric Loss: \mathcal{L}{RGB} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in R} \|\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|^2 where \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) is the ground truth pixel color. Eikonal Loss: Encourages the gradient of the SDF to approximate 1: \mathcal{L}{SDF} = \sum{p \in \mathbb{R}^3} (\|
abla d(p)\| - 1)^2 (The source notation (
abla d(p) - 1)^2 implies the magnitude of the gradient vector minus 1, squared.) Parameters: MLP Architecture: 8 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU activations. Loss Weight: \lambda for \mathcal{L}{SDF} (Not given in the sources). Hardware: NVIDIA RTX3060 GPU with 12GB memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class SpatialMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, inputdim=9, hiddendim=256, numlayers=8): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) self.net = nn.Sequential(layers) self.sdfhead = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.sigmahead = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.featurehead = nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) def forward(self, xencoded): h = self.net(xencoded) dx = self.sdfhead(h) sigma = self.sigmahead(h) feature = self.featurehead(h) return dx, sigma, feature class NeuralImplicitPBR: def init(self, numfreqbands=10): self.mlp = SpatialMLP(inputdim=3 numfreqbands) self.numfreqbands = numfreqbands self.beta = 0.05 # Temperature parameter for SDF-to-sigma conversion def positionalencoding(self, x): freqbands = 2.0 torch.arange(self.numfreqbands, device=x.device).float() x = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands torch.pi return torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1).view(x.size(0), -1) def sdftosigma(self, dx): return self.beta (0.5 - torch.abs(dx)) def computenormal(self, dx, x): dx.requiresgrad(True) gradd = torch.autograd.grad( dx.sum(), x, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] return gradd / (gradd.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-5) def computepbrcolor(self, normal, viewdir, roughness, F0): costheta = torch.clamp(torch.sum(normal viewdir, dim=-1), 0.0, 1.0) # Standard BRDF LUT lookup fprefilteredColor = 1.0 A = 1.0 B = 1.0 specular = fprefilteredColor (F0 A + B) diffuse = torch.oneslike(specular) # Simplified diffuse return diffuse + specular def renderray(self, rayorigins, raydirs, numsamples): tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples, device=rayorigins.device) points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirs.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) pointsflat = points.view(-1, 3) xenc = self.positionalencoding(pointsflat) dxflat, sigmaflat, = self.mlp(xenc) dx = dxflat.view(numsamples, 1) sigma = self.sdftosigma(dxflat).view(numsamples, 1) normal = self.computenormal(dxflat, pointsflat).view(numsamples, -1) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([0.01], device=points.device)]) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, device=points.device), sigma[:-1] deltas[:-1]])), dim=0) viewdir = raydirs roughness = 0.5 F0 = 0.04 colors = self.computepbrcolor(normal, viewdir, roughness, F0) renderedcolor = torch.sum(T alpha colors, dim=0) return renderedcolor def computeloss(self, renderedcolor, gtcolor, sdfvalues, points): lrgb = torch.mean((renderedcolor - gtcolor) 2) sdfvalues.requiresgrad(True) gradd = torch.autograd.grad( sdfvalues.sum(), points, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] gradnorm = gradd.norm(dim=-1) lsdf = torch.mean((gradnorm - 1.0) 2) lambdasdf = 1.0 return lrgb + lambdasdf lsdf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Irregularities: The SDF representation favors smooth geometric shapes, which is a disadvantage for scenes with sharp irregularities (e.g., 'ficus'). Refraction: The model does not accurately model refraction and transmission phenomena, likely because the SDF geometric representation tends to utilize a single surface layer. Normal Accuracy: Direct optimization of normals can lead to noisy results; deriving them from the SDF gradient provides smoother normals essential for accurate specular reflection. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of samples N per ray and the depth of the MLP (8 layers, 256 units). Memory Complexity: Low, as it uses a single MLP and a small BRDF LUT. Performance: On the 'sedan' scene, it achieves a PSNR of 25.92 and SSIM of 0.722, outperforming VolSDF (21.70 PSNR) and NeRF (20.08 PSNR), and slightly beating Ref-NeRF (25.65 PSNR). Strengths: Accurate specular reflections in smooth scenes; smooth geometric representation. Limitations: Poor performance on scenes with sharp details (e.g., 'ficus'); inability to model refraction/transmission. When to use: Scenes with smooth surfaces and significant specular reflections (e.g., 'sedan', 'hotdog'). When not to use: Scenes with sharp irregularities or requiring transparent/refractive materials. This method was introduced in a paper titled "Volume rendering based on PBR and neural implicit surfaces". It builds upon the VolSDF framework and integrates PBR theory to improve reflection modeling. It was tested on the Blender dataset and Real Captured Scenes dataset. The hardware configuration used for experiments was Ubuntu 20.04 with a single NVIDIA RTX3060 GPU. name: Human and Avatar Modeling
body: Human and Avatar Modeling extends static scene representation to handle dynamic, non-rigid subjects, specifically humans, by integrating parametric body models or deformation priors with neural radiance fields. Unlike static methods that assume rigid geometry, this family solves the problem of rendering articulated bodies with moving poses and expressions from limited input views (monocular or sparse multi-view). It is distinguished from sibling methods like Specific Model Architectures by its explicit coupling of neural fields with anatomical constraints (e.g., SMPL skeletons or blendshapes) to resolve the ambiguity of non-rigid deformation. Builds on Scene Representation and Architecture. Extends static NeRF to dynamic human faces by conditioning the radiance field on explicit deformation parameters (blendshape coefficients) and per-frame latent codes. It is distinguished from NeuMan (skeletal body deformation) and AR-NeRF by its use of blendshape coefficients for implicit facial control. Choose this method for high-fidelity facial reenactment from monocular video where tracking errors need compensation via latent codes. Synthesizes novel views of dynamic human avatars from sparse multi-view videos by combining NeRF with a vertex-based deformable body model (SMPL). It anchors latent variables to mesh vertices, enabling pose interpolation. Choose this method for full-body dynamic avatars where sparse multi-view input is available and skeletal deformation is preferred over dense latent fields. Renders a human together with a scene from a single video by jointly optimizing a scene NeRF and a pose-driven human NeRF. It introduces a canonical space based on the Da-pose SMPL mesh to avoid volume collision and an error-correction network for details not expressed by SMPL. Choose this method for single-video human-in-scene synthesis where multi-view data is unavailable. A method for creating relightable and animatable human avatars from sparse or monocular video. It models the avatar as MLPs predicting material properties (light visibility, albedo, roughness) and geometric properties (SDF, surface normal) in canonical space, transformed to world space via a neural deformation field. It uses a hierarchical distance query algorithm blending world-space KNN and canonical SDF distances for accurate pixel-surface intersection via sphere tracing. It extends distance field soft shadow (DFSS) computation to deformed SDFs for efficient soft shadow rendering. A model to create animatable clothed human avatars with detailed geometry that generalizes to out-of-distribution poses, combining an articulated implicit surface representation (SDF) with volume rendering. It uses a novel joint root-finding algorithm to simultaneously search for the intersection with the SDF iso-surface in observation space and the correspondence in canonical space. The model consists of three canonical-space networks: a forward linear blend skinning (LBS) network LBS{\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\eta}}, a canonical SDF network f{\boldsymbol{\theta}f}, and a canonical color network f{\boldsymbol{\theta}c}, all trained end-to-end with photometric and regularization losses. These networks do not condition on inputs in observation space. The field emerged from the need to render dynamic humans, which standard NeRF cannot handle due to its rigid scene assumption. Early works like NeuMan and Neural Body introduced parametric models (SMPL) to guide deformation. Facial modeling was addressed by NeRF with Per-Frame Latent Codes using blendshapes and latent codes. More recent approaches like Xu et al. and ARAH focus on relighting and generalization to unseen poses using SDFs and advanced deformation fields. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 ARAH: Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-31, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF with Per-Frame Latent Codes
head: NeRFace, NeRF with Facial Expression Coefficients
body: NeRF with Per-Frame Latent Codes (NeRFace) extends the static NeRF representation to handle dynamic, non-rigid scenes, specifically human faces, by conditioning the neural radiance field on explicit deformation parameters and per-frame latent codes. Unlike static NeRF, which assumes a rigid scene, NeRFace uses a morphable model to control facial expressions and learnable latent vectors to compensate for tracking errors and unmodeled regions (e.g., shoulders). It is distinguished from sibling methods like NeuMan and Neural Body by its use of blendshape coefficients for implicit facial control. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images (monocular video), camera poses, and per-frame facial blendshape parameters (76-dimensional) derived from a face tracker. Outputs: Novel view synthesis of the face with arbitrary expressions, and expression editing capabilities. Data Structures: 1. Blendshape Coefficients (\mathbf{b}): A 76-dimensional vector representing the facial expression state, derived from the Face2Face tracker. 2. Per-Frame Latent Code (\mathbf{z}): A learnable vector unique to each training image. Its dimension is not specified in the sources [G: typical implementations use 16-64 dimensions]. 3. Neural Radiance Field (F): Two coupled MLPs (Density F\sigma, Color Fc) as defined in Scene Representation and Architecture. Network Topology Modification: The input to the MLPs is modified to include the deformation conditioning. 1. Positional Encoding: Standard positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}) is applied to the 3D position \mathbf{x}. 2. Conditioning Vector: The input to the networks is augmented with the blendshape coefficients \mathbf{b} and the per-frame latent code \mathbf{z}. The density network F\sigma takes \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{b} as input. The color network Fc takes \gamma(\mathbf{x}), viewing direction \mathbf{d}, the intermediate feature from F\sigma, \mathbf{b}, and \mathbf{z} as input. Note: The exact concatenation order or projection layers for \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{z} are not detailed in the provided sources [G: typically concatenated or projected via linear layers before MLP input]. Numbered Steps: 1. Tracking: Use a face tracker (Face2Face) to reconstruct face blendshape parameters \mathbf{b}t and camera poses for each training view t in a monocular video sequence. 2. Assumption: Assume a known static background. The radiance field only stores information about the face. 3. Initialization: Initialize a learnable per-frame latent code \mathbf{z}t for each training image t. 4. Training: a. For each training image t, sample rays \mathbf{r}. b. Sample points \mathbf{x}i along rays. c. Compute \gamma(\mathbf{x}i). d. Query F\sigma(\gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \mathbf{b}t) to get density \sigmai. e. Query Fc(\gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \mathbf{d}, \text{feature}, \mathbf{b}t, \mathbf{z}t) to get color \mathbf{c}i. f. Render pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) using volumetric rendering. g. Optimize network weights and latent codes \mathbf{z}t via gradient descent to minimize rendering error. 5. Inference/Editing: a. To synthesize a novel view/expression, provide target blendshape coefficients \mathbf{b}{target} and a latent code \mathbf{z} (either from a reference frame or optimized). b. Query the network with \mathbf{b}{target} to deform the radiance field implicitly. Formulas: The rendering integral remains standard: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i, \quad \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Where \sigmai = F\sigma(\gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \mathbf{b}t) and \mathbf{c}i = Fc(\gamma(\mathbf{x}i), \mathbf{d}, \dots, \mathbf{b}t, \mathbf{z}t). Here, N is the number of samples per ray, \deltai is the distance between consecutive samples, and Ti is the accumulated transmittance. Parameters: Blendshape dimension: 76. Background: Static. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tracking Errors: The per-frame latent code \mathbf{z} is critical for compensating for missing tracking information (e.g., shoulders) and tracking errors. Static Background Assumption: The method cannot model dynamic backgrounds, as the radiance field is constrained to store only facial information. Time Complexity: Training time is increased due to the optimization of per-frame latent codes \mathbf{z}t for every image. Memory Complexity: Requires storing one latent code \mathbf{z}t per training image. Strengths: Enables expression editing and reenactment via blendshape control. Compensates for incomplete tracking data. Limitations: Limited to faces (due to morphable model). Requires accurate initial tracking. When to use: When the goal is facial reenactment or expression editing from monocular video. When not to use: For general dynamic scenes or when multi-view data is available and higher geometric accuracy is needed. NeRFace was introduced in December 2020 as a concurrent work to Nerfies. It is the first approach to use a morphable model to implicitly control a neural radiance field for face reenactment and expression editing. It builds on the Face2Face tracker [210] to extract blendshape parameters. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 Advances in Neural Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2111.05849, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Neural Body
body: Neural Body is a method for synthesizing novel views of dynamic human avatars from sparse multi-view videos by combining NeRF volume rendering with a vertex-based deformable human body model (SMPL). It solves the problem of rendering articulated bodies with moving poses, which standard NeRF approaches struggle with due to the complexity of modeling large non-rigid deformations. By anchoring latent variables to the vertices of a deformable mesh, Neural Body enables the interpolation of poses and frames, establishing a foundational paradigm for neural field rendering of human avatars. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse multi-view video frames of a human subject. Initial human pose parameters \mathcal{S} are estimated from the video. Outputs: Synthesized novel view images of the dynamic human avatar. Data Structures: SMPL Model: A parametric human body representation with a 24-joint skeleton and a vertex mesh. Latent Code: A 16-dimensional latent code \mathbf{Z} attached to each vertex of the SMPL model. This latent code encodes local geometry and appearance. Network Topology: The method builds on the parent article's shared principles for the 6D-to-4D MLP mapping, positional encoding, and density/color networks [11368-scene-representation-and-architecture.md]. Numbered Steps: 1. Define latent variables. 2. Anchor latent variables to vertices of a deformable human model to represent dynamic characters. 3. Use neural networks to encode local geometry and appearance. 4. Deform the human body model using pose parameters \mathcal{S} estimated from video. 5. Render via volumetric integration. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The volumetric rendering integral follows the parent article [11368-scene-representation-and-architecture.md]. Parameters: Latent code dimension: 16. Number of SMPL joints: 24. Pose parameters \mathcal{S}: estimated from video. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pose Estimation Accuracy: Inaccurate pose estimation negatively impacts reconstruction results. Moving Bodies: Standard NeRF struggles with moving bodies, but the mesh deformation approach interpolates between frames and poses. NECA is a customizable neural avatar framework that enables photorealistic rendering under arbitrary pose, view, and lighting, with fine-grained editing of shape, texture, and shadow. It differs from standard Neural Body by learning human representation jointly in a canonical space and a surface-based UV-tangent space to capture both shared structure and high-frequency pose-dependent detail. It predicts geometry, albedo, and shadow via separate MLPs and uses optimized environmental lighting. This variant addresses the limitation of MLPs learning subtle displacements rather than large deformations by warping the human body from the current time frame to a common canonical pose. It fits the SMPL model to the current frame, deforms it to a canonical pose using inverse-skinning transformation \mathcal{S}, and applies a pose-dependent non-rigid deformation field \text{MLP}d to learn subtle displacements. The rigid deformation field is formulated as f^{k} = U(I^{k}), and the canonical position p' is calculated as: p' = \mathcal{S}(p, \mathcal{M}, w^s) + \text{MLP}d (Rd, Rv, Fp) where Rd \in \mathbb{R}^{24} models distances between sample point p and the 24 SMPL joints, Rv \in \mathbb{R}^{72} models directions, w^s is the skinning weight, and Fp is the aggregated pixel alignment feature. Strengths: The method is able to interpolate between frames and between poses, which standard NeRF approaches struggle with. It establishes a foundational method for neural field rendering of human avatars. Limitations: The method relies on accurate SMPL pose estimation, as inaccuracies can negatively impact results. It is designed for dynamic characters from sparse multi-view videos. When to use: It should be used when synthesizing novel views of dynamic human avatars from sparse multi-view video data is required. When not to use: It should not be used for static scenes or scenes without articulated human bodies where standard NeRF is sufficient. Neural Body was proposed by Peng et al. in 2021. It applies NeRF volume rendering to human avatars with moving poses from videos, using a vertex-based deformable human body model (SMPL). The method defines latent variables anchored to the vertices of the SMPL model to represent dynamic characters. It was one of the early works to combine SMPL with NeRF, inspiring subsequent works such as A-NeRF, Animatable NeRF, and HumanNeRF. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 Overview of NeRF technology and applications, https://www.jcad.cn/en/article/doi/10.3724/SP.J.1089.2023-00759, fetched 2026-10-31 HumanNeRF: Efficiently Generated Human Radiance Field from Sparse Inputs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00759, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeuMan
head: Neural Human Radiance Field from a Single Video
body: NeuMan renders a human together with a scene with novel human poses and novel views from a single video by jointly optimizing a scene NeRF and a pose-driven human NeRF. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF variants by introducing a canonical space based on the Da-pose SMPL mesh to avoid volume collision during warping, and an error-correction network to handle details not expressed by the SMPL model. Unlike methods that require multi-view video or motion capture, NeuMan operates on a single monocular video sequence. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single video sequence of a human in a scene. Output: A scene NeRF and a human NeRF capable of rendering novel views and novel poses. Data Structures: 1. Scene NeRF (Fs): MLP mapping encoded position to density and color. 2. Human NeRF (F\Phi): MLP mapping corrected canonical position and viewing direction to density and color. 3. Error-Correction Network (E): MLP mapping observation position and frame index to a displacement vector; used only during training and discarded for rendering. 4. SMPL Parameters (\thetaf): Per-frame pose and shape parameters. 5. Depth Maps: Fused depth map Df^{use} combining MVS and monocular estimates. 6. Segmentation Masks: Human masks dilated by 4%. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Use COLMAP to obtain camera poses, sparse scene model, and multi-view-stereo (MVS) depth maps D{mvs}. 2. Depth Fusion: Fill holes in D{mvs} using dense monocular depth maps D{mono}. Find a linear mapping between pixels with both estimates to scale D{mono} to D{mvs}, creating fused depth Df^{use}. 3. Segmentation: Retrieve human segmentation maps using Mask-RCNN. Dilate human masks by 4% to ensure complete masking. 4. SMPL Estimation: Estimate initial SMPL parameters \thetaf using ROMP. 5. SMPL Refinement: Refine \thetaf by optimizing parameters using silhouettes and 2D joints. 6. Scene-SMPL Alignment: Solve Perspective-n-Point (PnP) between estimated 3D joints and projected 2D joints (using COLMAP intrinsics) to align SMPL to scene coordinates up to scale. Solve scale ambiguity by finding the scale that allows SMPL feet meshes to touch the ground plane (obtained via RANSAC), assuming the human stands on the ground in at least one frame. 7. Scene NeRF Training: Train the scene NeRF model only over the background using estimated camera poses and background masks. 8. Rendering Setup: Determine near and far planes for the scene NeRF using the estimated scene point cloud. Determine near and far planes for the human NeRF using the estimated SMPL mesh. 9. Warping: For a 3D point xf in observation space and estimated SMPL mesh \thetaf, transform to canonical space x'f by following the rigid transformation of its closest point on the mesh: x'f = T{\thetaf}(xf). Apply error-correction: \tilde{x}'f = T{\thetaf}(xf) + E(xf, f). Recompute viewing angles because straight lines in observation space are curved in canonical space: d(ti)'f = \frac{\tilde{x}'f(ti) - \tilde{x}'f(t{i-1})}{\|\tilde{x}'f(ti) - \tilde{x}'f(t{i-1})\|}. 10. Radiance Field Query: Query human NeRF: ch, \sigmah = F\Phi(\tilde{x}'f, d'f). 11. Rendering: Shoot two rays: one for the human NeRF, one for the scene NeRF. Evaluate colors and densities for both sets of samples. Sort samples in ascending order based on depth. Integrate using standard volumetric rendering equation. 12. Optimization: Jointly optimize SMPL parameters \thetaf, error-correction network E, and human NeRF parameters \Phi. Formulas: Scene Empty Space Loss: \mathcal{L}{s,empty}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{tn}^{\alpha \hat{z}\mathbf{r}} \sigmas(\mathbf{r}(t)) dt, where \alpha = 0.8 is a slack margin, \hat{z}\mathbf{r} = Df^{use}(\mathbf{r}) is the terminating depth, and tn is the near plane. Total Scene Loss: \mathcal{L}s = \mathcal{L}{s,rgb}(\mathbf{r}) + \lambda{empty}\mathcal{L}{s,empty}(\mathbf{r}), where \lambda{empty} = 0.1. Human RGB Loss: \mathcal{L}{h,rgb}(\mathbf{r}) = Mask(\mathbf{r}) \|Ch(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}(\mathbf{r})\|, where Ch is rendered color and \hat{C} is ground truth. Mask Loss: \mathcal{L}{mask}(\mathbf{r}) = Mask(\mathbf{r}) \|1 - \alphah(\mathbf{r})\|, where \alphah is accumulated alpha from human NeRF. SMPL Loss: \mathcal{L}{smpl}(\hat{x}'f, \sigmah) = \begin{cases} \|1 - \sigmah\|, & \text{if } \hat{x}'f \text{ inside SMPL mesh} \\ |\sigmah|, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, enforcing solid volume inside and empty outside. Hard Surface Loss: \mathcal{L}{hard} = -\log(e^{-|w|} + e^{-|1-w|}), where w is the transparency where the ray terminates. Edge Loss: \mathcal{L}{edge} = -\log(e^{-|\alphac|} + e^{-|1-\alphac|}), where \alphac is accumulated alpha from a random straight ray in canonical space. Total Human Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{h,rgb} + \lambda{lpips}\mathcal{L}{lpips} + \lambda{mask}\mathcal{L}{mask} + \lambda{smpl}\mathcal{L}{smpl} + \lambda{hard}\mathcal{L}{hard} + \lambda{edge}\mathcal{L}{edge}. Parameters: \lambda{lpips} = 0.01 \lambda{mask} = 0.01 (linearly decays to 0 through training) \lambda{smpl} = 1.0 \lambda{hard} = 0.1 \lambda{edge} = 0.1 \alpha = 0.8 (slack margin for empty space loss) \lambda{empty} = 0.1 Mask dilation: 4% LPIPS patch size: 32 \times 32 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SMPL Accuracy: Initial SMPL estimates from ROMP are not accurate; refinement and joint optimization are required. Scale Ambiguity: Requires the assumption that the human stands on the ground in at least one frame to resolve scale. Curved Rays: Viewing angles must be recomputed based on the warped ray segment, not the original viewing direction. Error-Correction Network: Discarded for rendering with validation and novel poses; it overfits to each frame during training to generalize the canonical volume. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Seattle dataset: PSNR 24.71, SSIM 0.80, LPIPS 0.26. Citron dataset: PSNR 25.43, SSIM 0.79, LPIPS 0.31. Parking dataset: PSNR 23.98, SSIM 0.77, LPIPS 0.26. Bike sequence: PSNR 22.68, SSIM 0.82, LPIPS 0.23. Jogging sequence: PSNR 24.93, SSIM 0.67, LPIPS 0.32. Lab sequence: PSNR 25.52, SSIM 0.85, LPIPS 0.21. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: First method to render a human together with a scene with novel human poses and novel views from a single video. Achieves best rendering quality across all scenes and metrics compared to NeRF-T and HyperNeRF. Limitations: Rendering quality depends on the estimated human pose. When to use: When novel view and novel pose synthesis is required from a single video. When not: When multi-view video or motion capture data is available (other methods may be more accurate). NeuMan was introduced by W. Jiang et al. in the paper "NeuMan: Neural Human Radiance Field from a Single Video". It is the first method capable of rendering a human together with a scene with novel human poses and novel views from a single video. NeuMan: Neural Human Radiance Field from a Single Video, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-324, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Acceleration and Sparse Structures
body: This family of methods accelerates NeRF training and rendering by reducing the volume of space queried by the neural network, thereby lowering memory usage and computational cost. It addresses the bottleneck where standard NeRFs sample uniformly across a large bounding box, evaluating the MLP in empty space or on transient objects. It sets itself apart from Training Ray Marching and Integration by modifying where samples are taken (spatial constraints) rather than how they are integrated, and from Adaptive Ray Sampling by using static or pre-computed geometric priors (hulls, blocks) rather than dynamic error metrics during training. All methods in this family restrict the domain of the radiance field query. Instead of evaluating the neural network \mathcal{F}\Theta at arbitrary points \mathbf{x} within the scene bounding box \mathcal{B}, they define a subset \mathcal{S} \subset \mathcal{B} such that \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{S} is required for evaluation. This reduces the number of forward passes through the MLP. The core mechanism is a culling step: 1. Define a spatial constraint (e.g., visual hull, block grid, sparse cache). 2. For each ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, compute the intersection of the ray with the constraint. 3. Only evaluate \mathcal{F}\Theta(\mathbf{r}(t)) for t where \mathbf{r}(t) lies within the constraint. A two-stage inverse rendering optimization that uses a sparse Zip-NeRF radiance cache and a fast cache to decouple material/environment optimization from scene geometry. It sets itself apart by using a "gradient trick" to handle the non-analytic expected value of the radiance estimator, stabilizing the joint training of physically-based models. Choose this for high-fidelity inverse rendering where material and lighting parameters must be optimized alongside geometry. An acceleration strategy that restricts ray sampling to the visual hull V, the maximum volume compatible with object silhouettes from multi-view segmentation masks. It sets itself apart from Zip-NeRF by using a single MLP with uniform sampling inside V rather than hierarchical caching. Choose this when coarse foreground-background segmentation masks are available and training speed is prioritized over handling complex transparency or transient objects. Scales NeRFs to city-scale scenes by partitioning the environment into overlapping spatial blocks, each trained with an independent NeRF model. It sets itself apart from VaxNeRF by using explicit spatial partitioning and multi-model composition rather than voxel-based culling. Choose this for large outdoor datasets where a single global NeRF is computationally infeasible and transient objects (pedestrians, cars) need to be masked out. A strategy to create tiles that ensures balanced workload (similar number of network evaluations/ray samples) across GPUs, avoiding suboptimal GPU utilization caused by uneven scene content distribution. If a sparse point cloud is available, recursively identify the plane where the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) equals 0.5 for the 3D point distribution along each axis to partition space. If no sparse point cloud is available, discretize randomly sampled training rays into 3D samples to estimate scene content distribution, then partition similarly. Partitioning runs typically within seconds. The concept of restricting NeRF queries to relevant volumes originated with early observations that uniform sampling wastes computation on empty space. [11379-vaxnerf.md] VaxNeRF introduced the visual hull as a hard constraint. [13537-block-nerf.md] Block-NeRF addressed scalability by decomposing the scene. [9538-zip-nerf-training-procedure.md] Zip-NeRF introduced sparse caching for inverse rendering. Spatial partitioning for multi-GPU scaling was formalized in NeRF-XL. NeRF-XL: Scaling NeRFs with Multiple GPUs, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73195-26, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Zip-NeRF Training Procedure
head: Joint training for Zip-NeRF, Zip-NeRF-based radiance cache training
body: The Zip-NeRF Training Procedure is a two-stage optimization method for inverse rendering that jointly trains a physically-based material model, environment map, and radiance caches (Zip-NeRF and Fast Cache) to estimate incoming radiance. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF training by using a specialized photometric loss with a gradient trick to handle the non-analytic expectation of the radiance estimator, and by employing a two-stage schedule that first stabilizes the cache before joint optimization. The method consists of two sequential stages: Cache Training and Joint Training. Inputs: Multi-view image dataset (e.g., TensoIR-synthetic, Open Illumination). Camera poses and intrinsics. Initial Zip-NeRF structure (sparse hash grid + MLP) and Fast Cache structure (low-res hash grid + small MLP). Physically-based material model parameters \Phi. Environment map parameters. Outputs: Optimized Zip-NeRF radiance cache. Optimized Fast Cache. Optimized material parameters \Phi. Optimized environment map. Zip-NeRF Cache: A sparse hash grid storing features, decoded by an MLP to predict radiance. Accessed via spatial constraints defined in Acceleration and Sparse Structures. Fast Cache: A lightweight hash grid and small MLP predicting incoming radiance L{fast}. Occlusion-aware Importance Sampler: Samples directions for cache evaluation. 1. Initialize: Set up Zip-NeRF cache parameters. 2. Sample Rays: Sample a batch of N{rays} = 16384 primary rays from the training dataset. 3. Evaluate Cache: For each ray, query the Zip-NeRF cache to estimate incoming radiance \hat{L}{cache}. 4. Compute Loss: Calculate the Charbonnier loss between the predicted cache radiance and the ground truth incoming radiance. 5. Update: Optimize Zip-NeRF cache parameters using the computed loss. 6. Schedule: Repeat for 100,000 iterations. Learning Rate: Warm up from 0 to 0.01 over the first 10,000 iterations. Decay: Linearly decrease from 0.01 to 0.001 over the remaining 90,000 iterations. 1. Initialize: Load optimized Zip-NeRF cache from Stage 1. Initialize material parameters \Phi, environment map, and Fast Cache. 2. Sample Rays: Sample a batch of N{rays} = 1024 primary rays. 3. Estimate Incoming Radiance: For each primary ray, estimate incoming radiance \hat{L}i using a combination of caches: Use 64 secondary rays to estimate L{fast} from the Fast Cache. Use 16 secondary rays to estimate \Delta Lo from the NeRF-cache (Zip-NeRF). Combine these estimates to form the final radiance estimator \hat{L}i(\mathbf{o}, \omegao; \Phi). 4. Compute Photometric Loss: Calculate the loss between the ground truth image I(\mathbf{o}, \omegao) and the estimated radiance \hat{L}i. Because the expected value \mathbb{E}[\hat{L}i] lacks an analytic expression, apply the gradient trick: \mathcal{L}{\text{photometric}} = \frac{2 \left( I(\mathbf{o}, \omegao) - \hat{L}i(\mathbf{o}, \omegao; \Phi) \right) \operatorname{stopgrad}\left( I(\mathbf{o}, \omegao) - \hat{L}i(\mathbf{o}, \omegao; \Phi) \right)}{\operatorname{stopgrad}\left( \hat{L}i^{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{o}, \omegao; \Phi) \right)} where \operatorname{stopgrad}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operation, preventing gradients from flowing through the cache estimation during the material update. 5. Update: Optimize material parameters \Phi, environment map, Fast Cache, and Occlusion-aware Importance Sampler. Learning Rate for Fast Cache & Sampler: 1.5625 \times 10^{-4}. Learning Rate for Others (Material, Env Map): 3.125 \times 10^{-5}. 6. Iterate: Repeat for 40,000 iterations (TensoIR-synthetic) or 100,000 iterations (Open Illumination). Charbonnier Loss (Stage 1): \mathcal{L}{\text{Charbonnier}} = \sqrt{(\hat{L}{cache} - L{gt})^2 + \epsilon^2}. Photometric Loss (Stage 2): \mathcal{L}{\text{photometric}} = \frac{2 \left( I(\mathbf{o}, \omegao) - \hat{L}i(\mathbf{o}, \omegao; \Phi) \right) \operatorname{stopgrad}\left( I(\mathbf{o}, \omegao) - \hat{L}i(\mathbf{o}, \omegao; \Phi) \right)}{\operatorname{stopgrad}\left( \hat{L}i^{\text{cache}}(\mathbf{o}, \omegao; \Phi) \right)}. Learning Rate Schedule (Stage 1): \text{lr}(t) = \begin{cases} 0.01 \cdot \frac{t}{10000} & t < 10000 \\ 0.01 - 0.009 \cdot \frac{t - 10000}{90000} & t \ge 10000 \end{cases} where t is the iteration number. Stage 1 Batch Size: 16384 rays. Stage 1 Iterations: 100,000. Stage 1 Learning Rate: Warmup 0 to 0.01 (10k iters), then linear decay to 0.001 (90k iters). Stage 2 Batch Size: 1024 rays. Stage 2 Iterations: 40,000 (TensoIR-synthetic), 100,000 (Open Illumination). Stage 2 Learning Rate (Fast Cache & Sampler): 1.5625 \times 10^{-4}. Stage 2 Learning Rate (Material & Env Map): 3.125 \times 10^{-5}. Fast Cache Samples: 64 secondary rays. NeRF Cache Samples: 16 secondary rays. Non-analytic Expectation: The expected value of the radiance estimator \mathbb{E}[\hat{L}i] cannot be computed analytically. Direct minimization of the squared error between I and \mathbb{E}[\hat{L}i] is impossible. The gradient trick must be used to obtain correct gradients in expectation. Precision: The use of stopgrad on the cache estimates is critical to prevent unstable gradients from the Monte Carlo sampling process from affecting the cache training during joint optimization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainzipnrfstage1(dataset, zipnrfcache, iterations=100000, batchsize=16384): """Stage 1: Optimize Zip-NeRF radiance cache.""" optimizer = Optimizer(zipnrfcache.parameters()) for step in range(iterations): # Learning rate schedule if step < 10000: lr = 0.01 (step / 10000.0) else: lr = 0.01 - (0.009 (step - 10000) / 90000.0) optimizer.setlr(lr) # [Comment: Sample rays from dataset] rays = samplerays(dataset, batchsize) # Evaluate Zip-NeRF cache Lcache = zipnrfcache.forward(rays) # [Comment: Retrieve ground truth incoming radiance from dataset] Lgt = getgroundtruthincomingradiance(rays) # Charbonnier Loss loss = charbonnierloss(Lcache, Lgt) # Backprop and update optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() def trainzipnrfstage2(dataset, zipnrfcache, fastcache, materialmodel, envmap, iterations, batchsize=1024, numfastsamples=64, numnerfsamples=16): """Stage 2: Joint training of material, environment, and caches.""" lrfast = 1.5625e-4 lrother = 3.125e-5 optimizerfast = Optimizer(fastcache.parameters() + materialmodel.sampler.parameters(), lr=lrfast) optimizerother = Optimizer(materialmodel.parameters() + envmap.parameters(), lr=lrother) for step in range(iterations): # [Comment: Sample rays from dataset] rays = samplerays(dataset, batchsize) # Estimate incoming radiance using caches # 1. Fast Cache estimation (64 samples) Lfast = fastcache.estimateincomingradiance(rays, numsamples=numfastsamples) # 2. Zip-NeRF Cache estimation (16 samples) Lnerf = zipnrfcache.estimateincomingradiance(rays, numsamples=numnerfsamples) # Combine estimates to form final estimator Lhati Lhati = combinecaches(Lfast, Lnerf) # [Comment: Retrieve ground truth image color] Igt = getgroundtruthimagecolor(rays) # Photometric Loss with Gradient Trick diff = Igt - Lhati diffstopgrad = stopgrad(diff) Lcachestopgrad = stopgrad(Lhati) # Loss formula loss = (2.0 diff diffstopgrad / Lcachestopgrad).mean() # Backprop and update optimizerfast.zerograd() optimizerother.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizerfast.step() optimizerother.step() A computationally efficient approximation of incoming radiance using a lightweight hash grid and small MLP, serving as a control variate to correct bias in the NeRF cache. A rendering procedure for specular reflections that casts reflected rays through a volume representation and uses a lightweight decoder, differing by explicitly approximating the reflection cone via a von Mises-Fisher distribution. Estimates expected volume-rendered features over a vMF distribution of reflected rays, avoiding Monte Carlo integration costs by modeling angular spread via conical sampling. Time Complexity: Stage 1 takes 5.5 hours on a single A100 for 100,000 iterations. Stage 2 takes 6.5 hours on a single A100 for 100,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces bias in radiance caching by using a control variate (Fast Cache). Joint training allows for consistent optimization of material and environment. Limitations: Requires significant GPU time (12+ hours total for full training). Relies on the quality of the initial Zip-NeRF cache. When to Use: When high-fidelity inverse rendering with accurate specular reflections is required, and computational resources allow for multi-stage optimization. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is required during training, or when hardware is limited (e.g., no A100-class GPU). The Zip-NeRF Training Procedure is described in "Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering". It builds upon the Zip-NeRF acceleration structure and addresses the bias issues in radiance caching for inverse rendering. The method integrates concepts from RawNeRF's loss function and gradient trick. Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73390-12, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Fast Cache (Control Variate Radiance Cache)
head: Fast Cache architecture, Flash Cache fast cache
body: Fast Cache is a computationally efficient approximation of the incoming radiance used in radiance caching for inverse rendering, designed to replace or augment the expensive NeRF-based cache. It solves the bottleneck of evaluating high-fidelity neural radiance fields for every importance sampling direction by using a lightweight, low-resolution hash grid and a small MLP to predict incident radiance. It sets itself apart from the standard NeRF-based cache by using a fixed, small number of samples (8) and direct distance prediction, while maintaining accuracy by serving as a control variate to correct the bias of the NeRF cache. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{x}, outgoing direction \omegao, incoming direction \omegai, surface normal \mathbf{n}, importance sampling PDF p(\omega), BRDF f(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao), and scene geometry. Output: Estimated outgoing radiance \hat{L}o. Data Structures: 1. Low-resolution NGP Grid: A multi-resolution hash grid (Neural Graphics Primitive) storing features \mathbf{f}k for sample points. 2. Sampling MLP (g{\text{sample}}): A small MLP that takes ray origin and direction, outputting sample distances t'k and unnormalized weights w'k. 3. Color MLP (\text{MLP}{\text{color}}): A small MLP that takes the aggregated ray feature vector and outputs incident radiance \hat{L}i^{\text{fast}}. 4. Environment MLP (\text{MLP}{\text{env}}): A small MLP taking direction \omegai to output far-field illumination. Parameters: S: Number of samples for the fast cache ray integration. Value: S=8. M': Number of directions sampled for the fast cache estimate. M: Number of additional independent directions sampled for the error correction term (M \ll M'). p(\omega): Importance sampling distribution for incoming directions. Steps: 1. Fast Cache Ray Integration: For a given ray origin \mathbf{x} and direction \omegai: a. Compute sample distances and weights using the sampling function: \{t'k, w'k\}{k=1}^{S} = g{\text{sample}}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) b. Compute sample positions: \mathbf{x}'k = \mathbf{x} + t'k \omegai c. Query features from the low-resolution NGP grid at each \mathbf{x}'k to get \mathbf{f}k. d. Normalize weights using softmax: \tilde{w}'k = \frac{\exp(w'k)}{\sum{j=1}^{S} \exp(w'j)} e. Compute the ray feature vector: \mathbf{F}{\text{ray}} = \sum{k=1}^{S} \tilde{w}'k \mathbf{f}k f. Decode incident radiance: \hat{L}i^{\text{fast}}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) = \text{MLP}{\text{color}}(\mathbf{F}{\text{ray}}) 2. Control Variate Estimation: To estimate outgoing radiance \hat{L}o, sample M' directions \{\omega'i\}{j=1}^{M'} and M additional independent directions \{\omegai\}{j=1}^{M} from the importance sampling distribution p(\omega). a. Evaluate the fast cache \hat{L}i^{\text{fast}} for all M' + M directions. b. Evaluate the accurate NeRF-based cache \hat{L}i^{\text{NeRF}} for the M additional directions only. c. Compute the fast outgoing radiance estimate: \hat{L}o^{\text{fast}} = \frac{1}{M'} \sum{j=1}^{M'} f(\mathbf{x}, \omega'i, \omegao) \hat{L}i^{\text{fast}}(\mathbf{x}, \omega'i) \frac{(\mathbf{n} \cdot \omega'i)}{p(\omega'i)} d. Compute the delta (error) outgoing radiance: \Delta \hat{L}o = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} f(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao) \left( \hat{L}i^{\text{NeRF}}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) - \hat{L}i^{\text{fast}}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) \right) \frac{(\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai)}{p(\omegai)} e. Combine estimates: \hat{L}o = \hat{L}o^{\text{fast}} + \Delta \hat{L}o 3. Far-Field Illumination: Add environment lighting to the cache radiance. Compute transparency T = 1 - \sum{k=1}^{N} wk using the weights from the NeRF-based cache integration. Compute environment radiance L{\text{env}i}(\omegai) = \text{MLP}{\text{env}}(\omegai) and multiply by T. Add the result to the cache radiance contribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastcacheradiance(x, omegao, n, pfunc, mprime, m, gsample, ngpfast, mlpcolor, mlpenv, mlpnerf, brdfeval): """ Computes outgoing radiance using Fast Cache as a control variate. """ # Sample M' + M directions and their PDFs from importance distribution p # Note: Exact sampling algorithm is not specified in the source dirsfast, pdfsfast = sampledirections(pfunc, mprime + m) dirsnerf, pdfsnerf = sampledirections(pfunc, m) # Evaluate fast cache for all M' + M directions Lifastall = [] for omega in dirsfast: tprime, wprime = gsample(x, omega) xprime = x + tprime omega features = [ngpfast.query(xpos) for xpos in xprime] wnorm = softmax(wprime) Fray = sum(wnorm[k] features[k] for k in range(len(tprime))) Lifast = mlpcolor(Fray) Lifastall.append(Lifast) # Evaluate NeRF cache for M directions Linerfall = [] for omega in dirsnerf: Linerf = mlpnerf(x, omega) # Full Zip-NeRF evaluation Linerfall.append(Linerf) # Compute fast outgoing radiance estimate Lofast = 0.0 for j in range(mprime): omega = dirsfast[j] pdf = pdfsfast[j] Lifast = Lifastall[j] fval = brdfeval(x, omega, omegao) Lofast += fval Lifast dot(n, omega) / pdf Lofast /= mprime # Compute delta outgoing radiance DeltaLo = 0.0 for j in range(m): omega = dirsnerf[j] pdf = pdfsnerf[j] Lifast = Lifastall[mprime + j] Linerf = Linerfall[j] fval = brdfeval(x, omega, omegao) diff = Linerf - Lifast DeltaLo += fval diff dot(n, omega) / pdf DeltaLo /= m # Combine estimates Lo = Lofast + DeltaLo # Add far-field illumination # Transparency T is computed from the NeRF-based cache integration weights # Note: Exact transparency calculation method is not specified in the source T = computetransparency(mlpnerf, x) Lenv = mlpenv(omega) T Lo += Lenv return Lo Time Complexity: Requires M evaluations of the expensive NeRF-based cache and M + M' evaluations of the cheap fast cache. Memory Complexity: Uses a low-resolution NGP grid and small MLPs, significantly less memory than the full Zip-NeRF grid. Strengths: High efficiency due to low sample count (S=8) and lightweight network. Unbiased estimator when combined with the NeRF cache. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the fast cache; if the fast cache is inaccurate, the control variate correction may not fully compensate. When to use: When real-time or near-real-time inverse rendering is required, and the full NeRF-based cache is too slow. Fast Cache is part of the Flash Cache method, introduced in "Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering". It builds on the Zip-NeRF architecture and Ref-NeRF. The method addresses the bias and computational cost of radiance caching in inverse rendering by using a control variate approach. Flash Cache: Reducing Bias in Radiance Cache Based Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-73390-12, fetched 2026-10-27

name: NeRF-Casting Reflection Model
head: NeRF-Casting Specular Rendering, Reflection Cone Tracing
body: NeRF-Casting is a rendering procedure designed to model accurate, detailed specular reflections in neural radiance fields without the computational cost of evaluating expensive color MLPs along every reflected ray. It addresses the problem of rendering view-dependent specular highlights by casting a small number of reflected rays through a volume representation, accumulating features, and then using a lightweight decoder to produce final colors. It differs from its siblings by explicitly approximating the reflection cone via a von Mises-Fisher distribution and pulling the reflection origin closer to the surface for non-perfect mirrors to maintain intersection with the pixel cone, whereas Conical Reflected Features handles conical integration differently and Fast Cache (Control Variate Radiance Cache) uses control variates. The method builds on the Zip-NeRF representation, which uses a multi-scale hashgrid to store 3D features, a small MLP (1 layer, width 64) to decode density, and a larger MLP (3 layers, width 256) to decode color. The rendering process for a single camera ray with origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} proceeds as follows: Input: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o}, camera ray direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Final pixel color \bar{c}. The underlying representation is based on Zip-NeRF: Hashgrid: Multi-scale grid storing 3D features. Density MLP: 1 layer, width 64. Takes grid features, outputs density \rho(\mathbf{x}). Color MLP: 3 layers, width 256. Takes grid features, bottleneck features, mixing coefficients, and viewing direction to output RGB color. Reflection Feature: A single accumulated vector \mathbf{f} representing the integrated reflection appearance. 1. Sample and Encode Camera Ray: Sample N points \mathbf{x}i along the camera ray. Use the Zip-NeRF spatial encoder to encode each point into volume density \rho(\mathbf{x}i), roughness \kappa(\mathbf{x}i) (inverse-roughness parameter for the reflection distribution), and surface normal \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}i). 2. Alpha Composite Camera Ray Features: Alpha composite the sampled densities and features along the camera ray to compute an expected termination point \bar{\mathbf{x}}, an aggregated von Mises-Fisher distribution width \bar{\kappa} (inverse-roughness), and an aggregated surface normal \bar{\mathbf{n}}. 3. Construct Reflection Distribution: Reflect the camera direction \mathbf{d} around the aggregated surface normal \bar{\mathbf{n}} to define the center of the reflection distribution. Approximate the von Mises-Fisher distribution vMF(\mathbf{d}', \bar{\kappa}) over reflected rays by sampling a small set of M reflected rays \{\mathbf{d}'j\}{j=1}^M (where M=5 in the source). 4. Determine Reflection Ray Origins: For each reflected ray j, determine the origin \mathbf{o}'j. If the surface is not a perfect mirror (i.e., \bar{\kappa} is finite), the reflection cone widens. To maintain the same intersection with the pixel cone, the origin of the reflected ray cone must be pulled closer to the surface location \bar{\mathbf{x}}. 5. Trace Reflected Rays: Cast the M reflected rays defined by origins \mathbf{o}'j and directions \mathbf{d}'j. Sample points along these reflected rays and encode each point using the same Zip-NeRF spatial encoder to obtain densities \rho'(\mathbf{x}) and features \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}). 6. Accumulate Reflection Features: Alpha composite the features along each reflected ray j to get per-ray features \bar{\mathbf{f}}j. Average the composited features \bar{\mathbf{f}}j across all M reflected rays to produce a single reflection feature \mathbf{f}. 7. Decode Final Colors: Broadcast the single reflection feature \mathbf{f} over the original camera ray's samples. For each sample i along the original ray, pass the reflection feature \mathbf{f}, bottleneck features \mathbf{b} (from Zip-NeRF), mixing coefficients \alpha, and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to the color decoder to produce an RGB color c(\mathbf{x}i) for each point. 8. Alpha Composite Final Color: Alpha composite the colors c(\mathbf{x}i) and densities \rho(\mathbf{x}i) along the original camera ray to render the final pixel color \bar{c}. Unverified code. Zip-NeRF Color MLP: 3 layers, width 256. Number of Reflected Rays (M): 5. Roughness Parameter (\kappa): Inverse-roughness, used to define the width of the von Mises-Fisher distribution. For non-perfect mirrors, the reflection cone widens and the origin is pulled closer to the surface. Non-Perfect Mirrors: When the surface is not a perfect mirror, the reflection cone widens. The origin of the reflected ray cone must be pulled closer to the surface location to maintain the same intersection with the pixel cone. Failure to adjust the origin may result in incorrect reflection sampling. Precision: The method relies on accurate estimation of the surface normal and termination point from noisy volume samples. Degenerate inputs (e.g., empty space) should return black or background color. Computational Cost: While cheaper than full ray tracing, querying the hashgrid and MLPs for M reflected rays per camera ray sample still adds overhead. The cost is mitigated by using the small density MLP for sampling and only using the larger color MLP for the final composite step. Time Complexity: Proportional to N \times (1 + M), where N is the number of samples per camera ray and M is the number of reflected rays (typically 5). Each reflected ray requires sampling and feature encoding, but avoids the full color MLP evaluation until the final step. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the Zip-NeRF hashgrid storage. The reflection feature is a single vector per ray, requiring minimal additional memory. Strengths: Models accurate detailed reflections without expensive MLP evaluations along every reflected ray. Minimizes computation by querying density/features cheaply and only decoding color once per camera sample using accumulated reflection features. Limitations: Approximates the reflection cone with a discrete set of rays, which may introduce aliasing or inaccuracies for highly rough surfaces if M is too small. Relies on the quality of the Zip-NeRF representation for normal and roughness estimation. When to Use: When view-dependent specular reflections are important and computational resources are limited compared to full path tracing, but more accurate than simple environment map reflections. When Not to Use: For scenes with complex global illumination beyond first-order reflections, or where perfect mirror reflections are required without approximation. NeRF-Casting was introduced in the paper "NeRF-Casting: Improved View-Dependent Appearance with Consistent Reflections". It builds upon the Zip-NeRF representation, which itself improves upon standard NeRF by using a multi-scale hashgrid for efficient feature storage and decoding. The method was developed to address the high computational cost of rendering reflections in neural radiance fields by reducing the number of expensive MLP evaluations.
