name: Vision-Only Pose Filtering in a NeRF
head: Optimization-based Pose Filter for NeRF, Recursive SE(3) Optimization
body: This method is an optimization-based state estimation filter that estimates the 6-DoF pose and velocities of a robot within a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) using only onboard monocular RGB images. It addresses the limitation of single-shot pose estimators by treating the problem as recursive Bayesian estimation, balancing a NeRF-based photometric loss with a dynamics prediction loss to provide robustness in low-gradient regions and output state covariance. The method operates as a recursive filter at each timestep t, updating the robot's state belief based on a new image It, the previous action ut, and the prior state estimate. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current image It, previous action ut, prior state mean \mu{t-1}, prior state covariance \Sigma{t-1}, pre-trained NeRF model, and a subset of selected pixels I (identified via feature detection). Outputs: Updated state mean \mut, updated state covariance \Sigmat, and the robot pose Tt derived from \mut. Data Structures: State Vector \mut: Contains the robot's position, orientation (represented in SE(3)), and velocities. Covariance Matrix \Sigmat: A symmetric positive-definite matrix representing the uncertainty of the state estimate. Pixel Subset I: A set of 2D image coordinates (u, v) selected using an image feature detector (e.g., ORB) to bias sampling toward areas of high gradient information. Numbered Steps: 1. State Propagation (Prediction): Propagate the state mean and covariance forward using the system dynamics model f and the applied action ut. \mu{t|t-1} = f(\mu{t-1}, ut) A{t-1} = \left. \frac{\partial f(x, ut)}{\partial x} \right|{x=\mu{t-1}} \Sigma{t|t-1} = A{t-1} \Sigma{t-1} A{t-1}^T + Q{t-1} where Q{t-1} is the process noise covariance. 2. Pixel Selection: Select a subset of pixels I from the current image It using an image feature detector (e.g., ORB) to identify points of interest. 3. Optimization (Update): Minimize the cost function J(\mut) with respect to the state \mut to find the posterior mean \mut. The cost function combines a photometric loss and a process loss: J(\mut) = \| CI(Tt) - It(I) \|{St^{-1}}^2 + \| \mu{t|t-1} - \mut \|{\Sigma{t|t-1}^{-1}}^2 where: CI(Tt) represents the predicted pixel values for the selected subset I given the pose Tt (derived from \mut) and the NeRF. It(I) are the observed pixel values from the image It at locations I. St is the measurement noise covariance. The notation \| x \|M^2 = x^T M x denotes the weighted L2 norm. 4. Outlier Rejection: Perform outlier rejection on the per-pixel loss to reduce variance before or during the optimization step. 5. Covariance Update: Compute the posterior covariance \Sigmat using the Hessian of the loss function at the optimized mean: \Sigmat = \left( \left. \frac{\partial^2 J(x)}{\partial x^2} \right|{x=\mut} \right)^{-1} 6. Manifold Projection: During the optimization of \mut, project the pose back onto the SE(3) manifold after every gradient step. This "recursive SE(3)" approach is preferred over optimizing with respect to a reference pose and projecting once, as the multiplication of skew-symmetric matrices in the exponential map does not commute, and recursive projection converges quicker and more smoothly on the noisy photometric loss landscape. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.autograd.functional as AF def visiononlyposefilter( prevmu: torch.Tensor, prevSigma: torch.Tensor, actionu: torch.Tensor, currentimage: torch.Tensor, nerfmodel: callable, pixelsubsetI: list, Q: torch.Tensor, S: torch.Tensor, maxiterations: int, learningrate: float) -> tuple: # Step 1: State Propagation # Dynamics model f(mu, u) is problem-specific and not detailed in the sources. mupred = dynamicsmodel(prevmu, actionu) A = computejacobiandynamics(prevmu, actionu) Sigmapred = A @ prevSigma @ A.T + Q # Step 2: Pixel Selection # pixelsubsetI is provided as input, selected via ORB or similar feature detector. # Step 3 & 6: Optimization with Recursive SE(3) Projection muopt = mupred.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([muopt], lr=learningrate) for step in range(maxiterations): optimizer.zerograd() loss = costfunction(muopt, mupred, Sigmapred, S, currentimage, pixelsubsetI, nerfmodel) # Outlier rejection on per-pixel loss reduces variance. loss = applyoutlierrejection(loss, currentimage, pixelsubsetI, muopt, nerfmodel) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Recursive SE(3) projection after every gradient step. muopt = projectse3manifold(muopt) # Step 5: Covariance Update # Hessian of the loss function at the optimized mean. H = AF.hessian(costfunction, muopt, args=(mupred, Sigmapred, S, currentimage, pixelsubsetI, nerfmodel)) Sigmat = torch.inverse(H) return muopt.detach(), Sigmat def dynamicsmodel(mu: torch.Tensor, u: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Problem-specific dynamics f(mu, u). Not given in the sources. # Example: constant velocity model return mu + u def computejacobiandynamics(mu: torch.Tensor, u: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Jacobian A = df/dx at x=mu. return torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(lambda x: dynamicsmodel(x, u), mu) def costfunction(mu: torch.Tensor, mupred: torch.Tensor, Sigmapred: torch.Tensor, S: torch.Tensor, currentimage: torch.Tensor, pixelsubsetI: list, nerfmodel: callable) -> torch.Tensor: Tt = extractposefromstate(mu) predictedpixels = nerfmodel.render(Tt, pixelsubsetI) observedpixels = currentimage[pixelsubsetI] diffphoto = predictedpixels - observedpixels diffphotoflat = diffphoto.view(-1, 1) Sinv = torch.inverse(S) photometricloss = diffphotoflat.T @ Sinv @ diffphotoflat diffproc = mupred - mu diffprocflat = diffproc.view(-1, 1) Sigmapredinv = torch.inverse(Sigmapred) processloss = diffprocflat.T @ Sigmapredinv @ diffprocflat return (photometricloss + processloss).squeeze() def extractposefromstate(mu: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Extracts SE(3) pose from the state vector. # Layout depends on the specific state representation. return mu[:6] def projectse3manifold(state: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # Projects pose component back onto SE(3) manifold after every gradient step. # Uses standard SVD to enforce valid rotation matrices. pose = state[:6] R = pose[:3,:3] U,, Vt = torch.linalg.svd(R) Rproj = U @ Vt t = pose[:3, 3] newstate = state.clone() newstate[:3,:3] = Rproj return newstate def applyoutlierrejection(loss: torch.Tensor, currentimage: torch.Tensor, pixelsubsetI: list, mu: torch.Tensor, nerfmodel: callable) -> torch.Tensor: # Masks pixels with high photometric residuals before backpropagation. Tt = extractposefromstate(mu) predicted = nerfmodel.render(Tt, pixelsubsetI) observed = currentimage[pixelsubsetI] residuals = torch.abs(predicted - observed) mask = residuals < torch.median(residuals) + 3 torch.std(residuals) if not torch.any(mask): return loss return loss torch.mean(mask.float()) Parameters: Feature Detector: ORB is used to select pixels for photometric evaluation. Process Noise Covariance Q{t-1}: Covariance of the process noise in the state propagation step. Measurement Noise Covariance St: Covariance weighting the photometric loss term. Learning Rate: Hyperparameter for the optimizer; value not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SE(3) Manifold Optimization: Multiplication of skew-symmetric matrices in the exponential map does not commute. Optimizing with respect to a reference pose and projecting once is mathematically distinct from recursive projection. The recursive SE(3) approach is required for quicker and smoother convergence due to the noisy photometric loss landscape. Low Gradient Regions: The method is designed to be robust in regions with low photometric gradient information by relying more on the dynamics model (process loss). Implementation: Optimization on the manifold is implemented using the LieTorch library. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated in simulation with a quadrotor navigating through a jungle gym, the inside of a church, and Stonehenge, and with an omnidirectional ground robot navigating through a church. Strengths: Provides robust pose estimation in low-gradient regions; outputs state covariance useful for parallel algorithms like collision avoidance; integrates seamlessly with trajectory planning in an online replanning loop. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF model; computationally intensive due to NeRF rendering and optimization at each timestep; sensitive to the accuracy of the dynamics model f and noise covariances Q, S. When to Use: Online robot navigation in environments represented by NeRFs where only monocular vision is available and dynamics are known. When Not to Use: When high-frequency updates are not required and offline batch optimization is acceptable; when the environment is not well-represented by a NeRF; when dynamics are unknown or highly uncertain. The method was introduced by Mikhalkiewicz et al. in 2022 in the paper "Vision-Only Robot Navigation in a Neural Radiance World". It builds upon previous work on single-image camera pose estimation using NeRFs [19] (cited in) but extends it to recursive Bayesian estimation. The method is part of a larger navigation framework that combines trajectory planning (based on differential flatness) and pose filtering for online replanning. It was demonstrated in high-fidelity simulation environments including a playground, a church, and Stonehenge. name: Online Receding Horizon Replanning
head: Online Replanning Navigation Pipeline
body: Online Receding Horizon Replanning is a vision-based robot navigation pipeline that combines a trajectory planner and a pose filter in a receding horizon loop to provide dynamic maneuvering through an environment using only an RGB camera for feedback. It solves the problem of navigating a robot through a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation when the robot's initial pose is uncertain and subject to disturbances. Unlike static waypoint planners, this method allows the robot to change homotopy classes around obstacles in response to disturbances by continuously replanning the trajectory based on updated state beliefs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial state prior (\mu0, \Sigma0), goal state x{goal}, trained NeRF model N of the environment. Outputs: A sequence of control actions u executed by the robot. Data Structures: State Belief: Represented by mean \mu and covariance \Sigma. Waypoints: A sequence W of states. NeRF: A neural network f\theta representing the scene geometry and appearance, used for collision checking and image synthesis. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize waypoints W using A search between the initial state \mu0 and the goal state x{goal}. 2. Loop: While the robot is not at x{goal}: a. Trajectory Optimization: Optimize the trajectory W using trajOpt to minimize a NeRF-based collision metric. This produces a refined sequence of waypoints. b. Action Extraction: Get the states x and actions u from the optimized waypoints W. c. Execution: The robot applies the first control action u[0]. d. Perception: The robot receives a noisy image I from its onboard RGB camera. e. Pose Filtering: The state estimator uses the captured image I to generate a posterior belief over the new state. This updates the state estimate using poseFilter with inputs I, previous state (\mu{t-1}, \Sigma{t-1}), and the first action u[0]. f. Replanning Preparation: Update W by replacing the first waypoint with the new mean \mut and keeping the rest of the previous waypoints (W[2:end]) as a hot start. Formulas: The collision metric evaluated during trajOpt relies on the NeRF's ability to synthesize images and estimate depth or occupancy, though the specific mathematical formulation of the collision metric is not detailed in the provided text. The pose filter uses the NeRF as a nonlinear measurement model to update the belief (\mut, \Sigmat). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def onlinerecedinghorizonplanning(initialpriormu, initialpriorsigma, goalstate, nerfmodel): # Step 1: Initialize waypoints using A search between initial state and goal waypoints = astarsearch(initialpriormu, goalstate) currentmu = initialpriormu currentsigma = initialpriorsigma # Step 2: Receding Horizon Loop while not isatgoal(currentmu, goalstate): # a) Optimize trajectory to minimize NeRF-based collision metric waypoints = trajoptimization(waypoints, nerfmodel) # b) Extract states and actions from optimized waypoints states, actions = getstatesandactions(waypoints) # c) Execute first control action executeaction(actions[0]) # d) Capture noisy RGB image from onboard camera image = getcameraimage() # e) Update pose belief using NeRF as nonlinear measurement model currentmu, currentsigma = posefilter(image, currentmu, currentsigma, actions[0]) # f) Update waypoints: replace first waypoint with new mean, keep rest as hot start waypoints = [currentmu] + waypoints[2:] return def astarsearch(start, goal): return [start] # Not given in the sources. def isatgoal(state, goal): return np.allclose(state, goal) # Standard convergence check def trajoptimization(waypoints, nerf): return waypoints # Not given in the sources. def getstatesandactions(waypoints): return waypoints, waypoints # Not given in the sources. def executeaction(action): pass # Not given in the sources. def getcameraimage(): return None # Not given in the sources. def posefilter(image, mu, sigma, action): return mu, sigma # Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Model Mismatch: The method assumes a trained NeRF model. Performance may degrade if there is a mismatch between the real-world scene and the trained NeRF. Disturbances: The system is designed to handle disturbances, but severe disturbances may require significant replanning effort. Homotopy Changes: The method allows the robot to change homotopy classes around obstacles in response to disturbances, which is difficult for existing differential flatness-based planners that use static waypoints. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated in simulation with quadrotor and ground robots navigating through pre-trained NeRF models of a playground, a church, and Stonehenge. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows the robot to change homotopy classes around obstacles in response to disturbances, which is difficult for existing differential flatness-based planners that use static waypoints. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF model of the environment. When to use: Navigating a robot through a known environment represented by a pre-trained NeRF using only an RGB camera, especially in the presence of disturbances. When not: When real-time mapping is required (NeRF is pre-trained) or when the environment cannot be represented by a pre-trained NeRF. Origin: The method was introduced in "Vision-Only Robot Navigation in a Neural Radiance World". History and Development: The paper builds on related work in neural implicit representations and vision-only navigation systems. Usage: Demonstrated in high-fidelity simulation environments. name: NeRF-based Trajectory Optimization
head: Differential Flatness-based Trajectory Optimization with NeRF, NeRF-based collision penalty optimization, Proposed trajectory optimizer
body:
NeRF-based Trajectory Optimization is a planning method for differentially flat systems that optimizes a dense set of flat output waypoints directly using first-order gradient descent. It solves the problem of finding collision-free paths in complex environments by using Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) density as an implicit obstacle representation, replacing the need for closed-form polytopes or explicit mesh extraction. Unlike traditional pipelines that rely on quadratic programs with static, hand-designed waypoints and convex constraints, this method treats waypoint locations as differentiable decision variables, allowing the optimizer to navigate through narrow spaces by minimizing a combined objective of collision probability and control effort. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model \mathcal{N} representing the environment; a current robot pose P{start}; a goal pose P{goal}; robot dynamics parameters (defining flat outputs and control limits). Outputs: A sequence of optimized flat output waypoints \{\sigma1, \dots, \sigmah\} defining the trajectory. Data Structures: Waypoints: A list of h flat output vectors. For a quadrotor, each vector \sigmai contains position (x, y, z) and yaw angle \psi. The total number of decision variables is 4h (3 for position, 1 for yaw). NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to volume density \sigma and color C. The density \sigma is used as a proxy for collision probability. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate a preliminary set of h waypoints between P{start} and P{goal} using a heuristic such as a straight line or A search on a coarse grid. Let these initial waypoints be \sigma^{(0)}. 2. Objective Formulation: Define the loss function \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of collision cost and control effort: \mathcal{L}(\sigma) = \lambda{col} \mathcal{L}{col}(\sigma) + \lambda{ctrl} \mathcal{L}{ctrl}(\sigma) where \lambda{col} and \lambda{ctrl} are weighting coefficients. 3. Collision Cost Calculation: For each waypoint \sigmai, sample the NeRF density at the corresponding 3D position. The collision cost \mathcal{L}{col} is computed by summing the NeRF density along the trajectory segments or at the waypoints. The source notes that minimizing this objective correlates with minimizing the intersecting volume of ground-truth meshes. Specifically, the method minimizes a "NeRF collision loss" which serves as a differentiable proxy for physical collision. The collision probability at time t is bounded by p{coll} = \sum{bt \in B} ho(bt) s(bt), where B is a finite collection of points representing the robot body, ho(bt) is the NeRF density, and s(bt) is the distance traveled. 4. Control Effort Calculation: Compute the control effort \mathcal{L}{ctrl} based on the robot's dynamics. The control inputs 	au and states s are derived from the surrounding waypoints using the robot's differential flatness properties. For a quadrotor, this typically involves computing the required thrust and moments to transition between waypoints, often related to snap or jerk minimization. 5. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradients 
abla{\sigma} \mathcal{L} using automatic differentiation through the NeRF density evaluation and the dynamics model. 6. Optimization Update: Update the waypoints using the Adam optimizer: \sigma^{(k+1)} = \sigma^{(k)} - \alpha \cdot 	ext{Adam}(
abla{\sigma} \mathcal{L}) where \alpha is the learning rate. 7. Convergence: Repeat steps 3-6 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. The optimizer converges to a trajectory with zero intersections with ground-truth meshes in tested environments (e.g., Stonehenge) by iteration 49 in specific experiments. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerftrajectoryoptimization(nerfdensityfn, startpose, goalpose, numwaypoints, maxiterations, lr=0.01, lambdacol=1.0, lambdactrl=1.0): """ Optimizes a trajectory for a differentially flat system using NeRF density. Args: nerfdensityfn: Callable returning volume density for a 3D point. startpose: Initial robot pose [x, y, z, yaw]. goalpose: Goal robot pose [x, y, z, yaw]. numwaypoints: Number of intermediate waypoints h. maxiterations: Maximum number of gradient descent steps. lr: Learning rate. lambdacol, lambdactrl: Loss weighting coefficients. Returns: optimizedwaypoints: List of optimized flat output vectors. """ # Step 1: Initialize waypoints using linear interpolation waypoints = [] for i in range(numwaypoints + 2): # +2 for start and goal t = i / (numwaypoints + 1) pos = [startpose[j] + t (goalpose[j] - startpose[j]) for j in range(3)] yaw = startpose[3] + t (goalpose[3] - startpose[3]) waypoints.append(pos + [yaw]) # Step 2-6: Optimization Loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Calculate Collision Cost collisionloss = sum(nerfdensityfn(wp[:3]) for wp in waypoints) / len(waypoints) # Calculate Control Effort (simplified snap-based metric) controlloss = 0.0 for i in range(1, len(waypoints) - 1): prev = waypoints[i-1] curr = waypoints[i] nxt = waypoints[i+1] # Approximate acceleration/snap from position differences accel = [nxt[j] - 2curr[j] + prev[j] for j in range(3)] controlloss += sum(a2 for a in accel) # Combined Loss loss = lambdacol collisionloss + lambdactrl controlloss # Compute Gradients via automatic differentiation through the NeRF and dynamics model # (Framework-specific AD engine computes dL/dw for each waypoint parameter) grad = [[0.0 for in range(4)] for in range(len(waypoints))] # Placeholder for AD output # Update Waypoints for i in range(len(waypoints)): for j in range(4): waypoints[i][j] -= lr grad[i][j] if iteration % 100 == 0: print(f"Iteration {iteration}, Loss: {loss}") return waypoints Parameters: Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Iterations (Initial): 2500. Iterations (Online Replanning): 250. Time Step (Online): 0.1s. Flat Outputs: Position (x, y, z) and yaw angle \psi for quadrotors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Convexity: The optimization problem is fundamentally non-convex due to the complex geometry represented by the NeRF and the dynamics constraints. First-order methods like Adam are required, and convergence to a local minimum is possible. Initialization Sensitivity: Poor initialization (e.g., a straight line through a dense obstacle) may lead to slow convergence or failure to find a collision-free path. Heuristics like A on a coarse grid are recommended. NeRF Density Accuracy: The collision cost relies on the NeRF density accurately representing obstacles. Inaccuracies in the NeRF (e.g., floating artifacts, incomplete reconstruction) may lead to false positives or negatives in collision detection. Re-plans trajectories in real-time (e.g., every 0.1s) using fewer iterations (250) to correct for state estimation errors or dynamic changes. A local obstacle avoidance method that defines a repulsive potential directly from NeRF density, computing repulsive forces via automatic differentiation without mesh extraction. The repulsive potential is U{rep}(x) =  rac{1}{2\eta} \left(1 -  rac{d(x)}{d0}ight)^2 if d(x) \leq d0, and 0 otherwise, where d0 controls influence range and \eta controls strength. The pseudo-distance is derived from integrated density as d(x) = - rac{1}{\sigma{max}} \log\left(1 -  rac{\min(\sigma(x), \sigma{max})}{\sigma{max}}ight), where \sigma(x) is density and \sigma{max} is maximum density. The repulsive force F{rep} = -
ablax U{rep} is computed via automatic differentiation through the NeRF density network and combined with an attractive potential toward the goal. This extends prior work on aerial robots using density thresholds by directly differentiating through the NeRF density to obtain smooth repulsive gradients suitable for ground robot navigation. Online replanning takes ~2s for 250 iterations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the NeRF model and the number of waypoints. Performance: In the Stonehenge environment, the optimizer converges to a trajectory with zero intersections with ground-truth meshes by iteration 49. It outperforms minimum-snap planners (which clip obstacles) and RRT (which has high control effort) in terms of smoothness and collision avoidance. Strengths: Handles complex, implicit obstacle representations without explicit meshing; leverages differential flatness for efficient control computation; allows for arbitrary differentiable cost functions. Limitations: Computationally expensive for real-time applications on current hardware; sensitive to NeRF quality; non-convex optimization may get stuck in local minima. When to Use: Suitable for offline or semi-real-time planning in complex, unstructured environments where explicit obstacle models are unavailable or difficult to construct. The method was proposed in "Vision-Only Robot Navigation in a Neural Radiance World" (2022). It builds on the concept of differential flatness, commonly used in quadrotor trajectory planning (e.g., minimum-snap planners), but replaces the convex quadratic programming formulation with a non-convex gradient-based optimization using NeRF density for collision avoidance. The work demonstrates that NeRFs can serve as implicit obstacle representations for trajectory planning, enabling robots to navigate tight spaces without explicit mesh extraction. name: Online Replanning

It solves the problem of catastrophic collisions caused by external disturbances or state estimation errors during execution. Unlike open-loop execution, which follows a pre-computed plan regardless of deviations, online replanning uses feedback to generate new collision-free paths to the goal, ensuring robustness. name: Surrogate Objective-based Trajectory Planning
head: Ensemble Objective E, SOARNet, Surrogate Objectives for Active Radiance Fields Network, Trajectory Planning with SOARNet
body: Surrogate Objective-based Trajectory Planning selects informative camera poses for training radiance fields without requiring radiance field training or ground-truth mesh access during inference. It solves the active view planning problem by using a deep neural network, SOARNet, to predict surrogate objective scores for candidate poses given monocular images and camera parameters. Unlike in-flight or post-hoc methods that rely on uncertainty estimation from a trained model, this approach is prescriptive and model-agnostic, enabling trajectory generation in seconds rather than hours. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by decoupling view selection from radiance field optimization, allowing for rapid, training-free planning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of monocular 2D images \hat{M} = \{mk: k \le n\} taken from visited camera poses \hat{C} = \{\hat{c}k: k \le n\}, the camera parameters (extrinsics) for each image, and a set of candidate unvisited poses C^-. The method does not require the image of the unvisited pose or the ground-truth mesh. Outputs: A sequence of selected camera poses \hat{C} up to a budget B, and the predicted surrogate objective scores for visited and candidate poses. Data Structures: SOARNet Architecture: Encoder \mu(\cdot): A ResNet-18 encoder processing the input images \hat{M}. Camera Extrinsics Encoder o(\cdot): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) taking positionally encoded camera extrinsics. Prediction Heads G(\cdot) and H(\cdot): Simple MLPs for generating objective scores via regression. Output Format: The network outputs a set of scores Fg for g \in \{n, n+1\}, where Fg = \{f{Cg}, f{Qg}, f{Dg}, f{Tg}\}. Fn contains normalized cumulative scores of all poses seen so far. F{n+1} returns normalized cumulative scores for an unseen camera pose c{n+1} conditioned upon visited poses. Formulas: The surrogate objectives are defined as follows: 1. Surface Coverage (fC): Measures the ratio of seen faces to total faces. fC = \frac{1}{J} \sum{j}^{J} \sum{k}^{n} U(Vj^k) Where J is the total number of faces, n is the number of visited poses, U(\cdot) is the Heaviside step function, and Vj^k is an indicator of face j visibility from pose k. 2. Geometric Complexity (fQ): Quantifies variability in mesh surface normals. Not given in the sources. 3. Textural Complexity (fT): Measures photometric variation. Not given in the sources. 4. Ray Diversity (fD): Measures the diversity of viewing rays. Not given in the sources. The SOARNet prediction is formalized as: \text{SOARNet}(\hat{C}, \hat{M}, c{n+1}) = \{Fg: g \in \{n, n+1\}\} The training loss L for SOARNet is the sum of Huber losses on the predictions of each head: L = LG(\hat{F}n, Fn) + LH(\hat{F}{n+1}, F{n+1}) Where LG and LH are Huber losses. Parameters: Budget B: The maximum number of camera poses to select. Initialization Steps n{init}: Set to 3. Ensemble Objective Sequence E: [C, Q, Q, D, D, T]. Training Hardware: NVIDIA RTX8000 GPU, 64GB DRAM, 8 CPUs. Optimizer: Adam with AMSGrad enabled, no weight decay. Learning Rate: 3 \times 10^{-5}. Beta1: 0.9. Beta2: 0.999. Epsilon: 1 \times 10^{-8}. Scheduler: Step size 0.6, \gamma 0.5. Epochs: 12. Batch Size: 8. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For the first n{init} steps (3 steps), select poses at the extremum along each principal spatial axis (PseudoCoverage). 2. Loop: While the number of selected steps is less than the budget B: a. Determine the current objective index: idx = \text{step} \pmod{\text{len}(E)}. b. Select the objective function f from the ensemble sequence E at index idx. c. For each candidate unvisited pose cz \in C^-: i. Compute the score using SOARNet: Sz = \text{SOARNet}(\hat{C}, \hat{M}, cz). ii. Extract the score corresponding to the selected objective f. d. Select the candidate pose cz with the highest score as the next pose \hat{c}{n+1}. e. Add \hat{c}{n+1} to \hat{C} and its image to \hat{M}. f. Remove \hat{c}{n+1} from C^-. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def getextremumposes(candidateposes, ninit): """ Standard PCA-based extremity selection for initialization.""" posesarray = np.array(candidateposes) mean = np.mean(posesarray, axis=0) cov = np.cov(posesarray.T) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) principalaxes = eigenvectors[:, -3:] extremumindices = [] for axis in principalaxes: projections = posesarray @ axis extremumindices.append(np.argmax(projections)) extremumindices.append(np.argmin(projections)) selected = [] for idx in extremumindices: if len(selected) < ninit and idx not in selected: selected.append(idx) return [candidateposes[i] for i in selected] def soarnet(images, extrinsics, candidatepose): """ Stub for the trained SOARNet model. Returns predicted scores.""" return { 'Fn': {'fC': 0.0, 'fQ': 0.0, 'fD': 0.0, 'fT': 0.0}, 'F{n+1}': {'fC': 0.0, 'fQ': 0.0, 'fD': 0.0, 'fT': 0.0} } def capturepose(pose): """ Standard environment function to render image and record extrinsics at a given pose.""" return np.zeros((224, 224, 3)), pose def generatetrajectory(images, cameraextrinsics, candidateposes, budget, ensemblesequence, ninit=3): selectedposes = [] visitedimages = list(images) visitedextrinsics = list(cameraextrinsics) candidateset = list(candidateposes) # Initialization phase for step in range(ninit): if step < len(candidateset): nextpose = candidateset[step] selectedposes.append(nextpose) candidateset.remove(nextpose) newimg, newext = capturepose(nextpose) visitedimages.append(newimg) visitedextrinsics.append(newext) # Greedy selection phase step = ninit while len(selectedposes) < budget: idx = step % len(ensemblesequence) objectivename = ensemblesequence[idx] bestscore = -float('inf') bestpose = None for candidate in candidateset: scores = soarnet(visitedimages, visitedextrinsics, candidate) score = scores['F{n+1}'][f'f{objectivename}'] if score > bestscore: bestscore = score bestpose = candidate selectedposes.append(bestpose) candidateset.remove(bestpose) newimg, newext = capturepose(bestpose) visitedimages.append(newimg) visitedextrinsics.append(newext) step += 1 return selectedposes Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of Huber loss suggests robustness to outliers in objective score predictions. Boundaries: The method relies on the availability of monocular images and camera extrinsics. If extrinsics are inaccurate, the positionally encoded input to the MLP may be misleading. A surrogate objective function measuring the ratio of seen faces to total faces to characterize informative samples for training radiance fields. It optimizes for maximizing the number of unique faces seen across camera poses, given the mesh of an object. It is chosen when surface completeness is the primary goal for reconstruction. Time Complexity: The method provides a significant speed-up, generating trajectories in seconds instead of hours, offering an ~80x speed-up compared to baselines. This is due to the fast inference of SOARNet compared to iterative radiance field training or uncertainty estimation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: SOARNet outperforms baselines with comparable or better reconstruction qualities. Scaling: The method is model-agnostic, generalizing across fully neural-implicit (e.g., NeRF) to fully explicit approaches (e.g., Plenoxels). Strengths: Training-free, fast, interpretable objectives, model-agnostic. Limitations: Requires a set of candidate poses and monocular images; does not account for radiance field-specific uncertainties during planning. When to use: When rapid view selection is needed without the computational cost of training a radiance field first. When not to use: When the scene geometry is unknown and cannot be approximated by candidate poses, or when high-precision uncertainty quantification is required. The method was introduced in the paper "SO-NeRF: Active View Planning for NeRF using Surrogate Objectives" by Chen Feng et al.. It addresses the limitations of existing active perception methods for radiance fields, which often require in-flight training or post-hoc uncertainty estimation. The work is supported by NSF Awards 2238968 and 2322242. SO-NeRF: Active View Planning for NeRF using Surrogate Objectives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.03266, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: MELON
head: Modulo-Equivalent Latent Optimization of NeRF, NeRF with Unposed Images in SO(3)
body: MELON is a differentiable inverse rendering method that jointly optimizes a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and camera poses from a set of unposed images. It solves the problem of local minima in the low-dimensional SO(3) latent space by introducing a "modulo loss" that maps the encoder's output to a quotient space, effectively replicating the latent variables to match the object's rotational symmetries. Unlike adversarial approaches such as GNeRF, MELON uses an encoder-decoder architecture with amortized inference, allowing it to perform ab-initio reconstruction without pose initialization or pre-trained CNNs. Does not require a discriminator. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n unposed images \{Ii\}{i=1}^n. The method assumes known camera intrinsics and that cameras point towards the scene origin from a known distance r. Output: A NeRF parameterized by \psi (predicting density \sigma\psi and color c\psi) and a set of camera poses \{Ri\}{i=1}^n in SO(3). Data Structures: NeRF (f\psi): A coordinate-based neural network predicting (c\psi, \sigma\psi) for a given 3D point and viewing direction. Encoder (h\xi): A neural network with weights \xi that maps an input image Ii to a latent pose variable zi in the latent space SO(3). Latent Space (\Omega): Parameterized as SO(3) using azimuth \theta \in SO(2), elevation \phi \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2], and roll \alpha \in SO(2). Replication Order (N): Integer N \in \mathbb{N}^ defining the equivalence relation. Mathematical Formulation: The image formation model is: Ii(p) = C(p; f^, Ri^) where C is the rendering function, f^ = (c^, \sigma^) is the unknown ground truth field, and Ri^ is the unknown ground truth pose. Operations on \Omega are defined for R \sim (\theta, \phi, \alpha): \theta0 + R \sim (\theta0 + \theta, \phi, \alpha) \lambda R \sim (\lambda\theta, \phi, \alpha) for \theta0 \in SO(2), \lambda \in \mathbb{R}. The equivalence relation RN for N \in \mathbb{N}^ is: z RN z' \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{Z}, z = z' + \frac{2k\pi}{N} This creates a quotient space \Omega/RN which is N times smaller than \Omega, replicating cameras along the azimuthal dimension. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Initialize NeRF parameters \psi and Encoder parameters \xi. Set replication order N. 2. Encode: For each input image Ii, compute the latent estimate zi = h\xi(Ii). 3. Generate Equivalence Class: Compute the equivalence class [zi]{RN} = \{ z \mid z RN zi \}. 4. Render Synthetic Views: For each z \in [zi]{RN}, render a synthetic image C(\cdot; f\psi, z) using the current NeRF. Let \mathcal{C}i^R(\psi, \xi) be the set of these rendered images. 5. Compute Modulo Loss: Calculate the loss as the minimum L2 distance between the input image and any synthetic view in the equivalence class: \mathcal{L}R(\psi, \xi) = \sum{i=1}^n \min \{ \| C - Ii \|2^2 \mid C \in \mathcal{C}i^R(\psi, \xi) \} This loss is a lower bound of the standard L2 loss due to the reflexivity of RN. 6. Optimize: Update \psi and \xi using gradient descent (e.g., Adam) to minimize \mathcal{L}R. 7. Final Pose Estimation: After convergence, for each Ii, the final pose estimate zi^ is: zi^ = \arg \min \{ \| C(\cdot; f\psi, z) - Ii(\cdot) \|2^2 \mid z \in [h{\xi^}(Ii)]{RN} \} where \xi^ is the optimal encoder weight. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def posetorotation(pose): theta, phi, alpha = pose cx, sx = torch.cos(theta), torch.sin(theta) cy, sy = torch.cos(phi), torch.sin(phi) cz, sz = torch.cos(alpha), torch.sin(alpha) R = torch.stack([ cz cy, cz sy sx - sz cx, cz sy cx + sz sx, sz cy, sz sy sx + cz cx, sz sy cx - cz sx, -sy, cy sx, cy cx ]).reshape(3, 3) return R def generaterays(intrinsics, R, T, imageshape): H, W = imageshape f = intrinsics['focallength'] u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='xy') dx = (u - W / 2) / f dy = -(v - H / 2) / f dz = -torch.oneslike(u) directions = torch.stack([dx, dy, dz], dim=-1) directions = torch.einsum('ij,hwj->hwi', R, directions) origins = T.expand(H, W, 3) return origins, directions def volumerender(nerf, origins, directions, numsamples=128, near=0.1, far=10.0): tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) zvals = 0.5 (tvals[1:] + tvals[:-1]) points = origins[..., None,:] + directions[..., None,:] zvals[None, None,:] colors, densities = nerf(points, directions[..., 0, 0,:].expandas(points)) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-torch.relu(densities) (far - near) / numsamples) weights = alpha torch.cumprod(torch.oneslike(alpha) - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-2) weights[..., 0] = alpha[..., 0] color = torch.sum(weights colors, dim=-2) return color def modulolossstep(nerf, encoder, images, intrinsics, r, N, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0 for i, Ii in enumerate(images): zi = encoder(Ii) azimuth, elevation, roll = zi syntheticviews = [] for k in range(N): newazimuth = (azimuth + 2 torch.pi k / N) % (2 torch.pi) latentpose = torch.stack([newazimuth, elevation, roll]) R = posetorotation(latentpose) T = torch.tensor([0, 0, r], device=latentpose.device) rayso, raysd = generaterays(intrinsics, R, T, Ii.shape) renderedview = volumerender(nerf, rayso, raysd) syntheticviews.append(renderedview) dists = [torch.sum((Ii - view) 2) for view in syntheticviews] mindist = min(dists) totalloss += mindist totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() def poseestimation(nerf, encoder, images, intrinsics, r, N): poses = [] for Ii in images: zi = encoder(Ii) azimuth, elevation, roll = zi bestpose = None bestdist = float('inf') for k in range(N): newazimuth = (azimuth + 2 torch.pi k / N) % (2 torch.pi) latentpose = torch.stack([newazimuth, elevation, roll]) R = posetorotation(latentpose) T = torch.tensor([0, 0, r], device=latentpose.device) rayso, raysd = generaterays(intrinsics, R, T, Ii.shape) renderedview = volumerender(nerf, rayso, raysd) dist = torch.sum((Ii - renderedview) 2) if dist < bestdist: bestdist = dist bestpose = latentpose poses.append(bestpose) return poses Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 256 crops (in 1D experiments) or full images. Replication Order (N): Integer N \in \mathbb{N}^. Typical values tested are N \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}. The method performs best when N is a multiple of the dataset's symmetry order K. Neural Network Architecture (1D): Positional encoding and four fully-connected layers of size 64 with ReLU activation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: The low dimensionality of SO(3) induces local minima. The modulo loss mitigates this by making the loss landscape more convex. Unknown Translation: If both object-to-camera distances and in-plane translations are unknown, the latent space becomes SE(3). MELON fails to jointly infer rotation Ri and translation Ti in this setup. Symmetry Matching: If N does not match the object's symmetry, convergence may be poor. The fractional covering DR(f^) indicates the likelihood of convergence. Time Complexity: Compute time per gradient step increases linearly with the replication order N. For N=1, it takes 23 ms/it; N=2 takes 34 ms/it; N=3 takes 43 ms/it; N=4 takes 52 ms/it. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the 'lego' scene with 6 views, MELON achieves a PSNR of 35.4 and a mean angular error of 0.901°, outperforming GNeRF (PSNR 35.3, error 1.21°) and failing COLMAP. Strengths: Does not require CNN pre-training or pose initialization (ab-initio). Does not require a discriminator (unlike GNeRF). Robust to small datasets (works with as few as 6 views). Limitations: Fails when translation is unknown (SE(3)). Requires known intrinsics and object-to-camera distance. MELON was introduced in the paper "MELON: NeRF with Unposed Images in SO(3)". It addresses the limitations of adversarial methods like GNeRF, which require large datasets, complex training schedules, and discriminators. MELON uses amortized inference via an encoder to map images to poses, combined with a modulo loss to handle rotational symmetries. It has been evaluated on the 'NeRF-Synthetic' dataset, RGB-MELON (spheres with quasi-symmetric textures), and real-world datasets (Gold Cape, Ethiopian Head, Toytruck). MELON: NeRF with Unposed Images in SO(3), https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv62453.2024.00084, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Time-dependent NeRF with Continuous Camera Motion
head: COPE-NeRF training, Continuous Optimization of NeRF and poses, Joint Optimization Pipeline, Joint Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields and Continuous Camera Motion
body: This method jointly optimizes a time-dependent Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and continuous camera motion from monocular video, representing the scene as local Signed Distance Field (SDF) and appearance fields at each time step. Unlike methods that train a single global NeRF mapped via noisy initial transformations, this approach uses local time-dependent representations constrained by consistency losses to avoid local minima. It builds on Camera Pose and Extrinsic/Intrinsic Optimization by modeling camera motion as continuous velocities rather than discrete pose parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of monocular RGB images (video frames) with normalized timesteps t \in [-1, 1]. No initial camera poses or intrinsics are required. Output: A time-dependent NeRF model (\phig, \phic) representing scene geometry and appearance, and a continuous camera motion network (\phiv) providing angular and linear velocities. Derived camera poses for each frame and the full scene geometry in a world coordinate system. Data Structures: 1. Time-dependent SDF Network (\phig): An MLP taking 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and time t as input, outputting scalar SDF value s \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Time-dependent Appearance Network (\phic): An MLP taking 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction d \in \mathbb{R}^2 (in camera coordinates), and time t as input, outputting color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. 3. Camera Motion Network (\phiv): An MLP taking time t as input, outputting angular velocity \omega(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and linear velocity v(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Sampling: At each iteration, 1024 rays are sampled, with 128 3D points per ray within a pre-defined depth range. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Networks: Initialize \phig, \phic, and \phiv. Normalize input timesteps to [-1, 1]. 2. Compute Camera Velocities: For a given time t, compute angular velocity \omega(t) and linear velocity v(t): \omega(t), v(t) = \phiv(t) 3. Integrate Camera Motion: To find the relative transformation from time t to t+l (l>0), use the Euler method with step size \Delta t = l/U (where U=10): R{t \to t+l} = \prod{u=0}^{U-1} \psi(\omega(t + u\Delta t)\Delta t) t{t \to t+l} = \sum{u=0}^{U-1} v(t + u\Delta t)\Delta t where \psi(\cdot): \mathbb{R}^3 \to SO(3) converts rotation angles to a rotation matrix using right-matrix multiplication. 4. Compute Transformation Matrix: Define the transformation P{t1 \to t2} from time t1 to t2: P{t1 \to t2} = \begin{cases} B{t1 \to t2} & \text{if } t1 \le t2 \\ (B{t2 \to t1})^{-1} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where B{t1 \to t2} = \begin{bmatrix} R{t1 \to t2} & t{t1 \to t2} \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}. 5. Render Color: For a ray r at time t, compute the rendered color \hat{C}t(r) using volume rendering with the SDF s(x,t) = \phig(x,t) and color c(x,t) = \phic(x,d,t). 6. Compute Surface Point: Calculate the expected surface point \tilde{x}(r,t) \in \mathbb{R}^3 for ray r at time t: \tilde{x}(r, t) = \sum{i=1}^K Li \sigmai xi(r, t) where K is the number of samples, Li are weights, \sigmai are opacities, and xi are sample points. 7. Calculate Losses: Rendering Loss (L{rgb}): L{rgb} = \frac{1}{|\Omega|} \sum{r \in \Omega} \|\hat{C}t(r) - Ct(r)\|^2 where \Omega is the set of rays and Ct(r) is the ground truth color. Eikonal Loss (L{eik}): Enforces the Eikonal equation for the SDF: L{eik} = \frac{1}{|X|} \sum{x \in X} \left\| \frac{\partial s(x, t)}{\partial x} - 1 \right\|^2 where X is the set of sampled 3D points. Flow Consistency Loss (L{flow}): Constrains SDF flow to match scene flow derived from camera motion: L{flow} = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum{x \in S} \left\| \frac{\partial s(x,t)}{\partial t} + (\omega(t) \times x + v(t))^T n(x,t) \right\| where S is the set of surface points and n(x) = \nablax s(x,t) is the surface normal. Photometric Consistency Loss (L{photo}): Projects surface points to neighboring frames t+n (n \in \mathcal{N}) and compares colors: \tilde{x}'{t \to t+n}(r, t) = P{t \to t+n} \tilde{x}'(r, t) L{photo} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}||\Omega|} \sum{n,r} \| C{t+n}[K \tilde{x}{t \to t+n}] - Ct(r) \|1 where K is the intrinsic matrix and [\cdot] denotes sampling. SDF Consistency Loss (L{sdf}): Encourages consistency between local SDF and the world frame SDF (where the world frame is the middle time step tw): L{sdf} = \frac{1}{|X|} \sum{x \in X} \| s(x, t) - s(x{t \to tw}, tw) \| where x{t \to tw} is point x transformed to the world frame via P{t \to tw}. 8. Total Loss: L = L{rgb} + \lambda1 L{eik} + \lambda2 L{flow} + \lambda3 L{photo} + \lambda4 L{sdf} Set \lambda4 = 0 for the first 200 epochs to avoid noisy initial transformations, then gradually increase it. 9. Joint Optimization: Update \phiv, \phig, \phic using Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001. 10. Fine-tuning: After joint optimization, fix the camera motion (derive poses P{t \to tw}), fix t to the world time step tw, drop \lambda2, \lambda3, \lambda4, and fine-tune \phig, \phic using all training frames for 5000 additional epochs with gradually decaying learning rate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ l = tend - tstart dt = l / U R = np.eye(3) tvec = np.zeros(3) for u in range(U): tcurr = tstart + u dt omega, v = phiv(tcurr) # Returns (3,) and (3,) # Convert rotation vector to matrix (right-multiplication) # Assuming psi converts angle vector to rotation matrix deltaR = psi(omega dt) R = R @ deltaR tvec += v dt return R, tvec def computetransformation(phiv, t1, t2): """ Compute P{t1->t2} using integration from 0 or relative to each other. Render Color and SDF # Assume samplepoints, weights, sigmas are computed via volume rendering # using phig(x, t) and phic(x, d, t) renderedcolors, surfacepoints, sdfs, normals = rendervolume(phig, phic, rays) # Lrgb lrgb = np.mean((renderedcolors - gtcolors)2) # Leik # Compute gradient of SDF w.r.t x sdfgrads = computesdfgradient(phig, surfacepoints) leik = np.mean((np.linalg.norm(sdfgrads, axis=1) - 1)2) # Lflow # Compute time derivative of SDF and scene flow # dS/dt approx via finite difference or network output if available # Scene flow = omega x x + v tcurr = rays.time # Assuming rays have time attribute omega, v = phiv(tcurr) sceneflow = np.cross(omega, surfacepoints) + v sdfflow = computesdftimederivative(phig, surfacepoints, tcurr) #: Implementation detail for dS/dt lflow = np.mean(np.abs(sdfflow + np.sum(sceneflow normals, axis=1))) # Lphoto lphoto = 0 for n in Nintervals: tneighbor = tcurr + n P = computetransformation(phiv, tcurr, tneighbor) # Project surface point to neighbor frame homopoints = np.hstack([surfacepoints, np.ones((surfacepoints.shape[0], 1))]) neighborpointshomo = (P @ homopoints.T).T neighborpoints = neighborpointshomo[:,:3] # Project to image plane neighboruv = K @ neighborpoints.T neighboruv = neighboruv[:2,:] / neighboruv[2,:] # Sample color from neighbor frame neighborcolors = sampleimage(K, neighboruv, gtcolorsneighbor) #: Helper to sample GT color at UV lphoto += np.mean(np.abs(neighborcolors - renderedcolors)) lphoto /= len(Nintervals) # Lsdf # Transform points to world frame (tw) Ptoworld = computetransformation(phiv, tcurr, tw) homopoints = np.hstack([surfacepoints, np.ones((surfacepoints.shape[0], 1))]) worldpointshomo = (Ptoworld @ homopoints.T).T worldpoints = worldpointshomo[:,:3] sdfsworld = phig(worldpoints, tw) lsdf = np.mean(np.abs(sdfs - sdfsworld)) # Total Loss ltotal = (lrgb + lambdaweights['eik'] leik + lambdaweights['flow'] lflow + lambdaweights['photo'] lphoto + lambdaweights['sdf'] lsdf) return ltotal, lrgb, leik, lflow, lphoto, lsdf def trainjointoptimization(phig, phic, phiv, dataloader, epochs=200, lambdaweightsinit=None): """ Joint optimization phase. """ optimizer = Adam([phig.parameters(), phic.parameters(), phiv.parameters()], lr=0.001) for epoch in range(epochs): for rays, gtcolors in dataloader: optimizer.zerograd() loss, = computeloss(phig, phic, phiv, rays, gtcolors,...) loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Adjust lambdasdf after 200 epochs if epoch >= 200: lambdaweightsinit['sdf'] =... # Gradually increase def trainfinetuning(phig, phic, dataloader, tw, Nintervals, K, gtcolorsall, epochs=5000): """ Fine-tuning phase: Fix camera motion, update NeRF only. """ optimizer = Adam([phig.parameters(), phic.parameters()], lr=0.001) # Decaying LR for epoch in range(epochs): for rays, gtcolors in dataloader: optimizer.zerograd() # Recompute transformations based on fixed phiv # Only compute Lrgb and Leik (Lflow, Lphoto, Lsdf dropped) #: Implementation of Lrgb and Leik as defined above lrgb, leik = computerenderingandeikonallosses(phig, phic, rays, gtcolors) loss = lrgb + lambdaweightsinit['eik'] leik loss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: U = 10: Number of sub-intervals between consecutive frames for integration. tw: World time step, chosen as the middle frame in the training set. Learning rate: 0.001 for Adam during initial joint optimization. Fine-tuning epochs: 5000 additional epochs with gradually decaying learning rate. Sampling: 1024 rays and 128 3D points per ray within a pre-defined depth range. Input normalization: Timesteps normalized from -1 to 1. \lambda4 = 0 for the first 200 epochs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Initial Transformations: Early in training, camera poses are noisy. Setting \lambda4 = 0 for the first 200 epochs prevents the SDF consistency loss from hindering convergence. Local Minima: Using a single global NeRF with noisy initial transformations can get stuck in local minima. The time-dependent local representation avoids this. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On average, reduces depth square relative errors by at least 82% on Co3D and 78% on Scannet datasets compared to other methods. Strengths: Prior-free pipeline; does not rely on initial camera poses or intrinsics; handles complex camera motions (e.g., large rotations in Co3D). Limitations: Requires monocular video; performance depends on the quality of the continuous motion modeling. When to use: When initial camera poses are unavailable or unreliable, and high-quality geometry reconstruction is needed from monocular video. When not: When high-quality initial poses are available and a simpler global NeRF optimization suffices. Origin: The method was introduced in "Joint Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields and Continuous Camera Motion from a Monocular Video". History: It builds on SDF-based NeRF models [29] and continuous camera motion modeling. It addresses limitations of prior works like NeRFmm [31] and NoPe-NeRF [2] which either require initial poses or use global NeRFs prone to local minima with noisy transformations. Usage: Evaluated on ScanNet (4 scenes) and Co3D (5 scenes) datasets for novel-view synthesis and depth evaluation. name: Camera Preconditioning
head: CamP (Camera Preconditioning), Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields
body: Camera Preconditioning (CamP) is a technique to normalize and decorrelate camera parameters during Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) optimization by transforming the optimization problem from direct camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}i to latent preconditioned parameters \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i, using a preconditioner matrix Pi^{-1} derived from the covariance of projection derivatives. It addresses issues where parameters are correlated or have different units (e.g., translation in world units vs. focal length in pixels), which causes ill-conditioning in naive optimization. Unlike per-parameter scaling or adaptive optimizers like Adam, CamP decouples highly correlated coefficients by using the full covariance matrix, ensuring that parameter updates are scaled according to their sensitivity to the rendered image. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}i^0 for each camera i; a set of randomly sampled 3D points within each camera's frustum; hyperparameters \lambda and \mu. Outputs: Preconditioned camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}i used in the NeRF forward pass; latent parameters \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i optimized by the gradient descent algorithm. Data Structures: Camera Parameters (\boldsymbol{\phi}i): A vector containing the specific parameterization for camera i. Common parameterizations include: SE3: 6D screw-axis representation (rotation \mathbf{r}, translation \mathbf{v}). SE3+Focal+Intrinsics: SE3 augmented with focal length (f), principal point (u0, v0), and radial distortion (k1, k2). Focal length residual is multiplicative: f' = f \exp(\Delta f). FocalPose+Intrinsics: Joint pose and focal length parameterization, modified as a residual with respect to initial estimates, plus principal point and radial distortion. SCNeRF: 6D rotation, residual 3D translation (tx, ty, tz), focal lengths (fu, fv), principal point (u0, v0), and radial distortion (k1, k2). Preconditioner (Pi^{-1}): A k \times k matrix where k is the dimension of the camera parameter vector. Computed as Pi^{-1} = (\Sigma{\Pi} + \lambda \text{diag}(\Sigma{\Pi}) + \mu I)^{-1/2}. Covariance Matrix (\Sigma{\Pi}): A k \times k matrix representing the covariance of the derivatives of projected points with respect to camera parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Point Sampling: For each camera i, sample m points within its view frustum. Sample pixel positions \mathbf{p} = (u, v) uniformly. Sample normalized ray distances d \in [0, 1] uniformly between normalized near and far planes d \sim U(n, f). Unnormalize sampled depths using the power ladder transform of Zip-NeRF, with a curve identical to its ray sampling distribution. 2. Compute Jacobian: Compute the Jacobian matrix J{\Pi} \in \mathbb{R}^{2m \times k} of the projection function \Pi(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\phi}) with respect to the camera parameters \boldsymbol{\phi} at the current parameter estimate \boldsymbol{\phi}0. The rows correspond to the 2D coordinates of the m projected points. 3. Compute Covariance: Calculate the covariance matrix \Sigma{\Pi} = J{\Pi}^\top J{\Pi}. 4. Compute Preconditioner: Apply dampening to improve conditioning: Pi^{-1} = (\Sigma{\Pi} + \lambda \text{diag}(\Sigma{\Pi}) + \mu I)^{-1/2} where \lambda and \mu are dampening hyperparameters, and I is the identity matrix. 5. Reformulate Optimization: Define latent parameters \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i such that the actual camera parameters used in the NeRF are \boldsymbol{\phi}i = Pi^{-1} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i. This transforms the covariance of the projected points with respect to \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i to the identity matrix Ik (ZCA whitening). 6. Optimization Loop: For each iteration, compute the loss \mathcal{L} using \boldsymbol{\phi}i = Pi^{-1} \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i. Update \tilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}i using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). Shared Intrinsics: If intrinsic parameters are shared across cameras, add a variance loss term \mathcal{L}{\text{shared}} to minimize the variance of these shared parameters. 7. Static Preconditioner: The preconditioner Pi^{-1} is computed once at initialization and kept static during optimization to avoid invalidating the running averages of gradient moments in optimizers like Adam. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def projectpoints(params, points3d): """Standard pinhole projection with optional distortion. Returns 2D coordinates (2m,)""" # Standard differentiable projection implementation for the chosen parameterization pass def computejacobianprojection(params, points3d, eps=1e-5): """Compute Jacobian of projection w.r.t camera parameters via finite differences.""" k = len(params) m = len(points3d) J = np.zeros((2 m, k)) for j in range(k): paramsplus = params.copy() paramsplus[j] += eps projplus = projectpoints(paramsplus, points3d) projminus = projectpoints(params, points3d) J[:, j] = (projplus - projminus) / (2 eps) return J def computepreconditioner(params0, points3d, lambdaval, muval): """Compute the per-camera preconditioner matrix Pinv.""" k = len(params0) J = computejacobianprojection(params0, points3d) Sigma = J.T @ J DampedSigma = Sigma + lambdaval np.diag(np.diag(Sigma)) + muval np.eye(k) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(DampedSigma) eigenvalues = np.maximum(eigenvalues, 1e-10) Dinvsqrt = np.diag(1.0 / np.sqrt(eigenvalues)) Pinv = eigenvectors @ Dinvsqrt @ eigenvectors.T return Pinv def optimizecameras(camerasdata, points3d, lambdaval, muval, lr, warmupsteps, totalsteps): """Main optimization loop for Camera Preconditioning.""" optimizedlatentparams = [] for cam in camerasdata: phi0 = cam['params0'] camid = cam['id'] # 1. Compute static preconditioner at initialization Pinv = computepreconditioner(phi0, points3d[camid], lambdaval, muval) P = np.linalg.inv(Pinv) # 2. Initialize latent parameters tildephi = P @ phi0 grad = np.zeroslike(tildephi) # 3. Optimization loop for step in range(totalsteps): # Map latent parameters to actual camera parameters phi = Pinv @ tildephi # 4. Compute loss and gradient via differentiable rendering # Standard differentiable volume rendering forward/backward pass loss, gradphi = renderandbackprop(phi, points3d[camid]) # Transform gradient to latent space: dL/d(tildephi) = Pinv^T @ dL/d(phi) grad = Pinv.T @ gradphi # 5. Apply learning rate schedule warmupfactor = min(1.0, step / warmupsteps) cosinedecay = np.cos(np.pi step / (2 totalsteps)) currentlr = lr warmupfactor cosinedecay # 6. Update latent parameters tildephi -= currentlr grad # 7. Handle shared intrinsic variance loss if applicable if cam.get('sharedintrinsics'): sharedloss = computevarianceloss(cam['sharedparams']) gradshared = computegradient(sharedloss, cam['sharedparams']) cam['sharedparams'] -= currentlr gradshared optimizedlatentparams.append(tildephi) return optimizedlatentparams def renderandbackprop(phi, points3d): """Standard differentiable volume rendering. Returns loss and gradient w.r.t phi.""" # Standard differentiable rendering implementation pass def computevarianceloss(sharedparams): """Compute variance loss for shared intrinsic parameters.""" # Standard variance computation over shared parameters pass def computegradient(loss, params): """Compute gradient of loss w.r.t params.""" # Standard automatic differentiation or finite difference gradient pass Parameters: \lambda: Dampening parameter for the diagonal of the covariance matrix. Typical value: 10^{-1}. \mu: Dampening parameter for the identity matrix added to the covariance matrix. Typical value: 10^{-8}. Learning Rate for Camera Parameters: Logarithmically decays from 10^{-3} to 10^{-4} over training. Warmup Multiplier: Cosine-decayed from 10^{-8} to 1 for the first 2500 iterations. Variance Loss Weights (Shared Intrinsics): Focal length 10^{-1}, Principal Point 10^{-2}, Radial Distortion 10^{-2}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Re-parameterization: Avoid updating the preconditioner during optimization. Dynamic updates render the running averages of gradient moments used in optimizers like Adam inaccurate. Lens Distortion: Lens distortion parameters can cause very small changes to dramatically affect point projection, making the covariance matrix ill-conditioned. Dampening parameters \lambda and \mu are especially important in this case. Local Minima: Preconditioning does not always prevent falling into local minima (e.g., white floaters in synthetic NeRF dataset due to bad camera poses). Procrustes Alignment: The Procrustes alignment method breaks when focal length changes significantly, so it is omitted in evaluation. Time Complexity: The preconditioner computation involves eigendecomposition of a k \times k matrix, where k is the number of camera parameters (typically small, e.g., 10-20). Training time is approximately 2 hours on 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs for 25,000 steps. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the preconditioner matrix Pi^{-1} for each camera (O(k^2) per camera) and the sampled points. Measured Performance: On the perturbed 360 dataset, preconditioning improves PSNR between 4.3 and 6.8 dB for all camera parameterizations. On the perturbed synthetic dataset, FocalPose+Intrinsics with CamP achieves PSNR 28.29, SSIM 0.930, LPIPS 0.064, and camera metrics R=0.420^\circ, p=0.186, f=54.3 px. Strengths: Decorrelates parameter effects and normalizes their scale, leading to improved convergence and accuracy. Handles mixed units and correlated parameters better than per-parameter scaling or Adam. Limitations: Does not guarantee escape from local minima. The preconditioner is computed once at initialization based on the initial camera parameter estimate. Camera Preconditioning (CamP) was introduced by K. Park et al. in the paper "CamP: Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields" (ACM Trans. Graph., Vol. 42, No. 6, Article 208, December 2023). It builds on the observation that naive camera parameterizations in NeRF optimization are ill-conditioned due to differences in parameter magnitude (e.g., world units vs. pixels) and spurious correlations. The method draws inspiration from numerical methods, specifically the Zero Component Analysis (ZCA) whitening transform, to design a per-camera preconditioner. It is implemented on top of ZipNeRF and used on datasets like 360, Perturbed-360, Perturbed-Synthetic, and ARKit. CamP: Camera Preconditioning for Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3618321, fetched 2026-10-30

name: SPARF
head: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses, SPARF Joint Pose-NeRF Training Strategy, joint pose-NeRF optimization, pose-NeRF training
body: SPARF is a joint pose-NeRF training strategy designed for novel view synthesis from sparse input views (as few as 3) with noisy camera pose estimates. It solves the problems of overfitting and geometric inconsistency inherent in sparse-view regimes by enforcing multi-view geometry constraints, specifically multi-view correspondence and depth consistency losses, rather than relying solely on photometric loss. Unlike sibling methods that optimize poses and NeRF weights using independent per-image photometric supervision, SPARF explicitly connects training views through pixel correspondences to drive convergence to a globally accurate pose and scene solution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: n RGB images (typically n=3) with large viewpoint variations and noisy camera pose estimates. No prior on scene shape is assumed. Outputs: Optimized camera poses \hat{P} and NeRF parameters \Theta defining the radiance field. Data Structures and Layouts: Camera Pose P: Represented as a world-to-camera transformation matrix. Translation: A 3D embedding vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3 optimized directly. Rotation: A continuous 6D embedding vector r \in \mathbb{R}^6 optimized directly. The rotation matrix R is recovered from r using a Gram-Schmidt-like process. Given r = [a1^T, a2^T] where a1, a2 \in \mathbb{R}^3, the columns of R = [b1, b2, b3] are computed as: b1 = \frac{a1}{\|a1\|} b2 = \frac{a2 - (a2 \cdot b1)b1}{\|a2 - (a2 \cdot b1)b1\|} b3 = b1 \times b2 NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. The sources note that for LLFF joint optimization, a single coarse MLP suffices, reducing training time compared to hierarchical sampling. Correspondences: Dense matches q for each pixel p and confidence wp inferred from a pre-trained matching model (e.g., PDC-Net). Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-compute Correspondences: Extract dense matches between all pairs of training views using a pre-trained dense correspondence regression network (e.g., PDC-Net). Filter matches by confidence threshold \gamma = 0.95 (PR operator) and optionally by cyclic consistency < 1.5 pixels. 2. Initialize: Initialize NeRF weights and camera poses (noisy estimates). Set depth sampling bounds. For LLFF, use inverse depth space with lower bound 1/tn = 1 and upper bound 1/tf = 0.05. For DTU/Replica, use metric space [tn, tf]. If poses are noisy, expand depth range by factor \epsilon = 0.3, i.e., [(1-\epsilon)tn, (1+\epsilon)tf]. 3. Staged Training Loop: Iterate for total N iterations (typically 100K for joint optimization). Stage 1 (Iterations 0 to 0.3N): Jointly optimize camera poses \hat{P} and the coarse NeRF MLP \Thetac. Stage 2 (Iterations 0.3N to N): Freeze camera poses \hat{P}. Optimize both coarse and fine NeRF MLPs (\Thetac, \Thetaf) if hierarchical sampling is used. Per-Iteration Procedure: 1. Photometric Loss: Sample x random pixels from all training images. Compute rendered color \hat{I} and photometric loss \mathcal{L}{photo} against ground truth I. 2. Multi-View Correspondence Loss: Sample an image pair (Ii, Ij) and a subset of 1024 matches. For each match (p, q) with confidence wp: Backproject pixel p in Ii to 3D using rendered depth \hat{z}(p; \Theta, \hat{P}i) and pose \hat{P}i. Project the 3D point into view Ij using \hat{P}j to get predicted pixel \hat{q}. Compute re-projection error \rho(\|q - \hat{q}\|^2) using Huber loss \rho. Accumulate \mathcal{L}{MVCorr} = \sum wp \rho(\dots). 3. Depth Consistency Loss: Sample a training view Ii with pose \hat{P}i. Find the closest other training view and compute a virtual "unknown" pose P{un} by interpolating the poses of two close-by training views. Sample 1024 pixels p in Ii. Backproject p to 3D point r{un,y} using \hat{P}i and rendered depth \hat{z}(p; \Theta, \hat{P}i). Project r{un,y} into the virtual view P{un} to get pixel y and depth zy. Compute rendered depth \hat{z}(y; \Theta, P{un}) at y in the virtual view. Calculate visibility mask \gammay = T{un, zy} = \exp \left( -\sum{m'=1}^{m} \sigma{m'} \delta{m'} \right) evaluated at the virtual view ray, where T is accumulated transmittance. \gammay \approx 1 if unoccluded, \approx 0 if occluded. Compute \mathcal{L}{DCons} = \sum \gammay \rho(zy - \hat{z}(y; \Theta, P{un})). Note: Backpropagate through the pseudo-supervision zy and \hat{z}, but not through \hat{P}i. 4. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambdac \mathcal{L}{MVCorr} + \lambdad \mathcal{L}{DCons}. 5. Update: Update parameters using Adam optimizer. 4. Loss Weight Decay: After Stage 1 (poses frozen) or from start if poses are fixed, halve \lambdac every 10,000 iterations to gradually increase photometric loss importance and correct geometry errors. Formulas: Volume Rendering: \hat{I}{i,p} = \sum{m=1}^{M} \alpham cm, where \alpham = Tm (1 - \exp(-\sigmam \deltam)) and Tm = \exp \left( -\sum{m'=1}^{m} \sigma{m'} \delta{m'} \right). \deltam = t{m+1} - tm is the distance between adjacent samples. Visibility Mask: \gammay = T{un, zy} = \exp \left( -\sum{m'=1}^{m} \sigma{m'} \delta{m'} \right) evaluated at the unseen view ray. \gammay is close to 1 if no point with large density exists between camera center and 3D point, otherwise close to 0. Rotation Recovery: R = f(r) = [b1, b2, b3], where b1, b2, b3 are computed using a generalized cross product to ensure orthogonality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def huberloss(error, delta=1.0): abserr = torch.abs(error) quadratic = torch.min(abserr, torch.fulllike(abserr, delta)) return 0.5 quadratic2 + delta (abserr - quadratic) def constructrays(poses, u, v, intrinsics): # u, v are 1D tensors of shape (N,) B, N = u.shape[0], u.shape[0] ones = torch.oneslike(u) pixcoords = torch.stack([u, v, ones], dim=0).unsqueeze(0) # Shape: (1, 3, N) pixcoords = pixcoords / intrinsics[0,:3,:3].unsqueeze(-1) origins = poses[:,:3, 3].unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1).expand(1, 3, N) directions = torch.bmm(pixcoords, poses[:,:3,:3].transpose(1, 2)).squeeze(0) # Shape: (3, N) directions = directions / torch.norm(directions, dim=0, keepdim=True) return origins, directions def volumerender(nerfmodel, origins, directions, near, far, numsamples): # origins, directions: (B, 3, N) B,, N = origins.shape tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples, device=origins.device) # For LLFF, sample in inverse depth space; for DTU/Replica, linear depth. zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals pts = origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) zvals.view(1, -1, 1) ptsflat = pts.view(B, numsamples, N, 3) dirsflat = directions.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples, -1, -1).view(B, numsamples, N, 3) sigmaflat, rgbflat = nerfmodel(ptsflat, dirsflat) sigma = torch.nn.functional.softplus(sigmaflat).view(B, numsamples, N) rgb = rgbflat.view(B, numsamples, N, 3) deltas = zvals[1:] - zvals[:-1] deltainf = torch.tensor(1e10, device=origins.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf]) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = alpha T color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb, dim=1) depth = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=1) return color, depth, weights, T def project3dtopixel(pts, pose, intrinsics): # pts: (B, 3, N), pose: (B, 3, 4), intrinsics: (B, 3, 3) campts = torch.bmm(pose[:,:3,:3], pts) + pose[:,:3, 3].unsqueeze(-1) pix = torch.bmm(intrinsics, campts) return pix[:, 0,:], pix[:, 1,:], campts[:, 2,:] def interpolatepose(p1, p2, t=0.5): tun = (1 - t) p1[:,:3, 3] + t p2[:,:3, 3] R1 = p1[:,:3,:3] R2 = p2[:,:3,:3] Run = (1 - t) R1 + t R2 b1 = Run[:,:, 0] b1 = b1 / torch.norm(b1, dim=1, keepdim=True) b2raw = Run[:,:, 1] - torch.sum(b1 Run[:,:, 1], dim=1, keepdim=True) b1 b2 = b2raw / torch.norm(b2raw, dim=1, keepdim=True) b3 = torch.cross(b1, b2, dim=1) Run = torch.stack([b1, b2, b3], dim=2) Pun = torch.zeroslike(p1) Pun[:,:3,:3] = Run Pun[:,:3, 3] = tun return Pun def sparfstep(nerfmodel, poses, images, matches, config): B, C, H, W = images.shape optimizernerf, optimizerposes = config['optnerf'], config['optposes'] nerfmodel.train() optimizernerf.zerograd() optimizerposes.zerograd() # 1. Photometric Loss idx = torch.randint(0, H W, (B, config['numphoto'])) u = (idx % W).float() v = (idx // W).float() o, d = constructrays(poses, u, v, config['K']) cphoto,,, = volumerender(nerfmodel, o, d, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) gt = images[:,:, v.long(), u.long()] lossphoto = torch.mean((cphoto - gt) 2) # 2. Multi-View Correspondence Loss lossmvc = 0.0 pairidx = torch.randint(0, B, (2,)) i, j = pairidx[0], pairidx[1] midx = torch.randint(0, matches[i].shape[0], (config['nummvc'],)) pu, pv = matches[i][midx,:2].T qu, qv = matches[i][midx, 2:4].T w = matches[i][midx, 4] oi, di = constructrays(poses[i:i+1], pu, pv, config['K']), depthi,, = volumerender(nerfmodel, oi, di, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) pts3d = oi + di depthi.unsqueeze(1) qpredu, qpredv, = project3dtopixel(pts3d, poses[j:j+1], config['K']) error = torch.norm(torch.stack([qpredu - qu, qpredv - qv], dim=1), dim=1) lossmvc = torch.mean(w huberloss(error)) # 3. Depth Consistency Loss lossdc = 0.0 idc = torch.randint(0, B, (1,)).item() kdc = (idc + 1) % B Pun = interpolatepose(poses[idc:idc+1], poses[kdc:kdc+1]) udc, vdc = torch.rand(config['numdc']), torch.rand(config['numdc']) odc, ddc = constructrays(poses[idc:idc+1], udc, vdc, config['K']), depthdc,, = volumerender(nerfmodel, odc, ddc, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) ptsun = odc + ddc depthdc.unsqueeze(1) yu, yv, zy = project3dtopixel(ptsun, Pun, config['K']) oun, dun = constructrays(Pun, yu, yv, config['K']), depthun,, Tun = volumerender(nerfmodel, oun, dun, config['near'], config['far'], config['numsamples']) tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., config['numsamples'], device=oun.device) zvalsun = config['near'] (1. - tvals) + config['far'] tvals # Find index of zy in zvalsun for each pixel idxz = torch.argmin(torch.abs(zvalsun.unsqueeze(1) - zy.unsqueeze(0)), dim=0) # Correct indexing for Tun: (B, numsamples, N) -> (numsamples, N) gammay = Tun[0, idxz, torch.arange(config['numdc'])] lossdc = torch.mean(gammay huberloss(zy - depthun)) # Total Loss lambdac = config['lambdac'] lambdad = config['lambdad'] totalloss = lossphoto + lambdac lossmvc + lambdad lossdc totalloss.backward() optimizernerf.step() optimizerposes.step() return totalloss.item(), lossphoto.item(), lossmvc.item(), lossdc.item() Parameters: Training Duration: 100K iterations for joint pose-NeRF refinement. Hardware: ~10 hours on a single A100 GPU. Image Resolution: Resized to 360×600. Samples per Step: 1024 pixel rays for photometric loss, 1024 matches for correspondence loss, 1024 pixels for depth consistency loss. Loss Weights: \lambdac = 10^{-3}, \lambdad = 10^{-3}. On DTU with fixed GT poses, \lambdac = 10^{-4}, \lambdad = 10^{-3}. Optimizer: Adam. NeRF LR: 5 \times 10^{-4} decaying to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Pose LR: 1 \times 10^{-3} decaying to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Positional Encoding: Coarse-to-fine schedule. Joint optimization: frequency width linearly adjusted from 40% to 70% of iterations. Fixed poses: 10% to 50%. Depth Bounds: LLFF: inverse depth [1, 0.05]. DTU/Replica: metric [tn, tf]. Noisy poses: expand by \epsilon=0.3. Correspondence Filter: Confidence \gamma = 0.95, cyclic consistency < 1.5 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Direct photometric loss causes overfitting to training views, especially with noisy poses. Solved by using multi-view correspondence as the main signal. Occlusion: Depth consistency loss is invalid for occluded pixels or those projected outside the virtual view. Handled by visibility mask \gammay. Training Length: Training longer than necessary with fixed GT poses leads to overfitting. Recommended limits: 50K/70K iterations for 3 views (DTU/Replica/LLFF respectively), 100K/140K for 6 views, 150K/200K for 9 views. Degenerate Geometry: High-frequency positional encodings with standard NeRF on few views lead to degenerate geometry. Coarse-to-fine PE prevents this. General framework for optimizing poses and NeRF parameters jointly. SPARF is a specific instance tailored for sparse views. Camera Pose and Parameter Optimization Uses local optimization and multi-scale features for pose refinement. SPARF uses global multi-view geometry constraints. MELON Models continuous camera motion over time. SPARF assumes static scene with discrete poses. Time-dependent NeRF with Continuous Camera Motion Uses preconditioning to stabilize pose optimization. SPARF uses staged training and specific loss functions. Camera Preconditioning Uses view matching losses. SPARF uses multi-view correspondence and depth consistency. VMRF (View Matching Neural Radiance Fields) Optimizes poses and appearance factors. SPARF focuses on geometry and pose. NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization Optimizes poses at test time. SPARF optimizes during training. Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization Time Complexity: 100K iterations, ~10 hours on A100 GPU. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory usage plus storage for pre-computed correspondences. Performance: DTU (3 views, noisy poses): PSNR 17.74, SSIM 0.71, LPIPS 0.26, Rot 1.81°, Trans 5.0×100. Outperforms BARF (PSNR 10.71) and SCNeRF (PSNR 12.04). LLFF (3 views, identity poses): PSNR 19.58, SSIM 0.61, LPIPS 0.31, Rot 0.53°, Trans 2.8×100. Outperforms BARF (PSNR 17.47) and SCNeRF (PSNR 17.10). Replica (3 views, COLMAP poses): PSNR 26.98, SSIM 0.88, LPIPS 0.13, Rot 0.15°, Trans 0.36×100. Outperforms DS-NeRF (PSNR 24.75) and SCNeRF (PSNR 22.54). Strengths: Handles sparse views (3 images) and noisy poses effectively. Prevents overfitting through multi-view constraints. Limitations: Requires pre-computed dense correspondences. Performance degrades if correspondences are inaccurate. Limited to static scenes. When to Use: Sparse-view novel view synthesis with noisy initial poses. When Not to Use: Dense-view settings (other methods may be more efficient), dynamic scenes, or when high-quality initial poses are available (fixed pose optimization may suffice). SPARF was introduced in the paper "SPARF: Neural Radiance Fields from Sparse and Noisy Poses". It addresses the challenge of novel view synthesis in the sparse-view regime, where traditional NeRF methods overfit and fail to converge to a globally consistent geometry. The method builds on principles of multi-view geometry, specifically using pixel correspondences and depth consistency to constrain the optimization. It was evaluated on DTU, LLFF, and Replica datasets, setting new state-of-the-art results for few-view synthesis with noisy poses.
