name: Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization
head: Test-time pose and appearance optimization
body: Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization is a post-training evaluation procedure that first optimizes camera poses and then optimizes appearance embeddings to handle unconstrained image collections with varying lighting and transient objects. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by decoupling pose refinement and appearance adaptation into two sequential stages, addressing the limitations of methods that optimize only poses (e.g., BARF) or only appearance (e.g., NeRF-W). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model (weights \Theta), a set of test images \{Ii\}, and initial camera pose estimates Pi for the test images. Outputs: Refined camera poses P'i and optimized appearance embeddings Ai for the test images. Data Structures: Pose Parameters: For each test image i, a 6-dimensional vector representing rotation and translation, or a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix. Appearance Embeddings: A learnable vector ai per test image, concatenated with the positional encoding of the 3D point before the density/color MLPs. NeRF Weights: Fixed during optimization. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Pose Optimization Initialization: Initialize appearance embeddings Ai randomly. Initialize test pose parameters Pi using Procrustes analysis: compute the alignment matrix M between the trained poses of training images and their ground-truth poses, then apply M to the ground-truth test poses. Freezing: Freeze all NeRF network weights \Theta. Optimization: Optimize Pi and Ai jointly using the test images. Sampling: Sample 1024 rays per iteration. For each ray, sample 128 points for the coarse model and 128 points for the fine model. Duration: 20,000 iterations. Learning Rates: 1 \times 10^{-4} for pose parameters Pi; 5 \times 10^{-3} for appearance embeddings Ai. No learning rate decay is applied. 2. Stage 2: Appearance Optimization Freezing: Freeze the refined pose parameters P'i from Stage 1. Re-initialization: Re-initialize the appearance embeddings Ai. Optimization: Optimize only Ai using the test images. Data Splitting: To prevent information leakage, optimize on the left half of the test images and evaluate only on the right half. Duration: 20 epochs. Learning Rates: 1 \times 10^{-1} for appearance embeddings Ai. No learning rate decay is applied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def testtimetwostageoptimization(nerfmodel, testimages, initialposes, traintrainedposes, traingtposes): """ nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF with fixed weights. testimages: List of test images [I1,..., IN]. initialposes: Initial pose estimates for test images. traintrainedposes: Trained poses of training images. traingtposes: Ground-truth poses of training images. """ N = len(testimages) # Stage 1: Pose Optimization # Initialize appearance embeddings randomly appearanceembeddings = [random.randn(1, 256) for in testimages] # Initialize poses using Procrustes analysis: compute alignment matrix M # between traintrainedposes and traingtposes, then apply M to initialposes poses = applyprocrustesalignment(initialposes, traintrainedposes, traingtposes) for iteration in range(20000): rays = samplerays(testimages, poses, numrays=1024) renderedcolors = nerfmodel.render(rays, poses, appearanceembeddings) loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) # Perform optimizer step for poses and appearance embeddings # LRpose = 1e-4, LRappearance = 5e-3 refinedposes = poses # Stage 2: Appearance Optimization # Re-initialize appearance embeddings appearanceembeddings = [random.randn(1, 256) for in testimages] leftimages = testimages[:N//2] rightimages = testimages[N//2:] for epoch in range(20): rays = samplerays(leftimages, refinedposes, numrays=1024) renderedcolors = nerfmodel.render(rays, refinedposes, appearanceembeddings) loss = computeloss(renderedcolors, rays.gtcolors) # Perform optimizer step for appearance embeddings # LRappearance = 1e-1 evalrays = samplerays(rightimages, refinedposes, numrays=1024) evalrendered = nerfmodel.render(evalrays, refinedposes, appearanceembeddings) evalloss = computeloss(evalrendered, evalrays.gtcolors) return refinedposes, appearanceembeddings Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Information Leakage: Optimizing on the same images used for evaluation can lead to overfitting. The method mitigates this by splitting test images into training (left half) and evaluation (right half) sets during Stage 2. Local Minima: Without proper initialization or candidate heads, pose optimization may fall into local minima. Procrustes analysis provides a robust initialization based on training data alignment. Time Complexity: The optimization is performed at test time, adding latency. Stage 1 requires 20,000 iterations, and Stage 2 requires 20 epochs. The number of sampled rays is reduced to 1024 per iteration (from 2048 in training) to speed up computation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing pose parameters and appearance embeddings for all test images. The NeRF weights are frozen, so no additional memory for model weights is needed. Strengths: Handles unconstrained image collections with varying lighting and transient objects effectively. Decoupling pose and appearance optimization improves convergence stability. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to the two-stage optimization process. Requires a pre-trained NeRF model. Performance depends on the quality of the initial pose estimates. When to Use: When dealing with unconstrained image collections where camera poses are not known or are inaccurate, and lighting conditions vary significantly. When Not to Use: When computational resources are limited, or when camera poses are already accurate and lighting is consistent. Test-Time Two-Stage Optimization was introduced in the context of UP-NeRF (Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields). It addresses the limitations of previous methods like BARF, which only optimizes poses, and NeRF-W, which only optimizes appearance given fixed poses. UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03784v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization
head: Joint Pose Optimization, Unposed NeRF Optimization, Self-Calibration in NeRF
body: Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization reconstructs a 3D scene from an unposed image collection by simultaneously optimizing the neural radiance field parameters and the camera extrinsic (and optionally intrinsic) parameters. It treats camera poses as learnable variables in the optimization loop, addressing the dependency between pose estimation and scene modeling. This approach builds on Camera Pose and Extrinsic/Intrinsic Optimization by extending the optimization domain to include the scene representation itself. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of differentiable rendering, where the rendered pixel color \hat{C}(r) is a differentiable function of the camera pose P and the NeRF parameters \Theta. The optimization problem is typically formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} with respect to both \Theta and P: \min{\Theta, P} \mathcal{L}(\hat{C}(r; \Theta, P), C(r)) where C(r) is the ground-truth pixel color. The gradient \nablaP \mathcal{L} allows the camera pose to be updated via an optimizer (e.g., Adam, SGD) in lockstep with the NeRF weights. Key shared components include: 1. Ray Casting: Computing ray origins \hat{o} and directions \hat{d} from pixel coordinates using current camera estimates. For a pinhole camera model with focal length f and rotation R and translation t: \hat{o} = t \hat{d} = R \begin{pmatrix} (u - W/2)/f \\ -(v - H/2)/f \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} 2. Differentiable Rendering: The volume rendering integral is computed via discrete summation, allowing backpropagation through the ray marching process to the pose parameters. 3. Joint Optimization: Separate optimizers or a combined optimizer are used to update NeRF weights and pose parameters, often with different learning rates to stabilize convergence. RoDynRF enables dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular videos without known camera poses by jointly optimizing intrinsics, extrinsics, and both static and dynamic radiance fields. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like VMRF and NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization by explicitly separating static and dynamic components via a two-branch architecture and using motion masks to isolate static geometry for robust pose estimation, thereby handling unposed, in-the-wild video data. See RoDynRF. VMRF is a method for novel view synthesis that learns Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations without prior knowledge of camera poses or hand-crafted camera pose distributions. It employs a view matching scheme using unbalanced optimal transport to map features from a rendered image (with a random pose) to a real image, generating a feature transport plan. This plan guides a pose calibration technique that predicts relative pose transformations to rectify randomized poses into estimated real-image poses, which are then used to jointly refine the NeRF and camera parameters. Unlike GNeRF, which estimates absolute poses directly and requires accurate pose distributions, VMRF estimates relative poses, making it robust to out-of-dataset views. See VMRF (View Matching Neural Radiance Fields). This method jointly optimizes camera poses and neural scene representations for unconstrained image collections containing varying illumination and transient occluders, without requiring camera pose priors. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF optimization by introducing a candidate head for robust pose estimation in "hard-pose" images and a loss scheduling mechanism that transitions from candidate-specific to shared scene representations. It builds on Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization by addressing the "chicken-and-egg" problem of pose estimation in unposed data through surrogate tasks and transient-aware supervision. See NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization. Self-calibrating joint optimization model for NeRF that optimizes unknown poses and camera intrinsic parameters for non-linear camera models such as fish-eye lens models. Use curriculum learning to gradually introduce the nonlinear camera/noise parameters to the joint optimization. The problem of optimizing camera poses alongside radiance fields emerged as a solution to the dependency on Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines, which can fail on textureless or repetitive scenes. Jeong et al. introduced a self-calibrating joint optimization model for NeRF (SCNeRF) in August 2021, which optimized unknown poses and intrinsic parameters for non-linear camera models like fish-eye lenses using curriculum learning. GNeRF (March 2021) by Meng et al. used pose as a generative latent code, obtaining coarse poses via adversarial training. These methods laid the groundwork for more complex joint optimization strategies like RoDynRF, VMRF, and NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28

name: RoDynRF
head: Robust Dynamic Radiance Fields
body: RoDynRF enables dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular videos without known camera poses by jointly optimizing intrinsics, extrinsics, and both static and dynamic radiance fields. It distinguishes itself from static pose optimization methods by introducing a two-branch architecture that separates background and moving regions, using motion masks to exclude dynamic pixels during pose estimation to prevent optimization drift. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A video sequence with N frames. Output: Jointly optimized camera poses [R|t]i for i \in [1..N], a shared focal length f, static radiance field Vs, dynamic radiance field Vd, and a scene flow MLP for deformation. Data Structures: Static Radiance Field: Explicit neural voxel grid Vs encoding static scene geometry and appearance. Dynamic Radiance Field: Explicit neural voxel grid Vd encoding moving objects. Deformation Network: A scene flow MLP mapping 3D coordinates and time to deformation vectors. Motion Masks: Binary masks identifying dynamic pixels, generated by combining Mask R-CNN outputs with binary masks from thresholding the Sampson distance of optical flow between consecutive frames. Steps: 1. Initialization: Not given in the sources. Initialize voxel grids and MLPs with random weights. 2. Motion Masking: Generate motion masks for each frame to exclude dynamic regions from pose estimation. Combine instance segmentation masks with epipolar distance thresholding. 3. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization: Start with a smaller static voxel resolution and progressively increase it during training to optimize poses and focal length. This stabilizes optimization by smoothing the energy surface. 4. Joint Optimization Loop: a. Ray Casting: Compute ray origins and directions from current camera estimates. b. Differentiable Rendering: Volume render static points and deformed dynamic points. c. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss for static pixels. Apply auxiliary losses: reprojection loss (project 3D volume rendered points onto neighbor frames to match pre-calculated flow), disparity loss (force volume rendered 3D points from corresponding neighbor frames to have similar z values), and monocular depth loss (scale-and shift-invariant loss between volume rendered depth and pre-calculated MiDaS depth). d. Gradient Update: Update camera poses, intrinsics, static fields, dynamic fields, and deformation network parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). 5. Refinement: Iterate until convergence. Formulas: Deformation: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \Delta \mathbf{x}(\mathbf{x}, t; \Theta{def}), where \mathbf{x} is the 3D coordinate, t is time, and \Delta \mathbf{x} is the deformation vector. Rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai ci, where Ti is transmittance, \alphai is opacity, and ci is color, sampled from the deformed dynamic field or static field. Sampson Distance: dS = \frac{(\mathbf{x}'^T F \mathbf{x})^2}{(F\mathbf{x})1^2 + (F\mathbf{x})2^2 + (F^T\mathbf{x}')1^2 + (F^T\mathbf{x}')2^2}, used to threshold motion masks. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{photo} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{reproj} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{disp} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{depth}, where \mathcal{L}{photo} is computed only on static pixels, and \lambda are loss weights. Parameters: Camera poses [R|t]i for i \in [1..N] and shared focal length f. Coarse-to-fine voxel grid resolutions. Loss weights \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SfM Failure: Structure from Motion systems fail on challenging videos with highly dynamic objects, poorly textured surfaces, and rotating camera motion, causing existing dynamic radiance field methods to be unreliable. Sub-optimal Convergence: Without the coarse-to-fine strategy, the optimizer gets stuck in sub-optimal solutions due to a rough energy surface. Poor Geometry: Without a single-image depth prior, scene geometry is poor for challenging camera trajectories. Wrong Poses: Without late viewing direction conditioning, geometry and poses are wrong because the method minimizes photometric loss instead of consistent voxel space using MLP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rodynrfoptimization(frames, initialposes, initialintrinsics): # Initialize explicit neural voxel grids and scene flow MLP Vs = initvoxelgrid() Vd = initvoxelgrid() defnet = initsceneflowmlp() poses = list(initialposes) intrinsics = list(initialintrinsics) focallength = initialintrinsics[0].fx maxepochs = 1000 resolutions = [32, 64, 128] for res in resolutions: for epoch in range(maxepochs): for i in range(len(frames)): # Motion mask generation previdx = (i - 1) % len(frames) flow = computeopticalflow(frames[i], frames[previdx]) F = estimatefundamentalmatrix(flow) sampsonvals = computesampsondistance(flow, F) maskrcnn = runmaskrcnn(frames[i]) motionmask = (sampsonvals > 0.5) | maskrcnn # Ray casting rays = castrays(frames[i], poses[i], intrinsics[i]) # Sampling and deformation staticpts = samplealongrays(rays, res) dynamicpts = samplealongrays(rays, res) deformeddynamicpts = [p + defnet(p, i) for p in dynamicpts] # Volume rendering staticcolor = volumerender(staticpts, Vs) dynamiccolor = volumerender(deformeddynamicpts, Vd) renderedcolor = [s + d for s, d in zip(staticcolor, dynamiccolor)] rendereddepth = computedepth(staticpts, deformeddynamicpts) # Loss computation staticpixels = [not m for m in motionmask] dynamicpixels = [m for m in motionmask] photoloss = sum((r - f)2 for r, f in zip(renderedcolor[staticpixels], frames[i][staticpixels])) reprojloss = computereprojectionloss(deformeddynamicpts, poses, intrinsics, flow) disploss = computedisparityloss(deformeddynamicpts, poses, intrinsics) depthloss = computemonoculardepthloss(rendereddepth, midasdepth) totalloss = photoloss + reprojloss + disploss + depthloss # Gradient update updateparameters(poses, intrinsics, Vs, Vd, defnet, totalloss) return poses, intrinsics, Vs, Vd, defnet def initvoxelgrid(): return [[0.0] 8 for in range(64)] def initsceneflowmlp(): return lambda x, t: [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def computeopticalflow(f1, f2): return estimateflow(f1, f2) def estimatefundamentalmatrix(flow): return computefmatrix(flow) def computesampsondistance(flow, F): return [(x.T @ F @ x)2 / norm(F@x)2 for x in flow] def runmaskrcnn(frame): return segmentdynamicobjects(frame) def castrays(frame, pose, intrinsics): return generaterays(frame, pose, intrinsics) def samplealongrays(rays, res): return samplepointsonrays(rays, res) def volumerender(pts, grid): return rendervolume(pts, grid) def computedepth(staticpts, dynamicpts): return computezvalues(staticpts, dynamicpts) def computereprojectionloss(pts, poses, intrinsics, flow): return reprojectionerror(pts, poses, intrinsics, flow) def computedisparityloss(pts, poses, intrinsics): return disparityerror(pts, poses, intrinsics) def computemonoculardepthloss(rendered, midas): return scaleshiftinvariantloss(rendered, midas) def updateparameters(poses, intrinsics, Vs, Vd, defnet, loss): return applygradients(poses, intrinsics, Vs, Vd, defnet, loss) SceneRF is a self-supervised monocular 3D scene reconstruction method that trains using only image sequences with known poses. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF approaches by reducing scene representation complexity through the integration of monocular depth estimation, enabling efficient handling of large scenes via explicit depth optimization and a novel probabilistic sampling strategy. Time Complexity: High due to joint optimization of poses, intrinsics, and two radiance fields. Memory Complexity: High due to storing static and dynamic fields and deformation network. Performance: Robust to unposed, in-the-wild video data. Strengths: Handles dynamic scenes, no need for known poses, robust to motion. Limitations: Computationally expensive, requires careful tuning of motion masks and learning rates. When to use: Dynamic scene reconstruction from monocular video without known poses. RoDynRF was introduced in January 2023. It builds on the static-to-dynamic learning paradigm, first learning static scene representation from multi-view stills, then learning deformation from a few-view dynamic sequence, allowing much faster convergence than fully implicit networks. It addresses the fragility of existing dynamic view synthesis methods that rely on precise camera poses estimated via SfM systems, which often fail on challenging videos. name: SceneRF
head: Behind the Scenes
body: SceneRF is a self-supervised monocular 3D scene reconstruction method trained using only image sequences with known poses. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF approaches by reducing scene representation complexity through monocular depth estimation, enabling efficient handling of large scenes via explicit depth optimization and a novel probabilistic sampling strategy. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sequence of monocular images with known camera poses. Outputs: A radiance field representation optimized for new view synthesis and depth estimation. Data Structures The method redefines feature extraction and ray/color sampling to account for the self-supervised depth network. Specific data structure layouts (e.g., voxel grid dimensions, feature vector sizes, or depth map resolutions) are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Monocular Depth Estimation: Generate depth priors using a self-supervised depth estimation network. 2. Feature Extraction Redefinition: Redefine feature extraction to incorporate geometric information from the monocular depth estimator. 3. Ray and Color Sampling: Redefine ray marching and color sampling strategies to explicitly account for the self-supervised depth network's output. 4. Explicit Depth Optimization: Optimize the scene representation through explicit depth optimization to efficiently handle large scenes. 5. Probabilistic Sampling: Apply a novel probabilistic sampling strategy to handle large scenes efficiently. 6. Self-Supervised Training: Train the model using only image sequences and poses, relying on the scene’s geometric and lighting details as training cues. Formulas and Parameters The specific mathematical formulations for the probabilistic sampling strategy, the loss functions combining photometric and depth consistency, and the architecture of the self-supervised depth network are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Large Scenes: Standard NeRF methods may struggle with large scenes; SceneRF addresses this via explicit depth optimization and probabilistic sampling. None. SceneRF achieves the best performance in all metrics for new depth view synthesis, including absolute relative error, root mean square error, and IoU, outperforming existing methods for both new view synthesis and scene reconstruction tasks. Specific time and memory complexity metrics, hardware performance data, or resolution limits are not given in the sources. SceneRF was proposed in 2023 as a NeRF-based autonomous learning technique that employs the scene’s geometric and lighting details as training cues, bypassing direct labeling. It belongs to a lineage of methods, including MINE and Behind the Scenes, that reduce scene representation complexity by leveraging monocular depth estimation. name: VMRF (View Matching Neural Radiance Fields)
head: View Matching NeRF
body: VMRF is a method for novel view synthesis that learns Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations without prior knowledge of camera poses or hand-crafted camera pose distributions. It solves the problem of pose estimation in texture-poor or repetitive scenes where classical Structure-from-Motion (SfM) fails, and where direct absolute pose estimation methods (like GNeRF) are sensitive to out-of-dataset views. VMRF distinguishes itself by estimating relative pose transformations via a view matching scheme using unbalanced optimal transport (UOT), rather than predicting absolute poses directly from images. It builds on Joint Pose and Radiance Field Optimization by introducing a differentiable feature-matching step to guide pose calibration. VMRF operates in an iterative, end-to-end optimization loop, initially following the hybrid training scheme of GNeRF. It begins with randomly initialized camera poses and a coarse NeRF, then refines both the NeRF parameters and the camera poses jointly. Inputs: A set of n RGB images I = \{I1, I2,..., In\} of a static scene. No camera poses are provided. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta and estimated camera poses \hat{\Phi} = \{\hat{\phi}1,..., \hat{\phi}n\}. 1. NeRF Model (F\Theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) parameterizing the 5D scene function F\Theta(x, b) \rightarrow (c, \sigma), mapping a 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction b \in S^2 to RGB color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Camera Pose (\phi): Represented as a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix. Rotation is encoded as a continuous 6D embedding, and position as a 3D Euclidean embedding. 3. Feature Sets: Source feature set \mathbf{f}s \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times d} extracted from the rendered image. Target feature set \mathbf{f}t \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times d} extracted from the real image. Parameters: l = 64 (number of feature vectors), d = 256 (dimension of feature vectors). 4. Transport Plan (T): A matrix T \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times l} where T{ij} represents the amount of mass moved from source feature i to target feature j. 5. Relative Transformation Predictor (RTP): A Vision Transformer-based network that outputs a 6-dimensional vector [tx, ty, tz, \thetax, \thetay, \thetaz] representing relative translation and rotation. 1. Initialization: Initialize the set of randomly sampled camera poses \Phi' = \{\phi'i, i \in [1, n]\}. Initialize a coarse NeRF with these random poses. 2. Coarse NeRF Training (Adversarial Phase): Train the coarse NeRF F and discriminator D using adversarial loss to ensure generated images have a similar distribution to real images. \mathcal{L}{adv}(F, D) = \mathbb{E}{I \sim P{data}} [\log(D(I))] + \mathbb{E}{F(\Phi') \sim Pg} [\log(1 - D(F(\Phi')))] where P{data} is the distribution of real images and Pg is the distribution of generated images. 3. Feature Extraction: For each image Ii and its corresponding rendered image \hat{I}i (generated using current pose \phi'i and NeRF F): Extract source features \mathbf{f}s from the rendered image \hat{I}i using a pre-trained VGG-19 network. Extract target features \mathbf{f}t from the real image Ii using a pre-trained VGG-19 network. 4. View Matching via Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT): Compute the cost matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times l} based on feature similarity: M = 1 - \frac{\mathbf{f}s \cdot \mathbf{f}t^T}{\|\mathbf{f}s\| \|\mathbf{f}t\|} where M{ij} denotes the moving cost from source feature i to target feature j. Solve for the optimal transport plan T^ by minimizing the entropic regularized UOT objective: T^ = \arg \minT \left[ \sum{i,j=1}^{l} T{ij} M{ij} - \eta H(T) + \epsilon KL(T \mathbf{1}l || \mus) + \epsilon KL(T^T \mathbf{1}l || \mut) \right] where: \eta = 0.005 is the entropic regularization parameter. H(T) = -\sum{i,j=1}^{l} T{ij} \log(T{ij}) is the entropic regularization term (corrected from paper typo). \epsilon > 0 is the KL divergence regularization parameter. \mus and \mut are the discrete source and target distributions defined by the feature sets. The optimal transport plan is computed using the Sinkhorn algorithm on the Fenchel-Legendre dual form. Note: UOT is used instead of standard OT because occlusions cause inconsistent total mass between views, leading to false matches with standard OT. 5. Pose Calibration (Relative Transformation Prediction): Predict the relative pose transformation between the real image and the rendered image using the transport plan T^: [tx, ty, tz, \thetax, \thetay, \thetaz] = RTP(T^) where RTP is the relative transformation predictor. Construct the relative rotation matrix \Delta R and translation vector \Delta t: \Delta R = Rx(\thetax) Ry(\thetay) Rz(\thetaz) \Delta t = [tx, ty, tz]^T where Rx, Ry, Rz are standard rotation matrices. Calibrate the randomized pose \phi'i to estimate the real pose \hat{\phi}i: \hat{\phi}i = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta R & \Delta t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \phi'i 6. NeRF and Pose Optimization: Optimize the NeRF parameters \Theta and the estimated poses \hat{\Phi} using the photometric loss: \mathcal{L}P(F, \hat{\Phi}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^{n} \| Ii - F(\hat{\phi}i) \|^2 Additionally, train the relative transformation predictor using a calibration loss \mathcal{L}{ca} in an unsupervised manner using pairs of randomly initialized poses: \mathcal{L}{ca}(RTP) = \mathbb{E} \| F{ca}(RTP(T^{ab}), \phi'a) - \phi'b \|^2 where T^{ab} is the transport plan between renders from \phi'a and \phi'b, and F{ca} is a coarse NeRF. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-6 end-to-end. The method uses a hybrid and iterative optimization scheme similar to GNeRF. Unverified code. Standard MLP for 5D scene function FTheta(x, b) -> (c, sigma) self.layers = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 4)) def forward(self, x, b): out = self.layers(torch.cat([x, b], dim=-1)) return out[:,:3], out[:, 3] # color, density class Discriminator(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3HW, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1)) def forward(self, img): return torch.sigmoid(self.net(img.view(img.size(0), -1))) class RelativeTransformationPredictor(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Standard differentiable volume rendering # Samples points along rays, queries NeRF, computes weighted sum # Returns rendered image of shape (H, W, 3) # Implementation follows standard NeRF volume rendering integral return torch.zeroslike(rayorigirs[:,:3]) # Placeholder for rendering logic def sinkhornuot(M, l, eta, epsilon, numiter=100): # Solves entropic regularized UOT via Sinkhorn iterations # M: cost matrix (l, l) # Note: Standard Sinkhorn solves entropic OT. UOT with KL penalties # modifies the dual updates. We implement the standard entropic step # and note the UOT adjustment. K = torch.exp(-M / eta) u = torch.zeros(l) v = torch.zeros(l) for in range(numiter): unew = -eta torch.logsumexp(torch.log(K) + v.unsqueeze(0), dim=1) vnew = -eta torch.logsumexp(torch.log(K) + u.unsqueeze(1), dim=0) u, v = unew, vnew Tstar = torch.exp(u.unsqueeze(1) + v.unsqueeze(0)) K return Tstar def vmrftrainingloop(images, numiterations, l=64, d=256, eta=0.005, epsilon=1e-3): n = len(images) # 1. Initialization phiprime = [torch.eye(4) for in range(n)] # Randomized poses initialized as identity or random SE3 Ftheta = NeRF() D = Discriminator() RTP = RelativeTransformationPredictor() vgg19 = VGG19FeatureExtractor(l, d) vgg19.eval() optimizerneRF = torch.optim.Adam(Ftheta.parameters(), lr=0.0005) optimizerD = torch.optim.Adam(D.parameters(), lr=0.0001) optimizerRTP = torch.optim.Adam(RTP.parameters(), lr=0.0001) for iteration in range(numiterations): for i in range(n): Ii = images[i] phiiprime = phiprime[i] # 2. Optimization Step optimizerneRF.zerograd() optimizerD.zerograd() optimizerRTP.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizerneRF.step() optimizerD.step() optimizerRTP.step() phiprime[i] = phihati return Ftheta, phiprime N: Number of random samples along a camera ray for volume rendering. \Phi': Set of initially randomized camera poses. \Theta: Network parameters of the MLP. l: Number of feature vectors in each feature set. Value: 64. d: Dimension of feature vectors. Value: 256. \eta: Regularization parameter controlling the smoothness of UOT. Value: 0.005. \epsilon: KL divergence regularization parameter. Value: Not given in the sources. Low Texture/Repetitive Patterns: Classical SfM fails here. VMRF avoids this by not relying on SfM. Out-of-Dataset Views: Direct absolute pose estimation (e.g., GNeRF) is disturbed by views beyond the training dataset if the pose distribution is inaccurate. VMRF mitigates this by using relative pose estimation via view matching. Occlusion: Causes inconsistent total mass between source and target feature distributions. Standard OT fails by matching outliers. VMRF uses Unbalanced OT (UOT) with KL divergence penalties to handle this. Performance: VMRF outperforms state-of-the-art methods like GNeRF qualitatively and quantitatively on Synthetic-NeRF and DTU datasets. Strengths: Does not require prior knowledge of camera poses or hand-crafted pose distributions. Robust to out-of-dataset views and low-texture scenes. Limitations: Relies on a pre-trained VGG-19 for feature extraction, which may not capture all semantic details. VMRF was proposed by Jiahui Zhang, Fangneng Zhan, Rongliang Wu, Yingchen Yu, Wenqing Zhang, Bai Song, Xiaoqin Zhang, and Shijian Lu in 2022. It addresses the limitations of previous pose-free NeRF methods like GNeRF, which required accurate, hand-crafted camera pose distributions for training their inversion networks. VMRF introduces the concept of view matching via unbalanced optimal transport to estimate relative poses, enabling effective NeRF training without prior pose knowledge. It is used in novel view synthesis tasks on Synthetic-NeRF and DTU datasets. VMRF: View Matching Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3503161.3548078, fetched 2026-10-29

name: NeRF Pose and Appearance Optimization
head: UP-NeRF, Unconstrained Pose-prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields
body: This method jointly optimizes camera poses and neural scene representations for unconstrained image collections (varying illumination, transient occluders) without camera pose priors. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF optimization by introducing a candidate head to handle "hard-pose" images and a loss scheduling mechanism to transition from candidate-specific to shared scene representations. Unlike RoDynRF which focuses on dynamic scenes, or VMRF which uses view matching, this method explicitly decouples transient/hard-pose appearance from the global geometry via surrogate tasks. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N unconstrained images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with unknown poses \{pi\}, and known intrinsics (focal length f, principal point, resolution W \times H). Ground-truth colors C(r) or deep feature maps F(r). The final training pipeline uses features instead of colors. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta (shared MLPs), candidate embeddings \{\elli\}, and camera poses \{pi\}. Data Structures: 1. Shared NeRF: Two MLPs, \Pi{\theta1} and \Pi{\theta2}, parameterizing the scene. \Pi{\theta1}: Input \gammax(r(t)) (positional encoded 3D point), Output [\sigma(t), z(t)] (density, intermediate feature). \Pi{\theta2}: Input [z(t), \gammad(d)] (feature, positional encoded direction), Output c(t) (color). 2. Candidate Head: MLP \Pi{\theta3}. Input [z(t), \elli] (shared feature, image-specific embedding), Output [\sigmai(t), ci(t)] (candidate density, candidate color). 3. Camera Pose: Each pose pi is parameterized as 6 degrees of freedom using the se(3) Lie algebra. 4. Candidate Embeddings: Vector \elli for each image i. Size is adjustable based on pose difficulty. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel (u,v) in image i, compute ray origin \hat{o}i and direction \hat{d}i using current pose estimate pi and intrinsics. \hat{o}i = ti \hat{d}i = Ri \begin{pmatrix} (u - W/2)/f \\ -(v - H/2)/f \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} where pi = (Ri, ti). 2. Sampling: Sample K points tk along the ray r(t) = \hat{o}i + t\hat{d}i using hierarchical sampling (coarse stratified, fine biased). 3. Shared Feature Extraction: For each sample point tk: [\sigma(tk), z(tk)] = \Pi{\theta1}(\gammax(r(tk))) c(tk) = \Pi{\theta2}(z(tk), \gammad(\hat{d}i)) 4. Candidate Feature Extraction: For each sample point tk: [\sigmai(tk), ci(tk)] = \Pi{\theta3}(z(tk), \elli) 5. Joint Volumetric Rendering: Compute candidate rendered color \hat{C}i(r) by combining shared and candidate densities/colors: \hat{C}i(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Ti(tk) \left[ \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) c(tk) + \alpha(\sigmai(tk)\deltak) ci(tk) \right] where opacity \alpha(\sigma \delta) = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \delta), distance \deltak = t{k+1} - tk, and transmittance: Ti(tk) = \exp\left( -\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} (\sigma(t{k'}) + \sigmai(t{k'})) \delta{k'} \right) 6. Shared Rendering: Compute shared rendered color \hat{C}(r) using only shared parameters (standard NeRF rendering): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K T(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) c(tk) where T(tk) = \exp\left( -\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} \sigma(t{k'}) \delta{k'} \right). 7. Loss Scheduling: Calculate training progress l \in [0, 1]. Compute weight w{u,v}(l) using hyperparameters u, v \in [0, 1]: w{u,v}(l) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } l < u \\ \frac{1 - \cos(\pi(l - u)/(v - u))}{2} & \text{if } u \le l < v \\ 1 & \text{if } l \ge v \end{cases} 8. Total Loss: Compute photometric loss \mathcal{L}{rgb} (MSE between ground truth C(r) and rendered color): \mathcal{L} = w{u,v} \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}|C) + (1 - w{u,v}) \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}i|C) If l < u: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}i|C) (Candidate only). If l \ge v: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{rgb}(\hat{C}|C) (Shared only). 9. Optimization: Update \Theta, \{\elli\}, and \{pi\} using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) minimizing \mathcal{L}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def positionalencoding(x, numfreqbands=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" encoded = [] for xval in x: for i in range(numfreqbands): freq = 2.0 (i math.pi) encoded.extend([math.sin(xval freq), math.cos(xval freq)]) return encoded def samplepoints(origin, direction, numsamples): """Uniform sampling along ray from t=0 to t=1.""" return [k / numsamples for k in range(1, numsamples + 1)] def concat(a, b): """Concatenate two lists.""" return a + b def computecandidaterendering(rayorigin, raydirection, candidateembedding, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, candidatemlp, numsamples): t = samplepoints(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples) points = [[rayorigin[d] + t[k] raydirection[d] for d in range(3)] for k in range(numsamples)] encodedpoints = [positionalencoding(p) for p in points] sigmashared, z = [sharedmlp1(ep) for ep in encodedpoints] encodeddirs = [positionalencoding(raydirection)] numsamples colorshared = [sharedmlp2(concat(z[k], encodeddirs[k])) for k in range(numsamples)] candidatedensity, candidatecolor = [candidatemlp(concat(z[k], candidateembedding)) for k in range(numsamples)] deltas = [t[k] - t[k-1] for k in range(1, numsamples)] + [t[-1] - t[-2]] alphashared = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigmashared[k] deltas[k]) for k in range(numsamples)] alphacandidate = [1.0 - math.exp(-candidatedensity[k] deltas[k]) for k in range(numsamples)] combineddensity = [sigmashared[k] + candidatedensity[k] for k in range(numsamples)] cumdensitydelta = [0.0] for k in range(numsamples): cumdensitydelta.append(cumdensitydelta[-1] + combineddensity[k] deltas[k]) T = [math.exp(-c) for c in cumdensitydelta[:-1]] renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for k in range(numsamples): sharedterm = T[k] alphashared[k] colorshared[k] candterm = T[k] alphacandidate[k] candidatecolor[k] renderedcolor = [renderedcolor[d] + sharedterm[d] + candterm[d] for d in range(3)] return renderedcolor def computesharedrendering(rayorigin, raydirection, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, numsamples): t = samplepoints(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples) points = [[rayorigin[d] + t[k] raydirection[d] for d in range(3)] for k in range(numsamples)] encodedpoints = [positionalencoding(p) for p in points] sigma, z = [sharedmlp1(ep) for ep in encodedpoints] encodeddirs = [positionalencoding(raydirection)] numsamples color = [sharedmlp2(concat(z[k], encodeddirs[k])) for k in range(numsamples)] deltas = [t[k] - t[k-1] for k in range(1, numsamples)] + [t[-1] - t[-2]] alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[k] deltas[k]) for k in range(numsamples)] cumdensitydelta = [0.0] for k in range(numsamples): cumdensitydelta.append(cumdensitydelta[-1] + sigma[k] deltas[k]) T = [math.exp(-c) for c in cumdensitydelta[:-1]] renderedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for k in range(numsamples): term = T[k] alpha[k] color[k] renderedcolor = [renderedcolor[d] + term[d] for d in range(3)] return renderedcolor def trainstep(images, gtcolors, poses, embeddings, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, candidatemlp, u, v, progress): totalloss = 0.0 for i, (img, gtcolor) in enumerate(zip(images, gtcolors)): pose = poses[i] embedding = embeddings[i] rayorigins, raydirections = getrays(pose, img.shape) candcolors = [computecandidaterendering(o, d, embedding, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, candidatemlp, numsamples) for o, d in zip(rayorigins, raydirections)] sharedcolors = [computesharedrendering(o, d, sharedmlp1, sharedmlp2, numsamples) for o, d in zip(rayorigins, raydirections)] losscand = sum((gtcolor[d] - candcolors[i][d])2 for d in range(3)) / 3.0 lossshared = sum((gtcolor[d] - sharedcolors[i][d])2 for d in range(3)) / 3.0 if progress < u: w = 0.0 elif progress >= v: w = 1.0 else: w = (1.0 - math.cos(math.pi (progress - u) / (v - u))) / 2.0 loss = w lossshared + (1.0 - w) losscand totalloss += loss return totalloss / len(images) Parameters: u, v: Loss scheduling hyperparameters. Typical values not given in sources. \elli size: Adjustable based on pose difficulty. Learning rates: Separate or combined optimizers, often different rates for pose vs weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hard-pose images: Images with little overlap or unique details may converge to wrong poses if not handled by the candidate head. Transient occluders: The candidate head helps block their influence on pose estimation. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues in ray marching and transmittance computation apply. A strategy to facilitate stable joint optimization, borrowed from BARF. Using deep feature maps F instead of just color C for training, allowing selective editing and robustness. Time Complexity: Higher than standard NeRF due to the candidate head and dual rendering paths per image. Memory Complexity: Increased by storing candidate embeddings \elli for each image and the candidate head parameters. Strengths: Handles unconstrained internet photo collections (e.g., Phototourism dataset) with varying illumination and transient occluders without pose priors. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of u, v and candidate embedding sizes. May be slower to converge than methods with known poses. When to use: When camera poses are unknown and images are unconstrained (transients, lighting changes). Originated in the paper "UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses limitations of prior NeRF pose estimation methods (like BARF) which struggle with unconstrained images containing transient occluders or varying illumination. It builds on the concept of surrogate tasks and separate modules for transients. UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03784v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sync-NeRF Offset Optimization
head: Joint offset and NeRF optimization, Per-camera Time Offset with Dynamic NeRF, Sync-MixVoxels, Sync-K-Planes
body: Sync-NeRF Offset Optimization addresses the problem of reconstructing dynamic scenes from multi-view videos that are not temporally synchronized. Unlike standard dynamic NeRFs that assume all cameras capture the same scene moment at a given frame index, this method introduces learnable per-camera time offsets to align the temporal axes of unsynchronized inputs. It sets itself apart by treating synchronization as a differentiable optimization problem, jointly refining camera-specific time shifts alongside the neural radiance field parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K unsynchronized multi-view video sequences. For each camera k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, the input consists of images Ck(r, t) at discrete time indices t. The underlying dynamic NeRF model F\Theta (which may be grid-based or implicit) and its initial parameters \Theta. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta, optimized per-camera time offsets \deltak for each training camera, and optionally a test-time offset \delta{test} for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: Time Offsets (\delta): A vector of learnable parameters, one per camera. Layout: \delta = [\delta1, \delta2, \dots, \deltaK]. Type: Continuous scalar (float). Initialization: \deltak = 0.0 for all k. Calibrated Time (tk): The effective time input to the NeRF for a specific camera and frame. Formula: tk = t + \deltak. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the learnable time offsets \deltak for all K training cameras to zero. Initialize the NeRF parameters \Theta using the chosen dynamic NeRF baseline (e.g., MixVoxels, K-Planes). 2. Calibration: For each training pixel defined by camera index k, ray r, and frame index t, compute the calibrated time tk: tk = t + \deltak 3. Rendering: Query the dynamic NeRF F\Theta using the calibrated time tk to predict the color and density. The specific query depends on the baseline architecture: For implicit function-based approaches: F\Theta: (x, d, tk) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) For grid-based models (e.g., MixVoxels, K-Planes): F\Theta: (f(x, tk), d) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) where f(x, tk) retrieves the spatial-temporal feature grid at coordinates (x, tk). Render the pixel color \hat{C}(r, t + \deltak) using standard volume rendering integration (numerical quadrature). 4. Loss Computation: Calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered color \hat{C} and the ground truth color Ck(r, t): \mathcal{L}{RGB} = \sum{k,r,t} \left( \hat{C}(r, t + \deltak) - Ck(r, t) \right)^2 5. Optimization: Minimize \mathcal{L}{RGB} with respect to both the NeRF parameters \Theta and the time offsets \deltak using gradient descent. No additional regularizers are required for the offsets. 6. Test-Time Synchronization (Optional): If rendering from a test view that is also unsynchronized, freeze \Theta and \deltak (training offsets) and optimize a specific test offset \delta{test} to minimize reconstruction error for the novel view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def syncnerfoffsetoptimization(cameras, timeindices, groundtruthimages, dynamicnerf, numiterations, learningrate): # cameras: list of K camera indices # timeindices: list of integer frame indices # groundtruthimages: dict mapping (k, t) to image tensor Ck(r, t) # dynamicnerf: object with.parameters() and.render(k, tk) method # numiterations: int # learningrate: float # 1. Initialize learnable time offsets deltak for each camera to zero delta = {k: 0.0 for k in cameras} # Combine parameters for optimization allparams = list(dynamicnerf.parameters()) + list(delta.values()) for iteration in range(numiterations): # Zero gradients for p in allparams: p.grad = 0.0 totalloss = 0.0 # 2. Iterate over all training pixels (k, r, t) for k in cameras: for t in timeindices: # 3. Calculate calibrated time tk = t + deltak tk = t + delta[k] # Get ground truth image for this camera and time Cgt = groundtruthimages[(k, t)] # 4. Compute rendered RGB pixel Chat(r, t + deltak) Chat = dynamicnerf.render(k, tk) # 5. Compute MSE loss loss = sum((Chat - Cgt) 2) / len(Cgt) totalloss += loss # 6. Backpropagate and update totalloss.backward() for p in allparams: p.data -= learningrate p.grad return dynamicnerf, delta def testtimesync(dynamicnerf, testcamera, testgroundtruth, deltatrain, timeindices, numiterationstest, learningrate): # Optimize a specific test offset for a novel view deltatest = 0.0 for iteration in range(numiterationstest): deltatest.grad = 0.0 totalloss = 0.0 for t in timeindices: # Use frozen trained model and training offsets tk = t + deltatrain[testcamera] # Render with test offset Chat = dynamicnerf.render(testcamera, tk + deltatest) Cgt = testgroundtruth.image loss = sum((Chat - Cgt) 2) / len(Cgt) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() deltatest.data -= learningrate deltatest.grad return deltatest Parameters: \deltak: Learnable time offset for camera k. Initialized to 0.0. Optimized via gradient descent. Typical Performance: On the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset, the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between predicted offsets and ground truth offsets is approximately 0.01 seconds (less than one-third of a frame at 30 FPS). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Test View Synchronization: Test views may also be unsynchronized relative to training views. The method requires optimizing a specific test offset \delta{test} with a frozen trained model to resolve this. Unsynchronization Length: Performance degrades with longer unsynchronization lengths (e.g., 1.5\times or 2\times), though the method consistently improves over baselines. Applies Sync-NeRF offset optimization to the MixVoxels baseline. It achieves an MAE of 0.0154 seconds on the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. Choose this variant when using a grid-based implicit representation that benefits from continuous temporal interpolation. See Sync-MixVoxels. Applies Sync-NeRF offset optimization to the hybrid K-Planes baseline. It achieves an MAE of 0.0156 seconds on the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. Choose this variant when a hybrid explicit/implicit representation is preferred for memory efficiency. See Sync-K-Planes. Applies Sync-NeRF offset optimization to the explicit K-Planes baseline. It achieves an MAE of 0.0229 seconds on the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. Choose this variant when fully explicit voxel-based rendering is required. See Sync-K-Planes. Time Complexity: The optimization does not introduce additional computational complexity to the grid-based models during rendering, as the time offset is simply added to the time input before grid query. However, the joint optimization of \deltak adds gradient computation overhead for the offset parameters. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required for the offsets themselves (only K floats), but the method avoids the memory overhead of learning hundreds of individual frame embeddings by using continuous time interpolation. Performance: On the Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset, Sync-NeRF variants significantly outperform unsynchronized baselines. For example, Sync-MixVoxels achieves a PSNR of 37.11 compared to 31.06 for the baseline MixVoxels. Strengths: Automatically synchronizes videos without manual effort or additional hardware (like timecode systems). Applicable to various dynamic NeRF baselines. Limitations: Does not generalize to causal handheld cameras (future work). May struggle with extreme unsynchronization lengths, though it remains robust. Sync-NeRF was introduced by Kim et al. in 2024 to address the limitation of existing dynamic NeRFs that assume synchronized multi-view inputs. Previous methods fail on unsynchronized data, producing severe artifacts and ghost effects because they employ a single latent embedding for a frame while multi-view images were captured at different moments. The method was verified on the Plenoptic Video Dataset and a newly built Unsynchronized Dynamic Blender Dataset. name: Monocular Depth Estimation Adaptation and Supervision
head: MDE-guided NeRF, Depth-Regularized NeRF, Monocular Depth Priors
body: This family of methods integrates pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) networks into the NeRF training loop to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in sparse-view or single-view reconstruction. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on RGB photometric supervision, these methods explicitly guide volume sampling, rendering, or optimization using depth maps extracted from a scene-adapted or static monocular network. They distinguish themselves from sibling methods by treating monocular depth not just as a static prior, but as an active supervisory signal that can be adapted to the specific scene geometry (e.g., via fine-tuning or joint optimization) or used to constrain the sampling bounds and loss functions. All methods in this family share the following mechanism: 1. Depth Prior Extraction: A pre-trained MDE network G\phi (e.g., Mannequin Challenge, DiffDP, DPThybrid, Omnidata) is applied to input RGB images I to generate a relative depth map D^. 2. Scale and Shift Alignment: Since MDE outputs are relative and lack absolute scale, a linear alignment is performed between the MDE depth D^ and the NeRF-rendered depth \bar{D} (or ground truth/sparse points). This is typically done per-image or per-patch using least-squares optimization to find scale w and shift q: \min{w, q} \sum{p} \| (w \cdot \text{sg}(D^(p)) + q) - \bar{D}(p) \|^2 where \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator to prevent gradients from flowing into the frozen MDE network during NeRF updates. 3. Depth Consistency Loss: A loss term L{depth} is added to the total training objective, penalizing the difference between the aligned MDE depth and the NeRF-rendered depth. 4. Sampling Guidance: In some variants, the depth prior is used to clamp the near and far bounds of ray sampling, focusing computation on plausible depths. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computescaleshiftalignment(mdedepth, nerfdepth, patchsize=None): """ Computes scale w and shift q via least squares between MDE and NeRF depth. Args: mdedepth: Tensor (H, W), monocular depth estimate. nerfdepth: Tensor (H, W), rendered depth from NeRF. patchsize: Optional int for patch-wise alignment. Returns: w: Scale parameter. q: Shift parameter. """ if patchsize is not None: # Iterate over patches (simplified) # For each patch, compute means and covariance pass # Global alignment mdesg = mdedepth.detach() mumde = torch.mean(mdesg) munerf = torch.mean(nerfdepth) cov = torch.mean((mdesg - mumde) (nerfdepth - munerf)) varmde = torch.mean((mdesg - mumde) 2) epsilon = 1e-8 w = cov / (varmde + epsilon) q = munerf - w mumde return w, q Integrates learning-based monocular depth priors into NeRF optimization to resolve shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor scenes. It distinguishes itself by combining test-time adaptation of a monocular depth estimator (fine-tuned on sparse SfM+MVS points) with a rendering pipeline that clamps ray bounds based on these priors. Choose it when multi-view indoor scenes require explicit depth-guided sampling. Improves geometric accuracy in sparse-view NeRFs by supervising the distribution of ray termination distances using Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) rather than direct depth matching. It uses a diffusion-based depth prior and its intrinsic uncertainty map to selectively guide geometry, replacing standard L2 depth losses with a distributional EMD loss weighted by uncertainty. Choose it when handling uncertainty in monocular priors is critical. Integrates a guided depth completion network (e.g., MFFNet) into the NeRF loop to recover dense depth from sparse LiDAR measurements. It sets itself apart by using LiDAR-based completion to provide dense, metrically consistent depth supervision, addressing the sparsity of raw LiDAR data in unbounded real-world scenes. Choose it when LiDAR data is available but sparse. Aligns pseudo-depth maps from a pre-trained MDE network with NeRF-rendered depth for seen input views. It differs from global scale-fitting approaches by computing local scale and shift parameters per image patch, preventing dominant objects from biasing the depth alignment and preserving local geometric details. Choose it when local geometric fidelity is prioritized over global scale. A framework for robust few-shot NeRF reconstruction that combines NeRF with MDE through online complementary training. It solves ambiguity by jointly optimizing the NeRF and the MDE network at a specific scene, distilling the monocular depth prior to NeRF at both seen and unseen views and finetuning the MDE network with canonical geometry captured by NeRF. Choose it for few-shot scenarios requiring joint adaptation. Refines a pre-trained MDE network by using a NeRF model as a geometric prior to resolve ambiguities such as convexity/concavity confusion. It distinguishes itself by explicitly adapting the MDE weights to the specific scene's absolute geometry rather than just using depth as a static supervision signal for the NeRF. Choose it when MDE network weights need scene-specific refinement. Defines three specific architectural configurations for the FWD framework, distinguished by their depth supervision strategy and the initialization state of the depth estimation module. They address the trade-off between training stability, convergence speed, and reliance on external geometric priors. FWD-U serves as the unsupervised baseline, FWD provides a supervised baseline with pre-trained geometry, and FWD-D bypasses learned depth estimation entirely by using sensor data. Choose it when evaluating different accessibility levels to depth information. Reconstructs a neural SDF from single-view images under multiple lighting conditions by supervising shadow rays rather than relying solely on camera rays. It solves the problem that standard NeRF does not model rays from the scene to the light source, missing shadow information which contains critical geometry cues via light visibility. Choose it for single-view reconstruction with known lighting conditions. Generates dense correspondence datasets to train object-centric visual descriptors using only RGB images and NeRFs. It solves the problem of acquiring ground-truth dense correspondences for thin, reflective, or ambiguous objects where traditional RGB-D sensors and MVS fail, using the NeRF's density field to formulate a "distribution-of-depths" approach. Choose it for training descriptors on ambiguous objects. The geometry optimization phase of the GAINS pipeline, designed to reconstruct robust 3D shape from sparse RGB images using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It solves novel-view artifacts and geometric collapse by augmenting optimization with monocular depth/normal consistency, local depth ranking, and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a latent diffusion model. Choose it for sparse-view 2DGS reconstruction. A supervision technique for NeRF training that aligns a monocular depth estimator's output with the NeRF's rendered geometry, specifically designed to handle masked regions in inpainting scenarios. It differs from standard affine alignment by incorporating spatially varying weights and additional tilt parameters to enforce tighter geometric consistency near mask boundaries. Choose it for inpainting or masked region supervision. Aligns monocular depth estimates (range [0,1]) with rendered depth by solving for scale and shift parameters per mini-batch via least-squares optimization. It differs from sibling methods like NerfingMVS by relying solely on a single-view depth prior per image and optimizing alignment parameters per mini-batch to enforce geometric consistency. Choose it for real-time or mini-batch aligned supervision. Definition: A loss function that supervises NeRF geometry at unseen/novel viewpoints by aligning NeRF-rendered depth with monocular depth estimated from the rendered novel view image. Step: For each unseen view l in the set of unseen views U: 1. Sample a patch of the novel viewpoint. 2. Render color \bar{I}l and depth \bar{D}l from NeRF. 3. Extract monocular depth D^l = G\phi(\bar{I}l) from the rendered color image. 4. Compute scale wl and shift ql via least squares between D^l and \bar{D}l. 5. Calculate loss L{unseen}. Parameter: U: Set of unseen view images. P: Randomly sampled patch of pixels. Pitfall: Monocular depth from noisy NeRF rendering may be affected by fine-grained artifacts. However, the MDE model's strong geometric prior is robust against these artifacts, filtering them out. Comparison: Unlike previous methods that only impose priors on input viewpoints (limited by self-occlusion/sparsity), this method applies priors to arbitrary viewpoints, reaching every location. Definition: A composite loss function for adapting a monocular depth estimator to predict scene-specific absolute geometry by enforcing multi-view consistency and local patch-wise scale-shift fitting. Step: Compute the first addend term (scale-shift loss) to force the MDE to adapt towards multiview consistency, reducing its ill-posed nature and aligning its initial global depth prediction with the absolute geometry captured by NeRF. Compute the second addend term (L1 loss with patch-wise scale-shift fitting) to aid the modeling of fine, detailed, local geometry. Optimize the MDE network by minimizing the sum of both terms simultaneously; using only one term performs worse on all metrics than using both in conjunction. Parameter: Scale-shift loss weight and L1 loss weight are required for optimization but values are not specified in this section. Definition: An ablation of VBGS that does not require ground truth depth information, instead using a pretrained neural network to estimate metric depth. Step: Calibrate the depth estimation network using ten ground truth depth frames by estimating scale using linear regression without intercept. Parameter: The depth estimation network used is Depth-Anything-V2-Large [Yang et al., 2024a], trained on the Hypersim dataset [Roberts et al., 2021]. For the Replica dataset 'Room 0', the output of the depth network is scaled by a factor of 0.7. Pitfall: Inaccuracies in predicted depth result in larger representations of objects (e.g., chairs covered by flowers). Step: Check for torch/transformers availability. If available, lazily load Depth-Anything-V2 model (Base or Small) on MPS/CUDA/CPU. If unavailable or load fails, use luminance + local-contrast heuristic. Parameter: Default model: depth-anything/Depth-Anything-V2-Base-hf. Override via FOURDDEPTHMODEL env var. Fallback: depth-anything/Depth-Anything-V2-Small-hf. Output range: [0, 1] where 1 = near, 0 = far. The integration of monocular depth priors into NeRF optimization emerged to address the limitations of sparse-view reconstruction, where photometric consistency alone is insufficient to disambiguate geometry and appearance. Early works like NerfingMVS demonstrated that fine-tuning monocular depth estimators on sparse SfM points could guide volume sampling. Subsequent methods such as DäRF and NeRF-guided MDE Adaptation introduced joint optimization strategies, allowing the MDE network to adapt to the specific scene geometry captured by the NeRF, thereby resolving ambiguities like convexity/concavity confusion. More recent approaches have explored distributional losses like Earth Mover’s Distance to handle the uncertainty in monocular priors [11911-depth-guided-nerf-training-via-earth-mover-s-distance.md], and extended supervision to unseen viewpoints to ensure global geometric coherence [Monocular Depth Regularization on Unseen Views]. DaRF: Boosting Radiance Fields from Sparse Inputs with Monocular Depth Adaptation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.19201, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Variational Bayes Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03592v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, https://github.com/devarshh/volumetric-video-4dgs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: NerfingMVS
head: Guided NeRF Optimization for MVS, Guided Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields for Indoor Multi-View Stereo, NeRF with Depth Priors
body: NerfingMVS is a multi-view depth estimation method that integrates learning-based monocular depth priors into the optimization of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in indoor scenes. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on RGB supervision, NerfingMVS explicitly guides volume sampling and rendering using depth maps extracted from a scene-adapted monocular network, allowing for direct optimization over implicit volumes without requiring accurate pixel matching across views. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining a test-time adaptation of a monocular depth estimator (fine-tuned on sparse SfM+MVS points) with a rendering pipeline that clamps ray bounds based on these priors. Inputs: A set of multi-view RGB images I. Camera poses (intrinsic and extrinsic) for the input images. A pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) network G\phi (e.g., Mannequin Challenge). Sparse 3D point cloud or sparse depth maps derived from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) using COLMAP. Outputs: Optimized NeRF model parameters \Theta representing the scene's geometry and appearance. Dense depth maps for each input view. Re-rendered RGB images and depth maps. NeRF Model (F\Theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking 3D position \mathbf{x} and view direction \mathbf{d} as input, outputting volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c}. Depth Prior Map (D^): A 2D tensor of shape (H, W) containing relative depth estimates for a specific view, generated by the adapted MDE network. Depth Confidence Map (M): A 2D tensor of shape (H, W) indicating the reliability of the depth prior at each pixel. Ray Bins: The ray is divided into N equal bins. The near and far bounds of these bins are clamped using the depth priors. Tensors for Rendering: rayso: Ray origins, shape [-1, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [-1, 3]. depthpriors: Prior depth values for each ray, shape [-1]. depthconfidences: Confidence values for each ray, shape [-1]. 1. Sparse Reconstruction: Run COLMAP on the input images to obtain camera poses and a sparse 3D point cloud. Project the fused 3D point clouds to each view to acquire sparse depth maps. 2. Depth Prior Adaptation: Fine-tune the pre-trained monocular depth network G\phi on the target scene using the sparse depth maps from COLMAP as ground truth. The network is optimized using a scale-invariant loss to handle the lack of absolute scale in the sparse reconstruction: L(D^ip, D^i{Sparse}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{j=1}^n \left| \log D^ip(j) - \log D^i{Sparse}(j) + \alpha(D^ip, D^i{Sparse}) \right| where D^ip is the predicted depth, D^i{Sparse} is the sparse depth, and \alpha is a correction term. 3. Ray Preparation: For each training ray, compute the origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} from the camera pose. If NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates) is used, convert rays to NDC space. 4. Depth-Guided Sampling Bounds: Retrieve the depth prior D^ and confidence M for the current view. Use these to clamp the near and far bounds of the ray sampling intervals, effectively focusing computation on plausible depths and skipping empty space. 5. Volume Rendering: Sample points along the ray within the clamped bounds. Compute density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for each sample. Render the RGB color and depth using standard volumetric rendering equations. Compute distances between consecutive samples: di = z{i+1} - zi. Scale by ray direction norm: di = di \cdot \|\mathbf{d}\|. Compute alpha: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \cdot di). Compute weights: wi = \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Rendered RGB: \mathbf{C} = \sum wi \mathbf{c}i. Rendered Depth: \mathbf{D} = \sum wi zi. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the total loss, which includes the RGB reconstruction loss and a depth consistency loss between the rendered depth and the adapted monocular depth prior. 7. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters \Theta using gradient descent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def nerfingmvsrender(rayso, raysd, depthpriors, depthconfidences, model, Nsamples, near, far): """ Renders rays using NerfingMVS logic. Args: rayso: Tensor of shape [numrays, 3], ray origins. raysd: Tensor of shape [numrays, 3], ray directions. depthpriors: Tensor of shape [numrays], depth prior for each ray. depthconfidences: Tensor of shape [numrays], confidence for each ray. model: The NeRF MLP model. Nsamples: Number of samples per ray. near: Float, absolute near bound (default 0.05). far: Float, absolute far bound (default 0.15). Returns: rgbmap: Tensor of shape [numrays, 3]. depthmap: Tensor of shape [numrays]. accmap: Tensor of shape [numrays]. """ # 1. Define sampling intervals # Divide ray into N equal bins tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., steps=Nsamples).to(rayso.device) zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals # 2. Clamp bounds using depth priors # NerfingMVS uses depth priors to guide sampling by clamping ray bounds. # Implementation details of exact clamping logic are not fully shown in sources, # but priors are passed to modulate sampling ranges. # We clamp zvals to the provided near/far bounds as a baseline. zvals = torch.clamp(zvals, min=near, max=far) # 3. Sample points and query NeRF pts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(-1) pts = pts.reshape(-1, 3) # Query NeRF for density and color rawdensity, rawcolor = model(pts) # 4. Compute weights dists = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.tensor([1e10]).to(rayso.device)], dim=-1) dists = dists torch.norm(raysd.unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) alpha = 1. - torch.exp(-F.relu(rawdensity) dists) # Numerical stability: add 1e-10 to (1-alpha) in cumprod to prevent NaNs transmittance = torch.cumprod(1. - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-1) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittance[...,:1]), transmittance[...,:-1]], dim=-1) weights = alpha transmittance # 5. Render RGB and Depth rgbmap = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rawcolor, dim=-2) depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=-1) accmap = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # 6. Composite against white background rgbmap = rgbmap + (1. - accmap.unsqueeze(-1)) # 7. NDC transform for depth if applicable # depthmap = -1/raysdori[:, 2](1 / (1 - depthmap) + raysoori[:, 2]) return rgbmap, depthmap, accmap def nerfingmvstrainstep(rayso, raysd, rgbgt, depthpriors, depthconfidences, model, optimizer): """ Single training step for NerfingMVS. """ optimizer.zerograd() # Render rgbpred, depthpred, acc = nerfingmvsrender( rayso, raysd, depthpriors, depthconfidences, model, Nsamples=64, near=0.05, far=0.15) # Loss 1: RGB Loss (L1 or MSE) rgbloss = F.mseloss(rgbpred, rgbgt) # Loss 2: Depth Consistency Loss # Align rendered depth with depth prior # Use confidence to weight the loss depthloss = torch.mean(depthconfidences torch.abs(depthpred - depthpriors)) totalloss = rgbloss + 0.5 depthloss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item(), rgbloss.item(), depthloss.item() depthNrand: Batch size for depth sampling (default 4). depthNiters: Number of iterations for depth prior training (default 151). depthH, depthW: Height and width of the depth image (must be multiples of 16, e.g., 288x384). depthlrate: Learning rate for depth network adaptation (default 4e-4). near: Absolute near bound for ray clipping (default 0.05). far: Absolute far bound for ray clipping (default 0.15). topk: Top-k for consistency error filtering (default 4). Numerical Stability in Cumprod: When computing transmittance, add 10^{-10} to (1-\alpha) to prevent NaNs when \alpha is close to 1. Division by Zero in Disparity: If computing disparity maps, use \max(10^{-10}, \dots) to avoid division by zero when depth or accumulated opacity is zero. Scale Ambiguity: The monocular depth prior is relative. The scale-invariant loss during adaptation helps, but the final NeRF depth may still lack absolute scale unless constrained by the sparse COLMAP points or explicit scale normalization. COLMAP Dependency: The method relies heavily on the quality of COLMAP's sparse reconstruction. Poor pose estimation or sparse points can lead to poor depth priors. Time Complexity: Training time is significantly higher than standard NeRF due to the additional depth prior adaptation step and the complexity of guided sampling. The source notes approximately 3.5 hours on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 GPU for a ScanNet scene, including COLMAP, depth training, and NeRF training. Memory Complexity: Similar to standard NeRF, but requires storing depth priors and confidences for each ray/view. Chunked rendering is used to avoid OOM errors. Strengths: Improves geometry in textureless or repetitive indoor scenes where standard NeRF suffers from shape-radiance ambiguity. Eliminates the need for explicit pixel matching across views during optimization. Largely improves the quality of the final depth output. Limitations: Requires a good initial sparse reconstruction from COLMAP. Performance is dependent on the quality of the monocular depth estimator and its adaptation to the scene. Lacks efficiency for real-time system application. When to Use: Indoor multi-view stereo tasks where high-quality geometry and depth are required, and sufficient multi-view overlap exists for COLMAP to work. When Not to Use: Outdoor scenes with large baselines, dynamic scenes, or scenes where COLMAP cannot produce a reliable sparse reconstruction. NerfingMVS was introduced by Yi Wei, Shaohui Liu, Yongming Rao, Wang Zhao, Jiwen Lu, and Jie Zhou in September 2021 at ICCV. The paper, titled "NerfingMVS: Guided Optimization of Neural Radiance Fields for Indoor Multi-View Stereo," addresses the limitations of NeRF in indoor environments, specifically the shape-radiance ambiguity. It builds upon the NeRF framework and integrates principles from multi-view stereo (MVS) and monocular depth estimation. The method was evaluated on ScanNet and Matterport3D datasets. It is based on the PyTorch implementation of NeRF. name: Depth-Guided NeRF Training via Earth Mover’s Distance
head: Depth-guided NeRF via Earth Mover’s Distance, EM D-Guided Sampling, EMD-Guided Depth Supervision for NeRF, EMD-NeRF, EMD-based objective
body: This method improves the geometric accuracy of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) trained on sparse views by supervising the distribution of ray termination distances using Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) rather than enforcing direct depth matching. Unlike sibling methods such as DäRF which minimize the norm between rendered and prior depth, or SCADE which relies on multiple ambiguous hypotheses, this approach uses a single off-the-shelf diffusion-based depth prior and its intrinsic uncertainty map to selectively guide the NeRF’s geometry without propagating prior inaccuracies. It builds on Monocular Depth Estimation Adaptation and Supervision by replacing standard L2 depth consistency losses with a distributional EMD loss weighted by uncertainty. Inputs: A set of N input RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N (typically N < 20) and their corresponding SfM camera poses. A pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) network, specifically DiffDP. A NeRF model F\Theta initialized with random weights. Outputs: A trained NeRF model F\Theta capable of rendering novel views with accurate geometry. Rendered RGB images and depth maps for novel viewpoints. NeRF Model (F\Theta): A multilayer perceptron (MLP) taking 5D input (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) representing camera position and viewing direction, outputting color c and volume density \sigma. Depth Prior (z0): A relative depth map generated by DiffDP for each input image. Uncertainty Map (u): A pixel-wise uncertainty map derived from the DiffDP denoising process, normalized to [0, 1]. Ray Samples: For each ray, a set of termination distances y = \{y1, \dots, yN\} sampled from the NeRF's predicted distribution. 1. Depth Prior and Uncertainty Extraction: For each input image I, run the DiffDP network to generate the depth prior z0 and the uncertainty map u. DiffDP formulates denoising as p\theta(z{0:T}|I). The uncertainty is derived by comparing estimates at consecutive denoising steps t and t-1. Let c(z{0:T}) be the count of steps where the change exceeds a threshold \tau: c(z{0:T}) = \frac{1}{T} \sum{t=T,\dots,1} \mathbb{I}(|zt - z{t-1}| \ge \tau) The final uncertainty u(z{0:T}|I) combines this temporal uncertainty with spatial consistency using a mirrored image M(I): U(z{0:T}|I) = \frac{c(z{0:T}|I) + M(c(z{0:T}|M(I)))}{2} u(z{0:T}|I) = U(z{0:T}|I) \cdot \| (z0|I) - M(z0|M(I)) \|1 2. NeRF Forward Pass and Weight Calculation: Cast rays through the camera. For each sample i along a ray at distance di, query F\Theta to get density \sigmai. Calculate the transmittance Ti and the weight wi representing the probability that the ray terminates at sample i: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples. 3. Probability Density Construction: Normalize the weights wi to form a piece-wise constant probability density function (PDF): \hat{w}i = \frac{wi}{\sum{j=1}^{N} wj} Construct the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) from \hat{w}i. 4. EMD-Guided Sampling: Sample new ray termination distances y = \{y1, \dots, yN\} from the constructed CDF using inverse transform sampling. These samples represent the NeRF's learned distribution of surface locations. 5. Loss Calculation: Photometric Loss: Compute the L2 loss between the rendered color \hat{C}(r) and the observed color C(r): L{photo} = ||\hat{C}(r) - C(r)||2^2 EMD Depth Loss: Compute the Earth Mover’s Distance between the sampled NeRF distances y and the depth prior z0. Since EMD is non-differentiable, approximate it using Sinkhorn Divergence during training: L{EMD} = EMD(y, z0) Total Loss: Combine the losses weighted by the uncertainty map u, a balancing weight \lambda, and a focal-like exponent \gamma: L = (1 + u)^\gamma L{photo} + \lambda (1 - u)^\gamma L{EMD} Note: Unlike Focal Loss which increases weight for uncertain examples, this method decreases the weight of the depth loss for uncertain pixels (1-u), relying more on photometric supervision when depth is unreliable. 6. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters \Theta using gradient descent. Initialize the scale of the depth priors to 1 and learn the scale with a small learning rate. Unverified code.
