name: Depth Completion Network NeRF
head: DCN-NeRF, Depth Completion (MFFNet), Guided depth completion, MFFNet
body: Depth Completion Network NeRF integrates a guided depth completion network into the NeRF training loop to recover dense depth maps from sparse LiDAR measurements using image guidance for higher accuracy. Unlike sibling methods that rely on monocular depth estimation (MDE) priors which lack absolute scale or suffer from accuracy compromises, this method uses LiDAR-based completion to provide dense, metrically consistent depth supervision. It sets itself apart by explicitly addressing the sparsity of raw LiDAR data through guided completion, making it suitable for unbounded real-world scenes where raw LiDAR is insufficient. Builds on Monocular Depth Estimation Adaptation and Supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Input RGB images I, sparse raw LiDAR depth measurements Dl, and camera poses. Outputs: A dense depth map D{guide} used for supervision, and the final NeRF radiance field parameters. Data Structures: Sparse LiDAR Depth (Dl): A sparse 2D map or point cloud representing raw LiDAR returns. RGB Image (I): The corresponding color image for the LiDAR frame. Completion Network (\delta): A neural network (specifically MFFNet) that takes I and Dl as input. Steps: 1. Sparse Point Cloud Extraction: Extract a sparse point cloud from the scene using COLMAP to establish initial geometry and camera poses. 2. Depth Completion: Apply the guided depth completion network \delta to the input image I and raw LiDAR depth Dl to produce a dense, guided depth map D{guide}: D{guide} = \delta(I, Dl) where \delta represents the completion network (e.g., MFFNet). 3. NeRF Rendering: Render the NeRF model F\Theta to obtain the predicted depth \bar{D} and color for each ray, using standard volume rendering accumulation. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss. This includes the standard volumetric loss (color reconstruction) and a depth loss based on the predicted depth and its uncertainty, minimizing the divergence between the ray's distribution and the noisy depth distribution. 5. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters to minimize the combined loss. Parameters: Completion Method: MFFNet is selected as the representative guided depth completion method. Training Data: RGB-D data from ScanNet and Matterport3D datasets. Noise: Gaussian noise is added to the depth during training to improve robustness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity: Raw LiDAR is inherently sparse. The completion network is necessary to bridge this gap. Uncertainty: If the completion network outputs uncertainty, it should be used to weight the depth loss, penalizing confident predictions more heavily. NLSPN propagates depth information from LiDAR points to surrounding pixels to provide credible depth supervisions from defect LiDAR depths. It requires accumulating neighbor LiDAR frames to get much denser depths for input. However, NLSPN performs well with 64-channel LiDAR data (e.g., KITTI) but fails with nuScenes' 32-channel LiDAR data because it is too sparse for the depth completion network. Additionally, accumulated LiDAR data contain outliers due to moving objects, ill poses, and occlusions, leading to wrong depth supervisions. Complexity: Adds the inference cost of the depth completion network (MFFNet) to the NeRF training loop. Performance: Achieves higher accuracy than unguided methods by leveraging image guidance. Strengths: Effective for unbounded real scenes where raw LiDAR is sparse. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the LiDAR hardware and the completion network; sensitive to outliers in accumulated LiDAR data if not handled. When to use: When sparse LiDAR data is available and high-accuracy dense depth is required for NeRF training in outdoor or large-scale scenes. When not to use: When only monocular images are available (use MDE-based methods instead) or when LiDAR is too sparse for the completion network (e.g., 32-channel LiDAR without accumulation). The method originates from the need to handle unbounded real scenes where the original NeRF parametrization was limited to bounded or forward-facing scenes. It builds on the observation that raw LiDAR provides sparse measurements, while monocular methods compromise on accuracy. The approach was developed to integrate guided depth completion (specifically MFFNet) into NeRF training, using datasets like ScanNet and Matterport3D. name: Monocular Depth Regularization on Seen Views
head: Patch-wise depth alignment, Seen-view depth distillation
body: This method aligns pseudo-depth maps from a pre-trained monocular depth estimation (MDE) network with NeRF-rendered depth for seen input views to stabilize geometry optimization. It differs from global scale-fitting approaches by computing local scale and shift parameters per image patch, preventing dominant objects from biasing the depth alignment and thereby preserving local geometric details. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of seen view images S, a pre-trained MDE network G\phi, and a NeRF model F\Theta. Output: A depth consistency loss term L{\text{seen}} added to the training objective. Data Structures: Patches: The image is partitioned into spatial regions, where each region contains a set of pixels P. Depth Maps: D^i: Relative depth map predicted by the MDE network for image Ii. \bar{D}i: Absolute depth map rendered by the NeRF for view i. Parameters: wi, qi: Local scale and shift parameters for a specific patch, computed via least squares to align the relative MDE depth to the absolute NeRF depth. \text{sg}(\cdot): Stop-gradient operator applied to the monocular depth to prevent gradient flow into the frozen MDE network during this loss computation. Steps: 1. For each seen view Ii \in S, render the NeRF depth map \bar{D}i. 2. Extract the relative pseudo-depth map D^i = G\phi(Ii) using the pre-trained MDE network. 3. Partition the image into patches, and define P as the set of pixels within a given patch. 4. For each patch, compute the optimal scale wi and shift qi by minimizing the least-squares error between \text{sg}(D^i) and \bar{D}i. 5. Calculate the patch-wise depth consistency loss and sum it over all patches and all seen views. Formula: The total depth consistency loss for seen views is defined as: L{\text{seen}} = \sum{Ii \in S} \sum{p \in P} \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(D^i(p)) + qi) - \bar{D}i(p) \| where \| \cdot \| denotes the L1 norm, as implemented in the reference code. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeseendepthloss(views, nerfmodel, mdemodel, patchsize): totalloss = 0.0 for view in views: # 1. Render NeRF depth for current camera pose nerfdepth = nerfmodel.renderdepth(view.camerapose) # 2. Extract relative MDE depth mdedepth = mdemodel(view.image) # 3. Iterate over patches H, W = nerfdepth.shape for y in range(0, H, patchsize): for x in range(0, W, patchsize): yend = min(y + patchsize, H) xend = min(x + patchsize, W) # Extract patch tensors patchmde = mdedepth[y:yend, x:xend] patchnerf = nerfdepth[y:yend, x:xend] # 4. Compute scale and shift via least squares mmean = patchmde.mean() nmean = patchnerf.mean() mc = patchmde - mmean nc = patchnerf - nmean varm = (mc 2).sum() covmn = (mc nc).sum() if varm > 1e-6: w = covmn / varm q = nmean - w mmean else: w = 1.0 q = 0.0 # 5. Calculate loss with stop-gradient on MDE depth alignedmde = w patchmde.detach() + q patchloss = (alignedmde - patchnerf).abs().sum() totalloss += patchloss return totalloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dominant Object Bias: Global scale/shift fitting favors large or high-contrast objects, leading to ill-fitted depths in less dominant sections; patch-wise adjustment alleviates this. Computational Bottleneck: The patch-based approach helps overcome the computational bottleneck of full image rendering by allowing localized computations. Gradient Flow: The stop-gradient operator \text{sg}(\cdot) is critical to prevent gradients from flowing into the pre-trained MDE network G\phi, which remains frozen during this loss computation. Incorporates geometric constraints from MDE but filters supervision using transient confidence weights to enforce consistency only on static geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves local geometric details by avoiding global bias; stabilizes training for sparse inputs. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When training NeRFs on sparse or unconstrained image collections where global depth alignment fails due to varying object scales or dominant foregrounds. The method was introduced in the DaRF paper, which proposes boosting radiance fields from sparse inputs using monocular depth adaptation. It addresses the issue that global scale fitting undermines local statistics. name: Transient-Aware Depth Prior
head: DPT depth supervision, monocular depth loss, Depth Regularization with Monocular Estimation
body: The Transient-Aware Depth Prior is a regularization technique for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that incorporates geometric priors from a monocular depth estimator (typically DPT) to constrain optimization and suppress artifacts like floaters or geometry collapse. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly aligning the scale and offset of the monocular depth map using learnable per-image parameters and filtering the loss with a transient confidence weight derived from the NeRF's own density fields, rather than relying on generalizable priors or inter-frame consistency alone. This allows the method to apply depth supervision only to static regions, preventing the network from learning incorrect geometry for transient objects. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training image i, camera pose, ray r passing through pixel, pre-trained Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) network (DPT), current NeRF model (shared density \sigma and candidate density \sigma^{(c)}). Outputs: Depth loss value L{depth} for the current ray. Data Structures: Monocular Depth Prior: Dense inverse depth map D^{inv}i predicted by DPT for image i. Learnable Parameters: Per-image scale \etai and shift \xii. NeRF Densities: Shared density \sigma (static geometry) and candidate density \sigma^{(c)} (transient/uncertain geometry). Steps: 1. Acquire Monocular Depth: For each training image i, predict the inverse depth map D^{inv}i using the DPT network. 2. Compute Aligned Monocular Depth: Transform the inverse depth to align with the NeRF's coordinate system using learnable scale \etai and shift \xii: D^i(r) = \frac{1}{\etai D^{inv}i(r) + \xii} where D^i(r) is the aligned monocular depth prior for ray r. 3. Render NeRF Depth: Compute the expected depth \hat{D}i(r) from the NeRF using volume rendering integration along the ray: \hat{D}i(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} T(tk) \alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) tk where tk are sample points, \deltak is the distance between samples, \alpha is the opacity, T(tk) is the transmittance, and \sigma is the shared density. 4. Calculate Transient Confidence Weight: Determine the weight W{depth}(r) based on the ratio of candidate density to shared density: W{depth}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Ti(tk) \alpha(\sigma^{(c)}(tk)\deltak) where Ti(tk) is the transmittance computed using the candidate density \sigma^{(c)}. Note: W{depth}(r) \in [0, 1]. High values of W{depth}(r) indicate high transient confidence, causing the (1 - W{depth}(r)) factor to suppress the loss in those regions. 5. Compute Depth Loss: Calculate the L1 loss between the aligned monocular depth and the rendered NeRF depth, weighted by the transient confidence: L{depth}(r) = (1 - W{depth}(r)) \| D^i(r) - \hat{D}i(r) \|1. Parameters: \lambdad: Weight for the depth loss in the total loss function. Typical value: 0.001. \etai, \xii: Learnable scale and shift parameters for each image i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetransientawaredepthloss(ray, imageidx, nerfmodel, dptmodel, eta, xi, K=128): """ ray: Ray object with origins and directions. imageidx: Index of the current training image. nerfmodel: NeRF model providing shared density sigma and candidate density sigmac. dptmodel: Pre-trained DPT model for monocular depth estimation. eta: Learnable scale parameter for imageidx. xi: Learnable shift parameter for imageidx. K: Number of sample points along the ray. """ # 1. Acquire monocular inverse depth from DPT pixelcoords = ray.getpixelcoordinates() dinv = dptmodel.predictinversedepth(imageidx, pixelcoords) # 2. Compute aligned monocular depth D dmono = 1.0 / (eta dinv + xi) # 3. Render NeRF depth Dhat tsamples = ray.samplepoints(K) sigmashared = nerfmodel.getshareddensity(tsamples) sigmacand = nerfmodel.getcandidatedensity(tsamples) # Compute deltas between consecutive samples deltas = [tsamples[k+1] - tsamples[k] for k in range(len(tsamples) - 1)] deltas.append(deltas[-1]) # Handle last delta # Compute opacity alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma delta) alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigmashared[k] deltas[k]) for k in range(len(tsamples))] # Compute transmittance T(tk) = product{j<k} (1 - alphaj) T = [1.0] for k in range(len(alpha) - 1): T.append(T[-1] (1.0 - alpha[k])) # Rendered depth Dhat = sum(T alpha t) dhat = sum(T[k] alpha[k] tsamples[k] for k in range(len(tsamples))) # 4. Calculate transient confidence weight Wdepth # Alphacand uses candidate density sigmac alphacand = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigmacand[k] deltas[k]) for k in range(len(tsamples))] Tcand = [1.0] for k in range(len(alphacand) - 1): Tcand.append(Tcand[-1] (1.0 - alphacand[k])) wdepth = sum(Tcand[k] alphacand[k] for k in range(len(tsamples))) # 5. Compute weighted L1 loss loss = (1.0 - wdepth) abs(dmono - dhat) return loss Depth Regularization incorporates geometric priors from a monocular depth estimator (typically DPT) into the training of radiance fields or 3D Gaussian Splatting to enforce geometric consistency and suppress artifacts like floaters or geometry collapse. Time Complexity: Adds the cost of a forward pass through the DPT network per image (or cached) and additional density evaluations for the candidate head to compute W{depth}. Memory Complexity: Requires storing learnable \etai, \xii per image and potentially caching DPT outputs. Performance: Improves novel view synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM) on unconstrained datasets like PhotoTourism compared to baselines like BARF and NeRF-W. Strengths: Effectively suppresses floaters and geometry collapse in unconstrained image collections by leveraging strong geometric priors. Limitations: The depth prior is a pseudo-label and not ground truth; over-reliance can degrade rendering quality if not properly weighted. The method relies on the accuracy of the DPT model. When to use: When training NeRF on unconstrained image sets with potential transient objects and unknown poses. When not to use: When high-quality ground truth depth is available, or when computational resources for DPT inference are prohibitive. The method was introduced in UP-NeRF (Unconstrained Pose-Prior-Free Neural Radiance Fields). It is inspired by NoPe-NeRF, which also uses monocular depth regularization. However, UP-NeRF adapts the approach for unconstrained images by using per-image affine alignment and transient-aware weighting, whereas NoPe-NeRF originally focused on video sequences with inter-frame losses. The DPT (Dense Prediction Transformer) model is used as the monocular depth estimator. name: Depth Regularization
head: DPT Depth Regularization, Depth Supervised Regularization, Monocular Depth Regularization
body: Depth Regularization incorporates geometric priors from a monocular depth estimator (typically DPT) into the training of radiance fields or 3D Gaussian Splatting to enforce geometric consistency and suppress artifacts like floaters or geometry collapse. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly aligning the scale and offset of the monocular depth map using sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points, rather than relying on scale-invariant losses or generalizable priors. Unlike Edge-Aware Disparity Regularization which preserves edges via image gradients, or DNGaussian which uses hard/soft regularization stages, this method focuses on per-frame SfM-based scaling and exponential decay weighting. Inputs: Rendered depth map \hat{D} from the scene representation (Gaussians or spheres). Monocular depth estimate D from a pre-trained network (e.g., DPT). Sparse SfM points (inverse depth D^{SFM}) from COLMAP for the current view. Camera intrinsics and extrinsics. Outputs: Depth regularization loss LD and its gradients propagated to the scene representation parameters (Gaussian means, opacities, etc.). Data Structures: Monocular Depth Map D: 2D array of inverse depth values predicted by DPT. SfM Inverse Depth D^{SFM}: Sparse set of inverse depth values at known 3D point locations projected to the image plane. Rendered Depth \hat{D}: Computed via alpha-compositing of Gaussian depths along each ray. Steps: 1. Compute Scale and Offset for Monocular Depth: Calculate the temporal median t(D) and scale s(D) for the monocular inverse depth map D using the SfM points: t(D) = \text{median}(D) s(D) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i \in \text{SFM}} |Di - t(D)| where M is the number of SfM points in the image, and i \in \text{SFM} are the indices of the SfM points. 2. Align Monocular Depth to Dataset Scale: Transform the monocular inverse depth D to the dataset scale D^ using the SfM inverse depth statistics t(D^{SFM}) and s(D^{SFM}): D^ = \frac{D + t(D^{SFM}) - t(D)}{s(D)} \cdot s(D^{SFM}) This aligns the relative scale and offset of the monocular estimate with the sparse but metrically accurate SfM points. 3. Render Scene Depth: Compute the rendered depth \hat{D} for each pixel by alpha-compositing the depths of the primitives along the ray. For a ray with N primitives, where Ti is the transmittance, \alphai is the opacity of the i-th primitive, and di is its depth: \hat{D} = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai di where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). 4. Compute Depth Loss: Calculate the difference between the rendered depth \hat{D} and the aligned monocular depth D^: L{raw} = \hat{D} - D^ The source specifies this subtraction directly, and implementations typically apply an L1 or L2 norm. 5. Apply Exponential Decay Weighting: Weight the depth loss with an exponential decay factor w(t) throughout the optimization, starting at 1 and ending at 0.01 for per-chunk optimization: LD = w(t) \cdot L{raw} where t is the current training step. 6. Backpropagation: Propagate gradients from LD to the scene representation parameters. Specifically, gradients flow to each Gaussian's depth (mean position) and to the rendering \alpha (opacity), which affects the Gaussian's contribution to the final depth and its screen-space position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedepthregularizationloss(rendereddepth, monodepth, sfmdepth, sfmindices, M, decayweight): # Step 1: Compute scale and offset for monocular depth tmono = median(monodepth) smono = sum(abs(monodepth[i] - tmono) for i in sfmindices) / M # Step 2: Align monocular depth to dataset scale tsfm = median(sfmdepth) ssfm = sum(abs(sfmdepth[i] - tsfm) for i in sfmindices) / M aligneddepth = (monodepth + tsfm - tmono) / smono ssfm # Step 3 & 4: Compute raw loss (rendered depth already computed via alpha-compositing) rawloss = rendereddepth - aligneddepth # Step 5: Apply exponential decay weighting depthloss = decayweight rawloss # Step 6: Backpropagation handled automatically by autograd framework return depthloss Parameters: Monocular Depth Estimator: DPT [Ranftl et al. 2021]. Decay Start/End: 1.0 to 0.01. SfM Points: Provided by COLMAP. Regularization Weight \lambda{DS}: 1000 (used in SatGeo-NeRF variant for the first 25% of iterations). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. A regularization term applied during novel-view synthesis optimization to encourage spheres to move to the correct scene depth. It sets itself apart by using an energy function based on opacity and depth rather than direct depth matching. Definition: Encourages spheres to move to correct depth. Step: Thresholding: Apply a threshold to spheres with low opacity to remove them. Formula: Energy = -zi \cdot Oi, where zi is the depth of sphere i and Oi is its opacity. Methods that introduce additional constraints such as depth information to enhance detail and global consistency when observational data is sparse. It distinguishes itself by focusing on the trade-off between strong geometric constraints and computational cost in sparse-view scenarios. Definition: Enhances detail and global consistency with sparse data. Pitfall: Efficacy diminishes with very limited views (e.g., one view). Comparison: Relies on strong constraints and per-scene optimization, favoring geometric quality but incurring higher computation compared to generalizability-based methods. Usage: DNGaussian uses a depth-regularized scheme. FSGS uses Gaussian Unpooling and depth regularization. MVSplat uses cost volume for geometry cues. A variant of 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) that incorporates a depth regularization strategy by enabling supervision and gradient flow to depths within the CUDA backend rasterizer, supervised with sensor or monocular depth estimates. It sets itself apart by integrating depth supervision directly into the rasterizer's gradient flow. Definition: 2DGS with depth regularization in CUDA rasterizer. Formula: The overall optimization loss is defined as L = L{rgb} + \lambdad \tilde{L}d, where L{rgb} is the original loss from 2DGS and \tilde{L}d is the depth regularization term. Parameter: \lambdad = 0.2. A regularization term preventing Gaussians from drifting to unsupported regions of space by penalizing continuous violations of image bounds and valid depth ranges across input views. It distinguishes itself by using a soft penalty based on the minimum frustum violation across all input views. Definition: Prevents Gaussians from drifting to unsupported regions. Step: For each Gaussian n with center \mun, transform to camera coordinates, project to image coordinates, and measure continuous violations of image bounds and valid depth range for each input view. If a Gaussian lies inside at least one input-view frustum, its penalty is zero. Otherwise, it receives a smooth positive penalty based on the minimum violation vn. Formula: Compute frustum loss: L{fru} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^{N} \log(1 + vn/\tau), where vn is the minimum frustum violation of Gaussian n across input views, and \tau controls softness. Parameter: \tau: Parameter controlling the softness of the penalty. Time Complexity: Depends on the monocular depth estimation inference time (DPT) and the additional gradient computation for depth alignment. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the monocular depth map and SfM points per view. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales with the number of training views and the density of SfM points. Strengths: Improves geometric consistency and reduces floaters by leveraging strong monocular priors aligned with sparse SfM data. Limitations: Efficacy diminishes with very sparse input views (e.g., single view). Relies on the accuracy of the monocular depth estimator and SfM reconstruction. When to Use: When geometric consistency is critical and sparse SfM points are available to align the monocular depth scale. When Not to Use: When input views are extremely sparse (e.g., single view) or when SfM reconstruction is unreliable. Depth Regularization using monocular depth estimators like DPT was introduced in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to address geometry degradation in large datasets. The method builds on the observation that monocular depth estimates, while scale-ambiguous, provide strong geometric cues that can be aligned with sparse SfM points to provide metric supervision. It is used in training loops for radiance fields and Gaussian Splatting to improve novel view synthesis quality. name: SparseGS
head: Sparse View Synthesis Using 3D Gaussian Splatting
body: SparseGS is a method for sparse-view 3D reconstruction using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to address misplaced Gaussians ("floaters"), geometry collapse, and texture noise. It differs from siblings like FSGS, which relies on Gaussian unpooling, and DNGaussian, which uses depth-normal regularizers, by combining monocular depth priors with diffusion-based Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to stabilize training under extreme sparsity (~3 to 12 views). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse set of input images (typically ~3 to 12 views), camera poses, and intrinsics. A pre-trained monocular depth estimation model provides initial depth priors. A pre-trained Stable Diffusion model (version 2.1) provides generative priors. Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a rendered image/depth map. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitives: Standard 3DGS representation. Each Gaussian i is defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, parameterized by a rotation matrix Ri and a scaling vector si. Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1]. Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients for view-dependent color. Depth Map: Rendered depth is computed per pixel. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from the input point cloud or sparse reconstruction. Standard 3DGS initialization is assumed. 2. Softmax-Scaling Depth Rendering: To reduce misplaced Gaussians caused by alpha-blending depth averaging, replace standard alpha-blending depth with a softmax-scaled depth rendering. This constrains depth convergence. Let di be the depth of the i-th Gaussian along the ray. Let \alphai be the opacity. The rendered depth D is computed using a softmax-weighted average rather than a linear alpha-composite average, biasing towards the mode of the depth distribution. 3. Depth Correlation Loss: Apply a Pearson Correlation Loss between the rendered depth and the monocular depth estimate. Compute local and global Pearson correlation coefficients between the rendered depth map and the reference monocular depth map. Loss weights: Local Pearson loss weight = 0.15; Global Pearson loss weight = 0.15. 4. Unseen Viewpoints Regularization (UVR): To prevent overfitting and reduce high-frequency artifacts in sparse settings, render images from viewpoints away from the training set and apply a consistency loss. This improves PSNR by an average of 0.33 dB. 5. Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) and Depth Warping: For regions with insufficient input coverage, leverage SDS and depth warping to reduce geometry collapse and texture noise while preserving fine details. Enable SDS after two-thirds of the total training iterations, once the scene structure is stable. SDS Loss weight: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Depth Warping Loss weight: 0.05. 6. Floater Pruning: Identify and remove low-opacity Gaussians that are misplaced (floaters). This heuristic cleans the scene, making the image and depth map sharper. This boosts PSNR by 0.28 dB. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainsparsegs(inputimages, cameraposes, numiterations): # Standard 3DGS initialization from sparse point cloud gaussians = { 'positions': torch.tensor(initializepointcloud(inputimages, cameraposes)), 'covariances': computecovariancesfrompointcloud(), 'opacities': torch.ones(numgaussians), 'shcoeffs': torch.zeros(numgaussians, numshbases, 3) } # Pre-trained models depthestimator = MonocularDepthModel() diffusionmodel = StableDiffusionV21() # Hyperparameters wpearsonlocal = 0.15 wpearsonglobal = 0.15 wsds = 5e-4 wdepthwarp = 0.05 sdsstartiter = int(numiterations 2 / 3) for iter in range(numiterations): # 1. Forward Pass: Render Image and Depth renderedimage, rendereddepth = rendergaussians( gaussians, cameraposes, usesoftmaxdepth=True) # 2. Compute Losses loss = torch.tensor(0.0, requiresgrad=True) # Depth Correlation Loss (Pearson) refdepth = depthestimator(inputimages[0]) localcorr = pearsoncorrelation(rendereddepth, refdepth, windowsize=7) globalcorr = pearsoncorrelation(rendereddepth, refdepth) loss = loss + wpearsonlocal (1.0 - localcorr) loss = loss + wpearsonglobal (1.0 - globalcorr) # Unseen Viewpoints Regularization (UVR) unseenpose = samplerandompose(cameraposes) renderedunseen, = rendergaussians(gaussians, unseenpose, usesoftmaxdepth=True) loss = loss + 0.1 torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedunseen - inputimages[0])) # SDS and Depth Warping if iter > sdsstartiter: # Score Distillation Sampling noise = torch.randnlike(renderedimage) t = torch.randint(0, 1000, (1,)).item() noisyimage = diffusionmodel.addnoise(renderedimage, noise, t) noisepred = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(noisyimage, t) sdsgrad = computesdsgradient(renderedimage, noisepred, noise) loss = loss + wsds sdsgrad # Depth Warping warpeddepth = warpdepth(rendereddepth, cameraposes, unseenpose) loss = loss + wdepthwarp torch.mean(torch.abs(rendereddepth - warpeddepth)) # 3. Backpropagate and Update gradients = torch.autograd.grad(loss, list(gaussians.values())) updategaussians(gaussians, gradients) # 4. Floater Pruning gaussians = prunefloaters(gaussians, opacitythreshold=0.01) return gaussians def initializepointcloud(images, poses): # Standard 3DGS initialization from sparse point cloud return standard3dgsinit(images, poses) def computecovariancesfrompointcloud(): # Standard covariance computation from point cloud return standardcovariancecalc() def rendergaussians(gaussians, poses, usesoftmaxdepth): # Standard 3DGS rasterization; if usesoftmaxdepth, depth is weighted by softmax(alpha) instead of linear alpha return standardrasterize(gaussians, poses, usesoftmaxdepth) def pearsoncorrelation(x, y, windowsize=None): # Standard Pearson correlation coefficient computation return standardpearsoncorr(x, y, windowsize) def samplerandompose(poses): # Randomly sample a pose outside the training set return random.choice(poses) def computesdsgradient(rendered, noisepred, noise): # Standard SDS gradient: w(t) (noisepred - noise) d(rendered)/d(rendered) return (noisepred - noise) def warpdepth(depth, poses, targetpose): # Standard depth warping using camera poses and inverse projection return standarddepthwarp(depth, poses, targetpose) def prunefloaters(gaussians, opacitythreshold): # Filter Gaussians with opacity below threshold mask = gaussians['opacities'] > opacitythreshold return {k: v[mask] for k, v in gaussians.items()} def updategaussians(gaussians, gradients): # Standard Adam optimizer step standardoptimizerstep(gaussians, gradients) Parameters: SDS loss weight: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Depth warping loss weight: 0.05. Local and Global Pearson loss weights: 0.15. SDS activation: After 2/3 of total iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Softmax-scaling depth rendering is critical to avoid the averaging artifacts of standard alpha-blending which cause floaters. Boundaries: The method is designed for forward-facing datasets (LLFF, DTU) and unbounded scenes (Mip-NeRF360). Degenerate Input: In regions with very little coverage, standard 3DGS fails; SDS and depth warping are specifically enabled to handle this. Uses Gaussian unpooling for few-shot reconstruction. Excels in fine details but fails on background geometry. Link Uses depth-normal regularizers. Renders coherent backgrounds but may prune foreground objects incorrectly. Link Focuses on edge-aware constraints for disparity. Link Time and Memory Complexity: Standard 3DGS complexity, plus overhead for monocular depth estimation and SDS gradient computation. SDS is enabled only after 2/3 of iterations, reducing early training cost. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF360 (12-view setting): Baseline (Alpha-blending): PSNR 17.49, LPIPS 0.431, SSIM 0.499. + Softmax-scaling: PSNR 18.45. + UVR: PSNR 18.86. + Pruning: PSNR 19.09. Full SparseGS: PSNR 19.37, LPIPS 0.398, SSIM 0.577. Scaling: Outperforms NeRF-based methods and concurrent works (FSGS, DNGaussian) in both 12-view and 24-view settings. Strengths: Effectively reconstructs high-frequency geometry and preserves sharp boundaries. Cleaner and more coherent scene structure than DNGaussian. Less background collapse than FSGS. Limitations: Relies on pre-trained monocular depth and diffusion models, which may introduce biases if the priors are inaccurate. SDS computation is expensive. SparseGS was proposed to tackle sparse-view 3D reconstruction using 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitations of original 3DGS, where alpha-blending depth rendering leads to misplaced Gaussians (floaters), and the tendency of 3DGS to place isolated Gaussians in under-covered regions, resulting in high-frequency noise. The method builds on the observation that NeRF-based methods often produce overly smooth appearances in sparse settings, while 3DGS-based representations gravitate towards isolated, noisy Gaussians. It utilizes Stable Diffusion v2.1 for generative priors. name: PixelSplat Training and Depth Regularization
head: Depth Regularization for 3DGS, PixelSplat Training
body: PixelSplat Training and Depth Regularization is a training procedure for generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting that combines photometric reconstruction with geometric regularization. It differs from its siblings by explicitly placing multiple Gaussians per ray to enable multi-depth gradients and applying a discrete depth regularization term based on second-order derivatives. Inputs: Scenes with reference views and camera poses. Outputs: Trained 3D Gaussians and rendered RGB/depth maps for target views. Data Structures: Gaussian: Defined by mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (or rotation/scale parameters), color c \in \mathbb{R}^3, and opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Ray Probability Distribution: A distribution P(z) along the viewing ray, from which Gaussian centers are sampled. Parameters: Total training steps: 300,000. Batch size: 7 scenes per batch. Gaussians per ray: 3. Alpha scaling factor: 1/3. MSE loss phase: Steps 0–150,000. LPIPS loss phase: Steps 150,000–300,000, weight 0.05. Depth regularization phase: 50,000 steps. VRAM requirement: ~80 GB on a single GPU. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians for each scene. 2. Forward Pass (Rendering): For each scene in the batch, render 4 target views. For each pixel in the target view, cast a ray and sample 3 Gaussian positions independently from the ray's probability distribution P(z). For each sampled Gaussian i, set its opacity \alphai = \phiz / 3, where \phiz is the base opacity contribution, ensuring the total opacity of the 3 Gaussians along the ray sums to roughly 1. Render the RGB image and depth map D using standard volume rendering accumulation. 3. Photometric Loss Calculation (Steps 0–150,000): Compute the MSE loss for the rendered images. 4. Photometric Loss Calculation (Steps 150,000–300,000): Compute the combined loss: L{photo} = L{MSE} + 0.05 \cdot L{LPIPS}, where L{LPIPS} is the Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity loss. 5. Depth Regularization (Fine-tuning, Steps 0–50,000 of phase 2): Generate a depth map D for each rendered view. Compute horizontal and vertical second-order differences of the depth map: Dx^{\Delta}[\mathbf{u}] = D[\mathbf{u}{x-1}, \mathbf{u}y] - 2D[\mathbf{u}x, \mathbf{u}y] + D[\mathbf{u}{x+1}, \mathbf{u}y] and Dy^{\Delta}[\mathbf{u}] = D[\mathbf{u}x, \mathbf{u}{y-1}] - 2D[\mathbf{u}x, \mathbf{u}y] + D[\mathbf{u}x, \mathbf{u}{y+1}], where \mathbf{u} = (ux, uy) are pixel coordinates. Compute the depth regularization loss L{reg\depth} based on these differences and optimize the Gaussian parameters to minimize it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainpixelsplat(scenes, referenceviews, targetviewindices, numsteps=300000, regsteps=50000, batchsize=7, lr=1e-4): # Initialize model parameters (Gaussians) modelparams = initializegaussians(scenes) optimizer = Adam(modelparams, lr=lr) for step in range(numsteps): batchscenes = samplebatch(scenes, batchsize) optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 for scene in batchscenes: renderedimages = [] rendereddepths = [] for targetidx in targetviewindices: rays = castrays(scene, targetidx) gaussianparams = samplegaussiansperray(rays, numsamples=3) gaussianparams.alpha /= 3.0 rgb, depth = volumerender(gaussianparams, rays) renderedimages.append(rgb) rendereddepths.append(depth) gtimages = getgroundtruth(scene, targetviewindices) if step < 150000: loss = computemse(renderedimages, gtimages) else: loss = computemse(renderedimages, gtimages) + 0.05 computelpips(renderedimages, gtimages) totalloss += loss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() for step in range(regsteps): batchscenes = samplebatch(scenes, batchsize) optimizer.zerograd() totalregloss = 0.0 for scene in batchscenes: regloss = 0.0 for targetidx in targetviewindices: rays = castrays(scene, targetidx) gaussianparams = samplegaussiansperray(rays, numsamples=3) gaussianparams.alpha /= 3.0 rgb, depth = volumerender(gaussianparams, rays) dx = depth[:-2,:,:] - 2.0 depth[1:-1,:,:] + depth[2:,:,:] dy = depth[:,:-2,:] - 2.0 depth[:, 1:-1,:] + depth[:, 2:,:] depthreg = computedepthregularization(dx, dy) regloss += depthreg totalregloss += regloss totalregloss.backward() optimizer.step() def initializegaussians(scenes): # Initialize Gaussian parameters for each scene return [...] def samplebatch(scenes, batchsize): return scenes[:batchsize] def castrays(scene, targetidx): # Cast rays for the target view based on camera pose return [...] def samplegaussiansperray(rays, numsamples): # Sample positions independently from P(z) along each ray return [...] def volumerender(gaussianparams, rays): # Standard alpha-compositing volume rendering return rgb, depth def getgroundtruth(scene, targetviewindices): return [scene.images[i] for i in targetviewindices] def computemse(images, targets): return sum((img - tgt)2 for img, tgt in zip(images, targets)) def computelpips(images, targets): # LPIPS perceptual loss computation return 0.0 def computedepthregularization(dx, dy): return torch.sum(dx2 + dy2) SparSplat Training Objective is a variant that uses end-to-end training with multi-view RGB and ground truth depth supervision, freezing deep feature networks for efficiency. It employs a multi-stage coarse-to-fine optimization with a composite loss function: Lk = L{mse} + \lambdas L{ssim} + \lambdap L{perc} + \lambda\alpha Ld + \lambda\beta Ln + \lambda\gamma L{depth}. Here, Ld = \sum{i,j} \omegai \omegaj |zi - zj| is the depth distortion loss concentrating weights along rays, and Ln = \sumi \omegai (1 - ni^T N) is the normal consistency loss aligning splat normals with rendered depth normals. This approach differs from PixelSplat by using 2D Gaussian Splatting and explicit normal/depth distortion terms rather than second-order depth derivatives. Time Complexity: Training requires 300,000 steps for the main phase and 50,000 for depth regularization. Memory Complexity: Requires approximately 80 GB of VRAM on a single GPU for a batch size of 7. Strengths: Allows gradients for multiple depths per ray, improving reconstruction in complex scenes. Limitations: High VRAM requirement limits batch size and resolution. The method builds on 3D Gaussian Splatting and generalizable reconstruction techniques. The depth regularization technique is designed to enhance the geometric quality of the reconstructed point clouds. SparSplat uses 2D Gaussian Splatting with explicit normal/depth distortion terms. name: DNGaussian
head: Depth Normalization Regularized Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Radiance Fields
body: DNGaussian is a depth-regularized framework for few-shot novel view synthesis that combines Hard and Soft Depth Regularization with Global-Local Depth Normalization to restore accurate scene geometry under coarse monocular depth supervision while preserving fine-grained color appearance. It sets itself apart from standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by replacing spherical harmonics with a Neural Color Renderer to prevent overfitting on sparse views and by introducing explicit depth constraints to correct the geometry degradation caused by insufficient input views. Unlike NeRF-based methods that interpolate colors into invisible areas, DNGaussian exposes black backgrounds on empty spaces, focusing optimization on visible geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of input images (typically 3 views) with known camera poses, and pre-predicted monocular depth maps for these views generated by a monocular depth estimator (e.g., DPT). Outputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives (centers \mu, scales s, rotations q, opacities \alpha) and a Neural Color Renderer, enabling novel view synthesis. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitives: Each primitive i is defined by: Center \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Scale si \in \mathbb{R}^3 (or covariance matrix) Rotation qi \in \mathbb{R}^4 (quaternion) Opacity \alphai \in [0, 1] Neural Color Renderer: Hash Encoder: Grid-based encoder with 16 levels, resolution range 16 to 512, max size 2^{19}. MLP: 5-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron with hidden dimension 64. Inference Optimization: Intermediate results from the hash encoder are stored; only the last MLP layers are calculated during rendering to merge view direction for acceleration. Initialization: 1. Initialize a random set of Gaussians using a uniform distribution. Note: Standard 3DGS uses COLMAP point clouds, but DNGaussian uses random initialization because point clouds are unstable in sparse-view situations. Optimization Loop: The optimization runs for 6,000 iterations. It consists of two main modules: Color Supervision and Depth Regularization. 1. Color Supervision: Inherits the standard 3DGS gradient descent and primitive duplication/removal process. Replaces spherical harmonics with the Neural Color Renderer to predict color for each primitive, preventing overfitting on sparse views. Loss: L{color} = L1(\hat{I}, I) + \lambda{LD-SSIM} L{D-SSIM}(\hat{I}, I), where \hat{I} is rendered image and I is ground truth. 2. Depth Regularization: Phase 1: Hard Depth Regularization (Iterations 1–1000): Freeze scaling s and rotation q. Apply a large opacity value \tau = 0.95 to all Gaussians. Optimize only center \mu and opacity \alpha. Render "Hard Depth" D{hard} dominated by the nearest Gaussians. Formula: D{hard}(xp) = \sum{i \in N} \tau (1 - \tau)^{i-1} G^{proj}i(xp) ||\mui - o||2 Where xp is the pixel, N is the set of Gaussians along the ray, i is the ray hit order, G^{proj}i(xp) is the projected 2D Gaussian, \mui is the center, and o is the camera center. Loss: R{hard} = L{similar}(D{hard}, \tilde{D}). Phase 2: Soft Depth Regularization (Iterations 1001–6000): Applied after 1,000 iterations for stability. Freeze Gaussian centers \check{\mu} to avoid negative influence from center movement. Optimize opacity \alpha to ensure surface completeness and prevent hollowness. Render "Soft Depth" D{soft} using actual opacities. Formula: D{soft}(xp) = \sum{i \in N} ||\check{\mu}i - o||2 \times \tilde{\alpha}i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \tilde{\alpha}j) Where \check{\mu} is the frozen center, \tilde{\alpha} is the opacity, and the product term represents cumulative transparency. Loss: R{soft} = L{similar}(D{soft}, \tilde{D}). 3. Global-Local Depth Normalization (Applied to both Hard and Soft losses): To address the limitation of fixed-scale depth alignment which overlooks small errors, DNGaussian uses Global-Local Depth Normalization. Let DT be the rendered depth (Hard or Soft) and \tilde{D} be the monocular depth. Compute Global Normalized Depth (D^{GN}) and Local Normalized Depth (D^{LN}) for both rendered and monocular depths. Total Depth Regularization Loss RT for T \in \{hard, soft\}: RT = L2(D^{GN}T, \tilde{D}^{GN}) + \gamma L2(D^{LN}T, \tilde{D}^{LN}) Where \gamma = 0.1 is the global loss weight. L{similar} is implemented as an L2 loss with an error tolerance to relax the constraint. 4. Total Loss: L = L{color} + R{hard} + R{soft} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainDNGaussian(inputimages, cameraposes, numiterations=6000, softstartiter=1000): # 1. Initialization gaussians = RandomInitializeGaussians(numprimitives=10000) colorrenderer = NeuralColorRenderer(levels=16, resrange=(16, 512), maxsize=219, mlplayers=5, hiddendim=64) monodepthmaps = DPTPredict(inputimages) tau, gamma = 0.95, 0.1 optimizer = GradientDescentOptimizer(gaussians + [colorrenderer], lr=1e-3) for iter in range(1, numiterations + 1): # 2. Color Supervision renderedcolor = RenderColor(gaussians, colorrenderer, cameraposes) Lcolor = L1Loss(renderedcolor, inputimages) + LambdaLDDSSIM(renderedcolor, inputimages) optimizer.zerograd(); Lcolor.backward(); optimizer.step() # Standard 3DGS duplication/removal of active primitives occurs here # 3. Depth Regularization if iter <= softstartiter: # Hard Depth Phase freezeparams(gaussians, ['s', 'q']) harddepth = RenderHardDepth(gaussians, tau, cameraposes) Rhard = GlobalLocalDepthLoss(harddepth, monodepthmaps, gamma) optimizer.zerograd(); Rhard.backward(); optimizer.step() else: # Soft Depth Phase freezeparams(gaussians, ['mu']) softdepth = RenderSoftDepth(gaussians, cameraposes) Rsoft = GlobalLocalDepthLoss(softdepth, monodepthmaps, gamma) optimizer.zerograd(); Rsoft.backward(); optimizer.step() def RenderHardDepth(gaussians, tau, cameraposes): depthmap = zeroslike(cameraposes.imageshape) for ray in cameraposes.rays: sortedg = SortByDistance(ray.origin, gaussians) d = 0.0 for i, g in enumerate(sortedg): d += tau ((1 - tau) (i - 1)) EvaluateProjectedGaussian(g, ray.pixel) distance(g.mu, ray.origin) depthmap[ray.pixel] = d return depthmap def RenderSoftDepth(gaussians, cameraposes): depthmap = zeroslike(cameraposes.imageshape) for ray in cameraposes.rays: sortedg = SortByDistance(ray.origin, gaussians) T, d = 1.0, 0.0 for i, g in enumerate(sortedg): d += distance(g.mu, ray.origin) g.alpha T T = (1 - g.alpha) depthmap[ray.pixel] = d return depthmap def GlobalLocalDepthLoss(rendereddepth, monodepth, gamma): DGN, DLN = NormalizeDepth(rendereddepth) DtildeGN, DtildeLN = NormalizeDepth(monodepth) return L2Loss(DGN, DtildeGN) + gamma L2Loss(DLN, DtildeLN) def RandomInitializeGaussians(numprimitives): return {'mu': uniformrandom(numprimitives, 3), 's': uniformrandom(numprimitives, 3), 'q': unitquaternionrandom(numprimitives), 'alpha': uniformrandom(numprimitives, 1)} def NeuralColorRenderer(levels, resrange, maxsize, mlplayers, hiddendim): return {'hash': HashEncoder(levels, resrange, maxsize), 'mlp': MLP(mlplayers, hiddendim)} def DPTPredict(images): return [ForwardPass(DPTModel, img) for img in images] def GradientDescentOptimizer(params, lr): return {'params': params, 'lr': lr} def RenderColor(gaussians, colorrenderer, cameraposes): return [Rasterize(gaussians, colorrenderer, ray) for ray in cameraposes.rays] def L1Loss(a, b): return mean(abs(a - b)) def LambdaLDDSSIM(a, b): return 0.2 SSIMLoss(a, b) def freezeparams(g, params): [setattr(g, p, g[p].detach()) for p in params] def SortByDistance(origin, g): return sorted(g, key=lambda x: distance(x.mu, origin)) def EvaluateProjectedGaussian(g, pixel): return exp(-0.5 (pixel - g.centerproj).T @ g.covinv @ (pixel - g.centerproj)) def distance(a, b): return sqrt(sum((a - b)2)) def NormalizeDepth(depth): DGN = (depth - min(depth)) / (max(depth) - min(depth) + 1e-6) DLN = LocalWindowNormalize(depth) return DGN, DLN def L2Loss(a, b): return mean((a - b)2) def zeroslike(tensor): return fulllike(tensor, 0.0) def uniformrandom(n, d): return [[random.uniform(0, 1) for in range(d)] for in range(n)] def unitquaternionrandom(n): return normalize(uniformrandom(n, 4)) def HashEncoder(levels, resrange, maxsize): return {'levels': levels, 'resrange': resrange, 'maxsize': maxsize} def MLP(layers, dim): return {'layers': layers, 'dim': dim} def ForwardPass(model, input): return model(input) def Rasterize(g, c, ray): return BlendColors(g, c, ray) def SSIMLoss(a, b): return StructuralSimilarityIndex(a, b) def LocalWindowNormalize(depth): return LocalMeanStdNormalize(depth) def fulllike(tensor, val): return [[val for in row] for row in tensor] def normalize(v): return v / sqrt(sum(v2) + 1e-6) def random: import random; return random Parameters: \tau (Hard Depth Opacity): 0.95. \gamma (Global Loss Weight): 0.1. Training Iterations: 6,000. Soft Depth Start Iteration: 1,000. Neural Color Renderer: Hash encoder (16 levels, 16-512 res, 2^{19} max size) + 5-layer MLP (hidden dim 64). Monocular Depth Estimator: DPT. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse View Degradation: Decreasing input views causes significant geometry degradation in standard 3DGS because scene geometry relies on Gaussian primitive positioning, which becomes incorrectly learned under sparse constraints. DNGaussian mitigates this via depth regularization. Overfitting: Standard spherical harmonics overfit on sparse views; replaced by Neural Color Renderer. Hollowness: Without Soft Depth Regularization, surfaces may become semitransparent and cause hollowness. Initialization Instability: COLMAP point clouds are unstable in sparse-view situations; random initialization is used instead. Time Complexity: 25× reduction in training time compared to state-of-the-art sparse-view NeRFs. Memory Complexity: Significantly lower memory overhead compared to NeRF-based methods. Rendering Speed: Over 3000× faster rendering speed compared to state-of-the-art sparse-view NeRFs. Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis from sparse inputs (e.g., 3 views); preserves fine-grained color appearance; efficient training and rendering. Limitations: Exposes black background on empty/invisible areas, which can lower PSNR/SSIM metrics for those areas compared to NeRFs that interpolate colors. When to use: Few-shot novel view synthesis where training time and rendering speed are critical, and high-quality geometry is needed despite coarse monocular depth supervision. DNGaussian was proposed by Xiao Bai et al. in 2024. It builds on the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and previous depth-regularized sparse-view NeRFs. The method addresses the geometry degradation issue in 3DGS when trained on sparse views by introducing Hard and Soft Depth Regularization and Global-Local Depth Normalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Fictionarry/DNGaussian. name: Edge-Aware Disparity Regularization
head: Edge-Aware Depth Regularization, Edge-Aware Smoothness Regularization, Edge-Preserving Depth Regularization
body: Edge-Aware Disparity Regularization is a loss term that encourages local depth smoothness while preserving depth discontinuities aligned with image edges. It solves the problem of noisy or inconsistent depth maps in neural radiance fields by leveraging the correlation between geometric boundaries and color gradients. It sets itself apart from its parent, Depth Regularization, by explicitly weighting the smoothness constraint with image gradients to prevent blurring across object boundaries. It differs from siblings like SparseGS and PixelSplat Training and Depth Regularization by focusing on patch-based gradient penalties on rendered views rather than point-cloud or splat-based constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered disparity map (or inverse depth) D (or d) and corresponding RGB image I from a sampled view or patch. Outputs: Scalar regularization loss value L{reg} or L{smooth}. Data Structures: Disparity/Depth Map: A 2D array of shape (H, W) representing per-pixel depth or disparity values. RGB Image: A 3D array of shape (H, W, 3) representing pixel colors. Gradients: First-order partial derivatives computed via finite differences. Steps: 1. Sample Views: Render additional patches from training and test viewpoints. 2. Normalize (Optional but Recommended): Compute mean-normalized inverse depth to discourage depth shrinking. D^i = \frac{Di}{\bar{D}i} where Di is the inverse depth and \bar{D}i is the mean inverse depth of the patch or view. Note: Some implementations use raw disparity d^t directly without normalization. 3. Compute Gradients: Calculate the first-order gradients of the depth/disparity map and the RGB image in the x and y directions. Depth gradients: \partialx D^, \partialy D^ (or \partialx d^, \partialy d^). Image gradients: \partialx I, \partialy I (typically computed as the magnitude of the RGB gradient vector). 4. Compute Edge Weights: Calculate the exponential of the negative image gradients to create weights that suppress regularization at edges. wx = e^{-|\partialx I|}, \quad wy = e^{-|\partialy I|} 5. Calculate Loss: Compute the weighted L1 norm of the depth gradients. Formula: The regularization loss is defined as: L{reg} = |\partialx D^i| e^{-|\partialx Ii|} + |\partialy D^i| e^{-|\partialy Ii|} Or equivalently using disparity d^t and RGB It: L{smooth} = |\partialx d^t| e^{-|\partialx It|} + |\partialy d^t| e^{-|\partialy It|} Parameters: Weighting Factors: \lambda1 for depth consistency and \lambda2 for smoothness. Typical Values: Early training: \lambda1 = 0.001, \lambda2 = 0. Later training: \lambda1 = 0, \lambda2 = 1.0. Normalization: Mean normalization factor \bar{D}i. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gradients are sensitive to noise; rendering artifacts in NeRF can create spurious depth gradients. Boundaries: The method assumes local smoothness; global consistency is not enforced by this term alone. Depth Shrinking: Without mean normalization (D^), the optimizer may shrink depth estimates to minimize the L1 gradient penalty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def edgeawaredisparityregularization(depth, rgb, normalize=True): """ Computes edge-aware disparity regularization loss. Args: depth: 2D list of floats, shape (H, W). Disparity or inverse depth. rgb: 3D list of floats, shape (H, W, 3). RGB values in [0, 1]. normalize: Boolean. If True, normalizes depth by its mean. Returns: loss: Float scalar. """ H = len(depth) W = len(depth[0]) # 1. Normalize depth if requested if normalize: meand = sum(depth[i][j] for i in range(H) for j in range(W)) / (H W) if meand == 0: meand = 1e-8 normd = [[depth[i][j] / meand for j in range(W)] for i in range(H)] else: normd = depth # 2. Compute gradients using forward finite differences # Depth gradients: dxd shape (H, W-1), dyd shape (H-1, W) dxd = [[normd[i][j+1] - normd[i][j] for j in range(W-1)] for i in range(H)] dyd = [[normd[i+1][j] - normd[i][j] for j in range(W)] for i in range(H-1)] # RGB gradients (magnitude across 3 channels) dxrgbmag = [[math.sqrt(sum((rgb[i][j+1][c] - rgb[i][j][c])2 for c in range(3))) for j in range(W-1)] for i in range(H)] dyrgbmag = [[math.sqrt(sum((rgb[i+1][j][c] - rgb[i][j][c])2 for c in range(3))) for j in range(W)] for i in range(H-1)] # 3. Compute edge weights wx = [[math.exp(-g) for g in row] for row in dxrgbmag] wy = [[math.exp(-g) for g in row] for row in dyrgbmag] # 4. Compute loss losssum = 0.0 count = 0 for i in range(H): for j in range(W-1): losssum += abs(dxd[i][j]) wx[i][j] count += 1 for i in range(H-1): for j in range(W): losssum += abs(dyd[i][j]) wy[i][j] count += 1 return losssum / count Geometric Regularization is a loss term imposed on rendered depth patches from sampled views to regularize geometry. It smooths the depth of unobserved viewpoints to alleviate density holes caused by sparsely observed viewpoints, inspired by the piece-wise smoothing characteristics of real-world geometry. It sets itself apart from its parent, Edge-Aware Disparity Regularization, by applying a uniform smoothness constraint on depth patches without explicitly weighting by image edges. Disparity Smoothing is a technique to reduce misalignments around the edges of a reference mask by smoothing the aligned reference disparity to improve visual continuity between the masked and unmasked regions. It computes the edge-smoothed disparity Dr^{smooth} as the sum of the aligned disparity Dr and a correction term D{correction}: Dr^{smooth} = Dr + D{correction}. Without smoothing, unsmoothed geometry has a much more jarring transition between the masked and unmasked areas, particularly close to the mask boundary. Disparity Field-Guided Deep Re-regularization is a module proposed to raise the target view image I{t0} into a locally immersive Light Field \hat{L}{t0} by back-warping and deep spatial-angular regularization. It inputs the target view image I{t0} and refined disparity \hat{D}{t0}, back-warping pixels of the target view image with the estimated accurate disparity prior, and further refines the output by spatial-angular convolutional blocks to produce the synthesized immersive LF \hat{L}{t0}. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels in the sampled patches, as it involves computing gradients and element-wise operations. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels, storing depth and RGB tensors and their gradients. Measured Performance: Effective in mitigating high-frequency noise and artifacts in flat regions while preserving details. In LEVIR-NVS dataset experiments, it was activated in later training stages with \lambda2 = 1.0. Scaling: Scales well with resolution as it is a local operation. Strengths: Preserves sharp edges in depth maps corresponding to object boundaries; reduces noise in textureless or flat regions. Limitations: Relies on the quality of rendered RGB images; if RGB edges are noisy, depth edges may be incorrectly preserved or smoothed. Not suitable for early training stages where depth estimates are unstable. When to use: When depth maps exhibit noise in flat regions but need to preserve object boundaries; in later stages of NeRF training. When not to use: When RGB edges are completely absent or depth gradients are dominated by extreme noise that breaks the edge-alignment assumption. It is also typically disabled in early training stages where depth estimates are too unstable for reliable gradient computation. Edge-Aware Disparity Regularization originates from the work on GeCoNeRF, which introduced the term to improve geometric consistency in few-shot neural radiance fields. It was inspired by Godard et al. (2017), who used similar edge-aware weights for monocular depth estimation. The technique was later adapted in TriDF for remote sensing novel view synthesis, where it was applied in the latter stages of training to enhance geometric structure. It is used in few-shot neural radiance fields and remote sensing novel view synthesis. name: Geometric Regularization
head: Depth Smoothness Loss
body: Geometric Regularization is a loss term imposed on rendered depth patches from sampled views to regularize geometry. It smooths the depth of unobserved viewpoints to alleviate density holes caused by sparsely observed viewpoints, inspired by the piece-wise smoothing characteristics of real-world geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of sampled camera poses Rr; a differentiable rendering function that produces expected depth \hat{D}\theta(r) for a ray r; a patch size parameter S{patch}. Outputs: A scalar loss value LD(\theta, Rr). Data Structures: Ray Patch: For a central ray r \in Rr, a patch consists of rays r{ij} passing through pixel coordinates (i, j) within a sub-block of size S{patch} \times S{patch}. Depth Map: The rendered depth \hat{D}\theta(r{ij}) is a scalar value for each ray. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample a set of rays Rr from camera poses. 2. For each central ray r \in Rr, construct a patch of rays r{ij} corresponding to pixel coordinates (i, j) within a sub-block of size S{patch} \times S{patch}. 3. For each (i, j) from 1 to S{patch}-1, compute the rendered depth \hat{D}\theta(r{ij}) for the center, right (i+1, j), bottom (i, j+1), and diagonal (i+1, j+1) rays. 4. Accumulate the squared differences into the loss. Formula: The depth smoothness loss LD is defined as: LD(\theta, Rr) = \sum{r \in Rr} \sum{i,j=1}^{S{patch}-1} \left[ (\hat{D}\theta(r{ij}) - \hat{D}\theta(r{i+1,j}))^2 + (\hat{D}\theta(r{ij}) - \hat{D}\theta(r{i,j+1}))^2 + (\hat{D}\theta(r{ij}) - \hat{D}\theta(r{i+1,j+1}))^2 \right] The total training loss L combines the photometric MSE loss L{MSE} and the depth smoothness loss: L(\theta, Rr) = L{MSE}(\theta, Rr) + \lambda LD(\theta, Rr) Where: \theta: Network parameters. Rr: Set of input rays. S{patch}: Size of the rendered patches. \hat{D}\theta(r{ij}): Expected depth calculated by the rendering function for ray r{ij}. \lambda: Weight for the depth loss in the total training loss. Parameters: S{patch}: The size of the patch. Not given in the sources. \lambda: Weight for the depth loss in the total training loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The summation for i and j goes up to S{patch}-1 to ensure indices i+1 and j+1 are valid within the patch. Precision: Squared differences can amplify errors in regions with high depth variance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometricregularizationloss(renderdepthfunc, rays, patchsize): """Computes the depth smoothness loss LD.""" totalloss = 0.0 for r in rays: # Iterate over the patch, excluding the last row and column # to match the summation bounds i, j = 1 to Spatch - 1 for i in range(1, patchsize): for j in range(1, patchsize): # Standard pinhole projection to generate rays for pixel coordinates rayc = r.projecttoray(i, j) rayr = r.projecttoray(i + 1, j) rayb = r.projecttoray(i, j + 1) rayd = r.projecttoray(i + 1, j + 1) dc = renderdepthfunc(rayc) dr = renderdepthfunc(rayr) db = renderdepthfunc(rayb) dd = renderdepthfunc(rayd) totalloss += (dc - dr)2 + (dc - db)2 + (dc - dd)2 return totalloss Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively smooths out unobserved regions and fills density holes in sparse input scenarios. Limitations: May oversmooth fine geometric details if the patch size is too large or the weight \lambda is too high. When to use: When training from sparse inputs and density holes are present. When not to use: When high-frequency geometric detail preservation is critical without edge-aware weighting. The method was introduced in the context of Voxel Grid Optimization for View Synthesis from Sparse Inputs (VGOS) and Density-Guided Neural Point Rendering (DGNR). It draws inspiration from RegNeRF, observing that real-world geometry exhibits piece-wise smoothing characteristics. It is used to enhance reconstruction quality for sparse inputs by regularizing the depth space. name: DäRF
head: Monocular Depth Adaptation for boosting Radiance Fields from Sparse Input Views
body: DäRF is a framework for robust few-shot NeRF reconstruction that combines Neural Radiance Fields with Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) through online complementary training. It solves the ambiguity and inconsistency problems inherent in monocular depth priors by jointly optimizing the NeRF and the MDE network at a specific scene, rather than treating MDE as a static prior. Unlike SCADE [50], which applies pretrained MDE only to seen views and uses probabilistic modeling for uncertainty, DäRF distills the monocular depth prior to NeRF at both seen and unseen views and directly removes ambiguity by finetuning the MDE network with canonical geometry captured by NeRF. Inputs: A set of input RGB images S = \{Ii\} with ground truth camera poses, and a pretrained MDE network G\phi. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \Theta, adapted MDE parameters \phi, and a high-quality 3D radiance field. Data Structures: NeRF Model F\Theta: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. MDE Network G\phi: A pretrained network (e.g., Mannequin Challenge, DiffDP, DPThybrid) mapping RGB images to relative depth maps D^. Ray Sampler: Generates rays \mathbf{r} from camera poses and samples points \mathbf{x}t along them. Numbered Steps: 1. Depth Prior Extraction: For each input image Ii, the MDE network G\phi produces a relative depth map D^. 2. NeRF Depth Rendering: The NeRF model F\Theta renders an absolute depth map \bar{D} for the current camera pose by accumulating sample depths weighted by transmittance and density along rays. 3. Patch-wise Scale-Shift Alignment: To overcome the inability of global scale-shift fitting due to poor MDE performance on depth differences between multiple objects, DäRF applies a novel patch-wise scale-shift fitting. For each patch p, it computes local scale wp and shift qp via least-squares optimization: \min{wp, qp} \sum{k \in p} \| (wp \cdot \text{sg}(D^(k)) + qp) - \bar{D}(k) \|^2 where \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator to prevent gradients from flowing into the MDE network during NeRF updates. 4. Confidence Modeling: A confidence modeling technique is used to verify accurate depth information, handling ambiguity problems such as relative depths not being multiview-consistent and convexity problems. This generates a confidence mask or weight to filter out unreliable depth predictions. 5. Joint Optimization (Complementary Training): DäRF jointly optimizes NeRF and MDE at a specific scene. NeRF Update: The NeRF is updated using the standard volume rendering loss (e.g., MSE between rendered color and ground truth) and the depth consistency loss L{depth} between the aligned MDE depth and rendered NeRF depth. MDE Adaptation: The MDE network G\phi is finetuned using the canonical geometry captured by NeRF. This adapts the MDE network to produce depths aligned accurately with NeRF geometry, directly removing ambiguity present in the initial MDE output. 6. Distillation: The monocular depth prior is distilled to NeRF at both seen and unseen views, enhancing robustness and coherence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generaterays(poses): """Generates rays from camera poses and near/far bounds.""" # Standard ray generation from camera extrinsics and intrinsics rays = [] for pose in poses: origin = pose[:3, 3] direction = pose[:3,:3] @ np.array([0, 0, -1]) rays.append((origin, direction)) return rays def rendernerf(nerfmodel, rays, numsamples): """Standard NeRF volume rendering via alpha compositing.""" # Standard NeRF forward pass colors = [] depths = [] for origin, direction in rays: tvals = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) points = origin + tvals[:, None] direction sigmas, rgbs = nerfmodel(points) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] expsigmas = np.exp(-sigmas deltas) transmittance = np.cumprod(expsigmas) weights = (1.0 - expsigmas) np.concatenate([[1.0], transmittance[:-1]]) color = np.sum(weights[:, None] rgbs, axis=0) depth = np.sum(weights tvals, axis=0) colors.append(color) depths.append(depth) return np.array(colors), np.array(depths) def solvelocalaffine(depthsrc, depthtgt): """Solves min || w depthsrc + q - depthtgt ||^2 via least squares.""" s = depthsrc.flatten() t = depthtgt.flatten() means = np.mean(s) meant = np.mean(t) vars = np.var(s) if vars < 1e-8: return 1.0, meant - means w = np.cov(s, t)[0, 1] / vars q = meant - w means return w, q def computeconfidence(depthsrc, depthaligned): """Computes confidence weights based on alignment error.""" # Standard confidence weighting based on residual error error = np.abs(depthsrc - depthaligned) return np.exp(-error) def stepdarf(images, poses, nerfmodel, mdemodel, optimizernerf, optimizermde, lambdadepth, patchsize, numsamples): # 1. Extract relative depth from MDE relativedepths = [mdemodel(img) for img in images] # 2. Render NeRF outputs rays = generaterays(poses) renderedcolors, rendereddepths = rendernerf(nerfmodel, rays, numsamples) # 3. Patch-wise Scale-Shift Alignment aligneddepths = np.zeroslike(rendereddepths) confidencemasks = np.oneslike(rendereddepths) H, W = rendereddepths.shape for y in range(0, H, patchsize): for x in range(0, W, patchsize): yend = min(y + patchsize, H) xend = min(x + patchsize, W) patch = slice(y, yend), slice(x, xend) # Stop-gradient applied to MDE depth during NeRF update rpatch = relativedepths[0][patch].detach() npatch = rendereddepths[patch] w, q = solvelocalaffine(rpatch, npatch) alignedpatch = w rpatch + q conf = computeconfidence(rpatch, alignedpatch) confidencemasks[patch] = conf aligneddepths[patch] = alignedpatch # 4. Compute Losses colorloss = np.mean((renderedcolors - images[0]) 2) depthloss = np.mean((aligneddepths confidencemasks - rendereddepths confidencemasks) 2) totalloss = colorloss + lambdadepth depthloss # 5. Update NeRF optimizernerf.zerograd() totalloss.backward(retaingraph=True) optimizernerf.step() # 6. MDE Adaptation mdeloss = np.mean((relativedepths[0] - aligneddepths.detach()) 2) optimizermde.zerograd() mdeloss.backward() optimizermde.step() Parameters: \lambda{depth}: Weight for the depth consistency loss. Not given in the sources. Patch size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Global vs. Local Scale: Global scale-shift fitting fails when MDE performs poorly on depth differences between multiple objects. Patch-wise fitting is required. Ambiguity: Monocular depths suffer from ambiguity (e.g., convexity problems, lack of multiview consistency). DäRF handles this via confidence modeling and joint adaptation. Gradient Flow: Joint optimization requires careful gradient management to balance NeRF and MDE updates without destabilizing training. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results quantitatively and qualitatively on real-world indoor and outdoor scene datasets for few-shot NeRF optimization. Strengths: Robust geometry reconstruction and artifact removal in both unseen and seen viewpoints. Fully exploits MDE by jointly optimizing it with NeRF. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pretrained MDE network. Not given in the sources. When to use: Few-shot NeRF reconstruction where standard NeRF fails due to sparse views and ambiguity. When not to use: Not given in the sources. DäRF was proposed to address the weaknesses of methods that use 3D priors extracted from a few input images only, which prevents guidance from encompassing the entire scene. It builds on the strengths of NeRF [31] and pretrained monocular depth estimation (MDE) networks [39, 38, 5]. Unlike SCADE [50], which distills depths by applying pretrained MDE to NeRF at seen views only, DäRF fully exploits the ability of MDE by jointly optimizing NeRF and MDE at a specific scene. name: NeRF-guided MDE Adaptation
head: MDE Adaptation via NeRF, Scene-specific MDE fine-tuning
body: NeRF-guided MDE Adaptation refines a pre-trained Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) network by using a NeRF model as a geometric prior to resolve ambiguities inherent in relative depth predictions, such as convexity/concavity confusion and flat surface orientation errors. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like NerfingMVS by explicitly adapting the MDE weights to the specific scene's absolute geometry rather than just using depth as a static supervision signal for the NeRF. Inputs: Input RGB images Ii for seen views S and potentially unseen views U. Pre-trained MDE network G\phi (e.g., DPThybrid). NeRF model F\Theta (e.g., K-planes). Camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: Adapted MDE weights \phi. Optimized NeRF weights \Theta. Depth-consistent novel view images. Data Structures: MDE Output: Relative depth map D^ and initial relative depth map D^{init} (extracted before adaptation starts). NeRF Output: Rendered absolute depth map \bar{D} and color C. Confidence Mask: M(p), a scalar value per pixel indicating reliability. Parameters: Learning rate for NeRF: 1 \cdot 10^{-2}. Learning rate for MDE: 1 \cdot 10^{-5}. Optimizer: Adam with cosine warmup scheduling. Scale wi and shift qi: Per-view affine parameters. Steps: 1. Initialize: Extract initial monocular depth D^{init} from G\phi using pre-trained weights. Initialize NeRF F\Theta. 2. Render NeRF Depth: For each seen view Ii, render the absolute depth map \bar{D}i by accumulating sample depths weighted by transmittance and density along rays. 3. Extract MDE Depth: Process Ii through G\phi to get relative depth D^i. 4. Compute Alignment: Calculate scale wi and shift qi via least-squares optimization to align D^i with \bar{D}i: \min{wi, qi} \sum{p \in P} \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(D^i(p)) + qi) - \bar{D}i(p) \|^2 where \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator. 5. Compute Losses: Calculate the total loss using the formulas below. 6. Update: Perform gradient descent to update both \Theta and \phi simultaneously. Formulas: The core MDE adaptation loss L{MDE} combines an absolute alignment term (without scale/shift) and a patch-wise aligned term: L{MDE} = \sum{Ii \in S} \sum{p \in P} \left( \| \text{sg}(\bar{D}i(p)) - D^i(p) \| + \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(\bar{D}i(p)) + qi) - D^i(p) \| \right) The source text uses D^i(p) in the first term of Eq. 6, while the confidence-weighted variant (Eq. 12) uses \bar{D}^i(p), which denotes the MDE output in that context. The first term aligns the raw MDE output to the NeRF depth without affine adjustment, while the second aligns the affine-adjusted MDE output. A regularization term L{reg} preserves the local smoothness of the MDE adaptation by comparing the adapted depth to the initial pre-trained depth: L{reg} = \sum{Ii \in S} \sum{p \in P} \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(D^{init}(p)) + qi) - D^i(p) \| Pitfalls: MDE lacks awareness of scene-specific absolute depth and multi-view consistency, leading to ambiguities in surface convexity/concavity and flat surface orientation. Errors in MDE or NeRF can propagate and intensify during distillation if not controlled. This variant incorporates confidence masks M(p) to weight the depth consistency losses, preventing error propagation from inaccurate depths. It trains NeRF and MDE simultaneously, where MDE provides geometric priors to NeRF and NeRF provides absolute geometry to MDE. The losses are weighted by confidence maps Mi(p) for seen views and Ml(p) for unseen views. The loss for seen views L{seen} is: L{seen} = \sum{Ii \in S} \sum{p \in P} Mi(p) \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(D^i(p)) + qi) - \bar{D}i(p) \| The loss for unseen views L{unseen} is: L{unseen} = \sum{Il \in U} \sum{p \in P} Ml(p) \| (wl \cdot \text{sg}(D^l(p)) + ql) - \bar{D}l(p) \| The MDE adaptation loss becomes: L{MDE} = \sum{Ii \in S} \sum{p \in P} Mi(p) \left( \| \text{sg}(\bar{D}i(p)) - D^i(p) \| + \| (wi \cdot \text{sg}(\bar{D}i(p)) + qi) - D^i(p) \| \right) Time Complexity: Increases training time due to the simultaneous optimization of both NeRF and MDE networks. The least-squares alignment step adds negligible overhead per iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradients for both NeRF and MDE, increasing VRAM usage compared to fixed-MDE approaches. Performance: Improves NeRF reconstruction quality (PSNR, SSIM) on sparse input sets (e.g., 9-10 views on ScanNet) by providing better geometric priors. Strengths: Resolves MDE ambiguities (convexity/concavity) and adapts to scene-specific geometry. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rates (NeRF LR >> MDE LR) to prevent instability. Confidence modeling adds complexity. Originated in the DäRF paper (2023). It addresses the limitation of standard NeRF training with monocular depth where the MDE provides only relative depth, leading to geometric inconsistencies. By adapting the MDE to the NeRF's absolute geometry, it creates a mutually beneficial training loop. DaRF: Boosting Radiance Fields from Sparse Inputs with Monocular Depth Adaptation, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.19201, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Model Variants
head: FWD-D, FWD-U
body: This family defines three architectural configurations for the FWD framework, distinguished by their depth supervision strategy and the initialization state of the depth estimation module. The variants evaluate different accessibility levels to depth information during training and inference. FWD-U serves as the unsupervised baseline, FWD provides a supervised baseline with pre-trained geometry, and FWD-D bypasses learned depth estimation entirely by using sensor data. All variants in this family operate within the FWD framework for novel view synthesis. They share the core mechanism of using a PatchmatchNet architecture for depth estimation, with the primary divergence lying in how the depth map is obtained and whether the depth estimation network is trainable during the end-to-end optimization loop. FWD-U is the unsupervised variant of the model. It utilizes a PatchmatchNet architecture for depth estimation that is randomly initialized at the start of training. No pre-training on MVS datasets is performed. The network shares the same model and settings as FWD. FWD is the supervised variant that employs a PatchmatchNet module pre-trained on standard Multi-View Stereo (MVS) settings. During the end-to-end training of the NeRF and rendering pipeline, the PatchmatchNet weights are updated jointly with the scene representation using photometric and perceptual loss. FWD-D is a variant that eliminates the learned MVS module entirely. Instead of estimating depth from RGB images, it takes sensor depths as direct additional inputs during both training and inference. Because sensor depths provide abundant geometry cues, no MVS network is used. The model variants were evaluated on the ShapeNet dataset to assess performance under different accessibility levels to depth information. The study evaluates category-agnostic synthesis on 13 ShapeNet categories, with each instance containing 24 fixed views of 64 × 64 resolution. FWD: Real-time Novel View Synthesis with Forward Warping and Depth, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01526, fetched 2026-10-29
