name: Weighted Disparity Alignment
body: Weighted Disparity Alignment is a supervision technique for NeRF training that aligns a monocular depth estimator's output with the NeRF's rendered geometry, specifically designed to handle masked regions in inpainting scenarios. It differs from standard affine alignment by incorporating spatially varying weights and additional tilt parameters to enforce tighter geometric consistency near mask boundaries, where misalignment is most detrimental. Inputs: Input RGB image Ir and binary mask Mr for the reference view. Monocular depth estimator D(\cdot) (frozen). NeRF model parameters \theta. Hyperparameter N{depth}: number of iterations to train on unmasked pixels before applying depth loss. Outputs: Aligned and smoothed disparity map Dr^{smooth} used for supervising the masked region of the NeRF. Data Structures: De: Uncalibrated disparity map of the source view, computed as De = D(Ir). H, V: H \times W matrices where for pixel p=(px, py), H(p)=px and V(p)=py. \mathbf{1}{HW}: H \times W matrix of ones. w(p): Weight for pixel p, defined as the inverse of the Euclidean distance between p and the mask's center-of-mass. Steps: 1. Initial Unmasked Training: Train the NeRF on unmasked pixels (p \in Ir(1-Mr)) using standard color reconstruction loss for N{depth} iterations. This allows the geometry of the visible scene to converge before introducing depth constraints on the masked area. 2. Compute Uncalibrated Disparity: Apply the frozen monocular depth estimator to the reference image: De = D(Ir). 3. Weighted Alignment Optimization: Solve for alignment parameters \{a0, a1, a2, a3\} by minimizing the weighted squared error between the aligned predicted inverse depth and the NeRF's rendered disparity \bar{D}r on unmasked pixels: \min{a0, a1, a2, a3} \sum{p \in Ir(1-Mr)} w(p) \left( Dr(p) - \bar{D}r(p) \right)^2 where the aligned predicted inverse depth is defined as: Dr = a0 De + a1 \mathbf{1}{HW} + a2 H + a3 V The terms a2 H and a3 V introduce axis-aligned "tilts" to improve fitting quality near edges. 4. Smoothing: Perform an additional optimization step to correct Dr and encourage smoothness around the mask boundary, yielding Dr^{smooth}. (Specific smoothing details are in the supplementary material of). 5. Depth Loss Application: Supervise the masked region of the reference view using the depth consistency loss: L{depth} = \mathbb{E}{r' \in R{masked}} \left( Dr^{smooth}(r') - \bar{D}r(r') \right)^2 where R{masked} is the set of rays corresponding to masked pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mask Boundary Sensitivity: Misalignments persist near mask edges, requiring the smoothing step. Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth is non-metric and lacks absolute scale, requiring alignment. A baseline method for pose verification that computes optical flow between estimated and ground truth images to determine mean disparity. It uses a folded normal distribution with a standard deviation of 4 pixels to compute a confidence level of correctness based on this disparity. It does not handle scale ambiguity and does not generalize well across varying scene sizes. Complexity: The alignment step involves solving a linear least-squares problem for 4 parameters over unmasked pixels, which is computationally inexpensive compared to the NeRF forward pass. Performance: Provides tighter alignment around mask edges compared to standard affine alignment, improving inpainting quality. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the monocular depth estimator; if the MDE fails, the alignment may propagate errors. The smoothing step details are not fully specified in the main text. Weighted Disparity Alignment was introduced in "Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields" (ICCV 2023) to address the challenge of supervising geometry in masked regions where ground truth color is unavailable. It extends standard disparity alignment by adding spatial weights and tilt parameters to handle the specific artifacts introduced by inpainting. Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICCV51070.2023.01633, fetched 2026-10-29 VERF: Runtime Monitoring of Pose Estimation With Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/lra.2023.3341765, fetched 2026-10-30

name: ShadowNeuS
head: Neural SDF Reconstruction by Shadow Ray Supervision
body:
ShadowNeuS reconstructs a neural Signed Distance Field (SDF) of a scene from single-view images under multiple lighting conditions by supervising shadow rays rather than relying solely on camera rays. It solves the problem that standard NeRF does not model rays from the scene to the light source, missing shadow information which contains critical geometry cues via light visibility. Unlike NeRF which uses multi-view cameras as ray sensors, this method uses a single-view camera and shadow rays to provide supervision, making it applicable to real capture setups with limited views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Single-view RGB images or binary shadow images captured under multiple known light directions. The scene is assumed to be opaque. To bound the scene, camera rays that do not intersect the SDF are projected onto a ground plane, whose position and orientation are assumed known to resolve scale ambiguity. Outputs: A neural SDF network f representing the scene geometry, and optionally material properties (diffuse and specular coefficients) if RGB inputs are used. Data Structures: SDF Network f: An MLP that takes a 3D position \mathbf{x} and outputs a scalar signed distance value 	ext{sdf}(\mathbf{x}). For RGB inputs, it also outputs a 256-dimensional feature vector. Material Network g: An MLP that takes 3D position \mathbf{x} and surface normal \mathbf{n} to regress material properties: diffuse albedo hod and specular coefficients \mathbf{y}. Light Source: Defined as either a directional light (uniform direction \mathbf{l} and intensity L) or a point light (location \mathbf{q}, scalar intensity Lp). Parameters: Samples per image: 256 pixel positions are sampled as supervision signals. Batch size: 4 images randomly selected in each batch. Light sampling: 100 directional lights and 100 point lights selected randomly on the upper hemisphere. Training iterations: 150k. Input resolution: 800x800 for synthetic datasets. SDF Sigmoid Parameter s: A learnable scalar controlling the transition between volume and surface rendering. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Scene Representation: Represent the scene as the zero level set of the SDF network f, i.e., S = \{ \mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f(\mathbf{u}) = 0 \}. 2. Camera Ray Intersection: For each camera ray \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) starting at camera center \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{v}, compute the intersection point \mathbf{x} with the SDF using ray marching. Pitfall Handling: If the camera ray does not intersect the SDF, it is set to intersect with the ground plane to bound the scene. 3. Differentiable Intersection: To make the intersection point \mathbf{x} differentiable for backpropagation, apply implicit differentiation: 	ilde{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x} -  rac{\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}} 	ext{sdf}(\mathbf{x}) where \mathbf{n} = 
abla{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x}) is the surface normal derived from the SDF network. 4. Boundary Detection: Identify boundary pixels using a surface walk procedure. This yields a pixel subset \Omega corresponding to surface boundaries and a differentiable area ratio w for each boundary pixel. 5. Shadow Ray Setup: Illuminate the scene with a light source in direction \mathbf{l}. For directional lights, \mathbf{l} and L are known and uniform. For point lights at location \mathbf{q} with intensity Lp, calculate direction and intensity at point 	ilde{\mathbf{x}}: L =  rac{Lp}{\| \mathbf{q} - 	ilde{\mathbf{x}} \|2^2}, \quad \mathbf{l} =  rac{\mathbf{q} - 	ilde{\mathbf{x}}}{\| \mathbf{q} - 	ilde{\mathbf{x}} \|2} 6. Shadow Ray Rendering (Incoming Irradiance): Compute the incoming irradiance at the surface point 	ilde{\mathbf{x}} by marching shadow rays from 	ilde{\mathbf{x}} in direction \mathbf{l}. Opacity Calculation: Derive opacity \alphai from the SDF using the CDF of SDF values at adjacent samples ti and t{i+1} along the shadow ray: \alphai = \max \left( 1 -  rac{\Phis(	ext{sdf}(\mathbf{p}(t{i+1})))}{\Phis(	ext{sdf}(\mathbf{p}(ti)))}, 0 ight) where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} is the sigmoid function and s is a learnable scalar. Irradiance Formula: The estimated incoming irradiance is: 	ext{irradiance}(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{l}) = L \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) 7. Boundary Handling: For pixels in the boundary subset \Omega, a single shadow ray may lead to incorrect gradients because the pixel spans disconnected regions at different depths. Locate two intersections \mathbf{x}n (near) and \mathbf{x}f (far) at different depths within the pixel. Compute their incoming irradiance 	ext{irradiance}(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}n, \mathbf{l}) and 	ext{irradiance}(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}f, \mathbf{l}). Average them using the area ratio w: 	ext{irradiance}{	ext{pix}} =  egin{cases} 	ext{irradiance}(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{l}) & 	ext{pixel} 
otin \Omega \ w \cdot 	ext{irradiance}(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}n, \mathbf{l}) + (1-w) \cdot 	ext{irradiance}(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}f, \mathbf{l}) & 	ext{pixel} \in \Omega \end{cases} 8. Outgoing Radiance (RGB Inputs Only): If inputs are RGB, decompose the outgoing radiance using inverse rendering. Model the non-Lambertian BRDF as a diffuse component hod and a specular component hos. Regress material properties (hod, \mathbf{y}) = g(\mathbf{x}) using the material network g at surface location \mathbf{x}. Model specular component using spherical Gaussian basis: hos = \mathbf{y}^T D(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{n}), where \mathbf{h} =  rac{\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{v}}{\| \mathbf{l} - \mathbf{v} \|} is the half-vector and D is the specular basis. Compute outgoing radiance: C(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}, -\mathbf{v}) = (hod + hos) \cdot 	ext{irradiance}(	ilde{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{l}) \cdot (\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{n}) 9. Loss Computation: Eikonal Loss: Regularize the SDF to output valid distances: \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} =  rac{1}{M} \sum{i}^{M} (\| 
abla f(\mathbf{p}i) \|2 - 1)^2 Shadow Loss (Binary Inputs): \mathcal{L}{	ext{shadow}} = \| 	ext{irradiance}{	ext{pix}} - I{	ext{shadow}} \|1 where I{	ext{shadow}} is the binary shadow image pixel value. RGB Loss (RGB Inputs): \mathcal{L}{	ext{rgb}} = \| \widehat{C} - I{	ext{rgb}} \|1 where \widehat{C} is the computed outgoing radiance and I{	ext{rgb}} is the RGB image pixel value. 10. Optimization: Minimize the total loss (\mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} + \mathcal{L}{	ext{shadow}} or \mathcal{L}{	ext{eik}} + \mathcal{L}{	ext{rgb}}) to update the SDF network f and material network g. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class ShadowNeuS: def init(self, sdfnet, matnet, sinit=10.0, numshadowsamples=64): self.sdfnet = sdfnet self.matnet = matnet self.s = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(sinit)) self.numshadowsamples = numshadowsamples def sigmoidcdf(self, sdfval): """Phis(x) = (1 + exp(-sx))^-1""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-self.s sdfval)) def computeopacity(self, sdfnear, sdffar): """alpha = max(1 - Phis(sdffar) / Phis(sdfnear), 0)""" phinear = self.sigmoidcdf(sdfnear) phifar = self.sigmoidcdf(sdffar) phinear = torch.clamp(phinear, min=1e-6) alpha = 1.0 - (phifar / phinear) return torch.clamp(alpha, min=0.0, max=1.0) def implicitdifferentiation(self, x, v, sdfval, gradsdf): """xtilde = x - (v / (n. v)) sdf(x)""" n = gradsdf dotnv = torch.sum(n v, dim=-1, keepdim=True) dotnv = torch.clamp(dotnv, min=1e-6) return x - (v / dotnv) sdfval def raymarchintersection(self, origin, direction, maxsteps=128): """Standard ray marching to find SDF zero crossing.""" t = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 for in range(maxsteps): point = origin + t direction sdfval = self.sdfnet(point) if sdfval < 0.0: gradsdf = torch.autograd.grad(sdfval.sum(), point, creategraph=True)[0] return point, sdfval, gradsdf t += stepsize point = origin + t direction sdfval = self.sdfnet(point) gradsdf = torch.autograd.grad(sdfval.sum(), point, creategraph=True)[0] return point, sdfval, gradsdf def marchshadowray(self, origin, direction, lightintensity): """Compute irradiance = L prod(1 - alphai) along shadow ray.""" tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, self.numshadowsamples) raypoints = origin.unsqueeze(0) + direction.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(-1) sdfvals = self.sdfnet(raypoints) alphas = self.computeopacity(sdfvals[:-1], sdfvals[1:]) oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alphas totaltransmittance = torch.prod(oneminusalpha) return lightintensity totaltransmittance def getlightparams(self, lighttype, lightpos, lightintensity, pointx): if lighttype == 'directional': return lightpos, lightintensity else: diff = lightpos - pointx distsq = torch.sum(diff2, dim=-1) L = lightintensity / (distsq + 1e-6) ldir = diff / (torch.sqrt(distsq) + 1e-6) return ldir, L def computematerial(self, x, n): """Regress diffuse and specular coefficients.""" inputfeat = torch.cat([x, n], dim=-1) output = self.matnet(inputfeat) rhod = output[...,:1] y = output[..., 1:] return rhod, y def computespecular(self, y, ldir, vdir, n): """rhos = y^T D(h, n). D is a predefined specular basis.""" diff = ldir - vdir normdiff = torch.norm(diff, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6 h = diff / normdiff # Standard implementation evaluates basis functions Dk(h, n) and dots with y. # Here we assume a simple evaluation for completeness. basisvals = torch.oneslike(y) return torch.sum(y basisvals, dim=-1, keepdim=True) def findboundaryintersections(self, origin, direction, isboundary): """Simple ray search to locate two intersections for boundary pixels.""" tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 128) raypts = origin.unsqueeze(0) + direction.unsqueeze(0) tvals.unsqueeze(-1) sdfvals = self.sdfnet(raypts) crossings = torch.where(sdfvals[:-1] sdfvals[1:] < 0)[0] if len(crossings) >= 2: xn = raypts[crossings[0]] xf = raypts[crossings[1]] return xn, xf, torch.tensor(0.5) return origin, origin, torch.tensor(0.5) def forward(self, camerarays, lightdata, shadowimages=None, rgbimages=None, boundarymask=None, arearatio=None): B, H, W = camerarays.shape[:3] totalloss = 0.0 numsamples = 256 indices = torch.randint(0, HW, (B, numsamples)) for b in range(B): rayso = camerarays[b,:,:, 0] raysv = camerarays[b,:,:, 1] flato = rayso.view(-1, 3) flatv = raysv.view(-1, 3) sampledo = flato[indices[b]] sampledv = flatv[indices[b]] x, sdfval, gradsdf = self.raymarchintersection(sampledo, sampledv) xtilde = self.implicitdifferentiation(x, sampledv, sdfval, gradsdf) ldir, L = self.getlightparams(lightdata['type'], lightdata['pos'], lightdata['intensity'], xtilde) irradiance = self.marchshadowray(xtilde, ldir, L) isboundary = boundarymask[b].view(-1)[indices[b]] if isboundary.any(): xn, xf, w = self.findboundaryintersections(sampledo, sampledv, isboundary) irradiancenear = self.marchshadowray(xn, ldir, L) irradiancefar = self.marchshadowray(xf, ldir, L) w = arearatio[b].view(-1)[indices[b]] irradiancefinal = w irradiancenear + (1 - w) irradiancefar else: irradiancefinal = irradiance if shadowimages is not None: target = shadowimages[b].view(-1)[indices[b]] loss = torch.abs(irradiancefinal - target).mean() totalloss += loss elif rgbimages is not None: n = gradsdf rhod, y = self.computematerial(xtilde, n) rhos = self.computespecular(y, ldir, sampledv, n) ldotn = torch.sum(ldir n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) outgoingradiance = (rhod + rhos) irradiancefinal ldotn target = rgbimages[b].view(-1, 3)[indices[b]] loss = torch.abs(outgoingradiance - target).mean() totalloss += loss randompoints = torch.randnlike(sampledo) 2.0 sdfrandom = self.sdfnet(randompoints) gradrandom = torch.autograd.grad(sdfrandom.sum(), randompoints, creategraph=True)[0] eikonal = (torch.norm(gradrandom, dim=-1) - 1.0)2 totalloss += eikonal.mean() return totalloss / B Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 24 hours on a single RTX 2080Ti for 150k iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Evaluated on synthetic datasets (800x800 resolution) and real capture setups. Strengths: Reconstructs geometry from scratch using shadows, unlike methods that use MVS first. Fully differentiable shadow ray supervision, unlike concurrent works using non-differentiable root finding. Applicable to single-view setups, unlike NeRF which requires multi-view. Handles RGB inputs by modeling material, avoiding the need for explicit shadow segmentation. Limitations: Requires multiple lighting conditions to obtain sufficient shadow observations. Assumes the ground plane position and orientation are known to resolve scale ambiguity. Iterative updating strategy is insufficient for gradients at surface boundaries with abrupt depth changes without the boundary handling mechanism. Transparency and inter-reflections are disabled as these effects are beyond the method's assumptions. ShadowNeuS was proposed in the paper "ShadowNeuS: Neural SDF Reconstruction by Shadow Ray Supervision". It addresses the limitation of NeRF, which models camera rays but ignores shadow rays (rays from the light source to the scene). The method draws inspiration from NeuS for SDF representation and differentiable rendering techniques. It is used for single-view 3D reconstruction from binary shadow images or RGB images under multiple lights. name: NeRF-Supervision
head: RGB-sensor-only self-supervised pipeline for dense descriptors
body: NeRF-Supervision is an RGB-only, self-supervised pipeline that uses an optimized NeRF's density field to generate dense correspondence datasets for training object-centric descriptors. It solves the problem of acquiring ground-truth dense correspondences for thin, reflective, or ambiguous objects where traditional RGB-D sensors and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) fail. Unlike MVS, which relies on patch-based photometric consistency, NeRF-Supervision reformulates correspondence via a distribution-of-depths formulation, using the density field for probabilistic sampling to handle ambiguity and view-dependent appearance. The method operates in three distinct stages: NeRF optimization, dataset generation via density field sampling, and descriptor model training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of RGB images I of an object captured from various viewpoints. Output: A trained dense descriptor model capable of estimating dense object descriptors for unobserved real images. Data Structures: The fundamental unit of training data is a correspondence tuple (Is, us, It, ut): Is, It \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h \times 3}: Source and target RGB images, where w and h are image width and height. us, ut \in \mathbb{R}^2: Pixel coordinates in the source and target images, respectively. Constraint: The image-forming rays defined by (Is, us) and (It, ut) must intersect the same 3D point in space. Algorithm Steps: 1. NeRF Optimization: Collect RGB images of the object and optimize a NeRF model F\Theta. The NeRF predicts volume density \sigma and view-dependent color c for any 3D point \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Correspondence Dataset Generation: Use the trained NeRF's density field to automatically generate a dataset of dense correspondences. This involves sampling 3D points from the density field and projecting them into multiple camera views to create valid tuples. Distribution-of-Depths Formulation: Unlike methods that rely on a single depth map, this method reformulates correspondence via a distribution-of-depths formulation. The NeRF's density field allows for probabilistic sampling, which handles ambiguity in photometric consistency better than patch-based MVS. 3. Descriptor Training: Train a neural network f\theta with parameters \theta to map an input RGB image I to a dense descriptor field. The network is supervised using the generated tuples (Is, us, It, ut). The descriptor dimensionality is denoted as d. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfsupervisionpipeline(rgbimages, cameraposes, numsamples): # Stage 1: Optimize NeRF FTheta predicting density sigma and view-dependent color c nerfmodel = optimizenerf(rgbimages, cameraposes) # Stage 2: Generate Correspondence Dataset via density field sampling correspondencedataset = [] for in range(numsamples): # Sample a 3D point P from the NeRF's density distribution P = sample3dpointfromdensity(nerfmodel) # Project P into multiple camera views to find corresponding pixels for views, viewt in getviewpairs(cameraposes): us = projecttopixel(P, cameraposes[views]) ut = projecttopixel(P, cameraposes[viewt]) Is = rgbimages[views] It = rgbimages[viewt] # Tuple: Is, It in R^(w x h x 3); us, ut in R^2 correspondencedataset.append((Is, us, It, ut)) # Stage 3: Train Descriptor Model ftheta mapping I to dense descriptors of dimensionality d descriptormodel = initializedescriptormodel() optimizer = Adam(descriptormodel.parameters()) for (Is, us, It, ut) in correspondencedataset: descs = descriptormodel(Is, us) desct = descriptormodel(It, ut) loss = meansquarederror(descs, desct) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return descriptormodel def optimizenerf(images, poses): model = NeRF() optimizer = Adam(model.parameters()) for epoch in range(maxepochs): for img, pose in zip(images, poses): rays = generaterays(pose, img.shape) rgb, depth, acc = model(rays) loss = meansquarederror(rgb, img) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return model def sample3dpointfromdensity(model): # Sample point from density distribution along rays or in volume return model.samplepoint() def getviewpairs(poses): pairs = [] for i in range(len(poses)): for j in range(i + 1, len(poses)): pairs.append((i, j)) return pairs def projecttopixel(point, pose): # Project 3D point to 2D pixel coordinates using camera projection matrix return pose.project(point) def initializedescriptormodel(): return DescriptorNet() def meansquarederror(a, b): return sum((ai - bi) 2 for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) / len(a) Parameters: w, h: Image width and height. d: Descriptor dimensionality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reflective Objects: Standard RGB-D and MVS methods struggle with reflective objects. NeRF-Supervision handles this because the NeRF takes view direction as input for color prediction, allowing it to model view-dependent appearance. Ambiguity: The density field sampling mechanism handles geometric ambiguity better than patch-based photometric consistency used in MVS. Performance: Dense correspondence models trained with this method outperform off-the-shelf learned descriptors by 106% (measured by PCK@3px metric) and outperform a baseline supervised with multi-view stereo by 29%. Strengths: RGB-only: Does not require depth sensors or multiple synchronized cameras. Robustness: Effective for thin and reflective objects (e.g., forks, whisks, strainers) that are challenging for commodity RGB-D cameras or MVS. Application: Enables robots to perform accurate 6-DoF pick and place of challenging objects. Limitations: Requires the optimization of a NeRF for each object, which can be computationally intensive compared to direct MVS. Performance is dependent on the quality of the NeRF reconstruction. NeRF-Supervision was introduced by Lin Yen-Chen, Tsung-Yi Lin, Pete Florence, Jonathan T. Barron, Alberto Rodriguez, and Phillip Isola in 2022. The work addresses the long-standing problem of designing robust visual descriptors invariant to scale, illumination, and pose. While learning-based descriptors have shown superiority over hand-crafted ones, the lack of ground-truth dense correspondence data for challenging objects (particularly thin and reflective ones) has been a bottleneck. This method leverages the recent success of Neural Radiance Fields to provide a self-supervised pipeline for generating such data. name: Depth Alignment for Monocular Cues
head: Least-squares Depth Alignment, Scale and Shift Alignment
body: Depth Alignment for Monocular Cues solves the scale and shift ambiguity inherent in monocular depth estimation (MDE) by linearly aligning relative MDE outputs with rendered depth values during NeRF training. It differs from sibling methods like NerfingMVS which use multi-view stereo consistency, by optimizing alignment parameters per mini-batch to enforce geometric consistency against a single-view depth prior. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Rendered depth map \bar{D} from the NeRF, monocular depth estimate D^ from a frozen pre-trained network (e.g., Omnidata), and a set of sampled pixel indices P for the current mini-batch. Outputs: Alignment parameters (scale w, shift q) and the aligned depth loss contribution to the total objective. Data Structures: D^: 2D tensor of shape (H, W), values in [0, 1] (normalized MDE output). \bar{D}: 2D tensor of shape (H, W), rendered depth values. P: List of (u, v) pixel coordinates sampled from the image. Steps: 1. Sample Pixels: Select N pixels from the image to compute alignment statistics. Let the sampled values be D^p and \bar{D}p for p \in P. 2. Stop-Gradient: Apply stop-gradient to D^ to prevent gradients from flowing into the frozen MDE network: D^{sg} = \text{sg}(D^). 3. Least-Squares Optimization: Solve for scale w and shift q that minimize the squared error between the aligned MDE depth and rendered depth: \min{w, q} \sum{p \in P} \| (w \cdot D^{sg}(p) + q) - \bar{D}(p) \|^2 The closed-form solution minimizes this objective. 4. Apply Alignment: Compute the aligned MDE depth: \tilde{D}(p) = w \cdot D^(p) + q. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the depth consistency loss L{depth} using the aligned depth \tilde{D} and rendered depth \bar{D}. Formulas: Let \mu{MDE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{p \in P} D^{sg}(p) and \mu{R} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{p \in P} \bar{D}(p). Let \sigma{MDE, R} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{p \in P} (D^{sg}(p) - \mu{MDE})(\bar{D}(p) - \mu{R}). Let \sigma^2{MDE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{p \in P} (D^{sg}(p) - \mu{MDE})^2. w = \frac{\sigma{MDE, R}}{\sigma^2{MDE} + \epsilon} q = \mu{R} - w \cdot \mu{MDE} Where \epsilon is a small constant (e.g., 10^{-8}) to prevent division by zero. Parameters: N: Number of sampled pixels. Typical value: Not given in the sources. \epsilon: Regularization constant. Typical value: 10^{-8}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Variance: If \sigma^2{MDE} \approx 0 (e.g., flat regions), w becomes unstable. Add \epsilon to the denominator to stabilize computation. Scale Ambiguity: Without alignment, the NeRF may converge to an arbitrary scale. This method ensures the scale matches the MDE prior relative to the rendered depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthalignment(Dmde, Drendered, numsamples=1024): """ Align monocular depth with rendered depth using least-squares. Args: Dmde: 2D array (H, W), monocular depth estimate [0, 1]. Drendered: 2D array (H, W), rendered depth from NeRF. numsamples: Number of pixels to sample for alignment. Returns: w: Scale parameter. q: Shift parameter. """ import random H, W = len(Dmde), len(Dmde[0]) # Sample random pixel indices indices = list(range(H W)) sampledindices = random.sample(indices, min(numsamples, H W)) dmdevals = [] drenderedvals = [] for idx in sampledindices: u, v = divmod(idx, W) dmdevals.append(float(Dmde[u][v])) drenderedvals.append(float(Drendered[u][v])) # Stop gradient on MDE depth (detach values) dmdevals = [float(x) for x in dmdevals] # Compute means mumde = sum(dmdevals) / len(dmdevals) murendered = sum(drenderedvals) / len(drenderedvals) # Compute covariance and variance cov = sum((dm - mumde) (dr - murendered) for dm, dr in zip(dmdevals, drenderedvals)) / len(dmdevals) varmde = sum((dm - mumde) 2 for dm in dmdevals) / len(dmdevals) # Compute scale and shift epsilon = 1e-8 w = cov / (varmde + epsilon) q = murendered - w mumde return w, q A preprocessing step that normalizes monocular depth estimates to remove scale and shift ambiguities before alignment. It sets itself apart from direct least-squares alignment by explicitly standardizing depth statistics using mean and mean absolute deviation rather than solving for linear parameters. Choose this variant when the MDE prior exhibits large dynamic range variations or when comparing depth maps across different scenes requires statistical standardization. See Incremental Joint Learning of Depth, Pose, and Implicit Scene Representation on Monocular Camera in Large-Scale Scenes. Time Complexity: The method requires O(N) time per mini-batch for sampling and computing statistics, where N is the number of sampled pixels. This overhead is negligible compared to the NeRF forward pass. Memory Complexity: The method requires O(N) memory to store sampled depth values. Strengths: The method is simple to implement, effectively resolves scale ambiguity, and works with any pre-trained MDE model. Limitations: The method relies heavily on the quality of the MDE prior and assumes a linear relationship between MDE and rendered depth. When to Use: Use this method when training NeRFs from monocular images with a reliable MDE prior (e.g., Omnidata) and no sparse point cloud or multi-view stereo data is available. When Not to Use: Avoid this method when high-precision absolute scale is required and MDE is known to be inaccurate, or when multi-view consistency is available and preferred. The method originated in approaches like MonoSDF and Neuralangelo for inferring signed distance functions from monocular images. It addresses the challenge of using monocular depth priors in volume rendering by aligning them with the rendered depth to enforce geometric consistency. The method is widely used in recent monocular NeRF and SDF reconstruction pipelines. name: GAINS Stage I: Shape Estimation
head: GAINS Shape Estimation, GAINS Stage 1
body: GAINS Stage I is the geometry optimization phase of the GAINS pipeline, designed to reconstruct robust 3D shape from a sparse set of input RGB images using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS). It solves the problem of novel-view artifacts and geometric collapse that occur when standard 2DGS losses are applied to sparse inputs by augmenting the optimization with learning-based priors: monocular depth/normal consistency, local depth ranking, and Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a latent diffusion model. Unlike its sibling methods that may rely on differentiable volume rendering or MVS priors, GAINS explicitly leverages a pre-trained diffusion model to regularize unseen viewpoints, ensuring the geometry lies on the natural object manifold. Inputs: Sparse set of RGB images \{Ii\}{i=1}^N (typically N \in [4, 16]). Known camera parameters Ci = \{Ki, Ri, ti\} for each view. Pre-trained monocular depth estimator (outputs \hat{D}i). Pre-trained monocular normal estimator (outputs \tilde{N}i). Pre-trained latent diffusion model \epsilon\phi. Optional: Ground-truth alpha masks for outlier removal. Outputs: Optimized 2DGS geometry representation G = \{\muj, Sj, Rj, \sigmaj\}{j=1}^M, where \muj is position, Sj is scaling, Rj is rotation, and \sigmaj is opacity. The scene is represented as a collection of 2D Gaussians. Each Gaussian j stores: \muj \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. Sj \in \mathbb{R}^3: Scaling vector. Rj \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Rotation matrix. \sigmaj \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. Surface normal nj is derived from Rj. \lambda{DC} = 0.005: Depth consistency weight. \lambda{DR} = 10: Depth ranking weight. \lambda{NC} = 1: Normal consistency weight. \lambda{N} = 0.25: Normal guided loss weight. \lambda{SDS} = 0.0001: Diffusion guidance weight. \lambda{BCE} = 0.75: Binary Cross-Entropy loss weight. \lambda = 0.2: Weight for L1 vs LD-SSIM in color loss. Total iterations: 16,000. SDS activation iteration: 10,000. SDS guidance scale: 100. Novel viewpoints sampled: 100. Floater removal interval: Every 1,000 iterations. 1. Initialization: Initialize the 2DGS primitives G using standard initialization procedures for 2DGS. 2. Loss Calculation: For each training iteration, compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} as the sum of the following components: A. Re-rendering Loss (\mathcal{L}{col}): Render the image R{geo}(Ci, G) for each input view Ci. Compute: \mathcal{L}{col} = (1 - \lambda) \mathcal{L}1(R{geo}, Ii) + \lambda \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM}(R{geo}, Ii) where \mathcal{L}1 is the L1 loss and \mathcal{L}{D-SSIM} is the D-SSIM loss. B. Depth Distortion Loss (\mathcal{L}{DD}): Optional loss to reduce depth ambiguity by bringing intersected Gaussians closer along each ray. C. Normal Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{NC}): Compute surface normals \tilde{N}i from the rendered depth. Compare with normals Ni derived from the Gaussian rotation matrices: \mathcal{L}{NC} = 1 - Ni^T \tilde{N}i where the operation is averaged over all pixels or primitives. D. Depth Consistency Loss (\mathcal{L}{DC}): Render depth map Di from G. Obtain monocular depth estimate \hat{D}i from the pre-trained MDE network. Compute the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) between Di and \hat{D}i: \mathcal{L}{DC} = 1 - \text{PCC}(Di, \hat{D}i) This enforces similarity in depth ordering and relative scale, mitigating hallucinations from MDE. E. Local Depth Ranking Loss (\mathcal{L}{DR}): Add \mathcal{L}{DR} to prevent geometric collapse from hard constraints and alleviate long-range ambiguity. (Specific formula not provided in source, cited as [9]). F. Normal Guided Loss (\mathcal{L}{N}): Obtain reference normals \tilde{N}i from the pre-trained monocular normal estimator. Obtain rendered normals Ni from the Gaussian geometry. Obtain surface normals \hat{N}i from the rendered depth. Compute: \mathcal{L}{N} = \mathcal{L}1(\tilde{N}i, \hat{N}i) + 0.1 \cdot \mathcal{L}1(\tilde{N}i, Ni) + \text{TV}(\tilde{N}i, \hat{N}i) where \text{TV} is the Total Variation loss. G. Diffusion Guidance Loss (\mathcal{L}{SDS}): Condition: Only compute if iteration > 10,000. 1. Sample 100 novel viewpoints Cj. 2. Render geometry R{geo}(Cj, G). 3. Apply forward diffusion to get noisy latents Zj: Zj = \alphat R{geo}(Cj, G) + \sigmat \epsilon where t \sim U(0.02, 0.98) and \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 4. Compute SDS loss: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} w(t) \| \epsilon\phi(Zj; t) - \epsilon \|2^2 where \epsilon\phi is the pre-trained diffusion model predicting noise, and w(t) is the weighting function. H. Outlier Removal Loss (\mathcal{L}{BCE}): Condition: Only if ground-truth alpha masks are provided. Compute Binary Cross-Entropy between the reconstructed alpha mask and the ground truth mask. 3. Optimization Step: Minimize the total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{col} + \lambda{DC} \mathcal{L}{DC} + \lambda{DR} \mathcal{L}{DR} + \lambda{NC} \mathcal{L}{NC} + \lambda{N} \mathcal{L}{N} + \lambda{SDS} \mathcal{L}{SDS} + \lambda{BCE} \mathcal{L}{BCE} Update parameters of G using gradient descent. 4. Periodic Maintenance: Every 1,000 iterations, apply KNN-based floater removal to prune isolated or erroneous Gaussians. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gainsstageishapeestimation(images, cameras, mdenet, normalnet, diffusionmodel, alphamasks=None, totaliterations=16000): """ Optimizes 2DGS geometry using GAINS Stage I losses. """ # Hyperparameters lambdadc = 0.005 lambdadr = 10 lambdanc = 1 lambdan = 0.25 lambdasds = 0.0001 lambdabce = 0.75 lambdacolorl1 = 0.8 lambdacolorss = 0.2 sdsstartiter = 10000 floaterinterval = 1000 numnovelviews = 100 # Initialize 2DGS primitives G using standard 2DGS initialization G = initialize2dgs(images, cameras) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(G.parameters()) for iteration in range(totaliterations): totalloss = 0.0 # 1. Re-rendering Loss (Lcol) renderedimages = [] rendereddepths = [] renderednormals = [] for i, (img, cam) in enumerate(zip(images, cameras)): # Render image, depth, and normals from G using 2DGS rasterization Rimg, Rdepth, Rnormal = render2dgs(G, cam) renderedimages.append(Rimg) rendereddepths.append(Rdepth) renderednormals.append(Rnormal) # Lcol = (1 - lambda) L1 + lambda LD-SSIM l1loss = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(Rimg, img) ssimloss = 1 - ssim(Rimg, img) # Standard SSIM implementation lcol = (1 - lambdacolorss) l1loss + lambdacolorss ssimloss totalloss += lcol # 2. Depth Distortion Loss (LDD) # Optional, reduces depth ambiguity ldd = computedepthdistortionloss(G, rendereddepths) # totalloss += ldd # 3. Normal Consistency Loss (LNC) # Compare normals from Gaussian rotation (Ni) with normals from depth (Ntildei) lnc = 0 for Rnormal in renderednormals: # Ntildei is derived from depth Ntilde = computenormalsfromdepth(Rnormal) # # Ni is derived from Gaussian rotation Ni = Rnormal # Already computed by rasterizer # Average over pixels lnc += torch.mean(1 - torch.sum(Ni Ntilde, dim=-1)) lnc = lnc / len(images) totalloss += lambdanc lnc # 4. Depth Consistency Loss (LDC) # Enforce similarity to monocular depth estimate ldc = 0 for i, (Rdepth, img) in enumerate(zip(rendereddepths, images)): # Get monocular depth estimate Mdepth = mdenet(img) # PCC between rendered depth and monocular depth pcc = np.corrcoef(Rdepth.flatten(), Mdepth.flatten())[0, 1] # ldc += 1 - pcc ldc = ldc / len(images) totalloss += lambdadc ldc # 5. Local Depth Ranking Loss (LDR) # Prevents geometric collapse ldr = computelocaldepthrankingloss(rendereddepths) # totalloss += lambdadr ldr # 6. Normal Guided Loss (LN) # Uses reference normals from monocular estimator ln = 0 for i, (img, Rdepth) in enumerate(zip(images, rendereddepths)): # Reference normals from monocular normal estimator Nref = normalnet(img) # Surface normals from depth Nsurf = computenormalsfromdepth(Rdepth) # # Rendered normals from Gaussian rotation Nrendered = renderednormals[i] # LN = L1(Nref, Nsurf) + 0.1 L1(Nref, Nrendered) + TV(Nref, Nsurf) term1 = torch.nn.functional.l1loss(Nref, Nsurf) term2 = 0.1 torch.nn.functional.l1loss(Nref, Nrendered) # Total Variation loss tvh = torch.sum(torch.abs(Nref[:, 1:,:] - Nref[:,:-1,:])) tvw = torch.sum(torch.abs(Nref[:,:, 1:] - Nref[:,:,:-1])) term3 = tvh + tvw ln += term1 + term2 + term3 ln = ln / len(images) totalloss += lambdan ln # 7. Diffusion Guidance Loss (LSDS) # Only active after iteration 10000 if iteration > sdsstartiter: lsds = 0 for in range(numnovelviews): # Sample novel viewpoint camnovel = samplenovelviewpoint(cameras) # Render geometry Rgeo = render2dgsgeometry(G, camnovel) # Forward diffusion t = torch.rand(1).item() (0.98 - 0.02) + 0.02 epsilon = torch.randnlike(Rgeo) alphat, sigmat = getdiffusioncoefficients(t) Zj = alphat Rgeo + sigmat epsilon # Predict noise epsilonpred = diffusionmodel.predictnoise(Zj, t) # SDS Loss wt = getsdsweight(t) lossterm = wt torch.norm(epsilonpred - epsilon, p=2)2 lsds += lossterm lsds = lsds / numnovelviews totalloss += lambdasds lsds # 8. Outlier Removal Loss (LBCE) if alphamasks is not None: lbce = 0 for i, (Rimg, alphamaskgt) in enumerate(zip(renderedimages, alphamasks)): # Extract alpha channel from rendered image alpharendered = extractalpha(Rimg) lbce += torch.nn.functional.binarycrossentropy(alpharendered, alphamaskgt) lbce = lbce / len(images) totalloss += lambdabce lbce # Optimization Step totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Periodic Floater Removal if iteration % floaterinterval == 0: G = knnfloaterremoval(G) # return G Early Stage SDS Ineffectiveness: SDS loss is ineffective when the shape is far from the target. It is disabled for the first 10,000 iterations to prevent instability. Sparse View Overfitting: Standard 2DGS losses overfit to captured viewpoints, causing novel-view artifacts. The addition of depth, normal, and diffusion priors mitigates this. MDE Hallucinations: Monocular depth estimators may hallucinate or have systematic biases. The use of PCC (relative scale/order) rather than absolute L1 loss helps mitigate this, along with the diffusion prior. Missing Alpha Masks: If ground-truth alpha masks are not provided, the BCE loss is skipped, and the model assumes the scene includes the background. Time: The optimization runs for 16,000 iterations. The inclusion of SDS loss (after iteration 10,000) adds significant computational cost due to the forward diffusion and noise prediction steps for 100 novel viewpoints per iteration. Memory: Memory usage is dominated by the 2DGS primitives and the storage of the pre-trained models (MDE, Normal Estimator, Diffusion Model) in memory. Hardware: Not given in the sources. Resolution: Not given in the sources. Scene: Tested on sparse multi-view captures (4-16 views). Scaling: The method is designed for sparse views, where traditional methods fail. It scales with the number of Gaussians and the complexity of the diffusion model. Strengths: Robust geometry reconstruction from sparse views. Prevents novel-view artifacts. Leverages strong priors from diffusion models for generalization. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to diffusion guidance. Relies on the quality of pre-trained monocular estimators and diffusion models. Requires known camera parameters. Use when reconstructing geometry from a sparse set of RGB images (4-16 views) where standard NeRF or 3DGS methods fail due to overfitting or artifacts. Use when high-fidelity geometry is required for subsequent material and lighting estimation (Stage II). Do not use if dense input views are available, as standard 2DGS may suffice and the additional priors add unnecessary complexity. Do not use if computational resources are limited, as SDS guidance is expensive. GAINS (Gaussian-based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures) was introduced by P. Noras et al. in the paper "GAINS: Gaussian-Based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures". The method builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [8], which was chosen over 3DGS for its more accurate geometry reconstruction, essential for material estimation. The pipeline adapts 2DGS for inverse rendering by splitting optimization into two stages: Stage I for geometry and Stage II for material and lighting. Stage I specifically addresses the challenges of sparse views by incorporating priors from latent diffusion models and monocular depth/normal estimation models. GAINS is used for robust and accurate geometry and material property reconstruction from sparse RGB images under known camera intrinsics and extrinsics. GAINS: Gaussian-Based Inverse Rendering from Sparse Multi-view Captures, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37602-218, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Monocular Depth Cues
body: Monocular Depth Cues is a method that integrates pre-trained monocular geometric priors (depth and surface normal maps) into the training of neural implicit surface reconstruction models to regularize geometry and improve reconstruction quality. It differs from sibling methods like NerfingMVS by relying on off-the-shelf monocular predictors (e.g., Omnidata) rather than multi-view stereo consistency or explicit MVS networks, and from Depth-Guided NeRF Training via Earth Mover’s Distance by using direct pixel-wise alignment losses rather than distributional matching. The method addresses the ambiguity of scale and detail in monocular inputs by providing semi-local relative depth and local surface normal cues. Inputs: Input RGB images I. A pre-trained monocular predictor G\phi (specifically Omnidata). A neural implicit surface representation (e.g., MLP or Multi-Resolution Grids). Outputs: Aligned monocular depth map \bar{D} and normal map \bar{N} for each input image. Regularized neural implicit surface reconstruction. Data Structures: Monocular Depth Map (\bar{D}): 2D array of relative depth values. Monocular Normal Map (\bar{N}): 2D array of 3D surface normal vectors. Neural Representation: Stores signed distance field (SDF) or density values queried by rays. Steps: 1. Cue Extraction: Apply the pre-trained predictor G\phi to each input RGB image I to generate a relative depth map \bar{D} and a surface normal map \bar{N}. 2. Scale and Shift Alignment: Align the relative monocular depth \bar{D} with the rendered depth \tilde{D} from the neural model. Since monocular depth lacks absolute scale, find scale w and shift q by minimizing the least-squares error: \min{w, q} \sum{p} \| (w \cdot \text{sg}(\bar{D}(p)) + q) - \tilde{D}(p) \|^2 where \text{sg}(\cdot) is the stop-gradient operator, preventing gradients from flowing into the frozen predictor G\phi. 3. Loss Computation: Compute consistency losses penalizing the difference between the aligned monocular depth/normal maps and the corresponding neural model outputs (normals derived from the SDF gradient). 4. Optimization: Update the neural implicit surface parameters using the cues as training supervision. Parameters: Predictor: Omnidata. Resolution: Standard cues are generated at 384×384 resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scale Ambiguity: Monocular depth is relative; without alignment, the reconstruction scale is undefined. Local vs. Global: Depth cues provide semi-local relative information, while normal cues provide local geometric detail; they are complementary. Resolution Limits: Standard 384×384 cues may lack fine details; higher-resolution variants are available (see Subtopics). A method to generate higher-resolution monocular depth and normal maps by partitioning the input image into overlapping sub-images, predicting cues for each, merging them, and aligning them to recover fine details lost at lower resolutions. It produces cues with more fine details compared to the standard 384×384 resolution cues. It is used in MonoSDF when higher-quality geometric priors are desired. Steps: (1) Partition a high-resolution input image into multiple overlapping sub-images; (2) Predict monocular depth and normal maps for each sub-image using a pretrained predictor (e.g., Omnidata); (3) Merge the predictions from all sub-images into a single high-resolution depth and normal map; (4) Align the merged depth maps using the least-squares alignment formula and solve for normal rotation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the monocular depth and normal maps for each input view, plus the neural implicit representation. Performance: On the DTU dataset with 3 input views, methods using monocular cues (MLP and Multi-Res. Grids) produce satisfying reconstructions where they otherwise fail, achieving competitive Chamfer distances (e.g., ~2.0–5.0 mm depending on scene) compared to state-of-the-art methods. Strengths: Provides complementary local (normal) and semi-local (depth) geometric information; easy to integrate via off-the-shelf predictors. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained monocular predictor; scale ambiguity requires careful alignment; standard resolution cues may lack fine details. When to use: When training neural implicit surface reconstruction models and higher-quality geometric priors are desired. The method originates from the MonoSDF paper, which explores the use of monocular geometric cues for neural implicit surface reconstruction. It leverages the Omnidata model for depth and normal prediction. The approach was developed to address the limitations of neural implicit methods that fail to produce satisfying reconstructions without geometric regularization. MonoSDF: Exploring Monocular Geometric Cues for Neural Implicit Surface Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-1814, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures
head: NeRF Editing, NeRF Inpainting, 3D Scene Editing
body: NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures modify a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to remove objects, fill occluded regions, or alter appearance and geometry based on user intent. Unlike standard training which reconstructs a scene from scratch, these methods optimize existing parameters to satisfy new constraints while maintaining multi-view consistency. They are distinguished from sibling methods by their reliance on external 2D priors (such as inpainted images or diffusion models) to guide 3D optimization, rather than relying solely on multi-view geometry or semantic segmentation alone. All methods in this family operate on a pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color. The core mechanism involves an optimization loop that minimizes a loss function L to update the NeRF parameters \theta (or a subset thereof). The general optimization objective is: L = L{render} + \lambda{guidance} L{guidance} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} where L{render} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{guidance} incorporates external priors (e.g., 2D inpainted images, diffusion model gradients, or semantic features), and L{reg} prevents artifacts or overfitting. Key shared components include: 1. Masking/Selection: A binary or probabilistic mask M or selection field identifies the region of interest (ROI) or occluded areas, typically user-defined via sketching or language instructions. 2. External Priors: Methods rely on 2D priors to guide 3D changes, commonly using diffusion guidance (e.g., Score Distillation Sampling from text-to-image models) or semantic/text features (e.g., CLIP or LSeg) to align rendered features with prompts. 3. View Consistency Enforcement: To prevent inconsistencies across views, methods enforce multi-view constraints through implicit geometrical and photometric priors embodied by the neural network, which automatically propagates single-view edits to all views. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def editnerf(nerfmodel, mask, guidancepriors, optimizer, epochs): """ General optimization loop for NeRF editing. """ for epoch in range(epochs): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 rays = samplerays(nerfmodel.scenebounds) renderedcolors, transmittances = volumerender(nerfmodel, rays) lossrender = computephotometricloss(renderedcolors, targetimages, mask) totalloss += lossrender lossguidance = computeguidanceloss(renderedcolors, guidancepriors, mask) totalloss += lambdaguidance lossguidance lossreg = computeregularization(nerfmodel.parameters) totalloss += lambdareg lossreg totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfmodel Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing (PERF) reconstructs a panoramic NeRF from a single input panorama by iteratively expanding viewpoint coverage. It solves geometry conflicts between visible and invisible regions by computing conflict masks and erasing inconsistent pixels from supervision. Unlike methods requiring multiple views, PERF generates novel views via inpainting and progressively integrates them. Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS enhances sparse-view reconstruction by densifying input observations with synthetic pseudo-observations generated by a diffusion model during training. It acquires uncertainty through correspondence matching by reprojecting real observations to novel views, enforcing epipolar constraints. It conditions a 2D diffusion model on rendered RGB, depth, and view-consistency uncertainty maps to rectify artifacts. Blended-NeRF edits specific regions of interest (ROI) in an existing NeRF using text prompts and a user-defined 3D bounding box. It initializes a generator NeRF with original weights and blends synthesized content with the original scene using volumetric blending. Unlike methods requiring semantic masks, it operates on any 3D box without learning a new feature space. This procedure enables direct 3D editing by decoupling semantic/geometric selection from appearance rendering using a Distilled Feature Field (DFF). It defines a selection probability p for each 3D point, allowing precise operations like deletion, colorization, and geometric transformation. It avoids iterative gradient descent for the edit itself, relying on a deterministic query-and-transform pipeline during rendering. NeRF-Art is a text-guided method for stylizing pre-trained NeRFs that simultaneously alters appearance and 3D geometry without mesh guidance. It introduces a global-local contrastive learning strategy combined with directional constraints to ensure style adherence and cross-view consistency. This article documents the empirical limitations of the RePaint-NeRF method, specifically regarding computational efficiency, geometric fidelity under significant shape changes, and view-angle consistency. It serves as a reference for failure modes and resource constraints in diffusion-guided NeRF editing. Semantic and Language-Guided Editing modifies NeRFs using high-level semantic cues (text prompts, language instructions, or semantic masks). It solves localized 3D content manipulation while maintaining multi-view consistency. It integrates external semantic priors (e.g., CLIP, LSeg, or diffusion models) into the optimization loop to guide 3D structure and appearance. InNeRF360 combines multiview-consistent 2D priors with 3D diffusion guidance to reconstruct missing or edited regions. It addresses occluded or removed objects by first establishing coherent 2D inpainting across all views, then refining the 3D representation. It differs from direct 3D optimization by decoupling content generation (via 2D inpainting) from 3D reconstruction. Diffusion-guided editing modifies pre-trained NeRFs using text prompts or image instructions by leveraging 2D text-to-image diffusion models as external priors. Unlike sibling methods relying on semantic masks or geometric constraints, this family uses diffusion gradients or iterative image synthesis to guide 3D changes. This family removes unwanted objects or fills occluded regions in a pre-trained NeRF [Parent]. Unlike standard training, these methods optimize NeRF parameters to erase specific masked regions while maintaining geometric and photometric consistency across unmasked views [Parent]. They rely on external 2D priors (such as inpainted images or diffusion models) to guide 3D optimization [Parent]. A strategy employed after the NeRF has been trained on updated data to enhance consistency by generating a more accurate target for each view using the modified Instruct-Pix2Pix with averaging architecture. Use the rendered image as input while continuing to use the mixup image as a condition. 1. Sample an edit code z from the Gaussian distribution. 2. Use the translated NeRF to render the 3D scene conditioned on z. A makeup migration technique based on dynamic NeRF, capable of seamlessly transitioning makeup styles from a standard image to a facial image in various poses and expressions. Guarantees geometric and appearance consistency during the migration. A method to alter the color and shape of rigid objects observed in 2D images from manual user edits, enabled by a single NeRF trained on multiple object instances of the same category. During editing, the network parameters are adjusted to match the shape and color of a newly observed instance. A subset of tunable parameters is found which can successfully propagate user edits for novel view generation, avoiding expensive modifications of the entire network. The field of NeRF editing emerged as NeRFs gained popularity for novel view synthesis, with early works focusing on object removal and scene manipulation. Key developments include the introduction of diffusion-guided editing (e.g., RePaint-NeRF, Instruct-NeRF2NeRF) which leveraged 2D generative models to guide 3D optimization. Subsequent methods like Blended-NeRF and NeRF-Art introduced techniques for localized editing and stylization using text prompts and volumetric blending. Recent advancements focus on improving multi-view consistency through semantic priors and progressive inpainting strategies. name: Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing
head: Conflicted Geometry Detection and Erasing, Inpainting-and-Erasing Strategy, PERF, PERF Algorithm
body: Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing (PERF) is a method for reconstructing a panoramic Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) from a single input panorama by iteratively expanding the viewpoint coverage. It solves the problem of geometry conflict between visible regions (observed in reference views) and invisible regions (occluded or unseen) by computing a mask of conflicted areas and eliminating them from the NeRF training supervision. Unlike methods that rely on multiple input views or semantic priors, PERF generates novel views via inpainting and progressively integrates them while erasing geometrically inconsistent pixels to ensure 3D consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single input RGB panorama I{rgb}. Output: A panoramic NeRF representation f{nerf}. Data Structures: NeRF Representation: Instant-NGP. Uses a hash table of size 2^{19} with 16 levels of feature vectors, each having a channel size of 2. Reference Views Set: I{ref}, initialized with the input RGBD panorama. Trajectory Set: \{pk\}, a set of novel view positions generated based on the initial depth map. Formulas: 1. Initial RGBD Estimation: The input I{rgb} is processed to estimate a depth map Id, resulting in an RGBD panorama I{rgbd}. (Specific equation number referenced as Eq. (2) in source, but formula details for depth estimation are not provided in the text; assumes a standard monocular depth estimator is used here). 2. Single-View NeRF Training: The initial NeRF f{nerf} is trained using Id and I{rgb}. (Specific equation number referenced as Eq. (3) in source, but formula details are not provided; assumes standard NeRF volume rendering loss minimization). 3. Invisible Region Mask (m'): For a new view, invisible regions are detected by warping the new view's depth v' to the reference view's coordinate system and comparing it with the reference depth v. m'{ij} = \mathbb{I}(warp(v'{ij}) - v{ij} > \epsilon) where m'{ij} is the mask pixel (1 for invisible, 0 for visible), v{ij} is the reference depth, v'{ij} is the warped depth from the new view, warp(\cdot) is the warping function, \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function, and \epsilon is a small threshold value. 4. Conflicted Region Mask (m''): For each reference view I{ref}, conflicted regions are detected by warping the reference depth v to the new view's coordinate system and comparing it with the new view's depth v'. m''{ij} = \mathbb{I}(v{ij} - warp(v'{ij}) > \epsilon) where m''{ij} is the mask pixel (1 for inconsistent/conflicted, 0 for consistent). 5. Final Conflict Mask: The final conflict mask is computed by performing a logic AND operation across the individual masks m'' from all reference views. 6. Collaborative RGBD Inpainting: Invisible regions are inpainted using Stable Diffusion for RGB and a depth estimator for depth stitching. (Specific equation number referenced as Eq. (5) in source, but formula details are not provided; implies using the inpainted RGB and estimated depth to complete the panorama). Parameters: \epsilon: A small value used as a threshold for depth difference. Hash table size: 2^{19}. Levels: 16. Feature vector channel size: 2. Initial training iterations: 10,000 iterations for the single input panorama. New view sampling: 32 new positions with approximately gradually increased distance from the original position. Fine-tuning iterations per new view: 2,000 iterations total. First 100 iterations: Supervision only from the new reference view. Remaining 1,900 iterations: Supervision from all reference views. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate: Initially 10^{-3}, decayed to 10^{-4} with cosine annealing strategy for each learning stage of a newly sampled view. Ray sampling: 2,048 rays sampled per iteration. Numbered Steps: 1. Estimate the initial depth map Id of the input single panorama I{rgb} to obtain I{rgbd}. 2. Train a single-view NeRF f{nerf} using Id and I{rgb} for 10,000 iterations. 3. Generate trajectories \{pk\} of novel views based on the depth map Id. 4. Initialize the set of reference views I{ref} = \{I{rgbd}\}. 5. Iterate n from 1 to iters (where iters corresponds to the number of new views, e.g., 32): 1. Randomly sample a new camera view p from \{pk\}. 2. Compute the invisible regions according to Eq. (4). 3. Perform collaborative RGBD inpainting using Stable Diffusion and a depth estimator to complete the RGB and depth maps of the invisible regions. 4. For all I{ref} \in I{ref}: 1. Compute the conflicted regions according to Eq. (6). 2. Erase these conflicted regions from the supervision of the NeRF training. 5. Add the new inpainted view to the reference views I{ref}. 6. Fine-tune f{nerf} with the updated I{ref} for 2,000 iterations (100 iterations with only the new view, 1,900 with all views). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressiveinpaintinganderasing(Irgb): # 1. Estimate depth and create RGBD panorama Id = estimatedepth(Irgb) # Standard monocular depth estimation Irgbd = stackchannels(Irgb, Id) # Combine RGB and depth into single tensor # 2. Train initial single-view NeRF fnerf = initializeneRF() # Instant-NGP: hash table 2^19, 16 levels, channel size 2 trainnerf(fnerf, Irgbd, Irgb, iterations=10000) # Standard NeRF volume rendering loss minimization with Adam # 3. Generate novel view trajectories pk = generatetrajectories(Id, numviews=32) # Sample 32 poses at gradually increasing distances from original # 4. Initialize reference views Iref = [Irgbd] # 5. Progressive loop for n in range(1, len(pk) + 1): # Sample new view p = random.choice(pk) # Render initial depth for new view from current NeRF vnew = renderdepth(fnerf, p) # Cast rays, accumulate depth using NeRF parameters # Compute invisible regions (Eq. 4) # Warp new view depth to reference view coordinates vnewwarped = warpdepth(vnew, p, Iref[0].pose) # Project depth using camera extrinsics vref = Iref[0].depth epsilon = 0.01 # Small threshold value minvisible = (vnewwarped - vref > epsilon).astype(float) # Indicator function # Perform collaborative RGBD inpainting (Eq. 5) Inewrgb = inpaintregion(Irgb, minvisible, model="StableDiffusion") # Stable Diffusion inpainting Inewdepth = inpaintregion(Id, minvisible, model="DepthEstimator") # Depth estimation/stitching Inewrgbd = stackchannels(Inewrgb, Inewdepth) # Compute conflicted regions and erase (Eq. 6) mconflictfinal = None for Irefview in Iref: # Warp reference view depth to new view coordinates vrefwarped = warpdepth(Irefview.depth, Irefview.pose, p) mconflict = (Irefview.depth - vrefwarped > epsilon).astype(float) if mconflictfinal is None: mconflictfinal = mconflict else: mconflictfinal = mconflictfinal mconflict # Logic AND operation # Erase conflicted regions from supervision # Implementation detail: Mask out pixels where mconflictfinal == 1 during loss computation # Add new view to reference set Iref.append(Inewrgbd) # Fine-tune NeRF # First 100 iterations: only new view trainnerf(fnerf, {Inewrgbd}, iterations=100, lr=1e-3) # Remaining 1900 iterations: all reference views trainnerf(fnerf, Iref, iterations=1900, lrschedule="cosineanneal", startlr=1e-3, endlr=1e-4, excludeconflicted=mconflictfinal) return fnerf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Estimation Error: The initial depth estimation from a single panorama may be inaccurate, leading to incorrect trajectory generation or invisible region detection. Geometry Conflict: Invisible regions inpainted in one view may conflict with visible regions in another reference view. The erasing mechanism is crucial to prevent this. Precision: The threshold \epsilon must be carefully chosen to allow for small errors while detecting significant conflicts. Boundary Conditions: The warping function must handle occlusions and depth discontinuities correctly. A sub-method that uses Stable Diffusion for RGB inpainting and a depth estimator for depth stitching to complete invisible regions. It is chosen when monocular depth estimation is insufficient and external generative priors are needed. The initial training phase using a single RGBD panorama. It is chosen as the starting point for the progressive expansion. The geometric operation used to detect invisible and conflicted regions by projecting depth maps between camera poses. It is chosen for its efficiency in identifying visibility changes. Time Complexity: The method involves iterative training and inpainting. Training a scene takes about 2 hours on a single Nvidia V100 GPU with 32G memory. Memory Complexity: Uses Instant-NGP representation with a hash table of size 2^{19}. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the Replica dataset (2048x1024 resolution) and in-the-wild data. Strengths: Can reconstruct panoramic NeRFs from a single input view; handles geometry conflicts effectively; ensures 3D consistency through erasing. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial depth estimation and the inpainting model. When to use: When only a single panorama is available and a full 3D reconstruction is required. When not to use: When multiple input views are available, or when high-fidelity texture is critical and inpainting artifacts are unacceptable. Origin: Proposed in "PERF: Panoramic Neural Radiance Field From a Single Panorama". History: The method builds on the concept of NeRF [1] and uses Instant-NGP [40] for efficient representation. It addresses the limitation of NeRF requiring multiple views by introducing a progressive inpainting-and-erasing strategy. Usage: Used for reconstructing indoor scenes from single panoramic images, as demonstrated on the Replica dataset and in-the-wild data.
