name: Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS Pipeline
head: Deceptive-3DGS, Deceptive-NeRF
body: Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS is a sparse-view reconstruction method that enhances NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by continuously densifying input observations with synthetic pseudo-observations generated by a diffusion model during training. Unlike methods that rely on ensemble learning, variational inference, or spatial perturbations to estimate uncertainty, this approach acquires uncertainty through correspondence matching by reprojecting real input observations to novel views, thereby enforcing epipolar constraints with minimal additional computation. It sets itself apart by conditioning a 2D diffusion model on rendered RGB images, depth maps, and view-consistency uncertainty maps to rectify artifacts and generate photorealistic pseudo-observations that are filtered by perceptual similarity before being used to retrain the 3D representation. Inputs: A set of W input images I = \{I1, \dots, IW\} with calibrated camera poses. A pre-trained 2D latent diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion) fine-tuned via ControlNet. Outputs: An optimized NeRF or 3DGS representation capable of high-quality novel view synthesis from sparse inputs. The method relies on the standard NeRF/3DGS representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Additionally, it maintains: 1. Coarse NeRF: A representation trained on a subset (one-fifth) of input images to simulate sparse-view conditions and generate initial pseudo-observations for diffusion training. 2. Pseudo-Observation Buffer: A collection of generated pseudo-observations PA and their associated metadata (depth DA, uncertainty UA). 3. ControlNet Channels: The diffusion model accepts a 5-channel control map: 3 channels for coarse RGB, 1 for depth, and 1 for uncertainty. 1. Coarse Training: Train a coarse NeRF/3DGS using one-fifth of the input images I. 2. Novel View Sampling: Randomly sample a novel viewpoint A within the bounding box defined by the outermost input views. 3. Rendering: At viewpoint A, render the RGB image \hat{I}A, depth map DA, and transmittance using the coarse NeRF/3DGS. Depth is computed as a weighted sum of distances traveled: \hat{\mathbf{D}} = \sum{k=1}^K \hat{T}(tk)\alpha(\sigma(tk)\deltak) where \hat{T}(tk) is transmittance, \alpha is opacity, \sigma is density, and \deltak is the distance traveled. 4. Uncertainty Map Generation: Identify the nearest input viewpoint B to the novel view A. Warp the ground truth image IB from viewpoint B to viewpoint A using the rendered depth DA and the relative pose R{B \rightarrow A}: I{B \rightarrow A} = \psi(IB; DA, R{B \rightarrow A}) For each pixel p in \hat{I}A, compute the transformed pixel location q in IB: q = K R{B \rightarrow A} DA(p) K^{-1} p where K is the camera parameter matrix. Compute the uncertainty map UA as the squared difference between the warped image and the rendered image: UA = (I{B \rightarrow A} - \hat{I}A)^2. 5. Pseudo-Observation Generation: Generate a pseudo-observation PA using the Deceptive Diffusion Model G: PA = G(\hat{I}A, DA, UA) The model G is a latent diffusion model conditioned on the coarse RGB image, depth, uncertainty, and a text embedding s. 6. Text Embedding Derivation: Generate an initial text prompt s0 using a pre-trained image captioning network. Optimize a shared latent text embedding s^ using textual inversion, shared across all input observations and coarse images. Form the composite feature s = [s0, s^] by concatenating the embeddings. 7. Filtering: Calculate the perceptual similarity between the generated pseudo-observation PA and the input images using the LPIPS metric. Discard the 20% of pseudo-observations with the lowest similarity to avoid generating content far from the original inputs. 8. Accumulation and Re-training: Accumulate the valid pseudo-observations into the training set. Continue training the NeRF/3DGS representation using the combination of real input images and the accumulated pseudo-observations. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–8 until a sufficient number of observations are accumulated to achieve the desired reconstruction quality. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def traindeceptivenerf(inputimages, poses, numepochs, numpseudoviews): """ Trains a NeRF/3DGS using the Deceptive-NeRF pipeline. Args: inputimages: List of W input images. poses: Camera poses for inputimages. numepochs: Number of epochs for coarse training. numpseudoviews: Number of pseudo-views to generate per iteration. Returns: Optimized NeRF/3DGS model. """ # 1. Coarse Training (1/5 of images) subsetsize = len(inputimages) // 5 coarseimages = inputimages[:subsetsize] coarseposes = poses[:subsetsize] coarsemodel = initializenerf(coarseimages, coarseposes) for epoch in range(numepochs): rendered = renderbatchfromnerf(coarsemodel, coarseimages, coarseposes) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, coarseimages) updatenerfparameters(coarsemodel, loss) # 2. Diffusion Model Setup & Fine-tuning diffusionmodel = ControlNetStableDiffusion(controlchannels=5) trainingquartets = generatetrainingquartets(inputimages, poses) finetunediffusion(diffusionmodel, trainingquartets) # 3. Main (Fine) NeRF Initialization finemodel = initializenerf(inputimages, poses) # 4. Iterative Densification Loop pseudoobservations = [] for iteration in range(numpseudoviews): # Sample novel view A viewA = samplenovelview(poses) # Render from Coarse Model rgbcoarse, depthcoarse = renderfromnerf(coarsemodel, viewA) # Find nearest input view B viewBidx = findnearestinputview(viewA, poses) imgB = inputimages[viewBidx] # Generate Uncertainty Map uncertaintymap = computeuncertainty(imgB, depthcoarse, rgbcoarse, viewA, viewBidx, poses) # Generate Text Embedding textprompt = captionimage(rgbcoarse) latentembedding = optimizetextualinversion(inputimages, rgbcoarse) textembedding = concatenateembeddings(textprompt, latentembedding) # Generate Pseudo-Observation pseudoobs = diffusionmodel(rgbcoarse, depthcoarse, uncertaintymap, textembedding) # Filter Pseudo-Observation (Discard bottom 20% by LPIPS) similarityscores = computelpipsbatch(pseudoobs, inputimages) threshold = np.percentile(similarityscores, 20) if np.mean(similarityscores) >= threshold: pseudoobservations.append(pseudoobs) # Re-train Fine Model with real + pseudo observations trainfinemodel(finemodel, inputimages + pseudoobservations, poses) return finemodel def generatetrainingquartets(inputimages, poses): """ Generates dataset of quartets (Ifine, Icoarse, D, U) for diffusion training. Uses NeRF duos for major data, plus Gaussian noise augmentation. """ dataset = [] # Major dataset: 200 scenes from Hypersim and CO3D (~20k images) scenes = loadscenes(['Hypersim', 'CO3D']) for scene in scenes: # Train coarse NeRF on 1/5 images coarseimgs = scene.images[:len(scene.images)//5] coarsemodel = trainnerf(coarseimgs, scene.poses) coarsergb, coarsedepth = render(coarsemodel, scene.poses) # Train fine NeRF on all images finemodel = trainnerf(scene.images, scene.poses) finergb = render(finemodel, scene.poses) # Compute uncertainty for each view for i in range(len(scene.poses)): viewA = scene.poses[i] viewBidx = findnearestinputview(viewA, scene.poses) imgB = scene.images[viewBidx] warpedB = warpimage(imgB, coarsedepth[i], viewBidx, i, scene.poses) uncertainty = (warpedB - coarsergb[i]) 2 dataset.append((finergb[i], coarsergb[i], coarsedepth[i], uncertainty)) # Data Augmentation: Add Gaussian noise (std=0.3) to 60k Hypersim images noisyimages = addgaussiannoise(scene.images, std=0.3) for i in range(len(scene.images)): # Pair noisy image with original depth; uncertainty is not fed for augmented data dataset.append((scene.images[i], noisyimages[i], scene.depths[i], None)) return dataset def computeuncertainty(imgB, depthA, rgbA, viewA, viewBidx, poses): """Computes UA = (I{B->A} - IA)^2 using epipolar warping.""" K = getcameramatrix(poses) RBA = computerelativepose(poses[viewBidx], poses[0]) warpedB = warpimage(imgB, depthA, viewBidx, 0, poses) uncertainty = (warpedB - rgbA) 2 return uncertainty def warpimage(img, depth, viewsrcidx, viewdstidx, poses): """Warp source image to destination using depth and relative pose.""" K = getcameramatrix(poses) Rsrcdst = computerelativepose(poses[viewsrcidx], poses[viewdstidx]) H = K @ Rsrcdst @ np.linalg.inv(K) # Standard perspective warp using bilinear interpolation over warped coordinates h, w = img.shape[:2] coords = np.meshgrid(np.arange(w), np.arange(h)) coords = np.stack([coords[0].flatten(), coords[1].flatten(), np.ones(wh)], axis=1).T warpedcoords = H @ coords warpedcoords = warpedcoords[:2,:] / warpedcoords[2,:] # Bilinear interpolation omitted for brevity; standard graphics operation return np.zeroslike(img) def finetunediffusion(model, quartets): """Fine-tunes diffusion model using ControlNet objective.""" for batch in quartets: Icoarse, D, U, s = batch z = encodetolatent(Icoarse) t = np.random.randint(1, 1000) epsilon = np.random.normal(0, 1, z.shape) zt = addnoise(z, epsilon, t) prednoise = model.predictnoise(zt, t, Icoarse, D, U, s) loss = np.mean((epsilon - prednoise) 2) updatediffusionparameters(model, loss) def captionimage(rgb): """Generates text prompt s0 using pre-trained captioning network.""" return pretrainedcaptioner(rgb) def optimizetextualinversion(images, coarsergb): """Optimizes shared latent text embedding s via textual inversion.""" sstar = initializerandomembedding() for step in range(100): loss = computetextualinversionloss(sstar, images, coarsergb) sstar = updateembedding(sstar, loss) return sstar def concatenateembeddings(s0, sstar): """Concatenates embeddings to form composite feature s = [s0, s].""" return np.concatenate([s0, sstar], axis=-1) def computelpipsbatch(pseudoobs, referenceimages): """Computes LPIPS perceptual similarity metric.""" scores = [] for ref in referenceimages: # Standard LPIPS metric computation score = lpipsmetric(pseudoobs, ref) scores.append(score) return np.mean(scores) def initializenerf(images, poses): """Initializes NeRF/3DGS parameters theta [Parent].""" return NeRFModel(poses=poses) def renderbatchfromnerf(model, images, poses): """Renders RGB, depth, transmittance for a batch [Parent].""" return model.render(poses) def computerenderingloss(rendered, images): """Computes photometric reconstruction loss Lrender [Parent].""" return np.mean((rendered.rgb - images) 2) def updatenerfparameters(model, loss): """Gradient descent step for NeRF parameters theta [Parent].""" model.optimizer.step(loss) def samplenovelview(poses): """Randomly samples viewpoint within bounding box of input views.""" bounds = computeboundingbox(poses) return randompointinbox(bounds) def renderfromnerf(model, view): """Renders single view RGB and depth [Parent].""" return model.render(view) def findnearestinputview(viewA, poses): """Finds index of input view B closest to A.""" distances = [np.linalg.norm(viewA - p) for p in poses] return np.argmin(distances) def getcameramatrix(poses): """Extracts intrinsic camera matrix K.""" return poses[0].K def computerelativepose(viewB, viewA): """Computes R{B->A} from camera poses.""" return viewA.R @ viewB.R.T def addgaussiannoise(images, std): """Adds Gaussian noise with given standard deviation.""" noise = np.random.normal(0, std, images.shape) return np.clip(images + noise, 0, 1) def loadscenes(datasetnames): """Loads scenes from specified datasets.""" return [Dataset(name) for name in datasetnames] def trainnerf(images, poses): """Trains NeRF on provided images and poses [Parent].""" model = initializenerf(images, poses) for epoch in range(1000): rendered = renderbatchfromnerf(model, images, poses) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, images) updatenerfparameters(model, loss) return model def render(model, poses): """Renders batch of images and depths [Parent].""" return model.render(poses) def encodetolatent(image): """Encodes image to latent space z using diffusion encoder.""" return pretrainedencoder(image) def addnoise(z, epsilon, t): """Adds noise at diffusion time step t.""" alphat = getalphaschedule(t) return np.sqrt(alphat) z + np.sqrt(1 - alphat) epsilon def getalphaschedule(t): """Returns pre-computed alpha values for time step t.""" return diffusionalphatable[t] def updatediffusionparameters(model, loss): """Gradient descent step for diffusion denoiser epsilontheta.""" model.optimizer.step(loss) def updateembedding(sstar, loss): """Gradient step for textual inversion embedding.""" return sstar - 0.01 np.gradient(loss, sstar) def lpipsmetric(pseudo, ref): """Computes Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity.""" return pretrainedlpipsnetwork(pseudo, ref) def trainfinemodel(model, images, poses): """Trains main NeRF on combined real and pseudo observations.""" for epoch in range(500): rendered = renderbatchfromnerf(model, images, poses) loss = computerenderingloss(rendered, images) updatenerfparameters(model, loss) Discard Rate: 20% of pseudo-observations with the lowest LPIPS similarity are discarded. Coarse NeRF Data: Trained on one-fifth of input images. ControlNet Channels: 5 channels (3 RGB, 1 Depth, 1 Uncertainty). Image Resolution: Randomly cropped to 512 \times 512. Gaussian Noise Std: 0.3, added to 60,000 images for data augmentation. Training Dataset Size: 200 scenes, approx. 20,000 images (Hypersim and CO3D). Captioning Efficacy: Image captioning efficacy diminishes for low-quality images or those with pronounced artifacts. Textual inversion is used to optimize a shared latent text embedding to counteract this. Augmentation Data: When training with noisy RGB-depth data augmentation, uncertainty maps are not fed into the diffusion model. Precision: The uncertainty map calculation relies on accurate depth rendering and precise camera pose alignment (K matrix) to ensure valid epipolar constraints. Time Complexity: The method requires training a coarse NeRF, fine-tuning a diffusion model, and iteratively generating pseudo-observations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the coarse and fine NeRF representations (during dataset generation), the diffusion model, and its ControlNet weights. Performance: On the LLFF dataset with 3 views, Deceptive-NeRF achieves a PSNR of 19.87 and SSIM of 0.436, outperforming PixelNeRF (17.88 PSNR) and MVSNeRF (17.07 PSNR). Deceptive-3DGS achieves 19.95 PSNR. Strengths: Effectively densifies sparse views without requiring dense input data. Enforces 3D consistency via uncertainty maps derived from epipolar geometry. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pre-trained diffusion model. Computationally intensive due to iterative training and diffusion inference. Deceptive-NeRF/3DGS was introduced by Liu et al. in 2023. It addresses the challenge of high-quality novel view synthesis from sparse input views, a common limitation in NeRF and 3DGS applications. The method leverages the power of 2D diffusion models to "rectify" NeRF renderings, hence the term "deceptive," by generating pseudo-observations that are consistent with the input data and 3D geometry. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and inverse rendering, specifically focusing on optimization loops that incorporate external 2D priors. name: Blended-NeRF
head: Zero-Shot Object Generation and Blending in Existing Neural Radiance Fields, Blending-NeRF
body: Blended-NeRF is a framework for editing specific regions of interest (ROI) in an existing Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene using text prompts and a user-defined 3D bounding box. It differs from generative methods that synthesize objects from scratch (e.g., Dream Fields) by initializing a generator NeRF with the weights of the original scene and blending the synthesized content with the original scene using a novel volumetric blending technique. Unlike methods requiring semantic masks or feature decomposition, it operates on any region defined by a 3D box without learning a new feature space. Inputs: Pre-trained NeRF model F{\thetaO}: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigmaO, \mathbf{c}O) representing the original scene. A 3D Region of Interest (ROI) box B localized within the scene. A text prompt y describing the desired edit. A language-image model (e.g., CLIP) with image encoder E{img} and text encoder E{txt}. Outputs: Edited NeRF model F{\thetaE} (implicitly defined by the blending of F{\thetaO} and F{\thetaG}). Rendered views of the edited scene. Data Structures: F{\thetaO}: MLP mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. F{\thetaG}: MLP initialized with weights from F{\thetaO}, mapping (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) to density \sigmaG and color \mathbf{c}G. B: Axis-aligned 3D box defined by min/max coordinates. \gamma(\mathbf{x}): Sinusoidal positional encoding function. Parameters: \alpha: Hyperparameter for distance smoothing blending strength. Controls the weight given to the original scene vs. the edited scene based on distance from the ROI center. Typical values: 0, 0.5, 2, 4, 10. \lambdaT, \lambdaD: Weights for transmittance and depth losses. \tau: Max transmittance threshold for LT. \rho: Max variance threshold for LD. \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability in blending. \phi: Non-negative activation function (e.g., ReLU) for densities. S: Sigmoid function. e{max}: Maximum dimension of the ROI box. \gamma{fov}: Camera field of view angle. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the generator NeRF F{\thetaG} with the weights of the original scene model F{\thetaO}. 2. ROI Localization: Localize the 3D box B inside the scene using a GUI that renders the original NeRF and uses the output depth map for 3D understanding. 3. Training Loop: For each iteration: a. Pose Sampling: Sample a random camera pose around the scene with azimuth/elevation angles (\theta, \phi). The initial distance d from the ROI is calculated as d = \frac{e{max}}{2 \tan(\gamma{fov}/2)}, and the radius is randomly sampled around this value. b. Ray Casting: Cast rays r that pass through the box B. Sample points \mathbf{x}i along these rays. c. Forward Pass (Generator): Query F{\thetaG} for points \mathbf{x}i \in B. For points outside B, set density to zero. d. Rendering: Render the generated content inside the ROI I{ROI} using standard volume rendering on the blended/selected points: C(r) = \frac{\sum{\mathbf{x}i \in B} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) \mathbf{c}i}{\sum{\mathbf{x}i \in B} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai})} where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j < i} \sigmaj \deltaj), if \exists \mathbf{x}i \in r s.t. \mathbf{x}i \in B, else 0. e. Loss Calculation: Similarity Loss: L{sim} = -E{img}(I{ROI})^T E{txt}(y). Transmittance Loss: LT = -\min(\tau, \text{mean}(T(P))), where T(P) is the transmittance of the rendered view from pose P. Depth Loss: LD = -\min(\rho, \sigma^2(D(P))), where \sigma^2(D(P)) is the variance of the disparity map of the rendered view from pose P. Total Loss: L{total} = L{sim} + \lambdaT LT + \lambdaD LD. f. Optimization: Update \thetaG to minimize L{total}. g. Augmentations: Use random backgrounds (Gaussian noise, checkerboard, random Fourier textures) to prevent scene diffusion. Use directional dependent prompts by concatenating view-dependent text to the original caption. Gradually introduce LT and LD during training using an annealing strategy to prevent completely transparent or amorphous scenes. 4. Blending (Post-Training): After training, render the final edited scene by blending the sample points generated by F{\thetaO} and F{\thetaG} along each view ray. a. For points outside B, use F{\thetaO}. b. For points inside B, apply distance smoothing blending: f(\mathbf{x}) = 1 - \exp\left(-\alpha \frac{d(\mathbf{x})}{diag}\right) \sigma{blend}(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sigmaO(\mathbf{x}) + (1 - f(\mathbf{x})) \cdot \sigmaG(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}{blend}(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{c}O(\mathbf{x}) + (1 - f(\mathbf{x})) \cdot \mathbf{c}G(\mathbf{x}) where d(\mathbf{x}) is the Euclidean distance from the ROI center, diag is the box diagonal, and \alpha is the smoothing parameter. c. Render the final view xe using standard volume rendering with the blended densities and colors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Bmin[0], Bmax[1] - Bmin[1], Bmax[2] - Bmin[2]) gammafov = np.radians(60) dinit = emax / (2 np.tan(gammafov / 2)) center = (Bmin + Bmax) / 2.0 for in range(numiterations): r = np.random.uniform(dinit 0.8, dinit 1.2) theta = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi) phi = np.random.uniform(-np.pi/2, np.pi/2) raysorigin, raysdirection = samplecamerapose(r, theta, phi, center) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersection(raysorigin, raysdirection, Bmin, Bmax) validmask = tmax > 0 raysorigin = raysorigin[validmask] raysdirection = raysdirection[validmask] tmin = tmin[validmask] tmax = tmax[validmask] numsamples = 128 tsamples = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, numsamples) samples3d = raysorigin[:, np.newaxis,:] + raysdirection[:, np.newaxis,:] tsamples[:,:, np.newaxis] maskinsideB = (samples3d >= Bmin) & (samples3d <= Bmax) maskinsideB = np.all(maskinsideB, axis=2) pointsG = samples3d[maskinsideB] sigmaG = np.zeros((len(raysorigin), numsamples)) colorG = np.zeros((len(raysorigin), numsamples, 3)) if len(pointsG) > 0: posencG = sinusoidalencoding(pointsG) direncG = sinusoidalencoding(raysdirection[maskinsideB[:, 0]]) sigmaGraw, colorGraw = FthetaG(posencG, direncG) sigmaG[maskinsideB] = sigmaGraw colorG[maskinsideB] = colorGraw phiact = lambda x: np.maximum(x, 0) deltat = np.diff(tsamples, axis=1, prepend=np.zeros((tsamples.shape[0], 1))) deltat = np.maximum(deltat, 1e-8) # During training, only FthetaG is used inside B; outside B density is 0 renderedcolor, Tcum,, = volumerendernormalized(tsamples, sigmaG, colorG) roimask = np.any(maskinsideB, axis=1) IROI = renderedcolor[roimask] imgemb = clipmodel.encodeimage(IROI) txtemb = clipmodel.encodetext(textprompt) Lsim = -np.dot(imgemb, txtemb) meanT = np.mean(Tcum[:, -1]) LT = -np.minimum(tau, meanT) troi = tsamples[roimask] disparity = 1.0 / np.maximum(troi, 1e-8) LD = -np.minimum(rho, np.var(disparity)) Ltotal = Lsim + lambdaT LT + lambdaD LD FthetaG.update(Ltotal) diag = np.sqrt(np.sum((Bmax - Bmin)2)) # Post-training blending would re-cast rays and apply f(x) smoothing return renderedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene Diffusion: Using white/black backgrounds during optimization can cause the scene to populate the background. Flat Geometry: In forward-facing scenes, limited viewing intervals can lead to flat billboard geometry. Transparency: Without regularization, the scene can become completely transparent. Use transmittance loss and annealing. View Consistency: Without pose sampling, the object may not be consistent across views. Directional Dependence: The object may look different in different views. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations, number of rays, and number of samples per ray, similar to standard NeRF training. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the weights of F{\thetaO} and F{\thetaG}. Strengths: Can edit any region using a 3D box without semantic masks; blends naturally with the original scene; supports object insertion, replacement, and blending. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF; relies on CLIP for guidance, which may not always align perfectly with the user's intent; requires tuning of hyperparameters (\alpha, \lambdaT, \lambdaD). When to use: When you want to edit a specific region of an existing NeRF scene using text prompts and a bounding box. When not to use: When you need to generate a new object from scratch without an existing scene (use Dream Fields); when you need semantic segmentation-based editing (use other methods). Blended-NeRF was introduced by Ori Gordon, Omri Avrahami, and Dani Lischinski from The Hebrew University in 2023. It builds on the principles of NeRF [Parent] and Dream Fields, adapting them for local editing of existing scenes. It addresses the challenge of editing local regions in 3D scenes represented by NeRFs, which is difficult due to the implicit nature of the representation. name: NeRF Editing Procedure
head: Feature Field Distillation Editing, DFF-based Editing
body: This procedure enables direct 3D editing of a pre-trained NeRF by decoupling semantic or geometric selection from appearance rendering using a Distilled Feature Field (DFF). It solves the problem of inconsistent multi-view edits by defining a selection probability p for each 3D point based on external feature queries, allowing for precise operations like deletion, colorization, and geometric transformation that respect the underlying scene structure. It sets itself apart from standard optimization-based methods (e.g., RePaint-NeRF) by avoiding iterative gradient descent for the edit itself, instead relying on a deterministic query-and-transform pipeline during rendering. Inputs: Pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}). Pre-trained teacher network (e.g., LSeg or DINO) for feature extraction. User-defined editing parameters: selection threshold \tau (user-defined), colorization function b(\cdot), geometric transformation g(\cdot) and its inverse g^{-1}(\cdot). Ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for each pixel. Outputs: Edited image I'. Data Structures: DFF: A field storing feature embeddings or probability scores p for 3D coordinates. In the source, p is calculated by querying the DFF for each point. The exact internal layout of the DFF is not specified, but it outputs a scalar probability p \in [0, 1] representing the likelihood that coordinate \mathbf{x} matches the editing query. NeRF: Representation storing density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}, queried via f\theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample points \{\mathbf{x}i\} along the ray \mathbf{r} as in standard volume rendering. 2. Feature Query: For each point \mathbf{x}i, query the DFF to obtain the selection probability pi. 3. Selection Decision: Determine if \mathbf{x}i is "selected" by the edit query: if pi > \tau, \mathbf{x}i is selected; otherwise, it is not selected. The source also mentions an alternative mixture approach where results are blended in proportion to p without a threshold, but the primary procedure uses the threshold. 4. Transform Application: For each point \mathbf{x}i, compute the effective density \sigma'i and color \mathbf{c}'i: Case A: Not Selected: Query the vanilla NeRF: (\sigmai, \mathbf{c}i) = f\theta(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}). Set \sigma'i = \sigmai, \mathbf{c}'i = \mathbf{c}i. Case B: Selected: Deletion: Set \sigma'i = 0. Color Editing: Query the vanilla NeRF for (\sigmai, \mathbf{c}i). Apply colorization function b: \mathbf{c}'i = b(\mathbf{c}i). Keep \sigma'i = \sigmai. Translation / Rescaling: 1. Compute deformed coordinate \mathbf{x}0 = g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}i). 2. Query the DFF for \mathbf{x}0 to get probability p0. 3. If \mathbf{x}0 is selected (p0 > \tau): Query NeRF for (\sigma0, \mathbf{c}0) = f\theta(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{d}). Set \sigma'i = \sigma0, \mathbf{c}'i = \mathbf{c}0. 4. If \mathbf{x}0 is not selected: The source does not explicitly define the fallback for the original point \mathbf{x}i in this specific branch. 5. Boundary Mixing: If both \mathbf{x}i and \mathbf{x}0 are selected and have non-zero density (e.g., at object boundaries during deformation): mix colors \mathbf{c}i and \mathbf{c}0 in the ratio of their alphas \alphai and \alpha0. 5. Volume Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering using the modified tuples (\sigma'i, \mathbf{c}'i) along the ray. Formulas: Selection probability: pi = \text{DFF}(\mathbf{x}i). Selection condition: \mathbf{x}i is selected if pi > \tau. Deletion transform: \sigma'i = 0. Color editing transform: \mathbf{c}'i = b(\mathbf{c}i). Geometric transform: \mathbf{x}0 = g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}i). Boundary color mixing: \mathbf{c}'i = \frac{\alphai \mathbf{c}i + \alpha0 \mathbf{c}0}{\alphai + \alpha0} (Derived from "mix their colors... in the ratio of their alphas"). Volume rendering compositing: C = \sumi Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}'i, where Ti = \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) and \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigma'i \Delta t} (Standard volume rendering formula). Parameters: Selection threshold \tau: User-defined. Colorization function b(\cdot): User-defined. Geometric transformation g(\cdot): User-defined. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: The threshold \tau requires careful tuning to avoid partial selection artifacts. Boundaries: At deformation boundaries where both \mathbf{x}i and \mathbf{x}0 are selected, color mixing is applied to prevent visual discontinuities. Degenerate input: If g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}i) falls outside the training domain, the NeRF query may produce unreliable \sigma0, \mathbf{c}0. The source does not specify behavior when \mathbf{x}0 is not selected during translation/rescaling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendereditedray(rayo, rayd, nerfmodel, dffmodel, transformginv, colorfuncb, threshold, isdeletion=False, numsamples=64, near=0.0, far=1.0): # 1. Ray Sampling tvals = [near + (far - near) i / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] points = [(rayo[0] + t rayd[0], rayo[1] + t rayd[1], rayo[2] + t rayd[2]) for t in tvals] dist = (far - near) / (numsamples - 1) densities = [] colors = [] for x, t in zip(points, tvals): # 2. Feature Query p = dffmodel(x) # 3. Selection Decision issel = p > threshold if not issel: # Case A: Not Selected sigma, c = nerfmodel(x, rayd) densities.append(sigma) colors.append(c) else: # Case B: Selected if isdeletion: # 4-A: Deletion densities.append(0.0) colors.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) else: # Query original point for base values sigmaorig, corig = nerfmodel(x, rayd) # Check for geometric transformation (Translation/Rescaling) xdeformed = transformginv(x) pdeformed = dffmodel(xdeformed) isdeformedselected = pdeformed > threshold if isdeformedselected: # Get values from deformed location sigmadef, cdef = nerfmodel(xdeformed, rayd) # 4'-C: Boundary Mixing alphaorig = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmaorig dist) alphadef = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmadef dist) totalalpha = alphaorig + alphadef if totalalpha > 0: worig = alphaorig / totalalpha wdef = alphadef / totalalpha cfinal = [worig corig[j] + wdef cdef[j] for j in range(3)] else: cfinal = corig densities.append(sigmadef) colors.append(cfinal) else: # Deformed point not selected. Fallback not specified in sources. # Use original point values. if colorfuncb is not None: cfinal = colorfuncb(corig) else: cfinal = corig densities.append(sigmaorig) colors.append(cfinal) # 5. Volume Rendering accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] T = 1.0 for sigma, c in zip(densities, colors): alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma dist) weight = T alpha accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + weight c[j] for j in range(3)] T = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor A technique to edit specific objects within a NeRF without altering the background, using 2D segmentation masks propagated across views via depth information. It solves the problem where existing methods induce simultaneous changes in both background and foreground, contradicting user intentions to alter distinct objects. It sets itself apart by using depth-based reprojection to ensure multi-view consistency of the segmentation mask, allowing exclusive modification of the target instance while leaving the background intact. Choose it when precise object-level editing is required without background alteration. A strategy to efficiently warm up the editing process by blending edits directly before the entire process, accelerating editing while preserving consistency. It sets itself apart by projecting a single edited view onto all other views using a simple pixel-wise blend formula. Choose it to speed up the initial convergence of view-consistent editing. An application where scene editing is performed by setting the density inside a proposal bounding box (generated by a Region Proposal Network) to zero when rendering. It sets itself apart by leveraging 3D object detection proposals for direct density suppression. Choose it for object removal tasks guided by detection frameworks. A simple 3D inpainting method that trains a NeRF using pixel reconstruction loss, guided by 2D inpainted images generated by an MST inpainting network. It sets itself apart by relying on standard pixel loss rather than DFF-based selection or iterative optimization. Choose it for straightforward inpainting tasks where 2D priors are sufficient. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the additional DFF query per sample point. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the DFF in addition to the NeRF. The size of the DFF is not given in the sources. Strengths: Deterministic editing; no iterative optimization required for the edit itself; supports complex transformations (translation, colorization). Limitations: Relies on the quality of the teacher network (LSeg/DINO) for accurate selection; threshold tuning required. When to use: When precise, non-iterative editing of specific semantic or geometric regions is required. When not to use: When iterative optimization with external diffusion priors is preferred for high-fidelity generation. The method originates from "Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation". It utilizes pre-trained teacher networks like LSeg (ViT-L/16 image encoder, CLIP’s ViT-B/32 text encoder) and DINO to generate feature maps for distillation. name: Local Editing via SAM and Depth Propagation
head: Depth-propagated Mask Editing, SAM-based NeRF Editing
body: A technique to edit specific objects within a NeRF without altering the background, using 2D segmentation masks propagated across views via depth information. It solves the problem where existing methods induce simultaneous changes in both background and foreground, contradicting user intentions to alter distinct objects. It sets itself apart by using depth-based reprojection to ensure multi-view consistency of the segmentation mask, allowing exclusive modification of the target instance while leaving the background intact. Builds on NeRF Editing Procedure. Inputs: A trained NeRF, depth maps for each view, and a user interaction point on a target object in one or more views. Outputs: A modified NeRF where the target object is edited while the background remains unchanged. Data structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initial Segmentation: Employ the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to derive masks encompassing all components within each image. 2. User Selection: Users pinpoint the target instance with a single point to isolate it. 3. Key View Selection: Designate nearly all views as key views to facilitate propagation. 4. Depth-Based Projection: Utilize depth information to project the identified mask across different views progressively. Standard 3D reprojection maps pixels from a source view to a target view using camera intrinsics and extrinsics. 5. Reprojection Check: Continue the projection process as long as the projected mask sufficiently overlaps with the corresponding mask in the current view. 6. Mask Integration: Integrate the wrapped segmentation mask with the segmented masks in the current view. This results in a multi-view consistent segmentation mask set. 7. Editing: Apply the editing operation constrained by the integrated masks to modify only the target object. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Overlap threshold for sufficient overlap is not explicitly defined in the sources. Key view density designates nearly all views as key views, which leads to reduced efficiency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect depth estimation is handled robustly as long as the NeRF is built successfully, demonstrated on glossy surfaces and sparser views. Existing methods often induce simultaneous changes in both background and foreground, contradicting user intentions to alter distinct objects. A grid-based 3D editing method using a 3D mask grid trained on 2D masks from SAM. It introduces a 3D mask grid trained on the 2D masks from SAM to locate the target object accurately. Instead of utilizing SDS, it employs Variational Score Distillation (VSD) along with composited rendering and a coarse-to-fine editing strategy to improve editing quality. Efficiency: Designating nearly all views as key views leads to reduced efficiency. Robustness: The method demonstrates robustness to incorrect depth estimation, handling glossy surfaces and sparse input views (e.g., 20% or 50% of views) effectively. Consistency: It achieves multi-view consistent segmentation, permitting exclusive modification of the target object without changing the background. Originated in ViCA-NeRF (View-Consistency-Aware 3D Editing of Neural Radiance Fields). The method addresses the discrepancy in existing methods that fail to isolate foreground edits from background changes. It builds on the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and leverages depth information for view consistency. name: NeRF-In
body: NeRF-In is a 3D inpainting method that removes undesired objects from a scene by training a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) to match 2D inpainted images generated by a Masked Scene Transformer (MST) network. It differs from sibling methods like Local Editing via SAM and Depth Propagation by relying on a pre-trained 2D inpainting model to provide both color and depth guidance, rather than propagating edits through geometric constraints alone. The method solves the problem of 3D object removal by minimizing pixel reconstruction errors against these 2D guides. Inputs: 1. A pre-trained NeRF model representing the original scene. 2. A set of input images with known camera poses. 3. A single-view annotation (mask) identifying the object to be removed. Outputs: 1. An updated NeRF model representing the scene with the object removed. 2. Inpainted images and depth maps for the input views. Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP-based representation mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Mask: Binary or soft mask indicating the region of interest. Guiding Images: 2D RGB images generated by the MST inpainting network. Guiding Depth: 2D depth maps generated by the MST inpainting network. Steps: 1. Mask Generation: Generate an initial mask for the target object using a one-shot segmentation method. Methods include Mask R-CNN, Segment Anything Model (SAM), or GLIP. This is done from a single-view annotation. 2. 2D Inpainting: Use an inpainting network (specifically the MST network) to generate a guiding RGB image and a guiding depth image for each input view. The inpainting network takes the original image and the mask as input, producing a completed image and corresponding depth for the masked region. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the pixel reconstruction loss between the rendered output of the NeRF and the guiding images. The loss is defined as: L = \sum{v \in V} \| I{\text{rendered}}^v - I{\text{guide}}^v \|1 where V is the set of input views, I{\text{rendered}}^v is the color rendered by the NeRF for view v, and I{\text{guide}}^v is the MST-generated guiding image for view v. The depth guiding loss is also optimized, typically as a similar pixel-wise difference between rendered depth and guiding depth, though the specific weighting is not detailed in the sources. 4. Optimization: Update the NeRF parameters by minimizing the combined color-guiding and depth-guiding losses. The optimization is performed over the input views. Parameters: Inpainting Network: MST. Loss Function: Pixel reconstruction loss (L1 or L2). Segmentation Method: One-shot methods (Mask R-CNN, SAM, GLIP). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: 3D Inconsistency: The method does not fully resolve 3D inconsistencies inherent in the 2D inpainter's output. The 2D inpainting may produce results that are inconsistent across different viewpoints, leading to artifacts in the 3D reconstruction. View Selection: NeRF-In only minimizes the number of views used for optimization but does not inherently select the most consistent views. This can lead to suboptimal results if the inpainted regions are unreliable in certain views. Blurring: The method may suffer from blurring in the inpainted regions. Uses SAM for segmentation and propagates edits via depth consistency rather than relying on a separate 2D inpainting network for guidance. Choose when geometric consistency is prioritized over texture synthesis fidelity. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the optimization steps for the NeRF and the inference time of the MST inpainting network. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Standard NeRF memory requirements plus storage for guiding images and depth maps. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation; leverages powerful 2D inpainting models (MST) for high-quality texture synthesis. Limitations: Struggles with 3D consistency; relies on the quality of the 2D inpainter; does not actively resolve view-dependent inconsistencies. When to use: When high-quality 2D inpainting is available and 3D consistency is secondary or can be tolerated. When not to use: When strict 3D consistency is required or when the 2D inpainter produces perceptually inconsistent results across views. NeRF-In was introduced as a simple 3D inpainting method that trains a NeRF using pixel reconstruction loss guided by 2D inpainted images generated by an MST inpainting network. It builds on the premise that 2D inpainting results can be transferred to 3D scenes. It is often compared to SPIn-NeRF, which improves upon NeRF-In by using perceptual loss and depth supervision. The method is part of the broader field of NeRF-based 3D editing, which aims to remove or modify objects in 3D scenes while maintaining visual coherence. name: NeRF-Art
head: Text-Driven Neural Radiance Fields Stylization
body: NeRF-Art is a text-guided method for stylizing pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that simultaneously alters both the appearance and the 3D geometry of a scene without requiring mesh guidance. It distinguishes itself from prior approaches by introducing a global-local contrastive learning strategy combined with directional constraints, addressing the insufficiency of direct CLIP similarity supervision in ensuring strong style adherence and cross-view consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is 3D position, \mathbf{d} is viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color [Parent]. A target style text prompt T{\text{target}} and a set of negative style text prompts \{T{\text{neg}}^k\}. Output: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta' that render images matching the target style in both texture and geometry. Data Structures: The method operates on the standard NeRF MLP representation [Parent]. No additional explicit data structures (like grids or meshes) are introduced for the stylization process itself, though the method supports mesh extraction from the final \sigma field for evaluation. Optimization Objective: The optimization minimizes a total loss combining photometric reconstruction, a hybrid global-local contrastive style loss, and a weight regularization term. L = L{\text{rec}} + \lambda{\text{style}} L{\text{style}} + \lambda{\text{reg}} L{\text{reg}} where L{\text{rec}} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{\text{style}} is the hybrid global-local contrastive loss based on CLIP embeddings, and L{\text{reg}} is a weight regularization term. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Ray Marching & Rendering: For each camera ray, sample points along the ray and compute transmittance and density using the current NeRF f\theta. Render the image using the standard volume rendering equation. 2. CLIP Embedding Extraction: Pass the rendered image and text prompts through the CLIP image encoder EI and text encoder ET. Extract the target embedding from the target style prompt, and negative embeddings from pre-defined negative style prompts. Extract the rendered embedding from the generated image. 3. Global-Local Contrastive Loss Calculation: The style loss is defined as a combination of global and local contrastive terms. The global contrastive loss measures similarity between the entire rendered image and the target text, while pushing away from negative texts. To ensure uniformity of style over local details, the contrastive constraint is extended to a local framework by dividing the image into patches. 4. Directional Constraint: A directional constraint is applied to control the trajectory and strength of the style, ensuring consistent application across views. 5. Geometry Stylization and Regularization: To support joint geometry and appearance stylization, constraints on the density field are relaxed. Cloudy artifacts and geometry noise arise easily when the density field is transformed during geometry stylization. A weight regularization term is applied to the NeRF weights to suppress these artifacts. 6. Optimization Loop: Update \theta using gradient descent to minimize the combined loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ # Initialize optimizer optimizer = Optimizer(nerfparams, lr=lr) # Pre-compute CLIP text embeddings targetemb = encodetext(targettext) negembs = [encodetext(txt) for txt in negativetexts] for in range(steps): optimizer.zerograd() totalloss = 0.0 renderedimgs = [] for cam in cameras: rays = generaterays(cam) sigma, color = raymarch(nerfparams, rays) img = volumerender(sigma, color, rays.transmittance) renderedimgs.append(img) if refimages: totalloss += lambdarec sum((r - ref)2 for r, ref in zip(renderedimgs, refimages)) styleloss = 0.0 for img in renderedimgs: imgemb = encodeimage(img) simtarget = cosinesimilarity(imgemb, targetemb) simnegs = [cosinesimilarity(imgemb, neg) for neg in negembs] exptarget = exp(simtarget / tau) expnegs = sum(exp(s / tau) for s in simnegs) styleloss += -log(exptarget / (exptarget + expnegs)) # Local contrastive loss divides image into patches and computes similar contrastive terms # styleloss += computelocalcontrastive(renderedimgs, targetemb, negembs, tau) # Directional constraint controls style trajectory and strength across views # styleloss += computedirectionalloss(renderedimgs, targetemb, cameras) totalloss += lambdastyle styleloss totalloss += lambdareg sum(w2 for w in nerfparams) totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfparams Parameters: Negative Prompts: Pre-defined styles used as negative samples. Loss Weights (\lambda{\text{rec}}, \lambda{\text{style}}, \lambda{\text{reg}}): Balances reconstruction, style, and regularization. Temperature (\tau): Controls the sharpness of the contrastive loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cloudy Artifacts: Transforming the density field for geometry stylization can easily introduce cloudy artifacts and geometry noise; handled by weight regularization. Insufficient Style Strength: Direct CLIP similarity supervision is insufficient to ensure desired style strength; addressed with contrastive loss. View Consistency: Without proper constraints, style may vary inconsistently across views; enforced via the global-local framework and directional constraints. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simultaneous geometry and appearance stylization without mesh guidance; strong style adherence via contrastive learning; cross-view consistency. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization to avoid artifacts; dependent on CLIP's style understanding; slower than non-differentiable stylization methods. When to use: When text-driven stylization of both geometry and appearance is needed without mesh data. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical or when mesh-based stylization is preferred. NeRF-Art was introduced by Can Wang, Ruixiang Jiang, Mingming He, Dongdong Chen, and Jing Liao. It addresses the challenge of text-guided NeRF stylization, which is difficult due to the need for simultaneous geometry and appearance transformation. The method builds on the use of large-scale Language-Vision models (CLIP) with NeRF. name: RePaint-NeRF Limitations
head: NeRF editing constraints
body: This article documents the empirical limitations of the RePaint-NeRF method, specifically regarding computational efficiency, geometric fidelity under significant shape changes, and view-angle consistency. It distinguishes these failure modes from the core optimization mechanics detailed in RePaint-NeRF. The method is both time and memory intensive. Generating a high-quality 3D model at the object level requires more than 30 minutes of optimization. Due to these resource demands, the method cannot scale to larger resolutions or larger scenes. Training struggles when the target object shape differs drastically from the source object. In such cases, the edit may be incomplete, failing to fully replace the original geometry. Restricted view angles cause geometric artifacts at image edges during optimization. Objects generated at the periphery may incorrectly combine features from multiple source objects, whereas central regions remain consistent. RePaint-NeRF was introduced in to enable NeRF editing via semantic masks and diffusion model guidance. The limitations described herein were identified during the evaluation of this framework, which uses gradient guidance from a pre-trained 2D diffusion model to regenerate masked parts of the scene. RePaint-NeRF: NeRF Editting via Semantic Masks and Diffusion Models, https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2023/201, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Semantic and Language-Guided Editing
head: Semantic Inpainting, Feature Field Distillation, SDS-based Editing
body: Semantic and Language-Guided Editing modifies neural radiance fields using high-level semantic cues, such as text prompts, language instructions, or semantic masks, rather than relying solely on low-level geometric or photometric constraints. It solves the problem of localized 3D content manipulation—such as object deletion, appearance transformation, or semantic inpainting—while maintaining multi-view consistency and scene integrity. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures is the explicit integration of external semantic priors (e.g., CLIP, LSeg, or diffusion models) into the optimization loop to guide the 3D structure and appearance, rather than merely filling in missing geometry or color. All methods in this family operate on a pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color [Parent]. The core mechanism involves an optimization loop that minimizes a loss function L to update the NeRF parameters \theta (or a subset thereof) [Parent]. The general optimization objective is: L = L{render} + \lambda{guidance} L{guidance} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} where L{render} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{guidance} incorporates external priors (e.g., 2D inpainted images, diffusion model gradients, or semantic features), and L{reg} prevents artifacts or overfitting. Key shared components include: 1. Masking/Selection: A binary or probabilistic mask M or selection field identifies the region of interest (ROI) or occluded areas, typically user-defined via sketching or language instructions. 2. External Priors: Methods rely on 2D priors to guide 3D changes, commonly using diffusion guidance (e.g., Score Distillation Sampling from text-to-image models) or semantic/text features (e.g., CLIP or LSeg) to align rendered features with prompts. 3. View Consistency Enforcement: To prevent inconsistencies across views, methods enforce multi-view constraints through implicit geometrical and photometric priors embodied by the neural network, which automatically propagates single-view edits to all views. DFF enables 3D semantic segmentation and editable novel-view synthesis by distilling features from a pre-trained 2D teacher network (such as LSeg or DINO) into a neural radiance field [12068-dff-decomposing-nerf-for-editing-via-feature-field-distillat.md]. It solves the problem of decomposing scenes into semantic regions for editing, addressing challenges in surface decomposition, volume decomposition, and handling unobserved parts [12068-dff-decomposing-nerf-for-editing-via-feature-field-distillat.md]. Unlike naive usage of NeRF features which are entangled with low-level factors like color or spatial adjacency, DFF explicitly learns semantic similarity, allowing for multi-view consistent editing such as object deletion or appearance transformation [12068-dff-decomposing-nerf-for-editing-via-feature-field-distillat.md]. Choose this method when explicit semantic decomposition is required for editing, rather than just appearance transfer. Unverified code. dim=1)[:,:-1], dim=1) weights = T alpha renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1) renderedfeature = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) feature, dim=1) return renderedcolor, return targetfeatures def computeloss(self, renderedcolor, renderedfeature, targetcolor, targetfeature): lp = F.l1loss(renderedcolor, targetcolor) lf = F.mseloss(renderedfeature, targetfeature) return self.teacher.encodepatch(queryvalue) sims = computedinosimilarity(renderfn, queryvec) probs = (sims > threshold).float() return probs Semantic inpainting allows editing of neural fields through simple interfaces like free-form sketching or language instructions. Given a user-supplied edit in a single reference view, the encoding of a neural field automatically propagates this edit to all views. This propagation promotes consistency between all views thanks to the implicit geometrical and photometric priors embodied by the neural network, preserving the structure of the whole scene. Described in reference [19]. A baseline approach using CLIP for semantic guidance. CLIP provides weak guidance for NeRF optimization; after several epochs, the masked region develops unreasonable textures instead of converging to the target prompt. This method serves as a cautionary example of why diffusion-based guidance (like SDS) is often preferred over simple feature similarity for complex editing tasks. GenN2N introduces a latent distill module to map edited images to edit code vectors. It constrains edit code vectors to a Gaussian distribution through a KL loss. It performs NeRF-to-NeRF translation based on edit codes. It optimizes the translated NeRF using reconstruction loss, adversarial loss, and contrastive loss. CustomNeRF is a method that can utilize images as editing prompts in addition to text prompts. It introduces a local-global iterative editing (LGIE) training scheme to preserve background integrity. It proposes a class-guided regularization to improve consistency across different views. Vox-E is a grid-based method for localized 3D object editing guided by text prompts. It leverages SDS loss for object editing. It introduces a volumetric regularization to preserve the original structure. It optimizes a 3D cross-attention grid based on 2D cross-attention maps. It derives a binary volumetric mask to merge the initial and edited volumetric fields. It enhances the preservation of unaffected areas. Language-Guided Gaussian Editing modifies 2D images with language input using a diffusion model in the masked region generated by a recent 2D segmentation model. It updates attributes of Gaussians again as in the previous NeRF editing work InstructNeRF2NeRF. The concept of semantic inpainting in neural fields was described in reference [19], highlighting the ability to propagate single-view edits to all views via implicit priors. Recent developments in neural rendering have accelerated with synergies to generative approaches such as DreamFusion, which distills 2D generative knowledge to 3D geometry without 3D supervision. Surveys on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS detail the evolution from simple feature distillation (DFF) to complex diffusion-based guidance (SDS, VSD) and grid-based optimizations (Vox-E). name: DFF (Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation)
head: Feature Field Distillation, LSeg-DFF, DINO-DFF
body: DFF enables 3D semantic segmentation and editable novel-view synthesis by distilling features from a pre-trained 2D teacher network (such as LSeg or DINO) into a neural radiance field. It solves the problem that standard NeRF feature spaces are entangled with low-level factors like color or spatial adjacency rather than semantic similarity, making naive decomposition unreliable. Unlike methods that rely on semantic labels during training, DFF achieves this through unsupervised distillation, allowing for zero-shot text-based or image-patch-based editing without retraining the underlying radiance field geometry. Inputs: A set of posed training images Ir with camera poses r. A pre-trained NeRF radiance field f\theta (or a newly trained one). A 2D teacher network (LSeg or DINO) and its associated query mechanism (text prompt for LSeg, image patch for DINO). Outputs: A decomposed NeRF representation consisting of a radiance field (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}) and a feature field \mathbf{f}. Semantic segmentation probabilities for any 3D point or 2D pixel. Data Structures: The implementation uses two primary neural network architectures: 1. Radiance Field MLP (f\theta): Input: Positional encoded coordinate \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Structure: 8 hidden ReLU layers with 256 dimensions. Outputs: Density \sigma: Linear layer (1 output). Color \mathbf{c}: 3 hidden layers (256 dims) \to Linear layer (3 outputs, RGB). Feature \mathbf{f}: 3 hidden layers (256 dims) \to Linear layer (output dim depends on teacher, e.g., 256 for DINO, 128 for LSeg). Note: In the "branch-based" variant, the feature branch shares the first 8 layers with the radiance field. In the "independent" variant, the feature field is a separate MLP. 2. Independent Feature Field MLP (Optional): Used to avoid retraining the radiance field. Structure: 4 hidden layers. Skip connection: Added at the 3rd layer if positional encoding is used. Input: Positional encoded coordinate \mathbf{x} (and optionally \mathbf{d}). Output: Feature vector \mathbf{f}. Positional Encoding: Input coordinate \mathbf{x}: Length 10. Viewing direction \mathbf{d}: Length 4. Skip connections: Applied to the input coordinate. Sampling Strategy: Coarse MLP: Stratified sampling with Nc = 64 points. Fine MLP: Importance sampling with Nf = 128 points (total 192 points including coarse). Distillation Note: Feature fields are trained using coarse sampling to ensure smoothness. Rendering for editing uses fine sampling. Training Phases: 1. Phase 1: Radiance Field Training (Standard NeRF) Train the radiance field f\theta for 200,000 iterations. Loss: Photometric loss Lp (e.g., L1 or SSIM between rendered and input images). Optimizer: Adam, linearly decaying learning rate from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 8 \times 10^{-5}. Regularization: Gaussian noise added to density. Batch size: 1024 rays (Replica) or 2048 rays (others). Image resolution: 320×240 (Replica) or 1008×756 (others). 2. Phase 2: Feature Field Distillation (Finetuning) Initialize feature branch (either attached to radiance field or independent). Remove Gaussian noise from density. Set learning rate to 1 \times 10^{-4}. Train for 5,000 iterations. Loss: L = Lp + \lambda Lf. Note: Feature loss converges significantly faster than photometric loss; thus, short training is sufficient. Excessively increasing \lambda (e.g., \times 10) degrades view synthesis without improving segmentation. Feature Distillation Loss (Lf): The feature loss minimizes the distance between the rendered feature \mathbf{f}{render} and the target teacher feature \mathbf{f}{img}. Lf = \sum{r} \sum{i \in \text{pixels}} \| \mathbf{f}{render}(r, i) - \mathbf{f}{img}(Ir, r, i) \|^2 Where: \mathbf{f}{img}(Ir, r, i) is the feature map from the teacher network for image Ir at pixel i. Teacher feature maps are resized to the original image size to match the NeRF pixel grid. \mathbf{f}{render} is obtained by volume rendering the feature field \mathbf{f} along the ray, similar to color rendering: \mathbf{f}{render} = \sum{j=1}^{N} Tj (1 - \alphaj) \mathbf{f}j where Tj is the accumulated transmittance and \alphaj is the opacity at sample j. Semantic Probability Calculation: To perform segmentation or editing, the probability p that a 3D point (or rendered pixel) belongs to a query is computed differently for LSeg and DINO. 1. LSeg (Text Query): Encode text label t using LSeg text encoder to get \mathbf{t}{vec}. Compute cosine similarity between rendered feature \mathbf{f}{render} and \mathbf{t}{vec}. Probability p is derived via softmax over all possible labels (Equation 22 in). 2. DINO (Image Patch Query): Select a query patch from an image. Compute patch feature \mathbf{q} by averaging DINO features of all pixels in the patch. Compute cosine similarity between \mathbf{f}{render} and \mathbf{q}. Hard Decomposition: If similarity > \tau (threshold), p=1; else p=0. Note: DINO does not use softmax with negative queries; it uses direct thresholded cosine similarity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies): """Standard sine/cosine positional encoding.""" # x: [B, D], returns [B, D 2 numfrequencies] scales = torch.tensor([2 (i / numfrequencies) for i in range(numfrequencies)], device=x.device) x = x.unsqueeze(-1) scales.unsqueeze(0) x = torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1) return x class RadianceMLP(nn.Module): """8 hidden layers (256 dims), ReLU. Outputs sigma, color, feature.""" def init(self, hiddendim=256): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(8)]) self.sigmalayer = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1) self.colorlayers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(3)]) self.colorout = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3) self.featurelayers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(3)]) self.featureout = nn.Linear(hiddendim, 128) # Matches LSeg/DINO typical dims def forward(self, xpe, dpe): h = xpe for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = F.relu(layer(h)) if i < 3: # Skip connections at first 3 layers h = torch.cat([h, xpe], dim=-1) sigma = self.sigmalayer(h) c = h for layer in self.colorlayers: c = F.relu(layer(c)) color = self.colorout(c) f = h for layer in self.featurelayers: f = F.relu(layer(f)) feature = self.featureout(f) return sigma, color, feature class IndependentFeatureMLP(nn.Module): """4 layers, skip connection at 3rd if PE used.""" def init(self, hiddendim=256): super().init() self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim) for in range(4)]) def forward(self, xpe): h = xpe for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = F.relu(layer(h)) if i == 2: # Skip at 3rd layer h = torch.cat([h, xpe], dim=-1) return h class DFF: def init(self, teachertype='LSeg', useindependentfeature=False, featuredim=128): self.teachertype = teachertype self.useindependentfeature = useindependentfeature self.radiancemlp = RadianceMLP() if useindependentfeature: self.featuremlp = IndependentFeatureMLP() self.teacher = self.loadteacher(teachertype) self.optimizer = None self.lr = 1e-4 self.lambdaf = 1.0 self.threshold = 0.5 # Default for DINO hard decomposition def loadteacher(self, name): # Placeholder for actual LSeg/DINO model loading. # Returns an object with.encodeimage(img),.encodetext(txt),.encodepatch(patch) return None def encodeinput(self, x, d): xpe = torch.cat([x, positionalencoding(x, 10)], dim=-1) dpe = positionalencoding(d, 4) return xpe, dpe def renderray(self, origins, directions, sigmacoarse, colorcoarse, featcoarse, sigmafine, colorfine, featfine, near=0.0, far=1.0): """Standard differentiable volume rendering.""" # Standard ray marching implementation # Compute deltas, alphas, transmittance, weights for coarse and fine # Return rendered color, feature, and accumulated transmittance # For brevity, assumes a standard differentiable renderer is integrated here. # The formula matches: frender = sum(Tj (1 - alphaj) fj) pass def getteacherfeatures(self, image): rawfeatures = self.teacher.encodeimage(image) targetfeatures = F.interpolate(rawfeatures, size=image.shape[2:], mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) return targetfeatures def computeloss(self, renderedcolor, renderedfeature, targetcolor, targetfeature): lp = F.l1loss(renderedcolor, targetcolor) lf = F.mseloss(renderedfeature, targetfeature) return lp, lf def trainstep(self, images, poses, optimizer): optimizer.zerograd() # Sample rays from images/poses origins, directions, targetcolors = self.samplerays(images, poses, batchsize=1024) # Get teacher features aligned with rays teacherfeats = self.getteacherfeatures(images) targetfeats = self.interpolateteacherfeatures(teacherfeats, origins, directions) # Encode inputs xpe, dpe = self.encodeinput(origins, directions) # Coarse pass (used for feature training) sigmac, colorc, featc = self.radiancemlp(xpe, dpe) # Hierarchical sampling: use coarse weights to sample fine points # Then fine pass xpefine, dpefine = self.encodeinput(fineorigins, finedirections) sigmaf, colorf, featf = self.radiancemlp(xpefine, dpefine) # Render renderedcolor, renderedfeature = self.renderray( origins, directions, sigmac, colorc, featc, sigmaf, colorf, featf) lp, lf = self.computeloss(renderedcolor, renderedfeature, targetcolors, targetfeats) loss = lp + self.lambdaf lf loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() def editscene(self, querytype, queryvalue, renderfn): if querytype == 'text': queryvec = self.teacher.encodetext(queryvalue) probs = self.computelsegprobability(renderfn, queryvec) elif querytype == 'patch': queryvec = self.teacher.encodepatch(queryvalue) sims = self.computedinosimilarity(renderfn, queryvec) probs = (sims > self.threshold).float() return probs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Loss Weight: Excessively increasing the feature loss weight (\lambda \times 10) hurts view synthesis quality without improving segmentation. Sampling Mismatch: Using fine sampling for training feature fields introduces high-frequency artifacts. Coarse sampling is preferred for smooth decomposition. Naive NeRF Features: Using hidden layers of the original NeRF (e.g., the 8th layer) for decomposition is not robust; selections leak to regions with similar color/geometry but different semantics. Deletion Artifacts: Deleting foreground objects may leave floating artifacts and blurred volumes in the far distance behind the object. Training Duration: Feature loss converges much faster than photometric loss; 5K iterations is sufficient for distillation. Time Complexity: Distillation phase is short (5,000 iterations) compared to initial training (200,000 iterations). Memory Complexity: Branch-based DFF adds minimal overhead (3 extra layers). Independent DFF adds a separate small MLP (4 layers). Performance: DFF achieves 3D semantic segmentation performance comparable to or better than supervised sparse 3D convolution models (e.g., MinkowskiNet). Strengths: Enables zero-shot text-based and image-patch-based editing. Multi-view consistent results for deletion/extraction, unlike 2D inpainting baselines (LaMa). Independent feature field allows adding semantics to existing NeRFs without retraining geometry. Limitations: Struggles with "volume decomposition" smoothness if fine sampling is used for training features. Deletion can leave artifacts in occluded background regions. Original NeRF features are not semantically meaningful. DFF was introduced in the paper "Decomposing NeRF for Editing Via Feature Field Distillation". It addresses the limitations of editable NeRFs, which previously struggled with surface decomposition, volume decomposition, and estimating unobserved parts. The method leverages pre-trained 2D vision-language models (LSeg) and self-supervised models (DINO) as teachers to distill semantic information into the 3D field, bypassing the need for 3D semantic labels during training. name: InNeRF360
body: InNeRF360 is a 3D scene inpainting and editing method that reconstructs missing or edited regions in a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by combining multiview-consistent 2D priors with 3D diffusion guidance. It addresses the problem of generating geometrically and photometrically consistent content for occluded or removed objects by first establishing a coherent 2D inpainting across all views and then refining the 3D representation. It differs from direct 3D optimization methods by decoupling the generation of plausible content (via 2D inpainting) from the 3D reconstruction, using 3D diffusion priors primarily to eliminate artifacts and enforce consistency rather than generating the primary geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), a set of input images \{Ii\}, and binary masks \{Mi\} indicating regions to be inpainted or edited. Outputs: An updated NeRF parameter set \theta' representing the scene with inpainted content. Data Structures: Segmentation Mask: A binary mask M{2D} derived from 2D segmentation, refined for view consistency. Inpainted Image: A 2D image I{inpaint} generated by a 2D inpainting model. NeRF Parameters: \theta, typically including MLP weights for density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Steps: 1. Multiview Consistent Segmentation Initialization: Initialize segmentations for the target regions using the Segment Anything Model (SAM). Refine these segmentations using depth-warping to ensure they are consistent across multiple views, producing a set of view-consistent 2D masks \{Mi^{\text{consistent}}\}. 2. Multiview 2D Inpainting: Apply a 2D image inpainting model to each view i using the consistent masks \{Mi^{\text{consistent}}\} and the original images \{Ii\}. Generate inpainted images \{Ii^{\text{inpaint}}\} that fill the masked regions with plausible content. 3. NeRF Training from Inpainted Views: Train a new NeRF or fine-tune the existing one using the inpainted images \{Ii^{\text{inpaint}}\} as supervision. The optimization minimizes a photometric reconstruction loss on the inpainted regions to establish the initial geometry and appearance. 4. 3D Diffusion Prior Fine-tuning: Fine-tune the NeRF using 3D diffusion priors to eliminate artifacts and ensure 3D consistency. This involves computing gradients from a 3D diffusion model (typically via Score Distillation Sampling) to guide the NeRF parameters \theta towards distributions consistent with 3D generative priors. Formulas: The exact loss formulation is not given in the sources. The optimization follows the shared parent objective L = L{\text{render}} + \lambda{\text{guidance}} L{\text{guidance}} + \lambda{\text{reg}} L{\text{reg}}, where L{\text{render}} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{\text{guidance}} incorporates the 3D diffusion priors, and L{\text{reg}} prevents artifacts or overfitting NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures. Parameters: \lambda{\text{guidance}}: Weight for the diffusion prior loss. Not given in the sources. Learning rate for NeRF optimization. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inconsistency in 2D Inpainting: If the 2D inpainter generates inconsistent content across views, the initial NeRF training may produce geometric artifacts. Over-smoothing: Heavy reliance on diffusion priors may lead to over-smoothed or hallucinated details that deviate from the original scene's texture. Mask Accuracy: The quality of the final inpainting is heavily dependent on the accuracy of the initial SAM segmentation and the subsequent depth-warping refinement. ViCA-NeRF is a method for 3D editing that enhances efficiency and consistency by operating in the latent domain. It differs from standard NeRF editing by focusing on local editing via latent domain refinement rather than direct field optimization. It builds upon IN2N with improvements, initializing and refining a NeRF model within the latent domain using a refinement adapter with residual and self-attention mechanisms. It focuses on editing key views with IP2P, projecting them onto other views, and subsequently refining them with a blending model. It iteratively updates the training set with edited latents and employs a delta module for targeted editing guided by prompts. Time Complexity: The method involves multiple stages: SAM segmentation, depth-warping, 2D inpainting, NeRF training, and 3D diffusion fine-tuning, making the overall process computationally intensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF parameters, intermediate rendered images, and potentially latent representations if latent-domain optimizations are used. Strengths: Produces visually plausible and consistent inpainted content by leveraging strong 2D priors and refining with 3D consistency checks. Limitations: Computationally expensive. Relies on the quality of 2D inpainting, which may struggle with complex occlusions or lack of texture. The 3D diffusion prior may introduce artifacts if not tuned correctly. When to use: When high-quality inpainting of missing regions in a NeRF is required, and computational resources are available for multi-stage optimization. When not to use: For real-time applications or when strict geometric fidelity to the original scene (without generative hallucination) is critical. The method is described in a survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS. It represents a trend in 3D editing that combines 2D generative models with 3D scene representations to achieve high-quality results. The pipeline builds on earlier works like IN2N and incorporates advancements in multiview consistency and diffusion priors.
