name: Diffusion-guided editing
body: Diffusion-guided editing modifies pre-trained NeRFs by leveraging 2D text-to-image diffusion models as external priors to guide 3D appearance and geometry changes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by either iteratively updating the training dataset with diffusion-edited views [14365-repaint-nerf.md] or directly backpropagating photometric losses from edited renders to update NeRF parameters [15089-instruct-nerf2nerf-optimization.md], rather than relying solely on semantic masks or geometric constraints. This family builds on NeRF Editing and Inpainting Procedures. Iteratively alternates between editing input images with a diffusion model and retraining the NeRF on the updated dataset to propagate 2D edits into 3D space while preserving view consistency [14365-repaint-nerf.md]. Choose when scene integrity and multi-view consistency are prioritized over direct gradient guidance. Directly backpropagates photometric loss between rendered views and InstructPix2Pix-edited views to update NeRF parameters without iterative dataset replacement [15089-instruct-nerf2nerf-optimization.md]. Choose for instruction-based editing where classifier-free guidance weights control edit strength, accepting subjective termination due to stochastic diffusion outputs. Employs a per-scene customization latent diffusion model to generate inpainted images and iteratively updates the training set. It incorporates a masked patch-based adversarial training strategy with adversarial loss and discriminator feature matching losses to refine results, using a pixel-level regression loss for reconstruction. Diffusion-guided editing emerged to address inconsistencies when applying 2D edits to 3D scenes independently. Recent advancements increasingly explore inpainting techniques on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) due to its rendering efficiency and high-quality reconstruction, while methods like MALD-NeRF refine results through adversarial training and iterative dataset updates. A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: RePaint-NeRF
head: Iterative DU, Iterative Dataset Update
body: RePaint-NeRF is a framework for editing 3D content in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) using text prompts by leveraging a pre-trained diffusion model to guide changes in designated 3D content, ensuring view consistency and scene integrity. It operates by iteratively alternating between two phases: (1) editing the 'dataset' of NeRF input images using an image-conditioned diffusion model, and (2) updating the underlying 3D representation (NeRF) to incorporate the edited images through standard NeRF training. This iterative process allows for the gradual percolation of diffusion priors into the 3D scene, resolving inconsistencies that arise from applying 2D edits independently to each view. It builds on Diffusion-guided editing by using an iterative dataset update scheme rather than direct gradient-based guidance (like SDS) for the NeRF parameters. RePaint-NeRF consists of two distinct stages: Semantic Mask Extraction and Text-to-3D Content Editing. The method takes a pre-captured NeRF scene, its source data (images, camera poses, calibration), and a natural-language instruction as input, and produces an edited NeRF and edited input images. Inputs: Pre-trained NeRF model f\theta (typically Instant-NGP or Nerfacto). Training dataset: Set of images I^0v, camera poses, and calibration parameters (typically from COLMAP). Text instruction cT (e.g., "turn him into Albert Einstein"). Optional: Background prompt c{BGT} (e.g., "leaves" if editing a rose). Outputs: Edited NeRF parameters \theta. Edited dataset images I^iv. NeRF Model: Instant-NGP [Müller et al., 2022] based on multi-resolution hash grid structure. Stores color C and density \sigma [Parent]. Semantic Feature Field: A view-independent feature field s: \mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{f}, where \mathbf{f} is a high-dimensional vector with semantic information. Feature Map: Rendered feature map FI of size H \times W \times 512. Depth Map: Size H \times W \times 1, normalized to range [0, 1]. Mask: Binary mask I{mask}^{H \times W \times 1}. Dataset: List of images I^0v cached separately to serve as conditioning signals. The goal is to extract a view-consistent semantic mask for the target object. 1. Feature Distillation: Distill supervised semantic features from a pre-trained CLIP model using LSeg [Li et al., 2022]. Interpolate all feature maps to size H \times W \times 512. 2. Depth Supervision: Predict rough depth from monocular images using MiDAS [Ranftl et al., 2022]. 3. Optimization: Optimize the feature network s and NeRF parameters to minimize: L{\text{first-stage}} = L{\text{color}} + \lambda{\text{feature}} L{\text{feature}} + \lambda{\text{depth}} L{\text{depth}} where L{\text{color}} is the standard photometric loss, L{\text{feature}} aligns rendered features with CLIP features, and L{\text{depth}} aligns rendered depth with MiDAS predictions: L{\text{depth}} = \sum{r \in R} (D(r) - \hat{D}(r))^2 where D(r) is the depth predicted by MiDAS and \hat{D}(r) is the depth predicted by NeRF. 4. Training Settings: Use Adam optimizer with learning rate 1e-2 and batch size 4096 for 2000 steps. 5. Mask Generation: Render the feature map FI. Compute the mask using a selected patch feature F{\text{patch}} (mean feature of the selected patch) and a similarity function Sim (e.g., cosine similarity) with threshold \alpha: I{mask}^{H \times W \times 1} = 1(Sim(F{\text{patch}}, FI) > \alpha) Patch features are preferred over text features for more accurate segmentation with higher thresholds. The goal is to modify the masked area to conform to the text prompt while preserving the unmasked area and filling "black holes" (previously occluded regions exposed by the edit). 1. Base NeRF Training: Train the NeRF on the original dataset to establish a base model. Use Adan optimizer with learning rate 1e-3 decaying to 1e-4 and batch size 1. Train for 3000 steps. 2. Iterative Update Loop: Alternate between image updates and NeRF updates for up to 10,000 steps (or 30k total iterations in some implementations). Image Update (Editing): For a viewpoint v, edit the current render I^iv using InstructPix2Pix. Inputs: Conditioning image cI = I^0v (original unedited image), text instruction cT, and noisy input zt. Noise: zt is a noised version of I^iv, defined as a linear combination of \mathcal{N}(0,1) and z0 = E(I^iv), following SDEdit. Noise Level: t is chosen randomly from [t{\min}, t{\max}] = [0.02, 0.98]. Sampling: Use DDIM sampling with a fixed number of steps s=20. Output: I^{i+1}v \leftarrow U\theta(I^iv, t; I^0v, cT). Update Dataset: Replace the original image with the edited one: Dataset[v] = I^{i+1}v. NeRF Update: Train the NeRF on a set of random rays sampled from the entire updated dataset (mix of old cached images and newly updated images). Loss: L{\text{render}} (L1 and LPIPS losses). Additional Losses for Masked Region: L{\text{repaint}} = \lambda{\text{unmask}} L{\text{unmask}} + \lambda{\text{clip}} L{\text{clip}} Unmasked Color Loss: Preserves the unmasked region to prevent unwanted diffusion changes: L{\text{unmask}} = \sum{r \in R} (C(r){\text{unmask}} - \hat{C}(r){\text{unmask}})^2 where C(r){\text{unmask}} = C(r) \times 1(I{mask} < 0.5) and \hat{C}(r){\text{unmask}} = \hat{C}(r) \times 1(I{mask} < 0.5). CLIP Loss: Guides the filling of "black holes" (exposed unseen parts) by encouraging similarity with the background prompt: L{\text{clip}} = -Sim(ZI, Z{BGT}) where ZI is the latent feature of the rendered image I and Z{BGT} is the latent feature of the background prompt encoded by CLIP. Training Settings: Adan optimizer, learning rate 1e-3 decaying to 1e-4, batch size 1. Train for 10,000 steps. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def SampleRays(images, poses): return [(img, pose) for img, pose in zip(images, poses)] def CosineSimilarity(a, b): return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) np.linalg.norm(b)) def MeanFeature(patch): return np.mean(patch, axis=(0, 1)) def GradientStep(params, loss, lr=1e-3): return params - lr np.gradient(loss, params) def AddNoise(image, t): return np.sqrt(1-t) image + np.sqrt(t) np.random.randn(image.shape) def ReconstructImage(color, rays): return color def extractmask(nerf, featurenet, images, poses, depthmodel, clipmodel): featurenet = FeatureNetwork() wnerf = InitializeWeights() for step in range(2000): rays = SampleRays(images, poses) c, d, f = nerf(rays, wnerf) lcolor = np.sum((c - rays[0].color)2) ldepth = np.sum((d - depthmodel(rays[0].image))2) lfeature = np.sum(1 - CosineSimilarity(f, clipmodel(rays[0].image))) wnerf, featurenet = GradientStep(wnerf, featurenet, lcolor + lambdafeature lfeature + lambdadepth ldepth) FI = RenderFeatureMap(nerf, images, poses) Fpatch = MeanFeature(selectedpatch) mask = (CosineSimilarity(Fpatch, FI) > alpha).astype(float) return mask def editnerf(nerf, dataset, textprompt, backgroundprompt, mask): originalimages = dataset.copy() for step in range(3000): rays = SampleRays(dataset, dataset.poses) c = nerf(rays, nerf.weights) loss = np.sum((c - rays[0].color)2) nerf.weights = GradientStep(nerf.weights, loss) for iteration in range(10000): for viewpoint in RandomOrder(dataset.viewpoints): currentrender = nerf.render(viewpoint) t = np.random.uniform(0.02, 0.98) noisyinput = AddNoise(currentrender, t) editedimage = InstructPix2Pix(noisyinput, originalimages[viewpoint], textprompt) dataset[viewpoint] = editedimage for step in range(10): rays = SampleRays(dataset) c = nerf(rays, nerf.weights) lunmask = np.sum((c (mask < 0.5) - rays[0].color (mask < 0.5))2) renderedimg = ReconstructImage(c, rays) zI = clipencoder(renderedimg) zBGT = clipencoder(backgroundprompt) lclip = -CosineSimilarity(zI, zBGT) loss = lambdaunmask lunmask + lambdaclip lclip nerf.weights = GradientStep(nerf.weights, loss) Noise Range: [t{\min}, t{\max}] = [0.02, 0.98]. Denoising Steps: s = 20. Classifier-Free Guidance: sI = 1.5 (image), sT = 7.5 (text). Update Counts: d=1 (image update), n=10 (NeRF updates) per iteration. Max Iterations: 30,000. \lambda{\text{unmask}}: 100. \lambda{\text{clip}}: Not explicitly given, but used to balance change. \lambda{\text{feature}}: Not explicitly given. \lambda{\text{depth}}: Not explicitly given. Black Holes: If the new object is smaller, previously covered areas become unknown. Mitigated by background prompts and CLIP loss. Inconsistency: Early edits may be inconsistent across views. Mitigated by iterative retraining. Drift: Recurrent synthesis can cause drift. Mitigated by conditioning on un-edited images I^0v. Mask Noise: Depth estimation noise can cause imprecise masks. Mitigated by coarse depth supervision. Over-constraint: Too large \lambda{\text{unmask}} restricts diffusion model and slows generation. A scalar weight \lambda{\text{unmask}} applied to the loss function to constrain the unmasked region, preventing unwanted diffusion model changes. When \lambda{\text{unmask}} = 0, no constraints are applied, allowing the diffusion model to alter the background completely. Gradually increasing \lambda{\text{unmask}} enforces shape/appearance preservation. Typical value is 100; too large values severely restrict the diffusion model's generative ability and slow generation speed. A variant that uses Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from Stable Diffusion to guide the masked region instead of CLIP loss. Produces significantly better texture and shape than Mask+CLIP because SDS provides stronger gradient guidance for the diffusion model. A method enhancing editing consistency using cross-attention and editing consistency modules. Uses a cross-attention consistency module (CCM) to harmonize cross-attention maps across all views for coherent edits. Uses an editing consistency module (ECM) to calibrate inconsistent editing outputs by fine-tuning a source-cloned 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and rendering it back to images. Integrates an iterative pattern of editing rendered images and updating the 3DGS for refinement. Uses 3DGS for fast rendering and InfEdit for rapid processing. Time Complexity: High. The process is time-consuming and space-consuming. Memory Complexity: High. Requires storing original images, feature maps, depth maps, and the NeRF model. Performance: Effective for editing appearance, shape, and content in both real-world (LLFF) and synthetic (Blender) datasets. Strengths: View consistency, scene integrity, ability to edit invisible content, user-friendly text interface. Limitations: Time-consuming and space-consuming. RePaint-NeRF was proposed in 2023 by authors from IJCAI-23. It builds on DreamFusion [Poole et al., 2022] for 3D generation and DFF [Kobayashi et al., 2022] for semantic feature extraction. It leverages Stable Diffusion [Rombach et al., 2022] and CLIP [Radford et al., 2021] for guidance. It is used for editing 3D content in NeRF under different text prompts, including editing appearance, shape, and more. name: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF Optimization
head: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF optimization process, NeRF Editing via Diffusion Guidance
body: Instruct-NeRF2NeRF edits pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using natural language instructions by leveraging a 2D text-to-image diffusion model as a guidance signal. It modifies 3D scene appearance without retraining from scratch by rendering a single view, passing it to InstructPix2Pix along with a text instruction and classifier-free guidance weights to generate an edited image, and backpropagating the difference to update the NeRF parameters. Unlike sibling methods such as RePaint-NeRF that use different priors, this approach relies on classifier-free guidance weights to control edit strength and lacks a single convergence point due to the temporally varying nature of diffusion guidance. Inputs: 1. A pre-trained NeRF model f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), typically initialized using the 'nerfacto' model from NeRFStudio trained for 30,000 iterations. 2. A set of input images used for the initial NeRF training. 3. A natural language edit instruction (e.g., "turn the man into a bear"). 4. Classifier-free guidance weights for the diffusion model: sI (image guidance) and sT (text guidance). Outputs: 1. An edited NeRF model with updated parameters \theta that reflects the instruction. The method operates on the standard NeRF representation. The implementation relies on: NeRF Parameters \theta: Stored in the NeRFStudio optimizer state. Diffusion Model State: The InstructPix2Pix model weights and the Stable Diffusion autoencoder state. 1. Initialization: Load the pre-trained NeRF. Re-initialize the optimizers in the NeRF training framework before starting the editing process. 2. View Selection: For each optimization iteration, select a single camera view from the training dataset. 3. Rendering: Render the image \mathbf{I}{\text{render}} from the current NeRF f\theta at the selected view. 4. Diffusion Editing: Pass \mathbf{I}{\text{render}}, the edit instruction, and guidance weights sI, sT to InstructPix2Pix (via the Diffusers library) to generate the edited image \mathbf{I}{\text{edit}}. 5. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the difference between the edited image and the rendered NeRF view to update the NeRF parameters. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–5 for a specified number of iterations. 7. Termination: Stop optimization at a subjective iteration count based on scene size. Photometric Loss: L = \|\mathbf{I}{\text{render}} - \mathbf{I}{\text{edit}}\|^2, where \mathbf{I}{\text{render}} is the rendered image and \mathbf{I}{\text{edit}} is the diffusion-generated edited image. sI (Image Classifier-Free Guidance): Controls the influence of the input image on the edit. Typical range: 1.3 to 1.75. Specific examples: 1.5 (Tree, Tents, Person, Fig 1, Bear), 1.3–1.5 (Fig 7). sT (Text Classifier-Free Guidance): Controls the influence of the text instruction. Typical range: 6.5 to 12.5. Specific examples: 7.5–12.5 (Tree), 10.0 (Tents), 6.5–7.5 (Person, Fig 1, Bear), 6.5–8.5 (Fig 7). Training Iterations: Small scenes (<100 input images): 3,000 to 4,000 iterations. Large scenes (>200–300 input images): 7,000 to 8,000 iterations. Lack of Convergence: Diffusion guidance produces temporally varying images during optimization, so the process lacks a single convergence point. The edit type and strength vary over training, requiring subjective termination. Texture Blurriness: Using Stable Diffusion's autoencoder on input images before NeRF training causes gradual texture blurriness, as the autoencoder creates locally similar but non-3D-consistent textures. Double Faces: Single-view diffusion guidance can cause artifacts like double faces on added objects. View Inconsistency: Edit instructions may only be relevant to certain camera views, causing inconsistent or absent edits in other views. Spatial Manipulation Limits: The method inherits limitations from InstructPix2Pix, including the inability to perform large spatial manipulations or binding between objects. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def instructnerf2nerfedit(nerfmodel, optimizer, cameraparamslist, instruction, sI, sT, maxiterations): # Re-initialize optimizers in the NeRF training framework optimizer.reset() for step in range(maxiterations): # 1. Select a single view idx = random.randint(0, len(cameraparamslist) - 1) cam = cameraparamslist[idx] # 2. Render current NeRF view Irender = nerfmodel.render(cam) # 3. Diffusion Editing: Pass Irender, instruction, and weights to InstructPix2Pix Iedit = instructpix2pixforward(Irender, instruction, sI, sT) # 4. Loss Computation loss = math.sqrt(sum((Irender[i] - Iedit[i]) 2 for i in range(len(Irender)))) # 5. Backpropagation optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfmodel def instructpix2pixforward(image, instruction, sI, sT): # Sources do not provide the InstructPix2Pix forward pass algorithm; uses Diffusers library implementation return image Time: Each iteration requires one NeRF forward pass (rendering) and one diffusion model forward pass (InstructPix2Pix). Total time scales with the number of iterations (3,000–8,000). Memory: Requires memory for the NeRF parameters, the optimizer state, and the InstructPix2Pix/Stable Diffusion model. Small Scenes (<100 images): Subjectively converges in 3,000–4,000 iterations. Large Scenes (>200–300 images): Subjectively converges in 7,000–8,000 iterations. Quality: Edited scenes often contain slightly blurrier textures compared to the original NeRF due to autoencoder effects. Strengths: Allows editing via natural language without 3D annotations. Simple to implement using existing NeRFStudio and Diffusers libraries. Limitations: Cannot perform large spatial manipulations. Struggles with object binding. Single-view guidance leads to multi-view inconsistencies (e.g., double faces). Quality degrades over long optimization runs. When natural language editing is required. When the scene is relatively small or moderate in size. When the user can tolerate subjective termination and potential blurriness. When strict multi-view consistency is required without post-processing. When large spatial transformations (e.g., moving an object from one side of the room to another) are needed. When high-fidelity texture preservation is critical (due to autoencoder blurring). The method was introduced by Zhizhuo Zhou and Shubham Tulsiani in the paper "Instruct-NeRF2NeRF: Editing 3D Scenes with Instructions". The method leverages the Stable Diffusion autoencoder and InstructPix2Pix implementation from the Diffusers library. It was developed to address the limitations of previous NeRF editing methods that required complex 3D priors or manual segmentation. The authors noted that the diffusion guidance produces temporally varying images, distinguishing it from standard NeRF optimization which has a clear convergence point. It is used for 3D scene editing where users provide text instructions to modify the appearance or content of a NeRF reconstruction. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF: Editing 3D Scenes with Instructions, https://instruct-nerf2nerf.github.io/, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Customize your NeRF
head: Local-Global Iterative Editing with Diffusion Priors
body: Customize your NeRF enhances editing quality by integrating 2D diffusion models as generative priors to generate highly detailed and stylized textures. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like RePaint-NeRF and Instruct-NeRF2NeRF Optimization by explicitly alternating between local region fine-tuning and global scene consistency optimization. This approach addresses the limitation of standard NeRF editing where geometric foundations may be flawed, causing edits to appear distorted or inconsistent with the scene’s true 3D structure. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model, a target region for editing, a diffusion model (2D), and a reference image or prompt generated by the diffusion model. Outputs: An edited NeRF model with updated density and color fields reflecting the stylized or detailed local changes while maintaining global coherence. Data Structures: NeRF Model: Standard MLP or grid-based representation storing density (\sigma) and view-dependent color (c) at query points. Diffusion Model: Pre-trained 2D latent diffusion model used for generating high-fidelity texture priors. Numbered Steps: 1. Local Region Definition: Identify the spatial region within the NeRF scene to be edited. 2. Diffusion Prior Generation: Use the 2D diffusion model to generate a reference image for the local region based on user intent (text or image prompt). 3. Local Fine-Tuning: Optimize the NeRF parameters restricted to the local region to match the diffusion-generated image. This involves minimizing the reconstruction error between the rendered local view and the diffusion prior. 4. Global Optimization: Optimize the entire NeRF scene to ensure global consistency. This step aligns the locally edited region with the surrounding unedited geometry and appearance. 5. Iterative Loop: Repeat steps 3 and 4 (Local-Global Iterative Editing) until convergence or a fixed number of iterations is reached. 6. Inverse Optimization (Optional): For integrating new real-world imagery, project new input images into the latent space of the pre-trained NeRF by minimizing reconstruction error. Formulas: Local Loss: Minimize L{local} = || R{local}(\theta{local}) - I{diffusion} ||^2, where R{local} is the rendered image of the local region, \theta{local} are the NeRF parameters for that region, and I{diffusion} is the diffusion-generated image. Global Loss: Minimize L{global} = || R{global}(\theta{global}) - I{reference} ||^2, where R{global} is the rendered image of the full scene and I{reference} is the original or reference view. Total Loss: L{total} = \lambda1 L{local} + \lambda2 L{global}, where \lambda1, \lambda2 are weighting factors. Parameters: Iteration Count: Not given in the sources. Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Loss Weights (\lambda1, \lambda2): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Inconsistency: Diffusion models lack 3D awareness, leading to view-inconsistent details that cause flickering or "painted-on" effects at novel angles. Contradictory Gradients: Stylized features from diffusion models (e.g., non-physical shadows) conflict with physically-based volume rendering, creating contradictory gradients during NeRF optimization. Feature Compatibility: Inverse optimization faces challenges where stylized diffusion features conflict with NeRF latent space physical rendering characteristics. Convergence Speed: The local-global strategy induces contradictory gradient directions during inverse optimization, significantly slowing down convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def customizeyournerf(nerfmodel, diffusionmodel, localregion, prompt, iterations): """ Customizes a NeRF model using diffusion priors via local-global iterative editing. Args: nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF model. diffusionmodel: Pre-trained 2D diffusion model. localregion: Spatial bounds of the region to edit. prompt: Text or image prompt for diffusion model. iterations: Number of local-global iterations. Returns: Edited NeRF model. """ # Generate diffusion prior for the local region diffusionprior = diffusionmodel.generate(prompt, localregion) for i in range(iterations): # Step 1: Local Fine-Tuning # Optimize NeRF parameters within localregion to match diffusionprior localloss = computereconstructionloss( nerfmodel.render(localregion), diffusionprior) optimize(nerfmodel.parameters(localregion), localloss) # Step 2: Global Optimization # Optimize entire NeRF for global consistency globalloss = computereconstructionloss( nerfmodel.renderfullscene(), nerfmodel.renderfullscene() # Reference to original or current state) optimize(nerfmodel.parameters(), globalloss) # Note: Inverse optimization for real-world data integration would be applied here # if new imagery is provided, by projecting into latent space. return nerfmodel Alternates between local region fine-tuning and global scene optimization to balance detail and coherence. Choose when high-fidelity local edits are needed without breaking global structure. Projects new input images into the NeRF latent space by minimizing reconstruction error. Choose when integrating new real-world imagery into an existing NeRF. Time Complexity: Training time increases by 2.3–3.5 times due to the constant switching of optimization targets between local and global scopes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Generates highly detailed, stylized edits on object-centric images. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enhances editing quality with detailed and stylized textures; ensures both fine-grained control and overall coherence. Limitations: Diffusion models lack 3D awareness, leading to view-inconsistent details and flickering; stylized features conflict with physical rendering, causing contradictory gradients and slow convergence. When to Use: When high-fidelity, stylized local edits are required and computational cost is acceptable. When Not to Use: When real-time performance or strict 3D consistency is critical, or when integrating new real-world data with complex stylizations. Customize your NeRF was introduced in [18] (cited in) as a method to enhance editing quality by integrating 2D diffusion models. It addresses the challenge of bridging the domain gap between 2D generative priors and the 3D physical world of NeRF. The method is particularly relevant for applications requiring free-viewpoint navigation, such as UAV applications, where view consistency is critical. name: Inpainting and Object Removal
body: This family removes unwanted objects or fills occluded regions in a pre-trained NeRF representation [Parent]. Unlike standard NeRF training which reconstructs the entire scene from input views, these methods optimize the NeRF parameters to erase specific masked regions while maintaining geometric and photometric consistency across all unmasked views [Parent]. They are distinguished from sibling methods by their reliance on external 2D priors (such as inpainted images or diffusion models) to guide the 3D optimization, rather than relying solely on multi-view geometry or semantic segmentation alone [Parent]. All methods operate on a pre-trained NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) as defined in Parent. The core mechanism involves an optimization loop that minimizes a loss function L to update the NeRF parameters \theta [Parent]. The general optimization objective is: L = L{render} + \lambda{guidance} L{guidance} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} where L{render} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss on visible pixels, L{guidance} incorporates external priors (e.g., 2D inpainted images, diffusion model gradients, or semantic features), and L{reg} prevents artifacts or overfitting. Key shared components include: 1. Masking/Selection: A binary or probabilistic mask M or selection field identifies the region of interest (ROI) or occluded areas [Parent]. 2. External Priors: Methods rely on 2D priors to guide 3D changes, commonly using diffusion guidance (e.g., Score Distillation Sampling from text-to-image models) or semantic/text features (e.g., CLIP or LSeg) to align rendered features with prompts [Parent]. 3. View Consistency Enforcement: To prevent inconsistencies across views, methods enforce multi-view constraints through implicit geometrical and photometric priors embodied by the neural network, which automatically propagates single-view edits to all views [Parent]. The optimization loop proceeds as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizenerfinpainting(nerfmodel, rays, masks, guidancepriors, lambdaguidance, lambdareg, numsteps, lr): """ General optimization loop for NeRF inpainting. Args: nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF MLP. rays: Batch of camera rays with ground truth colors. masks: Binary masks (1 for masked/occluded, 0 for visible). guidancepriors: 2D prior colors for masked regions. lambdaguidance, lambdareg: Loss weights. numsteps: Optimization iterations. lr: Learning rate. Returns: Updated NeRF model. """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(nerfmodel.parameters(), lr=lr) for step in range(numsteps): optimizer.zerograd() # Render current NeRF predictions for the batch renderedcolors = nerfmodel.render(rays) # Photometric loss on visible pixels (mask = 0) lossrender = torch.mean((renderedcolors - rays.gtcolors)2 (1 - masks)) # Guidance loss on masked pixels (mask = 1) lossguidance = torch.mean((renderedcolors - guidancepriors)2 masks) # Regularization loss (e.g., weight decay or density smoothness) lossreg = torch.sum(torch.square(nerfmodel.parameters())) # Total loss loss = lossrender + lambdaguidance lossguidance + lambdareg lossreg loss.backward() optimizer.step() return nerfmodel A framework that removes objects using a single user-drawn mask and 2D color/depth guidance. It jointly minimizes color and depth losses to ensure consistency, avoiding the artifacts of using multiple inconsistent 2D priors. Addresses inconsistency by adaptively switching between 2D inpainting priors and multi-view geometry based on local texture gradients. It is chosen when maintaining multi-view consistency is critical to prevent flickering in textured regions. Uses a single inpainted reference view to guide geometry and appearance via back-projection and a bilateral solver. It ensures view-dependent effects (VDEs) and avoids the quality deterioration seen in methods requiring multiple inpainted views. Selects individual objects using instance labels and manipulates the nerflet structure directly (e.g., copy-and-paste for duplication, deletion for removal) without additional optimization. It supports real-time volume-rendered RGB or depth images at up to 320 × 240 resolution while adjusting object bounding boxes. Performance benchmarks show 31 FPS on 4 A100 GPUs with 64 nerflets, achieving 457 million sample evaluations per second at 192 samples/pixel. When deleting objects, empty scene regions will not carry any density after deletion, as there is nothing there to evaluate. The problem of 3D scene inpainting emerged as NeRFs became popular for novel view synthesis, where removing objects or filling holes required more than just 2D image editing. Early approaches adapted 2D inpainting techniques to 3D by optimizing NeRF parameters. The field has evolved to include diffusion-based guidance and reference-guided consistency. name: NeRF-In Inpainting Optimization
head: Free-Form NeRF Inpainting with RGB-D Priors, NeRF object removal
body: NeRF-In is a framework for removing unwanted objects or retouching undesired regions in a 3D scene represented by a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It operates by optimizing the NeRF parameters \Theta using color and depth guidance derived from 2D images, without requiring category-specific training data or procedures. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on multiple inpainted views or semantic segmentation, NeRF-In primarily uses a single user-drawn mask on one view, transferred to other views via video object segmentation, and guides the optimization with inpainted color and completed depth priors. It sets itself apart by jointly minimizing color and depth losses to ensure both visual plausibility and geometric consistency across views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model F\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}), where \mathbf{x} is a 3D coordinate, \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction, \sigma is volume density, and \mathbf{c} is color. A user-chosen camera position ou and a free-form binary mask Mu drawn on the rendered view Iu = F{\Theta{image}}(ou), where Mu = 1 for pixels outside the masked region (background/valid) and Mu = 0 inside (object to remove). Output: Updated NeRF parameters \tilde{\Theta} that remove the unwanted object in the masked region across all rendered views. Data Structures: NeRF Model F\Theta: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) taking position and direction as input, outputting density and color. The sources specify a batch size of 4,096, 128 sample points for the fine model, and 64 for the coarse model, but do not detail the MLP layer dimensions. Camera Trajectory: A set of K camera positions O = \{os \mid s = 1 \dots K\} sampled along a pre-set trajectory (e.g., LLFF test-set trajectory). Masks: Transferred masks M = \{Ms \mid s = 1 \dots K\} for each sampled view, generated by transferring Mu. Guidance Materials: Guiding color images I^G = \{Is^G \mid s = 1 \dots K\}, where Iu^G is the inpainted user view and Is^G for s \neq u are inpainted sampled views. Guiding depth images D^G = \{Ds^G \mid s = 1 \dots K\}, generated via depth completion. Numbered Steps: 1. User Input: The user selects a view ou from the pre-trained NeRF and draws a mask Mu to specify the region to remove. 2. View Sampling: Sample K camera positions O = \{os \mid s = 1 \dots K\} along a pre-set trajectory. 3. Initial Rendering: Render RGB images Is and depth images Ds for all sampled camera positions os \in O using the current NeRF model F\Theta. 4. Mask Transfer: Transfer the user-drawn mask Mu to the sampled views to generate transferred masks M = \{Ms \mid s = 1 \dots K\} using a video object segmentation method (e.g., STCN). 5. Guidance Generation: Generate guiding color images Is^G for each sampled view using an image inpainting method \rho (e.g., MST inpainting network): Is^G = \rho(Is, Ms). Generate guiding depth images Ds^G using a depth completion method \tau (e.g., Fast Bilateral Solver): Ds^G = \tau(Ds, Ms, Is^G). 6. Optimization Setup: Define the set of all views O{all} and outside views O{out}. In the main framework, set O{all} = \{ou\} (the user-chosen view) and O{out} = O (all other sampled views). 7. Loss Computation: Compute the color-guiding loss L{color}(\Theta) and depth-guiding loss L{depth}(\Theta) (see Formulas below). 8. Parameter Update: Optimize the NeRF parameters \Theta to obtain updated parameters \tilde{\Theta} by minimizing the joint loss L{color}(\Theta) + L{depth}(\Theta) using the Adam optimizer for 50,000 steps. Formulas: Volume Rendering: The expected color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) of a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is computed via numerical quadrature: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} T(ti)(1 - \exp(-\sigma(ti)\deltai))c(ti) where T(ti) = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(tj)\deltaj), N is the number of quadrature points, \deltai = t{i+1} - ti, and c(ti), \sigma(ti) are the color and density at point ti produced by F\Theta. Depth Rendering: The rendered depth Df(\mathbf{o}s) is computed by accumulating density \sigma from ray batches during volume rendering. Similarly, Dc(\mathbf{o}s) is the coarse depth. Color-Guiding Loss: The total color-guiding loss is the sum of the all-view color loss and the outside-view color loss: L{color}(\Theta) = L{all}^{color}(\Theta) + L{out}^{color}(\Theta) where: L{all}^{color}(\Theta) = \sum{\mathbf{o} \in O{all}} \| F{\Theta{image}}(\mathbf{o}) - I{\mathbf{o}}^G \|2^2 L{out}^{color}(\Theta) = \sum{\mathbf{o} \in O{out}} \| (F{\Theta{image}}(\mathbf{o}) - I{\mathbf{o}}^G) \odot M{\mathbf{o}} \|2^2 Here, F{\Theta{image}}(\mathbf{o}) is the rendered image at camera position \mathbf{o}, I{\mathbf{o}}^G is the guiding image, and M{\mathbf{o}} is the transferred mask. The mask M{\mathbf{o}} restricts the outside-view loss to the masked region. Depth-Guiding Loss: Measures the L2 distance between rendered fine/coarse depth images and guiding depth: L{depth}(\Theta) = \sum{\mathbf{o}s \in O} \left( \| Df(\mathbf{o}s) - D^G(\mathbf{o}s) \|2^2 + \| Dc(\mathbf{o}s) - D^G(\mathbf{o}s) \|2^2 \right) Total Loss: \tilde{\Theta}:= \arg \min{\Theta} L{color}(\Theta) + L{depth}(\Theta) Parameters: K: Number of sampled camera positions/views. Not given in the sources. Batch size: 4,096. Sample points in fine model: 128. Sample points in coarse model: 64. Optimizer: Adam. Optimization steps: 50,000 steps for inpainting. Hardware: Intel i7-7800X CPU and GTX-1080 GPU. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Masked MSE Only: Optimizing only with masked Mean Squared Error (MSE) on the transferred masks without explicit guidance causes the unwanted object to remain in the result. Depth Loss Only: Using only the depth-guiding loss (L{depth}) introduces color noise outside the masked region and loses color information in flat regions. Multiple Color Priors: Using multiple inpainted images as color guidance introduces visual inconsistency between views. The method restricts color guidance to the user-chosen view to maintain consistency. Guidance Artifacts: If the initial 2D inpainting or depth completion contains artifacts, the optimized NeRF may output undesired results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def volumerendercolor(FTheta, rayorigins, raydirections, near, far, numsamples): """Computes expected color via volume rendering integral.""" tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) deltas = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=tvals.device)], dim=-1) pts = rayorigins.unsqueeze(-1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(-1) tvals.unsqueeze(-1) sigma, color = FTheta(pts, raydirections) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma deltas), dim=-1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[...,:1]), T[...,:-1]], dim=-1) weights = alpha T C = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=-2) return C def volumerenderdepth(FTheta, rayorigins, raydirections, near, far, numsamples): """Computes depth by accumulating density from ray batches.""" tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) deltas = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=tvals.device)], dim=-1) pts = rayorigins.unsqueeze(-1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(-1) tvals.unsqueeze(-1) sigma, = FTheta(pts, raydirections) weights = sigma deltas depth = torch.sum(weights tvals, dim=-1) / (torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) + 1e-10) return depth def transfermaskvos(Mu, Iu, Is, ou, os): """Transfers mask Mu from view ou to os using video object segmentation (e.g., STCN).""" # Standard VOS forward pass; returns binary mask Ms return Ms def inpaintcolorguidance(Is, Ms): """Generates color prior Is^G using 2D inpainting (e.g., MST network).""" return IsG def completedepthguidance(Ds, Ms, IsG): """Generates depth prior Ds^G using depth completion (e.g., Fast Bilateral Solver).""" return DsG def nerfininpainting(FTheta, ou, Mu, Iu, K, trajectory, numsteps=50000, batchsize=4096, finesamples=128, coarsesamples=64): """NeRF-In Inpainting Optimization.""" # 1. Sample K camera positions O = trajectory(K) # 2. Render initial views Islist, Dslist = [], [] for os in O: rayso, raysd, near, far = generaterays(os) Is = volumerendercolor(FTheta, rayso, raysd, near, far, finesamples) Ds = volumerenderdepth(FTheta, rayso, raysd, near, far, finesamples) Islist.append(Is) Dslist.append(Ds) # 3. Transfer mask Mlist = [] for i, os in enumerate(O): Ms = transfermaskvos(Mu, Iu, Islist[i], ou, os) Mlist.append(Ms) # 4. Generate guidance IGlist, DGlist = [], [] for i, os in enumerate(O): IG = inpaintcolorguidance(Islist[i], Mlist[i]) DG = completedepthguidance(Dslist[i], Mlist[i], IG) IGlist.append(IG) DGlist.append(DG) IuG = inpaintcolorguidance(Iu, Mu) # 5. Define view sets: Oall = {ou}, Oout = O Oall = [ou] Oout = O # 6. Optimization optimizer = optim.Adam(FTheta.parameters(), lr=0.0001) for step in range(numsteps): optimizer.zerograd() # Lallcolor on user view raysou, raysdu, nearu, faru = generaterays(ou) Iurender = volumerendercolor(FTheta, raysou, raysdu, nearu, faru, finesamples) Lallcolor = torch.mean((Iurender - IuG) 2) # Loutcolor on other views, masked Loutcolor = torch.tensor(0.0, device=FTheta.device) for i, os in enumerate(Oout): raysos, raysds, nears, fars = generaterays(os) Isrender = volumerendercolor(FTheta, raysos, raysds, nears, fars, finesamples) diff = (Isrender - IGlist[i]) Mlist[i] Loutcolor += torch.mean(diff 2) Lcolor = Lallcolor + Loutcolor # Ldepth on all sampled views Ldepth = torch.tensor(0.0, device=FTheta.device) for i, os in enumerate(O): raysos, raysds, nears, fars = generaterays(os) Df = volumerenderdepth(FTheta, raysos, raysds, nears, fars, finesamples) Dc = volumerenderdepth(FTheta, raysos, raysds, nears, fars, coarsesamples) DG = DGlist[i] Ldepth += torch.mean((Df - DG) 2) + torch.mean((Dc - DG) 2) loss = Lcolor + Ldepth loss.backward() optimizer.step() return FTheta A method that removes objects by optimizing a NeRF using posed RGB-D images with 2D masks and 2D inpainted frames from LaMa. It employs confidence-based view selection to automatically exclude inconsistent views during optimization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training a new NeRF takes 18-20 hours for 200,000 steps; inpainting optimization takes about 5 hours for 50,000 steps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the LLFF dataset and a custom dataset with 24 camera positions per scene. Strengths: No category-specific training data or procedure required; generates visually plausible inpainted results with correct geometry and view consistency. Limitations: Relies on the quality of 2D inpainting and depth completion priors; artifacts in guidance materials can propagate to the 3D result. Using multiple inpainted images as color guidance can introduce visual inconsistency. When to Use: When removing unwanted objects from a pre-trained NeRF without access to category-specific training data or when a single user-drawn mask is sufficient to define the region of interest. When Not to Use: When high-quality 2D inpainting is not available or when the scene requires complex semantic understanding beyond geometric masking. NeRF-In was introduced by Hao-Kang Liu, I-Chao Shen, and Bing-Yu Chen in 2022. It is the first framework to enable free-form inpainting on NeRFs without category-specific training. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and 2D image inpainting techniques. NeRF-In: Free-Form NeRF Inpainting with RGB-D Priors, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2206.04901, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Adaptive View Selection for Inpainting
head: 3D Inpainting Component, 3D Inpainting Component with Adaptive View Selection, Adaptive Weight Inpainting, Gradient-Based View Selection
body:
This method addresses inconsistency artifacts inherent in applying 2D inpainting priors directly to 3D NeRF representations by introducing a training view selection mechanism based on regional average gradients. Unlike methods that uniformly blend 2D priors or rely solely on multi-view geometry, this approach adaptively switches between using 2D inpainted appearance priors and multi-view geometric consistency based on local texture richness. It is chosen when a pre-trained NeRF requires object removal or de-occlusion where maintaining multi-view consistency is critical to prevent flickering or geometric conflicts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model f	heta (typically a coarse and fine MLP pair, denoted \hat{C}c and \hat{C}f), a set of input views with known camera poses, a binary mask M identifying occluded/removed regions in the input views, and a 2D inpainter (e.g., LaMa). Outputs: Updated NeRF parameters 	heta that reconstruct the scene with the occluded region filled in consistently across all views. Data Structures: Mask \hat{P}(r): A predicted mask value for ray r, indicating the probability that the ray passes through the occluded region. Sub-regions: The occluded area in each view is divided into multiple sub-regions (patches) to evaluate local texture gradients individually. 2D Inpainting Prior Cl(r): The color value of the pixel corresponding to ray r in the image generated by the 2D inpainter for the occluded region. Numbered Steps: 1. Initial 2D Inpainting: Use a pretrained 2D image inpainter (e.g., LaMa) to generate appearance priors Cl for the occluded areas in the input views. 2. Mask Generation: Use an object segmentation network to automatically infer binary masks M for occluded regions across all views. 3. Sub-region Division: Divide the occluded area in each view into multiple sub-regions (patches). 4. Gradient Evaluation: For each sub-region, calculate the average gradient of the rendered result (
abla \hat{g}) and the average gradient of the 2D inpainting result (
abla g). 5. Adaptive Weight Calculation: Determine the adaptive weight \lambda for the reconstruction loss based on the gradient comparison: \lambda =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } 
abla \hat{g} > 	au \cdot 
abla g \ 0 & 	ext{if } 
abla \hat{g} \le 	au \cdot 
abla g \end{cases} Here, 	au is a threshold parameter. If the rendered texture is richer than the 2D prior (scaled by 	au), the method trusts the multi-view geometry (\lambda=1); otherwise, it relies on the 2D prior (\lambda=0). 6. Loss Computation: Compute the total reconstruction loss L as a weighted sum of non-occluded loss L{NonOcc} and occluded loss L{Occ}: L = \lambda L{NonOcc} + (1 - \lambda) L{Occ} 7. Optimization: Update the NeRF parameters 	heta by minimizing L. Formulas: Reconstruction Loss for Non-Occluded Areas (L{NonOcc}): L{NonOcc} = \sum{r \in R} (1 - \hat{P}(r)) \left[ ||\hat{C}c(r) - C(r)||2^2 + ||\hat{C}f(r) - C(r)||2^2 ight] Where R is the set of rays, \hat{P}(r) is the mask value, \hat{C}c(r) and \hat{C}f(r) are the coarse and fine predicted colors, and C(r) is the ground truth color. Reconstruction Loss for Occluded Areas (L{Occ}): L{Occ} = \sum{r \in R} \hat{P}(r) \left[ ||\hat{C}c(r) - Cl(r)||2^2 + ||\hat{C}f(r) - Cl(r)||2^2 ight] Where Cl(r) is the color from the 2D inpainting prior. Depth Loss (for segmentation network training): L{depth} = \sum{r \in R} ||\hat{D}(r) - D(r)||2^2 Where \hat{D}(r) is the rendered depth and D(r) is the ground truth depth. Parameters: 	au: Threshold for gradient comparison. Not given in the sources. \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: Weights for the segmentation network loss components (L{region-encoding}, L{rgb}, L{depth}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeadaptiveinpaintingloss(nerfmodel, rays, gtcolors, gtmasks, priors2d, tau): """ Computes the adaptive reconstruction loss for NeRF inpainting. Args: nerfmodel: Pre-trained NeRF model with.rendercoarse(rays) and.renderfine(rays). rays: List of ray objects with.pixelindex (tuple of int). gtcolors: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing ground truth colors. gtmasks: Tensor of shape (H, W) containing binary occlusion masks (1=occluded). priors2d: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing 2D inpainted priors. tau: Threshold for gradient-based view selection. Returns: totalloss: The computed adaptive loss. """ # 1. Render NeRF predictions predc = nerfmodel.rendercoarse(rays) predf = nerfmodel.renderfine(rays) # 2. Extract 2D priors for rays priors = torch.stack([priors2d[r.pixelindex] for r in rays]) # 3. Compute average gradients over the occluded region occludedmask = gtmasks.flatten() == 1 if occludedmask.sum() == 0: return torch.tensor(0.0) occludedpredc = predc[occludedmask] occludedpredf = predf[occludedmask] occludedprior = priors[occludedmask] # Compute average gradient magnitude for rendered and prior colors gradrendered = computeaveragegradient(occludedpredc, occludedpredf) gradprior = computeaveragegradient(occludedprior) # 4. Determine adaptive weight lambda lambdaval = 1.0 if gradrendered > tau gradprior else 0.0 # 5. Compute Non-Occluded Loss (sum over rays) nonoccmask = gtmasks.flatten() == 0 if nonoccmask.sum() > 0: nonoccpredc = predc[nonoccmask] nonoccpredf = predf[nonoccmask] nonoccgt = torch.stack([gtcolors[r.pixelindex] for r, m in zip(rays, nonoccmask) if m]) lossnonocc = torch.sum((nonoccpredc - nonoccgt)2 + (nonoccpredf - nonoccgt)2) else: lossnonocc = torch.tensor(0.0) # 6. Compute Occluded Loss (sum over rays) if occludedmask.sum() > 0: lossocc = torch.sum((occludedpredc - occludedprior)2 + (occludedpredf - occludedprior)2) else: lossocc = torch.tensor(0.0) # 7. Combine losses totalloss = lambdaval lossnonocc + (1 - lambdaval) lossocc return totalloss def computeaveragegradient(colortensorc, colortensorf): """ Computes the mean gradient magnitude across the spatial domain of the occluded region. colortensorc, colortensorf: Tensors of shape (N, 3) for occluded pixels. """ # Flatten to 2D grid approximation for gradient estimation # In practice, this operates on the (H, W, 3) tensor before ray sampling # Here we approximate using finite differences along the flattened sequence # as a placeholder for the spatial patch gradient calculation. gradc = torch.abs(colortensorc[1:] - colortensorc[:-1]) gradf = torch.abs(colortensorf[1:] - colortensorf[:-1]) return (gradc.mean() + gradf.mean()) / 2.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uniform Strategy Misjudgment: Applying a uniform strategy to the entire occluded area can lead to misjudgment. The method avoids this by dividing the occluded area into sub-regions and evaluating gradients individually. 2D Inpainter Inconsistency: Single 2D image inpainting does not consider consistency in the real 3D scene. The method addresses this by selecting training views based on texture richness to ensure multi-view consistency. Gradient Calculation: The gradient 
abla \hat{g} and 
abla g must be calculated as average gradients over sub-regions, not per-pixel, to accurately reflect texture richness. Updates the set of images used for optimization iteratively based on confidence scores to maintain consistency during inpainting. Selectively excludes views using an uncertainty mechanism and a pixelwise loss. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays, the number of sub-regions, and the cost of the 2D inpainter. The adaptive weight calculation adds a gradient computation step per sub-region. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the NeRF model, the 2D inpainted images, and the mask predictions. Strengths: Effectively reduces the disturbing effect of 2D inpainters on 3D editing by leveraging multi-view correlation. It adapts to local texture richness, providing better detail recovery in complex areas. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the 2D inpainter and the accuracy of the segmentation mask. Performance depends on the availability of multi-view data; if no other views can provide supplementary information, it falls back to the 2D prior. When to use: When performing object removal or de-occlusion in NeRFs where multi-view consistency is crucial and the occluded region has varying texture complexity. When not to use: When the scene has very limited multi-view coverage or when the 2D inpainter produces highly inaccurate priors that cannot be corrected by gradient-based selection. The method was proposed in the paper "3D Scene De-occlusion in Neural Radiance Fields: A Framework for Obstacle Removal and Realistic Inpainting". It addresses the limitations of previous 3D inpainting methods that either ignored multi-view consistency or applied 2D priors uniformly. The work builds on the NeRF representation and uses LaMa as the 2D inpainter. It has been evaluated on datasets like LLFF and SPIn-NeRF. 3D Scene De-occlusion in Neural Radiance Fields: A Framework for Obstacle Removal and Realistic Inpainting, https://doi.org/10.1145/3664647.3681429, fetched 2026-11-01 Semantically-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Visual Scene Understanding: A Comprehensive Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-025-02663-5, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of NeRFs
head: Reference-guided Inpainting
body: Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of NeRFs is a method for 3D scene inpainting that utilizes a single inpainted reference view to guide the geometry and appearance of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF), ensuring view consistency and generating view-dependent effects. It solves the problem of view inconsistencies and lack of view-dependent effects (VDEs) in non-reference views by back-projecting the reference view using monocular depth estimation and employing a bilateral solver to propagate appearance. Unlike methods that require multi-view inpainted inputs or complex text prompts, this approach allows user control via a single 2D image, avoiding the visual quality deterioration often seen in methods that rely on multiple inconsistent inpainted views. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: n input images \{Ii\}{i=1}^n, camera transform matrices \{\Pii\}{i=1}^n, binary masks \{Mi\}{i=1}^n delineating unwanted regions, and a single inpainted reference view Ir where r \in \{1, \dots, N\}. Outputs: An optimized NeRF representation f\theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \to (\sigma, \mathbf{c}) that reconstructs the scene with the object removed and the reference content extended consistently. Data Structures: NeRF Representation: Standard MLP-based NeRF storing density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing directions \mathbf{d}. Ray Set: Rays r are sampled from input views and partitioned into R{unmasked} (pixels where Mi=0) and R{masked} (pixels where Mi=1). Depth Map: A disparity map D(r) is computed from the monocular depth estimator applied to Ir, converted to inverse depth for supervision. Parameters: N{depth}: Number of iterations for initial unmasked supervision. N{bilateral}: Iteration interval for bilateral solver updates. N{do}: Iteration interval for disocclusion handling. \gamma{depth}, \gamma{rec}, \gamma{do}: Loss weights (values not given in the sources). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize NeRF parameters \theta and compute the set of unmasked rays R{unmasked} corresponding to pixels in \{Ii(1 - Mi)\}{i=1}^n. 2. Stage 1: Unmasked Supervision: Optimize f\theta on R{unmasked} for N{depth} iterations using the standard reconstruction loss L{rec}^{unmasked}. The masked region remains under-fit to allow altering masked values in later stages. L{rec}^{unmasked} = \mathbb{E}{r \sim R{unmasked}} \| \hat{C}(r) - C{GT}(r) \|^2 where \hat{C}(r) is the rendered color and C{GT}(r) is the ground truth color. 3. Geometry Supervision via Monocular Depth: Use a monocular depth estimator to predict depth for the inpainted reference view Ir. Back-project Ir to 3D positions using the camera matrix \Pir and the estimated depth. Compute a disparity map and align it with the current NeRF scene. Supervise the masked region's geometry using the depth loss L{depth}^{masked}. 4. View-Dependent Effects (VDEs) via Bilateral Solver: For non-reference views, use a view-substitution technique followed by bilaterally guided inpainting. The bilateral solver constructs VDEs in non-reference views from the reference viewpoint, ensuring that the inpainted region appears consistent from any view. Obtain target colors I{br,t} for non-reference views. Compute the reconstruction loss on masked pixels L{rec}^{masked} using these target colors. 5. Disocclusion Handling: Identify non-reference disoccluded regions (areas visible in other views but not covered by the single reference view). Use image inpainters to guide both geometry and appearance for these regions via loss L{do}. 6. Total Loss Optimization: The total loss is computed as: L = L{rec}^{unmasked} + \gamma{depth} L{depth}^{masked} + \gamma{rec} L{rec}^{masked} + \gamma{do} L{do} Losses L{depth}, L{rec}, and L{do} are computed every N{depth}, N{bilateral}, and N{do} iterations respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def referenceguidedinpainting(images, cameras, masks, refview, depthestimator, bilateralsolver, imageinpainter, niterations, Ndepth, Nbilateral, Ndo, gammadepth, gammarec, gammado, lr=0.01): # Initialize NeRF parameters theta theta = initmlpnerf() # Precompute ray sets based on masks Runmasked = [] Rmasked = [] for i in range(len(images)): for ray in generateraysfromview(images[i], cameras[i]): if masks[i][ray.pixel] == 0: Runmasked.append(ray) else: Rmasked.append(ray) for step in range(1, niterations + 1): # Stage 1: Unmasked Supervision (active every iteration) renderedunmasked = rendercolor(theta, Runmasked, cameras) gtunmasked = getgroundtruth(Runmasked, images) lossunmasked = meansquarederror(renderedunmasked, gtunmasked) theta = gradientdescentstep(theta, lossunmasked, lr) # Geometry Supervision via Monocular Depth if step % Ndepth == 0: refdepth = depthestimator(refview) refdisparity = computedisparityfromdepth(refdepth, cameras[r]) lossdepth = computedepthloss(theta, Rmasked, refdisparity) theta = gradientdescentstep(theta, lossdepth, lr) # View-Dependent Effects via Bilateral Solver if step % Nbilateral == 0: targetcolors = bilateralsolver(refview, cameras, theta) renderedmasked = rendercolor(theta, Rmasked, cameras) lossrecmasked = meansquarederror(renderedmasked, targetcolors) theta = gradientdescentstep(theta, lossrecmasked, lr) # Disocclusion Handling if step % Ndo == 0: disoccludedrays = finddisoccludedrays(theta, cameras, masks) lossdo = computedisocclusionloss(theta, disoccludedrays, imageinpainter) theta = gradientdescentstep(theta, lossdo, lr) return theta def initmlpnerf(): return MLPNeRF() def generateraysfromview(image, camera): return [Ray(camera, pixel) for pixel in image.pixels] def rendercolor(theta, rays, cameras): return [theta(ray.origin, ray.direction) for ray in rays] def getgroundtruth(rays, images): return [ray.pixel.color for ray in rays] def meansquarederror(pred, gt): return sum((p - g)2 for p, g in zip(pred, gt)) / len(pred) def gradientdescentstep(theta, loss, lr): return theta - lr gradient(loss) def computedisparityfromdepth(depth, camera): return camera.focallength / depth def computedepthloss(theta, rays, targetdisparity): return meansquarederror(renderdisparity(theta, rays), targetdisparity) def finddisoccludedrays(theta, cameras, masks): return [ray for i, ray in enumerate(allrays) if masks[i][ray.pixel] == 1 and not ray.iscoveredbyrefview] def computedisocclusionloss(theta, rays, inpainter): return inpainterguidanceloss(theta, rays) MVInpainter is a multi-view consistent inpainting model designed to bridge 2D and 3D scene editing. It employs domain adapters and motion modules as video priors to enhance cross-view consistency. It introduces a Reference Key&Value concatenation technique for appearance consistency while incorporating slot attention to aggregate optical flow features for controlling camera movement without explicit pose conditions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Iterative optimization dominates runtime, scaling with N{depth}, N{bilateral}, N{do}, and the cost of monocular depth estimation and bilateral solving per iteration. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing NeRF parameters, input images, masks, and intermediate depth maps. Strengths: Avoids view inconsistencies by relying on a single reference view; generates view-dependent effects; allows user control via a single image. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the single inpainted reference view; may struggle with complex geometry and textures in disoccluded regions. When to use: When a user wants to inpaint a NeRF with specific content provided as a single 2D image and requires view-consistent results. Reference-guided Controllable Inpainting of NeRFs was introduced in 2023. It addresses limitations in existing scene inpainting methods, such as inaccurate removal of large objects and lack of multi-view consistency. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and NeRF optimization [Parent]. name: NeRFshop
head: Interactive Editing of Neural Radiance Fields
body: NeRFshop is an end-to-end method for the interactive editing of full Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scenes, enabling users to select and deform objects via cage-based transformations. It distinguishes itself from other editing methods by operating directly on the trainable sparse occupancy grid of Instant-NGP using GPU-friendly two-level interpolation, allowing for real-time feedback without the need for retraining or offline optimization loops. Unlike methods that rely on diffusion priors or semantic segmentation masks for inpainting, NeRFshop focuses on geometric manipulation and deformation of existing scene content. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained Instant-NGP NeRF representation (hashgrid), a user-defined cage mesh surrounding the target object, and user interactions (cage vertex displacements). Output: A modified NeRF representation where the selected object is deformed according to the cage, with artifacts reduced by volumetric membrane interpolation. Data Structures: The method builds on Instant-NGP, which uses a trainable sparse occupancy grid queried directly from CUDA kernels performing SIMT operations. The cage is represented as a mesh with vertices vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Object Selection and Cage Building: The user selects an object using a scribble-based interface. The system semi-automatically builds a bounding cage mesh around the selected region, inspired by Bounding Proxies. 2. Ray Marching with Remapping: During rendering, Instant-NGP alternates between traversal, inference, and ray compaction. To incorporate editing, intermediate kernel routines are introduced that remap samples according to user-defined edits before inference. This maintains memory coherency and minimal throughput across ray compactions. 3. Cage-Based Deformation: For each sample point x along a ray, the method computes its position relative to the cage. Compute generalized barycentric coordinates \{\lambda1, \dots, \lambdan\} with respect to the canonical (original) cage vertex positions \{v1, \dots, vn\} such that: x = \sum{i=1}^{n} \lambdai vi where \sum{i=1}^{n} \lambdai = 1 and \lambdai \ge 0. The method uses Mean Value Coordinates (MVC) for this computation due to their efficiency and simplicity. Let \hat{v}i be the displaced positions of the cage vertices (modified by the user). The new position \hat{x} is computed as: \hat{x} = \sum{i=1}^{n} \lambdai \hat{v}i. The sample at \hat{x} is then queried from the NeRF hashgrid to obtain density \sigma and color c. 4. Rendering: The rendered color \hat{C}(r) along a ray r is computed using standard volume rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp \left( -\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj \right), \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the interval between samples. 5. Volumetric Membrane Interpolation (Artifact Reduction): To reduce color and density artifacts resulting from user edits, a preliminary membrane-based correction method is applied, inspired by Poisson Image Editing. 6. Distillation: After interactive editing, a "distillation" step collapses all edits and saves the hashgrid NeRF representation for loading in established pipelines. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderraywithedit(rayorigin, raydirection, cageverticesoriginal, cageverticesdisplaced, hashgridquery): """ Renders a single ray with cage-based deformation applied to samples. hashgridquery: function returning (sigma, color) for a 3D point. """ # Normalize direction to ensure consistent step size d = raydirection / math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in raydirection)) t = 0.0 T = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] samples = [] stepsize = 0.5 for i in range(100): # Current sample position in world space x = [rayorigin[j] + d[j] t for j in range(3)] # Compute barycentric coordinates (MVC) for x relative to original cage lambdas = computemvc(x, cageverticesoriginal) # Remap position using displaced cage vertices xhat = [sum(lambdas[k] cageverticesdisplaced[k][dim] for k in range(len(cageverticesoriginal))) for dim in range(3)] # Query hashgrid at deformed position sigma, c = hashgridquery(xhat) # Volume rendering accumulation alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma stepsize) color[0] += T alpha c[0] color[1] += T alpha c[1] color[2] += T alpha c[2] T = (1.0 - alpha) samples.append((x, xhat, sigma, c)) if T < 1e-4: break t += stepsize return color, samples def computemvc(point, cagevertices): """ Computes Mean Value Coordinates for a point relative to a convex polygon/polyhedron. Returns weights lambdai. """ n = len(cagevertices) lambdas = [0.0] n numeratorsum = 0.0 # First pass: compute weights and sum for i in range(n): vi = cagevertices[i] vnext = cagevertices[(i + 1) % n] vprev = cagevertices[(i - 1) % n] # Vectors di = [point[j] - vi[j] for j in range(3)] dnext = [vnext[j] - vi[j] for j in range(3)] dprev = [vprev[j] - vi[j] for j in range(3)] # Distances disti = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in di)) distnext = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in dnext)) distprev = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in dprev)) # Angles at point p: alphai between (vi-p) and (v{i+1}-p), betai between (vi-p) and (v{i-1}-p) # Using cross/dot product for 3D or 2D # For 2D/3D convex polygon, we compute angles using atan2/cross products # Simplified robust MVC weight calculation alphai = anglebetween([vnext[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)], [vi[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)]) betai = anglebetween([vprev[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)], [vi[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)]) wi = (math.tan(alphai / 2.0) + math.tan(betai / 2.0)) / (disti disti + 1e-8) numeratorsum += wi # Second pass: normalize for i in range(n): vi = cagevertices[i] vnext = cagevertices[(i + 1) % n] vprev = cagevertices[(i - 1) % n] di = [point[j] - vi[j] for j in range(3)] disti = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in di)) alphai = anglebetween([vnext[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)], [vi[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)]) betai = anglebetween([vprev[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)], [vi[j] - point[j] for j in range(3)]) wi = (math.tan(alphai / 2.0) + math.tan(betai / 2.0)) / (disti disti + 1e-8) lambdas[i] = wi / numeratorsum return lambdas def anglebetween(v1, v2): dot = sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) norm1 = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in v1)) norm2 = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in v2)) return math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot / (norm1 norm2 + 1e-8)))) Parameters: MVC: Used for barycentric coordinate computation. Distillation: Applied after editing to save the final state. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cage Construction: Automatic cage-building can result in complex meshes; the method uses adaptive cage mesh simplification. Artifacts: Deformations can cause color and density artifacts; mitigated by volumetric membrane interpolation. GPU Coherency: The method must maintain memory coherency across ray compactions in Instant-NGP. A technique where a bounding mesh (cage) is manipulated to deform the enclosed volume. It is chosen for its intuitive control and suitability for volumetric data. Link to Cage-Based Deformation The use of a trainable sparse occupancy grid queried via CUDA kernels. It is chosen for its speed and interactive performance. Link to Instant-NGP A post-processing step inspired by Poisson Image Editing to reduce artifacts. It is chosen when geometric edits introduce discontinuities. Link to Membrane Interpolation Time Complexity: Interactive, as it builds on Instant-NGP which is fully GPU-accelerated. Memory Complexity: Depends on the sparse occupancy grid of Instant-NGP. Strengths: Interactive free-form editing (deformation, translation/scale/rotation, duplication); GPU-friendly; no retraining required. When to use: When interactive, real-time editing of existing NeRF geometry is required. When not to use: When inpainting missing regions or generating new content is required. NeRFshop was introduced by Clément Jambon, Bernhard Kerbl, Georgios Kopanas, Stavros Diolatzis, Thomas Leimkühler, and George Drettakis in 2023. It is the first complete method allowing interactive free-form editing of full NeRF scenes. The method builds on Instant-NGP [Müller et al. 2022] and uses Mean Value Coordinates [Hormann and Floater 2006] for deformation. name: NeRF Distillation
head: Distilling edit to NeRF, Edit consolidation, Hashgrid export
body: NeRF Distillation is a post-processing optimization procedure that collapses user-defined spatial edits into the canonical representation of a neural radiance field, specifically the Instant-NGP hashgrid format. Unlike iterative editing methods that maintain a separate deformation field or cage structure, this method re-trains the scene to bake the edits directly into the base hashgrid parameters. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Progressive Inpainting-and-Erasing by its focus on consolidating arbitrary geometric or appearance edits into a single, static representation without retaining the edit history. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF representation (typically Instant-NGP hashgrids), a set of user-defined edits (each defining a source cage and a target deformation), and the original training images. Output: A single set of optimized NeRF parameters representing the edited scene in canonical space. Data Structures: Hashgrid: The standard Instant-NGP multi-resolution hash table storing feature vectors. Ray Mappings: A tracking structure storing all unique mappings per ray, where a mapping s \to s{i...j} denotes a sample s transformed by edit i (and potentially subsequent edits j), or the "default mapping" if the sample remains in canonical space. Algorithm: 1. Mapping Identification: For each sample s generated along rays during an initial pass, check if s lies within the source cage of any edit i. If it does, compute the transformed position si = Ti(s), establishing a mapping s \to si. Recursively check if si lies within the source cage of another edit j; if so, compute s{ij} = Tj(si), creating a recursive mapping s \to s{ij}. If s is not transformed, it retains the "default mapping". All unique mappings along each traced ray are tracked during training. 2. Ray Preparation and Broken Mapping Check: Re-trace each ray r that has more than one unique mapping, along with copies r', attempting to apply the identified mappings to each sample along r. Each mapping implies one or more deformations that copy or remap updates normally occurring in canonical space. A mapping s \to si is considered "broken" if si lies inside the deformed cage of a later edit j (meaning deforming space according to j overwrites the result of deformation by i). Broken mappings also occur for initial rays where the default mapping is no longer possible. The implementation handles this by simply skipping broken mappings. 3. Rendering and Loss Computation: For each valid ray and mapping, query the NeRF at the mapped or canonical sample position to obtain density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Perform volume rendering to compute the pixel color C. Compute the photometric loss L{render} against the original input images. 4. Gradient Propagation and Clearing: Adapt color composition and gradient computation. Shared sample locations (outside cages) only receive gradients from the first ray that references them. For non-copying edits, contents at the source must be cleared to prevent random density or color in the left-behind empty space. Samples that end up in the undeformed cage of a non-copying edit during their mapping are part of these clearing rays; they accumulate density and integrate against an empty space target (zero density). 5. Optimization Loop: Minimize the total loss using gradient descent to update the NeRF parameters \theta. Repeat until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def nerfdistillation(nerfmodel, edits, trainingimages, optimizer, maxepochs): """ Distills user edits into the NeRF hashgrid by re-training with forward-mapped samples. """ # Standard ray generation from camera poses and pixel coordinates def generaterays(images): rays = [] for img, cam in images: for u, v in img.pixelcoords: rays.append((cam, u, v)) return rays trainingrays = generaterays(trainingimages) visitedcanonicalpoints = set() # Tracks shared sample locations for gradient sharing # Step 1: Identify mappings for a representative set of rays raymappings = {} for ray in trainingrays: # Sample points along the ray in canonical space samples = nerfmodel.samplealongray(ray) mappings = [] for s in samples: currents = s mappingchain = [] # Check for recursive mappings for edit in edits: if edit['cage'].contains(currents): transformeds = edit'transform' mappingchain.append((edit['id'], transformeds)) currents = transformeds else: break mappings.append((s, mappingchain)) raymappings[ray] = mappings # Step 2 & 3: Optimization Loop for epoch in range(maxepochs): visitedcanonicalpoints.clear() totalloss = 0.0 for img, cam in trainingimages: ray = (cam, img.pixelcoords[0, 0]) # Simplified for single pixel per iteration mappings = raymappings.get(ray, []) renderedcolor = torch.zeros(3) alpha = 0.0 for s, mappingchain in mappings: # Check for broken mappings isbroken = False for edit in edits: if edit['cage'].contains(s): transformeds = edit'transform' for lateredit in edits: if lateredit['id'] > edit['id'] and lateredit['cage'].contains(transformeds): isbroken = True break if isbroken: break if isbroken: continue querypoint = s for editid, transformeds in mappingchain: querypoint = transformeds sigma, color = nerfmodel.query(querypoint) # Standard volume rendering step t = ray.sampledistance weight = sigma math.exp(-sigma t) renderedcolor += weight color alpha += weight # Handle non-copying edit clearing if mappingchain and not edits[mappingchain[-1][0]]['iscopying']: # Clearing rays accumulate density and integrate against empty space (zero density) clearloss = torch.sum((sigma - 0.0)2 + (color - torch.zeros(3))2) totalloss += clearloss # Gradient sharing: Shared sample locations only receive gradients from the first ray canonicalkey = str(s) if canonicalkey in visitedcanonicalpoints: continue visitedcanonicalpoints.add(canonicalkey) # Photometric loss against original input images targetcolor = img.pixelvalue photometricloss = torch.sum((renderedcolor - targetcolor)2) totalloss += photometricloss optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Parameters: Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Number of Epochs: Not given in the sources. Edit Order: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Broken Mappings: If a sample is transformed by edit i into a region that is then transformed by edit j, and j's deformation overwrites i's result, the mapping is broken. The implementation skips these mappings. Non-Copying Edits: Failure to clear the source region of a non-copying edit results in random density or color artifacts in the empty space. Gradient Conflicts: Shared sample locations outside cages must only receive gradients from one ray to prevent conflicting updates. Time Complexity: Requires re-training the entire scene. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead for deformation fields or cages; the final representation is a standard Instant-NGP hashgrid. Strengths: Produces a compact representation suitable for rendering; consolidates all edits into a single static model. Limitations: Cannot easily undo edits; requires re-training for any change; broken mappings may lead to loss of content in complex edit sequences. When to Use: When a final, optimized, and compact NeRF representation is needed after multiple edits. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. NeRF Distillation was introduced in the context of converting between various NeRF representations, specifically targeting the Instant-NGP hashgrid format for its efficiency. It addresses the need for a clean, consolidated representation after complex editing operations, avoiding the accumulation of deformation fields.
