name: FlipNeRF Training Pipeline
head: FlipNeRF Ablation Sequence
body: FlipNeRF is a training procedure for few-shot novel view synthesis that enhances the standard mip-NeRF representation by introducing flipped reflection rays and consistency-based regularization. It solves the problem of overfitting and unreliable depth estimation in sparse-view settings by enforcing geometric and feature consistency between original viewing rays and their hypothetical flipped counterparts. Unlike standard NeRF training which relies solely on photometric loss from observed views, FlipNeRF distinguishes itself by leveraging reflection symmetry priors and bottleneck feature consistency to regularize the radiance field, achieving higher reliability and lower negative log-likelihood (NLL) than mixture-model baselines like MixNeRF. The method builds on the NeRF Training Loop and Scene Representation and Architecture (specifically mip-NeRF). It extends the standard ray marching process by generating auxiliary "flipped" rays and applying specific loss functions to enforce consistency. Inputs: A set of N sparse input images with known camera poses. The scene is represented by a neural radiance field (MLP) parameterized by \theta, taking position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} as input. Outputs: Optimized network parameters \theta that minimize the combined loss, producing novel view renderings with reduced artifacts and accurate depth. The implementation relies on standard NeRF data structures: Ray Buffer: Stores tuples (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}, t{near}, t{far}) for each sampled ray. Flipped Ray Buffer: Stores corresponding flipped rays (\mathbf{o}', \mathbf{d}', t{near}, t{far}). The flipped ray \mathbf{r}' is generated by reflecting the viewing direction \mathbf{d} across the surface normal estimated at the intersection point, or by a predefined reflection symmetry operation relative to the scene geometry. Bottleneck Features: Intermediate feature vectors extracted from the MLP before the final color/density prediction layer. These are used for consistency constraints. 1. Baseline Initialization: Initialize the mip-NeRF representation. 2. Ray Generation: For each training batch, sample standard rays \mathbf{r} from the input views. Simultaneously, generate flipped reflection rays \mathbf{r}' corresponding to \mathbf{r}. 3. Uncertainty-Aware Regularization (LUE): Apply the Uncertainty-aware Loss (LUE) to both the original rays \mathbf{r} and the flipped rays \mathbf{r}'. This loss models the ray's output as a mixture of distributions or uses an uncertainty term to prevent overconfident predictions in unobserved regions, improving reliability compared to naive empirical losses. 4. Bottleneck Feature Consistency (LBFC): Apply the Bottleneck Feature Consistency Loss (LBFC) using the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) on the bottleneck features of the original and flipped rays. This encourages the network to produce similar internal representations for geometrically symmetric viewpoints. 5. Feature Consistency Enforcement: Enforce consistency between the bottleneck features of the original ray pair \mathbf{r} and the flipped ray pair \mathbf{r}'. This step ensures that the learned features respect the reflection symmetry prior. 6. Normal Refinement (LOri): Integrate the Orientation Loss (L{Ori}) from Ref-NeRF to refine normal estimation. Accurate normals are crucial for generating meaningful flipped rays. 7. Optimization: Update network parameters \theta using an optimizer to minimize the total loss, which is the sum of photometric loss, LUE, LBFC, and L{Ori}. Total Loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{color} + \lambda{UE} \mathcal{L}{UE} + \lambda{LBFC} \mathcal{L}{LBFC} + \lambda{Ori} \mathcal{L}{Ori} Where \mathcal{L}{color} is the standard photometric reconstruction loss. Uncertainty-Aware Loss (LUE): The sources indicate LUE improves upon naive empirical loss (L{Emp}) by modeling uncertainty, resulting in lower NLL. The exact formula for LUE is not given in the sources. Bottleneck Feature Consistency (LBFC): Uses Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) between the bottleneck feature distributions of original and flipped rays. \mathcal{L}{LBFC} = JSD(P{feat}(\mathbf{r}) || P{feat}(\mathbf{r}')) Orientation Loss (L{Ori}): From Ref-NeRF, used to supervise the predicted surface normals. The exact formula is not given in the sources. Loss Weights: The specific weights \lambda{UE}, \lambda{LBFC}, \lambda{Ori} are not given in the sources. Performance Metrics (Full Model): On the Realistic Synthetic 360° dataset, the full model achieves PSNR 19.55, SSIM 0.767, LPIPS 0.180, Average Error 0.101, and NLL 2.56. Naive Empirical Loss: Applying naive empirical loss (L{Emp}) without the uncertainty-aware component (LUE) leads to inferior results compared to MixNeRF. Reduced Feature Dimension: Reducing the feature dimension of the bottleneck reduces the capacity of feature representations and prevents the model from improving robustness. Degenerate Results: Using only flipped reflection rays without the consistency losses (LUE, LBFC) leads to overall performance degradation compared to the baseline. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainflipnerf(inputimages, cameraposes, numiterations): # 1. Initialize mip-NeRF representation model = initializemipnerf() # Standard MLP initialization for radiance fields optimizer = Adam(model.parameters(), lr=5e-4) # Standard stochastic gradient descent optimizer for iteration in range(numiterations): # 2. Sample standard rays r and generate flipped reflection rays r' raysr = samplerays(inputimages, cameraposes) # Standard ray sampling from camera intrinsics and extrinsics raysrprime = generateflippedrays(raysr, model) # Reflect viewing direction d across estimated surface normal # Forward pass for original and flipped rays colorsr, densitiesr, featuresr = model.forward(raysr) colorsrprime, densitiesrprime, featuresrprime = model.forward(raysrprime) # 3. Apply Uncertainty-Aware Loss (LUE) to both r and r' # Exact formula not given in sources lossue = computeuncertaintyloss(colorsr, densitiesr) + \ computeuncertaintyloss(colorsrprime, densitiesrprime) # 4 & 5. Apply Bottleneck Feature Consistency Loss (LBFC) with JSD losslbfc = computejsddivergence(featuresr, featuresrprime) # 6. Integrate Orientation Loss (LOri) from Ref-NeRF # Exact formula not given in sources lossori = computeorientationloss(model, raysr) # Photometric loss (standard) losscolor = computephotometricloss(colorsr, groundtruthcolors) # 7. Optimize parameters theta totalloss = losscolor + lossue + losslbfc + lossori optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return model def initializemipnerf(): return NeRFMLP() def samplerays(images, poses): return [generaterayfrompose(p) for p in poses] def generateflippedrays(rays, model): return [reflectdirection(r.direction, model.predictnormal(r.origin)) for r in rays] def computephotometricloss(rendered, groundtruth): return mean((rendered - groundtruth)2) def computeuncertaintyloss(colors, densities): return -log(sigmoid(densities) + 1e-8) # LUE formula not in sources def computejsddivergence(feat1, feat2): return 0.5 (kldivergence(feat1, (feat1+feat2)/2) + kldivergence(feat2, (feat1+feat2)/2)) def computeorientationloss(model, rays): return mean(abs(model.predictnormal(rays.origin) - rays.normal)) # LOri formula not in sources FrugalNeRF is a few-shot NeRF framework designed to synthesize novel views from extremely sparse inputs (e.g., 2 views) without relying on learned external priors. It solves the problems of overfitting and long training times inherent in extreme few-shot scenarios by leveraging weight-sharing voxels across multiple scales and a cross-scale geometric adaptation scheme. Unlike methods that require complex scheduling or pre-trained models, FrugalNeRF uses reprojection errors to select pseudo-ground truth depth, enabling fast convergence and robust regularization. ESNeRF is a sparse neural rendering method designed to address the ill-posed nature of novel view synthesis in extremely sparse-view settings. It builds on the FreeNeRF backbone but introduces a hybrid loss function incorporating pixel-based, depth-based, and regularization losses to mitigate overfitting and reduce artifacts such as solid floaters. Unlike standard NeRF training, ESNeRF leverages depth maps generated by a pretrained DPT model for supervision and employs frequency regularization to stabilize high-frequency signal learning. 360FusionNeRF is a training method for panoramic neural radiance fields using a single 360° RGB-D image, incorporating color, geometric, and semantic consistency losses. It generates new training images and depth maps with various virtual camera poses by reprojecting the input panorama. Network parameters \theta are optimized using the Adam optimizer. The learning rate is initialized to 5 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially reduced to 5 \times 10^{-5}, over 200,000 epochs with a batch size of 1,400 on a DGX A100 GPU. Unlike OmniNeRF which is estimated from scratch per scene, this method uses geometric and semantic priors to generalize better to unseen views and avoid overfitting. FrameNeRF is a teacher-student approach for sparse view synthesis where a teacher model learns coarse geometry from sparse inputs to generate pseudo-groundtruth views, which regularize a student model that refines high-quality reconstruction. Step 1: Train the teacher model on sparse input views to learn coarse geometry using FreeNeRF for 30K iterations at 1/4 resolution (400x300px). Step 2: Generate 49 dense multi-view images of the object from the teacher model to serve as pseudo-groundtruths. Step 3: Train the student model (based on Zip-NeRF) on the pseudo-groundtruth images for 5K iterations at full resolution to regularize geometry. Step 4: Fine-tune the student model on the original sparse input images for 5K iterations to remove teacher-induced artifacts like floaters. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the Realistic Synthetic 360° dataset, the full FlipNeRF model achieves PSNR 19.55, SSIM 0.767, LPIPS 0.180, Average Error 0.101, and NLL 2.56. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces artifacts and improves depth map accuracy compared to MixNeRF. Provides more reliable outputs with lower NLL than mixture-model baselines. Limitations: Performance degrades if naive empirical loss is used instead of LUE. Reduced bottleneck feature dimension harms robustness. When to use: Few-shot novel view synthesis where reliability and accurate depth estimation are critical. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of generating flipped rays and computing JSD is prohibitive, or when the scene lacks reflection symmetry priors. FlipNeRF was introduced in the paper "FlipNeRF: Flipped Reflection Rays for Few-shot Novel View Synthesis". It addresses the challenges of few-shot NeRF training by incorporating reflection symmetry priors through flipped rays and consistency-based regularization. The method builds upon the mip-NeRF representation and integrates concepts from Ref-NeRF for normal estimation. name: FrugalNeRF
head: FrugalNeRF
body: FrugalNeRF is a few-shot NeRF framework designed to synthesize novel views from extremely sparse inputs (e.g., 2 views) without relying on learned external priors. It solves the problems of overfitting and long training times inherent in extreme few-shot scenarios by leveraging weight-sharing voxels across multiple scales and a cross-scale geometric adaptation scheme. Unlike methods that require complex scheduling or pre-trained models, FrugalNeRF uses reprojection errors to select pseudo-ground truth depth, enabling fast convergence and robust regularization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A small set of training views (typically 2) with known camera parameters, and optionally COLMAP-generated sparse point clouds. Outputs: A neural radiance field represented by multi-scale voxels, capable of rendering novel views. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a pair of voxels: density (VD) and appearance (VA). Base Voxel: A single high-resolution voxel grid serves as the base. Multi-scale Voxels: L+1 scales are constructed by hierarchical subsampling of the base voxel with a downsample ratio s=4. L=2 is the typical setting, resulting in 3 total scales (LL, L, H). Lower resolutions capture global geometry; higher resolutions capture fine details. Weights are shared across scales, meaning the higher-resolution voxels are subsampled versions of the base, ensuring consistent scene representation without increasing model size. Voxel Resolution: 640^3 for LLFF and RealEstate10K datasets. 300^3 for DTU dataset. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample rays from training views (r{train}). Sample rays from randomly generated novel views (r{novel}) along a spiral trajectory around the training views. Batch size: 4,096 rays for both training and novel view rays. Number of novel poses: 120. 2. Multi-scale Volume Rendering: For each ray r, compute rendered RGB color \hat{C}l(r) and depth \hat{D}l(r) at each scale l \in \{0, \dots, L\} using the corresponding subsampled voxels V{D,l} and V{A,l}. 3. Cross-Scale Geometric Adaptation (Training Views): For each pixel pi in a training view i: Compute depth \hat{D}l(pi) at each scale l. Lift pi to 3D point x^li using intrinsic Ki and depth \hat{D}l(pi). Transform x^li to world coordinates, then to the nearest training view j to find projected coordinate p{l \to j}. Calculate reprojection error el(pi): el(pi) = Ci(pi) - Cj(p{l \to j}) where Ci, Cj are input RGB images. Identify optimal scale l': l'(r{train}) = \arg \minl el(r{train}) Set pseudo-ground truth depth: D'(r{train}) = \hat{D}{l'}(r{train}) Pitfall/Guard: If the reprojection error exceeds a threshold of 0.5, the pixel is excluded from loss computation to ensure robustness. 4. Cross-Scale Geometric Adaptation (Novel Views): For each ray r{novel} from a novel view n at pixel pn: Compute rendered color \hat{C}n(pn). Warp to nearest training view j to find p{l \to j}. Calculate reprojection error using rendered color instead of input RGB: el(pn) = \hat{C}n(pn) - Cj(p{l \to j}) Identify optimal scale l': l'(r{novel}) = \arg \minl el(r{novel}) Set pseudo-ground truth depth: D'(r{novel}) = \hat{D}{l'}(r{novel}) 5. Loss Computation: Multi-scale Color Loss (L{ms-color}): MSE between rendered RGB and input RGB for training rays at all scales: L{ms-color} = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{r{train} \in R{train}} \| \hat{C}l(r{train}) - C(r{train}) \|2^2 Geometric Adaptation Loss (L{geo}): MSE between rendered depth and pseudo-ground truth depth for both training and novel rays: L{geo}(r{train}) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \| \hat{D}l(r{train}) - D'(r{train}) \|2^2 L{geo}(r{novel}) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \| \hat{D}l(r{novel}) - D'(r{novel}) \|2^2 L{geo} = L{geo}(r{train}) + L{geo}(r{novel}) Global Regularization Loss (L{reg}): Includes total variation, patch-wise depth smoothness, L1 sparsity, and distortion losses to suppress floaters and background collapse. Sparse Depth Loss (L{sd}): Uses COLMAP-generated sparse point cloud for absolute scale constraints. Dense Depth Loss (Ld): (Optional) Uses Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) to generate depth maps from training views. 6. Total Loss: L = L{ms-color} + \lambda{geo} L{geo} + \lambda{reg} L{reg} + \lambda{sd} L{sd} + \lambda{d} L{d} 7. Optimization: Use Adam optimizer. Initial learning rate: 0.08, decaying to 0.002. Iterations: 5,000 per scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def frugalnerftrainingloop(trainingviews, novelviewcount=120, iterations=5000, voxelres=640, L=2, downsampleratio=4, lambdageo=0.01, lambdasd=0.5, lambdad=0.01, reprojectionthreshold=0.5): """ FrugalNeRF Training Loop. Args: trainingviews: List of training view data (RGB images, camera intrinsics/extrinsics). novelviewcount: Number of novel views to sample. iterations: Number of training iterations. voxelres: Base voxel resolution. L: Number of scales minus 1 (e.g., L=2 means 3 scales). downsampleratio: Ratio for subsampling voxels. lambdageo: Weight for geometric adaptation loss. lambdasd: Weight for sparse depth loss. lambdad: Weight for dense depth loss. reprojectionthreshold: Threshold for excluding unreliable reprojection errors. Returns: Trained voxel models (VD, VA). """ # 1. Initialize Multi-scale Voxels # Base voxels for density and appearance VD = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(voxelres, voxelres, voxelres, 1)) VA = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(voxelres, voxelres, voxelres, 3)) # Create L+1 scales by hierarchical subsampling scales = [] currentres = voxelres for i in range(L + 1): # Downsample by ratio s=4 at each step # Note: In practice, this is done via strided convolution or pooling # Here we assume a helper function for subsampling VDl = subsample(VD, currentres, downsampleratio) VAl = subsample(VA, currentres, downsampleratio) scales.append((VDl, VAl)) currentres = currentres // downsampleratio optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([VD, VA], lr=0.08) # Optional: Load sparse point cloud for Lsd sparsepoints = loadcolmapsparsepoints(trainingviews) # Optional: Load DPT depth maps for Ld densedepthmaps = loaddptdepths(trainingviews) for step in range(iterations): optimizer.zerograd() # 2. Sample Rays # Sample rays from training views rtrain, Ctrain = sampleraysfromviews(trainingviews, batchsize=4096) # Sample rays from novel views (spiral trajectory) rnovel, Cnovelgt = samplenovelviews(trainingviews, count=novelviewcount, batchsize=4096) # Note: Cnovelgt is not used for loss, only for evaluation or if using teacher forcing (not standard here) # 3. Volume Rendering at All Scales # Render RGB and Depth for training rays Chattrain = [] Dhattrain = [] for l in range(L + 1): VDl, VAl = scales[l] Chat, Dhat = volumerender(VDl, VAl, rtrain) Chattrain.append(Chat) Dhattrain.append(Dhat) # Render RGB and Depth for novel rays Chatnovel = [] Dhatnovel = [] for l in range(L + 1): VDl, VAl = scales[l] Chat, Dhat = volumerender(VDl, VAl, rnovel) Chatnovel.append(Chat) Dhatnovel.append(Dhat) # 4. Compute Multi-scale Color Loss (Training Views) Lmscolor = 0 for l in range(L + 1): # MSE between rendered and input RGB Lmscolor += F.mseloss(Chattrain[l], Ctrain) # 5. Cross-Scale Geometric Adaptation # For Training Views Lgeotrain = 0 for l in range(L + 1): # Calculate reprojection error # Warp view i to nearest view j using depth Dhat[l] # This requires camera parameters from trainingviews # pltoj is the projected coordinate in frame j # el = Ci - Cj(pltoj) # Helper: get reprojection error mask and error values # Returns: validmask, errorvalues validmask, errorvalues = computereprojectionerror( rtrain, trainingviews, Chattrain[l], Dhattrain[l]) # Find optimal scale l' for each pixel # l' = argminl(el) # We need to aggregate errors across scales to find l' # Note: The paper defines l' per pixel based on min error across l # So we first compute all el, then find min # Aggregate errors for all scales to find l' # errorvalues shape: (batch, H, W) for each l # We need to stack them to find argmin pass # Implementation detail: stack errors across l to find l' # Simplified logic for Lgeo based on paper description: # 1. Lgeo = MSE(Dhat[l'], D'). # Let's implement the aggregation properly allerrorstrain = [] alldepthstrain = [] for l in range(L + 1): validmask, errorvalues = computereprojectionerror( rtrain, trainingviews, Chattrain[l], Dhattrain[l]) allerrorstrain.append(errorvalues) alldepthstrain.append(Dhattrain[l]) # Stack errors: (L, batch, H, W) allerrorstrainstacked = torch.stack(allerrorstrain, dim=0) # Find optimal scale index l' for each pixel # argmin along dim 0 lprimetrain = torch.argmin(allerrorstrainstacked, dim=0) # Gather depths at l' # D' = Dhat[l'] # This requires gathering from alldepthstrain using lprimetrain Dprimetrain = gatherdepths(alldepthstrain, lprimetrain) # Compute Lgeo for training views # Only for pixels where error < threshold # First, find min error for each pixel minerrortrain = torch.min(allerrorstrainstacked, dim=0).values validmasktrain = minerrortrain < reprojectionthreshold # Masked MSE Lgeotrain = F.mseloss( Dhattrain[lprimetrain] validmasktrain, Dprimetrain validmasktrain) # For Novel Views Lgeonovel = 0 allerrorsnovel = [] alldepthsnovel = [] for l in range(L + 1): # Warp novel view n to nearest training view j # Use rendered color Chatnovel[l] instead of input RGB validmask, errorvalues = computereprojectionerrornovel( rnovel, trainingviews, Chatnovel[l], Dhatnovel[l]) allerrorsnovel.append(errorvalues) alldepthsnovel.append(Dhatnovel[l]) allerrorsnovelstacked = torch.stack(allerrorsnovel, dim=0) lprimenovel = torch.argmin(allerrorsnovelstacked, dim=0) Dprimenovel = gatherdepths(alldepthsnovel, lprimenovel) minerrornovel = torch.min(allerrorsnovelstacked, dim=0).values validmasknovel = minerrornovel < reprojectionthreshold Lgeonovel = F.mseloss( Dhatnovel[lprimenovel] validmasknovel, Dprimenovel validmasknovel) Lgeo = Lgeotrain + Lgeonovel # 6. Global Regularization Loss Lreg = computeglobalregularization(VD, VA) # 7. Sparse Depth Loss Lsd = computesparsedepthloss(VD, sparsepoints) # 8. Dense Depth Loss (Optional) Ld = 0 if densedepthmaps is not None: Ld = computedensedepthloss(VD, densedepthmaps) # 9. Total Loss Ltotal = Lmscolor + lambdageo Lgeo + lambdareg Lreg + lambdasd Lsd + lambdad Ld # 10. Backpropagation Ltotal.backward() optimizer.step() # Decay learning rate adjustlearningrate(optimizer, step, initiallr=0.08, finallr=0.002, totaliters=iterations) def subsample(voxel, res, ratio): """ Subsample voxel by ratio. """ # Assuming voxel is (res, res, res, channels) # Use strided convolution or pooling # For density (1 channel) and appearance (3 channels) if voxel.shape[-1] == 1: # Use avg pooling for density kernel = ratio stride = ratio # Add batch and channel dims for pooling voxel4d = voxel.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) pooled = F.avgpool3d(voxel4d, kernelsize=kernel, stride=stride) return pooled.squeeze(0).squeeze(0) else: # For appearance, use trilinear interpolation or similar # Or simply strided slicing if exact division newres = res // ratio # Strided slicing return voxel[::ratio,::ratio,::ratio,:] def computereprojectionerror(rays, views, Chat, Dhat): """ Compute reprojection error for training views. """ # rays: (batch, H, W, 3) or similar # views: list of view data # Chat: (batch, H, W, 3) # Dhat: (batch, H, W, 1) # 1. Lift pixels to 3D # x3d = unproject(rays, Dhat, intrinsics) # 2. Transform to world, then to nearest view j # xworld = transformtoworld(x3d, extrinsicsi) # xj = transformtoviewj(xworld, extrinsicsj) # 3. Project to 2D in view j # pj = project(xj, intrinsicsj) # 4. Sample Cj at pj # Cjsampled = sampleimage(Cj, pj) # 5. Error # e = Chat - Cjsampled # 6. Mask pixels outside bounds or with invalid depth # validmask = (depth > 0) and (pj within bounds) # Return validmask and error pass def computereprojectionerrornovel(rays, views, Chat, Dhat): """ Compute reprojection error for novel views. Uses rendered color Chat instead of input RGB. """ # Similar to training, but Ci is replaced by Chat (rendered color of novel view) # Ci(pi) -> Chat(pi) pass def computeglobalregularization(VD, VA): """ Compute total variation, patch-wise depth smoothness, L1 sparsity, and distortion losses. """ # Total Variation tvD = computetotalvariation(VD) tvA = computetotalvariation(VA) # L1 Sparsity l1D = torch.mean(torch.abs(VD)) # Distortion Loss (requires sampling along rays) # This is complex to implement without ray marching # Placeholder for distortion loss distortion = 0 # Patch-wise depth smoothness # Requires rendering depth and computing smoothness depth = volumerenderdepth(VD, VA) smoothness = computedepthsmoothness(depth) return tvD + tvA + l1D + distortion + smoothness def computesparsedepthloss(VD, sparsepoints): """ Compute loss against sparse point cloud from COLMAP. """ # Sample depth at sparse points # Compare with sparse point depths pass def computedensedepthloss(VD, densedepthmaps): """ Compute loss against DPT depth maps. """ # Render depth from VD # Compare with DPT depth maps pass def adjustlearningrate(optimizer, step, initiallr, finallr, totaliters): """ Linear decay of learning rate. """ lr = initiallr - (initiallr - finallr) (step / totaliters) for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = lr Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than previous few-shot methods. On LLFF 2-view setting, it takes 10 minutes compared to FreeNeRF's 1.5 hours and TensoRF's 6 minutes (though TensoRF has lower quality). Memory Complexity: Weight-sharing voxels reduce model size compared to independent multi-scale voxels. Memory usage is comparable to TensoRF (183.04 MB). Performance: LLFF 2-view: PSNR 18.07, SSIM 0.54, LPIPS 0.35. Outperforms FreeNeRF, ViP-NeRF, SimpleNeRF, ZeroRF, SparseNeRF, and FSGS in PSNR and LPIPS with comparable SSIM. Strengths: Fast convergence, no learned priors required, robust to overfitting in extreme few-shot scenarios, handles diverse geometric details via multi-scale voxels. Limitations: Relies on accurate camera parameters. Performance may degrade if reprojection errors are noisy (mitigated by thresholding). When to use: Extreme few-shot novel view synthesis (2-4 views) where training time and lack of priors are constraints. When not to use: Dense input scenarios where other methods might be more efficient, or when ground truth depth is available and dense depth loss is preferred. FrugalNeRF was introduced in 2025 by authors publishing in CVPR 2025. It builds on TensoRF for fast training and addresses limitations of existing few-shot NeRF methods like FreeNeRF and SparseNeRF, which struggle with complex scheduling and bias from learned priors. It is evaluated on LLFF, DTU, and RealEstate10K datasets. name: ESNeRF
head: Extremely Sparse Neural Radiance Fields
body: ESNeRF is a sparse neural rendering method designed to address the ill-posed nature of novel view synthesis in extremely sparse-view settings. It builds on the FreeNeRF backbone but introduces a hybrid loss function incorporating pixel-based, depth-based, and regularization losses to mitigate overfitting and reduce artifacts such as solid floaters. Unlike standard NeRF training, ESNeRF leverages depth maps generated by a pretrained DPT model for supervision and employs frequency regularization to stabilize high-frequency signal learning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse set of input images I, camera poses, and intrinsics. Outputs: Rendered color images \hat{C} and depth maps \hat{d} for novel views. Data Structures: Ray Set \mathcal{R}: Set of rays sampled for training. Density \sigmaK: Density values of K points sampled along a ray from near to far. Mask mK: Binary mask vector of length K. Depth Map d: Depth map generated by the pretrained DPT model. Rendered Depth \hat{d}: Depth estimated by volume rendering. Frequency Mask \boldsymbol{\alpha}: Vector controlling positional encoding visibility. Parameters: w1, w2, w3: Weights for Total Variation, Ranking, and Continuity losses. Not given in the sources. k: Tolerance constant for depth ranking penalty. Not given in the sources. M: Regularization range index for occlusion penalty. Not given in the sources. T: Final iteration for frequency regularization (e.g., 40,000). t: Current iteration for frequency regularization. L: Number of bits in the positional encoding frequency table. Not given in the sources. Training Resolution: 1/4 of the original image resolution. Training Iterations: 5,000 per scene. Batch Size: 1,024. Numbered Steps: 1. Depth Supervision Generation: Generate ground-truth depth maps d using a pretrained DPT model. 2. Frequency Regularization Setup: Initialize positional encoding. The visible frequency is controlled by a mask \boldsymbol{\alpha}(t, T, L). Start with raw inputs without positional encoding. As training progresses (t increases), the visible frequency increases linearly by 3 bits each step to avoid unstable high-frequency signals early in training. 3. Ray Sampling: Sample rays r \in \mathcal{R} and compute coarse (\hat{C}c) and fine (\hat{C}f) rendered colors and depths (\hat{d}) using the current NeRF model. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}{total} as defined below. 5. Occlusion Regularization: Apply a penalty to dense fields near the camera to reduce solid floaters. The mask mk is set to 1 for indices up to M and 0 for the rest. 6. Optimization: Update model parameters using the computed loss. 7. Upsampling: After training, upsample the generated target views bilinearly to full resolution. Formulas: The total loss is a weighted sum of the NeRF reconstruction loss and three regularization terms: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{NeRF} + w1 \mathcal{L}{TV} + w2 R{rank} + w3 R{cont} The NeRF reconstruction loss uses both coarse and fine network outputs: \mathcal{L}{NeRF} = \sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \left\| \hat{C}c(r) - C(r) \right\|^2 + \left\| \hat{C}f(r) - C(r) \right\|^2 where C(r) is the ground-truth pixel color for ray r. Total Variation Loss promotes spatial consistency in depth: \mathcal{L}{TV} = \sum{i,j} \left( |d{i,j} - d{i+1,j}|^2 + |d{i,j} - d{i,j+1}|^2 \right) where d{i,j} is the depth at pixel (i, j) from the DPT model. Depth-Guided Ranking Regularisation penalizes incorrect depth ordering between random points: R{rank} = \sum{di \leq dj} \max \left( \hat{d}i - \hat{d}j + k, 0 \right) where di, dj are depths from the DPT model and \hat{d}i, \hat{d}j are rendered depths. If di \leq dj but \hat{d}i > \hat{d}j, a penalty is applied. Depth-Guided Continuity Regularisation controls frequency visibility: \gamma 'L = \gamma L (x) \odot \boldsymbol {\alpha } (t, T, L) where the mask \boldsymbol{\alpha} is defined element-wise for bit index i as: \boldsymbol {\alpha }i (t, T, L) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if}\ i \leq \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 3 \\ \frac {t \cdot L}{T} & \text{if}\ \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 3 < i \leq \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \\ 0 & \text{if}\ i > \frac {t \cdot L}{T} + 6 \end{cases} Occlusion Regularisation penalizes density near the camera: \mathcal{L}{occ} = \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \sigmak \cdot mk where \sigmak is the density at the k-th sample point (near to far), and mk=1 for k \leq M and 0 otherwise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainesnerf(inputimages, poses, intrinsics, Tfreq=40000, Lbits=10, Mrange=100, ktol=0.1, wtv=1.0, wrank=1.0, wcont=1.0): """Train ESNeRF model.""" # Initialize FreeNeRF backbone and pretrained DPT model model = FreeNeRFBackbone() dpt = DPTModel() batchsize = 1024 res = (originalwidth // 4, originalheight // 4) optimizer = GradientDescent(model.parameters(), lr=0.0005) for t in range(5000): alphamask = computealphamask(t, Tfreq, Lbits) rays = samplerays(inputimages, poses, intrinsics, batchsize, res) gtdepths = dpt(inputimages) gtdepths = bilinearresize(gtdepths, res) coarsecolors, coarsedepths, coarsedensities = nerfforward(model, rays, alphamask) finecolors, finedepths, finedensities = nerfforward(model, rays, alphamask) lossnerf = mse(coarsecolors, rays.gtcolors) + mse(finecolors, rays.gtcolors) losstv = computetotalvariation(gtdepths) lossrank = computerankingloss(gtdepths, coarsedepths, ktol) losscont = 0.0 # Continuity regularization uses alphamask lossocc = computeocclusionloss(coarsedensities, Mrange) totalloss = lossnerf + wtv losstv + wrank lossrank + wcont losscont + lossocc optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return model def computealphamask(t, T, L): """Compute frequency visibility mask alpha(t, T, L).""" alpha = [] thresholdlow = (t L) / T + 3 thresholdhigh = (t L) / T + 6 for i in range(L): if i <= thresholdlow: alpha.append(1.0) elif i <= thresholdhigh: alpha.append((t L) / T) else: alpha.append(0.0) return alpha def computetotalvariation(depthmap): """Compute LTV = sum{i,j} (|d{i,j} - d{i+1,j}|^2 + |d{i,j} - d{i,j+1}|^2).""" tv = 0.0 H, W = depthmap.shape for i in range(H - 1): for j in range(W - 1): tv += (depthmap[i+1, j] - depthmap[i, j])2 + (depthmap[i, j+1] - depthmap[i, j])2 return tv def computerankingloss(gtdepths, rendereddepths, k): """Compute Rrank = sum{di <= dj} max(dhati - dhatj + k, 0).""" loss = 0.0 numsamples = 1000 H, W = gtdepths.shape for in range(numsamples): idxi = (random.randint(0, H-1), random.randint(0, W-1)) idxj = (random.randint(0, H-1), random.randint(0, W-1)) di = gtdepths[idxi] dj = gtdepths[idxj] dhati = rendereddepths[idxi] dhatj = rendereddepths[idxj] if di <= dj: loss += max(dhati - dhatj + k, 0) return loss / numsamples def computeocclusionloss(densities, M): """Compute Locc = (1/K) sum{k=1}^K sigmak mk.""" occsum = 0.0 B, K = densities.shape for b in range(B): for k in range(K): mk = 1.0 if k < M else 0.0 occsum += densities[b, k] mk return occsum / (B K) def samplerays(images, poses, intrinsics, batchsize, res): rays = [] for in range(batchsize): u, v = randompixelcoordinates(res) ray = generaterayfrompixel(u, v, poses, intrinsics) gtcolor = bilinearresize(images, res)[u, v] rays.append({'u': u, 'v': v, 'direction': ray.direction, 'origin': ray.origin, 'gtcolors': gtcolor}) return rays def nerfforward(model, rays, alphamask): """Volumetric rendering with frequency mask applied to positional encoding.""" colors, depths, densities = [], [], [] for ray in rays: zvals = samplezvals(ray.origin, ray.direction) posenc = applyfrequencymask(positionalencoding(zvals), alphamask) # Query MLP for density and color sigma, rgb = querymlp(model, posenc) weights = computetransmittance(sigma) c = sum(weights rgb) d = sum(weights zvals) colors.append(c) depths.append(d) densities.append(sigma) return colors, depths, densities Edge Cases and Pitfalls: DPT Inaccuracy: The DPT-generated depth maps may be inaccurate and lack detail. Using them solely for supervision can deteriorate render quality, necessitating the hybrid loss. High-Frequency Instability: Training with full positional encoding from the start can lead to unstable and susceptible high-frequency signals. The frequency regularization is critical to avoid this. Floaters: Sparse views often result in solid floaters near the camera. The occlusion regularization is specifically designed to address this. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method was evaluated in the AIM 2024 Sparse Neural Rendering Challenge, Track 1. Scaling: Training is performed at 1/4 image resolution, followed by bilinear upsampling to full resolution. Strengths: Addresses overfitting and ill-posedness in sparse-view settings; reduces solid floaters; stabilizes high-frequency learning. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the pretrained DPT model; requires careful tuning of regularization weights (not provided). ESNeRF was proposed by the team "zongqihe" for the AIM 2024 Sparse Neural Rendering Challenge. It builds on the FreeNeRF backbone and incorporates techniques from [18] (pixel-based losses) and [28] (depth-based losses). The method was part of the challenge submissions, with the team participating in Track 1. The source notes 44K total iterations with frequency regulation ending at 40K iterations, while training is explicitly done at 1/4 image resolution for 5K iterations per scene. name: MLI-NeRF
head: Intrinsic-Aware NeRF (Stage 2), Multi-Light Intrinsic-Aware Neural Radiance Fields, Stage 2 Training
body: MLI-NeRF is a two-stage optimization procedure that learns an intrinsic-aware Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) capable of novel view synthesis, relighting, and intrinsic decomposition (separating reflectance and shading) without relying on statistical priors or ground-truth intrinsic labels. It differs from standard NeRF variants by explicitly modeling multiple light sources to generate physics-based pseudo-labels, and it differs from prior intrinsic NeRF methods by leveraging 3D geometric constraints and multi-light visibility rather than chromaticity or semantic statistical constraints. The method solves the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by decoupling the geometry learning (Stage 1) from the intrinsic component separation (Stage 2), using pseudo-labels derived from the Stage 1 model to guide the decomposition. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of images captured from various camera positions and multiple light source positions. Outputs: A trained model capable of rendering novel views under arbitrary lighting, and decomposing scenes into reflectance (R), shading (S), and residual (Re) components. Data Structures and Network Layout: The method builds upon the Neuralangelo architecture, which uses 3D hashing encoding and Signed Distance Fields (SDF). 1. Geometry Network (f): Predicts the SDF value sdf = f(x) for a spatial position x. It also provides features (feat) and normals (n) derived from the gradient of the SDF. 2. Color Network (MLP{color}): Used in Stage 1. Inputs: spatial position x, normal n, features feat, view direction d, and light position l. Output: color c. 3. Reflectance Network (MLP{reflectance}): Used in Stage 2. Inputs: spatial position x, normal n, features feat. It does not take light position or view direction as input. Output: reflectance r. 4. Shading Network (MLP{shading}): Used in Stage 2. Inputs: spatial position x, normal n, features feat, and light position l. It does not take view direction as input due to the Lambertian assumption. Output: shading s. 5. Residual (Re): Accounts for specularities and undirected light, calculated as Re = I - R \otimes S. Numbered Steps: Stage 1: Neural Multi-Light Implicit Representation 1. Train the geometry network f and color network MLP{color} using images from multiple camera angles and light positions. 2. Optimize the Stage 1 loss L{S1}: L{S1} = w{rgb} L{rgb} + w{eik} L{eik} + w{curv} L{curv} Where L{rgb} is the rendered image loss, L{eik} is the Eikonal loss, and L{curv} is the curvature loss. 3. Post-processing (Pseudo Label Generation): Step A (Normals and Visibility): Derive normals n from the gradient of the SDF network. Use geometry network depth and sphere tracing to estimate intersection points. Compute light visibility V (whether a point is directly illuminated) by sphere tracing from the light position to the intersection point. Step B (Pseudo Shading): Compute pseudo-shading S^ using the Lambertian cosine law and visibility, adjusted for gamma correction: S^ = (\max(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}, 0) \otimes V)^\gamma Where \mathbf{N} is the normal ray, \mathbf{L} is the light ray, \otimes is pixel-wise product, and \gamma is the gamma correction exponent. Step C (Pseudo Reflectance): Infer high-fidelity pseudo-reflectance R^ using multiple lighting conditions. For each pixel, use the equation: R^ = I \oslash S^ Where I is the input image and \oslash is pixel-wise division. This ignores the residual component Re initially, assuming diffuse dominance. Stage 2: Intrinsic-Aware NeRF 1. Freeze the geometry network f. 2. Initialize and train the new modules MLP{reflectance} and MLP{shading}. 3. Render predicted reflectance \hat{R} and shading \hat{S} using the new networks. 4. Compute the residual \hat{Re} from the rendered image \hat{I} and the predicted components: \hat{I} = \hat{R} \otimes \hat{S} + \hat{Re} 5. Optimize the Stage 2 loss L{S2}: L{S2} = w{rgb} L{rgb} + w{intrinsic} L{intrinsic} + w{reg} L{reg} Intrinsic Loss (L{intrinsic}): Guides the separation using pseudo-labels R^ and S^: L{intrinsic} = WR \cdot \|\hat{R} - R^\|1 + WS \cdot \|\hat{S} - S^\|1 Where WR and WS are weight maps derived during pseudo-label generation. Regularization Loss (L{reg}): Prevents convergence to local minima (e.g., R=0, S=0, Re=I): L{reg} = \|\hat{Re}\|1 Weights: Typical values are w{intrinsic} = 1.0, w{reg} = 1.0. origin) sdfval = geometrynet(pos) if sdfval < 1e-4: return 1.0 if t > 100.0: break t += sdfval return 0.0 def volumerender(positions, colors, alphas, numrays): # Standard alpha compositing along rays T = np.ones(numrays) rendered = np.zeroslike(colors[0]) for i in range(len(positions)): alpha = alphas[i] rendered += T alpha colors[i] T = (1.0 - alpha) return rendered def samplerays(pose, imageshape): # Generate camera rays from pose and image dimensions # Returns positions and directions pass def trainstage1(geometrynet, colornet, dataset, lr=1e-4, wrgb=1.0, weik=0.1, wcurv=5e-4): optimizerparams = list(geometrynet.parameters()) + list(colornet.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, pose, lightpos in dataset: rays = samplerays(pose, image.shape) positions, directions = rays sdf = geometrynet(positions) feat = geometrynet.getfeatures(positions) normals = normalize(computegradient(geometrynet, positions)) colors = colornet(positions, normals, feat, directions, lightpos) alphas = geometrynet.getalphas(positions) # Alpha prediction from NeRF renderedimage = volumerender(positions, colors, alphas, len(rays)) lossrgb = np.mean((renderedimage - image) 2) losseik = np.mean((np.linalg.norm(computegradient(geometrynet, positions), axis=-1) - 1.0) 2) losscurv = computecurvature(geometrynet, positions) # Curvature from SDF totalloss = wrgb lossrgb + weik losseik + wcurv losscurv for p in optimizerparams: if p.grad is not None: p -= lr p.grad return geometrynet, colornet def generatepseudolabels(geometrynet, dataset, gamma=2.2): pseudoshadings = [] pseudoreflectances = [] for image, pose, lightpos in dataset: rays = samplerays(pose, image.shape) positions, directions = rays normals = normalize(computegradient(geometrynet, positions)) visibility = spheretracevisibility(geometrynet, positions, lightpos) lightdir = normalize(lightpos - positions) cosineterm = np.maximum(np.sum(normals lightdir, axis=-1), 0.0) pseudoshading = (cosineterm visibility) gamma pseudoreflectance = image / pseudoshading pseudoshadings.append(pseudoshading) pseudoreflectances.append(pseudoreflectance) return pseudoshadings, pseudoreflectances def trainstage2(geometrynet, reflectancenet, shadingnet, pseudoshadings, pseudoreflectances, WR, WS, dataset, lr=1e-4, wrgb=1.0, wintrinsic=1.0, wreg=1.0): for param in geometrynet.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False optimizerparams = list(reflectancenet.parameters()) + list(shadingnet.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for i, (image, pose, lightpos) in enumerate(dataset): rays = samplerays(pose, image.shape) positions, directions = rays feat = geometrynet.getfeatures(positions) normals = normalize(computegradient(geometrynet, positions)) predreflectance = reflectancenet(positions, normals, feat) predshading = shadingnet(positions, normals, feat, lightpos) alphas = geometrynet.getalphas(positions) # Alpha prediction renderedimage = volumerender(positions, predreflectance predshading, alphas, len(rays)) predresidual = renderedimage - (predreflectance predshading) lossrgb = np.mean((renderedimage - image) 2) lossintrinsic = np.mean(WR np.abs(predreflectance - pseudoreflectances[i])) + \ np.mean(WS np.abs(predshading - pseudoshadings[i])) lossreg = np.mean(np.abs(predresidual)) totalloss = wrgb lossrgb + wintrinsic lossintrinsic + wreg lossreg for p in optimizerparams: if p.grad is not None: p -= lr p.grad return reflectancenet, shadingnet Parameters: \gamma: Gamma correction exponent used to adapt pseudo-shading to nonlinear digital image representation. w{eik}: Eikonal loss weight (0.1). w{curv}: Curvature loss weight (5 \times 10^{-4}). w{intrinsic}: Intrinsic loss weight (1.0). w{reg}: Regularization loss weight (1.0). w{rgb}: RGB loss weight (Not explicitly isolated in Stage 2 snippet, but present in L{S2}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: The optimization may converge to trivial solutions where R=0, S=0, Re=I. This is mitigated by the L{reg} term which penalizes the residual norm. Ill-Posed Inverse Rendering: Traditional inverse rendering is computationally intensive and ambiguous. MLI-NeRF avoids this by using intrinsic decomposition with pseudo-labels, limiting the scope to object-specific or well-lit scenes where diffuse dominance holds. Specularities: The pseudo-reflectance generation ignores the residual component, which entangles specularities and undirected light. This may lead to inaccuracies in highly specular regions. A pipeline to generate high-fidelity pseudo reflectance and shading labels from a trained multi-light NeRF model to guide intrinsic decomposition training in Stage 2. Unlike previous statistical priors, this physics-based pipeline provides a more reliable basis for disentanglement by leveraging explicit geometric and illumination models. It serves as the bridge between the implicit representation learned in Stage 1 and the intrinsic-aware NeRF in Stage 2. Time Complexity: Stage 1 training time follows Neuralangelo. Stage 2 training takes approximately 19 hours on a single Nvidia RTX 3090 for the tested datasets. Memory Complexity: Uses 3D hashing encoding and SDF storage similar to Neuralangelo. The addition of two MLPs (reflectance and shading) increases parameter count slightly, but the geometry network is frozen in Stage 2. Strengths: Does not require ground-truth intrinsic labels; leverages 3D geometric constraints for robustness; enables relighting and intrinsic editing. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to multi-light rendering and sphere tracing; limited to scenes where diffuse reflection dominates (Lambertian assumption); struggles with highly specular or complex non-diffuse effects without residual compensation. When to use: When intrinsic decomposition and relighting are required without ground-truth labels, and the scene has controllable or known multiple light sources. When not to use: For real-time applications (training is slow); for scenes with strong specularities where the Lambertian assumption fails significantly; when ground-truth intrinsic data is available (other methods may be more direct). MLI-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of existing intrinsic decomposition methods that rely on statistical priors (like chromaticity) and struggle with real-world data. It builds on the idea that varying light source positions, similar to how mineralogists illuminate specimens, reveals intrinsic scene details. The method integrates multiple light information into Neural Radiance Fields, generating pseudo-labels to guide intrinsic decomposition without statistical constraints. It was validated on synthetic (Blender-based) and real-world datasets, outperforming methods like IntrinsicNeRF, InvRender, and TensoIR in intrinsic decomposition and relighting tasks. name: Physics-based Pseudo Label Generation
head: Post-processing of Stage 1, Pseudo reflectance generation, Pseudo shading generation
body: This method generates high-fidelity pseudo reflectance and shading labels from a trained multi-light NeRF model to guide intrinsic decomposition training in Stage 2. Unlike previous statistical priors, this physics-based pipeline provides a more reliable basis for disentanglement by leveraging explicit geometric and illumination models. It serves as the bridge between the implicit representation learned in Stage 1 and the intrinsic-aware NeRF in Stage 2. Inputs: Trained SDF network and RGB MLP from Stage 1. Camera poses and light positions for multiple lighting conditions. Rendered RGB images I for each light condition. Outputs: Pseudo shading image S. Pseudo reflectance image R. Weight maps WR and WS for reliability estimation. Data Structures: Points: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) sampled along camera rays. Normals: Surface normal vectors \vec{N} derived from SDF gradients. Light Visibility: Binary or continuous mask V indicating if a point is illuminated by a specific light source. Images: 2D arrays of RGB values for I, S, and R. Steps: 1. Obtain Normal and Light Visibility: Use the trained SDF network from Stage 1 to perform sphere tracing and volume rendering to get normals and light visibility for each point. For each point along the camera ray, compute the surface normal \vec{N} via the gradient of the SDF. Determine light visibility V by checking if the point is occluded from the light source. 2. Generate Pseudo Shading: Compute the dot product of the normal \vec{N} and the light ray direction \vec{L}. Apply gamma correction to adapt the pseudo-shading to the nonlinear representation of digital images, mimicking sensor response. The shading S is calculated as: S = (\max(\vec{N} \cdot \vec{L}, 0) \otimes V)^\gamma where: \vec{N} is the normal ray. \vec{L} is the light ray direction. V is the light visibility mask. \gamma is the gamma value (Not given in the sources.). \otimes denotes pixel-wise product. (\cdot)^\gamma represents gamma correction. 3. Generate Pseudo Reflectance: Calculate initial reflectance for each light condition using pixel-wise division, ignoring the residual component (specular and indirect light): R = I \oslash S where \oslash denotes pixel-wise division. To handle multiple light conditions, use K-means clustering at the pixel level. Incorporate weights of each pseudo shading to select the most probable pseudo reflectance, creating a merged reflectance image. 4. Hole Filling: Identify regions in the merged reflectance that appear as holes due to the absence of direct illumination in all lighting conditions. Compute a weighted distance between hole pixels and non-hole pixels based on spatial distance in the image, angular difference of their normals, and RGB color difference. Assign the color of the nearest non-hole pixel (based on weighted distance) to the hole pixel. This is a rough supplementary approach with minimal impact on overall results, as hole regions are typically small under multi-light settings. 5. Compute Weight Maps: Compute weight maps WR and WS for pseudo reflectance and shading respectively. Weights are based on edges of pseudo shading and visibility. Areas with higher pseudo shading values or further from visibility edges have greater credibility. Areas closer to visibility edges or with lower pseudo shading values are deemed less reliable. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def generatepseudolabels(sdfnetwork, rgbmlp, cameraposes, lightpositions, gamma=2.2): pseudoshadings = [] pseudoreflectances = [] allnormals = [] allvisibilities = [] for pose, lightpos in zip(cameraposes, lightpositions): # Step A: Obtain Normal and Light Visibility points, normals, visibilities = spheretraceandrender( sdfnetwork, cameraposes=pose, lightpositions=lightpos) allnormals.append(normals) allvisibilities.append(visibilities) # Compute light ray direction lightray = normalize(lightpos - points) # Step B: Generate Pseudo Shading dotproduct = np.maximum(np.sum(normals lightray, axis=-1), 0) visibilities shading = dotproduct gamma pseudoshadings.append(shading) # Render RGB image for this light condition rgbimage = renderrgb(rgbmlp, points) # Step C: Generate Pseudo Reflectance (Initial) safeshading = np.maximum(shading, 1e-6) initialreflectance = rgbimage / safeshading[:, np.newaxis] pseudoreflectances.append(initialreflectance) # Merge reflectances using K-means clustering with weights mergedreflectance = kmeansmerge(pseudoreflectances, pseudoshadings) # Step D: Hole Filling holemask = ishole(mergedreflectance, pseudoshadings) filledreflectance = fillholes(mergedreflectance, holemask, allnormals[0]) # Compute Weight Maps weightshading = computeshadingweight(pseudoshadings) weightreflectance = computereflectanceweight(filledreflectance, weightshading) return filledreflectance, pseudoshadings[0], weightreflectance, weightshading def spheretraceandrender(sdfnetwork, cameraposes, lightpositions): # Sources do not specify the exact sphere tracing implementation. # Standard routine iterates along rays, queries SDF, computes normals via gradient, # and checks visibility. Returns arrays of shape (H, W, 3) and (H, W). return np.zeros((100, 100, 3)), np.zeros((100, 100, 3)), np.zeros((100, 100)) def renderrgb(rgbmlp, points): # Standard MLP forward pass to predict RGB from points and features return np.random.rand(points.shape[0], 3) def normalize(v): return v / (np.linalg.norm(v, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8) def kmeansmerge(reflectances, shadings, k=3, maxiter=10): # Weighted K-means clustering at pixel level across light conditions npixels = reflectances[0].shape[0] nlights = len(reflectances) flatref = np.vstack([r.flatten() for r in reflectances]) flatshad = np.vstack([s.flatten() for s in shadings]) weights = flatshad / (np.max(flatshad) + 1e-6) centroids = flatref[:k] for in range(maxiter): dists = np.linalg.norm(flatref[:, np.newaxis] - centroids[np.newaxis,:], axis=2) labels = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) newcentroids = np.zeroslike(centroids) for i in range(k): mask = labels == i if np.sum(mask) > 0: newcentroids[i] = np.average(flatref[mask], weights=weights[mask], axis=0) centroids = newcentroids merged = centroids[labels].reshape(reflectances[0].shape) return merged def ishole(reflectance, shadings): # Identify regions where shading was near zero for all lights minshading = np.min(np.stack(shadings, axis=0), axis=0) return minshading < 1e-3 def fillholes(reflectance, holemask, normals): filled = reflectance.copy() holeindices = np.argwhere(holemask) nonholeindices = np.argwhere(~holemask) for hole in holeindices: mindist = float('inf') bestpixel = None for nonhole in nonholeindices: dspatial = np.linalg.norm(hole - nonhole) dangle = 1.0 - np.abs(np.dot(normals[hole[0], hole[1]], normals[nonhole[0], nonhole[1]])) dcolor = np.linalg.norm(reflectance[hole[0], hole[1]] - reflectance[nonhole[0], nonhole[1]]) dist = dspatial + dangle + dcolor if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestpixel = nonhole if bestpixel is not None: filled[hole[0], hole[1]] = reflectance[bestpixel[0], bestpixel[1]] return filled def computeshadingweight(shadings): # Weights based on edges of pseudo shading and visibility avgshading = np.mean(np.stack(shadings, axis=0), axis=0) edges = np.abs(np.gradient(avgshading)) weight = avgshading / (edges + 1e-6) return weight def computereflectanceweight(reflectance, shadingweight): # Reflectance weight inherits shading reliability return shadingweight Exact time and memory complexity bounds are Not given in the sources. Qualitatively, time complexity depends on the number of light conditions and pixels, with K-means clustering adding per-pixel overhead across light conditions. Memory complexity requires storing normals, visibilities, and intermediate images for all light conditions. The method provides a physically grounded basis for intrinsic decomposition, reducing reliance on statistical priors. It handles multi-light scenarios effectively. The method relies on the accuracy of Stage 1 SDF and RGB networks. Hole filling is a heuristic and may introduce artifacts in complex scenes, though impact is minimal. Accuracy of visibility estimation affects shading quality. It is used when training an intrinsic-aware NeRF (Stage 2) and high-fidelity pseudo labels are needed for supervision. It is not recommended if computational resources are extremely limited, as it requires additional post-processing steps. If the scene has significant specular or indirect lighting that cannot be ignored in the residual component, the simplified R = I \oslash S may be inaccurate. Originated in the MLI-NeRF paper (2024). It addresses the need for reliable supervision signals for intrinsic decomposition in neural radiance fields, moving away from statistical priors used in earlier methods. The method leverages the physics of light transport (Lambert's cosine law) and sensor characteristics (gamma correction) to generate pseudo labels. MLI-NeRF: Multi-Light Intrinsic-Aware Neural Radiance Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.17235v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Diffusion-guided Optimization
body: Diffusion-guided optimization methods train Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by leveraging pretrained 2D or 3D diffusion models as priors to guide the optimization of 3D geometry and texture. These methods solve the problem of 3D data scarcity and underconstrained reconstruction by distilling generative knowledge from 2D image distributions into 3D scene representations. They set themselves apart from standard NeRF training by backpropagating gradients from a frozen or jointly trained diffusion model through a differentiable renderer, rather than relying solely on photometric reconstruction losses from input images. Builds on NeRF Training Loop. All methods in this family optimize a NeRF representation \theta (or latent codes x) by minimizing a loss derived from a diffusion model \phi. The core mechanism involves rendering an image (or latent) from the current NeRF state, perturbing it with noise, and computing gradients based on the diffusion model's prediction of that noise. The general optimization loop is: 1. Render an image x from the NeRF at a random viewpoint. 2. Sample a diffusion timestep t and Gaussian noise \epsilon. 3. Create a noisy version zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon. 4. Predict noise \hat{\epsilon} = \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; \text{condition}, t). 5. Compute gradients \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} using the difference between predicted and actual noise. The specific form of the gradient and the conditioning mechanism varies by child method. Optimizes a NeRF using Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) from a frozen 2D text-to-image diffusion model. It sets itself apart by introducing SDS to backpropagate gradients from a 2D prior to 3D geometry without explicit 3D supervision. Choose it for text-to-3D generation. Generates 3D human avatars using SDS but constrains the NeRF with an SMPL parametric shape prior. It is distinguished by its explicit geometric topology constraints, unlike DreamFusion's implicit representation. Choose it for human avatar generation. Jointly optimizes scene latent codes, a diffusion prior, and a NeRF decoder in a single loop. It solves the bias of two-stage methods by treating diffusion parameters as trainable. Choose it for multi-view reconstruction with a diffusion prior. Uses a multiview-conditioned latent diffusion model to regularize few-view reconstruction. It differs from SDS by sampling a new image at each iteration using a denoising U-Net conditioned on input views, reducing volumetric artifacts. Choose it for few-view 3D reconstruction. Applies a local 3D geometric diffusion prior to remove floaters. It distinguishes itself by using a 3D U-Net on voxelized patches (Density Score Distillation Sampling) rather than a 2D image prior. Choose it for cleaning up casually captured NeRFs. The concept of distilling 2D diffusion priors into 3D representations was introduced by DreamFusion. Subsequent works adapted this principle for specific domains: DreamAvatar for humans, Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF Training for joint optimization, ReconFusion for few-view reconstruction, and Nerfbusters for artifact removal.

name: DreamFusion
head: Diffusion-guided NeRF Optimization, Score Distillation Sampling, Text-to-3D NeRF Optimization, Text-to-3D diffusion NeRF
body: DreamFusion is a text-to-3D generation method that optimizes a parametric 3D scene representation (specifically a NeRF) to match a given textual description or image without requiring explicit 3D training data. It solves the problem of 3D data scarcity by distilling priors from a frozen 2D text-to-image diffusion model into the 3D geometry and appearance. What sets it apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives is its use of Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), which backpropagates gradients from the 2D diffusion model’s noise prediction through the differentiable renderer to update the 3D scene parameters. Unlike Instruct 3D-to-3D, which edits existing geometry, DreamFusion generates scenes from scratch. DreamFusion optimizes a NeRF representation \theta by minimizing a loss derived from a 2D diffusion model \phi. The core mechanism involves rendering an image from the current NeRF state, perturbing it with noise, and computing gradients based on the diffusion model's prediction of that noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A text prompt y (e.g., "a red apple") or a reference image. Input: A frozen 2D text-to-image diffusion model \phi (e.g., Imagen). Input: A NeRF representation \theta initialized from scratch. In DreamFusion, surface color is parameterized by an MLP instead of standard radiance. Output: An optimized NeRF \theta that renders images consistent with the prompt y. Data Structures: NeRF (\theta): A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. The specific architecture used in DreamFusion is mipNeRF 360. Diffusion Model (\phi): A pretrained text-to-image diffusion model (e.g., Imagen). It takes a noisy image zt, a timestep t, and a text condition y as input, and outputs a predicted noise \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t). Numbered Steps: 1. Random Viewpoint Selection: Sample a random camera viewpoint (position and orientation) for the current optimization step. 2. Differentiable Rendering: Render an image x from the NeRF \theta at the sampled viewpoint. 3. Noise Sampling: Sample a diffusion timestep t uniformly from [1, T] and a Gaussian noise vector \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 4. Noise Addition: Create a noisy version of the rendered image zt using the forward diffusion process: zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon where \alphat and \sigmat are timestep-dependent coefficients. 5. Diffusion Prediction: Pass the noisy image zt, timestep t, and text prompt y into the frozen diffusion model \phi to predict the noise: \hat{\epsilon} = \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t). 6. Gradient Computation: Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) gradient with respect to the NeRF parameters \theta: \nabla\theta \mathcal{L}{\text{SDS}} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon}\left[ w(t)\,(\hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t) - \epsilon)\,\frac{\partial zt}{\partial \theta} \right] where w(t) is a timestep weighting function. The term \frac{\partial zt}{\partial \theta} is the gradient of the rendered noisy image with respect to the NeRF parameters, obtained via backpropagation through the differentiable renderer. 7. Optimization Step: Update the NeRF parameters \theta using the computed gradient (e.g., via Adam optimizer). Formulas: SDS Loss Gradient: \nabla\theta L{SDS}(\phi, x) \triangleq \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} w(t) \left[ \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; y, t) - \epsilon \right] \frac{\partial zt}{\partial \theta}. Noisy Image: zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon. Parameters: Diffusion Model: Imagen was used in the original DreamFusion implementation. Resolution: Imagen images were generated at a 64x64 resolution. Viewpoint Control: Text prompts can include keywords such as "overhead view", "front view", and "back view" to control the viewpoint at the diffusion generation stage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Resolution: Because the source diffusion model (Imagen) generated images at 64x64 resolution, the resulting NeRF model lacked the capability to produce finer details. Janus Problem: The method suffers from the "Janus problem," where the generated 3D object exhibits multiple faces or inconsistent features from different viewpoints. Oversaturation and Oversmoothing: SDS tends to produce saturated colors and oversmoothed textures, leading to insufficient detail. Slow Optimization: The optimization process is slow, taking hours per scene. Instruct 3D-to-3D is a method for performing 3D scene editing or conversion guided by natural language instructions. It solves the problem of transforming an existing 3D scene into a new one that adheres to specific textual descriptions while maintaining structural coherence. It distinguishes itself from text-to-3D generation methods like DreamFusion by conditioning the optimization on a source 3D scene rather than generating geometry from scratch, and from other 3D editing methods like SKED by leveraging InstructPix2Pix for instruction following. Time Complexity: Optimization is slow, typically taking hours per scene. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DreamFusion produces photorealistic and semantically faithful 3D objects from text prompts without 3D supervision. However, the output resolution is limited by the resolution of the 2D diffusion model (e.g., 64x64 in the original implementation). Scaling: Scaling to higher resolutions requires multi-stage approaches (e.g., Magic3D) or latent-space methods (e.g., Latent-NeRF). Strengths: No 3D training data required; leverages powerful 2D diffusion priors; allows text-based control over viewpoint and semantics. Limitations: Slow optimization; Janus problem (multi-face artifacts); saturated colors; oversmoothing; insufficient detail due to low-resolution diffusion inputs. When to use: When generating novel 3D objects from text descriptions is required, and high-fidelity detail is not the primary concern, or when used as a coarse initialization for refinement. When not to use: When high-resolution details are critical, or when editing existing 3D scenes is required (use Instruct 3D-to-3D instead). DreamFusion was introduced in September 2022. It was proposed as a text-to-3D diffusion NeRF model that uses images from 2D diffusion models (specifically Imagen) to train a NeRF from scratch. The method addresses the lack of large-scale 3D training datasets by sidestepping explicit 3D supervision altogether. It builds on Diffusion-guided Optimization by introducing Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) as the specific gradient computation method. Subsequent works like Latent-NeRF and Magic3D built upon DreamFusion to address its limitations regarding resolution and detail. name: Instruct 3D-to-3D
body: Instruct 3D-to-3D is a method for performing 3D scene editing or conversion guided by natural language instructions. It realizes 3D-to-3D conversions following text instructions. It distinguishes itself from text-to-3D generation methods like DreamFusion by conditioning the optimization on a source 3D scene rather than generating geometry from scratch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source 3D scene (represented as a NeRF or similar implicit representation) and a text instruction. Output: An optimized target 3D scene that reflects the text instruction. Data Structures: Source Scene: The initial 3D representation (e.g., NeRF parameters). Text Instruction: A string of natural language. Optimization State: The parameters of the target 3D scene, initialized from the source scene. Steps: 1. Conditioning: Integrate the source 3D scene as a conditional input to the optimization process. 2. Loss Calculation: Utilize the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss [89] to guide the optimization. The SDS loss is computed using a text-to-image diffusion model (specifically InstructPix2Pix, as cited in) to evaluate how well the rendered images from the current 3D scene match the text instruction. 3. Geometry Modification: Integrate dynamic scaling to effectively modify scene geometry. This mechanism allows the method to adjust the scale of geometric elements during optimization to better fit the textual description. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Integrate source 3D scene as conditional input targetparams = copyparams(sourcenerf.parameters) # Load InstructPix2Pix model ip2pmodel = loadinstructpix2pix() optimizer = optim.Adam(targetparams, lr=0.01) for step in range(numiterations): # 2. Utilize SDS loss to optimize target scene renderedimages = render(targetparams, cameraposes) sdsloss = computesdsloss(renderedimages, textinstruction, ip2pmodel) # 3. Integrate dynamic scaling to effectively modify scene geometry scale = dynamicscale(step) gradients = computegradients(sdsloss scale, targetparams) targetparams = updateparameters(targetparams, gradients, optimizer) return targetparams Parameters: Text Instruction: The natural language command describing the desired 3D modification. Source Scene: The initial 3D object or scene to be edited. Dynamic Scaling: A mechanism to adjust geometry; specific values or formulas are not provided in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The quality of the output depends heavily on the capability of the InstructPix2Pix model to interpret the text instruction in the context of the source scene. Boundaries: The method relies on the source scene as a conditional input; if the source scene is significantly different from the target concept, the optimization may struggle to converge. A network translating images to a 3D model, based on a pix2pix convolutional and deconvolutional ResNet, outputting vertex offsets from a base model. It predicts offsets from a base model (uniform sphere with predefined topology) rather than absolute coordinates to improve convergence smoothness. It optionally predicts symmetry by splitting the model into four quarters, predicting shifts for one quarter, mirroring it, and predicting shifts for the mirrored quarter until all four are predicted. It also predicts uniform translation and scaling values to reduce offset magnitude and improve stability. Regularization on the 3D mesh considers angles between normals, edge lengths, and curvature. Input: Images. Internal State: Single representative image (from pix2pix component). Output: 3 \times \#vertices values from two fully connected layers, passed through a sigmoid layer, then linearly transformed to range [-1, 1]. A text-based 3D facial alteration technique utilizing malleable NeRF. It manages facial distortion by instructing a scene manipulator to use hidden codes and adapt to depict different latent codes for scene manipulation using a Positional Conditional Anchor Combiner (PAC). It successfully mirrors the visual characteristics of descriptive and emotionally charged texts, preserving the visual integrity and essence of 3D faces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages powerful text-to-image models (InstructPix2Pix) for instruction following. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the source scene and the diffusion model. When to use: When editing an existing 3D scene based on text instructions is required. When not to use: When generating 3D content from scratch without a source scene is required (use DreamFusion instead). Instruct 3D-to-3D was introduced as a method for 3D editing following text instructions. It utilizes InstructPix2Pix for instruction following and SDS loss for optimization. It is part of a series of 3D editing works that utilize the SDS algorithm. name: Focaldreamer
head: GSEditor-DDS, GSEditor-iN2N
body: Focaldreamer (also known as GSEditor-DDS and GSEditor-iN2N) is a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) editing method that performs localized geometric and textural modifications guided by text prompts. It solves the problem of precise, focal-region editing in existing 3D scenes without degrading the background. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like I3DS by explicitly utilizing rendered normal maps as shape encodings for the text-to-image (T2I) model and employing a pixelwise discriminative mask to unify base and editable textures, thereby ensuring geometric consistency during optimization. Inputs: An existing 3D Gaussian Splatting scene (base shape). A text prompt describing the desired edit. A mask defining the focal region for editing. Outputs: An edited 3D Gaussian Splatting scene with modified geometry and textures in the focal region. Data Structures: 3DGS Scene: Standard 3DGS representation containing Gaussian primitives with position, covariance, opacity, spherical harmonics coefficients, and scale. Editable Ellipsoids: A set of Gaussian primitives initialized in the focal regions to allow for geometric deformation. Pixelwise Discriminative Mask: A binary or soft mask M of image resolution, where M=1 indicates the focal region and M=0 indicates the background. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initiate the editing process with the base 3DGS shape. Initialize editable ellipsoids (Gaussian primitives) specifically within the focal regions defined by the user or prompt. 2. Rendering: Render the scene from the current camera viewpoint. This rendering includes both the base shape textures and the editable textures of the ellipsoids. The final pixel color C is computed by compositing these layers, weighted by the discriminative mask M. 3. Normal Map Generation: Render the normal maps of the current 3DGS scene. These normal maps serve as the shape encoding for the T2I model, providing geometric constraints to the diffusion prior. 4. Loss Computation: SDS Loss: Compute the Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) loss [89] using the T2I model. The input to the T2I model is the rendered image (or a latent representation thereof) combined with the normal maps as conditioning. The loss guides the optimization towards the text prompt semantics. Regularization: Incorporate additional regularization terms to improve editing quality. These typically include constraints on Gaussian opacity, scale, and position to prevent artifacts and maintain structural integrity. 5. Optimization: Update the parameters of the editable ellipsoids (position, scale, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients) using gradient descent on the combined loss. The base shape parameters are typically frozen or heavily regularized to preserve background integrity. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 for a fixed number of iterations or until convergence. Formulas: SDS Loss: \mathcal{L}{SDS} = \mathbb{E}{t, \epsilon} \left[ w(t) (\epsilon\theta(zt; y, t) - \epsilon) \right], where zt is the noisy latent, y includes the rendered image and normal maps, and \epsilon\theta is the denoiser. Composite Image: I = M \cdot I{editable} + (1 - M) \cdot I{base}. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Number of iterations: Not given in the sources. SDS weight w(t): Standard cosine schedule or constant, as per [89]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Normal map rendering must be accurate to provide meaningful shape encoding. Boundaries: The discriminative mask M must be smooth or carefully handled to avoid visible seams between edited and base regions. Degenerate Input: If the focal region is too small, the edit may not be perceptible; if too large, it may overwrite significant parts of the scene. RealmDreamer utilizes diffusion priors from inpainting and depth estimation models to generate different viewpoints of a scene iteratively. Unlike Focaldreamer which focuses on editing a single scene with a mask, RealmDreamer uses these priors to synthesize consistent multi-view data for scene composition or generation. It is chosen when iterative viewpoint generation is required for scene-level consistency rather than localized editing. 3D Prior (Zero-1-to-3) uses Zero-1-to-3, a view-dependent diffusion model finetuned on Objaverse, as the 3D prior. It takes a reference image Ir and novel view camera poses (R, T) as input to generate a novel view, thereby encouraging 3D consistency. The 3D SDS loss is formulated as \mathcal{L}{3D} = \mathbb{E}{t,\epsilon} w(t) \frac{\partial I}{\partial \theta} (\epsilon\phi(zt; Ir, t, R, T) - \epsilon). Unlike the 2D prior which uses text embedding, the 3D prior uses the reference view and camera poses as guidance to enable the usage of more 3D information. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations and the cost of rendering normal maps and images per iteration. Memory Complexity: Standard 3DGS memory plus overhead for storing normal maps and intermediate gradients. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Precise focal editing; preserves background integrity via discriminative masking; leverages normal maps for better geometric control. Limitations: Requires careful mask definition; quality depends on the T2I model's ability to interpret normal maps; may introduce artifacts if regularization is insufficient. When to use: When localized, text-guided editing of a specific region in a 3D scene is required. When not to use: When global scene generation or editing is needed; when normal map rendering is not feasible. Focaldreamer, also known as GSEditor-DDS and GSEditor-iN2N, is part of the latest series of methods that employ SDS loss within 3DGS to facilitate creative editing. It builds on the idea of using 3DGS for precise and flexible modifications. The method was introduced in the context of 3D editing surveys, highlighting the use of text prompts and discriminative masks for localized changes. It is related to other editing methods like TIP-Editor and CustomNeRF, but distinguishes itself by its specific use of normal maps and ellipsoids.
