name: I3DS
head: I3DS (Iterative 3D Diffusion Synthesis), Iterative 3D Diffusion Synthesis, Iterative 3D Synchronization
body: I3DS is an iterative framework for super-resolving a Low-Resolution (LR) Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a Super-Resolution (SR) NeRF by alternating between 2D image upscaling via diffusion models and 3D NeRF synchronization to ensure view consistency. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity, view-consistent 3D geometry and texture from LR inputs without requiring large multi-view image datasets or high-resolution reference images. Unlike Focaldreamer, DITTO-NeRF, and Text-to-Image-to-3D Reconstruction, I3DS segregates the process into distinct upscaling and synchronization stages rather than jointly optimizing 2D and 3D parameters in a single loop, achieving higher quality than prior-based methods while being significantly faster than diffusion-guided methods like DreamFusion. Inputs: \omega{lr}: The initial low-resolution NeRF weights. I{lr}: The set of low-resolution reference images. P{tr}: The set of training camera poses. y{text}: A fixed text prompt embedding (e.g., "subject, high resolution, 4K, photo"). Outputs: \omega{sr}: The super-resolved NeRF weights. Data Structures: NeRF (\omega): Represents the radiance field. The implementation uses Instant-NGP as the default backbone. Latent Space: Images are encoded into latent vectors z using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). Ray Data: Each ray is defined by origin ro, direction rd, and center color ctr. Parameters: max\stage\iter: Total number of I3DS cycles. Default is 4. max\sync\iter: Number of synchronization steps per stage. Not given in the sources. batch\size: Number of patches processed during upscaling. Default is 16. \eta: Learning rate for all learnable parameters. Default is 1e-2. patch\size: Resolution of random crops in latent space. Default is 128 \times 128 in latent space, corresponding to 512 \times 512 image patches. Algorithm: The method iterates through stages. In each stage, it first upscales the rendered images using a Refinement Step Diffusion (RSD) model, then synchronizes the NeRF to these new images. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def I3DS(ωlr, Ilr, Ptr, maxstageiter): ω = ωlr for stageiter in range(maxstageiter): # Upscaling stage x0 = RENDERIMAGE(ω, Ptr) x0 = INTERPOLATEX4(x0) z0 = VAEENCODE(x0) z0prime = RSD(z0, Ilr) x0prime = VAEDECODE(z0prime) Itr = x0prime # Synchronization stage # maxsynciter not given in sources for synciter in range(maxsynciter): ro, rd, ctr = SAMPLERAYS(Itr, Ptr) chat = RENDERRAYS(ro, rd) # Gradient descent step on ω to minimize ||chat - ctr|| ω = ω - η ∇ω ||chat - ctr||^2 ωold = ω return ωsr = ω RSD Refinement Details: The RSD step refines the latent z0 to be consistent with LR images I{lr} while adding high-frequency details guided by diffusion. It is related to Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) but operates on latent residuals. Input to RSD: Latent z0, text prompt y{text}, noise level y{noise\level}, min timestep t{min}, max timestep t{max}, LR images I{lr}. Output: Refined latent residuals h\theta. The RSD objective is derived from the difference of latent vector residuals z{t-1} and \hat{z}{t-1} (the one-step denoised estimate). The loss is defined as L{RSD} = \|z{t-1} - \hat{z}{t-1}\|. \hat{z}{t-1} is obtained directly from the predicted noise \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt, y, t) using the DDPM denoising equation, avoiding re-noising \hat{z}0. In practice, RSD is applied to random crops of size 128 \times 128 in latent space (corresponding to 512 \times 512 image patches) with a batch size of 16. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the stability of the VAE encode/decode cycle and the diffusion model's denoising process. Ensure that the VAE latent space normalization matches the diffusion model's expected input distribution. Boundaries: The 4x interpolation step assumes the LR NeRF output is compatible with standard image interpolation. If the NeRF output contains NaNs or extreme values, interpolation may fail; clamp or filter invalid pixels before encoding. Time Complexity: The optimization time is dominated by the diffusion upscaling and NeRF synchronization steps. Memory Complexity: Uses dynamic ray sampling to increase ray count when the occupancy grid is pruned, optimizing GPU memory usage. Patch-based processing (128 \times 128 latent crops) reduces memory footprint during upscaling. Measured Performance: On the LLFF dataset, DiSR-NeRF achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM scores among prior-based methods (DiSR-NeRF, IN2N, DreamFusion-SDS, SDx4). NIQE scores improve with increasing I3DS cycles, indicating convergence to high-quality details. Scaling: The method scales with the number of stages (default 4) and sync iterations. Increasing stages improves quality but increases time linearly. Strengths: View-consistent super-resolution without high-res reference images; faster than DreamFusion due to segregated stages; high detail generation via diffusion. Limitations: Longer optimization time than NGP, SDx4, NeRF-SR, and IN2N due to RSD optimization. Relies on the quality of the LR NeRF and LR images. When to use: When super-resolving a NeRF from LR inputs without high-res references is required, and view consistency is critical. When not to use: When computational speed is the primary constraint and high resolution is not needed; use standard NeRF training or simple upsampling instead. I3DS was introduced in the paper "DiSR-NeRF: Diffusion-Guided View-Consistent Super-Resolution NeRF". It builds on the Instant-NGP backbone and utilizes Stable Diffusion for upscaling. The method was developed to address the limitations of existing NeRF super-resolution methods that either require high-resolution reference images or suffer from view inconsistency. The research was supported by the National Research Foundation, Singapore under its AI Singapore Programmes. name: DITTO-NeRF
head: Diffusion-based Iterative Text To Omni-directional 3D Model
body: DITTO-NeRF is a pipeline for generating high-quality 3D Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) from a single text prompt or a reference image. It solves the trade-off between fidelity and diversity in text-to-3D generation by constructing a high-quality partial 3D object for limited "in-boundary" (IB) angles and iteratively reconstructing the remaining "outer-boundary" (OB) angles using an inpainting latent diffusion model. Unlike DreamFusion, which uses a proprietary diffusion model (Imagen), DITTO-NeRF leverages Stable Diffusion via a Latent NeRF representation, achieving higher fidelity and computation-efficient diversity within reasonable training times. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Text prompt y; optional reference image I. If I is absent, it is synthesized from y and a background prompt y{bg}. Outputs: A video V{out} of rendered views of the 3D object, derived from the trained NeRF model \mathcal{N}. Data Structures: NeRF Model \mathcal{N}: A latent NeRF that outputs a 4-channel latent vector zr and weight values P{ws} for each point on a ray, rather than direct RGB. IB Pre-rendered Data: A set of N pre-rendered latent vectors Zp and masks M corresponding to uniform angles within the IB region. Camera Parameters: Principal points cx, cy = 256; focal lengths fx, fy \approx 45\text{mm} (assumed equivalent); image dimensions 512 \times 512. Parameters: t{total}: Total iterations. Typical value: 5000. tu: End of PGVS beta decrease. Value: 0.3 \times t{total} (1500). i{refine}: Iteration threshold for refinement. Value: 1500. N: Number of pre-rendered IB views. Value: 64. \alpha0, \beta0: Initial beta distribution parameters. Values: 2, 8. \lambda{iSDS}: Weight for iSDS loss. Not given in the sources. \lambda{sp}: Weight for sparsity loss. Value: 5 \cdot 10^{-5}. \zeta: Reliability guide parameter. Value: 2. \lambda\eta: Decay rate for reliability guide. Value: 8. N{patch}: Number of patches in refinement. Value: 256. k (or S{patch}): Patch size. Value: 16. \epsilon: Clipping bound for sparsity loss. Value: 10^{-5}. f{ref}: Parameter for dimension refinement rate. Not given in the sources. f{scale}: Scaling factor for non-IB mask. Not given in the sources. Step 1: IB 3D Object Construction If no reference image I is provided, generate one: 1. Concatenate text y and background text y{bg} to form y{image}. 2. Pass y{image} through CLIP to get text embedding. 3. Generate latent z{image} using Inpainting-LDM. 4. Decode z{image} using decoder D to create image I. Generate IB 3D object from I: 1. Extract relative depth map from I using MiDaS monocular depth estimation. 2. Compose a point cloud from the depth map using camera intrinsics (cx, cy, fx, fy). 3. Remove outlier vertices based on proximity to other vertices using a predetermined standard deviation. 4. Apply Poisson surface reconstruction to generate a mesh. 5. Remove mesh parts with density less than a certain quantile. 6. Render N views (uniformly distributed within IB angles) to obtain RGB images, depth, and latent vectors Zp using the VAE encoder of the LDM. Store corresponding masks M. Step 2: Training Loop For iteration i = 1 to t{total}: 1. View Sampling: Determine camera angles \theta, \phi using Progressive Global View Sampling (PGVS). 2. Ray Casting: Obtain ray origin o and direction d via Render-ray(\theta, \phi). 3. NeRF Rendering: The NeRF model \mathcal{N} renders latent zr and weights P{ws} for each point on the ray based on o and d. 4. IB Handling: If the angle is in the IB region: Use Find-closest to retrieve pre-rendered zp and M. Else (OB region), no pre-rendered data is used directly in the loss calculation for IB, but zr is used for OB. 5. Phase Selection: If i \le i{refine}, execute Training. If i > i{refine}, execute Refinement. Training Procedure (i \le i{refine}): 1. Create training text embedding y{train} = \text{CLIP}(y, y{dir}), where y{dir} is direction info. 2. Calculate Inpainting SDS Loss (L{iSDS}): If IB: L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zp, y{train}, M). If OB: Define mask M0 = J / (H \cdot f{scale}) (where J is a constant or identity, f{scale} is a scaling factor). L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zr, y{train}, M0). 3. Calculate Reliability Guidance (LR): LR = [\zeta \cdot M + \eta(t) \cdot (1 - M)] \|zr - zp\|1, where \eta(t) = e^{-t/\lambda\eta}. Note: LR is applied to correct zr towards zp in IB regions, with reliability increasing over time. 4. Calculate Sparsity Loss (L{sp}): \alpha is the weighted sum of a ray clipped to [\epsilon, 1-\epsilon]. L{sp} = -\mathbb{E}[\alpha \log(\alpha) + (1-\alpha) \log(1-\alpha)]. 5. Total Loss: L{total} = \lambda{iSDS} L{iSDS} + \deltaR(\theta, \phi) LR + \lambda{sp} L{sp}. 6. Update \mathcal{N} with L{total}. Refinement Procedure (i > i{refine}): 1. Create refinement text embedding y{refine} = \text{CLIP}(y, y{dir}). 2. Calculate dimensions H, W using Dimension-Refine(i): \text{rate} = \frac{i - t{total} \cdot f{ref}}{t{total} \cdot (1 - f{ref})}. H = 64 \times (1 + \text{rate}), W = 64 \times (1 + \text{rate}). 3. Resize M and zp to H \times W if IB. 4. Apply Add-Patch(M): For j = 1 to N{patch}: Pick random coordinates Px, Py within mask size S{mask}. Set M[Px: Px + k, Py: Py + k] = 1. 5. Calculate L{iSDS}: If IB: L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zp, y{refine}, M). If OB: L{iSDS} = \text{inpainting-LDM}(zr, y{refine}, M0). 6. Calculate L{sp}. 7. Total Loss: L{total} = \lambda{iSDS} L{iSDS} + \lambda{sp} L{sp} (Reliability guidance omitted). 8. Update \mathcal{N} with L{total}. Rendering Output: For each rendering angle: 1. Get o, d via Render-ray. 2. Get zr from \mathcal{N}(o, d). 3. Decode I{out} = D(zr). 4. Append I{out} to V{out}. PGVS Formula: Sampling viewing position x at time t: f(x; t) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^{\alpha(t)-1} (1-x)^{\beta(t)-1}}{B(\alpha(t), \beta(t))} & \text{if } t < tu \\ U(0, 1) & \text{if } t \ge tu \end{cases} Where \alpha(t) = \alpha0 + (1 - \alpha0) \frac{t}{tu} and \beta(t) = \beta0 + (1 - \beta0) \frac{t}{tu}. Angles are sampled via inverse CDF: \theta, \phi = ( \int f(x; t) dx)^{-1} (U{\theta,\phi}(0, 1)) \cdot \text{range}(\theta, \phi). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def DITTONeRF(y, I=None): # Step 1: Generate IB 3D Object if I is None: yimage = CLIP(y + ybg) zimage = InpaintingLDM(yimage) I = Decoder(zimage) Zp, M = GenerateIB3D(I) # Uses MiDaS, Poisson Reconstruction # Step 2: Training Loop for i in range(1, ttotal + 1): theta, phi = PGVS(i, alpha0, beta0, tu, ttotal) if IBCheck(theta, phi): zp, M = FindClosest(Zp, M, theta, phi) IBFlag = True else: IBFlag = False o, d = RenderRay(theta, phi) zr, Pws = NeRFN(o, d) if i <= irefine: TrainingStep(NeRFN, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IBFlag) else: RefinementStep(NeRFN, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IBFlag, i) # Step 3: Rendering Vout = [] for theta, phi in RenderingAngles: o, d = RenderRay(theta, phi) zr = NeRFN(o, d) Iout = Decoder(zr) Vout.append(Iout) return Vout def TrainingStep(N, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IB): ytrain = CLIP(y, DirectionInfo(theta, phi)) if IB: LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zp, ytrain, M) LR = ReliabilityGuide(zp, zr, M, t=i) else: M0 = J / (H fscale) # H, fscale not fully defined in source for training phase, assumed constant or derived LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zr, ytrain, M0) Lsp = SparsityLoss(Pws) Ltotal = lambdaiSDS LiSDS + deltaR(theta, phi) LR + lambdasp Lsp N.Update(Ltotal) def RefinementStep(N, zp, M, zr, Pws, y, theta, phi, IB, i): yrefine = CLIP(y, DirectionInfo(theta, phi)) H, W = DimensionRefine(i, ttotal, fref) if IB: M = Resize(M, H, W) M = AddPatch(M, Npatch, k, Smask) zp = Resize(zp, H, W) LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zp, yrefine, M) else: M0 = J / (H fscale) LiSDS = InpaintingLDM(zr, yrefine, M0) Lsp = SparsityLoss(Pws) Ltotal = lambdaiSDS LiSDS + lambdasp Lsp N.Update(Ltotal) def ReliabilityGuide(zp, zr, M, t): etat = exp(-t / lambdaeta) return (zeta M + etat (1 - M)) L1Norm(zr - zp) def DimensionRefine(iter, ttotal, fref): rate = (iter - ttotal fref) / (ttotal (1 - fref)) H = 64 (1 + rate) W = 64 (1 + rate) return H, W def AddPatch(M, Npatch, k, Smask): for in range(Npatch): Px = Random(Smask) Py = Random(Smask) M[Px: Px + k, Py: Py + k] = 1 return M def CLIP(text1, text2): # Standard CLIP text encoder returning concatenated embedding return textencoder(text1 + text2) def InpaintingLDM(latent, textcond, mask): # Inpainting Latent Diffusion Model returning SDS loss gradient return diffusionmodel.sdsloss(latent, textcond, mask) def Decoder(latent): # VAE decoder converting latent to RGB image return vaedecoder(latent) def GenerateIB3D(I): # Uses MiDaS, point cloud, outlier removal, Poisson, renders N views depth = midas(I) points = depthtopointcloud(depth, cx, cy, fx, fy) points = removeoutliers(points, stdthreshold) mesh = poissonreconstruction(points) mesh = removelowdensity(mesh, quantilethreshold) Zp, M = renderviews(mesh, N, IBangles) return Zp, M def PGVS(i, alpha0, beta0, tu, ttotal): # Samples angles using beta distribution PDF alpha = alpha0 + (1 - alpha0) (i / tu) beta = beta0 + (1 - beta0) (i / tu) if i < tu: x = samplebeta(alpha, beta) else: x = uniform(0, 1) theta, phi = inversecdf(x) range(theta, phi) return theta, phi def RenderRay(theta, phi): # Computes origin and direction from spherical angles o = cameraorigin(theta, phi) d = cameradirection(theta, phi) return o, d def FindClosest(Zp, M, theta, phi): # Nearest neighbor lookup in pre-rendered set idx = argmin(dist(Zp, theta, phi)) return Zp[idx], M[idx] def SparsityLoss(Pws): # Computes sparsity loss formula alpha = clip(weightedsum(Pws), epsilon, 1 - epsilon) return -mean(alpha log(alpha) + (1 - alpha) log(1 - alpha)) def IBCheck(theta, phi): # Checks if angle falls within IB region return theta in IBthetarange and phi in IBphirange def DirectionInfo(theta, phi): # Converts angles to directional text prompt return f"view from theta={theta}, phi={phi}" def Resize(tensor, H, W): # Resizes tensor to H x W return interpolate(tensor, size=(H, W)) def Random(size): # Returns random integer in [0, size) return randint(0, size) def L1Norm(x): # Returns L1 norm return sum(abs(x)) def weightedsum(Pws): # Returns weighted sum of ray weights return sum(Pws) def clip(x, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, x)) def mean(x): return sum(x) / len(x) def log(x): return math.log(x) def uniform(a, b): return random.uniform(a, b) def samplebeta(alpha, beta): return random.betavariate(alpha, beta) def inversecdf(x): # Approximates inverse CDF for angle mapping return x def cameraorigin(theta, phi): return [0, 0, 0] def cameradirection(theta, phi): return [sin(theta)cos(phi), sin(theta)sin(phi), cos(theta)] def dist(Zp, theta, phi): return abs(Zp - target) def interpolate(tensor, size): return tensor.resize(size) def randint(a, b): return random.randint(a, b) def mathlog(x): return math.log(x) def randombetavariate(alpha, beta): return random.betavariate(alpha, beta) def randomuniform(a, b): return random.uniform(a, b) def randomrandint(a, b): return random.randint(a, b) def random(): return random.random() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Estimation: MiDaS relies on shadows and model priors. Images with minimal shadows or out-of-distribution inputs lead to inaccurate depth, causing inadequate IB 3D objects. Diffusion Quality: Poor quality or low-probability images from the diffusion model may not follow image priors, causing convergence issues and discontinuity between the image prior and diffusion-generated parts. IB Angle Width: If the IB angle is too narrow, matching between IB and OB is insufficient. If too wide, the Find-closest process becomes a bottleneck. Pre-rendering Count (N): Too small N leads to insufficient IB training; too large increases computational burden. N=64 is optimal. Patch Refinement: Insufficient N{patch} fails to produce appropriate refinement; excessive N{patch} may disrupt existing IB structures. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses Latent NeRF, which is more computation-efficient than standard NeRF. It achieves satisfactory quality within reasonable training time compared to Stable-DreamFusion. Scaling: The refinement stage linearly increases resolution from 64 \times 64 to 128 \times 128. Strengths: Higher fidelity and quality in image-to-3D correspondence; higher fidelity and computation-efficient diversity in text-to-3D generation compared to Stable Diffusion-based studies. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the monocular depth estimation and the diffusion model's ability to generate high-quality images. Convergence issues may arise with low-probability diffusion outputs. DITTO-NeRF was introduced in the paper "DITTO-NeRF: Diffusion-based Iterative Text To Omni-directional 3D Model". It builds on the DreamFusion approach but replaces the proprietary Imagen model with Stable Diffusion via Latent NeRF. The sparsity loss used in the method was introduced in Dreamfields and employed in Latent-NeRF. The method is supported by NRF grants. DITTO-NeRF: Diffusion-based Iterative Text To Omni-directional 3D Model, https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02827v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Text-to-Image-to-3D Reconstruction
head: Text-to-3D using 2D Diffusion, Two-step Text-to-3D
body: A method for synthesizing 3D models from text prompts by first generating a 2D image using a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model and then reconstructing that image into a 3D representation using RealFusion. It differs from one-step methods like DreamFusion by decoupling the semantic generation from the geometric reconstruction, offering easier user control and potentially addressing diversity issues. The method operates in two distinct stages: 2D image synthesis and 3D reconstruction. Inputs: Text prompt P. Pretrained 2D text-to-image diffusion model (e.g., Stable Diffusion). RealFusion model for single-image 3D reconstruction. Outputs: A 3D model (typically a NeRF or mesh) representing the object described by P. Data Structures: 2D Image: A single RGB image I{2D} generated by the diffusion model. 3D Representation: A Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) parameterized by an MLP, initialized from the single image I{2D} using RealFusion. Steps: 1. 2D Image Generation: Use the text prompt P to generate a single 2D image I{2D} using a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model. The user may sample multiple images and select the most suitable one. 2. 3D Reconstruction (RealFusion): Initialize a NeRF-like model with random weights or using the generated image I{2D} as a prior. Optimize the NeRF parameters to reconstruct the 3D geometry and appearance from I{2D} using the RealFusion algorithm. RealFusion uses a 360° reconstruction approach, lifting the single 2D image into a full 3D scene. Parameters: Diffusion Model: Pretrained text-to-image model (e.g., Stable Diffusion). RealFusion Settings: Standard RealFusion optimization parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Janus Problem: The method is susceptible to the "Janus problem," where reconstructions have two or more faces, because the loss function tries to make every view look like the input image. View-specific prompting (e.g., “back view”) partially alleviates this but does not eliminate it. Floaters: Floaters (small, disconnected geometry) are a significant issue, appearing in the majority of reconstructions. Image-specific prompts greatly alleviate this issue. Dream Fields is a zero-shot 3D generation method that synthesizes diverse 3D objects from natural language descriptions by optimizing a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It differs from sibling methods like Difix 3D Generation Pipeline by relying solely on multi-view CLIP score constraints to guide the radiance field, without requiring 3D shape priors or multi-view input data. The Difix 3D Generation Pipeline is a method for 3D-aware image generation and editing that processes multi-view or single-view inputs using a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with skip connections and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), combined with a 1-step UNet denoiser. It differs from standard diffusion pipelines by operating at a fixed diffusion timestep to enable single-step generation, and by explicitly handling multi-view tensor rearrangements to maintain consistency across views. Time Complexity: The method involves two stages: 2D image generation and 3D reconstruction. The time complexity depends on the diffusion model and RealFusion optimization steps. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the diffusion model and the NeRF representation. Strengths: Easier user control compared to one-step methods; potential to address diversity of generation issues. Limitations: Susceptible to the Janus problem and floaters. When to Use: When user control over the 2D image is desired or when diversity in generation is a concern. When Not to Use: When real-time generation is required or when high geometric accuracy without artifacts is critical. The method was introduced in the context of exploring text-to-3D generation by combining 2D diffusion models with 3D reconstruction techniques. It builds on the idea of using 2D priors to guide 3D synthesis, offering an alternative to direct 3D optimization methods like DreamFusion. DreamFusion: Text-to-3D using 2D Diffusion, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2209.14988, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) RealFusion 360° Reconstruction of Any Object from a Single Image, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00816, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Dream Fields
body: Dream Fields is a zero-shot 3D generation method that synthesizes diverse 3D objects from natural language descriptions by optimizing a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It guides the optimization using multi-view constraints based on CLIP image-text scores, without requiring 3D shape priors or multi-view input data. It builds on Text-to-Image-to-3D Reconstruction and differs from siblings like Difix 3D Generation Pipeline by relying exclusively on frozen CLIP embeddings for text-to-3D guidance rather than diffusion priors or explicit 3D supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A natural language text caption. Output: A trained NeRF radiance field representing the 3D object. Data Structures: NeRF Model: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) parameterized by weights \theta. It takes a 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 as input. CLIP Model: A pre-trained vision-language model that maps images and text to a shared embedding space. It is used as a frozen guidance signal. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF radiance field parameters \theta randomly. 2. Sampling: For each optimization step, sample a set of camera viewpoints around the object. 3. Rendering: For each viewpoint, render a 2D image by ray-marching through the NeRF. 4. CLIP Scoring: Pass each rendered image and the input text caption into the CLIP model to compute the image-text similarity score. 5. Optimization: Update the NeRF parameters \theta to maximize the aggregate CLIP score across all sampled views. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence or a fixed number of iterations. Formulas: The objective maximizes the mean CLIP score over N sampled views: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \text{CLIP}(Ii(\theta), T) where N is the number of sampled views, T is the text caption, and \text{CLIP}(I, T) denotes the cosine similarity between the image embedding EI and text embedding ET in the shared space: \frac{EI \cdot ET}{\|EI\| \|ET\|}. Gradient ascent updates \theta to maximize this objective. Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Number of views N: Not given in the sources. Optimization steps: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Adversarial Generations: Using a single CLIP model may lead to adversarial artifacts or poor geometric structure. An ensemble of CLIP models can mitigate this issue. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed for NeRF and CLIP operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dreamfields(textcaption, numviews, numiterations, lr): # Initialize NeRF MLP parameters theta randomly theta = [random.uniform(-0.1, 0.1) for in range(numparams)] # Load frozen CLIP model clipmodel = CLIPModel() # Pre-encode text caption txtemb = clipmodel.encodetext(textcaption) for step in range(numiterations): gradaccum = [0.0] numparams for in range(numviews): # Sample random camera pose around origin campos = randomspherepoint() camdir = randomunitvector() # Ray-march through NeRF to render image image = raymarch(theta, campos, camdir) # Compute CLIP image-text similarity score imgemb = clipmodel.encodeimage(image) score = dot(imgemb, txtemb) / (norm(imgemb) norm(txtemb)) # Compute gradient of score w.r.t. theta via automatic differentiation grad = gradient(score, theta) gradaccum = [g1 + g2 for g1, g2 in zip(gradaccum, grad)] # Average gradients and perform gradient ascent step theta = [p + lr (g / numviews) for p, g in zip(theta, gradaccum)] return theta Time Complexity: High, due to iterative optimization and repeated CLIP inference for multiple views per step. Memory Complexity: Moderate, storing the NeRF parameters and CLIP model weights. Strengths: Zero-shot generation from text only; no 3D data required. Limitations: May suffer from adversarial artifacts if not using ensemble guidance; computationally expensive optimization loop. When to use: When only text prompts are available and 3D data is absent. When not to use: When high-fidelity geometry is critical without ensemble guidance, or when computational resources are limited. Dream Fields was introduced by [JMB 21] as an optimization-based framework combining NeRF with CLIP. It leverages a pre-trained CLIP model to guide the generation process, enabling zero-shot 3D object creation from natural language captions. It is part of the broader trend of using 2D diffusion models and vision-language models for 3D generation. name: Difix 3D Generation Pipeline
head: Difix
body: The Difix 3D Generation Pipeline is a method for 3D-aware image generation and editing that processes multi-view or single-view inputs using a modified Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with skip connections and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), combined with a 1-step UNet denoiser. It differs from standard diffusion pipelines by operating at a fixed diffusion timestep to enable single-step generation, and by explicitly handling multi-view tensor rearrangements to maintain consistency across views. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A text prompt (string), an input tensor x of shape (b, v, c, h, w) where b is batch size, v is number of views, c is channels, h is height, and w is width. Optional prompttokens can be provided directly. Outputs: A denoised output tensor of shape (b, v, c, h, w) with values clamped to [-1, 1]. Data Structures VAE: A modified VAE with LoRA adapters. The decoder includes specific skip connections: skipconv1 (512->512), skipconv2 (256->512), skipconv3 (128->512), and skipconv4 (128->256). These are 1x1 convolutions with bias=False, initialized to 10^{-5}. UNet: A 1-step denoiser. If mvunet is True, a multi-view variant is used. Scheduler: A diffusion scheduler (e.g., DDIM) configured for single-step sampling. Parameters lorarankvae: Rank for VAE LoRA adapter. Default: 4. mvunet: Boolean flag to use multi-view UNet variant. Default: False. timestep: Fixed diffusion timestep for 1-step generation. Default: 999. scalingfactor: Scaling factor for VAE latent space (value not specified in sources). Steps 1. Text Encoding: Encode the text prompt using a tokenizer and CLIPTextModel to obtain captionenc. If prompttokens are provided, use them directly instead. 2. Input Rearrangement: Rearrange the input tensor x from shape (b, v, c, h, w) to (b \cdot v, c, h, w) to process all views as a single batch. 3. VAE Encoding: Encode the rearranged input through the VAE encoder: z = \text{vae.encode}(x{\text{rearranged}}).\text{latent\dist}.\text{sample}() \times \text{scaling\factor}. 4. Caption Repetition: Repeat captionenc across the view dimension to match the batch size of the latents: \text{caption\enc}{\text{repeated}} = \text{repeat}(\text{caption\enc}, 'b \ n \ c \rightarrow (b \ v) \ n \ c', v=\text{num\views}). 5. UNet Denoising: Pass the latent z and repeated caption to the UNet at the fixed timestep: \text{model\pred} = \text{unet}(z, \text{timesteps}, \text{encoder\hidden\states}=\text{caption\enc}{\text{repeated}}).\text{sample}. 6. Scheduler Step: Step the scheduler to obtain the denoised latent: z{\text{denoised}} = \text{sched.step}(\text{model\pred}, \text{timesteps}, z, \text{return\dict}=\text{True}).\text{prev\sample}. 7. Skip Connection Handling: Pass the encoder's currentdownblocks to the decoder's incomingskipacts to enable skip connections. 8. VAE Decoding: Decode the denoised latent: \text{output\image}{\text{rearranged}} = (\text{vae.decode}(z{\text{denoised}} / \text{scaling\factor}).\text{sample}).\text{clamp}(-1, 1). 9. Output Rearrangement: Rearrange the output back to shape (b, v, c, h, w) and return. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def difixforward(x, textprompt, prompttokens=None, scalingfactor=0.18215, timestep=999): """ x: Tensor of shape (b, v, c, h, w) textprompt: String prompttokens: Optional Tensor """ # 1. Text Encoding if prompttokens is not None: captionenc = prompttokens else: # Placeholder for tokenizer and CLIPTextModel implementation details not provided in source captionenc = encodetext(textprompt) # 2. Rearrange input: (b, v, c, h, w) -> (bv, c, h, w) b, v, c, h, w = x.shape xflat = x.reshape(b v, c, h, w) # 3. VAE Encode # latentdist.sample() returns noise from the distribution z = vae.encode(xflat).latentdist.sample() scalingfactor # 4. Repeat caption across views # captionenc shape: (b, seqlen, d) # Target shape: (bv, seqlen, d) captionencrepeated = repeat(captionenc, 'b n c -> (b v) n c', v=v) # 5. UNet Denoising at fixed timestep timesteps = torch.tensor([timestep]) modelpred = unet(z, timesteps, encoderhiddenstates=captionencrepeated).sample # 6. Scheduler Step # Assuming a standard scheduler interface like DDIMScheduler scheduleroutput = sched.step(modelpred, timesteps, z, returndict=True) zdenoised = scheduleroutput.prevsample # 7. Prepare Skip Connections # Pass encoder's down blocks to decoder's skip acts # Implementation detail: vae.decode handles this internally or via explicit hook # Assuming vae.decode accepts skipacts or has internal hook mechanism decoderskipacts = vae.encoder.currentdownblocks # 8. VAE Decode # Decode and clamp outputflat = vae.decode(zdenoised / scalingfactor, skipacts=decoderskipacts).sample outputflat = torch.clamp(outputflat, -1, 1) # 9. Rearrange output: (bv, c, h, w) -> (b, v, c, h, w) output = outputflat.reshape(b, v, c, h, w) return output Edge Cases and Pitfalls Input image dimensions (h, w) must be divisible by 8. The VAE sample method automatically rounds down width and height to the nearest multiple of 8 before processing. Time Complexity: Single-step generation reduces inference time significantly compared to iterative diffusion, but the multi-view processing and VAE/UNet overhead remain substantial. Memory Complexity: Depends on batch size b, number of views v, and resolution. The rearrangement to (b \cdot v, c, h, w) increases peak memory usage for the UNet pass compared to single-view processing. Strengths: Enables fast, single-step 3D-aware generation and editing. The modified VAE with skip connections and LoRA allows for efficient fine-tuning and adaptation. Limitations: Requires input dimensions to be multiples of 8. Performance depends on the quality of the 1-step denoiser and scheduler configuration. The Difix 3D Generation Pipeline is part of the Difix3D project by NVIDIA-Tlabs, released as an open-source repository. It builds upon techniques from differentiable rendering and diffusion models to enable efficient 3D content creation. nv-tlabs/Difix3D, https://github.com/nv-tlabs/Difix3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: DreamAvatar
body: DreamAvatar is a diffusion-based 3D avatar generation method that synthesizes text-guided 3D human avatars by combining a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representation with a pre-trained 2D diffusion model. It addresses the challenge of generating high-fidelity, personalized 3D human models from text prompts by leveraging an SMPL model as a geometric shape prior. Unlike general scene generation methods, DreamAvatar is specifically designed for human avatars, using the SMPL prior to constrain the NeRF optimization to plausible human geometries. DreamAvatar follows a DreamFusion-like optimization loop where a NeRF is trained to render images that match the distribution of a text-conditioned diffusion model. The key distinction is the integration of an SMPL parametric model to provide a strong shape prior for the human body/head. Inputs: Text prompt P describing the desired avatar. Pre-trained 2D diffusion model \phi. SMPL model parameters (initial guess or fixed template). NeRF parameters \theta (representing the radiance field). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta and SMPL parameters defining the 3D avatar. Data Structures: NeRF: Standard multi-layer perceptron mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. SMPL Model: Parametric human body model providing a mesh surface and pose/shape parameters. Diffusion Model: U-Net architecture conditioned on text embeddings. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize NeRF parameters \theta and SMPL parameters. 2. Viewpoint Sampling: Sample a random camera viewpoint around the avatar. 3. Rendering: Render a 2D image x from the current NeRF state at the sampled viewpoint. 4. Noise Addition: Sample a diffusion timestep t and Gaussian noise \epsilon. 5. Latent Perturbation: Create a noisy version zt = \alphat x + \sigmat \epsilon. 6. Noise Prediction: Pass zt, the text prompt P, and timestep t into the diffusion model \phi to predict the noise \hat{\epsilon} = \hat{\epsilon}\phi(zt; P, t). 7. Loss Computation: Compute gradients \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} using the difference between predicted and actual noise, adapted with Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) and the SMPL shape prior. 8. Optimization: Update NeRF parameters \theta (and SMPL parameters) using gradient descent. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–8 for a fixed number of iterations or until convergence. Formulas: The core loss is derived from Score Distillation Sampling (SDS), adapted to incorporate the SMPL shape prior. Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. AvatarStudio is a text-based editing method for dynamic head avatars using NeRF and diffusion. It is distinguished from its siblings by its focus on time-varying multi-view performance captures and its use of View- and Time-aware Score Distillation Sampling (VT-SDS) for personalized editing across the time and view domains. Choose this method when editing dynamic, time-varying head avatars from multi-view video data with text prompts. Link: AvatarStudio. Time Complexity: High, due to the iterative nature of NeRF optimization and the computational cost of diffusion model inference at each step. Memory Complexity: High, storing the NeRF weights, SMPL parameters, and intermediate rendering buffers. Performance: Generates high-fidelity 3D avatars with good text alignment. Strengths: Strong geometric priors via SMPL reduce artifacts; text-guided control. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: For generating personalized 3D human avatars from text. DreamAvatar was introduced in April 2023. It emerged as part of the growing research area of diffusion-based 3D avatar generation with text guidance, powered by neural fields and NeRF. It is conceptually similar to DreamHuman (June 2023) and AvatarVerse (August 2023), all of which use an SMPL model as a shape prior and text-guided 2D image generation via diffusion to create training data in a DreamFusion-like pipeline. name: Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF Training
head: Joint optimization of NeRF and Diffusion Prior, SSDNeRF training
body: Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF Training (SSDNeRF) jointly optimizes scene codes, a diffusion prior, and a NeRF decoder in a single training stage to minimize a combined loss of rendering fidelity and diffusion prior consistency. Unlike two-stage methods that ignore the prior term during autoencoder training—effectively setting the render-to-prior weight ratio to infinity and resulting in biased and noisy scene codes—this approach constrains codes with both terms simultaneously. It builds on Diffusion-guided Optimization by integrating the prior directly into the latent space optimization loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A dataset of images \{y{ij}^{gt}\} with corresponding rays \{r{ij}^{gt}\}, where i indexes the scene and j indexes the ray (pixel). Outputs: Optimized scene codes \{xi\}, diffusion prior parameters \phi, and NeRF decoder parameters \psi. Data Structures: Scene Codes (xi): Represented as triplanes with shape \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 6 \times 128 \times 128}. Diffusion Prior (\phi): A U-Net based Gaussian diffusion model that takes a noisy code xi^{(t)} and timestep t as input, outputting a denoised code \hat{x}i. NeRF Decoder (\psi): A decoder that maps scene codes and ray coordinates to pixel RGB values y{\psi}(x, r). Formulas: The total loss function is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{\text{rend}} \mathcal{L}{\text{rend}}(\{xi\}, \psi) + \lambda{\text{diff}} \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}}(\{xi\}, \phi) where \mathcal{L}{\text{rend}} is the rendering loss against known observations and \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}} is the approximate upper bound of the diffusion negative log-likelihood (NLL). The empirical weighting factors are calculated as: \lambda{\text{diff}}:= \frac{c{\text{diff}}}{\text{EMA} \|xi\|F^2} \lambda{\text{rend}}:= \frac{c{\text{rend}} (1 - e^{-0.1 Nv})}{Nv} where c{\text{diff}} and c{\text{rend}} are constant scales, Nv is the number of available views, and \text{EMA} \|xi\|F^2 is the exponential moving average of the scene codes' Frobenius norms. The rendering weight calibration prevents the loss from scaling linearly with the number of rays under the ray independence assumption. Algorithm: The training uses a nested loop structure with prior gradient caching to address the computational expense of the diffusion loss. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. X = initializescenecodes() phi = initializediffusionprior() psi = initializenerfdecoder() emanormsq = 0.0 lr = 0.01 # Learning rate for kout in range(1, Kout + 1): batchscenes = samplebatchscenes(Bsc) # Compute gradients for diffusion loss w.r.t. phi and X gphi, gxdiff = computegradients(lambdadiff Ldiff(X, phi), [phi, batchscenes]) # Update diffusion parameters using Adam optimizer phi = phi - lr gphi # Cache the prior gradient for reuse in inner loop cachedgxdiff = gxdiff for kin in range(1, Kin + 1): batchrays = samplebatchrays(Bray) # Compute gradients for rendering loss w.r.t. X gxrend = computegradients(lambdarend Lrend(X, psi, batchrays), [batchscenes]) # Combine cached diffusion gradient with current rendering gradient gxtotal = gxrend + cachedgxdiff # Update scene codes using Adam optimizer batchscenes = batchscenes - lr gxtotal # Update EMA of scene codes' Frobenius norms for dynamic weighting for xi in batchscenes: emanormsq = 0.9 emanormsq + 0.1 frobeniusnorm(xi)2 lambdadiff = cdiff / emanormsq # If this is the last inner iteration, update decoder parameters if kin == Kin: gpsi = computegradients(lambdarend Lrend(X, psi, batchrays), [psi]) psi = psi - lr gpsi Parameters: K{out}: Number of outer iterations. K{in}: Number of inner iterations per outer loop. c{\text{diff}}, c{\text{rend}}: Constant scales for empirical weighting. Nv: Number of available views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: The diffusion loss \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}} is computationally expensive to evaluate compared to the rendering loss \mathcal{L}{\text{rend}}, which reduces overall efficiency. The method mitigates this via prior gradient caching, reusing \nablax \lambda{\text{diff}} \mathcal{L}{\text{diff}} for multiple Adam steps while refreshing rendering gradients each step. Bias in Two-Stage Methods: If the prior term is ignored during initial training (as in two-stage methods), the resulting scene codes become biased and noisy. Time Complexity: The method is less efficient than rendering-only optimization due to the expensive diffusion loss evaluation. However, prior gradient caching reduces the number of diffusion passes required, accelerating reconstruction. Memory Complexity: Requires storing scene codes \{xi\}, diffusion parameters \phi, and decoder parameters \psi. Strengths: Produces more generalizable and less noisy scene codes compared to two-stage methods by constraining codes with both rendering and prior terms. Limitations: Higher computational cost per iteration compared to standard NeRF training. SSDNeRF was introduced in the paper "Single-Stage Diffusion NeRF: A Unified Approach to 3D Generation and Reconstruction". It addresses the limitations of previous two-stage generative neural field methods, which ignore the prior term during autoencoder training, leading to biased and noisy scene codes. The method is related to score distillation techniques. name: ReconFusion
body: ReconFusion is a 3D reconstruction method that recovers high-quality scenes from a limited number of input images (few-view setting) by regularizing a NeRF-based pipeline with a diffusion prior trained for novel view synthesis. Unlike methods that rely solely on geometric constraints or text-guided score distillation, ReconFusion explicitly trains a diffusion model to predict plausible novel views conditioned on input images and poses, then uses this model to supervise the NeRF optimization at unobserved viewpoints. It sets itself apart from siblings like DreamFusion by using a multiview-conditioned diffusion prior rather than a text-conditioned one, and from SparseFusion by sampling a new image at each iteration rather than using multistep sampling from a noisy encoding of the current rendering. ReconFusion consists of two main components: a diffusion model for novel view synthesis and a NeRF optimization loop. The method optimizes a NeRF representation \psi (using Zip-NeRF as the backbone) to minimize two losses: a reconstruction loss on observed views and a sample loss on novel views predicted by the diffusion model. Inputs: A set of N input images x{obs} = \{xi\}{i=1}^N with corresponding camera poses \pi{obs} = \{\pii\}{i=1}^N. A pretrained Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) encoder E, denoising U-Net \epsilon\theta, and decoder D. A pretrained CLIP image encoder. A PixelNeRF-style encoder R\phi. Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \psi. Rendered images from novel viewpoints. 1. NeRF (\psi): Standard Zip-NeRF representation. 2. PixelNeRF Encoder (R\phi): A small U-Net that takes input images of resolution 512 \times 512 and outputs a feature map f of resolution 64 \times 64 with 128 channels. 3. Diffusion Model: VAE: Encodes images to latents of dimension 64 \times 64 \times 8 from 512 \times 512 \times 3 input images. U-Net (\epsilon\theta): Takes noisy latents, feature maps, and CLIP embeddings as input. CLIP Embeddings: Text/image embeddings used for cross-attention in the U-Net. Before reconstruction, the diffusion model is finetuned for novel view synthesis. 1. Conditioning: For a target novel view \pi, select the 3 nearest camera positions from the observed inputs \pi{obs}. 2. Feature Rendering: Use the PixelNeRF encoder R\phi to render a feature map f for the target view \pi using the input images and poses: f = R\phi(x{obs}, \pi{obs}, \pi) 3. Latent Encoding: Encode the input images and the target view image (from dataset) into latents using the VAE encoder E. 4. Diffusion Process: Add noise to the target latent z to create zt at timestep t. 5. Cross-Attention: Compute CLIP embeddings of the input images and inject them into the U-Net via cross-attention. 6. Loss: Train the U-Net \epsilon\theta to predict the noise or clean latent. The model is finetuned on a mixture of RealEstate10K, CO3D, MVImgNet, and Objaverse datasets. 7. Classifier-Free Guidance: During training, set input images to all zeros with probability 10% to enable classifier-free guidance. For each training iteration of the NeRF: 1. Sample Observed View: Randomly select an observed pose \pi{obs} and image x{obs}. 2. Render Observed View: Render image x{render} from the current NeRF \psi at \pi{obs}. 3. Compute Reconstruction Loss: Calculate the Charbonnier loss between x{render} and x{obs}: L{recon}(\psi) = \mathbb{E}{x{obs},\pi{obs}} \ell(x(\psi, \pi{obs}), x{obs}) 4. Sample Novel View Pose: Select a novel pose \pi from a distribution based on the input poses (e.g., nearest 3 inputs). 5. Render Novel View Feature Map: Use the PixelNeRF encoder R\phi to generate the feature map f for \pi using the input images. 6. Render Novel View Image: Render image x from the current NeRF \psi at \pi. 7. Compute Noisy Latent: Compute a noisy latent by adding noise to the current NeRF rendering from the sample pose. 8. Diffusion Sampling: Input the noisy latent, feature map f, and CLIP embeddings to the U-Net \epsilon\theta. Perform k=10 DDIM sampling steps to generate a denoised latent \hat{z}. Decode \hat{z} to image \hat{x} using VAE decoder D. Apply classifier-free guidance with scale 3.0. 9. Compute Sample Loss: Calculate the loss between the rendered image x and the diffusion-generated sample \hat{x}: L{sample}(\psi) = \mathbb{E}{\pi,t} w(t) (\|x - \hat{x}\pi\|1 + Lp(x, \hat{x}\pi)) where Lp is the perceptual distance (LPIPS). 10. Total Loss: Combine losses with a weighting factor w(t) that decays linearly from 1 to 0.1 over training: L{total} = L{recon} + w(t) L{sample} 11. Update: Update NeRF parameters \psi using gradient descent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F nerf = ZipNeRF() pixelnerfencoder = PixelNeRFEncoder() vaeencoder = VAEEncoder() vaedecoder = VAEDecoder() diffusionunet = DenoisingUNet() clipencoder = CLIPEncoder() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(nerf.parameters(), lr=1e-4) def charbonnierloss(pred, target, epsilon=1e-3): """Compute Charbonnier loss.""" return torch.sqrt(F.mseloss(pred, target) + epsilon2) def samplenovelpose(observedposes, k=3): """Select k nearest camera positions from observed inputs.""" # Compute pairwise distances between observedposes and a candidate distribution # Return the pose with minimum average distance to the k nearest observed poses pass def addnoise(latent, t, alphat, sigmat): """Add Gaussian noise to latent at timestep t.""" noise = torch.randnlike(latent) return alphat(latent, t) latent + sigmat(latent, t) noise def diffusionsample(noisylatent, featuremap, clipemb, t, guidancescale=3.0, steps=10): """Perform DDIM sampling to denoise latent.""" currentlatent = noisylatent for i in range(steps): # Predict noise using U-Net with cross-attention for featuremap and clipemb noisepred = diffusionunet(currentlatent, featuremap, clipemb, t) # Apply classifier-free guidance by interpolating conditional and unconditional predictions if guidancescale > 1.0: noisepred = noisepred + guidancescale (noisepred - unconditionalnoisepred) # Update currentlatent using standard DDIM step currentlatent = ddimupdate(currentlatent, noisepred, t) return currentlatent def perceptualloss(img1, img2): """Compute LPIPS perceptual distance.""" # Forward pass through pretrained LPIPS network return lpipsnet(img1, img2) def trainreconfusion(inputimages, observedposes, numiterations=1000): """ Train NeRF using ReconFusion. inputimages: List of input images (N images) observedposes: List of observed poses (N poses) """ # Precompute CLIP embeddings for input images clipemb = clipencoder(inputimages) # Annealing schedule for tmin tminstart = 1.0 tminend = 0.0 for step in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample observed view idx = torch.randint(0, len(inputimages), (1,)).item() obsimg = inputimages[idx] obspose = observedposes[idx] # 2. Render observed view renderimgobs = nerf.render(obspose) # 3. Compute Reconstruction Loss (Charbonnier) reconloss = charbonnierloss(renderimgobs, obsimg) # 4. Sample novel view pose novelpose = samplenovelpose(observedposes) # 5. Render feature map for novel view featmap = pixelnerfencoder(inputimages, observedposes, novelpose) # 6. Render novel view image renderimgnovel = nerf.render(novelpose) # 7. Encode to latent latentnovel = vaeencoder(renderimgnovel) # 8. Add noise # tmax is fixed at 1.0 # tmin is annealed tmin = tminstart - (tminstart - tminend) (step / numiterations) t = torch.rand(1).item() (1.0 - tmin) + tmin noisylatent = addnoise(latentnovel, t, alphat=lambda z, t: 1.0 - t, sigmat=lambda z, t: t) # 9. Diffusion Sampling # Use classifier-free guidance scale 3.0 # k=10 steps denoisedlatent = diffusionsample( noisylatent, featmap, clipemb, t, guidancescale=3.0, steps=10) # Decode to image sampleimg = vaedecoder(denoisedlatent) # 10. Compute Sample Loss l1loss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderimgnovel - sampleimg)) lpipsloss = perceptualloss(renderimgnovel, sampleimg) sampleloss = l1loss + lpipsloss # 11. Weighting decay # Linear decay from 1 to 0.1 wt = 1.0 - 0.9 (step / numiterations) # 12. Total Loss totalloss = reconloss + wt sampleloss # 13. Update optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Diffusion Model: Latent Diffusion Model [42] with 64 \times 64 \times 8 latent space, 512 \times 512 \times 3 input resolution. PixelNeRF Encoder: Outputs 64 \times 64 feature map with 128 channels. Classifier-Free Guidance Scale: 3.0. Sampling Steps (k): 10 DDIM steps. Timesteps: t{max} = 1.0 fixed; t{min} annealed from 1.0 to 0.0. Loss Weighting (w(t)): Linearly decayed from 1 to 0.1 over training. Batch Size: 256 (for diffusion model training). Learning Rate: 10^{-4} (for joint training of PixelNeRF and U-Net). NeRF Training Iterations: 1000. Nearest Neighbors: 3 nearest camera positions used for conditioning. Reconstruction Loss: Charbonnier loss. Sample Loss: L1 + LPIPS. Few-View Scenarios: With 3 or 9 views, the reconstruction problem is severely underconstrained. The diffusion prior prevents catastrophic failures and improves robustness. Dense Capture: With 54 views, the method helps reduce "fog" and "floater" artifacts common in NeRF while preserving well-sampled regions. Novel View Selection: Views should not be placed inside objects or behind walls. The method uses a distribution based on known input poses to select reasonable novel views. Time Complexity: The method requires training a diffusion model (250k iterations) and then optimizing the NeRF (1000 iterations). Each NeRF iteration involves rendering, diffusion sampling (10 steps), and loss computation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the NeRF size and the diffusion model (U-Net, VAE, CLIP). The latent space is 64 \times 64 \times 8. Performance: Outperforms existing baselines on forward-facing and 360-degree scenes with few input views (3, 6, 9 views). Strengths: Effective regularizer for few-view NeRFs; reduces artifacts in dense captures; supports any number of input images via PixelNeRF conditioning. Limitations: Requires training a diffusion model on multiview data; relies on the quality of the diffusion prior. When to Use: When only a few photos are available for 3D reconstruction. When Not to Use: When dense capture is available and artifacts are minimal, the overhead may not be justified. ReconFusion was introduced in 2023/2024 by researchers aiming to reduce the need for dense capture in 3D reconstruction. It builds on the idea of using diffusion models as priors for 3D generation, similar to DreamFusion [36] and SparseFusion [67], but specifically conditions the diffusion model on input images and poses for novel view synthesis. The method uses Zip-NeRF as the backbone. name: Nerfbusters
head: Density Score Distillation Sampling (DSDS), Nerfbusters method
body: Nerfbusters is a 3D diffusion-based regularization method that improves scene geometry and removes ghostly artifacts (floaters) from Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) trained on casually captured images. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like DreamFusion by using a local 3D geometric prior learned from synthetic surface patches rather than a global scene prior or 2.5D RGB-D priors. This local approach is category-agnostic, simpler to model, and explicitly 3D-consistent, making it suitable for arbitrary scenes without requiring complex conditioning. The core innovation is the Density Score Distillation Sampling (DSDS) loss, which regularizes NeRF densities against a pre-trained 3D diffusion model without backpropagating through the diffusion network. The method consists of two phases: training a local 3D diffusion prior on synthetic data, and applying this prior to a NeRF during optimization via the DSDS loss and a visibility loss. Inputs: Training images Ij and camera poses Cj. Pre-trained 3D diffusion model \epsilon\theta (trained on ShapeNet cubes). Hyperparameters: Diffusion timestep t \in [10, 50], density threshold \tau = 0.01, density weight w = 0.01, visibility threshold V{thresh} = 2 (in normalized bounds). Outputs: Optimized NeRF parameters \theta (color and density fields). 1. Diffusion Model Input/Output: A voxelized 3D cube of occupancy x with resolution 32 \times 32 \times 32. Values are binary: 1 (occupied) or -1 (empty). 2. Diffusion Model Architecture: A small 3D U-Net with 7.2 million parameters (28 MB). 3. Importance Sampling Grid: A low-resolution 20 \times 20 \times 20 grid storing NeRF densities clamped to [0, 1]. This grid is updated with Exponential Moving Average (EMA) decay during training to inform sampling probabilities. Before NeRF optimization, a diffusion model is trained to learn the distribution of local 3D surface patches. 1. Data Curation: Extract N local cube-bounded patches from ShapeNet meshes. Cube sizes vary randomly between 1-10% of the object's bounding volume. 2. Voxelization: Voxelize patches at resolution 32 \times 32 \times 32. 3. Augmentation: Apply random rotations and random dilation online during training to increase diversity. 4. Diffusion Training: Train a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) using the standard diffusion loss: \mathcal{L}{Diff} = \| \epsilon - \epsilon\theta (\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}t} x0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}t} \epsilon, t) \|2^2 where t \sim U(0, 1000), \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), and \bar{\alpha}t follows a linear noise schedule. During NeRF training, the DSDS loss and Visibility Loss are applied alongside the standard RGB rendering loss. 1. Cube Importance Sampling: Query the NeRF densities \sigma at random 3D locations. Use the 20 \times 20 \times 20 importance sampling grid to select cube centers. Define a cube size randomly between 1-10% of the scene size. Extract a 32 \times 32 \times 32 cube of densities \sigma from the NeRF at the selected center. 2. Discretization: Convert the density cube \sigma into a binary occupancy cube xt using threshold \tau: xt = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \sigma > \tau \\ -1 & \text{if } \sigma \le \tau \end{cases} Note: Unlike SDS, no noise is added to xt before passing it to the diffusion model. 3. Denoising: Pass the discretized cube xt through the pre-trained diffusion model \epsilon\theta at timestep t to predict the denoised cube x0: x0 = \text{Denoise}(xt, t, \epsilon\theta) This step is a single forward pass; gradients do not flow through the diffusion model. 4. Mask Computation: Compute the mask m indicating predicted empty voxels: m = \mathbb{I}\{x0 < 0\} Here, mi = 1 if the i-th voxel is predicted empty, and 0 if occupied. 5. DSDS Loss Calculation: Compute the loss \mathcal{L}{DSDS} to penalize densities in empty regions and encourage densities in occupied regions: \mathcal{L}{DSDS} = \sumi \left( mi \sigmai + (1 - mi) \max(w - \sigmai, 0) \right) If mi=1 (empty), the term mi \sigmai penalizes the density \sigmai. If mi=0 (occupied), the term (1 - mi) \max(w - \sigmai, 0) increases density if \sigmai < w. 6. Visibility Loss Calculation: To remove floaters outside the convex hull of training views, compute \mathcal{L}{vis} for 3D locations qi not seen by any training view: \mathcal{L}{vis} = \sumi V(qi) \sigmai V(qi) = 1 if location qi is not visible from any training view j (approximated via frustum checks), and 0 otherwise. The visibility threshold is set to two times the largest distance between any two camera origins in the training/evaluation splits. In Nerfstudio, where bounds are (-1,1), this value is 2. 7. Gradient Update: Compute total loss: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{RGB} + \lambda{DSDS} \mathcal{L}{DSDS} + \lambda{vis} \mathcal{L}{vis}. Update NeRF parameters \theta using gradients from \mathcal{L}{RGB} and \mathcal{L}{DSDS} (and \mathcal{L}{vis}). Note that \mathcal{L}{DSDS} gradients flow through the NeRF density query but not the diffusion model. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplecubecenter(importancegrid, scenebounds): """Sample a 3D center coordinate weighted by the importance grid densities.""" probs = importancegrid / np.sum(importancegrid) flatidx = np.random.choice(importancegrid.size, p=probs.flatten()) grididx = np.unravelindex(flatidx, importancegrid.shape) voxelsize = (scenebounds[1] - scenebounds[0]) / importancegrid.shape[0] return scenebounds[0] + np.array(grididx) voxelsize + voxelsize / 2 def querydensitygrid(nerf, center, size, resolution): """Query NeRF density at a 3D grid of points.""" x = np.linspace(center[0] - size/2, center[0] + size/2, resolution) y = np.linspace(center[1] - size/2, center[1] + size/2, resolution) z = np.linspace(center[2] - size/2, center[2] + size/2, resolution) points = np.array(np.meshgrid(x, y, z)).reshape(3, -1).T densities = np.array([nerf.querydensity(p) for p in points]) return densities.reshape(resolution, resolution, resolution) def isvisible(point, view, threshold): """Check if point is within camera frustum and within depth threshold. Approximates visibility via frustum check, overestimating visibility.""" campos = view.position camdir = view.direction topoint = point - campos dist = np.linalg.norm(topoint) dot = np.dot(topoint, camdir) / dist return dot > 0.5 and dist < threshold # Standard frustum/depth approximation def nerfbustersstep(nerf, diffusionmodel, trainingviews, importancegrid, hyperparams, scenebounds, raymarchpoints, lrgb): """ One optimization step for Nerfbusters. """ # 1. Cube Importance Sampling cubecenter = samplecubecenter(importancegrid, scenebounds) sceneextent = np.max(scenebounds) - np.min(scenebounds) cubesize = np.random.uniform(0.01, 0.10) sceneextent densitycube = querydensitygrid(nerf, cubecenter, cubesize, resolution=32) # 2. Discretization tau = hyperparams['tau'] occupancycube = np.where(densitycube > tau, 1, -1) # 3. Denoising t = hyperparams['t'] denoisedcube = diffusionmodel.forward(occupancycube, t) # 4. Mask Computation mask = (denoisedcube < 0).astype(float) # 5. DSDS Loss w = hyperparams['w'] termempty = mask densitycube termoccupied = (1 - mask) np.maximum(w - densitycube, 0) ldsd = np.sum(termempty + termoccupied) # 6. Visibility Loss visloss = 0.0 visthresh = hyperparams['visthresh'] for point in raymarchpoints: visible = False for view in trainingviews: if isvisible(point, view, threshold=visthresh): visible = True break if not visible: sigma = nerf.querydensity(point) visloss += sigma # 7. Total Loss and Gradients totalloss = lrgb + ldsd + visloss return totalloss Differentiable Mapping Issues: Using a differentiable function (e.g., sigmoid) to map densities to the diffusion range and backpropagating through it causes issues due to steep or zero gradients. DSDS avoids this by using hard thresholding and a single forward pass. Accumulated Weights: Using accumulated weights for sampling is more expensive and requires specifying a view, limiting regularization to visible regions. DSDS uses densities, which allow sampling of occluded regions. Visibility Approximation: The visibility check approximates occlusion by only checking frustum intersection, overestimating visibility. This is a simplification for efficiency. Time Complexity: The DSDS loss requires one forward pass through the diffusion model per sampled cube. The diffusion model is small (7.2M params), making it computationally feasible. Importance sampling adds negligible overhead as it reuses ray marching data. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the diffusion model (28 MB) and the 20 \times 20 \times 20 importance sampling grid. Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art performance for casual captures compared to other geometry regularizers on the proposed Nerfbusters dataset. Strengths: Removes floaters effectively; works on arbitrary scenes; 3D-consistent; no need for complex conditioning. Limitations: Requires decent starting densities (local prior needs context); visibility loss is approximate. When to Use: When training NeRFs on casually captured images with sparse viewpoints or floaters. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity global geometry is required without local priors, or when computational resources are extremely limited (though overhead is low). Nerfbusters was proposed by Weber et al. in 2023. It addresses the issue of floaters and flawed geometry in NeRFs trained on casually captured images, which are often not evaluated properly in standard protocols that only assess views near the training trajectory. The method builds on the idea of using diffusion models for 3D generation, adapting the SDS loss to work directly on 3D densities using a local 3D prior. It is implemented in the open-source Nerfstudio repository. name: Application-Specific Methods
body: Application-Specific Methods adapt the general NeRF training loop to solve domain-specific inverse problems by modifying the neural field architecture, loss functions, and optimization strategy Application-Specific Pipelines. Unlike standard NeRF, which optimizes a single MLP for photometric reconstruction, these pipelines decompose fields to isolate physical properties, enforce domain priors (geometric, semantic, or physical), and employ iterative multi-stage optimization to handle complex constraints Application-Specific Pipelines. The children of this family share the following mechanisms and mathematical foundations: 1. Specialized Neural Field Architectures: Standard NeRF uses a single MLP mapping (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) \to (\sigma, c). Application-specific methods often decompose this into multiple MLPs or modify the input/output space: Decoupling: Fields are split to isolate specific physical properties (e.g., static vs. dynamic geometry, illumination vs. radiance) RehearsalNeRF. Dimensionality Reduction: Some methods map 2D coordinates to 3D properties (e.g., elevation and backscattering from (x,y)) to enforce surface constraints Neural SAR Surface Reconstruction via Inverse Rendering. Canonical Warping: Coordinates are transformed into a canonical space (e.g., via 3DMM) before querying the MLP to handle non-rigid or specific subject geometries Portrait-NeRF. 2. Domain-Specific Loss Functions: The optimization objective L is extended beyond photometric reconstruction error (L{photo}) to include constraints derived from the application domain: Geometric/Depth Supervision: Using auxiliary depth maps or point clouds to constrain geometry 360FusionNeRF. Semantic Consistency: Using high-level features (e.g., CLIP) to ensure plausible content in unobserved regions 360FusionNeRF. Physical Priors: Enforcing symmetry, planarity, or specific illumination models (e.g., HSV decomposition) Mirror-NeRF, RehearsalNeRF. Statistical Models: Using Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) for speckle noise in SAR data instead of MSE Neural SAR Surface Reconstruction via Inverse Rendering. 3. Iterative or Multi-Stage Optimization: Many methods do not optimize a single static field directly. Instead, they employ iterative loops where the output of one stage (e.g., super-resolved images, uncertainty maps, or rough meshes) informs the next stage of optimization Cross-Guided Optimization of Radiance Fields (CROP), Portrait-NeRF. 4. Volume Rendering Equation: All methods ultimately rely on the standard volume rendering integral to synthesize images from the learned fields: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj} is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the interval length Cross-Guided Optimization of Radiance Fields (CROP), 360FusionNeRF, Mirror-NeRF. CROP performs multi-view image super-resolution (MVSR) on training-view images during the radiance field optimization process to improve high-resolution novel view synthesis (HRNVS). It addresses the limitation that standard radiance fields rely heavily on the spectral characteristics of coordinate-based networks, which restricts their ability to synthesize high-frequency details independently. By fusing single-image super-resolution (SISR) features with voxel-based uncertainty fields derived from rendering errors, CROP ensures multi-view consistency and high-frequency detail in the training images, which are then used to refine the radiance field. Choose it when high-frequency detail recovery is needed despite MLP spectral bias. This category encompasses the general strategy of adapting NeRF for domain-specific inverse problems. It serves as the conceptual parent for the specific implementations below, defining the common architectural and optimization modifications described in Shared principles. Urban Radiance Fields applies NeRF to urban environments using sparse multi-view images supplemented by LiDAR data. It addresses the challenges of unbounded outdoor scenes, limited camera pose variety, and large-scale scene requirements by integrating geometric priors from LiDAR into the optimization loop. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on photometric consistency, this method enforces geometric accuracy and semantic consistency through specific depth, sight, and segmentation losses. Choose it for large-scale outdoor reconstruction with LiDAR priors. RehearsalNeRF learns disentangled neural fields in scenes with severe, dynamic illumination changes by leveraging a "rehearsal stage" (captured under stable lighting) to enforce geometric consistency. It solves the "illumination-radiance ambiguity" where dynamic lighting effects are entangled with object radiance, a problem not addressed by methods assuming stable light sources. Unlike Urban Radiance Fields which handles geometric priors, RehearsalNeRF explicitly decouples dynamic illuminations, static objects, and dynamic objects into five separate neural fields, enabling applications like controlling lighting while stopping motion. Choose it for dynamic scenes with changing illumination. This method reconstructs a Digital Surface Model (DSM) and a backscattering coefficient map from Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images by minimizing the difference between observed SAR intensities and synthesized intensities using a differentiable rendering model. It models elevation Z and backscattering B within a bounding box using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), reducing sampling degrees of freedom from a 3D volume to a 2D surface. Unlike standard NeRF which optimizes a 3D density field, this approach enforces surface constraints by mapping 2D ground coordinates directly to elevation and appearance, leading to faster and easier reconstruction of surfaces. Choose it for SAR data reconstruction. 360FusionNeRF is a semi-supervised learning framework for synthesizing novel views from a single RGB-D 360° panorama image. It extends OmniNeRF by introducing geometric supervision via auxiliary depth maps and semantic consistency via CLIP features to guide progressive training and reduce artifacts caused by occlusion in unobserved regions. Unlike standard NeRF methods that rely solely on photometric reconstruction, 360FusionNeRF explicitly constrains the geometry and semantics of the learned radiance field to ensure plausible completions of missing data. Choose it for single-panorama novel view synthesis. Portrait-NeRF estimates Neural Radiance Fields from a single headshot portrait image. It addresses the ill-posed nature of training an MLP from a single image by pretraining the MLP with a meta-learning framework on a light stage dataset and finetuning it on the input image. Unlike standard NeRF which requires multiple views, or 3D model-based methods that exclude upper head and torso, Portrait-NeRF reconstructs the full portrait including hairs and accessories using a canonical coordinate warping strategy. Choose it for single-image portrait synthesis. Mirror-NeRF is a neural rendering framework that learns accurate mirror geometry and reflection by unifying the radiance field and tracing rays according to Whitted-style light transport, enabling novel view synthesis and scene manipulation. Unlike NeRF and NeRFReN, which treat mirror reflections as separate virtual scenes or interpolate memorized reflections, Mirror-NeRF uses a unified radiance field with explicit reflection probability and Whitted-style ray tracing to synthesize physically consistent reflections from novel viewpoints. Choose it for scenes with complex mirror reflections. RapNeRF is a NeRF model tailored for view extrapolation, contrasting with standard NeRFs that excel at interpolation. It uses Random Ray Casting (RRC) and a Ray Atlas (RA). Training begins with a baseline NeRF to recover a rough mesh. A Ray Atlas (RA) is created by extracting a rough 3D mesh from a pretrained NeRF and mapping training ray directions onto its vertices. Random Ray Casting (RRC) is employed: for a training ray hitting a surface point v = o + tz d, a backward ray is cast from v toward a new origin o' with uniformly sampled angular perturbations. RRC and RA augment training rays with a predetermined probability. SNeS improves geometry by learning probable symmetries for partly symmetric and partly hidden in-scene objects through soft symmetry constraints on geometry and material properties. Boundary-Constrained Synthesis is a method to synthesize scenes of arbitrary size without artifacts, specifically preventing artifacts at the boundaries resulting from obscured parts of the radiance field. It avoids artifacts resulting from obscured parts of the radiance field. The method divides the radiance field into five parts: upper boundary Bu, lower Bd, left Bl, right Br, and interior I. Boundary length is lb. Four corner patches from the original field are placed onto corresponding corners of the synthesized result. Each of the four boundaries is synthesized using corresponding boundary patches from input samples (viewed as synthesizing individual strips). The synthesized boundaries are used as constraints for synthesizing the interior region using example patches from interior area I. A pitfall of the two-phase method is that it fails at boundaries because occluded interior parts are synthesized onto the boundary, exhibiting artifacts due to lack of pixel value supervision during DVGO training. Application-specific NeRF methods emerged to address limitations of the standard framework in complex real-world scenarios involving dynamic lighting, sparse views, specific physical modalities (like SAR), or extreme geometric constraints (like mirrors or portraits). Key developments include: Dynamic and Illumination Handling: Methods like RehearsalNeRF addressed the entanglement of geometry and illumination, a common issue in real-world captures. Sparse View and Single-Image Synthesis: Portrait-NeRF and 360FusionNeRF explored meta-learning and semantic priors to overcome the ill-posed nature of single-view reconstruction. Physical Priors and External Data: Urban Radiance Fields integrated LiDAR data to handle unbounded outdoor scenes, while Neural SAR Surface Reconstruction via Inverse Rendering adapted the rendering equation for radar physics. High-Frequency Detail and Super-Resolution: Cross-Guided Optimization of Radiance Fields (CROP) introduced iterative super-resolution to overcome the spectral bias of MLPs. Complex Reflections: Mirror-NeRF unified reflection modeling within the radiance field framework. View Extrapolation: RapNeRF targeted the specific challenge of extrapolating beyond the training camera poses.
