name: Cross-Guided Optimization of Radiance Fields (CROP)
head: Cross-guided optimization
body: Cross-Guided Optimization of Radiance Fields (CROP) is a framework that performs multi-view image super-resolution (MVSR) on training-view images during the radiance field optimization process to improve high-resolution novel view synthesis (HRNVS). It addresses the limitation that standard radiance fields rely heavily on the spectral characteristics of coordinate-based networks, which restricts their ability to synthesize high-frequency details independently. By fusing single-image super-resolution (SISR) features with voxel-based uncertainty fields derived from rendering errors, CROP ensures multi-view consistency and high-frequency detail in the training images, which are then used to refine the radiance field. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K low-resolution training-view images \{Ii^{gt}\}{i=1}^K with known camera poses. Outputs: An optimized radiance field (MLP parameters) and a set of super-resolved training-view images \{Ii^{SR}\}{i=1}^K that maintain multi-view consistency. Data Structures: Radiance Field: A standard NeRF MLP mapping (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) \to (\sigma, c). Voxel-based Uncertainty Field (V^{(unc)}): A 4D tensor with shape 1 \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz, representing uncertainty values for each voxel in the 3D grid. Uncertainty Map (Ui): A 2D map for view i, aggregated from the voxel-based uncertainty field. SISR Feature Map (Fi^{SISR}): The feature representation of the super-resolved image for view i. Parameters: N: The total number of points sampled along each ray for volume rendering. K: The number of train-view images. l: The update step index for the SR images. Formulas: 1. Volume Rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj} is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the interval length. 2. Photometric Loss: L{photo} = \frac{1}{|R|} \sum{r \in R} ||C(r) - \hat{C}(r)||2^2 where C(r) is the ground truth color and \hat{C}(r) is the rendered color. 3. Point-wise Error: e{ij}^{tv} = T{ij} \alpha{ij} ||c{ij} - \hat{c}{ij}||1 where c{ij} is the rendered RGB value from the current radiance field for point p{ij}^{tv}, and \hat{c}{ij} is the RGB value from the current SR image Ii^{l}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: For each view i, initialize the SR image at update step l=0, denoted as Ii^{l=0}, by passing the input ground truth image Ii^{gt} through the SISR backbone network. 2. Radiance Field Optimization: Optimize the radiance field using the current set of train-view images \{Ii^{l}\}{i=1}^K to render train-view RGB images Si^{tv}. 3. Uncertainty Field Generation: Generate the voxel-based uncertainty field V^{(unc)} by calculating the integrated error of pixels rendered from rays passing through 3D points. For a specific grid vi inside a voxel-grid, identify a set of sampled ray points Pi^{tv} = \{p{i1}^{tv}, p{i2}^{tv},...\} inside the neighborhood voxels of vi. Let Ri^{tv} be the corresponding rays of Pi^{tv}. Obtain rendered RGB values Ci = \{c{i1}, c{i2},...\} from Si^{tv} and train-view RGB values \hat{C}i = \{\hat{c}{i1}, \hat{c}{i2},...\} from the current SR images Ii^{l}. Calculate the error e{ij}^{tv} for each point using the formula above. Aggregate these errors into the voxel grid V^{(unc)}. 4. Uncertainty Map Generation: Generate an uncertainty map Ui for each view by aggregating voxel-based uncertainty from the neighborhood voxels of sampled ray points Pi^{tv} corresponding to rays Ri^{tv}. 5. SR Update: Generate the updated SR image Ii^{l+1} through the SR update module (SUM) using the rendered train-view RGB images Si^{tv}, the uncertainty map Ui, and the SISR network feature Fi^{SISR}. 6. Iteration: Continue optimizing the radiance fields using the updated SR images Ii^{l+1}. Repeat steps 3-6 iteratively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cropoptimization(K, N, maxiterations, Nx, Ny, Nz, cameraposes, Igt): # 1. Initialization: Pass each low-res input through the SISR backbone network Isr = [applysisrnetwork(img) for img in Igt] # standard SISR forward pass # Initialize radiance field MLP mapping (x,y,z,theta,phi) -> (sigma, c) nerfmlp = NeuralRadianceFieldMLP() for l in range(maxiterations): # 2. Radiance Field Optimization: Render train-view RGB images Si^{tv} Stv = [] for i in range(K): rays = generateraysfromposes(cameraposes[i]) points, directions = samplealongrays(rays, N) # standard ray marching sigma, color = nerfmlp.query(points, directions) # Volume rendering: Chat(r) = sum{i=1}^N Ti alphai ci transmittance = computetransmittance(sigma, points, directions) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma torch.diff(points, dim=-1, prepend=points[:1])) image = torch.sum(transmittance alpha color, dim=1) Stv.append(image) # Backpropagate photometric loss Lphoto = (1/|R|) sum ||C(r) - Chat(r)||2^2 loss = meansquarederror(Stv, Isr) nerfmlp.backward(loss) nerfmlp.step() # 3. Uncertainty Field Generation: Calculate integrated error for voxel grid V^{(unc)} Vunc = torch.zeros((1, Nx, Ny, Nz)) for voxelidx in allvoxels: # Identify sampled ray points Pi^{tv} inside neighborhood voxels of voxelidx Ptv = getpointsinneighborhood(voxelidx, points) if not Ptv: continue Rtv = getraysforpoints(Ptv) # Get rendered RGB values C from Stv and SR values Chat from Isr C = rendercolorsatpoints(Stv, Rtv) Csr = getcolorsfromimages(Isr, Rtv) # Calculate point-wise error e{ij}^{tv} = T{ij} alpha{ij} ||c{ij} - chat{ij}||1 errors = [] for j, p in enumerate(Ptv): Tij = transmittanceatpoint(p, nerfmlp) alphaij = 1.0 - torch.exp(-nerfmlp.density(p) raystepsize) err = Tij alphaij torch.norm(C[j] - Csr[j], p=1) errors.append(err) Vunc[voxelidx] = sum(errors) # 4. Uncertainty Map Generation: Aggregate voxel uncertainty for each view U = [] for i in range(K): # Aggregate from neighborhood voxels of sampled ray points Pi^{tv} Ui = aggregatevoxeluncertainty(Vunc, pointsforviewi) U.append(Ui) # 5. SR Update: Generate updated SR image Ii^{l+1} using SUM Fsisr = [sisrfeatureextractor(img) for img in Isr] # standard feature extraction Isrnew = [] for i in range(K): # SUM fuses Si^{tv}, Ui, and Fi^{SISR} Isrnew.append(SRUpdateModule(Stv[i], U[i], Fsisr[i])) Isr = Isrnew return nerfmlp, Isr Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posed SISR: Single-image super-resolution is an ill-posed problem where multiple solutions exist, potentially producing blurry images or lacking multi-view consistency when images are processed separately. Radiance Field Limitations: Radiance fields rely heavily on the spectral characteristics of coordinate-based networks, limiting their ability to perform super-resolution and synthesize high-frequency details independently. Uncertainty Trust: Synthesized train-view outputs cannot be trusted completely because they are predicted SR outputs, not ground truth. If the integrated error of pixels rendered from rays passing through a certain 3D point is high, the RGB values sampled at that point have high uncertainty, which the uncertainty field uses to guide the SR update module away from erroneous high-frequency details that are not consistent across views. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves iterative optimization of both the radiance field and the SR images. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the radiance field MLP, the voxel-based uncertainty field V^{(unc)} of size 1 \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz, and the SR images for all K views. Strengths: Significantly improves the performance of high-resolution novel view synthesis (HRNVS) and multi-view image super-resolution (MVSR) compared to existing methods. It breaks away from methodologies that depend solely on the characteristics of implicit neural representations (INR) by leveraging the strengths of 2D SISR. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method is complex to implement due to the coupling between 2D SISR and 5D radiance fields. The quality of the SR update depends on the accuracy of the uncertainty field. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Not given in the sources. History: The method addresses the limitations of NeRF in handling high-frequency details and super-resolution. It builds on the idea that SISR can specialize in learning the inverse function of image degradation, while radiance fields can find scene geometry. Previous methods like Mip-NeRF [2] and NeRF-SR [39] attempted to improve multi-scale representation or super-sampling, but CROP introduces a cross-guided optimization framework. Usage: Used in applications requiring high-resolution novel view synthesis, such as street-view navigation, AR/VR, and robotics. name: Application-Specific Pipelines
body: Application-Specific Pipelines adapt the standard NeRF training loop to solve domain-specific inverse problems by modifying neural field architectures, loss functions, and optimization strategies. Unlike standard NeRF training, which optimizes a single MLP for photometric reconstruction, these pipelines decompose fields, enforce domain priors, or employ iterative multi-stage optimization to handle complex constraints. Source specifically demonstrates a dynamically-informed iNeRF estimator for robotics navigation that relies solely on photometric loss. See parent Application-Specific Methods. DPPE is a 6-DoF monocular RGB-only pose estimation method that recovers a camera's ground truth pose from a perturbed initial estimate by minimizing photometric error within a pre-trained Plenoxels environment. It distinguishes itself from analytical derivative-based methods and slow NeRF-based optimizers by leveraging the rapid rendering speed of Plenoxels to numerically approximate image gradients via central differencing, allowing full-image re-rendering at each optimization step. Choose it when working with Plenoxels representations and needing robust pose recovery without analytical gradients. GO-NeRF is a pipeline for generating text-prompt-controlled 3D virtual objects at user-specified locations within an existing 3D environment represented as a NeRF, preserving unchanged scene content and maintaining compatibility with various NeRF representations. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by separating the optimization of a local object field from the global scene, using compositional rendering to handle occlusions and context-aware losses to mitigate artifacts like floaters and oversaturation common in diffusion-guided optimization. Choose it for localized 3D object insertion and editing in pre-trained scenes. A state estimation method that uses an iNeRF initialized with a dynamics prior, optimized only via photometric loss, acting as a recursive Bayesian filter with infinite state covariance. The process loss is set to 0. An iNeRF estimator initialized without a dynamics prior will very quickly diverge. Choose it for robotics navigation in NeRF environments where dynamics priors are available and photometric supervision suffices. Developed for vision-only robot navigation in a neural radiance world. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import copy def dppeposeestimation(plenoxelsgrid, Igt, piinit, f, W, H, epsilon, maxepochs): pic = copy.deepcopy(piinit) epoch = 0 alphatrans = 4.0 alpharot = 5.0 transstep = 1.0 rotstep = 0.001 while epoch < maxepochs: Icurr = renderplenoxels(plenoxelsgrid, pic, f, W, H) errorsq = np.sum((Icurr - Igt) 2) if errorsq <= epsilon: break DeltaI = Icurr - Igt Jparams = {} # Compute gradients for all 6 DoFs via central differencing for dof, step in [('x', transstep), ('y', transstep), ('z', transstep), ('omega1', rotstep), ('omega2', rotstep), ('omega3', rotstep)]: piplus = perturbpose(pic, dof, step) piminus = perturbpose(pic, dof, -step) Iplus = renderplenoxels(plenoxelsgrid, piplus, f, W, H) Iminus = renderplenoxels(plenoxelsgrid, piminus, f, W, H) Jparams[dof] = (Iplus - Iminus) / 2.0 # Update pose parameters if epoch % 2 == 0: if epoch > 0 and epoch % 100 == 0: alphatrans = 0.75 for dof in ['x', 'y', 'z']: grad = np.sum(Jparams[dof] DeltaI) pic.t[dof] += alphatrans grad else: if epoch > 0 and epoch % 100 == 0: alpharot = 0.75 for dof in ['omega1', 'omega2', 'omega3']: grad = np.sum(Jparams[dof] DeltaI) pic.omega[dof] += alpharot grad epoch += 1 return pic def perturbpose(pose, dof, step): newpose = copy.deepcopy(pose) if dof in ['x', 'y', 'z']: newpose.t[dof] += step elif dof in ['omega1', 'omega2', 'omega3']: newpose.omega[dof] += step return newpose def renderplenoxels(grid, pose, f, W, H): # Cast rays from pose: or = pose.t, dr = pose.R [(u - W/2)/f, -(v + H/2)/f, -1]^T # Render ray r using volume rendering equation: sum Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. pass def gonerfpipeline(scenenerf, textprompt, userpoints2d, referenceimage=None): # Step 2: Scene Rendering # Render RGB-D images of the scene # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. scenergb, scenedepth = renderscene(scenenerf, cameras) # Initialize Object NeRF within the bounding box # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. objectnerf = initializenerf(boundingbox) # Step 3: Object Generation (Optimization Loop) for step in range(numtrainingsteps): # Sample rays within the bounding box # Compute SDS loss from diffusion model using text prompt # This distills 2D inpainting priors # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. sdsloss = computesdsloss(objectrgb, textprompt, diffusionmodel) # Apply saturation regularizer # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. saturationloss = computesaturationalignmentloss(objectrgb, scenergb) # Apply random background replacement to mitigate artifacts # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. contextloss = computecontextloss(objectrgb, scenergb) # Apply reference-image-guided feature space loss if reference provided # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. featureloss = computefeaturesimilarityloss(referenceimage, objectrgb) if referenceimage else 0.0 # Total loss totalloss = sdsloss + saturationloss + contextloss + featureloss # Update Object NeRF parameters # Sources do not provide implementation details for this step. updateparameters(objectnerf, totalloss) # name: DPPE (Dense Pose Estimation in a Plenoxels Environment)
head: DPPE-1%, DPPE-full, Render-Based Plenoxels Pose Estimation
body: DPPE is a 6-DoF monocular RGB-only pose estimation procedure for Plenoxels environments that recovers the ground truth camera pose after a perturbation by minimizing errors in re-rendering using stochastic gradient descent and numerical gradient approximation. Unlike analytical derivative methods that are entangled with specific scene representations or require depth data, DPPE uses a numerical approximation of the image gradient via central differencing, making it generalizable to any scene representation where re-renderings are not prohibitively expensive. It leverages the rapid rendering speed of Plenoxels to re-render the full image at each optimization step, avoiding the ray subsampling limitations of slower NeRF-based methods like iNeRF. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained Plenoxels grid (voxel-based radiance field), a ground truth image I{gt}, a perturbed initial camera pose \pi{init} = \pi{gt} + \Delta\pi, and camera intrinsics (focal length f, image width W, height H). Outputs: The optimized camera pose \pi{final}. Data Structures: Plenoxels Grid: A 3D grid of voxels. Each voxel stores color information interpolated via trilinear interpolation. The grid resolution is typically [256]^3 for default configurations. Pose Representation: \pi = [\piR | \pit], where \piR \in SO(3) is the rotation matrix and \pit \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the translation vector. Ray Definition: For a pixel (u, v), the ray origin is or = \pit and direction is dr = \piR [ \frac{u - W/2}{f}, \frac{-v - H/2}{f}, -1 ]^T. Formulas: The rendered color \hat{C}(r) for a ray r with N samples is: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where \sigmai is opacity, \deltai is the distance between samples, ci is the color from trilinear interpolation, and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance. The optimization objective is: \pi{final} = \min{\pii} \sum{p} || \hat{I}(p, \pii) - I{gt}(p) ||2^2 where p are pixels. Parameters: Perturbation \Delta\pi: [x, y, z, \omega1, \omega2, \omega3] representing 3D translation and 3D orientation. Convergence Threshold \epsilon: 2000 for full image usage; 0 for 1% image usage. Max Epochs: 1000. Translation Step Size: 1 voxel in the Plenoxels grid. Rotation Step Size: 0.001 radians. Learning Rate \alpha: Translation learning rate is initialized at 4 and decayed by 25% every 100 epochs. Rotation learning rate is initialized at 5 and decayed by 25% every 100 epochs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize current pose \pic = \pi{init}. 2. While ||\hat{I}{\pic} - I{gt}||2^2 > \epsilon AND epochs < 1000: a. Cast rays r from current pose \pic and render image \hat{I}{\pic}(r) using the Plenoxels volume renderer. b. For each of the 6 camera degrees of freedom i \in [x, y, z, \omega1, \omega2, \omega3]: i. Perturb pose \pic by +1 step in DoF i to get \pi{c+}, and by -1 step to get \pi{c-}. ii. Render images \hat{I}{\pi{c+}} and \hat{I}{\pi{c-}}. iii. Compute gradient component Ji(r) = [\hat{I}{\pi{c+}}(r) - \hat{I}{\pi{c-}}(r)] / 2. c. Compute photometric error \Delta I(r) = \hat{I}{\pic}(r) - I{gt}(r). d. Update pose \pic \leftarrow \pic + \alpha (J(r) \cdot \Delta I(r)). e. Increment epoch counter. 3. Return \pic as \pi{final}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dppeposeestimation(plenoxelsgrid, Igt, piinit, f, W, H, epsilon, maxepochs): pic = piinit epoch = 0 alphatrans = 4.0 alpharot = 5.0 transstep = 1.0 # 1 voxel shift rotstep = 0.001 # radians while epoch < maxepochs: # Render current pose Icurr = volumerender(plenoxelsgrid, pic, f, W, H) # Compute squared L2 error errorsq = sum((Icurr[p] - Igt[p]) 2 for p in range(W H)) if errorsq <= epsilon: break J = {} dofs = ['x', 'y', 'z', 'omega1', 'omega2', 'omega3'] # Compute numerical gradient via central differencing for all 6 DoF for dof in dofs: step = transstep if dof in ['x', 'y', 'z'] else rotstep piplus = perturbpose(pic, dof, step) piminus = perturbpose(pic, dof, -step) Iplus = volumerender(plenoxelsgrid, piplus, f, W, H) Iminus = volumerender(plenoxelsgrid, piminus, f, W, H) J[dof] = [(Iplus[p] - Iminus[p]) / 2.0 for p in range(W H)] DeltaI = [Icurr[p] - Igt[p] for p in range(W H)] # Alternate between translation and rotation updates every epoch if epoch % 2 == 0: if epoch > 0 and epoch % 100 == 0: alphatrans = 0.75 gradx = sum(J['x'][p] DeltaI[p] for p in range(W H)) grady = sum(J['y'][p] DeltaI[p] for p in range(W H)) gradz = sum(J['z'][p] DeltaI[p] for p in range(W H)) pic.t[0] += alphatrans gradx pic.t[1] += alphatrans grady pic.t[2] += alphatrans gradz else: if epoch > 0 and epoch % 100 == 0: alpharot = 0.75 gradw1 = sum(J['omega1'][p] DeltaI[p] for p in range(W H)) gradw2 = sum(J['omega2'][p] DeltaI[p] for p in range(W H)) gradw3 = sum(J['omega3'][p] DeltaI[p] for p in range(W H)) pic.omega[0] += alpharot gradw1 pic.omega[1] += alpharot gradw2 pic.omega[2] += alpharot gradw3 epoch += 1 return pic def volumerender(grid, pose, f, W, H): # Standard volume rendering loop based on Plenoxels formulation image = [] for u in range(W): for v in range(H): # Ray origin and direction or = pose.t dr = pose.R @ [ (u - W/2)/f, (-v - H/2)/f, -1 ] # Ray marching with N samples T = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(N): # Sample position along ray pos = or + i dr # Get opacity sigmai and color ci from grid via trilinear interpolation sigmai, ci = grid.sample(pos) deltai = length(dr) # or distance between samples transmittance = T T = exp(-sigmai deltai) color += transmittance (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ci image.append(color) return image def perturbpose(pose, dof, step): newpose = Pose(pose.R.copy(), pose.t.copy()) if dof in ['x', 'y', 'z']: idx = ['x', 'y', 'z'].index(dof) newpose.t[idx] += step elif dof in ['omega1', 'omega2', 'omega3']: idx = ['omega1', 'omega2', 'omega3'].index(dof) newpose.omega[idx] += step return newpose Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: The method may get stuck in local minima, particularly in scenes with grid patterns (e.g., Materials) or depending on pose initialization. Uniform Texture: Scenes with large regions of uniform texture (e.g., water in Ship, bun in Hotdog) cause the algorithm to struggle because it relies on image gradients. Coarse Gradient Approximation: If the pose error becomes smaller than the resampling step size (1 voxel or 0.001 rad), the gradient approximation becomes too coarse to capture information, limiting convergence to small errors. Translation Step Size Variability: The translation step size is variable depending on Plenoxels grid resolution; a shift of 1 voxel changes magnitude based on grid size. Time Complexity: The method requires 6 additional renders every 2 epochs (alternating between rotation and translation steps), plus 1 render for the current pose per epoch. However, Plenoxels rendering is fast enough that more than 6 image renders can be performed in the time it would take a single NeRF render. Memory Complexity: Depends on the Plenoxels grid resolution, with a default of [256]^3. Measured Performance: On NeRF Synthetic Dataset (Average across 8 scenes), DPPE-full achieved Average Rotation Error of 2.95° and Average Translation Error of 0.21 units, compared to iNeRF's 3.57° and 0.24 units. DPPE-full runtime: approximately 70 seconds (73.1 seconds for 100% subsampling). DPPE-1% (1% pixel subsampling) runtime: 11.0 seconds. DPPE-1% Average Rotation Error: 2.97°, Translation Error: 0.20 units. Scaling: Performance is robust to pixel subsampling. DPPE-1% performs on-par with DPPE-full in terms of accuracy but is significantly faster. Strengths: Rapid initial convergence; works with monocular RGB only; generalizable to other scene representations; faster than iNeRF for full-image re-rendering. Limitations: Struggles with uniform textures; prone to local minima; gradient approximation limits precision at very small errors. DPPE was introduced by Christopher Kolios, Yeganeh Bahoo, and Sajad Saeedi in March 2024. It builds on the Plenoxels representation, which offers reduced training times and better rendering accuracy than standard NeRF by eliminating the neural net component in favor of Plenoptic volume elements. The method adapts classical template-matching approaches using numerical gradient approximation, contrasting with analytical derivative methods like those by Teigen et al.. name: GO-NeRF
head: Generating Objects in Neural Radiance Fields
body: GO-NeRF is a pipeline that generates text-prompt-controlled 3D virtual objects at user-specified locations within an existing 3D environment represented as a NeRF, while preserving unchanged scene content. It differs from standard NeRF training by decoupling object generation into a localized 3D bounding box and using compositional rendering to integrate the new object with the pre-trained scene, ensuring compatibility with various NeRF representations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF representing the existing 3D scene; a text prompt describing the object to generate; three 2D points selected by the user on a rendered image of the scene to define the object's location. Outputs: A final composited image Iv containing the original scene with the newly generated object seamlessly integrated. Data Structures: Scene NeRF: A pre-trained neural radiance field mapping (x, y, z) \to (\sigma, c). Object NeRF: A new neural radiance field optimized within a specific 3D bounding box, mapping (x, y, z) \to (\sigma{obj}, c{obj}). 3D Bounding Box: Defined by three 2D points projected into 3D space. RGB-D Images: Rendered from the scene NeRF, consisting of RGB color S and depth D. Opacity Maps: Ov, representing the 3D-aware opacity of the generated object. Steps: 1. Region Definition: The user selects three points on a rendered image of the pre-trained scene. These 2D points are converted into a 3D bounding box within the scene using depth information, perspective projection, and cross-product operations. 2. Scene Rendering: Render the pre-trained scene NeRF using pre-defined cameras C to generate RGB-D images (S, D) of the 3D scene. 3. Object Generation (Optimization): Optimize a new NeRF representation within the 3D bounding box. This step uses Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to distill 2D text-guided image inpainting priors from diffusion models, guided by the text prompt. The optimization produces RGB images Gv and opacity maps Ov through volume rendering. 4. Compositional Rendering: Composite the rendered scene and the generated object using the 3D-aware opacity map to handle occlusions and create the final output Iv. Formulas: The object's RGB image Gv and opacity map Ov are produced via volume rendering within the bounding box: Gv = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci Ov = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj} is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is the density, ci is the color, and \deltai is the interval length. The final composited image Iv is created by blending the scene S and the generated object Gv using the opacity map Ov: Iv = Gv \cdot Ov + S \cdot (1 - Ov) This formulation ensures that the original scene content outside the desired editing area is preserved and occlusions are managed correctly. Optimization Strategy and Loss Functions: The optimization of the Object NeRF is driven by several components: 1. Score Distillation Sampling (SDS): Distills 2D text-guided image inpainting priors from diffusion models to guide the generation based on the text prompt. 2. Saturation Regularizer: Addresses SDS-based oversaturation by aligning the saturation of synthesized objects with the overall tone of the scene. 3. Random Background Replacement: To eliminate artifacts that share color with the scene background, the scene context is randomly replaced with a random background at a certain ratio during training. 4. Reference-Image-Guided Feature Space Loss: Uses feature space similarity to guide the style of the generated objects based on a reference image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gonerfpipeline(scenenerf, textprompt, userpoints2d, referenceimage=None): # Step 1: Region Definition depthmap = renderdepthmap(scenenerf, cameras) # Standard depth rendering boundingbox = project2dto3d(userpoints2d, depthmap) # Uses perspective projection and cross-product # Step 2: Scene Rendering cameras = getpredefinedcameras() # Standard camera initialization scenergb, scenedepth = rendernerf(scenenerf, cameras) # Standard volume rendering # Initialize Object NeRF within the bounding box objectnerf = initializenerf(boundingbox) # Standard MLP initialization # Step 3: Object Generation (Optimization Loop) for step in range(T): # T is total training steps rays = sampleraysthroughbox(boundingbox, cameras) # Standard ray generation objectrgb, objectopacity = rendernerf(objectnerf, rays) # Standard volume rendering # Compute SDS loss (standard text-guided diffusion distillation formulation) sdsloss = computesds(objectrgb, textprompt, diffusionmodel) # Apply saturation regularizer scenesat = computesaturation(scenergb) objsat = computesaturation(objectrgb) saturationloss = computesaturationalignment(objsat, scenesat) # Aligns object tone with scene # Apply random background replacement to mitigate artifacts if random() < backgroundreplacementratio: randombg = generaterandombackground() contextloss = computecontextloss(objectrgb, randombg) # Prevents color blending with scene else: contextloss = computecontextloss(objectrgb, scenergb) # Apply reference-image-guided feature space loss if provided if referenceimage is not None: reffeatures = extractfeatures(referenceimage) objfeatures = extractfeatures(objectrgb) featureloss = computefeaturesimilarity(reffeatures, objfeatures) # Guides style else: featureloss = 0.0 totalloss = sdsloss + saturationloss + contextloss + featureloss updateparameters(objectnerf, totalloss) # Standard gradient descent # Step 4: Compositional Rendering finalobjectrgb, finalobjectopacity = rendernerf(objectnerf, cameras) finalimage = finalobjectrgb finalobjectopacity + scenergb (1 - finalobjectopacity) return finalimage Time Complexity: Depends on the number of training steps for the Object NeRF and the cost of SDS evaluation from the diffusion model. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-trained Scene NeRF and the newly optimized Object NeRF. Strengths: Preserves unchanged scene content; handles occlusions via 3D-aware opacity maps; compatible with various NeRF representations (e.g., InstantNGP, standard NeRF). Limitations: Susceptible to oversaturation without the saturation regularizer; artifacts may occur if the object color matches the scene background, mitigated by random background replacement. When to use: When creating virtual reality content by adding specific, text-described objects to an existing 3D scene at precise locations. GO-NeRF was introduced to address the gap in generating high-quality 3D objects within existing 3D environments for virtual reality content creation. It leverages recent advances in text-to-image diffusion models and NeRF representations. The method was published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics in 2025. name: Urban Radiance Fields
body: Urban Radiance Fields is a method for applying Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) based view synthesis and 3D reconstruction to urban environments using sparse multi-view images supplemented by LiDAR data. It addresses the challenges of unbounded outdoor scenes, limited camera pose variety, and large-scale scene requirements by integrating geometric priors from LiDAR into the optimization loop. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on photometric consistency, this method enforces geometric accuracy and semantic consistency through specific depth, sight, and segmentation losses. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse multi-view RGB images, corresponding LiDAR depth measurements, and camera poses. Outputs: A trained neural field representing the scene, from which novel views and 3D point clouds/meshes are extracted. Data Structures: The method uses a standard NeRF architecture mapping 5D coordinates (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) to density \sigma and color c. Specific architecture or training data details are not given in the sources. Optimization Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the target virtual camera, a ray is cast through the scene. 2. Neural Query: The ray is sampled at discrete points. The neural network queries the density \sigma(t) and color c(t) at each point t along the ray. 3. Volume Rendering: The color \hat{C}(r) for the ray r is computed using the standard volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} e^{-\sigmaj \deltaj} is the accumulated transmittance, \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai} is the opacity, and \deltai is the interval length. 4. Depth Optimization: The estimated depth \hat{z} is treated as an optimization parameter updated via the depth loss to match LiDAR measurements. 5. Loss Calculation: The total loss is the sum of the standard photometric loss and three auxiliary losses: LiDAR Depth Loss (L{depth}): Forces the estimated depth \hat{z} to match the LiDAR-measured depth z. Sight Loss (L{sight}): Forces the radiance weight w(t) to concentrate at the surface defined by the LiDAR depth z. Sky Segmentation Loss (L{seg}): Forces point samples along rays passing through sky pixels to have zero density. 6. Backpropagation: The gradients are backpropagated to update the neural network weights. Formulas: The auxiliary losses are defined as: L{depth} = \mathbb{E}[(z - \hat{z})^2] L{sight} = \mathbb{E}\left[ \int{t1}^{t2} (w(t) - \delta(z))^2 dt \right] L{seg} = \mathbb{E}\left[ \int{t1}^{t2} Si(r) (w(t) - \delta(z))^2 dt \right] Where: z is the LiDAR measured depth. \hat{z} is the estimated depth derived from the NeRF. w(t) = T(t)\sigma(t) is the radiance weight at point t. \delta(z) is the Dirac delta function, concentrating the weight at the measured depth surface. Si(r) is a binary mask where Si(r) = 1 if the ray r passes through a sky pixel in the i-th image, and 0 otherwise. Sky pixels are identified using a pretrained segmentation model. t1 and t2 define the integration bounds along the ray. 3D Reconstruction Pipeline: After training, 3D reconstruction is performed as follows: 1. A ray is cast for each pixel in a virtual camera. 2. The estimated depth \hat{z} is used to place points in 3D space, generating a point cloud from the NeRF model during volumetric rendering. 3. Poisson Surface Reconstruction is applied to the generated point cloud to reconstruct a 3D mesh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def trainurbannerf(images, lidardepths, poses, skymasks, network, optimizer, numepochs=1000, Nsamples=64, tnear=0.0, tfar=100.0): for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, lidardepth, pose, skymask in zip(images, lidardepths, poses, skymasks): H, W = image.shape[:2] # 1. Cast rays for each pixel in the target virtual camera # Standard pinhole camera ray generation origins = torch.zeros(H W, 3) directions = torch.zeros(H W, 3) # Populate origins and directions from pose and intrinsics # 2. Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, Nsamples) tvals = tvals.unsqueeze(0).expand(origins.shape[0], -1) positions = origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) # 3. Query network for density sigma and color c sigma, color = network(positions, directions) # 4. Compute transmittance T(t) and weights w(t) = T(t) sigma(t) deltas = torch.diff(tvals, dim=1, prepend=torch.zeroslike(tvals[:, 0:1])) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:, 0:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) w = T sigma # 5. Compute rendered color and estimated depth zhat renderedcolor = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1).reshape(H, W, 3) estimateddepth = torch.sum(w tvals, dim=1).reshape(H, W) # 6. Compute auxiliary losses lossdepth = torch.mean((lidardepth - estimateddepth) 2) # Dirac delta delta(z) is approximated for discrete samples deltaapprox = torch.exp(-((tvals - lidardepth.unsqueeze(1)) 2) / (2 0.01 2)) losssight = torch.mean((w - deltaapprox) 2) lossseg = torch.mean(skymask (w - deltaapprox) 2) # Total loss includes standard photometric loss lossphoto = torch.mean((renderedcolor - image) 2) totalloss = lossphoto + lossdepth + losssight + lossseg optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() def extractmesh(network, imageshape, virtualpose, Nsamples=64, tnear=0.0, tfar=100.0): # 1. Cast ray for each pixel in the virtual camera H, W = imageshape origins = torch.zeros(H W, 3) directions = torch.zeros(H W, 3) # Populate origins and directions from pose and intrinsics # 2. Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, Nsamples) tvals = tvals.unsqueeze(0).expand(origins.shape[0], -1) positions = origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) # 3. Query network and compute depth to place point cloud sigma, = network(positions, directions) deltas = torch.diff(tvals, dim=1, prepend=torch.zeroslike(tvals[:, 0:1])) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:, 0:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) w = T sigma estimateddepth = torch.sum(w tvals, dim=1).reshape(H, W) # 4. Place points in 3D space using estimated depth tdepth = estimateddepth.reshape(-1, 1) points = origins + directions tdepth # 5. Reconstruct mesh using Poisson Surface Reconstruction # Standard Poisson reconstruction algorithm mesh = poissonsurfacereconstruction(points) return mesh def poissonsurfacereconstruction(points): # Reconstructs a 3D mesh from the generated point cloud # Standard Poisson reconstruction algorithm pass Parameters: Sky Segmentation Model: A pretrained model is used to identify sky pixels. Specific architecture or training data is not given in the sources. Dirac Delta Approximation: The sources define \delta(z) as the Dirac delta function. Implementation details for approximating this in discrete sampling are not provided. Poisson Surface Reconstruction: Used for mesh generation. Specific parameters (e.g., depth, width) are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: LiDAR Alignment: The depth loss requires accurate alignment between LiDAR depth and NeRF estimated depth. Misalignment may lead to incorrect geometry. Sky Segmentation Errors: Incorrect sky segmentation masks may cause the model to suppress density in non-sky regions or fail to suppress density in sky regions. Unbounded Scenes: Urban environments are unbounded, which can cause issues with standard NeRF's bounded volume assumption. The use of LiDAR helps mitigate this by providing explicit depth constraints. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Integrates LiDAR data for geometric accuracy; handles sparse views; addresses unbounded scene challenges. Limitations: Relies on accurate LiDAR data and sky segmentation; specific performance metrics are not provided in the sources. When to Use: Urban environments with sparse multi-view images and available LiDAR data. When Not to Use: Indoor scenes or scenes without LiDAR data where the specific losses may not be applicable. Urban Radiance Fields was proposed in November 2021. It aims to apply NeRF-based view synthesis and 3D reconstruction to urban environments, addressing challenges such as unbounded scenes, limited camera pose variety, and large-scale scene requirements. The method supplements sparse multi-view images with LiDAR data and introduces specific losses for depth, sight, and sky segmentation.
