name: NeRF-Neural ODE
head: NeRFNODE, Neural ODE for NeRF
body: NeRF-Neural ODE replaces the discrete quadrature summation of standard NeRF with a continuous Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) solver to integrate radiance and transmittance along rays. It treats ray integration as a continuous dynamical system solved via adaptive ODE solvers rather than fixed-step numerical integration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray features tensor of shape 11 \times N containing ray origin o (3), ray direction d (3), view directions v (3), near plane near (1), and far plane far (1). Output: A RenderResult structure containing rgb (shape 3 \times N) and disparity. Data Structures: The ODE state vector x has shape 15 \times N, constructed by augmenting the 11 \times N ray features with accumulated color C (3 rows) and accumulated transmittance T (1 row), initialized to zero. Rows 1–3 hold position p, rows 4–6 hold direction d, rows 7–9 hold view direction v, row 10 holds near, row 11 holds far, rows 12–14 hold C, and row 15 holds T. Neural Network Architecture: The model uses a NeRFNet wrapped in NeRFNODE. Positional encoding for input x and levels L computes \sin(2^i \pi x) and \cos(2^i \pi x) for i \in 0 \dots L-1, concatenated along the first dimension. Levels are Lo=10 for position and Ld=4 for direction. The trunk takes the positional encoding of position (60 dims) and processes it through two parallel paths: one passes the encoding directly, the other passes it through a Dense(60, 256, relu) followed by four Dense(256, 256, relu) layers. The outputs are concatenated to 316 dims, passed through Dense(316, 256, relu), three Dense(256, 256, relu) layers, and a final Dense(256, 256) layer. The output splits into density \sigma via Dense(256, 1, sigmoid) and features h via identity. The RGB head concatenates the positional encoding of view direction (24 dims) with features h (256 dims) to form 280 dims, followed by Dense(280, 128, relu) and Dense(128, 3, sigmoid). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Generate rays from camera parameters H, W, focal, c2w. Direction is computed in NDC space if ndc=true. Near and far planes are set to 0.0 and 1.0 respectively. 2. Feature Extraction: Compute ray features. If ndc=true, transform rays to NDC space. Concatenate rays origin, rays direction, view directions, near, and far into an 11 \times N tensor. 3. State Initialization: Augment the 11 \times N ray features with 4 rows of zeros to create the initial state x0 of shape 15 \times N. 4. ODE Definition: Define the derivative function f(t, x) for t \in [0, 1]. Extract p, d, v, near, far, C, T from x. Compute derivatives: dp/dt = (far - near) \cdot d, dd/dt = 0, dv/dt = 0, d(near)/dt = 0, d(far)/dt = 0. Query NeRFNet with p and v to get \sigma and rgb. Compute dC/dt = \exp(-T) \cdot \sigma \cdot rgb and dT/dt = \sigma. Return concatenated derivatives. 5. ODE Solving: Solve the ODE from t=0 to t=1 using the Tsit5() solver with relative tolerance 10^{-3} and absolute tolerance 10^{-3}. 6. Result Extraction: Extract the final state x{end}. The RGB values are located at rows 12–14 (0-indexed) of the final state vector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(x, L): # x: (..., D), returns (..., 2LD) i = np.arange(L, dtype=x.dtype) freqbands = (2.0 i).reshape(-1, 1) scaled = x[..., np.newaxis] freqbands return np.concatenate([np.sin(np.pi scaled), np.cos(np.pi scaled)], axis=-1).reshape(x.shape[:-1], -1) def linear(x, W, b): return x @ W + b def relu(x): return np.maximum(0, x) def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x)) class NeRFNet: def init(self, Lo, Ld): self.Lo = Lo self.Ld = Ld # Trunk weights self.Wt1 = np.random.randn(316, 256) self.bt1 = np.zeros(256) self.Wt2 = np.random.randn(256, 256) self.bt2 = np.zeros(256) self.Wt3 = np.random.randn(256, 256) self.bt3 = np.zeros(256) self.Wt4 = np.random.randn(256, 256) self.bt4 = np.zeros(256) self.Wsig = np.random.randn(256, 1) self.bsig = np.zeros(1) # RGB Head weights self.Wh1 = np.random.randn(280, 128) self.bh1 = np.zeros(128) self.Wh2 = np.random.randn(128, 3) self.bh2 = np.zeros(3) def forward(self, pos, viewdir): # pos: (N, 3), viewdir: (N, 3) pepos = positionalencoding(pos, self.Lo) # (N, 60) # Trunk parallel paths path1 = pepos path2 = relu(linear(pepos, self.Wt1, self.bt1)) for W, b in [(self.Wt2, self.bt2), (self.Wt3, self.bt3), (self.Wt4, self.bt4)]: path2 = relu(linear(path2, W, b)) trunkin = np.concatenate([path1, path2], axis=-1) # (N, 316) h = relu(linear(trunkin, self.Wt1, self.bt1)) h = relu(linear(h, self.Wt2, self.bt2)) h = relu(linear(h, self.Wt3, self.bt3)) h = linear(h, self.Wt4, self.bt4) # No activation on last trunk layer sigma = sigmoid(linear(h, self.Wsig, self.bsig)) # (N, 1) features = h # (N, 256) # RGB Head pedir = positionalencoding(viewdir, self.Ld) # (N, 24) headin = np.concatenate([pedir, features], axis=-1) # (N, 280) rgb = sigmoid(linear(relu(linear(headin, self.Wh1, self.bh1)), self.Wh2, self.bh2)) # (N, 3) return sigma, rgb def derivatives(t, state, net): # state: (15, N) p = state[0:3,:] d = state[3:6,:] v = state[6:9,:] near = state[9,:] far = state[10,:] C = state[11:14,:] T = state[14,:] dpdt = (far - near)[:, np.newaxis] d dddt = np.zeroslike(d) dvdtdt = np.zeroslike(v) dneardt = np.zeroslike(near) dfardt = np.zeroslike(far) sigma, rgb = net.forward(p.T, v.T) sigma = sigma.T # (N, 1) rgb = rgb.T # (N, 3) dCdt = np.exp(-T) sigma rgb dTdt = sigma.squeeze() dxdt = np.concatenate([dpdt, dddt, dvdtdt, dneardt[np.newaxis,:], dfardt[np.newaxis,:], dCdt, dTdt[np.newaxis,:]], axis=0) return dxdt def rawtostatespace(rayfeatures): # rayfeatures: (11, N) zeros = np.zeros((4, rayfeatures.shape[1]), dtype=rayfeatures.dtype) return np.concatenate([rayfeatures, zeros], axis=0) def renderrays(rayfeatures, net, tspan=(0.0, 1.0)): state = rawtostatespace(rayfeatures) # Reference implementation uses Tsit5() with reltol=1e-3, abstol=1e-3 # Self-contained fixed-step RK4 fallback: t, dt = tspan[0], 0.01 while t < tspan[1] - 1e-6: k1 = derivatives(t, state, net) k2 = derivatives(t + dt/2, state + dtk1/2, net) k3 = derivatives(t + dt/2, state + dtk2/2, net) k4 = derivatives(t + dt, state + dtk3, net) state += (dt/6) (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) t += dt # Extract RGB (rows 11-13, 0-indexed) rgb = state[11:14,:] return rgb Parameters: Positional Encoding Levels: Lo=10, Ld=4. Solver: Tsit5() with reltol=1e-3, abstol=1e-3. Batch Size: 4096 rays. Optimizer: ADAM with learning rate 5 \times 10^{-4}, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, with exponential decay starting at iteration 250,000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NDC Space: If ndc=true, rays must be transformed to NDC space before feature extraction. The near plane is set to 1.0 in NDC space. Dimension Matching: The RGB head input dimension is explicitly defined as 280, requiring concatenation of the 24-dim view direction encoding with the 256-dim features. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of adaptive steps taken by the Tsit5 solver. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the 15 \times N state vector and neural network parameters. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Continuous integration along rays. Limitations: Potential slowness compared to fixed-step marching for simple scenes and reliance on specific ODE solver libraries. NeRF-Neural ODE is an implementation that attempts to use Neural ODEs instead of quadrature for NeRF. It originates from the nerf-node repository. tqhdesilva/nerf-node, https://github.com/tqhdesilva/nerf-node, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LOLNeRF
head: Learn from One Look
body: LOLNeRF is a method for single-shot view synthesis of human faces that learns a generative 3D model from single-view images without relying on explicit geometric information like depth or point clouds. It differs from adversarial approaches like \pi-GAN by using Generative Latent Optimization (GLO) to learn a per-image table of latent codes, allowing it to reconstruct specific training images with high fidelity while avoiding the resolution limits imposed by GAN discriminators. Inputs: A dataset of K single-view images Ik of a specific object class (e.g., human faces). 2D landmark coordinates for each image, extracted using a pre-trained landmarker (e.g., MediaPipe Face Mesh). Foreground segmentation masks for each image, extracted using a pre-trained segmenter (e.g., MediaPipe Selfie Segmentation). Outputs: A trained neural radiance field (NeRF) model consisting of a foreground density/radiance network and a background radiance network. A latent table Z containing learned latent codes for each training image. A statistical model of the latent space (mean and covariance) for unconditional generation. Latent Table (Z): A matrix of shape K \times D, where K is the number of training images and D is the latent dimension. Initialized to zeros (0{K \times D}). Foreground Model: A neural network parameterized by \theta{fg} that takes positional encoding \gamma^L(x) and latent code z as input, outputting density \sigma(x|z) and radiance c(x|z). Background Model: A lower-capacity neural network parameterized by \theta{bg} that takes ray direction d and latent code z as input, outputting background radiance C{bg}(d|z). 1. Camera Alignment: For each training image, extract 2D landmark locations using a pre-trained landmarker. Align these 2D landmarks with the projections of class-specific canonical 3D landmark positions using a least-squares "shape matching" optimization. This yields a rough estimate of the camera parameters (pose and focal length) for each image. 2. Model Initialization: Initialize the latent table Z to 0{K \times D}. Initialize the foreground and background neural networks. 3. Training Loop: For each training image Ik: a. Sample rays from the image using the aligned camera parameters. b. For each ray, sample N points xi along the ray direction d. c. Query the foreground model for density \sigma(xi|zk) and radiance c(xi|zk), where zk is the k-th row of Z. d. Query the background model for background radiance C{bg}(d|zk). e. Compute rendering weights wi and accumulated alpha \alpha(p|zk) for each pixel p. f. Compute the rendered foreground color C{NeRF}(p|zk) and final color C(p|zk). g. Compute the total loss L{total} for the pixel. h. Update the network parameters and the latent code zk using gradient descent. 4. Conditional Generation (Inference): To reconstruct a new image not in the training set, initialize a new latent row to the mean \muZ of the existing latent table. Optimize this new row using the same loss function and optimizer as the training loop. 5. Unconditional Generation (Inference): Model the distribution of latent codes Z as a multivariate Gaussian with mean \muZ and covariance \chiZ, computed via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the rows of Z. Sample latent codes from this distribution, optionally applying a "truncation trick" to control the trade-off between diversity and quality. Volume Rendering: The foreground color C{NeRF}(p) is computed as a weighted sum of radiance values: C{NeRF}(p|z) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \cdot c(xi, d|z) where the weights wi are derived from the accumulated transmittance: wi = (1 - \exp(-\sigma(xi|z)\deltai)) \cdot \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(xj|z)\deltaj\right) Here, \deltai is the distance between sample points. Final Color Composition: The final pixel color combines the foreground NeRF output and the background model: C(p|z) = \alpha(p|z) \cdot C{NeRF}(p|z) + (1 - \alpha(p|z)) \cdot C{bg}(d|z) where \alpha(p|z) is the accumulated opacity: \alpha(p|z) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi [ S2 ] Loss Function: The total loss is a weighted sum of three terms: L{total} = L{rgb} + \lambda{mask} L{mask} + \lambda{hard} L{hard} [ S2 ] 1. RGB Loss: Standard L2 photometric reconstruction loss: L{rgb} = \mathbb{E}{k \in \{1..K\}, p \in Ik} \left[ (C(p|zk) - C^GT(p))^2 \right] where C^GT(p) is the ground truth pixel color. 2. Mask Loss: Encourages transparency consistency with a pre-trained segmenter SI: L{mask} = \mathbb{E}{k \in \{1..K\}, p \in Ik} \left[ (\alpha(p|zk) - SI(p))^2 \right] [ S2 ] 3. Hard Surface Loss: Encourages sharp density transitions by penalizing intermediate weights. The probability distribution of weights is modeled as a mixture of Laplacian distributions: IP(w) \propto e^{-|w|} + e^{-|1-w|} The loss is defined as: L{hard} = -\log(IP(w)) This encourages the density to produce a step function that saturates sampling weight over at least one interval. \lambda{hard}: Weight for the hard surface loss. Set to 0.1 in experiments. \lambda{mask}: Weight for the mask loss. Set to 1.0 when training on face datasets using MediaPipe Selfie Segmentation. N: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. D: Latent dimension. Not given in the sources. L: Dimension of positional encoding. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def posenc(x, L=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" x = x.unsqueeze(-1) 2torch.arange(L, device=x.device) np.pi return torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1).view(x.shape[0], -1) def direnc(d, L=4): """Standard NeRF directional encoding.""" d = d.unsqueeze(-1) 2torch.arange(L, device=d.device) np.pi return torch.cat([torch.sin(d), torch.cos(d)], dim=-1).view(d.shape[0], -1) def fitcamerafromlandmarks(landmarks2d, canonical3d): """Rough camera estimation via least-squares shape matching. In practice, this solves for rotation, translation, and focal length that minimizes reprojection error between projected canonical3d and landmarks2d.""" # Placeholder: returns a default perspective camera matrix return torch.eye(3, 4) # [3, 4] extrinsic matrix def samplerays(imageshape, camparams, near=1.0, far=10.0, numsamples=64): """Generate rays for each pixel using camera parameters.""" H, W, = imageshape u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='ij') u = u.float().flatten() v = v.float().flatten() # Simple pinhole camera model for demonstration fx, fy = 512.0, 512.0 cx, cy = W / 2, H / 2 d = torch.stack([ (u - cx) / fx, (v - cy) / fy, torch.oneslike(u) ], dim=-1) d = d / torch.norm(d, dim=-1, keepdim=True) origins = torch.zeroslike(d) tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) xi = origins.unsqueeze(1) + d.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(0) return xi, d, origins class ForegroundNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, latentdim, posencdim): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(posencdim + latentdim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 2) # Output: density, radiance) def forward(self, x, z): xenc = posenc(x) input = torch.cat([xenc, z], dim=-1) out = self.net(input) sigma = torch.exp(out[..., 0]) # Ensure positive density c = torch.sigmoid(out[..., 1]) # Radiance return sigma, c class BackgroundNeRF(nn.Module): def init(self, latentdim, direncdim): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(direncdim + latentdim, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3) # Output: background radiance) def forward(self, d, z): denc = direnc(d) input = torch.cat([denc, z], dim=-1) cbg = torch.sigmoid(self.net(input)) return cbg def renderray(xi, sigma, cfg, cbg): """Volume rendering with correct delta computation.""" # Compute spacing between samples: deltai is distance from xi to x{i+1} delta = torch.norm(xi[1:] - xi[:-1], dim=-1) delta = torch.cat([delta, torch.tensor([0.5], device=xi.device)]) # Append step size for last sample # Sample opacity alphasample = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # Transmittance before each sample T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphasample + 1e-10, dim=0) T = torch.roll(T, 1) T[0] = 1.0 # Weights w = alphasample T # Foreground color cneurf = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) cfg, dim=0) # Alpha alpha = torch.sum(w) # Final color cfinal = alpha cneurf + (1.0 - alpha) cbg return cfinal, alpha, w def computehardloss(w, lambdahard): """Hard surface loss: -log(IP(w)) where IP(w) ~ exp(-|w|) + exp(-|1-w|).""" a = -torch.abs(w) b = -torch.abs(1.0 - w) logip = torch.logsumexp(torch.stack([a, b], dim=-1), dim=-1) Lhard = -torch.mean(logip) return lambdahard Lhard def trainlolnerf(images, landmarks, segments, latentdim, posencdim, direncdim, lambdamask=1.0, lambdahard=0.1, numiters=10000): K = len(images) D = latentdim # Initialize models fgmodel = ForegroundNeRF(D, posencdim) bgmodel = BackgroundNeRF(D, direncdim) # Initialize latent table Z = torch.zeros(K, D) # Optimizer optimizer = optim.Adam(list(fgmodel.parameters()) + list(bgmodel.parameters()) + [Z], lr=1e-4) for step in range(numiters): # Select a random image index k = torch.randint(0, K, (1,)).item() zk = Z[k] # Get image, landmarks, segment for image k Ik = images[k] lmk = landmarks[k] # [L, 2] segk = segments[k] # [H, W] # 1. Camera Alignment camparams = fitcamerafromlandmarks(lmk) # 2. Sample Rays xi, d, origins = samplerays(Ik.shape, camparams) # 3. Forward Pass sigma, cfg = fgmodel(xi, zk) cbg = bgmodel(d, zk) # 4. Render crender, alpha, w = renderray(xi, sigma, cfg, cbg) # 5. Compute Losses # Gather ground truth colors for sampled pixels (simplified to full image for clarity) gtcolors = Ik.flatten(0, 1) Lrgb = torch.mean((crender - gtcolors) 2) # Mask Loss segvalues = segk.flatten() Lmask = torch.mean((alpha - segvalues) 2) # Hard Surface Loss Lhard = computehardloss(w, lambdahard) # Total Loss loss = Lrgb + lambdamask Lmask + Lhard # 6. Backward Pass optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return fgmodel, bgmodel, Z def generateconditional(newimage, fgmodel, bgmodel, Z, posencdim, direncdim): # Initialize new latent code to mean of Z muZ = torch.mean(Z, dim=0) znew = muZ.clone().detach().requiresgrad(True) optimizer = optim.Adam([znew], lr=1e-4) # Optimize znew to reconstruct newimage for step in range(1000): # Sample rays from newimage xi, d, origins = samplerays(newimage.shape, torch.eye(3, 4)) # Render sigma, cfg = fgmodel(xi, znew) cbg = bgmodel(d, znew) crender, alpha, w = renderray(xi, sigma, cfg, cbg) # Compute RGB Loss gtcolors = newimage.flatten(0, 1) Lrgb = torch.mean((crender - gtcolors) 2) loss = Lrgb optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return znew def generateunconditional(Z, posencdim, direncdim, fgmodel, bgmodel, truncation=1.0): # Compute mean and covariance of Z muZ = torch.mean(Z, dim=0) # PCA to find covariance covZ = torch.cov(Z.T) # Sample from Gaussian noise = torch.randnlike(muZ) zsample = muZ + truncation torch.linalg.cholesky(covZ) @ noise return zsample Flat Representation: Without multi-view consistency, NeRF methods can collapse to a flat representation. LOLNeRF mitigates this with the hard surface loss and camera alignment. Surface Blurring: In single-view cases, the surface may blur along the view direction. The hard surface loss helps enforce sharp transitions. Segmentation Errors: If the segmentation module fails to remove non-subject foreground objects or erroneously removes parts of the subject, reconstruction quality degrades. Camera Fitting Errors: Unreasonable camera estimates (e.g., too short focal lengths) can lead to distorted reconstructions. Memory: Training complexity is decoupled from image resolution. Unlike GAN-based methods that supervise on inter-pixel relationships (requiring memory proportional to image size for discriminators), LOLNeRF trains on individual pixels, allowing arbitrary image sizes without increasing memory requirements during training. Time: Training involves optimizing latent codes for each image alongside network parameters. The time complexity is proportional to the number of images and the number of optimization steps per image. Reconstruction (CelebA subset): On a 200-image subset of the \pi-GAN training set (CelebA), LOLNeRF trained on FFHQ achieves PSNR 29.0, SSIM 0.913, LPIPS 0.199 at 128^2 resolution. Reconstruction (FFHQ Test): On test images from FFHQ, LOLNeRF trained on CelebA-HQ at 256^2 achieves PSNR 26.2, SSIM 0.856, LPIPS 0.363. Novel View Synthesis (HUMBI): On the HUMBI dataset, LOLNeRF trained on CelebA-HQ achieves PSNR 26.6, SSIM 0.930, Mask-LPIPS 0.0989. Strengths: Works with single-view images without explicit geometric supervision. Higher resolution capability than GAN-based methods due to pixel-wise supervision. Learns per-image latent codes, enabling high-quality reconstruction of specific images. Limitations: Requires pre-trained models for landmarks and segmentation, which may fail on out-of-distribution data. Camera fitting is approximate and can produce errors. Limited to specific object classes (e.g., faces) where canonical landmarks are available. Use when you have single-view images of a specific object class (e.g., faces) and want to generate novel views or reconstruct the 3D shape. Use when you need high-resolution output and cannot use GAN-based methods due to memory constraints. Do not use if you have multi-view data and want to use standard NeRF, which may be more robust. Do not use if the input images contain significant background clutter or non-subject foreground objects that the segmentation model cannot handle. LOLNeRF was introduced in November 2021. It was built similarly to \pi-GAN but used Generative Latent Optimization (GLO) instead of adversarial training. The method addresses the bottleneck of requiring multi-view data for NeRF training by leveraging approximate camera poses derived from 2D landmarks. It is used for single-shot view synthesis of human faces. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 LOLNeRF: Learn from One Look, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00161, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Robustness and Generalization
body: This family encompasses methods that improve NeRF training stability against adversarial perturbations Aug-NeRF, novel view synthesis quality through ensemble compression NeRF Ensemble with Conjoint Pruning, and handling of unconstrained "in-the-wild" data with transient occluders or synthetic-to-real domain gaps NeRF in the Wild, ContraNeRF. Unlike standard NeRF training which assumes a static, consistently lit scene, these methods introduce mechanisms for implicit regularization, multi-model aggregation, or explicit disentanglement of static and transient scene components. The methods in this family share the goal of improving generalization beyond the training set or robustness to data inconsistencies. They generally operate by modifying the optimization landscape or the scene representation: 1. Implicit Regularization: Methods like Aug-NeRF inject worst-case perturbations during training to smooth the loss landscape, avoiding the over-constraining of explicit smoothness regularizers. 2. Ensemble and Compression: Methods like NeRF Ensemble with Conjoint Pruning combine multiple models of different resolutions and compress them to reduce variance and memory footprint while maintaining quality. 3. Disentanglement: Methods like NeRF in the Wild separate the scene into static geometry and image-dependent transient/appearance components to handle non-static elements. 4. Cross-View Consistency: Methods like ContraNeRF use contrastive learning and geometry-aware feature aggregation to ensure multi-view consistency without per-scene optimization. Aug-NeRF addresses the generalization gap by injecting worst-case adversarial perturbations at three levels: input coordinates, intermediate MLP features, and pre-rendering outputs. It uses a min-max optimization game to induce a smooth loss landscape, enhancing generalization to unseen views without sacrificing detail, unlike explicit smoothness regularizers. This method improves novel view synthesis by combining two NeRF models of different grid resolutions (DVGO architecture). It uses a three-stage process: independent training, fine-tuning of the averaged output (Ens-FT), and compression via conjoint pruning (CPE). It outperforms vanilla ensembling while maintaining similar parameter counts. NeRF-W handles unconstrained photo collections by disentangling the scene into a shared static geometry and image-dependent components (appearance embeddings and a transient head). It uses a data-dependent uncertainty field to discount transient regions (e.g., moving objects, variable lighting), allowing robust synthesis of static structures. ContraNeRF improves synthetic-to-real generalization by eliminating per-scene optimization. It uses a shared CNN and contrastive learning to aggregate information from nearby source views for any unseen target view, addressing the tendency of synthetic-trained models to produce sharp but inaccurate volume densities on real data. RoGUENeRF is a post-processing enhancer that improves visual quality and high-frequency texture reconstruction. It aligns features from neighboring training views to a novel test view using geometry, refines them with non-rigid optical flow, and fuses them via geometry-aware attention. It is robust to inaccurate camera calibration and requires less training data than methods like NeRFLiX. The need for robustness and generalization in NeRF arises from the sensitivity of neural radiance fields to overfitting, limited view coverage, and non-ideal data conditions such as transient occluders or domain shifts. Aug-NeRF, NeRF Ensemble with Conjoint Pruning, NeRF in the Wild, ContraNeRF, and RoGUENeRF represent distinct approaches to these challenges, ranging from adversarial training to ensemble methods and explicit scene decomposition.

name: Aug-NeRF
head: Aug-NeRF Training Pipeline, Augmented NeRF, Triple-Level Physically-Grounded Augmentations
body: Aug-NeRF is a training framework for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that enhances generalization to unseen views and robustness to data inconsistencies by injecting worst-case adversarial perturbations at three distinct levels of the rendering pipeline: input coordinates, intermediate MLP features, and pre-rendering outputs. Unlike explicit smoothness regularizers (e.g., Laplacian or Total Variation) that aggressively constrain MLP flexibility and often degrade performance, Aug-NeRF uses these perturbations as a data-adaptive implicit regularization to induce a smooth loss landscape without sacrificing representation capacity. It builds on NeRF by treating the training objective as a min-max game where perturbations maximize the photometric loss, which is then minimized with respect to network parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N training images I = \{Ii\}{i=1}^N with corresponding camera poses P = \{\phii\}{i=1}^N. The neural radiance field F\Theta is parameterized by weights \Theta. Outputs: Updated network weights \Theta that minimize the combined photometric and adversarial regularization loss. Data Structures and Layout: Ray Representation: A ray is defined as r = (o, d, \theta), where o \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the optical center, d \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the direction, and \theta \in [-\pi, \pi]^2 is the angular view direction. Radiance Field: F\Theta: (p, \theta) \mapsto (c, \sigma), where p \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the spatial coordinate, c \in \mathbb{R}^3 is RGB color, and \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+ is density. MLP Structure: F\Theta = \gamma \circ \text{MLP}\Theta, where \gamma is a Fourier feature mapping network. The MLP consists of a shared feature encoder f(\cdot) mapping coordinates to a D-dimensional feature vector, followed by a color branch g(\cdot) and a density branch h(\cdot). Sampling: Points are sampled along rays using coarse uniform sampling (K/2 points) and fine density-proportional sampling (K/2 points), totaling K points per ray. Formulas: 1. Volume Rendering: C(r | \Theta) = \sum{k=1}^{K} T(k) (1 - \exp(-\sigmak \Delta tk)) ck where T(k) = \exp(-\sum{l=1}^{k-1} \sigmal \Delta tl) is the transmittance, and \Delta tk = t{k+1} - tk. 2. Training Objective (Min-Max Game): \min{\Theta} \mathbb{E}{(r, \hat{C}) \sim P(\mathcal{R})} \left[ \| C(r | \Theta) - \hat{C} \|2^2 + \lambda \max{\delta} \| C^\dag(r | \Theta, \delta) - \hat{C} \|2^2 \right] where \delta = (\deltap, \deltaf, \deltar) represents perturbations for coordinates, features, and output respectively, and \lambda = 0.1. 3. Perturbation Search (Projected Gradient Descent): \delta^{(t+1)} = \text{Proj}{\|\delta\|\infty \le \epsilon} \left[ \delta^{(t)} + \alpha \cdot \text{sgn}(\nabla\delta \mathcal{L}(\Theta | \mathcal{R}, \delta)) \right] where \alpha is the step size and \epsilon is the perturbation radius. Parameters: K: Total number of depth intervals (sum of coarse and fine samples). \lambda: Regularization weight, set to 0.1. PGD Configuration: Coordinate level uses 3 steps with step size 10^{-2}; Feature level uses 1 step with 10^{-3}; Pre-rendering level uses 1 step with 10^{-5}. Perturbation Bounds: \deltat: Constrained by |\alphat (t{k+1} - tk)|. \delta{xyz}: Constrained to a ball B(0, \epsilonp) along the ray. \delta\theta: Constrained to a conical frustum [-\epsilonp/2f, \epsilonp/2f]^2, where f is focal length and \epsilonp is pixel size. \deltac, \delta\sigma: Constrained to [-\epsilonc, \epsilonc]^3 \times [-\epsilon\sigma, \epsilon\sigma], clamped to keep ck, \sigmak \in [0, 1]. \deltaf: Constrained to [-\epsilonf, \epsilonf]^D. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def augnerftrain(images, poses, Ftheta, K, lambdareg, pgdcfg): """ images: List of N training images. poses: List of N camera poses (3x4 matrices). Ftheta: Neural Radiance Field function Ftheta(p, theta) -> (c, sigma). K: Total number of samples per ray. lambdareg: Weight for adversarial regularization (0.1). pgdcfg: Dict with keys 'coord', 'feat', 'output', each containing {'steps': int, 'stepsize': float, 'epsilon': float}. """ rays = [] for i in range(len(images)): # Cast rays for each pixel in image i using pose i # Returns list of rays r = (o, d, theta) and ground truth colors Chat raypixels = castrays(images[i], poses[i]) rays.extend(raypixels) for iteration in range(500000): # 500K iterations # 1. Sample a batch of rays (batch size 1 assumed for simplicity) ray, Chat = rays[random.randint(0, len(rays)-1)] o, d, theta, Chat = ray # 2. Generate worst-case perturbations using PGD # Coordinate Perturbation deltat, deltaxyz, deltatheta = pgdsearchcoordinate( ray, Ftheta, Chat, pgdcfg['coord']) # Feature Perturbation deltaf = pgdsearchfeature( ray, Ftheta, Chat, pgdcfg['feat']) # Pre-rendering Output Perturbation deltac, deltasigma = pgdsearchoutput( ray, Ftheta, Chat, pgdcfg['output']) # 3. Coarse Sampling tcoarse = uniformsample(K // 2, ray.tnear, ray.tfar) # 4. Fine Sampling (proportional to coarse densities) # Query coarse points to get densities for importance sampling pcoarse = o + tcoarse d, sigmacoarse = Ftheta(pcoarse, theta) tfine = importancesample(K // 2, tcoarse, sigmacoarse) # Combine and sort all depth intervals tall = sort(concat(tcoarse, tfine)) # 5. Compute Perturbed Points and Features # Apply coordinate perturbations tdag = tall + deltat thetadag = theta + deltatheta pdag = o + tdag d + deltaxyz # Query network for perturbed features features = Ftheta.featureencoder(pdag) # 6. Compute Perturbed Outputs # Color branch cdag = Ftheta.colorbranch(features + deltaf, thetadag) + deltac # Density branch sigmadag = Ftheta.densitybranch(features + deltaf) + deltasigma # Clamp outputs to valid range [0, 1] cdag = clamp(cdag, 0, 1) sigmadag = clamp(sigmadag, 0, 1) # 7. Volumetric Rendering # Compute intervals dt = diff(tall) dtdag = diff(tdag) # Compute transmittance T = [1.0] for k in range(1, len(tall)): T.append(T[-1] exp(-sigmacoarse[k-1] dt[k-1])) Tdag = [1.0] for k in range(1, len(tdag)): Tdag.append(Tdag[-1] exp(-sigmadag[k-1] dtdag[k-1])) # Render perturbed color alphadag = 1.0 - exp(-sigmadag dtdag) Cdag = sum(Tdag[k] alphadag[k] cdag[k] for k in range(len(tall))) # Clean render for photometric loss Cclean = renderclean(ray, Ftheta) # 8. Compute Loss L = mse(Cclean, Chat) + lambdareg mse(Cdag, Chat) # 9. Update Network Parameters gradients = computegradients(L, Ftheta) Ftheta.update(gradients) def pgdsearchcoordinate(ray, Ftheta, Chat, cfg): deltat, deltaxyz, deltatheta = 0.0, zeros(3), zeros(3) for step in range(cfg['steps']): # Compute gradient of loss w.r.t perturbations tdag = ray.t + deltat thetadag = ray.theta + deltatheta pdag = ray.o + tdag ray.d + deltaxyz # Render with these perturbations Cperturbed = renderraywithcoords(ray, Ftheta, deltat, deltaxyz, deltatheta) grad = gradient(mse(Cperturbed, Chat), [deltat, deltaxyz, deltatheta]) # Update deltat += cfg['stepsize'] sign(grad.deltat) deltaxyz += cfg['stepsize'] sign(grad.deltaxyz) deltatheta += cfg['stepsize'] sign(grad.deltatheta) # Project to constraints deltat = projectdeltat(deltat, ray) deltaxyz = projectball(deltaxyz, cfg['epsilon']) deltatheta = projectcone(deltatheta, cfg['epsilon'], ray.focallength) return deltat, deltaxyz, deltatheta def pgdsearchfeature(ray, Ftheta, Chat, cfg): deltaf = 0 for step in range(cfg['steps']): # Query features at perturbed coordinates (from coord PGD result) features = Ftheta.featureencoder(pdag) cperturbed = Ftheta.colorbranch(features + deltaf, thetadag) sigmaperturbed = Ftheta.densitybranch(features + deltaf) Cperturbed = renderray(cperturbed, sigmaperturbed,...) grad = gradient(mse(Cperturbed, Chat), deltaf) deltaf += cfg['stepsize'] sign(grad) deltaf = projectbox(deltaf, cfg['epsilon']) return deltaf def pgdsearchoutput(ray, Ftheta, Chat, cfg): deltac = 0 deltasigma = 0 for step in range(cfg['steps']): # Perturb final color and density before integration Cperturbed = renderray(c + deltac, sigma + deltasigma,...) gradc = gradient(mse(Cperturbed, Chat), deltac) gradsigma = gradient(mse(Cperturbed, Chat), deltasigma) deltac += cfg['stepsize'] sign(gradc) deltasigma += cfg['stepsize'] sign(gradsigma) deltac = projectbox(deltac, cfg['epsilon']) deltasigma = projectbox(deltasigma, cfg['epsilon']) return deltac, deltasigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perturbation Strength: Using excessively strong worst-case perturbations (e.g., PGD-10) can deteriorate training performance instead of improving it. Batch Size: The algorithm description assumes a batch size of 1 for simplicity; implementation for larger batches requires averaging gradients or perturbations appropriately. Feature Injection Point: Injecting feature perturbation into the middle layer of the NeRF MLP contributes most significantly to performance gains; other layers may be less effective. A data augmentation technique that overlays randomly positioned and colored squares on training images to test and improve model robustness to in-the-wild transient occlusions. It sets itself apart from standard augmentation by explicitly simulating the physical presence of temporary objects that obscure underlying geometry, forcing the neural radiance field to learn to ignore or represent these artifacts as non-permanent features. Time Complexity: Training requires 500K iterations, which is comparable to standard NeRF but includes the overhead of PGD steps for perturbation generation at each iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires standard NeRF memory footprint plus storage for perturbation vectors \delta during the inner maximization loop. Performance: On the LLFF dataset, Aug-NeRF reduces average error by 14.3%–26.0% and improves PSNR by up to 1.5dB (e.g., +1.34 on "fern", +1.37 on "trex") compared to baseline NeRF. On the 360° NeRF-Synthetic dataset, it reduces average error by 12.5%–44.7%. PSNR improvements include +1.33 on "drums" and +0.87 on "chair". Robustness: When trained on noisy supervision images (Gaussian and Shot noise), Aug-NeRF achieves 6.5%–26.9% average error reduction compared to vanilla NeRF. Hardware: Evaluated on NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU with 48 GB memory. Strengths: Implicitly regularizes the model without sacrificing representation flexibility; improves geometry smoothness and generalization to unseen views; robust to noisy input data. Limitations: Sensitive to perturbation strength; requires careful tuning of PGD parameters; computationally more expensive per iteration than vanilla NeRF due to adversarial search. Aug-NeRF was proposed by Tianlong Chen, Peihao Wang, Zhiwen Fan, and Zhangyang Wang from The University of Texas at Austin in 2022. It addresses the generalization gap in NeRF where interpolated novel views often yield inconsistent and visually non-smooth geometric results. The method is inspired by robust data augmentations used in convolutional neural networks, adapting the concept of worst-case adversarial perturbations to the specific physics of volumetric rendering. It contrasts with explicit regularizers like Laplacian or Total Variation, which are found to constrain MLP flexibility too aggressively. name: Occluder simulation augmentation
head: Transient occluder simulation
body: Occluder simulation augmentation is a data augmentation technique that overlays randomly positioned and colored squares on training images to test and improve model robustness to in-the-wild transient occlusions. It sets itself apart from standard augmentation by explicitly simulating the physical presence of temporary objects that obscure underlying geometry, forcing the neural radiance field to learn to ignore or represent these artifacts as non-permanent features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training images \{Ii\} for a static scene. Output: An augmented dataset \{I'i\} where transient occluders are simulated. Data Structures: Occluder: A rectangular region defined by its top-left coordinate (x, y), width w, and height h in pixel space. Stripes: The occluder is composed of 10 vertical stripes. Each stripe has a random color Cj \in \mathbb{R}^3 (RGB). Steps: 1. Reference Image: Leave the first training image I0 untouched to serve as a reference for evaluation. 2. Iteration: For each subsequent training image Ii (i > 0): a. Position Selection: Randomly select a position (x, y) for the occluder square within the image boundaries. b. Color Generation: Generate 10 random colors \{C1,..., C{10}\} for the vertical stripes. c. Overlay: Draw a square at (x, y) filled with the 10 vertical stripes of the generated colors. d. Result: The resulting image I'i contains the occluder. Parameters: Stripes per Occluder: 10. Occluder Shape: Square. Occluder Position: Random. Occluder Color: Random. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Consistency: The occluders must not have a consistent 3D location across images. If they do, the model represents them as colored fog in 3D space rather than transient noise. Evaluation Bias: Standard metrics like PSNR, MS-SSIM, and LPIPS are unable to ignore transient objects. Evaluating against reference images that contain occluders will yield poor scores because the NeRF model is designed to generate clean scenes without such occlusions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import numpy as np def applyoccluderaugmentation(image: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Applies transient occluder simulation to a single training image. Args: image: Input training image (H, W, 3) in RGB. Returns: Augmented image with a random occluder. """ augmentedimage = image.copy() h, w, = augmentedimage.shape # Square size not specified in sources squaresize = max(1, int(min(h, w) 0.1)) x = random.randint(0, w - squaresize) y = random.randint(0, h - squaresize) numstripes = 10 stripewidth = max(1, squaresize // numstripes) for j in range(numstripes): color = np.random.randint(0, 256, size=3, dtype=np.uint8) stripexstart = x + j stripewidth stripexend = min(x + (j + 1) stripewidth, x + squaresize) if j == numstripes - 1: stripexend = x + squaresize ystart = max(0, y) yend = min(h, y + squaresize) xstart = max(0, stripexstart) xend = min(w, stripexend) if xend > xstart and yend > ystart: augmentedimage[ystart:yend, xstart:xend] = color return augmentedimage def augmentdataset(images: list) -> list: """ Augments a list of training images. The first image is left untouched. """ augmentedimages = [] for i, img in enumerate(images): if i == 0: augmentedimages.append(img) else: augmentedimages.append(applyoccluderaugmentation(img)) return augmentedimages A training technique to promote robustness against image attacks by applying differentiable augmentations to the fully rendered image before passing it to a watermark decoder. Unlike occluder simulation which modifies input training data, this method modifies the output of the renderer. It selects a random pair of augmentations from a set including brightness, contrast, color jiggle, gaussian blur, gaussian noise, hue, posterize, RGB shift, saturation, median blur, box blur, motion blur, sharpness, and differentiable JPEG compression. This ensures the embedded watermark survives typical image processing attacks. Performance Impact: On the Lego dataset, this variation reduces NeRF's PSNR by 14 dB on average. Reason for Degradation: NeRF and NeRF-A represent occluders as colored fog in 3D space, thereby causing the underlying geometry (e.g., the Lego figure) to be obscured. Strengths: Tests model robustness to in-the-wild occlusions. Limitations: Standard evaluation metrics (PSNR, MS-SSIM, LPIPS) are biased against this augmentation because they compare against clean reference images, while the model is trained to ignore the occluders. Originated in the context of "NeRF in the Wild" (NeRF-W), where unconstrained photo collections contain transient objects like people and vehicles. The technique was introduced to test model robustness to in-the-wild occlusions, as standard image comparison metrics are unable to ignore transient objects. It is a component of the Aug-NeRF framework, which injects worst-case perturbations into the NeRF pipeline Aug-NeRF. name: NeRF Ensemble with Conjoint Pruning
head: CPE, Ens-FT, IPM
body: NeRF Ensemble with Conjoint Pruning (CPE) improves novel view synthesis by combining two Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models of different grid resolutions, specifically using the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) architecture. It addresses the high computational requirements and parameter inefficiency of single large NeRF models by demonstrating that ensembling multiple models at different scales requires fewer parameters to achieve the same image quality constraint compared to training and compressing one large model directly. Unlike vanilla ensembling, which may yield suboptimal results, CPE employs a specific fine-tuning and compression strategy to maintain a similar memory footprint and parameter count to a single model while outperforming it. The method operates in three distinct stages: independent training, ensemble fine-tuning, and conjoint pruning. It relies on the DVGO architecture, where the scene is represented by explicit voxel grids optimized directly, avoiding the implicit MLP bottleneck of standard NeRFs. Inputs: Training dataset D{train}, validation dataset D{val}, and the ensemble size, which is fixed at 2 models. Outputs: An ensemble of two compressed NeRF models (DVGO variants) that can be rendered jointly. The ensemble consists of two separate NeRF models, denoted as n=1 and n=2. Each model n maintains its own set of parameters wn and a voxel grid. The models are trained with different grid resolutions. The source specifies two different resolutions but does not list exact numerical values. Stage 1: Independent Training 1. Initialize two NeRF models with different grid resolutions. 2. Train each model independently on the training set D{train} for a fixed number of iterations. 3. Minimize the standard NeRF loss function for each model n: L(wn) = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^{M} \| Cm - C(wn, xm, \omegam) \|^2 Where: wn: Model parameters for the n-th NeRF. M: Total number of training samples. Cm: Ground truth color of the m-th pixel. C(wn, xm, \omegam): Predicted color by the n-th NeRF for the 3D point xm and viewing direction \omegam. Stage 2: Ensemble Fine-Tuning (Ens-FT) 1. Construct the ensemble by averaging the outputs of the two trained models. 2. Optimize the ensemble parameters by minimizing the difference between the ground truth and the averaged ensemble output. 3. The ensemble output C{avg, m} for a sample m is: C{avg, m} = \frac{1}{2} \sum{n=1}^{2} C(wn, xm, \omegam) (Note: The source defines n=1,2 and uses a simple average). 4. The loss function for this stage is: L{Ens-FT} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^{M} \| Cm - C{avg, m} \|^2 5. Continue fine-tuning until performance on the validation set begins to drop. Stage 3: Conjoint Pruning (CPE) 1. Compress the ensemble using the validation set D{val} via conjoint pruning. 2. Return the final pruned ensemble. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainnerfensemble(Dtrain, Dval, numiterations): # Stage 1: Independent Training w1 = initializemodel(resolution="high") w2 = initializemodel(resolution="low") for in range(numiterations): batch = samplebatch(Dtrain) loss1 = computeloss(w1, batch) w1 = optimizerstep(w1, loss1) loss2 = computeloss(w2, batch) w2 = optimizerstep(w2, loss2) # Stage 2: Ensemble Fine-Tuning (Ens-FT) while not earlystop(Dval, w1, w2): batch = samplebatch(Dtrain) pred1 = rendermodel(w1, batch) pred2 = rendermodel(w2, batch) predavg = [(p1 + p2) / 2.0 for p1, p2 in zip(pred1, pred2)] lossens = computelossensemble(batch, predavg) w1 = optimizerstep(w1, lossens) w2 = optimizerstep(w2, lossens) # Stage 3: Conjoint Pruning (CPE) w1, w2 = applyconjointpruning(w1, w2, Dval) return w1, w2 def computeloss(w, batch): predictions = rendermodel(w, batch) return meansquarederror(batch.colors, predictions) def computelossensemble(batch, predavg): return meansquarederror(batch.colors, predavg) def meansquarederror(target, prediction): return sum((t - p) 2 for t, p in zip(target, prediction)) / len(target) def samplebatch(dataset): return random.choice(dataset) def earlystop(Dval, w1, w2): # Standard validation metric check return False def applyconjointpruning(w1, w2, Dval): # Conjoint pruning formulation to prevent performance degradation # Specific algorithm details are not provided in the sources return w1, w2 def initializemodel(resolution): return {"params": [0.0] resolution} def rendermodel(w, batch): # Standard DVGO volumetric rendering return [0.0] len(batch) def optimizerstep(w, loss): # Standard gradient descent update return w Ensemble Size: 2 NeRF models. Grid Resolution: Two different resolutions are used. Training Iterations: Fixed number for Stage 1. Vanilla Ensembling: Simply averaging two independently trained models without fine-tuning and pruning yields suboptimal results. Pruning Degradation: Without the proposed conjoint pruning formulation, compression may lead to significant performance degradation. Precision: The source does not specify numerical precision requirements (e.g., FP16 vs FP32). Time Complexity: Requires training two models independently, then fine-tuning the ensemble, which is computationally more expensive than training a single model but achieves better quality under the same parameter count constraint. Memory Footprint: The method aims to maintain a similar memory footprint and parameter count to a single model by compressing the ensemble. Performance: Beats vanilla approaches under the same parameter's cardinality constraint. Strengths: Improves novel view synthesis performance; requires fewer parameters than training and compressing one large model directly for the same quality. Limitations: Higher training complexity due to the multi-stage process. Origin: Proposed by Francesco Di Sario, Riccardo Renzulli, Enzo Tartaglione, and Marco Grangetto in 2023 for ICIAP 2023. Context: Addresses the high computational requirements and limited scene diversity of standard NeRFs. It builds on Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO). History: It is described as the first work proposing a joint ensembling and compression scheme for NeRF models. Two is Better than One: Achieving High-Quality 3D Scene Modeling with a NeRF Ensemble, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-43153-127, fetched 2026-10-26

name: NeRF in the Wild
head: Martin-Brualla et al, NeRF-W (NeRF in the Wild), Neural Radiance Fields for Unconstrained Photo Collections
body: NeRF in the Wild (NeRF-W) is an extension of Neural Radiance Fields designed to handle unconstrained, "in-the-wild" photo collections where strict consistency assumptions fail due to variable illumination, auto-exposure, and transient occluders. It disentangles the scene into a shared static geometry and image-dependent components: a learned low-dimensional appearance embedding for photometric variations and a secondary volumetric radiance field with uncertainty modeling for transient objects. Unlike its siblings, NeRF-W explicitly models both appearance and transient geometry simultaneously, whereas Aug-NeRF focuses on robustness via perturbations, NeRF Ensemble with Conjoint Pruning on compression, and ContraNeRF on cross-view consistency without per-scene optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N images \{Ii\} of the same scene; 3D position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and image index i. Camera poses are estimated using COLMAP during experimental setup. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}i(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r}; static density \sigma(\mathbf{x}), static color \mathbf{c}i(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}), transient density \sigmai^{(\tau)}(\mathbf{x}), transient color \mathbf{c}i^{(\tau)}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}), and uncertainty variance \betai(\mathbf{r})^2. Data Structures: 1. Static MLP (MLP{\theta1}): Takes \mathbf{x} and positional encoding \gamma(\mathbf{x}). 2. Appearance Embedding (\mathbf{l}i^{(a)}): A learnable vector of length n^{(a)} for each image i. 3. Color MLP (MLP{\theta2}): Takes \mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}), viewing direction \mathbf{d} (encoded), and \mathbf{l}i^{(a)}. 4. Transient MLP (MLP{\theta3}): Takes \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}, and a transient embedding \mathbf{l}i^{(\tau)} (length n^{(\tau)}). 5. Uncertainty MLP (MLP{\theta4}): Takes \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize MLPs with random weights and embeddings to small random values. 2. Sampling: For each training image Ii, sample rays \mathbf{r}. Sample K points \{tk\}{k=1}^K along each ray using stratified sampling or importance sampling based on a coarse model. 3. Static Query: For each point tk, query MLP{\theta1} to get \sigma(tk) and \mathbf{z}(tk). 4. Static Color Query: Query MLP{\theta2} with \mathbf{z}(tk), \mathbf{d}, and \mathbf{l}i^{(a)} to get static color \mathbf{c}i(tk). 5. Transient Query: Query MLP{\theta3} with tk, \mathbf{d}, and \mathbf{l}i^{(\tau)} to get transient density \sigmai^{(\tau)}(tk) and transient color \mathbf{c}i^{(\tau)}(tk). 6. Uncertainty Query: Query MLP{\theta4} with tk and \mathbf{d} to get variance \betai(tk)^2. 7. Rendering (Composite): Compute the expected color \hat{C}i(\mathbf{r}) by alpha-compositing both static and transient components: \hat{C}i(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^K \alphak \mathbf{c}i(tk) + \sum{k=1}^K \alphak^{(\tau)} \mathbf{c}i^{(\tau)}(tk) where the transmittance Ti(tk) accounts for both static and transient densities: Ti(tk) = \exp\left( -\sum{k'=1}^{k-1} (\sigma(t{k'}) + \sigmai^{(\tau)}(t{k'})) \delta{k'} \right) and weights are \alphak = Ti(tk)(1 - \exp(-\sigma(tk)\deltak)) and \alphak^{(\tau)} = Ti(tk)(1 - \exp(-\sigmai^{(\tau)}(tk)\deltak)). 8. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss Li(\mathbf{r}) for the ray: Li(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\|Ci(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}i(\mathbf{r})\|^2}{2\betai(\mathbf{r})^2} + \frac{\log \betai(\mathbf{r})^2}{2} + \frac{\lambdau}{2K} \sum{k=1}^K \sigmai^{(\tau)}(tk) The first two terms are the negative log-likelihood of the color difference assuming Gaussian noise with variance \betai(\mathbf{r})^2. The third term is an L1 regularization on transient density to prevent it from explaining static features. 9. Coarse Loss: Additionally, compute a coarse rendering \hat{C}c^i(\mathbf{r}) using only the static head and appearance embeddings, and add \frac{1}{2} \| Ci(\mathbf{r}) - \hat{C}c^i(\mathbf{r}) \|^2 to the loss. 10. Optimization: Minimize the total loss over all rays and images using Adam optimizer. Optimize MLP parameters \theta and embeddings \{\mathbf{l}i^{(a)}\}, \{\mathbf{l}i^{(\tau)}\}. 11. Test-Time Evaluation: For a test image, optimize a single appearance embedding \mathbf{l}^{(a)} using only the left half of the image to avoid leakage, then evaluate metrics on the right half. Render only static \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) by omitting transient and uncertainty fields. Parameters: \lambdau: Regularization weight for transient density. Not given in the sources. \beta{min}: Hyperparameter >0 added to the softplus activation for \betai(\mathbf{x})^2 to ensure minimum importance. n^{(a)}, n^{(\tau)}: Dimensions of appearance and transient embeddings. Not given in the sources. Batch size: 2048. Training steps: 300,000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softplus(x, betamin): # Shifted softplus to ensure minimum variance return np.where(x > 20, x, np.log1p(np.exp(x))) + betamin def positionalencoding(x, numfreqs): scales = 2.0 np.arange(numfreqs) shaped = x.reshape(-1, 1, 3) scales.reshape(1, -1, 1) shaped = shaped.reshape(-1, 3 numfreqs) return np.concatenate([np.sin(shaped), np.cos(shaped)], axis=-1) def samplerays(imageindex, numrays, K): # Standard ray casting from camera pose and image grid # Returns x: (numrays, K, 3), d: (numrays, 3), Ci: (numrays, 3) pass def renderray(x, d, la, ltau, betamin, lambdau, mlpstatic, mlpcolor, mlptransient, mlpuncertainty, K, delta): # 1. Static Query sigma, z = mlpstatic(x) # sigma: (B, K), z: (B, K, D) # 2. Static Color Query cstatic = mlpcolor(z, d, la) # (B, K, 3) # 3. Transient Query sigmatau, ctau = mlptransient(x, d, ltau) # sigmatau: (B, K), ctau: (B, K, 3) # 4. Uncertainty Query betasq = softplus(mlpuncertainty(x, d), betamin) # (B, K) # 5. Alpha Compositing sigmatotal = sigma + sigmatau cumsum = np.cumsum(sigmatotal delta, axis=1) # Transmittance at start of each segment T = np.exp(-np.concatenate([np.zeros((x.shape[0], 1)), cumsum[:,:-1]], axis=1)) alpha = T (1 - np.exp(-sigma delta)) alphatau = T (1 - np.exp(-sigmatau delta)) chat = np.sum(alpha[:,:, None] cstatic + alphatau[:,:, None] ctau, axis=1) # (B, 3) # 6. Loss Calculation (matches S1 Eq. 13) # Variance is per-ray; we average per-sample predictions per ray betaraysq = np.mean(betasq, axis=1) # (B,) return chat, betaraysq, sigmatau def trainnerfw(images, poses, mlpstatic, mlpcolor, mlptransient, mlpuncertainty, la, ltau, betamin, lambdau, batchsize, numsteps, K, delta): N = len(images) for step in range(numsteps): batchindices = np.random.choice(N, batchsize) totalloss = 0.0 for i in batchindices: x, d, Ci = samplerays(i, batchsize, K) emba = la[i] embtau = ltau[i] chat, betaraysq, sigmatau = renderray( x, d, emba, embtau, betamin, lambdau, mlpstatic, mlpcolor, mlptransient, mlpuncertainty, K, delta) # S1 Eq. 13: Li(r) = ||C - Chat||^2 / (2beta^2) + log(beta^2)/2 + (lambdau / 2K) sum(sigmatau) likelihood = np.sum((Ci - chat)2, axis=-1) / (2 betaraysq) + np.log(betaraysq) / 2 reg = (lambdau / (2 K)) np.sum(sigmatau, axis=1) totalloss += np.mean(likelihood + reg) # S1 Eq. 14: Add coarse loss term: 0.5 ||Ci - Chatc||^2 # Standard Adam optimizer step on [mlpstatic, mlpcolor, mlptransient, mlpuncertainty, la, ltau] return mlpstatic, mlpcolor, mlptransient, mlpuncertainty, la, ltau def testnerfw(testimage, testpose, mlpstatic, mlpcolor, betamin): # Standard optimization to fit appearance embedding to test image latest = optimizeembedding(testimage, mlpstatic, mlpcolor, betamin) x, d, = samplerays(testimage, 1000, K) sigma, z = mlpstatic(x) cstatic = mlpcolor(z, d, latest) # Render only static components (omit transient and uncertainty) cumsum = np.cumsum(sigma delta, axis=1) T = np.exp(-np.concatenate([np.zeros((x.shape[0], 1)), cumsum[:,:-1]], axis=1)) alpha = T (1 - np.exp(-sigma delta)) chat = np.sum(alpha[:,:, None] cstatic, axis=1) return chat An architectural variant (e.g., in UP-NeRF) that uses a candidate head to predict transient properties (color, density, beta) alongside static properties, enabling robust pose optimization by filtering out transient occluders. It predicts transient color \mathbf{c}i^{(\tau)}, transient density \sigmai^{(\tau)}, and variance \betai using predicted candidate features \mathbf{f}i and candidate embeddings \mathbf{l}i^{(c)}. Unlike NeRF-W, which does not isolate the transient network and relies on different architecture assumptions, this method isolates the transient network and uses deep features (DINO) for candidate filtering. Merging transient and candidate heads degrades performance, causing failures in pose estimation and rendering quality. Time and Memory Complexity: Training requires optimizing per-image embeddings (N vectors) alongside MLP weights, increasing memory usage compared to standard NeRF. Training takes 300,000 steps. Measured Performance: On 6 landmark scenes from the Phototourism dataset, NeRF-W improves over the previous state-of-the-art (NRW) by an average margin of 4.4dB in PSNR and up to 40% in MS-SSIM. Strengths: Handles variable illumination, auto-exposure, and transient occluders (pedestrians) in unconstrained photo collections. Enables controllable appearance by interpolating in the latent space. Limitations: Cannot handle major appearance changes (e.g., seasonal changes). Camera poses are estimated using COLMAP during experimental setup. Test-time evaluation requires optimizing an appearance embedding for each test image, which can be slow. When to use: Unconstrained internet photo collections of static landmarks with varying lighting and transient objects. When not to use: Scenes with significant structural changes over time or where camera poses are unknown/unreliable. NeRF in the Wild (NeRF-W) was introduced by Martin-Brualla et al. in 2021. It was developed to address the limitations of NeRF in controlled settings, specifically its inability to model real-world phenomena like variable illumination and transient occluders in unstructured image collections. It was tested on large-scale image collections of tourist landmarks such as the Brandenburg Gate and the Trevi Fountain. A subsequent development by Sun et al. (2022) used appearance embeddings but sought output in meshes rather than radiance fields. name: ContraNeRF
body: ContraNeRF is a generalizable neural radiance field method designed to improve synthetic-to-real novel view synthesis by learning multi-view consistent features with geometric constraints. It addresses the failure of vanilla NeRF to generalize to new scenes by introducing geometry-aware contrastive learning and cross-view attention, which mitigate the artifacts caused by inaccurate volume density predictions typical of synthetic-trained models. Unlike per-scene optimization methods, ContraNeRF renders novel views for unseen scenes without per-scene optimization, relying on a shared encoder and contrastive loss to enforce consistency across views. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of training scenes \mathcal{D}{train} = \{\mathcal{I}i, \mathcal{K}i, \mathcal{E}i\}{i=1}^{N{train}}, where \mathcal{I}i = \{Ij\}{j=1}^{N^{view}i} are images, \mathcal{K}i = \{Kj\}{j=1}^{N^{view}i} are camera intrinsics, and \mathcal{E}i = \{Ej = [Rj, tj]\}{j=1}^{N^{view}i} are camera extrinsics for the i-th scene. Output: A rendered image \hat{I}r for a target view defined by intrinsic Kr and extrinsic Er. Data Structures: Features: Fi is the feature map extracted from source image Ii using a shared CNN. Enhanced Features: F'i is the geometrically enhanced feature map for source view i, obtained by aggregating information from other source views. Ray Representation: A ray R in world coordinates is parametrized by depth \delta. Parameters: N{train}: The number of training scenes. N^{view}i: The number of camera views of the i-th scene. N{near}: The number of source views used for rendering a target view. Algorithm: The model M\theta is trained by minimizing the L2 loss between rendered images and ground truth: \mathcal{M}\theta = \arg\min \| \hat{I}r - Ir \|^22 1. Feature Extraction: For each source view i in the set of N{near} nearby views, use a shared CNN to extract features Fi from the input image Ii. 2. Geometry-Aware Feature Aggregation: For each source view i, compute enhanced features F'i by querying and aggregating features from other source views using cross-view attention to enhance geometry perception. Let ui = [u, v]^\top be the 2D coordinate of a point on the i-th source view, and obtain the ray R of point ui in world coordinates parametrized by \delta. 3. Contrastive Loss Computation (GeoContrast): For each pair of source views (i, j), compute a contrastive loss. For a pixel in the i-th source view, project it to the j-th source view and sample a collection of projections to get positive and negative samples. Calculate the weighted contrastive loss considering the distance between the positive sample and the negative samples. 4. Rendering: For each ray in the target view, compute colors and densities for a set of samples along the ray by aggregating local features from the enhanced source features \{F'i\}{i=1}^{N{near}}. Accumulate colors and densities to render the image \hat{I}r. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traincontranerf(trainingdata, Nnear, lambdac, lr, epochs): # Initialize model parameters theta theta = inittheta() for epoch in range(epochs): for scene in trainingdata: images, intrinsics, extrinsics = scene # Select Nnear source views (e.g., closest by camera distance) sourceindices = selectnearbyviews(images, intrinsics, extrinsics, Nnear) srcimgs = [images[i] for i in sourceindices] srcKs = [intrinsics[i] for i in sourceindices] srcEs = [extrinsics[i] for i in sourceindices] # Step 1: Feature Extraction features = [sharedcnnforward(img, theta.cnnw) for img in srcimgs] # Step 2: Geometry-Aware Feature Aggregation enhancedfeatures = [] for i in range(len(srcimgs)): Fi = features[i] # Query features from other source views and aggregate to get F'i Fprimei = crossviewattentionforward(Fi, features, srcKs, srcEs, excludeindex=i, theta.attw) enhancedfeatures.append(Fprimei) # Step 3: Contrastive Loss Computation (GeoContrast) contrastiveloss = 0.0 for i in range(len(srcimgs)): for j in range(len(srcimgs)): if i == j: continue # Project pixels from view i to view j, sample positive/negative, compute weighted loss lossij = geocontrastlossforward(srcimgs[i], srcimgs[j], srcKs[i], srcEs[i], srcKs[j], srcEs[j], theta.conw) contrastiveloss += lossij # Step 4: Rendering and L2 Loss Ihatr = renderforward(enhancedfeatures, Kr, Er, theta.renderw) l2loss = sum((Ihatr[p] - Ir[p]) 2 for p in pixels) totalloss = l2loss + lambdac contrastiveloss # Optimization step grad = computegradients(totalloss, theta) theta = theta - lr grad def selectnearbyviews(images, intrinsics, extrinsics, Nnear): # Select Nnear source views closest to the target camera return sorted(range(len(images)), key=lambda i: cameradistance(intrinsics[i], extrinsics[i]))[:Nnear] def sharedcnnforward(img, weights): # Standard CNN forward pass to extract feature map Fi return convpoollayers(img, weights) def crossviewattentionforward(Fi, features, Ks, Es, excludeindex, weights): # Query features from other source views and aggregate to get F'i aggregated = 0.0 for j, (Fj, Kj, Ej) in enumerate(zip(features, Ks, Es)): if j == excludeindex: continue # Cross-view attention mechanism to enhance geometry perception aggregated += attentionquery(Fi, Fj, Kj, Ej, weights) return aggregated def geocontrastlossforward(imgi, imgj, Ki, Ei, Kj, Ej, weights): # Project pixels from view i to view j, sample positive/negative, compute weighted loss loss = 0.0 for pixel in imgi: proj = projectpixel(pixel, Ki, Ei, Kj, Ej) possamples = samplearound(proj, positive=True) negsamples = samplearound(proj, positive=False) loss += weightedcontrastiveloss(possamples, negsamples, weights) return loss def renderforward(enhancedfeatures, Kr, Er, weights): # Aggregate local features from enhancedfeatures along rays, compute colors/densities, accumulate rendered = {} for ray in rays(Kr, Er): samples = samplealongray(ray) color, density = aggregatefeaturesandaccumulate(samples, enhancedfeatures, weights) rendered[ray.id] = color return rendered Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Synthetic-to-Real Gap: Models trained on synthetic data tend to predict sharper but less accurate volume densities. If the geometry prediction is incorrect, this leads to severe artifacts, despite providing better fine-grained details when correct. Geometry Errors: The method relies on geometric constraints; incorrect geometry prediction can degrade performance significantly. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: ContraNeRF outperforms existing generalizable novel view synthesis methods in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS under the synthetic-to-real setting. When trained on real data, it also achieves state-of-the-art results. Strengths: Improves generalization from synthetic to real data; reduces artifacts caused by inaccurate density predictions; enhances fine-grained details. Limitations: Relies on accurate geometry perception; synthetic-trained models may still suffer from artifacts if geometry is wrong. When to use: Synthetic-to-real novel view synthesis; generalizable NeRF without per-scene optimization. When not to use: Not given in the sources. ContraNeRF was proposed by Hao Yang, Lanqing Hong, Aoxue Li, Tianyang Hu, Zhenguo Li, Gim Hee Lee, and Liwei Wang. It was published in CVPR 2023 (arXiv:2303.11052v3, 23 Jun 2023). The work addresses the limitation of vanilla NeRF, which is designed to fit the continuous 5D radiance field of a given scene and often fails to generalize to new scenes and datasets. It builds on previous generalizable NeRF methods such as pixelNeRF, IBRNet, MVSNeRF, and GeoNeRF, which leverage deep MVS techniques but overlook the negative effects of using synthetic data.
