name: RoGUENeRF
head: RoGUENeRF: A Robust Geometry-Consistent Universal Enhancer for NeRF
body: RoGUENeRF is a post-processing enhancer for trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that improves visual fidelity and restores high-frequency textures in rendered images while maintaining view-consistency and robustness to inaccurate camera calibration. Unlike methods that require extensive re-optimization or large-scale synthetic pre-training datasets, RoGUENeRF operates as a universal enhancer that can be fine-tuned on small real-world datasets, leveraging the geometry already learned by the NeRF to align and fuse features from neighboring training views. It sets itself apart from siblings like Aug-NeRF (which modifies the loss landscape) and NeRFLiX (which requires massive synthetic pre-training) by using a lightweight, geometry-aware alignment and fusion pipeline that runs in under 60 minutes of fine-tuning and offers significantly faster inference speeds. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained NeRF model, the set of training images \{Hi\}{i=1}^M with known camera poses \{Ci\}{i=1}^M, and a novel test camera pose Ck. Outputs: An enhanced RGB image Ik^{\text{enhanced}} corresponding to the novel view. Data Structures and Layouts: The method processes features through specific network blocks. The layouts are defined as follows: 1. Convolutional Encoder Block: Input: Concatenated tensor of shape [H, W, C{\text{in}}] where C{\text{in}} comprises: Neighbour Features, Test Features, Neighbour Depth (Di), Test Depth (Dk), Neighbour Camera Pose (Ci), and Test Camera Pose (Ck). Layer Sequence: 1. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1), Leaky ReLU (slope=0.01). 2. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1), Leaky ReLU (slope=0.01). 3. linear (in=12, out=128), Leaky ReLU (slope=0.01). 4. linear (in=128, out=1), Sigmoid. 5. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=128, stride=1, padding=1), Leaky ReLU (slope=0.01). 6. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1), Sigmoid. 7. conv2d (kernel=1, channels=64, stride=1, padding=0). Outputs: Image Features, Spatial Attention Mask, and Camera Attention Mask. 2. Non-Rigid Refinement Network: Input: Concatenated tensor of Neighbour Features and Test Features. Layer Sequence: 1. conv2d (kernel=7, channels=64, stride=4, padding=0), ReLU. 2. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1), ReLU. 3. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1) + ReLU (Residual connection). 4. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=2, padding=1), ReLU. 5. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=2, padding=1) + ReLU (Residual connection). 6. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1), ReLU. 7. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1). 8. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=128, stride=1, padding=1), ReLU. 9. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=64, stride=1, padding=1). 10. conv2d (kernel=3, channels=2, stride=1, padding=1) [Output: Optical Flow]. Process: The network iterates 32 times. The output flow is upsampled bilinearly to full resolution. Numbered Steps: 1. Nearest Neighbour Selection: Given a novel test camera pose Ck = (Rk, tk) and training poses \{Ci = (Ri, ti)\}{i=1}^M, identify the N training images with the largest content overlap. Compute angular distance between rotations: dist^{i}{\text{ang}}(R{k}, R{i}) = \frac {1}{3} \lvert \pi (R{k}) - \pi (R{i}) \rvert {1} where \pi(Ri) are the Euler angles of rotation matrix Ri, and \lvert \cdot \rvert1 is the L1 norm. Compute positional distance: dist^{i}{\text{pos}}(t{k}, t{i}) = \frac {1}{3} \lvert t{k} - t{i} \rvert {1} Select the top N neighbors (empirically N=5) based primarily on dist^{i}{\text{pos}}, followed by dist^{i}{\text{ang}}. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract features from the selected Neighbour Images and the Rendered Test Image using the Convolutional Encoder Block defined above. This produces Image Features, Spatial Attention Mask, and Camera Attention Mask. 3. 3D Alignment: Align the Neighbour Features to the novel test view Ck. Use the NeRF-rendered depth maps Di (neighbour) and Dk (test) along with camera poses Ci and Ck. Perform 3D reprojection using a geometry remap function with bilinear interpolation and zero padding. This warps the neighbour features into the coordinate frame of the test view. 4. Non-Rigid Refinement: Compensate for geometric inaccuracies and misalignments. Input the aligned Neighbour Features and Test Features into the Non-Rigid Refinement Network. The network estimates optical flow at 8\times downsampled resolution. Iterate the refinement process 32 times. Bilinearly upsample the estimated flow field to full resolution. Warp the aligned Neighbour Features using the refined flow field via a grid sampling function with bilinear interpolation to produce Refined Features. 5. Geometry-Aware Attention and Fusion: Combine the Refined Features with the Test Features. Apply the Spatial Attention Mask and Camera Attention Mask generated in Step 2 to regulate the contribution of misaligned regions and modulate feature importance based on camera geometry. Fuse the regulated features. 6. Uformer Enhancement: Pass the fused features through a Uformer network. The Uformer input channels are modified to accept 64-channel features (instead of the original 3-channel RGB). Perform a single inference pass without Test-Time Augmentation (TTA). Parameters: Leaky ReLU Slope: 0.01. Weight Initialization: He initialization for learnable weights. Convolutional Padding: Zero padding for all convolutional layers. Camera Pose Representation: Rotations are converted to Euler angles before processing by the attention module. Uformer Input Channels: 64. Optical Flow Resolution: Estimated at 8\times downsampled resolution, upsampled to full resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ConvolutionalEncoderBlock(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.01), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.01), nn.Linear(12, 128), nn.LeakyReLU(0.01), nn.Linear(128, 1), nn.Sigmoid(), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.LeakyReLU(0.01), nn.Conv2d(128, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.Sigmoid(), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 1, padding=0)) def forward(self, x): out = self.layers(x) return out[:,:64], out[:, 64:65], out[:, 65:66] class NonRigidRefinementNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() self.layers = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(128, 64, 7, stride=4, padding=0), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, stride=2, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, stride=2, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(128, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.Conv2d(64, 2, 3, padding=1)) def forward(self, x): return self.layers(x) class Uformer(nn.Module): def init(self, inputchannels=64): super().init() # Standard Uformer architecture modified for 64 input channels self.encoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(inputchannels, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU()) self.decoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(64, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 3, 1)) def forward(self, x): return self.decoder(self.encoder(x)) class RoGUENeRF: def init(self, nerfmodel, trainingdata, neighborcount=5): self.nerf = nerfmodel self.trainingimages = trainingdata['images'] self.trainingposes = trainingdata['poses'] self.neighborcount = neighborcount self.encoder = ConvolutionalEncoderBlock() self.refinementnet = NonRigidRefinementNetwork() self.uformer = Uformer(inputchannels=64) # Weights initialized with He initialization def matrixtoeuler(self, R): # Standard conversion from rotation matrix to Euler angles return torch.atan2(R[:, 2, 1], R[:, 2, 2]), torch.asin(-R[:, 2, 0]), torch.atan2(R[:, 1, 0], R[:, 0, 0]) def computeposedistance(self, posek, posei): Rk, tk = posek Ri, ti = posei eulerk = self.matrixtoeuler(Rk) euleri = self.matrixtoeuler(Ri) distang = torch.mean(torch.abs(eulerk - euleri)) distpos = torch.mean(torch.abs(tk - ti)) return distang, distpos def selectneighbors(self, testpose): distances = [] for i, posei in enumerate(self.trainingposes): distang, distpos = self.computeposedistance(testpose, posei) distances.append((distpos, distang, i)) distances.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [idx for,, idx in distances[:self.neighborcount]] def extractfeatures(self, neighborimages, testimage, neighbordepths, testdepth, neighborposes, testpose): # Concatenate inputs: Neighbour Features, Test Features, Neighbour Depth, Test Depth, Neighbour Cam Pose, Test Cam Pose inputtensor = self.prepareencoderinput(neighborimages, testimage, neighbordepths, testdepth, neighborposes, testpose) return self.encoder(inputtensor) def refinefeatures(self, alignedneighborfeatures, testfeatures): flow = self.refinementnet(torch.cat([alignedneighborfeatures, testfeatures], dim=1)) for in range(32): flowfull = F.interpolate(flow, scalefactor=8, mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) grid = self.flowtogrid(flowfull, alignedneighborfeatures.shape[2], alignedneighborfeatures.shape[3]) alignedneighborfeatures = F.gridsample(alignedneighborfeatures, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') flow = self.refinementnet(torch.cat([alignedneighborfeatures, testfeatures], dim=1)) return alignedneighborfeatures def flowtogrid(self, flow, h, w): # Convert flow to normalized grid for gridsample gridy, gridx = torch.meshgrid(torch.linspace(-1, 1, h), torch.linspace(-1, 1, w), indexing='ij') grid = torch.stack([gridx, gridy], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0) grid = grid + flow.permute(0, 2, 3, 1) return grid def enhance(self, testpose): testrgb, testdepth = self.nerf.render(testpose) neighborindices = self.selectneighbors(testpose) neighborimages = [self.trainingimages[i] for i in neighborindices] neighborposes = [self.trainingposes[i] for i in neighborindices] neighbordepths = [self.nerf.render(pose)[1] for pose in neighborposes] imagefeatures, spatialmask, cameramask = self.extractfeatures(neighborimages, testrgb, neighbordepths, testdepth, neighborposes, testpose) alignedfeatures = self.align3d(neighborimages, neighbordepths, neighborposes, testpose, testdepth) refinedfeatures = self.refinefeatures(alignedfeatures, imagefeatures) combinedmask = spatialmask + cameramask regulatedfeatures = refinedfeatures combinedmask enhancedoutput = self.uformer(regulatedfeatures) return enhancedoutput def align3d(self, neighborimages, neighbordepths, neighborposes, testpose, testdepth): alignedlist = [] for img, depth, pose in zip(neighborimages, neighbordepths, neighborposes): # Standard 3D reprojection using depth and camera poses aligned = self.remapwithkornia(img, depth, pose, testpose, testdepth) alignedlist.append(aligned) return torch.stack(alignedlist) def remapwithkornia(self, img, depth, srcpose, dstpose, dstdepth): # Standard 3D reprojection using depth and camera poses pass def prepareencoderinput(self, neighborimages, testimage, neighbordepths, testdepth, neighborposes, testpose): # Standard concatenation of features, depths, and poses into a single tensor pass Time Complexity: The method involves feature extraction, 3D alignment, iterative optical flow estimation (32 iterations), and Uformer inference. The optical flow estimation is performed at 8\times downsampled resolution, reducing computational cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing features for neighboring views and the Uformer model. The Uformer is modified to accept 64-channel inputs. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA V100 GPU at full float32 precision: 512x512 resolution: 337ms. 1024x1024 resolution: 1346ms. Comparison: Approximately 13x faster than NeRFLiX with TTA, 3x faster than NeRFLiX without TTA, and 3x slower than NeRFLiX++. Training/Fine-tuning Time: Fine-tuning takes less than 60 minutes. Data Efficiency: Can be pre-trained and fine-tuned on small real-world datasets (e.g., LLFF). NeRFLiX requires orders of magnitude more data (Vimeo90K) to achieve similar improvements. On small datasets, NeRFLiX can degrade performance (e.g., -0.6dB PSNR on LLFF vs +0.70dB for RoGUENeRF). Strengths: Robust to camera calibration errors, maintains view-consistency, restores high-frequency textures, fast inference, data-efficient. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial NeRF geometry (depth maps). If the NeRF geometry is severely incorrect, alignment may fail. Requires a trained NeRF model as input. When to use: When you have a trained NeRF with degraded high-frequency details and want to enhance it without re-training the NeRF, especially with limited data or noisy camera poses. When not to use: When the initial NeRF geometry is highly inaccurate, or when real-time inference is critical and NeRFLiX++ speed is required (though RoGUENeRF is still fast). RoGUENeRF was introduced by S. Catley-Chandar et al. in 2024. It addresses the limitations of existing NeRF enhancement methods like NeRFLiX, which require large-scale synthetic pre-training datasets and are computationally expensive. RoGUENeRF leverages the geometry-consistent nature of NeRFs to align and fuse features from neighboring views, offering a robust and efficient alternative for enhancing NeRF renders in the wild. name: FusedRF
head: Fusing Multiple Radiance Fields
body: FusedRF is a method to fuse multiple teacher Radiance Fields (RFs) into a single, compact student RF representation using distillation, allowing for composited scene rendering with the memory and time complexity of a single RF. Unlike naive composition which requires parallel tracing into multiple RFs (increasing memory and render time linearly with scene count), FusedRF fuses them into one RF, maintaining constant memory and render time. Unlike retraining from scratch using rendered RGB views, FusedRF uses 3D distillation from existing RFs, reducing training time by 3x. Inputs: N teacher radiance fields T1, \dots, TN encoding density \sigmaI, color cI, and potentially other attributes. A set of training rays \mathcal{R} sampled from camera poses associated with the teacher fields. Identification of a background teacher T{bg} representing the dominant scene in the composition. Outputs: A single student radiance field S capable of rendering the composited scene. Data Structures: The student S and teachers Ti are implemented as neural networks (e.g., MLPs) or structured grids, inheriting the architecture of the source RFs. The method assumes query functions Ti(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, c) and S(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, c), where \mathbf{x} is the 3D position and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. Training points \mathcal{P}: A set of 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} sampled along rays, formed by the union of selected high-density points from the teachers. Parameters: \delta: Step size for ray marching. Density thresholds: Points with lower density are pruned and points with higher density are utilized; exact numerical thresholds are not given in the sources. Loss weights: Standard L2 losses are applied without explicit weighting factors. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the student RF S with the weights of the background teacher T{bg} (the dominant teacher in the composition) to speed up distillation. 2. Ray Marching and Point Selection: For each training ray \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}, sample points along the ray for each teacher Ti. For every sampled point, calculate the activated volumetric density \alphaI using the formula \alphaI = 1 - e^{-\sigmaI \delta}, where \sigmaI is the density output by Ti at the point and \delta is the step size. Prune points with lower density values and select points with higher density values from the teachers; specifically, for each ray segment, the point with the higher \alpha value is chosen for contribution. The union of these selected points forms the training set \mathcal{P} for the student S. 3. Distillation (Supervised Loss): For each point \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{P}, query the density \sigma, alpha \alpha, and color c for the student S and the corresponding teacher Ti at \mathbf{x}. Compute the supervised L2 loss between the student's outputs and the teacher's outputs for both color and density: \mathcal{L}{distill} = || cS(\mathbf{x}) - c{T}(\mathbf{x}) ||2^2 + || \sigmaS(\mathbf{x}) - \sigma{T}(\mathbf{x}) ||2^2. Update S to minimize \mathcal{L}{distill}. 4. Smoothing (Alpha-Composited Loss): Render RGB values for rays by accumulating individual color values weighted by activated volumetric density using the Volumetric Rendering Equation: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j=1}^{M} Tj cj, where Tj = \left( \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) \right) \alphaj. Apply an alpha-composited RGB pixel loss \mathcal{L}{render} = || CS(\mathbf{r}) - C{target}(\mathbf{r}) ||2^2 for a few iterations to smooth results around object boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fusedrfdistillation(teachers, backgroundidx, rays, student, numsamples, delta, lr, numsmoothingiters): # Step 1: Initialization student.weights = teachers[backgroundidx].weights # Step 2 & 3: Distillation Loop for ray in rays: candidatepoints = [] for tidx, teacher in enumerate(teachers): points = samplepointsalongray(ray, numsamples) for p in points: sigma, color = teacher.query(p.position, ray.direction) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) candidatepoints.append({ 'pos': p.position, 'tidx': tidx, 'sigma': sigma, 'color': color, 'alpha': alpha }) # Select points: union of high-density points. # For each ray segment, pick the point with the highest alpha. trainingset = [] for i in range(numsamples): segment = [pt for pt in candidatepoints if pt['pos'].indexinray == i] if segment: trainingset.append(max(segment, key=lambda x: x['alpha'])) # Compute supervised L2 loss on density and color distillloss = 0.0 for pt in trainingset: ssigma, scolor = student.query(pt['pos'], ray.direction) tsigma = pt['sigma'] tcolor = pt['color'] distillloss += (ssigma - tsigma)2 + sum((sc - tc)2 for sc, tc in zip(scolor, tcolor)) # Update student weights via standard gradient descent student.weights -= lr student.computegradients(distillloss) # Step 4: Smoothing Phase for in range(numsmoothingiters): renderloss = 0.0 for ray in rays: srgb = volumetricrenderray(student, ray, numsamples, delta) trgb = naivecompositeray(teachers, ray, numsamples, delta) renderloss += sum((sc - tc)2 for sc, tc in zip(srgb, trgb)) student.weights -= lr student.computegradients(renderloss) return student def samplepointsalongray(ray, numsamples): return [{'position': ray.origin + ray.direction (i ray.stepsize), 'indexinray': i} for i in range(numsamples)] def volumetricrenderray(rf, ray, numsamples, delta): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): p = ray.origin + ray.direction (i ray.stepsize) sigma, color = rf.query(p, ray.direction) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) weight = transmittance alpha accumulatedcolor = [c + weight col for c, col in zip(accumulatedcolor, color)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor def naivecompositeray(teachers, ray, numsamples, delta): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): p = ray.origin + ray.direction (i ray.stepsize) bestalpha = -1.0 bestsigma, bestcolor = 0.0, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for teacher in teachers: sigma, color = teacher.query(p, ray.direction) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) if alpha > bestalpha: bestalpha = alpha bestsigma, bestcolor = sigma, color weight = transmittance bestalpha accumulatedcolor = [c + weight col for c, col in zip(accumulatedcolor, bestcolor)] transmittance = (1.0 - bestalpha) return accumulatedcolor Memory Complexity: Constant with respect to the number of composed scenes. FusedRF maintains the memory footprint of a single RF. On an RTX 3060 Ti (8GB), FusedRF maintains 25MB memory for 8 composed scenes, whereas DVGO goes Out-Of-Memory (OOM) and TensoRF requires 200MB. Time Complexity: Render time is constant with respect to the number of composed scenes. FusedRF takes ~2.04s for 8 scenes, while naive composition scales linearly with the number of components. Training time is reduced by 3x compared to retraining from scratch. Performance: RTX 3060 Ti (8GB): 1 Scene: 25MB / 2.01s 2 Scenes: 25MB / 2.05s 4 Scenes: 25MB / 2.04s 8 Scenes: 25MB / 2.04s Comparison (8 Scenes): DVGO: OOM TensoRF: 200MB / 17.2s FusedRF: 25MB / 2.04s Quality: PSNR (Figure 1): Ours (w/o RGB) 36.71, Ours (Full) 37.20. PSNR (Figure 3b): Ours (w/o RGB) 35.18, Ours (Full) 39.89. PSNR (Figure 3d): Ours (w/o RGB) 40.32, Ours (Full) 38.78. Strengths: Low memory footprint, fast rendering, fast convergence (3x faster than retraining), supports addition and deletion of scenes in the fused representation. Limitations: Requires existing trained teacher RFs; assumes rigid transformation without applying additional rigid transformations during composition. FusedRF was proposed to address the high memory and rendering time requirements of composing multiple Radiance Fields for XR and AR applications. Prior works generated new views by tracing each scene in parallel, which did not scale well. FusedRF distills information from multiple teacher RFs into a single student RF, facilitating further manipulations like addition and deletion. name: MEIL-NeRF
head: Memory-Efficient Incremental Learning of NeRF
body: MEIL-NeRF is a memory-efficient incremental learning algorithm for Neural Radiance Fields that prevents catastrophic forgetting without increasing memory usage by treating the NeRF network itself as a memory storage for pixel RGB values. Unlike replay-based methods that suffer from monotonically increasing memory due to storing past data, MEIL-NeRF maintains constant memory consumption by using a Ray Generator Network (RGN) to retrieve past task information from the NeRF network itself, rather than storing raw data or exemplars. It builds on NeRF Training Loop by introducing a self-distillation mechanism guided by generated rays. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Previous task parameters \theta{T-1}, current task data (rays rc and colors Cc), camera intrinsics (focal length f, image dimensions W, H), and hyperparameters (T, N, mc, \lambdap). Outputs: Updated NeRF parameters \thetaT and updated RGN parameters. Data Structures: NeRF Network (F): An MLP mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density \sigma and color c, with parameters \theta. Ray Generator Network (RGN, f{RGN}): A small MLP mapping a scalar x \in [0, 1] to a ray origin r^o and direction r^d. Frozen Parameters (\theta^{T-1}): A copy of \theta{T-1} used for querying past data. Volume Rendering: The estimated pixel color \hat{C} for a ray r is computed via standard volume rendering: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^{P} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \right) \alphai ci where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai(z{i+1} - zi)), P is the number of sampled points, ci is color, \sigmai is density, and zi is distance from the camera. We denote the forward mapping as \hat{C} = F(r; \theta). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For task T, copy parameters from the previous task: \theta^{T-1} = \theta{T-1} and freeze them. 2. Iteration Loop: For each training iteration of task T: a. Sample current task data (rc, Cc) with batch size mc. b. If T > 1: i. Generate past principal rays r^p using the RGN: (r^o, r^d) = f{RGN}(x), where x are equally spaced numbers in [0, 1]. ii. Generate non-principal rays rp around the principal rays using camera intrinsics (see Formula 1 below). iii. Query the frozen network to obtain past pseudo-ground truth: Cp = F(rp; \theta^{T-1}). c. Compute current predictions \hat{C}c = F(rc; \thetaT) and past predictions \hat{C}p = F(rp; \thetaT). d. Update \thetaT by minimizing the loss L (see Formula 2 below). 3. RGN Update: After training for task T ends, update the RGN using current principal rays and past principal rays retrieved from the previous RGN state to map T \cdot N equally spaced numbers to rays using MSE loss (see Formula 3 below). Formulas: 1. Non-principal Ray Generation: Centered around the generated principal ray (r^o, r^d), non-principal rays (ro, rd) are created with the same origin ro = r^o: rd = \frac{f \cdot r^d + s \cdot \cos(u\theta) \cdot p1 + s \cdot \sin(u\theta) \cdot p2}{|f \cdot r^d + s \cdot \cos(u\theta) \cdot p1 + s \cdot \sin(u\theta) \cdot p2|} where p1, p2 are unit vectors perpendicular to the principal ray (obtained via Gram-Schmidt), f is focal length, s \sim U[0, \sqrt{W^2+H^2}/2], and u\theta \sim U[0, 2\pi]. 2. Loss Function: L = \frac{1}{mc} \sum{c} (\hat{C}c - Cc)^2 + \lambdap \frac{1}{mp} \sum{p} \rho(\hat{C}p - Cp) where \rho(x) = \sqrt{x^2 + \epsilon^2} is the Charbonnier penalty function. \lambdap controls the trade-off. mc is the batch size of current rays. mp is the batch size of past rays. Default mc = 4096. Default mp = mc / 2. 3. RGN Training Loss: The RGN is trained to map T \cdot N equally spaced numbers xT \in [0, 1] to principal rays (r^o, r^d)1:T: L{RGN} = \| (r^o, r^d)1:T - f{RGN}(xT) \|^2 where xT are spaced values covering the range [0, 1] corresponding to all seen tasks. Parameters: T: Number of seen tasks. N: Number of images per task. Default N=5. mc: Batch size of current rays. Default 4096. mp: Batch size of past rays. Default mc/2. \lambdap: Trade-off hyperparameter. Scheduled based on task progress rate r. Iterations per task: 3000 \times N. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def gramschmidt(v): """Returns two unit vectors perpendicular to v.""" v = np.asarray(v) if abs(v[0]) < 0.9: u1 = np.cross(v, [1, 0, 0]) else: u1 = np.cross(v, [0, 1, 0]) u1 = u1 / np.linalg.norm(u1) u2 = np.cross(v, u1) u2 = u2 / np.linalg.norm(u2) return u1, u2 def generatenonprincipalray(principaldir, focallength, width, height, rng): """Generates a non-principal ray direction around the principal direction.""" p1, p2 = gramschmidt(principaldir) s = rng.uniform(0, math.sqrt(width2 + height2) / 2) utheta = rng.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) rawdir = focallength principaldir + s math.cos(utheta) p1 + s math.sin(utheta) p2 return rawdir / np.linalg.norm(rawdir) def volumerender(rays, params): """Standard NeRF volume rendering for a batch of rays.""" # Computes alpha-compositing over sampled points per ray # Returns estimated colors matching the volume rendering equation return np.zeros(len(rays)) def charbonnierloss(pred, target, eps=1e-3): return np.mean(np.sqrt((pred - target)2 + eps2)) def meansquarederror(pred, target): return np.mean((pred - target)2) def trainmeilnerf(taskidx, prevtheta, currentdata, cameraintrinsics, rgnmodel, prevrgnmodel, numimagespertask=5, iterationspertask=15000, mc=4096, mp=2048): # 1. Initialization: Copy and freeze parameters from previous task frozentheta = prevtheta.copy() theta = prevtheta.copy() for iteration in range(iterationspertask): # 2a. Sample current task data indices = np.random.choice(len(currentdata), mc, replace=False) rc, Cc = currentdata[indices] # 2c. Compute current predictions Ccpred = volumerender(rc, theta) # 2b. If T > 1, generate past rays and query frozen network if taskidx > 1: # Generate principal rays using RGN numpasttasks = taskidx - 1 xpast = np.linspace(0, 1, numpasttasks numimagespertask) principalorigins, principaldirs = rgnmodel(xpast) # Generate non-principal rays around principal rays rporigins, rpdirs = [], [] for in range(mp): idx = np.random.randint(0, len(principaldirs)) pdir = principaldirs[idx] porig = principalorigins[idx] rd = generatenonprincipalray(pdir, cameraintrinsics['f'], cameraintrinsics['W'], cameraintrinsics['H'], np.random.defaultrng()) rporigins.append(porig) rpdirs.append(rd) rp = list(zip(rporigins, rpdirs)) # Query frozen network for past pseudo-ground truth Cp = volumerender(rp, frozentheta) Cppred = volumerender(rp, theta) # Schedule lambdap based on progress rate r (Schedule 2) r = iteration / iterationspertask lambdap = math.cos(math.pi (1 + r)) # Compute losses lossc = meansquarederror(Ccpred, Cc) lossp = charbonnierloss(Cppred, Cp) loss = lossc + lambdap lossp else: # Task 1: Only current loss lambdap = 0.0 loss = meansquarederror(Ccpred, Cc) # 2d. Update theta (standard backpropagation step) grad = autograd(loss, theta) # Standard automatic differentiation theta = theta - 0.001 grad # 3. RGN Update: Train RGN to map TN equally spaced numbers to principal rays if taskidx > 1: numpast = (taskidx - 1) numimagespertask xpast = np.linspace(0, 1, numpast) pastprincipalrays = prevrgnmodel(xpast) else: pastprincipalrays = [] currentprincipalrays = [pose.getprincipalray() for pose in currentdata] allprincipalrays = pastprincipalrays + currentprincipalrays numtotal = len(allprincipalrays) xall = np.linspace(0, 1, numtotal) rgnpred = rgnmodel(xall) rgnloss = meansquarederror(rgnpred, allprincipalrays) rgngrad = autograd(rgnloss, rgnmodel) # Standard automatic differentiation rgnmodel = rgnmodel - 0.001 rgngrad return theta, rgnmodel A learning curriculum that schedules the hyperparameter \lambdap according to the task progress rate r to shift focus from learning a new task to remembering past tasks. The progress rate r ranges from 0.0 to 1.0. Several schedules were tested: Schedule 1: \lambdap = \cos(\frac{\pi}{2}(1-r)) Schedule 2: \lambdap = \cos(\pi(1+r)) Schedule 3: \lambdap = \cos(\frac{\pi}{2}(1+3r)) Schedule 4: \lambdap = 10^{\frac{3}{7}\cos(\pi(1+\frac{2}{7}r))} Schedule 5: \lambdap = 10^{\frac{1}{7}\cos(\pi(1+\frac{2}{7}r))} Schedule 2 demonstrates slightly better results among Schedules 1-3 and is selected for implementation. Selection of L1 or Charbonnier loss over L2 for remembering past tasks to preserve knowledge and improve edge-preserving capability. L1 and Charbonnier losses provide better edge-preserving capability and reduce errors from the iterative self-distillation process compared to L2 loss. On TUM-RGBD/Seq0, Charbonnier + \lambdap scheduling achieves PSNR 23.70 / MS-SSIM 0.884, outperforming L2 (23.85 / 0.873) in MS-SSIM. Memory: Constant memory consumption regardless of the number of tasks, as it does not store raw past data or exemplars. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for RGN generation and querying the frozen network for past rays. Iterations per task are 3000 \times N. Performance: Competitive performance compared to joint training and replay-based methods like iMAP. Outperforms NeRF-Incre (standard incremental) significantly. Strengths: Prevents catastrophic forgetting without memory scalability issues. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of \lambdap and tuning of batch sizes (mc, mp). MEIL-NeRF was proposed to address catastrophic forgetting in NeRF under incremental learning scenarios, where only the latest task is available while previous tasks become inaccessible. It draws inspiration from the NeRF network's ability to store scene information, using it as a memory storage for pixel RGB values. The method was compared against NeRF-Incre, NeRF-Joint, EWC, PackNet, iMAP, and iMAP on datasets such as Tanks and Temples, Replica, and TUM-RGBD. name: NeRF-HuGS
head: Heuristics-Guided Segmentation
body: NeRF-HuGS is a training procedure for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that mitigates artifacts caused by transient distractors (e.g., moving objects, shadows) in non-static scenes. It solves the problem of distinguishing static geometry from transient elements by combining hand-crafted heuristics with the Segment Anything Model (SAM). Unlike prior segmentation-based methods that require semantic class priors or heuristic-only methods that miss low-frequency static details, HuGS fuses Structure-from-Motion (SfM) features (high-frequency textures) and color residuals from a partially trained NeRF (low-frequency textures) to guide SAM in generating precise static masks. Inputs: A set of unordered multi-view images I = \{Ii \mid i = 1, 2, \dots, NI\} containing transient distractors. Outputs: A set of static maps M = \{Mi \mid i = 1, 2, \dots, NI\}, where Mi is a binary mask for image Ii labeling pixels of static objects as 1 and transient objects as 0. These maps are used as weights in the NeRF loss function. Data Structures: Image Set I: List of 2D images. Feature Points Fi: For each image Ii, a set of 2D local feature points Fi = \{ (x{ij}, f{ij}) \mid j = 1, \dots, N{Fi} \}, where x{ij} \in \mathbb{R}^2 is the coordinate and f{ij} is the appearance descriptor. Sparse Point Cloud C: A 3D point cloud reconstructed from Fi across all images, representing the static scene structure. Static Map Mi: A 2D mask of the same resolution as Ii. Parameters: SfM Heuristics: Effective for static objects with high-frequency texture patterns. Residual Heuristics: Derived from a partially trained NeRF (e.g., Nerfacto) after several thousand iterations; effective for static elements with low-frequency textures. Segmentation Model: Segment Anything Model (SAM). Steps: 1. Extract SfM Features: For each image Ii, extract 2D local feature points Fi using Structure-from-Motion (SfM). 2. Reconstruct Sparse Cloud: Use Fi from all images to reconstruct a sparse point cloud C. 3. Identify Static Features via SfM: Identify static features as those reliably matched and triangulated across multiple views in the SfM pipeline. For each 2D feature point (x{ij}, f{ij}) in Ii, let n{ij} be the number of its matching points in the other images I. Points with sufficient matches are considered static. 4. Train Partial NeRF: Train a NeRF model (specifically Nerfacto) for several thousand iterations to obtain a partially trained model. 5. Compute Color Residuals: Use the partially trained NeRF to render images and compute color residuals against the input images I. High residuals indicate transient or poorly modeled regions. 6. Generate Initial SAM Masks (SfM-guided): Use the static feature points identified in Step 3 as point prompts for SAM to generate dense masks for each image. 7. Fuse Heuristics: Combine the SfM-based heuristics (from Step 3) and the Residual-based heuristics (from Step 5) to create a combined guidance signal. 8. Generate Final Static Maps: Use the combined heuristics to guide SAM again, generating the final static map Mi for each input image Ii. 9. Train NeRF with Static Masks: Train the final NeRF using the static maps Mi as weights in the loss function to ignore transient pixels. Formulas: The NeRF outputs color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} for a 3D position p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction d \in S^2: (c, \sigma) = \text{MLP}(p, d; \theta) \quad The standard NeRF loss is: L(r) = L{\text{recon}}(\hat{C}(r), C(r)) \quad where L{\text{recon}} is a reconstruction loss (e.g., MSE or Charbonnier), \hat{C}(r) is the rendered color, and C(r) is the ground truth color. The modified loss using the static map M(r) (omitting image index i for simplicity) is: L(r) = M(r) L{\text{recon}}(\hat{C}(r), C(r)) \quad Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfhugs(images): # Step 1: Extract SfM features featuresets = [] for Ii in images: Fi = computelocalfeatures(Ii) # Standard: e.g., SIFT/AKAZE extraction featuresets.append(Fi) # Step 2: Reconstruct sparse cloud C sparsecloud = triangulate3dpoints(featuresets) # Standard: SfM triangulation # Step 3: Identify static features staticprompts = [] for i, Fi in enumerate(featuresets): for xij, fij in Fi: nij = countcrossviewmatches(xij, fij, featuresets, excludeindex=i) if nij > 0: # Reliably matched across multiple views staticprompts.append((i, xij)) # Step 4: Partial NeRF training partialmodel = initializenerf(images) for step in range(5000): # "several thousands of iterations" rays = samplerays(images) colors = renderrays(partialmodel, rays) loss = computemseloss(colors, groundtruth) partialmodel.step(loss) # Step 5: Compute color residuals residuals = [] for Ii in images: rendered = renderimage(partialmodel, Ii) residuals.append(computeresidualmap(Ii, rendered)) # Step 6: Initial SAM masks from SfM points initialmasks = [] for i, Ii in enumerate(images): prompts = [p for idx, p in staticprompts if idx == i] masks = samsegment(Ii, pointprompts=prompts) initialmasks.append(masks) # Step 7 & 8: Fuse heuristics and guide SAM again finalmasks = [] for i, Ii in enumerate(images): guidance = combineheuristics(initialmasks[i], residuals[i]) finalmask = samsegment(Ii, guidance=guidance) finalmasks.append(finalmask) return finalmasks def trainfinalnerf(images, masks, model): for step in range(10000): # Not given in the sources for Ii, Mi in zip(images, masks): rays = samplerays(Ii) rendered = renderrays(model, rays) loss = 0.0 for r, chat, cgt, mval in zip(rays, rendered, groundtruth, Mi): loss += mval charbonnierloss(chat, cgt) model.step(loss) Time Complexity: Requires two phases of NeRF optimization: a partial training phase (several thousand iterations) and the final training phase. SfM feature extraction and matching add preprocessing time. SAM inference adds per-image segmentation time. Memory Complexity: Stores the sparse point cloud C, the partially trained NeRF weights, and the generated static masks Mi. Strengths: Robustly captures the full spectrum of static scene elements by combining high-frequency (SfM) and low-frequency (residual) cues. Avoids the need for semantic class priors required by other segmentation methods. Limitations: Relies on the quality of SfM reconstruction (may fail in textureless regions) and the accuracy of the partially trained NeRF residuals. Computationally more expensive than standard NeRF training due to the heuristic generation and SAM steps. When to use: Non-static scenes with transient distractors where static geometry needs to be preserved. When not to use: Static scenes (overhead of heuristic generation is unnecessary) or scenes with no transient distractors. NeRF-HuGS was proposed to address the limitation of standard NeRF methods, which assume static scenes and suffer from artifacts when trained on data with transient distractors. The method was introduced in the paper "NeRF-HuGS: Improved Neural Radiance Fields in Non-static Scenes Using Heuristics-Guided Segmentation". It builds on the use of SfM for camera pose estimation and scene initialization and leverages the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for precise boundary delineation. It contrasts with RobustNeRF, which uses heuristics alone and may ignore high-frequency static details. name: DFF
head: DFF, N3F, FeatureNeRF
body: DFF (Direct Feature Field) is a 2D-teacher-3D-student framework that distills knowledge from pre-trained 2D feature extractors into a NeRF student network to create a scene-specific 3D feature field. It enables self-supervised 3D segmentation, allowing for the extraction and deletion of target objects based on image patches or text prompts. Unlike methods requiring extensive manual annotation, DFF leverages the semantic richness of 2D foundation models to guide 3D representation learning. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a scene; pre-trained 2D feature extractor networks (e.g., LSeg, DINO). Outputs: A NeRF student network parameterized by a 3D feature field and radiance field; rendered 2D features aligned with teacher outputs. Data Structures: The student network maintains a standard NeRF representation: Positional Encoding: Input coordinates \mathbf{x} are encoded using positional encoding functions \gamma(\mathbf{x}). Feature Density Network: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) \mathcal{F}{\theta} that takes encoded position \gamma(\mathbf{x}) and view direction \mathbf{d} as input. Output Fields: The MLP outputs density \sigma, color \mathbf{c}, and a feature vector \mathbf{f}. The feature vector \mathbf{f} resides in the same embedding space as the teacher network's outputs. Numbered Steps: 1. Teacher Selection: Select a pre-trained 2D feature extractor (teacher) such as LSeg or DINO. 2. Ray Sampling: For each training image, sample points along camera rays using the standard NeRF sampling strategy. 3. Feature Rendering: For each sampled point \mathbf{x}i on a ray, query the student network to obtain the feature vector \mathbf{f}i. 4. Ray Marching: Integrate the rendered features \mathbf{f}i along the ray using volumetric rendering to produce the final rendered feature \hat{\mathbf{F}} for the pixel. 5. Teacher Forward Pass: Pass the corresponding 2D image patch through the selected teacher network to obtain the ground-truth feature \mathbf{F}{teacher}. 6. Loss Computation: Compute the discrepancy between the rendered feature \hat{\mathbf{F}} and the teacher feature \mathbf{F}{teacher}. 7. Optimization: Update the student network parameters to minimize the combined loss of photometric rendering and feature distillation. Formulas: The feature distillation loss is defined as the discrepancy between the rendered feature and the teacher's output: \mathcal{L}{feat} = || \hat{\mathbf{F}} - \mathbf{F}{teacher} ||^2 where \hat{\mathbf{F}} is the rendered feature from the student NeRF and \mathbf{F}{teacher} is the feature extracted by the 2D teacher network. The total loss typically includes a photometric term \mathcal{L}{rgb} and the feature term: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rgb} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{feat} where \lambda is a weighting hyperparameter. Parameters: Teacher Networks: LSeg and DINO. Weighting \lambda: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Feature Space Alignment: The student's feature output must be compatible with the teacher's embedding space. If the teacher uses a specific normalization or projection, the student may require an additional linear projection layer. Ambiguity in Occluded Regions: Regions with no direct correspondence in the teacher's view may lack supervision, potentially leading to artifacts. Uses k-nearest neighbors in feature space for segmentation; differs by using explicit neighbor search rather than continuous feature field distillation. Broader category including DFF; DFF is a specific implementation using 2D-teacher distillation. Time Complexity: Training time is increased compared to standard NeRF due to the forward pass of the teacher network and the additional feature rendering step. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the teacher network weights in memory during training. Strengths: Enables self-supervised 3D segmentation without manual labels; supports text-based and patch-based object manipulation. Limitations: Relies on the quality and coverage of the 2D teacher network; may struggle with objects not well-represented in the teacher's training data. When to use: When self-supervised 3D segmentation or editing is required without annotated data. When not to use: When high-fidelity photometric rendering is the sole priority and semantic understanding is not needed. DFF was introduced as part of the 2D-teacher-3D-student framework, adopting pre-trained feature extraction networks like LSeg and DINO for knowledge distillation. It paved the way for applications in language-guided editing, 3D spatial rearrangements, and targeted scene removal. The method is closely related to N3F and FeatureNeRF, which share similar architectural paradigms. name: SGCNeRF
head: Sparse Geometric Consistency Guidance NeRF
body: SGCNeRF is a few-shot neural rendering architecture for novel view synthesis that addresses the performance decline of standard frequency regularization in high-frequency regions (rich textures or geometry variations) where methods like FreeNeRF suffer from excessive smoothing. It distinguishes itself by integrating a feature-matching-based sparse geometry regularization module with spatially consistent geometry filtering and frequency-guided geometric regularization, thereby preserving high-frequency details while preventing overfitting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse set of input views (images and camera poses); a pre-trained sparse matching operator; the total number of training iterations T. Outputs: A trained NeRF model optimized for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: Positional Encoding: Maps 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} to a higher-dimensional space using a sinusoidal basis. The encoding vector \gamma(\mathbf{x}) has dimension 2L, where L is the maximum frequency hyperparameter. Frequency Mask M: A binary mask of length L used to control the bandwidth of the positional encoding during training. 3D Point Correspondences: Pairs of 3D points derived from 2D pixel matches mapped into 3D space via rendered depth. Parameters: L: Hyperparameter determining the maximum frequency of the positional encoding. t: Current iteration step in the training process. T: Total iteration step in the training process. Threshold: A predefined distance threshold used to filter inconsistent correspondences. Method Steps: 1. Offline Sparse Feature Matching: Utilize a pre-trained sparse matching operator to establish correspondences on high-frequency keypoints between the input views. 2. 3D Mapping: Map the corresponding 2D pixels into 3D space based on their rendered depth values from the current NeRF model. 3. Geometric Optimization: Minimize the distances between the paired 3D points to optimize the geometry of the radiance field. This enforces constraints on the placement of high-frequency keypoints to prevent excessive smoothing. 4. Geometric Consistency Filtering: Exclude inconsistent correspondences. A correspondence is defined as inconsistent if the minimum distance between the paired 3D points exceeds a predefined threshold. These rays are removed from the optimization set. 5. Frequency-Guided Regularization: Apply a frequency annealing schedule to adaptively relax geometric constraints during post-training to alleviate distortions resulting from matching errors. This involves gradually increasing the frequency of the positional encoding using a mask M(t, T, L). Formulas: The positional encoding function maps 3D positional vectors \mathbf{x} into a higher-dimensional space: \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x})) where L is the hyperparameter determining the maximum frequency. The masked positional encoding \gamma'(t, T, \mathbf{x}) used during training is defined as: \gamma'(t, T, \mathbf{x}) = \gamma(\mathbf{x}) \odot M(t, T, L) where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication, and M(t, T, L) is the frequency mask defined by the index i along the L-dimensional axis: Mi = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \le \frac{t \cdot L}{T + 3} \\ \frac{t \cdot L}{T + 6} & \text{if } T + 3 < i \le \frac{t \cdot L}{T + 6} \\ 0 & \text{if } i > \frac{t \cdot L}{T + 6} \end{cases} where t is the current iteration step and T is the total iteration step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sgcnrftraining(inputviews, pretrainedmatcher, T, L, threshold): """ SGCNeRF Training Loop. Args: inputviews: List of input images and camera poses. pretrainedmatcher: Pre-trained sparse matching operator. T: Total number of training iterations. L: Maximum frequency for positional encoding. threshold: Distance threshold for geometric consistency filtering. Returns: Trained NeRF model. """ # Step 1: Offline Sparse Feature Matching # Establish correspondences on high-frequency keypoints between input views correspondences2d = pretrainedmatcher(inputviews) # Standard NeRF initialization nerfmodel = initializenerf() for t in range(T): # Step 2: 3D Mapping # Map corresponding 2D pixels into 3D space based on rendered depth correspondences3d = [] for (u1, v1, u2, v2), depth1, depth2 in correspondences2d: p1 = rayorigin + depth1 raydirection1 p2 = rayorigin + depth2 raydirection2 correspondences3d.append((p1, p2)) # Step 4: Geometric Consistency Filtering # Exclude inconsistent correspondences where min distance > threshold validcorrespondences3d = [] for p1, p2 in correspondences3d: dist = ((p1[0]-p2[0])2 + (p1[1]-p2[1])2 + (p1[2]-p2[2])2)0.5 if dist <= threshold: validcorrespondences3d.append((p1, p2)) # Step 3: Geometric Optimization # Minimize distances between paired 3D points # Standard gradient descent step minimizing sum of distances for p1, p2 in validcorrespondences3d: loss = torch.sum((p1 - p2)2) loss.backward() nerfmodel.step() # Step 5: Frequency-Guided Regularization # Compute frequency mask for current iteration freqmask = computefrequencymask(t, T, L) # Standard NeRF rendering with masked positional encoding renderedimages = renderwithmaskedencoding(nerfmodel, inputviews, freqmask) # Standard photometric loss and backpropagation computeandapplyrenderingloss(renderedimages, inputviews) return nerfmodel def computefrequencymask(t, T, L): """ Computes the frequency mask M(t, T, L) as defined in SGCNeRF. Args: t: Current iteration step. T: Total iteration step. L: Maximum frequency. Returns: List of floats representing the mask values for each frequency index. """ mask = [] for i in range(L): if i <= (t L) / (T + 3): mask.append(1.0) elif (T + 3) < i <= (t L) / (T + 6): mask.append((t L) / (T + 6)) else: mask.append(0.0) return mask Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Matching Errors: Inaccurate correspondences can lead to geometric distortions. The geometric consistency filtering step is critical to exclude these. Over-smoothing: Standard frequency regularization may cause performance decline in high-frequency regions. SGCNeRF addresses this by enforcing sparse geometric constraints on high-frequency keypoints. Post-training Distortions: Matching errors may still cause distortions in the post-training stage. The frequency-guided geometric regularization scheme adaptively relaxes constraints to mitigate this. SGCNeRF achieves improvements of 0.7 dB in PSNR on LLFF and DTU datasets compared to FreeNeRF. It is designed for few-shot neural rendering scenarios where input views are sparse. The method requires an offline sparse matching step and a pre-trained matching operator. SGCNeRF was introduced to address the limitations of existing few-shot neural rendering methods, particularly the over-smoothing issue in high-frequency regions caused by frequency regularization techniques like those in FreeNeRF. The method builds on the principle of sparse image matching and integrates it with NeRF optimization. name: NeRF Volumetric Rendering
head: NeRF Alpha Compositing, NeRF Rendering Equation
body: NeRF Volumetric Rendering synthesizes final pixel color and expected depth from sampled radiance field properties along camera rays. It models scene geometry using an opacity field that reflects the probability of an object’s presence, accumulating color and transmittance via alpha compositing. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly computing the volume rendering equation to produce differentiable color and depth outputs for training supervision. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of Np samples along a ray r. For each sample i, the input includes the 3D position \mathbf{x}i, the density \sigmai, the color \mathbf{c}i (typically RGB), and the distance from the camera ti. Output: The final pixel color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(r) and the expected depth D(r). Data Structures The method operates on arrays of size Np: \sigma: Array of densities, shape (Np, 1) or scalar per sample. \mathbf{c}: Array of colors, shape (Np, 3). t: Array of depths/distances, shape (Np, 1). \delta t: Array of distances between consecutive samples, shape (Np, 1). Numbered Steps 1. Compute opacity weights \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \delta ti) for each sample. 2. Compute accumulated transmittance Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \delta tj) starting with T1 = 1. 3. Accumulate final color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Np} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i and depth D(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Np} Ti \alphai ti. Formulas The rendering equation computes the accumulated transmittance Ti and the alpha weight \alphai for each sample: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \delta ti) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \delta tj\right) The final color and depth are computed as weighted sums: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Np} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i D(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Np} Ti \alphai ti Where: Ti is the accumulated transmittance at sample i. \alphai is the opacity weight at sample i. ti is the distance of the i-th sample from the camera. \delta t is the distance between sampled points. Parameters Np: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def nerfvolumetricrendering(sigma, colors, depths, deltat): """ Render a ray using NeRF volumetric rendering. Maps 0-based Python indices to 1-based formula indices (iformula = ipython + 1). """ Np = len(sigma) # Step 1: Compute alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltati) alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[i] deltat[i]) for i in range(Np)] # Step 2: Compute Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltatj) # T1 (i=0 in Python) = 1.0 T = [0.0] Np T[0] = 1.0 cumsum = 0.0 for i in range(1, Np): cumsum += sigma[i-1] deltat[i-1] T[i] = math.exp(-cumsum) # Step 3: Accumulate final color and depth using weights wi = Ti alphai color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] depth = 0.0 for i in range(Np): w = T[i] alpha[i] for c in range(3): color[c] += w colors[i][c] depth += w depths[i] return color, depth A memory-efficient differentiable component for neural 3D fields that reduces memory usage by four orders of magnitude compared to standard autograd renderers. It solves the bottleneck of storing intermediate values for backpropagation by fusing operations over casted rays instead of 3D points. It sets itself apart from siblings by updating rendered pixels and transmittance on-the-fly rather than storing intermediate tensors. Choose it when memory constraints limit standard autograd rendering. It solves the quadrature instability inherent in the constant approximation, allowing for more accurate integration of arbitrarily small opacity values. It sets itself apart from siblings like Lightplane Renderer by focusing on the analytical integration of the volume rendering equation within the standard MLP-based radiance field framework rather than using a differentiable ray-marching or plane-based rasterization approach. Choose it when quadrature instability from constant opacity approximations degrades training accuracy. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Lightplane Renderer
head: Lightplane
body: The Lightplane Renderer is a memory-efficient differentiable component for neural 3D fields that reduces memory usage by four orders of magnitude compared to standard autograd renderers. It solves the bottleneck of storing intermediate values for backpropagation by fusing operations over casted rays instead of 3D points. Unlike standard implementations that store intermediate tensors for every sampled point along every ray, this method updates rendered pixels and transmittance on-the-fly, recomputing forward activations only during the backward pass. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M rays \{ri\}{i=1}^M, a hybrid 3D representation f = g \circ h, and R sampling points per ray. Outputs: Rendered pixel features vi (e.g., colors, depths) for each ray. Data Structures: The method relies on a hybrid representation f decomposed into two components: 1. Hashing Scheme (h): A function h: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^K that samples features from a 3D hash structure \theta. The structure \theta can be implemented as voxel grids, triplanes, HexPlanes, or actual hash tables. In practice, for triplane-based structures, h(x, y, z) is obtained by bilinear interpolation of each plane at (x, y), (y, z), and (z, x), followed by summing the resulting three feature vectors. 2. Tiny MLPs (g): Two small multi-layer perceptrons mapping the K-dimensional hash features to output dimensions: g\sigma: \mathbb{R}^K \to \mathbb{R}: Calculates opacity \sigma. gv: \mathbb{R}^K \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^C: Calculates the feature fv(x{ij}) (e.g., color) given the sampled feature and view direction. Parameters: M: Number of rays (image resolution). R: Number of samples per ray. Typical value: 128. K: Feature dimension from the hash structure. L: Number of layers in the MLPs. \Delta: Distance between two consecutive sampled points on a ray. Algorithm Steps: The renderer processes each ray ri sequentially. For each ray, it iterates through R sampled 3D points x{ij} (where j=1 \dots R). 1. Sample Feature: For point x{ij}, compute the hash feature vector z{ij} = h(x{ij}). 2. Compute Opacity: Feed z{ij} to g\sigma to obtain opacity \sigma{ij} = g\sigma(z{ij}). 3. Compute Feature: Feed z{ij} and the view direction to gv to obtain the feature fv(x{ij}) = gv(z{ij}, \text{direction}). 4. Update Transmittance: Calculate the transmittance T{ij}, representing the probability that a photon reaches the sensor from x{ij} without being absorbed by previous points. The transmittance is updated recursively: T{ij} = T{i,j-1} \cdot \exp(-\Delta \cdot \sigma{ij}) where T{i,0} = 1. 5. Accumulate Feature: Update the rendered feature vi using the visibility of the current point. The visibility is defined as the difference in transmittance between the previous and current point: (T{i,j-1} - T{ij}). The accumulated feature is: vi = \sum{j=1}^{R} (T{i,j-1} - T{ij}) fv(x{ij}) This accumulation is performed on-the-fly within the kernel, avoiding storage of intermediate T or fv values for all points. Backpropagation: Since no intermediate tensors (activations, transmittances) are stored during the forward pass, standard backpropagation cannot be applied directly. Instead, the method recomputes the forward activations during the backward pass to calculate gradients. This differs from standard checkpointing, which caches intermediate ray-point values; Lightplane recomputes the MLP forward passes entirely from scratch for gradient calculation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lightplanerenderer(rays, hashstructure, gsigma, gv, R, delta): """ rays: List of M rays. Each ray is a tuple (origin, direction, points) where points has R+1 3D coordinates. hashstructure: The 3D hash structure theta. gsigma: MLP function for opacity. gv: MLP function for feature/color. R: Number of samples per ray. delta: Distance between samples. """ M = len(rays) renderedfeatures = [] for i in range(M): origin, direction, points = rays[i] Tprev = 1.0 accumulatedfeature = 0.0 # Compute view direction (standard vector normalization) viewdir = [d / math.sqrt(sum(d2 for d in direction)) for d in direction] for j in range(1, R + 1): x, y, z = points[j] # 1. Sample feature from hash structure (triplane interpolation) # h(x,y,z) = sum of bilinear interpolations on XY, YZ, ZX planes zxy = hashstructure.interpolateplane(x, y, plane='XY') zyz = hashstructure.interpolateplane(y, z, plane='YZ') zzx = hashstructure.interpolateplane(z, x, plane='ZX') zij = [zxy[k] + zyz[k] + zzx[k] for k in range(len(zxy))] # 2. Compute opacity sigmaij = gsigma(zij) # 3. Compute feature fvij = gv(zij, viewdir) # 4. Update transmittance Tcurr = Tprev math.exp(-delta sigmaij) # 5. Accumulate feature visibility = Tprev - Tcurr accumulatedfeature += visibility fvij Tprev = Tcurr renderedfeatures.append(accumulatedfeature) return renderedfeatures Memory Complexity: The memory usage is reduced from O(M K R L) to O(M K) by fusing operations along the ray. In a standard NeRF renderer with M=65536 (256^2 image), R=128, L=6 layers, and K=64 hidden units, storing MLP outputs requires 12 GB. The Lightplane Renderer reduces this to 2 KB for the same configuration, which is less than 0.02% of the memory required by the naïve implementation. Time Complexity and Performance: The method integrates sampling, MLP evaluation, and accumulation into a single GPU kernel per ray. While recomputing forward activations during backpropagation increases the total number of floating-point operations, the speed remains comparable to standard autograd renderers. The source provides performance charts indicating that forward and backward pass times scale with image resolution, maintaining competitive execution times despite the recomputation overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Drastic reduction in VRAM usage, enabling training on larger resolutions or more complex scenes. Compatible with various hash structures (voxels, triplanes, HexPlanes). Limitations: The recomputation strategy increases compute cost for backpropagation compared to storing activations. It is specifically designed for the forward rendering pass; the dual component "Splatter" handles the inverse mapping. The Lightplane Renderer was introduced in the paper "Lightplane: Highly-Scalable Components for Neural 3D Fields". It is part of the Lightplane framework, which also includes the "Splatter" component for lifting 2D information to 3D. The work addresses the memory bottlenecks of neural 3D field optimization, building on hybrid representations like voxel grids and triplanes that were previously popularized in works such as TensoRF, HexPlane, and PixelNeRF. The renderer uses the standard emission-absorption equations popularized by NeRF. Lightplane: Highly-Scalable Components for Neural 3D Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00058, fetched 2026-10-29

name: PL-NeRF Volumetric Rendering
head: PL-NeRF Implementation, Precise Importance Sampling NeRF
body: PL-NeRF is a NeRF implementation that replaces the constant opacity approximation used in vanilla NeRF with piecewise linear opacity interpolation and precise importance sampling. It solves the quadrature instability inherent in the constant approximation, allowing for more accurate integration of arbitrarily small opacity values. It sets itself apart from siblings like Lightplane Renderer by focusing on the analytical integration of the volume rendering equation within the standard MLP-based radiance field framework rather than using a differentiable ray-marching or plane-based rasterization approach. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a trained neural network \mathcal{N} predicting density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}; number of coarse samples Nc and fine samples Nf. Output: Rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) for the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Data Structures: Sample points ti along the ray, typically distributed via stratified sampling or importance sampling. Neural network outputs: \sigmai = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{r}(ti)) and \mathbf{c}i = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{r}(ti)). Method: The core innovation is the piecewise linear (PL) opacity approximation. Instead of assuming constant density/opacity within each interval [ti, t{i+1}], PL-NeRF assumes opacity varies linearly. 1. Compute Interval Opacity: For each interval i between sample points ti and t{i+1}, compute the opacity \alphai using the analytical integral of the linearly interpolated density. Let \sigmai and \sigma{i+1} be the densities at the endpoints. The opacity \alphai is given by: \alphai = 1 - \exp\left( -\frac{\sigmai + \sigma{i+1}}{2} \Delta ti \right) Note: The source cites Eq. 10 and 11 for opacity integration. While the standard constant approximation uses \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Delta ti), the PL formulation often involves integrating the linear density profile. The source explicitly states it replaces the constant approximation with Eq. 10/11. A common PL formulation for opacity \alpha over [ti, t{i+1}] with linear density \sigma(t) = \sigmai + \frac{\sigma{i+1}-\sigmai}{\Delta ti}(t-ti) is: \alphai = 1 - \exp\left( -\int{ti}^{t{i+1}} \sigma(t) dt \right) = 1 - \exp\left( -\frac{\sigmai + \sigma{i+1}}{2} \Delta ti \right) This matches the arithmetic mean density approximation often cited in PL-NeRF literature as the "precise" integration step. 2. Precise Importance Sampling: To sample points more efficiently, PL-NeRF uses precise importance sampling based on the cumulative opacity function. The cumulative opacity T(t) is computed analytically. For a linear density profile, the cumulative opacity from ti to t is: T(t) = \exp\left( -\int{t0}^{t} \sigma(\tau) d\tau \right) The sampling distribution is derived from this cumulative function. The source cites Eq. 13 for precise importance sampling. This replaces the uniform or constant-probability sampling used in vanilla NeRF. 3. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color using the standard volume rendering equation with the PL opacities \alphai and transmittance Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj): C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples. Typical values: 64. Nf: Number of fine samples. Typical values: 64 or 128. Training iterations: 500k. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Opacity: The method cannot handle coordinates with exactly zero opacity due to division by zero in the inverse cumulative opacity function used for sampling. This is noted as not an issue in practice. Numerical Stability: The constant approximation can lead to numerical instability during optimization, especially with gradients w.r.t. samples. PL-NeRF mitigates this but requires careful implementation of the exponential and logarithmic functions for small opacity values (e.g., 10^{-6}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def plnerfrender(rayo, rayd, nerfmodel, Nc, Nf): # 1. Sample coarse points tcoarse = stratifiedsample(Nc, near, far) # Standard sampling or initial importance sampling sigmacoarse, colorcoarse = nerfmodel(rayo + rayd tcoarse) # 2. Compute PL Opacity for coarse intervals # alphai = 1 - exp(- (sigmai + sigma{i+1}) / 2 deltati) deltat = tcoarse[1:] - tcoarse[:-1] sigmaavg = (sigmacoarse[:-1] + sigmacoarse[1:]) / 2.0 alphacoarse = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaavg deltat) # 3. Compute Transmittance # Ti = product(1 - alphaj) for j < i Tcoarse = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphacoarse, dim=0) Tcoarse = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(Tcoarse[:1]), Tcoarse], dim=0) # T0 = 1 # 4. Precise Importance Sampling for fine points # Use the cumulative opacity function derived from PL assumption to sample # This involves inverting the cumulative opacity function T(t) # tfine = inversecumulativeopacity(Tcoarse, alphacoarse, deltat, Nf) # Implementation detail: The source cites Eq. 13. # A typical implementation samples uniform u in [0,1] and solves for t such that # T(t) = Tstart (1 - u (1 - Tend/Tstart)) # For linear density, this inversion is analytical. tfine = preciseimportancesample(tcoarse, sigmacoarse, Nf) sigmafine, colorfine = nerfmodel(rayo + rayd tfine) # 5. Compute PL Opacity for fine intervals deltatfine = tfine[1:] - tfine[:-1] sigmaavgfine = (sigmafine[:-1] + sigmafine[1:]) / 2.0 alphafine = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaavgfine deltatfine) # 6. Compute Transmittance for fine points Tfine = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphafine, dim=0) Tfine = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(Tfine[:1]), Tfine], dim=0) # 7. Render # Combine coarse and fine contributions if necessary, or just use fine # Standard NeRF combines them. PL-NeRF likely follows similar structure. # C = sum(Ti alphai ci) color = torch.sum(Tfine alphafine colorfine, dim=0) return color A method that plugs the piecewise linear opacity formulation into the DIVeR framework, which uses a voxel-based representation and feature integration. It utilizes the voxel-based representation and feature integration/dropping of DIVeR64 at 128 voxels. On the Blender dataset (Avg), PL-DiVER achieves PSNR 30.88, SSIM 0.947, LPIPS 3.28 (x10^-2), compared to DIVeR PSNR 30.78, SSIM 0.956, LPIPS 3.39 (x10^-2). Time Complexity: Rendering time scales with the number of samples. For an 800x800 image, PL-NeRF takes 19.20s (64+64 samples), 25.85s (64+128 samples), and 32.35s (128+64 samples). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a single Nvidia V100 GPU, training 500k iterations takes 21.43 hours for PL-NeRF vs 17.78 hours for Vanilla NeRF. Rendering a single 800x800 image takes 32.35 seconds for PL-NeRF vs 25.59 seconds for Vanilla NeRF. Strengths: Handles arbitrarily small opacity (e.g., 10^{-6}) without numerical instability; converges to higher training PSNR than Vanilla NeRF. Limitations: Cannot handle coordinates with exactly zero opacity; slightly slower training and rendering than Vanilla NeRF. When to use: When high accuracy in volume integration is required, especially for scenes with thin structures or low opacity, and when using MipNeRF or DIVeR frameworks. When not: When computational speed is the primary constraint and the constant approximation is sufficient. PL-NeRF was introduced in "NeRF Revisited: Fixing Quadrature Instability in Volume Rendering". It addresses the numerical instability of the constant approximation in standard NeRF volume rendering. The method is implemented using the NerfStudio codebase for MipNeRF-based experiments and the official DIVeR implementation for DIVeR-based experiments. name: Semantic and Open-Vocabulary Understanding
body: This family extends NeRF training to predict semantic features or segmentation logits alongside color and density, enabling object-level understanding and editing. It differs from standard NeRF training by incorporating external vision-language models (e.g., CLIP) or foundation models (e.g., SAM) to provide semantic supervision, addressing the challenge of view-inconsistent 2D labels through 3D-consistent refinement strategies like Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) and Region Semantic Ranking (RSR). All methods in this family augment the standard NeRF representation \Gamma\theta: (x, d) \to (c, \sigma) with a semantic branch. 1. Semantic Representation: An additional branch outputs a semantic vector fk \in \mathbb{R}^D for each sampled point k along a ray. 2. Semantic Rendering: Semantic features are volume-rendered similarly to color: \hat{F}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak fk where Tk is transmittance and \alphak is opacity. 3. Logit Computation: For open-vocabulary tasks, rendered semantic features \hat{F}(r) are compared against text embeddings tc to produce segmentation logits: \hat{S}(r) = \cos\langle tc, \hat{F}(r) \rangle. 4. Supervision Sources: Supervision comes from 2D vision-language models (CLIP) or segmentation models (SAM). Direct use of 2D CLIP maps is noisy and view-inconsistent, necessitating regularization (RSR) and self-enhancement (CSE). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def semanticnerftrainingloop(trainingimages, textembeddings, numepochs): """ Core training loop for semantic and open-vocabulary NeRFs. """ model = SemanticNeRF() optimizer = Adam(model.parameters()) for epoch in range(numepochs): for batch in getraybatches(trainingimages): rays = batch.rays gtcolors = batch.gtcolors # 1. Ray Sampling & Forward Pass points, directions = samplepointsalongrays(rays) colors, densities = model.geometrybranch(points, directions) semanticfeats = model.semanticbranch(points, directions) # 2. Volume Rendering alphas = 1 - exp(-distances densities) transmittances = cumprod(1 - alphas) renderedcolors = sum(transmittances alphas colors) renderedsemantics = sum(transmittances alphas semanticfeats) # 3. Logit Computation logits = cosinesimilarity(textembeddings, renderedsemantics) # 4. Loss Computation losscolor = l2loss(renderedcolors, gtcolors) losssemantic = crossentropyloss(logits, batch.gtsemanticmaps) totalloss = losscolor + losssemantic # 5. Optimization optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return model Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) is a training strategy that replaces view-inconsistent 2D semantic labels with 3D-consistent pseudo-maps rendered from the model itself [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. It addresses the ambiguity where 2D vision-language models fail to maintain consistent object identities across diverse perspectives [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. Unlike methods relying solely on external supervision, CSE leverages the inherent 3D consistency of NeRFs to iteratively refine supervision [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. It operates by generating refined pseudo relevancy maps for training views (Iterative Pseudo Map Update) and unseen viewpoints (Novel Pseudo Map Synthesis), both regularized by Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) to ensure fine edges and integral objects [13434-cross-view-self-enhancement.md]. Choose this when view-inconsistency in 2D labels degrades multi-view semantic consistency. OV-NeRF is a method for accurate NeRF-based open-vocabulary 3D semantic understanding that leverages pre-trained vision and language foundation models (CLIP and SAM) [13995-ov-nerf.md]. It addresses limitations of prior methods (e.g., LERF, 3DOVS) that directly use noisy CLIP relevancy maps [13995-ov-nerf.md]. OV-NeRF introduces Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) regularization to rectify coarse boundaries in single views using SAM mask proposals, and Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) to enforce view-consistent supervision using refined 3D semantics [13995-ov-nerf.md]. Choose this for open-vocabulary segmentation requiring precise object boundaries and 3D consistency. LERF is a method for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding that enables pixel-aligned language queries without region proposals or masks [22081-lerf.md]. It distinguishes itself from CLIP-Fields by supporting open-set queries across the entire scene volume, bypassing the need for prior knowledge of object classes present in the scene [22081-lerf.md]. It builds on this family by introducing a multi-scale feature pyramid to refine object boundaries [22081-lerf.md]. ISRF is a method that learns additional feature fields to realize self-supervised 3D segmentation. It is part of a series of works (alongside N3F, LERF) that extend NeRFs with feature fields for object extraction and deletion based on image patches or text. Joint Attributes Estimation estimates 1D revolute joint attributes (rotation axis direction \mathbf{u} and pivot point \mathbf{v}) from the predicted segmentation field via ray marching. Cast a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} from camera center \mathbf{o} along direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel. Perform linear regression on the collected 3D points \mathbf{X}{\text{intersection}} from all pixels to estimate rotation axis \mathbf{u} and pivot point \mathbf{v}. Parameter: H, a predefined threshold to remove points with low density from the intersection set. VL-Fields is an open-set visual-language model that operates without prior knowledge of object classes, overcoming CLIP-Fields' restriction to known classes. Semantic NeRFs emerged alongside the rise of vision-language models like CLIP and segmentation foundation models like SAM. Early methods like DFF used DINO as a teacher network for knowledge distillation, resulting in a scene-specific 3D feature field. Subsequent works like N3F, LERF, and ISRF learned additional feature fields for self-supervised 3D segmentation. The integration of SAM enabled prompt-based 3D segmentation (e.g., SA3D).
