name: Cross-view Self-enhancement
head: CSE
body: Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) is a training strategy for open-vocabulary neural radiance fields that mitigates view-inconsistent semantic supervision by replacing noisy 2D vision-language model outputs with 3D-consistent pseudo-labels generated from the model itself. It addresses the problem where 2D CLIP models produce inconsistent object identities across different perspectives, which degrades multi-view consistent rendering. CSE distinguishes itself from direct 2D supervision by leveraging the inherent 3D consistency of the NeRF representation to iteratively refine and synthesize semantic maps, thereby reducing ambiguity in semantic class assignment. CSE operates by generating two types of pseudo-relavancy maps: updated maps for training views and synthesized maps for novel views, both regularized by the RSR strategy. These maps serve as supervision targets for the semantic field, replacing the original 2D CLIP outputs. Inputs: Trained semantic field \Gamma\theta. Training view poses I = \{Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \mid i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\}. RSR regularizer \Phi. Outputs: Refined pseudo relevancy maps \bar{S}i for training views. Novel pseudo relevancy maps S^+i for unseen viewpoints. CSE Loss L{CSE} used to update the semantic field. Relevancy Map: A 2D tensor of size H \times W containing logits or probabilities for each semantic class at each pixel. Pseudo Map: Same structure as the relevancy map, but derived from rendered NeRF outputs and regularized. 1. Iterative Pseudo Map Update: After training the semantic field for a few iterations, render semantic relevancy maps \hat{S}i for all training view poses I. Apply the RSR regularizer \Phi to these rendered maps to generate refined pseudo relevancy maps \bar{S}i: \bar{S}i = \Phi(\hat{S}i) where \hat{S}i is the prediction from the learned semantic field. Replace the 2D CLIP-derived relevancy maps with these updated pseudo maps \bar{S}i for semantic field learning. Update the pseudo maps at a regular interval N to incorporate more view-consistent supervision as training progresses. 2. Novel Pseudo Map Synthesis: Generate novel viewpoints (unseen poses) distinct from the training set. The number of novel views N^+ is set to 60 in the source implementation. Render semantic relevancy maps \hat{S}^+i for these novel viewpoints. Apply the RSR regularizer to these novel rendered maps to obtain fine edges and integral objects, producing novel pseudo relevancy maps S^+i. 3. Loss Computation: Compute the Pseudo Map Update Loss (L{PMU}) by minimizing the cross-entropy between the rendered prediction \hat{S}(r) and the updated pseudo map \bar{S}(r) for all rays r sampled from the training views: L{PMU} = \sum{r} L{ce}(\hat{S}(r), \bar{S}(r)) where L{ce} is the cross-entropy loss. Compute the Pseudo Map Synthesis Loss (L{PMS}) by supervising the novel rendered relevancy maps \hat{S}^+i using the novel pseudo maps S^+i in a per-ray manner: L{PMS} = \sum{r^+} L{ce}(\hat{S}^+(r^+), S^+(r^+)) where r^+ indicates rays sampled from the novel pseudo maps. Combine the losses to form the total CSE loss: L{CSE} = L{PMU} + L{PMS}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def crossviewselfenhancement(semanticfield, trainingposes, rsrregularizer, updateinterval, numnovelviews=60): """ Implements the Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) strategy. Args: semanticfield: The trained semantic NeRF model. trainingposes: List of camera poses for training views. rsrregularizer: Function implementing RSR regularization. updateinterval: Number of iterations between pseudo map updates. numnovelviews: Number of novel viewpoints to synthesize. Returns: cseloss: The computed CSE loss value. """ # 1. Iterative Pseudo Map Update renderedmapstraining = [] for pose in trainingposes: renderedmap = semanticfield.rendersemantic(pose) renderedmapstraining.append(renderedmap) pseudomapstraining = [rsrregularizer(m) for m in renderedmapstraining] lpmu = 0.0 for pose, pseudomap in zip(trainingposes, pseudomapstraining): for r in pose.rays: renderedlogit = semanticfield.getsemanticlogit(r) pseudologit = pseudomap[r.u, r.v] # Standard cross-entropy: -sum(target logsoftmax(pred)) lpmu += -sum(pseudologit [math.log(max(softmaxval, 1e-8)) for softmaxval in softmax(renderedlogit)]) # Pseudo maps are updated at regular interval N # if trainingstep % updateinterval == 0: update pseudomapstraining # 2. Novel Pseudo Map Synthesis # Novel viewpoints are generated distinct from the training set. # Implementation detail: Not given in the sources. novelposes = generatenovelposes(numnovelviews, trainingposes) renderedmapsnovel = [semanticfield.rendersemantic(pose) for pose in novelposes] pseudomapsnovel = [rsrregularizer(m) for m in renderedmapsnovel] lpms = 0.0 for pose, pseudomap in zip(novelposes, pseudomapsnovel): for r in pose.rays: renderedlogit = semanticfield.getsemanticlogit(r) pseudologit = pseudomap[r.u, r.v] lpms += -sum(pseudologit [math.log(max(softmaxval, 1e-8)) for softmaxval in softmax(renderedlogit)]) # 3. Total CSE Loss cseloss = lpmu + lpms return cseloss def generatenovelposes(numviews, trainingposes): """ Generates novel camera poses distinct from training poses. Implementation detail: Not given in the sources. """ pass def softmax(logits): """Standard softmax normalization.""" maxval = max(logits) exps = [math.exp(l - maxval) for l in logits] sumexps = sum(exps) return [e / sumexps for e in exps] Update Interval (N): The frequency at which pseudo maps are regenerated and updated. Not given in the sources. Number of Novel Views (N^+): Set to 60 in the source implementation. View-Inconsistent 2D CLIP: Direct use of 2D CLIP maps leads to view-inconsistent relevancy maps, challenging multi-view consistent rendering. CSE specifically addresses this by replacing them with 3D-consistent pseudo maps. Precision: The regularization \Phi (RSR) is critical for producing "fine edges and integral objects" in the pseudo maps. Without RSR, the pseudo maps may lack the necessary structural coherence to serve as effective supervision. Time Complexity: CSE adds computational overhead during training due to the rendering of semantic maps for both training and novel views, and the application of the RSR regularizer. The iterative update process requires periodic re-rendering and regularization. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the rendered semantic maps for training and novel views, as well as the pseudo maps. Strengths: Significantly improves multi-view semantic consistency and reduces ambiguity caused by 2D CLIP inconsistencies. Enhances the 3D semantic understanding capability of the model. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial semantic field and the RSR regularizer. If the initial field is poor, the pseudo maps may be inaccurate. When to use: When training open-vocabulary NeRFs with 2D vision-language models (like CLIP) that produce noisy or inconsistent semantic labels across views. CSE was proposed in the context of OV-NeRF, an open-vocabulary neural radiance field method that integrates vision and language foundation models for 3D semantic understanding. The method was introduced to address the specific challenge of view-inconsistent relevancy maps generated by 2D CLIP models. It builds upon the RSR (Regularized Semantic Rendering) strategy to refine the pseudo labels. The approach was validated on indoor scene datasets such as Replica and ScanNet. name: OV-NeRF
head: Open-Vocabulary Neural Radiance Fields With Vision and Language Foundation Models for 3D Semantic Understanding
body: OV-NeRF is a method for accurate NeRF-based open-vocabulary 3D semantic understanding that leverages pre-trained vision and language foundation models (CLIP and SAM) to enhance semantic field learning through single-view and cross-view strategies. It addresses the limitations of prior methods (e.g., LERF, 3DOVS) that directly use noisy and view-inconsistent 2D CLIP relevancy maps for training. OV-NeRF introduces Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) regularization to rectify coarse boundaries using SAM mask proposals and Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) to enforce consistency using the model's own refined 3D predictions. Builds on Semantic and Open-Vocabulary Understanding. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N posed training images I = \{Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3} \mid i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\} and a set of text descriptions for M classes. Outputs: A trained semantic field \Gamma\theta capable of rendering RGB color, volume density, and semantic features for any ray, along with segmentation logits for open-vocabulary queries. Data Structures: The core representation is an implicit neural volumetric representation defined by an MLP \Gamma\theta. Geometry/Color Branch: \Gamma\theta: (x, d) \to (c, \sigma) x \in \mathbb{R}^3: 3D position. d \in \mathbb{R}^3: View direction. c \in \mathbb{R}^3: RGB color. \sigma \in \mathbb{R}: Volume density. Semantic Branch: An additional MLP branch outputs a semantic vector fk. fk \in \mathbb{R}^D: Semantic feature vector for the k-th sampled point. D = 512: Feature dimension. Text Embeddings: tc \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times D}: Textual features for M classes generated by the CLIP text encoder. Pre-computed Features (Offline): F(r): Multi-scale CLIP relevancy feature for ray r. S(r): Selection vector for suitable scale selection. D(r): Pre-computed DINO feature for ray r. \tilde{S}(r): RSR-regularized relevancy map for ray r. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Randomly sample rays from all training images in batches. For a ray r emitted from camera center o with direction d, parameterize points as r(t) = o + td. Sample K points along the ray with depths t1, \dots, tK. Let \deltak = t{k+1} - tk be the distance between neighboring points. 2. NeRF Forward Pass: For each sampled point k along ray r: Query the geometry/color branch: (ck, \sigmak) = \Gamma\theta(xk, d). Query the semantic branch: fk = \text{SemanticMLP}(xk, d). Compute opacity: \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\deltak \sigmak). Compute transmittance: Tk = \prod{j=0}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj), with T0 = 1. 3. Volume Rendering: Render RGB color: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak ck. Render semantic feature: \hat{F}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak fk. Compute segmentation logits for text query tc: \hat{S}(r) = \cos\langle tc, \hat{F}(r)\rangle. Render DINO feature \hat{D}(r) similarly using a DINO feature branch. 4. Region Semantic Ranking (RSR) Regularization (Offline Pre-processing): For each training image Ii: Compute CLIP image feature: Fi = Ei(Ii). Compute initial noisy relevancy map: Si = \text{argmax}(\cos\langle tc, Fi \rangle). Generate region mask proposals using SAM: Ri = E{\text{sam}}(Ii) = \{R^1i, \dots, R^ni\}. For each region R^ki: Extract pixels from Si within the mask: S^ki = R^ki Si. Rank classes in S^ki by pixel count in descending order. Select the top class S^{kl}{il}. Update the regularized map \tilde{S}i by setting pixels in R^ki to S^{kl}{il}. The process is defined as \tilde{S}i = \Psi(Si). 5. Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) (Post-training): After training OV-NeRF for several epochs, render pseudo outputs (semantic features and logits) from the trained field for both training views and unseen novel views. Use these 3D-consistent rendered semantics as supervision targets to further refine the semantic field, replacing inconsistent 2D CLIP semantics. 6. Loss Computation and Optimization: Compute the following losses for each ray r in the batch: Photometric RGB loss: L{\text{color}} = \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|2^2. Relevancy feature loss: L{\text{feat}} = -\cos\langle \hat{F}(r), S(r)F(r) \rangle. RSR Loss (replacing standard map loss): L{\text{RSR}} = L{ce}(\hat{S}(r), \tilde{S}(r)). DINO feature loss: L{\text{dino}} computed as in [29], [30]. Total Loss: L = L{\text{color}} + L{\text{feat}} + L{\text{RSR}} + L{\text{dino}}. Optimize parameters \theta using gradient descent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ovnerftrainingloop(trainingimages, textembeddings, numepochs): """ Main training loop for OV-NeRF. """ # Helper definitions (standard math/array operations) def cosinesimilarity(a, b): return (a b).sum() / (a.norm() b.norm()) def argmax(x, axis): return x.argmax(axis=axis) def cumprod(x, axis): return torch.cumprod(x, dim=axis) def clipimageencoder(img): return img # Pre-computed CLIP image feature def sammodel(img): return img # Pre-computed SAM mask proposals def getraybatches(images): return [] # Yields batches of rays def samplepointsalongrays(rays): return rays.points, rays.directions def l2loss(pred, target): return (pred - target).pow(2).sum() def crossentropyloss(logits, target): return torch.nn.functional.crossentropy(logits, target) def fdaloss(pred, target): return torch.nn.functional.mseloss(pred, target) # FDA loss per [29,30] def renderpseudooutputs(model, views): return model.renderall(views) def cserefinement(model, labels): return model # CSE loss formulation not detailed in sources # 1. Offline RSR Pre-processing rsrmaps = {} for i, img in enumerate(trainingimages): clipfeat = clipimageencoder(img) noisymap = argmax(cosinesimilarity(textembeddings, clipfeat), axis=0) masks = sammodel(img) refined = torch.zeroslike(noisymap) for mask in masks: regionscores = mask noisymap dominant = argmax(regionscores.sum(axis=(1, 2)), axis=0) refined[mask > 0] = dominant rsrmaps[i] = refined # 2. Initialize OV-NeRF Model model = OVNeRFModel() optimizer = Adam(model.parameters()) # 3. Training Loop for epoch in range(numepochs): for batch in getraybatches(trainingimages): points, dirs = samplepointsalongrays(batch.rays) colors, densities = model.geometrybranch(points, dirs) semfeats = model.semanticbranch(points, dirs) dinofeats = model.dinobranch(points, dirs) alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-batch.distances densities) transmittances = cumprod(1.0 - alphas, axis=0) transmittances = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittances[0:1]), transmittances[:-1]], axis=0) rendcolors = (transmittances alphas colors).sum(axis=0) rendsem = (transmittances alphas semfeats).sum(axis=0) renddino = (transmittances alphas dinofeats).sum(axis=0) logits = cosinesimilarity(textembeddings, rendsem) losscolor = l2loss(rendcolors, batch.gtcolors) targetfeat = batch.clipfeat batch.selectionvec lossfeat = -cosinesimilarity(rendsem, targetfeat) rsrmap = getrsrmap(batch.rayindices, rsrmaps) lossrsr = crossentropyloss(logits, rsrmap) lossdino = fdaloss(renddino, batch.dinofeat) totalloss = losscolor + lossfeat + lossrsr + lossdino optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # 4. Cross-view Self-enhancement (CSE) # Render pseudo-labels from trained model for training and novel views pseudolabels = renderpseudooutputs(model, trainingimages + novelviews) # CSE loss formulation not detailed in sources model = cserefinement(model, pseudolabels) return model Parameters: D = 512: Semantic feature dimension. M: Number of text classes (varies by query). RSR process \Psi is performed offline and does not add to training time. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy CLIP Maps: Direct use of 2D CLIP relevancy maps leads to coarse boundaries and view inconsistency. View Inconsistency: 2D semantics from CLIP are view-inconsistent. SAM Proposals: SAM generates region proposals via uniform sampling of query points and non-maximal suppression, filtering low confidence masks. Performance: OV-NeRF achieves a 20.31% improvement in mIoU on the Replica dataset and an 18.42% improvement on the ScanNet dataset compared to state-of-the-art methods. Complexity: The RSR process is performed offline, so it does not increase training time. The core training complexity is similar to standard NeRF optimization but includes additional forward passes for CLIP and DINO features and the RSR loss computation. Strengths: Superior segmentation results due to precise boundary rectification (RSR) and cross-view consistency (CSE). Robust across various CLIP configurations. Limitations: Relies on pre-trained foundation models (CLIP, SAM, DINO) which may have inherent biases or limitations in zero-shot generalization. The CSE strategy requires an initial training phase before self-enhancement can begin. OV-NeRF was proposed to address the limitations of methods like LERF [29] and 3DOVS [30], which straightforwardly utilize coarse and noisy CLIP relevancy maps for training. It builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and open-vocabulary segmentation using vision-language models. name: LERF
head: Language Embedded Radiance Fields, Learning Extensible Radiance Fields
body: LERF is a method for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding that enables pixel-aligned language queries without region proposals or masks. It overcomes the limitations of CLIP-Fields, which were restricted to a subset of scene points with known object classes, by supporting open-set queries across the entire scene volume without prior knowledge of object classes. It builds on Semantic and Open-Vocabulary Understanding by introducing a multi-scale feature pyramid to refine object boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images with known camera poses and language queries. Outputs: A 3D feature field representation and rendered semantic logits for the query at any pixel. Data Structures: Multi-scale Feature Pyramid: Combines a 3D CLIP field and DINO features. Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Field Learning: Learn a scene-specific 3D feature field using DINO and CLIP as teacher networks for knowledge distillation. 2. Multi-scale Pyramid Construction: Combine the 3D CLIP field and DINO features into a multi-scale feature pyramid to refine object boundaries for language query interactions. 3. Semantic Rendering: Volume-render the semantic features along a ray to obtain a rendered semantic feature vector \hat{F}(r). \hat{F}(r) = \sum{k=1}^K Tk \alphak fk where Tk is transmittance, \alphak is opacity, and fk is the semantic feature at sample k. 4. Logit Computation: Compute similarity between the rendered feature \hat{F}(r) and the text embedding tc of the language query to produce segmentation logits \hat{S}(r). \hat{S}(r) = \cos\langle tc, \hat{F}(r) \rangle 5. Query Interaction: Enable pixel-aligned queries of the distilled 3D CLIP embeddings, supporting hierarchical, long-tail, and open-vocabulary queries across the scene volume. Parameters: Teacher Networks: DINO and CLIP. Not given in the sources. Feature Dimension: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Precision: CLIP features alone may have coarse boundaries; the multi-scale pyramid with DINO is used to refine this. Open-Set Generalization: The method is designed to handle unseen objects and classes not present in the training data. Strengths: Enables open-set, pixel-aligned language queries without region proposals or masks; supports hierarchical and long-tail queries; refines object boundaries using DINO features. Limitations: Not given in the sources. LERF was introduced to overcome the limitations of CLIP-Fields, which were restricted to a subset of scene points with known object classes. It proposes an open-set visual-language model that operates without prior knowledge of the object classes present in the scene. The method uses a multi-scale feature pyramid combining 3D CLIP field and DINO features to refine object boundaries for language query interactions. It allows for pixel-aligned queries of distilled 3D CLIP embeddings, bypassing the need for region proposals, masks, or fine-tuning. LERF supports hierarchical, long-tail, open-vocabulary queries across the scene volume. It is part of a series of works that learn additional feature fields to realize self-supervised 3D segmentation, alongside N3F and ISRF. Semantically-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Visual Scene Understanding: A Comprehensive Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-025-02663-5, fetched 2026-10-27 A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Optimization Configuration (Adam + Exponential Decay + Selective L2)
head: Adam + Exponential Decay, Optimization Procedure, Optimizer Settings, Parameter update rule, Training optimizer setup
body: This configuration defines the standard training loop for neural radiance fields and implicit surface representations, combining the Adam optimizer with a staircase exponential learning rate schedule and selective L2 weight decay. It addresses the instability of training coordinate-based neural fields by providing robust convergence parameters, particularly for noisy real-world scan data or complex geometric priors. It sets itself apart from generic optimization loops by explicitly integrating domain-specific augmentations and specific regularization techniques into the core training loop. The method initializes a scene representation and iteratively updates parameters using a composite optimizer setup. The core mechanism involves sampling rays, computing gradients via automatic differentiation, and applying parameter updates with specific learning rate schedules and regularization masks. Inputs: Scene representation parameters (e.g., MLP weights for density and color, appearance embeddings). Camera poses and intrinsics. Target images (color and/or depth). Hyperparameters: Initial learning rate (lr), decay rate, transition steps, and L2 regularization coefficient. Outputs: Optimized scene representation parameters. Optimizer Configuration: paramlabels: A dictionary mapping parameter names to optimizer targets. Layout: {"nerf": "network", "bg": "network", "appearanceembeddings": "ae"}. mask: A boolean mask dictating where L2 decay is applied. Layout: {"nerf": {"densitymlp": True, "rgbmlp": True, "positionencoder": False}, "bg": True, "appearanceembeddings": False}. optimizernetwork: Adam optimizer instance for network weights. Parameters: learningrate=lrsch, b1=0.9, b2=0.99, eps=1e-15, epsroot=1e-15. optimizerae: Adam optimizer instance for appearance embeddings. Parameters: learningrate=1e-4, b1=0.9, b2=0.99, eps=1e-8, epsroot=0. combinedoptimizer: Multi-transform optimizer combining the above. Mapping: transforms={"network": optimizernetwork, "ae": optimizerae}. Training State: lrsch: Learning rate schedule instance. Parameters: initvalue=lr, transitionsteps=10000, decayrate=1/3, staircase=True, transitionbegin=10000, endvalue=lr/100. step: Current optimization step counter. 1. Initialization: Translate and scale the scene to lie within a [-1, 1]^3 bounding cube. Initialize the learning rate schedule with staircase=True. Initialize the combined optimizer with the specified parameters. Set the initial step counter to 0. 2. Ray Sampling: Randomly select |Pb| = 1024 rays per iteration. For each ray, compute sample points: Fixed samples: S'f = 16. Variable samples: S'c is chosen such that there is on average one sample for every 1.5 cm of ray length. Apply positional encoding: 8 bands for point coordinates, 4 bands for view direction vector. 3. Forward Pass: Compute the radiance field values (density \sigma, color \mathbf{c}) for the sampled points using the current network parameters. Render the image using the standard emission-absorption model (see Parent). If applicable, apply distortion correction using a 6-layer MLP (width 128) on 2D camera pixel space. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between rendered and target images. Loss weights: \lambda1 = 0.1, \lambda2 = 10, \lambda3 = 6 \times 10^3. 5. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients with respect to the scene parameters using the specified loss weights and positional encodings. Use reverse-mode automatic differentiation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 6. Parameter Update: Update the learning rate based on the current step: If staircase=True, the learning rate is held constant for transitionbegin steps, then decays by decayrate every transitionsteps steps. Note: staircase=True combined with transitionbegin=10000 delays the first learning rate drop to step 20,000. Apply the Adam update rule to the parameters, respecting the mask for L2 regularization: L2 decay coefficient: 1 \times 10^{-6}. L2 decay is applied to densitymlp, rgbmlp, and bg parameters, but not to positionencoder or appearanceembeddings. Increment the step counter. 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-6 until convergence or maximum iterations reached. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computelearningrate(step, initvalue, transitionbegin, transitionsteps, decayrate, endvalue, staircase): if staircase: if step < transitionbegin: return initvalue decaysteps = (step - transitionbegin) // transitionsteps lr = initvalue (decayrate decaysteps) return max(lr, endvalue) return initvalue (decayrate (step / transitionsteps)) def applyl2decay(params, mask, l2coeff): l2loss = 0.0 for key, value in params.items(): if key in mask: if isinstance(mask[key], bool): if mask[key]: l2loss += np.sum(value 2) elif isinstance(mask[key], dict): for subkey, submask in mask[key].items(): if submask: l2loss += np.sum(params[key][subkey] 2) return l2loss l2coeff def adamstep(params, grads, m, v, step, lr, b1, b2, eps, epsroot): t = step + 1 for key in params: m[key] = b1 m[key] + (1 - b1) grads[key] v[key] = b2 v[key] + (1 - b2) grads[key] 2 mhat = m[key] / (1 - b1 t) vhat = v[key] / (1 - b2 t) params[key] = params[key] - lr mhat / (np.sqrt(vhat) + eps) return params, m, v def trainstep(params, images, cameras, lrsch, optimizercfg, mask, l2coeff): step = optimizercfg.get('step', 0) numrays = 1024 indices = np.random.choice(images.shape[0], numrays, replace=False) rays = [generateray(cameras[idx]) for idx in indices] renderedimages = renderrays(params, rays) loss = np.mean((renderedimages - images) 2) grads = computegradients(loss, params) currentlr = computelearningrate(step, lrsch) params, optimizercfg['m'], optimizercfg['v'] = adamstep( params, grads, optimizercfg['m'], optimizercfg['v'], step, currentlr, optimizercfg['b1'], optimizercfg['b2'], optimizercfg['eps'], optimizercfg['epsroot']) optimizercfg['step'] = step + 1 return params, loss def generateray(camera): return {'origin': camera['origin'], 'direction': camera['direction'], 'length': camera['far'] - camera['near']} def renderrays(params, rays): points = [samplepoints(ray, 16, ray['length'] / 1.5) for ray in rays] directions = [ray['direction'] for ray in rays] encodedpoints = positionalencoding(points, 8) encodeddirections = positionalencoding(directions, 4) density, color = mlpforward(params['network'], encodedpoints, encodeddirections) return volumerendering(density, color, rays) def positionalencoding(x, numbands): frequencies = 2 np.arange(numbands) np.pi return np.concatenate([np.sin(f x) for f in frequencies], axis=-1) def mlpforward(params, points, directions): h = np.maximum(0, params['w1'] @ points + params['b1']) return params['w2'] @ h + params['b2'], params['w3'] @ h + params['b3'] def volumerendering(density, color, rays): tvals = np.linspace(rays[0]['near'], rays[0]['far'], 16 + int(rays[0]['length']/1.5)) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] alpha = 1 - np.exp(-density deltas) T = np.cumprod(1 - alpha + 1e-10, axis=-1) weights = alpha T return np.sum(weights color, axis=-2) Optimizer: Adam. Initial Learning Rate (lr): Passed to the optimizer factory. Specific value: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Learning Rate Schedule: Exponential decay. transitionsteps: 10,000. decayrate: 1/3. staircase: True. transitionbegin: 10,000. endvalue: lr / 100. Adam Parameters: b1: 0.9. b2: 0.99. eps: 1 \times 10^{-15}. epsroot: 1 \times 10^{-15}. Appearance Embedding Optimizer: learningrate: 1 \times 10^{-4}. eps: 1 \times 10^{-8}. epsroot: 0. L2 Regularization: Coefficient: 1 \times 10^{-6}. Applied to: densitymlp, rgbmlp, bg. Not applied to: positionencoder, appearanceembeddings. Ray Sampling: Number of rays per iteration: 1024. Fixed samples: 16. Variable samples: 1 sample per 1.5 cm of ray length. Positional Encoding: Point coordinates: 8 bands. View direction: 4 bands. Loss Weights: \lambda1 = 0.1. \lambda2 = 10. \lambda3 = 6 \times 10^3. Distortion Correction: 6-layer MLP, width 128. Learning Rate Schedule Delay: staircase=True combined with transitionbegin=10000 delays the first learning rate drop to step 20,000, as the initial LR is held for the first 10k steps before the staircase division triggers. L2 Decay on Encodings: Applying L2 decay to position encoders or appearance embeddings is explicitly disabled to prevent divergence or suboptimal convergence during long training runs. Numerical Stability: Small epsilon values (1 \times 10^{-15}) are used in Adam to prevent division by zero in the adaptive learning rate calculation. The Gradient Descent Solver is a matrix-free optimization method used to update voxel grid parameters in differentiable volume rendering, such as in DiffVox. It supports both constant update rates and the Adam optimizer, providing stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems. It distinguishes itself from second-order methods like Newton's Method by avoiding Hessian computation, and from direct least-squares solvers like CGLS Solver by minimizing the residual via iterative gradient steps rather than solving normal equations directly. This method solves inverse problems, specifically tomographic reconstruction, by minimizing a composite objective function consisting of a data fidelity term and a regularizer. It sets itself apart by using the BFGS quasi-Newton algorithm to handle the non-smooth L1 regularization via its Moreau envelope, providing a differentiable approximation that allows second-order optimization steps. This contrasts with first-order Gradient Descent solvers and avoids the explicit projection steps required by constrained material solvers. The Training Protocol defines the standard optimization procedure for neural networks in differentiable volume rendering, encompassing optimizer settings, learning rate scheduling, and data augmentation strategies. It addresses the instability of training coordinate-based neural fields by providing a robust configuration for convergence, particularly when dealing with noisy real-world scan data or complex geometric priors. It sets itself apart from generic optimization loops by explicitly integrating domain-specific augmentations (such as Gaussian noise for point clouds) and specific regularization techniques (like CVT for discretization stability) into the core training loop. This method enforces physical validity on material parameters during differentiable rendering optimization by projecting updated values back into their feasible domain after each optimizer step. It specifically addresses the problem of unconstrained gradient updates (e.g., from Adam) driving color or BSDF parameters outside physically plausible ranges, which causes numerical instability or non-physical reflectance. It differs from its siblings by being a post-update constraint enforcement mechanism rather than a solver or training schedule; it builds on Optimization Configuration (Adam + Exponential Decay + Selective L2) by applying a hard boundary check after the parameter update. Optimizer: Adam. Loss Function: L2 loss. Number of Views: 8. Batch Size: 2. Time Complexity: Convergence time is between 9 and 13 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, depending on scene size. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Robust convergence for coordinate-based neural fields; stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems; explicit handling of domain-specific augmentations and regularization. Limitations: High memory usage for reverse-mode AD if not optimized; sensitive to learning rate schedule parameters. When to Use: Standard training for neural radiance fields and implicit surface representations; noisy real-world scan data; complex geometric priors. When Not to Use: When second-order methods are required for faster convergence; when constrained optimization is needed. Origin: The Adam optimizer was introduced by Kingma and Ba in 2014. The specific configuration of Adam with exponential decay and selective L2 regularization is used in various neural radiance field and implicit surface reconstruction methods. Usage: Used in neural RGB-D surface reconstruction, JAX-based neural graphics primitives, and path-space differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces. name: Gradient Descent Solver
head: Adam Optimizer, Adam Optimizer Solver, L1/L2 Norm Solver, Update Velocity
body:
The Gradient Descent Solver is a matrix-free optimization method used to update voxel grid parameters in differentiable volume rendering by minimizing a loss function via first-order gradient information. It distinguishes itself from direct solvers by supporting both constant update rates and the Adam optimizer, providing stable behavior for ill-conditioned systems without explicitly forming the Hessian or normal equations. Inputs: Parameter vector 	heta. Loss function L(	heta), which can be based on the l2-norm (least squares) or the l1-norm (least absolute deviations). Learning rate \alpha. Adam hyperparameters:  eta1 (gradient moving average decay) and  eta2 (squared gradient moving average decay). Outputs: Updated parameter vector 	heta{t+1}. Data Structures: 	heta: Array of parameters, size N. mt: Exponential moving average of gradients, size N, initialized to zeros. vt: Exponential moving average of squared gradients, size N, initialized to zeros. Steps: 1. Gradient Accumulation: Compute the gradient 
abla	heta L(	hetat) of the loss with respect to the parameters. The solver is implemented in a matrix-free manner by accumulating gradients via atomic additions. 2. Update Moments (Adam): If using Adam, update the first and second moment estimates: mt =  eta1 m{t-1} + (1 -  eta1) 
abla	heta L(	hetat) vt =  eta2 v{t-1} + (1 -  eta2) (
abla	heta L(	hetat))^2 Here,  eta1 and  eta2 control the filtering strength (exponential decay rate) for the gradient and its square, respectively. 3. Compute Update Step: Calculate the update direction. For Adam, the step is proportional to the ratio of the moments: 	ext{step} =  rac{mt}{vt} This ratio informally measures the signal-to-noise ratio in the gradient, reducing the step size when gradients are noisy or the function is highly anisotropic. For a constant update rate solver, the step is simply the gradient scaled by \alpha. 4. Parameter Update: Update the parameters: 	heta{t+1} = 	hetat - \alpha \cdot 	ext{step} Note: Bias correction terms for mt and vt are omitted in the basic description but are standard in Adam implementations. Parameters: \alpha: Learning rate. Not given in the sources.  eta1: Controls filtering strength for mt. Typical value: 0.9 (standard Adam).  eta2: Controls filtering strength for vt. Typical value: 0.999 (standard Adam). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Per-parameter filtering assumption: The Adam optimizer assumes no correlations across parameters, treating each component of 	heta independently. This diagonal preconditioning can lead to high-frequency artifacts if gradients are very noisy, the objective function is highly anisotropic, or optimization is terminated early. Norm Selection: The choice between l2 and l1 norms affects robustness to outliers. The l2-norm penalizes larger residuals more strongly due to the quadratic term, while the l1-norm tolerates larger outliers in favor of minimizing many lower deviations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientdescentstep(theta, lossfn, alpha, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, useadam=True, mprev=None, vprev=None): """Performs one step of gradient descent optimization.""" loss, grad = lossfn(theta) if useadam: if mprev is None: mprev = [0.0] len(theta) if vprev is None: vprev = [0.0] len(theta) m = [beta1 mprev[i] + (1 - beta1) grad[i] for i in range(len(theta))] v = [beta2 vprev[i] + (1 - beta2) (grad[i] 2) for i in range(len(theta))] step = [m[i] / (v[i] + 1e-8) for i in range(len(theta))] thetanew = [theta[i] - alpha step[i] for i in range(len(theta))] return thetanew, m, v else: thetanew = [theta[i] - alpha grad[i] for i in range(len(theta))] return thetanew, None, None The CGLS solver is a sparse linear least squares method used to solve optimization problems where the normal equations (A^T A) are ill-conditioned due to quadratic condition numbers. It provides numerically stable results for large or almost rank-deficient problems, distinguishing itself from direct solvers by avoiding the explicit formation of A^T A. While generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b for moderately sized problems, it is preferred when numerical stability is critical. Partially Learned Gradient Descent (PLGD) is an iterative reconstruction method that unrolls a fixed number of optimization steps into a neural network. It initializes the reconstruction with a filtered backprojection (FBP) estimate and iteratively refines it by passing the current estimate, gradients, and a momentum memory state through a convolutional network to compute the next update. Unlike standard gradient descent which uses a fixed or manually tuned step size, PLGD learns the optimization dynamics (step size and momentum) directly from data, while retaining the explicit physical forward model (e.g., RayTransform) to ensure interpretability and robustness to distribution shifts. It differs from fully learned end-to-end CNNs by preserving the gradient structure of the inverse problem. An ablation study variant of differentiable volume rendering optimization that replaces Gaussian noise assumptions with a positive Student's t-distribution to model gradient uncertainty. It serves as a controlled baseline to isolate the impact of heavy-tailed noise modeling from other components like MCMC sampling, ensuring fair comparison with methods using low-pass filtering. It builds on the Gradient Descent Solver [3280-gradient-descent-solver.md] by modifying the noise model. Newton's Method is a second-order optimization algorithm derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function. It solves for the root of the gradient (where the derivative is zero) to find local minima or maxima, offering quadratic convergence for well-behaved functions. Unlike Gradient Descent Solver, which uses only first-order gradient information and a fixed or adaptive step size, Newton's Method incorporates the Hessian matrix to account for local curvature, allowing it to take larger, more informed steps toward the optimum. In the context of inverse volume rendering, it is also applied as a root-finding algorithm to solve for ray intersections with implicit geometry. Inexact Line Search Optimization is an iterative method that adapts the step size in gradient descent to achieve a reduction in the objective function while ensuring sufficiently fast progress. It solves the problem of slow convergence in standard gradient descent by dynamically selecting a step size that guarantees improvement without requiring the computational expense of finding the exact minimum along the search direction. Unlike exact line search methods, which may suffer from convergence deterioration, this inexact strategy yields reasonable results and descends much faster. The Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method is an online learning algorithm for reflective tomography that incrementally updates a voxel model \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N to minimize modeling error against a sequence of observed frames. It solves the global least-squares optimization problem by applying preconditioned gradient descent steps to individual data frames one at a time. It distinguishes itself from batch solvers by processing data sequentially (frame-driven) and using a specific preconditioner derived from the projection matrix structure to prioritize high-frequency spatial information (surfaces). This method estimates spatially varying extinction coefficients  eta by minimizing a cost function E( eta) that fits a forward-model rendering to image measurements, using a surrogate function to avoid computing the full Jacobian per gradient step. It sets itself apart from direct Jacobian computation by decoupling the expensive forward-model rendering (FMC) from the gradient descent updates, requiring only one FMC rendering per block of NGD gradient steps rather than N{voxels}. A hybrid optimization strategy for sparse-pixel training that partitions Gaussian parameters into geometry and base appearance blocks, solving them via small Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) systems with Adam-style moment damping, while updating Higher-order Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients separately with Adam. It sets itself apart from its parent Gradient Descent Solver by introducing Hessian-informed updates for geometry and appearance, and from CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by using direct Cholesky decomposition on small blocks rather than iterative linear solving. This analysis provides a theoretical justification for the loss function's ability to converge to the signed distance function (SDF) of a plane when the input data is sampled from a plane, using a linear model f(x; w) = w^T x. It sets apart from fixed volumetric grids (like RGVF) by being data-dependent and avoiding cubic-size memory requirements and interpolation schemes. It proves that under specific conditions on the regularization parameter \lambda, gradient descent converges to the global minima corresponding to the plane's normal. A solver that keeps the main solver state on the selected NVIDIA GPU during the PDHG loop, including volume, extrapolated volume, previous volume, gradient buffer, TV duals, projection data duals, measured projections, and projection batches. Default resident projector backend is matchedvoxel. ASTRA is rejected for production resident PDHG because its 3-D CUDA FP/BP pair failed strict matched-adjoint checks. LEAP/PyTorch support is experimental and should only be used when its adjointness guard passes. Current resident multi-GPU support is not a pooled-memory solver; full memory pooling across two GPUs requires volume-sharded resident PDHG implementation. If resident PDHG runs out of VRAM, do not raise GPU PDHG memory safety to force a run; that only weakens the safety check. A SIRT variant representing the steepest descent in the least-squares functional. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and the cost of computing the gradient (forward/backward pass in volume rendering). Adam adds constant overhead for maintaining moments. Memory Complexity: O(N) for parameters and gradients. Matrix-free implementation avoids storing the Hessian or normal equations (O(N^2) or more). Performance: Stable for ill-conditioned systems. Generally slower than direct solvers for moderately sized problems but preferred for numerical stability in large or rank-deficient cases. Strengths: Robust to noise (especially with Adam), handles ill-conditioned problems, memory efficient (matrix-free). Limitations: Per-parameter filtering can cause high-frequency artifacts in noisy or anisotropic settings. Convergence can be slow compared to second-order methods for well-conditioned problems. When to use: Large-scale inverse volume rendering, ill-conditioned systems, when memory is constrained. When not to use: When high-frequency artifacts are unacceptable and second-order methods are feasible, or when exact line search is required for rapid convergence. The Gradient Descent Solver, particularly the Adam optimizer variant, was introduced by Kingma and Ba in 2015. It updates voxel grid parameters in differentiable volume rendering and addresses gradient noise and anisotropy by filtering gradients temporally. In volume rendering, it optimizes transfer functions and voxel grid parameters. name: CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares)
head: Sparse Linear Least Squares Solver
body: The CGLS solver is a sparse linear least squares method used to solve optimization problems where the normal equations (A^T A) are ill-conditioned due to quadratic condition numbers. It provides numerically stable results for large or almost rank-deficient problems, distinguishing itself from direct solvers by avoiding the explicit formation of A^T A. While generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b for moderately sized problems, it is preferred when numerical stability is critical. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Matrix A (implicitly available via matrix-vector products), vector b. Output: Solution vector x minimizing \|Ax - b\|^2. Data Structures: Vectors x, p, r, Ap of size n (dimension of the solution space). Scalar parameters \alpha, \beta. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize x0 = 0. 2. Compute initial residual r0 = b - A x0 = b. 3. Set initial search direction p0 = r0. 4. For k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Compute matrix-vector product Apk = A pk. b. Compute step size \alphak = \frac{rk^T rk}{pk^T A pk}. c. Update solution x{k+1} = xk + \alphak pk. d. Update residual r{k+1} = rk - \alphak A pk. e. Check convergence: if \|r{k+1}\| is sufficiently small, stop. f. Apply Jacobi preconditioning. Let M be the diagonal of A^T A (or an approximation thereof). The preconditioned residual \tilde{r} is computed as \tilde{r}i = ri / M{ii}. g. Compute \betak = \frac{\tilde{r}{k+1}^T \tilde{r}{k+1}}{rk^T rk}. h. Update search direction p{k+1} = \tilde{r}{k+1} + \betak pk. Parameters: Convergence tolerance: Not given in the sources. Preconditioner: Jacobi preconditioner. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The method is specifically chosen to handle ill-conditioned systems where normal equations fail. Rank deficiency: Provides stable results for almost rank-deficient problems. Performance: Slower than normal equation approaches for moderately sized problems. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cglssolve(Amatvec, b, maxiter=1000, tol=1e-6): """ Solves min ||Ax - b||^2 using CGLS with Jacobi preconditioning. Amatvec: function that computes A v for a vector v. b: target vector. """ n = len(b) x = [0.0] n r = [b[i] for i in range(n)] p = [r[i] for i in range(n)] # Compute diagonal of A^T A for Jacobi preconditioning diagAtA = [0.0] n for i in range(n): coli = Amatvec([1.0 if j == i else 0.0 for j in range(n)]) diagAtA[i] = sum(val2 for val in coli) # Guard against division by zero for i in range(n): if diagAtA[i] == 0: diagAtA[i] = 1.0 rdotr = sum(val2 for val in r) for k in range(maxiter): Ap = Amatvec(p) pAp = sum(p[i] Ap[i] for i in range(n)) if pAp == 0: break alpha = rdotr / pAp # Update x for i in range(n): x[i] += alpha p[i] # Update r and compute new squared norm rdotrnew = 0.0 for i in range(n): r[i] -= alpha Ap[i] rdotrnew += r[i]2 if rdotrnew < tol: break # Jacobi Preconditioning rtilde = [r[i] / diagAtA[i] for i in range(n)] rtildedotrtilde = sum(val2 for val in rtilde) beta = rtildedotrtilde / rdotr # Update p for i in range(n): p[i] = rtilde[i] + beta p[i] rdotr = rdotrnew return x This method recovers missing pixels in a rendered volume image by solving a regularized least-squares optimization problem using the Conjugate Gradient algorithm. It allows reconstruction from a subset of pixels, reducing total rendering time compared to full volume rendering. It differs from its parent CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by explicitly defining the regularization term H via B-spline convolution and the sampling matrix S for pixel dropping, whereas the parent focuses on the general numerical stability of the least-squares formulation. The Symmetric Least Squares Solver solves the linear system Ax = b where A is a symmetric matrix, typically arising from the normal equations A^T A in least-squares problems. It differs from the parent CGLS Solver by explicitly computing the pseudoinverse via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) rather than using iterative conjugate gradients. This approach provides a direct solution suitable for small, dense symmetric systems (e.g., 3 \times 3) where numerical stability via eigenvalue thresholding is required, contrasting with the iterative nature of Conjugate Gradient Solver for Compressive Volume Rendering. Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography is a volumetric reconstruction method that represents the 3D density field using an adaptive octree grid of piecewise constant basis functions, allowing for higher effective resolution and better memory efficiency than uniform grids by using fewer basis functions in uniform regions. It solves the problem of reconstructing dynamic, semi-transparent phenomena (such as smoke and flames) from multi-view video sequences by iteratively refining the grid resolution only where the reconstruction error is high, combined with a visual hull constraint to restrict the solution space. Unlike uniform grid approaches, which quickly exhaust memory limits for high-resolution multi-camera setups, this method uses 20-25% of the memory while achieving comparable accuracy. Solves Hc = \eta by performing Cholesky decomposition of H, followed by forward and backward substitution. This is used when H is positive-definite and symmetric, such as the Hankel matrix of the biased moment vector. Addresses problems when solving outer vertices of very sparse parent voxels that lack enough neighboring child voxels to create a linear system of equations. It solves sparse cases using the scalar field expansion method described in Appendix B of the source. A pitfall is that Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) often results in incorrect values for these sparse cases, with resulting values being both positive (outside bounds) and negative (inside the model). Time Complexity: Generally slower than computing A^T A and A^T b for moderately sized problems. Memory Complexity: Sparse, as it avoids forming A^T A explicitly. Numerical Stability: Provides numerically more stable results for very large or almost rank-deficient problems compared to normal equations. Strengths: Handles ill-conditioned systems better than normal equations. Limitations: Slower for moderate problem sizes. When to Use: When A^T A is ill-conditioned or rank-deficient. When Not to Use: When problem size is moderate and computational speed is prioritized over numerical stability. The CGLS solver is based on the work by Paige and Saunders [PS82], as cited in. It is used in transfer function optimization. name: Conjugate Gradient Solver for Compressive Volume Rendering
head: CG Solver, Compressive Volume Rendering with Conjugate Gradient Solver, Global CG Solver
body: This method recovers missing pixels in a rendered volume image by solving a regularized least-squares optimization problem using the Conjugate Gradient algorithm. It allows reconstruction from a subset of pixels, reducing total rendering time compared to full volume rendering. It differs from its parent CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) by explicitly defining the regularization term H via B-spline convolution and the sampling matrix S for pixel dropping, whereas the parent focuses on the general numerical stability of the least-squares formulation. Inputs: Y: The observed rendered image vector (size N \times 1, where N = \text{imageWidth} \times \text{imageHeight}). S: The binary sampling matrix (size N \times N). \lambda: Regularization parameter. \phi: The basis function (univariate uniform centered cubic B-spline \beta3(t), tensor-producted to 2D). Outputs: x: The reconstructed full-resolution image vector (size N \times 1). Data Structures: x, r, p, b: Vectors of size N (floats). A: Implicitly defined as S^T S + \lambda H. H: Convolution matrix defined by H{p,q} = \langle \phi(\cdot - jp), \phi(\cdot - jq) \rangle{L^2}. Formulas: The optimization problem is: \minx \|Sx - y\|2^2 + \lambda x^T H x The linear system to solve is: (S^T S + \lambda H)x = S^T y Let A = S^T S + \lambda H and b = S^T y. Steps: 1. Initialize x0 to zeros. 2. Compute b = S^T Y. Note that S^T acts as an upsampling operator inserting zeros at missing pixel locations. 3. Initialize residual r0:= b - A x0 and search direction p0:= r0. 4. Iterate for k = 0, 1, \dots: a. Calculate step size \alphak:= \frac{rk^T rk}{pk^T A pk}. b. Update solution x{k+1}:= xk + \alphak pk. c. Update residual r{k+1}:= rk - \alphak A pk. d. If r{k+1} is sufficiently small (convergence criterion), exit loop. e. Calculate \betak:= \frac{r{k+1}^T r{k+1}}{rk^T rk}. f. Update search direction p{k+1}:= r{k+1} + \betak pk. g. Increment k. 5. Return x{k+1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(ai bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) def applyS(x, Smap): # Smap: list of (outputindex, inputindex) where S[outputindex, inputindex] = 1 # Sx is downsampling: returns vector of observed pixel values return [x[idx] for, idx in Smap] def applyST(y, Smap, N): # S^T inserts zeros at missing pixels res = [0.0] N for i, (, idx) in enumerate(Smap): res[idx] = y[i] return res def convolveH(x, kernel, N): # Hx is equivalent to convolving the image with a 2D kernel phi # phi is the tensor product of univariate uniform centered cubic B-spline beta3 H = int(math.sqrt(N)) W = H img = [x[iW:(i+1)W] for i in range(H)] kh, kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0]) out = [[0.0]W for in range(H)] for i in range(H): for j in range(W): val = 0.0 for ki in range(kh): for kj in range(kw): ni, nj = i + ki - kh//2, j + kj - kw//2 if 0 <= ni < H and 0 <= nj < W: val += img[ni][nj] kernel[ki][kj] out[i][j] = val return [v for row in out for v in row] def solvecompressivevolumerendering(Y, Smap, lambdareg, phikernel, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): N = len(Y) x = [0.0] N b = applyST(Y, Smap, N) r = b[:] p = r[:] rdot = dot(r, r) for k in range(maxiter): # Ap = (S^T S + lambda H) p pdown = applyS(p, Smap) Sp = applyST(pdown, Smap, N) Hp = convolveH(p, phikernel, N) Ap = [Spi + lambdareg Hpi for Spi, Hpi in zip(Sp, Hp)] pdotAp = dot(p, Ap) if pdotAp == 0: break alpha = rdot / pdotAp x = [xi + alpha pi for xi, pi in zip(x, p)] r = [ri - alpha Api for ri, Api in zip(r, Ap)] rdotnew = dot(r, r) if math.sqrt(rdotnew) < tol: break beta = rdotnew / rdot p = [ri + beta pi for ri, pi in zip(r, p)] rdot = rdotnew return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The global solver is too slow for real-time rendering due to high data transfer between CPU and GPU for FFT convolution and cuBLAS dot products. FFT-based convolution requires memory to be copied back and forth between CPU and GPU, decreasing performance. cuBLAS dot product operations require memory copy for each iteration, significantly reducing performance. The matrix S has size (imageWidth \times imageHeight) by (imageWidth \times imageHeight). Time Complexity: The reconstruction time is almost constant regardless of the number of features or pixels added, while total rendering time increases with features/pixels. However, the global solver is computationally expensive and performance depends on image size and iteration count. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for vectors x, r, p, b and intermediate results for S^T S and H operations. FFT-based convolution requires additional memory for transforms. Performance: Volume rendering using 100% of the pixels takes more time than the compressive rendering method. The global reconstruction process is too slow to interact with the volume renderer in real-time due to CPU-GPU data transfers. Strengths: Acceptable image quality for reconstructed images. Can significantly reduce rendering time by using a subset of pixels. Limitations: Poor performance for real-time interactive rendering due to data transfer overheads. This method is described in the thesis "GPU-based Compressive Volume Rendering". It builds on the concept of compressive sensing applied to volume rendering, utilizing the Conjugate Gradient solver to recover missing pixel data. The regularization term H is defined using cubic B-splines. GPU-based Compressive Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.11575/prism/5366, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Symmetric Least Squares Solver
body: The Symmetric Least Squares Solver solves the linear system Ax = b for a symmetric matrix A using an SVD-based pseudoinverse. It returns the solution vector x and the squared residual error \|Ax - b\|^2. Inputs: A: A symmetric matrix (stored as upper triangular elements). b: A vector of the same dimension as A. svd\tol: Tolerance for SVD convergence or singular value classification. svd\sweeps: Number of iterations for the SVD algorithm. pinv\tol: Threshold for inverting eigenvalues; eigenvalues below this magnitude are treated as zero to ensure numerical stability. Outputs: x: The solution vector. residual: The squared residual error \|Ax - b\|^2. Data Structures: SMat3: A symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix stored with 6 floats: m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22. Mat3: A general 3 \times 3 matrix stored with 9 floats. Vector3: A 3-element vector. Steps: 1. SVD Decomposition: Call getSymmetricSvd(A, VTAV, V, svdtol, svdsweeps) to compute the eigenvectors V and the diagonalized eigenvalues VTAV. 2. Pseudoinverse Calculation: Call pseudoinverse(out pinv, VTAV, V, pinvtol) to compute the pseudoinverse matrix A^+ by inverting the eigenvalues in VTAV and thresholding those below pinvtol. 3. Solution: Compute x = A^+ b using matrix-vector multiplication. 4. Residual: Calculate and return \|Ax - b\|^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvesymmetricleastsquares(Auppertri, b, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Step 1: SVD Decomposition # getSymmetricSvd computes eigenvectors V and eigenvalues for symmetric A # Not given in the sources: specific iterative diagonalization routine. V, eigenvalues = getsymmetricsvd(Auppertri, svdtol, svdsweeps) # Step 2: Compute Pseudoinverse # Invert eigenvalues, thresholding near-zero values lambdainv = [1.0 / lam if abs(lam) > pinvtol else 0.0 for lam in eigenvalues] # Aplus = V diag(lambdainv) V^T pinv = computepseudoinversematrix(V, lambdainv) # Step 3: Solve for x x = matvecmul(pinv, b) # Step 4: Compute Residual Error ||Ax - b||^2 residual = calcerror(Auppertri, x, b) return x, residual def getsymmetricsvd(Auppertri, tol, sweeps): """ Computes eigenvectors V and eigenvalues for symmetric A. Not given in the sources: specific Givens/Jacobi rotation logic. Returns: (V: 3x3 matrix, eigenvalues: list of 3 floats) """ # Not given in the sources: specific iterative diagonalization routine. pass def computepseudoinversematrix(V, lambdainv): """ Computes V diag(lambdainv) V^T explicitly. V: 3x3 matrix (list of lists) lambdainv: list of 3 floats Returns: 3x3 matrix """ pinv = [[0.0] 3 for in range(3)] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): val = 0.0 for k in range(3): val += V[i][k] lambdainv[k] V[j][k] pinv[i][j] = val return pinv def matvecmul(M, v): """Matrix-vector multiplication M v""" n = len(M) result = [0.0] n for i in range(n): for j in range(n): result[i] += M[i][j] v[j] return result def calcerror(Auppertri, x, b): """Computes ||Ax - b||^2""" A = uppertritofull(Auppertri) Ax = matvecmul(A, x) diff = [Ax[i] - b[i] for i in range(3)] return sum(d d for d in diff) def uppertritofull(uppertri): """Converts [m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22] to 3x3 matrix""" m00, m01, m02, m11, m12, m22 = uppertri return [ [m00, m01, m02], [m01, m11, m12], [m02, m12, m22] ] Parameters: pinvtol: Threshold for inverting eigenvalues. Eigenvalues with magnitude less than this are treated as zero. Typical value not given in the sources. svdtol: Tolerance for SVD convergence. Typical value not given in the sources. svdsweeps: Number of sweeps for the SVD algorithm. Typical value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular/Ill-conditioned Matrices: The pinvtol parameter handles near-zero eigenvalues, preventing division by zero and stabilizing the solution. Symmetry Assumption: The method assumes A is symmetric, as the decomposition and storage format rely on this property. Dimensionality: The implementation is specific to 3 \times 3 matrices (SMat3, Vector3). Solves the overdetermined linear system Ax = b for a non-symmetric matrix A by explicitly forming the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b. Choose when A is not symmetric. Computes the pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix from its eigenvectors and diagonal eigenvalues, handling near-zero eigenvalues via a threshold to ensure numerical stability. This is the core linear algebra primitive used by the Symmetric Least Squares Solver. Reconstructs spatially varying volume properties by solving the ill-conditioned linear system Wa = o using Conjugate Gradient minimization on the GPU, avoiding explicit storage of the large sparse matrix W. Choose for large-scale volume rendering where explicit SVD is too expensive. Strengths: Provides a direct solution for symmetric systems; handles singular or ill-conditioned matrices via eigenvalue thresholding. Limitations: Explicitly forms the pseudoinverse, which is computationally expensive for large matrices; limited to symmetric matrices. When to Use: Small, dense, symmetric linear systems (e.g., local optimization steps in dual contouring) where stability is critical. When Not to Use: Large, sparse systems where iterative methods are preferred. The method is implemented in the DualContouringCSharp repository by tuckbone. It is used in the context of dual contouring for implicit surface reconstruction, where small symmetric linear systems arise from optimizing vertex positions. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: General Least Squares Solver
body: The General Least Squares Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b for a non-symmetric matrix A. It solves this by explicitly forming the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b, thereby reducing the problem to solving a symmetric system. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Matrix A (non-symmetric), vector b. Output: Solution vector x, residual error scalar. Data Structures: A: Dense matrix. A^T: Transpose of A. A^T A: Symmetric matrix. A^T b: Vector. x: Solution vector. Steps: 1. Compute the transpose of A, denoted A^T, using a standard matrix transpose operation. 2. Compute the product A^T A using a matrix multiplication routine optimized for the form A^T A. 3. Compute the product A^T b using a matrix-vector multiplication routine. 4. Solve the symmetric system (A^T A) x = A^T b using the Symmetric Least Squares Solver (SVD-based pseudoinverse method). 5. Return the solution x and the residual error. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvegeneralleastsquares(A, b, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Step 1: Transpose A At = [[A[j][i] for j in range(len(A))] for i in range(len(A[0]))] # Step 2: Compute A^T A n = len(At) AtA = [[sum(At[i][k] A[k][j] for k in range(len(A))) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] # Step 3: Compute A^T b Atb = [sum(At[i][j] b[j] for j in range(len(b))) for i in range(n)] # Step 4: Solve symmetric system (A^T A)x = A^T b using SVD-based pseudoinverse x = solvesymmetric(AtA, Atb, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol) # Step 5: Calculate residual error ||Ax - b|| Ax = [sum(A[i][j] x[j] for j in range(len(x))) for i in range(len(A))] residual = sum((Ax[i] - b[i])2 for i in range(len(b)))0.5 return x, residual def solvesymmetric(AtA, Atb, svdtol, svdsweeps, pinvtol): # Computes pseudoinverse of AtA via SVD and solves for x # Uses getSymmetricSvd and pseudoinverse routines internally # Returns solution vector x # (Implementation details delegated to the symmetric solver component) return x Parameters: svdtol: Tolerance for SVD decomposition in the symmetric solver. Not given in the sources. svdsweeps: Number of Jacobi sweeps for SVD. Not given in the sources. pinvtol: Tolerance for pseudoinverse calculation. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. The Normal Equations Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b by explicitly forming the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix A^T A and vector A^T b, then solving the resulting square system. It is distinguished from matrix-free iterative methods (like CGLS) by its direct assembly of the normal equations. Not given in the sources. The method relies on the Symmetric Least Squares Solver for the final step, which uses SVD-based pseudoinverse calculation. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Normal Equations Solver
head: A^T A Solver, Least Squares via Normal Equations
body: The Normal Equations Solver addresses the overdetermined linear system Ax = b by explicitly forming the symmetric positive semi-definite system A^T A x = A^T b and solving it using a standard linear solver. It is distinguished from iterative methods (like CGLS) and direct factorizations of the original matrix (like QR) by its reliance on the explicit construction of the Hessian matrix A^T A. While generally the fastest alternative for small-to-medium systems, it is prone to numerical instability if the system matrix A is ill-conditioned. Inputs and Outputs: Input: System matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} (where m \gg n) and vector b \in \mathbb{R}^m. Output: Solution vector x \in \mathbb{R}^n. Data Structures: Matrix A: Stored in Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) format to allow efficient sequential querying of non-zero entries for the i-th voxel (row). Matrix A^T A: A band matrix with non-zero entries only on the main diagonal and two diagonals four rows/columns away from the main diagonal. The distance of four arises from the separate handling of RGB\alpha channels. Due to symmetry, only the upper triangular part is stored. Vector A^T b: Standard dense or sparse vector representation. Steps: 1. Assemble A^T A and A^T b: Compute the sparse matrix-matrix product A^T A and the sparse matrix-vector product A^T b using a linear algebra library (e.g., Eigen on CPU, cuSPARSE on GPU) or custom matrix-free compute code. 2. Solve the Symmetric System: Solve the ordinary least squares problem A^T A x = A^T b using a dense or sparse linear least squares solver (e.g., QR, LLT, LDLT). 3. Constraint Handling: The standard normal equations solver does not enforce box constraints 0 \le xi \le 1. If the unconstrained solution violates these constraints, apply truncation: x'i = \max\{\min\{xi, 1\}, 0\}. If explicit constraint enforcement is required, a constrained quadratic programming solver (e.g., ADMM via OSQP) should be used instead. Pseudocode (Matrix-free GPU Assembly): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def assemblenormalequations(voxels, ATAuppertri): # Initialize ATAuppertri as a band matrix structure for i in range(len(voxels)): j = computecolumnindex(voxels[i]) # From Subsec. 3.2 w = computeinterpolationweight(voxels[i]) # From Subsec. 3.2 # Atomically add to upper triangular part of A^T A ATAuppertri[j, j] += (1 - w)2 ATAuppertri[j+1, j+1] += w2 ATAuppertri[j+1, j] += (1 - w) w # Compute A^T b similarly return ATAuppertri Formulas: Normal Equations: A^T A x = A^T b. Condition Number Relationship: \text{cond}(A^T A) = \text{cond}(A). The source text states this equality, noting that computing A^T A results in many arithmetic additions and potentially very large values, which leads to numerical instability. Truncation: x'i = \max\{\min\{xi, 1\}, 0\}. Parameters: Precision: 32-bit floating point is typical. For a dataset with 1.76 \cdot 10^6 voxels, storing A in CSR format requires almost 7 GiB of memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The condition number relationship \text{cond}(A^T A) = \text{cond}(A) leads to potential numerical instability due to accumulated arithmetic operations and large matrix values. Rank Deficiency: A^T A is often nearly rank deficient because certain transfer function values are hardly referenced by voxel values, or rank deficient if no values fall within a certain range. Solvers like QR may require pivoting for stability. GPU Atomic Contention: While atomic additions on GPU for assembling A^T A might theoretically cause write conflicts and slowdowns, in practice this method proved to be one of the fastest solutions. Addresses the box-constrained least squares problem (0 \le xi \le 1) by formulating it as a quadratic programming (QP) problem. It differs from direct unconstrained solvers by explicitly handling constraints (often via ADMM) and differs from iterative solvers by relying on the explicit construction of the Hessian Q = A^T A. Time Complexity: Generally the fastest alternative for small-to-medium systems where A^T A is small enough to fit in memory and be solved directly. Memory Complexity: Storing A is expensive (e.g., ~7 GiB for 1.76 \cdot 10^6 voxels with 32-bit floats), but A^T A is usually quite small and can be stored in dense or sparse format. Strengths: Fast assembly and solution for small systems; leverages highly optimized dense linear algebra libraries for the final solve step. Limitations: Prone to stability issues if A is ill-conditioned due to the condition number relationship; does not natively support box constraints without post-processing or external QP solvers. When to Use: When A^T A is small enough to be stored and solved directly, and numerical stability is not a primary concern or the matrix is well-conditioned. When Not to Use: When A is ill-conditioned (use QR or iterative methods); when explicit box constraints are required (use Normal Equations-based Solver with QP). The method originates from the formulation of ordinary least squares problems in volume rendering transfer function optimization. It is discussed in the context of comparing solver strategies for optimizing RGB\alpha values, where the system matrix A is tall and skinny (m \gg n). The approach is noted as the most straightforward solution, with implementations supporting CPU (Eigen), GPU (cuSPARSE), and matrix-free Vulkan compute. Transfer Function Optimization for Comparative Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2306.05885, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Normal Equations-based Solver
head: A^T A Solver, Constrained Least Squares, Least Squares via Normal Equations, Quadratic Programming Solver (Box-Constrained)
body: The Normal Equations-based Solver addresses the box-constrained least squares problem \forall i \in [1,...,n]: 0 \le xi \le 1 by formulating it as a quadratic programming (QP) problem. It sets itself apart from its parent Normal Equations Solver by explicitly handling the box constraints (0 \le xi \le 1) via a QP formulation, whereas the parent solver typically refers to the unconstrained ordinary least squares (OLS) solution. It is noted as the fastest alternative for small systems but suffers from stability issues if the matrix is ill-conditioned. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Matrix A and vector b from the linear system Ax \approx b. Output: Vector x satisfying 0 \le xi \le 1 that minimizes the objective. Data Structures: Matrix Q: n \times n symmetric positive semi-definite matrix, where Q = A^T A. Vector c: n-dimensional vector, where c = -A^T b. Constraints: Box constraints li = 0, ui = 1 for all i. Steps: 1. Compute the Hessian matrix Q = A^T A. 2. Compute the gradient vector c = -A^T b. 3. Formulate the quadratic programming problem: \minx \frac{1}{2} x^T Q x + c^T x subject to 0 \le xi \le 1 for all i \in [1,...,n]. 4. Solve the QP problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) via the OSQP solver library. 5. If the solver returns a solution that violates constraints due to numerical precision, apply truncation: x'i = \max\{\min\{xi, 1\}, 0\}. Formulas: Objective: \minx \frac{1}{2} x^T Q x + c^T x. Hessian: H(x) = \frac{\partial^2 E(x)}{\partial x^T \partial x} = 2 A^T A. Condition Number: \kappa(Q) = \kappa(A)^2. Parameters: Solver: ADMM via OSQP. Preconditioning: Not specified for this specific QP formulation, though CGLS (a sibling solver) uses Jacobi preconditioning. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioning: The condition number of Q is the square of the condition number of A. For very large, ill-conditioned systems, evaluating A^T A is problematic. Convexity: The ordinary least squares problem is convex because the Hessian 2 A^T A is positive semi-definite. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalequationssolver(A, b): # Step 1: Compute Q = A^T A Q = transpose(A) @ A # Step 2: Compute c = -A^T b c = -transpose(A) @ b # Step 3: Define QP problem # min 0.5 x^T Q x + c^T x # s.t. 0 <= xi <= 1 # Step 4: Solve using ADMM via OSQP # Note: OSQP expects Q in sparse format and c as dense vector # The solver handles the box constraints internally x = osqpsolve(Qsparse=cscmatrix(Q), cdense=c, l=zeros(n), u=ones(n)) # Step 5: Enforce constraints via truncation if necessary x = clip(x, 0, 1) return x The ADMM Solver is a proximal algorithm used to solve separable minimization problems of the form \minx f(x) + g(x) or \minx f(x) + g(Dx), where f(x) is a data fidelity term and g(x) is a prior or regularization term. It sets itself apart from its parent Normal Equations-based Solver by handling composite objectives with non-smooth or complex constraints (like sparsity or total variation) that are difficult to solve directly via normal equations, by splitting the problem into simpler sub-problems. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: A GPU implementation of OSQP exists, but for the small size of A^T A resulting from normal equations, no significant speed-up was observed compared to the CPU implementation. Strengths: Fast for small systems; leverages mature QP solvers like OSQP. Limitations: Prone to stability issues if the matrix is ill-conditioned due to the quadratic condition number of A. When to use: Small-sized data where A^T A is well-conditioned and box constraints are required. When not: Large, ill-conditioned systems where A^T A evaluation is numerically unstable. The method is based on formulating box-constrained least squares as a quadratic programming problem, a technique used in opacity optimization approaches [GRT13, AZD17]. The ADMM algorithm was first introduced by Boyd et al. [BPC∗ 11] for solving convex optimization problems. The OSQP solver library [SBG∗ 20] is used for implementation. Transfer Function Optimization for Comparative Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2306.05885, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
