name: ADMM Solver
head: Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, Standard ADMM
body: The ADMM Solver is a proximal algorithm used to solve separable minimization problems of the form \minx f(x) + g(x) or \minx f(x) + g(Dx), where f(x) is a data fidelity term and g(x) is a prior or regularization term. It sets itself apart from its parent Normal Equations-based Solver by splitting composite objectives into simpler sub-problems that are solved via proximal operators or constrained minimization. Inputs: Objective functions f(x) and g(\cdot), where f is typically a quadratic data term (e.g., \|Ax - p\|2^2) and g is a convex prior (e.g., \ell1 norm or Total Variation). Linear operator D (identity I for standard form, or a transform matrix for generalized form). Penalty parameter \rho > 0. Proximal parameter \mu (required for Linearized ADMM, optional for Standard ADMM depending on implementation). Maximum iterations T or convergence tolerance \epsilon. Outputs: Reconstructed volume x. Data Structures: x \in \mathbb{R}^n: Current primal variable (reconstruction). z \in \mathbb{R}^m: Auxiliary variable for the prior term. u \in \mathbb{R}^m: Scaled dual variable (Lagrange multiplier). y \in \mathbb{R}^m: Dual variable (used in Linearized ADMM). Numbered Steps (Standard ADMM for \minx f(x) + g(Dx)): 1. Initialize x^0, z^0, u^0. 2. For k = 0 to T-1: a. x-update: Solve x^{k+1} = \operatorname{argmin}x \left( f(x) + \frac{\rho}{2} \|Dx - z^k + u^k\|2^2 \right). b. z-update: Solve z^{k+1} = \operatorname{argmin}z \left( g(z) + \frac{\rho}{2} \|Dx^{k+1} - z + u^k\|2^2 \right). c. u-update: u^{k+1} = u^k + Dx^{k+1} - z^{k+1}. 3. Return x^T. Special Case: Standard Form (D=I): When D=I, the updates simplify to proximal operators: 1. x^{k+1} = \operatorname{prox}{\rho f}(x^k - u^k) 2. z^{k+1} = \operatorname{prox}{\rho g}(x^{k+1} + u^k) 3. u^{k+1} = u^k + x^{k+1} - z^{k+1}. Pseudocode (Standard ADMM with CG for x-update): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def admmsolver(A, p, D, proxf, proxg, rho, maxiter, tol): """ Solves minx f(x) + g(Dx) using Standard ADMM. Assumes f(x) = 0.5 ||Ax - p||^2. proxf and proxg are functions implementing the proximal operators. """ n = len(p) m = len(p) # Assuming D is square/compatible for simplicity x = [0.0] n z = [0.0] m u = [0.0] m zprev = [0.0] m for k in range(maxiter): # x-update: argminx f(x) + (rho/2) ||Dx - z + u||^2 # For f(x) = 0.5 ||Ax - p||^2, this solves (A^T A + rho D^T D) x = A^T p + rho D^T (z - u) # Solved via Conjugate Gradient as in RTK rhs = [0.0] n for i in range(n): rhs[i] = matvecmul(A.T, p)[i] + rho matvecmul(D.T, [z[j] - u[j] for j in range(m)])[i] H = lambda v: matvecmul(A.T, matvecmul(A, v)) + rho matvecmul(D.T, matvecmul(D, v)) x = conjugategradientsolve(H, rhs, maxinner=100) # z-update: prox{rho^{-1} g}(D x + u) Dzplusu = matvecmul(D, x) for i in range(m): Dzplusu[i] += u[i] z = proxg(Dzplusu, 1.0 / rho) # u-update: u + Dx - z Dx = matvecmul(D, x) for i in range(m): u[i] = u[i] + Dx[i] - z[i] # Convergence check if k > 0: rpri = norm([x[i] - z[i] for i in range(min(n, m))]) rdual = norm([z[i] - zprev[i] for i in range(m)]) if rpri < tol and rdual < tol: break zprev = z.copy() return x def conjugategradientsolve(H, b, maxinner=100): """Solves H x = b using Conjugate Gradient.""" n = len(b) x = [0.0] n r = b[:] pvec = r[:] rdotr = dot(r, r) for in range(maxinner): Hp = H(pvec) alpha = rdotr / dot(pvec, Hp) x = [x[i] + alpha pvec[i] for i in range(n)] r = [r[i] - alpha Hp[i] for i in range(n)] rdotrnew = dot(r, r) if rdotrnew < 1e-10: break beta = rdotrnew / rdotr pvec = [r[i] + beta pvec[i] for i in range(n)] rdotr = rdotrnew return x def matvecmul(M, v): """Standard matrix-vector multiplication.""" return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))] def dot(v1, v2): """Dot product of two vectors.""" return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def norm(v): """L2 norm of a vector.""" return dot(v, v) 0.5 Parameters: \rho: Augmented Lagrangian penalty parameter. \mu: Proximal parameter for Linearized ADMM. Constraint: \mu \rho \|K\|^2 \le 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: For tomography, f(x) = \|Ax - p\|2^2, making the x-update a least-squares problem solved via Conjugate Gradient (CG) in implementations like RTK. If A^T A + \rho I is ill-conditioned, CG convergence may be slow. Convergence is not guaranteed for non-convex problems. This method solves the L1 shearlet regularized computed tomography (CT) reconstruction problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). It minimizes a composite objective consisting of a weighted L1 norm of shearlet coefficients and a quadratic data fidelity term, subject to non-negativity constraints on the image. It sets itself apart from standard filtered backprojection by enforcing sparsity in the shearlet domain to handle limited-angle artifacts, and from its parent ADMM Solver by specifically structuring the proximal steps for shearlet shrinkage and non-negativity clamping. A proximal algorithm used to solve optimization problems of the form \arg \minv F(v) + G(Kv). It modifies the standard ADMM x-update to avoid solving a linear system by linearizing the quadratic term, at the cost of introducing a proximal parameter \mu. Initialization: v^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^N, z^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^d, y^{(0)} = 0d. Iterations (t = 1 to T1): 1. v^{(t+1)} = \text{prox}{\mu F}(v^{(t)} - \mu \rho K^T (K v^{(t)} - z^{(t)} + y^{(t)})). 2. z^{(t+1)} = \text{prox}{\rho G}(K v^{(t+1)} + y^{(t)}). 3. y^{(t+1)} = y^{(t)} + K v^{(t+1)} - z^{(t+1)}. Parameters: \mu (proximal parameter) and \rho (penalty parameter) must satisfy \mu \rho \|K\|^2 \le 1. T1 is the number of iterations. z and y are additional variables of size d. Metrics used to track the convergence of the ADMM optimization loop by measuring violations of primal and dual feasibility. Primal Residual: \text{RMSE}(A xt, pt). Dual Residual: \text{RMSE}(A xt, A x{t-1}). Comparison: Raskar codes yield slightly faster convergence (lower residuals per iteration) compared to boxcar codes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing x, z, u (and v, y for LADMM). Strengths: Handles non-smooth regularizers (like \ell1) efficiently by splitting them into simple proximal steps. Limitations: Convergence can be slow for ill-conditioned problems. The x-update may require an iterative solver (like CG), adding inner-loop complexity. When to use: When the objective function is separable into a data term and a prior term, and the prior term has a simple proximal operator (e.g., sparsity, total variation). When not to use: When the problem is strictly convex and smooth, and a direct solver (like Cholesky) is feasible and faster. ADMM was introduced as a technique to solve separable minimization problems. It is implemented in the Reconstruction ToolKit (RTK) for total variation-regularized reconstruction. Linearized ADMM (LADMM) was developed to avoid solving linear systems in the x-update, making it suitable for large-scale problems. The method has been applied in electron microscopy tilt-series reconstruction and joint temporal de-blurring and tomographic reconstruction. Industrial Computed Tomography using Proximal Algorithm, https://doi.org/10.25781/kaust-th10i, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Accelerated 3D Tomographic Reconstruction and Visualization From Noisy Electron Microscopy Tilt-Series., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2022.3230445, fetched 2026-10-28 CodEx: A Modular Framework for Joint Temporal De-blurring and Tomographic Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.06069v3, fetched 2026-10-26

name: L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM)
head: ADMM Shearlet Reconstruction, Bubba et al. Algorithm
body: This method solves the L1 shearlet regularized computed tomography (CT) reconstruction problem using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). It minimizes a composite objective consisting of a weighted L1 norm of shearlet coefficients and a quadratic data fidelity term, subject to non-negativity constraints on the image. It sets itself apart from standard filtered backprojection by enforcing sparsity in the shearlet domain to handle limited-angle artifacts, and from its parent ADMM Solver by specifically structuring the proximal steps for shearlet shrinkage and non-negativity clamping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: y (measured sinogram), radon (forward Radon projection operator R), shearlet (shearlet transform operator SH). Output: f (reconstructed image volume). Data Structures: f: Image tensor, shape matching the backprojected image bp. bp: Backprojected image tensor, shape matching f. sc: Shearlet coefficients of bp, shape matching shf. u1, z1: Dual and primal variables for shearlet constraint, shape matching sc. u2, z2: Dual and primal variables for non-negativity constraint, shape matching bp. cgy: Right-hand side vector for the conjugate gradient linear system. w: Weight vector for the L1 norm, shape matching shf. Parameters: p0: Data fidelity weight. Typical value: 0.02. p1: Regularization weight. Typical value: 0.1. numiterations: Number of ADMM iterations. Not given in the sources. maxiter: Maximum iterations for the inner Conjugate Gradient solver. Typical value: 50. nscales: Number of shearlet scales. Typical value: 5. w calculation: w = 3^{\text{scales}} / 400, reshaped to (1, -1, 1, 1) for broadcasting. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize u2, z2, u1, z1, f to zero tensors with shapes matching bp and sc respectively. Compute initial backprojection bp = radon.backward(y). Compute initial shearlet coefficients of backprojection sc = shearlet.forward(bp). Compute weights w = 3nscales / 400 and reshape to broadcastable dimensions (1, -1, 1, 1). 2. ADMM Loop (for i in range(numiterations)): Compute CG RHS: cg\y = p0 \cdot bp + p1 \cdot \text{shearlet.backward}(z1 - u1) + (z2 - u2) Solve for f (Primal Update): Solve the linear system for f using Conjugate Gradient Least Squares (CGLS): \minf \left( p0 \cdot \| R f - y \|2^2 + (1 + p1) \cdot \| f \|2^2 \right) This is equivalent to solving: (p0 \cdot R^T R + (1 + p1) \cdot I) f = cg\y Using the solver: f = cg(lambda x: p0 radon.backward(radon.forward(x)) + (1 + p1) x, f.clone(), cgy, maxiter=50). Shearlet Transform: Compute shearlet coefficients of the new f: sh\f = \text{shearlet.forward}(f) Update z1 (Shearlet Proximal Step): Apply soft-thresholding (shrinkage) to update the primal variable for the shearlet constraint: z1 = \text{shrink}(sh\f + u1, \frac{p0}{p1} \cdot w) Update z2 (Non-negativity Proximal Step): Project onto the non-negative orthant: z2 = \max(0, f + u2) Implemented as z2 = (f + u2).clampmin(0). Update Dual Variables: u1 = u1 + sh\f - z1 u2 = u2 + f - z2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def l1shearletadmm(y, radon, shearlet, numiterations=100, maxcgiter=50): p0 = 0.02 p1 = 0.1 nscales = 5 bp = radon.backward(y) sc = shearlet.forward(bp) u2 = zeroslike(bp) z2 = zeroslike(bp) u1 = zeroslike(sc) z1 = zeroslike(sc) f = zeroslike(bp) w = (3 nscales) / 400 w = reshape(w, (1, -1, 1, 1)) def linearop(x): return p0 radon.backward(radon.forward(x)) + (1 + p1) x for i in range(numiterations): cgy = p0 bp + p1 shearlet.backward(z1 - u1) + (z2 - u2) f = conjugategradient(linearop, f.clone(), cgy, maxiter=maxcgiter) shf = shearlet.forward(f) threshold = (p0 / p1) w z1 = shrink(shf + u1, threshold) z2 = clamp(f + u2, min=0.0) u1 = u1 + shf - z1 u2 = u2 + f - z2 return f def zeroslike(tensor): return fulllike(tensor, 0.0) def fulllike(tensor, val): return [val] tensor.size def conjugategradient(A, x0, b, maxiter): x = x0.copy() r = b - A(x) p = r.copy() rsold = dot(r, r) for in range(maxiter): Ap = A(p) alpha = rsold / dot(p, Ap) x = x + alpha p r = r - alpha Ap rsnew = dot(r, r) if sqrt(rsnew) < 1e-6: break p = r + (rsnew / rsold) p rsold = rsnew return x def shrink(a, b): return clamp(abs(a) - b, min=0.0) sign(a) def clamp(tensor, min=None, max=None): if min is not None: tensor = maximum(tensor, min) if max is not None: tensor = minimum(tensor, max) return tensor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The implementation supports single and half precision. Relative error between single and half precision for the Shepp-Logan phantom is 1.40 \cdot 10^{-4}, and reconstruction MSE error difference is negligible (2.0566 \cdot 10^{-4} vs 2.0567 \cdot 10^{-4}). Limited Angles: The method is designed for limited-angle tomography where R represents forward projection with limited angles. Numerical Stability: The inner CG solver requires a well-conditioned system. The term (1+p1)I acts as a regularization term to ensure invertibility. A GPU-based cone-beam CT reconstruction method that uses TIGRE for forward/backward projections and an ADMM solver with restarted GMRES for the x-update step to handle numerical mismatch between TIGRE's Ax and A^Tb operators. It sets itself apart from its parent L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM) by returning to TIGRE reconstruction physics, using matched A and A^T operators from TIGRE, and employing GMRES to solve the linear system arising from the ADMM x-update due to potential numerical mismatch between the forward and adjoint operators. Time Complexity: The dominant cost per iteration is the forward/backward Radon projections and the shearlet transform, plus the conjugate gradient solve. The CG solve converges in up to maxiter (50) steps per ADMM iteration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for f, bp, sc, u1, z1, u2, z2, and cgy. Measured Performance: On a Tesla V100 GPU, the implementation runs in 1.6 seconds per reconstruction, compared to 2.5 minutes on an Intel i7 CPU in the original paper, representing a 125x speedup. With batch processing, the average time is 1.2 seconds per image. Strengths: All operations (including shearlet transforms) are performed on the GPU, maximizing execution speed. No CPU-GPU memory copies occur in the main loop. Supports batch processing for parallel sinogram handling. Limitations: Performance depends on the convergence of the inner CG solver. The method is specific to L1 shearlet regularization and may not be optimal for other priors. The method is based on the work of Bubba et al. [4], who proposed solving the L1 shearlet regularized CT reconstruction problem as a preprocessing step for deep learning-based inverse problems. The original implementation was on CPU, but a GPU-accelerated version using TorchRadon was developed to leverage modern hardware. The algorithm uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to decouple the data fidelity term from the sparsity-promoting shearlet prior and the non-negativity constraint. name: TomoAnchor V3 Z-Sharded ADMM-GMRES
head: V3 solver
body: A GPU-based cone-beam CT reconstruction method that uses TIGRE for forward/backward projections and an ADMM solver with restarted GMRES for the x-update step to handle numerical mismatch between TIGRE's Ax and A^Tb operators. It sets itself apart from its parent L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM) by returning to TIGRE reconstruction physics, using matched A and A^T operators from TIGRE, and employing GMRES to solve the linear system arising from the ADMM x-update due to potential numerical mismatch between the forward and adjoint operators. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data y, forward projection operators As, backprojection operators Bs, weight matrix W, regularization parameter \rho, and initial volume estimate x. Output: Reconstructed volume x, split into shards xs. Data Structures: ShardedVolume: A dataclass with fields shards (tuple of arrays), volumeshards (tuple of VolumeShard objects), and xp (array library, default np). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize volume x and shards xs. Verify that the number of arrays matches the number of volume shards, raising ValueError if mismatched. Verify that shard local shape matches array shape, raising ValueError if tuple(int(value) for value in array.shape) != tuple(int(value) for value in shard.localshape). 2. ADMM Loop: For each ADMM iteration: a. x-update: Solve the linear system using restarted GMRES. The core matrix-vector product computes the global projection first, then the shard-wise residual. b. z-update: Update auxiliary variables based on current x and dual variable u. c. u-update: Update dual variable u based on current x and z. 3. Termination: Check convergence criteria (e.g., relative change in x, residual norm). If converged, stop; otherwise, return to step 2. Formulas: Each matvec computes the global projection first, then the shard output: y = \sums As xs \text{out}s = Bs W^2 y + \rho (G^T G x)s where As is the forward projection for shard s, Bs is the backprojection for shard s, W is the weight matrix, \rho is the regularization parameter, G is a linear operator, xs is the shard of volume x, and y is the global projection. Parameters: Residency mode: Determines host/device data management. stagedtigre: Production default. Uses stock TIGRE NumPy wrappers with pinned/staged host buffers. Preserves TIGRE physics but is not strict GPU-resident. devicetigre: Strict native bridge backend. Keeps ADMM-GMRES solver vectors host-resident, streams one z-shard at a time to GPU, and calls TIGRE CUDA kernels through the TomoAnchor native CuPy device-pointer bridge. Requires running python tools/buildtigredevicebackend.py --preflight-only then python tools/buildtigredevicebackend.py --tigre-source tools/TIGRE. devicetigreresident: Full CuPy-resident backend. Keeps all V3 solver shards on selected GPUs. Only appropriate when the whole ADMM-GMRES state fits in aggregate VRAM. auto: Uses devicetigre only when available, otherwise stagedtigre unless strict residency is required. Number of GMRES restarts: Not given in the sources. Tolerance for GMRES convergence: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mismatch between the number of arrays and volume shards raises a ValueError. Mismatch between shard local shape and array shape raises a ValueError. Numerical mismatch between TIGRE's Ax and A^Tb operators necessitates GMRES instead of CG. The volume is split only along the z-axis; slabs are not reconstructed independently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def admmgmresxupdate(xshards, As, Bs, W, rho, G): # Compute global projection y = sums As xs y = sum(Asi for i in range(len(xshards))) # Compute RHS for each shard: outs = Bs W^2 y + rho (G^T G x)s rhs = [] for i in range(len(xshards)): rhsi = Bsi + rho (G.T @ G @ xshards[i]) rhs.append(rhsi) # Define matvec for the linear system def matvec(vshards): vproj = sum(Asi for i in range(len(vshards))) return Bs[i + rho (G.T @ G @ vshards[i]) for i in range(len(vshards))] # Note: The sources do not provide the GMRES solver implementation. # A standard restarted GMRES implementation should be used here. xnew = gmresrestarted(matvec, rhs, xshards) return xnew Strengths: Uses TIGRE for accurate forward and backward projections, handles numerical mismatch between operators using GMRES, supports GPU acceleration via residency modes. Limitations: Numerical mismatch between operators may require careful tuning of GMRES parameters, residency modes may impact performance and memory usage. When to Use: Suitable for cone-beam CT reconstruction where TIGRE's physics are desired and GPU acceleration is needed. When Not to Use: Not suitable when strict GPU residency is required and the whole ADMM-GMRES state does not fit in aggregate VRAM, or when TIGRE's numerical mismatch cannot be handled by GMRES. Originated as part of the TomoAnchor V3 project, which aims to provide a flexible and efficient framework for CT reconstruction. The method builds on the L1 Shearlet Regularized CT Reconstruction (ADMM) algorithm, adapting it to use TIGRE for projections and GMRES for the x-update step. It is used in research and production environments for high-quality CT reconstruction. alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, https://github.com/alidarbandi/TomoAnchor-V3, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Symmetric Pseudo-Inverse Calculation
head: Pseudoinverse Calculation
body: Computes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix A given its eigen-decomposition (eigenvectors V and eigenvalues D), inverting the eigenvalues while handling near-zero values via a threshold to ensure numerical stability. It differs from general least squares solvers by exploiting the symmetry of A to use eigen-decomposition instead of full SVD or QR decomposition, and from CGLS by providing a direct algebraic solution rather than an iterative approximation. Inputs: A: A symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix (represented as SMat3 or Mat3 with symmetry constraint). V: A 3 \times 3 matrix where columns are the eigenvectors of A. D: A diagonal matrix (or vector) containing the eigenvalues of A on the diagonal (d{00}, d{11}, d{22}). tol: A floating-point threshold for truncating small eigenvalues. Outputs: Out: A 3 \times 3 matrix representing the pseudoinverse A^+. Data Structures: Mat3: A 3 \times 3 matrix with fields m00 through m22. SMat3: A symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix, typically storing only the upper triangle or diagonal, but here accessed as diagonal elements m00, m11, m22. Vector3: A 3-element vector. Steps: 1. Truncate Eigenvalues: For each diagonal element di of D (where i \in \{0, 1, 2\}), compute the truncated inverse d'i using the function pinv(di, tol). 2. Construct Pseudoinverse: Compute the elements of Out using the formula: Out{ij} = \sum{k=0}^{2} V{ik} \cdot d'k \cdot V{jk} Specifically, for all i, j \in \{0, 1, 2\}: Out{ij} = V{i0} d'0 V{j0} + V{i1} d'1 V{j1} + V{i2} d'2 V{j2} 3. Return: The matrix Out. Formulas: The core truncation function is defined as: pinv(x, tol) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } |x| < tol \text{ or } |1/x| < tol \\ 1/x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Parameters: tol: The threshold for considering an eigenvalue zero. Typical values are not explicitly given in, but uses an absolute magnitude of 0.1 for singular values in a related QEF context. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near-Zero Eigenvalues: If an eigenvalue is close to zero, its inverse becomes large, leading to numerical instability. The threshold tol prevents this by setting the inverse to zero. Symmetry: The input matrix A must be symmetric. If A is not symmetric, the eigen-decomposition may not yield an orthogonal matrix V, and the method may fail or produce incorrect results. Precision: Using absolute truncation (as in) can be robust for normalized vectors but may lose features if area-weighted normals are used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pinv(x: float, tol: float) -> float: """ Computes the truncated inverse of x. Returns 0 if |x| < tol or |1/x| < tol, else 1/x. """ if abs(x) < tol or abs(1.0 / x) < tol: return 0.0 return 1.0 / x def symmetricpseudoinverse(V: Mat3, Ddiag: Vector3, tol: float) -> Mat3: """ Computes the pseudoinverse of a symmetric matrix A given its eigen-decomposition. Args: V: 3x3 matrix of eigenvectors (columns). Ddiag: Vector of eigenvalues [d00, d11, d22]. tol: Threshold for truncating small eigenvalues. Returns: Mat3: The pseudoinverse matrix A+. """ # Step 1: Truncate eigenvalues d0 = pinv(Ddiag.x, tol) d1 = pinv(Ddiag.y, tol) d2 = pinv(Ddiag.z, tol) # Step 2: Construct the pseudoinverse matrix # Outij = sumk (Vik dk Vjk) # We compute all 9 elements of the 3x3 matrix # Row 0 outm00 = V.m00 d0 V.m00 + V.m01 d1 V.m01 + V.m02 d2 V.m02 outm01 = V.m00 d0 V.m10 + V.m01 d1 V.m11 + V.m02 d2 V.m12 outm02 = V.m00 d0 V.m20 + V.m01 d1 V.m21 + V.m02 d2 V.m22 # Row 1 outm10 = V.m10 d0 V.m00 + V.m11 d1 V.m01 + V.m12 d2 V.m02 outm11 = V.m10 d0 V.m10 + V.m11 d1 V.m11 + V.m12 d2 V.m12 outm12 = V.m10 d0 V.m20 + V.m11 d1 V.m21 + V.m12 d2 V.m22 # Row 2 outm20 = V.m20 d0 V.m00 + V.m21 d1 V.m01 + V.m22 d2 V.m02 outm21 = V.m20 d0 V.m10 + V.m21 d1 V.m11 + V.m22 d2 V.m12 outm22 = V.m20 d0 V.m20 + V.m21 d1 V.m21 + V.m22 d2 V.m22 return Mat3(outm00, outm01, outm02, outm10, outm11, outm12, outm20, outm21, outm22) Computes the pseudo-inverse of a 3x3 symmetric matrix by leveraging its eigen-decomposition. It uses auxiliary arrays w for inverse eigenvalues and u for eigenvectors, and can minimize towards a specified midpoint. Computes the pseudoinverse of A^T A (where A^T A is symmetric) by inverting singular values si and truncating 1/si to 0 if |si| < 0.1. It uses normalized vectors instead of area-weighted normals to ensure robustness against noise, as singular values become proportional to the number of vectors aligning with the eigenvector. Time Complexity: O(1) for 3 \times 3 matrices, as the size is fixed. The dominant cost is the eigen-decomposition, which is not part of this method but is a prerequisite. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only a few 3 \times 3 matrices and vectors. Strengths: Numerically stable due to thresholding; efficient for small symmetric matrices; direct solution. Limitations: Requires the matrix to be symmetric; requires pre-computed eigen-decomposition; not suitable for non-symmetric or large matrices. When to use: When solving symmetric linear systems in 3D (e.g., QEF in dual contouring) and eigen-decomposition is already available. When not to use: For non-symmetric matrices, or when iterative methods are preferred for very large systems. Originated in the context of dual contouring and implicit modeling, where symmetric matrices arise from quadratic error functions (QEF). The method is used to find the minimizer of the QEF by computing the pseudoinverse of the system matrix. It is a key component in real-time mesh generation and volume reconstruction algorithms. tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, https://github.com/tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChessQian/DualContouring, https://github.com/ChessQian/DualContouring, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Dual Contouring: "The Secret Sauce", https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~jrs/meshpapers/SchaeferWarren2.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Volume Reconstruction via Conjugate Gradient
head: Implicit Matrix Solution, Ray Marching Back-Projection
body: This method reconstructs spatially varying volume properties (albedo, emission, extinction) by solving the ill-conditioned linear system Wa = o using Conjugate Gradient (CG) minimization on the GPU. It avoids explicit storage of the large sparse matrix W by implicitly computing matrix-vector products via ray marching. Inputs: Target images o (observation pixels). Initial volume estimate a (stored in 3D textures). Camera poses and intrinsics. Optional: Per-pixel constraint weights, visual hull masks, regularization weights. Outputs: Reconstructed volume properties a (albedo, emission, extinction) in 3D textures. Data Structures: Volume Properties (a): Stored in 3D textures representing vectors. Fields correspond to albedo, emission, and extinction. Precision can be 16-bit to reduce bandwidth. Target Images (o): 2D textures or buffers. Residual (c): 2D buffer storing Wa - o. Gradient/Direction Vectors: 3D textures for volume updates. Formulas: The objective is to minimize the quadratic error function: E(a) = ||Wa - o||^2 With regularization terms \Omega(a): E{reg}(a) = ||Wa - o||^2 + \lambdaL ||La||^2 + \lambda0 ||a||^2 + \lambda1 ||a - 1||^2 Where: W is the sparse rendering matrix. L is the Laplacian operator. \lambdaL, \lambda0, \lambda1 are user-defined weights (typically weak, e.g., 2^{-9}). Constraint weights wp are applied per pixel by multiplying the residual vector: minimize || (Wa - o) \odot wp ||^2. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a (e.g., zeros or previous estimate). Compute initial gradient g0 = W^T(Wa0 - o). Set search direction p0 = -g0. 2. Iteration Loop: For k = 0, 1, \dots until convergence: a. Forward Pass (Wpk): Render the volume with properties pk to generate an image via ray marching. b. Back-Projection (W^T(Wpk)): Distribute the rendered image back to the volume voxels via ray marching with accumulation. c. Step Size: Compute \alphak = \frac{pk^T pk}{pk^T W^T W pk}. d. Update Solution: a{k+1} = ak + \alphak pk. e. Update Residual: g{k+1} = gk + \alphak W^T W pk. f. Convergence Check: If ||g{k+1}|| < \epsilon, stop. g. Beta: Compute \betak = \frac{g{k+1}^T g{k+1}}{gk^T gk}. h. Update Direction: p{k+1} = g{k+1} + \betak pk. Pseudocode: The core operations are implemented as shaders. The unified ray marching loop handles both forward (rendering) and backward (back-projection) passes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvevolumecg(targetimages, initialvolume, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): a = initialvolume.copy() # Compute initial gradient: g = W^T(Wa - o) Wa = raymarchforward(a) residualimg = Wa - targetimages g = raymarchbackward(residualimg) p = -g.copy() pdotp = dotproduct(p, p) for k in range(maxiter): if pdotp < tol: break # Compute W^T(Wp) Wp = raymarchforward(p) WTWp = raymarchbackward(Wp) pdotWTWp = dotproduct(p, WTWp) if pdotWTWp == 0: break alpha = pdotp / pdotWTWp a = a + alpha p g = g + alpha WTWp newpdotp = dotproduct(g, g) if newpdotp < tol: break beta = newpdotp / pdotp p = g + beta p pdotp = newpdotp return a def raymarchforward(volumeproperties): outputimage = zeroslike(targetimageshape) for pixel in allpixels: ray = getcameraray(pixel) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedradiance = 0.0 tmin, tmax = ray.intersectvolume() t = tmin while t < tmax: position = ray.origin + t ray.direction emission = textureread3d(volumeproperties.emission, position) extinction = textureread3d(volumeproperties.extinction, position) weight = accumulatedtransmittance (1.0 - exp(-extinction)) accumulatedradiance += weight emission accumulatedtransmittance = exp(-extinction) t += ray.stepsize outputimage[pixel] = accumulatedradiance return outputimage def raymarchbackward(imageresidual): volumegradient = zeroslike(volumeproperties) # Interleaved 6x6 pattern to avoid synchronization stalls from data scattering # Process pixels in blocks, advancing by 6 each round to minimize conflicts for offsety in range(6): for offsetx in range(6): for y in range(offsety, height, 6): for x in range(offsetx, width, 6): pixel = (x, y) ray = getcameraray(pixel) residual = imageresidual[pixel] accumulatedbackproj = 0.0 accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 tmin, tmax = ray.intersectvolume() t = tmin while t < tmax: position = ray.origin + t ray.direction extinction = textureread3d(volumeproperties.extinction, position) weight = accumulatedtransmittance (1.0 - exp(-extinction)) accumulatedbackproj += weight residual accumulatedtransmittance = exp(-extinction) t += ray.stepsize texturewriteadd3d(volumegradient, position, accumulatedbackproj) return volumegradient def dotproduct(u, v): return sum(u[i] v[i] for i in range(len(u))) def textureread3d(tex, pos): return tex.sample(pos) def texturewriteadd3d(tex, pos, val): tex[pos] = tex[pos] + val def zeroslike(shape): return [0.0] shape def getcameraray(pixel): return CameraRay(pixel, intrinsics, extrinsics) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Synchronization Stalls: Data scattering during back-projection (texture writes) causes stalls because neighboring rays write to the same voxels. Precision: Use 16-bit textures instead of 32-bit to reduce bandwidth and speed up computation by ~25%. Resolution Mismatch: Albedo and emission can use lower resolution than extinction to accelerate computation and reduce memory, though this may affect quality. Refractive Rays: For non-constant refractive indices, use arbitrary integration curves computed via Euler forward scheme. Visual Hulls: Limit solution domain to voxels with non-zero extinction (for albedo/emission) or user-defined masks (for extinction) to improve quality and performance. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of CG iterations and the cost of ray marching per iteration. Memory Complexity: O(Nv) for volume storage, where Nv is the number of voxels. Performance: 16-bit textures provide ~25% speedup. Interleaved pixel pattern provides ~10% speedup by reducing synchronization stalls. Strengths: Handles large sparse systems without explicit matrix storage. Flexible regularization. Supports refraction and visual hulls. Limitations: Ill-conditioned systems may require careful regularization. Synchronization issues in back-projection can limit parallel efficiency. When to Use: When reconstructing volume properties from multiple views and explicit matrix storage is infeasible. When Not to Use: When high precision is critical and 16-bit textures are insufficient. This method was introduced in "Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor" (2014). It builds on the linearity of light transport and the sparsity of the rendering operator. The use of Conjugate Gradient for volume reconstruction allows for efficient optimization of volume properties without the memory overhead of direct matrix inversion. Property and Lighting Manipulations for Static Volume Stylization Using a Painting Metaphor, https://doi.org/10.1109/TVCG.2014.13, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography
head: Adaptive Tomography, Adaptive reconstruction algorithm, Octree-based Optical Tomography, Octree-based adaptive CT
body: Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography is a volumetric reconstruction method that represents the 3D density field using an adaptive octree grid of piecewise constant basis functions, allowing for higher effective resolution and better memory efficiency than uniform grids by using fewer basis functions in uniform regions. It solves the problem of reconstructing dynamic, semi-transparent phenomena (such as smoke and flames) from multi-view video sequences by iteratively refining the grid resolution only where the reconstruction error is high, combined with a visual hull constraint to restrict the solution space. Unlike uniform grid approaches, which quickly exhaust memory limits for high-resolution multi-camera setups, this method uses 20-25% of the memory while achieving comparable accuracy. Inputs: A synchronized multi-video sequence of nc cameras. Camera calibration parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics) for all cameras. A set of background images for each camera. A visual hull (or silhouette masks) for each camera, derived from the background-subtracted foreground images. Outputs: A sparse system matrix S representing the projection of the current octree basis functions onto the image planes. A coefficient vector a representing the density values of the active basis functions. The final adaptive octree structure defining the 3D density field. Sparse Matrix S: Layout: Index-stored sparse matrix (coordinate format). Stores two indices (row, column) and the matrix value for each non-zero entry. Rows: Correspond to pixels in the image plane across all cameras. Total rows np is the number of pixels in one frame multiplied by the number of cameras nc. Columns: Correspond to basis functions (octree leaves) in the 3D volume. Entries: S{ij} is the integral of basis function \phij over the ray/pixel area for pixel i. Non-zero only if the support of \phij projects onto pixel i. Octree Node Structure: Used to track the splitting process and identify geometry. Fields: splitlevel: Integer, depth from the root of the octree. leafindex: Integer, the index the leaf would have in a uniformly split octree under a fixed traversal order (e.g., Morton order). This structure allows the algorithm to determine the position and size of new basis functions generated during splitting and to compute the integral values for the new columns of S. Coefficient Vector a: Vector of density coefficients corresponding to the columns of S. Constrained to be non-negative (ai \ge 0). Residual Vector r: r = p - S a, where p is the background-subtracted pixel vector. k: Number of basis functions to split per iteration. Typical value: \sqrt{nb}, where nb is the current number of basis functions. Max Split Level: Maximum depth of the octree. Non-negative Constraint: Applied during the solver step. 1. Preprocessing (Background Subtraction): Record background images for all cameras. Compute the median background image and standard deviation per pixel for each camera. Classify pixels as foreground or background based on the standard deviation. For foreground pixels, subtract the background value. For background pixels, set the value to zero. This computes the target vector p (representing p{original} - b) in advance. 2. Initialization: Initialize a uniform grid of box basis functions at the coarsest level (root of the octree). Construct the initial sparse projection matrix S where rows correspond to pixels and columns to basis functions. S{ij} is non-zero if basis function \phij projects onto pixel pi. Apply Visual Hull Restriction to S (see Substeps 2.1 and 2.2 below) to remove columns corresponding to basis functions with non-zero support completely outside the visual hull. 2.1. Visual Hull Restriction (Column Pruning): For each camera, create a binary vector marking basis functions that have non-zero support in the camera's silhouette (generalized cone). Compute the element-wise logical AND of all camera binary vectors to find the intersection of generalized cones (the visual hull). Restrict matrix S to only include columns (basis functions) that are inside the visual hull intersection. 2.2. Visual Hull Restriction (Row Handling): Note: Rows corresponding to pixels outside the silhouette are kept but will have zero entries in the right-hand side vector p (after background subtraction). The basis functions on the boundary of the visual hull are likely to be split, allowing the boundary to be represented accurately. 3. Adaptive Iteration Loop: Repeat the following steps until convergence or maximum split level is reached: Step 1: Solve for Coefficients Solve the linear least squares system using the CGLS (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) solver. The system is: S a = p. In every iteration of CGLS, project the solution to the subspace of non-negative solutions by setting all negative entries of the solution vector a to zero. The theoretical least squares solution is given by: a = (S^T S)^{-1} S^T (p - b) where p is the background-subtracted pixel vector and b is the background (already subtracted in preprocessing, so effectively p in the code represents p{orig}-b). Step 2: Compute Residual and Error Measure Compute the residual error vector: r = p - S a Project the residual error onto the basis functions to get a measure of where to split. For each basis function \phij, compute the error measure e{\phij}: e{\phij} = \frac{\sum{i} S{ij} |ri|}{n{\phij}} where the sum is over all pixels i for which S{ij} \neq 0, and n{\phij} is the number of cameras in which basis function \phij is visible (i.e., the number of non-zero entries in column j of S). Note: This formula weights the residual by the projection strength S{ij} to provide a better measure than simply summing absolute residuals. Step 3: Split Basis Functions Identify the k basis functions with the largest error measures e{\phij}. k is typically set to \sqrt{nb}, where nb is the current number of basis functions. Split the selected k basis functions uniformly. For box basis functions, this involves replacing the column in matrix S with columns for the new sub-boxes (children in the octree). For linear basis functions, asymmetric basis functions must be introduced where splitting levels overlap. Update matrix S: Remove the columns corresponding to the split basis functions. Insert new columns for the new basis functions. Recalculate the integral values for the new columns using the octree node structure (split level and leaf index). Re-apply Visual Hull Restriction to the updated matrix S to ensure new basis functions outside the visual hull are removed. Step 4: Termination Check Check if the estimate is good enough. Stop splitting if: A maximum split level is reached. A basis function projects to less than two pixels in all images (Nyquist limit). If not converged, go back to Step 1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivegridopticaltomography(cameras, backgroundimages, maxsplitlevel): """ Reconstructs a 3D density field from multi-view video using adaptive octree grid. Args: cameras: List of camera objects with calibration and projection functions. backgroundimages: List of background images for each camera. maxsplitlevel: Maximum depth of the octree. Returns: octree: The final adaptive octree structure. coefficients: The density coefficients for the active basis functions. """ # 1. Preprocessing medianbackgrounds = [] stddevs = [] for bgimg in backgroundimages: medianbackgrounds.append(computemedian(bgimg)) stddevs.append(computestd(bgimg)) p = [] for camidx, cam in enumerate(cameras): currentframe = getcurrentframe(cam) bg = medianbackgrounds[camidx] std = stddevs[camidx] for pixel in currentframe: if isforeground(pixel, bg, std): p.append(pixel - bg) else: p.append(0.0) # 2. Initialization octree = Octree(rootlevel=0) S = buildsparsematrix(cameras, octree) S = applyvisualhullrestriction(S, cameras, octree) a = [0.0] len(S.columns) # 3. Adaptive Iteration Loop while True: # Step 1: Solve using CGLS with non-negative projection a = cglssolve(S, p, a, nonnegative=True) # Step 2: Compute Residual and Error Measure r = [p[i] - sum(S[i][j] a[j] for j in range(len(S.columns))) for i in range(len(p))] e = computeerrormeasure(S, r) # Step 3: Split Basis Functions nbasis = len(S.columns) k = int(nbasis 0.5) splitindices = gettopkindices(e, k) cansplit = True for idx in splitindices: bf = octree.getbasisfunction(idx) if bf.projectstolessthan2pixels(cameras) or bf.splitlevel >= maxsplitlevel: cansplit = False break if not cansplit: break S, octree, a = splitbasisfunctions(S, octree, a, splitindices, cameras) S = applyvisualhullrestriction(S, cameras, octree) if isconverged(r, S): break return octree, a def computemedian(image): return sorted(image)[len(image) // 2] def computestd(image): mean = sum(image) / len(image) variance = sum((x - mean) 2 for x in image) / len(image) return variance 0.5 def getcurrentframe(cam): return cam.capture() def isforeground(pixel, bg, std): return abs(pixel - bg) > 2 std class Octree: def init(self, rootlevel): self.rootlevel = rootlevel self.nodes = [] def getbasisfunction(self, idx): return self.nodes[idx] def addchildren(self, children): self.nodes.extend(children) def buildsparsematrix(cameras, octree): # Constructs S where Sij = integral of basis function phij over ray/pixel area # Implementation involves ray-tracing each basis function through each camera pass def applyvisualhullrestriction(S, cameras, octree): binaryvectors = [] for cam in cameras: vec = [0] len(S.columns) for j in range(len(S.columns)): if basisfunctioninsilhouette(octree.getbasisfunction(j), cam): vec[j] = 1 binaryvectors.append(vec) hullmask = [1] len(S.columns) for vec in binaryvectors: hullmask = [h & v for h, v in zip(hullmask, vec)] S = S[:, [i for i, m in enumerate(hullmask) if m]] return S def computeerrormeasure(S, r): nphi = [sum(1 for val in S[i] if val != 0) for i in range(len(S.columns))] nphi = [n if n > 0 else 1 for n in nphi] weightedabsr = [[abs(r[i]) S[i][j] for j in range(len(S.columns))] for i in range(len(r))] sumweighted = [sum(weightedabsr[i][j] for i in range(len(r))) for j in range(len(S.columns))] return [sw / n for sw, n in zip(sumweighted, nphi)] def gettopkindices(e, k): indexede = sorted(enumerate(e), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) return [idx for idx, in indexede[:k]] def splitbasisfunctions(S, octree, a, splitindices, cameras): mask = [1 if i not in splitindices else 0 for i in range(len(S.columns))] S = S[:, [i for i, m in enumerate(mask) if m]] a = [val for i, val in enumerate(a) if mask[i]] newbasisfunctions = [] for idx in splitindices: parent = octree.getbasisfunction(idx) newbasisfunctions.extend(parent.split()) octree.addchildren(newbasisfunctions) newScols = [computecolumnforbasisfunction(child, cameras) for child in newbasisfunctions] S = S + newScols a.extend([0.0] len(newbasisfunctions)) return S, octree, a def computecolumnforbasisfunction(bf, cameras): # Computes integral values for new columns using split level and leaf index pass def cglssolve(S, p, a, nonnegative=False): # Standard CGLS algorithm solving min ||Sa - p||^2 # Projects a to non-negative subspace (a = max(a, 0)) in each iteration if nonnegative=True pass def basisfunctioninsilhouette(bf, cam): return bf.supportintersectssilhouette(cam) def isconverged(r, S): return sum(x2 for x in r) < 1e-6 Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method uses 20-25% of the memory required by a uniform grid approach. A uniform grid with 8 cameras at 320x240 resolution reaches the 2 GB memory limit on a 32-bit machine quickly, whereas the adaptive grid mitigates this by using fewer basis functions. Time: The method is more computationally intensive per iteration than filtered backprojection. The complexity involves solving a sparse linear system (CGLS) and updating the sparse matrix S during splitting. The number of non-zero elements in S is O(\sqrt{nb} \cdot np) per row, where nb is the number of basis functions and np is the number of pixels. Scaling: The number of basis functions grows sub-exponentially with the number of iterations when k = \sqrt{nb}. The method allows for higher resolution input images and reconstructed models compared to uniform grids due to the memory savings. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Higher effective resolution than uniform grids for the same memory budget. Handles dynamic scenes (time-varying volumetric models). Mathematically sound error projection heuristic (though noted as heuristic in future work). The visual hull restriction scheme is accurate up to the pixel level. Limitations: More computationally intensive per iteration than traditional methods like filtered backprojection. The error projection is a heuristic; a mathematically sound error projection is identified as future work. Splitting linear basis functions requires introducing asymmetric basis functions, complicating the implementation. Non-negative constraint is enforced by projection, which may not be optimal for all basis function types (e.g., wavelets). When to Use: Reconstructing thin smoke and flames volumetrically from synchronized multi-video recordings. Scenes where memory is a constraint for high-resolution multi-camera setups. Dynamic scenes requiring adaptive resolution. When Not to Use: When computational speed is more critical than memory usage or resolution. When the scene does not benefit from adaptive resolution (e.g., uniformly dense volumes). Origin: The method was presented by Ivo Ihrke and Marcus Magnor from the Max-Planck-Institut für Informatik, Saarbrücken, Germany. It was published in 2005 in the Eurographics proceedings. History and Development: The method builds upon a basic computerized tomography (CT) technique presented in [IM04] (Ihrke and Magnor, 2004), which used an algebraic formulation for fire reconstruction. The adaptive grid approach was developed to overcome the memory limitations of uniform grids and to improve reconstruction quality for dynamic phenomena. Future work mentioned in the source includes deriving a mathematically sound error projection, using wavelet bases, and modeling occluding objects in flames and smoke. Usage: Used for reconstructing dynamic volumetric models of flames and thin smoke from multi-camera video sequences. Applicable to other tomography problems, such as real X-ray data, as suggested by the authors. Adaptive Grid Optical Tomography, https://core.ac.uk/works/26024869, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Matrix-Free PCG Solver
head: Implicit normal operator PCG, Matrix-Free PCG, Triangle-Structured Matrix-Free PCG Solver, Vertex-Block Preconditioned PCG
body: The Matrix-Free PCG Solver is a method for solving the global normal system Hx=g arising in closed-form radiance-field optimization. It evaluates the matrix-vector product Hu directly from rasterization records without constructing the global observation or normal matrices H. Unlike factorization-based solvers that explicitly assemble and decompose the normal matrix, this variant maintains smaller GPU memory by never materializing A and H. Inputs: Set of calibrated RGB images \{Ik\}{k=1}^K. Rasterization records R containing, for each valid pixel p{k,r} in view k: triangle vertex indices \{i{s,k,r}\}{s=0}^2, observation vectors \{\phi{s,k,r}\}{s=0}^2 (SH basis evaluations at the pixel), and weight w{k,r} (grazing-angle down-weighting). Global SH regularizer \Lambda, composed of vertex blocks \Lambdai \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times q} for each vertex i. Tolerance \delta: Prescribed relative residual tolerance for PCG termination. T{max}: Maximum iteration count for PCG (typically 300). Outputs: Estimated appearance coefficients X^ \in \mathbb{R}^{q Nv \times 3}, where Nv is the number of vertices and q is the SH dimension per channel. Vertex Blocks: The solution vector X and right-hand side G are partitioned by vertex. Gi \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times 3} stores the accumulated RHS for vertex i. Preconditioner Blocks: Pi \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times q} stores the diagonal block of the normal matrix for vertex i. Cholesky Factors: Li \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times q} such that Pi = Li Li^\top. PCG Vectors: X^{(\tau)} (solution), r (residual), p (search direction), z (preconditioned residual), h (normal product result). 1. Construct the right-hand side G and the vertex-block preconditioner P. 2. Initialize Gi = 0 for all vertices i=1 \dots Nv. 3. Initialize Pi = \Lambdai for all vertices i=1 \dots Nv. 4. For each view k = 1 \dots K and each valid pixel p{k,r}: 5. For each vertex s \in \{0, 1, 2\} of the covering triangle: 6. Update RHS: G{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow G{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} Ik(p{k,r})^\top. 7. Update Preconditioner: P{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow P{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \phi{s,k,r}^\top. 8. Compute Cholesky factor Li such that Pi = Li Li^\top. 9. Evaluate the matrix-vector product h = Hu without forming H. 10. Update: h{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow h{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \left( \sum{t=0}^2 \phi{t,k,r}^\top u{i{t,k,r}} \right). 11. Solve H X^{(\tau)} = G^{(\tau)} using Preconditioned Conjugate Gradients. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TriangleSetup(R, K, Nv, q, Lambda): G = [zeros(q, 3) for in range(Nv)] P = [copy(Lambda[i]) for i in range(Nv)] for k in range(K): for pkr in R[k]: for s in range(3): i = pkr.vertexindices[s] w = pkr.weight phi = pkr.observationvectors[s] Ival = pkr.imagevalue G[i] += w phi Ival.T P[i] += w phi phi.T L = [] for i in range(Nv): L.append(cholesky(P[i])) return G, L def TriangleNormal(u, R, K, Nv, q, Lambda): h = [copy(Lambda[i] @ u[i]) for i in range(Nv)] for k in range(K): for pkr in R[k]: for s in range(3): i = pkr.vertexindices[s] w = pkr.weight phis = pkr.observationvectors[s] inner = sum(phit.T @ u[pkr.vertexindices[t]] for t in range(3)) h[i] += w phis inner return h def PCGLoop(G, L, R, K, Nv, q, Lambda, delta, Tmax): X = [zeros(q, 3) for in range(Nv)] for tau in range(3): g = [G[i][tau] for i in range(Nv)] r = copy(g) eta = sum(dot(v, v) for v in r) z = solvepreconditioner(L, r) p = copy(z) sigma = dot(r, z) for t in range(1, Tmax + 1): h = TriangleNormal(p, R, K, Nv, q, Lambda) alpha = sigma / dot(p, h) for i in range(Nv): X[i][tau] += alpha p[i] for i in range(Nv): r[i] -= alpha h[i] if sum(dot(v, v) for v in r) <= delta eta: break z = solvepreconditioner(L, r) sigmanew = dot(r, z) beta = sigmanew / sigma for i in range(Nv): p[i] = z[i] + beta p[i] sigma = sigmanew return X RHS Accumulation: G{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow G{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} Ik(p{k,r})^\top. Preconditioner Accumulation: P{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow P{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \phi{s,k,r}^\top. Cholesky Decomposition: Pi = Li Li^\top. Regularization Term: hi \leftarrow \Lambdai ui. Pixel Contribution to Normal Product: h{i{s,k,r}} \leftarrow h{i{s,k,r}} + w{k,r} \phi{s,k,r} \left( \sum{t=0}^2 \phi{t,k,r}^\top u{i{t,k,r}} \right). Termination Condition: \sum{i=1}^{Nv} \|Gi^{(\tau)} - Hi Xi^{(\tau)}\|2^2 \le \delta \sum{i=1}^{Nv} \|Gi^{(\tau)}\|2^2. \delta: Relative residual tolerance. Tighter tolerances reduce final residual error but require more iterations. T{max}: Maximum iterations. Set to 300 in evaluations to prevent infinite loops on ill-conditioned systems. Ill-conditioning: Without adaptive SH regularization, weakly supported SH components cause ill-conditioning, making the unregularized system difficult to solve within T{max} iterations. Memory: The method processes views sequentially during matrix-free evaluation, so peak memory does not grow with the number of views K. Memory Complexity: M{GPU} = O(Nv q + HW q). Peak memory depends on vertices and image resolution, not the number of views K. Computational Complexity: Setup: O(KHWq^2 + Nv q^3). Per Iteration: O(KHWq + Nv q^2). Total solve time grows linearly with K. Strengths: Maintains smaller GPU memory than factorization-based solvers by never materializing A and H. The vertex-block preconditioner preserves coupling among all SH coefficients of the same vertex, improving numerical efficiency over scalar Jacobi preconditioners. Limitations: Requires T{max} iterations; convergence depends on the conditioning provided by adaptive SH regularization. Accuracy: At tight stopping tolerances, the residual MAE approaches that of the explicitly assembled factorization-based solver, confirming high numerical accuracy. The Matrix-Free PCG Solver was introduced in CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors. It addresses the computational and memory costs of explicitly constructing the global normal matrix H for large-scale scenes. The method exploits the three-vertex support of each pixel to evaluate the normal operator directly from rasterization records. CF-Splat: Closed-Form Triangle Splatting with Mesh Priors, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22108, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: CGLS with Non-Negativity Projection
head: CGLS with projection, Conjugate Gradient Least Squares (CGLS) with Non-Negativity Projection, regularized conjugate gradient
body: This method solves the linear least squares problem S a = p for the coefficient vector a by applying the Conjugate Gradient Least Squares (CGLS) algorithm. It is specifically designed for tomographic reconstruction where the physical quantity (density) must be non-negative. Unlike the standard CGLS Solver (Conjugate Gradient Least Squares) which operates in the full space, this variant projects the solution onto the non-negative subspace at every iteration to enforce physical validity, using the number of iterations as an implicit regularization parameter. Inputs: S: The forward projection matrix (basis function contributions to pixels). Columns correspond to basis functions; rows correspond to pixels. p: The vector of observed pixel values (e.g., from multi-view images). n: The number of basis functions (size of a). m: The number of pixels (size of p). Outputs: a: The reconstructed non-negative coefficient vector. Data Structures: a \in \mathbb{R}^n: Coefficient vector. p \in \mathbb{R}^m: Observation vector. r \in \mathbb{R}^m: Residual vector. d \in \mathbb{R}^n: Search direction vector. S: Matrix-free or sparse representation. Explicit computation of S^T S is avoided to save memory, as S^T S is typically dense. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set k = 0. a0 = \mathbf{0} r0 = p - S a0 = p d0 = S^T r0 2. Iteration Loop: For k = 1, 2, \dots: a. Compute the step size \alphak: \alphak = \frac{\|S^T r{k-1}\|2^2}{\|S d{k-1}\|2^2} b. Update the solution: ak = a{k-1} + \alphak d{k-1} c. Update the residual: rk = r{k-1} - \alphak S d{k-1} d. Compute the next step size \betak: \betak = \frac{\|S^T rk\|2^2}{\|S^T r{k-1}\|2^2} e. Update the search direction: dk = S^T rk + \betak d{k-1} f. Non-Negativity Projection: Set any negative entries of ak to zero: ak = \max(ak, 0) This ensures the density field remains non-negative, assuming non-negative basis functions are used. 3. Termination: The iteration stops when the L-curve criterion indicates the optimal trade-off between solution smoothness and data fidelity. Plot the curve of points (\log \|ak\|2, \log \|S ak - p\|2) for k=1, \dots, K{max}. Identify the point of highest curvature on this curve. The number of iterations k at this point serves as the regularization parameter. Parameters: Regularization: The number of iterations acts as the regularization parameter. No explicit regularization term (like Tikhonov) is added to the equations; instead, early stopping prevents overfitting and ghosting artifacts. Basis Functions: Non-negative basis functions (e.g., box functions) are required to ensure that non-negative coefficients yield a non-negative density field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting Artifacts: If the number of views is insufficient to constrain the solution, the full system may produce ghosting artifacts. Restricting the linear system to the visual hull (removing columns for basis functions outside the visual hull) mitigates this. Precision: The method avoids forming S^T S, which is crucial for numerical stability and memory efficiency when n is large. Projection Impact: Projecting ak to zero affects the subsequent residual and search direction calculations. The standard CGLS recurrence relations are applied after the projection in the described variant, or the projection is applied to the solution vector while the residual update uses the unprojected step. The source text implies the projection is applied to ak after the update step ak = a{k-1} + \alphak d{k-1}, but the residual rk and direction dk updates follow the standard CGLS formulas based on the current residual. Note: Standard CGLS does not include projection. The specific variant described applies projection to ak but continues the CG process on the normal equations. The exact interaction of projection with the conjugacy of d is a deviation from pure CGLS, but the source specifies this sequence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cglsnonnegative(S, p, maxiter=1000, tol=1e-6): """ Solves S @ a = p with non-negativity constraint using CGLS. S is a function or object that computes S @ v and S^T @ w. """ n = len(p) # Number of basis functions (size of a) # Note: S is m x n. p is m x 1. # Initialization a = [0.0] n r = list(p) # r0 = p - S @ a0 = p d = transposemultiply(S, r) # d0 = S^T @ r0 k = 0 # Store L-curve points for termination lcurvepoints = [] while k < maxiter: # Compute S @ d{k-1} Sd = multiply(S, d) # Compute norms normSTrprevsq = dotproduct(transposemultiply(S, r), transposemultiply(S, r)) # Wait, standard CGLS uses ||S^T r{k-1}||^2 / ||S d{k-1}||^2 for alpha # But we need S^T r{k-1} for beta later. # Let's follow the source formula strictly: # alphak = ||S^T r{k-1}||2^2 / ||S d{k-1}||2^2 STrprev = transposemultiply(S, r) normSTrprevsq = dotproduct(STrprev, STrprev) normSdsq = dotproduct(Sd, Sd) if normSdsq == 0: break alpha = normSTrprevsq / normSdsq # Update solution for i in range(n): a[i] = a[i] + alpha d[i] # Project to non-negative subspace for i in range(n): if a[i] < 0: a[i] = 0.0 # Update residual # rk = r{k-1} - alpha S @ d{k-1} for i in range(len(r)): r[i] = r[i] - alpha Sd[i] # Compute L-curve point norma = dotproduct(a, a) 0.5 normr = dotproduct(r, r) 0.5 if normr > 1e-12: lcurvepoints.append((norma, normr)) # Check termination via L-curve curvature (simplified check for implementation) # In practice, compute curvature for all points and pick max. # For this pseudocode, we assume an external evaluator or loop finishes. # Compute betak STrcurr = transposemultiply(S, r) normSTrcurrsq = dotproduct(STrcurr, STrcurr) if normSTrprevsq == 0: break beta = normSTrcurrsq / normSTrprevsq # Update search direction # dk = S^T rk + beta d{k-1} for i in range(n): d[i] = STrcurr[i] + beta d[i] k += 1 return a, lcurvepoints def multiply(S, v): # Computes S @ v pass def transposemultiply(S, w): # Computes S^T @ w pass def dotproduct(u, v): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(u, v)) Uses CG for compressive sensing; differs by focusing on sparsity-promoting norms rather than non-negativity projection in the linear solver loop. Solves symmetric systems; CGLS is preferred for rectangular S where S^T S is formed implicitly. Uses adaptive grids for efficiency; CGLS with projection is the solver used within such frameworks for the linear step. Preconditioned CG; CGLS is a specific variant of PCG without preconditioning, tailored for least squares. Time Complexity: Each iteration requires two matrix-vector multiplications (S d and S^T r) and several vector operations. Convergence depends on the condition number of S^T S. Memory Complexity: O(m + n) for storing vectors a, r, d, p. Avoids storing S^T S (O(n^2)), which is critical for large n. Strengths: Enforces physical non-negativity constraints directly during iteration; numerically stable for ill-conditioned systems; memory efficient. Limitations: Convergence can be slow for ill-conditioned problems; the projection step may disrupt the conjugacy of search directions, potentially affecting convergence rate compared to unconstrained CGLS. When to use: Tomographic reconstruction of density fields (e.g., flames, smoke) where negative values are physically meaningless and the system is underdetermined or noisy. The method originates from image-based tomographic reconstruction of flames, specifically addressing the need for non-negative density fields from multi-view video sequences. It builds on the CGLS variant developed by Hanke [Han98] to solve normal equations without explicit matrix formation. The L-curve criterion for termination is adapted from Åström [Å96] and Hanke [Han98]. The approach is particularly relevant for visual hull-restricted systems to reduce ghosting artifacts caused by insufficient view counts. name: Partially Learned Gradient Descent
head: Learned Gradient Descent, Learned iterative reconstruction, Partially learned gradient descent without regularizer, Unrolled Optimization with Learned Updates, Unrolled optimization
body: Partially Learned Gradient Descent (PLGD) is an iterative reconstruction method that unrolls a fixed number of optimization steps into a neural network. It initializes the reconstruction with a filtered backprojection (FBP) estimate and iteratively refines it by passing the current estimate, gradients, and a momentum memory state through a convolutional network to compute the next update. Unlike standard gradient descent which uses a fixed or manually tuned step size, PLGD learns the optimization dynamics (step size and momentum) directly from data, while retaining the explicit physical forward model (e.g., RayTransform) to ensure interpretability and robustness to distribution shifts. It differs from fully learned end-to-end CNNs by preserving the gradient structure of the inverse problem. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Noisy measurement data y (e.g., sinograms), initial estimate x0 (typically FBP of y), and the forward operator \mathcal{A} (and its adjoint \mathcal{A}^). Output: Reconstructed volume x. Parameters: Number of iterations n{iter}, number of memory channels n{memory}, network weights W1, b1, W2, b2, W3, b3. Data Structures: State Tensor x: Shape [batch, height, width, 1]. Memory Tensor s: Shape [batch, height, width, nmemory], initialized to zeros. Network Weights: W1: [3, 3, C{in}, 32], b1: [1, 1, 1, 32] W2: [3, 3, 32, 32], b2: [1, 1, 1, 32] W3: [3, 3, 32, n{memory} + 1], b3: [1, 1, 1, n{memory} + 1] Where C{in} is the number of input channels to the network (2 for "No Regularizer" variant, 3 for "With Regularizer" variant). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute x0 = \text{FBP}(y). Initialize s = 0 with shape [batch, height, width, nmemory]. Normalize the forward operator \mathcal{A} and its pseudoinverse by the operator norm \|\mathcal{A}\| for scale invariance: \mathcal{A}{norm} = \frac{1}{\|\mathcal{A}\|} \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{A}{pinv} = \mathcal{A}{pinv} \cdot \|\mathcal{A}\|. 2. Iteration Loop (i = 0 to n{iter}-1): Compute Gradients: Forward projection: y{pred} = \mathcal{A}(x). Data Gradient: For linear models: g{data} = \mathcal{A}^(y - y{pred}). For nonlinear models (e.g., CT with attenuation): y{pred} = \exp(-\mu{water} \cdot \mathcal{A}(x)), then g{data} = \mu{water} \cdot \mathcal{A}^(y - y{pred}). Regularization Gradient (optional, see variants): g{reg} = \mathcal{R}^(x), where \mathcal{R}^ is the adjoint of the regularizer (e.g., Laplacian: (\partial0^ \partial0 + \partial1^ \partial1)(x)). Concatenate Inputs: Form input tensor u by concatenating along the channel axis: No Regularizer: u = \text{concat}(x, g{data}, s). With Regularizer: u = \text{concat}(x, g{data}, g{reg}, s). Neural Network Update: Layer 1: h1 = \text{ReLU}(W1 u + b1). Layer 2: h2 = \text{ReLU}(W2 h1 + b2). Layer 3 (Linear): h3 = W3 h2 + b3. Split Output: Step size: dx = h3[:,:,:, 0:1]. New Memory: s{new} = \text{ReLU}(h3[:,:,:, 1:]). Update State: s \leftarrow s{new}. x \leftarrow x + dx. 3. Training (if learning weights): Loss: Mean Squared Error between final x and ground truth x{true}: \text{Loss} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{b=1}^{N} \sum{i,j} (x{b,i,j} - x{true,b,i,j})^2. Optimizer: RMSProp with inverse time decay. Starter learning rate: 10^{-3}. Decay rate: 1.0. Decay steps: 500. Staircase: True. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partiallylearnedgradientdescent(x0, y, operatoradjoint, operatorforward, niter, nmemory, useregularizer=False, muwater=0.02, operatornorm=1.0, w1=None, b1=None, w2=None, b2=None, w3=None, b3=None): """ Implements Partially Learned Gradient Descent. Args: x0: Initial estimate tensor [batch, H, W, 1] y: Measurement tensor [batch, Hsin, Wsin, 1] operatoradjoint: Function computing A^(residual) operatorforward: Function computing A(x) niter: Number of unrolled iterations nmemory: Number of memory channels useregularizer: Boolean, whether to include regularization gradient in input muwater: Attenuation coefficient for nonlinear forward model operatornorm: Norm of the forward operator for scaling w1, b1, w2, b2, w3, b3: Convolutional weights and biases Returns: x: Final reconstruction tensor """ import numpy as np # Initialize memory state s to zeros batchsize = x0.shape[0] H, W = x0.shape[1], x0.shape[2] s = np.zeros((batchsize, H, W, nmemory)) x = x0.copy() # Ensure weights are provided if w1 is None: raise ValueError("Weights must be provided or initialized.") for i in range(niter): # 1. Compute forward projection ypred = operatorforward(x) / operatornorm # 2. Compute data gradient # Nonlinear model: ypred = exp(-muwater A(x)) # Residual: y - ypred # Gradient: muwater A^(y - ypred) residual = y - np.exp(-muwater ypred) gradx = operatoradjoint(residual) muwater # 3. Compute regularization gradient (if enabled) if useregularizer: gradreg = computelaplacianadjoint(x) updateinput = np.concatenate([x, gradx, gradreg, s], axis=-1) else: updateinput = np.concatenate([x, gradx, s], axis=-1) # 4. Neural Network Layers h1 = np.maximum(0, conv2d(updateinput, w1) + b1) h2 = np.maximum(0, conv2d(h1, w2) + b2) h3 = conv2d(h2, w3) + b3 # 5. Split output dx = h3[:,:,:, 0:1] snew = np.maximum(0, h3[:,:,:, 1:]) # 6. Update states s = snew x = x + dx return x def conv2d(x, W, stride=(1, 1)): """Standard 2D convolution with SAME padding.""" # x: [B, H, W, Cin], W: [kh, kw, Cin, Cout] # Returns: [B, H, W, Cout] B, H, W, Cin = x.shape kh, kw,, Cout = W.shape out = np.zeros((B, H, W, Cout)) for b in range(B): for cout in range(Cout): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): hstart = max(0, h - kh // 2) hend = min(H, h + (kh + 1) // 2) wstart = max(0, w - kw // 2) wend = min(W, w + (kw + 1) // 2) patch = x[b, hstart:hend, wstart:wend,:] out[b, h, w, cout] = np.sum(patch W[:,:,:, cout]) return out def computelaplacianadjoint(x): """ Computes the adjoint of the Laplacian operator: (partial0.adjoint partial0 + partial1.adjoint partial1)(x) Implemented as a discrete convolution kernel. """ # Kernel for 2D Laplacian adjoint (which is the Laplacian itself for symmetric operators) # Standard 5-point stencil: # 0 -1 0 # -1 4 -1 # 0 -1 0 kernel = np.array([[[[0, -1, 0], [-1, 4, -1], [0, -1, 0]]]]) # Expand kernel for batch/channel dimensions if necessary # Assuming x is [B, H, W, 1], kernel should be [3, 3, 1, 1] kernelexpanded = np.expanddims(kernel, axis=-1) return conv2d(x, kernelexpanded) Parameters: n{memory}: Number of memory channels. Typical value: 5. n{iter}: Number of unrolled iterations. Typical value: 10. n{angles}: Number of projection angles. Typical value: 30. \mu{water}: Attenuation coefficient. Typical value: 0.02. photons{per\pixel}: For Poisson noise simulation. Typical value: 10,000. \epsilon: Small constant for log/noise. Value: 1/photons{per\pixel}. Noise level: 5% of mean absolute data value. Pitfalls: Nonlinear Saturation: The exponential function in the nonlinear forward model can saturate if the input is not scaled correctly or if \mu{water} is incorrect. Ensure proper scaling of the forward projection before applying exp. Momentum Sign: The memory state s is updated using ReLU, ensuring it remains non-negative. This prevents oscillatory behavior from negative momentum values. Operator Norm: Failure to normalize the operator by its norm can lead to scale-dependent convergence issues. The operator and pseudoinverse must be scaled by \|\mathcal{A}\| and 1/\|\mathcal{A}\| respectively. Includes a Tikhonov-like regularization term (adjoint of partial derivatives) in the network input concatenation. Input channels are n{memory} + 3 (estimate, data gradient, regularization gradient, memory). Weights W1 shape: [3, 3, nmemory + 3, 32]. A technique to reuse samples from the previous gradient-descent iteration at the current iteration by merging reservoirs from current and previous iterations, treating different iterations as different frames. Handles sign changes by reusing both positive and negative samples for both reservoirs. M{cap} is typically 32 for base color, 16 otherwise. A recursive inference step to refine noisy primitive positions by updating offsets \Delta \mui based on previous estimation \Delta \mu{prev}. Update rule: \Delta \mui^k = \text{Tanh}(\mathcal{D}{pos}(\mathbf{f}i)) \cdot v{size}, where \mathbf{f}i = \mathcal{F}(\mui^{init} + \Delta \mui^{k-1}). Stabilizes at a stationary point. On Waymo dataset, first inference increases PSNR by ~0.46 dB, subsequent updates maintain stable PSNR of 23.78 dB. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of unrolled iterations n{iter}. Each iteration involves one forward projection, one adjoint projection, and a small convolutional network pass. Memory Complexity: Proportional to n{memory} channels for the state tensor s, plus the memory for the convolutional weights. Performance: Outperforms standard gradient descent and FBP in terms of reconstruction quality (PSNR/SSIM) on medical imaging and phantom data. Strengths: Retains physical model interpretability; learns adaptive step sizes and momentum; robust to noise. Limitations: Requires training data to learn the network weights; inference speed depends on n{iter} and network depth; sensitive to operator norm scaling. When to use: When a physics-based model is available but standard optimization converges slowly or gets stuck in local minima, and end-to-end learning is undesirable due to lack of interpretability. Partially Learned Gradient Descent originates from the field of learned iterative reconstruction for medical imaging and tomography. It was developed to bridge the gap between model-based iterative reconstruction (which is interpretable but slow/hard to tune) and end-to-end deep learning (which is fast but lacks physical guarantees). The method unrolls the optimization steps of gradient descent into a neural network, allowing the network to learn the update rule (step size and momentum) while keeping the data fidelity term fixed. It is implemented in the learnedgradienttomography repository. adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, https://github.com/adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Parameter-space ReSTIR for Differentiable and Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3588432.3591512, fetched 2026-10-27 EVolSplat: Efficient Volume-based Gaussian Splatting for Urban View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR52734.2025.01054, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Velocity Reconstruction (VelRecon)
head: VelRecon
body: Velocity Reconstruction (VelRecon) is an optimization-based method for estimating 3D velocity fields from temporal sequences of volumetric density fields. Unlike tracer-based techniques (e.g., tomographic PIV) that require specialized hardware and physical tracers, VelRecon is a tracer-free approach that infers motion directly from captured video data by solving a constrained primal-dual optimization problem. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric density fields at two consecutive time steps, \rho{t-2} and \rho{t-1}. Output: Estimated velocity field u{t-1} at time step t-1. Data Structures: The method operates on voxel grids representing the density and velocity fields. Exact bit-packing or memory layout details are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: VelRecon solves the velocity estimation problem using a fast primal-dual approach. The optimization is governed by Equations (11)–(13) as constraints and solved via Equations (14)–(16). The iterative procedure is as follows: 1. Initialize iteration loop for k from 0 to \text{maxIter}. 2. Update the velocity estimate u{t-1}^{k+1} using the proximal operator of the constraint function g, a scaling parameter \gamma, and an auxiliary variable Xk. Formula: u{t-1}^{k+1} = \text{prox}{\gamma g} (u{t-1}^k - \gamma Xk). 3. Update the auxiliary variable Y{k+1} using a momentum term \theta and the difference between the current and previous velocity estimates. Formula: Y{k+1} = u{t-1}^{k+1} + \theta (u{t-1}^{k+1} - u{t-1}^k). 4. Compute the residual r{k+1} as the difference between the current and previous velocity estimates. Formula: r{k+1} = u{t-1}^{k+1} - u{t-1}^k. 5. Update the error threshold e by adding 3 times the absolute value of the new residual to the previous error. Formula: e{k+1} = ek + 3 |r{k+1}|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zeroslike(arr): # Returns an array of zeros with the same shape as arr return [[0.0 for in range(len(row))] for row in arr] def proximaloperatorg(x, gamma): # Computes prox{gammag}(x) enforcing physical constraints from # Exact formulation not provided in sources return x def VelRecon(rhotminus2, rhotminus1, maxiter, gamma, theta): uprev = zeroslike(rhotminus1) X = zeroslike(rhotminus1) e = 0.0 for k in range(maxiter): # Step 2: Update velocity estimate ucurr = proximaloperatorg(uprev - gamma X, gamma) # Step 3: Update auxiliary variable with momentum Y = ucurr + theta (ucurr - uprev) # Step 4: Compute residual r = ucurr - uprev # Step 5: Update error threshold e = e + 3.0 abs(r) # Update for next iteration uprev = ucurr # Note: Dual variable X update rule is not specified in the provided notes return ucurr Parameters: \gamma: Scaling parameter for the proximal operator. Value not given in sources. \theta: Momentum term. Value not given in sources. \text{maxIter}: Maximum number of iterations. Value not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise if the proximal operator is not well-conditioned. Boundary conditions for the velocity field are not explicitly detailed in the sources. This variant recovers the roughness texture of a metallic plate from a single reference image using noisy gradients. It employs 16 samples per pixel for the primal update and 1 sample per pixel for the gradient update. The method uses Adam optimization with hyperparameters \alpha = 0.01 and \beta1 = 0.2. Time and Memory Complexity: The method uses a fast primal-dual approach, suggesting linear or near-linear complexity with respect to the number of voxels per iteration. Memory complexity is proportional to the storage of density fields, velocity fields, and auxiliary variables. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics (FPS, accuracy) are not provided in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: The method is tracer-free and does not require specialized hardware or complex camera setups. It couples density and velocity reconstruction in a physics-constrained manner for robustness. Solving the optimization problem at each step may be computationally intensive compared to direct methods. The accuracy relies on the quality of the input density fields. When to Use: Use when estimating fluid motion from monocular video without access to tracer particles or specialized PIV hardware. Origin: The method is described in the context of physics-based differentiable rendering for fluid modeling. It is part of a coupled density and velocity estimation framework where velocity reconstruction is called to estimate velocity fields from previous density fields to perform advection. History and Development: The approach contrasts with traditional tracer-based methods like tomographic PIV, synthetic aperture PIV, and structured-light PIV, which require careful particle choice and complex setups. VelRecon represents a tracer-free alternative leveraging differentiable rendering and optimization. Usage: Used in differentiable rendering frameworks for fluid simulation and reconstruction from monocular video.
