name: Reparameterized Stochastic Gradient Descent
head: Reparameterized SGD, Reparameterized Stochastic Gradient Descent for Parameter Optimization
body: Reparameterized Stochastic Gradient Descent (Reparam-SGD) is an optimization technique designed to find altered scattering parameters (g, \sigmas) that minimize the error between a rendered image and a target image. It addresses the problem of SGD getting trapped in local minima with small gradients caused by low-frequency lighting, which leads to solutions that generalize poorly to high-frequency lighting. It sets itself apart from standard SGD by reparameterizing the search space to regularize the error surface and using sequential 1D searches to escape ill-conditioned regions. Inputs: Target image I0. Initial guess for scattering parameters (g, \sigmas). Error function d(g, \sigmas) defined in the source (Eq. 21). Outputs: Optimized scattering parameters (g^, \sigmas^). Data Structures: Parameters: g (anisotropy factor), \sigmas (scattering coefficient). Reparameterized variable: \tilde{\sigma}s (reduced scattering coefficient). Formulas: The reparameterization replaces the horizontal axis with the reduced scattering coefficient: \tilde{\sigma}s:= (1 - g)\sigmas This ensures both axes (g and \tilde{\sigma}s) have the same units and regularizes the error surface. Steps: 1. Reparameterize: Transform the search space from (g, \sigmas) to (g, \tilde{\sigma}s) using the formula above. 2. First 1D Search: Fix \sigmas and perform a one-dimensional SGD search to find \tilde{\sigma}s that minimizes the error d. This step selects an equivalence class based on the order-1 similarity relation. 3. Second 1D Search: Keep the found \tilde{\sigma}s fixed and perform another one-dimensional SGD search to find the best \sigmas within the selected equivalence class. 4. Result: The pair (g, \sigmas) derived from the second step is the solution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterizedsgd(targetimage, initialg, initialsigmas, learningrate, numiterations): currentg = initialg currentsigmas = initialsigmas currenttildesigmas = (1 - currentg) currentsigmas # Step 2: First 1D Search - Optimize tildesigmas while fixing sigmas sigmasfixed = currentsigmas for in range(numiterations): # Gradient w.r.t tildesigmas is estimated via Monte Carlo simulation gradtildesigmas = 0.0 # Monte Carlo gradient estimation not provided in source currenttildesigmas -= learningrate gradtildesigmas currentg = 1.0 - currenttildesigmas / sigmasfixed # Step 3: Second 1D Search - Optimize sigmas while keeping tildesigmas fixed tildesigmasfixed = currenttildesigmas for in range(numiterations): # Gradient w.r.t sigmas is estimated via Monte Carlo simulation gradsigmas = 0.0 # Monte Carlo gradient estimation not provided in source currentsigmas -= learningrate gradsigmas currentg = 1.0 - tildesigmasfixed / currentsigmas if currentsigmas <= 0: currentsigmas = 1e-6 return currentg, currentsigmas Parameters: Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Number of iterations: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low-frequency lighting: Creates large regions where the error function d(g, \sigmas) is close to zero with very small gradients, dominated by Monte Carlo or measurement noise, trapping SGD. Local Minima: Solutions found in low-error regions under low-frequency lighting generalize poorly to high-frequency lighting. Physical Validity: Parameters g and \sigmas must remain within physical bounds (\sigmas > 0, g \in [-1, 1]). A reparameterization technique for optimizing translucent material properties that resolves ambiguities caused by similarity equivalence classes. It sets itself apart from standard gradient descent by warping the non-linear parameter space to separate indistinguishable parameter sets, thereby preventing the optimization from stalling in ill-conditioned regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method finds solutions that generalize better to high-frequency lighting compared to standard SGD, which gets trapped in local minima under low-frequency lighting. Strengths: Regularizes the error surface; avoids local minima caused by low-frequency lighting; improves generalization to high-frequency lighting. Limitations: Relies on Monte Carlo simulations for gradients, which can be noisy. When to use: When optimizing scattering parameters (g, \sigmas) for translucent materials, especially under low-frequency lighting conditions where standard SGD fails to generalize. Origin: The method is described in the paper "High-order similarity relations in radiative transfer". History: The paper discusses the application of forward rendering for optically dense and forward-scattering materials. Usage: Used for inverse rendering of translucent materials, specifically optimizing scattering parameters. name: Similarity-Based Inverse Rendering
head: Inverse Rendering Reparameterization
body: Similarity-Based Inverse Rendering is a reparameterization technique for optimizing translucent material properties that resolves ambiguities caused by similarity equivalence classes. It sets itself apart from standard gradient descent by warping the non-linear parameter space to separate indistinguishable parameter sets, thereby preventing the optimization from stalling in ill-conditioned regions. Inputs: Target image I{\text{target}}, initial material parameters \theta0 = (g, \sigmas), forward rendering function R(\theta). Outputs: Optimized material parameters \theta^ that minimize the error between rendered and target images. Data Structures: Parameter vector \theta storing scattering properties. Warped parameter vector \phi representing transformed search space coordinates. Exact layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Method: 1. Identify Ambiguity Locations: Use similarity theory to determine where in the parameter space equivalence classes exist. 2. Apply Non-Linear Warp: Transform the original parameters \theta into a warped space \phi using a non-linear mapping W. 3. Gradient Descent in Warped Space: Run gradient descent optimization in the warped space to recover material properties. Formulas: The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the warp function W or the error metric. Parameters: Typical values for the scattering parameters g and \sigmas are not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Inverse rendering is ill-conditioned because different parameters in the same equivalence class produce very similar appearances, creating ambiguities that stall standard optimization. Large Steps reparameterization is a gradient preconditioning technique for inverse rendering of geometry that handles sparse silhouette gradients and prevents mesh topology errors such as flipped triangles. It achieves fast convergence by preconditioning the bias of gradient steps toward smooth solutions without enforcing smoothness in the final result. It sets itself apart from standard optimizers by treating the optimization as a spatiotemporal process using Laplacian smoothing and infinity-norm filtering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Greatly improves the efficiency of gradient descent algorithms by resolving ambiguities that stall standard optimization. Limitations: Described as a "proof-of-concept," suggesting it may not be a general-purpose solver without specific derivation of similarity relations for the material class. When to use: When optimizing translucent materials where similarity equivalence classes are known or can be derived, and standard gradient descent fails to converge due to parameter ambiguity. The method originates from the work on high-order similarity relations in radiative transfer. It was proposed as a solution to the difficulty of inverse rendering of translucent media, where the search space is high-dimensional and the presence of equivalence classes makes the problem ill-conditioned. The authors note that forward rendering is their main application, but this approach has the potential to benefit a wide range of future applications in simulating and acquiring volume-based appearance. name: Large Steps reparameterization
head: Nicolet et al. 2021 method, Nicolet et al. Large Steps, Shape Reconstruction with Large Steps
body:
Large Steps reparameterization is a gradient preconditioning technique for inverse rendering of geometry that handles sparse silhouette gradients and prevents flipped triangles. It achieves fast convergence by preconditioning the bias of gradient steps toward smooth solutions without enforcing smoothness in the final result. It sets itself apart from standard optimizers by treating optimization as a spatiotemporal process that applies Laplacian smoothing and infinity-norm filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current vertex positions x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N}, Laplacian matrix L \in \mathbb{R}^{3N 	imes 3N}, hyperparameter \lambda > 0, and loss gradient 
ablax f. Output: Updated vertex positions x. Data Structures: Reparameterized Variable (u): u \in \mathbb{R}^{3N}, defined as u = (I + \lambda L)x. Optimizer State (mu, vu): First and second moment estimates for u, initialized to zero vectors of size 3N. Parameters: \lambda: Controls the strength of regularization introduced by the Laplacian matrix. \alpha,  eta1,  eta2, \epsilon: Standard Adam hyperparameters for learning rate, decay rates, and numerical stability. Steps: 1. Reparameterization: Compute the transformed variable u from the current geometry x: u = (I + \lambda L)x. 2. Gradient Transformation: Compute the gradient with respect to u using the chain rule: 
ablau f = (I + \lambda L)^{-1} 
ablax f. 3. UniformAdam Update: Perform an update on u using the UniformAdam variant of Adam. 4. Inverse Reparameterization: Convert the updated u back to the physical space x: x = (I + \lambda L)^{-1} u. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvelinearsystem(A, b): # Standard linear algebra routine to solve A y = b pass def largestepsupdate(x, L, lambdareg, gradx, mu, vu, alpha, beta1, beta2, epsilon, t): # 1. Reparameterization: u = (I + lambda L) x I = identitymatrix(L.shape[0]) A = I + lambdareg L u = A @ x # 2. Gradient transformation: gradu = (I + lambda L)^-1 gradx gradu = solvelinearsystem(A, gradx) # 3. UniformAdam update on u mu = beta1 mu + (1 - beta1) gradu vu = beta2 vu + (1 - beta2) (gradu 2) bias1 = 1 - beta1 t bias2 = 1 - beta2 t mhat = mu / bias1 vhat = vu / bias2 # UniformAdam: replace element-wise division by vhat with scalar infinity norm vinf = max(vhat) deltau = -alpha mhat / ((vinf 0.5) + epsilon) u = u + deltau # 4. Inverse reparameterization: x = (I + lambda L)^-1 u x = solvelinearsystem(A, u) return x, mu, vu Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse silhouette gradients cause local vertex perturbations that quickly lead to flipped triangles and tangled meshes. The matrix (I + \lambda L) requires \lambda > 0 and a positive semi-definite L to guarantee invertibility. Implementations must adjust \lambda and the step size when switching differentiable rendering backends. Time Complexity: Dominated by two linear system solves per step. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of vertices for storing L and optimizer states. Strengths: Prevents mesh topology errors and enables higher learning rates. Limitations: Requires Laplacian computation and careful hyperparameter tuning. When to use: Shape reconstruction in inverse rendering where mesh topology preservation is critical and gradients are sparse. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and iterative linear solves are too slow. The Large Steps reparameterization was introduced by Nicolet et al. in 2021 to stabilize gradient-based mesh reconstruction. Subsequent implementations adapt the method for different differentiable rendering engines, requiring hyperparameter adjustments. name: Newton's Method
head: Newton-Raphson method, Newton-Raphson method for inverse rays, Root Finding Based Algorithm
body: Newton's Method is a second-order optimization algorithm derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function. It solves for the root of the gradient (where the derivative is zero) to find local minima or maxima, offering quadratic convergence for well-behaved functions. Unlike Gradient Descent Solver, which uses only first-order gradient information and a fixed or adaptive step size, Newton's Method incorporates the Hessian matrix to account for local curvature, allowing it to take larger, more informed steps toward the optimum. In the context of inverse volume rendering, it is also applied as a root-finding algorithm to solve for ray intersections with implicit geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current parameter vector \thetat, objective function f(\theta), gradient function g(\theta) = \nabla f(\theta), Hessian function H(\theta) = \nabla^2 f(\theta). Output: Updated parameter vector \theta{t+1}. Data Structures: \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n: Parameter vector. g \in \mathbb{R}^n: Gradient vector. H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}: Hessian matrix. v \in \mathbb{R}^n: Newton direction vector. \alpha \in \mathbb{R}: Step length scalar. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Gradient and Hessian: Evaluate the gradient g(\thetat) and the Hessian matrix H(\thetat) at the current point \thetat. 2. Check Positive Semi-Definiteness (PSD): Verify if H(\thetat) is positive semi-definite. If not, apply Hessian modification to ensure PSD, or use a trust region method. 3. Compute Newton Direction: Solve the linear system H(\thetat) v = -g(\thetat) for v. The update direction is v = -H^{-1}(\thetat)g(\thetat). Note: For root-finding applications (e.g., inverse rays), solve JF(xn)(x{n+1} - xn) = -F(xn) for the root approximation x{n+1}, where JF is the Jacobian of the residual function F. 4. Determine Step Length: In standard Newton's Method, a fixed step size \gamma is often used, or \alpha=1 is assumed if the quadratic approximation is valid. In Newton Conjugate Gradient, \alpha is derived analytically by minimizing the quadratic approximation along v: \alpha = - \frac{g(\thetat)^T v}{v^T H(\thetat) v}. 5. Apply Trust Region (Optional but Recommended): To prevent divergence if the Hessian is not well-conditioned, truncate the step: \alpha = \min(\alpha, \Delta \|v\|^{-1}), where \Delta is the trust region radius. 6. Update Parameters: \theta{t+1} = \thetat + \alpha v. Formulas: Second-Order Taylor Expansion: f(\theta) \approx f(\thetat) + g(\thetat)^T (\theta - \thetat) + \frac{1}{2} (\theta - \thetat)^T H(\thetat) (\theta - \thetat) Optimality Condition (Root of Gradient): \frac{d}{d\theta} f(\theta) = 0 \approx g(\thetat) + H(\thetat)(\theta - \thetat) Newton Direction: v = -H^{-1}(\thetat)g(\thetat) Update Rule: \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \gamma H^{-1}(\thetat)g(\thetat) Newton Conjugate Gradient Step Length: \alpha = - \frac{g(\theta)^T v}{v^T H(\theta) v} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def norm(v): return sum(x2 for x in v)0.5 def dot(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def ensurepsd(H): # Shift diagonal until positive semi-definite mineig = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).min() if mineig < 0: H = H + (-mineig + 1e-6) np.eye(len(H)) return H def solvelinearsystem(A, b): return np.linalg.solve(A, b) def hessvectorproduct(theta, v, grad, eps=1e-5): # Central difference approximation return (grad(theta + eps v) - grad(theta - eps v)) / (2 eps) def newtonmethod(theta, f, grad, hess, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6, trustradius=None): for t in range(maxiter): g = grad(theta) H = hess(theta) if norm(g) < tol: break H = ensurepsd(H) v = solvelinearsystem(H, -g) alpha = 1.0 if trustradius is not None: if norm(v) > 1e-12: alpha = min(alpha, trustradius / norm(v)) else: alpha = 0.0 theta = theta + alpha v return theta def newtonconjugategradient(theta, f, grad, hess, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): v = -grad(theta) r = v for t in range(maxiter): Hv = hessvectorproduct(theta, v, grad) g = grad(theta) numerator = -dot(g, v) denominator = dot(v, Hv) if abs(denominator) < 1e-12: break alpha = numerator / denominator theta = theta + alpha v rnew = r - alpha Hv if norm(rnew) < tol: break beta = dot(rnew, rnew) / dot(r, r) v = rnew + beta v r = rnew return theta Parameters: \gamma: Step size multiplier (often 1 in pure Newton, but used in damped variants). \Delta: Trust region radius. \epsilon: Perturbation magnitude for central-difference Hessian-vector product approximation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hessian Inversion Cost: Computing, storing, and inverting the full Hessian H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} is O(n^3) and requires O(n^2) memory, becoming a bottleneck in high-dimensional problems. Negative Definiteness: If the Hessian is not positive semi-definite, the Newton direction may point towards a maximum or saddle point, causing divergence. This is handled by Hessian modification (ensuring PSD) and trust region step truncation. Root Finding Failure: In inverse ray tracing, naive Newton-Raphson can fail if the starting point is not close to the root or if the Jacobian is singular. Quasi-Newton methods utilize second-order information for optimization by approximating the Hessian matrix using zero- or first-order information. Unlike Newton's Method, which requires explicit computation of the Hessian, these methods build an approximation iteratively. In the context of differentiable rendering, they are distinguished by their sensitivity to noise; while they can converge on smooth tasks, they often fail on noisy derivative estimations common in rendering without specific damping or line-search modifications. Naive Newton fails if the Hessian is not positive semi-definite (PSD), as negative eigenvalues can flip the gradient vector and cause divergence. This is handled by ensuring positive semi-definiteness via Hessian modification and step truncation to a trust region: \alpha = \min(\alpha, \Delta \|v\|^{-1}). For example, in a negated 2D Gaussian convolution, analytic Hessians can be computed and compared with estimates, with mean error within 1 \times 10^{-4} for 100 samples across the interval (-3,3)^2. An upgrade to Newton's method that solves for the Newton direction iteratively using conjugate directions and determines the step length scalar \alpha. It avoids explicit Hessian inversion by solving H(\theta)v = -g(\theta) iteratively. The direction v and residual r are initialized to the negative gradient (v0 = r0 = -g(\thetat)). The step length is derived from the Taylor expansion derivative set to zero: \alpha = - \frac{g^T(\theta)v}{v^T H(\theta)v}. The residual is updated as r{t+1} = rt - \alpha H(\thetat) vt, and the new direction is computed using the Fletcher-Reeves formula: \beta = \frac{r{t+1}^T r{t+1}}{rt^T rt} and v{t+1} = r{t+1} + \beta vt. Time Complexity: O(n^3) per iteration for standard Newton's Method due to Hessian inversion. Newton Conjugate Gradient reduces this to O(n^2) per iteration if Hessian-vector products are O(n), but requires multiple iterations to converge to the Newton direction. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) for storing the Hessian matrix. Convergence: Quadratic convergence near the optimum for well-behaved functions. Strengths: Fast convergence near the solution; accounts for curvature. Limitations: High computational cost for large n; sensitive to non-PSD Hessians; requires smooth, differentiable objective functions. When to Use: Small to medium-scale optimization problems where the Hessian is affordable to compute and invert; when high precision is required near the optimum. When Not to Use: Large-scale problems where Hessian storage is prohibitive. The method can also fail in certain situations, such as poor starting points or singular Jacobians. Newton's Method is one of the most-used second-order optimizers, derived from the second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function. It has been applied to several optimization tasks in vision and graphics. The Newton-Raphson method is also a standard method for finding approximations of the roots of functions, such as in inverse ray tracing for volume rendering. Hessian-vector product approximations, such as central differences, have been discussed by Pearlmutter and Werbos to avoid explicit Hessian computation. name: Quasi-Newton Methods (BFGS/LBFGS)
head: BFGS, BFGS/LBFGS Optimization, LBFGS
body: Quasi-Newton methods utilize second-order information for optimization by approximating the Hessian matrix using zero- or first-order information. Unlike Newton's Method, which requires explicit computation of the Hessian, these methods build an approximation iteratively. In differentiable rendering, they are distinguished by their sensitivity to noise; while they can converge on smooth tasks, they often fail on noisy derivative estimations common in rendering without specific damping or line-search modifications. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Objective function f(\theta), initial parameter vector \theta0, and iteration parameters. Output: Optimized parameter vector \theta^. Data Structures: \theta: Parameter vector of size d (problem sizes are typically large, e.g., neural network weights). B: d \times d matrix approximating the inverse Hessian. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set \theta0, B0 = I (identity matrix), and iteration counter k=0. 2. Gradient Evaluation: Compute the gradient gk = \nabla f(\thetak). 3. Search Direction: Compute search direction pk = -Bk gk. 4. Line Search: Determine step size \alphak satisfying Wolfe conditions (e.g., Armijo-Wolfe). Update \theta{k+1} = \thetak + \alphak pk. 5. Curvature Update: Compute difference vectors sk = \theta{k+1} - \thetak and yk = g{k+1} - gk. 6. Hessian Update: Update the approximation B{k+1} using the BFGS rank-2 update formula: B{k+1} = Bk + \frac{yk yk^T}{yk^T sk} - \frac{Bk sk sk^T Bk}{sk^T Bk sk} Note: If yk^T sk \leq 0, the update is skipped to maintain positive definiteness. 7. Iteration: Increment k. If convergence criteria are not met, return to Step 2. Parameters: Line search tolerance: Standard Wolfe conditions. Damping: Used in "Damped BFGS" to handle non-positive semi-definite (non-PSD) Hessians or noisy gradients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Derivatives: Vanilla BFGS, BFGS with Armijo-Wolfe line search, and LBFGS only converge for smooth tasks (e.g., the QUAD task) but fail on noisy derivative estimations typical in rendering. Non-PSD Hessians: Non-PSD Hessians are not necessarily a problem if the right combination of estimator and optimizer is used, as demonstrated in sphere's Phong BRDF optimization. Scale: Problem sizes are typically large (e.g., neural network weights) compared to the number of physical rendering parameters. Pseudocode (BFGS with Inverse Hessian Approximation): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def outer(a, b): return [[x y for y in b] for x in a] def matvec(M, v): return [sum(row[j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for row in M] def norm(v): return dot(v, v) 0.5 def identity(n): return [[1 if i == j else 0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] def bfgsupdate(B, s, y): sy = dot(s, y) if sy <= 1e-10: return B Bs = matvec(B, s) yBs = dot(y, Bs) term1 = outer(y, y) term2 = outer(Bs, Bs) return [[B[i][j] + (term1[i][j] / sy) - (term2[i][j] / yBs) for j in range(len(B))] for i in range(len(B))] def solvebfgs(f, gradf, theta0, maxiter=1000, tol=1e-6): d = len(theta0) theta = theta0[:] B = identity(d) for k in range(maxiter): g = gradf(theta) if norm(g) < tol: break p = matvec(B, g) p = [-x for x in p] # Sources specify Armijo-Wolfe line search, but do not provide implementation details. # A standard backtracking line search is used here as a placeholder. alpha = 1.0 while f(theta + [alpha x for x in p]) > f(theta) + 1e-4 alpha dot(g, p): alpha = 0.5 thetanew = [theta[i] + alpha p[i] for i in range(d)] s = [thetanew[i] - theta[i] for i in range(d)] gnew = gradf(thetanew) y = [gnew[i] - g[i] for i in range(d)] B = bfgsupdate(B, s, y) theta = thetanew return theta A variant of BFGS that modifies the update step to handle cases where the Hessian is not positive semi-definite or gradients are noisy. It was tested in differentiable rendering contexts but did not improve convergence over vanilla BFGS for tasks beyond the smooth QUAD task. A variant that uses adaptive finite differences to estimate gradients or Hessians within the BFGS framework. Like Damped BFGS, it was tested for noisy derivative estimation in rendering but failed to change convergence behavior for other tasks compared to standard methods. An optimization algorithm used to solve configuration selection objectives by approximating gradients and Hessians via least squares. It generates a search direction from these approximations and solves a system of linear equations to update variables. It is prone to producing unreasonable resource allocation on complex scenes due to poor initial assumption values and inherent approximation errors in the least-squares estimation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Convergence: Converges on smooth tasks like the QUAD task, but fails on noisy derivative estimations typical in rendering. Limitations: Highly sensitive to noise in gradient estimation; vanilla variants fail on noisy rendering derivatives without damping or specialized line searches. When to use: Smooth optimization problems where second-order information provides acceleration. When not to use: Noisy derivative estimation (e.g., stochastic rendering gradients) without damping or specialized line searches. Quasi-Newton methods, specifically the BFGS family, are well-established optimization algorithms. They were tested in the context of differentiable rendering to leverage second-order information while avoiding the explicit computation of the Hessian. The family includes vanilla BFGS, BFGS with Armijo-Wolfe line search, and LBFGS. Variants like Damped BFGS and Adaptive Finite Difference BFGS were also explored in this context. name: Inexact Line Search Optimization
head: Line Search
body: Inexact Line Search Optimization is an iterative method that adapts the step size in gradient descent to achieve a reduction in the objective function while ensuring sufficiently fast progress. It solves the problem of slow convergence in standard gradient descent by dynamically selecting a step size that guarantees improvement without requiring the computational expense of finding the exact minimum along the search direction. Unlike exact line search methods, which may suffer from convergence deterioration, this inexact strategy yields reasonable results and descends much faster. Inputs: xk: Current point (e.g., feature opacity values) at iteration k. dk: Descent direction at iteration k. f(\cdot): Objective function to minimize (e.g., visibility-weighted saliency error). M: Maximum iteration count for the line search. Outputs: \gammam: The chosen step size. x{k+1}: The updated point xk + \gammam dk. Data Structures: Integer counter m: Tracks the current power of 2 for the step size. Integer M: Upper bound for m. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize m = 0 and set M to the maximum iteration count. 2. Check the condition: f(xk + \gamma{m+1} dk) < f(xk + \gammam dk) where \gammam = 2^m. 3. If the condition is met AND m < M - 1: Increment m \leftarrow m + 1. Repeat step 2. 4. Otherwise (condition fails OR m = M - 1): Terminate the line search. Set the chosen step size to \gammam. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inexactlinesearch(xk, dk, f, M): """ Performs inexact line search to find step size gamma. Args: xk: Current point (vector). dk: Descent direction (vector). f: Objective function callable. M: Maximum iteration count. Returns: gamma: The chosen step size. """ m = 0 gammam = 1 # 2^0 while m < M - 1: gammanext = gammam 2 fcurrent = f(xk + gammam dk) fnext = f(xk + gammanext dk) if fnext < fcurrent: m = m + 1 gammam = gammanext else: break return gammam Parameters: M: Maximum iteration count. \gammam: Step size defined as 2^m. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the objective function evaluation is expensive, the overhead of multiple evaluations may outweigh the benefits of faster convergence. The method assumes the objective function allows for meaningful comparison between f(xk + \gamma{m+1} dk) and f(xk + \gammam dk). Parallel Inexact Line Search is a variant that evaluates the objective function at different candidate points in parallel along the line search direction to accelerate optimization on multi-core processors. It differs from the sequential version by always evaluating all candidate points and picking the one with the least objective function value, whereas the sequential version terminates early if the condition is not met. It is beneficial when the objective function evaluation is more expensive than the overhead of parallel processing, such as when computing visibility fields requires a pass of slice-based volume rendering. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate a list of M step sizes S = \{\gamma0, \gamma1,..., \gamma{M-1}\} where \gammam = 2^m. 2. Evaluate f(xk + \gammam dk) in parallel for each \gammam in S using multiple threads. 3. Find the index m of the minimum f(xk + \gammam dk), and \gammam is the chosen step size. Pitfalls: The number of threads should not exceed the number of processor cores to avoid performance impact from sharing cores. Parallel search is only beneficial when objective function evaluation is more expensive than thread overhead. Golden-Section Search is a gradient-free iterative optimization algorithm used to locate the minimum of a unimodal function by successively narrowing the search range. It is employed to efficiently search for optimal bandwidth parameters in Anisotropic Fourier Features Mapping, replacing computationally prohibitive brute-force grid searches. Unlike its siblings, it reduces the number of expensive network training runs from polynomial to logarithmic time by leveraging the golden ratio and requires no gradient calculations. Choose it when optimizing bandwidth parameters in neural implicit representations without gradient access. Golden-Section Search Time Complexity: The sequential version performs up to M evaluations of the objective function. The parallel version performs M evaluations simultaneously, reducing wall-clock time for the line search phase but increasing total computational work if thread overhead is significant. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Compared to standard gradient descent, line search takes many fewer iterations to converge to a desired target. It descends much faster than gradient descent. Strengths: Adapts step size to achieve reduction in objective function while making sufficiently fast progress. Avoids convergence deterioration associated with exact line search methods. Limitations: Requires multiple evaluations of the objective function per iteration. Parallel version has overhead from thread management. When to use: When objective function evaluation is expensive (e.g., involves volume rendering passes) and parallel hardware is available. When faster convergence than standard gradient descent is needed. When not to use: When objective function evaluation is cheap, making parallel overhead unjustified. When exact minimum is required (though inexact is preferred for stability). The method was introduced in the context of transfer function optimization for volume rendering, specifically for optimizing feature opacities based on a combined model of visibility and saliency. It was proposed to reduce the number of iterations required in optimization compared to standard gradient descent. The approach is based on the work of Vrahatis et al. [2000] and Zhou et al. [2006], citing advantages of inexact strategies over exact methods. name: Golden-Section Search
head: 2D Golden-Section Search, GSS for Bandwidth, GSS-based bandwidth searching scheme, Golden-Section Search (GSS) for Bandwidth, Golden-Section Search (GSS) for Bandwidth Selection, Linear GSS
body: Golden-Section Search (GSS) is a gradient-free iterative optimization algorithm used to locate the minimum of a unimodal function by successively narrowing the range of values inside which the minimum is known to exist. In the context of volume rendering and neural implicit representations, it is specifically employed to efficiently search for optimal bandwidth parameters in Anisotropic Fourier Features Mapping (AFFM), replacing computationally prohibitive brute-force grid searches. Unlike its siblings, it reduces the number of expensive network training runs from polynomial time to logarithmic time by leveraging the golden ratio to shrink the search interval, requiring no gradient calculations with respect to the bandwidth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An initial search interval [a, b] for 1D, or an initial search box [a1, b1] \times [a2, b2] for 2D, containing the optimal bandwidth(s). A cost function that returns the training loss or validation error for a given bandwidth, which requires a full network training run to evaluate. Output: The estimated optimal bandwidth \beta^ (or pair \beta^1, \beta^2) and the final search interval/box. Data Structures: 1D Case: Two scalar values a, b representing the current search interval bounds. Two scalar values x1, x2 representing the candidate points within the interval. 2D Case: Four scalar values a1, b1, a2, b2 representing the current search box bounds. Four candidate points forming a grid of 4 pairs. Constants: Golden ratio conjugate \phi = \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2} \approx 0.618. Complementary ratio 1-\phi \approx 0.382. Numbered Steps (1D Linear GSS): 1. Initialize the search interval [a, b]. 2. Calculate two candidate points: x1 = a + (1-\phi)(b-a) x2 = a + \phi(b-a) Note: x1 is at 0.382 and x2 is at 0.618 of the interval. 3. Evaluate the cost function at x1 and x2 by training the network with these bandwidths. 4. Compare the costs: If cost(x1) < cost(x2), the minimum lies in [a, x2]. Set b = x2 and x2 = x1. Recalculate x2 using the new interval. The old x1 is reused, saving one evaluation. If cost(x1) \ge cost(x2), the minimum lies in [x1, b]. Set a = x1 and x1 = x2. Recalculate x1 using the new interval. The old x2 is reused. 5. Repeat steps 3-4 until convergence or a fixed number of iterations is reached. Numbered Steps (2D GSS): 1. Initialize the search box [a1, b1] \times [a2, b2]. 2. Define the 1D split points for each dimension using \phi and 1-\phi. 3. Generate 4 candidate pairs by combining the split points of dimension 1 with those of dimension 2. 4. Evaluate the cost for all 4 candidates. 5. Identify the candidate C{best} with the lowest cost. 6. Shrink the search box. The new bounds for each dimension are determined by the coordinates of C{best} and the previous bounds, effectively reducing the box area by a factor of \phi^2 (approx 0.618^2). Specifically, if C{best} is at (x^1, x^2), the new interval for dimension 1 is determined by the subset of previous candidates that contained x^1, and similarly for dimension 2. 7. Repeat steps 2-6 until convergence. Formulas: 1D Interval Width: After k iterations, the width of the search interval is (0.618)^k. 1D Evaluations: The number of network trainings is k + 1. 2D Box Area: After k iterations, the parameter box area is 0.618^{2k}. 2D Evaluations: The number of network trainings is 3^k + 1. Parameters: Iterations: Empirically, 5 iterations are sufficient to achieve good practice convergence. Shrinkage Factor: 0.618 (golden ratio conjugate) for 1D; 0.618^2 for 2D area reduction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Unimodal Functions: GSS assumes the cost function is unimodal within the search interval. If the loss landscape has multiple local minima, GSS may converge to a suboptimal local minimum. Evaluation Cost: Each evaluation requires a full network training run, which is expensive. The algorithm's efficiency relies on minimizing these evaluations. Precision: The reuse of candidates relies on precise interval updates. Floating-point errors in interval boundary calculations can accumulate, though the logarithmic convergence rate mitigates this over the typical 5 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def goldensectionsearch1d(costfunc, a, b, maxiter=5): """ Performs 1D Golden-Section Search. costfunc: A function that takes a bandwidth beta and returns the training loss. a, b: Initial search interval [a, b]. maxiter: Maximum number of iterations. Returns: The estimated optimal bandwidth. """ phi = (math.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2.0 # ~0.618 invphi = 1.0 - phi # ~0.382 # Initialize candidates x1 = a + invphi (b - a) x2 = a + phi (b - a) # Evaluate initial candidates f1 = costfunc(x1) f2 = costfunc(x2) for in range(maxiter): if f1 < f2: # Minimum is in [a, x2] b = x2 x2 = x1 f2 = f1 x1 = a + invphi (b - a) f1 = costfunc(x1) else: # Minimum is in [x1, b] a = x1 x1 = x2 f1 = f2 x2 = a + phi (b - a) f2 = costfunc(x2) # Return the better of the two if f1 < f2: return x1 else: return x2 def goldensectionsearch2d(costfunc, a1, b1, a2, b2, maxiter=5): """ Performs 2D Golden-Section Search. costfunc: A function that takes a tuple (beta1, beta2) and returns the training loss. a1, b1: Initial search interval for dimension 1. a2, b2: Initial search interval for dimension 2. maxiter: Maximum number of iterations. Returns: The estimated optimal bandwidth tuple (beta1, beta2). """ phi = (math.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2.0 invphi = 1.0 - phi # Initial candidates for dimension 1 x11 = a1 + invphi (b1 - a1) x21 = a1 + phi (b1 - a1) # Initial candidates for dimension 2 x12 = a2 + invphi (b2 - a2) x22 = a2 + phi (b2 - a2) # Generate 4 candidates candidates = [ (x11, x12), (x11, x22), (x21, x12), (x21, x22) ] # Evaluate all 4 costs = [costfunc(c) for c in candidates] for in range(maxiter): # Find best candidate bestidx = costs.index(min(costs)) bestc = candidates[bestidx] # Shrink bounds based on best candidate (1D logic per dimension) if bestc[0] == x11: b1 = x21 x21 = x11 x11 = a1 + invphi (b1 - a1) else: a1 = x11 x11 = x21 x21 = a1 + phi (b1 - a1) if bestc[1] == x12: b2 = x22 x22 = x12 x12 = a2 + invphi (b2 - a2) else: a2 = x12 x12 = x22 x22 = a2 + phi (b2 - a2) # Regenerate candidates and evaluate only the new ones newcandidates = [(x11, x12), (x11, x22), (x21, x12), (x21, x22)] newcosts = [] for i, c in enumerate(newcandidates): if c == candidates[bestidx]: # Reuse best candidate from previous iteration newcosts.append(costs[bestidx]) else: newcosts.append(costfunc(c)) candidates = newcandidates costs = newcosts # Return the best candidate from the last iteration bestidx = costs.index(min(costs)) return candidates[bestidx] The 1D variant of the algorithm. It is chosen when a single bandwidth parameter needs to be optimized. It reduces the search space exponentially by the golden ratio. The extension to two dimensions. It is chosen when two bandwidth parameters (e.g., spatial and angular) need to be optimized simultaneously. It reduces the search box area by the square of the golden ratio per iteration. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of searches from polynomial time (in grid search) to logarithmic time. Specifically, for 1D, the interval width decreases as (0.618)^k. For 2D, the area decreases as 0.618^{2k}. Memory Complexity: Low. It only stores the current search interval/box and a few candidate points. Measured Performance: In a neural relighting task with the 'kneeling knight' imageset (253 reflectance images), 2D GSS provided a 7x speed-up over Grid search. Strengths: Gradient-free (avoids expensive gradient calculations w.r.t bandwidth), no need for initial point selection, saves function evaluations per iteration. Limitations: Assumes unimodality. Convergence is slower than Newton's method if gradients are available, but in this context, gradients are not available or too expensive. When to use: When optimizing bandwidth parameters for Fourier feature mappings in neural rendering, where each evaluation is a full network training. When not to use: When the cost function is not unimodal or when gradients are cheap and available. Golden-Section Search was introduced in the context of Anisotropic Fourier Features for Neural Image-Based Rendering and Relighting by the authors of. It was developed to address the computational overload of brute-force grid search for bandwidth selection in AFFM. The method leverages the mathematical properties of the golden ratio to efficiently narrow down the search space for optimal bandwidths in both spatial and angular domains. name: Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method
head: Incremental ART, Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method for Reflective Tomography, Online Learning for Reflective Tomography
body: The Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method is an online learning algorithm for reflective tomography that incrementally updates a voxel model \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N to minimize modeling error against a sequence of observed frames. It solves the global least-squares optimization problem by applying preconditioned gradient descent steps to individual data frames one at a time. It distinguishes itself from batch solvers by processing data sequentially (frame-driven) and using a specific preconditioner derived from the projection matrix structure to prioritize high-frequency spatial information (surfaces). Inputs: Training dataset: A set of S camera configurations \{Cs\}{s=1}^S and corresponding observed images \{gs\}{s=1}^S, where gs \in \mathbb{R}^{Ms} and Ms is the number of pixels in frame s. Voxel grid: Defined by a bounding box with corners a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3 and voxel side length h. Parameters: Learning rate \omega, regularization \sigma, inner solver tolerance, stopping criteria. Outputs: Updated voxel model \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N, where N is the number of voxels. Data Structures: \phi: Vector of size N, storing voxel values. Initialized to zero. gs: Vector of size Ms, storing pixel intensities for frame s. XC: Linear projection operator mapping \phi to image space. In implementation, this is handled via ray-tracing backprojection and projection steps. Formulas: The cost function J for a single occurrence (C, g) is defined as: J(\phi, C, g) = \frac{1}{2} (XC XC^ + \sigma I)^{-\frac{1}{2}} (XC \phi - g) where \sigma > 0 is a regularization parameter. The gradient of J with respect to \phi is: \frac{\partial J}{\partial \phi}(\phi, C, g) = XC^ (XC XC^ + \sigma I)^{-1} (XC \phi - g) The model update for iteration k, using frame sk, is: \phi^{(k+1)} = \phi^{(k)} - \omega \frac{\partial J}{\partial \phi}(\phi^{(k)}, C{sk}, g{sk}) where \omega > 0 is the learning rate. The global problem solved incrementally is: \inf{\phi \in \mathbb{R}^N} \sum{s=1}^S J(\phi, Cs, gs) Parameters: \omega: Relaxation parameter. Suggested value \omega = 0.5 for reflective tomography to prioritize high-frequency spatial information (surfaces). Standard ART uses smaller values like 0.05. \sigma: Regularization parameter. Chosen on the order of Lh, where L is the characteristic length of the box (e.g., diagonal L = \|b-a\|) and h is the voxel side length. Inner solver tolerance: For the conjugate gradient solver used to approximate the inverse terms, a relative residual tolerance of 1\% and a maximum bound of 10 iterations are used. Stopping criterion: Either a fixed number of cycles \kappa (e.g., \kappa=2) or a decay rate threshold \tau (e.g., \tau=5\%) on the RMSE between successive cycles, with a safety bound \kappa{max} (e.g., \kappa{max}=8). Ray ordering: To simulate random ordering, use a step p relatively prime to S: s{k+1} - 1 = (sk + p - 1) \pmod S, starting with s0 = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalpreconditionedgradientmethod(S, cameras, images, boxcorners, voxelsize, omega, sigma, kappamax, tauthreshold): """ S: Total number of training frames cameras: List of camera configurations Cs images: List of observed images gs boxcorners: Tuple (a, b) defining the bounding box voxelsize: h, side length of voxels omega: Learning rate sigma: Regularization parameter kappamax: Maximum number of cycles tauthreshold: Threshold for RMSE decay rate """ # 1. Initialize voxel model N = calculatevoxelcount(boxcorners, voxelsize) phi = zeros(N) # 2. Determine ray ordering step # Choose p relatively prime to S. A safe generic choice for implementation if not specified: # find smallest p > 1 such that gcd(p, S) == 1. If S=1, p=1. p = findrelativelyprimestep(S) currentframeindex = 0 # s0 = 1 implies index 0 in 0-based list, but formula uses 1-based indexing for sk # Formula: s{k+1} - 1 = (sk + p - 1) mod S. # Let idxk be 0-based index. sk = idxk + 1. # idx{k+1} + 1 - 1 = (idxk + 1 + p - 1 - 1) mod S ? # Source: s{k+1} - 1 = (sk + p - 1) mod S. # If sk is 1-based index, then sk - 1 is 0-based index. # Let idx = s - 1. # idx{k+1} = ( (idxk + 1) + p - 1 - 1) mod S ? Compute residual and gradient # Project model to image space: r = XC phi - g # Note: XC phi is computed via forward projection (ray tracing) # XC^ v is computed via backprojection # The term (XC XC^ + sigma I)^{-1} requires solving a linear system # Let v = XC phi - g # We need to solve (XC XC^ + sigma I) y = v for y # Then gradient = XC^ y v = forwardprojection(phi, C) - g # Solve (XC XC^ + sigma I) y = v using Conjugate Gradient # Inner solver tolerance: 1% relative residual, max 10 iterations y = conjugategradientsolve(XCXCstarplussigmaI, v, tolerance=0.01, maxiter=10) # Compute gradient gradient = backprojection(y, C) # 5. Update model phi = phi - omega gradient # 6. Select next frame # s{k+1} - 1 = (sk + p - 1) mod S sk = ((sk + p - 1) % S) + 1 # End of one cycle (S iterations) cyclecount += 1 # 7. Check stopping criterion # Compute RMSE for the current cycle # RMSE is computed over the test set or training set? # Source mentions RMSE for test set S^{[i]} in cross-validation context. # For stopping criterion, it says "decay rate of the RMSE between two successive cycles". # This implies computing RMSE on the training data or a validation set. # Assuming training data for the loop control as per "successive cycles" in training. currentrmse = computermse(phi, cameras, images) if cyclecount > 1: decayrate = (prevrmse - currentrmse) / prevrmse if decayrate <= tauthreshold: break prevrmse = currentrmse return phi def findrelativelyprimestep(S): if S <= 1: return 1 for p in range(2, S): if gcd(p, S) == 1: return p return 1 # Should not happen for S > 1 def forwardprojection(phi, C): # Ray tracing to compute XC phi # Returns vector of size Ms pass def backprojection(v, C): # Backprojection to compute XC^ v # Returns vector of size N pass def conjugategradientsolve(A, b, tolerance, maxiter): # Solves Ax = b # A is implicitly (XC XC^ + sigma I) # Matrix-vector product for A: # def matvec(x): # temp = forwardprojection(backprojection(x, C), C) # XC XC^ x # return temp + sigma x pass def computermse(phi, cameras, images): # Computes RMSE over all training frames # eta = sqrt( (1 / sum(Ms)) sum( ||XC phi - g||^2)) totalsqerror = 0 totalpixels = 0 for C, g in zip(cameras, images): pred = forwardprojection(phi, C) diff = pred - g totalsqerror += dot(diff, diff) totalpixels += len(g) return sqrt(totalsqerror / totalpixels) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on double precision for \phi to maintain accuracy, consuming 8N bytes. Boundary Conditions: The bounding box must contain the scene; voxel size h should satisfy h \ge r (object space resolution) to ensure well-resolved MIP images. Degenerate Input: If S=1, the ordering step p is trivial. The regularization \sigma must be non-zero to ensure invertibility of (XC XC^ + \sigma I). A batch solver using conjugate gradients on the normal equations. Choose when memory allows loading all data and a single global solution is preferred over incremental updates. A variant that may use learned parameters. Choose when adaptive learning rates are needed beyond the fixed \omega. Uses a different sampling distribution for noise or updates. Choose for robustness against outliers in a stochastic setting. Uses second-order derivatives. Choose when the Hessian is available and the problem is well-conditioned, accepting higher per-iteration cost. Dynamically adjusts step size. Choose when a fixed \omega is insufficient for convergence stability. Time Complexity: One cycle of S iterations costs O(M n) operations, where M = S m^2 is the total number of pixels and n estimates the number of diagonal voxels (or contributing voxels per ray). One iteration costs O(22 m^2 n). Memory Complexity: Dominated by the unknown \phi \in \mathbb{R}^N, requiring 8N bytes for double precision. Total RAM usage is approximately 16N bytes including intermediate steps. Performance: The method is efficient for large-scale tomography due to its frame-driven approach, loading only one image at a time. Strengths: Handles large datasets incrementally; preconditioning improves convergence for reflective tomography by emphasizing surfaces. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \omega and \sigma; convergence depends on the ordering of frames. When to use: Reflective tomography reconstruction where data arrives sequentially or memory is limited. When not to use: When exact global solutions are required without iterative approximation, or when the problem is not ill-conditioned in a way that benefits from the specific preconditioner. The Incremental Preconditioned Gradient Method was introduced in the context of flexible algebraic techniques for multiview reconstruction. It is based on the work of (2019), which proposes an online learning approach for reflective tomography using a preconditioned gradient descent on a least-squares cost function. The method adapts the Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (ART) by incorporating a preconditioner derived from the projection matrix structure. Flexible algebraic technique for multiview reconstruction: incremental learning in reflective tomography, https://doi.org/10.1117/1.OE.58.10.103102, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gradient-based Optimization with Surrogate Function
head: Iterative optimization using surrogate function, NGD-based optimization
body: This method estimates spatially varying extinction coefficients \beta by minimizing a cost function E(\beta) that fits a forward-model rendering to image measurements, using a surrogate function to avoid computing the full Jacobian per gradient step. It sets itself apart from direct Jacobian computation by decoupling the expensive forward-model rendering (FMC) from the gradient descent updates, requiring only one FMC rendering per block of NGD gradient steps rather than N{voxels}. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Measured images \{i{c,\mu}^{measured}\} for views c=1 \dots N{views} and channels \mu \in \{R, G, B\}; camera parameters; physical constants (\sigma{\mu}^{aerosol}, \beta{\mu}^{air}); regularization weight \eta; step size \Delta; number of gradient steps per surrogate update NGD. Outputs: Estimated aerosol extinction field \hat{\beta}^{aerosol}. Data Structures: \beta^{(q)}: 3D grid of aerosol extinction coefficients at iteration q. j{all}^{(q)}: Field of radiance values \{j{c,\mu}^{(q)}\} computed via Forward Monte Carlo (FMC) at iteration q. Qc: Diagonal weighting matrix for view c, where element (k,k) is R{c,p}^{(q)}, the number of rays passing through voxel k in view c. L: 3D Laplacian matrix. W: Diagonal altitude-dependent weight matrix. Mc: Sun-mask binary matrix for view c. Formulas: 1. Channel Extinction: \beta{\mu} = \beta{\mu}^{air} + \tilde{\sigma}{\mu} \beta{G}^{aerosol} where \tilde{\sigma}{\mu} = \sigma{\mu}^{aerosol} / \sigma{G}^{aerosol}. 2. Cost Function: E(\beta) = \sum{c=1}^{N{views}} \sum{\mu=R,G,B} Mc \left[ i{c,\mu}^{measured} - ic(\beta{\mu}) \right]^2 + \eta \Psi(\beta{G}^{aerosol}) where ic(\beta{\mu}) is the modeled intensity. 3. Regularization Term: \Psi(\beta{G}^{aerosol}) = \| W \beta{G}^{aerosol} \|^2 Gradient: 2 L^T W^T W \beta{G}^{aerosol}. 4. Gradient of Cost Function: \frac{\partial E}{\partial \beta} = 2 \sum{c=1}^{N{views}} \sum{\mu=R,G,B} \tilde{\sigma}{\mu} Qc Mc Jc(\beta{\mu}) Mc \left[ ic(\beta{\mu}) - i{c,\mu}^{measured} \right] + \eta \frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial \beta} When j{all} is fixed, the Jacobian Jc degenerates to a simple calculation based on the surrogate field. 5. Surrogate Update: \hat{\beta}^{(q+1)} = \arg \min{\beta \in C} E(\beta | j{all}^{(q)}) This minimization is performed using Gradient Descent steps. 6. Gradient Descent Step: \beta{d+1} = \betad - \Delta \frac{\partial E(\beta | j{all}^{(q)})}{\partial \beta} where d indexes the gradient descent step within the current surrogate block. 7. Camera Noise Simulation (for input preparation): i{c,\mu}^{measured} \leftarrow \left( i{c,\mu}^{measured} + o{noise} \right) \cdot \frac{2^{10}}{\max(\{Mc \cdot i{c,\mu}^{measured}\})} Clipped to [0, 1024] and rounded. o{noise} is white noise with standard deviation 0.4. Parameters: \Delta (Step size): 10^{-3}. NGD (Gradient steps per surrogate update): 5. \eta (Regularization weight): Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbasedoptimizationwithsurrogate(measuredimages, cameras, physicalconstants, eta, delta, ngd, maxiterations, gridshape): """ Estimates aerosol extinction beta using surrogate function optimization. """ # Precompute physical constants sigmatilde = {mu: physicalconstants['sigmaaerosol'][mu] / physicalconstants['sigmaaerosol']['G'] for mu in ['R', 'G', 'B']} # Precompute masks and weighting matrices sunmasks = {c: computesunmasks(cameras[c]) for c in range(len(cameras))} weightingmatrices = {c: computeweightingmatrices(cameras[c], gridshape) for c in range(len(cameras))} laplacianmatrix = compute3dlaplacian(gridshape) altitudeweights = computealtitudeweights(gridshape) # Initialize beta (e.g., null initialization) beta = betagrid 0.0 q = 0 while q < maxiterations: # 1. Forward Model Rendering (FMC) to compute surrogate field # This is not an inverse problem; complexity does not increase with Nvoxels jall = fmctrace(beta, cameras, physicalconstants) # 2. Gradient Descent Block for d in range(ngd): gradient = computegradientsurrogate( beta=beta, jall=jall, measuredimages=measuredimages, sunmasks=sunmasks, weightingmatrices=weightingmatrices, sigmatilde=sigmatilde, laplacianmatrix=laplacianmatrix, altitudeweights=altitudeweights, eta=eta) beta = beta - delta gradient q += 1 return beta def computegradientsurrogate(beta, jall, measuredimages, sunmasks, weightingmatrices, sigmatilde, laplacianmatrix, altitudeweights, eta): """ Computes gradient of E(beta | jall) where jall is fixed. """ gradient = beta 0.0 # Regularization gradient: 2 L^T W^T W beta reggradient = 2.0 matvecmul(laplacianmatrix.T, matvecmul(altitudeweights.T, matvecmul(altitudeweights, beta.flatten()))) gradient += reggradient.reshape(beta.shape) for c in range(len(measuredimages)): for mu in ['R', 'G', 'B']: jcmu = jall[c][mu] # Modeled intensity is directly the radiance field values when jall is fixed icmodeled = jcmu # Residual residual = icmodeled - measuredimages[c][mu] # Masking maskedresidual = sunmasks[c] residual # Weighting Qc = weightingmatrices[c] # Jacobian-vector product degenerates to a simple calculation based on the fixed field # It scales the residual by the ray-voxel intersection counts or path lengths jacobianterm = Qc sunmasks[c] # Accumulate gradient: 2 sigmatilde Qc Mc Jc Mc residual weightedjac = Qc (sunmasks[c] jacobianterm) gradient += 2.0 sigmatilde[mu] weightedjac return gradient def fmctrace(beta, cameras, physicalconstants): """ Computes radiance field jall using Forward Monte Carlo (FMC). """ jall = {} for c in range(len(cameras)): jall[c] = {} for mu in ['R', 'G', 'B']: jall[c][mu] = traceraysthroughmedium(beta, cameras[c], physicalconstants[mu]) return jall def computesunmasks(camera): """Returns binary mask Mc for pixels around the Sun.""" return createbinarymask(camera.sunposition, camera.lensflareradius) def computeweightingmatrices(camera, gridshape): """Returns diagonal matrix Qc where Qc[k,k] = number of rays through voxel k.""" raycounts = countrayvoxelintersections(camera, gridshape) return creatediagonalmatrix(raycounts) def compute3dlaplacian(gridshape): """Returns 3D Laplacian matrix L.""" return buildlaplacianmatrix(gridshape) def computealtitudeweights(gridshape): """Returns diagonal matrix W with altitude-dependent weights.""" altitudes = getvoxelaltitudes(gridshape) return creatediagonalmatrix(altitudefunction(altitudes)) def matvecmul(matrix, vector): """Matrix-vector multiplication.""" result = [0.0] len(matrix) for i in range(len(matrix)): for j in range(len(vector)): result[i] += matrix[i][j] vector[j] return result def creatediagonalmatrix(diagvalues): """Creates a diagonal matrix from a 1D array.""" n = len(diagvalues) return [[diagvalues[i] if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)] def createbinarymask(sunposition, flareradius): """Creates a binary mask for pixels near the sun.""" return [[1.0 if pixeldistance(p, sunposition) < flareradius else 0.0 for p in pixels] for pixels in imagegrid] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sun Masking: Pixels around the Sun are masked (Mc) because Monte Carlo estimates have high variance due to forward scattering phase function sampling. Additionally, physical sun occluders cause saturation. Ill-conditioning: Voxels near cameras have unstable \beta estimates because they affect more pixels, leading to higher gradient magnitudes. This is solved by the diagonal weighting matrix Qc, where element (k,k) is the number of rays passing through voxel k. Convergence: Starting from \beta^{aerosol}=0, satisfactory convergence occurs after several hundred iterations. Time Complexity: Direct Jacobian computation requires O(N{voxels}) FMC renderings per iteration, which is computationally expensive. The surrogate approach requires only one FMC rendering per NGD gradient descent steps, significantly reducing cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the radiance field j{all} and the extinction field \beta. The weighting matrices Qc are diagonal, requiring O(N{voxels}) memory per view. Performance: On Atm1 (Haze blobs), \delta{mass} = 1.7\% (null init) vs 3.4\% (single scattering init); \epsilon = 6.3\% (null), 10\% (single). On Atm4 (Haze front), \delta{mass} = 14\% (null init) vs 4.1\% (single scattering init); \epsilon = 23\% (null), 2.4\% (single). Strengths: Effective gradient calculation without N{voxels} rendering processes; handles ill-conditioning via weighting. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \Delta and NGD; sensitive to noise in forward scattering regions (mitigated by sun mask). This method was developed for in-situ multi-scattering tomography, specifically for recovering aerosol distributions from multi-view images. It builds on the concept of surrogate functions to avoid the computational burden of direct Jacobian computation in heterogeneous media. The method was compared against a baseline reconstruction using a single scattering approximation. In-situ multi-scattering tomography, https://archive.org/details/arxiv-1512.02110, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Moment-Damped Levenberg-Marquardt Optimizer
head: Hybrid LM-Adam Optimizer, Moment-LM Optimizer, TurboGS Optimizer, hybrid moment-damped LM, sparse moment-damped Levenberg-Marquardt
body: A hybrid optimization strategy for sparse-pixel training that partitions Gaussian parameters into geometry and base appearance blocks, solving them via small Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) systems with Adam-style moment damping, while updating Higher-order Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients separately with Adam. It sets itself apart from its parent Gradient Descent Solver by introducing Hessian-informed updates for geometry and appearance to stabilize convergence under sparse supervision. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current Gaussian parameters \theta, Adam first moment m, Adam second moment v, Jacobians Jg and Ja for geometry and base appearance blocks, loss gradient moments m{SH} for SH coefficients. Output: Parameter updates \Delta g, \Delta a, and \Delta \theta{SH}. Data Structures: Gaussian parameters \theta are partitioned into: Geometry block g \in \mathbb{R}^{10}: position (3), scale (3), rotation (4 quaternion). Base appearance block a \in \mathbb{R}^{4}: RGB DC coefficients (3), opacity (1). Higher-order SH coefficients: updated separately. Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability (standard Adam value, e.g., 10^{-8}). \eta: Learning rate for Adam update of SH coefficients. \sqrt{v}: Element-wise square root of the second moment vector v, serving as an adaptive diagonal damping term. Steps: 1. Partition Parameters: Separate \theta into geometry block g and base appearance block a. 2. Compute Jacobians: Calculate Jg and Ja with respect to the rendered loss. 3. Solve LM System for g and a: For each block b \in \{g, a\}, solve the linear system: (Jb^\top Jb + \text{diag}(\sqrt{vb} + \epsilon)) \Delta b = -mb where mb is the Adam first moment for block b, and vb is the Adam second moment for block b. The term \text{diag}(\sqrt{vb} + \epsilon) acts as a moment-based diagonal damping term to stabilize sparse gradients. 4. Solve via Cholesky: Perform Cholesky decomposition on the matrix (Jb^\top Jb + \text{diag}(\sqrt{vb} + \epsilon)) to solve for \Delta b efficiently. 5. Update SH Coefficients: Update higher-order SH coefficients \theta{SH} using Adam-style moment damping. 6. Apply Updates: Apply \Delta g, \Delta a, and \Delta \theta{SH} to the respective parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def momentdampedlmupdate(g, a, thetash, mg, ma, msh, vg, va, vsh, Jg, Ja, eta, epsilon, stepcount): """ Perform one step of Moment-Damped Levenberg-Marquardt optimization. Args: g: Geometry parameters (R^10) a: Base appearance parameters (R^4) thetash: Higher-order SH coefficients mg, ma, msh: Adam first moments for respective blocks vg, va, vsh: Adam second moments for respective blocks Jg, Ja: Jacobians of loss w.r.t g and a eta: Learning rate for SH update epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability stepcount: Current training step for bias correction Returns: Updated g, a, thetash """ # Step 1: Solve LM system for geometry block g Hg = Jg.T @ Jg dampingg = np.sqrt(vg) + epsilon Ag = Hg + np.diag(dampingg) bg = -mg Lg = np.linalg.cholesky(Ag) yg = np.linalg.solve(Lg, bg) deltag = np.linalg.solve(Lg.T, yg) # Step 2: Solve LM system for base appearance block a Ha = Ja.T @ Ja dampinga = np.sqrt(va) + epsilon Aa = Ha + np.diag(dampinga) ba = -ma La = np.linalg.cholesky(Aa) ya = np.linalg.solve(La, ba) deltaa = np.linalg.solve(La.T, ya) # Step 3: Update SH coefficients using Adam beta1, beta2 = 0.9, 0.999 mhatsh = msh / (1 - beta1stepcount) vhatsh = vsh / (1 - beta2stepcount) deltash = -eta (mhatsh / (np.sqrt(vhatsh) + epsilon)) # Step 4: Apply updates gnew = g + deltag anew = a + deltaa thetashnew = thetash + deltash return gnew, anew, thetashnew Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ignoring SH cross-parameter correlations is a practical trade-off; joint optimization would substantially increase Jacobian size and memory overhead. Sparse gradients can be unstable; the moment-based damping \sqrt{v} is critical for stabilization. A tailored optimizer that couples Hessian-informed updates with Adam moment damping to stabilize and improve convergence under sparse supervision. It integrates Adam moments with Hessian-informed updates. Time Complexity: Solving small LM systems via Cholesky decomposition is efficient for the fixed small block sizes (10 and 4 dimensions). The overall complexity is dominated by Jacobian computation and Cholesky factorization, which is lightweight for these small blocks. Memory Complexity: Low memory overhead compared to full Newton methods due to block partitioning and ignoring SH correlations. Measured Performance: On Mip-NeRF 360, Moment-LM achieves 29.50dB PSNR vs 29.42dB for Sparse Adam-only, with identical training time (90s) and NGS (0.64M). Scaling: Suitable for sparse-pixel training scenarios where full dense optimization is too costly. Strengths: Higher PSNR/SSIM, lower LPIPS, and more stable high-frequency details compared to sparse Adam-only optimization under similar training times. Limitations: Trade-off in accuracy due to ignoring SH cross-parameter correlations. Originated in TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization. It is used in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to accelerate training while maintaining or improving rendering quality. TurboGS: Accelerating 3D Gaussian Splatting via Error-Guided Sparse Pixel Sampling and Optimization, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.15924, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Linear Model Analysis for Plane Reproduction
head: Geometric Initialization Justification, Theorem 1 Analysis
body:
This analysis provides a theoretical justification for the loss function's ability to converge to the signed distance function (SDF) of a plane when input data is sampled from a plane, using a linear model f(x; w) = w^T x. It differs from fixed volumetric grids (like RGVF) by being data-dependent and avoiding cubic-size memory requirements and interpolation schemes. Inputs: Point cloud X = \{xi\}{i \in I} in \mathbb{R}^d, where xi = yi + \epsiloni. yi spans a (d-1)-dimensional hyperplane H containing the origin, and \epsiloni are small deviations with \|\epsiloni\| < \delta. Regularization parameter \lambda. Outputs: Weight vector w (or q in transformed coordinates) representing the approximate SDF normal. Data Structures: Covariance matrix components: Eigenvalues \lambdaj and eigenvectors uj from spectral decomposition. Transformed coordinates q = U^T w. Steps: 1. Spectral Decomposition: Compute the spectral decomposition of the covariance matrix of the point cloud: \sum{i \in I} xi xi^T = U D U^T where U = (u1, \dots, ud) is the orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors and D = 	ext{diag}(\lambda1, \dots, \lambdad) with 0 \le \lambda1 < \lambda2 \le \dots \le \lambdad. 2. Coordinate Transformation: Change coordinates to q = U^T w. The loss function becomes diagonalized: \ell(q) = q^T D q + \lambda (\|q\| - 1)^2 3. Critical Point Identification: Find critical points by setting the gradient to zero. For q 
eq 0, critical points satisfy: 2\lambda(\|q\| - 1) = -\lambdaj This yields critical points qj = \pm \sqrt{1 -  rac{\lambdaj}{2\lambda}} ej for j \in [d], and q=0, where ej is the j-th standard basis vector. 4. Global Minima Selection: If \lambda >  rac{\lambda1}{2}, the global minima are \pm q = \pm \sqrt{1 -  rac{\lambda1}{2\lambda}} e1. These correspond to the approximate SDF to the plane. Formulas: Linear Loss: \ell(w) = \sum{i \in I} (w^T xi)^2 + \lambda (\|w\| - 1)^2 This is a simplified version of the general loss using squared error and removing normal data terms. Gradient in Transformed Coordinates: 
ablaq \ell(q)^T = 2(D + 2\lambda(\|q\| - 1)I)q Hessian in Transformed Coordinates: 
abla^2q \ell(q) = 2D + 4\lambda(\|q\| - 1)I + 8\lambda q q^T Parameters: \lambda: Regularization parameter. Must satisfy \lambda >  rac{\lambda1}{2} for the global minima to exist in the form of the SDF. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \lambda \le  rac{\lambda1}{2}, the term 1 -  rac{\lambda1}{2\lambda} becomes non-positive, and the global minima corresponding to the SDF do not exist in this form. The parameter \lambda must be chosen sufficiently large compared to the deviation from planarity \delta. The analysis assumes the point cloud is sampled approximately from a plane. In the general MLP case, this analysis holds locally, where the deviation from planarity is quantified by surface curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def linearmodelanalysis(pointcloud, lambdareg): """ Analyze linear model for plane reproduction. Args: pointcloud: numpy array of shape (N, d) lambdareg: float, regularization parameter Returns: wopt: numpy array of shape (d,), optimal weight vector """ # Step 1: Spectral Decomposition # Compute covariance matrix: sum{i in I} xi xi^T covmatrix = pointcloud.T @ pointcloud # Eigen decomposition (eigh returns sorted eigenvalues ascending) eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covmatrix) lambda1 = eigenvalues[0] U = eigenvectors D = np.diag(eigenvalues) # Edge case check if lambdareg <= lambda1 / 2: raise ValueError("Lambda must be greater than lambda1 / 2 for global minima to exist.") # Step 2 & 3: Identify Global Minima in Transformed Coordinates # The global minima in transformed coordinates are +/- q1 # q1 = sqrt(1 - lambda1 / (2 lambdareg)) e1 factor = np.sqrt(1 - lambda1 / (2 lambdareg)) qopt = np.zeros(pointcloud.shape[1]) qopt[0] = factor # Corresponds to e1 # Step 4: Transform back to original coordinates # w = U q wopt = U @ qopt return wopt A theoretical proof technique using a Liapunov function to demonstrate that continuous gradient flow converges to global minima of the loss function for plane reproduction in non-noisy data. It initializes q0 randomly from a continuous probability distribution in \mathbb{R}^d, ensuring with probability 1 that q0 is not orthogonal to e1. It selects v such that v^T q0 > 0, where v = \pm \sqrt{1 -  rac{\lambda1}{2\lambda}} e1 from Theorem 1. It verifies Liapunov conditions on the domain \Omega = \{q \in \mathbb{R}^d \mid e1^T q > 0\}: Energy (h(v)=0 and h(q)>0 for q \in \Omega \setminus \{v\}), Decreasing (
abla h(q) \cdot  rac{dq}{dt}(q) < 0 for q \in \Omega \setminus \{v\}), and Bounded (level-sets \{q \mid h(q)=c\} are bounded). The Liapunov function is h(q) =  rac{\|q - v\|^2}{1 + \|q\|^2}. The derivative proves the decreasing property: 
abla h \cdot  rac{dq}{dt} = - rac{8 v^T q}{(1+\|q\|^2)^2} (q^T D q + \lambda(\|q\|^2 - 1)) \le 0, using v^T q = q1 > 0 and D positive semi-definite. It concludes that q(t) 	o q^ as t 	o \infty, where q^ is a global minimum of the loss, and the limit model approximates the signed distance function to the hyperplane. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides theoretical guarantee for convergence to the plane's SDF under specific conditions. Data-dependent, avoiding fixed grid memory costs. Limitations: Requires \lambda to be chosen carefully relative to the data's deviation from planarity. Analysis is for linear models; extension to MLPs is local. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "Implicit Geometric Regularization for Learning Shapes". The analysis is presented as Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, justifying the use of the Eikonal regularization term alone for implicitly regularizing the zero level set. It contrasts with previous works that used Eikonal regularization in combination with other explicit reconstruction terms. The analysis uses perturbation theory for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Hermitian matrices. Implicit Geometric Regularization for Learning Shapes, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2002.10099, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Observed-Only Momentum Updates
head: Observed Variable Updates, Sparse Momentum
body: Observed-Only Momentum Updates is a modification to the Adam optimizer that restricts momentum and moment updates to variables receiving nonzero gradients in the current iteration, preventing noisy momentum from accumulating on unobserved variables. It differs from standard Adam by filtering updates based on direct observation rather than applying stochastic noise to all parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current parameters \theta, first moment estimate m, second moment estimate v, learning rate \alpha, decay rates \beta1, \beta2, stability constant \epsilon, iteration count t, and gradient g. Output: Updated parameters \theta', updated moments m', v'. Data Structures: Parameters \theta, moments m, v, and gradient g: Tensors of identical shape, initialized to zero. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute gradient g for the current batch. 2. Identify observed indices \mathcal{O} = \{ i \mid gi \neq 0 \}. 3. For i \in \mathcal{O}: update mi \leftarrow \beta1 mi + (1 - \beta1) gi and vi \leftarrow \beta2 vi + (1 - \beta2) gi^2. 4. For i \in \mathcal{O}: compute bias-corrected estimates \hat{m}i = mi / (1 - \beta1^t), \hat{v}i = vi / (1 - \beta2^t). 5. For i \in \mathcal{O}: update \thetai \leftarrow \thetai - \alpha \hat{m}i / (\sqrt{\hat{v}i} + \epsilon). 6. For j \notin \mathcal{O}: leave mj, vj, \thetaj unchanged. Formulas: Moment updates (observed i): mi^{(t)} = \beta1 mi^{(t-1)} + (1 - \beta1) gi^{(t)}, vi^{(t)} = \beta2 vi^{(t-1)} + (1 - \beta2) (gi^{(t)})^2. Parameter update (observed i): \thetai^{(t)} = \thetai^{(t-1)} - \alpha \frac{\hat{m}i^{(t)}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}i^{(t)}} + \epsilon}. Parameters: \alpha (learning rate), \beta1, \beta2 (exponential decay rates), \epsilon (numerical stability constant), t (iteration count). Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noisy Momentum Accumulation: Without this method, Adam maintains moment estimates from previous iterations' stochastic noise, which remains fixed for unobserved variables and impedes convergence. Indirect Gradients: In differentiable path tracing, gradients for indirectly observed parameters are extremely noisy due to low sampling probability of long light paths; restricting updates to directly observed variables mitigates this. Sparse Updates: Variables not observed in a batch do not receive updates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def observedonlymomentumupdate(theta, m, v, g, alpha, beta1, beta2, epsilon, t): observedmask = (g != 0) m[observedmask] = beta1 m[observedmask] + (1 - beta1) g[observedmask] v[observedmask] = beta2 v[observedmask] + (1 - beta2) (g[observedmask] 2) biascorrection1 = 1 - beta1 t biascorrection2 = 1 - beta2 t mhat = m / biascorrection1 vhat = v / biascorrection2 theta[observedmask] = theta[observedmask] - alpha (mhat[observedmask] / (vhat[observedmask] 0.5 + epsilon)) return theta, m, v A momentum scaling rule proposed to maintain high update cosine similarity and similar update magnitude when switching to larger training batch sizes in 3D Gaussian Splatting training. Compared to leaving momentum coefficients unchanged, the exponential momentum scaling rule keeps update cosine similarity higher across different training batch sizes. Time Complexity: O(N) per iteration, where N is the number of parameters, due to element-wise operations and masking. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing parameters and moments, identical to standard Adam. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Effectiveness depends on the sparsity of observed gradients. Strengths: Reduces noise accumulation for unobserved variables, improving convergence in scenes with sparse observations or indirect lighting. Limitations: May require more iterations to update all variables if observations are sparse. When to use: Differentiable rendering with path tracing where indirect gradients are noisy and many variables are not directly observed per batch. When not to use: Dense gradient scenarios where all variables are observed every step, or when masking overhead is prohibitive. Originated in material and lighting reconstruction for complex indoor scenes using texture-space differentiable rendering. The method addresses noisy momentum accumulation in the Adam optimizer when applied to differentiable rendering, where not all parameters are observed in every batch due to light transport characteristics.
