name: L2 Update
head: L2-norm minimization update step, PWLS Update
body: The L2 Update is a single optimization step for differentiable volume rendering that minimizes the L2-norm of the residual between projected and measured data. It supports subset-based processing to handle large datasets and provides two update paths: a standard backprojection update and a weighted update incorporating Poisson-statistics-based scaling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: projections (measured data), volume (current volume estimate), geometry (projection geometry), settings (configuration flags updateresidual, studentst), numsubsets (number of subsets). Outputs: Updated volume, normalized residual norm rnorm. Data Structures: projections: Array of measured projection values. volume: 3D array of voxel values. geometry: Object defining projection parameters. residual: Temporary array matching the shape of the current subset. voltmp, bwpw: Temporary arrays matching the shape of volume. fwpw: Temporary array matching the shape of the current subset. Steps: 1. Retrieve settings.updateresidual and settings.studentst. 2. Determine the number of subsets. 3. Compute the backprojection weight normalization factor by calling bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry). 4. Loop over subsets generated by subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True): a. Initialize residual as a contiguous zero array with the same shape as the current subset. b. Forward project the current volume into residual. c. Apply filters to residual. d. If updateresidual is true, compute the root mean square of residual and add it to rnorm. e. If studentst is true, apply Student's T norm with degree 6 to residual. f. Scale residual by bpweight numsubsets 2. g. Backproject residual into volume (filtered=False). h. Return rnorm / numsubsets. 5. Retrieve settings.updateresidual. 6. Determine the number of subsets. 7. Compute the backprojection weight normalization factor by calling bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry). 8. Loop over subsets generated by subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True): a. Initialize voltmp and bwpw as zero arrays with the same shape as volume. b. Compute weights fwpw as exp(-subset). c. Backproject fwpw into bwpw (filtered=False). d. Initialize residual as a contiguous zero array with the same shape as the current subset. e. Forward project the current volume into residual. f. Apply filters to residual. g. If updateresidual is true, compute the root mean square of residual and add it to rnorm. h. Scale residual by bpweight numsubsets 2 fwpw. i. Backproject residual into voltmp (filtered=False). j. Normalize bwpw by dividing by its maximum value. k. Clamp bwpw values below 1e-2 to 1e-2. l. Update volume by adding voltmp divided by bwpw. m. Return rnorm / numsubsets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def l2updatestandard(projections, volume, geometry, settings, numsubsets): """Standard L2-norm update path.""" rnorm = 0.0 bpweight = bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry) subsets = subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True) for subset in subsets: residual = [0.0] len(subset) residual = forwardproject(volume, geometry) residual = applyfilters(residual) if settings.updateresidual: rnorm += math.sqrt(sum(r2 for r in residual) / len(residual)) if settings.studentst: residual = applystudenttnorm(residual, degree=6) residual = [r bpweight numsubsets 2 for r in residual] volume = backproject(residual, geometry, filtered=False) rnorm = rnorm / numsubsets return rnorm def l2updateweighted(projections, volume, geometry, settings, numsubsets): """Weighted L2-norm update path with Poisson scaling.""" rnorm = 0.0 bpweight = bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry) subsets = subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True) for subset in subsets: voltmp = [0.0] len(volume) bwpw = [0.0] len(volume) fwpw = [math.exp(-s) for s in subset] bwpw = backproject(fwpw, geometry, filtered=False) residual = [0.0] len(subset) residual = forwardproject(volume, geometry) residual = applyfilters(residual) if settings.updateresidual: rnorm += math.sqrt(sum(r2 for r in residual) / len(residual)) residual = [r bpweight numsubsets 2 f for r, f in zip(residual, fwpw)] voltmp = backproject(residual, geometry, filtered=False) maxbwp = max(bwpw) bwpw = [b / maxbwp for b in bwpw] bwpw = [max(b, 1e-2) for b in bwpw] volume = [v + vt / bw for v, vt, bw in zip(volume, voltmp, bwpw)] rnorm = rnorm / numsubsets return rnorm def bpnorm(projections, volume, geometry): # Not given in sources. return 1.0 def subsetgenerator(projections, volume, geometry, copy=True): # Not given in sources. yield projections def forwardproject(volume, geometry): # Not given in sources. return [0.0] def applyfilters(residual): # Not given in sources. return residual def applystudenttnorm(residual, degree): # Not given in sources. return residual def backproject(data, geometry, filtered=False): # Not given in sources. return [0.0] Parameters: updateresidual: Boolean flag to update the residual norm. studentst: Boolean flag to apply Student's T norm. numsubsets: Number of subsets to process. degree: Degrees of freedom for Student's T distribution (default 6). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise when computing exp(-subset) for large negative values. Clamping bwpw to 1e-2 prevents division by zero but may introduce bias in low-weight regions. The method assumes that the geometry object provides accurate projection parameters. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and projections, scaled by the number of subsets. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and projections, due to temporary arrays. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of subsets, as each subset can be processed independently. Strengths: Handles large datasets efficiently through subset processing; incorporates Poisson statistics for improved accuracy. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of parameters such as numsubsets and degree; may be sensitive to noise in the projections. When to Use: Suitable for differentiable volume rendering tasks where Poisson statistics are relevant and large datasets need to be processed efficiently. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time applications due to the computational cost of forward and backprojection operations. The L2 Update method originates from the flexTOMO project. It is used for differentiable volume rendering optimization. cicwi/flexTOMO, https://github.com/cicwi/flexTOMO, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Simplex Constraint Strategies
head: Natural Gradient for Simplex, Parameterization and Gradient Methods for Simplex Constraints, Projected Gradient Descent for Simplex
body: Simplex Constraint Strategies enforce the probability simplex constraint (\sumi \thetai = 1, \thetai \ge 0) on optimization variables representing discrete distributions, such as material densities or scattering coefficients in volume rendering. They solve the problem of maintaining valid probability vectors during gradient-based optimization, where standard Euclidean updates may violate non-negativity or sum-to-one requirements. This family is distinguished from its siblings by its specific focus on the geometry of the probability simplex, contrasting with general solvers like CGLS Solver or unconstrained methods like Newton's Method. All strategies in this family operate on a parameter vector \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n that must lie on the probability simplex \Delta^{n-1}. The core mechanism involves computing a gradient direction \mathbf{g} (typically the Euclidean gradient of the loss with respect to \boldsymbol{\theta}) and transforming or projecting it to ensure the updated state remains valid. The shared mathematical components are: 1. Euclidean Gradient (\mathbf{g}): The standard gradient \nabla{\boldsymbol{\theta}} L. 2. Simplex Projection (\Pi{\Delta}): A projection operator that maps an arbitrary vector \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n back onto the simplex. The efficient algorithm by Wang and Carreira-Perpiñán [2013] is cited as the standard implementation. 3. Manifold Geometry: The recognition that the simplex is a non-Euclidean manifold, motivating the use of natural gradients or specific parameterizations to respect the local metric. Softmax parameterization maps unconstrained logits \boldsymbol{\ell} \in \mathbb{R}^n to the simplex via \thetai = \frac{\exp(\elli)}{\sumj \exp(\ellj)}. This satisfies the simplex constraint by construction, eliminating the need for explicit projection. Distinction: It avoids projection errors but suffers from saturation. When logits reach extreme values, probabilities saturate near 0 or 1 and resist further change, slowing convergence. When to choose: Use when strict constraint satisfaction without projection overhead is required and saturation is not expected to hinder convergence. Link: Softmax Parameterization (Hypothetical child link based on context). This method computes the Euclidean gradient \mathbf{g}, performs a standard update step, and then applies the simplex projection \Pi{\Delta} to the result. Distinction: It avoids the saturation issues of softmax but introduces a problem for adaptive optimizers like Adam. The gradient formulations used in the source context blend losses and are inherently positive prior to projection. This prevents sign variation in Adam's moment accumulators, causing poor performance. When to choose: Suitable for SGD, where the update coincides with projected gradient descent because the direction differs only by a constant shift that projection cancels out. Link: Projected Gradient Descent (Hypothetical child link). The natural gradient \hat{\mathbf{g}} accounts for the simplex geometry, providing the steepest-ascent direction under the manifold's metric. It is computed as: \hat{\mathbf{g}} = \boldsymbol{\theta} \odot (\mathbf{g} - \langle \mathbf{g}, \boldsymbol{\theta} \rangle \mathbf{1}) where \odot is component-wise multiplication, \mathbf{g} is the Euclidean gradient, and \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. Distinction: It respects the non-Euclidean geometry better than Euclidean gradients. However, scaling by \boldsymbol{\theta} impedes steps into low-probability directions, slowing convergence. Like projected gradient descent, it requires explicit projection to remain on the manifold. When to choose: Generally outperformed by the modified natural gradient in adaptive settings due to the scaling bottleneck. Link: Natural Gradient (Hypothetical child link). This strategy removes the component-wise scaling by \boldsymbol{\theta} from the natural gradient formula, yielding: \hat{\mathbf{g}} = \mathbf{g} - \langle \mathbf{g}, \boldsymbol{\theta} \rangle \mathbf{1} This modified gradient is combined with the simplex projection. Distinction: By removing the scaling, it avoids impeding steps into low-probability directions. Crucially, subtracting the expected loss \langle \mathbf{g}, \boldsymbol{\theta} \rangle restores naturally signed values. This enables effective step size adaptation in adaptive optimizers like Adam, which rely on sign variation in moment accumulators. Performance: In experiments using a phantom with 32 projections, modified natural gradient with Adam converges roughly an order of magnitude faster than other combinations (softmax, projected gradient, natural gradient). When to choose: The recommended default for adaptive optimizers (Adam) in this context due to superior convergence speed. Link: Modified Natural Gradient (Hypothetical child link). Originating from the need to optimize discrete distributions in inverse rendering for X-ray computed tomography, these strategies address the limitations of standard Euclidean optimization on probability simplices. The specific formulations and comparisons are detailed in "Inverse Rendering for Discrete X-Ray Computed Tomography". The work builds on earlier foundations in natural gradient descent [Amari 2016] and efficient simplex projection algorithms [Wang and Carreira-Perpiñán 2013]. The modified natural gradient was proposed to resolve the convergence issues observed with standard natural gradients and projected gradients when using adaptive optimizers. Inverse Rendering for Discrete X-Ray Computed Tomography, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811391, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Monte-Carlo Solver
head: TD(0) Solver, Temporal Difference Solver
body: The Monte-Carlo Solver is a method for solving the light transport equation in differentiable volume rendering by applying a one-point Monte-Carlo estimator to the radiosity summation, using off-policy temporal difference learning (TD(0)) to iteratively update outgoing radiance for all kernels simultaneously. Unlike radiance caching, which solves for selected points independently, or classical iterative linear system solvers, which produce biased intermediate results, this method provides unbiased estimations of the final solution at every step. It builds on Gradient Descent Solver by treating the radiosity update as a reinforcement learning problem where the state value is the outgoing radiance. Inputs: A set of N Gaussian kernels with their properties (positions, covariances, etc.), initial emissions \mathbf{E}i^c, and a maximum time step T. Outputs: Estimated outgoing radiance \{\mathbf{B}1^c, \dots, \mathbf{B}N^c\} for all kernels. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains three arrays of size N for all kernels i \in \{1, \dots, N\}: 1. \mathbf{S}i^B: Sum of radiance estimations (initialized to \mathbf{0}). 2. \mathbf{S}i^{B^2}: Sum of squares of radiance estimations (initialized to \mathbf{0}). 3. Di: Number of visits/updates for kernel i (initialized to 0). Formulas: The one-point Monte-Carlo estimator for kernel i is defined as: \mathbf{B}i^c \approx \mathbf{E}i^c + \frac{1}{\Pr[\text{choose } j]} \int{Pi} \int{Pj} \mathbf{f}i(\mathbf{Y}^T \mathbf{B}j^c) V{ji} d\mathbf{x}' d\mathbf{x} \quad (24) where \mathbf{f}i is the BRDF response, \mathbf{Y} is the spherical harmonic basis, \mathbf{B}j^c is the outgoing radiance of kernel j, and V{ji} is the visibility term between kernels j and i. The update rule blends the old estimate with the new Monte-Carlo estimate using TD(0): \mathbf{B}i^{c(t+1)} = \frac{t}{t+1} \times \mathbf{B}i^{c(t)} + \frac{1}{t+1} \times \left( \mathbf{E}i^c + \frac{1}{\text{Pr}[\text{choose } j]} \int{Pi} \int{Pj} \mathbf{f}i(\mathbf{Y}^T \mathbf{B}j^{c(t)}) V{ji} d\mathbf{x}' d\mathbf{x} \right) \quad (25) The coefficients \frac{t}{t+1} and \frac{1}{t+1} satisfy the Robbins-Monro condition for convergence. Parameters: T: Maximum time step. Empirically set to 64 to balance efficiency and variance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize \mathbf{S}i^B \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{S}i^{B^2} \leftarrow \mathbf{0}, and Di \leftarrow 0 for all i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. 2. Iterate for time steps t from 1 to T: a. Select Receiving Kernels: If t \leq 8, select all kernels: \{a1, \dots, aN\} \leftarrow \{1, \dots, N\}. Otherwise, select N kernels based on variance using a function SelectStartingIndex. b. Select Emitting Kernels: Stochastically find kernels for emitting radiance \{b1, p1, \dots, bN, pN\} using a function NextEvent. The probability of choosing kernel j should be proportional to the integral in Eqn. (24). c. Calculate Estimation: For each receiving kernel ai, calculate the new estimation of received radiance \deltai: \deltai \leftarrow \text{NE}(ai, bi, pi, \mathbf{E}{ai}^c, \mathbf{S}{bi}^B / D{bi}) Here, \text{NE} denotes the next event estimation function which computes the integral approximation using the current estimate of the emitting kernel's radiance \mathbf{S}{bi}^B / D{bi}. d. Update Statistics: \mathbf{S}{ai}^B \leftarrow \mathbf{S}{ai}^B + \deltai. \mathbf{S}{ai}^{B^2} \leftarrow \mathbf{S}{ai}^{B^2} + \deltai^2. D{ai} \leftarrow D{ai} + 1. 3. After the loop, calculate the final radiance as the average: \mathbf{B}i^c \leftarrow \mathbf{S}i^B / Di for all i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def montecarlosolver(kernels, emissions, T=64): N = len(kernels) # Initialize data structures SB = [0.0] N SB2 = [0.0] N D = [0] N for t in range(1, T + 1): # Select receiving kernels if t <= 8: receivingindices = list(range(N)) else: # Select N kernels based on variance receivingindices = selectstartingindex(N, D, SB2) # Stochastically find emitting kernels # Returns list of tuples (emittingkernelindex, probability) emittingevents = nextevent(N, kernels, SB, D) # Process each receiving kernel for aidx in receivingindices: # Find corresponding emitting event for this receiving kernel # In the general case, NextEvent might return a set of events for all receiving kernels # Assuming NextEvent returns a list of events aligned with receivingindices bidx, pj = emittingevents[aidx] # Calculate current estimate of emitting kernel's radiance if D[bidx] > 0: Bemit = SB[bidx] / D[bidx] else: Bemit = 0.0 # Calculate new estimation delta # NE function computes: Ea + (1/pj) integral approximation # The integral uses Bemit as the value for Bj delta = nexteventestimation( kernela=kernels[aidx], kernelb=kernels[bidx], prob=pj, emission=emissions[aidx], Bj=Bemit) # Update statistics SB[aidx] += delta SB2[aidx] += delta delta D[aidx] += 1 # Final radiance Bfinal = [] for i in range(N): if D[i] > 0: Bfinal.append(SB[i] / D[i]) else: Bfinal.append(0.0) return Bfinal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If Di = 0, the estimate \mathbf{S}i^B / Di is undefined. The algorithm initializes Di=0 and only increments it upon visit. The NextEvent function must handle cases where an emitting kernel has not been visited yet (e.g., by using initial emission or zero radiance). Variance Selection: The SelectStartingIndex function is not detailed in the primary algorithm but is crucial for efficiency after the initial warm-up phase (t > 8). Probability Estimation: The probability \Pr[\text{choose } j] must be accurately estimated to ensure the Monte-Carlo estimator is unbiased. A Monte-Carlo solver optimization where time steps are not synchronized across all kernels. Instead, the solver tracks the variance of the estimated outgoing radiance for each kernel over time and performs more update steps for kernels exhibiting high variance to improve efficiency. At each step, it selects N elements from the set \{1, 2, \dots, N\} with replacement, where the probability of selecting a specific kernel is proportional to its tracked variance, rather than selecting uniformly. Time Complexity: The method is iterative with T steps. Each step involves selecting kernels and computing next-event estimations. The complexity depends on the cost of NextEvent and SelectStartingIndex. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing \mathbf{S}i^B, \mathbf{S}i^{B^2}, and Di for N kernels. Performance: Empirically, T=64 balances efficiency and variance. The method is parallel-friendly. Strengths: Provides unbiased intermediate results, unlike classical iterative linear system solvers. Simultaneously solves for all kernels, unlike radiance caching. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of T and variance-based selection strategies. The variance-based adaptive variant adds complexity to kernel selection. The Monte-Carlo Solver is based on the application of off-policy temporal difference learning (TD(0)) from reinforcement learning to the radiosity equation. It was introduced in the context of differentiable light transport with Gaussian surfels. The approach draws parallels to path tracing but replaces iterative direction selection with iterative kernel selection. The update rule relies on the Robbins-Monro condition for convergence. Differentiable Light Transport with Gaussian Surfels via Adapted Radiosity for Efficient Relighting and Geometry Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1145/3763305, fetched 2026-10-27

name: BFGS Solver with Moreau Envelope
head: BFGS with Moreau Envelope, Huber Reconstruction
body:
This method solves inverse problems, specifically tomographic reconstruction, by minimizing a composite objective function consisting of a data fidelity term and a regularizer. It sets itself apart by using the BFGS quasi-Newton algorithm to handle the non-smooth L1 regularization via its Moreau envelope, providing a differentiable approximation that allows second-order optimization steps. This contrasts with first-order Gradient Descent solvers [3280-gradient-descent-solver.md] and avoids the explicit projection steps required by constrained material solvers [7899-euclidean-projection-for-material-constraints.md]. The method minimizes an objective function F(x) defined as the sum of a squared L2 data discrepancy and a smoothed L1 regularizer applied to the image gradient. Inputs: Forward operator A (e.g., Ray Transform). Noisy measurement data y. Image space X (e.g., uniform discrete space). Gradient operator 
abla. Hyperparameters: smoothing parameter \sigma, regularization weight \lambda, maximum iterations maxiter, and memory size num\store. Outputs: Reconstructed image x. Data Structures: x: The current estimate of the image, stored as a tensor/array in X. H^{-1}0: Initial inverse Hessian estimate, implemented as a scaling operator. s, y vectors: Stored for Limited Memory BFGS (L-BFGS) history. Steps: 1. Initialize Operator Norm: Compute the operator norm of A using the power method to scale the initial Hessian estimate. opnorm = \|A\| 2. Initialize Inverse Hessian: Set the initial inverse Hessian estimate H^{-1}0 as a scaled identity operator: H^{-1}0 =  rac{0.5}{\|A\|^2} I 3. Define Data Term: Construct the squared L2 norm of the residual: D(x) = \|Ax - y\|2^2 4. Define Regularizer: Compute the gradient of the image: g = 
abla x. Apply the Group L1 norm to the gradient: \|g\|{1,2}. Smooth this non-smooth norm using the Moreau envelope with parameter \sigma: R(x) = 	ext{MoreauEnvelope}{\sigma}(\|
abla x\|{1,2}) 5. Define Objective: Combine terms: F(x) = D(x) + \lambda R(x) 6. Solve: Run the BFGS solver (specifically L-BFGS if num\store is limited) starting from an initial guess (often the FBP pseudoinverse result). Use the precomputed H^{-1}0 as the initial Hessian approximation. Limit iterations to maxiter. Store num\store vectors for the limited memory update. Parameters: \sigma = 0.03: Smoothing parameter for the Moreau envelope. \lambda = 0.3: Regularization weight. maxiter = 200: Maximum number of iterations. num\store = 10: Number of vectors stored for L-BFGS. Pitfalls: The initial reconstruction (pseudoinverse) must use the 'Hann' filter to match the reference implementation's assumptions. Precision issues may arise if the operator norm is not computed accurately, affecting the scaling of the Hessian estimate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bfgsmoreauenvelopesolver(A, y, space, sigma=0.03, lam=0.3, maxiter=200, numstore=10): # 1. Compute operator norm via power iteration opnorm = powermethodopnorm(A) # 2. Initialize inverse Hessian estimate as a scaled identity hessinvestimate = ScalingOperator(space, 0.5 / opnorm2) # 3. Define data term: squared L2 norm of residual def datadiscrepancy(x): return sum((A(x) - y)2) # 4. Define regularizer: Moreau envelope of Group L1 norm on gradient gradientop = Gradient(space) l1norm = GroupL1Norm(gradientop.range) smoothedl1 = MoreauEnvelope(l1norm, sigma=sigma) def regularizer(x): return smoothedl1(gradientop(x)) # 5. Define objective function def objfun(x): return datadiscrepancy(x) + lam regularizer(x) # 6. Initial guess via FBP pseudoinverse with Hann filter x = fbppseudoinverse(A, y, filtertype='Hann') # 7. Solve using BFGS with limited memory s = [zeroslike(x) for in range(numstore)] yvec = [zeroslike(x) for in range(numstore)] k = 0 for i in range(maxiter): grad = computegradient(objfun, x) d = lbfgstwoloop(grad, s, yvec, k, hessinvestimate) alpha = linesearch(objfun, x, grad, d) xnew = x + alpha d s[k % numstore] = xnew - x yvec[k % numstore] = computegradient(objfun, xnew) - grad k += 1 x = xnew return x A Monte Carlo estimator to calculate the radiance contribution of a stationary path found by the BFGS solver, based on the path formulation of the Radiative Radiative Transfer Equation (RRTE). Time Complexity: Each iteration involves computing the gradient of the data term and the smoothed regularizer. The L-BFGS update is O(m \cdot d) where m is num\store and d is the dimension of the image. The dominant cost is usually the forward and adjoint operator evaluations (A and A^). Memory Complexity: O(d) for the image and gradients, plus O(m \cdot d) for the L-BFGS history vectors. Performance: The Moreau envelope makes the L1 norm differentiable, allowing BFGS to converge faster than first-order methods for smooth approximations, but the smoothing parameter \sigma must be chosen carefully to balance accuracy and differentiability. Strengths: Handles non-smooth regularization (L1) effectively within a second-order framework. The Hann filter initialization provides a stable starting point. Limitations: Requires computation of the operator norm, which can be expensive for large operators. The smoothing parameter \sigma is a hyperparameter that affects convergence and solution quality. When to use: Suitable for tomographic reconstruction and other inverse problems where L1 regularization on gradients is desired and second-order convergence is beneficial. When not to use: If the operator norm is too expensive to compute or if the problem size is extremely large, first-order methods might be preferred. The method is based on the reference implementation from the learnedgradienttomography repository. It combines classical tomographic reconstruction techniques (FBP with Hann filter) with modern optimization methods (BFGS with Moreau envelope) to solve inverse problems. The use of the Moreau envelope to smooth the L1 norm is a standard technique in convex optimization to enable the use of gradient-based methods. adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, https://github.com/adler-j/learnedgradienttomography, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Monte Carlo Path Contribution Estimation
head: Caustic contribution estimation, RRTE path estimator
body: This method estimates the radiance contribution of a stationary light path found by the BFGS solver, based on the path formulation of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RRTE). It differs from standard path tracing by evaluating contributions for specific, optimized stationary paths rather than sampling paths stochastically from the camera, and it differs from the parent BFGS solver by handling the final radiance accumulation and variance reduction. Inputs: Stationary path \bar{\mathbf{x}}k = (\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1, \dots, \mathbf{x}n) found by the BFGS solver, where \mathbf{x}0 is the receiver (camera) and \mathbf{x}n is the light source. Refractive Index Field (RIF) \eta(\mathbf{x}) describing the media. Extinction coefficient \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Final inverse Hessian matrix from the BFGS solver. Scene geometry for occlusion testing. Outputs: Estimated radiance contribution I for the path. Data Structures: Path points \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Generalized geometric factor G. Transmittance T. Exact layouts, fields, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Numerically integrate the transmittance along each ray section \Gammak between \mathbf{x}k and \mathbf{x}{k+1}. 2. Trace a shadow ray from \mathbf{x}0 in the direction of \mathbf{x}1 to check for intersections with the rest of the scene or bubbles inside the panel. 3. Compute the generalized geometric factor G(\mathbf{x}1 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}{n-1}) for the specular interfaces using the implicit function theorem and the final inverse Hessian matrix from the BFGS solver. 4. Regularize G by clamping it to a minimum \epsilon value to prevent instability. 5. Estimate the inverse probability 1/p(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k) of the BFGS solver converging to the path using the unbiased iterative procedure described in [21]. 6. Compute the contribution function f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k) using the integrated transmittance, regularized geometric factors, and estimated probability. 7. Sum the weighted contributions over K samples to obtain the final radiance estimate. Formulas: Transmittance: T(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{x}{k+1}) = \exp \left( - \int{tk}^{t{k+1}} \sigmat(\mathbf{x}(\tau)) \eta(\mathbf{x}(\tau)) d\tau \right). Integration method: Composite Simpson rule, assuming \sigmat varies slowly within a single tetrahedral cell. Regularized geometric factor: \bar{G}(\mathbf{x}1 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}{n-1}) = \max(G(\mathbf{x}1 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow \mathbf{x}{n-1}), \epsilon). Contribution function: f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k) = We(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) \eta^2(\mathbf{x}n) Le(\mathbf{x}n, \mathbf{x}{n-1}) G(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) T(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) \prod{i=1}^{n-1} G(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) T(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}) fc(\mathbf{x}{i-1}, \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{x}{i+1}). Final estimator: I \simeq \sum{k=1}^K \frac{f(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k)}{p(\bar{\mathbf{x}}k)}. Symbol definitions: We is the exitance weight, \eta(\mathbf{x}n) is the refractive index at the source, Le is a radiance term, fc is a scattering term, G is the geometric factor, T is transmittance, p is the sampling probability, and i is the product index running from 1 to n-1. The source formula explicitly places G(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) and T(\mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1) outside the product despite \mathbf{x}0 being the camera. Parameters: \epsilon: Regularization constant for G. Typical values: 10^{-2} to 10^{-3}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The computation of G can be unstable, leading to high variance, necessitating regularization. The BFGS solver initialization does not guarantee finding all possible paths in regions with strong RIF variations, which may cause local underestimation of transmitted lighting. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is used in conjunction with BFGS optimization. The text mentions 1M samples per pixel at 1024x1024 resolution for the final images, but this refers to the overall rendering pipeline, not just this estimator. Strengths: Provides an unbiased estimate of the contribution of stationary paths. Regularization helps eliminate highly contributing outliers. Limitations: Can locally underestimate the brightest parts of the transmitted caustic due to regularization. May miss paths in regions with strong RIF variations. This method is part of a pipeline for rendering old glass windows, where ancient windows were composed of several smaller fragments of glass assembled with lead. The method builds on the path formulation of the RRTE. name: Training Protocol
head: DCCVT Optimization Setup, DCCVT Training Configuration
body: The Training Protocol defines the standard optimization procedure for neural networks in differentiable volume rendering, encompassing optimizer settings, learning rate scheduling, and data augmentation strategies. It addresses the instability of training coordinate-based neural fields by providing a robust configuration for convergence, particularly when dealing with noisy real-world scan data or complex geometric priors. It sets itself apart from generic optimization loops by explicitly integrating domain-specific augmentations (such as Gaussian noise for point clouds) and specific regularization techniques (like CVT for discretization stability) into the core training loop. The protocol establishes a baseline configuration for training neural implicit representations, with specific variations for different architectural needs (e.g., pilot networks, variable views). Inputs: Input data (point clouds, voxel grids, or radiographic projections), target values (SDF, density, color), and hyperparameters (optimizer settings, batch size, epochs). Outputs: Trained neural network weights and biases. Optimizer State: Maintains first and second moment estimates for Adam/AdamW. Learning Rate Scheduler: Tracks current learning rate based on epoch/step count. Pilot Network (Optional): A small MLP used for early-stage coarse geometry estimation. 1. Initialization: Initialize the main neural network parameters. For methods like DCCVT, initialize both the main model and auxiliary structures (like MTet sites) with the same initial sites. If using a Pilot Network, initialize it with two hidden layers, each containing 64 neurons. Normalize input coordinates and target values to the range [-1, 1] to match the output range of activation functions like \sin(\cdot). Initialize weights using a standard scheme (e.g., Kaiming uniform or the protocol by Sitzmann et al. for SIREN-like networks). 2. Early Training (Pilot Phase - Optional): If a Pilot Network is employed, use it for the first N{pilot} steps (e.g., 300 steps). The pilot network functions as a standard volume rendering model to aid in finding coarse geometry, preventing convergence failure caused by feature integration of all samples in the early stage. After N{pilot} steps, discard the pilot network and switch to the main framework (e.g., VFR) for the remaining training steps. 3. Main Training Loop: For each epoch or iteration: a. Data Augmentation: Apply random scaling and translation to input data. For point cloud inputs, add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \sigma = 0.5 (assuming unit cube cells) to simulate real scan noise. For variable-view methods (e.g., X-GRM), randomly select the number of views from a set (e.g., \{6, 8, 10\}) evenly sampled from available projections. b. Forward Pass: Compute the rendered output (e.g., SDF, density, color) using the current network weights. If using structured latent codes, compute their contribution with a higher learning rate multiplier (e.g., 10\times). c. Loss Computation: Compute the loss using the same functions as the baseline method (e.g., UNDC). For DCCVT, incorporate CVT regularization to maintain discretization stability, distinct from pure Chamfer distance optimization. d. Backward Pass: Compute gradients with respect to network parameters. e. Optimization Step: Update parameters using the Adam or AdamW optimizer. Apply learning rate decay as specified (e.g., halve every 100 epochs, cosine annealing, or multistep). 4. Post-Training: Save the model weights. For MoE-INR, use 16-bit floating point for storage while training/inference uses 32-bit. Adam Optimizer Update: \theta{t+1} = \thetat - \frac{\eta \cdot \hat{m}t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}t} + \epsilon} Where \eta is the learning rate, \hat{m}t is the bias-corrected first moment, and \hat{v}t is the bias-corrected second moment. Gaussian Noise Augmentation: p{noisy} = p{clean} + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) Where \sigma = 0.5 for point cloud inputs. Optimizer: Adam or AdamW. Learning Rate (\eta): Standard: 1 \times 10^{-4} or 5 \times 10^{-4} or 0.0001. MoE-INR: 2 \times 10^{-5}. UVA: Decay from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-6}. Beta Coefficients (\beta1, \beta2): Common: (0.9, 0.999). DCCVT: (0.8, 0.99). Batch Size: Standard: 1 (per shape). UVA: 1024. MoE-INR: 16,000. Iterations/Epochs: DCCVT: 1000 iterations. Neural Dual Contouring: 400 epochs (SDF/voxel) or 250 epochs (point cloud). UVA: 300K iterations. MoE-INR: 30 pre-training epochs + 270 training epochs. Precision: Standard: 32-bit float. X-GRM: bFloat16. Convergence Failure: In early training, feature integration of all samples can cause convergence failure. Using a pilot network for the first 300 steps mitigates this. Noisy Data: Real scan data requires heavy augmentation, including Gaussian noise (\sigma=0.5) and random transformations, to prevent overfitting to artifacts. Discretization Stability: For methods like DCCVT, omitting CVT regularization can lead to instability, especially with non-uniform site distributions. This method addresses the inefficiency of optimizing coordinate-based neural networks from random weights for each new signal by applying meta-learning to derive optimal initial weight parameters. It sets itself apart from standard training protocols by decoupling the initialization phase from the specific instance optimization, allowing the network to start closer to the solution manifold of a target signal class (e.g., faces, 3D shapes). This results in faster convergence and improved generalization when only partial observations are available. This protocol defines a specific training schedule for differentiable volume rendering that combines background augmentation with density regularization to suppress floating artifacts and stabilize convergence. It addresses the instability of immediate background augmentation and the emergence of scene-matching floaters by enforcing a strict temporal sequence: constant-color initialization, followed by augmented backgrounds, and finally density priors. It differs from standard training by explicitly decoupling the learning of general scene structure from the refinement of density bias and object compactness. This article specifies the activation functions, dropout regularization, and latent space dimensionality validation for neural networks in radiance-field optimization. It addresses stabilizing training and preventing overfitting in differentiable rendering pipelines by defining architectural hyperparameters. It builds on Training Protocol. A small neural network used during the early training stage to aid the model in finding coarse geometry, preventing convergence failure caused by feature integration of all samples. It uses two hidden layers, each with 64 neurons, and is only used in the first 300 training steps. After 300 steps, the pilot network is discarded, and the main framework (e.g., VFR) takes over for the remaining training steps (e.g., total 20K steps). Optimizes the UVA model using Adam with learning rate decay from 5 \times 10^{-4} to 5 \times 10^{-6}. Structured latent codes have a 10\times learning rate relative to the base rate. The motion field and canonical field are jointly trained for 300K iterations with a batch size of 1024. Training takes about 10 hours using two NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs. Optimizes the X-GRM model using AdamW with a batch size of 8 for 100 epochs. The initial learning rate is 2 \times 10^{-5}, with \beta1 = 0.9 and \beta2 = 0.999. It uses bFloat16 precision for model storage, while training uses 32-bit float. It employs variable-view learning, randomly selecting views from available projections. Pre-trains the model for 30 epochs, then trains for 270 epochs. Coordinates and target values are normalized to [-1, 1]. Uses Adam with initial learning rate 2 \times 10^{-5}, \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.999, and a multistep scheduler for decay. Uses 32-bit float for training/inference and 16-bit for storage. Batch size is 16,000. Parameter initialization follows the protocol by Sitzmann et al.. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and batch size. For example, UVA training takes ~10 hours on two V100s for 300K iterations. Memory Complexity: Large batch sizes (MoE-INR: 16,000) require significant memory. Strengths: Robust to noisy data with appropriate augmentation. Pilot networks prevent early-stage convergence failure. CVT regularization ensures discretization stability. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of learning rate schedules and augmentation parameters. Pilot networks add complexity to the early training phase. When to Use: Use for training neural implicit representations in volume rendering, especially when dealing with noisy point clouds or requiring stable discretization. Use pilot networks for difficult initial geometry estimation. The training protocol for neural volume rendering has evolved from standard optimization techniques (Adam, learning rate decay) to more specialized configurations addressing the unique challenges of implicit representations. Early work focused on basic convergence, while later methods introduced specific regularizations (CVT), pilot networks for stability, and large-scale configurations for efficiency. The protocol is widely used in differentiable rendering pipelines for tasks like surface reconstruction, view synthesis, and 3D shape editing. name: Learned Initializations for Neural Fields
head: Learned Initializations for Optimizing Coordinate-Based Neural Representations, Learned Weight Initialization, Meta-learning for Neural Field Initialization
body: This method addresses the inefficiency of optimizing coordinate-based neural networks from random weights for each new signal by applying meta-learning to derive optimal initial weight parameters. It sets itself apart from standard training protocols by decoupling the initialization phase from the specific instance optimization, allowing the network to start closer to the solution manifold of a target signal class (e.g., faces, 3D shapes). This results in faster convergence and improved generalization when only partial observations are available. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of signals belonging to a specific class (e.g., 2D images of faces or 3D models of chairs). Output: A set of initial weight parameters \theta0 for a fully-connected neural network. Data Structures: The network is a standard fully-connected multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The learned initialization is a fixed tensor of weights and biases corresponding to the network architecture. Steps: 1. Meta-Training Phase: Apply standard meta-learning algorithms to learn the initial weight parameters for fully-connected networks based on the underlying class of signals being represented. The goal is to find \theta0 such that a few gradient steps on any new signal from the class yield a good approximation. 2. Instance Optimization Phase: For a new target signal (e.g., a specific 3D shape or image), initialize the network weights with the learned \theta0. Perform standard gradient descent (or Adam) to optimize the network parameters \theta to fit the new signal's observations. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Class Mismatch: Not given in the sources. Overfitting to Meta-Training Data: The learned initialization might overfit to the specific distribution of the meta-training set, reducing generalization to unseen variations within the class. Generates a geometric prior by pre-training a randomly initialized network to match a target SDF shape (specifically an inverted sphere) before scene reconstruction. It addresses the inefficiency of optimizing coordinate-based networks from random weights when the architecture lacks direct positional encoding for initialization. Unlike methods that hardcode SDF geometry into MLP weights, this relies on a dedicated optimization phase to embed the initialization. Choose it when a geometric prior is needed before full scene reconstruction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the learned initialization weights, which is negligible compared to the network weights themselves. Strengths: Faster convergence, better generalization with partial data, strong prior for the signal class. Limitations: Requires a diverse and representative meta-training dataset. When to Use: When optimizing multiple instances from the same signal class (e.g., reconstructing multiple faces). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Mildenhall et al. as part of their work on generalizing neural radiance fields and coordinate-based representations. It builds on the observation that coordinate-based MLPs suffer from slow convergence when trained from scratch. The approach leverages meta-learning to transfer knowledge across signals of the same class. It builds on Training Protocol. name: SDF Initialization via Overfitting
head: Inverted Sphere Pre-training, Neural Field Pre-training via Overfitting
body: This method initializes a Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation by overfitting a neural network to a target geometric shape (typically an inverted sphere) before commencing the primary scene reconstruction optimization. It addresses the challenge of initializing neural fields that do not accept position coordinates as direct inputs to the MLP, where hardcoding weights is not feasible. It is distinguished from alternatives like NeuS-facto and Neuralangelo, which hardcode the inverted sphere directly into MLP weights by leveraging position inputs, by requiring a dedicated pre-training phase to embed the initialization. Inputs: Randomly initialized model weights W0. Target SDF shape definition (e.g., inverted sphere). Pre-training hyperparameters: number of epochs E{init}. Outputs: Optimized weights W{init} that encode the target SDF shape. Data Structures: The neural network architecture (e.g., RING-NeRF). Loss function measuring the difference between the network's output and the target SDF values. Steps: 1. Initialize the model weights randomly. 2. Define the target SDF function S{target}(\mathbf{x}) corresponding to the desired initialization shape (e.g., an inverted sphere). 3. Perform optimization to minimize the loss between the network output S{net}(\mathbf{x}) and S{target}(\mathbf{x}) for E{init} epochs. 4. Use the resulting weights W{init} as the starting point for the "true" training on the actual scene data. Parameters: Pre-training epochs: 1000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializesdfviaoverfitting(network, targetsdffunction, epochs=1000): """ Initializes network weights by overfitting to a target SDF shape. Args: network: The neural network to initialize (e.g., RING-NeRF). targetsdffunction: A function S(x) returning the target SDF value for point x. epochs: Number of pre-training epochs (default 1000). Returns: network: The network with initialized weights. """ # Step 1: Initialize weights randomly network.randominitialize() # Step 2 & 3: Overfit to the target initialization scheme # The target scheme is typically an inverted sphere for epoch in range(epochs): # Sample points x from the domain of interest points = samplepoints() # Compute target SDF values targets = targetsdffunction(points) # Forward pass to get current network predictions predictions = network(points) # Compute loss (e.g., MSE) between predictions and targets loss = meansquarederror(predictions, targets) # Backpropagate and update weights network.updateweights(loss) # Step 4: Return network ready for true scene training return network Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Architecture Dependency: This method is specifically required for architectures like RING-NeRF that do not input position directly to the MLP, making weight hardcoding impossible. Failure without Initialization: Training without this initialization can lead to catastrophic failure or significantly noisier results (lower PSNR) compared to initialized counterparts. This method initializes a Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation by overfitting a neural network to an input point cloud. It leverages the Hotspot architecture to create a precise geometric prior before beginning the main scene reconstruction optimization. It is distinguished from generic overfitting by the specific use of the Hotspot network structure. Time Complexity: Adds a pre-training phase of 1000 epochs before the main training loop. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead beyond the standard network weights during pre-training. Performance: Prevents catastrophic failure in scenes where training without initialization fails. Results in higher PSNR metrics and less noise in RGB and depth compared to non-initialized training. Strengths: Effective for architectures that cannot hardcode initialization into weights. Limitations: Requires extra pre-training time. Not applicable to architectures that support direct weight hardcoding via position inputs (e.g., NeuS-facto, Neuralangelo). This method was introduced in the context of RING-NeRF, which rethinks inductive biases for versatile and efficient neural fields. It was developed to handle the specific constraints of RING-NeRF's architecture, which does not input position directly to the MLP, unlike NeuS-facto and Neuralangelo. The approach was evaluated against baselines without initialization and those with scene-specific initialization using SDF inverted spheres. name: SDF Initialization with Hotspot
head: Hotspot-based SDF Initialization
body: This method initializes a Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation by overfitting a neural network to an input point cloud. It leverages the Hotspot architecture to establish a geometric prior before scene reconstruction begins. Inputs: Input point cloud P. Training iterations T (typically 10,000 for full convergence or 500 for imprecise initialization). Outputs: A trained neural network model \mathcal{N} serving as the initialized SDF representation. Data Structures: The Hotspot neural network. Internal architecture details (layer sizes, activations) are not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Apply a random perturbation of magnitude 0.005 to point positions in P to avoid coplanarity. Normalize P and initial site positions to the cube [-1, 1]^3. 2. Overfitting: Train the Hotspot network \mathcal{N} to match the input point cloud P. 3. Selection: Select the trained model based on desired precision: use the model trained for T=10,000 iterations for a precise SDF, or the model trained for T=500 iterations to evaluate performance under an imprecise representation. 4. Initialization: Assign the selected model \mathcal{N} as the initial SDF representation for subsequent optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method may fail to produce a reliable SDF for certain shapes (e.g., shape ID 398259). Initialization quality is directly controlled by the iteration count T. Initializes the SDF using a coarser, unconverged state rather than a fully converged one to prevent optimization from trapping in local minima. It sets itself apart by explicitly leveraging the regularization benefits of an incomplete initialization. Choose this variant when complex scenes risk catastrophic failure from overly precise geometric priors. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The fully converged variant (10k iterations) yields a precise SDF representation. The unconverged variant (500 iterations) is used to benchmark performance under imprecise SDF conditions. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides a state-of-the-art neural network initialization for SDFs. Limitations: Fails to produce reliable SDFs for specific shapes (e.g., shape ID 398259). When to Use: When a precise SDF prior is required for neural field optimization. When Not to Use: When the input geometry matches known failure cases for Hotspot (e.g., shape ID 398259). Origin: The method adopts the Hotspot neural network. The original Hotspot paper is cited as [40] within the source. History and Development: Introduced in the DCCVT paper. Where it is Used: Used to initialize SDF representations in neural field optimization pipelines. name: SDF Initialization via Coarse-to-Fine Strategy
head: Coarse SDF Initialization, SDF State Initialization Pitfall, Unconverged SDF Initialization
body: This method initializes the Signed Distance Field (SDF) using a coarser, unconverged state rather than a fully converged one to prevent the optimization process from trapping in local minima. While a fully converged SDF provides a precise geometric prior, it can lead to catastrophic failure in complex scenes by restricting the optimization landscape. This approach builds on SDF Initialization with Hotspot by explicitly leveraging the regularization benefits of an incomplete initialization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A neural field model initialized with SDF values derived from a coarse or partially trained state. Output: A refined SDF field that avoids local minima traps associated with over-regularized initial states. Data Structures: The SDF field is represented as a continuous function f(\mathbf{x}) mapping 3D coordinates to signed distances. The "coarse" state implies that the network weights have not been optimized to minimize the SDF loss to convergence, leaving the field less constrained. Steps: 1. Initialize SDF State: Instead of training the SDF component until convergence (which yields a "hotspot" or highly refined surface), halt the initial training phase early. 2. Begin Optimization Loop: Start the main differentiable volume rendering optimization loop using this unconverged SDF as the prior. 3. Regularization Effect: The unconverged state acts as a regularizer. Because the initial surface is not perfectly fitted to the training data, the optimization has more freedom to explore the solution space, avoiding the local minima that a fully converged SDF would enforce. Pitfalls: Catastrophic Failure: Using a fully converged SDF initialization can trap the optimizer in a local minimum, leading to significant reconstruction errors (e.g., Mesh ID 252119 in). Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializesdfcoarsetofine(model, trainingdata, earlystopthreshold): """Initializes the SDF model using a coarse, unconverged state.""" for epoch in range(earlystopthreshold): sdfloss = computesdfloss(model, trainingdata) updateweights(model, sdfloss) if sdfloss < earlystopthreshold: break return model def computesdfloss(model, trainingdata): """Computes the loss for the SDF component.""" # Standard SDF loss computation (e.g., L1 distance to surface points or Eikonal regularization) return model.evaluatesdfloss(trainingdata) def computerenderingloss(model, trainingdata): """Computes the loss for the volume rendering component.""" # Standard differentiable volume rendering loss (e.g., MSE between rendered and target images) return model.evaluaterenderingloss(trainingdata) def updateweights(model, loss): """Performs a standard gradient descent step.""" # Standard gradient descent step gradients = computegradients(model, loss) model.applygradients(gradients) def computegradients(model, loss): """Computes gradients via backpropagation.""" # Standard automatic differentiation return model.backward(loss) def mainoptimizationloop(model, trainingdata, totalepochs): """Continues optimization from the coarse initialization.""" for epoch in range(totalepochs): renderingloss = computerenderingloss(model, trainingdata) updateweights(model, renderingloss) A training strategy that progressively transitions the scene representation from pure volumetric density to SDF to handle limited image overlap and complex urban scenes, avoiding the need for full scene observability required by bounded sphere initialization. Unlike StreetSurf, which initializes SDF based on road-surface, this method transitions from density to SDF, making it better suited for driving scenes with linear trajectories and reduced overlap. Choose this method when working with driving sequences or urban environments where camera trajectories are linear and image overlap is limited. See ViiNeS for implementation details. Strengths: Prevents catastrophic failure in complex scenes by avoiding local minima traps associated with fully converged SDFs. Provides better regularization for the optimization loop. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Performance: Results in significantly improved surface discretization compared to converged initializations in near-sampling and upsampling settings. This method addresses the "SDF State Initialization Pitfall" identified in differentiable volume rendering research. It was highlighted in the context of DCCVT (Differentiable Clipped Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation), where fully converged SDFs were found to cause catastrophic failures in specific mesh reconstructions (e.g., Mesh ID 252119 and 398259). The approach contrasts with progressive initialization methods like ViiNeS, which handle limited overlap by transitioning from density to SDF, whereas this method focuses on the state of the SDF itself during the initialization phase of a standard optimization loop. name: Training Protocol with Augmented Backgrounds and Density Prior
head: Gradient Descent Optimization with Augmented Backgrounds and Density Prior
body: This protocol defines a training schedule for neural volume rendering that combines background augmentation with density regularization to suppress floating artifacts and stabilize convergence. It addresses the instability of immediate background augmentation and the emergence of scene-matching floaters by enforcing a strict temporal sequence: constant-color initialization, followed by augmented backgrounds, and finally density priors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Neural network parameters (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}), camera poses, target images, and optimization step limit. Output: Optimized neural network parameters. Data Structures: Step Counter: Integer t tracking optimization iterations. Background Color: Vector \mathbf{b} used for compositing. Parameters: \lambda1 = 2 \cdot 10^{-5}: Weight for density regularization. \lambda2 = 8 \cdot 10^{-4}: Weight for color regularization. T{\text{bg}} = 25: Step threshold to switch from constant gray to augmented backgrounds. T{\text{prior}} = 100: Step threshold to begin applying density prior. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize network parameters and set t = 1. 2. Select background \mathbf{b}: if t < T{\text{bg}}, set \mathbf{b} to a random shade of gray; otherwise, sample \mathbf{b} from a distribution containing pure white, pure black, or random noise. 3. Render the image \hat{\mathbf{C}} by compositing the network's predicted density and color along camera rays against background \mathbf{b} using standard volume rendering integration. 4. Compute the color reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{\text{color}} between \hat{\mathbf{C}} and the target image \mathbf{C}{\text{target}}. 5. Compute the total loss \mathcal{L}: if t < T{\text{prior}}, \mathcal{L} = \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{color}}; if t \ge T{\text{prior}}, \mathcal{L} = \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{color}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{density}}, where \mathcal{L}{\text{density}} is a regularization term that encourages the volume material to be less transparent for important structures. 6. Perform a gradient descent update on the network parameters using \mathcal{L}. 7. Increment t and repeat until the step limit is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainwithaugmentedbackgroundsanddensityprior(networkparams, targetimages, cameraposes, numsteps, learningrate): # Parameters from lambdadensity = 2e-5 lambdacolor = 8e-4 tbgstart = 25 tpriorstart = 100 for t in range(1, numsteps + 1): # 1. Select Background if t < tbgstart: # Random shade of gray for stability in early steps background = [random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) for in range(3)] else: # Augmented background (e.g., white, black, or noise) augchoice = random.choice(['white', 'black', 'noise']) if augchoice == 'white': background = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] elif augchoice == 'black': background = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: background = [random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) for in range(3)] # 2. Render renderedcolor = standardvolumerender(networkparams, cameraposes, background) # 3. Compute Loss # Standard L2 color reconstruction loss colorloss = sum((r - t) 2 for r, t in zip(renderedcolor, targetimages)) / len(targetimages) totalloss = lambdacolor colorloss # 4. Apply Density Prior if step threshold reached if t >= tpriorstart: # Density prior encourages materials to be less transparent densityloss = sum(networkparams.density) / len(networkparams.density) # Simplified density regularization totalloss += lambdadensity densityloss # 5. Update Network gradients = computegradients(totalloss, networkparams) for param in networkparams: param -= learningrate gradients[param] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instability: Applying background augmentation immediately causes instability in the first few steps of gradient descent. Using a constant gray background for the first 25 steps mitigates this. Floaters: Simply compositing generated objects with the scene background introduces artifacts resembling the background, such as green floaters in a tree/grass scene. Augmenting the background with pure white or black during training makes these floaters apparent, allowing the optimization to suppress them. A variant strategy that combines sparsity loss to encourage compact object generation with background augmentation to eliminate artifacts. Sparsity loss is introduced during optimization to force the generated object to be compact, reducing floaters. Background augmentation with pure white or black is used to make remaining floaters apparent and easier to suppress. This approach specifically addresses the pitfall where compositing objects with complex scene backgrounds hides artifacts like green floaters in tree/grass scenes. Strengths: Stabilizes early training by avoiding aggressive background augmentation. Effectively reduces floating artifacts and "foggy" opacity patterns by making them visible against high-contrast backgrounds (white/black). Refines density bias after the general scene structure is established. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of step thresholds (T{\text{bg}}, T{\text{prior}}) and regularization weights (\lambda1, \lambda2). The density prior may over-regularize if applied too early, preventing the scene from being well-represented. When to Use: When training neural radiance fields for object insertion or scene editing where floating artifacts are a concern. When standard training produces unstable convergence in the first few steps. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The protocol originates from research on text-based transfer function design for semantic volume rendering and GO-NeRF for virtual reality content creation. The density prior component compares against existing methods like Beta prior, Dream Field, and Entropy-based priors, noting that Entropy and Beta produce higher opacity peaks. The background augmentation strategy was developed to address specific artifacts in object generation within neural radiance fields, such as green floaters in natural scenes. name: Network Training Settings
head: Activation and Dropout, General Network Configuration
body: This article specifies the activation functions, dropout regularization, and latent space dimensionality validation for neural networks in radiance-field optimization. It addresses stabilizing training and preventing overfitting in differentiable rendering pipelines by defining architectural hyperparameters. It builds on Training Protocol. Inputs: Network architecture definition (layer types, residual blocks) and training dataset. Outputs: A trained network with optimized weights and a validated latent space dimensionality. Not given in the sources. 1. Initialize Network: Construct the network using convolutional layers and residual blocks. 2. Apply Activation: Use Parametric ReLU (PReLU) for all hidden layers and a sigmoid function for the final output layer. 3. Apply Dropout: During training, apply dropout with probability p=0.5 after every convolutional layer, excluding layers within residual blocks. 4. Validate Latent Dimensionality: Test latent space dimensions d \in \{4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}. Modify the architecture to produce 64 \times 64 resolution images by removing the last few upsampling layers to reduce computational cost. Set the loss weight \lambda = 0 in the loss function to remove the L1 loss influence, as the latent space primarily impacts shape rather than color. Evaluate performance on the Combustion dataset without illumination. Select the dimension that minimizes color image RMSE, as latent space dimensionality has minimal impact on opacity image quality. 5. Finalize Configuration: Use the validated dimension (typically 8) for full-resolution training. Modified Loss Function: L = L{\text{adv}} + \lambda L{\text{L1}}, where \lambda = 0 during latent dimension validation to isolate shape impact from color. Dropout: Applied with probability p=0.5. Activation: PReLU for hidden layers, Sigmoid for output. Dropout Probability: 0.5. Latent Space Dimensions Tested: 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Optimal Latent Dimension: 8. Validation Resolution: 64 \times 64. Loss Weight (\lambda): 0 during validation. Overestimating Dimensionality: Using a latent space dimension larger than necessary results in poorer generalization and makes the TF latent space more difficult to sample. Color vs. Shape: Latent space dimensionality has minimal impact on opacity image quality but significant impact on color image quality. Computational Burden: Full-resolution training for all dimensions is computationally expensive; validation uses reduced resolution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializenetwork(layerdefinitions): network = [] for i, layer in enumerate(layerdefinitions): islast = (i == len(layerdefinitions) - 1) convop = lambda x: standardconvolution(x, layer['outchannels'], layer['kernelsize'], layer['stride']) if islast: activation = lambda x: 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-x)) else: activation = lambda x: max(0.01 x, x) network.append({'op': convop, 'act': activation, 'isresidual': layer.get('residual', False)}) return network def applydropout(network, training=True): if not training: return network for layer in network: layer['dropoutactive'] = not layer['isresidual'] return network def forwardpass(network, inputtensor): x = inputtensor for layer in network: x = layer'op' if layer['dropoutactive']: x = applydropoutmask(x, probability=0.5) x = layer'act' return x def validatelatentdimension(dataset, dimensions=[4, 8, 16, 32, 64], epochs=10): bestdim = None bestcolorrmse = float('inf') for dim in dimensions: model = buildmodel(latentdim=dim, outputresolution=(64, 64)) for in range(epochs): for batch in dataset: output = forwardpass(model, batch) # Lambda=0 removes L1 loss; only adversarial loss is computed loss = computeadversarialloss(output, batch) gradientdescentstep(model, loss) colorrmse = computermse(output, batch) if colorrmse < bestcolorrmse: bestcolorrmse = colorrmse bestdim = dim return bestdim def buildmodel(latentdim, outputresolution): # Remove last upsampling layers to match target resolution layerdefs = definearchitecture(latentdim, outputresolution) return initializenetwork(layerdefs) def applydropoutmask(tensor, probability): mask = randomuniform(tensor.shape) > probability return tensor mask / (1.0 - probability) def standardconvolution(tensor, outchannels, kernelsize, stride): # Standard convolution operation return tensor # Operation defined by standard convolution rules def computeadversarialloss(output, batch): # Adversarial loss computation return abs(output - batch) # Placeholder for specific adversarial metric def gradientdescentstep(model, loss): # Update model weights using gradient descent pass # Implementation depends on optimizer configuration def computermse(output, batch): # Root Mean Square Error calculation return sqrt(mean((output - batch) 2)) def definearchitecture(latentdim, outputresolution): # Define layer definitions based on latent dimension and resolution return [{'outchannels': 8, 'kernelsize': 5, 'stride': 2, 'residual': False}, {'outchannels': 16, 'kernelsize': 3, 'stride': 2, 'residual': False}, {'outchannels': 16, 'kernelsize': 3, 'stride': 1, 'residual': True}] # Example structure A validation process comparing networks with different latent space dimensionalities (4, 8, 16, 32, 64) to determine the optimal dimension for capturing shape variations. It sets \lambda=0 in the loss function to isolate shape impact from color. The optimal dimension found was 8, as higher dimensions lead to poorer generalization and sampling difficulties. Use this when determining the capacity of the latent space for a new dataset. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Strengths: PReLU and Dropout help stabilize training and prevent overfitting. Validating latent dimensionality ensures a balance between detail capture and generalization. Limitations: High-dimensional latent spaces are difficult to sample and may generalize poorly. Validation requires reduced resolution, which may not fully reflect full-resolution performance. Use: When training deep convolutional networks for differentiable rendering, especially when dealing with 3D shape and color reconstruction. Do Not Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and latent space validation is not feasible; consider using a fixed, smaller dimension (e.g., 4) with caution. Originated in the context of differentiable rendering and neural radiance fields. The activation and dropout settings are based on (RenderNet, 2018). The latent space dimensionality validation is based on (A Generative Model for Volume Rendering, 2018). These methods are used in volume rendering pipelines that require generative models for shape and color synthesis. name: X-GRM Training Configuration
head: X-GRM Implementation Details
body: X-GRM is a large Gaussian reconstruction model designed for sparse-view X-ray to Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction. This configuration defines the specific optimization protocol, including the AdamW optimizer settings, learning rate scheduling, and variable-view learning strategy, to train the model on synthetic radiographic projections. It distinguishes itself from other training protocols by employing a variable-number-of-views strategy during training to enhance robustness against sparse input views, combined with bFloat16 precision and gradient checkpointing for memory efficiency on large-scale GPU clusters. Inputs and Outputs Input: Synthetic radiographic projections. The dataset consists of 50 high-definition views (256x256 resolution) distributed uniformly throughout the complete angular spectrum [0^\circ, 360^\circ]. Output: Reconstructed 3D volumetric data (CT volume). Data Structures and Model Architecture The model consists of two Vision Transformer (ViT) components: 1. Encoder ViT (F{enc}): Uses ViT-B/16 architecture. Initialized from DINO pre-trained weights. 2. Fusion ViT (F{fuse}): Uses ViT-B/16 architecture. Initialized from scratch. Configuration: 16x16 patch size, 12 layers, 12 heads, embedding dimension 768, MLP ratio 4.0. Training Parameters Optimizer: AdamW. Batch Size: 8. Epochs: 100. Learning Rate Schedule: Cosine annealing. Initial Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-4}. Final Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-6}. Optimizer Hyperparameters: \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.95. Precision: bFloat16. Memory Optimization: Gradient checkpointing enabled. Hardware: 4 NVIDIA A100 (40G) GPUs for training. Algorithm Steps 1. Data Preparation: Generate or load synthetic radiographic projections. The source data includes 50 views with noise integration combining Gaussian and Poisson distributions to replicate quantum photon effects and Compton scatter phenomena. 2. Variable-View Selection: For each training step, randomly select the number of input views N from the set \{6, 8, 10\}. 3. View Sampling: Evenly sample N perspectives from the 50 available projections. 4. Forward Pass: Process the selected views through the Encoder ViT and Fusion ViT to generate the reconstruction. 5. Loss Computation: Calculate the loss based on the reconstructed volume and the ground truth. 6. Backward Pass: Compute gradients using bFloat16 precision with gradient checkpointing to reduce memory usage. 7. Update: Update model parameters using the AdamW optimizer with the current learning rate determined by the cosine annealing schedule. 8. Repeat: Iterate for 100 epochs. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainxgrm(): # Hyperparameters numepochs = 100 batchsize = 8 initiallr = 1e-4 finallr = 1e-6 beta1 = 0.9 beta2 = 0.95 availableviews = 50 # Total available projections viewoptions = [6, 8, 10] # Model Initialization encodervit = ViTB16(weights='DINOPRETRAINED') fusionvit = ViTB16( patchsize=16, layers=12, heads=12, embeddim=768, mlpratio=4.0, init='scratch') # Optimizer optimizer = AdamW( params=chain(encodervit.parameters(), fusionvit.parameters()), lr=initiallr, betas=(beta1, beta2)) # Learning Rate Scheduler (Cosine Annealing) scheduler = CosineAnnealingLR( optimizer=optimizer, Tmax=numepochs, etamin=finallr) # Training Loop for epoch in range(numepochs): for batch in dataloader: # Variable-view learning strategy numviews = random.choice(viewoptions) # Evenly sample views from the 50 available projections # Note: Implementation detail for 'evenly sampled' is not explicitly # defined in sources, assumed to be deterministic spacing or # pre-defined subsets. selectedindices = evenlysampleindices(availableviews, numviews) inputviews = batch['projections'][:, selectedindices,:,:] # Forward pass # encodervit and fusionvit process inputviews reconstructedvolume = forwardpass( inputviews, encodervit, fusionvit) # Compute loss (e.g., L1/L2 or perceptual loss in 3D space) # Source mentions PSNR calculated in 3D volumetric space loss = computeloss(reconstructedvolume, batch['groundtruth']) # Backward pass with gradient checkpointing loss.backward() # Optimizer step optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() # Update learning rate scheduler.step() SinGRAF uses a tri-plane representation with StyleGAN2 generator modulated by a noise vector z \sim \mathbb{R}^{128}. The tri-plane spatial resolution is 256x256 with feature channel count C=32. Rendering involves bilinear interpolation of features from the three planes followed by concatenation, processed by a decoder MLP (two shared linear layers, one density layer, two RGB layers, 64 hidden units with leakyReLU) to obtain color and density. Volume rendering uses 96 samples per ray without importance sampling. Training is performed on 64x64 patches, but a patch scale of s=0.25 allows effective 256x256 resolution rendering without 2D upsampling. Regularization balancing parameters are \lambda1 = 0.5 and \lambda2 = 50. The discriminator is a StyleGAN2 architecture with additional concatenation of patch scale. Inference Time: 0.928 seconds on one A100 GPU for 10-view input. Performance (10-View Input): PSNR of 29.21 and SSIM of 0.886. Performance (6-View Input): PSNR of 28.39 and SSIM of 0.873. Performance (8-View Input): PSNR of 28.86 and SSIM of 0.879. Memory Efficiency: Utilizes bFloat16 precision and gradient checkpointing to improve GPU memory and computational efficiency. Scalability: Trained on 4 NVIDIA A100 (40G) GPUs. X-GRM was introduced to address the challenge of reconstructing high-quality CT volumes from sparse-view X-ray projections. The method leverages large Gaussian reconstruction models and Vision Transformers. The training configuration was designed to handle synthetic radiographic data with clinical authenticity enhancements, including noise integration to replicate quantum photon effects and Compton scatter.
