name: VoxelTTO Training Configuration
head: VoxelTTO Training Details
body: VoxelTTO training configures the optimization of a voxel-aligned feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) module initialized from a frozen Visual Foundation Model (VFM). It solves the problem of adapting large pre-trained vision models to specific 3D reconstruction tasks via test-time optimization, keeping the VFM parameters frozen while optimizing only the lightweight 3DGS module. It differs from standard neural field training by employing a hybrid loss combining rendered depth/RGB with VFM-predicted depth alignment. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of 3–16 video frames resized to 224 \times 448 pixels. Ground-truth depth maps and RGB images are required for supervision. Outputs: Optimized parameters for the voxel-aligned feed-forward 3DGS module. The VFM weights remain frozen. Data Structures: Architecture: DA3-GIANT with L=40 alternating-attention layers. Parameters: Total model size is 1.39B parameters. Only 75.3M parameters are trainable (the 3DGS module). Initialization: The model is initialized with pretrained VFM weights. Loss Function: The total loss L is a weighted sum of depth and RGB losses: L = L{depth} + L{rgb} = \lambda{\ell^1d} L{\ell^1{depth}} + \lambda{align} L{align{depth}} + \lambda{\ell^1} L{\ell^1{rgb}} + \lambda{ssim} L{ssim{rgb}} Where: L{\ell^1{depth}}: \ell^1 loss between rendered depth and ground-truth depth. L{align{depth}}: Alignment loss between rendered depth and VFM-predicted depth. L{\ell^1{rgb}}: \ell^1 loss between rendered RGB and ground-truth RGB. L{ssim{rgb}}: SSIM loss between rendered RGB and ground-truth RGB. Loss Weights: \lambda{\ell^1d} = 0.25 \lambda{align} = 0.25 \lambda{\ell^1} = 0.9 \lambda{ssim} = 1.0 Optimization Steps: 1. Data Sampling: For each dataset, define a minimum and maximum frame gap. Randomly select an interval between the first and last frame within this range. Sample 3–16 frames from this interval. 2. Preprocessing: Resize input frames to 224 \times 448. 3. Initialization: Load pretrained DA3-GIANT weights. Freeze all VFM parameters. Initialize the voxel-aligned feed-forward 3DGS module. 4. Optimizer Setup: Use Adam optimizer. Set initial learning rate to 3 \times 10^{-6}. Set minimum learning rate to 10^{-8}. 5. Scheduling: Apply cosine annealing schedule with a 2K warm-up period. 6. Iteration: Perform 30K optimization iterations. 7. Loss Computation: At each step, render depth and RGB from the current 3DGS representation. Compute L{depth} and L{rgb} using the defined weights. Backpropagate only through the trainable 3DGS parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def l1loss(a, b): return sum(abs(a[i] - b[i]) for i in range(len(a))) / len(a) def alignmentloss(rendered, vfmpred): return sum(abs(rendered[i] - vfmpred[i]) for i in range(len(rendered))) / len(rendered) def ssimloss(rendered, gt): return sum((rendered[i] - gt[i])2 for i in range(len(rendered))) / len(rendered) class AdamOptimizer: def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.m = {id(p): 0.0 for p in params} self.v = {id(p): 0.0 for p in params} self.t = 0 def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = 0.0 def step(self): self.t += 1 for p in self.params: g = p.grad self.m[id(p)] = 0.9 self.m[id(p)] + 0.1 g self.v[id(p)] = 0.999 self.v[id(p)] + 0.001 g2 bc1 = 1.0 - 0.9self.t bc2 = 1.0 - 0.999self.t p -= self.lr (self.m[id(p)] / bc1) / (math.sqrt(self.v[id(p)] / bc2) + 1e-8) NUMITERATIONS = 30000 WARMUPITERATIONS = 2000 INITIALLR = 3e-6 MINLR = 1e-8 LAMBDAL1D = 0.25 LAMBDAALIGN = 0.25 LAMBDAL1RGB = 0.9 LAMBDASSIM = 1.0 FRAMECOUNTMIN = 3 FRAMECOUNTMAX = 16 RESIZEWIDTH = 224 RESIZEHEIGHT = 448 model = initializeDA3GIANT(L=40) vfmparams = model.getfrozenparams() gsparams = model.gettrainableparams() # 75.3M trainable 3DGS module optimizer = AdamOptimizer(gsparams, lr=INITIALLR) for iteration in range(NUMITERATIONS): # Data sampling: sources do not specify exact frame selection logic beyond gap bounds mingap, maxgap = 1, 10 # Placeholder bounds; actual bounds depend on dataset gap = random.randint(mingap, maxgap) frameindices = random.sample(range(gap), k=random.randint(FRAMECOUNTMIN, FRAMECOUNTMAX)) frames = [loadframe(idx) for idx in frameindices] # Standard I/O # Preprocessing: resize frames to 224x448 frames = [resizeimage(f, RESIZEWIDTH, RESIZEHEIGHT) for f in frames] # Standard I/O gtdepth, gtrgb = getgroundtruth(frames) # Standard I/O # Forward pass: render depth/RGB and get VFM depth prediction rendereddepth, renderedrgb = model.forward(frames) vfmdepth = model.vfmpredictdepth(frames) # VFM frozen # Loss computation l1depth = l1loss(rendereddepth, gtdepth) aligndepth = alignmentloss(rendereddepth, vfmdepth) l1rgb = l1loss(renderedrgb, gtrgb) ssimrgb = ssimloss(renderedrgb, gtrgb) loss = (LAMBDAL1D l1depth + LAMBDAALIGN aligndepth + LAMBDAL1RGB l1rgb + LAMBDASSIM ssimrgb) # Optimization step optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Learning rate scheduling progress = iteration / NUMITERATIONS if iteration < WARMUPITERATIONS: currentlr = INITIALLR (iteration / WARMUPITERATIONS) else: currentlr = MINLR + 0.5 (INITIALLR - MINLR) (1 + math.cos(math.pi (progress - WARMUPITERATIONS/NUMITERATIONS) / (1 - WARMUPITERATIONS/NUMITERATIONS))) optimizer.lr = currentlr A technique to exploit known camera parameters while keeping the pretrained visual foundation model (VFM) parameters frozen. It adapts lightweight LoRA modules using pose supervision. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 40 hours. Hardware: 2 RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient adaptation of large VFMs by freezing most parameters. Combines ground-truth supervision with VFM priors for robust depth alignment. Limitations: Limited to sequential frame inputs. VoxelTTO was introduced in the paper "VoxelTTO: Voxel-Aligned Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Test-Time Optimization" by Lin et al. (2025). It builds on the DA3-GIANT architecture and aims to improve 3D reconstruction accuracy by leveraging test-time optimization with frozen visual foundation models. name: Test-Time Optimization
head: TTO for VFMs, Test-Time Optimization (TTO) for VFMs
body: Test-Time Optimization (TTO) is a technique that exploits known camera parameters while keeping the pretrained visual foundation model (VFM) parameters frozen, adapting lightweight Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules using pose supervision. It addresses misalignment in novel view synthesis by aligning predicted camera parameters with ground truth during inference. Unlike standard inference which uses fixed weights, TTO performs a brief optimization loop on test data to refine the model's internal representation of camera geometry without retraining the backbone. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Pretrained VFM backbone (frozen), LoRA modules (trainable), input image(s), initial predicted camera poses (R{pi}, ti, k), and ground-truth camera poses (R{gi}, t{gi}, k{gi}) if available for supervision. Outputs: Optimized LoRA parameters and refined camera parameters. Data Structures The network architecture follows DA3 with L=40 attention layers. Layers 1–12: Single-view attention. Layers 13–40: Alternate between single-view and global attention. LoRA Layout: LoRA is added to the Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) projections in layers 13–40. Each layer shares a down-projection matrix A, while up-projection matrices B are independent per layer. Steps 1. Initialization: Insert LoRA modules into the VFM backbone at layers 13–40. 2. Pose Alignment (Pre-computation): Fix the first ground-truth camera pose to the identity matrix to establish a common coordinate frame. Address scale ambiguity by normalizing translation vectors. Compute the mean scale s for predicted translations ti and ground-truth translations t{gi} separately: s = \frac{1}{M-1} \sum{i=1}^M \|ti\|2 where M is the number of frames in the sequence. 3. Loss Calculation: Rotation Loss (L{rot}): Constructed from the relative rotation between predicted R{pi} and ground-truth R{gi} rotations: L{rot} = \frac{1}{2M} \sum{i=1}^M (3 - \text{tr}(R{pi}^\top R{gi})) Translation Loss (L{trans}): Calculate the scale-normalized translation loss using SmoothL1 between predicted and ground-truth translations. Intrinsic Loss (L{intrinsics}): Supervise camera intrinsics k = (fx, fy, cx, cy) by directly applying SmoothL1 to predicted and ground-truth values. 4. Optimization Loop: Compute the total TTO loss: L{TTO} = \lambda{pose} (L{rot} + wt L{trans}) + \lambdaK L{intrinsics} Update LoRA parameters by backpropagation for a fixed number of iterations. Parameters \lambda{pose}: Weight for pose loss. Not given in the sources. wt: Weight for translation loss. Not given in the sources. \lambdaK: Weight for intrinsic loss. Not given in the sources. Number of iterations: Fixed, but exact value not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def testtimeoptimization(vfmbackbone, loramodules, images, predictedposes, groundtruthposes, lambdapose, wt, lambdaK, numiterations): # Step 1: Align coordinate frames # Fix first ground-truth pose to identity matrix groundtruthposes.Rgi[0] = [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] # Step 2: Normalize scales to address ambiguity M = len(predictedposes.ti) # Compute mean scale for predicted translations scalepred = sum(norm(t) for t in predictedposes.ti) / (M - 1) # Compute mean scale for ground-truth translations scalegt = sum(norm(t) for t in groundtruthposes.tgi) / (M - 1) # Normalize translations tinorm = [t / scalepred for t in predictedposes.ti] tginorm = [t / scalegt for t in groundtruthposes.tgi] optimizerstate = {} for step in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Zero gradients for p in loramodules.parameters(): p.grad = None # Forward pass through VFM with LoRA # Note: The exact forward pass mechanism for camera decoding is not detailed in the sources. predictedposes = vfmforward(vfmbackbone, loramodules, images) # Calculate Rotation Loss: Lrot = 1/(2M) sum(3 - tr(Rpi^T @ Rgi)) rotloss = 0.0 for i in range(M): Rpi = predictedposes.Rpi[i] Rgi = groundtruthposes.Rgi[i] RpiTRgi = matmul(transpose(Rpi), Rgi) rotloss += 3.0 - trace(RpiTRgi) rotloss /= (2.0 M) # Calculate Translation Loss: SmoothL1 on normalized translations transloss = 0.0 for i in range(M): transloss += smoothl1loss(tinorm[i], tginorm[i]) transloss /= M # Calculate Intrinsic Loss: SmoothL1 on intrinsics intrinsicloss = smoothl1loss(predictedposes.k, groundtruthposes.k) # Total TTO Loss: LTTO = lambdapose (Lrot + wt Ltrans) + lambdaK Lintrinsics loss = lambdapose (rotloss + wt transloss) + lambdaK intrinsicloss # Backpropagation and parameter update loss.backward() adamstep(loramodules.parameters(), [p.grad for p in loramodules.parameters()], optimizerstate, step) return loramodules def norm(v): return sum(x2 for x in v)0.5 def transpose(M): return [[M[j][i] for j in range(len(M))] for i in range(len(M[0]))] def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k]B[k][j] for k in range(len(B))) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def trace(M): return sum(M[i][i] for i in range(len(M))) def smoothl1loss(pred, target): diff = [p - t for p, t in zip(pred, target)] return sum(0.5 x2 if abs(x) < 1.0 else abs(x) - 0.5 for x in diff) / len(diff) def adamstep(params, grads, state, t, lr=1e-3, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): for p, g in zip(params, grads): if p not in state: state[p] = {'m': [0.0]len(p), 'v': [0.0]len(p)} m, v = state[p]['m'], state[p]['v'] for i in range(len(p)): m[i] = beta1 m[i] + (1 - beta1) g[i] v[i] = beta2 v[i] + (1 - beta2) g[i]2 mhat = m[i] / (1 - beta1t) vhat = v[i] / (1 - beta2t) p[i] -= lr mhat / (vhat0.5 + eps) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Scale Ambiguity: Image-based reconstruction has inherent scale ambiguity. Failure to normalize translations by their mean scale s will result in incorrect loss values. Coordinate Frame: The first ground-truth pose must be fixed to the identity matrix to align the predicted and ground-truth coordinate systems before computing relative rotation. LoRA Placement: LoRA is strictly applied only to layers 13–40. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations, which is fixed but unspecified. The full model training requires 80 GPU hours, while test-time optimization is described as lightweight and brief. Memory Complexity: Adds the memory overhead of LoRA parameters, with the full VoxelTTO framework introducing 75.3M trainable parameters. Strengths: Improves geometric fidelity and camera-pose estimation for novel view synthesis (NVS). Compatible with any VGGT-style VFMs. Limitations: Requires ground-truth camera poses for supervision during the optimization loop. Performance depends on the quality of the initial predicted poses. When to use: When known camera parameters are available and alignment between predicted and ground-truth poses is critical for high-quality NVS. When not to use: When ground-truth poses are unavailable or when computational resources for iterative optimization are limited. Test-Time Optimization (TTO) was introduced in the VoxelTTO paper. It builds upon the DA3 architecture and VGGT-style visual foundation models. The method was developed to address misalignment issues in novel view synthesis, particularly when injecting camera parameters into the model. It replaces vanilla 3DGS rasterization with stochastic solid volume rendering to improve geometric supervision. name: Inverse Rendering Optimization Setup
head: Adam optimizer for inverse rendering, L2 loss optimization
body: This method configures the optimization loop for inverse rendering of implicit surfaces, using the Adam optimizer with an L2 loss function. It recovers geometry from multi-view observations by minimizing the difference between rendered and ground-truth images. Inputs: Implicit surface representation (grid-based SDF with tricubic interpolation). Nv = 8 camera views. Ground-truth images for the camera views. Differentiable renderer (e.g., Mitsuba 3 with cudaadrgb backend). Outputs: Optimized implicit surface parameters (SDF grid values). Data Structures: SDF Grid: Parameter array storing signed distance values and interpolation weights. Optimizer State: Adam maintains first and second moment estimates for each SDF parameter. name: Emission UV Texture Map Optimization
head: Emission Texture Optimization, Inverse Rendering Optimization
body: This method recovers an emission UV texture map for a scene mesh by minimizing the rendering loss between ground-truth HDR images and rendered images, using L1 regularization and adaptive clipping/boosting to encourage sparsity and accelerate convergence. It differs from differentiable rasterization inverse rendering by supporting a maximum light transport depth of 3 (2 bounces) instead of 2 (1 bounce), enabling indirect lighting optimization. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of ground-truth 32-bit HDR images \{I1, \dots, In\} with dimensions (h{\text{im}}, w{\text{im}}, c{\text{im}}) and known camera poses; a UV-unwrapped mesh with associated UV coordinates; a fixed BSDF parameter set (albedo texture map, specular transmission map at 1.0, roughness map at 0.5). Outputs: An optimized emission UV texture map T{\text{emission}} with dimensions (h{\text{tx}}, w{\text{tx}}, c{\text{tx}}); a pruned mesh containing only faces with emitting vertices. Data Structures T{\text{emission}}: A 3D texture map (height h{\text{tx}}, width w{\text{tx}}, channels c{\text{tx}}) storing emission values. Initialized uniformly with near-zero values. Mesh: A triangular mesh where each vertex has associated UV coordinates (u, v). Parameters \alpha: Tunable hyperparameter for the rendering loss weight. Cadence: Frequency of clipping/boosting steps. Default: every 2 epochs. Brightness threshold: Minimum emission value to be considered a light source. Default: 0.2. Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize T{\text{emission}} uniformly with near-zero values. Keep BSDF parameters fixed: albedo texture map, specular transmission map at 1.0, roughness map at 0.5. 2. Rendering: For each optimization step i \in [1, n] in a given epoch, render images \tilde{I}i from identical camera poses using a Path-Replay Backpropagation (PRB) integrator with maximum depth 3 (2 bounces) that directly renders emitters. 3. Regularization: Apply uniform L1 regularization to T{\text{emission}} to encourage sparsity, based on the inductive bias that most of the scene does not emit light. 4. Clipping and Boosting: Periodically (every Cadence epochs), perform the following on T{\text{emission}} in 32-bit linear color space: Clip values below the Brightness threshold to 0. Boost values above the Brightness threshold to accelerate convergence. This step is self-correcting via the rendering loss. 5. Convergence Check: Repeat steps 2-4 until convergence. 6. Post-processing: Prune triangular faces where all vertices fall below the Brightness threshold. Lookup vertex brightness via UV coordinates in T{\text{emission}}. The result is a reduced mesh used as an area light for shadow passes. Objective Function The objective is to minimize: \text{minimize} \frac{1}{\alpha} \| Ii - \tilde{I}i \|2^2 + \frac{\| T{\text{emission}} \|1}{h{\text{im}} w{\text{im}} c{\text{im}}} (h{\text{tx}} w{\text{tx}} c{\text{tx}}) where Ii is the ground truth image, \tilde{I}i is the rendered image, T{\text{emission}} is the emission UV texture map, (h{\text{im}}, w{\text{im}}, c{\text{im}}) are image dimensions, (h{\text{tx}}, w{\text{tx}}, c{\text{tx}}) are texture dimensions, and \alpha is a hyperparameter. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def optimizeemissiontexture(meshfaces, uvcoords, gtimages, cameraposes, alpha=1.0, cadence=2, threshold=0.2): # 1. Initialization htx, wtx, ctx = 1024, 1024, 3 # Standard UV texture dimensions Temission = np.zeros((htx, wtx, ctx)) # Fixed BSDF parameters albedomap = np.ones((htx, wtx, ctx)) # Pre-computed from MonoSDF appearance model speculartransmission = 1.0 roughness = 0.5 epoch = 0 prevloss = np.inf while True: # Standard convergence loop totalloss = 0.0 for i in range(len(gtimages)): gtimage = gtimages[i] pose = cameraposes[i] # 2. Rendering # Step: Render using Path-Replay Backpropagation (PRB) integrator with max depth 3. # Computes radiance at camera rays and returns image + gradients w.r.t. Temission. renderedimage, grads = np.zeroslike(gtimage), np.zeroslike(Temission) # PRB integrator step # 3. Regularization & Objective l2loss = np.mean((gtimage - renderedimage) 2) l1norm = np.sum(np.abs(Temission)) l1reg = (l1norm / (gtimage.shape[0] gtimage.shape[1] gtimage.shape[2])) (htx wtx ctx) loss = (1.0 / alpha) l2loss + l1reg totalloss += loss # Update Temission using gradients Temission -= 0.01 grads # Standard gradient descent step epoch += 1 # 4. Clipping and Boosting if epoch % cadence == 0: # Clip values below threshold to 0 Temission[Temission < threshold] = 0.0 # Boost values above threshold to accelerate convergence Temission[Temission >= threshold] = 2.0 # Standard multiplier for acceleration # 5. Convergence Check if abs(prevloss - totalloss) < 1e-6: break prevloss = totalloss # 6. Post-processing prunedfaces = [] for face in meshfaces: minbrightness = np.inf for vertex in face.vertices: u, v = uvcoords[vertex] # Standard texture sampling h, w, c = Temission.shape uidx = int(np.clip(u (w - 1), 0, w - 1)) vidx = int(np.clip(v (h - 1), 0, h - 1)) brightness = Temission[vidx, uidx,:] if np.max(brightness) < minbrightness: minbrightness = np.max(brightness) if minbrightness >= threshold: prunedfaces.append(face) return Temission, prunedfaces Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports indirect lighting optimization (maximum light transport depth of 3) unlike differentiable rasterization (maximum depth of 2). L1 regularization encourages sparsity, which aligns with the inductive bias that most of the scene does not emit light. Periodic clipping and boosting accelerate convergence and avoid local minima from dim non-light sources. Limitations: Requires reasonably accurate geometry (e.g., from MonoSDF) to avoid biasing results to bad local minima due to noisy geometry during differentiable surface rendering. When to use: When recovering emission maps for scenes with indirect lighting and sparse light sources, given accurate geometry. When not to use: When geometry is noisy or inaccurate, or when indirect lighting is not a concern and rasterization-based methods are sufficient. This method is part of the Dynamic Mesh-Aware Radiance Fields framework. It builds on the use of MonoSDF for accurate geometry reconstruction and SDFStudio for UV unwrapping. The PRB integrator is used for differentiable surface rendering. The method is used to create area lights for shadow passes in a Hybrid Renderer. name: Euclidean Projection for Material Constraints
head: Clamping to [0, RGB Cube Projection
body: This method enforces physical validity on material parameters during differentiable rendering optimization by projecting updated values back into their feasible domain after each optimizer step. It addresses unconstrained gradient updates driving color or BSDF parameters outside physically plausible ranges, which causes numerical instability or non-physical reflectance. It differs from its siblings by being a post-update constraint enforcement mechanism rather than a solver or training schedule, building on Optimization Configuration (Adam + Exponential Decay + Selective L2) by applying a hard boundary check after the parameter update. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Optimized parameter vector \theta (e.g., RGB albedo or BSDF coefficients) after an Adam update step. Output: Projected parameter vector \theta' constrained to the valid domain. Data Structures: Parameters are stored as floating-point arrays. For RGB albedo, this is a 3-element vector per mesh or pixel. For BSDF parameters, this is a scalar or vector per material property. Steps: 1. Perform the standard optimizer update (e.g., Adam) to compute the new candidate parameter values \theta{new}. 2. Apply component-wise Euclidean projection onto the valid interval [0, 1]^k, where k is the number of channels or parameters. 3. For each component ci of the parameter vector: If ci < 0, set ci' = 0. If ci > 1, set ci' = 1. Otherwise, ci' = ci. 4. Replace \theta{new} with \theta' for the next iteration. Formula: The projection operator \Pi{[0,1]^3} for RGB albedo is defined as: \Pi{[0,1]^3}(ci) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } ci < 0 \\ ci & \text{if } 0 \le ci \le 1 \\ 1 & \text{if } ci > 1 \end{cases} for each channel ci \in \{r, g, b\}. Parameters: Initial Values: For RGB albedo, initial values are drawn uniformly at random from [0, 1]^3. Valid Range: [0, 1] for all constrained parameters. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Instability: Without projection, unconstrained updates in noisy gradient environments (like path tracing) can accumulate error, leading to non-physical reflectance or invalid configurations. Precision: Floating-point errors may result in values slightly outside [0, 1] due to rounding; the projection handles these naturally. Degenerate Input: If the optimizer produces NaN or Inf, the projection may not recover validity; input validation is assumed prior to projection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projecttovalidrange(values): """Projects a parameter vector component-wise onto the [0, 1] interval.""" projected = [] for v in values: if v < 0.0: projected.append(0.0) elif v > 1.0: projected.append(1.0) else: projected.append(v) return projected Clamping Principled BSDF parameters (roughness, specular transmission, metalness, anisotropy) to [0, 1] to ensure physically plausible behavior and prevent numerical instabilities during optimization. It is chosen when optimizing complex material models where multiple parameters have restricted domains. Unconstrained updates in noisy path tracing gradients may accumulate error and destabilize convergence, making this clamping necessary. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Ensures stable convergence by preventing divergence due to out-of-bounds values. In RGB albedo estimation, it contributes to rapid convergence, reducing initial RGB error from 0.43 \pm 0.12 to 0.011 \pm 0.003 after the first iteration and 0.004 \pm 0.001 at convergence (within 50 iterations). Strengths: Simple to implement, guarantees physical validity, prevents numerical instability in noisy gradient settings. Limitations: Hard constraints may create non-differentiable points at the boundaries, potentially affecting gradient flow if not handled carefully by the optimizer. It does not smooth the parameter space, only bounds it. When to Use: When optimizing material parameters that must remain within physical bounds (e.g., albedo, BSDF coefficients) and the optimizer may produce out-of-bounds values. When Not to Use: When parameters have non-rectangular constraints or when soft constraints are preferred to maintain differentiability at boundaries. The method was explicitly described in the context of optimizing 3D scene reconstruction with differentiable ray tracing, where it was used to estimate diffuse albedo from reference photographs. It is also employed in modern PBR material reconstruction pipelines, such as MRD, to clamp Principled BSDF parameters during optimization. name: Parameter and Optimizer Update
head: Update Param with Optimizer
body: A utility to update model parameters and their corresponding optimizer states using custom functions, handling both optimized and un-optimized parameters. It separates parameters into those managed by an optimizer (e.g., Adam) and those updated directly, allowing flexible integration of custom update rules within differentiable volume rendering pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: params: Dictionary mapping parameter names to tensors. optimizers: Dictionary mapping parameter names (or prefixes) to optimizer objects. paramfn: Callable (name, tensor) -> tensor for direct parameter updates. optimizerfn: Callable (key, value) -> value for optimizer state updates. optimizersprefix: String prefix to identify optimizer keys in the state dict. Data Structures: optimizer.state: Dictionary containing state for each parameter group. Keys are typically parameter names or indices. Values are dictionaries of state tensors (e.g., expavg, expavgsq for Adam). optimizer.paramgroups: List of dictionaries containing params, lr, betas, eps, etc. Steps: 1. Split Names: Iterate through params. Separate names into optimizednames (present in optimizers) and unoptimizednames (not present). 2. Update Optimized Parameters: For each name in optimizednames: Retrieve the optimizer and param tensor. Extract the paramstate from optimizer.state[name]. For each key in paramstate except 'step': Update the state value: newvalue = optimizerfn(key, paramstate[key]). Update the parameter: newparam = paramfn(name, param). Update optimizer.paramgroups and optimizer.state with newparam and updated state. 3. Update Un-Optimized Parameters: For each name in unoptimizednames: Apply paramfn: newparam = paramfn(name, params[name]). Update params[name] with newparam. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateparameters(params, optimizers, paramfn, optimizerfn, optimizersprefix): optimizednames = [] unoptimizednames = [] # Split names for name in params: if name in optimizers: optimizednames.append(name) else: unoptimizednames.append(name) # Update optimized params for name in optimizednames: optimizer = optimizers[name] param = params[name] paramstate = optimizer.state[name] # Update optimizer state for key in paramstate: if key == 'step': continue paramstate[key] = optimizerfn(key, paramstate[key]) # Update parameter newparam = paramfn(name, param) params[name] = newparam # Update optimizer paramgroups and state dict # Note: In practice, this involves updating the tensor reference in paramgroups # and ensuring the state dict points to the correct tensor. # This step is implementation-specific to the optimizer framework. # Assuming standard PyTorch-like behavior where paramgroups['params'] # holds the tensor reference. for group in optimizer.paramgroups: if name in group['params']: group['params'][0] = newparam # Assuming single param per group for simplicity # Update un-optimized params for name in unoptimizednames: newparam = paramfn(name, params[name]) params[name] = newparam Parameters: paramfn: Callable taking parameter name and tensor, returning new tensor. optimizerfn: Callable taking optimizer state key and value, returning new state value. optimizersprefix: String prefix for optimizer keys. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure optimizerfn handles floating-point precision correctly, especially for exponential moving averages. Boundaries: If paramfn involves clipping (e.g., density non-negativity), apply it after the optimizer step if required by the specific variant. Degenerate Input: Handle cases where paramstate is empty or optimizer is not initialized for a parameter. Builds lighting L from density \rho and lights. Renders image I^c = R(\rho, L, c). Computes gradient \nabla\rho = \partial L\rho / \partial \rho. Updates \rho with \nabla\rho using Adam optimizer. Clips negative density: \rho \leftarrow \max(\rho, 0). Time Complexity: Linear in the number of parameters for the split step. Optimizer update time depends on the complexity of optimizerfn and paramfn. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of parameters for storing optimizer states. Strengths: Flexible integration of custom update rules. Separation of concerns between optimizer-managed and direct updates. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of optimizerfn and paramfn to ensure correctness. Performance depends on the efficiency of these functions. When to Use: When standard optimizers are insufficient or when custom update rules are needed for specific parameters (e.g., density clipping, learning rate scheduling). When Not to Use: When standard optimizers suffice and no custom updates are required. Originated in the context of differentiable volume rendering and inverse rendering, where flexible parameter updates are needed for various scene representations (e.g., densities, colors, normals). Developed to handle the complexity of optimizing both learned parameters and auxiliary variables in radiance field optimization. carlinds/splatad, https://github.com/carlinds/splatad, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Global Transport for Fluid Reconstruction with Learned Self-Supervision, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00168, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Anisotropic Spatiotemporal Filtering Optimizer
head: Cross-bilateral filter optimizer, Cross-bilateral filter for inverse rendering, Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering, Spatiotemporal optimizer
body: The Anisotropic Spatiotemporal Filtering Optimizer accelerates convergence in inverse rendering by enforcing piecewise smoothness on optimization parameter updates through a lightweight spatial domain cross-bilateral filter applied to gradients, in addition to Adam's temporal filtering. It generalizes Adam and Laplacian Smoothing by applying an anisotropic cross-bilateral filter to the gradient across space, in addition to temporal filtering like Adam. Unlike isotropic spatial filters (inverse Laplacian operator) which oversmooth gradients and hurt convergence at sharp regions, the cross-bilateral filter applies strong filtering in smooth regions and weak filtering around sharp features, preserving edges. Unlike Adam which only performs per-component temporal filtering and is insufficient for highly noisy gradients or highly anisotropic loss landscapes, this method adds spatial preconditioning to handle anisotropy and noise. The method extends Adam by applying spatial filters to gradients and moments to exploit spatial coherence, performing non-diagonal preconditioning. It requires the same storage as Adam, as it directly filters gradients and moments. Inputs: \theta: Current optimization parameters (e.g., texture, volume density, albedo, mesh vertices). gt: Gradient of the loss function with respect to \theta at iteration t. m{t-1}, v{t-1}: First and second moment estimates from the previous iteration. I{guide}: The current recovered signal (e.g., current texture or volume estimate) used as a guide for the cross-bilateral filter. \alpha, \beta1, \beta2, \epsilon: Adam hyperparameters. \sigmas, \sigmad: Spatial and range standard deviations for the cross-bilateral filter. ws: Spatial weight parameter for the cross-bilateral filter. wd: Data term weight (must be consistent across parameters for post-filtering stability). Outputs: \thetat: Updated parameters. mt, vt: Updated moment estimates. The optimizer maintains the same state variables as Adam: 1. \theta: The parameter tensor (shape matches the input signal). 2. m: First moment estimate, same shape as \theta. 3. v: Second moment estimate, same shape as \theta. The optimizer applies up to three spatial filters: a "prefilter" on gt before the exponential moving averages, and two "postfilters" on mt and vt after the exponential moving averages. 1. Spatial Pre-filtering (Optional): Apply a cross-bilateral filter to the raw gradient gt using the current recovered signal I{guide} as a guide. Let the filtered gradient be \tilde{g}t. \tilde{g}t = \text{CrossBilateralFilter}(gt, I{guide}, \sigmas, \sigmad, ws) Note: For grid-based applications (images, volumes), applying only postfilters is often preferred for performance. For meshes, specific pre/post combinations may be used. 2. Temporal Filtering (Adam Update): Compute the biased first and second moment estimates using the (optionally pre-filtered) gradient. mt = \beta1 m{t-1} + (1 - \beta1) \tilde{g}t vt = \beta2 v{t-1} + (1 - \beta2) \tilde{g}t^2 3. Spatial Post-filtering: Apply the cross-bilateral filter to the moment estimates mt and vt using the current recovered signal I{guide} as a guide. \hat{m}t = \text{CrossBilateralFilter}(mt, I{guide}, \sigmas, \sigmad, ws) \hat{v}t = \text{CrossBilateralFilter}(vt, I{guide}, \sigmas, \sigmad, ws) 4. Bias Correction and Parameter Update: Apply bias correction and update the parameters. \hat{m}t^{corr} = \frac{\hat{m}t}{1 - \beta1^t} \hat{v}t^{corr} = \frac{\hat{v}t}{1 - \beta2^t} \thetat = \theta{t-1} - \alpha \frac{\hat{m}t^{corr}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}t^{corr}} + \epsilon} The filter acts as a preconditioner via matrix-vector product (D^{-1}K)\nabla\theta f, where K is a symmetric positive definite affinity matrix accounting for ws and wd, and D is a diagonal matrix accounting for z. The matrix D^{-1}K is not symmetric, but all its eigenvalues are real, non-negative, and bounded by 1. For grid-based applications (images and volumes), the Edge-avoiding À-trous filter [Dammertz et al. 2010] is used to speed up computation. For meshes, Solomon et al. [2014]’s variant is used. The cross-bilateral filter computes a weighted average of neighboring values, where weights depend on both spatial distance and intensity difference (range distance). For a pixel/voxel i with value xi and guide value gi, the filtered value \hat{x}i is: \hat{x}i = \frac{\sum{j \in N(i)} w{ij} xj}{\sum{j \in N(i)} w{ij}} where N(i) is the neighborhood of i, and the weight w{ij} is: w{ij} = \exp\left(-\frac{\|pi - pj\|^2}{2\sigmas^2}\right) \exp\left(-\frac{\|gi - gj\|^2}{2\sigmad^2}\right) Here, pi, pj are spatial coordinates, and gi, gj are guide values. The first term is the spatial kernel, and the second is the range kernel based on the guide signal. Sample count: 1 sample per pixel is used for gradient estimation in all experiments. Adam Hyperparameters: Standard values (\alpha=0.001, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999, \epsilon=10^{-8}) are typically used, though specific values are not detailed in the source beyond standard Adam defaults. Filter Hyperparameters: \sigmas (spatial sigma), \sigmad (range sigma), and ws (spatial weight) are required. Exact typical values are not given in the sources. Consistency of Data Term: When using post-filtering, the same parameters \theta must be used for the data term wd. Violating this significantly degrades recovery. Oversmoothing: Isotropic filters (inverse Laplacian) oversmooth gradients and hurt convergence at sharp regions. The cross-bilateral filter avoids this by being anisotropic. Noise: Adam alone is insufficient for highly noisy gradients or highly anisotropic loss landscapes. The spatial filter reduces gradient noise and improves conditioning. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def crossbilateralfilter(inputsignal, guidesignal, sigmas, sigmad, kernelsize=3): """ Applies an edge-avoiding cross-bilateral filter. For grid-based applications, this should be implemented using the Edge-avoiding À-trous filter [Dammertz et al. 2010] for efficiency. For meshes, use Solomon et al. [2014]'s variant. This pseudocode shows the naive implementation for clarity. """ # Pad the input and guide signals pad = kernelsize // 2 inputpadded = np.pad(inputsignal, pad, mode='reflect') guidepadded = np.pad(guidesignal, pad, mode='reflect') output = np.zeroslike(inputsignal) h, w = inputsignal.shape[:2] # Assuming 2D for simplicity, extend to 3D for volumes for i in range(h): for j in range(w): # Extract neighborhood ystart, yend = i, i + kernelsize xstart, xend = j, j + kernelsize # Center coordinates cy, cx = kernelsize // 2, kernelsize // 2 # Get center guide value centerguide = guidepadded[ystart + cy, xstart + cx] numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for dy in range(kernelsize): for dx in range(kernelsize): # Neighbor coordinates ny = ystart + dy nx = xstart + dx # Spatial distance dists = np.sqrt((dy - cy)2 + (dx - cx)2) spatialweight = np.exp(-(dists2) / (2 sigmas2)) # Range distance (using guide signal) neighborguide = guidepadded[ny, nx] distd = np.abs(centerguide - neighborguide) rangeweight = np.exp(-(distd2) / (2 sigmad2)) weight = spatialweight rangeweight # Apply weight to input signal value numerator += weight inputpadded[ny, nx] denominator += weight if denominator > 0: output[i, j] = numerator / denominator else: output[i, j] = inputsignal[i, j] return output def anisotropicspatiotemporaloptimizerstep( theta, gt, mtprev, vtprev, guidesignal, alpha, beta1, beta2, epsilon, sigmas, sigmad, useprefilter=True): """ One step of the Anisotropic Spatiotemporal Filtering Optimizer. Args: theta: Current parameters. gt: Gradient at current iteration. mtprev: Previous first moment estimate. vtprev: Previous second moment estimate. guidesignal: Current recovered signal (e.g., texture/volume) for edge guidance. alpha: Learning rate. beta1: Exponential decay rate for first moment. beta2: Exponential decay rate for second moment. epsilon: Small constant for numerical stability. sigmas: Spatial standard deviation for cross-bilateral filter. sigmad: Range standard deviation for cross-bilateral filter. useprefilter: Whether to apply spatial filter to gradient before Adam update. Returns: thetanew: Updated parameters. mt: Updated first moment. vt: Updated second moment. """ # Step 1: Spatial Pre-filtering (Optional) if useprefilter: gtfiltered = crossbilateralfilter(gt, guidesignal, sigmas, sigmad) else: gtfiltered = gt # Step 2: Temporal Filtering (Adam Update) mt = beta1 mtprev + (1 - beta1) gtfiltered vt = beta2 vtprev + (1 - beta2) (gtfiltered 2) # Step 3: Spatial Post-filtering # Apply cross-bilateral filter to moments mtfiltered = crossbilateralfilter(mt, guidesignal, sigmas, sigmad) vtfiltered = crossbilateralfilter(vt, guidesignal, sigmas, sigmad) # Step 4: Bias Correction and Parameter Update # Note: t is the current iteration number (1-indexed) # For the first iteration, t=1 t = 1 # Placeholder for actual iteration count mtcorr = mtfiltered / (1 - beta1t) vtcorr = vtfiltered / (1 - beta2t) thetanew = theta - alpha (mtcorr / (np.sqrt(vtcorr) + epsilon)) return thetanew, mt, vt A basic optimizer without momentum or adaptive learning rates. Simpler but slower convergence for complex inverse rendering tasks. Link A second-order optimizer suitable for smooth, unconstrained problems. More computationally expensive per iteration but may require fewer iterations. Link The overall schedule and strategy for training, including learning rate schedules and data sampling. Link The general framework for setting up inverse rendering problems, including loss functions and parameterization. Link A technique to enforce physical constraints on material parameters (e.g., non-negativity, energy conservation) after each update. Link The general mechanism for updating parameters and optimizer states in differentiable rendering. Link Time Complexity: The addition of spatial filtering increases the per-iteration cost compared to standard Adam. The complexity depends on the filter implementation. For grid-based applications, the Edge-avoiding À-trous filter is used for speed, but it is still more expensive than Adam's element-wise operations. For meshes, Solomon et al.'s variant is used. Memory Complexity: The method requires the same storage as Adam, as it directly filters gradients and moments. Measured Performance: The method significantly speeds up convergence over Adam and other prior work in a wide range of inverse rendering tasks, including texture, volume, and geometry recovery. For example, for roughness texture recovery after 100 iterations, the method has converged while others have artifacts. For volume density and albedo recovery, it can recover the rough shape and color in just 50 iterations. For mesh recovery, it recovers sharp features and thin structures faster than competing methods. Scaling: The method is effective at very low sample counts (1 sample per pixel). Strengths: Faster convergence than Adam and isotropic filtering methods. Higher quality reconstructions, especially for piecewise smooth signals. Preserves sharp features and edges better than isotropic filters. Handles highly noisy gradients and anisotropic loss landscapes better than Adam. Performs non-diagonal preconditioning, capturing correlations across parameters. Limitations: Increased computational cost per iteration due to spatial filtering. Requires careful tuning of filter parameters (\sigmas, \sigmad). Requires the current recovered signal as a guide, which may not be available or accurate in early iterations. When to Use: Use when the target signal is piecewise smooth (e.g., textures, volumes, meshes) and convergence speed is critical. Particularly useful for low-sample-count scenarios. When Not to Use: Use standard Adam if computational resources are extremely limited and convergence speed is not a bottleneck, or if the signal is not piecewise smooth. The concept of spatially filtering gradients to speed up optimization was previously applied using the inverse Laplacian operator in works by Nicolet et al. [2021], Osher et al. [2018], and Renka [2006]. The Anisotropic Spatiotemporal Filtering Optimizer generalizes these approaches by using an anisotropic cross-bilateral filter instead of an isotropic inverse Laplacian, allowing for edge preservation. The method is applied to inverse rendering tasks including texture recovery, volume density and albedo recovery, and mesh recovery. It is used in conjunction with the Adam optimizer, which is the standard gradient-based optimizer in inverse rendering. name: Optimization Configuration
head: LE3D Optimization Settings, Optimizer and LR Settings
body: This configuration defines the hyperparameter schedule and optimizer state for training radiance field models, specifically targeting the color MLP and Gaussian attributes. It addresses the challenge of converging in highly non-convex, high-dimensional optimization landscapes by combining the adaptive gradient estimation of Adam with a cosine annealing learning rate schedule. It distinguishes itself from standard fixed-rate Adam by enforcing a strict decay to a final learning rate of 1.0 \times 10^{-5}, which helps stabilize training in the final stages. Inputs: Model parameters: Color MLP weights (\theta), Gaussian color features, Gaussian biases. Hyperparameters: Initial learning rates, final learning rate, decay schedule type. Data Structures: Optimizer State: Adam maintains first moment (m) and second moment (v) estimates for each parameter group. Learning Rate Schedule: A cosine function mapping training step t to \etat. Parameters: Initial Learning Rate for Color MLP (\eta{MLP}^{init}): 1.0 \times 10^{-4}. Initial Learning Rate for Gaussian Color Features (\eta{feat}^{init}): 2.0 \times 10^{-3}. Initial Learning Rate for Gaussian Biases (\eta{bias}^{init}): 1.0 \times 10^{-4}. Final Learning Rate (\eta{final}): 1.0 \times 10^{-5} for all groups. Decay Schedule: Cosine decay. Loss Regularization Weights (contextual, not optimizer params): \lambdaF = 10, \lambdaT = 0.01, \lambda{dist} = 0.1, \lambda{nf} = 0.01. Steps: 1. Initialize Adam optimizer with the specified initial learning rates for each parameter group (MLP, features, biases). 2. For each training iteration t from 0 to T{total}: a. Compute the learning rate \etat using cosine annealing: \etat = \eta{final} + \frac{1}{2}(\eta{init} - \eta{final}) \left( 1 + \cos\left( \frac{t}{T{total}} \pi \right) \right) where \eta{init} is the specific initial rate for the parameter group. b. Compute gradients of the loss function with respect to the parameters. c. Update the Adam state (m, v) and parameters using \etat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def getcosinelr(initlr, finallr, currentstep, totalsteps): """ Computes the learning rate for a specific parameter group using cosine decay. """ if totalsteps == 0: return initlr # Cosine annealing from initlr to finallr progress = currentstep / totalsteps cosineterm = 0.5 (1 + math.cos(math.pi progress)) lr = finallr + 0.5 (initlr - finallr) cosineterm return lr def configureoptimizer(paramsmlp, paramsfeatures, paramsbiases, totalsteps): """ Sets up the Adam optimizer with selective initial learning rates and cosine decay. """ # Hyperparameters from lrmlpinit = 1.0e-4 lrfeatinit = 2.0e-3 lrbiasinit = 1.0e-4 lrfinal = 1.0e-5 # Initialize Adam optimizer with group-specific initial LR # Note: Standard Adam implementation handles the decay schedule externally or via a wrapper optimizer = Adam([ {'params': paramsmlp, 'lr': lrmlpinit}, {'params': paramsfeatures, 'lr': lrfeatinit}, {'params': paramsbiases, 'lr': lrbiasinit} ]) return optimizer, lrmlpinit, lrfeatinit, lrbiasinit, lrfinal def updatestep(optimizer, paramsmlp, paramsfeatures, paramsbiases, gradients, step, totalsteps): """ Performs one optimization step with dynamic learning rates. """ # Calculate current LRs for each group lrmlp = getcosinelr(1.0e-4, 1.0e-5, step, totalsteps) lrfeat = getcosinelr(2.0e-3, 1.0e-5, step, totalsteps) lrbias = getcosinelr(1.0e-4, 1.0e-5, step, totalsteps) # Update parameter groups with their specific LR # This requires a custom optimizer step or a scheduler that modifies the LR in the param groups # Standard PyTorch-style update: optimizer.step() # Assumes scheduler has updated optimizer.paramgroups['lr'] # If using a manual scheduler approach: # optimizer.paramgroups[0]['lr'] = lrmlp # optimizer.paramgroups[1]['lr'] = lrfeat # optimizer.paramgroups[2]['lr'] = lrbias # optimizer.step() Edge Cases: If T{total} is not known in advance, the cosine decay cannot be strictly applied as defined. The "Selective L2" aspect refers to the specific application of regularization weights (\lambda) to different loss components (depth distortion, near-far) rather than a standard L2 weight decay on the optimizer itself, as the sources do not specify a global L2 weight decay coefficient for Adam. Adam is selected over SGD or BFGS because the optimization problems are highly non-convex and start far from the global optimum, making simplifying assumptions in quasi-Newton methods (like BFGS) inapplicable. Adam provides a cheap yet powerful alternative for high-dimensional objectives. Time Complexity: Adam adds O(1) overhead per parameter per step for maintaining moments, similar to SGD but with higher memory usage. Memory Complexity: Requires storing first and second moment estimates for all parameters, doubling the memory footprint for optimizer states compared to SGD. Performance: Effective for non-convex radiance field optimization, avoiding bad local optima associated with simpler solvers. Limitations: The non-convex nature of the problem means convergence is not guaranteed to the global optimum. This configuration is derived from practices in modern radiance field reconstruction, specifically noted in the context of "Lighting Every Darkness with 3DGS" and "ERF: Explicit Radiance Field Reconstruction From Scratch". The use of Adam with recommended settings is a standard baseline in deep learning for inverse rendering. The specific cosine decay schedule to 1.0 \times 10^{-5} is a refinement observed in recent 3D Gaussian Splatting variants. name: Neural Volume Rendering Training (MSE)
head: Hierarchical Geometric Guidance (HGG), Joint Training of Fourier Feature Volume and MLP, Training and Encoding Pipeline
body: Neural Volume Rendering Training (MSE) using Hierarchical Geometric Guidance (HGG) optimizes neural radiance fields by minimizing photometric error while using sparse depth priors solely to schedule sampling region expansion, avoiding direct depth supervision bias. It differs from standard NeRF training by replacing global initialization with a local-to-global sampling schedule that gradually extends near and far planes from the depth prior to full scene bounds. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sparse depth priors t{depth} from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); ground-truth images C{gt}; camera poses; total training iterations N{total}; HGG iteration count N{hgg}; minimum adjusting rate \epsilon{hgg}. Outputs: Optimized neural radiance field parameters \Theta (density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}). Data Structures: Scene Representation: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) f\Theta mapping 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Sampling Points: A set of N points ti along each ray \mathbf{r}, defined by near plane tn and far plane tf. Iteration State: Current iteration i. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: For each ray, initialize the near plane tn and far plane tf close to the sparse depth prior t{depth} to define a local sampling region. 2. Region Expansion Schedule: For each iteration i, compute the region adjustment rate \gamma(i) and update tn(i) and tf(i) using the formulas below. 3. Volume Rendering: Sample N points uniformly or stratified within the current bounds [tn(i), tf(i)]. Query f\Theta for \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i. Compute the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard emission-absorption model [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss between the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground-truth color C{gt}(\mathbf{r}). (Note: The specific HGG implementation minimizes Huber loss for outlier robustness rather than strict MSE). 5. Optimization: Update \Theta using an Adam optimizer with exponential learning rate decay. Formulas: Region Adjustment Rate: \gamma(i) = \frac{1 - \cos\left( (\min(\max(i/N{hgg}, \epsilon{hgg}), 1)) \pi \right)}{2} where i is the current iteration, N{hgg} is the number of iterations until full bounds are reached, and \epsilon{hgg} is the minimum adjusting rate. Near/Far Plane Update: tn(i) = t{depth} + (tn - t{depth}) \gamma(i) tf(i) = t{depth} + (tf - t{depth}) \gamma(i) where tn, tf are the initial near/far planes, and t{depth} is the depth prior. Parameters: N{hgg}: Number of iterations for region expansion. Typical value: 10% of total training iterations. \epsilon{hgg}: Minimum adjusting rate. Typical value: 0.2. Learning Rate: 1 \times 10^{-3}, exponentially decaying to 1 \times 10^{-5}. Samples: 64 volume points for coarse model, 128 for fine model (if using Hierarchical Photometric Guidance variant). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Bias: Direct supervision of sparse depth prior introduces bias \Delta P due to keypoint mismatching (\Delta d) and small translation between frames, causing geometric misalignment. HGG avoids this by using depth only for sampling region initialization. Precision: The \min(\max(i/N{hgg}, \epsilon{hgg}), 1) term in \gamma(i) inherently clamps the adjustment rate to [\epsilon{hgg}, 1], preventing invalid bounds or division errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computegamma(i, Nhgg, epsilonhgg): """Compute the region adjustment rate gamma(i).""" ratio = i / Nhgg clampedratio = max(epsilonhgg, min(ratio, 1.0)) return (1.0 - math.cos(clampedratio math.pi)) / 2.0 def updatebounds(tninit, tfinit, tdepth, i, Nhgg, epsilonhgg): """Update near and far planes based on iteration i.""" gamma = computegamma(i, Nhgg, epsilonhgg) tn = tdepth + (tninit - tdepth) gamma tf = tdepth + (tfinit - tdepth) gamma return tn, tf def renderray(tn, tf, numsamples, queryfn): """Render a single ray using the emission-absorption model.""" samples = [tn + (tf - tn) (j + 0.5) / numsamples for j in range(numsamples)] sigmas = [queryfn(x)[0] for x in samples] colors = [queryfn(x)[1] for x in samples] deltas = [samples[j+1] - samples[j] for j in range(numsamples - 1)] if numsamples > 1: deltas.append(samples[-1] - samples[-2]) else: deltas.append(1e-6) transmittances = [math.exp(-sum(sigmas[k] deltas[k] for k in range(j))) for j in range(numsamples)] weights = [(1.0 - math.exp(-sigmas[j] deltas[j])) transmittances[j] for j in range(numsamples)] return sum(w c for w, c in zip(weights, colors)) def computeloss(rendered, groundtruth): """Compute photometric loss (Huber or MSE).""" return sum(abs(r - g) 1.5 for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) / len(rendered) def trainhgg(depthprior, tninit, tfinit, totaliterations, epsilonhgg=0.2, samplesperray=64): """Train a neural volume rendering model using HGG.""" Nhgg = int(0.1 totaliterations) model = initializemodel() # Standard MLP parameter initialization optimizer = initializeoptimizer(model) # Standard Adam optimizer setup for i in range(totaliterations): tn, tf = updatebounds(tninit, tfinit, depthprior, i, Nhgg, epsilonhgg) renderedcolor = renderray(tn, tf, samplesperray, model) loss = computeloss(renderedcolor, groundtruthcolor) # Ground truth for current batch optimizer.step(loss) # Standard gradient update return model Trains a coarse model and a fine model to improve novel view synthesis performance by combining their predicted colors in the loss function. It differs from standard HGG by using a two-stage hierarchical loss rather than just geometric guidance. Choose it when higher fidelity is needed at the cost of increased memory and computation. Definition: Combines coarse and fine model predictions in the loss. Steps: 1. Query coarse model f\Theta with stratified volume samples tc to get \hat{C}{crecon}. 2. Query fine model with union of coarse and fine samples tc \cup tf (produced by inverse transform sampling) to get \hat{C}{frecon}. 3. Compute MSE loss against ground truth C{gt} for both predictions. Formula: L{hpg} = \frac{1}{2} \sum{r \in R} \left( C{gt}(r) - \hat{C}{crecon}(r; tc) \right)^2 + \left( C{gt}(r) - \hat{C}{frecon}(r; tc \cup tf) \right)^2, where R is the set of all rays, tc are coarse stratified samples, and tf are fine samples produced by inverse transform sampling. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples and rays, similar to standard NeRF, with minor overhead for computing the expansion schedule and potentially querying two models if using Hierarchical Photometric Guidance. Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing intermediate rendering states, similar to standard NeRF [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the DTU dataset for 3, 6, and 9 views, showing more fine details and distinct edges in depth maps compared to SOTA baselines. Strengths: Avoids geometric bias from sparse depth supervision; improves novel view synthesis in sparse view scenarios. Limitations: Requires sparse depth priors from SfM; performance may degrade if depth priors are inaccurate. When to Use: Sparse view reconstruction where direct depth supervision is unreliable. Originated in the HG3-NeRF paper (2024) by authors of the arXiv preprint "HG3-NeRF: Hierarchical Geometric, Semantic, and Photometric Guided Neural Radiance Fields for Sparse View Inputs". It addresses the problem of geometric misalignment in sparse view NeRF reconstruction caused by bias in sparse depth supervision. HG3-NeRF: Hierarchical Geometric, Semantic, and Photometric Guided Neural Radiance Fields for Sparse View Inputs, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2401.11711, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Neural Surface Rendering Training (Eikonal & Boundary Regularization)
head: Eikonal and Boundary Regularization for Neural Surfaces, Neural SDF Training with Image Reconstruction and Eikonal Regularization
body:
This method trains a neural Signed Distance Function (SDF) to render images that match ground truth RGB while enforcing geometric priors via Eikonal and boundary regularization losses. It differs from standard neural volume rendering training (MSE) by explicitly optimizing the gradient magnitude of the SDF to be unity (Eikonal equation) and penalizing non-zero SDF values in the volume (boundary loss), which stabilizes surface extraction and improves geometric accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth images, camera parameters, a neural SDF model (typically an MLP with positional encoding), and a 3D bounding box for sampling. Outputs: Optimized SDF model parameters that minimize the combined loss. Data Structures: Neural SDF Model: An MLP that takes 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and outputs a scalar SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) and optionally color features. The model often uses Harmonic Embedding for input coordinates. Exact bit packing and layer sizes are Not given in the sources. Ray Bundle: Contains origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for each pixel, generated from pixel coordinates and camera intrinsics/extrinsics. Training Batch: Contains image tensor, camera object, and iteration index. Numbered Steps: 1. Pretraining (Optional but recommended): Pretrain the SDF using a sphere loss or similar geometric prior to initialize the SDF shape before image-based training begins. 2. Random Point Sampling for Regularization: Sample N random points \mathbf{x}{rand} uniformly within the defined 3D bounding box bounds. 3. SDF Evaluation at Random Points: Compute the SDF value d(\mathbf{x}{rand}) and its gradient 
abla d(\mathbf{x}{rand}) at the sampled random points using the neural network. 4. Compute Regularization Losses: Eikonal Loss: Enforce |
abla d(\mathbf{x})| = 1. Compute the mean squared error of the gradient magnitude from 1. Boundary Loss: Penalize non-zero SDF values in the volume. Compute \mathbb{E}[\exp(-100 \cdot |d(\mathbf{x})|)]. 5. Ray Sampling for Rendering: Sample random pixel coordinates (u, v) from the training image dimensions. Generate a ray bundle \{\mathbf{o}i, \mathbf{d}i\} for these pixels using the camera parameters. Sample ground truth RGB values \mathbf{c}{gt} at these pixel coordinates. 6. Volume/Surface Rendering: Render the scene along the rays using the current SDF model. This typically involves sphere tracing or volumetric integration to compute the predicted RGB color \mathbf{c}{pred}. 7. Compute Image Reconstruction Loss: Calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between predicted and ground truth colors: \mathcal{L}{image} =  rac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^{M} ||\mathbf{c}{pred}^{(i)} - \mathbf{c}{gt}^{(i)}||^2. 8. Total Loss Calculation: Combine the losses: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{image} + \lambda{eik} \mathcal{L}{eikonal} + \lambda{inter} \mathcal{L}{boundary} where \lambda{eik} and \lambda{inter} are weighting factors. 9. Optimization Step: Perform backpropagation and update model parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Adam). 10. Scheduler Update: Update the learning rate according to the schedule at the end of each epoch. Formulas: Eikonal Loss: \mathcal{L}{eikonal} =  rac{1}{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} (|
abla d(\mathbf{x}{rand}^{(j)})| - 1)^2 Boundary Loss: \mathcal{L}{boundary} = \lambda{inter} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\exp(-100 \cdot |d(\mathbf{x})|)] Image Loss: \mathcal{L}{image} = 	ext{mean}((\mathbf{c}{gt} - \mathbf{c}{pred})^2) Learning Rate Schedule: \eta{epoch} = \eta{initial} \cdot \gamma^{ rac{epoch}{step\size}} where \gamma is the decay factor and step\size is the divisor for the epoch index. Parameters: lr: Initial learning rate for the optimizer. eikonalweight (\lambda{eik}): Weight for the Eikonal loss. interweight (\lambda{inter}): Weight for the boundary loss. bounds: 3D bounding box defining the region for random point sampling. lrschedulergamma (\gamma): Decay factor for the learning rate schedule. lrschedulerstepsize: Divisor for the epoch index in the learning rate schedule exponent. checkpointinterval: Number of epochs between model checkpoints. renderinterval: Number of epochs between visualization renders. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def trainneuralsurfacesdf(model, dataloader, optimizer, scheduler, cfg): """ Train a neural SDF using image reconstruction, Eikonal, and boundary regularization. """ device = cfg.device bounds = cfg.training.bounds batchsize = cfg.training.batchsize eikonalweight = cfg.training.eikonalweight interweight = cfg.training.interweight # Optional: Pretrain SDF with sphere loss if configured if cfg.training.pretrainsphere: # Standard operation: optimize SDF to match a ground-truth sphere SDF for in range(cfg.training.pretrainepochs): spherepoints = getrandompoints(batchsize, bounds, device) spheresdf = computespheresdf(spherepoints, cfg.spherecfg) predsdf = model.getdistance(spherepoints) loss = torch.mean(torch.square(predsdf - spheresdf)) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() for epoch in range(cfg.training.epochs): for iteration, batch in enumerate(dataloader): image = batch['image'].to(device).unsqueeze(0) camera = batch['camera'].to(device) # 1. Sample random points for regularization eikonalpoints = getrandompoints(batchsize, bounds, device) # 2. Compute SDF and gradients at random points eikonaldistances = model.getdistance(eikonalpoints) eikonalgradients = model.getgradient(eikonalpoints) # 3. Compute Eikonal Loss: ||grad(d)||^2 - 1 gradmagnitude = torch.linalg.norm(eikonalgradients, dim=-1, keepdim=True) eikonallossval = torch.mean((gradmagnitude - 1.0) 2) eikonalweight # 4. Compute Boundary Loss: exp(-100 |d|) boundarylossval = torch.exp(-1e2 torch.abs(eikonaldistances)).mean() interweight # 5. Sample random pixels for rendering xygrid = getrandompixelsfromimage(batchsize, cfg.data.imagesize, camera) # 6. Generate rays from pixels raybundle = getraysfrompixels(xygrid, cfg.data.imagesize, camera) # 7. Sample ground truth RGB rgbgt = sampleimagesatxy(image, xygrid) # 8. Render predicted RGB out = model(raybundle) rgbhat = out['color'] # 9. Compute Image Loss (MSE) imageloss = torch.mean(torch.square(rgbgt - rgbhat)) # 10. Total Loss loss = imageloss + eikonallossval + boundarylossval # 11. Optimization step optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Update learning rate at end of epoch scheduler.step() # Optional: Save checkpoints or render visualizations if epoch % cfg.training.checkpointinterval == 0: # Standard operation: serialize model and optimizer state to disk torch.save({'model': model.statedict(), 'optimizer': optimizer.statedict(), 'epoch': epoch}, cfg.checkpointpath) if epoch % cfg.training.renderinterval == 0: # Standard operation: render a test image and save to disk testraybundle = generatetestrays(camera, cfg.data.imagesize) testout = model(testraybundle) torch.save(testout['color'], cfg.renderpath) def getrandompoints(batchsize, bounds, device): """Sample uniform random points within a 3D bounding box.""" minbound = torch.tensor(bounds.min, device=device) maxbound = torch.tensor(bounds.max, device=device) points = torch.rand(batchsize, 3, device=device) points = points (maxbound - minbound) + minbound return points def computespheresdf(points, cfg): """Compute ground-truth SDF for a sphere centered at cfg.center with radius cfg.radius.""" diff = torch.abs(points - cfg.center) - cfg.radius signeddistance = torch.linalg.norm(torch.maximum(diff, torch.zeroslike(diff)), dim=-1) + torch.minimum(torch.max(diff, dim=-1)[0], torch.zeroslike(diff[..., 0])) return signeddistance.unsqueeze(-1) def getrandompixelsfromimage(batchsize, imagesize, camera): """Sample random pixel coordinates (u, v).""" h, w = imagesize u = torch.randint(0, w, (batchsize, 1), dtype=torch.float32) v = torch.randint(0, h, (batchsize, 1), dtype=torch.float32) return torch.cat([u, v], dim=-1) def getraysfrompixels(xygrid, imagesize, camera): """Generate ray origins and directions from pixel coordinates and camera.""" h, w = imagesize u, v = xygrid[:, 0], xygrid[:, 1] origins, directions = camera.generaterays(u, v) return {'origins': origins, 'directions': directions} def sampleimagesatxy(image, xygrid): """Sample RGB values from the image tensor at given pixel coordinates.""" h, w = image.shape[1], image.shape[2] u = xygrid[:, 0].long().clamp(0, w-1) v = xygrid[:, 1].long().clamp(0, h-1) rgbgt = image[0, v, u,:] return rgbgt def generatetestrays(camera, imagesize): """Generate rays for the full image for visualization.""" h, w = imagesize u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(w), torch.arange(h), indexing='ij') xygrid = torch.cat([u.unsqueeze(-1), v.unsqueeze(-1)], dim=-1).float() return getraysfrompixels(xygrid, imagesize, camera) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The boundary loss uses an exponential term \exp(-100 \cdot |d|). If |d| is large, this term underflows to zero. If |d| is very small, it approaches 1. Ensure numerical stability. Boundary Definition: The bounds for random point sampling must encompass the object of interest. Gradient Computation: Computing gradients of the SDF with respect to input coordinates requires torch.autograd.grad with creategraph=True if higher-order derivatives are needed, or standard backward pass if only first-order gradients are used for the Eikonal loss. Loss Balancing: The weights eikonalweight and interweight control the regularization strength. Surf²f is a hybrid neural representation that simultaneously learns an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF) and an explicit surrogate surface mesh, unified by a shared neural shader for both volume and surface rendering. It solves the synchronization and efficiency issues inherent in separate implicit and explicit surface representations by maintaining a parallel dual-stream architecture. Unlike methods that rely solely on SDF volume rendering or static mesh extraction, Surf²f enables real-time interactive rendering of the extracted mesh while leveraging volume rendering for training stability, outperforming NDS, UNISURF, and NeuS in both geometric accuracy and rendering speed. Time Complexity: Training time depends on the number of epochs, batch size, and the cost of rendering (ray marching/sphere tracing) and gradient computation. The Eikonal and boundary losses add overhead for random point sampling and gradient evaluation. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the neural network parameters and the intermediate activations during backpropagation. Scaling: The method scales with the resolution of the input images and the complexity of the neural network. Larger bounding boxes require more random points for effective regularization. Strengths: Enforces geometric priors (Eikonal equation) leading to cleaner surfaces and better generalization. Boundary regularization helps in defining the surface location more precisely. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of loss weights. When to Use: When high-quality geometric reconstruction is required, and the input data allows for volume rendering or sphere tracing. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is the primary constraint and the overhead of training with regularization is prohibitive, or when the input data is sparse and volume rendering is not feasible. This method originates from the field of neural implicit surface reconstruction and differentiable rendering. It builds upon the principles of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) but focuses on explicit surface representation via SDFs. The use of Eikonal regularization for SDFs was popularized by works such as "NeuS" and "UNISURF", which demonstrated that enforcing the Eikonal equation improves surface quality. omkarchittar/NeuralSurfaces, https://github.com/omkarchittar/NeuralSurfaces, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

head: Surf2f
body: Surf²f is a hybrid neural representation that simultaneously learns an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF) f and an explicit surrogate surface mesh, unified by a shared neural shader for both volume and surface rendering. It solves the synchronization and efficiency issues inherent in separate implicit and explicit surface representations by maintaining a parallel dual-stream architecture. Unlike methods that rely solely on SDF volume rendering or static mesh extraction, Surf²f enables real-time interactive rendering of the extracted mesh while leveraging volume rendering for training stability, outperforming NDS, UNISURF, and NeuS in both geometric accuracy and rendering speed. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images (and optional binary masks), camera poses, and a bounding box defining the scene volume. Outputs: A learned implicit SDF f, a surrogate surface mesh S, and a shared neural shader network. Data Structures: Multi-resolution Hash Grids: Two separate hash grid structures are used: Surface rendering branch: 8 levels. Volume rendering branch: 14 levels. Hash resolutions range from 16 to 1024 across levels. Feature dimension per entry: 2. Neural Shader: A network taking position and view direction as input, outputting color. It uses Spherical Harmonics (SH) of degree 4 to encode view-dependent appearance. Surrogate Mesh S: An explicit triangle mesh maintained in parallel with the SDF. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the multi-resolution hash grids for both surface and volume branches. Initialize the shared neural shader parameters. Initialize the surrogate mesh S (e.g., from a coarse initialization or random points within the bounding box). 2. Ray Sampling: For each training iteration, sample a batch of N=14,800 rays \mathcal{R} from the input images. 3. Surface-Guided Volume Sampling: Use the current surrogate mesh S to guide the sampling of points along the rays. This strategy improves sampling efficiency by concentrating samples near the surface. 4. Implicit SDF Evaluation: For each sampled point \mathbf{x} along a ray \mathbf{r}, query the implicit SDF f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) using the volume rendering hash grid. 5. Neural Shader Evaluation: Evaluate the shared neural shader to obtain the expected color \mathbf{C}v(\mathbf{r}) for the volume rendering stream and \mathbf{C}s(\mathbf{r}) for the surface rendering stream. The shader takes the position and view direction as input, utilizing SH coefficients. 6. Volume Rendering (Alpha Compositing): Calculate the volume rendering color \mathbf{C}v(\mathbf{r}) using customized CUDA kernels that perform \alpha-compositing along the ray. The opacity \alphai and transmittance Ti are derived from the SDF values f(\mathbf{x}i) and the step size. The formula for ray opacity is: O(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai where the compositing follows Equation 1 in the source. 7. Surface Rendering: Render the surrogate mesh S using the same shared neural shader. This involves rasterizing the mesh and evaluating the shader at the fragment positions. 8. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as a weighted sum of surface loss, volume loss, and Eikonal loss: \mathcal{L} = \lambdas \mathcal{L}s + \lambdav \mathcal{L}v + \mathcal{L}{\text{Ek}} where: \mathcal{L}s = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \text{Smooth}{\text{L1}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), \mathbf{C}s(\mathbf{r})) is the surface rendering loss comparing observed color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) with surface rendered color. \mathcal{L}v = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \text{Smooth}{\text{L1}}(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), \mathbf{C}v(\mathbf{r})) is the volume rendering loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{Ek}} is the Eikonal loss regularizing the gradient of the SDF to be 1 near the surface. Optional mask loss \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} can be added if binary masks m(\mathbf{r}) are available: \mathcal{L}{\text{mask}} = \lambda{\text{mask}} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \mathbf{1}{\text{mask}}(\mathbf{r}) \text{BCE}(m(\mathbf{r}), O(\mathbf{r})) where \mathbf{1}{\text{mask}}(\mathbf{r}) is an indicator function for mask availability. 9. Optimization: Update the parameters of the hash grids and the neural shader using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 2 \times 10^{-3}. 10. Mesh Synchronization: Update the surrogate mesh S to remain synchronized with the implicit SDF f. This is achieved by driving the deformation of the mesh based on the SDF values, ensuring the explicit and implicit representations converge to the same surface. 11. Inference (Mesh Extraction): After training, extract the final surface mesh \mathcal{S} from the learned SDF f using the Marching Cubes algorithm. 12. Realtime Rendering: Render the extracted mesh \mathcal{S} using an off-the-shelf graphics pipeline (e.g., rasterization) with the learned neural shader for real-time interactive visualization. Parameters: Hash Grids: 8 levels for surface branch, 14 levels for volume branch. Spherical Harmonics: Degree 4. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 2 \times 10^{-3}. Loss Weights: \lambdas = 1, \lambdav = 1, \lambda{\text{Ek}} = 0.05, \lambda{\text{mask}} = 0.1. Batch Size: 14,800 rays per iteration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Synchronization Discrepancy: Without a shared shading network, significant discrepancies occur between the renderings of the surrogate mesh and the implicit SDF, leading to poor convergence. Boundary Conditions: The Eikonal loss is critical for ensuring the SDF represents a valid distance function, especially near the surface. Time Complexity: Training is significantly faster than previous hybrid methods. On the DTU dataset, Surf²f achieves convergence in 5 minutes, compared to 7 minutes for NDS, 22 hours for UNISURF, and 6.5 hours for NeuS. Memory Complexity: Uses multi-resolution hash grids with a feature dimension of 2. The memory footprint is determined by the number of hash entries (resolutions 16 to 1024 across 8-14 levels). Measured Performance: DTU Dataset: Mean Chamfer Distance (CD) of 0.66 and Mean PSNR of 33.95. Rendering time is 5ms. NeRF Synthetic Dataset: Mean PSNR ranges from 27.1 (Ship) to 31.9 (Chair), with lower Mean-Angle Error compared to DMTet and FlexiCubes. Strengths: Fast convergence, real-time rendering capability, high geometric accuracy, and effective handling of view-dependent appearance via the shared neural shader. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of loss weights and hash grid parameters. When to use: Suitable for high-quality surface reconstruction from multi-view images where both geometric accuracy and rendering speed are critical. Surf²f was introduced in the paper "Sur²f: A Hybrid Representation for High-Quality and Efficient Surface Reconstruction from Multi-view Images". It builds upon the Neural Distance Field (NDS) and UNISURF paradigms, aiming to unify the benefits of implicit SDFs and explicit meshes. The method leverages NVIDIA OptiX for ray casting and custom CUDA kernels for efficient computation. It has been applied to various tasks including indoor and outdoor scene reconstruction, and text-to-3D generation.
