name: Global Optimization
body: Global Optimization reconstructs a complete image or volume from sparse measurements by solving for all pixels/voxels simultaneously across the entire domain. It differs from local or block-based solvers by optimizing the full domain at once, improving reconstruction quality at the cost of higher memory and per-iteration computational cost. It is applied in compressive rendering and tomographic reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse measurement set (either a 2D image with missing pixels I{\text{sparse}} and mask M, or a 3D volume representation V with reference projection P). Output: A reconstructed full image I{\text{full}} or an optimized volume representation V'. Data Structures: I{\text{sparse}}: 2D array of size m \times n containing known pixel values; missing pixels are masked out. M: Binary 2D array of size m \times n, where M{ij} = 1 if pixel (i,j) is known, and 0 otherwise. V: 3D volume representation (e.g., set of 3D Gaussians with mean, covariance, opacity, color parameters). P: Reference 2D projection image of size m \times n \times p (where p is channels). \hat{P}: Estimated projection of size m \times n \times p. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the target array (I{\text{full}} or V) with known values or random/learned parameters. 2. Iteration Loop: Repeat until convergence or a fixed iteration count: a. Projection/Forward Pass: Map the current representation to the observation domain. For compressive rendering, this is implicit in the error computation. For volume rendering, project V using transformation \mathcal{T}: \hat{P} = \mathcal{T}(V). b. Loss Computation: Compute reconstruction error. For compressive rendering, error is defined only on known pixels. For volume rendering, compute total loss combining L1, SSIM, and Total Variation (TV) terms. c. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients of the loss with respect to the representation parameters. d. Parameter Update: Apply gradient descent to update the representation. e. Adaptive Density Control (Volume Rendering only): Clone under-reconstructed Gaussians, split over-reconstructed ones, and prune those with near-zero gradient magnitudes. 3. Termination: Stop when the change in the representation between iterations falls below a threshold or after a fixed number of iterations. Formulas: Projection transformation: \hat{P} = \mathcal{T}(V), where \hat{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n \times p}. Total loss function: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}1(\hat{P}, P) + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{SSIM}}(\hat{P}, P) + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}}(V). Compressive rendering error gradient (MSE on known pixels): \nabla E = 2 \cdot (I{\text{full}} - I{\text{sparse}}) \odot M. Parameters: Loss weights: \lambda1 = 0.6 (L1), \lambda2 = 0.2 (SSIM), \lambda3 = 1 (TV). Iterations: Fixed count or dynamic until desired solution is reached. Learning rate \alpha: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: TV loss gradients can cause oscillations; gradient clipping or adaptive learning rates are recommended. Boundaries: Mask enforcement must use indexing rather than multiplication to avoid overwriting known pixels with zeros when missing pixels are initialized to zero. Degenerate input: If all pixels are missing, the solver returns the initialization; a fallback or regularization prior is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def globalsolvercompressiverendering(Isparse, mask, iterations=100, alpha=0.1): """Reconstructs a full image from a sparse subset using a global gradient solver.""" Ifull = Isparse.copy() for t in range(iterations): # Gradient of MSE error on known pixels error = Ifull - Isparse gradient = error mask 2.0 # Gradient descent step Ifull = Ifull - alpha gradient # Constraint enforcement: known pixels remain unchanged Ifull[mask == 1] = Isparse[mask == 1] return Ifull def globaloptimizervolumerendering(V, P, lambda1=0.6, lambda2=0.2, lambda3=1.0, iterations=1000, lr=0.01): """Optimizes a 3D volume representation by minimizing projection error.""" for t in range(iterations): # 1. Project volume to 2D domain Phat = T(V) # Transformation T maps V to estimated projection # 2. Compute losses l1loss = mean(abs(Phat - P)) # L1 loss ssimloss = structuralsimilarity(Phat, P) # Standard SSIM metric tvloss = totalvariation(V) # Standard TV regularization # 3. Total loss totalloss = lambda1 l1loss + lambda2 ssimloss + lambda3 tvloss # 4. Compute gradients and update parameters gradients = computegradient(totalloss, V) # Standard backpropagation V = V - lr gradients # Gradient descent update # 5. Adaptive density control # Clone under-reconstructed, split over-reconstructed, prune near-zero gradients # Exact heuristics not specified in sources return V A variant of global optimization specifically for reconstructing images from sparse pixel data. It uses a gradient solver that operates on the entire image, as opposed to block-based approaches. It is chosen when global consistency is more important than computational speed per iteration. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and the cost of gradient computation. For compressive rendering, convolution dominates runtime and scales linearly with iteration count. For volume rendering, each iteration projects the 3D volume and computes losses, avoiding the 30K iterations required by standard approaches. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full image or volume representation, which grows with resolution. Strengths: Produces higher quality reconstructions by leveraging global context and is compatible with Fan-Beam, Cone-Beam, Sparse-View, and Limited-Angle CT geometries. Limitations: Slower per-iteration runtime and high memory usage; CPU-GPU memory transfers further slow compressive rendering solvers if not optimized. When to use: When reconstruction quality and global consistency are prioritized over speed, and for sparse-view or limited-angle CT reconstruction. When not to use: When real-time performance is required or when memory is constrained. Global optimization in compressive rendering was proposed in a thesis on GPU-based compressive volume rendering, which suggested a parallel-based reconstruction approach. In neural volume rendering, global optimization using differentiable rendering and adaptive density control was introduced for discretized Gaussian representation in tomographic reconstruction, demonstrating substantial improvement over standard methods. name: Neural Volume Rendering Training Setup
head: Training and Optimization Setup
body: This article details the hyperparameters, data preprocessing, and hardware configurations required to train neural volume rendering models, focusing on the implicit neural representation (INR) approach for medical volume data. It establishes the baseline training loop for reconstructing high-resolution volumes from downsampled inputs using an L1 loss and Adam optimizer. A minor variant, Mobile-GS, adapts this setup for 3D Gaussian Splatting with distillation and quantization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D medical volume scan (e.g., FLAIR MRI) denoted as x, typically with dimensions such as 155 \times 240 \times 240. Output: A reconstructed volume y with resolution close to the original x. Data Structures and Preprocessing: 1. Normalization: Scale voxel values of x to the range [0, 1]. 2. Patch Segmentation: Segment the normalized volume into non-overlapping patches of size 64 \times 64 \times 64. 3. HR Patch Selection: Calculate the ratio of non-zero voxels in each patch. Classify a patch as High-Resolution (HR) if \ge 70\% of its voxels are non-zero. Select one HR patch as the input for the training pipeline. Training Loop Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.0015. Loss Function: L1 loss between reconstructed volume y and original volume x: \mathcal{L} = \| y - x \|1. Duration: 5,000 epochs. Hardware: NVIDIA A4000 16GB GPU with CUDA support. Framework: PyTorch. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the input volume has uniform voxel values, normalization requires a zero-division guard. Volume dimensions (e.g., 155 \times 240 \times 240) may not be divisible by the patch size (64), requiring boundary handling during segmentation. If no patch meets the 70\% non-zero threshold, the pipeline fails to select an input. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def preprocessandselectpatch(volume: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: # 1. Normalize to [0, 1] minval = volume.min() maxval = volume.max() if maxval == minval: normalized = torch.zeroslike(volume) # Guard for constant volume else: normalized = (volume - minval) / (maxval - minval) # 2. Segment into 64x64x64 patches patchsize = 64 D, H, W = normalized.shape patches = [] for d in range(0, D, patchsize): for h in range(0, H, patchsize): for w in range(0, W, patchsize): dend = min(d + patchsize, D) hend = min(h + patchsize, H) wend = min(w + patchsize, W) patch = normalized[d:dend, h:hend, w:wend] # 3. HR Patch Selection: >= 70% non-zero nonzeroratio = (patch != 0).sum() / patch.numel() if nonzeroratio >= 0.7: patches.append(patch) if not patches: raise ValueError("No High-Resolution patches found") # Guard return patches[0] def trainloop(model, x: torch.Tensor, epochs: int = 5000, lr: float = 0.0015): optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr) criterion = nn.L1Loss() device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.isavailable() else "cpu") model, x = model.to(device), x.to(device) for epoch in range(epochs): optimizer.zerograd() y = model(x) # Forward pass loss = criterion(y, x) # L1 loss between y and x loss.backward() optimizer.step() A variant for 3D Gaussian Splatting on mobile devices. It initializes the MLP \phi to output 1 to stabilize training. It uses Mini-Splatting as a teacher model for distillation. Neural vector quantization is launched at iteration 35,000. It adopts multi-view training for stronger constraints. Training runs for 60,000 iterations on an RTX 3090 GPU using PyTorch. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method reduces data size while preserving essential information for medical imaging. Strengths: Normalization and patching streamline computations. Limitations: The downsampling scale is fixed (1/2, 1/4, and 1/8) and not learned, which limits adaptability. When to use: When training INR-based volume reconstruction on medical data with limited computational resources (e.g., single GPU). The method is based on an end-to-end implicit neural representation architecture for medical volume data. It addresses the challenge of compressing and reconstructing high-resolution 3D medical scans (like FLAIR MRI) efficiently. The pipeline combines a non-trainable 3D downsampling module (Fourier Transform, low-pass filter, Inverse Fourier Transform) with a CNN and attention mechanism for super-resolution. The Mobile-GS variant extends these principles to real-time Gaussian Splatting for mobile deployment. An end-to-end implicit neural representation architecture for medical volume data., https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0314944, fetched 2026-10-26 Mobile-GS: Real-time Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Devices, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.11531, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Handpainted Reference Image Inversion
head: Reference Image Inversion, Semantic Colorization via Inversion
body: Handpainted Reference Image Inversion is a training task where a volume rendering model learns to reproduce a user-edited 2D reference image from a 3D volume, demonstrating the ability to learn complex classification features that are difficult to define with traditional multidimensional transfer functions. It solves the problem of tedious trial-and-error transfer function adjustments by allowing the model to automatically learn the parameters required to replicate a user-provided visual effect. The method builds on scribble-based transfer function interactions where users modify appearance via 2D image space edits. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (e.g., Bonsai3, Pig) and a set of reference images. The reference images are created by rendering the volume with an initial intensity-based transfer function to generate base images, then editing them in an image editor to create exemplary semantic colorization (e.g., removing spurious structures, adapting colors for consistency). Output: A trained rendering model (e.g., DVRNet, VNet variants, RenderNet, or Lookup table) capable of generating images that match the semantic content of the reference images. Data Structures: Volume Data: 3D scalar fields (e.g., CT data). Reference Images: 2D RGB images of 200 × 200 resolution. Model Architectures: The method is evaluated on several architectures: Lookup Table (standard multidimensional transfer function representation), RenderNet (MLP-based projection layer), VNet Variants (convolutional neural networks like VNet4-4, VNetL16-4, VNetL16-17), and DVRNet (Deep Direct Volume Rendering network). Numbered Steps: 1. Dataset Creation: Render the 3D volume using an initial intensity-based transfer function to generate base images. Edit these images in an image editor to create the target reference images. For example, in the Bonsai-H dataset, spurious green structures from a CT scanning table are removed, and colors are adapted for consistency (brown/orange for pot/stem, blue for grass). In the Pig-H dataset, coin visibility and brightness are adapted to bright yellow, and the coin slot is colored green. 2. Model Selection: Choose a rendering model architecture (Lookup, RenderNet, VNet, or DVRNet). 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between the rendered image Y{pred} and the reference image Y using a combination of Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM): L(Y, Y{pred}) = L{MSE}(Y, Y{pred}) + (1 - SSIM(Y, Y{pred})) The SSIM term is included to help recreate finer details. 4. Optimization: Train the model to minimize the loss function for 200 epochs. 5. Evaluation: Assess the model's ability to reproduce semantic attributes (e.g., distinct coloring, brightness) and consistency across views. Parameters: Training Duration: 200 epochs. Lookup Table: Batch size = 32, Learning rate = 0.03. RenderNet: Batch size = 10, Learning rate = 0.05. VNet Variants and DVRNet: Batch size = 2, Learning rate = 0.003. Hardware Constraint: Batch sizes were adapted to maximize usage of 32GB GPU memory. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lookup Table Limitations: Converges to a minimum achieving only general visual qualities, failing to find an adequate transfer function for complex semantic colorization. RenderNet Issues: Suffers from excessive overblurring due to low image resolution during projection and lacks explicit opacity handling, leading to inconsistent coloring between views. VNet Limitations: May assign general semantics but miss specific coloring details (e.g., tree stem, grass) and object brightness (e.g., coin brightness). DVRNet Limitations: While performing best overall, it may have minor issues with consistent coloring (e.g., green coloring for the coin slot) across all views. A technique that approximates a desired rendering setting (viewpoint, color, opacity, light direction/magnitude) from a single reference image by optimizing transformation parameters of a pre-trained composed iVR-GS model. It solves the problem of tedious trial-and-error transfer function adjustments by allowing the model to automatically learn the parameters required to replicate a user-provided visual effect. This method enables editing of lighting and appearance via optimization, achieving perceptual fidelity even from reference images. Time Complexity: DVRNet shows considerably better training speed compared to full VNet variants, attributed to the reduced cost of performing upsampling. Memory Complexity: Batch sizes are constrained by available GPU memory (e.g., 32GB). Lookup and RenderNet can train with higher batch sizes (32 and 10 respectively) compared to VNet and DVRNet (batch size 2). Measured Performance: DVRNet and VNetL16-17 perform very similarly regarding LPIPS and FID metrics, while VNetL16-4 performs best in terms of SSIM on the Bonsai3-H dataset. Strengths: Capable of learning complex classification features and semantic colorization that are difficult to define with traditional multidimensional transfer functions. Limitations: Performance varies significantly by architecture; Lookup tables and RenderNet are unsuitable for complex semantic tasks. Consistency across views can be challenging for some architectures. When to Use: When the goal is to replicate complex semantic colorization or visual effects from hand-painted reference images rather than pure photometric accuracy. When Not to Use: When simple intensity-based transfer functions are sufficient, or when strict consistency across all views is required without the computational overhead of deep learning models. The method was introduced in the paper "Deep Direct Volume Rendering: Learning Visual Feature Mappings From Exemplary Images". It builds on previous work involving scribble-based transfer function interactions where users can modify the transfer function via interactions in the 2D image space. The authors created two new datasets, Bonsai-H and Pig-H, based on the original Bonsai3 and Pig datasets to demonstrate the power of deeper architectures in learning complex classification features. Deep Direct Volume Rendering: Learning Visual Feature Mappings From Exemplary Images, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.05429, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Volume Exploration
head: Automatic Approximation, Reference Image Optimization
body: Inverse Volume Exploration is a technique that approximates a desired rendering setting (viewpoint, color, opacity, light direction/magnitude) from a single reference image by optimizing transformation parameters of a pre-trained composed iVR-GS model. It solves the problem of tedious trial-and-error transfer function adjustments by allowing the model to automatically learn the parameters required to replicate a user-provided visual effect. Unlike base 3D Gaussian Splatting which bakes the scene appearance, this method enables editing of lighting and appearance via optimization, achieving perceptual fidelity even from poor viewpoint reference images. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A composed iVR-GS model (formed by composing multiple basic iVR-GS models), a target reference image, and its corresponding camera pose. Output: A transformed iVR-GS model with optimized transformation parameters for color, opacity, and lighting, capable of replicating the reference image and generating novel view synthesis (NVS) results under those learned settings. Data Structures: The method operates on a composed iVR-GS model consisting of multiple basic iVR-GS models. Each basic model contains Gaussian primitives with editable attributes. The optimization targets specific transformation parameters rather than the primitive attributes themselves. Parameters: Learning rate: 0.01. Optimization iterations: 1,000 iterations on the reference image until convergence. Steps: 1. Composition: Compose all related basic iVR-GS models into a single composed model. 2. Reference Generation: Render a target reference image using settings (viewpoint, color, opacity, light direction/magnitude) that differ from the training images used to create the basic models. Ensure that the visible voxel value ranges in the reference image are covered by the composed model. 3. Freezing: Freeze all Gaussian primitive attribute values (including position, covariance, etc.) of all editable Gaussian attributes. 4. Optimization: Optimize multiple transformation parameters to modify the scene's color, opacity, and light settings using the reference image as the target. The optimization uses a combination of L1 and SSIM loss. Color: Make the global parameter cp learnable for each basic iVR-GS model. Opacity: Multiply and optimize a scaling factor for each basic iVR-GS model to control their contribution to the VolVis scene. Lighting (Magnitude): Optimize lighting globally for the composed model using two learnable parameter vectors \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 1} and b \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 1} applied to the basic iVR-GS attributes \{ka, kd, ks, \beta\} (ambient, diffuse, specular coefficients, and exponent) via the linear transformation: \{ka', kd', ks', \beta'\} = \lambda \{ka, kd, ks, \beta\} + b. Lighting (Direction): If the reference image employs an orbital light, optimize the light direction using two learnable parameters denoting polar and azimuthal light angles in the spherical coordinate system. 5. Evaluation: Render 181 images from the volume under novel viewpoints using the learned settings to evaluate reconstruction quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inversevolumeexploration(composedmodel, referenceimage, camerapose): # Step 1: Compose basic models (handled by composedmodel input) # Step 2: Freeze all Gaussian primitive attributes for basicmodel in composedmodel.basicmodels: basicmodel.freezeprimitiveattributes() # Step 3: Initialize learnable transformation parameters # Color: Global parameter cp for each basic model for basicmodel in composedmodel.basicmodels: basicmodel.cp = [0.0] len(basicmodel.cp) # Opacity: Scaling factor for each basic model for basicmodel in composedmodel.basicmodels: basicmodel.opacityscale = 1.0 # Lighting Magnitude: Global vectors lambda and b for the composed model # Attributes: {ka, kd, ks, beta} composedmodel.lambdavec = [0.0] 4 composedmodel.biasvec = [0.0] 4 # Lighting Direction: If orbital light is used if referenceimage.requiresorbitallightoptimization: composedmodel.lightpolarangle = 0.0 composedmodel.lightazimuthalangle = 0.0 # Step 4: Optimization Loop lr = 0.01 for iteration in range(1000): # Render current view renderedimage = composedmodel.render(camerapose) # Compute Loss: L1 + SSIM loss = l1loss(renderedimage, referenceimage) + ssimloss(renderedimage, referenceimage) # Gradient descent update (simplified) updateparameters(composedmodel, loss, lr) # Step 5: Apply optimized parameters to the model return composedmodel def l1loss(rendered, target): return sum(abs(r - t) for r, t in zip(rendered, target)) / len(rendered) def ssimloss(rendered, target): # Standard structural similarity metric computation return 1.0 - computestructuralsimilarity(rendered, target) def updateparameters(model, loss, lr): # Placeholder for automatic differentiation step # In practice, gradients are computed via backpropagation for param in model.getlearnableparams(): param -= lr param.gradient Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel Range Coverage: The visible voxel value ranges of the reference image must be covered by the composed model; otherwise, the approximation may fail. Poor Viewpoints: The method can achieve perceptual fidelity even when the reference image is associated with a poor viewpoint, though reconstruction quality may vary. Orbital Light: Optimization of light direction is conditional; it is only performed if the reference image employs an orbital light. The fundamental unit of the composed model, containing Gaussian primitives with editable transfer function attributes. It serves as the base for composing complex scenes. Choose it when isolating individual transfer function behaviors is required before composition. Link A structure formed by combining multiple basic iVR-GS models to represent complex volumetric data with multiple transfer functions. It allows for global lighting optimization. Choose it when managing multiple transfer functions simultaneously is necessary. Link Time Complexity: Optimization time scales with the total number of primitives. For the tested datasets, optimization took between 48 and 122 seconds. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Combustion Dataset: 5,432,519 primitives, PSNR 27.62 dB, LPIPS 0.033, Optimization time 88 s. Five-Jet Dataset: 1,484,642 primitives, PSNR 25.86 dB, LPIPS 0.046, Optimization time 48 s. Vortex Dataset: 7,104,441 primitives, PSNR 30.49 dB, LPIPS 0.031, Optimization time 122 s. Strengths: Eliminates tedious trial-and-error transfer function adjustments; allows automatic approximation of intended rendering settings; achieves perceptual fidelity even from poor viewpoint reference images; enables novel view synthesis under learned settings without access to original volume data. Limitations: Requires a composed iVR-GS model; optimization time increases with the number of primitives; relies on the composed model covering the visible voxel ranges of the reference image. Inverse Volume Exploration was introduced in the iVR-GS (Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting) paper. It is part of the iVR-GS framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting for volume visualization by allowing editable transfer functions. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of manual scene editing in volumetric visualization, providing a way to automatically learn rendering parameters from reference images. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Coarse-to-fine Sparse Volume Training
head: Coarse-to-fine reconstruction, Sparse volume finetuning with pruning, Training and Optimization
body: This method defines the training and optimization pipeline for sparse neural radiance fields, specifically focusing on the fine-tuning stage that refines a pre-constructed sparse volume V^g per scene. It solves the problem of achieving high-fidelity novel view synthesis with significantly reduced training time compared to dense per-scene optimization methods like NeRF. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a coarse-to-fine iterative pruning and subdivision strategy during optimization, rather than static initialization or global optimization over the entire dataset. It builds on Neural Volume Rendering Training (MSE). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A pre-constructed sparse neural volume V^g containing per-voxel neural features and an MLP decoder R; a set of captured reference images with known camera poses; ground truth pixel colors \hat{C}. Outputs: An optimized sparse neural volume V^g and updated MLP decoder R parameters. Data Structures: Sparse Volume V^g: A sparse mapping of 3D voxel coordinates to neural feature vectors. MLP Decoder R: A multi-layer perceptron that maps spatial position, view direction, and voxel features to volume density and view-dependent radiance. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with the sparse volume V^g and decoder R obtained from the pre-training phase (local reconstruction and end-to-end fusion training). 2. Per-Scene Optimization Loop: Iterate for a maximum of 25,000 iterations. 3. Rendering: For each iteration, render novel view images from both the current global volume V^gt and the local volume Vt using differentiable ray marching, supervising with ground truth. 4. Loss Calculation: Compute the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between rendered colors and ground truth colors. 5. Backpropagation: Update the per-voxel neural features in V^g and the MLP decoder weights using gradient descent. 6. Coarse-to-Fine Refinement: Every 10,000 iterations, perform the following structural updates: Pruning: Remove unnecessary voxels from V^g based on a threshold criterion (referenced as Eqn. 8 in the source). Subdivision: Subdivide each remaining voxel into 8 sub-voxels. This increases the spatial resolution of the representation. 7. Termination: Stop after 25,000 iterations. Formulas: The optimization minimizes the rendering loss. The core loss component cited for the fusion/training phase is: \mathcal{L}{\text{fuse}} = \sumt \|Ct - \hat{C}\|2^2 + \|Ct^g - \hat{C}\|2^2 Where: t indexes the input frames/views. \hat{C} is the ground truth pixel color. Ct is the pixel color rendered from the local volume Vt. Ct^g is the pixel color rendered from the global volume V^gt after fusing frame t. During the specific fine-tuning phase described, the primary objective is to minimize the error between the rendered global volume and the ground truth, effectively optimizing the features to match \hat{C}. Parameters: Optimization Iterations: Less than 25,000. Pruning/Subdivision Interval: Every 10,000 iterations. Subdivision Factor: 8 sub-voxels per parent voxel. Training Time: Less than 1 hour per scene on standard hardware. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofinesparsevolumetraining(Vg, R, images, poses, maxiterations=25000, interval=10000): """ Fine-tunes a sparse neural volume and MLP decoder per scene. Args: Vg: Sparse mapping of voxel coordinates to neural feature vectors. R: MLP decoder function(position, direction, feature) -> (density, radiance). images: List of ground truth RGB arrays. poses: List of camera extrinsics/intrinsics. maxiterations: Total optimization steps. interval: Steps between pruning and subdivision. Returns: Vg: Optimized sparse volume. R: Optimized MLP decoder. """ for step in range(1, maxiterations + 1): totalloss = 0.0 # Gradient accumulators (conceptual for pseudocode) gradVg = {} gradR = {} for img, pose in zip(images, poses): # 1. Generate rays from camera pose rays = generateraysfrompose(pose, img.shape) # 2. Differentiable ray marching renderedcolors = [] for ray in rays: samples = samplealongray(ray, numsamples=128) densities = [] radiances = [] for pos in samples: feat = Vg.get(voxelkey(pos), defaultzerovector) dens, rad = R(pos, ray.direction, feat) densities.append(dens) radiances.append(rad) color = volumerendercomposite(densities, radiances) renderedcolors.append(color) # 3. Compute MSE loss loss = sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(renderedcolors, img.flatten())) totalloss += loss # 4. Backpropagation and parameter update # Automatic differentiation updates Vg features and R weights Vg = sgdupdate(Vg, gradVg, lr=0.01) R = sgdupdate(R, gradR, lr=0.01) # 5. Coarse-to-fine refinement if step % interval == 0: # Prune unnecessary voxels (source references Eqn. 8 for criterion) Vg = prunevoxelsbythreshold(Vg, threshold=0.01) # Subdivide each remaining voxel into 8 sub-voxels Vg = subdividevoxels(Vg, factor=8) return Vg, R def generateraysfrompose(pose, imgshape): # Standard pinhole camera projection to generate ray origins and directions return [(pose.origin + (u, v, 1) @ pose.invintrinsics) for u, v in grid(imgshape)] def samplealongray(ray, numsamples): return [ray.origin + ray.direction t for t in linspace(ray.near, ray.far, numsamples)] def volumerendercomposite(densities, radiances): # Alpha compositing: C = sum(Ti alphai ci) alphas = 1.0 - exp(-densities) transmittances = [1.0] + [prod(1.0 - a for a in alphas[:i]) for i in range(1, len(alphas))] return sum(t a c for t, a, c in zip(transmittances, alphas, radiances)) def sgdupdate(structure, grads, lr): return {k: v - lr grads.get(k, 0) for k, v in structure.items()} def prunevoxelsbythreshold(Vg, threshold): # Removes voxels whose density or feature magnitude falls below threshold # Exact threshold formula from Eqn. 8 not provided in sources return {k: v for k, v in Vg.items() if magnitude(v) > threshold} def subdividevoxels(Vg, factor): # Splits each voxel into 8 children, initializing child features newVg = {} for k, v in Vg.items(): for dx, dy, dz in product([-1, 1], repeat=3): newk = tuple(k[i] + dx/2 for i in range(3)) newVg[newk] = v / 2.0 # Standard feature interpolation for subdivision return newVg The initial training of the local reconstruction network and radiance field decoder using \mathcal{L}{\text{local}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{fuse}} to initialize the model before fine-tuning. The underlying sparse data structure that allows for efficient storage and dynamic modification (pruning/subdivision) of the neural features. Time Complexity: Optimization requires less than 25,000 iterations and takes less than 1 hour per scene, significantly faster than dense per-scene methods like NeRF. Memory Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of V^g, with pruning reducing memory usage and subdivision increasing it. Strengths: Fast per-scene optimization and dynamic resolution refinement. Limitations: Requires a good initial reconstruction from the pre-training phase. When to use: When high-quality novel view synthesis is needed for a specific scene with limited computational resources or time constraints, and a pre-trained model is available. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the NeRFusion paper, which introduces a framework for fusing radiance fields for large-scale scene reconstruction. The coarse-to-fine training strategy is adapted from NSVF. It was developed to address the computational bottleneck of training neural radiance fields per scene, offering a faster alternative to pure per-scene optimization methods like NeRF. The approach is used in large-scale indoor scene reconstruction (e.g., ScanNet) and small object reconstruction (e.g., DTU). NeRFusion: Fusing Radiance Fields for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00537, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Inverse Rendering for Texture/Attribute Refinement
head: Photometric Loss Refinement, TexF Refinement via Inverse Rendering, UV Supervised Refinement
body: This method refines the attributes of a surface-aligned texture field (TexF) by propagating image-space supervision through a differentiable rendering process. It minimizes a photometric loss between reference images (generated from standard UV mapping) and rendered images (generated by querying the TexF at rasterized surface positions). This approach reduces transfer and discretization errors during representation construction and refines the compressed neural field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A surface-aligned texture field (TexF) defined on a sparse set of active voxels Q, where each voxel stores texture attributes. A set of reference images rendered from a 2D UV atlas. Camera parameters for the reference views. Output: Refined voxel attributes for the active set Q. Data Structures: Active Set Q: A sparse collection of voxel indices q \in \mathbb{Z}^3 such that 0 \le q < K, where K is the grid resolution. Only voxels intersecting the mesh surface are included. The dense K^3 grid is not allocated. Voxel Attributes: Each q \in Q stores a vector of attributes. The specific dimensionality is not given in the sources [G: typically 3 for RGB color]. Steps: 1. Rasterization: For each reference view, rasterize the mesh surface to obtain 2D screen coordinates and corresponding 3D surface positions. 2. TexF Query: For each rasterized surface position, query the TexF. The attributes are obtained by trilinearly interpolating the attributes of the neighboring voxels in the sparse grid. 3. Rendering: Construct the rendered image from the queried attributes. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric loss \mathcal{L}{photo} between the rendered image I{TexF} and the reference UV image I{UV}: \mathcal{L}{photo} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \| I{TexF}^{(i)} - I{UV}^{(i)} \|^2. 5. Optimization: Update the voxel attributes in Q using gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}{photo}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def refinetexfattributes(texf, mesh, referenceimages, cameras, numiterations, learningrate): # texf: dict mapping voxelindex (tuple) to attributevector # mesh: object with.vertices and.faces # referenceimages: list of 2D arrays # cameras: list of camera objects with.project() method gradaccum = {idx: np.zeroslike(attr) for idx, attr in texf.items()} for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0.0 for refimg, camera in zip(referenceimages, cameras): # 1. Rasterize mesh to obtain screen coordinates and 3D surface positions screencoords, surfacepositions = rasterize(mesh, camera) # 2. Query TexF at surface positions using trilinear interpolation renderedcolors = [trilinear(texf, pos) for pos in surfacepositions] # 3. Construct rendered image from queried attributes renderedimg = np.zeroslike(refimg) for (u, v), color in zip(screencoords, renderedcolors): renderedimg[v, u] = color # 4. Compute photometric loss loss = np.mean((renderedimg - refimg) 2) totalloss += loss # 5. Backpropagate and update attributes # Gradients flow through interpolation and rasterization to texf attributes grad = 2.0 (renderedimg - refimg) / refimg.size for (u, v), pos, g in zip(screencoords, surfacepositions, grad): updategradients(texf, pos, g) # Apply accumulated gradients for idx in texf: texf[idx] -= learningrate gradaccum[idx] gradaccum[idx] = np.zeroslike(texf[idx]) return texf def rasterize(mesh, camera): # Standard rasterization: project vertices, sort faces by depth, fill screen. # Returns list of (u, v) and corresponding 3D positions. # The sources do not specify the rasterization implementation. def trilinear(texf, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation from 8 neighboring active voxels. # Handles boundary conditions by clamping or zero-padding if neighbors are missing. # The sources do not specify the interpolation implementation. def updategradients(texf, pos, grad): # Distribute grad to contributing voxels based on interpolation weights. # The sources do not specify the gradient distribution implementation. Parameters: Learning Rate: Not given in the sources. Number of Iterations: Not given in the sources. Trilinear Interpolation: Standard 3D trilinear interpolation is used for querying the sparse grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Grid Boundaries: Since the grid is sparse and surface-aligned, queries near the boundary of the active set Q must handle missing neighbors. The sources do not specify the boundary condition (e.g., zero-padding, clamping) [G: typically zero-padding or clamping to nearest valid voxel]. Discretization Errors: The method aims to reduce discretization errors, but the quality of refinement depends on the initial voxelization accuracy. Repaint123 uses a progressive controllable repainting mechanism to refine generated mesh textures. It incorporates textural information from a reference image via attention feature injection and employs a visibility-aware repainting process to refine overlap regions with varying strengths. The refined images are then used as ground truths to directly optimize the texture through an MSE loss, achieving fast optimization. This variant differs from standard TexF refinement by using diffusion-based repainting and attention mechanisms for texture injection, rather than direct voxel attribute optimization via trilinear queries. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method uses a sparse voxel grid, avoiding the allocation of a dense K^3 grid. Memory usage is proportional to the number of active voxels intersecting the mesh surface, comparable to 2D texture maps. Time: Each optimization step requires rasterization, trilinear interpolation, and MSE computation. The complexity per step is linear in the number of pixels and active voxels involved in the query. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The sparse support allows high-resolution texture representation with sample counts comparable to 2D texture maps, avoiding the high memory cost of dense volumetric textures. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces transfer and discretization errors; efficient memory usage due to sparsity; direct optimization of 3D attributes. Limitations: Requires differentiable rendering. When to Use: Use when refining texture attributes for a surface-aligned sparse voxel grid (TexF) where memory efficiency is critical and high-resolution texture is needed. When Not to Use: Do not use if the texture representation is a dense 3D volume or a 2D UV atlas without 3D attributes. Inverse rendering optimizes geometry or appearance by propagating image-space supervision through a differentiable rendering process. The TexF method applies this to surface-aligned texture fields, organizing texture attributes in a sparse voxel grid derived from the mesh surface. This allows surface positions to directly query the 3D field, providing a common spatial basis for texture representation, compression, and rendering. The method was proposed to overcome limitations of conventional 2D UV atlas compression. name: INR Training Loop
body: The INR Training Loop optimizes an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) to approximate a discrete volumetric dataset. It learns a continuous function f\theta that maps 3D coordinates to scalar values by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between network predictions and ground-truth samples drawn uniformly from the volume domain. Inputs: Volume V of size N \times N \times N; neural network f\theta with parameters \theta; encoding function \gamma; learning rate \eta; batch size B. Outputs: Trained network f\theta representing V as a continuous function. Data Structures: Coordinates: Set of B tuples \{(xj, yj, zj)\}{j=1}^B; Encodings: Vector ej = \gamma(xj, yj, zj); Predictions: Scalar \hat{v}j = f\theta(ej); Ground Truth: Scalar vj obtained via trilinear interpolation. Steps: 1. Sample B coordinates \{(xj, yj, zj)\}{j=1}^B uniformly from the volume domain. 2. For each coordinate, compute encoding ej \leftarrow \gamma(xj, yj, zj). 3. Compute network output \hat{v}j \leftarrow f\theta(ej). 4. Retrieve ground truth vj \leftarrow \text{trilinear}(V, xj, yj, zj). 5. Compute MSE loss L \leftarrow \frac{1}{B} \sum{j=1}^B (\hat{v}j - vj)^2. 6. Perform gradient update \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla\theta L. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def traininr(V, ftheta, gamma, eta, B, numiterations): """ V: 3D array of shape (N, N, N) ftheta: neural network function taking encoded coordinates gamma: encoding function eta: learning rate B: batch size numiterations: number of training steps """ N = V.shape[0] for in range(numiterations): # 1. Sample B coordinates uniformly from the volume domain [0, N-1] coords = [(random.uniform(0, N - 1), random.uniform(0, N - 1), random.uniform(0, N - 1)) for in range(B)] losses = [] for (x, y, z) in coords: # 2. Encode e = gamma(x, y, z) # 3. Predict vhat = ftheta(e) # 4. Ground Truth via trilinear interpolation v = trilinear(V, x, y, z) # 5. Accumulate squared error losses.append((vhat - v) 2) # 6. Compute MSE loss L = sum(losses) / B # Compute gradients ∇θ L via automatic differentiation # Update parameters θ ← θ - η∇θ L for param in ftheta.parameters: param -= eta grad[param] return ftheta def trilinear(V, x, y, z): # Standard trilinear interpolation for continuous coordinates in [0, N-1] # Clamps coordinates to volume bounds to prevent out-of-bounds access x = max(0, min(V.shape[0] - 1, x)) y = max(0, min(V.shape[1] - 1, y)) z = max(0, min(V.shape[2] - 1, z)) # Extract grid points and interpolation weights x0, y0, z0 = int(x), int(y), int(z) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 # Fetch values with boundary checks def val(ix, iy, iz): ix = max(0, min(V.shape[0] - 1, ix)) iy = max(0, min(V.shape[1] - 1, iy)) iz = max(0, min(V.shape[2] - 1, iz)) return V[ix, iy, iz] # Trilinear interpolation formula c00 = val(x0, y0, z0) (1 - dx) + val(x1, y0, z0) dx c01 = val(x0, y0, z1) (1 - dx) + val(x1, y0, z1) dx c10 = val(x0, y1, z0) (1 - dx) + val(x1, y1, z0) dx c11 = val(x0, y1, z1) (1 - dx) + val(x1, y1, z1) dx c0 = c00 (1 - dy) + c10 dy c1 = c01 (1 - dy) + c11 dy return c0 (1 - dz) + c1 dz Parameters: \eta: Not given in the sources. B: Not given in the sources. \gamma: Positional or hash encoding. Edge Cases: Boundary Conditions: Trilinear interpolation requires coordinates to be within the volume bounds; coordinates sampled uniformly over a continuous domain may fall outside discrete indices and require clamping. Precision: Trilinear interpolation introduces smoothing artifacts compared to nearest-neighbor sampling, which may affect high-frequency reconstruction. A pretraining strategy using meta-learning to optimize initial network parameters from a sparse, spatiotemporally subsampled volumetric dataset, enabling rapid adaptation to unseen similar volumes via few gradient steps. It differs from standard INR training by optimizing a shared initialization that serves as a strong prior for generalizability, rather than training each volume independently from scratch. This approach significantly reduces the computational overhead of encoding new volumes in time-varying or ensemble datasets, achieving encoding speeds approximately 5.87× faster than training from scratch while maintaining higher reconstruction quality. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Algorithm 1 is described in as "INR training for volumetric data." Hash encodings are noted as a replacement for positional encoding in modern implementations. name: Meta-INR
head: Few-shot INR Adaptation, MAML-based INR Training
body:
Meta-INR is a pretraining strategy for Implicit Neural Representations (INR) that uses meta-learning to optimize initial network parameters from a sparse, spatiotemporally subsampled volumetric dataset, enabling rapid adaptation to unseen similar volumes via few gradient steps. It differs from standard INR training by optimizing a shared initialization that serves as a strong prior for generalizability, rather than focusing on network architecture design or training each volume independently from scratch. This approach significantly reduces the computational overhead of encoding new volumes in time-varying or ensemble datasets, achieving encoding speeds approximately 5.87× faster than training from scratch while maintaining higher reconstruction quality. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volumetric dataset D consisting of T timesteps or ensembles. Each volume di is a set of coordinate-value pairs (Ci, Vi), where Ci contains spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and Vi contains corresponding voxel values. Output: Optimized meta-model parameters 	hetam. Data Structures Network Architecture (\Phi): Maps a 3D spatial coordinate to a scalar voxel value: \Phi: \mathbb{R}^3 ightarrow \mathbb{R}. The implementation uses a seven-layer SIREN model with a hidden layer dimension of 256. Meta-Model Parameters (	hetam): The shared weights initialized randomly and optimized via meta-learning. Cloned Parameters (	heta'): A copy of 	hetam used for inner-loop adaptation. Parameters Spatial subsampling interval (\lambdas): 4. Temporal subsampling interval (\lambdat): 2. Inner-loop steps (K): 16. Inner-loop learning rate (\alpha): 0.0001 during meta-pretraining. Outer-loop learning rate ( eta): 0.0001 during meta-pretraining. Batch size: 50,000 coordinate-value pairs per iteration for both meta-pretraining and finetuning. Finetuning learning rates (\alpha,  eta): 0.00001. Algorithm Steps 1. Subsampling: Create a downsampled dataset \hat{D} = \{\hat{d}1,..., \hat{d}{T'}\} from D by subsampling spatially with interval \lambdas and temporally with interval \lambdat. This configuration retains approximately 0.78% of the original data samples. 2. Initialization: Randomly initialize meta-model parameters 	hetam. 3. Meta-Pretraining Loop: Iterate until convergence: a. Initialize outer-loop gradients 
abla{	hetam} = 0. b. For each subsampled volume \hat{d}i in \hat{D}: i. Clone parameters: 	heta' \leftarrow 	hetam. ii. Randomly sample a batch of coordinate-value pairs (Ci, Vi) from \hat{d}i. iii. Perform K inner-loop gradient steps: 1. Compute loss: L \leftarrow 	ext{MSE}(\Phi(Ci; 	heta'), Vi). 2. Update cloned parameters: 	heta' \leftarrow 	heta' - \alpha 
abla{	heta'} L. iv. Accumulate gradients for the outer loop: 
abla{	hetam} \leftarrow 
abla{	hetam} + (	hetam - 	heta'). c. Update meta-model parameters: 	hetam \leftarrow 	hetam -  eta  rac{
abla{	hetam}}{T'}. 4. Volume-Specific Finetuning: For a specific target volume, take the pre-trained 	hetam and update it in K gradient steps using all available (non-subsampled) data points from that volume, using the finetuning learning rates. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def metainrpretraining(D, lambdas, lambdat, alpha, beta, K, batchsize): # Step 1: Subsample dataset D spatially by lambdas and temporally by lambdat Dhat = [vol[::lambdas] for vol in D[::lambdat]] Tprime = len(Dhat) # Step 2: Randomly initialize meta-model parameters thetam thetam = [0.01 (2 random.random() - 1) for in range(1000)] # Step 3: Meta-pretraining loop while True: # Convergence check omitted for brevity gradthetam = [0.0] len(thetam) for dhati in Dhat: thetaprime = thetam[:] # Clone # Randomly sample batch idx = random.sample(range(len(dhati)), batchsize) coords = [dhati[i][0] for i in idx] values = [dhati[i][1] for i in idx] for in range(K): # Forward pass and MSE loss preds = [phi(c, thetaprime) for c in coords] loss = sum((p - v)2 for p, v in zip(preds, values)) / len(values) # Gradient computation gradthetaprime = computegrad(loss, thetaprime) # Inner-loop update thetaprime = [p - alpha g for p, g in zip(thetaprime, gradthetaprime)] # Accumulate outer-loop gradient: thetam - thetaprime gradthetam = [g + (tm - tp) for g, tm, tp in zip(gradthetam, thetam, thetaprime)] # Outer-loop update thetam = [tm - beta (g / Tprime) for tm, g in zip(thetam, gradthetam)] return thetam def metainrfinetuning(thetam, volumedata, alphaft, K, batchsize): thetaadapted = thetam[:] for in range(K): idx = random.sample(range(len(volumedata)), batchsize) coords = [volumedata[i][0] for i in idx] values = [volumedata[i][1] for i in idx] preds = [phi(c, thetaadapted) for c in coords] loss = sum((p - v)2 for p, v in zip(preds, values)) / len(values) gradtheta = computegrad(loss, thetaadapted) thetaadapted = [p - alphaft g for p, g in zip(thetaadapted, gradtheta)] return thetaadapted import random def phi(coords, params): return [sum(c w for c, w in zip(c, params[:3])) for c in coords] def computegrad(loss, params): return [0.0] len(params) Time Complexity: Meta-pretraining requires significant upfront computation (e.g., 2h 14m on half-cylinder), but volume-specific finetuning is extremely fast. The encoding time of adapted INRs is 5.87× faster on average across datasets compared to training from scratch. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Half-cylinder: PSNR 55.92 dB, LPIPS 0.0705, CD 0.2989, Encoding Time 43m 45s. Ionization: PSNR 51.30 dB, LPIPS 0.0576, CD 0.4622, Encoding Time 3h 15m. Tangaroa: PSNR 48.68 dB, LPIPS 0.1969, CD 0.5499, Encoding Time 33m 59s. Vortex: PSNR 48.19 dB, LPIPS 0.0294, CD 0.2029, Encoding Time 5m 10s. Strengths: Reduces computational overhead; enhances interpretability of adapted INR parameters for simulation analysis; captures intrinsic patterns from partial observation better than vanilla pretraining. Limitations: Validated only with MLP-based SIREN backbones; transfer to hash-grid or feature-grid encoders is untested. Vanilla pretraining (without inner-loop updating) produces block-like artifacts and significant deviations from Ground Truth. Meta-INR was proposed to address the computational inefficiency of training INRs from scratch for each new volume in large-scale time-varying or ensemble datasets. It is the first application of meta-learning techniques to volume data representation. The method adapts Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) principles to learn initial INR parameters from partial observation. It builds on INR Training Loop by introducing a meta-learning optimization loop. Meta-INR: Efficient Encoding of Volumetric Data via Meta-Learning Implicit Neural Representation, https://doi.org/10.1109/pacificvis64226.2025.00030, fetched 2026-10-26 PDF Deep Learning Methods and Neural Representations for Scientific Volume..., https://www.cs.uoregon.edu/Reports/AREA-202603-Mathai.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Optimization Baselines
head: Baselines, CMA-ES, Classical Optimization Baselines, Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy
body: This family provides black-box optimization strategies for inverse rendering problems where the forward rendering operator f is non-differentiable or gradient computation is prohibitively expensive. Unlike gradient-based siblings that rely on automatic differentiation or adjoint methods, these methods treat the renderer as an opaque function, minimizing a photometric loss \mathcal{L} by iteratively sampling and evaluating parameter candidates. The family is distinguished by its reliance on population-based search distributions (typically Gaussian) that adapt to the local loss landscape without explicit gradient information, offering robustness against local minima and Monte Carlo noise. All methods in this family operate within the standard inverse rendering loop defined by Optimization Loops and Training Procedures, minimizing a photometric loss \mathcal{L} between rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and ground-truth C(\mathbf{r}). The core mechanism involves maintaining a search distribution \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) over the parameter space \mathbb{R}^d, where \boldsymbol{\mu} is the mean and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is the anisotropic covariance matrix capturing correlations between parameters. The optimization proceeds in iterations. In each iteration, k candidates \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=0}^{k} are drawn from the current distribution \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}). These candidates are evaluated using the black-box renderer f to compute a cost ci = \mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}i), \mathbf{y}^). The distribution parameters \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} are then updated by computing a weighted average of the candidates, ranked by their cost. Higher weights are assigned to top-scoring candidates to adapt the search distribution to the local loss landscape. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def cmaesbaseline(renderer, targetimage, d, k=500, N=50, sigma0=1.0/6.0): """ Implements the CMA-ES baseline for black-box inverse rendering. Args: renderer: Black-box function f: R^d -> Image targetimage: Target image y d: Dimensionality of parameter space k: Population size N: Number of iterations sigma0: Initial standard deviation Returns: mu: Optimized parameters (mean of final distribution) """ mu = np.zeros(d) Sigma = sigma0 np.eye(d) for in range(N): # 1. Sampling: Draw k candidates from N(mu, Sigma) candidates = np.random.multivariatenormal(mu, Sigma, size=k) # 2. Evaluation: Compute photometric loss for each candidate costs = np.array([np.mean((renderer(x) - targetimage) 2) for x in candidates]) # 3. Ranking: Sort candidates by cost (ascending) sortedindices = np.argsort(costs) rankedcandidates = candidates[sortedindices] # 4. Weighting: Assign higher weights to top-scoring candidates weights = np.zeros(k) weights[:k//10] = 2.0 weights[k//10:] = 0.5 weights /= weights.sum() # 5. Update mean: Weighted average of ranked candidates mu = np.dot(weights, rankedcandidates) # 6. Update covariance: Rank-one/rank-mu style update using centered candidates centered = rankedcandidates - mu Sigma = np.sum(weights[:, None, None] (centered[:,:, None] centered[:, None,:]), axis=0) return mu A fully black-box framework combining a diffusion-based inverse prediction model with CMA-ES. It conditions the proposal distribution on dense visual features extracted from the target image, avoiding the information bottleneck of scalar loss values and mitigating mode averaging in ill-posed inverse problems. CMA-ES: The classical evolutionary baseline using covariance matrix adaptation. It serves as the primary reference for population-based search, adapting the Gaussian distribution to the loss landscape without auxiliary models. Dual Annealing: Combines simulated annealing with a local search strategy to improve convergence. It uses a standard implementation (e.g., SciPy) and does not maintain an explicit covariance matrix. ZeroGrads: Trains a differentiable surrogate of the black-box function’s loss landscape and uses it to derive optimization gradients. It bridges the gap between black-box and gradient-based methods by learning the gradient field. DiBO: A diffusion-based method that combines a diffusion prior with a learned reward proxy to sample candidates from an approximate posterior over high-performing solutions. It differs from FIDE by using a reward proxy rather than dense image features for conditioning. The family originates from the need to solve inverse rendering problems where differentiable rendering is unavailable or unstable. CMA-ES [Hansen 2006] serves as the primary evolutionary baseline, inheriting the ability to adapt to the local loss landscape via covariance updates and providing robustness against local minima without explicit gradient information. Dual annealing [Tsallis and Stariolo 1996] combines simulated annealing with a local search strategy to improve convergence; the standard SciPy implementation [Virtanen et al. 2020] is commonly used. From more recent methods, ZeroGrads [Fischer and Ritschel 2024] trains a differentiable surrogate of the black-box function’s loss landscape and uses it to derive optimization gradients. DiBO [Yun et al. 2025] is a diffusion-based method that combines a diffusion prior with a learned reward proxy to sample candidates from an approximate posterior over high-performing solutions. Classical Bayesian Optimization (BO) is not typically compared directly because its performance overhead is non-linear with iterations and several orders of magnitude higher than that of all other methods. name: Feature-Guided Diffusion for Inverse Rendering
head: Diffusion-CMA-ES Inverse Rendering, Diffusion-based CMA-ES, FGD, FIDE, Feature-Guided Diffusion, Feature-Guided Diffusion for Non-Differentiable Inverse Rendering, Feature-Informed Diffusion Evolution
body: Feature-Guided Diffusion for Inverse Rendering (FIDE) is a fully black-box optimization framework that solves non-differentiable inverse rendering problems by combining a diffusion-based inverse predictor with a Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES). Unlike scalar-loss baselines like Optimization Baselines or Bayesian optimization methods such as DiBO, FIDE extracts dense visual features from the target image to guide candidate proposal, thereby avoiding the information bottleneck of single-number loss values and the mode-averaging pitfalls of direct regression. It is specifically designed to handle the multi-modal ambiguity inherent in inverse graphics, where multiple parameter sets can produce identical images, by approximating the inverse function as a multi-modal conditional distribution. FIDE operates within the standard inverse rendering loop defined by Optimization Loops and Training Procedures, minimizing a photometric loss \mathcal{L} between rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and ground-truth C(\mathbf{r}). The core mechanism alternates between an inverse prediction step using a diffusion model conditioned on image features and an evolution step using CMA-ES to refine the search space. Inputs: Black-box renderer f: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathcal{I}, where \mathcal{I} is the image space. Target image \mathbf{y}^ \in \mathcal{I}. Pretrained frozen feature extractor E: \mathcal{I} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times c} (default: DINOv3). Hyperparameters: population size k=500, iterations N=50, initial standard deviation \sigma0 = 1/6. Outputs: Optimized parameters \boldsymbol{\mu} (mean of the final CMA-ES distribution). 1. CMA-ES State: Mean \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^d, initialized to \mathbf{0}d. Covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}, initialized to \sigma0 \mathbf{I}{d \times d}. 2. Diffusion Model \tilde{f}{\theta}^{-1}: Transformer-based architecture. Input Tokens: Image features \mathbf{F} = E(\mathbf{y}) flattened into tokens with learned positional embeddings. Noisy parameters \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^d projected into tokens via a learned linear layer. Processing: Four self-attention blocks on parameter tokens, followed by cross-attention with image tokens. Conditioning: Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) injects timestep information into each attention block. Output: Parameter tokens concatenated and projected back to \mathbb{R}^d via a linear layer. 3. Training Data: Dataset of pairs (\mathbf{z}i, \mathbf{y}i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) generated from CMA-ES samples. 1. Initialization: Set \boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0}d, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \sigma0 \mathbf{I}{d \times d}. Initialize diffusion weights \theta. Normalize all task parameters to [0, 1] and initialize at 0.5. 2. Iteration Loop (for i = 1 to N): 1. Sampling: Draw k candidates \{\mathbf{x}j\}{j=0}^{k-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}). 2. Inverse Prediction (Partial Denoising): Select the first k/2 candidates. Compute the timestep proxy \mathbf{s} = \sqrt{\text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})}. Denoise these candidates using the diffusion model: \{\mathbf{x}'j\}{j=0}^{k/2-1} = \tilde{f}{\theta}^{-1}(\{\mathbf{x}j\}{j=0}^{k/2-1}, E(\mathbf{y}^), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}). The denoising is performed by solving the reverse-time ODE using Euler's method with 3 steps and schedule [0.3, 0.2, 0.1]. The remaining k/2 candidates are passed through unmodified to preserve diversity and prevent mode collapse. Combine denoised and undenoised candidates to form the new population \{\mathbf{x}j\}{j=0}^{k-1}. 3. Evaluation: Render all candidates to obtain images \{\mathbf{y}j\}{j=0}^{k-1} = f(\{\mathbf{x}j\}{j=0}^{k-1}). 4. Feature Extraction: Extract features \{\mathbf{e}j\}{j=0}^{k-1} = E(\{\mathbf{y}j\}{j=0}^{k-1}). 5. Online Training: Train the diffusion model \tilde{f}{\theta}^{-1} on the current dataset \{(\mathbf{x}j, \mathbf{e}j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\} for T epochs (default 20) using the training objective: \mathcal{L}{diff} = \| \tilde{f}{\theta}^{-1}(z, \mathbf{e}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) - x \|2^2 where z \sim \mathcal{N}(x, \sigma(s)^2) is the noisy version of x. Use Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001. 6. CMA-ES Update: Compute cost cj = \mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}j), \mathbf{y}^) for all j. Rank candidates by cost. Update \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} using standard CMA-ES weighted update rules based on the ranked candidates. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def fideinverserendering(renderer, targetimage, d, k=500, N=50, sigma0=1.0/6.0, epochs=20, lr=0.001, featureextractor=None): """ Implements Feature-Guided Diffusion for Inverse Rendering (FIDE). Args: renderer: Black-box function f: R^d -> Image targetimage: Target image y d: Dimensionality of parameter space k: Population size N: Number of evolution cycles sigma0: Initial standard deviation epochs: Number of training epochs for diffusion model per iteration lr: Learning rate for diffusion model training featureextractor: Frozen feature extractor E (e.g., DINOv3) Returns: mu: Optimized parameters (mean of final distribution) """ # 1. Initialization mu = np.zeros(d) Sigma = sigma0 np.eye(d) # Diffusion model weights theta initialized to zeros theta = np.zeros(1) # Pre-compute target features targetfeatures = featureextractor(targetimage) for iteration in range(N): # 2. Sampling: Draw k candidates from N(mu, Sigma) candidates = np.random.multivariatenormal(mu, Sigma, size=k) # 3. Inverse Prediction (Partial Denoising) halfk = k // 2 noisyparams = candidates[:halfk] # Compute timestep proxy from covariance diagonal timestepproxy = np.sqrt(np.diag(Sigma)) # Denoise using diffusion model conditioned on target features # xdenoised = ftheta^-1(noisyparams, targetfeatures, Sigma) # This involves solving the reverse-time ODE with Euler's method (3 steps) denoisedcandidates = reverseodestep(noisyparams, targetfeatures, timestepproxy, steps=3) # Combine denoised and undenoised candidates candidates = np.concatenate([denoisedcandidates, candidates[halfk:]]) # 4. Evaluation: Render all candidates renderedimages = np.array([renderer(x) for x in candidates]) # 5. Feature Extraction imagefeatures = featureextractor(renderedimages) # 6. Online Training: Train diffusion model on current dataset # Generate noisy versions for training: z ~ N(x, sigma(s)^2) noise = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=candidates.shape) # sigma(s) approximated by timestepproxy for simplicity z = candidates + noise timestepproxy # Train for 'epochs' for epoch in range(epochs): # Forward pass: predict x from z, features, timestep predictedx = diffusionforward(z, imagefeatures, timestepproxy, theta) # Loss: || predictedx - x ||^2 loss = np.mean((predictedx - candidates) 2) # Backpropagate and update theta (standard optimizer step) grad = np.gradient(loss, theta) theta = theta - lr grad # 7. CMA-ES Update # Compute costs (using LPIPS or MSE as per source) costs = np.array([computeloss(renderedimages[i], targetimage) for i in range(k)]) # Rank candidates sortedindices = np.argsort(costs) rankedcandidates = candidates[sortedindices] # Weights: higher for top candidates weights = np.zeros(k) weights[:k//10] = 2.0 weights[k//10:] = 0.5 weights /= weights.sum() # Update mean mu = np.dot(weights, rankedcandidates) # Update covariance centered = rankedcandidates - mu Sigma = np.sum(weights[:, None, None] (centered[:,:, None] centered[:, None,:]), axis=0) return mu def reverseodestep(z, features, timestep, steps=3): # Simplified Euler reverse ODE solver for diffusion current = z.copy() schedule = [0.3, 0.2, 0.1] for i in range(steps): # Predict clean parameters pred = diffusionforward(current, features, timestep, thetaplaceholder) # Euler step towards prediction current = current + schedule[i] (pred - current) return current def diffusionforward(z, features, timestep, theta): # Placeholder for transformer architecture: # 1. Flatten features to tokens with pos embeddings # 2. Project z to tokens via linear layer # 3. 4 self-attention blocks on param tokens # 4. Cross-attention with image tokens # 5. FiLM conditioning with timestep # 6. Concat and project back to d # Returns predicted parameters return np.zeroslike(z) def computeloss(rendered, target): return np.mean((rendered - target) 2) Population Size (k): 500. Iterations (N): 50. Initial Standard Deviation (\sigma0): 1/6, chosen because the parameter space [0, 1] is within 3\sigma of the initialization at 0.5. Training Epochs: 20 (default), varies from 4 to 20. Learning Rate: 0.001. Reverse ODE Steps: 3 steps with schedule [0.3, 0.2, 0.1]. Feature Extractor: DINOv3 (small) is default; VGG-19 is an alternative. Mode Averaging: Naïve inverse predictors return the numerical average of multiple valid solutions, which is invalid. FIDE avoids this by using a diffusion model to represent the multi-modal posterior. Mode Collapse: Relying exclusively on denoising predictions risks the network overfitting to current estimates. FIDE mitigates this by denoising only half the candidates and passing the rest through unmodified. Non-Injectivity: Inverse rendering is often non-injective (e.g., lighting/material ambiguity). FIDE handles this by sampling distinct valid solutions rather than collapsing to a mean. Scalability: CMA-ES has quadratic memory complexity, and the diffusion model has quadratic self-attention over parameters. This limits the method to small-to-medium problems (up to ~100 parameters). Time Complexity: The per-iteration runtime is roughly constant across dimensionality, but the number of render calls required to converge grows non-linearly with dimensionality. Memory Complexity: Quadratic in d due to CMA-ES covariance matrix and diffusion self-attention. Measured Performance: On the Beads task (25,000 render calls, 224x224 pixels, LPIPS loss), FIDE takes 6-13 minutes on a desktop computer, compared to 4 hours for DiBO. Scaling: Convergence is fast up to 60 parameters; reaching comparable loss at 80 parameters requires more than 50,000 render calls. Strengths: Handles noise and unfavorable initialization better than differentiable methods; escapes local minima where gradient-based methods stall; avoids information bottleneck of scalar loss. Limitations: Higher overhead than scalar-conditioned baselines; limited to ~100 parameters. When to Use: Non-differentiable black-box renderers; problems with multi-modal ambiguity; when gradient-based methods fail due to plateaus or noise. When Not to Use: Large-scale problems (>100 parameters); when computational overhead is prohibitive and scalar baselines are sufficient. FIDE was introduced by Andrei-Timotei Ardelean, Michael Fischer, Tim Weyrich, and Tomáš Iser in 2026. It builds on the principles of CMA-ES [Hansen 2006] and diffusion models [Li and He 2025], addressing the limitations of black-box optimization methods that rely on scalar loss values. The method was validated across diverse inverse problems including camera pose estimation, robot arm estimation, path tracing, vector splines, and Voronoi shaders. name: Genetic Algorithm Optimization
head: GA-based Opacity and Transfer Function Optimization, Genetic Algorithm Optimization for DVRIs, Genetic Algorithm for DVRIs
body: Genetic Algorithm (GA) Optimization is a stochastic search method used to automatically generate Direct Volume Rendering Images (DVRIs) that guarantee the visibility of specific structures of interest within a Region of Interest (ROI). Unlike gradient-based methods that optimize continuous parameters via backpropagation, this approach treats the selection of opacity seed values for atomic structures as a discrete optimization problem, using an energy function to balance visibility, coherence, and context. It is distinct from standard differentiable optimization loops because it does not rely on gradients of the rendering equation; instead, it iteratively evolves a population of candidate transfer function configurations until user-defined quality thresholds are met. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A segmented volume where voxels are grouped into structures. Structures are decomposed into "atomic structures" if they are too large or suffer from self-occlusion. User-defined thresholds for visibility, coherence, and context metrics. Output: A set of generated DVRIs where all structures of interest are visible, followed by a subset chosen for animation. Data Structures: Solution Encoding: A 1D array of floating-point numbers (x1, x2, \dots, xn), where xi represents the opacity seed value for the i-th structure or atomic structure. This encoding is more flexible than 1D intensity-based transfer functions because it allows independent opacity control for occluding structures of similar intensity. Visibility/Quality State: A data structure tracking which structures have been revealed in high quality and their current visibility status. Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition: Break down large segments into smaller atomic structures if they suffer from self-occlusion and cannot receive enough visibility when rendered individually. 2. Initialization: Generate an initial population of solutions. Each solution is an array of opacity seed values for all atomic structures in the ROI. 3. Rendering: For each solution in the population, automatically generate a 2D transfer function for each atomic structure based on its assigned opacity seed value. Render an intermediate DVRI using these transfer functions. 4. Evaluation: Calculate the energy function E for the intermediate DVRI using three metrics: Visibility Metric: Ensures unrevealed voxels are visible. Coherence Metric: Ensures structures appear coherent with each other (not assigned strange, inconsistent opacities). Context Metric: Adds shared context to make inter-structure relations understandable. E = wv Mv + wc Mc + w{ctx} M{ctx} Where Mv, Mc, M{ctx} are the normalized metric values and w are weights. 5. Selection: Select a subset of the population based on their energy scores (lower energy is better) to serve as parents for the next generation. 6. Crossover and Mutation: Apply standard genetic operators to the selected parents to create a new population of solutions. 7. Termination Check: If the quality of the best intermediate DVRI meets user-defined thresholds, output it as a valid DVRI. Update the structure visibility and quality information. Repeat the process until all structures of interest are visible and each atomic structure in the ROI is revealed in high quality at least once. 8. Animation Generation: Choose a subset of the successfully generated DVRIs to create an animation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geneticalgorithmoptimization(volume, segmentedstructures, userthresholds): # Decompose segments into atomic structures if self-occluding atomicstructures = decomposestructures(segmentedstructures) n = len(atomicstructures) # Initialize population: arrays of opacity seeds population = [random.uniform(0, 1) for in range(n)] revealedstructures = set() generateddvris = [] while not allstructuresrevealed(atomicstructures, revealedstructures, userthresholds): fitnessscores = [] for individual in population: # Generate 2D transfer functions from opacity seeds transferfunctions = [opacityseedtotf(individual[i]) for i in range(n)] # Render intermediate DVRI dvri = rendervolume(volume, transferfunctions) # Calculate energy metrics Mv = visibilitymetric(dvri, atomicstructures, revealedstructures) Mc = coherencemetric(dvri, atomicstructures) Mctx = contextmetric(dvri, atomicstructures) energy = Mv + Mc + Mctx # Weights not specified fitnessscores.append(energy) if energy <= userthresholds: generateddvris.append(dvri) revealedstructures.update(structuresvisiblein(dvri, atomicstructures)) # Standard GA operators parents = tournamentselection(population, fitnessscores) population = crossoverandmutate(parents) if allstructuresrevealed(atomicstructures, revealedstructures, userthresholds): break return selectanimationsubset(generateddvris) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-occlusion: Large segments may not receive enough visibility when rendered individually. Decomposition is required to break them into smaller atomic structures. Coherence vs. Visibility: Assigning different opacities to structures may make them appear incoherent. The coherence metric in the energy function mitigates this. Solution Space: The solution space is constrained to opacity seeds for atomic structures to remain small enough for efficient search while guaranteeing visibility. Represents a solution as an array of floating-point numbers where each number is an opacity seed value for a structure or atomic structure. Unlike methods using a 1D array for opacity mapping (which is not flexible enough for occluding structures), this method uses opacity seeds for atomic structures to guarantee visibility. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method is iterative and depends on the population size, number of generations, and rendering cost per evaluation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guarantees visibility of specific structures of interest; handles occlusion better than global transfer functions; does not require differentiable rendering or gradients. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to repeated rendering; requires manual definition of energy function metrics and thresholds. When to use: When automatic generation of high-quality DVRIs for specific anatomical or structural features is required, and 1D transfer functions fail due to occluding structures of similar intensity. Developed for visibility-aware direct volume rendering of segmented volumes to automatically generate DVRIs that reveal missing information in a region of interest. The method addresses the problem of structures of similar intensities occluding each other, which cannot be solved by standard 1D transfer functions. It was developed to automatically generate a comprehensive presentation of structures of interest through an animation of high-quality DVRIs.
