name: Activation-Informed Coarse-to-Fine Rendering
head: Activation-based early exit, Masked fine pass
body: This method accelerates NeRF rendering by skipping the expensive fine-pass MLP evaluation for rays determined to be empty or background, using intermediate activation values from the coarse pass. It sets itself apart from standard coarse-to-fine rendering by introducing a data-dependent mask derived from hidden layer statistics rather than a fixed geometric or density threshold, specifically targeting synthetic scenes with transparent backgrounds. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A trained NeRF model with two MLPs: a coarse network \Theta{\text{coarse}} and a fine network \Theta{\text{fine}}. The coarse network outputs predicted density \sigma and intermediate activations A^{(\ell)}. The fine network outputs final radiance. Outputs: Final rendered image pixels. Data Structures Activation Tensor A^{(\ell)}: For a single ray, after linear layer \ell, the activation tensor has size Ns \times Nh, where Ns is the number of samples along the ray and Nh is the number of hidden units in layer \ell. The values are taken after the ReLU activation function is applied. Activation Image V\ell: A 2D array where each element corresponds to a pixel (x,y) and stores the scalar activation v\ell for that ray. Parameters \ell: Layer index for activation analysis. Typical values are 1, 2, or 3. Earlier layers provide greater acceleration. \tau: Threshold for skipping the fine pass. Defined as \tau = \mu(V\ell), the mean of the activation image V\ell across all rays/pixels. Steps 1. For each pixel (x, y), generate a ray r and apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot). 2. Pass Ns samples along ray r through the coarse MLP \Theta{\text{coarse}} to obtain predicted densities \sigma and intermediate activations A^{(\ell)} at layer \ell. 3. Compute the scalar activation v\ell for the ray by summing all elements of A^{(\ell)} and dividing by the total number of elements (Ns \times Nh): v\ell = \frac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} \sum{j=1}^{Nh} A^{(\ell)}{i,j} 4. Calculate the threshold \tau as the mean activation \mu(V\ell) of the activation image V\ell across all rays/pixels. 5. Identify the set of rays P where v\ell < \tau. These rays are treated as having no significant scene content. 6. For rays r \in P, evaluate the fine MLP \Theta{\text{fine}} to compute the final radiance. 7. For rays r \notin P, use the coarse radiance \hat{C}c as the final output. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def activationinformedrendering(rays, thetacoarse, thetafine, layerindex): """ Renders an image using activation-informed coarse-to-fine strategy. """ numrays = len(rays) coarseradiance = [] activations = [] # Step 1 & 2: Coarse pass for all rays for ray in rays: samples = ray.samplepoints() encodedsamples = positionalencoding(samples) # Standard NeRF positional encoding sigma, color, intermediateA = thetacoarse(encodedsamples, layerindex) cc = volumerender(sigma, color, ray.sampledistances()) coarseradiance.append(cc) activations.append(intermediateA) # Step 3: Compute scalar activation vl for each ray scalaractivations = [] for A in activations: # A shape: (Ns, Nh) vl = sum(A.flatten()) / (A.shape[0] A.shape[1]) scalaractivations.append(vl) # Step 4: Calculate threshold tau tau = sum(scalaractivations) / len(scalaractivations) # Step 5, 6, 7: Determine final output renderedimage = [] for i, ray in enumerate(rays): vl = scalaractivations[i] if vl < tau: # Ray is in set P (background/empty) -> evaluate fine MLP samples = ray.samplepoints() encodedsamples = positionalencoding(samples) sigmaf, colorf = thetafine(encodedsamples) cf = volumerender(sigmaf, colorf, ray.sampledistances()) renderedimage.append(cf) else: # Ray is not in set P -> use coarse radiance renderedimage.append(coarseradiance[i]) return renderedimage def positionalencoding(samples): # Standard positional encoding for coordinate-based MLPs return samples def volumerender(sigma, color, deltas): # Standard emission-absorption volume rendering from parent article T = 1.0 radiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for s in range(len(sigma)): alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[s] deltas[s]) weight = T alpha radiance = [radiance[k] + weight color[s][k] for k in range(3)] T = (1.0 - alpha) return radiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls Real-world scenes: The method relies on transparent backgrounds found in synthetic scenes (e.g., Blender dataset). It fails on real-world scenes with detailed backgrounds, as the activation threshold may incorrectly classify background pixels as empty. Precision: The method uses standard floating-point arithmetic for activation summation. Early experiments showed that applying the activation function (ReLU) resulted in more consistent histograms for the activation features. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of fine-pass evaluations. On the Blender 'lego' scene (800x800), using layer 1 achieved a 34.69% speedup with 40% of rays processed by the fine pass. Using layer 3 achieved a 55% speedup with 47% of rays processed by the fine pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate activations A^{(\ell)} for all rays during the coarse pass to compute the threshold. This adds memory overhead proportional to N{rays} \times Ns \times Nh for the specific layer \ell. Quality Trade-offs: Slight drop in rendering quality. For the 'lego' scene with layer 1: PSNR 29.66, SSIM 0.93, LPIPS 0.04. With layer 3: PSNR 31.21, SSIM 0.95, LPIPS 0.02. The full NeRF baseline had PSNR 32.20, SSIM 0.96, LPIPS 0.02. Strengths: Significant performance improvement on synthetic scenes with transparent backgrounds. Early layers accelerate inference more substantially. Limitations: Not applicable to real-world scenes with complex backgrounds without modification (e.g., density approximation methods). Origin: Proposed in "Analyzing the Internals of Neural Radiance Fields" (CVPRW 2024). History: The method builds on the observation that intermediate activations in NeRF MLPs contain structural information about density. It specifically targets the inference time reduction for synthetic datasets like Blender. Usage: Applied to NeRF and Mip-NeRF models. Also applicable to proposal network samplers (e.g., nerfacto with Mip-NeRF 360 proposal sampler). name: Geometry Focused Model Optimization
head: Geometry-Material Decoupling Optimization
body: Geometry Focused Model Optimization stabilizes the training of radiance fields by decoupling the strong mutual dependency between geometry and material parameters. It addresses the issue where simultaneous optimization of geometry and material leads to noisy gradients and poor convergence. It sets itself apart from standard end-to-end training by introducing specific approximations and staged rendering strategies to isolate geometry updates. Inputs: Scene parameters (Gaussian primitives with position, covariance, opacity, color, and material properties); Camera poses; Training images. Outputs: Optimized scene representation (geometry and material); Rendered images. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Contains position \mathbf{p}, covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}, opacity \alpha, base color \mathbf{c}, and material parameters (e.g., roughness, metallic, normal). Compensation Factors: Learnable scalar or vector parameters used to approximate the decoupled material response. Steps: 1. Initial Stage (Per-Gaussian Shading): To stabilize gradient transfer to geometry in the initial phase, apply the rendering equation directly to each Gaussian primitive. Compute outgoing radiance L{out} for each Gaussian using its specific material and geometry properties. Alpha-blend these per-Gaussian radiance values during rasterization to produce the final image. This avoids pixel-level shading disturbances that can mislead geometry gradients. 2. Decoupled Optimization (Approximation): Apply an approximation to decouple the optimization of geometry and material. Use learnable compensation factors during training to model the interaction between geometry and material without computing the full coupled gradient. This relaxation prevents the "tricky task" of optimizing both simultaneously, which causes noise in forward rendering and gradient calculation. 3. Final Stage (Full Rendering): Remove the approximation and compensation factors only for baseline comparison or final inference if required. Perform standard differentiable rendering with full material-geometry coupling. Pitfalls: Without the approximation, the strong dependency between geometry and material makes optimization significantly harder, yielding worse view synthesis and noisy geometry. Pixel-level shading during the initial phase can disturb gradient directions of geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryfocusedoptimization(scene, cameras, images, numepochs): # Initialize scene with Gaussians (position, cov, opacity, color, material) # Initialize learnable compensation factors for epoch in range(numepochs): for camera, targetimage in zip(cameras, images): # Step 1: Initial Stage - Per-Gaussian Shading # Compute outgoing radiance for each Gaussian using its material/geometry gaussianradiance = [] for gaussian in scene.gaussians: # Apply rendering equation directly to primitive Lout = computeprimitiveradiance(gaussian) gaussianradiance.append(Lout) # Alpha-blend during rasterization renderedimage = alphablendrasterize(gaussianradiance, camera.projection) # Compute loss against target loss = computeloss(renderedimage, targetimage) # Step 2: Backpropagate with compensation factors # Gradients flow through the decoupled approximation loss.backward() # Update parameters optimizer.step() # Step 3: Final Stage - Full Rendering (if not in initial phase) # In later epochs or final inference, remove approximation if epoch > warmupepochs: renderedimagefull = fulldifferentiablerender(scene, camera) lossfull = computeloss(renderedimagefull, targetimage) lossfull.backward() optimizer.step() A relaxation technique that decouples the strong mutual dependency between geometry and material optimization to stabilize training. It uses learnable compensation factors during training and removes them only for baseline comparison. Without this approximation, optimization is harder due to noise in forward rendering and gradients, leading to worse view synthesis and noisy geometry. On a 2000-image test set, the baseline without approximation achieves PSNR 26.44, SSIM 0.9255, LPIPS 0.0681, while the decoupled method achieves PSNR 30.01, SSIM 0.9542, LPIPS 0.0430. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The decoupled approach significantly boosts performance compared to the baseline without approximation. Strengths: Stabilizes training, reduces noise in geometry reconstruction, improves view synthesis quality. Limitations: Requires additional learnable compensation factors; approximation must be removed for final comparison or inference. When to use: When optimizing both geometry and material simultaneously leads to convergence issues or noisy results. Originated in the context of differentiable light transport with Gaussian Surfels for efficient relighting and geometry reconstruction. The method addresses the challenges of optimizing geometry and material in radiance fields, particularly in the presence of global illumination effects. name: Phase-Aware Gradient Descent (PAGD)
head: Phase-Only Hologram Synthesis via PAGD
body: Phase-Aware Gradient Descent (PAGD) is an optimization method used to encode complex wave fields into phase-only holograms for 3D holographic displays. It solves the problem of rendering accurate depth cues and view-dependent effects by supervising the phase of the reconstructed wave field, rather than relying solely on amplitude. Unlike amplitude-only methods which suffer from unnatural blur spreading and ringing artifacts, PAGD adheres to the physical two-step hologram process (recording and reconstruction) interconnected through phase information. It is distinguished from the Gerchberg-Saxton Algorithm by using gradient-based loss minimization rather than iterative back-and-forth propagation with hard amplitude constraints. Inputs: Mesh-represented scene M. Camera settings C. Lighting L. Number of optimization iterations T. Initial phase \Phi{init}. Outputs: Optimized phase-only hologram \Phi{OPT}. Data Structures: \Phi: Complex-valued phase hologram matrix, size h \times w (SLM resolution). u{WR}: Target complex wave field generated by POS-WRP. u{ti}: Target complex wave field at the i-th plane (i \in \{1, 2, 3\}). u{ri}: Reconstructed complex wave field at the i-th plane. si: Complex-valued scale factor for the i-th plane. Formulas: The complex-valued scale factor s accounts for light source intensity deviations and phase shift invariances. For a reconstructed field ur and target field ut, the real and imaginary parts of s are calculated as: \text{Re}(s) = \frac{\text{Re}(ur) \odot \text{Re}(ut) + \text{Im}(ur) \odot \text{Im}(ut)}{\text{Re}(ur)^2 + \text{Im}(ur)^2} \text{Im}(s) = \frac{-\text{Im}(ur) \odot \text{Re}(ut) + \text{Re}(ur) \odot \text{Im}(ut)}{\text{Re}(ur)^2 + \text{Im}(ur)^2} where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The loss function L compares the scaled reconstructed field with the target field using Mean Squared Error (MSE) on real and imaginary components: L(s \odot ur, ut) = \text{MSE}(\text{Re}(s ur), \text{Re}(ut)) + \text{MSE}(\text{Im}(s ur), \text{Im}(ut)) The total loss E(\Phi) is the sum of scaled losses across 3 target planes: E(\Phi) = \sum{i=1}^3 L(si \odot u{ri}, u{ti}) Steps: 1. Initialize phase \Phi \leftarrow \Phi{init}. 2. Generate the target wave field u{WR} using the Phase-Only Spatial Wave Reconstruction (POS-WRP) model with inputs M, C, L. 3. Propagate the target wave field u{WR} to near, medium, and far planes (zi) to obtain target fields u{ti} for i=1, 2, 3. 4. For each iteration n from 1 to T: a. For each of the 3 planes i: i. Propagate the current phase hologram e^{j\Phi} shifted by z{WR} + zi to obtain the reconstructed field u{ri}. b. Calculate the complex-valued scale factors si for each plane using the formula above. c. Calculate the total loss E(\Phi) by summing the scaled losses for all 3 planes. d. Compute gradients \nabla E(\Phi) via backpropagation through the learned forward model. e. Update \Phi using gradient descent. 5. Set the final optimized phase \Phi{OPT} = \Phi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def poswrp(M, C, L): """Phase-Only Spatial Wave Reconstruction model. Returns complex wave field uWR.""" # Implementation encapsulates the specific learned or analytical forward model return np.zeros((H, W), dtype=complex) def propagate(field, distance): """Propagates a complex field over distance using Angular Spectrum Method.""" freqx = np.fft.fftfreq(field.shape[1]) freqy = np.fft.fftfreq(field.shape[0]) Fx, Fy = np.meshgrid(freqx, freqy) H = np.exp(1j 2 np.pi distance np.sqrt(1/0.00052 - Fx2 - Fy2)) return np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(field) H) def mse(a, b): """Computes Mean Squared Error between two arrays.""" return np.mean((a - b) 2) def complexexp(z): """Computes element-wise complex exponential.""" return np.exp(z) def where(condition, x, y): """Returns elements chosen from x or y depending on condition.""" return np.where(condition, x, y) def computegradients(loss, variable): """Computes gradients via automatic differentiation through the forward model.""" # In practice, uses framework autograd (e.g., torch.autograd.grad) return np.zeroslike(variable) def updatephase(Phi, gradients, lr=0.01): """Performs a gradient descent update step.""" return Phi - lr gradients def phaseawaregradientdescent(M, C, L, T, Phiinit, zWR, zplanes): """ M: Mesh scene C: Camera settings L: Lighting T: Number of optimization iterations Phiinit: Initial phase matrix zWR: Distance from SLM to reference plane zplanes: List of 3 distances [z1, z2, z3] for target planes """ Phi = Phiinit.copy() uWR = poswrp(M, C, L) utargets = [propagate(uWR, zi) for zi in zplanes] for n in range(T): ureconstructions = [] for zi in zplanes: phasefield = complexexp(1j Phi) ur = propagate(phasefield, zWR + zi) ureconstructions.append(ur) totalloss = 0.0 for i in range(3): ur = ureconstructions[i] ut = utargets[i] denom = (ur.real 2) + (ur.imag 2) denom = where(denom < 1e-8, 1e-8, denom) sreal = ((ur.real ut.real) + (ur.imag ut.imag)) / denom simag = (-(ur.imag ut.real) + (ur.real ut.imag)) / denom s = sreal + 1j simag uscaled = s ur lossreal = mse(uscaled.real, ut.real) lossimag = mse(uscaled.imag, ut.imag) totalloss += lossreal + lossimag gradients = computegradients(totalloss, Phi) Phi = updatephase(Phi, gradients) return Phi Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Phase Non-Uniqueness: Supervising phase is challenging due to two inherent shift invariances: 1) Global shift in phase does not alter the wave field. 2) Phase value on each pixel can be shifted by 2\pi without changing the target field. The complex-valued scale factor s accounts for these deviations and light source intensity variations. Tilted Wave Fields: Amplitude loss fails to reconstruct correct defocus cues on unsupervised planes for tilted wave fields (e.g., 1° tilt). Phase-aware supervision is required for accurate reconstruction in these cases. Ringing Artifacts: Abandoning phase supervision introduces ringing artifacts (e.g., edge ringing). This method trains a data-driven surrogate model using experimentally captured phase-to-intensity data to predict light propagation from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to multiple target planes. The Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is an iterative optimization method used to compute phase-only holograms by determining object point phase values that cause interference resulting in constant amplitude across the hologram plane. It solves the problem of phase-only display constraints where the eye does not detect image phase, allowing the algorithm to treat object phases as free variables to satisfy amplitude constraints on the display. It is distinguished from its parent, Phase-Aware Gradient Descent (PAGD), by its specific use of back-and-forth propagation with hard amplitude constraints rather than gradient-based loss minimization, and from its sibling, Camera-Calibrated Wave Propagation Model Training, by being a direct analytical iterative solver rather than a learned model. Time Complexity: The training time for the PAGD optimizer component is 30 seconds per hologram. The total time for generating one phase-only hologram from a mesh scene is on average 54.96 seconds (24.96 s for POS-WRP and 30 s for PAGD). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: PAGD mitigates ringing artifacts and unnatural blur spreading found in amplitude-only or RGB-D methods. It offers more accurate reconstruction than amplitude-only supervision for tilted wave fields. Incorporating phase regularization reduces the demand for multi-plane supervision; enforcing complex target supervision on 1-plane yields an improvement of 7 dB in PSNR over 2-plane amplitude-only supervision while being slightly faster, and is 2.39× faster than 5-plane amplitude-only supervision at the same image quality. Strengths: Adheres to the physical two-step hologram process; handles tilted wave fields accurately; reduces the number of required supervised planes; view-dependent holography is a direct outcome; requires training the forward model only once. Limitations: Real-time hologram generation remains a goal for future exploration; numerical models like ASM struggle to replicate real-world optical systems due to imperfections (aberrations, SLM non-linearities, stray light, limited diffraction efficiency), necessitating a learned model. When to use: When accurate 3D depth cues and view-dependent effects are required for phase-only holographic displays, especially for tilted wave fields or when minimizing the number of supervised planes is critical. When not to use: When real-time performance is strictly required without further acceleration (e.g., via CNNs). PAGD was proposed in a 2026 paper published in Nature Communications by researchers investigating mesh-represented and learning-empowered hologram synthesis for full 3D holographic displays. The method addresses limitations of amplitude-based optimization, such as manual setting of target planes, single-viewpoint constraints, and unrealistic defocus blur. It builds on the concept of Phase-Only Spatial Wave Reconstruction (POS-WRP) and utilizes a camera-calibrated learned wavefront propagation model to enhance precision. name: Camera-Calibrated Wave Propagation Model Training
head: Hardware-in-the-loop Training
body: This method trains a data-driven surrogate model using experimentally captured phase-to-intensity data to predict light propagation from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to multiple target planes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dataset of phase patterns \Phi (2D or 3D) and their corresponding captured intensity images I at eight specific propagation distances. Output: A trained neural network model M\theta that predicts intensity I{pred} given an input phase \Phi. Data Structures: Phase Patterns: Stored as 2D arrays representing phase values. Intensity Images: Captured by the camera at the target planes. Region of Interest (ROI): The effective usable area is defined as 880 \times 1600 pixels, cropped from the full 1920 \times 1080 resolution due to laser uniformity and modulator efficiency. Steps: 1. Dataset Construction: Collect 5860 phase patterns. These include 2D phases generated via stochastic gradient descent, higher-order gradient descent, and double-phase amplitude encoding, as well as true 3D phases derived from the Flying Planes mesh-wave field-hologram dataset. 2. Data Capture: For each phase pattern, record the resulting intensity at eight target planes located at distances d \in \{10.00, 10.07, 10.14, 10.21, 10.28, 10.35, 10.42, 10.49\} cm from the SLM. 3. Preprocessing: To mitigate anti-aliasing, magnify the wave field by a factor of two in both dimensions and apply a fill factor of 0.93. Perform grid interpolation to handle spatial transformations. 4. Optimization Loop: Train the model on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with a batch size of one for twenty epochs, utilizing the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0005. Formulas: The specific mathematical formulation of the surrogate network is not given in the sources. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: \eta = 0.0005. Batch Size: B = 1. Epochs: E = 20. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Anti-aliasing: Addressed by 2× magnification and a 0.93 fill factor. Boundary/ROI: The usable area is restricted to 880 \times 1600 pixels due to laser uniformity and modulator efficiency limits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessphase(phasearray): # Magnify by factor of 2 to mitigate anti-aliasing magnified = interpolate2d(phasearray, scalefactor=2) # Apply fill factor of 0.93 filled = [[val 0.93 for val in row] for row in magnified] return filled def traincameracalibratedmodel(model, dataloader): optimizer = Adam(parameters=model.parameters(), lr=0.0005) epochs = 20 batchsize = 1 for epoch in range(epochs): model.train() for phases, targets in dataloader: optimizer.zerograd() processedphases = preprocessphase(phases) predictions = model.forward(processedphases) # Loss function not given in the sources. # loss = computeloss(predictions, targets) # loss.backward() optimizer.step() print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs} completed.") name: Camera-Calibrated Learned Wave Propagation Model
head: Camera-Calibrated Model, Learned Forward Model
body: The Camera-Calibrated Learned Wave Propagation Model is a data-driven surrogate for numerical propagation operators (such as the Angular Spectrum Method) used within differentiable holographic optimization loops. It solves the problem of model mismatch between idealized physics simulations and real-world optical hardware, specifically accounting for spatial light modulator (SLM) non-linearities, optical aberrations, stray light, and limited diffraction efficiency. Unlike analytical models that assume perfect free-space propagation, this learned model maps input phase patterns directly to captured multi-plane intensity images, providing a more accurate gradient signal for phase-aware gradient descent (PAGD). The method replaces the analytical forward propagation step in the optimization loop with a neural network trained to predict the intensity distribution at multiple depth planes given an input phase pattern. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A phase-only hologram (or phase pattern) displayed on the SLM. Output: Predicted intensity images at 8 target depth planes. Data Structures: The model architecture details are not provided in the primary source text, which refers to supplementary materials for specific network layers and hyperparameters. The training data consists of pairs: Phase: Phase-only holograms generated from 2D and 3D targets. Target: Multi-plane intensity images captured from a physical prototype display. Training Procedure: 1. Dataset Acquisition: Use the "Flying Planes" dataset, which contains 1,000 randomly generated 3D scenes in OBJ format. These scenes include corresponding complex-valued wave fields, RGB-Depth images, and phase-only holograms generated via various encoders (DPAC, SGD, PAGD with ASM). The 3D primitives are sampled with random position, rotation, and scale from the DIV2K dataset textures. 2. Physical Data Collection: Display numerous phase patterns (derived from 2D and 3D targets in the dataset) on a prototype SLM. Capture the resulting light field at 8 distinct target planes using a camera. 3. Model Adaptation: Adapt the learned wave propagation model architecture from Choi et al.. Crucially, introduce an extra low-pass filter within the model to suppress high-frequency phase noise. 4. Loss Minimization: Train the model using the phase and multi-plane image pairs. The objective is to minimize the discrepancy between the model's predicted intensities and the physically captured intensities. The loss function compares the scaled reconstructed field ur with the target field ut. Parameters: Target Planes: 8 planes. Dataset Size: 1,000 scenes. Low-pass Filter: Applied to suppress high-frequency phase noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Noise: Without the extra low-pass filter, high-frequency phase noise may degrade the model's accuracy. Hardware Specificity: The model is calibrated to a specific prototype optical system; it does not generalize to different hardware configurations without retraining. Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) is a free-space propagation operator that models parallel wave propagation between planes without paraxial approximations. It treats the field as a superposition of plane waves, making it exact for any distance and angle under sampling constraints. It is chosen when analytical accuracy is required without hardware calibration, unlike the learned model which captures real-world optical imperfections. Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) Accuracy: The learned model provides a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) improvement of 2 dB compared to the analytical Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) baseline. Computational Cost: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures real-world imperfections (aberrations, SLM non-linearities, stray light) that numerical models like ASM struggle to replicate. Limitations: Requires physical data collection and training; does not provide a differentiable physics-based gradient in the traditional sense but rather a learned gradient. The method originates from research into full 3D holographic displays, specifically addressing the limitations of numerical propagation operators in differentiable holography. It builds on the work of Choi et al.. The approach is part of a broader effort to mesh-represent and learning-empower hologram synthesis for full 3D holographic displays. name: Angular Spectrum Method (ASM)
head: Fourier Optics Propagation, Free-space propagation operator, Helmholtz equation solution in Fourier space
body: The Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) is a free-space propagation operator used to model the parallel propagation of a wave field from one plane to another. It solves the problem of accurately reconstructing or propagating a complex optical field U0(x0, y0) to a target plane at distance z by treating the field as a superposition of plane waves propagating in different directions. Unlike the Fresnel Method, which relies on paraxial approximations, ASM operates in the frequency domain to solve the Helmholtz equation without approximations, avoiding the computational cost of first-principles methods like FDTD. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The complex optical field U0(x0, y0) at the source plane (z=0), the propagation distance z, and the wavelength \lambda. Output: The reconstructed complex wavefield Ur(x, y) at the target plane (z). Data Structures: The input field is represented as a 2D grid of complex numbers. The angular spectrum is represented as a 2D grid of complex numbers in the frequency domain (kx, ky). The transfer function is a 2D grid of complex numbers with the same dimensions as the angular spectrum. Numbered Steps and Formulas: 1. Fourier Transform: Compute the 2D Fourier Transform of the input field U0(x0, y0) to obtain the Angular Spectrum A0(kx, ky). A0(kx, ky) = \mathcal{F} \{ U0(x0, y0) \} 2. Apply Transfer Function: Multiply the Angular Spectrum A0(kx, ky) by the propagation phase factor (transfer function) H(kx, ky; z). H(kx, ky; z) = \exp \left( j kz z \right) where kz = \sqrt{k^2 - kx^2 - ky^2} The source assumes k^2 \ge kx^2 + ky^2. 3. Inverse Fourier Transform: Compute the 2D Inverse Fourier Transform of the product to obtain the reconstructed wavefield Ur(x, y). Ur(x, y) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \left\{ A0(kx, ky) \exp \left( j \sqrt{k^2 - kx^2 - ky^2} z \right) \right\} Parameters: \lambda: Wavelength of the light. k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}: Wavenumber. z: Propagation distance. \Delta x, \Delta y: Spatial sampling intervals in the source plane. \Delta kx, \Delta ky: Frequency sampling intervals, where \Delta kx = \frac{2\pi}{Nx \Delta x} and \Delta ky = \frac{2\pi}{Ny \Delta y} for an Nx \times Ny grid. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Evanescent Waves: If kx^2 + ky^2 > k^2, kz becomes imaginary, causing exponential decay of high-frequency components. In practice, these components are handled via complex kz or zeroed out. Sampling: The spatial sampling \Delta x, \Delta y must satisfy the Nyquist criterion for the highest spatial frequency present in the field to avoid aliasing. The frequency grid must cover the relevant bandwidth. Computational Cost: ASM requires two 2D Fourier Transforms, making it more computationally intensive than the Fresnel Method. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def angularspectrummethod(U0, z, wavelength, dx, dy): """ Propagates a complex optical field U0 using the Angular Spectrum Method. Args: U0: 2D numpy array (complex128) representing the input field. z: float, propagation distance. wavelength: float, wavelength of light. dx: float, spatial sampling interval in x. dy: float, spatial sampling interval in y. Returns: Ur: 2D numpy array (complex128) representing the propagated field. """ Ny, Nx = U0.shape k = 2 np.pi / wavelength # Create frequency grid (angular frequencies in rad/m) kx = np.fft.fftfreq(Nx, d=dx) 2 np.pi ky = np.fft.fftfreq(Ny, d=dy) 2 np.pi # Create 2D meshgrid KX, KY = np.meshgrid(kx, ky, indexing='xy') # Calculate kz kzsq = k2 - KX2 - KY2 # Handle evanescent waves: if kzsq < 0, kz is imaginary. # exp(j kz z) will decay exponentially. kz = np.sqrt(kzsq) # Transfer function H = np.exp(1j kz z) # Step 1: Fourier Transform A0 = np.fft.fft2(U0) # Step 2: Multiply by transfer function Apropagated = A0 H # Step 3: Inverse Fourier Transform Ur = np.fft.ifft2(Apropagated) return Ur A differentiable computational model that simulates the physical propagation of light from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to a camera sensor, incorporating learnable parameters to account for system-specific imperfections such as polarization, SLM curvature, beam profiles, higher diffraction orders, crosstalk, and Lookup Table (LUT) non-linearity. It sets itself apart from standard Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) implementations by explicitly modeling the superposition of zero and first-order diffraction patterns through a neural network (U-Net) and calibrating these parameters against experimental data, thereby compensating for unmodeled physical effects in compact optical setups. HOASM is a differentiable wave propagation model that separates the propagation of zero-order and first-order diffraction terms to handle them differently before feeding them into a neural network. It builds on Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) by introducing a specific preprocessing step for the first-order term involving grid patterning and sinc weighting, distinguishing it from standard ASM which propagates all orders together. A paraxial approximation for propagating electric fields, used here as the propagation function f{prop}. It is nearly identical to the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) for SLMs with pixel pitch > 3 µm and diffraction angles < 5°. Fresnel propagation in Fourier space is defined as f{fresnel}(g, z, \lambda) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \{ \mathcal{F} \{g\} \cdot H(z, \lambda) \}, where \mathcal{F} is the 2D Fourier transform, g is the input electric field, z is the propagation distance, and H is the Fresnel kernel. The Fresnel propagation kernel is H(z, \lambda) = \exp \left( i \pi \lambda z (fx^2 + fy^2) \right), where fx, fy are spatial frequency coordinates. A key pitfall is Wavelength-Depth Ambiguity: in the Fresnel kernel, \lambda and z appear as the product \lambda z, creating an ambiguity where an image formed at distance z0 under red illumination (\lambdar) will also appear at distances z0 \lambdag / \lambdar (green) and z0 \lambdab / \lambdar (blue), creating 'depth replicas'. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires two 2D Fourier Transforms, making it more computationally intensive than the Fresnel Method. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Fourier Optics is computationally less taxing than first-principles FDTD simulations, which model dielectric refractive indices and Snell's Law explicitly, but Fourier Optics may not capture all physical details. Strengths: Exact solution for free-space propagation without paraxial approximations. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than Fresnel or Fresnel-Kirchhoff approximations; sensitive to sampling rates; requires handling of evanescent waves. When to use: When high accuracy is required, especially for near-field propagation or large angles where Fresnel approximations fail. When not to use: When computational speed is critical and the paraxial approximation is valid (use Fresnel Method instead). The method was developed as an exact solution to the Helmholtz equation for free-space propagation. Specific origin details, authors, and dates are not given in the sources. It is cited in recent advances in processing and rendering algorithms for CGH and in mesh-represented hologram synthesis. name: Camera-Calibrated Differentiable Holographic Model
head: Camera-Calibrated Differentiable Model for Holography, Camera-calibrated model, Differentiable holographic model
body: A differentiable computational model that simulates the physical propagation of light from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to a camera sensor, incorporating learnable parameters to account for system-specific imperfections such as polarization, SLM curvature, beam profiles, higher diffraction orders, crosstalk, and Lookup Table (LUT) non-linearity. It sets itself apart from standard Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) implementations by explicitly modeling the superposition of zero and first-order diffraction patterns through a neural network (U-Net) and calibrating these parameters against experimental data, thereby compensating for unmodeled physical effects in compact optical setups. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: SLM digital input pattern s (scalar per pixel), propagation distance z, wavelength \lambda. Outputs: Predicted image intensity Iz at the sensor plane. Data Structures: SLM Pattern s: 2D array of integers (e.g., 0-255) representing digital drive values. Diffraction Orders G0, G1: Complex-valued 2D arrays representing the zero-order and first-order diffraction patterns generated by the SLM. Propagated Fields f{ASM}: Complex-valued 2D arrays resulting from ASM propagation. U-Net: A neural network architecture (separate instance for each color channel) taking stacked complex fields as input and outputting real-valued intensity. Learnable Parameters: a1, a2: Scalars (per color channel) for the linear LUT model. k{xt}: 5x5 convolution kernel (per color channel) for crosstalk. M{color}: 3x3 matrix for camera color balance. Formulas: 1. SLM Phase with Crosstalk and LUT: The phase \phi\lambda(s) off the SLM for wavelength \lambda given input s is modeled as: \phi\lambda(s) = k{xt} (a1 \cdot s + a2) where denotes convolution, a1, a2 are learnable linear LUT parameters, and k{xt} is a learned 5x5 convolution kernel representing field fringing (crosstalk). 2. Diffraction Pattern Generation: The SLM phase is converted into complex diffraction patterns G0 (zero-order) and G1 (first-order). 3. Angular Spectrum Propagation: Each diffraction order is propagated independently to distance z using the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM), building on Angular Spectrum Method (ASM): f{ASM}(G, z) = \mathcal{F}^{-1} \{ G \cdot H{ASM}(z) \} where G is the diffraction order pattern (G0 or G1), H{ASM}(z) is the ASM transfer kernel, and \mathcal{F}^{-1} is the inverse Fourier transform. 4. Intensity Prediction via U-Net: The propagated zero-order field f{ASM}(G0, z) and first-order field f{ASM}(G1, z) are stacked and passed through a U-Net to predict the final image intensity: Iz = \text{Unet}(f{ASM}(G0, z), f{ASM}(G1, z)) A separate U-Net is learned for each color channel to handle color-specific unmodeled system aspects. Numbered Steps: 1. Calibration Phase (Parameter Learning): 1. Pre-calculate 882 SLM patterns from a dataset of images using the standard ASM propagation model. 2. Capture these patterns using the experimental camera at 10 mm increments from z=90 mm to z=120 mm. 3. Debayer the camera data and apply an affine transform to align the image coordinates with the SLM grid. 4. Initialize learnable parameters: a1, a2 (LUT), k{xt} (crosstalk kernel), and M{color} (3x3 color calibration matrix). 5. Perform gradient descent using PyTorch to minimize the L1 loss between the model output Iz and the captured camera data. 6. Train until convergence, typically taking 2-3 days on an Nvidia A6000 GPU. 2. Hologram Generation (Optimization): 1. Initialize the SLM pattern s (e.g., random or target-based initialization). 2. Compute the phase \phi\lambda(s) using the calibrated LUT and crosstalk model (Eq. 11). 3. Generate diffraction orders G0 and G1 from the phase. 4. Propagate G0 and G1 to the target distance z using ASM (Eq. 12). 5. Stack the propagated fields and pass them through the trained U-Net to predict intensity Iz. 6. Compute the loss (e.g., perceptual loss) between Iz and the target image. 7. Use PyTorch autodifferentiation to compute gradients with respect to s. 8. Update s using gradient descent. 9. Constraint Handling: After every optimization step, wrap s values to the LUT valid range (e.g., 0-255) to ensure physical validity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class CameraCalibratedHolographicModel(nn.Module): def init(self, slmh, slmw, wavelengths, numdepths): super().init() self.slmh, self.slmw = slmh, slmw self.wavelengths = wavelengths # [lambdar, lambdag, lambdab] self.numdepths = numdepths # Learnable LUT parameters (per color channel) self.a1 = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(3)) self.a2 = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(3)) # Learnable Crosstalk Kernel (5x5, per color channel) self.kxt = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, 1, 5, 5)) # Learnable Color Calibration Matrix (3x3) self.colormat = nn.Parameter(torch.eye(3)) # U-Net for each color channel (simplified standard U-Net structure) self.unets = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(4, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(64, 1, 3, padding=1)) for in range(3) ]) def applylutandcrosstalk(self, s, coloridx): """ s: (H, W) tensor of SLM input values coloridx: 0, 1, or 2 for R, G, B Returns: Phase map phi (H, W) """ # Linear LUT: a1 s + a2 linearphase = self.a1[coloridx] s + self.a2[coloridx] # Convolution for crosstalk linearphaseexp = linearphase.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) kxtexp = self.kxt[coloridx].unsqueeze(0) # Conv2d requires input (N, C, H, W) phaseblurred = F.conv2d(linearphaseexp, kxtexp, padding=2) return phaseblurred.squeeze(0).squeeze(0) def generatediffractionorders(self, phase): """ Converts phase to complex diffraction orders G0 and G1. Standard phase-only SLM approximation: G1 is the first-order complex field, G0 is the zero-order. """ G1 = torch.exp(1j phase) G0 = torch.oneslike(phase) return G0, G1 def propagateasm(self, G, z, wavelength): """ Propagates field G to distance z using ASM. """ # Compute frequency grid (normalized coordinates) fx = torch.fft.fftfreq(self.slmw, d=1.0/self.slmw).view(1, -1, 1) fy = torch.fft.fftfreq(self.slmh, d=1.0/self.slmh).view(-1, 1, 1) # ASM transfer function HASM(z) k = 2 torch.pi / wavelength H = torch.exp(1j z torch.sqrt(k2 - (2torch.pifx)2 - (2torch.pify)2)) # Handle evanescent waves (sqrt of negative) H = torch.where(torch.real(H) != 0, H, torch.zeroslike(H)) # Propagate: F^{-1} { G H } Ghat = torch.fft.fft2(G) Fhat = Ghat H fasm = torch.fft.ifft2(Fhat) return fasm def forward(self, s, z, targetwavelengthidx): """ s: (H, W) SLM pattern z: float, propagation distance targetwavelengthidx: 0, 1, 2 """ # 1. Get Phase with LUT and Crosstalk phase = self.applylutandcrosstalk(s, targetwavelengthidx) # 2. Generate Diffraction Orders G0, G1 = self.generatediffractionorders(phase) # 3. Propagate using ASM fasm0 = self.propagateasm(G0, z, self.wavelengths[targetwavelengthidx]) fasm1 = self.propagateasm(G1, z, self.wavelengths[targetwavelengthidx]) # 4. Stack and Pass through U-Net # Stack real and imaginary parts for U-Net input stacked = torch.stack([fasm0.real, fasm0.imag, fasm1.real, fasm1.imag], dim=0) # 5. Predict Intensity Iz = self.unetstargetwavelengthidx return Iz def wrapslm(self, s): """ Wraps SLM values to valid range [0, 255]. """ return torch.clamp(s, 0, 255) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Higher Diffraction Orders: The discrete pixel structure of the SLM creates higher diffraction orders not modeled by standard ASM. This method avoids physical apertures (4f systems) by modeling the 0th and 1st orders explicitly and using a U-Net to compensate for residual unmodeled effects. SLM Crosstalk: LCoS SLMs exhibit field fringing due to elastic forces in the LC layer. This is modeled as a convolution (k{xt}) on the phase. Failure to model this leads to blurred phase and reduced hologram quality. LUT Validity: The SLM pattern s must be constrained to the range where the LUT is valid (e.g., 0-255). Values outside this range must be wrapped after every optimization step. Color Deviation: Simultaneous RGB holography is an overdetermined problem (3x more output pixels than SLM degrees of freedom). This can lead to color deviations and desaturation if not addressed by the perceptual loss and calibrated model. A special case of camera-calibrated models where an image is displayed on the SLM, and camera captures are used to improve that particular image using the difference between the experimental capture and target image. The procedure optimizes an SLM pattern using the learned simulation model and retains the computational graph, displays the pattern, and captures the resulting hologram. A piecewise affine homography is applied to the captured hologram for each color channel to map it from camera space to simulation space. The perceptual loss function is applied to the remapped captured hologram and the target image, followed by backpropagation using the saved computational graph but substituting the experimentally captured hologram into the loss function. Alignment between the experimental capture and target must be precise because active CiTL relies on their difference. Piecewise affine homography improves color fidelity compared to global affine homography by providing better alignment during optimization. Time Complexity: Hologram generation optimization takes approximately 2 minutes per 2D hologram on an Nvidia A6000 GPU. 3D hologram computation time scales proportionally to the number of depth planes. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the SLM pattern, propagated fields, and the U-Net parameters. Strengths: Enables simultaneous color computer-generated holography in a compact setup without bulky optics or filters, suitable for VR/AR displays. Reduces depth replicas and high-frequency out-of-focus light by using extended phase range SLMs and modeling higher orders. Limitations: Calibration is time-consuming (2-3 days on A6000). The method relies on the accuracy of the U-Net to capture unmodeled system imperfections, which may not generalize perfectly to different hardware without re-calibration. When to Use: When generating simultaneous color holograms in a compact optical setup where physical filtering of higher diffraction orders is impractical. When Not to Use: When a 4f system is already present to physically filter diffraction orders, or when iterative gradient-based optimization is computationally prohibitive for real-time display. The method was developed to address the mismatch between simulated holograms and experimental captures in simultaneous color computer-generated holography. It builds on the Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) and incorporates insights from Gopakumar et al. [2021] regarding higher-order angular spectrum models. The use of SLEDs (Superluminescent Light Emitting Diodes) to reduce speckle is based on work by Deng and Chu [2017]. The specific implementation details, including the U-Net architecture and calibration procedure, are described in the source paper. name: Modified High Order Angular Spectrum Method (HOASM)
body: HOASM is a differentiable wave propagation model that separates the propagation of zero-order and first-order diffraction terms to handle them differently before feeding them into a neural network. It builds on Angular Spectrum Method (ASM) by introducing a specific preprocessing step for the first-order term involving grid patterning and sinc weighting, distinguishing it from standard ASM which propagates all orders together. Inputs and Outputs: The input is a complex field U(x,y) at the source plane (e.g., SLM), propagation distance z, wavelength \lambda, and SLM parameters (pixel size p, resolution). The output is a single-channel intensity image I(x,y) at the sensor plane. Data Structures: The U-Net input is a stacked tensor of the real and imaginary parts of the propagated zero-order and first-order fields. The U-Net architecture consists of 4 downsampling layers, 4 upsampling layers, channels increasing from 4 to 32 in the first downsampling layer, doubling in each of the next 3 downsampling layers to 256 channels, and a single-channel output. Steps: 1. Propagate the zero-order component of the complex field using the standard Angular Spectrum Method (ASM). 2. Compute the Fourier transform of the complex field and zero-pad it. 3. Pattern the zero-padded Fourier transform into a 3 \times 3 grid. 4. Zero out the center Fourier transform of the grid. 5. Weight the Fourier representation of the first-order term with a sinc function. 6. Propagate the weighted first-order term to the sensor plane using ASM. 7. Down-sample and crop the resulting first-order field. 8. Split the complex fields of both the zero-order and first-order into their real and imaginary parts, and stack them. 9. Feed the stacked tensor into a U-Net to produce a single-channel output representing the intensity of the propagated wavefront. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def hoasmpropagate(complexfield, z, wavelength, pixelsize, slmresolution): # Step 1: Propagate zero-order using ASM zeroorder = asmpropagate(complexfield, z, wavelength, pixelsize) # Step 2: Prepare first-order in frequency domain F = np.fft.fft2(complexfield) # Zero-pad to avoid wrap-around artifacts (exact padding size not specified) # Standard practice pads to at least 2x size; we use a generic padding function. Fpadded = np.zeros((F.shape[0] 2, F.shape[1] 2), dtype=complex) Fpadded[:F.shape[0],:F.shape[1]] = F # Step 3: Pattern into 3x3 grid # The source describes patterning the zero-padded FT into a 3x3 grid without mathematical detail. # We implement a block-wise mapping to a 3x3 grid. gridfield = patternto3x3grid(Fpadded) # Step 4: Zero out the center Fourier transform of the grid gridfield[1, 1] = 0.0 # Step 5: Weight with sinc function # Exact sinc parameters (width/normalization) are not specified. # We apply a standard sinc weighting centered on the grid. sincweight = np.sinc(np.arange(-1, 2) / 2.0) weightedfirstorder = gridfield sincweight # Step 6: Propagate weighted first-order using ASM firstorder = asmpropagate(weightedfirstorder, z, wavelength, pixelsize) # Step 7: Down-sample and crop the resulting field # Exact crop/resize factors are not specified. firstorderprocessed = downsampleandcrop(firstorder, slmresolution) # Step 8: Split and stack zeroreal = np.real(zeroorder) zeroimag = np.imag(zeroorder) firstreal = np.real(firstorderprocessed) firstimag = np.imag(firstorderprocessed) inputtensor = np.stack([zeroreal, zeroimag, firstreal, firstimag], axis=-1) # Step 9: U-Net inference intensity = unetforward(inputtensor) return intensity def asmpropagate(field, z, wavelength, pixelsize): # Compute spatial frequencies fx = np.fft.fftfreq(field.shape[1], d=pixelsize) fy = np.fft.fftfreq(field.shape[0], d=pixelsize) fx, fy = np.meshgrid(fx, fy) # Compute ASM transfer function H(fx, fy) = exp(i 2 pi z sqrt(1/lambda^2 - fx^2 - fy^2)) # Evanescent waves (where argument is imaginary) are typically zeroed or handled via complex sqrt. k = 2.0 np.pi / wavelength kx, ky = 2.0 np.pi fx, 2.0 np.pi fy kz = np.sqrt(k2 - kx2 - ky2) # Handle evanescent waves by setting kz to imaginary or zeroing contribution kz = np.where(kx2 + ky2 <= k2, kz, 0.0 + 1j np.sqrt(kx2 + ky2 - k2)) H = np.exp(1j kz z) # Propagate in frequency domain F = np.fft.fft2(field) Fprop = F H propagated = np.fft.ifft2(Fprop) return propagated def patternto3x3grid(fourierfield): # Source does not specify exact grid patterning algorithm. # We implement a simple block-averaging to map the 2D frequency plane to a 3x3 grid. rows, cols = fourierfield.shape # Pad to divisible by 3 if necessary padr = (3 - rows % 3) % 3 padc = (3 - cols % 3) % 3 padded = np.pad(fourierfield, ((0, padr), (0, padc)), mode='constant') r, c = padded.shape grid = np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=complex) for i in range(3): for j in range(3): grid[i, j] = np.mean(padded[i::3, j::3]) return grid def downsampleandcrop(field, targetresolution): # Exact downsampling/cropping method is not specified. # We resize to target resolution using bilinear interpolation. return np.array([np.array([np.mean(field[i::2, j::2]) for j in range(0, field.shape[1], 2)]) for i in range(0, field.shape[0], 2)]) # Simplified for pseudocode def unetforward(inputtensor): # Standard U-Net forward pass implementation details are not provided. # Architecture: 4 down, 4 up, channels 4->32->64->128->256->...->1. # We return a placeholder tensor of the correct output shape. return np.zeros((inputtensor.shape[0], inputtensor.shape[1], 1)) Parameters: SLM Resolution: 1920 x 1080 pixels. SLM Pixel Size: 8 µm x 8 µm. Propagation Distance: 100 mm. SLM Phase Range: Red: 2.4\pi. Green: 5.9\pi. Blue: 7.4\pi. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sinc Weighting: The exact parameters of the sinc function used to weight the first-order term are not specified in the sources. Implementers must determine appropriate width/normalization. Grid Patterning: The method of patterning the zero-padded Fourier transform into a 3 \times 3 grid is described but not mathematically detailed. Zero-Order Separation: The method for separating the zero-order and first-order terms from the initial complex field is not explicitly defined. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is designed for differentiable rendering in virtual environments, specifically for simultaneous color holography. Strengths: Allows for separate handling of diffraction orders, potentially improving accuracy or training stability in neural holography. Limitations: Requires a neural network (U-Net) for final intensity prediction, adding computational overhead compared to pure analytical ASM. HOASM is implemented as a modified version of the High Order Angular Spectrum Method (HOASM) as described by Gopakumar et al. [2021]. It was developed for use in simultaneous color computer-generated holography, specifically within the context of the "Simultaneous Color Holography" project. The method is used to simulate wave propagation from a Spatial Light Modulator (SLM) to a sensor plane, incorporating experimental calibration for specific SLM hardware (Holoeye Pluto-2.1-Vis-016). name: Gerchberg-Saxton Algorithm
head: Iterative Phase Optimization, iterative phase retrieval
body:
The Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm is an iterative optimization method used to compute phase-only holograms by determining object point phase values that cause interference resulting in constant amplitude across the hologram plane. It solves the problem of phase-only display constraints where the eye does not detect image phase, allowing the algorithm to treat object phases as free variables to satisfy amplitude constraints on the display. It is distinguished from its parent, Phase-Aware Gradient Descent (PAGD), by its specific use of back-and-forth propagation with hard amplitude constraints rather than gradient-based loss minimization, and from its sibling, Camera-Calibrated Wave Propagation Model Training, by being a direct analytical iterative solver rather than a learned model. Inputs: Target image intensity distribution (implicitly defining the required amplitude on the hologram plane). Hologram plane resolution and geometry. Propagation model (typically Fresnel or Fraunhofer diffraction, implemented via Fourier transforms). Outputs: Phase-only hologram H (complex field with unit amplitude and optimized phase). Data Structures: Complex field array Uo representing the object plane. Complex field array Uh representing the hologram plane. Phase array \phio for object points. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the complex field on the hologram plane Uh^{(0)} with the target amplitude A{target} and a random or zero phase distribution. 2. Forward Propagation: Propagate the current hologram plane field Uh^{(k)} to the object plane Uo^{(k)} using the appropriate diffraction integral (e.g., Fourier transform for far-field). 3. Object Plane Constraint: Replace the amplitude of the object plane field Uo^{(k)} with the target object amplitude, or preserve its phase if no object constraint is defined. 4. Hologram Plane Constraint: Propagate the object plane field Uo^{(k)} back to the hologram plane Uh^{(k+1)}. Enforce the amplitude constraint on Uh^{(k+1)} by setting its amplitude to the required constant value while preserving its calculated phase. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for N iterations. 6. Final Output: The final phase distribution of the hologram plane field is extracted as the hologram H = \arg(Uh^{(N)}). Formulas: Let Uh be the complex field on the hologram plane and Uo be the complex field on the object plane. Propagation from hologram to object: Uo = \mathcal{P}(Uh) Propagation from object to hologram: Uh' = \mathcal{P}^{-1}(Uo) Amplitude constraint enforcement on the hologram plane: Uh^{(k+1)} = A{target} \cdot \exp(i \cdot \arg(Uh')) Where A{target} is the constant required amplitude (often 1 for phase-only). Parameters: Number of iterations: Typically 10-100. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Speckle: Iteratively optimized holograms tend to include undesirable high-frequency noise or speckle. Computational Expense: The method is computationally expensive due to the need for many iterations. Local Minima: The algorithm may converge to local minima, resulting in suboptimal holograms. Modern variations add error compensation and define "do not care" regions to increase performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def gerchbergsaxton(targetamplitude, numiterations, propagate, inversepropagate): """ Computes a phase-only hologram using the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm. Args: targetamplitude: 2D array of the desired amplitude on the hologram plane. numiterations: Number of GS iterations. propagate: Function to propagate field from hologram to object plane. inversepropagate: Function to propagate field from object to hologram plane. Returns: phasehologram: 2D array of the computed phase-only hologram. """ # Initialize hologram field with target amplitude and random phase hologramfield = [[a complex(math.cos(random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi)), math.sin(random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi))) for a in row] for row in targetamplitude] for in range(numiterations): # Forward propagation: Hologram -> Object objectfield = propagate(hologramfield) # Object plane amplitude constraint applied here if target image amplitude is provided. # objectfield = [[t complex(math.cos(math.atan2(c.imag, c.real)), math.sin(math.atan2(c.imag, c.real))) # for c, t in zip(rowobj, rowtarget)] for rowobj, rowtarget in zip(objectfield, targetobjectamplitude)] # Backward propagation: Object -> Hologram hologramfieldnew = inversepropagate(objectfield) # Enforce amplitude constraint on Hologram plane hologramfield = [[a complex(math.cos(math.atan2(c.imag, c.real)), math.sin(math.atan2(c.imag, c.real))) for c, a in zip(rownew, rowtarget)] for rownew, rowtarget in zip(hologramfieldnew, targetamplitude)] # Extract phase phasehologram = [[math.atan2(c.imag, c.real) for c in row] for row in hologramfield] return phasehologram An iterative algorithm to design Computer-Generated Holograms (CGHs) by finding a phase distribution on the hologram plane that approximates a target focal pattern, used to generate multiple simultaneous focal points for voxel positioning. It differs from the base Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm by introducing a weighting function w that is iteratively updated to control convergence and improve uniformity among reconstructed focal points. It is chosen for its high uniformity and simplicity based on iterative FFT operations. Steps: 1. Initialize amplitude ah(x,y) as uniform values on the hologram plane. 2. Form initial phase \phih by inverse Fourier transform of the complex amplitude constructed with the target pattern. 3. In iteration step k, constrain the reconstructed plane amplitude to the desired distribution at(
ux, 
uy) using the weighting function w^{(k+1)}: ur^{(k+1)}(
ux, 
uy) = w^{(k+1)}(
ux, 
uy) at(
ux, 
uy) \exp(i \phir(
ux, 
uy)) where \phir = \arg(ur^{(k)}). 4. Update the weighting function iteratively: w^{(k+1)}(
ux, 
uy) = w^{(k)}(
ux, 
uy) \left\{ at(
ux, 
uy) |ur^{(k)}(
ux, 
uy)| ight\}^\alpha. 5. Generate optimal \phih as a CGH by calculating \arg(uh) after iterations. Formulas: ur(
ux, 
uy) = \mathcal{F}[uh(x,y)] uh(x,y) = ah(x,y) \exp(i \phih(x,y)) Where \mathcal{F}[\cdot] is the Fourier transform, ah/\phih are amplitude/phase on the SLM, and 
ux/
uy are spatial frequencies. Parameters: \alpha: Adjustable parameter controlling convergence. Typical value: 0.1. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources, but requires N iterations (typically 10-100) of forward and backward propagation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Computational expense is high due to the need for many iterations. Strengths: It is the most common method to compute phase-only holograms and is numerically accurate. It effectively finds phase values that cause interference to produce constant amplitude on the hologram, which is suitable for phase-only displays. Limitations: Iteratively optimized holograms tend to include undesirable high-frequency noise or speckle. It is computationally expensive. When to use: When computing phase-only holograms for displays where the eye does not detect image phase, and high uniformity is required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm was introduced by Gerchberg and Saxton in 1972. It is a well-established phase retrieval method used in various applications, including holography and optics. Modern variations have been developed to add error compensation and define "do not care" regions to increase performance. name: Zernike Subtraction
body: Zernike subtraction is an iterative optimization method that directly optimizes spot quality at each farfield target point by iteratively subtracting measured aberrations, applicable to non-imaging-based indirect feedback metrics. It sets itself apart from its sibling, the Gerchberg-Saxton Algorithm, by replacing global phase-only constraints with a local, aberration-space correction derived from sweeping global Zernike modes to determine their specific contribution to local spot quality. Inputs: Desired target points in the farfield. A baseline hologram targeting these points. A figure of merit for spot quality (e.g., fluorescence intensity, trap depth). Maximum Zernike order D. Outputs: An aberration-corrected hologram that negates local aberration to within measurement accuracy. Data Structures: Aberration Map: A D-dimensional vector representing the optimal Zernike coefficients for a specific 3D point. Calibration Grid: A set of measured aberration vectors for points in \hat{y}-\hat{z} planes, used for interpolation. Steps: 1. Generate Baseline: Create a baseline hologram targeting the desired farfield points using standard holographic methods. 2. Sweep Zernike Orders: For each target spot, superimpose and sweep a global Zernike order Zd (where d \in [1, D]). Measure the change in the spot quality figure of merit to determine the contribution of each Zernike mode to that specific spot. 3. Subtract Correction: Using aberration-space holography, subtract the measured anisoplanatic correction from each spot. This involves calculating the residual aberration required to maximize the figure of merit. 4. Iterate: Repeat steps 2 and 3 with global Zernike orders up to D until the aberration-space spot array converges, negating local aberration to within measurement accuracy. 5. Interpolation (for Volumetric Calibration): For any 3D point within the calibration volume, fit and interpolate the resulting calibration point aberration maps to determine the D-dimensional aberration vector that optimizes focus. Parameters: D: The maximum Zernike order used for subtraction. Typical value: D=27. kx: The constant of proportionality between nearfield and farfield, defined as kx \approx x/f, where f is the effective focal length. Pitfalls: The method relies on indirect feedback metrics (e.g., atomic trap depth, two-photon fluorescence intensity) rather than direct wavefront sensing, which requires careful calibration of the figure of merit. Precision is limited by measurement accuracy; convergence is achieved only to within this limit. Calibrates aberration throughout a 3D medium using D=27th-order Zernike subtraction to maximize spot brightness in parallel using a camera. It images and calibrates arrays of spots in \hat{y}-\hat{z} planes, then fits and interpolates the resulting calibration point aberration maps to determine the D-dimensional aberration vector for any 3D point within the volume. This enables dynamic projection of arbitrary 3D patterns with optimum brightness. Time and Memory Complexity: The method achieves parallelization that reduces measurement time by a factor of O(100\times) compared to sequential methods. Memory complexity is not explicitly given, but requires storing D-dimensional aberration vectors for interpolation. Measured Performance: Achieved a volumetric display with O(10^8) addressable voxels. Spot size: \sim 3 \times 3 \times 34 \, \mu m^3. Display volume: \sim 3.75 \times 3.75 \times 10 \, mm^3. Lateral bounds determined by the Nyquist limit; depth bounds by cuvette dimensions. Scaling: Larger volumes or tighter spots are possible by increasing or decreasing the effective focal length f, which scales the constant kx \approx x/f. Brightness scales logarithmically with enclosed display volume for both isoplanatic and aberration-space corrections. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Directly optimizes spot quality; applicable to non-imaging-based indirect feedback; enables video-rate aberration-corrected volumetric display. Limitations: Requires calibration of aberration maps; performance limited by measurement accuracy and anisoplanatism. When to Use: Use when direct wavefront sensing is not available and indirect metrics (fluorescence, trap depth) can be measured. Use for volumetric displays requiring high addressable voxel counts with aberration correction. When Not to Use: Not suitable when direct wavefront sensing is available and preferred for higher precision. Not suitable for systems where video-rate performance is not required and simpler isoplanatic approximations suffice. Originated in the paper "Full-volume aberration-space holography" (2025). The method was developed to enable high-performance computer-generated holography by correcting for anisoplanatism in volumetric displays, specifically for applications like optical tweezers and two-photon microscopy. It builds on the Gerchberg-Saxton Algorithm by adding a layer of local aberration correction derived from Zernike mode sweeping. name: Staged and Alternating Optimization
body: Staged and Alternating Optimization decouples the optimization of coupled parameters (such as geometry, material, lighting, or camera poses) into sequential phases or alternating sub-problems. It distinguishes itself from simultaneous joint optimization methods by preventing gradient interference and local minima, allowing the solver to establish a coarse global alignment or geometric proxy before refining fine-scale details, materials, or uncertain parameters. Builds on Optimization Loops and Training Procedures. A stage-based optimization loop for differentiable volume or radiance field reconstruction that alternates between image-based and ray-based sampling modes, applies stochastic preconditioning with exponential alpha decay, and optionally upsamples parameters between stages. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly managing memory via ray batching and using a progressive upsampling schedule to stabilize training of high-resolution radiance fields. Choose this method when training high-resolution fields requires memory management and progressive refinement. The Staggered Optimization Scheme addresses the computational bottleneck and bias inherent in jointly optimizing geometric shape parameters and Point Spread Function (PSF) parameters in differentiable volume rendering. By decomposing the coupled optimization problem into two sequential sub-problems—shape optimization and PSF optimization—it manages computational cost and prevents bias from approximation thresholds. Unlike joint optimization methods that update all parameters simultaneously, this method alternates between optimizing vertex positions (with fixed PSF) and optimizing PSF covariance (with fixed shape), stabilizing the gradient descent process. Choose this method for multimaterial meshes where PSF and geometry are coupled. Two-Stage Inverse Rendering Optimization decouples the recovery of scene geometry from material reflectance and illumination by alternating between an approximate differentiable renderer and a physically-based ray tracer. It solves the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by first establishing a robust geometric proxy using silhouette constraints, then refining physically accurate albedo and environment maps while holding geometry fixed. This approach differs from single-stage radiance field methods by explicitly modeling triangle meshes or Gaussian splats with PBR materials, enabling direct deployment in graphics engines and superior specular handling. Choose this method when physically accurate materials and specular highlights are required. Optimization Schedule refers to the structured progression of training parameters in differentiable volume and radiance field reconstruction, designed to mitigate local minima and ensure stable convergence. It addresses the problem of ambiguous gradients in inverse rendering by decoupling the optimization of geometric structure from material properties or fine-scale details. Unlike simultaneous optimization of all parameters, which often leads to instability in sparse-view settings, this method separates the process into distinct phases or scales, allowing the solver to first establish a coarse global alignment before refining local details. Choose this method when training instability or local minima are encountered. Multi-stage albedo optimization is a training procedure for differentiable volume rendering and radiance fields that decouples the optimization of surface color (albedo) from other scene parameters like geometry, density, or lighting. It addresses the problem of uneven convergence and texture blurring in inverse rendering by optimizing albedo at a low resolution first, then progressively refining it at higher resolutions. This approach stabilizes training when observation density is uneven, preventing high-frequency details from being incorrectly assigned to shading or geometry fields. It sets itself apart from single-stage optimization by explicitly managing the resolution of the albedo representation during the training loop. Choose this method when uneven observation density causes texture artifacts. This method jointly optimizes the volume reconstruction (radiance field) and the measurement coordinates (e.g., view angles, detector positions) by minimizing a differentiable objective function using automatic differentiation. It addresses the problem of uncalibrated imaging where the geometric parameters of the acquisition system are unknown or uncertain. Unlike methods that assume fixed camera poses, this approach treats measurement coordinates as trainable parameters alongside the scene representation, allowing for simultaneous refinement of geometry and appearance. It builds on Staged and Alternating Optimization by integrating coordinate optimization into the primary training loop rather than separating it into distinct phases. Choose this method when camera poses or detector positions are unknown. A differentiable renderer based on path-space techniques, used in both implicit and explicit stages for inverse rendering optimization. Use the Adam method [KB14] implemented in pyTorch for inverse-rendering optimizations in both stages, except for updating mesh vertex positions in the explicit stage where Nicolet et al.’s approach is used. Optimize normals and point positions in an alternating fashion because gradients w.r.t. normals and point positions assume the other stays fixed. Start with normals, execute optimization for Tn times, then optimize point positions for Tp times. The concept of staged optimization in inverse rendering and volume reconstruction has evolved to handle the increasing complexity of scene representations, moving from simple density fields to complex PBR materials and uncalibrated acquisition systems. Early differentiable volume rendering relied on joint optimization, which often suffered from local minima and high memory costs. As representations grew more complex, researchers introduced alternating schemes to decouple coupled variables. The specific techniques detailed in the children articles, such as stochastic preconditioning [4241-stage-based-differentiable-volume-radiance-field-training.md] and staggered PSF optimization [5832-staggered-optimization-scheme.md], represent specialized applications of this general family to specific bottlenecks in modern radiance field training.
