name: Last Layer Re-training
head: Instant NeRF Editing, Last Layer Fine-tuning
body: Last Layer Re-training is a technique to instantly propagate a color edit from a single view to the entire Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) by selectively retraining only the last layer of the color Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). It solves the problem of efficient NeRF editing by reducing the number of parameters requiring modification compared to full retraining, while preserving existing view-dependent information. It sets itself apart from full MLP retraining by avoiding the loss of useful pre-trained information. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained NeRF model (specifically its color MLP weights \phic and density MLP weights \phi\sigma) and a single edited view image I{edit} \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times H \times 3}. Output: Updated NeRF parameters where the last layer of the color MLP is replaced by \phi'{last}, producing a new rendered color c'{x,\theta}. Data Structures: The color MLP takes as input the concatenation of multiresolution hash grid features fx and a view direction encoding \gamma(\theta). The feature encoding fx is a concatenation of features from each resolution level L: fx = \{f{x,0} \oplus f{x,1} \oplus \dots \oplus f{x,L}\} where \oplus denotes concatenation. The last layer maps the penultimate layer output h{x,\theta} to the final color. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract Penultimate Output: For each ray sampled from the edited view, compute the hidden vector h{x,\theta} from the penultimate layer of the pre-trained color MLP. This vector depends on the position x and view direction \theta. 2. Initialize Last Layer: Initialize a new set of parameters \phi'{last} for the last layer of the color MLP. The rest of the network (density MLP and earlier layers of the color MLP) remains frozen. 3. Compute Loss: Render the color C'{ij} for each pixel (i,j) in the edited view using the volume rendering equation with the updated last layer. Compute the photometric loss against the ground truth edited image C{ij}: L = \sum{i,j} \| C{ij} - C'{ij} \|^2 where C{ij} is the original RGB value from the training image (the edited view) and C'{ij} is the volume rendered RGB value. 4. Optimize: Minimize L with respect to \phi'{last} using the Adam optimizer. 5. Update Model: Replace the original last layer weights \phic with the optimized \phi'{last}. Formulas: The naive approach would retrain the full color MLP: MLPc(hx, \gamma(\theta), \phi'c) = c'{x,\theta} However, Last Layer Re-training uses: MLP{last}(h{x,\theta}, \phi'{last}) = c'{x,\theta} where h{x,\theta} is the output of the penultimate layer. Parameters: Learning Rate: 0.01. Optimizer: Adam. Iterations: 200 iterations per scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Bleeding: Since the information encoded in the color MLP is global, modifying only the last layer may lead to undesired edits in regions not targeted by the user edit. This is addressed by IReNe using a soft 3D segmentation step to restrict edits to target regions. View-Dependent Effects: Editing only the last layer must preserve view-dependent effects (e.g., specularities) present in the pre-trained NeRF. The method relies on the view-dependent information already present in the pre-trained model's earlier layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lastlayerretraining(pretrainednerf, editedimage, numiterations=200, learningrate=0.01): """ Retrain only the last layer of the color MLP to match the edited image. Args: pretrainednerf: Pre-trained NeRF model with frozen density MLP and color MLP layers except last. editedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) representing the single edited view. numiterations: Number of optimization steps. learningrate: Learning rate for Adam optimizer. Returns: updatednerf: NeRF model with updated last layer weights. """ # Extract last layer of color MLP lastlayer = pretrainednerf.colormlp.layers[-1] # Freeze all parameters except the last layer for param in pretrainednerf.colormlp.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False for param in lastlayer.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = True # Initialize Adam optimizer state for the last layer m = {id(p): 0.0 for p in lastlayer.parameters()} v = {id(p): 0.0 for p in lastlayer.parameters()} t = 0 for step in range(numiterations): t += 1 # Forward pass: volume render rays for the edited view Cprime = volumerender(pretrainednerf, editedimage, lastlayer) Cgt = editedimage # Compute loss: L = sum ||Cij - C'ij||^2 loss = sum((Cgt - Cprime) 2) # Backward pass: compute gradients of loss w.r.t. lastlayer parameters gradients = computegradients(loss, lastlayer) # Adam update step for param in lastlayer.parameters(): grad = gradients[id(param)] m[id(param)] = 0.9 m[id(param)] + 0.1 grad v[id(param)] = 0.999 v[id(param)] + 0.001 (grad 2) mhat = m[id(param)] / (1 - 0.9 t) vhat = v[id(param)] / (1 - 0.999 t) param -= learningrate mhat / (math.sqrt(vhat) + 1e-8) return pretrainednerf def volumerender(nerf, editedimage, lastlayer): """Standard volume rendering using the emission-absorption model.""" renderedcolors = [] for y in range(editedimage.height): for x in range(editedimage.width): ray = generateray(editedimage, x, y) samples = samplealongray(ray) transmittance = 1.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for sample in samples: # Extract hash grid features and view direction encoding features = nerf.hashgrid.getfeatures(sample.position) viewdir = nerf.viewencoding(ray.direction) # Concatenate features and view direction hxtheta = nerf.colormlp.penultimatelayer(features, viewdir) # Map to color using the updated last layer alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-nerf.densitymlp(sample.position) sample.stepsize) c = lastlayer(hxtheta) color += transmittance alpha c transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) renderedcolors.append(color) return renderedcolors def computegradients(loss, targetmodule): """Standard automatic differentiation through the computational graph.""" return {id(p): p.grad for p in targetmodule.parameters()} IReNe is a method for instant 360-degree recoloring of pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using a single user-edited image. It addresses the limitations of prior methods by preventing color bleeding at object boundaries and ensuring multi-view consistency for view-dependent effects, such as specularities. Unlike ICE-NeRF, which suffers from color bleeding, or Palette-NeRF, which requires hours to train, IReNe achieves high-quality edits in under 5 seconds by selectively fine-tuning only the diffuse neurons in the last layer of the color MLP. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than full MLP retraining because only the last layer parameters are optimized. Memory Complexity: Lower memory footprint during training compared to full retraining as gradients are only computed for the last layer. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Rapid edits, preserves view-dependent information, prevents color bleeding (when combined with segmentation). Limitations: May still suffer from global color bleeding if not combined with segmentation techniques. When to use: When instant editing of a pre-trained NeRF is required, and view-dependent effects must be preserved. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Last Layer Re-training was introduced in the IReNe paper (Mazzucchelli et al., CVPR 2024) as a method for instant recoloring of Neural Radiance Fields. It builds on the Instant-NGP implementation. The method was developed to address the challenges of near real-time NeRF editing, specifically the trade-off between edit speed and quality. name: IReNe
head: Instant Recoloring of Neural Radiance Fields
body: IReNe is a method for instant 360-degree recoloring of pre-trained Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) using a single user-edited image. It addresses the limitations of prior methods by preventing color bleeding at object boundaries and ensuring multi-view consistency for view-dependent effects, such as specularities. Unlike ICE-NeRF, which suffers from color bleeding, or Palette-NeRF, which requires hours to train, IReNe achieves high-quality edits in under 5 seconds by selectively fine-tuning only the diffuse neurons in the last layer of the color MLP. Inputs: A pre-trained NeRF model (specifically Instant-NGP), consisting of a density MLP \sigma, multiresolution hash features f, and a color MLP c. A single training image I{edit} containing user-applied color edits. Outputs: An edited image I{render} generated via volumetric rendering. Data Structures: Multiresolution Hash Grid Features (fx): The feature vector for a 3D point x is a concatenation of features from L levels of a multiresolution hash grid. fx = \{f{x,0} \oplus f{x,1} \oplus \dots \oplus f{x,L}\} where \oplus denotes concatenation. Density MLP (MLP\sigma): Takes feature fx and outputs density \sigmax and hidden feature hx. MLP\sigma(fx, \phi\sigma) = \sigmax, hx Color MLP (MLPc): Takes hidden feature hx and encoded view direction \gamma(\theta) to output color c{x,\theta}. MLPc(hx, \gamma(\theta), \phic) = c{x,\theta} Instant-NGP uses spherical harmonics for the view direction encoding \gamma(\cdot). Segmentation MLP (MLPs): A lightweight, trainable MLP ruled by features f to estimate a volumetric soft-segmentation \alpha of the edited region. Neuron Classification: Neurons in the last layer of MLPc are classified as either "diffuse" or "view-dependent". Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Load the pre-trained Instant-NGP NeRF. 2. Detect Diffuse Neurons: Automatically detect diffuse neurons in the last layer of the color MLP c. This is done by analyzing the activations of the last layer neurons across different view directions. Diffuse neurons exhibit color consistency across views, while view-dependent neurons (e.g., specularities) change color with the viewing angle. 3. Train Segmentation: Train the segmentation MLP MLPs using the multiresolution hash features f to estimate the volumetric soft-segmentation mask \alpha for the edited region. The optimization minimizes the RGB loss between the rendered image and the user-edited image I{edit}. 4. Fine-tune Diffuse Neurons: Fine-tune only the weights corresponding to the identified diffuse neurons in the last layer of MLPc. The view-dependent neurons remain frozen to preserve view-specific effects. 5. Compute Blended Color: For any 3D point x and view direction \theta, compute the final color C{final} as a linear combination of the color predicted by the frozen weights (c{x,\theta}) and the color predicted by the retrained weights (c'{x,\theta}), blended using the segmentation mask \alphax: C{final} = (1 - \alphax) c{x,\theta} + \alphax c'{x,\theta} where c{x,\theta} is the output of the original frozen MLPc and c'{x,\theta} is the output of the MLPc with the fine-tuned last layer. 6. Volumetric Rendering: Perform standard volumetric rendering using the density \sigmax and the blended color C{final} to obtain the edited image I{render}. Optimization: The segmentation MLP MLPs and the trainable last-layer diffuse neurons are optimized simultaneously. The loss function is the standard RGB loss between the rendered image I{render} and the user-edited image I{edit}: L = \sum \| C{ij} - C'{ij} \|^2 where C{ij} is the pixel value in I{edit} and C'{ij} is the rendered pixel value. Parameters: Optimization Time: Approximately 5 seconds. Input Resolution: Depends on the input image I{edit}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color Bleeding: Without the segmentation module \alpha, color edits bleed into adjacent objects. The trainable segmentation module prevents this by providing spatial control over the edit. View-Dependent Consistency: If all neurons in the last layer were fine-tuned, view-dependent effects like specularities would be distorted or lost. Classifying and freezing view-dependent neurons ensures multi-view consistency. Complex 360-Degree Scenes: Unlike methods relying on reprojection which fail in complex 360-degree scenes, IReNe handles them consistently by operating directly in the 3D volume representation. Time Complexity: Extremely fast optimization, typically under 5 seconds per edit. This is 5× to 500× faster than competitors like Palette-NeRF (hours) and ICE-NeRF (seconds, but with quality issues). Memory Complexity: Low additional memory overhead due to the lightweight segmentation MLP and the fact that only a subset of the last layer weights are trained. Strengths: Near real-time interactive editing, prevention of color bleeding, multi-view consistency for specularities, and support for partial and multi-object edits. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained Instant-NGP model; relies on the accuracy of the automatic diffuse neuron classification. When to use: When instant, high-quality color editing of a NeRF is required, especially for scenes with complex boundaries or view-dependent effects. When not to use: When the underlying NeRF is not trained with Instant-NGP or when global scene reconstruction (not just color editing) is needed. IReNe was introduced by Mazzucchelli et al. in 2024. It builds upon the Instant-NGP architecture and addresses limitations in previous NeRF editing methods such as Palette-NeRF and ICE-NeRF. The method was validated on a new dataset with edited object colors, demonstrating significant quantitative and qualitative advancements. IReNe: Instant Recoloring of Neural Radiance Fields, https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/MazzucchelliIReNeInstantRecoloringofNeuralRadianceFieldsCVPR2024paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Temporal Optimization Heuristics
head: Dynamic DiffBMP, Dynamic DiffBMP for Videos, Dynamic DiffBMP heuristics, Dynamic Rendering with Spatial Constraint, Frame-wise Fidelity Heuristic, Sequential Optimization for Video
body:
Temporal Optimization Heuristics is a method for modeling dynamic content in differentiable bitmap primitive (DiffBMP) rendering by optimizing video frames sequentially to achieve both per-frame fidelity and temporal anti-flicker. It addresses two specific failure modes in sequential optimization: "stuck" primitives that block gradients in changing regions, and parameter drift in static regions that causes flicker. Unlike standard sequential optimization which simply warm-starts from the previous frame, this method applies three lightweight heuristics—warm-starting, removing stuck primitives, and freezing unchanged regions—to balance these competing goals. The method operates on a sequence of target images I^f{target} for frames f=1 \dots N. It maintains a set of N bitmap primitives per frame, where each primitive i is defined by parameters \Thetai = (xi, yi, si, 	hetai, 
ui, ci), representing position, scale, rotation, opacity logit, and color. The opacity is computed as \alphai = \alpha{max} \sigma(
ui), where \sigma is the sigmoid function. Inputs: Sequence of target images \{I^f{target}\}{f=1}^N. Previous frame's optimized parameters \Theta{f-1}^\star (for f > 1). Spatial grid dimensions (nh, nw). Thresholds: scale 	au{scale}, opacity 	au\alpha, z-order percentile \zeta. Intervention cap K (top-K primitives per region). Decay factor \eta \in (0, 1). Outputs: Optimized parameters \Thetaf^\star for each frame f. Primitive List: Array of N primitives. Each primitive i stores (xi, yi, si, 	hetai, 
ui, ci). Freeze Mask: Boolean array freeze of size N, where freeze[i] is true if the primitive is frozen. Inter-frame Difference Mask: Binary mask D \in \{0, 1\}^{H 	imes W}, where D[x,y]=1 if pixel (x,y) changed between frames. Spatial Grid: The image canvas is partitioned into nh 	imes nw regions Rj. The optimization for frame f proceeds as follows: 1. Warm-Start Initialization: Initialize the parameters for frame f (\Thetaf) using the optimized parameters from the previous frame (\Theta{f-1}^\star). The "stuck" heuristic helps mitigate this by decaying dominant primitives that might otherwise block correct optimization. Time Complexity: The heuristics add negligible overhead compared to the optimization step itself. The difference mask computation is O(HW). The freeze mask computation is O(N). The stuck primitive identification involves sorting primitives within regions, which is O(N \log N) in the worst case but typically O(N) if regions are small. The decay step is O(N). This is minimal compared to the memory required for storing primitive parameters and intermediate rendering states. The approach is inspired by sequential optimization techniques used in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [32], but adapted for the specific characteristics of bitmap primitives, which do not explicitly distinguish background. The heuristics address the unique failure modes of DiffBMP, such as primitives getting "stuck" and recoloring instead of relocating. name: Framework and Baseline Implementations
body: This family defines the software architectures and training protocols for executing differentiable volume rendering optimization. It is distinct from its siblings by specifying the low-level execution model (e.g., graph-based Vulkan submission vs. eager-mode) and high-level training schedules (e.g., distractor separation, multi-stage optimization) rather than the mathematical loss functions or camera models themselves. A define-and-run differentiable rendering optimization framework that constructs a computational graph, marks variables for gradient tracking, and executes forward/backward passes using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). It distinguishes itself from standard AD libraries by packing the computational graph into Vulkan command buffers for execution, allowing for hardware-agnostic differentiable rendering. Unlike general-purpose AD which may suffer from high memory usage due to storing intermediate states, DressiAD manages graph staticity and rebuilds stages only when necessary, optimizing for the specific constraints of GPU-based rendering. Choose this method when hardware-agnostic execution and explicit graph staticity management are required for GPU-based rendering pipelines. A protocol that defines the training loop, parameter initialization, and optimization hyperparameters for decomposed Gaussian splatting methods, specifically targeting distractor-free rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling and optimizing distractor elements alongside static scene Gaussians to improve background reconstruction and reduce artifacts, using specific learning rate schedules and regularization weights. Choose this method when distractor elements degrade background reconstruction and require joint optimization with static geometry. This variant optimizes multi-view video sequences using a two-stage process. First, the first frame is optimized for 3,000 iterations. Second, the full multi-view video sequence is optimized for 14,000 iterations. Not given in the sources. name: DressiAD Optimization Loop
head: Dressi-AD Computational Graph Execution, DressiAD Training Loop, Optimization Loop
body: The DressiAD Optimization Loop is a define-and-run differentiable rendering optimization framework that constructs a computational graph, marks variables for gradient tracking, and executes forward/backward passes using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). It distinguishes itself from standard AD libraries by packing the computational graph into Vulkan command buffers for execution, allowing for hardware-agnostic differentiable rendering. The method operates by defining a computational graph of rendering and loss functions, then executing an iterative optimization loop that handles data transfer between CPU and GPU, graph traversal for gradient computation, and Vulkan command submission. Inputs: Scene data: Vertex positions, UVs, faces, model/view/projection matrices, environment map, albedo, metallic, roughness, normal maps, and background. Target image: The ground-truth image to minimize loss against. HardSoftRas parameters: K (number of peeling steps), r (radius), \sigma (blending parameter), \delta (silhouette edge width). Learning rate: lr. Outputs: Optimized scene parameters (e.g., vertex positions, normal maps) saved as a GLTF file. CpuImage: A simple buffer representing a 2D image used to store scene data on the CPU. It holds vertex positions, UVs, faces, matrices, environment maps, albedo, metallic, roughness, normal, and background data. Variable: A data structure representing inputs and outputs of functions in the computational graph. Fields: type: Enum indicating data type (VEC3, VEC2, IVEC3, MAT4, FLOAT, VEC4). size: Dimensions of the variable. value: Current numerical value of the variable. requiresgrad: Boolean flag indicating if the variable is an optimization target. dirty: Boolean flag indicating if the variable's data has changed since the last GPU sync. creator: Reference to the Function that produced this variable. DressiAD Class: Manages the optimization state. Fields: mlossvar: The loss variable. minitstatus: Enum tracking initialization phase (BACKWARD, STAGE, SUBSTAGE, FINISHED). mgraphstaticcnt: Counter for static graph iterations. mvkcmdbuf: Vulkan command buffer. minputvars: List of input variables. minputgradvars: List of gradient variables for inputs. lr: Learning rate for SGD. Typical value: 0.01. K: Number of peeling steps for HardSoftRas. Typical value: 2. r: Radius parameter for HardSoftRas. Typical value: 0.01. \sigma: Blending parameter for HardSoftRas. Calculated as r / 7. \delta: Silhouette edge width for HardSoftRas. Equal to r. 1. Initialization: Create a DressiBasicRenderer instance and load scene data from files (e.g.,.gltf,.png) into CPU memory as CpuImage buffers. 2. Graph Construction: Call buildGraph with scene variables and HardSoftRas parameters (K, r, \sigma, \delta). This calls BuildBasicRenderGraph to assemble operators and F:: functions into a computational graph. 3. Loss Definition: Compute the L1 loss between the target image and the rendered image: L = \text{Mean}(|I{\text{target}} - I{\text{rendered}}|) Set this loss variable in the DressiAD instance. 4. Optimizer Definition: Define an SGD optimizer function that updates variables x using gradients gx: x{\text{new}} = x - gx \cdot lr Set this optimizer in the DressiAD instance. 5. Target Marking: Mark specific variables (e.g., vertex positions, normal maps) as optimization targets by setting their requiresgrad flag. 6. Optimization Loop: For each iteration: a. Dirty Check: Check if any input variable has changed dirty flags. If so, reset mgraphstaticcnt to 0. b. Rebuild Check: If mgraphstaticcnt equals FASTREBUILDCOUNT, set minitstatus to STAGE. If mgraphstaticcnt equals FULLREBUILDCOUNT, set minitstatus to SUBSTAGE. c. Data Transfer: If missent is false, send CPU images to GPU using sendImg, which marks variables as dirty and transfers data. d. Execution: Call execStep(). e. Backward Pass Construction: Inside execStep, if minitstatus <= BACKWARD: Initialize fwdbwdsmap (mapping forward variables to backward gradients) and funcqueue. Set the gradient of the loss variable to 1.0: fwdbwdsmap[lossvar] = {1.0}. Push the loss variable's creator function to funcqueue. While funcqueue is not empty: Pop function f from queue. Call f.buildBwd() to generate backward graph nodes. For each input x of f with gradient gx: Append gx to fwdbwdsmap[x]. If x has a creator, push it to funcqueue. f. Gradient Aggregation: Sum gradients for each input variable: g{\text{total}} = \sum gx Store pairs of (inputvar, totalgradient). g. Optimizer Step: Apply the optimizer function to update the input variables. h. Vulkan Submission: Submit the command buffer mvkcmdbuf using VkQueueSubmit. i. Cleanup: Mark all input variables as clean recursively (setDirtyRecursively(false)) and set minitstatus to FINISHED. j. Increment mgraphstaticcnt. 7. Finalization: Save the optimized scene data as a GLTF file. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FASTREBUILDCOUNT = 10 # Not given in the sources. FULLREBUILDCOUNT = 100 # Not given in the sources. class F: @staticmethod def Float(val): return val @staticmethod def Abs(x): return abs(x) @staticmethod def Mean(x): return sum(x) / len(x) if isinstance(x, list) else x @staticmethod def SumPixelWise(grads): if not grads: return 0.0 if isinstance(grads[0], list): return [sum(g) for g in zip(grads)] return sum(grads) class Variable: def init(self, name, vartype, size): self.name = name self.type = vartype self.size = size self.value = None self.requiresgrad = False self.dirty = False self.creator = None self.grads = [] def setrequiresgrad(self): self.requiresgrad = True if self.creator: self.creator.setrequiresgrad() def setdirty(self, val): self.dirty = val def setdirtyrecursively(self, val): self.dirty = val if self.creator: self.creator.setdirtyrecursively(val) class Function: def init(self, name, forwardfunc, backwardgenerator): self.name = name self.forwardfunc = forwardfunc self.backwardgenerator = backwardgenerator self.inputs = [] self.outputs = [] def buildbwd(self, outputgrads): # Generates backward graph nodes and returns list of (inputvar, gradient) pairs return [] class DressiAD: def init(self): self.lossvar = None self.optimizerfunc = None self.initstatus = 0 # BACKWARD self.graphstaticcnt = 0 self.vkcmdbuf = [] self.inputvars = [] self.inputgradvars = [] self.fwdbwdsmap = {} self.funcqueue = [] def setlossvar(self, lossvar): self.lossvar = lossvar self.initstatus = 0 # BACKWARD def setoptimizer(self, optimizerfunc): self.optimizerfunc = optimizerfunc def execstep(self): # Check dirty flags of input variables if any(v.dirty for v in self.inputvars): self.graphstaticcnt = 0 # Check rebuild condition if self.graphstaticcnt == FASTREBUILDCOUNT: self.initstatus = 1 # STAGE elif self.graphstaticcnt == FULLREBUILDCOUNT: self.initstatus = 2 # SUBSTAGE # Build backward pass if needed if self.initstatus <= 0: # BACKWARD self.fwdbwdsmap = {} self.funcqueue = [] # Set loss gradient to 1.0 self.fwdbwdsmap[self.lossvar] = [F.Float(1.0)] # Push loss creator if self.lossvar.creator: self.funcqueue.append(self.lossvar.creator) while self.funcqueue: func = self.funcqueue.pop() # Get gradients for this function's outputs outputgrads = [] for out in func.outputs: if out in self.fwdbwdsmap: outputgrads.extend(self.fwdbwdsmap[out]) # Build backward gradinputs = func.buildbwd(outputgrads) for inp, grad in gradinputs: if inp not in self.fwdbwdsmap: self.fwdbwdsmap[inp] = [] self.fwdbwdsmap[inp].append(grad) if inp.creator: self.funcqueue.append(inp.creator) # Aggregate gradients inputvars = [] inputgradvars = [] for var, grads in self.fwdbwdsmap.items(): if var.requiresgrad: inputvars.append(var) # Sum gradients pixel-wise totalgrad = F.SumPixelWise(grads) inputgradvars.append(totalgrad) # Apply optimizer if self.optimizerfunc and inputvars: updatedvars = self.optimizerfunc(inputvars, inputgradvars) # Update variable values for var, newval in zip(inputvars, updatedvars): var.value = newval # Vulkan submission submitvulkancommandbuffer(self.vkcmdbuf) # Cleanup for var in self.inputvars: var.setdirtyrecursively(False) self.initstatus = 3 # FINISHED self.graphstaticcnt += 1 def submitvulkancommandbuffer(cmdbuf): # Submits the Vulkan command buffer for execution pass class DressiBasicRenderer: def init(self): self.dressiad = DressiAD() self.varmap = {} self.imgmap = {} self.issent = False def loadscene(self, scenefile, targetimgfile): # Load scene data into CpuImage buffers pass def buildgraph(self, K, r, sigma, delta, lr): # Build rendering computational graph renderedimg = BuildBasicRenderGraph( self.varmap["vtxpos"], self.varmap["vtxuv"], self.varmap["faces"], self.varmap["modelmat"], self.varmap["viewmat"], self.varmap["prjmat"], self.varmap["envimg"], self.varmap["albedo"], self.varmap["metallic"], self.varmap["roughness"], self.varmap["normal"], self.varmap["background"], K, r, sigma, delta) # Compute L1 loss loss = F.Mean(F.Abs(self.varmap["target"].value - renderedimg.value)) # Set loss and optimizer self.dressiad.setlossvar(loss) # Define SGD optimizer def sgdoptimizer(xs, gxs): updatedxs = [] for x, gx in zip(xs, gxs): updatedxs.append(x - gx lr) return updatedxs self.dressiad.setoptimizer(sgdoptimizer) def setrequiresgrad(self, name): self.varmap[name].setrequiresgrad() def execstep(self): if not self.issent: for name, var in self.varmap.items(): if name in self.imgmap: var.setdirty(True) sendhostimagetodevice(var, self.imgmap[name]) self.issent = True self.dressiad.execstep() def savescene(self, outputfile): # Save optimized data as GLTF pass def sendhostimagetodevice(var, cpuimg): # Transfers image data from CPU to GPU pass def BuildBasicRenderGraph(args): # Assembles operators and F:: functions into a computational graph pass def main(): renderer = DressiBasicRenderer() renderer.loadscene("initialscene.gltf", "targetimg.png") K = 2 r = 0.01 sigma = r / 7.0 delta = r lr = 0.01 renderer.buildgraph(K, r, sigma, delta, lr) renderer.setrequiresgrad("vtxpos") renderer.setrequiresgrad("normal") for in range(1000): renderer.execstep() renderer.savescene("optimizedscene.gltf") Graph Staticity: The graph rebuild logic relies on mgraphstaticcnt reaching specific thresholds (FASTREBUILDCOUNT, FULLREBUILDCOUNT). Dirty Flags: Variables must be correctly marked as dirty when CPU data changes. Gradient Aggregation: Gradients for the same variable from multiple paths must be summed. Vulkan Command Buffer: The command buffer must be properly submitted and reset. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance is hardware-dependent due to the use of Vulkan. Strengths: Define-and-run approach simplifies implementation. Limitations: Requires manual graph construction. The DressiAD Optimization Loop is part of the Dressi renderer, a hardware-agnostic differentiable renderer with reactive shader packing and soft rasterization. It was introduced in the paper "Dressi: A Hardware‐Agnostic Differentiable Renderer with Reactive Shader Packing and Soft Rasterization". The system is designed to be similar to common AD libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow but is optimized for differentiable rendering. name: Training & Optimization Protocol
head: Splatfacto Training Protocol
body: This protocol defines the training loop, parameter initialization, and optimization hyperparameters for decomposed Gaussian splatting methods targeting distractor-free rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling distractor elements alongside static scene Gaussians, using specific learning rate schedules and regularization weights. Inputs: Training images and corresponding camera poses. Initial static point cloud from COLMAP. Hyperparameters for optimizer, scheduler, and regularization. Outputs: Optimized parameters for static Gaussians (means, opacities, scales, rotations, spherical harmonics). Optimized parameters for distractor Gaussians (means, opacities, scales, rotations, RGB colors). The method maintains two sets of Gaussian primitives: 1. Static Gaussians: Initialized from COLMAP point cloud. Parameters include mean \mu, opacity \alpha, scale s, rotation q (quaternion), and spherical harmonic coefficients c{lm}. 2. Distractor Gaussians: Initialized with 1000 points per training image. Parameters include mean \mu, opacity \alpha, scale s, rotation q, and RGB color \mathbf{c}. 1. Initialization: Initialize static Gaussians using the standard COLMAP point cloud method. Initialize 1000 distractor points per training image. Initialize appearance embeddings if using appearance modeling: per-image embedding ej \in \mathbb{R}^{32} and per-Gaussian embedding zi \in \mathbb{R}^{24} with Fourier frequencies. 2. Forward Pass: Render images using the current set of static and distractor Gaussians. Compute photometric and perceptual losses against ground truth. 3. Loss Computation: The total loss L for a batch of M novel views is L = \sum{m=1}^M \left( L{MSE}(I{render}^{(m)}, I{gt}^{(m)}) + \lambda L{LPIPS}(I{render}^{(m)}, I{gt}^{(m)}) \right), where \lambda = 0.05. Apply regularization terms for distractor Gaussians with weights \lambdas = 0, \lambdad = 0.01, and \lambda{bg} = 0.15. The threshold T\epsilon for regularization is set to 0.003. 4. Backward Pass and Optimization: Compute gradients with respect to all parameters. Update parameters using the Adam optimizer. Apply an Exponential decay scheduler with decay rates of 0.0001, 0.0002, and 0.00001. 5. Distractor Densification: Densify distractor Gaussians for the first 15,000 iterations. Stop densification after 15,000 iterations. 6. Training Duration: Train for 30,000 iterations on RobustNeRF, On-the-go, and Mip-NeRF-360 datasets. Train for 200,000 iterations on Photo Tourism datasets. Unverified code. g) 2 for r, g in zip(renderedimages, images)) / len(images) # Standard MSE losslpips = computelpips(renderedimages, images) # Standard LPIPS metric lossperceptual = lambdalpips losslpips # # Regularization losses: Formulas for distance and background regularization are not provided in the sources regdist = lambdadreg computedistanceregularization(distractorgaussians) regbg = lambdabgreg computebackgroundregularization(distractorgaussians) totalloss = lossmse + lossperceptual + regdist + regbg # optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() distractorgaussians.quaternions.lr = 0.01 # distractorgaussians.scales.lr = 0.05 # distractorgaussians.rgb.lr = 0.025 # # Means and opacities use Splatfacto defaults optimizer.step() scheduler.step() if iteration < maxdensificationiter: densifydistractorgaussians(distractorgaussians) # Standard densification procedure Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rates (Distractors): Quaternions=0.01, Scales=0.05, RGB=0.025. Means and opacities use Splatfacto defaults. Scheduler: Exponential decay with rates 0.0001, 0.0002, 0.00001. Regularization Weights: \lambdas=0, \lambdad=0.01, \lambda{bg}=0.15. Threshold: T\epsilon=0.003. Perceptual Loss Weight: \lambda=0.05. Distractor Densification: Must stop after 15,000 iterations to prevent overfitting or instability. Learning Rate Mismatch: Distractor points require specific learning rates different from static points; using defaults for all may lead to poor convergence. Regularization Threshold: The threshold T\epsilon=0.003 is critical for controlling the influence of regularization terms. Uses LPIPS loss with weight \lambda=0.05 to improve perceptual quality during optimization. A data augmentation technique for single-view reconstruction of roughly symmetric objects (e.g., shoes) by mirroring input images to simulate opposite viewpoints. This allows training on combined original and mirrored datasets to reconstruct full 3D mesh despite lacking back-side samples. Highly ill-posed problem; reconstruction quality for unseen parts remains lower compared to multi-view training. Evaluates method stability and degradation over extended sequence lengths by scaling training iterations and densification/pruning schedules proportionally. Tested on sequence lengths {300, 600, 900, 1200} frames using the flamesalmon scene from N3DV. CC-4DGS PSNR degrades from 29.62 dB (300f) to 29.12 dB (1200f, \Delta = -0.50 dB), while Swift4D degrades from 29.48 dB to 28.24 dB (\Delta = -1.25 dB). CC-4DGS retains up to a +0.88 dB advantage at 1200 frames. This single-scene stress test does not prove general long-duration scalability, but indicates that frequency-based time encoding with depth-3 TimeMLP avoids disproportionate long-sequence failure modes compared to 4D hash-grid baselines. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians and samples per ray. Training duration is 30k iterations for standard datasets and 200k for Photo Tourism. Memory Complexity: Higher than standard Gaussian Splatting due to the addition of distractor Gaussians and appearance embeddings. Strengths: Reduces distractor artifacts and improves background reconstruction. Limitations: Increased training time and memory usage due to distractor optimization and densification. Single-view reconstruction is ill-posed and less accurate than multi-view. When to Use: When distractor artifacts are prominent. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated from DeSplat: Decomposed Gaussian Splatting for Distractor-Free Rendering. The method extends standard Gaussian Splatting by explicitly modeling distractors. name: Multi-scale L2 Loss Optimization with Random Variable Perturbation
head: Multi-scale L2 Loss Optimization, Optimization, Ours, Pyramid L2 Loss, Resolution Alternating Loss
body: This method optimizes shader parameters to match a target image by minimizing a multi-scale L2 loss while using random variable perturbation to escape local minima. It is specifically designed for differentiable rendering pipelines where parameters (such as Dirac parameters) define geometry or appearance, and the rendering output is compared against a ground-truth image. Unlike methods that rely on a single resolution or fixed parameter ordering, this approach alternates between low-resolution and full-resolution loss objectives and perturbs non-ray-marching parameters to smooth the optimization landscape, particularly for discontinuous or binary targets. It differs from NeRF Training Loop by focusing on explicit shader parameter optimization rather than neural field weights, and from Optimization Configuration (Adam + Exponential Decay + Selective L2) by explicitly introducing stochastic perturbation to handle flat landscapes caused by sparse gradient signals. The method optimizes a set of shader parameters \theta to minimize the difference between a rendered image \hat{I} and a target image I{target}. The optimization is performed using a differentiable rendering operator that supports both forward and backward passes. Inputs: Target image I{target} (RGB, resized from source). Initial shader program with parameterized primitives (e.g., rings, knots). Initial parameter values \theta0 (randomly initialized). Outputs: Optimized shader program with optimized parameters \theta^. GLSL code with unused computations removed. Parameter Vector \theta: Contains all shader parameters. Dirac Parameters: Parameters not dependent on ray marching (e.g., position, radius, color, stroke width). These are subject to random perturbation. Ray-Marching Parameters: Parameters dependent on the ray path (e.g., Z-ordering that varies per pixel). These are not perturbed. Random Variable Scales \sigma: A vector of scales corresponding to each Dirac parameter. These are optimized alongside \theta. Resolution Pyramid: A list of resolutions R0, R1, \dots, Rk where R0 is the lowest resolution and Rk is the target rendering resolution. 1. Initialization: Initialize \theta with 100 random restarts. Initialize random variable scales \sigma to small positive values. 2. Optimization Loop (per restart): Run for 2000 iterations. Within each restart, alternate the loss objective 5 times. Loss Alternation: For each alternation step j \in \{0, \dots, 4\}: Define current resolution R = Rj. Compute the multi-scale L2 loss \mathcal{L}: \mathcal{L} = \sum{r=0}^{j} \text{L2}(\text{Downsample}(I{render}, Rr), \text{Downsample}(I{target}, Rr)) where \text{Downsample}(I, R) reduces the image to resolution R. The sum includes all resolutions from the lowest (R0) up to the current resolution Rj. Perform gradient descent step on \theta and \sigma using \mathcal{L}. Random Variable Perturbation: For every Dirac parameter \thetai (not dependent on ray marching), add a random variable \epsiloni: \thetai^{perturbed} = \thetai + \epsiloni, \quad \epsiloni \sim \mathcal{U}(-\sigmai, \sigmai) where \mathcal{U} is the uniform distribution and \sigmai is the optimized scale for parameter i. The scales \sigmai are updated via gradient descent to minimize the loss. Upon convergence, \sigmai typically approaches zero. 3. Post-Optimization (Dead Code Elimination): The compiler outputs the shader program with optimized parameters to a GLSL backend. During optimization, computations for extra primitives (added to avoid local minima) are wrapped in an EliminateIfUnused() annotation. Upon convergence, the compiler progressively removes computations within EliminateIfUnused() if they do not increase the optimization error. This effectively prunes primitives that are pushed outside the image or occluded by background color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizeshader(targetimage, initialparams, numrestarts=100, iterationsperrestart=2000, numalternations=5): bestparams = None bestloss = infinity for restart in range(numrestarts): # Initialize parameters and random variable scales theta = randominitialize(initialparams) sigma = randominitializescales(theta) # Define resolution pyramid (e.g., [H/8, H/4, H/2, H]) resolutions = getresolutionpyramid(targetimage.shape) for iteration in range(iterationsperrestart): # Alternate loss objectives for altstep in range(numalternations): # Current resolution index ridx = altstep currentres = resolutions[ridx] # Compute multi-scale L2 loss up to current resolution loss = 0.0 for r in range(ridx + 1): res = resolutions[r] # Downsample target and rendered image to resolution res targetds = downsample(targetimage, res) # Render with perturbed parameters perturbedtheta = applyrandomperturbation(theta, sigma) renderedds = downsample(render(perturbedtheta, res), res) loss += l2loss(renderedds, targetds) # Compute gradients and update parameters gradientstheta, gradientssigma = computegradients(loss, theta, sigma) theta = update(theta, gradientstheta) sigma = update(sigma, gradientssigma) # Evaluate final loss without perturbation finalloss = l2loss(render(theta), targetimage) if finalloss < bestloss: bestloss = finalloss bestparams = theta # Post-processing: Dead code elimination optimizedshader = compileshader(bestparams) optimizedshader = eliminateunusedprimitives(optimizedshader, targetimage) return optimizedshader Number of restarts: 100. Iterations per restart: 2000. Loss alternation repetitions: 5 times per restart. Random variable distribution: Uniform \mathcal{U}(-\sigmai, \sigmai). Local Minima: The optimization landscape can be flat, especially for binary or high-contrast targets (e.g., Celtic Knot) where gradients are sparse and noisy. The random variable perturbation alleviates this by generating a "fuzzy" rendering, increasing the number of pixels with differently branched neighbors and allowing more frequent sampling of discontinuities. Convergence of Scales: The scales of the random variables \sigmai should converge close to zero. If they do not, the perturbation may prevent precise convergence. Flat Landscape: In cases with poor alignment, the gradient contribution is noisy, leading to a flat landscape. The method's success relies on the random variables to escape this flatness. Ray-Marching Parameters: Random perturbation is not applied to parameters dependent on ray marching (e.g., parametric Z-ordering) to maintain geometric consistency. Time Complexity: The method is computationally intensive due to multiple restarts and iterations. However, it is significantly faster than baseline methods like FD and SPSA. Olympic Rings (10 rings): Median success time 1.4s, Expected time to success 5.0s. Celtic Knot: Median 2.3s, Expected 17.3s. SIGGRAPH Logo: Median 2.6s, Expected 6.1s. TF RayMarch: Median 0.7s, Expected 40.3s. TF RayCast: Median 4.3s, Expected 13.9s. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given, but the method uses standard differentiable rendering memory overhead. Scaling: The method scales with the complexity of the shader. For example, the 5-ring Olympic Rings variant has a median success time 0.5x that of the 10-ring variant, but converges less often (Expected time 1.6x higher) due to faster runtime but lower convergence rate. Strengths: Effectively escapes local minima in flat optimization landscapes. Fast convergence compared to gradient-free baselines (FD, SPSA). Produces clean GLSL code via dead code elimination. Limitations: Requires multiple restarts (100) to ensure convergence. Performance degrades on targets with sparse gradients (e.g., black and white images) without the random variable perturbation. The ablation without random variables (O/wo) fails to converge on challenging targets like Celtic Knot. The method was introduced in the paper "A δ". It is designed for differentiable rendering pipelines where users define parametric shapes (e.g., rings, knots) and optimize their parameters to match target images. The method addresses the challenge of optimizing discrete or discontinuous structures where traditional gradient-based methods struggle due to sparse gradients and local minima. It is particularly useful for artistic and illustrative workflows where manual animation is difficult due to the high dimensionality of parameters. The method allows for parametric Z-ordering, unlike DVG which requires a single Z value per shape. A δ, https://doi.org/10.1145/3528223.3530125, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Submap Optimization
head: Gaussian refinement loop
body: Submap Optimization is a training procedure for Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems that manages memory and accuracy by dividing the scene into local submaps and refining them iteratively. It solves the problem of unbounded memory growth and optimization instability in large-scale scenes by limiting the optimization scope to a local region around the camera. It differs from global optimization methods by focusing on local radiance field refinement and camera pose updates only when the camera approaches the boundary of the current local field. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of keyframes with ground truth color and depth images, a Gaussian model (containing positions \mathbf{xyz}, opacities, scaling, rotation, and spherical harmonics features), and optimization hyperparameters (total iterations, pruning threshold, loss weights). Outputs: An optimized Gaussian model and a dictionary of loss values per iteration. Data Structures: The Gaussian model maintains optimizable tensors for: xyz: 3D positions. fdc, frest: Spherical harmonics coefficients. opacity: Scalar opacity values. scaling: Scaling factors. rotation: Quaternion rotations. xyzgradientaccum: Accumulated gradient norms for densification. denom: Denominator for gradient normalization. maxradii2D: Maximum projected radius for culling. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set iteration counter iter = 0 and initialize an empty losses dictionary. 2. View Distribution: Calculate currentframeiterations as the product of currentviewoptiterations and totaliterations. Compute the probability distribution of views to optimize over using computeoptviewsdistribution, which depends on the number of keyframes, total iterations, and current frame iterations. 3. Optimization Loop: While iter \leq iterations: a. Gradient Reset: Zero gradients in the Gaussian model optimizer. b. View Selection: Randomly select a keyframe ID from the available keyframes based on the precomputed distribution probability. c. Data Retrieval: Retrieve the frame ID and keyframe data. Fetch ground truth color I{gt} and depth D{gt} from the keyframe. d. Rendering: Render the Gaussian model using the keyframe's render settings to obtain rendered color I{render} and depth D{render}. e. Masking: Create a validity mask M where M{ij} = 1 if D{gt, ij} > 0 AND D{render, ij} is not NaN; otherwise M{ij} = 0. Squeeze depth dimensions if necessary. f. Loss Calculation: Color Loss: L{color} = (1 - \lambda{dssim}) L1(I{render}, I{gt}) + \lambda{dssim} (1 - SSIM(I{render}, I{gt})) where \lambda{dssim} is a hyperparameter (e.g., self.opt.lambdadssim), L1 is the L1 norm, and SSIM is the Structural Similarity Index. Depth Loss: L{depth} = L1(D{render}, D{gt}) computed only on pixels where M=1. Regularization Loss: L{reg} = L{isotropic}(S) where S represents the Gaussian scaling parameters. Total Loss: L{total} = L{color} + L{depth} + L{reg}. g. Logging: Store L{color}, L{depth}, and L{total} as Python floats in the losses dictionary keyed by frame ID. h. Pruning: Enter a no-gradient context. If iter \geq \frac{iterations}{2} OR iter == iterations, prune Gaussians with opacity below self.pruningthre. i. Optimization Step: If iter < iterations, perform an optimizer step (e.g., Adam) and then zero gradients again. j. Increment: iter \leftarrow iter + 1. 4. Finalization: Calculate total optimization time and average time per iteration. Add these metrics to the losses dictionary and return it. Parameters: iterations: Total number of optimization steps. currentviewoptiterations: Multiplier for view distribution calculation. pruningthre: Opacity threshold for pruning Gaussians. lambdadssim: Weight for the SSIM component in the color loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NaN Depth: The mask explicitly handles NaN values in rendered depth to prevent gradient explosions. Zero Depth: Ground truth depth must be greater than 0 to be considered valid. Pruning Timing: Pruning is performed only at specific iterations (halfway and end) to avoid destabilizing the optimization process prematurely. A variant where the scene is represented by local radiance fields of resolution 64^3. When the camera reaches the boundary of the current local field, the system refines the current local radiance fields and camera pose for 600 iterations per frame. After refinement, the resolution of the local radiance fields is upsampled to 640^3. This approach is suitable for large-scale scenes where global optimization is infeasible. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of iterations and the number of Gaussians per frame. The view distribution calculation adds a small overhead per iteration. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active Gaussians. Pruning reduces memory usage over time. Performance: Depends heavily on the efficiency of the Gaussian rasterization and the chosen optimizer. Strengths: Prevents memory overflow in large scenes; focuses optimization on relevant local areas. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of pruning thresholds and iteration counts; may suffer from discontinuities at submap boundaries if not handled properly. When to Use: Large-scale SLAM applications with limited memory resources. When Not to Use: Small-scale scenes where global optimization is feasible and provides better consistency. Submap Optimization is primarily associated with Gaussian-SLAM, a system for real-time dense 3D reconstruction and pose estimation using Gaussian Splatting. It was developed to address the scalability issues of NeRF-based SLAM methods in large environments. The method builds on the differentiable rendering capabilities of Gaussian Splatting. name: Differentiable Optimisation via Back-Propagation
head: TomOpt optimisation
body: Differentiable Optimisation via Back-Propagation is a method for optimizing scene or system parameters by computing gradients of a task-specific loss function with respect to those parameters using automatic differentiation. It solves the problem of finding optimal configurations (e.g., detector geometry, material properties) where the forward process is differentiable. It is distinguished from standard differentiable rendering by its focus on end-to-end task performance optimization (e.g., fill-level prediction) rather than proxy metrics like image fidelity, leveraging standard deep learning optimizers to update parameters directly. Inputs: A differentiable forward model (inference and hit-recording steps) parameterized by \theta. A task-specific loss function L computed from the model output. An optimization algorithm (e.g., SGD, Adam). Outputs: Updated parameters \theta' that minimize L. Data Structures: Parameters \theta: Tensors managed by the deep learning framework (e.g., PyTorch). Loss L: Scalar value derived from the model output. Steps: 1. Forward Pass: Compute the model output and the loss L based on the current parameters \theta. 2. Backward Pass: Compute the gradients \frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} by back-propagating the derivative of the loss through the inference and hit-recording steps. 3. Update: Update \theta by stepping in the direction of steepest descent of the loss surface using a standard optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for epoch in range(numepochs): # 1. Forward pass optimizer.zerograd() # Clear existing gradients output = model(theta) # Inference and hit-recording steps loss = lossfn(output, target) # Compute task-specific loss # 2. Backward pass loss.backward() # Back-propagate derivative of loss through inference and hit-recording steps # 3. Update parameters optimizer.step() # Step in direction of steepest descent Parameters: Optimizer: Standard optimizers like SGD or Adam. Learning rate: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases: The loss function must be computed under conditions representative of actual operation (e.g., number of muons) to ensure valid gradients. A variant that uses a two-stage annealing strategy for detector geometry and decouples transverse (xy) and longitudinal (z) optimization phases. Memory: Requires storing the computational graph for back-propagation, leading to high memory usage proportional to the number of operations [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Time: Gradient computation is O(1) with respect to the number of parameters but depends on the complexity of the forward model [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Strengths: Ensures parameter changes directly impact final task performance; no balancing coefficients required between performance and cost in the loss function. Limitations: High memory consumption due to storing intermediate states [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Originated in the context of particle detector design for muon tomography, specifically in the TomOpt framework. It leverages automatic differentiation techniques from deep learning. name: TomOpt Two-Stage Differentiable Optimization
head: TomOpt
body: TomOpt is a differentiable optimization pipeline that updates detector panel positions and budget assignments by minimizing a task-specific loss function using automatic differentiation. It ensures that parameter changes directly impact final task performance (e.g., fill-level prediction) rather than optimizing proxy metrics like track resolution. It is distinguished from standard differentiable rendering by its specific two-stage annealing strategy for detector geometry and the explicit decoupling of transverse (xy) and longitudinal (z) optimization phases. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial detector configuration (panel xy positions, z positions, budget assignments), a differentiable forward model of muon tomography, and a task-specific loss function (e.g., mean squared error of fill-level prediction). Outputs: Optimized detector parameters (panel positions and budget weights). Data Structures: The trainable parameters are grouped into five families: 1. xy positions of detector panels above the passive volume. 2. xy positions of detector panels below the passive volume. 3. z positions of detector panels above the passive volume. 4. z positions of detector panels below the passive volume. 5. Budget assignment (weight) per panel. Sigmoid Detector Model: Detector efficiency and resolution are modeled using a sigmoid function. The smoothness parameter of this sigmoid decreases across optimization, transitioning from a smooth approximation to a sharp, physical distribution. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gradient Monitoring: Monitor gradients received by the trainable parameters over 5 epochs. 2. Nominal Learning Rate Calculation: Compute nominal learning rates corresponding to: Position updates: 1 cm per epoch. Budget weight updates: 0.1 (dimensionless). 3. Stage One (Global Optimization): Run for 10 epochs. Update all trainable parameters (xy positions, z positions, budget assignments). Apply 1-cycle learning rate annealing: nominal rates increase initially for large updates, then decrease to allow convergence. Anneal the sigmoid detector model from smooth to sharp. 4. Stage Two (Refinement): Fix xy positions at the center (directly above and below the passive volume) based on Stage One results and domain knowledge. Run for 10 epochs. Update only z positions and budget assignments. Use smaller update steps (derived from re-monitoring gradients for 5 epochs). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tomoptoptimize(initialdetector, lossfn, forwardmodel): """ initialdetector: dict containing 'xyabove', 'xybelow', 'zabove', 'zbelow', 'budgets' lossfn: differentiable function returning scalar loss forwardmodel: differentiable function returning prediction given detector config """ # Stage One # 1. Monitor gradients for 5 epochs to set nominal rates nominallrpos = 1.0e-2 # 1 cm per epoch nominallrbudget = 0.1 # dimensionless # 2. Initialize sigmoid smoothness parameter (high/smooth) sigmoidsmoothness = highvalue # 3. Run 10 epochs for epoch in range(10): # Anneal learning rate using 1-cycle schedule lrpos = nominallrpos onecycleschedule(epoch, totalepochs=10) lrbudget = nominallrbudget onecycleschedule(epoch, totalepochs=10) # Anneal sigmoid smoothness (decrease to make sharper) sigmoidsmoothness = annealsigmoid(epoch, totalepochs=10) # Compute loss and gradients prediction = forwardmodel(initialdetector, sigmoidsmoothness) loss = lossfn(prediction) gradients = computegradients(loss, initialdetector) # Update all parameters initialdetector['xyabove'] -= lrpos gradients['xyabove'] initialdetector['xybelow'] -= lrpos gradients['xybelow'] initialdetector['zabove'] -= lrpos gradients['zabove'] initialdetector['zbelow'] -= lrpos gradients['zbelow'] initialdetector['budgets'] -= lrbudget gradients['budgets'] # Stage Two # 1. Fix xy positions to center initialdetector['xyabove'] = centerxy initialdetector['xybelow'] = centerxy # 2. Re-monitor gradients for 5 epochs to compute new nominal rates for remaining params # (Assuming smaller steps as per source) nominallrposstage2 = nominallrpos reductionfactor # reductionfactor < 1 nominallrbudgetstage2 = nominallrbudget reductionfactor # 3. Run 10 epochs for epoch in range(10): # Smaller update steps lrpos = nominallrposstage2 onecycleschedule(epoch, totalepochs=10) lrbudget = nominallrbudgetstage2 onecycleschedule(epoch, totalepochs=10) # Compute loss and gradients (only for z and budgets) prediction = forwardmodel(initialdetector, sigmoidsmoothness) loss = lossfn(prediction) gradients = computegradients(loss, initialdetector) # Update only z positions and budgets initialdetector['zabove'] -= lrpos gradients['zabove'] initialdetector['zbelow'] -= lrpos gradients['zbelow'] initialdetector['budgets'] -= lrbudget gradients['budgets'] return initialdetector Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Stage One allows large updates to escape poor initial configurations. Physical Validity: The sigmoid annealing ensures the model approximates physical detectors only near the end of training, preventing premature convergence to non-physical solutions. Hardware Constraints: The method was demonstrated on a CPU (Intel i7, 2018 MacBook Pro) taking ~30 minutes; GPU acceleration is not specified but implied to be beneficial for differentiable pipelines. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in asymptotic terms. Empirical measurement: ~30 minutes for the full two-stage process on a 2018 Intel i7 CPU without GPU. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Stage One: Mean MSE of 0.0014 m², average absolute error on fill-level prediction of 2.8 cm. Stage Two: Mean MSE of 0.0011 m², average absolute error on fill-level prediction of 2.5 cm. Strengths: Directly optimizes for task-specific performance (fill-level prediction) rather than proxy metrics; can refine human-designed detectors. Limitations: Requires a differentiable forward model; computational cost depends on the complexity of the forward model and the number of epochs. When to use: When detector design parameters (positions, weights) can be parameterized and differentiated, and the goal is to maximize a specific task metric. When not to use: When the forward model is not differentiable or when computational resources are extremely limited relative to the cost of training. TomOpt was developed for muon tomography, specifically for estimating the fill-level of furnace ladles at metal refineries. It was introduced to allow detector designers to specify end goals numerically and optimize designs using automatic differentiation, ensuring changes have a genuine impact on final performance. The method was compared against human-designed baselines, including a paired configuration with 5 cm separation and 25 cm inter-pair spacing, and an even 10 cm spacing configuration. name: Domain-Specific Optimization Pipelines
body: Domain-Specific Optimization Pipelines are specialized training procedures that adapt the general differentiable volume rendering framework to specific physical or geometric constraints, rather than optimizing a generic radiance field. While the parent family relies on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and gradient propagation [44-radiance-field-optimization.md], these pipelines modify the optimization loop, scene representation, or loss formulation to address domain-specific challenges such as mesh manifold validity, camera occlusion ambiguities, or multi-wavelength physical interactions. They are distinguished from general radiance-field optimization by their explicit integration of external domain tools (e.g., mesh cleaners, specific physical simulators) or structured data partitioning. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the volume rendering equation and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD): Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing O(kn) intermediate states (where n is pixels and k is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 2. Adjoint Method: Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. 3. Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients: Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. An iterative optimization pipeline that initializes a 3D mesh, refines its geometry through subdivision and cleaning, and performs differentiable rendering optimization to align the mesh with projection data. It is distinguished from general radiance-field optimization by its explicit mesh-based representation and the use of external mesh-cleaning tools to maintain manifold validity during refinement. The Camera Group Optimization Pipeline is a domain-specific training strategy for differentiable volume rendering and radiance-field optimization that partitions the camera dataset into disjoint groups to enable parallel optimization and reduce occlusion-related ambiguities. By processing cameras in localized clusters rather than globally, the method minimizes conflicting gradient signals caused by self-occlusion and view-dependent artifacts, which is particularly beneficial for geometry reconstruction from sparse or unstructured views. It serves as a foundational loop structure within domain-specific pipelines, distinct from shape-from-projection methods that rely on analytical back-projection [13355-shape-from-projections-optimization-pipeline.md] or antagonistic methods that use adversarial losses [19675-antagonistic-dual-wavelength-optimization.md]. Antagonistic Dual-Wavelength Optimization is a domain-specific training procedure for volumetric additive manufacturing that synthesizes inhibition projector patterns against fixed activation projector patterns to achieve a target volumetric polymerization state. It differs from general radiance-field optimization by explicitly modeling the antagonistic interaction of two distinct wavelengths (activation and inhibition) to define an effective volume, rather than optimizing a single radiance field. Definition: A feedback algorithm used to produce optimized tomographic projections by replacing standard Radon/inverse Radon functions with custom tomographic projection and dose computation functions. Steps: Replace the Radon and inverse Radon functions with custom functions that compute the tomographic projections and dose computation. Add a histogram equalization step after the final projection calculation but before the final dose simulation to improve contrast relative to the projector black level. Clip projection values exceeding three standard deviations from the mean projection value, then rescale within the 8-bit greyscale range. Parameters: Termination condition: Optimization terminates when the absolute relative error between the target dose and the simulated dose is below 0.5 percent. The concept of domain-specific pipelines in volume rendering optimization emerged from the need to handle complex physical constraints that generic radiance field optimizers cannot address directly. The Object-Space Model Optimization (OSMO) feedback algorithm, originally described by Rackson et al. [10] and adapted in, represents an early integration of custom tomographic projection functions into the optimization loop for volumetric additive manufacturing. The adaptation involved replacing standard Radon transforms with custom dose computation functions and adding histogram equalization to handle projector black levels. More recently, the Camera Group Optimization Pipeline has been introduced to address occlusion ambiguities in sparse-view reconstruction by partitioning camera datasets into disjoint groups. These methods highlight a shift from purely mathematical optimization of neural fields to physically constrained optimization loops that incorporate domain-specific tools and constraints. name: Shape-from-Projections Optimization Pipeline
head: run/ours.py main loop
body: An iterative optimization pipeline that initializes a 3D mesh, refines its geometry through subdivision and cleaning, and performs differentiable rendering optimization to align the mesh with projection data. It is distinguished from general radiance-field optimization by its explicit mesh-based representation and the use of external mesh-cleaning tools to maintain manifold validity during refinement. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Projection dataset, physical dimensions, initial mesh, and hyperparameters (args.niter0, args.niter, args.nmu0, args.wlap, args.wflat, args.subdiv). Outputs: Optimized mesh (vertices, faces, labels) and attenuation values, saved to HDF5. Data Structures: Model: Encapsulates the differentiable renderer and mesh representation. mus: Array of initial attenuation values for the mesh materials. args: Configuration object containing optimization parameters. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the dataset and compute physical dimensions. Initialize the coarse mesh using saveinitmesh. 2. Coarse Refinement Loop: If args.niter0 > 0, execute the following sequence: a. Create a Model instance. b. Estimate and set initial attenuation values mu using args.nmu0. c. Run the optimization routine optimize.run. d. Extract the optimized vertices, faces, and material labels from the model. e. Update the mus values based on the refined geometry. f. Save the subdivided mesh. g. Clean the mesh using pymeshfix (with maxiters=10, innerloops=3) and the manifold tool to ensure manifold validity. Note that manifold requires the outresolution parameter from the first refinement pass. 3. Final Optimization: Run the final optimization phase with args.niter iterations using the cleaned mesh from the coarse stage. 4. Saving: Save the final results (mesh, labels, parameters) to an HDF5 file. Parameters: args.niter0: Threshold controlling whether the coarse refinement loop runs. args.niter: Number of iterations for the final optimization phase. args.nmu0: Initial attenuation values. args.wlap: Laplacian regularization weight. args.wflat: Flatness regularization weight. args.subdiv: Subdivision level for mesh refinement. Pitfalls: Mesh cleaning relies on external executables (pymeshfix, manifold). manifold requires the outresolution parameter from the first refinement pass. pymeshfix cleans with maxiters=10, innerloops=3. Refines the 6D pose (position and orientation) and scale of segmented 3D objects within a scene by minimizing the discrepancy between rendered and observed image data. It is distinguished from general radiance-field optimization by focusing specifically on rigid body transformations of pre-segmented objects rather than optimizing continuous volumetric fields. It is chosen when coarse pose initialization must be solved by optimizing object parameters in image space. Takes a coarse geometric prior, such as a mesh decimated from a MobileNeRF output using QEM. Initializes the DiffSoup optimization with this decimated mesh. Iteratively prunes transparent primitives during optimization to obtain a clean triangle soup. Training time with QEM initialization averages 8 minutes and 40 seconds. Using QEM initialization achieves comparable reconstruction fidelity with a drastically reduced triangle count and significantly less time than retraining MobileNeRF (which takes over 6 hours). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicit mesh representation allows for downstream processing. Mesh cleaning ensures topological validity. Limitations: Relies on external tools for mesh cleaning, which can be a bottleneck or source of failure. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: With QEM initialization, training takes an average of 8 minutes and 40 seconds, achieving comparable reconstruction fidelity with a drastically reduced triangle count and significantly less time than retraining MobileNeRF (which takes over 6 hours). The pipeline originates from the "ShapeFromProjections" project by Jakeoung. It is designed for reconstructing 3D shapes from 2D projections. The method integrates differentiable rendering with traditional mesh processing techniques to refine geometry iteratively. jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, https://github.com/jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DiffSoup: Direct Differentiable Rasterization of Triangle Soup for Extreme Radiance Field Simplification, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.27151, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Object Pose Optimization
head: Joint Pose Optimization for Objects, Object Pose Refinement via Differentiable Rendering, Refining Geometry
body: This method refines the 6D pose and scale of segmented 3D objects by minimizing the discrepancy between rendered and observed image data. It addresses coarse pose initialization by optimizing object parameters directly in image space using differentiable rendering. It operates as a sub-component of the Shape-from-Projections Optimization Pipeline. Inputs: Segmented 3D objects with initial coarse poses and geometry. Target images containing segmentation masks (M{it}) and depth maps (Dt). Object pose parameters \theta{obj} for each object, comprising scaling, horizontal translation, and rotation around the vertical axis. Outputs: Refined object poses \theta{obj} that minimize the loss function. Data Structures: Object Pose Parameters (\theta{obj}): Vector containing scale factor, 2D translation vector (horizontal plane), and 1D rotation angle (around vertical axis). Rendered Mask (M{ir}): Soft mask generated by the differentiable renderer. Rendered Depth (Dr): Depth map generated by the differentiable renderer, normalized to unit range. Target Mask (M{it}): Estimated segmentation mask for the object. Target Depth (Dt): Estimated depth for the object, normalized to unit range. Loss Function: The optimization minimizes a composite loss L{obj} defined as: L{obj} = \sumi L1(M{ir}(\theta{obj}) Dr(\theta{obj}), M{it} Dt) + \sumi L1(G(M{ir}(\theta{obj})), G(M{it})) Where: i iterates over the set of objects. denotes element-wise multiplication. L1 is the mean absolute error. G is a 2D Gaussian convolution pyramid applied to the mask. M{ir} and Dr are functions of the current pose parameters \theta{obj}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Poses: Initialize object poses based on segmented point clouds or coarse geometry predictions. 2. Define Constraints: For objects on the floor/ceiling: Constrain optimization to scaling, horizontal translation, and vertical-axis rotation to preserve alignment with the room floor/ceiling. For objects on walls: Constrain optimization to transformations and scaling along the wall plane. 3. Render: Use a differentiable renderer to generate the rendered mask M{ir} and rendered depth Dr for the current object poses \theta{obj}. The renderer must generate masks with anti-aliasing to ensure non-zero gradients for mask comparison losses. 4. Compute Loss: Calculate L{obj} using the formula above. The first term combines mask and depth errors (weighted by depth), and the second term compares blurred versions of the masks to capture structural similarity. 5. Optimize: Update \theta{obj} using gradient descent to minimize L{obj}. 6. Iterate: Repeat steps 3–5 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Pitfalls: Zero Gradients: If the differentiable renderer does not produce anti-aliased masks, the gradient of the mask loss with respect to pose parameters may be zero, preventing optimization. ShAPO extracts comprehensive 3D details (shape, 6D pose, scale, and appearance) of multiple objects from a single RGB-D observation. It uses an octree-based differentiable optimization and draws on pose, texture, and masks derived from an FPN backbone. This method is part of the PSDR-Room pipeline, which reconstructs rooms from single photos using differentiable rendering. It builds on the Shape-from-Projections Optimization Pipeline by adding a specific stage for refining object poses after coarse geometry prediction.
