name: Derivative-free Pose Estimation via Feature Matching
head: Feature-based differentiable rendering pose estimation, Gradient-free 6-DoF pose optimization
body: This method estimates the 6-DoF pose of a target from a single reference image by rendering multiple images at sampled pose perturbations, extracting feature correspondences, and computing a least-squares estimate for the pose using differential corrections to an initial guess. Unlike its sibling Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation, which explicitly constructs a numerical Jacobian of the image with respect to pose perturbations to drive gradient-based optimization, this method relies on differential corrections to an initial guess via feature matching. It bypasses the analytical description of the image formation model, which is complex due to lens and illumination dependencies, by seeking a local numerical solution in the feature space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A reference image I{ref} containing the target, a 3D model of the target (mesh or point cloud), an initial pose guess p{init}, and camera calibration parameters. Output: The optimized 6-DoF pose p^. Data Structures: Pose Vector p: Represented with a Gibbs vector q for orientation and translation components t. The relative pose difference is \Delta pi = [\Delta qi, \Delta ti]^T. Feature Vector x: For Nf key-point features, x is a vector of 2Nf coordinates: x = (x1, y1, \dots, x{Nf}, y{Nf}). The method requires at least three features, but uses four in the primary description. Pose Difference Matrix B: Size 6 \times Ns, where Ns is the number of sampled pose perturbations. Feature Difference Matrix E: Size 2Nf \times Ns, containing the differences between reference features and rendered features for each perturbation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with an informed initial pose guess p{init} for the target. This guess must be meaningful enough to find a minimum number of feature matches between the reference image and the image rendered at p{init}. 2. Pose Sampling: Generate Ns random pose perturbations \Delta pi for i = 1, \dots, Ns. Sample rotation axis uniformly on a spherical surface. Sample Gibbs vectors for orientation. Sample translation components. Construct the relative pose difference \Delta pi = [\Delta qi, \Delta ti]^T. Compute the sampled poses pi = p{init} \oplus \Delta pi. 3. Rendering: Render Ns images of the target using the current pose guess and the sampled pose perturbations pi. 4. Feature Extraction: Extract feature descriptors from the reference image I{ref} and the rendered images Ii using robust geometric feature detectors consistent with the image region type (e.g., SURF, Good Features to Track). Note: If rendered views are close to the reference camera, use the Kanade-Lucas-Tomasi (KLT) feature-based tracking algorithm for efficient real-time feature correspondence. 5. Feature Matching: Match features between the reference image and rendered images using the extracted descriptors. 6. Outlier Rejection: Reject outliers to block mismatched pairs and select the best few feature matches as sparse measurements. Let x{ref} be the feature vector from the reference image and xi be the feature vector from the i-th rendered image. 7. Compute Feature Differences: Compute the 2D feature differences \Delta xi between the reference and rendered images: \Delta xi = x{ref} - xi 8. Compute Pose Differences: For all pose perturbations, populate the difference between the reference pose p{ref} (the true pose corresponding to I{ref}, or the current estimate in an iterative loop) and the sampled pose pi. Compute rotation difference: \Delta Ri = R{ref}^T Ri. Compute translation difference: \Delta ti = t{ref} - ti. Combine into relative pose difference: \Delta pi = [\Delta qi, \Delta ti]^T. 9. Jacobian Estimation: Linearize the nonlinear transformation H from the image feature space to the pose space. The relationship is approximated as: \Delta x \approx Jf \Delta p where Jf is the Jacobian matrix of size 2Nf \times 6 (e.g., 8 \times 6 for four key-point features). Construct the matrix equation for Ns samples: E = Jf B where E is 2Nf \times Ns and B is 6 \times Ns. Solve for Jf using least squares: Jf = E B^T (B B^T)^{-1} Pitfall: Rank deficiency in B if perturbations do not cover all 6 degrees of freedom. Mitigation: Randomly and carefully perturb pose along all 6 axes. Note: Learning the inverse Jacobian Jf^{-1} is noted to result in better performance than inverting an estimate of the Jacobian. 10. Pose Optimization: Apply differential corrections to the initial pose guess to obtain the least-squares estimate of the 6-DoF pose. Compute the feature error \Delta x = x{ref} - x{init}, where x{init} is the feature vector from the image rendered at the initial pose guess. Compute the pose correction \Delta p{corr}: \Delta p{corr} = Jf^{-1} \Delta x Update the pose: p{new} = p{init} \oplus \Delta p{corr}. The process iteratively minimizes the feature errors by recomputing the Jacobian and applying corrections until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def derivativefreeposeestimation(Iref, model, pinit, K, Ns=10, maxiter=10): """ Estimate 6-DoF pose using derivative-free feature matching. Args: Iref: Reference image. model: 3D model of the target. pinit: Initial pose guess [qx, qy, qz, tx, ty, tz]. K: Camera intrinsic matrix. Ns: Number of pose perturbations. maxiter: Maximum number of optimization iterations. Returns: popt: Optimized pose. """ pcurr = pinit.copy() for iteration in range(maxiter): # 1. Render reference features at current pose xcurr = extractfeatures(renderimage(model, pcurr, K)) # 2. Check for minimum feature matches if len(xcurr) < 3: # Re-initialize with conservative pose samples pcurr = pinit continue # 3. Generate pose perturbations deltasp = generaterandomposeperturbations(Ns) # Shape: (Ns, 6) # 4. Render perturbed images and extract features xperturbed = [] for i in range(Ns): ppert = composepose(pcurr, deltasp[i]) Ipert = renderimage(model, ppert, K) xpert = extractfeatures(Ipert) xperturbed.append(xpert) # 5. Match features and compute differences xref = extractfeatures(Iref) # Compute feature differences E (2Nf, Ns) # And pose differences B (6, Ns) E = np.zeros((len(xref), Ns)) B = np.zeros((6, Ns)) for i in range(Ns): # Match xref with xperturbed[i] # Get corresponding coordinates xmatch = matchfeatures(xref, xperturbed[i]) if len(xmatch) < 3: continue # Skip if not enough matches # Feature difference E[:, i] = xref[:len(xmatch)2] - xmatch[:len(xmatch)2] # Flatten # Pose difference # Compute relative pose between pcurr and ppert[i] # Delta R = Rcurr^T Rpert # Delta t = tcurr - tpert # Convert to Gibbs vector if necessary deltap = computeposedifference(pcurr, ppert[i]) B[:, i] = deltap # 6. Estimate Jacobian Jf (2Nf, 6) # Solve E = Jf B for Jf # Jf = E B^T (B B^T)^-1 try: Jf = E @ B.T @ np.linalg.inv(B @ B.T) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: # Rank deficiency in B # Mitigation: Perturb along all 6 axes more carefully continue # 7. Compute pose correction # Delta x = xref - xcurr deltax = xref[:len(xmatch)2] - xcurr[:len(xmatch)2] # Delta pcorr = Jf^-1 deltax # Learning inverse Jacobian is better try: Jfinv = np.linalg.inv(Jf) deltapcorr = Jfinv @ deltax except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue # 8. Update pose pcurr = composepose(pcurr, deltapcorr) return pcurr def generaterandomposeperturbations(Ns): """Generate random pose perturbations covering all 6 DOFs.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def extractfeatures(I): """Extract features using robust geometric detectors or KLT.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def renderimage(model, pose, K): """Render image from model and pose.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def matchfeatures(xref, xpert): """Match features between two sets of keypoints.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def computeposedifference(p1, p2): """Compute relative pose difference in Gibbs vector representation.""" # Not given in the sources. pass def composepose(p1, deltap): """Compose pose p1 with deltap.""" # Not given in the sources. pass A method to numerically compute the Jacobian matrix Jf of the image formation model x = f(p) by generating random pose perturbations, rendering images, and solving a linear least-squares system. It bypasses analytical differentiation of the image formation process. Unlike methods that only track a target pose, this method estimates the pose by minimizing feature errors using the estimated Jacobian. Learning the inverse Jacobian is noted to result in better performance than inverting an estimate of the Jacobian. The rank deficiency in the pose difference matrix B can be avoided by randomly and carefully perturbing pose along all 6 axes. Time Complexity: The method is computationally expensive due to the rendering step, which is performed Ns times per iteration. Feature matching is also computationally inefficient, especially when images are far apart, but KLT tracking improves efficiency when views are close. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of features and samples. The matrices E and B scale with Ns and the number of features. Measured Performance: ISS Experiment: After 10 iterations, translation error was 0.12 m and rotation error was 0.116 degrees. Rheasilvia Experiment: Final translation error was 2.38 m and rotation error was 2.11 degrees. Strengths: Bypasses complex analytical image formation models; uses sparse 2D feature correspondences; efficient real-time correspondence with KLT when views are close. Limitations: Sensitive to establishing a minimum number of 2D feature correspondences; sensitive to illumination and shape mismatches which affect convergence accuracy; computationally expensive rendering step. When to Use: Proximity operations for space objects where a 3D model is available and real-time performance is not strictly constrained by the rendering cost. The method builds on KLT tracking [41] (Lucas, Kanade, 1981), robust feature detectors like SURF [39] (Bay et al., 2006) and Good Features to Track [40] (Shi et al., 1994), and least-squares differential corrections. It was proposed for proximity operations for space objects, specifically tested on the International Space Station (ISS) and the Rheasilvia basin on Vesta. The availability of a 3D model enables the rendering of images at different pose perturbations to facilitate feature-rich datasets for online learning. If a model is not readily available for an uncooperative target, a dense point cloud can be constructed from a LiDAR scanner or synthesized from multiview 3D reconstruction. name: Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation
head: DR-based pose estimation, Gradient-based pose optimization
body: Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation is a method for 6-DoF pose estimation that computes the derivative of the image rendering function with respect to rendering parameters (pose) using online learning of an approximate local gradient. It avoids analytical image formation models and 2D-to-3D correspondence solving by comparing rendered images only in the 2D feature space via sparse 2D feature correspondences. Unlike its sibling Derivative-free Pose Estimation via Feature Matching, which relies on differential corrections to an initial guess via feature matching, this method explicitly constructs a numerical Jacobian of the image with respect to pose perturbations to drive gradient-based optimization. Inputs: A 3D model of the target object. A reference image containing the target object. An initial guess for the 6-DoF pose (rotation R and translation t). Intrinsic camera matrix K. A feature extraction and matching algorithm (e.g., SIFT, ORB). Outputs: Optimized 6-DoF relative pose (rotation and translation). Data Structures: Pose Representation: The orientation matrix R is represented using Classical Rodrigues Parameters (CRPs) q = [q1, q2, q3]^T (Gibbs vector) to facilitate optimization via polynomial system solving, avoiding trigonometric functions. The rotation matrix R is derived from q using the Cayley transform. Camera Model: Perspective pinhole camera model. Intrinsic Matrix K: K = \begin{bmatrix} fx & \gamma & x0 \\ 0 & fy & y0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} where fx, fy are scaled focal lengths, \gamma is axis skew, and (x0, y0) is the principal point offset. Steps: 1. Initial Rendering: Utilize a rendering engine to synthesize an RGB image of the object at the initial pose guess. 2. Feature Extraction: Extract a set of reference features from the rendered image that match with features in the reference image. 3. Perturbation: Generate arbitrary views of the object by applying small perturbations to the current pose guess. 4. Gradient Computation: Numerically compute an approximate gradient (Jacobian) of the image with respect to the pose parameters using the registered poses from the perturbations and their respective image renderings. This involves tracking the reference features in the neighborhood of the pose guess. 5. Optimization: Utilize the computed gradient to optimize the view via gradient-based optimization to minimize misalignment error, reproducing the 2D view geometry and estimating the 6-DoF relative pose. Formulas: The perspective projection transformation from 3D reference points ai to view space 3D coordinates bi is given by: bi = R ai + t, \quad i = 1, 2,..., n where R^T R = I and \text{det}(R) = 1. The perspective projection extends to 2D homogeneous image projections li = [ui, vi, 1]^T via: s li = K [R | t] \begin{bmatrix} ai \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where s is the depth factor for the i-th point and K is the intrinsic camera matrix. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiablerenderingposeestimation(model, referenceimage, initialpose, K, featureextractor, featurematcher): currentpose = initialpose renderedimage = render(model, currentpose, K) reffeatures = featureextractor(referenceimage) renderedfeatures = featureextractor(renderedimage) matches = featurematcher(reffeatures, renderedfeatures) perturbationmagnitude = 1e-3 maxiterations = 100 convergencethreshold = 1e-6 for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Generate 6 orthogonal perturbations for 6-DoF perturbations = [[0.0] 6 for in range(6)] for i in range(6): perturbations[i][i] = perturbationmagnitude perturbedimages = [] for p in perturbations: perturbedpose = applyperturbation(currentpose, p) perturbedimages.append(render(model, perturbedpose, K)) gradient = computenumericalgradient(renderedimage, perturbedimages, currentpose, perturbations, featurematcher) learningrate = 0.01 currentpose = updatepose(currentpose, gradient, learningrate) renderedimage = render(model, currentpose, K) renderedfeatures = featureextractor(renderedimage) matches = featurematcher(reffeatures, renderedfeatures) if not converged(matches, convergencethreshold): break return currentpose def render(model, pose, K): # Standard perspective projection and rasterization pipeline return syntheticimage def applyperturbation(pose, delta): return [pose[i] + delta[i] for i in range(6)] def updatepose(pose, gradient, lr): return [pose[i] - lr gradient[i] for i in range(6)] def converged(matches, threshold): # Standard convergence check on feature alignment residuals return True def computenumericalgradient(refimg, perturbedimgs, currentpose, perturbations, matcher): # Source states gradient is computed numerically from registered poses and renderings # to minimize misalignment error in feature space. gradient = [0.0] 6 for i in range(6): # Standard finite difference approximation: (f(x+h) - f(x)) / h gradient[i] = 1.0 return gradient Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of CRPs avoids singularities associated with Euler angles but requires careful handling of the Cayley transform to ensure valid rotation matrices. Boundaries: The method relies on small perturbations; if the initial guess is too far from the true pose, the local gradient approximation may be invalid. A method to represent orientation using a 3D vector (Gibbs vector) to avoid trigonometric functions in optimization. A mathematical mapping used to convert CRPs into a rotation matrix. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids solving the conventional 2D-to-3D correspondence problem and computing reprojection errors directly; uses online learning of an approximate local gradient. Limitations: Relies on the availability of a 3D model and a rendering engine; requires a valid initial pose guess for the local gradient approximation to be effective. When to use: When a 3D model is available and an initial pose guess can be obtained, and when analytical derivatives are difficult to compute. When not to use: When no 3D model is available or when the initial pose guess is poor. The method was presented by Ramchander Rao Bhaskara, Roshan Thomas Eapen, and Manoranjan Majji in the paper "Differentiable Rendering for Pose Estimation in Proximity Operations" (arXiv:2212.12668v1, 24 Dec 2022). It is designed for proximity operations, such as satellite rendezvous, where 6-DoF relative pose estimation is critical. name: Lie Algebra (Tangent Plane) Pose Optimization
head: Manifold Optimization, Pose Optimization on Tangent Plane, SE(3) Pose Tracking, Tangent Plane Optimization, se(3) Optimization
body: This method estimates the current 6-DoF camera pose T \in SE(3) by optimizing in the tangent space of the special Euclidean group (Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3)) while keeping voxel embeddings and implicit network parameters fixed. It differs from direct optimization on the SE(3) manifold, which is prone to incorrect estimation results due to noisy photometric loss landscapes. By solving for the incremental update \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3) on the tangent plane, the method achieves smoother and quicker convergence. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: T0: Initial pose estimate (typically from the previous frame or a zero-motion model). K: Camera intrinsic parameters. R: A sampled set of pixel coordinates (sparse set of Nt pixels) from the input image. I(u): Observed image intensity at pixel u. \theta: Fixed parameters of the implicit network (SDF decoder) and voxel embeddings. F(\cdot; \theta): The rendering/compositing function that maps 3D coordinates to image space. Outputs: \hat{T}: The optimized camera pose transformation from camera coordinates to world coordinates. Data Structures: The optimization variable is \xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3), a 6-dimensional vector representing the twist (3 for rotation, 3 for translation). The pose T is an element of SE(3), typically represented as a 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the pose of the new frame T0 to be identical to the last tracked frame, assuming a zero motion model. Other motion models (e.g., constant motion) are applicable but zero motion is standard. 2. Sampling: Sample a sparse set of Nt pixels from the input images for tracking. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the photometric loss L between the rendered image and the observed image. The loss is defined as: L = \sum{u \in R} \| I(F(T K u; \theta)) - I(u) \|^2 where T is the current pose estimate, K are intrinsics, u are pixel coordinates, and I(\cdot) is the compositing function. 4. Optimization: Solve for the optimal tangent vector \hat{\xi} that minimizes the loss: \hat{\xi} = \arg \min{\xi \in \mathfrak{se}(3)} L(\xi | T0, I, \theta) This is performed via back-propagation. 5. Pose Update: Update the pose by exponentiating the optimal tangent vector and composing it with the initial pose: \hat{T} = \exp(\hat{\xi}) \hat{T}0 This represents applying the incremental transform \exp(\hat{\xi}) to the current estimate. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-5 until convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. T0: Initial pose transformation from camera coordinates to world coordinates. K: Camera intrinsic parameters. R: A sampled set of pixel coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interference from Mapping: A copy of the SDF decoder and voxel embeddings must be kept for the tracking process, updated only when a new frame is fused into the map, to prevent interference from ongoing mapping updates. Local Minima: Images are complex signals, making gradient descent prone to local minima. A truncated dynamic low-pass filter (TDLF) can be used to suppress high-frequency signals and escape local minima. Large Offsets: Localization performance degrades when translation error reaches large values (e.g., 16m) and rotation error is significant (e.g., 16°), due to small overlap between observed and rendered images. Error-state camera optimization refines camera poses and intrinsic parameters by optimizing residual corrections in the tangent space of the SE(3) manifold rather than updating the full transformation directly. It builds on Lie Algebra (Tangent Plane) Pose Optimization by specifically handling both extrinsic pose errors and intrinsic focal length perturbations within a differentiable rendering framework. This approach is distinct from direct manifold optimization by linearizing the update around a fixed initialization, ensuring smoother convergence for small residuals. Error-state Camera Optimization Time and Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the voxel embeddings and implicit network parameters, which are kept fixed during tracking. The method requires back-propagation through the volume rendering function, which is computationally intensive. Measured Performance: In experiments with initial translation errors up to 16m, the method achieved translation errors as low as 0.02m and rotation errors as low as 0.09° when combined with TDLF. Direct manifold optimization (iNeRF) failed or produced large errors (e.g., 22.78m translation error) under similar conditions. Scaling: The method scales with the number of sampled pixels Nt and the complexity of the implicit network. Strengths: Smoother and quicker convergence compared to direct optimization on SE(3). Robust to local minima when combined with TDLF. Limitations: Performance degrades with large initial pose errors due to limited overlap. Requires a copy of the network for tracking to avoid interference. The method builds on the principles of Lie group optimization, where updates are performed in the tangent space to maintain the manifold structure. The specific formulation using the tangent plane for SE(3) optimization was highlighted in as superior to direct manifold optimization for avoiding noisy photometric loss landscapes. The approach is used in systems like Vox-Fusion for dense tracking and mapping and LATITUDE for robotic global localization. name: Error-state Camera Optimization
head: Camera Parameterization, SE(3) Error-state Optimization, Tangent Plane Camera Optimization, Tangent space camera update
body: Error-state camera optimization refines camera poses and intrinsic parameters by optimizing residual corrections in the tangent space of the SE(3) manifold rather than updating the full transformation directly. It builds on Lie Algebra (Tangent Plane) Pose Optimization by specifically handling both extrinsic pose errors and intrinsic focal length perturbations within a differentiable rendering framework. This approach is distinct from direct manifold optimization by linearizing the update around a fixed initialization, ensuring smoother convergence for small residuals. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Initial camera poses \mathbf{T}c^{w,(0)} (fixed), initial focal lengths \mathbf{f}^{(0)}, principal point (cx, cy) (fixed), pixel coordinates (u, v), and rendered/observed images \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{C}^. Outputs: Optimized error states \boldsymbol{\xi} (pose) and \boldsymbol{\phi}f (focal lengths). Data Structures: Pose Error State: \boldsymbol{\xi} = [\boldsymbol{\xi}r, \boldsymbol{\xi}t] \in \mathbb{R}^6, where \boldsymbol{\xi}r \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the rotation perturbation and \boldsymbol{\xi}t \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the translation perturbation. Focal Error State: \boldsymbol{\phi}f \in \mathbb{R}^2, representing the log-space correction for focal lengths. Intrinsic Matrix: \mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} fx & 0 & cx \\ 0 & fy & cy \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set fixed odometry initialization \mathbf{T}c^{w,(0)} and initial focal lengths \mathbf{f}^{(0)}. Fix principal point (cx, cy). 2. Compute Ray Directions: For a pixel (u, v), compute the camera-space ray direction: \mathbf{r}^{\text{cam}} \propto \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{K} is updated using the current log-space focal estimate: \mathbf{f} = \exp(\log \mathbf{f}^{(0)} + \boldsymbol{\phi}f). 3. Differentiable Rendering: Render the image \mathbf{C} using the current pose \mathbf{T}c^w and intrinsics \mathbf{K}. The pose is computed as: \mathbf{T}c^w = \exp(\boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge) \mathbf{T}c^{w,(0)} where \exp(\cdot) is the exponential map from se(3) to SE(3) and (\cdot)^\wedge is the hat operator mapping \mathbb{R}^6 to se(3). 4. Compute Loss: Calculate the photometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{cam}} between rendered image \mathbf{C} and observed image \mathbf{C}^: \mathcal{L}{\text{cam}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{rgb}}(\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{C}^) + \lambda \dots (Note: The specific regularization term is truncated in the source). 5. Backpropagation: Backpropagate the loss through the differentiable renderer to compute gradients with respect to \boldsymbol{\xi} and \boldsymbol{\phi}f. The trilinear density and vertex-interpolated DC appearance provide dense gradients with respect to camera parameters. 6. Update: Update the error states \boldsymbol{\xi} and \boldsymbol{\phi}f using an optimizer (e.g., Levenberg-Marquardt or Adam). The final pose and intrinsics are reconstructed from the error states and fixed initialization. Parameters: \lambda: Weight for regularization terms (value not specified in sources). \mathbf{T}c^{w,(0)}: Fixed odometry initialization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: Focal lengths are optimized in log-space (\log \mathbf{f}) to ensure positivity and stability. Fixed Initialization: The method assumes the initial poses \mathbf{T}c^{w,(0)} are metrically plausible. Large initial errors may lead to poor convergence as the error-state approximation is local. Principal Point: The principal point (cx, cy) is fixed at its initialized value and not optimized. Complexity: Depends on the differentiable renderer and the number of pixels/voxels. The error-state formulation reduces the optimization problem to a local linear update, improving convergence speed compared to global SE(3) optimization. Strengths: Handles residual odometry errors effectively; provides dense gradients for camera parameters via differentiable rendering; numerically stable focal length optimization. Limitations: Relies on good initialization; principal point cannot be optimized; assumes a shared pinhole model per intrinsic group. When to Use: When refining poses and focal lengths in a differentiable volume rendering pipeline (e.g., SpaRV) where initial poses are known but have small errors. Error-state camera optimization is used in systems like SpaRV (Sparse Radiance Voxels) for scalable geometrically consistent LiDAR-visual mapping and rendering. It alternates camera optimization with map training to sharpen textures. The method leverages the tangent space of SE(3) to handle pose corrections, a technique common in visual odometry and SLAM. name: Shonan Averaging for Pose Synchronization
head: Global pose configuration, Pose Synchronization (Global Alignment), Pose Synchronization via Shonan Averaging, Shonan averaging, global pose estimation, pose averaging
body: Shonan Averaging for Pose Synchronization is a method for finding a global alignment of camera poses given a set of noisy relative pose measurements from local mini-scenes. It solves the non-convex optimization problem of registering local coordinate frames into a common global reference frame by iteratively relaxing the problem into higher-dimensional special-orthogonal spaces. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly handling the non-convexity of the rotation component via Shonan relaxation, whereas Lie Algebra (Tangent Plane) Pose Optimization relies on local linearization and Derivative-free Pose Estimation via Feature Matching avoids gradient-based optimization entirely. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N local mini-scenes. For each mini-scene, LU-NeRF provides local camera poses and geometry. Relative pose observations P{ij} (rotation R{ij} and translation t{ij}) between overlapping mini-scenes are derived from these local estimates. Confidence metrics (PSNR) for these relative poses are also provided. Output: A set of global poses P = \{P1, \dots, PN\} where Pi \in SE(3), representing the cameras in a common global reference frame. Data Structures: Relative Pose Graph: Nodes represent mini-scenes. Edges represent relative pose measurements between overlapping mini-scenes. Scale Reference: A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) constructed over mini-scene centers to propagate scale consistency. Steps: 1. Scale Consistency Resolution: The scale of each mini-scene is unique to its local reference frame. To resolve scale ambiguity: Construct an MST connecting the centers of all mini-scenes. Fix the scale of one reference mini-scene. Propagate the scale to other mini-scenes through the MST edges, ensuring that overlapping edges share a consistent scale. 2. Heuristic Selection for Relative Poses: Multiple relative pose measurements may exist for a pair of cameras (Ci, Cj) because they may appear in multiple overlapping mini-scenes. To select a single measure: For cameras Ci and Cj with i < j, compare the PSNR of the rendering of Ci in the mini-scene centered at Ci versus the rendering of Ci in the mini-scene centered at Cj. If PSNR(Ii | Ci) > PSNR(Ii | Cj), select the relative pose estimation from the mini-scene centered at Ci. Apply this same heuristic to select the relative translation measure. 3. Shonan Rotation Averaging: Solve for the global rotations Ri \in SO(3) by applying Shonan averaging. This method solves a convex relaxation of the rotation synchronization problem by iteratively converting the problem to higher-dimensional special-orthogonal spaces SO(n) until convergence. The input to this step is the set of selected relative rotations and their associated confidence weights. 4. Translation Optimization: With the global rotations Ri fixed from Step 3, solve for the global translations ti. The problem is formulated as a linear system based on the relative translation observations t{ij}: tj - ti = Ri t{ij} where t{ij} is the relative translation between camera i and j from LU-NeRF, and Ri is the global rotation of camera i. This linear system is solved using least-squares optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shonanaveragingposesynchronization(miniscenes, relativeposes, confidences): """ miniscenes: List of mini-scene objects, each containing local poses and PSNR metrics. relativeposes: Dict mapping (i, j) to list of relative pose objects (Rij, tij). confidences: Dict mapping (i, j) to list of confidence scores (PSNR). """ # Step 1: Resolve Scale Ambiguity # Construct MST over mini-scene centers mstedges = constructmst(miniscenes) # Fix reference scale and propagate referencescene = miniscenes[0] referencescale = referencescene.scale propagatescalethroughmst(mstedges, referencescale) # Step 2: Select Best Relative Poses selectedrotations = {} selectedtranslations = {} for (i, j), poselist in relativeposes.items(): if i > j: continue # Handle each pair once bestpose = None bestpsnr = -infinity for pose in poselist: # Heuristic: Compare PSNR of camera i in its own mini-scene vs j's # Note: pose comes from a specific mini-scene context psnriini = getpsnr(miniscenes[i], miniscenes[i]) psnriinj = getpsnr(miniscenes[i], miniscenes[j]) if psnriini > psnriinj: currentconfidence = psnriini else: currentconfidence = psnriinj if currentconfidence > bestpsnr: bestpsnr = currentconfidence bestpose = pose selectedrotations[(i, j)] = bestpose.R selectedtranslations[(i, j)] = bestpose.t # Step 3: Shonan Rotation Averaging # Input: selectedrotations and their confidences # Output: Global rotations Ri for all i globalrotations = shonanrotationaveraging(selectedrotations, confidences) # Step 4: Translation Optimization # Solve linear system: tj - ti = Ri tij # Construct matrix A and vector b for least squares A = [] b = [] for (i, j), tij in selectedtranslations.items(): Ri = globalrotations[i] # Equation: tj - ti = Ri tij # Reshape to linear constraints for ti and tj # Let t be the flattened vector of all translations # Add rows to A and b corresponding to this constraint # Row for ti: -I # Row for tj: I # RHS: Ri tij A.append([-eye(3), eye(3)]) # Simplified representation b.append(Ri @ tij) # Solve least squares: min ||Ax - b||^2 globaltranslations = solveleastsquares(A, b) # Construct final global poses globalposes = [] for i in range(len(miniscenes)): Pi = SE3(globalrotations[i], globaltranslations[i]) globalposes.append(Pi) return globalposes Parameters: Shonan Relaxation Dimension: The method iteratively increases the dimension n of the SO(n) space. The specific stopping criterion or maximum dimension is not given in the sources, but it continues until convergence. BARF Refinement: After synchronization, a final global optimization is performed using BARF [30] for 200k iterations with a coarse-to-fine positional encoding strategy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence Failure: Shonan averaging may fail to converge to a reasonable global pose configuration if depth regularization is not used during the local LU-NeRF optimization, even if the maximum relative rotation error is small. Scale Ambiguity: Without the MST-based scale propagation, the global solution remains ambiguous in scale. A robust step that registers local mini-scene poses into a common global reference frame using noisy relative pose measurements from overlapping mini-scenes. It computes a globally optimal positioning of all cameras from these noisy relative pose measurements. It is chosen when local estimates (e.g., from LU-NeRF) are inconsistent due to unique local reference frames and estimation errors. A key pitfall is that relative poses between images in overlapping mini-scenes will not perfectly agree due to these estimation errors and unique local scales. Time Complexity: The pose synchronization step runs on CPU and has a negligible running time compared to the neural network training stages (e.g., 3.18 seconds vs. hours for LU-NeRF-1/2 and refinement). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On an NVIDIA Tesla P100, the synchronization step takes approximately 3.18 seconds on average. Strengths: It handles the general SE(3) pose setting without restrictive assumptions on pose priors, outperforming prior attempts at unposed NeRF. It is complementary to feature-based SfM pipelines, comparing favorably to COLMAP on low-texture and low-resolution images. Limitations: It relies on the quality of local relative pose estimates; if depth regularization is omitted in the local stage, global convergence may fail. When to use: When local pose estimates are available but inconsistent across overlapping regions, and a global consistent frame is required for further refinement (e.g., by BARF). When not to use: When high-quality depth regularization is not available for local estimates, as convergence is not guaranteed. Shonan Averaging for Pose Synchronization is used in the LU-NeRF pipeline to bridge local mini-scene optimizations into a global scene representation. The method utilizes the off-the-shelf Shonan averaging technique [20] to solve the non-convex rotation synchronization problem. The specific application to NeRF pose synchronization was introduced in the LU-NeRF paper. name: Feature-metric Bundle Adjustment Pose Estimation
head: Feature-metric BA
body: Feature-metric Bundle Adjustment (FBA) Pose Estimation is a pose estimation method that optimizes relative pose \{\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}\} by minimizing feature residuals between consecutive frames, using learned high-level features instead of raw RGB pixels to improve robustness against illumination and viewpoint changes. It sets itself apart from standard photometric BA by operating in a semantic feature space extracted via a Unet-like encoder-decoder network, allowing it to handle large illumination variations and poor initial pose estimates more effectively. It builds on Levenberg-Marquardt Pose Optimization by defining the error metric in terms of feature map distances rather than pixel intensity differences. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two consecutive image frames \mathbf{I}a, \mathbf{I}b; a set of 3D points \mathbf{P}i observed in both frames; an initial pose estimate \{\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}\}; a robust cost function \rho(\cdot); a damping factor \lambda. Outputs: Optimized relative pose \{\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}\}. Data Structures: Feature Maps: For each level l \in \{L, \dots, 1\}, a multi-channel feature map \mathbf{F}^l \in \mathbb{R}^{Wl \times Hl \times Dl} is extracted. L is the number of feature levels. Resolution decreases as l increases (coarse to fine). Lookup Table: Feature maps support sub-pixel interpolation (bilinear) for arbitrary coordinate queries. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Encode consecutive frames \mathbf{I}a and \mathbf{I}b into multi-channel feature maps \mathbf{F}a^l and \mathbf{F}b^l at each level l using a Unet-like encoder-decoder network. The network also estimates per-pixel confidence to select robust features. 2. Residual Calculation: For each 3D point \mathbf{P}i observed in both frames, compute the projected pixel coordinate in frame b using the current pose estimate: \mathbf{p}i^a = \Pi(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P}i + \mathbf{t})b, where \Pi is the projection operator. 3. Feature Lookup: Sample the feature values at the projected location in frame b and the corresponding location in frame a using sub-pixel interpolation: \mathbf{F}b[\mathbf{p}i^a] and \mathbf{F}a[\mathbf{p}a]. 4. Error Computation: Calculate the feature residual \mathbf{r}a^i and the total weighted error E(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}). 5. Optimization: Use the Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) algorithm to iteratively minimize the error from the initial estimate. 6. Pose Update: Parametrize the pose update \boldsymbol{\delta} on the SE(3) manifold using its Lie algebra. Update the final pose by left-multiplication on the manifold SE(3). Formulas: The feature residual for point i at level l is defined as: \mathbf{r}a = \mathbf{F}b [\Pi(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P}i + \mathbf{t})b] - \mathbf{F}a [\mathbf{p}a] where \mathbf{p}i^a = \Pi(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P}i + \mathbf{t})b is the projection of point \mathbf{P}i from frame b given the current pose estimate \{\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}\}, and [\cdot] denotes lookup with sub-pixel interpolation. The total error over N observations is: E(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}) = \sum{i,a} wa^i \rho \left( \|\mathbf{r}a^i\|2^2 \right) where \rho(\cdot) is a robust cost function with derivative \rho', and wa^i is a per-residual weight. The LM update step is: \boldsymbol{\delta} = -(\mathbf{H} + \lambda \text{diag}(\mathbf{H}))^{-1} \mathbf{J}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{r} where \lambda is the damping factor, \mathbf{H} is the Hessian matrix, \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian, \mathbf{W} is the weight matrix, and \mathbf{r} is the residual vector. Parameters: \lambda: Damping factor for LM. Typical values are not specified in the sources. \rho(\cdot): Robust cost function. Specific form (e.g., Huber, Cauchy) is not explicitly named for the BA loss, though Huber is used for the training loss. \gamma: Huber cost function parameter used in the FBA training loss to weight supervision adaptively. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Poor Initial Pose: The method is designed to handle poor initial estimates due to the robustness of high-level features. Interpolation: Sub-pixel interpolation is required for accurate feature lookup. Confidence: The network estimates pixel confidence to select robust features, implying that low-confidence pixels should be down-weighted or excluded. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def featuremetricbaposeestimation(Ia, Ib, Ppoints, Rinit, tinit, levels, robustcost, dampingfactor): """ Optimizes relative pose {R, t} using feature-metric bundle adjustment. Args: Ia, Ib: Input image frames. Ppoints: Array of 3D points Pi. Rinit, tinit: Initial rotation and translation. levels: List of feature levels l from L down to 1. robustcost: Function rho(r^2) and its derivative rhoprime. dampingfactor: Lambda for LM. Returns: Ropt, topt: Optimized pose. """ # 1. Feature Extraction # Extract feature maps for all levels using Unet-like network # Fa[l], Fb[l] are feature maps of shape (Wl, Hl, Dl) Fa = extractfeatures(Ia, levels) Fb = extractfeatures(Ib, levels) # Initialize pose R = Rinit t = tinit # 2. Levenberg-Marquardt Optimization Loop converged = False while not converged: residuals = [] jacobians = [] weights = [] for l in levels: Fal = Fa[l] Fbl = Fb[l] for i, Pi in enumerate(Ppoints): # Project point Pi from frame b to frame a's coordinate system? # Note: Formula says pi^a = Pi(R Pi + t)b. # This implies Pi is in frame b's coordinate system? # Or R,t transform from a to b? # Standard BA: Pi is in world/camera frame. # Let's follow the formula strictly: # pi^a is the projection of Pi in frame b given pose {R,t}. # This suggests Pi is defined in frame a's space, and we project it to b? # Or Pi is in world, and we project to b using pose of b relative to world? # The text says "projection of frame b given its current pose estimate". # Let's assume Pi is a 3D point. # pi^a = Pi(R Pi + t) -> This looks like transforming Pi by R,t then projecting. # If R,t is pose of b relative to a, then Pi (in a) -> RPi+t (in b) -> project. # Project Pi to frame b Pb = R @ Pi + t pia = project(Pb) # pi^a # Lookup features with sub-pixel interpolation # Fb[pi^a] gets feature at projected location in image b # Fa[pa] gets feature at corresponding location in image a? # The formula uses Fa[pa]. pa is likely the projection of Pi in frame a directly. pa = project(Pi) # Assuming Pi is in frame a's space for direct projection? # Or pa is the same pixel location in image a? # "Fa[pa]" where pa is not defined in the snippet but implied to be the location in a. # Usually, for consecutive frames, we match feature at p in a to feature at p' in b. # Here, pi^a is the location in b. The corresponding location in a is pa. # If Pi is the 3D point, pa = Pi(Pi). featb = bilinearinterpolate(Fbl, pia) feata = bilinearinterpolate(Fal, pa) # Residual r = featb - feata residuals.append(r) # Jacobian calculation (J) # J = d(r)/d(delta) where delta is Lie algebra of SE(3) # This requires differentiating the feature lookup and projection Ji = computejacobianfeaturemetric(Fal, Fbl, Pi, R, t, pa, pia) jacobians.append(Ji) # Weight w = computeweight(pia, pa) # From confidence map weights.append(w) # Stack residuals, jacobians, weights Rvec = stack(residuals) Jmat = stack(jacobians) Wmat = diag(stack(weights)) # Hessian approximation H = J^T W J H = Jmat.T @ Wmat @ Jmat # LM Update # delta = -(H + lambda diag(H))^-1 J^T W r delta = solvelinearsystem(H + dampingfactor diag(H), Jmat.T @ Wmat @ Rvec) # Update Pose on SE(3) manifold R, t = updatese3pose(R, t, delta) # Check convergence if norm(delta) < tolerance: converged = True return R, t def extractfeatures(I, levels): # Unet-like encoder-decoder # Returns dict of feature maps for each level pass def project(P3d): # Standard pinhole projection pass def bilinearinterpolate(F, uv): # Sub-pixel interpolation pass def computejacobianfeaturemetric(Fa, Fb, P, R, t, pa, pb): # Derivative of feature residual w.r.t SE(3) parameters # Requires chain rule through projection and feature interpolation pass def computeweight(pa, pb): # Use confidence map from network pass def updatese3pose(R, t, delta): # Left-multiplication on SE(3) manifold # delta is 6D vector (3 rot, 3 trans) in Lie algebra expmap = se3exp(delta) Rnew = expmap[:3,:3] @ R tnew = expmap[:3,3] + expmap[:3,:3] @ t return Rnew, tnew Uses feature matching without gradient-based optimization. Choose when Jacobian computation is too expensive or unstable. Link Parametrizes pose updates in the tangent space of SE(3). This is the manifold handling used in FBA. Link Solves global pose synchronization from pairwise relative poses. Choose for global consistency across many frames. Link Time Complexity: Depends on the number of 3D points N and feature levels L. Each LM iteration involves Jacobian computation and matrix inversion (O(N \cdot D^2) or similar, where D is state dimension). Memory Complexity: Storage for feature maps at all levels L and Jacobian/Hessian matrices. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Coarse-to-fine strategy (levels L to 1) improves robustness and accuracy. Strengths: Robust to large illumination and viewpoint changes; handles poor initial pose estimates; accurate in indoor and outdoor environments. Limitations: Requires training a Unet-like network for feature extraction; relies on learned features which may not generalize to unseen domains without retraining. When to use: When photometric consistency is unreliable due to lighting/viewpoint changes. When not: When computational resources for deep learning inference are unavailable. Originated in the paper "Incremental Joint Learning of Depth, Pose, and Implicit Scene Representation on Monocular Camera in Large-Scale Scenes" (2025). It is inspired by prior work [51] (not cited in the provided sources) and integrates feature extraction with bundle adjustment for monocular large-scale scene reconstruction. name: Token-level Bundle Adjustment
head: TokenBA
body: Token-level Bundle Adjustment (TokenBA) is a per-scene refinement procedure that fits a frozen ZipSplat decoder to input views by jointly optimizing camera poses and scene tokens, recovering fine detail and correcting initial pose errors in a few seconds. It exploits the persistent 2D–3D correspondences established by the cone loss to refine cameras via robust Perspective-n-Point (PnP) and update scene tokens through the frozen decoder using photometric error. Unlike methods that optimize raw Gaussians or require pose supervision, TokenBA achieves faster convergence and higher quality by leveraging the built-in correspondence of scene tokens. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N unposed, uncalibrated input images I = \{In\}{n=1}^N, a pre-trained ZipSplat encoder producing scene tokens Z, and an initial estimate of camera poses. The decoder MLP is frozen. Outputs: Refined camera poses and refined scene tokens Z. Data Structures: Scene Tokens (Z): Each token represents a surface region and contains a set of 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian is parameterized by center \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, scales s \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation quaternion q \in \mathbb{R}^4, opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], and color coefficients c \in \mathbb{R}^C. Correspondences: Derived from cluster assignments. Every Gaussian of a scene token is paired with the patch center of each member patch. Parameters: Learning Rates: Tokens use Adam with learning rate 10^{-3} during alternation and 2 \times 10^{-3} in the joint tail. Joint Tail Increment: The joint tail refines tokens and poses using an se(3) increment with learning rate 3 \times 10^{-4}. Compression Ratio (r): Controls Gaussian budget. r=1.0 keeps full capacity and skips clustering, while r=0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.05 progressively reduce the budget. Resolution: Feed-forward encoder runs at 252 \times 252. TokenBA rendering loss is resolution-agnostic and can be evaluated at higher resolutions (e.g., 448 \times 448 or 540 \times 540) to recover fine features. Precision: Decoder MLP body runs in half precision (bfloat16) while its readout stays in full precision. Algorithm Steps: TokenBA executes alternating rounds of optimization, each comprising a PnP snap, photometric polish, and token update, followed by a joint tail refinement. 1. PnP Snap (Camera Update): Construct 2D–3D correspondences by pairing every Gaussian of a scene token with the patch center of each member patch based on cluster assignments. Sample 2048 correspondences. Solve each pose using robust PnP with graduated non-convexity. Anneal robust scale from 64 to 12 to 4 pixels over 4 iterations per level. Generate seven rotation hypotheses per view: the current rotation and \pm 40^\circ about each camera axis. Solve hypotheses in one batched call and select the hypothesis with the most inliers within 2 patches. 2. Photometric Polish: Remove patch-center quantization error using a direct Levenberg–Marquardt solver on the photometric residual. Full Configuration (Pre-Refinement): Scan nine log-spaced global scale factors from 0.5 to 2.0. Run a four-level pyramid (1/8, 1/4, 1/2, full resolution) with 12, 10, 8, and 6 steps per level. Apply Gaussian blur at the two coarse levels. Use accept-reject steps with a trust-region clamp on the pose twist. Keep the best full-resolution pose across levels. Inside TokenBA: Only the two fine levels (1/2, full) run, without verification or scale scan. Aligner Step: Each step renders at the current pose and takes a Gauss–Newton update on the brightness-constancy linearization with the analytic image-warp Jacobian. Uses one render per step and no autograd. Execution: Run two steps at half resolution and one at full resolution. 3. Token Update: Refine scene tokens by minimizing the \ell1 rendering loss on the input views. Gradients propagate through the renderer and frozen decoder to the tokens. Optimizing tokens instead of raw Gaussians retains the decoder as a learned scene prior. 4. Joint Tail Refinement: Jointly refine tokens and poses for at most 96 steps, reusing the same Adam state. Exits early once a block of 8 steps improves the loss by less than 2%. 5. Termination: Alternating rounds stop once the PnP snap moves every pose by less than 0.3^\circ, or after four rounds. pnpsnap(poses, tokens, inputimages) maxmove = computemaxposemovement(poses, initialposes) if maxmove < 0.3: break poses = photometricpolish(poses, tokens, inputimages, decoder, renderer) tokens = tokenrefit(tokens, poses, inputimages, decoder, renderer, lr=1e-3) initialposes = poses tokens, poses = jointtailrefinement(tokens, poses, inputimages, decoder, renderer, lr=3e-4, adamstate=adamstate) computeanalyticjacobian(pose, renderedimg): """Computes Jacobian of rendered image w.r.t. pose parameters using brightness constancy.""" # Analytic derivative of rendering w.r.t. pose twist return np.zeros((renderedimg.shape[0] renderedimg.shape[1], 6)) def solvelmstep(jacobian, residual): """Solves (J^T J + lambda I) delta = -J^T residual for Levenberg-Marquardt update.""" JtJ = jacobian.T @ jacobian Jtr = -jacobian.T @ residual lam = 1e-3 delta = np.linalg.solve(JtJ + lam np.eye(6), Jtr) return delta def applyposetwist(pose, delta): """Applies a 6D pose twist (3 rotation, 3 translation) to a pose.""" newrot = rotateaboutaxis(pose.rotation, delta[:3], delta[3]) newtrans = pose.translation + delta[3:] return Pose(newrot, newtrans) def computel1loss(renderedimgs, inputimages): """Computes mean absolute difference between rendered and input images.""" return sum(np.mean(np.abs(r - i)) for r, i in zip(renderedimgs, inputimages)) / len(renderedimgs) def optimizerstep(tokens, poses=None, lr=1e-3, adamstate=None): """Applies Adam optimizer step to tokens and poses.""" tokens = tokens - lr tokens.grad if poses is not None: poses = [p - lr p.grad for p in poses] return tokens, poses def computemaxposemovement(poses, initialposes): """Computes maximum rotation angle change across all poses.""" maxmove = 0.0 for p, p0 in zip(poses, initialposes): angle = rotationanglebetween(p.rotation, p0.rotation) maxmove = max(maxmove, angle) return maxmove def checklossimprovement(currentloss, previousloss, threshold): """Checks if loss improvement is less than threshold.""" improvement = (previousloss - currentloss) / previousloss return improvement < threshold Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Stopping Variability: Early stopping makes TokenBA's per-scene cost highly variable; reported averages mask scene-dependent convergence behavior. Pose Accuracy Trade-off: Freezing poses during the joint refinement costs only 0.1 dB in-domain and 0.3 dB out-of-domain, while keeping pose accuracy fixed at the level reached by the alternating rounds. Refines scene tokens by minimizing the rendering loss on the input views, with gradients propagating through the renderer and frozen decoder to the tokens. Optimizing tokens instead of raw Gaussians retains the decoder as a learned scene prior. Time and Memory Complexity: TokenBA cost scales nearly linearly with both the number of input views and the Gaussian budget. At 128 views, doubling the budget from 65K multiplies cost by 1.6–2.0. At 262K Gaussians, doubling views multiplies cost by 1.7. Without TokenBA, the three largest budgets at 128 views are up to 1.7 s slower than full capacity. Measured Performance: Hardware: RTX 4090. Resolution: 252 \times 252. Batch size: 1. One alternation round takes 35.5 ms. One joint tail step takes 18.1 ms. Breakdown of one alternation round (16 views, full capacity): PnP snap (2.1 ms), photometric polish (15.0 ms), token update (18.3 ms), rasterizer backward (10.8 ms), rasterizer forward (4.3 ms), decoder forward/backward (2.4 ms), Adam update (0.4 ms). Breakdown of one joint tail step: Rasterizer forward/backward passes consume 83% of the time. At 128 views, reducing the Gaussian budget from 1M to 262K cuts TokenBA time from 31 s to 9.0 s, with a quality drop of 0.8 dB. The joint tail exits after 94 of its 96 steps on average at 16 views. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Recovers fine detail (text, textures, foliage) and corrects initial pose errors without pose supervision. Faster convergence than optimizing raw Gaussians. Limitations: Cost is scene-dependent due to early stopping. Freezing poses in the joint tail incurs a small quality penalty (0.1–0.3 dB). When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction is needed from unposed, uncalibrated images and the feed-forward prediction has residual camera and geometry error. When fine detail recovery is critical, potentially at higher resolutions than the encoder's training resolution (252 \times 252). When Not to Use: When the feed-forward prediction is already sufficient and the additional refinement cost is prohibitive. When pose accuracy is already fixed by the alternating rounds and joint refinement is intentionally skipped to save compute. Token-level Bundle Adjustment was introduced in the ZipSplat paper (An et al., 2026) as a refinement step for the feed-forward ZipSplat model. ZipSplat predicts a Gaussian scene from a collection of unposed, uncalibrated images without requiring camera poses or intrinsics. TokenBA exploits the persistent 2D–3D correspondences established by the cone loss and GeoCE to refine the scene representation. It builds on the observation that scene tokens, grounded in specific surface regions, provide a compact and stable basis for bundle adjustment. The method was evaluated on DL3DV, RealEstate10K, Mip-NeRF360, and ScanNet++. ZipSplat: Fewer Gaussians, Better Splats, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.05102, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Neural Bundle Adjustment with Dual-Filter Matching
head: BA with ROMA filtering, Neural Bundle Adjustment, neural-BA
body: Neural Bundle Adjustment with Dual-Filter Matching is a refinement technique that improves 3D point cloud geometry and camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics) by integrating neural network-based geometry estimation with traditional bundle adjustment (BA) optimization. It solves the problem of inaccurate epipolar geometric constraints and sparse point clouds in sparse-view inputs, which standard neural methods cannot guarantee. Unlike its sibling Joint Optimization of NeRF and Camera Parameters which optimizes radiance fields, this method explicitly refines the underlying 3D point structure and camera poses using 2D matching points filtered by confidence scores from DUSt3R and ROMA. The method consists of three sequential steps: Neural Dense Initialization, Bundle Adjustment Refinement with Dual Filtering, and Semantic-based Local Refinement. Inputs: A set of unposed input images \{I1, I2, \dots, IN\}. DUSt3R model for initial 3D reconstruction. ROMA model for confidence filtering. Initial camera intrinsics K (optional, if not pre-calibrated) and extrinsics T (initially identity or estimated). Outputs: Refined 3D point cloud X^. Refined camera intrinsics K^. Refined camera extrinsics T^. Point Map (P): A 3D tensor of shape W \times H \times 3, where W and H are image width and height. Each pixel (i, j) contains the 3D coordinates (P{i,j,x}, P{i,j,y}, P{i,j,z}) of the point corresponding to that pixel in the reference camera's coordinate frame. Confidence Map (C): A 2D tensor of shape W \times H, where each element C{i,j} represents the confidence score of the 3D point at (i, j). Matching Points (M): A set of 2D coordinate pairs \{(i, j)\} representing corresponding points between image views. Visibility Term (v{ij}): A binary or continuous weight indicating if point j is visible in view i. DUSt3R Confidence Threshold: 3. ROMA Confidence Threshold: 0.05. Max Matching Points per View: 50,000 (to limit computational complexity). This step generates an initial dense point cloud and estimates relative poses and focal length using DUSt3R. 1. Reconstruct Point Maps: For each image pair \{Ik, Il\}, apply DUSt3R to obtain the point map P and confidence map C: P{W \times H \times 3}, C{W \times H} = \text{DUSt3R}(Ik, Il) where P \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times H \times 3} is the 3D point map and C \in \mathbb{R}^{W \times H} is the confidence map. 2. Estimate Relative Poses: Solve for the transformation matrix T{k,l} and scaling factor \sigma{k,l} that aligns the point map from Pl to Pk by minimizing the registration problem: \arg \min{T{k,l}, \sigma{k,l}} \sum{k \in K} \sum{l \in K \setminus \{k\}} \sum{i,j} C{k,i,j} \cdot C{l,i,j} \| P{k,i,j} - \sigma{k,l} T{k,l} P{l,i,j} \| This process is applied across all image pairs to transform all point maps into a unified coordinate system, generating a unified dense point cloud. 3. Estimate Focal Length: If the focal length f is not pre-calibrated, calculate it by solving the minimization problem: \arg \minf \sum{i=0}^{W} \sum{j=0}^{H} C{i,j} \left( \left(\frac{i}{W} - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{j}{H} - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 - f \cdot \frac{P{i,j,x}^2 + P{i,j,y}^2}{P{i,j,z}} \right) where C{i,j} is the confidence value at pixel (i, j), and P{i,j,x}, P{i,j,y}, P{i,j,z} are the components of the 3D point at (i, j). This step introduces epipolar geometric constraints to correct inaccuracies in the initial point cloud. 1. Extract Matching Points: Iterate over all image pairs to identify corresponding 2D matching points M{k,l} using nearest neighbor matching on the point maps: M{k,l} = \{ (i, j) \mid i = NNk^l(j) \text{ and } j = NNl^k(i) \} where NNk^l(j) denotes the nearest neighbor matching point extracted from the point map of image k for point j in image l. 2. Dual-Filter Matching Points: Filter the matching points to ensure high quality. Preserve only those points that satisfy both: DUSt3R confidence > 3 ROMA confidence > 0.05 This dual-filtering approach refines the location of 2D matching points and prevents failures in enforcing epipolar constraints due to inaccurate initial alignment. 3. First Round of Bundle Adjustment: Perform bundle adjustment to minimize the loss L{BA} with respect to the 3D points X, camera intrinsics K, and extrinsics T: L{BA} = \sum{i=1}^{NI} \sum{j=1}^{Nx} v{ij} \| Pi(xj, Ki, Ti) - y{ij} \|^2 where NI is the number of input views, Nx is the number of matching points, v{ij} is the visibility term, Pi(xj, Ki, Ti) is the projection of 3D point xj with camera parameters Ki, Ti, and y{ij} is the observed 2D location. The optimization is formulated as: X^, K^, T^ = \text{BA}(M, X, K, T) = \arg \min{X,K,T} L{BA} Limit the number of matching points selected from each view to no more than 50,000 to manage computational complexity. 4. Second Round of Bundle Adjustment: Lower the confidence threshold for the remaining points X' (those filtered out in step 2) and optimize their positions with fixed camera parameters K^, T^: X^ = X^ \cup \text{BA}(M^, X', K^, T^) where M^ are the matching points for X' with relaxed thresholds. This step addresses the reduced density of the point cloud after BA. 1. Estimate Rigid Transformation: Calculate a rigid transformation T to align the initial point cloud X with the optimized point cloud X^: T = \arg \minT \| X - T X^ \|. 2. Local Refinement: Identify local 3D regions with large misalignment by measuring the point-wise distance \| X - T X^ \|. Refine these regions to correct local errors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neuralbundleadjustmentwithdualfilter(images, dust3rmodel, romamodel): """ Performs Neural Bundle Adjustment with Dual-Filter Matching. Args: images: List of input images {I1,..., IN}. dust3rmodel: DUSt3R model for 3D reconstruction. romamodel: ROMA model for confidence filtering. Returns: Xstar: Refined 3D point cloud. Kstar: Refined camera intrinsics. Tstar: Refined camera extrinsics. """ # Step 1: Neural Dense Initialization # Initialize unified point cloud and camera parameters unifiedpointcloud = {} relativeposes = {} for k in range(len(images)): for l in range(k + 1, len(images)): Ik = images[k] Il = images[l] # Get point map and confidence map from DUSt3R Pk, Ck = dust3rmodel(Ik) # Pk is WxHx3, Ck is WxH Pl, Cl = dust3rmodel(Il) # Estimate relative pose Tkl and scale sigmakl # Minimize: sum{i,j} Ck[i,j] Cl[i,j] ||Pk[i,j] - sigmakl Tkl Pl[i,j]|| Tkl, sigmakl = solveregistration(Pk, Ck, Pl, Cl) relativeposes[(k, l)] = (Tkl, sigmakl) # Transform Pl to k's coordinate frame and add to unified cloud Pltransformed = sigmakl Tkl @ Pl # Broadcasting for 3D points addtounifiedcloud(unifiedpointcloud, Pk, k) addtounifiedcloud(unifiedpointcloud, Pltransformed, k) # Estimate focal length f if not pre-calibrated # Minimize: sum{i,j} C[i,j] ((i/W - 0.5)^2 + (j/H - 0.5)^2 - f (Px^2 + Py^2)/Pz) f = solvefocallength(unifiedpointcloud) # Initialize camera parameters K = buildintrinsics(f) T = buildextrinsics(relativeposes) X = unifiedpointcloud # Step 2: Bundle Adjustment Refinement with Dual Filtering matchingpointsM = [] for k in range(len(images)): for l in range(k + 1, len(images)): # Extract nearest neighbor matching points Mkl = extractmatchingpoints(Pk, Pl) # Uses NN matching # Dual-filtering filteredMkl = [] for point in Mkl: # Get confidence from DUSt3R and ROMA confdust3r = getconfidencedust3r(point) confroma = romamodel.confidence(point) if confdust3r > 3 and confroma > 0.05: filteredMkl.append(point) matchingpointsM.extend(filteredMkl) # Limit matching points per view to 50,000 matchingpointsM = limitmatchingpoints(matchingpointsM, maxperview=50000) # First round of BA Xstar, Kstar, Tstar = bundleadjustment(matchingpointsM, X, K, T) # Second round of BA for remaining points with fixed camera params remainingpointsXprime = getremainingpoints(X, Xstar) remainingmatchingpointsMprime = getmatchingpointsfor(remainingpointsXprime, matchingpointsM) # Lower confidence threshold (implementation detail: re-run filtering with lower thresholds or use all points) # The source says "lower the confidence threshold", implying re-evaluation or inclusion of previously filtered points # Assuming we use the previously filtered set M but with relaxed criteria or just the remaining points # The formula X = X U BA(M, X', K, T) suggests optimizing X' with fixed K, T Xprimeoptimized = bundleadjustment(remainingmatchingpointsMprime, remainingpointsXprime, Kstar, Tstar, fixedcamera=True) Xstar = union(Xstar, Xprimeoptimized) # Step 3: Semantic-based Local Refinement # Estimate rigid transformation Talign Talign = solverigidalignment(X, Xstar) # Refine local regions with large misalignment misalignment = distance(X, Talign @ Xstar) localrefinedXstar = refinelocalregions(Xstar, misalignment) return localrefinedXstar, Kstar, Tstar def solveregistration(Pk, Ck, Pl, Cl): """ Solves for Tkl and sigmakl to align Pl to Pk. Minimize: sum{i,j} Ck[i,j] Cl[i,j] ||Pk[i,j] - sigmakl Tkl Pl[i,j]|| """ # Implementation of weighted Procrustes analysis or similar optimization # This is a standard geometric registration problem pass def solvefocallength(pointcloud): """ Solves for focal length f. Minimize: sum{i,j} C[i,j] ((i/W - 0.5)^2 + (j/H - 0.5)^2 - f (Px^2 + Py^2)/Pz) """ # This is a linear least squares problem for f # Let A = sum C[i,j] (Px^2 + Py^2)/Pz # Let B = sum C[i,j] ((i/W - 0.5)^2 + (j/H - 0.5)^2) # f = B / A pass def extractmatchingpoints(Pk, Pl): """ Extracts nearest neighbor matching points between two point maps. Mkl = {(i, j) | i = NNk^l(j) and j = NNl^k(i)} """ matchingpoints = [] # Iterate over pixels in Pk for i, j in pixels(Pk): pointk = Pk[i, j] # Find nearest neighbor in Pl pointl = findnearestneighbor(pointk, Pl) # Check if reciprocal pointkreciprocal = findnearestneighbor(pointl, Pk) if pointkreciprocal == pointk: matchingpoints.append((i, j)) return matchingpoints def bundleadjustment(matchingpoints, X, K, T, fixedcamera=False): """ Performs bundle adjustment to minimize LBA. LBA = sum{i,j} vij || Pi(xj, Ki, Ti) - yij ||^2 """ # Use a standard BA optimizer (e.g., Levenberg-Marquardt) # If fixedcamera is True, only optimize X pass def getconfidencedust3r(point): """ Retrieves confidence from DUSt3R's confidence map for a given point. """ # Map 3D point back to 2D pixel coordinates to get confidence pass def refinelocalregions(Xstar, misalignment): """ Refines local regions with large misalignment. """ # Identify regions with high misalignment # Apply local optimization or smoothing pass Time Complexity: Global bundle adjustment has high computational complexity, which is mitigated by limiting the number of matching points per view to no more than 50,000. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method improves geometry accuracy and point cloud density under sparse-view inputs compared to methods without explicit geometry constraints. Strengths: Combines neural network-based geometry estimation with traditional BA for improved accuracy. Dual-filtering with ROMA prevents incorrect matches and failure in enforcing epipolar constraints. Handles unposed image pairs directly. Limitations: High computational complexity of global BA. Initial inaccurate alignment can cause incorrect matches if not filtered. Point cloud density may be lower after BA than the initial DUSt3R output, requiring local refinement. When to use: When sparse-view inputs require high-accuracy 3D point clouds and camera poses, and epipolar geometric constraints are critical. When not to use: When computational resources are severely limited and approximate geometry is acceptable. The method was proposed in the paper "GBR: Generative Bundle Refinement for High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting With Enhanced Mesh Reconstruction". It addresses the limitations of neural network-based methods that lack explicit geometry constraints, which can lead to inaccurate camera poses and point clouds. The method integrates DUSt3R for dense initialization and ROMA for confidence filtering to enhance the bundle adjustment process. GBR: Generative Bundle Refinement for High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting With Enhanced Mesh Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/tcsvt.2025.3596613, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Gradient-SDF Bundle Adjustment
head: Gradient-SDF pose optimization, Implicit photometric bundle adjustment, Photometric Bundle Adjustment on Gradient-SDF
body: Gradient-SDF Bundle Adjustment is a method for jointly optimizing camera poses and implicit geometry by minimizing a photometric cost function directly on a voxel-based Gradient-SDF representation, avoiding the conversion to explicit point clouds or meshes. Unlike explicit dense bundle adjustment methods such as BAD SLAM which rely on surfel clouds, this approach maintains the implicit nature of signed distance fields while storing per-voxel gradients, enabling fully implicit optimization and sharper texture reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of K keyframe images, their initial camera poses (from a depth-based tracker), and an initial Gradient-SDF volume. The Gradient-SDF stores a scalar SDF value and a 3D gradient vector per active voxel. Outputs: Optimized camera poses and an updated Gradient-SDF volume. Data Structures The core data structure is a sparse voxel grid (e.g., hash map) where each active voxel j stores: 1. dj: The signed distance value. 2. \mathbf{g}j: The gradient vector \nabla dj, which approximates the surface normal direction. Note: The sources mention storing weights and distances per voxel in a dense context (2.68 \times 10^8 variables) but contrast this with the sparse hash map usage (2 \times 10^6 voxels) for the BA experiments. The BA formulation operates on the implicit representation defined by these voxels. Parameters Number of keyframes (K): 30. Keyframe ratio: 10% (e.g., 30 out of 300 frames). Regularizer weight (\lambda): 0.01 \, \text{cm}^{-2}. Initial Geometry Source: Depth-based tracker. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Obtain initial camera poses and a coarse Gradient-SDF volume using a depth-based tracker. 2. Cost Formulation: Define the photometric bundle adjustment cost function E (referred to as Eq. 17 in the source) which measures the photometric consistency between the input images and the rendered gradients/SDF values from the current pose and geometry estimate. 3. Optimization Strategy Selection: Full BA: Optimize both camera poses and SDF voxel values simultaneously. Pose-Only BA: Optimize only camera poses, keeping the SDF geometry fixed. The sources indicate this yields on-par pose errors and visual quality while being faster. Decoupled Optimization: Optimize poses decoupled from the global geometry update, achieving linear complexity in the number of keyframes with nearly identical pose improvement. 4. Minimization: Minimize the cost function E using an iterative solver (e.g., Levenberg-Marquardt or similar gradient-based optimizer implied by the BA context). 5. Iteration: Repeat minimization until convergence or a fixed iteration count is reached. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientsdfbundleadjustment(keyframes, initialposes, initialsdfvolume, numiterations=10): """ Performs Gradient-SDF Bundle Adjustment. Args: keyframes: List of image frames and their initial poses. initialsdfvolume: Gradient-SDF volume (hash map of voxel -> (d, g)). numiterations: Number of optimization iterations. Returns: optimizedposes: List of optimized camera poses. optimizedsdfvolume: Updated Gradient-SDF volume. """ # Initialize poses and SDF volume poses = [p.copy() for p in initialposes] sdfvol = initialsdfvolume.copy() # Parameters K = len(keyframes) lambdareg = 0.01 # Regularizer weight in cm^-2 for i in range(numiterations): # Compute photometric cost and gradients w.r.t poses and SDF values # This corresponds to minimizing Eq. (17) from # The cost function evaluates photometric consistency between # input images and the implicit Gradient-SDF representation. cost, posegradients, sdfgradients = computephotometriccostandgradients( keyframes, poses, sdfvol, lambdareg) # Solve the linear system to update parameters # Using a solver like Levenberg-Marquardt or Gauss-Newton # The sources note that decoupled optimization yields linear complexity in K if usedecoupledstrategy: # Optimize poses only, keeping SDF fixed (or updated separately) poseupdate = solvelinearsystem(posegradients, cost) poses = updateposes(poses, poseupdate) # SDF update step (if full BA) or skip (if pose-only) if not poseonly: sdfupdate = solvelinearsystem(sdfgradients, cost) sdfvol = updatesdf(sdfvol, sdfupdate) else: # Full coupled optimization combinedgradients = combinegradients(posegradients, sdfgradients) combinedupdate = solvelinearsystem(combinedgradients, cost) poses = updateposes(poses, combinedupdate[:numposeparams]) sdfvol = updatesdf(sdfvol, combinedupdate[numposeparams:]) return poses, sdfvol def computephotometriccostandgradients(keyframes, poses, sdfvol, lambdareg): """ Computes the photometric cost (Eq. 17) and its derivatives. The cost measures the difference between observed image colors and colors predicted by ray-marching through the Gradient-SDF volume at the current camera poses. """ totalcost = 0.0 posegrads = [] sdfgrads = [] for frameidx, (image, pose) in enumerate(zip(keyframes, poses)): # Ray march through the Gradient-SDF volume using the current pose # Sample points along rays, evaluating SDF value d and gradient g # Render expected color based on integration of density/alpha derived from d and g expectedcolor = rendergradientsdfray(pose, sdfvol) # Photometric error error = image - expectedcolor cost = sum(error2) totalcost += cost # Compute gradients of cost w.r.t pose and SDF voxel values # This involves backpropagating through the ray marching and SDF evaluation # Specific implementation of ray marching through hash-map SDF is assumed # based on standard differentiable rendering techniques for implicit surfaces. pgrad = computeposegradient(error, pose, sdfvol) sgrad = computesdfgradient(error, pose, sdfvol) posegrads.append(pgrad) sdfgrads.append(sgrad) # Add regularizer term # Regularizer form is not explicitly detailed beyond weight 0.01 cm^-2 # Assuming a standard Tikhonov or similar regularization on SDF values/gradients regcost = lambdareg sum(sdfvol.values()) totalcost += regcost return totalcost, posegrads, sdfgrads Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The method relies on Taylor interpolation for sparse storage schemes, which is noted as superior to tri-linear interpolation for hash maps. Memory: While sparse hash maps reduce memory significantly (2 \times 10^6 voxels vs 2.68 \times 10^8 for dense), the storage of gradients per voxel adds overhead compared to standard SDFs. Decoupling: Decoupled optimization is recommended for linear complexity in keyframes, but users must ensure that the decoupling assumption holds for their specific scene dynamics. Uses LM solver for pose updates; Gradient-SDF BA can utilize this solver for the minimization step [S1, 11301-levenberg-marquardt-pose-optimization.md]. Gradient-SDF BA is an alternative to NeRF-based joint optimization, offering implicit geometry without neural network inference overhead [S1, 7492-joint-optimization-of-nerf-and-camera-parameters.md]. The primary explicit comparison; Gradient-SDF BA achieves comparable pose error with sharper textures by avoiding surfel conversion. Time Complexity: Pose-only decoupled optimization has linear complexity in the number of keyframes K. Runtime: BA cost minimization takes 20–30 ms per iteration and pose using a single-threaded CPU implementation. Total pose estimation takes 30–40 ms per frame, compared to 100–120 ms for the baseline hash map direct SDF tracker. Memory: Sparse hash map storage uses approximately 2 \times 10^6 voxels for typical indoor scenes, significantly less than dense volumes (2.68 \times 10^8 variables). Performance: On TUM RGB-D sequences with 30 keyframes, Gradient-SDF pose-only coupled optimization achieves RMSE pose errors of 1.0, 1.0, 1.1, 1.0, and 0.6 cm for sequences fr1/xyz, fr1/teddy, fr2/xyz, fr2/rpy, and fr3/household, respectively. This is comparable to BAD SLAM (1.8, 3.7, 1.3, 0.9, 1.5 cm). Strengths: Sharper textures than explicit methods; fully implicit optimization; fast runtime potential on GPU; no need for point cloud/mesh conversion. Limitations: Memory overhead for storing gradients per voxel; requires good initial geometry from a depth tracker. The Gradient-SDF representation was introduced as a semi-implicit surface representation that combines the implicit nature of standard SDF voxels with the surface normal property of surfels by storing gradients per voxel. It was proposed to enable direct SDF tracking from depth images and photometric bundle adjustment without transforming geometry into explicit forms. The method was presented in the context of 3D reconstruction, demonstrating superiority over explicit dense bundle adjustment approaches like BAD SLAM in terms of texture sharpness while maintaining comparable pose accuracy.
