name: Neural Radiance Field Integration
head: Bundle-Adjusting NeRF, Joint Optimization of NeRF and Poses
body: Neural Radiance Field Integration refers to the family of optimization procedures that simultaneously refine inaccurate camera poses and optimize the parameters of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF). It solves the problem of reconstruction failure when initial camera poses are erroneous, which causes standard NeRF training to converge to local minima or produce artifacts. It differs from standard NeRF optimization by treating camera parameters as learnable variables alongside the neural network weights, and from pure pose estimation methods by leveraging the geometric consistency of the learned 3D representation. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of differentiable volume rendering to compute gradients with respect to both the NeRF parameters \theta and the camera pose parameters Pi. The rendering equation for a ray \mathbf{r} is: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \left( 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai} \right) \mathbf{c}i, \quad Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} where \sigmai and \mathbf{c}i are the density and color predicted by the NeRF \mathcal{F}\theta at sample point i. The total loss \mathcal{L} is typically the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between rendered colors \hat{C} and ground truth images I: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \| \hat{C}i - Ii \|^2 Gradients \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial Pi} are computed via backpropagation through the differentiable renderer. Camera poses are typically parametrized in the Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3) as a 6D vector n (rotation \omega and translation t), which is exponentiated to a transformation matrix N = \exp(n) for composition with reference poses. Uses a coarse-to-fine frequency schedule for positional encoding to prevent high-frequency noise from misleading the optimizer when poses are inaccurate. Choose when initial pose errors are moderate and computational resources are limited. Combines local non-parametric photometric alignment with global parametric geometric alignment to handle large displacements and poor initialization. Choose when initial poses are very poor (e.g., identity) or when large camera movements exist. Extends BARF with a cascaded bundle-adjustment structure and distinct modulation factors for each stage to handle larger initial pose errors (e.g., 30.4° rotation) without overfitting. Choose when BARF fails to converge due to large initial pose deviations. The concept of joint optimization of NeRF and camera poses was introduced by. Early work demonstrated that standard NeRF optimization is highly sensitive to initial pose accuracy, often failing with even small errors. Subsequent developments like L2G-NeRF and CBARF addressed limitations regarding large displacements and overfitting, respectively. These methods are primarily used in Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines where initial pose estimates from traditional methods may be insufficient for high-fidelity NeRF reconstruction.

name: BARF (Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields)
head: Bundle-Adjusting NeRF
body: BARF reconstructs a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and refines inaccurate camera poses given multi-view images with pose errors. It differs from standard NeRF optimization by using a coarse-to-fine refinement strategy that gradually increases the high-frequency part of positional encoding. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images \{Ii\}, initial camera poses \{Pi\} (with errors), and a NeRF model \mathcal{F}\theta. Outputs: Refined camera poses \{\hat{P}i\} and optimized NeRF parameters \hat{\theta}. Data structures: NeRF Model \mathcal{F}\theta: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mapping 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Positional Encoding \Gamma: Standard Fourier feature mapping used to embed \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{d}. Optimization State: Parameters \theta for the MLP and pose parameters (rotation \mathbf{R}, translation \mathbf{t}) for each camera. Method: The core innovation is a coarse-to-fine refinement strategy that gradually introduces high-frequency information into the positional encoding. This allows the optimizer to first converge on low-frequency structures (which are robust to pose errors) before refining high-frequency details (which require accurate poses). 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF parameters \theta and camera poses Pi using the provided (potentially inaccurate) initial poses. 2. Coarse-to-Fine Schedule: Define a schedule for the number of frequency bands L(t) used in the positional encoding \Gamma at training step t. 3. Optimization Loop: For each training step t: a. Set the positional encoding frequency limit L(t) based on the schedule. b. Sample rays through the scene using the current camera poses Pi. c. Render colors \hat{C} using the NeRF \mathcal{F}\theta with positional encoding \Gamma{L(t)}. d. Compute the loss \mathcal{L} between rendered colors \hat{C} and ground truth images Ii (typically Mean Squared Error). e. Perform gradient descent to update both NeRF parameters \theta and camera pose parameters. f. Increment t and update L(t) if the schedule dictates. Formulas: Positional Encoding with frequency limit L: \GammaL(\mathbf{x}) = [\sin(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \pi \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \pi \mathbf{x})] Rendering equation (standard volume rendering): \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \left( 1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai} \right) \mathbf{c}i, \quad Ti = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} Loss function: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N \| \hat{C}i - Ii \|^2 Parameters: Initial frequency bands: Not given in the sources. Final frequency bands: Not given in the sources. Learning rate: Not given in the sources. Optimization algorithm: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: The gradual introduction of frequencies prevents the optimizer from being misled by high-frequency noise in the presence of pose errors. Boundaries: The schedule must be smooth enough to allow convergence at each frequency level. Degenerate input: If initial poses are extremely poor, even the coarse stages may fail to converge. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def barfoptimization(images, initialposes, nerfmlp, schedulefn, numsteps): # Initialize learnable parameters theta = list(nerfmlp.parameters()) poses = [p.clone().requiresgrad(True) for p in initialposes] optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(theta + poses, lr=1e-4) # for t in range(numsteps): Lt = schedulefn(t) optimizer.zerograd() renderedimages = [] for i, gtimg in enumerate(images): # Standard ray sampling through camera frustum rayso, raysd = sampleraysthroughposes(poses[i], gtimg.shape) # Apply positional encoding with limited frequency bands encodedrays = applypositionalencoding(rayso, raysd, L=Lt) # Standard differentiable volume rendering color = volumerender(nerfmlp, encodedrays) renderedimages.append(color) loss = computemseloss(renderedimages, images) loss.backward() optimizer.step() return poses, theta def applypositionalencoding(rayso, raysd, L): # Standard Fourier features up to frequency band L encoded = [] for i in range(L): freq = 2i torch.pi encoded.extend([torch.sin(freq rayso), torch.cos(freq rayso), torch.sin(freq raysd), torch.cos(freq raysd)]) return torch.cat(encoded, dim=-1) def computemseloss(rendered, groundtruth): return torch.mean((torch.stack(rendered) - torch.stack(groundtruth)) 2) The Iterative Alignment Strategy is a post-processing and data-generation technique used to mitigate reconstruction artifacts in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) caused by inaccurate camera poses and non-rigid scene motion. It addresses the "domain gap" where NeRF-rendered views are blurry due to misalignment, violating the sharp-pair assumption of standard optical flow estimators. Unlike direct alignment methods that optimize a loss function during training, this strategy iteratively warps ground truth images using optical flow to create a better-aligned training set, leveraging the sharpening effect of improved alignment to refine flow estimates in subsequent rounds. This method performs the final optimization step in the LU-NeRF pipeline to achieve high-fidelity novel view synthesis by jointly refining camera poses and the neural radiance field (NeRF) representation. It solves the problem of residual errors in camera poses and scene geometry that remain after the initial synchronization stage. Unlike the Iterative Alignment Strategy, which focuses on sequential alignment, this method leverages the global consistency provided by synchronization to apply a comprehensive bundle adjustment-style refinement. It sets itself apart by using the BARF optimization procedure as its core engine, treating the synchronized poses as a sufficiently accurate initialization to converge to the ground truth. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Robust to initial pose errors by decoupling frequency optimization. Limitations: Requires a coarse-to-fine schedule. When to use: When camera poses are inaccurate or sparse. BARF (Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced in ICCV 2021. It addresses the issue of NeRF's sensitivity to camera pose accuracy, which is a common problem in real-world scenarios where poses are estimated from SfM pipelines and may contain errors. The method was developed to improve the robustness of NeRF reconstruction under pose uncertainty. NeRF的基础及后续扩展, https://pengsida.net/files/NeRFTutorial.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Iterative Alignment Strategy
head: Misalignment Correction via Optical Flow
body: The Iterative Alignment Strategy is a post-processing and data-generation technique used to mitigate reconstruction artifacts in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) caused by inaccurate camera poses and non-rigid scene motion. It addresses the "domain gap" where NeRF-rendered views are blurry due to misalignment, violating the sharp-pair assumption of standard optical flow estimators. Unlike direct alignment methods that optimize a loss function during training, this strategy iteratively warps ground truth images using optical flow to create a better-aligned training set, leveraging the sharpening effect of improved alignment to refine flow estimates in subsequent rounds. The method operates as an iterative loop to generate aligned training and testing data. It assumes access to a NeRF model (e.g., mip-NeRF 360) and a set of input images with potentially erroneous camera poses. Inputs: Current NeRF model parameters (MLPs). Original ground truth images I{gt}. Original camera poses P. Optical flow estimator (PWC-Net). Outputs: Warped ground truth images I{warped}. Updated NeRF model parameters. Data Structures: Images: 2D arrays of pixel values (RGB). Optical Flow: 2D vector fields (u, v) representing displacement from source to target. Steps: 1. Render: Render images I{render} from the current NeRF model using the original camera poses P. 2. Estimate Flow: Calculate the optical flow from the rendered views I{render} to the ground truth views I{gt} using PWC-Net. Note: The rendered images are often blurry due to misalignment, which violates the general optical flow assumption of sharp paired inputs. However, PWC-Net produces reasonable results based on global structures and shapes. 3. Warp: Warp the ground truth images I{gt} using the estimated optical flows to build a new, better-aligned training set I{warped}. The warping aligns the ground truth content with the geometry estimated by the NeRF. 4. Retrain: Train the NeRF model using the new aligned training set I{warped}. 5. Iterate: Repeat steps 1-4 for 2-3 iterations. Each iteration leverages sharper images (from the improved NeRF) to improve flow accuracy, which in turn enables better alignment for the next round. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativealignmentstrategy(nerfmodel, gtimages, poses, numiterations=3): """Iteratively aligns ground truth images to NeRF geometry using optical flow.""" currentimages = gtimages for in range(numiterations): # Step 1: Render current NeRF model using original poses renderedimages = [nerfmodel.render(p) for p in poses] # Step 2: Calculate optical flow from rendered to ground truth using PWC-Net flowfields = [estimateflow(rendered, gt) for rendered, gt in zip(renderedimages, currentimages)] # Step 3: Warp ground truth images using estimated flows to build aligned training set alignedimages = [warp(gt, f) for gt, f in zip(currentimages, flowfields)] # Step 4: Retrain NeRF on aligned images nerfmodel.train(alignedimages, poses) currentimages = alignedimages return currentimages def estimateflow(source, target): # Compute optical flow field F from source to target using PWC-Net # Returns 2D vector field of displacements return PWCNet(source, target) # External optical flow estimator def warp(image, flow): # Sample image pixels at coordinates displaced by flow field using bilinear interpolation h, w = image.shape[:2] gridy, gridx = np.meshgrid(np.arange(h), np.arange(w), indexing='ij') # Flow is (dy, dx) y = gridy + flow[:,:, 0] x = gridx + flow[:,:, 1] # Clamp and sample y = np.clip(y, 0, h - 1) x = np.clip(x, 0, w - 1) return bilinearsample(image, x, y) Parameters: Iterations: 2-3 iterations are typically sufficient to reach best quality. Optical Flow Network: PWC-Net. RAFT was considered but rejected due to memory constraints on high-resolution images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: PWC-Net may run out of memory on high-resolution images. Alternative flow networks like RAFT were rejected for the same reason. Blurry Inputs: NeRF rendered images are often blurry due to misalignment, violating the sharp-pair assumption of optical flow estimators. This can reduce flow accuracy, though global structures help mitigate this. Non-Rigid Motion: The strategy addresses misalignment from camera pose errors and non-rigid motion. Non-Rigid Refinement is a post-processing alignment step that uses an iterative optical flow network to correct non-rigid deformations or misalignments in NeRF features by warping neighbor features to test features. It addresses the domain gap between blurry rendered novel views and sharp neighboring images, which causes standard 3D alignment to fail due to camera pose errors and geometry estimation inaccuracies. Unlike general-purpose alignment, this method is trained end-to-end specifically for the task of refining feature correspondences in the presence of these domain gaps. Direct Alignment is a training technique that applies a direct alignment loss between rendered images and input RGB images to improve camera pose estimation and structure reconstruction in neural radiance fields. For every frame, it selects a surrogate view from a neighborhood starting from 2 frames till 5 frames on either side of the keyframe to perform direct alignment. It is trained for 100k iterations. Unlike methods that require expansive optic-flow depth or foundation models for regularization, direct alignment avoids local minima in joint camera pose estimation without them. However, violations of photo-consistency can hamper reconstructions, particularly with semi-transparent objects. It has been applied to LLFF and DTU datasets, showing average boosts of 60% in rotation and 53% in translation error reduction. Time Complexity: The method requires multiple iterations of NeRF training and optical flow estimation. Each iteration involves rendering all training views, running PWC-Net, and warping images. The total time scales with the number of iterations (typically 2-3) multiplied by the cost of one NeRF training epoch plus flow estimation. Memory Complexity: High memory usage due to the need to store and process high-resolution images and optical flow fields. PWC-Net may run out of memory on high-resolution images, and RAFT was rejected for the same reason. Performance: The strategy improves PSNR by +0.62dB on the warped test set for large MLPs (4096 channels) and +0.23dB for smaller models (1024 channels). It also improves LPIPS and SSIM metrics. Strengths: Effectively reduces artifacts caused by misalignment; leverages the self-improving nature of NeRF rendering (sharper images lead to better flow). Limitations: Does not represent the core proposed algorithm of the AligNeRF paper (which is a loss function); serves primarily for analysis and data generation. Relies on the quality of the optical flow estimator; fails if the initial NeRF is too poor to provide useful global structures for flow estimation. When to Use: When camera poses are inaccurate and cause significant blurring in NeRF renders, and when computational resources allow for iterative retraining and flow estimation. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained for high-resolution images; when the scene has severe non-rigid motion that cannot be captured by global optical flow. The Iterative Alignment Strategy was introduced in the AligNeRF paper. It was developed to address the issue of misalignment in NeRF training, particularly in the context of the mip-NeRF 360 dataset. The authors observed that standard NeRF training with inaccurate poses leads to blurry renders, which in turn hampers the accuracy of optical flow estimation if used for alignment. The iterative approach was proposed to break this cycle by progressively aligning the training data. The strategy was used for analysis and data generation in the experiments, rather than as the primary algorithm of the work, which focused on an alignment-aware training loss. name: Non-Rigid Refinement
head: iterative flow network
body: Non-Rigid Refinement is a post-processing alignment step that uses an iterative optical flow network to correct non-rigid deformations or misalignments in NeRF features by warping neighbor features to test features. It addresses the domain gap between blurry rendered novel views and sharp neighboring images, which causes standard 3D alignment to fail due to camera pose errors and geometry estimation inaccuracies. Unlike general-purpose alignment, this method is trained end-to-end specifically for the task of refining feature correspondences in the presence of these domain gaps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pair of feature maps: Neighbour Features (H^f{i\rightarrow k}) and Test Features (I^fk). The neighbour features are the reprojected features from adjacent views, and the test features are from the novel view. Output: Refined Neighbour Features (H^{f'}{i\rightarrow k}) and an estimated 2D optical flow field. Data Structures: Feature Maps: 2D tensors representing features extracted from images. The specific channel depth is not explicitly defined in the source, but the architecture processes them as multi-channel inputs. Flow Field: A 2-channel tensor representing the horizontal and vertical displacement vectors for each pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Resolution Reduction: The input feature maps are downsampled by a factor of 8. The optical flow estimation is performed at this 8x downsampled resolution. 2. Flow Estimation: The downsampled neighbour features and test features are passed through the optical flow network \mathcal{F} to estimate the flow field f{H^f{i\rightarrow k}}: f{H^f{i\rightarrow k}} = \mathcal{F}(H^f{i\rightarrow k}, I^fk) 3. Warping: The neighbour features are warped using the estimated 2D flow field via a 2D warping function warp{2D}: H^{f'}{i\rightarrow k} = warp{2D}(H^f{i\rightarrow k}, f{H^f{i\rightarrow k}}) 4. Iteration: The estimation and warping process is iterated 32 times to refine the alignment progressively. Network Architecture (\mathcal{F}): The network \mathcal{F} is a lightweight convolutional neural network. The architecture is identical to the original formulation in [6] but adapted to accept multi-channel features instead of 3-channel RGB images. The layers are as follows: 1. Conv2d: kernel size 7, 64 channels, stride 4. Followed by ReLU. 2. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 3. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Skip connection added to previous output. Followed by ReLU. 4. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels, stride 2. Followed by ReLU. 5. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Skip connection added to previous output. Followed by ReLU. 6. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 7. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 8. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 128 channels. Followed by ReLU. 9. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 64 channels. Followed by ReLU. 10. Conv2d: kernel size 3, 2 channels (representing the optical flow vector). Followed by ReLU. Upsampling: The estimated flow field from the network is at the reduced resolution. It is upsampled to full resolution using bilinear upsampling before being used in the warping step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class NonRigidRefinementNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels): super(NonRigidRefinementNetwork, self).init() # Layer 1: Conv2d k7 c64 s4 -> ReLU self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 64, kernelsize=7, stride=4, padding=3) self.relu1 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 2: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu2 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 3: Conv2d k3 c64 + skip -> ReLU self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu3 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 4: Conv2d k3 c64 s2 -> ReLU self.conv4 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, stride=2, padding=1) self.relu4 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 5: Conv2d k3 c64 + skip -> ReLU self.conv5 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu5 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 6: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv6 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu6 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 7: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv7 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu7 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 8: Conv2d k3 c128 -> ReLU self.conv8 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu8 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 9: Conv2d k3 c64 -> ReLU self.conv9 = nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu9 = nn.ReLU() # Layer 10: Conv2d k3 c2 -> ReLU self.conv10 = nn.Conv2d(64, 2, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu10 = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, neighbourfeatures, testfeatures): # Concatenate inputs along channel dimension x = torch.cat([neighbourfeatures, testfeatures], dim=1) # Layer 1 x = self.relu1(self.conv1(x)) # Layer 2 x = self.relu2(self.conv2(x)) # Layer 3 (Skip connection) xskip = x x = self.relu3(self.conv3(x) + xskip) # Layer 4 x = self.relu4(self.conv4(x)) # Layer 5 (Skip connection) xskip = x x = self.relu5(self.conv5(x) + xskip) # Layer 6 x = self.relu6(self.conv6(x)) # Layer 7 x = self.relu7(self.conv7(x)) # Layer 8 x = self.relu8(self.conv8(x)) # Layer 9 x = self.relu9(self.conv9(x)) # Layer 10 flow = self.relu10(self.conv10(x)) return flow def warp2d(features, flow): """ Warps the input features using the provided 2D flow field via bilinear sampling. """ B, C, H, W = features.shape # Create normalized grid coordinates [-1, 1] y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.linspace(-1, 1, H), torch.linspace(-1, 1, W), indexing='ij') grid = torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1).to(features.device) # Flow is in pixel coordinates; convert to normalized [-1, 1] flownorm = flow.permute(0, 2, 3, 1) 2.0 / max(H, W) grid = grid + flownorm grid = torch.clamp(grid, -1, 1) return F.gridsample(features, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') def nonrigidrefinement(neighbourfeatures, testfeatures, numiterations=32): """ Performs non-rigid refinement iteratively at 8x downsampled resolution, then warps the full-resolution features with the final upsampled flow. """ h, w = neighbourfeatures.shape[2], neighbourfeatures.shape[3] smallh, smallw = h // 8, w // 8 # Downsample inputs by 8x smallneighbour = F.interpolate(neighbourfeatures, size=(smallh, smallw), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) smalltest = F.interpolate(testfeatures, size=(smallh, smallw), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) flownet = NonRigidRefinementNetwork(inchannels=smallneighbour.shape[1]) currentfeatures = smallneighbour # Iterative refinement loop at reduced resolution for in range(numiterations): flowsmall = flownet(currentfeatures, smalltest) currentfeatures = warp2d(currentfeatures, flowsmall) # Final flow estimation and upsampling to full resolution finalflowsmall = flownet(currentfeatures, smalltest) finalflowfull = F.interpolate(finalflowsmall, size=(h, w), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False) # Warp original full-resolution neighbour features refinedfeatures = warp2d(neighbourfeatures, finalflowfull) return refinedfeatures, finalflowfull Parameters: Optical flow estimation resolution: 8x downsampled relative to the input feature resolution. Number of iterations: 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Domain Gap: Standard optical flow methods expect clean images, but NeRF renders can be blurry, creating a domain gap. This method is specifically trained to handle this. Camera Pose Errors: Errors in COLMAP pose estimation can lead to misalignments that 3D alignment cannot fully correct. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves 32 iterations of a lightweight convolutional network and warping operations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing the feature maps and the flow field. Strengths: Effectively reduces ghosting artifacts caused by misalignment from camera pose errors and non-rigid motion. It handles the domain gap between blurry rendered images and sharp neighbours better than general-purpose optical flow. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the initial 3D alignment and feature extraction. Performance depends on the specific training of the flow network. When to use: When there are significant misalignments due to camera pose errors or non-rigid motion that 3D alignment cannot resolve, and when the domain gap between rendered and real images is significant. Non-Rigid Refinement was introduced in the RoGUENeRF paper by S. Catley-Chandar et al.. It builds upon the Iterative Alignment Strategy [6957-iterative-alignment-strategy.md] and is part of the broader effort to enhance NeRF quality by addressing alignment issues. The optical flow network architecture is based on the work presented in [6]. name: Global Pose and Scene Refinement
head: LU-NeRF+Sync, final refinement
body: This method performs the final refinement step in the LU-NeRF pipeline to achieve accurate poses and scene representation for novel view synthesis, leveraging the good initial poses from synchronization. It applies BARF optimization using the global poses estimated from the synchronization stage as initialization. It sets itself apart by using the BARF optimization procedure as its core engine, treating the synchronized poses as a sufficiently accurate initialization to converge to the ground truth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Global camera poses estimated from the synchronization stage (rotation and translation for each view), multi-view images corresponding to these poses, and the initial NeRF MLP parameters. Outputs: Refined camera poses (rotation and translation) and an optimized NeRF MLP representing the scene. Data Structures: The method utilizes standard neural radiance field structures: NeRF MLP: A multi-layer perceptron mapping 3D coordinates and viewing directions to color and density. Camera Poses: A list of SE(3) transformation matrices or separate rotation (quaternion/axis-angle) and translation vectors for each image. Images: A list of RGB images aligned with the camera poses. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeRF MLP and camera poses using the outputs from the synchronization stage. The synchronization ensures poses are close to ground truth, satisfying BARF's requirement for initialization. 2. Joint Optimization: Perform joint training of the NeRF MLP and refinement of the camera poses. 3. Coarse-to-Fine Positional Encoding: Apply a coarse-to-fine positional encoding strategy during the optimization process. 4. Iteration: Repeat the joint optimization for a fixed number of iterations. Parameters: Refinement Iterations: 200,000 iterations. Positional Encoding: Coarse-to-fine strategy as defined in BARF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def globalposeandscenerefinement(synchronizedposes, images, initialnerfparams): # Initialize poses and NeRF from synchronization results poses = synchronizedposes nerfparams = initialnerfparams # Standard differentiable volume rendering of rays through the NeRF def renderimages(poses, nerfparams, freq): # Cast rays, sample points, query MLP, accumulate color/density # Returns rendered images matching input resolution pass # Mean squared error between rendered and ground truth images def calculatephotometricloss(rendered, groundtruth): return sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, groundtruth)) / len(rendered) # Coarse-to-fine positional encoding scheduler class CoarseToFineScheduler: def getfrequency(self, iteration, totaliterations=200000): return min(1.0, iteration / (totaliterations 0.5)) # Standard gradient-based optimizer update class Optimizer: def init(self, params, lr=0.001): self.params = params self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): for p in self.params: p.grad = [0.0] len(p) def step(self): for p in self.params: for i in range(len(p)): p[i] -= self.lr p.grad[i] optimizer = Optimizer([poses, nerfparams]) scheduler = CoarseToFineScheduler() for iteration in range(200000): currentfreq = scheduler.getfrequency(iteration) renderedimages = renderimages(poses, nerfparams, currentfreq) loss = calculatephotometricloss(renderedimages, images) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return poses, nerfparams This variant refers to the specific application of the BARF optimization within the global refinement stage. It is distinguished by its reliance on the global consistency provided by the synchronization step, allowing it to handle larger initial pose errors compared to local methods. It is chosen when high-accuracy novel view synthesis is required after global synchronization. It uses the default BARF settings: 200k iterations with coarse-to-fine positional encoding. Time Complexity: The method runs for 200,000 iterations. Each iteration involves rendering and backpropagation through the NeRF, which is computationally expensive. The total time depends on the scene complexity and hardware. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the NeRF MLP, camera poses, and intermediate rendering buffers. Performance: The method achieves accurate poses and scene representation suitable for realistic novel view synthesis. Strengths: High accuracy in both pose and scene reconstruction; leverages global consistency; robust to initial pose errors provided by synchronization. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to the large number of iterations; requires good initialization from the synchronization stage. When to use: When high-fidelity novel view synthesis is the primary goal and global pose estimates are available from a synchronization step. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or real-time performance is required. The method originates from the LU-NeRF paper, which proposes a pipeline for scene and pose estimation by synchronizing local unposed NeRFs. The global pose and scene refinement step is the final stage of this pipeline, referred to as LU-NeRF+Sync. It builds on the BARF (Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields) method, which was introduced to handle pose errors in NeRF optimization. The approach was developed to address the limitations of existing methods that struggle with large pose errors or require precise initial poses. The method has been evaluated on datasets such as Blender and Objectron, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving accurate pose and scene reconstruction. name: L2G-NeRF
head: Local-to-Global Registration for Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields
body: L2G-NeRF is a bundle-adjusting method for Neural Radiance Fields that jointly optimizes neural 3D representations and camera poses by combining a local photometric alignment objective with a global geometric alignment objective. It solves the problem of suboptimal solutions caused by poor initialization, which plagues purely parametric methods, and the inability to handle large displacements, which affects purely non-parametric methods. It sets itself apart by using a two-stage process: first, a pixel-wise flexible alignment (non-parametric) to initialize the solution, followed by a frame-wise constrained parametric alignment (global) to enforce geometric consistency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of M images \{Ii\}{i=1}^M, query pixel coordinates \{xj\}{j=1}^N (for 2D) or 3D ray coordinates (for 3D), and initial camera poses (typically identity). Outputs: Optimized neural field parameters \Theta, optimized camera poses \{Ti\}{i=1}^M, and local transformation fields \{T{ji}\}. Data Structures: 1. Neural Field MLP (fR): 3D NeRF: Input is 3D coordinate z \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output is 4D vector [c; \sigma] \in \mathbb{R}^4, where c is RGB color and \sigma is volume density. 2D Image: Input is 2D coordinate x \in \mathbb{R}^2. Output is 3D vector (RGB color). 2. Warp Neural Field MLP (fW): Input is 2D coordinate x \in \mathbb{R}^2 and frame-dependent embedding \elli \in \mathbb{R}^d. Output is a Lie algebra vector (se(2) for 2D rigid or sl(3) for 2D homography). 3. Camera Pose: Ti \in SE(3) for 3D, parametrized as [R|t]. R = \exp(r) via exponential map from \mathfrak{so}(3) to SO(3), t \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Local Transformation: T{ji} \in SE(2) or SL(3) for 2D, modeled by W(xj; \elli, \Phi). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize all camera poses to identity: Ti = I \quad \forall i. Perturb initial poses using right multiplication to alter viewing directions and distances. Additive noise is sampled from r \sim \mathcal{N}(0, nr I) and t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, nt I), where nr and nt are base multipliers. Initialize neural field parameters \Theta and warp field parameters \Phi. 2. Stage 1: Local Alignment (Non-Parametric): For each image i and pixel j, predict a local transformation T{ji} using the warp neural field: T{ji} = W(xj; \elli, \Phi) = \exp(fW(xj; \elli, \Phi)) where \exp(\cdot) maps the Lie algebra output to the Lie group (SE(2) or SL(3)). Optimize \Theta, \Phi, and \{\elli\} by minimizing the photometric reconstruction error between the rendered image and the target image Ii: \mathcal{L}{local} = \sum{i=1}^M \sum{j=1}^N \| R(T{ji} xj; \Theta) - Ii(xj) \|^2 For 3D NeRF, the rendering function R(T{ji} xj; \Theta) is computed via volume rendering. Given a ray defined by pixel x and depth z, the 3D point is z x. The color is: R(x) = \int{z{near}}^{z{far}} T(x, z) \sigma(zx) c(zx) dz where T(x, z) = \exp(-\int{z{near}}^z \sigma(z'x) dz'). Numerically, this is discretized using K points sampled along the ray at depths \{z1,..., zK\}: R(x) = g(y1,..., yK), \quad yk = fR(T zk x; \Theta) where g is the differentiable and deterministic compositing function. 3. Stage 2: Global Alignment (Parametric): Solve for the global frame-wise transformation T^i for each image i by minimizing the alignment error between the local transformations T{ji} and the global transformation Ti applied to the coordinates. This is an orthogonal Procrustes problem: T^i = \arg \min{Ti} \sum{j=1}^N \| T{ji} xj - Ti xj \|^2 The optimal rigid transformation T=[R|t] is computed in closed form using SVD. Let \bar{x} and \overline{Tx} be the centroids of \{xj\} and \{T{ji} xj\} respectively. Compute the covariance matrix H: H = \sum{j=1}^N (xj - \bar{x})(T{ji} xj - \overline{Tx})^T = U S V^T Then: R = V U^T, \quad t = -R\bar{x} + \overline{Tx} (Note: For homography, a similar linear system Aj h = 0 is solved). Apply a soft constraint to the local alignment by adding the global objective to the loss: \mathcal{L}{global} = \lambda \sum{i=1}^M \sum{j=1}^N \| T{ji} xj - T^i xj \|^2 Jointly optimize \Theta, \{Ti\}, \Phi, and \{\elli\} by minimizing the combined loss: \min{\{T{ji}\}, \Theta, \{Ti\}} \mathcal{L}{local} + \mathcal{L}{global} The pipeline executes sequentially: Stage 1 optimizes local transformations, and Stage 2 solves for global transformations to constrain them. 4. Convergence Schedule: Linearly increase noise multipliers nr and nt by a common factor \{nc\}{c=2}^9 starting from base values nr=0.01, nt=0.1 to aid convergence. Parameters: \lambda: Weighting factor for the global constraint. Set to 1 \times 10^2 for synthetic/object-centric scenes. For forward-facing LLFF scenes, floated between 1 \times 10^2 and 1 \times 10^5. nr: Base rotation noise multiplier. Scene-dependent, typically 0.01 to 0.09. nt: Base translation noise multiplier. Scene-dependent, typically 0.3 to 0.7. K: Number of points sampled along a ray for volume rendering discretization. \Theta: Neural field MLP weights. \Phi: Warp neural field MLP weights. \elli: Frame-dependent embedding for frame i. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Poor Initialization: Parametric methods alone fail if initialized poorly. Large Displacements: Non-parametric methods alone fail with large displacements. Identity Initialization for 360° Scenes: L2G-NeRF fails to recover camera poses from identity transformation for inward-facing 360° scenes with large rotation displacements. High \lambda: A large \lambda (1 \times 10^5) improves geometric accuracy but reduces robustness, potentially causing divergence (e.g., on the Flower scene). Removing Global Objective: Removing the global alignment objective causes the optimization to get stuck at suboptimal poses and produce ghosting artifacts. Time Complexity: More efficient than global registration methods (like BARF) because it computes gradients w.r.t. local pose rather than global pose. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti, L2G-NeRF takes ~4.5 hours for synthetic objects and ~8 hours for real-world scenes. BARF takes ~8 and ~10.5 hours respectively. Robustness: Tolerates larger noise perturbations before divergence than BARF (fails at nc=8 vs nc=4 for L2G-NeRF vs BARF). Strengths: High-fidelity reconstruction, resolves large camera pose misalignment, robust to poor initialization. Limitations: Fails on inward-facing 360° scenes with large rotations from identity init; sensitive to \lambda setting. When to use: When camera poses are unknown or poorly estimated, and standard NeRF optimization fails due to initialization issues. Suitable for both 2D neural images and 3D NeRF. L2G-NeRF was proposed in the paper "Local-to-Global Registration for Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the limitations of existing bundle-adjusting NeRF methods, which are susceptible to suboptimal solutions if poorly initialized (parametric methods) or unable to handle large displacements (non-parametric methods). The method builds on the concept of photometric bundle adjustment. name: CBARF
head: CBARF, Cascaded BA
body: CBARF is a 3D reconstruction method that optimizes imperfect camera poses using a cascaded bundle-adjustment (BA) structure to progressively refine poses and rectify erroneous ones. It builds on BARF by introducing a coarse-to-fine optimization strategy with distinct modulation factors for each stage, allowing it to handle larger initial pose errors (e.g., 30.4° rotation deviation) where standard BARF may overfit. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of images with imperfect camera poses \hat{P}, a NeRF backbone (BARF), and scene geometry parameters. Outputs: Refined camera poses Q, a trained NeRF model, and optionally synthetic images via a Voxel Grid Module (DVGO). Data Structures: Camera Pose: Represented as P \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}, defined as P = [Rp \ tp] where Rp \in SO(3) and tp \in \mathbb{R}^3. The last row of the standard 4 \times 4 projection matrix is dropped. Noise/Refinement Parameters: Represented in the Lie algebra \mathfrak{se}(3) as n \in \mathbb{R}^6. Transform Matrix: Derived from \mathfrak{se}(3) parameters, represented as N = [Rn \ tn]. Numbered Steps: 1. Simulate Imperfect Poses (Initialization): Generate noise n \in \mathfrak{se}(3) from a 6-dimensional random normal distribution: n = 0.35 \mathcal{N}(0, I) \in \mathbb{R}^6 Transform n into a camera transform matrix N = [Rn \ tn]. Compose this with the reference pose P = [Rp \ tp] to obtain the imperfect pose \hat{P}: \hat{P} = [Rp Rn \ tp + tn] Note: The coefficient 0.35 corresponds to an average deviation of 30.4° in rotation and 0.56 in translation. 2. Define Refined Pose Composition: Optimize camera poses by training camera refine parameters p \in \mathfrak{se}(3). Convert p into a transform matrix Pr = [Rr \ tr]. Compose Pr with \hat{P} to obtain the refined pose Q: Q = [Rp Rn Rr \ tp + tn + tr] 3. Cascaded Optimization Structure: Use a coarse-to-fine structure with compact BA modules, using the BARF network as the backbone. The process consists of three stages: Coarse, Recursive, and Fine. 4. Learning Rate Schedule: Calculate the learning rate using exponential interpolation with a modulation factor \alpha to bias learning towards the initial high value. The modulation factors for the three stages are: Coarse stage: \alpha = 10.0 Recursive stage: \alpha = 3.0 Fine stage: \alpha = 1.0 A factor of 1.0 corresponds to the original exponential learning rate used in BARF. 5. Handling Incomplete Poses (Optional): For incomplete camera poses, randomly drop 10% of poses to form a test set F, assigning an initial pose P{ini} to F. The remaining images form the training set T. Jointly optimize poses for both T and F during training. 6. Evaluation Alignment: Use Procrustes analysis to align optimized poses with ground-truth before evaluation to remove global offset. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation as R def se3exp(v): """Convert 6D se(3) vector to 3x4 transform matrix [R t]. """ omega, t = v[:3], v[3:] return np.hstack([R.fromrotvec(omega).asmatrix(), t.reshape(3, 1)]) def composeposes(Pref, N): """Compose reference pose Pref [3x4] with transform N [3x4]. """ Rp, tp = Pref[:,:3], Pref[:, 3:] Rn, tn = N[:,:3], N[:, 3:] return np.hstack([Rp @ Rn, tp + tn]) def procrustesalign(A, B): """Align set A to set B using Procrustes analysis. """ Ac, Bc = A - np.mean(A, axis=0), B - np.mean(B, axis=0) U,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Ac.T @ Bc) Ropt = Vt.T @ U.T if np.linalg.det(Ropt) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1; Ropt = Vt.T @ U.T return (B - np.mean(B, axis=0)) @ Ropt.T + np.mean(A, axis=0) def sampleraysatres(images, poses, res): """Sample rays and target colors at reduced resolution. """ # Standard ray marching implementation omitted for brevity; # returns rays (N, 3) and targets (N, 3) tensors. pass def cbarfoptimize(images, refposes, stagesconfig, incomplete=False): """ images: list of image tensors refposes: list of 3x4 matrices [Rp tp] stagesconfig: list of dicts {'iters': int, 'modulation': float, 'res': int} """ # 1. Simulate imperfect poses noise = 0.35 np.random.normal(0, 1, 6) N = se3exp(noise) imperfectposes = [composeposes(P, N) for P in refposes] # 2. Handle incomplete poses if incomplete: testindices = np.random.choice(len(images), size=int(0.1 len(images)), replace=False) trainsetT = [images[i] for i in range(len(images)) if i not in testindices] currentposes = imperfectposes else: trainsetT = images currentposes = imperfectposes # 3. Cascaded optimization nerf = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3, 256), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(256, 3)) # optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(nerf.parameters()), lr=1e-3) for stage in stagesconfig: iters = stage['iters'] mod = stage['modulation'] res = stage['res'] for step in range(iters): rays, targets = sampleraysatres(trainsetT, currentposes, res) pred = nerf(rays) loss = torch.nn.functional.mseloss(pred, targets) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # LR schedule with modulation currentlr = 1e-3 mod np.exp(-step / iters) for pg in optimizer.paramgroups: pg['lr'] = currentlr # Update poses with refined parameters p refinedp = optimizer.paramgroups[-1]['params'][0].detach().numpy() Pr = se3exp(refinedp) currentposes = [composeposes(P, Pr) for P in currentposes] # 4. Evaluation alignment alignedposes = procrustesalign(currentposes, refposes) return alignedposes, nerf Parameters: Noise Coefficient: 0.35 (for simulation). Iterations: 20k for Coarse and Recursive stages; 200k for Fine stage. Image Resolution: 400×400 during pose optimization (half of 800×800 training resolution). Modulation Factors: 10.0 (Coarse), 3.0 (Recursive), 1.0 (Fine). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Standard BARF may encounter overfitting before completing optimization with large initial errors; CBARF mitigates this via the cascaded structure. Global Offset: Optimized poses may have a misalignment with the ground-truth coordinate system. Procrustes analysis is required for evaluation but does not correct the pose during optimization. Incomplete Poses: Randomly dropping 10% of poses requires joint optimization of training and test sets, using rendering quality as an indirect metric for pose error in the absence of ground-truth for the test set. Total Iterations: 240k per scene (20k coarse + 20k recursive + 200k fine). Memory Usage: Uses the BARF backbone, which stores the NeRF MLP and camera parameters. Image resolution is reduced to 400×400 during optimization to improve efficiency. Performance: Successfully optimizes poses initialized with 30.4° average rotation deviation, whereas standard BARF overfits before completion. Rendering quality is comparable to ground-truth images. Strengths: Handles large initial pose errors; progressive refinement prevents overfitting. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of modulation factors; Procrustes alignment is needed for evaluation, implying the absolute pose is not directly optimized to a global frame without post-processing. CBARF was proposed in 2024 by authors publishing in the IEEE Transactions on Multimedia. It addresses the limitations of BARF in handling imperfect camera poses by introducing a cascaded BA structure. The method is used for 3D reconstruction from imperfect camera poses, including scenarios with incomplete pose data. CBARF: Cascaded Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Fields From Imperfect Camera Poses, https://doi.org/10.1109/tmm.2024.3388929, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adversarial and GAN-based Optimization
head: GAN-based NeRF, Adversarial Radiance Field Optimization
body: Adversarial and GAN-based Optimization methods enhance the photorealism and structural consistency of radiance fields by integrating a discriminator network into the training loop. Unlike standard photometric optimization which minimizes pixel-wise reconstruction errors, these methods enforce that rendered image patches follow the distribution of real image patches, thereby suppressing artifacts and improving high-frequency details. This family is distinct from pure geometric or photometric approaches [44-radiance-field-optimization.md] by introducing a game-theoretic component that provides gradient feedback for perceptual quality rather than just color accuracy. All methods in this family extend the standard radiance field optimization by adding an adversarial loss term. The core mechanism involves a discriminator D that distinguishes between real image patches and those rendered by the generator (the radiance field G or F\Theta). The optimization problem becomes a minimax game where the radiance field parameters \Theta are updated to fool the discriminator, while the discriminator parameters \eta are updated to correctly classify real vs. fake patches. The general adversarial loss formulation follows the minimax objective: \min\Theta \max\eta LA(\Theta, \eta) = \mathbb{E}{I \sim P{real}}[\log(D(I; \eta))] + \mathbb{E}{\hat{I} \sim P{fake}}[\log(1 - D(\hat{I}; \eta))] where P{real} is the distribution of real image patches and P{fake} is the distribution of generated patches. Common variations include patch-based discrimination to reduce memory usage and focus on local texture consistency GANeRF, gradient penalty terms (e.g., R1 penalty) to stabilize training and prevent mode collapse GANeRF, and VGG-based perceptual losses to ensure semantic consistency GANeRF. GNeRF is a two-phase framework that jointly optimizes camera poses and neural radiance fields from uncalibrated images using adversarial training GNeRF. It is designed for scenarios where Structure-from-Motion (SfM) fails due to low texture or complex outside-in configurations GNeRF. Unlike methods requiring rough initialization, GNeRF uses an inversion network to decouple pose estimation from direct photometric gradient propagation, which is prone to local minima GNeRF. It builds on Radiance-field optimization by introducing a GAN-based generator-discriminator pair GNeRF. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GNeRF(images, numiterations, lambdaweight, batchsize): """ GNeRF implementation. images: List of n RGB images. numiterations: Total optimization steps. lambdaweight: Weight for the inversion network penalty in hybrid loss. batchsize: Number of random poses sampled per iteration. """ # Framework-specific initialization FTheta = initializeNeRF() # MLP dim 360 DNu = initializeDiscriminator() # GRAF architecture EThetaE = initializeInversionNetwork() # Vision Transformer Phi = [IdentityPose() for in images] PriorPoseDist = getpriordistribution() optG = RMSprop(lr=0.0005) # Generator (NeRF) optD = RMSprop(lr=0.0001) # Discriminator optE = Adam(lr=0.0001) # Inversion Network optP = Adam(lr=0.005) # Camera Poses for iteration in range(numiterations): # --- Phase A: Adversarial Training --- randomposes = [PriorPoseDist.sample() for in range(batchsize)] renderedimages = [renderNeRF(FTheta, pose) for pose in randomposes] realpatches = dynamicpatchsample(images, size=16) fakepatches = dynamicpatchsample(renderedimages, size=16) lossD = adversarialloss(DNu, realpatches, fakepatches) DNu.update(lossD, optD) lossGadv = adversarialloss(DNu, realpatches, fakepatches, generator=True) FTheta.update(lossGadv, optG) predictedposes = [EThetaE(patch) for patch in fakepatches] lossE = sum(l2norm(pred - true) for pred, true in zip(predictedposes, randomposes)) EThetaE.update(lossE, optE) # --- Phase B: Photometric Refinement --- renderedestimates = [renderNeRF(FTheta, phi) for phi in Phi] lossN = sum(l2norm(img - est) for img, est in zip(images, renderedestimates)) estimatedposesfromE = [EThetaE(img) for img in images] lossPosePenalty = sum(l2norm(estphi - phi) for estphi, phi in zip(estimatedposesfromE, Phi)) lossR = lossN + lambdaweight lossPosePenalty FTheta.update(lossR, optG) for i in range(len(Phi)): Phi[i].update(lossR, optP) # Explicit pose embedding update loop GANeRF optimizes a 3D radiance field using a 2D adversarial loss to enforce 3D-consistent photorealism GANeRF. It differs from non-adversarial refinement methods like NeRFLiX by using direct backpropagation from a discriminator to a full-resolution NeRF GANeRF. It builds on Neural Radiance Fields by integrating a discriminator into the training loop with adversarial, VGG perceptual, and gradient penalty losses GANeRF. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainiteration(self, batch, outputs): # 1. Zero gradients self.optimizers.zerogradall() # 2. Check if adversarial loss is active if self.config.advlossmult > 0.0: # 3. Extract patches realpatches, fakepatches = self.getpatches(outputs, batch) # 4. Discriminator Loss predreal = self.rundiscriminator(realpatches) predfake = self.rundiscriminator(fakepatches) # Standard GAN loss terms (implied by getdiscriminatortrainlossdict) dlossdict = self.computedloss(realpatches, fakepatches) # Gradient Penalty gploss = self.computesimplegradientpenalty(realpatches) dlossdict["gploss"] = gploss self.config.gplossmult # Sum discriminator loss dloss = functools.reduce(torch.add, dlossdict.values()) # Update Discriminator dloss.backward() assert hasfinitegradients(self.discriminator.parameters()) self.discriminatoroptimizer.step() # 5. NeRF Loss nerflossdict = self.getnerftrainlossdict(outputs, batch) # Merge discriminator loss if active if self.config.advlossmult > 0.0: # Add adversarial loss to NeRF dict advloss = self.computeadvloss(fakepatches) nerflossdict["advloss"] = advloss self.config.advlossmult # Add VGG perceptual loss if configured if self.config.vgglossmult > 0.0: vggloss = self.computevggloss(outputs, batch) nerflossdict["vggloss"] = vggloss self.config.vgglossmult loss = functools.reduce(torch.add, nerflossdict.values()) # Update NeRF loss.backward() self.nerfoptimizer.step() This variant uses a patch discriminator to regularize 2D image fidelity, addressing view-inconsistent rendered color and texture. To overcome discriminator memorization due to limited training data, it employs differentiable augmentation T applied to both real and fake samples. The GAN loss components are: \mathcal{L}\text{D} =\mathbb{E}{\boldsymbol{x} \sim p{\text{data}}(\boldsymbol{x})}\left[f{D}(-D(T(\boldsymbol{x})))\right] +\mathbb{E}{\boldsymbol{z} \sim p(\boldsymbol{z})}\left[f{D}(D(T(G(\boldsymbol{z}))))\right] \mathcal{L}\text{G} =\mathbb{E}{\boldsymbol{z} \sim p(\boldsymbol{z})}\left[f{G}(-D(T(G(\boldsymbol{z}))))\right] \mathcal{L}\text{adv} = \mathcal{L}\text{D} + \mathcal{L}\text{G} where T refers to the augmentation applied on both real and fake samples. The GAN framework is trained using Hinge loss, so fD(x) = \max(0, 1 + x) and fG(x) = x. The discriminator architecture consists of a cascade of convolutional layers. This variant removes the GAN inversion step from the training pipeline. Renderings become blurry and uncanny because this step connects π-GAN training and reconstruction, significantly affecting overall performance. The integration of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) into volume rendering and NeRF optimization emerged to address the "blurry" or artifact-prone results of standard photometric loss minimization. Early works like SinNeRF demonstrated that adversarial training with local texture guidance could recover geometry and poses from uncalibrated single images. Subsequent works like Pix2NeRF focused on unsupervised conditional π-GAN translation for single-image to NeRF translation, while GANeRF GANeRF refined existing NeRFs for higher photorealism. The approach has become a standard component in high-fidelity radiance field training pipelines, often combined with perceptual losses and gradient penalties to stabilize the adversarial game. name: GNeRF
head: GAN-based Neural Radiance Field without Posed Camera
body: GNeRF is a method for novel view synthesis and camera pose estimation that operates without known camera poses. It solves the problem of reconstructing a neural radiance field and estimating camera extrinsics simultaneously in complex scenes, including those with low texture or repeated patterns where traditional Structure-from-Motion (SfM) fails. Unlike sibling methods like GANeRF which may rely on posed initialization or different adversarial strategies, GNeRF uniquely employs a two-phase hybrid optimization scheme: an initial adversarial phase to obtain coarse poses and a radiance field, followed by a regularized photometric refinement phase, interleaved iteratively to escape local minima. GNeRF jointly optimizes a neural radiance field F\Theta and a set of camera poses \Phi = \{\phi1, \dots, \phin\} for n input images I = \{I1, \dots, In\}. The method treats camera poses as latent variables and uses a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework combined with an inversion network to bootstrap the optimization. Inputs: A set of n uncalibrated RGB images I. No camera poses are provided; shared intrinsics are assumed fixed. Outputs: A trained neural radiance field F\Theta and estimated camera poses \Phi. Camera Pose Representation: To avoid discontinuities in quaternions or Euler angles, poses are represented using continuous embeddings: Translation (t): A 3D vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the camera position in Euclidean space. Rotation (r): A 6D vector r \in \mathbb{R}^6. Given a rotation matrix R = [a1, a2, a3] \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, r is formed by dropping the last column (r = [a1, a2]). The original matrix can be recovered via Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization. Intrinsics: The method assumes a SIMPLE PINHOLE model with shared intrinsics across all views: focal length f, and principal point (cx, cy). Neural Radiance Field (F\Theta): Input: 3D location x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction d \in [-\pi, \pi]^2. Output: Emitted color c \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma. Architecture: Based on the original NeRF [32] with hierarchical sampling. Both coarse and fine sampling use 64 points. The MLP dimension is increased from 256 to 360 to maintain parameter count parity with the original NeRF while aligning coarse and fine pose spaces. Discriminator (D\eta): Architecture: Follows GRAF. Uses instance normalization over features and spectral normalization over weights. Input: Image patches. Inversion Network (E{\thetaE}): Architecture: Vision Transformer. The final layer is modified to output a camera pose (translation and rotation embeddings). Input: Image patches. Output: Estimated camera pose. 1. Initialization: Set all camera extrinsics to the identity matrix. Initialize the NeRF model F\Theta and discriminator D\eta. Define a prior pose distribution P(\phi) for random sampling. For Synthetic-NeRF, cameras are uniformly distributed on the upper hemisphere towards the origin. For DTU, cameras are on the upper hemisphere with azimuth [0, 150]^\circ and lookat points from N(0, 0.012). 2. Phase A: Pose-free NeRF Estimation (Adversarial Training): Generator: Sample a random camera pose \phi \sim P(\phi). Query F\Theta with \phi to render an image \hat{I} = G(\phi; F\Theta) using NeRF volume rendering. Dynamic Patch Sampling: Decompose \hat{I} and real images I into patches of fixed size 16 \times 16 with dynamic scale and random offset. Discriminator Update: Train D\eta to distinguish real patches Pd(I) from generated patches Pg(I|\Theta) using the adversarial loss LA: \min\Theta \max\eta LA(\Theta, \eta) = \mathbb{E}{I \sim Pd}[\log(D(I; \eta))] + \mathbb{E}{\hat{I} \sim Pg}[\log(1 - D(\hat{I}; \eta))] Inversion Network Training: Train E{\thetaE} to map generated image patches back to their corresponding sampled poses \phi using self-supervised loss LE: LE(\thetaE) = \mathbb{E}{\phi \sim P(\phi)} \| E(G(\phi; F\Theta); \thetaE) - \phi \|2^2 Repeat until convergence to obtain a coarse radiance field and initial pose estimates \Phi^0 = \{ E(Ii; \thetaE) \}{i=1}^n for the real training images. 3. Phase B: Regularized Learning Strategy (Photometric Refinement): Static Patch Sampling: For pose optimization, uniformly sample patches of fixed size 64 \times 64 across the whole image domain to estimate poses. Intrinsic Scaling: Scale camera intrinsics at the beginning to maximize receptive field, then progressively increase to the original value to focus on fine details. Hybrid Loss Optimization: Refine F\Theta and \Phi by minimizing the hybrid loss LR: LR(\Theta, \Phi) = LN(\Theta, \Phi) + \lambda \sum{i=1}^n \| E(Ii; \thetaE) - \phii \|2^2 where LN is the photometric reconstruction error: LN(\Theta, \Phi) = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n \| Ii - \hat{I}i \|2^2, \quad \hat{I}i = G(\phii; F\Theta) and \lambda is a weighting coefficient. 4. Iterative Hybrid Optimization: Interleave Phase A and Phase B in the pattern 'A, AB...AB, B'. This iterative scheme overcomes local minima that arise from directly propagating photometric loss to pose parameters, which is sensitive to low-texture conditions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GNeRF(images, numiterations, lambdaweight): # 1. Initialization FTheta = NeRFMLP(dim=360) # Hierarchical sampling: 64 coarse + 64 fine points DNu = DiscriminatorGRAF() # Instance normalization on features, spectral normalization on weights EThetaE = VisionTransformerPose() # Outputs 9D pose embedding (3 translation + 6 rotation) Phi = [IdentityPose() for in images] # Initialize extrinsics to identity matrix PriorPoseDist = UpperHemispherePrior() # Synthetic-NeRF: uniform upper hemisphere towards origin for iteration in range(numiterations): # --- Phase A: Adversarial Training --- batchsize = 16 randomposes = [PriorPoseDist.sample() for in range(batchsize)] renderedimages = [rendervolume(FTheta, pose) for pose in randomposes] realpatches = dynamicpatchsample(images, size=16) fakepatches = dynamicpatchsample(renderedimages, size=16) lossD = computeadversarialloss(DNu, realpatches, fakepatches) updateparameters(DNu, lossD, lr=0.0001, optimizer='RMSprop') lossGadv = computeadversarialloss(DNu, realpatches, fakepatches, generator=True) updateparameters(FTheta, lossGadv, lr=0.0005, optimizer='RMSprop') predictedposes = [EThetaE(patch) for patch in fakepatches] lossE = sum(l2norm(pred - true) for pred, true in zip(predictedposes, randomposes)) updateparameters(EThetaE, lossE, lr=0.0001, optimizer='Adam') # --- Phase B: Photometric Refinement --- scaleintrinsics(iteration, startscale=2.0, endscale=1.0) renderedestimates = [rendervolume(FTheta, phi) for phi in Phi] lossN = sum(l2norm(img - est) for img, est in zip(images, renderedestimates)) estimatedposesfromE = [EThetaE(img) for img in images] lossPosePenalty = sum(l2norm(estphi - phi) for estphi, phi in zip(estimatedposesfromE, Phi)) lossR = lossN + lambdaweight lossPosePenalty updateparameters(FTheta, lossR, lr=0.0005, optimizer='RMSprop') updateparameters(Phi, lossR, lr=0.005, optimizer='Adam') def NeRFMLP(dim): return MLP(hiddendim=dim, sampling=64) def DiscriminatorGRAF(): return CNN(norm=['instance', 'spectral']) def VisionTransformerPose(): return ViT(outputdim=9) def IdentityPose(): return np.eye(4) def UpperHemispherePrior(): return UniformUpperHemisphere() def rendervolume(model, pose): return volumerendering(model, pose) def dynamicpatchsample(imgs, size): return randomcrop(imgs, size=size, scale=True) def computeadversarialloss(D, real, fake, generator=False): if generator: return -mean(log(D(fake))) return mean(log(D(real))) + mean(log(1 - D(fake))) def updateparameters(params, loss, lr, optimizer): grad = computegradients(params, loss) if optimizer == 'RMSprop': params -= lr grad / (sqrt(runningmean(grad2)) + 1e-8) else: # Adam params -= lr (momentum + grad) / (sqrt(variance + 1e-8)) def scaleintrinsics(iter, start, end): pass # Progressive scaling logic def l2norm(a, b): return np.linalg.norm(a - b) Local Minima: Directly propagating photometric loss to camera poses is prone to local minima, especially in low-texture scenes. The hybrid iterative scheme is required to mitigate this. Inversion Network Limitations: The inversion network accepts limited-size patches, restricting pose accuracy. It may underperform COLMAP on scenes with sufficient reliable keypoints. Rotation Representation: Quaternions and Euler angles are avoided due to discontinuities; the 6D embedding is used instead. Intrinsic Scaling: Failure to progressively scale intrinsics may hinder convergence on fine details. Time Complexity: Training is computationally intensive. On a single Nvidia RTX TITAN GPU, training takes approximately 30 hours per scene. Memory Complexity: Uses dynamic patch sampling (16 \times 16) for GAN training to reduce memory usage compared to full-image discrimination. Performance: On the DTU dataset, GNeRF outperforms COLMAP-based NeRF. On Synthetic-NeRF, it is slightly outperformed by COLMAP-based NeRF but handles challenging scenes (repeated patterns, low texture) better. Strengths: Does not require camera pose initialization or masks. Robust to low-texture and repeated pattern scenes where SfM fails. Limitations: Pose accuracy is lower than COLMAP on standard scenes with good keypoints. GNeRF was introduced in 2021 by Meng et al. as a GAN-based framework for unposed neural radiance field reconstruction and camera pose estimation. It extends the NeRF framework by integrating adversarial training and an inversion network to handle scenarios where camera poses are completely unknown. It is evaluated on Synthetic-NeRF and DTU datasets. name: GANeRF
head: Adversarial Loss for GANerf, Adversarial NeRF Training, GAN-based NeRF Optimization, GANeRF Adversarial Training Loop, GANeRF
body:
GANeRF optimizes a 3D radiance field representation using a 2D adversarial loss, where a discriminator learns the distribution of image patches and provides gradient feedback to the NeRF to enforce 3D-consistent photorealism. It solves the problem of quality degradation in novel view synthesis caused by imperfect input data, such as limited coverage, image distortion, or illumination changes. Unlike standard NeRF optimization which relies solely on photometric reconstruction losses, GANeRF distinguishes itself by directly backpropagating gradients from a 2D patch discriminator into the 3D scene representation. It differs from GNeRF by focusing on patch-based discrimination for local realism, and from Test-time Adversarial Optimization by its integration directly into the training loop rather than a post-processing stage. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of posed input images capturing a static 3D scene; a base NeRF architecture (e.g., Nerfacto). Outputs: An optimized 3D radiance field representation capable of synthesizing photorealistic novel views. Data Structures: The implementation relies on the Nerfstudio framework structures: GanerfPipelineConfig: Extends VanillaPipelineConfig to include discriminator components. GanerfModelConfig: Extends the base model to include discriminator loss computation hooks. GanerfTrainerConfig: Extends the trainer to handle the adversarial training loop. Discriminator: A discriminator network that distinguishes between real and fake image patches. Patches: Extracted from rendered RGB images and ground truth images. Patches are reshaped from (B, H, W, 3) to (B, 3, H, W) and potentially unfolded to match the discriminator's resolution. Parameters: advlossmult: Multiplier for the adversarial loss. Default: 0.0003. vgglossmult: Multiplier for VGG perceptual loss. Default: 0.0003. gplossmult: Multiplier for gradient penalty loss. Default: 0.2. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set up the NeRF model and the 2D discriminator. Initialize optimizers for both the NeRF parameters \Theta and the discriminator parameters \eta. 2. Iteration Start: For each training iteration, retrieve a batch of rays and corresponding ground truth images. 3. NeRF Forward Pass: Render the scene using the current NeRF parameters \Theta to generate predicted RGB images \hat{I}. 4. Patch Extraction: Extract patches from the rendered images \hat{I} and the ground truth images I. Reshape patches to (B, 3, Hp, Wp) and normalize if required (e.g., 2.0 \cdot x - 1.0). 5. Discriminator Forward Pass (Fake): Pass the fake patches \hat{P} through the discriminator D to get predictions pred{fake} = D(\hat{P}; \eta). 6. Discriminator Forward Pass (Real): Pass the real patches P through the discriminator D to get predictions pred{real} = D(P; \eta). 7. Compute Discriminator Loss: Calculate the discriminator loss LD using the real and fake predictions. This includes the standard adversarial loss and a gradient penalty (R1) to stabilize training. L{adv} = 	ext{mean}(	ext{softplus}(-pred{fake})). Gradient penalty is computed on real patches. 8. Update Discriminator: Zero gradients for the discriminator optimizer. Compute LD. Backpropagate LD to update \eta. Verify gradients are finite. Step the discriminator optimizer. 9. Compute NeRF Loss: Calculate the standard reconstruction loss (e.g., L1) between \hat{I} and I. Calculate the adversarial loss for the NeRF: L{adv
erf} = 	ext{mean}(	ext{softplus}(-D(\hat{P}; \eta))). Calculate VGG perceptual loss if enabled. Combine losses: L{total} = L{rec} + \lambda{adv} L{adv
erf} + \lambda{vgg} L{vgg}. 10. Update NeRF: Zero gradients for the NeRF optimizer. Backpropagate L{total} through the discriminator (if using the discriminator's output directly) and into the NeRF parameters \Theta. Step the NeRF optimizer. Formulas: Adversarial Loss (for NeRF): L{adv} = \mathbb{E}{\hat{P} \sim P{fake}}[	ext{softplus}(-D(\hat{P}; \eta))] where 	ext{softplus}(x) = \log(1 + e^x). Gradient Penalty (R1): L{gp} =  rac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}{P \sim P{real}}[\|
ablaP D(P; \eta)\|2^2] where 
ablaP is the gradient of the discriminator output with respect to the input patch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softplus(x): return torch.log(1 + torch.exp(x)) def trainiteration(model, discriminator, batch, config): """ Performs one training iteration for GANeRF. model: The NeRF model (generator). discriminator: The 2D patch discriminator. batch: Dictionary containing 'rays' and 'gtimages'. config: Configuration object with advlossmult, vgglossmult, gplossmult. """ # 1. Render scene rays = batch['rays'] gtimages = batch['gtimages'] renderedoutputs = model(rays) renderedimages = renderedoutputs['rgb'] # Shape: (B, H, W, 3) # 2. Extract patches # getpatches handles reshaping to (B, 3, Hp, Wp) and normalization realpatches, fakepatches = model.getpatches(renderedoutputs, batch) # 3. Discriminator Training if config.advlossmult > 0.0: discriminator.zerograd() predreal = discriminator(realpatches) predfake = discriminator(fakepatches) # Standard GAN loss for discriminator dlossreal = softplus(-predreal).mean() dlossfake = softplus(predfake).mean() # R1 Gradient Penalty realpatches.requiresgrad(True) predrealgp = discriminator(realpatches) gradients = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=[predrealgp.sum()], inputs=[realpatches], creategraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] r1penalty = gradients.square().sum([1, 2, 3]).mean() gploss = config.gplossmult r1penalty / 2 dloss = dlossreal + dlossfake + gploss dloss.backward() discriminator.optimizer.step() # 4. NeRF Training model.zerograd() # Reconstruction Loss (L1) recloss = torch.mean(torch.abs(renderedimages - gtimages)) # Adversarial Loss for NeRF predfakenerf = discriminator(fakepatches) advloss = softplus(-predfakenerf).mean() # VGG perceptual loss computation (not given in sources) # vggloss =... # Total Loss totalloss = recloss + config.advlossmult advloss + config.vgglossmult vggloss # Backprop and step NeRF totalloss.backward() model.optimizer.step() return totalloss, advloss, dloss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Limited Coverage: In regions with sparse input observations, the discriminator may overfit to the observed distribution, requiring careful tuning of loss multipliers to maintain 3D consistency. Gradient Verification: Gradients must be verified as finite after the discriminator update to prevent NaN propagation into the NeRF parameters. Conditional Adversarial Loss is a regularization term used in differentiable volume rendering optimization to enforce photorealism and suppress blurry or distorted artifacts in rendered novel views. It distinguishes itself from standard reconstruction losses by employing a conditional discriminator that evaluates image pairs (rendered vs. target) from the same viewpoint, thereby preventing GAN mode collapse and ensuring 3D consistency across edited scenes. FENeRF uses semantic masks to edit the volume field via GAN inversion to enhance 3D GAN perception technology editability. Measured Performance: Evaluated on challenging indoor scenes from the ScanNet++ and Tanks and Temples datasets. GANeRF achieves significant improvements in perceptual metrics like LPIPS (reductions between 28-48%) while maintaining consistently better PSNR and SSIM scores compared to baselines like Nerfacto. Strengths: Mitigates quality degradation from imperfect input data (limited coverage, distortion, illumination changes). Enforces 3D-consistent photorealism. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of adversarial loss multipliers. May introduce artifacts if the discriminator is not well-trained. When to use: When photorealism and texture detail are critical, and the input data is imperfect or limited. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited, or when strict geometric accuracy is prioritized over photorealism. GANeRF was introduced by Barbara Roessle, Norman Müller, Lorenzo Porzi, Samuel Rota Bulò, Peter Kontschieder, and Matthias Nießner. It builds on the Nerfacto model. The method leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to improve NeRF quality in challenging real-world scenarios. It is related to concurrent work like NeRFLiX but differs in its adversarial formulation.
