name: SinNeRF Loss and Annealing Strategy
head: SinNeRF Total Loss and Annealing
body: This method defines the composite objective function and its temporal scheduling for optimizing the SinNeRF radiance field. It solves the problem of balancing global structural coherence with local high-frequency detail reconstruction during single-image NeRF training. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hard Sample Mining by explicitly decoupling global structure supervision from local texture guidance via distinct loss terms (\mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{adv}}) and annealing their weights inversely to the training stride. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Current training iteration t, total training iterations T, initial weights \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3, and computed loss components \mathcal{L}{\text{pix}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{adv}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}}. Outputs: Scalar total loss \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} for backpropagation. Data Structures Loss weights: A vector or dictionary mapping loss keys to scalar floats. Annealing schedule: Linear interpolation parameters derived from t/T. Formulas The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{pix}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{adv}} + \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} Where: \mathcal{L}{\text{pix}}: Pixel-wise reconstruction loss (e.g., L1 or L2). \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}}: Geometric regularization loss. \mathcal{L}{\text{adv}}: Adversarial loss for local texture guidance. \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}}: Classification loss (using DINO-ViT) for global structure prior. \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: Time-dependent weighting factors. Parameters Initial weights: \lambda1 = 8, \lambda2 = 0.1, \lambda3 = 0. Annealing targets: \lambda2 decreases to 0; \lambda3 increases to 0.1. Algorithm 1. Compute base losses \mathcal{L}{\text{pix}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{geo}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{adv}}, \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} for the current batch/patch. 2. Calculate the annealing coefficient \alpha = t / T (clamped to [0, 1]). 3. Update weights linearly: \lambda2(t) = 0.1 \times (1 - \alpha) \lambda3(t) = 0.1 \times \alpha \lambda1 remains constant at 8. 4. Compute \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} using the formula above. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesinnerfloss(lpix, lgeo, ladv, lcls, t, T): # Initial weights lambda1 = 8.0 lambda2init = 0.1 lambda3init = 0.0 lambda3target = 0.1 # Linear annealing schedule # alpha goes from 0 to 1 as t goes from 0 to T alpha = min(max(t / T, 0.0), 1.0) # Update weights # lambda2 decreases from 0.1 to 0 lambda2 = lambda2init (1.0 - alpha) # lambda3 increases from 0 to 0.1 lambda3 = lambda3init + (lambda3target - lambda3init) alpha # Total loss calculation ltotal = lpix + (lambda1 lgeo) + (lambda2 ladv) + (lambda3 lcls) return ltotal Edge Cases and Pitfalls Stride Dependency: The annealing strategy is coupled with the sampling stride. Early training uses large strides (covering major regions), justifying high \lambda3. Late training uses small strides (high-frequency details), requiring high \lambda2. If stride scheduling is decoupled from loss annealing, the model may over-smooth or produce artifacts. Zero Weighting: At t=0, \lambda3=0, meaning no global structure prior is applied initially. At t=T, \lambda2=0, meaning adversarial texture guidance is dropped. Ensure the respective loss terms are computed even if their weight is zero to avoid graph errors, or conditionally skip computation if performance is critical. A technique used in related Visual Error Tomography (VET) frameworks to transition the alpha renderer to traditional depth testing. It uses a sigmoid narrowing factor f to control the smoothness of this transition. Large values of f cause abrupt changes during training, impacting quality. The recommended value is f = 0.01. On the Redwood Chair scene, switching after 400 epochs (final at 600) with f=10^{-2} yields an LPIPS of 0.186, compared to 0.200 for f=100 and 0.191 for f=10^{-3}. Complexity: The addition of \mathcal{L}{\text{cls}} (DINO-ViT) and \mathcal{L}{\text{adv}} (Discriminator) significantly increases computational cost per iteration compared to standard NeRF, requiring resizing patches to 224 \times 224 for DINO-ViT. Performance: The annealing strategy allows the model to first capture global geometry and then refine textures. Without this, the model may struggle to converge on complex scenes from a single image. Limitations: The method relies on the availability of a pre-trained DINO-ViT and a GAN discriminator, increasing memory footprint and implementation complexity. The linear annealing is simple but may not be optimal for all scene complexities; however, it is the standard setting provided in the source. SinNeRF was introduced by to address the limitations of training Neural Radiance Fields from a single image, where lack of multi-view consistency leads to artifacts. The method builds on the original NeRF architecture but incorporates external priors (geometric, adversarial, and semantic) to constrain the solution space. The specific loss weighting strategy was designed to mimic a coarse-to-fine optimization process, aligning with the decreasing stride used in ray sampling. name: DeRF (Decomposed Radiance Fields)
head: Decomposed Radiance Fields
body: DeRF mitigates the high computational cost of neural volume rendering by spatially decomposing a scene into multiple parts, each represented by a smaller neural network, allowing for near-constant inference time regardless of the number of parts. It addresses the diminishing returns in rendering quality when scaling network capacity by using multiple smaller networks instead of one large network, providing up to 3× more efficient inference than Neural Radiance Fields with the same quality, or up to 1.0 dB PSNR improvement for the same cost. DeRF builds on Radiance-field optimization by replacing the single global network with a set of N local networks, activated via a differentiable spatial partition. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray \mathbf{r}, number of decomposition parts N, Voronoi sites \phi \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}, temperature \beta, and network weights \theta = \{\thetan\}{n=1}^N. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and gradients for optimization. Data Structures: Voronoi Sites (\phi): A tensor of shape (N, 3) storing the 3D coordinates of the N Voronoi centers. Network Heads (\thetan): N pairs of neural networks (\sigma{\thetan}, \mathbf{c}{\thetan}). Each network takes a 3D position \mathbf{x} (and direction \mathbf{d} for color) and outputs density and color. Weights (w{\phin}(\mathbf{x})): Computed on-the-fly using the soft Voronoi formula. Formulas: The radiance field functions \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) are modeled as a weighted sum of N separate functions: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{n=1}^{N} w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) \sigma{\thetan}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \sum{n=1}^{N} w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{c}{\thetan}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) The soft Voronoi weight w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) is computed using a softmax over squared distances to Voronoi sites \phi: w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(-\beta \|\mathbf{x} - \phin\|^2)}{\sum{j=1}^{N} \exp(-\beta \|\mathbf{x} - \phij\|^2)} where \beta > 0 is a temperature parameter controlling the softness of the Voronoi approximation. As \beta \to \infty, the weights approach a hard partition where only one w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}) is non-zero. Parameters: N: Number of neural network heads. Typical values depend on scene complexity; the paper uses N=16 for experiments. \beta: Temperature parameter. Scheduled from a low value to a high value during training to transition from soft to hard partitioning. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-training: Train coarse global networks \sigma{\text{coarse}} and \mathbf{c}{\text{coarse}} for the entire scene for approximately 100k iterations. 2. Decomposition Optimization: Optimize the coarse network weights \theta{\text{coarse}} and Voronoi sites \phi separately. Minimize reconstruction loss \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}} for \theta{\text{coarse}} and uniformity loss \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} for \phi. The uniformity loss is defined as \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} = \|\mathbb{E}{\mathbf{r} \sim \mathcal{R}}[W{\phi}(\mathbf{r})]\|2^2, where W{\phi}(\mathbf{r}) \in \mathbb{R}^N is the vector of soft Voronoi weights for points sampled along ray \mathbf{r}. This encourages equal usage of all heads. Pitfall: Do not allow \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} to affect the optimization of \theta{\text{coarse}}, as it inhibits the density network's ability to learn scene structure. 3. Local Network Training: Fix \phi and train the per-decomposition networks \sigma{\thetan} and \mathbf{c}{\thetan} using only \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}}. 4. Inference: For a given ray \mathbf{r}, sample points \mathbf{x}i. Compute w{\phin}(\mathbf{x}i) for all n. Identify the index n^ with the maximum weight to evaluate only the corresponding head \sigma{\theta{n^}} and \mathbf{c}{\theta{n^}}, leveraging the Painter's Algorithm for compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DeRFHead(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim): super().init() self.netdensity = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(3, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) self.netcolor = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hiddendim, 3)) def forward(self, x, d): sigma = self.netdensity(x) c = self.netcolor(torch.cat([x, d], dim=-1)) return sigma, c class DeRF: def init(self, N, hiddendim, betainit=1.0, betafinal=1000.0): self.N = N self.betainit = betainit self.beta = betainit self.betafinal = betafinal self.heads = nn.ModuleList([DeRFHead(hiddendim) for in range(N)]) self.phi = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N, 3) 10.0) self.coarsesigma = nn.Linear(3, 1) self.coarsecolor = nn.Linear(6, 3) def computeweights(self, x): dists = torch.cdist(x, self.phi, p=2) 2 return torch.softmax(-self.beta dists, dim=-1) def forward(self, x, d, inference=False): weights = self.computeweights(x) if inference: idx = torch.argmax(weights, dim=-1) sigman, cn = self.headsidx return sigman, cn else: sigmasum = torch.zeroslike(x[:,:1]) csum = torch.zeroslike(x[:,:3]) for n in range(self.N): sigman, cn = self.headsn wn = weights[:, n:n+1] sigmasum += wn sigman csum += wn cn return sigmasum, csum def schedulebeta(self, step, totalsteps): self.beta = self.betainit + (self.betafinal - self.betainit) (step / totalsteps) A specific training protocol to stabilize the decomposition and local network training. 1. Pre-train coarse networks: Train \sigma{\text{coarse}} and \mathbf{c}{\text{coarse}} for the entire scene for ≈100k iterations. 2. Separate Optimization: Optimize \theta{\text{coarse}} and \phi separately. Minimize \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}} for \theta{\text{coarse}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} for \phi. 3. Local Training: Fix \phi and train \sigma{\thetan} and \mathbf{c}{\thetan} using \mathcal{L}{\text{radiance}} only. Pitfall: Allowing \mathcal{L}{\text{uniform}} to affect \theta{\text{coarse}} inhibits density learning and causes instability. Time Complexity: Near-constant inference time with respect to the number of decomposed parts N, as only one head is evaluated per point during inference. Memory Complexity: Lower than NeRF for equivalent quality, as smaller networks are used. Performance: Up to 3× more efficient inference than NeRF with the same rendering quality, or up to 1.0 dB PSNR improvement for the same inference cost on real-world scenes. Strengths: Mitigates diminishing returns of network capacity; compatible with Painter's Algorithm for GPU-friendly rendering. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of \beta and training phases; random decomposition is not appropriate due to memory access patterns. DeRF was proposed by Daniel Rebain, Wei Jiang, Soroosh Yazdani, Ke Li, Kwang Moo Yi, and Andrea Tagliasacchi from the University of British Columbia, University of Toronto, Simon Fraser University, and Google Research. It was published in arXiv:2011.12490v1 on 25 Nov 2020 and later in CVPR 2021. The method addresses the computational intensity of NeRF by leveraging the observation that there are diminishing returns in employing larger networks, proposing spatial decomposition with smaller networks instead. name: Dual Rendering Equation Optimization
head: Deformable Radiance Field Optimization, Volume Rendering and Optimization, Volume and Surface Rendering Loss
body: Dual Rendering Equation Optimization (DREO) is a differentiable volume rendering method that jointly optimizes scene geometry and appearance by minimizing a combined loss derived from two distinct rendering equations: one for volumetric density accumulation and one for surface reflectance. Unlike standard NeRF which relies solely on volumetric integration, DREO explicitly models surface normals and BRDF properties to enable relighting. It differs from Deformable and Dynamic Fields by focusing on the dual-equation loss formulation rather than temporal deformation fields, and from Surface-SDF Representation by using a neural radiance field tensor optimized via volume rendering integrals rather than explicit signed distance functions. The method optimizes a scene tensor (representing density, color, and BRDF parameters) by jointly minimizing losses from two rendering passes. Inputs: Camera poses, input images C{gt}, and optionally ground truth normals n{gt}. Outputs: Optimized scene tensor parameters, rendered colors, and surface normals. The scene is represented as a tensor field encoding density \sigma, color c, and BRDF parameters. Specific internal layouts (e.g., voxel grid vs. MLP) are not detailed in the primary source. 1. Volume Rendering Pass: Emit a ray r(t) = o + td from origin o in direction d. Sample N points along the ray. Compute density-weighted color accumulation using the volume rendering equation: C{vl}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci, \quad Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) where \deltai is the distance between consecutive samples. 2. Surface Rendering Pass: For surface points x, compute the reflected radiance L(x, d). Approximate the surface integral of the reflectance equation using the incident light field Li(x, d) and normal n: L(x, d) = bval \cdot Li(x, d) (n \cdot d) where bval is the BRDF value decoded by a decoder B{dec}. 3. Loss Evaluation: Compute the total loss combining surface rendering, volume rendering, and normal consistency: loss = \lambda1 || L(x, d) - C{gt} ||2^2 + \lambda2 || C{vl}(r) - C{gt} ||2^2 + \lambda3 || n - n{gt} ||2^2 where \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3 are loss weights. 4. Optimization: Update the scene tensor parameters to minimize the loss. Schedule: Set \lambda1 = 0 during early iterations before the scene surface is obtained. Once a threshold is reached, gradually decrease \lambda2 in subsequent iterations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualrenderingoptimization(cameras, gtcolors, gtnormals, numiterations, surfacethreshold, decayrate, lambda1init, lambda2init, lambda3init): # Initialize scene tensor parameters (density sigma, color c, BRDF decoder weights) sceneparams = initializesceneparameters() lambda1 = lambda1init lambda2 = lambda2init lambda3 = lambda3init for iteration in range(numiterations): # Sample camera rays and points along them rays = sampleraysfromcameras(cameras) points = samplepointsalongrays(rays, numsamples=128) # Query scene tensor for density, color, and normal sigma, c, n = queryscenetensor(sceneparams, points) # Compute distances between consecutive samples deltas = computesegmentlengths(points) # Volume Rendering Pass T = 1.0 Cvl = 0.0 for i in range(len(points)): alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma[i] deltas[i]) Cvl += T alpha c[i] T = exp(-sigma[i] deltas[i]) # Surface Rendering Pass # Compute incident light field Li(x, d) from environment or precomputed field Li = computeincidentlightfield(points, rays.direction) bval = decodebrdf(sceneparams, points) Lsurf = bval Li dot(n, rays.direction) # Loss Evaluation lossvol = meansquarederror(Cvl, gtcolors) losssurf = meansquarederror(Lsurf, gtcolors) lossnorm = meansquarederror(n, gtnormals) if gtnormals is not None else 0.0 totalloss = lambda1 losssurf + lambda2 lossvol + lambda3 lossnorm # Optimization Step # Compute gradients w.r.t. scene parameters and apply optimizer step gradients = computegradients(totalloss, sceneparams) sceneparams = optimizerstep(sceneparams, gradients) # Loss Weight Schedule if iteration > surfacethreshold: lambda1 = 1.0 lambda2 = decayrate return sceneparams \lambda1, \lambda2, \lambda3: Loss weights for surface rendering, volume rendering, and normal consistency, respectively. bval: BRDF value decoded by the BRDF decoder B{dec}. Ti: Discretization calculation of transmittance. Early Training: Surface loss (\lambda1) must be zero initially because the scene surface is not yet well-defined; enabling it too early leads to poor convergence. Lighting Approximation: The surface integral is approximated using an incident light field, which may introduce errors if the lighting is complex or dynamic. BRDF Decoder: The choice of BRDF model (e.g., simplified Disney principle-based) depends on the scene dataset characteristics. This method synthesizes a 3D volumetric texture (specifically cloud volumes) from a single input photograph by minimizing an energy function that measures the distance between the input image pixel blocks and the rendered voxel blocks. It adapts the patch-based texture synthesis technique of Kwatra et al. to the 3D volume domain, treating voxel blocks as the fundamental units of synthesis. Unlike standard volume rendering which uses fixed parameters, this method optimizes the voxel values themselves to match visual evidence. It is distinguished from its parent Dual Rendering Equation Optimization by explicitly solving for the volume geometry/appearance via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework rather than optimizing only lighting parameters. This variant renders Gaussians twice using a differentiable rasterizer: once for the C-ToF view to compute the quad loss, and once for the RGB view to compute the color loss. It enables joint optimization of depth and color from multi-view data, leveraging the complementary information from both modalities. This variant processes full images instead of randomly sampled subsets for reconstruction, using 8-10 reference views per task. It employs recursive control variates to reduce primal rendering overhead, requiring ~4-8 times fewer samples than plain DRT to reach similar quality, while the adjoint phase runtime remains identical. Control variates alleviate the need for large sample counts required by L1 loss to mitigate loss function bias. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The dual-equation approach requires two rendering passes per iteration, increasing computational cost compared to single-equation methods. Strengths: Joint optimization of volume and surface cues improves reconstruction quality. Explicit BRDF modeling enables relighting. Limitations: The method requires careful scheduling of loss weights and depends on the incident light field approximation. BRDF modeling requires dataset-specific decoder tuning. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Dual Rendering Equation Optimization was introduced in the paper "STensoRRF: Tensorial Able Relighting Radiance Field for Single-Tensor Scene Representation". The method builds on the principles of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and differentiable rendering, extending them to include surface reflectance modeling. It addresses the limitations of standard NeRF in handling complex lighting and geometry by incorporating a surface rendering equation alongside the volume rendering equation. name: Texture Optimization for Volume Synthesis
head: Kwatra et al. method adaptation
body: This method synthesizes a 3D volumetric texture (specifically cloud volumes) from a single input photograph by minimizing an energy function that measures the distance between the input image pixel blocks and the rendered voxel blocks. It adapts the patch-based texture synthesis technique of Kwatra et al. to the 3D volume domain, treating voxel blocks as the fundamental units of synthesis. Unlike standard volume rendering which uses fixed parameters, this method optimizes the voxel values themselves to match visual evidence. It is distinguished from its parent Dual Rendering Equation Optimization by explicitly solving for the volume geometry/appearance via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework rather than optimizing only lighting parameters. Inputs: I{ph}: Input photograph (2D image). V{ex}: Example cloud volume database containing N example volumes. C{ex} = \{C1, \dots, CK\}: Set of K voxel blocks extracted from V{ex}. Each block has dimensions w \times w \times Nz. L0^, La^: Optimized lighting parameters obtained by solving a nonlinear least square problem. Outputs: V: Synthesized cloud volume. Data Structures: Voxel Block (zV): A 3D array of size w \times w \times Nz representing density/extinction values. Rendered Image Block (zI): A 2D array of size w \times w representing pixel values. Vector z: Concatenation of rendered image block and voxel block: z = \{zI, zV\}. Vector xp: Concatenation of input image pixel block xp^I and corresponding voxel block xp^V: xp = \{xp^I, xp^V\}. Distance Metric d(xp, z): d(xp, z) = \|xp^V - zV\|^2 + \lambda \|xp^I - zI\|^2 where \lambda is a relative weighting coefficient (default 100). Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Extract voxel blocks C{ex} from the example database V{ex}. Ensure grid resolution in the Z-direction is equal to Nz. Render all example volumes in V{ex} using L0^ and La^ to populate the set of candidate vectors z. 2. Sorting: Sort all voxel blocks in the order in which incident sunlight reaches them. This ensures that transmittance \tau can be calculated for voxels closer to the sun first. 3. Optimization Loop (EM Steps): Repeat until energy converges or a specified number of iterations is reached: E-step (Expectation Step): Minimize energy with respect to xp (specifically xp^V) keeping zp fixed. This results in a least squares problem. The derivative of the energy function E(x; \{z\}) = \sum{p \in X{ph}} d(xp, zp) with respect to xp^V is set to zero. The solution simplifies to a weighted average computation of neighbor voxel blocks. Update xp^V and accumulate the best zp^V into the corresponding voxels in V. M-step (Maximization Step): Minimize energy with respect to zp keeping xp fixed. This involves searching for the closest vector zp from the set of all vectors z. Acceleration Strategy: Since searching all K vectors is expensive, use a two-pass search: 1. For each xp^V, find k nearest neighbor vectors z1^V, \dots, zk^V from the database using the FLANN library. 2. Render each zi^V to compute zi^I. 3. Search for the closest vector zp from the set \{z1, \dots, zk\} based on the distance metric d(xp, z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def synthesizevolume(inputimage, examplevolumes, lightingparams, sundirection, w, Nz, kneighbors, lambdaweight, maxiterations, tolerance): # 1. Preprocessing: Extract voxel blocks from example database voxelblocksdb = [] for vol in examplevolumes: for y in range(0, vol.shape[0] - w + 1, w): for x in range(0, vol.shape[1] - w + 1, w): voxelblocksdb.append(vol[y:y+w, x:x+w,:]) volh, volw = inputimage.shape[:2] cols = volw // w rows = volh // w volume = [[[0.0] Nz for in range(cols)] for in range(rows)] # 2. Sorting: Sort blocks by sunlight incidence order sortedindices = sorted(range(rows cols), key=lambda i: (i // cols) sundirection[0] + (i % cols) sundirection[1]) # 3. Optimization Loop for iteration in range(maxiterations): totalenergy = 0.0 for idx in sortedindices: r, c = idx // cols, idx % cols ystart, xstart = r w, c w xpI = inputimage[ystart:ystart+w, xstart:xstart+w] xpV = volume[r][c] # --- E-step --- # Minimize energy w.r.t xp^V keeping zp fixed. # Results in a least squares problem solved by a weighted average of neighbor voxel blocks. neighbors = getneighbors(volume, r, c, rows, cols, w, Nz) xpV = weightedaverage(xpV, neighbors) volume[r][c] = xpV # --- M-step --- # Find closest zp from candidates using acceleration. xpVflat = [v for row in xpV for col in row for v in col] kindices = findknearestneighbors(xpVflat, voxelblocksdb, kneighbors) bestcandidate = None mindist = float('inf') for i in kindices: candV = voxelblocksdb[i] candI = renderblock(candV, lightingparams, sundirection) distV = sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(xpVflat, [v for row in candV for col in row for v in col])) distI = sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip([v for row in xpI for col in row for v in col], [v for row in candI for col in row for v in col])) dist = distV + lambdaweight distI if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestcandidate = candV volume[r][c] = bestcandidate totalenergy += mindist if totalenergy < tolerance: break return volume def renderblock(zV, lightingparams, sundirection): # Computes transmittance and radiance along the sun direction h, w, Nz = zV.shape out = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] # Standard volume rendering accumulation return out def getneighbors(vol, r, c, rows, cols, w, Nz): # Returns adjacent voxel blocks in the synthesized volume neighbors = [] for dr in [-1, 0, 1]: for dc in [-1, 0, 1]: if dr == 0 and dc == 0: continue nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols: neighbors.append(vol[nr][nc]) return neighbors def weightedaverage(current, neighbors): # Returns the weighted average of the current block and its neighbors if not neighbors: return current avg = [[[0.0]Nz for in range(w)] for in range(w)] count = 1 for n in neighbors: for i in range(w): for j in range(w): for k in range(Nz): avg[i][j][k] += n[i][j][k] count += 1 for i in range(w): for j in range(w): for k in range(Nz): avg[i][j][k] = (current[i][j][k] + avg[i][j][k]) / count return avg def findknearestneighbors(query, db, k): # Standard k-NN search dists = [sum((a - b)2 for a, b in zip(query, vec)) for vec in db] return sorted(range(len(dists)), key=lambda i: dists[i])[:k] Parameters: \lambda: Relative weighting coefficient for the pixel difference term. Default value is 100. k: Number of nearest neighbors searched in the M-step acceleration strategy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transmittance Calculation: Requires voxel values of blocks closer to the sun to be computed first. Incorrect sorting order leads to incorrect lighting/shadowing. Computational Cost: Rendering zV for every candidate is expensive. The k-nearest neighbor acceleration is critical for feasibility. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes specific boundary handling for the weighted average in the E-step. An extension of the texture optimization method to synthesize a cloud volume such that rendered images from two orthogonal directions (e.g., xy and xz planes) match two input images. It augments the vector xp and z to include pixel values from the second image plane (I{xz}). The distance metric becomes: d(xp, z) = \|xp^V - zV\|^2 + \lambda \|xp^I - zI\|^2 + \mu \|xp^{I{xz}} - zI^{I{xz}}\|^2 where \mu is a relative weighting coefficient (e.g., 10 in experiments). A method to synthesize a new texture patch Pn by pasting an example patch En from an input image I{in} into the output I{out}, ensuring boundary matching to avoid feature mismatches. It uses an overlap region to initialize optimized kd-trees for accelerating approximate nearest neighbors (ANN) search. The matching condition is d(\partial(Pn), \partial(En)) < \eta, where \partial(\cdot) is the boundary zone and \eta is a prescribed constant. A probability density function (PDF) is computed based on the L2 distance of boundaries, and a patch is randomly chosen according to the PDF, then pasted and blended. Time Complexity: The method is iterative (EM steps). Each iteration involves rendering k candidate blocks per pixel block. Rendering is O(Nz) per block. The ANN search is O(K \log K) or better with FLANN. Overall complexity is high due to repeated rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the example volume database and pre-rendered candidates. Memory scales with K \times w^2 \times Nz. Performance: On a desktop PC (Intel Core-i7 4790 3.60 GHz), preprocessing takes about 4 minutes for 137 example volumes. Synthesis time depends on resolution and iteration count. Strengths: Produces visually consistent textures that match input photographs. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to rendering in the loop. Requires a database of example volumes. The method is based on the texture optimization technique proposed by Kwatra et al. [11] (referenced in). It was adapted for 3D cloud volume synthesis by Iwasaki, Dobashi, and Okabe in 2017. The approach leverages the similarity between 2D patch-based synthesis and 3D voxel-based synthesis, extending the EM framework to volumetric data. name: Two-Phase Method
body: The Two-Phase Method is a synthesis technique designed to ensure both geometric and appearance continuity in synthesized results, particularly for complex texture and geometry. It decouples the patch selection process into two stages: first filtering candidates for geometric continuity, then selecting one for appearance continuity. The method operates on a set of candidate patches derived from an exemplar volume. It requires a density field V^{(d)} and a color feature field V^{(f)} from the exemplar, along with a shading map to guide lighting consistency. Inputs: Candidate patch set \mathcal{P} (filtered by shading similarity). Exemplar density field V^{(d)}. Exemplar color feature field V^{(f)}. Synthesis target patch Pn. Outputs: Selected patch P{selected} from \mathcal{P}. Data Structures: Patches are represented as 3D voxel blocks. Density field V^{(d)} stores scalar density values. Color feature field V^{(f)} stores color/feature vectors. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Geometry-based Synthesis For each candidate patch Pi \in \mathcal{P}, calculate the geometric continuity error against the target Pn using the density field V^{(d)}. Select a subset of kg candidate patches that exhibit the highest geometric continuity. 2. Phase 2: Appearance-based Synthesis For each of the kg candidates from Phase 1, calculate the appearance continuity error against the target Pn using the color feature field V^{(f)}. Select the single patch P{selected} that best matches the target in color features. Formulas: Geometric Error Eg(Pi, Pn): Not given in the sources. Appearance Error Ea(Pi, Pn): Not given in the sources. Parameters: kg: Number of candidates retained after Phase 1. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary artifacts may occur if patches are not constrained at scene edges. Precision issues in density or color feature comparison may lead to suboptimal selections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twophasesynthesis(targetpatch, candidatepatches, densityfield, colorfield): # Phase 1: Geometry-based Synthesis geometricerrors = [] for patch in candidatepatches: err = boundaryl2(patch, targetpatch, densityfield) geometricerrors.append((patch, err)) geometricerrors.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) kg = 10 # Not given in the sources topcandidates = [x[0] for x in geometricerrors[:kg]] # Phase 2: Appearance-based Synthesis appearanceerrors = [] for patch in topcandidates: err = boundaryl2(patch, targetpatch, colorfield) appearanceerrors.append((patch, err)) bestpatch, = min(appearanceerrors, key=lambda x: x[1]) return bestpatch def boundaryl2(patch1, patch2, field): """Computes L2 distance between boundary voxels of two patches using a field.""" # Not given in the sources # Standard implementation: mean squared difference of boundary voxels b1 = field[patch1.boundaryindices] b2 = field[patch2.boundaryindices] return ((b1 - b2) 2).mean() A variant for textures without sharp boundaries that introduces an edge error factor into the synthesis process to measure and balance average edge discontinuities. It calculates edge errors Ee by measuring average edge discontinuities for composed textures, considering that discontinuities along an edge come from 2 vertical pairs of adjacent cube faces (e.g., A(E)-C(E) and C(N)-D(N) for edge a1-b2-c3-d4). For each face of a cube, errors of the 4 edges are calculated from all cubes having the same color on the adjacent face, collecting the 2 face errors of the 12 edges from all combinations once and only once. The accumulated synthesis error is Es = pi \times Ei + pe \times Ee, where Ei is the inside error, Ee is the edge error, and pi, pe are weights set as the inverse of their cutting path size to balance the errors. The method ensures geometric and appearance continuity, which is crucial for complex texture and geometry. Performance details such as time and memory complexity are not explicitly provided in the sources. The method is suitable for synthesizing large-scale scenes with reasonable lighting. The Two-Phase Method was proposed in the context of NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance. It addresses high-dimensional texture synthesis problems inspired by traditional exemplar-based methods. name: Nerflets
head: Local Radiance Fields
body: Nerflets is a scene representation method that decomposes a 3D environment into a set of small, local neural radiance fields, termed "nerflets," to achieve efficient, structure-aware reconstruction. Unlike global NeRF models that rely on a single large MLP, Nerflets uses local fields with defined spatial ranges and orientations, enabling 2D-supervised training and facilitating direct scene editing and decomposition. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 2D image observations and corresponding camera poses. Outputs: Rendered novel views and the optimized set of nerflet parameters. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a collection of N nerflets. Each nerflet i stores: 1. Spatial Position: A 3D center coordinate \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Orientation: A rotation matrix or quaternion \mathbf{R}i defining the local coordinate frame. 3. Range/Influence: A spatial extent or radius ri determining the volume of influence. 4. Neural Weights: Parameters for a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) fi. Influence Function: Each nerflet has an influence function wi(\mathbf{x}) that determines its contribution to a point \mathbf{x} in space. The exact mathematical form is not detailed in the sources, but it acts as a weighting mechanism based on the point's proximity to the nerflet's range. A standard implementation uses a Gaussian falloff based on distance to \mathbf{c}i and ri. Rendering Steps: 1. Sampling: For a given ray, sample a set of 3D points \{\mathbf{x}j\} along a segment [t{\text{near}}, t{\text{far}}]. 2. Local Evaluation: For each sampled point \mathbf{x}j, evaluate all N nerflets. Each nerflet i uses its small MLP fi to predict a local density \sigma{i}(\mathbf{x}j) and color \mathbf{c}{i}(\mathbf{x}j). 3. Weighting: Compute the influence weight wi(\mathbf{x}j) for each nerflet at point \mathbf{x}j. 4. Aggregation: Combine the local predictions into a global density and color for the point using weighted averaging: \sigma(\mathbf{x}j) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} wi(\mathbf{x}j) \sigma{i}(\mathbf{x}j)}{\sum{i=1}^{N} wi(\mathbf{x}j)} \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}j) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} wi(\mathbf{x}j) \mathbf{c}{i}(\mathbf{x}j)}{\sum{i=1}^{N} wi(\mathbf{x}j)} 5. Volume Rendering: Use the aggregated density and color in standard volume rendering integration along the ray to produce the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, nerflets, numsamples, tnear=0.0, tfar=10.0): """ Renders a single ray using the Nerflets representation. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. nerflets: List of Nerflet objects. Each has: position: 3D vector orientation: Rotation matrix range: Float (influence radius) mlp: Function mapping (position) -> (density, color) numsamples: Integer, number of points to sample along the ray. tnear: Float, near clipping plane distance. tfar: Float, far clipping plane distance. Returns: finalcolor: 3D vector, the rendered color. finalalpha: Float, accumulated alpha. """ if numsamples < 2: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 # Sample points along the ray segment [tnear, tfar] tvals = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] points = [rayorigin + raydirection t for t in tvals] deltat = (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for point in points: localdensitysum = 0.0 localcolorsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] weightsum = 0.0 for nerflet in nerflets: # Compute influence weight based on distance to nerflet center and range dist = math.sqrt(sum((p - c)2 for p, c in zip(point, nerflet.position))) weight = math.exp(-dist2 / (2 nerflet.range2)) # Evaluate local MLP for density and color localdensity, localcolor = nerflet.mlp(point) localdensitysum += weight localdensity localcolorsum += weight localcolor weightsum += weight if weightsum > 1e-6: globaldensity = localdensitysum / weightsum globalcolor = localcolorsum / weightsum else: globaldensity = 0.0 globalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Standard volume rendering alpha compositing alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-globaldensity deltat) transmittance = 1.0 - accumulatedalpha accumulatedcolor += transmittance alpha globalcolor accumulatedalpha += transmittance alpha if accumulatedalpha > 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha Parameters: Number of Nerflets (N): Not specified in the sources. MLP Size: Described as "small" but specific layer counts or hidden dimensions are not given. Range (ri): Determines the spatial extent of each nerflet and is updated via data association across frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: Influence weights must decay to zero outside the range to prevent undefined contributions. Overlap: Multiple nerflets influence the same point; weighted averaging resolves this, but smooth transitions require careful influence function design. 2D Supervision: Training uses only 2D images, which requires the optimization procedure to handle depth ambiguity. Efficiency: Provides a more efficient and compact representation than global NeRF, particularly for outdoor environments. Performance: Achieves a PSNR more than one point higher on KITTI-360 and ScanNet datasets compared to baseline methods. Scalability: Local evaluation allows parallel processing across nerflets. Strengths: Enables direct scene editing and decomposition; supports 2D supervision; handles complex object instances. Limitations: Requires determining the number and placement of nerflets; the influence function definition is critical but not fully specified in the sources. Nerflets was introduced to address the limitations of global NeRF, which requires 3D supervision and lacks semantic/instance information. It builds on the concept of local radiance fields to provide a structure-aware representation. The method is discussed in reviews of semantically-aware neural radiance fields and surveys on improving NeRF quality. Semantically-aware Neural Radiance Fields for Visual Scene Understanding: A Comprehensive Review, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-025-02663-5, fetched 2026-10-27 Methods and Strategies for Improving the Novel View Synthesis Quality of Neural Radiation Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3382997, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Tetra-NeRF
head: Tetrahedra Field
body: Tetra-NeRF is a radiance field representation that replaces uniform voxel grids or sparse point clouds with a dense set of non-overlapping tetrahedra generated by Delaunay triangulation of an input point cloud. It solves the problem of empty regions in sparse point-based methods and the fixed-resolution limitations of voxel-based methods by providing a continuous, adaptive representation that is naturally denser near surfaces. Unlike Point-NeRF which requires growing the point cloud during training to fill gaps, Tetra-NeRF uses a fixed set of points and constant parameter count, ensuring the representation complexity does not grow. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud (typically from Structure from Motion/SfM like COLMAP) and camera poses. Output: Novel view images synthesized via volumetric rendering. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud: A set of 3D points P. Each point has a position and an initial feature vector. Feature Vector: Size 64. Initialization: Dimensions 0-3: RGBA color values from the point cloud, rescaled to [0, 1]. Original points have \alpha=1; randomly added points have \alpha=0. Dimensions 4-63: Uniformly sampled from [-10^{-4}, 10^{-4}]. 2. Tetrahedra Field: A set of non-overlapping tetrahedra \mathcal{T} covering the convex hull of P, generated via Delaunay triangulation. 3. Acceleration Structure: An acceleration structure (e.g., OptiX) for fast ray-triangle intersection to identify intersected tetrahedra. 4. MLP: Density/Appearance MLP: 3 layers, hidden size 128, Kaiming uniform initialization. Color MLP: Concatenate appearance features with ray direction encoded via Fourier features, pass through a single linear layer to get raw RGB. Numbered Steps: 1. Point Cloud Preprocessing: If the number of points |P| > 10^6, subsample to 10^6 points randomly. If |P| \le 10^6 (e.g., Blender dataset), add |P|/2 random points to prevent edge artifacts. To add a random point: Sample x0 \in P, a random normal n, and \alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar{d}, \bar{d}^2/4), where \bar{d} is the average spacing of P. Add x = x0 + \alpha n. 2. Triangulation: Perform Delaunay triangulation on P to generate the set of tetrahedra \mathcal{T}. 3. Ray Casting and Intersection: For each pixel in a virtual view, project a ray r from the camera plane. Compute intersections between r and all faces of tetrahedra in \mathcal{T} using an acceleration structure (e.g., OptiX). Limit to the first 512 intersected triangles per ray. Determine the corresponding tetrahedra and order them along the ray to allow marching. 4. Barycentric Coordinate Computation: For each ray-tetrahedron intersection, compute the 2D barycentric coordinates \lambda{2D} with respect to the triangle face. Obtain the 3D barycentric coordinates \lambda{3D} for the tetrahedron by setting the coordinate for the vertex opposite to the intersected face to 0. For a query point x inside a tetrahedron, compute its barycentric coordinates \lambda by linearly interpolating between the barycentric coordinates of the two ray-tetrahedron intersections. Alternatively, compute \lambda directly via volume ratios: \lambda = \left(\frac{V{x234}}{V{1234}}, \frac{V{1x34}}{V{1234}}, \frac{V{12x4}}{V{1234}}, \frac{V{123x}}{V{1234}}\right) where V{1234} is the volume of the tetrahedron and V{x234} etc. are volumes formed by replacing one vertex with x. 5. Feature Interpolation: Interpolate the feature vectors fv at the four vertices of the containing tetrahedron using \lambda: fx = \sum{i=1}^{4} \lambdai f{vi} This yields the feature vector fx for the query point x. 6. Network Query: Pass fx through the 3-layer MLP (hidden size 128) to compute raw density \bar{\sigma} and appearance features a. Encode the ray direction d using Fourier features. Concatenate a and the encoded d, then pass through the single linear layer to get raw RGB color \bar{c}. 7. Activation: Map raw density to volume density: \sigma = \text{softplus}(\bar{\sigma}). Map raw color to RGB: c = \text{sigmoid}(\bar{c}). 8. Sampling: Coarse Stage: Use stratified uniform sampling along the ray, limited to the space occupied by tetrahedra. Fine Stage: Use density weights from the coarse stage to bias sampling towards potential surfaces. Use the same network as the coarse stage. Merge coarse and fine samples. 9. Rendering: Compute accumulated weights \bar{w}i for each sample i: \bar{w}i = (1 - \exp (-\sigmai \deltai))\exp \left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1}\sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. Normalize weights to wi and render final color C: \mathbf {C} = \sum {i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp (\sigma i \delta i))\mathbf {c}i, \quad Ti = \exp (-\sum {j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) Backpropagate MSE loss to update features and MLP weights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softplus(x): return np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(x))) + np.maximum(x, 0) def sigmoid(x): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x)) def tetravolume(a, b, c, d): return np.abs(np.dot(a - d, np.cross(b - d, c - d))) / 6.0 def computebarycentriccoords(v1, v2, v3, v4, x): V = tetravolume(v1, v2, v3, v4) if V == 0: return np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]) return np.array([ tetravolume(x, v2, v3, v4) / V, tetravolume(v1, x, v3, v4) / V, tetravolume(v1, v2, x, v4) / V, tetravolume(v1, v2, v3, x) / V ]) def raytriangleintersect(rayo, rayd, a, b, c): edge1 = b - a edge2 = c - a h = np.cross(rayd, edge2) det = np.dot(edge1, h) if abs(det) < 1e-8: return None, None invdet = 1.0 / det s = rayo - a u = np.dot(s, h) invdet if u < 0 or u > 1: return None, None q = np.cross(s, edge1) v = np.dot(rayd, q) invdet if v < 0 or u + v > 1: return None, None t = np.dot(edge2, q) invdet if t > 1e-6: return t, np.array([1.0 - u - v, u, v]) return None, None def raytetraintersect(rayo, rayd, v1, v2, v3, v4): faces = [(v1, v2, v3), (v1, v2, v4), (v1, v3, v4), (v2, v3, v4)] ts = [] lambdas = [] for a, b, c in faces: t, lam = raytriangleintersect(rayo, rayd, a, b, c) if t is not None: ts.append(t) # Map triangle barycentrics to tet barycentrics (opposite vertex gets 0) if np.allclose([a, b, c], [v1, v2, v3]): tetlam = np.array([lam[0], lam[1], lam[2], 0.0]) elif np.allclose([a, b, c], [v1, v2, v4]): tetlam = np.array([lam[0], lam[1], 0.0, lam[2]]) elif np.allclose([a, b, c], [v1, v3, v4]): tetlam = np.array([lam[0], 0.0, lam[1], lam[2]]) else: tetlam = np.array([0.0, lam[0], lam[1], lam[2]]) lambdas.append(tetlam) if len(ts) >= 2: idx = np.argsort(ts) return ts[idx[0]], ts[idx[1]], lambdas[idx[0]], lambdas[idx[1]] return None, None, None, None def inversecdfsample(weights, tmin, tmax, numsamples): cdf = np.cumsum(weights) cdf /= cdf[-1] u = np.random.uniform(0, 1, numsamples) indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, u) tfine = tmin + (tmax - tmin) u return np.sort(tfine) def tetranerfforward(rayorigin, raydirection, tetrahedra, vertexfeatures, mlpdensityappearance, mlpcolor, numcoarsesamples=64, numfinesamples=48): # 1. Find intersected tetrahedra and compute segments tetsegments = [] for idx, tet in enumerate(tetrahedra): v1, v2, v3, v4 = tet tin, tout, lamin, lamout = raytetraintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, v1, v2, v3, v4) if tin is not None: tetsegments.append((idx, tin, tout, lamin, lamout)) # Limit to 512 triangles/tetrahedra as per source tetsegments = sorted(tetsegments, key=lambda x: x[1])[:512] if not tetsegments: return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # 2. Coarse Sampling bounds tmin = max(0.0, min(seg[1] for seg in tetsegments)) tmax = max(seg[2] for seg in tetsegments) coarset = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, numcoarsesamples) coarsesigma = [] coarsec = [] coarseweights = [] for tq in coarset: # Find containing tetrahedron segment tetidx = -1 lamq = None for i, (idx, tin, tout, lamin, lamout) in enumerate(tetsegments): if tin <= tq <= tout: tetidx = idx # Linear interpolation of barycentric coordinates along ray frac = (tq - tin) / (tout - tin) lamq = (1.0 - frac) lamin + frac lamout break if tetidx == -1: coarsesigma.append(0.0) coarsec.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) coarseweights.append(0.0) continue tet = tetrahedra[tetidx] v1, v2, v3, v4 = tet feats = vertexfeatures[tetidx] # (4, 64) # Interpolate features fx = np.dot(lamq, feats) # MLP: Density and Appearance rawsigma, appearance = mlpdensityappearance(fx) sigma = softplus(rawsigma) # MLP: Color # Fourier encoding placeholder for direction encodeddir = np.concatenate([np.sin(raydirection 2np.arange(10)), np.cos(raydirection 2np.arange(10))]) rawc = mlpcolor(np.concatenate([appearance, encodeddir])) c = sigmoid(rawc) coarsesigma.append(sigma) coarsec.append(c) coarsesigma = np.array(coarsesigma) coarsec = np.array(coarsec) # 3. Compute coarse weights for fine sampling bias deltas = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], coarset])) alphacoarse = 1 - np.exp(-coarsesigma deltas) transmittancecoarse = np.exp(-np.cumsum(coarsesigma deltas)) weightscoarse = alphacoarse transmittancecoarse # 4. Fine Sampling finet = inversecdfsample(weightscoarse, tmin, tmax, numfinesamples) finesigma = [] finec = [] for tq in finet: tetidx = -1 lamq = None for idx, tin, tout, lamin, lamout in tetsegments: if tin <= tq <= tout: tetidx = idx frac = (tq - tin) / (tout - tin) lamq = (1.0 - frac) lamin + frac lamout break if tetidx == -1: finesigma.append(0.0) finec.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) continue tet = tetrahedra[tetidx] v1, v2, v3, v4 = tet feats = vertexfeatures[tetidx] fx = np.dot(lamq, feats) rawsigma, appearance = mlpdensityappearance(fx) sigma = softplus(rawsigma) encodeddir = np.concatenate([np.sin(raydirection 2np.arange(10)), np.cos(raydirection 2np.arange(10))]) rawc = mlpcolor(np.concatenate([appearance, encodeddir])) c = sigmoid(rawc) finesigma.append(sigma) finec.append(c) finesigma = np.array(finesigma) finec = np.array(finec) # 5. Merge and Render allt = np.concatenate([coarset, finet]) allsigma = np.concatenate([coarsesigma, finesigma]) allc = np.concatenate([coarsec, finec]) sortidx = np.argsort(allt) allt = allt[sortidx] allsigma = allsigma[sortidx] allc = allc[sortidx] deltas = np.diff(np.concatenate([[0], allt])) alpha = 1 - np.exp(-allsigma deltas) transmittance = np.exp(-np.cumsum(allsigma deltas)) weights = alpha transmittance finalcolor = np.sum(weights[:, None] allc, axis=0) return finalcolor Parameters: Feature Vector Size: 64. MLP Hidden Sizes: 128. Batch Size: 4,096 random rays. Optimizer: RAdam. Learning Rate: Exponential decay from 10^{-3} to 10^{-4} in 300k steps. Max Intersections: 512 triangles per ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed Triangle Limit: Limiting to 512 triangles can degrade results in large scenes or those with fine-grained tetrahedralization, as more intersections may be needed. Mitigation: Consider more triangles at the cost of runtime. Edge Artifacts: With low point counts, some pixels on edges may not intersect any tetrahedra, causing artifacts. Mitigation: Add randomly generated points near the original point cloud. Empty Regions: Unlike Point-NeRF, Tetra-NeRF does not suffer from empty regions due to sparse points because the triangulation covers the convex hull continuously. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of tetrahedra, vertices, and scene structure. Training speed ranges from 15k to 30k rays per second on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. Memory Complexity: Fixed number of parameters. Feature vectors are stored at vertices. The number of parameters stays constant during training, unlike Point-NeRF or Plenoxels which grow complexity. Strengths: Adaptive resolution (denser near surfaces), continuous representation avoiding empty regions, fixed parameter count. Limitations: Performance degrades if the fixed triangle intersection limit (512) is insufficient for the scene complexity. When to Use: When a high-quality point cloud (e.g., from SfM) is available, and adaptive resolution is desired without the overhead of growing representations or fixed grid resolutions. When Not to Use: In very large scenes where the fixed intersection limit causes significant artifacts, or when no initial point cloud is available. Tetra-NeRF was introduced in the paper "Tetra-NeRF: Representing Neural Radiance Fields Using Tetrahedra". It builds on the idea of using classical surface reconstruction methods (Delaunay triangulation) to create a dense, non-overlapping tetrahedral mesh from a point cloud, extending the triangle-rendering pipeline to neural radiance fields. It addresses limitations of MLP-based NeRFs (costly queries, hard to modify) and voxel/grid-based methods (fixed resolution, non-local effects) by storing features freely in 3D space on a tetrahedral mesh. name: Light Field and Lumigraph Methods
head: Opacity Light Field Volume Viewing, Unstructured Lumigraph Rendering
body: Light Field and Lumigraph Methods synthesize novel views by treating a set of key views as an opacity light field parameterized on a geometric proxy surface. The method uses unstructured lumigraph rendering (ULR) to visualize the opacity field interactively on standard graphics hardware. Inputs and outputs: Input consists of a triangular mesh (geometric proxy) and a set of RGBA key views with corresponding camera parameters. The output is a rendered novel view image. Data structures: The method stores the triangular mesh proxy, RGBA key view textures, and a pre-computed BSP tree for back-to-front triangle traversal. Numbered steps: 1. For each mesh vertex v, determine the set of visible key views. A key view is visible if all neighboring triangles around v are completely unoccluded in that view. 2. For each vertex v, select the k (k \le 3) visible views closest to the new viewing direction \mathbf{d}. These are designated as the closest views for vertex v. 3. Compute blending weights for the closest views using unstructured lumigraph interpolation, assigning higher weights to views closer to \mathbf{d}. 4. Render each triangle by blending the key views from the closest views of its three vertices, amounting to blending up to nine textures per triangle. Formulas and parameters: The exact ULR interpolation formula is not provided in the sources. The method uses a fixed maximum of k=3 closest views per vertex. Edge cases and pitfalls: Triangles must be rendered in back-to-front order to ensure correct alpha blending; a BSP tree for the geometric proxy is pre-computed and traversed during rendering. For geometric proxies with relatively small occlusions, considering all camera views for blending at each vertex yields higher image quality at a slight performance cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderopacitylightfield(mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection): # Pre-compute BSP tree for back-to-front triangle traversal bsptree = computebsptree(mesh) renderedimage = emptyimage() for triangle in traversebacktofront(bsptree): v1, v2, v3 = triangle.vertices # Step 1 & 2: Find visible and closest views for each vertex closestv1 = getclosestvisibleviews(v1, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection, k=3) closestv2 = getclosestvisibleviews(v2, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection, k=3) closestv3 = getclosestvisibleviews(v3, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, newviewdirection, k=3) # Step 3: Compute blending weights using ULR interpolation w1 = computeulrweights(closestv1, newviewdirection) w2 = computeulrweights(closestv2, newviewdirection) w3 = computeulrweights(closestv3, newviewdirection) # Step 4: Blend up to nine textures per triangle via GPU hardware tricolor = blendtriangletextures(triangle, [closestv1, closestv2, closestv3], [w1, w2, w3]) rasterizetriangle(triangle, tricolor) return renderedimage def getclosestvisibleviews(vertex, mesh, keyviews, cameraparams, viewdirection, k=3): visibleviews = [] for view in keyviews: neighbors = getneighboringtriangles(vertex, mesh) # A key view is visible if all neighboring triangles around v are completely unoccluded if all(not isoccluded(tri, view, cameraparams) for tri in neighbors): visibleviews.append(view) # Sort by angular distance to viewdirection, return top k visibleviews.sort(key=lambda v: dotproduct(v.direction, viewdirection), reverse=True) return visibleviews[:k] def computeulrweights(views, viewdirection): # Higher blending weights are assigned to views closer to d weights = [1.0 - dotproduct(v.direction, viewdirection) for v in views] total = sum(weights) return [w / total for w in weights] if total > 0 else [1.0 / len(views)] len(views) def blendtriangletextures(triangle, closestviewspervertex, weightspervertex): # Blends up to nine textures per triangle (3 vertices 3 closest views) # Carried out solely by graphics hardware using standard barycentric interpolation and alpha compositing pass def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def isoccluded(triangle, view, cameraparams): # Standard ray-triangle intersection test from camera center through triangle pass def computebsptree(mesh): # Standard BSP tree construction for mesh pass def traversebacktofront(bsptree): # Standard recursive BSP traversal pass def emptyimage(): # Initialize output buffer pass def rasterizetriangle(triangle, color): # Standard GPU rasterization pass def getneighboringtriangles(vertex, mesh): # Standard adjacency lookup pass Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) is a method designed to produce photorealistic novel views for well-sampled, forward-facing scenes by predicting a discretized frustum-sampled RGB\alpha grid (Multiplane Image or MPI) for each input view. It differs from its siblings, such as Neural Lumigraph Rendering and Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields, by explicitly generating per-view MPI representations that are subsequently blended, rather than optimizing a single global implicit field or using a fixed light field parameterization. Neural Lumigraph Rendering (NLR) is a neural rendering framework that jointly optimizes an implicit signed distance function (SDF) for geometry and a radiance field for appearance, supervised exclusively by posed 2D images. It enables the export of view-dependent textured meshes for real-time rasterization, achieving rendering speeds two orders of magnitude faster than standard neural volume rendering methods like NeRF while maintaining comparable image quality. Unlike sibling methods that rely on dense volumetric sampling or local light field fusion, NLR uses sphere tracing on an SDF to find the surface and applies unstructured lumigraph rendering to blend projective textures, preserving view-dependent effects without runtime volumetric integration. Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields (i-NOLF) is a real-time neural rendering method that represents scenes as local neural opacity light fields to achieve one-query-per-pixel rendering. It combines spatial hash encoding with light field properties to avoid the computational overhead of hundreds of neural network forward passes per pixel, which is typical in standard neural radiance fields. Unlike its siblings, i-NOLF decouples the outgoing radiance into view-independent diffuse and view-dependent specular components, using a cached density texture for efficient hit-point estimation and Perfect Spatial Hashing (PSH) specifically for the specular encoder to balance memory efficiency and rendering speed. A technique to generate high-quality light field representation and integrate it into the GPU-based raycasting pipeline to provide novice audiences access to interactive volume renditions. The method is interactive on PCs using current graphics hardware, as texture blending is carried out solely by the GPU. Rendering each triangle blends up to nine textures (3 vertices \times 3 closest views). Considering all camera views for blending at each vertex yields higher image quality at a slight performance cost, particularly for proxies with small occlusions. Exact time and memory complexity metrics are not given in the sources. The method originates from image-based volume rendering research that parameterizes an opacity light field on a proxy surface. It builds on the system by Vlasic et al. and Unstructured Lumigraph Rendering (ULR) to visualize the opacity light field interactively. In volume visualization, the approach has been adapted to handle volumetric data, providing interactive capabilities for novice users by integrating high-quality light field representations into GPU-based raycasting pipelines. name: Local Light Field Fusion
head: LFLF, LLFF, Layered Light Field Fusion
body: Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) is a view synthesis method designed for producing photorealistic novel views for well-sampled, forward-facing scenes. It differs from its siblings by using a trained 3D convolutional network to directly predict a discretized frustum-sampled RGB\alpha grid (Multiplane Image or MPI) for each input view, then rendering novel views by alpha compositing and blending nearby MPIs. Unlike Neural Lumigraph Rendering which optimizes a separate network per scene, LLFF applies a single trained network to predict the MPIs directly from input images. Inputs: A set of input images from a forward-facing capture. Outputs: High-resolution novel view images. Data Structures: MPI (Multiplane Image): A discretized frustum-sampled RGB\alpha grid representing color and opacity at specific depth intervals within the camera frustum. 3D Convolutional Network: A trained neural network that takes an input image and outputs the parameters for the MPI planes. Steps: 1. Input Preparation: Collect a set of input images from a forward-facing scene. 2. MPI Prediction: Pass each input image through the trained 3D convolutional network to predict the RGB and \alpha values for the discretized frustum-sampled planes for that specific view. 3. Novel View Rendering: To render a novel viewpoint: a. Identify the nearby input views whose predicted MPIs are relevant to the novel viewpoint. b. Warp or project the MPIs from these nearby input views into the coordinate system of the novel viewpoint. c. Perform alpha compositing of the warped MPIs to combine the color and opacity information. d. Blend the results from the different MPIs to produce the final image. Parameters: Disparity Limit: The method provides a sampling guideline not to exceed 64 pixels of disparity between input views. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Disparity: The method frequently fails to estimate correct geometry in datasets with up to 400-500 pixels of disparity between views, as it exceeds the 64-pixel guideline. Inconsistency: Blending between different scene representations (MPIs) for rendering different views can result in perceptually-distracting inconsistency and repeated edges. Artifacts: The method exhibits banding artifacts on object edges and ghosting artifacts in complex geometry (e.g., masts, internal structures). Time Complexity: All compared single-scene methods take at least 12 hours to train per scene, whereas LLFF processes a small input dataset in under 10 minutes. Memory Complexity: LLFF produces a large 3D voxel grid for every input image, resulting in enormous storage requirements (over 15GB for one "Realistic Synthetic" scene). Strengths: Fast processing time; capable of recovering fine details in geometry and appearance (e.g., non-Lambertian reflectance, fine rigging) for well-sampled forward-facing scenes. Limitations: High storage requirements; fails with high disparity (>64 pixels); perceptual inconsistencies due to blending; artifacts like banding and ghosting. When to use: When fast processing of well-sampled, forward-facing scenes is required and storage is not a constraint. When not to use: For scenes with large baseline disparities, or when storage efficiency and view consistency are critical. Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF) was introduced as a method for view synthesis, specifically targeting forward-facing captures of real scenes. It was compared against baselines such as Scene Representation Networks (SRN) and Neural Volumes (NV). SRN is limited by selecting only a single depth and color per camera ray, while NV is limited by its explicit 128^3 voxel grid. LLFF was shown to outperform these baselines in qualitative and quantitative metrics for suitable scenes, although it suffered from storage and consistency issues. A sibling method that optimizes a separate network per scene. It is chosen when per-scene optimization is feasible and higher view consistency is required than LLFF can provide. See Neural Lumigraph Rendering. A sibling method focusing on instant rendering capabilities. It is chosen when speed of inference is critical. See Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields. name: Two-plane light field parameterization with re-parameterization
head: EPI-based parameterization, Epipolar Plane Images parameterization, Local affine transform embedding, Ray-space embedding, Two-plane light field parameterization, Two-plane parameterization
body: This method parameterizes a light field using two planes, \pi{xy} and \pi{uv}, and learns a re-parameterization to align the neural network's interpolation kernels with the object surface \pi{st}. It solves the problem of misaligned interpolation kernels in standard two-plane parameterizations, which degrades view synthesis quality when the distance between the view plane and the object surface is large. It sets itself apart from standard two-plane methods by explicitly optimizing the embedding space to minimize the discrepancy between the parameterized coordinates and the true surface coordinates. Inputs: A set of input images with known camera poses. A scene geometry (implicitly or explicitly defined, e.g., via a textured plane \pi{st} or a voxel grid). Two initial parameterization planes: \pi{xy} (view plane) and \pi{uv} (viewpoint plane). Outputs: A re-parameterized light field representation where rays are mapped to a latent space aligned with the object surface. A neural network (MLP) that maps the re-parameterized ray coordinates to color and density. Data Structures: Ray Representation: A ray r is defined by its origin on \pi{xy} and its intersection with \pi{uv}. Alternatively, each ray is parameterized by intersection points on a camera plane (u, v) and an image plane (s, t). Voxel Grid: For subdivided models, a 3D grid of voxels \upsilon is used to cover the scene space (e.g., NDC space). Embedding Network: An MLP that takes the re-parameterized ray coordinates as input and outputs the ray's color and density. Steps: 1. Initial Parameterization: Define \pi{xy} and \pi{uv}. For the Stanford Light Field dataset, \pi{xy} is set to z = -1 and \pi{uv} is set to z = 0. Camera positions are scaled to lie between [-0.25, 0.25] in x and y, and pixel coordinates on \pi{uv} are scaled to lie between [-1, 1]. For each ray r originating at (\hat{x}, \hat{y}) on \pi{xy} and passing through a point (\hat{s}, \hat{t}) on the object surface \pi{st}, calculate its intersection (\hat{u}, \hat{v}) with \pi{uv} using similar triangles: \hat{u} - \hat{x} = (\hat{s} - \hat{x}) \frac{z{uv}}{z{st}} \hat{v} - \hat{y} = (\hat{t} - \hat{y}) \frac{z{uv}}{z{st}} where z{st} and z{uv} are the depths of \pi{st} and \pi{uv} respectively, and the depth of \pi{xy} is assumed to be 0. 2. Re-parameterization (Subdivided Model): For a subdivided model, re-parameterize each ray r within a voxel \upsilon. Transform space so that the voxel center lies at the origin. Intersect the transformed ray with the voxel’s front and back planes. Take the xy coordinates of these intersections as the parameterization, which lie within the range [-\text{voxel width}, +\text{voxel width}] in all dimensions. 3. Learning Re-parameterization: Learn a re-parameterization that moves \pi{uv} towards \pi{st}, reducing the distance z{st} - z{uv}. The finite capacity of the light field MLP drives the embedding network to map rays intersecting the same 3D point to the same point in latent space. This process aligns the color network's interpolation kernels with the object surface \pi{st}. 4. EPI Alignment (Redundancy Reduction): A 3D point is determined by coordinates (u, v, s, t, \theta), where \theta is the slope of the line on the us or st slice of the light field (EPI). The parameterization is redundant because v and t are correlated for fixed planes. To align all points to a fixed (u^, v^), compute s0 = s + \arctan \frac{u-u^}{\tan\theta} and t0 = t + \arctan \frac{v-v^}{\tan\theta}. Each point is now parameterized by a 3D vector (s0, t0, \theta). Parameters: Stanford Light Field Dataset: \pi{xy} at z = -1, \pi{uv} at z = 0. Camera positions scaled to [-0.25, 0.25] in x and y. Pixel coordinates on \pi{uv} scaled to [-1, 1]. Real Forward-Facing and Shiny Datasets: Experiments performed in NDC space. A 32^3 voxel grid covers all NDC space, except for CD/Lab scenes which use a coarser 4^3 grid. Pitfalls: If the distance z{st} - z{uv} is large, the difference between (\hat{u}, \hat{v}) and (\hat{s}, \hat{t}) increases, causing the network's interpolation kernels to become misaligned with the object surface, degrading reconstruction quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def parameterizeray(x, y, s, t, zst, zuv): """ Calculates the intersection (u, v) on plane piuv for a ray originating at (x, y) on pixy and passing through (s, t) on pist. """ u = x + (s - x) (zuv / zst) v = y + (t - y) (zuv / zst) return u, v def alignepipolarcoordinates(u, v, s, t, theta, ustar, vstar): """ Reduces redundancy by aligning ray coordinates to a fixed (ustar, vstar). Returns the aligned 3D vector (s0, t0, theta). """ tantheta = math.tan(theta) s0 = s + math.atan((u - ustar) / tantheta) t0 = t + math.atan((v - vstar) / tantheta) return s0, t0, theta Not given in the sources. This method originates from the paper "Learning Neural Light Fields with Ray-Space Embedding Networks". It addresses the limitations of standard two-plane parameterization by introducing a learnable re-parameterization to improve view synthesis quality. name: Neural Lumigraph Rendering
head: Deep Surface Light Field, Neural Radiance Fields with SDF export, Neural Surface Light Field, SIREN-based Neural Rendering
body:
Neural Lumigraph Rendering (NLR) is a neural rendering framework that jointly optimizes an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF) for shape and a radiance field for appearance, supervised exclusively by posed 2D images. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric rendering methods like NeRF by exporting a triangular mesh with view-dependent textures, enabling real-time rasterization via OpenGL while maintaining state-of-the-art image quality. Unlike Local Light Field Fusion which relies on explicit light field parameterization, NLR learns an implicit neural representation that is subsequently discretized for rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of m multi-view 2D images I \in \mathbb{R}^{m 	imes w 	imes h 	imes 3} and corresponding binary object masks M \in \mathbb{R}^{m 	imes w 	imes h} (where 1 marks foreground). Camera poses are defined by view matrix V \in \mathbb{R}^{4 	imes 4} and projection matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{4 	imes 4}. Outputs: Optimized parameters 	heta (SDF) and \phi (appearance); optionally, a triangular mesh and projective textures for real-time rendering. Data Structures: SDF Network S: A SIREN (Sinusoidal Representation Network) MLP with 5 layers and 256 hidden units each. Input: position x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: scalar S(x; 	heta) \in \mathbb{R}. Radiance Field Network E: A SIREN MLP with 5 layers and 256 hidden units each. Input: position x \in \mathbb{R}^3, view direction rd \in \mathbb{R}^3, and local normal n \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: RGB color E(x, rd, n; 	heta, \phi) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Fourier Features: The view direction rd is embedded using Fourier features \{\sin(2k\pi rd), \cos(2k\pi rd) \mid k \in 1 \dots 4\} before entering E. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For a pixel at relative projection plane location u \in [-1, 1]^2, compute ray origin ro and direction rd: ro = (V^{-1} \cdot [0, 0, 1, 0]^T){x,y,z} rd = 
u((P \cdot V)^{-1} \cdot [ux, uy, 0, 1]^T) where 
u(\omega) = \omega{x,y,z} / \|\omega{x,y,z}\| is vector normalization. 2. Sphere Tracing: Find the zero-level set S0 closest to the camera along the ray using iterative updates: x0 = ro x{i+1} = xi + S(xi)rd The surface point is S0 = \{xn \mid S(xn) \approx 0\} for step count n=16. A small residual |S(xn)| < 0.005 is tolerated. To save memory, gradients are retained only for the last step n. 3. Normal Computation: Compute the local normal n via automatic differentiation of the SDF at the surface point: n = 
ablax S(xn; 	heta). 4. Appearance Sampling: Sample the radiance field at the surface point: c = E(xn, rd, n; 	heta, \phi). 5. Loss Calculation: Minimize the total loss L = LR + wE LE + wM LM + wS LS: Reconstruction Loss (LR): L1 error for foreground pixels Uf = U \cap S0 \cap \{U \mid MU = 1\}: LR =  rac{1}{|U|} \sum{c \in I{Uf}} |E(x, rd, n; 	heta, \phi) - c|. Eikonal Loss (LE): Enforces metric properties for sphere tracing by regularizing the gradient of S to unit length. Random points xr are uniformly sampled from a cube encapsulating the object's bounding unit radius sphere: LE =  rac{1}{|U|} \sum{xr} (\|
ablax S(xr; 	heta)\|2^2 - 1)^2. Soft Mask Loss (LM): Restricts coarse shape to object mask boundaries for non-foreground pixels U \setminus Uf. S{min} is the minimum SDF value along the ray: LM =  rac{1}{\alpha |U|} \sum{m \in M{U \setminus Uf}} 	ext{BCE}(	ext{sigmoid}(-\alpha S{min}), m) where \alpha is a softness parameter. Smoothness Loss (LS): Linearizes angular behavior to prevent overfitting: LS =  rac{1}{|U|} \sum \|
abla^2{rd} E(x, rd, n; 	heta, \phi)\|2^2. 6. Optimization: Parameters 	heta and \phi are optimized using the Adam solver with initial learning rate 10^{-4}, decreased by factor of 2 every 40,000 batches, for 150,000 batches. Batch size is 50,000 rays. Weights: wE = 0.1, wM = 100, wS = 0.01. 7. Mesh Extraction (Optional for Real-Time): Voxelize S at 512^3 resolution and extract mesh using marching cubes. Offset the iso-surface by 0.5% of the object radius in the outside direction. Resample E to synthesize projective textures Ti for N camera poses. 8. Real-Time Rendering (NLR-RAS): Rasterize the mesh using OpenGL. Compute angles 	aui between the rendering camera ray and rays to each projective texture viewpoint. Blend contributions from the first k=5 textures sorted by 	aui ascending: \hat{w}i =  rac{1}{	aui} \left(1 -  rac{	aui}{	auk}ight) wi =  rac{\hat{w}i}{\sum{j=1}^k \hat{w}j}. Discard occluded textures by setting wi=0 if the pre-rendered depth indicates occlusion. Parameters: n=16: Sphere tracing steps. wE = 0.1, wM = 100, wS = 0.01: Loss weights. \alpha: Softness parameter for mask loss. Hidden units: 256 per layer. Layers: 5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: SIRENs tend to overfit to training views. Mitigated by large batch size (50,000) and uniform ray distribution. High-Frequency Artifacts: Large values of wS cause high-frequency artifacts in S. Initialization: S is initialized to a unit sphere of radius 0.5 by pretraining to a procedural shape. Defines the end-to-end differentiable optimization objective for the Neural Lumigraph Representation (NLR++), which jointly reconstructs shape via a Signed Distance Function (SDF) and appearance via a radiance field from posed 2D images. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric rendering losses by introducing a soft mask loss on the SDF minimum along rays and a specific training schedule that decouples shape approximation from feature refinement to accelerate convergence. Time Complexity: Training is slower than some baselines; NLR is slower to converge in shape reconstruction than MetaNLR++ and IDR. Memory Complexity: Model size is compact. On DTU scan 65 at 1600x1200, NLR-ST is 2.07 MB and NLR-RAS is 34.68 MB, compared to NeRF's 2.27 MB and IDR's 11.13 MB. Performance: NLR-ST (sphere-traced) renders at 13s per image on DTU scan 65, while NLR-RAS (rasterized) achieves real-time performance (>60 fps at HD). This is 10x faster than NeRF (150s). Image Quality: NLR-RAS achieves 33.33 dB PSNR on DTU Scan 65, comparable to NeRF (34.87 dB) and superior to Colmap (32.13 dB) and IDR (33.50 dB). Strengths: Real-time rendering capability via mesh export; high image quality; compact model size; view-dependent textures. Limitations: Slower convergence during training compared to some implicit surface methods; requires posed images and masks. Neural Lumigraph Rendering was introduced by Kellnhofer et al. in CVPR 2021. It builds on sinusoidal representation networks (SIREN) and unstructured lumigraph rendering techniques from Buehler et al.. Fourier features for angular resolution are adopted from prior work. The method was implemented in PyTorch and rendered using OpenGL. name: NLR++ Training Loss and Supervision
