body: NLR++ Training Loss and Supervision defines the end-to-end differentiable optimization objective for the Neural Lumigraph Representation (NLR++), which jointly reconstructs shape via a Signed Distance Function (SDF) and appearance via a radiance field from posed 2D images. It distinguishes itself from standard volumetric rendering losses by introducing a soft mask loss on the SDF minimum along rays and a specific training schedule that decouples shape approximation from feature refinement to accelerate convergence. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A batch of k \le N input images \{In\}{n=1}^k, their corresponding binary object masks \{Mn\}{n=1}^k, and viewpoint parameters \{Cn\}{n=1}^k. Outputs: A synthesized target image \hat{I}t, a rendered mask \hat{M}t, and updated model parameters after minimizing the total loss. Data Structures SDF (\Phi\theta): An implicit function mapping 3D coordinates to signed distance values, initialized as a unit sphere of radius 0.5 using a pre-trained SIREN. Radiance Field: Defined by the encoder E\xi, decoder D\psi, and aggregator \Gamma\zeta, which map view-dependent features to color. Model Parameters: \Theta = [\xi, \psi, \zeta, \theta]. Numbered Steps 1. Batch Sampling: For each training iteration, sample a set of k \le N images \{In\}{n=1}^k from the available N input images. 2. Target Selection: Designate one image as the ground-truth target It, with its mask Mt and viewpoint Ct. 3. Multi-Target Gradient Computation: To improve gradient accuracy, treat l < k images in the batch as target images, computing gradients for each from the other images in the batch, limited by GPU memory. 4. Synthesis: Generate the synthesized target image \hat{I}t and rendered mask \hat{M}t from viewpoint Ct using the NLR++ image formation model. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the total loss \mathcal{L} as the sum of image reconstruction loss, soft mask loss, and eikonal regularization. 6. Scheduled Shape Supervision: Enforce shape-related losses \mathcal{L}M and \mathcal{L}E only for the first t1 iterations, and then every t2 iterations thereafter, allowing initial shape approximation before refining with better feature encoding. 7. Optimization: Update parameters \Theta using the Adam optimizer. Formulas The total loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}(\{\hat{I}t, \hat{M}t\}, \{It, Mt\}, \Phi\theta) = \mathcal{L}R(\hat{I}t, \{It, Mt\}) + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}M(\Phi\theta, Mt) + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}E(\Phi\theta) 1. Image Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}R): A masked L1 loss on rendered images: \mathcal{L}R(\hat{I}t, \{It, Mt\}) = \frac{1}{P} \sum{p | Mt[p]=1} |It[p] - \hat{I}t[p]| where P is the number of pixels where Mt[p]=1. 2. Soft Mask Loss (\mathcal{L}M): Applied to bootstrap neural shape learning from object masks: \mathcal{L}M(\Phi\theta, Mt) = \frac{1}{\alpha \cdot N{\text{valid}}} \sum{p \in \mathcal{P}{\text{valid}}} \text{BCE}(\text{sigmoid}(-\alpha \Phi{\min}[p]), Mt[p]) where \mathcal{P}{\text{valid}} = \{p \mid Mt[p]=0 \lor \Phi{\min}[p]<\tau\} and N{\text{valid}} = |\mathcal{P}{\text{valid}}|. \Phi{\min}[p] is the minimum SDF value along the ray traced from pixel p. \tau is a threshold for whether the zero level set L0(\Phi\theta) has been intersected. \alpha is a softness hyperparameter. \text{BCE}(y, \hat{y}) = -[y \log(\hat{y}) + (1-y) \log(1-\hat{y})] is the Binary Cross Entropy. 3. Eikonal Regularization (\mathcal{L}E): Enforces the eikonal constraint on randomly sampled points pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 in a unit cube containing the scene: \mathcal{L}E(\Phi\theta) = \frac{1}{P} \sum{i=0}^{P} ||(||\nabla{pi} \Phi\theta(pi)||^2 - 1)||^22 Parameters \alpha: Softness hyperparameter for mask loss. Starting value: 50. \tau: Threshold for zero level set intersection. Starting value: 1 \times 10^{-3}. \lambda1: Weight for mask loss. Calculated as 1 \times 10^2 / \alpha. \lambda2: Weight for eikonal regularization. Starting value: 3. t1: Number of initial iterations to enforce shape losses. Starting value: 50. t2: Frequency (in iterations) to enforce shape losses after t1. Starting value: 7. Learning Rates: Adam optimizer with starting LR 1 \times 10^{-4} for \Phi and 5 \times 10^{-4} for E, D, \Gamma. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trainnlrplusplus(batchimages, batchmasks, batchcameras, modelparams, optimizer, hyperparams, currentiter): """ Performs one training step for NLR++. Args: batchimages: List of k images {In} batchmasks: List of k masks {Mn} batchcameras: List of k camera parameters {Cn} modelparams: Parameters [xi, psi, zeta, theta] for E, D, Gamma, Phi optimizer: Adam optimizer instance hyperparams: Dict containing alpha, tau, lambda1, lambda2, t1, t2, l, Peikonal currentiter: Global iteration counter Returns: lossvalue: Scalar loss value """ k = len(batchimages) l = hyperparams['l'] t1 = hyperparams['t1'] t2 = hyperparams['t2'] alpha = hyperparams['alpha'] tau = hyperparams['tau'] lambda1 = hyperparams['lambda1'] lambda2 = hyperparams['lambda2'] Peikonal = hyperparams['Peikonal'] totalloss = 0.0 # Multi-Target Gradient Computation: treat l < k images as targets for idx in range(l): It = batchimages[idx] Mt = batchmasks[idx] Ct = batchcameras[idx] # Synthesis: generate synthesized target image and mask # NLR++ image formation model uses context images excluding the target itself context = [img for i, img in enumerate(batchimages) if i != idx] Ihatt, Mhatt = synthesizeimage(Ct, context, modelparams) # Image Reconstruction Loss (Masked L1) maskpixels = [p for p in range(len(It)) if Mt[p] == 1] nummaskpixels = len(maskpixels) lrloss = sum(abs(It[p] - Ihatt[p]) for p in maskpixels) / nummaskpixels if nummaskpixels > 0 else 0.0 # Scheduled Shape Supervision lmloss = 0.0 leloss = 0.0 if currentiter <= t1 or currentiter % t2 == 0: # Soft Mask Loss validpixels = [] for p in range(len(Mt)): rayorigin = Ct.origin raydirection = Ct.direction phimin = findminsdfalongray(rayorigin, raydirection, modelparams.phi) if Mt[p] == 0 or phimin < tau: validpixels.append((p, phimin)) denom = len(validpixels) num = sum(binarycrossentropy(sigmoid(-alpha phimin), Mt[p]) for p, phimin in validpixels) lmloss = num / (alpha denom) if denom > 0 else 0.0 # Eikonal Regularization points = samplerandompoints(Peikonal, bounds=[-1, 1]) leloss = sum((norm(computegradient(modelparams.phi, pi))2 - 1)2 for pi in points) / len(points) # Combine Losses loss = lrloss + lambda1 lmloss + lambda2 leloss totalloss += loss totalloss /= l optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def binarycrossentropy(ypred, ytrue): return -(ytrue math.log(ypred + 1e-8) + (1 - ytrue) math.log(1 - ypred + 1e-8)) def norm(v): return math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) def computegradient(phi, p, eps=1e-5): grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): pplus = [p[j] + (eps if j == i else 0.0) for j in range(3)] pminus = [p[j] - (eps if j == i else 0.0) for j in range(3)] grad[i] = (phi(pplus) - phi(pminus)) / (2 eps) return grad def samplerandompoints(n, bounds): return [[uniform(bounds[0], bounds[1]) for in range(3)] for in range(n)] def getrayfrompixel(p, C): return [C.origin[i] + p C.direction[i] for i in range(3)] def findminsdfalongray(rayorigin, raydirection, phi, numsamples=64, tmin=0.0, tmax=2.0): minval = float('inf') for t in [tmin + (tmax - tmin) i / numsamples for i in range(numsamples + 1)]: pt = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] val = phi(pt) if val < minval: minval = val return minval def synthesizeimage(C, context, params): # NLR++ image formation model: renders image from viewpoint C using context images and network params pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls Compute Bottleneck: \mathcal{L}M requires finding the minimum of \Phi\theta along a ray, which necessitates dense sampling of the network and accounts for most of the compute time of each forward pass. Precision: The threshold \tau must be small enough to detect the zero level set but large enough to avoid noise. The softness parameter \alpha controls the sharpness of the mask boundary; if too high, gradients may become unstable. MetaNLR++ uses meta-learning to learn a prior over feature encoding, decoding, aggregation, and shape representation by optimizing the initial network weights \Theta0 for fast convergence on unseen scenes. It differs from standard NLR++ by using the Reptile algorithm to update \Theta0 based on inner-loop optimization on sampled tasks. The meta-learning objective is to find initial weights \Theta0^ that minimize the expected loss after m optimization steps on an unseen scene T: \Theta0^ = \arg \min{\Theta0} \mathbb{E}{T \sim \mathcal{T}} [\mathcal{L}(\Thetam(\Theta0, T))]. The update rule is \Theta0^{j+1} = \Theta0^j + \beta(\Thetam(\Theta0^j, Tj) - \Theta0^j), where \beta is the meta-learning rate (starting value 1 \times 10^{-1}) and m is the fixed number of inner-loop steps. This approach significantly reduces training time; for example, on the ShapeNet chairs split, MetaNLR++ reaches 30dB PSNR in 1.5 minutes compared to NLR++'s 3.6 minutes. Time Complexity: Training is dominated by dense sampling for \mathcal{L}M, accounting for most compute time per forward pass. Multi-target batching adds forward passes to \Gamma and D, which are fast to evaluate. Memory Complexity: Number of target images l treated as targets is limited by GPU memory. Performance: On ShapeNet, NLR++ converges slower than MetaNLR++; on chairs split, NLR++ takes 3.6 min to reach 30dB PSNR vs MetaNLR++'s 1.5 min. Strengths: Scheduled shape supervision decouples shape approximation from feature refinement for faster initial convergence. CNN encoder/decoder increases image loss receptive field for more meaningful gradients. Limitations: Dense sampling for \mathcal{L}M is computationally expensive. NLR++ without meta-learning converges slower than MetaNLR++. When to Use: Use NLR++ for standard neural lumigraph representation without meta-learning overhead. Use MetaNLR++ when rapid convergence on unseen scenes is critical. NLR++ was introduced as an end-to-end differentiable neural lumigraph representation optimized to reconstruct target views from posed 2D images using a CNN encoder/decoder and an SDF for shape. It serves as the baseline for MetaNLR++, which improves upon it using meta-learning. The implementation details, including hyperparameters and training schedules, are described in the supplementary material of the source paper. Experiments were conducted on Nvidia Quadro RTX8000 and RTX6000 GPUs. Fast Training of Neural Lumigraph Representations using Meta Learning, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.14942, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields
head: Neural Opacity Light Field, PSH Implementation for i-NOLF
body: Instant Neural Opacity Light Fields (i-NOLF) is a real-time neural rendering method that represents scenes as local neural opacity light fields to achieve one-query-per-pixel rendering. It combines spatial hash encoding with light field properties to avoid the computational overhead of hundreds of neural network forward passes per pixel, which is typical in standard NeRF-based renderers. Unlike Local Light Field Fusion which relies on explicit light field structures, and Neural Lumigraph Rendering which uses neural radiance fields on lumigraphs, i-NOLF decouples diffuse and specular components and uses a proxy geometry with opacity refinement to handle complex details like hair and boundaries efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A surface mesh or proxy geometry M, view direction v, and ray origin. Outputs: Final outgoing radiance color c and opacity \alpha. Data Structures: 1. Density Texture Cubes: A set of small dense texture cubes representing the density field. Base Grid: Uniform indexing grid of resolution b (Typical value: 128) to index valid grid cells. Valid Cubes Table: Maps valid grid cells to addresses in a table of valid cubes. Cube Content: Uniform grid of resolution r (Typical value: 16) storing queried densities. Storage: Moved to texture memory for hardware-accelerated linear interpolation. 2. Hash Tables: Specular Hash Encoder (Es): Uses Perfect Spatial Hashing (PSH). Stores features only for voxels surrounding hit points. Diffuse Hash Encoder (Ed): Uses standard hash grid encoding. 3. Neural Networks: Specular MLP (Fs): Takes Es(p), view direction v, and coarse opacity \alphac as input. Outputs specular color cs and opacity \alpha. Diffuse MLP (Fd): Takes Ed(p) as input. Outputs diffuse color cd and specular tint t. Numbered Steps: 1. Hit Point Estimation: Perform ray marching on the cached density texture cubes to find the ray-object hit point Ph. To avoid noisy hit points on object boundaries or hair (common in standard NeRF blending), select the sample point with the largest blending weight wi as the hit point. Accumulate sample weights into a coarse opacity \alphac for the ray. The blending weight is defined as: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the distance between adjacent samples, and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance. 2. Feature Encoding: Encode the hit point coordinate Ph to a feature vector Es(Ph) using the specular hash encoder Es. Encode the hit point coordinate Ph to a feature vector Ed(Ph) using the diffuse hash encoder Ed. 3. Network Inference: Specular Path: Concatenate Es(Ph), the normalized view direction v (in 3D Cartesian space), and the coarse opacity \alphac. Pass this through the Specular MLP Fs: Fs: (Es(p), v, \alphac) \rightarrow (cs, \alpha) This outputs the view-dependent specular color cs and the refined opacity \alpha. Diffuse Path: Pass Ed(Ph) through the Diffuse MLP Fd: Fd: Ed(p) \rightarrow (cd, t) This outputs the view-independent diffuse color cd and the specular tint t. 4. Radiance Combination: Combine the diffuse and specular components to obtain the final outgoing radiance c: c = cd + t \cdot cs This decoupling helps keep specular effects during compression and leverages the compressibility of the residual specular component. 5. Training: Optimize parameters of hash grids Es, Ed and networks Fs, Fd using an L2 loss on a batch of N rays sampled according to an optimizable error map: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (\|c - c{gt}\|^2 + \|\alpha - \alpha{gt}\|^2) where c{gt} and \alpha{gt} are ground truth color and alpha values. Use the Adam optimizer with parameter settings similar to i-NGP. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hashfunction(p, hfunc): """ Simple hash function for integer coordinate p. In PSH, two hash functions h0 and h1 are used. This is a placeholder for the specific hashing logic described in PSH. """ # Implementation details of Perfect Spatial Hashing are complex; # here we assume a standard integer hash for the feature lookup index. return hash(p) % HASHTABLESIZE def getdensityfromtexturecube(x, y, z, basegrid, cubetable, cuberes): """ Retrieve density from cached density texture cubes. """ # 1. Find base grid cell baseidx = (basegridwidth basegridheight (y // cuberes) + basegridwidth (x // cuberes) + (z // cuberes)) # 2. Get cube address from table cubeaddr = cubetable[baseidx] # 3. Local coordinates within the cube localx = x % cuberes localy = y % cuberes localz = z % cuberes # 4. Linear interpolation (hardware accelerated in practice) # Simplified: return value at nearest neighbor or interpolated return cubetable[cubeaddr][localx, localy, localz] def raymarchinghitpoint(rayorigin, raydirection, basegrid, cubetable, cuberes): """ Estimate hit point and coarse opacity using density texture cubes. """ maxsteps = 100 stepsize = 0.01 currentpos = rayorigin coarseopacity = 0.0 maxweight = 0.0 hitpoint = currentpos for i in range(maxsteps): # Get density at current position density = getdensityfromtexturecube( currentpos.x, currentpos.y, currentpos.z, basegrid, cubetable, cuberes) # Calculate blending weight # wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) # Ti is transmittance from previous steps # For simplicity, assuming deltai is stepsize deltai = stepsize sigmai = density # Transmittance calculation would require accumulating previous densities # Here we assume Ti is passed or calculated in a loop # Ti = exp(-sum(sigmaj deltaj)) # Approximate weight for hit point selection # In full implementation, Ti must be tracked weight = 0.0 # Placeholder for actual weight calculation if weight > maxweight: maxweight = weight hitpoint = currentpos # Accumulate coarse opacity # alphai = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) # coarseopacity += alphai currentpos += raydirection stepsize return hitpoint, coarseopacity def encodepositionpsh(p, hashtable, offsettable, h0, h1): """ Perfect Spatial Hashing encoding. """ # Find voxel corners corners = getvoxelcorners(p) # Hash corner coordinates indices = [h0(corner) + offsettable[h1(corner)] for corner in corners] # Look up features features = [hashtable[idx] for idx in indices] # Tri-linear interpolation return interpolate(features, p) def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, basegrid, cubetable, cuberes, hashtables, offsettables, h0s, h1s, hashtabled, offsettabled, h0d, h1d, specularmlp, diffusemlp): """ One-query-per-ray rendering. """ # Step 1: Hit point estimation hitpoint, coarseopacity = raymarchinghitpoint( rayorigin, raydirection, basegrid, cubetable, cuberes) # Step 2: Specular Encoding Es = encodepositionpsh(hitpoint, hashtables, offsettables, h0s, h1s) # Step 3: Diffuse Encoding Ed = encodepositionpsh(hitpoint, hashtabled, offsettabled, h0d, h1d) # Step 4: Specular MLP # Fs: (Es(p), v, alphac) -> (cs, alpha) viewdir = normalize(raydirection) cs, alpha = specularmlp(Es, viewdir, coarseopacity) # Step 5: Diffuse MLP # Fd: Ed(p) -> (cd, t) cd, t = diffusemlp(Ed) # Step 6: Combine c = cd + t cs return c, alpha Parameters: M: Surface mesh or proxy geometry. S^2: Sphere of unit vectors representing view directions. Es: Spatial hash encoder for specular component. Ed: Extra spatial hash encoder for diffuse component. v: Normalized view direction in 3D Cartesian space. cs: View-dependent specular color output. \alpha: Refined opacity output. \alphac: Coarse opacity accumulated from sample weights. \deltai: Distance between adjacent samples. cd: Diffuse color output. t: Specular tint output. N: Number of rays in a batch. c{gt}: Ground truth color. b: Resolution of base uniform indexing grid (Typical: 128). r: Resolution of each density texture cube (Typical: 16). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Proxy Geometry Ambiguity: Learning an opacity light field with a bounding box as proxy geometry is difficult because spatially adjacent points have similar encoded features but different lumispheres (one-to-many mapping). Noisy Hit Points: Standard NeRF hit depth estimation generates noisy hit points on object boundaries and hair objects. The largest blending weight strategy mitigates this. Memory Efficiency: PSH is used for specular because it offers superior memory efficiency and speed, while diffuse is cached in texture cubes, making the hash grid sufficient for diffuse. An ultra-fast renderer that marries opacity light fields with i-NGP to conduct one-query-per-ray rendering, avoiding redundant computational overhead. It uses density texture cubes for fast hit point estimation and decouples diffuse/specular components for efficient encoding. A caching mechanism representing the density field as a set of small dense texture cubes to skip empty space and accelerate hit point estimation (ray marching) by leveraging hardware-accelerated linear interpolation in texture memory. It uses a base uniform indexing grid (resolution b=128) to index valid cells, which map to a table of valid cubes (resolution r=16). Hit point estimation takes less than 0.1ms for a 1920x1080 image. Time Complexity: One-query-per-ray rendering, significantly faster than standard NeRF which requires hundreds of forward passes per pixel. Hit point estimation takes less than 0.1ms for 1920x1080. Memory Complexity: Uses Perfect Spatial Hashing (PSH) for specular to improve memory efficiency and speed. Diffuse is cached in texture cubes. Hash tables store features only for voxels surrounding hit points, allowing finer grid resolution with acceptable parameter scale. Performance: Achieves real-time rendering speeds suitable for cloud platforms and interactive applications. Strengths: Ultra-fast rendering, handles complex details (hair, boundaries) better than standard NeRF hit estimation, memory efficient via PSH and texture cubes. Limitations: Requires proxy geometry M. Learning with poor proxy geometry (e.g., simple bounding boxes) can lead to artifacts due to one-to-many mappings. Slightly degraded rendering quality compared to non-optimized NeRF due to approximations. When to Use: Real-time neural rendering, cloud rendering platforms, scenes with complex geometry and view-dependent effects. When Not to Use: Scenes where proxy geometry is unavailable or highly inaccurate, or when maximum possible rendering quality is prioritized over speed. i-NOLF was introduced in the paper "NEPHELE: A Neural Platform for Highly Realistic Cloud Radiance Rendering" by Luo et al. in 2023. It builds on the i-NGP renderer [Müller et al. 2022] and aims to accelerate real-time neural rendering by combining opacity light fields with instant neural graphics primitives. The method addresses the computational bottlenecks of standard NeRF rendering and the limitations of multiresolution hash encoding on GPUs. NEPHELE: A Neural Platform for Highly Realistic Cloud Radiance Rendering, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04086v1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Generalizable Radiance Fields
body: Generalizable Radiance Fields solve the problem of per-scene optimization latency by learning a data prior from a large-scale dataset, enabling immediate novel view synthesis on unseen scenes without iterative training. They differ from standard radiance-field optimization methods by replacing per-scene gradient descent with a feedforward neural network that aggregates multi-view features or cost volumes to predict density and color directly. Generalizable radiance fields share the goal of bypassing per-scene optimization by learning a representation from a large-scale dataset that can be adapted to unseen objects or scenes. This is achieved by learning generalizable geometric priors from source images, typically obtained using feature volumes or transformer-based attention modules to aggregate source view information. Recent methods also leverage deep multiview stereo (MVS) strategies to enforce generalization within the NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines. NeRF-SDP is a generalizable neural radiance field designed for high-fidelity novel view synthesis with sparse sampling points NeRF-SDP. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly incorporating monocular depth estimation for geometry features and a depth-encoded ray transformer to maintain quality with fewer sampling points NeRF-SDP. Choose it when balancing rendering speed and quality is critical for sparse input views NeRF-SDP. IBRNet is a feedforward neural network for generalizable view synthesis that bypasses per-scene optimization by learning a data prior from a training set IBRNet. It differs from sibling methods by using a Ray Transformer to predict density directly from aggregated multi-view features IBRNet. Choose it when a data-driven prior from a large training set is available for fast inference on unseen scenes IBRNet. A generalizable approach aiming to learn a representation from a large-scale dataset that can be fine-tuned for unseen objects, using feature volumes to obtain generalizable geometric priors. A scene representation architecture that combines 2D feature planes (tri-planes) and a 3D voxel grid to improve reconstruction quality while maintaining compact parameter counts. Ablation on Synthetic-NeRF dataset: Tri-plane (13.7M, 31.44 PSNR, 0.949 SSIM), Voxel (13.6M, 32.35 PSNR, 0.956 SSIM), Hybrid (13.2M, 32.64 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM). Compared to a pure 2D tri-plane representation (13.7M params, 31.44 PSNR, 0.949 SSIM) and a pure 3D voxel representation (13.6M params, 32.35 PSNR, 0.956 SSIM), the hybrid grid uses 13.2M parameters to achieve 32.64 PSNR and 0.958 SSIM, confirming superior compactness and quality. Original implicit radiance field representations lack cross-scene generalization capabilities and typically overlook relations between views, requiring long per-scene optimization. To mitigate this, methods following a generalizable approach aim to learn a representation from a large-scale dataset that can be fine-tuned and adapted to unseen objects or scenes. This is achieved by learning generalizable geometric priors from source images, obtained using feature volumes or transformer-based attention modules to aggregate source view information. Recent methods further enforce generalization by leveraging deep multiview stereo (MVS) strategies incorporated into the original NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines. name: NeRF-SDP
body: NeRF-SDP is an efficient generalizable neural radiance field that achieves high-fidelity novel view synthesis with sparse sampling points by incorporating scene depth perception via geometry feature extraction and a depth-encoded ray transformer. It solves the problem of balancing rendering speed and quality in generalizable NeRFs, where existing methods either rely on complex networks leading to inefficient rendering or use simpler networks and fewer sampling points leading to artifacts. It differs from its siblings, such as IBRNet, by explicitly using monocular depth estimation to extract geometry features during the feature extraction stage and employing a depth-encoded ray transformer to infer volume density, thereby maintaining quality with fewer sampling points. Inputs: A set of N reference images Ii for i=1, \dots, N. Outputs: A rendered image for a target camera pose, derived from volume density \sigma and color c along rays. Data Structures: Feature Volume (V^fi): A 3D tensor representing features for a single view, derived from the total feature map Fi. Cost Volume (Vc): A 3D tensor constructed from multiple feature volumes, encoding multi-view consistency. Depth Probability Volume (Vp): A 3D tensor where each voxel contains the probability of a surface existing at that depth layer. 3D Feature Volume (F{cv}): A 3D tensor containing aggregated features for volume rendering, derived from the cost volume. Geometry Feature Map (F^{geo}i): A 2D map per view containing geometric priors. Texture Feature Map (F^{fe}i): A 2D map per view containing appearance priors. Steps: 1. Geometry Feature Extraction: For each reference image Ii, a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model H{mono} estimates the relative depth map \tilde{D}i. This depth map is passed through a shared feature extraction network G{fe} to calculate the geometry feature map F^{geo}i: F^{geo}i = G{fe}(H{mono}(Ii)), \quad i = 1, \dots, N The output F^{geo}i has the same spatial dimensions as the input image but encodes geometric structure. 2. Texture Feature Extraction: For each reference image Ii, a network extracts the texture feature map F^{fe}i. 3. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the texture feature map F^{fe}i and the geometry feature map F^{geo}i of the i-th view to form the total feature map Fi: Fi = \text{Concat}(F^{fe}i, F^{geo}i) Concatenation occurs along the channel dimension. 4. Feature Volume Construction: Obtain a feature volume V^fi for each view using its total feature map Fi. This is typically achieved by extruding the 2D feature map along the depth axis using a fixed set of depth planes. 5. Cost Volume Construction: Construct the cost volume Vc from the set of feature volumes \{V^fi\}: Vc = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (V^fi - \bar{V}^f)^2 where \bar{V}^f denotes the mean feature volume of the N views, and the square is an element-wise operation. 6. Depth Probability and 3D Feature Volume Generation: Use a 3D CNN network to convert the cost volume Vc into a depth probability volume Vp and a 3D feature volume F{cv}. 7. Depth and Confidence Estimation: Calculate the estimated depth d and confidence interval s on a ray r from the depth probability volume Vp: d = \sum{j=1}^{L} pj dj s = \sum{j=1}^{L} pj (dj - d)^2 Here, d and s represent the estimated depth and confidence interval on ray r. pj and dj represent the depth probability in Vp and the depth value at the j-th layer on ray r, respectively. L is the number of depth layers. 8. Volume Density Inference: Use a Depth-Encoded Ray Transformer (DERT) to infer the volume density \sigma of each query point. The DERT aggregates features from N views for each point and uses the estimated depth d and confidence s as positional encodings or inputs to guide density prediction, allowing for accurate reconstruction with fewer sampling points. 9. Volume Rendering: Render the image by integrating color and density along rays using the inferred \sigma and color c. Parameters: N: Number of reference views. L: Number of depth layers/hypotheses. Typical Performance: On the dataset in, NeRF-SDP achieves PSNR 26.95dB in 5.16s. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Monocular depth accuracy affects geometry features; inaccurate estimates may lead to artifacts. Extreme sparsity may challenge generalization. Element-wise operations in cost volume construction and depth estimation require careful numerical precision handling. Constructs a 3D cost volume from multiple input views to enable generalizable NeRFs by encoding multi-view consistency. It differs from standard NeRFs by replacing per-ray MLP optimization with a differentiable 3D convolutional encoding of a pre-computed cost volume, and from other generalizable methods by explicitly using homographic warping for feature alignment. Choose it when multi-view consistency is critical and homographic warping is applicable. Rendering time is efficient compared to other generalizable NeRFs, achieving 5.16s per image versus 7.44s for MVSNeRF and 15.48s for IBRNet. Memory complexity is not given in the sources. Measured performance on the comparison dataset shows NeRF-SDP achieves PSNR 26.95dB, outperforming MVSNeRF (25.33dB) and IBRNet (26.29dB). Strengths include high fidelity with sparse sampling points, efficient rendering, and improved geometry understanding via scene depth perception. Limitations include reliance on a pre-trained monocular depth estimation model and potential failure when depth estimation is unreliable. Use it when high-quality novel view synthesis is required from sparse input views with limited rendering resources. Avoid it when per-scene optimization is acceptable and higher accuracy is needed, or when input views are dense. NeRF-SDP was proposed by researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China. It was published in 2023. The method addresses the challenge of balancing rendering speed and quality in generalizable NeRFs by introducing scene depth perception. It is the first generalizable method to use estimated depth during the feature extraction stage. NeRF-SDP: Efficient Generalizable Neural Radiance Field with Scene Depth Perception, https://doi.org/10.1145/3595916.3626380, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Cost Volume Construction for Neural Radiance Fields
head: Homographic warping cost volume, Variance-based cost volume
body: This method constructs a 3D cost volume from multiple input views to enable generalizable neural radiance fields by encoding multi-view consistency. It infers scene geometry and appearance without per-scene optimization by warping 2D features from input views to a reference view across a range of depths and aggregating their variance. It replaces per-ray MLP optimization with a differentiable 3D convolutional encoding of a pre-computed cost volume, and uses homographic warping for feature alignment rather than simple depth projection or attention mechanisms. Inputs: N input views, each an image Ii \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi \times Wi \times 3} for i=1 \dots N. Camera parameters for each view i: intrinsic matrix Ki, rotation matrix Ri, translation vector ti. A reference view (typically view 1) with parameters K1, R1, t1. A set of discrete depth values g defining the scanning volume. Hyperparameters: feature channel count C, number of input views N. Outputs: Cost volume P with spatial dimensions matching the downsampled reference view, depth steps, and feature channels. Neural feature volume S = B(P), where B is a 3D CNN (see Subtopics). Data Structures: Feature maps Fi: Extracted via CNN, layout \mathbb{R}^{Hi/4 \times Wi/4 \times C}. Warped feature maps F{i,g}: Same layout as Fi, aligned to reference view coordinates. Cost volume P: 4D tensor with dimensions corresponding to reference view spatial resolution (downsampled by 4), depth steps, and feature channels. Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: For each input view Ii, pass through a deep CNN with down-sampling convolutional layers to extract a high-dimensional feature map Fi \in \mathbb{R}^{Hi/4 \times Wi/4 \times C}. The CNN typically uses stride-2 convolutions to achieve the 1/4 resolution reduction. 2. Homographic Warping: For each view i and each depth sample g: a. Compute the homographic deformation matrix Qi(g) to warp features from view i to the reference view at depth g: Qi(g) = Ki Ri R1^T + \frac{(t1 - ti)n}{n1} \mathbf{1}^T K1^{-1} Where Ki, K1 are intrinsic matrices, Ri, R1 are rotation matrices, ti, t1 are translation vectors, n is the normal vector, n1 is the depth component of n, and \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones. For a fixed depth g in the reference frame, n is typically [0,0,1]^T and n1 = g. b. Warp the feature map Fi to the reference view at depth g using bilinear interpolation: F{i,g}(a, b) = Fi(Qi(g)[a, b, 1]^T) where (a, b) is the pixel position in the reference view. 3. Cost Volume Aggregation: For each voxel at position (a, b, g) in the cost volume, collect the warped feature vectors from all N views and compute the variance across the views to determine the cost feature vector P(a, b, g): P(a, b, g) = \text{Var}(F{i,g}(a, b)) \text{Var}(\cdot) is computed channel-wise. For each channel c, P(a, b, g)c = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N (F{i,g}(a, b)c - \muc)^2, where \muc is the mean across views for channel c. This results in a vector of size C. 4. Neural Encoding: Process the cost volume P with a 3D CNN B with a UNet structure to extract scene geometry and appearance characteristics, producing a neural feature volume S = B(P). Parameters: C: The desired number of feature channels in the extracted feature maps. N: The total number of input views used to compute the variance in the cost volume. Depth range and sampling count: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusions: Homographic warping assumes consistent depth; occlusions cause mismatches in warped features, increasing variance incorrectly. Precision: Bilinear interpolation during warping introduces smoothing, potentially losing high-frequency details. Camera Parameters: Accurate K, R, t are critical; errors lead to misalignment and incorrect cost volume. A variant step where the cost volume P is processed by a 3D CNN B with a UNet structure to extract scene geometry and appearance characteristics, producing a neural feature volume S = B(P). This step transforms the raw variance-based cost features into a high-dimensional feature space where channels represent distinct attributes (lighting, textures, materials), enabling inference of volume density and brightness dependent on viewpoint. It sets itself apart by adding a learnable 3D convolutional encoder to the static cost volume, allowing the network to refine geometric and appearance cues before rendering. Choose this when high-fidelity rendering of complex materials and lighting is required, as opposed to using the raw cost volume directly. Time Complexity: Dominated by feature extraction (O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C)) and warping (O(N \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C)). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D \cdot H \cdot W \cdot C) to store intermediate warped features or the final cost volume. Performance: Enables fast novel view synthesis as it avoids per-scene optimization. Strengths: Generalizable to unseen scenes; leverages multi-view consistency; differentiable end-to-end. Limitations: Sensitive to camera calibration errors; struggles with occlusions and non-Lambertian surfaces; resolution limited by the cost volume size and warping accuracy. When to use: Sparse view synthesis, real-time applications where per-scene optimization is too slow. When not to use: Scenes with significant occlusions, dynamic content, or when high-precision depth is required without additional regularization. Originated in the context of generalizable neural radiance fields, specifically in the work by (2024/2025). It builds on earlier work in multi-view stereo and homography-based warping [37] (cited in) and UNet-based 3D CNNs [38] (cited in). The method addresses the limitation of traditional NeRFs that require per-scene optimization, by introducing a cost volume that encodes multi-view consistency, allowing for generalizable rendering. name: IBRNet
head: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with Image-Based Rendering Networks
body: IBRNet is a feedforward neural network method for novel view synthesis that generalizes to unseen scenes without per-scene optimization. It differs from standard NeRF and siblings like NeRF-SDP by replacing iterative volume rendering optimization with a CNN-based feature extraction and a Ray Transformer that predicts density directly from multi-view features. It builds on Generalizable Radiance Fields by using a data prior learned from a large dataset to bypass scene-specific training. The input consists of a target camera pose and N source images from the training set with similar viewing directions. The output is the density \sigma for query points along rays from the target camera. The feature volume is implicitly constructed via feature aggregation. No explicit 3D grid is stored, and features are projected from 2D image features. The Ray Transformer is a sequence model that processes concatenated features along a ray. 1. View Selection: For a target view, the method selects N source views from the training set with the most similar viewing directions. 2. Feature Extraction: A CNN extracts feature maps Fi from each of the N source images. 3. Query Point Projection: For a query point x along a ray from the target camera, the method projects x onto each source image i using the known camera matrix Ki to obtain pixel coordinates. 4. Feature Sampling: The method samples the color ci and feature vector fi from the CNN features at the projected coordinates for each view i. 5. Feature Refinement and Weighting: Each feature fi is passed through an MLP to produce a refined multi-view aware feature f'i and a pooling weight wi. 6. Feature Aggregation: The method computes the aggregated feature F{agg} for point x by summing the refined features weighted by wi: F{agg}(x) = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi f'i This step is repeated for all query points along the ray. 7. Ray Transformer Processing: The method concatenates the aggregated features F{agg}(x) for all query points along the ray into a sequence. This sequence is fed into a Ray Transformer. 8. Density Prediction: The Ray Transformer outputs the density \sigma for each query point. Color prediction details are not provided in the sources. The number of source views N is not given in the sources. The CNN backbone is not given in the sources. The MLP dimensions are not given in the sources. View selection relies on choosing N source views with the most similar viewing directions. Projection accuracy depends on camera calibration. IBRNet is limited by COLMAP for camera pose estimation. A denoising method that incorporates inter-view and spatial awareness to enhance noise robustness, achieving state-of-the-art results in burst denoising under challenging conditions like large motion and high noise. It avoids per-scene training by building on IBRNet, which generalizes to unseen scenes with minimal input. Feedforward inference is significantly faster than iterative NeRF optimization. Memory usage depends on the number of source views N and the CNN feature size, with no explicit 3D volume storage required. The method is widely used in benchmarks for view synthesis. It reduces the number of iterations compared to per-scene NeRF. Generalization to unseen scenes without per-scene optimization and fast inference are primary strengths. Limitations include the requirement for a training dataset and performance dependence on the availability of similar source views. The method should be used for novel view synthesis where per-scene optimization is too slow. It is not suitable for scenes with no similar training views. IBRNet was published in February 2021 as a NeRF-adjacent method for view synthesis. It was introduced to address the slow training speed of NeRF by using a feedforward model to learn a data prior. It is widely used in benchmarks. name: 2D-3D Hybrid Feature Grid
head: Hybrid Tri-Plane and Voxel Grid
body: The 2D-3D Hybrid Feature Grid is a scene representation architecture that combines 2D feature planes (tri-planes) and a 3D voxel grid to improve reconstruction quality while maintaining compact parameter counts. It addresses the trade-off between the geometric expressiveness of 3D voxels and the computational efficiency of 2D planes. Compared to a pure 2D tri-plane representation and a pure 3D voxel representation, the hybrid grid achieves superior compactness and quality, using fewer parameters to reach higher PSNR and SSIM scores. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of source images used for training; a query ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for rendering. Output: Volume density \sigma and view-dependent color \mathbf{c} for sample points along the ray. Data Structures: The representation consists of a hybrid feature grid \Psi. The architecture uses two resolution levels and two feature dimensions. 2D Feature Planes (Tri-planes): Three 2D grids storing spatial features. 3D Feature Grid: A 3D volume storing features. Density Features fd: A vector in \mathbb{R}^4. Appearance Features fc: A vector in \mathbb{R}^8. Positional Encoding \gamma(\cdot): Applied to the view direction \mathbf{d}, using 6 frequencies. Parameters: Feature dimensions = 2. Resolution levels = 2. d = 256: The final grid resolution dimension for the 3D component. fd \in \mathbb{R}^4: Number of density feature channels. fc \in \mathbb{R}^8: Number of appearance feature channels. N\gamma = 6: Number of frequencies in the positional encoding function \gamma(\cdot). Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample points pi along the query ray. 2. Coarse Interpolation: At the coarse resolution level, perform bilinear interpolation on the 2D feature planes and trilinear interpolation on the 3D voxel grid for each pi. 3. Fine Interpolation: At the fine resolution level, perform trilinear interpolation exclusively on the 3D voxel grid for each pi. 4. Feature Combination: Combine the coarse and fine interpolated features to form the input for the MLP decoders. 5. Density & Color Prediction: Process the combined features through MLPs \pid and \pic to estimate raw density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. Formulas: \sigmai = \pid(\mathbf{f}{\text{combined}}) \mathbf{c}i = \pic(\mathbf{f}{\text{combined}}, \gamma(\mathbf{d})) where \mathbf{f}{\text{combined}} is the concatenated output of the coarse and fine interpolation stages. Pitfalls: Hardware Efficiency: The number of features for each network must be a multiple of four to maximize texture efficiency, as one hardware-accelerated texture read fetches four channel values. Precision & Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryhybridgrid(grid3d, planes2d, point, viewdirection): # 1. Coarse scale: bilinear on 2D planes, trilinear on 3D grid coarse2d = bilinearinterpolate(planes2d, point.xy) coarse3d = trilinearinterpolate(grid3d, point) coarsefeatures = concatenate(coarse2d, coarse3d) # 2. Fine scale: trilinear on 3D grid only finefeatures = trilinearinterpolate(grid3d, point) # 3. Combine scales combinedfeatures = concatenate(coarsefeatures, finefeatures) # 4. Density prediction sigma = mlpdensity(combinedfeatures) # 5. Color prediction viewencoding = positionalencoding(viewdirection, numfrequencies=6) colorinput = concatenate(combinedfeatures, viewencoding) color = mlpcolor(colorinput) return sigma, color def trilinearinterpolate(grid, p): x, y, z = p x0, y0, z0 = floor(x), floor(y), floor(z) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 v000 = grid[x0, y0, z0]; v100 = grid[x1, y0, z0] v010 = grid[x0, y1, z0]; v110 = grid[x1, y1, z0] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1]; v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1]; v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1] c00 = lerp(v000, v100, dx); c10 = lerp(v010, v110, dx) c01 = lerp(v001, v101, dx); c11 = lerp(v011, v111, dx) c0 = lerp(c00, c10, dy); c1 = lerp(c01, c11, dy) return lerp(c0, c1, dz) def bilinearinterpolate(planes, uv): u, v = uv u0, v0 = floor(u), floor(v) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 du, dv = u - u0, v - v0 features = [] for plane in planes: v00 = plane[u0, v0]; v10 = plane[u1, v0] v01 = plane[u0, v1]; v11 = plane[u1, v1] c0 = lerp(v00, v10, du); c1 = lerp(v01, v11, du) features.append(lerp(c0, c1, dv)) return concatenate(features) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def concatenate(args): return sum(args) # Standard vector concatenation def positionalencoding(v, numfrequencies): encoded = [] for i in range(numfrequencies): scale = 2.0 i encoded.append(sin(2 pi scale v)) encoded.append(cos(2 pi scale v)) return concatenate(encoded) def mlpdensity(features): return exp(features @ Wd + bd) # Small MLP for density def mlpcolor(features): return tanh(features @ Wc + bc) # Small MLP for color A model architecture combining a 3D feature grid with small MLP decoders to leverage hardware texture interpolation and cache coherence for efficient real-time rendering. It uses a 3D feature grid \psi of dimension f \times d^3 and small MLPs \pid and \pic for density and color, respectively. This design achieves higher computational efficiency due to better cache coherence for sampling. It is critical to use multiples of four for the number of features for each network to maximize texture efficiency, as one hardware-accelerated texture read fetches four channel values. The grid resolution is set to d=256, with fd \in \mathbb{R}^4 and fc \in \mathbb{R}^8. The view direction \mathbf{d} is encoded using a positional encoding function \gamma(\cdot) with 6 frequencies. To address aliasing artifacts and high-resolution query costs in virtual reality, a hierarchy of feature grids is introduced by trilinearly downsampling the full-resolution grid to multiple levels of lower resolutions, similar to mipmaps. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The hybrid grid uses 13.2M parameters, which is fewer than the tri-plane (13.7M) and voxel (13.6M) representations. The 3D component has a resolution of 256^3. Time: The compact representation leads to better cache coherence, improving computational efficiency. Sparsity loss can improve rendering time in both training and inference with a minor decrease in reconstruction quality. Measured Performance: Synthetic-NeRF Dataset: Tri-plane: 13.7M params, 31.44 PSNR, 0.949 SSIM. Voxel: 13.6M params, 32.35 PSNR, 0.956 SSIM. Hybrid: 13.2M params, 32.64 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM. Dynamic Scene Reconstruction (D-NeRF/HyperNeRF): Ours-B2 (w/o sparsity loss): 6.4m train time, 3.3 fps inference, 32.69 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM. Ours-B2 (w/ sparsity loss): 6.1m train time, 3.8 fps inference, 32.64 PSNR, 0.958 SSIM. Ours-B8 (w/o sparsity loss): 14.7m train time, 2.2 fps inference, 33.60 PSNR, 0.964 SSIM. Ours-B8 (w/ sparsity loss): 13.9m train time, 2.7 fps inference, 33.59 PSNR, 0.964 SSIM. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Superior compactness and quality compared to pure 2D or 3D representations. Efficient real-time rendering potential due to hardware texture interpolation and cache coherence. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Use when high reconstruction quality is needed with compact parameter counts. Use when real-time rendering efficiency is critical, leveraging hardware texture interpolation. The 2D-3D Hybrid Feature Grid was introduced in "Binary Radiance Fields". It was developed to improve radiance field reconstruction quality while maintaining compact feature encoding. The hardware-guided variant was presented in "Neural Assets: Volumetric Object Capture and Rendering for Interactive Environments". name: Instant-NeRF
head: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives
body: Instant-NeRF is a multi-resolution feature voxel grid-based radiance field that enables the rendering of higher-quality radiance with significantly faster rendering speeds compared to standard MLP-based NeRFs. It sets itself apart from its parent Generalizable Radiance Fields by focusing on efficient spatial encoding for rapid optimization and rendering, rather than generalization from large datasets, and differs from siblings like NeRF-SDP and IBRNet by utilizing a dense multi-resolution grid structure for local feature storage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses. Output: A radiance field representation allowing for volume rendering of novel views. Data Structures: The core data structure is a multi-resolution feature voxel grid. Unlike standard NeRF which maps coordinates directly to an MLP, Instant-NeRF stores feature vectors in a 3D grid. Grid Layout: The grid consists of multiple resolutions (levels). At each level l, the grid has dimensions 2^l \times 2^l \times 2^l. Feature Vector: Each voxel stores a fixed-size feature vector (e.g., 8 or 16 floats). Lookup: For a query point \mathbf{x}, features are retrieved from all resolution levels using trilinear interpolation and concatenated to form the input to a small MLP. Steps: 1. Grid Initialization: Initialize multi-resolution voxel grids with random or zero-initialized feature vectors. 2. Sampling: For each pixel, cast a ray and sample points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. 3. Feature Extraction: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i: Query the feature vector \mathbf{f}i from the multi-resolution grid via trilinear interpolation. Concatenate features from all resolution levels: \mathbf{F}i = [\mathbf{f}i^{(1)}; \mathbf{f}i^{(2)}; \dots; \mathbf{f}i^{(L)}]. 4. MLP Processing: Pass \mathbf{F}i through a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict density \sigmai and view-dependent color \mathbf{c}i. \sigmai, \mathbf{c}i = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{F}i) 5. Volume Rendering: Compute the pixel color C using standard volume rendering integration: C = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj), and \deltai is the distance between samples. 6. Optimization: Minimize the difference between rendered and ground truth images using gradient descent. The gradients flow through the volume rendering equation back to the voxel features and MLP weights. Parameters: Grid Resolutions: Typically powers of 2, e.g., 128, 256, 512. Feature Dimension: 8–16 floats per voxel per level. MLP Size: Small, e.g., 2–3 hidden layers with 64–128 units. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Trilinear interpolation is differentiable but may introduce slight blurring at boundaries. Boundaries: Query points outside the grid bounds must be handled (e.g., clamping or returning zero features). Degenerate Input: If camera poses are inaccurate, the grid features may not align correctly, leading to artifacts. Multi-feature Radiance Baking Neural Network (MRBNN) is a neural volumetric rendering method that achieves real-time performance by leveraging analytic decomposition of scattering with an efficient learned representation. Time Complexity: Rendering is faster than standard NeRF due to the smaller MLP and efficient grid lookups. Training is also faster as the MLP is smaller. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is dominated by the voxel grid. For a grid of size S and feature dimension d, memory is O(S^3 \cdot d). Multi-resolution adds a constant factor. Measured Performance: Instant-NeRF achieves significantly faster rendering speeds than standard NeRF while maintaining comparable or higher quality. Strengths: Fast training and rendering; high quality. Limitations: Memory usage scales with grid resolution; less flexible than implicit representations for complex geometries. When to use: When fast training and rendering are required for static scenes. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained or for dynamic scenes requiring high flexibility. Instant-NeRF was developed by Müller et al.. It builds on the idea of using voxel grids to store feature vectors, which allows the radiance function to be decomposed into smaller, local functions. This approach reduces the complexity load on the MLP, enabling faster rendering and optimization. A community-driven implementation of Instant-NeRF is known as Nerfacto. name: Multi-feature Radiance Baking Neural Network
head: MRPNN, Multi-feature Radiance Baking
body: Multi-feature Radiance Baking Neural Network (MRBNN) is a neural volumetric rendering method that achieves real-time performance by leveraging analytic decomposition of scattering with an efficient learned representation. It reformulates the in-scattering integral in the Volumetric Radiance Transfer Equation (VRTE) into a diagonal scaling operator in the spherical harmonics spectrum, eliminating explicit spherical integration. Unlike its parent Instant-NeRF and sibling MRPNN, MRBNN operates without the low-density volume assumption, supports spatially varying albedo and heterogeneous phase functions, and achieves a 4–5× speedup over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high visual fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position, viewing direction \omega, volume bounding box, scattering coefficients (albedo \alpha, phase function parameter g), and light direction \omegas. Outputs: Radiance S(p, \omega) at point p. Data Structures: 1. Feature Grids: Multi-resolution voxel grids storing features. Base Grid (\mathcal{B}): Stores base features. Sampled via towards-light sampling. Transmittance Map (\mathcal{T}): Stores optical depth normalized by maximum density. Mipmapped. Light Grid (\mathcal{L}): Stores spherical harmonic coefficients L{i,l}^m(p). View Grid (\mathcal{V}): Stores view-dependent features. Geometry Grid (\mathcal{G}): Stores geometry features. Albedo Grid (\mathcal{A}): Stores albedo features. Note: For production volumes, scattering and extinction coefficients are stored as scalar voxels (direction-independent). 2. Latent Features (Oi): Intermediate representations fused across levels. O0 is a zero vector. 3. MLPs: Lightweight networks for feature fusion and decoding. Each MLP consists of two 64-neuron fully-connected layers. Parameters: M1: Number of grid levels and total steps towards light to sample \mathcal{B}. Typical value: 4. M2: Number of steps to sample \mathcal{T}. Typical value: 4. K: Order of spherical harmonics expansion. Coordinate Mapping: \cos \theta \in [-1, 1] is mapped to [0, 1] by (x+1)/2. Grid Resolution Mapping: Finer grid resolution is allocated for media with higher albedo using the non-linear mapping (e^x - 1)/(e - 1). Activation: ReLU6 is used as the final layer activation in MLPs for numeric stability. Algorithm Steps: 1. Reformulate Scattering: The in-scattering integral in the VRTE is reformulated as a diagonal scaling operator in the spherical harmonics spectrum. This allows the scattering operator to be approximated by a low-rank, factorized representation in latent space. 2. Sample Base and Transmittance Features: Perform towards-light sampling (cone tracing) to sample the Base feature \mathcal{B} and Transmittance feature \mathcal{T}. Sample \mathcal{B} at M1 points pi along the towards-light direction. Sample \mathcal{T} at M2 points pj along the towards-light direction. The step size increases exponentially. 3. Extract Multi-Feature Components: For each level i \in \{1, \dots, M1\}, extract the following features at the current shading point p and view direction \omega: Base Feature: \mathcal{B}i(pi) sampled at the i-th towards-light point. Light Feature: Approximated by summing spherical harmonics: \sum{l=0}^K g(p)^l \sum{m=-l}^l \mathcal{L}{i,l}^m(p)Yl^m(\omegas). View Feature: \mathcal{V}i(\omega). Geometry Feature: \mathcal{G}i(g(p), \cos \theta). Albedo Feature: \mathcal{A}i(\alpha(p, \omega), \cos \theta). Transmittance Vector: A vector of M2 samples [\mathcal{T}i(pj, \omegas)]{j=1}^{M2}. 4. Construct Feature Vector: Concatenate the components to form the feature vector \mathcal{F}i(p, \omega): \mathcal{F}i(p, \omega) = \left( \mathcal{B}i(pi), \sum{l=0}^K g(p)^l \sum{m=-l}^l \mathcal{L}{i,l}^m(p)Yl^m(\omegas), \mathcal{V}i(\omega), \mathcal{G}i(g(p), \cos \theta), \mathcal{A}i(\alpha(p, \omega), \cos \theta), [\mathcal{T}i(pj, \omegas)]{j=1}^{M2} \right) 5. Fuse Features Hierarchically: Use hierarchical residual blocks to fuse features across levels. For level i, compute the fused feature \overline{Oi} and update the latent feature Oi: \overline{Oi}(p, \omega) = \text{Concat}(\mathcal{F}i(p, \omega), O{i-1}(p, \omega)) Oi(p, \omega) = \mathcal{S}i(\overline{Oi}(p, \omega)) + \overline{Oi}(p, \omega) where \mathcal{S}i is an MLP with input and output dimension D. O0 is initialized to a zero vector. 6. Decode Radiance: After aggregating all M1 levels, use the final MLP \mathcal{S}{M1+1} to decode the final latent representation O{M1} into radiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Lcoeffs: list of lists, Lcoeffs[l][m] is the coefficient for degree l, order m. """ total = 0.0 for l in range(lmax + 1): term = gval l for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Yl^m(omegas) is assumed to be precomputed or available via a helper # For implementation, this requires a SH evaluation function Ylm = evaluatesh(l, m, omegas) term += Lcoeffs[l][m] Ylm total += term return total def evaluatesh(l, m, omegas): """ Placeholder for Spherical Harmonic evaluation. Sample Base Feature B at i-th towards-light point pi pi = sampletowardslight(p, i, M1) Bi = griddata['B'].query(pi) # 2. Sample Transmittance T at all M2 towards-light points Tsamples = [] for j in range(1, M2 + 1): pj = sampletowardslight(p, j, M2) Tsamples.append(griddata['T'].query(pj, omegas=volumeparams['omegas'])) # 3. Extract other features at current point p # Light Feature: SH sum Lcoeffs = griddata['L'].query(p) lightfeat = sphericalharmonicsum(K, volumeparams['g'], Lcoeffs, volumeparams['omegas']) # View Feature Vi = griddata['V'].query(omega) # Geometry Feature costheta = dot(omega, volumeparams['normal']) # Assuming normal available or derived costhetamapped = (costheta + 1.0) / 2.0 Gi = griddata['G'].query(volumeparams['g'], costhetamapped) # Albedo Feature alpha = volumeparams['alpha'] Ai = griddata['A'].query(alpha, costhetamapped) # 4. Construct Feature Vector Fi # Concatenate: Bi, lightfeat, Vi, Gi, Ai, Tsamples Fi = Bi + [lightfeat] + Vi + Gi + Ai + Tsamples # 5. Fuse Features # Concatenate Fi and Oprev Oprevdim = len(Oprev) Fidim = len(Fi) concatvec = Oprev + Fi # Apply MLP Si # Note: In practice, Si takes the concatenated vector and outputs a residual # The paper says Si has input/output R^D. Here we assume D is the latent dim. # If Fi and Oprev are not same dim, there's a projection. # Based on Eq 10: Oi = Si(overline{Oi}) + overline{Oi} # overline{Oi} is the concatenation. # Simulate MLP processing # In real impl, Si is a specific MLP. Here we just pass through for structure residual = mlptwolayer64(concatvec) # Update Oprev (Oi) # Note: Dimensions must match. Assuming residual is projected to match Oprev dim or Oprev is expanded. # For this pseudocode, we assume compatible dimensions or a projection layer exists. Oprev = [residual[k] + concatvec[k] for k in range(len(Oprev))] # Simplified addition # 6. Decode Radiance # Final MLP S{M1+1} decodes O{M1} radiance = mlptwolayer64(Oprev) return radiance def sampletowardslight(p, step, totalsteps): """ Simulates towards-light sampling (cone tracing). Step size increases exponentially. """ # Placeholder for actual ray marching logic return p # Returns current point for simplicity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-frequency Ambient Lighting: Stochastic light direction drawing causes severe flickering and requires seconds to converge. Baking ambient lighting (treating it as self-emission) stabilizes this. Low-Density Assumption: MRBNN does not assume low-density volumes, avoiding over-illumination artifacts in fragmented-volume scenarios where MRPNN fails. Albedo/Phase Variation: MRBNN supports spatially varying albedo and heterogeneous phase functions, whereas MRPNN requires consistent parameters throughout the scene. Time Complexity: The method achieves real-time performance. MRBNN renders complex multi-scattering effects of dense volumes at 200 FPS for 1024 × 1024 resolution with three-channel albedo. Memory Complexity: Uses compact latent-space neural baking with low-rank compression, offering practical space complexity. Performance: Achieves a 4–5× speedup over the state-of-the-art (MRPNN). Sampling strategy yields ~1.6× speedup; network inference achieves >20× speedup compared to MRPNN. MRPNN (single) takes 1.09ms delta tracking, 4.12ms sampling, 13.19ms MLP inference, <0.5ms post-process (51.1 FPS). MRBNN (single) takes 0.653ms MLP inference. MRPNN (full) takes 19.0ms MLP inference (40.5 FPS). MRBNN (full) takes 0.753ms MLP inference, 203ms post-process (5.01x), resulting in higher FPS. Strengths: Real-time rendering, support for spatially varying albedo and heterogeneous phase functions, temporal stability, no low-density assumption. Limitations: Requires training (10 epochs per scene, ~4 hours on RTX 4090). High-frequency ambient lighting requires baking to avoid flickering. When to Use: Real-time volumetric rendering of complex, dense volumes with varying material properties. When Not to Use: Scenes with high-frequency ambient lighting if baking is not feasible, or when offline path-tracing quality is required without neural approximation. MRBNN was introduced by Jiaming Liang, Hongliang Yuan, Meng Gai, Guoping Wang, and Sheng Li in 2026 at SIGGRAPH Conference Papers '26. It builds on the limitations of MRPNN, which assumed fragmented volumes to be continuous low-density volumes (causing over-illumination) and required consistent albedo and phase function parameters. MRBNN addresses these by using analytic decomposition of scattering and a compact factorized representation.
