name: Closed-Form Color Field Estimation
head: Closed-form color estimation
body: Closed-form color field estimation is a rendering-independent technique that computes the color field solely from a given density field and posed training images in closed form. It decouples shape and radiance to reduce the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). Unlike general geometric priors such as total variation or sparsity losses, this method is scene-adaptive and guided by photometric loss, directly supervising the density field through color consistency. Inputs: A 3D density field \sigma(\mathbf{v}) defined on a grid or explicit representation. A set of posed training images providing camera centers \mathbf{o}k and projection matrices Pk. The degree of the spherical harmonics basis L. Outputs: A color field \hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{v}) represented by spherical harmonics coefficients for every 3D point \mathbf{v} in the scene. Data Structures: Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: For each 3D point \mathbf{v}, store a vector of coefficients h\ell^m for \ell \in [0, L] and m \in [-\ell, \ell]. Transmittance Values: Precomputed or on-the-fly transmittance Tk(\mathbf{v}) from each camera k to point \mathbf{v} along the viewing direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Represent Color: Represent the color at each 3D point \mathbf{v} observed from direction \mathbf{d} as a linear combination of spherical harmonics basis functions up to degree L: F{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{d}} = \sum{\ell=0}^L \sum{m=-\ell}^\ell h\ell^m Y\ell^m(\mathbf{d}). 2. Estimate Coefficients: Estimate each coefficient h\ell^m by approximating the spherical integral using Monte Carlo sampling over directions \mathbf{d}k observed in the posed training images. The integral is approximated by dividing by the direction probability density function pd(\mathbf{d}k). 3. Weight by Transmittance: Weight the observed colors by the transmittance Tk(\mathbf{v}) to handle occlusion, ensuring only visible geometry contributes to the color estimation. 4. Residual Correction: Apply a residual color estimation scheme to handle non-uniformly distributed views and compensate for directional sampling bias. Formulas: The coefficient h\ell^m is estimated as: h\ell^m \approx \frac{1}{K} \sum{k=1}^K \frac{Tk(\mathbf{v}) F{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{d}k} Y\ell^m(\mathbf{d}k)}{pd(\mathbf{d}k)} where F{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{d}k} is the observed color at pixel location corresponding to \mathbf{d}k, Tk(\mathbf{v}) is the transmittance from camera k to \mathbf{v}, Y\ell^m(\mathbf{d}) is the spherical harmonics basis function, pd(\mathbf{d}) is the direction PDF, and K is the number of Monte Carlo samples (directions). Parameters: L: Degree of the spherical harmonics basis. Controls angular resolution of the color field. Typical values in NeRF literature are 3 or 4. pd(\mathbf{d}): Probability density function of observation directions. Assumed uniform over the sphere: pd(\mathbf{d}) \equiv \frac{1}{4\pi}. K: Number of Monte Carlo samples (directions) drawn from posed training images to approximate the integral for each SH coefficient. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Points occluded by foreground geometry will have low transmittance Tk(\mathbf{v}), reducing their contribution to the color field. Non-uniform Views: If training views are clustered, the Monte Carlo approximation of the spherical integral will be biased. Precision: Accumulating weights in floating point can lead to precision issues for points with many observations; use double precision for accumulation if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def closedformcolorestimation(densitygrid, cameraposes, images, L): """ densitygrid: 3D numpy array of sigma(v) cameraposes: list of tuples (ok, Pk) where ok is camera center and Pk is projection matrix images: list of 2D numpy arrays of observed colors L: Degree of spherical harmonics Returns: shcoeffs: 2D numpy array of shape (numvoxels, (L+1)^2) """ numvoxels = densitygrid.size numcoeffs = (L + 1) 2 shaccum = np.zeros((numvoxels, numcoeffs), dtype=np.float64) samplecounts = np.zeros(numvoxels, dtype=np.float64) pd = 1.0 / (4.0 np.pi) # Uniform direction PDF for k, (ok, Pk) in enumerate(cameraposes): img = images[k] # Standard ray marching over the grid to collect points and transmittance for u in range(img.shape[1]): for v in range(img.shape[0]): raydir = Pk.unproject(u, v) rayorig = ok points, transmittances = raymarch(rayorig, raydir, densitygrid) for pt, T in zip(points, transmittances): if T < 1e-6: continue observedcolor = img[v, u] dk = pt - ok dk /= np.linalg.norm(dk) # Standard SH basis evaluation for l=0..L, m=-l..l basis = evaluateshbasis(dk, L) # Accumulate weighted contributions weight = (T observedcolor basis) / pd idx = getvoxelindex(pt, densitygrid) shaccum[idx] += weight samplecounts[idx] += 1 # Normalize by K (number of samples per point) safecounts = np.maximum(samplecounts, 1.0) shcoeffs = shaccum / safecounts[:, np.newaxis] return shcoeffs def evaluateshbasis(d, L): """Evaluates spherical harmonics basis functions Yl^m(d) for l=0..L, m=-l..l.""" # Standard implementation depends on SH convention (e.g., Nayar, Healy) # Returns flattened array of basis values pass def raymarch(origin, direction, densitygrid): """Traces a ray through a 3D grid, returning points and transmittances.""" # Standard volumetric ray marching implementation pass def getvoxelindex(point, densitygrid): """Maps a 3D point to a voxel index in the grid.""" # Standard coordinate-to-index mapping pass Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot (L+1)^2) to store the SH coefficients for all points, where N is the number of 3D points (voxels). Strengths: Decouples shape and radiance, reducing ambiguity. Provides a photometric regularization term that is adaptive to the scene geometry. Limitations: Requires a pre-existing density field. Not given in the sources. When to use: As a regularization term for explicit NeRF representations like Plenoxels and Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO). When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed to address the shape-radiance ambiguity in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). It was introduced in the paper "Reducing Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in Radiance Fields with a Closed-Form Color Estimation Method". The authors note that existing regularization methods (TV, sparsity, distortion) are based on general assumptions and are not adaptive to specific scenes. This method was applied to explicit NeRF representations, specifically Plenoxels and DVGO, demonstrating improvements on NeRF Synthetic, LLFF, and DTU datasets. Reducing Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in Radiance Fields with a Closed-Form Color Estimation Method, https://doi.org/10.52202/075280-2570, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Surface-SDF Representation
body: Surface-SDF Representation methods reconstruct 3D geometry and appearance by modeling the scene as a continuous implicit surface defined by a Signed Distance Function (SDF), rather than a volumetric density field [6060-neus.md][10715-volsdf.md]. This approach disentangles geometry from appearance, enabling high-fidelity surface reconstruction and direct mesh extraction [6060-neus.md][7385-surface-nerf.md]. It differs from standard NeRF-like methods by enforcing geometric consistency through the SDF constraint, and from explicit mesh methods by avoiding explicit mesh extraction during the training phase, instead rendering differentiable images directly from the implicit field [6060-neus.md]. Builds on Radiance-field optimization. All methods in this family represent scene geometry using a learnable SDF f(\mathbf{x}), compute surface normals as \mathbf{n} = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) / \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|, and convert SDF values into a probability distribution (e.g., via sigmoid or Laplace CDF derivatives) to compute segment alphas and transmittance along rays [6060-neus.md][10715-volsdf.md][12440-instant-nsr.md]. NeuS represents a surface as the zero-level set of an SDF and trains it using a novel volume rendering scheme to avoid geometric bias inherent in standard volume rendering [6060-neus.md]. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality 3D surfaces from multi-view 2D images by combining the robustness of neural radiance fields with the geometric precision of implicit SDFs [6060-neus.md]. Unlike siblings that also use SDFs, NeuS introduces a specific S-density formulation based on the derivative of the sigmoid function to ensure unbiased surface reconstruction in the first-order approximation [6060-neus.md]. Choose it when high-quality surface reconstruction from multi-view images is needed without explicit mesh extraction during training [6060-neus.md]. Surface NeRF converts a pre-trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) into a 3D mesh and a surface light field, reducing per-pixel rendering cost by evaluating the NeRF only at the surface isosurface rather than via volumetric raycasting [7385-surface-nerf.md]. It achieves this by extracting an isosurface from the density field and optimizing both the geometry and the network parameters to maintain image quality, reducing per-pixel computational cost from 226 MFLOPS to 1.7 MFLOPS and runtime by more than 100x compared to baseline NeRF [7385-surface-nerf.md]. Choose it when rendering speed is critical and a pre-trained NeRF is available, as it reduces per-pixel cost by evaluating the network only at the isosurface [7385-surface-nerf.md]. VolSDF is a neural inverse rendering method that decouples geometric representation and appearance by modeling scene density as a function of a learnable Signed Distance Function (SDF) [10715-volsdf.md]. It solves the problem of noisy, low-fidelity geometry reconstruction inherent in standard density-based NeRF approaches, where geometry is extracted via arbitrary level sets of generic density functions [10715-volsdf.md]. Unlike siblings that model geometry as a function of density, VolSDF provides a useful inductive bias for geometry, bounds opacity approximation error, and enables efficient unsupervised disentanglement of shape and appearance [10715-volsdf.md]. Choose it when disentanglement of shape and appearance is required, or when stable geometry gradients and opacity error bounds are needed [10715-volsdf.md]. Instant-NSR is a neural surface reconstruction method that improves 3D geometry quality by incorporating a Signed Distance Function (SDF) representation into a hash-encoded neural network framework [12440-instant-nsr.md]. It solves the convergence instability inherent in applying SDFs to hash coding by employing a Truncated Signed Distance Function (TSDF) via a sigmoid output activation [12440-instant-nsr.md]. It sets itself apart from its sibling NeuS by using the spatial hashing acceleration of Instant-NGP while retaining NeuS's SDF-based rendering formulation, and from Surface NeRF by its specific handling of hash-grid numerical overflow through truncation [12440-instant-nsr.md]. Choose it when fast training and inference are required via hash-grid acceleration, and numerical stability with hash coding is a concern [12440-instant-nsr.md]. Originated from the integration of neural implicit fields with inverse volume rendering. VolSDF [10715-volsdf.md] was one of the early works to explicitly model the SDF for volume rendering, aiming to overcome the ambiguity of density-based representations. NeuS [6060-neus.md] and Surface NeRF [7385-surface-nerf.md] further refined this by introducing specific architectures and optimization strategies (such as hierarchical sampling and alternating optimization) to stabilize training and improve geometric fidelity. Instant-NSR [12440-instant-nsr.md] later adapted the approach for hash-grid acceleration. These methods are primarily used in multi-view stereo reconstruction, 3D asset creation, and augmented reality applications where accurate geometry is as important as photorealistic appearance [6060-neus.md][7385-surface-nerf.md][10715-volsdf.md][12440-instant-nsr.md]. Not given in the sources.

name: NeuS
head: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces by Volume Rendering for Multi-view Reconstruction, NeuS
body:
NeuS is a neural surface reconstruction method that represents scene geometry as the zero-level set of a learnable Signed Distance Function (SDF) and trains it using a novel volume rendering scheme. It solves the problem of inherent geometric bias that occurs when standard volume rendering is naively applied to SDF-associated density. Unlike Surface NeRF which uses occupancy grids, or VolSDF which uses a fixed variance, NeuS introduces an unbiased volume rendering formulation with a trainable sharpness parameter, allowing for high-quality surface extraction without foreground mask supervision. NeuS builds on Radiance-field optimization by replacing the density-outputting MLP with an SDF-outputting MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of posed RGB images \{Ik\} of a 3D object. Output: A reconstructed triangular mesh extracted from the learned SDF zero-level set, and rendered novel views. Data Structures: The scene is represented by two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): 1. SDF Network (f): Maps spatial position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 to a scalar signed distance value d = f(\mathbf{x}). Architecture: 8 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Activation: Softplus with  eta=100 (replacing ReLU). Skip connection: From input to the output of the 4th layer. Output: Tuple (d, \mathbf{g}) where d is the SDF value and \mathbf{g} \in \mathbb{R}^{15} is a geometry feature vector. 2. Color Network (c): Maps position \mathbf{x}, viewing direction \mathbf{v}, normal \mathbf{n}, and feature \mathbf{g} to RGB color. Architecture: 4 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Inputs: Spatial location \mathbf{p}, view direction \mathbf{v}, normal \mathbf{n} = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}), and feature \mathbf{g}. Positional Encoding: Applied to \mathbf{p} (6 frequencies) and \mathbf{v} (4 frequencies). 3. Variance Parameter: A single learnable scalar variance controlling the sharpness of the SDF-to-alpha conversion. Inverse temperature: inv\s = \exp(variance 	imes 10.0). Clipped to [10^{-6}, 10^6] to prevent numerical instability. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}, sample n points. NeuS uses hierarchical sampling: uniformly sample 64 points initially, then perform importance sampling for k=4 iterations, adding 16 points per iteration, totaling 128 points. For the 'w/o mask' setting, sample an extra 32 points outside the bounding sphere to represent the background using NeRF++. 2. SDF and Gradient Query: For each sampled point \mathbf{p}i, query the SDF network to get f(\mathbf{p}i) and the geometry feature \mathbf{g}i. Compute the normal \mathbf{n}i = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}i) / \|
abla f(\mathbf{p}i)\|. 3. Alpha Computation (Unbiased Volume Rendering): Compute the opacity \alphai for the segment between section points qi and q{i+1} using the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the S-density. Define the S-density function (derivative of Sigmoid): \phis(x) =  rac{s e^{-sx}}{(1 + e^{-sx})^2} where s is a trainable parameter (or derived from variance). Define the Sigmoid CDF: \Phis(x) =  rac{1}{1 + e^{-sx}} Compute alpha for segment i: \alphai = \max\left(  rac{\Phis(f(qi)) - \Phis(f(q{i+1}))}{\Phis(f(qi))}, 0 ight). Note: 10^{-5} is added to numerator and denominator to prevent division by zero. 4. Color Computation: Compute the color ci at the midpoint pi = \mathbf{o} +  rac{ti + t{i+1}}{2}\mathbf{v} using the Color Network with inputs \mathbf{p}i, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{g}i. 5. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color along the ray using standard alpha compositing: C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) = \sumi Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance. 6. Loss Calculation: Minimize the total loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{	ext{color}} +  eta \mathcal{L}{	ext{eikonal}} \mathcal{L}{	ext{color}}: Huber loss between rendered color and ground truth pixel. \mathcal{L}{	ext{eikonal}}: Regularizes the SDF gradient magnitude to 1: \mathcal{L}{	ext{eikonal}} =  rac{1}{mn} \sum{k,i} (\|\mathbf{n}{k,i}\| - 1)^2. 7. Optimization: Train using ADAM optimizer. Learning rate: Linear warmup from 0 to 5 	imes 10^{-4} in first 5k iterations, then cosine decay to minimum 2.5 	imes 10^{-5}. Total iterations: 300k. Weight normalization is used to stabilize training. Parameters: s (or variance): Trainable sharpness parameter. Standard deviation of \phis is 1/s, approaching 0 as training converges.  eta: Weight for Eikonal loss. Typical value not explicitly stated in sources, but described as indispensable. Softplus  eta: 100. initval: Initial value for variance parameter. modulate: Boolean to enable modulation of inv\s during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Bias: Naive application of standard volume rendering to SDF density causes inherent geometric errors. Spectral Bias: Random initialization causes axis-aligned artifacts due to positional encoding spectral bias. Textureless Regions: Textureless areas are ambiguous and may fail to reconstruct correctly. Numerical Stability: inv\s must be clipped to [10^{-6}, 10^6]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(o, v, sdffn, colorfn, s, tstarts, tends): """ Renders a single ray using NeuS unbiased volume rendering. o: ray origin (3,) v: ray direction (3,) sdffn: function returning (d, g) for a point colorfn: function returning RGB for (p, v, n, g) s: sharpness parameter tstarts, tends: arrays of section point distances along ray """ # Standard math helpers def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-x)) def clip(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) T = 1.0 # Initialize transmittance accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(len(tstarts)): qi = o + tstarts[i] v qnext = o + tends[i] v pi = o + (tstarts[i] + tends[i]) / 2.0 v # Query SDF and compute normal d, g = sdffn(qi) n = normalize(gradient(sdffn, qi)) # gradient computed via autograd or finite differences # Compute alpha using S-density CDF phiprev = sigmoid(s d) dnext, = sdffn(qnext) phinext = sigmoid(s dnext) alpha = clip((phiprev - phinext) / (phiprev + 1e-5), 0.0, 1.0) if alpha > 1e-4: c = colorfn(pi, v, n, g) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + T alpha c[j] for j in range(3)] T = T (1.0 - alpha) if T < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor HAME-NeRF is a two-stage framework for extracting high-fidelity, textured surface meshes from RGB images by defining volume density as a Secant Hyperbolic Function applied to a Signed Distance Function (SDF). It builds on NeuS by introducing a spatially-varying sharpness parameter  eta(\mathbf{x}) learned via an MLP, which enhances flexibility for complex surfaces compared to methods using fixed  eta values. Unlike NeuS which focuses on differentiable volume rendering for surface representation, HAME-NeRF explicitly optimizes a mesh through differentiable rendering and iterative refinement, achieving superior geometric accuracy and visual quality on synthetic benchmarks compared to NeRF2Mesh. D-NeuS is a volume rendering-based neural implicit surface reconstruction method that recovers fine-level geometric details by extending NeuS with two additional loss functions: a geometry bias loss and a multi-view feature consistency loss. It addresses the ambiguity in geometry and appearance representation inherent in volume rendering by ensuring consistency between the rendered surface points (derived from alpha compositing) and the underlying signed distance field (SDF) zero-crossings. Unlike its parent NeuS, which suffers from geometry bias due to the non-linear transformation of SDF to density, D-NeuS explicitly penalizes this bias and enforces feature consistency on surface points rather than all sampled points, distinguishing it from siblings like HAME-NeRF and NeuS2. NeuS2 is a fast neural surface reconstruction approach for multi-view RGB input that achieves two orders of magnitude improvement in training speed over NeuS without compromising reconstruction quality, applicable to both static and dynamic scenes. It sets itself apart by parameterizing the neural network-encoded Signed Distance Field (SDF) using multi-resolution hash tables of learnable feature vectors, as introduced in Instant-NGP, and by calculating second-order derivatives using a novel lightweight formula tailored to ReLU-based MLPs to leverage CUDA parallelism and reduce memory footprint. HF-NeuS is an improvement on NeuS that separates low-frequency details into a base SDF and high-frequency details into a displacement function to increase reconstruction quality. It builds on NeuS by addressing the smoothness limitations of standard implicit SDF representations, which often fail to capture sharp geometric features. SparseNeuS is a neural rendering-based method for surface reconstruction from multi-view images that generalizes to new scenes and works with sparse inputs (as few as 2 or 3 images). It improves upon NeuS by introducing a geometry encoding volume with learnable image features as a hybrid representation, allowing it to recover surfaces in a coarse-to-fine manner without requiring dense views or time-consuming per-scene optimization from scratch. Unlike NeuS, which suffers from distorted and incomplete geometry with only three images due to radiance ambiguity, SparseNeuS produces high-quality, complete meshes by leveraging generalizable priors learned from image features. NeuDA is a neural implicit surface reconstruction method that utilizes hierarchical deformable anchors to encode local geometry, building on the NeuS [6060-neus.md] framework. It distinguishes itself by replacing standard positional encoding with Hierarchical Positional Encoding (HPE) and employing a shallower SDF network (4 layers vs. 8 for NeuS). OmniSDF is a neural 3D reconstruction method for static indoor and outdoor scenes captured by omnidirectional video with small circular sweep baselines. It estimates geometry as a signed distance field (SDF) within an adaptive spherical binoctree to handle large depth ranges and narrow baselines where traditional ray-crossing methods fail. Unlike its sibling NeuS, which uses a fixed coordinate space, OmniSDF adapts the spatial subdivision dynamically during optimization, allowing it to refine incorrect initial depth estimates and reduce geometry error by 38% compared to fixed binoctree approaches. Time Complexity: NeuS is slower than standard NeRF because SDF queries require more network evaluations per ray (gradient computation). Rendering a 1600x1200 image takes ~320 seconds on an Nvidia 2080Ti GPU in default settings, or ~60 seconds with sphere tracing acceleration. On an A100 GPU at 1080p, it renders at 0.8 ± 0.2 FPS. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two MLPs (SDF and Color) and their gradients. Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, NeuS achieved PSNR = 28.4 ± 0.8 dB. On the DTU dataset, it achieved the most accurate surface reconstruction with Chamfer distance = 0.62 ± 0.08 mm. Strengths: Unbiased surface reconstruction; high geometric accuracy; works without foreground mask supervision; robust optimization for complex structures. Limitations: Slow training and rendering speed compared to hash-encoded variants; struggles with textureless regions; sensitive to initialization (requires geometric init to avoid artifacts). When to use: When high-quality, watertight surface meshes are required from multi-view images and training time is not the primary constraint. When not to use: When real-time rendering is needed (use Instant-NSR or NeuS2) or when input views are very sparse (use SparseNeus). NeuS was introduced in 2021 by Yen-Chen Lin et al. in the paper "NeuS: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces by Volume Rendering for Multi-view Reconstruction". It was developed to address the limitations of previous implicit surface representations (like UNISURF) and the geometric bias inherent in applying standard NeRF volume rendering to SDFs. The method combines the robustness of volume rendering with the accuracy of SDF-based surface extraction. It has become a foundational method for neural surface reconstruction, leading to numerous variants such as Instant-NSR, NeuS2, and HF-Neus. name: HAME-NeRF
head: High Accuracy Mesh Extraction Leveraging Neural Radiance Fields
body: HAME-NeRF is a two-stage framework for extracting high-fidelity, textured surface meshes from RGB images by defining volume density as a Secant Hyperbolic Function applied to a Signed Distance Function (SDF). It builds on NeuS by introducing a spatially-varying sharpness parameter \beta(\mathbf{x}) learned via an MLP, which enhances flexibility for complex surfaces compared to methods using fixed \beta values. Unlike NeuS which focuses on differentiable volume rendering for surface representation, HAME-NeRF explicitly optimizes a mesh through differentiable rendering and iterative refinement, achieving superior geometric accuracy and visual quality on synthetic benchmarks compared to NeRF2Mesh. HAME-NeRF operates in two stages: initialization of geometry and appearance using a grid-based NeRF, followed by mesh refinement via differentiable rendering. Inputs: A set of N RGB images with known camera poses. Outputs: A textured triangular mesh (vertices, faces, and diffuse/specular textures) and a learned scene representation. 1. Geometry Representation: Multi-resolution feature grid E^{\text{geo}} storing spatial features for SDF computation. A shallow MLP that maps features from E^{\text{geo}} to the SDF value. 2. Appearance Representation: Multi-resolution feature grid E^{\text{app}} storing spatial features for appearance. MLP1: Maps E^{\text{app}}(\mathbf{x}) to diffuse color \mathbf{c}d and specular feature \mathbf{f}s. MLP2: Maps \mathbf{f}s and view direction \mathbf{d} to specular color \mathbf{c}s. MLP\beta: Maps spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} to the sharpness parameter \beta(\mathbf{x}). 3. Mesh Data: Vertices \mathbf{V} with per-vertex offsets learned during refinement. Faces \mathbf{F} with adaptive resolution based on rendering error. The volume density \sigma is derived from the SDF and the spatially varying parameter \beta(\mathbf{x}): \sigma(\text{SDF}, \beta) = \frac{1}{4\beta} \cdot \frac{1}{\cosh^2\left(\frac{\text{SDF}}{2\beta}\right)} \quad (2) where \beta(\mathbf{x}) is output by MLP\beta(\mathbf{x}). Appearance is decomposed into diffuse and specular components: \mathbf{c}d, \mathbf{f}s = \psi(\text{MLP}1(E^{\text{app}}(\mathbf{x}))) \quad (4) \mathbf{c}s = \psi(\text{MLP}2(\mathbf{f}s, \mathbf{d})) \quad (4) \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}d + \mathbf{c}s \quad (5) where \psi denotes a sigmoid activation, \mathbf{f}s encodes specular information, and \mathbf{d} is the view direction. \lambda{\text{elk}}: Weight for the Eikonal Loss. \lambda\beta: Weight for the Beta Regularization Loss. Typical values: Not given in the sources. 1. Train Grid-based NeRF: Initialize a grid-based NeRF structure with an SDF component. Compute SDF using E^{\text{geo}} and a shallow MLP. Compute density \sigma using Equation (2). Compute appearance using Equations (4) and (5). 2. Optimize: Minimize the total loss (defined below) to converge the NeRF representation. 3. Extract Coarse Mesh: Apply Marching Cubes to the converged SDF field to generate an initial coarse mesh. 1. Differentiable Rendering: Use a differentiable rasterizer to render the current mesh and compute the photometric rendering loss against input images. 2. Vertex Optimization: Optimize vertex positions by learning per-vertex offsets using gradients from the pixel-wise rendering loss. 3. Adaptive Mesh Resolution: Identify faces with high rendering errors using k-means clustering. Subdivide high-error faces to increase resolution. Simplify low-error regions to decrease resolution. 4. Iterate: Repeat the refinement loop (rendering, vertex optimization, adaptive resolution) until convergence. 5. Unbounded Scene Handling: For unbounded scenes, partition the environment into regions of progressively lower resolution away from the center and apply regularization terms for smooth surfaces and bounded vertex displacements. images.shape[1:]) - images) 2, dim=-1) higherrorfaces = kmeanscluster(errors, k=1)[0] self.mesh.subdividefaces(higherrorfaces) lowerrorfaces = kmeanscluster(errors, k=1)[1] self.mesh.simplifyfaces(lowerrorfaces) self.optimizer.step() Unbounded Scenes: Requires partitioning the environment into regions of progressively lower resolution away from the center to maintain efficiency and accuracy. Beta Instability: Without regularization, \beta(\mathbf{x}) may vary unstably. The L1 penalty \lambda\beta |\beta(\mathbf{x})| is used to prevent this. Precision: The density formula involves division by \beta. If \beta approaches zero, numerical instability may occur. The sources do not specify a lower bound for \beta, but the regularization encourages smooth transitions. The parent method that introduced differentiable volume rendering for surface representation using SDFs. HAME-NeRF extends this by optimizing a mesh directly and learning spatially varying \beta. See NeuS. A baseline method that applies Marching Cubes directly to a density field. HAME-NeRF improves upon this by using an SDF for mesh extraction and adaptive mesh refinement. See NeRF2Mesh. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training involves two stages: NeRF initialization and mesh refinement. The refinement stage includes iterative k-means clustering and mesh subdivision, which may increase computational cost compared to static NeRF methods. Memory Complexity: Uses multi-resolution feature grids for geometry and appearance, which are memory-efficient compared to dense voxel grids. The mesh size adapts to scene complexity. Measured Performance: On the NeRF-Synthetic dataset, HAME-NeRF outperforms NeRF2Mesh in Chamfer Distance, Normal Consistency, PSNR, and visual quality. On the Mip-NeRF 360 dataset, it achieves comparable, though slightly lower, performance than NeRF2Mesh. Strengths: High-fidelity surface extraction, spatially varying sharpness control, adaptive mesh resolution, and compatibility with real-time graphics via mesh output. Limitations: Slightly lower performance on complex real-world scenes (Mip-NeRF 360) compared to NeRF2Mesh. Requires careful tuning of loss weights \lambda{\text{elk}} and \lambda\beta. When to use: When high-quality, editable 3D meshes are required for real-time rendering or simulation, and the scene is well-lit or pre-baked lighting is acceptable. When not to use: For unbounded scenes with extreme dynamic range or complex lighting without pre-baking, as the method relies on baked lighting. HAME-NeRF was proposed to address the difficulty of extracting accurate and editable 3D meshes from NeRFs, which are inherently volumetric and incompatible with polygonal meshes needed for real-time graphics and simulation. The method builds on the NeRF2Mesh pipeline but introduces an SDF-based density modeling and a learned spatially varying \beta parameter. It was evaluated on the NeRF-Synthetic and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets. HAME-NeRF: High Accuracy Mesh Extraction Leveraging Neural Radiance Fields, https://zenodo.org/records/18469075, fetched 2026-10-26

name: D-NeuS
head: Details recovering Neural implicit Surface reconstruction
body: D-NeuS is a volume rendering-based neural implicit surface reconstruction method that recovers fine-level geometric details by extending NeuS with two additional loss functions: a geometry bias loss and a multi-view feature consistency loss. It addresses the ambiguity in geometry and appearance representation inherent in volume rendering by ensuring consistency between the rendered surface points (derived from alpha compositing) and the underlying signed distance field (SDF) zero-crossings. Unlike its parent NeuS, which suffers from geometry bias due to the non-linear transformation of SDF to density, D-NeuS explicitly penalizes this bias and enforces feature consistency on surface points rather than all sampled points, distinguishing it from siblings like HAME-NeRF and NeuS2. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multi-view images of a static scene. Outputs: A trained implicit neural network representing the scene geometry (SDF) and appearance (radiance), from which a mesh can be extracted. Data Structures and Network Layout: 1. Geometry Network (f): An MLP mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}. Architecture: 8 hidden layers, each with 256 units. Skip connections: From input to the output of the 4th hidden layer. Initialization: Weights initialized to approximate the SDF field of a unit sphere. 2. Radiance Network (g or c): An MLP mapping spatial position, view direction, normal, and feature vector to color \mathbb{R}^3. Architecture: 4 hidden layers, each with 256 units. Inputs: Spatial point \mathbf{x}, view direction \mathbf{v}, normal \mathbf{n}, and feature vector \mathbf{z}. 3. Position Encoding: Spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}: 6 frequencies. View direction \mathbf{v}: 4 frequencies. 4. Feature Consistency: Feature channels: Nc = 32. Neighboring views: Nv = 2 source views compared against each reference view. Mathematical Formulation: The surface \mathcal{S} is defined as the zero-level set of the SDF f: \mathcal{S} = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \} \quad (1) A 3D point on a ray from camera center \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{v} is: \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}, \quad t \ge 0 \quad (2) The normal \mathbf{n} is computed via automatic differentiation of the SDF: \mathbf{n} = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) The opaque density \sigma(t) is derived from the SDF using a sigmoid function \Phis: \sigma(t) = \max \left( -\frac{d\Phis}{dt}(f(\mathbf{x}(t))), 0 \right) \quad (5) where \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1} and s^{-1} is a trainable standard deviation. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampling: For each iteration, sample 512 rays. For each ray, generate 64 coarse points, 64 fine points, and 32 additional points outside the unit sphere (following NeRF++ strategy). 2. SDF Evaluation: Query the geometry network f for all sampled points to obtain SDF values f(\mathbf{x}(t)). 3. Density and Alpha Compositing: Compute density \sigma(t) using Eq. (5). Perform volume rendering to accumulate color Cr and alpha weights w(t). 4. Surface Point Interpolation: Find the first zero-crossing of the SDF along the ray. Instead of recursive ray tracing, use locally differentiable linear interpolation between adjacent sampled points where the SDF sign changes to estimate the surface point \mathbf{x}s. 5. Feature Extraction: Extract feature vectors \mathbf{z} from the geometry network f at the surface point \mathbf{x}s. 6. Loss Calculation: Photometric Loss: Standard difference between rendered color and ground truth. Eikonal Loss: Regularizes the gradient of the SDF to be unit length. Weight \alpha = 0.1. Geometry Bias Loss: Generate additional distance maps during rendering. Back-project these distances to 3D points. Penalize the absolute SDF values predicted by f at these points to encourage consistency between the rendered surface and the implicit surface. Weight \beta varies by stage. Multi-view Feature Consistency Loss: Compare feature vectors \mathbf{z} of the surface point \mathbf{x}s from the reference view with those from Nv=2 neighboring source views. Use CNNs for robust feature representation. Weight \gamma varies by stage. 7. Optimization: Update network weights using the Adam optimizer. 8. Mesh Extraction: After training, apply Marching Cubes to the SDF field f in a bounding box of size 512^3 voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim class GeometryMLP(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 8 hidden layers, 256 units, skip connection from input to 4th layer output self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(256, 256) for in range(8)]) self.inputlayer = nn.Linear(9, 256) # 3 coords + 6 freq pos enc self.skiplayer = nn.Linear(9, 256) # Skip connection input def forward(self, x): h = self.inputlayer(x) hskip = self.skiplayer(x) for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): h = torch.relu(layer(h)) if i == 3: # After 4th layer (index 3), add skip connection h = h + hskip return h # Returns SDF value class RadianceMLP(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # 4 hidden layers, 256 units self.layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Linear(256, 256) for in range(4)]) self.inputlayer = nn.Linear(256, 256) # Feature vector z size assumed 256 or similar from f # Note: Input to radiance also includes view dir and normal, # but D-NeuS paper specifies z from geometry network. # Standard NeuS/D-NeuS usually concatenates v, n, z. # Assuming input dim matches hidden dim for simplicity in this abstract representation. def forward(self, z, v, n): # Concatenate features if necessary, here simplified to z input h = self.inputlayer(z) for layer in self.layers: h = torch.relu(layer(h)) return h # Returns color c def sigmoiddensity(sdf, s): # Phis(x) = (1 + exp(-sx))^-1 phi = 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-s sdf)) # dPhis/dt = dPhis/df df/dt # dPhis/df = s exp(-sdf) / (1 + exp(-sdf))^2 # However, the paper defines sigma(t) = max(-dPhis/dt(f(x(t))), 0) # In practice, this is often implemented as the derivative of the sigmoid w.r.t the argument # sigma = s exp(-s sdf) / (1 + exp(-s sdf))2 # But the paper writes max(-dPhis/dt, 0). Since Phis is decreasing with sdf? # Actually, Phis is increasing. The density is related to the derivative of the CDF. # NeuS paper Eq 5: sigma(t) = max(-dPhis/dt(f(x(t))), 0). # If f(x(t)) is the argument, and we differentiate w.r.t t: # dPhis/dt = (dPhis/df) (df/dt). # The paper likely implies the density is the derivative of the sigmoid CDF w.r.t distance. # Standard implementation: sigma = s torch.exp(-s sdf) / (1 + torch.exp(-s sdf))2 # Let's stick to the explicit formula provided in text: # sigma(t) = max( - derivative of sigmoid w.r.t its argument derivative of argument w.r.t t, 0) # But usually, the "unbiased opaque density" is just the PDF of the sigmoid distribution. # We will use the standard PDF form which matches the "unbiased" claim in NeuS/D-NeuS context. pdf = s torch.exp(-s sdf) / (1 + torch.exp(-s sdf))2 return torch.clamp(pdf, min=0.0) def findzerocrossing(tvals, sdfvals): # Linear interpolation to find t where sdf=0 # Find indices where sign changes signs = torch.sign(sdfvals) change = (signs[:-1] signs[1:]) < 0 if not torch.any(change): return None # Get the first change idx = torch.argmax(change) t0, t1 = tvals[idx], tvals[idx+1] s0, s1 = sdfvals[idx], sdfvals[idx+1] # Linear interpolation ts = t0 - s0 (t1 - t0) / (s1 - s0) return ts def traindneus(geometrynet, radiancenet, images, cameras, numiters=300000): optimizer = optim.Adam(list(geometrynet.parameters()) + list(radiancenet.parameters()), lr=5e-4) s = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(0.3)) # Trainable standard deviation inverse for i in range(numiters): # Stage-based loss weights if i < 50000: beta = 0.01 gamma = 0.0 elif i < 150000: beta = 0.1 gamma = 0.5 else: beta = 0.01 gamma = 0.05 alpha = 0.1 # Eikonal weight fixed # 1. Sample Rays rayso, raysd = samplerays(cameras, numrays=512) # 2. Hierarchical Sampling tcoarse = samplepoints(rayso, raysd, numsamples=64) tfine = samplepoints(rayso, raysd, numsamples=64) tout = samplepointsoutsideunitsphere(rayso, raysd, numsamples=32) tall = torch.cat([tcoarse, tfine, tout], dim=-1) # 3. Evaluate SDF xall = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + tall.unsqueeze(2) raysd.unsqueeze(1) sdfvals = geometrynet(xall) # Shape: [numrays, numsamples] # 4. Compute Density and Render sigma = sigmoiddensity(sdfvals, s) # Alpha compositing to get rendered color Cr Cr = volumerender(rayso, raysd, sigma, tall, geometrynet, radiancenet) # 5. Find Surface Points for Losses # Interpolate zero crossing ts = findzerocrossing(tcoarse, sdfvals[:,:64]) # Use coarse points for speed/robustness # Get surface points xs xs = rayso + ts.unsqueeze(1) raysd.unsqueeze(1) # Get features z at surface points zs = geometrynet(xs) # Feature vector from geometry network # 6. Compute Losses # Photometric Loss lossphoto = torch.mean((Cr - images)2) # Eikonal Loss # Gradient of SDF w.r.t x gradf = torch.autograd.grad(sdfvals.sum(), xall, creategraph=True)[0] losseikonal = torch.mean((gradf.norm(dim=-1) - 1)2) # Geometry Bias Loss # Back-project distance maps to 3D points (simplified here as using sampled points) # Penalize absolute SDF values at points derived from distance maps # Note: The paper mentions generating additional distance maps. # Implementation detail: Use the sampled points tall and their SDF values. # The bias is minimized by encouraging SDF to be 0 at the "rendered" surface. # The rendered surface is approximated by the zero crossing. # The bias loss penalizes |f(x)| for points x that should be on surface. # A common implementation is to penalize |sdf| at the interpolated surface point. lossbias = torch.mean(torch.abs(sdfvals[:,:64])) # Simplified: penalize sdf at coarse points near surface? # More accurately: The paper says "penalize their absolute SDF values predicted by the geometry MLP network" # for points back-projected from distance maps. # We will assume this is approximated by the Eikonal or a specific term on the zero-crossing vicinity. # Given the pseudocode constraint, we use a placeholder comment for the exact back-projection logic. # lossbias = computegeometrybiasloss(geometrynet, tall, xall) # For the sake of a complete, runnable pseudocode, we approximate bias loss as # minimizing the SDF magnitude at the zero-crossing points across all rays. sdfatsurface = torch.zeroslike(ts) # Ideally 0 # Since we interpolated to find ts, sdf at ts is ~0. # The bias loss in D-NeuS specifically targets the discrepancy between # the alpha-composited surface and the SDF zero-crossing. # We will use the mean absolute SDF of the coarse samples as a proxy for the bias term # if the zero-crossing is not perfectly aligned, or simply rely on the interpolation. # Let's use the mean absolute SDF of the coarse samples as the bias term # as it encourages the SDF to be small in the region where alpha is high. lossbias = torch.mean(torch.abs(sdfvals[:,:64])) # Multi-view Feature Consistency Loss # Compare zs from reference view with zs from neighboring views # This requires rendering/evaluating the same 3D point in other views lossfeature = computefeatureconsistencyloss(zs, cameras, geometrynet, Nv=2, Nc=32) # Total Loss loss = lossphoto + alpha losseikonal + beta lossbias + gamma lossfeature optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Learning rate decay adjustlearningrate(optimizer, i, initiallr=5e-4, minlr=2.5e-5, warmup=5000, totaliters=300000) def extractmesh(geometrynet, resolution=512): # Marching Cubes on SDF field in bounding box # Grid generation x = torch.linspace(-1, 1, resolution) y = torch.linspace(-1, 1, resolution) z = torch.linspace(-1, 1, resolution) xx, yy, zz = torch.meshgrid(x, y, z) coords = torch.stack([xx, yy, zz], dim=-1).view(-1, 3) # Query SDF sdfgrid = geometrynet(coords) sdfgrid = sdfgrid.view(resolution, resolution, resolution) # Marching Cubes vertices, faces = marchingcubes(sdfgrid.numpy(), level=0) return vertices, faces Parameters and Typical Values: s (Trainable standard deviation inverse): Initialized to 0.3. Learning Rate: 5 \times 10^{-4} with warm-up of 5k iterations, cosine decay to 2.5 \times 10^{-5}. Optimizer: Adam. Iterations: 300k. Eikonal Weight (\alpha): 0.1 (fixed). Geometry Bias Weight (\beta): 0.01 (0-50k), 0.1 (50k-150k), 0.01 (150k-300k). Feature Consistency Weight (\gamma): 0.0 (0-50k), 0.5 (50k-150k), 0.05 (150k-300k). Feature Channels (Nc): 32. Neighboring Views (Nv): 2. Mesh Extraction Resolution: 512^3 voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The linear interpolation for zero-crossing must be locally differentiable to allow backpropagation through the surface point selection. Boundaries: The inclusion of 32 points outside the unit sphere helps handle boundaries and occlusions. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a static scene. Dynamic scenes require extensions (e.g., D-NeRF, though not explicitly detailed in D-NeuS notes, the parent NeuS is static). MS-NeuS integrates the Multi-Space (MS) module into the NeuS framework to address multi-view inconsistency, specifically improving novel view synthesis and the reconstruction of mirror surfaces. It distinguishes itself from its parent D-NeuS by focusing on view-dependent appearance consistency via sub-space decomposition rather than explicit geometric bias or feature consistency losses. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 19 hours on a single NVIDIA Titan RTX for 300k iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rendering an image of resolution 1200 \times 1600 takes approximately 7 minutes on the described hardware. Mesh extraction takes about 57 seconds. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Recovers high-accuracy surface geometry, especially fine details and complex scenes. Outperforms NeRF, VolSDF, and NeuS in Chamfer distance on the DTU dataset (mean 32.22 vs 31.97 for NeuS). Achieves higher PSNR on pixels inside object masks. Limitations: Computationally expensive training and inference (7 mins per image). Relies on multi-view consistency which may struggle with highly reflective or textureless surfaces without additional priors (though MS-NeuS addresses this). When to use: When high-fidelity geometric reconstruction is required from multi-view images, particularly for complex scenes with fine details. When not: When real-time rendering is required or when only a small number of views are available (though it uses neighboring views, sparse views may degrade performance). D-NeuS was introduced in a paper presented at WACV 2023. It builds upon the NeuS method, which itself was designed to improve geometric reconstruction quality by using a signed distance field (SDF) representation. The key insight of D-NeuS is the analysis of geometry bias arising from the transformation of SDF to density for volume rendering, and the proposal of a novel constraint to regularize this bias. It also incorporates multi-view feature consistency using CNNs, inspired by MVSDF, to recover fine local geometric details. The method was evaluated on the DTU and BlendedMVS datasets. name: MS-NeuS
head: Multi-Space NeuS
body: MS-NeuS integrates the Multi-Space (MS) module into the NeuS framework to resolve multi-view inconsistency for novel view synthesis and improve the reconstruction of mirror surfaces. It distinguishes itself from its parent D-NeuS by enforcing view-dependent appearance consistency through feature sub-space decomposition rather than explicit geometric bias or multi-view feature consistency losses. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-view images of a scene containing reflective or mirror surfaces. Output: A neural implicit signed distance function (SDF) and a view-dependent radiance field for novel view synthesis. Data Structures: The method extends the NeuS architecture by replacing the standard feature representation with an MS module. Sub-spaces: The feature space is partitioned into K independent sub-spaces. Feature Dimension: d denotes the dimensionality of features within each sub-space. Hidden Dimension: h denotes the hidden dimension of the associated MLPs. Parameter Layout: The source reports grid parameters and MLP parameters separately using the notation "A|B". Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize the NeuS backbone (SDF MLP and Color MLP) and the MS module parameters. 2. Sampling: For each pixel, sample points along the camera ray through the scene volume. 3. Sub-space Decomposition: Query the MS module to project scene coordinates into K sub-spaces, yielding decomposed features instead of a single monolithic feature vector. 4. Rendering: Perform volumetric rendering by aggregating the decomposed features to compute density and view-dependent color. 5. Optimization: Minimize the standard NeuS loss functions (photometric, SDF, etc.) while the MS module implicitly enforces multi-view consistency across the decomposed sub-spaces. Parameters: K = 4: Number of sub-spaces. d = 16: Feature dimension per sub-space. h = 32: Hidden dimension of the MLPs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Cleanliness: The method struggles to reconstruct clean geometry because the MS module is primarily designed for novel view synthesis and lacks explicit geometric constraints on the sub-spaces. Mirror Surfaces: While it reconstructs mirror geometry better than standard NeuS, artifacts may persist due to the absence of geometric regularization within the sub-spaces. Geo-NeuS introduces multi-view constraints for SDF supervised by a NeRF, specifically a multi-view geometry constraint supervised by a sparse point cloud and a multi-view photometric consistency constraint. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: MS-NeuS requires more parameters than the baseline NeuS. On the synthesized dataset, NeuS uses 0.16 \times 10^{-1} M parameters, while MS-NeuS uses 0.37 \times 10^{-1} M parameters. Time: The method performs multiple volumetric rendering operations per pixel, making time consumption dependent on the importance sampling strategy and backbone network inference. Measured Performance: On a synthesized dataset with circle paths: PSNR: MS-NeuS achieves 28.65, compared to NeuS 25.86. SSIM: MS-NeuS achieves 0.859, compared to NeuS 0.831. LPIPS: MS-NeuS achieves 0.195, compared to NeuS 0.258. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly improves novel view synthesis quality and reconstructs better geometry for mirror surfaces compared to standard NeuS. Limitations: Fails to produce clean geometry due to the absence of geometric constraints on the sub-spaces. MS-NeuS is a generalization of the MS-NeRF scheme applied to the NeuS framework. It was developed to solve multi-view inconsistency for novel view synthesis, particularly in scenes with reflective surfaces. The implementation is based on the NeuS code from [66] (cited in). name: NeuS2
head: NeuS2 Dynamic Reconstruction, NeuS2 Static Reconstruction
body: NeuS2 is a fast neural surface reconstruction approach for multi-view RGB input that achieves two orders of magnitude improvement in training speed over NeuS without compromising reconstruction quality, applicable to both static and dynamic scenes. It sets itself apart by parameterizing the neural network-encoded Signed Distance Field (SDF) using multi-resolution hash tables of learnable feature vectors, as introduced in Instant-NGP, and by calculating second-order derivatives using a novel lightweight formula tailored to ReLU-based MLPs to leverage CUDA parallelism and reduce memory footprint. Inputs: Multi-view RGB images. For dynamic scenes, a sequence of such views. Outputs: A neural implicit surface representation (SDF and color) parameterized by multi-resolution hash encodings. Data Structures: Multi-resolution Hash Table: A set of hash tables, one for each resolution level l \in \{0, \dots, L-1\}, mapping 3D coordinates to learnable feature vectors. MLP: A ReLU-based Multi-Layer Perceptron that takes the hashed features as input and outputs the SDF value and color. Parameters: Training time for dynamic scenes: up to 20 seconds per frame. Typical training time for static scenes: minutes. Steps: 1. Hash Encoding: For a given 3D point \mathbf{x}, query the multi-resolution hash tables to retrieve feature vectors at different resolutions and combine them. 2. MLP Forward Pass: Pass the combined features through the ReLU-based MLP to predict the SDF value d(\mathbf{x}) and color c(\mathbf{x}). 3. Second-Order Derivative Calculation: Compute the second-order derivatives of the SDF required for the surface constraint using a novel lightweight formula tailored to ReLU-based MLPs to enable efficient CUDA implementation with a small memory footprint. 4. Progressive Learning (Static): Optimize the multi-resolution hash encodings from coarse to fine to stabilize and expedite training convergence. 5. Incremental Learning (Dynamic): Train the first frame of the sequence. For subsequent frames, sequentially fine-tune the representation, exploiting similarity in shape and appearance. If the movement between consecutive frames is large, predict a global transformation to roughly align the frames before learning the representation of the new frame, addressing issues where occluded regions get stuck in the previous frame's SDF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neuus2trainstatic(images, hashtables, mlp, numlevels): # Initialize hash tables and MLP weights for level in range(numlevels): # Progressive learning: optimize coarse to fine for image in images: # Sample points along rays (standard volume rendering step) points = samplerays(image) # Hash encoding features = [queryhashtable(hashtables[l], points) for l in range(numlevels)] combinedfeatures = combinefeatures(features) # MLP forward pass sdf, color = mlp(combinedfeatures) # Volume rendering to get pixel colors renderedcolor = volumerender(points, sdf, color) # Compute loss against ground truth image loss = colorloss(renderedcolor, image) + sdfconstraint(sdf) # Compute gradients # Second-order derivative calculation uses lightweight formula for ReLU MLPs # Update hash table features and MLP weights optimizer.step(loss) def neuus2traindynamic(sequences, hashtables, mlp): # Train first frame neuus2trainstatic(sequences[0], hashtables, mlp) for i in range(1, len(sequences)): # Estimate rigid transformation to align current frame with previous frame # using standard point cloud registration (e.g., SVD on matched features) transformation = estimaterigidalignment(sequences[i-1], sequences[i]) # Apply transformation to camera poses or points alignedsequence = applyalignment(sequences[i], transformation) # Fine-tune representation for the new frame neuus2trainstatic(alignedsequence, hashtables, mlp) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Movements in Dynamic Scenes: If the movement between consecutive frames is large, occluded regions may get stuck in the previous frame's SDF. The method addresses this by predicting a global transformation to align frames. Precision: The method aims to reduce memory footprint and computational cost, but specific precision details are not provided. Time Complexity: Two orders of magnitude faster than NeuS. Over 3x faster than Voxurf. 100x faster than Neuralangelo. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory footprint due to the lightweight calculation of second-order derivatives. Measured Performance: Static scenes reconstructed in minutes; dynamic scenes up to 20 seconds per frame. Strengths: Fast training, high-quality geometry, applicable to both static and dynamic scenes. Limitations: Not explicitly stated in the sources. When to Use: When fast training of neural implicit surfaces is required for multi-view reconstruction, especially for dynamic scenes. When Not to Use: When extremely dense geometry is required and training time is not a constraint (Neuralangelo might be better). NeuS2 was proposed as a fast neural surface reconstruction approach to address the long training time of NeuS, which takes an extremely long time (8 hours) and makes it almost impossible to apply to dynamic scenes with thousands of frames. It builds on the multi-resolution hash encodings introduced in Instant-NGP. The method was presented in the paper "NeuS2: Fast Learning of Neural Implicit Surfaces for Multi-view Reconstruction". name: HF-NeuS
head: High-Frequency NeuS
body: HF-NeuS is an improvement on NeuS that separates low-frequency details into a base SDF and high-frequency details into a displacement function to increase reconstruction quality. It builds on NeuS by addressing the smoothness limitations of standard implicit SDF representations, which often fail to capture sharp geometric features. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Calibrated multi-view images (intrinsics \{Ki\}, extrinsics \{Ti\}), camera poses. Outputs: Reconstructed 3D surface (SDF) and appearance (light field). Data Structures: The method decouples geometry and appearance. Geometry is represented by an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF) \Phi, and appearance by a light field encoded via a color network c: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{S}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3. The specific high-frequency displacement mechanism is described as a separation of low-frequency base SDF and high-frequency displacement, but the exact architectural layout of the displacement network is not detailed in the provided sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Definition: For a given pixel, define the ray r(s) = o + sv for s \ge 0, where o is the camera center and v is the unit direction vector. 2. Sampling: Uniformly sample points along the ray within the bounding volume \Omega. Additionally, uniformly sample 500 points per iteration in the bounding volume \Omega for the off-surface loss calculation. 3. Density and Color Evaluation: Evaluate the density \sigma(r(t)) and color c(r(t), v) at sampled points r(t). The density is formulated to be an unbiased and occlusion-aware function, as in NeuS. 4. Volume Rendering: Integrate color along the ray using the accumulated transmittance T(t): \hat{C}(r) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) c(r(t), v) dt where sn and sf are the near and far bounds of the ray. 5. Transmittance Calculation: Compute accumulated transmittance: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{sn}^{t} \sigma(r(u)) du\right). 6. Mask Estimation: Compute the predicted mask \hat{M}(r) as the sum of transmittance weights along the ray. 7. Loss Optimization: Optimize network parameters by minimizing the total loss L: L = L{color} + \alpha L{eikonal} + \beta L{mask} + \gamma L{off}. Formulas: Color Loss (L{color}): L{color} = \frac{1}{\#R} \sum{r \in R} \| M(r) (\hat{C}(r) - C(r)) \|1 where R is the ray set constructed from all images, C(r) is ground truth color, and M(r) is the ground truth object mask. Eikonal Loss (L{eikonal}): L{eikonal} = \frac{1}{\#X} \sum{p \in X} (\|\nablax \Phi(p)\|^2 - 1)^2 where X is the set of sample points on rays. Mask Loss (L{mask}): L{mask} = \frac{1}{\#R} \sum{r \in R} BCE(\hat{M}(r), M(r)) where BCE is binary cross entropy. Off-Surface Loss (L{off}): L{off} = \frac{1}{\#\Omega} \sum{x \in \Omega} \psi(\Phi(x), \beta0) where \Omega is the bounding volume, \beta0 = 100, and \psi is a penalty function encouraging off-surface points to have non-zero values. Parameters: \alpha, \beta, \gamma: Weights for the respective loss terms. Values are not given in the sources. \beta0: Parameter for the off-surface loss, set to 100. Sampling points: 500 points per iteration in \Omega for L{off}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The sources note that baseline geometry representations (like NGP) can lead to non-smooth reconstruction results with poor gradient continuity. HF-NeuS aims to mitigate this via high-frequency separation, though specific numerical stability guards for the displacement function are not provided. The mask term L{mask} is optional. A framework that decouples geometry (SDF) and appearance (light field) from calibrated multi-view images, using volume rendering to generate images and minimizing the difference between rendered and input images. It utilizes the NeuS volume rendering framework to render 2D images based on the neural implicit SDF and light field. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: HF-NeuS outperformed the baseline NeRF model and provided theoretical and experimental justifications for its SDF-based scene density implementation. It greatly increased reconstruction quality compared to standard NeuS. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Improves geometric reconstruction quality by separating low-frequency and high-frequency details. Limitations: The specific computational overhead of the displacement function is not quantified in the sources. When to use it: Use when high-frequency geometric details are required and standard NeuS reconstruction quality is insufficient. HF-NeuS was introduced in June 2022. It is an improvement on NeuS, which was designed to improve geometric reconstruction quality through volume rendering. Concurrently, other methods like Geo-NeuS and SparseNeus were introduced to address multi-view constraints and sparse-view reconstruction, respectively. name: SparseNeus
head: SparseNeuS
body: SparseNeuS is a neural rendering-based method for surface reconstruction from multi-view images that generalizes to new scenes and works with sparse inputs (as few as 2 or 3 images). It improves upon NeuS by introducing a geometry encoding volume with learnable image features as a hybrid representation, allowing it to recover surfaces in a coarse-to-fine manner without requiring dense views or time-consuming per-scene optimization from scratch. Unlike NeuS, which suffers from distorted and incomplete geometry with only three images due to radiance ambiguity, SparseNeuS produces high-quality, complete meshes by leveraging generalizable priors learned from image features. The pipeline consists of three parts: Geometry reasoning, Appearance prediction, and Per-scene fine-tuning. Inputs: N input images \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} (typically N=3). Camera parameters for each input image. A bounding box covering the region of interest, defined in the camera coordinate system of the centered input image and gridded into regular voxels. Outputs: A Signed Distance Function (SDF) field representing the surface geometry. Synthesized views of the scene. 1. Geometry Encoding Volume (M): A 3D sparse convolutional volume implemented with a U-Net-like architecture using torchsparse. Coarse Volume: Resolution 96 \times 96 \times 96. Fine Volume: Resolution 192 \times 192 \times 192. 2. Cost Volume (B): A 3D volume where each voxel v stores the variance of projected features. 3. Feature Maps (Fi): 2D feature maps extracted from input images Ii using a 2D feature extraction network. 4. SDF Prediction Network (f\theta): An MLP that takes 3D coordinates and interpolated features from M as input to predict SDF values. This stage constructs cascaded geometry encoding volumes to recover surfaces in a coarse-to-fine manner. 1. Feature Extraction: Extract 2D feature maps \{Fi\}{i=0}^{N-1} from the input images \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} using a 2D feature extraction network. 2. Projection: For each vertex v of the bounding box, project it to each feature map Fi using the camera parameters of image Ii. Let \pii(v) denote the projected pixel location. Obtain the features Fi(v) = Fi(\pii(v)) by interpolation. 3. Cost Volume Construction: Calculate the variance of all projected features for each vertex v to build the cost volume B: B(v) = \operatorname{Var}\left( \{Fi(v)\}{i=0}^{N-1} \right) where \operatorname{Var} computes the variance across the N feature vectors. 4. Geometry Encoding Volume Generation: Apply a sparse 3D CNN \Psi to the cost volume B to obtain the geometry encoding volume M: M = \Psi(B). 5. Surface Extraction (Coarse): For an arbitrary 3D location q, apply positional encoding \operatorname{PE} to its 3D coordinates. Interpolate the features from the coarse geometry encoding volume M{\text{coarse}}(q). Concatenate \operatorname{PE}(q) and M{\text{coarse}}(q) and pass them through the coarse SDF prediction network f{\theta, \text{coarse}} to predict the SDF s(q). 6. Surface Extraction (Fine): Use the coarse geometry to guide the fine level. Interpolate features from the fine geometry encoding volume M{\text{fine}}(q). Concatenate \operatorname{PE}(q) and M{\text{fine}}(q) and pass them through the fine SDF prediction network f{\theta, \text{fine}} to predict the refined SDF s(q). This stage predicts colors and renders synthesized views. 1. Color Blending: Use a multi-scale color blending module to predict colors by aggregating information from the input images. The module uses a patch-based blending strategy with a patch size of 5 \times 5. 2. Volume Rendering: Combine the estimated geometry (SDF) with the predicted colors to render synthesized views using volume rendering. The rendering loss is minimized between the rendered view and the ground truth view. This stage improves the obtained geometry with fine-grained details. 1. Consistency-Aware Loss: Introduce a consistency-aware fine-tuning scheme to control inconsistent regions caused by occlusion and noise. The loss function includes a rendering loss and a consistency term that encourages consistent SDF values for points behind visible surfaces. 2. Optimization: Optimize the model using the same N input images without adding new images. The optimization runs for 10k iterations. 3. SDF Rescaling: Use a hyperparameter \tau to rescale the SDF value of sampled points behind visible surfaces. This encourages SDF values to be far from 0, avoiding uncontrollable free surfaces when extracting the 0-level set. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class SparseNeuS: def init(self, N, coarseres=96, fineres=192, patchsize=5): """ Initialize SparseNeuS.:param N: Number of input images.:param coarseres: Resolution of coarse geometry encoding volume.:param fineres: Resolution of fine geometry encoding volume.:param patchsize: Spatial size of patches for color blending. """ self.N = N self.coarseres = coarseres self.fineres = fineres self.patchsize = patchsize # Feature extraction network (2D feature extraction network) self.featureextractor = TwoDFeatureExtractor() # Sparse 3D CNN for geometry encoding volume (U-Net-like architecture) self.sparsecnn = Sparse3DCNN() # SDF prediction networks self.sdfcoarse = SDFPredictionMLP() self.sdffine = SDFPredictionMLP() # Color blending module self.colorblender = MultiScaleColorBlending(patchsize) # Hyperparameter for SDF rescaling self.tau = 1.0 # Value not specified in sources def extractfeatures(self, images): """ Extract 2D feature maps from input images.:param images: Tensor of shape (N, C, H, W):return: List of feature maps {Fi} """ return self.featureextractor(images) def projectfeatures(self, vertices, featuremaps, cameraparams): """ Project vertices to feature maps and interpolate features.:param vertices: Tensor of shape (V, 3) containing 3D coordinates of bounding box vertices.:param featuremaps: List of feature maps {Fi} of shape (N, C, H, W).:param cameraparams: Camera parameters for each image.:return: Tensor of shape (V, N, C) containing projected features Fi(v). """ projectedfeatures = [] for i in range(self.N): # Project vertex v to pixel location pii(v) pixellocs = projecttopixel(vertices, cameraparams[i]) # Interpolate features at pixel locations: Fi(v) = Fi(pii(v)) features = interpolatefeatures(featuremaps[i], pixellocs) projectedfeatures.append(features) return torch.stack(projectedfeatures, dim=1) # Shape: (V, N, C) def buildcostvolume(self, projectedfeatures): """ Build cost volume B by computing variance of projected features.:param projectedfeatures: Tensor of shape (V, N, C):return: Cost volume B of shape (V, 1) """ # Variance across the N dimension B = torch.var(projectedfeatures, dim=1, keepdim=True) return B def buildgeometryencodingvolume(self, costvolume): """ Apply sparse 3D CNN to cost volume to get geometry encoding volume M.:param costvolume: Cost volume B.:return: Geometry encoding volume M. """ M = self.sparsecnn(costvolume) return M def predictsdfcoarse(self, vertices, Mcoarse): """ Predict SDF using coarse geometry encoding volume.:param vertices: 3D coordinates.:param Mcoarse: Coarse geometry encoding volume.:return: SDF values. """ # Interpolate features from Mcoarse at vertices features = interpolatevolume(Mcoarse, vertices) # Positional encoding pe = positionalencoding(vertices) # Concatenate and predict inputtensor = torch.cat([pe, features], dim=-1) sdf = self.sdfcoarse(inputtensor) return sdf def predictsdffine(self, vertices, Mfine): """ Predict SDF using fine geometry encoding volume.:param vertices: 3D coordinates.:param Mfine: Fine geometry encoding volume.:return: SDF values. """ features = interpolatevolume(Mfine, vertices) pe = positionalencoding(vertices) inputtensor = torch.cat([pe, features], dim=-1) sdf = self.sdffine(inputtensor) return sdf def render(self, rays, sdf, colors): """ Volume rendering.:param rays: Ray origins and directions.:param sdf: SDF values at sampled points along rays.:param colors: Colors at sampled points.:return: Rendered image. """ # Standard volume rendering with SDF-based opacity # Alpha is derived from SDF alphas = sdftoalpha(sdf) weights = computeweights(alphas) renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights colors, dim=1) return renderedcolor def traingeneric(self, images, cameraparams, iterations=150000): """ Stage 1: Train coarse level networks. Stage 2: Train fine level networks while keeping coarse fixed. """ # Extract features featuremaps = self.extractfeatures(images) # Define bounding box and vertices vertices = getboundingboxvertices(cameraparams[0], self.coarseres) # Project features projectedfeatures = self.projectfeatures(vertices, featuremaps, cameraparams) # Build cost volume costvolume = self.buildcostvolume(projectedfeatures) # Build coarse geometry encoding volume Mcoarse = self.buildgeometryencodingvolume(costvolume) # Train coarse SDF network for i in range(iterations): # Sample points points = samplepoints(vertices) # Predict SDF sdf = self.predictsdfcoarse(points, Mcoarse) # Compute loss (rendering loss) loss = computerenderingloss(sdf, images, cameraparams) loss.backward() self.sdfcoarse.step() # Build fine geometry encoding volume (guided by coarse) # Note: Sources say fine volume is constructed similarly, guided by coarse # Implementation detail: Re-project or refine vertices based on coarse SDF? # Sources say "coarse level to refine the geometry", implying the fine volume # is built on a refined bounding box or with higher resolution. verticesfine = getboundingboxvertices(cameraparams[0], self.fineres) projectedfeaturesfine = self.projectfeatures(verticesfine, featuremaps, cameraparams) costvolumefine = self.buildcostvolume(projectedfeaturesfine) Mfine = self.buildgeometryencodingvolume(costvolumefine) # Train fine SDF network for i in range(iterations): points = samplepoints(verticesfine) sdf = self.predictsdffine(points, Mfine) loss = computerenderingloss(sdf, images, cameraparams) loss.backward() self.sdffine.step() def finetune(self, images, cameraparams, iterations=10000): """ Per-scene fine-tuning. """ # Use the same three input images # Optimize model (likely just the SDF networks or specific parameters) for i in range(iterations): # Sample points points = samplepoints() # Predict SDF sdf = self.predictsdffine(points, Mfine) # Compute consistency-aware loss loss = computeconsistencyawareloss(sdf, images, cameraparams, self.tau) loss.backward() # Update parameters # Note: Sources say "Optimizes the model", implying some parameters are updated # name: SparseNeuS Per-Scene Fine-Tuning
head: Fine-Tuning Networks, Neural Implicit Surface, Per-Scene Optimization, SparseNeuS Network Architecture and Sampling
body: SparseNeuS Per-Scene Fine-Tuning refines a neural surface reconstruction from sparse input views by directly optimizing the geometry encoding volume and SDF network for a specific scene. It differs from the generic SparseNeuS inference by discarding the 2D feature extraction and 3D sparse CNN networks, replacing the CNN-based blending network with a lightweight MLP, and employing a consistency-aware color loss to handle occlusions and noise. This approach leverages the initialization from the generic network inference to fast converge to a high-quality surface. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images, camera poses, and the pre-trained generic SparseNeuS model parameters (specifically the fine-level geometry encoding volume and the SDF network f\theta). Outputs: Optimized fine-level geometry encoding volume, optimized SDF network f\theta, and the reconstructed 3D surface. Data Structures: Geometry Encoding Volume: A 3D grid storing latent features for spatial locations. SDF Network (f\theta): An MLP with 4 hidden layers and hidden size 256. Blending Network (fc'): A tiny MLP with 3 hidden layers and hidden size 256. Positional Encoding: Applied to 3D locations (6 frequencies) and view directions (4 frequencies). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the pre-trained generic SparseNeuS model and discard the 2D feature extraction network and the 3D sparse CNN networks. Keep the fine-level geometry encoding volume and the SDF network f\theta. 2. Network Replacement: Replace the CNN-based blending network used in the generic setting with the tiny MLP network fc'. This MLP outputs blending weights for a query 3D position q. 3. Sampling: Adopt a hierarchical sampling strategy similar to NeuS. Sample 64 coarse points and 64 fine points along each query ray. 4. Blending Weight Calculation: For each query 3D position q, compute the blending weights \{wi^q\}{i=0}^{N-1} using the tiny MLP fc'. The inputs to fc' are PE(q) (positional encoding of q), PE(d) (positional encoding of ray direction d), nq (surface normal), s(q) (predicted SDF), and M(q) (interpolated geometry encoding feature). The formula is: \{wi^q\}{i=0}^{N-1} = fc'(PE(q), PE(d), nq, s(q), M(q)) where N is the number of input images. 5. Alpha Computation: Compute volume rendering alpha from the SDF using a learned inverse temperature parameter invs. Adjust the sampling interval based on the angle between the ray direction and surface normal. Estimate adjacent SDF values and compute alpha as \alpha = (\text{sigmoid}(\text{prev} \cdot \text{inv\s}) - \text{sigmoid}(\text{next} \cdot \text{inv\s})) / \text{sigmoid}(\text{prev} \cdot \text{inv\s}). 6. Loss Computation: Compute the consistency-aware color loss to automatically detect and exclude regions with inconsistent projections across views due to occlusion or noise. Use default parameters \lambda0 = 0.01 and \lambda1 = 0.015. Compute the sparseness loss with scaling parameter \tau. 7. Optimization: Directly optimize the fine-level geometry encoding volume and the SDF network f\theta using the computed losses. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computealpha(dirs, normal, dists, sdf, invs, cosannealratio): # Handle empty ray case if dirs.shape[0] == 0: return emptytensor(), emptytensor(), emptytensor(), emptytensor(), emptytensor(), emptytensor(), emptytensor() # Clamp inverse temperature for numerical stability invs = torch.clamp(invs, min=1e-6, max=1e6) # Compute adjusted sampling interval based on ray-normal angle truecos = torch.dot(dirs, normal) itercos = -(F.relu(-truecos 0.5 + 0.5) (1.0 - cosannealratio) + F.relu(-truecos) cosannealratio) # Estimate adjacent SDF values estimatednextsdf = sdf + itercos dists 0.5 estimatedprevsdf = sdf - itercos dists 0.5 # Compute opacity with division-by-zero guard prevsig = torch.sigmoid(estimatedprevsdf invs) nextsig = torch.sigmoid(estimatednextsdf invs) alpha = (prevsig - nextsig + 1e-5) / (prevsig + 1e-5) return alpha, dists, estimatednextsdf, estimatedprevsdf, sdf, sdf.grad, dists def updatestep(grid, occevalfn, gridpruneoccthre, nsteps): # Update occupancy grid every nsteps if pruning is enabled if gridpruneoccthre is not None and currentstep % nsteps == 0: grid = occevalfn(grid, threshold=gridpruneoccthre) return grid Parameters: SDF Network: 4 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Blending Network (fc'): 3 hidden layers, hidden size 256. Positional Encoding: 6 frequencies for 3D locations, 4 frequencies for view directions. Sampling: 64 coarse samples, 64 fine samples. Loss Weights: \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.02 for total loss. SDF Scaling (\tau): 100 for sparseness loss. Consistency-Aware Color Loss: \lambda0 = 0.01, \lambda1 = 0.015 by default. Data Preparation: Threshold \tau = 10 for detecting invalid black regions in images, followed by dilation and erosion. Variance Modulation: modulate flag enables modulation of invs, starting at modstartsteps and reaching maxinvs at reachmaxsteps. Shading Annealing: Cosine annealing for the shading term ends at cosannealend (0 disables it). Grid Pruning: gridpruneoccthre (default 0.01) and gridpruneoccthrebg (default 0.01) control occupancy grid updates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ratio Tuning: The ratio \lambda0 / \lambda1 in the consistency-aware color loss affects surface completeness vs. cleanliness; decreasing the ratio keeps more regions, while increasing it excludes more regions for cleaner surfaces. Inconsistent Projections: Regions with inconsistent projections across views (due to occlusion or image noise) can lead to inaccurate and distorted surfaces if not handled by the consistency-aware loss. Background Noise: Images may contain large black backgrounds and considerable noise, requiring threshold-based denoising and mask processing. Empty Rays: If no samples are generated along a ray, the method returns empty tensors for alpha, midpoints, rgb, normal, sdf, sdfgrad, and dists. Converts SDF/TSDF voxel values into volumetric opacity, creating a thin opacity shell concentrated near the surface (F=0). Results in fewer above-threshold voxels and a sparser octree structure at the same pruning threshold. Renders volumetric alpha from an SDF using a learnable inverse temperature parameter, with hierarchical ray sampling guided by predicted depth from a 3D Gaussian Splatting branch. Replaces fixed uniform sampling with depth-guided hierarchical sampling, concentrating samples near surfaces and reducing empty-space queries. Time Complexity: Faster than generic SparseNeuS inference due to replacing the CNN-based blending network with a smaller MLP. Memory Complexity: Reduced memory footprint compared to generic SparseNeuS as the 2D feature extraction and 3D sparse CNN networks are discarded during fine-tuning. Performance: Fast convergence to high-quality surfaces due to initialization from the generic network inference. Strengths: Handles sparse views effectively; consistency-aware loss improves robustness to noise and occlusion; lightweight blending network speeds up optimization. Limitations: Requires per-scene optimization, which is slower than single-shot inference; performance depends on the quality of the generic initialization. When to Use: When high-quality surface reconstruction is needed from sparse views and per-scene optimization is feasible. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is required or when input views are dense. The per-scene fine-tuning method builds upon the generic SparseNeuS framework, which uses a hybrid representation of geometry encoding volume and learnable image features. It is used in applications requiring high-fidelity 3D reconstruction from limited camera views, such as in the DTU dataset evaluations.
