name: Differentiable Neural Radiosity
head: DNR
body: Differentiable Neural Radiosity (DNR) is a method for solving the differential rendering equation using a neural network to represent the differential radiance field. It addresses the problem of computing gradients of rendered images with respect to arbitrary scene parameters (such as geometry, material properties, or illumination) by minimizing the residual of the differential rendering equation. Unlike traditional differentiable rendering methods that simulate light transport per optimization step, DNR pre-trains a neural network to cache the differential radiance distribution, enabling view-independent gradient computation with constant time and memory complexity relative to path length. It distinguishes itself from Radiative Backpropagation (RB) by avoiding quadratic time complexity in path length and from Path Replay Backpropagation (PRB) and Automatic Differentiation (AD) by not requiring the storage of per-bounce data or complete light path construction. Inputs: Scene geometry, materials (BRDFs), and illumination. A set of scene parameters p with respect to which derivatives are desired (e.g., BRDF roughness, diffuse albedo, index of refraction). A pre-trained primal radiance network L\phi. Outputs: A trained neural network \partialp L\theta(x, \omegao) representing the differential radiance field. Gradients \partialp Ik for inverse rendering tasks. Data Structures: 1. Primal Radiance Network (L\phi): A neural network with fixed parameters \phi that approximates the outgoing radiance L(x, \omegao). Exact layout and sizes are not given in the sources. 2. Differential Radiance Network (\partialp L\theta): A neural network with learnable parameters \theta that approximates the differential radiance \partialp L(x, \omegao). Exact layout and sizes are not given in the sources. 3. Scene Parameters (p): A vector of parameters defining the scene state. Formulas: The differential rendering equation is derived by differentiating the standard rendering equation with respect to p: \partialp L(x, \omegao) = \partialp E(x, \omegao) + \int{H^2} f(x, \omegai, \omegao) \partialp L(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp + \int{H^2} \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) L(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp Where: L(x, \omegao) is the outgoing radiance. E(x, \omegao) is the emitted radiance. f(x, \omegai, \omegao) is the BRDF. x'(x, \omegai) is the next intersection point along direction \omegai. H^2 is the projected solid angle hemisphere. \partialp denotes the derivative with respect to parameter set p. The residual r\theta is defined as the difference between the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) of the differential equation, using the neural network approximations: r\theta(x, \omegao) = \partialp L\theta(x, \omegao) - \partialp E(x, \omegao) - \int{H^2} f(x, \omegai, \omegao) \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp - \int{H^2} \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) L\phi(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) d\omegai^\perp The loss function is the L2 norm of this residual: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \| r\theta \|^2 Steps: 1. Pre-train Primal Radiance: Train the network L\phi to approximate the primal radiance field L(x, \omegao) for the given scene. Fix parameters \phi. 2. Initialize Differential Network: Initialize the network \partialp L\theta with parameters \theta. 3. Compute Residual: For a sample point x and direction \omegao: a. Query L\phi to get incident primal radiance L\phi(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai). b. Compute \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) analytically or via automatic differentiation of the BRDF function with respect to p. c. Compute \partialp E(x, \omegao) analytically or via automatic differentiation. d. Query \partialp L\theta at x'(x, \omegai) to get \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai). e. Evaluate the integrals over the hemisphere H^2. f. Calculate the residual r\theta(x, \omegao) using the formula above. 4. Optimize: Minimize \mathcal{L}(\theta) with respect to \theta using gradient descent. 5. Inverse Optimization: For a new inverse rendering task, use the pre-trained \partialp L\theta to compute gradients \partialp Ik for the measurement equation: \partialp Ik = \intA \int{H^2} Wk(x, \omega) \partialp L\theta(x, \omega) d\omegai^\perp dx Use the pre-trained network to compute gradients for inverse optimization tasks. Parameters: \theta: Learnable parameters of the differential radiance network. \phi: Fixed parameters of the primal radiance network. p: Scene parameters (e.g., roughness, albedo). Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Discontinuities: The method ignores visibility-related discontinuities (occlusions) for simplicity. Pre-training Dependency: The accuracy of the differential gradients depends on the quality of the pre-trained primal radiance network L\phi. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class DifferentiableNeuralRadiosity: def init(self, primalnetwork, differentialnetwork): self.primalnetwork = primalnetwork self.differentialnetwork = differentialnetwork self.primalnetwork.eval() for param in self.primalnetwork.parameters(): param.requiresgrad = False def computeresidual(self, x, wo, p, sceneops, numsamples=100): # LHS: differential radiance at current point dLtheta = self.differentialnetwork(x, wo) # Differential emission dE = sceneops.computeemissionderivative(x, wo, p) # Sample directions in hemisphere H^2 wisamples, cosweights = sceneops.samplehemisphere(wo, numsamples) # RHS integral 1: f dLtheta term1 = torch.zeroslike(dLtheta) for i in range(numsamples): wi = wisamples[i] xprime = sceneops.traceray(x, wi) dLprime = self.differentialnetwork(xprime, -wi) f = sceneops.brdf(x, wi, wo) term1 += f dLprime cosweights[i] # RHS integral 2: df/dp Lphi term2 = torch.zeroslike(dLtheta) dfdp = sceneops.computebrdfderivative(x, wisamples, wo, p) for i in range(numsamples): wi = wisamples[i] xprime = sceneops.traceray(x, wi) Lphi = self.primalnetwork(xprime, -wi) term2 += dfdp[i] Lphi cosweights[i] # Residual rtheta = dLtheta - dE - term1 - term2 residual = dLtheta - dE - term1 - term2 return residual def train(self, optimizer, numiterations, sceneops): for in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() x, wo, p = sceneops.sampletrainingdata() residual = self.computeresidual(x, wo, p, sceneops) loss = torch.norm(residual) 2 loss.backward() optimizer.step() def computeinversegradients(self, p, sceneops): # Integrate differential radiance over pixel area and hemisphere to get dIk/dp # Implementation depends on specific pixel sampling strategy pass Optimizes scene parameters by minimizing the distance between rendered and reference images, using a neural network to cache the differential radiance field. It amortizes global light transport costs and avoids independent simulations per step. Represents the differential radiance field using learnable feature vectors at mesh vertices, reducing memory consumption and avoiding grid artifacts by leveraging geometric priors. Time Complexity: Constant in path length given pre-trained networks, as it queries the network at the first intersection rather than building complete light paths. In contrast, PRB and AD are linear in path length, and RB is quadratic. Memory Complexity: Constant in path length, similar to RB and PRB, as it does not store per-bounce data in an adjoint transcript. Measured Performance: Gradient computation time per iteration is 0.002s, compared to 0.009s for RB, 0.017s for PRB, and 0.088s for AD. View-Independence: Provides view-independent solutions, meaning sensor parameter changes do not require recomputation unless sensor parameters are being optimized. Strengths: Faster convergence, lower gradient computation time, view-independence, constant complexity in path length. Limitations: Ignores visibility-related discontinuities (occlusions), which can lead to incorrect gradients. Requires pre-training of the primal radiance network. Differentiable Neural Radiosity was introduced by Saeed Hadadan and Matthias Zwicker from the University of Maryland, College Park, USA. The method was published as a preprint on arXiv in January 2022. It builds on the concept of Neural Radiosity, which uses a neural network to solve the rendering equation, by extending it to the differential rendering equation. The method aims to provide a more efficient and accurate way to compute gradients for inverse rendering problems compared to existing differentiable rendering techniques. name: Inverse Rendering with Neural Radiosity
body: Inverse rendering with Neural Radiosity optimizes scene parameters p by minimizing an objective function z(\cdot) that measures the distance between a candidate rendered image and a reference image. It distinguishes itself from differentiable path tracing methods by caching the differential radiance distribution in a neural network, which amortizes the cost of resolving global light transport and avoids independent light transport simulations per optimization step. Inputs: Scene parameters p (e.g., roughness, position, emission intensity). Reference image. Pre-trained primal radiance network L\phi. Differential radiance network \partialp L\theta. Camera geometry and scene primitives. Outputs: Optimized scene parameters p. Updated networks \partialp L\theta and L\phi. Data Structures: Neural Networks: MLPs with 6 fully-connected layers and 512 neurons per hidden layer. Network Inputs: Position x, outgoing direction \omegao, surface normal, diffuse reflectance, and specular reflectance. Sparse Grids: Multiresolution learnable feature vectors stored in sparse grids within the scene. Sampling: Hemispherical samples \omega{i,j,k} for incident directions, importance sampled from emitter directions and BSDF distributions in primal space. Steps: 1. Compute a non-differentiable candidate primal rendering y = g(p) and calculate the loss z (e.g., L2 or L1 distance) between y and the reference image. 2. Compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the pixels of the primal image, \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}. 3. Compute the gradient of the rendered image with respect to parameters, \frac{\partial y}{\partial p}, equivalent to the measurement vector [\partialp I0 \dots \partialp In]. Trace rays from the sensor to find the first hit point x, query the differential radiance network \partialp L\theta, and integrate over the surface area A and hemisphere H^2: \partialp I{k,\theta} = \intA \int{H^2} Wk(x, \omega) \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omega)) \, dx \, d\omega{i\perp} where Wk is the window function and x'(x, \omega) is the point on the surface visible from x in direction \omega. 4. Compute the total gradient of the loss w.r.t. parameters \frac{\partial z}{\partial p} by multiplying the gradients from steps 2 and 3: \frac{\partial z}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial p}. 5. Update scene parameters p using an optimizer (e.g., Adam) and a learning rate. 6. Fine-tune the networks \partialp L\theta and L\phi to adapt to the new parameter state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inverserenderingstep(p, Iref, Lphi, dLtheta, camera, scene, optimizer, lr): # Step 1: Primal rendering y = renderprimal(p, Lphi, camera, scene) # loss = computeloss(y, Iref) # e.g., L2 or L1 distance # Step 2: Pixel gradient dzdy = computegradient(loss, y) # # Step 3: Differential radiance integration dydp = 0.0 for each pixel k: x, omega = traceray(camera, k) # dL = dLtheta(x, omega) # Query network integral = integrate(Wk(x, omega) dL, over=A, over=H2) # dydp += integral # Step 4: Gradient accumulation dzdp = dzdy dydp # # Step 5: Parameter update p = optimizer.step(p, dzdp, lr) # # Step 6: Network fine-tuning or RHS fallback if userhsfallback: # Use RHS of differential solution instead of fetching gradients from dLtheta # RHS adapts faster with one extra ray-tracing step using updated parameters pass # else: finetunenetworks(dLtheta, Lphi, p) # return p, dLtheta, Lphi Formulas: The differential radiance is reparameterized to separate the network output from the differential emission term: \partialp L\theta(x, \omegao) = N\theta(x, \omegao) + \partialp E(x, \omegao) where N\theta is the network output and E is emission. The residual of the differential rendering equation r\theta is defined as: r\theta(x, \omegao) = N\theta(x, \omegao) - T\{N\theta + \partialp E\}(x, \omegao) - T'\{N\phi + E\}(x, \omegao) where T and T' are transport operators. The transport operators are defined as integrals over the hemisphere H^2: T\{\partialp L\theta\}(x, \omegao) = \int{H^2} f(x, \omegai, \omegao) \partialp L\theta(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) \, d\omega{i\perp} T'\{L\phi\}(x, \omegao) = \int{H^2} \partialp f(x, \omegai, \omegao) L\phi(x'(x, \omegai), -\omegai) \, d\omega{i\perp} where f is the BSDF and L\phi is the primal radiance. Parameters: Sampling: Importance sample emitter directions and BSDF distributions in primal space to obtain incident directions \omegai. Samples are detached (static w.r.t. perturbations in scene parameters). Optimizer: Adam. Network Architecture: 6 fully-connected layers, 512 neurons per hidden layer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fine-tuning Bottleneck: Fine-tuning networks after every parameter update is computationally expensive. Mitigation: Keep networks intact in their initial state and use the Right-Hand Side (RHS) of the differential solution instead of fetching gradients from \partialp L\theta. The RHS adapts faster to parameter changes because it requires only one extra ray-tracing step with updated parameters, updating terms \partialp f and f in scattering integrals. This introduces bias but improves performance. Gradient Computation: All gradient terms, including \partialp f and \partialp E, are computed using automatic differentiation frameworks during optimization. Performs volumetric inverse rendering by jointly optimizing a neural medium field and a neural light field. It uses a Volumetric Radiance Error (VRE) loss to integrate radiance along primary viewing rays, counteracting oversmoothing from local constraints, and amortizes global light transport resolution. Time Complexity: Avoids the high cost of differentiating through generic Monte Carlo rendering by using an adjoint-like approach with a cached neural representation. Fine-tuning networks at every iteration is a bottleneck. Using the RHS approximation reduces this cost but introduces bias. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two neural networks (primal and differential) and sparse feature grids. The computation graph size is vastly reduced compared to generic differentiable path tracing. Performance: Efficient for scenes where global light transport is complex, as it amortizes the transport solution. Suitable for optimizing material properties (e.g., roughness) and illumination. Strengths: Avoids independent light transport simulations per scene instance; handles global illumination via the neural network; reduces computation graph size. Limitations: Fine-tuning bottleneck if not using the RHS approximation; potential bias from using the RHS approximation; requires pre-training of the primal radiance network. The method is based on "Differentiable Neural Radiosity" by Hadadan et al. (2022). It builds on the Neural Radiosity method by Hadadan et al. (2021). The approach was developed to address the computational costs of differentiable rendering by caching the differential radiance distribution in a neural network. head: Neural RTE Inverse Rendering, Ours
body: This method performs volumetric inverse rendering by jointly optimizing a neural medium field and a neural light field to reconstruct scene geometry, optical properties, and illumination from multi-view observations. It distinguishes itself from differentiable path tracing methods like Differential Ratio Tracking (DRT) by amortizing global light transport resolution through a learned light field representation, avoiding the need for independent light transport simulations per scene instance. Unlike purely local supervision methods, it employs a Volumetric Radiance Error (VRE) loss to integrate radiance along primary viewing rays, counteracting the oversmoothing induced by local constraints. The method solves for the volumetric scene properties and illumination by minimizing a composite objective function. It operates in two stages: an initialization stage and a joint optimization stage. Inputs: A set of posed observations \{I{l,k}\}, where l indexes scenes and k indexes images within each scene. For reconstruction, a single scene is assumed; for generation, multiple scenes are used. Outputs: Neural medium field M\phi (encoding scattering \sigmas, absorption \sigmaa, and phase function parameter g) and neural light field L\theta (encoding outgoing radiance). 1. Neural Hash Grid (F\xi): Initialized in Stage 1. Uses a neural hash grid architecture [MESK22] to store emission-absorption features. 2. Neural Medium Field (M\phi): Parameterized by a SIREN network [SMB20]. 3. Neural Light Field (L\theta): Parameterized by a SIREN network [SMB20]. Inputs are spatial coordinates x and direction \omega. 4. Optimization State: Adam optimizer state [KB15]. Stage 1: Initialization 1. Train the emission-absorption reconstruction model F\xi using the neural hash grid architecture [MESK22] on the input observations. 2. Discard the color output of F\xi. Stage 2: Joint Optimization 1. Initialize M\phi and L\theta using SIREN networks [SMB20]. 2. For each optimization iteration: a. Sample Collocation Points: Draw 10,000 random points xt from the volumetric domain. b. Compute Medium Properties: i. Query F\xi(xt) to get the volumetric density. ii. Query M\phi(xt) to get modulation factors. iii. Compute scattering coefficient \sigmas(xt) = \exp(M\phi(xt){\sigmas}) \cdot F\xi(xt). iv. Compute absorption coefficient \sigmaa(xt) = \exp(M\phi(xt){\sigmaa}) \cdot F\xi(xt). v. Compute total coefficient \sigmat(xt) = \sigmas(xt) + \sigmaa(xt). vi. Compute phase function parameter g(xt) = \tanh(M\phi(xt)g). c. Evaluate RTE Residual (L{RTE}): i. For each collocation point xt, approximate the in-scattering integral using 32 directional samples \omega' drawn randomly from the angular domain S^2. ii. Query L\theta(xt, \omega') for incoming radiance. iii. Compute the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) residual. d. Evaluate Boundary Conditions (L{BC}): i. Draw 10,000 random points on the scene boundary. ii. Evaluate boundary conditions (Eq. 5 in). e. Evaluate Observation Loss (L{obs}): i. Compute observation loss L{obs}. f. Evaluate Volumetric Radiance Error (L{VRE}): i. For each viewing ray defined by origin ok and direction \omegak(q): 1. Draw 100 samples along the ray randomly from the continuous domain. 2. For each sample point xt on the ray, compute the in-scattering radiance by querying L\theta(xt, -\omegak(q)). 3. Approximate the in-scattering integral using 32 directional samples \omega' drawn randomly from S^2. 4. Crucial: Draw independent samples for the forward and backward passes of the in-scattering direction integration to avoid optimization gradient bias. 5. Compute the VRE loss term: L{VRE}(\theta,\phi) = \mathbb{E}{k,q} \left[ \int0^{tb} \sigmas(xt) \left( Ik(q) - \int0^t \exp\left(-\int0^s \sigmat(xs) ds\right) \int{S^2} fp(xt, -\omegak(q), \omega') L\theta(xt, \omega') d\omega' ds \right)^2 dt \right] where Ik(q) is the observed radiance, fp is the phase function, and x\tau lies on the primary viewing ray ok + \tau \omegak(q). g. Update Parameters: Minimize the total objective using the Adam optimizer with default settings. Total Objective: L(\theta, \phi) = L{RTE}(\theta, \phi) + \lambda{BC} L{BC}(\theta) + \lambda{obs} L{obs}(\theta) + \lambda{VRE} L{VRE}(\theta, \phi) VRE Loss: L{VRE}(\theta,\phi) = \mathbb{E}{k,q} \left[ \int0^{tb} \sigmas(xt) \left( Ik(q) - \int0^t \exp\left(-\int0^s \sigmat(xs) ds\right) \int{S^2} fp(xt, -\omegak(q), \omega') L\theta(xt, \omega') d\omega' ds \right)^2 dt \right] \lambda{BC} = 1: Weight for boundary condition loss. \lambda{obs} = 1: Weight for observation loss. \lambda{VRE} = 70: Weight for volumetric radiance error loss. Gradient Bias: Stochastic sampling of in-scattering directions can introduce optimization gradient bias. Initialization: Scene initialization is crucial for high-quality solutions. Positivity Constraints: \sigmas and \sigmaa must be positive. Phase Function Bounds: The anisotropy parameter g is bounded using a hyperbolic tangent. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim import numpy as np def henyeygreenstein(costheta, g): """Standard Henyey-Greenstein phase function.""" g2 = g g denom = 1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g costheta return (1.0 - g2) / (4.0 np.pi np.power(denom, 1.5)) def samplesphere(N, device): """Uniform sampling on unit sphere S^2.""" u = torch.rand(N, 1, device=device) v = torch.rand(N, 1, device=device) theta = 2 np.pi u phi = torch.acos(1 - 2 v) x = torch.sin(phi) torch.cos(theta) y = torch.sin(phi) torch.sin(theta) z = torch.cos(phi) return torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=1) def computemediumproperties(x, Fxi, Mphi): """Computes optical properties from coordinates x.""" rhobase = Fxi(x) mediumout = Mphi(x) sigmas = torch.exp(mediumout[:, 0]) rhobase sigmaa = torch.exp(mediumout[:, 1]) rhobase sigmat = sigmas + sigmaa g = torch.tanh(mediumout[:, 2]) return sigmas, sigmaa, sigmat, g def computeinscattering(x, viewdir, Ltheta, sigmas, sigmat, g, numsamples=32): """Approximates in-scattering integral using Monte Carlo sampling.""" omegaprime = samplesphere(numsamples, x.device) Lout = Ltheta(x, omegaprime) costheta = torch.sum(viewdir omegaprime, dim=1) fp = henyeygreenstein(costheta, g) return torch.mean(fp Lout) def computevreloss(viewingrays, observations, Fxi, Mphi, Ltheta, lambdavre=70): """Computes the Volumetric Radiance Error loss.""" loss = 0.0 for k, (origin, direction) in enumerate(viewingrays): tsamples = torch.linspace(0, 1.0, 100, device=origin.device) # 100 samples per ray xt = origin + direction.unsqueeze(0) tsamples.unsqueeze(1) sigmast, sigmaat, sigmatt, gt = computemediumproperties(xt, Fxi, Mphi) dt = tsamples[1] - tsamples[0] opticaldepth = torch.cumsum(sigmatt dt, dim=0) transmittance = torch.exp(-opticaldepth) inscatteringvals = [] for i, xpoint in enumerate(xt): dirin = -direction inscat = computeinscattering(xpoint, dirin, Ltheta, sigmast[i], sigmatt[i], gt[i]) inscatteringvals.append(inscat) inscatteringtensor = torch.stack(inscatteringvals) weights = transmittance sigmast inscatteringtensor cumulativeintegral = torch.cumsum(weights dt, dim=0) error = observations[k] - cumulativeintegral vreintegrand = sigmast error2 rayvre = torch.sum(vreintegrand dt) loss += rayvre return lambdavre loss def optimize(Fxi, Mphi, Ltheta, viewingrays, observations, numiterations=10000): optimizer = optim.Adam(list(Mphi.parameters()) + list(Ltheta.parameters()), lr=0.001) for i in range(numiterations): optimizer.zerograd() xcolloc = torch.rand(10000, 3) # 10k collocation points sigmasc, sigmaac, sigmatc, gc = computemediumproperties(xcolloc, Fxi, Mphi) # LRTE: Compute RTE residual using 32 directional samples per point # [Comment: Source does not provide explicit formula for LRTE residual computation steps.] lrte = torch.tensor(0.0, requiresgrad=True) # LBC: Evaluate boundary conditions using 10k boundary samples # [Comment: Source does not provide explicit formula for LBC computation steps.] lbc = torch.tensor(0.0, requiresgrad=True) # Lobs: Compute observation loss # [Comment: Source does not provide explicit formula for Lobs computation steps.] lobs = torch.tensor(0.0, requiresgrad=True) # LVRE: Compute VRE loss lvre = computevreloss(viewingrays, observations, Fxi, Mphi, Ltheta) lambdabc = 1 lambdaobs = 1 lambdavre = 70 totalloss = lrte + lambdabc lbc + lambdaobs lobs + lambdavre lvre totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() Time Complexity: The runtime is dominated by the evaluation of the four objective terms. On an A100 GPU, L{RTE} takes 38%, L{VRE} takes 53%, L{obs} takes 2%, and L{BC} takes 7%. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Quantitative evaluation on anisotropic scenes shows MSE (x10^-2) for \sigmaa is 1.99, \sigmas is 2.37, \sigmat is 1.33, and g is 1.21. Strengths: Amortizes global light transport resolution through the learned light field, making it more efficient than methods requiring independent light transport simulations per instance (like DRT). The VRE loss counteracts oversmoothing. Limitations: Requires careful initialization (two-stage optimization) to avoid poor local minima. Relies on stochastic sampling which can introduce gradient bias if not handled (mitigated by independent sampling). Origin: The method was introduced in "Volumetric Inverse Rendering via Neural Radiative Transfer". History: It builds on prior work in differentiable inverse rendering and neural radiative transfer. It extends the concept of neural radiosity to volumetric scenes. Usage: Used for volumetric scene reconstruction and generation. name: Neural Vertex Features for Global Illumination
head: Neural Radiosity with Vertex Features, Neural Vertex Features, Vertex Features for Neural Global Illumination
body: Neural Vertex Features is a method for representing the differential radiance field in neural rendering by storing learnable feature vectors directly at the vertices of an explicit mesh geometry, rather than in a 3D grid or hash table. It solves the problem of high memory consumption and inefficient feature representation inherent in uniform spatial distributions by leveraging geometric priors to concentrate computation on actual scene surfaces. Unlike multi-resolution hash grids, which allocate resources to empty space and suffer from hashing collisions, this method aligns features with the mesh topology, achieving over 5× memory reduction while maintaining comparable visual quality and avoiding grid-like artifacts. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scene mesh defined by vertices V and triangular faces; camera rays; surface properties (albedo, normal). Output: Approximated outgoing radiance L\theta(x, \omegao) for a shading point x and view direction \omegao. Data Structures Feature Array G: A learnable array G \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}, where n = |V| is the number of vertices and d is the feature vector dimension. Each vertex vi \in V is uniquely mapped to a feature vector gi \in G via its index i. For static scenes, d=4 learnable parameters per vertex; for dynamic scenes, d=8 learnable parameters per vertex. MLP: A Multi-Layer Perceptron with 4 hidden layers, each containing 256 neurons, used to decode features into radiance. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Intersection: Ray-intersect camera rays against the mesh to obtain the primary shading point x, view direction \omegao, and geometry information (surface normal, albedo). 2. Primitive Identification: Identify the triangle primitive P containing x and calculate the barycentric coordinates (u, v) of x relative to the triangle vertices \{vi, vj, vk\} using standard ray-triangle intersection or rasterization. 3. Feature Retrieval: Retrieve the neural features \tilde{g}i, \tilde{g}j, \tilde{g}k from array G corresponding to vertices vi, vj, vk. 4. Barycentric Interpolation: Compute the interpolated feature fx at point x using the formula: fx = (1 - u - v) \tilde{g}i + u \tilde{g}j + v \tilde{g}k where u, v are the barycentric coordinates and \tilde{g}i, \tilde{g}j, \tilde{g}k are the vertex features. 5. Feature Plane Combination (Dynamic Scenes): For dynamic scenes, combine spatial features with scene state variables v using multiple feature planes P: f{XV}(x, v) = \sumP P(p, v) where x is the spatial position and v is the scene state vector. 6. Input Encoding: Encode auxiliary inputs for the MLP: albedo is encoded using OneBlob encoding; the outgoing direction \omegao and surface normal are encoded using spherical harmonic basis functions. 7. Radiance Prediction: Feed the interpolated feature fx (and f{XV} for dynamic scenes) along with encoded auxiliary inputs into the MLP to predict the outgoing radiance L\theta(x, \omegao). 8. Reflectance Factorization: Decouple texture and radiance by factorizing reflectance out of the learning target, allowing the network to focus on texture-independent details. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class NeuralVertexFeatures: def init(self, numvertices, isdynamic=False): # G: Learnable feature vectors at vertices # Static: 4 params/vertex, Dynamic: 8 params/vertex dim = 8 if isdynamic else 4 self.G = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numvertices, dim)) # MLP: 4 hidden layers, 256 neurons each # Input dimension is projected to 256 before the first hidden layer self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3) # Output RGB radiance) self.isdynamic = isdynamic if isdynamic: # Feature planes P for dynamic scenes self.featureplanes = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(10, 256)) def encodealbedo(self, albedo): # OneBlob encoding # Standard binning/basis implementation return albedo def encodedirection(self, direction): # Spherical Harmonic basis functions return self.shencode(direction) def encodenormal(self, normal): # Spherical Harmonic basis functions return self.shencode(normal) def shencode(self, vec): # Standard 9-coefficient SH encoding x, y, z = vec[:, 0], vec[:, 1], vec[:, 2] c0, c1, c2, c3, c4 = 0.282095, 0.488603, 1.092548, -0.315392, 0.546274 sh = torch.zeros((vec.shape[0], 9), device=vec.device) sh[:, 0] = c0 sh[:, 1] = c1 y sh[:, 2] = c1 z sh[:, 3] = c1 x sh[:, 4] = c2 x y sh[:, 5] = c2 y z sh[:, 6] = c4 (3 z2 - 1) sh[:, 7] = c2 x z sh[:, 8] = c3 (x2 - y2) return sh def forward(self, shadingpoints, vertexindices, barycentriccoords, viewdirections, albedos, normals): # Step 3: Retrieve features gi = self.G[vertexindices[:, 0]] gj = self.G[vertexindices[:, 1]] gk = self.G[vertexindices[:, 2]] u, v = barycentriccoords[:, 0], barycentriccoords[:, 1] # Step 4: Barycentric Interpolation w = 1 - u - v fx = w.unsqueeze(1) gi + u.unsqueeze(1) gj + v.unsqueeze(1) gk # Step 5: Feature Plane Combination (Dynamic only) if self.isdynamic: # fXV(x, v) = sumP P(p, v) # Standard linear combination of planes fx = fx + self.featureplanes.mean(dim=0) # Step 6: Encode Auxiliary Inputs albedoenc = self.encodealbedo(albedos) direnc = self.encodedirection(viewdirections) normalenc = self.encodenormal(normals) # Concatenate features for MLP input # Project fx to match MLP input dimension if necessary if fx.shape[1] != 256: fx = nn.Linear(fx.shape[1], 256)(fx) # Combine spatial feature with encoded inputs combinedinput = torch.cat([fx, albedoenc, direnc, normalenc], dim=1) # Project to MLP input dim if concatenation exceeds 256 if combinedinput.shape[1] != 256: combinedinput = nn.Linear(combinedinput.shape[1], 256)(combinedinput) # Step 7: Radiance Prediction radiance = self.mlp(combinedinput) return radiance Parameters Learnable Parameters: 4 per vertex for static scenes, 8 per vertex for dynamic scenes. MLP Architecture: 4 hidden layers, 256 neurons each. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 1 \times 10^{-3}, decayed by 0.33 every one-third of total steps. RHS Sample Count (M): Starts at 32, doubles every 1/5 of training steps. LOD Factors: Updated 3 times early in training, limited to max 50% of original vertex count (100% for dynamic), clamped to [0, 30]. Probability Mixing Factor (\alpha): Fixed at 0.5. Rendering Samples: 32 rays/pixel for offline static rendering; 1 ray/pixel with FXAA for interactive dynamic rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Geometry Assumption: Assumes triangular faces. Quadrilaterals are mentioned as potential but not detailed. Discontinuities: Adjacent triangles with different LOD levels may cause feature discontinuities at boundaries. The network learns to smooth these over training time. High-Frequency Radiance: Regions with high-frequency radiance are difficult for the network to capture due to vertex-based encoding limitations. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory consumption to approximately one-fifth (or less) of grid-based representations. Performance: Achieves over 5× reduction in memory overhead while maintaining comparable image quality. Inference Overhead: Lower inference overhead compared to grid-based methods. Measured Performance (Static Dining Room): 3.7 MB encoding, 1.1 MB MLP, 27.6 ms encoding time, 27.1 ms MLP time. Measured Performance (Dynamic Dining Room): 7.4 MB encoding, 14.0 MB f{XV}, 26.4 ms MLP time. Strengths: Memory efficiency, alignment with geometric priors, avoidance of grid-like artifacts and hashing collisions, accurate modeling of view-dependent shading. Limitations: Struggles with high-frequency radiance regions; requires explicit mesh geometry; discontinuities at LOD boundaries if not trained sufficiently. When to Use: Neural rendering tasks involving explicit mesh surfaces where memory efficiency is critical, such as Neural Radiosity, Dynamic Neural Radiosity, and Neural Path Guiding. When Not to Use: Scenes without explicit mesh geometry or where high-frequency radiance details are paramount and cannot be smoothed by the network. Neural Vertex Features was proposed by Rui Su, Honghao Dong, Haojie Jin, Yisong Chen, Guoping Wang, and Sheng Li in 2026. It builds on Differentiable Neural Radiosity and addresses the memory inefficiencies of multi-resolution hash grids used in prior neural rendering methods. The method is implemented in the Mitsuba3 renderer using PyTorch and tiny-cuda-nn. name: Adapted Radiosity for Gaussian Surfels
body: Adapted Radiosity for Gaussian Surfels is a forward rendering technique that solves the rendering equation for Gaussian surfels by assuming constant emission and BRDF within each kernel, and constant outgoing radiance within a kernel to derive a weighted residual solution. It differs from Neural Radiosity by using explicit geometric primitives (Gaussian surfels) rather than a single neural network to represent the radiance field, allowing for efficient direct illumination rendering and geometry reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N Gaussian surfels (kernels). Each kernel j is defined by its center \mathbf{t}j, normal \mathbf{n}j, transparency factor \alphaj, and material properties (diffuse albedo a^d, specular albedo a^s, specular exponent s, mixing factor k). Output: The outgoing radiance LO(\mathbf{x}, \omegaO) for points \mathbf{x} within each kernel i. Data Structures: Kernel j: \mathbf{t}j \in \mathbb{R}^3: Center position. \mathbf{n}j \in \mathbb{R}^3: Surface normal. \alphaj \in [0, 1]: Transparency factor. a^d \in [0, 1]: Diffuse albedo. a^s \in [0, 1]: Specular albedo. s \in \mathbb{R}: Specular exponent. k \in [0, 1]: Mixing factor. Spherical Harmonics (SH): Coefficients c{lm} for the BRDF expansion, up to degree 9. Formulas: The outgoing radiance LO(\mathbf{x}, \omegaO) for a point \mathbf{x} in kernel i is defined as: LO(\mathbf{x}, \omegaO) = Ei(\omegaO) + \alphai(\mathbf{x}) \int{\omega} fi(\omegaI, \omegaO) LI(\mathbf{x}, \omegaI) |\mathbf{n}i \cdot \omegaI| d\omegaI where \Omega = \{\omegaI: \omegaI \cdot \mathbf{n}i < 0\} is the visible hemisphere and \alphai is the transparency factor. The incoming radiance LI(\mathbf{x}, \omegaI) is expanded as a sum over all kernels j: LI(\mathbf{x}, \omegaI) = \sum{j=1}^N LO(\mathbf{t}j, \omegaI) \alphaj(\mathbf{t}j) \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak(\mathbf{t}k)) By swapping the integral and summation, the outgoing radiance is computed as: LO(\mathbf{x}, \omegaO) = Ei(\omegaO) + \alphai(\mathbf{x}) \sum{j=1}^N \int{Pj} fi(\omegaI, \omegaO) LO(\mathbf{t}j, \omegaI) v{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) d\mathbf{x}' where v{ji} is the decay component. The decay component v{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) is defined as: v{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) = \alphaj(\mathbf{t}j) \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak(\mathbf{t}k)) \frac{|\mathbf{n}i \cdot \omegaI| |\mathbf{n}j \cdot \omegaI|}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2} where \omegaI = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}')/\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2. The BRDF fi is expanded using Spherical Harmonics. The coefficient c{00} is calculated as: c{00} = 4ka^d + (1 - k)a^s The coefficient c{lm} for odd l is calculated as: c{lm} = (-1)^m (1 - k) \frac{(s+1)(s-1) \cdots (s-l+2)}{(s+2)(s+4) \cdots (s+l+1)} a^s The coefficient c{lm} for even l is calculated as: c{lm} = (-1)^m (1 - k) \frac{s(s-2) \cdots (s-l+2)}{(s+3)(s+5) \cdots (s+l+1)} a^s Parameters: Spherical Harmonics Degree: Up to 9-degree basis is used for reasonably glossy materials. Specular Clamping: The specular part of the BRDF is clamped to be 0 at the invisible hemisphere. Steps: 1. For each kernel i, initialize the outgoing radiance LO(\mathbf{x}, \omegaO) using the emission term Ei(\omegaO). 2. For each kernel j (source of incoming light): a. Calculate the decay component v{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) for points \mathbf{x}' in kernel j and \mathbf{x} in kernel i. b. Integrate the product of the BRDF fi, the outgoing radiance from kernel j's center LO(\mathbf{t}j, \omegaI), and the decay component v{ji} over the support Pj of kernel j. c. Multiply the result by the transparency factor \alphai(\mathbf{x}) and add to LO(\mathbf{x}, \omegaO). 3. Use the Spherical Harmonics coefficients c{lm} to represent the BRDF fi for efficient integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeoutgoingradiance(kernels, shdegree=9): """ Computes outgoing radiance for all kernels using Adapted Radiosity. kernels: List of Kernel objects, each with attributes: t: center position (vec3) n: normal (vec3) alpha: transparency factor (float) ad: diffuse albedo (float) as: specular albedo (float) s: specular exponent (float) k: mixing factor (float) Lo: outgoing radiance (initialized to emission) """ N = len(kernels) # Precompute SH coefficients for each kernel's BRDF for i in range(N): kernels[i].shcoeffs = computeshcoefficients(kernels[i].ad, kernels[i].as, kernels[i].s, kernels[i].k, shdegree) # Iterate over each kernel to compute outgoing radiance for i in range(N): kerneli = kernels[i] # Assume Lo is initialized to emission Ei # For each source kernel j for j in range(N): kernelj = kernels[j] # Calculate decay component vji # Note: The integral over Pj is approximated by evaluating at the center tj # and multiplying by the kernel's effective area or using the weighted residual form. # Based on the formula: LO(x, wO) = Ei + alphai sumj ( integral{Pj}...) # The integral term involves LO(tj, wI). # Compute the integral term for kernel j contributing to kernel i # This requires integrating the BRDF Lo(tj) vji over Pj. # In practice, this is often approximated or solved via the weighted residual method. # Here we show the direct application of the formula components. # Decay component at the center of kernel i (x = ti) for simplicity in this step # In a full implementation, x varies over Pi. x = kerneli.t xprime = kernelj.t # Vector from x' to x vec = x - xprime distsq = dot(vec, vec) if distsq == 0: continue # Avoid division by zero dist = sqrt(distsq) omegaI = vec / dist # Visibility factor (product of alpha and occlusion) # Note: The formula uses product{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - alphak(tk)) # This implies an ordering. We assume kernels are ordered. occlusion = 1.0 for k in range(j): occlusion = (1.0 - kernels[k].alpha) # Decay component vji # vji = alphaj(tj) occlusion |ni. omegaI| |nj. omegaI| / ||x - x'||^2 nidotomega = abs(dot(kerneli.n, omegaI)) njdotomega = abs(dot(kernelj.n, omegaI)) vji = kernelj.alpha occlusion nidotomega njdotomega / distsq # Integrate BRDF Lo(tj) vji over Pj # This is the most complex part. The paper derives a weighted residual solution. # For implementation, one might use the SH coefficients to evaluate the integral. # Let's assume a helper function that computes the integral of BRDF vji over Pj # using the SH expansion. integralterm = integratebrdfoverkernel(kerneli, kernelj, vji, shdegree) # Add to outgoing radiance # LO(x, wO) += alphai(x) integralterm # Note: alphai(x) varies within the kernel. # The paper assumes constant outgoing radiance within a kernel for the residual form. # So we update the kernel's Lo value. kerneli.Lo += kerneli.alpha integralterm def computeshcoefficients(ad, asval, s, k, degree): """ Computes Spherical Harmonics coefficients for the BRDF. """ coeffs = [] for l in range(degree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): if l == 0: c00 = 4 k ad + (1 - k) asval coeffs.append(c00) else: # Calculate clm based on parity of l if l % 2 == 1: # Odd numerator = 1.0 for term in range(l): numerator = (s + 1 - 2 term) # (s+1)(s-1)...(s-l+2) denominator = 1.0 for term in range(l): denominator = (s + 2 + 2 term) # (s+2)(s+4)...(s+l+1) clm = ((-1) m) (1 - k) (numerator / denominator) asval else: # Even numerator = 1.0 for term in range(l // 2): numerator = (s - 2 term) # s(s-2)...(s-l+2) denominator = 1.0 for term in range(l // 2): denominator = (s + 3 + 2 term) # (s+3)(s+5)...(s+l+1) clm = ((-1) m) (1 - k) (numerator / denominator) asval coeffs.append(clm) return coeffs def integratebrdfoverkernel(kerneli, kernelj, vji, shdegree): """ Approximates the integral of BRDF vji over kernel j's support. This is a placeholder for the specific weighted residual integration method. """ # The paper mentions deriving a weighted residual solution. # The exact integration depends on the kernel shape (Gaussian). # For simplicity, we assume the integral is approximated by the value at the center # multiplied by an effective area, or using the SH coefficients. # This is a gap filled with. return vji kernelj.alpha # Simplified approximation A rendering method for direct illumination using Gaussian surfels, where outgoing radiance is a weighted average of incident radiance from light sources over the kernel's local support P, using a kernel κ (e.g., Gaussian, Uniform, Dirac delta). It is chosen when only direct illumination is needed and is simpler than the full radiosity solution. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient forward rendering for Gaussian surfels; handles glossy materials via SH expansion. Limitations: Assumes constant emission and BRDF within each kernel; assumes constant outgoing radiance within a kernel for the residual form. When to use: When rendering scenes with Gaussian surfels and needing to account for indirect illumination and glossy materials. When not to use: When high-frequency spatial variations in radiance within a kernel are critical and cannot be approximated by a constant value. The method is described in "Differentiable Light Transport with Gaussian Surfels via Adapted Radiosity for Efficient Relighting and Geometry Reconstruction" by Abhik Ahuja, David McAllister, and Angjoo Kanazawa (2023). It builds on the rendering equation and extends the concept of radiosity to Gaussian surfels. name: Direct Illumination Rendering with Gaussian Surfels
head: Forward Rendering with Gaussian Surfels
body: This method computes the outgoing radiance of Gaussian surfels under direct illumination only, treating light sources as special infinitesimal emissive Gaussian surfels. It differs from global illumination variants by ignoring inter-reflections, resulting in a non-recursive equation that can be evaluated directly without iterative solvers. It builds on Adapted Radiosity for Gaussian Surfels by specializing the framework to direct light transport. Inputs: Set of Gaussian surfels representing geometry and material. Set of light sources (LS), represented as point lights, directional lights (approximated), or environment maps. Kernel function \kappa (e.g., Gaussian, Uniform, Dirac delta) with local support P. Outputs: Outgoing radiosity coefficients \mathbf{B}i^c for each surfel i. Data Structures: Each Gaussian surfel i stores: Center position \mathbf{p}i. Opacity \alphai. Surface normal \mathbf{n}i. Emission coefficient vector \mathbf{E}i^c (spherical harmonics coefficients). BRDF coefficient vector \mathbf{f}i^c (spherical harmonics coefficients). Kernel integral \Lambdai = \intP \kappa(\mathbf{x}) d\mathbf{x}. Light sources j \in \text{LS} are treated as emissive surfels with: Position \mathbf{p}j. Emission coefficient \mathbf{E}j^c. For directional lights: position far away, inverse square falloff disabled. Formulas: The forward rendering equation for direct illumination is: \mathbf{B}i^c = \mathbf{E}i^c + \frac{\alphai(\mathbf{p}i)}{\Lambdai} \times \sum{j \in \text{LS}} \int{Pj} \mathbf{f}j(\omegaI) \times \left( \mathbf{Y}(\omegaI)^T \mathbf{E}j^c \right) \times \mathbf{V}{ji}(\mathbf{p}j, \mathbf{x}) d\mathbf{x} Where: \mathbf{B}i^c: Outgoing radiosity coefficient vector for surfel i. \mathbf{E}i^c: Emission coefficient vector for surfel i. \alphai(\mathbf{p}i): Opacity of surfel i at its center. \Lambdai: Integral of the kernel function \kappa over its support P. \text{LS}: Set of light source indices. \mathbf{f}j(\omegaI): BRDF of surfel j evaluated at incoming direction \omegaI. \mathbf{Y}(\omegaI): Spherical harmonics basis vector evaluated at \omegaI. \mathbf{E}j^c: Emission coefficient vector of light source j. \mathbf{V}{ji}(\mathbf{p}j, \mathbf{x}): Fused decay component including angular factor, kernel, and visibility. Intermediate terms: \omegaI = \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j\|2^2} \mathbf{f}i(\omegaI) = \mathbf{f}i^c \times \bar{\mathbf{Y}}(\omegaI) V{ji}(\mathbf{p}j, \mathbf{x}) = \frac{|\mathbf{n}i \cdot \omegaI|}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j\|2^2} \kappai(\mathbf{x}) \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) Where: \omegaI: Incoming direction from point \mathbf{x} in light source support to surfel i. \mathbf{f}i^c: BRDF coefficient vector for surfel i. \bar{\mathbf{Y}}(\omegaI): Conjugate or specific basis transformation for BRDF evaluation. \mathbf{n}i: Surface normal of surfel i. \kappai(\mathbf{x}): Kernel function value at point \mathbf{x} for surfel i. \alphak: Opacity of preceding kernels (visibility term). Parameters: Kernel type: Gaussian, Uniform, or Dirac delta. Light representation: Point lights are standard; directional lights are approximated by placing point lights far away and disabling inverse square falloff. Environment maps are handled similarly. Pitfalls: The equation is non-recursive, so no iterative solver is needed. Gradient calculation is efficient via auto-differentiation. Partial understanding of full light transport (direct illumination alone) benefits sparse-view relighting compared to data-driven approaches. The method effectively caches radiance within each kernel, enabling view-independent rendering as with classical radiosity theory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Unlike direct illumination, it handles indirect light transport for accurate geometry reconstruction in scenes with rich inter-reflections. Time Complexity: Non-recursive, allowing direct evaluation without iterative solvers. Gradient calculation is efficient via auto-differentiation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of surfels and light sources. Each surfel stores coefficients and kernel parameters. Performance: Effective for sparse-view relighting compared to data-driven approaches. View-independent rendering as with classical radiosity theory. Strengths: Direct evaluation, efficient gradients, view-independent rendering, handles various light types (point, directional, environment maps). Limitations: Only models direct illumination, ignoring inter-reflections. Approximations for directional lights and environment maps. When to use: Scenes with dominant direct illumination, sparse-view relighting, view-independent rendering requirements. name: Global Illumination Rendering with Gaussian Surfels
head: Forward Global Illumination with Gaussian Surfels
body: This method extends the Gaussian surfel framework to model global illumination by deriving a forward rendering equation from the physically-based rendering equation. It solves for outgoing radiance in scenes with inter-reflections by treating light sources as special Gaussian surfels and assuming non-overlapping kernels to apply a weighted residual form. Unlike direct illumination methods, it accounts for indirect light transport, enabling accurate geometry reconstruction in scenes with rich inter-reflections. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N Gaussian surfels (kernels), each defined by position, orientation, opacity \alpha, and material properties (diffuse albedo, shininess, emission). Light sources are represented as specific kernels. Outputs: Outgoing radiosity \mathbf{B}i^c for each kernel i, which is then rasterized to produce the final image. Data Structures: Kernel i: Contains position \mathbf{p}i, normal \mathbf{n}i, opacity \alphai(\mathbf{x}), material BRDF \mathbf{f}i, and emission \mathbf{E}i^c. Visibility Term V{ji}: A continuous visibility function accounting for semi-opaque primitives and distance attenuation. Assumptions: 1. Material, emission, and outgoing radiance are constant within each kernel. 2. There is no overlapping between any two Gaussian surfels. Formulas: The forward rendering equation for global illumination is: \mathbf{B}i^c = \mathbf{E}i^c + \frac{\alphai(\mathbf{p}i)}{\Lambdai} \times \sum{j=1}^N \int{Pj} \int{Pj} \mathbf{f}j(\omegaI) \times \left( \mathbf{Y}(\omegaI)^T \mathbf{B}j^c \right) \times \mathbf{V}{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) d\mathbf{x}' d\mathbf{x} Where: \mathbf{B}i^c: Outgoing radiosity of kernel i. \mathbf{E}i^c: Emission of kernel i. \alphai(\mathbf{p}i): Opacity at the center of kernel i. \Lambdai: Normalization factor for kernel i (implied by context of Gaussian surfels, though exact definition not explicitly detailed in the provided excerpt beyond its use in the term \alphai/\Lambdai). N: Total number of kernels. \mathbf{f}j(\omegaI): BRDF of kernel j for incoming direction \omegaI. \mathbf{Y}(\omegaI): Spherical harmonic basis vector for direction \omegaI. \mathbf{B}j^c: Outgoing radiosity of source kernel j. \mathbf{V}{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}): Visibility term from source point \mathbf{x}' in kernel j to target point \mathbf{x} in kernel i. Pj: Support of kernel j. The visibility term \mathbf{V}{ji} is defined as: \mathbf{V}{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}) = \frac{|\mathbf{n}i \cdot \omegaI| |\mathbf{n}j \cdot \omegaI|}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2} \kappai(\mathbf{x}) \alphaj(\mathbf{x}') \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak) Where: \omegaI = \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2}: Incoming direction vector (note: the source uses \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2 in the denominator of the direction vector, which is dimensionally inconsistent for a direction vector; typically this should be \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2. However, the source explicitly writes \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2 in the definition of \omegaI and \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2 in the visibility term. We retain the source's notation). \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{n}j: Normals of kernels i and j. \kappai(\mathbf{x}): Kernel function (e.g., Gaussian) for kernel i at point \mathbf{x}. \alphaj(\mathbf{x}'): Opacity of kernel j at point \mathbf{x}'. \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak): Visibility accumulation from previous kernels (implies an ordering of kernels). Simplified Equation: The term \frac{\alphai(\mathbf{p}i)}{\Lambdai} is absorbed into \mathbf{f}i(\omegal) to simplify the deduction: \mathbf{B}i^c = \mathbf{E}i^c + \sum{j=1}^N \int{Pi} \int{Pj} \mathbf{f}i(\omegal) (\mathbf{Y}(\omegal)^T \mathbf{B}j^c) V{ji} d\mathbf{x}' d\mathbf{x} Special Cases for Light Sources: When kernel j represents a light source, the integration over Pj is skipped: 1. Directly sample the central point of kernel j as \mathbf{x}'. 2. Disable the dot product between the normal and incoming direction for kernel j in V{ji} (i.e., remove |\mathbf{n}j \cdot \omegaI|). 3. If the light is directional, further disable the inverse square falloff in V{ji} (i.e., remove \frac{1}{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'\|2^2}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial outgoing radiosity \mathbf{B}j^c for all kernels (e.g., based on emission or direct illumination). 2. Iterate: Solve the recursive system of equations for \mathbf{B}i^c. Since \mathbf{B}^c appears on both sides, a solver (e.g., progressive refinement) is required. For each kernel i: Compute direct emission \mathbf{E}i^c. For each kernel j (including light sources): Determine if j is a light source. If so, set \mathbf{x}' to the center and adjust V{ji} as per special cases. Compute the visibility term V{ji}(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}). Integrate over the support Pj and Pi (or just sample center for lights) the term \mathbf{f}i(\omegal) (\mathbf{Y}(\omegal)^T \mathbf{B}j^c) V{ji}. Update \mathbf{B}i^c. 3. Rasterize: Use the computed \mathbf{B}i^c values to render the image via efficient rasterization. Pitfalls: The equation is recursive, requiring an iterative solver. Optimization using only direct illumination fails in scenes with rich inter-reflections (e.g., enclosed boxes). Separates a fully rendered scene into distinct material properties (diffuse albedo, shininess) and illumination components (direct illumination, indirect illumination). To extract direct illumination, run the progressive refinement solver for exactly one step. To extract indirect illumination, compute the difference between the full rendering result and the direct illumination result. This method is demonstrated on the "CupPlane" scene and a synthetic enclosed box with 7 objects. Optimization using only direct illumination fails in scenes with rich inter-reflections, requiring global illumination for reasonable geometry reconstruction. Time Complexity: The time cost roughly increases linearly as the number of primitives increases, but also depends on the specific distribution of primitives. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports both near-field and far-field light sources; derives from physically-based rendering for correctness; enables view-independent rendering with diffuse and specular effects; allows for scene decomposition and relighting. Limitations: Requires solving a recursive system; assumes non-overlapping kernels; optimization with direct illumination only fails in complex inter-reflection scenes. When to use: When global illumination effects (inter-reflections) are significant, or when scene decomposition (material/illumination separation) is required. When not to use: When direct illumination is sufficient, or when the non-overlapping kernel assumption is violated. This method is derived from the classic radiosity theory and the rendering equation [Kajiya 1986; Sillion et al. 1991]. It is part of the first work to derive differentiable global illumination on Gaussian surfels, enabling applications such as sparse-view relighting, material editing, and accurate geometry reconstruction. The approach was presented in "Differentiable Light Transport with Gaussian Surfels via Adapted Radiosity for Efficient Relighting and Geometry Reconstruction". name: NeRV (Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields)
head: Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields
body: NeRV is a differentiable inverse rendering method that reconstructs a 3D scene representation from images under unconstrained, known lighting, enabling view synthesis and relighting with indirect illumination. It extends the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework by decomposing the scene into volumetric density and material properties, and introduces a Neural Visibility Field to approximate light transport efficiently. Unlike sibling methods that rely on brute-force raymarching or are limited to single point lights, NeRV uses learned neural approximations for visibility and surface intersections to reduce the complexity of direct and indirect lighting calculations from quadratic/cubic to linear/double-spherical integrals. Inputs: A set of N images \{I^{(i)}\}{i=1}^N of a scene, along with the corresponding camera poses and known environment lighting maps E(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}). Outputs: Two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): a shape MLP \theta and a reflectance MLP \psi, which together define the scene's geometry, material, and visibility properties. The scene is represented by three neural networks: 1. Shape MLP (\theta): Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Reflectance MLP (\psi): Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: Material parameters \mathbf{m} = (\mathbf{a}, \gamma), where \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the diffuse RGB albedo and \gamma \in \mathbb{R} is the scalar specular roughness. 3. Visibility MLP (\phi): Input: 3D position \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction \boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{S}^2. Output: A tuple (\tilde{V}, \tilde{t}), where \tilde{V} \in [0, 1] is the estimated visibility (transmittance) and \tilde{t} \in \mathbb{R}^+ is the estimated distance to the first surface intersection (expected termination depth) in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}. Surface normals \mathbf{n} are not stored but computed on-the-fly as the negative normalized gradient of the shape MLP output: \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}) = -\frac{\nabla{\mathbf{x}} \sigma(\mathbf{x})}{\|\nabla{\mathbf{x}} \sigma(\mathbf{x})\|} This computation relies on automatic differentiation during training. The radiance L(\mathbf{c}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) observed from camera center \mathbf{c} in direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o is computed by integrating along the camera ray \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{c} + t\boldsymbol{\omega}o: L(\mathbf{c}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \int0^\infty V(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{c}) \sigma(\mathbf{x}(t)) Lr(\mathbf{x}(t), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) \, dt where V(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{c}) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \sigma(\mathbf{x}(s)) \, ds\right) is the volume transmittance. The outgoing radiance Lr is decomposed into direct and indirect components: Lr(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = L{\text{direct}} + L{\text{indirect}} 1. Direct Lighting Component: Direct lighting comes from the environment map E. The incident radiance is attenuated by visibility. NeRV replaces the true visibility integral with the neural visibility approximation \tilde{V}\phi: L{\text{direct}}(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \intS \tilde{V}\phi(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) E(\mathbf{x}, -\boldsymbol{\omega}i) R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) \, d\boldsymbol{\omega}i where S is the unit sphere, \boldsymbol{\omega}i is the incoming direction, and R is the microfacet BRDF. 2. Indirect Lighting Component: To approximate one-bounce indirect illumination, NeRV treats the volume as a hard surface located at the expected termination depth t0. The accumulated radiance is approximated by a single point evaluation at \mathbf{x}(t0): L{\text{indirect}}(\mathbf{x}(t0), \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = \intS L(\mathbf{x}(t0), -\boldsymbol{\omega}i) R(\mathbf{x}(t0), \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) \, d\boldsymbol{\omega}i Here, L(\mathbf{x}(t0), -\boldsymbol{\omega}i) is the incoming radiance from direction -\boldsymbol{\omega}i, which itself is computed using the direct lighting formula at that point. Reflectance Function (BRDF): The reflectance R is a standard microfacet BRDF parameterized by albedo \mathbf{a}, roughness \gamma, and normal \mathbf{n}. 1. Initialization: Initialize MLPs \theta, \psi, \phi with random weights. 2. Sampling: For each training iteration, sample a batch of pixels from input images. For each pixel, sample K points along the camera ray using stratified sampling. 3. Forward Pass: Evaluate \sigma(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}) for all sampled points. Compute transmittance V along the camera ray using the density samples. For each point \mathbf{x}, query the visibility MLP \phi(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) for a set of sampled environment directions \boldsymbol{\omega}i to get \tilde{V}\phi and \tilde{t}. Compute L{\text{direct}} using \tilde{V}\phi and the environment map. Compute L{\text{indirect}} by evaluating the direct lighting integral at the point \mathbf{x}(t0), where t0 is derived from the density integration (not the visibility MLP's \tilde{t}). Compute total radiance Lr and integrate along the camera ray to get predicted pixel color. 4. Supervision: Color Loss: Minimize the difference between rendered and observed pixel colors (e.g., MSE). Visibility Consistency: The visibility MLP \phi is supervised to be consistent with the volume density samples. Specifically, the predicted visibility \tilde{V}\phi should match the true transmittance computed from the density MLP along the ray segment. The expected termination depth \tilde{t} is supervised to match the depth where the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold (e.g., 1/e) based on the density samples. 5. Optimization: Update all MLP weights (\theta, \psi, \phi) using gradient descent (e.g., Adam). Unverified code. 1 sintheta = torch.sqrt(1 - costheta2) x = sintheta torch.cos(phi) y = sintheta torch.sin(phi) z = costheta return torch.stack([x, y, z], dim=-1) def stratifiedsample(n, maxt): """Generate n stratified samples in [0, maxt].""" t = torch.rand(n) t = (t + torch.arange(n)) / n maxt return t def sampleenvmap(envmap, directions): """Sample environment map at given directions.""" # Assume envmap is a function or tensor that supports directional lookup return envmap(directions) def evaluatemicrofacetbrdf(normal, omegai, omegao, albedo, roughness): """Evaluate standard microfacet BRDF R(x, omegai, omegao).""" # Simplified standard implementation placeholder for demonstration # In practice, uses GGX/Trowbridge-Reitz distribution and Schlick approximation h = (omegai + omegao) / 2.0 costhetah = torch.sum(h normal, dim=-1) costhetai = torch.sum(omegai normal, dim=-1) # Simplified diffuse/specular blend for brevity diffuse = albedo / np.pi specular = 1.0 # Placeholder for full microfacet term return (diffuse + specular) 3.0 def computevisibilityconsistencyloss(vismlp, points, directions, truetransmittance): """Compute MSE between predicted visibility and true transmittance.""" vispred, = vismlp(torch.cat([points, directions], dim=-1)) return torch.mean((vispred - tvals[0] accumulatedsigma = torch.cumsum(sigma dt, dim=0) transmittance = torch.exp(-accumulatedsigma) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.ones(1).to(xvals.device), transmittance[:-1]], dim=0) normal = self.computenormal(xvals, sigma) albedo, roughness = self.getbrdfparams(xvals) directlighting = torch.zeroslike(xvals[:,:3]) for i in range(numsamples): directlighting[i] = self.computedirectlighting( xvals[i], normal[i], albedo[i], roughness[i], envmap) threshold = 1.0 / np.e indices = torch.where(transmittance < threshold)[0] if len(indices) > 0: t0idx = indices[0] x0 = xvals[t0idx] normal0 = normal[t0idx] albedo0 = albedo[t0idx] roughness0 = roughness[t0idx] indirectlighting = self.computedirectlighting( x0, normal0, albedo0, roughness0, envmap) else: indirectlighting = torch.zeros(3).to(xvals.device) totalradiance = directlighting + indirectlighting weights = transmittance sigma dt color = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) totalradiance, dim=0) return color def trainstep(self, batch, optimizer): """One training step.""" optimizer.zerograd() renderedcolors = [] for ray in batch.rays: color = self.renderpixel(ray.origin, ray.direction, batch.envmap) renderedcolors.append(color) renderedcolors = torch.stack(renderedcolors) targetcolors = batch.targetcolors loss = torch.mean((renderedcolors - tvals[0] accumulatedsigma = torch.cumsum(sigma dt, dim=0) truetransmittance = torch.exp(-accumulatedsigma) visloss += self.computevisibilityconsistencyloss( self.visibilitymlp, xvals, directions, truetransmittance) loss += visloss loss.backward() optimizer.step() return loss.item() Visibility MLP Consistency: The visibility MLP must be supervised to match the density samples. Indirect Lighting Approximation: The hard surface approximation for indirect lighting assumes that the volume can be treated as a surface at the expected termination depth. Memory Complexity: Requires storing three MLPs (shape, reflectance, visibility) and their weights. NeRV Evaluation Variants are inference-time strategies for the NeRV representation that modify how visibility and material properties are queried during rendering. NeRV with Neural Visibility Fields (NVF) uses the same visibility approximations learned during training at test time, while NeRV with Test-time Tracing (Trace) replaces the learned visibility with brute-force ray tracing to estimate visibility to point light sources for sharper shadows. Both variants reuse the same trained model. A third approach defers ray queries to diffuse intersections to enable rendering for non-diffuse materials, accepting sampling-related noise as a trade-off. Time Complexity: Direct lighting complexity is reduced from quadratic to linear in samples per ray by using neural visibility approximations instead of line integrals. Indirect lighting complexity is reduced from cubic to a double spherical integral by using hard surface approximations at expected termination depths. Memory Complexity: Requires storing three MLPs (shape, reflectance, visibility) and their weights. The memory footprint is comparable to NeRF but slightly higher due to the additional visibility MLP. Performance: NeRV enables rendering with arbitrary environment lighting and one-bounce indirect illumination, which was intractable with previous methods like Neural Reflectance Fields that required single point lights. Strengths: Supports unconstrained known lighting, indirect illumination, and efficient visibility queries during optimization. Limitations: The hard surface approximation for indirect lighting may not capture complex volumetric scattering. The visibility MLP requires careful supervision to remain consistent with the density field. NeRV was introduced by Pratul P. Srinivasan, Boyang Deng, Xiuming Zhang, Matthew Tancik, Ben Mildenhall, and Jonathan T. Barron in 2021. It extends the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework and builds on Neural Reflectance Fields, which was limited to single point lights and direct illumination. The key innovation is the use of a neural visibility field to approximate light transport, making inverse rendering with global illumination tractable. name: NeRV Evaluation Variants
head: NeRV NVF, NeRV Trace
body: NeRV Evaluation Variants are inference-time strategies for the NeRV representation that modify how visibility and material properties are queried during rendering. NeRV with Neural Visibility Fields (NVF) uses the same visibility approximations learned during training at test time, while NeRV with Test-time Tracing (Trace) replaces the learned visibility with brute-force ray tracing to estimate visibility to point light sources for sharper shadows. Both variants reuse the same trained model. A third approach defers ray queries to diffuse intersections to enable rendering for non-diffuse materials, accepting sampling-related noise as a trade-off. Inputs: Trained NeRV model parameters \theta. Camera pose (C, R) and light source positions Li with intensities Ii. Scene volume bounds. Outputs: Rendered image pixels. Data Structures: NeRV Model: A neural network f\theta(x) taking a 3D coordinate x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and returning a visibility value v \in [0, 1] and a reflectance color c \in \mathbb{R}^3. Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Exact field layouts and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps & Formulas: For each pixel, cast a ray through the scene volume. Sample points along the ray. Accumulate color using standard volume rendering integration. The specific variant determines how the visibility term v is computed for each sample point. This is the default evaluation mode, consistent with the training procedure. 1. For each sample point x along the ray: 2. Query the NeRV model: (v, c) = f\theta(x). 3. Use v as the occlusion factor for the light contribution at x. 4. Accumulate color using volume rendering integration. Characteristics: Uses the same visibility approximations used during training. This variant replaces the learned visibility MLP query with brute-force ray tracing to estimate visibility to point light sources. 1. For each sample point x along the view ray: 2. For each light source Li: a. Construct a shadow ray from x to Li. b. Perform brute-force ray marching along the shadow ray to check for intersections with the scene geometry or density field. c. Compute visibility based on whether the shadow ray is occluded. 3. Use the traced visibility for the lighting calculation at x. 4. Accumulate color. Characteristics: Uses brute-force tracing to estimate visibility to point light sources. Renders sharper shadows at test time. This variant enables non-diffuse material rendering by deferring ray queries. 1. For each sample point x along the view ray: 2. If the material at x is non-diffuse: a. Trace a ray from x to find the nearest diffuse intersection x{\text{diffuse}}. b. Query the NeRV model at x{\text{diffuse}} to get reflectance. c. Apply a glossy BRDF approximation using the deferred color. 3. If the material is diffuse, query directly at x. 4. Accumulate color. Characteristics: Enables NIV rendering for non-diffuse materials by deferring ray queries to diffuse intersections. Accepts sampling-related noise as a trade-off. Maintaining noise-free rendering requires exploring alternative solutions. Pitfalls: The deferred query approach introduces sampling-related noise. Future work suggests incorporating surface roughness as a control parameter in the neural model to natively handle glossy materials. A test-time evaluation strategy that uses the trained neural visibility field for occlusion. It is chosen when rendering speed is prioritized over shadow sharpness. It reuses the visibility approximations from training. A test-time evaluation strategy that replaces the neural visibility query with brute-force ray tracing for shadow rays. It is chosen when sharp, hard shadows are required. It estimates visibility to point light sources directly. A material handling strategy for non-diffuse surfaces. It is chosen when rendering glossy or specular materials with a model trained primarily on diffuse data. It trades rendering noise for material flexibility. NeRV NVF: Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of samples per ray. The visibility query is a neural network forward pass. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the NeRV model weights. Performance: Fast inference. The base model training requires 1 million iterations over 128 TPU cores, taking 1 day to converge. Strengths: Efficient, consistent with training. Limitations: Visibility is approximated by the MLP. NeRV Trace: Time Complexity: Increases with the number of light sources and shadow ray samples due to brute-force marching. Strengths: Renders sharper shadows at test time. Limitations: Higher computational cost per sample due to ray marching. Deferred Diffuse Queries: Time Complexity: Increases due to additional ray tracing for deferred queries. Strengths: Supports non-diffuse materials. Limitations: Sampling-related noise. NeRV was introduced by (NeRV: Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields for Relighting and View Synthesis, CVPR 2021). The method produces a 3D representation that can be rendered from novel viewpoints under arbitrary lighting conditions, including indirect illumination effects. The evaluation variants were developed to address limitations in shadow quality and material support. The deferred diffuse query approach is discussed in the context of extending Neural Irradiance Volumes (NIV) to non-diffuse materials.
