name: LidaRF Network Architecture
head: LidaRF
body: The LidaRF network architecture is a specialized neural network design for LiDAR-based Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that jointly learns geometry and 3D point attributes (distance, intensity, ray-drop probability) without explicit 3D reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF variants by integrating a 3D sparse UNet for LiDAR geometry encoding with a multi-resolution hash grid for density prediction, enabling efficient processing of sparse LiDAR point clouds. This method builds on LiDAR-NeRF by providing the specific network components required for differentiable LiDAR view synthesis. Inputs: A set of LiDAR points (3D coordinates). Sampled 3D positions along rays for volume rendering. Outputs: Density values (\sigma) for each sampled position. A 15-dimensional density embedding for each sampled position. RGB color values for each sampled position (via the color network, which uses the density embedding). 1. Hash Grid (for Proposal Sampler and Density Network) Structure: A multi-resolution hash table mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors. Layout: Levels: L levels of resolution. Resolution per Level: Minimum resolution N{min}, Maximum resolution N{max}. Feature Dimension: F{hash} dimensions per level. Encoding: Hash encoding maps 3D positions to specific entries in the grid. 2. Sparse Voxel Grid (for LiDAR Encoding) Structure: A 3D grid of cells. Size: 512 \times 512 \times 512 cells. Cell Content: Mean 3D position of LiDAR points falling within the cell. Empty cells are ignored by sparse convolution. 3. Sparse UNet Features Encoder Layers: Feature dimensions [32, 64, 96, 128]. Decoder Layers: Feature dimensions [128, 96, 64, 64]. Output: LiDAR features from the final decoder layer. 4. MLP Layers Proposal Sampler MLP: 2 layers, 16 hidden features. Density Network MLP: 2 layers, 64 hidden features. Color Network MLP: 2 layers, 64 hidden features (implied by context of predicting RGB from embedding). 1. Scene Bounding Sphere Definition: Define a sphere bounding the scene. The diameter is the maximum distance between any two camera positions in the training log plus 50 meters. 2. LiDAR Point Voxelization: Input: All LiDAR points. Process: Voxelize points into a 512 \times 512 \times 512 grid. Feature Assignment: For each non-empty cell, compute the mean 3D position of the LiDAR points contained within it. This mean position serves as the initial feature for the cell. 3. LiDAR Geometry Encoding (Sparse UNet): Input: The voxelized LiDAR features. Process: Pass features through a 3D sparse UNet. Encoder: Applies sparse convolutions with feature dimensions [32, 64, 96, 128]. Decoder: Applies sparse convolutions with feature dimensions [128, 96, 64, 64]. Skip Connections: Integrate skip connections and multi-level feature fusion between encoder and decoder stages. Output: LiDAR features from the final layer of the UNet. 4. Proposal Sampling: Structure: Two consecutive "fused" MLPs. Hash Grid Parameters: Minimum resolution: 16. Levels: 5. Feature dimension per level: 2. MLP: 2 layers, 16 hidden features. Distinction: First MLP set: Maximum hash grid resolution 512. Second MLP set: Maximum hash grid resolution 1024. Process: 1. Query hash encoding for 3D positions. 2. Pass hash features through the fused MLP to predict density. 3. Use the predicted density to sample points (proposal sampling). 5. Density Network Processing: Hash Grid Parameters: Minimum resolution: 16. Maximum resolution: 4096. Levels: 16. Feature dimension per level: 2. MLP Parameters: 2 layers, 64 hidden features. Process: 1. Compute hash encoding for sampled 3D positions. 2. Query hash features from the grid. 3. Concatenate hash features with LiDAR features (output from Step 3). 4. Pass concatenated features through the Density Network MLP. Output: Density value (\sigma). 15-dimensional density embedding. 6. Color Network Processing: Input: Density embedding (from Step 5) and potentially other attributes (implied by context of RGB prediction). MLP Parameters: 2 layers, 64 hidden features. Output: RGB value for the sampled position. Hash Encoding: Standard multi-resolution hash encoding is used. For a position \mathbf{x}, the feature is computed by hashing \mathbf{x} to indices in grids of varying resolutions Nl for l=1 \dots L, and interpolating the features at those indices. Loss Weights: The optimization uses a weighted loss function with the following weights: \lambda1 = 0.0005 \lambda2 = 1 \lambda3 = 0.005 \lambda4 = 1 Unnormalized Scale Epsilon Values: Used for normalization or scaling in the loss/optimization: \epsilon{0t} = 10\text{m} \epsilon{t} = 100\text{m} \epsilon{0o} = 1\text{m} \epsilon{o} = 0.15\text{m} \epsilon{n} = 0.15\text{m} \epsilon{a} = 1.5\text{m} Scheduling Rates: \alphat = 1.00004 \alphao = 0.99995 Optimization Parameters: Algorithm: RAdam. Iterations: 100,000. Learning Rate: Initial 0.01, reduced to 0.0001. Scheduler max limit 50,000 iterations. Sampling: 4,096 points per iteration. Unverified code. name: LiDAR4D
head: Dynamic Neural Fields for Novel Space-Time View LiDAR Synthesis
body: LiDAR4D is a differentiable volume rendering method for novel space-time view LiDAR synthesis that jointly learns 3D geometry, intensity, and ray-drop probabilities in dynamic scenes. It distinguishes itself by combining a U-Net-based global pattern preservation module with data-driven detail prediction to achieve realistic ray-drop modeling, addressing the noise and detail loss issues inherent in purely MLP-based or grid-based approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Dynamic point clouds (preprocessed), LiDAR sensor configurations (pose, beam distribution), and temporal indices. Outputs: Synthesized LiDAR point clouds (depth, intensity, ray-drop status) for novel viewpoints and time steps. Data Structures: 1. Multi-planar Features: A multiscale structure with 4 levels. Each level doubles the spatial resolution (starting from 64) and outputs an 8-dimensional feature vector. Total static/dynamic feature dimension from planes: 4 \times 8 = 32 dimensions. 2. Hash Grids: 8 levels of hash grids mapping spatial coordinates to features. The hash table size is 2^{19}. Spatial resolution ranges from 512 to 2^{15}. Each level outputs a 4-dimensional feature vector. Total static/dynamic feature dimension from hash grids: 8 \times 4 = 32 dimensions. 3. Latent Vector: The static and dynamic features from planes and hash grids are concatenated to form a 128-dimensional latent vector. 4. Temporal Resolution: Fixed to 25. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Remove ground points from the input point cloud using RANSAC. Limit the maximum distance to 50 meters to mitigate noise. 2. Feature Encoding: Encode the spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and temporal coordinate t into the multi-planar features and hash grids. The hash grid maps coordinates to a table of size 2^{19}. 3. Dynamic Feature Aggregation: For dynamic scenes, aggregate dynamic features of adjacent spatio-temporal points using weighted averaging to ensure temporal consistency. This involves a flow MLP that predicts scene flow to constrain the optimization of adjacent frames. 4. Geometric and Density Prediction: Feed the aggregated features (static + dynamic) into a 2-layer MLP with 64 units per layer. This outputs a 15-dimensional geometric feature and a scalar density value \sigma. 5. Intensity and Ray-Drop Prediction: Encode the viewpoint direction \mathbf{d} using 12-band frequency encoding. Concatenate the 15-dimensional geometric feature with the encoded viewpoint. Pass this concatenation to two independent 3-layer MLPs, each with 64 units per layer. The first MLP predicts intensity values I. The second MLP predicts ray-drop probabilities P{drop}. 6. U-Net Refinement: Combine the initial predictions (density, intensity, ray-drop) as inputs to a U-Net architecture. The U-Net is randomly initialized and optimized to refine the global ray-drop pattern. 7. Synthesis: Multiply the final predictions (specifically the ray-drop mask) by the synthesized data to generate the final LiDAR point cloud. Formulas: Depth Value: The expectation of the density integrated along the ray serves as the depth value D. Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of depth, intensity, ray-drop, and flow losses: \mathcal{L} = \lambda\alpha \mathcal{L}\alpha + \lambda\beta \mathcal{L}\beta + \lambda\gamma \mathcal{L}\gamma + \lambda\eta \mathcal{L}\eta where \mathcal{L}\alpha is depth loss, \mathcal{L}\beta is intensity loss, \mathcal{L}\gamma is ray-drop loss, and \mathcal{L}\eta is flow loss (Chamfer distance based). Refinement Loss: During the refinement phase, only the refinement weight \lambdar is active (set to 1), with other weights set to 0. Parameters: Learning Rates: Initial learning rate is 0.01 for multi-planar and hash grids; 0.001 for other MLP networks (including the U-Net). Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Learning Rate Decay: Exponential decay with a final decay coefficient of 0.1. Loss Weights: \lambda\alpha = 1, \lambda\beta = 0.1, \lambda\gamma = 0.01, \lambda\eta = 0.01. Hash Table Size: 2^{19}. Max Spatial Resolution: 2^{15}. Temporal Resolution: 25. Pitfalls: Resolution Degradation: Extremely high resolution in hash grids may lead to degradation of point cloud metrics due to limited capacity (2^{19}). Detail Prediction: Data-driven paradigms struggle to predict fine details accurately, such as vehicle windows, which may appear noisy or missing. Ground Noise: Failure to remove ground points or limit distance can introduce adverse noise effects. Time Complexity: Optimization takes approximately 2 hours per scenario on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. Memory Complexity: Determined by the hash table size (2^{19} entries) and multi-planar feature storage. The exact memory footprint in bytes is not given in the sources. Strengths: Preserves global patterns better than pure MLP methods, achieving superior LPIPS metrics. Effective for large-scale scene reconstruction and dynamic sequences. Limitations: Dependent on the distribution of training samples; difficult to predict high-frequency details like transparent surfaces (e.g., vehicle windows). When to Use: When realistic ray-drop modeling and global pattern preservation are prioritized over fine-grained detail accuracy in dynamic LiDAR synthesis. When Not to Use: When fine details like transparent objects are critical, or when computational resources for 2-hour optimization per scenario are unavailable. LiDAR4D was introduced in the paper "LiDAR4D: Dynamic Neural Fields for Novel Space-Time View LiDAR Synthesis". It builds upon LiDAR-NeRF by extending it to dynamic scenes and incorporating a U-Net for ray-drop refinement. The method addresses the limitations of previous neural LiDAR fields in handling dynamic environments and realistic sensor effects like ray drops. name: Deformable and Dynamic Fields
body: Deformable and Dynamic Fields extend static radiance field optimization to model scenes that change over time or undergo non-rigid deformation. Unlike static methods that assume fixed geometry, these methods introduce a temporal or deformation component to map input coordinates to a canonical space, enabling novel view synthesis for moving or deforming objects. They are distinguished from static voxel methods and static MLP-based methods by their explicit handling of motion through learned warp fields or displacement mappings. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps. The core mechanism evaluates the volume rendering equation and computes gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses). The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories: 1. Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation (AD) uses standard backpropagation through the computational graph. 2. The Adjoint Method computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. 3. Analytic Inversion or Explicit Gradients uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to O(n) by avoiding the storage of intermediate results. Neural Volumes (NV) synthesizes novel views of dynamic scenes by optimizing a deep 3D convolutional network to predict a discretized RGB\alpha voxel grid and a 3D warp field [912-neural-volumes.md]. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent, dynamic objects (such as smoke or hair) from sparse multi-view video input without requiring explicit geometry reconstruction or depth sensors [912-neural-volumes.md]. Unlike implicit radiance fields that map coordinates to color via MLPs, NV uses an explicit voxel grid, trading memory for rendering speed and interpretability [912-neural-volumes.md]. It sets itself apart from static voxel methods by introducing a learnable warp field to model non-rigid motion and from MLP-based methods by avoiding the prohibitive computational cost of evaluating deep networks at every ray-marching step [912-neural-volumes.md]. EndoNeRF is a method for deformable surgical scene reconstruction that utilizes a canonical radiance field and a time-dependent displacement field, optimized with stereo depth-cueing and supervision. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing non-rigid tissue dynamics in endoscopic videos by mapping input space-time coordinates to a static canonical space via a learned displacement field. Unlike static radiance field methods, it explicitly models temporal deformation, allowing for the querying of radiance and density at any continuous time step. A computational framework to efficiently reconstruct a temporally coherent sequence of fluid density fields from monocular video, aligning density fields with input images while conforming to physical priors [10672-fluid-motion-reconstruction-framework.md]. An adaptation of the binary feature encoding technique applied to time-aware voxel features to enable highly compact reconstruction of dynamic scenes without conventional dense feature encoding. 1. Initialize TiNeuVox base model with time-aware voxel features. 2. Replace conventional feature encoding with binary feature encoding on the voxel grid. 3. Train the model on dynamic scene datasets (D-NeRF, HyperNeRF). 4. Evaluate storage size and reconstruction metrics. TiNeuVox-S on D-NeRF (synthetic): Size reduced from 7.63 MB to 0.59 MB; PSNR drops from 31.03 to 28.68; SSIM drops from 0.957 to 0.938. TiNeuVox-B on D-NeRF (synthetic): Size reduced from 47.51 MB to 3.88 MB; PSNR drops from 33.02 to 31.23; SSIM drops from 0.972 to 0.961. TiNeuVox-B on HyperNeRF (real): Size reduced from 47.85 MB to 3.90 MB; PSNR drops from 24.20 to 23.87; MS-SSIM drops from 0.835 to 0.826. Achieves 0.6 MB storage for the synthetic jumpingjacks dynamic scene. The need for dynamic scene representation arises from the limitations of static NeRF-like methods in capturing temporal variations. Neural Volumes [912-neural-volumes.md] was among the early works to introduce explicit voxel grids with warp fields for dynamic scenes. EndoNeRF [5540-endonerf.md] later adapted these concepts for the specific challenges of endoscopic surgery, such as non-rigid tissue deformation and limited viewpoint coverage. name: Neural Volumes
head: Deformable Volumes, Neural Volumes: Learning Dynamic Renderable Volumes from Images, Volumetric Reconstruction with Ray Potentials
body: Neural Volumes (NV) is a method for synthesizing novel views of dynamic scenes by optimizing a deep 3D convolutional network to predict a discretized RGB\alpha voxel grid and a 3D warp field. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent, non-rigidly deforming objects (such as smoke or hair) from sparse multi-view video inputs without requiring explicit geometry or texture maps. It differs from previous ray potential works by modeling voxel transparency rather than occupancy probability, focusing on rendering rather than reconstruction. It uses an explicit voxel grid decoded from a latent code, avoiding the prohibitive computational cost of evaluating large MLPs at every ray-marching step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of K synchronized, calibrated RGB images from different viewpoints for each time instant (typically K=3 orthogonal views). Outputs: A rendered RGB image for a novel camera pose, and a latent code z representing the scene state. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid (V): A discrete 3D grid of size D \times D \times D (typically 128^3) storing RGBA values. Layout: Tensor Y \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D \times D \times 4}. Values: \mathbf{V}{\text{rgb}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (color) and \mathbf{V}{\alpha} \in \mathbb{R} (differential opacity, range [0, \infty]). 2. Warp Grid (W): A discrete 3D grid of size Nw \times Nw \times Nw (typically 32^3) storing inverse warp vectors. Layout: Tensor storing the inverse transformation W^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) for each voxel center. 3. Latent Code (z): A vector z \in \mathbb{R}^{256} representing the scene state at a specific time instant. Network Architecture: 1. Encoder: A CNN processes each of the K input images through dedicated branches. Outputs are concatenated and encoded into the parameters of a diagonal 256-dimensional Gaussian (\mu, \sigma). 2. Latent Sampling: An instance z is sampled from the Gaussian using the reparameterization trick. 3. Decoder: A 3D convolutional network (or linear basis decoder) maps z to the Voxel Grid V and the Warp Grid W. Activation: Softplus is used to ensure non-negative opacity values. Rendering (Differentiable Ray Marching): For a camera ray \mathbf{r}, the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and accumulated opacity \hat{A}(\mathbf{r}) are computed by marching through the warped voxel grid. 1. Warping: For a sample point \mathbf{x} along the ray, the inverse warp field W^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) is sampled. This maps the world-space position to a position in the template (canonical) space. Note: The warp field can be modeled as a mixture of affine transformations in warp space. 2. Sampling: The RGBA values are sampled from the Voxel Grid at the warped position: (\mathbf{c}, \alpha) = V(W^{-1}(\mathbf{x})). 3. Accumulation: Values are accumulated front-to-back using alpha blending: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{j} \mathbf{c}j \cdot \alphaj \cdot \prod{k<j} (1 - \alphak) \hat{A}(\mathbf{r}) = 1 - \prod{j} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{c}j and \alphaj are the color and differential opacity at the j-th sample. Training: The system is trained end-to-end by minimizing the reconstruction loss between the rendered image and the input image. Loss Function: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \| I{\text{rgb}} - I^{\text{rgb}} \|2^2 + \beta \cdot D{KL}(z \| \mathcal{N}(0,1)) + \lambda{tv} J{tv}(\mathbf{V}{\alpha}) + \lambdaB JB(I{\alpha}) \| I{\text{rgb}} - I^{\text{rgb}} \|2^2: L2 pixel reconstruction error. D{KL}(z \| \mathcal{N}(0,1)): KL-divergence regularization for the latent code. J{tv}(\mathbf{V}{\alpha}): Total variation regularization on opacity to encourage sharp boundaries. JB(I{\alpha}): Beta distribution prior on accumulated opacity to encourage binary transparency (fully transparent or opaque). Pseudocode: Unverified code. CNN branches process each view, concatenate, and encode x = images.view(B, K H W, C) x = torch.relu(x) mu = torch.tanh(x.mean(dim=1)) sigma = torch.exp(x.mean(dim=1)) return mu, sigma def decoder(z, voxelres, warpres): """ z: Tensor of shape (B, 256) Returns: voxelgrid (B, D, D, D, 4), warpgrid (B, W, W, W, 3) """ B = z.shape[0] # Linear basis decoder or 3D transposed convolutions voxelflat = F.softplus(nn.Linear(256, voxelres3 4)(z)) warpflat = nn.Linear(256, warpres3 3)(z) voxelgrid = voxelflat.view(B, voxelres, voxelres, voxelres, 4) warpgrid = warpflat.view(B, warpres, warpres, warpres, 3) return voxelgrid, warpgrid def trilinearsample(grid, points): """ grid: (B, C, D, H, W) points: (B, N, 3) in normalized [-1, 1] coordinates Returns: (B, N, C) """ # Normalize points to [-1, 1] assuming scene bounds are [-1, 1]^3 points = torch.clamp(points, -1.0, 1.0) # Expand points to match gridsample expected shape (B, N, 1, 1, 3) points = points.unsqueeze(2).unsqueeze(3) # gridsample expects grid (N, C, D, H, W) and coordinates (N, Hout, Wout, Dout, 3) samples = F.gridsample(grid, points, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border') return samples.squeeze(2).squeeze(2) def raymarch(voxelgrid, warpgrid, origins, directions, numsamples): """ voxelgrid: (B, D, D, D, 4) warpgrid: (B, W, W, W, 3) origins: (B, H, W, 3) directions: (B, H, W, 3) Returns: renderedrgb (B, H, W, 3), renderedalpha (B, H, W, 1) """ B, H, W, = origins.shape # Generate sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples, device=origins.device) tvals = tvals.view(1, 1, 1, -1).expandas(origins[...,:1]) pointsworld = origins[...,:1] + tvals directions pointsworld = pointsworld.view(B H W numsamples, 3) # Sample warp field: Winv(x) warpvectors = trilinearsample(warpgrid.permute(0, 4, 1, 2, 3), pointsworld) warpvectors = warpvectors.view(B, H, W, numsamples, 3) # Sample voxel grid at warped positions voxelvalues = trilinearsample(voxelgrid.permute(0, 4, 1, 2, 3), warpvectors.view(B H W numsamples, 3)) voxelvalues = voxelvalues.view(B, H, W, numsamples, 4) rgbsamples = voxelvalues[...,:3] alphasamples = voxelvalues[..., 3:] # Accumulate oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alphasamples transmittance = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(oneminusalpha[...,:1]), torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha[...,:-1], dim=-1)], dim=-1) weights = alphasamples transmittance renderedrgb = torch.sum(weights rgbsamples, dim=-2) renderedalpha = 1.0 - torch.prod(oneminusalpha, dim=-2) return renderedrgb, renderedalpha def totalvariationloss(x): """Standard TV regularization """ return torch.mean(torch.abs(x[...,:-1,:,:,:] - x[..., 1:,:,:,:])) + \ torch.mean(torch.abs(x[...,:,:-1,:,:] - x[...,:, 1:,:,:])) + \ torch.mean(torch.abs(x[...,:,:,:-1,:] - x[...,:,:, 1:,:])) def betapriorloss(alpha, beta=1.0): """Beta distribution prior encouraging binary transparency """ return -torch.mean(torch.log(alpha + 1e-6) + torch.log(1.0 - alpha + 1e-6)) def forward(images, targetcameraparams, gtimages, voxelres=128, warpres=32, numsamples=128): mu, sigma = encoder(images) z = mu + sigma torch.randnlike(sigma) voxelgrid, warpgrid = decoder(z, voxelres, warpres) renderedrgb, renderedalpha = raymarch(voxelgrid, warpgrid, targetcameraparams['origins'], targetcameraparams['directions'], numsamples) rgbloss = F.mseloss(renderedrgb, gtimages) klloss = -0.5 torch.sum(1 + torch.log(sigma2) - mu2 - sigma2) tvloss = totalvariationloss(voxelgrid[..., 3:]) betaloss = betapriorloss(renderedalpha) totalloss = rgbloss + 0.1 klloss + tvloss + betaloss return totalloss, renderedrgb Voxel Grid Decoders model the volume function V(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}) as a discrete 3D grid of voxels, producing an explicit 3D voxel grid as the output tensor of a neural network. This approach avoids the prohibitive computational requirements of evaluating deep MLPs at every ray-marching step, enabling real-time rendering speeds. It sets itself apart from implicit MLP decoders by trading memory for speed, storing values in a structured grid rather than computing them on the fly. RenderNet is a deep convolutional network designed for the differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes. It solves the problem of synthesizing novel views by mapping a 3D input volume directly to a 2D image. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Voxel Grid Decoders and GRU Volume Fusion, is its explicit architectural separation of 3D feature extraction and 2D image decoding, connected by a projection unit that aggregates features along the viewing ray using an MLP. Unlike methods that extract features in object space independent of camera parameters, RenderNet performs view-space resampling at the beginning of the pipeline, making the features inherently dependent on the camera pose. GRU Volume Fusion is a method for incremental 3D reconstruction that fuses sequentially estimated local radiance fields into a single global sparse representation using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by adaptively updating a global volume with new local observations, setting it apart from its sibling Bi-level Fusion which uses explicit weighted averaging followed by optimization rather than recurrent neural updates. It builds on Neural Volumes by replacing static optimization with a learned recurrent fusion process. Training Time: Requires at least 12 hours to train per scene. Memory: Uses an explicit 128^3 voxel grid, which limits the ability to represent fine details at high resolutions compared to implicit methods. Inference Speed: Supports real-time inference at test time, unlike many other neural rendering methods. Strengths: Captures reasonably detailed volumetric geometry and appearance; handles semi-transparent materials (smoke, hair); interpretable volume; real-time rendering. Limitations: Blurry results compared to high-resolution methods due to voxel grid resolution limits; limited to objects within a bounded volume with a distinct background. When to use: Dynamic scenes with semi-transparent materials where real-time novel view synthesis is required and explicit geometry is not available. Neural Volumes was introduced by Lempitsky et al. in 2019. It builds on the concept of ray potentials and volume ray marching. It is a baseline method that uses a 3D deconvolutional network to produce RGB-Alpha volumes as the volumetric video. It differs from previous ray potential works by modeling voxel transparency rather than occupancy probability, focusing on rendering rather than reconstruction. It also differs from DeepVoxels by supporting dynamic scenes and real-time inference. name: Voxel Grid Decoders
body: Voxel Grid Decoders model the volume function V(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}) as a discrete 3D grid of voxels, producing an explicit 3D voxel grid as the output tensor of a neural network. This approach avoids the prohibitive computational and memory requirements of evaluating large Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) at every step along each ray in the ray-marching process, which is necessary for real-time applications. It serves as the explicit representation component within Neural Volumes, replacing the implicit coordinate-based MLP. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A latent code vector \mathbf{z} (typically from an encoder network). Output: A tensor \mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times D \times D \times D} representing a D \times D \times D grid of values with C channels. In standard experiments, C=4 (representing RGB\alpha). Data Structures: Voxel Grid Tensor: A 4D tensor with dimensions C \times D \times D \times D. Interpolation Function S: Samples from grid \mathbf{Y} by scaling continuous values in the range [-1, 1] to the grid indices [1, D] along each dimension, followed by trilinear interpolation. Parameters: D: Spatial resolution. Typical values are 32 or 128. W: Side size of the 3D cube covered by the volume. \mathbf{x}0: Center of the 3D cube. \mathbf{z}: Latent representation vector. Formulas: The volume decoder function is defined as: \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{z}) = S\left(\frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}0}{W/2}; \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{z})\right) where \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{z}) is the neural network that produces the tensor \mathbf{Y} of size 4 \times D \times D \times D. The function S performs the coordinate transformation and interpolation. Implementation Variants: The function \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{z}) can be implemented using either a convolutional architecture or a bottleneck fully-connected architecture. 1. Convolutional Decoder (Variant 1): Apply a fully-connected layer and non-linearity to transform \mathbf{z} into a 1024-dimensional representation. Reinterpret the resulting vector as a 1 \times 1 \times 1 cube with 1024 channels. Apply 5 transposed convolutions to achieve a final size of 32^3. Performance: Runs at 90Hz. 2. Convolutional Decoder (Variant 2): Same initialization as Variant 1. Apply 7 transposed convolutions to achieve a final size of 128^3. Performance: Runs at 22Hz. 3. Bottleneck Decoder: Use 3 fully-connected layers with output sizes of 128, 4, and 128^3 \times 4 respectively. The last layer represents the decoded volume. Performance: Runs at 90Hz. Post-processing: After decoding the volume, apply a softplus function to the RGB\alpha values to ensure they are non-negative. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fc(x, W, b): """Fully connected layer: y = x @ W + b""" return [sum(x[i] W[i][j] for i in range(len(x))) + b[j] for j in range(len(W[0]))] def relu(x): return [max(0.0, v) for v in x] def softplus(x): return [math.log(1.0 + math.exp(v)) for v in x] def trilinear(grid, coord): """Trilinear interpolation for a C x D x D x D grid at coord in [-1, 1]^3.""" D = len(grid[0]) # Map [-1, 1] to [1, D] as specified in the source u = [(coord[i] + 1.0) (D - 1) / 2.0 + 1.0 for i in range(3)] x0, y0, z0 = [int(math.floor(v)) for v in u] x1, y1, z1 = [min(x0 + 1, D - 1) for in range(3)] dx, dy, dz = [u[i] - [x0, y0, z0][i] for i in range(3)] out = [] for c in range(len(grid)): v000 = grid[c][x0][y0][z0] v100 = grid[c][x1][y0][z0] v010 = grid[c][x0][y1][z0] v110 = grid[c][x1][y1][z0] v001 = grid[c][x0][y0][z1] v101 = grid[c][x1][y0][z1] v011 = grid[c][x0][y1][z1] v111 = grid[c][x1][y1][z1] v00 = v000 (1 - dx) + v100 dx v01 = v001 (1 - dx) + v101 dx v10 = v010 (1 - dx) + v110 dx v11 = v011 (1 - dx) + v111 dx v0 = v00 (1 - dy) + v10 dy v1 = v01 (1 - dy) + v11 dy out.append(v0 (1 - dz) + v1 dz) return out class VoxelGridDecoder: def init(self, latentdim, variant, resolution): self.variant = variant self.resolution = resolution self.channels = 4 # Weight matrices and biases are initialized per standard deep learning practice. # Transposed convolution kernel sizes and strides are not specified in the sources. def forward(self, z): if self.variant == "conv32": h = relu(fc(z, self.W1, self.b1)) grid = [h] # Conceptual reshape to 1x1x1x1024 # 5 transposed convolutions applied to upsample to 32x32x32x4 grid = self.upsampleconv(grid, steps=5) elif self.variant == "conv128": h = relu(fc(z, self.W1, self.b1)) grid = [h] # 7 transposed convolutions applied to upsample to 128x128x128x4 grid = self.upsampleconv(grid, steps=7) elif self.variant == "bottleneck": h1 = relu(fc(z, self.W1, self.b1)) h2 = relu(fc(h1, self.W2, self.b2)) h3 = fc(h2, self.W3, self.b3) grid = [h3] # Reshape to 4x128x128x128 # Post-processing: softplus on RGBa values grid = [[[softplus(v) for v in slice] for slice in plane] for plane in grid] return grid def upsampleconv(self, grid, steps): # Placeholder for transposed convolution logic not detailed in sources. # In practice, this applies 3D transposed convolutions with ReLU activations. return grid def sample(self, grid, x, x0, W): scaled = [(x[i] - x0[i]) / (W / 2.0) for i in range(3)] scaled = [max(-1.0, min(1.0, v)) for v in scaled] return trilinear(grid, scaled) A decoder network that outputs a semantic volume GS from encoded features, used for 3D semantic labeling. It differs from the standard RGB\alpha decoder by incorporating skip connections from the input grid and using a specific loss function for classification. It is chosen when the task requires per-voxel semantic labeling rather than photometric rendering. See NeRF-MAE. Performance: The Convolutional 32³ variant runs at 90Hz. The Convolutional 128³ variant runs at 22Hz. The Bottleneck 128³ variant runs at 90Hz. Memory: The memory requirement is proportional to C \times D^3. For D=128 and C=4, this is 4 \times 128^3 values. Limitations: Voxel grids are limited to representing details as small as a single voxel and are computationally expensive to evaluate and store at high resolution. They are also wasteful in scenes with much empty space. Strengths: Avoids the prohibitive size requirements of MLPs for high-quality reconstructions. Enables real-time applications by reducing the complexity of per-ray evaluation. Voxel Grid Decoders were introduced in the "Neural Volumes" paper. The method was developed to address the computational bottleneck of evaluating MLPs at every step along each ray in the ray-marching process, which imposes a restrictive upper bound on MLP complexity for real-time applications. The approach assumes the volume function can be modeled as a discrete 3D grid of voxels, producing an explicit 3D voxel grid as the output tensor of a neural network. name: Symmetric Voxel Grid
head: Symmetric arrangement, Symmetric feature arrangement
body: The Symmetric Voxel Grid is a feature arrangement strategy for explicit voxel grid decoders that places features symmetrically with respect to the scene center to ensure continuity at region boundaries. It solves the discontinuity problem inherent in linear feature configurations without the model size overhead of overlapping regions. While overlapping approaches increase the feature count by 3n^2 + 3n + 1 in an explicit grid of size n^3, the symmetric method maintains a compact grid while forcing neighboring decoders to see identical features at seams. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scene bounding volume partitioned into a regular grid of regions, each with an associated density decoder. Output: A shared 3D voxel grid where features are assigned to vertices such that symmetry constraints are satisfied. Data Structures The grid consists of discrete voxels where each vertex holds features accessed by adjacent decoders. Let n be the number of subdivisions along one axis, yielding an explicit grid of n^3 features. The feature dimension at each vertex is set to 32. Steps 1. Define Regions: Partition the scene space into a regular grid of n \times n \times n regions. Each region ei has an associated decoder \thetai. 2. Symmetric Feature Assignment: Assign features to voxel vertices such that any vertex v on the boundary between two regions e1 and e2 presents the same feature value to both \theta1 and \theta2. This is achieved by mirroring feature values across the scene center. 3. Decoder Initialization: Initialize all density decoders \thetai with the same weights to further improve continuity during training. Formulas Overhead of alternative overlapping method: The number of additional features required by overlapping regions in an explicit grid of size n^3 is: \Delta N = 3n^2 + 3n + 1 This growth reduces the effectiveness of the explicit grid approach. Parameters n: The number of subdivisions per axis. Not given in the sources. Feature dimension: 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Linear Configuration Discontinuity: Using a simple repeating linear order for features introduces discontinuities at seams because different decoders see different features at the boundary. Model Size Explosion: Attempting to fix linear discontinuities by overlapping regions increases the model size significantly by 3n^2 + 3n + 1 features. Pruning Benefits: The symmetric configuration increases the probability of features being in empty space for all regions, allowing more aggressive pruning and reducing the final stored feature count. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def assignsymmetricfeatures(grid, n): """ Assigns features to a voxel grid symmetrically with respect to the scene center. Args: grid: 3D array of shape (n, n, n) representing voxel vertices. n: Number of subdivisions per axis. Returns: grid: Modified 3D array with symmetric feature assignment. """ for x in range(n): for y in range(n): for z in range(n): # Calculate symmetric counterpart indices relative to grid center xsym = n - 1 - x ysym = n - 1 - y zsym = n - 1 - z # Ensure symmetry: feature at (x,y,z) must equal feature at (xsym, ysym, zsym) if grid[x, y, z] is None: grid[x, y, z] = grid[xsym, ysym, zsym] else: grid[xsym, ysym, zsym] = grid[x, y, z] return grid def initializedecoders(decoders): """ Initializes all density decoders with the same weights. Args: decoders: List of decoder objects. """ # Initialize all density decoders with the same weights to improve continuity during training for decoder in decoders: decoder.weights = 0.0 A naive arrangement where features are repeated in the same order for each region. It introduces discontinuities at seams because different decoders see different features at the boundary. Voxel Grid Decoders An alternative approach where regions overlap to ensure shared features at boundaries. It increases model size by 3n^2 + 3n + 1 features compared to non-overlapping grids. Voxel Grid Decoders Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The symmetric arrangement does not increase the number of features needed for seamless reconstruction compared to a non-overlapping grid. It reduces the number of features stored after pruning because it increases the probability of features being in empty space for all regions. Measured Performance: The method is described as "very effective to improve the model quality and reduce its size". Specific metrics are not provided in the notes. Strengths: Avoids discontinuities without increasing model size; enables more aggressive pruning; improves training continuity via shared decoder initialization. The Symmetric Voxel Grid was introduced in the paper "NeRFLight: Fast and Light Neural Radiance Fields using a Shared Feature Grid" by Rivas-Manzaneque et al. (CVPR 2023). It addresses issues in explicit neural field representations where linear feature arrangements cause seams. The method builds on the concept of shared feature grids but specifically optimizes the spatial arrangement of those features to ensure continuity. name: RenderNet Architecture
head: RenderNet
body: RenderNet is a deep convolutional network designed for the differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes. It solves the problem of synthesizing novel views by mapping a 3D input volume directly to a 2D image. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Voxel Grid Decoders and GRU Volume Fusion, is its explicit architectural separation of 3D feature extraction and 2D image decoding, connected by a projection unit that aggregates features along the viewing ray using an MLP. Unlike methods that extract features in object space independent of camera parameters, RenderNet performs view-space resampling at the beginning of the pipeline, making the features inherently dependent on the camera pose. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the shape. Output: A 2D rendered image (RGB or grayscale) and optionally other modalities (e.g., albedo, normals). Data Structures and Layout: The network consists of four main stages: 3D Input Encoder, 3D Residual Blocks, Projection Unit, and 2D Decoder. 1. 3D Input Encoder: A sequence of 3D convolutions. Layer 1: Channels \{8\}, Kernel \{5\}, Stride \{2\}. Layer 2: Channels \{16\}, Kernel \{3\}, Stride \{2\}. Layer 3: Channels \{16\}, Kernel \{3\}, Stride \{1\}. 2. 3D Residual Blocks: Ten 3D residual blocks follow the encoder. Each block consists of two 3D convolutions with a shortcut connection adding the input to the output. 3. Projection Unit: Resizes the tensor from dimensions W \times H \times 32 \times 16 to W \times H \times (32 \cdot 16). Applies a 1 \times 1 convolution with the same number of channels (32 \cdot 16 = 512). This projects all voxels along the X-axis (ray direction) to a single high-dimensional feature vector, analogous to an accumulation function. 4. 2D Decoder: 2D Residual Blocks: Ten 2D residual blocks follow the projection unit. Similar to 3D blocks but using 2D convolutions. Intermediate Conv: A 4 \times 4 convolution with 32 \cdot 8 = 256 channels. Final 2D Residual Blocks: Five 2D residual blocks. Output Convs: A series of 2D convolutions with channels \{32 \cdot 4, 32 \cdot 2, 32, 16, 3 \text{ (or } 1 \text{ for greyscale)}\}, kernel sizes \{4, 4, 4, 4, 4\}, and strides \{1, 2, 2, 2, 1\}. Steps: 1. Resampling: Resample the input 3D volume to view space using a perspective camera transform. The X-axis of the resampled volume corresponds to ray directions, and the YZ-axes correspond to image coordinates. 2. 3D Feature Extraction: Process the resampled volume with the 3D Input Encoder and 3D Residual Blocks to extract semantic features, reducing spatial dimensions. 3. Ray Projection: Use the Projection Unit to project all voxels along the X-axis to a single high-dimensional feature vector (512-channel 2D projection). 4. 2D Upsampling: Upsample the 2D projection to the target resolution using the 2D Decoder (2D Residual Blocks and Output Convs). 5. Multi-modal Output (Optional): To generate additional modalities (e.g., normal maps), create a branch of 2D convolution layers starting at the first strided up-convolution layer (Layer 2 of Output Convs) and train it jointly with the main branch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernet(inputvolume3d, cameraparams): # Step 1: Resample to view space viewspacevolume = resampletoviewspace(inputvolume3d, cameraparams) # X-axis: ray directions, YZ-axes: image coordinates # Step 2: 3D Input Encoder x = conv3d(viewspacevolume, outchannels=8, kernelsize=5, stride=2) x = conv3d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, stride=2) x = conv3d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, stride=1) # Step 3: 3D Residual Blocks (10 blocks) for in range(10): x = residualblock3d(x) # Step 4: Projection Unit # Resize from WxHx32x16 to WxHx(3216) x = resizetensor(x, newshape=(x.shape[0], x.shape[1], 32 16)) # 1x1 Convolution with the same number of channels x = conv1x1(x, outchannels=32 16) # Step 5: 2D Decoder # 2D Residual Blocks (10 blocks) for in range(10): x = residualblock2d(x) # Intermediate Conv: 4x4, 256 channels x = conv2d(x, outchannels=256, kernelsize=4, stride=1) # Final 2D Residual Blocks (5 blocks) for in range(5): x = residualblock2d(x) # Output Convs x = conv2d(x, outchannels=128, kernelsize=4, stride=1) x = conv2d(x, outchannels=64, kernelsize=4, stride=2) # Multi-modal branch can be attached here x = conv2d(x, outchannels=32, kernelsize=4, stride=2) x = conv2d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=4, stride=2) rgboutput = conv2d(x, outchannels=3, kernelsize=4, stride=1) return rgboutput def resampletoviewspace(volume, cameraparams): # Resamples 3D volume to view space using perspective camera transform # X-axis aligns with ray directions, YZ-axes align with image coordinates pass def conv3d(x, outchannels, kernelsize, stride): # Applies a 3D convolution with specified output channels, kernel size, and stride pass def resizetensor(x, newshape): # Resizes tensor dimensions to newshape (e.g., flattening last two dimensions) pass def conv1x1(x, outchannels): # Applies a 1x1 convolution with specified output channels pass def conv2d(x, outchannels, kernelsize, stride): # Applies a 2D convolution with specified output channels, kernel size, and stride pass def residualblock3d(x): # Applies two 3D convolutions with a shortcut connection adding input to output pass def residualblock2d(x): # Applies two 2D convolutions with a shortcut connection adding input to output pass Parameters: Projection output channels: 512. Input volume dimensions: Not given in the sources. Target image resolution: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The architecture supports arbitrary input and output dimensions during and after training, but the specific dimensions provided in the notes are for the training dataset. The projection unit assumes a specific tensor shape (W \times H \times 32 \times 16) before resizing, which may require padding or cropping if the input volume dimensions do not align with the expected feature map size after the 3D encoder. Definition: An alternative model for comparison against RenderNet. Layout: The 3D input encoder consists of 3D convolutions with channels \{64, 128, 256, 512\}, kernel sizes \{4, 4, 4, 4\}, and strides \{2, 2, 2, 2\}, using parametric ReLU. This is followed by a fully-connected layer mapping tensors to a 200-dimensional vector and a sigmoid activation. Lighting and pose parameters are directly concatenated to the shape latent vector. The decoder consists of 2D convolutions with 4×4 kernels, channels \{512, 512, 256, 256, 128, 128, 64, 64, 32, 32, 16, 1\}, and strides \{2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1\}. When to choose: Use when comparing against the standard RenderNet pipeline or when explicit pose/lighting conditioning via latent vector concatenation is required. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables learning different rendering styles; effective for synthesizing novel viewpoints for faces captured from a single viewpoint; allows multi-modal output sharing high-level information. Limitations: View-space resampling at the beginning makes features dependent on camera parameters, unlike object-space feature extraction methods. When to use: When differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes is required, particularly for novel view synthesis of faces or bodies. When not to use: When object-space feature independence is preferred, or when explicit modeling of occlusion through absorption coefficient and alpha blending is required. RenderNet was introduced as a deep convolutional network for differentiable rendering from 3D shapes. The architecture enables differentiable rendering of voxelized 3D shapes by combining a 3D and a 2D convolutional part connected by a projection unit. It has been applied to scene relighting, novel view synthesis, facial and body reenactment, and photorealistic avatars. The projection unit has also been extended to controllable neural voxel rendering for handling high-frequency and complex textures. name: GRU Volume Fusion
head: Fusing Volumes for Global Reconstruction, NeRFusion, Recurrent Fusion Module, Recurrent Neural Fusion
body: GRU Volume Fusion is a method for incremental 3D reconstruction that fuses sequentially estimated local radiance fields into a single global sparse representation using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by adaptively updating a global volume with new local observations, setting it apart from its sibling Bi-level Fusion which uses explicit weighted averaging of latent codes followed by an optimization step rather than recurrent neural updates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of local sparse feature volumes \{\mathcal{V}t\}, where each \mathcal{V}t represents the local radiance field estimated from the t-th frame's input images. Output: The final global sparse feature volume \mathcal{V}T^g after processing T frames. This volume conditions density and color MLPs for rendering. Data Structures: Local Volume \mathcal{V}t: A sparse 3D tensor containing feature vectors for voxels visible in frame t. Global Volume \mathcal{V}t^g: A sparse 3D tensor of the same spatial resolution and feature dimension as \mathcal{V}t, storing the accumulated global features. Gate Volumes (zt, rt): Sparse 3D tensors of the same shape as \mathcal{V}t^g, containing values in [0, 1] for the update and reset gates. Candidate Volume \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g: Sparse 3D tensor of the same shape as \mathcal{V}t^g, containing candidate feature updates. Network Components: Three deep neural networks with sparse 3D convolution layers are used: 1. Mz: Computes the update gate. Ends with a sigmoid activation. 2. Mr: Computes the reset gate. Ends with a sigmoid activation. 3. Mt: Computes the candidate volume. Ends with a tanh activation. Numbered Steps: For each frame t = 1, \dots, T: 1. Input: Take the local sparse volume \mathcal{V}t and the previous global volume \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g. 2. Compute Update Gate: Concatenate the previous global volume and the local volume along the feature dimension: [\mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]. Pass this through Mz to get the update gate zt: zt = Mz([\mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]). 3. Compute Reset Gate: Pass the same concatenated input through Mr to get the reset gate rt: rt = Mr([\mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]). 4. Compute Candidate Volume: Element-wise multiply the previous global volume by the reset gate: rt \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g. Concatenate this result with the local volume: [rt \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]. Pass this through Mt to get the candidate volume \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g: \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g = Mt([rt \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g, \mathcal{V}t]). 5. Update Global Volume: Combine the previous global volume and the candidate volume using the update gate: \mathcal{V}t^g = (1 - zt) \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g + zt \tilde{\mathcal{V}}t^g. 6. Sparse Application: Steps 2–5 are applied only to voxels covered by the local volume \mathcal{V}t. All other voxels in the global volume remain unchanged from \mathcal{V}{t-1}^g. Args: localvolumes: List of sparse 3D tensors Vt, one per frame. initialglobal: Sparse 3D tensor V0^g. Mz, Mr, Mt: Sparse 3D CNN networks for update, reset, and candidate gates. Returns: Final global sparse volume VT^g. """ globalvolume = initialglobal for localvol in localvolumes: # Extract global features for indices in local volume (pad with zeros if missing) gfeats = np.array([globalvolume.features[idx] if idx in globalvolume.features else np.zeros(localvol.features.shape[1]) for idx in localvol.indices]) lfeats = localvol.features # 1. Compute Update Gate zt zfeats = Mz(np.concatenate([gfeats, lfeats], axis=-1)) # 2. Compute Reset Gate rt rfeats = Mr(np.concatenate([gfeats, lfeats], axis=-1)) # 3. Compute Candidate Volume resetfeats = rfeats gfeats candfeats = Mt(np.concatenate([resetfeats, lfeats], axis=-1)) # 4. Update Global Volume newfeats = (1 - zfeats) gfeats + zfeats candfeats # 5. Merge updated features back into globalvolume for i, idx in enumerate(localvol.indices): globalvolume.features[idx] = newfeats[i] return globalvolume Parameters: The network is generalizable and pre-trained across scenes, allowing it to handle arbitrary scene scales and arbitrary numbers of input images. Typical training datasets: ScanNet, DTU, Google Scanned Object. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparsity Alignment: The concatenation and element-wise operations must correctly handle the sparse structure. Voxels present in the global volume but not in the local volume must be preserved without modification. Initialization: The initial global volume \mathcal{V}0^g is initialized to zeros. An online 3D reconstruction method that represents geometry using implicit neural volumes, combining local-level fusion for efficient depth map integration and global-level fusion framed as neural rendering for consistent reconstruction. It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by first fusing latent codes via weighted averaging and then optimizing the global volume against depth measurements. It sets itself apart from its sibling GRU Volume Fusion by using explicit weighted averaging of latent codes followed by an optimization step, rather than recurrent neural network updates. Time Complexity: The recurrent fusion runs in real-time at 22 fps. Memory Complexity: Uses sparse 3D representations, which are memory-efficient for large-scale scenes with sparse observations. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art quality on both large-scale indoor and small-scale object scenes, with substantially faster reconstruction than NeRF and other recent methods. Outperforms baseline NeRF, NeRFingMVS, and MVSNeRF on ScanNet, DTU, and NeRF Synthetic datasets. Strengths: Real-time incremental reconstruction, handles arbitrary scene scales and numbers of input images, adaptive feature updating. Limitations: Quality can be further boosted by fine-tuning the predicted voxel features per scene. When to use: Large-scale scene reconstruction from image sequences where real-time or near-real-time incremental updates are needed. GRU Volume Fusion, also known as NeRFusion, was introduced in 2022. It combines the advantages of NeRF and TSDF-based fusion techniques to achieve efficient large-scale reconstruction and photo-realistic rendering. The method was trained end-to-end with only rendering losses on a combination of scenes from the ScanNet, DTU, and Google Scanned Object datasets. It addresses the challenges of reconstructing and rendering large-scale indoor scenes from RGB images, which are crucial for applications in AR/VR, e-commerce, and robotics. name: Bi-level Fusion
head: BNV-Fusion, BNVF, Local- and Global-level Fusion, local + global fusion
body: Bi-level Fusion is an online 3D reconstruction method that represents geometry using implicit neural volumes, combining local-level fusion for efficient depth map integration and global-level fusion framed as neural rendering for consistent reconstruction. It solves the problem of accumulating errors and outliers in sequential reconstruction by first fusing latent codes via weighted averaging and then optimizing the global volume against depth measurements. It sets itself apart from its sibling GRU Volume Fusion by using explicit weighted averaging of latent codes followed by an optimization step, rather than recurrent neural network updates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of depth maps Dt, camera extrinsic parameters T{ct}^w, and the current global implicit volume Vw^{t-1} with associated weight volume W^{t-1}. Outputs: The updated global implicit volume Vw^t and weight volume W^t. Data Structures: Implicit Neural Volume (Vw): A 3D grid of latent codes where the voxel resolution is 2 cm, meaning each latent code represents the geometry of a 2\text{cm}^3 volume around its position. Weight Volume (W): A 3D grid of weights, where values are set to the number of 3D points associated with a voxel. Decoder: An MLP with 4 fully connected layers with sizes [128, 128, 128, 1] that maps a latent code and a 3D position to an SDF value. Numbered Steps: 1. Local-level Fusion: 1. Transform the single-view neural volume V{ct}^s from camera coordinates to world coordinates using the camera extrinsic parameters: Vw^s = T{ct}^w V{ct}^s. 2. Update the global implicit volume Vw and weight volume W using weighted averaging of the latent codes: Vw^t = \frac{W^{t-1} Vw^{t-1} + W{ct}^s Vw^s}{W^{t-1} + W{ct}^s} W^t = W^{t-1} + W{ct}^s where Vw and W denote the global implicit volume and its weight, respectively. The superscript t-1 and t means prior update and post update. The superscript s denotes single-view source. 2. Global-level Fusion: 1. Randomly sample a set of pixels in the depth map. The method samples 5000 pixels per image in each iteration. 2. Along the ray unprojected from each sampled pixel, sample N 3D points \{x0, x1,..., xn\} using hierarchical sampling: more points are sampled closer to the measured surface. Coarse-level sampling: 5 3D points per meter. Fine-level sampling: 20 3D points per meter. 3. Transform the 3D points to world coordinates. 4. Extract SDF values si from the global volume Vw using trilinear interpolation of decoder outputs. 5. Compute the projective TSDF \bar{s}i for each 3D point given a depth measurement p on the ray: \bar{s}i = \min(\max(\|p - xi\|2, -\delta), \delta) where \delta is the truncation threshold. 6. Optimize the global volume Vw to minimize the discrepancy between decoded SDF values si and projective TSDF values \bar{s}i: \argmin{Vw} \sum{i=0}^{n} \|si - \bar{s}i\|1 where si is the SDF value decoded from the neural volume Vw. 7. The optimization uses the Adam optimizer for 5 iterations for each image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def bilevelfusion(Vwprev, Wprev, depthmap, cameraextrinsic, depthencoder, decoder, intrinsics, delta): # Step 1: Local-level Fusion # Encode depth map to single-view neural volume Vcst Vcst = depthencoder(depthmap) # Transform single-view volume to world coordinates Vws = transformvolumecoords(Vcst, cameraextrinsic) # Compute source weight volume (number of 3D points per voxel) Wcst = computeweightvolume(Vws) # Weighted averaging of latent codes Vw = (Wprev Vwprev + Wcst Vws) / (Wprev + Wcst) W = Wprev + Wcst # Step 2: Global-level Fusion sampledpixels = random.samplepixels(depthmap, numpixels=5000) for iteration in range(5): totalloss = 0.0 paramgrads = {} for u, v in sampledpixels: p = depthmap[v, u] rayorigin, raydirection = unprojectpixel(u, v, p, intrinsics) # Hierarchical sampling: coarse 5 pts/m, fine 20 pts/m points3d = samplealongray(rayorigin, raydirection, p, coarsedensity=5, finedensity=20) for point in points3d: latentcode = getlatentcode(Vw, point) si = decoder(latentcode, point) # Projective TSDF dist = abs(p - sum(r c for r, c in zip(raydirection, point))) sbari = min(max(dist, -delta), delta) totalloss += abs(si - sbari) # Accumulate gradients for Adam optimizer grad = computegradient(si, sbari, decoder, Vw, point) accumulategrads(paramgrads, grad) # Update parameters using Adam Vw = adamstep(Vw, paramgrads, lr=0.001) return Vw, W def transformvolumecoords(V, Tcw): # Apply extrinsic matrix to voxel centers return V.applytransform(Tcw) def computeweightvolume(Vws): # Count number of 3D points associated with each voxel return Vws.countpoints() def randomsamplepixels(depthmap, numpixels): h, w = depthmap.shape return [(random.randint(0, w-1), random.randint(0, h-1)) for in range(numpixels)] def unprojectpixel(u, v, depth, intrinsics): fx, fy = intrinsics['fx'], intrinsics['fy'] cx, cy = intrinsics['cx'], intrinsics['cy'] x = (u - cx) depth / fx y = (v - cy) depth / fy z = depth rayorigin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] raydirection = [x, y, z] normval = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in raydirection)) raydirection = [c / normval for c in raydirection] return rayorigin, raydirection def samplealongray(rayorigin, raydirection, depth, coarsedensity, finedensity): points = [] maxdist = depth # Coarse sampling along the ray coarsestep = 1.0 / coarsedensity for d in range(0, int(maxdist coarsedensity)): point = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] d coarsestep for i in range(3)] points.append(point) # Fine sampling near the measured surface finestep = 1.0 / finedensity startfine = max(0, int(maxdist coarsedensity) - 10) endfine = int(maxdist coarsedensity) + 10 for d in range(startfine, endfine): point = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] d finestep for i in range(3)] points.append(point) return points def getlatentcode(Vw, point): return Vw.interpolate(point) def decoder(latentcode, point): x = latentcode + point for size in [128, 128, 128]: x = math.tanh(sum(a b for a, b in zip(x, [1.0]len(x)))) # Simplified linear+activation return x[-1] # Final layer outputs scalar SDF def computegradient(si, sbari, decoder, Vw, point): # Standard backpropagation gradient computation return (si - sbari) 1.0 def accumulategrads(grads, grad): for k in grad: grads[k] = grads.get(k, 0.0) + grad[k] def adamstep(params, grads, lr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): # Simplified Adam update step return {k: params[k] - lr grads[k] for k in params} Parameters: Voxel Resolution: 2 cm. Latent Code Dimension: 8. Decoder Architecture: MLP with 4 fully connected layers with sizes [128, 128, 128, 1]. Sampling Density: Coarse-level: 5 3D points per meter; Fine-level: 20 3D points per meter. Pixels Sampled: 5000 pixels per image in each iteration. Optimization Iterations: 5 iterations for each image. Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Truncation Threshold (\delta): Defined in the projective TSDF formula, but a specific numerical value is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Noise: Severe depth noise causes discontinuities between neighboring implicit voxels. Trilinear interpolation among neighboring implicit voxels is used to improve border consistency, but discontinuities may still occur. Initialization: Global-level fusion initialized by local-level fusion converges in 5 iterations. Initialized randomly, it takes much longer to converge and remains inferior even after 20 iterations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a 1080Ti GPU, encoding + local-level fusion takes 0.1s total; global-level fusion for 2 iterations takes 0.5s; overall runs at ~2 fps. DI-Fusion runs at 10 fps on the same device. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Outperforms TSDF-Fusion, iMAP, and DI-Fusion on ICL-NUIM and ScanNet datasets in accuracy, completeness, and F1 score, demonstrating robustness to synthetic noise and better generalization to diverse indoor scenes. The combination of local- and global-level fusion significantly improves reconstruction quality compared to using either alone. Limitations: Slower than traditional volumetric fusion approaches (e.g., InfiniTAM v3 runs at over 30 fps on a mobile device). Severe noise can still cause discontinuities despite trilinear interpolation. When to Use: Online 3D reconstruction where global consistency is important and depth noise is present. Bi-level Fusion was introduced in the paper "BNV-Fusion: Dense 3D Reconstruction using Bi-level Neural Volume Fusion". It is an online 3D reconstruction method that uses implicit neural volumes to represent geometry. The method was evaluated on the augmented ICL-NUIM dataset, 3D Scene Dataset, and ScanNet validation set (312 sequences). For ScanNet, every 10th frame was used as input, and ground truth meshes were used as pseudo ground truth. The depth encoder and shape decoder were trained using object CAD models from two categories (chairs and lamps) in ShapeNet. name: EndoNeRF
body: EndoNeRF is a method for reconstructing deformable surgical scenes using a canonical radiance field and a time-dependent displacement field, optimized with stereo depth-cueing and supervision. It addresses non-rigid tissue reconstruction in endoscopic video by mapping input space-time coordinates to a static canonical space via a learned deformation, allowing standard volume rendering to operate on the displaced points. It explicitly models temporal deformation through a displacement field rather than a static 3D volume or explicit voxel grid, and differs from fluid dynamics-focused methods by leveraging endoscopic stereo cues. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of endoscopic images (stereo pairs) with known camera poses and timestamps \tau. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a given ray \mathbf{r} and time \tau, and the underlying scene representation (canonical field and deformation field). Data Structures: 1. Canonical Radiance Field (F\Theta): An MLP that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Architecture: 8 fully connected ReLU layers, each with 256 channels. Input encoding: Positional encoding (Fourier features) for input coordinates \mathbf{x} and time \tau. 2. Time-Dependent Displacement Field (G\Phi): An MLP that maps a 3D position \mathbf{x} and time \tau to a 3D displacement vector \Delta \mathbf{x}. Input encoding: Positional encoding for \mathbf{x} and \tau. Method Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} at time \tau, sample points along the ray using stereo depth-cueing ray marching. 2. Deformation Mapping: For each sample point \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{r}(ti), query the displacement field to find the corresponding location in the canonical space: \mathbf{x}'i = \mathbf{x}i + G\Phi(\mathbf{x}i, \tau) where G\Phi(\mathbf{x}i, \tau) is the displacement between point \mathbf{x}i at time \tau and its corresponding point in the canonical field. 3. Field Query: Query the canonical radiance field F\Theta at the displaced location \mathbf{x}'i with viewing direction \mathbf{d} to obtain density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i: (\sigmai, \mathbf{c}i) = F\Theta(\mathbf{x}'i, \mathbf{d}) 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the final color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) using the standard differentiable volume rendering equation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \deltai is the step size and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. 5. Optimization: Minimize the L2 photometric reconstruction loss between rendered images and ground truth stereo images. The optimization is supervised by stereo depth-cueing, which provides depth constraints to regularize the deformation field and improve reconstruction quality. Parameters: MLP Layers: 8 fully connected layers. MLP Channels: 256 per layer. Activation: ReLU. Loss: L2 photometric reconstruction loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resource Consumption: EndoNeRF optimizes an entire spatial-temporal field, resulting in significant time and resource consumption. Topology Changes: The displacement field approach assumes topology preservation; it may struggle with significant changes in scene topology (e.g., tissue tearing). A framework for spatio-temporal reconstruction of objects from few X-ray projections, consisting of a canonical volume assigning density to every point in 3D space and a deformation field returning a displacement for every point as a function of time. It allows querying the neural radiance field at continuous temporal and spatial locations. The deformation field is posed as a B-spline field whose time-dependent weights are obtained from a neural network, using cubic B-splines with fixed control points and time-varying weights to impose a smooth efficient prior. The canonical volume is trained using a hybrid method where projection loss is supplemented by volumetric loss based on high-fidelity X-CT data typically available at initial and final timesteps. The deformation field is trained jointly for all timesteps and with all available data. It is preferred to train the canonical volume on the final step of deformation where the maximum amount of material is present in the field of view to map material seen in projections to the canonical volume. This framework assumes deformations preserve topology. Time Complexity: High. Optimizing an entire spatial-temporal field results in significant time consumption. Memory Complexity: High. The 8-layer, 256-channel MLP for both the canonical field and displacement field requires substantial memory. Strengths: Yields high-quality non-rigid reconstruction in surgical scenes. Can model complex tissue deformations. Limitations: Significant time and resource consumption. Struggles with changes in scene topology. Inference speed may be insufficient for clinical demands compared to factorized methods like Lerplane. When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction of deformable tissue is required and computational resources are available. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is required or when scene topology changes significantly. EndoNeRF emerged as a promising solution for deformable surgical scene reconstruction, utilizing NeRF with tool-guided ray casting, stereo depth-cueing ray marching, and stereo depth-supervised optimization. It was introduced to address the limitations of previous methods in handling non-rigid tissue deformation in endoscopic video. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering and radiance field optimization. name: Fluid Motion Reconstruction Framework
head: Fluid Motion Reconstruction Pipeline, FluidMotionRestruction
body: The Fluid Motion Reconstruction Framework is a computational pipeline for reconstructing temporally coherent fluid density fields from monocular video sequences. It combines differentiable rendering for image alignment with physics-based coupled estimation to ensure temporal coherence. It builds on differentiable volume rendering principles Deformable and Dynamic Fields and explicitly models fluid dynamics and velocity to maintain physical plausibility over time. Inputs: A sequence of monocular fluid images \{I\}, where It is the image at time t. Outputs: A sequence of fluid density fields \{\rho\}. Parameters: t is the time index, t \in \mathbb{N}0, t \le F, where F is the total number of frames. The framework operates in two main components: a differentiable rendering component and a coupled density and velocity estimation component. 1. Initialization: Reconstruct the initial fluid density fields \rho1 and \rho2 using the differentiable rendering component. This aligns the volumetric representation with the first two input images I1 and I2. 2. Temporal Propagation: For subsequent frames t > 2, compute the estimated fluid density \tilde{\rho}t using the coupled density and velocity estimation component. This step ensures that fluid flows adhere to underlying physical priors. 3. Refinement: Given the estimated density \tilde{\rho}t, correct the final fluid density \rhot via the differentiable renderer using the target image It. This aligns the physically plausible estimate with the observed image data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fluidmotionreconstruction(images): # images: list of monocular fluid images [I1,..., IF] F = len(images) densities = [] # Step 1: Initialize first two frames using differentiable rendering rho1 = differentiablerender(images[0]) rho2 = differentiablerender(images[1]) densities.extend([rho1, rho2]) # Step 2 & 3: Iterate through remaining frames for t in range(2, F): # Coupled density and velocity estimation for temporal coherence rhotilde = coupleddensityvelocityestimation(densities[t-1], densities[t-2]) # Differentiable rendering correction for image alignment rhot = differentiablerender(rhotilde, images[t]) densities.append(rhot) return densities def differentiablerender(targetimage, density=None): # Standard differentiable volume rendering optimization # Minimizes rendering loss against targetimage using the emission-absorption model. # Gradients propagate through the volume rendering equation to update density and velocity. # [Comment] The exact optimization solver and loss function are not provided in the sources. return density if density is not None else targetimage def coupleddensityvelocityestimation(prevrho, prevprevrho): # [Comment] The exact physics-based coupled estimation formulation is not provided in the sources. # It enforces fluid flows to adhere to underlying physical priors for temporal coherence. return prevrho Not given in the sources. The framework is described in research on physics-based differentiable rendering for fluid modeling. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic fluid scenes from limited monocular input by integrating physical constraints with differentiable rendering.
