name: HDR-NeRF
head: High Dynamic Range Neural Radiance Fields
body: HDR-NeRF is a method for high dynamic range (HDR) view synthesis that recovers an HDR radiance field from a set of low dynamic range (LDR) training images captured with variable exposure times. It solves the problem of limited sensor dynamic range by modeling the physical imaging process as two implicit functions: a radiance field that encodes scene radiance (values from 0 to +\infty) and a learned tone mapper that predicts pixel values from radiance and exposure time. Unlike baseline NeRF, which is limited to low dynamic range outputs, HDR-NeRF enables the generation of novel HDR views and novel LDR views under arbitrary exposures, while avoiding the ghost artifacts common in traditional multi-exposure stack-based HDR synthesis when the camera is hand-held. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of LDR images \{Ii\} captured from various camera poses Pi with known exposure times \Delta ti. The exposure is defined as the product of exposure time and radiance. Outputs: An HDR radiance field capable of rendering novel views at arbitrary exposure times, producing both HDR radiance values and tone-mapped LDR pixel values. Data Structures: The method consists of two neural network modules: 1. Radiance Field (F): An eight-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 256 channels per layer. It maps a 5D input (ray origin \mathbf{o}=(x,y,z) and ray direction \mathbf{d}=(\theta,\phi)) to a 4D output: HDR radiance \mathbf{e} \in 0, \infty) and density \sigma. 2. Tone Mapper: Three separate one-layer MLPs, each with 128 channels. These process the Red, Green, and Blue channels independently because RGB channels are tone-mapped with different Camera Response Functions (CRFs). The tone mapper takes the radiance \mathbf{e} and exposure time \Delta t as inputs to predict the final pixel color \mathbf{c}. Positional Encoding: To handle high-frequency variations in color and geometry, positional encoding is applied to the ray origins and ray directions, identical to the baseline NeRF strategy. Sampling Strategy: The method optimizes two models: a coarse model and a fine model, where densities from the coarse model bias the sampling of the fine model. The coarse model samples 64 points along each ray. The fine model samples 128 points for synthetic datasets and 64 points for real-world datasets. Formulas: The expected color \widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}) of a ray \mathbf{r} is computed via volume rendering: \widehat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \int{sn}^{sf} T(s) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(s), \mathbf{d}) \, ds \quad (1) where sn and sf are the near and far boundaries of the ray, and T(s) is the accumulated transmittance: T(s) = \exp \left( - \int{sp}^s \sigma(\mathbf{r}(p)) \, dp \right) \quad (2) The radiance field F outputs the HDR radiance \mathbf{e} and density \sigma: (\mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r}), \sigma(\mathbf{r})) = F(\mathbf{r}) \quad (5) The tone mapper models the Camera Response Function (CRF). The relationship between pixel value Z, irradiance H (approximated as radiance \mathbf{e}), and exposure time \Delta t is: Z = f(H\Delta t) \quad (4) To optimize the network, the method operates in the logarithmic domain. Assuming the tone mapper f is monotonic and invertible, the color prediction for a specific channel is derived from: \ln f^{-1}(\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t)) = \ln \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{r}) + \ln \Delta t(\mathbf{r}) \quad (7) Loss Function: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a combination of Color Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}c) and Unit Exposure Loss (\mathcal{L}u): \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}c + \lambdau \mathcal{L}u \quad (13) 1. Color Reconstruction Loss (\mathcal{L}c): Minimizes the [Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the rendered LDR views and the ground truth LDR views for both coarse and fine models: \mathcal{L}c = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{P})} \left( \|\widehat{C}c(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t) - C(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t)\|2^2 + \|\widehat{C}f(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t) - C(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t)\|2^2 \right) where \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{P}) is the set of camera rays at target position \mathbf{P}, and C(\mathbf{r}, \Delta t) is the ground truth pixel value. 2. Unit Exposure Loss (\mathcal{L}u): Constrains the tone mapper output g(0) to a constant C0 to fix the scale factor. This assumes pixels with value C0 correspond to unit exposure: \mathcal{L}u = \|g(0) - C0\|2^2 The weight \lambdau is fixed at 0.5. The constant C0 is set to 0.5 for real scenes (midway of pixel values) and to C{GT0} (the pixel value of the ground truth CRF when input logarithm radiance is 0) for synthetic scenes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def posenc(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, includeinput=True): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg)]) xb = torch.reshape((x.float()[:, None,:] scales[None,:, None]), (x.shape[0], -1, x.shape[1])) freqbands = 2 torch.pi xb enc = torch.cat((torch.sin(freqbands), torch.cos(freqbands)), dim=-1) if includeinput: enc = torch.cat((x, enc), dim=-1) return enc class RadianceFieldMLP(nn.Module): """Eight-layer MLP with 256 channels.""" def init(self): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(8): inch = 5 if i == 0 else 256 layers.append(nn.Linear(inch, 256)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(256, 4)) self.net = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, xyzdir): out = self.net(xyzdir) return out[:,:3], out[:, 3] # e, sigma class ToneMapperMLP(nn.Module): """One-layer MLP with 128 channels.""" def init(self): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1)) def forward(self, loge, logdt): return self.net(torch.cat([loge, logdt], dim=1)) def volumerendering(rayso, raysd, near, far, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb, dt, numsamples, coarseweights=None): """Renders a ray using discrete volume integration.""" if coarseweights is None: tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples) zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals else: # Importance sampling from coarse weights zvalsmid = (zvals[:-1] + zvals[1:]) / 2.0 zvals = torch.cat([zvals[:1], zvalsmid, zvals[-1:]], dim=-1) zvals = zvals coarseweights + (1. - coarseweights) zvals pts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) ptsflat = pts.reshape(-1, 3) ptsenc = posenc(ptsflat) raysdenc = posenc(raysd) inputpts = torch.cat([ptsenc, raysdenc.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples, -1)], dim=-1) inputpts = inputpts.reshape(pts.shape[0], -1, inputpts.shape[1]) e, sigma = radiancefield(inputpts) deltas = zvals[1:] - zvals[:-1] alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma[:,:-1] deltas) transmittances = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphas + 1e-10, dim=1) transmittances = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(transmittances[:,:1]), transmittances], dim=1) weights = alphas transmittances[:,:-1] loge = torch.log(e + 1e-8) logdt = torch.log(dt + 1e-8).unsqueeze(0).expand(loge.shape[0], 1) logcr = tonemapperr(torch.cat([loge[:,:,0:1], logdt], dim=1)) logcg = tonemapperg(torch.cat([loge[:,:,1:2], logdt], dim=1)) logcb = tonemapperb(torch.cat([loge[:,:,2:3], logdt], dim=1)) c = torch.exp(torch.cat([logcr, logcg, logcb], dim=2)) C = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) c, dim=1) return C, sigma, weights def trainstep(rayso, raysd, near, far, gtcolors, dt, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb): """Single training step.""" # Coarse rendering Ccoarse, sigmacoarse, weightscoarse = volumerendering(rayso, raysd, near, far, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb, dt, 64) # Fine rendering (coarse densities bias fine sampling) Cfine, sigmafine, = volumerendering(rayso, raysd, near, far, radiancefield, tonemapperr, tonemapperg, tonemapperb, dt, 128, weightscoarse) # Color Reconstruction Loss lossc = torch.sum((Ccoarse - gtcolors)2) + torch.sum((Cfine - gtcolors)2) # Unit Exposure Loss: evaluate tone mapper at logradiance=0, logexposure=0 gr = tonemapperr(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, 1), torch.zeros(1, 1)], dim=1)) gg = tonemapperg(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, 1), torch.zeros(1, 1)], dim=1)) gb = tonemapperb(torch.cat([torch.zeros(1, 1), torch.zeros(1, 1)], dim=1)) C0 = 0.5 lossu = (gr - C0)2 + (gg - C0)2 + (gb - C0)2 return lossc + 0.5 lossu Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Frequency Details: Naively feeding 5D coordinates into the MLP results in renderings that struggle to represent high-frequency variation in color and geometry; positional encoding is required. Ghost Artifacts: Traditional multi-exposure HDR methods produce ghost artifacts when the camera is hand-held or the scene is dynamic. HDR-NeRF handles varying camera poses implicitly through the radiance field, avoiding this issue. Channel-Specific CRFs: RGB channels are tone-mapped with different CRFs. Using a single MLP for all channels degrades performance; three separate MLPs are necessary. Scale Ambiguity: Without the Unit Exposure Loss, the scale of the recovered radiance field is ambiguous. The constraint g(0)=C0 fixes this scale. Time Complexity: Training requires 200K iterations on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU, taking approximately one day. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Synthetic Scenes: PSNR 39.07, SSIM 0.973, LPIPS 0.026 for LDR-OE (exposures t1, t3, t5). Real Scenes: PSNR 30.37, SSIM 0.944, LPIPS 0.075 for LDR-OE (exposures t1, t3, t5). Strengths: Recovers HDR radiance fields from LDR images without requiring HDR ground truth supervision. Enables novel view synthesis with arbitrary exposure control. Handles non-rigid scenes and camera motion better than stack-based methods by learning a continuous 3D representation. Limitations: Requires known exposure times from EXIF metadata. Performance on real-world scenes is lower than on synthetic scenes, likely due to unmodeled noise and complex lighting. Cannot render views with novel exposure times if the training data does not cover the desired exposure range effectively, though it interpolates better than NeRF-W. HDR-NeRF was introduced by Xin Huang, Qi Zhang, Ying Feng, Hongdong Li, Xuan Wang, and Qing Wang, with work conducted during an internship at Tencent AI Lab. It was published in November 2021. The method builds upon the baseline NeRF [1] and addresses the limitations of NeRF's low dynamic range output and the view-inconsistency of image-based HDR methods. It differs from "NeRF in the Dark" (RawNeRF), which recovers radiance fields from raw noisy images, by using LDR images with variable exposures. It also improves upon NeRF-W, which cannot render novel exposure times, by explicitly modeling exposure time \Delta t. The method was evaluated on a new forward-facing HDR dataset containing synthetic scenes (rendered with Blender) and real-world scenes captured by a digital camera. Neural Radiance Fields in 3D Vision: A Comprehensive Review, https://doi.org/10.26599/cvm.2026.9450535, fetched 2026-10-28 HDR-NeRF: High Dynamic Range Neural Radiance Fields, https://xhuangcv.github.io/hdr-nerf/, fetched 2026-10-27

name: GNeuVox
head: General Neural Voxels, Generalizable Neural Voxels
body: GNeuVox is a differentiable volume rendering framework for fast human radiance field optimization that replaces implicit MLPs with explicit neural voxel grids to accelerate training from hours to minutes. It distinguishes itself by maintaining two separate voxel grids: general voxels (Vg) pretrained across multiple subjects to provide geometric priors, and individual voxels (Vi) optimized per subject to capture unique differential textures. This separation allows the model to converge rapidly during fine-tuning while maintaining rendering quality comparable to methods requiring significantly longer training times. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Monocular video frames of a human subject, initial pose estimates P (joint positions J and rotation angles \Omega), camera intrinsics, and ray origins/directions. Outputs: Rendered pixel colors \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and densities \sigma for novel views. Data Structures: 1. General Voxel Grid (Vg): A 3D tensor of shape Cv \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Cv = 6 (feature channels). Nx = Ny = Nz = 160 (resolution). Initialized via pretraining on multiple subjects. 2. Individual Voxel Grid (Vi): A 3D tensor of shape Cv \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Initialized to zero for each new subject. 3. Deformation Embedding (Z): A learnable vector/tensor used to compute blend weights for the deformation network. Initialized to zero for each new subject. 4. Radiance Field (\Phir): A small MLP mapping concatenated voxel features, encoded coordinates, direction, and timestamp to color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma. Numbered Steps: 1. Pose Refinement: Correct the initial pose P = (J, \Omega) to Pc = (Jc, \Omegac) using a pose refinement network \Phip. Pc = (J, \Omega \otimes \Delta\Omega) where \Delta\Omega = \Phip(\Omega), and \otimes denotes the composition of rotation matrices and translation vectors: (Ri \cdot \Delta Ri, Ti + \Delta Ti). 2. Coordinate Deformation: Map observation space coordinates \mathbf{x}o = (xo, yo, zo) to canonical T-pose coordinates \mathbf{x}c = (xc, yc, zc) using the pose deformation network \mathbf{F}d. \mathbf{x}c = \mathbf{F}d(\mathbf{x}o, Pc) The deformation is defined as a weighted sum of rigid transformations: T{skel}(\mathbf{x}, Pc) = \sum{i=1}^K w^i(\mathbf{x})(Rc^i \mathbf{x} + Tc^i) where w^i(\mathbf{x}) are blend weights obtained by mapping the embedding Z through 3D convolutional layers and trilinear interpolation. 3. Voxel Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation on the canonical coordinates \mathbf{x}c to extract feature vectors from both voxel grids. \mathbf{v}g = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}c, Vg) \mathbf{v}i = \text{interp}(\mathbf{x}c, Vi) where \text{interp} denotes multi-distance interpolation (MDI). 4. Feature Concatenation and Encoding: Concatenate the features: \mathbf{v}{cat} = [\mathbf{v}g; \mathbf{v}i]. Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the voxel features, coordinates, and direction. Voxel features \mathbf{v}: Frequency L=2. Coordinates (x, y, z): Frequency L=10. Direction \mathbf{d}: Frequency L=4. \gamma(\mathbf{x}) = (\sin(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^0 \mathbf{x}), \dots, \sin(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x}), \cos(2^{L-1} \mathbf{x})). 5. Radiance Field Prediction: Feed the encoded voxel features, encoded coordinates, direction \mathbf{d}, and timestamp t into the radiance field \Phir. \mathbf{c}, \sigma = \Phir(\gamma(\mathbf{v}g), \gamma(\mathbf{v}i), \gamma(t), \gamma(\mathbf{x}o), \gamma(\mathbf{d})). 6. Volume Rendering: Sample N=128 points along each ray. Compute transmittance Ti and alpha \alphai. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 7. Loss Computation: \mathcal{L} = \lambdaM \|\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r})\|2^2 + \lambdaL \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} where \mathcal{L}{LPIPS} is computed on G=6 patches of size 32 \times 32. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with \beta=(0.9, 0.99). Learning Rates: Voxel grids (Vg, Vi): 2 \times 10^{-2}. Radiance field \Phir: 5 \times 10^{-4}. Other parameters: 5 \times 10^{-5}. LR Decay: Factor of 0.1 every 500k iterations. Loss Weights: Pretraining/Scratch: \lambdaM=0.2, \lambdaL=1. Fine-tuning (first 300 iters): \lambdaM=10, \lambdaL=0. Fine-tuning (remaining): \lambdaM=0.2, \lambdaL=1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class GNeuVox: def init(self, voxelres=160, featuredim=6, numbones=24): self.voxelres = voxelres self.featuredim = featuredim self.numbones = numbones # General Voxels (Pretrained) self.Vg = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(featuredim, voxelres, voxelres, voxelres)) # Individual Voxels (Per-subject, zero-init) self.Vi = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(featuredim, voxelres, voxelres, voxelres)) # Deformation Embedding (Per-subject, zero-init) self.Z = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, 1, 1)) # Pose Refinement Network (Shared) self.poserefine = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(1, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv3d(64, 1, 3, padding=1)) # Deformation Network (Shared) self.deformnet = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv3d(1, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv3d(64, numbones, 3, padding=1)) # Radiance Field MLP self.radiancemlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(featuredim 2 20 + 20 + 20 + 20, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3), nn.Sigmoid()) self.densitymlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(featuredim 2 20 + 20 + 20 + 20, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1)) def positionalencoding(self, x, L): """Standard positional encoding.""" freqbands = 2.0 torch.linspace(0, L-1, L).to(x.device) x = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands x = torch.cat([torch.sin(x), torch.cos(x)], dim=-1) return x.flatten(1) def refinepose(self, P, deltaomega): """Correct initial pose P using delta rotation/translation.""" # P contains joint positions J and rotations Omega # deltaomega contains delta rotations and translations # Returns corrected pose Pc = (J, Omega @ deltaomega) # Simplified implementation for demonstration Pc = P.clone() # Apply delta rotation to joints return Pc def deformcoordinates(self, xo, Pc, Z): """Deform observation coordinates to canonical space.""" # Get blend weights from Z via conv layers w = self.deformnet(Z) # Apply rigid transformations derived from Pc xc = torch.zeroslike(xo) for i in range(self.numbones): # Rc^i, Tc^i derived from Pc # xc += w^i(xo) (Rc^i @ xo + Tc^i) # Note: Exact bone transformation derivation from Pc is not specified in sources pass return xc def interpolatevoxels(self, xc, V): """Trilinear interpolation of voxel grid.""" # Normalize coordinates to [-1, 1] xnorm = 2.0 xc - 1.0 # Grid sample with trilinear interpolation v = F.gridsample(V.unsqueeze(0), xnorm.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), mode='trilinear', aligncorners=True) return v.squeeze() def forward(self, rayso, raysd, P, Z, t): """ rayso: (Nrays, 3) raysd: (Nrays, 3) P: Initial pose Z: Deformation embedding t: Timestamp """ # 1. Pose Refinement deltaomega = self.poserefine(Z) Pc = self.refinepose(P, deltaomega) # 2. Deformation # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0, 1, 128).to(rayso.device) pointso = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) # Deform to canonical space pointsc = self.deformcoordinates(pointso, Pc, Z) # 3. Interpolation vg = self.interpolatevoxels(pointsc, self.Vg) vi = self.interpolatevoxels(pointsc, self.Vi) # 4. Encoding vcat = torch.cat([vg, vi], dim=-1) encv = self.positionalencoding(vcat, L=2) encx = self.positionalencoding(pointso, L=10) encd = self.positionalencoding(raysd, L=4) enct = self.positionalencoding(t.unsqueeze(1), L=2) inputfeat = torch.cat([encv, encx, encd, enct], dim=-1) # 5. Radiance Field sigma = self.densitymlp(inputfeat) color = self.radiancemlp(inputfeat) # 6. Rendering delta = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta.unsqueeze(-1)) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha[:,:-1]], dim=1), dim=1) rendercolor = torch.sum(T alpha color, dim=1) return rendercolor, sigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Collapse: Training from scratch can lead to collapse or big variance in quantitative results. Pretrained general voxels alleviate this by providing prior knowledge for stable fitting. Face Rendering Vagueness and Distortion: Due to few fine-tuning iterations (≤3k) and reliance on SMPL pose/skeleton priors, complex non-rigid deformations of the face are hard to learn accurately. Boundary Conditions: Trilinear interpolation requires coordinates to be within the voxel grid bounds; out-of-bounds coordinates should be handled (e.g., clamped or padded). Explicit 3D feature grids that replace implicit MLPs for faster optimization. They store learnable features at discrete grid points and use interpolation for continuous queries. Choose when training speed is critical and the scene has a bounded volume. Link Networks that map observation-space coordinates to a canonical space using skeletal priors. They enable the representation of dynamic humans in a static canonical frame. Choose when dealing with articulated subjects like humans. Link Methods that learn a shared representation across multiple instances (e.g., different humans) to enable fast adaptation to new instances. Choose when you need to render novel instances with minimal per-instance training time. Link Time Complexity: Pretraining takes 15-50 minutes on multiple subjects. Fine-tuning for a new subject takes 1-5 minutes (1k-3k iterations). This is significantly faster than implicit NeRF methods which take hours to days (e.g., HumanNeRF takes 288 hours). Memory Complexity: Requires storing two 160^3 voxel grids with 6 channels each. This is more memory-intensive than compact MLPs but allows for faster gradient updates due to explicit structure. Performance: On ZJU-MoCap, GNeuVox-ZJU achieves PSNR 29.93 in 5 minutes, comparable to HumanNeRF (30.41 PSNR, 288 hours). Strengths: Extremely fast training time; explicit representation allows for easier debugging and modification; generalization across subjects. Limitations: Face rendering shows vagueness and distortion to some degree due to limited fine-tuning iterations and reliance on SMPL priors. When to Use: When rapid training of human radiance fields from monocular video is required, and high-frequency facial details are less critical than overall body shape and motion. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity facial animation is required, or when the scene volume is unbounded or highly irregular, making voxel grid definition difficult. GNeuVox was introduced in the paper "Generalizable Neural Voxels for Fast Human Radiance Fields". It builds upon concepts from Anim-NeRF, Neural Body, and HumanNeRF, which established the use of pose deformation and canonical space for human rendering. The key innovation is the introduction of generalizable neural voxels, which leverage the commonalities among human bodies (e.g., basic skeleton) to accelerate optimization. The method addresses the high computational cost of previous NeRF-based human rendering methods, which often require hours or days of training. Generalizable Neural Voxels for Fast Human Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.15387, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: NeRFifyMesh
body: NeRFifyMesh is a pipeline for converting textured 3D mesh models into Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by generating a ground-truth point-based radiance field from mesh geometry and texture. It eliminates the need for multi-view image rendering or camera pose supervision during training, making it suitable for robotics scene building where mesh assets are abundant. Unlike Neural Radiance Fields or Instant-NGP which optimize photometric loss from images, NeRFifyMesh decouples color, normals, and opacity into separate networks trained directly on mesh-derived samples. This results in lower PSNR but superior perceptual similarity (LPIPS) and explicit surface normal prediction. Inputs: A textured mesh model \Omega with surface S, texture images, and vertex normals. Outputs: Three neural networks: f\theta (color), f\phi (normals), and f\zeta \circ f\psi (opacity), along with saved voxel indices I. Data Structures: 1. Surface Voxel Grids: N grids G1, \dots, GN. 2. Hash Tables: Hl for each grid level l. 3. Default Latent Vector: v{l, \text{default}} for points outside the occupied voxel region of Gl. 4. Voxel Indices: I = [i,j,k] for occupied voxels in each Gl, saved with the model to allow reconstruction without the original mesh. Parameters: \tau: Threshold parameter for importance weighting. Typical value: 0.1. N: Number of grid levels. Training iterations: 300,000. Batch size: 4,096 samples. Samples per mesh: 2 million points (inside, outside, on surface). Assumptions: 1. Mesh appearance is view-independent (view-direction parameters \phi, \theta are omitted). 2. Meshes are opaque (opacity is binary). Steps: 1. Generate Ground Truth Data: Sample points x=(x,y,z) within the bounding box of \Omega. Calculate Signed Distance Function (SDF) for each point. Let S be the mesh surface and (x', y', z') be the nearest point on S. Color/Normal GT: c{gt}(x) = \begin{cases} cS(x', y', z') & \text{if } SDF < 0 \\ cS(x, y, z) & \text{if } SDF = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} \vec{n}{gt}(x) = \begin{cases} \vec{n}S(x', y', z') & \text{if } SDF < 0 \\ \vec{n}S(x, y, z) & \text{if } SDF = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} where cS is texture color and \vec{n}S is barycentrically interpolated vertex normal. Opacity GT: \alpha{gt}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } SDF \le 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} Importance Weights: wc(x) = w{\vec{n}}(x) = \begin{cases} \exp(-|SDF|/\tau) & \text{if } SDF \le 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} w\alpha(x) = \begin{cases} \exp(-|SDF|/\tau) & \text{if } SDF \le 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } SDF > 0 \end{cases} These weights prioritize points near the surface and suppress external points. 2. Initialize Opacity Network: Initialize N surface voxel grids G1, \dots, GN from mesh surface points. Assign trainable latent vectors vl[i,j,k] (dim 2) to grid vertices corresponding to occupied voxels. Save indices I. 3. Train Networks: Color/Normal Networks: Apply positional encoding (sine/cosine) to input x. Feed to f\theta (color) and f\phi (normals), composed of SIREN layers. Opacity Network: 1. Query each grid Gl: Multiply x by resolution Rl. If x \in Gl, use corner indices as hash keys to retrieve vl from Hl. Else, use v{l, \text{default}}. 2. Trilinearly interpolate to get v'l(x). 3. Concatenate: V(x) = [v'1(x), \dots, v'N(x)]. 4. Decode: f\psi(V(x)). 5. Predict Opacity: \alpha(x) = f\zeta([f\psi(V(x)), x]). 4. Loss Functions: Color Loss: Lc = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n w{c,i} (ci - c{gt,i})^2. Normal Loss: L{\vec{n}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n w{\vec{n},i} (1 - \cos \deltai)^2, where \cos \deltai = \vec{n}{gt,i} \cdot \vec{n}i. Opacity Loss: L\alpha = \lambda1 L{BCE} + \lambda2 L{reg}. L{BCE} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum{i=1}^n w{\alpha,i} [\alpha{gt,i} \log \alphai + (1-\alpha{gt,i}) \log(1-\alphai)] L{reg} = \sum{l=1}^N \|vl\|^2 \lambda1, \lambda2 are weighting terms. 5. Rendering: Sample points \{ti\}{i=1}^M along camera rays with intervals \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Color: \hat{C}(r) \approx \sum{i=1}^M Ti \alphai ci. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10): """Standard NeRF positional encoding.""" scales = [2i for i in range(numfrequencies)] scaledx = np.outer(x, scales) encoded = np.concatenate([np.sin(scaledx), np.cos(scaledx)], axis=-1) return np.concatenate([x, encoded], axis=-1) def trilinearinterpolate(v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111, xfrac): """Trilinear interpolation of 8 corner vectors.""" x, y, z = xfrac v00 = v000 (1-x) + v100 x v01 = v010 (1-x) + v110 x v10 = v001 (1-x) + v101 x v11 = v011 (1-x) + v111 x v0 = v00 (1-y) + v01 y v1 = v10 (1-y) + v11 y return v0 (1-z) + v1 z def getopacityfeatures(x, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors): """Get concatenated features for opacity network.""" features = [] for l, resolution in enumerate(grids): indices = np.floor(x resolution).astype(int) if np.all((indices >= 0) & (indices < resolution)): corners = [] for dx in [0, 1]: for dy in [0, 1]: for dz in [0, 1]: idx = indices + np.array([dx, dy, dz]) key = tuple(idx) corners.append(hashtables[l].get(key, defaultvectors[l])) frac = x resolution - indices vinterp = trilinearinterpolate(corners, frac) features.append(vinterp) else: features.append(defaultvectors[l]) return np.concatenate(features, axis=-1) def computesdfweights(sdf, tau=0.1): """Compute importance weights based on SDF.""" abssdf = np.abs(sdf) wcn = np.where(sdf <= 0, np.exp(-abssdf / tau), 0.0) walpha = np.where(sdf <= 0, np.exp(-abssdf / tau), 1.0) return wcn, walpha def trainstep(samples, sdf, gtcolor, gtnormal, gtopacity, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors, colornet, normalnet, opacitynet, tau, lambda1=1.0, lambda2=1.0): """Single training step.""" wcn, walpha = computesdfweights(sdf, tau) encx = positionalencoding(samples) predcolor = colornet(encx) prednormal = normalnet(encx) features = getopacityfeatures(samples, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors) opacityinput = np.concatenate([features, samples], axis=-1) predopacity = opacitynet(opacityinput).squeeze(-1) colorloss = np.mean(wcn (predcolor - gtcolor)2) cossim = np.sum(prednormal gtnormal, axis=-1) cossim = np.clip(cossim, -1.0, 1.0) normalloss = np.mean(wcn (1 - cossim)2) eps = 1e-7 predopacityclamped = np.clip(predopacity, eps, 1-eps) bce = -np.mean(walpha (gtopacity np.log(predopacityclamped) + (1 - gtopacity) np.log(1 - predopacityclamped))) regloss = 0.0 for table in hashtables.values(): for vec in table.values(): regloss += np.sum(vec2) totalopacityloss = lambda1 bce + lambda2 regloss return colorloss, normalloss, totalopacityloss def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, maxdist, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors, colornet, normalnet, opacitynet, numsamples=128): """Render a single ray.""" tvals = np.linspace(0.0, maxdist, numsamples) points = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, np.newaxis] encx = positionalencoding(points) predcolor = colornet(encx) features = getopacityfeatures(points, grids, hashtables, defaultvectors) opacityinput = np.concatenate([features, points], axis=-1) predopacity = opacitynet(opacityinput).squeeze(-1) transmittance = np.ones(numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples): transmittance[i] = transmittance[i-1] (1 - predopacity[i-1]) weights = transmittance predopacity finalcolor = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] predcolor, axis=0) return finalcolor A method for assembling multiple independent radiance-field models (specifically NeRFifyMesh or iVR-GS representations) into a single unified global scene without retraining. It solves the problem of scalable scene building by allowing pre-converted mesh-based models to be placed in a global coordinate system or integrated with existing NeRF models. It differs from monolithic training approaches by treating each model as an independent, transformable primitive that is composited at render time via depth-based blending. A hybrid representation method that combines a textured mesh with a sparse voxel grid to achieve real-time view synthesis while preserving comprehensive scene information. It solves the trade-off between the geometric precision of meshes and the volumetric completeness of neural radiance fields by using the mesh for surface details and the voxels for thin structures and background volume. Unlike Adaptive Shells, which constrain volume rendering to regions near the surface, Vosh allows pure volume rendering where necessary, making it suitable for outdoor scenes. It differs from VMesh by reconstructing a volumetric density field, enabling the mesh to represent thin structures like fishing nets that are difficult to capture with Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). A neural radiance field representation that synthesizes novel images efficiently using standard polygon rasterization pipelines, avoiding specialized volumetric ray marching. It represents the NeRF as a set of textured polygons with binary opacities and feature vectors, interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color. Unlike classic NeRF which uses volumetric density compositing, MobileNeRF uses opacity compositing on a mesh. Unlike semi-transparent mesh rendering which requires per-frame sorting, MobileNeRF uses binary opacity and z-buffering, which is order-independent. It is 10x faster than SNeRG with the same output quality and consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures. A surface estimation technique used in point cloud rendering to determine the precise 3D position of a ray-surface intersection from discrete point data. It solves the problem of inaccurate depth sampling in sparse or noisy point clouds by correcting the raw depth value based on the angle between the viewing ray and the scene's primary axis. Unlike standard depth buffering which assumes a planar intersection perpendicular to the view ray, this method accounts for surface orientation, enabling photorealistic rendering from discrete points by providing accurate input coordinates for subsequent neural radiance mapping. It serves as the foundational geometry estimation step in the End-to-End Rendering Pipeline, preceding the frequency-modulated radiance mapping stage. A method to fill a user-selected area on a neural implicit field with a texture template (e.g., furry hair or golden metal) from a pre-captured object model. First, the target UV-map of the selected area is obtained by unwrapping in Blender. A texture template from a pre-trained NeuMesh model (e.g., a small squared patch with ~10 vertices) is repeatedly filled into the target UV-map in a sliding-window manner. Texture codes in target vertices are assigned with interpolated codes from the template, and the radiance decoder is bound to the one from the pretrained model because target and template texture codes do not share the same latent radiance space. For smooth transitions near the area boundary, color contributions from different decoders are fused with inverse distance weighting for query points having texture codes/decoders from different sources. A method to attach realistic surface structures modeled by NeRFs onto a 3D mesh by deforming a voxel grid and using a deformation field. First, a scene is synthesized on a plane with desired lighting using a specific shading map guider. The corresponding voxel grid is deformed to match the 3D mesh using a deformation field \Psi: x \rightarrow \Delta x, which maps points in the deformed space to the canonical space. The deformation field is bent to synthesize a large-scale V(d) onto the 3D mesh, and a ray-tracing-based method computes the shading map guider on the surface. The shading map guider synthesizes a new scene with desired lighting and deforms it to match the target mesh surface. The ARAP parametric method establishes the mapping between the 3D mesh and the undersurface of the scene, defining corresponding directions for each vertex along the normal direction to collect discrete corresponding points. A neural network fits the deformation field using MSE loss on the coordinates of corresponding points as supervision. Time and Memory Complexity: Training time: ~2 hours per model on an NVIDIA P100 GPU with 50 GB RAM. Model Size: 4.7 ± 0.2 MB on the Objaverse dataset, achieving a 14.4x compression ratio compared to the original mesh size of 67.3 ± 60.6 MB. Memory usage depends on the number of hash table entries and grid levels. Measured Performance (Objaverse dataset): PSNR: 31.70 (lower than Instant-NGP 35.62 and NeRF 32.20). LPIPS: 0.037 (better than Instant-NGP 0.043 and NeRF 0.083). SSIM: 0.958 (better than NeRF 0.927, lower than Instant-NGP 0.965). Surface Normal Accuracy: RMSAE of 4.59 ± 1.84 degrees. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: No need for multi-view images or camera poses. Explicit surface normal prediction enables relighting. High perceptual quality (LPIPS). Significant model compression. Limitations: Lower PSNR compared to image-optimized methods. Assumes view-independent appearance and opaque meshes. Requires watertight meshes for SDF calculation. When to use: When converting existing mesh assets (e.g., from Objaverse, Poly Haven) to NeRFs for robotics or simulation. When explicit normals are needed for shading/relighting. When model size is a constraint. When not to use: When photometric accuracy (PSNR) is the primary metric. For scenes with translucent objects or view-dependent effects (e.g., glossy reflections). NeRFifyMesh was introduced to address the need for tools to convert existing 3D mesh models into NeRF representations for rapid algorithm development and testing, particularly in robotics. It builds on the principles of Radiance-field optimization but diverges by using mesh-derived ground truth instead of image-based optimization. The method leverages hash encoding inspired by Instant-NGP and SIREN networks for color/normal prediction. name: Scene Composition
head: Composed iVR-GS
body: Scene Composition assembles multiple independent radiance-field models (NeRFifyMesh or iVR-GS representations) into a unified global scene without retraining. It solves scalable scene building by allowing pre-converted mesh-based models to be placed in a global coordinate system or integrated with existing NeRF models. It differs from monolithic training approaches by treating each model as an independent, transformable primitive composited at render time. Inputs: N pre-trained local radiance-field models (NeRFifyMesh or iVR-GS). For each model i, a pose transformation matrix T{wi} \in SE(3) defining its position and orientation in the global world frame. For iVR-GS models: quantized attribute data, exact values for mean \mu and normal n, shared codebook indices for other attributes, and a global palette color cp. Outputs: A single composed radiance field representation. Rendered 2D images with correct occlusion handling between models. Data Structures: Local Model Parameters: NeRFifyMesh stores implicit neural network weights. iVR-GS stores explicit Gaussian primitives with \mu (exact floats), n (exact floats), other attributes (shared codebook indices), and cp (global palette color). Global Scene List: A single parameter list formed by concatenating the decompressed attribute values of all primitives from all basic models. Steps: 1. Normalization: Each NeRFifyMesh model is normalized to fit within a unit cube and defined in a local coordinate frame. 2. Storage (iVR-GS specific): Save exact values of \mu and n, and indices with shared codebooks for other attributes for each editable Gaussian. Store palette color cp as a global parameter for each basic scene. 3. Ray Casting: Cast rays from a virtual camera in the global frame. The ray is defined as rw(t) = ow + t\vec{d}w, where ow is ray origin and \vec{d}w is ray direction. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the world-frame ray into the local coordinate frame of each model i using the inverse transformation: ri(t) = T^{-1}{wi} rw(t), where T{wi} \in SE(3) is the pose of model i in the world frame. 5. Local Evaluation: Evaluate each local NeRF model using the transformed ray ri(t). Each model returns RGB and depth values for the transformed rays. 6. Decompression and Composition (iVR-GS specific): Decompress each model from the quantized format and append attribute values of primitives from basic iVR-GS models into a single parameter list to form the composed model. 7. Depth-Based Blending: Composite per-model renderings in the 2D image plane using depth-based ordering to resolve occlusions. For each pixel, blend RGB outputs from different models back-to-front using the corresponding depth values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def invertse3(T): # T is a 4x4 list of lists representing an SE(3) matrix. # Returns the inverse matrix. R = [T[i][:3] for i in range(3)] t = [T[i][3] for i in range(3)] Rt = [[R[j][i] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)] invt = [-sum(Rt[i][j] t[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] inv = [[0.0] 4 for in range(4)] for i in range(3): inv[i][:3] = Rt[i] inv[i][3] = invt[i] inv[3][3] = 1.0 return inv def transformpoint(M, p): x, y, z = p return (M[0][0]x + M[0][1]y + M[0][2]z + M[0][3], M[1][0]x + M[1][1]y + M[1][2]z + M[1][3], M[2][0]x + M[2][1]y + M[2][2]z + M[2][3]) def transformvector(M, v): x, y, z = v return (M[0][0]x + M[0][1]y + M[0][2]z, M[1][0]x + M[1][1]y + M[1][2]z, M[2][0]x + M[2][1]y + M[2][2]z) def composeandrender(models, cameraorigin, cameradirection, poses): # Step 3 & 4: Cast ray and transform to local frames results = [] for i, model in enumerate(models): Tinv = invertse3(poses[i]) localorigin = transformpoint(Tinv, cameraorigin) localdir = transformvector(Tinv, cameradirection) # Step 5: Local evaluation # The sources do not specify the exact evaluation routine; standard radiance field sampling is used. rgb, depth = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 # Placeholder for model.evaluate() results.append({'rgb': rgb, 'depth': depth}) # Step 7: Depth-based blending results.sort(key=lambda r: r['depth'], reverse=True) finalrgb = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for res in results: rgb = res['rgb'] alpha = res.get('alpha', 1.0) finalrgb = [finalrgb[j] + rgb[j] alpha (1.0 - sum(finalrgb[k] for k in range(3))) for j in range(3)] return finalrgb def composeivrgsmodels(basicmodels): # Step 6: Decompress and append primitives composedprimitives = [] for model in basicmodels: decompressed = model.decompress() composedprimitives.extend(decompressed.primitives) return composedprimitives Parameters: T{wi}: Pose matrix. Not given in the sources. Depth threshold: Not given in the sources. Early termination threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Incorrect depth sorting leads to visual artifacts where models intersect incorrectly. Depth-based ordering is critical. Coordinate Systems: Failure to correctly invert T{wi} results in models appearing in wrong positions or orientations. Quantization Loss (iVR-GS): While VQ provides ~4× compression, decompression must be exact for \mu and n to maintain geometric fidelity. Boundary Artifacts: Models normalized to a unit cube may have discontinuities at their boundaries if not handled by the underlying radiance field. Time Complexity: Rendering time scales linearly with the number of models N and the number of primitives per model. Each ray must be evaluated against all models before blending. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is the sum of the memory required for all individual models. For iVR-GS, this includes the decompressed primitives and codebooks. Performance: The composition pipeline itself is lightweight; the cost is dominated by the individual model evaluations. NeRFifyMesh models capture interior features due to geometry-based sampling. Strengths: Enables real-time scene editing for iVR-GS by adjusting editable Gaussian attributes. Allows modular scene building without retraining. Limitations: Requires pre-computation/normalization of each model. Occlusion handling is simplified to depth-based blending, which may not account for complex inter-model lighting or shadows. Scene Composition was introduced as part of the NeRFifyMesh pipeline and the iVR-GS framework. NeRFifyMesh was developed to convert textured mesh models into NeRF representations for robotics scene building, addressing the need for scalable scene assembly. iVR-GS extended this concept to editable 3D Gaussian Splatting, allowing for composability and real-time editing. iVR-GS: Inverse Volume Rendering for Explorable Visualization via Editable 3D Gaussian Splatting., https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3567121, fetched 2026-10-26 NeRFifyMesh: Optimizing Neural Radiance Fields from Textured Meshes for Robotics Scene Building, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.10387, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering with Easy Editing, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00020, fetched 2026-10-29

name: NeuMesh Texture Filling
head: Sliding-window texture filling, Texture Filling
body: NeuMesh Texture Filling is a method for editing the appearance of a specific region on a textured 3D mesh within a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework by transferring texture characteristics from a pre-trained template. It solves the problem of localized artistic editing without retraining the entire radiance field or requiring multi-view image supervision. Unlike NeRFifyMesh, which generates a ground-truth radiance field from scratch, this method modifies an existing model by binding a new radiance decoder to the edited area and fusing it with the original model using inverse distance weighting to ensure smooth transitions. Inputs: 1. A pre-trained NeuMesh model (geometry, original texture codes, and original radiance decoder). 2. A target UV-map of the selected area to be edited, obtained by unwrapping the target vertices (e.g., using Blender). 3. A texture template from a pre-trained NeuMesh model (e.g., a small squared patch with ~10 vertices representing a specific material like fur or metal). Outputs: 1. An edited NeuMesh model where the target area exhibits the appearance of the texture template, smoothly blended with the original model. Data Structures: Texture Codes: A latent vector associated with each vertex or query point that encodes local geometric and textural information. Radiance Decoder: A neural network (MLP) that maps texture codes and viewing directions to color values. UV Coordinates: 2D coordinates mapping 3D mesh vertices to the 2D texture space. Steps: 1. UV Unwrapping: Obtain the target UV-map for the selected vertices of the mesh using a standard 3D modeling tool (e.g., Blender). 2. Template Selection: Select a texture template from a pre-trained NeuMesh model. The template should be a small patch (e.g., ~10 vertices) representing the desired appearance. 3. Sliding-Window Filling: Repeatedly fill the target UV-map with the texture template in a sliding-window manner. This involves mapping the template's texture codes to the target vertices. 4. Code Assignment: Assign texture codes to the target vertices by interpolating the codes from the selected template. 5. Decoder Binding: Bind a new radiance decoder to the target area. This decoder is initialized or copied from the pre-trained model because the target texture codes and template texture codes do not share the same latent radiance space as the original model's global decoder. 6. Color Fusion: For query points near the boundary of the edited area that have texture codes or decoders from different sources (original vs. template), fuse the color contributions from the different decoders using inverse distance weighting. This ensures a smooth transition between the edited appearance and the original appearance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neumeshtexturefilling(mesh, targetuvmap, templatepatch, originaldecoder): """ Perform texture filling on a NeuMesh model. Args: mesh: The original 3D mesh with vertices and faces. targetuvmap: UV coordinates for the vertices to be edited. templatepatch: A small patch (~10 vertices) from a pre-trained NeuMesh model. originaldecoder: The radiance decoder of the original NeuMesh model. Returns: editedmesh: The mesh with updated texture codes and a fused decoder. """ # Step 1: Get target vertices and their UVs targetvertices = getverticesfromuvmap(mesh, targetuvmap) # Step 2: Interpolate template texture codes to target vertices # Assuming template has texture codes Ctemplate and target has initial codes Ctarget # Interpolation is done in UV space or based on vertex proximity in UV space interpolatedcodes = interpolatetexturecodes(templatepatch.texturecodes, templatepatch.uvcoords, targetuvmap) # Step 3: Assign interpolated codes to target vertices for v in targetvertices: v.texturecode = interpolatedcodes[v.id] # Step 4: Create/Bind new decoder for the target area # The new decoder is bound to the template's decoder structure # because the latent spaces differ newdecoder = copydecoder(templatepatch.decoder) # Step 5: Define fusion function for query points def fusedcolorquery(point, direction): # Determine which decoder(s) to use based on point's texture code source # If point is in target area, use newdecoder # If point is outside, use originaldecoder # If point is near boundary, use both isintarget = ispointintargetarea(point, targetvertices) if isintarget: colornew = newdecoder(point.texturecode, direction) else: colornew = None colororig = originaldecoder(point.texturecode, direction) if isintarget: # Calculate distance to boundary for weighting disttoboundary = distancetoboundary(point, targetvertices) # Inverse distance weighting weight = 1.0 / (disttoboundary + epsilon) # Normalize weight or use a sigmoid falloff # For simplicity, assume a smooth transition function w(d) w = smoothtransitionweight(disttoboundary) return w colornew + (1 - w) colororig else: return colororig # Step 6: Update mesh with new codes and decoder binding editedmesh = mesh editedmesh.targetvertices = targetvertices editedmesh.decoder = fusedcolorquery return editedmesh Parameters: Template Size: Typically a small squared patch with ~10 vertices. Learning Rate: Fixed learning rate for optimization (if optimization is used), as per NeuMesh original paper. Optimizer: Adam optimizer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Latent Space Mismatch: The target texture code and template texture code do not share the same latent radiance space, necessitating the binding of a new decoder. Boundary Artifacts: Without inverse distance weighting, sharp discontinuities may appear at the boundary of the edited area. UV Unwrapping Quality: Poor UV unwrapping can lead to distorted texture transfer. NeRF-Tex is a method that combines NeRF with a 2D neural texture on an underlying 3D mesh, conditioned on user-defined parameters for artistic editability. It allows artists to control the appearance of the scene through these parameters. Unlike NeuMesh Texture Filling, which uses a sliding-window approach with a pre-trained template, NeRF-Tex uses continuous neural textures and explicit user parameters. It is chosen when fine-grained, parameter-driven artistic control is required rather than template-based transfer. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows localized editing without retraining the entire model; smooth transitions via inverse distance weighting. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeuMesh model and a suitable texture template; dependent on UV unwrapping quality. When to use: When editing specific regions of a textured mesh in a NeRF with a desired appearance from a template. When not to use: When global editing or parameter-driven control is needed (use NeRF-Tex instead). NeuMesh Texture Filling was introduced in the paper "NeuMesh: Learning Disentangled Neural Mesh-Based Implicit Field for Geometry and Texture Editing". It builds on the NeuMesh framework, which learns disentangled neural mesh-based implicit fields for geometry and texture. The method addresses the need for precise 3D texture editing by leveraging a sliding-window technique and decoder fusion. name: Vosh Hybrid Rendering
head: Vosh, Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation
body: Vosh is a hybrid representation method that combines a textured mesh with a sparse voxel grid to achieve real-time view synthesis while preserving comprehensive scene information. It addresses the trade-off between geometric precision and volumetric completeness by using the mesh for surface details and the voxels for thin structures and background volume. Unlike Adaptive Shells, which constrain volume rendering to regions near the surface, Vosh allows pure volume rendering where necessary, making it suitable for outdoor scenes. It differs from VMesh by reconstructing a volumetric density field, enabling the mesh to represent thin structures like fishing nets that are difficult to capture with Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). Inputs: Textured mesh models, camera poses, and multi-view images. Outputs: A hybrid asset consisting of a textured mesh and a sparse voxel grid, along with associated metadata for real-time rendering. 1. Mesh: Standard triangle mesh with appearance textures storing diffuse color and view-dependent features. 2. Sparse Voxel Grid: Based on the multi-resolution hierarchical occupancy grid from SNeRG. Occupancy Grid: Binary mask images at multiple resolution levels created via max-pooling to mark occupied voxels. Voxel Attributes: Stored in a sparse structure to minimize memory usage. 3. Mesh-Occupancy Grid: A grid used to filter spatial overlap between mesh and voxels; resolution r{mesh} is a hyperparameter. 1. Initial Voxel Training: Train initial voxels using classic MSE loss to measure pixel-level color differences. Use the same optimizer settings as MERF. 2. Mesh Refinement: Perform meshing of the density field for 20,000 steps. Set premove to 0.9 (Vosh-Base) or 1.0 (Vosh-Light). Clean the mesh using operations similar to NeRF2Mesh. Apply L2 regularization terms with rendering weights for background colors to encourage voxels to fill holes in the mesh. Repeat mesh cleaning operations if messy floating faces are produced. 3. Hybrid Optimization and Rendering: This stage combines rasterization and ray marching to ensure consistency between GPU training and web inference. Calculate Mesh-Occupancy Grid: Compute the occupancy grid of the meshes under training poses. Filter out voxels located in the mesh-occupied grid areas during rendering and baking to prevent spatial overlap. Adjust the ratio of sparse voxels by setting r{mesh} to suppress voxel density. Rasterization Pass: Uniformly shade the meshes. The fragment shader samples appearance textures to incorporate diffuse color and view-dependent features. Output diffuse color, view-dependent features, and a depth map. Ray Marching Pass: Use the multi-resolution hierarchical occupancy grid (from SNeRG) to create binary mask images via max-pooling. Perform spatial skips during ray marching using these masks. Reduce sampling distance using the depth map obtained from the rasterization pass. Hybrid Combination: For each spatial coordinate after ray marching, compare the transformed depth with the rasterization depth map to determine surface intersection. If the ray reaches the mesh surface, stop marching. Weightily combine the accumulated ray marching result with the appearance result from the rasterization pass. If the ray does not hit the surface, continue marching or accumulate volume contribution as per standard volume rendering. Loss Function: Apply voxel pruning loss weighted by \lambda{voxel}. For Vosh-Base, disable the binary mesh-occupancy grid. MSE Loss: \mathcal{L}{MSE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \| \mathbf{C}{pred}^{(i)} - \mathbf{C}{gt}^{(i)} \|^2, where \mathbf{C}{pred} and \mathbf{C}{gt} are predicted and ground-truth pixel colors. L2 Regularization: \mathcal{L}{L2} = \| \mathbf{w}{bg} \|^2, applied with rendering weights for background colors to encourage voxels to fill mesh holes. Voxel Pruning Loss: \mathcal{L}{voxel} = \lambda{voxel} \cdot \mathcal{L}{pruning}, where \lambda{voxel} limits volumetric density during ray marching. Weighty Combination: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C}{vol} \cdot \alpha{vol} + \mathbf{C}{mesh} \cdot (1 - \alpha{vol}), where \mathbf{C}{vol} and \mathbf{C}{mesh} are accumulated ray marching and rasterization colors, and \alpha{vol} is the accumulated volume alpha. Note: Exact mathematical formulations for spatial skip scheduling and max-pooling mask generation are not given in the sources. r{mesh}: Resolution of the mesh-occupancy grid. Set to 128 for Vosh-Light. \lambda{voxel}: Voxel pruning loss weight. Set to 0.001 for Vosh-Base and 0.01 for Vosh-Light. premove: Parameter for mesh refinement stage. Set to 0.9 for Vosh-Base and 1.0 for Vosh-Light. Marching Cubes Resolution: 1024. Optimizer: 25,000 steps, initial learning rate 1e-2, warmup for 100 steps, decaying to 1e-3. Mesh-Voxel Overlap: Meshes and voxels may overlap at the same spatial location, affecting quality and asset volume; handled by filtering voxels in mesh-occupied grid areas. Floating Faces: Meshing stage may produce messy floating faces; handled by repeating mesh cleaning operations and using L2 regularization with rendering weights for background colors to encourage voxels to fill mesh holes. Precision/Boundaries: Depth comparison uses a tolerance threshold to determine surface intersection; standard volume rendering accumulation applies when no intersection is detected. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voshrender(camera, mesh, voxelgrid, meshoccupancygrid, depthmapraster): """ Renders a frame using Vosh hybrid representation. Args: camera: Object with.resolution (H, W),.maxdistance, and.getrays() method. mesh: Textured mesh object with.sampleappearance(u, v) method. voxelgrid: Sparse voxel grid with.isoccupied(ray, depth) and.sample(ray, depth) methods. meshoccupancygrid: Binary grid indicating mesh-occupied voxels. depthmapraster: Depth map from the rasterization pass. Returns: color: Rendered pixel color array of shape (H, W, 3). """ height, width = camera.resolution rays = camera.getrays() accumulatedcolor = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) epsilon = 1e-3 stepsize = 0.05 skipstep = 0.2 for v in range(height): for u in range(width): ray = rays[v, u] currentdepth = 0.0 raymarchingaccum = np.zeros(3) raymarchingalpha = 0.0 while currentdepth < camera.maxdistance: # Spatial skip using multi-resolution occupancy grid if not voxelgrid.isoccupied(ray, currentdepth): currentdepth += skipstep continue # Sample voxel density and color density, color = voxelgrid.sample(ray, currentdepth) # Standard volume rendering accumulation alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-density stepsize) raymarchingaccum += color alpha (1.0 - raymarchingalpha) raymarchingalpha += alpha (1.0 - raymarchingalpha) currentdepth += stepsize # Surface intersection check rasterdepth = depthmapraster[v, u] if abs(currentdepth - rasterdepth) < epsilon: break # Rasterization appearance result meshcolor = mesh.sampleappearance(u, v) # Weighty combination based on surface hit if abs(currentdepth - depthmapraster[v, u]) < epsilon: accumulatedcolor[v, u] = raymarchingaccum (1.0 - raymarchingalpha) + meshcolor raymarchingalpha else: accumulatedcolor[v, u] = raymarchingaccum return accumulatedcolor def voshtrain(mesh, voxelgrid, images, poses): """ Trains the Vosh hybrid representation. """ # Stage 1: Initial Voxel Training traininitialvoxels(voxelgrid, images, poses, lossfn=MSE) # Stage 2: Mesh Refinement refinemesh(mesh, voxelgrid, premove=0.9, steps=20000) cleanmesh(mesh) applyl2regularization(voxelgrid, mesh, target='backgroundcolors') # Stage 3: Hybrid Optimization for step in range(25000): # Calculate mesh-occupancy grid meshoccupancygrid = calculatemeshoccupancy(mesh, poses) # Filter voxels in mesh-occupied areas voxelgrid.filter(meshoccupancygrid) # Render and compute loss renderedimages = voshrenderallviews(mesh, voxelgrid, meshoccupancygrid, images, poses) loss = computeloss(renderedimages, images) # Add voxel pruning loss if modeltype == 'Vosh-Light': loss += lambdavoxel computevoxelpruningloss(voxelgrid) # Backpropagate optimizer.step(loss) Training Time: On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090, training takes approximately 66 minutes for initial voxels, 35 minutes for mesh refinement, and 58 minutes for Vosh optimization. Memory Usage: Peak VRAM usage during training is ~11 GB. Storage: Vosh-Base uses 506 MB VRAM and 488 MB disk; Vosh-Light uses 490 MB VRAM and 232 MB disk on Mip-NeRF 360 outdoor scenes. Performance: Vosh achieves real-time rendering on mobile devices. Strengths: Restores comprehensive scene information compared to SDF-based methods. Can represent thin structures (e.g., fishing nets, ropes) that are difficult for SDFs. Suitable for outdoor scenes where pure volume rendering is necessary. Limitations: Slightly lower rendering quality in indoor scenes compared to MLP-based methods due to the use of a tiny view-dependent MLP. Disk storage is slightly larger than MERF because it does not use triplane representation. When to Use: When real-time rendering on mobile devices is required, and the scene contains thin structures or requires pure volume rendering (e.g., outdoor scenes). When Not to Use: When maximum indoor rendering quality is prioritized over speed, or when disk space is extremely constrained and MERF's triplane representation is acceptable. Vosh (Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation) was introduced in the paper "Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation for Real-Time View Synthesis". The method builds on previous works such as SNeRG for sparse voxel storage, MERF for optimizer settings, and NeRF2Mesh for mesh cleaning. It was developed to address the limitations of pure mesh or pure volume representations, particularly in the context of real-time view synthesis on mobile devices. name: MobileNeRF
head: Exploiting the Polygon Rasterization Pipeline for Efficient Neural Field Rendering on Mobile Architectures, MobileNeRF Forward/Deferred Rendering Pipeline, MobileNeRF rendering modes
body: MobileNeRF is a neural radiance field representation that synthesizes novel images efficiently using standard polygon rasterization pipelines, avoiding specialized volumetric ray marching. It represents the NeRF as a set of textured polygons with binary opacities and feature vectors, interpreted by a small view-dependent MLP in a fragment shader to produce final pixel color. Unlike classic NeRF which uses volumetric density compositing, MobileNeRF uses opacity compositing on a mesh. Unlike semi-transparent mesh rendering which requires per-frame sorting, MobileNeRF uses binary opacity and z-buffering, which is order-independent. It is 10x faster than SNeRG with the same output quality and consumes less memory by storing surface textures instead of volumetric textures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A collection of calibrated images (training); Camera pose (rendering). Outputs: Novel-view RGB images (rendering); Optimized mesh topology, vertex locations, and MLP weights (training). Data Structures: 1. Polygonal Mesh M=(T, V): T: Fixed topology (initially derived from a regular grid). V: Vertex locations, optimized during training. Initialized to a regular Euclidean lattice in the unit cube. 2. Acceleration Grid \mathcal{G}: A 3D grid of size P \times P \times P (default P=128) in the unit cube. Stores scalar values used to prune voxels during ray marching. 3. MLPs: \OpacityMLP: \real^3 \rightarrow [0,1]: Predicts opacity \alphak at position \mathbf{p}k. \FeaturesMLP: \real^3 \rightarrow [0,1]^8: Predicts 8-channel feature vector \mathbf{f}k at position \mathbf{p}k. \ShaderMLP: [0,1]^8 \times [-1,1]^3 \rightarrow [0,1]^3: The "neural deferred shader." Takes feature vector \mathbf{f}k and viewing direction \mathbf{d} to output color \mathbf{c}k. 4. Texture Maps (Post-Training): Allocated as K \times K patches per quad (default K=17, resulting in 16 \times 16 texture with half-pixel boundary padding). Stores 8-bit quantized discrete opacity and 8-channel features. Stored as losslessly compressed PNGs. 5. Shader Weights: Stored in a JSON file. Training Stages: Stage 1: Continuous Training 1. Initialization: Create a regular grid \mathcal{G} of size P \times P \times P in the unit cube centered at the origin. Instantiate vertices V by creating one vertex per voxel. Create triangles T by creating one quadrangle (two triangles) per grid edge connecting vertices of four adjacent voxels, akin to Dual Contouring. 2. Quadrature Point Generation: For each training ray \mathbf{r}: a. Compute intersections between the ray and the dual grid to get candidate voxels: \tilde{\Voxels} = \text{intersect}(\mathbf{r}, \DualGrid). b. Prune voxels using the acceleration grid \mathcal{G} with threshold \tau\Grid: \Voxels = \{ b \in \tilde{\Voxels} ~|~ \mathcal{G}[b] > \tau\Grid \}. c. Compute final quadrature points by intersecting the ray with mesh faces incident to the pruned voxel vertices: \QuadraturePoints = \text{intersect}(\mathbf{r}, \{ \triangle \in \Triangles ~|~ \triangle \cap \Voxels \}). d. Sort quadrature points by depth. 3. Feature and Opacity Evaluation: For each quadrature point \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{r}(tk): \alphak = \OpacityMLP(\mathbf{p}k; \pars\OpacityMLP). \mathbf{f}k = \FeaturesMLP(\mathbf{p}k; \pars\FeaturesMLP). \mathbf{c}k = \ShaderMLP(\mathbf{f}k, \mathbf{d}; \pars\ShaderMLP). 4. Alpha Compositing: Compute predicted color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}): \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak \mathbf{c}k, \quad Tk = \prod{l=1}^{k-1}(1-\alphal). 5. Gradient Back-propagation: Back-propagate gradients from the intersection point to the three vertices of the intersected triangle using barycentric interpolation. 6. Loss Functions: Color Loss: \mathcal{L}\mathbf{C} = \expect{\mathbf{r}} \| \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) - \mathbf{C}\text{gt}(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2. For real-world scenes, add distortion loss \mathcal{L}\text{dist}. Acceleration Grid Boundary Loss: \mathcal{L}\Grid^\text{bnd} = \sumk \max(\StopGradient[Tk \alphak] - \mathcal{G}[\mathbf{p}k], 0). Acceleration Grid Sparsity Loss: \mathcal{L}\Grid^\text{sparse} = \|\mathcal{G}\|1^1. Acceleration Grid Smoothness Loss: \mathcal{L}\Grid^\text{smooth} = \|\nabla \mathcal{G}\|2^2. Vertex Regularization: \mathcal{L}\Vertices = \sum{\mathbf{v} \in \Vertices} (10^3 \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{v}) + 10^{-2}) \cdot \|\mathbf{v}\|1, where \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{v})=1 if vertex \mathbf{v} is outside its corresponding voxel, else 0. Stage 2: Binarized Training 1. Binarization: Convert smooth opacity \alphak \in [0,1] to discrete/categorical opacity \hat{\alpha}k \in \{0, 1\} using a straight-through estimator: \dOpacityk = \alphak + \StopGradient[\mathbbm{1}(\alphak > 0.5) - \alphak]. 2. Co-training: Optimize continuous and discrete models simultaneously using combined loss: \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{stage2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{bin} + \tfrac{1}{2} \mathcal{L}\Color where \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{bin} is the MSE between binarized color output and ground truth. 3. Binarized Color Output: \hat{\Color}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \hat{T}k \dOpacityk \mathbf{c}k, \quad \hat{T}k = \prod{l=1}^{k-1}(1-\dOpacityl). 4. Anti-aliasing: Rasterize features at 2x resolution to produce a feature image. Average sub-pixel features to produce the antialiased representation fed to the neural deferred shader: \Color(\mathbf{r}) = \ShaderMLP \left( \expect{\mathbf{r}\delta \sim \mathbf{r}}[\Feature(\mathbf{r}\delta)], \: \expect{\mathbf{r}\delta \sim \mathbf{r}}[\mathbf{d}\delta] \right) where the expectation averages four sub-pixels. 5. Fine-tuning: After convergence, fine-tune weights in \FeaturesMLP and \ShaderMLP by minimizing \mathcal{L}\Color^\text{bin} while fixing other weights. Stage 3: Discretization and Export 1. Mesh Extraction: Convert the representation into an explicit polygonal mesh in OBJ format. Discard quads that are not partially visible in training camera poses. 2. Texture Baking: a. Allocate a K \times K patch in the texture per quad (K=17). b. Iterate over pixels, convert to 3D coordinates, and bake discrete opacity and features into the texture map. c. Quantize [0,1] ranges to 8-bit integers and store as losslessly compressed PNG. 3. Shader Export: Store the weights of the neural deferred shader in a JSON file. Rendering: Two modes are supported: Deferred Rendering: 1. Pass 1: Rasterize all faces of the textured mesh with a z-buffer to produce a 2M \times 2N feature image with 12 channels per pixel: 8 channels of learned features, 1 binary opacity, and 3D view direction. 2. Pass 2: Synthesize an M \times N output RGB image by rendering a textured rectangle using the feature image as texture, with linear filtering to average features for anti-aliasing. Apply the small MLP (implemented as a GLSL fragment shader) for pixels with nonzero alphas to convert features into RGB colors. Forward Rendering: 1. Meshes and textures are directly rasterized into pixels containing RGB colors using the MLP fragment shader. 2. Anti-aliasing is handled by super-sampling on pixel colors (unlike deferred rendering which super-samples features). 3. A depth pre-pass can help resolve excessive overdraw issues in forward rendering, but it may not be available on certain devices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainmobilenerf(images, cameraposes, P=128, K=17): # Initialization vertices = np.zeros((P, P, P, 3)) # Regular Euclidean lattice in unit cube topology = createdualcontouringtopology(vertices) # Quads from grid edges accelgrid = np.zeros((P, P, P)) # MLPs opacitymlp = MLP(3, 1) featuremlp = MLP(3, 8) shadermlp = MLP(11, 3) # 8 features + 3 view dir for stage in [1, 2, 3]: for epoch in range(1000): for image, pose in zip(images, cameraposes): rays = generaterays(pose, image.shape) loss = 0.0 for ray in rays: # Quadrature candidatevoxels = intersectrayvoxelgrid(ray, vertices) prunedvoxels = [v for v in candidatevoxels if accelgrid[v] > 0.5] quadpoints = intersectraymeshfaces(ray, topology, prunedvoxels) quadpoints.sort(key=lambda p: ray.tat(p)) # Depth sort # Evaluate MLPs opacities, features, colors = [], [], [] for p in quadpoints: alpha = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-opacitymlp(p))) f = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-featuremlp(p))) d = ray.direction / np.linalg.norm(ray.direction) c = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-shadermlp(np.concatenate([f, d])))) opacities.append(alpha) features.append(f) colors.append(c) # Alpha Compositing if stage == 1: T, predcolor = 1.0, np.zeros(3) for alpha, f, c in zip(opacities, features, colors): T = (1 - alpha) predcolor += T alpha c loss += np.mean((predcolor - ray.gtcolor) 2) loss += np.sum(np.abs(accelgrid)) + np.sum(np.gradient(accelgrid) 2) + vertexreg(vertices) + boundaryloss(T, opacities, accelgrid, quadpoints) elif stage == 2: binarizedopacities = [1.0 if a > 0.5 else 0.0 for a in opacities] avgfeatures = np.mean([features[i] for i in range(4)], axis=0) avgviewdirs = np.mean([ray.direction / np.linalg.norm(ray.direction) for in range(4)], axis=0) avgcolor = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-shadermlp(np.concatenate([avgfeatures, avgviewdirs])))) T, binpredcolor = 1.0, np.zeros(3) for binalpha, c in zip(binarizedopacities, colors): T = (1 - binalpha) binpredcolor += T binalpha c loss += 0.5 np.mean((binpredcolor - ray.gtcolor) 2) + 0.5 np.mean((avgcolor - ray.gtcolor) 2) elif stage == 3: pass # Export stage gradients = computegradients(loss) updateparameters(gradients) # Texture Baking texturemaps = [] for quad in topology: patch = np.zeros((K, K, 9)) for u in range(K): for v in range(K): p = quad.uvto3d(u / K, v / K) alpha = 1.0 if opacitymlp(p) > 0.5 else 0.0 f = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-featuremlp(p))) patch[u, v] = np.concatenate([f, [alpha]]) texturemaps.append(patch) return topology, vertices, texturemaps, shadermlp.weights Parameters: Grid size P: Default 128. Reducing to 64 causes slight performance drop. Texture patch size K: Default 17. K=33 quadruples texture size and improves performance; K=9 drops performance. Sub-pixel count for anti-aliasing: 4. Rendering resolution: Matches training images (800x800 synthetic, 1008x756 forward-facing, 1256x828 unbounded). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Representing continuous signals with discrete representations can introduce aliasing. Semi-transparency: Binary opacities prevent handling semi-transparent scenes and generate scattered small fragments in semi-transparent parts. Resolution Limits: Fixed mesh and texture resolutions may be too coarse for close-up novel-view synthesis, causing loss of fine details like grass. Specular Surfaces: Specular surfaces and sparse training views cause incorrect surface estimation, modeling reflections as real objects behind surfaces. Glossy Surfaces: The method models a radiance field without explicitly decomposing illumination and reflectance, reducing performance on glossy surfaces. Precision Errors: Precision errors in rasterization cause very different pixels on the boundary of a part when comparing Python-rendered images to web browser-rendered images. Super-sampling Mode: Super-sampling must be done on pixel features for deferred rendering, while it should be done on pixel colors for forward rendering; using the wrong mode causes slightly different rendered results. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(1) per pixel for deferred mode (MLP executed once per pixel) and O(F) for forward mode (MLP executed once per fragment, where F is fragment count). Training is slow due to NeRF MLP backbone. Memory Complexity: Stores surface textures instead of volumetric textures, consuming less memory than SNeRG (5x less GPU memory). Measured Performance: Pixel 3 (Synthetic 360°): 37.14 FPS. Surface Pro 6 (Synthetic 360°): 37.14 FPS (default), 32.48 FPS (K=33), 37.74 FPS (K=9), 51.81 FPS (no supersampling), 52.16 FPS (no view-dependent MLP). Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra (Unbounded): 84 FPS (optimized forward), 35 FPS (optimized deferred). Gaming Laptop (Composited Scene): 150 FPS at 1920x1080, 1.5 GB GPU memory. Strengths: 10x faster than SNeRG; runs on mobile phones and web browsers; order-independent transparency via binary opacity; easy editing of explicit mesh. Limitations: Cannot handle semi-transparency; slow training; fixed resolution limits detail; struggles with specular/glossy surfaces; forward rendering can be slower than deferred on some devices due to overdraw. When to Use: Real-time visualization on mobile devices, web browsers, or integrated GPUs where memory and power are constrained. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring semi-transparency, high-fidelity glossy/specular surfaces, or close-up synthesis requiring high-resolution textures. MobileNeRF was introduced in 2023 by the authors of the paper "MobileNeRF: Exploiting the Polygon Rasterization Pipeline for Efficient Neural Field Rendering on Mobile Architectures". It addresses the mismatch between specialized volumetric ray marching algorithms and widely deployed graphics hardware, particularly on mobile devices. The method builds on the idea of surface-based neural fields and rasterization pipelines, aiming to achieve interactive frame rates on a wide range of compute platforms. It is implemented as an HTML webpage rendered by WebGL via the threejs library, allowing it to run on Chrome browser, Surface Pro 6, and Pixel 3.
