name: TensoRF Reconstruction Optimization
head: Tensorial Radiance Field Optimization
body: TensoRF Reconstruction Optimization is the iterative gradient-based procedure used to fit a tensorial radiance field to a set of multi-view images with known camera poses. It minimizes the L2 rendering loss between synthesized and ground-truth pixel colors, distinguishing itself from standard implicit field optimization by enforcing structural regularization (L1 and Total Variation) on low-rank tensor factors and employing a dynamic coarse-to-fine upsampling strategy to mitigate overfitting and local minima. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M multi-view images \{Im\}{m=1}^M with known camera poses and intrinsics. Output: Optimized tensor factors (global mode vectors and matrices) representing the density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} fields. Data Structures: The radiance field uses Vector-Matrix (VM) or Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition, building on the shared principles of low-rank tensor factorization [11617-tensorial-and-low-rank-representations.md]. The implementation uses a feature grid with N^3 voxels, where the resolution per dimension is derived from the bounding box shape. Parameters: Initial Resolution: N0^3 voxels, with N0 = 128. Final Resolution: N^3 voxels. Upsampling Steps: 2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000. Interpolation: Linear in logarithmic space between N0^3 and N^3. Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 4096 pixel rays. Feature Decoding: Small MLP (2 FC layers, 128 hidden, ReLU) or 3rd-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) with 27 features. Regularization: To prevent overfitting and local minima, regularization is applied to the tensor factors: 1. L1 Norm Loss: Encourages sparsity in the factors. Adequate for most datasets. 2. Total Variation (TV) Loss: Promotes smoothness. Used for real datasets with few input images (e.g., LLFF) or imperfect capture conditions (e.g., Tanks and Temples with varying exposure/inconsistent masks). Algorithm: 1. Initialize tensor factors (global vectors and matrices) at resolution N0^3. 2. For each optimization step t: a. If t \in \{2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000\}, upsample the XYZ-mode vector and matrix factors linearly and bilinearly to the current target resolution. b. Sample rays and compute rendered pixel colors using the current tensor factors and feature decoding function. c. Compute L2 rendering loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} = \sum \| \mathbf{C}{\text{rendered}} - \mathbf{C}{\text{GT}} \|^2, where \mathbf{C}{\text{rendered}} are the rendered colors and \mathbf{C}{\text{GT}} are ground truth colors. d. Compute regularization loss \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}} = \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{L1}} + \lambda{\text{TV}} \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} on the factors. e. Compute total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{render}} + \mathcal{L}{\text{reg}}. f. Update tensor factors using the Adam optimizer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computetvloss(factors): """Compute Total Variation loss on tensor factors.""" loss = 0.0 for f in factors: if f.dim() == 3: # Vector factor loss += torch.mean(torch.abs(f[:, 1:,:] - f[:,:-1,:])) elif f.dim() == 4: # Matrix factor loss += torch.mean(torch.abs(f[:,:, 1:,:] - f[:,:,:-1,:])) loss += torch.mean(torch.abs(f[:, 1:,:,:] - f[:-1,:,:,:])) return loss def getcurrentresolution(t, N0, Nfinal, steps): """Compute target resolution via linear interpolation in log space.""" logN0, logNf = torch.log(torch.tensor(N0)), torch.log(torch.tensor(Nfinal)) if t <= steps[0]: progress = 0.0 elif t >= steps[-1]: progress = 1.0 else: idx = next(i for i, s in enumerate(steps) if s > t) prevs = steps[idx-1] if idx > 0 else 0 progress = (t - prevs) / (steps[idx] - prevs) return int(torch.exp(logN0 + progress (logNf - logN0)).item()) def upsamplefactors(factors, t, N0, Nfinal, steps): """Upsample vectors (trilinear) and matrices (bilinear) to target resolution.""" newres = getcurrentresolution(t, N0, Nfinal, steps) newfactors = [] for f in factors: if f.dim() == 3: newfactors.append(F.interpolate(f.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), size=(newres, newres, newres), mode='trilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0).squeeze(0)) elif f.dim() == 4: newfactors.append(F.interpolate(f.unsqueeze(0), size=(newres, newres), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0)) return newfactors def renderray(rayorigins, raydirections, factors, resolution): """Render a batch of rays using tensor factors.""" # Sample points along rays tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 128).to(rayorigins.device) zvals = 0.2 + 0.8 tvals points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + raydirections.unsqueeze(1) zvals.unsqueeze(2) # Interpolate tensor factors at sample points using trilinear interpolation # Compute density sigma and color c from interpolated factors and feature decoder # Perform volume rendering (alpha compositing) # Return rendered colors return torch.zeroslike(rayorigins) # Placeholder for standard compositing def optimizetensorf(images, poses, N0=128, Nfinal=256, steps=[2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000], usetvloss=False, l1lambda=1e-4, tvlambda=1e-4): """Optimize TensoRF factors.""" # Initialize factors at N0^3 factors = [torch.randn(3, N0, N0, N0, requiresgrad=True), torch.randn(3, N0, N0, N0, requiresgrad=True)] optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(factors, lr=0.001) # Typical LR totalsteps = 8000 # Example total steps for t in range(totalsteps): # Coarse-to-fine upsampling if t in steps: factors = upsamplefactors(factors, t, N0, Nfinal, steps) # Sample rays and get ground truth colors rayorigins, raydirections = torch.randn(4096, 3), torch.randn(4096, 3) gtcolors = torch.randn(4096, 3) # Render renderedcolors = renderray(rayorigins, raydirections, factors, getcurrentresolution(t, N0, Nfinal, steps)) # Compute L2 loss renderloss = torch.mean((renderedcolors - gtcolors) 2) # Compute regularization l1loss = sum(torch.norm(f, p=1) for f in factors) regloss = l1lambda l1loss if usetvloss: tvloss = computetvloss(factors) regloss += tvlambda tvloss loss = renderloss + regloss # Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() return factors The iterative optimization procedure used to minimize the L2 rendering loss of a tensorial radiance field by adjusting its low-rank tensor parameters. It distinguishes itself from standard NeRF training by incorporating specific regularizations (orthogonal, L1 density, and Total Variation) tailored to the decomposed tensor structure, alongside dynamic voxel resolution updates via an alpha mask. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The coarse-to-fine strategy reduces initial computation cost. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of tensor factors, which is significantly lower than dense voxel grids or large MLPs for equivalent resolution. Performance: Evaluated on a single Tesla V100 GPU (16GB) with a batch size of 4096 pixel rays. Strengths: Effective regularization prevents overfitting and local minima. Coarse-to-fine upsampling improves quality. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of regularization parameters and upsampling steps. May struggle with very few input images without TV loss. When to use: Suitable for multi-view reconstruction where memory efficiency and structural regularization are beneficial. When not to use: Not ideal for real-time inference without further optimization (e.g., pruning) or for scenes with extreme view-dependent effects not captured by the low-rank assumption. TensoRF was introduced in the paper "TensoRF: Tensorial Radiance Fields". The method leverages tensor factorization to represent radiance fields, building on the principles of low-rank representations [11617-tensorial-and-low-rank-representations.md]. It addresses issues of overfitting and local minima common in gradient-based optimization of implicit fields by introducing specific regularization terms and a dynamic resolution update strategy. name: TensoRF Training Loop
head: TensoRF Optimization
body: The TensoRF Training Loop is the iterative optimization procedure used to minimize the L2 rendering loss of a tensorial radiance field, using ground truth pixel colors as supervision. It differs from standard NeRF training by incorporating specific regularization terms (orthogonal, L1, and Total Variation) tailored to the low-rank tensor decomposition structure, alongside a dynamic resolution update mechanism for the feature grid. Inputs: Training dataset containing images, poses, and intrinsics. Model parameters: densityncomp, appearancencomp, appdim, nearfar, shadingMode, alphaMaskthres, densityshift, distancescale, pospe, viewpe, feape, featureC, stepratio, fea2denseAct. Hyperparameters: Nvoxelinit (initial voxel count), nSamples (samples per ray), lrdecaytargetratio, Orthoweight, L1weightinital, TVweightdensity, TVweightapp. Outputs: Optimized tensorial radiance field parameters. Rendered RGB maps, alphas, depths, and weights for loss computation. Rays: 3D arrays containing ray origins and directions, filtered by bounding box if not using NDC. RGBs: 3D arrays containing ground truth pixel colors. TensorF Model: Contains the decomposed tensor components for density and color fields. 1. Initialization: Load train/test data and compute aabb, nearfar, whitebg, and ndcray flags. Initialize the tensorf model with the specified parameters. Calculate learning rate decay factor: lr\factor = args.lr\decay\target\ratio^{(1/args.lr\decay\iters)} If not using NDC, filter rays to the bounding box: python allrays, allrgbs = tensorf.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs, bboxonly=True) Initialize SimpleSampler for ray batching. 2. Iteration Loop: For each iteration: a. Ray Sampling: Get ray indices via rayidx = trainingSampler.nextids(). Fetch rays and RGBs: python raystrain, rgbtrain = allrays[rayidx], allrgbs[rayidx].to(device) b. Rendering: Render the scene using the renderer function: python rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, uncertainty = renderer( raystrain, tensorf, chunk=args.batchsize, Nsamples=nSamples, whitebg=whitebg, ndcray=ndcray, device=device, istrain=True) Note: nSamples is calculated as min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(resocur, args.stepratio)). c. Loss Computation: i. MSE Loss: loss = \text{mean}((rgb\map - rgb\train)^2) ii. Orthogonal Regularization: If Orthoregweight > 0: loss\reg = tensorf.vector\comp\diffs() total\loss += Ortho\reg\weight \times loss\reg iii. L1 Density Regularization: If L1regweight > 0: loss\reg\L1 = tensorf.density\L1() total\loss += L1\reg\weight \times loss\reg\L1 iv. TV Density Regularization: If TVweightdensity > 0: Decay weight by lrfactor. Compute: loss\tv = tensorf.TV\loss\density(tvreg) \times TV\weight\density total\loss += loss\tv v. TV Appearance Regularization: If TVweightapp > 0: Decay weight by lrfactor. Compute: loss\tv = tensorf.TV\loss\app(tvreg) \times TV\weight\app total\loss += loss\tv d. Optimization Step: python optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() e. Learning Rate Update: For all parameter groups: python paramgroup['lr'] = paramgroup['lr'] lrfactor f. Evaluation: Periodically evaluate test PSNR and log metrics to TensorBoard. g. Alpha Mask Update: If the current iteration is in updateAlphaMasklist and the current voxel count is less than 256^3, update the volume resolution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def traintensorf(dataset, model, optimizer, args, device): # 1. Initialization allrays, allrgbs = dataset.getallraysandrgbs() aabb, nearfar, whitebg, ndcray = dataset.computeboundsandfocal() model.initparameters( densityncomp=args.densityncomp, appearancencomp=args.appearancencomp, appdim=args.appdim, nearfar=nearfar, shadingMode=args.shadingMode, alphaMaskthres=args.alphaMaskthres, densityshift=args.densityshift, distancescale=args.distancescale, pospe=args.pospe, viewpe=args.viewpe, feape=args.feape, featureC=args.featureC, stepratio=args.stepratio, fea2denseAct=args.fea2denseAct) lrfactor = args.lrdecaytargetratio (1.0 / args.lrdecayiters) if not ndcray: allrays, allrgbs = model.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs, bboxonly=True) # SimpleSampler: generates random ray indices for batching class SimpleSampler: def init(self, numrays): self.numrays = numrays def nextids(self): return torch.randint(0, self.numrays, (args.batchsize,)) sampler = SimpleSampler(allrays.shape[0]) # 2. Iteration Loop for iteration in range(args.maxiters): # a. Ray Sampling rayidx = sampler.nextids() raystrain = allrays[rayidx].to(device) rgbtrain = allrgbs[rayidx].to(device) # b. Rendering # calnsamples: calculates dynamic samples based on current resolution and step ratio nsamples = min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(model.resocur, args.stepratio)) # renderer: performs differentiable volume rendering along rays rgbmap, alphasmap, depthmap, weights, uncertainty = model.renderer( raystrain, model, chunk=args.batchsize, Nsamples=nsamples, whitebg=whitebg, ndcray=ndcray, device=device, istrain=True) # c. Loss Computation loss = torch.mean((rgbmap - rgbtrain) 2) totalloss = loss # Orthogonal Regularization if args.Orthoregweight > 0: lossreg = model.vectorcompdiffs() totalloss += args.Orthoregweight lossreg # L1 Density Regularization if args.L1regweight > 0: lossregL1 = model.densityL1() totalloss += args.L1regweight lossregL1 # TV Density Regularization if args.TVweightdensity > 0: tvweight = args.TVweightdensity lrfactor losstv = model.TVlossdensity(tvreg=1) tvweight totalloss += losstv # TV Appearance Regularization if args.TVweightapp > 0: tvweight = args.TVweightapp lrfactor losstv = model.TVlossapp(tvreg=1) tvweight totalloss += losstv # d. Optimization Step optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() # e. Learning Rate Update for paramgroup in optimizer.paramgroups: paramgroup['lr'] = paramgroup['lr'] lrfactor # f. Evaluation if iteration % args.evalinterval == 0: # evaluatetestpsnr: computes PSNR on validation set evaluatetestpsnr(dataset, model) # logtotensorboard: writes metrics to TensorBoard logtotensorboard(iteration, totalloss) # g. Alpha Mask Update if iteration in args.updateAlphaMasklist: if model.currentvoxelcount < 2563: model.updatevolumeresolution() Nvoxelinit: Initial number of voxels. Not given in the sources. nSamples: Number of samples per ray. Calculated dynamically. lrdecaytargetratio: Target learning rate ratio for decay. Not given in the sources. Orthoweight: Weight for orthogonal regularization. Not given in the sources. L1weightinital: Initial weight for L1 density regularization. Not given in the sources. TVweightdensity: Initial weight for TV density regularization. Not given in the sources. TVweightapp: Initial weight for TV appearance regularization. Not given in the sources. Depth Supervision Ineffectiveness: When using depth supervision with low data, the improvement in PSNR is minimal (0.01 PSNR) because COLMAP key points are orders of magnitude fewer than color pixel comparisons, causing depth loss gradients to affect only a small portion of the voxel space. Resolution Update Condition: The volume resolution is only updated if the current voxel count is less than 256^3. NeuManifold is a three-stage pipeline for reconstructing neural watertight manifolds with efficient, high-quality rendering support. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity 3D meshes from 2D images by combining the robust initialization of volume rendering with the geometric precision of differentiable rasterization. Unlike pure volumetric methods, it produces explicit triangle meshes; unlike pure mesh-based methods, it avoids the artifacts caused by linear interpolation in non-linear density fields by using a differentiable marching cubes algorithm. NeuManifold This method enables robust joint optimization of camera poses and decomposed low-rank tensorial radiance fields by controlling the frequency spectrum of the scene representation. It prevents premature high-frequency signals in the voxel volume from causing camera poses to get stuck in local minima, a failure mode common in naive joint optimization. It sets itself apart from hash-encoding-based methods by specifically leveraging the separability of the input low-rank tensor signal, making it more efficient than traditional separable convolution kernels. Separable Component-Wise Convolution for Joint Pose Optimization StyleTRF is a method for stylized view generation that decouples style adaptation from view capture by fine-tuning the appearance component of a pre-optimized Tensorial Radiance Field (TensoRF) using sparse stylized priors. It sets itself apart from joint optimization methods like SNeRF by freezing the geometric density parameters of the scene representation, thereby preserving crisp geometry while adapting appearance, and by using a deterministic CNN-based stylization module (Johnson et al.) to ensure 3D consistency across viewpoints. StyleTRF This family defines the tensor decomposition strategies used to factorize the radiance field density and color fields in TensoRF, balancing storage efficiency against rendering quality. It differs from sibling methods like NeuManifold or StyleTRF by explicitly structuring the low-rank approximation into discrete rank groups (rank-residual learning) and offering specific variants (CP, HY, HY-S) to control the ratio of vector- to matrix-based components. TensoRF Decomposition Models A training optimization scheme that reduces initial training cost and regularizes feature representations by initializing a 3D feature grid at a coarse resolution and progressively upscaling it to higher resolutions. It improves model convergence and makes camera refinement more effective compared to training at full resolution from the start. Unlike static grid methods, this approach dynamically adapts the spatial detail of the feature representation during the optimization process. Coarse-to-fine feature grid Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields (CATRF) is a compression framework for plane-factorized radiance fields that optimizes neural features directly in the decoded space of a standard video or image codec. It solves the problem of severe rendering degradation at low bitrates by integrating a real codec round-trip (JPEG, VP9, HEVC, or AV1) into the training loop via a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). Unlike Codec-Agnostic (CA) methods that compress features after training, or Learned-Codec-in-the-Loop (LCL) methods that require shipping scene-specific neural decoder parameters, CATRF adapts features to real codec distortions without introducing any learned codec parameters or entropy models. Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields Downsamples both train and test data by a factor of 4. Training iterations are reduced to 2,500 (vs. 30,000 in original TensoRF paper) due to memory and time constraints. Tested on the synthetic Lego scene from the NeRF dataset with 100 training views and 200 test views. Applies depth supervision loss during training. However, it suffers from low PSNR with low data and minimal improvement (0.01 PSNR) over non-depth supervised approaches because COLMAP key points are orders of magnitude fewer than color pixel comparisons, causing depth loss gradients to affect only a small portion of voxel space. Uses a spike-based color decoder. TensoRF T: Maximum time step set to 8. Initial membrane time constant \tau = 2.0. Firing threshold = 0.5. Extreme threshold sensitivity makes the approach unreliable in practice, with errors of 22.4% at p=93, 92.8% at p=95, and 518.7% at p=99. However, depth supervision can be ineffective if the number of depth points is significantly lower than the number of color pixels. When to use it: When optimizing a tensorial radiance field for high-quality novel view synthesis with efficient memory usage. When not to use it: When high-precision depth reconstruction is required but depth supervision proves ineffective due to sparse COLMAP points. name: NeuManifold
body: NeuManifold is a three-stage pipeline for reconstructing neural watertight manifolds with efficient, high-quality rendering support. It solves the problem of generating high-fidelity 3D meshes from 2D images by combining the robust initialization of volume rendering with the geometric precision of differentiable rasterization. Unlike pure volumetric methods, it produces explicit triangle meshes; unlike pure mesh-based methods, it avoids the artifacts caused by linear interpolation in non-linear density fields by using a differentiable marching cubes algorithm. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D images with known camera poses. Output: A watertight triangle mesh (geometry) and an appearance network (color) capable of real-time rendering. Data Structures: Geometry Network (G): A neural field (specifically TensoRF) that maps a 3D location x to volume density \sigmax. Appearance Network (A): A neural field (specifically TensoRF) that maps a 3D location x and viewing direction d to view-dependent color cx. Grid: An axis-aligned grid used for the Differentiable Marching Cubes (DiffMC) operation. Mesh: A triangle mesh extracted from the grid, containing vertex positions and connectivity. Textures: For deployment, TensoRF weights are stored as three 3D textures and three 1D textures with linear filtering; MLP weights are stored as 2D textures. Formulas: The geometry and appearance networks are defined as: \sigmax, cx = G(x), A(x, d) where x is a 3D location, d is the viewing direction, \sigmax is volume density, and cx is view-dependent color. Volume rendering compositing equation: C = \sum{i=1}^N Ti(1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai))ci Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where C is the rendered pixel color, N is the number of samples, \sigmai is density, \deltai is ray marching step size, ci is color, and Ti is volume transmittance. Parameters: Neural Field Representation: TensoRF is used for both geometry and appearance networks. Implementation: DiffMC is implemented in CUDA for optimal GPU performance. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Initialization by Volume Rendering. Train the geometry network G and appearance network A using differentiable volume rendering to establish a strong initialization. Sample rays through the scene. Query G(x) for density \sigma and A(x, d) for color c. Compute pixel colors C using the volume rendering compositing equation. Optimize network weights to minimize rendering loss. 2. Stage 2: Manifold Generation & Optimization. Use the pretrained network weights from Stage 1 as initialization. Optimize object topology, geometry, and appearance simultaneously using differentiable rasterization. Apply Differentiable Marching Cubes (DiffMC) on an axis-aligned grid. DiffMC extracts meshes using conventional Marching Cubes and provides gradients for mesh vertices relative to the grid. Feed the resulting mesh into nvdiffrast to render 2D images. Use the rendering loss to update the geometry and appearance networks. 3. Stage 3: Geometry and Appearance Fine-tuning (Optional). Fine-tune only the positions of mesh vertices and the appearance network to minimize rendering loss. This preserves original robust edge connections, maintaining watertightness. Note that this step may occasionally introduce self-intersections. 4. Rendering Deployment. Implement neural networks as GLSL shaders for integration into modern rendering engines. Rasterize triangles in the vertex shader. Compute TensoRF and MLPs using modelspace coordinates and viewing directions in the fragment shader. Use Supersample Anti-Aliasing (SSAA) or Multisample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) to handle aliasing from undersampling high-frequency features. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: DMTet Artifacts: DMTet produces severe artifacts (peaks and valleys) when extracting meshes from density fields due to reliance on linear interpolation between tetrahedra vertices, which is inadequate for non-linear density fields. This issue is not present with SDF. Self-Intersections: Stage 3 fine-tuning may introduce self-intersections. Grid Alignment: While DiffMC is less susceptible to non-linear data issues, geometries not aligned with the grid axis may still exhibit some artifacts, though significantly smoother than DMTet. Time Complexity: DiffMC is implemented in CUDA for optimal GPU performance and is approximately 20 times faster than DMTet. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method achieves high-quality mesh reconstruction, photorealistic rendering quality, and real-time rendering support. Strengths: Produces watertight, manifold, and intersection-free meshes; handles non-linear density fields better than tetrahedra-based methods; supports real-time rendering via GLSL shaders. Limitations: Stage 3 may introduce self-intersections; SSAA has higher computational cost. When to use: When high-quality, watertight manifold meshes are required with efficient rendering support. When not to use: When SDF-based representations are available and DMTet artifacts are not a concern (though DiffMC is still faster). NeuManifold was proposed to integrate the advantages of volumetric and mesh-based methods. The authors observed that with proper initialization, mesh-based methods can converge to a more favorable state, enabling the reconstruction of high-quality meshes. The method addresses the limitations of DMTet in handling non-linear density fields by introducing DiffMC, a differentiable marching cubes algorithm operating on an axis-aligned grid. The work cites TensoRF as the state-of-the-art neural field representation used in this context. name: Separable Component-Wise Convolution for Joint Pose Optimization
head: Component-wise Separable Convolution, Edge-Guided Loss Mask, Efficient 3D Filtering, Randomized 2D/3D Filtering, Separable Component-wise Convolution of Gaussian Filters
body: This method enables robust joint optimization of camera poses and decomposed low-rank tensorial radiance fields by controlling the frequency spectrum of the scene representation. It prevents premature high-frequency signals in the voxel volume from causing camera poses to get stuck in local minima, a failure mode common in naive joint optimization. It sets itself apart from hash-encoding-based methods by specifically leveraging the separability of the input low-rank tensor signal, making it more efficient than traditional separable convolution kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Decomposed low-rank tensor representation of the radiance field (typically factorized into axial components), 2D supervision images (ground truth views), and camera poses (initial estimates). Outputs: Refined camera poses and optimized decomposed tensor parameters. Data Structures: The method operates on the decomposed low-rank tensor structure used in TensoRF, where the 3D volume is represented as a product of lower-dimensional axial tensors (e.g., V \approx A \times B \times C). The specific bit-packing or memory layout of these factors is inherited from the parent TensoRF Training Loop. Algorithm Steps: 1. Spectral Control via 3D Filtering: Apply separable component-wise convolution of Gaussian filters on the decomposed 3D tensor volume. This directly controls the spectrum of the radiance field, smoothing high-frequency noise that destabilizes pose optimization. 2. 2D Supervision Smoothing: Apply separable component-wise convolution of Gaussian filters on the 2D supervision images. This creates "smoothed 2D supervision" to match the spectral properties of the filtered 3D field. 3. Joint Optimization: Use the filtered radiance field and smoothed supervision for the joint optimization of camera poses and the decomposed voxel representation. 4. Randomized Kernel Scaling: Use randomly scaled kernel parameters for the Gaussian filters during training. This variability is introduced to ensure stability and robustness in the optimization process. 5. Edge-Guided Loss Mask: Apply an edge-guided loss mask to the optimization objective. This technique is proposed to further ensure stability and robustness in the optimization process. Formulas and Parameters: Gaussian Filter: The core operation is a convolution with a Gaussian kernel. The specific kernel size (k) and standard deviation (\sigma) are not explicitly detailed in the provided text but are implied to be configurable. Randomized Scaling: The kernel parameters (likely \sigma or k) are randomly scaled at each step or epoch. Separability: The method utilizes the separability of the input signal (the decomposed tensor) to achieve an equivalent effect to brute-force 3D convolution with little computational overhead. This implies that instead of convolving the full 3D volume, the convolution is applied component-wise to the factorized tensors, exploiting their structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generategaussiankernel1d(sigma): """Generates a normalized 1D Gaussian kernel.""" radius = max(1, int(3 sigma)) x = list(range(-radius, radius + 1)) kernel = [math.exp(-0.5 (xi / sigma) 2) for xi in x] total = sum(kernel) return [k / total for k in kernel] def convolve1d(signal, kernel): """Convolves a 1D signal with a kernel using zero-padding.""" n = len(signal) klen = len(kernel) pad = klen // 2 padded = [0.0] pad + signal + [0.0] pad result = [] for i in range(n): val = 0.0 for j in range(klen): val += padded[i + j] kernel[j] result.append(val) return result def applyseparablecomponentwiseconvolution(tensorfactors, sigma): """Applies 1D Gaussian convolution to each axial factor of the decomposed tensor.""" filteredfactors = [] kernel = generategaussiankernel1d(sigma) for factor in tensorfactors: filteredfactors.append(convolve1d(factor, kernel)) return filteredfactors def smooth2dimages(images, sigma): """Applies separable 2D Gaussian smoothing to a list of images.""" kernel1d = generategaussiankernel1d(sigma) smoothedimages = [] for img in images: smoothedrows = [convolve1d(row, kernel1d) for row in img] cols = list(zip(smoothedrows)) smoothedcols = [convolve1d(col, kernel1d) for col in cols] smoothedimg = list(zip(smoothedcols)) smoothedimages.append(smoothedimg) return smoothedimages def renderviews(tensorfactors, poses): """Renders 2D views from decomposed tensor factors and camera poses.""" # Standard volume rendering or tensor factor evaluation given poses. return [rendersingleview(factor, pose) for factor, pose in zip(tensorfactors, poses)] def rendersingleview(factor, pose): # Evaluates the radiance field at camera ray origins and integrates. return [[0.0 for in row] for row in factor] def computeedgeguidedloss(rendered, target, edgemask): """Computes edge-guided mean squared error loss.""" totalloss = 0.0 count = 0 for rrow, trow, erow in zip(rendered, target, edgemask): for rval, tval, eval in zip(rrow, trow, erow): diff = rval - tval totalloss += diff diff eval count += 1 return totalloss / max(count, 1) def updateparameters(poses, tensorfactors, gradients, lr=0.01): """Updates parameters using gradient descent.""" # Standard parameter update step. for i in range(len(poses)): poses[i] = [p - lr g for p, g in zip(poses[i], gradients[i])] for i in range(len(tensorfactors)): tensorfactors[i] = [v - lr g for v, g in zip(tensorfactors[i], gradients[i])] return poses, tensorfactors def jointposeoptimization(tensorfactors, images, poses, edgemask, numiterations=50000): """Main loop for joint optimization with randomized filtering.""" basesigma = 1.0 for step in range(numiterations): # Randomly scale kernel parameter for stability scale = 0.5 + (step % 100) / 100.0 # Deterministic pseudo-random scaling for reproducibility currentsigma = basesigma scale # Step 1: Filter 3D tensor volume filteredfactors = applyseparablecomponentwiseconvolution(tensorfactors, currentsigma) # Step 2: Filter 2D supervision images smoothedimages = smooth2dimages(images, currentsigma) # Step 3: Optimize renderedviews = renderviews(filteredfactors, poses) loss = computeedgeguidedloss(renderedviews, smoothedimages, edgemask) # Gradients are computed via standard backpropagation through the rendering and filtering operations. gradients = computegradients(loss, poses, tensorfactors) poses, tensorfactors = updateparameters(poses, tensorfactors, gradients) return poses, tensorfactors def computegradients(loss, poses, tensorfactors): # Standard autodiff routine. Returns gradients for poses and tensor factors. return [[0.0] for in poses], [[0.0] for in tensorfactors] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premature High Frequencies: Naively applying joint optimization on voxel-based NeRFs leads to dramatic failure because premature high-frequency signals in the voxel volume curse the camera poses to get stuck in local minima. Inapplicability to Hash Encoding: This method is specifically designed for decomposed low-rank tensors and is not directly applicable to multi-resolution hash encoding, which requires different interpolation schemes or curriculum learning. Time Complexity: The method is more efficient than traditional separable convolution kernels because it utilizes the separability of the input signal (the decomposed tensor). It achieves an equivalent effect to brute-force 3D convolution with little computational overhead. Memory Complexity: Inherits the memory complexity of the underlying TensoRF representation, which uses decomposed low-rank tensors instead of dense 3D grids. Performance: The proposed framework requires only 50k training iterations, whereas previous methods typically need 200k iterations. It demonstrates superior performance in novel view synthesis and rapid convergence for optimization. Strengths: Robust joint pose refinement, efficient spectral control, rapid convergence. Limitations: Not applicable to hash-based representations. Origin: The method was proposed in the paper "Improving Robustness for Joint Optimization of Camera Pose and Decomposed Low-Rank Tensorial Radiance Fields". History: It addresses the challenge of joint optimization of camera poses and radiance fields, which is prone to local minima due to high-frequency artifacts. The method builds on the TensoRF representation. Usage: It is used in the Joint-TensoRF project for robust joint pose refinement. name: StyleTRF
head: StyleTRF (S3)
body: StyleTRF is a method for stylized view generation that decouples style adaptation from view capture by fine-tuning the appearance component of a pre-optimized Tensorial Radiance Field (TensoRF) using sparse stylized priors. It sets itself apart from joint optimization methods like SNeRF by freezing the geometric density parameters of the scene representation, thereby preserving crisp geometry while adapting appearance, and by using a deterministic CNN-based stylization module (Johnson et al.) to ensure 3D consistency across viewpoints. Inputs: A set of posed ground-truth images of a scene. A reference style image. Camera poses (obtained via COLMAP for real scenes or Blender for synthetic scenes). Outputs: A fine-tuned TensoRF representation capable of rendering stylized novel views. Data Structures: The scene is represented using the VM-48 variant of TensoRF, which employs Vector-Matrix decomposition (a special case of Block Term Decomposition). Density Tensor (T\sigma): Stores volumetric density. These parameters are frozen during the style adaptation phase. Appearance Tensor (TC): Stores color/appearance vectors. These parameters are optimized during the style adaptation phase. Voxel Grid: The effective resolution starts at 128^3 and is upsampled to 640^3 for real-world scenes (or 300^3 for synthetic scenes). Interpolation: Bi-linear interpolation is used for matrices, and linear interpolation is used for vectors within the VM-decomposed representation during ray queries and upsampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def styletrf(groundtruthimages, cameraposes, styleimage): # Phase 1: Pre-optimization of TensoRF # Initialize VM-48 representation: density grid (128^3) and appearance grid (128^3) densitygrid = createvoxelgrid(shape=(128, 128, 128)) appearancegrid = createvoxelgrid(shape=(128, 128, 128)) optimizer = Adam(parameters=[densitygrid, appearancegrid], lr=0.02) for iteration in range(15000): # Sample 4096 rays from camera poses rays = generaterays(cameraposes, count=4096) # Render colors using volumetric rendering renderedcolors = volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, rays) # Calculate losses l1loss = meanabsoluteerror(renderedcolors, groundtruthimages[rays]) tvloss = computetvloss(densitygrid, appearancegrid) totalloss = l1loss + tvloss # Update parameters optimizer.step(totalloss) # Upsampling schedule: start at 2000, every 1000 until 5000 if 2000 <= iteration <= 5000 and iteration % 1000 == 0: densitygrid = upsamplegrid(densitygrid, factor=2) appearancegrid = upsamplegrid(appearancegrid, factor=2) optimizer.lr = 0.02 # Re-initialize LR after upsampling # Phase 2: Preprocessing Stylization Module # Train Johnson et al. CNN for the specific style on COCO2014 dataset # Note: Sources do not provide implementation details for the CNN training loop. stylizationcnn = traincnn(styleimage, dataset="COCO2014") # Phase 3: Generate and Stylize Priors # Render sparse novel views (20-30 views in spiral trajectory) novelcameras = generatespiraltrajectory(count=30) novelviews = volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, novelcameras) # Stylize these views using the pre-trained CNN stylizedpriors = [stylizationcnn(view) for view in novelviews] # Phase 4: Fine-tuning Appearance # Freeze density parameters densitygrid.requiresgrad = False # Optimize only appearance vectors using stylized priors appearanceoptimizer = Adam(parameters=[appearancegrid], lr=0.02) for iteration in range(1000): rays = generaterays(novelcameras, count=len(stylizedpriors)) renderedcolors = volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, rays) styleloss = meanabsoluteerror(renderedcolors, stylizedpriors) appearanceoptimizer.step(styleloss) return densitygrid, appearancegrid def volumetricrender(densitygrid, appearancegrid, rays): """ Computes color C from transmittance tauq, color cq, density sigma, and step size Delta. C = sum{q=1}^{Q} tauq cq tauq = product{p=1}^{q-1} exp(-sigmap Deltap) """ colors = [] for ray in rays: color = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # Q samples along the ray (0-based indexing maps to 1-based formula) for q in range(ray.Q): sigmaq = querygrid(densitygrid, ray.position[q]) cq = querygrid(appearancegrid, ray.position[q]) deltaq = ray.stepsize[q] color += transmittance cq transmittance = exp(-sigmaq deltaq) colors.append(color) return colors def computetvloss(densitygrid, appearancegrid): """ LTV = (1/N) sum( sqrt(Delta^2 Tsigma) + 0.1 sqrt(Delta^2 TC)) Delta^2 is squared difference between neighboring values. N is total number of parameters. Density and appearance weighted in ratio 10:1. """ N = densitygrid.numel() + appearancegrid.numel() tvsigma = sum((densitygrid[i] - densitygrid[i+1])2 for i in range(N-1)) tvC = sum((appearancegrid[i] - appearancegrid[i+1])2 for i in range(N-1)) return (1/N) (sqrt(tvsigma) + 0.1 sqrt(tvC)) Formulas: Volumetric Rendering: C = \sum{q=1}^{Q} \tauq cq where \tauq = \prod{p=1}^{q-1} \exp(-\sigmap \Deltap). C is the final color, \tauq is the transmittance, cq is the color, \sigma is the density, and \Delta is the step size. Total Variation Loss: L{TV} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \left( \sqrt{\Delta^2 T\sigma} + 0.1 \sqrt{\Delta^2 TC} \right) where \Delta^2 is the squared difference between neighboring values in the tensors, N is the total number of parameters in the TensoRF representation T, T\sigma represents the density value, and TC represents the appearance value. The density and appearance are weighted in a ratio of 10:1. Parameters: TensoRF Variant: VM-48 (Vector-Matrix decomposition). Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 0.02 (re-initialized to 0.02 after upsampling). Voxel Grid Resolution: Effective resolution starts at 128^3. Upsampled every 1000 iterations starting at iteration 2000 until 5000 iterations, reaching 640^3 for real-world scenes and 300^3 for synthetic scenes. Training Iterations (Pre-optimization): 15,000 iterations. Training Iterations (Style Fine-tuning): 1,000 iterations. Rays per Iteration: 4,096 rays. Number of Stylized Priors: 20–30 (or 30–40) randomly sampled camera positions around the object. Stylization Module: Johnson et al. [20] (trained on COCO2014). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimizing from scratch (Strategy S1): Fails because stylized priors may not share exact geometry with ground truth, leading to geometric artifacts. Unconstrained optimization (Strategy S2): Optimizing both density and appearance simultaneously leads to fuzzy geometry and artifacts in thin structures because limit-free optimization alters geometry components. Stylization Module Choice: Using Gatys et al. [10] causes inconsistencies across nearby viewpoints because it starts with white noise and depends on initialization/optimizer, making it unreliable for 3D consistency. Micro-details: Strategy S2 struggles to capture micro-details and may lose geometry. Time Complexity: Pre-optimization of TensoRF: 10–15 minutes. Stylization Module Training (per style): ~20 minutes. Style Fine-tuning: 40–50 seconds. Rendering (800x800 image): 4–5 seconds. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint of TensoRF VM-48: 10–15 MB. Strengths: Decouples style adaptation from view capture. Preserves crisp geometry by freezing density. Fast style adaptation (40–50 seconds). Low memory footprint compared to MLP-based NeRFs (~1GB). Stable stylization across close-by viewpoints using Johnson et al.. Limitations: Requires pre-optimization of the scene. Relies on the quality of the sparse priors; insufficient priors may lead to incomplete style transfer. When to use: When crisp geometry preservation is critical and fast style adaptation is desired. When 3D consistency across viewpoints is required. When not to use: When joint optimization of geometry and style is preferred (e.g., if the style implies geometric changes). When real-time training is required (pre-optimization takes 10-15 mins). StyleTRF was introduced in the paper "StyleTRF: Stylizing Tensorial Radiance Fields" presented at ICVGIP’22 in December 2022. It builds upon the TensoRF representation [6] and the Johnson et al. stylization method [20]. It addresses limitations in previous methods like SNeRF [29], which uses Gatys et al. [10] and joint optimization, leading to higher training times and potential 3D inconsistencies. name: TensoRF Decomposition Models
head: CP model, HY model, HY-S model, Rank-Residual Decomposition Models (CP, HY-S)
body: This family defines the tensor decomposition strategies used to factorize the radiance field density and color fields in TensoRF, balancing storage efficiency against rendering quality. It differs from sibling methods like NeuManifold or StyleTRF by explicitly structuring the low-rank approximation into discrete rank groups (rank-residual learning) and offering specific variants (CP, HY, HY-S) to control the ratio of vector- to matrix-based components. The core mechanism is Rank-Residual Decomposition, where the radiance field is approximated as a sum of M groups of components. Each group m contains a specific number of rank components for density and color. The decomposition supports two types of components: Vector-based (CP) uses only 1D vectors for each spatial dimension. Hybrid (HY) uses both vector- and matrix-based components. The HY decomposition allows arbitrary adjustment of the ratio of vector- to matrix-based rank components, providing greater flexibility in model size control compared to TensoRF's fixed 1:1 VM ratio. A scalable variant of HY that allows adjustable model size. Both density and color initially use 96 vector components. Four additional groups for color append matrix components {4, 16, 32, 64} gradually. Total M=5 groups (first has 96 vector components). The total field value at a point is the sum of contributions from all groups. The model size is controlled by the number of groups M and the rank distribution within each group. The decomposition is optimized using an Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.02 for the factorized matrices and 0.001 for the singular values. Reconstructs a radiance field from sparse input views by factorizing geometry and appearance tensors into a fixed number of components equal to the number of input views (n), rather than a small fixed constant. It differs from TensoRF by binding each tensor component to a specific input view, enabling robust point cloud fusion that substitutes inaccurate depth-derived points with accurate ones from other views. The approach uses Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition for spatial factors and a global appearance dictionary to abstract commonalities across the scene. Models radiance and geometry by decomposing feature probes into shared core factors and probe-specific basis factors. It distinguishes itself from standard CP decomposition by introducing a hybrid structure where a Vector-Matrix (VM) core captures multilinear interactions shared across local probes, while a Matrix (M) basis factor handles individual probe details, enabling efficient spatial sharing and multi-scale pyramid storage. Decomposes 3D tensors into plane and line features at multiple resolutions to reconstruct scenes from coarse to fine scales. It improves shape and appearance reconstruction accuracy and convergence speed over single-scale TensoRF while using fewer parameters. Unlike TensoRF, which performs decomposition at a single scale, MTD leverages multiscale representations to explore local smoothness at varying scales, allowing higher-resolution representations to capture richer details with fewer total parameters. Initializes the shared basis B with Fourier-Bessel (FB) bases for faster convergence, with the number of bases r set to 6 by default. The bases B are updated during training to make them specific to the scene. A smaller value of r achieves a higher compression ratio. The Rank-Residual Decomposition models were introduced in "Compressible-Composable NeRF Via Rank-Residual Decomposition". The work addresses the limitations of the standard TensoRF VM decomposition, which requires a fixed 1:1 ratio of vector- to matrix-based ranks, limiting flexibility in model size control. The HY decomposition allows arbitrary adjustment of this ratio, and the HY-S model provides a scalable range of model sizes without requiring retraining for optimal configurations. name: Factorized Radiance Field with Fixed View-Dependent Components
head: Point Cloud Fusion NeRF, VM Decomposition NeRF
body: This method reconstructs a radiance field from sparse input views by factorizing geometry and appearance tensors into a fixed number of components equal to the number of input views (n), rather than a small fixed constant. It differs from TensoRF by binding each tensor component to a specific input view, enabling robust point cloud fusion that substitutes inaccurate depth-derived points with accurate ones from other views. The approach uses Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition for spatial factors and a global appearance dictionary to abstract commonalities across the scene. Inputs: n input views, each containing an RGB image, a depth map, and camera parameters (intrinsic matrix K, rotation matrix R, translation vector t). Hyperparameters: \lambda{depth} (balance between color and depth loss), \omega{reg} (L1 regularization weight), P (feature decoding MLP dimension, set to 27), N0 (initial grid size, set to 128), N (final grid size), Q (number of shading points per ray). Outputs: Rendered RGB images and depth maps for novel viewpoints. 1. Geometry Grid (G\sigma) A factorized 3D tensor representing volume density \sigma. It is decomposed into n components, one per input view. Each component r (1 \le r \le n) consists of: Three 1D vectors: v{\sigma,r}^X \in \mathbb{R}^I, v{\sigma,r}^Y \in \mathbb{R}^J, v{\sigma,r}^Z \in \mathbb{R}^K. Three 2D matrices: M{\sigma,r}^{XY} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J}, M{\sigma,r}^{XZ} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times K}, M{\sigma,r}^{YZ} \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times K}. The grid dimensions are I \times J \times K. 2. Appearance Grid (Gc) A factorized 3D tensor representing color c. It is also decomposed into n components. Each component r involves: Three 1D vectors: v{c,r}^X \in \mathbb{R}^I, v{c,r}^Y \in \mathbb{R}^J, v{c,r}^Z \in \mathbb{R}^K. Three 2D matrices: A{c,r}^X \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J}, A{c,r}^Y \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times K}, A{c,r}^Z \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times K}. Three basis vectors: b{3r-2}, b{3r-1}, b{3r} \in \mathbb{R}^P. 3. Global Appearance Dictionary (B) A matrix of size P \times 3n formed by stacking the 3n basis vectors br. 1. NDC Mapping: Map depth values to Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space to ensure all visible locations fit within a predetermined cubic space. 2. Point Cloud Generation: For each input view r, map every 2D pixel location xp to a 3D world location xw using the camera parameters: xw = R^{-1} (K^{-1} xp D - t) where D is the depth value at xp. 3. Grid Assignment: Geometry: For each point xw from view r, identify the corresponding voxel indices (i,j,k) in the I \times J \times K grid. Set the elements of v{\sigma,r}^X, v{\sigma,r}^Y, v{\sigma,r}^Z and M{\sigma,r}^{XY}, M{\sigma,r}^{XZ}, M{\sigma,r}^{YZ} corresponding to these projections to 1. All other elements are set to 0. Appearance: For the same projections, assign the average RGB color of the projected points to the elements of A{c,r}^X, A{c,r}^Y, A{c,r}^Z. Assign random values to v{c,r}^X, v{c,r}^Y, v{c,r}^Z. 4. Dictionary Initialization: Initialize the basis vectors br (and thus matrix B). To render a pixel, march along a ray and sample Q shading points xq with step size \Deltaq. 1. Density Interpolation: Calculate \sigmaq = G\sigma(xq) using trilinear interpolation of the factorized geometry grid. For a single component r, the interpolated value follows A{\sigma,r}(x) = v{\sigma,r}(x) M{\sigma,r}(y, z). 2. Color Interpolation: Calculate the feature vector fq by concatenating the interpolated appearance factors for component r, then multiplying by the dictionary B: fq = B \oplus [A{c,r}(xq)]{r} The color cq is obtained by passing fq through a feature decoding MLP S: cq = S(fq, dq) where dq is the view direction at xq. 3. Volume Rendering: Compute the pixel color C and transmittance \tauq: \tauq = \exp\left(-\sum{p=1}^{q-1} \sigmap \Deltap\right) C = \sum{q=1}^{Q} \tauq (1 - \exp(-\sigmaq \Deltaq)) cq \tau{Q+1} = \exp\left(-\sum{p=1}^{Q} \sigmap \Deltap\right). The model is optimized using a composite loss function L: L = L{RGB} + \lambda{depth} L{depth} 1. RGB Loss (L{RGB}): L{RGB} = \|C - \hat{C}\|2^2 + \omega{reg} L{reg} where \hat{C} is the ground truth color, C is the predicted color, and L{reg} is the L1 regularization term applied to all tensor factors to promote sparsity and eliminate floaters. 2. Depth Loss (L{depth}): L{depth} = \|D - \hat{D}\|2^2 where D is the rendered depth and \hat{D} is the ground truth depth. Training starts with a grid of size N0^3 (N0=128). The grid is upsampled at specific training steps (2000, 3000, 4000, 5500, 7000) to the final size N^3. Upsampling is performed by linearly and bilinearly upsampling the XYZ-mode vector and matrix factors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def bilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y): """Interpolate 2D grid at continuous coordinates x, y in [0, W], [0, H].""" x0, x1 = torch.floor(x).long(), torch.ceil(x).long() y0, y1 = torch.floor(y).long(), torch.ceil(y).long() x0 = torch.clamp(x0, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) x1 = torch.clamp(x1, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) y0 = torch.clamp(y0, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) y1 = torch.clamp(y1, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) wa = (x1.float() - x) wb = (x - x0.float()) hc = (y1.float() - y) hd = (y - y0.float()) val = (wa hc grid[:, x0, y0] + wb hc grid[:, x1, y0] + wa hd grid[:, x0, y1] + wb hd grid[:, x1, y1]) return val def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """Interpolate 3D grid at continuous coordinates x, y, z in [0, D], [0, H], [0, W].""" x0, x1 = torch.floor(x).long(), torch.ceil(x).long() y0, y1 = torch.floor(y).long(), torch.ceil(y).long() z0, z1 = torch.floor(z).long(), torch.ceil(z).long() x0 = torch.clamp(x0, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) x1 = torch.clamp(x1, 0, grid.shape[1] - 1) y0 = torch.clamp(y0, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) y1 = torch.clamp(y1, 0, grid.shape[2] - 1) z0 = torch.clamp(z0, 0, grid.shape[3] - 1) z1 = torch.clamp(z1, 0, grid.shape[3] - 1) wa, wb = (x1.float() - x), (x - x0.float()) hc, hd = (y1.float() - y), (y - y0.float()) sc, sd = (z1.float() - z), (z - z0.float()) val = (wa hc sc grid[:, x0, y0, z0] + wb hc sc grid[:, x1, y0, z0] + wa hd sc grid[:, x0, y1, z0] + wb hd sc grid[:, x1, y1, z0] + wa hc sd grid[:, x0, y0, z1] + wb hc sd grid[:, x1, y0, z1] + wa hd sd grid[:, x0, y1, z1] + wb hd sd grid[:, x1, y1, z1]) return val class FactorizedRadianceField: def init(self, nviews, I, J, K, P, N0=128): self.n = nviews self.I, self.J, self.K = I, J, K self.P = P # Geometry Grid Factors: n components self.vsigmaX = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, I)) self.vsigmaY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, J)) self.vsigmaZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, K)) self.MsigmaXY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, I, J)) self.MsigmaXZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, I, K)) self.MsigmaYZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, J, K)) # Appearance Grid Factors: n components self.vcX = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, I)) self.vcY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, J)) self.vcZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, K)) self.AcX = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, I, J)) self.AcY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, J, K)) self.AcZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(nviews, I, K)) # Global Appearance Dictionary B: P x 3n self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(P, 3 nviews)) # Feature Decoding MLP self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(P, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 3)) self.lambdadepth = 1.0 self.omegareg = 1e-4 def getdensity(self, x, y, z): # Interpolate vectors vx = trilinearinterpolate(self.vsigmaX.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1), x, y, z) vy = trilinearinterpolate(self.vsigmaY.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1), x, y, z) vz = trilinearinterpolate(self.vsigmaZ.unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(1), x, y, z) # Interpolate matrices Myz = bilinearinterpolate(self.MsigmaYZ, y, z) Mxz = bilinearinterpolate(self.MsigmaXZ, x, z) Mxy = bilinearinterpolate(self.MsigmaXY, x, y) # VM decomposition sum: sigma = sumr (vX MYZ + vY MXZ + vZ MXY) sigma = torch.sum(vx Myz + vy Mxz + vz Mxy, dim=0) return sigma def getcolor(self, x, y, z, d): # Interpolate appearance matrices Ayz = bilinearinterpolate(self.AcY, y, z) Axz = bilinearinterpolate(self.AcZ, x, z) Axy = bilinearinterpolate(self.AcX, x, y) # Concatenate features for each view r (3 matrices per view -> 3n features) features = torch.cat([Axy.flatten(1), Ayz.flatten(1), Axz.flatten(1)], dim=1) # Multiply by Dictionary B features = torch.matmul(features, self.B.T) # Pass through MLP colors = self.mlp(features) return colors def renderray(self, rayorigins, raydirections, tnear, tfar, Q=128): # Sample points along ray tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, Q).unsqueeze(0) tvals = tvals.expand(rayorigins.shape[0], -1) points = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + tvals.unsqueeze(2) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # Map NDC world coordinates to grid coordinates [0, I], [0, J], [0, K] # Assuming points are in NDC [-1, 1]^3 xgrid = (points[:,:, 0] + 1) 0.5 self.I ygrid = (points[:,:, 1] + 1) 0.5 self.J zgrid = (points[:,:, 2] + 1) 0.5 self.K sigma = self.getdensity(xgrid, ygrid, zgrid) colors = self.getcolor(xgrid, ygrid, zgrid, raydirections) # Volume rendering deltas = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.zeroslike(deltas[:,:1])], dim=1) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma deltas), dim=1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), 1.0 - T], dim=1) weights = alpha T[:,:-1] C = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(2) colors[:,:-1], dim=1) return C def loss(self, predcolor, preddepth, gtcolor, gtdepth): Lrgb = torch.mean((predcolor - gtcolor)2) + self.omegareg torch.mean(torch.abs(self.vsigmaX)) Ldepth = torch.mean((preddepth - gtdepth)2) return Lrgb + self.lambdadepth Ldepth Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The number of tensor components is fixed to the number of input views n. Memory scales with n \times (I \cdot J + J \cdot K + I \cdot K) for geometry and appearance matrices, plus P \times 3n for the dictionary. Time: Rendering involves interpolating factors for each sample point. The number of components n adds a summation loop during density/color calculation. Measured Performance: LLFF Dataset (2 views): PSNR 17.83, SSIM 0.5512, LPIPS 0.3832. LLFF Dataset (4 views): PSNR 20.86, SSIM 0.5967, LPIPS 0.3247. DTU Dataset (0% noise): PSNR 19.34, SSIM 0.7431, LPIPS 0.2576. DTU Dataset (10% depth noise): PSNR 16.63, SSIM 0.4144, LPIPS 0.5561. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Robust to inaccurate depth values through point cloud fusion; eliminates floaters via L1 regularization; performs well on sparse views. Limitations: Performance degrades with noisy depth maps (e.g., 10% noise significantly reduces PSNR). When to Use: Sparse view reconstruction where depth maps are available but potentially noisy. Scenes where view-dependent appearance can be abstracted into a global dictionary. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Depth-Guided Robust and Fast Point Cloud Fusion NeRF for Sparse Input Views" presented at the Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-24). History and Development: It builds upon TensoRF but modifies the decomposition to fix the number of components to the number of input views, enabling explicit point cloud fusion. It uses NDC normalization similar to DSNeRF. Usage: Implemented in PyTorch, optimized on NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with a batch size of 4096 pixel rays. name: Vector-Matrix-Matrix (VMM) Factorization
head: VMM decomposition
body: Vector-Matrix-Matrix (VMM) factorization is a compact representation technique for light field tensors that models radiance and geometry by decomposing feature probes into shared core factors and probe-specific basis factors. It distinguishes itself from standard CP decomposition by introducing a hybrid structure where a Vector-Matrix (VM) core captures multilinear interactions shared across local probes, while a Matrix (M) basis factor handles individual probe details, enabling efficient spatial sharing and multi-scale pyramid storage. Input: A set of L discrete spherical probes \mathcal{T} = \{\taul \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}\}{l=1}^L, where each probe \taul represents a D-layered spherical grid located at position pl. Output: A continuous feature field \taul(\mathbf{x}) for any 3D coordinate \mathbf{x}, reconstructed via weighted blending of neighboring probes. The decomposition utilizes three types of factor tensors. The layout and typical resolutions for optimization are: 1. Core Vector (\ddot{V}{c,r}): Shape: \mathbb{R}^D Role: Shared among all local probes; captures depth interactions. Resolution: Starts at 64, upscaled to 1024 during optimization. 2. Core Matrix (\ddot{M}{c,r}): Shape: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} Role: Shared among all local probes; captures angular interactions. Resolution: Starts at (64, 128), upscaled to (128, 256) during optimization. 3. Basis Matrix (M{l,r}): Shape: \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} Role: Specific to probe l; designated exclusively for each individual probe. Resolution: Fixed at (256, 512) during optimization. Parameters: R: Number of factor components (rank). Set to 32. F: Number of basis factor components reduced via a linear layer before aggregation. Set to 2. D: Dimension of the core vector (depth of spherical grid). H, W: Spherical dimensions of the matrix factors, providing full angular coverage. To query values on the low-dimensional factors, the input 3D coordinate \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) is transformed into local normalized depth and spherical coordinates relative to a probe center p: \tilde{t} = \|\mathbf{x} - p\|2 t = \frac{1}{\tilde{t} + 1} \tilde{\mathbf{v}} = \left( \arccos \left( \frac{z}{\tilde{t}} \right), \arctan \left( \frac{y}{x} \right) \right) Here, t represents the normalized depth, and \tilde{\mathbf{v}} represents the spherical angles. The discrete tensor element \taul^{ijk} for probe l at indices i, j, k is factorized as a sum of R scalar products using the Hadamard product (\circ): \taul^{ijk} = \sum{r=1}^R \ddot{V}{c,r}^k \circ \ddot{M}{c,r}^{ij} \circ M{l,r}^{ij} Where: \ddot{V}{c,r} \in \mathbb{R}^D is the core vector component r for core index c. \ddot{M}{c,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} is the core matrix component r for core index c. M{l,r} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W} is the basis matrix component r for probe l. c, l are core and basis factor indices respectively. i, j, k denote the three modes (angular and depth). For continuous field reconstruction, linear interpolation (\cdot) is applied to each vector and matrix when querying a target position \mathbf{x}: \taul(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{r=1}^R \ddot{V}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}) \circ \ddot{M}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}) \circ M{l,r}(\mathbf{x}) To simplify computation, scalar values are concatenated into an R-channel vector: \ddot{V}c(\tilde{t}c) = [\ddot{V}{c,1}(\tilde{t}c), \dots, \ddot{V}{c,R}(\tilde{t}c)]. Similarly for \ddot{M}c and Ml. The combined feature for probe l at \mathbf{x} is denoted as Gl(\mathbf{x}) = \ddot{V}c(\tilde{t}c) \circ \ddot{M}c(\tilde{v}c) \circ Ml(vl). The final tensor value is recovered via summation: \taul(\mathbf{x}) = \sum Gl(\mathbf{x}), though a neural decoder may be included instead. 1. Neighbor Selection: For a target camera center, select K neighboring feature probes based on the distance between the target camera center and the probe centers. Use \hat{L}=16 neighboring basis factors for representation. 2. Coordinate Transformation: For each selected probe l and target point \mathbf{x}, compute local coordinates t and \tilde{\mathbf{v}} using the transformation equations above. 3. Factor Interpolation: Perform linear interpolation on the core vector \ddot{V}{c,r}, core matrix \ddot{M}{c,r}, and basis matrix M{l,r} using the local coordinates to obtain interpolated values \ddot{V}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}), \ddot{M}{c,r}(\mathbf{x}), and M{l,r}(\mathbf{x}). 4. Weighted Blending: Apply efficient weighted blending on each factor group (core and basis) across the K selected probes. This is done before performing the final matrix multiplication to avoid multiplying factors for each probe individually. 5. Factor Multiplication: Compute the Hadamard product of the blended core vector, blended core matrix, and blended basis matrix for each rank r. 6. Summation: Sum the results over all R ranks to obtain the feature tensor \taul(\mathbf{x}). 7. Decoding (Optional): Pass the aggregated features through a neural network \Phi to predict density \alphai and blended radiance weights w{i,l}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def vmmfactorizationquery(probes, corevectors, corematrices, basismatrices, targetpoint, probecenters, weights): """ Reconstructs the feature tensor at a target point using VMM factorization. Args: probes: List of probe indices selected (size K). corevectors: Tensor of shape (C, R, D) - Core vectors for C cores. corematrices: Tensor of shape (C, R, H, W) - Core matrices for C cores. basismatrices: Tensor of shape (L, R, H, W) - Basis matrices for L probes. targetpoint: 3D coordinate (x, y, z). probecenters: Array of probe center coordinates (L, 3). weights: Blending weights for the K selected probes (K,). Returns: featuretensor: Reconstructed feature tensor of shape (H, W, D). """ K = len(probes) R = corevectors.shape[1] D = corevectors.shape[2] H, W = corematrices.shape[2], corematrices.shape[3] # Initialize blended factors blendedcorevec = np.zeros((R, D)) blendedcoremat = np.zeros((R, H, W)) blendedbasismat = np.zeros((R, H, W)) for k in range(K): probeidx = probes[k] probecenter = probecenters[probeidx] w = weights[k] # 1. Coordinate Transformation distsq = np.sum((targetpoint - probecenter) 2) ttilde = np.sqrt(distsq) t = 1.0 / (ttilde + 1.0) # Spherical coordinates if ttilde < 1e-8: theta = 0.0 phi = 0.0 else: theta = np.arccos(targetpoint[2] / ttilde) phi = np.arctan2(targetpoint[1], targetpoint[0]) # 2. Linear Interpolation of Factors c = 0 interpcorevec = interp1d(corevectors[c], t, D) interpcoremat = interp2d(corematrices[c], theta, phi, H, W) interpbasismat = interp2d(basismatrices[probeidx], theta, phi, H, W) # 3. Weighted Blending blendedcorevec += w interpcorevec blendedcoremat += w interpcoremat blendedbasismat += w interpbasismat # 4. Factor Multiplication (Hadamard Product) # product shape: (R, H, W) product = blendedcoremat blendedbasismat # Expand V to (R, 1, 1, D) and multiply productexpanded = product[:,:,:, np.newaxis] blendedcorevec[:, np.newaxis, np.newaxis,:] # Sum over R to get (H, W, D) featuretensor = np.sum(productexpanded, axis=0) return featuretensor def interp1d(tensor, t, dimsize): """Standard linear interpolation along a 1D grid.""" idx = t (dimsize - 1) i = int(np.floor(idx)) f = idx - i i = np.clip(i, 0, dimsize - 2) return tensor[i] (1.0 - f) + tensor[i + 1] f def interp2d(tensor, theta, phi, H, W): """Standard bilinear interpolation on a spherical grid.""" i = np.clip((theta / np.pi) (H - 1), 0, H - 2).astype(int) j = np.clip(((phi + np.pi) / (2 np.pi)) (W - 1), 0, W - 2).astype(int) fi = ((theta / np.pi) (H - 1)) - i fj = ((phi + np.pi) / (2 np.pi)) (W - 1) - j val = (tensor[i, j] (1 - fi) (1 - fj) + tensor[i + 1, j] fi (1 - fj) + tensor[i, j + 1] (1 - fi) fj + tensor[i + 1, j + 1] fi fj) return val Division by Zero: When the target point coincides with a probe center, \tilde{t} = 0. The formula for t involves division by \tilde{t}+1, which is safe, but the spherical coordinate calculation \arccos(z/\tilde{t}) requires handling \tilde{t}=0 explicitly to avoid NaNs. Precision: Linear interpolation on low-resolution core factors (starting at 64) may introduce aliasing if not upscaled properly. The method uses progressive upscaling to mitigate this. Boundary Conditions: The spherical coordinates \theta and \phi must be correctly mapped to the matrix indices H and W to ensure full angular coverage. A minor variant that enables fast reconstruction and aliasing-free rendering by blending factors before multiplication. It selects K neighboring feature probes based on the Euclidean distance between the target camera center and each probe's center. Blending weights are computed for the selected probes and applied to each factor group (core VM and basis M) before multiplication. Linear factor interpolation is used for query points to achieve continuous light field factorization, inspired by TensoRF. This approach provides aliasing-free rendering and fast reconstruction by avoiding the need to load the entire representation into memory or trace cones/multiple samples. Time Complexity: The factorization reduces the complexity of storing and querying light field tensors. By sharing core factors, the number of parameters is significantly reduced compared to storing full tensors for each probe. The weighted blending before multiplication reduces the number of matrix multiplications from K \times R to 1 \times R (after blending). Memory Complexity: The memory usage is dominated by the core factors (shared) and the basis factors (per probe). With R=32, D=1024, H=128, W=256 for cores and H=256, W=512 for basis, the memory footprint is compact relative to the scene size. Strengths: Compactness: Achieves compact encoding while preserving locality. Efficiency: Fast reconstruction and aliasing-free rendering via soft localization and blending. Multi-scale: Stores 3D points in a multi-scale pyramid (mipmaps) format, modeling nearby areas at higher resolution and distant areas at lower resolution. Limitations: Resolution Dependency: Performance depends on the resolution of the core and basis factors. Lower resolutions may lose detail. Probe Selection: Requires selecting K neighboring probes, which adds computational overhead during query time. When to Use: Suitable for novel view synthesis in scenes with arbitrary scales where compact representation and efficient rendering are prioritized. Origin: The Vector-Matrix-Matrix (VMM) factorization was introduced in the paper "NeLF-Pro: Neural Light Field Probes for Multi-Scale Novel View Synthesis". Development: It was developed to improve grid-based representations for handling scenes with arbitrary scales within a compact and efficient framework. It builds on the concept of light field feature probes and introduces a novel factorization technique to uncover hidden relationships and patterns within the scene. Usage: It is used in novel view synthesis tasks, particularly for large-scale scenes like Google Earth, KITTI360, and City Walk, as demonstrated in the evaluation section of the source paper. NeLF-Pro: Neural Light Field Probes for Multi-Scale Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01875, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Multiscale Tensor Decomposition
body: Multiscale Tensor Decomposition (MTD) is a radiance field representation method that decomposes 3D tensors into plane and line features at multiple resolutions to reconstruct scenes from coarse to fine scales. It improves shape and appearance reconstruction accuracy and convergence speed over single-scale TensoRF while using fewer parameters. Unlike TensoRF, which performs decomposition at a single scale, MTD leverages multiscale representations to explore local smoothness at varying scales, allowing higher-resolution representations to capture richer details with fewer total parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point x = (x, y, z) and a view direction d. Output: Density \sigma and color c (diffuse and specular components) for the point. Data Structures: The representation consists of L levels. At each level l, the 3D tensor is decomposed into three plane feature maps F{xy}^l, F{xz}^l, F{yz}^l with resolution Nl \times Nl and three line feature vectors F{z}^l, F{y}^l, F{x}^l with length Nl. The total number of parameters is determined by the number of levels, base resolution, growth factor, and feature channels per level. Parameters: N{min}: Base resolution (16). N{max}: Maximum resolution (512). L: Total number of levels (16). b: Growth factor, calculated as b = \exp\left(\frac{\ln N{max} - \ln N{min}}{L-1}\right). C{app}: Feature channels for appearance field (4). C{den}: Feature channels for density field (2). Spatial MLP: 3 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU activation. Directional MLP: 6 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU activation. Bottleneck feature b size: 128. Specular encoding feature ai size: 2. Optimizer: Adam with learning rate 2 \times 10^{-3} for MTDs and 1 \times 10^{-3} for MLPs. Steps: 1. Calculate Resolution: For each level l \in [0, L-1], compute the resolution Nl: Nl = \lfloor N{min} b^l \rfloor 2. Feature Extraction: For a point x at level l: Decompose coordinates into 2D projections (x, y), (x, z), (y, z) and 1D projections z, y, x. Perform linear interpolation (bilinear for planes, linear for lines) on the feature maps/vectors: f{xy}^l = \text{Interp2D}(F{xy}^l, (x, y)) f{z}^l = \text{Interp1D}(F{z}^l, z) (Similarly for f{xz}^l, f{y}^l, f{yz}^l, f{x}^l). Compute the feature vector for level l by element-wise multiplication (Hadamard product) of the corresponding plane and line features. For example, for the xyz component: f{xyz}^l = f{xy}^l \odot f{z}^l 3. Concatenation and Spatial MLP: Concatenate feature vectors from all levels: f{concat} = [f{xyz}^0, \dots, f{xyz}^{L-1}]. Feed f{concat} into the Spatial MLP to predict parameters P = \{cd, s, n, b, ai, \lambdai, \mui\}. 4. Density Prediction: Sum the feature vectors from all levels for the density field and apply softplus activation: \sigma = \text{softplus}\left(\sum{l=0}^{L-1} f{den}^l\right) 5. Color Prediction: Construct an encoded feature vector g by concatenating encoded view direction features. Feed g and the bottleneck feature b (from P) into the Directional MLP to predict specular color cs. Predict diffuse color cd and specular weight s from the Spatial MLP output P. Compute final color: c = \text{Sigmoid}(cd + s \odot cs) 6. Volume Rendering Weights: For a ray sampled at points xi with depth ti and interval \Deltai, compute composition weights: wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Deltai)) Only compute colors for points where wi exceeds a predefined threshold to reduce computational cost. Rendered pixel color is the weighted sum: \hat{c} = \sumi wi ci Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def bilinearinterp(x, y, featmap): # featmap: [H, W, C], x,y: [B, 1] in [0, 1] H, W, C = featmap.shape x0 = torch.floor(x (W - 1)) x1 = x0 + 1 y0 = torch.floor(y (H - 1)) y1 = y0 + 1 x0 = torch.clamp(x0, 0, W - 2).long() x1 = torch.clamp(x1, 1, W - 1).long() y0 = torch.clamp(y0, 0, H - 2).long() y1 = torch.clamp(y1, 1, H - 1).long() Ia = featmap[y0, x0,:] Ib = featmap[y1, x0,:] Ic = featmap[y0, x1,:] Id = featmap[y1, x1,:] wa = (x1 - x) (y1 - y) wb = (x1 - x) (y - y0) wc = (x - x0) (y1 - y) wd = (x - x0) (y - y0) return wa[:, None] Ia + wb[:, None] Ib + wc[:, None] Ic + wd[:, None] Id def linearinterp(t, featvec): # featvec: [N, C], t: [B, 1] in [0, 1] N, C = featvec.shape t0 = torch.floor(t (N - 1)) t1 = t0 + 1 t0 = torch.clamp(t0, 0, N - 2).long() t1 = torch.clamp(t1, 1, N - 1).long() Ia = featvec[t0,:] Ib = featvec[t1,:] wa = t1 - t wb = t - t0 return wa[:, None] Ia + wb[:, None] Ib class MultiscaleTensorDecomposition(nn.Module): def init(self, Nmin=16, Nmax=512, L=16, Capp=4, Cden=2): super().init() self.Nmin = Nmin self.Nmax = Nmax self.L = L self.Capp = Capp self.Cden = Cden self.b = torch.exp((torch.log(torch.tensor(Nmax)) - torch.log(torch.tensor(Nmin))) / (L - 1)) self.appplanes = nn.ParameterList() self.applines = nn.ParameterList() self.denplanes = nn.ParameterList() self.denlines = nn.ParameterList() for l in range(L): Nl = int(torch.floor(self.Nmin (self.b l))) self.appplanes.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Nl, Capp))) self.applines.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Capp))) self.denplanes.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Nl, Cden))) self.denlines.append(nn.Parameter(torch.randn(3, Nl, Cden))) inputdim = L Capp 3 self.spatialmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(inputdim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256)) self.directionalmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3)) def forward(self, x, d): B = x.shape[0] allfeatures = [] densitysum = torch.zeros(B, self.Cden, device=x.device) for l in range(self.L): Nl = int(torch.floor(self.Nmin (self.b l))) # Extract features for level l appp = self.appplanes[l] appl = self.applines[l] denp = self.denplanes[l] denl = self.denlines[l] # Interpolate fxy = bilinearinterp(x[:, 0:1], x[:, 1:2], appp[0]) fz = linearinterp(x[:, 2:3], appl[0]) fxyz = fxy fz fxz = bilinearinterp(x[:, 0:1], x[:, 2:3], appp[1]) fy = linearinterp(x[:, 1:2], appl[1]) fxzy = fxz fy fyz = bilinearinterp(x[:, 1:2], x[:, 2:3], appp[2]) fx = linearinterp(x[:, 0:1], appl[2]) fyzx = fyz fx # Concatenate for spatial MLP levelfeat = torch.cat([fxyz, fxzy, fyzx], dim=-1) allfeatures.append(levelfeat) # Accumulate density features dxy = bilinearinterp(x[:, 0:1], x[:, 1:2], denp[0]) dz = linearinterp(x[:, 2:3], denl[0]) dxyz = dxy dz densitysum += dxyz fconcat = torch.cat(allfeatures, dim=-1) P = self.spatialmlp(fconcat) cd = P[:,:3] s = P[:, 3:4] bfeat = P[:, 4:132] # Encode view direction (simplified placeholder for REE logic per evidence) g = torch.cat([d, bfeat], dim=-1) cs = self.directionalmlp(g) sigma = torch.nn.functional.softplus(densitysum) c = torch.sigmoid(cd + s cs) return sigma, c This variant integrates the MTD representation with a specific volume rendering pipeline. It models density and appearance fields separately using two MTD representations. Density \sigmai is the softplus of the sum of feature vectors at all levels. Color composition weights wi are computed based on densities and sampling intervals \Deltai. To reduce computational cost, colors are only computed for sampled points where wi exceeds a predefined threshold. The final color is a weighted sum of predicted colors. The specular color is predicted by a directional MLP fed with an encoded feature vector g and a bottleneck feature b, while diffuse color and specular weight are predicted by the spatial MLP. The spatial MLP has 3 layers and the directional MLP has 6 layers. Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the number of levels L and the resolution Nl at each level for interpolation. Memory complexity is proportional to the total number of parameters in the plane and line features across all levels. Performance: MTD achieves better view synthesis quality than single-scale TensoRF with fewer parameters. For example, a configuration with 16 levels, max resolution 512, and 4 feature channels uses 8.5M parameters, compared to 13M parameters for single-scale TensoRF with resolution 300 and 48 channels. Convergence: Scene geometry appears fast in coarse-scale representations, leading to faster convergence than single-scale representations. Strengths: Better exploration of local smoothness at varying scales; fewer parameters for high-resolution details; faster convergence. Limitations: More complex implementation due to multiple scales; interpolation overhead at multiple resolutions. When to use: When high-quality reconstruction of wide-ranging computer vision tasks (nature scenes) is required with limited parameters and faster training convergence. When not to use: When computational resources for interpolation at multiple scales are constrained, or if single-scale accuracy is sufficient. Multiscale Tensor Decomposition was proposed in the paper "Multiscale Tensor Decomposition and Rendering Equation Encoding for View Synthesis" (CVPR 2023). It was developed to address the limitations of single-scale tensor decomposition in TensoRF, which performs decomposition only at a single scale. The method draws inspiration from multiscale methods in computer vision and aims to represent scenes from coarse to fine scales. It differs from Multiresolution Hash Encoding (MHE), which uses multiresolution to mitigate hash collisions, by using multiresolution to explore local smoothness at varying scales.
