name: Rendering Equation Encoding (REE)
head: Anisotropic Spherical Gaussian (ASG) Encoding, encode the rendering equation in the feature space
body: Rendering Equation Encoding (REE) is a technique for modeling view-dependent effects by encoding the rendering equation directly into the feature space using predicted Anisotropic Spherical Gaussian (ASG) mixture parameters, rather than encoding view directions. Unlike standard NeRF approaches that use frequency or spherical harmonic encoding for view directions, REE allows the subsequent MLP to be aware of the underlying rendering physics, facilitating the learning of complex specular reflections. It builds on Multiscale Tensor Decomposition by using the multiscale features to predict the physical parameters required for this encoding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Spatial bottleneck feature vector b (size 128) and a comprehensive feature vector g formed by concatenating encoded feature vectors from N samples. Output: Final color c. Data Structures: Spatial Bottleneck Feature (b): A vector of size 128. Feature Vector (ai): A vector of size 2. Parameters (P): Predicted by the spatial MLP. Includes diffuse color cd, specular weight s, surface normal n, spatial bottleneck b, ASG feature vectors ai, and ASG bandwidths \lambdai, \mui for i \in [0, N-1]. Numbered Steps: 1. Feature Aggregation: Obtain the spatial bottleneck feature vector b and the comprehensive feature vector g from the multiscale tensor decomposition. The vector g is formed by concatenating encoded feature vectors gi for all N samples: g = [g0, g1,..., g{N-1}]. 2. Parameter Prediction: Feed b and g into a spatial MLP to predict the parameter set P = \{cd, s, n, b, ai, \lambdai, \mui\}. The spatial MLP has 3 layers with 256 hidden units and ReLU activation. 3. View Direction Reparameterization: Reparameterize the view direction \omegao to align with the reflective direction. Let d be the camera direction and n be the surface normal predicted in Step 2. Compute: \omegao = 2(d \cdot n)n - d This ensures \omegao aligns with the lobe direction \omegai for specular reflection. 4. Sample Lobes: Sample N lobes on a unit sphere. In experiments, N = 128 (specifically 8 \times 16). For each sample i, define the primary axis \omegai = (\theta, \phi). 5. Define Orthonormal Axes: For each \omegai, define the tangent axis \omega{i\lambda} = (\theta + \pi/2). Rotate \omega{i\lambda} around \omegai by \pi/2 using a quaternion operation to obtain the bi-tangent axis \omega{i\mu}. The axes [\omegai, \omega{i\lambda}, \omega{i\mu}] are predefined orthonormal axes satisfying \omegai \cdot \omega{i\lambda} = \omegai \cdot \omega{i\mu} = \omega{i\lambda} \cdot \omega{i\mu} = 0. 6. Compute Specular Feature Representation: Calculate the feature representation of the specular integral c's(\omegao; x) using the ASG mixture model: c's(\omegao; x) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ai S(\omegao; \omegai) \exp\left(-\lambdai (\omegao \cdot \omega{i\lambda})^2 - \mui (\omegao \cdot \omega{i\mu})^2\right) where S(\omegao; \omegai) = \max(\omegao \cdot \omegai, 0), ai is the feature vector, and \lambdai, \mui > 0 are the bandwidths. 7. Predict Final Color: Apply a directional MLP (6 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU) to predict the specular color cs using the inputs b and g. The final color c is computed as: c = \text{Sigmoid}(cd + s \odot cs) where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class REE: def init(self, N=128): self.N = N # Spatial MLP: 3 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU self.spatialmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(128 + N 2, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU()) # Directional MLP: 6 layers, 256 hidden units, ReLU self.directionalmlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(128 + N 2, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3)) def samplelobes(self, N): """Sample N lobes and compute orthonormal axes.""" phi = torch.rand(N) 2 math.pi costheta = torch.rand(N) 2 - 1 theta = torch.acos(costheta) omegai = torch.stack([ torch.sin(theta) torch.cos(phi), torch.sin(theta) torch.sin(phi), costheta ], dim=1) # Define tangent axis omegailambda = (theta + pi/2) costhetal = torch.cos(theta + math.pi / 2) sinthetal = torch.sin(theta + math.pi / 2) omegailambda = torch.stack([ sinthetal torch.cos(phi), sinthetal torch.sin(phi), costhetal ], dim=1) # Rotate omegailambda around omegai by pi/2 to get omegaimu # For orthogonal unit vectors, cross product implements the pi/2 rotation omegaimu = torch.cross(omegai, omegailambda, dim=1) return omegai, omegailambda, omegaimu def forward(self, b, g, d): # b: (128,), g: (N2,), d: (3,) camera direction spatialinput = torch.cat([b, g], dim=0) spatialout = self.spatialmlp(spatialinput) # Unpack parameters P from spatialout # Assumed layout: cd(3), s(1), n(3), b(128), ai(N2), lambdai(N), mui(N) offset = 0 cd = spatialout[offset:offset+3]; offset += 3 s = spatialout[offset:offset+1]; offset += 1 n = spatialout[offset:offset+3]; offset += 3 bpred = spatialout[offset:offset+128]; offset += 128 ai = spatialout[offset:offset+self.N2].reshape(self.N, 2); offset += self.N2 lambdai = spatialout[offset:offset+self.N]; offset += self.N mui = spatialout[offset:offset+self.N]; offset += self.N # Normalize normal for numerical stability n = n / (torch.norm(n) + 1e-8) # Reparameterize view direction omegao = 2 torch.dot(d, n) n - d # Sample lobes omegai, omegailambda, omegaimu = self.samplelobes(self.N) # Compute ASG encoding doti = torch.sum(omegao.unsqueeze(0) omegai, dim=1) S = torch.clamp(doti, min=0.0) dotl = torch.sum(omegao.unsqueeze(0) omegailambda, dim=1) expl = torch.exp(-lambdai dotl 2) dotm = torch.sum(omegao.unsqueeze(0) omegaimu, dim=1) expm = torch.exp(-mui dotm 2) weights = S expl expm cprimes = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) ai, dim=0) # Directional MLP predicts specular color cs directionalinput = torch.cat([b, g], dim=0) cs = self.directionalmlp(directionalinput) # Final color c = torch.sigmoid(cd + s cs) return c Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential terms in the ASG encoding can underflow if bandwidths \lambdai, \mui are large and dot products are small. Ensure numerical stability in the exponential calculation. Boundary Conditions: The reparameterization \omegao = 2(d \cdot n)n - d assumes n is a unit vector. Normalize n if necessary. Degenerate Input: The reparameterization of view direction depends on the accuracy of the predicted normal n. If d and n are parallel, the reflection is straightforward. If they are orthogonal, the reflection direction is perpendicular to both. The quaternion rotation for \omega{i\mu} requires \omegai and \omega{i\lambda} to be non-parallel. Since \omega{i\lambda} is defined as (\theta + \pi/2), it is orthogonal to \omegai on the sphere, so the cross product is well-defined. Time Complexity: The method involves sampling N lobes and computing dot products and exponentials for each. With N=128, this is a constant overhead per point. The MLPs have fixed sizes (3 and 6 layers, 256 units). Memory Complexity: The feature vectors ai (size 2) and bandwidths \lambdai, \mui (size 1) are stored for each lobe. The bottleneck b is size 128. Performance: The method uses 16 levels of multiscale tensor decomposition, with base resolution 16 and max resolution 512. The number of feature channels is 4 for appearance and 2 for density. The spatial MLP has 3 layers, and the directional MLP has 6 layers, all with 256 hidden units. Strengths: Encodes the rendering equation in the feature space, making the MLP aware of rendering physics. Reduces the channels of the feature representation compared to direct color prediction. Limitations: Requires predicting additional parameters (n, ai, \lambdai, \mui). The reparameterization of view direction depends on the accuracy of the predicted normal n. Rendering Equation Encoding (REE) was proposed in the paper "Multiscale Tensor Decomposition and Rendering Equation Encoding for View Synthesis" (CVPR 2023). It is part of the Neural Radiance Feature Field (NRFF) method, which combines multiscale tensor decomposition with learnable feature representations. The method addresses the limitation of standard NeRF approaches that encode view directions but neglect the rich information in the rendering equation. By encoding the rendering equation in the feature space, the method aims to better model complex view-dependent effects. name: Coarse-to-fine feature grid
head: Progressive Upscaling of Feature Grids, Coarse-to-fine grid optimization
body: A training optimization scheme that reduces initial training cost and regularizes feature matrices and vectors by initializing a 3D feature grid at a coarse resolution and progressively upscaling it to higher resolutions. It improves model convergence and makes camera refinement more effective compared to training at full resolution from the start. Unlike static grid methods, this approach dynamically adapts the spatial detail of the feature representation during the optimization process. Inputs and Outputs Input: Initial coarse 3D feature grid (matrices and vectors), current iteration count. Output: Updated feature grid parameters at the current resolution stage. Data Structures The method operates on the 3D feature grid components defined in the parent TensoRF Decomposition Models, which consist of feature matrices and feature vectors. Feature Matrices: 2D tensors representing features along specific axes. Feature Vectors: 1D tensors representing features at grid nodes. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the 3D feature grid with a coarse resolution. 2. Start Optimization: Begin model optimization with an initial grid resolution of d = 32. 3. Iterative Upscaling: Check if the current iteration count is a multiple of 5,000. If yes, upsample the grid to a resolution that is two times larger in each dimension. Apply bi-linear upscaling to the feature matrices. Apply linear upscaling to the feature vectors. Initialize the new grid entries with interpolated values from the coarse grid. 4. Repeat: Continue the optimization and upscaling process every 5,000 iterations. 5. Termination: Stop upscaling when the final dimension reaches d = 256 or the desired fine resolution determined by scene complexity. Formulas Upsampling Interval: Upsampling occurs at iterations k where k \mod 5000 = 0. Resolution Progression: d{new} = 2 \times d{old}. Matrix Upscaling: Bi-linear interpolation is used for 2D feature matrices. Vector Upscaling: Linear interpolation is used for 1D feature vectors. Parameters Initial Resolution (d{init}): 32. Final Resolution (d{final}): 256 or determined by scene complexity (input DVR or IR images). Upsampling Frequency: Every 5,000 iterations. Upsampling Factor: 2x per step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Scene Complexity: If the scene is simple, a lower final resolution may suffice, reducing memory usage. Camera Refinement: Coarse-to-fine optimization is critical for effective camera refinement; skipping it may lead to poor pose estimation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofinefeaturegrid(initialresolution=32, finalresolution=256, upsampleinterval=5000): resolution = initialresolution iteration = 0 # Initialize coarse feature matrices and vectors featurematrices = createtensor(resolution, resolution, resolution) featurevectors = createtensor(resolution, resolution, resolution) while resolution < finalresolution: # [Comment] Perform standard gradient descent optimization for the current resolution # optimizestep(featurematrices, featurevectors, lossfn, optimizer) iteration += 1 if iteration % upsampleinterval == 0: newresolution = resolution 2 # Bi-linear upscaling for feature matrices featurematrices = interpolate2d(featurematrices, newresolution, mode='bilinear') # Linear upscaling for feature vectors featurevectors = interpolate1d(featurevectors, newresolution, mode='linear') resolution = newresolution return featurematrices, featurevectors A transition strategy from a coarse feature grid to a fine grid to improve shape refinement, triggered at a specific iteration count. At iteration 5000, it samples the coarse color feature at each grid coordinate and copies it to the new R{min} level (fine grid). It reinitializes the alpha feature during this transition to avoid oversaturated alpha values from coarse-stage training hindering shape refinement. The transition iteration is fixed at 5000. Time Complexity: Reduces initial training cost by starting with a smaller grid. Total training time may increase due to upscaling steps, but convergence is faster. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Regularizes the optimization process, prevents overfitting in early stages, and improves camera refinement. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of upscaling frequency and final resolution. When to Use: When training cost is a concern, or when camera refinement is critical. Originated in the context of TensoRF and HexPlane representations to address the high computational cost of training large 3D feature grids. It was adopted in ViSNeRF for efficient multidimensional neural radiance field representation and in Neural Assets for volumetric object capture. The method reduces initial training cost and regularizes matrices and vectors, while improving model convergence and making camera refinement more effective. name: Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields
head: CATRF, SCL, Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop
body: Codec-Adaptive TriPlane Radiance Fields (CATRF) is a compression framework for plane-factorized radiance fields that optimizes neural features directly in the decoded space of a standard video or image codec. It solves the problem of severe rendering degradation at low bitrates by integrating a real codec round-trip (JPEG, VP9, HEVC, or AV1) into the training loop via a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). Unlike Codec-Agnostic (CA) methods that compress features after training, or Learned-Codec-in-the-Loop (LCL) methods that require shipping scene-specific neural decoder parameters, CATRF adapts features to real codec distortions without introducing any learned codec parameters or entropy models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained plane-factorized radiance field backbone (TensoRF for static scenes, DVGO for dynamic scenes). Output: A compressed bitstream of the radiance field features decodable by standard codecs, and the ability to render the scene from this compressed representation. Data Structures: The method operates on plane-factorized radiance fields. The scene is represented by three orthogonal feature planes P = \{P{xy}, P{xz}, P{yz}\} and a 3D density grid D. Each feature plane P{ax} (where ax \in \{xy, xz, yz\}) has layout P{ax} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}, where C is the channel dimension, and H, W are height and width. The density grid is D \in \mathbb{R}^{Dy \times Dx \times Dz}. These tensors are quantized and packed into 2D canvases (images with integer pixel values) suitable for standard codecs. The default packing format is FlattenGray, which avoids cross-channel mixing to reduce codec artifact sensitivity. Quantization uses AbsMax quantization by default. Channelwise quantization is avoided as it increases bitrate by ~45x. Parameters: Codec: Off-the-shelf codecs (JPEG, VP9, HEVC, AV1). Total-variation regularization weight (\lambda{tv}): Controls the trade-off between codec compatibility and high-frequency detail preservation. Default value: 5 \times 10^{-5}. Cache refresh interval (M): The number of training steps before the cached decoded planes are refreshed. Default value: 128. Algorithm Steps: The method employs a two-stage pipeline: 1. Backbone Training: Train the vanilla backbone (TensoRF for static, DVGO for dynamic) for each scene or video segment to convergence. 2. SCL Finetuning: Finetune the radiance fields using the Standard-Codec-in-the-Loop (SCL) framework under a fixed codec configuration. During the SCL finetuning phase, each training step proceeds as follows: 1. Quantize and Pack: Quantize the multi-channel appearance planes and density grid into 2D canvases using AbsMax quantization and FlattenGray packing. 2. Codec Round-Trip: Encode the canvases using the selected standard codec, then decode them to obtain reconstructed features. 3. Unpack and Dequantize: Unpack the decoded canvases back into feature planes and dequantize them. 4. Render and Loss: Render the radiance fields from the decoded features to compute the reconstruction loss. 5. Regularization: Apply spatial total-variation and temporal-consistency regularization terms to encourage smoother, codec-friendly patterns. The total loss includes the reconstruction loss and \lambda{tv} \times \text{TV}(P). 6. Backpropagation: Pass gradients across the entire codec round-trip using a Straight-Through Estimator (STE). The codec is treated as a black box with an identity gradient (i.e., \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{Input}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \text{Output}}). 7. Caching: Cache the decoded planes across training steps to avoid per-minibatch codec round trips. The cache is refreshed every M steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class StraightThroughCodec(nn.Module): """Straight-Through Estimator for non-differentiable codec round-trip.""" def forward(self, x): # Forward: encode then decode bitstream = codecencode(x) return codecdecode(bitstream) def codecencode(x): """Simulate codec encoding: quantize to uint8.""" return torch.clamp(x.round(), 0, 255).to(torch.uint8) def codecdecode(bitstream): """Simulate codec decoding: convert back to float.""" return bitstream.float() def quantizeabsmax(tensor): """AbsMax quantization: scale to [0, 255] uint8.""" absmax = tensor.abs().max() if absmax == 0: absmax = 1e-8 scale = absmax / 255.0 quantized = (tensor / scale).round().clamp(0, 255).to(torch.uint8) return quantized, scale def dequantizeabsmax(quantized, scale): """Dequantize: scale back to original range.""" return quantized.float() scale def packflattengray(planes): """Pack list of (C, H, W) planes into a single 2D canvas (H, WC).""" return torch.cat([p.flatten(0, 1) for p in planes], dim=1) def unpackflattengray(canvas, numplanes, channelsperplane): """Unpack canvas back to list of planes.""" planes = [] for i in range(numplanes): start = i channelsperplane end = start + channelsperplane planes.append(canvas[:, start:end].reshape(-1, canvas.shape[0], canvas.shape[1])) return planes def mseloss(pred, target): """Mean Squared Error loss.""" return torch.mean((pred - target) 2) def tvloss(tensor): """Spatial total variation regularization.""" dx = tensor[:,:, 1:] - tensor[:,:,:-1] dy = tensor[:, 1:,:] - tensor[:,:-1,:] return dx.abs().mean() + dy.abs().mean() class CATRF: def init(self, backbone, optimizer, lambdatv=5e-5, cacherefreshinterval=128): self.backbone = backbone self.optimizer = optimizer self.codec = StraightThroughCodec() self.lambdatv = lambdatv self.cacherefreshinterval = cacherefreshinterval self.stepcount = 0 self.cachedcanvases = None self.cachedscales = None def trainstep(self, rays, gtimages): # 1. Get planes and density from backbone planes, densitygrid = self.backbone.getplanesanddensity() # 2. Check cache if self.cachedcanvases is None or self.stepcount % self.cacherefreshinterval == 0: # Quantize and pack self.cachedscales = [] canvases = [] for p in planes: q, s = quantizeabsmax(p) self.cachedscales.append(s) canvases.append(q) # Pack density grid similarly qd, sd = quantizeabsmax(densitygrid) self.cachedscales.append(sd) canvases.append(qd) # Codec round-trip bitstream = self.codec(canvases) self.cachedcanvases = bitstream # Unpack and dequantize decodedcanvases = self.cachedcanvases decodedplanes = [] for i, canvas in enumerate(decodedcanvases[:-1]): decodedplanes.append(dequantizeabsmax(canvas, self.cachedscales[i])) decodeddensity = dequantizeabsmax(decodedcanvases[-1], self.cachedscales[-1]) # 3. Render renderedimages = self.backbone.render(decodedplanes, decodeddensity, rays) # 4. Compute Loss reconloss = mseloss(renderedimages, gtimages) tvreg = tvloss(torch.cat(decodedplanes, dim=0)) totalloss = reconloss + self.lambdatv tvreg # 5. Backpropagate totalloss.backward() self.optimizer.step() self.optimizer.zerograd() self.stepcount += 1 return totalloss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Codec Sensitivity: Feature planes are highly sensitive to codec distortions (quantization, block transforms, in-loop filtering). Training without codec exposure (Codec-Agnostic) causes severe rendering degradation at low bitrates. Bitrate vs. Quality: Standard codecs are sensitive to artifacts. CATRF adapts to various quality levels, operating at lower bitrates with modest detail loss or higher bitrates for sharper edges. Quantization Choice: Channelwise quantization increases bitrate by ~45x and is unsuitable for streaming. FlattenGray with AbsMax quantization is the default. Cache Refresh: The cache refresh interval M balances training time and bitrate. M=128 is the empirical default. Time and Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is dominated by the encoded feature planes. On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, CATRF uses 70.04 MB total, with 69.95 MB for encoded feature planes, 0.05 MB for feature vectors, and 0.04 MB for hash embeddings. It requires 0 MB for neural codec parameters, entropy model parameters, anchor features, and MLPs. Measured Performance: Static Scenes: CATRF-JPEG achieves a 43% BD-rate reduction over state-of-the-art LCL compression methods. On NeRF Synthetic, it achieves a 23% bitrate reduction over CNC at matched PSNR. On Tanks and Temples, it achieves a 43% bitrate saving over CNC. Dynamic Scenes: CATRF achieves BD-rate reductions of 40.5% (AV1), 63.3% (HEVC), and 51.8% (VP9) compared to TeTriRF on the N3D dataset. It achieves 17% bitrate savings over HAC++ and 39% BD-rate reduction over GIFStream. Decoding Speed: CATRF-HEVC reconstructs radiance fields at 138 FPS, compared to 2.94 FPS for GIFStream and 0.35 FPS for HAC++. This is because CATRF reconstruction is neural-free, relying only on standard-codec decoding. Strengths: No need to transmit scene-specific decoding parameters (unlike LCL). Neural-free reconstruction (unlike 3DGS methods). High decoding throughput. Limitations: Requires a two-stage training process. Relies on the quality of the underlying backbone (TensoRF/DVGO). When to Use: Volumetric content delivery, free-viewpoint video streaming, 3D video playback, and telepresence. CATRF was introduced as the first standard-codec-in-the-loop (SCL) training framework for plane-factorized radiance fields. It overturns the prevailing assumption that the codec must be differentiable, instead treating the real codec round trip as a black box and using STE to pass gradients. It differs from Learned-Codec-in-the-Loop (LCL) methods like NeRFCodec and CNC, which require learned neural codecs and entropy models, and from Codec-Agnostic (CA) methods that compress features after training. name: TensoRF with Density-Shift Fix
head: Corrected TensoRF, Corrected TensoRF Density Parameterization, Density shift correction, Novelty I, TensoRF density shift correction
body: TensoRF with Density-Shift Fix is a parameter correction for the TensoRF [13296-tensorf-decomposition-models.md] density parameterization that prevents the density field from collapsing to zero during training. It replaces the default configuration (\Delta = -10, s = 25) which causes degenerate attenuation geometry and zero gradient flow, with a corrected configuration (\Delta = 0, s = 1) that stabilizes volumetric reconstruction and thresholding. Unlike the default TensoRF which may achieve high photometric fidelity (PSNR 32.0 dB) but unstable geometry, this fix yields stable volumetric errors across adjacent percentiles. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: TensoRF model parameters \theta (including feature planes/lines Pi, Li and MLP weights). Camera poses and intrinsics. Target images I. Outputs: Corrected volumetric density field \sigma(x). Optimized model parameters \theta. Data Structures: TensoRF Model: Uses Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition. Feature planes Pi (48 per axis, 27-dim features). Feature lines Li (16 per axis, VM rank-16). MLP: 2 \times 128 hidden units, ReLU activation, 6 frequencies. Scene AABB: x \in [-2.5, 3.5], y \in [-1.5, 1.5], z \in [-2.0, 1.5]. Voxel grid: 64^3 voxels (\approx 3.75 mm per voxel). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize TensoRF model parameters \theta using Kaiming initialization. 2. Set density shift \Delta = 0 and scale s = 1 in the TensoRF configuration. 3. Render views using the corrected density parameterization \sigma(x) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(x)). 4. Compute photometric loss \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}}, sparsity loss \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}}, and total variation loss \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}}. 5. Update parameters \theta via gradient descent to minimize \mathcal{L}. 6. After training, perform a threshold sweep on the resulting density field for volumetric extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes). Formulas: The corrected density \sigma(x) at position x is computed as: \sigma(x) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(x) + \Delta) \cdot s where f\theta(x) is the raw output of the TensoRF density network. With the correction (\Delta=0, s=1): \sigma(x) = \text{ReLU}(f\theta(x)) The total loss function is defined as: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} + \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}} + \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{photo}} = \text{MSE}(\hat{I}, I), \mathcal{L}{\text{sparse}} is an \ell1 penalty on density, and \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} is total variation regularization on density planes: \mathcal{L}{\text{TV}} = \sumi \left( \|\Deltah Pi\|1 + \|\Deltav Pi\|1 \right) where \Deltah, \Deltav are horizontal and vertical finite differences. Parameters: \Delta (density shift): Corrected value is 0 (Default is -10). s (distance scale): Corrected value is 1 (Default is 25). \lambda1 (sparsity weight): 1 \times 10^{-4}. \lambda2 (TV regularization weight): 1 \times 10^{-5}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dead-Zone Failure: Using the default \Delta = -10 with Kaiming initialization (f\theta(x) \in [-1, 1]) results in f\theta(x) + \Delta \in [-11, -9]. The ReLU output is zero, gradients are zero, and density remains zero throughout training. Photometric vs. Geometric Fidelity: The default parameterization may achieve high PSNR (32.0 dB) because the appearance MLP can still update, but the density field remains uniformly zero, leading to unstable marching cubes results (e.g., 204% error at p=97). Threshold Sensitivity: The corrected version stabilizes errors across adjacent percentiles (e.g., 13.8% at p=99 and 14.3% at p=97 on patient LIDC-IDRI-0001), confirming that the parameterization is a prerequisite for downstream reconstruction quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def relu(x): return max(x, 0.0) def mse(a, b): return sum((ai - bi) 2 for ai, bi in zip(a, b)) / len(a) def l1norm(x): return sum(abs(xi) for xi in x) def computetotalvariation(planes): tv = 0.0 for plane in planes: for i in range(len(plane) - 1): for j in range(len(plane[0]) - 1): tv += abs(plane[i + 1][j] - plane[i][j]) + abs(plane[i][j + 1] - plane[i][j]) return tv def correctedtensorfdensity(fthetax, delta=0.0, s=1.0): return [relu(f + delta) s for f in fthetax] def traincorrectedtensorf(modelparams, images, poses, lambda1=1e-4, lambda2=1e-5, iterations=3000): delta, s = 0.0, 1.0 for i in range(iterations): # [Comment] Standard volume rendering forward pass to produce rendered views rendered = forwardpass(modelparams, poses) lphoto = mse(rendered, images) density = correctedtensorfdensity(modelparams.ftheta, delta, s) lsparse = l1norm(density) ltv = computetotalvariation(modelparams.densityplanes) loss = lphoto + lambda1 lsparse + lambda2 ltv # [Comment] Standard gradient descent step to update model parameters updateparams(modelparams, loss) return modelparams Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On patient LIDC-IDRI-0001, the corrected method achieves 13.8% error at one percentile and 14.3% at an adjacent percentile. The default method achieves 8.0% error at p=99 but 204% at p=97. Strengths: Restores gradient flow immediately; stabilizes volumetric reconstruction; robust to variation in initialization range c. Limitations: May reduce photometric fidelity (PSNR) compared to the default configuration which can "learn" to reproduce pixel intensities via the appearance branch despite zero density. When to Use: When stable volumetric extraction (e.g., for medical nodule volumetry) is required, and the default TensoRF density collapse is observed. When Not to Use: When only photometric rendering quality is needed and geometric consistency is not critical. Origin: Identified in "Sparse-View Lung Nodule Volumetry from Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs via AReT: Anatomy-Regularized TensoRF". History: The default TensoRF parameterization (\Delta = -10, s = 25) was found to cause a critical failure mode where density collapses to zero due to the interaction with Kaiming initialization. The fix (\Delta = 0, s = 1) was proposed as "Novelty I" in this work. Usage: Applied in medical imaging, specifically for lung nodule volumetry from sparse-view X-ray projections (LIDC-IDRI dataset). name: TensoIR
head: TensoRF-based inverse rendering, Tensorial Inverse Rendering
body: TensoIR is a differentiable inverse rendering method that reconstructs geometry, material properties (albedo, roughness), and lighting from multi-view images by combining radiance field rendering with physically-based shading. It solves the problem of jointly optimizing scene appearance and illumination without explicit geometry inputs, leveraging the efficiency of tensor factorization. It differs from its parent TensoRF Training Loop by introducing a physically-based rendering path that estimates surface points from volume density and computes indirect lighting via secondary ray sampling, while maintaining the low-rank tensor structure for memory efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images of a static scene, camera poses, and optionally environmental maps for relighting. Outputs: Density field, appearance field, normal field, BRDF parameters (albedo, roughness), and estimated lighting. Data Structures: The method uses tensor factorization for the radiance field. Density Tensor: Uses 48 tensor components, distributed as 16 components per dimension (16 \times 16 \times 16). Appearance Tensor: Uses 144 tensor components, distributed as 48 components per dimension (48 \times 48 \times 48). Spatial Resolution: Typically 300^3. For complex thin structures (e.g., Ficus), 400^3 is used. MLP Decoder: A two-layer MLP with 128 channels in each hidden layer and ReLU activation. Radiance Net: Inputs are appearance feature and viewing direction. Normal Net & BRDF Net: Inputs are intrinsic feature and 3D location. Encoding: Frequency encoding is applied to directions and locations. Algorithm Steps: 1. AlphaMask Generation (Pre-training): Run radiance field rendering only (no physically-based rendering) for the first 10,000 iterations. Generate an alpha mask to identify empty space. This step takes approximately 5 minutes and reduces GPU memory usage, allowing larger batch sizes later. 2. Ray Sampling: Sample camera rays with a batch size of 4096 rays (enabled by the alpha mask). For a grid resolution of 300^3, sample approximately 1000 points per ray. 3. Radiance Field Rendering: Compute volume density \sigmaj and view-dependent radiance cj for each sample point j along the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Calculate transmittance Tj and rendering weights wj: Tj = \exp\left(-\sum{q=1}^{j-1} \sigmaq \deltaq\right) wj = Tj (1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj)) Compute radiance field color C{\text{RF}}: C{\text{RF}}(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}) = \sum{j=1}^N wj cj 4. Surface Point Estimation: Estimate the expected surface intersection point \hat{\mathbf{x}} using the weighted sum of sample positions: \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \sum{j=1}^N wj \mathbf{r}(tj) 5. Physically-Based Rendering (PBR): At surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}}, compute shading color C{\text{PB}} using the rendering equation: C{\text{PB}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{d}) = \int{\Omega} Li(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) fr(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{d}, \boldsymbol{\beta}) (\boldsymbol{\omega}i \cdot \mathbf{n}) d\boldsymbol{\omega}i where Li is incident illumination, fr is the BRDF, \boldsymbol{\beta} are material parameters, and \mathbf{n} is the normal. Visibility and Indirect Lighting Calculation: Sample 512 secondary rays from \hat{\mathbf{x}}. Filter rays: only keep those in the upper hemisphere relative to the surface normal \mathbf{n} (256 rays). Points per secondary ray: 96. Direction generation: stratified sampling by dividing the environmental map into equal 2D area grids and picking a random direction per grid. Gradients for visibility and indirect lighting are detached to save memory. 6. Relighting Sampling (Optional): If ground-truth environmental maps are available for relighting, use lighting-intensity importance sampling instead of stratified sampling to prioritize directions with stronger lighting. 7. Loss Computation: Radiance Field Loss: Compare C{\text{RF}} with ground truth. Weight \alpha{RF} = 1.0. Physically-Based Loss: Compare C{\text{PB}} with ground truth. Weight \alpha{PB} = 0.2. BRDF Smoothness Loss (\ell\beta): Encourage spatial coherence of material properties. \ell\beta = \sum{j, \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{r}(tj)} wj \left\| \frac{\beta{\mathbf{x}} - \beta{\mathbf{x}+\xi}}{\max(\beta{\mathbf{x}}, \beta{\mathbf{x}+\xi})} \right\|2^2 where \xi is a random translation vector from a normal distribution (mean 0, variance 0.01). Weight: 0.001. Normal Back-Facing Loss (\elld): Penalize normals facing away from the camera. \elld = \sumj wj \max(0, \mathbf{n}j \cdot \mathbf{d}) Weight \alphan \in [4 \times 10^{-4}, 6 \times 10^{-3}]. 8. Optimization: Use Adam optimizer. Initial learning rate: 0.02 for tensor factors, 0.001 for MLPs. Total iterations: 80,000. Coarse-to-fine reconstruction: start from 128^3, upsample vectors linearly and matrices bilinearly at steps 10000, 20000, 30000, 40000 to final resolution (300^3 or 400^3), with voxels interpolated linearly in logarithmic space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import math class TwoLayerMLP(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddenchannels=128): super().init() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(hiddenchannels, hiddenchannels) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hiddenchannels, hiddenchannels) self.relu = nn.ReLU() def forward(self, x): return self.relu(self.fc2(self.relu(self.fc1(x)))) def tensoirtraining(scenedata, numiterations=80000): # Initialization densitytensor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(16, 16, 16, 128)) appearancetensor = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(48, 48, 48, 128)) mlpdecoder = TwoLayerMLP(hiddenchannels=128) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(list(densitytensor.parameters()) + list(appearancetensor.parameters()) + list(mlpdecoder.parameters()), lr=0.02) mlpoptimizer = torch.optim.Adam(mlpdecoder.parameters(), lr=0.001) alphamask = None currentresolution = 128 finalresolution = 300 # Phase 1: AlphaMask Generation (First 10k iterations) for step in range(10000): rays = samplecamerarays(batchsize=4096) colorsrf = renderradiancefield(rays, densitytensor, appearancetensor, mlpdecoder, currentresolution) loss = torch.mean((colorsrf - scenedata.gtimages) 2) loss.backward() optimizer.step() mlpoptimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() mlpoptimizer.zerograd() if step % 1000 == 0: alphamask = generatealphamask(densitytensor, resolution=currentresolution) # Phase 2: Coarse-to-Fine Upsampling and PBR Training upsamplingsteps = [10000, 20000, 30000, 40000] pointsperray = 1000 # For 300^3 grid for step in range(10000, numiterations): # Coarse-to-fine upsampling if step in upsamplingsteps: currentresolution = interpolateresolution(currentresolution, finalresolution, step, upsamplingsteps) densitytensor = upsampletensor(densitytensor, currentresolution, mode='linear') appearancetensor = upsampletensor(appearancetensor, currentresolution, mode='bilinear') rays = samplecamerarays(batchsize=4096, alphamask=alphamask) samples = samplepointsalongrays(rays, pointsperray) # Radiance Field Rendering sigma, c = queryradiancefield(samples, densitytensor, appearancetensor, mlpdecoder) delta = samples.delta T = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigma delta, dim=1)[:,:-1]) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T], dim=1) w = T[:, 1:] (1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma delta)) colorsrf = torch.sum(w c, dim=1) # Surface Point Estimation surfacepoints = torch.sum(w.unsqueeze(-1) samples.positions, dim=1) # Physically-Based Rendering normals, brdfparams = querymaterialproperties(surfacepoints, appearancetensor, mlpdecoder) # Secondary Ray Sampling for Indirect Lighting secondaryrays = samplesecondaryrays(surfacepoints, normals, numrays=512) validsecondaryrays = filterupperhemisphere(secondaryrays, normals) with torch.nograd(): visibility = computevisibility(validsecondaryrays, densitytensor) indirectlighting = computeindirectlighting(validsecondaryrays, densitytensor, appearancetensor) colorspb = computepbrcolor(surfacepoints, normals, brdfparams, visibility, indirectlighting) # Loss Computation lossrf = torch.mean((colorsrf - scenedata.gtimages) 2) 1.0 losspb = torch.mean((colorspb - scenedata.gtimages) 2) 0.2 lossbeta = computebrdfsmoothnessloss(brdfparams, w) 0.001 lossd = computenormalbackfacingloss(normals, rays.direction, w) alphan totalloss = lossrf + losspb + lossbeta + lossd totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() mlpoptimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() mlpoptimizer.zerograd() def samplecamerarays(batchsize, alphamask=None): # Generate batchsize camera rays from scenedata.cameras # Apply alphamask to filter rays passing through empty space pass def renderradiancefield(rays, densitytensor, appearancetensor, mlpdecoder, resolution): # Standard volume rendering loop using queryradiancefield and compositing pass def generatealphamask(densitytensor, resolution): # Render density field, threshold transmittance to create binary mask pass def interpolateresolution(current, final, step, steps): # Linear interpolation of resolution between current and final based on step index pass def upsampletensor(tensor, newres, mode='linear'): # Interpolate tensor factors: linear for vectors, bilinear for matrices # Voxels interpolated linearly in logarithmic space pass def samplepointsalongrays(rays, numpoints): # Uniformly sample numpoints along each ray's near/far bounds pass def queryradiancefield(samples, densitytensor, appearancetensor, mlpdecoder): # Decode density and color from tensor factors + MLP decoder pass def querymaterialproperties(points, appearancetensor, mlpdecoder): # Decode normals and BRDF parameters from intrinsic features + MLP pass def filterupperhemisphere(secondaryrays, normals): # Keep rays where dot(raydir, normal) > 0 pass def computevisibility(secondaryrays, densitytensor): # Render transmittance along secondary rays pass def computeindirectlighting(secondaryrays, densitytensor, appearancetensor): # Render color along secondary rays for indirect illumination pass def computepbrcolor(surfacepoints, normals, brdfparams, visibility, indirectlighting): # Evaluate rendering equation integral using visibility and indirectlighting pass def computebrdfsmoothnessloss(brdfparams, weights): # Compute relative difference loss with random perturbation xi pass def computenormalbackfacingloss(normals, raydirs, weights): # Compute max(0, dot(normal, raydir)) loss pass This method computes the incident illumination Li at a surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}} for a specific direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i by combining direct lighting with physically-based indirect effects. It solves the problem of accurately modeling secondary shading (bounces) in inverse rendering without the prohibitive computational cost of traditional neural radiance field (NeRF) methods. It differs from its parent TensoIR by explicitly separating the visibility and indirect components using the radiance field's own transmittance and color outputs, enabling efficient online Monte Carlo integration via tensor factorization. This method estimates the 3D surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}} for physically-based rendering by calculating the rendering weight wj for each sample point j using the transmittance and density, and then computing the expected surface intersection point as the weighted sum of sample positions. It differs from its siblings by providing a differentiable approximation of surface geometry directly from the volume density, which is then used as the anchor for physically-based shading calculations. Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 5 hours on an RTX 2080 Ti (11 GB) for 80k iterations. The first 10k iterations are fast (~5 minutes) as they only involve radiance field rendering. Memory Complexity: The use of tensor factorization (48 components for density, 144 for appearance) significantly reduces memory compared to dense voxel grids. The alpha mask generation allows increasing the batch size from 1024 to 4096 rays, improving throughput. Performance: On synthetic datasets, TensoIR achieves higher PSNR and SSIM for novel view synthesis and relighting compared to baselines like NeRFactor and InvRender. For example, on the Ficus scene, it achieves a PSNR of 27.130 for novel view synthesis and 24.296 for relighting, outperforming NeRFactor (21.664 and 20.684 respectively). Strengths: Efficient memory usage due to tensor factorization; accurate material and lighting estimation; ability to handle complex thin structures with higher resolution (400^3). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of loss weights (e.g., \alphan) to balance normal accuracy and high-frequency detail; large \alphan can damage high-frequency detail prediction. TensoIR was introduced in the paper "TensoIR: Tensorial Inverse Rendering". It builds upon the TensoRF framework, which uses tensor decomposition for efficient radiance field representation. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous inverse rendering methods that either lacked efficiency or struggled with accurate material and lighting estimation. It is used in computer vision and graphics for tasks such as novel view synthesis, relighting, and 3D reconstruction from multi-view images. name: TensoIR Incident Illumination Calculation
head: Light visibility and indirect illumination
body: This method computes the incident illumination Li at a surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}} for a specific direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i by combining direct lighting with physically-based indirect effects. It solves the problem of accurately modeling secondary shading (bounces) in inverse rendering without the prohibitive computational cost of traditional neural radiance field (NeRF) methods. It differs from its parent TensoIR by explicitly separating the visibility and indirect components using the radiance field's own transmittance and color outputs, enabling efficient online Monte Carlo integration via tensor factorization. The method calculates incident illumination by evaluating a physically-based rendering integral. It relies on the radiance field representation to provide both visibility (transmittance) and indirect illumination (radiance color) along secondary rays. Inputs: Surface point position \hat{\mathbf{x}}. Incident direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i. Radiance field parameters (tensor factors). Spherical Gaussian (SG) parameters for the environment map. Number of secondary rays N (for Monte Carlo integration). Outputs: Incident illumination Li(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i). Data Structures: Spherical Gaussians (SG): The direct illumination environment map is represented as a mixture of SGs. Each SG is defined by an amplitude a, a center direction \mathbf{c}, and a sharpness \sigma. Radiance Field: The tensorial representation stores volume density and color. It allows efficient evaluation of transmittance T and color C{\text{RF}} along any ray. Formulas: The incident illumination is the sum of direct and indirect components: Li(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) = V(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i)Ld(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) + L{\text{ind}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) \quad (7) where: V(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) is the light visibility. Ld(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) is the direct illumination from direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i. L{\text{ind}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) is the indirect illumination. Visibility and indirect illumination are derived directly from the radiance field: V(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) = T(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) L{\text{ind}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) = C{\text{RF}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) \quad (8) Here, T(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) is the volume transmittance of the final point sampled on the secondary ray \mathbf{r}i(t) = \hat{\mathbf{x}} + t\boldsymbol{\omega}i, and C{\text{RF}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) is the radiance field color along that ray. Steps: 1. Sample Secondary Rays: For each surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}} during training, generate N secondary rays with directions \boldsymbol{\omega}i using stratified sampling over the hemisphere or sphere. 2. Evaluate Direct Illumination: For each direction \boldsymbol{\omega}i, compute Ld(\boldsymbol{\omega}i) by evaluating the mixture of Spherical Gaussians. Note that SGs are used here only for compact parameterized representation, not for closed-form integral approximation. 3. Compute Visibility: Evaluate the volume transmittance T(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) along the secondary ray \mathbf{r}i(t) = \hat{\mathbf{x}} + t\boldsymbol{\omega}i to the final sampled point. This serves as the light visibility V. 4. Compute Indirect Illumination: Evaluate the radiance field color C{\text{RF}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) along the same secondary ray. This serves as the indirect illumination L{\text{ind}}. 5. Combine Components: Calculate the incident illumination for each ray using Equation (7). 6. Monte Carlo Integration: Average the incident illumination values over the N sampled rays to approximate the rendering integral for physically-based rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeincidentillumination(surfacepoint, radiancefield, sgenvmap, numsamples): """ Computes incident illumination Li at surfacepoint for directions sampled via stratified sampling, using the radiance field for visibility and indirect light. """ totalillumination = 0.0 # Stratified sampling for secondary rays directions = stratifiedsamplehemisphere(numsamples, surfacepoint.normal) for omegai in directions: # 1. Direct Illumination from SGs # Ld is evaluated by summing the SG contributions at direction omegai Ld = evaluatesphericalgaussians(omegai, sgenvmap) # 2. Define secondary ray # ri(t) = surfacepoint + t omegai # The ray extends to the final point sampled for transmittance/color # 3. Visibility (Transmittance) # T is the volume transmittance along the ray to the final point # This is computed efficiently via tensor factorization T = radiancefield.computetransmittance(surfacepoint, omegai) # 4. Indirect Illumination (Radiance Color) # CRF is the radiance field color along the ray CRF = radiancefield.computecolor(surfacepoint, omegai) # 5. Combine: Li = V Ld + Lind # V = T, Lind = CRF Li = T Ld + CRF totalillumination += Li # Monte Carlo integration: average over samples return totalillumination / numsamples Parameters: numsamples: Number of secondary rays for Monte Carlo integration. Not given in the sources. SG parameters: Amplitude, center, sharpness for the environment map. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Previous NeRF-based methods found this process expensive, requiring 128 TPUs or days of offline pre-computation with extra MLPs. TensoIR avoids this by performing the calculation online using efficient tensor factorization. SG Usage: Unlike previous methods that use SGs for closed-form integral approximation, TensoIR uses SGs solely for compact representation. This variant refers to the specific implementation of the Monte Carlo integration step where multiple secondary rays are marched from each surface point \hat{\mathbf{x}} during training. It uses stratified sampling for the secondary rays. For each ray, it obtains direct illumination from Spherical Gaussians (SGs) and computes visibility T(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) and indirect illumination C{\text{RF}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) using the radiance field rendering equation directly. This approach is notable because it performs second-bounce ray marching online, achieving higher accuracy than previous methods that required 128 TPUs or days of offline pre-computation with extra MLPs. Time Complexity: The method is efficient enough to be performed online during training, unlike previous NeRF-based methods. This efficiency is attributed to the highly efficient tensor factorization-based representation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Achieves higher accuracy than methods using offline pre-computation or heavy hardware requirements. Strengths: Online computation of physically-based rendering integral; avoids expensive offline pre-computation or massive hardware requirements (128 TPUs); no extra MLPs required for this step. Limitations: Requires a radiance field representation that supports efficient transmittance and color evaluation along arbitrary rays. When to use: When accurate secondary shading (indirect illumination) is required in inverse rendering, and computational resources for offline pre-computation or massive parallel hardware are unavailable. When not to use: When real-time inference is required without pre-computation and the tensor factorization overhead is prohibitive (though the source emphasizes efficiency, it is a training-time optimization). The method originates from the TensoIR paper, which introduces a tensorial inverse rendering framework. It addresses the limitations of previous NeRF-based inverse rendering methods that struggled with the computational cost of physically-based rendering integrals. By leveraging tensor factorization, TensoIR enables efficient online computation of incident illumination, including indirect effects, without the need for extra MLPs or offline pre-computation. name: ZeroRF
head: ZeroRF
body: ZeroRF is a per-scene optimization method for sparse-view (specifically 36° or 6-view) 360° reconstruction that integrates a tailored Deep Image Prior into a factorized NeRF representation, specifically TensoRF-VM [8644-tensorf-training-loop.md]. It parametrizes spatial feature grids using untrained deep generator networks driven by frozen standard Gaussian noise, eliminating the need for pretraining, handcrafted regularization, or progressive upsampling. Unlike generalizable NeRFs or methods relying on pretrained priors (e.g., RegNeRF, DietNeRF), ZeroRF avoids data bias and resolution limits, while outperforming non-pretrained priors (e.g., InfoNeRF, FlipNeRF) in robustness and quality on both synthetic and real-world data. Inputs: Sparse set of input images (e.g., 6 views), camera poses, and intrinsics. Outputs: A radiance field representation (generated feature volume) and rendered novel views. Data Structures: 1. Generator Network (G): A deep neural network based on the Stable Diffusion (SD) VAE decoder architecture. It is modified to be smaller in width and depth for speed. Layers are adapted from 2D to 1D/3D as needed for the factorization. It takes frozen Gaussian noise as input. 2. Feature Volume (\mathcal{T}): A decomposed tensorial feature volume in TensoRF-VM style. For a 3D tensor \mathcal{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{I, J, K}, it is decomposed into vector and matrix factors: \mathcal{T} = \sum{r=1}^{R1} vr^1 \circ Mr^{2,3} + \sum{r=1}^{R2} vr^2 \circ Mr^{1,3} + \sum{r=1}^{R3} vr^3 \circ Mr^{1,2} where vr^a are vector factors and Mr^{b,c} are matrix factors. These factors are generated by G. 3. Decoder MLP: A multi-layer perceptron that maps sampled features to density and color. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the generator network G with random weights. Set the input to G to a frozen standard Gaussian noise sample \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), fixed for the duration of training. 2. Feature Generation: Use G to produce the planes and vectors that form the decomposed tensorial feature volume \mathcal{T} in the TensoRF-VM style. 3. Ray Sampling: For each ray r, uniformly sample N=1024 points along the ray. Accelerate this process using occupancy pruning and occlusion culling. 4. Feature Sampling: For each sampled point xi on ray r, sample the feature field F{xi} from the generated volume \mathcal{T} using linear interpolation (bilinear/trilinear depending on dimension). 5. Density Prediction: Decode F{xi} to predict volume density \sigma{xi}: \sigma{xi} = \exp(\Theta\sigma(\text{SiLU}(\Thetab(F{xi})))) where \Thetab and \Theta\sigma are linear layers, and SiLU is the activation function. 6. Color Prediction: Encode the view direction d with Sphere Harmonics (SH). Predict color c{xi}: c{xi} = \sigma(\Thetac(\text{SiLU}(\Thetab(F{xi}) + \Thetad(\text{SH}(d))))) where \Thetad and \Thetac are linear layers, \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, and SH denotes Sphere Harmonics encoding. Note: No positional encoding is added to the input of the decoder to prevent leakage of position information outside the deep prior. 7. Volume Rendering: Compute the predicted RGB color \hat{C}(r) for ray r using differentiable volume rendering: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the volume transmittance, \sigmai is density, ci is color, and \deltai is the ray marching step size. 8. Optimization: Minimize the plain Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between rendered colors and ground truth colors C(r) by optimizing the generator network parameters: \mathcal{L} = \sum{r \in R} \|\hat{C}(r) - C(r)\|2^2 Use the AdamW optimizer with \beta1 = 0.9, \beta2 = 0.98, weight decay of 0.2, and a learning rate starting at 0.002 decaying to 0.001 with a cosine schedule. name: Joint Optimization of Camera Pose and Decomposed Low-Rank Tensorial Radiance Fields
head: Joint TensoRF
body: Joint TensoRF is a method for the joint refinement of camera poses and scene geometry represented by decomposed low-rank tensors, using only 2D image supervision. It solves the problem that naive joint optimization on voxel-based radiance fields leads to suboptimal solutions because voxel-based methods lack the spectral bias inherent in MLPs, causing them to overemphasize sharp edges and get trapped in local optima. Unlike TensoRF, which assumes known camera poses, this method integrates efficient spectral filtering into the training loop to enable stable pose optimization. Inputs: A set of 2D images with initial camera poses and intrinsics; a decomposed low-rank tensor representation of the radiance field. Outputs: Refined camera poses and an optimized radiance field. Data Structures: The scene is represented by decomposed low-rank tensors. For density \sigma and color features \mathbf{c}, the method uses mode vectors and matrices. The core mechanism applies convolutional Gaussian filters on these fields to control the frequency spectrum during training. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the decomposed low-rank tensor factors and camera poses. 2. Spectral Filtering (Coarse-to-Fine): Apply convolutional Gaussian filters to both the 2D supervision images and the 3D radiance fields to enable a coarse-to-fine training schedule. Efficient 3D Convolution: Leverage the decomposition property of the low-rank tensor to achieve an equivalent effect to brute-force 3D convolution with minimal computational overhead. The convolution is applied to the individual mode vectors and matrices. Filter Parameters: Use Gaussian kernels with randomly scaled parameters during training to improve robustness. 3. Rendering: Render the filtered 2D images from the current camera poses using differentiable volume rendering. 4. Loss Computation: Compute the loss between the rendered images and the ground truth 2D images. Smoothed 2D Supervision: Apply smoothing to the supervision images to reduce high-frequency noise that could destabilize pose optimization. Edge-Guided Loss Mask: Use an edge-guided loss mask to focus optimization on structural details, improving stability. 5. Optimization: Update both the camera poses and the tensor factors using gradient descent. The joint optimization is performed for 50,000 iterations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def applygaussian2d(image, kernelsize, sigma): """Apply 2D Gaussian filter for smoothed supervision.""" kernel = [math.exp(-0.5 ((i - kernelsize//2)2) / sigma2) for i in range(kernelsize)] blurred = [] for row in image: blurredrow = [] for j in range(len(row)): acc = sum(row[max(0, j-kernelsize//2):min(len(row), j+kernelsize//2+1)] kernel[max(0, kernelsize//2-j):min(len(kernel), kernelsize//2+1-j)]) blurredrow.append(acc) blurred.append(blurredrow) return blurred def applygaussian3dseparable(factors, kernelsize, sigma): """Leverage decomposition to apply 3D Gaussian filter efficiently.""" kernel = [math.exp(-0.5 ((i - kernelsize//2)2) / sigma2) for i in range(kernelsize)] filteredfactors = [] for factor in factors: if len(factor.shape) == 1: filteredfactors.append([sum(factor[max(0, i-kernelsize//2):min(len(factor), i+kernelsize//2+1)] kernel[max(0, kernelsize//2-i):min(len(kernel), kernelsize//2+1-i)] for i in range(len(factor)))]) else: filteredfactors.append([[sum(row[max(0, j-kernelsize//2):min(len(row), j+kernelsize//2+1)] kernel[max(0, kernelsize//2-j):min(len(kernel), kernelsize//2+1-j)] for j in range(len(row))) for row in factor]]) return filteredfactors def computeedgemask(image): """Generate edge-guided loss mask.""" return [[1.0 if abs(image[i][j] - image[i][j+1]) > 0.1 else 0.0 for j in range(len(image[0])-1)] for i in range(len(image))] def volumerender(factors, pose): """Differentiable volume rendering using interpolated tensor factors.""" return [sum(f p for f, p in zip(factors, pose)) / len(factors)] def jointoptimization(images, initialposes, initialfactors, numiterations=50000): poses = initialposes factors = initialfactors lr = 0.01 # Standard learning rate kernelsize = 3 basesigma = 1.0 for step in range(numiterations): # 1. Spectral Filtering & Smoothed Supervision currentsigma = basesigma (0.5 + 0.5 random.random()) filteredimages = [applygaussian2d(img, kernelsize, currentsigma) for img in images] # 2. Efficient 3D Convolution on Tensor Factors filteredfactors = applygaussian3dseparable(factors, kernelsize, currentsigma) # 3. Rendering renderedimages = [volumerender(filteredfactors, pose) for pose in poses] # 4. Loss Computation with Edge-Guided Mask totalloss = 0.0 for rendered, gt in zip(renderedimages, filteredimages): mask = computeedgemask(gt) totalloss += sum((r - g)2 for r, g in zip(rendered, gt)) / len(rendered) # 5. Optimization gradsposes = [lr random.random() for in poses] # Gradient computation placeholder gradsfactors = [lr random.random() for in factors] poses = [p - g for p, g in zip(poses, gradsposes)] factors = [f - g for f, g in zip(factors, gradsfactors)] return poses, factors Parameters: Training iterations: 50,000. Previous methods typically require 200,000 iterations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Optima: Naive joint optimization on voxel-based NeRFs easily leads to suboptimal solutions due to the lack of spectral bias, which causes the model to overemphasize sharp edges. The proposed Gaussian filtering and coarse-to-fine schedule are critical to avoid this. Precision: The efficiency relies on the decomposition property; if the rank is too high, the computational overhead of the "efficient" convolution may approach that of brute-force 3D convolution. Time Complexity: The method reduces training time by 25% compared to previous MLP-based methods. This is attributed to the efficient spectral filtering algorithm which requires only a single reusable voxel grid. Memory Complexity: Inherits the low memory usage of decomposed low-rank tensors (TensoRF). Performance: Achieves superior performance in novel view synthesis and rapid convergence. Strengths: Robust joint pose refinement; efficient computation via separable component-wise convolution; reduced training iterations (50k vs 200k). Limitations: Requires careful tuning of filter parameters and edge-guided masks for stability. Joint TensoRF was proposed by Bo-Yu Cheng, Wei-Chen Chiu, and Yu-Lun Liu from National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University. It addresses the limitations of voxel-based NeRFs in joint pose optimization, which lack the spectral bias of MLPs. The method builds on the TensoRF framework [3026-tensorf.md] and incorporates techniques from TensoRF Reconstruction Optimization for upsampling. The source code is available at https://github.com/Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF. name: Strivec Fast Variant
head: Multi(0.6, 0.3) with TopK=2
body: The Strivec Fast Variant is a computationally optimized configuration of the Strivec method, designed to accelerate training and inference while maintaining competitive rendering quality. It achieves this by reducing the number of multi-scale levels and the number of top-k candidates considered during ray sampling. It serves as a faster alternative to the standard Strivec configuration, offering a speed profile closer to Vector-Matrix (VM) decomposition while outperforming Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition in efficiency. Builds on Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations. The method builds on the shared principles of Tensorial and Low-Rank Representations, specifically using sparse tri-vector radiance fields. The "Fast Variant" is defined strictly by its hyperparameters rather than a change in the underlying mathematical formulation of the radiance field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera poses, image observations, and the specified hyperparameters (scales, TopK). Output: Rendered images and optimized tensor factors. Data Structures: The radiance field is represented using a multi-scale tri-vector structure. The specific configuration for the Fast Variant is: Number of Scales: 2. Scale Lengths: The tensor lengths for the two scales are 0.6 and 0.3. TopK: The number of top-k candidates selected per sample point along a ray is 2. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the tri-vector tensor factors for the two scales with lengths 0.6 and 0.3 as an ablation variant of the default 3-scale configuration. 2. Ray Sampling: For each ray, sample points along the path. 3. Sparse Selection: For each sample point, identify the relevant tensor components by selecting only the top 2 candidates (TopK=2) based on their relevance or magnitude. 4. Interpolation and Rendering: Interpolate the values from the selected tensor components to compute density and color, then perform volume rendering. 5. Optimization: Update the tensor factors using gradient descent, applying regularization as per the parent method's principles. Parameters: numscales: 2. scalelengths: [0.6, 0.3]. topk: 2. Note: The standard Strivec model uses 3 scales (0.15, 0.3, 0.6) and TopK=4. The Fast Variant reduces these to accelerate computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reducing TopK from 4 to 2 reduces the computational load significantly but may slightly impact the ability to capture high-frequency details if the scene is complex. Reducing scales from 3 to 2 simplifies the multi-resolution hierarchy, which may affect the smoothness of the rendered output compared to the 3-scale variant. This is the standard multi-scale configuration of Strivec, serving as the baseline from which the Fast Variant is derived. It uses 3 scales with tensor lengths of 0.15, 0.3, and 0.6. It typically employs 24 appearance components by default. This configuration provides more smoothness and better rendering quality than single-scale counterparts, consistent with findings in iNGP. A multi-scale model with 24 components outperforms a single-scale model with more parameters. The benefit of adding more components becomes marginal when the number reaches 48. Time and Memory Complexity: The Fast Variant reduces computation by lowering the number of tensor ranks and the number of TopK candidates per sample point. This results in faster training and inference times compared to the standard Strivec configuration and TensoRF-CP. Measured Performance: Evaluated on the NeRF Synthetic dataset: Training Time: 959 seconds. Inference Time: 1.67 seconds per iteration. Parameters: 6.20 Million. PSNR: 33.09. Comparison: vs. TensoRF-CP: Faster training (959s vs 1914s), faster inference (1.67s/it vs 2.01s/it), more parameters (6.20M vs 0.98M), but higher PSNR (33.09 vs 31.56). vs. TensoRF-VM: Similar training time (959s vs 915s), slightly slower inference (1.67s/it vs 1.60s/it), significantly fewer parameters (6.20M vs 17.95M), and comparable PSNR (33.09 vs 33.14). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Achieves a balance between speed and quality. It becomes faster than CP and close to VM in speed, while maintaining competitive quality. It improves quality, training time, and compactness together with proper hyper-parameters. Limitations: The reduction in scales and TopK may limit the model's capacity to learn very high-frequency details compared to the full 3-scale, TopK=4 configuration. The Strivec method (Sparse Tri-Vector Radiance Fields) was introduced in 2023. The Fast Variant is an ablation study result from the same work, demonstrating that reducing the number of scales and TopK candidates accelerates the method without significant quality loss. The method is part of the broader family of tensorial and low-rank representations for neural radiance fields. name: Multi-scale Tri-Vector Radiance Fields
body: Multi-scale Tri-Vector Radiance Fields is a low-rank volume representation that extends the Strivec Fast Variant by employing a multi-scale tensor decomposition to improve rendering smoothness and quality. It differs from its parent method by combining multiple tensor resolutions to capture both coarse structures and fine details, outperforming single-scale counterparts with fewer parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D images with known camera poses. Output: A radiance field model capable of synthesizing novel views. Data Structures: The model consists of S scales. For each scale s \in \{1, \dots, S\}, the radiance field is represented by a set of tri-vectors. Tensor Lengths: Each scale s has a specific tensor length Ls. The default configuration uses three scales with lengths L1 = 0.15, L2 = 0.3, and L3 = 0.6. Components: Each scale maintains K appearance components. The default ablation setting uses K=24 components. Tri-Vector Representation: For each component k and scale s, the density and color are factorized into three vectors: \mathbf{u}{s,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{Ls}, \mathbf{v}{s,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{Ls}, and \mathbf{w}{s,k} \in \mathbb{R}^{Ls}, corresponding to spatial dimensions x, y, z. The density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} at position \mathbf{p} = (x,y,z) are computed by summing contributions across scales and components. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize tri-vectors for each scale s and component k. The tensor lengths are fixed as Ls \in \{0.15, 0.3, 0.6\} for S=3 scales. 2. Evaluation: For a query point \mathbf{p}, compute the density and color by interpolating the tri-vectors. The multi-scale approach aggregates information from all scales, providing smoother gradients than single-scale models. 3. Optimization: Minimize the photometric loss between rendered and input images. The multi-scale structure allows the model to capture high-frequency details more effectively than single-scale models with comparable parameter counts. Parameters: Number of scales S=3. Tensor lengths: 0.15, 0.3, 0.6. Number of appearance components K=24 (default). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Adding more than 48 components yields marginal performance gains, as the model struggles to learn high-frequency details despite increased capacity. Single-scale models with more parameters may underperform the multi-scale model with fewer components due to lack of smoothness. TensoRF represents a 3D radiance field by factorizing the volume into a sum of outer products between functions of one or more spatial dimensions, significantly reducing memory usage compared to dense voxel grids. Time and Memory Complexity: The multi-scale structure reduces memory usage compared to dense voxel grids by factorizing the volume. The specific complexity depends on the tensor lengths and number of components. Measured Performance: On the NeRF Synthetic dataset, the multi-scale model with 24 components outperforms single-scale models with more parameters. Strengths: Provides more smoothness and better rendering quality than single-scale counterparts. Limitations: The benefit of adding more components becomes marginal when the number reaches 48. The method is part of the Strivec family, which uses sparse tri-vector radiance fields for efficient volume rendering. The multi-scale variant was introduced to address the limitations of single-scale representations, drawing inspiration from iNGP findings on multi-scale benefits. name: TensoRF Volume Representation
head: Static TensoRF, Tensorial Radiance Fields
body: TensoRF represents a 3D radiance field by factorizing the volume into a sum of outer products between functions of one or more spatial dimensions, significantly reducing memory usage compared to dense voxel grids. It differs from its parent method, Multi-scale Tri-Vector Radiance Fields, by using a specific low-rank tensor decomposition structure for both density and appearance, enabling efficient optimization of static scenes. Inputs: Spatial coordinates xk = (xk, yk, zk) for sample points along a ray. Ray direction \vec{\omega} for color evaluation. Hyperparameters: M: Output dimension of the vector-valued functions (rank). Nx, Ny, Nz: Spatial resolution of the discretized arrays. Outputs: Density \sigma(xk) at each sample point. Spherical harmonic coefficients A(xk) at each sample point. Final color Le(xk, \vec{\omega}) computed from coefficients and direction. Data Structures: The representation consists of six sets of vector-valued functions discretized into arrays. For a single component of the vector output (dimension M): f1: Stored as a 2D array of size Nx \times Ny. g1: Stored as a 1D array of size Nz. f2: Stored as a 2D array of size Nx \times Nz. g2: Stored as a 1D array of size Ny. f3: Stored as a 2D array of size Ny \times Nz. g3: Stored as a 1D array of size Nx. h1, k1, h2, k2, h3, k3: Same layout as f/g pairs, used for density. B1, B2, B3: Linear transforms mapping the element-wise products to the spherical harmonic coefficient space. Algorithm: 1. Evaluate Appearance Coefficients: Compute the spherical harmonic coefficients A(xk) for point xk using the following factorization: A(xk) = B1(f1(xk, yk) \odot g1(zk)) + B2(f2(xk, zk) \odot g2(yk)) + B3(f3(yk, zk) \odot g3(xk)) Here, \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. fj and gj are vector-valued functions with output dimension M. Bj are linear transforms. 2. Evaluate Density: Compute the density \sigma(xk) using a similar factorization: \sigma(xk) = \mathbf{1}^\top(h1(xk, yk) \odot k1(zk)) + \mathbf{1}^\top(h2(xk, zk) \odot k2(yk)) + \mathbf{1}^\top(h3(yk, zk) \odot k3(xk)) Here, \mathbf{1} is a vector of ones, and hj, kj are vector-valued functions with output dimension M. The term \mathbf{1}^\top(\cdot) sums the elements of the resulting vector. 3. Compute Color: Compute the color Le(xk, \vec{\omega}) by taking the dot product of the coefficients A(xk) and the spherical harmonic basis functions evaluated at the ray direction \vec{\omega}. 4. Volume Rendering: Use the computed color Le(xk, \vec{\omega}) and density \sigma(xk) for all sample points \{xk\} along a ray to render the final pixel color, typically via standard volume rendering integration (e.g., Eq. 2 in). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluatetensorrf(x, y, z, B1, B2, B3, f1, g1, f2, g2, f3, g3, h1, k1, h2, k2, h3, k3, shbasisfunc): """ Evaluates TensoRF representation for a batch of points. Args: x, y, z: 1D arrays of coordinates, shape (N,) B1, B2, B3: Linear transform matrices, shape (Msh, M) f1: Array, shape (Nx, Ny) g1: Array, shape (Nz,)... (other arrays follow similar layout) shbasisfunc: Function evaluating spherical harmonics at direction omega. Note: This implementation assumes omega is handled externally or passed if needed. For pure spatial evaluation, we return A. Returns: A: Spherical harmonic coefficients, shape (N, Msh) sigma: Density, shape (N,) """ # Interpolate functions at coordinates # f1(x, y) -> shape (N, M) assuming M channels per array element or # M separate arrays. The source says "M different 2D and 1D arrays". # We assume f1 is a list of M arrays or a single array with last dim M. # For clarity, we assume f1 has shape (Nx, Ny, M). # Interpolation helper def interp2d(arr2d, xcoords, ycoords): # Bilinear interpolation # Returns shape (N, M) if arr2d is (Nx, Ny, M) pass def interp1d(arr1d, zcoords): # Linear interpolation # Returns shape (N, M) if arr1d is (Nz, M) pass # Evaluate terms for Appearance # Term 1: f1(x,y) g1(z) f1val = interp2d(f1, x, y) # (N, M) g1val = interp1d(g1, z) # (N, M) term1 = f1val g1val # Element-wise, (N, M) # Term 2: f2(x,z) g2(y) f2val = interp2d(f2, x, z) g2val = interp1d(g2, y) term2 = f2val g2val # Term 3: f3(y,z) g3(x) f3val = interp2d(f3, y, z) g3val = interp1d(g3, x) term3 = f3val g3val # Sum and apply linear transforms # B1, B2, B3 are (Msh, M) A = np.zeros((len(x), B1.shape[0])) A += (term1 @ B1.T) A += (term2 @ B2.T) A += (term3 @ B3.T) # Evaluate terms for Density # Term 1: h1(x,y) k1(z) h1val = interp2d(h1, x, y) k1val = interp1d(k1, z) dterm1 = h1val k1val sigma1 = np.sum(dterm1, axis=1) # Sum over M # Term 2: h2(x,z) k2(y) h2val = interp2d(h2, x, z) k2val = interp1d(k2, y) dterm2 = h2val k2val sigma2 = np.sum(dterm2, axis=1) # Term 3: h3(y,z) k3(x) h3val = interp2d(h3, y, z) k3val = interp1d(k3, x) dterm3 = h3val k3val sigma3 = np.sum(dterm3, axis=1) sigma = sigma1 + sigma2 + sigma3 return A, sigma def computecolor(A, omega): """ Computes color from SH coefficients and direction. """ # Evaluate SH basis at omega shbasis = shbasisfunc(omega) # Shape (Msh,) # Dot product for each point color = A @ shbasis return color Extends TensoRF to parameterize volumetric snapshots at discrete time steps (keyframes) by making the gj and kj functions dependent on time \taui, in addition to one spatial dimension. The spatial functions fj remain static. Formula: A(xk, \taui) = B1(f1(xk, yk) \odot g1(zk, \taui)) + B2(f2(xk, zk) \odot g2(yk, \taui)) + B3(f3(yk, zk) \odot g3(xk, \taui)) \sigma(xk, \taui) = \mathbf{1}^\top(h1(xk, yk) \odot k1(zk, \taui)) + \mathbf{1}^\top(h2(xk, zk) \odot k2(yk, \taui)) + \mathbf{1}^\top(h3(yk, zk) \odot k3(xk, \taui)) Layout: Memory layout uses spatial resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz) and number of keyframes Nt. f1 is stored as Nx \times Ny. g1 is stored as Nz \times Nt. Since Nt \ll Nx/y/z, the time-dependent arrays do not significantly increase model size. Parameters: For dynamic datasets, every 4th frame is used as a keyframe. Input videos are split into 50-frame chunks for training. Memory: The memory footprint is significantly lower than dense voxel grids because it stores low-rank factors. For dynamic scenes, the memory footprint is similar to a static TensoRF for a single frame, assuming the number of keyframes is small relative to spatial resolution. Performance: Specific FPS and PSNR numbers are provided in comparisons against other methods (e.g., DoNeRF dataset) in the source, but exact hardware specs for the TensoRF baseline are not detailed in the provided text. Strengths: Memory efficiency for static and dynamic scenes; ability to handle high-resolution volumes via factorization. Limitations: Requires discretization of functions into arrays; dynamic scenes require keyframe selection and chunking. TensoRF (Tensorial Radiance Fields) was introduced as a memory-efficient approach to represent 3D volumes by factorizing them into outer products of functions. It builds on the concept of low-rank tensor decomposition applied to radiance fields. The dynamic extension, Keyframe-Based Dynamic Volume Representation, was developed to handle 6-DoF video by adapting TensoRF to parameterize volumetric snapshots at discrete time steps.
