name: Hybrid Multi-Space Module
head: Hybrid MS Module, MS module for grid-based methods, MS-NeRF Hybrid MS Module, MS-TensoRF, MS-iNGP, multi-space iNGP
body: The Hybrid Multi-Space Module extends grid-based Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) methods to handle scenes with complex light paths, such as reflections and refractions, by decomposing the rendering process into multiple sub-spaces. Unlike pure feature-field approaches that are incompatible with high-performance grid structures, this module integrates a small "Gate" MLP to compute composition weights while using multiple radiance fields (density and color) within the explicit grid backbone. It sets itself apart from siblings like Hybrid Representation by explicitly modeling K distinct radiance fields for sub-spaces rather than just feature fields, enabling accurate rendering of virtual images and refractive surfaces in grid-based frameworks like iNGP and TensoRF. The method modifies the standard grid-based NeRF pipeline by introducing a parallel "Gate" MLP branch and expanding the output layer to support K sub-spaces. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Sampled 3D points \{pi\} along a ray, ray direction d, explicit grid parameters V (from the parent Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Representations), and positional encoding \gamma(pi). Outputs: Final rendered color C and optional per-sub-space color maps \{Ck\}. Data Structures: 1. Explicit Grid (V): Inherits the layout from the parent method (e.g., hash table or voxel grid) storing feature vectors. 2. Gate MLP (\ThetaG): A small Multi-Layer Perceptron with parameters \ThetaG. Input dimension: Dimension of positional encoding \gamma(p). Hidden layer dimension: h. Output dimension: d (feature vector size for gating). 3. Radiance Fields Branch: The main grid-based NeRF backbone. Output: For each sub-space k \in \{1, \dots, K\}, outputs density \sigma{ik} and color c{ik} for point pi. Parameters: K: Total number of sub-spaces. Typical value: 4. d: Dimension of output features for the Gate MLP. Typical value: 8. h: Hidden layer dimension of the Gate MLP. Typical value: 32. \gamma(\cdot): Positional encoding function (as defined in standard NeRF literature, e.g., Eq. 1). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Gate MLP: Construct a small MLP \ThetaG with hidden dimension h and output dimension d, initializing it similarly to the main branch's MLP but with smaller capacity. 2. Query Gate Features: For each sampled point pi and view direction d, compute positional encoding \gamma(pi). Pass \gamma(pi) and d through \ThetaG to obtain a feature vector fi \in \mathbb{R}^d. One feature vector is recorded per position due to model capacity constraints. 3. Query Radiance Fields: For each sampled point pi and view direction d, retrieve the base feature vector v{pi} from the explicit grid V using query function Q(V, pi). Pass v{pi} and d through the main radiance field decoder to predict K pairs of density and color: \{(\sigma{i1}, c{i1}), \dots, (\sigma{iK}, c{iK})\}. 4. Multi-Space Integration (Color Maps): Perform volumetric rendering along the ray for each sub-space k independently. Use the densities \{\sigma{ik}\}i and colors \{c{ik}\}i to compute transmittance and opacity. Integrate to form K color maps \{Ck\}. Formula: Ck = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{ik} (1 - e^{-\sigma{ik} \deltai}) c{ik}, where T{ik} is the accumulated transmittance up to point i for sub-space k, and \deltai is the distance between samples. 5. Multi-Space Integration (Feature Maps): Perform volumetric rendering using the Gate features \{fi\} and the sub-space densities \{\sigma{ik}\}i. Compute K feature maps \{Fk\} for each sub-space. Formula: Fk = \sum{i=1}^{N} T{ik} (1 - e^{-\sigma{ik} \deltai}) fi. 6. Decode Composition Weights: Decode the pixel-wise composition weight map \{wk\} from the feature maps \{Fk\}. Formula: wk = \text{Softmax}(\text{Reduce}(Fk)), where \text{Reduce} projects the d-dimensional feature map to a scalar (e.g., linear projection or sum). 7. Compose Final Output: Combine the K color maps \{Ck\} using the decoded weights \{wk\}. Formula: C = \sum{k=1}^{K} wk Ck. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridmultispacerender(rayorigin, raydirection, gridV, gatemlp, radiancedecoder, K, d, h, tnear, tfar, Nsamples): """ Renders a single ray using the Hybrid Multi-Space Module. Args: rayorigin: (3,) float32, origin of the ray. raydirection: (3,) float32, normalized direction of the ray. gridV: Explicit feature storage (e.g., HashGrid or VoxelGrid). gatemlp: Small MLP with hidden dim h, output dim d. radiancedecoder: Main decoder mapping grid features + direction to K (sigma, color) pairs. K: Number of sub-spaces. d: Output dimension of gatemlp. h: Hidden dimension of gatemlp. tnear, tfar: Ray bounds. Nsamples: Number of samples per ray. Returns: finalcolor: (3,) float32, rendered color. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray tvals = tnear + (tfar - tnear) np.arange(Nsamples) / Nsamples points = rayorigin + raydirection tvals[:, np.newaxis] deltas = (tfar - tnear) / Nsamples # 2. Compute Gate Features gammapoints = positionalencoding(points) directions = np.broadcastto(raydirection, (Nsamples, 3)) gateinput = np.concatenate([gammapoints, directions], axis=-1) gatefeatures = gatemlp(gateinput) # Shape: (Nsamples, d) # 3. Query Radiance Fields for K sub-spaces gridfeatures = gridV.query(points) sigmas, colors = radiancedecoder(gridfeatures, raydirection) # sigmas: (N, K), colors: (N, K, 3) # 4. Multi-Space Integration colormaps = np.zeros((K, 3)) featuremaps = np.zeros((K, d)) for k in range(K): sigmak = sigmas[:, k] colork = colors[:, k,:] alphak = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmak deltas) transmittancek = np.ones(Nsamples) transmittancek[1:] = np.cumprod(1.0 - alphak[:-1]) sampleweights = transmittancek alphak colormaps[k] += np.sum(sampleweights[:, np.newaxis] colork, axis=0) featuremaps[k] += np.sum(sampleweights[:, np.newaxis] gatefeatures, axis=0) # 5. Decode Composition Weights scalarfeatures = np.sum(featuremaps, axis=1) weights = softmax(scalarfeatures) # 6. Compose Final Result finalcolor = np.sum(weights[:, np.newaxis] colormaps, axis=0) return finalcolor def positionalencoding(points, numfrequencies=10): # Standard NeRF positional encoding scales = np.array([2i for i in range(numfrequencies)]) scaledpoints = np.einsum('ij,k->ikj', points, scales) scaledpoints = np.reshape(scaledpoints, (scaledpoints.shape[0], -1)) return np.concatenate([np.sin(scaledpoints), np.cos(scaledpoints)], axis=-1) def softmax(x): ex = np.exp(x - np.max(x)) return ex / ex.sum(axis=0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Grid-based feature retrieval assumes continuous variation; sharp discontinuities in sub-space boundaries may require higher grid resolution or specialized handling. Boundaries: Points outside the defined storage domain must be handled (e.g., clamping or zero-padding) as per the parent method's requirements. Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the scene may result in sparse feature storage, requiring efficient sparse data structures or padding strategies. Weight Decoding: The exact reduction of feature maps Fk (size d) to scalar weights wk is not explicitly defined in the source text, only that they are "decoded". Implementation requires a choice (e.g., linear projection or sum). An implementation of the Hybrid Multi-Space Module integrated with Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (iNGP). It uses the iNGP hash grid and proposal estimator. Choose when rendering unbounded scenes with reflections/refractions requiring fast convergence. An implementation of the Hybrid Multi-Space Module integrated with Tensor Decomposition-based NeRF (TensoRF). It uses 2D/3D tensor grids. Choose when rendering bounded scenes with complex light paths where memory efficiency of tensor decomposition is prioritized. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the MS-TensoRF-grid ablation, the method achieved PSNR 32.07 and SSIM 0.932. In Mip-NeRF 360-based experiments, it showed a 4.15 dB PSNR improvement over baselines with minimal extra cost. Strengths: Compatible with high-performance grid-based methods (iNGP, TensoRF); handles reflections and refractions effectively; small Gate MLP keeps parameter count low. Limitations: Requires tuning of K, d, h; performance depends on the underlying grid's ability to resolve sub-space boundaries. When to use: Scenes with complex light paths (mirrors, glass) where grid-based methods are preferred for speed/memory. When not to use: Simple scenes without multi-space effects, where standard grid-based NeRF suffices. The Hybrid Multi-Space Module was introduced in "MS-NeRF: Multi-Space Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the limitation of previous multi-space modules that relied on MLP-based feature fields, which are not compatible with the high-performance grid-based representations (like iNGP and TensoRF) that dominate modern NeRF optimization. By decomposing the multi-space composition information into a small MLP branch (Gate) and modeling the sub-spaces using multiple radiance fields within the grid, it enables efficient rendering of reflective and refractive surfaces in grid-based frameworks. MS-NeRF: Multi-Space Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3540074, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DVGO (Deep Voxel Grids)
head: Deep Voxel Grids, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization
body: DVGO is a super-fast radiance field method that uses a hybrid representation: explicit for density inference and implicit for color inference, chosen for its potential for real-time applications. It speeds up NeRF by replacing the density MLP with voxel grids, allowing for efficient trilinear interpolation and volume rendering. Unlike completely implicit NeRF representations which are not fast enough for real-time applications due to querying costs, DVGO achieves competitive results and speed by leveraging the efficiency of grid-based explicit representations for density. DVGO operates in two stages: a coarse stage and a fine stage. The coarse stage uses two explicit volumes for density and color, while the fine stage refines the density grid and replaces the color volume with a feature grid and a shallow MLP for view-dependent color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera parameters (ray origin o and direction d), near and far planes, scene images (for supervision). Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}(r) for each ray r. Data Structures: 1. Coarse Stage: V^{(\sigma,c)}: A 3D voxel grid storing raw density values \ddot{\sigma}^{(c)}. Dimensions: Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Initialized with zero raw density to prevent suboptimal geometry. V^{(rgb,c)}: A 3D voxel grid storing color values c^{(c)}. Dimensions: Nx \times Ny \times Nz. 2. Fine Stage: V^{(\sigma,f)}: A higher-resolution 3D voxel grid storing raw density values \ddot{\sigma}^{(f)}. Initialized with the optimized coarse geometry V^{(\sigma,c)}. V^{(feat,f)}: A 3D voxel grid storing color features. Dimensions: Nx \times Ny \times Nz. MLP{\Theta{rgb}}: A shallow multi-layer perceptron for view-dependent color inference. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: For a pixel-rendering ray r, sample n points xi between pre-defined near and far planes. Let \deltai be the distance between adjacent sampled points. 2. Coarse Stage Query (Optional/Initial): Query density: \ddot{\sigma}^{(c)} = \text{interp}(x, V^{(\sigma,c)}). Query color: c^{(c)} = \text{interp}(x, V^{(rgb,c)}). Activate density: \sigma^{(c)} = \text{softplus}(\ddot{\sigma}^{(c)}) = \log(1 + \exp(\ddot{\sigma}^{(c)} + b)), where b is a shift hyperparameter. 3. Fine Stage Query: Density Retrieval: Interpolate raw density from the refined grid: \ddot{\sigma}^{(f)} = \text{interp}(x, V^{(\sigma,f)}) where \text{interp} denotes trilinear interpolation. Density Activation: Apply shifted softplus to obtain final density: \sigma = \text{softplus}(\ddot{\sigma}^{(f)}) = \log(1 + \exp(\ddot{\sigma}^{(f)} + b)) where b is a hyperparameter. Feature Retrieval: Interpolate color features from the feature grid: v = \text{interp}(x, V^{(feat,f)}) where v \in \mathbb{R}^C. Color Decoding: Map the color feature to a view-dependent color emission using the shallow MLP: c^{(rgb)} = MLP{\Theta{rgb}}(v, x, d) Positional encoding is applied to encode x and d for the MLP{\Theta{rgb}}. 4. Volume Rendering: Calculate light termination probability (opacity) for each point: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where \sigmai is the density at point i and \deltai is the distance to the adjacent point. Calculate accumulated transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) with T1 = 1. Accumulate results into a single color \hat{C}(r): \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \alphai ci + T{n+1} c{bg} where ci is the color at point i, and c{bg} is a pre-defined background color. Parameters: b: A shift hyperparameter in the softplus activation function for density. Grid Resolution: Nx, Ny, Nz for coarse and fine grids. MLP Architecture: Shallow MLP for color decoding. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: V^{(\sigma,c)} must be initialized with zero raw density to prevent suboptimal geometry. Precision: Trilinear interpolation assumes continuous variation between voxels; sharp discontinuities may require higher resolution. Boundaries: Points outside the defined storage domain must be handled (e.g., clamping, zero-padding, or out-of-bounds flags). Degenerate Input: Empty regions in the scene may result in sparse feature storage, requiring efficient sparse data structures or padding strategies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softplus(x, b=0.0): """Shifted softplus activation.""" return np.log(1 + np.exp(x + b)) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, points): """ Perform trilinear interpolation for points in a 3D grid. grid: np.array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) or (Nx, Ny, Nz, C) points: np.array of shape (N, 3) with coordinates in [0, 1] relative to grid bounds Returns: interpolated values. If grid has C channels, returns (N, C). """ Nx, Ny, Nz = grid.shape[:3] coords = points np.array([Nx - 1, Ny - 1, Nz - 1]) x0, y0, z0 = np.floor(coords).astype(int) x1, y1, z1 = np.ceil(coords).astype(int) x0 = np.clip(x0, 0, Nx - 1) x1 = np.clip(x1, 0, Nx - 1) y0 = np.clip(y0, 0, Ny - 1) y1 = np.clip(y1, 0, Ny - 1) z0 = np.clip(z0, 0, Nz - 1) z1 = np.clip(z1, 0, Nz - 1) fx, fy, fz = coords - np.floor(coords) def getval(x, y, z): return grid[x, y, z] v000 = getval(x0, y0, z0) v100 = getval(x1, y0, z0) v010 = getval(x0, y1, z0) v110 = getval(x1, y1, z0) v001 = getval(x0, y0, z1) v101 = getval(x1, y0, z1) v011 = getval(x0, y1, z1) v111 = getval(x1, y1, z1) w000 = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) w100 = fx(1-fy)(1-fz) w010 = (1-fx)fy(1-fz) w110 = fxfy(1-fz) w001 = (1-fx)(1-fy)fz w101 = fx(1-fy)fz w011 = (1-fx)fyfz w111 = fxfyfz return (w000v000 + w100v100 + w010v010 + w110v110 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) def dvgorenderray(rayorigin, raydirection, nearplane, farplane, Vsigmaf, Vfeatf, mlprgb, b, bgcolor, numsamples=128): """ Render a single ray using the fine stage of DVGO. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array raydirection: (3,) array nearplane: float farplane: float Vsigmaf: 3D grid of raw densities Vfeatf: 3D grid of color features mlprgb: function taking (features, position, direction) -> color b: shift hyperparameter for softplus bgcolor: (3,) array numsamples: int Returns: color: (3,) array """ # 1. Sample points along the ray t = np.linspace(nearplane, farplane, numsamples) points = rayorigin + t[:, np.newaxis] raydirection # 2. Query Density rawdensities = trilinearinterpolate(Vsigmaf, points) densities = softplus(rawdensities, b) # 3. Query Color Features and Decode features = trilinearinterpolate(Vfeatf, points) # Positional encoding is applied to points and direction colors = np.zeros((numsamples, 3)) for i in range(numsamples): colors[i] = mlprgb(features[i], points[i], raydirection) # 4. Volume Rendering # Calculate delta distances correctly deltas = np.full(numsamples, (farplane - nearplane) / (numsamples - 1)) # Calculate alpha alphas = 1 - np.exp(-densities deltas) # Calculate transmittance Ti = prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) transmittances = np.ones(numsamples) for i in range(1, numsamples): transmittances[i] = transmittances[i-1] (1 - alphas[i-1]) # Accumulate color contribution = transmittances[:, np.newaxis] alphas[:, np.newaxis] colors accumulatedcolor = np.sum(contribution, axis=0) # Add background: T{n+1} = Tn (1 - alphan) finaltransmittance = transmittances[-1] (1 - alphas[-1]) finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + finaltransmittance bgcolor return finalcolor The general class of methods combining explicit and implicit storage. DVGO is a specific instance using voxel grids for density and MLPs for color. See Hybrid Explicit-Implicit Representations. A sibling method that may use different explicit storage mechanisms (e.g., hash tables) or decoder structures. See Hybrid Representation. Time Complexity: Faster than completely implicit NeRF representations because querying density from voxel grids is efficient compared to MLP evaluation for every sample point. The coarse stage allows fast convergence, and the fine stage provides high-quality reconstruction. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: DVGO demonstrates super-fast radiance field capabilities, suitable for real-time applications. It achieves competitive results and speed when compared to other hybrid representations. Strengths: Real-time potential, efficient density computation, dual-stage design for flexibility in level of detail. Limitations: Memory usage scales with grid resolution; view-dependent color requires an MLP, which is slower than direct color lookup but faster than full NeRF. When to Use: When real-time or near real-time rendering is required, and the scene can be represented with sufficient resolution in voxel grids. DVGO (Direct Voxel Grid Optimization) was proposed as a method to speed up NeRF by replacing the density MLP with voxel grids. It is part of a family of "super fast radiance fields" that use hybrid representations (implicit for light field, explicit for density field). It has been used in applications such as ActiveRMAP for active mapping and planning. The method builds on the principles of neural radiance fields but optimizes for query efficiency. name: SpikingNeRF-D
head: DVGO-based SpikingNeRF, SpikingNeRF based on DVGO
body: SpikingNeRF-D is a differentiable volume rendering method that integrates spiking neural network (SNN) principles into the Deep Voxel Grids (DVGO) framework. It replaces the standard density Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with explicit voxel grids for density and feature storage, while using a spiking MLP (sMLP) to predict RGB colors from the features. This approach aims to improve hardware efficiency by producing regular, condensed data structures suitable for neuromorphic hardware and DNN accelerators, distinguishing it from standard NeRF variants that rely on dense MLP queries for all volumetric parameters. Inputs: Density voxel grid V\sigma and feature voxel grid Vf. Spiking MLP sMLP(\cdot). Camera view direction v. Rays R^N = \{r1, r2,..., rN\} from camera origins to pixel directions for N pixels. Number of sampled points per ray M. Ground-truth RGB images C = \{C1, C2,..., CN\} (for training). Outputs: Rendered RGB image \hat{C} = \{\hat{C}1, \hat{C}2,..., \hat{C}N\}. Training loss L. Data Structures: V\sigma: 3D voxel grid storing learnable density values. Vf: 3D voxel grid storing learnable feature vectors. P^{N \times M}: Tensor of sampled 3D coordinates. \alpha^{N \times M}: Tensor of opacity weights. w^{N \times M}: Tensor of accumulation weights. P': Filtered set of coordinates (variable length per ray). T: Temporal length, defined as the maximum number of points among the batched rays after filtering. Parameters: N: Number of pixels in the scene. M: Number of sampled points per ray. T: Temporal length (dynamic, based on batch). Typical values for N and M are not specified in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample M points along each of the N rays to form the coordinate tensor P^{N \times M} = \{p{1,1}, p{1,2},..., p{N,M}\}. 2. Density Query & Weighting: Query V\sigma at coordinates P to compute opacity weights \alpha^{N \times M} and accumulation weights w^{N \times M}. The specific formulas for \alpha and w are referenced as Eq. 6 and Eq. 3 in the source, which correspond to standard volumetric rendering weight calculations based on density. 3. Masking: Filter P using \alpha and w to remove irrelevant points (e.g., those with negligible contribution), resulting in filtered coordinates P'. The masking logic is referenced as Eq. 8. 4. Feature Extraction: Query Vf at coordinates P' and incorporate view direction v to extract volumetric parameters InputMLP. This step is referenced as Eq. 7 and Eq. 2. 5. Temporal Length Calculation: Determine T, the maximum number of points among the batched rays in P'. 6. Transformation: Apply Temporal Padding (TP) or Temporal Condensing with Padding (TCP) to InputMLP to create InputsMLP with shape compatible for the sMLP. This transformation handles the variable number of points per ray by padding or condensing them to the fixed length T. This is referenced as Eq. 14 and Section TCP. 7. Color Prediction: Pass InputsMLP through the spiking MLP sMLP to compute RGB values c^{N \times T}. 8. Accumulation: Accumulate the RGB values c using the weights \alpha and w and filtered coordinates P' to produce the final rendered image \hat{C}. This follows standard volume rendering integration, referenced as Eq. 9. 9. Loss Calculation: If training, calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss L between the rendered image \hat{C} and ground truth C, referenced as Eq. 5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SpikingNeRFD(Vsigma, Vf, sMLP, v, R, M, Cgt): """ Vsigma: Density voxel grid Vf: Feature voxel grid sMLP: Spiking MLP function v: View direction vector R: List of N rays M: Number of samples per ray Cgt: Ground truth RGB image (N, H, W, 3) or flattened (N, 3) """ N = len(R) # Step 1: Sample points # P shape: (N, M, 3) P = Sample(R, M) # Step 2: Query density and compute weights # alpha shape: (N, M), w shape: (N, M) # Note: Exact formulas for alpha and w depend on Vsigma interpolation # and standard volume rendering equations (Eq. 6, Eq. 3 in source) alpha, w = Weigh(P, Vsigma) # Step 3: Mask irrelevant points # Pprime is a list of arrays, where Pprime[i] contains points for ray i # that have significant weight. Length varies per ray. Pprime = Mask(P, alpha, w) # Step 4: Extract features for filtered points # InputMLP contains features for all points in Pprime # Shape is variable, handled by subsequent transformation InputMLP = ExtractFeatures(Pprime, Vf, v) # Step 5: Determine temporal length T # T is the max number of points across all rays in the batch T = max(len(pts) for pts in Pprime) # Step 6: Transform InputMLP to fixed size T # Uses TP (Temporal Padding) or TCP (Temporal Condensing with Padding) # InputsMLP shape: (N, T, featuredim) InputsMLP = Transform(InputMLP, T, mode='TCP') # Step 7: Predict RGB values using sMLP # c shape: (N, T, 3) c = sMLP(InputsMLP) # Step 8: Accumulate RGB values to form final image # Re-associate weights with filtered points for accumulation # Chat shape: (N, 3) Chat = Accumulate(Pprime, alpha, w, c) # Step 9: Calculate loss L = MSE(Chat, Cgt) return Chat, L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variable Point Counts: The number of valid points per ray varies after masking. The TP or TCP transformation is required to handle this irregularity for the sMLP. Hardware Overhead: While data condensing incurs overhead, the resulting regular structure benefits hardware accelerators. Dependency on DVGO: The method relies on the specific voxel grid querying mechanisms of DVGO. Time Complexity: Dominated by voxel grid queries and sMLP inference. The masking step reduces the number of points processed by the sMLP, potentially saving computation compared to processing all M points. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for V\sigma and Vf. The sMLP parameters are stored separately. Strengths: Hardware-friendly due to regular data structures after TCP/TP transformation; compatible with neuromorphic hardware. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the voxel grid initialization and the sMLP's ability to model complex radiance fields. The masking and transformation steps add computational overhead. When to use: When hardware efficiency (especially for neuromorphic or specific DNN accelerators) is a priority and the scene can be well-represented by voxel grids. SpikingNeRF-D was proposed as part of the SpikingNeRF framework, which integrates bio-inspired spiking neural networks into neural radiance fields. It is built upon the DVGO (Deep Voxel Grids) framework by Sun, Sun, and Chen (2022), which accelerates NeRF by using voxel grids for density. The method was designed to leverage the efficiency of spiking networks and regular data structures for better hardware compatibility, including neuromorphic chips. name: MixRT
head: Mixed Neural Representations For Real-Time NeRF Rendering
body: MixRT is a hybrid neural representation designed to enable real-time Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering on edge devices by decomposing the scene into three complementary components: a low-quality triangle mesh for coarse geometry, a view-dependent displacement map for surface calibration, and a compressed NeRF model stored in an Instant-NGP hash table for density and color. It distinguishes itself from other hybrid approaches by explicitly leveraging distinct graphics hardware units—rasterizers, texture mapping units, and SIMD units—via WebGL APIs to bypass the computational bottlenecks of dense ray-marching, achieving real-time frame rates on edge devices. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A low-quality triangle mesh, a view-dependent displacement map, and a compressed NeRF model in Instant-NGP format. Outputs: Rendered color and density for each pixel along camera rays. Data Structures: 1. Triangle Mesh: Standard format containing geometric vertex coordinates, texture coordinates, and polygonal face elements. Per-vertex appearance parameters are not stored. The mesh is post-processed with vertex order optimization to improve cache hit rates for neighboring triangles. 2. View-Dependent Displacement Map: A texture map storing spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients and scale factors, accessed via texture coordinates associated with the mesh vertices. 3. Compressed NeRF Model: An Instant-NGP representation consisting of a 3D embedding grid stored as a compact 1D hash table, followed by a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Hash Table: Configured with a shrunk number of levels and an enlarged table size to optimize for rendering speed. MLP: 2 hidden layers with 64 units each. Scene Configuration: The unbounded scene domain is mapped into a finite sphere using a contraction function for the NeRF model components, while the low-quality mesh and displacement map remain in their original unbounded space to leverage optimized rasterization pipelines common in graphics hardware. Rendering Pipeline (Numbered Steps): 1. Mesh Rasterization: Use rasterizer hardware to rasterize the low-quality triangle mesh and determine the ray-mesh intersection point p. 2. Displacement Calibration: Leverage texture mapping units to access the displacement map using the texture coordinates associated with p. Retrieve the SH coefficients and scale, then compute the calibrated point p{cali} by applying the displacement to p. 3. Feature Retrieval: Process p{cali} using SIMD units to query the 3D embedding grid (stored as a hash table) and retrieve embeddings for the eight closest vertices to p{cali}. 4. Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation of the eight retrieved embeddings to obtain the final feature vector for p{cali}. 5. Color and Density Prediction: Feed the interpolated embeddings into the small MLP (2 layers, 64 hidden units) to obtain the corresponding density and view-dependent color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpixel(cameraray, mesh, displacementmap, hashtable, mlp): # Step 1: Mesh Rasterization # Standard ray-triangle intersection returning point p and UV coordinates p, texcoords = raytriangleintersection(cameraray, mesh) # Step 2: Displacement Calibration # Retrieve spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients and scale from displacement map shcoeffs, scale = sampletexturemap(displacementmap, texcoords) # Compute calibrated point pcali using SH basis functions and scale # Note: Exact SH basis evaluation is not specified in the sources pcali = p + scale evaluateshdisplacement(shcoeffs, cameraray.direction) # Step 3 & 4: Feature Retrieval and Interpolation # Query hash table for 8 closest vertices to pcali neighborindices = hashtable.query8neighbors(pcali) neighborembeddings = [hashtable.getembedding(idx) for idx in neighborindices] # Trilinear interpolation of the 8 embeddings features = trilinearinterpolate(neighborembeddings, pcali) # Step 5: MLP Prediction # MLP: 2 layers, 64 hidden units density, color = mlp.forward(features) return color, density def raytriangleintersection(ray, mesh): # Standard ray-triangle intersection returning point and UV coordinates # Not given in the sources. pass def sampletexturemap(texturemap, uv): # Standard texture sampling returning SH coefficients and scale # Not given in the sources. pass def evaluateshdisplacement(shcoeffs, direction): # Evaluate spherical harmonics basis functions for the given direction # Not given in the sources. pass def trilinearinterpolate(embeddings, point): # Standard trilinear interpolation of 8 voxel embeddings # Not given in the sources. pass Parameters and Typical Values: Mesh Complexity: Approximately 15 MB storage size. MLP Architecture: 2 layers, 64 hidden units per layer. Hash Table Configuration: Number of levels is shrunk; hash table size is enlarged. Resolution: 1280x720. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Real-Time Failure: Directly combining a low-quality mesh with a standard Instant-NGP hash table retains storage efficiency but fails to achieve real-time rendering speeds due to bottlenecks in the number of hash table levels. The hash table structure must be modified (shrinking levels, enlarging size) to boost speed. Geometry Quality: High-quality geometry (many triangles) is not necessary for photorealistic rendering if supported by the displacement map and hash table color field. Performance: Achieves over 30 FPS at 1280x720 resolution on a MacBook M1 Pro laptop. Quality: Achieves 0.2 PSNR higher than state-of-the-art methods in indoor scenes of the Unbounded-360 dataset. Storage: Consumes less than 80% of the storage size of state-of-the-art methods (e.g., BakedSDF uses >300 MB, MixRT uses ~15 MB). Scaling: The method is designed for edge devices and leverages WebGL APIs, making it compatible with cross-platform graphics libraries and existing computer graphics toolchains. Strengths: Maximizes utilization of diverse hardware resources (Rasterizer, Texture Mapping Units, SIMD Units); small storage footprint; real-time speed on consumer hardware. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the low-quality mesh for coarse geometry; performance depends on WebGL implementation efficiency on the target device. MixRT addresses the limitation of NeRF's slow rendering speed on edge devices, challenging the convention that high-quality geometry (substantial triangles) is necessary for photorealistic rendering. The method builds on the observation that a low-quality mesh combined with a hash table color field can achieve higher PSNR than a high-quality mesh with 5x more triangles while consuming only 0.26x the storage size. It further refines Instant-NGP by modifying its hash table structure to align with WebGL frameworks, enabling real-time rendering on devices equipped with browsers. name: LidaRF Hybrid Representation
head: LidaRF
body: LidaRF is a neural radiance field method for street scenes that fuses explicit LiDAR point cloud features with an implicit hash-based grid representation to improve geometry and rendering quality under sparse and collinear camera trajectories. It differs from prior LiDAR-only NeRF approaches by avoiding low-resolution and incomplete rendering caused by sparse LiDAR coverage and limited field of view; instead, it combines explicit LiDAR geometry with a high-resolution implicit grid. Inputs: A set of LiDAR point clouds from all frames of a sequence. Camera poses and intrinsics for the frames. Image observations for color supervision. Outputs: Rendered images via standard volume rendering. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid constructed from aggregated LiDAR points. Each occupied voxel cell stores a 3-dimensional feature vector representing the averaged spatial position of all LiDAR points assigned to that cell. 2. LiDAR Embeddings (P): A set \{(pi, fi) \mid i = 1, \dots, N\}, where pi is the 3D spatial position and fi is an n-dimensional neural feature vector extracted by a 3D sparse UNet. 3. Hash-based Feature Grid: An implicit grid storing features for the background and regions not covered by LiDAR. The specific hash function and grid resolution are not detailed in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Aggregate LiDAR Data: Aggregate LiDAR point clouds from all frames of the entire sequence to construct a denser point cloud set. 2. Voxelize: Voxelize the aggregated point clouds into a voxel grid. For each voxel cell, average the spatial positions of all points falling into that cell to produce a single 3-dimensional feature vector per voxel. 3. Encode Geometry: Encode the scene geometry features using a 3D sparse UNet operating on the voxel grid to capture local and global contextual information. The 3D sparse UNet takes the voxel grid along with its 3-dim features as input and outputs neural volumetric features. 4. Form LiDAR Embeddings: Yield LiDAR embeddings P = \{(pi, fi) \mid i = 1, \dots, N\}, where each point i is located at pi and associated with a vector fi, which is the neural feature of the voxel cell it resides in, encoding the local and global geometry around pi. 5. Query and Fuse Features: For a sample point x along a ray, query its LiDAR feature if it resides within the voxel grid. Fuse the extracted LiDAR features with the hash-based feature grid. The exact fusion operation (e.g., concatenation or addition) is not specified beyond this step. 6. Decode: Feed the hybrid features into MLPs to decode color c and density \sigma. 7. Render: Apply standard volume rendering to generate the final image. Formulas: Volume rendering follows the standard discrete integral approximation: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^n Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci, where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is the volume density, \deltai is the step length along the ray, and ci is the view-dependent color. Parameters: LiDAR Aggregation: All frames of the sequence are used. Voxel Feature Dimension: 3 dimensions (averaged spatial position) before UNet encoding. UNet Architecture: 3D sparse UNet. Feature Dimension after UNet: n dimensions (not specified). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse LiDAR Coverage: Relying on LiDAR features alone results in low-resolution rendering due to the sparse nature of LiDAR points. Limited Field of View: LiDAR does not cover the entire scene (e.g., building surfaces above a certain height), yielding blank rendering in those regions if not fused with the implicit grid. Occlusion: Depth supervision from LiDAR must account for occlusion. Strengths: Improves geometry and rendering quality in street scenes, particularly under sparse and collinear camera trajectories. Combines the geometric guidance of LiDAR with the completeness of a high-resolution implicit grid. Limitations: Requires LiDAR data. Performance depends on the quality and density of the aggregated LiDAR point clouds. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory: Not given in the sources. LidaRF was introduced in the paper "LidaRF: Delving into Lidar for Neural Radiance Field on Street Scenes". It addresses the limitations of previous LiDAR-only NeRF approaches, such as [9], which suffered from low-resolution rendering and incomplete coverage due to sparse LiDAR data and limited field of view. The method leverages denser LiDAR points accumulated across frames as depth supervision while accounting for occlusion, leading to extra losses L{ds} and L{aug} in addition to the original losses from Nerfactor L{nerfacto}. name: Explicit Stage for Inverse Rendering
head: Explicit Stage, Mesh-based Refinement
body: The Explicit Stage refines a coarse shape and appearance reconstruction obtained from an implicit stage by converting a continuous implicit field into a discrete mesh and jointly optimizing vertex positions and spatially varying BRDF (SVBRDF) maps. Unlike purely implicit methods, this stage uses a mesh-based framework, allowing for better handling of complex light transport and avoiding the stair-case artifacts associated with low-resolution marching cubes in implicit-only approaches. Inputs: Optimized implicit geometric function \phi(\cdot; \theta^g) and reflectance field B(\cdot; \theta^a) from the implicit stage. n input images Ij with known illumination and viewing conditions \thetas for j=1, \dots, n. Optional: Anti-aliased mask images Sj for each input image. Outputs: Refined mesh geometry M (vertex positions). Refined SVBRDF maps (diffuse albedo kd, specular albedo ks, surface roughness \alpha). Optimized parameters (\theta^g, \theta^a). Data Structures: Mesh M: Defined by vertex positions and connectivity, with BRDF parameters cached at each vertex. SVBRDF Maps: 2D texture maps generated via UV parameterization of the mesh. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iso-surface Extraction: Convert the implicit representation \phi(\cdot; \theta^g) into an initial explicit mesh \tilde{M}0 using iso-surface extraction (e.g., marching cubes). This step is not differentiable. 2. UV Parameterization: Use the Boundary First Flattening (BFF) method [SC17] to UV-parameterize the mesh \tilde{M}0. 3. SVBRDF Initialization: Generate initial SVBRDF maps based on the reflectance field B(\cdot; \theta^a) from the implicit stage. Cache BRDF parameter values (kd, ks, \alpha) at each mesh vertex. 4. Joint Optimization: Perform a second inverse-rendering optimization using a mesh-based framework [LZBD21] that jointly optimizes the position of each mesh vertex and the value of each pixel in the SVBRDF maps. 5. Vertex Update: Update mesh vertex positions using the approach by Nicolet et al. [NJJ21] to avoid expensive continuous collision detection and handling. 6. Mask Supervision (Optional): If mask images Sj are available, include an extra loss term \lambda{\text{mask}} L{\text{mask}}(\thetag). Formulas: The optimization solves for (\theta^g, \theta^a): (\theta^g, \theta^a) = \arg \min{\thetag, \thetaa} L(\thetag, \thetaa) where the total loss L is: L(\thetag, \thetaa) = L{\text{img}}(\thetag, \thetaa) + \lambda{\text{reg}} L{\text{reg}}(\thetag, \thetaa) The image loss L{\text{img}} is: L{\text{img}}(\thetag, \thetaa) = \sum{j=1}^n \| R(\thetag, \thetaa, \thetas^{(j)}) - Ij \|^2 The regularization loss L{\text{reg}} encourages \phi to be a signed-distance function (unit-length gradients): L{\text{reg}}(\thetag, \thetaa) = \sumi (\|\nablax \phi(xi; \thetag)\| - 1)^2 If mask supervision is used, the additional term is: \lambda{\text{mask}} L{\text{mask}}(\thetag) = \sum{j=1}^n \| R{\text{mask}}(\thetag, \thetas^{(j)}) - Sj \|^2 where R{\text{mask}} renders only an anti-aliased mask, R renders the scene, \lambda{\text{reg}} and \lambda{\text{mask}} are loss weights, and xi are sample points. Parameters: \lambda{\text{reg}}: Hyper-parameter controlling the weight of the regularization term, \lambda{\text{reg}} \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}. \lambda{\text{mask}}: Weight for the mask supervision loss (if used). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiable Extraction: The initial iso-surface extraction does not need to be differentiable, but errors here propagate to the optimization. Collision Handling: Using older geometric processing libraries (e.g., elTopo [BB09]) requires expensive continuous collision detection, which the recommended approach [NJJ21] avoids. Performance: Caching BRDF parameters at vertices and reusing the mesh for multiple camera views in a minibatch reduces computational overhead. A two-stage inverse rendering pipeline that combines implicit and explicit geometric representations to solve physics-based inverse rendering problems, supporting topology changes and differentiable rendering of complex effects. It separates the reconstruction into a coarse implicit stage for robust topology handling and a fine explicit stage for high-fidelity appearance and shape refinement using mesh-based differentiable rendering. Unlike purely implicit methods (e.g., DVR, IDR) that struggle with complex light transport, or purely explicit methods that require good initialization, this pipeline leverages the topological flexibility of implicit fields and the rendering efficiency of explicit meshes. Choose it when high-fidelity appearance and geometry are required, and the scene allows for mesh-based representation. Complexity: The optimization jointly updates vertex positions and SVBRDF pixels, which can be computationally intensive, but caching BRDF values and reusing meshes for minibatches amortizes overhead. Strengths: Handles complex light transport better than implicit-only methods; avoids stair-case artifacts from low-resolution marching cubes; supports topology changes during optimization. Limitations: Requires a good initial implicit reconstruction; mesh-based optimization can be sensitive to initialization; UV parameterization may introduce distortions. When to use: When high-fidelity appearance and geometry are required, and the scene allows for mesh-based representation. Particularly useful when complex light transport effects are significant. The method originates from the work by Cai et al. (2022) on physics-based inverse rendering using combined implicit and explicit geometries. It builds upon the implicit stage framework by Yariv et al. [YKM20] (idr) and the mesh-based inverse rendering framework by Luan et al. [LZBD21]. The approach leverages MeshSDF [RLR20] for iso-surface extraction and Nicolet et al. [NJJ21] for efficient vertex updates. Physics‐Based Inverse Rendering using Combined Implicit and Explicit Geometries, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14592, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Combined Implicit and Explicit Inverse Rendering Pipeline
head: Two-stage Inverse Rendering Pipeline
body: This method solves physics-based inverse rendering problems by combining implicit and explicit geometric representations to support topology changes and differentiable rendering of complex light-transport effects. It separates the reconstruction into a coarse implicit stage for robust topology handling and a fine explicit stage for high-fidelity appearance and shape refinement using mesh-based differentiable rendering. Unlike purely implicit methods (e.g., DVR, IDR) that struggle with complex light transport, or purely explicit methods that require good initialization, this pipeline leverages the topological flexibility of implicit fields and the rendering efficiency of explicit meshes. The pipeline consists of two sequential stages: an implicit optimization stage followed by an explicit refinement stage. Inputs: A collection of N geometrically calibrated input images I1, \dots, IN. Camera poses and intrinsics for each image. Initial geometric parameters \thetag for the implicit field. Initial optical parameters \thetaa for the appearance field. Outputs: A reconstructed 3D mesh M representing the object surface. SVBRDF maps (diffuse albedo kd, specular albedo ks, roughness \alpha) associated with the mesh. 1. Implicit Field (\phi): A function \phi: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \Thetag \to \mathbb{R} defining the surface as the zero level set. In practice, this is implemented as a Signed Distance Function (SDF) controlled by parameters \thetag. 2. Explicit Mesh (M): A triangle mesh defined by vertex positions V and connectivity F. Vertices are updated during the explicit stage. 3. Appearance Field (B): A reflectance field mapping surface points to BRDF parameters. Implemented as SVBRDF maps storing kd, ks, \alpha, controlled by parameters \thetaa. 4. Lighting Model: The incident radiance Li(x, \omegai) supports environmental illumination, soft shadows, and interreflections. Stage 1: Implicit Optimization 1. Initialize: Define the object surface M(\thetag) as the zero level set of \phi(x; \thetag) = 0. 2. Render: For each input image, compute the rendered radiance L{rendered} using a differentiable renderer that supports implicit surfaces. The source notes that Monte Carlo sampling over implicit surfaces is challenging, but this stage focuses on coarse shape recovery where topology changes are critical. 3. Compute Loss: Calculate a reconstruction loss between L{rendered} and the target image. 4. Optimize: Update geometric parameters \thetag to minimize the loss. This stage allows topology changes without remeshing. 5. Extract: Once convergence is reached, obtain the coarse implicit geometry. Stage 2: Explicit Refinement 1. Iso-surface Extraction: Apply a non-differentiable iso-surface extraction algorithm (specifically MeshSDF, a differentiable marching cubes variant) to convert the implicit surface \phi(x; \thetag) = 0 into an explicit triangle mesh M. 2. Initialize Appearance: Initialize SVBRDF maps (kd, ks, \alpha) for the mesh. 3. Differentiable Rendering: Render the mesh M using physics-based differentiable rendering. This involves solving the rendering equation and its differential form. Rendering Equation: L(x, \omegao) = \int{S^2} Li(x, \omegai) fr(x, \omegai, \omegao) d\sigma(\omegai) where Li is incident radiance, fr is the cosine-weighted BRDF, and \sigma is the solid-angle measure. Differential Rendering Equation: \frac{d}{d\theta} L(x, \omegao) = \int{S^2} \frac{d}{d\theta}[Li fr] d\sigma(\omegai) + \int{\partial S^2} v\perp(\omegai) \Delta Li fr d\ell(\omegai) where \partial S^2 is the domain of jump discontinuity points of Li, v\perp captures the change rate of the discontinuity boundary, and \Delta Li is the difference in Li across the boundary. 4. Optimize: Jointly optimize: Shape: Update mesh vertex positions. Appearance: Update pixel values in SVBRDF maps (\thetaa). 5. Output: Return the final mesh and SVBRDF maps. Unverified code. Args: inputimages: List of calibrated input images. cameraposes: List of camera poses corresponding to inputimages. initialthetag: Initial parameters for the implicit field phi. initialthetaa: Initial parameters for the appearance field B. lrg: Learning rate for geometric optimization. lra: Learning rate for appearance optimization. maxiterg: Maximum iterations for implicit stage. maxitera: Maximum iterations for explicit stage. Returns: finalmesh: Reconstructed triangle mesh. finalsvbrdf: SVBRDF maps (kd, ks, alpha). thetag) = 0 # Returns triangle mesh with vertices V and faces F pass def renderexplicit(mesh, thetaa, pose): # Performs physics-based differentiable rendering on mesh # Solves rendering equation and differential equation pass def computeshapegradient(loss, mesh): # Computes d(loss)/d(vertexpositions) using boundary integral term pass def computeappearancegradient(loss, thetaa): # Computes d(loss)/d(SVBRDFpixels) pass def updatemeshvertices(mesh, gradient): # Moves vertices along negative gradient direction mesh.vertices = mesh.vertices - learningrate gradient return mesh Max Implicit Iterations: Not given in the sources. Max Explicit Iterations: Not given in the sources. BRDF Model: Microfacet BRDF model is used. Iso-surface Extraction: MeshSDF is specified. Topology Changes: Explicit mesh representations suffer from difficulty in handling topology changes during gradient-based optimization, requiring good initial geometry or frequent remeshing. The implicit stage mitigates this. Implicit Rendering Difficulty: Implicit representations are difficult to use for physics-based differentiable rendering because Monte Carlo sampling over implicitly expressed surfaces is challenging due to difficulty in parameterization. The pipeline avoids this by switching to explicit meshes for the final rendering stage. Discontinuity Boundaries: In differentiable rendering, the boundary integral term in the differential rendering equation is crucial when the parameter \theta controls scene geometry (e.g., mesh vertex positions), as it can be the major contributor to the resulting gradient. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The pipeline is computationally more efficient than existing differentiable-sphere-tracing based methods (e.g., DVR, IDR). Strengths: Supports topology changes during optimization. Supports complex light-transport effects such as environmental illumination, soft shadow, and interreflection. Enables high-fidelity 3D reconstruction of objects with complex topologies. Limitations: Requires two stages, potentially increasing implementation complexity. Implicit stage may be less accurate for fine details compared to explicit methods. When to Use: When reconstructing objects with complex topologies that may change during optimization, or when high-fidelity appearance with complex lighting effects is required. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and topology changes are not expected, or when simple lighting models suffice. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Physics-Based Inverse Rendering using Combined Implicit and Explicit Geometries". History: Inverse rendering has been a long-standing problem in computer vision and graphics. Previous mesh-based techniques struggled with topology changes, while implicit methods struggled with differentiable rendering. This method bridges the gap by combining both. name: NeRF-Editing
head: Geometry Editing of Neural Radiance Fields
body: NeRF-Editing is a method that allows users to perform user-controlled shape deformation on the implicit representation of a scene (NeRF) and synthesizes novel view images of the edited scene without re-training the network. It is the first mesh-based shape deformation method, leveraging explicit representations for scene geometry edits and implicit representations for realistic rendering effects. Unlike EditingNeRF which is limited to color modification or removal of parts, and ObjectNeRF which only supports duplication, movement, or rotation, this method supports substantial shape deformation. Inputs: 1. A trained NeRF model (implicit representation) of a scene. 2. Multi-view images used to train the NeRF. 3. User-defined deformation constraints on an extracted explicit mesh. Outputs: 1. Rendered images of the edited scene from novel viewpoints. Data Structures: 1. Triangular Mesh (M{tri}): An explicit surface representation extracted from the NeRF. 2. Tetrahedral Mesh (M{tet}): A volumetric proxy mesh wrapping around M{tri}, used to propagate deformations into the surrounding space. 3. Deformation Field (D(x)): A continuous vector field defined over the volume, derived from the discrete deformations of M{tet}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Extract Explicit Mesh: Extract a triangular mesh representation (M{tri}) from the trained NeRF. 2. User-Driven Deformation: Users apply intuitive deformations to M{tri} using classic mesh deformation methods, such as As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) deformation. Let the deformed mesh be M'{tri}. 3. Build Tetrahedral Proxy: Construct a tetrahedral mesh (M{tet}) that wraps around the original triangular mesh M{tri}. This mesh serves as a spatial proxy to propagate the surface deformation into the volume. 4. Propagate Deformation to Tetrahedral Mesh: Drive the deformation of M{tet} based on the deformation of M'{tri}. The vertices of M{tet} are displaced to reflect the geometric changes of the surface, creating a discrete deformation field. Let the deformed tetrahedral mesh be M'{tet}. 5. Interpolate to Continuous Deformation Field: Use tetrahedral vertex interpolation to transform the discrete deformation field from M'{tet} into a continuous deformation field D(x) defined for any point x in 3D space. For a query point x inside a tetrahedron T with vertices vi and deformation vectors di, the deformation D(x) is computed by interpolating di using the barycentric coordinates of x within T. Points outside M{tet} are assumed to have zero deformation. 6. Ray Bending: During rendering, camera rays passing through the tetrahedral mesh are bent according to the continuous deformation field D(x). Sampling positions along the ray are displaced by D(x) to query the implicit NeRF at the deformed locations. This ensures that the implicit NeRF is queried at locations corresponding to the deformed geometry, effectively "bending" the ray to match the user's edit. 7. Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering integration along the bent rays. The NeRF decoder predicts density \sigma and color c at the sampled points, and the final color is computed via alpha compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def sub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def barycentrictet(p, v0, v1, v2, v3): # Compute barycentric coordinates of p in tetrahedron v0,v1,v2,v3 # Returns (w0, w1, w2, w3) or None if outside vol = dot(sub(v0, v1), cross(sub(v2, v1), sub(v3, v1))) if abs(vol) < 1e-9: return None w0 = dot(sub(p, v1), cross(sub(v2, v1), sub(v3, v1))) / vol w1 = dot(sub(v0, p), cross(sub(v2, v0), sub(v3, v0))) / vol w2 = dot(sub(v0, p), cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v3, v0))) / vol w3 = dot(sub(v0, p), cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v2, v0))) / vol if 0.0 <= w0 <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= w1 <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= w2 <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= w3 <= 1.0: return (w0, w1, w2, w3) return None def nerfeditingrender(rayorigin, raydirection, nerfmodel, tetmesh, deformationvectors): """ Renders a single ray for the edited scene. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the camera ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the camera ray. nerfmodel: Function that queries NeRF for (sigma, color) at a point. tetmesh: List of 4-tuples, each containing vertices (v0, v1, v2, v3). deformationvectors: List of 4-tuples, each containing deformation vectors (d0, d1, d2, d3). Returns: color: 3D vector, the final rendered color. """ tmin = 0.1 tmax = 10.0 numsamples = 128 dt = (tmax - tmin) / (numsamples - 1) tvals = [tmin + i dt for i in range(numsamples)] points = [[rayorigin[j] + t raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] for t in tvals] deformations = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in points] for i, p in enumerate(points): for tetidx, tet in enumerate(tetmesh): v0, v1, v2, v3 = tet bary = barycentrictet(p, v0, v1, v2, v3) if bary is not None: d0, d1, d2, d3 = deformationvectors[tetidx] deformations[i] = [ bary[0]d0[j] + bary[1]d1[j] + bary[2]d2[j] + bary[3]d3[j] for j in range(3) ] break bentpoints = [[points[i][j] + deformations[i][j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(numsamples)] sigmas = [] colors = [] for p in bentpoints: sigma, c = nerfmodel(p) sigmas.append(sigma) colors.append(c) alphas = [1.0 - math.exp(-s dt) for s in sigmas] transmittances = [1.0] for i in range(1, numsamples): transmittances.append(transmittances[i-1] (1.0 - alphas[i-1])) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): weight = alphas[i] transmittances[i] for j in range(3): color[j] += weight colors[i][j] return color Parameters: Deformation Method: ARAP (As-Rigid-As-Possible) is used for the initial mesh deformation. Interpolation: Tetrahedral vertex interpolation (barycentric interpolation) is used to create the continuous field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts from Direct Interpolation: Directly transferring deformation from the surface mesh to the implicit volume by simple interpolation (without the tetrahedral proxy) leads to obvious artifacts. The two-step strategy using a tetrahedral proxy is necessary to avoid these. Boundary Handling: Points outside the tetrahedral mesh volume are assumed to have zero deformation. This is handled explicitly to prevent undefined behavior. Precision: The quality of the continuous deformation field depends on the resolution of the tetrahedral mesh. Coarse tetrahedral meshes may result in blocky or inaccurate deformations. Time Complexity: The method requires no network re-training, making the editing phase fast. The rendering phase involves an additional interpolation step for the deformation field, adding minor overhead to standard NeRF rendering. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports substantial shape deformation (not just color or rigid transforms); works on arbitrary shapes (animals, man-made objects), not limited to humans. Intuitive user control via mesh editing. Limitations: Requires an initial mesh extraction step, which can be noisy or incomplete for complex scenes. The quality of deformation propagation depends on the tetrahedral mesh generation. When to use: When substantial geometric changes to a NeRF scene are required without re-training. When not to use: When only color or texture edits are needed (EditingNeRF is simpler); when rigid body transforms are sufficient (ObjectNeRF is simpler). NeRF-Editing was proposed in 2022. It is cited as the first mesh-based shape deformation method for NeRFs. It addresses the limitation of prior editing methods that were restricted to color modification, part removal, or rigid transformations (translation, rotation, scaling). The method establishes a correspondence between an extracted explicit mesh and the implicit neural representation, allowing users to leverage well-developed mesh-based deformation tools. It is applicable to arbitrary shapes, including animal models and general man-made objects. NeRF-Editing: Geometry Editing of Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01781, fetched 2026-10-26 A survey on 3D editing based on NeRF and 3DGS, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11704-025-41176-9, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Vosh (VOxel-meSH)
head: Voxel-Mesh Hybrid Representation
body: Vosh is a hybrid neural rendering representation that combines a voxel grid and a triangle mesh to achieve real-time view synthesis on mobile devices. It addresses the trade-off between voxel rendering quality and mesh rasterization speed by converting portions of the volumetric density field into a surface mesh based on rendering quality differences. Unlike VMesh, which relies on Signed Distance Functions (SDF) and manual hyperparameter tuning, Vosh uses only the implicit volumetric density field, making it suitable for unbounded scenes and complex backgrounds. Vosh constructs a hybrid representation through a three-stage training process followed by WebGL-based inference. Inputs: A set of multi-view images of the scene. Outputs: A hybrid asset containing sparse voxels and textured meshes, optimized for real-time rendering. 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D grid storing neural radiance field values (density \sigma and color features c) for volumetric regions. 2. Mesh: A triangle mesh representing surfaces extracted from the density field, storing vertex positions and texture coordinates. 3. Hybrid Ratio: A scalar parameter controlling the balance between voxel and mesh components. The training consists of three stages: 1. Grid Training: Initialize a voxel grid model and train it via volume rendering using the multi-view images. 2. Meshing Density Field: Calculate the difference in rendering quality between the current voxel grid volume and the potential surfaces it contains. Regions where the rendering quality of the volume is similar to the underlying surface are converted into a mesh, replacing the volumetric density values at those positions. 3. Optimization: Perform joint optimization of the remaining voxels and the mesh using hybrid rendering. This stage includes voxel pruning to remove redundant voxels and refine the final hybrid representation. The trained assets (sparse voxels and textured meshes) are exported and rendered using WebGL. The mesh component handles simple geometry and textures for fast rendering, while the voxel component handles intricate regions for high-quality rendering. Standard volume rendering integration along a ray r computes the color C(r) as: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci, \quad Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \sigmai is the density, ci is the color, and \deltai is the step size between samples. The hybrid rendering blends the mesh rasterization C{mesh}(r) and voxel volume rendering C{voxel}(r) using the hybrid ratio \alpha \in [0, 1]: C{hybrid}(r) = \alpha C{mesh}(r) + (1 - \alpha) C{voxel}(r) Hybrid Ratio: A flexible parameter allowing users to adjust the balance between voxel and mesh components, controlling the trade-off between rendering quality and speed. Complex Backgrounds: Unlike SDF-based methods (e.g., VMesh), Vosh's density-field-only approach avoids low-quality reconstruction in cluttered backgrounds. Mobile Compatibility: Vosh avoids CUDA-specific APIs required by 3D Gaussian Splatting, enabling real-time rendering on mobile devices. Precision: Tri-linear interpolation assumes continuous variation between voxels; sharp discontinuities may require higher resolution or specialized handling. Boundaries: Points outside the defined storage domain must be handled via clamping or zero-padding. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainvosh(multiviewimages, numepochs, hybridratio): # Stage 1: Grid training for initial voxels voxelgrid = VoxelGrid(dim=64) # 3D array storing density σ and color features c for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, camerapose in multiviewimages: # Standard differentiable volume rendering along rays renderedimage = volumerender(voxelgrid, camerapose) loss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, image) voxelgrid.applygradients(loss) # Stage 2: Meshing density field # Determine regions of meshing based on rendering quality difference # between the voxel grid volume and potential surfaces it contains qualitydiff = computerenderingqualitydifference(voxelgrid, multiviewimages) meshregions = thresholdregions(qualitydiff, threshold=0.1) # Standard thresholding # Convert density field in meshregions to a textured mesh mesh = extractmeshfromdensity(voxelgrid, meshregions) # Marching cubes on density field # Stage 3: Optimization # Joint optimization of voxels and mesh via hybrid rendering and voxel pruning for epoch in range(numepochs): for image, camerapose in multiviewimages: # Hybrid rendering: rasterize mesh + volume render remaining voxels meshcolor = rasterizemesh(mesh, camerapose) voxelcolor = volumerender(voxelgrid, camerapose) hybridimage = blend(meshcolor, voxelcolor, hybridratio) loss = meansquarederror(hybridimage, image) voxelgrid.applygradients(loss) mesh.applygradients(loss) voxelgrid.prune(lowdensitythreshold=0.01) # Remove redundant voxels return voxelgrid, mesh def rendervosh(voxelgrid, mesh, camerapose, hybridratio): # Inference Phase: Real-time hybrid rendering via WebGL meshcolor = rasterizemesh(mesh, camerapose) voxelcolor = volumerender(voxelgrid, camerapose) # Combine based on hybrid ratio and visibility finalimage = blend(meshcolor, voxelcolor, hybridratio) return finalimage def volumerender(grid, pose): # Standard differentiable volume rendering integration pass def rasterizemesh(mesh, pose): # Standard triangle rasterization with texture lookup pass def blend(c1, c2, ratio): return ratio c1 + (1 - ratio) c2 # def computerenderingqualitydifference(grid, images): # pass def thresholdregions(diff, threshold): return diff < threshold # def extractmeshfromdensity(grid, regions): # pass def prune(grid, threshold): # pass Performance: Achieves real-time view synthesis on mobile devices. Memory: Reduces space occupation compared to SDF-based methods. Flexibility: The hybrid ratio allows users to control the balance between rendering quality and speed. Strengths: Excels in fast rendering for simple geometry/texture via the mesh component and high-quality rendering for intricate regions via the voxel component. Suitable for unbounded outdoor scenes and complex backgrounds. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Complexity: Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Vosh was proposed to address the limitations of using voxels or meshes individually for neural radiance field-based view synthesis. It was developed as a hybrid representation that optimizes a voxel grid based on neural rendering and strategically meshes a portion of the volumetric density field to surface. The method is designed to enable real-time view synthesis on mobile devices, leveraging WebGL for inference.
