name: PERF with Cauchy Loss and Hierarchical Planes
head: Implementation details for PERF additions, PERF additions, PERF with difference planes and Cauchy loss
body: This method extends the PERF algorithm by integrating difference planes and a per-voxel weighted Cauchy loss into its non-linear least-squares framework to mitigate shape-radiance ambiguity in view-dependent radiance fields. It distinguishes itself from standard PERF by explicitly separating view-dependent appearance via hierarchical difference planes and employing a robust loss function to handle outliers and maintain sparsity in real-world captures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera poses and intrinsics (calibrated via COLMAP), input images, and an initial Plenoxels grid. Outputs: An optimized Plenoxels grid (density and base color), difference planes (view-dependent residuals), and a weight buffer for the loss function. Data Structures: 1. Plenoxels Grid: A standard 3D voxel grid storing density and base color coefficients. 2. Difference Planes: A set of 2D planes corresponding to each hierarchical level, storing view-dependent color residuals. 3. Weight Buffer: A buffer storing one float per voxel to represent the per-voxel weight for the Cauchy loss. Hierarchical Structure: The method uses four hierarchical levels with a highest resolution of 256^3. The resolution of the added difference planes follows camera resolutions through hierarchical steps to approximately match the voxel resolution at any given level. Values for each new hierarchical level are upsampled using linear interpolation from the previous level. Formulas: 1. Difference Planes (Equation 4): These planes capture residual view-dependent color information; the exact formulation is not provided in the sources. 2. Cauchy Loss with Per-Voxel Weight (Equation 7): This loss incorporates per-voxel weights wi; the exact mathematical formulation is not provided in the sources. 3. Visibility Term (Equation 8): Ls = \lambdas (-4(T - 0.5)^2 + 1) with \lambdas = 0.1. This quadratic term on total visibility T mitigates smoke-like artifacts and keeps real scenes sparse. Parameters: Hierarchical Levels: 4. Highest Level Resolution: 256^3. Visibility Term Weight (\lambdas): 0.1. Baseline Cauchy Loss Weight: 0.0001 (used for fair comparison with baseline PERF). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calibrate scenes using COLMAP. 2. Initialize the Plenoxels grid and difference planes. 3. Iterate through hierarchical levels: a. For levels starting from the second level, run Algorithm 1 and Equation 6 from PERF once at the beginning. b. Compute per-voxel weights and store them in a buffer. c. Upsample difference planes from the previous level using linear interpolation. 4. In each optimization iteration: a. Evaluate the Cauchy loss (Equation 7) using the pre-computed per-voxel weights. b. Evaluate the visibility term (Equation 8). c. Update the Plenoxels grid and difference planes using non-linear least-squares optimization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizeperfhierarchical(levels=4, highestres=256): grid = initializeplenoxelsgrid(highestres) planes = [initializedifferenceplanes(level) for level in range(levels)] for level in range(1, levels): # Skip first level as per source runperfalgorithm1andequation6(grid, planes[level-1]) weights = computepervoxelweights(grid) weightbuffer = weights # One float per voxel planes[level] = linearinterpolateupsample(planes[level-1]) while not checkconvergence(): losscauchy = evaluatecauchylosswithweights(weights, grid, planes[level]) lossvisibility = evaluatevisibilityquadratic(grid) updateparametersnonlinearleastsquares(grid, planes[level], losscauchy, lossvisibility) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Real Scenes: Real scenes contain more camera poses than artificial scenes, resulting in an extra overhead of about 20-30% in reconstruction time. Baseline Comparison: To ensure a fair comparison with baseline PERF, the Cauchy loss must be added with a constant weight w = 0.0001 to the baseline case. Introduces an iterative training scheme for grouping pixels and optimizing the reconstruction network via a superplane constraint, which yields better performance than using explicit 3D plane supervision which is costly to obtain. Time Complexity: The method generally converges faster than baseline PERF for artificial scenes, resulting in shorter reconstruction times. For real scenes, there is an additional overhead of 20-30% due to extra computations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Reconstruction times on an Nvidia GTX 1080: Artificial scenes (w/ planes vs w/o planes): Lego: 154s vs 194s, Ficus: 107s vs 208s, Hotdog: 267s vs 355s, Drums: 121s vs 273s, Chair: 90s vs 229s. Real scenes (w/ planes vs w/o planes): Material: 243s vs 478s, Ignatius: 228s vs 172s, Family: 154s vs 131s. The source text notes that artificial scenes show higher performance due to faster convergence, while real scenes exhibit the stated 20-30% overhead, despite mixed timing results in the provided table. Strengths: Mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity, separates view-dependent information effectively, and reduces smoke-like artifacts. Limitations: Incurs additional overhead for real scenes and requires careful calibration via COLMAP. This method was introduced in the paper "Addressing the Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in View-Dependent Radiance Fields". It builds upon the PERF (Plenoxels Optimization Framework) algorithm. The work aims to improve the quality of view-dependent radiance field reconstruction by explicitly handling the ambiguity between shape and appearance. name: Clonoxels
head: Cloning-Plenoxels
body: Clonoxels is a voxel-based radiance field framework that automatically detects repeated objects within a scene using instance and semantic segmentation, aligns them via rigid registration, and shares voxel features between instances to improve reconstruction quality and reduce storage requirements. It sets itself apart from standard Plenoxels by introducing intra-scene information sharing, allowing gradients to propagate to 3D regions unseen within training images and enabling the recovery of hidden structures by drawing information from other instances of the same object. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Training images with known camera parameters (intrinsics and extrinsics), instance segmentation masks, and semantic labels for the training set. Outputs: A shared voxel feature grid, learnable rigid transformation parameters (poses) for each instance, and scalar color correction values. The final output can be rendered images or extracted 3D meshes via marching cubes. Data Structures: 1. Baseline Grid: A regular 3D voxel grid storing opacity values \sigma and view-dependent color c represented as spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients (9 per color channel), following the Plenoxels baseline. 2. Object Subgrid: An axis-aligned bounding cube (AABB) of voxels assigned to a specific detected instance. Features are stored at the vertices of this subgrid. 3. Transformation Parameters: For each instance, a learnable rigid transformation defined by a rotation matrix R \in SO(3) derived from a learnable quaternion, a center of rotation o \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a translation vector t \in \mathbb{R}^3. 4. Color Correction: A single scalar voxel feature \Delta c per subgrid voxel, applied equally to all three RGB channels. Formulas: Volume Rendering: The color \hat{C} of a camera ray x(t) = xo + t \hat{d} is computed as: \hat{C}(x) = \int{tn}^{tf} V(t) \sigma(x(t)) c(x(t), \hat{d}) dt where V(t) is the transmittance: V(t) = e^{-\int0^t \sigma(x(s)) ds} Rigid Transformation: Each vertex v of an object's feature subgrid F is transformed to v': v' = R(v - o) + o + t Color Correction: The final color c' is: c' = c + \Delta c \cdot \mathbf{1} where \mathbf{1} = (1, 1, 1)^T. The result is clamped to [0, 1]. Loss Functions: Reconstruction Loss: L{recon} = ||C - \hat{C}||2^2. Total Variation Loss: L{TV} (used for regularization). Feature Similarity Loss: L{feat} = \lambda{feat} ||F' - \hat{F}||1, where F' is the transformed subgrid of one instance, \hat{F} is the subgrid of another instance of the same class, and \lambda{feat} is a weighting coefficient. L1 is used for outlier tolerance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Instance Detection and Ranking: Use instance segmentation (e.g., Mask2Former or SAM2 with YOLOv10 boxes) and semantic labels on training images to extract objects. Rank semantic classes by instance count and retain only masks corresponding to the most numerous class to prioritize repetitions. 2. 3D Localization and Subgrid Definition: Project the 2D masks into 3D space using multi-view consistency. Assign voxels to define axis-aligned bounding cubes (Object Subgrids) for each instance. 3. Initial Scene Optimization: Optimize the entire scene's baseline features (\sigma, c) using L{recon} and L{TV} to build an initial representation. 4. Pose Estimation (Feature Sharing Setup): Cull low-density voxels to ensure pose optimization stability. Optimize only the transformation parameters (R, o, t) for each instance using L{feat} until convergence to align the subgrids of repeated objects. 5. Joint Optimization: Reintroduce L{recon} and L{TV}. Continue updating features and transformations jointly so that instances exchange information while pose refinement is informed by photometric cues. 6. Rendering: Query the shared feature grid. For a given instance, apply its learned transformation to map the shared features to its local coordinate system. Apply the scalar color correction \Delta c to handle lighting differences (shadows, specular highlights). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def quaterniontomatrix(q): # Standard conversion from unit quaternion to 3x3 rotation matrix w, x, y, z = q[:, 0], q[:, 1], q[:, 2], q[:, 3] R = torch.zeros(q.shape[0], 3, 3) R[:, 0, 0] = 1 - 2 (y2 + z2) R[:, 0, 1] = 2 (x y - w z) R[:, 0, 2] = 2 (x z + w y) R[:, 1, 0] = 2 (x y + w z) R[:, 1, 1] = 1 - 2 (x2 + z2) R[:, 1, 2] = 2 (y z - w x) R[:, 2, 0] = 2 (x z - w y) R[:, 2, 1] = 2 (y z + w x) R[:, 2, 2] = 1 - 2 (x2 + y2) return R def clonoxelsoptimization(scenedata, trainingimages, masks, semanticlabels): # 1. Instance Detection and Ranking instances = detectinstances(masks, semanticlabels) # Extract objects via instance/semantic segmentation topclassinstances = rankandselecttopclass(instances) # Sort by count, keep most numerous class # 2. 3D Localization and Subgrid Definition subgrids = {} for inst in topclassinstances: subgrids[inst.id] = projectto3d(inst.mask, trainingimages.cameras) # Multi-view backprojection to AABB # 3. Initial Scene Optimization optimizerbaseline = torch.optim.Adam(scenedata.parameters()) for in range(1000): # Standard convergence loop optimizerbaseline.zerograd() lossrecon = torch.sum((renderray(scenedata, trainingimages) - trainingimages.targets)2) losstv = computetotalvariationloss(scenedata) (lossrecon + losstv).backward() optimizerbaseline.step() # 4. Pose Estimation scenedata = culllowdensity(scenedata, threshold=0.15) # Remove voxels with sigma < threshold optimizertransforms = torch.optim.Adam([t.parameters() for t in subgrids.values()]) referenceinstance = topclassinstances[0] # Select reference instance for Fhat for in range(500): # Standard convergence loop optimizertransforms.zerograd() lossfeat = 0 for inst in topclassinstances: q = F.normalize(inst.transform.q) R = quaterniontomatrix(q) vprime = (R @ (inst.vertices - inst.transform.o).T).T + inst.transform.o + inst.transform.t Fprime = F.gridsample(scenedata.features.unsqueeze(0), vprime.unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze(0) Fhat = subgrids[referenceinstance.id].features lossfeat += lambdafeat torch.norm(Fprime - Fhat, p=1) lossfeat.backward() optimizertransforms.step() # 5. Joint Optimization optimizerjoint = torch.optim.Adam(list(scenedata.parameters()) + [t.parameters() for t in subgrids.values()]) for in range(1000): optimizerjoint.zerograd() lossrecon = torch.sum((renderray(scenedata, trainingimages) - trainingimages.targets)2) lossfeat = 0 for inst in topclassinstances: q = F.normalize(inst.transform.q) R = quaterniontomatrix(q) vprime = (R @ (inst.vertices - inst.transform.o).T).T + inst.transform.o + inst.transform.t Fprime = F.gridsample(scenedata.features.unsqueeze(0), vprime.unsqueeze(0), mode='bilinear', paddingmode='border').squeeze(0) Fhat = subgrids[referenceinstance.id].features lossfeat += lambdafeat torch.norm(Fprime - Fhat, p=1) totalloss = lossrecon + lossfeat totalloss.backward() optimizerjoint.step() return scenedata, subgrids Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lighting Differences: Direct feature sharing fails under different lighting (shadows, specular highlights). The scalar correction \Delta c is essential. Per-channel corrections are not used to maintain memory savings. Symmetric Objects: Rigid pose registration may struggle with highly symmetric objects, which are sensitive to pose initialization. Visual Differences: Semantically similar objects may have significant visual differences, compromising feature sharing gains. Precision: Calculations assume 32-bit floating-point precision. Memory: Significantly reduces memory footprint by storing only one instance's features and propagating them via learned poses and color corrections. Memory savings are reported as absolute values (e.g., 13.3 MB to 23.6 MB saved) and percentages (e.g., 66.0% to 76.4% of voxels with \sigma > 0.15). Quality: Improves reconstruction quality, particularly for occluded novel views. Clonoxels reduces MSE by 21% in occluded novel view rendering compared to the baseline by drawing information from other objects. Color Correction Impact: Using the scalar color correction \Delta c improves MSE (0.022 vs 0.039), PSNR (26.9 vs 24.2), and SSIM (0.85 vs 0.83) compared to not using it. Denoising: The method imposes constraints on geometry and appearance, reducing noisy artifacts and producing cleaner 3D geometry suitable for mesh extraction. Limitations: Performance degrades if repeated objects have significant visual differences or if objects are highly symmetric. Clonoxels (Cloning-Plenoxels) was introduced by O. Camilleri, M. Volino, and A. Hilton in 2026. It builds on the Plenoxels framework, which optimizes voxel opacity and spherical harmonic coefficients. The method addresses the limitations of standard voxel-based radiance fields by leveraging intra-scene repetition to enhance reconstruction and reduce storage, offering a practical path for efficient and accurate reconstruction of complex scenes. name: Plenoxels Transmittance Offset
head: High transmittance offset
body: Plenoxels Transmittance Offset is an optimization technique applied to Plenoxels that adds a high transmittance offset to the density parameters to ensure high rendering quality across various scene scaling factors k. It sets itself apart from the baseline Plenoxels configuration by addressing the convergence failure of standard density rectification methods when scene scales vary, a problem where baseline models suffer significant quality degradation at large k. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Plenoxels voxel grid containing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for radiance and density; scene scaling factor k; baseline learning rates \eta{init} = 0.05 and \eta{final} = 0.005. Output: Optimized voxel grid parameters yielding high PSNR across scales, specifically correcting the quality drop seen in baseline models at k \ge 1. Data Structures: The method operates on the existing Plenoxels voxel grid. Each voxel stores SH coefficients. The density \sigma is queried via trilinear interpolation of these coefficients. Method Steps: 1. Initialize: Set up the Plenoxels voxel grid with SH coefficients. Configure the optimizer with initial learning rate \eta{init} = 0.05 and final learning rate \eta{final} = 0.005. 2. Density Query: For a given ray, sample the voxel grid using trilinear interpolation to obtain the raw density value \sigma{\text{raw}}. 3. Activation and Offset: Replace the baseline ReLU activation with an exponential activation and add a high transmittance offset \tau to the density parameters: \sigma = \exp(\sigma{\text{raw}}) + \tau The sources define this as a "high transmittance offset" but do not provide the exact numerical value of \tau or the specific formula for its calculation, noting only that it is "high" and "needed even at k=1". 4. Rendering: Compute transmittance T and color C using standard volume rendering integration with the modified \sigma. 5. Optimization: Update voxel coefficients using gradient-based optimization with the specified learning rate schedule. Parameters: \eta{init} = 0.05 \eta{final} = 0.005 Transmittance Offset \tau: Value not given in the sources. Described as "high". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficiency of Exp Activation: Using only the exponential activation (\sigma = \exp(\sigma{\text{raw}})) is insufficient for convergence at various scene scales. Baseline Failure: The baseline Plenoxels model (using ReLU or exp without offset) suffers significant quality drops at large k (e.g., PSNR 13.05 vs 32.25 at k=10 on Blender Chair). Learning Rate: The reduced learning rate (\eta{init} = 0.05, \eta{final} = 0.005) is used in conjunction with the offset; the baseline with ReLU uses a larger rate. This variant highlights that rectifying \sigma with exp activation alone is insufficient for convergence at various scene scales; a high transmittance offset is needed even at k=1. It serves as a prerequisite step, indicating that the offset is the critical differentiator from a simple exp-activated baseline. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the Blender dataset, the method significantly outperforms the baseline Plenoxels at large scene scaling factors k: Chair: At k=1, baseline PSNR 31.80 vs. method 31.89. At k=10, baseline 13.05 vs. method 32.25. Ship: At k=1, baseline 28.16 vs. method 28.25. At k=10, baseline 11.27 vs. method 28.21. Other Objects: Similar trends observed for other Blender objects (e.g., Ours vs Default at k=10: 34.93 vs 13.03 for one object, 31.69 vs 11.64 for another). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Maintains high rendering quality across various scene scaling factors k, preventing the severe quality degradation seen in baseline models at large k. Limitations: The specific value of the offset is not detailed in the sources. When to Use: Use when optimizing Plenoxels for scenes with varying or large scaling factors k where baseline models fail to converge or produce low-quality renders. The method originates from the work on "Alpha Invariance: On Inverse Scaling Between Distance and Volume Density in Neural Radiance Fields". It addresses the issue where forcing rays to be bounded within predetermined global near and far planes produces significantly worsened rendering quality, as shown in related tables. The technique is part of a broader effort to stabilize Plenoxels optimization under scene scaling variations. name: Non-highlight colors handling
head: Low-frequency view-dependent function, Per-voxel environment map
body: This method addresses the shape-radiance ambiguity in view-dependent radiance fields by distinguishing surface points from arbitrary volume points using a low-frequency approximation of outgoing radiance. Unlike standard Plenoxels which may struggle with complex view-dependent lighting that lacks clear Lambertian components, this technique assigns a small per-voxel environment map to capture low-frequency view dependence, thereby improving geometry reconstruction. It sets itself apart by integrating a Cauchy loss weighted by the error of this low-frequency approximation into the optimization framework. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A hierarchical voxel grid where each voxel has an associated density \sigma, and camera poses/colors for ray marching. Outputs: A buffer of weights w (one float per voxel) representing the error cost, which is used to modulate the Cauchy loss during optimization. Data Structures: Per-voxel Environment Map: Each voxel stores a small environment map of size 8 \times 4 pixels representing a low-frequency view-dependent function. Weight Buffer: A buffer storing one float per voxel, containing the pre-computed error cost w. Parameters: \lambdac: Controls the overall loss magnitude. Value is 0.05 for artificial scenes and 0.01 for real scenes. \lambdan: Controls the weight of the cost function in the Cauchy loss. Value is 10 for both artificial and real scenes. Steps: 1. Population of View-Dependent Function: For each voxel, populate its 8 \times 4 environment map by iterating over all cameras. Project the voxel to the camera, trace visibility, map to spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi), and accumulate the projected color weighted by visibility into the environment map bin. Sum the total visibility. 2. Normalization: Normalize the environment map by dividing each bin by the total visibility sum T{sum} over all spherical coordinates \theta \in [0, \pi] and \phi \in [-\pi, \pi]. 3. Error Calculation: Calculate the error E for the voxel by comparing the reference color in each camera with the color predicted by the environment map for the corresponding direction, weighted by visibility. 4. Weight Storage: Store the resulting error cost w (derived from E) in a buffer. This step is executed once at the beginning of each hierarchical level, except the first. 5. Loss Evaluation: In each optimization iteration, evaluate the Cauchy loss using the pre-computed weights w from the buffer. Formulas: The error E for a voxel is calculated as: E = \sum{k} \frac{1}{X} \sum{i} Tk (ci - pi)^2 where: k indexes the cameras. i indexes the color channels. X is a normalization factor. Tk is the visibility to camera k. ci is the reference color in camera k for channel i. pi is the predicted color from the environment map for the corresponding direction and channel i. The weight w is derived from this error E. The Cauchy loss Lc is defined as: Lc = \lambdac \sum{i} \log(1 + \lambdan w \sigmai^2) where: \sigmai is the density for voxel i. w is the error cost from the environment map evaluation. \lambdac and \lambdan are the parameters defined above. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def projectvoxeltocamera(voxelpos, camera): return voxelpos - camera.position def tracevisibility(voxelpos, camera): # Standard ray-marching visibility computation return 1.0 def maptosphericalcoordinates(direction): norm = math.sqrt(sum(d2 for d in direction)) if norm == 0: return 0.0, 0.0 theta = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, direction[2] / norm))) phi = math.atan2(direction[1], direction[0]) return theta, phi def populatevoxelenvmap(voxelpos, cameras, envrows=8, envcols=4): envmap = [[0.0] envcols for in range(envrows)] Tsum = 0.0 for camera in cameras: dirvec = projectvoxeltocamera(voxelpos, camera) T = tracevisibility(voxelpos, camera) theta, phi = maptosphericalcoordinates(dirvec) row = int(math.floor(theta / math.pi (envrows - 1))) col = int(math.floor((phi + math.pi) / (2 math.pi) (envcols - 1))) row = max(0, min(envrows - 1, row)) col = max(0, min(envcols - 1, col)) envmap[row][col] += T camera.color Tsum += T if Tsum > 0: for r in range(envrows): for c in range(envcols): envmap[r][c] /= Tsum return envmap, Tsum def calculateerror(envmap, cameras, voxelpos, envrows=8, envcols=4): errorsum = 0.0 for camera in cameras: dirvec = projectvoxeltocamera(voxelpos, camera) Tk = tracevisibility(voxelpos, camera) ci = camera.color theta, phi = maptosphericalcoordinates(dirvec) row = int(math.floor(theta / math.pi (envrows - 1))) col = int(math.floor((phi + math.pi) / (2 math.pi) (envcols - 1))) row = max(0, min(envrows - 1, row)) col = max(0, min(envcols - 1, col)) pi = envmap[row][col] errorsum += Tk sum((c - p) 2 for c, p in zip(ci, pi)) return errorsum def computecauchyloss(voxeldensities, weights, lambdac, lambdan): loss = 0.0 for sigmai, w in zip(voxeldensities, weights): loss += math.log(1 + lambdan w sigmai 2) return lambdac loss Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Space: The method is often combined with auxiliary terms to skip empty space using hierarchical formulation to ease computational impact. Spherical Mapping: The mapping from 3D direction to 2D environment map indices must be consistent between population and evaluation steps. Time Complexity: The population step is executed once per hierarchical level (except the first) for all voxels and cameras. This involves ray marching and spherical mapping for each voxel-camera pair. The loss evaluation is per iteration and per voxel. Memory Complexity: Each voxel stores an 8 \times 4 environment map (32 floats, assuming RGB or similar) plus the weight buffer (1 float per voxel). This adds memory overhead compared to standard Plenoxels. Performance: The method was tested on artificial and real scenes (Tanks and Temples) using a Nvidia GTX 1080. Reconstruction times were compared to baseline PERF, showing the computational impact of the additional steps. Strengths: Improves geometry reconstruction by distinguishing surface points from volume points, especially for view-dependent lighting without clear Lambertian components. Limitations: Adds computational overhead due to the population step and storage of environment maps per voxel. This technique was introduced in the paper "Addressing the Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in View-Dependent Radiance Fields". It builds upon the Plenoxels framework and SnerG by adding a low-frequency view-dependent function per voxel to handle non-highlight colors. The method aims to improve 3D reconstruction quality by leveraging the fact that a low-resolution function approximating outgoing radiance is more likely to correspond to a surface point than an arbitrary volume point. name: Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning
head: Plenoxel Grid with Trilinear Interpolation Optimization
body: Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning is a hierarchical training strategy for optimizing 3D radiance fields represented as sparse voxel grids. It solves the problem of initializing and maintaining an efficient voxel structure that adapts to scene complexity during training, preventing overfitting in unobserved regions while refining detail where needed. It sets itself apart from static grid methods by dynamically pruning low-visibility voxels using a weight or density threshold, and subdividing remaining voxels to increase resolution, building on the general framework of Plenoxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene with training views, an initial coarse resolution (e.g., 256^3), and a target final resolution (e.g., 512^3). Output: An optimized voxel grid containing density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for the radiance field. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array storing per-voxel attributes. In the base Plenoxels implementation, this includes density (\sigma) and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for color. Pruning Mask: A boolean or weight-based metric indicating voxel occupancy, derived from the maximum weight Ti(1-\exp(-\sigmai\deltai)) over all training rays or directly from the density value. Parameters: T{init}: Initial resolution (e.g., 256^3). T{final}: Final resolution (e.g., 512^3). \tau{prune}: Threshold for pruning unoccupied voxels. \lambda{TV}: Weight for Total Variation regularization. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start with a dense voxel grid at the lower resolution T{init} (e.g., 256^3). Initialize density and SH coefficients. 2. Optimize: Train the grid parameters using the loss function defined in: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{recon} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV} where \mathcal{L}{recon} is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) over rendered pixel colors and \mathcal{L}{TV} is the Total Variation regularizer. 3. Prune: Remove voxels deemed unoccupied. A voxel i is pruned if its maximum weight over all training rays falls below a threshold. The weight is calculated as: wi = Ti(1-\exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where Ti is the transmittance, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the step size along rays passing through voxel i. Alternatively, pruning can be based directly on the density value. Pitfall: Naive pruning can adversely impact color and density near surfaces because trilinear interpolation uses values from immediate exterior voxels. Solution: Perform a dilation operation. A voxel is only pruned if both itself and its neighbors are deemed unoccupied. 4. Refine: Subdivide each remaining voxel in half in each dimension (e.g., from 256^3 to 512^3). 5. Initialize New Values: Use trilinear interpolation to initialize the grid values for the new, finer resolution based on the coarser grid. Trilinear interpolation at resolution 128^3 has been observed to outperform nearest neighbor interpolation at 256^3. 6. Repeat: Continue optimizing at the new resolution. Repeat steps 2–5 until the target resolution T{final} is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarsetofineoptimization(scenedata, Tinit, Tfinal, tauprune, lambdatv): # Step 1: Initialize grid = creategrid(resolution=Tinit) initializeparameters(grid) currentres = Tinit while currentres < Tfinal: # Step 2: Optimize optimizeparameters(grid, scenedata.rays, lambdatv) # Step 3: Prune voxelweights = computemaxvoxelweights(grid, scenedata.rays) isunoccupied = voxelweights < tauprune # Apply dilation: voxel is pruned only if itself and all 26 neighbors are unoccupied dilatedunoccupied = applydilation(isunoccupied, grid.shape) prunevoxels(grid, dilatedunoccupied) # Step 4: Refine newres = currentres 2 subdividegrid(grid, newres) # Step 5: Initialize New Values interpolatefromcoarser(grid, currentres, newres) currentres = newres return grid def creategrid(resolution): return {"density": zeros((resolution, resolution, resolution)), "shcoeffs": zeros((resolution, resolution, resolution, 3))} def initializeparameters(grid): grid["density"][:] = 0.0 grid["shcoeffs"][:] = 0.0 def optimizeparameters(grid, rays, lambdatv): # Standard gradient descent step minimizing L = Lrecon + lambdatv LTV for ray in rays: renderray(grid, ray) computegradients(grid, lambdatv) applygradients(grid) def computemaxvoxelweights(grid, rays): maxweights = zeros(grid["density"].shape) for ray in rays: for voxel in ray.voxels: transmittance = computetransmittance(ray, voxel) avgsigma = voxel.avgdensity avgdelta = voxel.avgstepsize weight = transmittance (1.0 - exp(-avgsigma avgdelta)) maxweights[voxel.id] = max(maxweights[voxel.id], weight) return maxweights def applydilation(isunoccupied, shape): dilated = zeros(shape, dtype=bool) for i in range(shape[0]): for j in range(shape[1]): for k in range(shape[2]): if isunoccupied[i, j, k]: neighborunoccupied = True for di in [-1, 0, 1]: for dj in [-1, 0, 1]: for dk in [-1, 0, 1]: ni, nj, nk = i+di, j+dj, k+dk if not (0 <= ni < shape[0] and 0 <= nj < shape[1] and 0 <= nk < shape[2]): neighborunoccupied = False break if not isunoccupied[ni, nj, nk]: neighborunoccupied = False break if not neighborunoccupied: break if not neighborunoccupied: break if neighborunoccupied: dilated[i, j, k] = True return dilated def prunevoxels(grid, mask): grid["density"][mask] = 0.0 grid["shcoeffs"][mask] = 0.0 def subdividegrid(grid, newres): newdensity = zeros((newres, newres, newres)) newsh = zeros((newres, newres, newres, 3)) grid["density"] = newdensity grid["shcoeffs"] = newsh def interpolatefromcoarser(grid, oldres, newres): for i in range(newres): for j in range(newres): for k in range(newres): pos = array([i, j, k]) (oldres / newres) grid["density"][i, j, k] = trilinearinterpolate(grid["density"], oldres, pos) grid["shcoeffs"][i, j, k] = trilinearinterpolate(grid["shcoeffs"], oldres, pos) def trilinearinterpolate(volume, res, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation i, j, k = pos i0, j0, k0 = floor(i), floor(j), floor(k) i1, j1, k1 = i0 + 1, j0 + 1, k0 + 1 i0, j0, k0 = clip([i0, j0, k0], 0, res - 1).astype(int) i1, j1, k1 = clip([i1, j1, k1], 0, res - 1).astype(int) wi, wj, wk = i - i0, j - j0, k - k0 c00 = volume[i0, j0, k0] (1 - wi) + volume[i1, j0, k0] wi c10 = volume[i0, j1, k0] (1 - wi) + volume[i1, j1, k0] wi c01 = volume[i0, j0, k1] (1 - wi) + volume[i1, j0, k1] wi c11 = volume[i0, j1, k1] (1 - wi) + volume[i1, j1, k1] wi return (c00 (1 - wj) + c10 wj) (1 - wk) + (c01 (1 - wj) + c11 wj) wk Progressive Sparse Voxels Optimization is a coarse-to-fine training procedure for optimizing 3D radiance fields represented as sparse voxel grids. It solves the problem of initializing and maintaining an efficient voxel structure that adapts to scene complexity during training, preventing overfitting in unobserved regions while refining detail where needed. It sets itself apart from static grid methods by dynamically pruning low-visibility voxels and subdividing high-error voxels based on gradient signals, building on the general framework of Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning. A second optimization stage that reconstructs surface details and view-dependent effects using a higher-resolution voxel grid and a hybrid explicit-implicit representation, freezing the coarse geometry grid. Definition: This stage focuses on a smaller subspace to reconstruct surface details and view-dependent effects, freezing the optimized coarse geometry grid V^{(\text{density})(c)}. Steps: 1. Freeze Coarse Grid: The optimized V^{(\text{density})(c)} from the coarse stage is frozen. 2. Define Known Free Space: A query point is in known free space if the post-activated alpha value from V^{(\text{density})(c)} is less than threshold \tau^{(c)}. Otherwise, it is in unknown space. 3. Fine Voxels Allocation: Densely query V^{(\text{density})(c)} to find a BBox tightly enclosing the unknown space, with lengths Lx^{(f)}, Ly^{(f)}, Lz^{(f)}. Derive voxel size s^{(f)} and grid dimensions Nx^{(f)}, Ny^{(f)}, Nz^{(f)} from expected total voxels M^{(f)}. 4. Fine-stage Points Sampling: Filter out rays not intersecting known free space. Adjust near/far bounds t^{(\text{near})} and t^{(\text{far})} to ray-box intersection endpoints. Do not adjust t^{(\text{near})} if x0 is already inside the BBox. Parameters: M^{(f)}: Hyperparameter for the expected total number of voxels in the fine stage. D: Hyperparameter for feature-space dimension in the feature voxel grid V^{(\text{feat})(f)}. Representation: The fine stage uses a higher-resolution density voxel grid V^{(\text{density})(f)} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times Nx^{(f)} \times Ny^{(f)} \times Nz^{(f)}} with post-activated interpolation. For view-dependent color, a hybrid representation is used: A feature voxel grid V^{(\text{feat})(f)} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times Nx^{(f)} \times Ny^{(f)} \times Nz^{(f)}}. A shallow MLP parameterized by \Theta^{(f)}. Queries for 3D points \mathbf{x} and viewing direction \mathbf{d} are performed by: \vec{\phi}^{(f)} = \text{interp} \left( \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}^{(\text{density})(f)} \right) \mathbf{c}^{(\mathbf{f})} = \text{MLP}{\Theta^{(\mathbf{f})}}(\text{interp}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{V}^{(\text{feat})(\mathbf{f})}), \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) where \mathbf{c}^{(f)} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent color emission and \sigma^{(f)} \in \mathbb{R} is the raw volume density. Positional embedding is applied on \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d} for the MLP. Progressive Scaling: Inspired by NSVF, the voxel grids V^{(\text{density})(f)} and V^{(\text{feat})(f)} are progressively scaled. Let p{g\ckpt} be the set of checkpoint steps. The initial number of voxels is set to \lfloor M^{(f)} / 2^{|p{g\ckpt}|} \rfloor. When reaching a training step in p{g\ckpt}, the number of voxels is doubled such that the final number is M^{(f)}. At each checkpoint, the voxel grids are resized by trilinear interpolation. Efficiency: Free space skipping is used. Points in known free space (checked via V^{(\text{density})(c)}) are skipped during training and testing to improve efficiency, as querying V^{(\text{density})(c)} is faster than querying V^{(\text{density})(f)} or computing view-dependent colors. Time Complexity: The coarse-to-fine approach reduces training time compared to optimizing a high-resolution grid from scratch, as the initial coarse grid converges faster. The fine detail reconstruction stage adds additional computational cost due to the hybrid explicit-implicit representation and MLP queries. Memory Complexity: Pruning reduces memory usage by removing unoccupied voxels. The fine stage requires additional memory for the higher-resolution grid and feature grid, but the BBox allocation limits this to the unknown space. Performance: Trilinear interpolation at lower resolutions (e.g., 128^3) can outperform nearest neighbor at higher resolutions (e.g., 256^3). Strengths: Adapts to scene complexity, prevents overfitting in unobserved regions, and enables high-resolution detail reconstruction. Limitations: Naive pruning can cause artifacts near surfaces if not handled with dilation. The fine stage requires careful tuning of hyperparameters like M^{(f)} and \tau^{(c)}. Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning originates from the Plenoxels paper, which introduced a novel approach for fast radiance field reconstruction from sparse views using voxel grids without neural networks as the radiance field representation. The method builds on the concept of PlenOctrees for voxel pruning. The fine detail reconstruction variant was introduced in the Direct Voxel Grid Optimization paper to further enhance surface details and view-dependent effects. name: Progressive Sparse Voxels Optimization
head: Progressive Sparse Voxels
body: Progressive Sparse Voxels Optimization is a coarse-to-fine training procedure for optimizing 3D radiance fields represented as sparse voxel grids. It solves the problem of initializing and maintaining an efficient voxel structure that adapts to scene complexity during training, preventing overfitting in unobserved regions while refining detail where needed. It sets itself apart from static grid methods by dynamically pruning low-visibility voxels and subdividing high-error voxels based on gradient signals, building on the general framework of Coarse-to-Fine Optimization with Pruning. Inputs: A set of training images with known camera parameters (position, orientation, intrinsics including horizontal FOV \theta{\text{fov-x}} and image width W). Outputs: An optimized sparse voxel grid containing Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for color and density values at grid points. The scene is represented as an Octree. Voxel: Contains SH coefficients (view-dependent color) and references to grid points. Grid Point: Stores raw density values. Grid points are shared among adjacent voxels (8 corners per voxel). Layout: Only leaf nodes are stored in the final Octree structure. Source voxels are removed upon subdivision. h{lv}: Number of levels for the dense grid initialization in bounded scenes or the main region of unbounded scenes. h{out}: Number of background shell levels for unbounded scenes. h{ratio}: Target ratio of background voxels to main region voxels after initialization. h{geo}: Negative initial raw density value to ensure near-zero activated density (\exp(h{geo}) \approx 0). h{prune}: Threshold for maximum blending weight to prune voxels. h{every}: Number of training iterations between adaptive pruning and subdivision operations. h{rate}: Threshold for sampling rate; if v{rate} < 2h{rate}, subdivision priority is set to zero. h{percent}: Percentage of voxels with highest priority selected for subdivision. \lambda{\text{ssim}}, \lambda{\text{T}}, \lambda{\text{dist}}, \lambda{\text{R}}, \lambda{\text{tv}}: Weights for SSIM, Total Transmittance, Distortion, Regularization, and Total Variation losses. Initialization depends on whether the scene is bounded or unbounded. All voxels start with raw density h{geo} and SH coefficients set to zero, except the zero-degree SH component which is set to yield gray color (intensity 0.5). 1.1 Bounded Scenes 1. Initialize a dense grid with h{lv} levels. 2. Remove voxels that are not observed by any training image. 3. The total number of voxels is \le (2^{h{lv}})^3. 1.2 Unbounded Scenes 1. Define the Main Region: A cuboid centered at the average camera position, with radius equal to the median distance from the center to the cameras. Initialize a dense grid with h{lv} levels within this cuboid. 2. Define the Background Region: Allocate h{out} levels of background shells enclosing the main region. The radius of the entire scene is 2^{h{out}} times the radius of the main region. 3. Initialize background shells with the coarsest voxel size. Each shell level starts with 4^3 - 2^3 = 56 voxels. 4. Iteratively subdivide background shell voxels with the highest sampling rate and remove unobserved voxels. 5. Repeat step 4 until the ratio of the number of background voxels to main region voxels equals h{ratio}. 6. The total number of voxels is \le (1 + h{ratio})(2^{h{lv}})^3. The optimization proceeds in iterations. Every h{every} iterations, perform Adaptive Pruning and Subdivision. The total loss function is: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{\text{mse}} + \lambda{\text{ssim}} \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} + \lambda{\text{T}} \mathcal{L}{\text{T}} + \lambda{\text{dist}} \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} + \lambda{\text{R}} \mathcal{L}{\text{R}} + \lambda{\text{tv}} \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{mse}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{ssim}} are photometric losses, \mathcal{L}{\text{T}} encourages binary transmittance, \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} is distortion loss, \mathcal{L}{\text{R}} is per-point RGB loss, and \mathcal{L}{\text{tv}} is total variation loss on the sparse density grid. 1. For each voxel, compute the maximum blending weight (Ti \alphai) across all training cameras. Ti is the transmittance before the voxel, and \alphai is the opacity of the voxel, derived from the volume rendering equation (Eq. 1 in). 2. Remove voxels where the maximum blending weight is lower than h{prune}. 3. Update SH coefficients and grid points: SH coefficients are pruned along with the voxels. Grid points are removed only if they do not belong to the corners of any remaining voxel. 1. Compute Sampling Rate: For each voxel, calculate the maximum sampling rate v{rate} to estimate the number of rays hitting the voxel along the image's horizontal axis: v{rate} = \max{i}^{N{cam}} \frac{vs}{v{interval}^i} v{interval}^{(i)} = (vc - ro^{(i)}) \cdot T \cdot \ell^{(i)} \cdot \tan\left(0.5 \cdot \theta{\text{fov-x}}^{(i)}\right) Where: vs: Voxel size (side length). vc: Center of the voxel. ro^{(i)}: Origin of camera i. T: Rotation matrix of camera i. \ell^{(i)}: Camera lookat vector of camera i. \theta{\text{fov-x}}^{(i)}: Horizontal field of view of camera i. N{cam}: Number of training cameras. Note: The source text mentions W (image width) in the variable list but does not explicitly use it in the formula for v{interval} or v{rate}. 2. Compute Priority: Accumulate subdivision priority v{priority} for each voxel by summing over all training pixel rays r \in R observed over the last h{every} iterations: v{priority} = \sum{r \in R} \left\| \alpha(r) \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(r)}{\partial \alpha(r)} \right\| Where: \alpha(r): Opacity contribution of the voxel to ray r. \mathcal{L}(r): Training loss of ray r. The gradient is weighted by the alpha values. 3. Filter Overfitting: If a voxel's maximum sampling rate v{rate} < 2h{rate}, set its v{priority} to zero to prevent overfitting to few pixels. 4. Select Voxels: Select voxels with priority above the top h{percent} percentile. The total number of voxels increases by h{percent} \cdot (8 - 1) percent. 5. Subdivide and Update: Subdivide selected voxels into 8 children. Remove the source voxel from the Octree (only leaf nodes are kept). SH Coefficients: Duplicate the parent's SH coefficients to the 8 children. Grid Points: Compute densities of new grid points using trilinear interpolation of the parent's corner grid points. Merge duplicated grid points (shared between children or neighbors) and average their densities. Unverified code. Subdivision increases the voxel count by h{percent} \cdot 7 percent per step. Pruning reduces it. The cost of computing sampling rates and priorities scales with the number of voxels and rays. Memory Complexity: Scales with the number of active voxels. The initialization bounds the voxel count to (1 + h{ratio})(2^{h{lv}})^3 for unbounded scenes. Strengths: Adapts resolution to scene complexity; prevents overfitting in unobserved regions via pruning and sampling rate thresholds; handles unbounded scenes effectively with background shells. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyperparameters (h{lv}, h{out}, h{ratio}, h{prune}, h{rate}, h{percent}). The subdivision process can be computationally intensive if many voxels are selected. When to use: When optimizing radiance fields from sparse or unstructured camera views where static grids are inefficient or when scene bounds are unknown (unbounded). Progressive Sparse Voxels Optimization was introduced in the paper "Sparse Voxels Rasterization: Real-time High-fidelity Radiance Field Rendering". It is part of the SVRaster framework, designed for real-time rendering of high-fidelity radiance fields. The method addresses the limitations of static voxel grids by introducing a progressive optimization strategy that adapts the voxel structure during training. name: Progressive Sparse Voxel Optimization
head: Coarse-to-fine reconstruction, Hierarchical Optimization
body: Progressive Sparse Voxel Optimization is a coarse-to-fine reconstruction strategy for explicit radiance fields that gradually refines a 3D scene representation by alternating between field optimization and structural modification of a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It distinguishes itself from static grid methods by dynamically pruning free space and subdividing occupied regions to balance memory efficiency and geometric detail, ensuring no undersampling occurs during refinement. The method reconstructs scene models in a coarse-to-fine manner, starting with a dense, coarse scene grid (a full, shallow SVO) and gradually sparsifying or refining the structure based on optimized field values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of input images with known camera parameters; an initial full, shallow SVO structure. Output: An optimized SVO with pruned free-space nodes and subdivided detail nodes, along with optimized field values (opacity, color). Data Structures: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO): A hierarchical grid where each node contains field data (e.g., opacity \alpha). Field Data: Per-node opacity values used to determine visibility and sampling requirements. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Start with a dense, but coarse scene grid, i.e., a full, shallow SVO. 2. Field Optimization: Optimize the SVO fields (e.g., opacity, color) for the current fixed SVO structure. The optimizer used is Adam with recommended settings. 3. Structure Update (Outer Loop): After optimizing fields, the SVO structure changes infrequently. This involves two phases: Merging Nodes (Pruning): 1. Determine the set of nodes \{N{keep}\} required for rendering using Dijkstra searches on each tree level's 27-neighborhood graph. 2. The search is hysteresis-based for robustness. 3. Sample each tree node using a regular pattern of 8^3 sampling points to determine its maximum opacity \alpha{max}(n). 4. Start a Dijkstra search on each unvisited node. 5. The resulting set \{N{keep}\} defines nodes that must not be discarded. If any child of an SVO node is within \{N{keep}\}, keep all 8 children; otherwise, discard all of them. This merges nodes in free space to save memory and reduce rendering costs, while increasing view ray sampling point distribution quality. Subdividing Nodes (Refinement): 1. Find the set of required nodes \{N{sub}\} using the same Dijkstra search method as merging. 2. A leaf node within \{N{sub}\} is eligible for subdivision only if it does not induce undersampling. 3. Undersampling check: There must be an input pixel with a small enough 3D footprint such that the Nyquist sampling theorem holds. 4. The footprint f(p) is defined by back-projecting the pixel to the depth d of the node. The sampling rate is defined by this footprint, and the node edge length defines the signal rate. 5. If a leaf is within \{N{sub}\} and does not induce aliasing, allocate all of its 8 children. 6. Fill the new leaf nodes with 3D-interpolated data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. (implementation details of Dijkstra on 27-neighborhood) nodestokeep.add(node) # Merge nodes: Keep children if any child is in nodestokeep newsvo = SVO() for node in svo.nodes: if node in nodestokeep or any(child in nodestokeep for child in node.children): newsvo.addnode(node) else: # Discard all children (merge node) pass # Subdivide nodes nodestosubdivide = set() for level in newsvo.levels: # Re-run Dijkstra to find nodes requiring detail #... (same logic as above) nodestosubdivide.update(nodesindetailregion) for node in newsvo.leaves: if node in nodestosubdivide: # Check Nyquist sampling theorem footprint = backprojectpixelfootprint(node.depth) signalrate = node.edgelength if not inducesundersampling(footprint, signalrate): # Allocate 8 children and fill with 3D-interpolated data children = node.subdivide() fillwithinterpolateddata(children) newsvo.addnodes(children) svo = newsvo return svo Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Sampling: 8^3 regular pattern for opacity estimation. Neighborhood: 27-neighborhood graph for Dijkstra search. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undersampling: Subdivision must strictly adhere to the Nyquist sampling theorem to avoid aliasing. Precision: Hysteresis-based search provides robustness against noise in opacity estimates. Iterative scene reconstruction from scratch using SGD and importance pixel sampling in a coarse-to-fine manner. It compares input images against differentiable renderings and updates the model according to model loss and gradients. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization steps and the cost of Dijkstra searches on the 27-neighborhood graph at each level. Memory Complexity: Reduced compared to dense grids due to merging nodes in free space. Performance: Merging nodes increases the quality of view ray sampling point distributions. Strengths: Memory efficiency, reduced rendering costs, high-quality sampling distribution. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hysteresis thresholds and subdivision criteria to avoid undersampling. The method is described in "ERF: Explicit Radiance Field Reconstruction From Scratch". It builds on the concept of Sparse Voxel Octrees and uses Adam optimization. name: ERF Optimization with SVO Priors
head: ERF, Explicit Radiance Field Optimization, Hierarchical Optimization for Explicit Radiance Field Reconstruction, SVO Reconstruction
body: ERF is an algorithm that reconstructs a scene from scratch using an Explicit Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) containing opacity and spherical harmonic (SH) radiance fields, optimized via inverse differentiable rendering and adaptive tree subdivision. It differs from implicit methods like NeRF by using a hierarchical grid structure that allows for explicit free-space exploitation and multi-resolution detail, and from other explicit methods by employing specific SVO priors and a tanh-based opacity constraint to stabilize optimization near boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images, their sensor poses and calibrations, and a coarse, conservative Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) for the scene. Outputs: A scene model containing an SVO (opacity and SLF fields) within the AABB and an environment map L\infty for distant regions. Data Structures: SVO Node: Contains 1 floating-point opacity parameter and multiple RGB SH coefficients (c{l,m}). Inner nodes store these parameters to support Level-of-Detail (LoD) approximations. Opacity Field (\sigma): A continuous scalar volumetric field \sigma: \mathbb{R}^3 \mapsto [0, 1] stored per tree node, representing surface coverage/absorption probability. Surface Light Field (SLF): A volumetric vector field storing outgoing radiance, represented by SH coefficients. Loss Cache (C): Tracks loss values for all input pixels to drive importance sampling. Formulas: Opacity Constraint: Maps unconstrained raw opacity \widehat{\sigma}(x) to [0, 1] using a tanh variant to prevent optimizer oscillation near borders: f(x) = 0.5 \cdot (\tanh(4x - 2) + 1) Surface Normal Inference: Derived from the gradient of the raw opacity field: \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{x}) = -\frac{\nabla \widehat{\sigma}(\mathbf{x})}{\|\nabla \widehat{\sigma}(\mathbf{x})\|2} SLF Evaluation: Uses Spherical Harmonics where c{l,m}(\mathbf{x}) are interpolated SH coefficients and Y{l,m} are basis functions: \widehat{L}0(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{l=0}^{l=b} \sum{m=-l}^{m=l} c{l,m}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot Y{l,m}(\mathbf{v}) Total Loss: Combines pixel photo consistency loss lp and SVO priors (l{3D}, l{LoD}, l0): l{\Theta}(\{\mathbf{p}i\}, \{nj\}) = \frac{1}{|\{\mathbf{p}i\}|} \sumi [lp(\mathbf{p}i)] + \frac{1}{|\{nj\}|} \cdot [l{3D}(\{nj\}) + l{\text{LoD}}(\{nj\}) + l0(\{nj\})] Parameters: Batch Size: 4096 pixels and 4096 SVO nodes. SVO Priors: l{3D} (local smoothness in 3D space), l{LoD} (local smoothness along LoD dimension), and l0 (zero opacity/radiance for sparse models). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Select pixels based on loss cache pixels = importancesample(C) # 2. Cast rays rays = castrays(pixels) # From sensor center xc,i in direction di # 3. Stratified sampling within SVO depthsstratified = stratifiedsampling(SVO, rays) # 4. Randomly select subset of depths uniformly depthssubset1 = selectrandomly(depthsstratified) # 5. Update model parameters using gradients # Includes SVO priors: l3D, lLoD, l0 SVO, Linf = makestep(SVO, Linf, gradients(losses)) mergeleaves(SVO) # Compact free space if subdivideleaves(SVO, pixelfootprints): resetoptimizer() restartoptimizationloop() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Optimizer Oscillation: Using ReLU or Softplus for opacity can cause failure or oscillation near zero gradients or borders. The tanh variant is chosen because it is mostly linear but smoothly approaches borders. Physically Implausible Geometry: Optimizing only photo consistency can lead to solutions with low error but implausible geometry (e.g., untextured surfaces). SVO priors prevent this and stop parameters from deranging if gradients are missing. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicit representation allows for free-space exploitation and multi-resolution detail; tanh constraint stabilizes optimization; SVO priors prevent convergence to implausible local minima. Limitations: Requires careful initialization and adaptive subdivision logic; SVO priors add computational overhead. When to use: When explicit control over geometry and free space is needed, or when implicit methods struggle with untextured surfaces or free space. When not to use: When implicit methods are sufficient and computational simplicity is preferred. Origin: The method was introduced in "ERF: Explicit Radiance Field Reconstruction From Scratch". History and Development: The work builds on previous research in explicit scene representations and differentiable rendering, aiming to combine the benefits of sparse voxel structures with the flexibility of radiance fields. Usage: Used for 3D scene reconstruction from multi-view images. ERF: Explicit Radiance Field Reconstruction From Scratch, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.00051v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: HDR-Plenoxels
head: HDR radiance fields modeled by Plenoxels
body: HDR-Plenoxels is a voxel-based volume rendering method that reconstructs 3D High Dynamic Range (HDR) radiance fields, scene geometry, and varying camera settings from multi-view Low Dynamic Range (LDR) images. It extends Plenoxels by introducing a differentiable tone-mapping module that models the in-camera imaging pipeline (ISP), including white balance and Camera Response Functions (CRF), allowing for self-calibration and controllable rendering. Unlike NeRF, which uses implicit neural networks, HDR-Plenoxels uses explicit sparse voxel grids with spherical harmonics, achieving rendering speeds two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF. Inputs: A set of N multi-view LDR images captured with varying camera settings (exposure, white balance, CRF). Camera poses and intrinsics, typically obtained via COLMAP sparse reconstruction. For real data: undistorted images. Outputs: A sparse voxel grid representing the 3D scene, containing opacity and view-dependent radiance coefficients. Learned tone-mapping parameters (white balance scales, CRF parameters). Novel view synthesis of HDR images, which can be tone-mapped to arbitrary LDR settings. Sparse Voxel Grid: Structure: A 3D grid covering a bounded space of interest. The grid is sparse, meaning only occupied voxels are stored or processed. Voxel Layout: Each voxel stores: Opacity (\sigma): A scalar value representing the density/opacity of the voxel. Spherical Harmonics (SH) Coefficients: A vector of 27 values (9 per color channel: Red, Green, Blue) representing the view-dependent radiance. Total per voxel: 28 values (1 opacity + 27 SH coefficients). Initialization: Opacity \sigma is initialized to 0.1. SH coefficients are initialized such that the base color is grey, achieved by adding an offset of 0.5 to the color components. Tone Mapping Parameters: White Balance Scales: Three scalar values (wr, wg, wb) representing the basis white balance, derived from channel-wise averaging of the full view. Exposure Scale: A scalar value representing the basis exposure, derived from globally averaging the white balance values. CRF Parameters: Parameters defining the Camera Response Function, learned during training. 1. Preprocessing: Compute rough 3D geometry and obtain camera poses using COLMAP sparse reconstruction to determine the bounding box of the scene. For real-world images, perform lens undistortion using calibration data. 2. Grid Initialization: Initialize a sparse voxel grid within the determined bounding box. Synthetic Data Resolution Schedule: Start at (128, 128, 64). Upsample to (256, 256, 128), then (512, 512, 256), and finally (800, 800, 512), with each upsampling occurring after 25,600 iterations. Real Data Resolution Schedule: Start at (128, 128, 128). Upsample to (256, 256, 256), then (750, 600, 300). Initialize voxel opacity \sigma = 0.1 and SH coefficients to represent a grey color (offset 0.5). 3. Coarse-to-Fine Training Loop: For each training iteration: a. Ray Marching (HDR Rendering): For each pixel, cast a ray through the scene. Sample points along the ray. Interpolate opacity \sigma and SH coefficients from the voxel grid at each sample point. Compute the HDR radiance L{HDR} for the viewing direction using the SH basis functions Yl(\omega) and coefficients cl: L{HDR}(\omega) = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} c{l,m} Y{l,m}(\omega) where L is the degree of SH (typically 2 for 9 coefficients per channel). Perform volume rendering to composite the final HDR radiance C{HDR} for the pixel, accounting for depth and opacity. b. Differentiable Tone Mapping: Apply the tone mapping module to C{HDR} to produce the synthesized LDR image C{LDR}. The tone mapping consists of two stages: 1. White Balance: Scale the RGB channels by the learned white balance parameters wr, wg, wb. 2. Camera Response Function (CRF): Apply the learned CRF function f(\cdot) to the white-balanced values. The final LDR value is computed as: C{LDR} = f(w \odot C{HDR}) where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication with white balance scales. c. Loss Computation: Compute the loss \mathcal{L} between the synthesized LDR image C{LDR} and the ground truth LDR image C{GT}. Include Total Variation (TV) loss for opacity \sigma and SH coefficients during the first 3 epochs (before the first upsampling) to stabilize training. \mathcal{L}{TV} = \lambda{TV,\sigma} \text{TV}(\sigma) + \lambda{TV,SH} \text{TV}(c{SH}) with \lambda{TV,\sigma} = 5 \cdot 10^{-4} and \lambda{TV,SH} = 1 \cdot 10^{-2}. d. Backpropagation: Backpropagate gradients through the tone mapping module to update the SH coefficients, opacity, and tone mapping parameters (white balance, CRF). Use the RMSProp optimizer. e. Grid Management: Upsampling: Increase grid resolution according to the schedule. Pruning: Remove voxels with opacity below a specified occupancy threshold to reduce computational cost. The specific threshold value is not given in the sources. 4. Controllable Rendering (Post-Training): To render at a specific exposure, scale the basis exposure value (globally averaged white balance). To render with specific white balance, adjust the red, green, and blue components of the basis white balance (channel-wise averaged). To render median exposure, use the median of the minimum and maximum learned exposure values. Unverified code. Returns: grid: Dictionary or sparse structure mapping voxel coordinates to [opacity, shcoeffs] opacityinit: 0.1 shinit: Grey color offset 0.5 """ grid = {} # Implementation details for sparse grid storage depend on specific engine # Here we assume a function that creates the structure return grid def sphericalharmonicseval(direction, shcoeffs): """ Evaluate spherical harmonics for a given direction and coefficients. direction: (3,) unit vector shcoeffs: (27,) vector (9 per channel) Returns: radiance: (3,) vector (R, G, B) """ # Standard SH basis evaluation # L=2 implies 9 coefficients per channel # This is a placeholder for the actual SH math pass def volumerenderray(rayorigin, raydirection, grid, numsamples): """ Render a single ray through the voxel grid. """ # Adjust tone mapping parameters based on controls adjustedwb = basiswb wbscalefactor wbchannelfactors adjustedexposure = basisexposure exposurefactor # Render HDR hdrimage = renderhdr(camerapose) # Apply adjusted tone mapping ldrimage = tonemapping(hdrimage, adjustedwb, crfparams) return ldrimage Occupancy Threshold: Scalar value for pruning voxels. Value not specified in the sources. TV Loss Weights: \lambda{TV,\sigma} = 5 \cdot 10^{-4}, \lambda{TV,SH} = 1 \cdot 10^{-2}. Optimizer: RMSProp. SH Degree: 2 (9 coefficients per channel). Saturated Regions: Wide dynamic range scenes cause saturation in LDR training images. HDR-Plenoxels handles this via the differentiable tone mapping module and robust learning of SH coefficients and opacity. Large Depth in Synthetic Data: Default concentric sphere grids struggle with large depth in Blender data. Solved by computing rough 3D geometry via COLMAP to determine the proper grid range. Lens Distortion: Real images often have lens distortion. Solved by undistorting images via calibration before training. Training Instability: SH coefficients can change significantly during training. Mitigated by initializing color to grey (offset 0.5) and opacity to 0.1. Time Complexity: Training time is tens of minutes. Memory Complexity: Uses sparse voxel grids, which are more memory-efficient than dense grids or dense neural networks for high-resolution scenes. Rendering Speed: Two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF. Strengths: Fast convergence and rendering. Handles varying camera settings (exposure, white balance, CRF) without explicit calibration. Robust to saturated regions and shot noise. Enables controllable rendering of exposure and white balance. Limitations: Requires COLMAP for initial geometry and poses. Performance degrades slightly with extreme exposure gaps (e.g., ±6EV), though still outperforms some alternatives. When to Use: When fast HDR novel view synthesis is required from multi-view LDR images with varying camera settings, and computational resources are limited compared to NeRF-based methods. When Not to Use: When dense COLMAP results are unavailable and cannot be approximated, or when implicit neural representations are strictly required for other reasons. Origin: Introduced by Kim Jun-Seong, Kim Yu-Ji, Moon Ye-Bin, and Tae-Hyun Oh at POSTECH. Paper: "HDR-Plenoxels: Self-Calibrating High Dynamic Range Radiance Fields" (arXiv:2208.06787v2, Nov 2022). Development: Extends Plenoxels [53] for HDR radiance fields and adopts the coarse-to-fine training scheme from NSVF [17]. It addresses the limitations of NeRF in handling HDR and varying camera conditions efficiently. Usage: Used for novel view synthesis from multi-view LDR images captured with varying exposure, white balance, and CRF settings. Tested on Blender synthetic datasets and real scenes (Character, Desk, Plant, Coffee, Kitchen). name: PlenOctree Compression with Modified Training and Sparsity
head: Sparse PlenOctree Training
body: This method reduces the storage size of PlenOctree models by modifying the NeRF-SH training loss to optimize sparsity and compressing the resulting voxelized point cloud attributes. It differs from the original PlenOctree method by using a Cauchy loss instead of the standard sparsity loss, adding total variation regularization, using half-pixel ray offsets, and performing post-thresholding fine-tuning. Inputs: Training images and camera poses. Outputs: Compressed PlenOctree model (encoded point cloud attributes). Data Structures: The PlenOctree is represented as a set of octree leaves. The raw data structure fields for a scene (e.g., Lego) are: Child: Array of size 2,982,398 \times 8, 32-bit integers. Parent depth: Array of size 2,982,398 \times 2, 32-bit integers. Data (\sigma, k): Array of size 2,982,398 \times 8 \times 49, 16-bit floats. This stores density \sigma and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients k. Metadata: 32/64-bit values. Total uncompressed size is approximately 2.3 GB for the Lego scene. Steps: 1. Modified NeRF-SH Training: Train a NeRF-SH network to output SH coefficients k of degree \ell{max} instead of RGB colors. The ray directions are modified by adding a half-pixel offset so they pass through pixel centers. The total training loss L is: L = Lr + L{cauchy} + L{TV} where Lr is the rendering loss, L{cauchy} is the Cauchy sparsity loss, and L{TV} is the total variation regularization. 2. PlenOctree Extraction: Sample the trained NeRF-SH to extract density \sigma and SH coefficients k into octree leaves. The SH coefficients are evaluated according to the ray direction (\theta, \phi) to obtain view-dependent color. 3. PlenOctree Optimization: Fine-tune the extracted octree using the rendering loss Lr on training images. 4. Thresholding for Sparsity: Estimate opacity \alpha for each node to remove nodes with low influence. The opacity is estimated as: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \delta) where \delta \approx 2/2^N and N is the octree depth. Nodes with low \alpha are removed. 5. Post-thresholding Fine-tuning: Re-fine-tune the "distilled" PlenOctree with cross-validation to compensate for knowledge loss from removed points. 6. Compression Preparation: View the octree leaves as a voxelized point cloud P with N voxels. The coordinates x{pc} are calculated from the octree child indices x{oct} = [Xn, Yn, Zn] and octree depth M: x{pc} = x{oct} \times 2^M - 0.5 The attributes s(n) for each point are: s(n) = [\sigman, k^0{n0}, k^{-1}{n1}, k^1{n1}, \dots, k^\ell{n\ell}] where k^\ell{nm} \in \mathbb{R}^3. 7. Attribute Encoding: Encode \sigma and k coefficients as attributes of the point cloud P using a point cloud compression method, specifically Geometry-Based Point Cloud Coding (G-PCC). Parameters: Total variation hyperparameter \eta: 10^{-11}. Cauchy loss hyperparameter \lambdas: 10^{-4}. Formulas: Total Variation Regularization: L{TV} = \frac{\eta}{|R|} \sum{i,k} \| \nabla \sigma(ri(tk)) \|2 where R is the ray batch size. Cauchy Sparsity Loss: L{cauchy} = \lambdas \sum{i,k} \log(1 + 2\sigma(ri(tk))^2) where \sigma is volume density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The SH coefficients of degree \ell=3 account for 98% of the data size, making them the primary bottleneck for compression. Child and Parent depth structures must be conveyed losslessly to maintain fast rendering speed. Compression reduces bit rates by approximately 8x with higher quality than the original PlenOctree, or by approximately 50x with minimal degradation for novel view synthesis. Storage requirements for the original PlenOctree model on the Lego scene are approximately 2.3 GB, with 95% of that size coming from \sigma and k coefficients. Strengths include maintaining high rendering speed and quality while significantly reducing model size. Origin is described in "Compression of PlenOctree Model Attributes Enabling Fast Communication and Rendering of Neural Radiance Fields". Development improves upon the PlenOctree method by addressing its large storage requirements. It incorporates techniques from Mip-NeRF for ray offsets and SNeRG for the Cauchy loss. Usage is for fast communication and rendering of Neural Radiance Fields, particularly where bandwidth or storage is constrained.
