name: Gaussian Process Occupancy Model
head: GP occupancy, Probabilistic implicit surface
body:
The Gaussian Process Occupancy Model defines voxel occupancy as the probability that a point lies on or inside an object, derived from a Gaussian Process (GP) over a geometric classification function. It differs from deterministic implicit models by providing a probabilistic interpretation of occupancy, enabling robust optimization through orientation assignment based on the expected gradient of the mean function. Inputs and Outputs Input: A grid-based texture storing the mean implicit function values \mu(\mathbf{x}) at voxel centers. Output: Occupancy probability \alpha(\mathbf{x}) for any point \mathbf{x}, and the background surface  ar{S} defined by the zero-level set of \mu(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures The model relies on a 3D grid (texture) where each cell stores a scalar value \mu(\mathbf{x}). In the cited implementation, cubic interpolation is used to query \mu(\mathbf{x}) at arbitrary positions. Parameters \sigma: Constant variance for the Gaussian Process. The sources assume \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma for all \mathbf{x}. \gamma: Parameter for the squared exponential kernel, used to define spatial correlation. However, this parameter is not used in the core occupancy calculation or surface extraction described. Formulas The geometric classification function \Phi(\mathbf{x}) is modeled as a Gaussian random variable: \Phi(\mathbf{x}) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu(\mathbf{x}), \sigma^2) The occupancy \alpha(\mathbf{x}) is the probability that \Phi(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0: \alpha(\mathbf{x}) = 	ext{Pr}\{\Phi(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0\} =  rac{1}{2} \left[ 1 - \operatorname{erf} \left(  rac{\mu(\mathbf{x})}{\sqrt{2\sigma^2}} ight) ight] The orientation  eta(\mathbf{x}) at point \mathbf{x} is defined by the normalized expected gradient of the mean:  eta(\mathbf{x}) =  rac{
abla\mu(\mathbf{x})}{\|
abla\mu(\mathbf{x})\|} The background surface  ar{S} is the isosurface where \mu(\mathbf{x}) = 0 (equivalently \alpha(\mathbf{x}) = 0.5). Steps 1. Query Mean: For a given point \mathbf{x}, retrieve \mu(\mathbf{x}) from the grid using cubic interpolation. 2. Compute Occupancy: Calculate \alpha(\mathbf{x}) using the error function formula above with the constant \sigma. 3. Compute Orientation (Optional): Calculate 
abla\mu(\mathbf{x}) (e.g., via finite differences on the grid) and normalize it to get  eta(\mathbf{x}). This improves optimization robustness. 4. Surface Extraction (Optional): To visualize or interact with the background surface  ar{S}, apply Marching Cubes to the grid of \mu(\mathbf{x}) values. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Gradient Vanishing: If 
abla\mu(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}, the orientation  eta(\mathbf{x}) is undefined. This occurs at critical points of the implicit function. Spatial Correlation Ignored: The implementation does not model the auto-correlation 	ext{corr}(\Phi(\mathbf{x}), \Phi(\mathbf{y})) = \exp(-\gamma\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|^2) because it only requires pointwise probability evaluations and surface extraction, not sampling concrete surface realizations. Variance Assumption: The model assumes constant variance \sigma. If the true uncertainty varies spatially, this assumption may lead to inaccurate occupancy probabilities. Complexity: Querying occupancy is O(1) per point given the grid. Computing gradients adds a small constant factor. Strengths: The orientation assignment  eta(\mathbf{x}) significantly improves the robustness and speed of optimizations. The probabilistic formulation allows for a natural interpretation of uncertainty. Limitations: The assumption of constant variance may not capture complex uncertainty structures. The model does not inherently handle spatial correlations between points, which might be necessary for tasks involving sampling multiple surface realizations. When to use: When robust optimization of implicit surfaces is needed and a probabilistic interpretation of occupancy is beneficial. When not to use: When spatial correlation between points is critical (e.g., sampling realistic surface variations) or when variance varies significantly across the scene. The Gaussian Process Occupancy Model is part of the "Many-Worlds Inverse Rendering" framework. It was introduced to handle the ambiguity in inverse rendering by treating the scene geometry as a distribution of surfaces rather than a single deterministic surface. The use of Gaussian Processes allows for a principled way to define occupancy probabilities and orientations, which are crucial for stable optimization in inverse rendering scenarios. Many-Worlds Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1145/3767318, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural Residual Field (ReRF)
head: Neural Residual Field (ReRF) Training, Neural Residual Radiance Fields
body: Neural Residual Field (ReRF) is a method for generating compact neural representations of dynamic scenes from RGB video inputs by sequentially optimizing explicit feature grids, motion grids, and residual grids. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and rendering long-duration dynamic scenes by avoiding a global canonical space, instead warping features from the previous frame and encoding only the differences. Unlike Neural Radiance Fields which model static scenes, or Deformable and Dynamic Fields which may use complex deformation fields, ReRF explicitly separates motion estimation and residual compensation into distinct grid structures to maintain sparsity and smoothness. ReRF operates in a two-stage sequential training scheme: first optimizing an explicit feature grid for the initial frame, then iteratively optimizing motion and residual grids for subsequent frames. Inputs: A sequence of RGB images (video frames) It for t=0, 1, \dots, T. Outputs: A sequence of feature grids ft (containing density and color features) for each frame, and a global MLP \Phi. 1. Explicit Feature Grid (V\sigma, Vc): V\sigma: Explicit density grid. Dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Vc: Color feature grid. Dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Total feature dimension C=13 (union of density and color features). 2. Dense Motion Field (Dt): Dimensions 3 \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Contains warping information (position offset) from frame t to t-1. 3. Compact Motion Grid (Mt): Generated from Dt via motion pooling. Represents the position offset from the current frame to the previous. 4. Residual Grid (rt): Dimensions C \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Initialized to zero. Stores residuals to compensate for warping errors and newly observed regions. 5. Global MLP (\Phi): Two hidden layers, 128 channels each. Decodes color features to RGB. Grid Resolution: Progressive upscaling from 125^3 to 150^3 (step 1000), 200^3 (step 2000), and 250^3 (step 4000). Optimizer: Adam. Batch Size: 10,192 rays. Learning Rates: Global MLP \Phi: 0.002. Explicit Grid (V\sigma, Vc): 0.1 (density), 0.11 (color). Motion Grid (Mt): 10^{-4}. Residual Grid (rt): 0.1 (density), 0.11 (color). Loss Weights: \lambda{TV} (Total Variation): 0.000016 for explicit and residual grids; 1 for motion grid. \lambda{residual} (L1 Residual): 0.01. TV Loss Activation: Only active during training iterations 1000 to 12,000. Stage 1: Explicit Feature Grid Optimization (Frame 0) 1. Construct an explicit density grid V\sigma and color feature grid Vc for the first frame using an initialization resolution (e.g., 125^3). 2. For each training iteration: a. Cast rays through pixels. Sample points p along rays. b. Query density \sigma(p) and color features c{feat}(p) via trilinear interpolation from V\sigma and Vc. c. Apply softplus activation to density: \sigma{final}(p) = \text{softplus}(\sigma(p)). d. Decode color features to RGB using global MLP \Phi: c{pred}(p) = \Phi(c{feat}(p)). e. Perform volume rendering to predict pixel color \hat{c}(l) for ray l. f. Compute loss \mathcal{L}{explicit} (see Formulas) and update V\sigma, Vc, \Phi. g. Train for 5,000 iterations (coarse) and 16,000 iterations (fine). Stage 2: Sequential Optimization for Frame t > 0 1. Motion Grid Estimation: a. Sample points pt along rays in frame t. b. Estimate dense motion field Dt by warping points from frame t-1 to t and minimizing photometric loss and TV loss on Dt. c. Progressively upscale Dt resolution as defined in parameters. d. Generate compact motion grid Mt from Dt using motion pooling strategy. e. Train for 3,000 iterations (coarse) and 16,000 iterations (fine). 2. Warping: a. Warp the previous frame's feature grid f{t-1} using Mt to generate base feature grid \hat{f}t. b. \hat{f}t is fixed during residual optimization. 3. Residual Grid Optimization: a. Initialize residual grid rt with zero values. b. For each training iteration: i. Sample points pt along rays in frame t. ii. Query base features \hat{f}t(pt) via trilinear interpolation from warped grid. iii. Query residual features rt(pt) via trilinear interpolation from rt. iv. Compute final feature ft(pt) = \hat{f}t(pt) + rt(pt). v. Decode ft(pt) using \Phi and render to get \hat{c}(l). vi. Compute loss \mathcal{L}{residual} (see Formulas) and update rt. vii. Train for 5,000 iterations (coarse) and 16,000 iterations (fine). Explicit Loss: \mathcal{L}{explicit} = \mathcal{L}{render{explicit}} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV{explicit}} \mathcal{L}{render{explicit}} = \sum{l \in L} \| c(l) - \hat{c}(l) \| \mathcal{L}{TV{explicit}} = \frac{1}{|V\sigma|} \sum{v \in V\sigma} \sqrt{\Deltax^2 v + \Deltay^2 v + \Deltaz^2 v} Where \Delta{x,y,z}^2 v is the squared difference between density values in adjacent voxels. Deformation (Motion) Loss: \mathcal{L}{deform} = \mathcal{L}{render{deform}} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV{deform}} \mathcal{L}{render{deform}} = \sum{l \in L} \| c(l) - \hat{c}(l) \| \mathcal{L}{TV{deform}} = \frac{1}{|Dt|} \sum{v \in Dt} \sqrt{\Deltax^2(v,d) + \Deltay^2(v,d) + \Deltaz^2(v,d)} Where \Delta{x,y,z}^2(v,d) is the squared difference of motion vectors in adjacent voxels. Residual Loss: \mathcal{L}{residual} = \mathcal{L}{render{residual}} + \lambda{TV} \mathcal{L}{TV{residual}} + \lambda{residual} \cdot \mathcal{L}{1residual} \mathcal{L}{render{residual}} = \sum{l \in L} \| c(l) - \hat{c}(l) \| \mathcal{L}{TV{residual}} = \frac{1}{|ft^d|} \sum{v \in ft^d} \sqrt{\Deltax^2 v + \Deltay^2 v + \Deltaz^2 v} \mathcal{L}{1residual} = \frac{1}{|rt|} \sum{v \in rt} (|vx| + |vy| + |vz|) Where ft^d represents the density component of the feature grid ft. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterp(grid, points): # grid: (D, D, D) or (D, D, D, C) # points: (N, 3) coordinates in [0, D-1] # Returns interpolated values at points x0 = floor(points[:, 0]) y0 = floor(points[:, 1]) z0 = floor(points[:, 2]) x1 = clamp(x0 + 1, max=grid.shape[0]-1) y1 = clamp(y0 + 1, max=grid.shape[1]-1) z1 = clamp(z0 + 1, max=grid.shape[2]-1) dx = points[:, 0] - x0 dy = points[:, 1] - y0 dz = points[:, 2] - z0 if grid.dim() == 3: v00 = grid[x0, y0, z0] v10 = grid[x1, y0, z0] v01 = grid[x0, y1, z0] v11 = grid[x1, y1, z0] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1] v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1] v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1] w000 = (1-dx)(1-dy)(1-dz) w100 = dx(1-dy)(1-dz) w010 = (1-dx)dy(1-dz) w110 = dxdy(1-dz) w001 = (1-dx)(1-dy)dz w101 = dx(1-dy)dz w011 = (1-dx)dydz w111 = dxdydz return (w000v00 + w100v10 + w010v01 + w110v11 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) else: v00 = grid[x0, y0, z0,:] v10 = grid[x1, y0, z0,:] v01 = grid[x0, y1, z0,:] v11 = grid[x1, y1, z0,:] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1,:] v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1,:] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1,:] v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1,:] w000 = (1-dx)(1-dy)(1-dz) w100 = dx(1-dy)(1-dz) w010 = (1-dx)dy(1-dz) w110 = dxdy(1-dz) w001 = (1-dx)(1-dy)dz w101 = dx(1-dy)dz w011 = (1-dx)dydz w111 = dxdydz return (w000v00 + w100v10 + w010v01 + w110v11 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) def volumerender(sigma, color, rayorigins, raydirs, near, far, numsamples): # Standard volume rendering logic # The sources do not provide the exact volume rendering implementation details. # Typically: sample points along ray, compute transmittance T, accumulate color. pass def tvloss(grid): # Total variation loss on grid diffx = grid[:, 1:,:] - grid[:,:-1,:] diffy = grid[:,:, 1:] - grid[:,:,:-1] diffz = grid[1:,:,:] - grid[:-1,:,:] return sqrt(diffx2 + diffy2 + diffz2).mean() class ReRF: def init(self, gridsize=125, channels=13): self.Vsigma = randn(gridsize, gridsize, gridsize) self.Vc = randn(gridsize, gridsize, gridsize, channels) self.mlp = Sequential( Linear(channels, 128), ReLU(), Linear(128, 128), ReLU(), Linear(128, 3)) self.optimizer = Adam(list(self.mlp.parameters()) + [self.Vsigma, self.Vc], lr=0.002) self.channels = channels self.gridsize = gridsize def trainframe0(self, rays, targets, numcoarse=5000, numfine=16000): # Stage 1: Explicit Feature Grid Optimization for i in range(numcoarse + numfine): self.optimizer.zerograd() rayorigins, raydirs, targets = rays sigma = trilinearinterp(self.Vsigma, rayorigins) cfeat = trilinearinterp(self.Vc, rayorigins) sigma = softplus(sigma) colors = self.mlp(cfeat) renderedcolors = volumerender(sigma, colors, rayorigins, raydirs, near=0.0, far=1.0, numsamples=128) lossrender = mean((renderedcolors - targets)2) losstv = 0 if 1000 <= i <= 12000: losstv = tvloss(self.Vsigma) loss = lossrender + 0.000016 losstv loss.backward() self.optimizer.step() def trainframet(self, prevfeaturegrid, currentrays, targets, motiongridsize=125, residualgridsize=125): # Stage 2: Sequential Optimization # 1. Motion Grid Optimization # Estimate dense motion field Dt and generate compact motion grid Mt via motion pooling. # Optimize Mt using Ldeform for 3000 (coarse) + 16000 (fine) iterations with lr=1e-4. # Motion pooling and dense field estimation details are implementation-specific. # 2. Warping fhatt = warp(prevfeaturegrid, Mt) # 3. Residual Grid Optimization rt = zeros(residualgridsize, residualgridsize, residualgridsize, self.channels) optimizerr = Adam([rt], lr=0.1) for i in range(5000 + 16000): optimizerr.zerograd() rayorigins, raydirs, targets = currentrays fhat = trilinearinterp(fhatt, rayorigins) r = trilinearinterp(rt, rayorigins) ffinal = fhat + r sigma = softplus(ffinal[..., 0]) cfeat = ffinal[..., 1:] colors = self.mlp(cfeat) renderedcolors = volumerender(sigma, colors, rayorigins, raydirs, near=0.0, far=1.0, numsamples=128) lossrender = mean((renderedcolors - targets)2) losstv = 0 if 1000 <= i <= 12000: rdensity = rt[..., 0] losstv = tvloss(rdensity) lossl1 = mean(abs(rt)) loss = lossrender + 0.000016 losstv + 0.01 lossl1 loss.backward() optimizerr.step() return rt A two-stage training scheme to efficiently obtain ReRF from RGB videos, maintaining smoothness and sparsity of motion/residual grids. It introduces a novel motion pooling strategy to maintain the smoothness and compactness of the inter-frame motion grid along with sparsity regularizers to improve the compactness of ReRF. Time Complexity: Sequential optimization per frame. Motion grid optimization takes 19,000 iterations (3k coarse + 16k fine). Residual grid optimization takes 21,000 iterations (5k coarse + 16k fine). Memory Complexity: Scales with grid resolution. Base resolution 125^3, up to 250^3. Feature dimension 13. Performance: Achieves three orders of magnitude compression rate compared to per-frame-based neural representations. Strengths: Compact representation, supports online streaming, allows pause/play/fast-forward like 2D video. Limitations: Requires sequential training; errors can accumulate if motion estimation is poor (mitigated by residual grid). ReRF was introduced in "Neural Residual Radiance Fields for Streamably Free-Viewpoint Videos" (CVPR 2023). It builds on the idea of using explicit grids (like DVGO) and extends it to dynamic scenes by decomposing the feature field into motion and residual components, inspired by video compression standards (H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC). Neural Residual Radiance Fields for Streamably Free-Viewpoint Videos, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00016, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Neural 3D Volume Decomposition
body: Neural 3D Volume Decomposition (Neural-PIL) is a method for jointly estimating 3D shape, spatially-varying BRDF (SVBRDF), and per-image illumination from a collection of images of an object captured under varying viewpoints and lighting conditions. It extends the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework by replacing the implicit view-dependent color output with an explicit physical material representation (Cook-Torrance BRDF parameters) and a latent illumination vector. Unlike standard NeRF which optimizes for novel view synthesis directly, this method solves the inverse problem of reflectance decomposition, enabling high-quality relighting and material-aware view synthesis. The method builds on Radiance-field optimization by introducing a physically-based rendering formulation within the neural volume. It uses a two-stage sampling strategy similar to NeRF but optimizes for material and lighting parameters rather than just color. Inputs: A set of q images Cj \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times 3} for j \in \{1, \dots, q\}, where s is the number of pixels per image. Per-pixel binary masks Mj \in \{0, 1\}^{s \times 1} indicating which pixels belong to the object. Outputs: A neural 3D volume V that, for any 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, estimates: Cook-Torrance BRDF parameters b \in \mathbb{R}^7: diffuse color bd \in \mathbb{R}^3, specular color bs \in \mathbb{R}^3, and roughness br \in \mathbb{R}. Unit-length surface normal n \in \mathbb{R}^3. Optical density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Per-image latent illumination vectors zl \in \mathbb{R}^{128} for each of the q images. The neural volume V is implemented as two Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Coarse MLP: Learns a coarse representation and samples the 3D volume in a fixed sampling pattern. Fine MLP: Uses the coarse density knowledge to sample the volume in high-density areas at a finer resolution. Input to MLPs: 3D coordinate x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output of MLPs: Predicts material and density parameters in a fixed tensor layout: indices 0-2 for bd, 3-5 for bs, 6 for br, 7-9 for n, and 10 for \sigma. Illumination Storage: A learnable tensor of shape q \times 128 storing zl for each image. The method replaces NeRF's direct color prediction with a rendering equation that integrates BRDF and illumination. 1. Ray Sampling: For a camera ray r(t) = o + td, sample points ti along the ray between near bound tn and far bound tf. 2. Neural Query: For each sample point ti, query the neural volume V to get b(ti), n(ti), and \sigma(ti). 3. Illumination Retrieval: Retrieve the latent illumination vector zl corresponding to the image index j of the camera ray. 4. BRDF Evaluation: Compute the Cook-Torrance BRDF fr using b(ti), the surface normal n(ti), the view direction d, and the light direction derived from zl. 5. Radiance Integration: Compute the outgoing radiance Lo at each sample point by integrating the incident illumination against the BRDF. 6. Volume Rendering: Composite the final color \hat{c}(r) using numerical quadrature: \hat{c}(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(t) c(t) dt with T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(t') dt'\right). Here, c(t) represents the outgoing radiance computed from the BRDF and illumination at sample t. The network is optimized by minimizing the difference between the rendered images and the input images Cj. The loss function typically includes a photometric term comparing \hat{c}(r) to the pixel color in Cj for pixels where Mj=1. The method may also use pre-trained networks (neural-PIL, light-SMAE, BRDF-SMAE) to regularize or initialize the optimization of BRDF and light parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class NeuralVolumeDecomposition: def init(self, numimages, coarsesamples=64, finesamples=128, near=0.1, far=10.0): self.numimages = numimages self.coarsesamples = coarsesamples self.finesamples = finesamples self.near = near self.far = far # Coarse MLP: maps (x, d) to material/density parameters self.coarsemlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 11)) # Fine MLP: refines sampling in high-density areas self.finemlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 11)) # Learnable per-image illumination latent vectors zl in R^128 self.illuminationlatents = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(numimages, 128)) def samplerays(self, origins, directions, numsamples): tvals = torch.linspace(self.near, self.far, numsamples, device=origins.device) originsexp = origins.unsqueeze(1) dirsexp = directions.unsqueeze(1) tvalsexp = tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) points = originsexp + dirsexp tvalsexp deltas = torch.diff(tvals, dim=0) deltainf = torch.tensor([self.far - tvals[-1]], device=origins.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], dim=0) deltas = deltas.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(origins.shape[0], numsamples, 1) return points, deltas def queryvolume(self, points, directions, mlp): inputs = torch.cat([points, directions], dim=-1) outputs = mlp(inputs) bd = outputs[:,:, 0:3] bs = outputs[:,:, 3:6] br = outputs[:,:, 6:7] n = outputs[:,:, 7:10] sigma = outputs[:,:, 10:11] n = n / (torch.norm(n, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-6) return bd, bs, br, n, sigma def render(self, origins, directions, imageidx): # Stage 1: Coarse fixed sampling coarsepoints, coarsedeltas = self.samplerays(origins, directions, self.coarsesamples),,,, coarsesigma = self.queryvolume(coarsepoints, directions, self.coarsemlp) coarsesigma = torch.clamp(coarsesigma, min=0.0) # Stage 2: Fine sampling (density-guided refinement) finepoints, finedeltas = self.samplerays(origins, directions, self.finesamples) finebd, finebs, finebr, finen, finesigma = self.queryvolume(finepoints, directions, self.finemlp) finesigma = torch.clamp(finesigma, min=0.0) # Use fine samples for final composition points = finepoints deltas = finedeltas bd, bs, br, n, sigma = finebd, finebs, finebr, finen, finesigma # Compute outgoing radiance c(t) from BRDF and illumination # The exact mapping from zl to light directions/intensity uses pre-trained networks (neural-PIL, light-SMAE) zl = self.illuminationlatents[imageidx] c = torch.zeroslike(bd) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma.squeeze(-1) deltas.squeeze(-1)) T = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigma.squeeze(-1) deltas.squeeze(-1), dim=1)) Tshifted = torch.cat([torch.ones(origins.shape[0], 1, device=origins.device), T[:,:-1]], dim=1) weights = Tshifted alpha.unsqueeze(-1) renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights c, dim=1) return renderedcolor Precision: The optimization of BRDF parameters (especially roughness br) can be sensitive to initialization. Pre-training with neural-PIL helps stabilize this. Boundaries: The near and far bounds tn and tf must be chosen to encompass the object. If the object is outside these bounds, it will not be rendered. Accelerates neural volume queries using a multi-resolution grid structure, reducing memory and computation compared to dense MLPs [1414-hierarchical-grid-optimization.md]. Details on integration with this method are not given in the sources. Represents scenes as explicit 3D Gaussians for faster rasterization, trading off the implicit neural volume representation for speed [1795-3d-gaussian-splatting.md]. Details on integration with this method are not given in the sources. The foundational coordinate-based MLP method for novel view synthesis, which Neural 3D Volume Decomposition extends by adding physical material parameters [4972-neural-radiance-fields.md]. The method explicitly builds on NeRF's two-MLP architecture. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables high-quality relighting and material-aware view synthesis. Can recover accurate shape and material properties from real-world datasets. Limitations: Requires images captured under varying illumination conditions. Optimization is complex and may require pre-trained networks for stability. When to use: When the goal is to recover physical material properties and illumination from a set of images, rather than just novel view synthesis. When not to use: When only novel view synthesis is needed, or when the input images do not have varying illumination. Neural 3D Volume Decomposition, also known as Neural-PIL, was introduced in the paper "Neural-PIL: Neural Pre-Integrated Lighting for Reflectance Decomposition". The method addresses the challenge of recovering 3D shape and SVBRDF from images captured under varying lighting conditions, a problem relevant to digitizing real-world objects like statues or landmarks. It builds on the success of NeRF in novel view synthesis and extends it to physical material decomposition. name: Shading-Guided NeRF Synthesis
head: Shading Map Guided Synthesis Pipeline, Shading vector synthesis
body: Shading-Guided NeRF Synthesis is a method for generating large-scale radiance fields from a smaller exemplar by controlling lighting effects using shading vectors, avoiding the need to decouple geometry, material, and lighting. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing repetitive 3D structures while maintaining consistent lighting across complex scenes. It sets itself apart from methods that rely solely on feature grid matching, which leads to discontinuous shading changes under complex lighting, by explicitly incorporating a shading map and shading map guider to ensure continuous lighting. Inputs: 1. Exemplar Radiance Field: Represented by a density field V^{(d)} and a color feature field V^{(f)}. 2. Exemplar Shading Map: A 3D volume where each voxel column stores a shading vector derived from the exemplar. 3. Target Scene Geometry: A geometrically continuous large scene (synthesized via geometry-based synthesis) used to generate the shading map guider. 4. Light Source Information: Position xl and intensity I of point light sources in the target scene. 5. Parameters: M: Number of viewpoints to approximate the shading vector (typically 50). ks: Number of closest shading patches to find in the exemplar. kg: Number of candidate patches with geometric continuity. np: Number of high-density points selected for ray tracing. ns: Number of sample points along the light path. nc: Number of shading vector channels retained (those with the lowest missing value rate). Outputs: A synthesized large-scale NeRF scene with density field and radiance field stitched from exemplar patches, guided by the target lighting. Data Structures: Shading Map: A 3D volume. Each voxel at position v contains a vector \mathbf{s}v \in \mathbb{R}^M, where M is the number of viewpoints. The m-th component is the shading value of the voxel column at viewpoint m. Shading Map Guider: A 3D volume of the same dimensions as the Shading Map, containing shading vectors derived from the target scene's geometry and light sources. Density Field V^{(d)}: 3D grid storing density values \sigma. Color Feature Field V^{(f)}: 3D grid storing color feature values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Extract Exemplar Shading Map: a. Perform intrinsic decomposition on multiple images of the exemplar using PIE-Net to derive shading and albedo. b. Apply Gaussian blurring and polynomial fitting to the shading image to smooth it and remove geometric interference. c. For each pixel in the smoothed shading image, project the shading value along the camera ray to a depth position d in the 3D voxel grid. d. Calculate depth d using the density grid: d = \sum{k} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ti where Ti is transmittance, \sigmai is density, \deltai is distance, and ti is a position/weight factor. e. Collect shading information from M viewpoints to form the shading vector for each voxel column. f. Post-processing: i. Fill holes in shading vector channels (caused by occlusions/limited pixels) using KNN interpolation with inverse distance weighting. ii. Repair noisy points using median filtering. iii. Retain only the nc channels with the lowest rate of missing values. 2. Generate Shading Map Guider: a. Synthesize a geometrically continuous large scene using geometry-based synthesis (matching density only) to create a base target scene. Then, apply ray tracing to generate the shading map guider for the target illumination. b. Select np points from this scene with high density. c. For each selected point x and a point light source xl: i. Sample ns points x1,..., x{ns} along the path between xl and x, where x{ns} = x. ii. Calculate the probability p{ns} of the ray propagating to x{ns}: p{ns} = T{ns} (1 - \exp(-\sigma{ns} \delta{ns})). iii. Calculate brightness b: b = p{ns} \frac{1}{ns} \frac{I}{\|x - xl\|2^2} where I is light intensity. d. The brightness values from M viewpoints (or equivalent lighting configurations) form the shading vector for each voxel column in the target scene, creating the Shading Map Guider. 3. Synthesize Scene (Patch Selection and Stitching): a. For a patch Pn to be synthesized in the target area: i. Compute the L2 distance between the shading vector of Pn and patches in the exemplar's Shading Map. ii. Accelerate search using a kd-tree. iii. Identify the ks closest shading patches from the exemplar. iv. Normalize the values of the exemplar's Shading Map and the target's Shading Map Guider to the same scale. v. Rotate the exemplar by 90, 180, and 270 degrees to obtain additional available patches, addressing selection limitations. b. Two-Phase Patch Selection: i. Phase 1 (Geometry): From the ks candidates, find kg candidate patches with geometric continuity based on the density field V^{(d)}. ii. Phase 2 (Color): From the kg candidates, select one patch for color continuity in the overlap area based on the color feature field V^{(f)}. c. Stitch the selected patch’s density field and radiance field onto the target area. d. Repeat until the target scene is fully synthesized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def shadingguidednerfsynthesis(exemplarshadingimages, exemplardensity, targetdensity, lightsources, M, ks, kg, np, ns, nc): # 1. Extract Exemplar Shading Map # Intrinsic decomposition to derive shading and albedo from images smoothedshading = [smoothshading(img) for img in exemplarshadingimages] # Initialize Shading Map volume (X, Y, Z, M) with NaN shadingmap = np.full((X, Y, Z, M), np.nan) for m in range(M): camera = getcameraparams(m) shadingimg = smoothedshading[m] for y in range(shadingimg.shape[0]): for x in range(shadingimg.shape[1]): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.unproject(x, y) # Ray march through exemplar density to get samples samples = raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, exemplardensity) # Depth formula: d = sumk Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltai)) ti d = sum(s.transmittance (1 - np.exp(-s.sigma s.delta)) s.t for s in samples) voxelcoords = rayorigin + d raydirection if isinsidegrid(voxelcoords): shadingmap[voxelcoords] = shadingimg[y, x] # Post-processing for m in range(M): channel = shadingmap[:,:,:, m] # KNN interpolation with inverse distance weighting for holes channel = knninterpolate(channel, weights='inversedistance') # Median filtering for noisy points channel = medianfilter(channel, size=3) shadingmap[:,:,:, m] = channel # Retain nc channels with lowest missing rate missingrates = np.mean(np.isnan(shadingmap), axis=(0,1,2)) bestchannels = np.argsort(missingrates)[:nc] exemplarshadingmap = shadingmap[:,:,:, bestchannels] # 2. Generate Shading Map Guider # Geometry-based synthesis to create base target scene basescenedensity = geometrybasedsynthesis(targetdensity) # Select np points with high density highdensitypoints = selecthighdensitypoints(basescenedensity, np) shadingmapguider = np.zeros((X, Y, Z, M)) for point in highdensitypoints: x = point for m in range(M): lightsource = getlightsource(m) I = lightsource.intensity xl = lightsource.position # Sample ns points along path pathpoints = samplepath(xl, x, ns) xns = pathpoints[-1] sigmans = getdensity(basescenedensity, xns) deltans = distance(xl, xns) / ns Tns = calculatetransmittance(xl, xns, basescenedensity) pns = Tns (1 - np.exp(-sigmans deltans)) distsq = np.linalg.norm(x - xl)2 brightness = pns (1/ns) (I / distsq) voxelcoords = getvoxelcoords(x) shadingmapguider[voxelcoords, m] = brightness # 3. Synthesize Scene synthesizeddensity = np.zeros(targetdensity.shape) synthesizedcolor = np.zeros(targetdensity.shape) for patch in targetgeometry.patches: # Normalize scales exemplarpatches = normalize(exemplarpatches) targetshadingvec = normalize(targetshadingvec) # Find ks closest patches using L2 distance (accelerated by kd-tree) distances, indices = kdtree.query(targetshadingvec, k=ks) candidatepatches = exemplarpatches[indices] # Two-phase selection # Phase 1: Geometric continuity based on density field geometriccandidates = filterbydensitycontinuity(candidatepatches, targetareapatch, kg) # Phase 2: Color continuity based on color feature field bestpatchidx = selectbycolorcontinuity(geometriccandidates, targetareapatch) # Stitch patch patchdensity = extractpatchdensity(exemplardensity, bestpatchidx) patchcolor = extractpatchcolor(exemplarcolor, bestpatchidx) stitch(synthesizeddensity, synthesizedcolor, patch, patchdensity, patchcolor) return synthesizeddensity, synthesizedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Shading Map: Occlusions and limited pixels cause missing values in shading vector channels. Addressed by KNN interpolation with inverse distance weighting. Noisy Points: Inaccurate depth values introduce noise. Addressed by median filtering. Channel Selection: Channels with high missing value rates have high interpolation error. Only retain nc channels with the lowest missing rate. Selection Limitations: Strict shading/geometry/texture requirements may limit patch selection. Addressed by rotating the exemplar by 90, 180, and 270 degrees to increase available patches. Scale Mismatch: Exemplar and target shading maps may have different scales. Must be normalized to the same scale before distance calculation. NeRF Synthesis via DVGO is a method for generating large-scale radiance fields by applying 2D texture synthesis algorithms to the flattened density and feature grids of a Differentiable Voxel Grid Object (DVGO) representation. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing repetitive 3D structures (e.g., vegetation) by exploiting the observation that only two spatial dimensions typically exhibit clear repeatability, thereby avoiding the inefficiency of full 3D synthesis. It sets itself apart from direct 3D synthesis by flattening the 3D grid along the Z-axis into 2D grids, allowing the use of established 2D texture synthesis techniques while treating each unit as storing density and feature values rather than RGB pixels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for the exemplar density/color fields, the exemplar shading map, and the target shading map guider. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Controls lighting effects using shading guidance without decoupling geometry, material, and lighting. Ensures continuous lighting in synthesized scenes under complex lighting. Can synthesize new scenes on curved surfaces with arbitrary lighting effects. Uses a two-phase method to ensure both geometric and appearance continuity. Limitations: Requires intrinsic decomposition (PIE-Net) and ray tracing for preprocessing. Sensitive to occlusions and limited pixels, requiring post-processing. Relies on the availability of multiple images of the exemplar for intrinsic decomposition. When to use: When synthesizing large-scale scenes with repetitive structures and complex lighting, where maintaining consistent lighting is critical. Origin: The method was proposed in "NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance". History: The paper addresses the limitations of physically-based rendering (PBR) in virtual reality, augmented reality, and video games, and the challenges of attaching realistic surface structures onto mesh surfaces. It builds on the concept of 3D texture synthesis and NeRF representations. Usage: Demonstrated for generating high-quality results with consistent geometry and appearance for scenes with complex lighting, including synthesis on curved surfaces. name: NeRF Synthesis via DVGO
head: 2D texture synthesis for 3D NeRF
body: NeRF Synthesis via DVGO is a method for generating large-scale radiance fields by applying 2D texture synthesis algorithms to the flattened density and feature grids of a Differentiable Voxel Grid Object (DVGO) representation. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing repetitive 3D structures (e.g., vegetation) by exploiting the observation that only two spatial dimensions typically exhibit clear repeatability, thereby avoiding the inefficiency of full 3D synthesis. It sets itself apart from direct 3D synthesis by flattening the 3D grid along the Z-axis into 2D grids, allowing the use of established 2D texture synthesis techniques while treating each unit as storing density and feature values rather than RGB pixels. Inputs: Source DVGO: Density grid V^{(d)} and feature grid V^{(f)}. Target dimensions: Width W{target}, Height H{target}. Synthesis parameters: Patch size S \times S, number of nearest neighbors kg, blending radius. Outputs: Synthesized Density grid I^{(d)} of size W{target} \times H{target}. Synthesized Feature grid I^{(f)} of size W{target} \times H{target}. Data Structures: The 3D grids are flattened into 2D grids along the Z-axis. For a voxel at (x, y, z), the corresponding 2D coordinate (x', y') is calculated as: x' = x y' = y \cdot D + z The resulting 2D grid I^{(d)} has dimensions W \times (H \cdot D). Each "pixel" in this 2D grid stores a scalar density value d and a feature vector \mathbf{f} instead of RGB. Algorithm (Two-Phase Method): The method prioritizes geometric continuity over appearance because the synthesis operates at the voxel column level, where color features inherently incorporate geometric information; ensuring geometric continuity first prevents density from affecting subsequent appearance considerations. 1. Flattening: Convert V^{(d)} and V^{(f)} into 2D grids I^{(d)} and I^{(f)} by flattening along the Z-axis. 2. Initialization: Initialize the target grids I^{(d)}{target} and I^{(f)}{target} with zeros. 3. Synthesis Loop: Iterate through each voxel patch Pn in the target grid in raster order. Phase 1 (Geometry Selection): Extract the boundary of the current density patch Pn^{(d)}, denoted \partial(Pn^{(d)}). Search the source grid I^{(d)} for candidate patches Ei^{(d)}. Calculate the similarity between the boundary of the target patch and the boundary of each candidate using a distance metric d(\cdot, \cdot) (L2 distance on flattened boundary vectors). Select the kg best matching density patches En^{(d)} = \{E1^{(d)}, \dots, E{kg}^{(d)}\} based on minimum distance. Phase 2 (Appearance Selection): For each of the kg selected density patches, retrieve the corresponding feature patch Ei^{(f)} from the source feature grid I^{(f)}. Calculate the similarity between the boundary of the target feature patch Pn^{(f)} and the boundary of each candidate feature patch \partial(Ei^{(f)}) using d(\partial(Pn^{(f)}), \partial(Ei^{(f)})). Convert these similarities into likelihoods for random selection. Randomly select one final patch En^ from the kg candidates based on these likelihoods. Blending: Copy the non-overlapping parts of En^ into Pn. For overlapping regions between En^ and the existing content in Pn, blend the values using inverse distance weighting. 4. Unflattening (Optional): If the final output requires a 3D grid, reshape I^{(d)}{target} and I^{(f)}{target} back to W \times H \times D{target} by reversing the flattening mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def synthesizedvgo(sourcedensity3d, sourcefeature3d, targetw, targeth, targetd, patchsize, kg): # Flatten 3D to 2D along Z-axis: (W, H, D) -> (W, HD) sourcedensity2d = flattenz(sourcedensity3d) sourcefeature2d = flattenz(sourcefeature3d) targetw2d = targetw targeth2d = targeth targetd targetdensity2d = zeros((targetw2d, targeth2d)) targetfeature2d = zeros((targetw2d, targeth2d)) # Iterate over target patches in raster order for y in range(0, targeth2d, patchsize): for x in range(0, targetw2d, patchsize): # Define current patch coordinates patchcoords = (x, y, patchsize, patchsize) # Phase 1: Geometry # Extract boundary of current target density patch currentboundaryd = getboundary(targetdensity2d, patchcoords) # Find kg best matches in source candidatesd = findknearestneighbors( sourcedensity2d, currentboundaryd, kg, patchsize) # Phase 2: Appearance # Calculate feature similarity for candidates currentboundaryf = getboundary(targetfeature2d, patchcoords) similarities = [] for candd in candidatesd: # Get corresponding feature patch from source candf = getfeaturepatch(sourcefeature2d, candd.coords, patchsize) candboundaryf = getboundary(candf, candd.coords) dist = l2distance(currentboundaryf, candboundaryf) similarities.append((dist, candd)) # Sort by distance (lower is better) similarities.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Convert distances to likelihoods (inverse distance weighting) likelihoods = [1.0 / (dist + 1e-6) for dist, in similarities] total = sum(likelihoods) likelihoods = [l / total for l in likelihoods] # Random selection based on likelihoods idx = weightedrandomchoice(len(similarities), likelihoods) selectedcandidate = similarities[idx][1] # Blend selected patch into target blendpatch(targetdensity2d, targetfeature2d, selectedcandidate, patchcoords) # Unflatten back to 3D targetdensity3d = unflattenz(targetdensity2d, targetw, targeth, targetd) targetfeature3d = unflattenz(targetfeature2d, targetw, targeth, targetd) return targetdensity3d, targetfeature3d def zeros(shape): return [[0.0] shape[1] for in range(shape[0])] def flattenz(grid3d): W, H, D = len(grid3d), len(grid3d[0]), len(grid3d[0][0]) grid2d = zeros((W, H D)) for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): idx = y D + z grid2d[x][idx] = grid3d[x][y][z] return grid2d def unflattenz(grid2d, W, H, D): grid3d = zeros((W, H, D)) for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): idx = y D + z grid3d[x][y][z] = grid2d[x][idx] return grid3d def getboundary(grid2d, coords): x, y, w, h = coords boundary = [] # Top and bottom rows for i in range(w): boundary.append(grid2d[x + i][y]) boundary.append(grid2d[x + i][y + h - 1]) # Left and right columns (excluding corners) for i in range(1, h - 1): boundary.append(grid2d[x][y + i]) boundary.append(grid2d[x + w - 1][y + i]) return boundary def l2distance(a, b): return math.sqrt(sum((ai - bi) 2 for ai, bi in zip(a, b))) def findknearestneighbors(sourcegrid, targetboundary, k, patchsize): candidates = [] W, H = len(sourcegrid), len(sourcegrid[0]) for y in range(0, H - patchsize + 1, patchsize): for x in range(0, W - patchsize + 1, patchsize): candboundary = getboundary(sourcegrid, (x, y, patchsize, patchsize)) dist = l2distance(targetboundary, candboundary) candidates.append((dist, (x, y))) candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [{"dist": d, "coords": c} for d, c in candidates[:k]] def getfeaturepatch(featuregrid, coords, patchsize): x, y = coords return [row[y:y+patchsize] for row in featuregrid[x:x+patchsize]] def weightedrandomchoice(n, weights): r = random.random() sum(weights) cumulative = 0.0 for i, w in enumerate(weights): cumulative += w if r <= cumulative: return i return n - 1 def blendpatch(targetd, targetf, sourcepatch, coords): x, y, w, h = coords for i in range(w): for j in range(h): tx, ty = x + i, y + j # Inverse distance weighting for overlaps dist = math.sqrt(ii + jj) + 1e-6 weight = 1.0 / dist targetd[tx][ty] = (targetd[tx][ty] + sourcepatch[i][j] weight) / (1.0 + weight) targetf[tx][ty] = (targetf[tx][ty] + sourcepatch[i][j] weight) / (1.0 + weight) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: The method struggles with boundary synthesis because occluded interior parts are synthesized onto the boundary, lacking pixel value supervision during DVGO training, leading to artifacts. Dimensionality: High dimensionality of the combined grid increases search time. Weighting: In the baseline combined method, high weight for density causes color inconsistencies, while high weight for color causes geometric inconsistencies. A baseline method that concatenates density and feature grids V^{(d)} and V^{(f)} into a combined 2D image I^{(d \oplus f)} and measures distance via L2. It suffers from weighting challenges between geometry and appearance. It prioritizes density over color because the synthesis operates at the voxel column level where color features inherently incorporate geometric information; ensuring geometric continuity first prevents density from affecting subsequent appearance considerations. The process involves Phase 1 (Geometry): selecting kg best density voxel patches En^{(d)} based on similarity of d(\partial(Pn^{(d)}), \partial(En^{(d)})); and Phase 2 (Appearance): calculating similarity d(\partial(Pn^{(f)}), \partial(En^{(f)})) for the selected patches, using these as likelihoods for random selection, and blending overlapping regions using inverse distance weighting. Pitfalls include high weight for density causing color inconsistencies, high weight for color causing geometric inconsistencies, and high dimensionality of I^{(d \oplus f)} increasing search time. Time Complexity: The search for nearest neighbors in the source grid dominates the complexity. With high dimensionality of the feature space, search time increases significantly. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the flattened 2D grids I^{(d)} and I^{(f)}, which have size W \times (H \cdot D). Strengths: Efficiently synthesizes repetitive 3D structures by leveraging 2D texture synthesis methods; avoids the inefficiency of full 3D synthesis. Limitations: Boundary artifacts due to lack of supervision for occluded parts; sensitivity to weighting in combined methods; high search time for high-dimensional features. When to use: Suitable for scenes with clear 2D repeatability (e.g., grass, trees) where 3D synthesis is inefficient. When not to use: Scenes with complex 3D structures lacking 2D repeatability or requiring precise boundary continuity without artifacts. The method originates from the paper "NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance". It builds on the DVGO representation, which uses a hybrid implicit-explicit structure. The approach was developed to address the inefficiency of 3D synthesis for objects like grass, where only two dimensions exhibit clear repeatability. name: Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering
body: Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering treats computed tomography (CT) not as a linear algebra problem to be solved via closed-form filters or static iterative solvers, but as an optimization problem where a differentiable forward renderer (the projector) is minimized against measured projection data. This approach unifies classical algebraic reconstruction techniques (ART, SIRT) with modern neural representations and compressive sensing priors under a single gradient-based framework. It distinguishes itself from Differentiable volume rendering by focusing specifically on the tomographic geometry (parallel/fan/cone beam) and the reconstruction of density/absorption fields from sparse or noisy sinograms, and from Radiance-field optimization by explicitly modeling the X-ray physics (Beer-Lambert law) rather than just RGB appearance. All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward projection operator \mathcal{P} and its adjoint (back-projection) \mathcal{P}^T. The core optimization problem is generally formulated as minimizing a loss function \mathcal{L} between the measured sinogram p and the rendered projection \hat{p} = \mathcal{P}(x) of the current volume estimate x: \minx \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}(x), p) + \lambda R(x) where R(x) is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and \lambda is a weighting factor. The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume x is computed via the chain rule: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = \mathcal{P}^T \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} \right) The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{p}} is the residual gradient in projection space (e.g., p - \hat{p} for MSE), and \mathcal{P}^T is the back-projection operator. Key shared components include: 1. Forward Projection: Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients. 2. Backward Projection (Adjoint): Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume. This is mathematically the transpose of the forward operator, ensuring stable convergence in iterative methods. 3. Optimization Loop: An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error. An adaptive, hierarchical neural rendering pipeline for multi-view inverse rendering, designed specifically for the tomographic reconstruction of semi-transparent volumetric scenes from X-ray images. It combines an adaptive explicit octree representation with neural features stored in leaf nodes to achieve efficient reconstruction and simultaneous self-calibration of geometric and photometric parameters. Unlike purely implicit neural representations, NeAT uses a hybrid explicit-implicit structure optimized via differentiable volume rendering, which outperforms alternatives in both quality and compute time for tomographic tasks where samples are widely scattered. A set of techniques designed to reconstruct high-quality volume renderings from a sparse subset of pixels, treating the problem as an image restoration or inpainting task. Unlike standard iterative reconstruction methods that solve for voxel values directly via linear systems, these methods exploit prior knowledge about the signal's structure—specifically sparsity in transform domains (wavelet, gradient) or smoothness (Total Variation)—to recover the image from undersampled measurements. A compressive sensing technique that renders discrete gradient components instead of pixel values to exploit sparsity in the gradient domain, then reconstructs the image using a Poisson solver. It differs from standard volume rendering by optimizing for gradient coefficients in the frequency domain rather than direct pixel intensities, allowing for reconstruction from fewer samples than the Nyquist rate. The mathematical adjoint (transpose) of the forward projection operator, used to accumulate 2D projection data into a 3D reconstruction volume. It solves the problem of mapping measured projection weights to volume expansion coefficients, serving as the core gradient computation step in differentiable tomographic reconstruction. Unlike direct methods like FDK which may suffer from artifacts with limited projections, back-projection provides the exact transpose required for stable iterative optimization over many iterations. A PyTorch-based framework for differentiable computed tomography projection and reconstruction. It implements a cell-constant attenuation field integrator along rays defined by per-view acquisition geometry, where the backprojector is the matched discrete adjoint of the forward projector. It distinguishes itself from analytical methods (like FBP/FDK) by supporting arbitrary trajectories, trainable geometry, and native first-order derivatives for iterative optimization, while avoiding the separable-footprint approximations of earlier releases. An iterative algebraic reconstruction technique that solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by minimizing the discrepancy between measured projections and forward-projected volume estimates. It distinguishes itself from simultaneous methods like SART by applying global normalization to both the ray residuals and the backprojected updates, ensuring stable convergence through nonnegativity constraints. It serves as a baseline differentiable reconstruction method within the Tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering framework. This framework formulates tomographic reconstruction as a regularized inverse problem, minimizing a data fidelity term against a regularizer to recover volumetric data from projections. It distinguishes itself from direct algebraic methods (like SIRT) by decoupling the data consistency and regularization steps via proximal splitting, allowing for complex, non-linear priors and flexible integration of physical constraints. It serves as the foundational solver for advanced applications including sparse-view reconstruction, 3D super-resolution, and dynamic fluid capture. A CPU-optimized implementation of the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, an analytical method for reconstructing a 3D volume from a stack of 2D cone-beam projection images. It solves the tomographic reconstruction problem by applying a specific convolution filter to weighted projections and back-projecting them into a 3D grid. It sets itself apart from its siblings by precomputing geometric weights and using a direct spatial-domain convolution filter to avoid the overhead of FFTs during the main reconstruction loop, prioritizing speed and memory locality on CPU architectures. Solves the coupled inverse problem of near-field holotomography by combining holographic phase retrieval with tomographic reconstruction using Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Unlike standard tomography that assumes far-field (Fraunhofer) propagation, HoloINR explicitly models near-field physics via Fresnel propagation between the object and the detector. It differs from sibling methods like NeAT or DuDoTrans by replacing discrete voxel grids with a continuous neural field, allowing for resolution-independent reconstruction and natural integration of wave-optics effects. A differentiable renderer designed for multi-line neural tomography, specifically recovering 3-D coronal electron density (ne) and temperature (Te) from multiview, multiline spectral-intensity images. It performs ray marching and Line-of-Sight (LOS) integration of emissivity coefficients derived from neural network models. It is distinguished from general volume renderers by its explicit physics-based emissivity computation using a Look-Up Table (LUT) for ion-specific spectral lines and its integration with occupancy grids for sparse volume representation. A tomographic reconstruction method that adapts 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to sparse-view X-ray imaging by rectifying an integration bias inherent in standard 3DGS splatting. It replaces the appearance-based 3DGS kernel with a radiative Gaussian kernel parameterized by density, position, and covariance, and derives new X-ray rendering functions to ensure accurate volume retrieval. Unlike siblings that use 3DGS only for data augmentation or replace rasterization with simulators, R2-Gaussian maintains efficient differentiable rasterization while enabling direct 3D density volume extraction. An inverse rendering technique that reconstructs the volumetric absorption coefficients of an object from a series of 2D X-ray projection images by optimizing scene parameters via gradient descent. It formulates Computed Tomography (CT) as an iterative optimization problem where the 3D volume is treated as a differentiable parameter space, allowing the use of auto-differentiable rendering engines to compute gradients of a projection loss. Unlike traditional algebraic or analytical methods, this approach relies on end-to-end differentiability of the forward projection, enabling the use of modern optimizers like ADAM without explicit derivation of the back-projection operator. It is distinct from neural implicit methods (e.g., HoloINR) by typically operating on explicit voxel grids rather than continuous neural fields, and from deep learning approaches by requiring no pre-trained models. An iterative algebraic method that minimizes the quadratic norm of the difference between acquired projections and projected reconstructed volume, avoiding explicit matrix storage. A staggered two-step iterative process that alternates between reconstructing a volume from a frozen displacement field and identifying the motion from a frozen estimate of the microstructure to handle deforming volumes in tomography. A volumetric display where multiple emitters surround the display area and project rays with programmed intensity for each direction; the intersection of rays in a scattering medium produces the graphics. An iterative reconstruction method that solves the inverse problem g = Af + n by combining a gradient descent step on the data fidelity term with a sparsity-promoting wavelet thresholding step. It is used to reconstruct images from noisy sinograms, particularly in sparse or limited angle scenarios. This family encompasses methods that replace or augment traditional algebraic regularizers with neural networks to solve the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from classical iterative methods (like SIRT or ART) by leveraging the expressive power of deep learning to enforce priors, either implicitly through network architecture (Deep Image Prior) or explicitly through learned features (Transformers), often enabling reconstruction from sparse or noisy data where traditional methods fail. Physics-Based Image Formation Models define the differentiable forward operator \mathcal{P} that maps a 3D (or 4D) volume representation to 2D projection images, serving as the core component in inverse rendering pipelines. Unlike generic differentiable renderers, these models are tailored to specific physical acquisition modalities (e.g., X-ray absorption, ultrasound wave propagation) to ensure physical consistency and computational efficiency. They distinguish themselves from siblings like Neural Adaptive Tomography by explicitly modeling the underlying physics (such as linear absorption or coupled wave equations) rather than relying solely on learned neural priors or adaptive sampling strategies. A physics-based tomographic reconstruction method employing Laplacian regularization for sparse view reconstruction, representing the state-of-the-art in physics-based smoke reconstruction. Multi-view variant uses 16 views; single-view variant uses only one input view. A CPU-based implementation of CT reconstruction used as a ground truth reference for validating GPU implementations. Input includes projections (std::vector<float>), P (number of projections), W (width), H (height), NX (volume width), NY (volume height/depth), voxelSize (float), pixelSize (float), sdd (source-to-detector distance), sod (source-to-origin distance). Output is std::vector<float> representing the reconstructed volume. A method to reconstruct an image from its tomographic scans (projections), producing a result that may be blurry-filtered compared to the original. Call reconstruct with scan data, width, and height to produce the destination image. For overscanned reconstruction, call reconstructoverscan with additional xover and yover parameters, then trim the result to the original dimensions. RMS error between source and reconstructed image is between 59.0 and 61.0 for a 35x40 ray/angle configuration, attributed to the blurry-filtered nature of the reconstruction. Reconstruction produces a blurry-filtered version of the original, resulting in higher RMS error compared to a perfect reconstruction, but better than a blank image baseline. Tomographic reconstruction has traditionally been dominated by analytical methods like Filtered Back Projection (FBP) and algebraic methods like ART and SIRT. The advent of differentiable rendering has allowed these problems to be framed as optimization problems, enabling the use of gradient-based optimizers and complex neural priors. The field continues to evolve with hybrid methods combining explicit structures (octrees, Gaussians) with neural features for efficient and high-quality reconstruction. name: Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods
head: Compressed Sensing Wavelet, Total Variation (TV) Minimization, Least-Squares (SS), CS-Wavelet, CS-Gradient
body: Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods are a family of image restoration techniques that reconstruct full-resolution volume-rendered images from a sparse subset of rendered pixels. They solve the problem of high rendering costs by leveraging the inherent smoothness or sparsity of volume-rendered images to recover missing pixel values via optimization. Unlike standard compressive sensing methods that rely on sparsity in transform domains (which can be incoherent with point sampling), smoothness-based methods like Total Variation (TV) minimization and Least-Squares (SS) are more resilient to missing information and generally outperform compressed sensing variants. The recovery process treats the volume rendering output as an image inpainting problem. Given a set of measured pixels y at specific locations defined by a sampling matrix S, the goal is to recover the full image vector x. Input: A vector y containing the rendered pixel values at sampled locations. The sampling pattern is defined by the matrix S (e.g., random, low-discrepancy, or partial Fourier). Output: The recovered full-resolution image vector x. Image Vector x: A column vector of size N \times 1, where N is the total number of pixels in the target resolution (e.g., 1200 \times 1200 = 1,440,000). Sampling Matrix S: An M \times N binary matrix (M < N) where M is the number of sampled pixels. S{ij} = 1 if pixel j is sampled, 0 otherwise. Transform Matrices: \Psi: Orthonormal transform matrix (e.g., DWT or DCT). \Phi: Gaussian blurring matrix (used in CS-Wavelet). W: DWT matrix (used in CS-Wavelet formulation in). The general measurement equation for compressed sensing approaches is: y = A \hat{x} where A is the sensing matrix and \hat{x} is the sparse coefficient vector. 1. CS-Wavelet: Assumes the image x is sparse in the wavelet domain. To ensure incoherence between the sampling basis (point sampling) and the wavelet basis, a blurred version xb is recovered. y = S \Phi^{-1} W^{-1} \hat{x}b where \hat{x}b is the DWT of the blurred image xb = \Phi x. The final image is reconstructed as: x = W \hat{x}b Note: Some sources define the transform as \Psi and the equation as y = S \Psi^{-1} \hat{x}. The blurring step is critical for CS-Wavelet to satisfy the Restricted Isometry Condition (RIC). 2. CS-Gradient: Assumes the image gradient is sparse in the Fourier domain. 3. TV Minimization: Minimizes the total variation seminorm, defined as: \|x\|{TV}:= \sum{i,j} |x{i+1,j} - x{i,j}| + |x{i,j+1} - x{i,j}| where x{i,j} is the pixel value at coordinates (i, j). The optimization problem is: \minx \|x\|{TV} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|Sx - y\|2 \leq \epsilon 4. Least-Squares (SS): Minimizes a smoothness norm based on second derivatives (variational minimization in a spline space). It solves a least-squares minimization problem with a regularization parameter \lambda. 1. Sampling: Render only a fraction of pixels (e.g., 20-50%) using a distribution algorithm (Random or Low-Discrepancy/LD). 2. Preprocessing (CS-Wavelet only): If using CS-Wavelet, apply Gaussian blurring to the target image domain to create xb. Set the standard deviation \sigma of the filter. 3. Optimization: Solve for the coefficients \hat{x} (or x directly for TV/SS) using an iterative solver: For CS-Wavelet, CS-Gradient, and TV: Use the NESTA solver for l1 minimization. For SS: Use a conjugate gradient solver for least-squares minimization. 4. Reconstruction: For CS-Wavelet: Apply the inverse DWT (W) to the recovered coefficients \hat{x}b to get x. For TV/SS/CS-Gradient: The output of the solver is the image x directly. Blurring Filter Standard Deviation (\sigma): 20 for CS-Wavelet. This value balances the trade-off between incoherence and blurring effects. NESTA Tolerance/Stopping Criteria: 10^{-2} (noted as 102 in some texts, likely a typo for 10^{-2} or 1e-2). SS Regularization Parameter (\lambda): 10^{-2} (noted as 102 in some texts). Resolution: Experiments typically use 1200 \times 1200 output images from datasets with resolution \approx 256 \times 256 \times 256. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressivevolumerenderingrecovery(measuredpixelsy, samplingmatrixS, method, resolution=(1200, 1200)): """ Reconstructs a full image from sparse pixel measurements. """ N = resolution[0] resolution[1] if method == 'CS-Wavelet': # 1. Define sensing matrix A = S Phi^-1 W^-1 # 2. Solve l1-minimization for xhatb using NESTA solver # Tolerance = 1e-2, Blurring sigma = 20 # (Source does not specify NESTA internals; standard first-order sparse recovery method [BBC11]) xhatb = None # Solve l1 minimization # 3. Reconstruct image using inverse DWT recoveredimage = None # Apply inverse DWT to xhatb elif method == 'CS-Gradient': # 1. Solve l1-minimization for gradient coefficients using NESTA solver # Tolerance = 1e-2 gradcoeffs = None # Solve l1 minimization # 2. Reconstruct image from gradient coefficients using Poisson solver # (Source does not specify Poisson solver internals) recoveredimage = None # Solve Poisson equation for gradient elif method == 'TV': # 1. Solve TV minimization: min ||x||TV s.t. ||Sx - y||2 <= epsilon using NESTA solver # Tolerance = 1e-2 # (Source does not specify TV solver internals) recoveredimage = None # Solve TV minimization elif method == 'SS': # 1. Solve Least-Squares minimization with smoothness prior using Conjugate Gradient solver # Regularization parameter lambda = 1e-2 # (Source does not specify SS solver internals) recoveredimage = None # Solve least-squares minimization else: raise ValueError("Unknown method") return recoveredimage High Missing Pixel Rates: CS-Wavelet and CS-Gradient deteriorate quickly when the fraction of missing pixels is high. CS-Wavelet is particularly sensitive to pixel distribution; random distribution leads to strong speckling artifacts. Non-Smooth Images: TV and SS methods fail on images with high and low frequencies alike (e.g., synthetic textures). They cannot produce acceptable recovery even with 10% missing pixels if the image lacks smoothness. Blurring Sensitivity: CS-Wavelet requires careful tuning of the Gaussian blurring filter variance (\sigma), which must be adjusted case-by-case. Directional Artifacts: Low-Discrepancy (LD) distribution in CS-Wavelet can exhibit directional artifacts. Renders discrete gradient components instead of pixel values to exploit sparsity in the Fourier domain, then reconstructs the image using a Poisson solver. It differs from standard volume rendering by optimizing for gradient coefficients in the frequency domain rather than direct pixel intensities, allowing for reconstruction from fewer samples than the Nyquist rate. Treats the entire image as a single unit for inverse rendering recovery, solving for missing pixel values by running a solver over the full image domain simultaneously. It addresses the problem of recovering high-quality volumes from images with high missing pixel rates. Renders a full-resolution image by tracing rays for only a sparse subset of pixels and reconstructing the remaining pixels using an image representation model. It extends the two-step compressive rendering proposal by Sen and Darabi by replacing compressed sensing with a smoothness-based recovery approach. A regularized inverse problem solver for CT reconstruction that addresses sparse sampling and noise. It alternates between gradient descent on the data fidelity term and sparsity-promoting soft-thresholding in the Haar wavelet domain. It is a specific instance of ISTA adapted for tomographic geometry. Time Complexity: Depends on the solver. CS-Wavelet is the slowest because it requires evaluating forward and inverse DWT at every iteration. TV and CS-Gradient have comparable performance trends. SS is the fastest due to the efficiency of the least-squares solver. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the full image vector x (N pixels) and the sampling matrix S (M \times N). For 1200 \times 1200, N \approx 1.44 \times 10^6. Measured Performance: Head Dataset (600x600): 1754.92s recovery time. Head Dataset (900x900): 3955.13s. Head Dataset (1200x1200): 7067.32s. Engine Dataset (600x600): 1093.61s. Engine Dataset (900x900): 2442.28s. Engine Dataset (1200x1200): 4249.44s. GPU TV-L1: 30 FPS for 320x240 resolution using iterative conjugate gradient solver. Strengths: Smoothness-based methods (TV, SS) are more resilient to missing information than CS-based methods and produce high-quality recovery with as little as 20% of pixels. SS is sharper in boundary regions; TV preserves edges better. Limitations: Performance degrades with high missing pixel rates for CS methods. All methods struggle with non-smooth images. CS-Wavelet is sensitive to pixel distribution and blurring parameters. When to Use: Use TV or SS for general volume rendering where smoothness is expected and high missing pixel rates are acceptable. Use CS-Wavelet/Gradient only if strict sparsity priors are justified and pixel distribution can be controlled (LD preferred for CS-Wavelet, Random for CS-Gradient). Compressive Volume Rendering was initially proposed by Sen and Darabi [SD11] for compressive rendering, leveraging the theory of compressed sensing. The specific methods discussed (CS-Wavelet, CS-Gradient, TV, SS) were further explored and compared by Liu and Alim. The NESTA solver used for l1 minimization was introduced by Becker, Bobin, and Candès [BBC11]. The concept of using pixel shuffling based on Fibonacci numbers for distribution was introduced by Anderson [And93]. Least-squares linear systems have a long history of GPU acceleration [PF05].
