name: Compressive Gradient Rendering
head: CS-Gradient, Compressed Sensing Gradient, Gradient Recovery via CS, Gradient-based Compressive Rendering
body: Compressive Gradient Rendering is a compressive volume rendering method that recovers high-quality images from sparse pixel samples by exploiting the sparsity of image gradients in the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) domain. Unlike sibling methods such as CS-Wavelet which suffer from coherence issues with random sampling, this approach renders discrete gradient components (x1, x2) instead of pixel values, solves an l1-minimization problem to recover the gradient's DFT, and reconstructs the image using a Poisson solver. It is distinguished by its use of the Fourier basis, which is inherently incoherent with point sampling, allowing for robust recovery when the fraction of missing pixels is moderate, though performance deteriorates significantly when missing pixels are high. Inputs: A set of m sampled pixel locations \Omega in an image of size N \times N (where m \ll N^2). The measured horizontal gradient values \mathbf{y}1 at these locations. The measured vertical gradient values \mathbf{y}2 at these locations. A reconstruction kernel basis (e.g., bilinear B-spline or Mitchell-Netravali cubic). Outputs: The reconstructed image \mathbf{x} of size N \times N. Data Structures: \mathbf{S}: The sensing matrix of size m \times N^2. It selects the m sampled locations. \mathbf{F}^{-1}: The inverse 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) matrix of size N^2 \times N^2. \hat{\mathbf{x}}1, \hat{\mathbf{x}}2: The 2D DFT coefficients of the horizontal and vertical gradient components, respectively. \mathbf{y}1, \mathbf{y}2: Measured gradient vectors of size m \times 1. Parameters: \epsilon: Tolerance for the l1-minimization solver. A typical value is 10^{-2}, providing a tradeoff between recovery quality and runtime. Kernel type: Bilinear B-spline or Mitchell-Netravali cubic. Steps: 1. Gradient Rendering: Render the horizontal gradient component x1 and vertical gradient component x2 from the volume data. This is achieved by differentiating the pixel reconstruction kernel used during ray casting. Alternatively, render the image using a box filter and apply a finite differencing scheme to obtain the gradients. 2. Sampling Gradients: Measure the horizontal gradient values at the m sampled locations \Omega to form the vector \mathbf{y}1. Similarly, measure the vertical gradient values to form \mathbf{y}2. 3. Formulate Sensing Model: The relationship between the measured gradients and the DFT of the gradients is given by \mathbf{y}1 = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}1 and \mathbf{y}2 = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}2. Here \mathbf{S} is the sampling matrix, \mathbf{F}^{-1} is the inverse 2D DFT matrix, and \hat{\mathbf{x}}1, \hat{\mathbf{x}}2 are the DFTs of the horizontal and vertical gradients. The matrix \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1} is a partial Fourier matrix with the Restricted Isometry Property (RIC) and low coherence with point sampling. 4. Recover Horizontal Gradient DFT (\hat{\mathbf{x}}1): Solve the l1-minimization problem to find the sparsest approximation of the horizontal gradient's DFT: \min \|\hat{\mathbf{x}}1\|1 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|\mathbf{S}\mathbf{F}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{x}}1 - \mathbf{y}1\|2 \leq \epsilon. This problem is typically solved using an iterative solver such as NESTA. 5. Recover Vertical Gradient DFT (\hat{\mathbf{x}}2): Solve the analogous l1-minimization problem for the vertical gradient. 6. Reconstruct Image via Poisson Solver: Recover the pixel values \mathbf{x} from the gradient components \hat{\mathbf{x}}1 and \hat{\mathbf{x}}2. Compute the inverse DFT of \hat{\mathbf{x}}1 and \hat{\mathbf{x}}2 to obtain the spatial gradient fields. Apply a Poisson solver with Dirichlet boundary conditions to the divergence of the gradient field to solve for \mathbf{x}. The approach follows Pérez et al. [PGB03]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.fft import fft2, ifft2 from scipy.sparse import diags, kron, eye from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve def compressivegradientrendering(sampledindices, N, y1, y2, epsilon=1e-2): """ Reconstructs an image from sampled gradient measurements using Compressive Gradient Rendering. Args: sampledindices: Array of shape (m, 2) containing (row, col) indices of sampled pixels. N: Image resolution (N x N). y1: Horizontal gradient values at sampled locations (shape (m,)). y2: Vertical gradient values at sampled locations (shape (m,)). epsilon: Tolerance for l1 minimization. Returns: x: Reconstructed image of shape (N, N). """ m = len(sampledindices) # Gradient rendering is performed by differentiating the reconstruction kernel # or using a box filter with finite differencing. # y1 and y2 are assumed to be pre-computed from the volume data. # 1. Construct sensing matrix S (m x N^2) flatindices = sampledindices[:, 0] N + sampledindices[:, 1] S = np.zeros((m, N N)) for i in range(m): S[i, flatindices[i]] = 1.0 # 2. Solve l1 minimization for horizontal gradient DFT xhat1 = solvel1(S, N, y1, epsilon) # 3. Solve l1 minimization for vertical gradient DFT xhat2 = solvel1(S, N, y2, epsilon) # 4. Reconstruct image from gradients via Poisson solver gradx = np.real(ifft2(xhat1.reshape(N, N))) grady = np.real(ifft2(xhat2.reshape(N, N))) x = poissonsolver(gradx, grady, N) return x def solvel1(S, N, y, epsilon): """ Solves min ||xhat||1 s.t. ||S @ Finv @ xhat - y||2 <= epsilon using Iterative Soft-Thresholding Algorithm (ISTA). """ xhat = np.zeros(N N) stepsize = 1.0 # Lipschitz constant for S @ Finv is 1.0 maxiter = 1000 threshold = epsilon 0.1 # Heuristic threshold for sparsity for in range(maxiter): # Compute spatial gradient from DFT coefficients spatialgrad = np.real(ifft2(xhat.reshape(N, N))) # Compute residual: S @ spatialgrad - y residual = S @ spatialgrad.flatten() - y # Compute gradient of data fidelity: F @ S^T @ residual errorspatial = S.T @ residual grad = np.real(fft2(errorspatial.reshape(N, N))) # Proximal gradient step xhatnew = xhat - stepsize grad # Soft thresholding xhat = np.sign(xhatnew) np.maximum(np.abs(xhatnew) - threshold, 0) return xhat def poissonsolver(gradx, grady, N): """ Solves for x given horizontal gradient gradx and vertical gradient grady. Uses Dirichlet boundary conditions. """ # Compute divergence of the gradient field: div(g) = d(gx)/dx + d(gy)/dy divg = np.zeros((N, N)) # d(gx)/dx using central differences for interior, forward/backward for boundaries divg[:, 1:-1] += (gradx[:, 2:] - gradx[:,:-2]) / 2.0 divg[:, 0] = gradx[:, 1] - gradx[:, 0] divg[:, -1] = gradx[:, -1] - gradx[:, -2] # d(gy)/dy divg[1:-1,:] += (grady[2:,:] - grady[:-2,:]) / 2.0 divg[0,:] = grady[1,:] - grady[0,:] divg[-1,:] = grady[-1,:] - grady[-2,:] # Construct 2D Laplacian matrix (5-point stencil) e = np.ones(N) T = diags([-1, 2, -1], [-1, 0, 1], shape=(N, N), format='csr') A = kron(eye(N), T) + kron(T, eye(N)) # Apply Dirichlet BCs: remove boundary rows/columns interiorindices = [] for i in range(1, N - 1): for j in range(1, N - 1): interiorindices.append(i N + j) Ainterior = A[np.ix(interiorindices, interiorindices)] binterior = divg.flatten()[interiorindices] # Solve linear system xinterior = spsolve(Ainterior, binterior) # Reconstruct full image x = np.zeros((N, N)) for idx, flatidx in enumerate(interiorindices): x[flatidx // N, flatidx % N] = xinterior[idx] return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Missing Pixel Fraction: Performance deteriorates quickly when the fraction of missing pixels is high. Boundary Conditions: The Poisson solver requires boundary conditions. Solver Tolerance: The tolerance \epsilon must be chosen carefully; 10^{-2} is recommended as a tradeoff between quality and runtime. Time Complexity: Dominated by the l1-minimization solver (e.g., NESTA) and the Poisson solver. The l1 minimization is iterative and scales with the number of samples m and image size N. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the DFT coefficients (O(N^2)) and the sensing matrix operations. Measured Performance: The method shows improvement over CS-Wavelet and Sen and Darabi's approach [SD11] in terms of recovery quality for moderate missing pixel fractions. Strengths: Exploits sparsity in the Fourier domain, which is inherently incoherent with point sampling, avoiding the coherence issues of wavelet-based methods. Gradient components are often sparser in the Fourier domain than the image itself. Limitations: Deteriorates significantly with high percentages of missing pixels. Requires solving two l1-minimization problems and a Poisson solver, which can be computationally expensive. When to Use: Suitable for compressive volume rendering when the fraction of missing pixels is moderate and high coherence with the sampling basis is a concern. When Not to Use: When the fraction of missing pixels is very high, or when computational resources are limited and iterative solvers are prohibitive. Compressive Gradient Rendering was introduced as part of the broader field of Compressive Volume Rendering. It extends the idea of Sen and Darabi [SD11] by rendering gradient components instead of the image itself. The method leverages the Restricted Isometry Property (RIC) of random partial Fourier matrices, which are known to have low coherence with point sampling. The approach was developed to address coherence issues found in CS-Wavelet methods and to exploit the natural sparsity of gradients in the Fourier domain. The Poisson solver step follows the approach of Pérez et al. [PGB03]. The method is discussed in the context of tomographic reconstruction as inverse rendering and is a key component of Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods. name: Laplacian Projection
head: Laplacian Regularization for Sparse View Reconstruction
body: Laplacian Projection is a physics-based tomographic reconstruction method employing Laplacian regularization for sparse view reconstruction. It represents the state-of-the-art in physics-based smoke reconstruction. It is evaluated against methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting to validate its effectiveness across different input configurations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 2D projection images (views). The method supports single-view (N=1) and multi-view (N=16) configurations. Output: A 3D volume grid representing the reconstructed physical property. Data Structures: The volume is represented as a 3D grid with a resolution of 128 \times 196 \times 128. Not given in the sources for other layout details. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the 3D volume field V (e.g., with zeros or a prior estimate). 2. Forward Projection: Render the current volume estimate V to generate synthetic 2D projections P{\text{syn}} for each input view angle. This involves integrating the volume along rays, potentially using directional samples. The source recommends 30 directional samples as the optimal balance between accuracy and performance. 3. Error Calculation: Compute the difference between the synthetic projections P{\text{syn}} and the observed input views P{\text{obs}}. 4. Regularization Term Calculation: Compute the Laplacian of the volume field, \nabla^2 V. This term penalizes curvature, enforcing smoothness. 5. Optimization Step: Update the volume field V by minimizing a combined cost function comprising a data fidelity term and a Laplacian regularization term. The update can be performed using gradient-based optimization or projection-based iterative solvers. Not given in the sources for the exact mathematical formulation or solver specifics. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-5 until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. The source investigates iteration limits of 250, 1000, and 5000 to analyze the quality-efficiency trade-off. Parameters: Number of views: 1 (single-view) or 16 (multi-view). Directional samples: 30 (recommended for optimal balance). Volume resolution: 128 \times 196 \times 128 (as used in experiments). Iteration limit: Variable (250, 1000, 5000 tested). Regularization weight \lambda: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse views can lead to significant artifacts if regularization is too weak. Precision issues may arise in the calculation of second-order derivatives on discrete grids. Over-regularization may blur sharp features. Enforces spatial smoothness on volume properties by penalizing their Laplacian, addressing the ill-posed nature of sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from standard Tikhonov regularization by directly penalizing second-order spatial derivatives (curvature) rather than first-order gradients, which better preserves sharp features while suppressing high-frequency noise. Choose it when second-order smoothness constraints are preferred over first-order gradient penalties. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and the cost of forward projection and Laplacian computation. The source notes that 30 directional samples are used for pre-computation. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the volume grid size (128 \times 196 \times 128) and the number of views. Performance: Evaluated on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU using the ScalarFlow dataset (300×531 pixels). It is described as state-of-the-art for physics-based smoke reconstruction. Strengths: Effective for sparse-view reconstruction; suitable for smoke and spray imaging. Limitations: Performance depends on the choice of regularization parameter and iteration count; may be computationally intensive for high-resolution volumes or large numbers of views. When to use: When reconstructing volumetric media like smoke from limited angular data. When not to use: When high computational resources are unavailable or when the input data is dense and standard methods suffice. The method has been evaluated against 3D Gaussian Splatting using the ScalarFlow dataset to demonstrate its effectiveness for smoke reconstruction. name: Laplacian Regularization
head: Laplacian Regularization for Sparse View Reconstruction
body: Laplacian Regularization enforces spatial smoothness on volume properties by penalizing their Laplacian, addressing the ill-posed nature of sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. It distinguishes itself from standard Tikhonov regularization by directly penalizing second-order spatial derivatives (curvature) rather than first-order gradients, which better preserves sharp features while suppressing high-frequency noise. Inputs: Training view images I, camera poses P, and initial neural field parameters \Theta. Outputs: Optimized parameters \Theta minimizing the combined loss. Data Structures: The volume is represented implicitly by a neural network F\Theta that outputs density \sigma\Theta(x) for spatial coordinates x \in [-1, 1]^3. Formulas: The regularization term R{Lap}(\Theta) is the L1 norm of the Laplacian of the density field over the domain: R{Lap}(\Theta) = \int{[-1,1]^3} |\Deltax \sigma\Theta(x)| dx \approx \sum{i=1}^N \sum{j=1}^N \sum{k=1}^N |\Deltax \sigma\Theta(\delta i, \delta j, \delta k)| \delta^3 where \Delta = \text{div} \cdot \nabla denotes the Laplacian operator, N is the grid resolution per dimension, and \delta is the uniform grid spacing. Steps: 1. Initialize training data and parameters \Theta. 2. Evaluate the density field \sigma\Theta(x) on a uniform 3D grid over [-1, 1]^3. 3. Compute the discrete Laplacian magnitude |\Deltax \sigma\Theta| at each grid point using finite differences. 4. Approximate the integral by summing the magnitudes weighted by the voxel volume \delta^3. 5. Backpropagate the regularization gradient through \Theta alongside the photometric loss to update parameters. Parameters: Grid resolution N: Not given in the sources. Grid spacing \delta: Not given in the sources. Regularization weight: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The absolute value |\cdot| renders the term non-differentiable at zero, requiring subgradient methods or a smooth approximation (e.g., \sqrt{\epsilon^2 + x^2}) during backpropagation. Boundary conditions for the discrete Laplacian stencil are not specified. Multi-parameter Regularization with Center-Axis Constraint: Stabilizes ill-posed inverse reconstruction of local extinction coefficients and radiative source terms in axisymmetric sprays by combining a global second-order Tikhonov smoothness penalty with a zero-gradient center-axis constraint. It preserves physical features near the symmetry axis where single-penalty Abel-type inversions fail, using regularization matrices with different null spaces. Choose this variant when reconstructing axisymmetric sprays from infrared radiance data to suppress numerical artifacts near the symmetry axis. Link Time Complexity: Scales with O(N^3) for grid evaluation and regularization, plus ray sampling costs. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing neural network parameters and the 3D density grid for regularization evaluation. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves continuity and generates smooth geometry representations, reducing severe noise compared to unregularized baselines. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the volume field is smooth; excessive regularization weight may oversmooth sharp discontinuities. When to use: Sparse-view tomographic reconstruction where high-frequency noise and artifacts are prevalent. When not to use: Scenes with inherently non-smooth, highly discontinuous volume properties where strong smoothing degrades fidelity. The method is employed in Aug-NeRF to enhance neural radiance fields with physically-grounded augmentations, specifically improving the smoothness of depth maps and geometry representations in scenes rendered with a physics-based renderer. name: Multi-parameter Regularization with Center-Axis Constraint
head: Center-axis constrained regularization, Multi-Parameter Regularized Inversion for Axisymmetric Tomography, Multi-parameter regularization, Multi-regularized Inversion, Tikhonov with axis constraint
body: This method stabilizes the ill-posed inverse reconstruction of local extinction coefficients and radiative source terms from infrared radiance data in axisymmetric sprays. It combines a global second-order Tikhonov smoothness penalty with a specific center-axis constraint (zero-gradient condition) to suppress numerical artifacts near the symmetry axis that plague single-penalty Abel-type inversions. Unlike single regularization terms which cause artifacts near the axis, this multi-penalty model preserves physical features by utilizing regularization matrices with different null spaces. Inputs: Line-of-sight IR radiance measurements y. Differential Infrared Thermography (DIT) emissivity \epsilon{DIT}. Radial grid spacing \Delta r. Regularization weights \mu2 and \mu0. Threshold for weakly radiating regions \epsilon{thresh}. Outputs: Local radiative source term vector x. Local extinction coefficient (reconstructed in Step 1). Data Structures: Radial grid points ri for i = 1 \dots N, where r1 = 0 is the symmetry axis. Unknown vector x of size N representing the local radiative source term. System matrix F encoding the attenuated line-of-sight integral operator. Regularization matrices L2 (global smoothness) and L0 (center-axis constraint). Step 1: Reconstruct Local Extinction Coefficient Use the DIT emissivity \epsilon{DIT} to reconstruct the local extinction coefficient. The DIT technique provides integrated emissivity, which is inverted to obtain attenuation information. Step 2: Formulate the Inverse Problem for Source Term The local radiative source term is recovered by solving the attenuated line-of-sight integral of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). The problem is ill-posed and sensitive to measurement noise, particularly near the symmetry axis. Step 3: Apply Multi-Parameter Regularization Stabilize the inversion by minimizing an objective function that combines two penalty terms: 1. Global Smoothness Penalty: Second-order Tikhonov regularization to suppress high-frequency oscillations caused by measurement noise. 2. Center-Axis Constraint: A constraint imposing the zero-gradient condition \frac{\partial x}{\partial r} = 0 at r=0, required by axisymmetry. The objective function \Phi(x) to minimize is: \Phi(x) = \|Fx - y\|2^2 + \mu2^2 \|L2 x\|2^2 + \mu0 \|L0 x\|2^2 Where: F is the system matrix representing the line-of-sight integration operator. y is the vector of measured radiance data. L2 is the second-order difference matrix for global smoothness. L0 is the matrix enforcing the zero-gradient condition at the axis. \mu2 and \mu0 are regularization parameters. Step 4: Boundary Masking Apply a mask based on \epsilon{DIT} to exclude weakly radiating regions below a prescribed threshold \epsilon{thresh}. This reduces boundary fluctuations that appear near the outer boundary where the extinction coefficient becomes small. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiparamregularization(y, F, dr, mu2, mu0, epsilonDIT, epsilonthresh): """ Reconstructs local source term x using multi-parameter regularization with center-axis constraint. """ N = len(y) # L2: Second-order difference matrix for global smoothness (size (N-2) x N) L2 = [[0.0] N for in range(N - 2)] for i in range(N - 2): L2[i][i] = 1.0 L2[i][i + 1] = -2.0 L2[i][i + 2] = 1.0 for i in range(N - 2): for j in range(N): L2[i][j] /= dr 2 # L0: Center-axis constraint matrix (size 1 x N) L0 = [[0.0] N] L0[0][0] = -1.0 L0[0][1] = 1.0 L0[0][0] /= dr L0[0][1] /= dr # Construct combined system matrix B^M = F^T F + mu2^2 L2^T L2 + mu0 L0^T L0 BM = matmul(transpose(F), F) BM = add(BM, scale(matmul(transpose(L2), L2), mu2 2)) BM = add(BM, scale(matmul(transpose(L0), L0), mu0)) # Construct right-hand side B^M x = F^T y rhs = matvecmul(transpose(F), y) # Solve the linear system using Cholesky factorization L = choleskydecompose(BM) z = solvetriangular(L, rhs, lower=True) x = solvetriangular(transpose(L), z, lower=False) # Apply boundary masking based on DIT emissivity mask = [1.0 if e >= epsilonthresh else 0.0 for e in epsilonDIT] x = [x[i] mask[i] for i in range(N)] return x def transpose(M): return [[M[j][i] for j in range(len(M))] for i in range(len(M[0]))] def matmul(A, B): return [[sum(A[i][k] B[k][j] for k in range(len(B))) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))] def add(A, B): return [[A[i][j] + B[i][j] for j in range(len(A[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def scale(M, s): return [[M[i][j] s for j in range(len(M[0]))] for i in range(len(M))] def choleskydecompose(A): n = len(A) L = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1): s = sum(L[i][k] L[j][k] for k in range(j)) if i == j: L[i][j] = (A[i][i] - s) 0.5 else: L[i][j] = (A[i][j] - s) / L[j][j] return L def solvetriangular(L, b, lower=True): n = len(b) x = [0.0] n for i in range(n): s = sum(L[i][j] x[j] for j in range(i)) x[i] = (b[i] - s) / L[i][i] return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Semi-convergence: Iterative techniques like ART suffer from slow convergence and semi-convergence, where the solution diverges as measurement noise is amplified. Boundary Fluctuations: Fluctuations appear near the outer boundary where the extinction coefficient becomes small, because the local radiance is obtained from the ratio of the radiative source term to the extinction coefficient. Axis Artifacts: Single global regularization terms cause numerical artifacts near the symmetry axis due to Abel-type inversion sensitivity. Grid Refinement: The L0 operator is only effective if the radial grid at the center is sufficiently refined; otherwise, it may not properly damp oscillations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves reconstruction near the axis without significantly influencing the overall radial distribution compared to single Tikhonov regularization. Suppresses high-frequency oscillations and non-physical artifacts near the symmetry axis. Limitations: Remaining fluctuations can still appear near the outer boundary where extinction is small. When to use: For tomographic reconstruction of IR radiance from axisymmetric sprays in hot environments, particularly when high accuracy near the symmetry axis is required and measurement noise is present. When not to use: For non-axisymmetric flows where the center-axis constraint is invalid. The method was introduced to address the limitations of single-penalty regularization in axisymmetric spray tomography. It builds on the concept that multi-penalty models with different null spaces can preserve various physical features of the target. The framework combines Differential Infrared Thermography (DIT) with multi-parameter regularized inversion to directly solve the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). Numerical phantom studies, including configurations relevant to evaporating cold sprays and flashing jets, demonstrated the method's accuracy under well-defined conditions and noisy measurement scenarios. name: Global Solver
body: The Global Solver is a compressive volume rendering reconstruction method that treats the entire image as a single unit for inverse rendering recovery. It solves for missing pixel values by running a solver over the full image domain simultaneously, contrasting with block-based partitioning strategies. It addresses the problem of recovering high-quality volumes from images with high missing pixel rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: volume rendering image with missing pixels. Output: reconstructed full-resolution image. Data Structures: The method operates on the entire image matrix as a single entity without partitioning it into blocks. Steps: 1. Initialize the solver for the entire image domain. 2. Set the iteration parameter, which can be fixed to a constant value or controlled via a flag to run until a desired solution is reached. 3. Execute the iterative solver loop. 4. Inside the loop, perform the convolution process, identified as the most time-consuming operation. 5. Update the image data iteratively until the fixed iteration count is met or the convergence flag indicates a desired solution is arrived at. Parameters: Number of iterations: Affects solver performance; can be fixed or set via a flag to run multiple times until a desired solution is arrived at. Pitfalls: FFT-based convolution overhead: Using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) for convolution causes memory to be copied back and forth from CPU to GPU for each iteration, resulting in very slow reconstruction time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def globalsolver(image, missingmask, maxiterations=None, convergenceflag=False): """Reconstructs the entire image globally with the solver running the entire image at once.""" currentimage = image.copy() if convergenceflag: # Allow the solver to run multiple times until it arrives at a desired solution while not checkconvergence(currentimage, missingmask): currentimage = updateimage(currentimage, missingmask) else: # Fixed number of iterations parameter for in range(maxiterations): currentimage = updateimage(currentimage, missingmask) return currentimage def updateimage(image, missingmask): # Perform convolution process, which is the most time-consuming operation # Using FFT-based convolution causes memory to be copied back and forth from CPU to GPU for each iteration # Apply standard convolution operation to the image matrix convolved = applystandardconvolution(image) # Update missing pixels while preserving known pixels updated = image.copy() updated[missingmask] = convolved[missingmask] return updated def checkconvergence(image, missingmask): # Check if the solver has arrived at a desired solution # Compare residual or error against a threshold return True def applystandardconvolution(image): # Standard convolution operation # In practice, this applies a kernel to the image matrix return image # Placeholder for actual convolution logic A parallel implementation that partitions the image into mutually exclusive blocks to reduce global memory access and improve performance using shared memory. It differs from the Global Solver by processing blocks independently, allowing for different numbers of iterations per block based on local convergence criteria. Time Complexity: High, as the convolution process is the most time-consuming operation. Memory Access: Inefficient when using FFT-based convolution due to frequent CPU/GPU memory transfers. Measured Performance: Reconstruction time of approximately 124 milliseconds (about 10 frames per second) when 60% of pixels are missing (40% present). The global solver takes 119 milliseconds using only 60% pixels. Scaling: Not well suited for interactivity due to the high reconstruction time. Strengths: Provides a global solution for the entire image, maintaining consistency across the full domain. Limitations: Very slow reconstruction time compared to local solvers; for example, the Local Solver takes 5.6 milliseconds for the same task, making it 24 times faster. When to use: When global consistency is prioritized over speed and interactivity is not required. When not to use: When interactive frame rates are needed. The Global Solver was proposed in a thesis on GPU-based compressive volume rendering as one of two parallel approaches to reconstruction, the other being the Local Solver. It builds on gradient solver techniques previously demonstrated by Liu and Alim et al., who measured reconstruction times using a CPU. The method was developed to address the limitations of CPU-based reconstruction and to provide a baseline for comparing block-based optimizations. name: Local Solver
head: Block-based Solver, Block-based gradient solver, Block-wise CG Solver, Compressive Rendering (Local Solver), Local Conjugate Gradient Solver, Tiled CG Solver, Tiled Solver
body: The Local Solver is a parallel optimization technique for compressive volume rendering that partitions the reconstruction image into smaller, mutually exclusive blocks to solve the inverse problem locally on each block. It solves the same regularized normal equations as the Global Solver but operates on reduced vector sizes (blockWidth \times blockHeight instead of imageWidth \times imageHeight). It is distinguished from its sibling Global Solver by processing blocks independently, which allows for different numbers of iterations per block based on local convergence and significantly reduces global memory traffic by leveraging CUDA shared memory. The method solves the regularized normal equation (S^T S + \lambda H)x = S^T y using a Conjugate Gradient (CG) solver, but applies it to tiled regions of the image rather than the entire image at once. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The sampling matrix S, the convolution filter H, the regularization parameter \lambda, and the observed image with missing pixels y. Output: The reconstructed volume density field, merged from individual block solutions. Data Structures: Shared Memory: Used per block to store intermediate vectors for the CG solver (residual, direction, etc.). Layout: Limited to approximately 48 KB per block. Constraint: Variables are copied for each individual block; threads from one block cannot access shared memory from another. Ghost Elements: A padded region surrounding each block containing known pixels from neighboring blocks to provide neighborhood information for convolution. Parameters: Thread Configuration: 16 \times 16 threads per block produces the best performance. Padding Size (P): P = kernelWidth / 2, where kernelWidth is the width of the convolution filter. Number of Blocks: The number of blocks in the x and y dimensions is calculated as: blockNumberx = \frac{imageWidth - P}{threadSizex + P} blockNumbery = \frac{imageHeight - P}{threadSizey + P} Algorithm Steps: 1. Partition: Divide the image data into mutually exclusive blocks of size blockWidth \times blockHeight. 2. Pad: For each block, create a padded region of size P around the block boundaries. Fill this region with "ghost elements" (known pixels) from the neighboring blocks in the original image y. This ensures the convolution filter has access to neighborhood data, eliminating boundary artifacts. 3. Load: Copy the block data (including ghost elements) into the block's shared memory. 4. Solve Locally: Run the standard Conjugate Gradient algorithm on the data within the shared memory. Because the solver runs locally, each block maintains its own state variables. Each block can converge independently, potentially requiring a different number of iterations. 5. Reduce: Perform block-wise vector dot product reductions using parallel reduction (complexity O(\log n)) to compute scalar products required by the CG algorithm. 6. Merge: Combine the reconstructed solutions from all blocks to form the final output image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localsolver(imagewidth, imageheight, samplingmatrixS, convolutionfilterH, lambdareg, observedimagey): # Parameters from evidence threadsizex = 16 threadsizey = 16 kernelwidth = convolutionfilterH.width paddingsize = kernelwidth / 2 # Calculate number of blocks using source formula numblocksx = (imagewidth - paddingsize) // (threadsizex + paddingsize) numblocksy = (imageheight - paddingsize) // (threadsizey + paddingsize) # Initialize output image reconstructedimage = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for blocky in range(numblocksy): for blockx in range(numblocksx): # Calculate block start coordinates startx = blockx (threadsizex + paddingsize) starty = blocky (threadsizey + paddingsize) # Extract padded region with ghost elements ystart = max(0, starty - paddingsize) yend = min(imageheight, starty + threadsizey + paddingsize) xstart = max(0, startx - paddingsize) xend = min(imagewidth, startx + threadsizex + paddingsize) paddedblock = [row[xstart:xend] for row in observedimagey[ystart:yend]] # Extract core block (remove padding) coreblock = [row[paddingsize:-paddingsize] for row in paddedblock] # Restrict matrices to the block's spatial domain localS = restrictmatrix(samplingmatrixS, startx, starty, threadsizex, threadsizey) localH = restrictmatrix(convolutionfilterH, startx, starty, threadsizex, threadsizey) localy = coreblock # Solve the local normal equation (S^T S + lambda H)x = S^T y localsystemmatrix = matrixmultiplytranspose(localS, localS) localrhs = matrixvectormultiplytranspose(localS, localy) localA = addmatrices(localsystemmatrix, scalematrix(localH, lambdareg)) blocksolution = conjugategradientsolve(localA, localrhs) # Merge result into global image for i in range(threadsizey): for j in range(threadsizex): reconstructedimage[starty + i][startx + j] = blocksolution[i][j] return reconstructedimage def restrictmatrix(matrix, startx, starty, width, height): # Extracts the submatrix corresponding to the block's spatial coordinates return [row[startx:startx + width] for row in matrix[starty:starty + height]] def conjugategradientsolve(A, b): # Standard CG solver for Ax = b n = len(b) x = [0.0] n r = [b[i] - sum(A[i][j] x[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)] p = r[:] rsold = sum(r[i] r[i] for i in range(n)) for in range(n): Ap = [sum(A[i][j] p[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)] pAp = sum(p[i] Ap[i] for i in range(n)) if pAp == 0: break alpha = rsold / pAp for i in range(n): x[i] += alpha p[i] r[i] -= alpha Ap[i] rsnew = sum(r[i] r[i] for i in range(n)) if abs(rsnew - rsold) < 1e-10: break for i in range(n): p[i] = r[i] + (rsnew / rsold) p[i] rsold = rsnew return x def matrixmultiplytranspose(A, B): # Computes A^T B rowsA, colsA = len(A), len(A[0]) rowsB, colsB = len(B), len(B[0]) result = [[0.0] colsB for in range(colsA)] for i in range(colsA): for j in range(colsB): for k in range(rowsA): result[i][j] += A[k][i] B[k][j] return result def matrixvectormultiplytranspose(A, v): # Computes A^T v return [sum(A[k][i] v[k] for k in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A[0]))] def addmatrices(A, B): return [[A[i][j] + B[i][j] for j in range(len(A[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def scalematrix(A, s): return [[A[i][j] s for j in range(len(A[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Without padding with ghost elements, the local solver generates incoherent results and boundary artifacts around the border of each block because the convolution lacks neighborhood information. Shared Memory Limits: The limited shared memory (48 KB) restricts the maximum block size. Race Conditions: Uncontrolled execution of threads within a block may lead to race conditions if multiple threads read/write the same memory location; syncthreads() must be used appropriately to maintain execution order. The GMRES Solver is an iterative Krylov subspace method used to solve the regularized normal equations arising from least-squares Computed Tomography (CT) reconstruction. It minimizes the residual between the forward-projected reconstruction and the observed sinogram data while applying Tikhonov regularization to enforce smoothness. Unlike direct solvers that explicitly construct the large, sparse system matrix, GMRES operates in a matrix-free manner to reduce memory overhead. It is distinguished from its sibling Local Solver by solving the global inverse problem rather than partitioning the image into independent blocks [Parent]. Choose GMRES when global convergence properties and matrix-free scalability are prioritized over block-wise parallelism [Parent]. Performance: The Local Solver is significantly faster than the Global Solver. In measurements using 60% pixel coverage, the Local Solver took 5.6 milliseconds, compared to 119 milliseconds for the Global Solver, a 24-fold speedup. Complexity: The computational complexity of the parallel reduction operation is O(\log n), compared to O(n) for sequential summation. The reduction in matrix size from imageWidth \times imageHeight to blockWidth \times blockHeight significantly reduces the computational cost per iteration. Memory: Reduces global memory access bottlenecks by utilizing fast shared memory (48 KB per block). Strengths: Enables interactive frame rates (e.g., ~10 fps) by reducing reconstruction time. Allows adaptive sampling strategies where each block can have independent sampling rates (e.g., 12.5% or 32 rays per block) to reduce warp divergence. Limitations: Requires careful management of shared memory and synchronization. Performance is sensitive to thread configuration (multiples of 16 are optimal). The Local Solver was proposed as an optimization for GPU-based compressive volume rendering to address the poor performance and high data transfer costs of global reconstruction methods. It builds on the conjugate gradient solver framework but introduces a tiling strategy to leverage CUDA's blocking scheme and shared memory. The method was developed to achieve interactivity in volume rendering, which was previously hindered by the computational cost of solving the large global system. name: GMRES Solver
head: GMRES Solver for CT Reconstruction, GMRES Solver for Regularized Normal Equations, Generalized Minimal Residual Method, Generalized Minimal Residual Method for CT, Iterative CT Reconstruction, Matrix-Free Regularized Least-Squares Solver
body:
The GMRES Solver is an iterative Krylov subspace method used to solve the regularized normal equations arising in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction. It addresses the ill-posed inverse problem of reconstructing a volume from sinogram data by minimizing a least-squares objective with Tikhonov regularization. Unlike direct solvers that require explicit matrix inversion, GMRES operates in a matrix-free manner, making it suitable for large-scale tomographic reconstruction where the system matrix is too large to store. Inputs: volgeom: Volume geometry object defining the reconstruction grid dimensions v 	imes h. projgeom: Projection geometry object defining the detector and source parameters. projectorid: Identifier for the forward projection operator (e.g., 'line', 'pixel'). g: Measured sinogram data. alpha: Regularization strength parameter. penalty: String specifying the regularization type: "tikhonov" (0-order) or "gradient" (1st-order). maxiter: Maximum number of iterations (default 700). Outputs: falpha: Reconstructed volume image reshaped to (v, h). Data Structures: The system is represented as a LinearOperator object A that does not store the full matrix A^T A + \alpha R but defines a matvec function that computes the product of the regularized normal matrix with a vector. The right-hand side vector is b = A^T g, computed using the adjoint projection operator. Steps: 1. Geometry Setup: Initialize volgeom and projgeom using the provided dimensions and angles. Compute the total number of pixels M = v 	imes h and N = M. 2. Compute Right-Hand Side: Calculate the vector b = A^T g by applying the adjoint projection operator to the sinogram data g. 3. Construct Linear Operator: Define a LinearOperator A with shape (M, M). Its matvec method must compute (A^T A + \alpha R) x for any input vector x: Compute y = A x using the forward projection operator. Compute z = A^T y using the adjoint projection operator. Apply regularization R: If penalty is "tikhonov", R = I (identity). The term is \alpha x. If penalty is "gradient", R is the Laplacian operator (discrete second derivative). The term is \alpha R x. Note that in the reference experiments, the gradient penalty uses a scaling factor of 2\alpha compared to the tikhonov penalty. Return z + \alpha R x. 4. Solve: Call the GMRES solver with the LinearOperator A, the flattened right-hand side vector b, and a callback function for monitoring convergence. 5. Reshape: Reshape the resulting solution vector to the 2D volume dimensions (v, h). Formulas: The solver minimizes the regularized least-squares objective: \minf \| A f - g \|^2 + \alpha \| R f \|^2 This leads to the regularized normal equations: (A^T A + \alpha R) f = A^T g Where: A is the forward projection matrix. g is the sinogram vector. R is the regularization operator. \alpha is the regularization parameter. For 0-order Tikhonov regularization: R = I For 1st-order Tikhonov (gradient) regularization: R = 
abla^2 where 
abla^2 is the discrete Laplacian operator. Parameters: penalty: "tikhonov" or "gradient". alpha: Regularization strength. The optimal value is often determined using the L-Curve method. maxiter: 700. Pitfalls: The regularization parameter \alpha significantly affects the trade-off between data fidelity and smoothness. The implementation relies on the ASTRA toolbox for projection operations. The callback function is optional but useful for monitoring convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import scipy.sparse.linalg as spla def forwardprojection(x2d, projgeom, projectorid): # Standard forward projection operator # Returns sinogram array of shape (nsamples, nangles) pass def adjointprojection(sinogram, projgeom, projectorid): # Standard adjoint projection operator # Returns image array of shape (v, h) pass def matvec(x, v, h, projgeom, projectorid, alpha, penalty): # Compute (A^T A + alpha R) x x2d = x.reshape(v, h) y = forwardprojection(x2d, projgeom, projectorid) z = adjointprojection(y, projgeom, projectorid).flatten() if penalty == "tikhonov": return z + alpha x elif penalty == "gradient": # Laplacian operator R = 
abla^2 lap = np.zeroslike(x2d) lap[1:-1, 1:-1] = (x2d[2:, 1:-1] + x2d[:-2, 1:-1] + x2d[1:-1, 2:] + x2d[1:-1,:-2] - 4 x2d[1:-1, 1:-1]) # Experiments use alpha2 for gradient penalty compared to tikhonov return z + 2 alpha lap.flatten() else: raise ValueError("Unknown penalty type") def gmressolver(volgeom, projgeom, projectorid, g, alpha, penalty, maxiter=700): v, h = volgeom.shape M = v h # Compute right-hand side b = A^T g b = adjointprojection(g, projgeom, projectorid).flatten() # Construct LinearOperator A = spla.LinearOperator((M, M), matvec=lambda x: matvec(x, v, h, projgeom, projectorid, alpha, penalty)) # Solve using GMRES solution, info = spla.gmres(A, b, maxiter=maxiter) return solution.reshape(v, h) A heuristic method for determining the optimal regularization parameter \alpha by identifying the corner of the L-shaped curve plotting the norm of the solution against the norm of the residual on a log-log scale. It is used to balance data fidelity and smoothness in ill-posed inverse problems like tomographic reconstruction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: GMRES is effective for large-scale problems where direct solvers are infeasible. Strengths: Matrix-free operation, handles large sparse systems, supports various regularization types. Limitations: Convergence can be slow for ill-conditioned problems without preconditioning. When to use: Large-scale tomographic reconstruction with sparse or limited-angle data. When not to use: Small-scale problems where direct solvers are faster, or when real-time performance is critical and convergence is slow. The GMRES (Generalized Minimal Residual) method is applied to the regularized normal equations to solve the inverse problem efficiently in CT reconstruction. imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans - GitHub, https://github.com/imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: L-Curve Regularization Parameter Selection
head: Alpha Sweep, L-curve, L-Curve Parameter Selection
body:
L-Curve Regularization Parameter Selection determines the optimal regularization parameter \alpha for ill-posed inverse problems by plotting the norm of the solution \|f\| against the norm of the residual \|r\| on a log-log scale and identifying the curve's corner. It solves the trade-off between data fidelity and solution smoothness without requiring a direct error metric like MSE, unlike grid search methods. Inputs: A range of regularization parameters \alpha, typically logarithmically spaced (e.g., 10^{	ext{linspace}(-3, 4, 15)}). The noisy sinogram data g. The forward projection operator A (Radon transform). The regularization type (e.g., 0-order or 1st-order Tikhonov). Solver and geometry parameters (number of angles, samples, volume dimensions). Outputs: The optimal regularization parameter \alpha{opt} corresponding to the L-curve corner. Arrays of solution norms \|f\alpha\| and residual norms \|r\alpha\| for all tested \alpha. Data Structures: alphas: 1D array of floats, logarithmically spaced values for \alpha. finorms: 1D array of floats, storing \|f\alpha\| for each \alpha. rnorms: 1D array of floats, storing \|r\alpha\| for each \alpha. keys: List of tuples/arrays, storing [finorm, rnorm, alpha] for each iteration. Steps: 1. Generate a logarithmic grid of regularization parameters \alpha. A common range is 10^{-3} to 10^{4} with 15 points. 2. For each \alpha in the grid: a. Solve the regularized inverse problem to obtain the reconstruction f\alpha. b. Compute the forward projection of the solution: p\alpha = A f\alpha. c. Compute the residual vector: r\alpha = g - p\alpha. d. Compute the solution norm: 	ext{fi
orm} = \|f\alpha\|. e. Compute the residual norm: 	ext{r
orm} = \|r\alpha\|. f. Store 	ext{fi
orm}, 	ext{r
orm}, and \alpha. 3. Plot 	ext{r
orm} versus 	ext{fi
orm} on a log-log scale. 4. Identify the "corner" of the curve, which represents the optimal trade-off between data fidelity and solution smoothness. In the provided implementation, this is manually selected by index (e.g., idxsp = 5 or idxlim = 6). Formulas: Residual: r\alpha = g - A f\alpha Solution Norm: 	ext{fi
orm} = \|f\alpha\| Residual Norm: 	ext{r
orm} = \|r\alpha\| Parameters: theta: Noise level for the sinogram. Typical value used in examples is 10000. alphas: Logarithmically spaced array. Example: 10.0np.linspace(-3, 4, 15). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The "corner" can be ambiguous in noisy data or for certain regularization types, often requiring manual index selection or curvature-based heuristics. The method assumes the L-curve shape is well-defined; for some ill-conditioned systems, the curve may not exhibit a clear corner. Computational cost increases linearly with the number of \alpha values tested, as each requires a full independent solve. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def lcurveselection(g, A, alphas, solvefunc, projectfunc): """ Selects optimal alpha using the L-curve method. Args: g: Noisy sinogram data (vector). A: Forward projection operator (matrix or callable). alphas: Array of regularization parameters to test. solvefunc: Function that solves the regularized inverse problem for a given alpha. projectfunc: Function that computes forward projection. Returns: alphaopt: Optimal regularization parameter. finorms: Array of solution norms. rnorms: Array of residual norms. """ nalphas = len(alphas) finorms = np.zeros(nalphas) rnorms = np.zeros(nalphas) for i, alpha in enumerate(alphas): # Solve the regularized problem falpha = solvefunc(g, A, alpha) # Compute forward projection palpha = projectfunc(falpha, A) # Compute residual and norms ralpha = g - palpha finorms[i] = np.linalg.norm(falpha) rnorms[i] = np.linalg.norm(ralpha) # Identify the corner of the L-curve # The source implementation manually selects the index (e.g., idxsp = 5) # Standard heuristic: maximize curvature of the log-log plot logfi = np.log(finorms) logr = np.log(rnorms) dx = np.gradient(logfi) dy = np.gradient(logr) ddx = np.gradient(dx) ddy = np.gradient(dy) numerator = np.abs(dx ddy - dy ddx) denominator = np.power(dx2 + dy2, 1.5) denominator = np.where(denominator == 0, 1e-10, denominator) kappa = numerator / denominator idxopt = np.argmax(kappa) alphaopt = alphas[idxopt] return alphaopt, finorms, rnorms Automated method to find the L-curve corner by maximizing curvature on the log-log plot, removing manual selection. Chosen when high-throughput parameter tuning is required. Extension using different norms or regularization terms when the standard L-curve lacks a clear corner. Chosen for non-standard ill-posed formulations. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot T), where N is the number of regularization parameters tested and T is the time to solve the inverse problem for one \alpha. Each solve is independent, allowing parallelization. Memory Complexity: O(N + M), where M is the memory required for one solution f\alpha and residual r\alpha. Strengths: Does not require knowledge of the noise level or true solution; provides a visual diagnostic of the regularization trade-off. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple solves; the "corner" can be ambiguous or non-existent for some problems; manual selection introduces subjectivity. When to use: When the noise level is unknown and a robust, visually interpretable method for parameter selection is needed. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and a single solve is preferred; when the L-curve does not exhibit a clear corner. The L-curve method was introduced by Per Christian Hansen as a tool for selecting regularization parameters in discrete ill-posed problems. It has been applied in various fields including image processing and tomography. In the provided source, it is used to select \alpha for Tikhonov regularization in CT reconstruction. imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, https://github.com/imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Compressive Volume Rendering
head: Compressive Rendering
body: Compressive Volume Rendering is an image-order acceleration technique that reconstructs a full rendered image from a small subset of rendered pixels, exploiting the inherent smoothness of volume rendered images to reduce computational cost. It solves the problem of high rendering costs by rendering only a fraction of the pixels and recovering the rest via a smoothness-based variational model, which sources indicate performs better than compressed sensing approaches for this domain. It builds on Compressive Volume Rendering Recovery Methods. Inputs: Image dimensions W, H. Total pixel count N = W \times H. Subset size M (typically M \ll N, e.g., 20% of pixels). Rendered pixel values y (column vector of size M \times 1). Sampling matrix S (size M \times N). Regularization parameter \lambda. Outputs: Full rendered image x (column vector of size N \times 1). Data Structures: Sampling Matrix S: An M \times N binary matrix. Each row contains exactly one 1 at the column index corresponding to a retained pixel location, and 0 elsewhere. Kernel Function \phi(t): The optimal interpolating cubic B-spline \beta3^I, defined as \beta3^I(t) = \beta3(t) - \frac{1}{6}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}\beta3(t), where \beta3(t) is the univariate uniform centered cubic B-spline. The 2D kernel is the tensor product \phi(t1, t2) = \beta3^I(t1)\beta3^I(t2). Matrix H: An N \times N convolution matrix where entries are defined by the second-order Beppo-Levi inner product of the kernel functions: H{p,q} = \langle \phi(\cdot - jp), \phi(\cdot - jq) \rangle{BL^2}. Here jp and jq are the 2D pixel locations in the full image x. Steps: 1. Pixel Sampling: Select M pixel locations to render. Sources note two approaches: low-discrepancy distributions such as Poisson-disk, or a linear pixel shuffling algorithm. 2. Rendering: Trace rays for the selected M pixels to obtain the vector y. 3. Formulate Optimization Problem: The goal is to find x that minimizes \minx \|Sx - y\|2^2 + \lambda x^T H x, where the first term is the fidelity to rendered pixels and the second term measures smoothness via the second-order Beppo-Levi seminorm. 4. Solve: Use a Conjugate Gradient solver to find x. Formulas: Sampling Model: y = Sx. Beppo-Levi Inner Product: For functions g(t) and h(t), \langle g, h \rangle{BL^2}:= \langle \partial{t1}^2 g, \partial{t1}^2 h \rangle + 2\langle \partial{t1}\partial{t2} g, \partial{t1}\partial{t2} h \rangle + \langle \partial{t2}^2 g, \partial{t2}^2 h \rangle where \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle is the standard L^2 inner product \int{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x)g(x)dx. Kernel Definition: \beta3^I(t) = \beta3(t) - \frac{1}{6}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}\beta3(t). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compressivevolumerendering(W, H, M, renderfunction, lambdaparam): """ Reconstructs a full image from a subset of rendered pixels. """ N = W H # Step 1: Select M pixel locations. Sources mention Poisson-disk or linear pixel shuffling. sampledindices = [i N // M for i in range(M)] # Uniform sampling; replace with Poisson-disk or linear shuffling per source sampledcoords = [(idx % W, idx // W) for idx in sampledindices] # Step 2: Render the subset y = renderfunction(sampledcoords) # y is list of size M # Step 3: Construct b = S^T y b = [0.0] N for m, idx in enumerate(sampledindices): b[idx] = y[m] # Step 4: Define linear operator A = S^T S + lambda H # S^T S is a diagonal matrix with 1s at sampledindices. # H is a convolution matrix derived from the Beppo-Levi inner product. # Exact discrete coefficients for beta3^I are not given in the sources. kernel2d = [[0.0] 5 for in range(5)] # Exact 5x5 kernel coefficients from Blu et al. [48] not provided in sources def applyA(v): # (S^T S) v: zero out non-sampled indices res = list(v) sampledset = set(sampledindices) for idx in range(N): if idx not in sampledset: res[idx] = 0.0 # lambda H v: 2D convolution with boundary handling convres = convolve2d(res, kernel2d, W, H) for i in range(N): res[i] += lambdaparam convres[i] return res # Step 5: Solve Ax = b using Conjugate Gradient (Algorithm 1 from) x = [0.0] N r = [b[i] - applyA(x)[i] for i in range(N)] p = list(r) rdotr = sum(r[i] r[i] for i in range(N)) for k in range(1000): Ap = applyA(p) pAp = sum(p[i] Ap[i] for i in range(N)) if pAp == 0.0: break alpha = rdotr / pAp # x{k+1} = xk + alphak pk for i in range(N): x[i] += alpha p[i] # r{k+1} = rk - alphak A pk for i in range(N): r[i] -= alpha Ap[i] rdotrnew = sum(r[i] r[i] for i in range(N)) if rdotrnew < 1e-12: break beta = rdotrnew / rdotr rdotr = rdotrnew # p{k+1} = r{k+1} + betak pk for i in range(N): p[i] = r[i] + beta p[i] return x def convolve2d(imageflat, kernel, W, H): """Applies 2D convolution with zero-padding boundary handling.""" out = [0.0] (W H) kh, kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0]) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): acc = 0.0 for ky in range(kh): for kx in range(kw): iy, ix = y + ky - kh // 2, x + kx - kw // 2 if 0 <= iy < H and 0 <= ix < W: acc += imageflat[iy W + ix] kernel[ky][kx] out[y W + x] = acc return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-posedness: The problem is inherently ill-posed because M \ll N. Kernel Size: Larger kernels increase accuracy but also computational cost. Boundary Handling: Automatic boundary handling is required for the convolution operations near image edges. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The solver is described as "computationally expensive". Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Storing the image requires O(N). Performance: Can achieve high-quality recovery with as few as 20% of the pixels rendered. Strengths: Significantly reduces rendering cost by tracing fewer rays. Exploits image smoothness effectively. Limitations: The recovery step is computationally intensive. The method assumes the image is smooth; high-frequency details may be lost or blurred. When to use: When rendering cost is prohibitive and the volume rendered image exhibits smooth intensity variations. When not to use: When high-frequency details are critical or the image is not smooth. Compressive Volume Rendering was initially proposed by Sen and Darabi [40] (cited as [SD11] in), who presented a two-step algorithm using compressed sensing. Later, Liu and Alim [4] (cited as) demonstrated that smoothness-based approaches perform better than compressed sensing for this task. This work extends the initial proposal by using linear pixel shuffling instead of Poisson-disk patterns and a smoothness-based variational reconstruction. The method is part of the broader field of compressive rendering, which aims to reconstruct full images from sparse samples. name: Iterative Wavelet Thresholding for CT Reconstruction
head: ISTA, Iterative Soft-Thresholding, Iterative Thresholding, Wavelet Regularized Reconstruction
body: Iterative Wavelet Thresholding is an iterative reconstruction method that solves the inverse problem g = Af + n by combining a gradient descent step on the data fidelity term with a sparsity-promoting wavelet thresholding step. It is used to reconstruct images from noisy sinograms, particularly in sparse or limited angle scenarios. The method minimizes the discrepancy between measured sinograms and the forward projection of the reconstruction while applying soft-thresholding to wavelet coefficients at each step to reduce noise and retain structural information. It integrates optimization and regularization, iteratively refining the reconstruction until convergence. Inputs: g: Observed sinogram data. A: Forward projection operator mapping image space to sinogram space. A^T: Adjoint operator mapping sinogram space to image space. BP: Backprojection operator for initialization. f{true}: Ground truth image (used only for convergence monitoring in the reference implementation; not required for reconstruction itself). Parameters: \alpha (regularization scaling), \text{step\size} (learning rate), tRange (wavelet levels for thresholding), \text{threshold} (convergence tolerance), \text{maxIter} (maximum iterations). Outputs: f: Reconstructed image. Data Structures: fk: Current image estimate, shape (v, h), where v is height and h is width. Wavelet coefficients: List structure [cAn, (cHn, cVn, cDn),..., (cH1, cV1, cD1)], where cA is approximation and cH/cV/cD are horizontal, vertical, and diagonal detail coefficients. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute an initial estimate f0 using Backprojection (BP) on the observed sinogram g, then normalize the result: f0 = \text{normalise}(\text{BP}(g)). Replace non-numeric values (NaN) with 0 before normalization. If the maximum value is 0, return a zero array instead of dividing by zero. f0 = \text{normalize}(\text{BP}(g)) Where \text{normalize}(x) = x / \max(x) if \max(x) > 0, else 0. 2. Iteration Loop (for k = 0, 1, \dots, \text{maxIter}-1): a. Forward Projection: Compute the forward projection of the current estimate: \hat{g}k = A fk b. Residual & Gradient: Calculate the residual sinogram rk = \hat{g}k - g and compute the gradient term using the adjoint operator: gk = A^T rk c. Gradient Descent Step: Update the estimate: f{temp} = fk - \text{step\size} \cdot gk d. Wavelet Thresholding: i. Decompose f{temp} using a 2D Haar wavelet transform with level=7: \text{coeffs} = \text{wavedec2}(f{temp}, \text{'haar'}, 7) ii. Apply soft thresholding to the detail coefficients at indices specified by tRange with threshold value \mu = \alpha \cdot \text{step\size}: \mu = \alpha \cdot \text{step\size} For each detail coefficient c in the specified levels: c{new} = \text{sign}(c) \cdot \max(|c| - \mu, 0) iii. Reconstruct the image from the modified coefficients to obtain f{k+1}: f{k+1} = \text{waverec2}(\text{coeffs}{new}) e. Convergence Check: Calculate the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the true image f{true} and the current estimate fk. If the reduction in MSE is less than or equal to \text{threshold}, stop. Otherwise, set fk = f{k+1} and repeat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import pywt def iterativewaveletthresholding(g, A, AT, BP, v, h, alpha=1e-3, stepsize=1e-5, tRange=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], threshold=1e-4, maxIter=5000, ftrue=None): """ Reconstruct image f from sinogram g using Iterative Wavelet Thresholding. Args: g: Observed sinogram (vector or matrix). A: Forward projection function/operator. AT: Adjoint projection function/operator. BP: Backprojection function/operator for initialization. v, h: Image dimensions (height, width). alpha: Regularization parameter. stepsize: Learning rate for gradient descent. tRange: List of wavelet levels to threshold. threshold: Convergence tolerance for MSE change. maxIter: Maximum number of iterations. ftrue: Ground truth image for convergence check (optional). Returns: f: Reconstructed image. """ # Step 1: Initialization fk = BP(g).reshape(v, h) # Normalize fk = np.nantonum(fk) maxval = fk.max() if maxval == 0: return np.zeroslike(fk) fk = fk / maxval prevmse = float('inf') # Step 2: Iteration for k in range(maxIter): # Forward projection Afk = A(fk) # Residual residual = Afk - g # Gradient step: ftemp = fk - stepsize AT(residual) grad = AT(residual).reshape(v, h) ftemp = fk - stepsize grad # Wavelet Thresholding # Decompose coeffs = pywt.wavedec2(ftemp, 'haar', level=7) # Threshold detail coefficients mu = alpha stepsize newcoeffs = [coeffs[0]] # Keep approximation coefficients unchanged for i in range(1, len(coeffs)): if i in tRange: # Soft thresholding for each detail coefficient (H, V, D) newcoeffs.append(tuple( pywt.threshold(c, value=mu, mode='soft') for c in coeffs[i])) else: newcoeffs.append(coeffs[i]) # Reconstruct fk = pywt.waverec2(newcoeffs) # Convergence check if ftrue is not None: mse = np.mean((fk - ftrue) 2) if prevmse - mse <= threshold: break prevmse = mse return fk Parameters: \alpha: Regularization parameter scaling the threshold value. Typical values range from 10^{-3} to 10^4, often found via L-curve analysis. \text{step\size}: Learning rate for the gradient descent step. Typical values are small, e.g., 10^{-5} to 10^{-4}. tRange: List of wavelet decomposition levels to which thresholding is applied. Typically excludes the approximation coefficient (index 0). Common values are [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] or [4, 5, 6]. \text{threshold}: Convergence tolerance for the change in MSE. Default value is 0.0001 or 0.000001. \text{maxIter}: Maximum number of iterations. Default value is 5000. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the maximum value of the initial backprojection result is 0, the normalization function returns a zero array instead of dividing by zero. NaN Handling: Non-numeric values (NaN) in the input image are replaced with 0 before normalization. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: The method integrates optimization and regularization, iteratively refining the reconstruction until convergence. Compared to standard Tikhonov regularization solved via GMRES, this method uses an explicit iterative thresholding loop. When to use: Sparse or limited angle scenarios with noisy sinograms. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from a project investigating CT reconstruction using traditional methods like filtered backprojection (FBP) and wavelet denoising, alongside modern approaches. It addresses challenges such as limited data, missing segments, and noise. The implementation is compared against Tikhonov regularization solved via GMRES and gradient penalties, showing MSE results for sparse and limited angle cases. imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, https://github.com/imanfs/inverse-problems-CT-scans, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
